name: Backward Differentiable Monte Carlo Voxelization
body: Computes backward-mode gradients of voxel occupancy with respect to mesh vertex positions using Monte Carlo sampling. It differs from Forward-Mode Derivative of Monte Carlo 2D Voxelization by propagating gradients from the output occupancy grid back to the input vertices, enabling geometry optimization from voxel supervision. Inputs: vertices: Array of shape (N, 3) containing vertex positions, type Float. faces: Array of shape (M, 3) containing vertex indices for each triangle, type uint32t. doccupancy: Input array of shape (H, W) for 2D or (D, H, W) for 3D, containing occupancy gradients, type Float. height, width, depth: Grid dimensions. Outputs: dvertices: Output array of shape (N, 3) containing vertex gradients, type Float. Initialized to zero. Data Structures: Temporary vectors for polygon splitting in barycentric coordinates: remainingx, polyx, tempbelow, tempabove, remainingy, polyxy, remainingz, polybary, polyxyz. dvnvec: Vector of shape (3) storing the derivative projected onto the normal direction. Steps: 1. Validate inputs using validatecommondifferentialvoxelizearguments. 2. Dispatch to 2D or 3D backward-mode implementation with DifferentiationMode::Backward. 3. For each face f with vertices v0, v1, v2: a. Compute edge vectors: e1 = v1 - v0, e2 = v2 - v0. b. Compute normal: n = e1 \times e2. c. Compute normal length: L = \|n\|. d. If L < 10^{-12}, skip face. e. Compute unit normal: \hat{n} = n / L. f. For Backward mode, set dvn\vec = \hat{n}. g. Perform Monte Carlo integration to compute gradients. The gradient contribution for each vertex is derived from the derivative of the occupancy function with respect to vertex positions, projected onto the normal direction. h. Accumulate gradients into dvertices for v0, v1, v2. Parameters: dvertices: Output array of shape (n, dim) containing vertex gradients, type Float. doccupancy: Input array of shape (h, w) or (d, h, w) containing occupancy gradients, type Float. Edge Cases: Zero-area triangles (L < 10^{-12}) are skipped. Pseudocode: Unverified code. a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def backwarddifferentiablemcvoxelize(vertices, faces, doccupancy, height, width, depth): dvertices = zeroslike(vertices) validatecommondifferentialvoxelizearguments(vertices, faces, doccupancy) dim = 2 if len(doccupancy.shape) == 2 else 3 if dim == 2: backward2d(vertices, faces, doccupancy, height, width, dvertices) else: backward3d(vertices, faces, doccupancy, height, width, depth, dvertices) return dvertices def backward2d(vertices, faces, doccupancy, height, width, dvertices): remainingx, polyx, tempbelow, tempabove = [], [], [], [] remainingy, polyxy = [], [] remainingz, polybary, polyxyz = [], [], [] polydvn = [] for faceidx in range(len(faces)): i0, i1, i2 = faces[faceidx] v0, v1, v2 = vertices[i0], vertices[i1], vertices[i2] e1 = [v1[j] - v0[j] for j in range(3)] e2 = [v2[j] - v0[j] for j in range(3)] normal = cross(e1, e2) normallen = norm(normal) if normallen < 1e-12: continue unitnormal = [n / normallen for n in normal] dvnvec = unitnormal # Monte Carlo integration: sources do not provide the exact sampling and accumulation formula gradcontribution = dvnvec dvertices[i0] = [dvertices[i0][j] + gradcontribution[j] for j in range(3)] dvertices[i1] = [dvertices[i1][j] + gradcontribution[j] for j in range(3)] dvertices[i2] = [dvertices[i2][j] + gradcontribution[j] for j in range(3)] def backward3d(vertices, faces, doccupancy, height, width, depth, dvertices): stepx = 2.0 / depth stepy = 2.0 / height stepz = 2.0 / width cellvolume = stepx stepy stepz centerk = width // 2 remainingx, polyx, tempbelow, tempabove = [], [], [], [] remainingy, polyxy = [], [] remainingz, polybary, polyxyz = [], [], [] polydvn = [] for faceidx in range(len(faces)): i0, i1, i2 = faces[faceidx] v0, v1, v2 = vertices[i0], vertices[i1], vertices[i2] e1 = [v1[j] - v0[j] for j in range(3)] e2 = [v2[j] - v0[j] for j in range(3)] normal = cross(e1, e2) normallen = norm(normal) if normallen < 1e-12: continue unitnormal = [n / normallen for n in normal] dvnvec = unitnormal # Monte Carlo integration: sources do not provide the exact sampling and accumulation formula gradcontribution = dvnvec dvertices[i0] = [dvertices[i0][j] + gradcontribution[j] for j in range(3)] dvertices[i1] = [dvertices[i1][j] + gradcontribution[j] for j in range(3)] dvertices[i2] = [dvertices[i2][j] + gradcontribution[j] for j in range(3)] This method converts a triangle mesh into a 3D voxel volume by casting random rays from voxel centers to the top plane of the bounding box, enabling gradient-based optimization of mesh geometry from voxel supervision. name: Differentiable Rasterization via Ray Casting
head: CUDA rasterize kernel, voxel2mesh rasterization
body: This method converts a triangle mesh into a 3D voxel volume by casting random rays from voxel centers to the top plane of the bounding box, enabling gradient-based optimization of mesh geometry from voxel supervision. It differs from standard rasterization by providing a backward pass that computes gradients with respect to vertex positions, allowing the mesh to be refined to match a target voxel occupancy. Unlike Backward Differentiable Monte Carlo Voxelization, which relies on Monte Carlo sampling for the backward pass, this method uses a deterministic ray-casting forward pass with a specialized geometric gradient approximation for the backward pass. Inputs: Mesh defined by vertices V \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3} and faces F \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times 3} (indices into V). Voxel grid dimensions W, H, D (width, height, depth). Bounding box depth D (used for gradient scaling). Outputs: Voxel occupancy volume Vol \in \{0, 1\}^{D \times H \times W}. Gradients \frac{\partial Loss}{\partial V} with respect to vertex positions. Data Structures: Vol[z][y][x]: Integer (0 or 1) indicating voxel occupancy. gradV: Tensor of shape (N, 3) storing gradients for each vertex. Parameters: diag: Scaling factor 1.732 \cdot D, approximating the diagonal of the voxel grid. borderintersection: Counter for ambiguous ray intersections. Steps: 1. Forward Pass (Occupancy): For each voxel at coordinates (x, y, z), initialize a random number generator state with seed S = H \cdot W \cdot z + W \cdot y + x. Generate a random point P1 on the top plane (z=D) with P1.x = W \cdot \text{rand\uniform}(S) and P1.y = H \cdot \text{rand\uniform}(S). Set ray origin P0 = (x, y, z). Initialize counters faceintersection = 0 and borderintersection = 0. Iterate over all faces: compute edge vectors u = V1 - V0, v = V2 - V0, and normal n = \text{cross}(u, v). Compute ray direction dir = P1 - P0 and vector w0 = P0 - V0. Calculate a = -\text{dot}(n, w0) and b = \text{dot}(n, dir). If |b| < 10^{-8}, skip (ray parallel to face). Calculate intersection distance r = a / b. If r < 0, skip (intersection behind ray origin). Compute intersection point I = P0 + r \cdot dir. Check if I is inside triangle V0 V1 V2 using barycentric coordinates: uu = \text{dot}(u, u), vv = \text{dot}(v, v), uv = \text{dot}(u, v). Compute w = I - V0, wu = \text{dot}(w, u), wv = \text{dot}(w, v). Calculate d = uv^2 - uu \cdot vv. Compute s = \frac{uv \cdot wv - vv \cdot wu}{d} and t = \frac{uv \cdot wu - uu \cdot wv}{d}. If s < 0 or s > 1 or t < 0 or s + t > 1, skip. If s == 0 or t == 0 or s + t == 1, increment borderintersection. Otherwise, increment faceintersection. After checking all faces, if borderintersection > 0, restart the ray for this voxel. If faceintersection is odd, set Vol[z][y][x] = 1 (inside); else set 0 (outside). 2. Backward Pass (Gradients): For each voxel (x, y, z), retrieve voxel = Vol[z][y][x] and grad\voxel = \frac{\partial Loss}{\partial Vol[z][y][x]}. For each face with vertices V0, V1, V2, compute gradients for each vertex using computegrad. In computegrad for vertex V2 (relative to ray origin P and other vertices V0, V1), define plane through P, V0, V1 and compute normal n = \text{cross}(V0 - P, V1 - P). For each axis axis \in \{x, y, z\}, calculate potential shifted position V2^{shifted} by intersecting the plane with a line parallel to the axis passing through V2. Example for x-axis shift: V2^{shifted}x = -\frac{ny V2.y + nz V2.z}{nx}, V2^{shifted}y = V2.y, V2^{shifted}z = V2.z (similar formulas apply for y and z shifts). Check if V2^{shifted} lies on the face triangle V0, V1, V2^{shifted} using Pisonface. The check solves a(V0 - V2^{shifted}) + b(V1 - V2^{shifted}) = P - V2^{shifted} for coefficients a, b. If n{axis} \neq 0 and the shift is non-zero and Pisonface returns true, update gradient: \text{grad}{V2}[axis] = -\text{grad}{\text{voxel}} \cdot \frac{|V2^{shifted} - V2|}{\text{diag}} if the sign of the shift relative to the voxel boundary matches the gradient direction (i.e., d \cdot \text{grad}{\text{voxel}} < 0 for outside voxels, > 0 for inside), where d = V2^{shifted} - V2. Else gradient contribution for this axis is 0. Formulas: Barycentric coordinate check for point I inside triangle defined by V0, V1, V2: s = \frac{uv \cdot wv - vv \cdot wu}{uv^2 - uu \cdot vv}, t = \frac{uv \cdot wu - uu \cdot wv}{uv^2 - uu \cdot vv}, where u=V1-V0, v=V2-V0, w=I-V0, uu=u\cdot u, vv=v\cdot v, uv=u\cdot v, wu=w\cdot u, wv=w\cdot v. Point is inside if s \ge 0, t \ge 0, s+t \le 1. Gradient update rule for a vertex component: \text{grad}{V2} = -\text{grad}{\text{voxel}} \cdot \frac{|V2{\text{shifted}} - V2|}{\text{diag}} if the sign of the shift relative to the voxel boundary matches the gradient direction (i.e., d \cdot \text{grad}{\text{voxel}} < 0 for outside voxels, > 0 for inside), where d = V2{\text{shifted}} - V2 and \text{diag} = 1.732 \cdot D. Pitfalls: Border Intersections: If the ray intersects any triangle edge or vertex, the borderintersection counter increments. If this counter is > 0 after checking all faces, the voxel result is discarded and the ray is re-cast to avoid ambiguity. Precision: The threshold 10^{-8} for parallel rays is critical; too small may cause division by zero, too large may miss valid intersections. Gradient Scaling: The diag factor 1.732 \cdot D approximates the grid diagonal; incorrect scaling may lead to unstable gradients. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forwardpass(meshvertices, meshfaces, W, H, D): Vol = np.zeros((D, H, W), dtype=np.int32) for z in range(D): for y in range(H): for x in range(W): seed = H W z + W y + x border = True while border: border = False u1 = randuniform(seed) u2 = randuniform(seed) P1 = np.array([W u1, H u2, D]) P0 = np.array([x, y, z]) dirvec = P1 - P0 facecount = 0 for face in meshfaces: V0, V1, V2 = meshvertices[face[0]], meshvertices[face[1]], meshvertices[face[2]] u = V1 - V0 v = V2 - V0 n = np.cross(u, v) w0 = P0 - V0 a = -np.dot(n, w0) b = np.dot(n, dirvec) if abs(b) < 1e-8: continue r = a / b if r < 0: continue I = P0 + r dirvec w = I - V0 uu = np.dot(u, u) vv = np.dot(v, v) uv = np.dot(u, v) wu = np.dot(w, u) wv = np.dot(w, v) d = uv uv - uu vv s = (uv wv - vv wu) / d t = (uv wu - uu wv) / d if s < 0 or s > 1 or t < 0 or s + t > 1: continue if s == 0 or t == 0 or s + t == 1: border = True break facecount += 1 if border: continue Vol[z, y, x] = 1 if (facecount % 2 == 1) else 0 return Vol def backwardpass(Vol, gradVol, meshvertices, meshfaces, W, H, D): gradV = np.zeroslike(meshvertices) diag = 1.732 D for z in range(D): for y in range(H): for x in range(W): voxelval = Vol[z, y, x] gvox = gradVol[z, y, x] P0 = np.array([x, y, z]) for face in meshfaces: V0, V1, V2 = meshvertices[face[0]], meshvertices[face[1]], meshvertices[face[2]] for Viidx, Vi in enumerate([V0, V1, V2]): # Compute gradient for Vi using the other two vertices and P0 # Determine the other two vertices for the plane definition others = [meshvertices[face[j]] for j in range(3) if j != face[Viidx]] Vp, Vq = others[0], others[1] n = np.cross(Vp - P0, Vq - P0) for axis in range(3): if n[axis] == 0: continue shifted = Vi.copy() shifted[axis] = -(n[(axis+1)%3]Vi[(axis+1)%3] + n[(axis+2)%3]Vi[(axis+2)%3]) / n[axis] # Check if P0 lies on triangle Vp, Vq, shifted # Solve a(Vp-shifted) + b(Vq-shifted) = P0-shifted e1 = Vp - shifted e2 = Vq - shifted w = P0 - shifted uu = np.dot(e1, e1) vv = np.dot(e2, e2) uv = np.dot(e1, e2) wu = np.dot(w, e1) wv = np.dot(w, e2) d = uvuv - uuvv if abs(d) < 1e-12: continue sa = (uvwv - vvwu) / d sb = (uvwu - uuwv) / d if sa >= 0 and sb >= 0 and sa + sb <= 1: dshift = shifted[axis] - Vi[axis] if (voxelval == 0 and dshift gvox < 0) or (voxelval == 1 and dshift gvox > 0): gradV[face[Viidx], axis] -= gvox abs(dshift) / diag return gradV Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot D \cdot M) per forward pass, where M is the number of faces. The backward pass is also O(W \cdot H \cdot D \cdot M) due to per-voxel gradient computation. Performance: Performance depends heavily on the number of faces and voxel resolution. The random ray casting allows for parallelization on GPUs. Strengths: Provides differentiable mesh optimization from voxel supervision; handles complex geometries via ray casting. Limitations: Stochastic nature requires multiple samples or careful seed management for reproducibility; border intersection handling adds complexity. When to use: When optimizing mesh geometry to match a target voxel volume is required. When not to use: When real-time rendering without gradients is needed; when exact analytical gradients are preferred over approximations. This method is part of the Voxel2Mesh framework, which aims to generate meshes from voxel data using deep learning. It was introduced in the context of differentiable rendering for 3D shape optimization. The technique leverages CUDA for efficient parallel ray casting and gradient computation. cvlab-epfl/voxel2mesh, https://github.com/cvlab-epfl/voxel2mesh, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable Voxelization (MC/CF)
head: Closed-form Voxelization, Convolution Filter Voxelization, Differentiable 3D Voxelization (Forward/Backward Mode), VoxelizeFunc
body: Differentiable Voxelization converts parametrically defined continuous geometric objects (2D polygons or 3D triangle meshes) into digital voxel grids of winding numbers or occupancy values, while providing closed-form gradients with respect to the input vertex positions. It solves the differentiability bottleneck in gradient-based optimization of surface representations by avoiding the non-differentiable nature of standard rasterization or discrete marching cubes. Unlike Monte Carlo 2D Voxelization which relies on stochastic sampling, or Analytic Moment Voxelization which computes polynomial moments, this method uses deterministic closed-form integration over triangle faces to compute both the primal voxel values and their derivatives. The method is implemented as a PyTorch autograd.Function that supports two primal modes: Marching Cubes (MC) and Convolution Filter (CF). The MC mode uses Monte Carlo integration for the forward pass and closed-form integration for the backward pass, while the CF mode uses a box filter approximation for both. Inputs: vertices: Array of shape (N, D) containing triangle/polygon vertices, type Float (float32 or float64). indices (or faces/edges): Array of shape (M, D) containing vertex indices for each simplex, type uint32t. gridshape: Tuple defining the output voxel grid dimensions (e.g., (H, W) for 2D or (D, H, W) for 3D). voxelsize: The physical size of a single voxel cell. numsamplespervoxel: Number of Monte Carlo samples per voxel for the MC forward pass. Default: 16. numsamplespersimplex: Number of Monte Carlo samples per simplex for the MC backward pass. Default: 64. filterradius: Radius of the filter. Default: halfvoxelsize. For CF, it must equal halfvoxelsize; otherwise, it has no effect. Outputs: occupancy: Output tensor of shape gridshape and dtype matching vertices, containing the voxel winding numbers or occupancy values. The implementation uses standard dense tensors for vertices, indices, and the output grid. The core algorithm also utilizes a Bitset structure for internal bookkeeping. The forward pass computes the occupancy/winding number for each voxel. 1. Validation: Validate inputs using validatecommonvoxelizearguments. 2. Dispatch: Select the primal function based on method ('mc' or 'cf') and dtype (float32/float64). 3. Initialization: Initialize the output voxel grid occupancy as a zero tensor of shape gridshape and dtype matching vertices. 4. Execution: Execute the primal voxelization function with vertices, indices, and the occupancy output tensor. Detailed Forward Logic (CF Mode): The CF method assumes a box filter the size of a voxel. 1. Iterate over all faces. For each face, extract vertices v0, v1, v2. 2. Compute edge vectors e1 = v1 - v0, e2 = v2 - v0. 3. Compute normal n = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(e1, e2)) and area A = 0.5 \times \|\text{cross}(e1, e2)\|. 4. Determine the bounding box in grid coordinates covering the triangle. 5. For each voxel in the bounding box, compute the intersection of the triangle with the voxel cell. This is done by splitting the triangle polygon in barycentric coordinates against the voxel planes. 6. Compute the contribution to the voxel occupancy based on the signed area of the intersection polygon and the normal direction. Detailed Forward Logic (MC Mode): 1. For each face, perform Monte Carlo integration over the triangle surface. 2. Generate uniform random samples u, v. If u + v > 1, reflect: u = 1 - u; v = 1 - v. 3. Compute sample point on triangle: p = v0 + u \cdot e1 + v \cdot e2. 4. Determine which voxel contains p and increment its occupancy count. 5. Normalize by the number of samples. The backward pass computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the vertex positions, \frac{\partial L}{\partial vi}, given the gradient of the loss with respect to the occupancy grid, \delta \text{occupancy}. 1. Save: Save vertices, indices, and voxels for the backward pass. 2. Dispatch: Select the appropriate backward function (voxelizebackwardmc or voxelizebackwardcf) based on method and dtype. 3. Initialization: Initialize gradient tensor for vertices \delta \text{vertices} as zeros with same shape and dtype. 4. Execution: Execute the backward function with vertices, indices, occupancy, \delta \text{vertices}, and \delta \text{occupancy}. Detailed Backward Logic (CF Mode): 1. Iterate over all faces. For each face, extract vertices v0, v1, v2. 2. Compute edge vectors e1 = v1 - v0, e2 = v2 - v0, normal n = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(e1, e2)), and area A = 0.5 \times \|\text{cross}(e1, e2)\|. 3. Determine the bounding box in grid coordinates. 4. For each voxel in the bounding box: a. Compute the filter weight (intersection area/volume contribution). b. If the weight is non-zero, compute the differential weight: w{diff} = \delta \text{occupancy}[voxel] \times \text{filter\weight} \times A / \text{num\samples\per\simplex}. c. Compute normal velocities for backward pass: \frac{\partial x{bn}}{\partial v0} = n \times (1 - u - v) \frac{\partial x{bn}}{\partial v1} = n \times u \frac{\partial x{bn}}{\partial v2} = n \times v. d. Add to vertex gradients: \delta \text{vertices}[3 \cdot v0 + d] += \frac{\partial x{bn}}{\partial v0}[d] \times w{diff} for all 3 vertices and 3 dimensions d. Detailed Backward Logic (MC Mode): 1. Iterate over all faces. For each face, extract vertices v0, v1, v2. 2. Compute edge vectors e1 = v1 - v0, e2 = v2 - v0, normal n = \text{normalize}(\text{cross}(e1, e2)), and area A = 0.5 \times \|\text{cross}(e1, e2)\|. 3. Perform Monte Carlo integration over the triangle surface. Generate uniform u, v. If u + v > 1, reflect: u = 1 - u; v = 1 - v. 4. Compute normal velocities for backward pass: \frac{\partial x{bn}}{\partial v0} = n \times (1 - u - v) \frac{\partial x{bn}}{\partial v1} = n \times u \frac{\partial x{bn}}{\partial v2} = n \times v. 5. In Forward mode (accumulating gradients from downstream), compute d{xbn} by dotting the vertex gradients with the normal velocities: d{xbn} += \text{dot}(\delta v0, \frac{\partial x{bn}}{\partial v0}) + \text{dot}(\delta v1, \frac{\partial x{bn}}{\partial v1}) + \text{dot}(\delta v2, \frac{\partial x{bn}}{\partial v2}). 6. Compute sample point on triangle: p = v0 + u \cdot e1 + v \cdot e2. Convert to grid coordinates and get support box. 7. Iterate over neighbor voxels (nx, ny, nz). Compute neighbor center n{center} = (nx + 0.5) \times \text{voxel\size} - 1. 8. Compute filter weight. If non-zero, update gradients. Forward: \delta \text{occupancy}[n{voxel\index}] += d{xbn} \times \text{filter\weight} \times A / \text{num\samples\per\simplex}. 9. Backward: Compute differential\weight = \delta \text{occupancy}[n{voxel\index}] \times \text{filter\weight} \times A / \text{num\samples\per\simplex}. Add to vertex gradients: \delta \text{vertices}[3 \cdot v0 + d] += \frac{\partial x{bn}}{\partial v0}[d] \times differential\weight for all 3 vertices and 3 dimensions. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def voxelizecfforward(vertices, indices, gridshape, voxelsize, numsamplespervoxel=16): # 1. Validate inputs # validatecommonvoxelizearguments(vertices, indices, gridshape) # 2. Initialize output occupancy = torch.zeros(gridshape, dtype=vertices.dtype, device=vertices.device) stepx = 2.0 / gridshape[0] stepy = 2.0 / gridshape[1] stepz = 2.0 / gridshape[2] if len(gridshape) == 3 else 1.0 cellvolume = stepx stepy stepz for i in range(indices.shape[0]): v0 = vertices[indices[i, 0]] v1 = vertices[indices[i, 1]] v2 = vertices[indices[i, 2]] e1 = v1 - v0 e2 = v2 - v0 normal = torch.cross(e1, e2) area = 0.5 torch.norm(normal) if area < 1e-12: continue unitnormal = normal / area # Bounding box in grid coordinates minx = torch.min(v0[0], torch.min(v1[0], v2[0])) maxx = torch.max(v0[0], torch.max(v1[0], v2[0])) miny = torch.min(v0[1], torch.min(v1[1], v2[1])) maxy = torch.max(v0[1], torch.max(v1[1], v2[1])) minz = torch.min(v0[2], torch.min(v1[2], v2[2])) maxz = torch.max(v0[2], torch.max(v1[2], v2[2])) bboxmini = max(0, int((minx + 1) / stepx)) bboxmaxi = min(gridshape[0] - 1, int((maxx + 1) / stepx)) bboxminj = max(0, int((miny + 1) / stepy)) bboxmaxj = min(gridshape[1] - 1, int((maxy + 1) / stepy)) bboxmink = max(0, int((minz + 1) / stepz)) bboxmaxk = min(gridshape[2] - 1, int((maxz + 1) / stepz)) # Initialize barycentric polygon for the triangle polybary = [torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]), torch.tensor([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]), torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])] for k in range(bboxmink, bboxmaxk + 1): xhi = -1.0 + (k + 1) stepz polybary = splitpolygonbary(polybary, torch.tensor([v0[2], v1[2], v2[2]]), xhi) if len(polybary) < 3: break for j in range(bboxminj, bboxmaxj + 1): yhi = -1.0 + (j + 1) stepy polybary = splitpolygonbary(polybary, torch.tensor([v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]]), yhi) if len(polybary) < 3: break for ivox in range(bboxmini, bboxmaxi + 1): zhi = -1.0 + (ivox + 1) stepx polybary = splitpolygonbary(polybary, torch.tensor([v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]]), zhi) if len(polybary) < 3: break # Compute contribution from intersection polygon contrib = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) pivot = polybary[0] / 3.0 for vi in range(1, len(polybary) - 1): pv0, pv1, pv2 = polybary[vi], polybary[vi+1], polybary[0] edge1 = pv1 - pv0 edge2 = pv2 - pv0 subarea = 0.5 torch.norm(torch.cross(edge1, edge2)) b1 = polybary[vi] / 3.0 b2 = polybary[vi+1] / 3.0 contrib += subarea (pivot + b1 + b2) occupancy[ivox, j, k] += contrib[0] / cellvolume return occupancy def splitpolygonbary(polygonbary, tricoords, value): below = [] above = [] n = len(polygonbary) for i in range(n): currbary = polygonbary[i] nextbary = polygonbary[(i + 1) % n] currval = torch.dot(currbary, tricoords) nextval = torch.dot(nextbary, tricoords) currbelow = currval <= value nextbelow = nextval <= value if currbelow: below.append(currbary) else: above.append(currbary) if currbelow != nextbelow: d = nextval - currval if torch.abs(d) > 1e-12: t = (value - currval) / d intersectionbary = currbary + t (nextbary - currbary) below.append(intersectionbary) above.append(intersectionbary) return below def voxelizecfbackward(vertices, indices, occupancygrad, gridshape, voxelsize): dvertices = torch.zeroslike(vertices) stepx = 2.0 / gridshape[0] stepy = 2.0 / gridshape[1] stepz = 2.0 / gridshape[2] if len(gridshape) == 3 else 1.0 cellvolume = stepx stepy stepz for i in range(indices.shape[0]): v0 = vertices[indices[i, 0]] v1 = vertices[indices[i, 1]] v2 = vertices[indices[i, 2]] e1 = v1 - v0 e2 = v2 - v0 normal = torch.cross(e1, e2) area = 0.5 torch.norm(normal) if area < 1e-12: continue unitnormal = normal / area minx = torch.min(v0[0], torch.min(v1[0], v2[0])) maxx = torch.max(v0[0], torch.max(v1[0], v2[0])) miny = torch.min(v0[1], torch.min(v1[1], v2[1])) maxy = torch.max(v0[1], torch.max(v1[1], v2[1])) minz = torch.min(v0[2], torch.min(v1[2], v2[2])) maxz = torch.max(v0[2], torch.max(v1[2], v2[2])) bboxmini = max(0, int((minx + 1) / stepx)) bboxmaxi = min(gridshape[0] - 1, int((maxx + 1) / stepx)) bboxminj = max(0, int((miny + 1) / stepy)) bboxmaxj = min(gridshape[1] - 1, int((maxy + 1) / stepy)) bboxmink = max(0, int((minz + 1) / stepz)) bboxmaxk = min(gridshape[2] - 1, int((maxz + 1) / stepz)) polybary = [torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]), torch.tensor([0.0, 1.0, 0.0]), torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0])] for k in range(bboxmink, bboxmaxk + 1): xhi = -1.0 + (k + 1) stepz polybary = splitpolygonbary(polybary, torch.tensor([v0[2], v1[2], v2[2]]), xhi) if len(polybary) < 3: break for j in range(bboxminj, bboxmaxj + 1): yhi = -1.0 + (j + 1) stepy polybary = splitpolygonbary(polybary, torch.tensor([v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]]), yhi) if len(polybary) < 3: break for ivox in range(bboxmini, bboxmaxi + 1): zhi = -1.0 + (ivox + 1) stepx polybary = splitpolygonbary(polybary, torch.tensor([v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]]), zhi) if len(polybary) < 3: break contrib = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) pivot = polybary[0] / 3.0 for vi in range(1, len(polybary) - 1): pv0, pv1, pv2 = polybary[vi], polybary[vi+1], polybary[0] edge1 = pv1 - pv0 edge2 = pv2 - pv0 subarea = 0.5 torch.norm(torch.cross(edge1, edge2)) b1 = polybary[vi] / 3.0 b2 = polybary[vi+1] / 3.0 contrib += subarea (pivot + b1 + b2) doccupancy = occupancygrad[ivox, j, k] differentialweight = doccupancy / cellvolume for d in range(3): dvertices[3 indices[i, 0] + d] += contrib[0] unitnormal[d] differentialweight dvertices[3 indices[i, 1] + d] += contrib[1] unitnormal[d] differentialweight dvertices[3 indices[i, 2] + d] += contrib[2] unitnormal[d] differentialweight return dvertices numsamplespervoxel: Number of samples per voxel for MC forward pass. Default: 16. numsamplespersimplex: Number of samples per simplex for MC backward pass. Default: 64. filterradius: Radius of the filter. Default: halfvoxelsize. For CF method, it must equal halfvoxelsize, otherwise it has no effect. Coordinate Convention: The CF method uses a different coordinate convention (width, height vs height, width), requiring a transpose of the output voxels (voxels.transpose(0, -1)), which regresses performance. Hardware Support: The implementation is CPU-only; GPU tensors are automatically moved to CPU for processing and moved back, issuing a warning. Degenerate Triangles: Triangles with zero area (normal length < 10^{-12}) are skipped in the backward pass. Method Selection: The 'auto' method selects 'cf' if filterradius equals halfvoxelsize, otherwise 'mc'. Differentiable Voxelization via Smoothed Winding Numbers (DVX) is a method for voxelizing triangle meshes into smoothed winding number voxel grids that provides closed-form gradients with respect to mesh vertex positions, enabling gradient-based optimization of surface representations based on volumetric properties. Unlike Differentiable Voxelization (MC/CF) which samples a non-smoothed winding number and uses automatic differentiation (yielding sparse near-surface derivative signals), this method yields a broader gradient pattern matching finite-difference references. This method provides a differentiable voxelizer \mathcal{V} that efficiently queries a 3D density volume V \in \mathbb{R}^{X \times Y \times Z} from a set of radiative Gaussians G3. It solves the computational bottleneck of mapping continuous Gaussian splats to a discrete grid, enabling 3D regularization priors for tomographic reconstruction. Unlike Differentiable Voxelization (MC/CF) which operates on polygonal meshes, this method operates directly on parametric Gaussian distributions, leveraging spatial tiling for acceleration. Silhouette fitting is a post-processing voxelization technique that refines an initial coarse voxel model by aligning its boundary with the silhouette of the input 3D mesh, thereby preserving shape accuracy. Unlike standard rasterization-based voxelization which produces blocky artifacts, this method minimizes an energy function based on distance, tangent, and gradient differences to carve or adjust the voxel boundary. It is distinct from Differentiable Voxelization (MC/CF) because it operates on a discrete voxel set using heuristic search rather than continuous gradient descent, and from Differentiable Voxelization via Smoothed Winding Numbers by focusing specifically on silhouette curve matching rather than volumetric field smoothing. Computes backward-mode gradients of voxel occupancy with respect to vertex positions using closed-form integration. Steps: Validate inputs using validatecommondifferentialvoxelizearguments. Dispatch to 2D or 3D backward-mode closed-form implementation. Parameters: dvertices: output array of shape (N, D) containing vertex gradients, type Float. doccupancy: input array of shape (H, W) or (D, H, W) containing occupancy gradients, type Float. Steps: Validate inputs using validatecommondifferentialvoxelizearguments. Dispatch to 2D or 3D forward-mode closed-form implementation. Parameters: dvertices: input array of shape (N, D) containing vertex gradients, type Float. doccupancy: output array of shape (H, W) or (D, H, W) containing occupancy gradients, type Float. Rasterizes a 2D polygon to a destination grid by computing polynomial density moments over the covered cells. Parameters: poly: The polygon to be rasterized. ibox: Minimum and maximum indices of the polygon, found with r2dgetibox(). Indices are from a virtual grid starting at the origin. destgrid: The rasterization buffer. A row-major grid patch starting at dibox[0] and ending at dibox[1]. Must have size at least (ibox[1].i-ibox[0].i)(ibox[1].j-ibox[0].j)(ibox[1].k-ibox[0].k)R2DNUMMOMENTS(polyorder). d: The cell spacing of the grid. polyorder: Order of the polynomial density field. 0 for constant (1 moment), 1 for linear (3 moments), 2 for quadratic (6 moments). Layout: r2ddestgrid struct: r2dreal moments[6] (row-major C order, size n.xn.y), r2dint polyorder, r2dorientation orient (size (n.x+1)(n.y+1), unused if compiled with -DUSETREE), r2dlong bufsz, r2ddvec2 n (grid dimensions), r2drvec2 d (cell size). Calculates an N \times N \times N voxel volume of signed distance values for a given mesh. The mesh is transformed to fit inside a cube ranging from -1 to 1. Steps: Check if the result is plausible by verifying if the difference in SDF is smaller than the difference in distance between any two points. If not, throw an exception. Parameters: voxelresolution: The resolution N of the resulting voxel volume. Default value is 64. pad: If True, the resulting array is padded with ones, ensuring a mesh without holes when reconstructing with Marching Cubes. Default value is False. Layout: Returns a numpy array of shape (N, N, N) or (N + 2, N + 2, N + 2) when using padding. If returngradients is True, additionally returns gradients in a numpy array of shape (N, N, N, 3) or (N + 2, N + 2, N + 2, 3) when using padding. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method is CPU-only in the provided implementation, which limits scalability for large grids or high-resolution meshes. Strengths: Provides closed-form gradients, enabling end-to-end differentiable rendering and optimization. Supports both MC and CF modes. Limitations: CPU-only implementation. CF mode has a coordinate convention pitfall. MC mode is stochastic and may require many samples for low noise. When to use: When gradient-based optimization of mesh vertices is required based on volumetric properties. When not to use: When GPU acceleration is critical, or when non-differentiable voxelization is sufficient. The method originates from the work on differentiable voxelization of surface representations, specifically the differentiable-voxelization repository. It builds on the principles of analytic voxelization, extending them to provide differentiable backward passes for gradient-based optimization. The CF method is related to convolution-based rasterization techniques, while the MC method leverages Monte Carlo integration for differentiability. name: Backward Differentiable Closed-form Voxelization
head: Backward-Mode Derivatives for Voxelization
body: Computes the adjoint (gradient) of the occupancy grid with respect to mesh vertex positions, given an occupancy adjoint. It propagates adjoints backwards through the voxelization process using closed-form integration. Unlike forward-mode derivatives which compute the tangent of occupancy from vertex tangents, this method computes vertex gradients from occupancy gradients, enabling efficient backpropagation in differentiable rendering pipelines. It builds on Differentiable Voxelization (MC/CF) by providing the specific backward pass implementation for the Convolution Filter (CF) method. Inputs: Mesh vertices V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}, where n is the number of vertices and d is the dimension (2 or 3). Simplices S (edges in 2D, triangles in 3D) defining the mesh connectivity. Grid resolution \mathbf{r} = (r1, \dots, rd). Occupancy adjoint \bar{O} \in \mathbb{R}^{r1 \times \dots \times rd}, containing the gradient of the loss with respect to the occupancy grid. Outputs: Vertex adjoint \bar{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}, containing the gradient of the loss with respect to the vertex positions. Data Structures: The algorithm processes each simplex \sigma \in S independently. For each simplex, it maintains a polytope \mathbf{P} represented in barycentric coordinates relative to the simplex vertices. \mathbf{V}\sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} is the vertex matrix of the simplex, where rows are the vertex coordinates (\mathbf{v}0, \dots, \mathbf{v}{d-1})^\top. Parameters: Voxel size \mathbf{h} = (2/r1, \dots, 2/rd). The grid spans [-1, 1]^d. Voxel volume m = \prod{\ell=1}^d h\ell. Threshold t{hi}^\ell = -1 + (i\ell + 1) \cdot h\ell for voxel index i\ell in dimension \ell. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute voxel size \mathbf{h} and volume m. Initialize the vertex adjoint accumulator \bar{V} to zeros. 2. Validation: Validate input arguments (dimensions, shapes). 3. Simplex Processing: For each simplex \sigma \in S: a. Extract vertices \mathbf{v}0, \dots, \mathbf{v}{d-1} and compute the unit outward normal \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \text{unit\normal}(\sigma). b. Compute the bounding box (b{\min}^1, \dots, b{\max}^d) of the simplex projected onto the grid axes using \text{BOUNDINGBOX}(V, h). c. Initialize the current polytope \mathbf{P}^{(0)} \leftarrow \sigma in barycentric coordinates (i.e., the simplex itself) and set \mathbf{V}\sigma \leftarrow (\mathbf{v}0, \dots, \mathbf{v}{d-1})^\top. d. Clipping Loop: Iterate over dimensions \ell from 1 to d: i. Iterate over voxel indices i\ell from b{\min}^\ell to b{\max}^\ell. ii. Compute the threshold t{hi}^\ell = -1 + (i\ell + 1) \cdot h\ell. iii. Split the current polytope \mathbf{P}^{(\ell-1)} by the plane defined by t{hi}^\ell in dimension \ell. This is done using \text{SPLITPOLYTOPE}(\mathbf{P}^{(\ell-1)}, \mathbf{V}\sigma, t{hi}^\ell, \ell, d), which returns the part below or equal to the threshold (\mathbf{P}^{(\ell)}) and the part above (\mathbf{P}{\text{above}}^{(\ell)}). iv. Update \mathbf{P}^{(\ell-1)} \leftarrow \mathbf{P}{\text{above}}^{(\ell)} for the next iteration. e. Adjoint Distribution: If \ell = d (last dimension): i. Set the voxel index \mathbf{i} = (i1, \dots, id). ii. Compute the adjoint weight \mathbf{w} = \bar{O}[\mathbf{i}] / m. iii. Compute the Cartesian coordinates of the clipped polytope vertices: \mathbf{V}^{(d)} = \mathbf{P}^{(d)} \mathbf{V}\sigma. iv. Distribute the adjoint to the simplex vertices using barycentric coordinates via \text{INTEGRATEBARYCENTRIC}(\mathbf{P}^{(d)}, \mathbf{V}^{(d)}), which returns barycentric weights (\bar{b}0, \dots, \bar{b}{d-1}) proportional to the surface area contribution of each vertex in the clipped polytope. v. Accumulate the gradient to the vertex adjoints in the normal direction: for j = 0 to d-1, \bar{\mathbf{v}}j \leftarrow \bar{\mathbf{v}}j + \mathbf{w} \cdot \bar{b}j \cdot \hat{\mathbf{n}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backwarddifferentiableclosedformvoxelization(V, S, r, doccupancy): """ V: Vertex positions, shape (n, d) S: List of simplices, each simplex is a list of vertex indices r: Grid resolution, tuple of length d doccupancy: Adjoint of occupancy grid, shape r Returns: dvertices: Adjoint of vertices, shape (n, d) """ d = V.shape[1] h = tuple(2.0 / ri for ri in r) m = 1.0 for hi in h: m = hi dvertices = torch.zeroslike(V) for simplexindices in S: v = V[simplexindices] # Shape (d, d) v0, v1, v2 = v[0], v[1], v[2] if d == 3 else (v[1], None, None) # Compute unit outward normal if d == 2: e1 = v1 - v0 normal = torch.tensor([-e1[1], e1[0]]) else: e1 = v1 - v0 e2 = v2 - v0 normal = torch.cross(e1, e2) normallen = torch.norm(normal) if normallen < 1e-12: continue nhat = normal / normallen # Compute bounding box # BOUNDINGBOX computes min/max voxel indices for each dimension bmin, bmax = computeboundingbox(v, h) # Initialize polytope in barycentric coordinates # For a simplex, barycentric coords are (1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1) P = torch.eye(d) # Shape (d, d) Vsigma = v # Shape (d, d) for l in range(1, d + 1): for il in range(bmin[l-1], bmax[l-1] + 1): thi = -1.0 + (il + 1) h[l-1] # Split polytope # SPLITPOLYTOPE splits P by the plane thi in dimension l # Returns Pbelow, Pabove # The split is done in barycentric coordinates Pbelow, Pabove = splitpolytope(P, Vsigma, thi, l, d) P = Pabove if l == d: # Compute voxel index i = tuple(il if lidx == l-1 else 0 for lidx in range(d)) # Reconstruct full index from loop variables # In practice, indices are accumulated in the loop # Here we assume i is constructed correctly from the nested loops # For simplicity, we assume i is available pass # Compute adjoint weight # doccupancy shape is r, so we need to map i to indices # i is 1-based in formula, 0-based in array # Formula: thi = -1 + (il + 1) hl => il is 0-based index # doccupancy[i1-1,..., id-1] if 1-based, but formula uses il from bmin to bmax # bmin/max are 0-based indices into the grid # So doccupancy[i1,..., id] # Note: The loop indices il in the source are 0-based grid indices # doccupancy shape is (r1,..., rd) # Reconstruct i from the nested loops # This is a simplification; in code, indices are tracked idx = tuple(0 for in range(d)) #... fill idx from loop variables... w = doccupancy[idx] / m # Compute Cartesian coords of clipped polytope Vd = torch.matmul(Pbelow, Vsigma) # Shape (k, d) where k is number of vertices in clipped poly # Integrate barycentric weights # INTEGRATEBARYCENTRIC returns barycentric weights for each vertex of the original simplex # proportional to the area/volume contribution bbar = integratebarycentric(Pbelow, Vd) # Shape (d,) # Accumulate to vertex adjoints for j in range(d): dvertices[simplexindices[j]] += w bbar[j] nhat return dvertices def splitpolytope(P, Vsigma, thi, l, d): """ Splits the polytope P (in barycentric coords) by the plane defined by thi in dimension l. P is a list of vertices in barycentric coordinates. Vsigma is the vertex matrix of the simplex. Returns Pbelow, Pabove (lists of vertices in barycentric coordinates) """ # Convert barycentric to Cartesian to check against thi # Vcart = P @ Vsigma.T # But we need to split in barycentric space? # The source says "Split polygon (in barycentric coords) by a Cartesian plane" # This implies we evaluate the Cartesian coordinate of each barycentric vertex # and split the polygon accordingly. # Get Cartesian coordinates of current polytope vertices # P is (k, d), Vsigma is (d, d) Vcart = torch.matmul(P, Vsigma.T) # Shape (k, d) # The plane is defined by the l-th Cartesian coordinate (0-indexed l-1) # thi is the threshold for the l-th dimension coordl = Vcart[:, l-1] belowmask = coordl <= thi abovemask = coordl > thi Pbelow = P[belowmask] Pabove = P[abovemask] # If the polytope is split, we need to add intersection points # This is a simplified version; a full implementation requires polygon clipping # The source mentions "SPLITPOLYTOPE" which likely handles the clipping # For the purpose of this article, we assume it returns the correct barycentric polygons # Note: The actual implementation in S2 uses a more complex polygon clipping algorithm # that maintains the polygon structure in barycentric coordinates. # Here we provide a conceptual representation. return Pbelow, Pabove def integratebarycentric(P, Vcart): """ Computes barycentric weights for the vertices of the original simplex based on the clipped polytope P (in barycentric coords) and its Cartesian coords Vcart. Returns bbar, shape (d,) """ # This function computes the integral of the barycentric coordinates over the clipped polytope # For a simplex, the integral of barycentric coordinate bj over a sub-polytope P' # is proportional to the volume/area of P' times the average value of bj in P' # A common approximation or exact formula for linear functions is used. # The source says "Distribute adjoint to simplex vertices via barycentric coords (surface area)" # For a triangle (2D), the barycentric weight for vertex j is proportional to the area of the sub-triangle # opposite to vertex j within the clipped polygon. # For a tetrahedron (3D), it's proportional to the volume of the sub-tetrahedron. # A simple implementation for a triangle: # If P is a triangle with barycentric coords (b0, b1, b2), the area is constant. # The integral of b0 over the triangle is Area/3. # If P is a polygon, we decompose it into triangles and sum the contributions. # This is a placeholder for the actual integration logic which depends on the dimension and polytope shape. # The source implies a closed-form integration exists. # For a simplex, the integral of bj over the simplex is Vol/d+1. # For a clipped polytope, it's more complex. # We assume INTEGRATEBARYCENTRIC returns the correct weights. # Example for 2D triangle clipped to a polygon: # Decompose polygon into triangles, compute barycentric weights for each, sum. # This function is implementation-specific and not fully detailed in the source. # We mark it as for the gap. # Return dummy weights for now return torch.ones(d) / d Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Simplices: If the normal length is near zero (e.g., collinear vertices in 2D, coplanar vertices in 3D), the simplex is skipped. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise during polygon splitting, especially for thin triangles or voxels. The threshold comparison thi should be handled carefully. Boundary Conditions: The grid spans [-1, 1]^d. Voxels outside this range are not processed. Uses smoothed winding numbers for differentiability, offering a different approach to handling boundaries. Voxelizes radiative Gaussians, suitable for Gaussian splatting. Fits a mesh to 2D silhouettes, not a general voxelization method. Converts 2D polygon edges to a sparse boundary representation. Computes occupancy tangents from vertex tangents, the dual of this method. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of simplices times the number of voxels they intersect. The clipping operation is linear in the number of vertices of the clipped polytope. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the grid size for the occupancy adjoint and temporary storage for polytope vertices during clipping. Strengths: Provides exact gradients for the CF voxelization method, enabling efficient optimization of mesh vertices in differentiable rendering. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-resolution grids or complex meshes due to the per-voxel clipping. When to Use: When differentiable mesh optimization is required and the CF voxelization method is used for the forward pass. When Not to Use: For real-time applications where performance is critical, or when the forward pass uses a different voxelization method (e.g., MC). The method is described in "Differentiable Voxelization of Surface Representations". It is part of a broader effort to make surface representations differentiable for use in optimization and rendering. The implementation details are also available in the associated GitHub repository. name: Differentiable Voxelization via Smoothed Winding Numbers
head: DVX, Smoothed Winding Number Voxelization
body: Differentiable Voxelization via Smoothed Winding Numbers (DVX) is a method for voxelizing triangle meshes into smoothed winding number voxel grids that provides closed-form gradients with respect to mesh vertex positions, enabling gradient-based optimization of surface representations based on volumetric properties. Unlike Differentiable Voxelization (MC/CF) which samples a non-smoothed winding number and uses automatic differentiation (yielding sparse near-surface derivative signals), this method yields a broader gradient pattern matching finite-difference references. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh defined by vertex positions V and connectivity; a 3D voxel grid of resolution N^3. Output: A voxel grid of smoothed winding numbers W; the gradient of a scalar objective function L with respect to vertex positions \nablaV L. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array of size N \times N \times N. Each cell stores a floating-point value representing the average winding number within that voxel volume. Mesh: Defined by a list of vertices vi \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a list of triangles tj = (va, vb, vc). Method: The core challenge is that point-sampling the raw winding number gives a piecewise-constant signal, so its derivative with respect to mesh motion is zero almost everywhere or undefined at the boundaries. DVX solves this by smoothing the winding-number field with a filter before sampling voxel values. 1. Voxel Value Computation: For a voxel-aligned box filter, a voxel's filtered value is the average winding number within the voxel. To compute this efficiently: Clip each triangle of the mesh against the boundaries of the voxel grid. For each triangle, determine its intersection with the voxel grid. Divide the intersections into sub-triangles. Add up their signed shadow-volume contributions along grid columns to compute the voxel value. The winding number w(p) for a point p is the signed count of how the surface wraps around p. The smoothed value W{ijk} for voxel (i,j,k) is: W{ijk} = \frac{1}{V{\text{voxel}}} \int{V{ijk}} w(p) \, dp where V{ijk} is the volume of the voxel and V{\text{voxel}} is the voxel volume. The algorithm computes this integral by summing the contributions of clipped sub-triangles. 2. Gradient Computation: The gradient is computed using Reynolds' transport theorem. The general derivation states that the moving boundary contributes a term, while the interior term vanishes because the integrand does not otherwise depend on the mesh parameter. This holds for general surfaces and allows self-intersections. For the efficient closed-form algorithm specialized for triangle meshes: Integrate the triangles' normal motion over the clipped pieces. Map those contributions back to mesh vertices. The gradient \frac{\partial W{ijk}}{\partial vm} for a vertex vm is non-zero only if vm is part of a triangle that intersects the voxel or its vicinity. The contribution is derived from the boundary term of the transport theorem, effectively integrating the displacement of the triangle edges against the voxel boundaries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def sub(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]) def scale(a, s): return (a[0]s, a[1]s, a[2]s) def add(a, b): return (a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]) def cliptriangletobox(v0, v1, v2, minc, maxc): """Clips a triangle against an AABB using Sutherland-Hodgman plane clipping.""" poly = [v0, v1, v2] bounds = [minc, maxc] for axis in range(3): newpoly = [] for i in range(len(poly)): curr = poly[i] prev = poly[i-1] currinside = curr[axis] >= bounds[0][axis] previnside = prev[axis] >= bounds[0][axis] if currinside: if not previnside: t = (bounds[0][axis] - prev[axis]) / (curr[axis] - prev[axis]) newpoly.append(add(prev, scale(sub(curr, prev), t))) newpoly.append(curr) elif previnside: t = (bounds[0][axis] - prev[axis]) / (curr[axis] - prev[axis]) newpoly.append(add(prev, scale(sub(curr, prev), t))) poly = newpoly if not poly: return [] newpoly = [] for i in range(len(poly)): curr = poly[i] prev = poly[i-1] currinside = curr[axis] <= bounds[1][axis] previnside = prev[axis] <= bounds[1][axis] if currinside: if not previnside: t = (bounds[1][axis] - Approximate nature: The method is approximate; the resulting shapes may not fill the whole volume or be intersection-free, and are described as 'near-tileable'. An optimization process that deforms a mesh to minimize the volume difference between the object and its extruded silhouettes from three orthogonal directions. Steps: Project the voxelized mesh along each of three orthogonal directions to obtain filled silhouettes. Extrude the silhouettes. Compare the resulting cut shape with the voxelized mesh to compute the objective. Parameters: An as-rigid-as-possible (ARAP) regularizer is used to discourage unnecessary deformation. Performance: On the TOSCA cat category, the average cut-volume difference (measured with the voxel-based objective) improves by 70.775%, going from 3.425 \times 10^3 to 0.454 \times 10^3. Relative improvements for four examples (voxel-based comparison) are 76.0%, 69.9%, 58.7%, and 62.8%. Optimizing repeated shapes toward space-filling tilings. Efficient closed-form algorithm for triangle meshes with voxel-aligned box filters. Limitations: Approximate; self-intersection removal and tiling optimization may not be perfect. name: Self-Intersection Removal via Mesh Deformation
head: Self-Intersection Resolving via Winding Number Energy
body: This method detects and resolves self-intersections in a triangle mesh by optimizing a voxelized representation of the mesh's smoothed winding number field. It minimizes an energy functional that penalizes voxels where the winding number exceeds one, using gradient descent to deform the mesh vertices. Unlike binary occupancy voxelization, this approach leverages the continuous gradient of the smoothed winding number to provide closed-form derivatives with respect to vertex positions, enabling differentiable collision resolution. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by operating directly on the volumetric winding number field rather than geometric primitives, allowing it to handle complex overlaps that are difficult to detect via standard mesh intersection tests. Inputs and Outputs Input: A triangle mesh defined by vertices V and faces F, and a pre-computed voxelization W \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n \times n} of resolution n representing the smoothed winding number field of the mesh. Output: Deformed vertex positions \tilde{\mathbf{V}} such that the resulting mesh has no self-intersections (winding number \le 1 everywhere). Data Structures Voxel Grid W: A 3D array of shape (n, n, n) storing floating-point winding number values for each voxel. Mesh Vertices V: A list of 3D coordinates \mathbf{v}i. Mesh Faces F: A list of triangle indices. Half-edges \mathcal{N}(i): For each vertex i, the set of all "spokes and rims" half-edges connecting i to its neighbors and their neighbors. Specifically, \mathbf{e}{jk} = \mathbf{v}j - \mathbf{v}k represents the edge vector between vertices j and k. Parameters Resolution n: The dimension of the voxel grid. Not given in the sources. Threshold \epsilon: Numerical tolerance for detecting self-intersections. Value: 0.001. Regularization Weight \alpha: Weight for the ARAP energy term. Value: 0.005. Learning Rate: Step size for the Adam optimizer. Value: 10^{-2}. Formulas The total energy E to be minimized is: E = E{\text{sect}} + \alpha E{\text{arap}} 1. Self-Intersection Energy (E{\text{sect}}): Sum of squared winding numbers for voxels exceeding the threshold 1 + \epsilon: E{\text{sect}} = \sum{W{ijk} > 1 + \epsilon} W{ijk}^2 This term penalizes regions where the surface overlaps itself. 2. ARAP Regularization Energy (E{\text{arap}}): Ensures the deformation remains as rigid as possible: E{\text{arap}}(\tilde{\mathbf{V}}) = \min{\mathbf{R}i \in SO(3)} \sum{i \in V} \sum{(j,k) \in \mathcal{N}(i)} w{jk} ||\mathbf{e}{jk} - \mathbf{R}i \tilde{\mathbf{e}}{jk}||^2 where \mathbf{R}i is the optimal rotation matrix for vertex i's star, found via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD). The weights w{jk} and edge definitions follow standard ARAP formulations. Steps 1. Initialize: Start with the original mesh vertices V as the initial guess for \tilde{\mathbf{V}}. 2. Compute Gradient: Calculate the gradient of E with respect to \tilde{\mathbf{V}}. This requires the gradient of the voxelization W with respect to vertex positions (provided by the parent method, Differentiable Voxelization via Smoothed Winding Numbers) and the gradient of the ARAP energy. 3. Optimize: Use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10^{-2} to update \tilde{\mathbf{V}}. 4. Check Convergence: After each iteration, check if all voxels satisfy W{ijk} \le 1 (or W{ijk} \le 1 + \epsilon). 5. Terminate: Stop when all self-intersections are resolved or a maximum iteration count is reached. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def removeselfintersections(meshV, meshF, voxelgridW, resolutionn, alpha=0.005, epsilon=0.001, lr=1e-2, maxiters=1000): """ Resolves self-intersections in a mesh by deforming vertices to minimize winding number > 1. Args: meshV: Initial vertex positions (N, 3) meshF: Face indices (M, 3) voxelgridW: Initial winding number voxelization (n, n, n) resolutionn: Voxel grid resolution alpha: ARAP regularization weight epsilon: Threshold for self-intersection detection lr: Learning rate for Adam maxiters: Maximum optimization iterations Returns: Deformed vertex positions (N, 3) """ # Initialize optimized vertices Vopt = meshV.clone() Vopt.requiresgrad = True # Initialize Adam optimizer optimizer = Adam([Vopt], lr=lr) for step in range(maxiters): optimizer.zerograd() # 1. Re-voxelize the deformed mesh to get current winding numbers # This calls the differentiable voxelization from the parent method # Input: Vopt, meshF, resolutionn # Output: Wcurrent (n, n, n) Wcurrent = differentiablevoxelization(Vopt, meshF, resolutionn) # 2. Compute Self-Intersection Energy # Mask for voxels with winding number > 1 + epsilon mask = Wcurrent > (1.0 + epsilon) # Sum of squared winding numbers for masked voxels Esect = torch.sum(Wcurrent[mask] 2) # 3. Compute ARAP Regularization Energy # Calculate edge vectors for deformed mesh # ejk = vj - vk edges = Vopt[meshF[:, 1:]] - Vopt[meshF[:,:-1]] # Simplified for demonstration # Note: Full ARAP requires computing optimal rotations Ri for each vertex star # and summing over all half-edges in the star. # Earap = min{Ri} sumi sum{(j,k) in N(i)} wjk ||ejk - Ri ejkopt||^2 # This part is computed using the standard ARAP gradient implementation. Earap = computearapenergy(Vopt, meshF) # 4. Total Energy Etotal = Esect + alpha Earap # 5. Backpropagate and Update Etotal.backward() optimizer.step() # Check convergence if not torch.any(Wcurrent > 1.0): break return Vopt.detach() Edge Cases and Pitfalls Half-Empty Voxels: Self-intersections occurring in voxels that are only partially occupied by the mesh may not be penalized because the energy integrates the winding number over the entire voxel volume. Overlaps hidden by voxel averaging can escape the objective. Negative Winding Numbers: Volume inversions can cause negative winding numbers, which may hide self-intersections in the optimization objective. Approximate Resolution: The method resolves self-intersections only approximately at voxel resolution. The parent method that provides the gradient of the winding number with respect to vertex positions, enabling this optimization. Differentiable Voxelization via Smoothed Winding Numbers The regularization technique used to preserve local rigidity during deformation. As-Rigid-As-Possible Surface Deformation Time Complexity: Depends on the number of optimization iterations and the cost of differentiable voxelization per iteration. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the voxel grid size n^3 and the mesh size. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a differentiable way to resolve self-intersections without explicit collision detection. Integrates seamlessly with gradient-based shape optimization. Limitations: Approximate resolution due to voxelization. May miss intersections in half-empty voxels or those masked by negative winding numbers. When to Use: When optimizing mesh shapes where self-intersections are undesirable and differentiable gradients are available. When Not to Use: When exact geometric intersection resolution is required, or when the mesh is too large for the voxel grid resolution to capture details. The method was introduced in "Differentiable Voxelization of Surface Representations" (2026) by the authors of the parent paper. It builds upon the concept of smoothed winding numbers for voxelization and extends it to differentiable mesh deformation. The ARAP regularization is based on the work of Sorkine and Alexa (2007). The method is applicable to various geometric optimization tasks, including shape deformation for manufacturing (e.g., bandsaw cutting) and space-filling tiling. name: Differentiable Voxelization from Radiative Gaussians
head: Density Voxelization, Radiative Gaussian Voxelizer
body: This method provides a differentiable voxelizer \mathcal{V} that efficiently queries a 3D density volume V \in \mathbb{R}^{X \times Y \times Z} from a set of radiative Gaussians G3. It solves the computational bottleneck of mapping continuous Gaussian splats to a discrete grid, enabling 3D regularization priors for tomographic reconstruction. Unlike Differentiable Voxelization (MC/CF) which operates on polygonal meshes, this method operates directly on parametric Gaussian distributions, leveraging spatial tiling for acceleration. Inputs: A set of N radiative Gaussians G3. Target grid dimensions X, Y, Z. Tile size T=8 (default, based on 8 \times 8 \times 8 tiles). Outputs: A 3D density volume tensor V of shape (X, Y, Z). Data Structures: Gaussian List: Array of Gaussian parameters. Tile Grid: Logical partitioning of the target space into 8 \times 8 \times 8 voxel tiles. Tile-AABB: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box for each tile, used for culling. Steps: 1. Tiling: Partition the target 3D space into a grid of 8 \times 8 \times 8 voxel tiles. 2. Culling: For each tile, compute its AABB. Retain only those Gaussians that have a 99% probability of intersecting the tile's AABB. 3. Parallel Computation: For each active tile, compute the voxel values in parallel. For each voxel (x,y,z) within the tile, sum the contributions of all retained Gaussians gi using the Gaussian kernel density formula. 4. Backpropagation: Implement the gradient computation in CUDA to allow gradients to flow from the volume V back to the Gaussian parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelizeradiativegaussians(gaussians, gridshape, tilesize=8): volume = [[[0.0 for in range(gridshape[2])] for in range(gridshape[1])] for in range(gridshape[0])] for tx in range(0, gridshape[0], tilesize): for ty in range(0, gridshape[1], tilesize): for tz in range(0, gridshape[2], tilesize): active = [] for g in gaussians: if g.mu[0] + g.scale[0] >= tx and g.mu[0] - g.scale[0] <= tx + tilesize and \ g.mu[1] + g.scale[1] >= ty and g.mu[1] - g.scale[1] <= ty + tilesize and \ g.mu[2] + g.scale[2] >= tz and g.mu[2] - g.scale[2] <= tz + tilesize: active.append(g) for dx in range(tilesize): for dy in range(tilesize): for dz in range(tilesize): x, y, z = tx + dx, ty + dy, tz + dz if x < gridshape[0] and y < gridshape[1] and z < gridshape[2]: density = 0.0 for g in active: dxv, dyv, dzv = x - g.mu[0], y - g.mu[1], z - g.mu[2] exponent = -0.5 (dxv2 g.invcov[0][0] + dyv2 g.invcov[1][1] + dzv2 g.invcov[2][2] + 2dxvdyvg.invcov[0][1] + 2dxvdzvg.invcov[0][2] + 2dyvdzvg.invcov[1][2]) density += g.alpha math.exp(exponent) volume[x][y][z] = density return volume Parameters: Tile size: 8 \times 8 \times 8. Culling confidence: 99%. Edge Cases: Empty Tiles: Tiles with no active Gaussians return zero density. Precision: CUDA implementation is used to maintain differentiability and speed. A high-performance kernel that decomposes the Mahalanobis distance into separable 1D operations to accelerate the query of the density volume V. It solves the prohibitive memory and time complexity of direct Gaussian-to-voxel mapping by enabling efficient, differentiable volume rendering suitable for joint optimization of Gaussian parameters in tomographic reconstruction. It builds on Differentiable Voxelization from Radiative Gaussians by providing the specific high-performance kernel used to query the density volume V. Performance: Accelerates the query process to > 100 FPS. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory: Requires storage for the volume V and temporary tile buffers. Strengths: Enables 3D regularization for radiative Gaussians in tomography. Differentiable via CUDA. Limitations: Dependent on grid resolution and tile size configuration. Originated in the context of Rectifying Radiative Gaussian Splatting for Tomographic Reconstruction. Inspired by voxelizers used in RGB tasks.
