name: R3D Polytope Splitting and Moment Reduction
head: voxel moment accumulation
body: R3D Polytope Splitting and Moment Reduction is a voxelization technique that computes exact coordinate moments of the intersection between a 3D polytope and a Cartesian grid by recursively splitting the polytope along grid axes until it fits within a single voxel, then reducing the polytope's moments to that voxel. It builds on Analytic Moment Voxelization by providing the specific geometric splitting and moment accumulation logic required to handle arbitrary convex polyhedra. It differs from Polynomial Field Integration via Coordinate Moments by focusing on the spatial decomposition of the domain (voxels) rather than the integration of a field over a fixed domain. Inputs: poly: A convex 3D polytope defined by a list of vertices and their connectivity. moments: An array to store the computed coordinate moments. polyorder: The highest order of moments to compute. destgrid: The output grid storing accumulated moments. d: Grid spacing vector (dx, dy, dz). ibox: The bounding box of the current polytope in voxel coordinates. dmax: The maximum dimension of the bounding box in voxels. Outputs: moments: Filled with the moments of the polytope's intersection with the current voxel. destgrid: Updated with the moments from the current voxel. The implementation relies on the following structures: r3drvec3: Contains x, y, z (real coordinates). r3ddvec3: Contains i, j, k (integer voxel indices). r3dplane: Contains d (real plane constant) and n.xyz (real normal vector). r3dvertex: Contains pos (r3drvec3) and pnbrs (array of 3 r3dint neighbor indices). r3dpoly: Contains nverts (r3dint) and verts (array of r3dvertex). r3dreal is double by default, or float if compiled with -DSINGLEPRECISION. R3DMAXVERTS limits the vertex buffer size (default 512). 1. Bounding Box Computation (r3dgetibox): Compute the integer bounding box ibox[2] for a polytope. Initialize rbox[0] to 1.0 \times 10^{30} and rbox[1] to -1.0 \times 10^{30} for all 3 dimensions. Iterate over all vertices to find min/max coordinates. Compute: \text{ibox}[0].\text{ijk}[i] = \lfloor \text{rbox}[0].\text{xyz}[i] / d.\text{xyz}[i] \rfloor \text{ibox}[1].\text{ijk}[i] = \lceil \text{rbox}[1].\text{xyz}[i] / d.\text{xyz}[i] \rceil 2. Clamping (r3dclampibox): Clamp the polytope's ibox to a clampbox. If ibox is completely outside clampbox (i.e., \text{ibox}[1].\text{ijk}[i] \le \text{clampbox}[0].\text{ijk}[i] or \text{ibox}[0].\text{ijk}[i] \ge \text{clampbox}[1].\text{ijk}[i]), clear ibox and set poly->nverts = 0. If \text{ibox}[0].\text{ijk}[i] < \text{clampbox}[0].\text{ijk}[i], add a clipping plane with d = -\text{clampbox}[0].\text{ijk}[i] \cdot d.\text{xyz}[i] and n.\text{xyz}[i] = 1.0. If \text{ibox}[1].\text{ijk}[i] > \text{clampbox}[1].\text{ijk}[i], add a plane with d = \text{clampbox}[1].\text{ijk}[i] \cdot d.\text{xyz}[i] and n.\text{xyz}[i] = -1.0. If planes were added, call r3dclip(poly, boxfaces, nboxclip). 3. Main Loop (Splitting): Maintain a stack of polytopes to process. For each polytope on the stack: If dmax == 1 (single voxel): Call r3dreduce(&stack[nstack].poly, moments, polyorder) to compute moments. Accumulate moments into destgrid using the index macro: \text{gind}(ii, jj, kk, mm) = \text{nmom} \cdot ((ii - \text{ibox}[0].i) \cdot \text{gridsz}.j \cdot \text{gridsz}.k + (jj - \text{ibox}[0].j) \cdot \text{gridsz}.k + (kk - \text{ibox}[0].k)) + mm If dmax > 1: Split the polytope along the axis spax at coordinate c = d.\text{xyz}[\text{spax}] \cdot (\text{stack}[nstack].\text{ibox}[0].\text{ijk}[\text{spax}] + \text{dmax}/2) using r3dsplitcoord. This produces two child polytopes children[0] and children[1]. Update the bounding box indices for the children. Copy the parent ibox to both. For children[0]: subtract (\text{dmax} - \text{dmax}/2) from \text{children}[0].\text{ibox}[1].\text{ijk}[\text{spax}]. For children[1]: add \text{dmax}/2 to \text{children}[1].\text{ibox}[0].\text{ijk}[\text{spax}]. Increment nstack by 2 to push children to the stack. 4. Coordinate Splitting (r3dsplitcoord): Calculate signed distances: \text{sdists}[v] = \text{vertbuffer}[v].\text{pos}.\text{xyz}[\text{ax}] - \text{coord} for all vertices. Mark \text{side}[v] = 1 if \text{sdists}[v] > 0.0. Count nright. Edge Cases: If nright == 0, copy inpoly to outpolys[0] and set outpolys[1]->nverts = 0. If nright == nverts, copy inpoly to outpolys[1] and set outpolys[0]->nverts = 0. Bisecting Edges: Iterate over all vertices vcur. If side[vcur] is false, iterate over its 3 neighbors np. If neighbor vnext has side[vnext] true, bisect the edge using linear interpolation to find the intersection point. Add new vertex to buffer, link it to vcur and vnext, increment nverts. Set side[nverts] = 1. Update neighbor pointers for vcur and vnext to include the new vertex. Face Traversal: For each new vertex (vstart from onv to nverts-1), traverse the face to find new neighbor links. Start at vcur = vstart, vnext = vertbuffer[vcur].pnbrs[0]. Loop: find np such that vertbuffer[vnext].pnbrs[np] == vcur. Move vcur = vnext. Set pnext = (np+1)%3. Set vnext = vertbuffer[vcur].pnbrs[pnext]. Continue while vcur < onv. Finally, link vertbuffer[vstart].pnbrs[2] = vcur and vertbuffer[vcur].pnbrs[1] = vstart. Compression: Iterate v from 0 to onv-1. Get cside = side[v]. Copy vertbuffer[v] to outpolys[cside]->verts[outpolys[cside]->nverts]. Update side[v] to the new index (outpolys[cside]->nverts++). Increment outpolys[cside]->nverts. Reindexing: For each vertex v in outpolys[0], update its 3 pnbrs entries using the side[] array: outpolys[0]->verts[v].pnbrs[np] = side[outpolys[0]->verts[v].pnbrs[np]]. Do the same for outpolys[1]. 5. Moment Reduction (r3dreduce): Compute the moments of the polytope. This involves decomposing the polytope into tetrahedra and computing the moments for each tetrahedron. The moments for a tetrahedron with vertices v0, v1, v2, v3 are computed using the local volume locvol and specific polynomial combinations of vertex coordinates. For example, moments 8, 9, and 10 are computed as: \text{moments}[8] += \text{locvol} \cdot 0.05 \cdot (v2.y \cdot v0.z + v2.y \cdot v1.z + 2 \cdot v2.y \cdot v2.z + v0.y \cdot (2 \cdot v0.z + v1.z + v2.z) + v1.y \cdot (v0.z + 2 \cdot v1.z + v2.z)) \text{moments}[9] += \text{locvol} \cdot 0.05 \cdot (v2.x \cdot v0.z + v2.x \cdot v1.z + 2 \cdot v2.x \cdot v2.z + v0.x \cdot (2 \cdot v0.z + v1.z + v2.z) + v1.x \cdot (v0.z + 2 \cdot v1.z + v2.z)) (Other moments follow similar patterns based on the polynomial order). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class r3dvertex: def init(self, pos, pnbrs): self.pos = pos self.pnbrs = pnbrs class r3drvec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def getitem(self, idx): return [self.x, self.y, self.z][idx] def sub(self, other): return r3drvec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def add(self, other): return r3drvec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def mul(self, s): return r3drvec3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def wav(p1, d1, p2, d2): # Linear interpolation to find intersection point on plane t = d1 / (d1 - d2) return p1 + (p2 - p1) t def r3dsplitcoord(inpoly, ax, coord, outpolys): nverts = inpoly.nverts vertbuffer = inpoly.verts side = [0] nverts sdists = [0.0] nverts for v in range(nverts): sdists[v] = vertbuffer[v].pos.xyz[ax] - coord if sdists[v] > 0.0: side[v] = 1 nright = sum(side) if nright == 0: outpolys[0] = inpoly outpolys[1].nverts = 0 return if nright == nverts: outpolys[1] = inpoly outpolys[0].nverts = 0 return # Bisect edges and create new vertices onv = nverts for vcur in range(nverts): if side[vcur] == 0: for np in range(3): vnext = vertbuffer[vcur].pnbrs[np] if side[vnext] == 1: newpos = wav(vertbuffer[vcur].pos, -sdists[vnext], vertbuffer[vnext].pos, sdists[vcur]) newv = r3dvertex(pos=newpos, pnbrs=[0,0,0]) vertbuffer.append(newv) side.append(1) onv += 1 # Traverse faces to update neighbor links for new vertices for vstart in range(nverts, onv): vcur = vstart vnext = vertbuffer[vcur].pnbrs[0] while vcur < onv: for np in range(3): if vertbuffer[vnext].pnbrs[np] == vcur: break vcur = vnext pnext = (np + 1) % 3 vnext = vertbuffer[vcur].pnbrs[pnext] vertbuffer[vstart].pnbrs[2] = vcur vertbuffer[vcur].pnbrs[1] = vstart # Compress vertices outpolys[0].nverts = 0 outpolys[1].nverts = 0 for v in range(onv): cside = side[v] outpolys[cside].verts[outpolys[cside].nverts] = vertbuffer[v] side[v] = outpolys[cside].nverts outpolys[cside].nverts += 1 # Reindex neighbor pointers for poly in outpolys: for v in range(poly.nverts): for np in range(3): poly.verts[v].pnbrs[np] = side[poly.verts[v].pnbrs[np]] R3DMAXVERTS: Static size array limit for storing vertices of 3D polyhedra. Default value is 512. Configurable via CMake command line: cmake -DR3DMAXVERTS=N... SHIFTPOLY: Boolean CMake option (-DSHIFTPOLY=True). Shifts polytopes to the origin to improve accuracy of moment calculations for small polytopes far from the origin. Computationally costly for high-order moments. If nright == 0 (polytope entirely on negative side), copy inpoly to outpolys[0] and set outpolys[1]->nverts = 0. If nright == nverts (entirely on positive side), copy inpoly to outpolys[1] and set outpolys[0]->nverts = 0. Precision issues may arise for small polytopes far from the origin; use SHIFTPOLY to mitigate. The vertex buffer size is limited by R3DMAXVERTS; ensure this is sufficient for the complexity of the polytopes being processed. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of voxels and the complexity of the polytopes. Strengths: Exact computation of moments, geometric robustness. Limitations: High computational cost for high-order moments, especially with SHIFTPOLY. Limited by R3DMAXVERTS. When to use: When exact moment computation is required for volume rendering, particularly for high-quality anti-aliasing. When not to use: When performance is critical and approximate methods are acceptable. The R3D library was developed by Devon Powell at Stanford University in 2014-2015. body: Analytic Tetrahedron Voxelization converts a parametrically defined continuous tetrahedral mesh into a digital voxel representation by computing physically conservative moments (volume, linear, quadratic) for each grid cell. Unlike standard binary voxelization which only stores occupancy, this method ensures that the total mass in each grid cell exactly equals the integral of the input density field over the cell, avoiding aliasing noise. It sets itself apart from Monte Carlo 2D Voxelization and Differentiable Voxelization (MC/CF) by providing exact, deterministic geometric intersection results rather than statistical approximations, and from Analytic Moment Voxelization by focusing specifically on the tetrahedral primitive and its robust clipping implementation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tetrahedral mesh defined by vertices. The mesh must have high quality: large minimum angle, no overlapping elements, and small variance in element quality. Output: A Cartesian grid containing moments. The grid stores moments (array of arrays for constant, linear, and quadratic orders) and orient (orientation flags). Data Structures: The implementation relies on specific structures for grid storage and geometric representation: 1. r3ddestgrid: r3dreal moments[10]: Gridded moments in row-major C order. Size is at least nx \times ny \times nz. r3dint polyorder: Polynomial order (0=constant, 1=linear, 2=quadratic). r3dorientation orient: Buffer for gridpoint orientation checks. Size is at least (nx+1) \times (ny+1) \times (nz+1). r3dlong bufsz: Buffer size. r3ddvec3 n: Grid dimensions (nx, ny, nz). 2. r3dorientation: r3dreal fdist[4]: Signed distances to the four clip planes. unsigned char fflags: Bit flags indicating inside/outside status for each of the 4 clip planes. 3. r3dplane (Face representation): r3ddvec3 n: Unit normal vector. r3dreal d: Signed distance to the origin. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preconditioning (Orientation): Ensure the tetrahedron vertices are oriented such that the volume is positive. Calculate the signed volume using the determinant of vectors spanning the tetrahedron. If the orientation function returns negative, swap vertices 2 and 3. \text{Signed Volume} = \frac{\det(\vec{AB}, \vec{AC}, \vec{AD})}{6} Exchanging two rows in the determinant leads to opposite signed volume. 2. Face Conversion: Convert the vertex representation to a face representation to obtain the four clip planes defining the tetrahedron. 3. Voxel Search: Identify voxels that need processing. Two methods are described: Brute-force: Check every grid point against each tetrahedron face. Scales as g^3. Binary Space Partitioning (BSP): Use a spatial tree. Scales as g^2 \log g. Note: Brute-force performs better for coarser grids due to BSP overhead; BSP overtakes brute-force at grid resolution 128^3. 4. Voxel Classification (Inside/Outside/Boundary): For each voxel, determine its relationship to the tetrahedron. Fully Inside: All 4 clip planes contain the voxel. Fully Outside: The voxel is outside at least one clip plane. Boundary: The voxel intersects the tetrahedron boundary. Classification using Philipp B's Algorithm: To test if a point P lies inside tetrahedron ABCD, define vectors \mathbf{a}=\vec{PA}, \mathbf{b}=\vec{PB}, \mathbf{c}=\vec{PC}, \mathbf{d}=\vec{PD}. Calculate determinants: Da = \det(\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{d}) Db = \det(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{d}) Dc = \det(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{d}) Dd = \det(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}) Point P is inside if: (Da > 0 \land Db < 0 \land Dc > 0 \land Dd < 0) \lor (Da < 0 \land Db > 0 \land Dc < 0 \land Dd > 0) 5. Moment Calculation (Reduction): Fully Inside Voxels: Compute analytic moments directly. For a voxel at grid index (i,j,k) with cell size d, the constant moment is volume V=d^3. Linear moments are V \cdot (i+0.5)d. Quadratic moments involve terms like V \cdot \frac{1}{3} d^2 (1+3i+3i^2). Boundary Voxels: Perform clipping and integration. 6. Clipping and Integration (Boundary Voxels): For boundary voxels, intersect the voxel (a convex polyhedron, typically a cube) with the tetrahedron. Clipping: Clip the voxel against the four faces of the tetrahedron. This is done by successively clipping one polyhedron against the faces of the other. Graph Traversal: Store polyhedra using only vertex locations and neighbors. Use a depth-first graph traversal on the planar graph representation to ensure topological validity and geometric robustness. This method inserts new vertices in the correct order on the fly, requiring no post-clipping reordering or face normals. Integration: Calculate moment integrals (constant, linear, quadratic) over the resulting clipped intersection domain. The results are accumulated into grid.moments. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Preconditioning: Ensure positive volume A, B, C, D = tetvertices vecAB = B - A vecAC = C - A vecAD = D - A signedvol = determinant(vecAB, vecAC, vecAD) / 6.0 if signedvol < 0: # Swap vertices 2 and 3 (C and D) to fix orientation tetvertices = [A, B, D, C] A, B, C, D = tetvertices vecAB = B - A vecAC = C - A vecAD = D - A signedvol = determinant(vecAB, vecAC, vecAD) / 6.0 # 2. Search and Process Voxels # Using brute-force for clarity, though BSP is faster for large grids for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): # Define voxel corners (8 corners) corners = [] for dx in [0, 1]: for dy in [0, 1]: for dz in [0, 1]: x = i d + dx d y = j d + dy d z = k d + dz d corners.append([x, y, z]) # 4. v2[2]v3[1]) - v1[1](v2[0]v3[2] - v2[2]v3[0]) + v1[2](v2[0]v3[1] - v2[1]v3[0]) def cross(v1, v2): return [ v1[1]v2[2] - v1[2]v2[1], v1[2]v2[0] - v1[0]v2[2], v1[0]v2[1] - v1[1]v2[0] ] def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return [v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag] This method voxelizes a single tetrahedron onto a Cartesian grid by computing physically conservative moments (volume, linear, quadratic) for a specified polynomial order. It ensures that the total mass in each grid cell exactly equals the integral of the input density field over the cell, avoiding aliasing noise. Unlike standard rasterization or Sutherland-Hodgman clipping, which can fail due to geometric degeneracy and roundoff errors, this scheme uses planar graph representations to maintain topological consistency during clipping, guaranteeing robustness even when vertices lie on clip planes. Platonic Solid Voxelization generates a 3D binary voxel array representing the interior of regular platonic solids (tetrahedron, cube, octahedron, dodecahedron, and icosahedron). It outputs a 3D array where the voxel value is 1 if inside the polyhedron and 0 otherwise. Unlike Analytic Tetrahedron Voxelization, which computes conservative moments for arbitrary tetrahedra, this method outputs a simple binary mask for specific regular polyhedra. It differs from Exact General Remeshing Scheme for Conservative Voxelization by using a direct half-space intersection test rather than remeshing. Time and Memory Complexity: Clipping and reduction operations scale roughly quadratically with the grid dimension g (linearly with surface area). Brute-force search scales as g^3. Binary space partitioning (BSP) search scales as g^2 \log g. Memory usage is dominated by the grid storage for moments and orientation flags. Measured Performance: On a 128^3 grid with 10^5 tetrahedra, the method produces 1.3 \times 10^4 interior and 1.5 \times 10^4 boundary voxels per tetrahedron on average. The proposed clipping operation is 3-4 times faster than López and Hernández (2008), with an overall speed-up of 2x. Philipp B's algorithm is faster than other point-in-tetrahedron algorithms. BSP overtakes brute-force at grid resolution 128^3. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Physically conservative (sum of voxel moments equals analytic moments up to floating-point precision). Immune to geometric degeneracies (e.g., vertices on clip planes). Does not require watertight or topologically closed meshes. Limitations: Cancellation errors arise when shifting voxels to a local coordinate frame, causing accuracy to be a few orders of magnitude away from machine precision despite the reduction process being accurate to machine precision. Requires high-quality input tetrahedral meshes (large minimum angle, no overlapping). When to Use: Use when physical conservation of mass/moments is critical (e.g., cosmological N-body systems). Use when exact geometric robustness is required for degenerate cases. Do not use if binary occupancy is sufficient and performance is paramount for very coarse grids (brute-force is simple). Analytic Tetrahedron Voxelization originates from the need for exact, mass-conservative voxelization in cosmological N-body systems. The specific clipping and integration framework was developed to address geometric degeneracies in polyhedron intersection, building on ideas from Sugihara (1994) regarding planar graph representations. The point-in-tetrahedron test known as "Philipp B's algorithm" was introduced by Philipp Beisel in June 2020 in response to a question by Denis Lolik, and was proven correct in the paper by. The C implementation r3d is available from Los Alamos National Laboratory. body: This method voxelizes a single tetrahedron onto a Cartesian grid by computing physically conservative moments (volume, linear, quadratic) for a specified polynomial order. It ensures that the total mass in each grid cell exactly equals the integral of the input density field over the cell, avoiding aliasing noise. Unlike standard rasterization or Sutherland-Hodgman clipping, which can fail due to geometric degeneracy and roundoff errors, this scheme uses planar graph representations to maintain topological consistency during clipping, guaranteeing robustness even when vertices lie on clip planes. The algorithm computes the intersection of a tetrahedron with a Cartesian grid cell (voxel) and integrates a polynomial density field over this intersection. It is divided into three phases: Searching, Clipping, and Reduction. Input: A tetrahedron defined by four vertices \mathbf{x}0, \mathbf{x}1, \mathbf{x}2, \mathbf{x}3; a Cartesian grid cell (voxel) defined by its eight vertices; a polynomial density field defined on the tetrahedron (typically up to quadratic order). Output: The conservative moments (integrals of 1, x, y, z, x^2, xy, \dots) of the density field over the voxel. Polyhedron Vertex: Each vertex in the planar graph representation contains: 1. Spatial coordinates (x, y, z). 2. Three pointers to neighboring vertices (forming the edges of the planar graph). 3. A byte flag indicating if the vertex has been clipped. 4. Four floating-point numbers storing the signed distance to each of the tetrahedron's four faces. Tetrahedron Faces: Each face f is defined by a vertex \mathbf{x}f and a unit normal \mathbf{n}f. The signed distance of a point \mathbf{x} to face f is: df = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}f) \cdot \mathbf{n}f Points with df \le 0 are "behind" or "outside" the face; points with df > 0 are "inside" or "in front". Determine which voxels intersect the tetrahedron boundary. 1. Classification: For each voxel, check the signed distances of its 8 vertices to all 4 faces of the tetrahedron. Type 1 (Outside): All 8 vertices have df \le 0 for at least one face f. Ignore these voxels. Type 2 (Inside): All 8 vertices have df > 0 for all 4 faces. These are fully contained. Type 3 (Boundary): Voxels that are neither Type 1 nor Type 2. These require clipping. 2. Optimization: Use Binary Space Partitioning (BSP) to find Type 3 voxels efficiently. Recursively split the grid bounding box along its longest dimension. Stop recursion if: 1. All 8 vertices of the box are outside one face (ignore box). 2. All 8 vertices are inside all faces (process box with a loop for Type 2 voxels). 3. The box contains a single voxel (process as Type 3). Complexity: O(g^2 \log g) vs O(g^3) for brute force, where g is the linear grid dimension. Construct the convex polyhedron resulting from the intersection of the voxel (cube) and the tetrahedron. 1. Initialization: Initialize the planar graph of the cubical voxel. Compute signed distances for all 8 vertices to the 4 tetrahedron faces. 2. Iterative Clipping: For each of the 4 faces of the tetrahedron: Find a vertex in the current graph with df \le 0 (behind the plane). If none exist, the polyhedron is entirely in front; skip this face. Perform a Depth-First Search (DFS) traversal starting from this vertex. For each vertex \mathbf{v} visited in the traversal: If \mathbf{v} is already marked clipped, continue. If \mathbf{v} is in front of the plane (df > 0): Identify the previous vertex \mathbf{v}{prev} in the edge traversal. Calculate the intersection point \mathbf{x}p between the edge (\mathbf{v}{prev}, \mathbf{v}) and the clip plane. Insert a new vertex at \mathbf{x}p into the graph, connecting it to \mathbf{v}{prev} and \mathbf{v}. Mark \mathbf{v}{prev} as clipped. Compute the signed distances of \mathbf{x}p to the remaining unclipped faces using weighted averaging (see Pitfalls). Mark \mathbf{v} as clipped. The traversal continues until all vertices behind the plane are processed and the graph topology is updated. 3. Result: The remaining graph represents the clipped polyhedron (intersection of voxel and tetrahedron). The graph structure preserves topological validity (faces are loops). Integrate the polynomial density field over the Type 1 and Type 3 voxels. 1. Type 1 (Inside): The voxel is a full axis-aligned cube. Integrate the polynomial analytically over the cube. 2. Type 3 (Clipped): Simplicial Decomposition: Decompose the clipped polyhedron into tetrahedra. Fix the origin \mathbf{0} as a common vertex for all tetrahedra. Traverse the planar graph to identify face loops. For each face loop, let the vertices be \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \dots, \mathbf{v}k in order. Form tetrahedra using the origin and each edge of the loop: Tetrahedron i has vertices \{\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}i, \mathbf{v}{i+1}\} (with \mathbf{v}{k+1} = \mathbf{v}2). Integration: Compute the integral of the polynomial density over each tetrahedron and sum the results. Coordinate Transformation: The integration formulas are given in barycentric coordinates. Convert Cartesian coordinates \mathbf{X} to barycentric coordinates \zetai: \mathbf{X} = \mathbf{X}0 \zeta0 + \mathbf{X}1 \zeta1 + \mathbf{X}2 \zeta2 + \mathbf{X}3 \zeta3 where \mathbf{X}i are the tetrahedron vertices. Polynomial Integral Formula: The integral of a monomial \zeta0^a \zeta1^b \zeta2^c \zeta3^d over a tetrahedron \Omegat with volume V is: \int{\Omegat} \zeta0^a \zeta1^b \zeta2^c \zeta3^d \, d\Omegat = 6 V \frac{a! b! c! d!}{(a + b + c + d + 3)!} Substitute the Cartesian expansion into this formula to compute moments like \int x^2 d\Omegat. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def signeddistance(vertex, facepoint, facenormal): """Calculate signed distance from vertex to face.""" return sum((vertex[i] - facepoint[i]) facenormal[i] for i in range(3)) def intersectedge(v0, d0, v1, d1): """ Calculate intersection point of edge (v0, v1) with plane. v0 is in front (d0 > 0), v1 is behind (d1 <= 0). """ denom = d0 - d1 return tuple((d0 v1[i] - d1 v0[i]) / denom for i in range(3)) def tetrahedronvolume(v0, v1, v2, v3): """Volume of tetrahedron with vertices v0, v1, v2, v3.""" m = [[v1[i]-v0[i], v2[i]-v0[i], v3[i]-v0[i]] for i in range(3)] det = (m[0][0] (m[1][1]m[2][2] - m[1][2]m[2][1]) - m[0][1] (m[1][0]m[2][2] - m[1][2]m[2][0]) + m[0][2] (m[1][0]m[2][1] - m[1][1]m[2][0])) return abs(det) / 6.0 def barycentricintegral(V, a, b, c, d): """Integral of barycentric monomial over tetrahedron.""" return 6.0 V math.factorial(a) math.factorial(b) math.factorial(c) math.factorial(d) / math.factorial(a + b + c + d + 3) def clippolyhedron(vertices, tetfaces): """ Clip a voxel (cube) against the 4 faces of a tetrahedron. Returns the planar graph of the resulting polyhedron. """ nodes = [] for v in vertices: nodes.append({'pos': v, 'neighbors': [], 'clipped': False, 'distances': []}) cubeedges = [(0,1), (1,2), (2,3), (3,0), (4,5), (5,6), (6,7), (7,4), (0,4), (1,5), (2,6), (3,7)] for i, j in cubeedges: nodes[i]['neighbors'].append(nodes[j]) nodes[j]['neighbors'].append(nodes[i]) for node in nodes: node['distances'] = [signeddistance(node['pos'], f['point'], f['normal']) for f in tetfaces] for i, face in enumerate(tetfaces): startnode = None for node in nodes: if node['distances'][i] <= 0 and not node['clipped']: startnode = node break if startnode is None: continue stack = [startnode] while stack: curr = stack.pop() if curr['clipped']: continue curr['clipped'] = True dcurr = curr['distances'][i] for neighbor in curr['neighbors']: if neighbor['clipped']: continue dnext = neighbor['distances'][i] if dcurr > 0 and dnext <= 0: newpos = intersectedge(curr['pos'], dcurr, neighbor['pos'], dnext) newnode = {'pos': newpos, 'neighbors': [], 'clipped': False, 'distances': []} curr['neighbors'].remove(neighbor) neighbor['neighbors'].remove(curr) curr['neighbors'].append(newnode) neighbor['neighbors'].append(newnode) newnode['neighbors'].extend([curr, neighbor]) newnode['distances'] = [signeddistance(newpos, f['point'], f['normal']) for f in tetfaces] newnode['distances'][i] = 0.0 curr['clipped'] = True elif dcurr <= 0: stack.append(neighbor) return [n for n in nodes if not n['clipped']] def integratepolyhedron(clippednodes): """ Integrate polynomial density over the clipped polyhedron. Uses simplicial decomposition (fan from origin). """ totalintegral = 0.0 visitededges = set() faceloops = [] for node in clippednodes: for neighbor in node['neighbors']: edge = (id(node), id(neighbor)) if edge in visitededges: continue visitededges.add(edge) loop = [node] curr = neighbor while curr != node: loop.append(curr) visitededges.add((id(curr), curr['neighbors'][0])) curr = curr['neighbors'][0] faceloops.append(loop) origin = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for loop in faceloops: v1 = loop[0]['pos'] for i in range(1, len(loop) - 1): v2 = loop[i]['pos'] v3 = loop[i+1]['pos'] V = tetrahedronvolume(origin, v1, v2, v3) totalintegral += barycentricintegral(V, 0, 0, 0, 0) return totalintegral Polynomial Order: The method supports moment integrals up to quadratic order (e.g., 1, x, y, z, x^2, xy, \dots). Constants (2D Demo): In the 2D demonstration, r0 = 0.45 (on a grid of side length 1.0), S0 = 0.2, and T0 = \pi/2. Geometric Degeneracy: Vertices lying on the clip plane within roundoff error can cause Sutherland-Hodgman to duplicate or omit vertices, creating invalid topology. This method avoids this by using topological consistency (planar graphs) and making geometric decisions combinatorially. Divide-by-Zero: The intersection formula \mathbf{x}p = \frac{d0 \mathbf{x}1 - d1 \mathbf{x}0}{d0 - d1} is safe because strict inequalities (d0 > 0, d1 \le 0) guarantee d0 - d1 > 0. Numerical Stability: The weighted averaging method for intersection points is more stable than parametric forms, especially when vertices are near the clip plane. Boundary Degeneracy: Near the boundaries of the domain, the old and new meshes may be exactly degenerate (lying on top of each other), which the method handles robustly. Time Complexity: Brute-force vertex checking scales as O(g^3), where g is the linear grid dimension. Binary space partitioning scales as O(g^2 \log g). Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of boundary voxels and the size of the planar graph representation. Each vertex stores coordinates, 3 pointers, 1 byte, and 4 floats. Performance: BSP is theoretically superior but has higher overhead; brute-force performs better practically on coarse grids. Strengths: Physically conservative (mass/momentum/energy conservation); robust to geometric degeneracy; supports higher-order polynomial interpolation; exact analytic integration. Limitations: Complex implementation due to graph management; higher overhead for BSP on coarse grids; limited to convex polyhedra intersections (tetrahedron vs. cube). When to use: When conservation of physical quantities (mass, momentum, energy) is critical, such as in cosmological N-body simulations, plasma physics, or hydrodynamics, and when aliasing noise from standard voxelization is unacceptable. The method was introduced by Devon Powell and Tom Abel in 2014 in the paper "An exact general remeshing scheme applied to conservative voxelization". It was developed for the analysis of cosmological N-body data, specifically for dark matter simulations, where global conservation of mass, momentum, and energy is required when solving Poisson equations. The core clipping algorithm is based on ideas by Sugihara (1994) regarding planar graph representations of convex polyhedra to ensure topological consistency. The method has applications in computer graphics, continuum mechanics, and hydrodynamics. name: Mesh Topology and Robust Digitization
body: This family of methods converts polygon meshes into discrete volumetric representations (voxel grids) while prioritizing topological validity and robustness against geometric defects. Unlike standard rasterization which may produce gaps or artifacts on non-watertight or low-quality meshes, these techniques enforce structural integrity, ensuring the resulting volume accurately reflects the mesh's interior or surface connectivity. They differ from primitive-based union methods by treating the mesh as a unified solid object rather than a collection of independent bounding volumes. Produces a binary UniformGrid from effectively 1D primitives (curves, surfaces) where occupied voxels form a 26-connected path. It distinguishes itself by using a target of three bisecting quadrilaterals per voxel to guarantee connectivity without gaps, unlike standard methods that may break thin structures. Choose this for flow simulation or fill operations on thin structures where topological continuity is critical. Transforms a polygon mesh into a UniformGrid using high-level library abstractions (e.g., PyVista). It enforces topological validity through built-in watertightness checks. Distinguished from explicit geometric decomposition methods, it relies on library functions like pyvista.voxelize. Choose this for rapid voxelization of valid, watertight meshes where ease of implementation is preferred over low-level control. Produces a single RectilinearGrid from a MultiBlock mesh input, labeling each voxel with the integer ID of the specific sub-mesh block it intersects. It differs from binary voxelization by preserving the topological identity of each mesh component through iterative enclosed-point testing or data sampling. Choose this when distinguishing between multiple overlapping or adjacent mesh components in a single volume is required. A robust framework that generates a high-quality tetrahedral mesh within a user-defined error bound to produce solid binary voxel data. It specifically addresses the failure of existing methods on low-quality, non-watertight, or topologically open meshes. Unlike centroid-connection methods, it combines background grid insertion with mesh improvement to maintain quality and speed, achieving near 100% success rates on difficult datasets. Choose this for robust voxelization of internet-sourced 3D models that are often non-watertight or low-quality. Definition: An extension to the base framework that uses PN-triangles and displacement mapping to voxelize low-resolution meshes with rugged surfaces at high resolution, achieving visual quality comparable to conventional voxelization of high-resolution meshes. Steps: Perform triangle subdivision using the hardware tessellator as in the base method. Use PN-triangles to reconstruct mesh details. Utilize the positions and normals of the PN-triangles to apply displacement mapping during the voxelization process. The need for robust mesh voxelization arises from the prevalence of low-quality, non-watertight, or topologically open meshes in internet 3D models, which cause standard voxelization methods to fail. Displacement voxelization was developed to maintain visual quality while achieving higher performance by voxelizing low-resolution versions of triangle meshes. It compares efficiency with pipeline-based and CUDA-based methods. Point-Tessellated Voxelization, http://www.cs.columbia.edu/cg/raymond/gi12/paper100.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Relaxed Connectivity Voxelization
head: 26-connected voxelization of 1D input
body: Relaxed Connectivity Voxelization is a method for voxelizing effectively one-dimensional input (1D, 2D, or 3D primitives) in 3D space that ensures the resulting voxels form a connected path, preventing gaps in flow simulation or fill operations. It produces a 26-connected path, allowing for fewer voxels than 6-connected methods while still maintaining connectivity. Unlike existing algorithms restricted to 1D primitives (e.g., line segments), this method works for input composed of 2D or 3D primitives that are effectively 1D. It builds on Mesh Topology and Robust Digitization and differs from Polygon Mesh Voxelization via Union of Sets, Labeled Volume Creation via MultiBlock Iteration, and Improved Tetrahedral Mesh Generation for Voxelization by targeting effectively 1D primitives with relaxed 26-connectivity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A continuous geometric object composed of 1D, 2D, or 3D primitives that is effectively one-dimensional (cannot produce separation in 3D space). Output: A set of voxels in a uniform grid that form a 26-connected path. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D uniform grid where each cell represents a voxel. Intersection Target: A geometric construct defined within each voxel to determine if the input intersects the voxel, consisting of three quadrilaterals that bisect the voxel along all three axes, subdividing space into cubes centered at voxel corners. Steps: 1. Define Intersection Target: For each voxel V, construct three quadrilaterals that bisect V along the x, y, and z axes. 2. Intersect Input with Target: Check if the input geometry intersects any of the three quadrilaterals within V. 3. Mark Voxels: If the input intersects the target in V, mark V as part of the voxelization. 4. Verify Connectivity: If the input intersects the target in V, parts of the intersection targets of the 26-neighbors of V form a closed box with side length twice that of a single voxel. 5. Ensure Path Continuity: Any continuous path from V to voxels outside immediate neighbors must intersect this enclosing box, and therefore intersect the target in N{26}(V). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def relaxedconnectivityvoxelization(inputsegments, gridbounds, voxelsize): """ Voxelizes effectively 1D input with 26-connectivity. Args: inputsegments: List of line segments, each ((x0,y0,z0), (x1,y1,z1)). gridbounds: Bounding box (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz). voxelsize: Size of each cubic voxel. Returns: Set of voxel coordinates (x, y, z) forming a 26-connected path. """ gridsize = [ int((gridbounds[3] - gridbounds[0]) / voxelsize), int((gridbounds[4] - gridbounds[1]) / voxelsize), int((gridbounds[5] - gridbounds[2]) / voxelsize) ] voxelizedvoxels = set() half = voxelsize / 2.0 for x in range(gridsize[0]): for y in range(gridsize[1]): for z in range(gridsize[2]): cx = gridbounds[0] + (x + 0.5) voxelsize cy = gridbounds[1] + (y + 0.5) voxelsize cz = gridbounds[2] + (z + 0.5) voxelsize # Three quadrilaterals bisecting the voxel along x, y, z axes quads = [ [(cx-half, cy-half, cz), (cx+half, cy-half, cz), (cx+half, cy+half, cz), (cx-half, cy+half, cz)], # XY [(cx-half, cy, cz-half), (cx+half, cy, cz-half), (cx+half, cy, cz+half), (cx-half, cy, cz+half)], # XZ [(cx, cy-half, cz-half), (cx, cy+half, cz-half), (cx, cy+half, cz+half), (cx, cy-half, cz+half)] # YZ ] intersects = False for p0, p1 in inputsegments: for q in quads: if intersectssegmentquad(p0, p1, q): intersects = True break if intersects: break if intersects: voxelizedvoxels.add((x, y, z)) return voxelizedvoxels def intersectssegmentquad(p0, p1, quad): v0, v1, v2 = quad[0], quad[1], quad[2] n = cross(sub(v1, v0), sub(v2, v1)) nlen = length(n) if nlen == 0: return False n = scale(n, 1.0/nlen) d = dot(n, v0) denom = dot(n, sub(p1, p0)) if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return False t = (d - dot(n, p0)) / denom if t < 0 or t > 1: return False ix = add(p0, scale(sub(p1, p0), t)) return pointinconvexquad(ix, quad) def sub(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) def add(a, b): return (a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]) def scale(v, s): return (v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]) def length(v): return (v[0]2+v[1]2+v[2]2)0.5 def pointinconvexquad(p, quad): v0, v1, v2 = quad[0], quad[1], quad[2] n = cross(sub(v1, v0), sub(v2, v1)) axes = [i for i in range(3) if abs(n[i]) < 1e-9] if len(axes) != 1: return False axis = axes[0] minv = [min(v[i] for v in quad) for i in range(3)] maxv = [max(v[i] for v in quad) for i in range(3)] return minv[0] <= p[0] <= maxv[0] and minv[1] <= p[1] <= maxv[1] and minv[2] <= p[2] <= maxv[2] Parameters: Voxel Size: Determines the resolution of the output grid. Not given in the sources. Grid Bounds: Defines the spatial extent of the voxelization. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The resulting voxelization may contain almost as many voxels as a cover produced by intersecting the input against the entire 3D voxel, making it potentially inefficient. The result is not thin in the same sense as the 2D crosshairs target; stepping along a curve in the dominant direction may produce fewer voxels. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Works for input composed of 2D or 3D primitives that are effectively 1D, unlike existing algorithms restricted to 1D primitives. Produces a 26-connected path, allowing for fewer voxels than 6-connected methods. Limitations: The resulting voxelization may contain almost as many voxels as a cover produced by intersecting the input against the entire 3D voxel, making it potentially inefficient. When to Use: When 26-connectivity is sufficient and the input is effectively 1D but composed of 2D or 3D primitives. When Not to Use: When 6-connectivity is strictly required for flow simulation, or when a thinner representation is needed (stepping along a curve in the dominant direction may yield fewer voxels). Origin: The method is described in "A Topological Approach to Voxelization" by Laine et al.. History and Development: The method is part of a broader topological approach to voxelization, which includes 6-connected voxelization and 26-separating voxelization. Usage: Used in applications requiring connected voxelizations of effectively 1D structures, such as flow simulation or fill operations. name: 3D Discrete Topology Fundamentals
head: Discrete Adjacency Definitions, Voxel Connectivity Types
body: 3D Discrete Topology provides the theoretical framework for defining topological properties, such as surface separation and connectivity, within a 3D discrete voxel grid. It solves the problem of "discrete disagreement," where standard continuous topology concepts fail in discrete space (e.g., 8-connected black curves can be penetrated by 8-connected white pixels without intersection). It sets itself apart from general graph theory by specifically addressing the geometric adjacency constraints of cubic voxels in 3D Euclidean space to ensure robust surface representation for volume rendering and ray tracing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D discrete space \Sigma, defined as a set of integral grid points in 3D Euclidean space with Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z). A subset of voxels S \subset \Sigma (typically "black" or opaque) and the background voxels W = \Sigma \setminus S ("white" or transparent). Output: Classification of connectivity (N-connected components), separation status (N-separating), and minimality of surfaces (N-minimal covers). Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array where each cell corresponds to a unit cubic volume centered at an integral grid point. Voxel Values: Mapped to a binary set \{0, 1\} where 1 represents "black" (opaque) and 0 represents "white" (transparent). Non-binary mappings to [0, 1] are supported for partial coverage or variable densities, enabling 3D antialiasing. Adjacency Definitions: Two voxels are defined as N-adjacent based on their geometric intersection: 1. 6-adjacent: Voxels share a face. Each voxel has 6 face-sharing neighbors. 2. 18-adjacent: Voxels share an edge or a face. Each voxel has 12 edge-sharing and 6 face-sharing neighbors. 3. 26-adjacent: Voxels share a vertex, an edge, or a face. Each voxel has 8 vertex-sharing, 12 edge-sharing, and 6 face-sharing neighbors. Connectivity and Paths: An N-path is a sequence of voxels with the same value where all consecutive pairs are N-adjacent. A set W is N-connected if there exists an N-path between every pair of voxels in W. An N-connected component is a maximal N-connected set. Separation and Minimality: N-Separating: A subset S is N-separating in \Sigma if \Sigma - S is not N-connected (i.e., \Sigma - S consists of at least two white N-connected components). N-Simple Voxel: For an N-separating surface W, a voxel p \in W is N-simple if W - p is still N-separating. N-Minimal Surface: An N-separating surface is N-minimal if it contains no N-simple voxels. Cover: A set of voxels such that every point of the continuous surface lies in a voxel of the cover. A minimal cover has no subset that is also a cover. Note that a cover is not necessarily separating, and a minimal cover is not necessarily N-minimal for any N. Avoiding Discrete Disagreement: To prevent the penetration of a closed surface by the background without intersection (discrete disagreement), "opposite" connectivity types must be used for the object and the background. In 3D space, 6 is "opposite" to 26 or to 18. Pseudocode: The following logic determines if a voxel is N-simple within an N-separating surface. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isnsimple(surfacevoxels, nadjacencytype, voxelspaceshape): """ Determines if a voxel p in surfacevoxels is N-simple. A voxel is N-simple if removing it from the surface leaves the surface still N-separating (i.e., the background remains disconnected). Args: surfacevoxels: Set of voxel coordinates (x,y,z) forming the surface W. nadjacencytype: Integer, 6, 18, or 26. voxelspaceshape: Tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) defining the bounds of Sigma. Returns: True if p is N-simple, False otherwise. """ # 1. Identify the background voxels (Sigma - Surface) # In a full grid implementation, this would be all voxels not in surfacevoxels. # For efficiency, we assume a function to get background components. background = getbackgroundvoxels(surfacevoxels, voxelspaceshape) # 2. Check if the original surface is N-separating # This implies the background has >= 2 N-connected components. if not isnseparating(surfacevoxels, nadjacencytype, voxelspaceshape): return False # Surface must be separating to have simple voxels # 3. Iterate through each voxel p in the surface for p in surfacevoxels: # 4. Create a temporary surface W' = W - {p} tempsurface = surfacevoxels - {p} # 5. Check if W' is still N-separating # This requires recomputing background connectivity for W' if not isnseparating(tempsurface, nadjacencytype, voxelspaceshape): # If removing p disconnects the background further or merges components # such that it is no longer separating (or changes separation status), # p is critical. If it remains separating, p is simple. # Note: The definition states p is simple if W-p is STILL N-separating. # So if isnseparating returns True for W-p, p is simple. pass else: # If W-p is still N-separating, then p is N-simple. return True return False def isnseparating(surfacevoxels, nadjacencytype, voxelspaceshape): """ Checks if the surface voxels separate the background into >= 2 N-connected components. """ background = getbackgroundvoxels(surfacevoxels, voxelspaceshape) if not background: return False # Find connected components in the background using N-adjacency components = findnconnectedcomponents(background, nadjacencytype) # Separating means the background is NOT N-connected (i.e., > 1 component) return len(components) >= 2 def findnconnectedcomponents(voxelset, nadjacencytype): """ Standard BFS/DFS to find connected components in a voxel set. """ visited = set() components = [] for voxel in voxelset: if voxel not in visited: component = set() queue = [voxel] visited.add(voxel) while queue: current = queue.pop(0) component.add(current) # Get N-neighbors neighbors = getnneighbors(current, nadjacencytype, voxelspaceshape) for neighbor in neighbors: if neighbor in voxelset and neighbor not in visited: visited.add(neighbor) queue.append(neighbor) components.append(component) return components def getnneighbors(voxel, nadjacencytype, voxelspaceshape): """ Returns all voxels adjacent to 'voxel' based on N-adjacency rules. """ x, y, z = voxel neighbors = [] # Offsets for 26-adjacency offsets = [] for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue offsets.append((dx, dy, dz)) for dx, dy, dz in offsets: nx, ny, nz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz # Filter by adjacency type if nadjacencytype == 6: # Face sharing: exactly one coordinate differs by 1 if abs(dx) + abs(dy) + abs(dz) == 1: neighbors.append((nx, ny, nz)) elif nadjacencytype == 18: # Edge or face sharing: max(|dx|,|dy|,|dz|) <= 1 and not vertex-only (sum of abs > 1? No) # Vertex sharing: all 3 differ by 1. Edge sharing: 2 differ by 1. Face: 1 differs by 1. # 18-adjacent includes face (1 diff) and edge (2 diffs). Excludes vertex (3 diffs). if max(abs(dx), abs(dy), abs(dz)) <= 1 and not (abs(dx)==1 and abs(dy)==1 and abs(dz)==1): neighbors.append((nx, ny, nz)) elif nadjacencytype == 26: # All 26 neighbors neighbors.append((nx, ny, nz)) # Boundary check if 0 <= nx < voxelspaceshape[0] and \ 0 <= ny < voxelspaceshape[1] and \ 0 <= nz < voxelspaceshape[2]: pass else: neighbors.remove((nx, ny, nz)) return neighbors 3D Discrete Topology is the theoretical framework for defining topological properties, such as surface separation and connectivity, within a 3D discrete voxel grid. It solves the problem of "discrete disagreement," where standard continuous topology concepts fail in discrete space (e.g., 8-connected black curves can be penetrated by 8-connected white pixels without intersection). It sets itself apart from general graph theory by specifically addressing the geometric adjacency constraints of cubic voxels in 3D Euclidean space to ensure robust surface representation for volume rendering and ray tracing. Time Complexity: Determining N-connectivity and separation requires graph traversal (BFS/DFS) on the voxel grid. Complexity is O(V + E) where V is the number of voxels and E is the number of adjacencies. For 26-adjacency, E \approx 26V. Checking N-minimality requires iterating over all surface voxels and recomputing connectivity, leading to O(S \cdot (V + E)) where S is the surface size. Memory Complexity: O(V) to store the voxel grid and visited sets for connectivity analysis. Strengths: Provides rigorous guarantees for topological correctness in discrete space, preventing artifacts like tunneling in ray tracing or incorrect surface extraction. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large volumes if minimality checks are performed frequently. The choice of N (6, 18, 26) significantly impacts performance and topological properties. When to use: When topological correctness is critical, such as in space subdivision for ray tracing or robust surface extraction. When not to use: For real-time rendering where performance is paramount and approximate topology is acceptable. The concept of 3D discrete topology was formalized to address the limitations of 2D discrete topology in three dimensions. The specific definitions of N-adjacency (6, 18, 26) and the concept of "opposite" connectivity to avoid discrete disagreement are detailed in foundational works on volume visualization. The text cites [94] and [43] for further details on covers and minimality, indicating a lineage of research in computational geometry and computer graphics. Volume Visualization and Volume Graphics, https://www3.cs.stonybrook.edu/~mueller/teaching/cse332/volvisChapter.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (book)

name: 3D Discrete Topology
body: 3D Discrete Topology is the theoretical framework for defining topological properties, such as surface separation and connectivity, within a 3D discrete voxel grid. It addresses "discrete disagreement," where topological properties in continuous space do not directly translate to discrete grids. Space Definition The 3D discrete space is a set of integral grid points in 3D Euclidean space defined by Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z). A voxel is the unit cubic volume centered at each integral grid point. Voxel Values In the binary case, voxel values are mapped to the set \{0, 1\}. Voxels assigned '1' are called black voxels representing opaque objects, and those assigned '0' are white voxels representing the transparent background. Adjacency and Connectivity Two voxels are 26-adjacent if they share a vertex, an edge, or a face. Every voxel has exactly 26 adjacent neighbors: 8 share a vertex, 12 share an edge, and 6 share a face. Face-sharing voxels are 6-adjacent, and edge-sharing and face-sharing voxels are 18-adjacent. The prefix N denotes the adjacency type, where N \in \{6, 18, 26\}. Connectivity and Paths An N-path is a sequence of voxels having the same value where all consecutive pairs are N-adjacent. A set of voxels W is N-connected if there is an N-path between every pair of voxels in W. An N-connected component is a maximal N-connected set. Opposite Connectivity To avoid penetration scenarios, opposite connectivity types are used for foreground and background sets. In 2D space, 4 and 8 are opposite, while in 3D space 6 is opposite to 26 or to 18. Separation and Minimality A subset S of black voxels is N-separating if it is not N-connected, meaning it consists of at least two white N-connected components. Let W be an N-separating surface. A voxel p \in W is N-simple if W \setminus \{p\} is still N-separating. An N-separating surface is N-minimal if it contains no N-simple voxels. Covering A cover of a continuous surface is a set of voxels such that every point of the continuous surface lies in a voxel of the cover. A cover is minimal if none of its subsets is also a cover. Discrete Disagreement In 2D, 8-connected black curves can be penetrated by 8-connected white pixels without intersection, unlike continuous curves. There are no analogous results in 3D space. Limitations A cover is not necessarily separating. Even a minimal cover is not necessarily N-minimal for any N. What it is: The foundational definitions of 3D discrete space, voxel geometry, and basic adjacency relations. Distinction: Provides the static geometric and set-theoretic definitions (coordinates, unit cubes, basic adjacency counts) without addressing dynamic topological properties like separation or minimality. When to choose: Use this as the starting point for understanding the coordinate system and voxel structure. Link: 3D Discrete Topology Fundamentals The theory of 3D discrete topology was formalized to address topological issues in 3D discrete space, such as defining the separation of both sides of a surface, which cannot be well-defined by employing 2D terminology. It originated in the context of volume visualization and voxelization, specifically to support applications like fast ray tracing where space subdivision is employed. The concepts were detailed by Arie Kaufman in the chapter "Fundamentals of 3D Discrete Topology" within the book Volume Visualization: Principles and Advances. The theory is essential for binary voxelization techniques that aim to generate N-separating, N-minimal, and covering surfaces. Volume Visualization: Principles and Advances, https://courses.cs.duke.edu/spring03/cps296.8/papers/KaufmanVolumeVisualization.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Polygon Mesh Voxelization via Union of Sets
head: PyVista Mesh Voxelization, PyVista Mesh Voxelization & Watertight Handling, Union of Sets Voxelization, VTK-based Mesh Voxelization
body: This method converts a continuous polygon mesh into a discrete UniformGrid voxel representation by computing the union of bounding volumes around vertices, edges, and faces. It solves the problem of robust surface digitization for volume rendering by enforcing separability guarantees and providing built-in watertightness validation. It differs from topological digitization methods (like Mesh Topology and Robust Digitization) by relying on geometric bounding volumes rather than explicit connectivity graphs, and from primitive-based union methods by treating the mesh as a unified solid object. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A polygon mesh (pyvista.PolyData). Point clouds require triangulation first, optionally via delaunay3d for simple surfaces. Output: A pyvista.UniformGrid object containing the voxelized representation. Data Structures: UniformGrid: Stores voxel bounds, dimensions, and point data. Implicit Distance: A scalar field that verifies voxel consistency relative to the mesh surface. Parameters: checksurface (bool, default True): Skips watertight validation when False, preventing errors on imperfect meshes but risking noise if large holes exist. Rc (radius for bounding volumes): Equals L/2 for 6-separability and L/(2\sqrt{3}) for 26-separability, where L is voxel width. Steps: 1. Validate mesh watertightness if checksurface=True; otherwise, proceed with pyvista.voxelize(inputmesh) to generate the UniformGrid. 2. Compute the union of bounding volumes: for each vertex, include voxels whose centers fall inside a bounding sphere of radius Rc. For each edge, include voxels inside a bounding cylinder of radius Rc and length equal to the edge length. For the mesh body, include voxels between two bounding planes G and H, plus planes perpendicular to each edge, forming a closed region. 3. Optionally compute implicit distances via computeimplicitdistance to verify consistency or filter internal voxels for a hollow representation. 4. Optionally replace cube glyphs with other primitives using voxelizedobject.glyph(geom=typeofprimitive()). Formulas: Rc = \frac{L}{2} \quad \text{(6-separability)} Rc = \frac{L}{2\sqrt{3}} \quad \text{(26-separability)} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import pyvista as pv import numpy as np def voxelizemeshunionofsets(mesh, checksurface=True, separability=6): """ Voxelize a polygon mesh using the Union of Sets method. Args: mesh: pyvista.PolyData mesh object. checksurface: bool, default True. Validates watertightness. separability: int, 6 or 26. Determines bounding volume radius. Returns: pyvista.UniformGrid: The voxelized volume. """ # Compute voxel width L from mesh bounds or desired resolution # Standard initialization: bounds = mesh.bounds; L = (bounds[1]-bounds[0])/resolution # Compute bounding volume radius Rc based on separability if separability == 6: Rc = L / 2.0 elif separability == 26: Rc = L / (2.0 np.sqrt(3.0)) else: raise ValueError("Separability must be 6 or 26.") # Step 1: Voxelization # pyvista.voxelize generates the UniformGrid and enforces checksurface validation voxelgrid = pv.voxelize(mesh, checksurface=checksurface) # Step 2: Union of Sets inclusion # The algorithm includes voxels whose centers fall inside: # 1. Bounding spheres at vertices (radius Rc) # 2. Bounding cylinders along edges (radius Rc, length = edge length) # 3. Bounding planes forming a closed slab around the mesh body # Implementation iterates over candidate voxels and tests geometric inclusion. # Step 3: Optional verification # implicitdist = voxelgrid.computeimplicitdistance() return voxelgrid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Watertight Meshes: PyVista expects watertight meshes by default; holes, overlapping edges, or incorrect geometry cause errors. Skipping Validation: Setting checksurface=False bypasses errors on imperfect meshes but may yield noise or incorrect voxelization if large holes or geometric imperfections exist. Intersection Holes: Using a distance parameter t instead of Rc for bounding volumes causes holes at intersections (e.g., 45-degree lines) because the intersection point may fall outside both bounding volumes. Point Cloud Input: Point clouds must be triangulated into a mesh before voxelization. Focuses on connectivity constraints rather than strict watertightness. Choose when 26-connectivity is required without surface validation. Relaxed Connectivity Voxelization Handles multiple mesh blocks with distinct labels. Choose when processing multi-part assemblies. Labeled Volume Creation via MultiBlock Iteration Uses tetrahedralization for complex geometries. Choose when high-fidelity internal structure is needed. Improved Tetrahedral Mesh Generation for Voxelization Time Complexity: Depends on the implementation; the authors use a linked list to store the volume model, with complexity influenced by the number of voxels and mesh complexity. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly defined in the sources. Measured Performance: On an SGI workstation (195MHz R10000, 640MB memory, 512x512x512 resolution), the pump model (3030 facets) took 67.8 seconds for 6-separability (21.8 voxels/ms) and 95.4 seconds for 26-separability (21.2 voxels/ms). Strengths: Simple interface, built-in watertightness checks, Python ecosystem integration. Limitations: Requires watertight meshes by default, may produce noise if validation is skipped, limited to mesh inputs. When to Use: Quick, robust voxelization of watertight meshes in Python. When Not to Use: Non-watertight meshes requiring high-fidelity internal structure, or performance-critical large meshes needing C++ optimization. This method is based on the PyVista library, which wraps VTK's geometric processing capabilities for mesh-to-UniformGrid transformation. The theoretical foundation uses bounding spheres, cylinders, and plane slabs to guarantee 6- or 26-separability for planar objects. How to Voxelize Meshes and Point Clouds in Python - Medium, https://medium.com/data-science/how-to-voxelize-meshes-and-point-clouds-in-python-ca94d403f81d, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) An Accurate Method for Voxelizing Polygon Meshes, https://web.eecs.utk.edu/~huangj/papers/polygon.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Labeled Volume Creation via MultiBlock Iteration
head: Labeled Volume Creation via Sample and Split
body: This method voxelize a MultiBlock mesh into a single RectilinearGrid volume where each voxel is labeled with the integer ID of the specific sub-mesh block it intersects, rather than using a binary inside/outside flag. It differs from Relaxed Connectivity Voxelization and Polygon Mesh Voxelization via Union of Sets by explicitly preserving block identity through iterative enclosure testing or sampling, enabling distinct material or region assignment per block in the final volume. It builds on Mesh Topology and Robust Digitization by enforcing topological consistency across multiple mesh blocks during discretization. Inputs and Outputs Input: mesh (pyvista.DataSet or MultiBlock), density (float or arraylike[float]), checksurface (bool, default True). Output: voi (pyvista.RectilinearGrid with InsideMesh cell data) for Method 1, or multiblock (MultiBlock of grids) for Method 2. Data Structures voi: pyvista.RectilinearGrid defined by coordinate arrays x, y, z. InsideMesh: cell data array of size voi.ncells, initialized to zero. maskvol: boolean array of size voi.npoints indicating enclosed grid points. cellids: 1D integer array of unique voxel indices interior to a sub-mesh. Parameters density: uniform voxel size. Defaults to mesh.length / 100 if None. checksurface: specifies whether to check the surface for closure. If True, raises a runtime error if the surface is not closed and manifold. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import pyvista as pv import collections.abc def voxelizevolumemultiblocklabel(mesh, density=None, checksurface=True): """Method 1: Iterative Enclosure""" mesh = pv.wrap(mesh) # Determine density if density is None: density = mesh.length / 100 if isinstance(density, (int, float, np.number)): densityx, densityy, densityz = [density] 3 elif isinstance(density, (collections.abc.Sequence, np.ndarray)): densityx, densityy, densityz = density else: raise TypeError(f"Invalid density {density!r}, expected number or array-like.") # Define grid bounds xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax = mesh.bounds x = np.arange(xmin, xmax, densityx) y = np.arange(ymin, ymax, densityy) z = np.arange(zmin, zmax, densityz) voi = pv.RectilinearGrid(x, y, z) voi["InsideMesh"] = np.zeros(voi.ncells) # Iterate over sub-meshes for i, submesh in enumerate(mesh): submeshnumber = i + 1 surface = submesh.extractgeometry() # Pre-processing if not surface.faces.size: raise ValueError("Input mesh must have faces for voxelization.") if not surface.isalltriangles: surface.triangulate(inplace=True) # Enclosure test selection = voi.selectenclosedpoints(surface, tolerance=0.0, checksurface=checksurface) maskvol = selection.pointdata["SelectedPoints"].view(np.bool) # Identify voxels cellids = np.unique(voi.extractpoints(np.argwhere(maskvol))["vtkOriginalCellIds"]) voi["InsideMesh"][cellids] = submeshnumber return voi def voxelizesamplesplitlabel(mesh, density=0.01, tolerance=1): """Method 2: Sampling and Split""" # Assume mesh already has cell data labels assigned (e.g., mesh['labels'] = blockindices) vox = pv.voxelize(mesh, density=density) sampled = vox.sample(target=mesh, tolerance=tolerance) sampled.setactivescalars('labels') # Convert point data to cell data sampled = sampled.ptc() sampled['labels'] = np.round(sampled['labels']) # Split into MultiBlock based on unique label values multiblock = sampled.splitvalues() return multiblock Edge Cases and Pitfalls Empty Mesh: If surface.faces.size == 0, the method raises ValueError. Non-Triangular Meshes: Non-triangular surfaces may cause artifacts; triangulation is recommended. Sampling Tolerance: In Method 2, if tolerance is too small, data may not be sampled correctly. Point vs. Cell Data: Method 2 requires ptc() conversion because sample only handles point data, which can introduce interpolation errors. Method 2 is more scalable for complex meshes but depends on the efficiency of pyvista.voxelize and sample. Strengths: Method 1 provides precise block identification without interpolation. Method 2 leverages existing PyVista filters for simplicity. Limitations: Method 1 can be slow for many blocks. Method 2 introduces interpolation artifacts and requires specific PyVista versions for splitvalues. This method originates from discussions in the PyVista GitHub repository regarding labeled volume creation for MultiBlock meshes. It was proposed as a solution to create voxel volumes where each voxel is labeled with the ID of the sub-mesh block it intersects, addressing limitations in standard voxelization methods that only provide binary inside/outside flags. name: Improved Tetrahedral Mesh Generation for Voxelization
head: Robust Tetrahedral Voxelization, Tetrahedral Mesh Voxelization
body: This method is a robust voxelization framework that converts a triangular mesh into solid binary voxel data by generating a high-quality intermediate tetrahedral mesh. It specifically addresses the failure of existing methods to handle low-quality, non-watertight, or topologically open meshes common in internet datasets. Unlike state-of-the-art approaches that connect triangle facets to a model centroid (producing faulty meshes for high-face models) or standard Delaunay triangulation (which suffers from boundary quality issues and high cost for sparse models), this method uses background grid insertion combined with mesh improvement to maintain quality and speed. It achieves near 100% success rate on testing datasets compared to ~50% for other methods. Inputs: 1. A triangular mesh M. 2. A user-defined error tolerance parameter \epsilon. Outputs: 1. A tetrahedral mesh T generated within the error bound. 2. Solid binary voxel data derived from T. Data Structures: Triangular Mesh M: Defined by vertices V and triangular faces F{tri}. Tetrahedral Mesh T: Defined by vertices VT and tetrahedral cells. Background Grid: A structured grid aligned with the bounding box of the input mesh, used as the base for insertion. Parameters: \epsilon (epsilon): User-defined tolerance for errors in tetrahedral mesh generation. It controls the magnitude of zigzag artifacts on straight lines. Typical tested values are 2 \times 10^{-3}, 5 \times 10^{-3}, and 1 \times 10^{-2}. Errors up to \epsilon = 10^{-2} (10x default) do not produce major differences in the final voxelized output. Algorithm Steps: 1. Input Validation/Preprocessing: Accept the triangular mesh M. 2. Initial Mesh Improvement: Perform mesh improvement processing on the input triangular mesh M to enhance quality. 3. Background Mesh Insertion: Insert the improved triangular mesh into a background grid (background mesh insertion). This creates an initial tetrahedral mesh structure. 4. Post-Insertion Mesh Improvement: Perform mesh improvement processing on the resulting tetrahedral mesh to refine element quality and satisfy the error bound \epsilon. 5. Voxelization: Rasterize the final tetrahedral mesh to produce solid binary voxel data. This step relies on the stronger assumption of mesh validity provided by the improved tetrahedral generation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def improvedtetrahedralvoxelization(triangularmesh, epsilon): # Step 1: Initial Mesh Improvement # Standard operation: Apply Laplacian smoothing and edge flips to improve triangle quality. improvedtrimesh = applylaplaciansmoothingandedgeflips(triangularmesh) # Step 2: Background Mesh Insertion # Standard operation: Subdivide a uniform grid aligned with the bounding box, then insert mesh vertices and edges. initialtetmesh = insertintouniformgrid(improvedtrimesh) # Step 3: Post-Insertion Mesh Improvement # Standard operation: Perform Delaunay refinement and edge swapping to satisfy quality and epsilon bound. finaltetmesh = applydelaunayrefinementandedgeswapping(initialtetmesh, epsilon) # Step 4: Voxelization # Standard operation: Evaluate each voxel center against the tetrahedral mesh to classify solid/empty. voxeldata = rasterizetetmeshtovoxels(finaltetmesh) return voxeldata Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zigzag Artifacts: Setting \epsilon too large causes visible zigzag artifacts on straight lines. However, the impact on the final voxel output is minimal even at \epsilon = 10^{-2}. Low-Quality Input: The method is designed to handle meshes that cause other methods to fail, including non-watertight or topologically open meshes. Sparse Models: Standard grid insertion is computationally expensive for sparse models; this method mitigates this by combining insertion with improvement. A method to convert a coarse voxel representation into a tetrahedral mesh by splitting each hexahedron (voxel) into 6 tetrahedra to ensure face-to-face consistency. Definition: A tetrahedron is a pyramid-like polyhedron with four vertices and four triangular faces. A hexahedron has eight vertices and six quadrilateral faces. Process: The voxel-based shape is represented as a hexahedral mesh H = (V, F{quad}) = (\cupc \{v{c,i}\}{i=1}^8, \cupc \{f{c,j}\}{j=1}^6), where V is the vertex set, F{quad} is the quadrilateral face set, v{c,i} is the i-th vertex of the c-th cube, and f{c,j} is the j-th quadrilateral face of the c-th cube. This is then split into a tetrahedral mesh T = (V, F{tri}) = (\cupc \cup{k=1}^6 \{v{c,k,i}\}{i=1}^4, \cupc \cup{k=1}^6 \{f{c,k,j}\}{j=1}^4), where V is the same vertex set, F{tri} is the triangular face set, v{c,k,i} is the i-th vertex of the k-th tetrahedron in the c-th cube, and f{c,k,j} is the j-th triangular face of the k-th tetrahedron in the c-th cube. Parameter: Number of tetrahedra per cube is 6. Success Rate: Achieved near 100% availability (success rate) on testing datasets (Princeton ModelNet and Thingi10k), whereas other methods achieved around 50%. Performance: Produces much higher quality tetrahedral meshes as an intermediate outcome, allowing for a faster voxelization algorithm based on stronger assumptions. Scalability: Combines background insertion with mesh improvement to maintain process speed, addressing the computational expense of standard grid insertion for sparse models. Strengths: Robustness to low-quality, non-watertight, or topologically open meshes; high success rate; ability to use \epsilon as a data augmentation technique for 3D CNNs. Limitations: Requires careful selection of \epsilon to balance zigzag artifacts and accuracy, though the method is tolerant up to \epsilon = 10^{-2}. The method was proposed by researchers from National Taiwan University. It is based on the work of [32] and [33] (cited in the source), which involve background mesh insertion with mesh improvement processing. The framework was tested on various datasets including Princeton ModelNet and Thingi10k. The work includes a proof that the algorithm performs better than the state-of-the-art method [1] (which connects every triangle facet to the model centroid).
