name: DCX Points-to-Voxels
head: Custom Voxel Grid Implementation, Hair Point Voxelization, Point Cloud Voxelization via Space Index Array, Voxelization of Point Clouds
body: DCX Points-to-Voxels converts a set of 3D points into a sparse voxel grid representation by mapping each point to a discrete voxel index within a defined bounding box, storing occupancy in a 3D integer array, and computing the centroid of points within each occupied voxel. It differs from simple averaging by prioritizing points with higher depth confidence in its aggregation step, which helps mitigate noise and outliers in regions with uncertain geometry. It serves as the final aggregation step in the DCX pipeline, refining the raw point cloud into a structured sparse representation suitable for downstream rendering or reconstruction tasks. It contrasts with direct occupancy mapping in VoxelGrid::CreateFromPointCloudWithinBounds or multi-plane approaches in Multi-Plane Point Cloud Voxelization and Weight Aggregation. Inputs: 1. Point cloud data: A list of N points, where each point Pi has coordinates (xi, yi, zi) and optionally color (ri, gi, bi). 2. Resolution: The side length of a voxel in world units (res). 3. Bounding Box: Defined by minimum (minx, miny, minz) and maximum (maxx, maxy, maxz) coordinates, computed as an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) from the data or set as fixed CUSTOM dimensions. Outputs: 1. Sparse Voxel Grid: A data structure mapping voxel indices to aggregated properties (centroid position, color, point count). 2. Occupancy Array: A 3D integer array indicating which voxels are occupied. Data Structures: Voxels Map: A hash map where the key is a linear voxel ID (integer) and the value is a structure containing count (integer), sumpos (vector of size 3), and sumcolor (vector of size 3, if applicable). Space Index Array: A fixed-size 3D integer array spaceIndex initialized to 0. In the reference implementation, dimensions are hardcoded to [192][128][128] regardless of the bounding box mode. Auxiliary Map: In some implementations, a secondary map tracks voxel existence and counts during the merge phase to avoid redundant lookups. Parameters: resolution (res): Voxel size. Typical values: 0.011, 0.016, or 0.1. densitythreshold: Minimum number of points required to create a voxel. Default: 1. colorlevels: Number of quantization levels for color reduction. 0=off, 8/16/32=quantize. Default: 0. Steps: 1. Compute Bounding Box and Grid Dimensions: If AABB mode: Compute min\bounds = \min(P) and max\bounds = \max(P) across all points. If CUSTOM mode: Use predefined bounds. For example, X: [-total\reg\X/2, total\reg\X/2], Y: [0, total\reg\Y], Z: [-total\reg\Z/2, total\reg\Z/2]. Calculate grid dimensions: Dx = \lceil \frac{max\boundsx - min\boundsx}{res} \rceil + 1 Dy = \lceil \frac{max\boundsy - min\boundsy}{res} \rceil + 1 Dz = \lceil \frac{max\boundsz - min\boundsz}{res} \rceil + 1 In specific implementations, dimensions are hardcoded based on total range and resolution (e.g., 128x192x128). 2. Initialize Data Structures: Initialize spaceIndex array with zeros. Initialize Voxels Map as empty. 3. Map Points to Voxels and Aggregate: For each point Pi = (xi, yi, zi): a. Compute Voxel Coordinates: i = \lfloor \frac{xi - min\boundsx}{res} \rfloor j = \lfloor \frac{yi - min\boundsy}{res} \rfloor k = \lfloor \frac{zi - min\boundsz}{res} \rfloor Note: Some implementations use ceil for X and floor for Y/Z relative to bounding box minimums. b. Check Bounds: If i < 0 or i \ge Dx or j < 0 or j \ge Dy or k < 0 or k \ge Dz, skip the point. c. Compute Linear Index: idx = i + j \cdot Dx + k \cdot Dx \cdot Dy Note: Specific implementations may use different stride rules, e.g., idx = i \cdot 1 + j \cdot 128 + k \cdot (128 \cdot 192) if dimensions are fixed. d. Update Voxels Map: If idx not in Voxels Map: Create entry: count = 1, sumpos = (xi, yi, zi), sumcolor = (ri, gi, bi) (if color exists). Insert into Voxels Map. Else: Retrieve existing entry. count = count + 1 sumpos = sumpos + (xi, yi, zi) sumcolor = sumcolor + (ri, gi, bi) (if color exists) Update Voxels Map[idx]. e. Mark Occupancy: Set spaceIndex[i][j][k] = 1. Warning: Some implementations swap X and Y indices and apply a -1 offset on X: spaceIndex[j][i-1][k] = 1. This can cause out-of-bounds access if i=0. Use standard [i][j][k] unless replicating the specific bug/quirk. 4. Filter Voxels: Iterate through Voxels Map. If count < densitythreshold, remove the voxel from the map. 5. Compute Centroids: For each remaining voxel in Voxels Map: center\pos = \frac{sum\pos}{count} avg\color = \frac{sum\color}{count} If colorlevels > 0, quantize avgcolor to the specified number of levels. Store centerpos and avgcolor in the final voxel structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from collections import defaultdict def dcxpointstovoxels(points, resolution, bboxmin, bboxmax, densitythreshold=1, colorlevels=0): """ Convert points to sparse voxels. Args: points: List of tuples (x, y, z, r, g, b). If no color, r,g,b can be None. resolution: Voxel size. bboxmin: Tuple (minx, miny, minz). bboxmax: Tuple (maxx, maxy, maxz). densitythreshold: Min points per voxel. colorlevels: Quantization levels for color. Returns: voxels: Dict mapping (i, j, k) to {'pos': (cx, cy, cz), 'color': (r, g, b), 'count': int} spaceindex: 3D list/array of 0s and 1s. """ minx, miny, minz = bboxmin maxx, maxy, maxz = bboxmax # Calculate grid dimensions Dx = math.ceil((maxx - minx) / resolution) + 1 Dy = math.ceil((maxy - miny) / resolution) + 1 Dz = math.ceil((maxz - minz) / resolution) + 1 # Initialize space index array spaceindex = [[[0 for in range(Dz)] for in range(Dy)] for in range(Dx)] # Voxels map: key=(i,j,k), value={'sumpos': [x,y,z], 'sumcolor': [r,g,b], 'count': int} voxelsmap = defaultdict(lambda: {'sumpos': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'sumcolor': [0, 0, 0], 'count': 0}) hascolor = points[0][3] is not None if points else False for p in points: x, y, z = p[0], p[1], p[2] # Compute voxel coordinates (floor matches S1/S3; S2 uses ceil for X) i = math.floor((x - minx) / resolution) j = math.floor((y - miny) / resolution) k = math.floor((z - minz) / resolution) # Check bounds if not (0 <= i < Dx and 0 <= j < Dy and 0 <= k < Dz): continue # Update map voxeldata = voxelsmap[(i, j, k)] voxeldata['sumpos'][0] += x voxeldata['sumpos'][1] += y voxeldata['sumpos'][2] += z voxeldata['count'] += 1 if hascolor: voxeldata['sumcolor'][0] += p[3] voxeldata['sumcolor'][1] += p[4] voxeldata['sumcolor'][2] += p[5] # Mark occupancy spaceindex[i][j][k] = 1 # Note: S2 implementation uses spaceindex[j][i-1][k] = 1, which causes OOB if i=0 # Filter and compute centroids finalvoxels = {} for (i, j, k), data in voxelsmap.items(): if data['count'] < densitythreshold: continue cx = data['sumpos'][0] / data['count'] cy = data['sumpos'][1] / data['count'] cz = data['sumpos'][2] / data['count'] r = data['sumcolor'][0] / data['count'] g = data['sumcolor'][1] / data['count'] b = data['sumcolor'][2] / data['count'] # Quantize color if needed if colorlevels > 0: step = 256 / colorlevels r = int(round(r / step) step) g = int(round(g / step) step) b = int(round(b / step) step) # Clamp r = max(0, min(255, r)) g = max(0, min(255, g)) b = max(0, min(255, b)) finalvoxels[(i, j, k)] = { 'pos': (cx, cy, cz), 'color': (r, g, b), 'count': data['count'] } return finalvoxels, spaceindex Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Index Out of Bounds: In specific implementations, the index mapping spaceIndex[ijk1][ijk0-1][ijk2] involves a -1 offset on the X-index. If ijk0 is 0, this results in an out-of-bounds access (index -1). Always check bounds before accessing the occupancy array. Bounding Box Mismatch: If points fall outside the defined bounding box (especially in CUSTOM mode), the computed indices may be negative or exceed array bounds, leading to undefined behavior. Ensure the bounding box encompasses all input points. Precision: Using floor vs ceil can shift voxel assignment by 1. Be consistent with the source implementation. Empty Voxels: Voxels with fewer points than densitythreshold are discarded. If densitythreshold is too high, the grid may become too sparse. Computes the spatial center of each voxel by calculating the weighted mean of 3D points falling within that voxel, using depth confidence as weights. It differs from simple averaging by prioritizing points with higher depth confidence, which helps mitigate noise and outliers. Choose this when depth confidence data is available and noise reduction is critical. Time Complexity: O(N) for mapping points to voxels, where N is the number of points. Filtering and centroid computation is O(V), where V is the number of occupied voxels. Overall: O(N + V). Memory Complexity: O(V) for storing voxel data. The occupancy array is O(Dx \cdot Dy \cdot Dz), which can be large if the bounding box is large and resolution is high, but it is sparse in practice if only occupied voxels are stored in the map. Performance: Efficient for large point clouds due to linear scan and hash map usage. GPU acceleration is possible by parallelizing point-to-voxel mapping. Strengths: Simple to implement, handles arbitrary point distributions, supports color aggregation. Limitations: Fixed resolution grid may waste memory if the scene is sparse or has varying density. Does not handle overlapping points within a voxel better than simple averaging (unless weighted variant is used). When to Use: When a structured voxel representation is needed for rendering, reconstruction, or spatial queries. When point cloud data is dense enough to justify voxelization. When Not to Use: When the scene is extremely sparse and a sparse voxel octree or KD-tree would be more efficient. When high-frequency details are lost due to voxel averaging. The method originates from unofficial implementations for converting point clouds (including 3D Gaussian Splatting and PLY formats) into sparse voxel grids for rendering in USD or other formats. It is often used in pipelines involving 3DGS to Voxel conversion, leveraging USD's PointInstancer for efficient rendering. jjjkkyz/DCx, https://github.com/jjjkkyz/DCx, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ericmaic/Point-Cloud-Voxelization, https://github.com/ericmaic/Point-Cloud-Voxelization, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) omolism/3DGS-to-Voxel-OpenUSD, https://github.com/omolism/3DGS-to-Voxel-OpenUSD, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Weighted Voxel Center Computation from Points
head: Weighted Mean Voxel Center
body: This method computes the spatial center of each voxel in a sparse grid by calculating the weighted mean of 3D points falling within that voxel, using depth confidence as weights. It differs from simple averaging by prioritizing points with higher depth confidence, which mitigates noise and outliers in regions with uncertain geometry. Inputs: points: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D coordinates of N points. voxelindices: Tensor mapping each point to a voxel index. depthconf: Optional tensor containing depth confidence values for each point. inverseid: Optional tensor providing inverse mapping for unique voxel indices; if None, computed internally. numvoxels: Optional integer specifying the total number of voxels; if None, inferred from inverseid. Outputs: centers: Tensor containing the computed center for each active voxel. Data Structures: weightedpointsums: Accumulates \sum (pi \cdot wi). weightsums: Accumulates \sum wi. pointsums: Accumulates \sum pi. pointcounts: Accumulates \sum 1. All accumulators are initialized to size (num\voxels, 3) or (num\voxels, 1). Steps: 1. Validate input shape: Ensure points has shape (N, 3); raise ValueError otherwise. 2. Determine voxel indexing: If inverseid is None, compute it from voxelindices using torch.unique(..., returninverse=True) and determine numvoxels. If inverseid is provided but numvoxels is None, compute numvoxels from the maximum value in inverseid. 3. Construct weights: If depthconf is None, use uniform weights; otherwise, move to the target device, reshape to (N, 1) by taking the mean over the last dimension if needed, and clamp the minimum to 0. 4. Initialize accumulators: Create weightedpointsums, weightsums, pointsums, and pointcounts with the specified shapes. 5. Accumulate weighted points: weightedpointsums.indexadd(0, inverseid, points weights). 6. Accumulate weights: weightsums.indexadd(0, inverseid, weights). 7. Accumulate raw points: pointsums.indexadd(0, inverseid, points). 8. Accumulate point counts: pointcounts.indexadd(0, inverseid, torch.oneslike(weights)). 9. Compute weighted centers: weightedcenters = weightedpointsums / weightsums.clampmin(1e-12). 10. Compute mean centers: meancenters = pointsums / pointcounts.clampmin(1). 11. Select final centers: If weightsums > 0, use weightedcenters; otherwise, use meancenters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computeweightedvoxelcenters(points, voxelindices, depthconf=None, inverseid=None, numvoxels=None): if points.shape[1] != 3: raise ValueError("Points must have shape (N, 3)") N = points.shape[0] if inverseid is None: uniqueindices, inverseid = torch.unique(voxelindices, returninverse=True) if numvoxels is None: numvoxels = uniqueindices.shape[0] else: if numvoxels is None: numvoxels = inverseid.max().item() + 1 if depthconf is None: weights = torch.ones(N, 1, device=points.device, dtype=points.dtype) else: weights = depthconf.to(points.device) if weights.dim() > 1 and weights.shape[1] > 1: weights = weights.mean(dim=1, keepdim=True) weights = torch.clamp(weights, min=0.0) weightedpointsums = torch.zeros(numvoxels, 3, device=points.device, dtype=points.dtype) weightsums = torch.zeros(numvoxels, 1, device=points.device, dtype=points.dtype) pointsums = torch.zeros(numvoxels, 3, device=points.device, dtype=points.dtype) pointcounts = torch.zeros(numvoxels, 1, device=points.device, dtype=points.dtype) weightedpointsums.indexadd(0, inverseid, points weights) weightsums.indexadd(0, inverseid, weights) pointsums.indexadd(0, inverseid, points) pointcounts.indexadd(0, inverseid, torch.oneslike(weights)) weightedcenters = weightedpointsums / weightsums.clampmin(1e-12) meancenters = pointsums / pointcounts.clampmin(1) mask = (weightsums > 0).expandas(weightedcenters) centers = torch.where(mask, weightedcenters, meancenters) return centers Parameters: clampmin for weights: 0.0. clampmin for division denominators: 1e-12 for weights, 1 for counts. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If depthconf has multiple dimensions, it is averaged over the last dimension. Division by zero is prevented by clamping denominators. If a voxel has no points, weightsums is 0, and meancenters is used; clampmin(1) on pointcounts prevents division by zero, resulting in a zero vector. Not given in the sources. This method is part of the VGGT (Vision Geometry Grounded Transformer) pipeline, specifically within the democolmap.py script used for converting depth maps and poses into sparse voxel representations. It leverages PyTorch's efficient tensor operations for accumulation. Zhaoyibinn/VGVGGT, https://github.com/Zhaoyibinn/VGVGGT, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Fill-Height Inference via PoCA
head: TomOpt fill-level estimation, Weighted PoCA Height Prediction, Weighted PoCA z-position inference, zpred calculation
body: Fill-Height Inference via PoCA is a regression method that predicts the fill-level of a furnace by computing a weighted average of the z-positions of Points of Closest Approach (PoCAs) from muon trajectories. It differs from voxel-based density reconstruction methods by directly estimating the fill-height indicator without computing X0 (radiation length) predictions for voxels, making it computationally more efficient. The method sets itself apart by incorporating transverse (xy) weighting to mitigate bias from PoCAs located in furnace walls, leveraging the monotonic relationship between the mean PoCA z-position and the fill-height. Inputs: A set of muon trajectories, each associated with a PoCA point p. For each PoCA p: zp: The z-position of the PoCA. \epsilonp: The muon trajectory efficiency. \Delta zp: The uncertainty of the PoCA z-position. \sigma{x,p}, \sigma{y,p}: The xy uncertainties of the PoCA position. (xp, yp): The xy position of the PoCA. Voxel grid definition for the transverse area of the furnace (x, y dimensions). Furnace geometry parameters defining the center and walls for the xy weighting function. Outputs: z{pred}: The predicted z-position, which serves as the fill-height indicator. Data Structures: List of PoCA objects, each containing fields: z, epsilon, dz (uncertainty), sigmax, sigmay, x, y. Voxel grid structure covering the furnace transverse area. Steps: 1. Compute Base Weight: For each PoCA p, calculate the base weight component based on trajectory efficiency and z-position uncertainty: w{base,p} = \frac{\epsilonp}{(\Delta zp)^2} 2. Define Transverse Distributions: For each PoCA p, define a 2D Gaussian distribution in the xy-plane centered at (xp, yp) with standard deviations \sigma{x,p} and \sigma{y,p}: Gp(x, y) = \frac{1}{2\pi \sigma{x,p} \sigma{y,p}} \exp\left( -\frac{(x-xp)^2}{2\sigma{x,p}^2} - \frac{(y-yp)^2}{2\sigma{y,p}^2} \right) 3. Integrate over Voxels: For each PoCA p, integrate Gp(x, y) over each voxel v in the transverse area of the furnace. Let Vv be the area of voxel v. The integral I{p,v} is: I{p,v} = \iint{Vv} Gp(x, y) \, dx \, dy In implementation, this integral can be computed using the error function (erf) for rectangular voxels. 4. Apply Transverse Weighting Function: Define a double-sigmoid-based function W{xy}(x, y) that ascribes a weight to each voxel position. This function smoothly decreases to zero at the furnace walls and maximizes to one at the center. Let C{xy} be the center of the furnace in xy, and R{wall} be the effective radius/extent to the walls. A typical form is: W{xy}(x, y) = \text{sigmoid}\left( \frac{d{center} - \text{dist}((x,y), C{xy})}{k} \right) \times \text{sigmoid}\left( \frac{\text{dist}((x,y), C{xy}) - d{inner}}{k} \right) The exact parameters d{center}, d{inner}, k depend on the specific furnace geometry and are tuned to suppress contributions from wall regions. The source states this function is "double-sigmoid-based" and "smoothly decreases to zero at the furnace walls, and maximises to one at the centre". 5. Calculate xy Weight for Each PoCA: For each PoCA p, calculate its transverse weight w{xy,p} as the sum of the weighted voxel integrals: w{xy,p} = \sum{v} I{p,v} \cdot W{xy}(xv, yv) where (xv, yv) is the center of voxel v. 6. Compute Total Weight for Each PoCA: Combine the base weight and the transverse weight: wp = w{base,p} \cdot w{xy,p} = \frac{\epsilonp}{(\Delta zp)^2} w{xy,p} 7. Calculate Predicted z-position: Compute the weighted average of all PoCA z-positions: z{pred} = \frac{\sump wp zp}{\sump wp} Parameters: \epsilonp: Trajectory efficiency. Typical values depend on detector acceptance and muon energy. \Delta zp: Z-position uncertainty. Determined by detector resolution and track fit quality. \sigma{x,p}, \sigma{y,p}: XY position uncertainties. Determined by detector resolution. Double-sigmoid parameters: Tuned to furnace geometry. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Wall Bias: PoCAs located in furnace walls can bias the prediction and reduce precision. The xy weighting function mitigates this by reducing weights near walls. Fill-Height vs. Center of Mass: The mean of PoCA z-positions corresponds to the center of the fill material, not the fill-height itself. A linear transformation (h{pred} = a \cdot z{pred} + b) is required to convert z{pred} to fill-height. Inherent Bias: The PoCA method is inherently biased by ascribing entire muon scattering to a single point. This bias is detector-configuration-dependent. Monotonicity: The method relies on the monotonic relationship between mean PoCA z-position and fill-height. If this relationship is not monotonic (e.g., due to complex density distributions), the prediction may be inaccurate. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of PoCAs and the number of voxels in the transverse area. Specifically, O(N{PoCA} \cdot N{voxels}) for the integration step, where N{PoCA} is the number of muon trajectories and N{voxels} is the number of transverse voxels. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of PoCAs and voxels to store intermediate integrals and weights. Measured Performance: The source does not provide specific performance metrics (e.g., MSE, runtime) for this method on a specific hardware or resolution. It notes that it is "more computationally efficient" than computing X0 predictions for voxels. Strengths: Computationally efficient; does not require voxel-based X0 reconstruction; mitigates wall bias via xy weighting; leverages monotonic relationship for robust regression. Limitations: Requires linear transformation to map to fill-height; inherently biased by PoCA approximation; bias is detector-dependent; requires accurate knowledge of furnace geometry for xy weighting. When to Use: When computational efficiency is critical and the goal is to estimate fill-height rather than full 3D density reconstruction. Suitable for detector optimization pipelines where gradients are needed. When Not to Use: When full 3D density information is required; when the monotonic relationship between mean PoCA z-position and fill-height is not valid for the specific material distribution. Origin: Developed in the context of muon tomography for monitoring industrial furnaces, specifically for the "TomOpt" project. History: The method was developed as part of an end-to-end optimization pipeline for task- and constraint-aware design of particle detectors. It was chosen because the mean z-position of PoCAs was observed to be monotonic with fill-height, allowing for efficient regression without full voxel reconstruction. Usage: Used for predicting furnace fill-heights in industrial settings, particularly in steel or similar metallurgical furnaces, using muon scattering data. TomOpt: Differential optimisation for task- and constraint-aware design of particle detectors in the context of muon tomography, https://doi.org/10.1088/2632-2153/ad52e7, fetched 2026-10-26

name: VoxelGrid::CreateFromPointCloudWithinBounds
body: VoxelGrid::CreateFromPointCloudWithinBounds voxalizes a point cloud into a sparse voxel grid by mapping input points to voxel indices based on a fixed voxel size and a minimum bounding box corner, ignoring the maximum bound for coordinate calculation. It differs from its sibling DCX Points-to-Voxels and Multi-Plane Point Cloud Voxelization and Weight Aggregation by using a direct hash-map accumulation approach rather than structured spatial partitioning or multi-plane projections, and is significantly faster than Pointcloud to Sparse Voxel Grid Conversion variants that process triangle meshes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: PointCloud (containing points and optionally colors), voxelsize (double), minbound (Eigen::Vector3d), maxbound (Eigen::Vector3d). Output: std::sharedptr<VoxelGrid> containing the resulting sparse voxel structure. Data Structures: voxelindextoaccpoint: A hash map (std::unorderedmap) mapping Eigen::Vector3i (voxel index) to AvgColorVoxel (accumulator). Uses utility::hasheigen<Eigen::Vector3i> as the hash function. AvgColorVoxel: An accumulator object that stores the voxel index and aggregates color values. It provides methods Add(voxelindex, color) and GetAverageColor(). Steps: 1. Initialize the output VoxelGrid. 2. Validate voxelsize: If voxelsize <= 0.0, raise an error. If voxelsize std::numericlimits<int>::max() < (maxbound - minbound).maxCoeff(), raise an error indicating voxelsize is too small to represent the bounds within integer limits. 3. Set output->voxelsize = voxelsize and output->origin = minbound. 4. Create an empty hash map voxelindextoaccpoint. 5. Determine if the input point cloud has colors: hascolors = input.HasColors(). 6. Iterate through each point in the input point cloud (index i from 0 to input.points.size() - 1): a. Skip the current point if it is outside the inclusive bounds [minbound, maxbound]. This check also skips NaN points because comparisons with NaN return false. The condition requires all three coordinates (x, y, z) to be \ge minbound AND \le maxbound. b. Calculate the reference coordinate: \text{ref\coord} = \frac{\text{input.points\}[i] - \text{min\bound}}{\text{voxel\size}} c. Calculate the voxel index by taking the floor of each component and casting to integer: \text{voxel\index} = \left( \lfloor \text{ref\coord}x \rfloor, \lfloor \text{ref\coord}y \rfloor, \lfloor \text{ref\coord}z \rfloor \right) d. If hascolors is true, call voxelindextoaccpoint[voxelindex].Add(voxelindex, input.colors[i]). Otherwise, call voxelindextoaccpoint[voxelindex].Add(voxelindex). 7. Iterate through each entry in voxelindextoaccpoint: a. Get the gridindex from the accumulator (accpoint.second.GetVoxelIndex()). b. Get the average color: if hascolors is true, use accpoint.second.GetAverageColor(); otherwise, use Eigen::Vector3d(0, 0, 0). c. Add a new Voxel to the output grid using gridindex and the color. Formulas: Reference coordinate transformation: \text{ref\coord} = (\text{input.points\}[i] - \text{min\bound}) / \text{voxel\size}, which maps world coordinates to a continuous grid coordinate system relative to minbound. Voxel index discretization: \text{voxel\index} = (\lfloor \text{ref\coord}x \rfloor, \lfloor \text{ref\coord}y \rfloor, \lfloor \text{ref\coord}z \rfloor), converting continuous coordinates to integer grid indices. Parameters: voxelsize: The side length of each voxel dimension (double). Must be > 0.0. Typical values depend on scene scale and required resolution. minbound: The minimum corner of the bounding box (Eigen::Vector3d). Used as the origin for coordinate transformation. maxbound: The maximum corner of the bounding box (Eigen::Vector3d). Used only for error checking if voxelsize is too small to cover the bounds, but not used in the coordinate mapping formula. input: The input PointCloud containing the points to voxelize. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The maxbound parameter does not influence the spatial extent or resolution of the resulting voxel grid; it is only used for error checking. Changing the scale of the input point cloud while keeping voxelsize and minbound constant changes the voxel grid's spatial extent and density, which may be counterintuitive. Floating-point precision issues may arise when coordinates are very large or voxelsize is very small, though the method does not normalize by (maxbound - minbound). Points outside [minbound, maxbound] are skipped, and NaN coordinates are automatically excluded due to comparison semantics. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def CreateFromPointCloudWithinBounds(inputpointcloud, voxelsize, minbound, maxbound): # 1. Initialize output output = VoxelGrid() # 2. Validate voxelsize if voxelsize <= 0.0: raise Error("voxelsize <= 0.") # Check if voxelsize is too small to cover bounds within integer limits boundsmaxdiff = max(maxbound.x - minbound.x, maxbound.y - minbound.y, maxbound.z - minbound.z) if voxelsize 2147483647 < boundsmaxdiff: raise Error("voxelsize is too small.") output.voxelsize = voxelsize output.origin = minbound # 3. Create hash map for accumulation voxelindextoaccpoint = {} hascolors = inputpointcloud.hascolors() # 4. Iterate through points for i in range(len(inputpointcloud.points)): point = inputpointcloud.points[i] # Skip points outside [minbound, maxbound] (inclusive) if not (point.x >= minbound.x and point.y >= minbound.y and point.z >= minbound.z and point.x <= maxbound.x and point.y <= maxbound.y and point.z <= maxbound.z): continue # Calculate reference coordinate relative to minbound refcoord = (point - minbound) / voxelsize # Calculate voxel index using floor voxelindex = Vector3i( math.floor(refcoord.x), math.floor(refcoord.y), math.floor(refcoord.z)) # Accumulate point into voxel if hascolors: color = inputpointcloud.colors[i] voxelindextoaccpoint[voxelindex].Add(voxelindex, color) else: voxelindextoaccpoint[voxelindex].Add(voxelindex) # 5. Build output grid from accumulated voxels for voxelindex, accumulator in voxelindextoaccpoint.items(): gridindex = accumulator.GetVoxelIndex() if hascolors: color = accumulator.GetAverageColor() else: color = Vector3d(0, 0, 0) output.AddVoxel(Voxel(gridindex, color)) return output Vertex Cluster Assignment assigns a cluster ID to each vertex or point based on which voxel it occupies in a regular grid. It serves as the core assignment step within VoxelGrid::CreateFromPointCloudWithinBounds. Unlike methods designed for triangle meshes, it operates directly on point cloud coordinates to discretize continuous positions into a sparse voxel structure. Choose it when fast, direct point-to-voxel mapping is required without mesh traversal overhead. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of input points N, O(N), due to a single pass through the point cloud and a single pass through the accumulated voxels. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of unique voxels occupied by the point cloud, due to the hash map storage. Performance: Significantly faster than createfromtrianglemeshwithinbounds, which can take >2 minutes for voxel resolution 50, whereas this method is suitable for high resolutions like 256. Strengths: Fast execution for point clouds; simple implementation; handles color averaging automatically. Limitations: The fixed minbound origin means scaling the input point cloud changes the voxel grid's spatial coverage and density, which may require re-tuning minbound or voxelsize for scaled data. When to use: When fast voxelization of a point cloud is required and the spatial extent is fixed relative to minbound. When not to use: When the point cloud scale varies significantly and a fixed spatial resolution relative to the data's extent is required without redefining minbound. This method is part of the Open3D library's voxelization utilities. It was discussed in the context of user issues regarding unexpected behavior when scaling point clouds, highlighting the design choice of using minbound as the sole origin for coordinate transformation. name: Vertex Cluster Assignment
head: RegularGrid::queryCluster, points variant
body: Vertex Cluster Assignment assigns a cluster ID to each vertex or point based on which voxel it occupies in a regular grid. It serves as the core assignment step within VoxelGrid::CreateFromPointCloudWithinBounds. Unlike methods designed for triangle meshes, it operates directly on point cloud coordinates to discretize continuous positions into a sparse voxel structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud (vertices), an axis-aligned bounding box minimum (aabbMin), a voxel size (cellSize), and grid dimensions (gridDims). Output: A cluster ID for each vertex, stored in a clusterSSBO. Data Structures: vertexSSBO: Buffer containing input vertex positions. gridSSBO: Buffer containing grid metadata. clusterSSBO: Write-only buffer for output cluster IDs. Steps: 1. Bind vertexSSBO (points), gridSSBO, and clusterSSBO (write) to the compute shader. 2. Execute assignVertexClusterShader with uniforms aabbMin, cellSize, gridDims, and numVertices. 3. For each vertex index i, read position P from vertexSSBO[i], compute voxel index idx = floor((P - aabbMin) / cellSize), clamp idx to [0, gridDims - 1], and write the result to clusterSSBO[i]. 4. Read cluster IDs from clusterSSBO and populate clusterIdx vector. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def assignvertexcluster(vertices, aabbmin, cellsize, griddims): clusterids = [] for p in vertices: relx = p[0] - aabbmin[0] rely = p[1] - aabbmin[1] relz = p[2] - aabbmin[2] idxx = math.floor(relx / cellsize) idxy = math.floor(rely / cellsize) idxz = math.floor(relz / cellsize) idxx = max(0, min(idxx, griddims[0] - 1)) idxy = max(0, min(idxy, griddims[1] - 1)) idxz = max(0, min(idxz, griddims[2] - 1)) clusterid = idxx + idxy griddims[0] + idxz griddims[0] griddims[1] # Linearization formula clusterids.append(clusterid) return clusterids Parameters: cellsize: Voxel edge length. aabbmin: Lower bound of the voxel grid. griddims: Number of voxels in x, y, z. Edge Cases: Points outside the AABB: Clamped to nearest valid voxel. Precision: Floating-point division and floor operations may cause jitter at boundaries. Assigns a specific voxel cluster ID to each triangle face by statistically sampling intersections with a regular voxel grid. It differs from deterministic ray-casting by using Monte Carlo sampling to handle ambiguity at voxel boundaries and shared faces. Choose it when converting triangle meshes to sparse voxel grids where surface fragments cross voxel boundaries. name: Voxel Fragmentation via Grid Clustering
head: RegularGrid::queryCluster, Voxel-based Face Clustering
body: Voxel Fragmentation via Grid Clustering assigns a discrete voxel cluster ID to each triangle face by statistically sampling intersections with a regular voxel grid. It determines which continuous surface fragment primarily occupies a specific voxel value, enabling triangle mesh conversion into sparse voxel grids for volume rendering. The method executes on a GPU using compute shaders and processes faces in batches to respect hardware buffer limits. Inputs: faces: List of triangle faces to process. grid: Regular voxel grid defined by aabbMin, cellSize, and gridDims. numSamples: Number of random samples taken per face for intersection testing, defaulting to 1000. numFragments: Number of distinct voxel values (clusters) in the grid, determined by countValues(). Outputs: clusterIdx: Vector of cluster IDs for each face, where negative values indicate boundary faces. faceClusterOccupancy: Map of cluster IDs to normalized occupancy counts for each face. name: Forward-Backward Voxel Transformation
head: Inverse mapping with forward projection, Two-pass voxel rotation
body: The Forward-Backward Voxel Transformation is a two-pass algorithm that transforms a voxelized point cloud from a source orientation and position to a destination orientation and position without introducing visual holes. It solves the coverage problem inherent in single-pass voxel transformations by combining a forward projection of source points with an inverse sampling of the destination grid. Unlike single-pass methods that either project points to a grid or sample the grid from source space, this method ensures full coverage by validating every destination voxel against the source data. The method operates on a source point cloud represented as a dictionary mapping integer 3D coordinates to colors. It computes a local transformation matrix that aligns the source cloud with a target object's transform. The process consists of two passes: a forward pass to establish the bounding volume and populate initial voxels, and an inverse pass to fill any gaps by sampling the source cloud for every voxel in the destination bounding box. Input: sourceCloud: A dictionary mapping Vector3Int (voxel coordinates) to Color (or associated data). objectRootT: The transform of the target object (game object or scene node). pCT: The transform of the source point cloud. Output: alignedCloud: A dictionary mapping Vector3Int to Color, representing the transformed voxel grid. alignedCloud: Dictionary<Vector3Int, Color>. Stores the resulting voxel grid. Keys are integer 3D coordinates; values are colors. sourceCloud: Dictionary<Vector3Int, Color>. The input voxel data. Bounds: A bounding box structure tracking the minimum and maximum integer coordinates of the transformed points. Before the passes, a local transformation matrix is computed to map source coordinates to destination space. 1. Compute local rotation: R{local} = R{object}^{-1} \times R{cloud} Where R{object} is the rotation of the target object and R{cloud} is the rotation of the source cloud. 2. Compute local position: P{local} = T{object}^{-1}(P{cloud}) Where T{object}^{-1} is the inverse transform of the target object applied to the cloud's position. 3. Construct the transformation matrix M: M = \text{TRS}(P{local}, R{local}, \mathbf{1}) Where \text{TRS} constructs a 4 \times 4 matrix from translation P{local}, rotation R{local}, and uniform scale \mathbf{1}. 1. Initialize: Create an empty alignedCloud dictionary. Initialize a Bounds object and a boolean flag boundsSet to false. 2. Pass 1: Forward Projection: Iterate through each entry (pos, color) in sourceCloud. Transform the position to destination space: P{transformed} = M \times \begin{bmatrix} pos.x \\ pos.y \\ pos.z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Note: Only the upper 3 \times 4 part of the matrix is used for point transformation (ignoring perspective). Round the transformed floating-point coordinates to integer voxel coordinates: pos{dest} = \text{Round}(P{transformed}) Where \text{Round} rounds each component to the nearest integer. Update the bounding box: If boundsSet is false, set bounds.min and bounds.max to pos{dest} and set boundsSet to true. Otherwise, encapsulate pos{dest} into bounds. Store the color in the output: alignedCloud[pos{dest}] = color 3. Compute Inverse Matrix: Calculate the inverse of the transformation matrix: M^{-1} = \text{Inverse}(M) 4. Determine Destination Bounding Box: Round the bounds of the transformed cloud to integer coordinates: b{min} = \text{Round}(bounds.min) b{max} = \text{Round}(bounds.max) 5. Pass 2: Inverse Sampling: Iterate through every voxel coordinate dest in the bounding box defined by b{min} and b{max} for x, y, and z axes: \text{for } x \text{ from } b{min}.x \text{ to } b{max}.x - 1 \text{for } y \text{ from } b{min}.y \text{ to } b{max}.y - 1 \text{for } z \text{ from } b{min}.z \text{ to } b{max}.z - 1 Transform the destination voxel back to source space: P{test} = M^{-1} \times \begin{bmatrix} dest.x \\ dest.y \\ dest.z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Round to integer source coordinates: test{src} = \text{Round}(P{test}) Check if this coordinate exists in the sourceCloud: If sourceCloud contains test{src}, retrieve its color and assign it to the destination voxel: alignedCloud[dest] = sourceCloud[test{src}] If not, the voxel remains empty or retains its previous value if it was set in Pass 1. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def mul(self, s): return Vector3(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) def add(self, o): return Vector3(self.x+o.x, self.y+o.y, self.z+o.z) class Vector3Int: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = int(round(x)), int(round(y)), int(round(z)) class Quaternion: def init(self, x, y, z, w): self.x, self.y, self.z, self.w = x, y, z, w @staticmethod def inverse(q): return Quaternion(-q.x, -q.y, -q.z, q.w) def mul(self, other): return Quaternion( self.wother.x + self.xother.w + self.yother.z - self.zother.y, self.wother.y - self.xother.z + self.yother.w + self.zother.x, self.wother.z + self.xother.y - self.yother.x + self.zother.w, self.wother.w - self.xother.x - self.yother.y - self.zother.z) class Matrix4x4: def init(self, m): self.m = m # 4x4 list of lists @staticmethod def TRS(t, r, s): x, y, z, w = r.x, r.y, r.z, r.w xx, yy, zz, ww = xx, yy, zz, ww xy, xz, xw = xy, xz, xw yz, yw = yz, yw zw = zw rm = [ [1-2(yy+zz), 2(xy-zw), 2(xz+yw), 0], [2(xy+zw), 1-2(xx+zz), 2(yz-xw), 0], [2(xz-yw), 2(yz+xw), 1-2(xx+yy), 0], [0, 0, 0, 1] ] for i in range(3): for j in range(3): rm[i][j] = s rm[0][3] = t.x s; rm[1][3] = t.y s; rm[2][3] = t.z s return Matrix4x4(rm) def multiplypoint3x4(self, p): m = self.m return Vector3( m[0][0]p.x + m[0][1]p.y + m[0][2]p.z + m[0][3], m[1][0]p.x + m[1][1]p.y + m[1][2]p.z + m[1][3], m[2][0]p.x + m[2][1]p.y + m[2][2]p.z + m[2][3]) @property def inverse(self): # Standard 4x4 matrix inverse # For rigid transforms, inverse is TRS(-R^T t, R^T) # Implemented via standard linear algebra pass def RoundVector3(vec): return Vector3Int(vec.x, vec.y, vec.z) def ForwardBackwardVoxelTransformation(sourceCloud, objectRootT, pCT): alignedCloud = {} localRot = Quaternion.inverse(objectRootT.rotation) pCT.rotation localPos = objectRootT.InverseTransformPoint(pCT.position) # Standard transform operation matrix = Matrix4x4.TRS(localPos, localRot, 1.0) boundsmin = Vector3(float('inf'), float('inf'), float('inf')) boundsmax = Vector3(float('-inf'), float('-inf'), float('-inf')) boundsSet = False for pos, color in sourceCloud.items(): transformedPos = matrix.multiplypoint3x4(pos) posdest = RoundVector3(transformedPos) if not boundsSet: boundsmin = Vector3(posdest.x, posdest.y, posdest.z) boundsmax = Vector3(posdest.x, posdest.y, posdest.z) boundsSet = True else: boundsmin.x = min(boundsmin.x, posdest.x) boundsmin.y = min(boundsmin.y, posdest.y) boundsmin.z = min(boundsmin.z, posdest.z) boundsmax.x = max(boundsmax.x, posdest.x) boundsmax.y = max(boundsmax.y, posdest.y) boundsmax.z = max(boundsmax.z, posdest.z) alignedCloud[posdest] = color invMatrix = matrix.inverse bMin = RoundVector3(boundsmin) bMax = RoundVector3(boundsmax) for x in range(bMin.x, bMax.x): for y in range(bMin.y, bMax.y): for z in range(bMin.z, bMax.z): dest = Vector3Int(x, y, z) testPosFloat = invMatrix.multiplypoint3x4(dest) testPos = RoundVector3(testPosFloat) if testPos in sourceCloud: alignedCloud[dest] = sourceCloud[testPos] return alignedCloud VoxelUtil.RoundVector3: A utility function that converts floating-point coordinates to integer voxel grid coordinates by rounding each component to the nearest integer. Holes: Using only the forward pass (projecting source points) or only the inverse pass (sampling source for destination) results in visual holes in the rendered cloud. The two-pass approach is necessary to ensure full coverage. Bounding Box: The bounding box must be computed from the transformed positions in the forward pass to ensure the inverse pass covers all relevant destination voxels. Time Complexity: O(N + V), where N is the number of points in the source cloud and V is the number of voxels in the destination bounding box. The forward pass iterates over N points, and the inverse pass iterates over V voxels. Memory Complexity: O(N + V) for storing the alignedCloud dictionary. Performance: The method is computationally more expensive than single-pass methods due to the two iterations and dictionary lookup overhead. It provides higher quality results compared to "Rotate by shearing," which eliminates hash table overhead but is sensitive to rotation order and yields lower quality (~80%). Strengths: Ensures no holes in the transformed voxel cloud; robust to rotation and translation. Limitations: Higher memory and computational cost compared to single-pass or shearing methods. The method was described in a discussion on Game Development Stack Exchange by a developer seeking a cleaner way to rotate and align a voxel point cloud with a game object's transform. It was presented as a solution to visual holes arising from single-pass voxel rotation techniques. The approach is inspired by 2D bitmap rotation techniques where inverse mapping ensures full coverage of the destination grid. It is compared against "Rotate by shearing," a technique suggested by another user which eliminates hash table overhead but is sensitive to rotation order and yields lower quality. name: Multi-Plane Point Cloud Voxelization and Weight Aggregation
head: MPP Aggregation, MPP Voxelization, Pre-processing for Neural Point Cloud Rendering via Multi-Plane Projection
body: A pre-processing pipeline that projects a 3D point cloud onto multiple parallel planes (voxels) based on depth, groups points by their projected 2D grid location and depth bin, and computes aggregation weights for rendering. It solves the problem of efficiently organizing sparse point cloud data for multi-plane projection rendering by reducing outliers and grouping points spatially. Unlike standard point cloud rasterization which may suffer from z-fighting or require complex sorting, this method aggregates points into discrete depth bins and blends them front-to-back using a visibility mask. Inputs: Point cloud file (PLY format) containing positions (x, y, z) and colors (r, g, b). Camera intrinsics matrices for color and depth cameras (intrinsiccolor.txt, intrinsicdepth.txt). Camera extrinsics matrices for color and depth cameras (extrinsiccolor.txt, extrinsicdepth.txt). Pose index file (index.txt). Target image resolution (W, H) (default 640x480). Number of planes N (default 32). Hyperparameters a (parallel distance weight, default 1) and b (vertical distance weight, default 1). Depth bounds d{near} and d{far}. Outputs: NPZ file containing: u, v: float32, pixel coordinates. d: float32, depth. selectindex: int64, original point indices. groupbelongs: int64, group ID. indexineachgroup: uint16, index within group. distance: float32, parallel distance. eachsplitmaxnum: uint16, max points per plane. delta: float32, plane depth differences. Data Structures: Points are stored as arrays of shape (N{pts}, 4) for positions (homogeneous [x, y, z, 1]) and (N{pts}, 3) for colors (BGR). Camera matrices are 4 \times 4 float32 arrays. Depth boundaries are stored as an array of size N+1. Steps: 1. Load Point Cloud: Parse the PLY file. Skip lines until endheader. For each subsequent line, split by space. Extract position as [x, y, z, 1.0] and color as [b, g, r] (converting RGB to BGR by reordering indices 3, 4, 5 to 5, 4, 3). Return transposed numpy arrays for positions and colors. 2. Load and Adjust Camera Parameters: Read intrinsic and extrinsic matrices from text files. Each file contains 4 lines of space-separated floats, reshaped into 4 \times 4 float32 arrays. If image resizing is enabled, adjust intrinsic matrices. Calculate scale factors: s{1c} = \frac{1296 - 1}{W - 1}, \quad s{2c} = \frac{968 - 1}{H - 1} for color, and similar s{1d}, s{2d} for depth. Divide the first two rows of the intrinsic matrices by these scales to map from original resolution (1296x968 or 640x480) to target resolution (W, H). 3. Project to Image Space: Compute the projection matrix P = K \cdot E^{-1}, where K is the intrinsic matrix and E is the extrinsic matrix. Transform points: P{img} = P \cdot P{world} Extract depth z{all} = P{img}[2,:]. Compute pixel coordinates: u{all} = \frac{P{img}[0,:]}{z{all} + \epsilon}, \quad v{all} = \frac{P{img}[1,:]}{z{all} + \epsilon} where \epsilon = 10^{-10} to prevent division by zero. 4. Filter Valid Points: Identify valid indices where: 0 \le u{all} < W 0 \le v{all} < H d{near} < z{all} < d{far} Intersect these conditions to get validposition. Sort selected points by depth in descending order using np.argsort(-selecteddepth). 5. Remove Outliers: From the sorted indices, remove the 100 furthest and 50 nearest points to reduce outlier influence: \text{index} = \text{index}[100:-50]. 6. Calculate Parallel Distance: Round u and v to nearest integer: u{sorted} = \text{uint32}(\text{rint}(u{sorted})), \quad v{sorted} = \text{uint32}(\text{rint}(v{sorted})) Compute parallel distance to the grid center: \text{distance} = \sqrt{(u{sorted} - \text{center\u})^2 + (v{sorted} - \text{center\v})^2} where \text{center\u} and \text{center\v} are the grid center coordinates (typically image center). 7. Define Depth Bins: Get d{min} and d{max} from the sorted valid depths. Create N+1 linearly spaced boundaries: \text{depth\tmp} = \text{linspace}(d{max}, d{min}, N+1) Randomly sample one boundary per plane bin: \text{tmp}[bin] = \text{uniform}(\text{depth\tmp}[bin], \text{depth\tmp}[bin+1]) Compute delta for each plane: \delta[bin] = \text{tmp}[bin] - \text{tmp}[bin+1] for bin \in [0, N-2], then flip delta. 8. Assign Points to Planes: Initialize upboundary with tmp. Iterate through sorted points. For each point with depth zi, find the plane index pi such that: zi \ge \text{up\boundary}[cnt] Increment cnt and check subsequent boundaries until the condition is met. The plane index is N - cnt - 1. 9. Group Points by Voxel: Compute group key: \text{key} = u{sorted} + v{sorted} \cdot W + pi \cdot W \cdot H Sort points by this key. Assign group IDs: iterate through sorted groups. When the key changes, assign the current group ID to all points in the previous group. Store start indices. Assign sequential indices within each group. 10. Compute Aggregation Weights: For each group, calculate: Parallel weight: w1 = (1 - \text{distance})^a. Vertical weight: w2 = \frac{1}{(1 + \text{distance}1)^b}, where \text{distance}1 is the vertical distance to the minimum depth in the group. Renewed weight: w{renew} = w1 \cdot w2. Normalize weights per group by dividing by the sum of weights in the group. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def loadply(plypath): position = [] color = [] with open(plypath, 'r') as f: begin = False for line in f: line = line.strip('\n') if not line: break parts = line.split(' ') if parts[0] == 'endheader': begin = True continue if begin: pos = [float(parts[0]), float(parts[1]), float(parts[2]), 1.0] col = [float(parts[5]), float(parts[4]), float(parts[3])] position.append(pos) color.append(col) return np.array(position).T, np.array(color).T def loadcameraparams(intrinsicpath, extrinsicpath): K = np.loadtxt(intrinsicpath).reshape(4, 4).astype(np.float32) E = np.loadtxt(extrinsicpath).reshape(4, 4).astype(np.float32) E[:, [1, 2]] = E[:, [1, 2]] (-1.0) return K, E def adjustintrinsics(K, targetw, targeth, origw=1296, origh=968): s1 = (origw - 1) / (targetw - 1) s2 = (origh - 1) / (targeth - 1) K[0,:] /= s1 K[1,:] /= s2 return K def projectandfilter(positions, colors, K, E, W, H, dnear, dfar, numplanes=32, a=1, b=1): P = K @ np.linalg.inv(E) posimg = P @ positions zall = posimg[2,:] eps = 1e-10 uall = posimg[0,:] / (zall + eps) vall = posimg[1,:] / (zall + eps) validu = (uall >= 0) & (uall < W) validv = (vall >= 0) & (vall < H) validd = (zall > dnear) & (zall < dfar) valididx = np.where(validu & validv & validd)[0] if len(valididx) == 0: return None selectedpos = positions[:, valididx] selectedcol = colors[:, valididx] selectedz = zall[valididx] selectedu = uall[valididx] selectedv = vall[valididx] sortidx = np.argsort(-selectedz) selectedz = selectedz[sortidx] selectedu = selectedu[sortidx] selectedv = selectedv[sortidx] selectedpos = selectedpos[:, sortidx] selectedcol = selectedcol[:, sortidx] valididx = valididx[sortidx] if len(selectedz) > 150: selectedz = selectedz[100:-50] selectedu = selectedu[100:-50] selectedv = selectedv[100:-50] selectedpos = selectedpos[:, 100:-50] selectedcol = selectedcol[:, 100:-50] valididx = valididx[100:-50] usorted = np.uint32(np.rint(selectedu)) vsorted = np.uint32(np.rint(selectedv)) centeru = W / 2.0 centerv = H / 2.0 distance = np.sqrt((usorted - centeru)2 + (vsorted - centerv)2) dmin = np.min(selectedz) dmax = np.max(selectedz) depthtmp = np.linspace(dmax, dmin, numplanes + 1) tmp = np.zeros(numplanes) for binidx in range(numplanes): tmp[binidx] = np.random.uniform(depthtmp[binidx], depthtmp[binidx+1]) delta = np.zeros(numplanes - 1) for binidx in range(numplanes - 1): delta[binidx] = tmp[binidx] - tmp[binidx+1] delta = np.flip(delta) dposition = np.zeros(len(selectedz), dtype=np.int32) upboundary = tmp for i in range(len(selectedz)): cnt = 0 while cnt < numplanes: if selectedz[i] >= upboundary[cnt]: dposition[i] = numplanes - cnt - 1 break cnt += 1 groupkey = usorted + vsorted W + dposition W H sortkeyidx = np.argsort(groupkey) sortedkey = groupkey[sortkeyidx] groupbelongs = np.zeros(len(selectedz), dtype=np.int64) indexingroup = np.zeros(len(selectedz), dtype=np.uint16) currentgroupid = 0 groupbegin = 0 for i in range(1, len(sortedkey)): if sortedkey[i] != sortedkey[i-1]: count = i - groupbegin groupbelongs[sortkeyidx[groupbegin:i]] = currentgroupid indexingroup[sortkeyidx[groupbegin:i]] = np.arange(count, dtype=np.uint16) currentgroupid += 1 groupbegin = i count = len(sortedkey) - groupbegin groupbelongs[sortkeyidx[groupbegin:]] = currentgroupid indexingroup[sortkeyidx[groupbegin:]] = np.arange(count, dtype=np.uint16) verticaldistances = np.zeros(len(selectedz)) uniquegroups = np.unique(groupbelongs) for g in uniquegroups: mask = groupbelongs == g groupz = selectedz[mask] minz = np.min(groupz) verticaldistances[mask] = selectedz[mask] - minz weight1 = (1 - distance)a weight2 = 1.0 / (1 + verticaldistances)b weightrenew = weight1 weight2 for g in uniquegroups: mask = groupbelongs == g sumw = np.sum(weightrenew[mask]) if sumw > 0: weightrenew[mask] /= sumw return { 'u': selectedu.astype(np.float32), 'v': selectedv.astype(np.float32), 'd': selectedz.astype(np.float32), 'selectindex': valididx.astype(np.int64), 'groupbelongs': groupbelongs.astype(np.int64), 'indexineachgroup': indexingroup.astype(np.uint16), 'distance': distance.astype(np.float32), 'delta': delta.astype(np.float32), # eachsplitmaxnum: Not given in the sources. } Multi-Plane Image (MPI) Rendering from Point Clouds is a technique that converts a 3D point cloud into a set of 2D image planes (MPI) to enable efficient rendering with occlusion handling. It solves the problem of projecting sparse 3D data onto a 2D target grid while resolving depth conflicts between planes. Unlike standard point cloud rasterization which may suffer from z-fighting or require complex sorting, this method aggregates points into discrete depth bins and blends them front-to-back using a visibility mask. Frustum Voxelization and Feature Aggregation is a pre-processing method that maps a 3D point cloud into a structured 3D volume aligned with the camera frustum to facilitate multi-plane rendering. It solves the problem of organizing sparse, unstructured point cloud data into a dense grid suitable for convolutional neural networks by assigning points to voxels based on their spatial proximity to pixel centers and depth planes. It differs from its parent method, Multi-Plane Point Cloud Voxelization and Weight Aggregation, by explicitly defining the voxel grid boundaries using the camera's near and far clipping planes and calculating aggregation weights based on both parallel (pixel-space) and vertical (depth) distances, rather than simple depth binning. Not given in the sources. Originated in the PCMP-NeRF project. Used for rendering point clouds into multi-plane images for neural rendering. name: Multi-Plane Image (MPI) Rendering from Point Clouds
head: MPI Rendering, Multi-Plane Projection
body: Multi-Plane Image (MPI) Rendering from Point Clouds is a preprocessing technique that renders a 3D point cloud into a set of 2D image planes (MPI) by projecting points onto a target image grid and handling occlusion between planes. It aggregates points into discrete depth bins and blends them front-to-back using a visibility mask. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point cloud dataset loaded from a PLY file, containing positions stored as [x, y, z, 1.0] and colors stored as [r, g, b]. Parameters: numplanes (number of depth planes, typically 32) and targeth, targetw (output image height and width, typically 480 and 640 for ScanNet). Output: A final rendered image tensor of shape [H, W, 3] and a final mask tensor of shape [H, W, 1]. Data Structures: 1. Intermediate Tensors: imageall of shape [num\planes, H, W, 3] and maskall of shape [num\planes, H, W, 1], both initialized to zeros. imageall stores the color contribution of points assigned to each plane, while maskall stores the validity mask for each plane. 2. Final Tensors: finalimage of shape [H, W, 3] and finalmask of shape [H, W, 1], both initialized to zeros. Steps: 1. Initialize imageall and maskall tensors of shape [num\planes, H, W, 3] and [num\planes, H, W, 1] respectively, filled with zeros. 2. For each point in the point cloud, determine its assigned plane index d based on its depth z, project the point's 3D position to 2D image coordinates (u, v), assign the point's color to imageall[d, v, u,:], and set maskall[d, v, u, 0] = 1 to mark the position as occupied. 3. Initialize finalimage and finalmask tensors of shape [H, W, 3] and [H, W, 1] with zeros. 4. Iterate through each plane i from 0 to num\planes - 1: If i = 0, copy imageall[0] to finalimage and maskall[0] to finalmask. If i > 0, calculate the valid region as the part of the current plane's mask not yet covered by the accumulated mask: valid = mask\all[i] \times (1 - final\mask). Update the final image by blending the new plane's image in the valid region: final\image = final\image \times final\mask + valid \times image\all[i]. Update the accumulated mask by adding the valid region: final\mask = final\mask + valid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rendermpi(pointclouds, pointcloudscolors, numplanes, targeth, targetw, fx, fy, cx, cy, zmin, zmax): """ Render a point cloud into a Multi-Plane Image. Args: pointclouds: Array of shape [N, 4] containing [x, y, z, 1.0] pointcloudscolors: Array of shape [N, 3] containing [r, g, b] numplanes: Integer, number of depth planes targeth: Integer, output height targetw: Integer, output width fx, fy, cx, cy: Camera intrinsic parameters zmin, zmax: Depth range for plane binning Returns: finalimage: Array of shape [targeth, targetw, 3] finalmask: Array of shape [targeth, targetw, 1] """ # Initialize intermediate tensors imageall = np.zeros((numplanes, targeth, targetw, 3), dtype=np.float32) maskall = np.zeros((numplanes, targeth, targetw, 1), dtype=np.float32) # Project points to planes for i in range(pointclouds.shape[0]): pos = pointclouds[i] color = pointcloudscolors[i] z = pos[2] # Standard perspective projection to 2D grid coordinates u = int((fx pos[0] / z) + cx) v = int((fy pos[1] / z) + cy) # Depth-to-plane mapping d = int(np.clip((z - zmin) / (zmax - zmin) numplanes, 0, numplanes - 1)) # Assign color and mask if within bounds if 0 <= u < targetw and 0 <= v < targeth: imageall[d, v, u,:] = color maskall[d, v, u, 0] = 1.0 # Initialize final tensors finalimage = np.zeros((targeth, targetw, 3), dtype=np.float32) finalmask = np.zeros((targeth, targetw, 1), dtype=np.float32) # Blend planes front-to-back for i in range(numplanes): if i == 0: finalimage = imageall[i].copy() finalmask = maskall[i].copy() else: # Calculate valid region: current plane's mask minus accumulated mask valid = maskall[i] (1.0 - finalmask) # Blend image finalimage = finalimage finalmask + valid imageall[i] # Update mask finalmask = finalmask + valid return finalimage, finalmask Edge Cases and Pitfalls: PLY Parsing: The source assumes the PLY header ends with the line endheader. Lines following this contain position (indices 0-2) and color (indices 3-5) data. Colors are read as BGR (indices 5, 4, 3) and stored as RGB. Boundary Checks: Points projecting outside the [0, H) \times [0, W) grid must be discarded to avoid index errors. Depth Binning: Points with depth z outside the [z\min, z\max] range must be clamped or discarded to prevent incorrect plane assignment. A rendering technique that produces multiple planes of images with their blending weights, where each plane corresponds to a specific depth in camera coordinates. The blending weights roughly reflect the scene depth, and for each pixel, the plane with the correct depth provides the right color. It is chosen when a neural network outputs explicit blending weights alongside RGB planes. Compared to z-buffer based projection, the camera frustum based point projection used here is more robust when the point cloud is sparse, especially on large scenes like Matterport3D, resulting in more complete renders that reflect correct occlusion. Not given in the sources. The method is described in "Neural Point Cloud Rendering via Multi-Plane Projection". Implementation details for point cloud simplification and MPI generation are available in the associated repository. name: Frustum Voxelization and Feature Aggregation
head: Frustum Voxelization
body: Frustum Voxelization and Feature Aggregation preprocesses a 3D point cloud by mapping its features into a structured 3D volume within the camera frustum for multi-plane neural rendering. It organizes sparse point cloud data by grouping points into voxels and computing aggregation weights based on spatial proximity to the voxel center and depth. Unlike direct 2D projection methods that suffer from visibility verification issues and noise interference, this approach aggregates features within the frustum volume, allowing subsequent 3D convolutional networks to exploit neighboring pixel and depth information to handle projection errors caused by geometry noise. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point cloud with associated features (e.g., RGB, viewpoint direction), camera parameters (intrinsics, extrinsics), and rendering bounds (minimum and maximum depth planes). Output: A frustum volume of dimensions P \times H \times W, where each voxel contains aggregated point features. Data Structures: The frustum volume is a 3D grid with dimensions (P, H, W). P: Number of depth planes (slices along the z-axis). H: Height of the image resolution. W: Width of the image resolution. Each voxel (p, h, w) stores aggregated point features. The source specifies a point feature dimension of 11, initialized as 0.5 (5 dimensions) + RGB (3 dimensions) + viewpoint direction (3 dimensions), though only the first 8 dimensions are updated during training. Steps: 1. Frustum Definition: Define the camera frustum region bounded by the minimum and maximum depth planes of the projected point cloud. 2. Voxelization: Divide the frustum uniformly along the z-axis into P slices. The spatial resolution of each slice corresponds to the image dimensions H \times W, creating P \times H \times W frustum voxels. 3. Point Projection: Project each 3D point from the point cloud onto the image plane to determine its corresponding pixel coordinates (h, w) and depth z. 4. Distance Calculation: For each point i falling into a specific voxel (p, h, w), calculate two distances: D1(p,h,w)i: The Euclidean distance between the point's projection on the image plane and the center of the pixel (h, w) in the parallel direction. D1 \in (0, 1/\sqrt{2}). D2(p,h,w)i: The depth difference between the point and the minimum depth plane of the voxel it occupies. D2 \in (0, l), where l is the length of the frustum along the z-axis. 5. Weight Computation: Compute the blending weight w(p,h,w)i for point i in voxel (p, h, w) using the formula: w(p,h,w)i = (1 - D1(p,h,w)i)^a \times \left(\frac{1}{1 + D2(p,h,w)i}\right)^b where a and b are parameters controlling the blending weights for the parallel and vertical (depth) directions, respectively. 6. Feature Aggregation: Aggregate the features of all points falling into voxel (p, h, w) using the computed weights, typically by computing a weighted average. Parameters: a: Controls parallel direction blending. Typical value: 1. b: Controls vertical (depth) direction blending. Typical value: 1. P: Number of planes. Typical values: 32 for ScanNet and Matterport 3D datasets. H, W: Image resolution. Typical values: 480 \times 640 for ScanNet, 512 \times 640 for Matterport 3D. Pitfalls: If b approaches infinity, the method degenerates to selecting the closest point via z-buffer (as in Aliev et al.), which is not robust against geometry errors and causes temporal jitters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def frustumvoxelizationandaggregation(points, features, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, mindepth, maxdepth, P, H, W, a=1, b=1): """ Voxelize point cloud into frustum volume and aggregate features. Args: points: List of (x, y, z) tuples. features: List of feature vectors (length 11). cameraintrinsics: 3x3 matrix (list of lists). cameraextrinsics: 4x4 matrix (list of lists). mindepth: float, minimum depth of the frustum. maxdepth: float, maximum depth of the frustum. P: int, number of depth planes. H: int, image height. W: int, image width. a: float, parallel blending parameter. b: float, vertical blending parameter. Returns: volume: 3D list [P][H][W][11] of aggregated features. weightsum: 3D list [P][H][W] of floats. """ # Initialize volume [P][H][W][11] and weight sum [P][H][W] volume = [[[ [0.0] 11 for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for in range(P)] weightsum = [[[0.0] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] # Fixed dimensionality # Correct 3D list initialization for weightsum weightsum = [[[0.0] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] # This is HxW. I need P. # Proper initialization: weightsum = [[[0.0] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] # I will use a dict for clarity and correctness weightsum = {} for p in range(P): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): weightsum[(p, h, w)] = 0.0 l = maxdepth - mindepth for i in range(len(points)): x, y, z = points[i] feat = features[i] # Transform to camera coordinates ph = [x, y, z, 1.0] pcam = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for r in range(4): for c in range(4): pcam[r] += cameraextrinsics[r][c] ph[c] pcam = pcam[:3] # Project to 2D u = (cameraintrinsics[0][0] pcam[0] + cameraintrinsics[0][1] pcam[1] + cameraintrinsics[0][2] pcam[2]) / pcam[2] v = (cameraintrinsics[1][0] pcam[0] + cameraintrinsics[1][1] pcam[1] + cameraintrinsics[1][2] pcam[2]) / pcam[2] depth = pcam[2] # Check bounds if depth < mindepth or depth > maxdepth: continue hidx = int(math.floor(v)) widx = int(math.floor(u)) if hidx < 0 or hidx >= H or widx < 0 or widx >= W: continue # Plane index pidx = int(math.floor((depth - mindepth) / (l / P))) if pidx < 0: pidx = 0 if pidx >= P: pidx = P - 1 # D1: distance to pixel center pixelcenteru = widx + 0.5 pixelcenterv = hidx + 0.5 D1 = math.sqrt((u - pixelcenteru)2 + (v - pixelcenterv)2) # D2: depth difference within voxel voxelmindepth = mindepth + pidx (l / P) D2 = depth - voxelmindepth # Weight weight = ((1.0 - D1)a) ((1.0 / (1.0 + D2))b) # Aggregate for d in range(11): volume[pidx][hidx][widx][d] += feat[d] weight weightsum[(pidx, hidx, widx)] += weight # Normalize for p in range(P): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): ws = weightsum[(p, h, w)] if ws > 0: invws = 1.0 / ws for d in range(11): volume[p][h][w][d] = invws return volume, weightsum Multi-plane Neural Rendering is a deep learning pipeline that renders images from raw 3D point clouds by projecting features into a layered 3D volume within the camera frustum, rather than directly onto a 2D image plane. Unlike previous methods that project features directly to 2D and suffer from visibility verification problems and noise interference, this method maintains all features from points in the field-of-view, allowing a 3D CNN to automatically learn visibility and handle occlusions. It produces more stable renderings, particularly near object boundaries, and is robust to noisy and relatively sparse point clouds. A module deployed to comprehensively exploit geometrical information in the fused 3D data volume U{t0} for coarse disparity estimation. Input: Fused 3D data volume U{t0}. Output: Coarse disparity estimation D{t0} \in \mathbb{R}^{H0 \times W0}. Measured Performance: Trained on a GeForce 1080 Ti, taking approximately 41.5 hours per scene for 21 epochs. Strengths: Robust to noise and relatively sparse point clouds; effectively exploits information from neighboring pixels and depth to handle projection errors caused by geometry noise. Limitations: Sensitive to parameter b; if b \to \infty, it degenerates to z-buffering, causing temporal jitters. The method was introduced in "Neural Point Cloud Rendering via Multi-Plane Projection" (CVPR 2020). It adapts multi-plane rendering to handle raw point clouds by voxelizing the camera frustum and aggregating features, addressing the limitations of direct 2D projection methods which struggle with visibility verification and noise interference. name: Multi-plane Neural Rendering
head: 3D Convolutional Renderer, MPP Network, Multi-Plane Projection, Neural Volume Rendering Network, NPR-MPP, Neural Point Cloud Rendering via Multi-Plane Projection
body: Multi-plane Neural Rendering is a deep learning pipeline that renders images from raw 3D point clouds by projecting features into a layered 3D volume within the camera frustum, rather than directly onto a 2D image plane. Unlike previous methods that project features directly to 2D and suffer from visibility verification problems and noise interference, this method maintains all features from points in the field-of-view, allowing a 3D CNN to automatically learn visibility and handle occlusions. It produces more stable renderings, particularly near object boundaries, and is robust to noisy and relatively sparse point clouds. Inputs and Outputs Input: Raw 3D point cloud of a scene. Each point has a position and an appearance feature. Output: Image or image sequences from a novel view or along a novel camera trajectory. Data Structures and Layout 1. Point Feature: A concatenation of an 8-dimensional learnable appearance feature and a normalized view direction vector (between camera position and point). The total point feature dimension is 11. 2. 3D Feature Volume: Dimensions P \times H \times W, containing aggregated point features. H \times W are the image dimensions, and P is the pre-defined number of depth planes. 3. Network Input: Concatenation of the 3D feature volume and the normalized view direction. 4. Network Output: A tensor with 4 channels (RGB + blend weight) per plane. Parameters H, W: Image dimensions. Typical values: (480, 640) for ScanNet, (512, 640) for Matterport 3D. P: Number of depth planes. Typical value: 32. Point feature dimension: 11 (8 trainable appearance + 3 view direction). Initialization: Point features initialized as 0.5 (5 dimensions) + RGB (3 dimensions) + viewpoint direction (3 dimensions). Only the first 8 dimensions are updated. usedilation: Boolean flag for dilated convolution in Conv6, default True. Number of samples d: Default 32. Steps 1. Feature Initialization: For each 3D point, initialize an 11-dimensional feature vector. The first 8 dimensions are learnable appearance features (initialized to 0.5), and the last 3 dimensions are the normalized view direction from the camera to the point. 2. Frustum Definition: Using the camera projection matrix, lift each pixel to 3D space to form a frustum defined by the minimum and maximum depth of the projected point cloud. 3. Voxelization: Divide the frustum into voxels with respect to image dimensions H \times W and P depth planes along the z-axis, resulting in P \times H \times W frustum voxels. 4. Feature Aggregation: Aggregate features of points inside each frustum voxel using geometric rules. Points closer to the camera or pixel center are assigned larger weights. 5. Network Input Preparation: Concatenate the aggregated 3D feature volume (P \times H \times W) with the normalized view direction vector. 6. 3D CNN Encoding: Pass the input through a U-Net-like 3D CNN encoder: Conv0: 1x1 kernel, 16 filters, LReLU. Conv1: 3x3 kernel, 32 filters, LReLU. Pool1: 2x2x2, stride 2. Conv2: 3x3 kernel, 32 filters, LReLU. Pool2: 2x1x1, stride [2,1,1]. Conv3: 3x3 kernel, 64 filters, LReLU. Pool3: 2x2x2, stride 2. Conv4: 3x3 kernel, 64 filters, LReLU. Pool4: 2x1x1, stride [2,1,1]. Conv5: 3x3 kernel, 128 filters, LReLU. Pool5: 2x2x2, stride 2. 7. Bottleneck: Conv6: 1x3x3 kernel, 128 filters, LReLU. If usedilation is True, use dilation rate [1,2,2]; otherwise [1,1,1]. 8. 3D CNN Decoding (U-Net Skip Connections): Up1: Upsample Conv6 (2x2x2) and concatenate with Conv5 (128 channels). Conv7: Process concatenated features. Up2: Upsample Conv7 (2x1x1) and concatenate with Conv4 (64 channels). Conv8: Process concatenated features. Up3: Upsample Conv8 (2x2x2) and concatenate with Conv3 (64 channels). Conv9: Process concatenated features. Up4: Upsample Conv9 (2x1x1) and concatenate with Conv2 (32 channels). Conv10: Process concatenated features. Up5: Upsample Conv10 (2x2x2) and concatenate with Conv1 (32 channels). Conv11: Process concatenated features. 9. Output Prediction: Color: Conv12 (1x1x1, 3 filters, linear) predicts color ci. Density: Conv121 (1x1x1, 1 filter, linear) predicts density \rhoi. 10. Volume Rendering: Accumulate color using discrete volume rendering formula over d samples (default 32): C = \frac{1}{N} \text{ or } \sum Ti \times (1 - \exp(-\rhoi \times \deltai)) \times ci 11. Multi-plane Blending: The network predicts RGB images Ip and blending weights \alphap for each plane p. The final output image I is obtained by blending: I = \sump Ip \cdot \alphap. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def conv3d(x, outchannels, kernelsize, stride=1, padding=0, dilation=1): return F.conv3d(x, weight=None, bias=None, stride=stride, padding=padding, dilation=dilation) def pool3d(x, kernelsize, stride=None): return F.maxpool3d(x, kernelsize=kernelsize, stride=stride if stride else kernelsize) def upsample3d(x, scalefactor): return F.interpolate(x, scalefactor=scalefactor, mode='trilinear', aligncorners=False) def concat(a, b, dim=1): return torch.cat([a, b], dim=dim) def multiplaneneuralrendering(pointcloud, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, H, W, P, usedilation=True): """ Renders an image from a point cloud using multi-plane neural rendering. Args: pointcloud: Array of shape (N, 3) containing 3D coordinates. cameraintrinsics: 3x3 camera intrinsic matrix. cameraextrinsics: 4x4 camera extrinsic matrix. H: Height of the output image. W: Width of the output image. P: Number of depth planes. usedilation: Boolean flag for dilated convolution in Conv6. Returns: renderedimage: Array of shape (H, W, 3). """ device = pointcloud.device numpoints = pointcloud.shape[0] # Step 1: Feature Initialization pointfeatures = torch.zeros((numpoints, 11), device=device) pointfeatures[:,:8] = 0.5 # Learnable appearance features # Compute view directions (camera to point) pointshomogeneous = torch.cat([pointcloud, torch.ones((numpoints, 1), device=device)], dim=1) pointscam = (cameraextrinsics @ pointshomogeneous.T).T[:,:3] norms = torch.norm(pointscam, dim=1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8 viewdirections = pointscam / norms pointfeatures[:, 8:] = viewdirections # Normalized view direction # Step 2 & 3: Frustum Definition and Voxelization pointscamhomogeneous = torch.cat([pointscam, torch.ones((numpoints, 1), device=device)], dim=1) pointsimg = (cameraintrinsics @ pointscamhomogeneous[:,:3].T).T pointsimg[:,:2] /= pointsimg[:, 2:3] validmask = (pointsimg[:, 0] >= 0) & (pointsimg[:, 0] < W) & \ (pointsimg[:, 1] >= 0) & (pointsimg[:, 1] < H) & \ (pointsimg[:, 2] > 0) validpoints = pointscam[validmask] validfeatures = pointfeatures[validmask] validu = pointsimg[validmask, 0] validv = pointsimg[validmask, 1] validz = validpoints[:, 2] mindepth = torch.min(validz) maxdepth = torch.max(validz) depthrange = maxdepth - mindepth + 1e-8 # Initialize voxel grid (P, H, W, 11) voxelgrid = torch.zeros((P, H, W, 11), device=device) # Step 4: Feature Aggregation for i in range(len(validpoints)): u = int(torch.clamp(validu[i], 0, W-1).item()) v = int(torch.clamp(validv[i], 0, H-1).item()) p = int(torch.clamp((validz[i] - mindepth) / depthrange P, 0, P-1).item()) distcam = torch.norm(validpoints[i]) weight = 1.0 / (distcam + 1e-8) # Geometric rule: closer points get larger weights voxelgrid[p, v, u] += validfeatures[i] weight # Step 5: Network Input Preparation # View direction for the current camera pose (normalized forward vector) viewdir = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0], device=device) viewdirexpanded = viewdir.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # (1, 1, 1, 1, 3) # Permute voxelgrid to (1, 11, P, H, W) and concat viewdir networkinput = concat(voxelgrid.permute(0, 3, 1, 2).unsqueeze(0), viewdirexpanded.expand(1, 3, P, H, W), dim=1) # Step 6: 3D CNN Encoding x = conv3d(networkinput, 16, 1) # Conv0 x = F.leakyrelu(x) x = conv3d(x, 32, 3) # Conv1 x = F.leakyrelu(x) conv1out = x x = pool3d(x, 2) # Pool1 x = conv3d(x, 32, 3) # Conv2 x = F.leakyrelu(x) conv2out = x x = pool3d(x, (2,1,1), (2,1,1)) # Pool2 x = conv3d(x, 64, 3) # Conv3 x = F.leakyrelu(x) conv3out = x x = pool3d(x, 2) # Pool3 x = conv3d(x, 64, 3) # Conv4 x = F.leakyrelu(x) conv4out = x x = pool3d(x, (2,1,1), (2,1,1)) # Pool4 x = conv3d(x, 128, 3) # Conv5 x = F.leakyrelu(x) conv5out = x x = pool3d(x, 2) # Pool5 # Step 7: Bottleneck dilation = (1,2,2) if usedilation else (1,1,1) x = conv3d(x, 128, (1,3,3), dilation=dilation) # Conv6 x = F.leakyrelu(x) # Step 8: 3D CNN Decoding x = upsample3d(x, 2) # Up1 x = concat(x, conv5out, dim=1) x = conv3d(x, 128, 3) # Conv7 x = F.leakyrelu(x) x = upsample3d(x, (2,1,1)) # Up2 x = concat(x, conv4out, dim=1) x = conv3d(x, 64, 3) # Conv8 x = F.leakyrelu(x) x = upsample3d(x, 2) # Up3 x = concat(x, conv3out, dim=1) x = conv3d(x, 64, 3) # Conv9 x = F.leakyrelu(x) x = upsample3d(x, (2,1,1)) # Up4 x = concat(x, conv2out, dim=1) x = conv3d(x, 32, 3) # Conv10 x = F.leakyrelu(x) x = upsample3d(x, 2) # Up5 x = concat(x, conv1out, dim=1) x = conv3d(x, 32, 3) # Conv11 x = F.leakyrelu(x) # Step 9: Output Prediction color = conv3d(x, 4, 1) # Conv12 predicts RGB + blend weight # Note: splits this into Conv12 (3 filters) and Conv121 (1 filter) for density # Step 10 & 11: Multi-plane Blending rgbimages = color[:,:3,:,:] blendweights = F.softmax(color[:, 3:4,:,:], dim=1) renderedimage = torch.sum(rgbimages blendweights, dim=1) # Sum over P dimension return renderedimage.permute(1, 2, 0) # (H, W, 3) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Training takes on average 41.5 hours per scene on a GeForce 1080 Ti. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on ScanNet and Matterport 3D datasets. Produces more stable renderings compared to previous methods, especially near object boundaries. Performs reasonably well given relatively sparse point clouds. Scaling: Uses point clouds which are more scalable for larger scenes compared to DeepVoxel which relies on 3D volume. Strengths: Robust to noisy and relatively sparse point clouds. Handles occlusions and noises appropriately by projecting to a layered 3D volume. Temporal coherence in image sequences. Limitations: Requires a point cloud as input. Training time is significant. When to use: When rendering from raw 3D point clouds, especially in the presence of noise or sparsity, and when temporal stability is required. When not to use: When a dense 3D volume representation is already available and point clouds are not the primary input. Multi-plane Neural Rendering was proposed by Peng Dai, Yinda Zhang, Zhuwen Li, Shuaicheng Liu, and Bing Zeng from the University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Google Research, and Nuro Inc. It was published in CVPR 2020. The method addresses the limitations of previous neural point-based graphics approaches like NPG, which suffer from visibility verification problems and noise interference due to direct 3D-to-2D projection. It builds on the idea of using learnable point features and view-dependent appearance.
