name: Ray Model Voxelization
head: LiDAR Voxelization, Ray Traversal Voxelization
body: Ray Model Voxelization converts sparse LiDAR point clouds into dense 3D occupancy grids by tracing rays from sensor origins to detected points, classifying voxels as free, occupied, or unobserved. It differs from Hard Voxelization by explicitly modeling the empty space between the sensor and the target points, rather than only marking voxels containing points, and from Point Cloud to Gaussian Converter by producing discrete grid states rather than continuous density fields. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: pointsorigin: Sensor origin positions, shape [N, 3]. points: LiDAR point coordinates, shape [N, 3+] (typically [N, 3] or [N, 4] with intensity). pointslabel: Semantic labels for points, shape [N]. pointcloudrange: 3D bounding box [x{min}, y{min}, z{min}, x{max}, y{max}, z{max}] in meters. voxelsize: Voxel dimensions [vx, vy, vz] in meters. Default: [0.2, 0.2, 0.2]. spatialshape: Output grid dimensions [H, W, D]. Default: [512, 256, 32]. Outputs: voxelstate: Integer grid [H, W, D] with values -1 (NOTOBSERVED), 0 (FREE), 1 (OCCUPIED). voxellabel: Integer grid [H, W, D] with semantic labels. Default label for free voxels is 0. invalidmask: Boolean grid [H, W, D] indicating unobserved voxels or voxels with no label. Data Structures The implementation uses CUDA kernels for parallel ray traversal. Key variables include: voxelocccount: Atomic counter for occupied voxels. voxelfreecount: Atomic counter for free voxels. ray[3]: Ray direction vector. step[3]: Step direction per axis (+1 or -1). tDelta[3]: Increment in t to move one voxel. tMax[3]: Next voxel boundary in t units. currentvoxel[3]: Current traversal position. targetvoxel[3]: End point voxel (LiDAR hit). Parameters voxelsize: [0.2, 0.2, 0.2] meters. pointcloudrange: [-51.2, -25.6, -2, 51.2, 25.6, 4.4] meters. spatialshape: [512, 256, 32]. apre/apost: Frames to aggregate before/after for ground truth. Default: 70/70. ppre/ppost: Input/prediction sequence lengths. Default: 10/10. freenthreshold: 0. occupiednthreshold: 1. Steps 1. Coordinate Transformation: Normalize point origins using the inverse pose matrix and rotate points based on dataset-specific conventions. For Lyft, rotate \pi around Z; for NuScenes, rotate -\pi/2 around Z. \text{points}{\text{norm}} = \text{pose\origin\inv} \times \text{points} \text{points}{\text{rot}} = \text{points}{\text{norm}} \times \text{rotation\matrix}^T 2. Temporal Aggregation: Aggregate input points from frames [index - p{pre}, index] and ground truth points from frames [index, index + p{post}]. For ground truth, further aggregate points from the window [i - a{pre}, i + a{post}] for each target frame i. 3. Ray Initialization: For each ray, calculate the direction vector from the sensor origin to the target point. Compute step (+1 or -1 per axis), tDelta (increment to move one voxel), and tMax (distance to the next voxel boundary). 4. Ray Traversal: Traverse the ray path using a while loop with bounds checks. Mark the target voxel by incrementing voxelocccount using atomicAdd. Mark all traversed voxels (excluding the target) by incrementing voxelfreecount using atomicAdd. Stop rays at a distance of 1 voxel to prevent over-traversal, and ignore voxels too close to the sensor or target using a distance threshold of 1.0m. 5. Voxel State Assignment: Assign states based on counts. If voxelocccount > 1, state = OCCUPIED (1). Else if voxelfreecount > 0, state = FREE (0). Else, state = NOTOBSERVED (-1). 6. Label Assignment: Calculate voxel indices for points within range. \text{pcds\voxel} = \lfloor (\text{points} - \text{range\min}) / \text{voxel\size} \rfloor Convert to scalar indices and assign point labels to voxellabelsqueeze. Default label for free voxels is 0. 7. Invalid Mask Generation: Generate a mask for voxels that are unobserved or have no label. 8. Compression: Compress binary occupancy data using bit packing. Reshape the boolean array [H, W, D] to 1D, compress 8 bools into 1 uint8, and save as.npy. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def raymodelvoxelization(pointsorigin, points, pointslabel, pointcloudrange, voxelsize, spatialshape, rotationmatrix=None, poseorigininv=None): """ Convert point cloud to voxel grid using ray traversal. Args: pointsorigin: [N, 3] sensor origins points: [N, 3] LiDAR points pointslabel: [N] semantic labels pointcloudrange: [6] [xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax] voxelsize: [3] [vx, vy, vz] spatialshape: [3] [H, W, D] rotationmatrix: [3, 3] optional rotation poseorigininv: [4, 4] optional inverse pose Returns: voxelstate: [H, W, D] int (-1, 0, 1) voxellabel: [H, W, D] int invalidmask: [H, W, D] bool """ # 1. Coordinate Transformation if poseorigininv is not None: pointsh = np.hstack([points, np.ones((points.shape[0], 1))]) pointsnorm = (poseorigininv @ pointsh.T).T[:,:3] else: pointsnorm = points if rotationmatrix is not None: pointsrot = pointsnorm @ rotationmatrix.T else: pointsrot = pointsnorm points = pointsrot # 2. Initialize Grids H, W, D = spatialshape voxelocccount = np.zeros(spatialshape, dtype=np.int32) voxelfreecount = np.zeros(spatialshape, dtype=np.int32) voxellabel = np.zeros(spatialshape, dtype=np.int32) # Default 0 rangemin = pointcloudrange[:3] # 3. Process Each Ray for i in range(points.shape[0]): origin = pointsorigin[i] target = points[i] # Skip if too close (1.0m threshold) dist = np.linalg.norm(target - origin) if dist < 1.0: continue raydir = (target - origin) / dist # Shift coordinates to voxel space origin originshifted = origin - rangemin targetshifted = target - rangemin # Calculate voxel indices for origin and target originvoxel = np.floor(originshifted / voxelsize).astype(np.int32) targetvoxel = np.floor(targetshifted / voxelsize).astype(np.int32) # Check bounds if not np.all(originvoxel >= 0) or not np.all(originvoxel < spatialshape): continue if not np.all(targetvoxel >= 0) or not np.all(targetvoxel < spatialshape): continue # Ray parameters in voxel space raydirvoxel = raydir / voxelsize step = np.where(raydirvoxel > 0, 1, -1).astype(np.int32) tdelta = 1.0 / np.abs(raydirvoxel) # tMax: distance to next boundary in t units tmax = np.zeros(3) for d in range(3): if raydirvoxel[d] > 0: tmax[d] = (originvoxel[d] + 1) - (originshifted[d] / voxelsize[d]) else: tmax[d] = originvoxel[d] - (originshifted[d] / voxelsize[d]) currentvoxel = originvoxel.copy() # Traverse ray # Stop 1 voxel before target to prevent over-traversal while not np.arrayequal(currentvoxel, targetvoxel): # Mark free voxel (simulates atomicAdd) voxelfreecount[currentvoxel[0], currentvoxel[1], currentvoxel[2]] += 1 # Find next voxel tnext = np.argmin(tmax) currentvoxel[tnext] += step[tnext] tmax[tnext] += tdelta[tnext] # Check bounds if not np.all(currentvoxel >= 0) or not np.all(currentvoxel < spatialshape): break # Mark target voxel as occupied (simulates atomicAdd) voxelocccount[targetvoxel[0], targetvoxel[1], targetvoxel[2]] += 1 # 4. Assign States voxelstate = np.full(spatialshape, -1, dtype=np.int32) # NOTOBSERVED occupiedmask = voxelocccount > 1 freemask = (voxelfreecount > 0) & ~occupiedmask voxelstate[occupiedmask] = 1 # OCCUPIED voxelstate[freemask] = 0 # FREE # 5. Assign Labels pcdsvoxel = np.floor((points - rangemin) / voxelsize).astype(np.int32) validpoints = np.all((pcdsvoxel >= 0) & (pcdsvoxel < spatialshape), axis=1) if np.any(validpoints): validvoxels = pcdsvoxel[validpoints] validlabels = pointslabel[validpoints] inds = validvoxels[:, 0] W D + validvoxels[:, 1] D + validvoxels[:, 2] voxellabelflat = voxellabel.reshape(-1) voxellabelflat[inds] = validlabels voxellabel = voxellabelflat.reshape(spatialshape) # 6. Invalid Mask # Unobserved or occupied voxels with no label (default 0) invalidmask = (voxelstate == -1) | ((voxelstate == 1) & (voxellabel == 0)) # 7. Compression (for binary occupancy) # binaryocc = (voxelstate == 1) # compressed = np.packbits(binaryocc.reshape(-1)) return voxelstate, voxellabel, invalidmask Performance: Implemented using CUDA kernels with NVRTC for high performance. Atomic operations ensure thread safety. Strengths: Explicitly models free space, which is critical for occupancy prediction. Handles multi-frame temporal aggregation for dense ground truth. Limitations: Requires careful handling of coordinate transformations for different datasets. Numerical precision issues can occur if TF32 is not disabled in CUDA operations. The Ray Model Voxelization method is part of the Occ4cast project, specifically designed for processing LiDAR data for occupancy forecasting. The implementation is optimized for GPU execution using CUDA. name: Two-stage training with adaptive point cloud generation
head: Adding extra points, Supplemental point cloud generation
body: This method expands a sparse scene representation by generating a supplemental point cloud based on the bounding volume of existing points. It splits training into two stages, using noise-injected UDF gradient descent to densify the point cloud after the first stage. Inputs: Initial point cloud positions P{init} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3} from stage 1. Ground truth points P{gt}. Hyperparameters: stability constant c=1.1, maximum supplemental points N{max}=200,000, noise scaling factor lowrange, UDF threshold dffilter, outlier distance outlier. Outputs: Combined point cloud P{combined} for stage 2 training. Data Structures: Bounding box defined by Q{min} and Q{max}, the element-wise minimum and maximum coordinates of P{init}. cKDTree for efficient nearest-neighbor queries during stage 2. Step 1: Calculate Supplemental Point Count Determine the number of points Np to generate based on the volume of the bounding box of the initial point cloud: Np = \text{min}\left(\frac{\text{prod}(Q{max} - Q{min})}{c^3}, N{max}\right) where \text{prod}(\cdot) returns the product of all values in the vector (Q{max} - Q{min}). Step 2: Generate Supplemental Points The process samples points, computes offsets and standard deviation, generates noise scaled by lowrange, adds noise to points, computes UDF and gradient, projects samples to surface, filters by udfsample < dffilter, and repeats until numpoints is reached. Step 3: Concatenate and Rebuild Concatenate ground truth points with generated points, build cKDTree, and update dataset for stage 2 training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def genextrapointcloud(Pinit, Pgt, Nmax=200000, c=1.1, lowrange=0.01, dffilter=0.05, outlier=0.1, numpoints=None, maxiterations=1000, learningrate=0.01): # Step 1: Calculate Np Qmin = Pinit.min(axis=0) Qmax = Pinit.max(axis=0) bboxvolume = np.prod(Qmax - Qmin) Np = min(bboxvolume / (c 3), Nmax) if numpoints is None: numpoints = int(Np) # Step 2: Generate points via UDF gradient descent # Initialize samples on a grid within the bounding box griddim = int(np.ceil(numpoints (1/3))) coords = np.linspace(Qmin, Qmax, griddim) X, Y, Z = np.meshgrid(coords[:, 0], coords[:, 1], coords[:, 2], indexing='ij') samples = np.stack([X.ravel(), Y.ravel(), Z.ravel()], axis=1) generatedpoints = [] for in range(maxiterations): # [Comment: UDF computation and gradient descent details are implementation-specific and not provided in the sources] udfvalues = np.zeros(len(samples)) # Placeholder for actual UDF values gradients = np.zeroslike(samples) # Placeholder for actual gradients noise = np.random.normal(0, lowrange, samples.shape) samples = samples - gradients learningrate + noise validmask = udfvalues < dffilter samples = samples[validmask] if len(samples) >= numpoints: break generatedpoints = samples[:numpoints] # Step 3: Remove outliers # Compute distances to nearest neighbor in Pgt and filter if len(Pgt) > 0 and len(generatedpoints) > 0: dists = np.linalg.norm(generatedpoints[:, np.newaxis,:] - Pgt[np.newaxis,:,:], axis=2) mindists = dists.min(axis=1) generatedpoints = generatedpoints[mindists < outlier] # Concatenate and rebuild KDTree Pcombined = np.concatenate([Pgt, generatedpoints], axis=0) # [Comment: cKDTree construction for stage 2 sampling is implementation-specific] return Pcombined Memory complexity increases by Np points, which is capped at 200,000. The method was introduced in "Deblurring 3D Gaussian Splatting" by B. Lee et al.. It addresses sparse point clouds in Gaussian Splatting by supplementing points to improve reconstruction quality. name: Hard Voxelization
body: Hard Voxelization discretizes a continuous 3D point cloud into a fixed-size 3D grid of cubic voxels by binning points based on their spatial coordinates and aggregating associated attribute values within each voxel. It solves the problem of converting unstructured point data into a regular grid structure suitable for convolutional neural networks or efficient spatial queries, differing from its siblings by enforcing a strict grid topology where points are assigned to specific voxels based on deterministic coordinate mapping, unlike probabilistic or sparse variants. The core mechanism maps continuous point coordinates (x, y, z) to discrete integer voxel indices (i, j, k) using floor division relative to a bounding box origin and voxel dimensions. Coordinate Mapping: For a point p with coordinates (x, y, z), a voxel size v = [vx, vy, vz], and a bounding box range R = [x{min}, y{min}, z{min}, x{max}, y{max}, z{max}], the voxel coordinates are calculated as: i = \left\lfloor \frac{x - x{min}}{vx} \right\rfloor, \quad j = \left\lfloor \frac{y - y{min}}{vy} \right\rfloor, \quad k = \left\lfloor \frac{z - z{min}}{vz} \right\rfloor Grid Dimensions: The grid dimensions are derived from the range and voxel size. While some implementations use ceiling division to ensure full coverage, others use rounding: \text{dim}x = \max(1, \lceil \frac{x{max} - x{min}}{vx} \rceil) \quad \text{or} \quad \text{round}\left(\frac{x{max} - x{min}}{vx}\right) Boundary Handling: Points with coordinates outside the range R are mapped to invalid indices (e.g., -1) and are typically discarded or filtered out before aggregation. Aggregation: Points falling into the same voxel are aggregated. Common strategies include storing all points up to a limit, averaging attributes, or computing a centroid. The output typically consists of voxels, coors, and numpointspervoxel. Determinism: Standard hard voxelization may rely on atomic operations which are non-deterministic. Deterministic variants use explicit sorting or unique-coordinate identification to ensure reproducible output order. Multiscale Hard Voxelization is a GPU-accelerated method that simultaneously voxelizes a LiDAR point cloud into multiple spatial resolutions (scales) in a single pass. It extends standard hard voxelization by iterating over a list of voxel sizes and point limits, outputting separate voxel feature tensors, coordinates, and point counts for each scale. It differs from single-scale voxelization by managing multiple memory blocks indexed by scale, offering a 10% speed improvement over ordinary single-scale CUDA operators on NVIDIA RTX 3090 hardware. Choose it when processing LiDAR data requires multiple spatial resolutions in a single pass to improve inference speed. Hard Voxelization (Deterministic) discretizes a continuous 3D point cloud into a fixed-size 3D grid of cubic voxels by binning points based on their spatial coordinates and aggregating associated attribute values within each voxel. It outputs a single representative point per occupied voxel calculated as the centroid of the aggregated attributes. Unlike its sibling Multiscale Hard Voxelization, which handles multiple resolutions, this method operates on a single fixed scale. It differs from the non-deterministic variant by guaranteeing reproducible output through explicit sorting and unique-coordinate identification, ensuring that the order of points within a voxel is preserved, whereas non-deterministic versions rely on atomic operations that may yield varying results across runs. Choose it when bit-identical, reproducible output order is required for debugging or training stability. Point Cloud Voxelization Visualization is a rendering pipeline that visualizes the occupancy of a point cloud after it has been downsampled into a 3D voxel grid using the Point Cloud Library (PCL). It solves the problem of visually verifying voxelization parameters and bounding box constraints by offering three distinct rendering modes: raw point cloud coloring, solid voxel cubes, and wireframe voxel cubes. It differs from its siblings by focusing specifically on the visualization of the filtered output rather than just the aggregation logic, and it relies on PCL's VoxelGrid filter for the downsampling step. Choose it when visually verifying voxelization parameters and bounding box constraints is needed. This method reduces point cloud density by grouping points into a 3D grid and probabilistically selecting a fixed number of points per voxel. It addresses the computational bottleneck of processing large-scale point clouds in volume rendering pipelines by ensuring uniform spatial distribution while preserving local density characteristics. Unlike deterministic hard voxelization which may arbitrarily discard points or retain all, this approach guarantees a controlled output size per voxel through random sampling weighted by the inverse of the local point count. Choose it when memory constraints require a predictable output size while preserving statistical point distribution. Computes voxel coordinates for each point. When maxpoints = -1, it skips duplicate handling and fixed grid assignment, outputting only the coordinate tensor. Calculate grid dimensions: gridx = round((coorsxmax - coorsxmin) / voxelx), etc. Launch dynamicvoxelizekernel to compute voxel coordinates for each point and store them in the coors tensor. NDim: Number of dimensions for coordinates, default 3. Hard voxelization is a fundamental preprocessing step in 3D computer vision, particularly for LiDAR-based object detection and autonomous driving perception systems. It was popularized by frameworks like MMDetection3D and PointPillars, which require regular grid inputs for 3D CNNs or 2D projection networks. The method originated from the need to efficiently process sparse point clouds by converting them into dense voxel grids, allowing the use of standard convolutional operations. Modern variants leverage GPU acceleration for real-time performance. Susie0909/MultiscaleVoxelizationCUDA, https://github.com/Susie0909/MultiscaleVoxelizationCUDA, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Multiscale Hard Voxelization
body:
Multiscale Hard Voxelization is a GPU-accelerated method that simultaneously voxelizes a LiDAR point cloud into multiple spatial resolutions in a single pass, outputting voxel features, coordinates, and point counts for each scale. It solves the inefficiency of invoking separate single-scale voxelization operators for different resolutions in 3D perception pipelines. Unlike standard single-scale hard voxelization, this method iterates over multiple voxel sizes and stores results in separate memory blocks indexed by scale, offering a 10% speed improvement over ordinary single-scale CUDA operators on an NVIDIA RTX 3090. It builds on Hard Voxelization by extending the coordinate mapping and aggregation logic to handle a list of voxel sizes and maximum point limits per scale. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud tensor points of shape [N, D], where N is the number of points and D is the number of features (e.g., x, y, z, reflectivity). Outputs: voxels: Tensor of shape [S, M{total}, M{max}, D], containing the point features grouped by voxel. xmin) / vx) cy = math.floor((y - ymin) / vy) cz = math.floor((z - zmin) / vz) # Progressive boundary masking per source if not (0 <= cx < gridx): pointcoors[i] = [-1, -1, -1] continue if not (0 <= cy < gridy): pointcoors[i] = [-1, -1, -1] continue if not (0 <= cz < gridz): pointcoors[i] = [-1, -1, -1] continue pointcoors[i] = [cz, cy, cx] # Deterministic O(N^2) linking num = 0 firstmatch = -1 for j in range(i): if pointcoors[j] == pointcoors[i]: num += 1 if num == 1: firstmatch = j if num >= maxpts: pointtovoxelidx[i] = -1 continue pointtovoxelidx[i] = num if num == 0: pointtopointidx[i] = i if voxelnum >= maxvoxels: pointtovoxelidx[i] = -1 continue vidx = voxelnum voxelnum += 1 coortovoxelidx[i] = vidx numpointspervoxel[s][vidx] = 1 else: pointtopointidx[i] = firstmatch coortovoxelidx[i] = coortovoxelidx[firstmatch] numpointspervoxel[s][coortovoxelidx[i]] += 1 # Aggregate features for i in range(N): if pointtovoxelidx[i] != -1: vidx = coortovoxelidx[i] pidx = pointtovoxelidx[i] voxels[s][vidx][pidx] = points[i] coors[s][vidx] = pointcoors[i] # Slice outputs to actual used voxel counts per scale voxelsout = [voxels[s][:voxelnum] for s in range(S)] coorsout = [coors[s][:voxelnum] for s in range(S)] numpointsout = [numpointspervoxel[s][:voxelnum] for s in range(S)] return voxelsout, coorsout, numpointsout Parameters: voxelsizes: e.g., [[0.16, 0.16, 4], [0.32, 0.32, 4], [0.64, 0.64, 4]] maxpointsforallscales: e.g., [32, 64, 128] pointcloudrange: e.g., [0, -39.68, -3, 69.12, 39.68, 1] maxvoxels: e.g., 20000 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out of Bounds: Points outside the pointcloudrange are discarded by progressively masking their coordinates to -1. Max Voxels/Points: If the number of voxels exceeds maxvoxels or points in a voxel exceed maxpoints, additional points are discarded. The source notes that users should shuffle points before calling the function because maxvoxels may drop points. Determinism: The method is deterministic by default, using explicit nested loops instead of atomic operations. Performance: The deterministic linking approach is O(N^2), which is inefficient for large point clouds. This variant uses Multiscale Hard Voxelization as a preprocessing step for LiDAR feature encoding. It encodes LiDAR features using PointNet++ with hidden feature dimensions mirroring those of a sparse UNet method. It samples points at different levels (4096, 1024, 256, and 56 points) using farthest point sampling (FPS). The FPS and neighbor point grouping are implemented using CUDA-based routines from PyTorch3D to enhance efficiency. This approach was found to underperform compared to sparse UNet-based encoding in the context of neural radiance fields for street scenes. Time Complexity: The coordinate mapping is O(N) per scale, but the deterministic point linking is O(N^2) per scale due to the nested loop approach, which is a significant bottleneck for large N. Memory Complexity: O(S \cdot M{total} \cdot M{max} \cdot D) for the output tensors, where S is the number of scales, M{total} is maxvoxels, M{max} is the maximum maxpoints, and D is the number of features. Performance: On an NVIDIA RTX 3090, the multiscale operator shows a 10% speed improvement over the ordinary single-scale voxelization CUDA operator. Strengths: Simultaneous multi-scale processing reduces API overhead and kernel launch latency, while deterministic output ensures reproducibility. Limitations: The O(N^2) linking step is inefficient for large point clouds, and the method requires pre-allocation of memory based on maxvoxels and maxpoints, which can lead to wasted memory if these limits are not tight. When to Use: When a 3D perception network requires multi-scale voxel inputs and deterministic behavior is critical. Not suitable for very large point clouds where the O(N^2) step becomes prohibitive. Multiscale Hard Voxelization was introduced as a CUDA operator to address the inconvenience of invoking single-scale voxelization operators multiple times for different resolutions in 3D perception pipelines. It builds on the work of normal voxelization methods and was implemented to improve speed and convenience. The implementation is based on the mmcv and mmdet open-source codebases. name: Hard Voxelization (Deterministic)
head: Voxelization (mmdet3d.ops.Voxelization), voxel_layer [S3, unofficial]
body: Hard Voxelization (Deterministic) converts an unstructured 3D point cloud into a fixed-size, regular voxel grid by partitioning space into cubic cells, aggregating point attributes within each cell, and outputting a single representative point (typically the centroid) per occupied voxel. It solves the problem of downsampling dense, irregular point clouds into a structured format suitable for efficient neural network processing or volume rendering. Unlike its sibling Fast Deterministic GPU Voxelization (Sort-Scatter), which uses parallel sorting for speed, this method relies on explicit coordinate quantization and unique-coordinate identification to guarantee bit-identical, reproducible output order regardless of hardware execution order. It differs from Grid Pooling (Max Pooling over Points) by computing centroids (averages) rather than maximum values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud dataset containing N points. Each point has spatial coordinates (x, y, z) and optional attributes (features) such as intensity, color, or labels. The input is typically a 2D array of shape (N, 3) or (N, 3+F). Parameters: voxelsize: A scalar or vector [vx, vy, vz] defining the physical dimensions of a voxel. Typical scalar value: 0.5. coorsrange: A bounding box [x{min}, y{min}, z{min}, x{max}, y{max}, z{max}] defining the spatial extent of the grid. If not provided, it is computed from the data. maxpoints: Maximum number of points allowed per voxel. If exceeded, points are dropped or capped. maxvoxels: Maximum number of voxels to create. Points in excess voxels are ignored. Typical value: 20,000. ignorelabel: An integer label value to exclude from aggregation (default: -1). Outputs: voxels: A tensor of shape [M, \text{max\points}, F] containing the aggregated features for M valid voxels. coors: A tensor of shape [M, 3] containing the integer voxel indices (i, j, k) for each valid voxel. numpointspervoxel: A tensor of shape [M] storing the count of points assigned to each voxel. pointtovoxel: A mapping array of length N indicating which voxel index each original point belongs to (or -1 if invalid). Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A dense 3D array of dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Dimensions are calculated as Dx = \max(1, \lceil (x{max} - x{min}) / vx \rceil). Accumulator: For each voxel, a structure stores sums of coordinates and attributes, plus a count integer. In CPU implementations, this is often implicit in temporary arrays vcnt (count) and vsum (sum). In GPU implementations, a Voxel struct contains sumx, sumy, sumz, sumintensity, sumring (floats) and count (int). Algorithm Steps: 1. Validation and Masking: Identify valid points. A point is valid if its coordinates and features are finite. Create a boolean mask finite where finite[i] is true if point i has no NaN or Inf values. Points failing this mask are excluded from aggregation but retain their index in the mapping array, assigned -1. 2. Bounding Box and Grid Dimensions: If coorsrange is not provided, compute it by iterating over all valid points to find x{min}, x{max}, y{min}, y{max}, z{min}, z{max}. Calculate grid dimensions: Dx = \max(1, \lceil \frac{x{max} - x{min}}{vx} \rceil), \quad Dy = \max(1, \lceil \frac{y{max} - y{min}}{vy} \rceil), \quad Dz = \max(1, \lceil \frac{z{max} - z{min}}{vz} \rceil). Note: Some implementations use rounding instead of ceiling. 3. Coordinate Quantization: Map each valid point's continuous coordinates to discrete voxel indices (i, j, k) using floor division relative to the bounding box origin: i = \left\lfloor \frac{x - x{min}}{vx} \right\rfloor, \quad j = \left\lfloor \frac{y - y{min}}{vy} \right\rfloor, \quad k = \left\lfloor \frac{z - z{min}}{vz} \right\rfloor. Points with coordinates outside [x{min}, x{max}] etc. map to indices <0 or \ge D. These are identified as invalid (often mapped to (-1, -1, -1)) and filtered out. 4. Unique Voxel Identification (Deterministic Step): To ensure deterministic output order, identify unique voxel coordinates from the set of mapped indices. Collect all valid voxel indices (i, j, k). Sort them lexicographically (or use a stable unique operation) to find the set of unique voxel coordinates uniquecoors. Generate a mapping array coorsmap of length N, where coorsmap[p] is the index in uniquecoors corresponding to point p's voxel. If point p is invalid, coorsmap[p] = -1. Note: The non-deterministic variant uses atomic operations here, which do not guarantee order. The deterministic variant uses np.unique or at::uniquedim which returns sorted unique values. 5. Feature Aggregation: Aggregate point attributes into the identified voxels. Centroid Calculation: For each voxel, sum the coordinates and features of all points mapping to it, then divide by the count to get the average. Numerical Stability: To prevent overflow when summing large numbers of points, or subnormal erasure when dividing early, use a scaled-mean reduction. 1. Find the maximum absolute feature value maxima for each voxel among its points. 2. Normalize features by dividing by maxima. 3. Accumulate normalized features. 4. Divide accumulated sums by the point count. 5. Rescale by multiplying by maxima. Label Aggregation: If labels are present, determine the majority label for each voxel. On ties, choose the smallest numeric label. 6. Output Construction: Construct the voxels tensor by copying the aggregated features for each unique voxel. Construct the coors tensor from uniquecoors. Construct numpointspervoxel from the counts. Enforce maxpoints and maxvoxels limits. If a voxel has more points than maxpoints, only the first maxpoints (in original order) are stored. If the number of unique voxels exceeds maxvoxels, only the first maxvoxels are kept. Pseudocode (CPU/NumPy Style): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def hardvoxelizedeterministic(points, voxelsize, coorsrange=None, maxpoints=35, maxvoxels=20000): """ points: np.ndarray of shape (N, 3) or (N, 3+F) voxelsize: float or list [vx, vy, vz] coorsrange: list [xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax] Returns: voxels, coors, numpointspervoxel, pointtovoxel """ N, numfeatures = points.shape if isinstance(voxelsize, (int, float)): voxelsize = [voxelsize, voxelsize, voxelsize] # 1. Validate points finitemask = np.isfinite(points).all(axis=1) validpoints = points[finitemask] validindices = np.where(finitemask)[0] if len(validpoints) == 0: return np.array([]), np.array([]), np.array([]), np.full(N, -1, dtype=np.int64) # 2. Compute Bounding Box if not provided if coorsrange is None: coorsrange = [ validpoints[:, 0].min(), validpoints[:, 1].min(), validpoints[:, 2].min(), validpoints[:, 0].max(), validpoints[:, 1].max(), validpoints[:, 2].max() ] xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax = coorsrange vx, vy, vz = voxelsize # 3. Compute Grid Dimensions dimx = max(1, int(np.ceil((xmax - xmin) / vx))) dimy = max(1, int(np.ceil((ymax - ymin) / vy))) dimz = max(1, int(np.ceil((zmax - zmin) / vz))) # 4. Quantize Coordinates # Calculate voxel indices for all valid points # Use float division then floor to int coors = np.floor((validpoints[:,:3] - np.array([xmin, ymin, zmin])) / np.array([vx, vy, vz])).astype(np.int64) # 5. Filter Out-of-Bounds Points # Points outside the grid map to negative or >= dim indices validvoxelmask = ( (coors[:, 0] >= 0) & (coors[:, 0] < dimx) & (coors[:, 1] >= 0) & (coors[:, 1] < dimy) & (coors[:, 2] >= 0) & (coors[:, 2] < dimz)) finalcoors = coors[validvoxelmask] finalvalidindices = validindices[validvoxelmask] finalfeatures = points[validvoxelmask] # Includes all features # 6. Identify Unique Voxels (Deterministic Sorting) # np.unique sorts lexicographically by default uniquecoors, inverseindices, counts = np.unique(finalcoors, axis=0, returninverse=True, returncounts=True) M = len(uniquecoors) if M > maxvoxels: # Keep only first maxvoxels unique voxels keepmask = np.zeros(M, dtype=bool) keepmask[:maxvoxels] = True # Adjust inverseindices for points in dropped voxels # Map dropped voxel indices to -1 droppedvoxelindices = np.where(~keepmask)[0] # Create a map from old unique index to new unique index newinverse = np.where(inverseindices < maxvoxels, inverseindices, -1) inverseindices = newinverse uniquecoors = uniquecoors[:maxvoxels] counts = counts[:maxvoxels] M = maxvoxels # 7. Aggregate Features # Initialize output arrays voxels = np.zeros((M, maxpoints, numfeatures), dtype=points.dtype) numpointspervoxel = np.zeros(M, dtype=np.int32) pointtovoxel = np.full(N, -1, dtype=np.int64) # Map original point indices to voxel indices # inverseindices maps each point in finalcoors to its index in uniquecoors # We need to map back to the original N points # finalvalidindices tells us which original points are in finalcoors # inverseindices tells us which voxel they belong to # Create a mapping from original index to voxel index # Only for valid points that are within bounds pointtovoxel[finalvalidindices] = inverseindices # Aggregate for vidx in range(M): # Get points belonging to this voxel # Find indices in finalcoors where inverseindices == vidx # This is inefficient for large N, but correct for description. # In practice, use np.bincount or scatteradd. mask = (inverseindices == vidx) voxelpoints = finalfeatures[mask] count = len(voxelpoints) if count == 0: continue # Cap points if count > maxpoints: voxelpoints = voxelpoints[:maxpoints] count = maxpoints numpointspervoxel[vidx] = count # Compute centroid (average) # Handle potential division by zero if count is 0 (already handled) avgfeatures = np.mean(voxelpoints, axis=0) voxels[vidx,:count,:] = avgfeatures return voxels, uniquecoors, numpointspervoxel, pointtovoxel A PyTorch-based method that achieves ~100× speedup over sequential CPU implementations while maintaining bit-identical output. It replaces O(N^2) kernels with a parallel pipeline of filtering, coordinate computation, stable sorting, and scattering. It guarantees reproducibility by preserving original point order within voxels via stable sorting, unlike the standard deterministic=False path which uses non-reproducible atomic operations. Aggregates point cloud features into a voxel grid by performing max-pooling within each cell. It differs from Hard Voxelization (Deterministic) by explicitly tracking the index of the point that achieved the maximum value to enable differentiable backpropagation. Generates cropped point cloud datasets by dividing a scene into a grid, applying padding, and precomputing K-nearest neighbor (KNN) relationships for points and voxels. It differs from siblings by precomputing KNN indices and relative coordinates for local feature grouping, rather than just aggregating values. Assigns attribute values to voxel centers by finding the single closest point in the cloud to each voxel center, rather than aggregating all points within the voxel volume. It is chosen when a specific point's value is preferred over an average. Converts points to a sparse voxel grid using hashing, dynamically allocating memory only for occupied voxels. It differs from fixed-grid approaches by avoiding pre-allocated dense memory, chosen when memory efficiency for sparse clouds is critical. Simplifies large point clouds by voxelizing and randomly sampling points within voxels to a target density, followed by re-projecting onto multi-planes. It sets itself apart by introducing probabilistic downsampling based on local density, rather than deterministic retention. Converts points to a fixed-size grid while enforcing strict limits on points per voxel and total voxels via rejection counters and chunk-based memory management. It differs from the standard deterministic variant by explicitly managing capacity constraints for bounded memory usage. A deterministic, CPU-based algorithm using NumPy that converts sparse clouds to dense grids by binning and averaging attributes. It differs from GPU sort-scatter methods by relying on CPU-side sorting and cumulative sums, and from simple hard voxelization by handling attribute averaging and density filtering in a single pass. Converts points to a grid and subsequently removes isolated, non-connected voxels to clean up noise. It extends Hard Voxelization (Deterministic) by adding a topological cleanup phase that eliminates single-voxel artifacts. A faster, non-reproducible variant that uses atomic operations or parallel reductions to assign points to voxels, avoiding the sorting/unique step of the deterministic version. It uses nondisterministicgetassignpos and nondisterministicassignpointvoxel kernels, which are faster but not reproducible. Converts a set of 3D points into a fixed-size voxel grid structure by assigning each point to a discrete voxel based on its coordinates and a specified voxel size and range. It handles duplicate points within the same voxel and limits the number of points per voxel and total voxels. A point cloud refinement algorithm that first coarsens a point cloud by voxel averaging, then removes outliers based on neighbor distance standard deviation, and finally refines positions by averaging neighbors. It uses an N \times N \times N grid partitioning. Time Complexity: O(N) for coordinate mapping and aggregation, where N is the number of points. The deterministic unique-sort step adds a factor related to the number of unique voxels M, typically O(M \log M) or O(M) with hash-based unique. Memory Complexity: O(Dx Dy Dz) for the dense grid if pre-allocated, or O(M) for the output structures where M is the number of occupied voxels. The sparse variant (Voxel Hashing) uses O(M) memory. Performance: Sequential CPU implementations (e.g., using std::unorderedmap) are slow for large N. GPU implementations (CUDA) provide significant speedups, with deterministic sort-scatter methods achieving ~100× speedup over naive CPU while maintaining reproducibility. Strengths: Deterministic output order; simple implementation; suitable for dense grids; handles arbitrary attributes. Limitations: Memory usage grows with grid resolution; empty space is wasted in dense grids; boundary handling requires care. When to Use: When reproducible output order is required for debugging or training stability. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained and the cloud is very sparse (use Voxel Hashing); when speed is critical and determinism is not required (use Non-Deterministic GPU variant). Hard Voxelization is a fundamental technique in point cloud processing, originating from the need to convert unstructured 3D data into a regular grid format for convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and volume rendering. The method is adapted from functions like voxels() originally written by J. Antonio Guzmán Q. for the rTLS package. It is used for benchmarking point cloud downsampling on the nuScenes dataset. head: fast GPU voxelizer, parallel sort + unique + scatter PyTorch path
body: Fast Deterministic GPU Voxelization is a PyTorch-based method for converting 3D point clouds into a fixed-size voxel grid that achieves bit-identical output to a reference C++/CUDA implementation while providing a ~100× speedup. It replaces an O(N^2) sequential CUDA kernel with a parallel pipeline of filtering, coordinate computation, stable sorting, and scattering. Unlike the standard deterministic=False path which relies on non-reproducible atomic operations, this method guarantees reproducibility by preserving original point order within voxels via stable sorting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: points tensor of shape (N, D), where N is the number of points and D \ge 3. rmin and rmax define the bounding box. voxelsize defines the grid resolution. maxvoxels is the global limit on occupied voxels. maxnumpoints is the limit on points per voxel. Outputs: voxels tensor, coors tensor, and numpointspervoxel tensor. Data Structures: points: Float tensor on GPU. inrange: Boolean mask of length N. voxelcoords: Integer tensor of shape (N', 3), where N' is the number of points within the range and valid grid bounds. sortkeys: Integer tensor of shape (N'), representing a linearized voxel index used for sorting. Parameters: voxelsize: Float scalar or vector (vx, vy, vz). rmin, rmax: Float vectors (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}). maxvoxels: Integer. If the number of points M exceeds maxvoxels, the method falls back to the existing C++ op to preserve bit-identity. maxnumpoints: Integer. Maximum points retained per voxel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Range Filtering: Compute a boolean mask for points inside the bounding box. The condition is inclusive of the lower bound and exclusive of the upper bound: pi \in [r{min}, r{max}) for all dimensions. 2. Coordinate Computation: For each point in the filtered set, compute its voxel coordinate c for each dimension d \in \{x, y, z\}: cd = \lfloor \frac{pd - r{min,d}}{vd} + 0.5 \rfloor This formula mirrors the C++ round() behavior exactly. 3. Grid Boundary Validation: Compute the grid dimensions Gd from the configuration. Filter out points where any coordinate cd < 0 or cd \ge Gd. This step is critical to handle non-integer grid sizes or points at the upper bound that might round up to an out-of-bounds index. 4. Linearization: Compute a unique linear key for each valid voxel coordinate to enable sorting. For 3D coordinates (x, y, z) and grid dimensions (W, H, D): key = z \cdot (W \cdot H) + y \cdot W + x This z-major linear key is an internal sort/group key only. 5. Stable Sorting: Sort the points (and their associated data) by the linear key using a stable sort algorithm. This preserves the original relative order of points that map to the same voxel. 6. Grouping and Truncation: Identify unique voxel keys. For each unique voxel, select the first maxnumpoints points from the sorted list. Points beyond this limit are discarded. 7. Scattering: Scatter the selected points into the output voxels tensor, populate coors with the voxel coordinates, and record the count of points per voxel in numpointspervoxel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def voxelizefastgpu(points, rmin, rmax, voxelsize, maxvoxels, maxnumpoints, griddims): """ points: (N, D) float tensor rmin: (3,) float tensor rmax: (3,) float tensor voxelsize: (3,) float tensor maxvoxels: int maxnumpoints: int griddims: (3,) int tensor (W, H, D) """ # 1. Range Filter: inclusive min, exclusive max inrange = torch.all((points[:,:3] >= rmin) & (points[:,:3] < rmax), dim=1) pts = points[inrange] if pts.shape[0] == 0: return torch.empty((0, maxnumpoints, pts.shape[1]), device=pts.device), \ torch.empty((0, 3), dtype=torch.long, device=pts.device), \ torch.empty((0,), dtype=torch.long, device=pts.device) # 2. Compute Voxel Coordinates: floor((p - rmin) / voxelsize + 0.5) coords = torch.floor((pts[:,:3] - rmin) / voxelsize + 0.5).long() # 3. Grid Boundary Validation: keep only 0 <= coord < griddim valid = torch.all((coords >= 0) & (coords < griddims), dim=1) pts = pts[valid] coords = coords[valid] if pts.shape[0] == 0: return torch.empty((0, maxnumpoints, pts.shape[1]), device=pts.device), \ torch.empty((0, 3), dtype=torch.long, device=pts.device), \ torch.empty((0,), dtype=torch.long, device=pts.device) # 4. Linearize Coordinates for Sorting: z (W H) + y W + x W, H, D = griddims keys = coords[:, 2] (W H) + coords[:, 1] W + coords[:, 0] # 5. Stable Sort sortedindices = torch.argsort(keys, stable=True) sortedpts = pts[sortedindices] sortedcoords = coords[sortedindices] sortedkeys = keys[sortedindices] # 6. Identify Unique Voxels and Counts uniquekeys, counts = torch.uniqueconsecutive(sortedkeys, returncounts=True) numvoxels = counts.numel() # Fallback check: if number of points M exceeds maxvoxels, fall back to C++ op if numvoxels > maxvoxels: raise NotImplementedError("Fallback to C++ op required when M > maxvoxels") # 7. Select Points per Voxel (first maxnumpoints) # Calculate start indices for each voxel group in the sorted list startindices = torch.cat([torch.tensor([0], device=counts.device), counts[:-1]]) # Calculate rank of each point within its voxel group ranks = torch.arange(pts.shape[0], device=pts.device) - startindices[torch.searchsorted(uniquekeys, sortedkeys)] # Mask for points to keep keepmask = ranks < maxnumpoints finalpts = sortedpts[keepmask] finalcoords = sortedcoords[keepmask] # 8. Scatter Output voxels = torch.zeros((numvoxels, maxnumpoints, finalpts.shape[1]), device=pts.device) coors = torch.zeros((numvoxels, 3), dtype=torch.long, device=pts.device) numpointspervoxel = torch.zeros((numvoxels,), dtype=torch.long, device=pts.device) # De-linearize unique keys to get x, y, z coordinates coors[:, 2] = uniquekeys // (W H) coors[:, 1] = (uniquekeys % (W H)) // W coors[:, 0] = uniquekeys % W # Fill voxels and counts # Map each kept point to its voxel ID and local rank keptvoxelids = torch.searchsorted(uniquekeys, sortedkeys[keepmask]) keptranks = ranks[keepmask] destindices = keptvoxelids maxnumpoints + keptranks # Flatten voxels for scatter voxelsflat = voxels.view(-1, finalpts.shape[1]) voxelsflat[destindices] = finalpts # Compute actual point counts per voxel numpointspervoxel = torch.bincount(keptvoxelids, minlength=numvoxels).long() return voxels, coors, numpointspervoxel Aggregates features within voxels using max pooling rather than truncation. Chosen when feature preservation is prioritized over strict point count limits. Link Focuses on spatial cropping and neighbor search precomputation rather than the voxelization step itself. Chosen for downstream neighbor queries. Link Time Complexity: O(N \log N) due to the stable sort step, where N is the number of points within the range. This is a significant improvement over the O(N^2) complexity of the reference C++ implementation which scans previous points for rank. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing intermediate tensors (masks, coordinates, keys). Performance: On an NVIDIA H100 with PyTorch 2.12, the method achieves 0.69–0.70 ms per frame for 250k points, compared to 69.8–70.1 ms for the C++ deterministic version, a ~100× speedup. In a full end-to-end training loop, this reduces per-step time from 2.61 s to 0.38 s (~6.9× faster). Strengths: Bit-identical output to the reference implementation; highly parallelizable; reproducible. Limitations: Falls back to the slower C++ implementation if the number of occupied voxels exceeds maxvoxels. Requires PyTorch and CUDA. When to use: BEVFusion training where deterministic, reproducible voxelization is required and performance is critical. When not to use: Deployment scenarios like Autoware which use different voxelizers (e.g., spconv hash voxelizer). The method was introduced in a pull request to the Tier4 AWML repository in June 2026 by Max-Bin. It was developed to address a bottleneck in BEVFusion training, where the existing deterministic CUDA voxelizer was too slow due to its sequential nature. The method leverages PyTorch's built-in sorting and scattering operations to achieve parallelism while maintaining the strict determinism required for reproducible research and training. perf(BEVFusion): faster bit-identical GPU voxelizer (training), https://github.com/tier4/AWML/pull/212, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Grid Pooling (Max Pooling over Points)
head: Point-to-Grid Max Pooling
body: Grid Pooling aggregates point cloud features into a fixed-size 3D voxel grid by performing max-pooling within each grid cell. It maps a set of N points with C-dimensional features to a W \times H \times D grid where each cell stores the maximum feature value among points falling into that cell. It differs from its sibling Hard Voxelization (Deterministic) by explicitly tracking the index of the point that achieved the maximum value to enable differentiable backpropagation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: points tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D coordinates. Input: featpoints tensor of shape (N, C) containing features for each point. Input: shape tensor of shape (3) containing grid dimensions (W, H, D). Input: gridsize float defining the physical size of each grid cell (typically 1.0). Output: featcell tensor of shape (W \times H \times D, C) storing the maximum feature values. Output: indices tensor of shape (W \times H \times D, C) storing the global point index that achieved the max value for each cell and feature channel. Data Structures: featcell: Float tensor, initialized to negative infinity (or zero if features are guaranteed positive, but negative infinity is safer for general max-pooling). indices: Long tensor, initialized to -1 to indicate empty cells or invalid states. Parameters: gridsize: Constant float, typically 1.0. eps: Constant float, typically 10^{-8}, declared for numerical stability in comparisons or divisions, though not explicitly used in the provided CPU implementation snippet. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize featcell with negative infinity and indices with -1 for all cells (i, j, k) where 0 \le i < W, 0 \le j < H, 0 \le k < D. 2. Forward Pass: For each grid cell (i, j, k): a. Identify all points p such that their coordinates (xp, yp, zp) satisfy: i \cdot \text{grid\size} \le xp < (i+1) \cdot \text{grid\size} j \cdot \text{grid\size} \le yp < (j+1) \cdot \text{grid\size} k \cdot \text{grid\size} \le zp < (k+1) \cdot \text{grid\size} Let P{cell} be the set of indices of these points. b. If P{cell} is empty, skip to the next cell. c. For each feature dimension c \in [0, C-1]: i. Find the point p^ \in P{cell} that maximizes featpoints[p, c]. ii. Set featcell[iHD + jD + k, c] = featpoints[p, c]. iii. Set indices[iHD + jD + k, c] = p. 3. Backward Pass: For each grid cell (i, j, k) and feature dimension c: a. Retrieve the stored index p = \text{indices}[i \cdot H \cdot D + j \cdot D + k, c]. b. If p < 0 (empty cell), skip. c. Propagate the gradient from the output gradient tensor gradoutput to the input feature gradient tensor gradfeatpoints: \text{grad\feat\points}[p, c] \leftarrow \text{grad\output}[i \cdot H \cdot D + j \cdot D + k, c] Note: The reference implementation uses an assignment operation (set2d), which overwrites the value. If multiple cells select the same point as their max (due to duplicate points or specific data distributions), only the last processed cell's gradient is retained. Standard max pooling backpropagation should sum gradients for all cells where the point was the max. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def gridpoolingforward(points, featpoints, shape, gridsize=1.0): """ points: Tensor of shape (N, 3) featpoints: Tensor of shape (N, C) shape: Tuple (W, H, D) gridsize: Float Returns: featcell (WHD, C), indices (WHD, C) """ N, C = featpoints.shape W, H, D = shape numcells = W H D # Initialize outputs featcell = torch.full((numcells, C), float('-inf'), dtype=featpoints.dtype, device=featpoints.device) indices = torch.full((numcells, C), -1, dtype=torch.long, device=points.device) for i in range(W): xmin = i gridsize xmax = (i + 1) gridsize for j in range(H): ymin = j gridsize ymax = (j + 1) gridsize for k in range(D): zmin = k gridsize zmax = (k + 1) gridsize cellidx = i H D + j D + k # Find points in this cell inx = (points[:, 0] >= xmin) & (points[:, 0] < xmax) iny = (points[:, 1] >= ymin) & (points[:, 1] < ymax) inz = (points[:, 2] >= zmin) & (points[:, 2] < zmax) mask = inx & iny & inz pointindicesincell = torch.nonzero(mask, astuple=False).squeeze(1) if pointindicesincell.numel() == 0: continue # Get features for these points cellfeatures = featpoints[pointindicesincell] # Max pooling over the point dimension (dim 0) maxvals, maxindiceslocal = torch.max(cellfeatures, dim=0) # Convert local indices to global point indices globalindices = pointindicesincell[maxindiceslocal] # Update output tensors featcell[cellidx,:] = maxvals indices[cellidx,:] = globalindices return featcell, indices def gridpoolingbackward(gradoutput, indices, N): """ gradoutput: Tensor of shape (WHD, C) indices: Tensor of shape (WHD, C) N: int, number of points Returns: gradfeatpoints (N, C) """ gradfeatpoints = torch.zeros((N, gradoutput.shape[1]), dtype=gradoutput.dtype, device=gradoutput.device) # Flatten for easier iteration indicesflat = indices.view(-1) gradflat = gradoutput.view(-1) # The reference implementation uses set2d (overwrite). # We replicate the overwrite behavior exactly as described in the source. validmask = indicesflat >= 0 validindices = indicesflat[validmask] validgrads = gradflat[validmask] # Overwrite: gradfeatpoints[ind] = grad for idx, grad in zip(validindices, validgrads): gradfeatpoints[idx] = grad return gradfeatpoints Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Cells: If no point falls into a grid cell, indices remains -1. The backward pass must check for p < 0 to prevent invalid memory access. Gradient Assignment Pitfall: The reference C implementation uses THFloatTensorset2d, which overwrites the gradient value. If multiple cells select the same point as their max, only the last processed cell's gradient is retained. Standard max pooling backpropagation should sum gradients for all cells where the point was the max. Precision: The eps parameter is declared but not used in the provided CPU snippet. Numerical stability should be ensured in comparisons if features are very close. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot D \cdot P{avg}) for the forward pass, where P{avg} is the average number of points per cell. The backward pass is O(W \cdot H \cdot D \cdot C). Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot D \cdot C) for featcell and indices. Strengths: Differentiable, allowing gradients to flow back to point features. Efficient for sparse point clouds mapped to dense grids. Limitations: The "overwrite" pitfall in the reference implementation can lead to incorrect gradients if not handled. Performance degrades if points are densely clustered in few cells, increasing P{avg}. When to use: When point cloud features need to be aggregated into a voxel grid for subsequent 3D CNN or grid-based processing, and differentiability is required. When not to use: If memory is constrained and the grid is very large, or if non-differentiable aggregation is sufficient. Grid Pooling is used in deep learning architectures for 3D point cloud processing, specifically in methods that combine point-based features with voxel-based representations. yiyiliao/deepmarchingcubes, https://github.com/yiyiliao/deepmarchingcubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Grid-based Scene Cropping with KNN Precomputation
head: scene_crop_pointcloud dataset, voxel KNN grouping
body: This method generates cropped point cloud datasets by dividing a normalized 3D scene into a structured grid, applying padding, and precomputing K-nearest neighbor (KNN) relationships for both input points and grid voxels to facilitate local feature grouping. It solves the problem of preparing fixed-size, spatially coherent data structures with relative coordinate offsets for deep learning models. It differs from its siblings, Fast Deterministic GPU Voxelization (Sort-Scatter) and Grid Pooling (Max Pooling over Points), by explicitly precomputing KNN indices and relative coordinates for both points and voxels within a cropped region. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D points normalized to a unit cube [-1, 1]^3. Outputs: pcKNNidx: 1D array of shape [N{pc} \times K], storing indices of KNN points. pcKNNxyz: 1D array of shape [N{pc} \times K, 3], storing relative coordinates of KNN points to the query point. voxelxyzint: 1D array of shape [N{vox}], storing integer coordinates of active voxels. voxelKNNidx: 1D array of shape [N{vox} \times K], storing indices of KNN points for each active voxel. voxelKNNxyz: 1D array of shape [N{vox} \times K, 3], storing relative coordinates of KNN points to each voxel. Parameters: inputpointnum: Number of points to sample per crop for training. outputgridsize: Base grid resolution per crop dimension (e.g., 32 or 64). KNNnum: Number of nearest neighbors to query (K). poolingradius: Radius for morphological dilation of the voxel grid to expand active cells. blockpadding: Padding added to crop bounds in grid units. Steps: 1. Normalization and Grid Setup: Normalize input points to the unit cube. Scale coordinates by blocknumperdim and multiply by outputgridsize to determine grid dimensions. 2. Crop Extraction: For each grid index (i, j, k), extract points within the bounds defined by the grid cell extended by blockpadding. The condition for a point p to be included in crop (i, j, k) is: \begin{aligned} & i \cdot G - P < px < (i+1) \cdot G + P \\ & j \cdot G - P < py < (j+1) \cdot G + P \\ & k \cdot G - P < pz < (k+1) \cdot G + P \end{aligned} where G is outputgridsize and P is blockpadding. 3. Empty Check: If the number of extracted points is less than 100, return arrays of shape [1] filled with zeros to avoid empty batches. 4. Local Coordinate Shift: Shift extracted points to local coordinates relative to the crop origin. 5. Sampling: Shuffle the extracted points and sample inputpointnum points. 6. Voxel Grid Construction: Create a 3D boolean grid of size outputgridsize. Assign points to voxels by converting their local coordinates to integer indices. 7. Morphological Dilation: Expand the active voxel region using poolingradius. For each iteration in the radius, perform a 3D dilation by OR-ing the grid with its shifted neighbors. 8. KNN Precomputation: Build a KDTree on the sampled points. Query KNN for each sampled point to get pcKNNidx and pcKNNxyz. Query KNN for each active voxel center to get voxelKNNidx and voxelKNNxyz. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.spatial import KDTree def gridbasedscenecropping(points, outputgridsize, KNNnum, poolingradius, blockpadding, inputpointnum): """ points: N x 3 array, normalized to [-1, 1] Returns: pcKNNidx, pcKNNxyz, voxelxyzint, voxelKNNidx, voxelKNNxyz """ # 1. Normalize and Scale (Assuming points are already normalized to [-1,1]) # Scale to grid units. Note: The source implies a specific scaling logic involving blocknumperdim. # For implementation, we assume points are in a space where gridsize defines the resolution. # 2. Extract Crop (Simplified for single crop logic as per source snippet) # Bounds calculation minx = -blockpadding maxx = outputgridsize + blockpadding miny = -blockpadding maxy = outputgridsize + blockpadding minz = -blockpadding maxz = outputgridsize + blockpadding mask = (points[:, 0] > minx) & (points[:, 0] < maxx) & \ (points[:, 1] > miny) & (points[:, 1] < maxy) & \ (points[:, 2] > minz) & (points[:, 2] < maxz) croppoints = points[mask] # 3. Empty Check if len(croppoints) < 100: pcKNNidx = np.zeros(1, dtype=np.int32) pcKNNxyz = np.zeros((1, 3), dtype=np.float32) voxelxyzint = np.zeros(1, dtype=np.int32) voxelKNNidx = np.zeros(1, dtype=np.int32) voxelKNNxyz = np.zeros((1, 3), dtype=np.float32) return pcKNNidx, pcKNNxyz, voxelxyzint, voxelKNNidx, voxelKNNxyz # 4. Local Coordinate Shift localpoints = croppoints - np.array([minx, miny, minz]) # 5. Sampling if len(localpoints) > inputpointnum: indices = np.random.choice(len(localpoints), inputpointnum, replace=False) sampledpoints = localpoints[indices] else: sampledpoints = localpoints # 6. Voxel Grid Construction gridsize = outputgridsize tmpgrid = np.zeros((gridsize, gridsize, gridsize), dtype=np.uint8) # Convert to integer indices and clip to valid array bounds [0, gridsize-1] pcxyzint = np.floor(localpoints).astype(np.int32) pcxyzint[:, 0] = np.clip(pcxyzint[:, 0], 0, gridsize - 1) pcxyzint[:, 1] = np.clip(pcxyzint[:, 1], 0, gridsize - 1) pcxyzint[:, 2] = np.clip(pcxyzint[:, 2], 0, gridsize - 1) # Assign to grid tmpgrid[pcxyzint[:, 0], pcxyzint[:, 1], pcxyzint[:, 2]] = 1 # 7. Morphological Dilation for in range(poolingradius): tmpmask = np.copy(tmpgrid) dilated = np.zeroslike(tmpmask) for i in range(3): for j in range(3): for k in range(3): dilated[i:gridsize-1+i, j:gridsize-1+j, k:gridsize-1+k] |= tmpmask tmpgrid = dilated # Identify active voxels and store as 1D index array to match [numvoxels] shape activevoxels = np.argwhere(tmpgrid > 0) voxelxyzint = activevoxels[:, 0] + activevoxels[:, 1] gridsize + activevoxels[:, 2] gridsize2 # 8. KNN Precomputation tree = KDTree(sampledpoints) distpc, idxpc = tree.query(sampledpoints, k=KNNnum) pcKNNidx = idxpc.flatten() K = KNNnum N = len(sampledpoints) pcKNNxyz = np.zeros((N K, 3), dtype=np.float32) for i in range(N): neighbors = idxpc[i] for k in range(K): neighboridx = neighbors[k] pcKNNxyz[i K + k] = sampledpoints[neighboridx] - sampledpoints[i] voxelcoords3d = np.unravelindex(voxelxyzint, (gridsize, gridsize, gridsize)) voxelcoords3d = np.stack(voxelcoords3d, axis=1).astype(np.float32) distv, idxv = tree.query(voxelcoords3d, k=KNNnum) voxelKNNidx = idxv.flatten() voxelKNNxyz = np.zeros((len(voxelcoords3d) K, 3), dtype=np.float32) for i in range(len(voxelcoords3d)): neighbors = idxv[i] for k in range(K): neighboridx = neighbors[k] voxelKNNxyz[i K + k] = sampledpoints[neighboridx] - voxelcoords3d[i] return pcKNNidx, pcKNNxyz, voxelxyzint, voxelKNNidx, voxelKNNxyz This method originates from the NDC (Neural Distance Field) project, specifically the scenecroppointcloud dataset generation code. It is designed to facilitate the training of neural networks for 3D shape representation by providing structured local patches with precomputed neighbor relationships. czq142857/NDC, https://github.com/czq142857/NDC, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Nearest Neighbour Interpolation for Voxelization
head: KDTree-based nearest neighbour voxelization
body: This method assigns attribute values (e.g., intensity, color) to voxel centers by identifying the single closest point in the original point cloud to each voxel center, rather than aggregating all points within the voxel volume. It is used when a specific point's value is preferred over an average, distinguishing it from histogramming methods that sum or average all points falling within a voxel. It builds on Hard Voxelization (Deterministic) by replacing volume-based aggregation with spatial nearest-neighbor lookup. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud array ar of shape (N, 4) containing coordinates (x, y, z) and an attribute value (e.g., amplitude/intensity) in the 4th column. A voxel grid structure vxl of shape (4, n, m, p) containing the coordinates of the voxel centers in the first three dimensions. A voxel width vwidth. Output: An array pntofs of shape (4, n, m, p) where the first three dimensions are the voxel coordinates and the fourth dimension contains the interpolated attribute values. Data Structures: ar: 2D NumPy array. Columns 0, 1, 2 are x, y, z. Column 3 is the attribute a. vxl: 4D NumPy array. vxl[0], vxl[1], vxl[2] are 3D arrays of shape (n, m, p) representing the x, y, z coordinates of each voxel center. vxl[3] is the target for attribute storage. tree: A KDTree data structure built from the point cloud coordinates. Parameters: vwidth: The side length of a voxel. In the source example, 0.7 is used. Steps: 1. Extract coordinates and attributes from the input point cloud ar. x = ar[:, 0], \quad y = ar[:, 1], \quad z = ar[:, 2], \quad a = ar[:, 3] 2. Construct a KDTree from the point cloud coordinates. \text{tree} = \text{cKDTree}(\text{np.c\}[x, y, z]) 3. Flatten the voxel center coordinate arrays to query all voxel centers at once. \text{centers} = \text{np.c\}[ \text{vxl}[0].\text{ravel}(), \text{vxl}[1].\text{ravel}(), \text{vxl}[2].\text{ravel}() ] 4. Query the KDTree for the nearest neighbor (k=1) to each voxel center. dd, ii = \text{tree.query}(\text{centers}, k=1) Where dd is the distance to the nearest neighbor and ii is the index of the nearest neighbor in the original point cloud. 5. Filter out points that are too far away. If the distance dd is greater than or equal to half the voxel width (vwidth/2), the point is considered too distant to represent the voxel center reliably. Set the corresponding attribute values to NaN. a[ii[dd \ge vwidth/2]] = \text{np.nan} 6. Reshape the retrieved attribute values to match the voxel grid shape. \text{vann} = a[ii].\text{reshape}(\text{vxl}[0].\text{shape}) 7. Stack the voxel coordinates and the interpolated attribute values into the output array. \text{pnt\ofs} = \text{np.stack}((\text{vxl}[0], \text{vxl}[1], \text{vxl}[2], \text{vann})) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.spatial import cKDTree def nearestneighbourvoxelization(ar, vxl, vwidth): """ Assigns attribute values to voxel centers using nearest neighbour interpolation. Parameters: ar: numpy.ndarray, shape (N, 4) Point cloud data. Columns 0-2 are x, y, z coordinates. Column 3 is the attribute. vxl: numpy.ndarray, shape (4, n, m, p) Voxel grid structure. vxl[0], vxl[1], vxl[2] are the x, y, z coordinates of voxel centers. vwidth: float The width (side length) of a voxel. Returns: pntofs: numpy.ndarray, shape (4, n, m, p) Voxel grid with interpolated attributes in the 4th dimension. """ # 1. Extract coordinates and attributes x = ar[:, 0] y = ar[:, 1] z = ar[:, 2] a = ar[:, 3] # 2. Construct KDTree tree = cKDTree(np.c[x, y, z]) # 3. Flatten voxel centers voxelcenters = np.c[vxl[0].ravel(), vxl[1].ravel(), vxl[2].ravel()] # 4. Query nearest neighbor dd, ii = tree.query(voxelcenters, k=1) # 5. Filter by distance threshold # Points further than half voxel width are set to NaN a[ii[dd >= vwidth / 2]] = np.nan # 6. Reshape attributes to voxel grid shape vann = a[ii].reshape(vxl[0].shape) # 7. Stack coordinates and attributes pntofs = np.stack((vxl[0], vxl[1], vxl[2], vann)) return pntofs Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distance Threshold: The threshold vwidth/2 is critical. Points exactly at the boundary are excluded. If the point cloud is sparse, many voxels may become NaN. Precision: Floating-point precision in distance calculations may affect which point is selected as the nearest neighbor in dense regions. Empty Voxels: Voxels with no points within vwidth/2 will have NaN values. Downstream processing must handle NaN appropriately. A technique where tiny dots of density and color are baked into a voxel grid one by one using antialiasing by smearing the dot across eight neighboring voxels. For a dot at position x{dot} with density \rho{dot} and color c{dot}, the 8 nearest voxels are identified by indices \{x{abc} | a=i, i+1, b=j, j+1, c=k, k+1\} where (i,j,k) is the voxel index containing x{dot}. The density and color are updated using trilinear interpolation weights \omega{abc}: \rho{abc} += \rho{dot} \cdot \omega{abc} c{abc} += c{dot} \cdot \omega{abc} This method is used in the 'Steps to Grow Point Wisps' algorithm to bake particle density and color into a voxel grid. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This method is described in the context of point cloud voxelization using Python (numpy & scipy). It is presented as a simple alternative to histogramming for assigning attribute values (like intensity) to voxel grids. The approach leverages the scipy.spatial.cKDTree for efficient nearest neighbor search. name: Point Cloud Voxelization via Discretization and Accumulation
head: Coverage Estimation and View Frustum Construction, LiDAR Point Cloud Voxelization, MATLAB voxel grid conversion, Sparse SfM Point Voxelization, Voxel-based Urban Vegetation Volume Analysis, binary occupancy grid from point cloud
body: This method converts an irregular 3D point cloud into a structured, binary 3D volume model (occupancy grid) by discretizing point coordinates into a regular grid and marking voxels as occupied if they contain at least one point. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on direct coordinate binning and accumulation to produce a binary occupancy map, rather than storing feature vectors or using sorting-based parallelization. It serves as a foundational step for spatial analysis and volume calculation, such as urban vegetation modeling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An N \times 3 matrix xyz containing (X, Y, Z) coordinates for N points. Input: A scalar voxelsize defining the cubic voxel edge length (e.g., 0.5 or 1.0). Output: A 3D binary logical array V where V(i,j,k) = 1 if occupied and 0 otherwise. Data Structures: xyz: N \times 3 floating-point matrix. V: 3D logical array of dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz derived from coordinate ranges and voxelsize. Parameters: voxelsize: Physical voxel edge length; typical values are 0.5 or 1.0. (X{min}, Y{min}, Z{min}): Minimum coordinates of the point cloud along each axis, establishing the voxel coordinate system origin. Steps: 1. Establish Coordinate System: Determine the minimum coordinates of the point cloud: X{min} = \min(X), Y{min} = \min(Y), Z{min} = \min(Z). The method ensures resulting voxel indices are non-negative. 2. Discretize Coordinates: For each dimension d \in \{X, Y, Z\}: extract the coordinate column tmp; define bin edges starting at \min(tmp), stepping by voxelsize, and ending at \max(tmp) + \text{voxelsize}; convert continuous coordinates to discrete bin indices using i = \text{Int}((X - X{min}) / \Delta i), j = \text{Int}((Y - Y{min}) / \Delta j), k = \text{Int}((Z - Z{min}) / \Delta k). Here \Delta i = \Delta j = \Delta k = \text{voxelsize}, and \text{Int}(\cdot) performs truncation towards zero (floor for non-negative values). 3. Accumulate and Threshold: Count the number of points assigned to each discrete bin index; threshold the counts to create a binary occupancy grid where V = 1 if count > 0 and 0 otherwise. 4. Visualization (Optional): Display the resulting binary volume V using a volume viewer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def pointcloudvoxelization(xyz: np.ndarray, voxelsize: float) -> np.ndarray: """ Convert a 3D point cloud to a binary voxel grid via discretization and accumulation. Args: xyz: (N, 3) array of point coordinates. voxelsize: Side length of the cubic voxels. Returns: V: 3D binary numpy array representing the voxel grid. """ if voxelsize <= 0: raise ValueError("voxelsize must be positive") mincoords = np.min(xyz, axis=0) indices = np.floor((xyz - mincoords) / voxelsize).astype(int) gridshape = np.max(indices, axis=0) + 1 V = np.zeros(gridshape, dtype=bool) V[tuple(indices.T)] = True return V Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point errors in coordinate calculations can cause points on voxel boundaries to be assigned to incorrect bins. Memory Usage: The output grid size scales with the bounding box range divided by voxelsize. Resolution Trade-off: High-resolution models (small voxelsize) provide detailed information but are slower for calculation and visual processing, whereas low-resolution models have fast response times but less detail. Negative Coordinates: The formula (X - X{min}) ensures non-negative numerators, guaranteeing non-negative voxel indices. Time Complexity: O(N) for discretization and accumulation, where N is the number of points. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the output grid, where V = Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Strengths: Deterministic; produces a clean binary occupancy grid suitable for volume calculations. Limitations: Does not preserve point attributes (e.g., intensity, color); memory usage scales with the bounding box size and inverse voxel size. When to use: When a binary occupancy representation is needed for volume analysis or as input for further voxel-based processing. When not to use: When preserving point features is required or when the scene is extremely large and sparse. This method originates from applications in urban vegetation analysis using LiDAR point clouds, where converting irregular point data into a structured 3D volume model facilitates spatial analysis and volume calculation. It is also commonly implemented in MATLAB environments for converting laser scanner point clouds into voxel grids for visualization and further processing. The approach relies on basic discretization and accumulation techniques, which are standard in computational geometry for converting continuous data to discrete grids.
