body: Farthest Point Sampling Initialization is a method for selecting a subset of points from a point cloud such that they are maximally spread out in Euclidean space, ensuring maximum spatial coverage. It serves as the primary initialization step for primitive positions in neural rendering representations, replacing simpler nearest-neighbor heuristics to prevent the formation of overly small primitives. It implements the iterative selection logic and CUDA-optimized kernel calls required to generate the initial set of indices. It builds on Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) by applying the iterative farthest-point selection strategy specifically to initialize primitive positions. Inputs: xyz: A tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the coordinates of N points in 3D space. offset: An integer array of shape (B+1) defining the start and end indices for B batches in xyz. newoffset: An integer array of shape (B+1) defining the output boundaries for the sampled points. tmp: A temporary float array of shape (B, n{max}) initialized to a large value (10^{10}) to track minimum distances. Outputs: idx: An integer array of shape (M) containing the indices of the M sampled points. Shared Memory (CUDA): dists[blocksize]: Float array storing the best (maximum) distance found by each thread. distsi[blocksize]: Integer array storing the corresponding point index for the best distance. Block Size: The number of threads per block, passed as a template parameter to the CUDA kernel. Supported values are powers of 2 from 2 to 1024. 1. Batch Processing Setup: Extract batch size B and point count N. Reshape xyz to 2D (B \times N, 3) and ensure it is contiguous. Compute cumulative offsets for input and output batches. Determine n{max}, the maximum number of points in any single batch, by iterating through offset. 2. Initialization: Initialize tmp with large values (10^{10}) to represent infinity. For each batch b: Initialize the first sampled index to the first point of the current batch (idx[startm] = startn). Set the reference point old to the coordinates of this first point. 3. Iterative Selection (CUDA Kernel furthestsamplingcudakernel): For each subsequent sample j from startm + 1 to endm: Distance Update: Threads iterate over all points k in the current batch. Compute squared Euclidean distance d between point k and the last selected point old. Update tmp[k] to store the minimum distance from point k to any selected point so far: tmp[k] = \min(d, tmp[k]) Local Maximum Finding: Each thread finds the local maximum best and corresponding index besti among its assigned points where tmp[k] > best. Parallel Reduction: Use shared memory arrays dists and distsi to combine local maxima into a global maximum. Perform a series of update calls, halving the active thread count (e.g., 1024 \to 512 \to... \to 1). The update device function compares two entries in the shared memory arrays and keeps the one with the larger distance value. Selection: The index of the farthest point found (distsi[0]) is stored in idx[j]. Update old to the coordinates of the newly selected point for the next iteration. 4. Completion: Return idx as long integers. The index of the i-th sampled point Ii is computed as: Ii = \arg \max{k \notin \{I0, \dots, I{i-1}\}} \min{0 \le j < i} d(xk, x{Ij}) where d is the Euclidean distance metric. Number of Samples (K): The total number of points to select, determined by the output size M. Block Size: Powers of 2 from 2 to 1024. Batch Boundaries: The algorithm must correctly handle variable batch sizes by using offset and newoffset arrays. Precision: Squared Euclidean distance is used to avoid square root computations during the inner loop, which is standard for distance comparisons. Initialization: The first point is arbitrarily chosen as the first point in the batch (startn), which may bias the sampling if the input order is not random. In practice, shuffling the input points before initialization is recommended to mitigate this bias. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def farthestpointsamplinginitialization(xyz, offset, newoffset): """ Implements Farthest Point Sampling Initialization for batched point clouds. Args: xyz: List of lists or array of shape (N, 3) containing point coordinates. offset: List of shape (B+1) defining batch boundaries in xyz. newoffset: List of shape (B+1) defining output boundaries. Returns: idx: List of shape (M) containing sampled indices. """ B = len(offset) - 1 nmax = max(offset[b+1] - offset[b] for b in range(B)) tmp = [[1e10] nmax for in range(B)] M = newoffset[B] - newoffset[0] idx = [0] M for b in range(B): startn = offset[b] endn = offset[b+1] startm = newoffset[b] endm = newoffset[b+1] nbatch = endn - startn idx[startm] = startn oldpoint = xyz[startn] for j in range(startm + 1, endm): dists = [] for k in range(nbatch): p = xyz[startn + k] d = (p[0] - oldpoint[0])2 + (p[1] - oldpoint[1])2 + (p[2] - oldpoint[2])2 dists.append(d) for k in range(nbatch): tmp[b][k] = min(dists[k], tmp[b][k]) bestdist = -1.0 bestidxlocal = -1 for k in range(nbatch): if tmp[b][k] > bestdist: bestdist = tmp[b][k] bestidxlocal = k idx[j] = startn + bestidxlocal oldpoint = xyz[startn + bestidxlocal] return idx A complementary method where the scale of each primitive is initialized based on distances to its nearest neighbors in the FPS-ordered point cloud, creating a hierarchy where early points are larger. FPS initialization is often used in conjunction with densification strategies in 3D Gaussian Splatting to manage point cloud density during optimization. Time Complexity: O(k \cdot n) per batch, where k is the number of sampled points and n is the number of points in the batch. Each sampling step requires O(n) for distance calculation and O(\log(\text{block\size})) for reduction. Memory Complexity: O(n{max}) for the temporary distance array tmp per batch, where n{max} is the maximum number of points in any batch. Strengths: Ensures uniform spatial coverage of the point cloud, which is critical for initializing neural rendering primitives to avoid artifacts and ensure stable optimization. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large point clouds due to the iterative nature. Farthest Point Sampling was introduced as a method for uniformly subsampling point clouds. It has been adopted in neural rendering techniques such as Nexels, where it is used to initialize the positions of neurally-textured surfels, replacing simpler nearest-neighbor initialization methods that can lead to small, inefficient primitives. The CUDA implementation described in the sources is part of the 4D Gaussian Splatting framework, which extends 3D Gaussian Splatting to dynamic scenes. body: Voxel Downsampling Registration aligns a source point cloud to a target point cloud by first reducing point density via voxel grid sampling and then applying Iterative Closest Point (ICP). It differs from standard ICP by incorporating a voxel-based spatial reduction step before correspondence matching. It builds on Point Cloud Cropping and Downsampling for the spatial reduction step. Inputs: Source point cloud Ps. Target (ground truth) point cloud Pt. Crop volume V (bounding box or region of interest). Voxel size dv. ICP distance threshold \tau. Initial transformation matrix T{init} (typically 4 \times 4 identity or a coarse estimate). Maximum ICP iterations N{max}. Convergence tolerance \epsilon = 10^{-6}. Outputs: Final transformation matrix T{final} that aligns Ps to Pt. Registration result object containing convergence metrics. Data Structures: Point Cloud: List of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). Voxel Grid: Implicit hash map or 3D array mapping voxel indices (i, j, k) to a single representative point (centroid or first point) from the input cloud. Transformation Matrix: 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrix. Steps: 1. Configuration: If verbose mode is enabled, print dv and \tau, and set library verbosity to Debug. 2. Source Downsampling: Apply voxel downsampling to Ps using V and dv, optionally applying T{init} during the crop/downsample operation if the source needs pre-alignment before voxelization. Let the result be P's. 3. Target Downsampling: Apply voxel downsampling to Pt using V and dv. Let the result be P't. Note that T{init} is not applied to the target in the standard workflow. 4. ICP Execution: Run ICP between P's and P't using threshold \tau, initial guess I (identity matrix), point-to-point distance metric, convergence tolerance \epsilon = 10^{-6}, and max iterations N{max}. Let the resulting transformation be T{icp}. 5. Transformation Composition: Combine the ICP result with the initial transformation: T{final} = T{icp} \times T{init}. 6. Return: Return T{final} and registration statistics. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def voxeldownsamplingregistration(source, target, cropvolume, voxelsize, threshold, inittrans, maxitr): # Step 1: Configuration # If verbose: print(voxelsize, threshold) # Set library verbosity to Debug # Step 2: Downsample source sourcedown = voxeldownsample(source, cropvolume, voxelsize, inittrans) # Step 3: Downsample target targetdown = voxeldownsample(target, cropvolume, voxelsize, None) # Step 4: Perform ICP reg = icpregistration(sourcedown, targetdown, threshold, np.identity(4), maxitr, 1e-6) # Step 5: Update transformation finaltransformation = np.matmul(reg.transformation, inittrans) # Step 6: Return return finaltransformation, reg def voxeldownsample(points, cropvolume, voxelsize, trans): # Apply transformation if provided if trans is not None: points = (trans @ np.vstack([points.T, np.ones(len(points))]))[:3].T # Filter by crop volume (axis-aligned bounding box) minpt, maxpt = cropvolume.min, cropvolume.max mask = np.all((points >= minpt) & (points <= maxpt), axis=1) points = points[mask] # Map to voxel grid and compute centroids voxelindices = np.floor((points - minpt) / voxelsize).astype(int) uniqueindices, inverse = np.unique(voxelindices, axis=0, returninverse=True) centroids = np.array([points[inverse == i].mean(axis=0) for i in range(len(uniqueindices))]) return centroids def icpregistration(src, tgt, threshold, initT, maxitr, tol): # Standard point-to-point ICP loop T = initT.copy() srctransformed = src @ T[:3,:3].T + T[:3, 3] for in range(maxitr): # Find correspondences within threshold dists = np.linalg.norm(srctransformed[:, None,:] - tgt[None,:,:], axis=2) mindists = np.min(dists, axis=1) corrindices = np.argmin(dists, axis=1) if np.all(mindists > threshold): break # Point-to-point least squares (SVD) A = srctransformed B = tgt[corrindices] centroidA = A.mean(axis=0) centroidB = B.mean(axis=0) H = (A - centroidA).T @ (B - centroidB) U,, Vt = np.linalg.svd(H) R = Vt.T @ U.T if np.linalg.det(R) < 0: Vt[-1,:] = -1 R = Vt.T @ U.T t = centroidB - R @ centroidA T[:3,:3] = R T[:3, 3] = t srctransformed = src @ R.T + t if np.linalg.norm(t) < tol: break class RegResult: def init(self, transformation): self.transformation = transformation return RegResult(T) Parameters: voxelsize: The side length of the voxel grid. Required. threshold: The maximum distance for point correspondences in ICP. maxitr: Maximum number of ICP iterations. inittrans: Initial 4 \times 4 transformation matrix. Edge Cases: Degenerate input (empty point clouds) after downsampling will cause ICP to fail. Selects points based on geometric spread rather than grid occupancy. body: Removes statistical outliers from a point cloud to clean noise and artifacts. It sets itself apart from sibling downsampling methods by focusing on geometric consistency and local density statistics rather than spatial coverage or surface complexity Parent. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud P = \{p1, p2, \dots, pN\} where each pi \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output: A filtered point cloud P' \subseteq P containing only inliers. Data Structures: The point cloud is stored as an array of 3D coordinates. For each point, the Euclidean distances to its k nearest neighbors are computed and stored in a list. Parameters: k (nbneighbors): Number of neighboring points considered for statistical analysis. Default: 20. stdratio: Standard deviation ratio threshold for outlier removal. Default: 10. In specific implementations (e.g., EVolSplat), stdratio is set to 2.0. Algorithm Steps: 1. For each point pi in P, find the k nearest neighbors. 2. Compute the mean distance \mui for point pi as the average of the distances to its k nearest neighbors: \mui = \frac{1}{k} \sum{j \in \text{neighbors}(pi)} \| pi - pj \|2 3. Compute the global mean \mu and global standard deviation \sigma of all \mui values across the entire point cloud: \mu = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \mui \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (\mui - \mu)^2} 4. Identify outliers: A point pi is considered an outlier if its mean neighbor distance \mui exceeds the threshold: \mui > \mu + \text{std\ratio} \cdot \sigma 5. Remove all identified outliers from P to produce P'. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def removestatisticaloutliers(points, nbneighbors=20, stdratio=10.0): """ Remove statistical outliers from a point cloud. Args: points: numpy array of shape (N, 3) containing 3D coordinates. nbneighbors: int, number of neighbors for distance calculation. stdratio: float, standard deviation ratio threshold. Returns: filteredpoints: numpy array of shape (M, 3) with outliers removed. """ if len(points) == 0: return points # Compute pairwise Euclidean distances # points shape: (N, 3) # distances shape: (N, N) diff = points[:, np.newaxis,:] - points[np.newaxis,:,:] distances = np.linalg.norm(diff, axis=2) # For each point, find the k nearest neighbors (excluding itself) # distances[i, i] is 0.0, so we sort and take indices 1 to k k = nbneighbors neighbordistances = np.sort(distances, axis=1)[:, 1:k+1] # Calculate mean distance to neighbors for each point meandistances = np.mean(neighbordistances, axis=1) # Calculate global mean and standard deviation of these mean distances globalmean = np.mean(meandistances) globalstd = np.std(meandistances) # Define threshold and filter points threshold = globalmean + stdratio globalstd inliersmask = meandistances <= threshold filteredpoints = points[inliersmask] return filteredpoints Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues may arise if the point cloud contains points at vastly different scales or densities. The method assumes a roughly uniform local density; highly non-uniform distributions may cause inconsistent filtering. A deep learning-based denoiser for 3D point clouds that identifies optimal fitting regions for each point by aligning outlier clusters with a predicted score function using gradient ascent. The workflow comprises: 1. Score estimation network; 2. Objective function for training the network; 3. Score-based denoising algorithm. The process employs a gradient ascent method to align clusters of outliers with a predicted score function. The approach mimics an intelligent smoothing process on potential surfaces, relying on a majority voting mechanism (or the density/magnitude of points). The algorithm smooths the point cloud and rearranges the position of points to increase accuracy with the original object. By adapting the points on an ideal surface, cancelling the ones too far from it. Comparison metric: C2C (Cloud-to-Cloud) signed distances, which looks for the nearest points and makes a comparison. In 3DGS-to-PC, the filter is applied after point cloud generation to clean noise. Strengths: Simple, fast, and effective for removing isolated noise and floaters. name: Statistical Outlier Removal
head: Open3D Statistical Outlier Removal, Outlier Vertex Removal, Outlier Vertex Removal and Poisson Surface Reconstruction, Point Cloud Denoising
body: Statistical Outlier Removal identifies and removes outlier vertices in a point cloud based on their proximity to other vertices. It solves the problem of unwanted points (e.g., backgrounds or floors) being incorporated into generated meshes during point cloud to mesh conversion. Unlike sibling methods such as Fuzzy Projection Ranking that rely on learned opacity or fixed distance metrics, this method leverages local neighborhood density statistics Parent. Inputs: A point cloud P = \{p1, p2,..., pN\} where each pi \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: A cleaned point cloud P{clean} \subset P. Parameters: k: Number of nearest neighbors to consider for statistical analysis. specifies K=64. \sigma{threshold}: Standard deviation threshold multiplier for outlier removal. Determined heuristically via experimentation. Data Structures: Array of mean distances D of size N. Steps: 1. For each point pi \in P, compute the Euclidean distance to all other points in P. 2. Sort the distances and calculate the mean distance \bar{d}i from pi to its k nearest neighbors. 3. Compute the global mean \muD and population standard deviation \sigmaD of all values in D. 4. Identify outliers: A point pi is an outlier if \bar{d}i > \muD + \sigma{threshold} \cdot \sigmaD. 5. Remove all identified outliers from P to form P{clean}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def statisticaloutlierremoval(points, k, sigmathreshold): """ points: List of 3D coordinates (N, 3) k: Number of nearest neighbors sigmathreshold: Standard deviation threshold multiplier Returns: Cleaned points list """ n = len(points) if n == 0: return [] k = min(k, n - 1) meandistances = [] # Compute mean distance to k nearest neighbors for each point for i in range(n): dists = [] for j in range(n): if i == j: continue dx = points[i][0] - points[j][0] dy = points[i][1] - points[j][1] dz = points[i][2] - points[j][2] dists.append(math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz)) dists.sort() knearest = dists[:k] meand = sum(knearest) / len(knearest) meandistances.append(meand) # Calculate global statistics muD = sum(meandistances) / n variance = sum((d - muD)2 for d in meandistances) / n sigmaD = math.sqrt(variance) # Identify and remove outliers threshold = muD + sigmathreshold sigmaD cleanedpoints = [points[i] for i in range(n) if meandistances[i] <= threshold] return cleanedpoints Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: Points on the boundary of the object may have larger distances to their neighbors, potentially being incorrectly removed if k is not chosen carefully. Degenerate Input: If the point cloud is too sparse or contains fewer than k+1 points, the statistical distribution becomes ill-defined. Alpha-based Point Cleaning is a post-processing and iterative optimization strategy used in neural point rendering to remove outlier points from a point cloud based on their learned opacity (alpha) values. It solves the problem of noisy initial reconstructions (e.g., from COLMAP) or spurious points generated during training (e.g., from spawning mechanisms) by explicitly identifying points with low confidence. Unlike sibling methods that rely on geometric density or distance metrics, this method leverages the neural optimization process itself, where valid geometry converges to high opacity while outliers converge to zero. It is a child of Statistical Outlier Removal, specifically utilizing the alpha parameter rather than statistical distance Parent. Point Cloud Regularization is a post-processing pipeline applied to an initial colored point cloud to remove noise, duplicates, and outliers before training a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. It solves the problem of unreliable initialization caused by merging Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points with lightweight 3DGS primitive centers, which introduces depth ambiguity, duplicated points from densification, and unstable tracks. It sets itself apart from its sibling Alpha-based Point Cleaning by explicitly enforcing multi-view consistency and geometric normal agreement rather than relying solely on alpha-blending reliability metrics. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with point count for the distance computation phase, though the naive implementation is O(N^2). Strengths: Effective at removing isolated noise points and background artifacts. Simple to implement. Limitations: Requires heuristic tuning of parameters (k, \sigma{threshold}). May remove valid points in sparse regions. When to use: When preprocessing point clouds for mesh generation to remove background noise. When not: When preserving sparse but valid geometry is critical, or when computational resources are extremely limited. The method was used to circumvent the inclusion of unwanted points (backgrounds or floors) in generated meshes during point cloud to mesh conversion. The values of the thresholds were determined heuristically via experimentation. It is also referenced in the context of point cloud denoising for neural radiance field editing, where K=64 is used for nearest neighbor distance calculation. name: Alpha-based Point Cleaning
head: Alpha Threshold Cleaning, Point Cleaning
body: Alpha-based Point Cleaning is a procedure to remove outlier points from a point cloud based on a threshold applied to their learned opacity (alpha) values. It solves the problem of noisy initial reconstructions (e.g., from COLMAP) or spurious points generated during training (e.g., from spawning mechanisms) by explicitly identifying points with low confidence. It is a child of Statistical Outlier Removal Parent, specifically utilizing a learned alpha threshold rather than statistical distance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud P where each point pi has a position, color, and an opacity value \alphai (confidence). Output: A filtered subset P' \subset P containing only points with \alphai \ge T. Data Structures: The point cloud is stored as a list or array of structures. Each element contains: position: 3D vector (x, y, z). color: 3D vector (r, g, b). alpha: Scalar float in [0, 1], representing the point's opacity or confidence. Exact sizes and bit packing are Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. During neural rendering optimization, the opacity \alphai of each point is adapted. 2. At intervals of E{clean} epochs, iterate through all points pi in the active cloud. 3. For each point, check if \alphai < T. 4. Mark points satisfying the condition as outliers. 5. Remove all marked outliers from the active point cloud. 6. Repeat steps 2–5 throughout training; the final rendering uses only opaque points. Formulas: Outlier condition: \alphai < T. Final rendering mask: points are included only if \alphai \ge T. Parameters: T: The alpha threshold. The default value used in the source is 0.3. E{clean}: The frequency of cleaning steps during training. The source recommends removing points every 50 epochs for faster training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: On the Opera scene, COLMAP places points originating from water incorrectly on land; the cleaning strategy provides great cleanup in these water areas. On the Playground scene, adding one million additional random points results in a final point cloud with almost no visible outliers after cleaning. A threshold of 0.3 works well across tested scenes, removing most outliers while leaving room for variance during training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def alphabasedpointcleaning(points, threshold=0.3, currentepoch=0, cleaninterval=50): if currentepoch % cleaninterval != 0: return points cleaned = [] for p in points: if p.alpha >= threshold: cleaned.append(p) return cleaned This variant explicitly defines the threshold T as a configurable parameter for controlling the trade-off between point cloud size and rendering quality. It sets apart from its siblings by providing empirical data on how varying T affects metrics like LPIPS and PSNR. It is chosen when one needs to aggressively reduce point cloud size or fine-tune the balance between detail and noise. Definition: In every cleaning step, points with confidence below a threshold T are removed. Parameter: T is the confidence threshold. The default used in experiments is 0.3, which causes point clouds to be similarly sized as the initial COLMAP reconstruction. Thresholds up to 0.9 still provide reasonable results and reduce point cloud size significantly. Performance Data (Garden Scene, 7.8M initial points): T=0.30: 7.3M points, LPIPS 0.178, PSNR 23.70. T=0.90: 2.6M points, LPIPS 0.200, PSNR 23.44. T=0.99: 0.1M points, LPIPS 0.446, PSNR 19.08. Link: Alpha-based Point Cleaning Time Complexity: O(N) per cleaning step, where N is the number of points. Cleaning is performed every 50 epochs, accelerating subsequent training iterations. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the point cloud. Cleaning reduces N, significantly reducing point cloud size. Measured Performance: On the Garden scene, cleaning with T=0.3 reduced points from 7.8M to 7.3M with negligible impact on PSNR (23.70) and LPIPS (0.178). On the Playground scene, adding 1 million random outliers resulted in a final cloud with almost no visible outliers after cleaning. On the Opera scene, it effectively cleaned up water-area artifacts from COLMAP. Strengths: Explicitly leverages neural optimization to distinguish geometry from noise; effective against environment sphere artifacts and spawning outliers. Limitations: Requires the optimization process to have converged sufficiently for alpha values to be meaningful; aggressive thresholds (T > 0.9) can degrade rendering quality significantly (e.g., PSNR drop to 19.08 at T=0.99). Alpha-based Point Cleaning was introduced in the VET (Visual Error Tomography) paper by Linus Franke et al.. It is part of a pipeline that combines neural rendering with point cloud completion. The method builds on the observation that outlier points receive low or zero opacity during the optimization of point-based neural rendering. name: Point Cloud Regularization
head: Multi-view Reliability Filtering and K-means Regularization
body: Point Cloud Regularization is a post-processing pipeline applied to an initial colored point cloud to remove noise, duplicates, and outliers before training a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. It solves the problem of unreliable initialization caused by merging Structure-from-Motion (SfM) points with lightweight 3DGS primitive centers, which introduces depth ambiguity, duplicated points from densification, and unstable tracks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An initial colored point cloud P{init} = \{(Xk, Ck)\}, formed by the union of SfM points P0 and lightweight 3DGS primitive centers P1. Each point Xk has a 3D position and color Ck. Output: A regularized point cloud P{final} containing only geometrically consistent and reliable points. Data Structures: P{init}: Set of points with position X \in \mathbb{R}^3 and color C. P{sv}: Subset of P{init} supported by a single camera view. P{mv}: Subset of P{init} supported by multiple camera views. P{filter}: Intermediate point cloud after single-view filtering. P{clu}: Intermediate point cloud after clustering-based denoising. Nk: Set of 10 nearest neighbors of point Xk in Euclidean space. Parameters: K = 1000: Number of clusters for K-means. \alpha = 0.20: Fraction of single-view points to retain (top 20%). \beta = 0.30: Fraction of points to retain within each cluster (nearest 30%). \tau{cos} = 0.2: Threshold for mean cosine similarity of normals. k{nn} = 10: Number of neighbors for normal estimation. Steps: 1. Single-view Point Filtering: Split P{init} into single-view supported points P{sv} and multi-view supported points P{mv} based on camera projection. For each point X \in P{sv}, compute a reliability score r(X) based on its proximity to P{mv}. Retain the top 20% of points from P{sv} ranked by r(X), denoted as P{sv}^. Create the filtered point cloud P{filter} = P{mv} \cup P{sv}^. 2. Clustering-Based Denoising: Apply K-means clustering with K=1000 clusters to P{filter}. For each cluster c with centroid \muc and point set Qc, retain the nearest 30% of points to \muc. The cluster-filtered cloud is defined as: P{clu} = \{ Xk \in P{filter} \mid k \in \text{Top30\%} \{ \|Xk - \muc\|^2: Xk \in Qc \}, c = 1, \dots, K \}. 3. Normal-based Consistency Filtering: For each point Xk \in P{clu}, estimate its surface normal nk via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on its 10 nearest neighbors Nk in Euclidean space. Let all normals be unit-length. Compute the mean cosine similarity: \bar{c}k = \frac{1}{|Nk|} \sum{j \in Nk} nk^\top nj. Retain point k if \bar{c}k \ge 0.2. The final set is: P{final} = \{ (Xk, Ck) \in P{clu} \mid \bar{c}k \ge 0.2 \}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointcloudregularization(Pinit, cameraprojections, K=1000, alpha=0.20, beta=0.30, taucos=0.2, knn=10): # Step 1: Single-view filtering Psv, Pmv = [], [] for i, pt in enumerate(Pinit): if len(cameraprojections[i]) == 1: Psv.append(pt) else: Pmv.append(pt) # Reliability r(X) = inverse distance to nearest point in Pmv reliability = [] for pt in Psv: mind = min(dist(pt.X, mv.X) for mv in Pmv) if Pmv else float('inf') reliability.append((pt, 1.0 / (mind + 1e-8))) reliability.sort(key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) nretain = max(1, int(len(reliability) alpha)) Psvstar = [p for p, in reliability[:nretain]] Pfilter = Pmv + Psvstar # Step 2: Clustering (Lloyd's K-means) centroids = randomsample(Pfilter, K) labels = [0] len(Pfilter) for in range(50): for i, pt in enumerate(Pfilter): labels[i] = min(range(K), key=lambda c: distsq(pt.X, centroids[c])) newcentroids = [] for c in range(K): pts = [Pfilter[i] for i in range(len(Pfilter)) if labels[i] == c] if pts: newcentroids.append(meanvec([p.X for p in pts])) else: newcentroids.append(centroids[c]) centroids = newcentroids Pclu = [] for c in range(K): clusterpts = [Pfilter[i] for i in range(len(Pfilter)) if labels[i] == c] if not clusterpts: continue dists = [(p, distsq(p.X, centroids[c])) for p in clusterpts] dists.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) nretainc = max(1, int(len(dists) beta)) Pclu.extend(p for p, in dists[:nretainc]) # Step 3: Normal filtering Pfinal = [] for pt in Pclu: neighbors = getknn(pt, Pclu, knn) nk = estimatenormal([n.X for n in neighbors]) cossims = [] for n in neighbors: nj = estimatenormal([nn.X for nn in getknn(n, Pclu, knn)]) cossims.append(dot(nk, nj)) meancos = sum(cossims) / len(cossims) if meancos >= taucos: Pfinal.append(pt) return Pfinal def dist(a, b): return math.sqrt(sum((x-y)2 for x, y in zip(a, b))) def distsq(a, b): return sum((x-y)2 for x, y in zip(a, b)) def meanvec(pts): return [sum(p[i] for p in pts)/len(pts) for i in range(3)] def dot(a, b): return sum(xy for x, y in zip(a, b)) def getknn(query, cloud, k): dists = [(p, distsq(p.X, query.X)) for p in cloud if p is not query] dists.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) return [p for p, in dists[:k]] def estimatenormal(pts): # PCA on 3D points: eigenvector of covariance matrix with smallest eigenvalue mu = meanvec(pts) cov = [[sum((pts[i][d]-mu[d])(pts[j][e]-mu[e]) for i in range(len(pts))) for e in range(3)] for d in range(3)] # Solve 3x3 symmetric eigenvalue problem for smallest eigenvalue a, b, c = cov[0][0], cov[1][1], cov[2][2] d, e, f = cov[0][1], cov[0][2], cov[1][2] T = a + b + c P = ab + ac + bc - d2 - e2 - f2 Q = abc + 2def - ae2 - bd2 - cf2 p = P - T2/3 q = 2T3/27 - PT/3 + Q if p >= 0: return [0, 0, 1] r = math.sqrt(-p3/27) phi = math.acos(-q/(2r)) roots = [2math.sqrt(-p/3)math.cos((phi + 2math.pik)/3) - T/3 for k in range(3)] minidx = min(range(3), key=lambda i: roots[i]) # Extract eigenvector for minidx (simplified back-substitution) # Standard 3x3 eigenvector extraction omitted for brevity; returns unit vector return [0, 0, 1] def randomsample(pts, k): import random return [pts[i].X for i in random.sample(range(len(pts)), k)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Multi-view Set: If P{mv} is empty, the reliability score r(X) cannot be computed as defined. The pseudocode handles this by assigning infinite distance, resulting in an empty P{sv}^. Small Clusters: If a cluster has fewer than 1/\beta points, the "nearest 30%" logic may retain all or none depending on rounding. The pseudocode uses max(1,...) to ensure at least one point is retained if possible, but the source does not specify this guard. Normal Estimation Degeneracy: PCA on collinear or coplanar neighbors may yield unstable normals. The source does not specify a fallback. Precision: The threshold \bar{c}k \ge 0.2 is specific to the source. Time Complexity: Dominated by K-means clustering (O(N \cdot K \cdot I) where I is iterations) and normal estimation (O(N \cdot k{nn} \cdot \log N) or O(N \cdot k{nn}) with spatial indexing). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the point cloud and intermediate subsets. Measured Performance: On MipNeRF360 and LLFF datasets, regularization increases computation time (e.g., from 1m32s to 4m16s training time in some configurations) but mitigates overfitting and improves reconstruction quality. Strengths: Removes noise from unstable 2-view SfM tracks and duplicated points from 3DGS densification. Enforces geometric consistency. Limitations: Computationally expensive compared to vanilla 3DGS. Initialization strength is more decisive than regularization gains. When to use: When initializing 3DGS with a merged point cloud from SfM and lightweight 3DGS, especially in sparse-view scenarios. When not to use: When computational resources are severely limited, as the method explicitly increases computation time. Point Cloud Regularization was introduced in the paper "Initialize to Generalize: A Stronger Initialization Pipeline for Sparse-View 3DGS" by CoR-GS authors. It addresses the initialization-limited nature of sparse-view 3DGS by refining the merged point cloud P{init} before final optimization. The method combines single-view filtering, clustering-based denoising, and normal-based consistency filtering to ensure uniform spatial coverage and multi-view consistency. body:
Fuzzy Projection Ranking (FPR) is a point cloud processing technique that projects 3D LiDAR points onto a 2D range image grid to compute a fuzzy rank for each point based on the range distribution of its neighbors, thereby filtering noise and enhancing features. It is designed for robust cloud voxelization and denoising in LiDAR odometry and mapping, particularly in adverse weather conditions such as rain, fog, and dust. Unlike sibling methods like Statistical Outlier Removal which rely on global or local statistical distributions in 3D space, FPR leverages the structured nature of LiDAR scans via 2D projection and rank-based voxelization to preserve geometric structure while removing outliers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A raw LiDAR point cloud containing points with fields x, y, z, intensity, timestamp, and ring index. Outputs: cloudtrimmed (points within valid range bounds), cloudranked (points with an added rank field), cloudvoxelized (voxelized point cloud), filtered (final denoised point cloud), and Neighbours (a 2D matrix mapping range image coordinates to point indices). Data Structures: PointType: Struct containing x, y, z (float), intensity (float), timestamp (double), and ring (uint16t). VoxelAccum: Struct containing weightedsum (Eigen::Vector3d), weightsum (double, initialized to 0.0001 to avoid division by zero), maxintensity (float, initialized to -1.0f), and maxpoint (PointType). VoxelHash: Hash function for voxel indices (i, j, k) computed as ((1 \ll 20) - 1) \& (i \cdot 73856093 \oplus j \cdot 19349663 \oplus k \cdot 83492791). Neighbours: Matrix of size N\SCAN 	imes Horizon\SCAN storing the index of the point projected to each pixel, initialized to -1. Parameters: N\SCAN: Number of vertical channels (rings). Typical values: 32 (Hesai) or 64 (HDL-64). anges\x: Horizontal angular resolution in degrees. Typical values: 0.18 (Hesai) or 0.2 (HDL-64). Horizon\SCAN: Number of horizontal columns, calculated as 360 / anges\x. Typical values: 2000 (bag files) or 1800 (bin files). maxange: Maximum valid range for point acceptance. Typical value: 30.0 (or 100.0 in some configurations). kernelow: Half-height of the 2D convolution kernel. Value: 1. kernel\col: Half-width of the 2D convolution kernel. Value: 5. voxel\size: Size of the voxel grid in meters. Typical value: 0.5. drop\percent: Percentage of lowest-rank points to drop. Typical value: 10. use\weighted: Boolean flag for voxelization mode (weighted centroid vs. max intensity). Steps: 1. Range Image Projection: For each point p in the input cloud, calculate range r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}. If r < 0.1 or r > maxange, skip the point. Calculate row: row = ring. Calculate horizontal angle: horizonAngle = 	ext{atan2}(x, y) \cdot 180 / \pi. Calculate column: col = -	ext{round}((horizonAngle - 90.0) / anges\x) + Horizon\SCAN / 2. Handle horizontal wrapping: if col \ge Horizon\SCAN, set col = col - Horizon\SCAN. If col < 0 or col \ge Horizon\SCAN, skip the point. Store the point index in Neighbours[row, col]. Overwrite p.intensity with r and add p to cloudtrimmed. 2. Rank Estimation: For each point p in cloudtrimmed, retrieve its projected coordinates (row, col) and current range range\curr = p.intensity. Initialize rank = 0.0 and count = 0. Iterate over neighbors defined by the kernel offsets (dy, dx) where dy \in [-kernelow, kernelow] and dx \in [-kernel\col, kernel\col], excluding (0,0). For each neighbor offset, calculate neighbor coordinates: y\ = row + dy, x\ = col + dx. Handle vertical boundary: if y\ < 0 or y\ \ge N\SCAN, continue. Handle horizontal wrapping: if x\ < 0, set x\ = Horizon\SCAN - 1 + x\. If x\ \ge Horizon\SCAN, set x\ = x\ - Horizon\SCAN - 1. If x\ < 0 or x\ \ge Horizon\SCAN, continue. Retrieve neighbor index idx

eigh = \sqrt{p

.z^2}. Calculate difference diff = r
eigh - range\curr. Update rank: rank += \exp(-0.5 \cdot diff^2). Increment count. If count > 0, normalize rank: rank = rank / count. Calculate weight: weight = range\curr / maxange. Finalize rank: rank = (1 + rank) \cdot (1 + weight). Store the rank in p.intensity. 3. Intensity Filtering: Calculate number of points to drop: num	o\drop = 	ext{int}((drop\percent / 100.0) \cdot len(cloudanked)). Sort points in cloudranked by rank (stored in intensity) in ascending order. Remove the first num	o\drop points (lowest rank) to produce filtered. 4. Voxelization: Initialize a hash map grid mapping voxel indices to VoxelAccum. For each point p in filtered, calculate voxel index: voxel = \lfloor p / voxel\size floor (integer division). Else (max intensity mode), if p.intensity > acc.max\intensity, set acc.max\intensity = p.intensity and acc.max\point = p. 90.0) / angresx) + HorizonSCAN // 2 if col >= HorizonSCAN: col -= HorizonSCAN rangecurr = pt.intensity rank = 0.0 count = 0 for dy, dx in kernel: y = row + dy x = col + dx if y < 0 or y >= NSCAN: continue if x < 0: x = HorizonSCAN - 1 + x if x >= HorizonSCAN: x = x - HorizonSCAN - 1 if x < 0 or x >= HorizonSCAN: continue idxn = Neighbours[y][x] if idxn > 0: pn = cloud[idxn] rneigh = math.sqrt(pn.x2 + pn.y2 + pn.z2) diff = rneigh - rangecurr rank += math.exp(-0.5 diff diff) count += 1 if count > 0: rank /= count weight = rangecurr / maxrange rank = (1 + rank) (1 + weight) pt.intensity = rank cloudranked.append(pt) return cloudranked def filterbyrankpercent(cloudranked, droppercent): if not cloudranked or droppercent <= 0: return cloudranked numtodrop = int((droppercent / 100.0) len(cloudranked)) sortedindices = sorted(range(len(cloudranked)), key=lambda i: cloudranked[i].intensity) keptindices = sortedindices[numtodrop:] return [cloudranked[i] for i in keptindices] def voxelize(filtered, voxelsize, useweighted): grid = {} for pt in filtered: vx = int(pt.x / voxelsize) vy = int(pt.y / voxelsize) vz = int(pt.z / voxelsize) voxel = (vx, vy, vz) if voxel not in grid: grid[voxel] = { 'weightedsum': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'weightsum': 0.0001, 'maxintensity': -1.0, 'maxpoint': None } acc = grid[voxel] if useweighted: acc['weightedsum'][0] += pt.intensity pt.x acc['weightedsum'][1] += pt.intensity pt.y acc['weightedsum'][2] += pt.intensity pt.z acc['weightsum'] += pt.intensity else: if pt.intensity > acc['maxintensity']: acc['maxintensity'] = pt.intensity acc['maxpoint'] = pt cloudvoxelized = [] for voxel, acc in grid.items(): if useweighted: centroid = [acc['weightedsum'][i] / acc['weightsum'] for i in range(3)] newpt = Point(centroid[0], centroid[1], centroid[2], acc['maxintensity'], 0) cloudvoxelized.append(newpt) else: if acc['maxpoint'] is not None: cloudvoxelized.append(acc['maxpoint']) return cloudvoxelized A sibling method that removes outliers based on the statistical distribution of distances to neighbors in 3D space. It does not use 2D projection or rank-based weighting. Choose FPR when LiDAR scan structure is reliable and adverse weather noise is prevalent; choose Statistical Outlier Removal for general-purpose noise reduction where scan structure may be irregular [17819-statistical-outlier-removal.md]. Time Complexity: Projection is O(N) where N is the number of points. Rank computation is O(N \cdot K) where K is the number of kernel neighbors (2 \cdot kernelow + 1 	imes 2 \cdot kernel\col + 1 - 1). Voxelization is O(N) on average using a hash map. Filtering is O(N \log N) due to sorting. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the point cloud and O(N\SCAN \cdot Horizon\SCAN) for the Neighbours matrix. Performance: The method is parallelized using TBB for rank computation. It is effective in adverse weather conditions (rain, fog, snow). Strengths: Preserves geometric structure better than simple statistical filtering in noisy conditions; leverages LiDAR scan structure. Limitations: Requires accurate LiDAR parameters (N\SCAN, anges\x); sensitive to horizontal wrapping errors; performance depends on kernel size. When to use: LiDAR odometry and mapping in adverse weather; when scan structure is consistent. When not to use: When LiDAR parameters are unknown or inaccurate; for non-LiDAR point clouds lacking ring structure. Fuzzy Projection Ranking (FPR) was introduced by Eugeniu Vezeteu as an unofficial implementation for robust cloud voxelization and denoising in LiDAR odometry and mapping. It is designed to handle adverse weather conditions such as rain, fog, and dust, which typically degrade LiDAR point cloud quality. The method leverages the structured nature of LiDAR data by projecting points onto a 2D range image, computing a fuzzy rank based on neighbor intensity distributions, and then performing rank-based voxelization. eugeniu1994/FPR, https://github.com/eugeniu1994/FPR, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Point Cloud Downsampling based on Geometry and Texture Complexity
body:
This method reduces the density of a point cloud by selecting a subset of points based on local geometric curvature and color texture complexity, ensuring that visually or structurally significant regions are preserved during downsampling. It differs from uniform voxel downsampling by using probabilistic sampling weighted by complexity metrics rather than simple spatial binning, and from uniform random downsampling by biasing selection toward high-complexity areas. It builds on Point Cloud Cropping and Downsampling. Inputs: pointcloudpath (path to input PLY), targetnum (integer, desired output point count), chunksize (integer, processing chunk size), kneighbors (integer, neighbor count for local estimation), geoweight (float, geometric complexity weight), texweight (float, texture complexity weight). Outputs: outputpath (path to save downsampled PLY), structured array with fields x,y,z (f4), nx,ny,nz (f4), r,g,b (u1), geo (f4), tex (f4). Data Structures: points (N, 3) float32, normals (N, 3) float32 or None, colors (N, 3) float32 in Lab space or None, geoscores (N,) float32, texscores (N,) float32, combinedscores (N,) float32, probabilities (N,) float32, selectedindices (targetnum,) int64. Steps: 1. Load and Preprocess: Read point cloud from pointcloudpath using Open3D. Extract points as points (N, 3) float32. Check for existence of colors and normals. If colors exist, scale RGB to 0-255 uint8, convert using cv2.cvtColor with cv2.COLORRGB2LAB, convert to float32, normalize L channel by dividing by 100, normalize a,b channels by adding 128 and dividing by 255. If no colors, set colors=None and disable texture computation. If normals do not exist, estimate them using Open3D's estimatenormals with a hybrid KDTree search parameter (radius=0.1, maxnn=kneighbors). Build a cKDTree spatial index on points. 2. Initialize Scores: Initialize geoscores and texscores arrays of size numpoints with zeros if respective computations are enabled. Initialize combinedscores to zeros. 3. Compute Complexity Scores (Chunked): Process points in chunks of size chunksize. For each chunk, query k-nearest neighbors (kneighbors+1 to include self) from the KDTree, obtaining distances and neighborindices. Get neighbor points for each point in the chunk. Compute difference vectors diffs between neighbors and their mean. Compute covariance matrices covs using einsum: np.einsum('nki,nkj->nij', diffs, diffs) / kneighbors. Compute eigenvalues of covariances using np.linalg.eigvalsh. Calculate curvature as eigenvalues[:, 0] / (eigenvalues.sum(axis=1) + 1e-6) (smallest eigenvalue divided by sum of eigenvalues). Store in geoscores. Get neighbor colors. Compute center color as the first neighbor (self). Compute L2 norm of difference between neighbor colors and center color for each neighbor. Average these norms across neighbors for each point. Store in texscores. 4. Normalize and Combine Scores: For each enabled score type (geo, tex), normalize to [0,1] using (score - min) / (max - min + 1e-6). Combine normalized scores using weighted sum: combinedscores += weight score for each score/weight pair. If no scores, set combinedscores to ones. 5. Probabilistic Sampling: Compute sampling probabilities: probabilities = combinedscores / combinedscores.sum(). Select targetnum points using np.random.choice with these probabilities, without replacement. 6. Output: Select downsampled points, normals, colors, and scores using the selected indices. Construct a structured numpy array for PLY output with fields: x,y,z (f4), nx,ny,nz (f4), r,g,b (u1), geo (f4), tex (f4). Write to outputpath as text PLY. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import open3d as o3d import cv2 from scipy.spatial import cKDTree def adaptivedownsample(pointcloudpath, targetnum, chunksize=1000, kneighbors=10, geoweight=1.0, texweight=1.0, outputpath="output.ply"): # 1. Load and Preprocess pcd = o3d.io.readpointcloud(pointcloudpath) points = np.asarray(pcd.points).astype(np.float32) numpoints = len(points) hascolors = pcd.hascolors() hasnormals = pcd.hasnormals() colors = None if hascolors: rgbuint8 = (np.asarray(pcd.colors) 255).astype(np.uint8).reshape(-1, 1, 3) labuint8 = cv2.cvtColor(rgbuint8, cv2.COLORRGB2LAB) labfloat = labuint8.astype(np.float32) L = labfloat[:,:, 0] / 100.0 ab = (labfloat[:,:, 1:] + 128) / 255.0 colors = np.concatenate([L.reshape(-1, 1), ab], axis=1) if not hasnormals: pcd.estimatenormals(searchparam=o3d.geometry.KDTreeSearchParamHybrid(radius=0.1, maxnn=kneighbors)) normals = np.asarray(pcd.normals).astype(np.float32) else: normals = np.asarray(pcd.normals).astype(np.float32) tree = cKDTree(points) geoscores = np.zeros(numpoints, dtype=np.float32) texscores = np.zeros(numpoints, dtype=np.float32) # 2. Compute Complexity Scores (Chunked) for start in range(0, numpoints, chunksize): end = min(start + chunksize, numpoints) # Query k-nearest neighbors (kneighbors+1 to include self) distances, neighborindices = tree.query(points[start:end], k=kneighbors+1) # Geometric Complexity if geoweight > 0: neighborpoints = points[neighborindices] meanneighbors = np.mean(neighborpoints, axis=1, keepdims=True) diffs = neighborpoints - meanneighbors covs = np.einsum('nki,nkj->nij', diffs, diffs) / kneighbors eigenvalues = np.linalg.eigvalsh(covs) curvature = eigenvalues[:, 0] / (eigenvalues.sum(axis=1) + 1e-6) geoscores[start:end] = curvature # Texture Complexity if texweight > 0 and colors is not None: neighborcolors = colors[neighborindices] centercolor = neighborcolors[:, 0,:] diffscolors = neighborcolors - centercolor[:, np.newaxis,:] l2norms = np.linalg.norm(diffscolors, axis=2) avgnorm = np.mean(l2norms, axis=1) texscores[start:end] = avgnorm # 3. Normalize and Combine Scores combinedscores = np.zeros(numpoints, dtype=np.float32) if geoweight > 0: mingeo = np.min(geoscores) maxgeo = np.max(geoscores) normgeo = (geoscores - mingeo) / (maxgeo - mingeo + 1e-6) combinedscores += geoweight normgeo if texweight > 0 and colors is not None: mintex = np.min(texscores) maxtex = np.max(texscores) normtex = (texscores - mintex) / (maxtex - mintex + 1e-6) combinedscores += texweight normtex if combinedscores.sum() == 0: combinedscores = np.ones(numpoints, dtype=np.float32) # 4. Probabilistic Sampling probabilities = combinedscores / combinedscores.sum() selectedindices = np.random.choice(numpoints, size=targetnum, replace=False, p=probabilities) # 5. Output selectedpoints = points[selectedindices] selectednormals = normals[selectedindices] selectedgeo = geoscores[selectedindices] selectedtex = texscores[selectedindices] selectedcolorsrgb = np.zeros((targetnum, 3), dtype=np.uint8) if colors is not None: selectedcolors = colors[selectedindices] Lback = selectedcolors[:, 0] 100.0 abback = (selectedcolors[:, 1:] 255.0) - 128 labuint8 = np.stack([Lback, abback[:, 0], abback[:, 1]], axis=1).astype(np.uint8).reshape(1, -1, 3) rgbuint8 = cv2.cvtColor(labuint8, cv2.COLORLAB2RGB) selectedcolorsrgb = rgbuint8.reshape(-1, 3) plydata = np.zeros(targetnum, dtype=[ ('x', '<f4'), ('y', '<f4'), ('z', '<f4'), ('nx', '<f4'), ('ny', '<f4'), ('nz', '<f4'), ('r', 'u1'), ('g', 'u1'), ('b', 'u1'), ('geo', '<f4'), ('tex', '<f4') ]) plydata['x'] = selectedpoints[:, 0] plydata['y'] = selectedpoints[:, 1] plydata['z'] = selectedpoints[:, 2] plydata['nx'] = selectednormals[:, 0] plydata['ny'] = selectednormals[:, 1] plydata['nz'] = selectednormals[:, 2] plydata['r'] = selectedcolorsrgb[:, 0] plydata['g'] = selectedcolorsrgb[:, 1] plydata['b'] = selectedcolorsrgb[:, 2] plydata['geo'] = selectedgeo plydata['tex'] = selectedtex # Write to outputpath as text PLY with open(outputpath, 'w') as f: f.write("ply
") f.write("format ascii 1.0
") f.write("element vertex %d
" % targetnum) f.write("property float x
property float y
property float z
") f.write("property float nx
property float ny
property float nz
") f.write("property uchar red
property uchar green
property uchar blue
") f.write("property float geo
property float tex
") f.write("endheader
") for i in range(targetnum): f.write("%f %f %f %f %f %f %d %d %d %f %f
" % ( plydata['x'][i], plydata['y'][i], plydata['z'][i], plydata['nx'][i], plydata['ny'][i], plydata['nz'][i], plydata['r'][i], plydata['g'][i], plydata['b'][i], plydata['geo'][i], plydata['tex'][i])) Parameters with typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: If targetnum exceeds numpoints, np.random.choice raises an error. If all scores are zero, combinedscores.sum() is zero, causing division by zero in probability normalization; the method initializes combinedscores to ones when no scores are enabled to prevent this. Precision issues in eigenvalue computation are mitigated by using np.linalg.eigvalsh for symmetric matrices. The k-NN approach with kneighbors+1 avoids boundary conditions where radius search might find fewer than 3 neighbors. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) for KDTree construction and O(N \cdot k) for complexity scoring, where N is point count and k is kneighbors. Sampling is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) for points, scores, and KDTree. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Linear with N for scoring, assuming efficient KDTree queries. Strengths: Preserves geometric and texture details better than uniform downsampling by biasing selection toward high-complexity areas. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than uniform downsampling and requires normals and colors for full functionality. When to use: When preserving visual and geometric fidelity is important and the point cloud is large enough to benefit from intelligent downsampling. When not to use: When computational resources are limited or the point cloud is already small. This method originates from the AVM-GS project, which focuses on adaptive volume rendering. It is designed to prepare point clouds for further processing, such as voxelization or rendering, by reducing redundancy while maintaining key features. Yang-SyZng/AVM-GS, https://github.com/Yang-SyZng/AVM-GS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Grid Partitioning by Cell Size
body: Grid Partitioning by Cell Size converts a point cloud into a regular 3D voxel grid by partitioning the spatial extent defined by the cloud's bounding box or a user-specified origin into uniform cubic cells. It solves the problem of discretizing continuous point data into a structured volume representation for downstream rendering or analysis. It differs from Octree Construction for Point Clouds by using a fixed-resolution regular grid rather than an adaptive hierarchical structure, and from Point Resampling with Neighbor Masking by not explicitly handling neighbor interactions during the initial partitioning step. All variants in this family share the core mechanism of mapping 3D coordinates (x, y, z) to integer voxel indices (vx, vy, vz) using a fixed spacing s (cell length). The mapping is generally defined as: vi = \lfloor (pi - oi) / s \rfloor where pi is the point coordinate, oi is the grid origin, and s is the cell size along axis i. The resulting indices are clamped or checked against the grid dimensions Dx, Dy, Dz. The output is typically a binary mask or a data array associated with the grid geometry. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mappointstovoxels(points, origin, spacing, dimensions): """ Map 3D points to voxel indices using fixed cell spacing. Args: points: List of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). origin: Tuple (ox, oy, oz) of grid origin. spacing: Float cell size s. dimensions: Tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) of grid dimensions. Returns: mask: 3D boolean array of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz). """ if spacing <= 0: raise ValueError("Spacing must be strictly positive for standard mapping.") invspacing = 1.0 / spacing mask = [[[False for in range(dimensions[2])] for in range(dimensions[1])] for in range(dimensions[0])] for p in points: vx = int(math.floor((p[0] - origin[0]) invspacing)) vy = int(math.floor((p[1] - origin[1]) invspacing)) vz = int(math.floor((p[2] - origin[2]) invspacing)) vx = max(0, min(vx, dimensions[0] - 1)) vy = max(0, min(vy, dimensions[1] - 1)) vz = max(0, min(vz, dimensions[2] - 1)) mask[vx][vy][vz] = True return mask Voxelize Point Cloud (Basic Mode) determines grid dimensions dynamically based on a user-specified target number of cells per axis (N) and the point cloud's bounding box. It applies a fixed padding factor of 1.002 to the bounding box extent after an initial preflight calculation, which can result in output dimensions that deviate from the requested N. Unlike the Existing Partition Grid Mode, it does not validate for zero spacing during preflight, risking division-by-zero errors on degenerate inputs. It is chosen when a target resolution is desired rather than a physical cell size. Voxelize Point Cloud (Advanced Mode) maps a 3D point cloud to a regular grid using a user-defined cell length (spacing) parameter. It differs from Basic Mode by explicitly accepting a spacing parameter rather than deriving it from geometry, and from Existing Partition Grid Mode by not requiring an existing image geometry as a reference. Unlike the Existing Partition Grid path, which rejects zero spacing with an error, Advanced Mode allows zero spacing, resulting in a silent failure where all points are skipped. This method voxelizes a point cloud by mapping points into a pre-existing destination grid geometry defined by its origin, spacing, and dimensions. It differs from Basic Mode by requiring the grid structure to be provided externally rather than computed from the point bounds, and from Advanced Mode by focusing on the fundamental mapping and validation against a fixed grid. It solves the problem of integrating point data into a specific, pre-defined volumetric coordinate system. Validation routines for grid parameters exhibit specific edge-case behaviors. DataCheckNumberOfPartitions takes int32 values but casts them to usize before checking against <= 0, causing negative values like -1 to become 2^64-1, pass validation, and request a very large geometry. DataCheckCellLength only rejects negative values, allowing zero cell length. DataCheckBoundingBoxCoords only rejects min > max, allowing min == max. The cell edge length should be about the average size of the objects, e.g., measured by their bounding box. Cells should be cuboid-like. Too many cells cause slow traversal, heavy memory usage, and bad cache utilization, while too few cells cause too many objects per cell. The methods are implemented within the VoxelizePointCloudFilter component. The implementation supports multiple input geometries including Vertex, Edge, Triangle, Quad, Tetrahedral, and Hexahedral. Not given in the sources. name: Voxelize Point Cloud (Basic Mode)
head: Basic partitioning mode
body: Voxelize Point Cloud (Basic Mode) is a voxelization method that determines grid dimensions dynamically based on a user-specified target number of cells per axis (N) and the point cloud's bounding box extent. It differs from sibling methods by applying a fixed percentage padding to the bounding box extent after an initial "preflight" calculation, which can result in output dimensions that deviate from the requested N. Unlike the Existing Partition Grid Mode, it does not validate for zero spacing during preflight, risking division-by-zero errors on degenerate inputs. Inputs: Point cloud data with 3D coordinates (x, y, z). User parameter N: Target number of cells per axis. Grid origin (ox, oy, oz) and cell size s are derived, not input directly. Outputs: A voxel grid (Image Geometry) with dimensions Dx, Dy, Dz. A binary mask or data array associated with the grid, indicating occupied voxels. The output geometry is an ImageGeometry object. Key fields include: spacing: A 3D vector (sx, sy, sz) representing cell dimensions. In Basic Mode, sx = sy = sz = s. dimensions: A 3D vector (Dx, Dy, Dz) representing the number of voxels along each axis. origin: The 3D coordinates of the grid's starting corner. 1. Calculate Bounding Box: Determine the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the input point cloud. Let Ex, Ey, Ez be the extents (max - min) along each axis. 2. Preflight Calculation: Calculate initial spacing s = \max(Ex, Ey, Ez) / N. This step is used for preflight validation but does not define the final output. 3. Apply Padding: Add a fixed padding factor to the extent. The source specifies a padding of 0.1\% to the extent, implemented as a multiplier of 1.002 in the dimension calculation step. Padded extent: E'i = Ei \times 1.002. 4. Recalculate Dimensions: The final dimensions are calculated using the preflight spacing s and the padded extent: Di = \lceil E'i / s \rceil = \lceil 1.002 \times Ei / s \rceil. Substituting s = \max(Ex, Ey, Ez) / N yields Di = \lceil 1.002 \times Ei \times N / \max(Ex, Ey, Ez) \rceil. 5. Voxelization: Map each point (px, py, pz) to voxel indices (vx, vy, vz) using the shared principles of the parent method: vi = \lfloor (pi - oi) / s \rfloor. Clamp indices to [0, Di - 1]. Mark the corresponding voxel in the output mask/array. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelizepointcloudbasic(points, N): """ Voxelize a point cloud using Basic Mode. Args: points: List of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). N: Target number of cells per axis. Returns: dimensions: Tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) spacing: Float s mask: 3D boolean array of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz) """ if not points: raise ValueError("Empty point cloud") # 1. Calculate Bounding Box xs = [p[0] for p in points] ys = [p[1] for p in points] zs = [p[2] for p in points] minx, maxx = min(xs), max(xs) miny, maxy = min(ys), max(ys) minz, maxz = min(zs), max(zs) ex = maxx - minx ey = maxy - miny ez = maxz - minz # 2. Preflight Spacing Calculation maxextent = max(ex, ey, ez) spacing = maxextent / N # 3 & 4. Recalculate Dimensions with Padding # Padding factor 1.002 applied to extent paddedex = ex 1.002 paddedey = ey 1.002 paddedez = ez 1.002 Dx = math.ceil(paddedex / spacing) Dy = math.ceil(paddedey / spacing) Dz = math.ceil(paddedez / spacing) # 5. Voxelization # Origin is typically the min corner of the bounding box originx, originy, originz = minx, miny, minz mask = [[[False for in range(Dz)] for in range(Dy)] for in range(Dx)] for p in points: px, py, pz = p vx = int(math.floor((px - originx) / spacing)) vy = int(math.floor((py - originy) / spacing)) vz = int(math.floor((pz - originz) / spacing)) # Clamp to grid bounds vx = max(0, min(vx, Dx - 1)) vy = max(0, min(vy, Dy - 1)) vz = max(0, min(vz, Dz - 1)) mask[vx][vy][vz] = True return (Dx, Dy, Dz), spacing, mask N: Target number of cells per axis. Typical values are not specified, but values < 500 exhibit dimension inflation. 1. Dimension Inflation: For N < 500, the executed dimensions are N+1, not N. For example, N=10 results in 11 \times 11 \times 11, and N=2 results in 4 \times 4 \times 4. 2. Zero Extent (Degenerate Input): If the bounding box has zero extent on an axis (e.g., a planar cloud at z=100), and the internal padding (noted as 1e-6 in some contexts, but 0.1\% in the formula) is smaller than half a float32 ULP (\approx 7.6e-6), the padded extent may remain. This results in spacing 0, causing a divide-by-zero in dimension calculation (\lceil distance/0 \rceil = \infty), leading to undefined behavior, badalloc, or incorrect grids. 3. Preflight Mismatch: Preflight dimensions and origin do not agree with the output dimensions, causing downstream filters to receive incorrect geometry information during preflight. 4. Zero Spacing Validation: Unlike the 'Existing Image Geometry' path, Basic mode allows zero spacing if not fixed, leading to division by zero. Generates a grid aligned to the shortest axis of a point cloud, with padding \epsilon. It computes the bounding box from min/max of points, identifies the shortest axis, and uses linspace for that axis while using arange for the other two axes with spacing derived from the shortest axis length. Returns a dictionary with keys: gridpoints (tensor [N, 3]), shortestaxislength (float), xyz (list of 1D arrays), and shortestaxisindex (int). Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement; user-friendly parameter (N) instead of spacing. Limitations: Unpredictable output dimensions due to padding and ceiling operations; prone to errors on degenerate (planar/point) clouds; preflight/output mismatch. When to use: When a rough grid resolution is desired and the point cloud is well-formed (non-degenerate, 3D extent). When not to use: When exact grid dimensions are required; when processing planar or point-like clouds; when preflight consistency is critical for downstream processing. This method is part of the simplnx library's voxelization filters. The implementation highlights gaps in preflight testing and error handling for degenerate cases, as noted in code reviews. FILT: Voxelize Point Cloud, https://github.com/BlueQuartzSoftware/simplnx/pull/1724, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) pbonazzi/guassian-diffusion, https://github.com/pbonazzi/guassian-diffusion, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Voxelize Point Cloud (Advanced Mode)
head: Advanced partitioning mode
body: Voxelize Point Cloud (Advanced Mode) maps a 3D point cloud to a regular grid using a user-defined cell length parameter. Unlike the Existing Image Geometry path which rejects zero spacing with error -45983, this mode allows zero spacing, resulting in a silent failure where all points are skipped. Inputs: Point cloud geometry (e.g., VertexGeom or TriangleGeom). Cell length parameter s. Grid origin o. Grid dimensions Dx, Dy, Dz. Outputs: A binary mask or data array associated with the grid geometry. The tuple shape is \{Dz, Dy, Dx\}. Data Structures: The output is an image geometry with dimensions Dx, Dy, Dz. The mask is stored as a 1D array of tuples with shape \{Dz, Dy, Dx\}. Formula: The mapping from point coordinates to voxel indices follows the parent principle: vi = \lfloor (pi - oi) / s \rfloor where pi is the point coordinate, oi is the grid origin, and s is the cell length along axis i. Steps: 1. Validate Input: Check if the cell length s is negative; DataCheckCellLength only rejects negative values. 2. Calculate Spacing: Set spacing s{calc} = s. 3. Compute Inverse Spacing: Calculate s{inv} = 1.0 / s{calc}. 4. Map Points to Voxels: For each point p = (px, py, pz), calculate voxel coordinates vi = (pi - oi) \times s{inv}. 5. Index and Clamp: Convert vi to integer indices (vx, vy, vz) and clamp to grid bounds [0, Di-1]. 6. Set Mask: Set the corresponding voxel in the output mask to 1 (or relevant data). 7. Finalize: If all points were skipped (e.g., due to s=0), the output mask is all zeros. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Zero Spacing: If s=0, the division 1.0/0 results in infinity/NaN, causing all points to be skipped. Negative Spacing: Rejected by DataCheckCellLength. Implementation Pitfalls: A sign error on the origin subtraction, a swapped x{inv}/y{inv}, or a units mistake can lead to incorrect voxel mapping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelizepointcloudadvanced(points, origin, celllength, dimensions): """ Voxelize point cloud using Advanced Mode. Args: points: List of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). origin: Tuple (ox, oy, oz) of grid origin. celllength: Float cell length s. dimensions: Tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) of grid dimensions. Returns: mask: 3D boolean array of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz). """ if celllength < 0: raise ValueError("Cell length must be non-negative.") spacing = celllength invspacing = 1.0 / spacing if spacing != 0 else float('inf') # Initialize mask with shape (Dx, Dy, Dz) mask = [[[False for in range(dimensions[2])] for in range(dimensions[1])] for in range(dimensions[0])] for p in points: # Calculate raw voxel coordinates vxraw = (p[0] - origin[0]) invspacing vyraw = (p[1] - origin[1]) invspacing vzraw = (p[2] - origin[2]) invspacing # Skip points that map to infinity or NaN (e.g., when spacing is 0) if math.isinf(vxraw) or math.isnan(vxraw) or \ math.isinf(vyraw) or math.isnan(vyraw) or \ math.isinf(vzraw) or math.isnan(vzraw): continue # Convert to integer indices and clamp to grid bounds vx = max(0, min(int(math.floor(vxraw)), dimensions[0] - 1)) vy = max(0, min(int(math.floor(vyraw)), dimensions[1] - 1)) vz = max(0, min(int(math.floor(vzraw)), dimensions[2] - 1)) mask[vx][vy][vz] = True return mask A voxelization mode that accepts min/max bounding box coordinates to determine grid extent. If min equals max on any axis, the spacing becomes zero, causing all points to be skipped. DataCheckBoundingBoxCoords only rejects min > max. If min == max, spacing is 0, CalculateImageVoxelMask calculates 1.0f / 0 = inf, causing coordinates to become inf or NaN, skipping all points. The filter completes with an all-zero mask and only a warning. Not given in the sources. This mode is part of the Voxelize Point Cloud filter family in the simplnx library. The behavior regarding zero spacing was noted in code review discussions, highlighting a discrepancy with the Existing Partition Grid path. name: Voxelize Point Cloud (Existing Partition Grid Mode)
head: Existing Image Geometry, Existing Partition Grid
body: This method voxelizes a point cloud by mapping points into a pre-existing destination grid geometry defined by its origin, spacing, and dimensions. It solves the problem of integrating point data into a specific, pre-defined volumetric coordinate system. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud geometry and an existing image geometry defining the destination grid. Output: A mask or data array associated with the grid geometry. Data Structures: The destination grid is defined by origin (ox, oy, oz), uniform spacing s, and dimensions Dx, Dy, Dz Grid Partitioning by Cell Size. The output array uses a tuple shape of \{dims[2], dims[1], dims[0]\}. Steps: 1. Validate Grid Spacing: Check that the grid spacing is strictly greater than zero. 2. Map Points to Indices: For each point p with coordinates (px, py, pz), compute the voxel indices (vx, vy, vz) using the parent's shared mapping formula: vi = \lfloor (pi - oi) / s \rfloor for each axis i Grid Partitioning by Cell Size. 3. Clamp/Check Bounds: Verify that 0 \le vi < Di for all axes. 4. Write to Grid: Set the corresponding voxel in the output array to the active value (e.g., True or 1). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mappointstovoxels(points, origin, spacing, dimensions): """ Map 3D points to voxel indices using fixed cell spacing. Args: points: List of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). origin: Tuple (ox, oy, oz) of grid origin. spacing: Float cell size s. dimensions: Tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) of grid dimensions. Returns: mask: 3D boolean array of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz). """ if spacing <= 0: raise ValueError("Spacing must be strictly positive for standard mapping.") invspacing = 1.0 / spacing mask = [[[False for in range(dimensions[2])] for in range(dimensions[1])] for in range(dimensions[0])] for p in points: vx = int(math.floor((p[0] - origin[0]) invspacing)) vy = int(math.floor((p[1] - origin[1]) invspacing)) vz = int(math.floor((p[2] - origin[2]) invspacing)) vx = max(0, min(vx, dimensions[0] - 1)) vy = max(0, min(vy, dimensions[1] - 1)) vz = max(0, min(vz, dimensions[2] - 1)) mask[vx][vy][vz] = True return mask Parameters: Grid Origin: Defined by the pre-existing destination grid geometry. Grid Spacing: Defined by the pre-existing destination grid geometry. Grid Dimensions: Defined by the pre-existing destination grid geometry. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Spacing: If the grid spacing is not larger than zero, the method rejects it with error code -45983. Shape Verification: The output tuple shape must be explicitly checked as \{dims[2], dims[1], dims[0]\} to ensure correct memory layout. Origin Precision: The grid origin may be padded (e.g., \approx -0.01) due to prior resizing operations; this padding is critical for correct alignment. A strategy to initialize the occupancy grid by treating geometry points as finite-sized entities that splat to nearby grid cells within a radius, rather than as infinitesimal points, to complete small missing regions. It addresses incomplete occupancy grids resulting from sparsity and errors in the geometry prior. The key parameter is the splatting radius, which defines the spatial extent for spreading point influence. A pitfall is the addition of empty grid cells, which is a trade-off for filling missing regions. This approach yields significant quantitative and qualitative performance improvements, though it cannot completely remove missing regions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Integrates point data into a pre-defined coordinate system; supports out-of-core processing with chunked data stores; validates grid spacing to prevent invalid mappings. Limitations: Requires a valid pre-existing grid geometry; sensitive to grid spacing validation. When to Use: When the target voxel grid geometry is already known or defined by another process. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This method is implemented as the VoxelizePointCloudFilter in the simplnx library, supporting geometry types including Edge, Triangle, Quad, Tetrahedral, and Hexahedral. It is designed to work with chunked data stores for out-of-core processing. The validation logic rejecting invalid spacing with error code -45983 is specific to this implementation.
