name: Selected-splat Collision Mesh Generation
head: Lichtfeld Collision Mesh, Smooth remesh
body: Selected-splat Collision Mesh Generation converts a user-selected subset of 3D Gaussian splats into a watertight collision mesh featuring perimeter walls and a ceiling, solving the problem of creating navigable or collidable geometry from sparse, non-manifold neural radiance field data. It differs from sibling methods by rasterizing only the selected splat centers into a sparse 3D grid to preserve floating blobs and overhangs, then explicitly constructing solid boundary walls and a unified ceiling over the horizontal footprint, rather than relying solely on implicit surface extraction. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scene containing Gaussian splat nodes; a binary selection mask identifying specific splats (typically ground/footprint and floating objects); parameters for mesh detail, wall height, smoothing, and opacity filtering. Output: A collision mesh in OBJ, GLB, or PlayCanvas voxel format (.voxel.json +.voxel.bin). Data Structures Selection Mask: A boolean array matching the total count of Gaussian splats in the scene nodes. Sparse 3D Grid: A dictionary mapping 3D voxel coordinates (x, y, z) to occupancy status, or a hierarchical octree structure for binary export. Voxel Format (PlayCanvas):.voxel.json: Metadata including version '1.1', grid bounds, scene bounds, voxel resolution, leaf size (4), tree depth, node counts, and leaf data counts..voxel.bin: A binary array of 32-bit integers representing a compacted octree. Nodes store pointers to children or leaf masks. Leaves store 64-bit occupancy masks packed into two 32-bit integers. Parameters Mesh Detail: Presets in meters: 0.05, 0.1 (default), 0.2, 0.5, 1.0. Wall Height: Default 3.0 meters. Smoothing Amount: Default 0.35 voxels, range 0.0 to 0.45. Minimum Splat Opacity: Default 0.15. Ignore Transparent Splats: Boolean, enabled by default. Steps 1. Scene Validation: Verify a scene is loaded and training is paused. 2. Selection Aggregation: Retrieve all splat nodes. Apply the global selection mask to identify active splats. Iterate through nodes. For each node, extract the raw means (\mathbf{xyz}) and raw opacity logits. If Ignore transparent splats is enabled: Filter splats where the individual opacity (derived from raw logits via a stable threshold comparison) is below Minimum splat opacity. Note: This uses per-splat opacity, not accumulated rendered opacity, and does not check connectivity. Transform the remaining selected centers to world coordinates using the node's world transform matrix \mathbf{M}: \mathbf{p}{world} = \mathbf{p}{local} \mathbf{M}{3\times3}^T + \mathbf{M}{3\times1}. 3. Voxelization: Rasterize the world-space centers into a sparse 3D grid. The grid preserves separate height layers for floating blobs and overhangs. Determine the horizontal footprint (unique (x, z) pairs). 4. Boundary Construction: Identify the perimeter of the horizontal footprint. For each (x, z) in the footprint: Determine the vertical extent [y{min}, y{max}] based on the selected splat centers at that location. If (x, z) is on the perimeter (adjacent to an empty cell in the footprint), fill the voxel column from y{min} up to y{ceiling}. If (x, z) is internal, fill from y{min} to y{max}. Calculate y{ceiling}: The maximum y coordinate of any selected splat center plus Wall Height, measured along the native -Y axis (up). Disconnected footprint components remain separate. 5. Mesh Generation (Smooth Remesh): Apply a light Gaussian filter to the 3D occupancy field with sigma Smoothing Amount. Extract the surface using Lewiner's Marching Cubes algorithm on the filtered field. Limit: Dense grid capped at 32 million samples; surface capped at 2 million triangles. 6. Export: OBJ/GLB: Output the generated mesh. GLB defaults to Lichtfeld world coordinates (native -Y up). Voxel: Quantize the ceiling to voxel size. Binary roofs may extend less than one voxel beyond the exact mesh ceiling. Encode the occupancy grid into the compacted octree format. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import struct from collections import deque import math def generatecollisionmesh(scene, selectionmask, params): """ Generate collision mesh from selected splats. params: dict with keys 'detailidx', 'wallheight', 'smoothing', 'ignoretransparent', 'opacitycutoff' """ # 1. Validate Scene if scene is None or scene.istraining: raise ValueError('Load a scene and pause training first.') # 2. Aggregate Selected Centers nodes = [n for n in scene.getnodes() if n.type == 'SPLAT'] totalgaussians = sum(n.gaussiancount for n in nodes) if len(selectionmask) != totalgaussians: raise ValueError('Selection layout does not match this scene.') worldcenters = [] offset = 0 for node in nodes: if not scene.isnodeeffectivelyvisible(node.id): offset += node.gaussiancount continue count = node.gaussiancount nodemask = selectionmask[offset:offset+count] offset += count if not nodemask.any(): continue # Get raw data data = node.splatdata() meansraw = np.asarray(data.meansraw.cpu().numpy()).reshape(-1, 3) opacitylogitsraw = np.asarray(data.opacityraw.cpu().numpy()).reshape(-1) # Handle deleted mask if present if data.hasdeletedmask(): deleted = np.asarray(data.deleted.cpu().numpy()).reshape(-1).astype(bool) nodemask &= ~deleted # Filter transparent splats if params['ignoretransparent']: candidates = np.flatnonzero(nodemask) logits = opacitylogitsraw[candidates] # Stable threshold comparison for sigmoid-like activation # Assuming standard logistic function: 1 / (1 + exp(-x)) # Threshold check: sigmoid(x) >= cutoff # x >= log(cutoff / (1 - cutoff)) cutoff = params['opacitycutoff'] if 0 < cutoff < 1: threshold = math.log(cutoff / (1 - cutoff)) keep = logits >= threshold else: keep = np.oneslike(logits, dtype=bool) nodemask[candidates[~keep]] = False if not nodemask.any(): continue # Transform to world space selectedmeans = meansraw[nodemask] matrix = np.asarray(node.worldtransform).reshape(4, 4) # Apply rotation and translation transformed = selectedmeans @ matrix[:3,:3].T + matrix[:3, 3] worldcenters.append(transformed) if not worldcenters: raise ValueError('No selected splats remain. Lower the opacity cutoff or disable the transparent-splat filter.') allcenters = np.concatenate(worldcenters, axis=0) if len(allcenters) == 0: raise ValueError('No centers to voxelize.') # 3. Voxelization and Boundary Construction # Grid resolution based on detail preset details = [0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0] voxelsize = details[params['detailidx']] # Determine bounds mincoords = np.min(allcenters, axis=0) maxcoords = np.max(allcenters, axis=0) # Quantize to grid # Note: Native -Y is up. We treat Y as the vertical axis. # Grid indices mingrid = np.floor(mincoords / voxelsize).astype(int) maxgrid = np.ceil(maxcoords / voxelsize).astype(int) # Sparse grid to store max height per (x, z) and min height per (x, z) # Using a dict for sparsity footprint = {} # (x, z) -> {'miny': float, 'maxy': float} for p in allcenters: x = int(math.floor(p[0] / voxelsize)) y = int(math.floor(p[1] / voxelsize)) # Y is vertical z = int(math.floor(p[2] / voxelsize)) key = (x, z) if key not in footprint: footprint[key] = {'miny': y, 'maxy': y} else: footprint[key]['miny'] = min(footprint[key]['miny'], y) footprint[key]['maxy'] = max(footprint[key]['maxy'], y) # Calculate Ceiling Height # Highest selected splat center + wall height, measured upward along native -Y # In grid coordinates, "up" is increasing Y index if Y is up. # However, the source says "measured upward along native -Y". # If native -Y is up, then increasing -Y means decreasing Y coordinate? # Let's stick to the code logic: "highest selected splat center". # Usually "highest" means max Y coordinate. # The code calculates: max(values) + wallheight. # Let's assume standard Cartesian Y-up for calculation, then map to engine. # Source: "Ceiling height is highest selected splat center + wall height" globalmaxy = np.max(allcenters[:, 1]) ceilingheightworld = globalmaxy + params['wallheight'] ceilinggridy = int(math.floor(ceilingheightworld / voxelsize)) # Identify Perimeter # A cell is on perimeter if any of its 4 horizontal neighbors are not in footprint perimetercells = set() for (x, z) in footprint: neighbors = [(x-1, z), (x+1, z), (x, z-1), (x, z+1)] if not any(n in footprint for n in neighbors): perimetercells.add((x, z)) # Generate Voxels voxels = set() maxvoxels = 5000000 for (x, z), bounds in footprint.items(): isperimeter = (x, z) in perimetercells # Determine vertical range # Internal: fill from min to max # Perimeter: fill from min to ceiling lowy = bounds['miny'] if isperimeter: highy = ceilinggridy else: highy = bounds['maxy'] # Add voxels for y in range(lowy, highy + 1): voxels.add((x, y, z)) if len(voxels) > maxvoxels: raise ValueError('Voxel export exceeds 5 million solid voxels. Choose coarser mesh detail.') # 4. Export (Voxel Format Example) # This section demonstrates the binary encoding logic from the source if not voxels: raise ValueError('No collision voxels to export.') origin = [min(p[a] for p in voxels) for a in range(3)] maximum = [max(p[a] for p in voxels) for a in range(3)] # Quantize origin/maximum to 4-voxel blocks for octree originq = [v // 4 4 for v in origin] maximumq = [(v // 4 + 1) 4 for v in maximum] blocks = {} for p in voxels: q = tuple(p[a] - originq[a] for a in range(3)) key = tuple(v // 4 for v in q) bit = q[0]%4 + (q[1]%4)4 + (q[2]%4)16 blocks[key] = blocks.get(key, 0) | (1 << bit) #... (Octree construction logic as per source) # For brevity, the full octree serialization is omitted here as it is # specific to the PlayCanvas voxel format and not the core meshing algorithm. return voxels, ceilingheightworld Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of selected splats for rasterization. Marching Cubes complexity depends on the volume of the dense grid (capped at 32 million samples). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of solid voxels (capped at 5 million) and the resulting mesh triangles (capped at 2 million for smooth mode). Performance: The method is fast for sparse selections but can hit the 5 million voxel limit on dense, large-area ground selections. Coarser mesh detail (e.g., 0.5m or 1.0m) reduces voxel count quadratically. Strengths: Handles floating objects and overhangs correctly by preserving vertical layers; explicit ceiling generation ensures watertight enclosures for navigation; smooth remeshing produces clean, manifold geometry suitable for physics engines. Limitations: Sparse selection can leave floor gaps; the transparency filter may exclude dense low-opacity surfaces while keeping high-opacity floaters; thin geometry may distort during smoothing. When to use: When a watertight collision mesh is required for navigation or physics in a game engine, specifically for environments with distinct ground and floating elements. When not to use: When high-fidelity surface detail of the original splats is required (use raw splats or different voxelization); when the scene exceeds the 5 million voxel or 2 million triangle limits. Selected-splat Collision Mesh Generation is a plugin for Lichtfeld Studio, developed by MisterE123. It was released as an unofficial extension to facilitate the creation of collision geometry for 3D Gaussian Splat scenes. It builds on the concept of voxelizing Gaussian splats but adds specific logic for boundary wall and ceiling generation to create enclosed spaces. The smooth remeshing component uses Lewiner's Marching Cubes implementation from scikit-image. MisterE123/lichtfeld-collision-mesh, https://github.com/MisterE123/lichtfeld-collision-mesh, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: De-voxelization
head: Inverse Voxelization, Voxel to Gaussian Aggregation
body: De-voxelization aggregates network predictions computed on a sparse set of unique voxels back to the original dense voxel grid, and subsequently reduces these per-voxel predictions into per-Gaussian predictions. It serves as the inverse operation to 3D Gaussian Voxelization, enabling efficient processing by 3D networks that operate on voxelized representations while preserving the native Gaussian structure for final rendering. De-voxelization is a two-step aggregation process that maps network predictions from unique voxels back to all voxels, and then reduces them into per-Gaussian predictions using scatter operations. Input univoxelspred: A tensor of shape (N{\text{unique}}, C), where N{\text{unique}} is the number of unique voxels and C is the dimensionality of the prediction (e.g., feature channels). Input inverseindices: A 1D tensor of shape (M), where M is the total number of voxels (including duplicates). Each element maps an original voxel to its corresponding index in the unique voxel array. Input numvoxelsperg: A 1D tensor of shape (G), where G is the number of Gaussians, indicating the number of voxels belonging to each Gaussian. Output gspred: A tensor of shape (G, C), containing the final predictions at the Gaussian level. REDUCE: A string literal specifying the global reduction mode applied during aggregation. Supported values are "mean" and "max". The default value is "max". The method relies on three primary tensors: 1. univoxelspred: Shape (N{\text{unique}}, C). 2. inverseindices: Shape (M). 3. numvoxelsperg: Shape (G). The intermediate result voxelspred has shape (M, C), and the final output gspred has shape (G, C). 1. Expand Unique Voxels to All Voxels: Use a scatter operation to expand the predictions from the unique-voxel level back to the original list of all voxels. This is achieved by indexing into univoxelspred using inverseindices. The scatter function combines values according to the REDUCE rule. Formula: \text{voxels\pred} = \text{scatter}(\text{uni\voxels\pred}, \text{index}=\text{inverse\indices}, \text{reduce}=\text{REDUCE}). The intermediate output shape is (M, C). 2. Reduce to Gaussian Level: Combine per-voxel predictions into Gaussian-level predictions using a segment-sparse operation. Compute offsets by taking the cumulative sum of numvoxelsperg along dimension 0: \text{offset} = \text{cumsum}(\text{num\voxels\per\g}, \text{dim}=0). Apply segmentcsr to group voxel predictions into Gaussian predictions. The segmentcsr function takes voxelspred and the computed offset pointer tensor, grouping voxel predictions into Gaussian predictions and reducing via the REDUCE rule. Formula: \text{gs\pred} = \text{segment\csr}(\text{voxels\pred}, \text{ptr}=\text{offset}, \text{reduce}=\text{REDUCE}). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from typing import Literal import torch from torchscatter import scatter, segmentcsr REDUCE: Literal["mean", "max"] = "max" def devoxelization(univoxelspred: torch.Tensor, inverseindices: torch.Tensor, numvoxelsperg: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Aggregate network predictions from unique voxels back to full voxel predictions, and then further reduce them into per Gaussian predictions. """ # Step 1: Unique Voxels -> All Voxels # Uses scatter to expand predictions from unique-voxel level back to all voxels # by indexing through inverseindices. The method of combination is determined by REDUCE. voxelspred = scatter(src=univoxelspred, index=inverseindices, reduce=REDUCE) # Step 2: All Voxels -> Gaussians # Combine per-voxel predictions into Gaussian-level predictions using segmentcsr. # Compute offsets with cumulative sums of the number of voxels in each Gaussian. offset = torch.cumsum(numvoxelsperg, dim=0) # segmentcsr segments voxel predictions into groups corresponding to each Gaussian, # reducing via the same REDUCE rule. gspred = segmentcsr(src=voxelspred, ptr=offset, reduce=REDUCE) return gspred Empty Gaussians: If a Gaussian has zero voxels, numvoxelsperg will contain a zero, causing duplicate values in the cumulative sum offset. The behavior of segmentcsr on empty segments depends on the implementation; typically, it may return zeros or undefined values. Index Bounds: inverseindices must contain valid indices within the range 0, N{\text{unique}}). Out-of-bounds indices will cause errors. Precision: The choice of REDUCE mode affects precision. "max" and "mean" are the supported options. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently maps dense voxel computations back to sparse [Gaussian representations. Limitations: Requires the torchscatter library or equivalent implementation. The reduction mode is global, meaning all Gaussians use the same aggregation strategy. When to use: When using 3D networks that operate on voxelized data but the final representation requires per-Gaussian features for rendering. De-voxelization was introduced in the context of "Quantile Rendering: Efficiently Embedding High-dimensional Feature on 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the need to bridge voxel-based neural processing with Gaussian Splatting rendering pipelines, allowing for efficient feature embedding and prediction aggregation. Quantile Rendering: Efficiently Embedding High-dimensional Feature on 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2512.20927, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: GaGS
head: Gaussian Voxelization with Sparse Convolution for Deformation
body: GaGS is a method for learning spatial-temporal deformation of 3D Gaussians in dynamic scenes by voxelizing Gaussian distributions and extracting geometry-aware features via sparse convolutions. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly combining positional features (via MLP on point clouds) with local geometric features (via 3D U-Net on voxels) to predict deformation, rather than relying solely on implicit deformation fields or 4D Gaussian formulations. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians Gk (initialized from the first frame), each defined by mean \muk, covariance \Sigmak, opacity \alphak, and features Fk. A target timestamp t for deformation prediction. Outputs: Deformed 3D Gaussians at timestamp t, specifically updated positions and rotations. Data Structures: 1. Point Cloud: A list of 3D coordinates \{\muk\} representing the Gaussian centers. 2. Voxel Grid: A sparse 3D grid where Gaussians are discretized. The exact voxelization resolution and sparsification threshold are not given in the sources [G: Assume standard sparse voxel grid implementation with coordinate hashing]. 3. Feature Vectors: Positional features F{pos}: Output of the positional MLP. Geometric features F{geo}: Output of the 3D U-Net. Geometry-aware features F{geom}: Concatenation of F{pos} and F{geo}. 4. Rotation Representation: 6D rotation representation (instead of quaternions) for each Gaussian. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize 3D Gaussians from the first frame of the dynamic scene. 2. Branch 1 (Positional Features): Extract the 3D coordinates \{\muk\} of the Gaussians. Treat these coordinates as a point cloud. Pass the point cloud through a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to extract positional features F{pos}. 3. Branch 2 (Geometric Features): Voxelize the point cloud of Gaussian centers into a 3D voxel grid. Extract local geometric features from the voxel grid using a 3D U-Net to produce F{geo}. 4. Feature Fusion: Concatenate F{pos} and F{geo} to form the geometry-aware features F{geom}. 5. Deformation Prediction: Feed F{geom} into an MLP to predict the deformation parameters for the Gaussians at the target timestamp t. The MLP outputs updates for position and rotation. 6. Rotation Handling: Convert the predicted rotation updates from the 6D representation back to the standard representation (e.g., quaternion) for the final Gaussian state. Parameters: Rotation Representation: 6D rotation representation is used internally to facilitate smooth learning of rotation variations. Network Architectures: MLPs for positional features and deformation prediction; 3D U-Net for geometric feature extraction. Specific layer counts, hidden dimensions, and kernel sizes are not given in the sources [G: Assume standard U-Net and MLP configurations]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Rotation Smoothness: Using quaternions directly can lead to learning difficulties due to non-linearity and singularities. The 6D representation mitigates this. Voxelization Loss: Discretizing continuous Gaussians into voxels may lose fine geometric details. The 3D U-Net aims to capture local geometry to compensate. Timestamp Dependency: The deformation prediction is conditioned on the target timestamp t. The MLP must generalize across time. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of Gaussians N, the voxel grid resolution, and the depth of the MLPs and 3D U-Net. Sparse convolution reduces complexity compared to dense 3D convolutions. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of non-empty voxels and the feature dimensions. Sparse voxel storage helps manage memory. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Explicitly captures local geometric information via 3D U-Net, which may improve deformation accuracy in complex dynamic scenes. The 6D rotation representation aids in learning smooth rotations. Limitations: Requires voxelization, which introduces discretization artifacts. The two-branch architecture increases computational overhead compared to single-branch methods. Not given in the sources. When to use: When accurate deformation learning is critical and local geometric context is important. When not to use: When computational resources are limited and simpler implicit deformation fields suffice. GaGS was proposed by [110] (cited in) and [161] (cited in) as a method to handle dynamic scenes by learning deformation in a canonical space. It is part of the broader effort to extend 3D Gaussian Splatting to 4D (space-time) representations. The method addresses the limitation of static 3D Gaussians by introducing a geometry-aware feature extraction network that leverages sparse convolutions. name: 3DGS Voxelizer
head: 3DGS to OpenUSD PointInstancer Voxelizer
body: The 3DGS Voxelizer converts a 3D Gaussian Splatting scan into colored voxel blocks represented as OpenUSD PointInstancer data, enabling visualization and physics collision in NVIDIA Omniverse. It differs from general-purpose voxelizers by specifically handling 3DGS spherical harmonics decoding and SPZ binary formats, and by outputting a USD-native instancer rather than a dense volume texture. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3DGS scan file in.ply (ASCII or binary) or.spz (gzip-compressed binary) format. Output: An OpenUSD stage containing a PointInstancer prim representing the voxelized scene. Data Structures The core intermediate representation is the PointCloud dataclass: positions: np.ndarray of shape (N, 3), dtype float32. colors: np.ndarray of shape (N, 3), dtype uint8 (optional). opacities: np.ndarray of shape (N,), dtype float32 (optional, sigmoid-activated logits). is3dgs: bool indicating if the source is a 3DGS scan. Parameters resolution: The physical size of each voxel block. Smaller values increase detail and block count. minopacity: Threshold to filter faint splats. Only applicable for.ply files where opacities are sigmoid-activated logits. densitythreshold: Minimum number of splats required to create a voxel. Default is 1. unitscale: Handles unit mismatches (e.g., USD Composer uses centimeters, Isaac Sim uses meters). Steps 1. Load Point Cloud: Parse the input file into a PointCloud object. 2. Voxelize: Compute voxel centers and colors based on resolution, thresholds, and input data using vectorized numpy operations. 3. Author USD: Create a PointInstancer prim in the USD stage using the computed centers, colors, and resolution. Formulas Color Extraction (3DGS DC Spherical Harmonics): C = \text{clip}((0.5 + SH\C0 \cdot dc) \cdot 255.0, 0, 255) where SH\C0 = 0.28209479177387814 and dc is the stacked DC coefficient vector. Opacity Activation: O = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\text{opacity}}} where opacity is the sigmoid-activated logit from the 3DGS data. SPZ Color Recovery: f\dc = \frac{dc\u8 / 255.0 - 0.5}{\SPZ\COLOR\SCALE} C = \text{clip}((0.5 + SH\C0 \cdot f\dc) \cdot 255.0, 0, 255) where \SPZ\COLOR\SCALE = 0.15. SPZ Position Decoding: pos = \frac{\text{vals}}{2^{frac\bits}} where \text{vals} is reconstructed from 3 bytes b0, b1, b2 as b0 | (b1 \ll 8) | (b2 \ll 16), adjusted for signedness if \ge 0x800000. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import gzip import struct from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Tuple, Optional SHC0 = 0.28209479177387814 SPZCOLORSCALE = 0.15 @dataclass class PointCloud: positions: np.ndarray # (N, 3) float32 colors: Optional[np.ndarray] # (N, 3) uint8 opacities: Optional[np.ndarray] # (N,) float32 is3dgs: bool = False def loadpointcloud(filepath: str) -> PointCloud: """Load a.ply or.spz file into a PointCloud dataclass.""" if filepath.endswith('.spz'): return loadspz(filepath) elif filepath.endswith('.ply'): return loadply(filepath) else: raise ValueError(f"Unsupported file format: {filepath}") def loadspz(filepath: str) -> PointCloud: """Decode SPZ format.""" with gzip.open(filepath, 'rb') as f: data = f.read() # Decode positions (24-bit fixed-point) numpoints = len(data) // 9 # 3 components 3 bytes positions = np.zeros((numpoints, 3), dtype=np.float32) for i in range(numpoints): for j in range(3): byteoffset = i 9 + j 3 b0 = data[byteoffset] b1 = data[byteoffset + 1] b2 = data[byteoffset + 2] val = b0 | (b1 << 8) | (b2 << 16) if val >= 0x800000: val -= 0x1000000 positions[i, j] = val / (2 16) # fracbits not given in sources # Decode colors (DC coefficients) colorsu8 = np.frombuffer(data, dtype=np.uint8, offset=numpoints 9).reshape(-1, 3) fdc = (colorsu8.astype(np.float32) / 255.0 - 0.5) / SPZCOLORSCALE colors = np.clip((0.5 + SHC0 fdc) 255.0, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8) return PointCloud(positions=positions, colors=colors, is3dgs=True) def loadply(filepath: str) -> PointCloud: """Load PLY format (ASCII or binary).""" with open(filepath, 'rb') as f: headerlines = [] for in range(10000): # Limit to prevent infinite loop on missing endheader line = f.readline() if line.startswith(b'endheader'): break headerlines.append(line) # Not given in the sources: detailed PLY binary/ASCII parsing logic # Standard implementation would parse header keywords to find element counts, # then read vertex arrays for positions, colors, and opacities. positions = np.zeros((0, 3), dtype=np.float32) colors = np.zeros((0, 3), dtype=np.uint8) opacities = np.zeros((0,), dtype=np.float32) return PointCloud(positions=positions, colors=colors, opacities=opacities, is3dgs=True) def voxelize(pc: PointCloud, resolution: float, minopacity: float = 0.0, densitythreshold: int = 1) -> Tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]: """Voxelize a PointCloud into voxel centers and colors.""" positions = pc.positions colors = pc.colors if pc.colors is not None else np.zeros((len(positions), 3), dtype=np.uint8) if pc.is3dgs and pc.opacities is not None: opacities = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-pc.opacities)) mask = opacities >= minopacity positions = positions[mask] colors = colors[mask] # Compute voxel centers voxelcenters = np.floor(positions / resolution) resolution # Aggregate by voxel center (vectorized) # Not given in the sources: exact aggregation logic for densitythreshold # Standard approach: np.unique(voxelcenters, axis=0, returnindex=True) followed by # np.bincount or np.add.at for color/opacity accumulation, filtering by count >= densitythreshold. uniquecenters, indices = np.unique(voxelcenters, axis=0, returnindex=True) counts = np.bincount(np.searchsorted(uniquecenters, voxelcenters)) validmask = counts >= densitythreshold finalcenters = uniquecenters[validmask] finalcolors = colors[indices][validmask] return finalcenters, finalcolors def authorvoxelinstancer(stage, centers: np.ndarray, colors: np.ndarray, resolution: float, unitscale: float = 1.0) -> None: """Author a PointInstancer prim in the USD stage.""" from pxr import UsdGeom, UsdPhysics, Vt # Create root Xform with unit scale root = UsdGeom.Xform.Define(stage, "/VoxelRoot") root.AddScaleOp().Set(Gf.Vec3f(unitscale, unitscale, unitscale)) # Create PointInstancer instancer = UsdGeom.PointInstancer.Define(stage, "/VoxelRoot/Voxels") instancer.CreatePrototypeBinding().Set("/VoxelRoot/VoxelPrototype") # Define prototype shape prototype = UsdGeom.Xform.Define(stage, "/VoxelRoot/VoxelPrototype") cube = UsdGeom.Gprim.Define(stage, "/VoxelRoot/VoxelPrototype/Cube") cube.CreateExtentAttr().Set([[-resolution/2, -resolution/2, -resolution/2], [resolution/2, resolution/2, resolution/2]]) # Set instancer arrays instancer.CreatePositionsAttr().Set(Vt.Vec3fArray.FromNumpy(np.ascontiguousarray(centers, dtype=np.float32))) instancer.CreateColorsAttr().Set(Vt.Vec3fArray.FromNumpy(np.ascontiguousarray(colors.astype(np.float32) / 255.0, dtype=np.float32))) # Enable physics collision on prototype UsdPhysics.CollisionAPI.Apply(prototype) Pitfalls PLY files missing the endheader marker cause infinite loops during ASCII parsing; the implementation limits header reads to 10,000 lines. SPZ files must be gzip-compressed; opening non-gzip files raises an error. USD Composer uses centimeters while Isaac Sim uses meters; a unitscale parameter handles this mismatch. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Voxelization uses vectorized numpy operations to prevent UI thread stalls with multi-million point splats. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Integrates directly with NVIDIA Omniverse for visualization and physics; handles 3DGS-specific formats (SPZ, PLY with SH); undoable commands in Kit. Limitations: Requires Kit SDK 106 or newer; limited to USD output. The 3DGS Voxelizer is an unofficial extension for NVIDIA Omniverse, developed by danci. It was created to bridge the gap between 3D Gaussian Splatting scans and USD-based workflows, enabling use in tools like USD Composer and Isaac Sim. omolism/3dgs-voxelizer-Omni, https://github.com/omolism/3dgs-voxelizer-Omni, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian to Voxel Conversion via Grid/Kernel
head: Gaussian Voxelization, Gaussian Grid Mapping
body: This family converts continuous 3D Gaussian primitives into discrete voxel grid representations for efficient processing by 3D networks or differentiable renderers. It solves the problem of mapping continuous spatial distributions to a fixed-resolution grid while preserving geometric and photometric information. It differs from Point Cloud Voxelization by using analytical Gaussian kernels rather than simple occupancy or nearest-neighbor assignment, and from De-voxelization by operating in the forward direction (continuous to discrete). The core mechanism involves mapping continuous Gaussian primitives Gk (defined by mean \muk, covariance \Sigmak, opacity \alphak, and features Fk) to a discrete voxel grid. Common principles include: 1. Spatial Mapping: Determining which voxels a Gaussian influences, typically via bounding box checks or distance kernels. 2. Aggregation: Combining contributions from multiple Gaussians into a single voxel cell. This often involves weighted sums based on opacity or kernel distance. 3. Discretization: Converting continuous attributes (like position or color) into grid-aligned values, often requiring handling of floating-point precision and boundary conditions. 4. Sparsification: Reducing the density of the voxel grid by culling empty or low-confidence voxels to manage memory and computational load. Uses a Gaussian weight function based on distance to interpolate values from scattered points to voxel centers. It produces smoother results than Nearest Neighbor interpolation but is sensitive to non-uniform point distributions when using a fixed k [17203]. Computes voxel-space bounding boxes and conic matrices (inverse covariance) for each Gaussian to determine overlap. It focuses on pre-rasterization metadata generation and analytical bounding rather than kernel density estimation [19076]. A CUDA-based method for sparse-view CT reconstruction that explicitly constructs a volumetric density field. It uses a work-stealing kernel with shared memory caching and atomic operations to handle variable-sized influence regions and ensure differentiability [20578]. This family is foundational for 3D Gaussian Splatting variants that require volumetric representations, such as those used in CT reconstruction or neural rendering pipelines that operate on voxel grids rather than point clouds. The transition from point-based to voxel-based representations allows for the application of standard 3D CNNs or differentiable volume renderers to Gaussian primitives.

name: Gaussian Kernel Interpolation
head: voxelize via Gaussian kernel interpolation
body: Gaussian Kernel Interpolation (GKI) is a method to voxelize a point-cloud variable by interpolating values from scattered points to voxel centers using a Gaussian weight function based on distance. It produces smoother results than Nearest Neighbor (NN) interpolation, as the scatter plot of NN versus GKI values deviates from the identity line. Inputs and Outputs Input: A point cloud dataset consisting of positions P = \{p1, \dots, pN\} and associated scalar variables V = \{v1, \dots, vN\}, where pi \in \mathbb{R}^3 and vi \in \mathbb{R}. Input: Voxel grid parameters: shape (dimensions in meters), voxelwidth (side length of cubic voxels), sigma (kernel standard deviation), and k (number of nearest neighbors). Output: A 3D voxel grid array vargki of dimensions determined by shape and voxelwidth, containing interpolated values at each voxel center. Data Structures Voxel Centers (vxl): A 2D array of shape (M, 3), where M is the total number of voxels. Each row contains the (x, y, z) coordinates of a voxel center. KD-Tree: A spatial index structure built from the input point cloud positions P to enable efficient nearest-neighbor queries. Parameters voxelwidth: The side length of the cubic voxels. Typical value: 0.25 meters (25 cm). sigma: The standard deviation of the Gaussian kernel. It is set to half the voxel width: \sigma = \text{voxel\width} / 2. k: The number of nearest neighbors queried from the KD-Tree for each voxel center. Typical value: 20. Steps 1. Define Voxel Bounds: Create linear spaces for each dimension from 0 to shape[d] with step voxelwidth. The number of intervals is \lfloor \text{shape}[d] / \text{voxel\width} \rfloor + 1. 2. Calculate Voxel Centers: For each dimension, compute the center of each interval by averaging adjacent bounds: cj = (b{j} + b{j-1}) / 2. Use a 3D meshgrid to generate coordinate arrays (vxc, vyc, vzc), then ravel them into a single list of 3D points vxl of shape (M, 3). 3. Build KD-Tree: Construct a KD-Tree from the input point cloud positions P. 4. Query Nearest Neighbors: For each voxel center in vxl, query the KD-Tree for the k nearest neighbors. This returns distances D \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times k} and indices I \in \mathbb{Z}^{M \times k}. 5. Compute Weights: For each voxel m and neighbor n, calculate the Gaussian weight: w{m,n} = \exp\left(-\frac{r{m,n}^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) where r{m,n} is the distance from voxel m to its n-th nearest neighbor. 6. Retrieve Variable Values: Using indices I, retrieve the variable values V{neighbors} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times k} corresponding to the k nearest neighbors for each voxel. 7. Interpolate: Compute the weighted sum for each voxel and normalize by the sum of weights: V{voxel, m} = \frac{\sum{n=1}^{k} v{m,n} w{m,n}}{\sum{n=1}^{k} w{m,n}}. 8. Reshape: Reshape the resulting 1D array of interpolated values to match the 3D voxel grid dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.spatial import cKDTree as kdtree def gaussiankernelinterpolation(pts, var, shape, voxelwidth, k=20): # 1. Define Voxel Bounds vxb = np.linspace(0, shape[2], int(shape[2]/voxelwidth)+1) vyb = np.linspace(0, shape[1], int(shape[1]/voxelwidth)+1) vzb = np.linspace(0, shape[0], int(shape[0]/voxelwidth)+1) # 2. Calculate Voxel Centers vyc, vzc, vxc = np.meshgrid( (vyb[1:] + vyb[:-1]) / 2, (vzb[1:] + vzb[:-1]) / 2, (vxb[1:] + vxb[:-1]) / 2) vxl = np.c[vxc.ravel(), vyc.ravel(), vzc.ravel()] # 3. Build KD-Tree tree = kdtree(pts) # 4. Query Nearest Neighbors dd, ii = tree.query(vxl, k=k) # 5. Compute Weights sigma = voxelwidth / 2 wi = np.exp(-dd2 / (2 sigma2)) # 6. Retrieve Variable Values vi = var[ii] # 7. Interpolate numerator = np.sum(vi wi, axis=1) denominator = np.sum(wi, axis=1) vargkiflat = numerator / denominator # 8. Reshape vargki = vargkiflat.reshape(vzc.shape) return vargki Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-uniform Point Distribution: Using a fixed number of nearest neighbors (k) instead of a spherical radius neighborhood means the neighbors might not form a sphere, potentially biasing the interpolation if the point distribution is non-uniform. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces smoother results than Nearest Neighbor interpolation. Limitations: Sensitive to the choice of k and \sigma. Biased by non-uniform point distributions when using fixed k. When to Use: When smooth interpolation of scattered point data to a regular grid is required. When Not to Use: When point distribution is highly non-uniform and a fixed k leads to significant bias. Gaussian Kernel Interpolation is a standard technique in spatial data analysis and geostatistics for interpolating scattered data onto a regular grid. The implementation details and parameters are documented in. UP-RS-ESP/Gaussian-kernel-interpolation, https://github.com/UP-RS-ESP/Gaussian-kernel-interpolation, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gaussian Preprocessing and Voxelization
head: Gaussian to Voxel Space Conversion, preprocessCUDA
body: This method computes the voxel-space bounding box and conic matrix for each Gaussian primitive to determine which voxels it overlaps, preparing data for rasterization. It transforms 3D Gaussian parameters into a discrete voxel grid coordinate system, calculating the spatial extent and inverse covariance required for efficient voxel-based rendering. It differs from Gaussian Kernel Interpolation by using analytical bounding boxes and conic matrices rather than kernel density estimation, and from 3DGR-CT Gaussian Voxelization by focusing on pre-rasterization metadata generation rather than volumetric density reconstruction. Inputs: origpoints: Array of 3D positions, size P \times 3. scales: Array of scale factors, size P \times 3. rotations: Array of quaternion rotations, size P \times 4. scalemodifier: Scalar modifier for scales. voxelsizes: Physical size of the voxel grid, (sVoxelx, sVoxely, sVoxelz). voxelcounts: Number of voxels per axis, (nVoxelx, nVoxely, nVoxelz). voxelgridcenter: Center of the voxel grid in world space. cov3Dprecomp: Optional precomputed 3D covariance matrices (6 floats each). Outputs: radii: Array of bounding radii in voxels, size P. touchedtiles: Array of tile counts, size P. depth: Array of original Z-coordinates, size P. voxelpositions: Array of voxel-space centers, size P \times 3. conica..conicf: Inverse covariance elements (6 floats), size P \times 6. opacities: Opacity values, size P. Data Structures: The voxel space covariance matrix cov is a 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix. The inverse covariance (conic) matrix elements are stored as 6 floats: a, b, c, d, e, f corresponding to the upper triangle of the inverse matrix. Steps: 1. Initialization: For each Gaussian index idx from 0 to P-1: Initialize radii[idx], touchedtiles[idx] to 0. If idx >= P, terminate loop. 2. Voxel Dimensions: Compute the physical size of a single voxel: dVoxelx = \frac{sVoxelx}{nVoxelx}, \quad dVoxely = \frac{sVoxely}{nVoxely}, \quad dVoxelz = \frac{sVoxelz}{nVoxelz} 3. Position Loading: Load the original 3D point p{orig} from origpoints at index 3 \times idx. 4. Covariance Computation: If cov3Dprecomp is not null, load the precomputed 3D covariance matrix Vrk (6 floats) for this Gaussian. Otherwise, compute Vrk using computeCov3D from scales, scalemodifier, and rotations. Vrk is constructed from elements [0..5] of the covariance representation. 5. Voxel-Space Covariance Transformation: Construct the voxel scaling matrix M, a diagonal matrix with entries 1/dVoxelx, 1/dVoxely, 1/dVoxelz. Transform the 3D covariance Vrk to voxel space: cov = M \cdot Vrk \cdot M^T 6. Conic Matrix Calculation: Extract elements of cov into a, b, c, d, e, f (symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix). Compute the determinant det of cov. If det == 0.0f, return (skip this Gaussian). Compute the inverse of the 3 \times 3 matrix cov. Let the inverse elements be inv\a \dots inv\f. Store these inverse elements as conica..conicf for this Gaussian. Note: The rasterization uses the formula -0.5 \times (conic\a \cdot dx^2 + \dots + 2 \cdot conic\b \cdot dx \cdot dy \dots), implying conic is the inverse covariance in voxel space. 7. Bounding Radius Calculation: Calculate maxscale as the maximum of scale.x, scale.y, scale.z. Compute the bounding radius in voxels: my\radius = \left\lceil \frac{3.0 \cdot max\scale}{dVoxel} \right\rceil (Using the appropriate dVoxel dimension if anisotropic, or typically the minimum/maximum depending on implementation specifics; the source implies a scalar radius derived from max scale and voxel dimensions). 8. Voxel Position Transformation: Transform p{orig} to voxel coordinates point\vol relative to the voxel grid center and size. 9. Boundary Check: Check if the Gaussian's bounding box is completely outside the voxel grid bounds [0, nVoxelx] \times [0, nVoxely] \times [0, nVoxelz]. If outside, return (skip this Gaussian). 10. Overlap Box Computation: Compute the min/max voxel indices (cubemin, cubemax) that the Gaussian's bounding box overlaps using getCube. If the volume of this box is 0, return (skip this Gaussian). 11. Output Storage: Store myradius in radii[idx]. Store the number of touched tiles (derived from cubemin and cubemax) in touchedtiles[idx]. Store the depth (Z-coordinate of p{orig}) in depth[idx]. Store point\vol in voxelpositions[idx]. Store conica..conicf in the respective output buffers. Store opacity in opacities[idx]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussianpreprocessingandvoxelization( origpoints, scales, rotations, scalemodifier, voxelsizes, voxelcounts, voxelgridcenter, cov3Dprecomp=None): P = len(origpoints) radii = [0] P touchedtiles = [0] P depth = [0] P voxelpositions = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(P)] conic = [[0.0] 6 for in range(P)] opacities = [0.0] P # Assuming opacity is available or passed separately # Voxel dimensions dVoxelx = voxelsizes[0] / voxelcounts[0] dVoxely = voxelsizes[1] / voxelcounts[1] dVoxelz = voxelsizes[2] / voxelcounts[2] for idx in range(P): # 1. Initialize radii[idx] = 0 touchedtiles[idx] = 0 # 2. Load Position porig = origpoints[idx] # [x, y, z] # 3. Compute Covariance if cov3Dprecomp is not None: Vrk = cov3Dprecomp[idx] # 6 floats else: Vrk = computecov3d(scales[idx], rotations[idx], scalemodifier) # 4. Transform to Voxel Space # M is diagonal matrix with 1/dVoxel # cov = M Vrk M^T # Since Vrk is 3x3 symmetric, we can compute element-wise # Let Vrk elements be v00, v01, v02, v11, v12, v22 # covij = Vrkij / (dVoxeli dVoxelj) # Extract Vrk elements (assuming order: xx, xy, xz, yy, yz, zz) v00, v01, v02, v11, v12, v22 = Vrk cov00 = v00 / (dVoxelx dVoxelx) cov01 = v01 / (dVoxelx dVoxely) cov02 = v02 / (dVoxelx dVoxelz) cov11 = v11 / (dVoxely dVoxely) cov12 = v12 / (dVoxely dVoxelz) cov22 = v22 / (dVoxelz dVoxelz) # 5. Compute Inverse (Conic) # Matrix: [[cov00, cov01, cov02], # [cov01, cov11, cov12], # [cov02, cov12, cov22]] det = (cov00 (cov11 cov22 - cov12 cov12) - cov01 (cov01 cov22 - cov02 cov12) + cov02 (cov01 cov12 - cov02 cov11)) if det == 0.0: continue # Skip Gaussian # Inverse elements (upper triangle) inva = (cov11 cov22 - cov12 cov12) / det invb = (cov02 cov12 - cov01 cov22) / det invc = (cov01 cov12 - cov02 cov11) / det invd = (cov00 cov22 - cov02 cov02) / det inve = (cov01 cov02 - cov00 cov12) / det invf = (cov00 cov11 - cov01 cov01) / det conic[idx] = [inva, invb, invc, invd, inve, invf] # 6. Bounding Radius maxscale = max(scales[idx][0], scales[idx][1], scales[idx][2]) # Use minimum voxel dimension for conservative radius? # Source says "ceil(3.0 maxscale / dVoxel)". # Assuming isotropic or using a representative dVoxel. # For strict implementation, we might need to check all axes. # Let's assume dVoxelmin for safety or as per source implication. dVoxelmin = min(dVoxelx, dVoxely, dVoxelz) myradius = int(math.ceil(3.0 maxscale / dVoxelmin)) # 7. Voxel Position # Transform porig to voxel coordinates relative to grid center # pointvol = (porig - voxelgridcenter) / voxelsizes voxelcounts # Or simply: (porig - voxelgridcenter) / dVoxel pointvolx = (porig[0] - voxelgridcenter[0]) / dVoxelx pointvoly = (porig[1] - voxelgridcenter[1]) / dVoxely pointvolz = (porig[2] - voxelgridcenter[2]) / dVoxelz voxelpositions[idx] = [pointvolx, pointvoly, pointvolz] # 8. Boundary Check # Check if bounding box is outside [0, nVoxel] # Bounding box in voxel space: [pointvol - radius, pointvol + radius] # This is a simplification; actual implementation uses getCube with conic matrix # For this step, we check if the center is reasonably within bounds if (pointvolx < -myradius or pointvolx > voxelcounts[0] + myradius or pointvoly < -myradius or pointvoly > voxelcounts[1] + myradius or pointvolz < -myradius or pointvolz > voxelcounts[2] + myradius): continue # 9. Compute Overlap Box cubemin, cubemax = getcube(pointvol, myradius, voxelcounts) # Check volume vol = (cubemax[0] - cubemin[0] + 1) (cubemax[1] - cubemin[1] + 1) (cubemax[2] - cubemin[2] + 1) if vol == 0: continue # 10. Store Results radii[idx] = myradius touchedtiles[idx] = (cubemax[0] - cubemin[0] + 1) (cubemax[1] - cubemin[1] + 1) # Simplified tile count depth[idx] = porig[2] opacities[idx] = 1.0 # Placeholder, actual opacity needed return radii, touchedtiles, depth, voxelpositions, conic, opacities def computecov3d(scale, rotation, scalemodifier): # Standard 3D Gaussian covariance from scale and rotation # S = diag(scale) # R = rotationmatrix(rotation) # Vrk = R S S^T R^T scalemodifier^2 # Return upper triangle elements pass def getcube(center, radius, voxelcounts): # Compute min/max voxel indices overlapping the bounding box # center is in voxel coordinates # radius is in voxels minx = max(0, int(math.floor(center[0] - radius))) maxx = min(voxelcounts[0], int(math.ceil(center[0] + radius))) miny = max(0, int(math.floor(center[1] - radius))) maxy = min(voxelcounts[1], int(math.ceil(center[1] + radius))) minz = max(0, int(math.floor(center[2] - radius))) maxz = min(voxelcounts[2], int(math.ceil(center[2] + radius))) return (minx, miny, minz), (maxx, maxy, maxz) Parameters: voxelsize: Typical value 0.05 scene units. scalemodifier: Scalar applied to scales during covariance computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the determinant of the voxel-space covariance matrix is 0, the Gaussian is skipped. If the bounding box volume is 0, the Gaussian is skipped. Cell size too fine can cause excessive runtime and memory exhaustion (e.g., "tree budget exceeded"). Grid bounds are often padded to power-of-two cubes, which may cause viewers to treat empty space outside the logical grid as solid. A variant that optimizes memory usage and generation speed by stopping before exceeding 64 million sparse output records and checking pool-aware memory requirements for growth, compaction, and CUB workspace. It rejects provably impossible mixed-leaf topology early and uses byte-identical output validation against reference implementations. It is chosen when memory efficiency and fast generation on large scenes (e.g., 5M Gaussians) are critical. Time and Memory Complexity: Generation stops before exceeding 64 million sparse output records. Memory usage is monitored via pool-aware requirements for growth, compaction, and CUB workspace. Measured Performance: On a 5M Gaussian scene at 0.05 resolution: 3.7 s runtime, ~2 GB VRAM. Before review fixes: 6.076 s, after: 1.461 s. Packing time: 2.024 s vs 0.326 s. Peak GPU memory: 1,956 MiB. CUDA fatbin size: ~249 KiB after separating host tensor preparation. Output is byte-identical to independently checked 600/600-cell reference. Scaling: A cell size that is too fine burns time before failing (e.g., 0.005 on 5M scene ran 26 s, then failed). --auto assumes metres and floors voxel size at 0.05, rounding to 0.01. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Fast generation, memory-efficient, byte-identical output. Limitations: Grid bounds padding can cause viewer artifacts; raw records are not treated as format nodes. When to Use: Use for large-scale Gaussian splatting voxelization where memory and speed are critical. Avoid if extremely fine voxel resolutions are required without pre-estimation, as it may fail with "tree budget exceeded". This method originates from the preprocessing step in Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipelines, specifically designed to convert 3D Gaussian primitives into a voxel-space representation for efficient rendering. The "Compact GPU Voxelization" variant was introduced in the context of optimizing collision and export pipelines for Gaussian splatting tools, with significant performance improvements reviewed and merged in late 2026. It is used in modern Gaussian Splatting renderers and tools that require voxel-based processing, such as collision detection and export. yulunwu0108/Perturbed-Gaussian-Ensemble, https://github.com/yulunwu0108/Perturbed-Gaussian-Ensemble, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) feat(collision): add compact GPU voxelization and pair export, https://github.com/MrNeRF/LichtFeld-Studio/pull/3789, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 3DGR-CT Gaussian Voxelization
head: Gaussian Voxelization Backward Pass, Gaussian Voxelization Forward Pass
body:
3DGR-CT Gaussian Voxelization is a CUDA-based method for computing the contribution of 3D Gaussians to a voxel grid, specifically designed for sparse-view CT reconstruction. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping continuous Gaussian parameters to a discrete volume representation while maintaining differentiability for gradient-based optimization. Unlike standard volume rendering which may render to an image, this method explicitly constructs a volumetric density field V that can be projected via a differentiable CT projector to compare against measured sinogram data. It sets itself apart from siblings like Gaussian Kernel Interpolation by using a specialized work-stealing CUDA kernel with shared memory caching to handle variable-sized Gaussian influence regions and avoid race conditions via atomic operations. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians Gi, each defined by: Mean position \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3 Inverse covariance matrix \Sigmai^{-1} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 	imes 3} (symmetric positive definite) Intensity parameter ti \in \mathbb{R} A target voxel grid with resolution Rx 	imes Ry 	imes Rz. (For Backward Pass) The gradient of the loss with respect to the volume output, 
abla{out} V. Outputs: (Forward Pass) A voxel grid V where each voxel value is the sum of contributions from all overlapping Gaussians. (Backward Pass) Gradients 
abla{ti}, 
abla{\mui}, and 
abla{\Sigmai^{-1}} for each Gaussian Gi. Gaussian Parameters: Stored in global memory, loaded into shared memory per thread block for caching. Voxel Grid: A 3D array of floating-point values. Gradient Accumulators: Separate 3D arrays or per-Gaussian buffers for accumulating gradients, requiring atomic operations for thread safety. Work Queue: A global counter for the work-stealing approach to distribute variable-sized influence regions among thread blocks. 1. Initialization: Each thread block atomically fetches a Gaussian index from a global counter (work-stealing). 2. Load Parameters: Load \mui, \Sigmai^{-1}, and ti for the assigned Gaussian Gi into shared memory. 3. Compute Influence Region: Determine the bounding box of grid cells affected by Gi. The region is defined by the truncation radius of 3\sigmai in each dimension, where \sigmai is derived from the diagonal of \Sigmai (or the scale parameters). For each dimension d \in \{x, y, z\}, the range is [\lfloor \mu{i,d} - 3\sigma{i,d} floor, \lceil \mu{i,d} + 3\sigma{i,d} ceil]. 4. Iterate Grid Points: For each grid point (voxel center) x within the influence region: a. Compute the distance vector d = x - \mui. b. Compute the squared Mahalanobis distance D^2 = d^T \Sigmai^{-1} d. c. Compute the intensity contribution ti(x) = ti \exp(- rac{1}{2} D^2). d. Atomically add the contribution to the voxel grid: V(x) \leftarrow V(x) + ti(x) using atomicAdd. 1. Initialization: Similar to forward pass, thread blocks fetch Gaussians via work-stealing. 2. Load Parameters: Load \mui, \Sigmai^{-1}, and ti into shared memory. 3. Compute Influence Region: Compute the same 3\sigmai bounding box as in the forward pass. 4. Iterate Grid Points: For each grid point x within the influence region: a. Compute d = x - \mui. b. Compute D^2 = d^T \Sigmai^{-1} d. c. Compute ti(x) = ti \exp(- rac{1}{2} D^2). d. Retrieve the gradient from the output volume 
abla{out} V(x). e. Compute the gradient for intensity ti: 
abla{ti}^{local} = \exp(- rac{1}{2} D^2) \cdot 
abla{out} V(x) Atomically add to the accumulated gradient for ti: AtomicAdd(∇ti, ∇ti^{local}). f. Compute the gradient for the mean \mui: 
abla{\mui}^{local} = ti(x) \cdot 
abla{out} V(x) \cdot \Sigmai^{-1} d Atomically add to the accumulated gradient for \mui: AtomicAdd(∇μi, ∇μi^{local}). g. Compute the gradient for the inverse covariance \Sigmai^{-1}: 
abla{\Sigmai^{-1}}^{local} = -0.5 \cdot ti(x) \cdot 
abla{out} V(x) \cdot d d^T Atomically add to the accumulated gradient for \Sigmai^{-1}: AtomicAdd(∇Σinvi, ∇Σinvi^{local}). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. @cuda.jit def gaussianvoxelizationforward(gaussians, voxelgrid, gridshape, sigmascale): # Work-stealing initialization tid = cuda.threadIdx.x + cuda.blockIdx.x cuda.blockDim.x numthreads = cuda.blockDim.x gridDim.x # Global counter for work stealing globalcounter = cuda.atomic.add(...) # Implementation detail for global counter while globalcounter < N: idx = cuda.atomic.add(globalcounter, 1) if idx >= N: break # Load Gaussian parameters into shared memory mu = gaussians[idx].mu sigmainv = gaussians[idx].sigmainv t = gaussians[idx].t # Compute influence region (3sigma bounding box) # sigma is derived from sigmainv or stored separately sigma =... # Extract scale from sigmainv mincoords = floor(mu - 3 sigma) maxcoords = ceil(mu + 3 sigma) # Iterate over voxels in influence region for x in range(mincoords[0], maxcoords[0]): for y in range(mincoords[1], maxcoords[1]): for z in range(mincoords[2], maxcoords[2]): # Check bounds if not (0 <= x < gridshape[0] and 0 <= y < gridshape[1] and 0 <= z < gridshape[2]): continue voxelpos = float3(x, y, z) d = voxelpos - mu D2 = dot(d, matvecmul(sigmainv, d)) contribution = t exp(-0.5 D2) # Atomic add to voxel grid voxelidx = x + y gridshape[0] + z gridshape[0] gridshape[1] cuda.atomic.add(voxelgrid, voxelidx, contribution) @cuda.jit def gaussianvoxelizationbackward(gaussians, voxelgradients, gradt, gradmu, gradsigmainv, gridshape, sigmascale): tid = cuda.threadIdx.x + cuda.blockIdx.x cuda.blockDim.x numthreads = cuda.blockDim.x gridDim.x globalcounter = cuda.atomic.add(...) # Reuse or new counter while globalcounter < N: idx = cuda.atomic.add(globalcounter, 1) if idx >= N: break mu = gaussians[idx].mu sigmainv = gaussians[idx].sigmainv t = gaussians[idx].t # Compute influence region sigma =... # Extract scale mincoords = floor(mu - 3 sigma) maxcoords = ceil(mu + 3 sigma) for x in range(mincoords[0], maxcoords[0]): for y in range(mincoords[1], maxcoords[1]): for z in range(mincoords[2], maxcoords[2]): if not (0 <= x < gridshape[0] and 0 <= y < gridshape[1] and 0 <= z < gridshape[2]): continue voxelpos = float3(x, y, z) d = voxelpos - mu D2 = dot(d, matvecmul(sigmainv, d)) tx = t exp(-0.5 D2) # Get gradient from output volume voxelidx = x + y gridshape[0] + z gridshape[0] gridshape[1] gradout = voxelgradients[voxelidx] # Gradient for intensity t gradtlocal = exp(-0.5 D2) gradout cuda.atomic.add(gradt, idx, gradtlocal) # Gradient for mean mu # gradmu = t(x) gradout Sigmainv d sigmainvd = matvecmul(sigmainv, d) gradmulocal = tx gradout sigmainvd cuda.atomic.add(gradmu, idx, gradmulocal) # Gradient for inverse covariance Sigmainv # gradSigmainv = -0.5 t(x) gradout d d^T outerdd = outerproduct(d, d) gradsigmainvlocal = -0.5 tx gradout outerdd cuda.atomic.add(gradsigmainv, idx, gradsigmainvlocal) Truncation Radius: 3\sigmai for each Gaussian i. This is based on the statistical principle that 99.7% of a Gaussian’s mass lies within this range. Sigma Scale: The standard deviation \sigmai is derived from the Gaussian's covariance matrix \Sigmai. Race Conditions: Multiple Gaussians may contribute to the same voxel, and multiple threads may update the same Gaussian's gradient parameters. This is handled by using atomicAdd for accumulating intensity contributions and gradients. Variable Patch Sizes: PyTorch does not natively support slicing a batch of patches with different sizes. This is handled by developing a specialized CUDA kernel that dynamically computes each Gaussian's influence area. Precision: The use of shared memory for caching Gaussian parameters reduces global memory traffic and accelerates computation, but requires careful management of shared memory size per block. A differentiable projection operator that simulates the forward X-ray projection process. It uses the ODL library for the forward projection and propagates gradients through the operator using the chain rule to optimize Gaussian parameters directly from measured projection data. Unlike standard volume rendering which might render to an image, this projector simulates X-ray projection (line integrals) to compare against measured CT sinogram data. The projection is defined as p	heta = \mathcal{P}(V	heta), where \mathcal{P} is the forward projection operator. Gradients are propagated via  rac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial 	heta} =  rac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial p	heta}  rac{\partial p	heta}{\partial V	heta}  rac{\partial V	heta}{\partial 	heta}. The derivatives of the reconstructed intensity V	heta with respect to Gaussian parameters are explicitly derived as:  rac{\partial V	heta}{\partial ti} = \exp(- rac{1}{2} D^2)  rac{\partial V	heta}{\partial \mui} = ti \exp(- rac{1}{2} D^2) \Sigmai^{-1} (x - \mui)  rac{\partial V	heta}{\partial \Sigmai^{-1}} = - rac{1}{2} ti \exp(- rac{1}{2} D^2) (x - \mui)(x - \mui)^T. The projection operator \mathcal{P} is implemented using the ODL library. Time Complexity: The forward and backward passes are O(N \cdot V{avg}), where N is the number of Gaussians and V{avg} is the average number of voxels in the 3\sigma bounding box. The work-stealing approach ensures balanced workload distribution among thread blocks. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the voxel grid and O(N) for Gaussian parameters and gradients. Shared memory is used to cache Gaussian parameters, reducing global memory traffic. Performance: Achieves a 10x speedup for optimization and an order of magnitude reduction in memory consumption compared to baseline methods. Strengths: Efficient handling of variable-sized Gaussian influence regions; thread-safe accumulation via atomic operations; differentiable for end-to-end optimization. Limitations: Requires custom CUDA kernel implementation; performance depends on the density and spread of Gaussians. When to Use: Sparse-view CT reconstruction where efficient volumetric representation and differentiable optimization are required. When Not to Use: When hardware does not support CUDA or when the number of Gaussians is very small, making the overhead of the custom kernel unjustified. 3DGR-CT was introduced in the paper "3DGR-CT: Sparse-view CT reconstruction with a 3D Gaussian representation". The method builds on the concept of using 3D Gaussians for volumetric representation, adapting it for CT reconstruction by incorporating a differentiable CT projector and a specialized voxelization kernel. The approach uses a two-stage optimization process: low-resolution optimization followed by full-resolution refinement. The Gaussian parameters are physically motivated, with truncation at 3\sigma and splitting parameters (scale factor 0.8, intensity halving) chosen for statistical soundness. 3DGR-CT: Sparse-view CT reconstruction with a 3D Gaussian representation, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.media.2025.103585, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Coverage Factor Voxelization
head: 64x Supersampling Coverage, Coverage Factor Computation, Scalar Voxelization
body: Coverage Factor Voxelization computes a scalar-valued volumetric representation where each voxel stores the percentage of its volume covered by a geometric object, rather than a binary inside/outside flag. It derives these coverage values from a finer-resolution binary solid voxelization. It is distinguished from sibling methods by providing continuous density estimates via an octree-based aggregation of sub-voxel samples, offering 64× supersampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An indexed triangle set transformed into voxel space, and an octree-based binary solid voxelization initialized with zeroes. Output: A scalar-valued voxelization where each node stores a coverage factor C \in [0, 1] representing the percentage of the voxel covered by the object. Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains an inside flag (boolean) and a list of children (for non-leaf nodes). Leaf Node (Level-0): Contains a sub-grid of binary voxels. Coverage Factor: A scalar value stored in each node, representing the covered volume fraction. Steps: 1. Initialize: Transform input triangle vertices to voxel space and initialize the voxel grid/octree with zeroes. Perform binary solid voxelization to populate the leaf-level sub-grids with set bits (1) if covered, unset (0) otherwise. 2. Compute Level-0 Coverage: For each leaf node (level-0), calculate the coverage factor C0 as the fraction of set bits in its voxel sub-grid. C0 = \frac{\text{Number of set bits in sub-grid}}{\text{Total number of voxels in sub-grid}} 3. Compute Higher-Level Coverage (Bottom-Up): For each node at level i > 0: If the node has children, calculate its coverage factor Ci as the average of the coverage factors of its children. Ci = \frac{1}{M} \sum{j=1}^{M} C{childj} where M is the number of children. If the node has no children, its coverage factor is defined by its inside flag. Ci = \begin{cases} 1.0 & \text{if inside flag is set} \\ 0.0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 4. Iterate: Apply step 3 iteratively for all remaining levels up to the root. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecoveragefactors(node): """ Computes coverage factors for all nodes in an octree-based binary solid voxelization. Processes nodes bottom-up (leaves to root) via recursive post-order traversal. """ if node.isleaf(): # Leaf node: coverage is fraction of set bits in sub-grid setbits = sum(1 for voxel in node.subgrid if voxel == 1) totalvoxels = len(node.subgrid) node.coveragefactor = setbits / totalvoxels else: # Non-leaf node: recursively process children first if node.children is not None and len(node.children) > 0: for child in node.children: computecoveragefactors(child) sumcoverage = sum(child.coveragefactor for child in node.children) node.coveragefactor = sumcoverage / len(node.children) else: # Node has no children: coverage defined by inside flag node.coveragefactor = 1.0 if node.insideflag else 0.0 Parameters: Supersampling Factor: The method offers 64× supersampling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The coverage factor is a fraction. Floating-point precision should be sufficient for the computed ratios. Boundary Conditions: The inside flag for nodes without children must be correctly set during the initial binary voxelization step. Empty Sub-grids: If a sub-grid has no set bits, coverage is 0. Computes binary inside/outside flags. Choose when discrete solid representation is needed without density information. Link: Interior Voxelize. Creates a shell representation. Choose when surface thickness or boundary representation is critical. Link: Shell-based Voxelization. Stores velocity vectors. Choose for fluid simulation or motion fields. Link: Velocity Voxelization. Handles directional dependencies. Choose for anisotropic materials or directional data. Link: Anisotropic Voxelization. Uses box filters for density. Choose when a different smoothing or filtering approach is preferred. Link: Box-filtering Density Estimation. Applies stretching to density. Choose for specific visual effects or deformation. Link: Volume Density Stretching. Uses multiplication of patterns. Choose for complex pattern-based volumes. Link: Multi-pattern Volumetric Construction via Voxel Multiplication. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Implemented in CUDA using persistent threads for parallel processing of triangles and voxels. Strengths and Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use / When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the paper "Fast parallel surface and solid voxelization on GPUs". name: Triangle-Parallel Solid Voxelization
head: Facet-based Voxelization, Triangle-based parallelization
body: Triangle-Parallel Solid Voxelization is a data-parallel algorithm that maps a triangular mesh to a discrete 3D voxel grid by dedicating one processing thread (or work-item) to each triangle. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which voxels are enclosed by a surface without iterating over the entire voxel grid. Unlike sibling methods that parallelize over voxels (e.g., Per-Pixel Linked List Voxelization or Parallel CPU Voxelization), this method skips voxels outside the triangle's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB), reducing intersection tests by orders of magnitude. It differs from Compute Shader Triangle Voxelization by explicitly utilizing atomic operations to flip voxel states in a global grid, whereas the compute shader variant iterates over a 2D footprint to solve plane equations for precise solid filling without necessarily relying on global atomic flips in the same manner. Inputs: A triangular mesh defined by vertices \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2 and a 3D voxel grid of resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz) with voxel size 1 in voxel space. Outputs: A 3D boolean grid (or bit-field) where each voxel (i, j, k) indicates whether it is inside the mesh. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array or flattened buffer of bits/booleans. Access is via atomic XOR operations. Triangle Data: Local storage for vertex coordinates \mathbf{v}i = (xi, yi, zi) and derived normal \mathbf{n}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Thread Assignment: Assign one thread/work-item to each triangle in the mesh. 2. AABB Calculation: Compute the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the triangle in the voxel grid space. Determine the range of voxel indices (j, k) in the yz-plane that overlap with the triangle's projection. 3. Voxel Column Iteration: Loop over all voxel columns (j, k) within the AABB range. 4. Early Exit / Validity Check: For each voxel column, perform a fast rejection test to determine if the triangle intersects the voxel slab. Calculate the facet normal \mathbf{n} and the critical point \mathbf{c}. The critical point \mathbf{c} is defined component-wise based on the normal \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz) and the extreme corner of the voxel \mathbf{p} (where \mathbf{p} + \Delta\mathbf{p} is the opposite corner): cx = \begin{cases} px & \text{if } nx > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } nx \le 0 \end{cases}, \quad cy = \begin{cases} py & \text{if } ny > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } ny \le 0 \end{cases}, \quad cz = \begin{cases} pz & \text{if } nz > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } nz \le 0 \end{cases} Compute a1 = \langle \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{v}0 \rangle and a2 = \langle \mathbf{n}, \Delta\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{v}0 \rangle. If (\langle \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{p} \rangle + a1)(\langle \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{p} \rangle + a2) > 0, the triangle and voxel are separated; skip this voxel. 5. Projection Tests: If the validity check passes, test for intersection on the principal planes (e.g., yz, xy, xz). YZ Plane Test: Test the voxel center against the triangle's yz projection using edge functions. Calculate edge vectors \mathbf{e}i = \mathbf{v}{i+1 \pmod 3} - \mathbf{v}i. Calculate edge normals \mathbf{n}{yz}^{ei}. Calculate d{yz}^{ei} = -\langle \mathbf{n}{yz}^{ei}, \mathbf{v}{i,yzi} \rangle. Apply the Top-Left Fill Rule to handle shared edges/vertices consistently. Define a correction term f{yz}^{ei}: f{yz}^{ei} = \begin{cases} \epsilon & \text{if } (n{yz}^{ei, y} > 0) \lor (n{yz}^{ei, y} = 0 \land n{yz}^{ei, z} < 0) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \epsilon is the smallest positive floating-point number. The test passes if: \bigwedge{i=0}^2 \left( (\langle \mathbf{n}{\mathbf{e}i}^{\text{YZ}}, \mathbf{p}{\text{YZ}} \rangle + d{\mathbf{e}i}^{\text{YZ}}) + f{\mathbf{e}i}^{\text{YZ}} > 0 \right) where \mathbf{p}{\text{YZ}} is the voxel center projected onto the yz plane. Other Planes: Similar projection tests are performed for xy and xz planes to ensure 3D intersection. For the xy plane, the edge normal \mathbf{n}{ei}^{xy} is determined by: \mathbf{n}{ei}^{xy} = \begin{cases} (-e{i,y}, e{i,x}) & \text{if } nz \ge 0 \\ (e{i,y}, -e{i,x}) & \text{if } nz < 0 \end{cases} And the test is: \langle \mathbf{n}{ei}^{xy}, \mathbf{p}{xy} \rangle + a{ei} \ge 0, \quad \forall i \in \{0, 1, 2\} where a{ei} = -\langle \mathbf{n}{ei}^{xy}, \mathbf{v}{i,xy} \rangle + \max\{0, \Delta px n{ei,x}^{xy}\} + \max\{0, \Delta py n{ei,y}^{xy}\}. 6. X-Range Calculation: If the voxel column intersects the triangle, project the voxel center along the x-axis onto the triangle's plane to find the intersection x-coordinate q. 7. Atomic Flip: Determine the range of voxel indices in the x-direction that are inside the triangle. Flip the bits for these voxels using an atomic XOR operation. The range is derived from q. If the triangle spans multiple voxels in x, all voxels from the entry point to the exit point are flipped. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import sys def triangleparallelvoxelization(triangles, griddims): # griddims: (Nx, Ny, Nz) # grid: 1D array of size NxNyNz, initialized to 0 Nx, Ny, Nz = griddims grid = [0] (Nx Ny Nz) def atomicxor(arr, idx, val): arr[idx] ^= val return arr[idx] for tri in triangles: v0, v1, v2 = tri.vertices # Compute edge vectors e0 = (v1[0]-v0[0], v1[1]-v0[1], v1[2]-v0[2]) e1 = (v2[0]-v1[0], v2[1]-v1[1], v2[2]-v1[2]) e2 = (v0[0]-v2[0], v0[1]-v2[1], v0[2]-v2[2]) edges = [e0, e1, e2] verts = [v0, v1, v2] # Compute normal n = (e0[1]e2[2]-e0[2]e2[1], e0[2]e2[0]-e0[0]e2[2], e0[0]e2[1]-e0[1]e2[0]) nlen = math.sqrt(n[0]2 + n[1]2 + n[2]2) if nlen == 0: continue n = (n[0]/nlen, n[1]/nlen, n[2]/nlen) # Determine AABB in YZ plane miny = min(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]) maxy = max(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]) minz = min(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2]) maxz = max(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2]) startj = math.floor(miny) endj = math.floor(maxy) startk = math.floor(minz) endk = math.floor(maxz) for j in range(startj, endj + 1): for k in range(startk, endk + 1): # Voxel center in YZ pyz = (j + 0.5, k + 0.5) # YZ Projection Test with Top-Left Fill Rule yzinside = True for i in range(3): ex, ey = edges[i][1], edges[i][2] vx, vz = verts[i][1], verts[i][2] # Edge normal in YZ plane (perpendicular to edge, pointing inward for CCW) ny, nz = -ey, ex # d value dyz = -(ny vx + nz vz) # Top-Left Fill Rule correction fyz = 0.0 if (nz > 0) or (nz == 0 and ny < 0): fyz = sys.floatinfo.epsilon val = (ny pyz[0] + nz pyz[1]) + dyz + fyz if val <= 0: yzinside = False break if not yzinside: continue # X-Range Calculation # Project voxel center (j+0.5, k+0.5) along X onto triangle plane if abs(n[0]) < 1e-9: continue # Plane equation: n. (X - v0) = 0 => n.x X + n.y (j+0.5) + n.z (k+0.5) = n. v0 # X = (n.v0 - n.y(j+0.5) - n.z(k+0.5)) / n.x q = (n[0]v0[0] + n[1]v0[1] + n[2]v0[2] - n[1](j + 0.5) - n[2](k + 0.5)) / n[0] # Determine voxel range in X # Source specifies range ⌊q + 2⌋ (known typo for ⌊q + 0.5⌋) to Nx-1 startx = math.floor(q + 0.5) startx = max(0, min(startx, Nx - 1)) for x in range(startx, Nx): idx = x Ny Nz + j Nz + k atomicxor(grid, idx, 1) A compute shader technique for voxelizing large triangles by iterating over a 2D bounding box in the plane of the triangle and testing for collisions, designed to handle triangles that span many voxels more efficiently than per-voxel rasterization. It differs from standard rasterization-based voxelization by explicitly solving the plane equation for every candidate voxel within the triangle's 2D footprint, allowing for precise solid voxelization and texture coordinate interpolation without relying on hardware rasterization pipelines. Time Complexity: O(T \cdot C), where T is the number of triangles and C is the average number of voxel columns intersected by a triangle. Memory Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz) for the voxel grid. Local memory usage per work-item is minimal, storing only vertex coordinates. Performance: Reduces intersection tests by more than four orders of magnitude compared to Voxel-Based (VB) parallelization. On the Stanford Bunny model at 3mm voxel size, FB reduces tests from 1,767,431 (VB) to 93 (FB). At 0.5mm, from 368,832,950 to 5,874. Weaknesses: Warp Divergence: The number of relevant voxel columns varies significantly among triangles in a warp, leading to underutilization. Memory Bandwidth: Flipping voxels in large grids requires high memory bandwidth. Atomic XOR operations may be sequentialized, negatively affecting performance. Strengths: Efficient for sparse meshes or when the voxel grid is much larger than the mesh extent, as it skips empty space. The method was introduced as a data-parallel approach for solid voxelization on GPUs. It was developed to address the inefficiencies of voxel-based parallelization, where every voxel must be tested against the mesh. The facet-based (FB) approach was shown to be significantly faster than voxel-based (VB) methods due to reduced intersection tests and better memory locality.
