name: Compute Shader Triangle Voxelization
head: Large Triangle DDA Voxelization
body: A compute shader technique for voxelizing large triangles by iterating over a 2D bounding box in the plane of the triangle and testing for collisions, designed to handle triangles that span many voxels more efficiently than per-voxel rasterization. It differs from standard rasterization-based voxelization by explicitly solving the plane equation for every candidate voxel within the triangle's 2D footprint, allowing for precise solid voxelization and texture coordinate interpolation without relying on hardware rasterization pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A buffer of triangle indices (largetriangles), global vertex arrays (vertices), index arrays (indices), a texture map (trianglemap), a Uniform Buffer Object (ubo) containing AABB bounds (aabbmin, aabbmax) and image size, and a texture atlas for diffuse colors. Output: A 3D voxelTexture (storage image) where voxel colors are written. Data Structures: largetriangles: A buffer or array where largetriangles[glWorkGroupID.x].triangleindex stores the index of the triangle assigned to the workgroup. vertices: Global array of vertex positions. indices: Global array of triangle indices. trianglemap: Array mapping triangle index to texture atlas index. ubo: Uniform buffer containing aabbmin (vec4), aabbmax (vec4), and implicitly the voxel grid resolution via imageSize(voxelTexture).x. shared uint triangleindex: Shared memory variable used to broadcast the triangle index from thread 0 to all threads in the workgroup. Parameters: NUMTHREADS: The number of threads per workgroup is set to 64 for the base method, while the Correct Texture Coordinates variant uses 32 threads per workgroup. Steps: 1. Triangle Index Broadcast: Thread 0 loads the triangle index from largetriangles[glWorkGroupID.x].triangleindex into the shared memory variable triangleindex, then a barrier synchronizes all threads. 2. Vertex Retrieval: All threads retrieve the three vertex positions from vertices using the shared triangleindex and the indices array, and get the texture index from trianglemap[triangleindex]. 3. Coordinate Transformation: Transform vertices to world space using pc.model, then convert to voxel space using min and voxelwidth derived from ubo.aabbmin, ubo.aabbmax, and imageSize(voxelTexture).x. 4. Bounding Box Calculation: Calculate the bounding box of the triangle in world space (minx, maxx, etc.) and determine dimensions xdim, ydim, zdim. 5. Plane Equation: Compute the plane equation in voxel space: normal via cross product of edge vectors, then coefficients planexcoefficient, planeycoefficient, and planeconstant derived from the normal and distance D. 6. 2D Bounding Box: Determine the 2D bounding box in voxel coordinates for the x and y axes (minxvoxel, maxxvoxel, etc.) and calculate total voxel count. 7. Voxel Iteration and Z-Computation: Calculate the z coordinate on the triangle plane for the current (i, j) position using the plane equation coefficients. 8. Collision Test: Construct the voxel coordinate voxelcoord using i, j, and the calculated zvalue, then perform a collision test voxeltrianglecollisiontest. 9. Texture Interpolation: Compute barycentric coordinates in voxel space and interpolate texture coordinates to sample the diffuse color from the texture atlas. 10. Output: Store the resulting voxel color (diffuse + alpha 1.0) into the voxelTexture at voxelcoord. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelizetriangle(triangleindex, largetriangles, vertices, indices, trianglemap, ubo, voxeltexture): # Thread 0 loads triangle index into shared memory (simulated) sharedtriangleindex = largetriangles[triangleindex].triangleindex # Barrier implied for shared memory sync # Retrieve vertices and texture index v0 = vertices[indices[sharedtriangleindex 3]] v1 = vertices[indices[sharedtriangleindex 3 + 1]] v2 = vertices[indices[sharedtriangleindex 3 + 2]] texidx = trianglemap[sharedtriangleindex] # Transform to world space v0w = ubo.modelmatrix v0 v1w = ubo.modelmatrix v1 v2w = ubo.modelmatrix v2 # Convert to voxel space voxelwidth = (ubo.aabbmax.x - ubo.aabbmin.x) / ubo.imagesizex v0v = (v0w - ubo.aabbmin) / voxelwidth v1v = (v1w - ubo.aabbmin) / voxelwidth v2v = (v2w - ubo.aabbmin) / voxelwidth # Bounding box in voxel space minx = min(v0v.x, v1v.x, v2v.x) maxx = max(v0v.x, v1v.x, v2v.x) miny = min(v0v.y, v1v.y, v2v.y) maxy = max(v0v.y, v1v.y, v2v.y) minz = min(v0v.z, v1v.z, v2v.z) maxz = max(v0v.z, v1v.z, v2v.z) # Plane equation in voxel space edge1 = v1v - v0v edge2 = v2v - v0v normal = cross(edge1, edge2) D = dot(normal, v0v) planex = normal.x planey = normal.y planez = normal.z planeconstant = D # 2D bounding box for iteration minxv = int(floor(minx)) maxxv = int(ceil(maxx)) minyv = int(floor(miny)) maxyv = int(ceil(maxy)) # Thread mapping to 2D grid localthreadid = glLocalInvocationID.x # Standard GPU invocation ID width = maxxv - minxv + 1 height = maxyv - minyv + 1 if localthreadid < width height: i = localthreadid % width + minxv j = localthreadid // width + minyv # Z coordinate on plane if planez != 0: zval = (planeconstant - planex i - planey j) / planez else: zval = 0.0 # Degenerate plane parallel to Z-axis voxelcoord = vec3(i, j, zval) # Collision test if pointintriangle(voxelcoord, v0v, v1v, v2v): # Barycentric coordinates bary = computebarycentric(voxelcoord, v0v, v1v, v2v) # Interpolate UVs (assuming u0, u1, u2 are available) uv = bary.x u0 + bary.y u1 + bary.z u2 # Sample color color = sampletextureatlas(texidx, uv) # Store output voxeltexture[voxelcoord] = vec4(color, 1.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: If the triangle is degenerate (area zero), the normal will be zero, leading to division by zero in the plane equation. Plane Parallel to Z-axis: If planezcoefficient is zero, the plane is vertical relative to the voxel grid's Z-axis, requiring special handling. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when calculating the plane equation and barycentric coordinates for large triangles or small voxel sizes. Boundary Conditions: The bounding box calculation must correctly handle voxels that are partially covered by the triangle, and the collision test must be robust to handle edge cases where the voxel center is exactly on the triangle edge. A compute shader variant for voxelizing triangles with correct texture coordinate interpolation, processing one triangle per thread group (or per invocation depending on launch configuration), focusing on accurate UV mapping. It differs from the Large Triangle DDA method by explicitly calculating and interpolating texture coordinates for each voxel, ensuring that the resulting voxel colors accurately reflect the original triangle's texture. It uses a local size of 32 threads per workgroup. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot A), where N is the number of triangles and A is the average area of the triangle in voxels, as each triangle is processed by a workgroup and each thread processes a voxel within the triangle's 2D bounding box. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the number of voxels in the output volume, with minimal shared memory usage limited to storing the triangle index. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with the number of triangles due to independent processing, though performance may be limited by memory bandwidth when writing to the voxelTexture. Strengths: Handles large triangles efficiently by avoiding per-voxel rasterization overhead and provides precise control over voxelization and texture interpolation. Limitations: Requires careful handling of degenerate cases, precision issues, and vertical planes. When to Use: Suitable for applications requiring high-quality solid voxelization with accurate texture mapping, such as voxel cone tracing or global illumination. When Not to Use: Not suitable for real-time applications with extremely large scenes where performance is critical and approximate voxelization is acceptable. Not given in the sources. name: Hybrid Triangle Voxelization
head: Bin-based Triangle Voxelization, Compute Shader Hybrid Voxelization
body: Hybrid Triangle Voxelization is a compute-shader-based technique for voxelizing triangles that dynamically selects between direct voxel filling and a two-stage binning process based on triangle size. It solves the problem of workload imbalance in parallel voxelization by avoiding the overhead of binning for small triangles while preventing excessive memory usage and atomic contention for large triangles. It builds on Compute Shader Triangle Voxelization by introducing a spatial binning stage for triangles that span more than two voxels. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Triangle index ixsrctriangle, global triangle count ntriangles, index buffer indices, vertex buffer vertices, model matrix, cascade anchor positions, voxel size, cascade dimensions, firstindex, firstvertex, and per-triangle diffuse color. Outputs: Voxel target buffer voxeltargets (for small triangles) and a buffered triangle list buf (for large triangles, to be processed in a subsequent pass). Data Structures: Vertex Struct (std430 alignment): position: [3]f32 aligned to 16 bytes (implicit padding to 4 floats). normal: [3]f32 aligned to 16 bytes (implicit padding to 4 floats). Triangle Struct (packed into buffer buf): p0[0]: half2 (xy of p0). p0[1]: half2 (z of p0, x of normal). p1[0]: half2 (xy of p1). p1[1]: half2 (z of p1, x of normal). p2[0]: half2 (xy of p2). p2[1]: half2 (z of p2, x of normal). diffuse: uint (packed from packDiffuseNormalOpacity). emissive: uint (set to 0). Numbered Steps: 1. Get triangle index ixsrctriangle from glGlobalInvocationID.x. If ixsrctriangle >= ntriangles, return. 2. Calculate vertex indices: indexoffset = firstindex + 3 ixsrctriangle; i0 = indices[indexoffset + 0] + firstvertex, i1 = indices[indexoffset + 1] + firstvertex, i2 = indices[indexoffset + 2] + firstvertex. 3. Fetch model-space positions p0model, p1model, p2model from vertices buffer using i0, i1, i2. 4. Transform to cascade-local space: p0 = (modelmatrix vec4(p0model, 1.0)).xyz - anchors[targetcascade].xyz (same for p1, p2). 5. Compute normal: normal = normalize(cross(p1 - p0, p2 - p0)). 6. Compute AABB bounds in cascade-local space: lowerbound = min(min(p0, p1), p2), upperbound = max(max(p0, p1), p2). 7. Pack attributes: packed = packDiffuseNormalOpacity(diffuse.rgb, abs(normal), 1.0). 8. Calculate voxel bounds: voxelsize = voxelSize(targetcascade); voxellowerbound = max(ivec3(floor(lowerbound / voxelsize)), -cascadesizehalf); voxelupperbound = min(ivec3(floor(upperbound / voxelsize)), cascadesizehalf - 1). 9. If triangleVolume(voxellowerbound, voxelupperbound) <= 2, execute direct voxelization loop and return. 10. Otherwise, calculate bin bounds: binsize = voxelSize(targetcascade) 4; binlowerbound = max(ivec3(floor(lowerbound / binsize)), -bincascadesizehalf); binupperbound = min(ivec3(floor(upperbound / binsize)), bincascadesizehalf - 1). 11. Increment bin counters: Loop over bin bounds, calculate binindex = binIndex(binpos), execute atomicAdd(binoffsets[binindex + bingroupoffset], 1). 12. Pack triangle data into Triangle struct: tri.p0[0] = packHalf2x16(p0.xy), tri.p0[1] = packHalf2x16(vec2(p0.z, normal.x)), etc. for p1, p2. Set tri.diffuse = packed, tri.emissive = 0. 13. Append to buffer: ix = atomicAdd(nbufferedtriangles[buffergroupindex], 1); buf[ix + buffergroupoffset] = tri. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def packhalf2x16(xy): # Packs two floats into a half2 representation (uint32) return int(xy[0] 65536) | int(xy[1] 65536) def packdiffusenormalopacity(diff, normal, opacity): # Packs diffuse, normal, and opacity into a uint return (int(diff[0]) << 16) | (int(normal[0]) << 8) | int(opacity) def setpackedopacity(packed, opacity): # Updates the opacity field in the packed uint return (packed & 0xFFFFFF00) | int(opacity) def trianglevolume(lower, upper): # Returns the number of voxels in the AABB return (upper.x - lower.x + 1) (upper.y - lower.y + 1) (upper.z - lower.z + 1) def binindexfrompos(pos): # Standard 3D to 1D index for bin grid return pos.x + pos.y bincascadesizehalf + pos.z bincascadesizehalf bincascadesizehalf def indexfromcascadepos(cascade, pos): # Standard 3D to 1D index for voxel grid return pos.x + pos.y cascadesizehalf + pos.z cascadesizehalf cascadesizehalf def atomicadd(arr, idx, val): arr[idx] += val def atomicor(arr, idx, val): arr[idx] |= val def hybridtrianglevoxelization(ixsrctriangle, ntriangles, indices, vertices, modelmatrix, anchors, targetcascade, voxelsize, cascadesizehalf, bincascadesizehalf, binoffsets, bingroupoffset, nbufferedtriangles, buffergroupindex, buf, voxeltargets, firstindex, firstvertex, diffuse): if ixsrctriangle >= ntriangles: return indexoffset = firstindex + 3 ixsrctriangle i0 = indices[indexoffset + 0] + firstvertex i1 = indices[indexoffset + 1] + firstvertex i2 = indices[indexoffset + 2] + firstvertex p0model = vertices[i0].position p1model = vertices[i1].position p2model = vertices[i2].position p0 = (modelmatrix vec4(p0model, 1.0)).xyz - anchors[targetcascade].xyz p1 = (modelmatrix vec4(p1model, 1.0)).xyz - anchors[targetcascade].xyz p2 = (modelmatrix vec4(p2model, 1.0)).xyz - anchors[targetcascade].xyz normal = normalize(cross(p1 - p0, p2 - p0)) lowerbound = min(min(p0, p1), p2) upperbound = max(max(p0, p1), p2) packed = packdiffusenormalopacity(diffuse.rgb, abs(normal), 1.0) voxellowerbound = max(ivec3(floor(lowerbound / voxelsize)), -cascadesizehalf) voxelupperbound = min(ivec3(floor(upperbound / voxelsize)), cascadesizehalf - 1) if trianglevolume(voxellowerbound, voxelupperbound) <= 2: for x in range(voxellowerbound.x, voxelupperbound.x + 1): for y in range(voxellowerbound.y, voxelupperbound.y + 1): for z in range(voxellowerbound.z, voxelupperbound.z + 1): voxelpos = ivec3(x, y, z) voxelindex = indexfromcascadepos(targetcascade, voxelpos) packedwithopacity = setpackedopacity(packed, 0.5) atomicor(voxeltargets[voxelindex], packedwithopacity) return binsize = voxelsize 4 binlowerbound = max(ivec3(floor(lowerbound / binsize)), -bincascadesizehalf) binupperbound = min(ivec3(floor(upperbound / binsize)), bincascadesizehalf - 1) for x in range(binlowerbound.x, binupperbound.x + 1): for y in range(binlowerbound.y, binupperbound.y + 1): for z in range(binlowerbound.z, binupperbound.z + 1): binpos = ivec3(x, y, z) binindex = binindexfrompos(binpos) atomicadd(binoffsets[binindex + bingroupoffset], 1) tri = Triangle() tri.p0[0] = packhalf2x16(p0.xy) tri.p0[1] = packhalf2x16(vec2(p0.z, normal.x)) tri.p1[0] = packhalf2x16(p1.xy) tri.p1[1] = packhalf2x16(vec2(p1.z, normal.x)) tri.p2[0] = packhalf2x16(p2.xy) tri.p2[1] = packhalf2x16(vec2(p2.z, normal.x)) tri.diffuse = packed tri.emissive = 0 ix = atomicadd(nbufferedtriangles[buffergroupindex], 1) buf[ix + buffergroupoffset] = tri Parameters: binsize: The spatial extent of a bin, calculated as voxelSize(targetcascade) 4. opacity: In the direct voxelization path, the opacity is hardcoded to 0.5 via setPackedOpacity(packed, 0.5). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Atomic Contention: Appending to the triangle buffer via atomicAdd(nbufferedtriangles[buffergroupindex], 1) may cause contention if many threads write simultaneously. Small Triangle Overhead: Direct voxelization is used for triangles spanning <= 2 voxels to avoid the overhead of binning for very fine geometry, but this requires an LOD system to prevent overloading the voxelization pass. name: Surface Voxel Texture Update
head: Surface Voxel Texture Generation, Surface Voxel to Texture Upload
body: Surface Voxel Texture Update converts discrete surface voxel data into a GPU-accessible 2D texture format for volume rendering. It differs from general voxelization methods by focusing on the specific data layout (position and normal) and OpenGL texture upload mechanics rather than the geometric intersection logic itself. Inputs: surfacevoxels: A list or array of voxel data. If None, a surface voxel structure is generated from volumedata. volumedata: The source volumetric data used to generate surface voxels when surfacevoxels is None. surfacedata.shape: The dimensions of the source data, used to determine texture width. Outputs: A 2D OpenGL texture (surfacevoxeltexture) containing surface voxel data. Data Structures: Surface Voxel Array: A numpy array of shape (N, 7) with float32 dtype, where each row is (x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, ?). Texture: A 2D texture with width W = \min(\text{surface\data.shape}[0], \text{GL\MAX\TEXTURE\SIZE}), height H = 1, internal format GLRGBA32F, format GLRGBA, type GLFLOAT, min/mag filter GLLINEAR, and S/T wrap mode GLCLAMPTOEDGE. Steps: 1. Generate Surface Voxels: If surfacevoxels is None, call createsurfacevoxelstructure(volumedata) to generate the voxel list. 2. Convert to Array: Convert the surfacevoxels list into a numpy array of shape (N, 7) cast to float32. 3. Extract Components: Extract the first 6 components (x, y, z, nx, ny, nz) from the array for texture data. 4. Determine Dimensions: Calculate texture width W as \min(\text{surface\data.shape}[0], \text{GL\MAX\TEXTURE\SIZE}) and set height H=1. 5. Upload Texture: Create a 2D texture with the calculated dimensions and formats. Upload the extracted data, padding or truncating to match the texture's W \times H \times 4 float capacity. 6. Set Filters: Set minification and magnification filters to GLLINEAR. 7. Set Wrapping: Set S and T wrapping modes to GLCLAMPTOEDGE. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import OpenGL.GL as gl def createsurfacevoxelstructure(voldata): """Stub for external voxel generation logic. name: Voxel Generation with Diffusion Models
head: DDPM-based Voxel Generation
body: This method generates discrete 3D volumetric shapes by training a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) to learn the distribution of voxelized objects. It learns a parameterized Markov chain that generates novel samples after a finite number of steps. The generated voxel grids serve as an initial coarse representation for downstream volumetric mesh extraction. Inputs and Outputs Input: A training dataset of voxelized shapes, where each shape is a binary tensor V \in \{0, 1\}^{r \times r \times r} representing a mesh discretized into a grid. Shapes are normalized to fit within a unit cube. Output: A generated binary tensor \hat{x}0 \in \{0, 1\}^{r \times r \times r} representing a novel 3D shape. Data Structures Voxel Tensor: A 3D array of size r \times r \times r with values 0 (unfilled) or 1 (filled). Noise Schedule: A sequence of variance parameters \betat for t \in [1, T], where \betat gradually decreases to 0 as t \to 0. Parameters r: Voxel resolution. Not given in the sources. T: Total number of diffusion steps. Not given in the sources. \betat: Noise schedule parameter. Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps 1. Forward Process (Diffusion): The forward Markov chain gradually diffuses a real data sample x0 to standard Gaussian noise xT over T steps. The joint distribution is q(x{0:T}) = q(x0) \prod{t=1}^T q(xt | x{t-1}). Each transition adds Gaussian noise: q(xt | x{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}(xt; \sqrt{1 - \betat} x{t-1}, \betat I). Using the reparameterization trick, any step t can be sampled directly from x0: xt = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}t} x0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}t} \epsilon, where \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I), \alphat = 1 - \betat, and \bar{\alpha}t = \prod{i=1}^t \alphai. 2. Model Parameterization: A 3D convolutional neural network \epsilon\phi predicts the noise \epsilon added to xt at step t. The architecture follows standard 3D CNN designs with modifications for voxel generation tasks. 3. Training Objective: The model maximizes the evidence lower bound (ELBO), which simplifies to a mean squared error loss between the predicted noise and the actual noise. The loss is L{ddpm} = \mathbb{E}{x0, t, \epsilon} [ || \epsilon - \epsilon\phi(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}t} x0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}t} \epsilon, t) ||^2 ]. Training samples x0 from the dataset, t uniformly from [1, T], and \epsilon from \mathcal{N}(0, I). 4. Sampling (Reverse Process): To generate a shape, start with \hat{x}T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) and iteratively denoise from t=T down to t=0. The reverse chain is p\phi(x{0:T}) = p(xT) \prod{t=1}^T p\phi(x{t-1} | xt). Each step samples from p\phi(x{t-1} | xt) = \mathcal{N}(x{t-1}; \mu\phi(xt, t), \betat I). The mean is computed as \mu\phi(xt, t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alphat}} (xt - \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}t} \epsilon\phi(xt, t)). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F def trainstep(model, x0, alphat, alphabart, betat, device): """ Computes the training loss for one batch. x0: Ground truth voxel tensor [B, 1, r, r, r] alphat: Tensor of alpha values [T] alphabart: Tensor of alphabar values [T] betat: Tensor of beta values [T] """ B, C, H, W, D = x0.shape # Sample time step t uniformly from [0, T-1] t = torch.randint(0, len(alphat), (B,), device=device).long() # Sample noise epsilon ~ N(0, I) epsilon = torch.randnlike(x0) # Create noisy sample xt using reparameterization trick # xt = sqrt(alphabart) x0 + sqrt(1 - alphabart) epsilon sqrtalphabar = torch.sqrt(alphabart[t]).view(B, 1, 1, 1, 1) sqrtoneminusalphabar = torch.sqrt(1 - alphabart[t]).view(B, 1, 1, 1, 1) xt = sqrtalphabar x0 + sqrtoneminusalphabar epsilon # Predict noise with 3D CNN predictedepsilon = model(xt, t) # Loss: MSE between predicted and actual noise loss = F.mseloss(predictedepsilon, epsilon) return loss def generatesample(model, alphat, alphabart, betat, device, resolution=32): """ Generates a voxel grid from noise. """ # Start with pure Gaussian noise xT ~ N(0, I) xt = torch.randn(1, 1, resolution, resolution, resolution, device=device) # Iteratively denoise from t = T-1 down to 0 for t in reversed(range(len(alphat))): # Predict noise predictedepsilon = model(xt, torch.tensor([t], device=device)) # Compute mean for reverse process # mu = 1/sqrt(alphat) (xt - sqrt(1 - alphabart) epsilonpred) alpha = alphat[t] alphabar = alphabart[t] sqrtalpha = torch.sqrt(alpha) sqrtoneminusalphabar = torch.sqrt(1 - alphabar) mu = (1.0 / sqrtalpha) (xt - sqrtoneminusalphabar predictedepsilon) # Add noise if t > 0, otherwise use deterministic mean if t > 0: beta = betat[t] z = torch.randnlike(xt) xt = mu + torch.sqrt(beta) z else: xt = mu # Threshold continuous output to binary voxel grid {0, 1} voxelgrid = (xt > 0.5).float() return voxelgrid Edge Cases and Pitfalls Binary Constraint: The diffusion process operates on continuous space, but the target representation is binary \{0, 1\}. Thresholding the final output is required to enforce the binary constraint. Resolution: The method assumes a fixed resolution r \times r \times r. Changing resolution requires retraining or interpolation, which is not detailed in the source. Normalization: Shapes must be normalized to a unit cube before voxelization for training. Training requires iterative 3D convolutional network forward passes over T steps per sample. Sampling time scales linearly with T. Memory usage scales with the voxel grid volume r^3 and the 3D CNN parameters. The method generates novel shapes with good generalization but is constrained by fixed resolution and the computational cost of 3D convolutions. This method was proposed by Yan Zheng, Lemeng Wu, Xingchao Liu, Zhen Chen, Qiang Liu, and Qixing Huang from the University of Texas at Austin in the paper "Neural Volumetric Mesh Generator" (2022). It builds on the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) framework introduced by Ho et al. (2020). It serves as the first module in the NVMG pipeline to produce coarse voxel representations for subsequent tetrahedral mesh generation. name: DDPM Sampling at Inference
head: DDPM Inference, DDPM Sampling
body: DDPM Sampling at Inference is the process of generating voxelized 3D shapes by reversing a learned Markov chain, as used in Voxel Generation with Diffusion Models. It differs from Sharf by relying on iterative denoising of a latent representation (typically triplane features) rather than direct geometric construction. The method produces occupancy fields that are subsequently decoded into meshes. Inputs: A noise tensor zT \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) of the same shape as the target latent representation (e.g., triplane features); the number of inference steps T; the precomputed noise schedule parameters \alphat and \bar{\alpha}t (alphascumprod). Outputs: A denoised latent representation z0, which represents the occupancy field or triplane features. Data Structures: Noise Schedule: A tensor of size T+1 containing \bar{\alpha}t = \prod{i=1}^t \alphai. In standard DDPM implementations, T=1000. Latent Tensor: Shape (B, C, H, W) for triplanes, where B is batch size, C is channels, and H, W are spatial dimensions. Steps: 1. Initialization: Sample zT from a standard normal distribution. 2. Iterative Denoising: For t = T, T-1, \dots, 1: a. Compute the variance term \sigmat^2 = \frac{1-\bar{\alpha}{t-1}}{1-\bar{\alpha}t} \frac{1-\bar{\alpha}t}{\bar{\alpha}t}. b. Predict the noise \epsilon\theta(zt, t) using the trained diffusion model (UNet). c. Compute the predicted mean \mu\theta(zt, t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}t}} (zt - \frac{1-\bar{\alpha}t}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}t}} \epsilon\theta(zt, t)). d. Sample z{t-1} = \mu\theta(zt, t) + \sigmat \epsilon, where \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I). 3. Decoding: Evaluate the resulting latent field using an MLP at resolution 128^3 and extract the mesh using marching cubes. Parameters: T: Number of iterations. Default is 1000. Can be reduced to 250 for faster generation with minor visual fidelity loss. Resolution: 128^3 for mesh extraction. Edge Cases: Precision: The noise schedule and intermediate tensors should be maintained in high precision to avoid accumulation errors during the 1000-step reverse process. Interpolation: Using DDIM for interpolation results in visually worse-quality meshes compared to DDPM sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def ddpmsample(model, T=1000, device="cuda"): """ Performs DDPM sampling for 3D shape generation. Args: model: The trained diffusion model (UNet) that predicts noise. T: Number of inference steps (default 1000). device: Device to run inference on. Returns: z0: The denoised latent representation (triplane features). """ # Step 1: Initialize noise # Assuming latent shape is (1, C, H, W) for a single example z = torch.randn(1, 3, 64, 64, device=device) # Typical triplane shape # Precompute noise schedule parameters # betat is usually linearly spaced in standard DDPM betas = torch.linspace(0.0001, 0.02, T, device=device) alphas = 1.0 - betas alphascumprod = torch.cumprod(alphas, dim=0) # Add alpha0 = 1 for convenience alphascumprod = torch.cat([torch.tensor([1.0], device=device), alphascumprod]) for t in range(T, 0, -1): tidx = t - 1 # 0-indexed for tensor access if needed, but t is 1..T # Step 2a: Predict noise # model takes (zt, t) and outputs predicted noise epsilon epsilonpred = model(z, t) # Step 2b: Compute coefficients # alphatbar is alphascumprod[t] alphatbar = alphascumprod[t] alphat = alphas[t] # Coefficient for zt coeff1 = 1.0 / math.sqrt(alphatbar) # Coefficient for epsilonpred # (1 - alphatbar) / sqrt(1 - alphatbar) = sqrt(1 - alphatbar) coeff2 = (1.0 - alphatbar) / math.sqrt(1.0 - alphatbar) # Step 2c: Compute mean mu = coeff1 (z - coeff2 epsilonpred) # Step 2d: Add noise if t > 1: # Variance sigmat^2 = (1 - alpha{t-1}) / (1 - alphat) (1 - alphat) / alphat # Simplifies to: (1 - alpha{t-1}) / alphat alphaprev = alphascumprod[t-1] sigmasq = (1.0 - alphaprev) / alphat sigma = torch.sqrt(sigmasq) noise = torch.randnlike(z) z = mu + sigma noise else: # No noise at the final step z = mu return z A variant that configures the DDPM scheduler for single-step inference by setting timesteps to 1 and moving alphascumprod to CUDA. It loads the scheduler from stabilityai/sd-turbo and sets timesteps to 1 via settimesteps(1, device="cuda"). This reduces generation time significantly but may alter the quality characteristics compared to the standard iterative approach. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of iterations T. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the latent volume size and the model size. Performance: Generating a set of triplane features for a single example takes roughly 20 seconds on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU with 1000 iterations. Decoding the resulting occupancy field and extracting a mesh at 128^3 resolution takes about 5 seconds per mesh, including MLP evaluation and marching cubes. Strengths: Produces high-fidelity 3D shapes; allows for interpolation (though DDIM is preferred for interpolation, DDPM is used for generation). Limitations: Slow generation time due to iterative nature; reducing iterations to 250 causes a small visual fidelity reduction. The method originates from "3D Neural Field Generation Using Triplane Diffusion", which introduced the use of DDPM to generate triplane features for 3D shape synthesis. The approach leverages the stability of DDPM sampling over DDIM for final shape generation, despite DDIM's faster convergence, due to better visual quality. 3D Neural Field Generation Using Triplane Diffusion, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.02000, fetched 2026-10-26 nv-tlabs/Difix3D, https://github.com/nv-tlabs/Difix3D, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Sharf
head: ShaRF, Shape-aware Radiance Fields
body: Sharf (Shape-aware Radiance Fields) generates novel 3D shapes and high-fidelity novel views by combining a generative model of voxelized shapes with a conditional neural radiance field (NeRF). It addresses the limitation of standard NeRFs, which represent a single static scene, by enabling the synthesis of diverse object instances within a category. Unlike sibling methods that may use continuous latent deformations or template-based approaches, Sharf explicitly discretizes shape generation into a voxel grid, which then conditions the radiance field for rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A shape latent code zs and an appearance latent code za. Output: A rendered image of a novel view of a generated 3D object. Data Structures: 1. Shape Latent Code (zs): A vector sampled from a learned distribution representing the geometric structure. 2. Appearance Latent Code (za): A vector representing visual properties (color, texture) independent of shape. 3. Voxel Grid: A 3D grid representing the occupancy of the object. The resolution is determined by the shape network's output. 4. NeRF Network: A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) that outputs color and density. Steps: 1. Shape Generation: A shape network (encoder/decoder or generator) maps the shape latent code zs into a 3D voxel grid V. This grid represents the occupancy of the object in the category. 2. Conditioning: The NeRF network is conditioned on two factors: The occupancy value o(x) estimated from the voxel grid V at the query point x. The appearance latent code za. 3. Rendering: The conditioned NeRF is rendered using standard volume rendering techniques to produce the final image. Formulas: The occupancy o(x) is derived from the voxel grid V. The NeRF function F\theta takes position x, viewing direction d, occupancy o(x), and appearance code za: (c, \sigma) = F\theta(x, d, o(x), za) where c is color and \sigma is density. Parameters: Resolution of the voxel grid: Not given in the sources. Dimension of latent codes: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discretization Artifacts: The voxel grid introduces discretization errors, potentially leading to jagged surfaces if the resolution is insufficient. Conditioning Consistency: The occupancy value must be accurately estimated from the voxel grid to ensure the NeRF renders the correct shape. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shaRFrender(shapelatentcode, appearancelatentcode, cameraparams): # Step 1: Generate voxel grid from shape latent code # Shape network maps zs to a 3D voxel grid V voxelgrid = shapenetwork(shapelatentcode) # Step 2: Define the conditioned NeRF # The NeRF takes position, direction, occupancy, and appearance code def neRF(position, direction): # Get occupancy from voxel grid at position occupancy = getoccupancyfromvoxelgrid(voxelgrid, position) # NeRF predicts color and density conditioned on occupancy and appearance color, density = neRFnetwork(position, direction, occupancy, appearancelatentcode) return color, density # Step 3: Render using volume rendering # Cast rays through cameraparams and integrate along rays image = volumerender(neRF, cameraparams) return image Uses a Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) to generate voxelized shapes. The goal is to learn a parameterized Markov chain that generates novel samples after finite time steps. [18300-ddpm-sampling-at-inference.md] Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables high-fidelity novel view synthesis by leveraging the explicit shape representation of the voxel grid. Limitations: The reliance on voxel grids may limit resolution and introduce discretization artifacts. When to use: When generating diverse 3D shapes within a category and requiring high-quality novel views. When not to use: When continuous, high-resolution shape representation is required without discretization artifacts. Sharf was introduced by [RMBF21] as a method to generate voxelized shapes of objects in a category, which condition a higher resolution neural radiance field for novel view synthesis. It builds on the idea of using latent codes to represent 3D structures, extending it to include explicit voxel-based shape generation. name: Voxel Operations and Tests
body: Voxel Operations and Tests provide the fundamental mechanisms for querying, modifying, and combining discrete volumetric data structures after they have been generated. While parent methods like Voxelization focus on mapping continuous sources into a grid, this family addresses how to interact with that grid: checking spatial containment, transferring data blocks, and performing boolean or arithmetic logic on voxel values. This family is distinct from generation techniques as it operates on the resulting data structure, enabling tasks such as collision detection, multi-field visualization, and volume editing. All methods in this family operate on a discrete 3D grid representation where each voxel is addressed by integer indices (i, j, k) corresponding to a spatial domain. The core mechanism involves: 1. Indexing and Addressing: Mapping continuous coordinates or block identifiers to discrete grid locations. Implementers must handle coordinate system conventions (e.g., XYZ vs ZYX) and boundary conditions (e.g., inclusive vs exclusive bounds). 2. Data Access and Type Handling: Reading or writing voxel values, which may be stored in various formats (e.g., single-channel occupancy, multi-channel RGBA, or multi-component vectors). Implementers must handle type conversions (e.g., integer to float, byte to short). 3. Spatial Logic: Applying geometric or logical rules to determine voxel states. This includes binary operations on sets of single-field features and block-based operations like union or Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG). Determines whether query points lie within occupied voxels of a pre-computed voxel grid. It solves the problem of spatial containment checking for point clouds or particle systems against a discrete volumetric representation. Unlike sibling methods that may use spatial acceleration structures or kernel approximations, this method performs a direct geometric containment check against the voxel grid's occupancy mask [1281-voxel-occupancy-test.md]. Definition: A technique to voxelize surface meshes for volume rendering and boolean operations to create occlusion-free multi-field visualizations. Usage: Used to perform binary operations on sets of single-field features in multi-field visualization. Definition: A 3D counterpart to bitblt operations, supporting the transfer of cuboidal voxel blocks with voxel-by-voxel operations between source and destination blocks. Step: Perform block-based operations on neighboring voxels during the voxelization stage. Definition: Helper functions to read and write voxel data from osg::Image objects, including boundary checks and type conversion. Step: setVoxel: Check if color is < 0 (set to 0) or > 255 (print warning). Check if pos is inside the image. Set data[0] to (unsigned char)color. Pitfall: Data Type Handling: getVoxel(osg::Vec3f pos) handles both GLUNSIGNEDBYTE and GLUNSIGNEDSHORT data types, reading intensity and occlusion from data[0] and data[1] respectively. The concept of voxel operations stems from the early days of volume visualization and computer graphics, where raster-based volume representations were first explored. Arie Kaufman's work on volume visualization principles highlights the utility of rasters for block-based operations like voxblt and Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG). More recently, techniques for multi-field visualization have utilized voxelization for boolean operations to handle complex acoustic simulations. Implementation details for data access are often found in open-source visualization toolkits like OpenSceneGraph (OSG). name: Voxel Occupancy Test
head: Voxel Mask, Voxel Mask Output
body: The Voxel Occupancy Test determines whether continuous query points lie within occupied voxels of a discrete 3D grid, producing a binary mask. It operates on a pre-constructed voxel grid structure rather than explicit axis-aligned bounds. Inputs: 1. An array of query points P with shape (N, 3), where each row is a continuous coordinate (x, y, z). Outputs: 1. A boolean array or binary UInt8 mask M of length N, where M[i] = 1 (or True) if point P[i] is inside an occupied voxel, and 0 (or False) otherwise. Data Structures: A voxel grid data structure representing the spatial domain, typically created from a point cloud or mesh with a defined voxelsize. The occupancy status is stored as a boolean or integer flag per voxel. Steps: 1. Coordinate Mapping: For each query point Pi = (x, y, z), map the continuous coordinates to discrete voxel indices (i, j, k) by subtracting the grid origin and dividing by the voxel size. The specific axis ordering must match the grid's storage convention. 2. Boundary Check: Verify if the computed indices (i, j, k) fall within the valid bounds of the voxel grid. If any component is negative or greater than or equal to the grid dimensions, the point is outside. 3. Occupancy Query: Access the voxel at (i, j, k) in the grid data structure. 4. Result Assignment: If the voxel is marked as occupied, set the corresponding output mask value to 1 (or True); otherwise, set it to 0 (or False). 5. Aggregation: If multiple points map to the same voxel, the mask records the status for each point individually. Duplicate points and multiple points per voxel collapse to a single 1 in a global mask, but the primary test returns per-point results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxeloccupancytest(voxelgrid, querypoints): """ Tests if query points are within occupied voxels. Args: voxelgrid: Object with attributes origin (tuple), voxelsize (float), dimensions (tuple), and isoccupied(i, j, k) method. querypoints: List of tuples or list of lists, shape (N, 3). Returns: mask: List of integers (0 or 1) of length N. """ N = len(querypoints) mask = [0] N origin = voxelgrid.origin vsize = voxelgrid.voxelsize dims = voxelgrid.dimensions for idx in range(N): p = querypoints[idx] # Check for non-finite coordinates if not (math.isfinite(p[0]) and math.isfinite(p[1]) and math.isfinite(p[2])): mask[idx] = 0 continue # Coordinate mapping i = int((p[0] - origin[0]) / vsize) j = int((p[1] - origin[1]) / vsize) k = int((p[2] - origin[2]) / vsize) # Boundary check if i < 0 or i >= dims[0] or j < 0 or j >= dims[1] or k < 0 or k >= dims[2]: mask[idx] = 0 continue # Occupancy query occupied = voxelgrid.isoccupied(i, j, k) # Result assignment if occupied: mask[idx] = 1 return mask Parameters: voxelsize: The side length of a voxel. Typical values depend on the scene scale (e.g., 0.05 in Open3D examples). origin: The world coordinate of the grid's (0,0,0) voxel. Default is often (0,0,0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out-of-Bounds Points: Points outside the destination grid are silently dropped with no warning, resulting in an all-zero mask if the origin or spacing is mismatched. Non-Finite Coordinates: Points with NaN or Inf coordinates are skipped. I/O Performance: If the mask is written in point order, a spatially unsorted cloud produces scattered writes, which is I/O-bound with out-of-core storage; pre-sorting the point cloud spatially helps. Coordinate Mismatch: If the origin or spacing of the query points does not match the voxel grid's geometry, points may be incorrectly classified or dropped. A method to determine if any scene geometry exists inside a voxel, used to flag voxels for subdivision. It differs from standard point-inclusion tests by using rendering techniques to detect geometry presence rather than geometric intersection. It determines if scene geometry intersects a voxel volume. The steps involve sampling scene depth at the voxel corners, where only some cubemap texels are used to test for intersection. Alternatively, it uses occlusion queries by placing the camera at the center of the voxel, rendering into each face of a cubemap (first drawing quads for the voxel faces, then the scene), and checking if any draw calls pass the occlusion query. It should be chosen for adaptive subdivision or irradiance volume computation where geometric presence within a volume is required, rather than point containment. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Fast for batched queries; performance degrades if the point cloud is unsorted and writes are scattered to memory. Strengths: Simple, efficient for point-in-voxel queries; supports batch processing. Limitations: Does not handle partial voxel occupancy (binary only); sensitive to coordinate system mismatches. When to use: When you need to know which points from a cloud lie inside a voxelized representation. When not to use: When you need to know which voxel a point is in for spatial indexing (use Mask Cache Lookup or index generation), or when you need to detect geometry inside a voxel using rendering (use Voxel Contains Scene Geometry Test). The Voxel Occupancy Test is a fundamental operation in voxel-based graphics and geometry processing. It is commonly used in point cloud processing pipelines to convert continuous point data into discrete voxel representations. The method checkifincluded is part of the Open3D library's voxel grid API, which allows testing if points are within an occupied voxel after voxelization. The concept is also used in game development for irradiance volume computation and adaptive subdivision. name: Point-in-Box Inclusion Test
head: Point Array Box Partitioning, annBoxSplit
body: The Point-in-Box Inclusion Test partitions a point array about an orthogonal bounding box, returning the count of points inside or on its boundary. It differs from sibling methods like 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation or Sparse AABB Collision Test by performing a direct, dimension-aware containment check optimized for in-place array partitioning rather than spatial acceleration or kernel approximation. Inputs: PP: An array of N points, where each point Pi has coordinates (xi, yi, zi). box: An axis-aligned bounding box with a method inside(dim, point) that returns true if the point lies within the box bounds along the specified dimension dim. dim: The axis index (0, 1, or 2) to test for containment. Outputs: nin: The number of points inside or on the boundary of the box. The array PP is reordered in-place such that the first nin points satisfy the containment condition, and the remaining points do not. Data Structures: PP is stored as a contiguous block of memory. Each point is a tuple or struct of three floating-point values. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize indices l = 0 and r = n - 1. 2. Loop while l < n and r >= 0: a. Increment l while l < n and box.inside(dim, PP[l]) is true. b. Decrement r while r >= 0 and box.inside(dim, PP[r]) is false. c. If l > r, break the loop. d. Swap PP[l] and PP[r]. e. Increment l and decrement r. 3. Set nin = l. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointinboxinclusiontest(PP, box, dim): """ PP: List of points, each point is a tuple/list of 3 floats (x, y, z). box: Object with method inside(dim, point). dim: Axis index (0, 1, or 2) to test. Returns: (nin, PP) where PP is partitioned in-place. """ n = len(PP) l = 0 r = n - 1 while l < n and r >= 0: while l < n and box.inside(dim, PP[l]): l += 1 while r >= 0 and not box.inside(dim, PP[r]): r -= 1 if l > r: break PP[l], PP[r] = PP[r], PP[l] l += 1 r -= 1 nin = l return nin, PP Parameters: dim: The spatial dimension to test. If not specified, all three dimensions are tested. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point comparisons for boundary inclusion must be consistent to avoid points being counted or missed due to rounding errors. Empty Array: If N=0, the loop condition l < n fails immediately, and nin is 0. All Inside/Outside: If all points are inside, l increments to n and the loop breaks, yielding nin = n. If all are outside, r decrements to -1 and the loop breaks, yielding nin = 0. This method performs point-in-box inclusion tests by pre-sorting point cloud coordinates along each axis and using binary search to determine occupancy. It differs from the parent method by explicitly leveraging sorted index arrays and bisect operations to handle range queries, rather than generic partitioning logic. Choose it when repeatedly querying static point sets for bounding box occupancy, as it reduces the search space to O(\log N) per axis at the cost of O(N \log N) preprocessing. This variant finds the spatial dimension with the largest spread among all dimensions in a point set. It is used to prioritize partitioning along the axis with the greatest variance, improving balance in subsequent hierarchical structures. Time Complexity: O(N) per query for the basic partitioning method, where N is the number of points. The sorted variant requires O(N \log N) preprocessing but O(\log N) per query. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space for the in-place partitioning method. The sorted variant requires O(N) space for indices. Strengths: Simple implementation, low memory overhead, and effective for one-time occupancy checks. Limitations: Linear scan is slow for repeated queries on large static datasets. When to use: Use the basic method for single-pass voxelization or memory-constrained environments. Use the sorted variant for scenes with static geometry and frequent occupancy queries. name: Point-in-Box Inclusion Test via Sorted Indices and Bisect
head: Efficient Voxel Query via Sorted Indices and Bisect, Range Query via Binary Search on Sorted Coordinates
body: This method performs point-in-box inclusion tests by pre-sorting point cloud indices along each axis and using binary search to determine occupancy. It solves the problem of efficiently querying which points lie within an orthogonal bounding box by reducing the search space to O(\log N) per axis. It differs from its parent, Point-in-Box Inclusion Test, by explicitly leveraging sorted index arrays and bisect operations to handle range queries, rather than generic partitioning logic. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N 3D points P = \{p1, \dots, pN\} where pi = (xi, yi, zi), and a query box defined by [x{min}, x{max}] \times [y{min}, y{max}] \times [z{min}, z{max}]. Output: A subset of points P{in} \subseteq P such that pi \in P{in} if and only if x{min} \le xi \le x{max}, y{min} \le yi \le y{max}, and z{min} \le zi \le z{max}. Data Structures: Three arrays of indices sorted by coordinate value are maintained: idxx: Indices of P sorted by x-coordinate. idxy: Indices of P sorted by y-coordinate. idxz: Indices of P sorted by z-coordinate. The corresponding sorted coordinate values are stored in sortedx, sortedy, and sortedz. Note: The provided code snippet in the source does not contain this method; the description relies on the source notes. Steps: 1. Initialization: Extract x, y, and z coordinates from P. Create index arrays [0, \dots, N-1]. Sort each index array based on its corresponding coordinate to form idxx, idxy, idxz. Extract sorted coordinate values into sortedx, sortedy, sortedz. 2. Query Processing: For a query box, use bisect.bisectleft to find the first index in each sorted array where the coordinate is \ge the lower bound, and bisect.bisectright to find the first index where the coordinate is > the upper bound. 3. Intersection: Map the sorted indices back to original point indices for each axis using the index arrays. Compute the set intersection of the three index sets to identify points satisfying all three bounds. 4. Return: Return the points corresponding to the intersected indices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import bisect class VoxelQuery: def init(self, points): """points: list of (x, y, z) tuples or 2D array-like""" self.points = points self.N = len(points) # Pre-sort indices by each coordinate self.idxx = sorted(range(self.N), key=lambda i: points[i][0]) self.idxy = sorted(range(self.N), key=lambda i: points[i][1]) self.idxz = sorted(range(self.N), key=lambda i: points[i][2]) # Extract sorted coordinate values for binary search self.sortedx = [points[i][0] for i in self.idxx] self.sortedy = [points[i][1] for i in self.idxy] self.sortedz = [points[i][2] for i in self.idxz] def getpointsinrange(self, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax): # Find ranges in sorted arrays xlo = bisect.bisectleft(self.sortedx, xmin) xhi = bisect.bisectright(self.sortedx, xmax) ylo = bisect.bisectleft(self.sortedy, ymin) yhi = bisect.bisectright(self.sortedy, ymax) zlo = bisect.bisectleft(self.sortedz, zmin) zhi = bisect.bisectright(self.sortedz, zmax) # Map back to original indices origx = set(self.idxx[xlo:xhi]) origy = set(self.idxy[ylo:yhi]) origz = set(self.idxz[zlo:zhi]) # Intersect sets to find points inside the 3D box finalindices = origx & origy & origz return [self.points[i] for i in finalindices] Note: The source notes describe returning "the slice of points between these indices," which implies a 1D query or a simplified description. The pseudocode implements the standard 3D intersection logic. Parameters: xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax: Float values defining the box boundaries. Edge Cases: Empty point cloud: Return empty set. Box outside point cloud bounds: bisect returns equal bounds, yielding empty slices. Duplicate coordinates: bisectleft and bisectright correctly define inclusive ranges for duplicates. Searchsorted finds the indices where query points v should be inserted into a sorted reference array a to maintain order. It serves as the core lookup mechanism for the parent method, enabling range queries on pre-sorted coordinate arrays. Unlike standard binary search which returns a single insertion point, this vectorized implementation explicitly computes both lower (idxlo) and upper (idxhi) bounds to handle edge cases and range queries robustly. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) for preprocessing (sorting). O(\log N) for each axis query. Total query time is O(\log N + K) where K is the number of candidate points before intersection. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the sorted index and coordinate arrays. Strengths: Fast query times for static point clouds. Simple to implement using standard library bisect functions. Limitations: Preprocessing time is significant for large datasets. Dynamic updates (insertions/deletions) are expensive (O(N)). The source notes do not specify how 3D intersection is handled efficiently beyond the index mapping. When to use: Static point clouds with frequent range queries. When not to use: Dynamic point clouds or when memory is constrained. This method is derived from standard computational geometry techniques for range searching. The specific implementation is referenced in the MasonAndrewHarrison/Point-Cloud-Voxelizer repository. It is used in voxelization pipelines to efficiently determine which points contribute to a voxel grid. name: Searchsorted
body: Searchsorted finds the indices where query points v should be inserted into a sorted reference array a to maintain order. It serves as the core lookup mechanism for the parent method, enabling range queries on pre-sorted coordinate arrays. Unlike standard binary search which returns a single insertion point, this vectorized implementation explicitly computes both lower (idxlo) and upper (idxhi) bounds to handle edge cases and range queries robustly. Inputs: a: Sorted reference points (keys). v: Query points. Outputs: idxlo: Indices of the maximum position in a where v >= a holds. idxhi: Indices of the minimum position in a where v < a holds. Data Structures: a: Array of floats or integers, sorted in ascending order. v: Array of floats or integers, same type as a. i: Index tensor for the last dimension of a. vgea: Boolean mask where v >= a. Steps: 1. Create an index tensor i corresponding to the last dimension of a. 2. Compute a boolean mask vgea where each element is true if the corresponding query point v is greater than or equal to the reference point a. 3. Compute idxlo as the maximum index i where vgea is true, handling out-of-range values. 4. Compute idxhi as the minimum index i where v < a, handling out-of-range values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def searchsorted(key, query): a = np.asarray(key) v = np.asarray(query) # Step 1: Create index tensor i for the last dimension of a i = np.arange(a.shape[-1]) # Step 2: Compute boolean mask vgea where v >= a vgea = v[..., np.newaxis] >= a # Step 3: Compute idxlo as max of indices where v >= a idxlo = np.zeros(v.shape, dtype=np.int64) for idx in np.ndindex(v.shape): valid = np.where(vgea[idx])[0] idxlo[idx] = valid[-1] if len(valid) > 0 else 0 # Step 4: Compute idxhi as min of indices where v < a idxhi = np.full(v.shape, len(a), dtype=np.int64) for idx in np.ndindex(v.shape): valid = np.where(~vgea[idx])[0] idxhi[idx] = valid[0] if len(valid) > 0 else len(a) return idxlo, idxhi Parameters: query: Query values v. key: Key values to search within. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If v is out of the range [a[0], a[-1]], idxlo and idxhi are clamped to the first or last index of a respectively. Specifically, if v < a[0], both are set to 0; if v > a[-1], both are set to len(a). The implementation uses a full comparison mask followed by reduction operations. Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. Strengths include a straightforward vectorized implementation. Limitations involve memory usage scaling with the product of query and reference array sizes due to the comparison mask. When to use it is not given in the sources. head: AdjacentNeighbors, Adjacent Neighbors in Dimension 1 of an Interval
body: This method determines the empty integer intervals immediately adjacent to a query interval I within a sorted collection of existing intervals I1. It returns a pair (Cl, Cr) representing the gap between I and its nearest left neighbor, and the gap between I and its nearest right neighbor, respectively. It is a subroutine for sweep-line algorithms in voxel data compression, distinguishing itself by explicitly handling the discrete integer boundaries and "sign" states of interval endpoints to define strict adjacency gaps. Inputs: I: The query interval, defined as [a, b] where a, b \in \mathbb{R} (typically integers in this context). I1: A sorted array of N intervals \{I1[1], \dots, I1[N]\}. Each interval Ik has a minimum endpoint \min(Ik) and maximum endpoint \max(Ik). Outputs: Cl: The interval strictly between the left endpoint of I and the right endpoint of the nearest left neighbor, or the left endpoint of I itself if no such gap exists. Cr: The interval strictly between the right endpoint of I and the left endpoint of the nearest right neighbor, or the right endpoint of I itself if no such gap exists. Data Structures: I1 is stored as a sorted array. Access to \min(Ik) and \max(Ik) is O(1). The binary search operates on indices 1 to N. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Boundaries: Set imin = \min(I) - 1 and imax = \max(I) + 1. These values define the search targets for the immediate left and right neighbors in the integer domain. 2. Find Left Neighbor (Cl): Perform a binary search for the interval in I1 with an endpoint closest to imin, searching in the -1 direction (left). This returns an interval Il and a sign signl. If signl = +1 (indicating the closest endpoint found was a right endpoint of some interval Il), then a gap exists between Il and I. Set: Cl = [\max(Il) + 1, imin] Else (if signl \neq +1, meaning the closest endpoint was a left endpoint or no valid right endpoint was found to the left), set: Cl = [imin + 1, imin + 1] This represents the single integer point at the left boundary of I. 3. Find Right Neighbor (Cr): Perform a binary search for the interval in I1 with an endpoint closest to imax, searching in the +1 direction (right). This returns an interval Ir and a sign signr. If signr = -1 (indicating the closest endpoint found was a left endpoint of some interval Ir), then a gap exists between I and Ir. Set: Cr = [imax, \min(Ir) - 1] Else (if signr \neq -1, meaning the closest endpoint was a right endpoint or no valid left endpoint was found to the right), set: Cr = [imax - 1, imax - 1] This represents the single integer point at the right boundary of I. 4. Return: Return the pair (Cl, Cr). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adjacentneighbors(I, I1): """ Finds adjacent empty intervals around I in sorted I1. I: tuple (minval, maxval) I1: list of tuples [(min1, max1), (min2, max2),...], sorted by minval Returns: (Cl, Cr) where Cl and Cr are tuples (start, end) """ # Step 1: Initialize boundaries imin = I[0] - 1 imax = I[1] + 1 # Step 2: Find Left Neighbor # Binary search for closest integer key to imin in I1, searching -1 direction Il, signl = binarysearchdim1(0, len(I1) - 1, imin, I1, -1) if signl == 1: # Gap exists between right endpoint of Il and left of I Cl = (Il[1] + 1, imin) else: # No gap, return left endpoint of I Cl = (imin + 1, imin + 1) # Step 3: Find Right Neighbor # Binary search for closest integer key to imax in I1, searching +1 direction Ir, signr = binarysearchdim1(0, len(I1) - 1, imax, I1, 1) if signr == -1: # Gap exists between right of I and left endpoint of Ir Cr = (imax, Ir[0] - 1) else: # No gap, return right endpoint of I Cr = (imax - 1, imax - 1) return (Cl, Cr) def binarysearchdim1(a1, b1, T1, I1, sign): """ Binary search within dimension 1. a1, b1: search range indices [a1, b1] T1: target integer I1: sorted array of intervals sign: -1 (search left) or +1 (search right) Returns: (interval, signo) """ m1 = (a1 + b1) // 2 if sign == -1: signo = -1 # Default to Left Endpoint while a1 < m1: # Check if max of mid interval is strictly less than target if I1[m1][1] < T1: a1 = m1 signo = 1 # Found a right endpoint < T1 # Check if min of mid interval is strictly less than target elif I1[m1][0] < T1: a1 = m1 signo = -1 # Found a left endpoint < T1 else: b1 = m1 m1 = (a1 + b1) // 1 else: # sign == 1 # Implementation for +1 direction mirrors -1 logic # Default to Right Endpoint for right search signo = 1 while a1 < m1: if I1[m1][0] > T1: b1 = m1 signo = -1 # Found a left endpoint > T1 elif I1[m1][1] > T1: b1 = m1 signo = 1 # Found a right endpoint > T1 else: a1 = m1 m1 = (a1 + b1) // 1 # Return the interval I1[m1] (or I1[a1] depending on convergence) # Note: The source pseudocode returns (Il, signl) where Il is the interval found # The exact interval index returned by the loop needs to be resolved. # Based on standard binary search convergence, a1 == b1 == m1 at end. return (I1[a1], signo) Parameters: I: Query interval. I1: Sorted collection of intervals. Typical values: Not specified. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The algorithm relies on integer arithmetic. If I contains non-integer coordinates, \min(I) and \max(I) must be cast or floored/ceiled appropriately before subtracting/adding 1, as the method assumes integer keys. Empty I1: If I1 is empty, the binary search must handle the empty range. The source does not explicitly define the behavior for N=0, but logically Cl and Cr would default to the boundary points of I (the else branches). Sign Logic: The sign signl = +1 specifically indicates that the closest interval to the left ends before imin. If the closest interval starts after imin (a left endpoint), signl is -1, and no gap Cl exists in the traditional sense, so Cl collapses to a point. Time Complexity: O(\log N) for the two binary searches, where N is the number of intervals in I1. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, assuming I1 is provided. Strengths: Efficiently identifies empty gaps for sweep-line processing without iterating through all intervals. Limitations: Requires I1 to be sorted. Relies on discrete integer coordinates. This method is described in the context of compressing voxelized vector field data. It serves as a subroutine for the "Sweep-Line Algorithm 5.2" implementation, specifically for determining adjacent neighboring intervals to facilitate data compression by boxes. name: 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation
head: 3D Binary Sphere Kernel
body: 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation produces binary occupancy masks or synthetic volume data representing a sphere within a voxel grid. It differs from its sibling Point-in-Box Inclusion Test by using a radial distance threshold rather than axis-aligned bounds, and from Voxel Filled Check by explicitly generating the kernel data structure rather than querying an existing one. The method supports two distinct output modes: a static binary occupancy field for general sphere representation and directional entry/exit offset arrays for optimized traversal. Inputs: 1. size: Integer dimension of the cubic kernel grid (N \times N \times N). Default: 3. 2. radius: Floating-point or integer radius of the sphere. Default: 1.0. For sampling masks, rad denotes the radius in voxel units. For world-space generation, radius is in world units and voxelsize converts it to voxel units. 3. direction (optional): A 3D vector (dirx, diry, dirz) specifying the traversal direction for sampling mask generation. 4. voxelsize (optional): Size of each voxel in world units (f32). 5. position (optional): Center of the sphere in voxel grid coordinates (IVec3). Outputs: Mode A (Static Binary): A 3D array of shape (size, size, size) where elements are 1.0 if within the sphere and 0.0 otherwise, with the center element explicitly set to 0. Mode B (Sampling Masks): Two sets of 3D vector offsets: idxadd (entering voxels) and idxremove (leaving voxels), stored as Vec3Array or std::vector<osg::Vec3>. Data Structures: Binary Kernel: float kernel[size][size][size] or uint8t kernel[size][size][size]. Sampling Masks: idxremove/idxadd for left->right, idxu/idxd for down->up, idxf/idxb for front->back. Steps: 1. Initialization: If generating sampling masks: Clear idxremove and idxadd arrays. If generating binary kernel: Initialize a zero-filled volume of shape (size, size, size). 2. Coordinate Generation: Create a linear space from -\lfloor size/2 \rfloor to \lfloor size/2 \rfloor. Generate a 3D meshgrid of coordinates (x, y, z) covering the kernel space. Calculate the center coordinates: cx = cy = cz = \lfloor size/2 \rfloor. For world-space generation, compute radius in voxel units as r = \lceil \text{radius} / \text{voxel\size} \rceil and calculate lefttopcorner as position - radius. 3. Distance Calculation and Masking: Compute the squared radial distance from the center for each voxel: d^2 = (x - cx)^2 + (y - cy)^2 + (z - cz)^2 For Binary Kernel: Set voxel value to 1.0 if d^2 < (size/4)^2 or if d \le radius. Explicitly set the center element (cx, cy, cz) to 0. For Sampling Masks: Iterate through a grid from -rad to rad with a step size of 4 (e.g., x, y, z \in \{-rad, -rad+4, \dots, rad\}). This step size reduces sample count for performance. Let pos = (x, y, z). If direction has an x-component (dirx \neq 0): If x == -rad, add pos to idxremove (leaving face). If x == rad, add pos to idxadd (entering face). If direction has a z-component (dirz \neq 0): If z == -rad, add pos to idxremove. If z == rad, add pos to idxadd. Note: The sources do not specify handling for the y-component (up/down) in the iteration logic, though storage structures idxu/idxd exist. Formulas: Sphere inclusion: x^2 + y^2 + z^2 \le r^2 where r = \lceil \text{radius} / \text{voxel\size} \rceil. Coordinates are shifted by lefttopcorner to align with the voxel grid origin. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Tuple, Union def generatefilledcirclekernel( size: int = 3, radius: Union[int, float] = 1.0, voxelsize: float = 1.0, position: Tuple[int, int, int] = (0, 0, 0), direction: Tuple[float, float, float] = None) -> Union[List[List[List[float]]], Tuple[List[Tuple[int, int, int]], List[Tuple[int, int, int]]]]: """ Generates a 3D filled circle (sphere) kernel. Args: size: Dimension of the cubic grid. radius: Radius of the sphere. voxelsize: Size of each voxel in world units. position: Center of the sphere in voxel grid coordinates. direction: Optional (x, y, z) vector for sampling mask generation. Returns: If direction is None: 3D list of floats (binary kernel). If direction is provided: Tuple of (idxadd, idxremove) lists of (x,y,z) offsets. """ if direction is None: # Mode A: Static Binary Kernel (S3, S4) halfsize = size // 2 kernel = [[[0.0 for in range(size)] for in range(size)] for in range(size)] cx, cy, cz = halfsize, halfsize, halfsize # Use explicit radius if provided, else fallback to size//4 logic from S4 thresholdsq = radius 2 if radius != 1.0 else (size // 4) 2 for z in range(size): for y in range(size): for x in range(size): dx, dy, dz = x - cx, y - cy, z - cz if dxdx + dydy + dzdz < thresholdsq: kernel[z][y][x] = 1.0 # Explicitly set center to 0 as per S3 and S4 kernel[cx][cy][cz] = 0.0 return kernel else: # Mode B: Sampling Masks (S1, S2) idxadd = [] idxremove = [] # S1: Compute radius in voxel units rad = math.ceil(radius / voxelsize) lefttopcorner = (position[0] - rad, position[1] - rad, position[2] - rad) dirx, diry, dirz = direction # S2: Iterate with step 4 coords = list(range(-rad, rad + 1, 4)) for x in coords: for y in coords: for z in coords: pos = (x, y, z) if dirx != 0: if x == -rad: idxremove.append(pos) elif x == rad: idxadd.append(pos) if dirz != 0: if z == -rad: idxremove.append(pos) elif z == rad: idxadd.append(pos) return (idxadd, idxremove) Generates a 3D Gaussian kernel for smoothing operations, with the center element explicitly set to zero. It differs from its parent 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation by using a continuous probability density function for weighted smoothing rather than a binary occupancy mask, and from Sphere Carving by providing isotropic decay rather than hard geometric boundaries. Sphere Carving is a voxelization post-processing method that removes solid voxels within a spherical radius from a specified center point in a voxel chunk or Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO). It solves the problem of creating destructible terrain or breakable objects by efficiently identifying and nullifying voxels intersecting a spherical volume. It sets itself apart from its parent 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation by operating on existing occupancy data to remove voxels rather than generating a static binary kernel, and from 3D Binary Sphere Kernel Generation by focusing on the destructive modification of a scene graph rather than kernel synthesis. This method procedurally generates a 3D binary scalar field (density texture) representing a sphere centered at the origin of a voxel grid, specifically designed as input for GPU-based Marching Cubes surface extraction. Unlike static voxelization, this implementation features a time-varying radius that oscillates, creating a dynamic volume. It differs from its parent 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation by explicitly targeting the DensityTexture property of a Marching Cubes component and utilizing a specific oscillating radius formula rather than a static threshold. Deterministic generation of cell write sets for box and sphere shapes, emitting writes in canonical (z, y, x) order. The sphere brush uses spallcore's fixed-point containscellcentre predicate over the shape's cell bounding box to determine included cells. The write set and order are byte-stable, guarded by pinned BLAKE3 digests and confirmed by a brute-force reference over a wider box. Both brushes are verified to touch exactly eight bricks when centred on the corner where eight bricks meet. A cell centre exactly on the sphere radius is included in the write set. Time Complexity: O(N^3) for full grid evaluation, where N is the kernel size. For sampling masks, the step-4 iteration reduces complexity to approximately O((N/4)^3). Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for the binary kernel. Sampling masks store only boundary offsets, requiring significantly less memory. Performance: The step-4 iteration reduces sample count for performance optimization. Strengths: Precomputing offsets optimizes ray casting by avoiding per-ray distance calculations. Limitations: The step-4 approximation may miss voxels or introduce boundary inaccuracies. The center element is explicitly set to 0. When to use: Use for optimizing volume rendering ray casting based on direction and radius. Use binary kernels for synthetic volume testing. The method originates from implementations in volume occlusion editing and rendering optimization, specifically within the volume-occlusion-editor project. The deterministic brush variant is part of the spall project's fixture and edit plan system. Static binary kernel generation is used for synthetic volume testing in reconstruction algorithms and Gaussian smoothing operations. mkmarek/svo-rs, https://github.com/mkmarek/svo-rs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) MPanknin/volume-occlusion-editor, https://github.com/MPanknin/volume-occlusion-editor, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) DanJbk/Plenoxels, https://github.com/DanJbk/Plenoxels, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ayush-chauhan-1202/physics-aware-ct-reconstruction, https://github.com/ayush-chauhan-1202/physics-aware-ct-reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) T03 — Fixture worlds, rays, and integer brushes, https://github.com/deranjer/spall/pull/4, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: 3D Gaussian Kernel Generation
body: Generates a 3D Gaussian kernel for smoothing operations, with the center element explicitly set to zero. It differs from its parent 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation by using a continuous probability density function for weighted smoothing rather than a binary occupancy mask, and from Sphere Carving by providing isotropic decay rather than hard geometric boundaries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: size (integer, kernel dimension), sigma (float, standard deviation). Optional: scale (float, ratio of grid size to AABB dimensions) and c2fparameter (float, width multiplier) if used within a conversion pipeline. Output: A 3D array of shape (size, size, size) containing normalized Gaussian weights with the center element equal to 0. Data Structures: The kernel is stored as a dense 3D array. Steps: 1. Define the coordinate range: Create a linear space from -(size // 2) to size // 2. Let this be vector v of length size. 2. Generate meshgrid: Create a 3D meshgrid of coordinates (x, y, z) from v. 3. Compute radial distance: Calculate the Euclidean distance d from the center (0,0,0) for each element: d = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}. 4. Compute Gaussian values: Calculate the unnormalized weight for each element: w = \exp\left(-\frac{d^2}{2\sigma^2}\right). If c2fmode is 'uniform-gaussian', the effective width is adjusted to scale c2fparameter, which modifies the grid spacing or \sigma. 5. Zero the center: Set the element at the center index (size // 2, size // 2, size // 2) to 0. 6. Normalize: Divide all elements by the sum of all elements to ensure the kernel sums to 1. Parameters: size: Kernel dimension. Default is 3. sigma: Standard deviation. Default is 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generate3dgaussiankernel(size=3, sigma=1.0): """ Generates a 3D Gaussian kernel with the center element set to 0. Args: size (int): The dimension of the cubic kernel. sigma (float): The standard deviation of the Gaussian distribution. Returns: numpy.ndarray: A 3D array of shape (size, size, size) with normalized weights. """ # 1. Create linear space from -(size//2) to size//2 half = size // 2 coords = np.linspace(-half, half, size) # 2. Generate 3D meshgrid of coordinates x, y, z = np.meshgrid(coords, coords, coords, indexing='ij') # 3. Compute radial distance d from center dsquared = x2 + y2 + z2 # 4. Compute Gaussian values: exp(-d^2 / (2sigma^2)) if sigma == 0: kernel = np.zeros((size, size, size)) else: kernel = np.exp(-dsquared / (2 sigma2)) # 5. Set center element to 0 centeridx = half kernel[centeridx, centeridx, centeridx] = 0.0 # 6. Normalize by sum of all elements kernelsum = np.sum(kernel) if kernelsum > 0: kernel = kernel / kernelsum else: kernel = np.zeros((size, size, size)) return kernel Generates spatially distributed light sources using either Poisson disk or uniform sampling, then constructs a luminance field by evaluating scaled multivariate Gaussian probability density functions (PDFs) at query points. It differs from its parent 3D Gaussian Kernel Generation by treating the Gaussian as an emission model for light sources rather than a smoothing kernel, and by supporting spatially varying elliptical covariances via eigen-decomposition. Separable component-wise convolution is a computationally efficient method for applying 3D Gaussian smoothing to volumes represented as decomposed low-rank tensors. It solves the problem of high computational cost and memory usage associated with naively convolving a 3D kernel on a reconstructed full tensor volume. Unlike traditional separated kernel convolution which only exploits kernel separability, this method distributes the convolution across individual vector and matrix components of the decomposed tensor, leveraging the input signal's inherent separability to maintain space compression and reduce time complexity. Time Complexity: O(N^3) where N is the kernel size size, as every element must be computed. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) to store the kernel. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides smooth, isotropic smoothing. Limitations: The center-zero constraint makes it unsuitable for standard blurring where the center should retain maximum weight; it is better suited for edge detection or specific gradient-based operations. Small kernel sizes (e.g., 3x3x3) may not capture long-range dependencies. When to use: When a smoothing kernel with a null center is required for specific volume rendering or voxelization steps. When not to use: For standard image/volume blurring where the center should be the peak. The method is implemented in voxel-based neural rendering and volume processing pipelines.
