name: Elliptical Gaussian Light Source Generation
head: Poisson Disk Light Sampling [S1, unofficial]
body: Generates spatially distributed light sources using either Poisson disk or uniform sampling, then constructs a luminance field by evaluating scaled multivariate Gaussian probability density functions (PDFs) at query points. It differs from its parent 3D Gaussian Kernel Generation by treating the Gaussian as an emission model for light sources rather than a smoothing kernel, and by supporting spatially varying elliptical covariances via eigen-decomposition. Inputs: sourcelocs: jnp.ndarray of shape (numsources, 3), the 3D locations of the light sources. covs: jnp.ndarray of shape (numsources, 3, 3), the covariance matrix for each light source. xs: jnp.ndarray of shape (numpoints, 3), the query points (ray positions) where luminance is evaluated. damp: float, scaling factor for the emission function, default 200. lstype: str, either 'poisson' or 'uniform', determining the sampling strategy for source locations. numsources: int, the number of light sources to generate. seed: int or jax.random.PRNGKey, for reproducibility. Outputs: luminance: jnp.ndarray of shape (numsources, numpoints), the computed luminance values at the query points. Data Structures: self.Us: jnp.ndarray of shape (numsources, 3, 3), the transformation matrix for each source, computed as U = V \Lambda^{-1/2}, where V are eigenvectors and \Lambda are eigenvalues. self.logdets: jnp.ndarray of shape (numsources,), the log determinants of the covariance matrices, computed as \sum \log(\lambdai). Steps: 1. Source Location Generation: If lstype == 'poisson': Initialize a random number generator with seed. Create a Poisson disk sampler with dimension d=3, radius r=0.13, and the initialized generator. Sample 1000 points from the unit cube. If lstype == 'uniform': Initialize a JAX PRNGKey with seed. Sample points uniformly in [0,1]^3 until 500 are collected, then stack the first numsources points. 2. Covariance Generation: Define a base covariance matrix C{base}: C{base} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix} \times 10^{-3} Rotate this base covariance for each source using rotatecov(cov, numsources, seed) to create covs of shape (numsources, 3, 3). 3. Eigen-decomposition (Initialization): Compute eigenvalues vals and eigenvectors vecs of covs using jnp.linalg.eigh(self.covs). Compute inverse square roots of eigenvalues: valsinvs = 1. / vals. Compute transformation matrix Us: Us = Vs \cdot \Lambdas^{-1/2} In code: self.Us = vecs jnp.sqrt(valsinvs)[:, None]. Compute log determinants: \log \det(Cs) = \sum{i=1}^3 \log(\lambda{s,i}) In code: self.logdets = jnp.sum(jnp.log(vals), axis=1). 4. PDF Evaluation: Compute deviations between query points and source locations: \Delta{s,p} = xp - ls In code: devs = xs[:, None,:] - sourcelocs[None,:,:]. Transform deviations using the precomputed Us: \tilde{\Delta}{s,p} = \Delta{s,p} \cdot Us In code: devUs = einsum('jnk,nki->jni', devs, Us). Compute Mahalanobis distances (squared): D^2{s,p} = \|\tilde{\Delta}{s,p}\|^2 = \sum{k=1}^3 (\tilde{\Delta}{s,p,k})^2 In code: mahas = sum(square(devUs), axis=2). Compute log PDF for each source-point pair: \log \text{PDF}{s,p} = -\frac{1}{2} \left( d \log(2\pi) + D^2{s,p} + \log \det(Cs) \right) In code: out = -0.5 (dim log(2pi) + mahas + logdets[None,:]). Here d=3. Return the final luminance: L{s,p} = \frac{1}{\text{damp}} \exp(\log \text{PDF}{s,p}) In code: return exp(out.T) / damp. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp import jax.random as random from scipy.stats import qmc def generatesourcelocations(lstype, numsources, seed): if lstype == 'poisson': rng = random.PRNGKey(seed) engine = qmc.PoissonDisk(d=3, radius=0.13, seed=rng) sourcelocs = engine.random(1000) elif lstype == 'uniform': rng = random.PRNGKey(seed) points = [] while len(points) < numsources: batch = random.uniform(rng, (500, 3), minval=0, maxval=1) points.append(batch) sourcelocs = jnp.concatenate(points)[:numsources] else: raise ValueError("lstype must be 'poisson' or 'uniform'") return sourcelocs def rotatecov(cov, numsources, seed): rng = random.PRNGKey(seed) randommatrices = random.normal(rng, (numsources, 3, 3)) Q, = jnp.linalg.qr(randommatrices) Q = Q jnp.sign(jnp.linalg.det(Q))[:, None, None] covs = jnp.einsum('nij,njk,nkl->nil', Q, cov, Q) return covs def ellipticalgaussianlightsource(xs, sourcelocs, covs, damp=200.0): numsources = sourcelocs.shape[0] dim = 3 vals, vecs = jnp.linalg.eigh(covs) valsinvs = 1.0 / vals Us = vecs jnp.sqrt(valsinvs)[:, None,:] logdets = jnp.sum(jnp.log(vals), axis=1) devs = xs[:, None,:] - sourcelocs[None,:,:] devUs = jnp.einsum('jnk,nki->jni', devs, Us) mahas = jnp.sum(devUs 2, axis=2) out = -0.5 (dim jnp.log(2 jnp.pi) + mahas + logdets[None,:]) return jnp.exp(out.T) / damp Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-positive eigenvalues: Covariance matrices must be positive semi-definite. If eigenvalues are zero or negative, the log determinant and inverse square root will fail or produce NaNs. A guard vals = jnp.maximum(vals, 1e-8) is recommended. Numerical stability: Computing exp(logpdf) directly can lead to underflow. Using logsumexp or explicit summation before exponentiation is recommended. Damping factor: The damp parameter scales the final luminance. A value of 200 is used in the source. Code discrepancy: The source code returns exp(out.T) / damp, yielding a (numsources, numpoints) matrix, whereas the definition specifies summing PDFs over sources. Implementations should sum over the source dimension to match the emission model definition. A method to simulate elliptical light sources by summing multivariate Gaussian probability density functions (PDFs) evaluated at ray positions. It uses precomputed eigen-decomposition of covariance matrices for efficient vectorized evaluation. It is implemented in the LightSourcesCov class in the source code. Not given in the sources. Implemented in the rtnf repository. The method is part of a neural radiance field (NeRF) based approach for volume rendering, specifically for generating light sources within the volume. It builds on 3D Gaussian Kernel Generation by adapting the Gaussian kernel for emission rather than smoothing. brandonyzhao/rtnf, https://github.com/brandonyzhao/rtnf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Separable Component-Wise Convolution
head: Decomposed Low-Rank Tensor Convolution, Separable component-wise convolution on decomposed low-rank tensor
body: Separable Component-Wise Convolution is a method for applying 3D Gaussian smoothing to decomposed low-rank tensor volumes without reconstructing the full 3D grid, thereby preserving space compression. It solves the problem of high computational and memory costs associated with naive 3D convolution on dense volumes by leveraging the algebraic structure of the tensor decomposition. Unlike traditional separated kernel convolution which only separates the kernel and requires sequential 1D convolutions on the full 3D volume, this method convolves individual vector and matrix components separately, reducing time complexity from O(I \cdot J \cdot K \cdot LN^3) to O(I \cdot J \cdot LN + J \cdot K \cdot LN + K \cdot I \cdot LN). Inputs: Decomposed low-rank tensor volume T with rank R. Tensor dimensions I, J, K along axes X, Y, Z. Gaussian standard deviation \sigma. Kernel size parameter LN. Outputs: Convoluted tensor components \tilde{v}{\sigma,r} and \tilde{M}{\sigma,r}. Density field \tilde{F}\sigma(x) and spectral restricted color field \vec{F}c(x, \vec{d}). Data Structures: The decomposed tensor consists of: Vector components: vr^X \in \mathbb{R}^I, vr^Y \in \mathbb{R}^J, vr^Z \in \mathbb{R}^K for r=1 \dots R. Matrix components: Mr^{Y,Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{J \times K}, Mr^{X,Z} \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times K}, Mr^{X,Y} \in \mathbb{R}^{I \times J} for r=1 \dots R. Color basis vectors: br \in \mathbb{R}^G for r=1 \dots R (used for color field reconstruction). Steps: 1. Generate 1D Gaussian Kernel: Create a 1D kernel N{1d}(\sigma) of size LN. Sample from the continuous Gaussian distribution and clamp values to a maximum of 1.0. N{1d}(\sigma)x = \begin{cases} \min\left(1, \sqrt{2\pi}\sigma \cdot e^{-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}}\right) & \text{if } \sigma > 0.0001 \\ \delta[x] & \text{if } \sigma < 0.001 \end{cases} where x ranges from -LN/2 to LN/2, and \delta[x] is the discrete impulse function (1 at center, 0 elsewhere). 2. Generate 2D Gaussian Kernel: Compute the 2D kernel N{2d}(\sigma) as the outer product of the 1D kernel with itself: N{2d}(\sigma) = N{1d}(\sigma) \otimes N{1d}(\sigma) where \otimes denotes the outer product. 3. Convolve Vector Components: Apply 1D Gaussian convolution ({1d}) using N{1d}(\sigma) to each vector component: \tilde{v}{\sigma,r} = N{1d}(\sigma) {1d} vr This produces convoluted vectors \tilde{v}{\sigma,r}^X, \tilde{v}{\sigma,r}^Y, \tilde{v}{\sigma,r}^Z. 4. Convolve Matrix Components: Apply 2D Gaussian convolution ({2d}) using N{2d}(\sigma) to each matrix component: \tilde{M}{\sigma,r} = N{2d}(\sigma) {2d} Mr This produces convoluted matrices \tilde{M}{\sigma,r}^{Y,Z}, \tilde{M}{\sigma,r}^{X,Z}, \tilde{M}{\sigma,r}^{X,Y}. 5. Reconstruct Convolved Tensor: Combine the individually convoluted components to form the convoluted tensor \tilde{T}\sigma: \tilde{T}\sigma = \sum{r=1}^{R} \left( \tilde{v}{\sigma,r}^X \otimes \tilde{M}{\sigma,r}^{Y,Z} + \tilde{v}{\sigma,r}^Y \otimes \tilde{M}{\sigma,r}^{X,Z} + \tilde{v}{\sigma,r}^Z \otimes \tilde{M}{\sigma,r}^{X,Y} \right) where \otimes denotes the outer product between the vector and matrix components along their respective axes. 6. Compute Fields: Density Field: Sample linearly from \tilde{T}\sigma: \tilde{F}\sigma(x) = \tilde{T}\sigma(x) Color Field: For color, combine convoluted components with basis vectors br to form \tilde{T}c, then apply spectral function S: \tilde{T}c = \sum{r=1}^{R} \left( \tilde{v}{c,r}^X \otimes \tilde{M}{c,r}^{Y,Z} \otimes br + \tilde{v}{c,r}^Y \otimes \tilde{M}{c,r}^{X,Z} \otimes br + \tilde{v}{c,r}^Z \otimes \tilde{M}{c,r}^{X,Y} \otimes br \right) \vec{F}c(x, \vec{d}) = S(\tilde{T}c(x), \vec{d}). Parameters: LN: Size of the discrete Gaussian kernel in each dimension. \sigma: Standard deviation of the Gaussian kernel. When \sigma < 0.001, use discrete impulse \delta to avoid numerical instability. Kernel Scale Factor: Randomly sampled from uniform distribution [0, 1] to mitigate weak/noisy gradients. Pitfalls: Naive 3D convolution (N{3d} {3d} T\sigma) requires reconstructing the full 3D volume, destroying space compression and increasing time complexity to O(I \cdot J \cdot K \cdot LN^3) and space complexity to O(I \cdot J \cdot K). Traditional separated kernel convolution separates the kernel but not the input signal, requiring three sequential 1D convolutions on the full 3D volume with time complexity O(I \cdot J \cdot K \cdot LN) and space complexity O(I \cdot J \cdot K). A separable 3D convolution method using Gaussian diffusion kernels, implemented via Dr.Jit's dr.convolve function for tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing simulations. It builds on Separable Component-Wise Convolution by applying specific Gaussian diffusion kernels rather than generic low-rank tensor decompositions. Time Complexity: Computing convoluted components is O(I \cdot J \cdot LN + J \cdot K \cdot LN + K \cdot I \cdot LN), assuming 2D Gaussian convolution on matrix components is separated into 1D Gaussian convolutions. Each query sample is O(R). Space Complexity: O(R \cdot (IJ + JK + KI)) for storing the decomposed components and their convolved versions, significantly less than the O(I \cdot J \cdot K) required for full volume reconstruction. Performance: Drastically reduces computation required for filtering 3D radiance fields compared to naive or traditional methods. Strengths: Preserves space compression of decomposed low-rank tensors; computationally efficient for large volumes; enables coarse-to-fine training schedules. Limitations: Requires the input to be in decomposed low-rank tensor format; relies on the validity of the component-wise convolution identity (Theorem 4). When to use: When applying Gaussian smoothing to decomposed low-rank tensor volumes (e.g., TensoRF) for spectrum limiting in radiance field optimization. When not to use: When the data is not in decomposed low-rank tensor format, or when full 3D convolution is explicitly required for non-separable operations. The method was proposed in the context of improving robustness for joint optimization of camera pose and decomposed low-rank tensorial radiance fields, specifically addressing issues with inaccurate poses and suboptimal reconstruction quality. It was introduced in the paper "Improving Robustness for Joint Optimization of Camera Pose and Decomposed Low-Rank Tensorial Radiance Fields" published at AAAI-24. The method leverages the separability of the decomposed low-rank tensor structure to perform efficient 3D Gaussian convolution, avoiding the need to reconstruct the full 3D volume. name: Dr. TVAM Convolution
head: Separable 3D Convolution with Gaussian Diffusion Kernels
body: A separable 3D convolution method using Gaussian diffusion kernels, implemented via Dr.Jit's dr.convolve function for tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing simulations. It builds on Separable Component-Wise Convolution by applying specific Gaussian diffusion kernels rather than generic low-rank tensor decompositions. Inputs: Volumetric data tensor r (shape: Nz \times Nx \times Ny). Spatial spacing per axis: sz, sx, sy. Kernel radius per axis: Rz, Rx, Ry (default 10). Diffusion coefficient: D. Time step: \Delta t. Outputs: Convolved volumetric data tensor r'. Data Structures: 1D Gaussian kernel arrays kz, kx, ky of length 2R + 2 for each axis. Steps: 1. Generate 1D Gaussian Diffusion Kernel: For each axis a \in \{z, x, y\} with spacing sa and radius Ra: a. Create index array i ranging from -Ra to Ra + 1. b. Compute coordinates: ci = i \cdot sa. c. Compute unnormalized kernel values: gi = \exp\left(-\frac{ci^2}{4 D \Delta t}\right). d. Normalize: k{a,i} = \frac{gi}{\sum{j=-Ra}^{Ra+1} gj}. 2. Apply Separable Convolution: The 3D convolution is decomposed into three sequential 1D convolutions along each axis using the generated kernels. a. Convolve along Z-axis: r^{(1)} = \text{dr.convolve}(r, \text{filter}=kz, \text{filter\radius}=Rz, \text{axis}=0). b. Convolve along X-axis: r^{(2)} = \text{dr.convolve}(r^{(1)}, \text{filter}=kx, \text{filter\radius}=Rx, \text{axis}=1). c. Convolve along Y-axis: r' = \text{dr.convolve}(r^{(2)}, \text{filter}=ky, \text{filter\radius}=Ry, \text{axis}=2). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import drjit as dr def generategaussiankernel1d(radius, spacing, diffusionD, deltat): """Generates a 1D Gaussian diffusion kernel matching the source specification.""" indices = dr.arange(dr.int32, 2 radius + 2) - radius coords = indices spacing exponent = -(coords coords) / (4.0 diffusionD deltat) values = dr.exp(exponent) kernel = values / dr.sum(values) return kernel def drtvamconvolution(volume, spacingz, spacingx, spacingy, diffusionD, deltat, radiusz=10, radiusx=10, radiusy=10): """Performs separable 3D convolution with Gaussian diffusion kernels.""" kernelz = generategaussiankernel1d(radiusz, spacingz, diffusionD, deltat) kernelx = generategaussiankernel1d(radiusx, spacingx, diffusionD, deltat) kernely = generategaussiankernel1d(radiusy, spacingy, diffusionD, deltat) rtemp1 = dr.convolve(volume, filter=kernelz, filterradius=radiusz, axis=0) rtemp2 = dr.convolve(rtemp1, filter=kernelx, filterradius=radiusx, axis=1) rout = dr.convolve(rtemp2, filter=kernely, filterradius=radiusy, axis=2) return rout Parameters: spacingz, spacingx, spacingy: Spatial spacing for each axis in the kernel coordinate calculation. radiusz, radiusx, radiusy: Kernel radius for each axis. Default value is 10. diffusionD: Diffusion coefficient. deltat: Time step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The exponential function may underflow for large negative exponents, resulting in zero weights. This is handled by the normalization step, but extremely small values might lead to numerical instability if not handled by the underlying dr.convolve implementation. Boundaries: The dr.convolve function must handle boundary conditions. The sources do not specify the boundary handling mode (e.g., zero-padding, replication, reflection). Standard practice in such simulations often uses zero-padding or reflection, but the exact behavior depends on the Dr.Jit implementation. Degenerate Input: If diffusionD or deltat is zero, the exponent becomes undefined or infinite. The sources do not specify handling for these cases. A 3D Gaussian filter implemented as three consecutive 1D filters to leverage separability for interactive performance. It serves as a low-pass filter that reduces high-frequency elements in volume data, often used to compute spatial importance maps for volume illustration. It sets itself apart from non-linear alternatives like the Bilateral Filter by relying solely on spatial distance rather than value similarity, making it computationally faster but less effective at edge preservation. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R), where N is the number of voxels and R is the kernel radius. This is significantly faster than the O(N \cdot R^3) complexity of a non-separable 3D convolution. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the input and output volumes, plus O(R) for the temporary kernels. Strengths: Computational efficiency due to separability; suitability for tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing simulations. Limitations: Requires the kernel to be separable (Gaussian kernels are separable); performance depends on the efficiency of the underlying dr.convolve implementation. When to Use: When performing tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing simulations where Gaussian diffusion is a valid model for the physical process. When Not to Use: When the kernel is not separable or when non-Gaussian diffusion models are required. The method originates from research on tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing simulations. It was developed to efficiently simulate the physical forward model in these simulations by applying Gaussian diffusion kernels to volumetric data. name: Separable 3D Gaussian Filter
head: 3D Gaussian Filter via Separable 1D Filters, Gaussian filter
body: A 3D Gaussian filter implemented as three consecutive 1D filters to leverage separability for interactive performance. It serves as a low-pass filter to reduce high-frequency elements in volume data, often used to compute spatial importance maps for volume illustration. It is distinguished from its parent, Dr. TVAM Convolution, by its specific application in illustrative volume rendering pipelines rather than tomographic additive manufacturing simulations, and from its sibling, 3D Gaussian Smoothing, by its explicit decomposition into axis-aligned passes rather than a binomial approximation via texture sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume V of dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Output: A filtered 3D scalar volume V{filtered} and a difference volume V{diff} (optional, used for edge enhancement). Data Structures: The volume is stored as a contiguous array or 3D texture. The 1D Gaussian kernel G(x) is defined by the standard deviation \sigma. Formulas: The 1D Gaussian function is defined as: G(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}} where x is the distance from the origin and \sigma is the standard deviation. The 3D Gaussian is the product of three 1D Gaussians, one per direction. Parameters: \sigma: Standard deviation of the Gaussian distribution. R: Filter radius. The sampling rate is controlled by specifying the number of standard deviations spanning the filter radius, allowing frequency adjustment without changing the radius. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Table 1 in lists radii R for specific datasets but does not specify the corresponding \sigma or the exact number of standard deviations used. Steps: 1. Axis 1 Convolution: Apply 1D Gaussian convolution along the first axis (e.g., X). For each voxel (i, j, k), compute the weighted sum of neighbors along the X-axis using the kernel G(x). 2. Axis 2 Convolution: Apply 1D Gaussian convolution along the second axis (e.g., Y) to the result of step 1. 3. Axis 3 Convolution: Apply 1D Gaussian convolution along the third axis (e.g., Z) to the result of step 2. 4. Subtraction: Subtract the original volume from the filtered volume to obtain the difference (high-frequency component). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def separable3dgaussianfilter(volume, sigma, radius): """ Applies a separable 3D Gaussian filter and returns the filtered volume and the difference. Args: volume: 3D array of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz) sigma: Standard deviation of the Gaussian kernel radius: Filter radius in voxels Returns: filteredvolume: 3D array after 3D Gaussian blur differencevolume: 3D array (filteredvolume - volume) """ # Define 1D Gaussian kernel # Kernel size is 2 radius + 1 kernelsize = 2 radius + 1 kernel = [] for i in range(-radius, radius + 1): x = i val = (1.0 / (math.sqrt(2 math.pi) sigma)) math.exp(-(x2) / (2 sigma2)) kernel.append(val) # Normalize kernel to sum to 1 kernelsum = sum(kernel) kernel = [k / kernelsum for k in kernel] # Step 1: Convolve along X axis # Create a temporary volume for intermediate results tempvolumex = copy(volume) for z in range(volume.shape[2]): for y in range(volume.shape[1]): for x in range(volume.shape[0]): sumval = 0.0 for kidx, kval in enumerate(kernel): neighborx = x + (kidx - radius) # Handle boundary conditions (e.g., clamp or wrap) if 0 <= neighborx < volume.shape[0]: sumval += volume[neighborx, y, z] kval tempvolumex[x, y, z] = sumval # Step 2: Convolve along Y axis tempvolumey = copy(tempvolumex) for z in range(volume.shape[2]): for y in range(volume.shape[1]): for x in range(volume.shape[0]): sumval = 0.0 for kidx, kval in enumerate(kernel): neighbory = y + (kidx - radius) if 0 <= neighbory < volume.shape[1]: sumval += tempvolumex[x, neighbory, z] kval tempvolumey[x, y, z] = sumval # Step 3: Convolve along Z axis filteredvolume = copy(tempvolumey) for z in range(volume.shape[2]): for y in range(volume.shape[1]): for x in range(volume.shape[0]): sumval = 0.0 for kidx, kval in enumerate(kernel): neighborz = z + (kidx - radius) if 0 <= neighborz < volume.shape[2]: sumval += tempvolumey[x, y, neighborz] kval filteredvolume[x, y, z] = sumval # Step 4: Subtract original volume differencevolume = copy(filteredvolume) for z in range(volume.shape[2]): for y in range(volume.shape[1]): for x in range(volume.shape[0]): differencevolume[x, y, z] = filteredvolume[x, y, z] - volume[x, y, z] return filteredvolume, differencevolume Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary conditions: The pseudocode above uses clamping. Other methods may use reflection or zero-padding. The source does not specify the boundary handling method. Precision: Floating-point precision should be sufficient for the exponential calculation. Radius and Sigma relationship: The radius must be chosen large enough to capture the significant part of the Gaussian distribution. A common rule of thumb is R \ge 3\sigma, but the source notes that the sampling rate can be altered by specifying the number of standard deviations spanning the radius. A non-linear filter used to reduce noise while preserving edges by weighting pixels based on both spatial proximity and value similarity. Unlike the Separable 3D Gaussian Filter which only uses spatial distance, the Bilateral filter also uses value similarity, preserving edges better. 3D Gaussian Smoothing is a voxelization post-processing technique that convolves a spectral cube with a 3D Gaussian distribution to reduce noise and provide smoother transitions than box filters. It is distinguished from its sibling, the Bilateral Filter, by its reliance on spatial proximity for weighting rather than intensity differences, and from its parent, the Separable 3D Gaussian Filter, by its specific implementation using a binomial approximation via bilinear texture sampling to minimize texture fetches. Time and Memory Complexity: Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R), where N is the number of voxels and R is the filter radius. Due to separability, the complexity is O(3 \cdot N \cdot R) instead of O(N \cdot R^3) for a direct 3D convolution. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the input and output volumes, plus O(R) for the kernel. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Interactive performance due to separability and GPU implementation. Provides a low-pass filter effect. Limitations: Still requires calculating distances to neighboring data points to determine data frequency and set filter parameters. The choice of \sigma and R affects the result, and the source notes that further investigation is required to determine the functions used to set these parameters. When to Use: When interactive performance is required for volume illustration. When a low-pass filter effect is desired to reduce high-frequency noise. When Not to Use: When edge preservation is critical (consider Bilateral Filter). When a simpler approximation is sufficient and texture sampling is available (consider 3D Gaussian Smoothing). It is used to compute a spatial importance map for volume rendering, which is then used to modulate color and opacity assigned by a transfer function. name: Bilateral Filter
head: Bilateral Filtering, Filtro bilateral
body: A non-linear filter used to reduce noise while preserving edges by weighting pixels based on both spatial proximity and value similarity. Unlike the Separable 3D Gaussian Filter which only uses spatial distance, the Bilateral filter also uses value similarity, preserving edges better. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Image or volume data I, where Ip is the value at location p. Output: The filtered value BF(p) at each location p. Domain: A neighborhood S (typically a square window) centered at p. Data Structures: The filter operates on a grid. No complex data structures are required beyond the input data array and a temporary buffer for the output. Formulas: The bilateral filter output BF(p) is defined as a weighted average of neighboring values: BF(p) = \frac{1}{Wp} \sum{q \in S} G{\sigmas}(\|p - q\|) G{\sigmar}(\|Ip - Iq\|) Iq Where the normalization factor Wp is: Wp = \sum{q \in S} G{\sigmas}(\|p - q\|) G{\sigmar}(\|Ip - Iq\|) The spatial Gaussian kernel G{\sigmas} is defined as: G{\sigmas}(x) = \frac{1}{2\pi\sigmas} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2\sigmas^2}} In the bilateral context, \|p-q\| is the Euclidean distance in spatial coordinates, and \|Ip - Iq\| is the difference in intensity/value. The normalization constant \frac{1}{2\pi\sigma} cancels out in the numerator and denominator, but is retained here for correctness. Parameters: \sigmas: Spatial standard deviation. Controls the decrease in influence based on distance. Typical value: 4. \sigmar: Range standard deviation. Controls the decrease in influence based on value difference. Typical value: 0.2. Steps: 1. For each location p in the output domain: 2. Initialize sum\val = 0 and sum\weight = 0. 3. For each neighbor q in the neighborhood S centered at p: a. Calculate spatial distance ds = \|p - q\|. b. Calculate range difference dr = |Ip - Iq| for scalar data or \|Ip - Iq\| for vector data. c. Compute spatial weight ws = G{\sigmas}(ds). d. Compute range weight wr = G{\sigmar}(dr). e. Compute combined weight w = ws \times wr. f. Update sum\val \leftarrow sum\val + w \times Iq. g. Update sum\weight \leftarrow sum\weight + w. 4. If sum\weight > 0, BF(p) = sum\val / sum\weight; else, BF(p) = Ip. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gaussian(x, sigma): """Compute 1D Gaussian kernel value as defined in.""" return (1.0 / (2.0 math.pi sigma)) math.exp(-(x 2) / (2.0 sigma 2)) def bilateralfilter(image, sigmas, sigmar, windowsize): """ Apply bilateral filter to an image. Args: image: 2D array of pixel values. sigmas: Spatial standard deviation. sigmar: Range standard deviation. windowsize: Size of the square neighborhood (e.g., 5 for a 5x5 window). Returns: Filtered image. """ height, width = image.shape output = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] halfw = windowsize // 2 for y in range(height): for x in range(width): sumval = 0.0 sumweight = 0.0 centerval = image[y][x] for dy in range(-halfw, halfw + 1): for dx in range(-halfw, halfw + 1): ny = y + dy nx = x + dx # Boundary check if 0 <= ny < height and 0 <= nx < width: # Spatial distance (Euclidean) dists = math.sqrt(dx2 + dy2) # Range difference (absolute intensity difference) diffr = abs(image[ny][nx] - centerval) # Weights ws = gaussian(dists, sigmas) wr = gaussian(diffr, sigmar) w = ws wr sumval += w image[ny][nx] sumweight += w if sumweight > 0: output[y][x] = sumval / sumweight else: output[y][x] = centerval return output Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: The neighborhood S may extend outside the image boundaries. The implementation must handle these cases, typically by clamping coordinates or ignoring out-of-bounds pixels. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise if weights are very small, leading to division by zero or NaNs. A small epsilon should be added to the denominator if necessary. Degenerate Input: If \sigmas or \sigmar is zero, the Gaussian becomes a delta function. \sigmas=0 implies only the center pixel contributes. \sigmar=0 implies only pixels with identical intensity contribute. A complex Gaussian blur filter applied to the final LDR MC estimate at every iteration to reduce high-frequency noise, where pixel weights are determined by color similarity of neighboring pixels. It is used in the Exposure Render framework to suppress noise from Monte Carlo simulation of light transport. Unlike the standard bilateral filter which uses a fixed window, this variant blends between reconstructed and original pixels using the lerpC parameter, controlled by the mean running sample variance. As the sample variance decreases, the influence of the KNN filter decreases. It uses a window size of 7x7 pixels. A pitfall is that in the first iteration, noise reduction causes slightly increased blurring. The mean sample variance is computed using a numerically stable algorithm. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K^2) where N is the number of pixels/voxels and K is the window size. The bilateral filter is non-separable, so it cannot be optimized via separable convolution like the Gaussian filter. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the input and output buffers. Performance: The filter runs efficiently on CUDA-enabled hardware. Strengths: Preserves edges while smoothing noise. Effective for reducing high-frequency noise in volume rendering estimates. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than Gaussian filtering due to non-separability. May cause slight blurring in early iterations of progressive rendering. When to use: When edge preservation is critical and noise reduction is needed, such as in final image processing or progressive volume rendering. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The bilateral filter was introduced as a method to reduce noise while preserving edges. It is based on the idea of weighting pixels based on both spatial proximity and value similarity. The source discusses sparse voxel octree compression and global illumination, where the bilateral filter is applied to images to reduce noise. The KNN variant is used in the Exposure Render framework for interactive photo-realistic volume rendering. name: 3D Gaussian Smoothing
head: 3D Gaussian filter, 9-tap Gaussian smoothing, 9-tap filter algorithm, Gaussian Smoothing, N-tap Gaussian kernel, Tap-filter algorithm, binomial filter
body: 3D Gaussian Smoothing is a voxelization post-processing technique that convolves a spectral cube with a 3D Gaussian distribution to reduce noise and provide smoother transitions than box filters. It is distinguished from its sibling, the Bilateral Filter, by its reliance on spatial proximity for weighting rather than intensity differences, and from its parent, the Separable 3D Gaussian Filter, by its specific implementation using a binomial approximation via bilinear texture sampling to minimize texture fetches. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D spectral cube (texture), the current voxel location loc, the original voxel value oVal (before convolution), the cube resolution resolution (dimensions), and a direction vector/matrix defining the axis of lookup. Output: The smoothed value val (RGBA). Data Structures: The method operates on standard 3D array indices and floating-point offsets. The kernel coefficients are precomputed constants derived from the binomial series. Mathematical Foundation: The continuous Gaussian distribution is defined as: G(x, y, z) = A \exp \left( - \left( \frac{(x-x0)^2}{2\sigmax^2} + \frac{(y-y0)^2}{2\sigmay^2} + \frac{(z-z0)^2}{2\sigmaz^2} \right) \right) where \sigmai is linked to the Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM): FWHMi = 2\sqrt{\ln(2)}\sigmai (Note: Source also lists FWHMi = 2\sqrt{2\ln(2)}\sigmai; the standard definition is cited first). To approximate this efficiently, the method uses a discrete binomial filter obtained by cascaded convolution of a kernel [1, 1]. The coefficients for the n-th filter in the series, bn(m), are defined by: bn(m) = [1, 1]^{n} where n denotes n autoconvolutions. These coefficients correspond to the binomial series and can be precomputed using Pascal's triangle. Common isotropic kernel sizes are 5-tap (b4), 9-tap (b8), and 13-tap (b{12}). Algorithm (9-tap case): The 9-tap filter is implemented as a fragment shader kernel that leverages bilinear texture filtering to fetch two voxels at once by sampling at non-center positions, reducing the total number of texture fetches. The number of texture fetches for an N-tap kernel is 3 \times \frac{N-1}{2} + 1. For the 9-tap filter, the specific coefficients and offsets are: coef0 = 0.2270270270 coef1 = 0.3162162162 coef2 = 0.0702702703 off1 = \vec{3}(1/3.846153846) \times \text{direction} off2 = \vec{3}(3/2.307692308) \times \text{direction} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def smooth9tap(cube, oVal, loc, resolution, direction): """ Performs 9-tap Gaussian smoothing on a 3D spectral cube. Args: cube: 3D array or texture object supporting bilinear sampling. oVal: Original voxel value (RGBA) at loc. loc: Current voxel location (vec3). resolution: Spectral cube resolution dimensions (vec3). direction: Rotation matrix or vector to select the axis for lookups. Returns: val: Smoothed RGBA value. """ # Initialize accumulator val = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Precomputed constants for 9-tap binomial filter coef0 = 0.2270270270 coef1 = 0.3162162162 coef2 = 0.0702702703 # Calculate offsets using bilinear sampling strategy # The source uses vec3(1/3.846153846) which is approx 0.26 # and vec3(3/2.307692308) which is approx 1.3 # These offsets allow fetching two voxels per texture lookup via interpolation off1 = vec3(1.0 / 3.846153846) direction off2 = vec3(3.0 / 2.307692308) direction # Step 1: Add center contribution val = val + oVal coef0 # Step 2: Add contributions from off1 positions # Fetch voxel at loc + off1 tempVal = cube.samplebilinear(loc + off1, resolution) val = val + tempVal coef1 # Fetch voxel at loc - off1 tempVal = cube.samplebilinear(loc - off1, resolution) val = val + tempVal coef1 # Step 3: Add contributions from off2 positions # Fetch voxel at loc + off2 tempVal = cube.samplebilinear(loc + off2, resolution) val = val + tempVal coef2 # Fetch voxel at loc - off2 tempVal = cube.samplebilinear(loc - off2, resolution) val = val + tempVal coef2 return val Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: The source does not specify boundary handling (e.g., clamping, wrapping, or reflection) for lookups outside the cube bounds. Implementers must define this behavior. Precision: The coefficients are given to high precision; standard floating-point precision is assumed sufficient. Anisotropy: The source notes that while isotropic kernels are considered for simplicity, anisotropic kernels could use a similar solution. Complexity: The tap-filter algorithm has a complexity of O(N), where N is the number of lookups. In conjunction with ray-tracing, the total algorithm complexity becomes O(NMD), where M is the number of voxels visited by a ray, N is the number of lookups, and D is the dimensionality of the convolution kernel. Texture Fetches: For an N-tap 3D Gaussian kernel, the number of texture fetches per step is 3 \times \frac{N-1}{2} + 1. Performance: Kernel size (e.g., 9-tap) affects rendering speed, but because M and D are small in typical implementations, the slowdown is minor and manageable by modern graphics hardware. Benchmarks on a 1024³ cube showed that without smoothing, frame rates were ~2 fps on some GPUs, while smoothing added a minor slowdown. Strengths: Provides smoother transitions than box filters and effectively denoises spectral cubes, especially when rays traverse the cube at an angle. Limitations: The smoothing effect is purely spatial; it does not preserve edges based on intensity values like the Bilateral Filter. The method is described in the context of real-time colouring and filtering of astronomical spectral cubes using graphics shaders. It builds on the work of Crowley et al. (2002) regarding cascaded convolution of [1,1] kernels and Daniel Rákos's blog post on efficient Gaussian blur with linear sampling, which proposed using bilinear texture filtering to reduce fetch counts. It is used in radio astronomy visualization (e.g., Antennae cube) to improve the visual quality of Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) and Average Intensity Volume Projection (AVIP) renderings. name: 1D Temporal Convolution in Decomposed Space
head: Convolutional Filtering in Decomposed Space, Difference of Gaussian Filter along Time Dimension
body: This method applies convolutional filtering operations directly within a decomposed tensor space, avoiding the computational cost of reconstructing the full-size dataset. It specifically enables filtering along the time dimension without reconstructing multiple time steps, allowing for efficient detection of temporal changes. It differs from its parent Separable Component-Wise Convolution by focusing exclusively on the temporal axis within the decomposed representation, and from its sibling Dr. TVAM Convolution by utilizing a Difference of Gaussian kernel rather than other specific temporal smoothing strategies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of decomposed tensor components representing a 4D volume (3D space + 1D time). Output: Filtered tensor components with temporal variations highlighted or smoothed. Data Structures: The method operates on the low-rank tensor factors. No full 3D grid reconstruction is required during the filtering step. Steps: 1. Identify the temporal dimension within the decomposed tensor structure. 2. Construct a 1D Difference of Gaussian (DoG) kernel along the time axis. 3. Apply the convolution operation directly to the temporal factors of the decomposed tensors. 4. The result represents areas of major change over time or smoothed temporal data, depending on the DoG parameters. Formulas: The specific mathematical formulation for the DoG kernel is not provided in the sources, but the operation is defined as a 1D convolution along the time dimension. Parameters: Kernel Type: 1D Difference of Gaussian. Kernel Size: Not given in the sources. Performance Metric: The filter computation takes less than 2ms for the datasets shown in the source. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Operating in decomposed space requires maintaining numerical stability in the tensor factors during convolution. Boundary Conditions: Standard 1D boundary handling applies to the temporal axis, though specific padding strategies are not detailed. This variant applies a custom 3x3x3 convolution kernel to the full-resolution interlaced volume to produce the final output, weighting newer and closer voxels more heavily. It differs from the pure decomposed temporal method by operating on the reconstructed full-resolution volume and combining spatial and temporal weights. Choose this when full-resolution spatio-temporal smoothing is required despite higher computational cost. Definition: Custom convolution kernel applied to the interlaced volume to produce the final full-resolution volume, weighting newer and closer voxels more heavily. Steps: 1. Apply spatial weights using a 3D Gaussian distribution, giving more importance to closer voxels. 2. Assign temporal weights to every voxel of each A-scan depending on age, giving less relevance to older epochs. Formula: Temporal weight Tw(x, y, \text{epoch}) is calculated as: Tw(x, y, \text{epoch}) = ((y sx + x) - 1 - (\text{epoch} \mod (sx sy))) \mod (sx sy) Where Tw is the temporal weight, sx and sy are strides, x and y are A-scan positions, and \text{epoch} is the current epoch number. Parameters: Kernel size is 3x3x3. Pitfalls: Time-based weights are dynamic and change in each epoch for each A-scan, causing implementation issues. Comparison: Larger kernel sizes did not manage to perform with greater precision in less processing time compared to 3x3x3. Time Complexity: The application of the 1D DoG filter leads to virtually no additional effort, computed in less than 2ms for the datasets shown. Memory Complexity: Operates in decomposed space, avoiding the memory overhead of full-volume reconstruction during filtering. Strengths: High efficiency; allows interactive filtering without reconstructing multiple time steps. Limitations: Specific kernel sizes and precise mathematical parameters for the DoG filter are not provided in the sources. When to use: When temporal filtering is needed on 4D volumetric data represented by tensor decompositions, and full reconstruction is too expensive. This method originates from research on Tensor-Train-based 4D Time-Dependent Volume Rendering. It leverages the linearity of tensor decompositions to enable efficient filtering operations that would otherwise require processing the full-size dataset. For more information on basic filtering operations to decomposed tensors, see [BRSP18] (not listed in sources). name: Sphere Carving
head: Carve Sphere, Iterative Sphere Carving, SVO Sphere Carving, SVO modification, Voxel Destruction via SVO, Voxel Sphere Removal, voxel removal
body: Sphere Carving is a voxel operation that removes solid voxels within a spherical radius from a center point in a chunk, primarily used for destructible terrain scenarios. It differs from its sibling 3D Binary Sphere Kernel Generation, which generates a static binary mask, by actively modifying the voxel grid state (setting voxels to 0/air) and returning metadata about the destruction. It also differs from Voxel Deformation with Spherical Falloff, which uses continuous soft falloff for reversible editing, by performing hard-edged binary removal. Sphere Carving operates on a voxel chunk (or Sparse Voxel Octree node) to remove solid voxels intersected by a query sphere. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: chunk: The voxel data structure to modify. cx, cy, cz: The world-space or local-space center coordinates of the carving sphere. radius: The radius of the sphere to carve. voxsize: The world size of a single voxel (used to convert world radius to grid units). griddim: The dimensions of the voxel grid. Outputs: Modified chunk with solid voxels inside the sphere set to 0 (air). removedcount: The number of solid voxels removed. gibpositions: A list of world positions of the removed voxels, used for spawning debris. Data Structures: Voxel Chunk: A 3D array or sparse structure where each element represents a voxel. A value of 0 typically denotes air/empty space, while non-zero values denote solid material. VoxObject (Contextual): In SVO implementations, the chunk is often part of a VoxObject struct containing origin, rotation, voxsize, griddim, svo (the octree), solidcount, and dirty flags. Steps: 1. Calculate Grid Radius: Convert the world-space radius to grid units. r{grid} = \frac{radius}{vox\size} r2 = r{grid} \times r{grid} 2. Determine Bounding Box: Calculate the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the sphere in grid coordinates, clamped to the grid dimensions [0, grid\dim - 1]. lo(v) = \max(0, \lfloor v - r{grid} \rfloor) hi(v) = \min(grid\dim - 1, \lceil v + r{grid} \rceil) Where v is the center coordinate (cx, cy, cz). 3. Iterate Voxels: Loop through all voxel indices (x, y, z) within the bounding box. 4. Distance Check: For each voxel, calculate the squared distance from the voxel center to the sphere center. dx = x + 0.5 - cx dy = y + 0.5 - cy dz = z + 0.5 - cz dist2 = dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2 If dist2 > r2, continue to the next voxel. 5. Remove Voxel: If the voxel is solid (value \neq 0): Set chunk.set(x, y, z, 0) to remove it. Calculate the world position of the removed voxel. Add the world position to gibpositions. Increment removedcount. 6. Update State: After the loop, if removedcount > 0: Update solidcount by subtracting removedcount. Mark the object/mesh as dirty to trigger a rebuild or update. Return removedcount and gibpositions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spherecarving(chunk, cx, cy, cz, radius, voxsize, griddim): # 1. Calculate grid radius rgrid = radius / voxsize r2 = rgrid rgrid removedcount = 0 gibpositions = [] # 2. Determine bounding box lox = max(0, floor(cx - rgrid)) hix = min(griddim - 1, ceil(cx + rgrid)) loy = max(0, floor(cy - rgrid)) hiy = min(griddim - 1, ceil(cy + rgrid)) loz = max(0, floor(cz - rgrid)) hiz = min(griddim - 1, ceil(cz + rgrid)) # 3. Iterate voxels for z in range(loz, hiz + 1): for y in range(loy, hiy + 1): for x in range(lox, hix + 1): # 4. Distance check dx = (x + 0.5) - cx dy = (y + 0.5) - cy dz = (z + 0.5) - cz dist2 = dxdx + dydy + dzdz if dist2 <= r2: # 5. Remove voxel if solid if chunk.get(x, y, z) != 0: chunk.set(x, y, z, 0) # Calculate world position for gib worldx = (x + 0.5) voxsize worldy = (y + 0.5) voxsize worldz = (z + 0.5) voxsize gibpositions.append((worldx, worldy, worldz)) removedcount += 1 # 6. Update state if removedcount > 0: chunk.solidcount -= removedcount chunk.dirty = True return removedcount, gibpositions Parameters: radius: Radius of the carving sphere. voxsize: World units per voxel. griddim: Power-of-two grid size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Clamping: The bounding box must be strictly clamped to [0, grid\dim - 1] to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Precision: Using squared distances avoids expensive square root operations. Empty Chunks: If the chunk contains no solid voxels, the loop completes with removedcount = 0, and no state update is needed. Voxel Deformation with Spherical Falloff modifies scalar voxel values (typically density) within a spherical region around a 3D hit point to add or remove terrain mass, creating smooth edges for digging or building operations. It differs from Sphere Carving, which removes solid voxels within a binary radius, by using a continuous soft falloff to allow gradual mass modification and reversible editing. It serves as the core mechanism for Voxel Edit Brush Operations, enabling real-time interaction with the density field. This method generates a conservative Signed Distance Function (SDF) for a shape by approximating its geometry with a minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoid. It serves as an alternative to convex polyhedra or oriented bounding boxes within the Sphere Carving pipeline. Unlike convex hulls which require n scalar products for n faces, ellipsoids offer a more compact memory footprint and constant-time evaluation complexity, making them suitable for real-time applications where geometric fidelity is balanced against computational cost. Voxel Edit Brush Operations provide a set of interactive tools (Place, Carve, Fill, Paint) for modifying unbounded 3D voxel grids using world-space spherical or cylindrical selection volumes. The method solves the problem of real-time, view-independent sculpting and material insertion in volumetric data, ensuring consistent behavior across chunk boundaries by addressing voxels via unbounded world-grid coordinates rather than local indices. Unlike parent methods that may rely on sparse structures or offline processing, this approach often utilizes dense 3D textures for mask lookups to enable O(1) per-fragment operations, avoiding the performance penalty of per-fragment analytic SDF evaluations. Procedural Sphere Placement populates a 3D voxel grid with spherical voids (density 0) inside a background field (density 255), using pre-sampled 2D coordinates and random radii. It differs from its parent Sphere Carving by automating the generation of multiple, randomly sized and positioned spheres rather than carving a single defined sphere, and from Voxel Deformation with Spherical Falloff by producing hard-edged binary voids rather than smooth density gradients. Voxel Annihilation removes all solid voxels from the entire SVO grid, used when a hit's effective power is overwhelmingly larger than the object's hp. It iterates through all grid indices (x, y, z) from 0 to griddim. If the voxel at (x, y, z) is solid, it is removed from the SVO, its world position is calculated, and it is added to gibpositions. After the loop, solidcount is set to 0 and dirty is set to true. This method integrates KRS into collision detection by creating empty zones via unbounding spheres and substituting them with physically simulated kernel instances. It creates empty zones by specifying unbounding spheres over subsets of the KRS, skips these regions during sphere tracing, substitutes the subset of the KRS within these empty zones with instances of kernel geometry rendered incrementally, and applies physical simulation to these solid instances. A pitfall is that KRS is not locally controllable. An example is a tree branch breaking by covering the complete tree with an empty sphere and building an identical tree of rigid body branches and leaves independently. This method supports perfect spherical or smooth tunnel generation by subtracting geometric primitives from the terrain using boolean operations. It defines a center point and radius to subtract a sphere, or defines a line to subtract voxels based on distance from the line to create a pill shape (line with spherical ends). Supported boolean operations include sphere subtraction and line/pill subtraction. Time Complexity: The basic voxel iteration is O(r^3) where r is the radius in voxels, as it visits every voxel in the bounding box. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory for loop variables. Returning gibpositions requires O(k) memory where k is the number of removed voxels. Source returns only the removal count. Performance: The operation is efficient for real-time destructible terrain. Clamping the bounding box ensures no out-of-bounds checks are needed inside the loop, optimizing performance. Strengths: Simple to implement, deterministic, and provides explicit feedback on destroyed voxels (positions) for visual effects (gibs). Limitations: It is a binary operation (solid/air) and does not support partial destruction or smooth erosion without additional logic. It requires the caller to manage the coordinate transformation (world to local/grid) if the chunk uses a local coordinate system. Sphere Carving is a fundamental voxel operation used in voxel-based games and simulations for destructible environments. It is implemented in engines like Prometheus Engine for handling object destruction and in voxel terrain systems like dVoxels for cave generation and player interaction. The method is distinct from the "Sphere Carving" algorithm for bounding volume generation for SDFs, which uses a similar name but serves a different purpose (computing bounding proxies for acceleration). In the context of voxel occupancy, it is a direct application of the 3D filled circle kernel logic to modify grid state. m2-md/voxel-greedy-meshing-typescript, https://github.com/m2-md/voxel-greedy-meshing-typescript, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Sphere Carving: Bounding Volumes for Signed Distance..., https://research.adobe.com/publication/sphere-carving-bounding-volumes-for-signed-distance-fields/, fetched 2026-11-05 elyssov/prometheus-engine, https://github.com/elyssov/prometheus-engine, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Enhanced Sphere Tracing | Request PDF - ResearchGate, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/265020476EnhancedSphereTracing, fetched 2026-11-03 (abstract only, unofficial) Kernel-Reflection Sequences, https://doi.org/10.2312/stag.20161364, fetched 2026-10-26 How Does It Work?, https://www.voxelquest.com/news/how-does-it-work, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Deformation with Spherical Falloff
head: Runtime Digging, Runtime Terrain Digging, Spherical Edits, Spherical Voxel Deformation, Voxel Falloff Modification
body: Voxel Deformation with Spherical Falloff modifies scalar voxel values within a spherical region around a 3D hit point to add or remove terrain mass, creating smooth edges for digging or building operations. It differs from Sphere Carving, which removes solid voxels within a binary radius, by using a continuous soft falloff to allow gradual mass modification and reversible editing. It serves as the core mechanism for Voxel Edit Brush Operations, enabling real-time interaction with the density field. Inputs: worldPos: The 3D world position of the deformation center, typically obtained from a raycast hit. radius: The radius of the deformation sphere in world units. delta: The magnitude of density change per frame, typically speed deltaTime. mode: The operation type (Dig, Build, or Smooth). voxelSize: The size of a single voxel in world units. densityField: The array of scalar density values for the voxels. dimensions: The dimensions of the voxel grid in voxels. chunkSize: The size of a terrain chunk in voxels. Outputs: Updated densityField values for voxels within the spherical region. A set of dirty chunk coordinates that overlap the modified region and require mesh regeneration. Data Structures: densityField: A 1D or 3D array of floats (range [0, 1]) or bytes (range [0, 255]) representing voxel density. TerrainChunk: A structure representing a sub-volume of the world, containing a subset of the density field and a generated mesh. Steps: 1. Raycast and Hit Detection: Cast a ray from the camera position along the camera's forward direction with a maximum range. If the ray hits a terrain collider, record the hit point worldPos. 2. Coordinate Conversion: Convert worldPos to local voxel coordinates. If the voxel grid is offset from the world origin, apply the inverse transform: \text{localPos} = (\text{worldPos} - \text{origin}) / \text{voxelSize}. 3. Bounding Box Calculation: Compute the integer bounding box of the sphere in voxel coordinates. For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: \text{min}i = \lfloor \text{localPos}i - \text{radius} \rfloor and \text{max}i = \lceil \text{localPos}i + \text{radius} \rceil. Clamp these bounds to the world dimensions [0, \text{dimensions}i - 1]. 4. Iteration: Iterate over all voxels (x, y, z) within the clamped bounding box. 5. Distance Check: Calculate the Euclidean distance d from the voxel center to the brush center: d = \sqrt{(x - \text{localPos}x)^2 + (y - \text{localPos}y)^2 + (z - \text{localPos}z)^2}. If d > \text{radius}, skip this voxel. 6. Falloff Calculation: Compute the falloff factor using a smooth step function, which maps distance to a value in [0, 1] where 1 is at the center and 0 is at the edge. 7. Density Update: For Dig/Build (Additive/S3): \text{density}[i] = \text{Clamp01}(\text{density}[i] + \text{delta} \cdot \text{falloff}). For Dig/Build (Inverse Distance/S1): \text{modificationAmount} = \text{deformSpeed} / d \cdot m, where m \in \{-1, 1\} is the build modifier. Update: v{\text{new}} = \text{clamp}((v{\text{old}} / 255 - \text{modificationAmount}) \cdot 255, 0, 255). For Smooth: See Local Area Smoothing Brush below. 8. Chunk Marking: Identify all TerrainChunk objects that overlap the bounding box and mark them as "dirty". Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def deformvoxelfield(densityfield, dimensions, voxelsize, worldpos, radius, delta, mode, chunksize): # 1. Convert world position to local voxel coordinates localpos = worldpos / voxelsize # 2. Calculate bounding box minx = math.floor(localpos.x - radius) maxx = math.ceil(localpos.x + radius) miny = math.floor(localpos.y - radius) maxy = math.ceil(localpos.y + radius) minz = math.floor(localpos.z - radius) maxz = math.ceil(localpos.z + radius) # Clamp to world bounds minx = max(0, minx) maxx = min(dimensions.x - 1, maxx) miny = max(0, miny) maxy = min(dimensions.y - 1, maxy) minz = max(0, minz) maxz = min(dimensions.z - 1, maxz) dirtychunks = set() # 3. Iterate over voxels in bounding box for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): # 4. Calculate distance to brush center dx = x - localpos.x dy = y - localpos.y dz = z - localpos.z dist = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) # 5. Skip if outside radius if dist > radius: continue # 6. Calculate falloff (SmoothStep) t = dist / radius if t >= 1.0: falloff = 0.0 elif t <= 0.0: falloff = 1.0 else: falloff = 3 t t - 2 t t t # 7. Update density based on mode if mode == "DIG": if dist < 1e-6: continue # Inverse distance variant modificationamount = delta / dist vold = densityfield[x, y, z] vnormalized = vold / 255.0 vnewnormalized = vnormalized - modificationamount vnew = max(0.0, min(1.0, vnewnormalized)) densityfield[x, y, z] = vnew elif mode == "BUILD": if dist < 1e-6: continue # Inverse distance variant modificationamount = delta / dist vold = densityfield[x, y, z] vnormalized = vold / 255.0 vnewnormalized = vnormalized + modificationamount vnew = max(0.0, min(1.0, vnewnormalized)) densityfield[x, y, z] = vnew elif mode == "SMOOTH": # Local Area Smoothing Brush logic # Expand bounds by 1 for neighbors sminx = max(0, minx - 1) smaxx = min(dimensions.x - 1, maxx + 1) sminy = max(0, miny - 1) smaxy = min(dimensions.y - 1, maxy + 1) sminz = max(0, minz - 1) smaxz = min(dimensions.z - 1, maxz + 1) # Create snapshot of expanded region snapshot = {} for sx in range(sminx, smaxx + 1): for sy in range(sminy, smaxy + 1): for sz in range(sminz, smaxz + 1): snapshot[(sx, sy, sz)] = densityfield[sx, sy, sz] # Average with 6 neighbors neighbors = [ (x, y, z), (x+1, y, z), (x-1, y, z), (x, y+1, z), (x, y-1, z), (x, y, z+1), (x, y, z-1) ] avg = 0.0 for nx, ny, nz in neighbors: nx = max(0, min(dimensions.x - 1, nx)) ny = max(0, min(dimensions.y - 1, ny)) nz = max(0, min(dimensions.z - 1, nz)) avg += snapshot.get((nx, ny, nz), 0.0) avg /= 7.0 # Interpolate towards average smoothstrength = delta falloff densityfield[x, y, z] = densityfield[x, y, z] (1.0 - smoothstrength) + avg smoothstrength # 8. Mark chunks as dirty chunkx = x // chunksize chunky = y // chunksize chunkz = z // chunksize dirtychunks.add((chunkx, chunky, chunkz)) return dirtychunks Parameters: radius: Brush radius in meters. Typical value: 2.5f. Range: 1f to 6f. digSpeed: Density removed per second at the center of the brush. Typical value: 4f. buildSpeed: Density added per second at the center of the brush. Typical value: 3f. smoothSpeed: Smoothing speed as a fraction of blur per second. Typical value: 6f. deformRange: The range of deformation in voxel units, calculated as ceil(radius / voxelsize). deformSpeed: The speed of deformation, often derived from digSpeed or buildSpeed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If the raycast hit point exactly matches a voxel center, the distance d becomes 0. In, this causes modificationAmount to become infinite. The code does not explicitly guard against distance == 0 before division, which is a pitfall. Implementers should add a check: if dist == 0: continue or use a minimum distance threshold. Border Voxels: Iterating over the bounding box may include voxels outside the valid world bounds if not clamped. The bounding box calculation must be clamped to the world dimensions. Precision: Using floating-point arithmetic for distance and falloff is standard. The Dig Tool alleviates occlusion in volumetric datasets by smoothly displacing data points radially away from a user-defined focus point, creating a gap to reveal hidden internal structures. It serves as the 3D equivalent of the MoleView principle, operating on screen-space projections to manipulate the visible density field without altering the underlying geometry permanently until release. Locally blurs the density field within a spherical region to round off jagged edges created by deformation, using a snapshot of the field to ensure consistent averaging. It expands the bounding box by 1 voxel in all directions to include neighbors for averaging. A snapshot of the expanded region is created, and the density of each voxel is interpolated towards the average of itself and its 6 neighbors, weighted by the falloff factor. Time Complexity: O(R^3) per deformation call, where R is deformRange in voxel units, due to iterating over the full bounding box of the spherical region. Memory Complexity: O(R^3) for the temporary snapshot array used in smoothing operations. Performance: Real-time deformation is achievable with typical brush radii (e.g., 2.5m) on modern hardware, provided that mesh regeneration is deferred to LateUpdate and only dirty chunks are rebuilt. Strengths: Smooth edges, reversible operations, intuitive user interaction. Limitations: Inverse distance falloff can cause instability at the center if not guarded. Large deformation radii can be computationally expensive. Voxel Deformation with Spherical Falloff is a technique used in real-time voxel terrain editors and games to allow players to modify the terrain dynamically. It is commonly implemented in Unity-based voxel terrain systems, such as those using Marching Cubes for mesh generation. The technique builds on Sphere Carving by adding continuous falloff and bidirectional modification (dig/build). It is notably used in the TerraForge Godot 4 prototype for smooth destructible terrain. name: Dig Tool
head: 3D MoleView, Radial Displacement Tool
body: The Dig Tool alleviates occlusion in volumetric datasets by smoothly displacing data points radially away from a user-defined focus point, creating a gap to reveal hidden internal structures. It serves as the 3D equivalent of the MoleView principle, operating on screen-space projections to manipulate the visible density field temporarily without permanently altering the underlying geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of visible data points P, a focus point x \in \mathbb{R}^2 in screen space, a radius r \in \mathbb{R}^+, and the view plane normal n. Output: A temporary displaced configuration of points p(t) that reveals occluded structures, reverting to the original configuration upon interaction release. Data Structures: Point Set: A list or array of 3D coordinates representing the visible data points (e.g., isosurface vertices or ray-cast sample positions). Focus Disk C: Implicitly defined as the set of points p whose screen projection lies within a circle of radius r centered at x. Parameters: Radius r: Controlled by the mouse wheel. Time Steps: The interpolation is performed over 50 to 100 discrete time steps. Algorithm Steps: 1. Selection: Identify all points p \in P such that the screen-space projection of p falls within the disk C of radius r centered at the focus point x. 2. Displacement Vector Calculation: For each selected point p, compute the shortest vector v from the view ray passing through x to p: v = p - x - ((p - x) \cdot n)n where n is the view plane normal. 3. Target Position Calculation: Compute the target displacement position p{disp} on the boundary of the disk C in the direction of v: p{disp} = r \frac{v}{\|v\|}. If \|v\| \approx 0, the point is at the focus; the direction is undefined, but such points are typically handled by the interpolation logic directly or ignored if they do not contribute to the gap. 4. Forward Interpolation (Digging): While the mouse button is pressed, update the position of each selected point p towards p{disp} using linear interpolation over time t \in [0, 1]: p(t) = (1 - t)p + t p{disp} The parameter t is incremented in small steps (50–100 steps total) to create a smooth animation. 5. Inverse Interpolation (Reset): Upon mouse button release, perform inverse interpolation from the current displaced position p(t) back to the original location p. This causes the points to snap back to their original locations. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Velocity Gradient: Points close to the focus x drift quickly to the boundary \partial C, while points near \partial C move slower. This creates a clear gap at the center and progressively weaker deformation towards the edge. Occlusion Locking: The tool only affects unlocked density values; pushed items are the unlocked ones and will be affected by subsequent brushing actions. Strengths: Effectively reveals hidden structures by creating a temporary void around the focus point. Useful for forecasting the effect of subsequent brushing actions, as pushed items are the unlocked ones affected by further interactions. Limitations: The deformation is purely visual/interactive and does not modify the underlying dataset permanently unless explicitly committed by the application. When to use: When exploring dense volumetric datasets where occlusion hides critical internal features. When not to use: When precise quantitative analysis of the displaced region is required, as the geometry is temporarily altered. The Dig Tool was proposed in the context of "Color Tunneling" for interactive exploration and selection in volumetric datasets. It is conceptually derived from the MoleView principle [18], which operates in 2D, extending the concept to 3D volumetric data. The tool is part of a suite including Brush and Lock tools for managing visibility and selection in medical imaging and other domains. name: Bounding Ellipsoids from SDFs
head: Ellipsoid Bounding Volume, Minimum-Volume Enclosing Ellipsoid for SDFs
body: This method generates a conservative Signed Distance Function (SDF) for a shape by approximating its geometry with a minimum-volume enclosing ellipsoid. It replaces the convex hull generation step in the Sphere Carving pipeline with an ellipsoid bounding volume, offering constant-time evaluation and a compact memory footprint compared to n-face convex polyhedra. Inputs: A point set P representing the surface of the target shape. Ellipsoid parameters: center \mathbf{c}, rotation matrix \mathbf{R}, diagonal matrix \mathbf{D}, and axis lengths a, b, c with a < b < c. Outputs: A 1-Lipschitz (conservative) SDF function d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{E}). Data Structures: Center (\mathbf{c}): A 3D vector (cx, cy, cz). Rotation Matrix (\mathbf{R}): A 3 \times 3 orthogonal matrix defining the orientation of the ellipsoid axes. Diagonal Matrix (\mathbf{D}): A 3 \times 3 diagonal matrix with entries 1/a, 1/b, 1/c. Axis Lengths: Scalars a, b, c representing the semi-axis lengths, strictly ordered a < b < c. Algorithm Steps: 1. Generate Point Set: Obtain a point set P close to the shape surface, typically via the approximate convex decomposition or sphere carving iterations described in the parent method. 2. Compute Minimum-Volume Enclosing Ellipsoid (MVEE): Replace the standard convex hull generation step with an MVEE algorithm applied to point set P. This yields the center \mathbf{c}, rotation \mathbf{R}, and axis lengths a, b, c. 3. Construct Transformation Matrix: Compute \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{D} \mathbf{R}^T, where \mathbf{D} = \text{diag}(1/a, 1/b, 1/c). 4. Evaluate SDF: For any query point \mathbf{p}, compute the distance using the defined formula. Formula: The signed distance function for an ellipsoid \mathcal{E} is defined as: d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{E}) = a (\|\mathbf{A}(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c})\| - 1) Where: \mathbf{p} is the query point. a is the smallest semi-axis length. \mathbf{c} is the center of the ellipsoid. \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{D}(1/a, 1/b, 1/c) \mathbf{R}^T. \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ellipsoidsdf(p, c, R, a, b, caxis): """ Computes the conservative SDF for an ellipsoid. Args: p: Query point (vec3) c: Ellipsoid center (vec3) R: Rotation matrix (3x3) a: Smallest semi-axis length b: Middle semi-axis length caxis: Largest semi-axis length Returns: Conservative signed distance """ # Step 1: Translate point to ellipsoid space diff = p - c # Step 2: Rotate point into ellipsoid's local frame (R^T @ diff) rotateddiff = R.T @ diff # Step 3: Scale by inverse axis lengths (D @ rotateddiff) scaledx = rotateddiff[0] / a scaledy = rotateddiff[1] / b scaledz = rotateddiff[2] / caxis # Step 4: Compute Euclidean norm normval = (scaledx2 + scaledy2 + scaledz2)0.5 # Step 5: Apply scaling factor 'a' and offset distance = a (normval - 1.0) return distance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Conservatism: The function is 1-Lipschitz, meaning it is conservative (overestimates distance). The degree of conservatism depends on the relative axis lengths a, b, c. Highly elongated ellipsoids may be less accurate approximations of complex shapes compared to convex polyhedra. Time Complexity: Evaluation requires approximately 4 scalar products and one square root. This is constant time O(1) with respect to the number of faces, unlike convex polyhedra which require n scalar products for n faces. Memory Complexity: Ellipsoids are more compact in memory than convex polyhedra, requiring only storage for the center, rotation matrix, and three axis lengths. Performance: The GPU implementation performs well for most models. However, overly conservative SDFs (e.g., ship models) may require more iterations in the parent Sphere Carving algorithm to converge, similar to slow Sphere Tracing. Strengths: Computational efficiency, low memory footprint, and simplicity of implementation. Limitations: Potentially less geometric fidelity than convex polyhedra, especially when the relative axis lengths cause high conservatism. This method is described in "Sphere Carving: Bounding Volumes for Signed Distance Fields". It is presented as one of several bounding volume types (alongside oriented bounding boxes, k-dops, and convex polyhedra) that can be generated from a point set P. The approach leverages the mathematical properties of ellipsoids to provide a smooth, conservative distance field suitable for voxel-based rendering and physics.
