name: Voxel Edit Brush Operations
head: Place/Carve/Fill/Paint
body: Voxel Edit Brush Operations provide a set of interactive tools (Place, Carve, Fill, Paint) for modifying unbounded 3D voxel grids using world-space spherical or cylindrical selection volumes. The method solves the problem of real-time, view-independent sculpting and material insertion in volumetric data, ensuring consistent behavior across chunk boundaries by addressing voxels via unbounded world-grid coordinates rather than local indices. Unlike parent methods that may rely on sparse structures or offline processing, this approach utilizes dense 3D textures for mask lookups to enable O(1) per-fragment operations. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D voxel grid (represented as a VolumeTex and a SculptMap mask texture), a brush center P, and a brush radius r. For cylindrical operations, a projection plane is also required. Outputs: Modified voxel occupancy or material values in the affected region. Data Structures: SculptMap: A 3D texture (sampler3D) storing mask information. The alpha channel (a) typically represents visibility or erasure masks, while the blue channel (b) may represent addition or insertion masks. VolumeTex: A 3D texture (sampler3D) storing the base volume data, including RGB color and alpha occupancy. Brush Parameters: P: A 4D vector (float4) where P.xyz is the 3D center of the brush and P.a is the tool radius r. For cylindrical tools, P represents a 2D point on a projection plane, with r as the cylinder radius. Steps: 1. Coordinate Addressing: Address voxels using unbounded world-grid coordinates to ensure consistent behavior across chunk boundaries (e.g., 32-cell boundaries). 2. Stroke Accumulation: Accumulate edits into a stroke across frames. On mouse release, push a single VoxelEditCommand to process the batch. 3. Selection Volume Definition: Spherical (Carve/Fill): Define a sphere with center P and radius r. Cylindrical (Eraser): Define a projection plane and a 2D point P on it, independent of viewing parameters. 4. Distance Calculation: Spherical: Calculate the 3D Euclidean distance d from the voxel center V to P: d = \text{distance}(P, V) If d < r, the voxel is selected. Cylindrical: Orthogonally project the voxel center V onto the projection plane to get V{proj}. Calculate the 2D Euclidean distance d from V{proj} to P: d = \text{length}(V{proj}.xy - P.xy) If d < r, the voxel is selected. 5. Operation Execution: Carve: If the voxel is selected, remove it by clearing its visibility mask. Fill: If the voxel is selected, check if it currently holds a background value; if so, insert material without overwriting existing material. Place/Paint: Modify specific channels of the mask texture (e.g., setting alpha or color channels) based on the selection. Pseudocode (Spherical Carve/Fill in Fragment Shader): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applybrush(voxelpos, brushcenter, brushradius, mode, sculptmap, volumetex): # 1. Calculate normalized 3D Euclidean distance d = length(voxelpos - brushcenter) / brushradius if d >= 1.0: return sculptmap(voxelpos) # Outside brush radius, return unchanged mask = sculptmap(voxelpos) volume = volumetex(voxelpos) if mode == "carve": # Remove voxel by clearing visibility mask mask.a = 0.0 elif mode == "fill": # Insert material only if voxel is background; do not overwrite if volume.r == 0.0 or mask.a == 0.0: mask.b = 1.0 # Mark for addition elif mode == "paint": # Modify mask channels for visual feedback or material stamping mask.a = 1.0 elif mode == "place": # Add material to empty space if volume.r == 0.0: mask.b = 1.0 return mask Parameters: Brush Radius (r): World-space radius defining the spherical area of influence. Brush Center (P): 3D point specifying the center of the selection volume. Projection Plane: Required for cylindrical operations; defines the axis and orientation of the brush. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Chunk Boundaries: Using chunk-local indices causes inconsistent behavior at boundaries; unbounded world-grid coordinates must be used. Overwriting: The Fill tool must check current voxel values to avoid overwriting existing material. Undo/Losslessness: Snapshots should capture whole chunks, not cell deltas, to allow lossless undo (removing a chunk entirely if it becomes empty). This variant implements real-time voxel carving in a browser-based 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renderer by injecting a discrete voxel occupancy mask into the fragment shader via a shader patching hook [12596-voxel-edit-brush-operations-place-carve-fill-paint-real-time.md]. It solves the problem of crisp, axis-aligned removal of splats using a discard instruction, avoiding the performance penalty of per-fragment analytic SDF evaluations or per-splat geometric tests [12596-voxel-edit-brush-operations-place-carve-fill-paint-real-time.md]. Unlike parent methods that may rely on sparse structures or offline processing, this approach uses a dense 3D texture sized to the voxel grid, enabling O(1) per-fragment lookup regardless of the number of carved cells [12596-voxel-edit-brush-operations-place-carve-fill-paint-real-time.md]. A fragment shader that implements the eraser tool for volume sculpting, modifying the alpha channel of a SculptMap texture based on the distance from a 3D point P to the current fragment. It uses a virtual hand metaphor, detaching the cursor from viewing parameters to allow free rotation and translation. Layout: Input Struct: vertex2fragment with field Tex0 (float2, TEXCOORD0). Uniforms: SculptMap (sampler3D, TEXUNIT0), VolumeTex (sampler3D, TEXUNIT1), P (float4, C0) where P.xyz is the 3D point and P.a is the tool radius. Steps: 1. Sample SculptMap at v2f.Tex0: Col = tex3D(SculptMap, v2f.Tex0). 2. Calculate normalized 3D Euclidean distance D between P and texCoord: D = \frac{\text{distance}(\text{float4}(P.xyz, 1), \text{texCoord})}{P.a}. 3. If D < \text{Col}.a, update Col.a to D. Applies a volumetric brush to a voxel world, then identifies and detaches disconnected support islands that lose structural integrity after the edit. Steps: 1. Convert spec to brush object via brushFromSpec(spec). 2. If lift is true, call liftGrid(w, brush) to extract matter before carving. 3. Call w.applyBrush(brush, { op, mat, hardness }) to modify the world. 4. If conn and op === 'carve' and r.changed, call findIslands(w, box, { erode, near }). 5. For each island, call detachIsland(w, isl, { keepGrid: !small }). 6. If island count < debris, add to reply.dust with center and removed count. 7. Else, call gridPrep(g, 0), transfer buffers, and add to reply.islands. Parameters: debris (minimum voxel count for an island to become a physics body instead of dust, default: 16), erode (erosion radius applied to island detection box, default: 0), lift (boolean flag to extract carved matter as a separate grid before removal, default: false). Carves a voxel body's grid using a world-space brush, transforming the brush's signed distance field into the body's local frame for evaluation. Steps: 1. Parse brush spec, world transform t, local frame f, and row-major matrix m. 2. Define local distance function: lx = x - f[0], ly = y - f[1], lz = z - f[2]; world\x = t[0] + m[0]lx + m[1]ly + m[2]lz, world\y = t[1] + m[3]lx + m[4]ly + m[5]lz, world\z = t[2] + m[6]lx + m[7]ly + m[8]lz; return b.d(world\x, world\y, world\z). 3. Call carveGrid(g, local, { hardness }). 4. Transfer g.sdf.buffer and g.mat.buffer. 5. Return { grid, removed, changed }. Sculpture actions (addition or subtraction of material) performed by intersecting tool and material voxels and modifying material voxel values based on filling percentage. Steps: 1. Perform a collision test between the bounding boxes of the tool and the material. 2. If collision occurs, find voxels of material and tool in the collision zone. 3. Extract the value of each tool voxel in the collision zone using discrete rotation. 4. Find which tool voxel intersects which material voxel in the collision zone. 5. Compute the filling percentage of the material voxel by the tool voxel. 6. In 'Adding material' mode: if tool voxel is not null, add filling percentage to material voxel value; clamp to 255 if greater. 7. In 'Subtracting material' mode: if tool voxel is not null, subtract filling percentage from material voxel value; clamp to 0 if negative. 8. Rebuild triangulated surface by marching cubes only for modified parts of the 3D object for each level of detail. Performance: Sculpting a chain with a ball, in 256x256x256, using spherical, cubic, and ring tools took less than 10 minutes. Sculpting a more complicated object using a previously designed tool took less than 5 minutes. Time Complexity: O(1) per-fragment lookup for mask access when using dense 3D textures. Stroke accumulation allows batch processing, pushing a single command on release. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of chunks affected by the edit, as only changed chunks are kept in snapshots for undo. Measured Performance: Byte-equality validated against voxlap C's setspans, ensuring identical behavior to the reference implementation. Sculpting a 256x256x256 chain with various tools completes in under 10 minutes. Strengths: View-independent, consistent across chunk boundaries, supports lossless undo via chunk snapshots. Limitations: Dense texture approach may consume significant memory for large grids. Cylindrical tools require additional projection plane calculations. When to Use: Real-time voxel sculpting, destructible terrain, interactive volume editing where view independence is critical. When Not to Use: Extremely large sparse volumes where dense textures are prohibitive, or when analytic SDFs are preferred for smooth surfaces. The concept of voxel editing brushes originated in 3D sculpting tools that use a virtual hand metaphor to detach the cursor from viewing parameters, allowing free rotation and translation. The specific implementation of Place/Carve/Fill/Paint operations over unbounded grids with chunk-based undo was developed for real-time voxel engines, such as those used in browser-based 3D Gaussian Splatting renderers. The FSEraser and related tools were described in academic literature on volume sculpting based on geometric tools. The runtime editing pipeline for spans, cubes, and spheres has been validated against reference implementations like voxlap's setspans. Virtual sculpture operations using Haar wavelets and voxel representations were later introduced to handle subtraction and addition of material efficiently. feat(terrain): DDA voxel raycast + editing brushes with undo/redo, https://github.com/drsnuggles8/OloEngineBase/pull/973, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Volume sculpting based on geometric tools, https://doi.org/10.1007/bf03194498, fetched 2026-10-26 roxlap-cli 0.32.0, https://docs.rs/crate/roxlap-cli/latest, fetched 2026-10-29 sh1ftmaker/voxel-wars, https://github.com/sh1ftmaker/voxel-wars, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial), https://www.scitepress.org/PublishedPapers/2006/13546/pdf/index.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Edit Brush Operations — Place/Carve/Fill/Paint, Real-time Voxel Editing, VoxelEdit
head: FragmentSdfShaderPatch, Voxel Carving via Shader Patching
body: This method implements real-time voxel editing on an unbounded voxel grid by injecting a binary occupancy mask into a fragment shader via shader patching. It solves the problem of performing crisp, axis-aligned carve operations on volumetric data (specifically 3D Gaussian Splatting) without modifying the underlying geometry or splat primitives. Unlike standard eraser tools that remove voxels through the entire depth of the volume, this approach limits removal to a specific spatial region defined by a 3D texture mask, enabling efficient, GPU-accelerated sculpting. The method operates by maintaining a 3D texture (uCarveMask) that stores the binary state of each voxel cell (carved or uncarved). This texture is sampled in the fragment shader to discard fragments that fall within carved regions. The system manages the state of these carves using a key-value store and updates the shader uniforms dynamically. Input: World-space coordinates of the brush center, brush radius, and current voxel grid parameters (origin, size, counts). Output: Modified fragment shader pipeline that discards pixels corresponding to carved voxels. 1. Carve Mask Texture (uCarveMask): Type: sampler3D (backed by a Uint8Array or bytearray). Layout: 1 byte per voxel. Value 255 indicates a carved voxel; 0 indicates an uncarved (solid) voxel. Dimensions: voxelcounts.x voxelcounts.y voxelcounts.z. 2. Carve State Map: A dictionary mapping unique keys to voxel indices (i, j, k). Used to track active carves for uncarve operations. 3. Uniforms Injected into Fragment Shader: sampler3D uCarveMask: The occupancy texture. vec3 uVoxelOrigin: World-space origin of the voxel grid. float uVoxelSizeInv: Inverse of the voxel size (for coordinate conversion). vec3 uVoxelCountsInv: Inverse of the voxel counts (for normalization). vec3 uCarveBoundsMin: Minimum world-space coordinates of the union of all active carves. vec3 uCarveBoundsMax: Maximum world-space coordinates of the union of all active carves. int uCarveCount: Number of active carves. 4. Uniforms Injected into Vertex Shader: mat4 uClipToLocal: Transformation matrix from clip space to local voxel space. out vec3 vWorldPos: Output world position of the vertex. 1. Carve Operation (carve(key, i, j, k)): Validate that key is not already in the Carve State Map. Validate that indices i, j, k are within the grid bounds [0, counts-1]. Calculate the linear index in the 3D texture: idx = 1 + 2w + 3wh (where w and h are grid dimensions). Set the texel at idx in uCarveMask to 255. Increment patch.count. Update the union AABB (uCarveBoundsMin, uCarveBoundsMax) to include the voxel center (voxelorigin + (i+0.5)size,...). Increment tex.version to trigger a texture update. 2. Uncarve Operation (uncarve(key)): Validate that key exists in the Carve State Map. Retrieve the stored indices (i, j, k). Set the texel at the corresponding linear index in uCarveMask to 0. Decrement patch.count. Update the union AABB. Increment tex.version. 3. Shader Compilation (compile(shader)): Inject fragment shader code containing a single texture lookup to uCarveMask. Gate the lookup on a union AABB check (uCarveBoundsMin/Max) for early-out. Move world-position computation to the vertex shader using uClipToLocal. Voxel Index to World Position: P{world} = P{origin} + (P{index} + 0.5) \times S{voxel} Where P{origin} is uVoxelOrigin, P{index} is the integer voxel coordinate, and S{voxel} is the voxel size. Linear Index in 3D Texture: idx = 1 + 2 \times w + 3 \times w \times h Where w and h are grid dimensions, as specified by the source. AABB Check: \text{if } (P{world}.x < uCarveBoundsMin.x \lor P{world}.x > uCarveBoundsMax.x \lor \dots) \text{ skip texture lookup} Fragments outside the union AABB skip the texture sample entirely with three float compares. uVoxelOrigin: World-space origin of the voxel grid. uVoxelSizeInv: Inverse voxel size for coordinate normalization. uVoxelCountsInv: Inverse voxel counts for normalization. uCarveBoundsMin/Max: Bounding box of all active carves. uCarveCount: Number of active carves. Out-of-Bounds Indices: Clamped safely by returning false and writing nothing. Missing Anchors: Throws if expected fragment anchors are missing in the shader. Shader Fragility: Anchor-based string injection is fragile to upstream changes in the rendering engine (e.g., Spark). Carve Capacity: Limited by the voxel grid size (counts.x \cdot counts.y \cdot counts.z bytes). No per-session cap on number of carves, but memory scales cubically with resolution. 2DGS Interaction: Carves while 2DGS is enabled may mis-mask due to different vNdc assignment forms. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def mul(self, scalar): return Vec3(self.x scalar, self.y scalar, self.z scalar) def vec3min(a, b): return Vec3(min(a.x, b.x), min(a.y, b.y), min(a.z, b.z)) def vec3max(a, b): return Vec3(max(a.x, b.x), max(a.y, b.y), max(a.z, b.z)) class VoxelEditBrush: def init(self, voxelcounts, voxelorigin, voxelsize): self.voxelcounts = voxelcounts self.voxelorigin = voxelorigin self.voxelsize = voxelsize self.voxelsizeinv = 1.0 / voxelsize self.voxelcountsinv = 1.0 / voxelcounts self.carvemask = bytearray(voxelcounts.x voxelcounts.y voxelcounts.z) self.carvemap = {} self.patchcount = 0 self.boundsmin = Vec3(math.inf, math.inf, math.inf) self.boundsmax = Vec3(-math.inf, -math.inf, -math.inf) self.texversion = 0 def linearindex(self, w, h): return 1 + 2 w + 3 w h def updatebounds(self, i, j, k, isadd): center = self.voxelorigin + Vec3(i + 0.5, j + 0.5, k + 0.5) self.voxelsize if isadd: self.boundsmin = vec3min(self.boundsmin, center - Vec3(0.5) self.voxelsize) self.boundsmax = vec3max(self.boundsmax, center + Vec3(0.5) self.voxelsize) else: self.boundsmin = Vec3(math.inf, math.inf, math.inf) self.boundsmax = Vec3(-math.inf, -math.inf, -math.inf) for, (ci, cj, ck) in self.carvemap.items(): ccenter = self.voxelorigin + Vec3(ci + 0.5, cj + 0.5, ck + 0.5) self.voxelsize self.boundsmin = vec3min(self.boundsmin, ccenter - Vec3(0.5) self.voxelsize) self.boundsmax = vec3max(self.boundsmax, ccenter + Vec3(0.5) self.voxelsize) def carve(self, key, i, j, k): if key in self.carvemap: return False if not (0 <= i < self.voxelcounts.x and 0 <= j < self.voxelcounts.y and 0 <= k < self.voxelcounts.z): return False idx = self.linearindex(self.voxelcounts.x, self.voxelcounts.y) self.carvemask[idx] = 255 self.carvemap[key] = (i, j, k) self.patchcount += 1 self.updatebounds(i, j, k, True) self.texversion += 1 return True def uncarve(self, key): if key not in self.carvemap: return False i, j, k = self.carvemap.pop(key) idx = self.linearindex(self.voxelcounts.x, self.voxelcounts.y) self.carvemask[idx] = 0 self.patchcount -= 1 self.updatebounds(i, j, k, False) self.texversion += 1 return True def compileshader(self, shadersource): uniforms = """ uniform sampler3D uCarveMask; uniform vec3 uVoxelOrigin; uniform float uVoxelSizeInv; uniform vec3 uVoxelCountsInv; uniform vec3 uCarveBoundsMin; uniform vec3 uCarveBoundsMax; uniform int uCarveCount; uniform mat4 uClipToLocal; """ vertexinjection = """ out vec3 vWorldPos; void main() { vec4 clipPos = glPosition; vec4 localPos = uClipToLocal clipPos; vWorldPos = localPos.xyz; } """ fragmentinjection = """ in vec3 vWorldPos; void main() { if (vWorldPos.x < uCarveBoundsMin.x || vWorldPos.x > uCarveBoundsMax.x || vWorldPos.y < uCarveBoundsMin.y || vWorldPos.y > uCarveBoundsMax.y || vWorldPos.z < uCarveBoundsMin.z || vWorldPos.z > uCarveBoundsMax.z) { return; } vec3 voxelCoord = (vWorldPos - uVoxelOrigin) uVoxelSizeInv - 0.5; voxelCoord = clamp(voxelCoord, vec3(0.0), uVoxelCountsInv - 1.0); float isCarved = texture(uCarveMask, voxelCoord).r; if (isCarved > 0.5) { discard; } } """ shadersource = shadersource.replace("// VoxelEditUniforms", uniforms) shadersource = shadersource.replace("// VoxelEditVertex", vertexinjection) shadersource = shadersource.replace("// VoxelEditFragment", fragmentinjection) return shadersource FSDigger is a fragment shader implementation of the 2D Digger tool for real-time volume sculpting, designed to carve semi-spherical holes into a volume starting from the first surface intersection along the line of sight. Unlike the Eraser tool which removes voxels through the entire depth of the volume, FSDigger limits removal to a depth determined by the cursor radius and viewing geometry, effectively creating a "dug" cavity rather than a tunnel. It builds on Voxel Edit Brush Operations — Place/Carve/Fill/Paint, Real-time Voxel Editing, VoxelEdit by injecting specific carving logic into the fragment shader pipeline. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment for the mask lookup, regardless of the number of carves. The AABB check is also O(1). Memory Complexity: O(N) where N is the total number of voxels in the grid (counts.x \cdot counts.y \cdot counts.z). At default resolution (64^3), this is 262 KB. Performance: ~4 × splat count / frame instead of ~pixels / frame for carving logic. Strengths: Crisp, axis-aligned carving; efficient GPU-based discard; no need to modify underlying geometry. Limitations: Memory scales cubically with resolution; fragile to shader engine changes; limited to binary (carved/uncarved) states. When to Use: Real-time voxel sculpting in web-based 3DGS viewers where crisp, axis-aligned cuts are required. When Not to Use: When smooth, continuous SDF-based carving is needed, or when memory constraints prevent storing a full 3D texture. The method was introduced by stevekwon211 in the splatcarve project. It leverages the Material.onBeforeCompile hook from Spark 2.0 to inject a voxel-cell-resolution occupancy mask into the fragment stage of a 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterizer. It is described as the first public open-source browser-based 3DGS demo to apply this technique for crisp, axis-aligned discard-based carves. The closest prior art, Santos & Soares (SVR 2025), targets modulation effects inside an SDF region rather than crisp removal. stevekwon211/splatcarve, https://github.com/stevekwon211/splatcarve, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: FSDigger
head: 2D Digger, Digger Tool, Volume Sculpting Digger
body: FSDigger is a fragment shader implementation of the 2D Digger tool for real-time volume sculpting, designed to carve semi-spherical holes into a volume starting from the first surface intersection along the line of sight. Unlike the Eraser tool which removes voxels through the entire depth of the volume, FSDigger limits removal to a depth determined by the cursor radius and viewing geometry, effectively creating a "dug" cavity rather than a tunnel. It builds on Voxel Edit Brush Operations — Place/Carve/Fill/Paint, Real-time Voxel Editing, VoxelEdit by injecting specific carving logic into the fragment shader pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: The shader operates on a fragment shader stage. Input: v2f struct containing Tex0 (float2, semantic TEXCOORD0). Uniforms: SculptMap: sampler3D at TEXUNIT0. Stores the current voxel state (alpha channel represents occupancy/depth mask). VolumeTex: sampler3D at TEXUNIT1. Stores the original volume data (color/alpha). P: float4 at C0. P.xyz is the 3D point representing the brush center in world/clip space, and P.a is the tool radius r. PolygonCoord: sampler2D at TEXUNIT1. Output: Col (float4, semantic COLOR0). The output contains the resulting color and alpha for the fragment. Data Structures: SculptMap: A 3D texture where the alpha channel Col.a acts as a mask. The value represents the remaining depth or occupancy. P: A uniform vector defining the brush. P.a is the radius r. Algorithm Steps: 1. Texture Sampling: Sample the PolygonCoord texture using v2f.Tex0 to obtain the 3D texture coordinates texCoord for the current fragment. \text{texCoord} = \text{tex2D}(\text{PolygonCoord}, \text{v2f.Tex0}) 2. Current State Retrieval: Sample the SculptMap texture at texCoord to get the current voxel state Col. \text{Col} = \text{tex3D}(\text{SculptMap}, \text{texCoord}) 3. Distance Calculation: Calculate the 3D Euclidean distance D between the brush center point P (homogeneous coordinate w=1) and the current fragment position texCoord, normalized by the tool radius r (P.a). D = \frac{\text{distance}(\text{float4}(P.xyz, 1), \text{texCoord})}{P.a} 4. Mask Update: If the calculated distance D is less than the current alpha value Col.a, update Col.a to D. This effectively carves out the voxel if the distance is within the brush radius, reducing the alpha mask. \text{if } (D < \text{Col.a}) \quad \text{Col.a} = D 5. Color Combination: Combine the original volume color with the sculpted mask. The output color Col.rgb is taken from VolumeTex, and the output alpha is the original volume alpha multiplied by the floor of the updated mask alpha (ensuring binary occupancy or stepped depth). \text{volume\voxel} = \text{tex3D}(\text{VolumeTex}, \text{v2f.Tex0}) \text{Col.rgb} = \text{volume\voxel.rgb} \text{Col.a} = \text{volume\voxel.a} \times \lfloor \text{Col.a} \rfloor Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class float4: def init(self, x, y, z, w): self.x, self.y, self.z, self.w = x, y, z, w def tex2D(tex, uv): # Standard 2D texture lookup returning a 4-component vector return tex.sample(uv) def tex3D(tex, uvw): # Standard 3D texture lookup returning a 4-component vector return tex.sample(uvw) def fsdigger(v2fTex0, SculptMap, VolumeTex, P, PolygonCoord): # Step 1: Get 3D texture coordinates from 2D screen coordinates texCoord = tex2D(PolygonCoord, v2fTex0) # Step 2: Sample current sculpt map state Col = tex3D(SculptMap, texCoord) # Step 3: Calculate normalized 3D Euclidean distance from brush center P to fragment # P.xyz is the 3D point, P.a is the radius r # We treat P as a homogeneous point (w=1) for distance calculation Phomogeneous = float4(P.x, P.y, P.z, 1.0) D = distance(Phomogeneous, texCoord) / P.a # Step 4: Update alpha mask if within brush radius # This carves the voxel by reducing its alpha value to the distance if D < Col.a: Col.a = D # Step 5: Sample original volume data volumevoxel = tex3D(VolumeTex, v2fTex0) # Step 6: Combine color and final alpha # Color comes from original volume Col.rgb = volumevoxel.rgb # Alpha is original volume alpha floor of sculpt mask alpha # floor() ensures binary removal (0 or 1) or stepped depth depending on interpretation Col.a = volumevoxel.a floor(Col.a) return Col Parameters: P.a (Radius r): The radius of the digging tool. The depth of the dig is constrained by this radius and viewing geometry. P.xyz: The 3D position of the brush center. For the 2D Digger, this is projected onto the volume surface along the line of sight. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Semi-spherical Constraint: The selection region is a semi-sphere constrained by viewing parameters. Its size varies according to the cursor radius and the position is determined by the intersection of the line of sight and the volume surface. Depth Calculation: The depth of the dig is not uniform; it is calculated based on the cursor radius r, the surface distance ds, and the view plane distance dv to the point of view, as given by Equation 1 in the source: \text{depth} = \frac{ds \cdot r}{dv} However, the shader implementation uses a direct Euclidean distance check normalized by radius, which approximates this geometric constraint in screen space. Texture Unit Conflict: The source lists VolumeTex and PolygonCoord both at TEXUNIT1. In implementation, these must be assigned to distinct texture units. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment. The shader performs a constant number of texture samples and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per fragment. The state is stored in the SculptMap texture. Performance: Real-time performance is achieved by leveraging the GPU fragment shader pipeline. The method avoids iterating over all voxels in the volume, instead processing only the fragments corresponding to the proxy geometry planes. Strengths: Efficient real-time sculpting; intuitive 2D interaction for 3D volume modification; creates natural-looking dug holes. Limitations: The digging depth is constrained by the viewing geometry and cursor radius, which may not provide precise control over the exact depth of the hole in world units. The semi-spherical shape may not be suitable for all sculpting needs (e.g., flat-bottomed holes). FSDigger originates from the "Volume sculpting based on geometric tools" paper by (2009). It is part of a suite of tools including Eraser, Clipper, and Combiner, designed for interactive volume editing. The 2D Digger tool was introduced to address the need for digging holes in volumes without erasing the entire path along the line of sight, which is the behavior of the Eraser tool. The implementation uses a fragment shader (Cg) to inject the carving logic into the rendering pipeline, using a 3D texture mask (SculptMap) to track the sculpted state. name: Procedural Sphere Placement
head: Bubble Generation, Voxel Sphere Carving
body: Procedural Sphere Placement populates a 3D voxel grid with spherical voids (density 0) inside a background field (density 255), using pre-sampled coordinates and random radii. Not given in the sources. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Grid dimensions (maxX, maxY, maxZ), sampling stride sep, and radius parameters. Output: A 3D voxel field array. Data Structures: field: A 3D numpy array of shape (maxZ, maxX, maxY) or (maxX, maxY, maxZ), dtype uint8. Memory order is row-major (C-style). Access pattern is field[z][x][y]. The field is initialized to 255 (opaque background). Parameters: r: Sphere radius. Typical values are 1–3 for small bubbles or 7–16 for large ones. sep: Sampling stride for seed points. Typical values are 1, 2, or 10. A, B: Squared semi-axes for elliptical variants (see Subtopics). Steps: 1. Initialize the 3D field array to 255. 2. Sample seed points (px, py, pz) across the grid using isin or random grid traversal with stride sep. 3. For each seed point: a. Pick a radius r from the distribution (e.g., randint(1, 3)). b. Define the bounding box for the sphere: i \in [px-r-1, px+r+1], j \in [py-r-1, py+r+1], k \in [pz-r-1, pz+r+1]. c. Iterate through every voxel (i, j, k) in the bounding box. d. Compute local coordinates relative to the center: i2 = i - px j2 = j - py k2 = k - pz. e. Perform the sphere inclusion test: i2^2 + j2^2 + k2^2 < r^2. f. If the test is true, clamp the coordinates to the grid bounds and set the voxel to 0 (transparent): x = \max(0, \min(i, maxX-1)) y = \max(0, \min(j, maxY-1)) z = \max(0, \min(k, maxZ-1)) field[z][x][y] = 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import random def proceduralsphereplacement(maxX, maxY, maxZ, sep=2, minr=1, maxr=3): # Initialize field to 255 (opaque) field = np.full((maxZ, maxX, maxY), 255, dtype=np.uint8) # Sample seed points using stride sep for pz in range(0, maxZ, sep): for px in range(0, maxX, sep): for py in range(0, maxY, sep): # Pick random radius r = random.randint(minr, maxr) # Define bounding box istart = max(0, px - r - 1) iend = min(maxX, px + r + 2) jstart = max(0, py - r - 1) jend = min(maxY, py + r + 2) kstart = max(0, pz - r - 1) kend = min(maxZ, pz + r + 2) # Iterate bounding box for i in range(istart, iend): i2 = i - px i2sq = i2 i2 for j in range(jstart, jend): j2 = j - py j2sq = j2 j2 for k in range(kstart, kend): k2 = k - pz k2sq = k2 k2 # Sphere inclusion test if i2sq + j2sq + k2sq < r r: # Clamp to grid bounds x = max(0, min(i, maxX - 1)) y = max(0, min(j, maxY - 1)) z = max(0, min(k, maxZ - 1)) # Set to 0 (transparent) field[z][x][y] = 0 return field Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary clamping is mandatory to prevent out-of-bounds array access when spheres are placed near grid edges. Not given in the sources. Removes voxels outside a specified elliptical cylinder boundary, effectively cropping the procedural volume to a specific shape. It differs from standard sphere placement by evaluating an elliptical condition along two axes rather than a spherical distance test. Choose this when a non-spherical, elongated void is required. Definition: Iterates over all voxels (i, j, k) and clears those satisfying the elliptical condition. Steps: 1. Iterate over all voxels (i, j, k) in the grid. 2. Compute centered coordinates with jitter: i2 = i - maxX/2.0 + \text{randint}(0, 3) j2 = j - maxY/2.0 + \text{randint}(0, 3) k2 = k - maxZ/2.0 + \text{randint}(0, 3). 3. Evaluate the elliptical condition: \frac{j2^2}{A} + \frac{k2^2}{B} > 1 If true, set field[i][j][k] = 0. Parameters: A, B: Squared semi-axes of the elliptical cylinder, typically 3000, 3500, or 4500. \text{randint}(0, 3): Adds slight jitter to the center offset. Pitfalls: The randint(0, 3) jitter shifts the cylinder center per-voxel, creating a noisy, irregular boundary rather than a smooth mathematical cylinder. The sources do not provide time complexity, memory complexity, measured performance, scaling, strengths, limitations, or usage guidelines. Originating from the webgl-volumetric project by rbaravalle, this method is used for generating volumetric data with procedural spherical voids. It is applied in WebGL-based volume rendering to create complex internal structures without explicit mesh data. rbaravalle/webgl-volumetric, https://github.com/rbaravalle/webgl-volumetric, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Sphere Generation & Distance Ordering
head: Bubble Generation, Voxel Sphere Carving
body:
This method generates a sparse, distance-ordered set of voxels representing a hollow or solid sphere by carving voids into a background field, building on Procedural Sphere Placement. It differs from standard voxelization by explicitly filtering out occluded voxels via raycasting and organizing the remaining voxels into a sorted dictionary keyed by their distance from the center, enabling ordered rendering or growth animations. Inputs: mcenter: World-space center of the sphere (Vector3). mmaxRadius: Maximum radius of the sphere in world units. mvoxelScale: Size of each voxel in world units. VoxelResolution: Resolution of the target grid (Vector3Int). GlobalBounds: Bounds of the scene/grid (Bounds). Outputs: VoxelsGrid: A 1D float[] array of size VoxelResolution.x 	imes VoxelResolution.y 	imes VoxelResolution.z, storing VoxelDistance at computed grid indices. morderedVoxels: A SortedDictionary<float, List<Voxel>> mapping distance order to lists of voxels. mvoxelsCache: A Dictionary<Vector3, Voxel> for fast lookup of existing voxels. Data Structures: Voxel struct: LocalPosition: Vector3 (local to sphere center). VoxelDistance: float (Euclidean distance from center). Order: float (used for sorting/animation timing). Parameters: mgrowthTime: Duration of the growth animation in seconds. mvoxelScale: Typical values depend on scene scale; must be consistent with VoxelResolution and GlobalBounds. Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Integer Radius: Compute the integer radius r in voxels: r = 	ext{round}\left( rac{m\maxRadius}{m\voxelScale}ight) 2. Generate Octant Voxels: Iterate tx, ty, tz from 0 to r-1. Compute squared magnitude: 	ext{sqrMag} = \sqrt{tx^2 + ty^2 + tz^2} If 	ext{sqrMag} < r, invoke a callback with voxel at (tx, ty, tz) and distance 	ext{sqrMag}. 3. Mirror to Full Sphere: For each valid voxel in the first octant, generate symmetric counterparts to fill all 8 octants. The source specifies mirroring rules: If tx 
eq 0, add (-tx, ty, tz). If tz 
eq 0, add (-tx, ty, -tz). If tz 
eq 0, add (tx, ty, -tz). If ty 
eq 0, add (tx, -ty, tz). Mirror remaining axes similarly to cover all sign combinations. Note: The source logic implies generating all 8 octants by flipping signs of non-zero coordinates. 4. Raycast Filtering: For each generated voxel at local position v.LocalPosition: Cast a Physics.Raycast from mcenter + Vector3.up 0.1f along v.LocalPosition. Discard the voxel if the ray hits any geometry. Add valid voxels to mvoxelsCache and morderedVoxels. Key morderedVoxels by Order = VoxelDistance. Track maxRadius and outLayerVoxels (voxels on the boundary). 5. Connectivity Expansion (Optional/Contextual): While deleted > 0: Iterate outLayerVoxels. For each, get 6 neighbors via GetConnectedVoxels. For each neighbor, check if not in cache and !Physics.CheckBox(center + neighbor.pos + up0.1f, scale0.5). If valid, set VoxelDistance = parent.VoxelDistance + 1, Order = order, add to cache/ordered dict, decrement deleted, increment order. Update maxRadius. Break if deleted == 0 or no connections found. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatevoxelsphere(mcenter, mmaxradius, mvoxelscale, voxelresolution, globalbounds): # Step 1: Calculate integer radius r = round(mmaxradius / mvoxelscale) voxelscache = {} orderedvoxels = {} outlayervoxels = [] deletedcount = 0 # Step 2 & 3: Generate and Mirror for tx in range(r): for ty in range(r): for tz in range(r): sqrmag = sqrt(tx2 + ty2 + tz2) if sqrmag < r: # Generate all 8 octants positions = [ (tx, ty, tz), (-tx, ty, tz) if tx != 0 else None, (tx, -ty, tz) if ty != 0 else None, (tx, ty, -tz) if tz != 0 else None, (-tx, -ty, tz) if tx != 0 and ty != 0 else None, (-tx, ty, -tz) if tx != 0 and tz != 0 else None, (tx, -ty, -tz) if ty != 0 and tz != 0 else None, (-tx, -ty, -tz) if tx != 0 and ty != 0 and tz != 0 else None ] for pos in positions: if pos is None: continue localpos = Vector3(pos[0] mvoxelscale, pos[1] mvoxelscale, pos[2] mvoxelscale) # Step 4: Raycast Filtering rayorigin = mcenter + Vector3(0, 0.1 mvoxelscale, 0) raydirection = localpos.normalized if not physicsraycast(rayorigin, raydirection): voxel = Voxel(localpos, sqrmag, sqrmag) voxelscache[localpos] = voxel orderkey = sqrmag if orderkey not in orderedvoxels: orderedvoxels[orderkey] = [] orderedvoxels[orderkey].append(voxel) outlayervoxels.append(voxel) deletedcount += 1 # Assuming initial state requires connection check # Step 5: Connectivity Expansion (if needed) while deletedcount > 0: currentlayervoxels = outlayervoxels outlayervoxels = [] for voxel in currentlayervoxels: neighbors = get6neighbors(voxel.localpos, mvoxelscale) for neighborpos in neighbors: if neighborpos not in voxelscache: # Check bounding box boxcenter = mcenter + neighborpos + Vector3(0, 0.1 mvoxelscale, 0) boxsize = Vector3(mvoxelscale, mvoxelscale, mvoxelscale) if not physicscheckbox(boxcenter, boxsize): newvoxel = Voxel(neighborpos, voxel.voxeldistance + 1, voxel.order + 1) voxelscache[neighborpos] = newvoxel orderkey = newvoxel.order if orderkey not in orderedvoxels: orderedvoxels[orderkey] = [] orderedvoxels[orderkey].append(newvoxel) outlayervoxels.append(newvoxel) deletedcount -= 1 if not outlayervoxels: break # Populate VoxelsGrid voxelsgrid = [0.0] (voxelresolution.x voxelresolution.y voxelresolution.z) for pos, voxel in voxelscache.items(): grididx = localtogridindex(pos, voxelresolution, globalbounds) voxelsgrid[grididx] = voxel.voxeldistance return voxelsgrid, orderedvoxels, voxelscache Time Complexity: O(r^3) for generation, where r is the integer radius in voxels. Raycasting adds a cost proportional to the number of surface voxels. Memory Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of valid voxels after filtering. The VoxelsGrid is O(VoxelResolution^3) but sparse in usage. Strengths: Explicit distance ordering allows for animated growth or ordered rendering. Raycasting ensures geometric accuracy against scene obstacles. Limitations: Raycasting is expensive for large spheres. The method is specific to Unity's physics system (Physics.Raycast, Physics.CheckBox), limiting portability. When to use: When dynamic, obstacle-aware voxel spheres are needed for effects like smoke or bubbles. When not to use: For static, high-resolution volumes where performance is critical and geometric accuracy against dynamic obstacles is not required. This method originates from the "VolumetricSmoke" project by Voltonik, an unofficial implementation of voxel-based smoke rendering in Unity. It is part of a pipeline that includes procedural sphere placement and raymarching. The technique is designed for real-time visual effects in game engines. name: VoxelDestruct Destruction
head: singular destruction, vox.destroy
body: VoxelDestruct is a method for performing voxelated destruction on specific parts or mesh parts, returning generated debris and affected walls. It differs from its sibling Sphere Carving by operating on arbitrary Part or MeshPart geometries rather than spherical volumes, and from Voxel Deformation with Spherical Falloff by focusing on discrete destruction events rather than continuous deformation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A focus part (Part or MeshPart) defining the shape, size, and position of the destruction. Optional parameters for filtering, voxelSize for resolution, debrisCount for quantity, and reset timer. Output: A table containing two lists: debris (generated debris parts) and walls (affected destructible parts). Data Structures: The module maintains a Cache for parts to prevent instancing lag. Parts are stored in this cache if Settings.PartCache is true. The hitbox object maintains collisions data and runtime parts lists. Parameters: focus: Part | MeshPart. Required. The geometry to destroy. parameters: OverlapParams?. Optional. Used for whitelisting/blacklisting. Example: FilterType = Enum.RaycastFilterType.Include, FilterDescendantsInstances = {game.Workspace.Baseplate}. voxelSize: number?. Optional. If nil: Intersections are not voxelized; raw intersections are returned. If 0 and Settings.Relativity is true: Settings.HitboxRelative is used for distance calculation. If 0 and Settings.Relativity is false: Settings.VoxelDefault is used. If > Settings.VoxelMinimum (default 1): Used as the voxel size. debrisCount: number?. Optional. Quantity of debris. If nil, all debris is returned. reset: number?. Optional. Timer until destruction is cleaned up. Settings: Settings.VoxelMinimum = 1: Minimum voxel size. Settings.HitboxRelative = 1/3: Relative distance to hitbox size required before destroying again. Settings.GreedyMeshing = true: Recommended to keep on. Settings.RunService = false: Recommended to keep off to avoid performance heavy frame-by-frame destruction. Settings.PartCache = true: Recommended to keep on to prevent instancing lag. Settings.CachePrecreated = 10000: Number of precreated parts in cache. Steps: 1. Initialize the module: local vox = require(game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage"):WaitForChild("VoxelDestruction")). 2. Call breaker.destroy(focus, parameters, voxelSize, debrisCount, reset). 3. The method processes the focus part, optionally voxelizing it based on voxelSize. 4. It generates debris and identifies affected walls. 5. Return the table of debris and walls. Pitfalls: Parts destroyed via standard:Destroy() cannot be returned to the cache. Must use the module's.cleanup() method to return parts to cache if useCache is true. Do not destroy debris and destructible parts when finished using them; use.cleanup() instead. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def destroy(focus, parameters=None, voxelSize=None, debrisCount=None, reset=None): """ Performs singular destruction on a focus part. Returns a table of debris and a table of affected walls. """ # Determine voxelization behavior if voxelSize is None: # Intersections are not voxelized and returned instead intersections = getintersections(focus, parameters) return {"debris": intersections, "walls": intersections} # Apply voxel size logic if voxelSize == 0: if Settings.Relativity: voxelSize = Settings.HitboxRelative else: voxelSize = Settings.VoxelDefault # Ensure minimum voxel size if voxelSize < Settings.VoxelMinimum: voxelSize = Settings.VoxelMinimum # Voxelize the focus part voxels = voxelizegeometry(focus, voxelSize, parameters) # Generate debris based on debrisCount if debrisCount is None: debris = generatealldebris(voxels) else: debris = generatedebris(voxels, debrisCount) # Identify affected walls walls = getaffectedwalls(voxels, parameters) # Handle caching if Settings.PartCache: cacheparts(debris) cacheparts(walls) return {"debris": debris, "walls": walls} def cleanup(parts): """ Cleans up parts by returning them to cache or destroying them. """ if isinstance(parts, Part): parts = [parts] for part in parts: if Settings.PartCache and part in cache: returntocache(part) else: part:Destroy() A system to create hitboxes from parts, meshparts, or models that trigger destruction upon interaction. It inherits parameters from.destroy(). Start: hitbox:Start() starts the hitbox. Can be restarted while active without calling:Stop() first. Fires hitbox.Started event. Stop: hitbox:Stop() stops the hitbox, disconnects connections, resets hitbox.collisions to 0 if revert is true, and fires hitbox.Stopped event with debris and walls. Fire: hitbox:Fire() activates the hitbox once. If destructible parts are detected, fires hitbox.Collision event with debris and affected parts. State: hitbox:IsActive() returns boolean. Runtime Data: hitbox:GetRuntimeParts() and hitbox:GetLifetimeParts() return all created debris and affected parts from runtime. Parameters: focus, parameters, voxelSize, debrisCount, reset. If voxelSize is passed and Relativity is true, Settings.HitboxRelative is used for distance before destroying again. Cleanup: The hitbox object itself can be garbage collected, but parts must be cleaned up using.cleanup(). Performance: Using Settings.RunService = true results in destruction every frame and is very performance heavy; it is recommended to keep this setting off. Caching: Settings.PartCache = true is recommended to prevent instancing lag. Parts must be cleaned up using.cleanup() to return them to cache; standard:Destroy() prevents this. Greedy Meshing: Settings.GreedyMeshing = true is recommended to keep on. VoxelDestruct is a module for Roblox game development, providing voxelated destruction physics with greedy meshing, hitboxes, and more. It was released as version 2.1 on the Roblox DevForum. name: 3D Binary Sphere Kernel Generation
head: Sphere Volume Generation for Marching Cubes
body: This method procedurally generates a 3D binary scalar field (density texture) representing a sphere centered at the origin of a voxel grid, specifically designed as input for GPU-based Marching Cubes surface extraction. Unlike static voxelization, this implementation features a time-varying radius that oscillates, creating a dynamic volume. It differs from its parent 3D Filled Circle Kernel Generation by explicitly targeting the DensityTexture property of a Marching Cubes component and utilizing a specific oscillating radius formula rather than a static threshold. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Resolution (integer, dimension of the cubic grid), Time.time (float, current simulation time). Output: A 3D texture densityTexture of size Resolution x Resolution x Resolution with format RFloat (single-channel float), and a 1D array colors of size Resolution^3 storing the density values in the red channel. Data Structures: colors: 1D array of size N^3 (where N = \text{Resolution}). Each element is a color/vector with a red channel r storing the binary density (0 or 1). densityTexture: 3D texture, dimensions N \times N \times N, format RFloat, wrap mode Clamp. Parameters: Resolution: Grid dimension. Not given in the sources. Time.time: Continuous time variable. Steps: 1. Initialize colors array of size N^3 with white values (or zero-initialized, as only the red channel is used). 2. Calculate the current radius resol using the oscillating formula: \text{resol} = \frac{N - 2}{2} \times \sin(0.25 \times \text{Time.time}) The radius oscillates between 0 and \frac{N-2}{2}. 3. Iterate through all voxel indices idx from 0 to N^3 - 1. This is typically done using nested loops for z, y, and x: \text{idx} = z \cdot N^2 + y \cdot N + x. 4. For each voxel (x, y, z), compute normalized coordinates relative to the center of the volume: sx = x - \frac{N}{2} sy = y - \frac{N}{2} sz = z - \frac{N}{2}. 5. Determine the density value amount by checking if the squared Euclidean distance from the center is less than or equal to the squared radius: \text{amount} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } sx^2 + sy^2 + sz^2 \le \text{resol}^2 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. 6. Store the density value in the red channel of the color array: \text{colors}[\text{idx}].r = \text{amount}. 7. Upload the computed colors array to the 3D texture densityTexture using SetPixels and Apply (or equivalent GPU upload mechanism). 8. Assign densityTexture to the Marching Cubes component's DensityTexture property. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generatespherekernel(Resolution, Timetime): N = Resolution numvoxels = N N N # Initialize colors array (R, G, B, A) # Only R channel is used for density colors = [[1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0] for in range(numvoxels)] # Calculate oscillating radius # Radius oscillates between 0 and (N-2)/2 resol = ((N - 2) / 2.0) math.sin(0.25 Timetime) resolsq = resol resol center = N / 2.0 for z in range(N): for y in range(N): for x in range(N): idx = z N N + y N + x # Normalized coordinates relative to center sx = x - center sy = y - center sz = z - center # Squared distance from center distsq = sxsx + sysy + szsz # Binary density: 1 if inside sphere, 0 otherwise if distsq <= resolsq: colors[idx][0] = 1.0 else: colors[idx][0] = 0.0 # Upload to 3D texture # densityTexture.SetPixels(colors) # densityTexture.Apply() # marchingcubescomponent.DensityTexture = densityTexture return colors Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The comparison distsq <= resolsq is sensitive to floating-point precision. For very large resolutions or small radii, this may cause aliasing or incorrect boundary voxels. Boundary Conditions: The radius formula uses (N-2)/2, leaving a 1-voxel border around the sphere. This ensures the sphere never touches the grid boundaries, which might be important for certain marching cubes implementations that assume a buffer. Time Variation: If Time.time is not continuous or resets, the sphere will jump. Ensure Time.time is a monotonically increasing value. Zero Radius: When sin(0.25 Time.time) == 0, the radius is 0, and the entire volume is empty (all zeros). A method that subtracts a sphere from an existing volume. Choose this when you need to hollow out a region rather than generate a solid sphere. Sphere Carving Time Complexity: O(N^3), where N is the resolution. Every voxel is visited once. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for the colors array and the 3D texture. Performance: The method is computationally lightweight per voxel (simple arithmetic and comparison). However, uploading the texture to the GPU every frame can be a bottleneck if done naively. Using a compute shader or persistent mapped memory can improve performance. Strengths: Simple to implement, produces a smooth sphere for Marching Cubes, dynamic radius. Limitations: Binary field may lead to aliasing artifacts in the extracted mesh if the resolution is too low. The oscillating radius is specific to this implementation and may not be suitable for static scenes. When to use: When a dynamic, procedurally generated sphere is needed for Marching Cubes surface extraction, and the oscillating behavior is desired. When not to use: For static spheres (use a static kernel), or when higher-order interpolation is needed (use a signed distance field). This method originates from an unofficial Unity-based implementation of GPU Marching Cubes by Pavel Kouril. It is designed to demonstrate procedural geometry generation within the Unity engine, leveraging the Marching Cubes component's ability to accept a DensityTexture. The oscillating radius is a visual effect to demonstrate the dynamic nature of the volume. pavelkouril/unity-marching-cubes-gpu, https://github.com/pavelkouril/unity-marching-cubes-gpu, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Filled Check
head: Filled, Intersection Detection, Voxel Occupancy Check
body: Voxel Filled Check determines whether a specific voxel coordinate within a structured grid or block is occupied by geometry. It serves as the fundamental occupancy test for ray traversal and rendering, returning a binary status to allow rays to skip free space. Unlike Point-in-Box Inclusion Test which tests continuous coordinates against bounding volumes, or Voxel Visibility Culling which determines visibility from a camera, this method operates on discrete integer grid indices and relies on pre-computed bitmask data structures. The method checks occupancy by accessing a compact bitmask representation of the voxel grid. Depending on the implementation configuration, it may consult additional metadata or perform strict boundary checks before testing the bit. Inputs: coord: A 3D integer coordinate (x, y, z) representing the voxel to test. voxelbatch: An array of integers storing the packed bits for the block. outputlb, outputub: Lower and upper bounds defining the valid coordinate range for the output grid. option.WithMeta(): A boolean flag indicating whether metadata is available and should be consulted. voxelmetas: An array of voxel metadata objects. Outputs: occupied: A boolean value or integer 0/1 indicating if the voxel is occupied. Data Structures: Bitmask Block: A contiguous memory region or texture where each bit corresponds to a voxel. Voxel Batch: An array of integers where each integer stores multiple bits. Steps: 1. Calculate Local Coordinates: Determine the position of the voxel within its local block using bitwise masking. local = coord \ \& \ (VX\MASK\EXT - 1) where VX\MASK\EXT is the block dimension size. 2. Calculate Linear Index: Compute the linear index of the voxel within the bitmask block. mask\linear\idx = local.x + local.y \cdot VX\MASK\EXT + local.z \cdot VX\MASK\EXT \cdot VX\MASK\EXT This maps the 3D coordinate to a 1D bit position. 3. Metadata Check (Optional): If option.WithMeta() is true, retrieve the metadata object for the voxel at masklinearidx and return the result of the Filled() method on that metadata. 4. Boundary Check: If metadata is not used, verify that coord lies within the valid output bounds [output\lb, output\ub]. If the coordinate is out of bounds, return 0. 5. Bit Test: Determine the integer index within the voxelbatch array and extract the bit. batch\index = mask\linear\idx / kBatchSize occupied = GETBIT(voxel\batch[batch\index], mask\linear\idx) Return occupied. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelfilledcheck(coord, voxelbatch, outputlb, outputub, usemeta, voxelmetas, vxmaskext, kbatchsize): """ Check if a voxel at coord is occupied. Args: coord: Tuple (x, y, z) of integers. voxelbatch: List or array of integers representing packed bits. outputlb: Tuple (x, y, z) lower bound. outputub: Tuple (x, y, z) upper bound. usemeta: Boolean flag for metadata usage. voxelmetas: Array of metadata objects (if usemeta is true). vxmaskext: Block dimension size. kbatchsize: Number of bits per integer in voxelbatch. Returns: bool: True if occupied, False otherwise. """ # Step 1: Calculate local coordinates within the block localx = coord[0] & (vxmaskext - 1) localy = coord[1] & (vxmaskext - 1) localz = coord[2] & (vxmaskext - 1) # Step 2: Calculate linear index masklinearidx = localx + localy vxmaskext + localz vxmaskext vxmaskext # Step 3: Metadata Check if usemeta: return voxelmetas[masklinearidx].filled() # Step 4: Boundary Check if not (outputlb[0] <= coord[0] <= outputub[0] and outputlb[1] <= coord[1] <= outputub[1] and outputlb[2] <= coord[2] <= outputub[2]): return False # Step 5: Bit Test batchindex = masklinearidx // kbatchsize bitoffset = masklinearidx % kbatchsize return (voxelbatch[batchindex] >> bitoffset) & 1 Parameters: VXMASKEXT: The dimension of the voxel block. kBatchSize: The number of bits packed into one integer of the voxelbatch array. outputlb, outputub: The bounding box of the valid output grid. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out-of-Bounds Access: If coord is outside outputlb and outputub, the method must return 0 to prevent invalid memory access or incorrect occupancy. Metadata Consistency: If WithMeta() is true, the metadata array must be aligned with the bitmask indices. Determines if a voxel's material is transparent for ray traversal. It differs from Voxel Filled Check by interpreting the unpacked material ID to return a semantic status or transparency flag. Validates if a sampled voxel contributes to opacity, reducing banding artifacts. It focuses on visual contribution rather than simple geometric containment. Iterates over the grid to return linear indices of voxels satisfying a predicate. It returns indices rather than boolean flags and supports arbitrary conditions beyond occupancy. Tallies occurrences of unique voxel values (fragment IDs), ignoring empty voxels. It provides statistical histograms rather than binary occupancy checks. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the bitmask. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Low overhead, suitable for dense traversal and early ray termination. Limitations: Only provides binary occupancy. Voxel Filled Check is a core component of voxel-based rendering systems, particularly those using hierarchical or block-based data structures like those in vxray. It enables efficient ray traversal by allowing rays to skip empty regions of space. name: Voxel Material Classification
head: ClassifyVoxel, Transparent Material Check
body: Voxel Material Classification determines whether a voxel material is transparent for ray traversal purposes, allowing rays to pass through. It differs from Voxel Filled Check, which only determines occupancy, by interpreting the unpacked material ID to return a semantic status or transparency flag. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A packed uint32t voxel value. Output: A classification status, either a boolean transparency flag or an enumeration (KnownAir, KnownLiquid, KnownSolid, UnknownBlocked). Data Structures: Voxel: A packed uint32t integer containing material identifiers. Material Index: An 8-bit unsigned integer (uint8t) returned by the unpacking function. Status Enum: CollisionSampleStatus with values KnownAir, KnownSolid, KnownLiquid, UnknownBlocked. Steps: 1. Unpack Material: Extract the material ID from the packed voxel using Utils::UnpackMaterial, which returns a uint8t. 2. Classify by Type (Semantic): Compare the unpacked material against predefined categories: If material equals Air, return KnownAir. If material equals Water, Lava, or Oil, return KnownLiquid. Otherwise, return KnownSolid. 3. Classify by Transparency (Boolean): Determine if the material allows ray traversal. A material m is considered transparent if: 5 \le m \le 12 m = 18 m = 35 (Specifically MATTURF, because blade cells are 90% air). Otherwise, the material is opaque. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def classifyvoxel(voxel: int) -> tuple: # Step 1: Unpack material from packed uint32t voxel # Exact bit-packing scheme not given in sources; assumes lowest 8 bits. materialid = voxel & 0xFF # Step 2: Semantic classification # Exact numeric values for material enums are implementation-specific. MATERIALAIR = 0 MATERIALWATER = 1 MATERIALLAVA = 2 MATERIALOIL = 3 if materialid == MATERIALAIR: status = "KnownAir" elif materialid in (MATERIALWATER, MATERIALLAVA, MATERIALOIL): status = "KnownLiquid" else: status = "KnownSolid" # Step 3: Transparency check istransparent = (5 <= materialid <= 12) or (materialid == 18) or (materialid == 35) return status, istransparent Parameters: Material 35 (MATTURF): Explicitly treated as transparent because the geometry consists of blade cells that are 90% air. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bit Packing Ambiguity: The exact bit layout of the uint32t voxel is not specified in the sources. Implementers must refer to the specific unpacking implementation in their codebase. Output Divergence: Source defines a boolean transparency check, while Source defines a semantic enum classification. These serve different pipeline stages (culling vs. shading) and can be used together. Generates a compact lookup table (palette) mapping discrete voxel values (1–255) to physically-based rendering (PBR) material definitions for each of the six voxel faces. It differs from per-voxel material instances by batching materials into atlases, thereby reducing memory overhead and draw calls. Choose this when memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and materials are shared across many voxels. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel. The operation involves a constant-time unpack and a few integer comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. No large tables are required for the classification logic itself. Strengths: Efficiently determines transparency for ray traversal culling. Limitations: Relies on hardcoded material IDs and ranges. When to use: During ray marching or traversal to skip empty space or handle liquid interactions. The method originates from voxel rendering engines that require efficient culling and shading of volumetric data. Source documents the transparency logic for ray traversal. Source documents the semantic classification pipeline for chunk generation tests. The distinction between "filled" (occupancy) and "material" (semantic/transparent) classification is a common optimization in voxel engines to separate coarse culling from fine-grained shading decisions. mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) asajid2-cell/voxelrender, https://github.com/asajid2-cell/voxelrender, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Material Palette Generation
body: This method generates a compact lookup table (palette) that maps discrete voxel values (1–255) to physically-based rendering (PBR) material definitions for each of the six voxel faces. It solves the problem of efficiently storing and accessing per-face material properties by packing material layer indices and flags into a single 2D texture atlas and a corresponding 3D palette array. It differs from per-voxel material instances by batching materials into atlases, thereby reducing memory overhead and draw calls. Inputs: materials: A dictionary mapping string voxel values ("1" to "255") to a list of material names for the 6 faces. materialdefinitions: A source (e.g., JSON) providing PBR texture paths and boolean flags (isopaque, hascolor, etc.) for each material name. atlaswidth, atlasheight: Dimensions of the output texture atlas in pixels. res: Resolution of each material tile in the atlas. Typical value: 512. Outputs: palette: A 3D NumPy array of shape (256, 6, 3) with type np.uint8. coloratlas, emissionatlas, normalatlas, rsmaatlas: 2D texture arrays containing the packed material channels. Data Structures: 1. Palette Texture: Shape (256, 6, 3). Each entry [voxel, face] contains: Index 0: layer & 255 (lower 8 bits of the material index). Index 1: layer >> 8 (upper 8 bits of the material index). Index 2: flag (bitmask of material properties). 2. Material Flags Bitmask: Bit 0: ISOPAQUE Bit 1: HASCOLOR Bit 2: HASEMISSION Bit 3: HASNORMAL Bit 4: HASRSMA. 3. Material Channels: color: RGBA texture. emission: RGB texture. normal: RGB texture (derived from RG source). rsma: RGBA texture (R=roughness, G=specular, B=metallic, A=ambient occlusion). Algorithm Steps: 1. Load and Sort Materials: Parse material definitions to extract unique material names. Sort unique names alphabetically to create a deterministic index i for each name. Calculate atlas grid dimensions: cols = \lfloor atlas\width / res \rfloor rows = \lfloor atlas\height / res \rfloor. 2. Build Atlas and Lookup Tables: Initialize empty atlas textures for color, emission, normal, and rsma with dimensions (rows res, cols res). For each unique material name name at index i: Calculate grid position: col = i \pmod{cols} row = \lfloor i / cols \rfloor. Calculate pixel coordinates: x = col \times res y = row \times res. Extract sub-region [y:y+res, x:x+res] from each atlas. Load the material's PBR channels. If a channel is missing, fill it with self.redx (default). Store the loaded textures in lists self.colortextures, etc.. Record the layer index: layers[name] = i. Compute the flag bitmask: flag = (IS\OPAQUE \text{ if } is\opaque \text{ else } 0) \ | \ (HAS\COLOR \text{ if } has\color \text{ else } 0) \ | \ (HAS\EMISSION \text{ if } has\emission \text{ else } 0) \ | \ (HAS\NORMAL \text{ if } has\normal \text{ else } 0) \ | \ (HAS\RSMA \text{ if } has\rsma \text{ else } 0). Record flags: flags[name] = flag. 3. Fill Palette: Initialize palette array of shape (256, 6, 3) with zeros. For each voxel value v (1 to 255): Get the list of material names for the 6 faces. If the list length is 1, replicate it to 6 faces: names = 6. If the list length is not 6, raise an error. For each face f (0 to 5): Get name = names[f]. Lookup layer = layers[name] and flag = flags[name]. Set palette[v, f] = [layer & 255, layer >> 8, flag]. 4. Verify Palette: Check for mixed opaque/transparent sides on a single voxel. Count opaque flags per voxel: opaquecounts = sum(flag & 1 for face in palette[v]). If 0 < opaquecounts < 6 for any voxel, raise an error. Mixed opacity on a single voxel is invalid. 5. Write Outputs: Save palette as a PNG texture. Save coloratlas, emissionatlas, normalatlas, and rsmaatlas as PNG textures. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatevoxelpalette(materials, materialdefs, atlaswidth, atlasheight, res=512): # 1. Load and Sort Materials allnames = set() for facenames in materials.values(): allnames.update(facenames) names = sorted(list(allnames)) cols = atlaswidth // res rows = atlasheight // res # Initialize atlases coloratlas = np.zeros((rows res, cols res, 4), dtype=np.uint8) emissionatlas = np.zeros((rows res, cols res, 3), dtype=np.uint8) normalatlas = np.zeros((rows res, cols res, 3), dtype=np.uint8) rsmaatlas = np.zeros((rows res, cols res, 4), dtype=np.uint8) layers = {} flags = {} # 2. Build Atlas and Lookup Tables for i, name in enumerate(names): col = i % cols row = i // cols x = col res y = row res # Load material properties mat = materialdefs[name] isopaque = mat.get('isopaque', True) hascolor = mat.get('hascolor', True) hasemission = mat.get('hasemission', False) hasnormal = mat.get('hasnormal', False) hasrsma = mat.get('hasrsma', False) # Load textures: if channel missing, fill with self.redx (default) color = mat.get('color', np.full((res, res, 4), 255, dtype=np.uint8)) emission = mat.get('emission', np.full((res, res, 3), 0, dtype=np.uint8)) normal = mat.get('normal', np.full((res, res, 3), 128, dtype=np.uint8)) rsma = mat.get('rsma', np.full((res, res, 4), 0, dtype=np.uint8)) # Store in atlas coloratlas[y:y+res, x:x+res] = color emissionatlas[y:y+res, x:x+res] = emission normalatlas[y:y+res, x:x+res] = normal rsmaatlas[y:y+res, x:x+res] = rsma # Compute flags flag = 0 if isopaque: flag |= 1 # ISOPAQUE if hascolor: flag |= 2 # HASCOLOR if hasemission: flag |= 4 # HASEMISSION if hasnormal: flag |= 8 # HASNORMAL if hasrsma: flag |= 16 # HASRSMA layers[name] = i flags[name] = flag # 3. Fill Palette palette = np.zeros((256, 6, 3), dtype=np.uint8) for voxelstr, facenames in materials.items(): voxel = int(voxelstr) if voxel < 1 or voxel > 255: raise ValueError(f"Invalid voxel value: {voxel}") if len(facenames) == 1: facenames = facenames 6 if len(facenames) != 6: raise ValueError(f"Invalid material names at voxel {voxel}: {facenames}") for f, name in enumerate(facenames): layer = layers[name] flag = flags[name] palette[voxel, f] = [layer & 255, layer >> 8, flag] # 4. Verify Palette opaquecounts = np.sum(palette[:,:, 2] & 1, axis=1, dtype=np.uint8) mixed = np.logicaland(opaquecounts > 0, opaquecounts < 6) if np.any(mixed): raise ValueError("ERROR: Palette contains voxels with mixed opaque/transparent sides.") return palette, coloratlas, emissionatlas, normalatlas, rsmaatlas Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mixed Opacity: A voxel cannot have both opaque and transparent faces. The system validates this and exits with an error if detected. Missing Channels: If a material lacks a specific channel, it must be filled with self.redx (default) to prevent atlas corruption. Voxel Value Range: Only voxel values 1–255 are supported. The system explicitly validates this range and raises an error for values outside it. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R^2 + V \cdot F), where N is the number of unique materials, R is the resolution of each tile, V is the number of voxel types (255), and F is the number of faces (6). The dominant cost is loading and packing textures for N materials. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot R^2 + V \cdot F). The atlas size is N \cdot R^2 pixels per channel. The palette size is fixed at 256 \times 6 \times 3 bytes. Performance: Reduces memory overhead and draw calls by batching materials into atlases instead of using per-voxel material instances. Strengths: Efficient storage for voxel worlds with many distinct materials; fast lookup during rendering. Limitations: Fixed voxel value range (1–255); mixed opacity per voxel is not supported; atlas size grows linearly with the number of unique materials. This method is part of the voxel material classification and storage system in the Godot Voxel plugin. It enables efficient PBR rendering for voxel-based games by mapping discrete voxel IDs to a shared set of material atlases. viktor-ferenczi/godot-voxel, https://github.com/viktor-ferenczi/godot-voxel, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Solidity Check
body: Voxel Solidity Check is a post-sampling validation step that verifies whether a sampled voxel actually contributes to the volume's opacity. It is used to reduce banding and rendering artifacts in raycasting pipelines. Input: A voxel grid (8-bit or 16-bit raw volumetric data) and a sampling position within a voxel. Output: A boolean flag or weighted value indicating if the voxel is solid enough to contribute to the render. The input is stored as raw volumetric data supporting 8-bit or 16-bit depth. The layout is a 3D array or texture indexed by (x, y, z) coordinates. 1. Sample Voxel Value: Retrieve the density or occupancy value at the current voxel coordinate (x, y, z). 2. Validate Contribution: Compare the sampled value against a threshold to determine if the voxel contains significant material. 3. Proceed or Skip: If the voxel is solid, proceed with raycasting or compositing; otherwise, skip or treat as transparent. No explicit mathematical formula is provided in the sources for the threshold comparison itself. The validation can be conceptually represented as: \text{Solid} = \begin{cases} \text{true} & \text{if } V(x,y,z) > T \\ \text{false} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where V(x,y,z) is the voxel value and T is the threshold. Threshold (T): Not given in the sources. Bit Depth: 8-bit or 16-bit. Banding: The primary pitfall this method addresses is banding artifacts. Precision: Using 16-bit data helps preserve subtle density variations that might be lost in 8-bit formats, reducing artifacts. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelsoliditycheck(voxelgrid, x, y, z, threshold): """Checks if a voxel at (x, y, z) is solid enough to contribute to rendering. Args: voxelgrid: 3D array of voxel values (8-bit or 16-bit). x, y, z: Coordinates of the voxel to check. threshold: Minimum value for the voxel to be considered solid. Returns: bool: True if the voxel is solid, False otherwise. """ # Bounds checking should be performed in the calling context value = voxelgrid[x][y][z] if value > threshold: return True return False Volume Fraction is a voxel occupancy determination method where a cell is considered solid if the majority (or a specific cutoff value) of its volume is filled by the object. This method requires calculating the volume of the intersection between the cube and the parametric surface to determine the fill ratio. Alternatively, it can be approximated by choosing a representative or random set of points inside the cube, testing if they are inside the parametric object, and declaring the voxel occupied if a cutoff percentage of points are inside. Binary Marching Cubes is described as a version of this method that specifically chooses the 8 corners of the cube as its test points and includes anti-aliasing. Fractional occupancy varieties can use intermediate cases linked to other cutoff values as an anti-aliasing technique. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage format of the voxel grid (8-bit or 16-bit per voxel). Strengths: Effectively reduces banding and rendering artifacts. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When rendering volumetric data that exhibits banding artifacts or when using raycasting on discrete voxel grids. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The term "Voxel Solidity Check" appears in the context of a C++/OpenGL volume rendering project that loads 8 and 16-bit raw volumetric data and displays it using raycasting. The project lists "voxel's solidity check" as a feature to reduce banding/artifacts, alongside ray jitter, gradient computation, and smoothing. The concept of using volume fraction or point occupancy for voxelization, which underpins the solidity check, was discussed in the context of rasterizing parametric solids in Minecraft voxel space. name: Voxel Filtering
head: Voxel Predicate Filter
body: Voxel Filtering iterates over a voxel grid to identify and return the linear indices of voxels that satisfy a user-defined predicate function. It solves the problem of isolating relevant data from a dense grid by discarding voxels that do not meet specific criteria. Inputs: grid: A 3D array of voxel data (e.g., CellType). func: A callable predicate that takes a single voxel as input and returns a boolean indicating whether the voxel satisfies the condition. Outputs: indices: A dynamic list (vector) of integers containing the linear indices of voxels where func returns True. Data Structures: The grid is accessed as a flat array for iteration, with linear index i mapping to the underlying voxel data. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty output vector outputindices. 2. Determine the total number of voxels N in the grid. 3. Iterate i from 0 to N-1: a. Retrieve the voxel value cell at linear index i. b. Evaluate result = func(cell). c. If result is True, append i to outputindices. 4. Return outputindices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelfilter(grid, func): """ Filters a voxel grid based on a predicate function. Args: grid: 3D array or flattened list of voxel data. func: Function taking a single voxel element and returning a boolean. Returns: List of linear indices where func returns True. """ outputindices = [] N = len(grid) for i in range(N): cell = grid[i] if func(cell): outputindices.append(i) return outputindices Parameters: func: A callable predicate that takes a single voxel (CellType) as input and returns a boolean indicating whether the voxel satisfies the condition. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the grid is empty, the function returns an empty list. Precision issues may arise if the predicate relies on floating-point comparisons without a tolerance threshold. The method assumes a contiguous memory layout for linear indexing; non-contiguous grids may require coordinate-to-index mapping. Generates a mixed set of voxel indices for volume rendering by combining uniformly sampled cells with cells known to be occupied by geometry. It filters out cells with invalid density values (specifically -1). It is chosen when a renderer needs to balance coverage of empty space with detail in occupied regions. Link: Sample Uniform and Occupied Cells. Reduces a dense 3D voxel grid to a sparse set of voxels that satisfy a user-defined predicate, typically based on a transfer function evaluating density and gradient. It solves the problem of rendering or processing large volumes by discarding empty or irrelevant voxels, storing the result as a 2D array of splat rows to enable efficient front-to-back or back-to-front traversal. It differs from Voxel Filtering by specifically structuring the output for splat-based rendering pipelines rather than returning a flat list of indices, and from Sample Uniform and Occupied Cells by using a continuous transfer function threshold rather than simple occupancy checks. Link: Volume Subset Extraction. Computes the voxel intensity threshold below which a volume brick is considered empty and can be skipped during streaming. Link: Empty-Brick Threshold Calculation. Connected Component Labeling (CCL) for Voxel Filtering identifies and retains only the largest connected components of occupied voxels in a 3D boolean grid, filtering out small noise or isolated artifacts. It operates by performing a flood-fill traversal with a configurable neighborhood distance, enforcing spherical connectivity within cubic bounds to determine adjacency. Unlike sibling methods that sample uniformly or extract arbitrary subsets, this method specifically targets topological coherence, making it suitable for cleaning sparse voxel representations where small disconnected clusters represent noise rather than signal. Link: Connected Component Labeling for Voxel Filtering. Sets all non-empty voxels to VOXELFREE, effectively removing fragment IDs and marking all occupied space as free. It iterates over all voxels and, if a voxel is not VOXELEMPTY, sets its value to VOXELFREE. Selects grid cells based on two disjoint value ranges for a physical property. Selection condition: (−200 \le \text{pressure} \le 20) \lor (500 \le \text{pressure} \le 1000), where pressure is measured in Pascal units. Not given in the sources.
