name: Local Short-Range Repulsion
head: Particle repulsion optimization, Tangential repulsive force iteration
body:
Local Short-Range Repulsion is a particle distribution optimization step that treats repulsive interactions as local short-range forces to optimize particle distribution. It consists of searching for neighboring particle sets, calculating the repulsive force, and iterating the tangential repulsive force. Inputs: Particle positions \mathbf{p}i and \mathbf{p}j, particle normal vectors \mathbf{n}i, voxel pyramid structure defining scale levels l and voxel sizes \sigmal, base cell size h{base}, and maximum scale level L. Outputs: Updated particle positions \mathbf{p}i'. The method relies on an adaptively subdivided voxel pyramid. The voxel unit is defined by scale level l with size \sigmal. The repulsion cutoff radius h{cutoff} is numerically equal to the voxel size \sigmal at the scale level l to which the target particle belongs. The source provides a formula h{cutoff} = h{base} \cdot 2^{i-1-i}, which contains a typographical error in the exponent but explicitly defines h{cutoff} as equal to \sigmal. 1. Neighbor Search: Traverse all voxels within the voxel unit containing the target particle i and its 26-neighborhood. Treat all other particles in these voxels as the neighboring particle set Ni. Map the coordinates of activated particles and their repulsion radii to the current scale to ensure consistency during force calculation. 2. Repulsive Force Calculation: For each neighbor j \in Ni, j 
eq i, calculate the relative position vector \mathbf{d}{ij} = \mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{p}j. Compute the radial distance r = \|\mathbf{d}{ij}\|. Calculate the repulsion weight factor \omega = (1 - r/h{cutoff})^2, which ensures the force is strong at close range and tends to zero as r 	o h{cutoff}. Normalize the relative position to obtain the unit vector \hat{\mathbf{d}}{ij} = \mathbf{d}{ij} / \|\mathbf{d}{ij}\|. Compute the individual repulsive force contribution \mathbf{f}j = \hat{\mathbf{d}}{ij} \cdot \omega. 3. Tangential Force Iteration: Compute the total repulsive force on particle i as the vector sum \mathbf{f}g = \sum{j \in Ni, j 
eq i} \mathbf{f}j. Project \mathbf{f}g onto the normal direction \mathbf{n}i of particle i to obtain the tangential component \mathbf{f}v^T = \mathbf{f}v - \mathbf{n}i(\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{n}i). The source uses \mathbf{f}v and \mathbf{f}g interchangeably in this context; \mathbf{f}g^T is used as the actual acting repulsive force to reduce impact on projection accuracy during iteration. 4. Displacement Update: Calculate the displacement \Delta \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{f}g^T \cdot 0.02, where 0.02 is the iteration step size chosen to balance accuracy and efficiency. Add the displacement to the current position \mathbf{p}i \leftarrow \mathbf{p}i + \Delta \mathbf{p}i to complete one iteration. Repeat iterations until equilibrium, defined as the state where the energy gradient is zero ( rac{d\mathbf{p}i}{dt} - 
abla E{total} = 0). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def localshortrangerepulsion(particles, voxelgrid, hbase, L): """ particles: List of dicts with keys 'pos' (vec3), 'normal' (vec3) voxelgrid: Spatial hash or grid structure mapping voxel coords to particle indices hbase: Base cell size at finest scale L: Maximum scale level """ stepsize = 0.02 for i, p in enumerate(particles): posi = p['pos'] normali = p['normal'] # Determine voxel level l for particle i # Standard grid lookup: find voxel coordinates containing posi voxelcoords = ( math.floor(posi[0] / hbase), math.floor(posi[1] / hbase), math.floor(posi[2] / hbase)) levell = voxelgrid.getlevel(voxelcoords) # Cutoff radius equals voxel size at level l # Assuming standard adaptive scaling: voxelsize = hbase 2^(L - levell) voxelsize = hbase (2 (L - levell)) hcutoff = voxelsize totalforce = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Search neighbors in 26-neighborhood of current voxel # Traverse all voxels within the voxel unit and its 26-neighborhood neighborindices = [] for dx in (-1, 0, 1): for dy in (-1, 0, 1): for dz in (-1, 0, 1): if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue targetvoxel = (voxelcoords[0] + dx, voxelcoords[1] + dy, voxelcoords[2] + dz) neighborindices.extend(voxelgrid.getparticlesinvoxel(targetvoxel)) for j in neighborindices: if i == j: continue posj = particles[j]['pos'] # Map coordinates to current scale # Scale positions relative to voxel origin for consistency scalefactor = 2 (L - levell) posiscaled = [c scalefactor for c in posi] posjscaled = [c scalefactor for c in posj] dij = [posiscaled[k] - posjscaled[k] for k in range(3)] r = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in dij)) if r >= hcutoff: continue omega = (1.0 - r / hcutoff) 2 if r == 0.0: continue dhatij = [c / r for c in dij] fj = [dhatij[k] omega for k in range(3)] totalforce = [totalforce[k] + fj[k] for k in range(3)] # Tangential projection per source: fvT = fv - ni (ni. ni) # Source uses fv and fg interchangeably; we use totalforce as fg ndotn = sum(normali[k] normali[k] for k in range(3)) ftangential = [ totalforce[k] - normali[k] ndotn for k in range(3) ] # Displacement update displacement = [ftangential[k] stepsize for k in range(3)] p['pos'] = [p['pos'][k] + displacement[k] for k in range(3)] Iteration Step Size: 0.02, chosen to balance iteration accuracy and efficiency. Cutoff Radius: Numerically equal to the voxel size \sigmal at the particle's scale level. Zero Distance: If r=0, normalization fails; skip the particle. Scale Consistency: Coordinates and radii must be mapped to the current scale before calculation. Projection Formula: The source defines the tangential component as \mathbf{f}v^T = \mathbf{f}v - \mathbf{n}i(\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{n}i), where \mathbf{f}v and \mathbf{f}g are used interchangeably for the total force. Not given in the sources. Origin: Introduced in Surface Extraction for Industrial CT Based On Adaptive Particle System. Purpose: Optimizes particle distribution by treating repulsive interactions as local short-range forces, addressing the weakness of repulsive forces at long distances. Development: Part of a pipeline involving adaptive voxel pyramids, neighbor search, and energy minimization for equilibrium. name: Moore Neighbourhood Sampling
body: Moore Neighbourhood Sampling reads all 27 voxels in a 3x3x3 block centered on a target voxel, returning their values and a bitmask of non-empty voxels. It provides a fixed, exhaustive 27-neighbor scope, distinguishing it from radius-based alternatives like PBF Displacement Calculation with Grid-Based Neighbor Search. Inputs: voxels: A flat array of 27 voxel values representing the 3x3x3 block. center: The 3D integer coordinates (vx, vy, vz) of the central voxel. VOXELEMPTY: The sentinel value representing an empty voxel. Outputs: neighbours: An array of 27 voxel values. mask: A 32-bit unsigned integer bitmask. Data Structures: The output is encapsulated in a MooreNeighbourhood struct: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class MooreNeighbourhood: neighbours: list[int] # Values of the 27 voxels mask: int # Bitmask: bit i is 1 if neighbours[i] != VOXELEMPTY Linear Indexing Logic: The 27 neighbors are indexed linearly from i = 0 to 26. The mapping between linear index i and 3D offset (dx, dy, dz) is defined as follows: 1. Linear to Offset: Given linear index i: z = \lfloor i / 9 \rfloor y = \lfloor (i \pmod 9) / 3 \rfloor x = i \pmod 3 The offset vector is (x-1, y-1, z-1). 2. Offset to Linear: Given offset vector v = (vx, vy, vz) where vx, vy, vz \in \{-1, 0, 1\}: \text{linear\index} = u32(vx + 1) + 3 \cdot u32(vy + 1) + 9 \cdot u32(vz + 1) Here, u32(\cdot) denotes casting to unsigned 32-bit integer to handle potential negative values in intermediate calculations if implemented in languages with signed arithmetic, though in Python-like pseudocode, standard integer arithmetic suffices. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize neighbours array of size 27 and mask to 0. 2. For each i from 0 to 26: a. Calculate offset (dx, dy, dz) using the Linear to Offset formula. b. Calculate neighbor position u = (vx + dx, vy + dy, vz + dz). c. Calculate linear index idx for u using the Offset to Linear formula. d. Read value = voxels[idx]. e. Set neighbours[i] = value. f. If value != VOXELEMPTY, set bit i in mask (i.e., mask |= (1 << i)). 3. Return MooreNeighbourhood(neighbours, mask). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mooreneighbourhoodsampling(voxels3x3x3, center, voxelempty): neighbours = [0] 27 mask = 0 for i in range(27): # Linear index i to 3D offset z = i // 9 y = (i % 9) // 3 x = i % 3 # Offset vector relative to center dx = x - 1 dy = y - 1 dz = z - 1 # Neighbor position ux = center[0] + dx uy = center[1] + dy uz = center[2] + dz # Neighbor position to linear index (maps offsets -1,0,1 to 0,1,2) linearidx = (dx + 1) + 3 (dy + 1) + 9 (dz + 1) # Read value from the 3x3x3 block value = voxels3x3x3[linearidx] neighbours[i] = value if value != voxelempty: mask |= (1 << i) return MooreNeighbourhood(neighbours, mask) The source provides the mapping logic for the 3x3x3 block but does not explicitly detail the global array bounds checking or the global-to-linear conversion for the voxels array itself. An implementer must add boundary checks for ux, uy, uz against the volume dimensions before accessing the global voxels array. Extracts the 6 face-adjacent voxels from a Moore neighbourhood result. It returns the values at specific indices corresponding to the \pm x, \pm y, \pm z directions. The indices in the 27-element Moore array are [12, 14, 10, 16, 4, 22], corresponding to directions -x, x, -y, y, -z, z respectively. A precomputed bitmask VONNEUMANNMASK (value 4281360u) has bits 12, 14, 10, 16, 4, and 22 set, allowing for efficient filtering of the Moore mask to identify which face neighbors are non-empty. Time Complexity: O(1), as it always accesses exactly 27 voxels. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring storage for 27 values and one 32-bit integer. Strengths: Provides complete local context for voxel-based algorithms; the bitmask allows for efficient conditional processing of only occupied neighbors. Limitations: Accesses empty voxels unnecessarily if the neighborhood is sparse; requires boundary handling for voxels at the edge of the volume. Originating from implementations in GPU-based voxel terrain rendering, this method is documented in the wgpu-voxel-terrain repository. It is used as a low-level primitive for spatial queries in voxel grids, enabling higher-level operations like neighbor searches for physics or rendering. statusfailed/wgpu-voxel-terrain, https://github.com/statusfailed/wgpu-voxel-terrain, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Collision Test
head: Grid Check, Voxel Column Collision, vertical column check
body: A Voxel Collision Test determines if a specific spatial region within a voxel grid contains any occupied (solid) voxels. It solves the problem of detecting intersections between geometric primitives (such as vertical slabs or particles) and a discrete voxelized environment. Unlike the parent Voxel Occupancy Test, which tests individual points for containment, this method tests a continuous range or volume against the grid structure. It differs from Raycasting (often implemented as line rasterization) by evaluating a column or volume rather than a single line, and from Sparse AABB Collision Test by operating on dense or structured grid coordinates rather than bounding volume hierarchies. The method operates by mapping world-space coordinates to local grid indices and iterating through the relevant voxels to check for occupancy. Inputs: World-space horizontal position (x, z). World-space height bounds y{lo} and y{hi} defining a vertical slab. Grid parameters: origin (ox, oy, oz), voxel size s, grid dimensions (Dx, Dy, Dz), rotation matrix R, and half-grid offset h. Occupancy data: A 3D array or hash map indicating solid voxels. Outputs: Boolean: true if any voxel in the tested region is solid; false otherwise. The grid is typically stored as a dense 3D array grid[Dx][Dy][Dz] where each element is a boolean or integer flag indicating occupancy. For sparse implementations, a hash map mapping (x, y, z) tuples to occupancy flags is used. 1. Coordinate Transformation: Convert world-space horizontal coordinates to the grid's local coordinate system. Construct a local position vector p = (x, 0, z). Apply the inverse rotation and subtract the origin: p{local} = R^{-1} \cdot (p - origin). 2. Grid Index Calculation: Convert local coordinates to floating-point grid indices. lxf = \frac{p{local,x} + h}{s} lzf = \frac{p{local,z} + h}{s} ly{lo,f} = \frac{y{lo} - oy + h}{s} ly{hi,f} = \frac{y{hi} - oy + h}{s} (Note: h represents half the physical grid size, aligning the grid center with the origin.) 3. Bounds Checking: Verify if the horizontal floating-point indices (lxf, lzf) fall within the grid dimensions 0, Dx) and [0, Dz). If outside, return false (no collision). 4. Index [Clamping: Clamp the floating-point Y indices to valid integer grid bounds. ly{lo} = \max(0, \lfloor ly{lo,f} \rfloor) ly{hi} = \min(Dy - 1, \lceil ly{hi,f} \rceil) 5. Iteration and Check: Iterate through all integer Y indices k from ly{lo} to ly{hi}. Check the voxel at (\lfloor lxf \rfloor, k, \lfloor lzf \rfloor). If the voxel is solid, return true. 6. Result: If the loop completes without finding a solid voxel, return false. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelcollisiontest(worldx, worldz, worldylo, worldyhi, grid): # 1. Transform to local coordinates local = grid.rotinv (Vec3(worldx, 0.0, worldz) - grid.origin) # 2. Calculate floating-point grid indices lxf = (local.x + grid.halfgrid) / grid.voxsize lzf = (local.z + grid.halfgrid) / grid.voxsize # 3. Check horizontal bounds if lxf < 0 or lxf >= grid.dimx or lzf < 0 or lzf >= grid.dimz: return False # 4. Convert Y bounds to local grid indices lylof = (worldylo - grid.origin.y + grid.halfgrid) / grid.voxsize lyhif = (worldyhi - grid.origin.y + grid.halfgrid) / grid.voxsize # 5. Clamp to integer bounds lylo = max(0, int(floor(lylof))) lyhi = min(grid.dimy - 1, int(ceil(lyhif))) # 6. Iterate and check ix = int(floor(lxf)) iz = int(floor(lzf)) for y in range(lylo, lyhi + 1): if grid.issolid(ix, y, iz): return True return False (Note: Vec3, matrix multiplication, floor, and ceil are standard mathematical/vector operations.) Voxel Size: Determines resolution. Smaller sizes increase accuracy but memory usage and iteration count. Precision: Floating-point to integer conversion must handle boundary cases carefully. Using floor for start and ceil for end ensures full coverage of the slab. Degenerate Input: If y{lo} > y{hi}, the range is invalid and should return false or raise an error. Out-of-Bounds: Horizontal coordinates outside the grid must be handled explicitly to avoid memory access violations. Entity Collision & Movement is a discrete-time physics solver for voxel-based environments that handles collision detection, response, step-height climbing, and crouching for dynamic hitboxes against static voxel chunks and other dynamic solid hitboxes. It differs from simple grid checks by integrating gravity, ground detection, and axis-aligned movement with wall-sliding collision detection against voxel blocks. It builds on Voxel Collision Test by extending simple occupancy checks into a full state-based simulation loop. A collision detection method for a sphere moving through a voxel grid that calculates a displacement vector representing the push-out needed to resolve penetration by averaging displacements from all intersected voxel faces. It differs from simple boolean occupancy tests by providing a continuous resolution vector, allowing the sphere to be pushed out of the voxel structure rather than merely detecting overlap. This method computes intersection points and force-feedback vectors between a haptic burr tool and a virtual object represented solely by a voxel set, enabling realistic tactile interaction during virtual carving. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by relying exclusively on volumetric data for collision resolution, avoiding supplemental polygonal mesh information. Unlike Entity Collision & Movement which may use complex physics engines, or Sphere-Voxel Collision Detection via Displacement Averaging which averages displacements, this method uses an "anchor-based" approach to determine force direction, ensuring stability in complex geometries like tight corners or pits. Time Complexity: O(Dy) for a vertical column test, where Dy is the height of the grid in voxels. For a full volume test, it is O(Dx Dy Dz). Memory Complexity: O(Dx Dy Dz) for dense grids. Sparse implementations use O(N) where N is the number of occupied voxels. Performance: Very fast for sparse checks or when early-out conditions are met. The bottleneck in particle systems is often the rendering (billboarding) rather than the collision test itself. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust for axis-aligned movements, handles concave geometry naturally. Limitations: Resolution-dependent; may miss thin features smaller than a voxel. Does not provide contact normals or penetration depth without extension. The Voxel Collision Test is a fundamental operation in voxel-based game engines and simulations. It is often referred to as a "simple grid check" in the context of early voxel engines like noa. It is used in physics simulations for entities and GPU particle systems. The method extends naturally from 2D collision checks used in tile-based games. name: Entity Collision & Movement
head: Entity Physics, Voxel Entity Physics, Player Movement & Collision, Entity Movement with Sub-stepping and Collision Resolution
body: Entity Collision & Movement is a discrete-time physics solver for voxel-based environments that handles collision detection, response, step-height climbing, and crouching for dynamic hitboxes against static voxel chunks and other dynamic solid hitboxes. It differs from simple grid checks by integrating gravity, ground detection, and axis-aligned movement with wall-sliding collision detection against voxel blocks. It builds on Voxel Collision Test by extending simple occupancy checks into a full state-based simulation loop. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Entity position, velocity, input direction (yaw, forward/strafe vectors), time delta (dt), and a collection of static voxel chunks and dynamic hitboxes. Outputs: Updated entity position, velocity, and grounded state. Data Structures: The core state is stored in a Hitbox struct: position: glm::vec3 (current world position) velocity: glm::vec3 (current velocity) halfsize: glm::vec3 (half-extents of the AABB) grounded: bool (is currently on ground) prevGrounded: bool (state from previous substep) prevVelocity: glm::vec3 prevPosition: glm::vec3 groundMaterial: string groundVelocity: glm::vec3 gravityScale: float stepHeight: float (maximum climbable step height) elasticity: float (coefficient of restitution) type: BodyType enum (STATIC, DYNAMIC, etc.) crouching: bool An AABB struct is used for collision checks: b: glm::vec3 (max bounds) Methods: scale(glm::vec3), translated(glm::vec3), intersects(AABB), min(), max(). Voxel access uses blockAt(goal, chunks): Computes chunk indices: x{chunk} = \lfloor x / \text{CHUNK\SIZE} \rfloor, z{chunk} = \lfloor z / \text{CHUNK\SIZE} \rfloor. Accesses chunk->blocks[localX][localY][localZ]. Returns 255 for air, otherwise the block ID. Parameters: E: Small epsilon for floating-point comparisons and AABB scaling (e.g., E \times 2.0f). MOVESPEED: 10. MAXFIX: Maximum distance for position correction. JUMPPOWER: 10. GRAVITY: 30 (downward acceleration per second). ENTITYHEIGHT: 2 (vertical size in blocks). substeps: Number of physics substeps per frame (e.g., 8). maxDeltaTime: Maximum time step size, set to 0.01 seconds. maxVelocityNormPerStep: Maximum allowed velocity magnitude per sub-step, set to 0.1. epsilon: Precision threshold for integer checks, set to 10^{-5}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization & Sub-stepping Setup: Clear groundMaterial. Set prevGrounded = grounded. Reset grounded = false. Store prevVelocity = velocity and prevPosition = position. Calculate substep delta: dt{sub} = dt / \text{substeps}. Initialize remainingDeltaTime = dt. Clamp localDeltaTime to maxDeltaTime: localDeltaTime = min(localDeltaTime, maxDeltaTime). Calculate fullVelocityNorm = velocity.length(). Calculate naiveStepVelocityNorm = remainingDeltaTime fullVelocityNorm. If naiveStepVelocityNorm <= maxVelocityNormPerStep, set localDeltaTime = remainingDeltaTime. Else, set localDeltaTime = remainingDeltaTime (maxVelocityNormPerStep / naiveStepVelocityNorm). 2. Gravity & Position Integration: Apply gravity to velocity: vy \leftarrow vy - \text{GRAVITY} \times dt{sub} \times \text{gravityScale}. Update position: p \leftarrow p + v \times dt{sub} + \frac{1}{2} g \times \text{gravityScale} \times dt{sub}^2. 3. Ground Detection: Check block at p - (0, \text{ENTITY\HEIGHT}, 0). If block \neq 255: Set onGround = true. If vy < 0, set vy = 0. Snap py = \lceil py \rceil. 4. Movement Calculation & Axis-Aligned Collision Resolution: Compute horizontal direction from yaw: \vec{front} = (\cos(\text{yaw}), 0, \sin(\text{yaw})). \vec{right} = \text{normalize}(\vec{front} \times (0,1,0)). Calculate change vector: \Delta \vec{p} = \vec{front} \times (-\text{MOVE\SPEED} \times dt{sub}) \times \text{move\dir}z + \vec{right} \times (\text{MOVE\SPEED} \times dt{sub}) \times \text{move\dir}x. Angle wrapping: if \text{yaw} \ge 2\pi or \text{yaw} \le -2\pi, reset to 0. Check collision at p + \Delta \vec{p}. If air (255), move there. Else, zero out X component of \Delta \vec{p} and recheck. Else, zero out Z component of \Delta \vec{p} and recheck. 5. Step-Up Climbing & Ceiling Checks: If stepHeight > 0 and vy \le 0: Check for obstacles ahead in movement direction by scaling AABB and iterating x/z coordinates. If obstacle is climbable (height \le stepHeight), adjust position and velocity to climb. If vy > 0, check for ceiling collisions against voxel chunks by iterating x/z coordinates and scaling the AABB. 6. Crouching: If not crouching or not grounded, return. Check ground contact at two axes (x and z) by checking obstacles at y = py - \text{halfsize}y - E. If no obstacle found at an axis, reset position and velocity at that axis to initial values and zero velocity. Force grounded = true after check. 7. Dynamic Hitbox Interaction: Find nearby solid hitboxes using spatial culling based on movement budget and extents. For each dynamic hitbox, call calcCollisions with stepHeight if previously grounded and gravityScale > 0. Check ceiling collisions if vy > 0 by iterating x/z coordinates and scaling AABB. 8. Edge Cases & Merging: If py < 0, teleport to y=100 and reset vy = 0. Floating-point precision issues are mitigated by using epsilon E in AABB scaling and distance checks. Subtract localDeltaTime from remainingDeltaTime and repeat loop. After the main loop, call applyAndMergeStep(0) three times to resolve any remaining static collisions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. It distinguishes itself from general-purpose physics engines by relying on abstracted boolean test functions for voxel properties rather than a pre-computed spatial structure, making it lightweight and engine-agnostic. Unlike its predecessor voxel-physical, it implements more physically accurate behaviors including semi-implicit Euler integration, axis-dependent friction, and buoyancy. Computes player velocity and position updates using directional acceleration, ground/air friction, gravity, and discrete time steps. It calculates forward and right vectors from yaw, builds a wish direction from WASD/Arrow keys, and normalizes it. Acceleration is scaled by ACCEL when grounded and AIRCONTROL in air, with deceleration applied when stationary. Gravity is applied per frame, and jump impulses are handled via JUMPFORCE. Strengths: Handles complex interactions like step-climbing, crouching, and dynamic hitboxes. Stable with discrete substeps. Limitations: Discrete nature can cause tunneling at high speeds. Requires careful tuning of stepHeight and MAXFIX. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. It evolved from simple raycasting prototypes to full state-based simulation with substeps to handle gravity, ground detection, and collision response. name: Voxel Physics Engine
head: Abstracted terrain physics engine for voxel games
body: The Voxel Physics Engine is a rigid-body simulation system designed for voxel-based game environments, handling collisions between entities and solid or liquid voxel terrain. It distinguishes itself from general-purpose physics engines by relying on abstracted boolean test functions for voxel properties rather than a pre-computed spatial structure, making it lightweight and engine-agnostic. Unlike its predecessor voxel-physical, it implements more physically accurate behaviors including semi-implicit Euler integration, axis-dependent friction, and buoyancy. Inputs: testSolid(x, y, z): A function returning true if the voxel at integer coordinates is solid. testFluid(x, y, z): A function returning true if the voxel at integer coordinates is fluid. options: Configuration object merging with DefaultOptions. dt: Time step in milliseconds. Outputs: Updated rigid body states (position, velocity, resting flags). Collision impact vectors passed to onCollide callbacks. RigidBody: aabb: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box defined by base (min corner) and vec (dimensions). mass: Scalar. Bodies with mass <= 0 are static. velocity: Vector [vx, vy, vz]. resting: Vector [rx, ry, rz] where each component is -1, 0, or 1 indicating contact direction (-1 for negative axis, 1 for positive, 0 for none). friction: Scalar coefficient. restitution: Scalar coefficient (0 to 1). gravityMultiplier: Scalar multiplier for global gravity. airDrag: Scalar. If >= 0, overrides global air drag. fluidDrag: Scalar. If >= 0, overrides global fluid drag. inFluid: Boolean flag. ratioInFluid: Scalar fraction of volume submerged. autoStep: Boolean flag enabling automatic stepping onto 1-unit obstructions. onCollide(impacts): Callback function receiving impact vector. Physics Engine: bodies: List of RigidBody instances. gravity: Vector [gx, gy, gz]. airDrag: Global default air drag coefficient. fluidDrag: Global default fluid drag coefficient. fluidDensity: Scalar density for buoyancy calculations. minBounceImpulse: Scalar threshold for bounce activation. DefaultOptions.airDrag: 0.1. DefaultOptions.fluidDrag: 0.4. DefaultOptions.fluidDensity: 2.0. DefaultOptions.gravity: [0, -10, 0]. DefaultOptions.minBounceImpulse: 0.5. 1. Initialization: Create Physics instance with testSolid, testFluid, and optional options. Merge options with DefaultOptions. 2. Body Addition: Add bodies via addBody(aabb, mass, friction, restitution, gravMult, onCollide). Defaults: AABB [0,0,0] to [1,1,1], mass 1, friction 1, restitution 0, gravMult 1. 3. Simulation Tick (tick(dt)): 1. Convert dt to seconds: dtsec = dt / 1000. 2. For each body b: 1. Static Check: If b.mass <= 0, set velocity, forces, and impulses to zero. Return. 2. Sleep Check: If bodyAsleep(b) returns true, skip processing. Decrement sleepFrameCount. 3. Fluid Forces: Call applyFluidForces(self, b). Check if corner (b.aabb.base[0], b.aabb.base[1], b.aabb.base[2]) is fluid. If not, b.inFluid = false. If fluid, count submerged voxels from y0 = b.aabb.base[1] up to y1 = b.aabb.base[1] + b.aabb.vec[1]. Calculate fluidLevel = y0 + submergedcount. Calculate heightInFluid = fluidLevel - b.aabb.base[1]. Calculate ratioInFluid = min(heightInFluid / b.aabb.vec[1], 1.0). Calculate displaced volume vol = b.aabb.vec[0] b.aabb.vec[1] b.aabb.vec[2]. Calculate buoyant force f = -gravity fluidDensity (vol ratioInFluid). Apply force f to body. Set b.inFluid = true, b.ratioInFluid = ratioInFluid. 4. Integration (Semi-implicit Euler): Acceleration: a = (forces / mass) + (gravity gravityMultiplier). Velocity Change: dv = (impulses / mass) + (a dtsec). Update Velocity: velocity = velocity + dv. 5. Friction Application: If b.friction is set, call applyFrictionByAxis for axes 0, 1, and 2. For axis i: Let restDir = resting[i], vNormal = dv[i]. If restDir == 0 or restDir vNormal <= 0, return. Calculate lateral velocity magnitude vCurr from velocity excluding axis i. If vCurr == 0, return. Calculate dvMax = abs(friction vNormal). Calculate scaler s = max(0, (vCurr - dvMax) / vCurr). Scale lateral velocity components by s. 6. Linear Drag: Determine drag: If b.airDrag >= 0 use it, else use global airDrag. If b.inFluid: If b.fluidDrag >= 0 use it, else use global fluidDrag. Multiply by (1 - ratioInFluid)^2. Calculate multiplier mult = max(1 - (drag dtsec / mass), 0). Scale velocity by mult. 7. Position Update: dx = velocity dtsec. 8. Reset Forces: Set forces and impulses to zero. 9. Collision Sweep: If b.autoStep, cache current AABB in tmpBox. Call sweep(testSolid, b.aabb, dx, callback). Callback: If collision detected on axis i with direction dir, set resting[i] = dir and zero the position component along i in dx (effectively stopping movement along that axis). 10. Auto-Stepping: If b.autoStep and resting[1] >= 0 (on ground) or b.inFluid, return. Check if X or Z movement is blocked. Check movement ratio abs(dx[0]/dx[2]) against cutoff 4. Move towards target until first X/Z collision (ignoring Y). Calculate Y step distance ydist = floor(b.aabb.base[1] + 1.001) - b.aabb.base[1]. Sweep up by upvec = [0, ydist, 0]. If collision, return. Sweep leftover X/Z movement. If no movement in blocked direction, return. Update AABB and resting. 11. Impact Calculation: Initialize impacts to zero. For each axis i: If resting[i] != 0 and oldResting[i] == 0, set impacts[i] = -velocity[i]. Set velocity[i] = 0 for all collided axes. 12. Bounce Resolution: Calculate impact magnitude mag = length(impacts). If mag > 0.001 (epsilon) and b.restitution > 0 and mag > minBounceImpulse: Scale impacts by b.restitution. Apply impulse impacts to body. 13. Sleep Check: If squaredlength(velocity) > 1e-5, mark body as active. Unverified code. options: dict = None): defaults = { 'airDrag': 0.1, 'fluidDrag': 0.4, 'fluidDensity': 2.0, 'gravity': [0, -10, 0], 'minBounceImpulse': 0.5 } if options: defaults.update(options) self.gravity = defaults['gravity'] self.airdrag = defaults['airDrag'] self.fluiddrag = defaults['fluidDrag'] self.fluiddensity = defaults['fluidDensity'] self.minbounceimpulse = defaults['minBounceImpulse'] self.bodies: List[RigidBody] = [] self.testsolid = testsolid self.testfluid = testfluid def addbody(self, aabb, mass=1, friction=1, restitution=0, gravmult=1, oncollide=None): b = RigidBody(aabb, mass, friction, restitution, gravmult, oncollide) self.bodies.append(b) return b def tick(self, dtms): dt = dtms / 1000.0 nogravity = (vecsquaredlength(self.gravity) == 0) for b in self.bodies: self.iteratebody(b, dt, nogravity) def iteratebody(self, b, dt, nogravity): oldresting = list(b.resting) if b.mass <= 0: vecset(b.velocity, 0, 0, 0) vecset(b.forces, 0, 0, 0) vecset(b.impulses, 0, 0, 0) return if self.bodyasleep(b, dt, nogravity): return b.sleepframecount -= 1 self.applyfluidforces(b) a = vecscale(b.forces, 1.0 / b.mass) vecscaleandadd(a, a, self.gravity, b.gravitymultiplier) dv = vecscale(b.impulses, 1.0 / b.mass) vecscaleandadd(dv, dv, a, dt) b.velocity = vecadd(b.velocity, dv) if b.friction: self.applyfrictionbyaxis(0, b, dv) self.applyfrictionbyaxis(1, b, dv) self.applyfrictionbyaxis(2, b, dv) drag = b.airdrag if b.airdrag >= 0 else self.airdrag if b.influid: drag = b.fluiddrag if b.fluiddrag >= 0 else self.fluiddrag drag = (1 - b.ratioinfluid) 2 mult = max(1 - (drag dt / b.mass), 0) b.velocity = vecscale(b.velocity, mult) dx = vecscale(b.velocity, dt) vecset(b.forces, 0, 0, 0) vecset(b.impulses, 0, 0, 0) tmpbox = None if b.autostep: tmpbox = AABB(list(b.aabb.base), list(b.aabb.vec)) self.processcollisions(b, dx) if b.autostep: self.tryautostepping(b, tmpbox, dx) impacts = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): if b.resting[i] != 0: if oldresting[i] == 0: impacts[i] = -b.velocity[i] b.velocity[i] = 0.0 mag = veclength(impacts) if mag > 0.001: if b.restitution > 0 and mag > self.minbounceimpulse: bounceimpulse = vecscale(impacts, b.restitution) b.applyimpulse(bounceimpulse) if b.oncollide: b.oncollide(impacts) if vecsquaredlength(b.velocity) > 1e-5: b.sleepframecount = 0 def bodyasleep(self, b, dt, nogravity): if vecsquaredlength(b.velocity) <= 1e-5 and b.sleepframecount <= 0: return True return False def applyfluidforces(self, b): x0, y0, z0 = b.aabb.base if not self.testfluid(x0, y0, z0): b.influid = False return submerged = 0 y1 = y0 + b.aabb.vec[1] for y in range(int(y0), int(y1)): if self.testfluid(x0, y, z0): submerged += 1 fluidlevel = y0 + submerged heightinfluid = fluidlevel - b.aabb.base[1] ratioinfluid = heightinfluid / b.aabb.vec[1] if ratioinfluid > 1.0: ratioinfluid = 1.0 vol = b.aabb.vec[0] b.aabb.vec[1] b.aabb.vec[2] displaced = vol ratioinfluid f = vecscale(self.gravity, -self.fluiddensity displaced) b.applyforce(f) b.influid = True b.ratioinfluid = ratioinfluid def applyfrictionbyaxis(self, axis, b, dvel): restdir = b.resting[axis] vnormal = dvel[axis] if restdir == 0: return if restdir vnormal <= 0: return lateralvel = list(b.velocity) lateralvel[axis] = 0 vcurr = veclength(lateralvel) if vcurr == 0: return dvmax = abs(b.friction vnormal) scaler = (vcurr - dvmax) / vcurr if vcurr > dvmax else 0 b.velocity[(axis + 1) % 3] = scaler b.velocity[(axis + 2) % 3] = scaler def processcollisions(self, b, dx): # Implements sweep(testSolid, box, velocity, callback) behavior from evidence # Callback sets resting[axis] = dir and zeros dx[axis] step = 0.05 remaining = veclength(dx) direction = vecscale(dx, 1.0 / remaining) if remaining > 0 else [0,0,0] currentpos = list(b.aabb.base) while remaining > 0.001: testpos = [currentpos[i] + direction[i] step for i in range(3)] if self.testsolid(int(testpos[0]), int(testpos[1]), int(testpos[2])): for i in range(3): if abs(direction[i]) > 0.1: b.resting[i] = 1 if direction[i] > 0 else -1 dx[i] = 0 return currentpos = testpos remaining -= step def tryautostepping(self, b, tmpbox, dx): if b.resting[1] >= 0 or b.influid: return if b.resting[0] == 0 and b.resting[2] == 0: return ratio = abs(dx[0] / dx[2]) if dx[2] != 0 else float('inf') if ratio > 4: pass ydist = math.floor(b.aabb.base[1] + 1.001) - b.aabb.base[1] upvec = [0, ydist, 0] # Sweep up logic placeholder: in practice calls sweep with upvec # If collision, return # Sweep leftover X/Z # Update AABB and resting pass Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K) per tick, where N is the number of bodies and K is the number of voxels checked during collision sweeps and fluid queries. Fluid queries require scanning the height of the body, so K scales with body size. Memory Complexity: O(N) for body data structures. No spatial acceleration structure is maintained by the engine itself; it relies on the caller's voxel storage. Strengths: Lightweight, no pre-processing required, handles fluid dynamics (buoyancy/drag) natively, supports auto-stepping for platformer mechanics. Limitations: Does not handle rigid body-to-rigid body collisions. Does not support non-cubic voxels. Performance degrades with large bodies due to voxel counting for buoyancy. When to Use: Voxel-based games (Minecraft-like) where terrain is the primary collision surface and rigid body interactions are minimal. When Not to Use: Games requiring complex rigid body collisions (e.g., ragdolls hitting each other), non-cubic terrain, or high-precision continuous collision detection beyond AABB sweeps. The Voxel Physics Engine was developed as a replacement for voxel-physical to provide more physically accurate behavior for voxel games. It was designed to work with the noa engine and voxel.js, but is abstracted to work with any engine providing boolean voxel test functions. The library has undergone several versions, with significant changes in version 0.8.0 (friction scaling) and 0.9.0 (drag renaming and per-body overrides). voxel-physics-engine, https://github.com/andyhall/voxel-physics-engine, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Sphere-Voxel Collision Detection via Displacement Averaging
head: sphereIntersect
body: A collision detection method for a sphere moving through a voxel grid that calculates a displacement vector representing the push-out needed to resolve penetration by averaging displacements from all intersected voxel faces. It differs from simple boolean occupancy tests by providing a continuous resolution vector, allowing the sphere to be pushed out of the voxel structure rather than merely detecting overlap. Inputs: sphere: A sphere defined by a center point (Vector3) and a radius (float). voxelmapCollider: An object providing access to voxel data, specifically getVoxel(voxel) which returns an EVoxelStatus enum (e.g., EMPTY, FULL). Outputs: null if no collision is detected. An object { normal: Vector3, depth: float } where normal is the unit vector of the average displacement and depth is the magnitude of that average displacement. Data Structures: displacements: An array of Vector3 objects storing individual face push-out vectors. voxel: A Vector3 representing integer voxel coordinates (x, y, z). sphereCenterProjection2dX/Y/Z: Objects with x and y fields representing 2D projections of the sphere center onto specific voxel faces. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize an empty list displacements. 2. Define a helper function addDisplacementIfNeeded(sphereCenterProjection): a. Calculate projectionToCenter = sphere.center - sphereCenterProjection. b. Calculate distanceFromCenter = projectionToCenter.length(). c. If distanceFromCenter < sphere.radius: i. Calculate pushVector = projectionToCenter.normalize() (sphere.radius - distanceFromCenter). ii. Push pushVector to displacements. 3. Calculate the bounding voxel coordinates containing the sphere: a. voxelFrom = floor(sphere.center - sphere.radius). b. voxelTo = floor(sphere.center + sphere.radius). 4. Iterate through all voxels in the bounding box: a. For voxel.z from voxelFrom.z to voxelTo.z: b. For voxel.y from voxelFrom.y to voxelTo.y: c. For voxel.x from voxelFrom.x to voxelTo.x: i. Calculate local sphere center relative to voxel: localSphereCenter = sphere.center - voxel. ii. Calculate 2D projections of the local sphere center onto the voxel faces: sphereCenterLocalProjection2dX (using z, y components). sphereCenterLocalProjection2dY (using x, z components). sphereCenterLocalProjection2dZ (using x, y components). iii. Calculate global 2D projection coordinates for each face by adding voxel indices: sphereCenterProjection2dX = { x: sphereCenterLocalProjection2dX.x + voxel.z, y: sphereCenterLocalProjection2dX.y + voxel.y }. sphereCenterProjection2dY = { x: sphereCenterLocalProjection2dY.x + voxel.x, y: sphereCenterLocalProjection2dY.y + voxel.z }. sphereCenterProjection2dZ = { x: sphereCenterLocalProjection2dZ.x + voxel.x, y: sphereCenterLocalProjection2dZ.y + voxel.y }. iv. Check if current voxel is full: voxelIsFull = (voxelmapCollider.getVoxel(voxel) != EVoxelStatus.EMPTY). v. Check neighbors for fullness: voxelBelowIsFull: status of (voxel.x, voxel.y - 1, voxel.z). voxelAboveIsFull: status of (voxel.x, voxel.y + 1, voxel.z). voxelLeftIsFull: status of (voxel.x - 1, voxel.y, voxel.z). voxelRightIsFull: status of (voxel.x + 1, voxel.y, voxel.z). voxelBackIsFull: status of (voxel.x, voxel.y, voxel.z - 1). voxelFrontIsFull: status of (voxel.x, voxel.y, voxel.z + 1). vi. If voxelIsFull != voxelBelowIsFull, call addDisplacementIfNeeded({ x: sphereCenterProjection2dY.x, y: voxel.y, z: sphereCenterProjection2dY.y }). vii. If voxelIsFull != voxelAboveIsFull, call addDisplacementIfNeeded({ x: sphereCenterProjection2dY.x, y: voxel.y + 1, z: sphereCenterProjection2dY.y }). viii. If voxelIsFull != voxelLeftIsFull, call addDisplacementIfNeeded({ x: voxel.x, y: sphereCenterProjection2dX.y, z: sphereCenterProjection2dX.x }). ix. If voxelIsFull != voxelRightIsFull, call addDisplacementIfNeeded({ x: voxel.x + 1, y: sphereCenterProjection2dX.y, z: sphereCenterProjection2dX.x }). x. If voxelIsFull != voxelBackIsFull, call addDisplacementIfNeeded({ x: sphereCenterProjection2dZ.x, y: sphereCenterProjection2dZ.y, z: voxel.z }). xi. If voxelIsFull != voxelFrontIsFull, call addDisplacementIfNeeded({ x: sphereCenterProjection2dZ.x, y: sphereCenterProjection2dZ.y, z: voxel.z + 1 }). 5. After loops, if displacements.length > 0: a. Sum all displacements into totalDisplacement. b. Calculate averageDisplacement = totalDisplacement / displacements.length. c. Calculate totalDepth = averageDisplacement.length(). d. Return { normal: averageDisplacement.normalize(), depth: totalDepth }. 6. If displacements.length is 0, return null. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spherevoxelcollision(sphere, voxelmapcollider): """ sphere: dict with 'center' (Vec3) and 'radius' (float) voxelmapcollider: object with getvoxel(voxel: Vec3) -> EVoxelStatus Returns: dict with 'normal' (Vec3) and 'depth' (float), or None """ displacements = [] def adddisplacementifneeded(spherecenterprojection): projectiontocenter = sphere['center'] - spherecenterprojection distancefromcenter = projectiontocenter.length() if distancefromcenter < sphere['radius']: pushvector = projectiontocenter.normalize() (sphere['radius'] - distancefromcenter) displacements.append(pushvector) voxelfrom = floorvec3(sphere['center'] - sphere['radius']) voxelto = floorvec3(sphere['center'] + sphere['radius']) for z in range(voxelfrom.z, voxelto.z + 1): for y in range(voxelfrom.y, voxelto.y + 1): for x in range(voxelfrom.x, voxelto.x + 1): voxel = Vec3(x, y, z) localspherecenter = sphere['center'] - 1, z)) != EVoxelStatus.EMPTY voxelaboveisfull = voxelmapcollider.getvoxel(Vec3(x, y + 1, z)) != EVoxelStatus.EMPTY voxelleftisfull = voxelmapcollider.getvoxel(Vec3(x - 1, y, z)) != EVoxelStatus.EMPTY voxelrightisfull = voxelmapcollider.getvoxel(Vec3(x + 1, y, z)) != EVoxelStatus.EMPTY voxelbackisfull = voxelmapcollider.getvoxel(Vec3(x, y, z - 1)) != EVoxelStatus.EMPTY voxelfrontisfull = voxelmapcollider.getvoxel(Vec3(x, y, z + 1)) != EVoxelStatus.EMPTY if voxelisfull != voxelbelowisfull: adddisplacementifneeded(Vec3(spherecenterproj2dy.x, y, spherecenterproj2dy.y)) if voxelisfull != voxelaboveisfull: adddisplacementifneeded(Vec3(spherecenterproj2dy.x, y + 1, spherecenterproj2dy.y)) if voxelisfull != voxelleftisfull: adddisplacementifneeded(Vec3(x, spherecenterproj2dx.y, spherecenterproj2dx.x)) if voxelisfull != voxelrightisfull: adddisplacementifneeded(Vec3(x + 1, spherecenterproj2dx.y, spherecenterproj2dx.x)) if voxelisfull != voxelbackisfull: adddisplacementifneeded(Vec3(spherecenterproj2dz.x, spherecenterproj2dz.y, z)) if voxelisfull != voxelfrontisfull: adddisplacementifneeded(Vec3(spherecenterproj2dz.x, spherecenterproj2dz.y, z + 1)) if len(displacements) > 0: totaldisplacement = sum(displacements) averagedisplacement = totaldisplacement / len(displacements) totaldepth = averagedisplacement.length() return {'normal': averagedisplacement.normalize(), 'depth': totaldepth} return None Parameters: sphere.radius: The radius of the sphere. The algorithm assumes floor is applied to the bounding box calculation. The algorithm assumes normalize handles zero-length vectors gracefully or that they do not occur. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of intersected faces, which is O(r^2). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales with the cube of the sphere radius. Strengths: Provides a continuous displacement vector for collision resolution, allowing for smooth movement and penetration recovery. Limitations: Requires checking multiple neighbors for each voxel in the bounding box, which can be computationally expensive for large spheres or dense voxel grids. When to use: When continuous collision resolution is needed for spheres in a voxel environment. When not to use: When only boolean collision detection is required, or when performance is critical and the sphere is very large. name: Haptic Collision Detection (Voxel-Only)
head: Voxel-Only Haptic Collision
body: This method computes intersection points and force-feedback vectors between a haptic burr tool and a virtual object represented solely by a voxel set, enabling realistic tactile interaction during virtual carving. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by relying exclusively on volumetric data for collision resolution, avoiding supplemental polygonal mesh information. Unlike Entity Collision & Movement which may use complex physics engines, or Sphere-Voxel Collision Detection via Displacement Averaging which averages displacements, this method uses an "anchor-based" approach to determine force direction, ensuring stability in complex geometries like tight corners or pits. Inputs: Burr tool position in world coordinates (P{burr}^{world}). Burr radius (R{burr}). Voxel model local-to-world transformation matrix (M{local}^{world}) and its inverse (M{world}^{local}). Set of cached voxels (V{cache}) representing the object's volume. Each voxel is defined by its center position in local coordinates (P{voxel}^{local}) and occupancy status. Anchor drag distance (D{drag}), a fixed scalar defining the search radius for alternate anchor points. Outputs: Force feedback vector in world coordinates (F{world}). Link distance (d{link}) between the burr center and the anchor point. Boolean collision status. Data Structures: Voxel: A structure containing center (vec3, local coords) and occupied (bool). Anchor: A vec3 representing the contact point approximation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Convert the burr's current position from world coordinates to the voxel model's local coordinate system. P{burr}^{local} = M{world}^{local} \times P{burr}^{world} 2. Collision Search: Iterate through the set of cached voxels (V{cache}). For each voxel v \in V{cache}: a. Calculate the Euclidean distance from the voxel center to the burr center: d = \| P{burr}^{local} - v.center \| b. If d \le R{burr}, a collision is detected. Halt iteration immediately. Set collision status to true. c. If the iteration completes without finding any voxel satisfying the condition, set collision status to false. 3. Anchor Initialization (No Collision): If no collision occurred: a. Set the anchor point (A) to the burr's current local position: A = P{burr}^{local} b. This anchor approximates the closest point to the burr head that does not intersect with any voxels. 4. Anchor Refinement (Collision Detected): If a collision occurred: a. Determine if an alternate anchor point exists within the anchor drag distance (D{drag}) that is closer to the burr head than the current anchor (A{old}). b. Generate 26 new candidate anchor positions (Ci) by applying the anchor drag distance in every combination of x, y, and z directions relative to A{old}. The directions correspond to the 26 neighbors in a 3D grid (excluding the center and the 6 face-adjacent neighbors if strictly diagonal, but the source specifies 26 candidates, implying all 3x3x3 neighbors excluding the center itself, or specifically the 26 surrounding voxels in a cubic lattice). Ci = A{old} + D{drag} \times \vec{d}i where \vec{d}i \in \{-1, 0, 1\}^3 \setminus \{(0,0,0)\}. c. Disqualify any candidate Ci that collides with one or more voxel points. A candidate collides if the distance from Ci to any voxel center in V{cache} is \le R{burr}. d. From the remaining valid candidates, select the one with the shortest Euclidean distance to the burr center P{burr}^{local} as the new anchor point A{new}. A{new} = \arg \min{Ci \in Valid} \| P{burr}^{local} - Ci \| e. If no valid candidates exist (all disqualified), retain A{old} as the anchor. 5. Force Vector Calculation: Compute the force vector and link distance using the established anchor A. \vec{F}{local} = A - P{burr}^{local} d{link} = \| \vec{F}{local} \| 6. Output Transformation: Convert the force vector from local coordinates to world coordinates. F{world} = M{local}^{world} \times \vec{F}{local} Send F{world} and d{link} to the haptic device. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hapticcollisiondetection(burrposworld, burrradius, voxelcache, transformlocaltoworld, transformworldtolocal, anchordragdist): # 1. Transform burr position to local space burrposlocal = transformworldtolocal(burrposworld) collisionfound = False anchor = burrposlocal # 2. Iterate through cached voxels to find collision for voxel in voxelcache: dist = distance(burrposlocal, voxel.center) if dist <= burrradius: collisionfound = True break if not collisionfound: # No collision: anchor is burr position anchor = burrposlocal else: # Collision detected: refine anchor currentanchor = anchor # From previous frame or initial guess # 3. Generate 26 candidates candidates = [] for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue candidate = currentanchor + vec3(dx, dy, dz) anchordragdist # Check if candidate collides with any voxel isvalid = True for voxel in voxelcache: if distance(candidate, voxel.center) <= burrradius: isvalid = False break if isvalid: candidates.append(candidate) # 4. Select best candidate if candidates: bestcandidate = None mindist = infinity for cand in candidates: d = distance(burrposlocal, cand) if d < mindist: mindist = d bestcandidate = cand anchor = bestcandidate else: # No valid candidates found, keep current anchor pass # 5. Calculate force vector and distance forcevectorlocal = anchor - burrposlocal linkdist = magnitude(forcevectorlocal) # 6. Transform force to world space forcevectorworld = transformlocaltoworld(forcevectorlocal) return forcevectorworld, linkdist, collisionfound Parameters: burrradius: Radius of the spherical burr head. Typical values depend on the simulation scale; not given in sources. anchordragdist: Fixed distance for searching alternate anchor points. Not given in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Distance calculations must handle floating-point precision carefully, especially when d \approx R{burr}. Boundaries: If the burr is entirely inside a solid voxel region, the collision detection will trigger, but the anchor refinement might fail to find a valid candidate if the anchordragdist is insufficient to reach the surface boundary. Degenerate Input: Empty voxel cache results in no collision and anchor equals burr position. A method for determining the direction of the haptic force vector using an 'anchor' point, preferred over nearest-voxel or voxel-summation methods to ensure stability in complex geometries. Nearest-voxel and voxel-summation methods perform erratically when the burr-head is in a tight corner or inside a pit. The anchor-based method performs as expected in these situations as well as on normal surface curvatures. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K), where N is the number of cached voxels and K is the number of candidate anchors (26). In the worst case, every candidate requires checking against all cached voxels. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the voxel cache. Performance: The method is computationally intensive due to the nested loop of candidate validation against the voxel set. However, it provides stable force feedback. Strengths: Provides stable force feedback in complex geometries (corners, pits) where other methods fail. Directly maps tool interaction to volumetric data. Limitations: Does not use polygonal mesh information, potentially missing fine surface details not captured by the voxel resolution. Computationally heavier than simple nearest-voxel checks. When to use: When using a voxel-only representation and stable force feedback in complex geometries is required. When not to use: When high-frequency surface details from a mesh are needed, or when computational resources are extremely limited. This method was introduced in the context of a Haptic-Based 3D Carving Simulator. It builds on William et al.’s graphical carving simulator. The system uses a pen-based haptic tool as a 3D mouse to "feel" the surface of the model and remove volume segments. The collision detection scheme is one of two presented, the other using supplemental polygonal mesh information. name: Mask Cache Lookup
body: Mask Cache Lookup determines the occupancy status of a set of 3D points by querying a pre-computed 3D boolean grid. It converts continuous world coordinates into discrete grid indices and performs a direct memory lookup to return a boolean array indicating whether each point lies within an occupied voxel. Inputs: world: A 3D boolean array of shape (szi, szj, szk) representing the occupancy grid. xyz: An (npts, 3) array of world coordinates for the points to test. xyz2ijkscale: A 3-element array defining the scaling factor from world units to grid units. xyz2ijkshift: A 3-element array defining the offset from world origin to grid origin. Outputs: out: An (npts,) boolean array where out[i] is True if the i-th point is inside an occupied voxel, False otherwise. Data Structures: The world grid is stored in row-major order. The index for a voxel at (i, j, k) is calculated as i \cdot szj \cdot szk + j \cdot szk + k. Steps: 1. For each point p with world coordinates (x, y, z) in xyz: a. Convert world coordinates to grid indices (i, j, k) using the scale and shift parameters: i = \text{round}(x \cdot \text{xyz2ijk\scale}[0] + \text{xyz2ijk\shift}[0]) j = \text{round}(y \cdot \text{xyz2ijk\scale}[1] + \text{xyz2ijk\shift}[1]) k = \text{round}(z \cdot \text{xyz2ijk\scale}[2] + \text{xyz2ijk\shift}[2]) b. Check if the indices are within the valid bounds of the grid: 0 \le i < szi \quad \text{and} \quad 0 \le j < szj \quad \text{and} \quad 0 \le k < szk c. If the point is within bounds, lookup the occupancy value in the world grid using row-major indexing: \text{index} = i \cdot szj \cdot szk + j \cdot szk + k \text{out}[p] = \text{world}[\text{index}] d. If the point is out of bounds, set \text{out}[p] = \text{False}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def maskcachelookup(world, xyz, xyz2ijkscale, xyz2ijkshift, szi, szj, szk): npts = xyz.shape[0] out = [False] npts szjk = szj szk for p in range(npts): x, y, z = xyz[p] i = round(x xyz2ijkscale[0] + xyz2ijkshift[0]) j = round(y xyz2ijkscale[1] + xyz2ijkshift[1]) k = round(z xyz2ijkscale[2] + xyz2ijkshift[2]) if 0 <= i < szi and 0 <= j < szj and 0 <= k < szk: index = i szjk + j szk + k out[p] = world[index] else: out[p] = False return out Parameters: szi, szj, szk: The dimensions of the 3D boolean world grid. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Out-of-bounds points: Points outside the grid bounds must be handled explicitly. Setting them to False assumes empty space outside the defined volume. Precision: The use of round for coordinate conversion can lead to aliasing artifacts if the grid resolution is low relative to the scene detail. Floating-point precision errors in coordinate transformation should be considered. Grid Resolution: If the grid is too coarse, multiple distinct points may map to the same voxel, leading to false positives for occupancy. This variant determines which rays intersect with the currently solved coarse geometry mask by combining bounding box containment checks with a 3D boolean grid lookup. It serves as a pre-filtering step in volume rendering pipelines, identifying valid sampling points before expensive density or color computations. Unlike the parent Mask Cache Lookup which handles general occupancy queries, this variant explicitly manages ray geometry and bounding box boundaries to optimize the lookup process for unbounded scenes. It is chosen when rays may originate from or pass through regions outside the primary grid volume, requiring an initial bounding box test to avoid unnecessary grid lookups or out-of-bounds errors. This variant involves iterating over a 3D occupancy grid stored as vector<vector<vector<bool>>> Grid on the CPU to transfer occupancy data to a chunk structure. The process iterates i from 0 to dim, j from 0 to dim, and k from 0 to dim, assigning c.filled[i][j][k] = Grid[i][j][k]. The parameter dim sets the grid resolution, with typical values being 32, 64, 128, 256, or 512. Higher values increase computation time linearly with the number of voxels. Not given in the sources. name: Mask Cache Lookup with Ray Bounding Box Check
head: DVGO Hit Coarse Geometry, DVGO Hit Coarse Geometry Check
body: This method checks whether rays intersect with the currently solved coarse geometry mask by combining ray sampling with a 3D boolean grid lookup. It identifies valid sampling points before subsequent volume rendering computations. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape [N, 3]. raysd: Ray directions, shape [N, 3]. xyzmin: Minimum corner of the bounding box, shape [3]. xyzmax: Maximum corner of the bounding box, shape [3]. near: Near clipping plane distance. far: Far clipping plane distance. stepsize: Base step size for sampling. voxelsize: Physical size of a single voxel in the grid. maskcache: A 3D boolean grid storing occupancy information. Outputs: hit: A boolean tensor of shape [N], where hit[i] is True if ray i intersects the coarse geometry within the bounding box. Data Structures: maskcache: A 3D boolean grid that supports indexing with world coordinates converted to grid indices. raypts: Tensor of sampled points on rays, shape [N, K, 3], where K is the number of samples per ray. maskoutbbox: Boolean tensor of shape [N, K], True if the point is outside the bounding box. rayid: Tensor mapping each sampled point back to its source ray index, shape [N, K]. Parameters: far: Set to 10^9 in the source implementation to prevent early stopping at the scene bounding box. Steps: 1. Reshape rayso and raysd to shape [-1, 3] and ensure they are contiguous in memory. 2. Set far to 10^9. 3. Calculate the effective step distance: stepdist = stepsize \times voxel\size. 4. Sample points along each ray using the bounding box limits and step distance. This yields raypts, maskoutbbox, and rayid. 5. Identify points inside the bounding box: mask\inbbox = \neg mask\outbbox. 6. Initialize a boolean tensor hit of zeros with length equal to the number of rays N. 7. For points inside the bounding box, query the maskcache using their world coordinates. 8. Mark rays as hit if the corresponding query points are inside the bounding box and pass the mask cache check: hit[ray\id[mask\inbbox][mask\cache(ray\pts[mask\inbbox])]] = 1 This operation sets hit[i] = 1 if any sample point on ray i is inside the bounding box and marked as occupied in the coarse geometry mask. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def hitcoarsegeo(rayso, raysd, xyzmin, xyzmax, near, far, stepsize, voxelsize, maskcache): # Reshape to [-1, 3] and ensure contiguous layout rayso = rayso.reshape(-1, 3) raysd = raysd.reshape(-1, 3) # Set far distance farval = 1e9 # Calculate step distance stepdist = stepsize voxelsize # Step not provided in sources; computes points along rays within bbox at stepdist intervals. # raypts, maskoutbbox, rayid = sampleptsonrays(rayso, raysd, xyzmin, xyzmax, near, farval, stepdist) # Identify points inside the bounding box maskinbbox = ~maskoutbbox # Initialize hit tensor of zeros hit = torch.zeros(len(rayso)) # Query mask cache for points inside bounding box occupied = maskcache(raypts[maskinbbox]) # Mark rays as hit if corresponding points are occupied hit[rayid[maskinbbox][occupied]] = 1 return hit Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure rayso and raysd are contiguous to avoid CUDA kernel errors. Bounding Box: The far distance is set to 10^9 in the source. Empty Rays: If no points are inside the bounding box or no points are occupied, the hit tensor remains all zeros. Multiple Hits: If multiple points on a single ray are occupied, the ray is marked as hit only once due to tensor indexing semantics. name: Occupancy Ground Truth Computation
head: Computing ground truth occupancy
body: This method computes the binary occupancy value (inside or outside) for arbitrary 3D coordinates by ray casting against a watertight mesh. It serves as the ground truth generator for training neural implicit representations, distinguishing itself from sibling methods like Mask Cache Lookup by operating on continuous geometric primitives (meshes) rather than discrete voxel grids. It is primarily used to create training datasets for 3D neural field generation. Inputs: A watertight mesh representing the 3D shape. A set of 3D query points \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z). Outputs: Binary occupancy values o \in \{0, 1\} for each query point. Data Structures: The watertight mesh is represented as a collection of triangles (faces) and vertices, extracted via the marching cubes algorithm. Steps: 1. Mesh Extraction: Generate a watertight mesh from the target shape using the marching cubes algorithm. 2. Query Point Sampling: Generate the set of query points \mathbf{P} using two strategies: Draw 50% of the points uniformly at random from the bounding volume of the mesh. Draw the remaining 50% of the points via importance sampling near the surface of the watertight mesh. 3. Ray Casting: For each query point \mathbf{p}i: Cast a ray starting at \mathbf{p}i along the positive z-axis direction \mathbf{d} = (0, 0, 1). Compute the intersection count N between this ray and the triangles of the watertight mesh. 4. Occupancy Determination: If N is odd, the point is inside the shape; set occupancy oi = 1. If N is even, the point is outside the shape; set occupancy oi = 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeoccupancy(mesh, querypoints): """ Compute occupancy for query points by ray casting along the z-axis. Args: mesh: A watertight mesh object containing triangles. querypoints: A list of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). Returns: A list of binary occupancy values (0 or 1). """ occupancies = [] # Pre-compute mesh triangles for intersection testing triangles = mesh.gettriangles() for point in querypoints: # Cast ray along positive z-axis rayorigin = point raydirection = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Count intersections with mesh triangles intersectioncount = 0 for triangle in triangles: if raytriangleintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, triangle): intersectioncount += 1 # Determine occupancy based on parity of intersections if intersectioncount % 2 == 1: occupancies.append(1) # Inside else: occupancies.append(0) # Outside return occupancies def raytriangleintersect(origin, direction, triangle): """ Standard ray-triangle intersection test. Returns True if the ray intersects the triangle, False otherwise. """ # Implementation details for ray-triangle intersection (e.g., Möller–Trumbore algorithm) # are assumed to be available as standard geometric primitives. # This function returns a boolean indicating intersection. pass Parameters: Ray direction: Fixed to the z-axis (0, 0, 1). Sampling ratio: 50% uniform, 50% importance sampled near surface. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The mesh must be watertight; non-watertight meshes may yield incorrect parity counts. Precision issues in ray-triangle intersection tests near vertices or edges may affect the intersection count. The method assumes the mesh is correctly oriented for consistent inside/outside determination. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot F), where N is the number of query points and F is the number of triangles in the mesh. Memory Complexity: O(F) to store the mesh geometry. Performance: The method is computationally expensive for large meshes and high numbers of query points due to the per-point ray casting. Strengths: Provides exact geometric ground truth for arbitrary coordinates. Limitations: Does not scale well to very high-resolution meshes or massive query sets compared to voxel-based methods. When to use: When generating training data for neural implicit representations where exact geometric occupancy is required. When not to use: When real-time inference or large-scale voxel-based lookups are needed. This method was implemented in the context of "3D Neural Field Generation Using Triplane Diffusion". It follows the implementation details described in Mescheder et al. [5] (cited within). The watertight mesh is extracted using the marching cubes algorithm [4] (cited within). The approach is used to generate ground truth occupancy labels for training triplane-based neural fields. 3D Neural Field Generation Using Triplane Diffusion, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.02000, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Composite Reference Volume Generation
head: ALL volume, ALL/ANY Volumes, ANY volume, Intersection/Union Composite Volumes
body: Composite Reference Volume Generation creates two binary composite volumes (ALL and ANY) from a set of reference expert volumes to define the maximal and minimal boundaries of expert performance. These composites serve as the ground truth against which resident test volumes are compared, accounting for variation in expert performance. Unlike Occupancy Ground Truth Computation, which computes occupancy for arbitrary coordinates via ray casting, this method aggregates a fixed set of discrete reference volumes using set-theoretic operations to establish mandatory and allowed removal zones. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of reference volumes R = \{V1, V2,..., VN\}, where each Vi is a binary volume of identical dimensions. Output: Two composite binary volumes: ALL and ANY, with the same dimensions as the input volumes. Data Structures Reference Volume (V): A 3D grid of voxels. Each voxel is binary: occupied (1) or empty (0). Composite Volumes (ALL, ANY): 3D grids of the same dimensions as V, initialized to empty (0). Numbered Steps 1. Define the set of reference volumes R. 2. Initialize the ALL volume grid to all zeros (empty). 3. Initialize the ANY volume grid to all zeros (empty). 4. Iterate through every voxel position (x, y, z) in the grid dimensions. 5. Check the occupancy of the voxel at (x, y, z) in all reference volumes V \in R. 6. Compute the state for the ALL volume: the voxel is occupied if and only if it is occupied in all reference volumes in R. 7. Compute the state for the ANY volume: the voxel is occupied if and only if it is occupied in any (at least one) reference volume in R. Formulas ALL = \bigcap{V \in R} V, \quad ANY = \bigcup{V \in R} V where R is the set of reference volumes and V represents a single reference volume. For binary grids, the intersection \bigcap corresponds to logical AND (all voxels must be 1) and the union \bigcup corresponds to logical OR (at least one voxel must be 1). Parameters Reference Set Size (N): The number of reference volumes in R. Typical value: 4. Volume Type: Binary. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Empty Reference Set: The method requires at least one reference volume to compute intersections and unions. Dimension Mismatch: All reference volumes must have identical dimensions to allow voxel-wise comparison. Binary Assumption: The method assumes binary inputs; non-binary values will break the logical aggregation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatecompositevolumes(referencevolumes): """ Generates ALL and ANY composite volumes from a set of reference binary volumes. Args: referencevolumes: List of 3D lists representing binary volumes. Each element is a 3D grid of 0s and 1s. All grids must have the same dimensions. Returns: allvolume: 3D grid representing the intersection of all reference volumes. anyvolume: 3D grid representing the union of all reference volumes. """ if not referencevolumes: raise ValueError("Reference set R cannot be empty.") # Determine grid dimensions from the first volume dimx = len(referencevolumes[0]) dimy = len(referencevolumes[0][0]) dimz = len(referencevolumes[0][0][0]) # Initialize output volumes with zeros allvolume = [[[0 for in range(dimz)] for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimx)] anyvolume = [[[0 for in range(dimz)] for in range(dimy)] for in range(dimx)] for x in range(dimx): for y in range(dimy): for z in range(dimz): # Check occupancy across all reference volumes at this coordinate states = [vol[x][y][z] for vol in referencevolumes] # ALL: occupied if in all reference volumes allvolume[x][y][z] = 1 if all(states) else 0 # ANY: occupied if in any reference volume anyvolume[x][y][z] = 1 if any(states) else 0 return allvolume, anyvolume Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and computationally inexpensive. It provides a clear, conservative (ALL) and permissive (ANY) boundary for expert performance. Limitations: It does not account for the frequency of expert agreement beyond binary presence/absence. It assumes all reference experts are equally valid. When to use: When a set of expert annotations is available and a binary ground truth range (mandatory vs. allowed) is needed for evaluating test subjects. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the context of virtual mastoidectomy performance evaluation. It was developed to compare surgical resident performances (test set) against known expert performances (reference set). The authors used 130 test volumes and 4 reference volumes to demonstrate the system's utility. The ALL volume represents mandatory bone removal areas (where all experts removed bone), and the ANY volume represents allowed removal areas (where at least one expert removed bone). This approach accounts for variation in expert performance by defining maximal and minimal boundaries of the reference set. name: Voxel Visibility Culling
head: Clipped Voxel Rejection, Ignoring Clipped Voxels, Inside/Outside Clipping, Structure Visibility, Visibility Metric
body: Voxel Visibility Culling determines which voxels in a volume dataset are perceptually relevant to the viewer, allowing the renderer to skip processing occluded or low-importance regions. It solves the problem of rendering unnecessary data by filtering voxels based on geometric position, structural coherence, or feature importance. It differs from its sibling Voxel Occupancy Test by not merely checking if a voxel is occupied, but evaluating its visibility relative to a camera or structural context. Voxels with high gradients (feature outlines) have higher importance. 2. Check Visibility: A voxel v is considered visible if its computed metric (e.g., opacity or scalar value) exceeds Tv. 3. It differs from sibling methods by using a downsampled, peak-based Gaussian approximation of opacity to achieve significant performance gains (from ~1-2s to ~10ms) while maintaining sufficient accuracy for camera framing. The Obstacle-Flag method is a dynamic job-scheduling mechanism used in distributed volume rendering to determine when a sub-volume is "combinable" (i.e., ready to be rendered and merged into the final image). It solves the inefficiency of sequential job-scheduling, where agents remain idle waiting for rigid, pre-computed visibility orders, by tracking real-time obscuration relationships between neighboring sub-volumes. Unlike static visibility culling, it updates its state as rendering progresses, allowing agents to immediately pick up the next available sub-volume as soon as its obscuring neighbors are completed. Voxel Visibility Propagation is a method for determining the visibility of voxels within a multi-resolution voxel cascade by inheriting occlusion data from coarser levels. It solves the problem of efficiently culling skylight or ambient occlusion contributions in high-resolution voxel grids by leveraging spatial coherence, avoiding expensive per-voxel ray marching. It differs from Near Plane Visibility Culling by operating on cascade hierarchy rather than camera frustum planes, and from Obstacle-Flag by using multiplicative opacity accumulation rather than binary flags. Removes voxels completely surrounded by other voxels on all 6 faces to reduce instance count without visual impact. It builds a hash set of occupied positions by packing each voxel's (x,y,z) into a unique long key. For each voxel, it checks if all 6 neighbors exist in the hash set. If all 6 neighbors are present, the voxel is marked as fully enclosed and excluded. It assumes coordinates fit in 20 bits each and handles negatives by adding a 1,000,000 offset. Complexity is O(N) for building the hash set and O(N) for culling. Filters voxels to only those within the physical cylindrical display area, discarding corner voxels that would not be visible on a spinning drum. It normalizes x and y coordinates, computes squared distance from the center, and compares it against a squared radius derived from the volume dimensions. Voxels within the radius are retained. Marks 3D Gaussian centers as visible or invisible based on their position relative to the view and projection matrices, returning a boolean tensor. It is a GPU-accelerated visibility test that determines which 3D Gaussian centers are within the camera frustum and projected onto the image plane, outputting a boolean mask. It initializes a present tensor, invokes a CUDA rasterization kernel with the Gaussian means and camera matrices, and returns the visibility flags. Interior: O(N) for hash set construction and O(N) for neighbor checks. Cylindrical: O(N) for coordinate transformation and distance check. body: Interior Voxel Culling removes voxels completely surrounded by other occupied voxels on all six faces to reduce instance count and draw calls without visual impact. It differs from view-dependent methods by relying solely on topological connectivity to the grid boundary, ignoring camera projection and ray casting entirely. Inputs: A 3D voxel grid or list of occupied coordinates, and a chunk dimension size. Outputs: A subset of voxels that expose at least one face to an empty neighbor or the grid boundary. Data Structures: 1. Occupied Set: A HashSet<Long> storing packed coordinate keys for fast neighbor lookup. 2. Voxel Grid: A 3D array [CHUNKSIZE][CHUNKSIZE][CHUNKSIZE] of Voxel structs, each containing a single int type field where -1 denotes AIR. 3. Enclosed Mask: A boolean array matching the grid dimensions, initialized to True (or oneslike(filled)). 4. Output Buffer: mpositionsLayered, a std::vector<glm::vec4> storing world coordinates and voxel type for the visible result. Packing Formula: \text{key} = (x{\text{shifted}} \ll 42) \mid (y{\text{shifted}} \ll 21) \mid z{\text{shifted}} where x{\text{shifted}} = x + 1,000,000, y{\text{shifted}} = y + 1,000,000, and z{\text{shifted}} = z + 1,000,000. Algorithm Steps: 1. Build Occupied Set: Iterate through all input voxel coordinates (x, y, z), pack each into a unique 64-bit key using the formula above, and insert into the hash set. 2. Initialize Enclosed Mask: Create a boolean array enclosed with the same dimensions as the voxel grid, initializing all entries to True. 3. Iterate Chunk: Loop through all voxels in the chunk using three nested loops for x, y, z from 0 to \text{CHUNK\SIZE}-1. 4. Skip Air: Retrieve the current voxel's type; if it equals \text{AIR} (-1), skip to the next iteration. 5. Check Neighbors: Verify the 6 immediate spatial neighbors (\pm x, \pm y, \pm z). Hash Lookup Method: Check if all 6 neighbor keys exist in the occupied set. Array Rolling Method: For each axis a \in \{0, 1, 2\} and shift s \in \{1, -1\}, roll the filled array by s along axis a, set the entering edge voxels (index 0 if s=1, index \text{shape}[a]-1 if s=-1) to False to treat out-of-bounds as empty, and update enclosed &= neighbor. 6. Mark Enclosed: If all 6 neighbors are present (or non-air), mark the voxel as fully enclosed. 7. Filter & Output: Return filled & ~enclosed. Compute world positions by adding chunk offsets to local coordinates, append (x+\text{offset}, y+\text{offset}, z+\text{offset}, \text{type}) to mpositionsLayered, and set mshouldRegen to false.
