name: Implicit Surface Voxelization
head: Iso-surface voxelization
body: Implicit Surface Voxelization converts an analytical implicit surface into a discrete voxel grid by rasterizing a sequence of rectangles within the Region of Interest (ROI) and evaluating the implicit function in the pixel shader. It differs from Parametric Surface Voxelization by evaluating the surface equation in the pixel shader rather than computing positions in the vertex shader, and from Rasterization and GPU Shaders by handling non-polygonal, analytically defined surfaces directly. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An implicit surface function f(\mathbf{x}), the Region of Interest (ROI) bounding the surface, and a target voxel grid resolution. Output: A voxel grid where each voxel is marked as occupied (binary) or contains a value (solid) based on the implicit function evaluation. Data Structures: Render Target: A 2D buffer or texture representing the projection of the ROI. Each pixel corresponds to a specific 3D coordinate in the voxel grid. Implicit Function: A mathematical function f(\mathbf{x}) defining the surface, evaluated in a shader program. Steps: 1. Generate Rectangles: The host application computes the ROI of the target surface and generates a sequence of rectangles embedded within it. 2. Rasterize Rectangles: Each rectangle is rasterized to the render target from front to back. 3. Evaluate Implicit Surface: For each pixel in the render target, the pixel's coordinates determine the corresponding 3D point \mathbf{x} in space. The implicit function f(\mathbf{x}) is evaluated. 4. Check Conditions: If the result satisfies given conditions, the pixel is output and transformed to the worksheet (voxel grid). 5. Voxelization Type: Binary Voxelization: Extracts the defined iso-surface. Solid Voxelization: Finds an interval that satisfies some inequation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def implicitsurfacevoxelization(implicitfunc, quads, voxelgrid, resolution): # Step 1: Generate a sequence of rectangles embedded in the ROI # The host application computes the ROI and provides a list of quads covering it. rectangles = quads # Step 2: Rasterize each rectangle to a render target from front to back # Render target is a 2D buffer mapping pixel indices to 3D coordinates. rendertarget = [[None for in range(resolution[0])] for in range(resolution[1])] for quad in rectangles: minx, maxx, miny, maxy = quad.screenbounds for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): # Standard inverse projection: ray = origin + direction (x, y, 1) rendertarget[y][x] = quad.rayorigin + quad.raydirection (x, y, 1.0) # Step 3 & 4: Evaluate implicit surface and check conditions for y in range(resolution[1]): for x in range(resolution[0]): point3d = rendertarget[y][x] if point3d is None: continue value = implicitfunc(point3d) if value <= 0.0: # Output pixel and transform to worksheet (voxel grid) # Mapping 2D pixel to 3D voxel slice depends on projection setup for z in range(len(voxelgrid[x][y])): voxelgrid[x][y][z] = 1.0 return voxelgrid Parameters: ROI: Defines the spatial extent of the surface. Computed by the host application. Instruction Slots: The shader program must support enough long instruction slots to handle very complex implicit surfaces. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complexity: Very complex implicit surfaces may exceed shader instruction limits. Precision: The accuracy of the voxelization depends on the precision of the implicit function evaluation and the rasterization process. Binary vs. Solid: Binary voxelization extracts the defined iso-surface, while solid voxelization requires finding an interval satisfying an inequation. An approach to rendering general-form implicit surfaces by sampling an analytical implicit into a regular grid by voxelization, followed by direct volume rendering. It is chosen when subvoxel surface detail is critical or when the implicit surface is defined analytically and needs to be rendered as a volume. Voxelization of a surface defined as the product of n filtered silhouette images. The surface is the isosurface S(\mathbf{p}) = 0.5, where S(\mathbf{p}) is the product of silhouette values projected into NVC space. It is used for image-based modeling from multiple camera views. The surface is defined by: S(\mathbf{p}) = \prodi \mathcal{I}i(\mathcal{C}i(\mathbf{p})) where \mathcal{I}i: \mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow [0, 1] is the filtered silhouette image for camera i, and \mathcal{C}i: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2 is the projective transform from NVC space to image space for camera i. The gradient \nabla S(\mathbf{p}) is normal to the surface, providing a smooth normal field if the silhouette images are smooth. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rectangles generated and the resolution of the render target. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Can handle very complex implicit surfaces given sufficient shader instruction slots. Real-time performance is achievable. Limitations: Limited by shader instruction length for very complex functions. When to Use: When the surface is defined analytically and real-time voxelization is required. When Not to Use: When shader instruction limits are insufficient for the implicit function complexity. The method was proposed in "Real-time Voxelization for Complex Models". It is part of a broader effort to enable real-time voxelization for complex models, including implicit and parametric surfaces. The approach leverages GPU rasterization and shader programming to evaluate implicit functions efficiently. name: Smooth Visual Hull Reconstruction
head: Smooth Visual Hull, Product Silhouette Voxelization
body: Smooth Visual Hull Reconstruction voxelize a 3D surface by defining it as the isosurface of a continuous scalar field constructed from the product of filtered 2D silhouette images from multiple camera views. Unlike discrete methods such as Visual Hull Construction which rely on binary octree subdivision, this method produces a smooth implicit surface where the gradient of the product field provides a continuous normal field. It solves the problem of generating high-resolution voxel data for image-based modeling by leveraging GPU rasterization and texture filtering to evaluate the implicit function efficiently. Inputs: n: Number of camera views. \mathcal{I}i: Filtered silhouette image for camera i, mapping \mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow [0, 1]. Ci: Projective transform from Normalized Device Coordinates (NVC) space to image space for camera i, mapping \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2. \mathcal{R}: Region of Interest (ROI) in NVC space to be voxelized. Outputs: A voxel grid representing the volume, where the surface is defined by the isosurface \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{p}) = 0.5. Data Structures: Silhouette Textures: Each \mathcal{I}i is stored as a 2D texture (e.g., a 2D texture array on the GPU). Values are floats in [0, 1]. Foreground pixels are 0, background pixels are 1. NVC Space: The 3D coordinate system in which the voxel grid is defined. Points \mathbf{p} are sampled within the ROI. Steps: 1. Silhouette Acquisition: For each camera i, segment the foreground and background from the input image. Assign value 0 to foreground pixels and 1 to background pixels. 2. Filtering: Apply a filter to the binary silhouette images to create smooth transitions at the boundaries. This results in the continuous functions \mathcal{I}i. 3. Voxelization via Rasterization: For each voxel center \mathbf{p} in the ROI (or during a rasterization pass where pixel shaders evaluate the function): Initialize the scalar value S = 1.0. For each camera i from 1 to n: Compute the 2D image coordinates \mathbf{u}i = Ci(\mathbf{p}). Sample the filtered silhouette texture \mathcal{I}i at \mathbf{u}i using bilinear (or appropriate) filtering. Let this value be vi. Update S = S \times vi. The resulting scalar field value is \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{p}) = S. 4. Surface Extraction: The implicit surface is defined by the isosurface \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{p}) = 0.5. The gradient \nabla \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{p}) is normal to this surface. Formula: The scalar field \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{p}) at a point \mathbf{p} in NVC space is defined as: \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{p}) = \prod{i=1}^{n} \mathcal{I}i(Ci(\mathbf{p})) The surface is the set of points \mathbf{p} such that: \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{p}) = \frac{1}{2} Parameters: Isosurface Value: Fixed at 0.5. Filtering: The specific filter used to generate \mathcal{I}i is not explicitly named in the provided text, but "filtered silhouette images" are required to ensure \nabla \mathcal{S} is smooth. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The product of many values in [0, 1] can underflow to zero if any silhouette value is exactly 0 (inside the object) or if the product becomes extremely small due to many cameras. However, since foreground is 0 and background is 1, any point inside the visual hull of any camera will have a product of 0. The isosurface at 0.5 effectively captures the boundary where the product transitions from 0 to non-zero. Note: If filtering creates values close to 0 but not exactly 0, numerical stability should be considered. Boundaries: The method assumes the ROI fully contains the object. Points outside all silhouettes will have \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{p}) = 1. Points inside any silhouette will have \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{p}) = 0. The transition occurs at the filtered edges. Degenerate Input: If a camera view has no foreground (all 1s), it does not constrain the volume. If a camera view has no background (all 0s), the entire volume is 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def smoothvisualhullvoxelization(roipoints, cameras, silhouettetextures): """ Voxelize the smooth visual hull. Args: roipoints: List of 3D points (x, y, z) in NVC space. cameras: List of camera objects, each with a method project(p) -> (u, v). silhouettetextures: List of 2D texture objects, each with a method sample(u, v) -> float. Returns: List of scalar values S(p) for each point in roipoints. """ results = [] for p in roipoints: svalue = 1.0 for i, camera in enumerate(cameras): # Project 3D point to 2D image coordinates u, v = camera.project(p) # Sample the filtered silhouette image # Assuming texture sampling handles coordinates in [0,1] or appropriate range # If u,v are in pixel coordinates, they must be normalized first silhouettevalue = silhouettetextures[i].sample(u, v) # Multiply into the product svalue = svalue silhouettevalue # Optimization: if svalue becomes 0, it will stay 0 if svalue == 0.0: break results.append(svalue) return results Generates a 3D representation by intersecting 3D cones from 2D silhouettes using discrete octree subdivision. Choose this when a binary, hierarchical representation is sufficient and smooth normals are not required. Aggregates soft foreground mattes into a continuous probability field, robust for wide-baseline captures. Choose this when handling inconsistent silhouettes or as a low-fidelity input for neural refinement. Time Complexity: O(V \cdot n), where V is the number of voxels (or rasterized pixels) and n is the number of cameras. Each voxel requires n texture lookups and multiplications. Memory Complexity: O(n \cdot W \cdot H) for storing the silhouette textures, where W, H are image dimensions. The voxel grid itself is O(V). Performance: Real-time high-resolution sparse voxelization is claimed. Performance depends heavily on GPU texture sampling speed and the number of cameras. Strengths: Produces smooth surfaces with continuous normals; leverages GPU rasterization and texture filtering for efficiency; simple to implement using standard graphics APIs. Limitations: Requires accurate silhouette extraction and filtering; sensitive to camera calibration errors (projective transform Ci); the product operation can lead to very small values, potentially affecting numerical precision in the transition region. When to use: When smooth surface normals are important and high-resolution voxel data is needed from multiple calibrated views. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and binary voxelization is sufficient, or when dealing with wide-baseline captures with significant occlusion inconsistencies where probabilistic methods are more robust. Originated in the context of real-time high-resolution sparse voxelization for image-based modeling. The method utilizes the property that the gradient of the product of silhouette images provides a smooth normal field, enabling high-quality surface reconstruction from 2D silhouettes. Real-time high-resolution sparse voxelization with application to image-based modeling, https://doi.org/10.1145/2492045.2492053, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Visual Hull Construction
head: Octree Visual Hull Construction, Octree carving, Photo Hull, Shape from Silhouette, Shape from Silhouette (SfS) / Octree Visual Hull Construction, Silhouette Intersection, Visual hull reconstruction
body: Visual Hull Construction generates a 3D representation of an object by intersecting multiple 3D cones created by back-projecting 2D silhouettes from different views onto 3D space. It is a Shape from Silhouette (SfS) technique that represents the resulting volume using an octree, where the object is defined as the intersection of all view-consistent volumes. Unlike Smooth Visual Hull Reconstruction, which uses a continuous product of filtered silhouette values to define an implicit surface, Visual Hull Construction relies on discrete octree subdivision and binary classification of spatial regions. Inputs: N 2D images (or precomputed binary silhouette masks), camera projection matrices for each view, and an initial 3D bounding cube enclosing the object. Outputs: An octree data structure representing the visual hull, where nodes are classified as inside, outside, or intersection. Data Structures: Octree Node: Represents a cubic volume in 3D space with fields for status (enum: OUTSIDE, INSIDE, INTERSECTION), children (array of 8 child nodes for INTERSECTION nodes), and bbox (bounding box coordinates). Silhouette Mask: Binary 2D image where 1 indicates the object silhouette and 0 indicates background. Parameters: \epsilon: Threshold for binary mask generation. Typical value: 0.04. \sigma{img}: Blur kernel size for image masks. Typical value: 1 pixel. \sigma{vol}: Blur kernel size for volume hulls. Typical value: 0.5 cells. K: Camera intrinsic matrix. Remains constant if the same camera is used. \theta: Rotational angle from reference position. tx, ty: X and Y translations at \theta=0. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: For each input image, perform background subtraction to isolate the object. Convert the result to a binary mask using threshold \epsilon. Apply a Gaussian blur with \sigma{img} to the binary masks to smooth edges. 2. Camera Model Setup: Define the projection matrix P(\theta) for each view. For circular motion (e.g., turntable), use: P(\theta) = K \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta & \sin \theta & 0 & tx \\ -\sin \theta & \cos \theta & 0 & ty \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} where \theta is the rotational angle, and tx, ty are translations at \theta=0. If only a single view is available, generate 4 auxiliary views by rotating the camera around the central Y-axis. Mirror the masks from these auxiliary views at the projected rotation axis to reduce cutoffs. 3. Octree Construction (Carving): Project the initial bounding cube onto multiple images. Split the cube into eight smaller cubes (octants) if the projection intersects a silhouette. Classify each octant as outside, inside, or intersection. Carve out octants classified as outside. Extract surfaces from the resulting octree. 4. Post-processing (Optional): Apply a Gaussian blur with \sigma{vol} to the resulting binary volume representation to smooth the hull. 5. Surface Extraction: Extract the surface from the final octree using the Marching Cubes (MC) algorithm. MC estimates surface triangles from INTERSECTION octants. The location of the triangles is determined by the configuration of inside vertices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class OctreeNode: def init(self, bbox, status='INSIDE'): self.bbox = bbox # (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) self.status = status self.children = [] def getbboxcorners(bbox): minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz = bbox return [ (minx, miny, minz), (maxx, miny, minz), (minx, maxy, minz), (maxx, maxy, minz), (minx, miny, maxz), (maxx, miny, maxz), (minx, maxy, maxz), (maxx, maxy, maxz) ] def project3dto2d(bbox, P): corners = getbboxcorners(bbox) projected = [] for x, y, z in corners: ph = [x, y, z, 1.0] projh = [ P[0][0]ph[0] + P[0][1]ph[1] + P[0][2]ph[2] + P[0][3]ph[3], P[1][0]ph[0] + P[1][1]ph[1] + P[1][2]ph[2] + P[1][3]ph[3], P[2][0]ph[0] + P[2][1]ph[1] + P[2][2]ph[2] + P[2][3]ph[3] ] if projh[2] != 0: projected.append((projh[0]/projh[2], projh[1]/projh[2])) if not projected: return None minu = min(p[0] for p in projected) minv = min(p[1] for p in projected) maxu = max(p[0] for p in projected) maxv = max(p[1] for p in projected) return (minu, minv, maxu, maxv) def checkoverlap(proj2d, mask): minu, minv, maxu, maxv = proj2d for u in range(int(minu), int(maxu) + 1): for v in range(int(minv), int(maxv) + 1): if 0 <= u < mask.width and 0 <= v < mask.height: if mask[v, u] == 1: return True return False def splitoctant(bbox): minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz = bbox midx, midy, midz = (minx+maxx)/2, (miny+maxy)/2, (minz+maxz)/2 children = [] for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): x0 = minx if i == 0 else midx x1 = midx if i == 0 else maxx y0 = miny if j == 0 else midy y1 = midy if j == 0 else maxy z0 = minz if k == 0 else midz z1 = midz if k == 0 else maxz children.append(OctreeNode((x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1), 'INSIDE')) return children def isleaf(bbox, minsize): minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz = bbox return (maxx - minx < minsize) or (maxy - miny < minsize) or (maxz - minz < minsize) def constructvisualhull(masks, projectionmatrices, initialbbox, minsize): root = OctreeNode(initialbbox, 'INSIDE') queue = [root] while queue: node = queue.pop(0) proj2ds = [project3dto2d(node.bbox, P) for P in projectionmatrices] if proj2ds is None: node.status = 'OUTSIDE' continue allintersect = True anyintersect = False for proj, mask in zip(proj2ds, masks): if proj is None: allintersect = False continue if checkoverlap(proj, mask): anyintersect = True else: allintersect = False if allintersect: node.status = 'INSIDE' elif anyintersect: node.status = 'INTERSECTION' else: node.status = 'OUTSIDE' if node.status == 'OUTSIDE': continue if node.status == 'INSIDE' or isleaf(node.bbox, minsize): continue node.children = splitoctant(node.bbox) queue.extend(node.children) return root Ambiguity and Pitfalls: Inside Vertex Identification: Ambiguity arises when only part of an octant edge is within a silhouette (case b) or the silhouette is entirely within an octant (case c). These cases frequently arise from imperfect silhouettes, projection matrix errors, or insufficient octree resolution. Projection Errors: Errors in \theta or wobbly rotational axes propagate to surface construction errors. Noise Robustness: Octree construction is robust against image noise because an octant is only removed if no nonzero-valued pixels are found in its projection. However, simple thresholding preserves non-convex details but degrades the subsequent Marching Cubes surface. Time Complexity: Depends on the octree depth and the number of views. Each node requires projection and intersection tests for all views. Complexity is roughly O(N \cdot V) where N is the number of views and V is the number of voxels/nodes in the octree. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of nodes in the octree. Sparse octrees save memory compared to dense voxel grids. Strengths: Robust against image noise. Simple thresholding preserves non-convex details during construction. Efficient representation for large volumes with sparse object presence. Limitations: Surface quality depends on octree resolution and the accuracy of silhouette extraction. Marching Cubes on octree leaves can produce degraded surfaces if silhouettes are imperfect. Single-view reconstruction requires symmetry assumptions which may not hold for arbitrary shapes. When to Use: When multiple views are available and computational efficiency is prioritized over high-fidelity surface detail. Suitable for objects with clear silhouettes. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity surface reconstruction is required from imperfect silhouettes without post-processing. Not suitable for single-view reconstruction of asymmetric objects without auxiliary assumptions. The concept of the 3D visual hull was introduced as the intersection of multiple 3D cones created by back-projecting 2D silhouettes. This technique is part of the broader Shape from Silhouette (SfS) family. The use of octrees for representing visual hulls became widely adopted due to their efficiency in handling sparse 3D data. The Marching Cubes algorithm, originally developed for medical imaging, is commonly used for surface extraction from these octrees. Recent applications include fluid reconstruction, where visual hulls guide density estimation. name: Probabilistic Visual Hull (PVH) Reconstruction
head: soft visual hull
body: Probabilistic Visual Hull (PVH) Reconstruction generates a voxel-based occupancy estimate by aggregating soft foreground mattes from multiple camera views, specifically designed to handle wide-baseline captures where traditional correspondence-based methods fail. Unlike the binary hard constraints of Visual Hull Construction, PVH produces a continuous probability field that serves as a robust, low-fidelity input for subsequent refinement stages, such as those performed by 3D Convolutional Autoencoder for PVH Refinement. Inputs: Capture volume defined by a set of voxels VL. C camera views with known extrinsic parameters \{Rc, COPc\} (rotation matrix and center of projection) and intrinsic parameters \{fc, o{xc}, o{yc}\} (focal length and 2D optical center). Soft foreground mattes BG derived from each camera image Ic via background subtraction. Outputs: A 3D volume VL where each voxel VLi has an associated occupancy probability p(VLi). Data Structures: The capture volume is decimated into voxels VLi = (v{ix}, v{iy}, v{iz}) for i = 1, \dots, |VL|. In the referenced implementation, each voxel is approximately 5\text{mm}^3 in size. The volume is typically processed as a sub-volume or "patch" to manage computational complexity. Algorithm Steps: 1. Voxel Decimation: Divide the studio capture volume into a grid of voxels VLi. 2. Coordinate Transformation: For each voxel i and each camera view c, compute the voxel's position relative to the camera frame: \begin{bmatrix} v'{ix} \\ v'{iy} \\ v'{iz} \end{bmatrix} = COPc - Rc^{-1} VLi where VLi is treated as a column vector of coordinates. 3. Projection: Project the transformed voxel coordinates onto the 2D image plane of view c: x[VLi] = \frac{fc \cdot v'{ix}}{v'{iz}} + o{xc} y[VLi] = \frac{fc \cdot v'{iy}}{v'{iz}} + o{yc} where (x[VLi], y[VLi]) is the point in image Ic corresponding to voxel VLi. 4. View Probability: Sample the soft foreground matte BG at the projected coordinates to determine the probability of the voxel belonging to the subject in view c: p(VLi|c) = BG(x[VLi], y[VLi]). 5. Aggregation: Compute the overall likelihood of occupancy for voxel i by aggregating probabilities across all C views. The source provides the following formula for the overall likelihood: p(VLi) = \sum{c=1}^{C} \frac{1}{1 + e^{p(VLi|c)}}. Note: The source text presents this as a summation of sigmoid-transformed view probabilities, though the exact mathematical interpretation of summing sigmoids of probabilities rather than combining them via product or average is specific to this implementation. 6. Efficiency Optimization: Limit the extent of VL to 3D patches. Ignore patches where the sum of p(VLi) equals 0 to avoid unnecessary processing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computepvh(voxels, cameras, bgmattes): """ Compute Probabilistic Visual Hull. Args: voxels: List of voxel coordinates VLi = (vix, viy, viz). cameras: List of camera parameters. Each camera c has: Rc: 3x3 rotation matrix. COPc: 3x1 center of projection vector. fc: float focal length. oxc, oyc: float optical center coordinates. bgmattes: List of background subtraction functions/mattes BGc. BGc(x, y) returns the soft foreground value at (x, y). Returns: pvh: Dictionary mapping voxel index i to probability p(VLi). """ pvh = {} for i, voxel in enumerate(voxels): vix, viy, viz = voxel totallikelihood = 0.0 for c in range(len(cameras)): cam = cameras[c] Rc = cam['R'] COPc = cam['COP'] fc = cam['f'] oxc = cam['ox'] oyc = cam['oy'] BGc = bgmattes[c] # Step 2: Coordinate Transformation # vprime = COPc - Rc^{-1} voxel # Note: voxel is treated as a column vector. # In practice, this involves matrix inversion and multiplication. Rinvc = invertmatrix(Rc) voxelvec = [vix, viy, viz] transformed = subtractvectors(COPc, multiplymatrixvector(Rinvc, voxelvec)) vprimex, vprimey, vprimez = transformed # Step 3: Projection # Avoid division by zero if voxel is at camera center if vprimez == 0: continue xproj = (fc vprimex / vprimez) + oxc yproj = (fc vprimey / vprimez) + oyc # Step 4: View Probability # Sample the soft matte. Assume BGc handles boundary checks or returns 0 outside. pview = BGc(xproj, yproj) # Step 5: Aggregation # Formula: 1 / (1 + e^(p(VLi|c))) # Note: The source formula sums these terms over c. term = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(pview)) totallikelihood += term pvh[i] = totallikelihood return pvh Parameters: Voxel size: Approximately 5\text{mm}^3. Patch size: Not given in the sources. Overlap: Not given in the sources, though dense sampling with overlap is evaluated in the source. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If a voxel lies exactly at the camera center of projection (v'{iz} = 0), the projection is undefined. The implementation should skip or handle these voxels. Wide Baselines: Standard correspondence methods fail with wide baselines; PVH is chosen specifically to mitigate this, but the resulting PVH may contain "phantom limbs and blocky false positive voxels" if not refined. Empty Patches: Patches with zero total probability can be ignored for efficiency, but care must be taken to ensure no valid surface voxels are missed due to sampling gaps. Refines low-fidelity PVHs into high-fidelity volumes using a convolutional autoencoder, hallucinating detail from limited viewpoints. Choose this when wide-baseline captures produce coarse occupancy estimates that require high-quality volumetric reconstruction from minimal camera counts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Processing is done per patch, making it tractable for large volumes, but the cost scales with the number of voxels and cameras. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method processes sub-volumes (patches) to avoid requiring excessively large receptive fields or up-convolutional layer counts in subsequent refinement steps. Strengths: Handles wide-baseline views that cause correspondence-based methods to fail; produces a soft probability field suitable for refinement. Limitations: The raw PVH contains phantom limbs and blocky false positives; it is a low-fidelity representation intended for further processing. When to use: When capturing performance with a limited number of cameras and wide baselines, and when a probabilistic input is required for a downstream refinement network. When not to use: When high-fidelity geometry is required directly from the reconstruction without refinement, or when correspondence-based methods are viable (narrow baselines) and faster binary hulls are sufficient. Probabilistic Visual Hull Reconstruction was introduced in the context of volumetric performance capture from minimal camera viewpoints. It builds on the concept of soft visual hulls, adapting them to handle the challenges of sparse, wide-baseline camera setups by treating the reconstruction as a probabilistic aggregation problem rather than a hard intersection of silhouettes. The method is often used as a pre-processing step for deep learning-based refinement, where the PVH serves as a low-fidelity input to a convolutional autoencoder. name: 3D Convolutional Autoencoder for PVH Refinement
head: Symmetric Autoencoder, Volumetric Autoencoder
body: This method refines a low-fidelity Probabilistic Visual Hull (PVH) into a high-fidelity PVH of identical dimensions by learning to hallucinate volumetric detail from limited camera viewpoints. It addresses the limitation of wide-baseline captures where sparse views produce coarse, low-resolution occupancy estimates, enabling high-quality volumetric reconstruction from minimal camera counts. Unlike correspondence-based methods that fail with wide baselines, this approach treats refinement as a supervised mapping problem, effectively simulating the benefit of additional viewpoints without requiring them during capture. The method employs a symmetric 3D convolutional autoencoder with skip connections to learn a mapping F from a low-camera-count input volume to a high-camera-count target volume. Input (VL): A 4D tensor \mathbb{R}^{X \times Y \times Z \times 1} representing a low-fidelity PVH patch. The single channel encodes the probability of volume occupancy p(X,Y,Z) derived from a small set of camera views. Output (VH): A 4D tensor \mathbb{R}^{X \times Y \times Z \times 1} representing the refined, high-fidelity PVH of identical dimensions. The network architecture is symmetric with 5 encoder stages and 5 decoder stages. Encoder Parameters: Filter counts (ne): [64, 64, 128, 128, 256] Kernel sizes (ke): [3, 3, 3, 3, 3] (all 3D kernels) Decoder Parameters: Filter counts (nd): [256, 128, 128, 64, 64] Kernel sizes (kd): [3, 3, 3, 3, 3] (all 3D kernels) Skip Connections: Locations (s): [0, 1, 0, 1, 0]. A value of 1 indicates a skip connection between the corresponding encoder and decoder layers. Mechanism: Feature maps from the encoder are summed element-wise with the up-convolutional feature maps in the decoder before passing to the next layer. Latent Space: The central fully-connected layer encodes a 100-dimensional latent representation. 1. Patch Extraction: The capture volume is divided into densely overlapping 3D sub-volumes (patches). Patches where the sum of occupancy probabilities is zero are ignored for efficiency. 2. Encoding: The input patch xi is passed through the encoder. This consists of successive 3D convolutional operations with non-linear activation layers, downsampling the spatial dimensions until the central fully-connected layer. 3. Latent Representation: The central fully-connected layer produces a 100-D latent vector. 4. Decoding: The latent vector is decoded using up-convolutional layers. At layers where s=1, the corresponding encoder feature maps are added element-wise to the decoder feature maps. 5. Output Generation: The final decoder layer produces the output tensor VH of the same spatial dimensions as the input. 6. Training Optimization: The network weights \phi are updated to minimize the Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the network output and the ground truth high-fidelity PVH. Loss Function: The objective is to minimize the MSE across all voxels in the patch: L(\phi) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} ||F(xi; \phi) - zi||2^2 Where: N = X \times Y \times Z is the number of voxels in the patch. xi is the input low-fidelity PVH patch. zi is the ground truth high-fidelity PVH patch. F(xi; \phi) is the network output. \phi represents the network weights. Optimizer: Adadelta is used. It restricts the window of accumulated past gradients to a fixed size w to prevent aggressive, radically diminishing learning rates associated with Adagrad. Optimizer: Adadelta. Epochs: 10. Convergence is typically small, occurring around 5 to 10 epochs. Patch Processing: Patches are processed independently at both training and inference time. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class ConvAutoencoder: def init(self, inputshape=(X, Y, Z)): """ Initialize the symmetric 3D convolutional autoencoder. inputshape: Tuple (X, Y, Z) defining the voxel dimensions of a patch. """ # Encoder filter counts and kernel sizes self.encoderfilters = [64, 64, 128, 128, 256] self.encoderkernels = [3, 3, 3, 3, 3] # Decoder filter counts and kernel sizes self.decoderfilters = [256, 128, 128, 64, 64] self.decoderkernels = [3, 3, 3, 3, 3] # Skip connection locations (1 means skip connection exists) self.skipconnections = [0, 1, 0, 1, 0] # Latent dimension self.latentdim = 100 # Initialize weights phi (not shown, assumed initialized by framework) self.phi = None def encode(self, x): """ Encode input PVH patch into latent representation. x: Tensor of shape (Batch, X, Y, Z, 1) """ # Stage 1 h = conv3d(x, filters=64, kernel=3, activation='relu') h = downsample(h) # Stage 2 (Skip connection 1) h = conv3d(h, filters=64, kernel=3, activation='relu') h = downsample(h) skip1 = h # Store for skip connection # Stage 3 h = conv3d(h, filters=128, kernel=3, activation='relu') h = downsample(h) # Stage 4 (Skip connection 2) h = conv3d(h, filters=128, kernel=3, activation='relu') h = downsample(h) skip2 = h # Store for skip connection # Stage 5 h = conv3d(h, filters=256, kernel=3, activation='relu') h = downsample(h) # Central Fully Connected Layer # Flatten spatial dimensions flat = flatten(h) latent = fullyconnected(flat, units=self.latentdim, activation='relu') return latent, skip1, skip2 def decode(self, latent, skip1, skip2): """ Decode latent representation to output PVH patch. latent: Tensor of shape (Batch, 100) skip1, skip2: Feature maps from encoder stages 2 and 4 """ # Reverse fully connected and reshape h = fullyconnected(latent, units=256 (X//8) (Y//8) (Z//8)) # Assuming specific downsampling factors h = reshape(h, targetshape=(Batch, X//8, Y//8, Z//8, 256)) # Stage 5 (Decoder) h = upconv3d(h, filters=256, kernel=3, activation='relu') # Stage 4 (Decoder) - Skip connection 2 h = conv3d(h, filters=128, kernel=3, activation='relu') h = upconv3d(h, filters=128, kernel=3, activation='relu') # Add skip connection h = elementwiseadd(h, skip2) # Stage 3 (Decoder) h = conv3d(h, filters=128, kernel=3, activation='relu') h = upconv3d(h, filters=128, kernel=3, activation='relu') # Stage 2 (Decoder) - Skip connection 1 h = conv3d(h, filters=64, kernel=3, activation='relu') h = upconv3d(h, filters=64, kernel=3, activation='relu') # Add skip connection h = elementwiseadd(h, skip1) # Stage 1 (Decoder) h = conv3d(h, filters=64, kernel=3, activation='relu') h = upconv3d(h, filters=64, kernel=3, activation='relu') # Final Output Layer output = conv3d(h, filters=1, kernel=3, activation=None) return output def forward(self, x): latent, skip1, skip2 = self.encode(x) return self.decode(latent, skip1, skip2) def trainstep(self, x, z): """ Perform one training step. x: Input low-fidelity PVH patch z: Ground truth high-fidelity PVH patch """ # Forward pass pred = self.forward(x) # Calculate MSE Loss # N = X Y Z loss = meansquarederror(pred, z) # Backpropagate using Adadelta optimizer # Adadelta updates weights phi based on accumulated gradients updateweightsadadelta(self.phi, loss, x, z) return loss def inferpatch(self, patch): """ Refine a single patch. """ return self.forward(patch) def refinevolume(self, lowfidelityvolume, patchsize, overlap): """ Refine the entire volume by processing densely overlapping patches. """ # Initialize output volume highfidelityvolume = zeroslike(lowfidelityvolume) countvolume = zeroslike(lowfidelityvolume) # Generate densely overlapping patches patches = generatepatches(lowfidelityvolume, patchsize, overlap) for patch in patches: # Ignore empty patches if sum(patch) == 0: continue refinedpatch = self.inferpatch(patch) # Accumulate results (handling overlap via averaging or simple sum) # Note: The source mentions "densely overlapping sub-volumes" but # does not specify the exact blending strategy for inference overlap. # Standard practice is averaging. highfidelityvolume += refinedpatch countvolume += 1 # Average overlapping regions # Guard against division by zero safecount = max(countvolume, 1) return highfidelityvolume / safecount Empty Patches: Patches where the sum of occupancy probabilities is zero are ignored to improve efficiency. Memory Constraints: Processing the entire volume at once is intractable due to memory constraints and large receptive fields. Patch-based processing is required. Vanishing Gradients: Deeper networks may suffer from vanishing gradients; skip connections help mitigate this. Detail Loss: Without skip connections, finer details may be lost or corrupted due to the compact latent feature abstraction. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but inference is performed per patch. Training requires 5-10 epochs. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is constrained by the patch size rather than the full volume, making it tractable for large capture volumes. Performance: The method allows for high-fidelity reconstruction from minimal camera viewpoints, effectively doubling or more the utility of the camera setup. Strengths: Handles wide-baseline views; reduces cost by requiring fewer cameras; mitigates memory issues via patching. Limitations: Requires training data (pairs of low and high fidelity PVHs); inference quality depends on the training data distribution. When to use: When camera count is limited (prosumer scenarios, sports events) or camera placement is restricted. When not to use: When high camera counts are available and direct PVH construction is feasible without refinement. The method was introduced in "Volumetric Performance Capture from Minimal Camera Viewpoints". It extends the space of use scenarios for volumetric capture to settings with low camera counts, such as prosumer scenarios or sports events where cost or placement restrictions limit the number of available views. The approach is inspired by 3D convolutional architectures used for visual content de-noising and up-scaling (super-resolution). name: Parametric Surface Voxelization
head: Directional Sheet Buffer Voxelization, Parametric field rasterization
body: Parametric surface voxelization converts a parametric surface into a voxel grid by rasterizing its 2D parameter domain in the vertex shader rather than the 3D object space. It differs from implicit surface voxelization by evaluating the surface function directly on a point boodle and projecting the results immediately, avoiding fragment-shader ray marching or interval solving. Inputs: Parametric surface function S(u, v) mapping 2D parameters to 3D space. A boodle of 2D points covering the parametric domain. Target voxel grid bounds and resolution. Outputs: A voxel grid (worksheet) populated with surface data. Data Structures: Parametric Boodle: An unordered list of 2D points \{(ui, vi)\} covering the parameter space. Worksheet: The target volume buffer where 3D positions are transcoded. Steps: 1. Build a boodle of points that cover the parametric field. 2. Consider each point as a vertex processed in the vertex shader. 3. Use texture coordinates in the parametric domain to calculate positions in 3D space. 4. Transcode these positions to the worksheet immediately. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parametricsurfacevoxelization(surfacefunc, parametricsamples, bounds, resolution): """ Voxelize a parametric surface by rasterizing its parameter domain. Args: surfacefunc: Callable taking (u, v) and returning (x, y, z). parametricsamples: List of (u, v) tuples covering the domain. bounds: Tuple (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz). resolution: Tuple (resx, resy, resz). """ minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz = bounds resx, resy, resz = resolution for u, v in parametricsamples: # Step 3: Calculate 3D position from parametric coordinates x, y, z = surfacefunc(u, v) # Step 4: Transcode position to voxel grid # Map continuous 3D coordinates to discrete voxel indices # Standard coordinate transform nx = (x - minx) / (maxx - minx) ny = (y - miny) / (maxy - miny) nz = (z - minz) / (maxz - minz) i = int(nx resx) j = int(ny resy) k = int(nz resz) # Clamp to valid range i = max(0, min(i, resx - 1)) j = max(0, min(j, resy - 1)) k = max(0, min(k, resz - 1)) # Store the transcoded position in the worksheet worksheet.set(i, j, k, value=(x, y, z)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Instruction Slot Limits: Handling very complex surfaces depends on the shader program supporting enough instruction slots. Shader Stage Selection: The method explicitly uses the vertex shader instead of the pixel shader for rasterization. This method converts a free-form object represented by a Catmull-Clark subdivision surface (CCSS) into a voxel grid by recursively subdividing the 2D parameter space of surface patches and sampling 3D points, rather than subdividing 3D object space. It ensures leak-free results for closed objects when a 3D flooding operation is performed by guaranteeing that voxels generated from a single patch satisfy specific N-adjacency properties. Unlike 3D space subdivision techniques which are computationally expensive due to distance computations between 3D points, this method performs subdivision in 2D parameter space, avoiding expensive 3D distance computations. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of points in the parametric boodle. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the worksheet size and parametric boodle size. Performance: The method leverages GPU vertex shader parallelism for surface evaluation and projection. Strengths: Enables rapid voxelization for applications like transparent illustration and CSG boolean operations on 2D textures. Limitations: Requires the surface to be defined parametrically and the shader to support sufficient instruction slots for complex evaluations. When to Use: When voxelizing parametric surfaces in real-time applications where GPU acceleration is available. When Not to Use: For implicit surfaces defined by scalar fields or polygonal meshes. The method was described in the context of real-time voxelization for complex models, including CSG models and parametric surfaces. It was proposed to solve rapid voxelization challenges, enabling techniques like transparent illustration and GPU-based boolean operations on voxelized worksheets. name: Recursive Parameter Space Voxelization for Catmull-Clark Subdivision Surfaces
head: CCSS Voxelization, Voxelization of Solids Represented by CCSSs
body: This method converts a free-form object represented by a Catmull-Clark subdivision surface (CCSS) into a voxel grid by recursively subdividing the 2D parameter space of surface patches and sampling 3D points, rather than subdividing 3D object space. It guarantees leak-free results for closed objects when a 3D flooding operation is performed by ensuring shared boundaries between patches or subpatches map to the same voxel and by recursively subdividing until the generated voxels satisfy specific N-adjacency conditions. Unlike 3D space subdivision techniques which are computationally expensive due to distance computations between 3D points, this method performs subdivision in 2D parameter space, avoiding expensive 3D distance computations. Inputs: A control mesh S defining a Catmull-Clark subdivision surface. Output voxel grid resolution M1 \times M2 \times M3. Adjacency requirement N \in \{6, 18, 26\}, specifying the connectivity of voxels generated from a subpatch (6 for face-sharing, 18 for edge/face-sharing, 26 for vertex/edge/face-sharing). Initial subdivision level k, an integer specifying that the parameter space [0,1] \times [0,1] is divided into k \times k subpatches before recursive processing begins. Outputs: A voxel grid of resolution M1 \times M2 \times M3 containing the voxelized representation of the CCSS. Data Structures: The control mesh S is stored as a collection of patches. Each patch pid is associated with a local 2D parameter domain [0,1] \times [0,1]. Parametrization techniques allow the explicit calculation of any 3D point \mathbf{S}(u,v), its position, normal, and partial derivatives on the limit surface given a patch ID and parameter coordinates (u,v). Steps: 1. Normalization: Normalize the control mesh S so that its bounding box aligns with the voxel grid coordinates [0, M1-1] \times [0, M2-1] \times [0, M3-1]. 2. Initialization: Iterate through each patch pid in the mesh S. 3. Initial Grid: For the parameter space of the patch, iterate u from 1/k to 1 with step 1/k, and v from 1/k to 1 with step 1/k. 4. Recursive Processing: For each initial subpatch defined by parameter ranges [u-1/k, u] and [v-1/k, v], call VoxelizeSubPatch(N, pid, u - 1/k, u, v - 1/k, v). 5. Subpatch Evaluation: Inside VoxelizeSubPatch, evaluate the 3D surface positions for the four corners of the current subpatch defined by (u1, v1), (u2, v1), (u2, v2), and (u1, v2) using the patch ID pid and the parametrization function \mathbf{S}(u,v). Let these points be \mathbf{V}1, \mathbf{V}2, \mathbf{V}3, \mathbf{V}4. 6. Voxel Conversion: Convert the 3D surface coordinates to voxel indices (i,j,k) using the formula: i = [\mathbf{S}(u, v).x + 0.5], \quad j = [\mathbf{S}(u, v).y + 0.5], \quad k = [\mathbf{S}(u, v).z + 0.5] where [\cdot] denotes the floor function, implementing rounding to the nearest integer via +0.5 truncation. Mark the resulting voxel indices in the output grid. 7. Termination Check: If the subpatch size is smaller than a voxel, return. Calculate the maximum differences in voxel indices among the four corners: \Delta i = \max{a,b \in \{1,2,3,4\}} |ia - ib| \Delta j = \max{a,b \in \{1,2,3,4\}} |ja - jb| \Delta k = \max{a,b \in \{1,2,3,4\}} |ka - kb| If N=6 and \Delta i + \Delta j + \Delta k \le 1, return (subpatch is small enough for 6-adjacency). If N=18 and \Delta i \le 1, \Delta j \le 1, \Delta k \le 1, and \Delta i + \Delta j + \Delta k \le 2, return (subpatch is small enough for 18-adjacency). If N=26 and \Delta i \le 1, \Delta j \le 1, \Delta k \le 1, return (subpatch is small enough for 26-adjacency). 8. Recursive Subdivision: If the subpatch is not small enough, compute midpoints u{12} = (u1 + u2)/2 and v{12} = (v1 + v2)/2. Recursively call VoxelizeSubPatch for the four quadrants: [u1, u{12}] \times [v1, v{12}] [u{12}, u2] \times [v1, v{12}] [u{12}, u2] \times [v{12}, v2] [u1, u{12}] \times [v{12}, v2] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelizeccss(controlmesh, N, M1, M2, M3, k): """ Voxelizes a Catmull-Clark Subdivision Surface. Args: controlmesh: List of patches, each patch has an ID and parametrization function. N: Adjacency requirement (6, 18, or 26). M1, M2, M3: Resolution of the output voxel grid. k: Initial subdivision level for parameter space. Returns: 3D boolean array of shape (M1, M2, M3). """ # Initialize voxel grid voxelgrid = [[[False] M3 for in range(M2)] for in range(M1)] # Normalize control mesh bounding box to [0, M1-1] x [0, M2-1] x [0, M3-1] normalizedmesh = controlmesh step = 1.0 / k for patch in normalizedmesh: pid = patch.id # Initial parameter space subdivision for i in range(1, k + 1): u = i step for j in range(1, k + 1): v = j step # Call recursive voxelization for the initial subpatch voxelizesubpatch(pid, u - step, u, v - step, v, N, voxelgrid) return voxelgrid def voxelizesubpatch(pid, u1, u2, v1, v2, N, voxelgrid): """ Recursively voxelizes a subpatch of a CCSS. """ # Evaluate 3D surface positions for the four corners using standard CCSS limit surface parametrization V1 = evaluateccss(pid, u1, v1) V2 = evaluateccss(pid, u2, v1) V3 = evaluateccss(pid, u2, v2) V4 = evaluateccss(pid, u1, v2) # Convert to voxel indices: i = floor(S.x + 0.5), etc. i1, j1, k1 = math.floor(V1[0] + 0.5), math.floor(V1[1] + 0.5), math.floor(V1[2] + 0.5) i2, j2, k2 = math.floor(V2[0] + 0.5), math.floor(V2[1] + 0.5), math.floor(V2[2] + 0.5) i3, j3, k3 = math.floor(V3[0] + 0.5), math.floor(V3[1] + 0.5), math.floor(V3[2] + 0.5) i4, j4, k4 = math.floor(V4[0] + 0.5), math.floor(V4[1] + 0.5), math.floor(V4[2] + 0.5) # Mark voxels in the output grid voxelgrid[i1][j1][k1] = True voxelgrid[i2][j2][k2] = True voxelgrid[i3][j3][k3] = True voxelgrid[i4][j4][k4] = True # Check if subpatch size is smaller than a voxel; if so, return # (Implementation detail: typically checked via bounding box or curvature, source omits exact test) # Calculate maximum differences in voxel indices deltai = max(i1, i2, i3, i4) - min(i1, i2, i3, i4) deltaj = max(j1, j2, j3, j4) - min(j1, j2, j3, j4) deltak = max(k1, k2, k3, k4) - min(k1, k2, k3, k4) # Termination conditions based on N if N == 6 and (deltai + deltaj + deltak) <= 1: return if N == 18 and deltai <= 1 and deltaj <= 1 and deltak <= 1 and (deltai + deltaj + deltak) <= 2: return if N == 26 and deltai <= 1 and deltaj <= 1 and deltak <= 1: return # Recursive subdivision u12 = (u1 + u2) / 2.0 v12 = (v1 + v2) / 2.0 voxelizesubpatch(pid, u1, u12, v1, v12, N, voxelgrid) voxelizesubpatch(pid, u12, u2, v1, v12, N, voxelgrid) voxelizesubpatch(pid, u12, u2, v12, v2, N, voxelgrid) voxelizesubpatch(pid, u1, u12, v12, v2, N, voxelgrid) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes: Holes appear if the voxels generated from the four corners of a subpatch are not N-adjacent. The algorithm prevents this by recursively subdividing until the N-adjacency condition is met. Shared Boundaries: Shared boundaries between patches or subpatches must map to the same voxel to ensure leak-free results. The algorithm guarantees this because shared boundary points are evaluated at the same parameter coordinates. Termination Test: The exact geometric test for "subpatch size is smaller than a voxel" is not specified in the sources. Time Complexity: The method avoids the exponential increase in faces associated with uniformly refining the control mesh, making it more efficient than direct sampling on subdivided surfaces. Memory Complexity: The output is a voxel grid of size M1 \times M2 \times M3. Strengths: Guarantees leak-free voxelization for closed objects when followed by 3D flooding. Works directly on parametric surfaces of arbitrary topology without requiring explicit polygonization first. Avoids expensive 3D distance computations inherent in 3D space subdivision techniques. Limitations: Requires efficient parametrization techniques to explicitly calculate surface points. Performance is sensitive to the initial subdivision level k and adjacency N; higher N or smaller k may increase computation time. When to use: Volume graphics applications involving free-form solids with arbitrary topology represented by Catmull-Clark subdivision surfaces. Origin: The method was presented in a paper titled "Voxelization of Free-Form Solids Represented by Catmull-Clark Subdivision Surfaces". History: Subdivision surfaces have become popular in graphical modeling, visualization, and animation due to their capability in modeling complex shapes of arbitrary topology and high visual quality. Traditional 3D scan-conversion methods extend 2D scan-line algorithms, but this method works directly on parametric surfaces. Recent parametrization techniques allow explicit calculation of points on the limit surface, enabling this efficient voxelization approach. Usage: Used for volume graphics applications. name: Rasterization and GPU Shaders
head: GPU-based Voxelization, Shader-based Voxelization
body: This family converts triangle meshes into discrete volumetric representations (voxels) by leveraging GPU hardware rasterization pipelines or programmable shaders, rather than CPU-based geometric intersection tests. It solves the problem of real-time or high-throughput voxelization for volume rendering and fluid simulation by mapping 2D rasterization concepts or explicit geometry generation to 3D grid occupancy. It differs from sibling methods like Voxel Carving or Implicit Surface Voxelization by utilizing the graphics pipeline's fragment processing or stream output to determine voxel inclusion and generate output geometry. All methods in this family map a conceptual or physical source into a discrete or analytic volumetric representation suitable for rendering. The core mechanism involves: 1. Domain Definition: Establishing a spatial domain, typically a 3D grid with resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz) and bounding box, or an infinite analytic space. 2. Value Assignment: Determining the value (density, distance, color) for each point in the domain based on the source method (geometric intersection, function evaluation, or physical state). 3. Storage/Access: Either storing the result in a discrete array (voxelization, simulation) or providing an interface to compute it on-the-fly (procedural). A technique that converts a triangle mesh into a discrete volumetric representation by projecting the geometry onto a 3D grid using hardware rasterization principles or hash-based spatial mapping. It solves the problem of generating surface-level voxel data (shell voxelization) for volume rendering or voxel art, differing from CPU-based geometric intersection methods by leveraging efficient spatial hashing or GPU fragment shaders to determine voxel occupancy. Unlike 3D Grid Rasterization which outputs a dense or sparse occupancy grid, this method often generates explicit cube mesh geometry or point clouds from the occupied voxels. A real-time technique that converts mesh geometry into discrete voxel-like cubes by iterating over integer grid positions within a triangle's bounding box and emitting cube geometry for positions close to the triangle plane. Unlike rasterization-based voxelization which fills pixels, this method explicitly generates cube geometry for every grid cell intersecting the triangle, resulting in significantly higher vertex and triangle counts. This family defines methods for converting continuous geometric primitives (points, lines, planes, triangles) into discrete volumetric representations (voxel grids) suitable for volume rendering. It solves the problem of accurately representing sharp geometric boundaries within a scalar field without the aliasing artifacts inherent in binary voxelization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Rasterization-based Voxelization by focusing on analytic slab definitions, optimal scanline criteria, and priority-based clipping rather than GPU rasterization pipelines or geometry shaders. This family converts continuous triangle meshes into discrete volumetric representations (voxel grids) by determining the occupancy of grid cells relative to triangle geometry. It differs from Rasterization-based Voxelization by explicitly separating surface shell generation (via AABB-triangle intersection) from volume filling (via scanlines) to ensure watertight interiors, and from Mesh-to-Voxel Geometry Shader by relying on CPU-side geometric tests rather than GPU shader pipelines for topological correctness. LPV Voxelization Sampling is a method to improve the simulation of direct illumination from area light sources within the Light Propagation Volumes (LPV) technique by voxelizing the area light source geometry into a voxel volume matching the LPV grid resolution. It generates one Virtual Point Light (VPL) sample for each LPV cell that intersects the light source triangles, providing an optimal distribution of samples that covers all necessary cells, unlike dense sampling which may under-sample or over-sample. This approach reduces the number of VPLs processed per frame compared to dense sampling strategies, offering performance advantages while maintaining plausible lighting. A technique to draw all voxelization slices in a single draw call using instancing. Use instancing to draw all slices in a single draw call. Use the instance ID to specify the target slice. A fragment shader that rasterizes geometry into a 3D grid volume by mapping clip-space coordinates to grid indices and writing a value to a structured buffer. Extract clip-space position: float3 xyz = i.vertex.xyz;. Handle reversed Z if applicable: #if defined(UNITYREVERSEDZ) xyz.z = 1 - xyz.z; #endif. Scale and clamp to grid resolution: xyz.z = CVCTGridResolutionI 0.99999;. Convert to integer grid coordinates: int3 pos = int3(xyz);. Calculate flat index: int index = dot(pos, int3(1, CVCTGridResolutionI, CVCTGridResolutionI CVCTGridResolutionI));. Write to buffer: CVCTgv[index] = 1;. CVCTGridResolutionI: integer resolution of the grid, used for coordinate scaling and indexing. CVCTgv: RWStructuredBuffer<int> storing grid values. Coordinate mapping: The shader multiplies Z by 0.99999 to ensure 0 \le pos.z < GridResolution, preventing out-of-bounds writes due to floating-point precision errors at the boundary. Algorithmic paradigm that warps and projects 3D scene elements onto a 2D imaging plane via algebraic transformations, then converts the 2D vector form to a discretized image buffer. Perform algebraic transformations to warp and project 3D scene elements onto a 2D imaging plane. Convert the now-2D vector form of the scene elements to a discretized representation on an image buffer. Favored in high-performance applications like video games for easy GPU parallelization, but implementing physically-based rendering (PBR) numerical methods atop it is markedly harder or impossible compared to ray-tracing. The use of GPU shaders for voxelization emerged with the availability of stream output and geometry shaders in the mid-2000s. Blythe (2006) described stream output as a mechanism to cache transformed vertices, allowing deforming meshes (like skinned characters) to be voxelized without recomputing transformations for each slice. This approach was adopted in real-time fluid simulation to voxelize obstacles at every frame using low-poly meshes to minimize performance cost. The technique evolved to include instancing for drawing multiple slices in a single draw call. Later implementations, such as those in Cascaded Voxel Cone Tracing, utilized fragment shaders with structured buffers to write directly to voxel grids, handling reversed-Z architectures and precision issues via coordinate scaling. name: Rasterization-based Voxelization
head: Cube Mesh Generation, Hash-based Surface Voxelization, Sparse Voxelization with PositionMap Hashing, Voxelizing a Triangle Mesh, madcad Voxelization
body: Rasterization-based Voxelization converts a triangle mesh into a discrete volumetric representation by rasterizing triangles into voxel locations and generating a surface mesh (cube mesh) or point cloud from the occupied voxels. It solves the problem of creating a voxelized surface representation suitable for volume rendering or voxel art, differing from CPU-based geometric intersection methods by leveraging hash-based spatial mapping or GPU fragment shaders to determine voxel occupancy. Unlike full surface reconstruction methods that solve for dual vertices or QEF, this method outputs binary presence or simple cube geometries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh defined by vertices V and faces F (indices). Parameters: voxsize: Voxel dimensions (vx, vy, vz). Typical values range from 0.1 to 1.0 units, or 1/256.0 in normalized space. voxorigin: The world-space coordinate of the bottom-left-back corner of the (0,0,0) voxel. Typically [0, 0, 0]. precision: A tolerance factor to reduce "holes" artifacts caused by rasterization gaps. Typical value: 0.01. gapfraction: The spacing between generated cubes in the output mesh. Typical value: 0.02. Output: A voxelized mesh (cube mesh) containing vertices and indices for each occupied voxel, or a point cloud of voxel centers. Data Structures: 1. Hash Table (Sparse Storage): Used to store occupied voxel coordinates to avoid dense 3D arrays. Key: Voxel center position or integer grid coordinates (i, j, k). Value: Voxel data structure containing position and optional color. Implementation: A hash table with buckets, where each bucket contains a linked list of nodes to handle collisions. 2. Output Mesh (vxmesht): vertices: Array of size N{voxels} \times 8, storing the 8 corners of each cube. normals: Array of size 6, storing predefined face normals for the 6 faces of a cube. colors: Array of size N{voxels} \times 8 (or NULL). indices: Array of size N{voxels} \times \text{VOXELIZER\INDICES\SIZE}. normalindices: Array of size N{voxels} \times \text{VOXELIZER\INDICES\SIZE}. Steps: 1. Load Mesh: Read vertices V and faces F from the input file (e.g., OBJ, PLY). 2. Compute Half-Voxel Size: Calculate hvs = vs \times 0.5, where vs = (vx, vy, vz). 3. Rasterize to Voxels: Iterate through each face (triangle) in the mesh. For each triangle, determine the set of voxel coordinates it intersects or covers. Method A (Hash-based/PositionMap): Use a PositionMap hasher to map triangle points to voxel grid keys and update a set/hash table with these keys. Method B (GPU Rasterization): Project the triangle onto the 3D grid using hardware rasterization; fragments generated correspond to occupied voxels, which are stored in a hash table. Precision Handling: Apply the precision parameter during rasterization/intersection to ensure conservative coverage and reduce holes. 4. Generate Geometry: Allocate output mesh arrays based on the number of unique voxels N{voxels} found in the hash table. Define the 8 corner offsets for a cube centered at the origin relative to hvs: \begin{aligned} &(-hvsx, hvsy, hvsz), (-hvsx, -hvsy, hvsz), (hvsx, -hvsy, hvsz), (hvsx, hvsy, hvsz), \\ &(-hvsx, hvsy, -hvsz), (-hvsx, -hvsy, -hvsz), (hvsx, -hvsy, -hvsz), (hvsx, hvsy, -hvsz) \end{aligned}. Iterate through the hash table buckets. For each occupied voxel: Extract the voxel center position P and color C. Compute the 8 world-space vertices by adding P to the corner offsets. Store these vertices in the output mesh array. Assign predefined normals to the cube faces. Generate indices to form the 6 faces of the cube (typically 12 triangles or 36 indices per voxel, or optimized for shared vertices). 5. Cleanup: Free the hash table and intermediate structures. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rasterizationbasedvoxelization(mesh, voxsize, voxorigin, precision=0.01, gapfraction=0.02): """ Converts a triangle mesh to a voxelized cube mesh. Args: mesh: Object with.vertices (N, 3) and.faces (M, 3) voxsize: Tuple (vx, vy, vz) voxorigin: Tuple (ox, oy, oz) precision: Float for hole reduction gapfraction: Float for spacing between cubes Returns: outputvertices: (V, 3) outputfaces: (F, 3) """ # 1. Compute half-voxel sizes hvs = [s 0.5 for s in voxsize] # 2. Initialize sparse hash table for occupied voxels occupiedvoxels = {} # 3. Rasterize triangles to voxels for face in mesh.faces: v0 = mesh.vertices[face[0]] v1 = mesh.vertices[face[1]] v2 = mesh.vertices[face[2]] # Determine bounding box of triangle in voxel space mini = int(min((v0[0]-voxorigin[0])/voxsize[0], (v1[0]-voxorigin[0])/voxsize[0], (v2[0]-voxorigin[0])/voxsize[0])) maxi = int(max((v0[0]-voxorigin[0])/voxsize[0], (v1[0]-voxorigin[0])/voxsize[0], (v2[0]-voxorigin[0])/voxsize[0])) minj = int(min((v0[1]-voxorigin[1])/voxsize[1], (v1[1]-voxorigin[1])/voxsize[1], (v2[1]-voxorigin[1])/voxsize[1])) maxj = int(max((v0[1]-voxorigin[1])/voxsize[1], (v1[1]-voxorigin[1])/voxsize[1], (v2[1]-voxorigin[1])/voxsize[1])) mink = int(min((v0[2]-voxorigin[2])/voxsize[2], (v1[2]-voxorigin[2])/voxsize[2], (v2[2]-voxorigin[2])/voxsize[2])) maxk = int(max((v0[2]-voxorigin[2])/voxsize[2], (v1[2]-voxorigin[2])/voxsize[2], (v2[2]-voxorigin[2])/voxsize[2])) # Iterate over bounding box voxels and test intersection for i in range(mini, maxi + 1): for j in range(minj, maxj + 1): for k in range(mink, maxk + 1): # Standard triangle-voxel intersection test (e.g., slab method or barycentric) if triangleintersectsvoxel(v0, v1, v2, i, j, k, voxsize, voxorigin, precision): center = [voxorigin[0] + i voxsize[0] + hvs[0], voxorigin[1] + j voxsize[1] + hvs[1], voxorigin[2] + k voxsize[2] + hvs[2]] occupiedvoxels[(i, j, k)] = center # 4. Generate cube mesh geometry outputvertices = [] outputfaces = [] # Predefined cube corner offsets relative to center corneroffsets = [ [-hvs[0], hvs[1], hvs[2]], [-hvs[0], -hvs[1], hvs[2]], [ hvs[0], -hvs[1], hvs[2]], [ hvs[0], hvs[1], hvs[2]], [-hvs[0], hvs[1], -hvs[2]], [-hvs[0], -hvs[1], -hvs[2]], [ hvs[0], -hvs[1], -hvs[2]], [ hvs[0], hvs[1], -hvs[2]] ] # Cube face definitions (indices into the 8 corners) cubefaces = [ [0, 1, 2], [0, 2, 3], [4, 6, 5], [4, 7, 6], [0, 4, 5], [0, 5, 1], [2, 6, 7], [2, 7, 3], [1, 5, 7], [1, 7, 3], [0, 3, 7], [0, 7, 4] ] vertexoffset = 0 for idx, center in occupiedvoxels.items(): # Generate 8 vertices for this voxel voxelvertices = [[center[0] + off[0], center[1] + off[1], center[2] + off[2]] for off in corneroffsets] outputvertices.extend(voxelvertices) # Generate faces for this voxel for faceindices in cubefaces: outputfaces.append([vertexoffset + faceindices[0], vertexoffset + faceindices[1], vertexoffset + faceindices[2]]) vertexoffset += 8 return outputvertices, outputfaces 3D Grid Rasterization converts a triangle mesh into a discrete 3D occupancy grid by projecting the mesh onto three orthogonal planes (XY, YZ, XZ) using hardware rasterization and combining the results. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which voxels in a fixed-resolution 3D grid are intersected by the mesh surface without performing explicit CPU-side raycasting or complex geometric intersection tests. It differs from Conservative Voxelization by relying on standard rasterization rules (which may miss thin features) and from A-Buffer Solid Voxelization by discarding occluded fragments rather than retaining depth lists, making it faster but potentially less watertight for complex internal structures. GPU Volume Kernel Voxelization is a technique that accelerates the voxelization of triangle meshes by parallelizing the iteration over the 2D XY plane of the voxel grid using a GPU compute shader. It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based voxelization, where nested loops over X and Y coordinates are executed sequentially. Unlike Rasterization-based Voxelization and 3D Grid Rasterization which project geometry into 3D textures, this method retains the explicit triangle-voxel intersection logic of CPU implementations but distributes the workload across GPU threads, achieving significant speedups (e.g., 50x) for high-resolution grids. GPU Voxelization via Compute Shaders converts a triangle mesh into a voxel grid by offloading the geometric intersection and occupancy logic to parallel compute kernels. It distinguishes itself from GPU Voxelization by separating surface generation (front/back facing) and interior filling into distinct compute dispatches, allowing for precise control over surface attributes and solid filling. GPU Voxelization converts a triangle mesh into a regular voxel grid representation by leveraging the GPU's hardware rasterization pipeline. It maps each fragment generated by the rasterizer to a specific cell in the voxel grid and writes data into that cell, typically using a 3D texture bound as an Unordered Access View (UAV) or a Shader Storage Buffer Object (SSBO). Unlike CPU-based ray-tracing methods which are slow due to serial intersection tests, this method parallelizes the conversion across the GPU. It distinguishes itself from its sibling 3D Grid Rasterization by using standard orthographic projection and viewport mapping rather than explicit 3D grid traversal, and from GPU Voxelization via Compute Shaders by relying on the fixed-function rasterizer rather than manual thread dispatch. CPU Mesh Voxelization converts a triangle mesh into a 3D grid of voxels by iterating over the bounding box of each triangle and testing each voxel center against the triangle's plane and edge constraints. It differs from its parent Rasterization-based Voxelization by outputting a binary occupancy grid or bit-packed table rather than generating a cube mesh per occupied voxel. It differs from 3D Grid Rasterization by using exact geometric overlap tests (SAT or plane/projection) rather than simple grid cell intersection, and from Voxelization via Triangle Scattering by iterating cells against triangles rather than scattering triangles into cells. Voxel Rasterization is a technique to rasterize triangle meshes into a 3D voxel grid by iterating over the surface of triangles, calculating points and normals, and writing them into a voxel buffer. It supports two primary modes: simple occupancy (binary marking of occupied voxels) and normal/color mapping (associating geometric attributes with voxels). It differs from its sibling 3D Grid Rasterization by explicitly iterating over triangle edges to sample points rather than projecting the entire mesh into a 3D texture volume, and from GPU Volume Kernel Voxelization by relying on a procedural sampling approach rather than a fixed kernel convolution. Conservative voxelization is a hardware-accelerated algorithm for polygonal models that guarantees conservative correctness: every voxel intersecting the input model is correctly recognized. It differs from standard rasterization-based voxelization by computing the exact depth range of the intersection between the triangle and the voxel column, rather than using a single depth value which leads to missed voxels. This method repairs holes in voxelized meshes caused by standard fixed-function rasterization, which only emits fragments for pixels whose centers lie inside the projected triangle. It expands the triangle in clip space within a geometry shader to ensure all potentially covered pixels are rasterized, then culls the overestimated coverage in the fragment shader. It is distinguished from exact bounding polygon methods by using a simple triangle expansion and fragment-shader culling, which is faster in practice despite higher fragment shader workload. Single-Pass Voxelization is a GPU-based method that converts triangle meshes into a sparse voxel representation in a single rendering pass by leveraging the geometry shader for axis selection and conservative rasterization for coverage. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by eliminating the need for multiple draw calls per object (via geometry shaders) and avoiding plain grid allocations (via sparse structures), making it suitable for dynamic scenes where objects are added at runtime. Multi-view projection voxelization converts a triangle mesh into a 3D voxel grid by rasterizing the geometry from multiple camera viewpoints, typically aligned with the principal axes of the scene's bounding box. It solves the problem of occlusion gaps and missing data inherent in single-view projections by ensuring volumetric coverage from multiple directions. It differs from Single 2D Projection Voxelization by using multiple views to cover all surface normals, and from 3D Grid Rasterization by relying on standard GPU rasterization pipelines rather than explicit 3D grid traversal. This family converts 2D rasterized surface data into 3D voxel grids by transferring world-space positions from a 2D texture (the "position map") into a 3D volume texture. It solves the problem of efficiently populating a 3D grid from 2D rasterization outputs, avoiding the computational cost of geometric intersection tests in 3D space. It differs from sibling methods by decoupling the rasterization of geometry (or instances) from the voxelization of the resulting surface points, using image-space coordinates as the bridge. Rasterization-based Volume Modeling is the process of building volume data voxel-by-voxel. It involves instancing the primitive representation, bounding it to find the region of voxels it overlaps, and sampling its density function at each voxel in the overlapping region. The main rasterization loop iterates over voxels in the discrete bounding box, transforms voxel position to world space, samples the primitive, and adds the value to the buffer if positive. Rasterization-based modeling pulls values into a voxel (similar to raytracing), whereas instantiation-based modeling pushes values into voxels (similar to micropolygon rendering). Time Complexity: Depends on the number of triangles Nt and the number of occupied voxels Nv. Memory Complexity: O(Nv) for the hash table and output mesh. Using a hash table makes it memory-efficient for sparse meshes compared to dense 3D arrays. Measured Performance: For a torus mesh (441 vertices, 800 faces, radius 20 units), a voxel size of 0.75 results in 61,312 vertices and 91,968 faces; a voxel size of 0.5 results in 144,968 vertices and 217,452 faces. For a bunny mesh (2503 vertices, 4968 faces), a voxel size of 0.2 results in 53,720 vertices and 80,580 faces. Strengths: Fast on GPU due to parallel rasterization; produces clean cube meshes suitable for voxel art; sparse storage handles large scenes efficiently. Limitations: Output mesh size scales with voxel density, impacting rendering performance if not managed. Standard rasterization may produce "holes" if precision is not handled, requiring conservative rasterization or expansion techniques. When to use: When a discrete voxel surface representation (cube mesh) is needed for volume rendering or voxel art, and GPU acceleration is available. When not to use: When deep (solid) voxelization is required, as this method typically performs shell voxelization (surface only). When exact geometric intersection without rasterization artifacts is critical without conservative techniques. Rasterization-based Voxelization is implemented in libraries such as Point-Cloud-Utils and the C-based voxelizer library by Karim Naaji. The technique is also used in Python via the madcad library's PositionMap hasher. It is considered a layer in the voxel modeling abstraction hierarchy, specifically for rasterization-based volume modeling. The method is often compared to geometry shader-based voxelization, with rasterization-based approaches generally providing better results.
