name: 3D Grid Rasterization
head: 3D Voxel Grid Rasterization, Grid-Snapped Voxelization
body: 3D Grid Rasterization converts a triangle mesh into a binary occupancy grid by projecting the mesh onto three orthogonal planes (XY, YZ, XZ) using hardware rasterization and combining the results. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which voxels in a fixed-resolution 3D grid are intersected by the mesh surface without performing explicit CPU-side raycasting or complex geometric intersection tests. It differs from Conservative Voxelization by relying on standard rasterization rules (which may miss thin features) and from A-Buffer Solid Voxelization by discarding occluded fragments rather than retaining depth lists, making it faster but potentially less watertight for complex internal structures. Inputs: A triangle mesh (vertices, indices, optional colors/normals), a target resolution (integer), and grid bounds. Outputs: A 3D occupancy grid (binary or colored) representing the voxelized mesh. Data Structures: Voxel Grid Storage: A compact 1-bit-per-voxel format. For a grid of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz, the storage is a std::vector<uint32t> of size \lceil (Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz) / 32 \rceil. Each uint32t stores 32 voxels. Memory order is linear in X, then Y, then Z. Projection Textures: Three 3D textures (xProjTextureId, yProjTextureId, zProjTextureId) used as intermediate buffers. Their dimensions are adjusted to store 32 slices per texture layer to match the bit-packing width. For example, xProjTextureId has dimensions (Ny, Nz, Nx/32). VoxelCoord: A struct with integer fields x, y, z. Hash function for sparse variants uses primes p1=73856093, p2=19349663, p3=83492791: hash = x \cdot p1 \oplus y \cdot p2 \oplus z \cdot p3. Parameters: resolution: Target grid resolution along the smallest bounding box dimension. Typical values: 64, 128, 256, 512. voxelsize: Calculated as \min(\text{boundingBoxSize}) / \text{resolution}. gridmin, gridmax: Integer bounds of the grid, typically \{0,0,0\} and \{\text{grid\size}, \text{grid\size}, \text{grid\size}\}. Steps: 1. Grid Initialization: Compute the mesh bounding box in world space. Calculate voxelsize based on the smallest dimension of the bounding box and the target resolution. Round the number of voxels in each dimension up to the nearest multiple of 32 to facilitate bit-packing. Calculate minCorner and maxCorner based on the bounding box center and the rounded voxel count: \text{minCorner} = \text{boundingBoxCenter} - 0.5 \times (\text{roundedNbVoxels} \times \text{voxelSize}) Allocate the three projection 3D textures and the final compact 1-bit grid. 2. X-Axis Projection (YZ Plane): Iterate through the X-axis in steps of 32 (slabs). For each slab index sliceX: Bind the corresponding slice of xProjTextureId to the framebuffer. Set viewport to (Ny, Nz). Clear the buffer. Set up an orthographic projection matrix looking down the X-axis. The view frustum covers the Y and Z extents of the grid, and the near/far planes cover the current 32-voxel slab in X: \text{viewProj} = \text{ortho}(\min Y, \max Y, \min Z, \max Z, \text{sliceX} \cdot \text{voxelSize}, (\text{sliceX} + 32) \cdot \text{voxelSize}) Apply rotation to align the mesh for X-projection: R = \text{rotate}(-90^\circ, \hat{x}) \times \text{rotate}(90^\circ, \hat{z}). Rasterize the mesh triangles into the 2D slice. Use GLOR logic operation or additive blending to set bits in the texture. 3. Y-Axis Projection (XZ Plane): Iterate through the Y-axis in steps of 32. For each sliceY: Bind slice of yProjTextureId (dimensions Nx \times Nz \times Ny/32). Set viewport to (Nx, Nz). Orthographic projection: \text{viewProj} = \text{ortho}(\min X, \max X, \min Z, \max Z, \text{sliceY} \cdot \text{voxelSize}, (\text{sliceY} + 32) \cdot \text{voxelSize}) Rotation: R = \text{rotate}(-90^\circ, \hat{x}). Rasterize mesh into the slice. 4. Z-Axis Projection (XY Plane): Iterate through the Z-axis in steps of 32. For each sliceZ: Bind slice of zProjTextureId (dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz/32). Set viewport to (Nx, Ny). Orthographic projection: \text{viewProj} = \text{ortho}(\min X, \max X, \min Y, \max Y, \text{sliceZ} \cdot \text{voxelSize}, (\text{sliceZ} + 32) \cdot \text{voxelSize}) Rotation: R = \text{rotate}(180^\circ, \hat{z}) \times \text{rotate}(180^\circ, \hat{y}). Rasterize mesh into the slice. 5. Combination (Compilation): Use a compileProjections shader. Bind xProjTextureId to unit 0, yProjTextureId to unit 1. For each sliceZ (step 32): Set uniform slice to sliceZ. Bind the target slice of zProjTextureId to the framebuffer. Draw a full-screen quad (or triangle strip) to combine the X and Y projections into the Z texture. The fragment shader computes the logical AND of the bits from the X and Y projections to determine final occupancy for the Z-slab. Note: Some implementations use a single pass per axis and combine later, or use a 3D texture with image stores for direct writing. The specific "compile" step described in combines X and Y to verify Z-intersection. 6. Result Retrieval: Read the final zProjTextureId (or the combined result) using glGetTexImage with format GLRGBAINTEGER and type GLUNSIGNEDINT8888 (or similar bit-packed format) into a CPU buffer. Unpack the bits into the final 1-bit grid or convert to a boolean array. Pseudocode: Unverified code. It differs from standard depth-buffer rasterization by retaining all fragment depth information rather than discarding occluded fragments, allowing it to output a linked list of starting and ending voxels for each row and column in the grid. This method rasterizes triangle meshes into a Morton-ordered sparse voxel grid by classifying each triangle into one of nine cases based on the thickness of its axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in grid coordinates. It solves the problem of efficiently determining intersected voxels while minimizing redundant depth tests, setting itself apart from general 3D grid rasterization by explicitly handling "thin" (1-voxel thick) triangles via 2D projection and "thick" triangles via 3D plane and projection tests. Geometry Shader Voxelization rasterizes polygonal meshes directly into a 3D voxel grid by leveraging the GPU's geometry shader stage to project triangles onto axis-aligned planes and iterate through occupied grid cells. It solves the problem of converting continuous surface geometry into discrete volumetric data without requiring explicit CPU-side raycasting or compute-shader-based brute-force intersection tests. Unlike sibling methods that rely on hardware rasterization of 2D fragments (e.g., Image-space Voxelization) or pure compute shaders (e.g., GPU Mesh Voxelization via AABB-Triangle Intersection), this method explicitly generates 3D voxel primitives or iterates grid bounds within the shader, offering a balance between implementation simplicity and watertightness control. This method generates a dense 3D voxel grid by computing the center coordinates of each voxel cell directly on the GPU using a compute shader. It solves the problem of converting a mesh's spatial extent into a fixed-width, height, and depth 3D grid structure, returning a flat array of voxel centers. Unlike rasterization-based approaches that project geometry onto slices, this method calculates grid dimensions from the mesh's bounding box and fills the grid with uniform cells, making it suitable for preprocessing steps where a regular grid topology is required. It builds on 3D Grid Rasterization by providing the specific grid generation mechanism. Derived Grid Rasterization converts an unstructured 3D volume mesh (e.g., tetrahedra, hexahedra) into a dense, regular 3D voxel grid spanning the mesh's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). This creates a structured data layout required for efficient volume ray-marching and axis-aligned slice planes on data that originally lacks a grid structure. Unlike sibling methods that may produce sparse structures or rely on different rasterization primitives, this method explicitly maps each voxel to its owning unstructured cell and local tetrahedron index, enabling direct lookup during rendering. It builds on 3D Grid Rasterization by handling unstructured cell topology rather than simple surface mesh voxelization. A pixelization routine that transforms variable-resolution unstructured mesh values into an image buffer by depositing values through nearest-neighbor interpolation with anti-aliasing, decoupling the pixelization step from the underlying data model. It differs from standard rasterization by using a geometric containment test based on dot product signs relative to element centroids, which eliminates the requirement for consistent vertex winding order (CW/CCW). Fast Solid Voxelization via Planar Raycasting is a rasterization-based method that generates a solid voxel mesh from an arbitrary polyhedron by casting rays along the three world coordinate planes (XY, YZ, XZ). It solves the problem of converting polygonal meshes into dense 3D grids by determining voxel occupancy through intersection parity, prioritizing raw computational speed over memory efficiency. It differs from its sibling A-Buffer Solid Voxelization and 3D Grid Rasterization by using pre-computed plane buffers and bit-shifting accumulation rather than per-voxel raycasting or hierarchical data structures, making it significantly faster but less accurate for complex internal structures. Image-space voxelization projects the vertices of a triangular mesh into a 2D image stored in a Frame Buffer Object (FBO) to determine voxel locations and colors. It solves the problem of converting boundary models into volumetric representations by leveraging GPU rasterization hardware, specifically using a single render pass and a single buffer to preserve original vertex colors, unlike methods requiring multiple passes or z-buffer stacks. A vertex shader that generates a full-screen quad to process each voxel slice, outputting non-normalized voxel coordinates for the fragment shader. It defines quad corners vec2(0,0), vec2(1,0), vec2(0,1), vec2(1,1), calculates voxel coordinate texelCoord = vec3(corner gridSize.xy, slice), and sets clip space position glPosition = vec4(corner2-1, 0, 1). Input uniforms are slice (current Z-slice index) and gridSize (voxel grid dimensions). A simplicial covering method that computes the minimal bounding box and centroid of the polygon/solid, constructs a tetrahedron (in 3D) or triangle (in 2D) between the origin vertex (centroid) and one edge (or face), and rasterizes the simplex in the P-Buffer (Presence Buffer), flipping all positions (bits) covered by it. It repeats this for all edges/faces until no edges are left, then transfers all positions from the P-Buffer within the minimal bounding box that have a presence value of 1 to the framebuffer, applying the corresponding color. The P-Buffer is a 3D buffer where each position stores a single bit representing the presence value of a voxel (1 if inside, 0 if outside). Time Complexity: O(N \cdot V) where N is the number of triangles in the mesh and V is the number of slices (proportional to grid resolution). Each slice renders the entire mesh. Memory Complexity: O(Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz / 32) for the compact 1-bit grid storage. Intermediate 3D textures require similar memory proportional to the grid volume. Measured Performance: On an Intel HD 4400 with a Suzanne model (31,000 vertices): 64^3 grid takes 2 ms; 128^3 takes 9 ms; 256^3 takes 10 ms; 512^3 takes 120 ms. A 1,000,000 vertex model at 128^3 takes 45 ms. On a CPU (Intel Xeon) vs GPU (NVIDIA A100) for a PegInsertionSide-v1 mesh (281K verts, 561K faces) at 1024^3 resolution: CPU takes 1.35s, GPU takes 0.56s (3x faster). Strengths: Leverages highly optimized GPU hardware rasterization; compact memory storage; simple implementation using standard OpenGL/Direct3D features. Limitations: Precision glitches on some hardware (e.g., Linux/Intel HD 4400); triangles outside the grid bounds are not voxelized; thin features may be missed due to rasterization gaps; additive blending assumes opaque mesh. When to use: When a fast, approximate occupancy grid is needed for global illumination (VXGI) or collision detection, and watertightness is not critical. When not to use: When exact surface reconstruction (dual vertices) is required, or when the mesh has transparency or complex internal structures that require depth sorting. Originating from hardware-accelerated voxelization techniques for global illumination (VXGI) and real-time rendering, this method utilizes the GPU's rasterization pipeline to project geometry onto 3D grids. It is a core component of the o-voxel pipeline, specifically the "intersect scanline" step, which discovers occupied voxels without performing the subsequent QEF (Quadratic Error Function) minimization or dual vertex solving steps. name: A-Buffer Solid Voxelization
body: A-Buffer Solid Voxelization is a GPU-based technique that voxelize a watertight mesh by rasterizing it into a fixed-width, height, and depth 3D grid and resolving multiple depth intersections per pixel using an A-buffer linked list structure. It differs from standard depth-buffer rasterization by retaining all fragment depth information rather than discarding occluded fragments, allowing it to output a linked list of starting and ending voxels for each row and column in the grid. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A watertight triangle mesh with vertex positions in the interval [-1, 1]. Output: A VoxelizerABufferLinkedList struct containing the grid dimensions, fragment count, and three arrays (headPointers, nodePointers, nodeData) representing a linked list of voxel intersections. Data Structures: The implementation relies on specific C structs and OpenGL resources: 1. Voxelizer: The main context. algorithm: Enum VOXELIZERABUFFER. width, height, depth: Grid dimensions. framebuffer: OpenGL framebuffer object ID. framebufferColor: OpenGL texture ID (GLRGBA, GLUNSIGNEDBYTE, size width x height). meshVertCount: Number of vertices. meshVertPositions: Pointer to vertex data. meshVertBuffer: OpenGL buffer object ID. data: Pointer to VoxelizerABufferData. 2. VoxelizerABufferData: Algorithm-specific state. voxelizer: Pointer to the parent Voxelizer struct. fragCountProgram: Shader program ID for counting fragments. makeFragListProgram: Shader program ID for building the linked list. sortFragListProgram: Shader program ID for sorting the linked list. screenQuadBuffer: OpenGL buffer ID for the screen quad. atomicCounter: OpenGL buffer ID for the atomic counter. headPtrSSBO: Shader Storage Buffer Object (SSBO) ID, size width height 4 bytes. nodePtrSSBO: SSBO ID, size fragmentCount 4 bytes. nodeDataSSBO: SSBO ID, size fragmentCount 4 bytes. fragmentCount: Integer count of fragments. 3. VoxelizerABufferLinkedList: Final output. width, height, depth: Grid dimensions. fragmentCount: Total number of fragments. headPointers: Array of GLint (size width height). nodePointers: Array of GLint (size fragmentCount). nodeData: Array of GLint (size fragmentCount). Steps: 1. Initialization: If voxelizerCount is 0, create an OpenGL window and context, then increment voxelizerCount. Allocate Voxelizer struct. Set width, height, depth. Create a framebuffer with a GLRGBA GLUNSIGNEDBYTE texture of size width x height. Allocate VoxelizerABufferData and initialize algorithm-specific data. 2. Mesh Setup: Upload meshVertPositions to a GLARRAYBUFFER (meshVertBuffer). Enable vertex attribute 0 with 3 floats per vertex. 3. Fragment Counting: Disable GLCULLFACE and GLDEPTHTEST. Bind the framebuffer and set viewport to width x height. Bind meshVertBuffer and use fragCountProgram. Reset the atomic counter to 0. Set modelTransformMatrix uniform. Draw triangles. Retrieve fragmentCount from the atomic counter. 4. Linked List Memory Setup: Map headPtrSSBO (size width height 4 bytes) with GLMAPWRITEBIT | GLMAPINVALIDATEBUFFERBIT. Initialize all entries to -1. Unmap headPtrSSBO. Allocate nodePtrSSBO and nodeDataSSBO (size fragmentCount 4 bytes each). Bind nodePtrSSBO and nodeDataSSBO to binding points 2 and 3 respectively. 5. Create Linked List: Reset atomic counter to 0. Use makeFragListProgram. Set framebufferWidth and modelTransformMatrix uniforms. Draw triangles. Issue GLSHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT memory barrier. 6. Sort Linked List: Bind screenQuadBuffer. Use sortFragListProgram. Set framebufferWidth uniform. Draw 6 vertices (one triangle). Issue GLSHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT memory barrier. 7. Retrieve Results: Allocate VoxelizerABufferLinkedList. Copy width, height, depth, fragmentCount. Allocate headPointers (size width height 4 bytes), nodePointers (size fragmentCount 4 bytes), and nodeData (size fragmentCount 4 bytes). Copy data from headPtrSSBO, nodePtrSSBO, and nodeDataSSBO using glGetBufferSubData. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def allocateintarray(size): return [0] size def setdepthtest(enabled): # Simulates glDisable(GLDEPTHTEST) or glEnable(GLDEPTHTEST) pass def setcullface(enabled): # Simulates glDisable(GLCULLFACE) or glEnable(GLCULLFACE) pass def bindframebuffer(id): # Simulates glBindFramebuffer(GLFRAMEBUFFER, id) pass def setviewport(x, y, w, h): # Simulates glViewport(x, y, w, h) pass def bindarraybuffer(id): # Simulates glBindBuffer(GLARRAYBUFFER, id) pass def enablevertexattrib(index, size, type, normalized, stride, offset): # Simulates glEnableVertexAttribArray(index) and glVertexAttribPointer pass def bindatomiccounterbuffer(id): # Simulates glBindBuffer(GLATOMICCOUNTERBUFFER, id) pass def resetatomiccounter(id): # Simulates clearing the atomic counter buffer to 0 pass def useprogram(id): # Simulates glUseProgram(id) pass def setuniform(loc, value): # Simulates glUniform pass def drawarrays(mode, first, count): # Simulates glDrawArrays(mode, first, count) pass def mapbuffer(id, access): # Simulates glMapBufferRange(id, 0, size, access) pass def unmapbuffer(id): # Simulates glUnmapBuffer(id) pass def bindssbobase(binding, id): # Simulates glBindBufferBase(GLSHADERSTORAGEBUFFER, binding, id) pass def memorybarrier(mask): # Simulates glMemoryBarrier(mask) pass def getbuffersubdata(id, offset, size, dest): # Simulates glGetBufferSubData(id, offset, size, dest) pass def voxelizerrunabuffer(voxelizer): data = voxelizer.data # 1. Fragment Counting setdepthtest(False) setcullface(False) bindframebuffer(voxelizer.framebuffer) setviewport(0, 0, voxelizer.width, voxelizer.height) bindarraybuffer(voxelizer.meshVertBuffer) enablevertexattrib(0, 3, 'FLOAT', False, 3 4, 0) bindatomiccounterbuffer(data.atomicCounter) resetatomiccounter(data.atomicCounter) useprogram(data.fragCountProgram) setuniform('modelTransformMatrix', voxelizer.modeltransformmatrix) drawarrays('TRIANGLES', 0, voxelizer.meshVertCount) ptr = mapbuffer(data.atomicCounter, 'READONLY') data.fragmentCount = ptr[0] unmapbuffer(data.atomicCounter) # 2. Setup Linked List Memory headptr = mapbuffer(data.headPtrSSBO, 'WRITEONLY') for i in range(voxelizer.width voxelizer.height): headptr[i] = -1 unmapbuffer(data.headPtrSSBO) nodesize = data.fragmentCount 4 bindssbobase(2, data.nodePtrSSBO) bindssbobase(3, data.nodeDataSSBO) # 3. Create Linked List resetatomiccounter(data.atomicCounter) useprogram(data.makeFragListProgram) setuniform('framebufferWidth', voxelizer.width) setuniform('modelTransformMatrix', voxelizer.modeltransformmatrix) drawarrays('TRIANGLES', 0, voxelizer.meshVertCount) memorybarrier('SHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT') # 4. Sort Linked List bindarraybuffer(data.screenQuadBuffer) useprogram(data.sortFragListProgram) setuniform('framebufferWidth', voxelizer.width) drawarrays('TRIANGLES', 0, 6) memorybarrier('SHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT') # 5. Retrieve Results linkedlist = allocateintarray(voxelizer.width voxelizer.height) linkedlist.width = voxelizer.width linkedlist.height = voxelizer.height linkedlist.depth = voxelizer.depth linkedlist.fragmentCount = data.fragmentCount headsize = voxelizer.width voxelizer.height 4 nodesize = data.fragmentCount 4 linkedlist.headPointers = allocateintarray(voxelizer.width voxelizer.height) linkedlist.nodePointers = allocateintarray(data.fragmentCount) linkedlist.nodeData = allocateintarray(data.fragmentCount) getbuffersubdata(data.headPtrSSBO, 0, headsize, linkedlist.headPointers) getbuffersubdata(data.nodePtrSSBO, 0, nodesize, linkedlist.nodePointers) getbuffersubdata(data.nodeDataSSBO, 0, nodesize, linkedlist.nodeData) return linkedlist Parameters: Grid Size: Defined by width, height, depth at creation. Vertex Range: Input mesh vertices must be in [-1, 1]. Mesh Type: Input triangle meshes must be watertight. Requirements: OpenGL 4.2 with GLARBshaderstoragebufferobject extension. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Z-axis Clipping: The algorithm does not clip the depth component in the voxel grid. If the mesh extends beyond the grid bounds, it can output an infinite number of voxels along the z-axis. Platform Support: Only Windows is supported at the time of writing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles multiple intersections per pixel accurately via the A-buffer linked list. Limitations: Requires OpenGL 4.2 and SSBO support. Does not clip depth, potentially leading to infinite voxel lists if bounds are exceeded. Only supports Windows. When to use: When accurate solid voxelization of watertight meshes is required on modern GPUs with OpenGL 4.2+. When not: When cross-platform support is needed or when the mesh is not watertight. The A-Buffer Solid Voxelization method is part of the "Voxelizer" library, a fast GPU-based solid voxelization library written in C by Kelsey Kurzeja (khkurzeja). The library was released under the MIT license. The author notes that while the library aims for cross-platform support, only Windows was supported at the time of writing. The method was designed to output a linked list of starting and ending voxels for each row and column in the voxel grid. khkurzeja/Voxelizer, https://github.com/khkurzeja/Voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Sparse Voxelization with Bounding Box Thickness Cases
head: Out-of-Core SVO Builder Voxelization, triangle rasterization via bounding box cases
body: This method rasterizes triangle meshes into a Morton-ordered sparse voxel grid by classifying each triangle into one of nine cases based on the thickness of its axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in grid coordinates. It solves the problem of efficiently determining intersected voxels while minimizing redundant depth tests, setting itself apart from general 3D grid rasterization by explicitly handling "thin" (1-voxel thick) triangles via 2D projection and "thick" triangles via 3D plane and projection tests. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A list of triangles (vertices v0, v1, v2 and optional colors), a partition defined by Morton code range [mortonstart, mortonend), a voxel physical size unitlength, and a sparseness limit sparsenesslimit. Outputs: A voxels array of size mortonend - mortonstart and an optional voxeldata vector. In binary mode, voxels stores EMPTYVOXEL or FULLVOXEL. In non-binary mode, voxels stores indices into voxeldata, which contains normals and colors. Data Structures: VoxelData: Struct containing normal (vec3) and color (vec3). Used only in non-binary mode. voxels array: Flat array indexed by index - mortonstart. Binary mode: uint8t or bool. Values: EMPTYVOXEL (0) or FULLVOXEL (1). Non-binary mode: sizet. Values: Index into voxeldata or EMPTYVOXEL. pbboxgrid: Partition bounding box in grid coordinates, derived from mortonstart and mortonend. Parameters: unitlength: Physical size of one voxel side. Used to convert grid to world coordinates via unitdiv = 1.0f / unitlength. sparsenesslimit: Float parameter (default 0.10) used to estimate max data side-array size: maxbytesdata = ((mortonend - mortonstart) sizeof(char)) sparsenesslimit. Steps: 1. Initialize Partition: Iterate i from 0 to mortonend - mortonstart - 1. Set voxels[i] = EMPTYVOXEL. 2. Compute Partition Bounds: Decode mortonstart and mortonend - 1 to get pbboxgrid.min and pbboxgrid.max. 3. Process Each Triangle: a. Compute Bounding Box: Calculate world-space AABB tbboxworld. Convert to grid coordinates tbboxgrid by multiplying min/max components by unitdiv and casting to int. b. Clamp Bounds: Clamp tbboxgrid.min and tbboxgrid.max to pbboxgrid.min and pbboxgrid.max. c. Determine Thickness: Compute onethick vector where onethick[axis] = 1 if tbboxgrid.min[axis] == tbboxgrid.max[axis], else 0. d. Compute Geometry: Calculate edges e0 = v1 - v0, e1 = v2 - v1, e2 = v0 - v2. Compute normal n = \text{normalize}(e0 \times e1). e. Case Classification & Rasterization: Case 1-3 (1D Bounding Box): If onethick.sum() >= 2 (thin in at least 2 axes): Iterate all voxels in tbboxgrid. For each voxel, compute index = mortonEncodeLUT(z, y, x). If voxels[index - mortonstart] == EMPTYVOXEL, mark as filled (FULLVOXEL or store index) and increment nfilled. No geometric overlap test is needed. Case 4-6 (2D Bounding Box): If onethick.sum() == 1: Identify the thin axis. Perform a 2D projection test on the plane perpendicular to the thin axis. Iterate voxels in the remaining 2D grid bounds. Compute edge normals for the projection plane. If the triangle's normal component in the thin axis is negative, negate all edge normal vectors. Compute edge distance de = (-1.0f \cdot (ne \cdot v{proj})) + \max(0.0f, \text{unitlength} \cdot ne[0]) + \max(0.0f, \text{unitlength} \cdot ne[1]). For each voxel center p{proj}, check if (ne \cdot p{proj}) + de < 0.0f for all 3 edges. If true for all edges, mark voxel as filled. Case 7-9 (3D Bounding Box): If onethick.sum() == 0: Compute critical point c where c[\text{axis}] = \text{unitlength} if n[\text{axis}] > 0, else 0. Compute d1 = n \cdot (c - v0) and d2 = n \cdot ((\deltap - c) - v0) where \deltap = (1, 1, 1) \cdot \text{unitlength}. Perform 3D plane test: if (n \cdot p + d1) \cdot (n \cdot p + d2) > 0.0f, the voxel is entirely on one side of the triangle plane; skip it. Perform 2D projection tests on all three planes (XY, YZ, XZ). For each plane, compute edge normals and distances, negating normals if the corresponding normal component is negative. If the voxel center passes all 3 edge tests for a specific plane, it is inside the triangle's projection. All three planes must pass their respective tests. If a voxel passes the plane test and all three projection tests, mark it as filled. In non-binary mode, compute barycentric coordinates and interpolate vertex colors to store in voxeldata. Pitfalls: Duplicate Voxel Marking: Always check if voxels[index - mortonstart] is already EMPTYVOXEL before processing to prevent double-counting and redundant writes. mortonstart if 0 <= offset < numvoxels and voxels[offset] == EMPTYVOXEL: voxels[offset] = FULLVOXEL if binarymode else len(voxeldata) if not binarymode: voxeldata.append(VoxelData(normal=n, color=average3Vec(tri.v0color, tri.v1color, tri.v2color))) nfilled += 1 elif thicknesssum == 1: thinaxis = next(i for i in range(3) if onethick[i] == 1) projaxes = [i for i in range(3) if i != thinaxis] edgenormals2d = [] for edge in [e0, e1, e2]: n2d = [-edge[projaxes[1]], edge[projaxes[0]]] if n[thinaxis] < 0.0: n2d = [-v for v in n2d] edgenormals2d.append(n2d) edgedistances = [] for i, edge in enumerate([e0, e1, e2]): vproj = [tri.v0[projaxes[0]], tri.v0[projaxes[1]]] ne = edgenormals2d[i] de = (-1.0 (ne[0]vproj[0] + ne[1]vproj[1])) + max(0.0, unitlengthne[0]) + max(0.0, unitlengthne[1]) edgedistances.append(de) for y in range(tbboxgridmin[projaxes[0]], tbboxgridmax[projaxes[0]] + 1): for z in range(tbboxgridmin[projaxes[1]], tbboxgridmax[projaxes[1]] + 1): pproj = [yunitlength, zunitlength] inside = True for i in range(3): if (edgenormals2d[i][0]pproj[0] + edgenormals2d[i][1]pproj[1] + edgedistances[i]) >= 0.0: inside = False break if inside: index = mortonencode(z, y, tbboxgridmin[thinaxis]) offset = index - mortonstart if 0 <= offset < numvoxels and voxels[offset] == EMPTYVOXEL: voxels[offset] = FULLVOXEL if binarymode else len(voxeldata) if not binarymode: voxeldata.append(VoxelData(normal=n, color=average3Vec(tri.v0color, tri.v1color, tri.v2color))) nfilled += 1 else: c = [unitlength if n[i] > 0.0 else 0.0 for i in range(3)] deltap = [unitlength, unitlength, unitlength] d1 = dot(n, [c[i] - tri.v0[i] for i in range(3)]) d2 = dot(n, [(deltap[i] - c[i]) - tri.v0[i] for i in range(3)]) projtests = [] planes = [(0,1), (1,2), (0,2)] planenormals = [2, 0, 1] for planeidx, (a1, a2) in enumerate(planes): edgenormals2d = [] edgedistances = [] for edge in [e0, e1, e2]: n2d = [-edge[a2], edge[a1]] if n[planenormals[planeidx]] < 0.0: n2d = [-v for v in n2d] edgenormals2d.append(n2d) vproj = [tri.v0[a1], tri.v0[a2]] ne = n2d de = (-1.0 (ne[0]vproj[0] + ne[1]vproj[1])) + max(0.0, unitlengthne[0]) + max(0.0, unitlengthne[1]) edgedistances.append(de) projtests.append((edgenormals2d, edgedistances)) for z in range(tbboxgridmin[2], tbboxgridmax[2] + 1): for y in range(tbboxgridmin[1], tbboxgridmax[1] + 1): for x in range(tbboxgridmin[0], tbboxgridmax[0] + 1): p = [xunitlength, yunitlength, zunitlength] nDOTp = dot(n, p) if (nDOTp + d1) (nDOTp + d2) > 0.0: continue inside = True for planeidx, (edgenormals2d, edgedistances) in enumerate(projtests): a1, a2 = planes[planeidx] pproj = [p[a1], p[a2]] for i in range(3): if (edgenormals2d[i][0]pproj[0] + edgenormals2d[i][1]pproj[1] + edgedistances[i]) >= 0.0: inside = False break if not inside: break if inside: index = mortonencode(z, y, x) offset = index - mortonstart if 0 <= offset < numvoxels and voxels[offset] == EMPTYVOXEL: voxels[offset] = FULLVOXEL if binarymode else len(voxeldata) if not binarymode: voxeldata.append(VoxelData(normal=n, color=average3Vec(tri.v0color, tri.v1color, tri.v2color))) nfilled += 1 NGLE Triangle Voxelization is a rasterization-based algorithm for converting triangle meshes into a sparse voxel data structure (specifically a Sparse Voxel DAG or Octree) by classifying triangles into nine cases based on the thickness of their axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in grid coordinates. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which voxels are intersected by a triangle while minimizing redundant depth tests, setting itself apart from general 3D grid rasterization by explicitly handling "thin" (1-voxel thick) triangles via 2D projection and "thick" triangles via 3D plane and projection tests. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(M), where M is the number of voxels in the partition (mortonend - mortonstart). Binary mode uses 1 byte per voxel; non-binary mode uses sizeof(sizet) per voxel plus VoxelData storage. Performance: Optimized for out-of-core processing by partitioning the grid into Morton-ordered chunks. Strengths: Efficient handling of thin triangles; sparse storage reduces memory usage for large scenes. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the "Out-Of-Core SVO Builder" by Jeroen Baert (Forceflow) and is also referenced in the "High Resolution Sparse Voxel DAGs" project. It is designed for building large-scale sparse voxel structures from triangle meshes, leveraging Morton ordering for efficient spatial indexing and out-of-core processing capabilities. name: NGLE Triangle Voxelization
head: N-gle
body: NGLE Triangle Voxelization is a rasterization-based algorithm for converting triangle meshes into a sparse voxel data structure (specifically a Sparse Voxel DAG or Octree) by classifying triangles into nine cases based on the thickness of their axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in grid coordinates. It efficiently determines which voxels are intersected by a triangle using plane and projection tests. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of triangles (each with 3 vertices in world space), a voxel side length unitlength, and a partition range defined by mortonstart and mortonend (Morton codes). Output: A sparse voxel grid where intersected voxels are marked. In binary mode, a boolean flag is set; in data-rich mode, normal and color data are stored. Data Structures: VoxelData: A struct containing normal (vec3) and color (vec3, computed as the average of the three vertex colors). Used only when BINARYVOXELIZATION is not defined. voxels: An array indexed by Morton code. If BINARYVOXELIZATION is defined, voxels is bool; otherwise, it is sizet (indices into a vector<VoxelData>). pbboxgrid: The bounding box of the current partition in grid coordinates, with min and max components. Parameters: unitlength: The side length of a voxel in world units. mortonstart, mortonend: The range of Morton codes allocated for the current partition. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Voxel Array: If BINARYVOXELIZATION is defined, allocate bool voxels. Otherwise, allocate sizet voxels and vector<VoxelData>& voxeldata. Clear the voxel entries for the range [mortonstart, mortonend) to EMPTYVOXEL (or false). 2. Compute Partition Bounding Box: Decode mortonstart and mortonend - 1 into 3D grid coordinates to determine pbboxgrid.min and pbboxgrid.max. 3. Process Each Triangle: Compute World AABB: Calculate the world-space bounding box tbboxworld of the triangle vertices. Convert to Grid AABB: Convert tbboxworld to grid coordinates tbboxgrid by multiplying by unitdiv (1.0f / unitlength) and casting to int. Clamp tbboxgrid to pbboxgrid to stay within the partition. Determine Thickness: Compute the onethick vector. For each axis i \in \{X, Y, Z\}: \text{one\thick}[i] = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } t\bbox\grid.min[i] == t\bbox\grid.max[i] \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Compute Triangle Geometry: Edges: e0 = v1 - v0, e1 = v2 - v1, e2 = v0 - v2. Normal: n = \text{normalize}(e0 \times e1). Case Classification and Voxelization: Cases 4-6 (2D Bounding Box): If \sum \text{one\thick} == 1, the triangle is thin in one axis. Identify the dominant axis (where onethick is 1). Perform a 2D projection test on the plane perpendicular to the dominant axis. Case 4 (Thin in X, Thick in Y, Z): Project onto YZ plane. Compute edge normals n{yz\e0} = \text{vec2}(-e0[Z], e0[Y]), etc. If n[X] < 0, negate all n{yz\ei}. Compute offsets d{yz\ei} = -1.0f \cdot (n{yz\ei} \cdot \text{vec2}(vi[Y], vi[Z])) + \max(0.0f, \text{unitlength} \cdot n{yz\ei}[0]) + \max(0.0f, \text{unitlength} \cdot n{yz\ei}[1]). Iterate y, z in tbboxgrid. Compute Morton index with fixed x = t\bbox\grid.min[X]. Test: For point p{yz} = \text{vec2}(y, z), if (n{yz\ei} \cdot p{yz} + d{yz\ei}) < 0 for all i \in \{0, 1, 2\}, skip. Otherwise, mark voxel. Case 5 (Thin in Y, Thick in X, Z): Project onto ZX plane. Compute edge normals n{zx\e0} = \text{vec2}(-e0[X], e0[Z]), etc. If n[Y] < 0, negate all n{zx\ei}. Compute offsets d{zx\ei} similarly. Iterate z, x in tbboxgrid. Compute Morton index with fixed y = t\bbox\grid.min[Y]. Test projection against all three edges. Mark if intersected. Case 6 (Thin in Z, Thick in X, Y): Project onto XY plane. Compute edge normals n{xy\e0} = \text{vec2}(-e0[Y], e0[X]), etc. If n[Z] < 0, negate all n{xy\ei}. Compute offsets d{xy\ei} similarly. Iterate x, y in tbboxgrid. Compute Morton index with fixed z = t\bbox\grid.min[Z]. Test projection against all three edges. Mark if intersected. Cases 7-9 (3D Bounding Box): If \sum \text{one\thick} == 0, the triangle has variable size in all dimensions. Determine the dominant axis of the normal n (the axis with the largest absolute component). Compute critical point c: c[i] = \begin{cases} \text{unitlength} & \text{if } n[i] > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Compute plane distances for the bounding box: d1 = n \cdot (c - v0) d2 = n \cdot ((\deltap - c) - v0), where \deltap = \text{vec3}(\text{unitlength}, \text{unitlength}, \text{unitlength}). Setup projection tests for all three planes (XY, YZ, ZX) as in Cases 4-6. Iterate x, y, z in tbboxgrid. Compute Morton index. Plane Intersection Test: Let p = \text{vec3}(x, y, z). If (n \cdot p + d1) \cdot (n \cdot p + d2) > 0.0f, skip. This checks if the voxel center is entirely on one side of the triangle plane (assuming the plane passes through the box, d1 and d2 have opposite signs). Projection Tests: If the plane test passes, test the voxel against all three 2D projection planes. If any projection test fails (voxel is outside the triangle's 2D shadow on that plane), skip. Otherwise, mark voxel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelizengle(triangles, unitlength, mortonstart, mortonend, binarymode=True): # 1. Initialize voxelcount = mortonend - mortonstart if binarymode: voxels = [False] voxelcount voxeldata = None else: voxels = [0] voxelcount voxeldata = [] unitdiv = 1.0 / unitlength # 2. Compute Partition Bounding Box pmin = decodemorton3d(mortonstart) pmax = decodemorton3d(mortonend - 1) for tri in triangles: # 3. Compute Grid AABB tbboxmin = clamp(int(floor(min(tri.v0.x, tri.v1.x, tri.v2.x) unitdiv)), pmin.x, pmax.x) tbboxmax = clamp(int(floor(max(tri.v0.x, tri.v1.x, tri.v2.x) unitdiv)), pmin.x, pmax.x) tbboxmin.y = clamp(int(floor(min(tri.v0.y, tri.v1.y, tri.v2.y) unitdiv)), pmin.y, pmax.y) tbboxmax.y = clamp(int(floor(max(tri.v0.y, tri.v1.y, tri.v2.y) unitdiv)), pmin.y, pmax.y) tbboxmin.z = clamp(int(floor(min(tri.v0.z, tri.v1.z, tri.v2.z) unitdiv)), pmin.z, pmax.z) tbboxmax.z = clamp(int(floor(max(tri.v0.z, tri.v1.z, tri.v2.z) unitdiv)), pmin.z, pmax.z) # 4. Determine Thickness onethick = [0, 0, 0] for axis in range(3): if tbboxmin[axis] == tbboxmax[axis]: onethick[axis] = 1 # 5. Compute Geometry e0 = tri.v1 - tri.v0 e1 = tri.v2 - tri.v1 e2 = tri.v0 - tri.v2 n = normalize(cross(e0, e1)) sumonethick = sum(onethick) if sumonethick == 1: # Cases 4-6: 2D Projection dominantaxis = onethick.index(1) if dominantaxis == 0: # Case 4: Thin X, Project YZ for z in range(tbboxmin.z, tbboxmax.z + 1): for y in range(tbboxmin.y, tbboxmax.y + 1): p2d = vec2(y, z) if test2dproj(p2d, tri, unitlength, axis=0): morton = encodemorton3d(tbboxmin.x, y, z) voxels[morton - mortonstart] = True if binarymode else addvoxeldata(voxels, voxeldata, tri, morton) elif dominantaxis == 1: # Case 5: Thin Y, Project ZX for x in range(tbboxmin.x, tbboxmax.x + 1): for z in range(tbboxmin.z, tbboxmax.z + 1): p2d = vec2(z, x) if test2dproj(p2d, tri, unitlength, axis=1): morton = encodemorton3d(x, tbboxmin.y, z) voxels[morton - mortonstart] = True if binarymode else addvoxeldata(voxels, voxeldata, tri, morton) elif dominantaxis == 2: # Case 6: Thin Z, Project XY for y in range(tbboxmin.y, tbboxmax.y + 1): for x in range(tbboxmin.x, tbboxmax.x + 1): p2d = vec2(x, y) if test2dproj(p2d, tri, unitlength, axis=2): morton = encodemorton3d(x, y, tbboxmin.z) voxels[morton - mortonstart] = True if binarymode else addvoxeldata(voxels, voxeldata, tri, morton) elif sumonethick == 0: # Cases 7-9: 3D Bounding Box absn = abs(n) dominantaxis = argmax(absn) c = vec3(0.0) for axis in range(3): if n[axis] > 0: c[axis] = unitlength deltap = vec3(unitlength, unitlength, unitlength) d1 = dot(n, c - tri.v0) d2 = dot(n, (deltap - c) - tri.v0) for z in range(tbboxmin.z, tbboxmax.z + 1): for y in range(tbboxmin.y, tbboxmax.y + 1): for x in range(tbboxmin.x, tbboxmax.x + 1): p = vec3(x, y, z) # Plane Intersection Test val = dot(n, p) + d1 val2 = dot(n, p) + d2 if val val2 > 0.0: continue # Projection Tests pxy = vec2(x, y) pyz = vec2(y, z) pzx = vec2(z, x) if (test2dproj(pxy, tri, unitlength, axis=2) and test2dproj(pyz, tri, unitlength, axis=0) and test2dproj(pzx, tri, unitlength, axis=1)): morton = encodemorton3d(x, y, z) voxels[morton - mortonstart] = True if binarymode else addvoxeldata(voxels, voxeldata, tri, morton) def test2dproj(p2d, tri, unitlength, axis): e0 = tri.v1 - tri.v0 e1 = tri.v2 - tri.v1 e2 = tri.v0 - tri.v2 n = normalize(cross(e0, e1)) if axis == 0: # YZ plane ne0 = vec2(-e0.z, e0.y) ne1 = vec2(-e1.z, e1.y) ne2 = vec2(-e2.z, e2.y) if n.x < 0: ne0 = -ne0; ne1 = -ne1; ne2 = -ne2 d0 = -dot(ne0, vec2(tri.v0.y, tri.v0.z)) + max(0.0, unitlength ne0.x) + max(0.0, unitlength ne0.y) d1 = -dot(ne1, vec2(tri.v1.y, tri.v1.z)) + max(0.0, unitlength ne1.x) + max(0.0, unitlength ne1.y) d2 = -dot(ne2, vec2(tri.v2.y, tri.v2.z)) + max(0.0, unitlength ne2.x) + max(0.0, unitlength ne2.y) elif axis == 1: # ZX plane ne0 = vec2(-e0.x, e0.z) ne1 = vec2(-e1.x, e1.z) ne2 = vec2(-e2.x, e2.z) if n.y < 0: ne0 = -ne0; ne1 = -ne1; ne2 = -ne2 d0 = -dot(ne0, vec2(tri.v0.z, tri.v0.x)) + max(0.0, unitlength ne0.x) + max(0.0, unitlength ne0.y) d1 = -dot(ne1, vec2(tri.v1.z, tri.v1.x)) + max(0.0, unitlength ne1.x) + max(0.0, unitlength ne1.y) d2 = -dot(ne2, vec2(tri.v2.z, tri.v2.x)) + max(0.0, unitlength ne2.x) + max(0.0, unitlength ne2.y) else: # XY plane ne0 = vec2(-e0.y, e0.x) ne1 = vec2(-e1.y, e1.x) ne2 = vec2(-e2.y, e2.x) if n.z < 0: ne0 = -ne0; ne1 = -ne1; ne2 = -ne2 d0 = -dot(ne0, vec2(tri.v0.x, tri.v0.y)) + max(0.0, unitlength ne0.x) + max(0.0, unitlength ne0.y) d1 = -dot(ne1, vec2(tri.v1.x, tri.v1.y)) + max(0.0, unitlength ne1.x) + max(0.0, unitlength ne1.y) d2 = -dot(ne2, vec2(tri.v2.x, tri.v2.y)) + max(0.0, unitlength ne2.x) + max(0.0, unitlength ne2.y) if dot(ne0, p2d) + d0 < 0: return False if dot(ne1, p2d) + d1 < 0: return False if dot(ne2, p2d) + d2 < 0: return False return True def addvoxeldata(voxels, voxeldata, tri, morton): normal = normalize(cross(tri.v1 - tri.v0, tri.v2 - tri.v1)) color = (tri.v0color + tri.v1color + tri.v2color) / 3.0 voxeldata.append(VoxelData(morton, normal, color)) return len(voxeldata) - 1 def encodemorton3d(x, y, z): m = 0 for i in range(10): m |= (x & (1 << i)) << (2 i) m |= (y & (1 << i)) << (2 i + 1) m |= (z & (1 << i)) << (2 i + 2) return m def decodemorton3d(m): x = y = z = 0 for i in range(10): x |= (m & (1 << (2 i))) >> (2 i) y |= (m & (1 << (2 i + 1))) >> (2 i + 1) z |= (m & (1 << (2 i + 2))) >> (2 i + 2) return vec3(x, y, z) Triangle-to-Grid Insertion is a simpler method where, for each triangle, the cells overlapped by the triangle's bounding box are determined, and a reference to the triangle is added to each of these cells. It uses a bounding box overlap test instead of an exact triangle-in-box test. While the exact test reduces triangle references by more than one third, it shrinks ray-triangle intersection tests by only a few percent after mailboxing, making the higher rebuild cost unjustified for most scenes. However, for scenes with dominantly long, skinny, and diagonal triangles, a more accurate test may still pay off. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels in the bounding box of each triangle, multiplied by the number of triangles. The 2D cases (4-6) are faster as they iterate over a 2D plane. The 3D cases (7-9) iterate over a 3D volume but use plane tests to skip empty regions. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of intersected voxels. Sparse storage (Morton codes) ensures only occupied voxels are stored. Strengths: Efficiently handles thin triangles via 2D projection. Robust 3D handling for thick triangles. Compatible with sparse data structures like DAGs/Octrees. Limitations: Bounding box approximation in the initial step can lead to overestimation of voxels (mitigated by the plane/projection tests). Precision issues may arise with very small unitlength or large coordinates. When to use: When building sparse voxel structures for ray tracing or volume rendering where triangle count is high and geometry varies in thickness. NGLE Triangle Voxelization is described in the context of building high-resolution Sparse Voxel DAGs. It is part of a pipeline that includes partitioning and octree building. The method is designed to efficiently populate a sparse voxel structure from triangle meshes, leveraging the properties of Morton codes for spatial locality. The approach is detailed in the GitHub repository leonzheng2/INF584-HighResolutionSparseVoxelDAGs. leonzheng2/INF584-HighResolutionSparseVoxelDAGs, https://github.com/leonzheng2/INF584-HighResolutionSparseVoxelDAGs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Ray Tracing Animated Scenes using Coherent Grid Traversal, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~thiago/papers/grid.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25

name: Dominant-Axis Triangle Voxelization
head: Bresenham Line Segment Voxelization, Dominant Axis Voxelization, Dominant-Axis Triangle Rasterization into Voxel Grid, Voxelization with Dominant Axis Projection
body:
Dominant-Axis Triangle Voxelization is a rasterization-based method for converting triangle meshes into a sparse voxel grid (such as a Sparse Voxel Octree or DAG) by projecting the triangle onto a 2D plane defined by its dominant normal axis. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which voxels are intersected by a triangle while minimizing redundant depth tests. It sets itself apart from general 3D grid rasterization by explicitly classifying triangles into "thin" (1-voxel thick in one axis) and "thick" categories, using 2D projection tests for thin triangles and column-casting with secondary plane checks for thick ones. Inputs: Triangle vertices in world space: v0, v1, v2. Triangle vertex attributes (color, normal). Voxel grid parameters: gridsize (resolution), unitlength (voxel side length). Bounding box of the partition or parent node: pbboxgrid (min/max voxel indices). Voxel storage: voxels array (indexed by Morton code offset) and voxeldata vector for non-binary mode. Outputs: Marked voxels in the voxels array. Voxel data (normal, color) in voxeldata vector (non-binary mode). Voxel Storage: voxels: An array indexed by mortoncode - mortonstart. In BINARYVOXELIZATION mode: stores boolean true if occupied. In non-binary mode: stores an index into voxeldata. voxeldata: A vector of structures. Each entry contains: normal: The triangle's normal vector. color: The average color of the triangle's vertices (average3Vec(v0, v1, v2)). Triangle Info: Vertices v0, v1, v2 and colors v{0\color}, v{1\color}, v{2\color}. tbboxgrid: The bounding box of the triangle in voxel indices. unitlength: The physical size of a single voxel, used to convert voxel indices to world coordinates and to expand edge distances for robustness. EMPTYVOXEL: A constant representing an unmarked voxel (e.g., false or 0). DISTFACTOR: Constant multiplier for distance in attenuation (used in lighting variants, not core voxelization). Value: 1.1f. pc.largetrianglethreshold: Threshold for voxel count to decide between direct rasterization and deferred processing. Value: Not given in the sources. WORKGROUPSIZE: Fixed constant for compute shader workgroup size. Value: 64. 1. Transform and Normalize: Transform vertices to voxel space: v{voxel} =  rac{v{world} - min}{unitlength}. Compute the triangle normal: n = normalize(cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0)). Compute the plane constant: d = -dot(n, v0). 2. Determine Dominant Axis: Calculate the absolute normal components: abs
 = |n|. Select the dominant axis based on the largest component: dominantaxis = X If abs
[Y] > abs
[dominant\axis], dominantaxis = Y. If abs
[Z] > abs
[dominant\axis], dominantaxis = Z. Note: In single-pass GPU modes, this is computed per triangle in the vertex shader. In multi-pass, it is pre-computed and stored. 3. Compute Bounding Box: Calculate voxel-space bounding box extents: x{dim} = \max(x0, x1, x2) - \min(x0, x1, x2) + 1 y{dim} = \max(y0, y1, y2) - \min(y0, y1, y2) + 1 z{dim} = \max(z0, z1, z2) - \min(z0, z1, z2) + 1. Determine mindim = min(xdim, ydim, zdim). 4. Classify and Rasterize: Case 1: Thin Triangle (1 voxel thick in one axis) If z{dim} == 1 (thin in Z): Perform 2D overlap test in XY plane. Compute edge normals for XY plane: n{xy\e0} = (-e0[Y], e0[X]), etc.. If n[Z] < 0, negate edge normals. Compute distances: d{xy\e0} = -dot(n{xy\e0}, v0[XY]) + \max(0, unitlength \cdot n{xy\e0}[X]) + \max(0, unitlength \cdot n{xy\e0}[Y]). Iterate x from t box\grid.min[X] to max[X] and y from min[Y] to max[Y]. For each (x,y), compute center p{xy} = (x \cdot unitlength, y \cdot unitlength). Test if inside: if (dot(n{xy\ei}, p{xy}) + d{xy\ei}) < 0 for any edge, skip. If inside, mark voxel at (x, y, z{min}). If y{dim} == 1 (thin in Y): Perform 2D overlap test in XZ plane. Compute edge normals n{zx\ei} = (-ei[Z], ei[X]). If n[Y] < 0, negate edge normals. Compute distances d{zx\ei} similarly. Iterate z, x; test center p{zx}; mark voxel if inside. If x{dim} == 1 (thin in X): Perform 2D overlap test in YZ plane. Compute edge normals n{yz\ei} = (-ei[Z], ei[Y]). If n[X] < 0, negate edge normals. Compute distances d{yz\ei} similarly. Iterate y, z; test center p{yz}; mark voxel if inside. Case 2: Thick Triangle (3D bounding box) Determine the iteration plane based on dominantaxis. If dominantaxis == X: Iterate y from t box\grid.min[Y] to max[Y] and z from min[Z] to max[Z]. Compute YZ edge normals n{yz\ei} = (-ei[Z], ei[Y]). If n[X] < 0, negate edge normals. Compute distances d{yz\ei}. Test voxel center p{yz} = (y \cdot unitlength, z \cdot unitlength) against YZ projection. If inside YZ projection: Calculate column range in X: Define voxel corners in YZ: min\corner = (y \cdot unitlength, z \cdot unitlength), max\corner = min\corner + (unitlength, unitlength). Swap components if normal components are negative: if n[Y] < 0, swap min\corner[0], max\corner[0]; if n[Z] < 0, swap min\corner[1], max\corner[1]. Project corners to plane: x{min\world} =  rac{n[Y] \cdot min\corner[0] + n[Z] \cdot min\corner[1] + d}{-n[X]} x{max\world} =  rac{n[Y] \cdot max\corner[0] + n[Z] \cdot max\corner[1] + d}{-n[X]} Convert to voxel indices: x{min} = x{min\world} / unitlength, x{max} = x{max\world} / unitlength. Clamp x{min}, x{max} to p box\grid.min[X], p box\grid.max[X]. Special Case: If x{min} == x{max}, compute Morton index for (z, y, x{min}). If not marked, mark it and continue. Range > 1: Iterate x from x{min} to x{max}. For each x, compute Morton index for (z, y, x). Check if already marked; if so, continue. Perform additional overlap tests in XY and ZX planes for the voxel center at (x, y, z). If inside both XY and ZX projections, mark the voxel. If dominantaxis == Y: Iterate z and x in t box\grid. Perform XZ plane projection tests (edge normals n{zx\ei} = (-ei[Z], ei[X])). If inside XZ projection, determine Y-range: y{min\world} =  rac{n[Z] \cdot min\corner[0] + n[X] \cdot min\corner[1] + d}{-n[Y]} (Note: min\corner components correspond to Z and X axes). Clamp y{min}, y{max} to p box\grid. Handle y{min} == y{max} as single voxel. For ranges > 1, test YZ and XY planes. Pitfall: Source code contains a bug where y{max} is clamped using y{min} instead of y{max}. If dominantaxis == Z: Iterate x and y in t box\grid. Perform XY plane projection tests (edge normals n{xy\ei} = (-ei[Y], ei[X])). If inside XY projection, determine Z-range: z{min\world} =  rac{n[X] \cdot min\corner[0] + n[Y] \cdot min\corner[1] + d}{-n[Z]} (Note: min\corner components correspond to X and Y axes). Clamp z{min}, z{max} to p box\grid. Handle z{min} == z{max} as single voxel. For ranges > 1, test XZ and YZ planes. 5. Mark Voxel: Compute Morton index: index = mortonEncode(z, y, x). Check if voxels[index - mortonstart] is EMPTYVOXEL. If not empty, continue. If empty: In BINARYVOXELIZATION: voxels[index - mortonstart] = true. In non-binary: Push VoxelData(normal, averagecolor) to voxeldata, store voxeldata.size() - 1 in voxels[index - mortonstart]. Increment nfilled. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dominantaxisvoxelization(triangles, gridsize, unitlength, mortonstart, voxels, voxeldata): """ Voxelize triangles using the dominant-axis method. """ nfilled = 0 for tri in triangles: v0, v1, v2 = tri.v0, tri.v1, tri.v2 e0, e1, e2 = v1 - v0, v2 - v1, v0 - v2 normal = normalize(cross(e0, e1)) d = -dot(normal, v0) absn = abs(normal) dominantaxis = 'X' if absn[1] > absn[0]: dominantaxis = 'Y' if absn[2] > absn[dominantaxis]: dominantaxis = 'Z' minx, maxx = int(min(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0])), int(max(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0])) miny, maxy = int(min(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1])), int(max(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1])) minz, maxz = int(min(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2])), int(max(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2])) xdim, ydim, zdim = maxx - minx + 1, maxy - miny + 1, maxz - minz + 1 if zdim == 1: rasterize2d(tri, normal, d, unitlength, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz, 'XY', voxels, voxeldata, mortonstart, nfilled) elif ydim == 1: rasterize2d(tri, normal, d, unitlength, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz, 'XZ', voxels, voxeldata, mortonstart, nfilled) elif xdim == 1: rasterize2d(tri, normal, d, unitlength, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz, 'YZ', voxels, voxeldata, mortonstart, nfilled) else: if dominantaxis == 'X': rasterizecolumn(tri, normal, d, unitlength, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz, 'X', voxels, voxeldata, mortonstart, nfilled) elif dominantaxis == 'Y': rasterizecolumn(tri, normal, d, unitlength, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz, 'Y', voxels, voxeldata, mortonstart, nfilled) else: rasterizecolumn(tri, normal, d, unitlength, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz, 'Z', voxels, voxeldata, mortonstart, nfilled) return nfilled def rasterize2d(tri, normal, d, unitlength, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz, plane, voxels, voxeldata, mortonstart, nfilled): e0, e1, e2 = tri.v1 - tri.v0, tri.v2 - tri.v1, tri.v0 - tri.v2 if plane == 'XY': ne0 = vec2(-e0[1], e0[0]) ne1 = vec2(-e1[1], e1[0]) ne2 = vec2(-e2[1], e2[0]) if normal[2] < 0.0: ne0, ne1, ne2 = -ne0, -ne1, -ne2 de0 = -dot(ne0, vec2(tri.v0[0], tri.v0[1])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(ne0[0])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(ne0[1])) de1 = -dot(ne1, vec2(tri.v1[0], tri.v1[1])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(ne1[0])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(ne1[1])) de2 = -dot(ne2, vec2(tri.v2[0], tri.v2[1])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(ne2[0])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(ne2[1])) for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): pxy = vec2(x unitlength, y unitlength) if (dot(ne0, pxy) + de0) < 0.0: continue if (dot(ne1, pxy) + de1) < 0.0: continue if (dot(ne2, pxy) + de2) < 0.0: continue abs(ne1[0])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(ne1[1])) de2 = -dot(ne2, vec2(tri.v2[0], tri.v2[2])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(ne2[0])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(ne2[1])) for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): for x e2[0]) if normal[1] < 0.0: nxze0, nxze1, nxze2 = -nxze0, -nxze1, -nxze2 dxze0 = -dot(nxze0, vec2(tri.v0[0], tri.v0[2])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(nxze0[0])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(nxze0[1])) dxze1 = -dot(nxze1, vec2(tri.v1[0], tri.v1[2])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(nxze1[0])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(nxze1[1])) dxze2 = -dot(nxze2, vec2(tri.v2[0], tri.v2[2])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(nxze2[0])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(nxze2[1])) pxz = vec2(x unitlength, z unitlength) if (dot(nxze0, pxz) + dxze0) < 0.0: continue if (dot(nxze1, pxz) + dxze1) < 0.0: continue if (dot(nxze2, pxz) + dxze2) < 0.0: continue # YZ Plane Test nyze0 = vec2(-e0[2], e0[1]) nyze1 = vec2(-e1[2], e1[1]) nyze2 = vec2(-e2[2], e2[1]) if normal[0] < 0.0: nyze0, nyze1, nyze2 = -nyze0, -nyze1, -nyze2 dyze0 = -dot(nyze0, vec2(tri.v0[1], tri.v0[2])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(nyze0[0])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(nyze0[1])) dyze1 = -dot(nyze1, vec2(tri.v1[1], tri.v1[2])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(nyze1[0])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(nyze1[1])) dyze2 = -dot(nyze2, vec2(tri.v2[1], tri.v2[2])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(nyze2[0])) + max(0.0, unitlength abs(nyze2[1])) pyz = vec2(y unitlength, z unitlength) if (dot(nyze0, pyz) + dyze0) < 0.0: continue if (dot(nyze1, pyz) + dyze1) < 0.0: continue if (dot(nyze2, pyz) + dyze2) < 0.0: continue markvoxel(x, y, z, tri, voxels, voxeldata, mortonstart, nfilled) def markvoxel(x, y, z, tri, voxels, voxeldata, mortonstart, nfilled): index = mortonencode(z, y, x) if voxels[index - mortonstart] != 0: return normal = tri.normal color = (tri.v0color + tri.v1color + tri.v2color) / 3.0 voxeldata.append(VoxelData(normal, color)) voxels[index - mortonstart] = len(voxeldata) - 1 nfilled += 1 def mortonencode(z, y, x): # Standard 10-bit Morton encoding (bit interleaving) def interleavebits(v): v = (v & 0x3FF) << 20 v = (v | ((v >> 1) & 0x3FF)) << 10 v = v | ((v >> 1) & 0x3FF) return v return interleavebits(x) | interleavebits(y) | interleavebits(z) def VoxelData(normal, color): return {'normal': normal, 'color': color} Division by Zero: The column range calculation divides by -n[domant\axis]. If the dominant axis component is exactly 0 (e.g., due to precision issues or a degenerate triangle normal), this causes division by zero. The algorithm assumes the dominant axis selection prevents this, but robust implementations should check for near-zero values. Clamping Bug: In the Y-dominant case, source code contains a bug where y{max} is clamped using y{min} instead of y{max}. Thin Triangle Handling: If a triangle is 1 voxel thick in an axis, the 2D projection test is used. If the triangle is not actually thin but the bounding box calculation results in a dimension of 1 due to integer truncation, the 2D test may miss voxels that the 3D column casting would find. However, the method relies on the bounding box dimensions to classify. Morton Index Overflow: The voxels array is indexed by mortoncode - mortonstart. If the Morton code exceeds the allocated array size, an out-of-bounds access occurs. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot A), where N is the number of triangles and A is the area of the triangle's projection in voxels. For thick triangles, the complexity is proportional to the projected area plus the column depth checks. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the number of voxels in the sparse grid. The voxels array size depends on the Morton code range, and voxeldata stores attributes for each filled voxel. Performance: The method is efficient for sparse voxel grids because it avoids testing voxels outside the triangle's projection. The dominant axis selection minimizes the number of plane tests required. Strengths: Efficient culling of empty columns. Handles thin triangles explicitly, reducing redundant tests. Supports both binary and non-binary voxelization. Limitations: Sensitive to numerical precision in plane tests and column range calculations. Requires careful handling of edge cases (thin triangles, degenerate normals). The clamping bug in the Y-dominant case can lead to incorrect voxel marking. Origin: The method is described in the context of Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) builders, specifically in the oocsvobuilder project and the INF584-HighResolutionSparseVoxelDAGs project. History: It is a rasterization-based approach that evolved from 2D triangle rasterization techniques adapted for 3D voxel grids. The dominant axis selection is a common optimization in voxelization to reduce the search space. Usage: Used in SVO builders for real-time ray tracing and global illumination, where efficient conversion of triangle meshes to voxel data is required. name: Geometry Shader Voxelization
head: GS Voxelization, OpenGL Geometry Shader Voxelization
body: Geometry Shader Voxelization rasterizes polygonal meshes directly into a 3D voxel grid by leveraging the GPU's geometry shader stage to project triangles onto axis-aligned planes and iterate through their bounding boxes. It differs from A-Buffer Solid Voxelization and Image-space Voxelization by writing directly to 3D textures (UAVs) from the geometry shader rather than using fragment shaders with depth buffering or atomic operations on 2D projections. Unlike GPU Mesh Voxelization via AABB-Triangle Intersection, it relies on hardware rasterization logic for coverage determination rather than explicit geometric intersection tests. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh (vertices and indices) and a voxel grid resolution dim (typically cubic, e.g., 64 \times 64 \times 64). Output: A 3D occupancy grid (e.g., GLR8UI) and optionally a 3D color grid (e.g., GLRGBA8). Data Structures: Mesh Data: Vertices V (3xN floats) and Faces F (3xM uint32s). Voxel Grid: Two 3D images bound via OpenGL Image Pipeline: voxelOccupancy: layout(r8ui, binding = 0) uniform uimage3D storing occupancy flags (uint8). voxelColor: layout(rgba8, binding = 1) uniform image3D storing color data (rgba8). Uniforms: voxelResolution (ivec3) specifying grid dimensions. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Load mesh vertices V and faces F. Compute the AABB of the mesh: xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax. Calculate dimensions dx, dy, dz and dmax = \max(dx, dy, dz). Normalize vertex coordinates to [0, 1] range: V{norm} = (V - min) / dmax. Set voxelResolution to the desired grid dimension (e.g., 64) for all axes. 2. Pipeline Setup: Bind the voxelization pipeline with Vertex Shader, Geometry Shader, and Fragment Shader (or just GS if no FS output is needed). Bind the 3D textures as images at bindings 0 and 1. Set primitive topology to TRIANGLELIST. 3. Rasterization (Geometry Shader Execution): For each input triangle (v0, v1, v2): Swizzling: Calculate the triangle normal n = \text{cross}(v1 - v0, v2 - v1). Determine the dominant axis of the normal (max component of |n|). Permute vertex coordinates and normal to align the dominant plane with the XY plane. Store the permutation matrix unswizzle to reverse the transformation later. Edge Normals: For each edge (e0=v1-v0, e1=v2-v1, e2=v0-v2), compute inward-facing 2D edge normals for the XY, YZ, and ZX planes. The direction depends on the sign of the normal component perpendicular to the plane. For the XY plane: n{e0,xy} = (nz \ge 0) ? \text{vec2}(-e{0,y}, e{0,x}): \text{vec2}(e{0,y}, -e{0,x}) Similar logic applies to YZ and ZX planes. Bounding Box: Compute the AABB of the triangle vertices in voxel space. Convert to voxel indices: minVoxIndex = \text{clamp}(\lfloor AABB{min} \rfloor, 0, voxelResolution) maxVoxIndex = \text{clamp}(\lceil AABB{max} \rceil, 0, voxelResolution). Edge Distances (Initial): Calculate initial edge distances for the projected plane. Thin Voxelization: de = \text{dot}(ne, 0.5 - v{proj}) + 0.5 \times \max(|n{e,x}|, |n{e,y}|) Fat Voxelization: de = -\text{dot}(ne, v{proj}) + \max(0, n{e,x}) + \max(0, n{e,y}) These are computed for all 3 edges and 3 planes (XY, YZ, ZX). Triangle Plane Distance: Thin: d{Tri} = \text{dot}(n{proj}, v0) - \text{dot}(n{proj,xy}, 0.5) Fat: d{Tri, min} = \text{dot}(n{proj}, v0) - \max(n{proj,x}, 0) - \max(n{proj,y}, 0) and d{Tri, max} = \text{dot}(n{proj}, v0) - \min(n{proj,x}, 0) - \min(n{proj,y}, 0). X-Y Loop: Iterate p.x from minVoxIndex.x to maxVoxIndex.x and p.y from minVoxIndex.y to maxVoxIndex.y. Update edge distances: dde = de + \text{dot}(ne, p{proj}). Check XY overlap: xy\overlap = (dd{e0,xy} \ge 0) \land (dd{e1,xy} \ge 0) \land (dd{e2,xy} \ge 0). Z-Range Calculation (if XY overlap): Thin: z{min} = (-\text{dot}(n{proj,xy}, p{xy}) + d{Tri}) / n{proj,z}. Apply floor/ceil boundary handling: zMin = \text{int}(zMinFloor) - \text{int}(zMinFloor == zMinInt) and zMax = \text{int}(zMaxCeil) + \text{int}(zMaxCeil == zMaxInt). Fat: z{min} = (-\text{dot}(n{proj,xy}, p{xy}) + d{Tri, fat, min}) / n{proj,z} and z{max} = (-\text{dot}(n{proj,xy}, p{xy}) + d{Tri, fat, max}) / n{proj,z}. Apply similar boundary handling. Z-Loop: Iterate p.z from zMin to zMax (clamped to grid bounds). Update edge distances for YZ and ZX planes: dde = de + \text{dot}(ne, p{proj}). Check overlaps: yz\overlap = (dd{e0,yz} \ge 0) \land \dots and zx\overlap = (dd{e0,zx} \ge 0) \land \dots. Write Voxel: If yz\overlap and zx\overlap are true, the voxel is occupied. Write occupancy: imageStore(voxelOccupancy, ivec3(unswizzlep), uvec4(1)). Write color: imageStore(voxelColor, ivec3(unswizzlep), vec4(unswizzlep/voxelResolution, 1)). 4. Synchronization: Call glMemoryBarrier(GLALLBARRIERBITS) to ensure the 3D texture write is complete before reading. Parameters: dim: Voxel resolution (e.g., 64). THICKNESS: Compile-time constant (THIN 0 or FAT 1) selecting voxel thickness. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Clamping: Voxel indices must be clamped to [0, voxelResolution] to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Overwrite Order: Multiple fragments mapping to the same voxel will overwrite previous values. The final value depends on rasterization depth and draw order. Degenerate Triangles: Triangles with zero area or collinear vertices may produce undefined edge normals or distances. Ensure input meshes do not contain degenerate triangles or handle them by skipping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometryshadervoxelization(mesh, voxelresolution, thicknessmode): """ Voxelize a mesh using Geometry Shader logic.:param mesh: Object with V (3xN floats) and F (3xM uint32s):param voxelresolution: int, dimension of the cubic grid:param thicknessmode: 'THIN' or 'FAT' """ V = mesh.V F = mesh.F # 1. Preprocessing xmin, xmax = min(V[0]), max(V[0]) ymin, ymax = min(V[1]), max(V[1]) zmin, zmax = min(V[2]), max(V[2]) dx, dy, dz = xmax - xmin, ymax - ymin, zmax - zmin dmax = max(dx, dy, dz) Vnorm = (V - [xmin, ymin, zmin]) / dmax # Initialize output buffers voxeloccupancy = [0] (voxelresolution 3) voxelcolor = [0.0] (voxelresolution 3 4) # 2. Rasterization (per triangle) for face in F: v0, v1, v2 = Vnorm[face[0]], Vnorm[face[1]], Vnorm[face[2]] # Swizzling n = cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v1) dominantaxis = argmax(abs(n)) v0, v1, v2, n = swizzle(v0, v1, v2, n, dominantaxis) unswizzle = getunswizzlematrix(dominantaxis) # Edge Normals e0, e1, e2 = v1 - v0, v2 - v1, v0 - v2 ne0xy, ne1xy, ne2xy = compute2dedgenormals(e0, e1, e2, n, 'XY') ne0yz, ne1yz, ne2yz = compute2dedgenormals(e0, e1, e2, n, 'YZ') ne0zx, ne1zx, ne2zx = compute2dedgenormals(e0, e1, e2, n, 'ZX') # Bounding Box minVoxIndex = clamp(floor(min(v0, v1, v2)), 0, voxelresolution - 1) maxVoxIndex = clamp(ceil(max(v0, v1, v2)), 0, voxelresolution - 1) # Initial Edge Distances if thicknessmode == 'THIN': de0xy = dot(ne0xy, 0.5 - v0[:2]) + 0.5 max(abs(ne0xy[0]), abs(ne0xy[1])) de1xy = dot(ne1xy, 0.5 - v1[:2]) + 0.5 max(abs(ne1xy[0]), abs(ne1xy[1])) de2xy = dot(ne2xy, 0.5 - v2[:2]) + 0.5 max(abs(ne2xy[0]), abs(ne2xy[1])) de0yz = dot(ne0yz, 0.5 - v0[1:]) + 0.5 max(abs(ne0yz[0]), abs(ne0yz[1])) de1yz = dot(ne1yz, 0.5 - v1[1:]) + 0.5 max(abs(ne1yz[0]), abs(ne1yz[1])) de2yz = dot(ne2yz, 0.5 - v2[1:]) + 0.5 max(abs(ne2yz[0]), abs(ne2yz[1])) de0zx = dot(ne0zx, 0.5 - v0[::2]) + 0.5 max(abs(ne0zx[0]), abs(ne0zx[1])) de1zx = dot(ne1zx, 0.5 - v1[::2]) + 0.5 max(abs(ne1zx[0]), abs(ne1zx[1])) de2zx = dot(ne2zx, 0.5 - v2[::2]) + 0.5 max(abs(ne2zx[0]), abs(ne2zx[1])) else: # FAT de0xy = -dot(ne0xy, v0[:2]) + max(0, ne0xy[0]) + max(0, ne0xy[1]) de1xy = -dot(ne1xy, v1[:2]) + max(0, ne1xy[0]) + max(0, ne1xy[1]) de2xy = -dot(ne2xy, v2[:2]) + max(0, ne2xy[0]) + max(0, ne2xy[1]) de0yz = -dot(ne0yz, v0[1:]) + max(0, ne0yz[0]) + max(0, ne0yz[1]) de1yz = -dot(ne1yz, v1[1:]) + max(0, ne1yz[0]) + max(0, ne1yz[1]) de2yz = -dot(ne2yz, v2[1:]) + max(0, ne2yz[0]) + max(0, ne2yz[1]) de0zx = -dot(ne0zx, v0[::2]) + max(0, ne0zx[0]) + max(0, ne0zx[1]) de1zx = -dot(ne1zx, v1[::2]) + max(0, ne1zx[0]) + max(0, ne1zx[1]) de2zx = -dot(ne2zx, v2[::2]) + max(0, ne2zx[0]) + max(0, ne2zx[1]) # Triangle Plane Distance if thicknessmode == 'THIN': dtri = dot(n, v0) - dot(n[:2], 0.5) else: dtrimin = dot(n, v0) - max(n[0], 0) - max(n[1], 0) dtrimax = dot(n, v0) - min(n[0], 0) - min(n[1], 0) # X-Y Loop for px in range(minVoxIndex[0], maxVoxIndex[0] + 1): for py in range(minVoxIndex[1], maxVoxIndex[1] + 1): pproj = [px, py] # Update Edge Distances dde0xy = de0xy + dot(ne0xy, pproj) dde1xy = de1xy + dot(ne1xy, pproj) dde2xy = de2xy + dot(ne2xy, pproj) if (dde0xy >= 0) and (dde1xy >= 0) and (dde2xy >= 0): # Z-Range Calculation if thicknessmode == 'THIN': zmin = (-dot(n[:2], pproj) + dtri) / n[2] zmax = zmin # Simplified for example, actual logic involves floor/ceil else: zmin = (-dot(n[:2], pproj) + dtrimin) / n[2] zmax = (-dot(n[:2], pproj) + dtrimax) / n[2] zminint = int(zmin) zmaxint = int(zmax) # Boundary handling zminfinal = zminint - int(zminint == zmin) zmaxfinal = zmaxint + int(zmaxint == zmax) # Z-Loop for pz in range(zminfinal, zmaxfinal + 1): pprojyz = [py, pz] pprojzx = [pz, px] # Update Edge Distances for YZ and ZX dde0yz = de0yz + dot(ne0yz, pprojyz) dde1yz = de1yz + dot(ne1yz, pprojyz) dde2yz = de2yz + dot(ne2yz, pprojyz) dde0zx = de0zx + dot(ne0zx, pprojzx) dde1zx = de1zx + dot(ne1zx, pprojzx) dde2zx = de2zx + dot(ne2zx, pprojzx) if (dde0yz >= 0) and (dde1yz >= 0) and (dde2yz >= 0) and \ (dde0zx >= 0) and (dde1zx >= 0) and (dde2zx >= 0): # Write Voxel voxelpos = unswizzle [px, py, pz] imagestore(voxeloccupancy, voxelpos, 1) imagestore(voxelcolor, voxelpos, [px/voxelresolution, py/voxelresolution, pz/voxelresolution, 1.0]) # 3. Synchronization barrierall() def swizzle(v0, v1, v2, n, axis): # Permute coordinates to align dominant axis with Z (XY plane projection) if axis == 0: # X dominant return [v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]], [v0[2], v1[2], v2[2]], [v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]], [n[1], n[2], n[0]] elif axis == 1: # Y dominant return [v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]], [v0[2], v1[2], v2[2]], [v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]], [n[0], n[2], n[1]] else: # Z dominant return v0, v1, v2, n def getunswizzlematrix(axis): # Returns permutation matrix to reverse swizzle if axis == 0: return [[0,0,1],[1,0,0],[0,1,0]] elif axis == 1: return [[1,0,0],[0,0,1],[0,1,0]] else: return [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]] def compute2dedgenormals(e0, e1, e2, n, plane): # Compute inward-facing 2D edge normals based on plane and normal sign if plane == 'XY': sign = 1 if n[2] >= 0 else -1 return [sign vec2(-e0[1], e0[0]), sign vec2(-e1[1], e1[0]), sign vec2(-e2[1], e2[0])] elif plane == 'YZ': sign = 1 if n[0] >= 0 else -1 return [sign vec2(-e0[2], e0[1]), sign vec2(-e1[2], e1[1]), sign vec2(-e2[2], e2[1])] else: # ZX sign = 1 if n[1] >= 0 else -1 return [sign vec2(-e0[0], e0[2]), sign vec2(-e1[0], e1[2]), sign vec2(-e2[0], e2[2])] def imagestore(buffer, pos, value): idx = pos[0] + pos[1] voxelresolution + pos[2] voxelresolution voxelresolution buffer[idx] = value def barrierall(): # GPU memory barrier to ensure writes are visible pass This method voxelizes a polygonal mesh by dispatching one compute shader thread per voxel grid cell, which then tests its Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) against every triangle in the mesh using the Separating Axis Theorem (SAT). It differs from Geometry Shader Voxelization by avoiding the overhead of generating geometry primitives and from GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics by relying on explicit geometric intersection tests rather than rasterization coverage. It is a brute-force approach that does not use spatial acceleration structures. GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics transforms continuous 3D polygonal meshes into a discrete, regular volumetric grid stored in GPU memory by projecting geometry along its dominant axis, rasterizing fragments without a traditional framebuffer, and utilizing fragment-stage image atomic operations to write directly into 3D textures. It solves the problems of projection loss (degenerate triangles perpendicular to the view plane) and race conditions (concurrent writes to the same voxel) inherent in standard rasterization pipelines. Unlike standard rasterization which projects onto a 2D viewport, this method decouples rasterization from the framebuffer, converting complex geometric meshes into solid or shell voxel structures in a single render pass. It differs from Geometry Shader Voxelization by explicitly handling concurrency via hardware atomics and dominant-axis projection to ensure watertightness, and from GPU Mesh Voxelization via AABB-Triangle Intersection by relying on rasterization primitives rather than explicit geometric intersection tests. GPU Mesh Voxelization via Axis-Aligned Projection converts a triangle mesh into a 3D voxel grid (typically a 3D texture or structured buffer) by projecting each triangle onto a 2D plane aligned with its dominant normal axis, rasterizing it, and writing the resulting fragments into the 3D volume. This method solves the "missing voxel" artifacts common in single-direction rasterization by ensuring that every triangle is viewed from the orientation that maximizes its projected surface area, thereby minimizing gaps caused by edge-on or thin polygons. It differs from GPU Mesh Voxelization via AABB-Triangle Intersection by relying on hardware rasterization rather than explicit geometric intersection tests, and from GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics by using a geometry shader to determine projection axes rather than a single fixed view or pure compute shaders. Single-Pass GPU Voxelization is a technique that maps 3D mesh vertices directly to a 3D grid (voxel space) in a single rasterization pass using a Frame Buffer Object (FBO), avoiding the multiple passes required by methods like Karabassi et al.. It sets itself apart from its sibling Geometry Shader Voxelization by encoding voxel indices into vertex attributes and the FBO alpha channel during the vertex shader stage, rather than rasterizing triangles into a 3D texture via a geometry shader. It is distinct from GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics by relying on standard rasterization depth testing and FBO downloads rather than atomic operations on 3D textures. Imperfect Volume Creation is a fast one-pass algorithm to create a rough approximation of the scene by converting geometry into a dense point cloud and rasterizing points into a 3D volume texture to mark occupancy and store lighting data. The geometry shader takes the triangle as input and emits N random points. For each emitted point, the appropriate slice of the 3D volume is calculated and the point is directly rendered to that slice, marking the corresponding voxel as occupied. Direct illumination is calculated using the interpolated normal from the input triangle and stored in the volume using a spherical harmonics representation. The parameter N controls the number of random points generated per triangle, but performance drops quickly as N increases due to geometry shader data amplification costs. There is no guarantee that every occupied voxel will receive a random point, but as the density of generated points increases, the probability that an occupied voxel does not receive a point tends to zero. Time Complexity: O(T \cdot B), where T is the number of triangles and B is the average number of voxels in the triangle's bounding box. The inner loops iterate over the bounding box, checking overlap with the triangle in 3D. Memory Complexity: O(R^3) for the 3D voxel grid, where R is the resolution. Performance: Efficient for dense meshes and moderate resolutions. The method relies on the GPU's rasterization pipeline to determine which voxels are covered, rather than explicitly iterating over a bounding box, making it simpler to implement but potentially less efficient for sparse triangles or large grids. Strengths: Simple implementation using standard graphics pipeline; no need for explicit intersection tests or complex data structures. Limitations: Overwrites voxel values if multiple fragments map to the same voxel; order depends on rasterization depth and draw order. May produce artifacts for thin or edge-on triangles if not handled with "fat" voxelization. When to Use: When a simple, GPU-accelerated voxelization method is needed and the mesh is not extremely sparse. When Not to Use: When exact watertightness is critical without post-processing, or when the mesh is very sparse and the bounding box iteration is too costly. Implementations such as the one by skanti use OpenGL Geometry Shaders to rasterize triangles directly into a 3D texture. It builds on the concept of using the GPU's rasterization pipeline for volume generation, avoiding the need for CPU-side traversal or complex compute shader logic. The method differs from compute shader-based voxelization by relying on the GPU's rasterization pipeline to determine which voxels are covered, rather than explicitly iterating over a bounding box. ivandrodri/gpu-voxelizer, https://github.com/ivandrodri/gpu-voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Oshanath/Voxel-Cone-Tracing, https://github.com/Oshanath/Voxel-Cone-Tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) StarsX/VoxelizerX12, https://github.com/StarsX/VoxelizerX12, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) skanti/Mesh-Voxelization-OpenGL-Geometry-Shader, https://github.com/skanti/Mesh-Voxelization-OpenGL-Geometry-Shader, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF Voxel Cone Tracing Evaluation for Real-Time Applications, https://kth.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1886204/FULLTEXT01.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) SCITEPRESS - SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY PUBLICATIONS, https://www.scitepress.org/PublishedPapers/2011/33186/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)
