It differs from Geometry Shader Voxelization by avoiding the overhead of generating geometry primitives and from GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics by relying on explicit geometric intersection tests rather than rasterization coverage. It is a brute-force approach that does not use spatial acceleration structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh defined by a vertex buffer (MeshVertices) and an index buffer (MeshTriangleIndices), and a 3D voxel grid defined by dimensions GridWidth, GridHeight, GridDepth, cell half-size CellHalfSize, and world-space minimum corner BoundsMin. Output: A structured buffer Voxels (or VoxelGridPoints) where each entry corresponds to a voxel, containing its position and a boolean isSolid (or intersects) flag. Data Structures: Triangle: float3 a, b, c (36 bytes). AABB: float3 center, float3 extents (24 bytes). Voxel: float3 position, float isSolid (16 bytes). MeshVertices: StructuredBuffer<float3>. MeshTriangleIndices: StructuredBuffer<int>. Voxels: RWStructuredBuffer<Voxel>. Parameters: CellHalfSize: Half the side length of a voxel. Typical value: 0.05f. WorldToLocalMatrix: Transforms world-space coordinates to local mesh space for intersection tests. TriangleCount: Total number of triangle indices in the mesh. Algorithm Steps: 1. Grid Setup: Calculate grid dimensions from the mesh bounds and CellHalfSize: xGridSize = \lceil bounds.extents.x / CellHalfSize \rceil yGridSize = \lceil bounds.extents.y / CellHalfSize \rceil zGridSize = \lceil bounds.extents.z / CellHalfSize \rceil. 2. Dispatch: Dispatch the compute shader with thread groups of size (4, 4, 4) covering the grid: numGroupsX = \lceil xGridSize / 4 \rceil, \quad numGroupsY = \lceil yGridSize / 4 \rceil, \quad numGroupsZ = \lceil zGridSize / 4 \rceil. 3. Thread Execution: For each thread with ID (id.x, id.y, id.z): a. Bounds Check: If id.x \ge GridWidth or id.y \ge GridHeight or id.z \ge GridDepth, return. b. Voxel AABB Construction: Calculate the voxel center in world space: centerPos = (id.x \cdot cellSize + CellHalfSize + BoundsMin.x, \quad id.y \cdot cellSize + CellHalfSize + BoundsMin.y, \quad id.z \cdot cellSize + CellHalfSize + BoundsMin.z) where cellSize = CellHalfSize \cdot 2.0. Define the voxel AABB: aabb.center = centerPos, aabb.extents = (CellHalfSize, CellHalfSize, CellHalfSize). Transform the AABB center to local mesh space if required by the intersection function: aabb.center = mul(WorldToLocalMatrix, centerPos). c. Triangle Intersection Test: Iterate through all triangles in the mesh (step 3). For each triangle T with vertices a, b, c: i. Test intersection between T and aabb using the Separating Axis Theorem (SAT). ii. If an intersection is found, set isSolid = 1.0 and break the loop. d. Output: Calculate the linear voxel index: voxelIndex = id.x + GridWidth \cdot (id.y + GridHeight \cdot id.z). Store the voxel position and isSolid in Voxels[voxelIndex]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def sub(self, o): return Vec3(self.x-o.x, self.y-o.y, self.z-o.z) def isub(self, o): self.x-=o.x; self.y-=o.y; self.z-=o.z; return self def mul(self, s): return Vec3(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) def dot(self, o): return self.xo.x + self.yo.y + self.zo.z def cross(self, o): return Vec3(self.yo.z-self.zo.y, self.zo.x-self.xo.z, self.xo.y-self.yo.x) def normalize(self): l = (self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2)0.5 return Vec3(self.x/l, self.y/l, self.z/l) if l > 0 else self class Triangle: def init(self, a, b, c): self.a, self.b, self.c = a, b, c class AABB: def init(self, center, extents): self.center, self.extents = center, extents class Voxel: def init(self, position, isSolid): self.position, self.isSolid = position, isSolid def VoxelizeMesh(idx, idy, idz): if idx >= GridWidth or idy >= GridHeight or idz >= GridDepth: return cellSize = CellHalfSize 2.0 centerPos = Vec3( idx cellSize + CellHalfSize + BoundsMin.x, idy cellSize + CellHalfSize + BoundsMin.y, idz cellSize + CellHalfSize + BoundsMin.z) aabb = AABB(center=centerPos, extents=Vec3(CellHalfSize, CellHalfSize, CellHalfSize)) intersects = False for i in range(0, TriangleCount, 3): tri = Triangle( a=MeshVertices[MeshTriangleIndices[i]], b=MeshVertices[MeshTriangleIndices[i+1]], c=MeshVertices[MeshTriangleIndices[i+2]]) if IntersectsTriangleAabb(tri, aabb): intersects = True break voxelIndex = idx + GridWidth (idy + GridHeight idz) Voxels[voxelIndex] = Voxel(position=centerPos, isSolid=1.0 if intersects else 0.0) def IntersectsTriangleAabb(tri, aabb): tri.a -= aabb.center tri.b -= aabb.center tri.c -= aabb.center ab = (tri.b - tri.a).normalize() bc = (tri.c - tri.b).normalize() ca = (tri.a - tri.c).normalize() axes = [] axes.append(Vec3(0.0, -ab.z, ab.y)) axes.append(Vec3(0.0, -bc.z, bc.y)) axes.append(Vec3(0.0, -ca.z, ca.y)) axes.append(Vec3(ab.z, 0.0, -ab.x)) axes.append(Vec3(bc.z, 0.0, -bc.x)) axes.append(Vec3(ca.z, 0.0, -ca.x)) axes.append(Vec3(-ab.y, ab.x, 0.0)) axes.append(Vec3(-bc.y, bc.x, 0.0)) axes.append(Vec3(-ca.y, ca.x, 0.0)) axes.append(Vec3(1, 0, 0)) axes.append(Vec3(0, 1, 0)) axes.append(Vec3(0, 0, 1)) axes.append(ab.cross(bc)) for axis in axes: if not IntersectsTriangleAabbSat(tri.a, tri.b, tri.c, aabb.extents, axis): return False return True def IntersectsTriangleAabbSat(v0, v1, v2, aabbExtents, axis): p0 = v0.dot(axis) p1 = v1.dot(axis) p2 = v2.dot(axis) maxP = max(p0, max(p1, p2)) minP = min(p0, min(p1, p2)) r = aabbExtents.x abs(axis.x) + aabbExtents.y abs(axis.y) + aabbExtents.z abs(axis.z) if max(-maxP, minP) > r: return False return True Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: The SAT implementation normalizes edge vectors. If a triangle has zero area, normalization produces NaNs or infinities, potentially causing incorrect results or GPU errors. Missing Axes: The SAT test checks the separating axes (9 cross products of edges with coordinate axes, 3 coordinate axes, and 1 triangle normal). Missing any axis can lead to false positives. Race Conditions: If multiple triangles write to the same voxel, the last thread to execute wins, as there is no atomic blend logic. This method converts a triangular mesh into a voxel grid by dispatching compute threads to test for intersections between mesh facets and voxel cubes. It distinguishes itself from CPU-based approaches by leveraging OpenCL for parallel execution, achieving up to 260 times faster computation. It builds on GPU Mesh Voxelization via AABB-Triangle Intersection by optimizing memory access patterns for the specific geometry of triangular facets. Time Complexity: O(N{cells} \cdot N{triangles}) per voxelization pass, where N{cells} is the number of voxels and N{triangles} is the number of triangles. This is a brute-force approach without spatial acceleration structures. Memory Complexity: O(N{cells}) for the output voxel buffer, plus O(N{vertices} + N{indices}) for input buffers. Performance: Performance scales linearly with grid size and triangle count. It is efficient for moderate-resolution grids and meshes but becomes prohibitive for high-resolution grids or complex meshes due to the O(N^2) nature. Strengths: Simple implementation, no spatial data structure maintenance, fully parallelizable at the voxel level. Limitations: Poor scalability for large scenes or high-resolution grids; no culling of empty space. This method is part of the Unity GPU Mesh Voxelizer series by bzgeb, introduced in 2021. It is designed for real-time voxelization in game engines, leveraging compute shaders for parallel intersection testing. name: OpenCL-based Voxelization
head: Parallelized Voxelization using OpenCL
body: This method converts a triangular mesh into a voxel grid by dispatching compute threads to test for intersections between mesh facets and voxel cubes. It distinguishes itself from conventional single-thread CPU approaches by leveraging OpenCL for parallel execution, achieving up to a 260-fold decrease in computation time. It builds on GPU Mesh Voxelization via AABB-Triangle Intersection by optimizing memory access patterns for the specific geometry of triangular facets. Inputs: A triangular mesh M with n triangles; user-defined voxel grid parameters (origin p0 \in \mathbb{R}^3, dimensions d \in \mathbb{N}^+, diagonal \Delta p \in \mathbb{R}^3). Outputs: A 1D array of length dx dy dz storing material-specific information for each voxel. Data Structures: 1. Preprocessed Mesh Array: A contiguous float array of length 9n. For triangle i, elements 9i to 9i+8 store the x,y,z coordinates of vertices v0, v1, v2 respectively. This ensures coalesced memory access. 2. Voxel Grid Representation: Defined by origin p0, dimensions d=(dx, dy, dz), and voxel diagonal \Delta p. The grid covers the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the mesh. 3. Output Array: 1D array of size dx dy dz. Index i corresponds to voxel (x,y,z) via i = x + y dx + z dx dy. Algorithm Steps: 1. Input Preparation: Construct the preprocessed mesh array. Sort vertex coordinates per triangle into a single contiguous buffer to avoid cluttered memory access caused by separate vertex/index arrays. 2. Grid Construction: Calculate the AABB of the mesh using min/max vertex coordinates. Define the voxel grid parameters p0, d, \Delta p. Allocate the output array. 3. Kernel Execution: Dispatch work-items. Each work-item processes voxel/facet intersections. Index Mapping: If processing by voxel index i, calculate grid coordinates: z = \lfloor i / (dx dy) \rfloor y = \lfloor (i - z dx dy) / dx \rfloor x = i - z dx dy - y dx Voxel Corner Calculation: Calculate the minimum corner o of voxel V(x,y,z): o = p0 + \langle \Delta p, (x, y, z) \rangle where \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle is the dot product. The voxel is defined by corners p=o and p+\Delta p. Facet/Voxel Overlap Test: For each triangle T with vertices v0, v1, v2: 1. Calculate normal n of T. 2. Calculate critical point c relative to the voxel's diagonal \Delta p: ck = \begin{cases} \Delta pk & \text{if } nk > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } nk \le 0 \end{cases} 3. Perform the overlap test based on the enhanced separating axis theorem variant. 4. If an intersection is detected, mark the voxel in the output array. Parameters: Local Size: Number of work-items per work-group. Best practice suggests maximization, but limited local memory often forces reliance on global memory. Global Size: Total number of work-items. Pitfalls: Memory Access: Standard mesh formats (separate vertex/index arrays) cause slow, uncoalesced access. Preprocessing into a contiguous float array is required. Global Memory Limits: Efficient OpenCL programming limits global memory access to a maximum of two per kernel execution (one read, one write). Excessive access compromises performance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelizationkernel(globalid, meshdata, p0, dx, dy, dz, dp, outputarray): i = globalid if i >= dx dy dz: return z = i // (dx dy) remainder = i - z dx dy y = remainder // dx x = remainder - y dx ox = p0[0] + dp[0] x oy = p0[1] + dp[1] y oz = p0[2] + dp[2] z pmin = (ox, oy, oz) pmax = (ox + dp[0], oy + dp[1], oz + dp[2]) numtriangles = len(meshdata) // 9 for t in range(numtriangles): baseidx = t 9 v0 = (meshdata[baseidx], meshdata[baseidx+1], meshdata[baseidx+2]) v1 = (meshdata[baseidx+3], meshdata[baseidx+4], meshdata[baseidx+5]) v2 = (meshdata[baseidx+6], meshdata[baseidx+7], meshdata[baseidx+8]) e1 = (v1[0]-v0[0], v1[1]-v0[1], v1[2]-v0[2]) e2 = (v2[0]-v0[0], v2[1]-v0[1], v2[2]-v0[2]) nx = e1[1]e2[2] - e1[2]e2[1] ny = e1[2]e2[0] - e1[0]e2[2] nz = e1[0]e2[1] - e1[1]e2[0] cx = dp[0] if nx > 0 else 0.0 cy = dp[1] if ny > 0 else 0.0 cz = dp[2] if nz > 0 else 0.0 # The source describes an enhanced separating axis theorem for facet/voxel overlap. # The exact boolean logic is not detailed beyond calculating n and c. # Perform SAT check here. If intersecting, mark voxel. # outputarray[i] = 1 # break Performance: Up to 99.6% reduction or 260 times decrease in computation time compared to conventional single-thread CPU approaches. Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of triangles and voxels, but heavily dependent on memory access patterns. Strengths: High parallelism on heterogeneous hardware (GPU/CPU); optimized memory access via data preprocessing. Limitations: Performance is constrained by the trade-off between local size maximization and global memory access limits. Limited local memory often forces reliance on slower global memory. When to use: When voxelizing large triangular meshes on hardware supporting OpenCL, and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck for standard CPU approaches. This method was developed in the context of heterogeneous computing for computer graphics, with planned integration into virtual orthopaedic surgery platforms. It adopts an enhanced version of the separating axis theorem from prior work, requiring fewer operations than standard implementations. name: GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics
head: Conservative Rasterization Voxelization, OpenGL Image Atomic Voxelization, Scene Voxelization using GPU Rasterization
body: GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics transforms continuous 3D polygonal meshes into a discrete, regular volumetric grid stored in GPU memory by projecting geometry along its dominant axis, rasterizing fragments without a traditional framebuffer, and utilizing fragment-stage image atomic operations to write directly into 3D textures. It solves the problems of projection loss (degenerate triangles perpendicular to the view plane) and race conditions (concurrent writes to the same voxel) inherent in standard rasterization pipelines. Unlike standard rasterization which projects onto a 2D viewport, this method decouples rasterization from the framebuffer, converting complex geometric meshes into solid or shell voxel structures in a single render pass. It differs from Geometry Shader Voxelization by explicitly handling concurrency via hardware atomics and dominant-axis projection to ensure watertightness, and from GPU Mesh Voxelization via AABB-Triangle Intersection by relying on rasterization primitives rather than explicit geometric intersection tests. Inputs and Outputs Input: A polygonal mesh (vertices and indices) and a target 3D voxel grid resolution (typically 128^3 or 256^3). Output: A 3D texture (e.g., GLR32UI) representing the voxel grid, where occupied voxels are marked via atomic operations. Data Structures Voxel Grid: A 3D texture with unsigned integer format GLR32UI. Layout: 3D array of 32-bit unsigned integers. Binding: Bound as a coherent image using glBindImageTexture with GLREADWRITE access. Attribute Grids (Optional): Separate 3D textures for accumulating attributes (e.g., color, normals) and a counter grid for averaging. Steps 1. Geometry Shader Processing: Calculate the triangle's face normal in the Geometry Shader using the cross product of two edges: \text{normal} = \text{cross}(v1 - v0, v2 - v0) Compute the absolute value of the normal components: \text{absNormal} = |\text{normal}| Determine the dominant projection plane by comparing the magnitudes of the normal components: If |Nz| \ge |Nx| and |Nz| \ge |Ny|, project onto the XY-plane. If |Nx| \ge |Ny| and |Nx| \ge |Nz|, swizzle coordinates to project onto the YZ-plane. If |Ny| \ge |Nx| and |Ny| \ge |Nz|, swizzle coordinates to project onto the ZX-plane. Apply an orthographic projection matrix matching the resolution of the target 3D voxel grid along the chosen axis. Pass the original world-space positions to the fragment shader as interpolants. Conservative Rasterization: Enable hardware conservative rasterization via GLNVconservativeraster (glEnable(GLCONSERVATIVERASTERNV)) or use a software fallback where the geometry shader expands the 2D projected triangle vertices outward along their edge normals by half a voxel's diagonal width. 2. Host Setup: Disable color writes and depth tests: c glColorMask(GLFALSE, GLFALSE, GLFALSE, GLFALSE); glDisable(GLDEPTHTEST); glDisable(GLCULLFACE); Initialize the voxel grid storage: c glTexStorage3D(GLTEXTURE3D, 1, GLR32UI, size, size, size); glBindImageTexture(0, voxelTexture, 0, GLTRUE, 0, GLREADWRITE, GLR32UI); 3. Fragment Shader Execution: Convert the interpolated world-space position into normalized coordinates within the voxel bounding box [0, 1], and then scale to integer grid coordinates: \text{voxelCoord} = \text{ivec3}(\text{normalizedWorldPos} \times \text{voxelGridResolution}) Declare the texture as a coherent image in the fragment shader: glsl layout(binding = 0, r32ui) uniform coherent uimage3D voxelGrid; Perform atomic writes based on the desired output type: Binary Occupancy: Use imageAtomicOr to mark a voxel as occupied: glsl imageAtomicOr(voxelGrid, voxelCoord, 1u); Averaging Attributes: Use imageAtomicAdd to accumulate values alongside a separate counter buffer (since atomic floating-point addition is not universally supported): glsl imageAtomicAdd(countGrid, voxelCoord, 1u); imageAtomicAdd(colorGridR, voxelCoord, uint(color.r 255.0)); Bit-Packed Composite Data: Pack values into a single 32-bit unsigned integer using bit-shifts (e.g., (R << 24) | (G << 16) | (B << 8) | A) and write using imageAtomicMax to preserve dominant high-intensity colors or surface markers. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def absvec(v): return tuple(abs(c) for c in v) def applyorthographicprojection(vertices, plane, gridsize): # Project vertices onto the dominant plane and scale to grid resolution projected = [] for v in vertices: if plane == "XY": projected.append((v[0], v[1], v[2])) elif plane == "YZ": projected.append((v[1], v[2], v[0])) else: projected.append((v[2], v[0], v[1])) return projected def expandverticesalongedgenormals(vertices, expansion): # Software fallback: expand triangle vertices along edge normals # Not given in the sources. Placeholder logic omitted. return vertices def imageatomicor(grid, coord, value): # Atomic bitwise OR to mark voxel as occupied index = coord[0] gridsize2 + coord[1] gridsize + coord[2] grid[index] |= value def setupvoxelization(gridsize, bboxmin, bboxmax): # Allocate 3D texture backing the voxel grid with GLR32UI format voxelgrid = [0] (gridsize 3) # Disable color writes and depth tests glcolormask(False, False, False, False) gldisable(GLDEPTHTEST) gldisable(GLCULLFACE) # Enable conservative rasterization if supported if glsupportsextension("GLNVconservativeraster"): glenable(GLCONSERVATIVERASTERNV) return voxelgrid, bboxmin, bboxmax def geometryshaderprocess(vertices, gridsize, conservativerasterizationenabled): v0, v1, v2 = vertices # Calculate face normal normal = cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0) absnormal = absvec(normal) # Determine dominant projection plane if absnormal[2] >= absnormal[0] and absnormal[2] >= absnormal[1]: projectionplane = "XY" elif absnormal[0] >= absnormal[1] and absnormal[0] >= absnormal[2]: projectionplane = "YZ" else: projectionplane = "ZX" # Apply orthographic projection along chosen axis projectedvertices = applyorthographicprojection(vertices, projectionplane, gridsize) # Software fallback for conservative rasterization if not conservativerasterizationenabled: projectedvertices = expandverticesalongedgenormals(projectedvertices, voxeldiagonal / 2) return projectedvertices, vertices def fragmentshaderprocess(interpolatedworldpos, gridsize, bboxmin, bboxmax, voxelgrid): # Map world position to [0, 1] bounding box normalizedpos = [(p - b) / (e - b) for p, b, e in zip(interpolatedworldpos, bboxmin, bboxmax)] # Scale to integer grid coordinates voxelcoord = tuple(int(coord gridsize) for coord in normalizedpos) # Atomic write to mark voxel as occupied imageatomicor(voxelgrid, voxelcoord, 1) Parameters voxelGridResolution: The resolution of the target 3D voxel grid, typically 128^3 or 256^3. GLR32UI: The unsigned integer format used for the 3D texture backing the voxel grid. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Projection Loss: A triangle perpendicular to the projection plane will degenerate into a line or disappear entirely, leaving holes in the voxel grid. This is solved by projecting along the dominant axis where the projected area is largest. Race Conditions: Multiple fragments originating from different triangles, or overlapping segments of the same triangle, may map to the identical voxel cell simultaneously. This is solved by using OpenGL image atomic operations instead of standard imageStore. Missing Voxels: Thin geometry or edges may cross a voxel's spatial bounds without covering the pixel center, resulting in missing voxels. This is solved by using conservative rasterization. A fragment-shader-based voxelization technique that accumulates per-fragment lighting and material properties into a 3D texture using hardware atomic operations to resolve race conditions and compute a moving average of samples per voxel. Choose this when you need to store averaged attributes (like color or normal) rather than just binary occupancy. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Single-pass voxelization; handles concurrency via hardware atomics; ensures watertightness with conservative rasterization; decouples from framebuffer. Limitations: Requires support for GLNVconservativeraster or software fallback; atomic operations may have performance overhead on some hardware; limited to integer formats for atomic operations (floating-point atomics not universally supported on images). When to use: When real-time voxelization of complex meshes is required and the target platform supports OpenGL image atomics and conservative rasterization. When not to use: When floating-point atomic operations are strictly required and not supported; when the mesh is extremely sparse and a sparse voxel structure is more appropriate. GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics is a technique developed to leverage modern OpenGL capabilities for real-time volumetric rendering. It builds on the principles of rasterization-based voxelization, specifically addressing the limitations of standard rasterization pipelines when applied to 3D grids. The method relies on the GLNVconservativeraster extension for hardware-accelerated conservative rasterization and OpenGL 4.2+ features for image atomics. It is commonly used in real-time ray tracing, volumetric rendering, and collision detection systems where fast conversion of polygonal meshes to voxel grids is necessary. otaku690/SparseVoxelOctree, https://github.com/otaku690/SparseVoxelOctree, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics - opengl, https://salivity.github.io/opengl/article/gpu-voxelization-using-open-gl-image-atomics, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: GPU Voxelization with Atomic Accumulation
head: Atomic RGBA8 Averaging, Atomic Average for Voxelization, Atomic RGBA8 average voxelization, Atomic Voxelization with Averaging, Atomic Running Average Voxelization, Voxelization with Atomic Running Average, Voxelization via Fragment Shader with Image Atomic Operations
body: A fragment-shader-based voxelization technique that accumulates per-fragment lighting and material properties into a 3D texture using hardware atomic operations to resolve race conditions and compute a moving average of samples per voxel. It differs from its parent, GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics, by explicitly implementing a moving average via imageAtomicCompSwap loops to prevent flickering when multiple primitives overwrite the same voxel, rather than relying solely on conservative rasterization or simple max operations. Inputs: 3D triangle mesh geometry. Material properties (diffuse color, emission, transparency mode). Light sources (position, color, intensity). Scene parameters (voxel resolution, view matrices, shadow maps). Outputs: A 3D texture (or array of 3D textures) storing voxel data in RGBA8 format (packed into uint). A sparse list of occupied voxel coordinates. Data Structures: 1. VoxelData (Internal struct): color: vec4 (RGBA8 scaled to 0-1). light: uint (4-bit shadow flag). count: uint (4-bit sample counter). 2. Packed Voxel Value (uint): Bits 28-31: light (4 bits). Bits 24-27: count (4 bits). Bits 16-23: R (8 bits). Bits 8-15: G (8 bits). Bits 0-7: B (8 bits). Note: Alpha is stored separately or implied by the averaging logic in some variants, but the primary packing for accumulation focuses on RGB, Light, and Count. 3. Sparse List Entry (uint): Packed XYZ coordinates using packRG11B10: R: 11 bits. G: 11 bits. B: 10 bits. Numbered Steps: 1. Rasterization and Voxel Coordinate Calculation: Project geometry along a dominant axis (e.g., X, Y, or Z) to generate fragments. Calculate base voxel coordinates in texture space: \text{baseVoxel} = \text{uvec3}(\text{floor}(\min(\text{In.posTexSpace}, \text{vec3}(0.999)) \times \text{voxelTexSize})) Clamp position to 0.999 to prevent floating-point errors from mapping to the maximum voxel index (out of bounds). Determine voxelCoord based on the dominant direction index (domInd): If domInd == 0: (depthCoord, glFragCoord.y, res - glFragCoord.x) If domInd == 1: (glFragCoord.x, depthCoord, res - glFragCoord.y) If domInd == 2: (glFragCoord.x, glFragCoord.y, depthCoord) Where depthCoord = glFragCoord.z res and res is the voxel resolution. 2. Lighting and Material Computation: Compute diffuse color from texture/material: \text{diffColor} = \text{texture}(\text{diffuseTex}, \text{vec2}(\text{In.uv.x}, 1.0 - \text{In.uv.y})) If no texture, use material.diffuseColor. Compute lighting per fragment: Loop over numlights = min(pointlightcount, MAXPOINTLIGHTS). Direction: \text{dir} = \text{normalize}(\text{light\pos} - \text{world\pos}). Distance: d = \|\text{light\pos} - \text{world\pos}\|. Attenuation: a = 1.0 / (1.0 + d \times d). Diffuse contribution: \text{cos\surf} = \max(\text{dot}(\text{normalize}(\text{normal}), \text{dir}), 0.0). Accumulate: \text{color} += \text{cos\surf} \times a \times \text{light.color} \times \text{light.intensity}. Combine with material: \text{color} = (\text{diffuse} \times \text{color}) + \text{emission}. Handle transparency: If illum is 4, 6, 7, or 9, set finaltrans = transmittance and alpha = dissolve; otherwise finaltrans = vec3(1.0) and alpha = 1.0. Clamp and convert: \text{final\color} = \text{clamp}(\text{vec4}(\text{final\trans} \times \text{color}, \text{alpha}), 0, 1). 3. Shadow Calculation: Transform light coordinates: \text{lightCoord} = (\text{shadowCoord.xyz} / 2.0) + 0.5. Sample shadow map: \text{shadowDepth} = \text{texture}(\text{shadowMap}, \text{lightCoord.xy}).r. Calculate bias: \text{bias} = \text{clamp}(0.005 \times \tan(\arccos(\text{clamp}(\text{dot}(\text{normalize}(\text{exNormal}), \text{normalize}(\text{scene.lightDir})), 0.0, 1.0))), 0.0, 0.01). If \text{shadowDepth} > \text{lightCoord.z} - \text{bias} AND \text{dot}(\text{lightDir}, \text{normal}) > 0.0, set data.light = 0x8. 4. Atomic Accumulation (Moving Average): Pack finalcolor into RGBA8 bytes. Initialize sample counter n=1. Loop with imageAtomicCompSwap (max 16 iterations, or MAXNUMAVGITERATIONS = 100): Call imageAtomicCompSwap(tex3D, voxelpos, currentval, newval). If successful (returned currentval equals expected old value): Compute new average: \text{rval} = (\text{rval} \times n + \text{val}) / ++n. Round to even: \text{rval} = \text{round}(\text{rval} / 2) \times 2. Repack and store. If failed (value changed): Reload previous value. Retry loop. This resolves flickering caused by multiple primitives overwriting the same voxel. 5. Sparse List Update: If the voxel was empty (prevData == 0): Atomically add 1 to drawCmd[0].instanceCount. Calculate nextIndex from the atomic add result. Pack voxelCoord using packRG11B10 and store in sparseList[nextIndex + drawCmd[0].baseInstance]. Update compute work group sizes if necessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def main(): # 1. Initialize VoxelData # GetColor() returns diffuse color or texture sample colordata = GetColor() data = VoxelData(color=colordata, light=0x0, count=0x8) # 2. Calculate Voxel Coordinates res = float(scene.voxelRes) depthcoord = glFragCoord.z res if scene.domInd == 0: voxelcoord = ivec3(depthcoord, glFragCoord.y, res - glFragCoord.x) elif scene.domInd == 1: voxelcoord = ivec3(glFragCoord.x, depthcoord, res - glFragCoord.y) else: voxelcoord = ivec3(glFragCoord.x, glFragCoord.y, depthcoord) # Clamp to prevent out-of-bounds access voxelcoord = clamp(voxelcoord, ivec3(0), ivec3(res - 1)) # 3. Compute Lighting finalcolor = vec4(0.0) numlights = min(scene.pointlightcount, 10) # MAXPOINTLIGHTS for i in range(numlights): light = scene.pointlights[i] dir = normalize(light.position - worldpos) d = length(light.position - worldpos) a = 1.0 / (1.0 + d d) cossurf = max(dot(normalize(normal), dir), 0.0) finalcolor.rgb += cossurf a light.color light.intensity # Combine with material finalcolor.rgb = (material.diffuse finalcolor.rgb) + material.emission # Handle transparency if material.illum in [4, 6, 7, 9]: finalcolor.rgb = material.transmittance finalcolor.rgb finalcolor.a = material.dissolve else: finalcolor.rgb = vec3(1.0) finalcolor.a = 1.0 finalcolor = clamp(finalcolor, 0.0, 1.0) # 4. Shadow Calculation lightcoord = shadowcoord.xyz / 2.0 + 0.5 shadowdepth = texture(shadowMap, lightcoord.xy).r costheta = clamp(dot(normalize(exnormal), normalize(scene.lightdir)), 0.0, 1.0) bias = clamp(0.005 tan(acos(costheta)), 0.0, 0.01) if shadowdepth > lightcoord.z - bias and dot(normalize(scene.lightdir), normalize(exnormal)) > 0.0: data.light = 0x8 # 5. Atomic Average Accumulation # Pack initial value for comparison outdata = packARGB8(data, finalcolor) # Loop for atomic average prevdata = 0 n = 1 for iter in range(16): # Max iterations # imageAtomicCompSwap returns the previous value prevdata = imageAtomicCompSwap(voxelTextures, voxelcoord, prevdata, outdata) if prevdata == outdata: # Success: value didn't change, we wrote our average break else: # Conflict: reload, re-average, retry # Decode prevdata to get current average and count currval = unpackARGB8(prevdata) # Re-average with new sample # Note: Simplified logic; real implementation requires careful unpacking/packing # rval = (rval n + val) / ++n # Repack and update outdata outdata = packARGB8(data, reaverage(currval, finalcolor)) n += 1 # 6. Sparse List Update if voxel was new if prevdata == 0: nextindex = atomicAdd(drawCmd[0].instanceCount, 1) sparseList[nextindex + drawCmd[0].baseInstance] = packRG11B10(uvec3(voxelcoord)) def packARGB8(data, color): # light: 4 bits, count: 4 bits, color: 8 bits per channel r = uint(color.r 31.0 data.count) & 0xFF g = uint(color.g 31.0 data.count) & 0xFF b = uint(color.b 31.0 data.count) & 0xFF return (data.light & 0x0F) << 28 | (data.count & 0x0F) << 24 | r << 16 | g << 8 | b def packRG11B10(coord): return (coord.r & 0x7FF) << 21 | (coord.g & 0x7FF) << 10 | (coord.b & 0x3FF) A variant that calculates direct light per fragment and stores it directly into a sparse 3D texture, approximating only indirect diffuse lighting, using hardware conservative rasterization and geometry shader projection to resolve overlaps and gaps, rather than using compute-shader-based atomic operations to resolve race conditions and compute moving averages. Time Complexity: O(N \times I), where N is the number of fragments and I is the average number of iterations in the atomic average loop. Contention increases I. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the 3D texture, where V is the voxel grid volume. Sparse list adds O(O) where O is the number of occupied voxels. Performance: The atomic average loop can be expensive under high contention (many fragments hitting the same voxel). However, it produces flicker-free results compared to simple overwriting. Strengths: Resolves flickering from multiple primitives overwriting the same voxel. Works with standard fragment shaders. Limitations: No atomic operations for floats in OpenGL, limiting HDR voxel storage to integer formats (RGBA8) or requiring software emulation. High contention can lead to shader execution stalls. When to use: When flicker-free voxelization is required and the scene has significant overlap or transparency. When not to use: When HDR voxel storage is critical and atomic float operations are not available, or when performance is paramount and flicker is acceptable. Originating from voxel cone tracing techniques, this method was developed to address the flickering artifacts inherent in simple rasterization-based voxelization where multiple triangles map to the same voxel. It leverages OpenGL's image atomic operations (imageAtomicCompSwap) to implement a moving average, a technique adapted from GPU computing to the fragment shader stage. latencyhiding/voxelconetracing, https://github.com/latencyhiding/voxelconetracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) AnotherHermit/VoxelConeTracingMobile, https://github.com/AnotherHermit/VoxelConeTracingMobile, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) league1991/Voxel-Cone-Tracing, https://github.com/league1991/Voxel-Cone-Tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Voxel Cone Tracing - GitHub, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/righier/gidemo/master/report.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GPU Voxelization with Lighting Accumulation
head: Light Injection & Opacity Voxelization, Voxelization and storing direct lighting
body: GPU Voxelization with Lighting Accumulation is a rasterization-based technique that converts scene triangle meshes into a 3D voxel grid to store direct lighting information and opacity for subsequent indirect lighting calculations, such as cone tracing. It differs from standard geometry voxelization by leveraging cube map depth maps for occlusion-aware radiance injection relative to each point light. Unlike GPU Voxelization with Atomic Accumulation, which uses hardware atomics to resolve race conditions and compute moving averages, this method relies on conservative rasterization and specific projection strategies to ensure complete coverage and correct lighting accumulation without explicit atomic operations for every sample. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene triangle meshes, light sources (spotlights, point lights, emissive materials), and a target 3D voxel grid. Outputs: A sparse 3D texture where each voxel stores direct lighting radiance and opacity. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: Implemented as a sparse 3D texture using the GLARBsparsetexture extension. Layout: RGBA format. Channels 0-2 (RGB): Encode the light radiance coming from the voxel. Channel 3 (A): Encodes voxel opacity (1.0 for opaque, 0.0 for empty). Memory Management: Chunks of the texture can be enabled or disabled. Enabled chunks consume memory; disabled chunks do not. Only areas containing voxels are enabled to optimize memory usage. Light Data: For point lights, a cube depth map is used to determine occlusion. Parameters: Voxel Type: Isotropic: Standard voxels sharing data for all faces. Anisotropic: Voxels with different data for each face. Increases memory usage sixfold compared to isotropic voxels but allows accurate illumination where light hits only one side of thin objects. Viewport Resolution: Must exactly match the voxel grid scale so that fragment size matches voxel size. Steps: 1. Vertex Transformation: Use a vertex shader to transform vertex positions into the voxel grid coordinate system. Apply an orthographic projection matrix that captures the entire scene in visible clip-space. 2. Depth Testing Disable: Disable all depth testing before rasterization. This ensures that all primitives, even occluded ones, are processed in the fragment shader. 3. Geometry Shader Projection: Use a geometry shader to project every primitive onto a 2D surface. Determine the axis with the largest face area (greatest "axis shadow") when looking through the camera perspective along one of the axes. Swizzle the X, Y, and Z components and substitute the depth to zero to project the primitive triangle on the 2D surface. This projection maximizes the area and prevents cracks between voxels. 4. Rasterization: Rasterize the transformed primitives. Ensure the viewport resolution exactly matches the voxel grid scale. Enable hardware conservative rasterization via the GLCONSERVATIVERASTERIZATIONNV extension. This expands the outer edges of triangle primitives so a fragment is considered covered if any part of it is touched by a primitive, fixing gaps where rendered geometry does not fill voxel fragments fully. 5. Fragment Shader Processing: For every surface, set all intersecting voxels to fully opaque. Calculate direct light information using the Lambertian model. For spotlights, calculate diffuse light using the Lambertian model, light falloff, and shadow maps. For point lights, use the cube depth map to inject lighting data with occlusion awareness. Add light emitted by emissive materials into the 3D texture. Store the computed RGBA value into the 3D texture using OpenGL's imageStore() command. Discard fragments (do not write to a conventional 2D render target). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(position, modelmatrix, voxelgridmatrix): # Transform vertex positions into the voxel grid coordinate system # using an orthographic projection matrix that captures the entire scene transformedposition = voxelgridmatrix modelmatrix position return transformedposition def geometryshader(trianglevertices): # Calculate face areas for each axis projection # Axis X, Y, Z projections areax = calculatefaceareaprojection(trianglevertices, axis='x') areay = calculatefaceareaprojection(trianglevertices, axis='y') areaz = calculatefaceareaprojection(trianglevertices, axis='z') # Select axis with largest face area (greatest 'axis shadow') if areax >= areay and areax >= areaz: axis = 'x' elif areay >= areax and areay >= areaz: axis = 'y' else: axis = 'z' # Swizzle components and substitute depth to zero # Project primitive on 2D surface projectedvertices = [] for v in trianglevertices: if axis == 'x': projectedvertices.append(vec4(v.y, v.z, 0.0, 1.0)) elif axis == 'y': projectedvertices.append(vec4(v.x, v.z, 0.0, 1.0)) else: projectedvertices.append(vec4(v.x, v.y, 0.0, 1.0)) return projectedvertices def fragmentshader(fragmentcoords, voxelgridtexture, lightsources): # fragmentcoords match voxel grid coordinates due to viewport resolution match # Initialize output lightradiance = vec3(0.0) opacity = 0.0 # Set voxel to fully opaque opacity = 1.0 # Calculate direct lighting for light in lightsources: if light.type == 'spotlight': # Calculate diffuse light using Lambertian model # Include light falloff and shadow map lookup diffuse = calculatelambertiandiffuse(light, fragmentcoords) falloff = calculatelightfalloff(light, fragmentcoords) shadow = checkshadowmap(light, fragmentcoords) lightradiance += diffuse falloff shadow elif light.type == 'point': # Use cube depth map for occlusion-aware radiance injection radiance = injectpointlightradiance(light, fragmentcoords) lightradiance += radiance elif light.type == 'emissive': # Add light emitted by emissive materials lightradiance += light.emissioncolor # Store RGBA value into 3D texture # RGB: light radiance, A: opacity outputcolor = vec4(lightradiance, opacity) # Discard fragment (do not write to screen) discardfragment() return outputcolor def calculatefaceareaprojection(vertices, axis): # Helper to calculate projected area of triangle on plane perpendicular to axis # Returns scalar area value pass def calculatelambertiandiffuse(light, coords): # Standard Lambertian reflection: max(0, dot(N, L)) lightintensity pass def calculatelightfalloff(light, coords): # Inverse square or linear falloff based on distance pass def checkshadowmap(light, coords): # Sample shadow map to determine if voxel is in shadow pass def injectpointlightradiance(light, coords): # Sample cube depth map to determine visibility # Return radiance if visible pass Point Light Voxel Injection accumulates point light radiance into a 3D voxel grid by rendering scene geometry to a depth buffer, then dispatching a compute shader that reads voxel albedo/normal/radiance textures and the light's cube depth map to inject lighting data. It differs from standard geometry voxelization by leveraging cube map depth maps for occlusion-aware radiance injection relative to each point light. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of enabled chunks in the sparse 3D texture. Memory is only consumed for areas with voxels. Anisotropic voxels increase memory usage sixfold compared to isotropic voxels. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient memory usage via sparse textures. Accurate illumination for thin objects using anisotropic voxels. Prevents cracks and gaps through conservative rasterization and smart projection. Limitations: Approximates only indirect diffuse lighting, not specular. Sparse textures are not optimized for very small chunks allocated, so enabling only areas with voxels might be slow. Requires specific OpenGL extensions (GLARBsparsetexture, GLCONSERVATIVERASTERIZATIONNV). When to use: When direct lighting needs to be precomputed and stored for later indirect lighting calculations (e.g., cone tracing), and memory efficiency is important. When not to use: When specular lighting or directional light directionality within the voxel is required. The technique was developed as part of research into real-time voxel cone tracing. It builds on the concept of voxelizing scene geometry to store lighting information, as described in works evaluating voxel cone tracing for real-time applications. The specific implementation details, including the use of sparse textures and conservative rasterization, are derived from NVIDIA Developer articles and practical implementations in projects like GIDemo. Voxel Cone Tracing Evaluation for Real-Time Applications, https://kth.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1886204/FULLTEXT01.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Voxel Cone Tracing - GitHub, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/righier/gidemo/master/report.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Point Light Voxel Injection
head: Point Light Capture, Point Light Injection
body: Point Light Voxel Injection accumulates point light radiance into a 3D voxel grid by rendering scene geometry to a depth buffer, then dispatching a compute shader that reads voxel albedo/normal/radiance textures and the light's cube depth map to inject lighting data. It differs from standard geometry voxelization by leveraging cube map depth maps for occlusion-aware radiance injection relative to each point light. Inputs: Scene geometry (vertices, indices, normals, UVs). Voxel grid data: Albedo texture, Normal texture, and Radiance texture (read-write). Point light parameters: Position, color, and attenuation cutoff (0.05f). Voxel grid resolution (m\PointLightInjectionRes) and compute shader group size (m\LightInjectionGroupSize). Outputs: Updated Voxel Radiance texture (3D texture, format GLR32UI). Uniform Buffer Layout (Point Light Capture): The uniform buffer stores transformation matrices and light parameters. Offset 0: glm::mat4 array of size 6 (Light view matrices for the 6 faces of the cube map). Offset 6 \times 16 bytes: glm::mat4 (Projection matrix). Offset 7 \times 16 bytes: glm::vec4 (Light position). Offset 7 \times 16 + 16 bytes: glm::vec2 (Capture range: near and far planes). Texture Bindings: Voxel Albedo: Read-only image texture. Voxel Normal: Read-only image texture. Voxel Radiance: Read-write image texture with format GLR32UI, bound at BINDINGPOINTSTARTVOXELIMG + VoxelChannel::TexVoxelRadiance. Cube Depth Map: Bound to texture unit 0, storing depth values from the geometry rasterization pass relative to the point light. Attenuation Cutoff (atten\cutoff): Threshold used to compute the point light cutoff radius. Value: 0.05f. Capture Range: Near and far planes for the light's cube map frustum. Value: (0.1f, rangefar), where rangefar is computed from the attenuation cutoff. 1. Iterate Active Lights: Loop over all active point lights in the scene. 2. Setup Depth FBO: For the current light, bind a depth FBO and its associated cube depth map. 3. Compute Cutoff: Calculate the light's cutoff radius using the attenuation threshold (0.05f). 4. Setup Frustum: Set the capture range to (0.1f, cutoff). 5. Generate Matrices: Generate 6 cube map view matrices and a projection matrix. 6. Upload Uniforms: Upload the 6 view matrices, projection matrix, light position, and capture range to the uniform buffer. 7. Clear Depth: Clear the depth buffer of the FBO. 8. Render Geometry: Render scene geometry for the point light injection pass. 9. Bind Textures: Bind voxel albedo and normal textures as read-only image textures. Bind the voxel radiance texture as a read-write image texture with format GLR32UI. Bind the cube depth map to texture unit 0. 10. Set Compute Uniforms: Set light position, color, and current light pass index uniforms. 11. Dispatch Compute Shader: Dispatch the compute shader with grid dimensions \lceil m\PointLightInjectionRes / m\LightInjectionGroupSize \rceil. 12. Barrier: Issue a GLSHADERIMAGEACCESSBARRIERBIT. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointlightvoxelinjection(scenegeometry, voxelalbedo, voxelnormal, voxelradiance, pointlights, gridresolution, groupsize, attencutoff=0.05): for light in pointlights: # Compute cutoff radius from attencutoff (formula not provided in sources) # Set capture range to (0.1, cutoff) capturerange = (0.1, 0.0) # # Generate 6 cube map view matrices and 1 projection matrix (implementation not provided in sources) viewmatrices = [None] 6 projectionmatrix = None # Setup Depth FBO and Render Geometry depthfbo = createdepthfbo() # bindfbo(depthfbo) # cleardepthbuffer() # for mesh in scenegeometry: setviewprojection(viewmatrices, projectionmatrix, light.position) # rendermesh(mesh) # unbindfbo() # # Bind Textures for Compute Shader bindimagetexture(voxelalbedo, access=READONLY) # bindimagetexture(voxelnormal, access=READONLY) # bindimagetexture(voxelradiance, binding=BINDINGPOINTSTARTVOXELIMG + TEXVOXELRADIANCE, access=READWRITE, format=GLR32UI) # bindtexture(depthfbo.cubemap, textureunit=0) # # Set Compute Shader Uniforms setuniform("uViewMatrices", viewmatrices) # setuniform("uProjectionMatrix", projectionmatrix) # setuniform("uLightPosition", light.position) # setuniform("uCaptureRange", capturerange) # setuniform("uLightColor", light.color) # setuniform("uLightPassIndex", currentlightindex) # # Dispatch Compute Shader dispatchcount = math.ceil(gridresolution / groupsize) dispatchcomputeshader(dispatchcount, dispatchcount, dispatchcount) # # Memory Barrier glshaderimageaccessbarrier() # Boundaries: The capture range is fixed at (0.1f, cutoff). Geometry closer than 0.1f to the light may be clipped or cause depth precision issues. Degenerate Input: If a point light has zero intensity or invalid position, the cutoff radius calculation may fail or produce undefined behavior. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently captures indirect diffuse lighting from point lights using GPU parallelism. Limitations: Approximates only indirect diffuse lighting, not specular GPU Voxelization with Lighting Accumulation. Limited by the precision of GLR32UI. Use when real-time indirect diffuse lighting from point lights is required and cone tracing is the chosen rendering technique. Not suitable for specular lighting or global illumination involving complex bounces beyond the first indirect diffuse pass GPU Voxelization with Lighting Accumulation. The method is implemented in the "HarshLight" project by MangoSister. The technique is described in the source code of the HarshLight repository as an implementation detail of a custom renderer rather than a widely published academic algorithm. Used in the HarshLight renderer for voxelizing scene lighting for cone tracing. MangoSister/HarshLight, https://github.com/MangoSister/HarshLight, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: GPU Mesh Voxelization via Axis-Aligned Projection
head: Dominant Axis Projection, Dominant Axis Projection Voxelization, Dominant Axis Voxelization, GPU Voxelization via Rasterization and Geometry Shader Axis Projection, Voxelization (Cozzi and Riccio), Voxelization with Dominant Axis Projection
body: GPU Mesh Voxelization via Axis-Aligned Projection converts triangle meshes into a 3D voxel grid (typically a 3D texture or structured buffer) by projecting each triangle onto a 2D plane aligned with its dominant normal axis, rasterizing it, and mapping the resulting fragments to 3D voxel indices. It solves the problem of "holes" in voxelization caused by edge-on triangles by ensuring every triangle is rasterized from the perspective that maximizes its projected area. Unlike Single-Pass GPU Voxelization which may use multiple passes or different projection strategies, this method processes each triangle individually in a single pass using a Geometry Shader to determine the projection axis dynamically. It differs from GPU Voxelization Using OpenGL Image Atomics by relying on the hardware rasterizer's fragment generation rather than pure compute-based intersection tests. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh (vertices, normals, colors) and a target voxel grid resolution r (e.g., 128^3) and physical scale s (bounding box size). Output: A 3D texture (RGBA) or a structured buffer where occupied voxels store color/lighting data and occupancy flags. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D texture RWTexture3D<float4> (or similar) bound as an Unordered Access View (UAV). Format is typically RGBA, where RGB stores direct diffuse lighting (Phong model) and Alpha stores solidity (0 for empty, 1 for occupied). Constant Buffer: Contains World, View, and Projection matrices. For axis-alignment, three view matrices (ViewX, ViewY, ViewZ) or a single orthographic view along Z is used. Fragment Attributes: The fragment shader receives interpolated 3D world positions (positionWS) and 2D clip-space positions (SVPOSITION). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a 3D texture of size r \times r \times r initialized to zero. Set the viewport to r \times r. Disable depth testing and color writes to the default render target (use a dummy 2D texture if required by the API to trigger fragment execution). Bind the 3D texture as a UAV. 2. Geometry Shader - Dominant Axis Selection: For each input triangle with vertices v0, v1, v2: Calculate the face normal \vec{n} using the cross product of two edges: \vec{n} = (\vec{v}1 - \vec{v}0) \times (\vec{v}2 - \vec{v}0) Determine the dominant axis by finding the component of \vec{n} with the largest absolute magnitude. Let lx = |nx|, ly = |ny|, lz = |nz|. Identify the axis v{axis} that maximizes l{x,y,z}. Projection: Rotate the triangle vertices so that the dominant axis aligns with the camera's view direction (typically Z). This is done by permuting the vertex coordinates: If |nx| is max: Swap Y and Z components of vertices (v.xyz = v.zyx). If |ny| is max: Swap X and Z components (v.xyz = v.xzy). If |nz| is max: Keep as is (v.xyz = v.xyz). Emit the transformed vertices. The rasterizer will now project this triangle onto the XY plane. 3. Rasterization: The hardware rasterizer generates fragments for the projected 2D triangle. Barycentric interpolation provides each fragment with: Clip-space position (for depth/viewport mapping). Interpolated 3D world position \vec{p} (from the original, unrotated vertex positions passed as attributes). Note: Using centroid qualifier on world position is recommended to prevent MSAA interpolation artifacts. 4. Fragment Shader - Voxel Mapping and Storage: For each fragment, compute the 3D voxel index \vec{i} from the interpolated world position \vec{p}: \vec{i} = \left( \frac{\vec{p}}{s} + 1 \right) \cdot \frac{r}{2} Where s is the physical scale of the volume (bounding box half-extent or full extent depending on coordinate system normalization, typically mapping [-s, s] to [0, 1]) and r is the grid resolution. Clarification on Formula: The source describes dividing by s, adding 1 (mapping to [0, 2]), dividing by 2 (mapping to [0, 1]), and multiplying by r (mapping to [0, r]). This assumes \vec{p} is in range [-s, s]. Clamp \vec{i} to [0, r-1] to handle boundary cases. Collision Handling: Multiple fragments may map to the same voxel. To prevent flickering, use an atomic operation. A common approach is to store the color in a buffer and use an atomic add or InterlockedCompareExchange to maintain a running average or keep the brightest color (using luminance in upper bits). Alternatively, simple overwriting is used in basic implementations, accepting artifacts. Write the voxel data (color, normal, or occupancy) to the 3D texture at index \vec{i} using imageStore or UAV write. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct VSOUTPUT { float4 posCS: SVPOSITION; float3 posWS: TEXCOORD0; // Original world position float3 normalWS: TEXCOORD1; // Original normal for lighting }; VSOUTPUT VertexShader(uint vertexID: SVVertexID) { // Load vertex data float3 pos = VertexBuffer[vertexID].position; float3 norm = VertexBuffer[vertexID].normal; // Transform to clip space for rasterization float4 posCS = mul(ProjectionViewMatrix, float4(pos, 1.0)); VSOUTPUT output; output.posCS = posCS; output.posWS = pos; output.normalWS = norm; return output; } [maxvertexcount(3)] void GeometryShader(triangle VSOUTPUT input[3], inout TriangleStream<VSOUTPUT> stream) { // 1. Calculate Normal float3 v0 = input[0].posWS; float3 v1 = input[1].posWS; float3 v2 = input[2].posWS; float3 edge1 = v1 - v0; float3 edge2 = v2 - v0; float3 normal = normalize(cross(edge1, edge2)); // 2. Determine Dominant Axis float3 absNormal = abs(normal); float maxComp = max(absNormal.x, max(absNormal.y, absNormal.z)); // 3. Project Vertices based on Dominant Axis // We want the dominant axis to become the Z-axis (view direction) // so the triangle is projected onto the XY plane. VSOUTPUT output[3]; for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { output[i].posWS = input[i].posWS; // Keep original for fragment shader output[i].normalWS = input[i].normalWS; // Keep original for lighting float3 pos = input[i].posWS; if (absNormal.x >= maxComp) { // X is dominant // Swap Y and Z so X becomes Z (view dir) // New XYZ = Old ZYX output[i].posCS = mul(ProjectionViewMatrix, float4(pos.z, pos.y, pos.x, 1.0)); } else if (absNormal.y >= maxComp) { // Y is dominant // Swap X and Z so Y becomes Z // New XYZ = Old XZY output[i].posCS = mul(ProjectionViewMatrix, float4(pos.x, pos.z, pos.y, 1.0)); } else { // Z is dominant // Keep as is output[i].posCS = mul(ProjectionViewMatrix, float4(pos.x, pos.y, pos.z, 1.0)); } } stream.Append(output[0]); stream.Append(output[1]); stream.Append(output[2]); stream.RestartStrip(); } struct PSINPUT { float4 posCS: SVPOSITION; float3 posWS: TEXCOORD0; float3 normalWS: TEXCOORD1; }; void FragmentShader(PSINPUT input, out float4 outColor: SVTarget) { // 1. Compute Voxel Index // Assuming posWS is in range [-s, s] float s = 1.0; // Scale parameter float r = 128.0; // Resolution // Formula: i = (p / s + 1) r / 2 float3 voxelIndex = (input.posWS / s + 1.0) (r / 2.0); // 2. Lighting Calculation (Phong) // Use original normal, not the rotated one float3 N = normalize(input.normalWS); float3 L = normalize(lightPosition - input.posWS); float diffuse = max(dot(N, L), 0.0); float3 color = diffuse lightColor; // 3. Write to 3D Texture (Atomic/Overwrite) // In HLSL: imageStore(voxelTexture, int3(voxelIndex), float4(color, 1.0)); // In GLSL: imageStore(voxelTexture, ivec3(voxelIndex), vec4(color, 1.0)); // For simplicity, we output to a dummy target if the API requires it, // but the real work is done via UAV write in the shader. outColor = float4(0, 0, 0, 0); } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes from Edge-On Triangles: Standard rasterization misses thin triangles. Solved by dominant axis projection. Overlapping Triangles: Triangles projecting to the same 2D pixel overwrite each other. Use atomic operations or post-processing to resolve. Lighting Errors: Do not use the rotated normal for lighting calculations; use the original vertex normal. MSAA Artifacts: MSAA can corrupt interpolated world positions. Use the centroid qualifier for position attributes. Conservative Rasterization: For "thin" (6-separating) voxelization, standard rasterization may miss voxels. Use conservative rasterization extensions (e.g., NVconservativeraster) to expand the triangle slightly. Uses conservative rasterization to ensure all intersecting voxels are marked, differing from standard projection by explicitly calculating geometric bounds. Renders the mesh slice-by-slice along an axis, differing from dominant axis projection by using explicit clipping planes rather than per-triangle axis selection. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of triangles, as each triangle is processed once in the geometry shader. Memory Complexity: O(R^3) for the 3D texture, where R is the resolution. Performance: Real-time performance is achievable for scenes with up to 2 million triangles at 256^3 resolution on modern GPUs. On an NVIDIA GTX 770, 512^3 voxelization took ~11.7 ms. Strengths: Single-pass, efficient use of hardware rasterizer, avoids complex rotation matrices. Limitations: Overlapping triangles cause artifacts; dense grid consumes significant memory; requires conservative rasterization for thin-voxel accuracy. Originating from techniques described by Cozzi and Riccio, this method leverages the OpenGL Geometry Shader and image load/store features (OpenGL 4.2+) to voxelize scenes in a single pass. It builds on the concept of projecting triangles to maximize rasterized area. Related historical works include "An Accurate Method for Voxelizing Polygon Meshes" by Huang et al. (1998) and "Fast Parallel Surface and Solid Voxelization on GPUs" by Michael et al. (2010). It is commonly used as a preprocessing step for Voxel Cone Tracing, Global Illumination, and Volumetric Effects. name: GPU-based Conservative Voxelization
head: voxelize::operator()
body: GPU-based Conservative Voxelization is a two-pass GPU algorithm that converts 3D triangle meshes into a list of voxels using conservative rasterization, followed by an octree construction step. It uses atomic counters to determine the voxel count for buffer allocation. It differs from standard rasterization by ensuring any voxel intersecting the triangle is marked as occupied, and differs from slicemap-based approaches by explicitly calculating geometric intersection bounds rather than relying on bitwise blending of discrete depth slices. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D triangle mesh, areaposition, areasize, and voxelsony. Output: A dynamic list of occupied voxel coordinates. Data Structures Scene Normalization Matrix: A 4 \times 4 matrix mapping the model's bounding box to the unit cube (0,0,0) to (1,1,1). Orthographic Projection Matrices: Three 4 \times 4 matrices for X, Y, and Z axes configured for conservative rasterization. Atomic Counter Buffer: A buffer bound to binding point 3 used to count occupied voxels. Voxel List Buffer: A storage buffer bound to binding points 1 and 2 storing the final voxel coordinates. Grid Dimensions: Uniform variables defining the voxel grid size, derived from areasize and voxelsony. Parameters ucanstore: A uniform integer flag set to 0 for Pass 1 (counting) and 1 for Pass 2 (storing). utransform: The scene normalization matrix. uxorthoprojection, uyorthoprojection, uzorthoprojection: The three orthogonal projection matrices. ugrid: The voxel grid dimensions. Viewport: Set to maxside x maxside, where maxside is the maximum dimension of the proportional grid. Steps 1. Disable depth testing, alpha testing, and face culling. 2. Compute the scene normalization matrix using createscenenormalizationmatrix(areaposition, areasize) and upload it to uniform utransform. 3. Compute three orthogonal projection matrices using createprojectionmatrices(proj) and upload them to uniforms uxorthoprojection, uyorthoprojection, uzorthoprojection. 4. Calculate proportional grid dimensions using calcproportionalgrid, determine maxside as the maximum dimension, set the viewport to maxside x maxside, and set grid dimensions via uniform ugrid. 5. Pass 1 (Count): Set uniform ucanstore to 0, reset the atomic counter to 0, bind it to binding point 3, bind the mesh geometry, and invoke the shader program. 6. Pass 2 (Store): Set uniform ucanstore to 1, reset the atomic counter to 0, bind it to binding point 3, bind the voxel list to binding points 1 and 2, and invoke the shader program. 7. Execute glMemoryBarrier(GLSHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT) to ensure storage buffer writes are visible. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpuconservativevoxelization(mesh, areaposition, areasize, voxelsony): # Helper definitions for standard operations def gldisable(target): state[target] = False def createscenenormalizationmatrix(pos, size): return glm.mat4(1.0) # Maps bbox to (0,0,0)-(1,1,1) def createprojectionmatrices(): return {'X': glm.mat4(1.0), 'Y': glm.mat4(1.0), 'Z': glm.mat4(1.0)} def calcproportionalgrid(size, voxelsony): return type('Grid', (), {'x': size.x, 'y': size.y, 'z': size.z})() def setviewport(w, h): viewport.width, viewport.height = w, h def setuniform(name, val): uniforms[name] = val def resetatomiccounter(bindingpoint): atomiccounters[bindingpoint] = 0 def bindatomiccounter(bindingpoint): activebuffers[bindingpoint] = atomiccounters def bindmesh(mesh): activevao = mesh.vao def drawtriangles(): rasterize(activevao, uniforms, activebuffers) def readatomiccounter(bindingpoint): return atomiccounters[bindingpoint] def bindvoxellistbuffer(bindingpoints): for bp in bindingpoints: activebuffers[bp] = voxellistbuffer def glmemorybarrier(flag): syncstorage(flag) # 1. Initialization gldisable(GLDEPTHTEST) gldisable(GLALPHATEST) gldisable(GLCULLFACE) normmatrix = createscenenormalizationmatrix(areaposition, areasize) projmatrices = createprojectionmatrices() griddims = calcproportionalgrid(areasize, voxelsony) maxside = max(griddims.x, griddims.y, griddims.z) setviewport(maxside, maxside) setuniform('ugrid', griddims) # 2. Pass 1 (Count) setuniform('ucanstore', 0) resetatomiccounter(bindingpoint=3) bindatomiccounter(bindingpoint=3) bindmesh(mesh) setuniform('utransform', normmatrix) setuniform('uxorthoprojection', projmatrices['X']) setuniform('uyorthoprojection', projmatrices['Y']) setuniform('uzorthoprojection', projmatrices['Z']) drawtriangles() voxelcount = readatomiccounter(bindingpoint=3) # 3. Pass 2 (Store) setuniform('ucanstore', 1) resetatomiccounter(bindingpoint=3) bindatomiccounter(bindingpoint=3) bindvoxellistbuffer(bindingpoints=[1, 2]) bindmesh(mesh) setuniform('utransform', normmatrix) setuniform('uxorthoprojection', projmatrices['X']) setuniform('uyorthoprojection', projmatrices['Y']) setuniform('uzorthoprojection', projmatrices['Z']) drawtriangles() # 4. Synchronization glmemorybarrier(GLSHADERSTORAGEBARRIERBIT) return voxellistbuffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Conservative rasterization behavior depends on GPU driver implementation. Buffer Allocation: The atomic counter must be read back to the CPU to allocate the voxel list buffer, introducing a synchronization stall. Duplicate Voxels: Conservative rasterization may generate multiple fragments for the same voxel if the triangle covers multiple pixels within the same grid cell. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Guarantees no missing voxels for intersected cells. Limitations: Requires two draw calls per mesh. The method is implemented in the open-source project loryruta/voxelizer. It leverages OpenGL's conservative rasterization extensions to perform voxelization directly on the GPU, avoiding the need for CPU-side ray casting or marching cubes. The technique is part of a pipeline that may include subsequent octree construction steps. loryruta/voxelizer, https://github.com/loryruta/voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Conservative Voxelization via Depth Range
head: Depth range voxelization
body: Conservative Voxelization via Depth Range is a GPU-based technique that converts 3D triangle meshes into a binary 3D grid of voxels by computing the depth range of a projected triangle over a fragment rectangle and encoding occupancy bits into a texture. It solves the problem of real-time voxelization by leveraging graphics hardware to test geometry for intersection with an encompassing grid of cells, allowing the tracking of all fragments in a single pass rather than discarding all but the closest. Unlike Slicemap Boundary Voxelization, which explicitly maps specific depth slices to specific bit positions, this method encodes depth ranges into occupancy bits, enabling efficient accumulation of all intersecting geometry via bitwise operations. Inputs: A 3D triangle mesh defined by vertices Pi = (xi, yi, zi) for i \in \{1, 2, 3\}. Outputs: A 3D voxel grid where a voxel is marked as occupied if it intersects the triangle. Data Structures: 1. Lookup Table Texture: A 2D texture storing bitmasks. Standard mode: Size 32 \times 32. Format RGBA8. Each texel stores 32 bits (one per voxel slice). Index (z^{min}, z^{max}) where z^ = z \times 32. MRT mode: Size 512 \times 128. Format RGBA8. Stores 128-bit bitmasks across four texels. 2. Frame Buffer: Render targets storing the voxel occupancy. Supports logical 'OR' operations to combine results from multiple triangles. Parameters: \epsilonm: Machine error constant for GPU precision. \epsilonI: Threshold for detecting parallel lines and degenerate edges. \epsilonS: Threshold for detecting degenerate triangles based on projected area. Floating point error constant: 10^{-5}, added to the computed depth range to address limited GPU precision. Steps: 1. Vertex Processing (Partial Derivatives): For each vertex Pi, compute the barycentric coordinate derivatives and depth derivatives. Compute signed area S of the projected triangle: S = x1 y2 - x2 y1 + x2 y3 - x3 y2 + x3 y1 - x1 y3 Compute barycentric derivatives: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial x} = \frac{(y2 - y3, y3 - y1, y1 - y2)}{S} \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial y} = \frac{(x3 - x2, x1 - x3, x2 - x1)}{S} Compute depth derivatives via dot product with vertex depths z = (z1, z2, z3): \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = z \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial x} \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = z \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial y} Compute \Delta \mathbf{C} and output C^ = C(Pi) - \Delta \mathbf{C} as a 3D vector. C^{min} is obtained via bilinear interpolation during rasterization. 2. Fragment Processing (Depth Range Calculation): For each fragment covered by the triangle, determine the depth range [z{min}, z{max}] of the triangle within the fragment rectangle R. Initialize enlarged width/height of R: xE, yE \leftarrow \epsilonm. For each edge Pi Pj of the triangle: Check for parallelism with horizontal/vertical edges of R. If |\frac{yj - yi}{xj - xi}| < \max(\epsilonI, \epsilonI |xj - xi|): Set a^y{ij} = 0, b^y{ij} = 2 to discard intersections with top/bottom edges eT, eB. Update yE \leftarrow \max(yE, \epsilonI). Else: Compute coefficients: a^y{ij} = \frac{1}{yj - yi}, b^y{ij} = \frac{-yi}{yj - yi}. Compute a^x{ij}, b^x{ij} similarly for vertical comparisons. Check for degenerate triangle: If |S| < \epsilonS: Set C^ \leftarrow (-1, -1, -1). Enlarge R: xE \leftarrow \max(xE, \sqrt{2}h), yE \leftarrow \max(yE, \sqrt{2}h), where h is the minimal triangle height. Compute intersection points Q between edge Pi Pj and edges of R. For edge eT (top), calculate t = a^y{ij} \cdot y{\max} + b^y{ij} and Q = \mathcal{L}(Pi, Pj, t). Validate Q: If Q lies on both the triangle edge and the fragment edge, set z(Q) = \mathcal{L}(zi, zj, t). Otherwise, assign z(Q) a huge value. Handle parallel case robustness: If Pi Pj is nearly horizontal, replace intersection with top edge QT with intersection with prolonged right edge QR to avoid numerical instability. Handle degenerate edges: If |xj - xi| < \epsilonI and |yj - yi| < \epsilonI, assume both vertices are inside R. Check if third vertex Pk is inside R using x{min} - \epsilonI \le xk \le x{max} + \epsilonI and y{min} - \epsilonI \le yk \le y{max} + \epsilonI. Compute z{min} and z{max} as the minimal and maximal depth values among the 12 intersection points (optimized using GPU 4D vector processing). Apply floating point error correction: z{max} \leftarrow z{max} + 10^{-5}. 3. Voxel Encoding: Map z{min}, z{max} to indices z^{min} = z{min} \times 32 and z^{max} = z{max} \times 32. Perform a texture lookup in the precomputed lookup table to retrieve the bitmask representing occupied voxels. Write the bitmask to the frame buffer using logical 'OR' to accumulate occupancy from multiple triangles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedepthrange(vertices, epsilonI, epsilonS, epsilonm, fragbounds): """ Computes the depth range [zmin, zmax] for a triangle within a fragment. vertices: list of 3 tuples (x, y, z) fragbounds: dict with keys 'xmin', 'xmax', 'ymin', 'ymax' """ x1, y1, z1 = vertices[0] x2, y2, z2 = vertices[1] x3, y3, z3 = vertices[2] # 1. Compute Signed Area S S = x1y2 - x2y1 + x2y3 - x3y2 + x3y1 - x1y3 # 2. Handle Degenerate Triangle if abs(S) < epsilonS: # Set C to (-1, -1, -1) and enlarge R by sqrt(2)h # h is minimal triangle height h = computeminimalheight(vertices) return None, None, True # 3. Compute Derivatives invS = 1.0 / S dCdx = ((y2 - y3) invS, (y3 - y1) invS, (y1 - y2) invS) dCdy = ((x3 - x2) invS, (x1 - x3) invS, (x2 - x1) invS) zvec = (z1, z2, z3) dzdx = zvec[0]dCdx[0] + zvec[1]dCdx[1] + zvec[2]dCdx[2] dzdy = zvec[0]dCdy[0] + zvec[1]dCdy[1] + zvec[2]dCdy[2] # 4. Initialize Enlargement xE = epsilonm yE = epsilonm # 5. Process Edges edges = [(vertices[0], vertices[1]), (vertices[1], vertices[2]), (vertices[2], vertices[0])] intersectiondepths = [] for Pi, Pj in edges: xi, yi, zi = Pi xj, yj, zj = Pj # Check for parallel/horizontal edge if abs(yj - yi) < max(epsilonI, epsilonI abs(xj - xi)): ayij = 0.0 byij = 2.0 yE = max(yE, epsilonI) else: ayij = 1.0 / (yj - yi) byij = -yi / (yj - yi) # Compute ax, bx similarly if abs(xj - xi) < max(epsilonI, epsilonI abs(yj - yi)): axij = 0.0 bxij = 2.0 xE = max(xE, epsilonI) else: axij = 1.0 / (xj - xi) bxij = -xi / (xj - xi) # Compute intersections with fragment edges (Top, Bottom, Left, Right) # Top edge (y = ymax) ttop = ayij fragbounds['ymax'] + byij Qtop = linearinterpolate(Pi, Pj, ttop) if isonsegment(Pi, Pj, Qtop) and isonfragmentedge(Qtop, 'top', fragbounds): ztop = linearinterpolatez(zi, zj, ttop) intersectiondepths.append(ztop) else: # Robustness: if nearly horizontal, use Right Edge intersection instead # The sources state QT is replaced by QR to maintain conservative correctness pass # Bottom, Left, Right edges computed similarly (omitted for brevity) # GPU optimization uses 4D vectors to compute 4 intersections simultaneously # 6. Determine Min/Max Depth if not intersectiondepths: # Fallback for degenerate or fully inside/outside cases intersectiondepths = [z1, z2, z3] zmin = min(intersectiondepths) zmax = max(intersectiondepths) # 7. Apply Floating Point Error Correction zmax += 1e-5 return zmin, zmax, False def computeminimalheight(vertices): # Standard geometric computation for minimal triangle height # h = 2 Area / baselength # Sources do not specify exact height calculation, using standard fallback return 1.0 def linearinterpolate(P1, P2, t): return (P1[0] + t(P2[0]-P1[0]), P1[1] + t(P2[1]-P1[1]), P1[2] + t(P2[2]-P1[2])) def isonsegment(P1, P2, Q): # Check if Q lies on segment P1P2 dotproduct = (Q[0]-P1[0])(Q[0]-P2[0]) + (Q[1]-P1[1])(Q[1]-P2[1]) + (Q[2]-P1[2])(Q[2]-P2[2]) return dotproduct <= 0 def isonfragmentedge(Q, edgetype, fragbounds): eps = 1e-6 if edgetype == 'top': return abs(Q[1] - fragbounds['ymax']) < eps and fragbounds['xmin'] - eps <= Q[0] <= fragbounds['xmax'] + eps elif edgetype == 'bottom': return abs(Q[1] - fragbounds['ymin']) < eps and fragbounds['xmin'] - eps <= Q[0] <= fragbounds['xmax'] + eps elif edgetype == 'left': return abs(Q[0] - fragbounds['xmin']) < eps and fragbounds['ymin'] - eps <= Q[1] <= fragbounds['ymax'] + eps elif edgetype == 'right': return abs(Q[0] - fragbounds['xmax']) < eps and fragbounds['ymin'] - eps <= Q[1] <= fragbounds['ymax'] + eps return False def linearinterpolatez(z1, z2, t): return z1 + t(z2-z1) Slicemap Boundary Voxelization is a technique to represent a binary 3D grid of voxels using a single 2D texture, where the k-th bit of the RGBA representation of pixel (i, j) encodes the occupancy of voxel (i, j, k). It solves the problem of real-time voxelization by leveraging graphics hardware to test geometry for intersection with an encompassing grid of cells, allowing the tracking of all fragments in a single pass rather than discarding all but the closest. Unlike Conservative Voxelization via Depth Range, which encodes depth ranges into occupancy bits, slicemaps explicitly map specific depth slices to specific bit positions, enabling efficient accumulation of all intersecting geometry via bitwise operations. Time and Memory Complexity: The method performs constant-time operations per fragment for derivative calculation and intersection checks, optimized by GPU 4D vector processing. Memory usage is dominated by the lookup table texture (32 \times 32 or 512 \times 128 texels) and the frame buffer. Measured Performance: The technique is implemented using standard graphics pipeline features (vertex processing, rasterization, fragment shaders) to compute depth ranges, avoiding explicit geometric intersection algorithms on the CPU. Strengths and Limitations: The method achieves real-time performance via GPU rasterization and conservative correctness ensures no voxels are missed. Efficient bitwise encoding allows processing 128 slices in a single pass with MRT. Limitations include sensitivity to GPU floating-point precision, requiring error correction constants, and the fact that alternative pre-computation approaches using lookup tables for intersection codes are faster in theory but expensive in hardware due to switch-case structures. When to Use: Use when real-time voxelization of triangle meshes is required and conservative accuracy is critical. Not suitable when hardware does not support MRT or logical 'OR' blending. The technique is implemented using standard graphics pipeline features (vertex processing, rasterization, fragment shaders) to compute depth ranges, avoiding explicit geometric intersection algorithms on the CPU. It builds on the need for efficient, hardware-accelerated voxelization techniques that maintain geometric accuracy.
