name: Slicemap Boundary Voxelization
head: GPU Boundary Voxelization, GPU friendly voxel representation, Slicemap
body: Slicemap Boundary Voxelization is a technique to represent a binary 3D grid of voxels using a single 2D texture, where the k-th bit of the RGBA representation of pixel (i, j) encodes the occupancy of voxel (i, j, k). It solves the problem of real-time voxelization by leveraging graphics hardware to test geometry for intersection with an encompassing grid of cells, allowing the tracking of all fragments in a single pass rather than discarding all but the closest. Unlike Conservative Voxelization via Depth Range, which encodes depth ranges into occupancy bits, slicemaps explicitly map specific depth slices to specific bit positions, enabling efficient accumulation of all intersecting geometry via bitwise operations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scene (meshes) and a camera frustum defining the voxel grid's spatial extent (x, y) and depth range (z). Output: A 2D texture (the slicemap) where each texel stores a 32-bit integer representing a column of 32 voxels. Data Structures: Slicemap Texture: A 2D texture with width W and height H. Texel Layout: Each texel at pixel coordinates (i, j) stores a 32-bit value derived from the RGBA channels. The bits are interpreted as a concatenated boolean vector: Bit 0 corresponds to voxel depth k=0, Bit 1 to k=1,..., Bit 31 to k=31. The x and y dimensions of the texture define the spatial extent of the voxel grid. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the slicemap texture with zeros. 2. Set Blending: Configure the graphics pipeline to use a bitwise OR blending operation for the color attachment(s). 3. Render Loop: For each fragment generated by rasterizing the scene geometry: a. Determine the fragment's depth d in the voxelization coordinate system. b. Map d to a slice index k (where k is an integer representing the depth layer). c. Calculate the output color value C such that only the k-th bit is set. If using a single 32-bit channel or combining RGBA, C = 2^k (assuming bit 0 is LSB) or equivalent bit manipulation. d. Output C to the framebuffer. 4. Combine: The hardware blending unit performs a bitwise OR between the new fragment value and the existing texel value, effectively setting the k-th bit to 1 if any fragment intersects that voxel column. Formulas: Output color: C = 2^k, where k is the quantized slice index and bit 0 is the least significant bit. Accumulation: T{new}(i, j) = T{old}(i, j) \lor C, where \lor denotes bitwise OR. Parameters: Blending Mode: Bitwise OR. This is critical to combine all fragments projecting to the same pixel without overwriting previous bits. Slices per Pass: Currently limited by hardware to 4 Multiple Render Targets (MRTs) \times 4 channels \times 32 bits = 128 slices per pass. Future hardware with 32-bit logical operations would allow 512 slices per pass. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Watertightness: The method requires the object to be watertight to obtain a filled voxel representation without iterative flood fill operations, which is necessary for applications like refraction. Depth Quantization: Depth is quantized to discrete slices, unlike multi-pass methods (e.g., depth peeling) which have full precision. Hardware Limits: The number of slices is limited by the number of MRTs and channels. Current hardware limits this to 128 slices per pass. Resolution Limits: Unlike methods that fuse several views (which reduces cracks but limits resolution), slicemaps do not fuse views, avoiding resolution limits imposed by view fusion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateslicemap(fragments, width, height): # 1. Initialize slicemap texture with zeros slicemap = [[0] width for in range(height)] # 2. Process each fragment from rasterization for frag in fragments: # 3a. Determine fragment depth in voxel space depthinvoxelspace = mapdepthtovoxellayer(frag.depth) # 3b. Map depth to integer slice index k k = int(depthinvoxelspace) # 3c. Guard against out-of-bounds slices if k < 0 or k >= 32: continue # 3d. Calculate output color with only k-th bit set bitmask = 1 << k # 4. Combine via bitwise OR accumulation slicemap[frag.y][frag.x] |= bitmask return slicemap Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of polygons, as it runs in a single pass. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H \times S) where W, H are texture dimensions and S is the number of slices (bits per texel). For a single texture, S=32 bits per texel. Performance: Voxelization of millions of polygons can be performed in real-time (order of milliseconds). Strengths: Single-pass generation, no need to predefine the number of peeling steps, GPU-friendly, supports deformed grids (local refinement). Limitations: Depth is quantized, requires watertight geometry for filled volumes, limited by hardware MRT/channel count. When to Use: Transmittance shadow maps, shadow volume culling/clamping, refraction/scattering effects. When Not to Use: When full depth precision per slice is required, or when geometry is not watertight and flood fill is undesirable. Slicemaps were introduced by as a GPU-friendly voxel representation of a scene. The technique builds upon earlier work in GPU boundary voxelization. It was developed to enable real-time voxelization of complex and dynamic scenes containing more than 1M polygons, with creation and storage performed on the graphics card to avoid unnecessary data transfer. The term "slicemap" was coined by [10] (cited in) to refer to the texture where bits form slices of the 3D grid. name: GPU-based Voxelization via Slice Rendering
head: Hardware Rasterization Voxelization
body: GPU-based Voxelization via Slice Rendering is a technique that computes the voxelization of a triangle mesh by leveraging hardware rasterization to fill a 3D grid. It solves the problem of converting surface representations into volumetric data by rendering the mesh slice-by-slice along a chosen axis, adjusting near and far clipping planes for each slice to correctly compute boundary voxels. Unlike CPU-based voxelization, all computation is handled on the GPU, and the result is stored directly in a 3D volume texture or structured buffer, allowing immediate use in hardware applications. It differs from GPU Mesh Voxelization via Axis-Aligned Projection by using explicit depth slicing and clipping planes rather than projecting triangles onto dominant axes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh (vertices, normals, indices) and a target resolution (grid dimensions). Output: A 3D voxel grid. The grid can be stored as a 3D volume texture or a bit-packed std::vector<uint32t>. Data Structures: 1. 3D Volume Texture: Stores volumetric data where each texel corresponds to a voxel. The origin is at the top-left corner. The center location of a voxel in camera coordinates is computed by transforming its texture coordinate. Example: If voxel physical size is 0.5 \times 0.5 \times 0.5, voxel indices (1,1,0) and (4,3,2) correspond to center positions (0.75, 0.75, 0.25) and (2.25, 1.75, 1.25). 2. Bit-Packed Grid (Alternative): A std::vector<uint32t> where each uint32t contains the state of 32 voxals (1 bit per voxel). Layout: Grid dimensions must be multiples of 32. Order: (X0,Y0,Z00-31) | (X1,Y0,Z00-31) |... | (Xmax,Y0,Z00-31) for the first Z-block, then (X0,Y1,Z00-31) |... for the next Y, up to (X0,Ymax,Z00-31). This pattern repeats for subsequent Z-blocks (Z32-63, etc.). Parameters: resolution: The target resolution for the voxel grid. precision: Default precision/resolution used in the Scene class, typically set to 32. voxelphysicalsize: Physical dimensions of each voxel (e.g., 0.5 \times 0.5 \times 0.5). Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Grid Dimensions: Determine the optimal 3D grid dimensions based on the mesh bounds and target resolution. 2. Transform Vertices: Transform vertex positions into camera coordinates and compute the depth value Z(v) for each vertex. 3. Iterate Slices: Fill the 3D grid by iterating through slices along a chosen axis. 4. Determine Slice Range: For each triangle, calculate the range of slices in the 3D volume texture that possibly intersect the triangle using the depth of all three vertices. 5. Duplicate Triangles: In the geometry shader, duplicate the triangle once for each slice in the possible range. 6. Set Clipping Planes: For each duplicated triangle instance destined for a specific slice index, set up the far and near clipping planes according to that slice index to correctly compute boundary voxels. 7. Rasterize: Render the clipped triangles. The hardware rasterizer fills the voxels corresponding to the projected area. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelizeslicerendering(mesh, resolution, axis='Z'): """ Voxelize a mesh using slice rendering. mesh: list of triangles, each triangle is [v0, v1, v2] where v is (x,y,z) resolution: (dimx, dimy, dimz) axis: The axis along which to slice ('X', 'Y', or 'Z') """ # 1. Compute grid dimensions # Ensure dimensions are multiples of 32 if using bit-packing griddims = alignto32(resolution) # Initialize output structure # Option A: 3D Texture (conceptual) # Option B: Bit-packed vector grid = [0] (griddims[0] griddims[1] griddims[2] // 32) # 2. Transform vertices to camera coordinates # Assume a standard camera looking down the slicing axis # For simplicity, assume identity view/projection for this abstract step # In practice, use viewProjMatrix cameravertices = [] for tri in mesh: camtri = [] for v in tri: # Transform v to camera space vcam = transformtocamera(v) camtri.append(vcam) cameravertices.append(camtri) # 3. Iterate through slices along the chosen axis for sliceidx in range(griddims[axisindex(axis)]): # Determine slice bounds in camera space # The slice corresponds to a specific depth range znear, zfar = getslicedepthbounds(sliceidx, griddims, axis) # 4. & 5. Process triangles for camtri in cameravertices: # Calculate depth of all three vertices depths = [v[axisindex(axis)] for v in camtri] mindepth = min(depths) maxdepth = max(depths) # Check if triangle intersects this slice if maxdepth >= znear and mindepth <= zfar: # 6. Set clipping planes # Clip the triangle to the slice volume clippedtri = cliptriangletoslice(camtri, znear, zfar) if clippedtri is not None: # 7. Rasterize # The hardware rasterizer handles the rest # We conceptually mark the voxels rasterizetriangletogrid(clippedtri, sliceidx, grid, griddims) return grid def alignto32(dim): return (dim + 31) // 32 32 def axisindex(axis): if axis == 'X': return 0 if axis == 'Y': return 1 if axis == 'Z': return 2 def getslicedepthbounds(sliceidx, griddims, axis): # Assuming uniform voxel size of 1.0 for simplicity in this abstract # In reality, scale by voxelphysicalsize voxelsize = 1.0 zmin = sliceidx voxelsize zmax = (sliceidx + 1) voxelsize return zmin, zmax def cliptriangletoslice(tri, znear, zfar): # Clip triangle against znear and zfar planes # Returns clipped polygon (list of vertices) or None # Implementation details depend on specific clipping algorithm # Standard Sutherland-Hodgman or similar 3D clipping pass def rasterizetriangletogrid(tri, sliceidx, grid, griddims): # Project tri to 2D plane perpendicular to axis # Mark voxels in grid # This step is handled by hardware rasterization in the actual GPU method # Here we simulate the result pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grid dimensions must be multiples of 32 to align with the bit-packing scheme if using uint32t storage. Precision issues may arise when computing boundary voxels if clipping planes are not set correctly. Converts high-poly convex/concave meshes into a 1024x1024x256 voxel format by slicing the scene into 256 depth slices and using the stencil buffer to generate silhouettes. It renders slices on the GPU, downloads and processes stencil buffer contents on the CPU, and uploads processed data back to the GPU. GPU memory footprint is ~4MB at any point. Pitfalls include floodfilled voxels near mesh edges requiring the same normal as the voxels forming the edges, and the renderer being based on Bresenham, requiring extra work for 'inner' mesh voxels. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of triangles and slices. Each triangle is processed for each slice it intersects. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the grid size (3D texture or bit-packed array). Stencil buffer variant uses ~4MB. Performance: Depends on GPU hardware rasterization speed. Slicing approach allows efficient use of GPU parallelism. Strengths: All computation on GPU; result stored in 3D texture for direct hardware use; handles complex meshes via rasterization. Limitations: Requires multiple passes (one per slice); potential for overdraw; stencil buffer variant requires CPU-GPU data transfer. When to use: When real-time voxelization is needed and GPU resources are available; when the result needs to be used directly in hardware rendering pipelines. When not to use: When CPU-only processing is required; when memory bandwidth is a severe bottleneck due to large grid sizes. Originated from the need for efficient GPU-based voxelization for real-time applications. The technique leverages the graphics pipeline's ability to clip and rasterize geometry, adapting it for volumetric representation. It was developed as an alternative to CPU-based voxelization, offering significant performance gains by utilizing hardware rasterization. The stencil buffer variant was explored for specific use cases like raytracing. piellardj/voxelizer-gpu, https://github.com/piellardj/voxelizer-gpu, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Real-time GPU-Based Voxelization and Applications, https://minds.wisc.edu/items/e8fdcf0a-3edc-4603-82ef-f91f70900877, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Forum archive / Ken Silverman / Real-time voxel raytracing, in development.., https://www.jonof.id.au/forum/topic-1433.html, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Single-Pass GPU Voxelization
head: LEGOr Voxelization, Voxelization: Vertex Shader
body: Single-Pass GPU Voxelization maps 3D mesh vertices directly to a 3D grid (voxel space) in a single rasterization pass using a Frame Buffer Object (FBO), avoiding the multiple passes required by methods like Karabassi et al.. It encodes voxel indices into the FBO alpha channel during the vertex shader stage, rather than rasterizing triangles into a 3D texture via a geometry shader. Inputs: vp: 3D vertex position (v{px}, v{py}, v{pz}). vc: 3D vertex color (v{cx}, v{cy}, v{cz}). size: Integer grid resolution (side length of the cubic voxel grid). Outputs: A 2D Frame Buffer Object (FBO) where each pixel corresponds to a projected vertex. The FBO channels store: Red (R) = v{cx}, Green (G) = v{cy}, Blue (B) = v{cz}, Alpha (A) = normalized voxel index. A Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) generated from the downloaded FBO data, used for subsequent polygonization. Data Structures: FBO Layout: A 2D texture or render target with RGBA format. The spatial resolution of the FBO must be sufficient to avoid overlapping projections of distinct vertices. Voxel Index: A linear integer index w representing the position in the 3D grid, calculated as w = ix \cdot size^2 + iy \cdot size + iz, where ix, iy, iz are the integer voxel coordinates. Steps: 1. Vertex Shader Execution: For each vertex of the input mesh: a. Compute the linear voxel index w from the vertex position vp and grid size: w = \lfloor v{px} \rfloor \cdot size^2 + \lfloor v{py} \rfloor \cdot size + \lfloor v{pz} \rfloor Note: The source uses int() which truncates toward zero; for positive voxel-space coordinates this is equivalent to floor. b. Check bounds: If w is outside the valid grid range [0, size^3 - 1], set the output alpha to NULL (or 0) and discard the vertex for further processing. c. Normalize the voxel index for storage in the alpha channel: \alpha = \frac{w}{size^3} d. Output the vertex color (v{cx}, v{cy}, v{cz}) to the RGB channels and \alpha to the Alpha channel. 2. Rasterization: The vertices are rasterized into the FBO. Standard depth testing (Z-buffer) is applied. Vertices closer to the camera overwrite those further away. Vertices projecting to the same pixel position are resolved by the Z-buffer, which keeps the closest vertex and discards others. 3. FBO Download and VBO Creation: a. Read the FBO data back to the CPU. b. Interpret each pixel in the FBO as a vertex. c. Construct a VBO where each vertex contains the RGB color and the Alpha value (which encodes the voxel index). 4. Polygonization (LEGOr Brick Generation): a. Use a Geometry Shader to process the VBO. b. Convert the normalized alpha value \alpha back to spatial coordinates (ix, iy, iz) to find the center of the cube. c. Generate the geometry (triangles) for the LEGOr brick (voxel) at that location. d. Discard vertices with illegal/null values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(vp: tuple, vc: tuple, size: int) -> tuple: # 1. Compute linear voxel index w ix = int(vp[0]) iy = int(vp[1]) iz = int(vp[2]) w = ix size size + iy size + iz # 2. Check bounds maxvoxels = size size size if w < 0 or w >= maxvoxels: return (vc[0], vc[1], vc[2], 0.0) # Null value for alpha # 3. Normalize voxel index for alpha channel alpha = w / maxvoxels # 4. Emit pixel with color in RGB and normalized index in Alpha return (vc[0], vc[1], vc[2], alpha) def reconstructandpolygonize(vbodata: list, size: int) -> list: bricks = [] for pixel in vbodata: alpha = pixel[3] if alpha == 0.0: continue # Discard illegal/null values w = int(alpha size size size) iz = w % size w //= size iy = w % size ix = w // size # Generate LEGOr brick geometry at (ix, iy, iz) bricks.append((ix, iy, iz, pixel[0], pixel[1], pixel[2])) return bricks Parameters: size: The grid resolution (e.g., 128, 256). FBO Resolution: Must be large enough to prevent overlapping projections of distinct vertices. Typical values are 512x512 for resolutions up to 128^3 voxels, and >1024x1024 for complex objects. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes in Back Surfaces: Because the method relies on vertex projection and Z-buffering, back-facing surfaces may be occluded by front-facing vertices, resulting in holes. This is mitigated by increasing the FBO size to reduce vertex overlap and ensure distinct vertices map to distinct pixels. Vertex Overlap: Complex objects may have many vertices projecting to the same pixel. The Z-buffer resolves this by keeping only the closest vertex, which may discard interior geometry information if the application requires it. Precision: The normalization of the voxel index into the alpha channel introduces quantization error. Using floating-point FBOs is recommended to preserve index integrity. This method transforms a surface-represented scene into a high-resolution voxel grid in a single GPU pass by using the geometry shader to duplicate geometry for intersecting slices and a 3D volume texture as the direct render target. It solves the inefficiency of multi-pass slicing algorithms and the projection artifacts or fixed-resolution limitations of grid encoding methods. Unlike encoding methods that induce errors, this approach uses a clipping plane algorithm to avoid projection artifacts. Time Complexity: O(V) for the vertex shader pass, where V is the number of vertices. The subsequent geometry shader pass is O(P), where P is the number of projected pixels (voxels). Memory Complexity: O(size^2) for the FBO storage (2D projection) and O(size^3) for the final voxel grid if explicitly stored, though the method primarily outputs a VBO of projected vertices. Performance: On an AMD Athlon 64 3500+ with 2GB RAM and GeForce 8800GTX, a 512x512 FBO produces good results for 128^3 voxel resolutions. Complex objects require FBO sizes >1024x1024. Speed: Up to 5 times faster than Passalis et al., which renders the model six times using multiple buffers. This method renders the model only once using a single frame buffer. Strengths: Single-pass rasterization; real-time performance; no preprocessing required. Limitations: Dependent on model surface complexity; prone to holes in back surfaces if FBO is too small; misses concavities in concave objects if not carefully tuned (though less prone than Karabassi et al.). The method was introduced in the "Legolizer" system, described in the paper Legolizer: A Real-Time System for Modeling and Rendering LEGO Representations of Boundary Models. It was developed to create LEGO-like representations of 3D models efficiently. The approach was compared against Passalis et al. and Karabassi et al.. name: Single-Pass GPU Voxelization via 3D Texture Render Target
head: Geometry Shader Voxelization via 3D Texture, Real-time GPU-Based Voxelization, Voxelization via 3D Texture Render Target, slicing-based voxelization using geometry shader [S2, unofficial]
body: This method transforms a surface-represented scene into a high-resolution voxel grid in a single GPU pass by using the geometry shader to duplicate geometry for intersecting slices and a 3D volume texture as the direct render target. It solves the inefficiency of multi-pass slicing algorithms and the projection artifacts or fixed-resolution limitations of grid encoding methods. Unlike encoding methods that induce errors, this approach uses a clipping plane algorithm to avoid projection artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A mesh defined by triangles (or quadrilaterals) with vertex positions, colors, and normals. Output: A 3D volume texture where each texel stores volumetric existence, color, surface normal, transmission coefficient, and refraction index. Data Structures: 3D Volume Texture: The primary storage for voxel data, with dimensions adjustable based on hardware limitations and application needs. Texel Layout: Each texel stores existence (implicit via render target or explicit flag), color, surface normal, transmission coefficient, refraction index, and an absorption coefficient. The absorption coefficient is computed according to the number of surface drawings in each voxel during voxelization. Numbered Steps: 1. Vertex Shader: Compute the positions of triangle vertices in camera coordinates. 2. Geometry Shader: Determine which slices along the z-axis intersect the triangle. Duplicate the triangle for each intersecting slice to rasterize in the pixel shader. 3. Pixel Shader: Rasterize the duplicated triangles onto the 3D texture render target. Store surfacial data (normal, color) and volumetric data (transmittance) in the corresponding texels. Update the absorption coefficient based on the number of surface drawings in each voxel. Formulas: Let zi be the camera-space z-coordinate of vertex i of a triangle. Let thickness be the slice depth parameter. The slice index range is computed as: maxslice = \max(z0, z1, z2) / thickness minslice = \min(z0, z1, z2) / thickness where maxslice and minslice define the inclusive range of z-axis slices that intersect the triangle. Parameters: Typical values are not given in the sources. The voxel resolution is determined by the dimensions of the 3D texture. The absorption coefficient is derived from the count of surface intersections per voxel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Deformable models are handled without preprocessing or sorting, overcoming limitations of previous encoding methods. The algorithm can be extended to handle quadrilaterals without major modification. The size of the 3D texture is adjustable but constrained by hardware limitations. Precision issues may arise when computing slice indices from floating-point z-coordinates, requiring careful rounding or floor/ceil operations. Degenerate triangles with zero area or coplanar vertices may produce invalid slice ranges and require explicit culling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. slicethickness = 1.0 # Not given in the sources. modelviewmatrix = [...] # Standard 4x4 matrix transforming world to camera space. def transformtocamera(position, mvmatrix): # Standard matrix-vector multiplication for camera-space conversion return mvmatrix @ position def writeto3dtexture(texture, x, y, zslice, color, normal, transmission, refractionidx, absorption): # Standard 3D texture render target write operation texture[x, y, zslice].color = color texture[x, y, zslice].normal = normal texture[x, y, zslice].transmission = transmission texture[x, y, zslice].refractionindex = refractionidx texture[x, y, zslice].absorption += absorption def vertexshader(position, normal, color, mvmatrix): camerapos = transformtocamera(position, mvmatrix) return camerapos, normal, color def geometryshader(trianglevertices, slicethickness): # trianglevertices: list of 3 camera-space positions z0 = trianglevertices[0].z z1 = trianglevertices[1].z z2 = trianglevertices[2].z maxslice = max(z0, z1, z2) / slicethickness minslice = min(z0, z1, z2) / slicethickness # Duplicate triangle for each intersecting slice for slicez in range(int(minslice), int(maxslice) + 1): yield trianglevertices, slicez def pixelshader(trianglevertices, slicez, normal, color, texture): # Standard triangle rasterization fills fragments (x, y) within the projected triangle bounds # Not detailed in sources. for x, y in trianglerasterization(trianglevertices, slicez): writeto3dtexture(texture, x, y, slicez, color, normal, 1.0, 1.5, 1.0) def trianglerasterization(vertices, zslice): # Compute bounding box and scanline fill for the triangle projected at zslice # Returns list of (x, y) fragment coordinates pass # Standard rasterization algorithm; not detailed in sources. Time Complexity: Single GPU pass, making it efficient for real-time applications. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the 3D texture, which is adjustable. Performance: Capable of real-time voxelization of highly complex scenes. Strengths: Avoids projection artifacts, handles deformable models without preprocessing, allows adjustable resolution, and stores rich surfacial and volumetric data. Limitations: Limited by hardware constraints on 3D texture size. When to Use: Real-time applications requiring transparent shadow, transmittance, and refraction effects. When Not to Use: When hardware does not support 3D texture render targets or geometry shaders. This method was proposed by Hsu-Huai Chang and Yu-Chi Lai in their paper "Real-time GPU-Based Voxelization and Applications". It leverages newly available GPU functionalities, specifically the geometry shader and 3D volume texture as render targets, to overcome limitations of previous slicing-based and encoding-based voxelization methods. The technique is used for rendering transparent shadow, transmittance, and refraction effects in real-time applications. name: GPU Mesh Voxelizer (Grid Generation)
head: Compute Shader Voxel Grid Generation, Grid-Snapped Voxelization via Compute Shader
body: This method generates a dense 3D voxel grid by computing the center coordinates of each voxel cell directly on the GPU using a compute shader. It converts a mesh's spatial extent into a fixed-width, height, and depth 3D grid structure, returning a flat array of voxel centers. Unlike rasterization-based approaches that project geometry onto slices, this method calculates grid dimensions from the mesh's bounding box and fills the grid with uniform cells. It builds on 3D Grid Rasterization by providing the specific grid generation mechanism. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A mesh (typically accessed via a MeshCollider or MeshFilter), the mesh's local-space bounding box extents, and a target voxel half-size parameter S. Output: A RWStructuredBuffer<float4> containing the center coordinates of every voxel in the grid, linearized in 3D order. Data Structures: Voxel Grid Buffer: A RWStructuredBuffer<float4> named VoxelGridPoints. Each element stores a 4D vector (x, y, z, w) where w=1.0. The layout is a 1D linearization of the 3D grid: index I = ix + W \cdot (iy + H \cdot iz), where W, H, D are the grid dimensions in x, y, and z respectively. Compute Shader Parameters: BoundsMin is a float4 representing the minimum corner of the mesh's local bounding box. CellHalfSize is a float representing the half-width of a voxel cell (S). GridWidth, GridHeight, GridDepth are int values defining the dimensions of the voxel grid. Thread Group: Defined as [numthreads(4,4,4)]. Steps: 1. Calculate Bounding Box: Determine the mesh's bounding box in local space. Let B{min} be the minimum corner and E be the extents. 2. Determine Grid Dimensions: Calculate the number of voxels required along each axis by dividing the extents by the cell half-size S and ceiling the result: W = \lceil Ex / S \rceil, \quad H = \lceil Ey / S \rceil, \quad D = \lceil Ez / S \rceil 3. Allocate Buffer: Allocate a ComputeBuffer of size W \times H \times D with element size 4 \times \text{sizeof(float)}. 4. Dispatch Compute Shader: Dispatch the VoxelizeMesh kernel with thread group counts calculated as \lceil W / 4 \rceil, \lceil H / 4 \rceil, \lceil D / 4 \rceil. 5. Compute Voxel Centers: Inside the shader, each thread computes the center of its assigned voxel using the formula below. Formula: The center coordinate C for a voxel at grid index (ix, iy, iz) is: Cx = B{min,x} + ix \cdot (2 \cdot S) Cy = B{min,y} + iy \cdot (2 \cdot S) Cz = B{min,z} + iz \cdot (2 \cdot S) where B{min} is the minimum bound of the mesh in local space, i is the thread's global index, and S is the cell half-size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelizemesh(meshcollider, halfsize): bounds = meshcollider.bounds boundsmin = transform.inversetransformpoint(bounds.min) extents = bounds.extents voxelcountx = math.ceil(extents.x / halfsize) voxelcounty = math.ceil(extents.y / halfsize) voxelcountz = math.ceil(extents.z / halfsize) width = voxelcountx height = voxelcounty depth = voxelcountz buffersize = width height depth voxelbuffer = ComputeBuffer(buffersize, 16) groupsize = 4 dispatchx = math.ceil(width / groupsize) dispatchy = math.ceil(height / groupsize) dispatchz = math.ceil(depth / groupsize) computeshader.dispatch(voxelizekernel, dispatchx, dispatchy, dispatchz) return voxelbuffer def voxelizemeshkernel(idx, idy, idz, gridwidth, gridheight, griddepth, cellhalfsize, boundsmin, voxelgridpoints): if idx >= gridwidth or idy >= gridheight or idz >= griddepth: return cellsize = cellhalfsize 2.0 index = idx + gridwidth (idy + gridheight idz) center = [ boundsmin[0] + idx cellsize, boundsmin[1] + idy cellsize, boundsmin[2] + idz cellsize, 1.0 ] voxelgridpoints[index] = center Parameters: halfSize (or CellHalfSize): The half-width of each voxel cell. Typical value: 0.05f. GridWidth, GridHeight, GridDepth: Integer dimensions of the output grid. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Checks: A boundary check (id.x >= GridWidth, etc.) is required in the compute shader to prevent out-of-bounds writes if the grid dimensions are not exact multiples of the thread group size (4). Precision: Floating-point precision in the bounding box calculation and grid indexing should be sufficient for typical scene scales. Empty Meshes: If the mesh has zero extents, the grid dimensions will be zero, and no buffer allocation or dispatch is needed. Generates solid voxels by accumulating coverage in an A-Buffer, handling transparency and depth. Choose when voxel opacity or partial coverage matters. A-Buffer Solid Voxelization Uses an octree-like structure to adapt resolution based on geometry complexity. Choose for large scenes with varying detail levels. Adaptive Sparse Voxelization with Bounding Box Thickness Cases Uses geometry shaders to generate voxels during rasterization. Choose for simpler pipelines without compute shader support. Geometry Shader Voxelization Rasterizes geometry onto a pre-defined grid structure. Choose when the grid topology is fixed and known in advance. Derived Grid Rasterization Handles unstructured meshes by checking element containment. Choose for non-standard mesh formats. Unstructured Mesh Pixelization via Convex Element Containment Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot D), where W, H, D are the grid dimensions. The complexity is linear with the number of voxels. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot D) for storing the voxel centers. Each voxel stores 4 floats (16 bytes). Measured Performance: Performance depends on the grid resolution and GPU compute throughput. For a typical voxel size of 0.05f, grid sizes can become large quickly, leading to high memory usage. Strengths: Simple implementation, parallelizable, no rasterization overhead, suitable for dense grids. Limitations: Memory-intensive for large bounding boxes or small voxel sizes. Does not handle geometry inside the bounding box; it fills the entire volume. When to Use: When a dense, regular grid is required for subsequent processing (e.g., marching cubes, density fields) and the bounding box is not excessively large. When Not to Use: For sparse scenes or when memory is constrained, as it allocates space for the entire bounding box volume. This method originates from an unofficial Unity tutorial series by bzgeb, demonstrating a GPU-based mesh voxelizer for Unity. It leverages Unity's Compute Shader infrastructure to offload the grid generation process from the CPU to the GPU, allowing for real-time or near-real-time voxelization of meshes. The approach is part of a broader effort to create efficient voxelization pipelines for real-time rendering applications. bzgeb/UnityGPUMeshVoxelizerPart1, https://github.com/bzgeb/UnityGPUMeshVoxelizerPart1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Derived Grid Rasterization
head: Derived Grid for Unstructured Volume Rendering, DerivedGrid, DerivedGrid construction, Tetrahedral Grid Construction, Unstructured Volume Grid, Unstructured Volume to Structured Grid Conversion, cell-to-voxel mapping
body: Derived Grid Rasterization converts an unstructured 3D volume mesh (e.g., tetrahedra, hexahedra) into a dense, regular 3D voxel grid spanning the mesh's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). It maps each voxel to its owning unstructured cell and local tetrahedron index, enabling direct structured lookup for volume ray-marching and axis-aligned slice planes. Unlike sibling methods that produce sparse structures or rely on different rasterization primitives, this method explicitly stores cell connectivity per voxel for subsequent rendering. Inputs: Unstructured mesh with volume cells (tetrahedra, hexahedra, etc.). Scalar field data associated with points or cells. Parameters: maxDim (default 192), maxVoxels (default 16 \ll 20 or 16 Mi). Outputs: DerivedGrid: Structured grid containing voxel-to-cell mappings and occupancy. ScalarGrid: Structured scalar field values with occupancy mask and slice min/max bounds. Data Structures: DerivedGrid layout: dimX, dimY, dimZ: int, grid dimensions in voxels. origin, extent: glm::dvec3, AABB origin and size in world units. cellId: std::vector<uint32t>, size dimX dimY dimZ. Stores the ID of the unstructured cell containing the voxel center. Empty voxels store kEmpty (0xFFFFFFFFu). tet: std::vector<uint8t>, size dimX dimY dimZ. Stores the local tetrahedron index within the owning cell. cellVoxelStart: std::vector<uint32t>, size numCells + 1. CSR-style start indices for voxel lists per cell. cellVoxels: std::vector<uint32t>, flattened list of voxel indices grouped by cell ID. kEmpty: Constant 0xFFFFFFFFu. ScalarGrid layout: value: std::vector<float>, size dimX dimY dimZ. Scalar values, valid where occupancy is true. occupancy: std::vector<std::uint8t>, boolean mask for occupied voxels. planeMin, planeMax: std::array<std::vector<float>, 3>, per-axis slice min/max values for occupied voxels, used for early ray termination. Steps: 1. Eligibility Check: Reject if vertices are empty, no unstructured volume cells exist, topology is invalid (e.g., CSR inconsistent), or bounding box extents are non-positive or zero within epsilon (rejects 2D meshes). 2. Grid Dimension Calculation: Compute spacing from the longest AABB extent and maxDim. Iterate to find dimensions such that total voxels \le maxVoxels. Clamp each dimension between 2 and maxDim. If spacing becomes non-positive or infinite, fail. 3. Cell Decomposition: For each volume cell, decompose it into tetrahedra using celltopology::tets. Skip cells if decomposition fails or returns empty. 4. Degeneracy Check: Compute scale-relative volume epsilon based on the maximum corner distance cubed. Skip tetrahedra with determinant magnitude \le volumeEps to avoid ill-conditioned barycentric solves. 5. Voxel Intersection (Rasterization): For each tetrahedron, compute its bounding box in grid coordinates: tmin[a] = \min(p0[a], p1[a], p2[a], p3[a]) tmax[a] = \max(p0[a], p1[a], p2[a], p3[a]) where pi are the cell's vertex positions. Calculate grid indices covering the bounding box: f0[a] = \frac{tmin[a] - origin[a]}{step[a]} - 0.5 i0[a] = \text{clamp}(\lfloor f0[a] \rfloor, 0, dim[a] - 1) i1[a] = \text{clamp}(\lfloor \frac{tmax[a] - origin[a]}{step[a]} - 0.5 \rfloor, 0, dim[a] - 1) Iterate over all voxels (x, y, z) in [i0, i1]. Compute voxel center in world space: point = origin + (x + 0.5, y + 0.5, z + 0.5) \times \frac{extent}{dims} This mapping matches the volume shader's UVW calculation: uvw = (pos - origin) / extent. Compute barycentric coordinates w of point relative to the tetrahedron vertices. If any weight wi < -kInsideTol or \sum wi \neq 1.0 (within tolerance), the voxel is outside. If all weights satisfy the condition, the voxel is inside. Mark voxel as occupied: cellId[idx] = cellID, tet[idx] = tetIndex. 6. Pin Thin Cells: For cells that are thinner than one voxel (do not contain any voxel center), pin them to the voxel containing their geometric center. Assign cellId and tet index 0 to that voxel. 7. Counting Sort (CSR Construction): Count occurrences of each cell ID in cellId: ++cellVoxelStart[id + 1]. Compute prefix sums: cellVoxelStart[c] += cellVoxelStart[c - 1]. Scatter voxel indices into cellVoxels using cursors initialized from cellVoxelStart: cellVoxels[cursor[id]++] = i. 8. Scalar Scattering: Scatter field values into ScalarGrid.value. If cellPlacement is false, remap point data from pre-split vertex space to post-split vertex space using vertexSourceIndex. If cellPlacement is true, treat values as one per cell. Compute per-slice min/max for occupied voxels into planeMin and planeMax. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Tuple, Any class DerivedGrid: def init(self, dimX, dimY, dimZ, origin, extent, cellId, tet, cellVoxelStart, cellVoxels): self.dimX, self.dimY, self.dimZ = dimX, dimY, dimZ self.origin = origin self.extent = extent self.cellId = cellId self.tet = tet self.cellVoxelStart = cellVoxelStart self.cellVoxels = cellVoxels self.kEmpty = 0xFFFFFFFF class ScalarGrid: def init(self, value, occupancy, planeMin, planeMax): self.value = value self.occupancy = occupancy self.planeMin = planeMin self.planeMax = planeMax def computeaabb(vertices): minv = [float('inf')] 3 maxv = [float('-inf')] 3 for v in vertices: for a in range(3): if v[a] < minv[a]: minv[a] = v[a] if v[a] > maxv[a]: maxv[a] = v[a] return minv, maxv def computegriddims(extent, maxdim, maxvoxels): maxextent = max(extent) spacing = maxextent / maxdim if spacing <= 0 or math.isinf(spacing): raise ValueError("Invalid spacing") dims = [max(2, min(maxdim, int(math.floor(e / spacing)))) for e in extent] while dims[0] dims[1] dims[2] > maxvoxels: maxidx = dims.index(max(dims)) dims[maxidx] = max(2, dims[maxidx] - 1) return dims def decomposecelltotets(cellverts): # Sources do not specify the exact cell-to-tet decomposition algorithm. # Standard approach: split polyhedra into tetrahedra via fan or dual-triangulation. return [] def barycentric(point, tetverts): v0, v1, v2, v3 = tetverts mat = [[v0[0]-v3[0], v1[0]-v3[0], v2[0]-v3[0]], [v0[1]-v3[1], v1[1]-v3[1], v2[1]-v3[1]], [v0[2]-v3[2], v1[2]-v3[2], v2[2]-v3[2]]] vec = [point[0]-v3[0], point[1]-v3[1], point[2]-v3[2]] det = (mat[0][0](mat[1][1]mat[2][2]-mat[1][2]mat[2][1]) - mat[0][1](mat[1][0]mat[2][2]-mat[1][2]mat[2][0]) + mat[0][2](mat[1][0]mat[2][1]-mat[1][1]mat[2][0])) if abs(det) < 1e-9: return [0, 0, 0, 0] w0 = ((vec[0](mat[1][1]mat[2][2]-mat[1][2]mat[2][1]) - mat[0][1](vec[1]mat[2][2]-mat[1][2]vec[2]) + mat[0][2](vec[1]mat[2][1]-mat[1][1]vec[2])) / det) w1 = ((mat[0][0](vec[1]mat[2][2]-mat[1][2]vec[2]) - vec[0](mat[1][0]mat[2][2]-mat[1][2]mat[2][0]) + mat[0][2](mat[1][0]vec[2]-vec[1]mat[2][0])) / det) w2 = ((mat[0][0](mat[1][1]vec[2]-vec[1]mat[2][1]) - mat[0][1](mat[1][0]vec[2]-vec[1]mat[2][0]) + vec[0](mat[1][0]mat[2][1]-mat[1][1]mat[2][0])) / det) w3 = 1.0 - w0 - w1 - w2 return [w0, w1, w2, w3] def computecentroid(vertices): return [sum(v[a] for v in vertices) / len(vertices) for a in range(3)] def scatterscalars(mesh, cellid, occupancy, origin, extent, dims, cellplacement, vertexsourceindex, pointdata, celldata): numvoxels = dims[0] dims[1] dims[2] value = [0.0] numvoxels occupancymask = [False] numvoxels planemin = [[float('inf')] dims[a] for a in range(3)] planemax = [[float('-inf')] dims[a] for a in range(3)] for idx in range(numvoxels): if not occupancy[idx]: continue occupancymask[idx] = True cid = cellid[idx] if cellplacement: val = celldata[cid] else: # Remap point data using vertexSourceIndex as per source notes. # Exact indexing depends on mesh data layout. val = pointdata[cid] value[idx] = val for a in range(3): if a == 0: ax = idx % dims[0] elif a == 1: ax = (idx // dims[0]) % dims[1] else: ax = idx // (dims[0] dims[1]) if val < planemin[a][ax]: planemin[a][ax] = val if val > planemax[a][ax]: planemax[a][ax] = val return ScalarGrid(value, occupancymask, planemin, planemax) def derivegrid(mesh, maxdim=192, maxvoxels=16 << 20, kinsidetol=1e-6): if not mesh.vertices or not mesh.cells: raise ValueError("Empty mesh") bboxmin, bboxmax = computeaabb(mesh.vertices) extent = [bboxmax[a] - bboxmin[a] for a in range(3)] if any(e <= 0 for e in extent): raise ValueError("Degenerate AABB") dims = computegriddims(extent, maxdim, maxvoxels) origin = bboxmin step = [extent[a] / dims[a] for a in range(3)] numvoxels = dims[0] dims[1] dims[2] cellid = [0xFFFFFFFF] numvoxels tetidx = [0] numvoxels occupancy = [False] numvoxels for c, cellverts in mesh.cells.items(): tets = decomposecelltotets(cellverts) if not tets: continue # Degeneracy check: compute scale-relative volume epsilon based on max corner distance cubed. # Skip tetrahedra with determinant magnitude <= volumeEps. cellbboxmin, cellbboxmax = computeaabb(cellverts) f0 = [(cellbboxmin[a] - origin[a]) / step[a] - 0.5 for a in range(3)] i0 = [max(0, min(dims[a] - 1, math.floor(f))) for a, f in enumerate(f0)] f1 = [(cellbboxmax[a] - origin[a]) / step[a] - 0.5 for a in range(3)] i1 = [max(0, min(dims[a] - 1, math.floor(f))) for a, f in enumerate(f1)] touched = False for x in range(i0[0], i1[0] + 1): for y in range(i0[1], i1[1] + 1): for z in range(i0[2], i1[2] + 1): idx = x + y dims[0] + z dims[0] dims[1] point = [origin[a] + (coord + 0.5) step[a] for a, coord in enumerate([x, y, z])] for tidx, tet in enumerate(tets): w = barycentric(point, tet) if all(wi > -kinsidetol for wi in w) and abs(sum(w) - 1.0) < kinsidetol: cellid[idx] = c tetidx[idx] = tidx occupancy[idx] = True touched = True break if not touched: center = computecentroid(cellverts) cx = max(0, min(dims[0] - 1, math.floor((center[0] - origin[0]) / step[0] - 0.5))) cy = max(0, min(dims[1] - 1, math.floor((center[1] - origin[1]) / step[1] - 0.5))) cz = max(0, min(dims[2] - 1, math.floor((center[2] - origin[2]) / step[2] - 0.5))) idx = cx + cy dims[0] + cz dims[0] dims[1] cellid[idx] = c tetidx[idx] = 0 occupancy[idx] = True cellvoxelstart = [0] (mesh.numcells + 1) for idx in range(numvoxels): cid = cellid[idx] if cid != 0xFFFFFFFF: cellvoxelstart[cid + 1] += 1 for c in range(1, len(cellvoxelstart)): cellvoxelstart[c] += cellvoxelstart[c - 1] cellvoxels = [0] sum(cellvoxelstart[:-1]) cursor = cellvoxelstart.copy() for idx in range(numvoxels): cid = cellid[idx] if cid != 0xFFFFFFFF: cellvoxels[cursor[cid]] = idx cursor[cid] += 1 scalargrid = scatterscalars(mesh, cellid, occupancy, origin, extent, dims, mesh.cellplacement, mesh.vertexsourceindex, mesh.pointdata, mesh.celldata) return DerivedGrid(dims[0], dims[1], dims[2], origin, extent, cellid, tetidx, cellvoxelstart, cellvoxels), scalargrid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty voxels (outside every volume cell) are marked with kEmpty (0xFFFFFFFFu) so that shaders can skip them, preventing fogging of the entire bounding box. The derived grid is static geometry; it does not change when the scalar field changes. Transient frames only re-scatter the field data into the grid structure. 2D mesh rejection: Meshes with zero z-extent (triangles/quads) are rejected by eligibility check to prevent degenerate 3D rasterization. Vertex index remapping: Point data may be indexed in pre-split vertex space (original mesh vertices) but rendered in post-split space (one value per rendered vertex). Use vertexSourceIndex to remap. [1189-a-buffer-solid-voxelization.md] [1686-adaptive-sparse-voxelization-with-bounding-box-thickness-cas.md] [2566-geometry-shader-voxelization.md] [11413-gpu-mesh-voxelizer-grid-generation.md] [11479-unstructured-mesh-pixelization-via-convex-element-containmen.md] Time Complexity: O(C \cdot T \cdot V) where C is the number of cells, T is the average number of tetrahedra per cell, and V is the average number of voxels in a tetrahedron's bounding box. Grid construction (CSR, scattering) is O(V{total}). Memory Complexity: O(V{total}) for the dense grid arrays (cellId, tet, occupancy, value). The CSR structures add O(C + V{occupied}). Performance: The method is static; the grid structure does not change when the scalar field changes, allowing transient frames to only re-scatter field data. Performance is limited by the dense nature of the grid; large maxVoxels can lead to high memory usage and cache misses during ray-marching if the volume is sparse. Strengths: Provides a simple, structured lookup for volume rendering. Efficient for dense volumes. Compatible with standard volume shaders. Limitations: Inefficient for sparse volumes due to dense grid storage. Sensitive to grid resolution; too fine a grid increases memory, too coarse loses detail. 2D meshes are explicitly rejected. When to use: When the volume is dense and fits within memory limits, and simple structured access is preferred. When not to use: For highly sparse volumes where sparse voxel octrees (like Adaptive Sparse Voxelization) would be more efficient. Derived Grid Rasterization is implemented in SciRender, an open-source scientific visualization tool. It is designed to handle unstructured volume meshes (like those from CFD simulations) by converting them into a format suitable for real-time volume rendering in OpenGL. The method addresses the need for structured data access in volume ray-marching shaders when the underlying data is unstructured. thermeng/SciRender, https://github.com/thermeng/SciRender, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Unstructured Mesh Pixelization via Convex Element Containment
body: A pixelization routine that transforms variable-resolution unstructured mesh values into an image buffer by depositing values through nearest-neighbor interpolation with anti-aliasing, decoupling the pixelization step from the underlying data model. It differs from standard rasterization by using a geometric containment test based on dot product signs relative to element centroids, which eliminates the requirement for consistent vertex winding order (CW/CCW). Inputs: A set of unstructured mesh elements (e.g., hexahedra, tetrahedra, wedges). Field data defined at element centroids. An interpolation kernel (initially nearest-neighbor). Image plane dimensions and view parameters. Outputs: An image buffer containing deposited values. Data Structures: Element: Defined by a centroid position \mathbf{c} and a set of face normal vectors \{\mathbf{n}i\}. Containment Signatures: For each element, a precomputed array of signs si = \text{sign}(\mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{n}i) for each face i. Image Buffer: A 2D array corresponding to the image plane pixels. Steps: 1. Bounding Box Culling: Apply coarse bounding box checks to the image plane and all supplied elements to filter out elements that do not intersect the view frustum. 2. Precompute Element Signatures: For each element, compute the sign of the dot product between the element centroid \mathbf{c} and each normal vector \mathbf{n}i defining its faces, storing these signs to determine internal containment without requiring clockwise/counter-clockwise vertex ordering. 3. Iterate Mesh Types: Iterate over each mesh type separately to deposit their fields in sequence, enabling interoperation of fields between mesh types without requiring uniform size. 4. Pixel Containment Test: For each pixel in the image plane that passed the bounding box check for a given element: a. Calculate the pixel's position \mathbf{p} in the same coordinate system as the element. b. Calculate the sign of the dot product between the pixel's position and each face normal vector: s'i = \text{sign}(\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n}i). c. Compare the pixel's sign array with the element's stored signature. d. If all the signs match, classify the pixel as internal to the convex element. 5. Value Deposition: If the pixel is internal, evaluate the appropriate interpolation kernel for the internal point and deposit the resulting value into the image plane. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def sign(x): return 1 if x >= 0 else -1 def zeros(shape): return [[0.0 for in range(shape[1])] for in range(shape[0])] def unstructuredmeshpixelization(elements, imagewidth, imageheight, kernel, viewbounds): """ Pixels values from unstructured mesh elements to an image buffer. """ imagebuffer = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) # Step 1: Bounding box culling # Filter elements that do not intersect the view frustum/image plane bounds. # Exact frustum math is implementation-dependent based on the coordinate handler. visibleelements = [e for e in elements if not (e['bboxmax'][0] < viewbounds[0] or e['bboxmin'][0] > viewbounds[3] or e['bboxmax'][1] < viewbounds[1] or e['bboxmin'][1] > viewbounds[4] or e['bboxmax'][2] < viewbounds[2] or e['bboxmin'][2] > viewbounds[5])] # Step 3: Iterate over mesh types (simplified here as a single loop over elements) for element in visibleelements: centroid = element['centroid'] normals = element['normals'] value = element['value'] # Step 2: Precompute element containment signature elementsignatures = [sign(dot(centroid, n)) for n in normals] # Step 4: Iterate over pixels in the image plane for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Map pixel coordinates to world space (simplified linear mapping) pixelpos = (x, y, 0.0) # Calculate pixel containment signature pixelsignatures = [sign(dot(pixelpos, n)) for n in normals] # Check if all signs match if all(ps == es for ps, es in zip(pixelsignatures, elementsignatures)): # Step 5: Deposit value imagebuffer[y][x] = kernel(pixelpos, centroid, value) return imagebuffer def kernel(pixelpos, centroid, value): # Nearest-neighbor interpolation kernel return value Parameters: interpolationkernel: The kernel used for value deposition; initially supports only nearest-neighbor. fielddefinitionlocation: The location where field data is defined within the element; initially supports only centroids, with edge and face support planned. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The containment test assumes convex elements; non-convex elements may fail the sign-matching test. Vertex ordering (CW/CCW) is not required for the containment test because it relies on dot product signs relative to the centroid. Not given in the sources. This method is described in YTEP-0031, an enhancement proposal for the yt unstructured mesh handling capabilities. It was developed to address the need for flexible pixelization of variable-resolution unstructured mesh data, allowing for the interoperation of fields between different mesh types without requiring uniform size. YTEP-0031: Unstructured Mesh — yt Enhancement Proposals 1.0 documentation, https://ytep.readthedocs.io/en/master/YTEPs/YTEP-0031.html, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Fast Solid Voxelization via Planar Raycasting
body: Fast Solid Voxelization via Planar Raycasting is a rasterization-based method that generates a solid voxel mesh from an arbitrary polyhedron by casting rays along the three world coordinate planes (XY, YZ, XZ). It solves the problem of converting polygonal meshes into dense 3D grids by determining voxel occupancy through intersection parity, prioritizing raw computational speed over memory efficiency. It differs from the '--safe' rasterizer by being optimized for pure speed but being less memory efficient and less accurate for complex internal structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A polygonal mesh (polyhedron) defined by vertices and faces, typically loaded from.stl or.obj files. Output: A 3D grid of uint8t values representing voxel states (0: empty, 1: shell, 2+: interior depth). Data Structures: The method relies on three pre-computed 3D buffers to accelerate raycasting. Each buffer stores face indices for a specific projection plane. buffer3d<mesh::face<idt>> xyplanebuffer, yzplanebuffer, xzplanebuffer: Three 3D buffers storing face indices for each plane orientation, used to accelerate raycasting. voxeldatat: A struct rasterresults<buffer3d<uint8t>, mesh::polyhedron<baset>> containing arrdim (glm::vec3), voxels (buffer3d<uint8t>), and mesh (mesh::polyhedron<baset>). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Calculate minfacearea as poly.avgfacearea() / 10. Determine grid dimensions dim by taking the ceiling of the polyhedron's bounding box dimensions: dim = glm::ceil(polyhedron.dim()). Call prepareindexbuffers(poly, dim, xyplanebuffer, yzplanebuffer, xzplanebuffer, minfacearea) to populate internal buffers and set polyhedron. 2. Buffer Setup: Create voxeldatat buf with dimensions dim, a 3D uint8t buffer initialized to 0, and the polyhedron. 3. Raycasting Loop: Execute planarraycast<yzx>(buf), then planarraycast<xzy>(buf), then planarraycast<xyz>(buf). 4. Planar Raycast Implementation (planarraycast<mode>): Iterate over the 2D plane dimensions (i, j) corresponding to the mode (e.g., for YZX, i corresponds to Y, j to Z). Parallelize this iteration using OpenMP (#pragma omp parallel for). For each pixel (i, j), retrieve the sorted list of intersection indices from the pre-computed plane buffer using checks::raycast::getintersectionsfast<mode>. Initialize isin = false and from = 0. Iterate through the sorted intersection indices inters: Clamp inters to the valid voxel range [0, \text{dim}-1] using constrain(0, \text{dim}-1, \text{inters}). Mark the voxel at the intersection as shell type (value 1). If from < inters: Iterate through intermediate voxels k from from to inters - 1. Update voxel value: if voxel != 0, left-shift by 1 (voxel = voxel << 1); if voxel == 0, set to 1. Check if the current seed position holds an interior voxel. If not, update the seed position to the current voxel coordinates (k, i, j) depending on the plane mode. Set from = inters + 1. Toggle isin = !isin. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constrain(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(val, maxval)) def planarraycast(mode, buf, mesh, dim, planebuffer): # Map mode to 2D iteration dimensions and 3D coordinate generation if mode == 'yzx': dimi, dimj = dim.y, dim.z getcoords = lambda k, i, j: (k, i, j) elif mode == 'xzy': dimi, dimj = dim.x, dim.z getcoords = lambda k, i, j: (i, k, j) elif mode == 'xyz': dimi, dimj = dim.x, dim.y getcoords = lambda k, i, j: (i, j, k) else: raise ValueError("Unknown mode") # Parallelize iteration over 2D plane dimensions using OpenMP for i in range(dimi): for j in range(dimj): # Retrieve sorted intersection indices from pre-computed plane buffer inters = getintersectionsfast(mode, i, j, planebuffer, mesh) if not inters: continue isin = False fromidx = 0 for intersidx in inters: # Clamp to valid voxel range [0, dim-1] currentidx = constrain(intersidx, 0, dim[mode] - 1) # Mark corresponding voxel as shell type coords = getcoords(currentidx, i, j) buf.voxels[coords] = 1 # Iterate through intermediate voxels between shells if fromidx < currentidx: for k in range(fromidx, currentidx): coords = getcoords(k, i, j) voxelval = buf.voxels[coords] if voxelval != 0: buf.voxels[coords] = voxelval << 1 else: buf.voxels[coords] = 1 # Check if current seed position holds interior voxel # Update seed position to (k, i, j) if needed pass fromidx = currentidx + 1 isin = not isin def voxelize(mesh, dim): # Constructor initialization minfacearea = mesh.avgfacearea() / 10.0 dim = [int(d) for d in dim] # glm::ceil approximation # Initialize plane buffers xybuf = buffer3d(mesh.face, dim[0], dim[1], 1) yzbuf = buffer3d(mesh.face, dim[1], dim[2], 1) xzbuf = buffer3d(mesh.face, dim[0], dim[2], 1) # Populate plane buffers prepareindexbuffers(mesh, dim, xybuf, yzbuf, xzbuf, minfacearea) # Initialize voxel data buffer buf = voxeldatat() buf.arrdim = dim buf.voxels = buffer3d(uint8, dim[0], dim[1], dim[2], 0) buf.mesh = mesh # Execute planar raycasts planarraycast('yzx', buf, mesh, dim, yzbuf) planarraycast('xzy', buf, mesh, dim, xzbuf) planarraycast('xyz', buf, mesh, dim, xybuf) return buf Parameters: seedsize: Initial size for the seed tracking mechanism, default value 128. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infill Issues: The method casts rays along world coordinate planes rather than checking every cell individually, potentially missing internal structures not aligned with these projections. Precision: Uses FLTEPSILON 10 as a precision bias for geometric checks. Memory: Allocates complete 3D buffers, which is not memory efficient for large resolutions. Time Complexity: The method is optimized for pure speed. Parallelization over the 2D plane dimensions using OpenMP reduces wall-clock time significantly. Memory Complexity: High memory usage due to the allocation of complete 3D buffers for voxel data and plane index buffers. Measured Performance: On an Intel i7 4770k (4 physical cores) with a Stanford Bunny mesh (112k faces): 64³ resolution: 59 ms 128³ resolution: 71 ms 256³ resolution: 134 ms 512³ resolution: 409 ms 1024³ resolution: 2918 ms 2048³ resolution: 28509 ms Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Very fast for solid voxelization; simple implementation; parallelizable. Limitations: Not memory efficient; less accurate for complex internal structures; prone to missing infill not aligned with world axes; does not handle edge collisions as robustly as the '--safe' mode. When to Use: Use when raw speed is the primary concern and the mesh is relatively simple or does not require precise internal structure representation. Avoid when memory is constrained or high accuracy for complex internal geometries is required. The method is part of the 3DStuff voxelizer project, an open-source tool for converting polygonal meshes into voxel data. It was developed as a high-performance alternative to more memory-intensive voxelization techniques, specifically targeting the '--fast' mode use case for generating solid voxel models. 3DStuff/voxelizer, https://github.com/3DStuff/voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Image-space Voxelization
head: FBO-based Voxelization, Legolizer Voxelization
body: Image-space voxelization projects the vertices of a triangular mesh into a 2D image stored in a Frame Buffer Object (FBO) to determine voxel locations and colors. It solves the problem of converting boundary models into volumetric representations by leveraging GPU rasterization hardware, specifically using a single render pass and a single buffer to preserve original vertex colors, unlike methods requiring multiple passes or z-buffer stacks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangular mesh M already residing on the GPU, a grid size parameter size, and a cube size parameter r. Output: A Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) containing the voxelized data, where each pixel in the FBO corresponds to a vertex in the VBO. Data Structures: FBO Layout: The Frame Buffer Object stores vertex color in the RGB channels (representing x, y, z coordinates) and the normalized voxel number in the Alpha channel. VBO Layout: Each pixel downloaded from the FBO becomes a vertex in the VBO. Parameters: size: The dimension of the cubic voxel grid. r: The cube size, used to determine voxel indices and geometry generation. Steps: 1. Create an FBO. 2. Set an orthogonal projection to the FBO. 3. Enable the mapping shader. 4. Draw the mesh M (which is already on the GPU). 5. Disable the mapping shader. 6. Download the FBO data. 7. Create a VBO from the downloaded FBO data. 8. Return the VBO pointer. Vertex Shader Logic: The vertex shader computes the voxel index for each vertex vp with color vc. 1. Let voxelxyz \leftarrow vc{xyz}. 2. Compute the linearized 3D grid index: voxelw = \text{int}(vpx) \times size^2 + \text{int}(vpy) \times size + \text{int}(vpz) where vpx, vpy, vpz are the projected vertex coordinates. 3. If voxelw is outside the valid grid range, set voxelw \leftarrow \text{NULL}. 4. Compute the normalized voxel number: voxelw{normalized} = \frac{voxelw}{size^3} This value is stored in the Alpha channel of the FBO. 5. Emit the voxel as a pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(vp: tuple, vc: tuple, size: int) -> tuple: # vp: Vertex 3D Position (projected coordinates) # vc: Vertex Color (RGB, representing xyz) # size: Grid size # Returns: (colorrgb, alphanormalizedvoxelindex) voxelxyz = vc voxelw = int(vp[0]) (size size) + int(vp[1]) size + int(vp[2]) if voxelw < 0 or voxelw >= size 3: return None, None # NULL value prevents invalid voxel generation voxelwnormalized = voxelw / (size size size) return vc, voxelwnormalized Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vertices outside the defined grid receive a null value for voxelw to prevent invalid voxel generation. Vertices written to the same position in the FBO are overwritten by the Z-buffer test, meaning only the front surface is completely displayed, while back surfaces may contain holes. Holes in back surfaces can be avoided by increasing the frame buffer resolution or mesh refinement. Uses accumulation buffers for solid voxelization. Choose when anti-aliasing or transparency handling is required. A-Buffer Solid Voxelization Adapts voxel density based on geometry complexity. Choose for memory efficiency in sparse scenes. Adaptive Sparse Voxelization with Bounding Box Thickness Cases Generates voxels directly in the geometry shader stage. Choose for fine-grained control over voxel generation per primitive. Geometry Shader Voxelization General GPU-based grid generation techniques. Choose for broader grid generation needs beyond image-space projection. GPU Mesh Voxelizer (Grid Generation) Rasterizes onto a derived grid structure. Choose when the grid structure is non-uniform or derived from scene data. Derived Grid Rasterization Handles unstructured meshes via containment tests. Choose for non-tetrahedral/unstructured input data. Unstructured Mesh Pixelization via Convex Element Containment Uses raycasting for solid voxelization. Choose for high-accuracy solid interiors. Fast Solid Voxelization via Planar Raycasting Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of vertices in the mesh, as it involves a single draw call and shader execution per vertex. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the FBO size (size^2 for the 2D image) and the resulting VBO size. Performance: Uses a single render pass and a single buffer, making it faster than methods requiring six passes and six z-buffers. Strengths: Preserves original voxel colors; efficient single-pass rasterization; leverages GPU hardware. Limitations: Back surfaces may contain holes due to Z-buffer occlusion; resolution limited by FBO size and mesh refinement. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method is part of the Legolizer system. It was developed to create LEGO representations from boundary models in real-time. The approach differs from earlier methods by Karabassi et al. and Passalis et al., which used six z-buffers and six passes, by utilizing a single render pass and buffer. The method relies on mesh subdivision to ensure vertices sample the surface well, allowing the image-space projection to create a good volumetric approximation. name: GPU Volume Kernel Voxelization
head: Compute Shader Voxelization, Parallel XY Voxelization
body: GPU Volume Kernel Voxelization is a technique that accelerates the voxelization of triangle meshes by parallelizing the iteration over the 2D XY plane of the voxel grid using a GPU compute shader. It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based voxelization, where nested loops over X and Y coordinates are executed sequentially. Unlike Rasterization-based Voxelization and 3D Grid Rasterization which project geometry into 3D textures, this method retains the explicit triangle-voxel intersection logic of CPU implementations but distributes the workload across GPU threads, achieving significant speedups (e.g., 50x) for high-resolution grids. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh (vertices and indices), voxel grid dimensions (Width, Height, Depth), and voxel unit size. Output: A GPUVoxelData object containing the populated voxel buffer and grid metadata. Data Structures: Voxel Buffer: A 1D array or structured buffer representing the 3D grid. Access is performed via a helper function getvoxelindex(x, y, z) which maps 3D coordinates to the buffer offset. Mesh Buffers: Vertex and triangle buffers (vertBuffer, triBuffer) are bound to the compute shader context before dispatch and released afterward. Parameters: Thread Group Size: 8×8×1 threads per group (ThreadX=8, ThreadY=8, ThreadZ=1). Grid Limits: Width, Height, and Depth define the maximum bounds of the voxel grid. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a compute shader kernel named "Volume" and bind the voxel buffer to it using a set buffer command. 2. Dispatch Calculation: Calculate the number of thread groups to dispatch. The X and Y group counts are derived from dividing the grid width and height by the thread group dimensions, adding 1 to each to handle remainders (ceiling division). GroupsX = \lfloor Width / ThreadX \rfloor + 1. GroupsY = \lfloor Height / ThreadY \rfloor + 1. GroupsZ = ThreadZ. 3. Kernel Execution: Dispatch the compute shader with the calculated group counts. 4. Per-Thread Processing (Inside Kernel): Retrieve the global thread ID (x, y, z) from SVDispatchThreadID. Clamp or check bounds: If x \ge Width or y \ge Height, return immediately. Iterate through all Z depths from 0 to Depth - 1. For each Z, calculate the voxel index and retrieve the voxel data from the buffer. Perform the voxelization logic (triangle-voxel intersection) similar to the CPU implementation. 5. Cleanup: Release the mesh data buffers (vertBuffer, triBuffer) as they are no longer needed after the kernel completes. 6. Return: Construct and return a GPUVoxelData object containing the voxel buffer, dimensions, and unit size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def Volume(idx, idy, idz, Width, Height, Depth, VoxelBuffer): x = int(idx) y = int(idy) if x >= Width: return if y >= Height: return for z in range(Depth): # getvoxelindex(x, y, z) maps 3D coordinates to buffer offset; implementation not provided in sources. voxelindex = getvoxelindex(x, y, z) voxel = VoxelBuffer[voxelindex] # The source states processing continues "Almost the same as in CPUVoxelizer.Voxelize", # but does not provide the specific triangle-voxel intersection algorithm details. def rungpuvoxelization(meshvertices, meshindices, Width, Height, Depth, Unit, VoxelBuffer): # 1. Initialize kernel and bind buffers # Create compute shader kernel "Volume" and bind VoxelBuffer to "VoxelBuffer" # 2. Dispatch ThreadX = 8 ThreadY = 8 ThreadZ = 1 GroupsX = (Width // ThreadX) + 1 GroupsY = (Height // ThreadY) + 1 GroupsZ = 1 # Dispatch compute shader with groups (GroupsX, GroupsY, GroupsZ) # 3. Cleanup # Release mesh vertex and index buffers (vertBuffer, triBuffer) # 4. Return result return GPUVoxelData(VoxelBuffer, Width, Height, Depth, Unit) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Remainder Handling: The dispatch calculation adds 1 to the X and Y group counts to ensure coverage of grid dimensions that are not exact multiples of the thread group size. Bounds Checking: Explicit checks (if x >= Width) are required inside the kernel because the dispatch may launch threads beyond the valid grid range due to the ceiling division. Memory Management: Mesh buffers must be explicitly released after the kernel execution to free GPU memory, as they are not automatically garbage collected in some contexts. Performance: Under test conditions (Windows 10, Core i7, 32GB RAM, GeForce GTX 980, mesh with 5319 vertices/9761 triangles, resolution 256), the GPU implementation runs approximately 50 times faster than the CPU implementation. Scaling: Performance depends heavily on the execution environment, the number of polygons in the mesh, and the voxel resolution. Strengths: Significant speedup for real-time applications; leverages GPU parallelism for the XY iteration loop. Limitations: Coloring/texture application is more difficult compared to rendering-based methods; the method relies on explicit triangle-voxel intersection which can be computationally intensive per voxel. When to use: When real-time voxelization of complex meshes is required and the primary bottleneck is the iteration over the voxel grid rather than the intersection calculation itself. When not to use: When accurate texture mapping or coloring of voxels is a primary requirement, as rendering-based methods (projecting to 3D texture) are easier for coloring. This method was introduced in the context of real-time GPU-based voxelization for Unity, specifically to accelerate the voxelization of mesh models for applications like particle systems. It builds upon the concept of CPU-based voxelization by replacing the sequential XY loops with a parallel compute shader kernel. The approach contrasts with methods that construct voxel data by rendering the model from XYZ directions into a 3D texture via parallel projection.
