name: GPU Mesh Voxelization via Plane/Projection Tests
head: GPU Voxelization via Plane and 2D Projection Tests, Solid Voxelization via Triangle Projection
body: This method converts a triangle mesh into a solid 3D voxel grid on the GPU by explicitly testing every voxel within a triangle's bounding box against the triangle's plane equation and its 2D projections on the XY, YZ, and ZX planes. It is distinguished from its sibling GPU Voxelization via Projection and Bitmasking by using full 3D plane and projection tests for every voxel rather than a compact bitmask per voxel to store depth occupancy, making it suitable for general solid voxelization where explicit geometric containment is required. Inputs: triangledata: A flat array of floats containing vertex positions. Each triangle consists of 9 floats (v{0x}, v{0y}, v{0z}, v{1x}, \dots, v{2z}). voxeltable: An array of unsigned int (32-bit) representing the voxel grid, where each bit corresponds to a voxel. gridsize: A 3D vector (Gx, Gy, Gz) defining the resolution of the voxel grid. bbox: An axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the mesh in world coordinates, defined by min and max vectors. mortonorder: A boolean flag determining if voxels are encoded using Morton codes (Z-order curve) or linear row-major indexing. morton256x, morton256y, morton256z: Device constants (lookup tables) for Morton encoding, each 256 uint32t elements, used if mortonorder is true. Outputs: voxeltable: Updated such that bits corresponding to filled voxels are set to 1. Data Structures: AABox<T>: A template struct with fields min and max of type T (typically float3). voxinfo: A struct containing bbox (AABox<float3>), gridsize (uint3), ntriangles (sizet), and unit (float3, the voxel size). Vec3(self.yo.z - self.zo.y, self.zo.x - self.xo.z, self.xo.y - self.yo.x) def length(self): return math.sqrt(self.dot(self)) def normalize(self): l = self.length(); return self if l == 0 else self (1.0/l) def min(self, o): return Vec3(min(self.x, o.x), min(self.y, o.y), min(self.z, o.z)) def max(self, o): return Vec3(max(self.x, o.x), max(self.y, o.y), max(self.z, o.z)) class Vec2: def dot(self, o): return self.xo.x + self.yo.y def neg(self): return Vec2(-self.x, -self.y) def mortonencode(x, y, z, morton256x, morton256y, morton256z): # Source uses 8-bit LUTs for Morton encoding return (morton256x[x & 0xFF] | (morton256y[y & 0xFF] << 8) | (morton256z[z & 0xFF] << 16)) def checkpointtriangle(p, v0, v1, v2): # Standard barycentric coordinate test d1 = (p.x - v2.x) (v0.y - v2.y) - (p.y - v2.y) (v0.x - v2.x) d2 = (p.x - v0.x) (v1.y - v0.y) - (p.y - v0.y) (v1.x - v0.x) d3 = (p.x - v1.x) (v2.y - v1.y) - (p.y - v1.y) (v2.x - v1.x) hasneg = (d1 < 0) or (d2 < 0) or (d3 < 0) haspos = (d1 > 0) or (d2 > 0) or (d3 > 0) return 0 if (hasneg and haspos) else 1 def setbit(voxeltable, index, mortonorder, morton256x, morton256y, morton256z, gridsize): if mortonorder: location = mortonencode(index.x, index.y, index.z, morton256x, morton256y, morton256z) else: location = index.x + index.y gridsize.x + index.z (gridsize.y gridsize.x) intlocation = location // 32 bitpos = 31 - (location % 32) voxeltable[intlocation] |= (1 << bitpos) def voxelizekernel(triangledata, voxeltable, info, morton256x, morton256y, morton256z): threadid = 0 # Simplified for Python; in CUDA: threadIdx.x + blockIdx.x blockDim.x stride = 1 # Simplified while threadid < info.ntriangles: t = threadid 9 v0 = Vec3(triangledata[t], triangledata[t+1], triangledata[t+2]) - info.bbox.min v1 = nyze2 = Vec2(-1.0 e2.z, e2.y) if n.x < 0.0: nyze0 = -nyze0 nyze1 = -nyze1 nyze2 = -nyze2 dyze0 = (-1.0 nyze0.dot(Vec2(v0.y, v0.z))) + max(0.0, info.unit.y nyze0.y) + max(0.0, info.unit.z nyze0.z) dyze1 = (-1.0 nyze1.dot(Vec2(v1.y, v1.z))) + max(0.0, info.unit.y nyze1.y) + max(0.0, info.unit.z nyze1.z) dyze2 = (-1.0 nyze2.dot(Vec2(v2.y, v2.z))) + max(0.0, info.unit.y nyze2.y) + max(0.0, info.unit.z nyze2.z) nzxe0 = Vec2(-1.0 e0.x, e0.z) nzxe1 = Vec2(-1.0 e1.x, e1.z) nzxe2 = Vec2(-1.0 e2.x, e2.z) if n.y < 0.0: nzxe0 = -nzxe0 nzxe1 = -nzxe1 nzxe2 = -nzxe2 dzxe0 = (-1.0 nzxe0.dot(Vec2(v0.z, v0.x))) + max(0.0, info.unit.z nzxe0.z) + max(0.0, info.unit.x nzxe0.x) dzxe1 = (-1.0 nzxe1.dot(Vec2(v1.z, v1.x))) + max(0.0, info.unit.z nzxe1.z) + max(0.0, info.unit.x nzxe1.x) dzxe2 = (-1.0 nzxe2.dot(Vec2(v2.z, v2.x))) + max(0.0, info.unit.z nzxe2.z) + max(0.0, info.unit.x nzxe2.x) tbboxworldmin = v0.min(v1.min(v2)) tbboxworldmax = v0.max(v1.max(v2)) tbboxgridmin = tbboxworldmin / info.unit tbboxgridmax = tbboxworldmax / info.unit tbboxgridmin = Vec3(max(0, int(tbboxgridmin.x)), max(0, int(tbboxgridmin.y)), max(0, int(tbboxgridmin.z))) tbboxgridmax = Vec3(min(info.gridsize.x, int(tbboxgridmax.x)), min(info.gridsize.y, int(tbboxgridmax.y)), min(info.gridsize.z, int(tbboxgridmax.z))) for z in range(tbboxgridmin.z, tbboxgridmax.z + 1): for y in range(tbboxgridmin.y, tbboxgridmax.y + 1): for x in range(tbboxgridmin.x, tbboxgridmax.x + 1): p = Vec3(x info.unit.x, y info.unit.y, z info.unit.z) nDOTp = n.dot(p) if (nDOTp + d1) (nDOTp + d2) > 0.0: continue pxy = Vec2(p.x, p.y) if (nxye0.dot(pxy) + dxye0 < 0.0) or \ (nxye1.dot(pxy) + dxye1 < 0.0) or \ (nxye2.dot(pxy) + dxye2 < 0.0): continue pyz = Vec2(p.y, p.z) if (nyze0.dot(pyz) + dyze0 < 0.0) or \ (nyze1.dot(pyz) + dyze1 < 0.0) or \ (nyze2.dot(pyz) + dyze2 < 0.0): continue pzx = Vec2(p.z, p.x) if (nzxe0.dot(pzx) + dzxe0 < 0.0) or \ (nzxe1.dot(pzx) + dzxe1 < 0.0) or \ (nzxe2.dot(pzx) + dzxe2 < 0.0): continue setbit(voxeltable, Vec3(x, y, z), info.mortonorder, morton256x, morton256y, morton256z, info.gridsize) threadid += stride Alternative Projection-Based Variant (from S2 notes): The sources also describe a variant that projects triangles onto the YZ plane, iterates over the 2D bounding box, and fills voxels along the X-axis up to the intersection. 1. Project vertices to YZ plane: v{yz} = (v.y, v.z). 2. Ensure counter-clockwise winding in YZ plane. 3. Compute 2D bounding box in grid indices. 4. Iterate over (y, z) in the 2D box. 5. Check if voxel center (y, z) is inside the projected triangle. 6. Calculate max X index (x{max}) by intersecting a ray from the voxel center along the X-axis with the triangle plane: x{max} = \lfloor \frac{\text{get\x\coordinate}(n, v0, \text{point})}{\text{info.unit.x}} - 0.5 \rfloor. 7. Iterate x from 0 to x{max} and set bits. Converts a mesh to a voxel grid by rasterizing triangles into a bitmask representation. It projects triangles onto 2D planes and tests voxel occupancy against triangle edges using plane equations, updating a 32-bit integer bitmask per voxel to represent occupancy along the depth axis (Z). It is distinguished by using a compact bitmask per voxel to store depth occupancy, reducing memory usage compared to storing a boolean or float per voxel, which is efficient for sparse or thin geometry. Not given in the sources. It builds on GPU Mesh Voxelization (Schwarz & Seidel 2010) by using compute shaders or CUDA kernels to parallelize the voxel testing process. The specific plane and projection test approach is detailed in unofficial sources related to CUDA voxelization implementations. name: GPU Voxelization via Projection and Bitmasking
head: hpsoar/voxelizer
body: This method converts a triangle mesh into a 3D voxel grid on the GPU by rasterizing triangles into a bitmask representation. It projects triangles onto 2D planes, tests voxel occupancy against triangle edges using plane equations, and updates a 32-bit integer bitmask per voxel to represent occupancy along the depth axis (Z). It is distinguished from its sibling GPU Mesh Voxelization via Plane/Projection Tests by using a compact bitmask per voxel to store depth occupancy, reducing memory usage compared to storing a boolean or float per voxel, which is efficient for sparse or thin geometry. Inputs: Triangle mesh vertices (vertices): array of floats, size 3 \times N{verts}. Triangle mesh indices (triangles): array of integers, size 3 \times N{tris}. Voxel grid parameters: bbox0: minimum bounds of the voxel grid (float[3]). delta: voxel size (float[3]). invdelta: inverse voxel size (float[3]). stride: stride for accessing voxels in memory (int[3]). vols: pointer to the voxel grid array (int). Outputs: vols: array of integers representing the voxel grid. Each voxel is a 32-bit integer. The bitmask at index (x, y, z) corresponds to the z-th bit of the integer at voxel(x, y, z). Data Structures: vols: int array. The layout is linearized 3D. Access to voxel (x, y, z) is calculated as vols + z stride[Z] + y stride[Y] + x stride[X]. tribbox0, tribbox1: bounding box of the current triangle in world space (float[3]). Steps: 1. Compute Triangle Bounding Box: For each triangle, determine its axis-aligned bounding box in world space, tribbox0 and tribbox1. 2. Map to Voxel Indices: Calculate the voxel grid range [start, end] for the triangle using the inverse voxel size. start[i] = (tri\bbox0[i] - bbox0[i]) \times inv\delta[i] end[i] = (tri\bbox1[i] - bbox0[i]) \times inv\delta[i] where i \in \{X, Y, Z\}. These values are floats representing the fractional voxel indices. 3. Calculate Integer and Bit Indices: Determine the range of 32-bit integer blocks along the Z-axis. int\begin = \lfloor start[Z] \rfloor \gg 5 bit\begin = \lfloor start[Z] \rfloor \ \& \ 31 int\end = \lfloor end[Z] \rfloor \gg 5 bit\end = \lfloor end[Z] \rfloor \ \& \ 31 Note: The source code uses start[Z] >> 5 which implies integer division by 32. Since start is float, it is cast to int (truncated) before shifting. 4. Preprocess for Optimization: Determine the primary axis (X, Y, or Z) for optimization based on the bounding box dimensions. If start[X] == end[X], the triangle is degenerate in X. If start[Y] == end[Y], the triangle is degenerate in Y. If start[Z] == end[Z], the triangle is degenerate in Z. The preprocessing logic sets an axis flag and handles degenerate cases by setting bits directly or returning early. 5. Iterate 2D Range: If not degenerate, iterate over the 2D range perpendicular to the primary axis. For a standard case, this involves iterating over x and y within [start[X], end[X]] and [start[Y], end[Y]]. 6. Projection Test: For each voxel (x, y) in the 2D range, perform a projection test to determine if the voxel's column intersects the triangle's projection on the XY plane. Compute edge vectors: e0 = v1 - v0, e1 = v2 - v1, e2 = v0 - v2. Compute plane distances for the triangle normal n and edges. The projection test checks if the point (x, y) is inside the triangle's 2D projection. This is done by evaluating the sign of the cross product or plane equation for each edge. Specifically, the code computes ndxy for each edge, which represents the plane equation parameters for the projection. If the projection test fails, skip this voxel. 7. Compute Bitmask: If the voxel is inside the triangle's projection, compute the bitmask of occupied voxels along the depth axis (Z). Iterate z from start[Z] to end[Z]. For each z, check if the point p = (x, y, z) is inside the triangle in 3D. The condition is: (n \cdot p + d1) \times (n \cdot p + d2) \le 0, where d1 and d2 are distances computed from the triangle vertices and normal. Additionally, perform projection tests on the YZ and ZX planes to ensure the point is within the triangle's extent in all dimensions. If the point is inside, set the z-th bit in the bitmask. 8. Atomic Update: Atomically OR the computed bitmask into the voxel's integer in the vols array. atomicOr(vol\ptr, bits) Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: GPU-based Voxelization via Compute Shader
head: PGP-Voxelize
body: A technique to convert 3D triangle meshes into a voxel grid representation using a GPU compute shader. It solves the problem of generating a 3D boolean occupancy grid from mesh geometry by offloading the marking logic to the GPU. Unlike CPU-based voxelization, this method leverages parallel compute shaders to mark occupied cells in a global grid buffer. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D model file (OBJ format) containing vertices (v) and faces (f), and a user-defined resolution parameter representing the number of voxels along the X-axis. Output: A 3D boolean grid indicating occupied voxels and a list of world positions for those occupied cells. Data Structures: 1. Model Data: vertices: List of 3D points (float x, y, z). triangles: List of vertex indices forming faces. boundboxmin, boundboxmax: Axis-aligned bounding box of the mesh. 2. GPU Buffers: SSBO 0 (Binding Point 0): Stores triangle vertex data. SSBO 1 (Binding Point 1): Voxel grid. Type: array of 32-bit integers (GLint). Size: gridsize sizeof(GLint) where gridsize = width height depth. Initialized to zero. Parameters: resolution: User-defined integer, voxels along X-axis. step: Voxel size (float). width, height, depth: Grid dimensions (integers). Steps: 1. Parse Model: Read OBJ file. Extract vertices and faces. Calculate boundboxmin and boundboxmax. 2. Calculate Grid Dimensions: step = (boundboxmax.x - boundboxmin.x) / resolution. width = resolution. height = ceil((boundboxmax.y - boundboxmin.y) / step). depth = ceil((boundboxmax.z - boundboxmin.z) / step). 3. Upload Data: Upload vertex data to SSBO 0. Allocate and zero-initialize SSBO 1 for the voxel grid. 4. Dispatch Compute Shader: Dispatch size in X: vbosize + 32 - (vbosize % 32) (rounded up to multiple of 32). Dispatch size in Y: 1. Dispatch size in Z: 1. The compute shader iterates over the input data and marks occupied voxels in SSBO 1. 5. Memory Barrier: Ensure writes to SSBO 1 are visible to subsequent host reads. 6. Readback: Map SSBO 1 to host memory. Iterate through the 3D grid (z, y, x). If voxels[zheightwidth + ywidth + x] == 1, compute world position: boundboxmin + (xstep, ystep, zstep). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class WPVector: def init(self, x=0.0, y=0.0, z=0.0): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): if isinstance(other, tuple): return WPVector(self.x + other[0], self.y + other[1], self.z + other[2]) return WPVector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def voxelize(objpath, resolution): # 1. Parse Model vertices = [] triangles = [] boundboxmin = WPVector(float('inf'), float('inf'), float('inf')) boundboxmax = WPVector(float('-inf'), float('-inf'), float('-inf')) with open(objpath, 'r') as f: for line in f: parts = line.split() if not parts: continue if parts[0] == 'v': x, y, z = float(parts[1]), float(parts[2]), float(parts[3]) vertices.append(WPVector(x, y, z)) if x < boundboxmin.x: boundboxmin.x = x if y < boundboxmin.y: boundboxmin.y = y if z < boundboxmin.z: boundboxmin.z = z if x > boundboxmax.x: boundboxmax.x = x if y > boundboxmax.y: boundboxmax.y = y if z > boundboxmax.z: boundboxmax.z = z elif parts[0] == 'f': triangles.append([int(idx.split('/')[0]) - 1 for idx in parts[1:4]]) # 2. Calculate Grid Dimensions step = (boundboxmax.x - boundboxmin.x) / resolution width = resolution height = math.ceil((boundboxmax.y - boundboxmin.y) / step) depth = math.ceil((boundboxmax.z - boundboxmin.z) / step) gridsize = width height depth # 3. Setup GPU Buffers vbosize = len(vertices) # SSBO 0: Vertex data (uploaded to GPU) ssbovertices = vertices # SSBO 1: Voxel grid (allocated and zero-initialized on GPU) ssbogrid = [0] gridsize # 4. Dispatch Compute Shader dispatchx = vbosize + 32 - (vbosize % 32) dispatchy = 1 dispatchz = 1 # The compute shader kernel runs here, iterating over triangles/vertices # and marking occupied voxels in ssbogrid. Exact rasterization logic is not provided. # 5. Memory Barrier # Host waits for GPU completion and ensures SSBO 1 visibility. # 6. Readback and Extract Voxels occupiedvoxels = [] for z in range(depth): for y in range(height): for x in range(width): index = z height width + y width + x if ssbogrid[index] == 1: pos = boundboxmin + (x step, y step, z step) occupiedvoxels.append(pos) return occupiedvoxels Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point calculations for step and bounding box extents may introduce small errors. Ensure consistent rounding modes when mapping grid indices to world coordinates. Boundary Conditions: The ceil function for height and depth ensures full coverage but may create empty voxels at the edges if the bounding box extents are not perfectly divisible by step. Dispatch Alignment: The dispatch size is rounded up to a multiple of 32 for wavefront/warp alignment. If vbosize is small, this may lead to idle threads. Uses a bit-packed voxel table and sparse extraction. Choose when memory efficiency for large grids is critical. Builds a DAG for sparse representation. Choose for highly sparse scenes. Focuses on surface voxels. Choose when only surface representation is needed. Uses plane tests. Choose for different rasterization strategies. Time Complexity: The compute shader dispatch is proportional to the number of vertices (rounded to a multiple of 32). Host readback is proportional to the grid size. Memory Complexity: O(gridsize) for the voxel grid SSBO. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Leverages GPU parallelism for marking occupied cells. Simple implementation structure. Limitations: Uses a dense grid representation, which is memory intensive for large volumes. No anti-aliasing or coverage information is mentioned. name: Multi-channel Surface Voxelization
body: Multi-channel surface voxelization is a real-time GPU technique that rasterizes 3D geometry into a uniform voxel grid while simultaneously computing and storing multiple surface attributes (such as albedo, normals, and spherical harmonics coefficients) per voxel. It distinguishes itself from binary occupancy voxelization methods by supporting partial occupancy, transparency, and rich multi-channel data in a single pass, albeit at a higher computational cost. The method generates a uniform spatial partitioning structure on the GPU using two distinct single-pass algorithms: Triangle Slicing and Pixel Shader Fragment Clipping. Both approaches rely on a geometry shader to prepare data for a pixel shader that writes to multiple render targets (MRTs). Inputs: 3D scene geometry (triangles), voxel grid resolution (N \times N \times N), viewing direction (for sweeping), and a list of requested attributes (e.g., albedo, normals, SH coefficients). Outputs: A set of floating-point buffers representing the voxel grid. One buffer stores occupancy (half-float, 16-bit), while others store the requested attributes (floating-point, 32-bit). Voxel Grid: A 3D array of size N^3. Occupancy Buffer: 16-bit half-float buffer indicating if a voxel is occupied. Attribute Buffers: 32-bit floating-point buffers for surface attributes, dynamic lighting, and radiance values represented as compact spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. This method splits triangles that intersect volume slices into smaller primitives to ensure accurate coverage. 1. Geometry Shader Processing: For each triangle, determine if it intersects the current sweeping direction's volume slices. If a triangle spans multiple slices, it is split. A quad-shaped triangle strip is generated for each split segment. The number of output vertices from the geometry shader is 3 + 4n, where n is the number of splits. The geometry shader emits the split primitives along with the slice boundaries in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC). 2. Pixel Shader Processing: The pixel shader is virtually empty; it does not perform complex lighting calculations but writes the pre-computed multi-channel data to the MRTs. Data is written to the appropriate volume layer based on the slice index provided by the geometry shader. This method avoids triangle splitting in the geometry shader, relying instead on fragment rejection in the pixel shader. 1. Geometry Shader Processing: For each triangle aligned with the current sweeping direction, the geometry shader rasterizes it into all volume slices it intersects. The geometry shader computes the slice boundaries in NDC: z{Min} \leftarrow \min(\text{depth of slice in NDC}) z{Max} \leftarrow \max(\text{depth of slice in NDC}) The geometry shader emits the triangle vertices with the computed z{Min} and z{Max} values as flat inputs to the pixel shader. 2. Pixel Shader Processing: For each fragment generated by rasterization, the pixel shader checks if its depth lies within the slice boundaries: python if fragdepth < zMin or fragdepth > zMax: discardfragment() else: writemultichanneldatatovolume() If the fragment is within bounds, the multi-channel data is written to the volume buffer. Geometry Shader Output Limit: The maximum number of vertices the geometry shader can output. A higher limit reduces holes in the voxelization but increases memory bandwidth usage. Voxel Grid Resolution: Typically tested at 64^3, 128^3, and 256^3. Number of MRTs: Depends on the number of attributes requested (e.g., 1 for occupancy, 2-3 for albedo/normals/SH). Holes in Voxelization: If the geometry shader output vertex limit is too low (e.g., 3 vertices), triangles may be partially sliced, resulting in empty voxels or holes. This is particularly problematic for dense volumes required by fluid effects. Performance Scaling: Running times vary significantly with the number of requested output vertices. For unified GPU architectures, the triangle count is indicative of the best approach. Animation Optimization: For slow or gradual animations, the three directional voxelization steps can be interleaved, recalculating only one axis pass per frame, reducing volume buffer creation time by a factor of 3. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of triangles, voxel grid resolution, and the number of MRTs. Performance scales with the number of output vertices from the geometry shader. Memory Complexity: Proportional to N^3 \times C, where N is the grid resolution and C is the number of channels (occupancy + attributes). Measured Performance: Tested on an Intel Core i7 860 @ 2.80GHz with an nVIDIA GeForce GTX 285 GPU. For a 64^3 grid with 3 MRTs, the Triangle Slicing method took 2.36 ms, while Pixel Shader Clipping took 1.33 ms. For a 256^3 grid with 3 MRTs, Triangle Slicing took 10.2 ms (slicing output used) or 25.1 ms (clipping output used), while Pixel Shader Clipping took 15.8 ms (clipping output used) or 24.3 ms (slicing output used). Strengths: Supports multi-channel data, partial occupancy, and transparency in a single pass. Faster than methods requiring multiple passes over geometry data. Limitations: Slower than binary occupancy-only voxelization methods. Requires careful tuning of geometry shader output limits to avoid holes. When to Use: Real-time deferred rendering, smoke/fluid simulations, visibility computations, and global illumination effects where multi-channel data is beneficial. When Not to Use: When binary occupancy is sufficient and performance is critical, or when the geometry shader output limit cannot be increased to avoid holes in dense volumes. The method was introduced in a 2011 short paper by the authors of "Two Simple Single-pass GPU methods for Multi-channel Surface Voxelization of Dynamic Scenes". It was integrated into a real-time deferred renderer using OpenGL and GLSL. The work compares favorably to earlier methods by Fang et al. [FC00] and Eisemann et al. [ED06], offering a balance between speed and data richness. Two Simple Single-pass GPU methods for Multi-channel Surface Voxelization of Dynamic Scenes, https://doi.org/10.2312/pe/pg/pg2011short/031-036, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: GPU Rasterization-based Octree Building
head: GPU-based Mesh Voxelization, Hierarchical Voxelization, Octree Build, Octree Generation from Voxel Data, Rasterization Octree Construction, Real-time Mesh Voxelization and Octree Building, Real-time Voxelization
body: GPU Rasterization-based Octree Building is a technique for constructing sparse voxel octrees directly on the GPU by exploiting the rasterization pipeline to identify occupied leaf nodes. It solves the problem of efficiently generating hierarchical voxel data for fully dynamic scenes by rasterizing geometry from multiple orthogonal directions to eliminate boundary holes inherent in single-pass methods. Unlike sibling methods that may require pre-processing or specific primitive types, this approach handles any hardware-supported rasterizable geometry in a single geometry submission pass, leveraging 32-bit integer textures and bitwise operations for high performance. It differs from GPU Voxelization via Compute Shaders by using rasterization fragments to drive the octree traversal rather than a purely compute-based atomic accumulation, and from GPU Mesh Voxelization (Schwarz & Seidel 2010) by explicitly building the hierarchical octree structure during the rasterization phase rather than just filling a flat voxel grid. The method constructs an octree representation of the voxel world by traversing from the root level to the leaf level, setting bits in a storage buffer to indicate occupied octants. It supports fully dynamic scenes by building the octree once for static parts and updating it interactively for moving objects. Inputs: Triangle mesh geometry (static and dynamic). Scene bounds and resolution parameters. A 3D texture of voxel data (texture3d<u32>) for reading voxel occupancy. Outputs: An octree structure stored in a global buffer, where nodes are allocated via atomic counters. Leaf values (bricks) stored in a shared brick buffer. The implementation relies on specific buffer layouts and texture formats. 1. Voxel Texture (voxels): A 3D texture of type texture3d<u32>. Each texel stores 4 voxels packed into 32 bits, with each voxel occupying 8 bits. Access requires bit-shifting based on the local position within the texel. 2. Octree Buffer (octreeBuffer): An array of 32-bit atomic integers. It stores the occupancy bits of the octree nodes. 3. Scene Data (sceneData): A uniform buffer containing worldWidth (total width of the voxel world), octantSize (size of the root octant), and other traversal parameters. 4. Node Buffer: A global shared buffer for allocating node structures. Nodes are allocated using an atomic increment of a global shared counter. 5. Brick Buffer: A shared buffer for leaf values, allocated similarly to nodes. 6. Thread List: A global list for deferred execution of threads that encounter mutex contention. The algorithm proceeds in rasterization passes and shader execution. Initialize traversal variables based on scene parameters: baseDim = sceneData.worldWidth / sceneData.octantSize texWidth = 256u (fixed for the implementation in) texHeight = baseDim level = 0u octSize = sceneData.octantSize The mesh is rasterized three times, along the three main axes of the scene. Viewport Resolution: Set to the maximum octree level resolution (e.g., 512 \times 512 for a 512^3 octree). Depth Test: Disabled to prevent early culling, ensuring at least one fragment shader thread is generated per potentially existing leaf node. Each thread corresponds to a potential leaf node position. The entry point uses a workgroup size of (8, 4, 8). It assumes a fragment shader context where id is the global invocation ID or fragment coordinate. Step 3.1: Early Exit Check If the voxel at the current position is empty, exit immediately: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. if GetVoxel(id) == 0u: return Note: GetVoxel extracts the 8-bit value from the packed 32-bit texture. Step 3.2: Octree Traversal Traverse the octree from the root to the leaf level. Loop through octree levels: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. while True: octantPos = id // octSize dimAtLevel = baseDim >> level # Check if position exceeds current level dimensions if any(octantPos >= vec3<u32>(dimAtLevel)): break # Calculate linear index in octree buffer zOffset = (sceneData.worldWidth / sceneData.octantSize) level texZ = octantPos.z + zOffset linearIndex = (texZ texHeight + octantPos.y) texWidth + octantPos.x # Calculate bit position within the 32-bit word wordIndex = linearIndex // 4 byteInWord = linearIndex % 4 bitOffset = byteInWord 8 # Set the bit using atomicOr atomicOr(&octreeBuffer[wordIndex], 1 << bitOffset) level += 1 octSize = 2 Step 3.3: Node Subdivision and Allocation When a node needs subdivision (determined by the traversal logic and occupancy): 1. Allocate a set of 2 \times 2 \times 2 sub-nodes in the global shared node buffer using an atomic increment of a global shared counter. 2. Write the address of the new sub-nodes to the 'child' pointer of the subdivided node. Step 3.4: Mutex Handling Use a per-node mutex to ensure subdivision is performed only by the first thread, preventing incoherent structures from parallel conflicts. Threads that cannot proceed due to mutex contention put themselves in the global thread list for deferred execution. Step 3.5: Leaf Value Writing Write values in leaves directly inside the brick associated with the nodes. Allocate bricks similarly to nodes inside a shared brick buffer. At the end of the rasterization pass, deferred threads are re-run (in a vertex shader) and values written in the tree. Repeat deferred passes as long as the global thread list is not empty. This mechanism avoids expensive active waiting loops. For animated objects: 1. Rasterize animated objects every frame. 2. New voxels cannot overwrite existing static parts. 3. Static elements are stored at the end of the buffers to allow fast clearing every frame and prevent overwriting. The following pseudocode combines the traversal logic from with the structural allocation and deferred execution strategy from. It assumes a fragment shader context where id is the global invocation ID or fragment coordinate. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. octreeBuffer = [] # Simulates array<atomic<u32>> nodeBuffer = [] # Simulates array<Node> brickBuffer = [] # Simulates array<Brick> threadList = [] # Simulates array<ThreadTask> nodeCounter = 0 # Simulates atomic<u32> brickCounter = 0 # Simulates atomic<u32> mutexBuffer = [] # Simulates array<atomic<u32>> for per-node mutex scenedata = { 'worldWidth': 0, 'octantSize': 0, 'baseDim': 0, 'texWidth': 256, 'texHeight': 0 } def GetVoxel(voxelpos): # Load from texture at (voxelpos[0] >> 1, voxelpos[1], voxelpos[2] >> 1) packed = textureLoad(voxelTexture, (voxelpos[0] >> 1, voxelpos[1], voxelpos[2] >> 1)) # Shift count based on local position shiftCount = (voxelpos[0] & 0x1) | ((voxelpos[2] & 0x1) << 1) # Mask and extract 8-bit value mask = 255 << (shiftCount << 3) return (packed & mask) >> (shiftCount << 3) def AllocateNode(): return atomicAdd(&nodeCounter, 1) def AllocateBrick(): return atomicAdd(&brickCounter, 1) def ComputeMain(id): # 1. Early Exit if GetVoxel(id) == 0: return # 2. Initialize Traversal baseDim = scenedata['worldWidth'] // scenedata['octantSize'] texWidth = 256 texHeight = baseDim level = 0 octSize = scenedata['octantSize'] # 3. Traverse and Build Octree while True: octantPos = id // octSize dimAtLevel = baseDim >> level # Check bounds if any(octantPos >= (dimAtLevel, dimAtLevel, dimAtLevel)): break # Calculate Linear Index in Octree Buffer zOffset = (scenedata['worldWidth'] // scenedata['octantSize']) level texZ = octantPos[2] + zOffset linearIndex = (texZ texHeight + octantPos[1]) texWidth + octantPos[0] # Calculate Bit Position wordIndex = linearIndex // 4 byteInWord = linearIndex % 4 bitOffset = byteInWord 8 # Set Bit atomicOr(&octreeBuffer[wordIndex], 1 << bitOffset) # Subdivision Logic # When a node needs subdivision, allocate 2x2x2 sub-nodes # Use per-node mutex to ensure only first thread subdivides mutexId = linearIndex # Simplified mutex ID mapping if atomicCompareExchange(&mutexBuffer[mutexId], 0, 1) == 0: childAddr = AllocateNode() # Write child pointer to parent node nodeBuffer[childAddr].child = AllocateNode() # Standard node layout update # Allocate bricks for leaves if level == 8: # Assuming max level 8 for 512^3 octree for i in range(8): brickAddr = AllocateBrick() # Write voxel data to brick brickBuffer[brickAddr].data[i] = GetVoxel(id) else: # Mutex Contention: Defer execution threadList.append(id) return # Move to next level level += 1 octSize = 2 def DeferredPass(): while not threadList.empty(): task = threadList.pop() # Re-run traversal logic for deferred threads ComputeMain(task) Viewport Resolution: Corresponds to the max octree level (e.g., 512 \times 512). Extensions: NVshaderbufferload and NVshaderbufferstore are used for CUDA-like video memory pointers and atomic operations in OpenGL shaders. Workgroup Size: (8, 4, 8). Mutex Contention: Active waiting loops are too expensive. A global thread list is required for deferred execution. Boundary Holes: Single-direction rasterization causes holes. Rasterizing three times along the main axes solves this. Overwriting Static Data: Dynamic updates must not overwrite static parts. Static elements are stored at the end of buffers to allow fast clearing. Precision: Bit manipulation in atomicOr requires careful calculation of wordIndex, byteInWord, and bitOffset to avoid race conditions on the same 32-bit word. This method constructs an octree from triangle meshes by recursively subdividing nodes and querying GPU-accelerated CUDA kernels for geometric intersection and signed distance calculations. It differs from fully GPU-side octree builds by performing the recursive subdivision logic on the CPU while offloading expensive geometric queries (bounding box computation, intersection tests, and signed distance calculations) to parallel CUDA kernels. Hierarchical Binary-Scene Voxelization is a robust, real-time method for computing a multi-resolution binary volumetric representation (octree) of a scene directly on the GPU. It solves the problem of generating voxel data for fully dynamic scenes by rasterizing geometry from three orthogonal directions and unioning the results, thereby eliminating the boundary holes inherent in single-direction rasterization methods like Eisemann and D´ecoret. Unlike sibling methods that may require pre-processing or specific primitive types, this approach handles any hardware-supported rasterizable geometry in a single geometry submission pass, leveraging 32-bit integer textures and bitwise operations for high performance. Time Complexity: The rasterization pass generates one thread per potentially occupied leaf node. Deferred execution adds overhead proportional to the number of mutex conflicts. Memory Complexity: The octree buffer size is proportional to the number of nodes in the octree. The node and brick buffers are allocated dynamically via atomic counters. Performance: Real-time performance is achieved by leveraging the GPU rasterization pipeline and atomic operations. Strengths: Supports fully dynamic scenes, handles any rasterizable geometry, eliminates boundary holes, and is efficient on GPU hardware. Limitations: Requires extensions for atomic buffer operations (e.g., NVshaderbufferload). Deferred execution can add latency if there is high contention. When to Use: Real-time indirect illumination, dynamic scenes, sparse voxel octrees. When Not to Use: Static scenes where offline precomputation is acceptable, or hardware without support for atomic buffer operations. The method was introduced in the paper "Interactive Indirect Illumination Using Voxel Cone Tracing". It was developed to enable real-time indirect illumination by efficiently building and filtering a sparse voxel octree from triangle meshes. The key contribution was the real-time mesh voxelization and octree-building algorithm that exploits the GPU rasterization pipeline. The method supports fully dynamic scenes by updating the octree interactively with moving objects or dynamic modifications. name: GPU Octree Voxelization via Triangle-AABB Intersection
head: CUDA Octree Voxelization, Parallel Voxelization via Octree Construction
body: This method constructs an octree from triangle meshes by recursively subdividing nodes and querying GPU-accelerated CUDA kernels for geometric intersection and signed distance calculations. It differs from fully GPU-side octree builds by performing the recursive subdivision logic on the CPU while offloading expensive geometric queries (bounding box computation, intersection tests, and signed distance calculations) to parallel CUDA kernels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of triangle meshes, where each triangle is represented as a glm::fmat3x3 (3x3 matrix of floats, where each row is a vertex glm::fvec3). Output: An octree structure rooted at mroot, where each node contains an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB), a node type, and a signed distance value. Data Structures: 1. AABB: Defined as struct AABB { glm::fmat2x3 mbox; glm::fvec3 mcenter; };. mbox: A 2x3 float matrix representing the minimum and maximum coordinates of the box. mcenter: The center point of the AABB. 2. Node: Defined as struct Node { AABB mbox; float msingeddist; int mnodetype; Node mparent; Node mchildren[8]; };. mnodetype: Enum values include NTLEAF, NTINTERNEL, NTEMPTY. msingeddist: Stores the shortest distance from the node center to the surface. 3. Triangle Mesh: Stored in device memory as an array of glm::fmat3x3. Parameters: voxelsize: Default value is 1. gridSize: CUDA grid dimension, default dim3(256). blockSize: CUDA block dimension, default dim3(256). The source uses dim3 which allows 3D dimensions, but 1D is implied by the loop logic. Algorithm Steps: 1. Memory Allocation: Allocate device memory for the triangle meshes and copy data from host to device. 2. Root Initialization: Create the root node and compute its AABB by calling the parallel bounding box kernel getBoundingBox. 3. Recursive Subdivision: Call recSubDivision on the root node. For each node, check for intersection with triangles using isBoxleIntersectsTriangle. If Intersection is True: If Leaf Condition Met (e.g., dim == voxeldim): Set node type to NTLEAF. Calculate signed distance using calcLeafNodeSignedDistance kernel. Store result in msingeddist. If Internal Node: Set node type to NTINTERNEL. Initialize 8 children. Set each child's AABB using setAABB. Recursively call recSubDivision on each child. If Intersection is False: Set node type to NTEMPTY. Calculate signed distance using calcLeafNodeSignedDistance kernel. Store result in msingeddist. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildoctree(trimeshes, voxelsize=1.0): # 1. Memory Allocation dtrimeshes = cudamalloc(len(trimeshes) sizeof(glmfmat3x3)) cudamemcpy(dtrimeshes, trimeshes, len(trimeshes) sizeof(glmfmat3x3)) # 2. Root Initialization root = Node() root.mbox = getboundingbox(dtrimeshes, len(trimeshes)) root.mparent = None root.mchildren = [None] 8 # 3. Recursive Subdivision recsubdivision(root, dtrimeshes, len(trimeshes), voxelsize) return root def recsubdivision(node, dtrimeshes, numtriangles, voxelsize): isintersect = isboxintersectstriangle(dtrimeshes, node.mbox.min, node.mbox.max) if isintersect: if node.dim == voxelsize: node.mnodetype = NTLEAF node.msingeddist = calcleafnodesigneddistance(dtrimeshes, node.mbox.center) else: node.mnodetype = NTINTERNEL node.msingeddist = 0.0 for i in range(8): child = Node() child.mparent = node child.mbox = setaabb(node.mbox, i) node.mchildren[i] = child recsubdivision(child, dtrimeshes, numtriangles, voxelsize) else: node.mnodetype = NTEMPTY node.msingeddist = calcleafnodesigneddistance(dtrimeshes, node.mbox.center) Geometric Kernels: 1. Bounding Box Reduction (findRecudedBoundingBox): Uses shared memory scache for parallel reduction. Uses a mutex (atomicCAS) to handle atomic min/max operations since CUDA lacks native atomic min/max for floats. Formula for min/max update: \text{box}{min} = \min(\text{box}{min}, \text{cache}{min}) \text{box}{max} = \max(\text{box}{max}, \text{cache}{max}). 2. Signed Distance Calculation (calcLeafNodeSignedDistance): Iterates over all triangles to find the closest point on any triangle to the node center. Uses findClosestPointOnTriangle to compute the closest point using barycentric coordinates. Formula for closest point: \text{closestPoint} = \text{triangle}[0] + s \cdot \text{edge0} + t \cdot \text{edge1} where edge0 = triangle[1] - triangle[0] and edge1 = triangle[2] - triangle[0]. Barycentric coordinates s and t are computed using dot products: a = \text{dot}(\text{edge0}, \text{edge0}) b = \text{dot}(\text{edge0}, \text{edge1}) c = \text{dot}(\text{edge1}, \text{edge1}) \text{det} = a \cdot c - b^2. The specific cases for s and t depend on the position of the projection relative to the triangle edges. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intersection Test Implementation: The isBoxleIntersectsTriangle function is declared but has an empty body in the source code, meaning intersection testing is not implemented. Memory Allocation Efficiency: calcLeafNodeSignedDistance allocates memory on host and device for every call, which is inefficient. Mutex Size: The source uses cudaMemset(dmutex, 0, sizeof(float)) instead of sizeof(int), which may cause issues if the mutex is expected to be an integer. Time complexity is not given in the sources. Memory complexity is not given in the sources. Strengths: Leverages GPU parallelism for expensive geometric queries. Limitations: The recursive CPU-side control flow may lead to kernel launch overhead. The source code has incomplete intersection testing. This method is described in the "ParallelVoxelizer" project by allenkim0129. It is a GPU-accelerated voxelization technique that constructs an octree from triangle meshes. allenkim0129/ParallelVoxelizer, https://github.com/allenkim0129/ParallelVoxelizer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical Binary-Scene Voxelization
head: GPU-based Hierarchical Voxelization, Real-Time Hierarchical Binary-Scene Voxelization
body: Hierarchical Binary-Scene Voxelization is a robust, real-time method for computing a multi-resolution binary volumetric representation (octree) of a scene directly on the GPU. It solves the problem of generating voxel data for fully dynamic scenes by rasterizing geometry from three orthogonal directions and unioning the results, thereby eliminating the boundary holes inherent in single-direction rasterization methods like Eisemann and D´ecoret. Unlike sibling methods that may require pre-processing or specific primitive types, this approach handles any hardware-supported rasterizable geometry in a single geometry submission pass, leveraging 32-bit integer textures and bitwise operations for high performance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of rasterizable geometric primitives and a defined world-space bounding box for the voxel grid. Output: A mipmapped 32-bit integer RGBA texture representing a hierarchical binary octree. Data Structures: The core data structure is a single mipmapped 32-bit integer RGBA texture attached to a Frame Buffer Object (FBO). Base Resolution: The width (w) and height (h) of the texture correspond to the viewport dimensions. Voxel Encoding: Each texel stores a 32-bit integer across its RGBA channels, representing a column of 32 voxels along the Z-axis, where one bit corresponds to one voxel in the column. Depth Extension: By using N Multiple Render Targets (MRTs), the total depth resolution becomes 32 \times N. For example, 8 MRTs provide a depth of 1024 cells. Hierarchy: Each mip-level L corresponds to an octree depth level. A texel at level L represents a 2 \times 2 block of texels from level L-1 in the X-Y plane. The value of a texel at level L is the bitwise OR of its four parent texels from level L-1. Parameters: Grid Resolution: Defined by viewport width w, height h, and depth discretization (32 cells per RGBA channel). A typical example is a 128^3 grid. Texture Format: 32-bit integer RGBA. Projection: Orthographic camera projection is required to ensure non-deformed voxelization. Rendering State: Face culling and z-test are disabled; no z-buffer is attached to the FBO. Algorithm Steps: 1. Geometry Transformation (Geometry Shader): The input geometry is processed by a Geometry Shader. The geometry is transformed and emitted three times, corresponding to three viewing directions: -X, -Y, and -Z. These three transformed versions are rendered into three layers of a layered texture in a single draw call to avoid multiple geometry submissions and reduce bandwidth. 2. Fragment Program Execution (Per Direction): For each fragment generated by the rasterization of the transformed geometry, the following logic is executed in the Fragment Program: a. World Space Z Calculation: Compute the world space Z coordinate (fPosW.z) of the fragment by transforming the fragment position using the viewport-to-world matrix. b. Grid Index Calculation: Map the world space Z coordinate to the grid's discrete Z-index. Let minZ and maxZ be the grid boundaries. Let gridParams.z be the scaling factor \frac{127}{maxZ - minZ}. index{local} = (fPosW.z - minZ) \times gridParams.z c. Channel and Bit Selection: Determine which color channel (Red, Green, Blue, Alpha) and which bit within that channel corresponds to index{local}. The channels represent ranges of 32 bits: Red: indices 0-31 Green: indices 32-63 Blue: indices 64-95 Alpha: indices 96-127 Let channel\offset be 0, 32, 64, or 96 based on the range containing index{local}. Let bit\index = index{local} - channel\offset. d. Mask Generation: Create a 32-bit mask with a single bit set at bit\index. mask = 1 \ll bit\index e. Framebuffer Update: Perform a bitwise OR between the generated mask and the existing content of the framebuffer pixel using the GPU's logical operation support for 32-bit integers. 3. Union of Directions (GPGPU Pass): After rendering the geometry from the three directions (-X, -Y, -Z), a GPGPU pass unions the three resulting grids into a final grid texture. This step ensures that voxels intersected by surfaces with slopes close to the grid axes are correctly filled, preventing holes. 4. Hierarchical Octree Generation (Mipmapping): The hierarchical structure is generated using standard GPU mipmapping operations. For each mip-level L > 0: Texel(L, x, y, z) = Texel(L-1, 2x, 2y, z) \lor Texel(L-1, 2x+1, 2y, z) \lor Texel(L-1, 2x, 2y+1, z) \lor Texel(L-1, 2x+1, 2y+1, z) where \lor denotes the bitwise OR operation. This process aggregates the binary occupancy from the finest level up to the root. The Z-resolution remains constant across all mip-levels in this basic representation, though Z-direction mip-reduction is possible by ORing groups of bits within a texel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevoxelmask(worldz, minz, scale): # Map world Z to grid index [0, 127] idx = (worldz - minz) scale if idx < 0 or idx >= 128: return 0 # Determine channel offset (0, 32, 64, 96) if idx >= 96: offset = 96 elif idx >= 64: offset = 64 elif idx >= 32: offset = 32 else: offset = 0 bit = int(idx - offset) return 1 << bit def hierarchicalvoxelization(geometry, minz, maxz, w, h, nummrts): # Grid: 2D array of 32-bit integers. Each int stores 32 voxels in Z. # Total depth = nummrts 32. grid = [[0] w for in range(h)] scale = 127.0 / (maxz - minz) vtwzrow = [0, 0, 1, 0] # Z-row of viewport-to-world matrix # Step 1 & 2: Render from three directions (-X, -Y, -Z) # Geometry is transformed by a Geometry Shader into 3 layers. directionalgrids = [] for in range(3): passgrid = [[0] w for in range(h)] # GPU rasterization step produces fragments with screen coords and world-space positions for frag in gpurasterize(geometry): worldz = (frag.pos[0] vtwzrow[0] + frag.pos[1] vtwzrow[1] + frag.pos[2] vtwzrow[2] + frag.pos[3] vtwzrow[3]) frag.pos[3] mask = computevoxelmask(worldz, minz, scale) x, y = frag.screencoords passgrid[y][x] |= mask directionalgrids.append(passgrid) # Step 3: Union the three grids finalgrid = [[0] w for in range(h)] for y in range(h): for x in range(w): finalgrid[y][x] = directionalgrids[0][y][x] | directionalgrids[1][y][x] | directionalgrids[2][y][x] # Step 4: Generate mipmaps (X-Y aggregation only, Z constant) mipmaps = [finalgrid] currw, currh = w, h while currw > 1 or currh > 1: neww = max(1, currw // 2) newh = max(1, currh // 2) nextlevel = [[0] neww for in range(newh)] for y in range(newh): for x in range(neww): val = 0 for dy in range(2): for dx in range(2): if y 2 + dy < currh and x 2 + dx < currw: val |= mipmaps[-1][y 2 + dy][x 2 + dx] nextlevel[y][x] = val mipmaps.append(nextlevel) currw, currh = neww, newh return mipmaps Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes in Boundary Representation: Single-direction rasterization creates holes where surface slopes are close to the grid's Z-axis. This method avoids this by rasterizing from three orthogonal directions and unioning the results. Precision: The method relies on 32-bit integer arithmetic. Correct mapping from floating-point world coordinates to integer grid indices is required to avoid off-by-one errors. Depth Range: The grid depth is limited by the number of MRTs and channels. For depths exceeding 1024, texture tiling must be used. Time Complexity: The voxelization is a hardware rasterization process, making it highly efficient. Performance is largely independent of the fragment processing complexity, as the bottleneck is the fixed-function rasterizer. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the grid resolution. A 512^3 grid requires 16 MB (using 4 MRTs). The theoretical maximum with 8 MRTs and tiling is a 4096^3 grid (8 GB). Measured Performance: On a G80 GPU, for a 128^3 grid: Knot model: 2.5 ms Tree model: 17.5 ms Spheres model: 1.5 ms Disabling fragment processing yields similar times, confirming the fixed-function bottleneck. Strengths: Robustness: No holes in the voxel representation. Speed: Real-time performance (milliseconds). Simplicity: No pre-processing of geometry required; works with any rasterizable primitive. Dynamic Scenes: Suitable for fully dynamic, animated, or deformed scenes. Limitations: Requires GPU support for 32-bit integer textures, geometry shaders, and logical operations. Orthographic projection is required for non-deformed voxelization. When to Use: Ideal for visibility computations, hierarchical collision detection, and CSG operations in dynamic scenes where speed and robustness are critical. When Not to Use: When perspective projection is strictly required without distortion correction, or when the hardware does not support the necessary 32-bit integer texture features. The method was introduced in a 2009 publication. It builds upon earlier work by Eisemann and D´ecoret (2006) and Zhao et al. (Dong et al., 2004). Eisemann and D´ecoret used a single slice map which suffered from holes, while Zhao et al. required pre-processing and was limited to triangles. This method leverages advanced GPU functionalities, such as geometry shaders and 32-bit integer formats, to achieve robust, single-pass voxelization. It is particularly well-suited for applications like constructive solid geometry (CSG), shape repair, and collision detection. name: GPU Voxelizer using Nearest Vertex and Normal Dot Product
head: Compute Shader Voxelizer, GPUVoxelizer
body: This method is a real-time voxelization technique that determines if a voxel is inside, on the edge, or outside a mesh by finding the nearest vertex on the mesh for each voxel and using the dot product between the ray from the vertex to the voxel and the vertex normal to determine interiority. It differs from sibling methods like GPU Mesh Voxelization (Schwarz & Seidel 2010) and Multi-channel Surface Voxelization by avoiding traditional rasterization for the voxelization pass, instead relying on direct vertex proximity checks executed in a compute shader. The source implementation explicitly notes that the dot-product interiority logic is considered buggy and is often superseded by distance-only checks in practice. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A mesh defined by an array of vertices (position and normal) and a voxel grid defined by an array of entities (voxel positions and scales). Output: A voxel grid where each voxel's scale (opacity/visibility) is updated based on its proximity to the mesh surface and interiority. Data Structures: The implementation uses two std430 buffers in a compute shader: 1. entities (Binding 0): An array of particle structs representing voxels. position: vec4 (xyz: voxel center, w: unused/padding). scale: vec4 (xyz: unused/padding, w: opacity/visibility factor). 2. meshdata (Binding 1): An array of meshData structs representing the mesh. position: vec4 (xyz: vertex position, w: unused/padding). normal: vec4 (xyz: vertex normal, w: unused/padding). Parameters: meshdataCount: Uniform integer specifying the number of vertices in the mesh to test against. voxelSize: Uniform float specifying the size of each voxel, used as the threshold for edge detection. Steps: 1. Initialize a compute shader with a local group size of (1024, 1, 1). 2. Each work item corresponds to one voxel, identified by the global invocation ID gid. 3. Retrieve the voxel's position p from the entities buffer at index gid. 4. Iterate through all meshdataCount vertices in the meshdata buffer to find the nearest vertex. 5. Calculate the squared Euclidean distance d between the voxel position p and each vertex position vi: d = (p.x - vi.x)^2 + (p.y - vi.y)^2 + (p.z - vi.z)^2 (Implemented as pow(d1, 2.0) + pow(d2, 2.0) + pow(d3, 2.0) in the source). 6. Track the minimum squared distance nearDist and the index nearestIndex of the closest vertex. 7. Calculate the vector from the nearest mesh vertex to the voxel: toCell = \text{normalize}(p - \text{meshdata}[nearestIndex].position). 8. Calculate the dot product between the normalized vector to the cell and the mesh vertex normal: dotProduct = \text{dot}(toCell, \text{meshdata}[nearestIndex].normal). 9. Determine the "inside" factor using a step function with a threshold of -0.9: isInside = 1 - \text{step}(-0.9, dotProduct) If dotProduct \le -0.9, the ray from the vertex to the voxel is opposed to the normal, indicating the voxel is inside the mesh. 10. Determine the "edge" factor based on the distance to the nearest vertex: fDist = 1 - \text{step}(voxelSize, \sqrt{nearDist}) If \sqrt{nearDist} < voxelSize, the voxel is considered on the edge. 11. Calculate the final voxel scale using the maximum of the edge factor and the inside factor: voxelScale = \max(fDist, isInside). 12. Write the calculated scale to the scale component (w) of the voxel entity in the entities buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processvoxel(gid, entities, meshdata, meshdataCount, voxelSize): # 1. Retrieve voxel position p = entities[gid].position.xyz # 2. Find nearest vertex by brute-force iteration neardistsq = float('inf') nearestindex = -1 for i in range(meshdataCount): vpos = meshdata[i].position.xyz dx = p.x - vpos.x dy = p.y - vpos.y dz = p.z - vpos.z distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz if distsq < neardistsq: neardistsq = distsq nearestindex = i # 3. Calculate vectors nearestvpos = meshdata[nearestindex].position.xyz nearestvnorm = meshdata[nearestindex].normal.xyz tocellx = p.x - nearestvpos.x tocelly = p.y - nearestvpos.y tocellz = p.z - nearestvpos.z # Normalize tocell, handling degenerate case where voxel center coincides with vertex mag = (tocellx2 + tocelly2 + tocellz2)0.5 if mag > 0.0: tocellx /= mag tocelly /= mag tocellz /= mag else: tocellx, tocelly, tocellz = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # 4. Dot product dotproduct = tocellx nearestvnorm.x + \ tocelly nearestvnorm.y + \ tocellz nearestvnorm.z # 5. Determine factors # isInside: 1 if dotproduct <= -0.9, else 0 isinside = 1.0 if dotproduct <= -0.9 else 0.0 # fDist: 1 if sqrt(neardistsq) < voxelSize, else 0 dist = neardistsq0.5 fdist = 1.0 if dist < voxelSize else 0.0 # 6. Final scale voxelscale = max(fdist, isinside) # 7. Write output entities[gid].scale.w = voxelscale Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Buggy Logic: The source explicitly notes that the dot-product method for determining interiority is considered "bugged" and that the final effective logic often relies primarily on the distance check (fDist) rather than the combination with isInside. Implementers should be aware that isInside may produce incorrect results for non-convex or complex meshes where the nearest vertex is not a reliable indicator of interiority. Precision: The squared distance calculation uses floating-point arithmetic. For very large meshes or high-precision requirements, precision loss in neardistsq tracking may occur. Degenerate Input: If a voxel center coincides exactly with a mesh vertex, the toCell vector has zero magnitude. The pseudocode handles this by setting the vector to zero, which results in a dot product of 0. Since 0 > -0.9, isInside becomes 0. The voxel will only be marked if it is within voxelSize of the vertex (which it is, distance 0), so fDist will be 1. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot V), where N is the number of voxels (work items) and V is the number of mesh vertices (meshdataCount), as each voxel iterates through all vertices to find the nearest one. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Tested on NVIDIA GTX 1070 and 1060 GPUs. The implementation is noted as not being the most optimized version. Strengths: Simple brute-force logic; fully GPU-accelerated via compute shaders. Limitations: Linear scaling with vertex count; dot-product interiority detection is unreliable for complex geometry and noted as buggy in the source. This technique originates from an unofficial implementation by alexr4 (Bonjour Lab) for the Processing.org environment, aiming to provide a real-time voxelization solution using GPU compute shaders. It was developed as a practical experiment for real-time rendering and voxel display, tested on consumer NVIDIA hardware. alexr4/Processing-GPUVoxelizer, https://github.com/alexr4/Processing-GPUVoxelizer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: GPU Voxelization
head: Basic GPU Voxelization, GPU Rasterization-based Voxelization, GPU Voxelization via GPU Rasterization, GPU Voxelization via Orthogonal Rasterization, Render-to-Volume, Voxelization using 3D Texture UAV, Voxelization via GPU Rasterization
body: GPU Voxelization converts a triangle mesh into a regular voxel grid representation by leveraging the GPU's hardware rasterization pipeline. It maps each fragment generated by the rasterizer to a specific cell in the voxel grid and writes data into that cell, typically using a 3D texture bound as an Unordered Access View (UAV) or a Shader Storage Buffer Object (SSBO). Unlike CPU-based ray-tracing methods which are slow due to serial intersection tests, this method parallelizes the conversion across the GPU. It distinguishes itself from its sibling 3D Grid Rasterization by using standard orthographic projection and viewport mapping rather than explicit 3D grid traversal, and from GPU Voxelization via Compute Shaders by relying on the fixed-function rasterizer rather than manual thread dispatch. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh (vertices, indices), voxel grid resolution (W, H, D), and voxel step size (edge length). Output: A voxel grid (3D texture or SSBO) marking occupied voxels, optionally with color or density data. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: A 3D texture bound as a UAV or a 1D SSBO int cnts[] of size W \times H \times D. 2. Projection Matrices: Clip-space projection matrix: Orthographic matrix mapping vertex positions to [-1, 1] for width/height and [0, 1] for depth (Device Normalized Coordinates). Voxel-space projection matrix: Orthographic matrix mapping input coordinates to [0, W] for width, [0, H] for height, and [0, D] for depth. 3. Camera: Orthographic camera positioned outside the mesh's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) along the projection axis, with a frustum slightly larger than the AABB range (e.g., 1.2 \times range). Steps: 1. Compute AABB: Iterate over all mesh vertices to find min/max x, y, z coordinates to determine the mesh's AABB. 2. Calculate Resolution: Determine voxel grid resolution based on the AABB range and a fixed step size (voxel edge length): \text{Resolution} = \lfloor \text{Range} / \text{step} \rfloor + 1 where Range is the extent of the AABB along each axis. 3. Setup Render Target: Allocate a 3D texture bound as a UAV or an SSBO of size W \times H \times D initialized to 0. Disable depth testing and back-face culling to ensure all triangles are processed regardless of orientation or depth. 4. Transform Vertices: In the Vertex Shader, transform vertex positions into the voxel grid coordinate system (or clip space for rasterization). 5. Rasterize: Rasterize the transformed primitives using a viewport matching the dimensions of the voxel grid's 2D projection (W \times H). The orthogonal viewport frustum covers the voxel grid exactly, such that rasterized pixel position/depth correspond to the X, Y, Z components of the voxel grid. 6. Write Voxels (Fragment Shader): Map each rasterized fragment to one or more voxels. Calculate the voxel index from the fragment's world position or rasterized coordinates. Write data (e.g., increment a counter or set a flag) to the voxel grid using atomic operations to handle concurrent writes. Formulas: Voxel Index Calculation (Fragment Shader): Given fragment world position FragPos, box minimum boxMin, step size step, and resolution resolution: x = \lfloor (FragPos.x - boxMin.x) / step \rfloor y = \lfloor (FragPos.y - boxMin.y) / step \rfloor z = \lfloor (FragPos.z - boxMin.z) / step \rfloor index = y \times (resolution.z \times resolution.x) + z \times resolution.x + x Homogeneous Coordinates (Voxel Space): After applying the voxel-space projection matrix, divide the x, y, z components of the resulting position vector by its w-component to map to voxel cell coordinates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(position, clipspaceprojectionmatrix): # Transform vertex to clip space using orthographic projection # Maps to [-1, 1] for x/y, [0, 1] for depth return clipspaceprojectionmatrix @ vec4(position, 1.0) def fragmentshaderssbo(fragworldpos, boxMin, step, resolution, voxelcounts): # Calculate voxel coordinates from world position x = floor((fragworldpos.x - boxMin.x) / step) y = floor((fragworldpos.y - boxMin.y) / step) z = floor((fragworldpos.z - boxMin.z) / step) # Calculate linear index in SSBO index = y (resolution.z resolution.x) + z resolution.x + x # Atomically increment the voxel counter voxelcounts[index] += 1 # Atomic increment assumed def fragmentshaderuav(clippos, primmin, primmax, voxpos, resolution, voxelextenth, voxelcenter, colordata, voxelgrid): # SVPosition.xy are pixel coordinates, SVPosition.z is depth # Map to voxel coordinates voxelposf = vec3(clippos.x, clippos.y, clippos.z resolution.z) voxelmin = voxelposf - Typical value depends on scene scale. Viewport: Must be aligned with a face of the voxel grid and have dimensions matching one of the 2D projections of the voxel grid. Scene Normalization Matrix: Scales the scene to fit in a 1 \times 1 \times 1 cube centered at the origin, then translates it. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cracks: Occur when the depth gradient of the primitive exceeds 1.0 (calculated via ddx(depth) and ddy(depth) in the pixel shader). This happens when triangles are parallel to the projection plane, projecting to lines/zero area. Holes: Changing projection directions per primitive can cause gaps where no primitive covers a pixel center. Extra Voxels: Manual conservative rasterization (edge expansion) shades extra pixels not covered by the primitive, leading to unnecessary pixel shader calls and incorrect voxels. VoxelPipe is a highly flexible, programmable software pipeline for triangle voxelization implemented in CUDA. It solves the problem of converting triangle meshes into voxel grids with support for fully conservative and thin voxelizations, arbitrary render targets (boolean, floating-point, vector), and user-defined shaders. It distinguishes itself from prior binary voxelizers by supporting arbitrary framebuffer types and programmability via vertex and fragment shaders, tackling load balancing via a tile-based algorithm instead of assigning individual triangles to single threads with global memory atomics, and optimizing the triangle/box overlap test. Conservative rasterization is a technique used during voxelization to prevent artifacts where small triangles (smaller than the voxel grid resolution) are ignored completely, resulting in holes in the voxelized mesh. It ensures that all voxels potentially intersected by a triangle are covered by rasterization. Two primary implementations exist: Geometric Dilatation, which explicitly enlarges triangles in clip space within the geometry shader, and MSAA Approximation, which leverages Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing to invoke the pixel shader if any subsample is covered, approximating conservative behavior without explicit edge expansion. The MSAA approach is often preferred for its simplicity and lack of redundant voxels compared to edge extension. An extension of single-view voxelization that uses three orthographic cameras (along X, Y, Z axes) and selects the best view for each triangle based on its normal vector to prevent cracks caused by degenerate projections. It creates three orthographic cameras looking along the negative X, negative Y, and negative Z axes, positioned outside the AABB. In the Geometry Shader, it computes the triangle face normal using the cross product of two edge vectors derived from input vertices. It selects the camera index by comparing the absolute values of the normal's components: n{DX} = |nx|, n{DY} = |ny|, n{DZ} = |nz|. Selection is based on \text{argmax}(n{DX}, n{DY}, n{DZ}). The triangle vertices are then transformed using the selected View-Projection matrix and emitted. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot D) for the voxel grid storage. Performance: Extremely fast due to parallelization on the GPU, leveraging existing rasterization hardware. However, it can be memory-intensive for high-resolution grids. Strengths: High speed, simplicity of implementation using standard graphics APIs, parallel processing. Limitations: Prone to cracks and holes if not handled with conservative rasterization or multi-view techniques. Single projection direction causes cracks when triangles are parallel to the projection plane. Manual conservative rasterization can produce extra voxels. When to use: When real-time or near-real-time voxelization of triangle meshes is required, and the hardware supports the necessary features (e.g., UAVs, MSAA, or conservative rasterization). When not to use: When exact geometric accuracy is required without hardware conservative rasterization support, or when memory bandwidth is severely constrained for very high-resolution grids. GPU Voxelization was popularized by Michael Schwarz and NVIDIA, leveraging the GPU's rasterization pipeline to convert triangle meshes into voxel grids. It emerged as a solution to the inefficiency of CPU-based ray-tracing voxelization methods, which required serial intersection tests for every voxel. The method is widely used in real-time global illumination techniques like Voxel Cone Tracing and in physics simulations such as Position Based Dynamics. name: VoxelPipe
body: VoxelPipe is a highly flexible, programmable software pipeline for triangle voxelization implemented in CUDA. It solves the problem of converting triangle meshes into voxel grids with support for fully conservative and thin voxelizations, arbitrary render targets (boolean, floating-point, vector), and user-defined shaders. It distinguishes itself from prior binary voxelizers by supporting arbitrary framebuffer types and programmability via vertex and fragment shaders, tackling load balancing via a tile-based algorithm instead of assigning individual triangles to single threads with global memory atomics, and optimizing the triangle/box overlap test. VoxelPipe implements two distinct pipelines depending on the output mode: a sort-middle tile-based rasterizer for blending-based (standard) voxelization, and a sort-last feedforward pipeline for A-buffer (bucketing) generation. Inputs: Triangle mesh (vertices, indices), voxel grid resolution, voxelization type (thin or conservative), render target type (boolean, float, vector), and optional user-defined vertex/fragment shaders. Outputs: A 3D voxel grid. In standard mode, each voxel contains a blended value (e.g., max-blended normal). In A-buffer mode, each voxel contains a list of all fragments belonging to it. The pipeline relies on efficient sorting primitives to avoid inter-thread communication queues. Coarse Tiles: The 3D grid is divided into coarse tiles. The tile size is limited by shared memory constraints; for floating-point buffers, the maximum tile size is 16^3. Triangle/Tile Pairs: Lists of triangles overlapping each coarse tile are generated during the coarse raster stage. Fragments: Generated in the fine raster stage. In A-buffer mode, fragments are sorted into voxels. This mode uses a sort-middle pipeline divided into two stages: coarse raster and fine raster. 1. Coarse Raster: The grid is divided into coarse tiles. Triangle setup is performed. An overlap test determines which triangles intersect which coarse tiles. Triangles overlapping each tile are emitted, creating a list of triangle/tile pairs. Triangles are sorted into tiles using efficient sorting primitives. 2. Fine Raster: Each coarse tile is assigned to a single GPU core (thread block). The core generates fragments for all triangles in its assigned tile list. Blending is performed in shared memory to resolve fragment conflicts (e.g., max-blending for normals). The resulting voxel values are written to global memory. Triangle/Box Overlap Test: The overlap test is an extension of the 2D variant by Möller and Aila [2005], as described by Schwarz and Seidel [2010], with factorized computations. It determines if a triangle intersects a voxel box. The specific implementation details of the factorization are not provided in the sources. This mode performs 3D binning of triangles over uniform grids using a sort-last pipeline. 1. Batching: Input triangles are batched by size and orientation. 2. Fragment Generation: Fragments are generated for all triangles. 3. Sorting: Fragments are sorted by voxel ID using efficient sorting primitives. 4. Fragment Storage: User-defined fragment shaders store specific fragment data, including interpolated attributes generated using barycentric coordinates, into the voxel lists. Unlike previous binning systems that store plain triangle ID lists, VoxelPipe stores full fragment data. Tile Size: Limited to 16^3 for floating-point buffers due to shared memory constraints. Voxelization Type: Fully conservative or thin. Separation: Supports accurate 6-separating and 26-separating voxelization. Hairball Scene Performance: In floating-point buffers, the Hairball scene (2.88M triangles) performs poorly (<2x better than Schwarz and Seidel 2010) at high resolutions. This is due to: 1) Limited tile size (16^3) increasing coarse raster work (sorting more triangle/tile pairs). 2) Many long/skinny triangles generating variable fragment counts, leading to low SIMT utilization in the fine raster stage. Shared Memory Constraints: The tile size limit for floating-point buffers is a hard constraint imposed by hardware shared memory limits. A sort-middle tile-based rasterization pipeline divided into coarse raster and fine raster stages. Coarse raster divides the grid into coarse tiles, performs triangle setup, and emits triangles overlapping each tile. Fine raster assigns each tile to a core, generates fragments, and performs blending in shared memory. Advantages include load balancing by breaking large triangles across multiple tiles and reduced expensive memory bandwidth by doing heavy-lifting in the upper memory hierarchy (shared memory). Performance: VoxelPipe is up to 28 times superior to state-of-the-art binary voxelizers (Schwarz and Seidel 2010) and up to 4 times faster than previous triangle binning implementations (Kalojanov and Slusallek 2009; Kalojanov et al. 2011). Hardware: Benchmarks were run on a GeForce GTX480 GPU with 1GB GPU memory and an Intel Core i7 860 @ 2.8GHz CPU with 4GB main memory. Timing Breakdown (Binary Voxelization): Conference (282k triangles): 128 res: Coarse 0.5ms, Sorting 0.7ms, Fine 2.2ms. 512 res: Coarse 0.5ms, Sorting 1.2ms, Fine 2.6ms. 1024 res: Coarse 0.6ms, Sorting 1.4ms, Fine 6.4ms. Hairball (2.88M triangles): 128 res: Coarse 2.1ms, Sorting 2.4ms, Fine 7.9ms. 512 res: Coarse 2.3ms, Sorting 4.8ms, Fine 10.7ms. 1024 res: Coarse 2.8ms, Sorting 6.9ms, Fine 24.0ms. Asia Dragon (7.21M triangles): 128 res: Coarse 4.8ms, Sorting 4.2ms, Fine 14.0ms. 512 res: Coarse 4.8ms, Sorting 7.5ms, Fine 10.1ms. 1024 res: Coarse 4.9ms, Sorting 8.6ms, Fine 10.1ms. Comparison with Kalojanov and Slusallek (KS) for Bucketing: Conference (282k): KS 13.5ms vs VP 3.8ms (3.55x speedup). Dragon (180k): KS 4.0ms vs VP 3.7ms (1.08x). Fairy (174k): KS 12.0ms vs VP 4.2ms (2.85x). Soda Hall (2.2M): KS 65.0ms vs VP 15.0ms (4.33x). Note: KS timings were divided by 2x to estimate GTX480 performance from GTX280 data. Strengths: High flexibility, programmability, efficient load balancing for uneven geometric density, and fast performance for both binary and A-buffer modes. Limitations: Performance degrades for scenes with many long/skinny triangles in floating-point buffers at high resolutions due to SIMT utilization issues and coarse raster overhead. VoxelPipe was introduced in. The source code is available at http://code.google.com/p/voxelpipe/. It is used in real-time global illumination systems (AnonGI) to create a scene proxy for tracing incoherent rays, rebuilt every frame for dynamic geometry, materials, and lighting, running at over 50 FPS at 1024x1024 resolution. body: Conservative rasterization is a technique used during voxelization to prevent artifacts where small triangles (smaller than the voxel grid resolution) are ignored completely, resulting in holes in the voxelized geometry. It ensures that all voxels potentially intersected by a triangle are covered by rasterization. Two primary implementations exist: Geometric Dilatation, which explicitly enlarges triangles in clip space within the geometry shader, and MSAA Approximation, which leverages Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing to invoke the pixel shader if any subsample is covered, approximating conservative behavior without explicit edge expansion. The MSAA approach is often preferred for its simplicity and lack of redundant voxels compared to edge extension. This section details the Geometric Dilatation method, as it provides a deterministic, algorithmic definition. The MSAA method is described as a parameterized alternative in Operating characteristics. Input: A triangle defined by three vertices P0, P1, P2 in clip space. Output: A dilated triangle with vertices P'0, P'1, P'2 in clip space, which is then transformed to world space for voxelization. Uniforms: halfPixel[3]: Array of vec2 representing half the pixel size in clip space, indexed by the selected view projection. viewProject[3]: Array of 3 mat4 matrices for view-projection transformations. viewProjectInverse[3]: Array of 3 mat4 matrices for inverse view-projection transformations. Edge Planes: Three vec3 values representing the homogeneous plane equations for the triangle edges. Triangle Plane: One vec4 representing the plane equation of the original triangle. Intersection Lines: Three vec3 values representing the direction vectors of the intersection lines between offset edge planes. Bounding Box: vec4 containing min/max x/y coordinates in clip space, used in the fragment shader for culling. 1. Select Projection Axis: Determine the dominant axis of the triangle's face normal to select the appropriate orthographic projection matrix from viewProject. Let this index be projectIndex. 2. Compute Triangle Plane: Calculate the normal N = (A, B, C) of the triangle in world/view space using the cross product of edge vectors: N = \text{normalize}((P1 - P0) \times (P2 - P0)) Compute the plane constant D: D = -P0 \cdot N The plane equation is Ax + By + Cz + D = 0. 3. Ensure Consistent Winding: Check if the triangle is back-facing relative to the camera. If the z-component of the normal is negative (Nz < 0), swap vertices P1 and P2 to ensure counter-clockwise winding. 4. Compute Homogeneous Edge Planes: For each edge i (connecting Pi to P{i+1}, with P3=P0), compute the homogeneous plane passing through the origin. The normal (Ai, Bi, Ci) is found via the cross product of the homogeneous vertex coordinates (using x, y, w components): \text{edgePlanes}[i] = \text{cross}(P{i+1}.xyw - Pi.xyw, Pi.xyw) Note: In orthographic projection, w=1, so this represents a 2D line in clip space. 5. Dilate Edge Planes: Offset each homogeneous plane to expand the triangle. Subtract the projection of the half-pixel size onto the plane's normal from the plane's z-component (distance): \text{edgePlanes}[i].z \leftarrow \text{edgePlanes}[i].z - \text{dot}(\text{halfPixel}[\text{projectIndex}], |\text{edgePlanes}[i].xy|). 6. Compute Intersection Lines: Calculate the direction vector of the intersection line between adjacent offset planes. The direction is the cross product of their normals. Normalize by dividing by the z-component: \text{intersection}[i] = \text{cross}(\text{edgePlanes}[i], \text{edgePlanes}[i+1]) \text{intersection}[i] \leftarrow \text{intersection}[i] / \text{intersection}[i].z. 7. Compute Dilated Vertices: The x and y coordinates of the new vertices are taken from the intersection line vectors. The z coordinate is solved using the original triangle's plane equation: zi = -( \text{intersection}[i].x \cdot A + \text{intersection}[i].y \cdot B + D) / C If C = 0 (triangle plane parallel to view direction), the algorithm returns early or handles the singularity. P'i = (\text{intersection}[i].x, \text{intersection}[i].y, zi). 8. Transform and Output: Transform the dilated vertices P'i back to world space using viewProjectInverse[projectIndex] for voxelization. Pass the clip-space positions to the fragment shader.
