Validate input types and shapes assert 1 <= nsamppervox <= 256 # C.MAXNSAMP exact value not given in sources assert voxcenters.shape == (voxcenters.size(0), 3) assert geos.shape == (geos.size(0), 8) assert rgbs.shape == (rgbs.size(0), 3) assert subdivp.shape == (subdivp.size(0), 1) # Device mismatch checks are enforced for w2cmatrix, c2wmatrix, voxcenters, voxlengths, geos, rgbs, and gtcolor # 2. Preprocess octree geometry via C++ extension nduplicates, geomBuffer = C.rasterizepreprocess( voxcenters, geos, subdivp, w2cmatrix, c2wmatrix, imagewidth, imageheight, tanfovx, tanfovy, cx, cy, nearplane) # 3. Identify voxels in frustum infrustsidx = torch.where(nduplicates > 0)[0] # 4. Forward voxel parameters to GPU campos = c2wmatrix[:, 3] # Standard extraction voxparams = voxfn(infrustsidx, campos, colormode) # C++/CUDA helper extracting geos, rgbs, subdivp # 5. Invoke differentiable rasterization numrendered, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, outcolor, outdepth, outnormal, outT, maxw = \ C.rasterizevoxels( infrustsidx, voxcenters, geos, rgbs, subdivp, nsamppervox, w2cmatrix, c2wmatrix, imagewidth, imageheight, tanfovx, tanfovy, cx, cy, bgcolor, nearplane, needdepth, neednormal, trackmaxw, lambdaRconcen, lambdaascending, lambdadist, gtcolor, debug) # 6. Save tensors for backward pass ctx.saveforbackward( octreepaths, voxcenters, voxlengths, geos, rgbs, geomBuffer, binningBuffer, imgBuffer, outT, outdepth, outnormal) # 7. Mark maxw as non-differentiable ctx.marknondifferentiable(maxw) return outcolor, outdepth, outnormal, outT, maxw @staticmethod def backward(ctx, gradoutcolor, gradoutdepth, gradoutnormal, gradoutT, gradmaxw): # Backward pass kernel implementation not provided in sources pass Parameters lambdadist (float): Enables distortion regularization when > 0. gtcolor (torch.Tensor): Ground truth color tensor of shape [3, H, W] used for color concentration loss in the backward pass. name: Direct Voxel Rasterization with Edge Fading
head: Max-blend voxel rasterization, Volume Sphere Rasterization, Voxel Sphere, Voxel-based sphere rendering
body: Direct Voxel Rasterization with Edge Fading renders 3D spheres into a voxel grid by iterating over axis-aligned bounding boxes, computing Euclidean distance to the sphere center, applying a linear edge fade, and blending colors using maximum blending. It differs from standard binary voxelization by introducing anti-aliased edges via intensity falloff, and from ray-marching volume rendering by using a direct, iterative rasterization approach that avoids complex traversal structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of spheres, each defined by a 3D position (cx, cy, cz), a radius r, and an RGB color (Cr, Cg, Cb). Output: A 4D voxel grid raster.data of dimensions (L, H, W) indexed as [z, y, x, channel]. Data Structures: raster.data: A 4D array with memory layout [z, y, x, channel]. Channel 0 stores Red, Channel 1 stores Green, Channel 2 stores Blue. Dimensions correspond to (length, height, width). Parameters: RENDERFADEMARGIN: A float controlling the width of the edge fade region relative to the sphere radius. Typical value: 0.2. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sphere Validation: If a sphere's radius r \le 0.1, skip it to avoid degenerate bounding boxes and unnecessary computation. 2. Bounding Box Calculation: For each sphere with center (cx, cy, cz) and radius r, compute integer bounds clamped to grid boundaries: \begin{aligned} x{min} &= \max(0, \lfloor cx - r \rfloor) \\ x{max} &= \min(W - 1, \lfloor cx + r \rfloor) \\ y{min} &= \max(0, \lfloor cy - r \rfloor) \\ y{max} &= \min(H - 1, \lfloor cy + r \rfloor) \\ z{min} &= \max(0, \lfloor cz - r \rfloor) \\ z{max} &= \min(L - 1, \lfloor cz + r \rfloor) \end{aligned} Clamping prevents out-of-bounds array access. 3. Voxel Iteration: Iterate z from z{min} to z{max}, y from y{min} to y{max}, and x from x{min} to x{max}. 4. Distance Calculation: For each voxel (x, y, z), compute deltas dx = x - cx, dy = y - cy, dz = z - cz, then compute Euclidean distance d = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2}. 5. Intensity and Color Calculation: Define fade start threshold: d{fade} = r \times (1.0 - \text{RENDER\FADE\MARGIN}). If d \le r, set intensity I = 1.0. Else if d > d{fade}, set intensity I = 1.0 - \frac{d - d{fade}}{r \times \text{RENDER\FADE\MARGIN}}. Else, set I = 0.0 and skip blending. Compute new color components: C'r = \lfloor Cr \times I \rfloor, C'g = \lfloor Cg \times I \rfloor, C'b = \lfloor Cb \times I \rfloor. 6. Maximum Blending: Update the voxel at [z, y, x] using maximum blending for each channel: \begin{aligned} \text{raster.data}[z, y, x, 0] &= \max(\text{raster.data}[z, y, x, 0], C'r) \\ \text{raster.data}[z, y, x, 1] &= \max(\text{raster.data}[z, y, x, 1], C'g) \\ \text{raster.data}[z, y, x, 2] &= \max(\text{raster.data}[z, y, x, 2], C'b) \end{aligned} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rasterizespheres(spheres, rasterwidth, rasterheight, rasterlength, fademargin=0.2): """ Renders spheres into a voxel grid using direct rasterization with edge fading. Args: spheres: List of dicts with keys 'x', 'y', 'z', 'radius', 'color' (dict with 'r', 'g', 'b'). rasterwidth: Width of the voxel grid (x-dimension). rasterheight: Height of the voxel grid (y-dimension). rasterlength: Length of the voxel grid (z-dimension). fademargin: Controls the width of the edge fade region (default 0.2). Returns: A 4D list of shape (length, height, width, 3) with integer values. """ # Initialize raster data with zeros. Layout: [z, y, x, channel] # Channel 0: Red, 1: Green, 2: Blue raster = [[[[0, 0, 0] for in range(rasterwidth)] for in range(rasterheight)] for in range(rasterlength)] for sphere in spheres: cx = sphere['x'] cy = sphere['y'] cz = sphere['z'] r = sphere['radius'] cr = sphere['color']['r'] cg = sphere['color']['g'] cb = sphere['color']['b'] # Pitfall: Skip degenerate spheres if r <= 0.1: continue # Calculate bounding box and clamp to grid boundaries xmin = max(0, int(cx - r)) xmax = min(rasterwidth - 1, int(cx + r)) ymin = max(0, int(cy - r)) ymax = min(rasterheight - 1, int(cy + r)) zmin = max(0, int(cz - r)) zmax = min(rasterlength - 1, int(cz + r)) # Precompute fade start distance and denominator fadestart = r (1.0 - fademargin) fadedenominator = r fademargin # Iterate over bounding box for z in range(zmin, zmax + 1): for y in range(ymin, ymax + 1): for x in range(xmin, xmax + 1): # Calculate distance dx = x - cx dy = y - cy dz = z - cz dist = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) # Calculate intensity if dist <= r: intensity = 1.0 elif dist > fadestart: intensity = 1.0 - (dist - fadestart) / fadedenominator else: continue # Outside fade region, no contribution # Calculate new color values newr = int(cr intensity) newg = int(cg intensity) newb = int(cb intensity) # Maximum blending if newr > raster[z][y][x][0]: raster[z][y][x][0] = newr if newg > raster[z][y][x][1]: raster[z][y][x][1] = newg if newb > raster[z][y][x][2]: raster[z][y][x][2] = newb return raster Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R^3), where N is the number of spheres and R is the average radius in voxels, because each sphere iterates over its axis-aligned bounding box volume. Memory Complexity: O(L \cdot H \cdot W) for the voxel grid storage. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of spheres and cubically with their radius. Strengths: Simple logic, no complex data structures required, produces smooth edges via fading. Limitations: Maximum blending can cause color bleeding if not handled carefully; performance degrades quickly with large radii or high voxel counts; no support for transparency or alpha blending in the basic form. This method originates from the volumetric-display project by fughilli, which targets rendering volumetric data for LED cube displays. It combines basic geometric rasterization with anti-aliasing techniques (edge fading) to improve visual quality on discrete voxel grids. name: WebGL Voxelization via Triangle Splitting and Instancing
head: Triangle Splitting Voxelization, WebGL Voxelizer
body: A method to calculate the distance field of a mesh in real-time on WebGL by converting mesh triangles into small points (particles) that fit within voxels, using instancing to handle adjacent voxels and depth testing to simulate atomic minimum-distance updates. It sets itself apart from GPU-native voxelization methods by avoiding compute shaders and atomic operations, which are unavailable in WebGL, by instead leveraging the rasterization pipeline, instancing, and depth buffering. It builds on Voxel Rasterization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh. Output: A 3D distance field stored in a 2D texture (simulating 3D data). Data Structures: Small Triangles Buffer: Contains triangles split until they meet a size threshold. Big Triangles Buffer: Contains triangles that exceed the threshold but are below a secondary threshold. Distance Texture: A 2D texture where each texel stores the minimum distance to the mesh. Steps: 1. Triangle Splitting (CPU): Split the original mesh triangles on the CPU until they meet a size threshold. Separate triangles that are still too large ("big triangles") into a different buffer. The threshold for "big" is a secondary, larger threshold. Rationale: CPU splitting is preferred over GPU splitting to avoid excessive memory usage and triangle generation for meshes with varying triangle sizes. 2. Small Triangle Voxelization (Vertex Shader + Instancing): Launch a draw call with points, where the number of points equals the number of small triangles. In the vertex shader, use glVertexID to read the three vertices of the triangle from a texture. Calculate the average position of the three vertices to define the center voxel. Use instancing (glInstanceID) to iterate over 27 instances representing the center voxel and its 26 adjacent neighbors in 3D. For each instance, calculate the offset from the center voxel and compute the distance from the triangle to that specific voxel. Map the 3D voxel position to a 2D texture coordinate and write the distance, using the depth test to ensure only the minimum distance is saved. 3. Big Triangle Voxelization (Fragment Shader): For big triangles, execute a fragment shader pass that evaluates the distance field for all voxels in the texture for up to 64 big triangles. Update the texture with the minimum distance via depth testing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Triangle: def init(self, v0, v1, v2): self.v0 = v0 self.v1 = v1 self.v2 = v2 # Placeholder for area calculation; in practice computed from vertex positions self.area = 0.0 def splitmesh(mesh, smallthreshold, bigthreshold): smalltriangles = [] bigtriangles = [] for tri in mesh.triangles: if tri.area > bigthreshold: bigtriangles.append(tri) elif tri.area > smallthreshold: splittrianglerecursive(tri, smallthreshold, smalltriangles) else: smalltriangles.append(tri) return smalltriangles, bigtriangles def splittrianglerecursive(tri, threshold, resultlist): if tri.area <= threshold: resultlist.append(tri) return mid0 = (tri.v0 + tri.v1) / 2.0 mid1 = (tri.v1 + tri.v2) / 2.0 mid2 = (tri.v2 + tri.v0) / 2.0 splittrianglerecursive(Triangle(tri.v0, mid0, mid2), threshold, resultlist) splittrianglerecursive(Triangle(tri.v1, mid1, mid0), threshold, resultlist) splittrianglerecursive(Triangle(tri.v2, mid2, mid1), threshold, resultlist) splittrianglerecursive(Triangle(mid0, mid1, mid2), threshold, resultlist) def readtrianglefromtexture(texture, vertexid): # Simulates reading triangle vertices from a texture buffer using glVertexID return texture.trianglebuffer[vertexid] def getneighboroffset(instanceid, voxelsize): # Maps 0-26 to a 3x3x3 grid offset centered at (0,0,0) dx = (instanceid % 3) - 1 dy = ((instanceid // 3) % 3) - 1 dz = (instanceid // 9) - 1 return (dx voxelsize, dy voxelsize, dz voxelsize) def distancetriangletovoxel(v0, v1, v2, voxelpos): # Standard point-to-triangle distance calculation e1 = v1 - v0 e2 = v2 - v0 n = cross(e1, e2) d = dot(v0 - voxelpos, n) / dot(n, n) proj = voxelpos + d n return math.dist(voxelpos, proj) def map3dto2d(pos, width, depth): # Standard 3D-to-2D texture coordinate packing (layer-by-layer) x, y, z = pos return (x + y width + z width depth, 0.0) def writemindistance(texture, coord, dist): # Simulates depth test / atomic minimum update current = texture.read(coord) if current is None or dist < current: texture.write(coord, dist) def voxelizesmalltriangles(smalltriangles, distancetexture, voxelsize): # Draw call launches points equal to number of small triangles for i, tri in enumerate(smalltriangles): # Vertex shader: read vertices using glVertexID v0, v1, v2 = readtrianglefromtexture(distancetexture, i) center = (v0 + v1 + v2) / 3.0 # Instancing loop: 27 instances (1 center + 26 neighbors) for instid in range(27): offset = getneighboroffset(instid, voxelsize) targetvoxel = center + offset dist = distancetriangletovoxel(v0, v1, v2, targetvoxel) texcoord = map3dto2d(targetvoxel, distancetexture.width, distancetexture.depth) writemindistance(distancetexture, texcoord, dist) def voxelizebigtriangles(bigtriangles, distancetexture): # Fragment shader pass over all voxels in the texture for voxelpos in distancetexture.allvoxels(): mindist = float('inf') # Evaluate up to 64 big triangles for tri in bigtriangles[:64]: dist = distancetriangletovoxel(tri.v0, tri.v1, tri.v2, voxelpos) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist texcoord = map3dto2d(voxelpos, distancetexture.width, distancetexture.depth) writemindistance(distancetexture, texcoord, mindist) Parameters: Max big triangles per shader pass: 64. Number of instances for 3D voxel neighborhood: 27 (1 center + 26 adjacent). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: WebGL lacks compute shaders, storage buffers, and atomic operations, requiring the use of the rasterization pipeline, 2D texture simulation for 3D data, and depth testing for min-distance updates. Large triangles cause performance bottlenecks in naive voxelization because the bounding box contains too many voxels to evaluate in a loop. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Works within WebGL constraints (no compute shaders/atomics); handles dense meshes well with small triangles; separates big triangles to avoid excessive voxel evaluation loops. Limitations: Requires CPU-side triangle splitting; limited to 64 big triangles per pass; 2D texture simulation for 3D data adds complexity. When to use: Real-time distance field calculation in WebGL environments. When not to use: When compute shaders and atomic operations are available (use CUDA or native GPU methods instead). Origin: The method was developed to implement real-time distance field voxelization in WebGL, adapting concepts from the TressFX shader to work around WebGL's lack of compute shaders, storage buffers, and atomic operations. The author discusses conversations with Vicente Lucendo regarding GPU triangle splitting, which led to the decision to perform splitting on the CPU to avoid excessive memory usage and triangle generation for meshes with varying sizes. name: Voxelizer Forward Pass
head: CUDA Gaussian Voxelization and Rendering, CudaVoxelizer::Voxelizer::forward
body: The Voxelizer Forward Pass is a CUDA-based voxelization and rendering pipeline that processes 3D Gaussians into a volume. It computes radii, generates tile/depth keys for sorting, identifies tile ranges, and renders the volume by blending Gaussians per tile. Inputs: P: Number of input 3D Gaussians. means3D: Array of P 3D mean positions (world space). opacities: Array of P opacity values. scales: Array of P scale vectors. scalemodifier: Scalar multiplier for scales. rotations: Array of P quaternions. cov3Dprecomp: Optional pre-computed 3D covariance matrices (or nullptr to compute internally). prefiltered: Boolean flag indicating if Gaussians are pre-filtered. nVoxelx, nVoxely, nVoxelz: Dimensions of the voxel grid (number of tiles in each dimension). sVoxelx, sVoxely, sVoxelz: Scale/size of each voxel/tile in world units. centerx, centery, centerz: Center coordinates of the voxel grid in world space. Outputs: outvolume: Output buffer for the rendered volume data. numrendered: Total number of rendered Gaussian instances (duplicates included). The method uses three main state structures allocated via callbacks (geometryBuffer, imageBuffer, binningBuffer). GeometryState (size P): depths: float[P] – Computed depth of each Gaussian. internalradii: int[P] – Radius of each Gaussian in tile units. means3Dnorm: vec3[P] – Normalized mean positions. cov3D: float[P6] – Covariance matrices (6 floats per Gaussian, symmetric upper triangle). conicopacity: float[P7] – Conic matrix (6 floats) + opacity (1 float). tilestouched: int[P] – Count of tiles touched by each Gaussian. pointoffsets: int[P] – Prefix sum of tilestouched, used for indexing duplicated Gaussians. scanningspace: void – Temporary allocation space. scansize: sizet – Size of scanning space. ImageState (size N, where N = nVoxelx \times nVoxely \times nVoxelz): ncontrib: int[N] – Number of Gaussians contributing to each tile. ranges: uint2[N] – Start and end indices in the sorted pointlist for each tile. BinningState (size num\rendered): pointlist: int[P] – Sorted Gaussian indices. pointlistunsorted: int[P] – Unsorted Gaussian indices. pointlistkeys: uint64t[P] – Sorted tile/depth keys. pointlistkeysunsorted: uint64t[P] – Unsorted tile/depth keys. listsortingspace: void – Temporary allocation space. sortingsize: sizet – Size of sorting space. 1. Allocate GeometryState: Allocate buffers for GeometryState using geometryBuffer callback with size required<GeometryState>(P). 2. Initialize GeometryState: Initialize fields depths (P floats), internalradii (P ints), means3Dnorm (P vec3), cov3D (P6 floats), conicopacity (P7 floats), and tilestouched (P ints). 3. Preprocess Gaussians: Launch FORWARD::preprocess kernel to compute radii, normalized means, depths, covariances, conic matrices, and count touched tiles per Gaussian. 4. Compute Offsets: Compute inclusive prefix sum of tilestouched to determine offsets for duplicated Gaussians. Store result in pointoffsets. 5. Allocate ImageState: Allocate ImageState buffers using imageBuffer callback with size required<ImageState>(nVoxelx nVoxely nVoxelz). Fields: ncontrib (N ints), ranges (N uint2). 6. Retrieve Render Count: Retrieve total number of rendered Gaussian instances (numrendered) from the last element of pointoffsets. 7. Allocate BinningState: Allocate BinningState buffers using binningBuffer callback with size required<BinningState>(numrendered). Fields: pointlist (P ints), pointlistunsorted (P ints), pointlistkeys (uint64t[P]), pointlistkeysunsorted (uint64t[P]). 8. Duplicate and Key Generation: Launch duplicateWithKeys2 kernel. For each Gaussian with radius > 0, compute bounding cube [cubemin, cubemax] using getCube. For each tile (x,y,z) in the cube, generate key = (z \cdot grid.y \cdot grid.x + y \cdot grid.x + x) \ll 32 \mid depth\bits. Store key and Gaussian index (idx) in unsorted buffers at offset determined by pointoffsets. 9. Calculate Sort Bits: Calculate bit depth for radix sort: bit = \text{getHigherMsb2}(tile\grid.x \cdot tile\grid.y \cdot tile\grid.z). 10. Sort: Sort pairs (keys, values) using CUB radix sort. Sort keys from bit 0 to 32+bit. Output sorted keys to pointlistkeys and sorted values (Gaussian indices) to pointlist. 11. Zero Ranges: Zero out imgState.ranges buffer. 12. Identify Tile Ranges: If numrendered > 0, launch identifyTileRanges2 kernel. For each index idx in sorted list, read tile ID from key >> 32. If idx==0, set range start to 0. If tile ID changes from previous, set previous tile's end to idx and current tile's start to idx. If idx==L-1, set current tile's end to L. 13. Render: Launch FORWARD::render kernel. Pass tilegrid, block, imgState.ranges, binningState.pointlist, voxel dimensions, means3Dnorm, conicopacity, ncontrib, and outvolume. 14. Return: Return numrendered. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelizerforwardpass( means3D: list, opacities: list, scales: list, scalemodifier: float, rotations: list, cov3Dprecomp: list, prefiltered: bool, nVoxelx: int, nVoxely: int, nVoxelz: int, sVoxelx: float, sVoxely: float, sVoxelz: float, centerx: float, centery: float, centerz: float) -> tuple: P = len(means3D) N = nVoxelx nVoxely nVoxelz # 1. Allocate GeometryState geo = { 'depths': [0.0] P, 'internalradii': [0] P, 'means3Dnorm': [(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)] P, 'cov3D': [0.0] (P 6), 'conicopacity': [0.0] (P 7), 'tilestouched': [0] P, 'pointoffsets': [0] P } # 2. Initialize GeometryState fields # (Initialized above) # 3. Preprocess Gaussians # Launch FORWARD::preprocess kernel to compute radii, normalized means, depths, covariances, conic matrices, and count touched tiles per Gaussian. # 4. Compute Offsets geo['pointoffsets'] = inclusiveprefixsum(geo['tilestouched']) # 5. Allocate ImageState img = { 'ncontrib': [0] N, 'ranges': [(0, 0)] N } # 6. Retrieve numrendered numrendered = geo['pointoffsets'][P - 1] # 7. Allocate BinningState binstate = { 'pointlist': [0] numrendered, 'pointlistunsorted': [0] numrendered, 'pointlistkeys': [0] numrendered, 'pointlistkeysunsorted': [0] numrendered } # 8. Duplicate and Key Generation off = 0 for idx in range(P): if geo['internalradii'][idx] > 0: # Compute bounding cube [cubemin, cubemax] using getCube cubemin, cubemax = getcube(geo['means3Dnorm'][idx], geo['internalradii'][idx], nVoxelx, nVoxely, nVoxelz) for z in range(cubemin[2], cubemax[2] + 1): for y in range(cubemin[1], cubemax[1] + 1): for x in range(cubemin[0], cubemax[0] + 1): key = (z nVoxely nVoxelx + y nVoxelx + x) << 32 # Bitcast depths[idx] to uint32t depthbits = int.frombytes(struct.pack('f', geo['depths'][idx]), 'little') & 0xFFFFFFFF key |= depthbits binstate['pointlistkeysunsorted'][off] = key binstate['pointlistunsorted'][off] = idx off += 1 # 9. Calculate Sort Bits bit = gethighermsb(nVoxelx nVoxely nVoxelz) # 10. Sort # Sort pairs (keys, values) using radix sort from bit 0 to 32+bit. combined = sorted(zip(binstate['pointlistkeysunsorted'], binstate['pointlistunsorted']), key=lambda x: x[0]) binstate['pointlistkeys'] = [x[0] for x in combined] binstate['pointlist'] = [x[1] for x in combined] # 11. Zero Ranges img['ranges'] = [(0, 0)] N # 12. Identify Tile Ranges if numrendered > 0: for idx in range(numrendered): key = binstate['pointlistkeys'][idx] currtile = key >> 32 if idx == 0: img['ranges'][currtile] = (0, img['ranges'][currtile][1]) else: prevtile = binstate['pointlistkeys'][idx - 1] >> 32 if currtile != prevtile: img['ranges'][prevtile] = (img['ranges'][prevtile][0], idx) img['ranges'][currtile] = (idx, img['ranges'][currtile][1]) if idx == numrendered - 1: img['ranges'][currtile] = (img['ranges'][currtile][0], numrendered) # 13. Render # Launch FORWARD::render kernel with tilegrid, block, imgState.ranges, binningState.pointlist, voxel dimensions, means3Dnorm, conicopacity, ncontrib, and outvolume. outvolume = [0.0] (N 4) # 14. Return return numrendered, outvolume def inclusiveprefixsum(arr): result = [0] len(arr) acc = 0 for i, val in enumerate(arr): acc += val result[i] = acc return result def gethighermsb(n): return n.bitlength() def getcube(mean, radius, nx, ny, nz): # Logic for getCube not given in the sources. # Returns (minx, miny, minz), (maxx, maxy, maxz) return (0, 0, 0), (nx - 1, ny - 1, nz - 1) nVoxelx, nVoxely, nVoxelz: Dimensions of the voxel grid. sVoxelx, sVoxely, sVoxelz: Scale/size of each voxel/tile in world units. centerx, centery, centerz: Center coordinates of the voxel grid in world space. scalemodifier: Multiplier applied to scales. prefiltered: Boolean flag indicating if Gaussians are pre-filtered. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Zero Radius: Gaussians with internalradii[i] == 0 are skipped during duplication. Precision: Depth bits are packed into the lower 32 bits of the key. Ensure depths are normalized or scaled appropriately to fit within 32 bits without collision. Boundary Conditions: The identifyTileRanges2 kernel handles the last tile explicitly by setting its end range to L (total number of rendered instances). Not given in the sources. The method is described in the x2-gaussian repository as a CUDA-based voxelization and rendering pipeline that processes 3D Gaussians into a volume. yuyouxixi/x2-gaussian, https://github.com/yuyouxixi/x2-gaussian, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Conservative Voxelization
body: Conservative voxelization is a hardware-accelerated algorithm for polygonal models that guarantees conservative correctness: every voxel intersecting the input model is correctly recognized. It differs from standard rasterization-based voxelization [Rasterization-based Voxelization] by computing the exact depth range of the intersection between the triangle and the voxel column, rather than using a single depth value which leads to missed voxels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangular model (tessellated from arbitrary polygons), a projection direction (typically orthogonal), and a volumetric resolution along the projection direction, resz. Output: A set of voxels (x, y, z^) corresponding to all voxels intersected by the triangles. Data Structures: Triangle Vertices: Three vertices P1, P2, P3 with 3D coordinates (xi, yi, zi). Projected Triangle (Tp): The 2D projection of T onto the viewing plane with vertices (xi, yi). Fragment Rectangle (R): The unit square in the viewing plane corresponding to a fragment (x, y). Intersection Polygon (I): The convex polygon resulting from the intersection of Tp and R, with up to seven vertices. Numbered Steps: 1. Tessellation: Tessellate arbitrary polygonal models into triangular models. 2. Rasterization: Rasterize the projected triangle Tp to generate fragments, where each fragment (x, y) corresponds to a column of voxels V(x, y) = \{x, y, z | z = 0,..., z{res} - 1\}. 3. Classification: For each fragment, determine if it is an interior fragment (fully covered by Tp) or a boundary fragment (partially covered by Tp). 4. Depth Range Calculation: Compute the minimal depth z{min} and maximal depth z{max} of the intersection between the triangle T and the prism formed by V(x, y). Interior Fragments: Use the center depth and partial derivatives. Boundary Fragments: Compute the intersection polygon I and evaluate depths at its vertices. 5. Voxel Generation: Convert the depth range [z{min}, z{max}] to voxel indices: z^{min} = z{min} \cdot resz and z^{max} = z{max} \cdot resz. Generate all voxels (x, y, z) for z \in [z^{min}, z^{max}]. Formulas: 1. Interior Fragment Depth Range: For an interior fragment, the depth range is calculated as: z{min} = zc - \Delta z z{max} = zc + \Delta z where zc is the depth value at the fragment center, and: \Delta z = \frac{1}{2} \left( \left| \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} \right| + \left| \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} \right| \right) 2. Partial Derivatives: The partial derivatives of depth and barycentric coordinates are computed using the triangle vertices (xi, yi, zi) for i=1,2,3: Signed area of Tp: S = x1 y2 - x2 y1 + x2 y3 - x3 y2 + x3 y1 - x1 y3 Partial derivative of barycentric coordinate vector \mathbf{C} with respect to x: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial x} = \frac{(y2 - y3, y3 - y1, y1 - y2)}{S} Partial derivative of barycentric coordinate vector \mathbf{C} with respect to y: \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial y} = \frac{(x3 - x2, x1 - x3, x2 - x1)}{S} Partial derivative of depth z with respect to x: \frac{\partial z}{\partial x} = (z1, z2, z3) \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial x} Partial derivative of depth z with respect to y: \frac{\partial z}{\partial y} = (z1, z2, z3) \cdot \frac{\partial \mathbf{C}}{\partial y} 3. Boundary Fragment Depth Range: The intersection polygon I vertices consist of: Intersection points between Tp and the edges of R. Vertices of Tp inside R. Vertices of R inside Tp. Let v{min} be the vertex of R such that z(v{min}) = \min{p \in R} z(p). If v{min} \in Tp, then z{min} = z(v{min}). (p2[1]-p1[1])(p4[0]-p3[0]) if d == 0: return None t = ((p4[0]-p3[0])(p3[1]-p1[1]) - (p4[1]-p3[1])(p3[0]-p1[0])) / d u = ((p2[0]-p1[0])(p3[1]-p1[1]) - (p2[1]-p1[1])(p3[0]-p1[0])) / d if 0 <= t <= 1 and 0 <= u <= 1: return (p1[0] + t(p2[0]-p1[0]), p1[1] + t(p2[1]-p1[1])) return None Parameters: resz: The volumetric resolution along the projection direction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Using the simple interior fragment depth range formula for boundary fragments leads to over-conservative results, especially when the voxelizing triangle is nearly parallel to the projection direction. Degenerate triangles (area S=0) must be handled to avoid division by zero. Measured Performance: Experiments show lower memory consumption than previous approaches and higher efficiency when the volume resolution is high. Strengths: Guarantees conservative correctness; no preprocessing required; suitable for deformable models; hardware-accelerated. Limitations: More complex implementation than simple rasterization-based methods; potential for over-conservative results if boundary handling is incorrect. When to Use: Collision detection, occlusion culling, visibility processing, and applications requiring guaranteed intersection detection. When Not to Use: When performance is the sole priority and missing some intersecting voxels is acceptable; when input is not polygonal. It addresses the limitations of previous hardware-accelerated voxelization algorithms that missed intersecting voxels, which is critical for applications like collision detection and occlusion culling. The method leverages GPU rasterization capabilities to achieve efficiency. name: Conservative Rasterization via Triangle Expansion
head: Conservative Rasterization via Geometry Shader Expansion, Hole Repair via Conservative Rasterization, Triangle Expansion Method, GS Edge Expansion, Manual Conservative Rasterization
body: This method repairs holes in voxelized meshes caused by standard fixed-function rasterization, which only emits fragments for pixels whose centers lie inside the projected triangle. It expands the triangle in clip space within a geometry shader to ensure all potentially covered pixels are rasterized, then culls the overestimated coverage in the fragment shader. It is distinguished from exact bounding polygon methods by using a simple triangle expansion and fragment-shader culling, which is faster in practice despite higher fragment shader workload. Inputs: A triangle mesh; projection matrix (orthographic assumed for simplicity in source formulas); pixel size in clip space. Outputs: A set of fragments covering the triangle and its immediate neighborhood, written to a voxel grid. Data Structures: pos[3]: The three vertices of the triangle in clip space (homogeneous coordinates vec4). edgePlanes[3]: Homogeneous plane representations of the triangle edges (vec3). aabb: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box in clip space (vec4, xy = min, zw = max). pixelDiagonal: Half the diagonal length of a pixel in clip space (vec2). Steps: 1. Calculate Clip-Space AABB: Compute the 2D bounding box of the triangle in clip space (x, y), ignoring z. 2. Expand AABB: Expand the bounding box by pixelDiagonal in all directions to ensure edge pixels are not missed during culling. 3. Compute Edge Planes: For each edge of the triangle, compute a homogeneous plane normal in clip space. 4. Expand Edge Planes: Shift each plane outward along its normal by a distance proportional to the pixel size. 5. Compute Expanded Vertices: Calculate the intersection of the expanded edge planes to find the new vertices of the expanded triangle. 6. Rasterize: Pass the expanded triangle to the fixed-function rasterizer. 7. Cull in Fragment Shader: For each generated fragment, determine if it lies within the original triangle. Discard fragments outside the original triangle but inside the expanded region. Formulas: AABB Expansion: AABB{expanded}.xy = AABB{original}.xy - pixelDiagonal AABB{expanded}.zw = AABB{original}.zw + pixelDiagonal Where pixelDiagonal is half the diagonal length of a pixel in clip space. Edge Plane Calculation: For an edge from vertex Pi to Pj, the homogeneous plane normal N is: N = (Pi.xyw - Pj.xyw) \times Pj.xyw Where \times denotes the 3D cross product, and xyw refers to the x, y, w components of the vertex. Plane Expansion: The z component (representing the plane offset in this homogeneous representation) is shifted: Nz' = Nz - \text{dot}(halfPixel, |N{xy}|) Where halfPixel is the pixel size vector and |N{xy}| is the absolute value of the x, y components of the normal. Fragment Culling: In the fragment shader, calculate barycentric coordinates or distance to the original triangle edges. If the fragment is outside the original triangle, discard it. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processtriangle(pos: list[vec4], pixeldiagonal: vec2) -> list[vec4]: """ pos: List of 3 vec4 vertices in clip space. pixeldiagonal: Half the diagonal length of a pixel in clip space. Returns: List of 3 vec4 vertices for the expanded triangle. """ # Step 3: Compute Edge Planes # Edge 0: P0 -> P2, Edge 1: P1 -> P0, Edge 2: P2 -> P1 edgeplanes = [ cross(pos[0].xyw - pos[2].xyw, pos[2].xyw), cross(pos[1].xyw - pos[0].xyw, pos[0].xyw), cross(pos[2].xyw - pos[1].xyw, pos[1].xyw) ] # Step 4: Expand Edge Planes halfpixel = vec2(pixeldiagonal.x, pixeldiagonal.y) expandedplanes = [] for i in range(3): plane = edgeplanes[i] shift = dot(halfpixel, abs(plane.xy)) plane.z -= shift expandedplanes.append(plane) # Step 5: Compute Expanded Vertices # Intersection of two 2D lines in homogeneous coordinates (A,B,C) is cross(A, B) v0 = cross(expandedplanes[1], expandedplanes[2]) v1 = cross(expandedplanes[2], expandedplanes[0]) v2 = cross(expandedplanes[0], expandedplanes[1]) # In orthographic projection w=1, so homogeneous coordinates are directly usable return [v0, v1, v2] def fragmentshader(originalpos: list[vec4], fragmentpos: vec4) -> bool: """ originalpos: The 3 original triangle vertices in clip space. fragmentpos: The position of the current fragment in clip space. Returns: True if fragment should be kept, False if discarded. """ # Calculate edge planes of the ORIGINAL triangle originaledgeplanes = [ cross(originalpos[0].xyw - originalpos[2].xyw, originalpos[2].xyw), cross(originalpos[1].xyw - originalpos[0].xyw, originalpos[0].xyw), cross(originalpos[2].xyw - originalpos[1].xyw, originalpos[1].xyw) ] # Check if fragment is on the inside of all three edge planes # For consistent counter-clockwise winding, inside is dot(plane, fragment.xyw) >= 0 for plane in originaledgeplanes: if dot(plane, fragmentpos.xyw) < 0: return False # Outside original triangle return True # Inside original triangle Parameters: pixelDiagonal: Half the diagonal length of a pixel in clip space, used as the shift vector for plane expansion. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Homogeneous calculations can suffer from precision issues near the clipping planes. Winding Order: The sign of the plane dot product depends on the winding order of the triangle. Overestimation: The expanded triangle covers more area than the original, leading to unnecessary fragment shader invocations for discarded pixels. Time Complexity: O(1) per triangle in the geometry shader (constant number of operations). O(N) in the fragment shader, where N is the number of pixels covered by the expanded triangle. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory in the geometry shader. Performance: Faster in practice than computing the exact bounding polygon in the geometry shader, despite the extra work in the fragment shader. Strengths: Simple to implement; leverages fixed-function rasterization; effective at eliminating holes. Limitations: Overestimates coverage, leading to wasted fragment shader cycles. This technique is described in the context of sparse voxelization using OpenGL, specifically addressing the issue of holes in voxelized meshes due to standard rasterization. It is presented as a practical solution for real-time voxelization on GPUs. name: Single-Pass Voxelization
head: Axis-Aligned Voxelization, Dynamic Voxelization, One pass voxelization pipeline, Thin surface voxelization
body: Single-Pass Voxelization is a GPU-based method that converts triangle meshes into a sparse voxel representation in a single rendering pass by leveraging the geometry shader for axis selection and conservative rasterization for coverage. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by eliminating the need for multiple draw calls per object (via geometry shaders) and avoiding plain grid allocations (via sparse structures), making it suitable for dynamic scenes where objects are added at runtime. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Triangle mesh data (vertices, normals) and a sparse voxel data structure (e.g., sparse octree or hash table). Output: Occupied voxels with attributes (position, color, normal) written to a 3D surface or texture. Data Structures: Sparse Voxel Structure: No plain grid allocation; uses a sparse octree or hash map to store only occupied voxels. Render Target: An MSAA (Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing) render target is required to prevent incorrect filling of empty cells. Steps: 1. Dominant Axis Selection: For each input triangle, the geometry shader calculates the projection of the triangle's normal onto the X, Y, and Z axes and selects the axis with the largest absolute projection value as the dominant axis. 2. Triangle Projection: The triangle is projected onto the 2D plane perpendicular to the dominant axis. 3. Edge Shifting: The edges of the projected triangle are shifted outward to account for voxel grid alignment, ensuring full coverage of intersected voxels. 4. Hardware Setup/Rasterization: The rasterizer processes the shifted triangle using conservative rasterization, generating fragments for all pixels that have any overlap with the triangle rather than only those whose centers are covered. 5. Fragment Shader Execution: For each generated fragment, the fragment shader computes thin surface voxelization attributes and writes them to a 3D surface. 6. Sparse Octree Construction: A post-processing step organizes voxels into a hierarchical structure via top-down subdivision and value MIP-mapping. Formulas: Dominant Axis Selection: Let \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz) be the triangle normal. The dominant axis A is: A = \arg \max{i \in \{x,y,z\}} |ni| Conservative Rasterization Condition: A fragment is generated for a pixel p if the triangle T intersects the pixel's coverage area, rather than just the pixel center. Parameters: Hardware Support: Requires hardware conservative rasterization support, available on Nvidia Maxwell architecture and later. RTX driver support is available for Turing and Pascal architectures. Performance: Dynamic objects are added at runtime in ~4-5ms, while static environments are pre-voxelized in ~20ms. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cracks: Without conservative rasterization, GPUs only generate fragments if a pixel's center is covered, leading to small cracks at triangle edges. Over-filling: Conservative rasterization generates too many fragments, incorrectly filling cells that should be empty. This is mitigated by using an MSAA render target. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def geometryshader(triangle): v0, v1, v2 = triangle.vertices normal = normalize(cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0)) absnormal = abs(normal) if absnormal.x >= absnormal.y and absnormal.x >= absnormal.z: dominantaxis = 'x' elif absnormal.y >= absnormal.x and absnormal.y >= absnormal.z: dominantaxis = 'y' else: dominantaxis = 'z' projected = project2d(triangle, dominantaxis) shifted = shiftedges(projected) yield shifted def project2d(triangle, axis): if axis == 'x': return Triangle([(0, v[1], v[2]) for v in triangle.vertices]) elif axis == 'y': return Triangle([(v[0], 0, v[2]) for v in triangle.vertices]) else: return Triangle([(v[0], v[1], 0) for v in triangle.vertices]) def shiftedges(triangle): # Expand triangle bounds to cover adjacent grid cells xs = [v[0] for v in triangle.vertices] ys = [v[1] for v in triangle.vertices] zs = [v[2] for v in triangle.vertices] minv = (min(xs) - 0.5, min(ys) - 0.5, min(zs) - 0.5) maxv = (max(xs) + 0.5, max(ys) + 0.5, max(zs) + 0.5) return Triangle([minv, maxv, (minv[0], maxv[1], minv[2])]) def computevoxelposition(fragment): # Map fragment screen coordinates to voxel grid indices return (int(fragment.screenx gridwidth), int(fragment.screeny gridheight), fragment.depth) def computecolor(fragment): # Barycentric interpolation of vertex colors return fragment.barycentric[0] fragment.color0 + fragment.barycentric[1] fragment.color1 + fragment.barycentric[2] fragment.color2 def fragmentshader(fragment): voxelpos = computevoxelposition(fragment) voxelcolor = computecolor(fragment) # Conceptual atomic write to sparse structure sparsevoxels[voxelpos] = voxelcolor Encodes directional data in voxels instead of isotropic data, improving quality when view-dependent changes occur. Choose when directional lighting or material properties vary significantly with viewing angle. Link. Post-processing step that organizes flat voxel data into a hierarchical tree structure via top-down subdivision and value MIP-mapping. Choose when hierarchical traversal or compression is required. Link. Performance: Dynamic objects are added at runtime in ~4-5ms, while static environments are pre-voxelized in ~20ms. Strengths: Reduces draw calls via geometry shaders, supports dynamic scene updates, and avoids plain grid memory overhead through sparse allocation. Limitations: Requires hardware conservative rasterization (Nvidia Maxwell architecture and later), incurs MSAA overhead, and risks over-filling empty cells without MSAA. When to Use: Real-time applications with dynamic scenes requiring efficient, single-pass voxelization. When Not to Use: Hardware lacking conservative rasterization support, or when exact voxel coverage is critical and MSAA cannot be used, as conservative rasterization inherently over-fills empty cells. Single-Pass Voxelization was introduced as part of the Voxel Cone Tracing pipeline for real-time indirect illumination. It was developed to address the inefficiencies of previous voxelization methods that required multiple passes or draw calls. The method leverages advancements in GPU hardware, specifically conservative rasterization, to achieve efficient and accurate voxelization. name: Multi-view projection
body: Multi-view projection voxelization converts a triangle mesh into a 3D voxel grid by rasterizing geometry from multiple camera viewpoints aligned with the scene's bounding box axes. It solves occlusion gaps from single-view projections by ensuring volumetric coverage, differing from Single 2D Projection Voxelization by using multiple views for all normals, and from 3D Grid Rasterization by relying on standard GPU rasterization rather than explicit 3D traversal. All methods in this family project 3D geometry onto 2D planes and aggregate the resulting fragments into a 3D voxel grid. The common mechanism consists of the following steps: 1. Camera Configuration: Orthographic cameras are positioned along specific axes (e.g., X, Y, Z) looking towards the scene's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). 2. Rasterization: Triangles are rasterized into 2D buffers or directly into a 3D texture [3892-orthographic-multi-view-voxelization.md]. 3. Aggregation: Fragments from different views are merged into the final voxel grid, typically using an atomic "OR" operation for occupancy [5300-3-pass-voxelization.md]. 4. Coordinate Mapping: Clip-space coordinates are transformed into voxel indices using a scale and offset derived from the scene's bounding box and the target resolution R = (Rx, Ry, Rz): i = \text{floor}\left( \frac{p{clip}.xyz - bb{min}}{bb{max} - bb{min}} \times R \right) [3892-orthographic-multi-view-voxelization.md]. Produces 6-separating voxelization using only one 2D projection along the dominant axis of a triangle's normal vector. It reduces computational cost by dynamically determining the projection direction based on geometry orientation, leveraging the thinness property of the resulting voxel set. It is chosen when performance is critical and the geometry is planar or thin. Rasters scene geometry into a 3D texture or a compressed 2D "worksheet" using three orthographic cameras aligned with the principal axes. It ensures every surface element is visible from at least one viewpoint. It differs from Single 2D Projection by using three views to cover all normals, and from 3-Pass Voxelization by typically performing synthesis in a single GPU-driven pass or via efficient 2D-to-3D transcoding. Eliminates cracks and missing data by projecting geometry from three orthogonal directions (X, Y, Z). It ensures complete volumetric coverage by aggregating fragments from all three principal axes, addressing geometric distortion inherent in 2D projections. It is chosen when strict topological correctness (no tunnels) is required for complex, non-planar meshes. Constructs a 3D volumetric representation from a sparse set of calibrated multi-view images by registering estimated depth maps into a voxel grid. It addresses non-Lambertian scenes using individual minimum cost per view and represents geometry as a sparse voxel cloud. It distinguishes itself by incorporating an iterative refinement loop that removes isolated voxels and smooths sharp corners. Definition: A cost volume Vc is constructed from feature volumes \{Vfi\} of N reference views to perceive coarse scene structure and provide scene priors for sampling, skipping blank areas. Parameter: L: Number of depth layers in the cost volume. Typical value: 16. Pitfall: Checkerboard artifacts caused by deconvolution layers in the Res-Unet processing the cost volume are eliminated by replacing deconvolution with combinations of upsampling and convolution layers. name: Single 2D Projection Voxelization
head: Dominant axis voxelization, Thin voxelization via single projection
body: Single 2D Projection Voxelization produces 6-separating voxel grids from planar triangles by leveraging the geometric "thinness" property. It solves volumetric coverage with minimal computational overhead by requiring only one 2D rasterization pass along the dominant axis of the triangle's normal, rather than three orthogonal passes. Unlike Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization, it relies on the fact that for any pixel center covered by the projection, the dominant axis projection uniquely determines the voxel in that column, handling edge cases via crosshair-segment intersection tests. Inputs: A planar triangle defined by three vertices in 3D space, a target voxel grid resolution R = (Rx, Ry, Rz), and the scene's axis-aligned bounding box defined by bb{min} and bb{max}. Outputs: A 3D voxel grid where occupied voxels are marked. Data Structures: A 3D voxel grid of size Rx \times Ry \times Rz storing occupancy and depth, and a 2D buffer for the projection plane. Algorithm Steps: 1. Identify the dominant axis of the geometric normal vector of the planar triangle. 2. Rasterize the triangle projected into 2D along the dominant axis of the normal. 3. For pixels where the projected triangle contains the pixel center, output the voxel whose center depth is closest to the depth of the triangle evaluated at the pixel center. 4. For pixels that contain an edge of the triangle but where the triangle does not overlap the center, find the extents of the triangle on a horizontal line bisecting the pixel. 5. Clamp these horizontal extents to the horizontal pixel extents. 6. Evaluate the depth of the triangle at these two clamped points. 7. If the evaluated depths are on different sides of a voxel's center depth, output the corresponding voxel. 8. If the horizontal test fails, repeat the test for the vertical direction (vertical line bisecting the pixel). Formulas: Coordinate mapping from the parent article transforms 3D points to voxel indices: i = \text{floor}\left( \frac{p{clip}.xyz - bb{min}}{bb{max} - bb{min}} \times R \right) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def single2dprojectionvoxelization(triangle, resolution, bbmin, bbmax): # triangle: list of 3 vertices, each (x, y, z) # resolution: (Rx, Ry, Rz) # bbmin, bbmax: (x, y, z) # 1. Identify dominant axis n = cross(triangle[1] - triangle[0], triangle[2] - triangle[0]) dominantaxis = 0 if abs(n[0]) >= abs(n[1]) and abs(n[0]) >= abs(n[2]) else (1 if abs(n[1]) >= abs(n[2]) else 2) # 2. Project and Rasterize projtri = dropaxis(triangle, dominantaxis) pixels = rasterize2d(projtri, resolution[dominantaxis]) voxelgrid = {} scale = resolution[dominantaxis] / (bbmax[dominantaxis] - bbmin[dominantaxis]) offset = -bbmin[dominantaxis] scale for u, v in pixels: center2d = (u + 0.5, v + 0.5) center3d = project2dto3d(projtri, dominantaxis, center2d) if center3d is not None: # 3. Pixel center covered depthtri = center3d[dominantaxis] idx = int(math.floor(depthtri scale + offset)) voxelidx = list(maptovoxel2d(center3d, resolution, bbmin, bbmax)) voxelidx[dominantaxis] = idx voxelgrid[tuple(voxelidx)] = True else: # 4. Edge pixel: triangle covers pixel but not center # Horizontal test hextents = getlineextents(projtri, dominantaxis, center2d, horizontal=True) if hextents: clampedh = clampextents(hextents, u, v) depthsh = sorted([project2dto3d(projtri, dominantaxis, p)[dominantaxis] for p in clampedh]) voxelidx = int(math.floor((u + 0.5) scale + offset)) voxelcenterdepth = (voxelidx + 0.5) / scale + bbmin[dominantaxis] if depthsh[0] < voxelcenterdepth < depthsh[1]: for p in clampedh: p3d = project2dto3d(projtri, dominantaxis, p) voxelgrid[tuple(maptovoxel2d(p3d, resolution, bbmin, bbmax))] = True else: # Vertical test vextents = getlineextents(projtri, dominantaxis, center2d, horizontal=False) if vextents: clampedv = clampextents(vextents, u, v) depthsv = sorted([project2dto3d(projtri, dominantaxis, p)[dominantaxis] for p in clampedv]) if depthsv[0] < voxelcenterdepth < depthsv[1]: for p in clampedv: p3d = project2dto3d(projtri, dominantaxis, p) voxelgrid[tuple(maptovoxel2d(p3d, resolution, bbmin, bbmax))] = True return voxelgrid def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def dropaxis(vertices, axis): return [(v[i] for i in range(3) if i != axis) for v in vertices] def rasterize2d(tri2d, res): # Standard scanline rasterization returning covered (u, v) pixel coordinates v0, v1, v2 = tri2d minu, maxu = int(min(v[0] for v in tri2d)), int(max(v[0] for v in tri2d)) + 1 minv, maxv = int(min(v[1] for v in tri2d)), int(max(v[1] for v in tri2d)) + 1 covered = [] for u in range(minu, maxu): for v in range(minv, maxv): if pointintriangle((u + 0.5, v + 0.5), tri2d): covered.append((u, v)) return covered def pointintriangle(p, tri): v0, v1, v2 = tri denom = (v1[0] - v0[0]) (v2[1] - v0[1]) - (v2[0] - v0[0]) (v1[1] - v0[1]) if denom == 0: return False w0 = ((v1[1] - v0[1]) (p[0] - v0[0]) + (v0[0] - v1[0]) (p[1] - v0[1])) / denom w1 = ((v2[1] - v0[1]) (p[0] - v0[0]) + (v0[0] - v2[0]) (p[1] - v0[1])) / denom w2 = 1.0 - w0 - w1 return w0 >= 0 and w1 >= 0 and w2 >= 0 def project2dto3d(projtri, dominantaxis, p2d): # Barycentric interpolation to reconstruct 3D point at 2D location v0, v1, v2 = projtri fulltri = [] for v in projtri: fullv = list(v) fullv.insert(dominantaxis, 0) fulltri.append(tuple(fullv)) denom = (fulltri[1][0] - fulltri[0][0]) (fulltri[2][1] - fulltri[0][1]) - (fulltri[2][0] - fulltri[0][0]) (fulltri[1][1] - fulltri[0][1]) if denom == 0: return None w0 = ((fulltri[1][1] - fulltri[0][1]) (p2d[0] - fulltri[0][0]) + (fulltri[0][0] - fulltri[1][0]) (p2d[1] - fulltri[0][1])) / denom w1 = ((fulltri[2][1] - fulltri[0][1]) (p2d[0] - fulltri[0][0]) + (fulltri[0][0] - fulltri[2][0]) (p2d[1] - fulltri[0][1])) / denom w2 = 1.0 - w0 - w1 if w0 < 0 or w1 < 0 or w2 < 0: return None return ( w0 fulltri[0][0] + w1 fulltri[1][0] + w2 fulltri[2][0], w0 fulltri[0][1] + w1 fulltri[1][1] + w2 fulltri[2][1], w0 fulltri[0][2] + w1 fulltri[1][2] + w2 fulltri[2][2]) def getlineextents(projtri, dominantaxis, center2d, horizontal): # Intersects triangle with line y=center2d[1] (horizontal) or x=center2d[0] (vertical) v0, v1, v2 = projtri lineval = center2d[1] if horizontal else center2d[0] linecoord = 1 if horizontal else 0 points = [] edges = [(v0, v1), (v1, v2), (v2, v0)] for a, b in edges: if (a[linecoord] - lineval) (b[linecoord] - lineval) <= 0: t = (lineval - a[linecoord]) / (b[linecoord] - a[linecoord] + 1e-9) othercoord = a[1 - linecoord] + t (b[1 - linecoord] - a[1 - linecoord]) points.append((othercoord, lineval) if horizontal else (lineval, othercoord)) return points def clampextents(extents, u, v): # Clamp x to [u, u+1] and y to [v, v+1] return [(max(u, min(u+1, p[0])), max(v, min(v+1, p[1]))) for p in extents] def maptovoxel2d(point3d, resolution, bbmin, bbmax): scale = [resolution[i] / (bbmax[i] - bbmin[i]) for i in range(3)] offset = [-bbmin[i] scale[i] for i in range(3)] return tuple(int(math.floor(point3d[i] scale[i] + offset[i])) for i in range(3)) Parameters: Resolution R: Determines the granularity of the voxel grid. Bounding Box: Defines the spatial extent of the voxel grid. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: Triangles with zero area or collinear vertices may produce invalid normals. Ensure normal computation handles degenerate cases by returning a default axis or skipping the triangle. Precision: Depth comparisons for the edge tests must be robust to floating-point errors. Use a small epsilon when comparing depths to voxel center depths. Boundary Conditions: The rasterization must ensure that pixels on the boundary of the projection are correctly handled to avoid missing voxels at the edges of the bounding box. Multi-pass Projection Voxelization is the initial surface voxelization step that projects input surface primitives onto 2D planes and rasterizes them into a 3D volume, producing an "incorrect" surface voxelization that includes hidden primitives. It differs from its parent, Single 2D Projection Voxelization, by using multiple orthogonal projection directions and compositing the results to handle surfaces perpendicular to the projection plane, which would otherwise have zero area and fail to rasterize. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significantly faster than multi-view methods due to the reduction in rasterization passes. It produces 6-separating voxelization, ensuring tunnel-freeness. Limitations: Relies on the "thinness" property, which may not hold for all geometric configurations or non-planar inputs. It is specifically designed for planar triangles. When to Use: When computational efficiency is critical and the input geometry consists of planar triangles. When Not to Use: For non-planar surfaces or when higher-order topological guarantees beyond 6-separation are required without additional processing. The method is derived from the "thinness" property of voxelization and the equivalence of 3-axis rasterization with the crosshairs target. It was presented in the paper "A Topological Approach to Voxelization" by Laine et al. (2013). The approach leverages the observation that projecting along the dominant axis of the normal is sufficient to capture the unique voxel in each column for pixel centers, with edge cases handled by crosshair-segment intersection tests. A Topological Approach to Voxelization, https://research.nvidia.com/sites/default/files/pubs/2013-06A-Topological-Approach/laine2013egsrpaper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Multi-pass Projection Voxelization
head: Primitive Voxelization
body: Multi-pass Projection Voxelization is the initial surface voxelization step that projects input surface primitives onto 2D planes and rasterizes them into a 3D volume, producing an "incorrect" surface voxelization that includes hidden primitives. It differs from its parent, Single 2D Projection Voxelization, by using multiple orthogonal projection directions and compositing the results to handle surfaces perpendicular to the projection plane, which would otherwise have zero area and fail to rasterize. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of surface primitives (e.g., triangles) after culling. Output: A 3D texture representing the initial voxelization, where voxels are marked if they intersect the projected primitives. Data Structures: 3D Texture: A single 3D texture with 32-bit RGBA format is used for volume encoding. For a resolution of 1024^3, this requires 128 MB of video memory. Multiple Render Targets (MRT): The GPU renders to 8 color buffers simultaneously. Parameters: Volumetric Resolution (n): The side length of the cubic volume. Typical value: 1024. View Volume Enlargement: The view volume is set slightly larger than the Minkowski sum bounding box to ensure outer voxels are connected. The enlargement percentage is calculated as: \text{Enlargement} = \frac{2(1 + \epsilon)}{n - 2(1 + \epsilon)} where n is the volumetric resolution and \epsilon is an infinitesimal number. Steps: 1. Project: Project each surface primitive onto a 2D plane using orthogonal projection. 2. Rasterize: Rasterize the projected surfaces to produce fragments containing depth information and 2D coordinates. 3. Map: Map each fragment to a corresponding voxel in the 3D volume using the 2D coordinates and depth. 4. Encode: Use a fragment shader to compute an RGBA color for each fragment based on its depth information, which is passed as a texture coordinate. 5. Render Passes: Render the vertex buffer object (VBO) multiple times using MRT to fill the 3D texture. For a 1024^3 resolution, render 4 times (1024 / 32 / 8). 6. Handle Perpendicular Surfaces: To address the failure of rasterizing surfaces perpendicular to the projection plane, project the model along three orthogonal directions (e.g., x, y, z). 7. Compose: Use a fragment shader to sample the x and y 3D textures and write the result to the z texture, then delete the x and y textures to free memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multipassprojectionvoxelization(primitives, resolution): # Initialize three 3D textures for x, y, z projection directions # Each texture has resolution^3 voxels with 32-bit RGBA format texx = [[[ [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(resolution)] for in range(resolution)] for in range(resolution)] texy = [[[ [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(resolution)] for in range(resolution)] for in range(resolution)] texz = [[[ [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(resolution)] for in range(resolution)] for in range(resolution)] # Calculate view volume enlargement to ensure outer voxels are connected epsilon = 1e-9 enlargementfactor = 2 (1 + epsilon) / (resolution - 2 (1 + epsilon)) bbmin = [min(p.mincoord[d] for p in primitives) for d in range(3)] bbmax = [max(p.maxcoord[d] for p in primitives) for d in range(3)] viewvolume = expandboundingbox(bbmin, bbmax, enlargementfactor) # Render along three orthogonal directions rendervbo(primitives, viewvolume, 'x', texx) rendervbo(primitives, viewvolume, 'y', texy) rendervbo(primitives, viewvolume, 'z', texz) # Compose results: sample x and y textures, write to z texture for i in range(resolution): for j in range(resolution): for k in range(resolution): texz[i][j][k] = [max(texx[i][j][k][c], texy[i][j][k][c]) for c in range(4)] # Free memory by clearing x and y textures for i in range(resolution): for j in range(resolution): for k in range(resolution): texx[i][j][k] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] texy[i][j][k] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return texz def expandboundingbox(bbmin, bbmax, factor): expandedmin = [bbmin[d] - (bbmax[d] - bbmin[d]) factor / 2 for d in range(3)] expandedmax = [bbmax[d] + (bbmax[d] - bbmin[d]) factor / 2 for d in range(3)] return expandedmin, expandedmax def rendervbo(primitives, viewvolume, direction, targettexture): # Projects primitives orthogonally along direction onto 2D plane # Rasterizes fragments with depth and 2D coordinates # Maps fragments to 3D volume slices using MRT (8 color buffers per pass) # Number of passes = resolution // 32 // 8 passes = resolution // 32 // 8 for p in range(passes): # Fragment shader computes RGBA color based on depth passed as texture coordinate # Writes to targettexture slice corresponding to pass p # Not given in the sources: exact GPU rasterization and MRT slice mapping logic pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perpendicular Surfaces: Surfaces perpendicular to the projection plane have zero area and are not rasterized. This is mitigated by using three orthogonal projections. Hidden Primitives: The initial voxelization includes hidden primitives, which are later used as a barrier for flood fill. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but the method takes approximately one second for a 1024^3 resolution on a GPU. Memory Complexity: Requires 128 MB of video memory for a 1024^3 resolution using a single 3D texture with 32-bit RGBA format. Strengths: Efficient use of GPU rasterization; reduces memory cost and number of render passes by using 3D textures and MRT. Limitations: Produces an "incorrect" surface voxelization that includes hidden primitives, requiring a subsequent flood fill step. Multi-pass Projection Voxelization, also known as Primitive Voxelization, was introduced in the paper "A GPU-based voxelization approach to 3D Minkowski sum computation". It is used as the first step in a voxelization algorithm for computing 3D Minkowski sums, providing an initial surface voxelization that serves as a barrier for subsequent flood fill operations. A GPU-based voxelization approach to 3D Minkowski sum computation, https://doi.org/10.1145/1839778.1839783, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization
head: 3-Direction Rasterization, 3-View Voxelization, Directional Sheet Buffer Voxelization, Orthogonal Voxelization Camera Setup, Orthographic 3D Texture Rasterization, Voxelization via Orthographic Projection, Worksheet Voxelization
body: Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization rasterizes scene geometry into a 3D texture using three orthographic cameras aligned with the scene's bounding box axes to create a voxelized representation for subsequent volume rendering. It differs from Single 2D Projection Voxelization by using three orthogonal views to ensure complete coverage and from 3-Pass Voxelization by utilizing intermediate "sheet buffers" and a final "worksheet" synthesis to handle discrete voxel encoding efficiently on GPU hardware. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Triangle mesh geometry, scene axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) defined by bbmin and bbmax, and target voxel grid resolution R = (Rx, Ry, Rz). Output: A 3D texture (Direct Method) or a 2D worksheet texture encoding 3D data (Indirect Method) representing the voxelized volume. Data Structures: 1. 3D Texture (Direct Method): A std::vector<GLfloat> of size 4 \times Rx \times Ry \times Rz, initialized to 0.0f, representing RGBA32F voxel data. 2. Sheet Buffers (Indirect Method): Three 2D buffers representing parts of the discrete voxel space, one for each axis direction (X, Y, Z). 3. Worksheet (Indirect Method): A 2D texture of resolution 2^W \times 2^H. It encodes the discrete voxel space (2^L \times 2^M \times 2^N) such that 2^L \times 2^M \times 2^N = 2^W \times 2^H \times C, where C is the number of voxels encoded in a single texel (e.g., C=32 for binary voxelization with four 8-bit components). Parameters: voxelTextureSize: Default resolution, e.g., glm::uvec3(64, 64, 64). offset: Camera extension distance beyond the bounding box, fixed at 0.2f. projectionscale: Frustum expansion factor applied to range, fixed at 1.02f (passed as 0.51f to half-width). C: Voxels per texel in the worksheet method. Steps: 1. Bounding Box and Camera Setup: Calculate the scene bounding box min/max. Compute the range Range = bb{max} - bb{min}. Set the camera offset to 0.2f beyond the max bounds along each axis. Configure three orthographic cameras looking towards the scene's AABB along the X, Y, and Z axes. Set the orthographic projection frustum bounds to 1.02 \times Range on the viewing planes, with near plane at 0.1f and far plane at 1.2 \times Range + offset. 2. Rasterization (Stage 1): For each of the three views (X, Y, Z): Pass the corresponding view-projection matrix to the voxelization shader uniform viewProject[i]. For each triangle, determine the axis direction along which it has the maximum projection area. Rasterize the triangle against this axis direction to avoid degenerate line segments caused by 2D linear interpolation when the triangle is parallel to the view. If using the Direct Method: Clear the 3D texture to RGBA(0,0,0,0), disable multisampling, depth testing, and face culling. Bind the texture as a read-write image buffer. Rasterize triangles directly into the 3D texture using atomic operations for occupancy. If using the Indirect Method: Rasterize triangles into the corresponding 2D Sheet Buffer. Only triangles intersecting the current slab are processed. 3. Texelization (Stage 2 - Indirect Method Only): Transform voxel positions to 3D volume coordinates immediately. Use these coordinates to find the correct position in the worksheet. Add voxels to the worksheet via a blending operation at the corresponding location. 4. Synthesis (Stage 3 - Indirect Method Only): Transcode the three directional sheet buffers to the final worksheet. Transform each element to discrete voxel space, then encode to the appropriate texel in the worksheet. Voxel Access Logic: To access a voxel at coordinates (px, py, pz): 1. Determine the patch by dividing pz by C. 2. Access the texel at (px, py) in the found patch. 3. Determine the bit offset within the texel component using pz and C. 4. Use a lookup table to facilitate accessing bits from the component. 5. Finalization: Generate mipmaps for the filled 3D texture (Direct Method) or the final worksheet (Indirect Method) to enable multi-resolution cone tracing. Pseudocode (Direct Method): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def orthographicmultiviewvoxelization(mesh, bbmin, bbmax, voxelsize): """ Voxelizes a mesh into a 3D texture using 3 orthographic views. """ # 1. Setup rangevec = [bbmax[i] - bbmin[i] for i in range(3)] offset = 0.2 scale = [voxelsize[i] / rangevec[i] for i in range(3)] maxextent = max(rangevec) center = [(bbmin[i] + bbmax[i]) / 2.0 for i in range(3)] # Initialize 3D texture (RGBA32F) texturesize = voxelsize[0] voxelsize[1] voxelsize[2] 4 voxeltexture = [0.0] texturesize # Camera configurations for X, Y, Z views cameras = [ {"pos": [center[0] + maxextent + offset, center[1], center[2]], "look": [-1.0, 0.0, 0.0], "up": [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]}, {"pos": [center[0], center[1] + maxextent + offset, center[2]], "look": [0.0, -1.0, 0.0], "up": [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]}, {"pos": [center[0], center[1], center[2] - maxextent - offset], "look": [0.0, 0.0, 1.0], "up": [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]} ] for cam in cameras: for tri in mesh.triangles: # Determine axis with max projection area to avoid degenerate rasterization v0, v1, v2 = tri.vertices normal = cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0) maxaxis = max(range(3), key=lambda i: abs(normal[i])) # Project vertices to clip space [-1, 1] clipcoords = [[(v[i] - cam["pos"][i]) / (0.51 maxextent) for i in range(3)] for v in (v0, v1, v2)] # Rasterize into 3D texture using atomic OR for occupancy # Not given in the sources. # Generate mipmaps for multi-resolution cone tracing # Not given in the sources. return voxeltexture def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] Pseudocode (Indirect/Worksheet Method): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def worksheetvoxelization(mesh, bbmin, bbmax, voxelres, texelvoxelsc): """ Voxelizes a mesh into a 2D worksheet texture using 3 sheet buffers. """ # 1. Setup rangevec = [bbmax[i] - bbmin[i] for i in range(3)] offset = 0.2 maxextent = max(rangevec) center = [(bbmin[i] + bbmax[i]) / 2.0 for i in range(3)] sheetbuffers = [[0] (voxelres[0] voxelres[1]) for in range(3)] cameras = [ {"pos": [center[0] + maxextent + offset, center[1], center[2]], "look": [-1.0, 0.0, 0.0], "up": [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]}, {"pos": [center[0], center[1] + maxextent + offset, center[2]], "look": [0.0, -1.0, 0.0], "up": [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]}, {"pos": [center[0], center[1], center[2] - maxextent - offset], "look": [0.0, 0.0, 1.0], "up": [0.0, 1.0, 0.0]} ] # 2. Rasterization Stage for viewidx, cam in enumerate(cameras): for tri in mesh.triangles: v0, v1, v2 = tri.vertices normal = cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0) maxaxis = max(range(3), key=lambda i: abs(normal[i])) if maxaxis == viewidx: clipcoords = [[(v[i] - cam["pos"][i]) / (0.51 maxextent) for i in range(3)] for v in (v0, v1, v2)] # Rasterize triangle to sheet buffer # Not given in the sources. # 3. Synthesis Stage worksheet = [0] (voxelres[0] voxelres[1] 4) # RGBA for viewidx in range(3): for element in sheetbuffers[viewidx]: # Transform sheet buffer coordinates to discrete 3D voxel space # Not given in the sources. voxelcoords = transformtovoxelspace(element, viewidx, bbmin, rangevec) px, py, pz = voxelcoords patchindex = pz // texelvoxelsc texelcoords = (px, py) # Encode voxel into worksheet texel using patch division and bit offset logic # Not given in the sources. # Generate mipmaps # Not given in the sources. return worksheet def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] Shadow Volume Voxelization generates a 3D shadow volume texture by voxelizing scene geometry into a 3D grid, where each voxel stores a bitmask representing which of its 8 constituent sub-voxels are occluded. It replaces standard occupancy flags with a bitmask per coarse voxel to enable multi-resolution shadow representation through mipmaps. Slicing-based voxelization rasterizes the model the same number of times as the resolution of the volume along the z-direction. This feature (rendering to 3D textures) has not been supported in consumer graphics hardware of PC platform at the time of writing. It is significantly slower than the proposed 2D texture method; for the Blade model at 256^3, it takes ~5 seconds compared to ~100ms for the proposed method. Voxelization via SRP Render Context creates a hidden orthographic camera with aspect ratio 1.0 and MSAA enabled. The far clip plane is set to 0.5 \times \text{bound}, the near clip plane to -0.5 \times \text{bound}, and the orthographic size to 0.5 \times \text{bound}, positioned at the voxel space center. It uses a temporary dummy render texture descriptor with format R8, dimension Tex2D, and memoryless flags for Color, Depth, and MSAA. Single-View Orthographic Voxelization converts an arbitrary polygonal scene into a voxelized representation by rendering it into a 2D texture where each pixel represents a column of voxels along the view ray. Each bit in the 32-bit pixel value indicates if a polygon crosses that voxel. It uses a single fragment shader where depth values index a bitmask texture, returning a 32-bit value with one bit set, which is OR-blended into the output RGBA8 texture. Applications include transmittance shadow maps, shadow volume culling, and refraction/attenuation of light. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot V), where N is the number of triangles and V is the number of views (3). The indirect method adds a synthesis step proportional to the number of fragments. Memory Complexity: O(Rx Ry Rz) for the direct method. The indirect method uses O(Rx Ry) for sheet buffers and O(Rx Ry / C) for the worksheet, reducing memory footprint. Performance: The worksheet method is significantly faster than slicing-based voxelization. For a 256^3 resolution, the worksheet method takes ~100ms, while slicing-based takes ~5 seconds. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated, real-time capable, handles complex models efficiently. Limitations: Requires careful handling of degenerate triangles (parallel to rasterization direction). The indirect method requires additional synthesis pass and lookup logic. When to use: Real-time volume rendering, shadow volume generation. When not to use: When high-precision solid voxelization is required without post-processing (requires 3D scan-filling). The method was introduced in "Real-time Voxelization for Complex Models" as a scheme to solve the problem of fast voxelization for interactive graphics applications by representing the resultant volume as 2D textures. The direct method implementation is found in "Voxel Cone Tracing". name: Shadow Volume Voxelization
head: Shadow Volume Texture Generation
body: Shadow Volume Voxelization generates a 3D shadow volume texture by voxelizing scene geometry into a 3D grid, where each coarse voxel stores an 8-bit bitmask representing which of its 8 constituent sub-voxels are occluded. It extends Orthographic Multi-View Voxelization by storing a full 8-bit occlusion mask per coarse voxel instead of a single occupancy bit, enabling fine-grained shadow information for subsequent volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry (meshes with model matrices), scene bounding box dimensions (W, H, D in world units), and a scale factor (e.g., 10 units per meter). Output: A 3D texture with internal format GLR8UI (unsigned byte, red channel only) containing 3 mip levels. Data Structures: ShadowVolume class fields: width, height, depth (integer dimensions of the finest mip level), volumetexture (OpenGL 3D texture handle), shadowvolumemip0 (pointer to Level 0 data, uint8t), scenexml and sceneroot (XML scene hierarchy representation). Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a 3D texture with 3 mip levels. Level 0 dimensions are (W, H, D), Level 1 are (W/2, H/2, D/2), and Level 2 are (W/4, H/4, D/4). Initialize Level 0 memory to zero. 2. Voxel Processing: For each voxel (xv, yv, zv) in the input shape: Calculate world position: \text{voxel\pos} = \text{vec3}(xv, yv, zv) + \text{vec3}(0.5, 0.5, 0.5), then transform: \text{voxel\pos} = \text{vec3}(\text{model\matrix} \times \text{vec4}(\text{voxel\pos}, 10.0)). Map to grid coordinates: x = \lfloor \text{voxel\pos}.x \rfloor + \text{width} / 2, y = \lfloor \text{voxel\pos}.y \rfloor, z = \lfloor \text{voxel\pos}.z \rfloor + \text{depth} / 2. Boundary check: If x < 0 or x \ge \text{width} or y < 0 or y \ge \text{height} or z < 0 or z \ge \text{depth}, skip the voxel. 3.
