name: Scanline and Geometric Primitives
body: This family defines methods for converting continuous geometric primitives (points, lines, planes, triangles) into discrete volumetric representations (voxel grids) suitable for volume rendering. It solves the problem of accurately representing sharp geometric boundaries within a scalar field without the aliasing artifacts inherent in binary voxelization. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Rasterization-based Voxelization by focusing on analytic slab definitions, optimal scanline criteria, and priority-based clipping rather than GPU rasterization pipelines or geometry shaders. Builds on the domain definition, value assignment, and storage mechanisms of Rasterization and GPU Shaders. Converts polygons into a volumetric dataset, combines them with existing data using volume matting, and renders the composite. Sets itself apart by pre-filtering geometry into the voxel grid to allow standard ray-casting while avoiding aliasing through analytic anti-aliasing. Choose when mixing explicit geometry with volumetric data. Generates topologically correct representations of lines and planes by defining a slab of voxels. Solves N-separability and N-minimality simultaneously. Sets itself apart by deriving thickness t from surface normal and grid resolution. Choose when topological correctness (no holes) is critical for lines/planes. Maps objects into voxels where distance to surface S is < t. Bypasses polygon conversion. Sets itself apart by using spatial proximity rather than scanline logic. Choose for regular shapes or surfaces where distance metrics are computable. Triangle-based voxelization slicing along a dominant axis and performing 2D line voxelizations. Sets itself apart by using an "optimal" distance criterion for tighter fit than standard grid-aligned lines. Choose for high-quality triangle voxelization. 3D generalization of scan-line algorithm for low-level processor implementation. Determines visible portions of primitives for the Compositing Frame Buffer (CFB). Sets itself apart by explicit priority-based occlusion culling during voxelization. Choose when writing to a priority-based CFB. Bandlimit the object to the Nyquist frequency in all three dimensions. Sample the object in a manner that limits losses due to quantization. Use volume rendering's partial opacity capability to handle the resulting voxel representation and avoid aliasing artifacts common in binary voxel representations. The method originates from the need to hybridize ray tracing and volume rendering. Early hybrid ray tracers used binary voxel representations for polyhedra and parametric surfaces, resulting in aliasing. To avoid these artifacts, Kaufman et al. proposed bandlimiting objects to the Nyquist frequency and using volume rendering's partial opacity to handle the resulting voxel representation. This approach allows polygons to be shaded, filtered, sampled, and combined with volumetric data, which is then rendered using standard techniques without supersampling. The method is described in a technical report on interactive visualization of 3D medical data. DTIC ADA208091: Interactive Visualization of 3D Medical Data, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA208091, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 3D Scan-conversion
head: Polygon-to-voxel conversion, Voxelization with geometric primitives
body: 3D scan-conversion is a rendering method that converts geometric primitives (polygons) into a volumetric dataset, combines them with existing volumetric data using volume matting operators, and renders the resulting composite ensemble using standard volume rendering techniques. It sets itself apart from hybrid ray tracing by pre-filtering and sampling geometry into the voxel grid, allowing the use of standard ray-casting for the final image while avoiding aliasing artifacts through analytic anti-aliasing. Inputs: 1. A volumetric dataset (scalar field) defined on an N \times N \times N voxel array. 2. A set of embedded geometric primitives (polygons). Outputs: 1. A final rendered image. 2. An intermediate composite volumetric dataset containing color and opacity for every voxel. Data Structures: Volumetric Buffer: An N \times N \times N array storing scalar values. Color/Opacity Buffers: Arrays storing the color cv and opacity ov for the volumetric data, and cp, op for the polygons. Light Strength Buffer: A 3D buffer storing fractional light strength for shadow calculations (optional). Steps: 1. Classify Volumetric Data: Shade and classify the volumetric data to yield a color cv and opacity ov for each voxel. 2. Shade and Filter Polygons: For each polygon: shade it (homogeneous color per source), apply a 3D edge filtering algorithm to bandlimit the data, and sample it at the volumetric resolution to yield a color cp and opacity op for each affected voxel. 3. Combine (Volume Matting): Combine the volumetric color/opacity (cv, ov) and polygon color/opacity (cp, op) using volume matting operators to yield a composite color cc and opacity oc for each voxel. 4. Render Composite: Ray trace, resample, and composite the composite dataset (cc, oc) without further consideration of the geometric data. 5. Shadow Calculation (Optional): If shadows are required, use a two-pass approach storing shadow information in a 3D light strength buffer instead of a 2D shadow depth buffer, computing fractional light strength at every point in space. Formulas: Volume matting (over operator): oc' = oc + op(1 - oc) Composite color: cc' = \frac{cc oc + cp op (1 - oc)}{oc'} (when oc' > 0). Parameters: Filter: 3D version of the edge filtering algorithm by Feibush et al. [1980]. Convolution Kernel: Constant weight ball, 2 voxels in diameter. Sampling Rate: One ray per pixel is usually sufficient to prevent aliasing artifacts. Pitfalls: Matting Order: Matting is not commutative. The order in which polygons are scan-converted affects the appearance of polygon-polygon intersections. Volumetric Interaction: Polygons may be matted over or under volumetric data, affecting appearance. Aliasing: If polygonal data is not sufficiently bandlimited prior to sampling, aliasing artifacts will appear. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def render3dscanconversion(volumetricdata, polygons, viewparams): """ Renders a mixture of volumetric data and geometric primitives using 3D scan-conversion. """ N = len(volumetricdata) # Step 1: Classify Volumetric Data cv = [[[ [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] ov = [[[0.0 for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for i in range(N): for j in range(N): for k in range(N): cv[i][j][k], ov[i][j][k] = classifyvolumetric(volumetricdata[i][j][k]) # Initialize composite buffers cc = [[[cv[i][j][k] for k in range(N)] for j in range(N)] for i in range(N)] oc = [[[ov[i][j][k] for k in range(N)] for j in range(N)] for i in range(N)] # Step 2 & 3: Process Polygons for polygon in polygons: # Shade polygon (homogeneous color per source) pcolor = polygon.color # Filter polygon using 3D edge filter (Feibush et al.) # Kernel: Constant weight ball, 2 voxels diameter (radius 1) pfiltered = apply3dedgefilter(polygon, radius=1) # Sample filtered polygon into voxel grid pcolorgrid, popacitygrid = samplepolygontovoxels(pfiltered, N) # Combine using volume matting operators cc, oc = volumemattingcombine(cc, oc, pcolorgrid, popacitygrid) # Step 4: Render Composite finalimage = raycastvolume(cc, oc, viewparams) return finalimage def classifyvolumetric(scalar): """Apply transfer function to scalar field to yield color and opacity per voxel.""" # Implementation depends on specific transfer function return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0 def apply3dedgefilter(polygon, radius): """Convolve polygon representation with constant weight ball kernel.""" # Standard 3D box blur or convolution over the polygon's voxel footprint return polygon def samplepolygontovoxels(filteredpolygon, N): """Rasterize filtered polygon into N x N x N grid to yield cp and op.""" cp = [[[ [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] op = [[[0.0 for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] # Iterate voxels, evaluate polygon contribution, store in cp and op return cp, op def volumemattingcombine(cc, oc, cp, op): """Combine existing composite with new polygon data using over operator.""" onew = [[[oc[i][j][k] + op[i][j][k] (1 - oc[i][j][k]) for k in range(N)] for j in range(N)] for i in range(N)] cnew = [[[ [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for i in range(N): for j in range(N): for k in range(N): if onew[i][j][k] > 0: cnew[i][j][k] = [(cc[i][j][k][d] oc[i][j][k] + cp[i][j][k][d] op[i][j][k] (1 - oc[i][j][k])) / onew[i][j][k] for d in range(3)] return cnew, onew def raycastvolume(cc, oc, viewparams): """Standard volume ray casting loop over the composite dataset.""" # Iterate rays, resample cc/oc, composite along ray return [] This family compares two distinct approaches for rendering mixtures of geometric primitives and volumetric data: hybrid ray tracing and 3D scan-conversion. Both methods are reasonably efficient and produce aliasing-free images, but they differ significantly in computational cost, image quality characteristics, and versatility. The choice between them depends on whether the application prioritizes the physical accuracy of ray-traced lighting and shadows or the structural clarity provided by scan-converted geometric backdrops. A rasterization technique that converts geometric primitives (lines and triangles) from standard 3-D data into a cylindrical voxel grid coordinate system, specifically designed for a volumetric display with a rotating screen. The raster engine, in conjunction with the host PC, scan-converts typical 3-D data into the device coordinate system, storing rasterized data in graphics memory (e.g., 3 Gbits DDR SDRAM). Traditional Cartesian scan-conversion algorithms do not apply because the display uses a cylindrical coordinate system, requiring proprietary efficient rasterization algorithms. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given. Requires shading, filtering, and sampling each polygon into the volume grid, followed by standard volume ray casting. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volumetric data, color/opacity buffers for the volume and polygons, and potentially a 3D light strength buffer for shadows. The 3D buffer is noted to require significantly more memory than a 2D shadow depth buffer. Performance: Designed to be efficient. The pre-filtering of polygons allows for standard sampling rates (one ray per pixel) without aliasing. Strengths: Produces images free from aliasing artifacts; allows use of standard volume rendering techniques for the final composite; convenient for adding shadows via 3D light strength buffers. Limitations: Matting is non-commutative, requiring careful ordering of polygons; high memory usage for 3D shadow buffers; continuous shading is noted as under investigation, implying potential limitations with current implementations. When to Use: When structural clarity of geometric backdrops is prioritized over physical accuracy of lighting; when aliasing-free rendering of mixed data is required without the cost of full hybrid ray tracing. When Not to Use: When physical accuracy of ray-traced lighting and shadows is the primary goal (use Hybrid Ray Tracer instead); when memory is severely constrained (due to 3D buffers). Originating from research in medical imaging and molecular graphics, this method was presented in a study comparing hybrid ray tracing and 3D scan-conversion for rendering mixtures of geometric and volumetric data. It builds on volume matting operators [Drebin et al., 1988] and edge filtering algorithms [Feibush et al., 1980]. The method was developed to provide an efficient alternative to hybrid ray tracing while maintaining high image quality and avoiding aliasing artifacts. name: Hybrid Ray Tracer vs 3D Scan-Conversion
body: This family compares two approaches for rendering mixtures of geometric primitives and volumetric data: hybrid ray tracing and 3D scan-conversion. Both methods are reasonably efficient and produce aliasing-free images, but differ in cost, image quality, and versatility. Both methods integrate explicit geometric primitives with volumetric datasets to produce a single coherent image without aliasing artifacts. They are both considered reasonably efficient for their respective use cases. Builds on 3D Scan-conversion. Renders mixtures of geometric and volumetric data. Reasonably efficient and aliasing-free. Specific implementation details, computational cost relative to 3D scan-conversion, and versatility characteristics are not given in the sources. Renders mixtures by embedding geometric primitives into the volumetric dataset. Polygons exhibit finite thickness when rotated, and their opacity varies with their angle relative to the view direction, enhancing shape and orientation comprehension. Embedding polygons improves comprehension of the volume, as a backdrop of known shape and pattern aids appreciation of fine internal structures during rotation. For example, bisecting a CT study of the head with a gridded, coronally-oriented polygon improves appreciation of fine structure in the sinuses and eye orbits. The implementation uses tri-linear interpolation for resampling 3D data, which can blur polygonal edges, and the shadow casting algorithm includes three successive resampling steps. The comparison was described in a DTIC report. The work highlights trade-offs in cost, image quality, and versatility between the two methods. It suggests improvements such as better filtering to reduce blurring during 3D scan-conversion and reorganizing shadow casting operations to eliminate one resampling step. name: Cylindrical Rasterization
head: Cylindrical voxel grid conversion, Line- and triangle-drawing algorithms for rotating screen coordinate space, Proprietary efficient rasterization algorithms, Raster Engine Coordinate Transformation and Rasterization, Volumetric Rasterization
body: Cylindrical Rasterization is a specialized scan-conversion technique that transforms standard 3D geometric primitives (lines and triangles) or volumetric data into a cylindrical voxel grid coordinate system, specifically designed for volumetric displays featuring a rotating screen. Unlike traditional Cartesian rasterization, this method accounts for the unique kinematics of a rotating projection plane and projector-induced keystoning, ensuring that voxels are correctly mapped to the physical display space. It is distinct from general 3D scan-conversion [1895-3d-scan-conversion.md] by its explicit handling of the cylindrical coordinate transformation required for rotating hardware, rather than static volume buffers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D geometric data (polygons/lines) or pre-existing volumetric data (e.g., MRI, seismic) from a host PC. Output: Voxel data in the 3D-display-specific coordinate system, stored in graphics memory for continuous display. Data Structures: Graphics Memory: Partitioned into volume buffers. In the reference implementation, this is 3 Gbits (expandable to 6 Gbits) of DDR SDRAM. Buffer Layout: Each buffer stores 198 slices of 768 x 768 imagery. Coordinate System: Defined as the composition of a rotating screen with a rotation in the plane of the screen. Steps: 1. Data Reception: The Raster Engine accepts volumetric or geometry-based 3D data from the host PC via a SCSI interface. 2. Pre-processing (Geometry Only): A Mesa-based OpenGL-like library splits polygons into triangles, clips polygons outside the cylindrical volume, and calculates parameters required to draw in the display's specific coordinate system. This involves proprietary algorithms to handle the non-Cartesian space and keystoning. 3. Pre-processing (Volumetric Data Only): The volumetric data is resampled so that points in volumetric space align with the cylindrical grid. Volumetric data may optionally be transformed into polygonal surfaces for rendering. 4. Rasterization/Conversion: The Raster Engine converts the prepared data into voxel data in the 3D-display-specific coordinate system. Traditional scan-conversion algorithms are not applicable due to the cylindrical coordinate system. 5. Memory Storage: The resulting voxel data is stored into graphics memory. 6. Synchronization: A motor controller pages through memory in tight synchronization with the position of the rotating screen. 7. Output: The graphics memory is read out to the projector subsystem (e.g., DMD formatter electronics) at a rate of 24 volumes/second. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cylindricalrasterization(hostdata, displayconfig): # 1. Receive data from host via SCSI interface data = hostdata # 2. Pre-process geometry or volumetric data if data.type == "geometry": # Split polygons into triangles triangles = [] for poly in data.polygons: triangles.extend(splitpolygontotriangles(poly)) # Clip triangles outside the cylindrical volume clippedtriangles = [tri for tri in triangles if isinsidecylinder(tri, displayconfig.radius)] # Calculate parameters for the specific coordinate system # Handles rotation and projector-induced keystoning rasterparams = [computerasterparams(tri, displayconfig) for tri in clippedtriangles] # Convert to voxel data in display coordinate system voxeldata = rasterizetrianglestovoxels(rasterparams, displayconfig.grid) elif data.type == "volumetric": # Resample volumetric data to the cylindrical grid voxeldata = resamplevolumetrictocylindrical(data.grid, displayconfig.grid) # 3. Store in graphics memory # Memory partitioned into two volume buffers, each storing 198 slices of 768x768 writevoxelstomemory(voxeldata, displayconfig.memorylayout) # 4. Synchronize with rotating screen and output while displayconfig.isrunning: # Motor controller pages through memory in sync with screen position screenangle = hardwarereadencoder() sliceindex = mapangletosliceindex(screenangle, displayconfig) slicedata = readslicefrombuffer(sliceindex, displayconfig.memorylayout) hardwarewritedmd(slicedata) def splitpolygontotriangles(poly): return [poly[i], poly[i+1], poly[i+2] for i in range(len(poly)-2)] def isinsidecylinder(tri, radius): return all(x2 + y2 <= radius2 for x, y, z in tri) def computerasterparams(tri, config): return transformtocylindrical(tri, config) def rasterizetrianglestovoxels(params, grid): return scanconverttogrid(params, grid) def resamplevolumetrictocylindrical(grid, config): return interpolatetocylindrical(grid, config) def writevoxelstomemory(voxels, layout): for i, slicedata in enumerate(voxels): layout.buffers[i % 2].slices[i % 198] = slicedata def hardwarereadencoder(): return getencodervalue() def mapangletosliceindex(angle, config): return int((angle % 360) / 360 198) def readslicefrombuffer(index, layout): return layout.buffers[index % 2].slices[index % 198] def hardwarewritedmd(slicedata): transmittodmd(slicedata) def getencodervalue(): return 0 def transmittodmd(data): pass def transformtocylindrical(tri, config): return tri def scanconverttogrid(params, grid): return [] def interpolatetocylindrical(grid, config): return [] Parameters and Typical Values: Memory: 3 Gbits DDR SDRAM (standard), up to 6 Gbits (high resolution). Resolution: 768 x 768 pixels per slice. Slices per Volume: 198 slices. Update Rate: 24 volumes/second. Interface: SCSI. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate Mismatch: Traditional scan-conversion algorithms fail because the display uses a cylindrical coordinate system rather than Cartesian. Keystoning: Projector-induced keystoning distorts the image, requiring specific parameter calculations during rasterization. Bottleneck: For volumetric data, the SCSI connection speed is the primary bottleneck, limiting update rates and image complexity. Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined in terms of Big-O, but the system supports 24 volumes/second for 198 slices of 768x768 imagery. Memory Complexity: Requires significant dedicated graphics memory (3-6 Gbits) to buffer the entire volume for continuous display. Performance: The system can support higher resolution imagery than the current projector generates, allowing for up to 6 Gbits of RAM. For volumetric data, performance is limited by the SCSI bandwidth. Strengths: Enables real-time 3D visualization on rotating cylindrical displays; handles both geometry and raw volumetric data. Limitations: Proprietary algorithms limit portability; SCSI bottleneck for volumetric data; requires custom hardware (DSP, motor controller). When to use: When rendering to a volumetric display with a rotating screen component. When not to use: Requires custom hardware and proprietary algorithms tailored to rotating cylindrical displays. Cylindrical Rasterization was developed for a 100-million-voxel volumetric display system. The hardware implementation uses a Texas Instruments TMS320C6201 DSP as the Raster Engine. The algorithms were created because existing line- and triangle-drawing algorithms were unsuitable for the display's unique coordinate space and projector-induced keystoning. The system was presented at SPIE Vol. 4297A, "Stereoscopic Displays and Virtual Reality Systems IX" in San Jose, CA, in January 2001. 100-million-voxel volumetric display, https://doi.org/10.1117/12.480930, fetched 2026-11-01 Volumetric three-dimensional display system with rasterization hardware, https://doi.org/10.1117/12.430821, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Voxelization of Lines and Planes
head: Slab-based Voxelization, N-separating Voxelization, 6-separating voxelization, 26-separating voxelization, 26-Separating Plane Voxelization
body: This method generates a discrete, topologically correct representation of 2D lines and 3D planes by defining a slab of voxels around the geometric primitive. It solves the problem of ensuring N-separability (preventing N-connected ray paths from penetrating the surface) and N-minimality (excluding redundant voxels) simultaneously, a guarantee that earlier scan-conversion algorithms lacked. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like 3D Scan-conversion by deriving a specific thickness parameter t from the surface normal and grid resolution, rather than relying on fixed thresholds or simple center-point inclusion. Inputs: Geometric primitive: A 2D line or 3D plane defined by coefficients. Grid resolution: Voxel width L (assumed uniform). Separability type N \in \{4, 8\} for 2D lines, N \in \{6, 26\} for 3D planes. Outputs: A set of voxel coordinates \tilde{S} representing the discretized primitive. Data Structures: The output is a set of integer coordinates (x, y, z) or (x, y). For mesh extensions, voxels are classified into Vertex Voxels, Edge Voxels, and Body Voxels. Parameters: L: Voxel width (grid spacing). tN: Thickness threshold for separability N. \alpha: Angle between the voxel diagonal and the plane normal (for 3D). \beta: Angle between the pixel diagonal and the line normal (for 2D). Steps: 1. Define the Primitive Equation: For a 3D plane, define the equation: Ap X + Bp Y + Cp Z + Dp = 0 The normal vector (Ap, Bp, Cp) must be normalized. 2. Calculate Thickness tN: Compute the slab thickness based on the desired separability and grid size. For 26-separating planes: t{26} = \frac{L}{2 \sqrt{3} \cos \alpha}. For 6-separating planes: t6 = \frac{L}{2 \cos \beta}. For 8-separating lines: t8 = \frac{L}{2 \cos \alpha}. For 4-separating lines: t4 = \frac{L}{2 \cos \beta}. 3. Define Slab Boundaries: Construct two parallel planes (or lines in 2D) offset from the original primitive by distance tN. 4. Voxel Inclusion Test: For each voxel center (x, y, z) within the bounding volume of the primitive: Calculate the signed distance value: val = Ap x + Bp y + Cp z + Dp Include the voxel in \tilde{S} if: -tN \leq val \leq tN. 5. Handle Degeneracies: If the primitive passes exactly through a voxel corner, edge, or face, use infinitesimal perturbation to ensure the intersection occurs strictly inside a voxel, never exactly on the boundary. This prevents ambiguity in connectivity. 6. Mesh Extension (Optional): For polygon meshes, classify voxels into three sets: \tilde{S}v: Vertex Voxels (within radius Rc of vertices). \tilde{S}e: Edge Voxels (within radius Rc of edges). \tilde{S}b: Body Voxels (from the plane slab method). The final representation combines these overlapping sets. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelizeplane(Ap, Bp, Cp, Dp, L, N, bounds): """ Voxelize a 3D plane for N-separability. Args: Ap, Bp, Cp, Dp: Plane equation coefficients Ax + By + Cz + D = 0. L: Voxel width. N: Separability type (6 or 26). bounds: Tuple (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) defining the grid region to check. Returns: List of voxel coordinates (x, y, z) included in the slab. """ # Normalize normal vector normlen = math.sqrt(Ap2 + Bp2 + Cp2) Ap /= normlen Bp /= normlen Cp /= normlen # Calculate thickness tN # Angle alpha: angle between voxel diagonal and plane normal # Voxel diagonal vector K can be (1, 1, 1) in local grid space # Normal vector N is (Ap, Bp, Cp) # cos(alpha) = |K. N| / (|K| |N|) # |K| = sqrt(3), |N| = 1 # Dot product = |Ap + Bp + Cp| # Note: The source defines alpha specifically for the worst-case diagonal. # For 26-separability, we use the diagonal that makes the smallest angle with the normal # to ensure no 26-holes. The formula uses cos(alpha). # If the normal is (Ap, Bp, Cp), the max projection onto a diagonal direction (signs of Ap, Bp, Cp) # is |Ap| + |Bp| + |Cp|. # However, the source formula is t26 = L / (2 sqrt(3) cos(alpha)). # Let's derive cos(alpha) from the normal. # The angle between the normal and the diagonal (1,1,1) is alpha. # cos(alpha) = (Ap1 + Bp1 + Cp1) / (sqrt(3)1) = (Ap + Bp + Cp) / sqrt(3) ? # Actually, to guarantee separation, we must consider the diagonal most aligned with the normal. # The source states: "alpha is the angle between the voxel diagonal K and the plane normal N". # And t26 = L / (2 sqrt(3) cos(alpha)). # If we assume K is the specific diagonal aligned with the normal's octant: # cosalpha = (|Ap| + |Bp| + |Cp|) / math.sqrt(3) cosalpha = (abs(Ap) + abs(Bp) + abs(Cp)) / math.sqrt(3) if N == 26: tN = L / (2 math.sqrt(3) cosalpha) elif N == 6: # For 6-separability, beta is angle between normal and face normal. # The worst case is the face normal most aligned with the plane normal. # cos(beta) = max(|Ap|, |Bp|, |Cp|) cosbeta = max(abs(Ap), abs(Bp), abs(Cp)) tN = L / (2 cosbeta) else: raise ValueError("N must be 6 or 26 for 3D planes") voxels = [] minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz = bounds for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): # Signed distance from voxel center to plane # Assuming voxel centers are at integer coordinates val = Ap x + Bp y + Cp z + Dp if -tN <= val <= tN: voxels.append((x, y, z)) return voxels def voxelizeline(Ap, Bp, Dp, L, N, bounds): """ Voxelize a 2D line for N-separability. Args: Ap, Bp, Dp: Line equation Ax + By + D = 0. L: Grid square size. N: Separability type (4 or 8). bounds: Tuple (minx, maxx, miny, maxy). Returns: List of pixel coordinates (x, y). """ # Normalize normlen = math.sqrt(Ap2 + Bp2) Ap /= normlen Bp /= normlen if N == 8: # alpha is angle between normal and pixel diagonal # cos(alpha) = (|Ap| + |Bp|) / sqrt(2) cosalpha = (abs(Ap) + abs(Bp)) / math.sqrt(2) tN = L / (2 cosalpha) elif N == 4: # beta is angle between normal and pixel axis (face normal equivalent) # cos(beta) = max(|Ap|, |Bp|) cosbeta = max(abs(Ap), abs(Bp)) tN = L / (2 cosbeta) else: raise ValueError("N must be 4 or 8 for 2D lines") voxels = [] minx, maxx, miny, maxy = bounds for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): val = Ap x + Bp y + Dp if -tN <= val <= tN: voxels.append((x, y)) return voxels A method to generate a discrete, 4-separating, and 4-minimal voxel representation of a 2D line segment. It solves the problem of ensuring topological correctness (no 4-holes) and efficiency (no redundant voxels) for line primitives in a grid. It sets itself apart from standard scanline algorithms by dynamically calculating a thickness threshold t4 based on the line's angle relative to the grid axes, rather than using a fixed width or simple midpoint tests. Choose it when 4-connected ray paths are sufficient and a thinner representation is desired. Time Complexity: O(V), where V is the number of voxels in the bounding volume. The method iterates over all candidate voxels and performs a constant-time distance check. Memory Complexity: O(V{out}), where V{out} is the number of voxels in the output set \tilde{S}. For mesh extensions, linked lists are used to store voxels, incurring overhead proportional to the voxel count. Performance: Measured in VPM (Voxels Per Millisecond). VPM decreases as voxel count increases due to linked list overhead. Non-optimized implementations are slow; efficient incremental algorithms are recommended for production. Strengths: Guarantees topological correctness (separability and minimality) for both lines and planes. Eliminates artifacts at edges and vertices when extended to meshes. Visually indistinguishable from 6-separating models despite topological differences. Limitations: 26-separating voxelization produces significantly more voxels (especially Vertex and Edge voxels) than 6-separating voxelization. Requires careful handling of degeneracies (perturbation). When to use: When topological correctness is critical (e.g., ray casting where penetration must be strictly prevented). Use 6-separating for visualization where speed is prioritized and 6-connected paths are sufficient. Use 26-separating for robust collision detection or ray tracing against thin surfaces. The method originates from the need to provide a comprehensive treatment of separability and minimality in voxelization, which earlier algorithms failed to guarantee simultaneously, especially for polygon meshes. Key theoretical foundations were laid by Cohen-Or and Kaufman [COK97, COK95], who analyzed 26-connected ray paths and 26-separating covers. The specific slab-based thickness derivation for N-separating planes and lines was presented in "An Accurate Method for Voxelizing Polygon Meshes". The approach uses the Jordan curve theorem to prove that connecting voxel corners via 1D intersection targets guarantees 26-separation for effectively 2D inputs. A Topological Approach to Voxelization, https://research.nvidia.com/sites/default/files/pubs/2013-06A-Topological-Approach/laine2013egsrpaper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) An Accurate Method for Voxelizing Polygon Meshes, https://web.eecs.utk.edu/~huangj/papers/polygon.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: 4-Separating Line Voxelization
head: 4-separating line representation, 4-minimal line voxelization
body: A method to generate a discrete, 4-separating, and 4-minimal voxel representation of a 2D line segment. It solves the problem of ensuring topological correctness (no 4-holes) and efficiency (no redundant voxels) for line primitives in a grid. It sets itself apart from standard scanline algorithms by dynamically calculating a thickness threshold t4 based on the line's angle relative to the grid axes, rather than using a fixed width or simple midpoint tests. Inputs: Line equation parameters Ap, Bp, Dp defining the line Ap x + Bp y + Dp = 0, where Ap^2 + Bp^2 = 1 (unit normal vector). Grid voxel size L (assumed uniform). Bounding box coordinates (x{min}, x{max}, y{min}, y{max}) covering the line segment. Outputs: A set of voxel centers \tilde{\mathcal{S}} representing the line. Data Structures: The output is a set of integer coordinate tuples (x, y) belonging to \tilde{\mathcal{S}}. Numbered Steps: 1. Calculate \cos\alpha from the line normal and the grid diagonal direction. 2. Compute the threshold t4 using the geometric formula. 3. Iterate over every integer coordinate (x, y) in the bounding box. 4. Evaluate the signed distance inequality for each coordinate. 5. Add coordinates satisfying the inequality to \tilde{\mathcal{S}}. Formulas: The threshold t4 is defined as: t4 = \frac{L}{2\sqrt{2}\cos\alpha} where \alpha is the angle between the line normal \mathbf{N}=(Ap, Bp) and the voxel diagonal vector \mathbf{K}=(1, 1). The inclusion condition for a voxel center (x, y) is: -t4 \leq Ap x + Bp y + Dp \leq t4 which is equivalent to checking if the absolute signed Euclidean distance from the center to the line is \leq t4. Parameters: t4: The half-thickness of the slab. \alpha: The angle between the normal vector \mathbf{N} to the line and the diagonal vector \mathbf{K} of the voxel. Typical values: L=1 for unit grids; t4 scales linearly with L and varies with \alpha. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the threshold t4 is not calculated correctly based on the angle \alpha, pixels that should be included might be excluded, creating 4-holes. The proof shows that if a pixel is intersected by the line but excluded, it leads to a contradiction regarding the distance from the center C to the line. Degenerate lines (zero length or undefined normal) must be handled to avoid division by zero in normalization. When \cos\alpha \approx 0 (line normal perpendicular to grid diagonal), t4 approaches infinity; a practical guard clamps t4 to a maximum reasonable value or falls back to L/2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelizeline4separating(Ap, Bp, Dp, L, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax): """ Voxelize a 2D line defined by Apx + Bpy + Dp = 0. Returns a set of (x, y) coordinates. """ # Ensure normal is unit length for Euclidean distance norm = math.hypot(Ap, Bp) if norm == 0: return set() An, Bn, Dn = Ap / norm, Bp / norm, Dp / norm # Angle alpha between normal (An, Bn) and grid diagonal (1, 1) # cos(alpha) = (An1 + Bn1) / (|N| |K|) = (An + Bn) / sqrt(2) cosalpha = (An + Bn) / math.sqrt(2) # Threshold t4 if abs(cosalpha) < 1e-9: t4 = L / 2.0 else: t4 = L / (2.0 math.sqrt(2) abs(cosalpha)) voxelset = set() for x in range(xmin, xmax + 1): for y in range(ymin, ymax + 1): val = An x + Bn y + Dn if abs(val) <= t4: voxelset.add((x, y)) return voxelset Extends the 4-separating concept to fill triangle slices by dynamically calculating step sizes to skip covered voxels. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the bounding box of the line segment. Each voxel requires a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(K) where K is the number of voxels in the final representation. Strengths: Guarantees 4-separability (no 4-holes) and 4-minimality (no redundant voxels) for 2D lines. Limitations: The method is defined for 2D lines. For 3D planes, the source indicates a similar slab-based approach is used but does not provide the specific 3D threshold formula in the provided text, only referencing 6- or 26-separating representations. When to use: When topological correctness (connectivity) of line primitives is critical and minimal voxel count is desired. Originated in the paper "An Accurate Method for Voxelizing Polygon Meshes". The method is part of a broader family of geometric voxelization techniques that rely on distance-based slab inclusion to ensure topological properties like separability and minimality. An Accurate Method for Voxelizing Polygon Meshes, https://web.eecs.utk.edu/~huangj/papers/polygon.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Optimal Scanline Voxelization (Floating-Point)
head: Optimal Scanline
body: Optimal Scanline Voxelization is a method for generating a discrete voxel representation of 2D line segments within a triangle slice. It solves the problem of filling the interior of a triangle slice with voxels while minimizing the total voxel count by ensuring no voxel exists between two parallel scanlines separated by a distance l. It sets itself apart from standard scanline algorithms by dynamically calculating the maximum safe step size l based on the scanline direction, thereby skipping intermediate voxels that are guaranteed to be covered by the projection of the scanline. Inputs: A triangle defined by vertices v1, v2, v3 in 3D space; the triangle's normal vector n = (nx, ny, nz); the plane constant D such that n \cdot p = D for any point p on the triangle. Outputs: A set of voxel coordinates representing the 2D line voxelization of the triangle slice. Data Structures: v1, v2, v3: 3D vectors (x, y, z). n: 3D normal vector (nx, ny, nz). dsl: 2D normalized scanline direction vector (d{sl,x}, d{sl,y}). l: Scalar distance threshold. li: Current scanline offset, initialized to 0. Steps: 1. Determine Scanline Direction (d{sl}): Check if all vertices v1, v2, v3 have the same integer z-coordinate. If yes, set d{sl} to the normalized direction of edge v1 \to v3. If no, calculate the gradient of the triangle with respect to z. The plane equation is z = \frac{D - nx x - ny y}{nz}. The gradient vector is d = \left( \frac{-nx}{nz}, \frac{-ny}{nz} \right). Normalize this vector: d{sl} = \frac{d}{|d|}. 2. Calculate Distance Threshold (l): Compute l = |d{sl,x}| + |d{sl,y}|. Alternatively, using the four cases for signs of d{sl}: l = \begin{cases} ((0, 1) - (1, 0)) \cdot d{sl} & \text{if } d{sl,x} < 0 < d{sl,y} \\ ((1, 0) - (0, 1)) \cdot d{sl} & \text{if } d{sl,y} < 0 < d{sl,x} \\ ((0, 0) - (1, 1)) \cdot d{sl} & \text{if } d{sl,x}, d{sl,y} < 0 \\ ((1, 1) - (0, 0)) \cdot d{sl} & \text{if } 0 < d{sl,x}, d{sl,y} \end{cases} These equations represent the dot product of the voxel diagonal aligned with d{sl}. 3. Iterate Scanlines: Initialize li = 0. While li is within the bounds of the triangle slice: Calculate endpoints for the current scanline offset li on the triangle edges. For edges connected to v1 (edges v1 \to v2 and v1 \to v3): Let de be the normalized direction of the edge. Calculate endpoint vp = v1 + de \frac{li}{de \cdot d{sl}}, where the dot product uses the x,y components of de and d{sl}. For the edge v2 \to v3: This edge does not share v1 as a base for the projection formula. Calculate a modified vertex v2' such that (v2' - v1) \cdot d{sl} = 0 and v2' - v2 is parallel to v3 - v2. v2' = v2 + (v3 - v2) \frac{(v1 - v2) \cdot d{sl}}{(v3 - v2) \cdot d{sl}}. Use v2' as the base vertex and edge direction v2 \to v3 in the projection formula: vp = v2' + de \frac{li}{de \cdot d{sl}}. Voxelize the line segment between the calculated endpoints. Increment li by l. 4. Merge Edges: The voxels on edge v1 \to v2 are merged with the voxels on edge v2 \to v3, counting them as a single edge to avoid double-counting or gaps at vertex v2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def optimalscanlinevoxelization(v1, v2, v3, n, D): def dot2d(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] def normalize2d(v): mag = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag) if mag > 0 else (0.0, 0.0) # Step 1: Determine scanline direction dsl if v1[2] == v2[2] == v3[2]: dsl = normalize2d((v3[0] - v1[0], v3[1] - v1[1])) else: if n[2] == 0: raise ValueError("Triangle parallel to z-axis, gradient undefined") dsl = normalize2d((-n[0]/n[2], -n[1]/n[2])) # Step 2: Calculate distance threshold l l = abs(dsl[0]) + abs(dsl[1]) # Step 3: Iterate scanlines li = 0.0 voxels = set() # Precompute v2' for edge v2-v3 v3minusv2 = (v3[0] - v2[0], v3[1] - v2[1]) v1minusv2 = (v1[0] - v2[0], v1[1] - v2[1]) denomv2p = dot2d(v3minusv2, dsl) v2prime = None if denomv2p != 0: factor = dot2d(v1minusv2, dsl) / denomv2p v2prime = (v2[0] + v3minusv2[0] factor, v2[1] + v3minusv2[1] factor) # Determine sweep bounds by projecting vertices onto dsl projv1 = dot2d((v1[0], v1[1]), dsl) projv2 = dot2d((v2[0], v2[1]), dsl) projv3 = dot2d((v3[0], v3[1]), dsl) minproj = min(projv1, projv2, projv3) maxproj = max(projv1, projv2, projv3) currentli = minproj while currentli <= maxproj: # Project onto v1-v2 de12 = normalize2d((v2[0] - v1[0], v2[1] - v1[1])) denom12 = dot2d(de12, dsl) ep1 = (v1[0] + de12[0] (currentli / denom12), v1[1] + de12[1] (currentli / denom12)) if denom12 != 0 else None # Project onto v1-v3 de13 = normalize2d((v3[0] - v1[0], v3[1] - v1[1])) denom13 = dot2d(de13, dsl) ep2 = (v1[0] + de13[0] (currentli / denom13), v1[1] + de13[1] (currentli / denom13)) if denom13 != 0 else None # Project onto v2-v3 using v2' ep3 = None if v2prime is not None: de23 = normalize2d((v3[0] - v2[0], v3[1] - v2[1])) denom23 = dot2d(de23, dsl) if denom23 != 0: ep3 = (v2prime[0] + de23[0] (currentli / denom23), v2prime[1] + de23[1] (currentli / denom23)) # Voxelize line segment between calculated endpoints endpoints = [ep for ep in [ep1, ep2, ep3] if ep is not None] if len(endpoints) >= 2: # Standard 2D line rasterization between endpoints voxels.add(tuple(endpoints[0])) voxels.add(tuple(endpoints[1])) currentli += l return voxels Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: If nz = 0, the triangle is parallel to the z-axis, and the gradient is undefined. Precision: Floating-point arithmetic may cause gaps or overlaps if l is not calculated with sufficient precision. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Minimizes the voxel count by skipping intermediate voxels that are guaranteed to be covered by the projection of the scanline. Limitations: Requires careful handling of the v2 \to v3 edge projection using the modified base vertex v2'. Optimal Scanline Voxelization was proposed in the context of triangle slice voxelization for volume rendering. It builds on the theory that there exists a maximum distance l between parallel scanlines such that no voxel can exist between them. A Comparison of Optimal Scanline Voxelization Algorithms, https://liu.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1459330/FULLTEXT01.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Distance-based Voxelization
head: Direct Voxelization of Geometric Objects, Distance-based Voxelization for Cubic Objects, Lagrangian Method Voxelization
body: Distance-based Voxelization is a method that voxelize objects directly without polygon conversion by including voxels where the distance to the surface S is smaller than a threshold t. Unlike 3D Scan-conversion which relies on polygon mesh intersection, this approach bypasses polygon conversion, offering efficiency and accuracy for regular shapes and surfaces where distance metrics are computable. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A geometric surface S defined analytically or parametrically; a voxel grid resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz); a distance threshold t; and a bounding box defining the search space. Output: A 6-connected or 26-connected voxel representation of the surface S. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz storing binary inclusion values. Surface Representation: For regular shapes (spheres, cylinders), implicit equations are used. For general surfaces, a parametric or implicit form allowing distance evaluation is required. Steps: 1. Define Search Space: Determine the bounding box of the object S and restrict the voxel scan to a subset of the voxel space in the vicinity of the surface to ensure efficiency. 2. Iterate Voxels: For each voxel center (x, y, z) within the search space, calculate the minimum distance to the surface S. 3. Distance Calculation: For regular shapes, compute the distance directly using geometric formulas. For general surfaces, use the Lagrangian Method to find the point (x0, y0, z0) on the surface that minimizes the distance to the voxel center (x, y, z). 4. Threshold Check: If the calculated distance is smaller than t, mark the voxel as part of the surface representation. Formulas: The distance minimization problem is defined by minimizing the squared Euclidean distance function: p(x, y, z) = (x - x0)^2 + (y - y0)^2 + (z - z0)^2 where (x0, y0, z0) is a point on the surface S and (x, y, z) is the voxel center. The goal is to find (x0, y0, z0) such that p(x, y, z) is minimized subject to the constraint that (x0, y0, z0) lies on S. Parameters: Threshold t: Determines the thickness of the voxelized surface. Typical values depend on grid resolution; e.g., for a 256 \times 256 \times 256 grid, specific t values are chosen to achieve 6-separability. Object Dimensions: Sphere radius: 61.4. Cylinder radius: 49.7 and height: 158.2. Function parameter k for x^2 + y^2 + kz = 0: 10.0. Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: Solving the Lagrangian Method for general surfaces may require solving high-order polynomial equations that lack analytical solutions. Numerical methods must be employed with high accuracy to avoid incorrect distance estimates. Efficiency: Scanning the entire voxel space is inefficient. The search must be restricted to the vicinity of the surface. Topological Correctness: For non-planar objects, topological correctness needs further proof and careful handling of the threshold t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def distancebasedvoxelization(surfacedistancefunc, gridresolution, threshold): """ Voxelize a surface S by including voxels within distance threshold. Args: surfacedistancefunc: Callable that takes a 3D point (x, y, z) and returns the minimum distance to the surface. gridresolution: Tuple (Nx, Ny, Nz) defining the voxel grid dimensions. threshold: Float, the maximum distance for a voxel to be included. Returns: A 3D list of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) with boolean values. """ Nx, Ny, Nz = gridresolution # Initialize 3D grid with False values voxelgrid = [[[False] Nz for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] # Sources do not specify the exact bounding box derivation algorithm # Assume the grid coordinates map directly to the search space for x in range(Nx): for y in range(Ny): for z in range(Nz): # Voxel center coordinates voxelcenter = (x + 0.5, y + 0.5, z + 0.5) # Calculate minimum distance to surface # For regular shapes, this is a direct formula. # For general surfaces, this involves the Lagrangian Method. # Sources state that numerical methods must be used for high accuracy dist = surfacedistancefunc(voxelcenter) # Include voxel if distance is within threshold if dist < threshold: voxelgrid[x][y][z] = True return voxelgrid A 3D object-space antialiasing technique that performs antialiasing once on a 3D view-independent representation during the modeling stage to produce alias-free 3D models stored in a volume buffer. It extends the distance-based approach by replacing the binary separability requirement with a 'uniform thickness' and using voxel values as a function of distance to the surface. Time Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz \cdot D), where D is the cost of computing the distance to the surface. For regular shapes, D is O(1). For general surfaces using the Lagrangian Method, D can be significantly higher due to iterative numerical solving. Memory Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz) for storing the voxel grid. Performance: The method is efficient for regular shapes like spheres and cylinders where distance measurement is straightforward. For general surfaces, performance depends on the efficiency of the numerical solver for the Lagrangian Method. Strengths: Allows direct voxelization without polygon conversion. Limitations: Requires efficient distance computation; numerical instability for high-order polynomials; topological correctness for non-planar objects is not fully proven. When to Use: When direct voxelization of analytic or regular geometric objects is desired, and polygon conversion is undesirable or inefficient. The method was introduced by Cohen and Kaufman as an extension of their accurate algorithm for voxelizing polygon meshes. It was presented in the paper "An Accurate Method for Voxelizing Polygon Meshes". The approach builds on the observation that voxelization can be viewed as a distance-based inclusion problem, allowing for the direct voxelization of geometric objects without intermediate polygon conversion. The project was partially supported by Ford Motor Company. An Accurate Method for Voxelizing Polygon Meshes, https://web.eecs.utk.edu/~huangj/papers/polygon.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Volume-Sampled Antialiasing
head: 3D Antialiasing (Object-Space), Density-based voxelization, Object-Space Antialiasing, Volume sampling technique
body: Volume-Sampled Antialiasing is a 3D object-space technique that performs antialiasing once on a view-independent representation during the modeling stage to produce alias-free 3D models stored in a volume buffer. Unlike 2D scan-converted graphics antialiasing, which focuses on aesthetically pleasing displays, this method emphasizes producing smooth, alias-free 3D models suitable for volume graphics manipulations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A geometric primitive defined in object space and a target voxel grid. Output: A 3D volume buffer where each voxel stores a density value mapped to the interval [0, 1]. Data Structures: Volume Buffer: A 3D array of floating-point values representing the density contribution of the geometric primitive to each voxel. Lookup Table (Optional): A precomputed 1D array of density values indexed by distance, used to improve performance. Method Steps: 1. Iterate Voxels: For each voxel in the target grid, determine if it is potentially intersected by the geometric primitive. 2. Calculate Distance: Compute the distance d between the center of the current voxel and the geometric primitive. 3. Determine Density: Estimate the density contribution by attenuating the voxel density with a filter weight function proportional to d. For performance, use d as an index into a precomputed lookup table to select the density value. 4. Store Density: Assign the calculated density value to the voxel in the volume buffer, mapping the value to the interval [0, 1]. Formulas: The density D of a voxel is attenuated by a filter weight function f(d) proportional to the distance d between the voxel center and the geometric primitive: D = f(d) where f is a filter weight function. Parameters: Non-binary Mapping: Voxel values are mapped to the interval [0, 1] to support 3D antialiasing and higher quality rendering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Binary Voxelization: Using point sampling (evaluating the continuous object at the voxel center and assigning 0 or 1) results in object space aliasing, manifesting as jagged surfaces. Precision: The non-binary [0, 1] mapping provides a larger dynamic range than binary classification, supporting higher quality rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumesampledantialiasing(primitive, griddims, lookuptable=None): """ Performs volume-sampled antialiasing for a geometric primitive. Args: primitive: An object with a method distancetopoint(point) returning the distance to the primitive. griddims: A tuple (nx, ny, nz) defining the output volume dimensions. lookuptable: An optional 1D list of density weights indexed by distance. Returns: volumebuffer: A 3D list of density values in [0, 1]. """ nx, ny, nz = griddims volumebuffer = [[[0.0 for in range(nz)] for in range(ny)] for in range(nx)] for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): voxelcenter = (i + 0.5, j + 0.5, k + 0.5) distance = primitive.distancetopoint(voxelcenter) if lookuptable is not None: idx = int(distance) density = lookuptable[idx] if idx < len(lookuptable) else 0.0 else: # Fallback filter weight function proportional to distance, attenuating density. density = max(0.0, min(1.0, 1.0 - distance)) volumebuffer[i][j][k] = density return volumebuffer Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces alias-free 3D models that are view-independent. The smoothness of the volume-sampled objects carries over into image space during volume rendering, improving silhouette quality. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Volume-Sampled Antialiasing was developed to address object space aliasing in 3D voxelization. Traditional point sampling methods result in jagged surfaces due to the binary classification of voxels. This technique was introduced as part of the modeling stage to produce view-independent representations that can be used for various volume graphics manipulations. name: Floating-Point Optimal Scanline
head: Optimal Scanline
body: The Floating-Point Optimal Scanline method is a triangle-based voxelization algorithm that fills the interior of a triangle by slicing it along a dominant axis and performing 2D line voxelizations between the sliced edges. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like 3D Scan-conversion by using an "optimal" distance criterion to determine which voxels are intersected by the scanlines, ensuring a tighter fit to the geometric surface than standard grid-aligned line algorithms. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single triangle defined by three vertices V0, V1, V2 in 3D space and the triangle's normal vector \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz). Output: A set of voxel coordinates (x, y, z) that intersect the triangle. Data Structures: Vertices: Array of 3 vectors, each containing 3 floating-point coordinates. Normal: Vector of 3 floating-point components. Edge Slices: List of pairs of 2D points representing the intersection of the triangle edges with integer planes of the dominant axis. Steps: 1. Determine Dominant Axis: Calculate the absolute values of the normal's components: |nx|, |ny|, |nz|. Identify the axis corresponding to the maximum value: if |nx| is max, dominant axis is X; if |ny| is max, dominant axis is Y; if |nz| is max, dominant axis is Z. The algorithm description assumes the dominant axis is Z for the subsequent steps. 2. Sort Vertices: Sort the triangle vertices V0, V1, V2 based on their coordinates along the dominant axis. Let the sorted vertices be V{min}, V{mid}, V{max} such that their dominant-axis coordinates satisfy z{min} \le z{mid} \le z{max} (assuming Z is dominant). 3. Voxelize Edges: Perform line voxelization between each pair of sorted vertices (V{min}, V{mid}) and (V{mid}, V{max}) using a Ray Casting Line Voxelization (RLV) algorithm to voxelize all edges. 4. Slice Edges: Split the voxelized edges into slices along the dominant axis. A slice is defined by an integer value k of the dominant axis. For each integer k between the minimum and maximum dominant-axis coordinates of the triangle, identify the two points on the triangle edges that lie on the plane z=k (or x=k or y=k). 5. Calculate Optimal Distance: For each slice k, calculate the optimal distance l using the formula l = |dslx| + |dsly|. Here, dsl is the voxel's diagonal projected onto the scanline direction. Specifically, if the scanline connects P{left} and P{right}, the direction vector is \mathbf{d} = P{right} - P{left}. The term dsl represents the projection of the unit voxel diagonal onto this direction. 6. Perform 2D Optimal Scanline Voxelization: For each slice k, determine the voxels intersected by the line segment between P{left}(k) and P{right}(k). Use the optimal distance l to decide voxel inclusion. The theorem states that if the distance between two parallel lines is less than l, no voxel can exist between them without being intersected. The algorithm classifies the scanline into four cases based on the signs of the components of dsl to determine the exact set of voxels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def floatingpointoptimalscanline(V0, V1, V2, n): # 1. Determine dominant axis nx, ny, nz = abs(n.x), abs(n.y), abs(n.z) if nx >= ny and nx >= nz: dominant = 'x' elif ny >= nx and ny >= nz: dominant = 'y' else: dominant = 'z' # 2. Sort vertices along dominant axis vertices = sorted([V0, V1, V2], key=lambda v: getattr(v, dominant)) Vmin, Vmid, Vmax = vertices # 3. Voxelize edges using RLV # The source does not provide the explicit RLV implementation. edge1 = raycastinglinevoxelization(Vmin, Vmid) edge2 = raycastinglinevoxelization(Vmid, Vmax) edge3 = raycastinglinevoxelization(Vmax, Vmin) # 4. Split edges into slices along dominant axis slices = {} for edge in [edge1, edge2, edge3]: for voxel in edge: k = int(getattr(voxel, dominant)) slices.setdefault(k, []).append(voxel) output = set() for k, edgevoxels in slices.items(): # Identify two points on triangle edges on plane dominant=k # Linear interpolation between edge voxels to find exact intersection points. Pleft, Pright = interpolateedgeintersections(edgevoxels, k, dominant) # 5. Calculate optimal distance l = |dslx| + |dsly| d = Pright - Pleft length = math.sqrt(d.x2 + d.y2) if length == 0: continue u = Vector(d.x / length, d.y / length, 0) dslx, dsly = u.x, u.y l = abs(dslx) + abs(dsly) # 6. Perform 2D optimal scanline voxelization # The source states the scanline is classified into four cases based on the signs of dsl, # but does not provide the explicit branching logic. voxelsinslice = voxelize2dlineoptimal(Pleft, Pright, l) output.update(voxelsinslice) return output Parameters: Voxel Size: Implicitly 1.0 in the normalized coordinate system where the diagonal projection is calculated. Dominant Axis: Determined dynamically per triangle. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: If the triangle is degenerate (area zero), the normal is undefined. The source does not specify handling for this case. A 2D scan-line algorithm that rasterizes a polygon into a P-buffer by decomposing it into triangles and flipping presence bits for covered positions. It sorts vertices by y-coordinate, sets xl=xr=C.x and y=C.y (where C is the vertex with the least y), initializes slopes il, ir for segments CA and CB, and swaps them if ir < il. It updates the slope at vertex B, adds or subtracts the triangle's sign to the P-buffer from (xl,y) to (xr,y), increments y, updates xl+=il and xr+=ir, and loops until y < A.y. It constructs triangles between the centroid and polygon edges, rasterizes them in the P-buffer by flipping bits, and transfers positions with presence value 1 to the framebuffer with corresponding color. This method is distinct from the 3D Floating-Point Optimal Scanline as it operates in 2D and uses a bit-flipping P-buffer approach rather than optimal distance-based voxel inclusion. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels intersected by the triangle, plus the cost of sorting vertices and slicing edges. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels in the triangle's bounding box. Strengths: Provides a tighter voxelization than standard grid-aligned line algorithms by using the optimal distance criterion. Limitations: Requires calculation of the triangle normal and sorting of vertices. When to use: When high-quality triangle voxelization is required and the computational cost of determining the optimal voxel set is justified. The Floating-Point Optimal Scanline algorithm was proposed by Zhang et al.. It is part of a family of optimal scanline voxelization techniques. The method builds on the concept of line voxelization and extends it to 2D slices within a 3D triangle. The theoretical basis involves a theorem regarding the maximum distance between parallel lines such that no voxel can exist between them without intersection. name: Polygon Rasterization (2D)
head: Edge Walking, Rasterization algorithm for polygons, Rasterization algorithms for triangles, Scan-line polygon rasterization, Scanline Triangle Rasterization, Triangle Filling
body: This method rasterizes a 2D polygon into a P-Buffer (presence buffer) by decomposing the polygon into triangles and flipping presence bits for covered positions. It differs from standard framebuffer rasterization by using a bit-flip parity mechanism to determine voxel inclusion, which is specifically designed for 3D voxelization workflows where the 2D projection serves as a slice or projection step. Inputs: A 2D polygon defined by a list of vertices V = \{v1, v2,..., vn\} in 2D space. A color value associated with the polygon. Outputs: A P-Buffer: A 2D grid of bits where each bit represents a voxel's presence (1 if inside, 0 if outside). A Framebuffer: The final colored voxels extracted from the P-Buffer. P-Buffer: A 2D array of bits. Dimensions: Corresponds to the minimal bounding box of the polygon. Value: 0 (empty) or 1 (filled). Operation: Bitwise XOR (flip) during rasterization. 1. Compute the minimal bounding box of the polygon. 2. Compute the centroid C of the polygon. 3. For each edge of the polygon: Construct a triangle using the centroid C and the current edge vertices. Rasterize this triangle into the P-Buffer (see Triangle Rasterization). Repeat until all edges are processed. 4. Transfer all positions from the P-Buffer in the minimal bounding box with presence value equal to 1 to the framebuffer, applying the corresponding color. The triangle rasterization uses a scanline approach with slope updates for edge walking. An alternative integer-based traversal using error accumulation is also described. Preprocessing: 1. Sort the triangle vertices by their y-coordinate such that yC \le yB \le yA (where C is the bottom vertex). Let the sorted vertices be v1, v2, v3 with coordinates (x1, y1), (x2, y2), (x3, y3). 2. Initialize scanline variables: xl = xr = x1, y = y1. 3. Calculate slopes: il = \frac{x3 - x1}{y3 - y1} (slope of left edge v1-v3), ir = \frac{x2 - x1}{y2 - y1} (slope of right edge v1-v2). 4. Ensure il \le ir. If ir < il, swap il and ir, and swap xl and xr. First Half (Upper Triangle): 1. Loop while y < y3: Flip the P-Buffer bits for the range [xl, xr] at row y. Increment y. Update xl \leftarrow xl + il, xr \leftarrow xr + ir. 2. If y1 == y2 (flat-top triangle), the first half loop does not execute. Second Half (Lower Triangle): 1. If y reaches y2, update the slope for the edge connecting v2 to v3: i{new} = \frac{x3 - x2}{y3 - y2}. 2. Assign i{new} to the variable corresponding to the edge connected to v2 and v3. If a swap occurred in preprocessing, update il; otherwise, update ir. 3. Continue the loop until y > y3. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rasterizepolygon2d(vertices, color, pbuffer): """ Rasterizes a 2D polygon into a P-Buffer using centroid decomposition. Args: vertices: List of (x, y) tuples. color: Color value to apply. pbuffer: 2D array of bits (0 or 1). """ # Step 1: Compute centroid n = len(vertices) cx = sum(v[0] for v in vertices) / n cy = sum(v[1] for v in vertices) / n centroid = (cx, cy) # Step 2: Decompose into triangles and rasterize for i in range(n): v1 = vertices[i] v2 = vertices[(i + 1) % n] rasterizetriangle(centroid, v1, v2, pbuffer) # Step 3: Transfer to framebuffer for y in range(pbuffer.height): for x in range(pbuffer.width): if pbuffer[y][x] == 1: pbuffer[y][x] = color def rasterizetriangle(p1, p2, p3, pbuffer): """ Rasterizes a single triangle into the P-Buffer using slope-based scanline. """ # Sort vertices by y: C (bottom), B (middle), A (top) pts = sorted([p1, p2, p3], key=lambda p: p[1]) C, B, A = pts xl = xr = C[0] y = C[1] # Calculate slopes (guard for horizontal edges) il = (A[0] - C[0]) / (A[1] - C[1]) if A[1] != C[1] else 0.0 ir = (B[0] - C[0]) / (B[1] - C[1]) if B[1] != C[1] else 0.0 # Ensure il <= ir if ir < il: il, ir = ir, il xl, xr = xr, xl while y < A[1]: # Flip bits in P-Buffer from xl to xr for x in range(int(xl), int(xr) + 1): pbuffer[y][x] ^= 1 y += 1 xl += il xr += ir # Update slope for the edge connected to B when reaching the middle vertex if y == B[1]: newslope = (A[0] - B[0]) / (A[1] - B[1]) if A[1] != B[1] else 0.0 if ir < il: # Swap occurred, so il originally held the right edge slope il = newslope else: ir = newslope Flat-top triangles: If y1 == y2, the first half loop does not execute. Horizontal edges: If dy = 0, the slope is undefined. The pseudocode handles this by setting the slope to 0.0. Non-unit cell size: Scaling coordinates to the target grid resolution is required, but exact scaling factors are Not given in the sources. Degenerate triangles: If vertices are collinear, the triangle has no area. Handling is Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation, suitable for voxelization where parity is sufficient. Limitations: Not optimized for modern GPUs; relies on CPU-side loop. This method originates from work on voxelization of solids. It is designed for 3D rasterization where the 2D algorithm serves as a core component for projecting 3D solids into a voxel grid. The use of a P-Buffer with bit-flipping is a key innovation for determining solid occupancy. name: Scan-line Clipping Algorithm
head: 3D Scan-line Clipping, CFB Clipping
body: The Scan-line Clipping Algorithm is a 3D generalization of the classic scan-line algorithm, designed for low-level processor implementation to determine which portions of a volumetric primitive (such as a room or figurine) are visible and should be written to the Compositing Frame Buffer (CFB). It solves the problem of priority-based occlusion culling during voxelization by processing a primitive scan-by-scan, ensuring that higher-priority existing data in the CFB is never overwritten. Unlike window-manager level algorithms that recursively subdivide space, this method explicitly identifies and writes only the visible segments, leaving invisible sections to be handled by the application. The algorithm processes a source primitive r against a set of higher-priority primitives already present in the CFB. It operates in a hierarchical scan-line order (Z, then Y, then X) to efficiently cull occluded regions. Input: The source primitive r (defined by its bounding box and voxel value), the current CFB state, and a priority list of existing primitives. Output: Updated CFB entries for the visible voxels of r. InterTable: A temporary table storing identifiers of all rooms/primitives that intersect with r and have higher priority. It is sorted by Z{min}, then Y{min}, then X{min}. Active Table: A subset of InterTable containing primitives intersecting with the current scan-line. Registers: ZoomX, ZoomY, ZoomZ: Scaling factors for voxel replication (default 1). Orient: Rotation angle (default 0 degrees). Colour Mode, Texture Mask, VoxelOps: Control final pixel blending and masking. 1. Initialize InterTable: Create InterTable containing identifiers of all primitives intersecting r with higher priority. Sort by Z{min}, Y{min}, X{min}. 2. Z-Scan Loop: Iterate Z{scan} from Z{min} to Z{max} of primitive r. Remove primitives from InterTable where Z{min} > Z{scan} (optimization based on sorted order). Update Active Table with primitives from InterTable that intersect the current Z{scan} plane. Sort Active Table primitives by Y then X. 3. Y-Scan Loop: Iterate Y{scan} from Y{min} to Y{max} of primitive r. Initialize LeftBound and RightBound based on the leftmost primitive in Active Table. X-Scan Clipping Loop: While LeftBound < RightBound and Active Table is not empty: Get the next "right" primitive from Active Table and update LeftBound to its left X-coordinate. If the current "left" and "right" primitives are adjacent in the sorted list: Write the voxel value of r to the CFB for the run from RightBound to LeftBound along the Y{scan} line. Get the next "left" and "right" primitives from Active Table. Else: Get the next "left" primitive. Update RightBound if the right edge of the new "left" primitive is to the right of the current RightBound. 4. Voxel Replication: Before writing, replicate voxels or intervals according to ZoomX, ZoomY, ZoomZ. 5. Write to CFB: Apply Colour Mode, Texture Mask, and VoxelOps (boolean operations) to determine the final value written to the CFB. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scanlineclip(primitiver, cfb, intertable, zoomx, zoomy, zoomz): # intertable: list of higher-priority primitives, sorted by Zmin, Ymin, Xmin # primitiver: source primitive with attributes Zmin, Zmax, Ymin, Ymax, Xmin, Xmax, value # Each primitive has attributes: Zmin, Ymin, Xmin, leftx, rightx, id, nextid # Save processor state (jacks) for zscan in range(primitiver.Zmin, primitiver.Zmax + 1): # Remove primitives from InterTable below current Zscan intertable = [p for p in intertable if p.Zmin <= zscan] # Sort primitives in InterTable by Y then X intersecting Zscan line activetable = sorted( [p for p in intertable if p.Zmin <= zscan <= p.Zmax], key=lambda p: (p.Ymin, p.Xmin)) for yscan in range(primitiver.Ymin, primitiver.Ymax + 1): if len(activetable) < 2: break # Initialize bounds with the leftmost primitive leftprim = activetable[0] rightbound = leftprim.rightx rightprim = activetable[1] leftbound = rightprim.leftx # X-Scan Clipping Loop while leftbound < rightbound and len(activetable) >= 2: # Get next 'right' primitive and update LeftBound # (rightprim is already the next one after leftprim) # Check adjacency in sorted list if rightprim.id == leftprim.nextid: # Set run from RightBound to LeftBound along Yscan line to voxel value of r for x in range(rightbound, leftbound): # Replicate voxels according to Zoom registers for dz in range(zoomz): for dy in range(zoomy): for dx in range(zoomx): # Apply Colour Mode, Texture Mask, VoxelOps cfb[x + dx, yscan + dy, zscan + dz] = primitiver.value # Get next 'left' and 'right' primitives from the list activetable.pop(0) activetable.pop(0) if len(activetable) >= 2: leftprim = activetable[0] rightbound = leftprim.rightx rightprim = activetable[1] leftbound = rightprim.leftx else: break else: # Get the next 'left' primitive and update RightBound activetable.pop(0) leftprim = activetable[0] if leftprim.rightx > rightbound: rightbound = leftprim.rightx # leftbound remains the left edge of the current rightprim # Restore processor state (jacks) Zoom/Orient: The sequence of clipping is affected by ZoomX, ZoomY, ZoomZ, and Orient registers. Voxels must be replicated according to Zoom registers before writing. Priority: Higher priority primitives in the CFB are never overwritten. Reading: When reading a room, overlapping is ignored and priorities play no role. Time Complexity: The algorithm is efficient for low-level hardware implementation. Sorting InterTable by Z{min} allows early termination of searches. The nested loops (Z, Y, X) process only visible segments, reducing unnecessary writes compared to full rasterization. Memory: Requires temporary storage for InterTable and Active Table. Strengths: Explicitly handles visible segments, leaving invisible sections to the application (e.g., room manager), which can reduce overhead in complex scenes. Limitations: The clipping sequence is not the order of the input stream, which can be drastically affected by transformation registers. The algorithm is a 3D generalization of the scan-line algorithm, adjusted for low-level processor implementation in the context of the Voxblt Engine. It was designed to handle room and figurine occlusion in a voxel frame buffer processor. It contrasts with Pike's algorithm, which operates at the window manager level and recursively subdivides windows into subrectangles. name: Mesh Rasterization and Triangle Intersection
body: This family covers methods that map continuous triangle meshes into discrete or analytic representations by computing geometric intersections between triangles and grid cells or pixels. It differs from Rasterization-based Voxelization by focusing on explicit triangle-grid intersection tests rather than GPU fragment shaders, and from Mesh-to-Voxel Geometry Shader by operating on CPU-side data structures or custom rasterization loops rather than fixed-function GPU pipelines. All methods in this family map a conceptual or physical source into a discrete or analytic volumetric representation suitable for rendering. The core mechanism involves: 1. Domain Definition: Establishing a spatial domain, typically a 3D grid with resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz) and bounding box, or an infinite analytic space. 2. Value Assignment: Determining the value (density, distance, color) for each point in the domain based on the source method (geometric intersection, function evaluation, or physical state). 3. Storage/Access: Either storing the result in a discrete array (voxelization, simulation) or providing an interface to compute it on-the-fly (procedural). This method converts a 3D triangle mesh into a solid, non-hollow voxel grid by first identifying surface voxels via Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) vs. Triangle intersection tests, and then filling the interior using a scanline fill algorithm. It differs from its siblings by explicitly separating the surface shell generation (using SAT-based intersection) from the volume filling (using parity-based scanlines), ensuring watertight interiors suitable for deep physical simulations like heat diffusion or fracture. Unlike Fake Voxelization via Triangle-Cube Intersection which outputs only surface voxels, this method produces a solid volume. Mesh Voxelization converts a continuous polygon mesh (typically STL or OBJ) into a discrete 3D grid of voxels, determining the occupancy (solid/empty) and optionally the signed distance field (SDF) for each cell. It solves the problem of discretizing surface geometry for volume rendering, simulation, or 3D printing preparation. Unlike Mesh to Voxel Generation via AABB-Triangle Intersection, which relies on bounding box overlap, or Template-based Voxelization, which uses precomputed patterns, this method uses ray casting to robustly determine topological inside/outside status, handling complex concavities and open meshes via multi-directional sampling. Template-based Voxelization computes the digitization of a continuous triangle or mesh by determining if a voxel belongs to the digitization based on whether a geometric template centered at the voxel intersects the triangle. It converts a continuous surface mesh into a discrete set of voxels (DigitalSet). This method is distinguished from sibling methods like AABB-triangle intersection by its reliance on topological separation properties (6- or 26-connectivity) to define the boundary, ensuring that the resulting digital surface separates the interior from the exterior in the specified connectivity sense. Triangle Rendering with Thickness renders a triangle as a volumetric shell by voxelizing grid points that lie within a specified distance from the triangle's plane or edges. It differs from solid triangle rasterization by including points outside the triangle boundary (up to the thickness limit) and from sphere-based thickness methods by using planar geometry defined by three vertices. This method is a specialized case of mesh rasterization where the primitive is a polygon. This method renders ground-truth normal maps by interpolating per-vertex normals across rasterized faces using barycentric coordinates and blending overlapping faces per pixel via a softmax function. It differs from standard hard-edge rasterization by providing smooth transitions between overlapping geometry, which is critical for training differentiable rendering pipelines where normal continuity aids gradient flow. A tensor indicating the extent to which a given triangle covers a given pixel, computed by checking if directed distances from the pixel to each edge are positive, smoothed via sigmoid. For each edge e=(v1,v2) of triangle T, calculate the directed distance from pixel (px,py) to the edge. Apply sigmoid \sigma to this distance scaled by steepness s. Multiply the results for all three edges to get V. To make the visibility tensor orientation invariant, add the term computed with negative directed distances (or sum over a \in \{-1,1\} as per the formula). V(px, py, T):= \prod{e=(v1,v2)\in T} \sigma\left( \frac{v{x,2}-v{x,1}}{s} (v{y,1}-py) + \frac{v{y,2}-v{y,1}}{s} (v{x,1}-px) \right) V{orient.inv.}(px, py, T) = \sum{a\in\{-1,1\}} \prod{e=(v1,v2)\in T} \sigma\left( a \cdot \frac{(v{x,2}-v{x,1})(v{y,1}-py) - (v{y,2}-v{y,1})(v{x,1}-px)}{s} \right) s: Steepness hyper-parameter for the sigmoid function in the visibility tensor calculation. The foundational concepts of mesh rasterization and triangle-grid intersection are rooted in computer graphics literature, specifically differentiable rendering and voxelization techniques. The visibility tensor approach was introduced in "Pix2Vex: Image-to-Geometry Reconstruction using a Smooth Differentiable Renderer". AABB-triangle intersection and scanline fill methods are standard in voxelization implementations. Ray casting for mesh voxelization is a standard technique in computational geometry. Template-based voxelization relies on digital topology and separation properties.
