name: Mesh to Voxel Generation via AABB-Triangle Intersection
head: AABB-Triangle Voxelization, Triangle Voxelization via AABB-Triangle SAT, Voxelization via Triangle-Cube Intersection, Triangle-Cube Intersection Voxelization, Triangle-to-Voxel Conversion, Triangle Mesh Voxelization, Bounding Box Voxelization
body: This method converts a triangle mesh into a solid 3D voxel grid by iterating over the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of each triangle and testing for intersection with every voxel cube within that box using the Separating Axis Theorem (SAT). It differs from Template-based Voxelization by using explicit geometric intersection tests rather than precomputed templates, and from Fake Voxelization via Triangle-Cube Intersection by typically being followed by a scanline fill to produce a solid interior rather than just a surface shell. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh (vertices and indices), a world-space transformation matrix, a voxel size s (float), and a bounding box for the output grid. Output: A 3D occupancy grid (voxel array) where each cell is marked as empty or solid. Data Structures: Triangle: Struct containing three 3D vector fields (p1, p2, p3) representing vertices in world space. voxels: A 3D integer array int[y, z, x] with dimensions derived from the bounding box and voxel size. Values are 0 (empty), 1 (intersected/shell), or 2 (occupied/filled). Alternatively, a HashSet<UVec3> can be used to store unique voxel coordinates. Bounds: A bounding box defined by min and max vectors in world space. Steps: 1. Grid Initialization: Transform all mesh vertices to world space using the transformation matrix. Compute the world-space bounding box of the transformed vertices by finding the component-wise minimum (v{min}) and maximum (v{max}) of all vertices. Round v{min} down to the nearest multiple of s and v{max} up to the nearest multiple of s. If any dimension of the bounding box is zero (i.e., maxi == mini), add s to maxi to ensure non-zero grid dimensions. Calculate the grid dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz) as \lceil (max - min) / s \rceil. Initialize the voxels array with zeros. 2. Shell Generation (Surface Voxelization): Iterate through each triangle in the mesh. Compute the triangle's bounding box in world space. Determine the range of voxel indices [x{min}, x{max}] \times [y{min}, y{max}] \times [z{min}, z{max}] that overlap with the triangle's bounding box by translating the bounding box min by subtracting the grid origin and dividing by s, then flooring/ceiling. For each voxel index (ix, iy, iz) in this range: Compute the voxel center in world space: c = (ix \cdot s + s/2, iy \cdot s + s/2, iz \cdot s + s/2) + bounds.min Perform an AABB-Triangle Intersection Test using the Separating Axis Theorem (SAT). Translate triangle vertices relative to the voxel center: vi \leftarrow vi - c. Compute edge vectors: e1 = v2 - v1, e2 = v3 - v2, e3 = v1 - v3. Compute the triangle normal: n{tri} = e1 \times e2. Define AABB axes: u0=(1,0,0), u1=(0,1,0), u2=(0,0,1). Test separation along 13 axes: 1. AABB Face Normals (u0, u1, u2): Project triangle vertices onto axis u: pi = vi \cdot u for i \in \{0,1,2\}. Compute the radius of the AABB projection: r = s/2 \cdot (|u \cdot u0| + |u \cdot u1| + |u \cdot u2|). Note: Since u is a basis vector, r = s/2. Separation condition: \max(\min(p0,p1,p2), -\max(p0,p1,p2)) > r. If true, the axis separates the triangle from the AABB. 2. Edge Cross Products (uk \times ej): Compute 9 cross-product axes a{kj} = uk \times ej for k,j \in \{0,1,2\}. For each axis a, compute the projection interval of the triangle: [minp, maxp] where minp = \min(vi \cdot a) and maxp = \max(vi \cdot a). Compute the radius of the AABB projection: ra = s/2 \cdot (|a \cdot u0| + |a \cdot u1| + |a \cdot u2|). Separation condition: minp > ra or maxp < -ra. 3. Triangle Normal (n{tri}): Project triangle vertices onto n{tri}: pi = vi \cdot n{tri}. Compute the radius of the AABB projection along n{tri}: rn = s/2 \cdot (|n{tri} \cdot u0| + |n{tri} \cdot u1| + |n{tri} \cdot u2|). Separation condition: \max(\min(p0,p1,p2), -\max(p0,p1,p2)) > rn. If all 13 axes pass the SAT test (no separation), the triangle intersects the voxel. If an intersection is found, mark voxels[iy, iz, ix] = 1 and break the triangle loop for this voxel (optimization: one intersection is sufficient to mark the voxel as part of the shell). 3. Solid Fill (Scanline Fill): Process the voxel grid slice by slice (e.g., along the Z-axis), and each slice row by row (e.g., along the X-axis). Initialize a 'pen' state to 'Up' (not filling) for each row. For each voxel in the row: If the voxel is empty (voxels == 0), continue to the next voxel without changing the pen state. If the voxel is part of the shell (voxels == 1): Cast a horizontal ray from left to right through the center of the voxel to find all intersecting triangles. Determine the orientation of T{last} relative to the scan direction (X-axis). Let nx be the x-component of the normal of T{last}. If nx > 0 (normal faces right, i.e., inward or exiting), set Pen = Up. Mark the current voxel as solid (voxels = 2) if the pen is Down. If the pen is Down, mark subsequent empty voxels as solid (voxels = 2) as the scan moves to the right. If the pen is Up, leave empty voxels empty. It identifies candidate voxels via vertex mapping rather than testing every voxel against every triangle, enabling parallel processing where each thread handles one triangle. Tessellation-based Voxelization is a GPU-accelerated method for generating 3D voxel grids from triangle meshes by leveraging the hardware tessellation pipeline to subdivide geometry before rasterization. It differs from fixed-function or CPU-based voxelizers by enabling adaptive triangle density and displacement mapping during the generation phase, allowing for higher fidelity in complex regions. Fake Voxelization via Triangle-Cube Intersection is a surface-only voxelization technique that digitizes a triangulated mesh by independently testing each triangle against a grid of axis-aligned cubes (voxels). Unlike solid voxelization methods that fill the interior volume using Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG), this approach outputs only the voxels intersected by the mesh surface, making it computationally simpler and suitable for generating surface representations. It is distinguished from its siblings by its independence from tessellation depth and its reliance on a template-based intersection test to control topological separability (6- or 26-connectivity). A mesh-native voxelizer that produces an occupancy grid or a signed-distance field (SDF) over a Piecewise Linear Complex (PLC)'s bounding box, using exact-predicate classification to avoid epsilon-ray speckle. Unlike Level 1 Triangle-Voxel Classification which may rely on approximate ray casting, this method uses Shewchuk's exact predicates for geometric calculations to ensure robust classification of watertight meshes in single precision. It differs from Tessellation-based Voxelization by operating directly on the input triangle mesh without prior subdivision, and from Fake Voxelization via Triangle-Cube Intersection by providing true inside/outside parity checks rather than mere intersection counts. Triangle Subdivision for Voxelization is a pre-processing method that recursively splits mesh triangles to ensure they are small enough to be voxelized efficiently and predictably. It solves the problem of variable voxel counts per triangle, which complicates memory allocation and parallel processing in out-of-core or batch-based voxelization pipelines. Unlike general-purpose mesh smoothing or tessellation, this method is geometry-driven, targeting specific edge-length or area thresholds relative to the voxel resolution to guarantee homogeneous voxel generation and compact Morton index ranges. It differs from Level 1 Triangle-Voxel Classification by actively modifying the mesh geometry rather than just classifying existing triangles, and from Tessellation-based Voxelization by using a deterministic, CPU/GPU-friendly iterative queue rather than hardware tessellation pipelines. This method determines which voxels within a triangle's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) are intersected by the triangle's plane and its edge tangent planes. It serves as the final rasterization step in mesh-to-voxel generation, refining the candidate voxels identified by coarse AABB tests. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on a discrete vertex-weight summation algorithm rather than continuous geometric intersection tests or tessellation, offering a brute-force but highly parallelizable approach suitable for CPU implementation. Mesh-based VCP Grid Generation computes a Vector-to-Closest-Point (VCP) from each grid point to the mesh triangles using barycentric coordinates of the perpendicular projection. If the projection is outside the triangle, it computes the closest point on the edges. Triangles are inserted into an empty grid, updating grid points if they are empty or point to a triangle with a greater VCP distance. The VCP data is then expanded using region growing, where grid points adopt the triangle of their neighbors if it results in a shorter VCP distance. An alternative voxelization method implemented in binvox, written by Eric Haines, using triangle overlap code by Tomas Akenine-Möller. A bug existed in version 1.17 where triangles completely at max x/y/z were not voxelized correctly. In version 1.02, the -e option caused triangles to be voxelized too thick. When using the -e method with.obj to.schematic conversion, the -mb parameter can be used to specify block IDs in material names. Time Complexity: O(Nt \cdot Nv) in the worst case, where Nt is the number of triangles and Nv is the number of voxels in the bounding box of each triangle. With the SAT test, each intersection check is constant time but involves 13 axis tests. The scanline fill is O(N{voxels}). Memory Complexity: O(Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz) for the voxel grid. Performance: The method is straightforward to implement and parallelize (e.g., per-voxel or per-triangle parallelism). However, it can be slow for high-resolution grids or complex meshes due to the large number of intersection tests. Strengths: Produces solid, watertight voxel models suitable for physics simulations. The SAT test is robust and handles arbitrary triangle orientations. Limitations: The brute-force intersection testing can be computationally expensive. The scanline fill requires ray casting for each shell voxel, which adds overhead. When to use: When a solid, volumetric representation is required for simulation (e.g., heat diffusion, fracture). When not to use: When only a surface representation is needed (use Fake Voxelization via Triangle-Cube Intersection). When performance is critical and the mesh is very complex (consider Tessellation-based Voxelization or Robust Mesh Voxelization via Exact Predicates). The method was popularized by David Rosen in a 2009 blog post describing voxelization for automatic skinning and physical simulations in games. It is based on the principle of solidifying a surface shell and then filling the interior using a scanline algorithm. The AABB-Triangle intersection test using the Separating Axis Theorem is a standard technique in computer graphics for collision detection and has been adapted for voxelization. The method is used in various game development contexts for creating destructible environments and physics bodies. body: Level 1 Triangle-Voxel Classification classifies input triangles into a coarse 3D voxel grid by mapping vertices to voxel indices and testing overlap with all candidate voxels the triangle spans. It solves the problem of spatial indexing for volume rendering by creating a list of candidate triangles for every voxel, enabling efficient downstream processing. Inputs: trianglesCUDAData: Flat float array, stride 9 per triangle (v0.x, v0.y, v0.z, v1.x, v1.y, v1.z, v2.x, v2.y, v2.z). objBoxMin, objBoxMax: Scene bounding box coordinates (float3). numDiv: 3D grid resolution (int3: numDiv.x, numDiv.y, numDiv.z). boxExtents: Voxel size parameter (float3). inOutCUDAData, voxelTriCountCUDAData, voxelTriIndexCUDAData: Buffers for voxel triangle lists. triBufferLen: Maximum number of triangles allocated per voxel in the buffer. Outputs: Populated voxelTriIndexCUDAData and voxelTriCountCUDAData indicating which triangles intersect which voxels. Data Structures: Voxel grid is indexed linearly: index = r numDiv.y numDiv.x + q numDiv.x + p, where (p, q, r) are the voxel coordinates. Each voxel maintains a list of triangle indices, capped at triBufferLen. Steps: 1. Each thread processes one triangle. Extract 3 vertices from trianglesCUDAData at offset t9. 2. Map each vertex to voxel indices. For vertex i \in \{0, 1, 2\}: \text{boxNumX}i = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{vertex}i.x - \text{objBoxMin}.x}{\text{objBoxMax}.x - \text{objBoxMin}.x} \times \text{numDiv}.x \right\rfloor \text{boxNumY}i = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{vertex}i.y - \text{objBoxMin}.y}{\text{objBoxMax}.y - \text{objBoxMin}.y} \times \text{numDiv}.y \right\rfloor \text{boxNumZ}i = \left\lfloor \frac{\text{vertex}i.z - \text{objBoxMin}.z}{\text{objBoxMax}.z - \text{objBoxMin}.z} \times \text{numDiv}.z \right\rfloor Clamp boundary: if \text{boxNumX}i == \text{numDiv}.x and \text{vertex}i.x == \text{objBoxMax}.x, then \text{boxNumX}i \leftarrow \text{boxNumX}i - 1. Repeat for Y and Z. 3. Compute min/max box indices across the 3 vertices: \text{minBoxX} = \min(\text{boxNumX}0, \text{boxNumX}1, \text{boxNumX}2) \text{maxBoxX} = \max(\text{boxNumX}0, \text{boxNumX}1, \text{boxNumX}2) Repeat for Y and Z. 4. Iterate p from \text{minBoxX} to \text{maxBoxX}, q from \text{minBoxY} to \text{maxBoxY}, r from \text{minBoxZ} to \text{maxBoxZ}. 5. For each voxel (p, q, r), compute box midpoint: \text{boxMidPoint}.x = (p + 0.5) \times \text{boxExtents}.x \times 2 + \text{objBoxMin}.x \text{boxMidPoint}.y = (q + 0.5) \times \text{boxExtents}.y \times 2 + \text{objBoxMin}.y \text{boxMidPoint}.z = (r + 0.5) \times \text{boxExtents}.z \times 2 + \text{objBoxMin}.z. 6. Call TriBoxOverlapCUDA(boxMidPoint, boxExtent, triVerts). If overlap, compute linear index: r \times \text{numDiv}.y \times \text{numDiv}.x + q \times \text{numDiv}.x + p. Add triangle index to voxel list via AddPointToVoxel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Calculates source triangle index ixsrctriangle = glGlobalInvocationID.x and returns if ixsrctriangle >= ntriangles. name: Level 2 Triangle-Voxel Classification
head: CUDAClassifyTessellationLevel2Kernel
body: Refines the coarse triangle classification from Level 1 into a finer 3D voxel grid by re-evaluating triangle overlaps and determining inside/outside status for sub-voxels. It builds on Level 1 Triangle-Voxel Classification by using Level 1 results to limit the search space, processing each Level 2 box against only the triangles assigned to its parent Level 1 box. Unlike Level 1, which maps vertices to coarse indices, Level 2 computes precise geometric intersections (ray casting) within the finer grid to resolve topology. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Triangle data (trianglesCUDAData), Level 1 voxel centers (level1MidPointCUDAData), Level 1 triangle counts (voxelTriCountCUDAData), Level 1 triangle flat indices (level1TriFlatIndexCUDAData), Level 1 triangle flat list (level1TriFlatCUDAData), Level 2 to Level 1 box mapping (level2IndexCUDAData), grid resolutions (numDiv, numDiv2), bounding boxes (objBoxMin, objBoxMax), and voxel extents (boxExtentsLevel1, boxExtentsLevel2). Outputs: Level 2 voxel buffers (level2InOutCUDAData, level2NormalCUDAData) storing inside/outside flags and/or normals. Data Structures: trianglesCUDAData: Flat array of floats, 9 values per triangle (3 vertices × 3 coordinates). level2IndexCUDAData: Array mapping Level 2 box index to Level 1 box index. level1TriFlatCUDAData: Flat array of triangle indices, concatenated per Level 1 box. level1TriFlatIndexCUDAData: Array of starting indices into level1TriFlatCUDAData for each Level 1 box. voxelTriCountCUDAData: Array of triangle counts per Level 1 box. level1MidPointCUDAData: Array of float3 centers for Level 1 boxes. Algorithm Steps: 1. Each thread b processes one Level 2 box. 2. Retrieve the parent Level 1 box index: level1BoxIndex = level2IndexCUDAData[b]. 3. Get the number of triangles in the parent box: numTriangles = voxelTriCountCUDAData[level1BoxIndex]. 4. Get the starting index in the flat triangle list: localIndex = level1TriFlatIndexCUDAData[level1BoxIndex]. 5. Retrieve the Level 1 box center: midPoint.x = level1MidPointCUDAData[b 3 + 0], midPoint.y = level1MidPointCUDAData[b 3 + 1], midPoint.z = level1MidPointCUDAData[b 3 + 2]. 6. Compute the Level 2 box coordinates (p, q, r) from the global Level 2 box index localBoxIndex: r = localBoxIndex / (numDiv2.x numDiv2.y) pqIndex = localBoxIndex - (r numDiv2.x numDiv2.y) q = pqIndex / numDiv2.x p = pqIndex % numDiv2.x 7. Compute the Level 2 box midpoint boxMidPoint: boxMidPoint.x = (2 p + 1) boxExtentsLevel2.x + midPoint.x - boxExtentsLevel1.x boxMidPoint.y = (2 q + 1) boxExtentsLevel2.y + midPoint.y - boxExtentsLevel1.y boxMidPoint.z = (2 r + 1) boxExtentsLevel2.z + midPoint.z - boxExtentsLevel1.z 8. Iterate through each triangle t in the Level 1 box (from localIndex to localIndex + numTriangles): a. Extract vertices v0, v1, v2 from trianglesCUDAData. b. Check for intersection between the triangle and a ray from the voxel center along the Z-axis using TriRayIntersectCUDA. c. If intersecting, increment numIntersections. If numIntersections % 2 == 1, mark the voxel as inside via AddPointToVoxelLevel2. d. For normal computation, calculate edge vectors e01 = v1 - v0 and e02 = v2 - v0, then compute faceNormal = normalize(cross(e01, e02)). e. Add the point and normal to the Level 2 voxel buffer via AddPointNormalToVoxelLevel2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. (r numdiv2[0] numdiv2[1]) q = pqindex // numdiv2[0] p = pqindex % numdiv2[0] boxmid = [ (2 p + 1) boxextentsl2[0] + midpoint[0] - boxextentsl1[0], (2 q + 1) boxextentsl2[1] + midpoint[1] - boxextentsl1[1], (2 r + 1) boxextentsl2[2] + midpoint[2] - boxextentsl1[2] ] numintersections = 0 for i in range(numtris): triidx = level1triflat[localidx + i] v0 = [triangles[triidx 9], triangles[triidx 9 + 1], triangles[triidx 9 + 2]] v1 = [triangles[triidx 9 + 3], triangles[triidx 9 + 4], triangles[triidx 9 + 5]] v2 = [triangles[triidx 9 + 6], triangles[triidx 9 + 7], triangles[triidx 9 + 8]] if trirayintersect(v0, v1, v2, boxmid, [0, 0, 1]): numintersections += 1 if numintersections % 2 == 1: level2inside[b] = True e01 = [v1[j] - v0[j] for j in range(3)] e02 = [v2[j] - v0[j] for j in range(3)] level2normals[b] = normalize(cross(e01, e02)) return level2inside, level2normals def trirayintersect(v0, v1, v2, origin, direction): # Standard Möller–Trumbore ray-triangle intersection e01 = [v1[j] - v0[j] for j in range(3)] e02 = [v2[j] - v0[j] for j in range(3)] h = cross(direction, e02) a = dot(e01, h) if a > -1e-6 and a < 1e-6: return False f = 1.0 / a s = [origin[j] - v0[j] for j in range(3)] u = f dot(s, h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return False q = cross(s, e01) v = f dot(direction, q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: return False return True def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 if mag == 0: return [0, 0, 0] return [v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag] Parameters: numDiv2: Resolution of the Level 2 grid (int3). boxExtentsLevel1/2: Size of Level 1 and Level 2 voxels. Edge Cases: Precision issues may occur if the ray origin is exactly on a coplanar edge during inside/outside determination. Vertices exactly on the object bounding box max limits require clamping to numDiv - 1 to avoid out-of-bounds indices. Determines inside/outside status for Level 2 voxels by casting a ray along the Z-axis from the voxel center and counting triangle intersections. It differs from the normal-based classification by using a topological ray-casting approach rather than geometric overlap. Choose this when topological correctness (winding number) is required over surface normal estimation. A pitfall is precision errors at coplanar edges; a small epsilon offset to the ray origin is suggested to avoid degenerate intersections. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of Level 2 boxes times the average number of triangles per parent Level 1 box. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of Level 2 boxes for output buffers and Level 1 triangle lists. Performance: Optimized for GPU execution via CUDA kernels, leveraging parallel processing of Level 2 boxes. Strengths: High precision due to finer grid; efficient culling via Level 1 parent mapping. Limitations: Higher memory usage than Level 1; sensitive to ray-casting precision issues. The method is implemented in the GPView project as a CUDA kernel for volume rendering tessellation. It extends the coarse voxelization method to provide detailed surface representation for volume rendering pipelines. idealab-isu/GPView, https://github.com/idealab-isu/GPView, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Occupancy Grid Voxelization
head: Occupancy grid computation, Grid Occupancy Voxelization, Voxelization from Triangle Mesh, Mesh Voxelization into Occupancy Grids, Scene Discretization to Occupancy Grid
body: Occupancy Grid Voxelization converts a triangle mesh into a 3D boolean occupancy grid by mapping vertex positions to discrete grid indices and marking voxels that intersect the mesh surface as occupied. It serves as a foundational step for generating volume data from polygonal models, providing a binary representation aligned with sensor resolution. Unlike Signed Distance Field (SDF) derived occupancy, which may miss thin surfaces due to interpolation or level-set thresholds, this method guarantees that any voxel intersecting the mesh geometry is explicitly marked as occupied. The method takes a triangle mesh and a target grid resolution, producing a 3D occupancy grid where each cell indicates the presence of the mesh surface. Input: A triangle mesh defined by a list of vertices V and faces F. Each face f \in F consists of three vertex indices. Optionally, a color flag preserves original mesh face colors by storing face IDs in occupied voxels instead of binary flags. Output: A 3D occupancy grid O of dimensions H \times W \times D (Height, Width, Depth). O[h][w][d] = 1 if the voxel intersects the mesh, 0 otherwise. The grid is typically stored as a dense 3D array. Layout: A 3D array voxelData of type bool or int. Dimensions: (SAMPLE\RATE + 1) \times (SAMPLE\RATE + 1) \times (SAMPLE\RATE + 1) in some implementations, though the active rendering loop often iterates only up to SAMPLE\RATE. Memory: Sequential allocation, e.g., voxelData[x][y][z]. Alternative Layout: For batch processing, an HDF5 tensor of shape N \times C \times H \times W \times D is used, where N is the number of files and C=2 (SDF and occupancy channels). Eigen Tensor: Eigen::Tensor<int, 3, Eigen::RowMajor> occ. 1. Initialize Bounds: Determine the bounding box of the mesh. Initialize minX, maxX, minY, maxY, minZ, maxZ to extreme values (e.g., \pm 99999999) and iterate over all vertices to update these bounds. 2. Compute Grid Parameters: Calculate the index spans for each axis based on the desired resolution (e.g., SAMPLERATE or user-defined H, W, D): X{span} = \frac{|maxX - minX|}{SAMPLE\RATE}, \quad Y{span} = \frac{|maxY - minY|}{SAMPLE\RATE}, \quad Z{span} = \frac{|maxZ - minZ|}{SAMPLE\RATE} Alternatively, scale the mesh to lie in the range [0, H] \times [0, W] \times [0, D] corresponding to the resolution. 3. Initialize Grid: Allocate the occupancy grid and set all entries to 0 (empty). 4. Voxelization (Triangle-Box Intersection): Iterate over all voxels in the grid. For each voxel (h, w, d), define its spatial bounds [minx, maxx] \times [miny, maxy] \times [minz, maxz]. Iterate over all mesh faces f. For each face with vertices v1, v2, v3: Perform a triangle-box intersection test: overlap = triangleboxintersection(min, max, v1, v2, v3). If an intersection is detected: Set O[h][w][d] = 1 (or store face ID/color if enabled). Break the face loop for this voxel to avoid redundant checks. 5. Post-Processing (Optional): If a solid volume is required, apply a connected components algorithm to fill the interior of the surface voxels, as the raw output only marks the surface. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def occupancygridvoxelization(vertices, faces, resolution): # 1. Initialize bounds minx = miny = minz = float('inf') maxx = maxy = maxz = float('-inf') for v in vertices: minx = min(minx, v[0]); maxx = max(maxx, v[0]) miny = min(miny, v[1]); maxy = max(maxy, v[1]) minz = min(minz, v[2]); maxz = max(maxz, v[2]) # 2. Compute voxel size dx = (maxx - minx) / resolution dy = (maxy - miny) / resolution dz = (maxz - minz) / resolution # 3. Initialize grid occgrid = [[ [0 for in range(resolution)] for in range(resolution)] for in range(resolution)] # 4. Voxelization for h in range(resolution): for w in range(resolution): for d in range(resolution): vminx = minx + w dx; vmaxx = vminx + dx vminy = miny + h dy; vmaxy = vminy + dy vminz = minz + d dz; vmaxz = vminz + dz occupied = False for face in faces: v1 = vertices[face[0]]; v2 = vertices[face[1]]; v3 = vertices[face[2]] if triangleboxintersect(v1, v2, v3, vminx, vmaxx, vminy, vmaxy, vminz, vmaxz): occupied = True break if occupied: occgrid[h][w][d] = 1 return occgrid def triangleboxintersect(v1, v2, v3, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz): # Standard Separating Axis Theorem for triangle-box intersection n = cross(v2-v1, v3-v1) if separatingaxis(v1, v2, v3, n, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz): return False for axis in [(1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1)]: if separatingaxis(v1, v2, v3, axis, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz): return False edges = [v2-v1, v3-v2, v1-v3] boxaxes = [(1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1)] for e in edges: for b in boxaxes: axis = cross(e, b) if separatingaxis(v1, v2, v3, axis, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz): return False return True def separatingaxis(p1, p2, p3, axis, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz): ax = axis t0 = dot(p1, ax); t1 = dot(p2, ax); t2 = dot(p3, ax) tmin = min(t0, t1, t2); tmax = max(t0, t1, t2) bmin = 0.0; bmax = 0.0 for i, (mn, mx) in enumerate([(minx, maxx), (miny, maxy), (minz, maxz)]): if ax[i] >= 0: bmin += mn; bmax += mx else: bmin += mx; bmax += mn return tmax < bmin or tmin > bmax def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0]+a[1]b[1]+a[2]b[2] def sub(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) Resolution (H, W, D): The number of voxels along each axis. Typical values are 32^3, 64^3, or higher depending on required detail. Color Flag: A boolean parameter. When set, the grid stores face IDs or colors instead of binary occupancy. Index Calculation Error: Incorrectly using abs(minY) instead of abs(minZ) in the z-index calculation can cause vertical misalignment in the voxel grid. Boundary Rendering: Allocating a grid of size SAMPLERATE + 1 but iterating strictly less than SAMPLERATE leaves the outermost layer of voxels unrendered or uninitialized. Surface vs. Volume: The method produces hollow occupancy grids (only surface voxels are marked). It does not fill the interior. A connected components algorithm is required to generate a solid volume. Empty Models: If the tetravoxelization variant yields no active voxels (e.g., due to misaligned AABB), it may fall back to a naive fill to prevent empty grids. This method extends standard occupancy grid voxelization by storing the index of the first intersecting mesh face in each occupied voxel, rather than a binary occupancy flag. This preserves color information by mapping face indices to voxel values, allowing the original mesh colors to be reconstructed from the voxel grid. It differs from Occupancy Grid Voxelization by retaining per-voxel identity data instead of simple presence/absence. The Adaptive Triangle-to-Voxel Overlap Test is a voxelization algorithm that determines which grid voxels overlap with a mesh triangle by classifying the triangle's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) thickness into three cases (1D, 2D, or 3D) to optimize the overlap test. It builds on Occupancy Grid Voxelization by replacing a naive intersection check with a hierarchical classification that skips geometric tests when the bounding box is thin in multiple dimensions, marking those voxels as fully occupied without further computation. Populates a regular voxel grid by tetravoxelizing input 3D models and mapping binary occupancy results to grid values. It initializes a tetravoxelizer with grid subdivisions, processes each model component to compute voxelization into a 1D array (voxelOpenGL), and then maps these results to a grid. If no active voxels are found, it falls back to a naive fill method to prevent empty grids. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W \cdot D) for the dense grid. Performance: The method is computationally expensive for high-resolution grids due to the large number of triangle-box intersection tests. It is suitable for moderate resolutions (e.g., 32^3 to 64^3). Strengths: Guarantees surface voxel inclusion; simple to implement; preserves geometric accuracy better than SDF-based methods for thin structures. Limitations: Does not fill interior volumes by default; sensitive to resolution; performance degrades with increasing resolution and triangle count. The method originates from basic volumetric rendering pipelines where mesh data needs to be converted to a voxel-based representation for raycasting or volume rendering. It is often implemented as a preliminary step in projects involving Marching Cubes or Sparse Voxel Octree Raycasting. The specific triangle-box intersection approach is attributed to Tomas Akenine-Möller, ensuring robust detection of surface voxels. It is used in various open-source projects for volumetric visualization and additive manufacturing simulations. name: Color-Preserving Occupancy Voxelization
head: Color Preservation in Occupancy Grids
body: This method computes an occupancy grid where voxel values store the index of the first mesh face intersecting the voxel, preserving color information by mapping face indices to voxel values. It differs from Occupancy Grid Voxelization by storing face indices instead of binary flags, and from Adaptive Triangle-to-Voxel Overlap Test by using a fixed parallel iteration over all voxels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A watertight triangular mesh in OFF format with optional per-face RGB colors. Output: An HDF5 file containing an N \times H \times W \times D tensor of integer face indices (0 for empty, f for occupied by face f). If the --color flag is set, a separate [int]color.h5 file stores the original mesh face colors. Data Structures: Occupancy Grid: 3D array of integers with dimensions H \times W \times D. Color File: HDF5 file storing RGB values for each face in the mesh. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize a parallel loop over all voxel indices i from 0 to H \times W \times D - 1. 2. Calculate voxel coordinates: d = i \bmod D, w = \lfloor i / D \rfloor \bmod W, h = \lfloor i / D \rfloor / W. 3. Define voxel bounds in grid coordinates: \text{min} = (w, h, d) and \text{max} = (w + 1, h + 1, d + 1). 4. Loop over all mesh faces f from 0 to N{\text{faces}} - 1. 5. Retrieve vertices v1, v2, v3 for face f. 6. Check intersection: \text{overlap} = \text{triangle\box\intersection}(\text{min}, \text{max}, v1, v2, v3). 7. If \text{overlap} is true, store face index f in the occupancy grid at (h, w, d) and break the face loop. 8. If color mode is enabled, write the original mesh face colors to [int]color.h5. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def colorpreservingvoxelization(mesh, height, width, depth): occgrid = [[[0] depth for in range(width)] for in range(height)] numfaces = mesh.numfaces() for i in range(height width depth): d = i % depth w = (i // depth) % width h = (i // depth) // width mincoord = (w, h, d) maxcoord = (w + 1, h + 1, d + 1) for f in range(numfaces): v1, v2, v3 = mesh.getfacevertices(f) # Perform triangle-box intersection test (implementation not provided in sources) overlap = triangleboxintersection(mincoord, maxcoord, v1, v2, v3) if overlap: faceid = f if f != 0 else numfaces occgrid[h][w][d] = faceid break return occgrid Parameters: --color: Enables color file output. Grid dimensions (H, W, D): Determined by mesh bounds and voxel size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Face Index 0: Face index 0 is treated as 'not voxelized' space by default; if face 0 overlaps a voxel, store numfaces() instead of 0 to distinguish it from empty space. Watertight Meshes: Input OFF files must contain watertight triangular meshes. Color File Ordering: When providing multiple color files to occtooff.py, the ordering is important. Assigns colors by sampling the nearest point on the mesh surface rather than the voxel center, avoiding color errors when voxel centers fall inside empty space. It differs from center-based sampling by ensuring that surface voxels receive colors derived from the actual geometry intersection. This method builds on Color-Preserving Occupancy Voxelization by utilizing the occupancy grid to identify which voxels require surface sampling. Time Complexity: O(V \times F), where V is the number of voxels and F is the number of faces, due to the nested loop structure. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the occupancy grid, plus O(F) for the color file if enabled. Strengths: Preserves color information directly in the voxel grid, enabling simple color reconstruction. Limitations: Only stores the first intersecting face, which may not be the most representative for thick surfaces; performance degrades with high face counts due to the linear scan per voxel. When to use: When color preservation is required and the mesh is watertight. When not to use: For non-watertight meshes or when multiple surface interactions per voxel are needed. Originating from the mesh-voxelization project by David Stutz, this method was developed to enhance standard occupancy grid voxelization by incorporating color data. It is used in contexts requiring colored voxel representations of 3D meshes, such as 3D reconstruction and visualization. name: Surface-based Voxel Color Sampling
head: Surface Voxel Color Assignment
body: Surface-based Voxel Color Sampling assigns colors to voxels by sampling the nearest point on the mesh surface rather than the voxel center, avoiding color errors when voxel centers fall inside empty space. It differs from center-based sampling by ensuring that surface voxels receive colors derived from the actual geometry intersection rather than potentially empty interior points. Inputs: A filled voxel grid (binary occupancy mask). A mesh object containing geometry, and optionally vertex colors or texture UVs. Voxel grid parameters: pitch (voxel size), voxelorigins (world coordinate of the grid origin). Resolution N (assumed cubic grid N \times N \times N). Outputs: A color array or voxel data structure containing RGB values for each surface voxel. Voxels not on the surface may be left empty or assigned a default color. Data Structures: filledmask: Boolean array of shape (N, N, N), true if the voxel intersects the mesh. surfacemask: Boolean array of shape (N, N, N), true if the voxel is on the surface. worldpoints: Array of shape (K, 3), world coordinates of the centers of surface voxels. closestpoints: Array of shape (K, 3), world coordinates of the nearest points on the mesh surface. faceindices: Array of shape (K,), indices of the mesh faces containing the closest points. colors: Array of shape (K, 3), RGB values for each surface voxel. Steps: 1. Identify Surface Voxels: Erode the filledmask to remove interior voxels, then subtract the eroded mask from the filled mask to isolate the surface layer. \text{eroded} = \text{erode}(\text{filled}) \text{surface} = \text{filled} \ \& \ \sim \text{eroded} Note: The erosion operation typically uses a 3x3x3 kernel or checks all 26 neighbors. If a voxel has any empty neighbor, it is considered surface. 2. Convert to World Coordinates: For each voxel index (i, j, k) where surface[i, j, k] is true, compute the world center coordinate: \mathbf{p}{world} = (i, j, k) \times \text{pitch} + \text{voxel\origins} + \frac{\text{pitch}}{2} Collect all such \mathbf{p}{world} into worldpoints. 3. Nearest Surface Query: Perform a nearest-neighbor query on the mesh surface for each point in worldpoints: \text{closest\points}, \, \text{face\indices} = \text{mesh.nearest.on\surface}(\text{world\points}) This returns the closest point on the mesh geometry and the index of the triangle (face) containing that point. 4. Color Assignment: Assign colors based on available mesh data: Case A: Vertex Colors If the mesh has vertex colors, for each surface voxel m with corresponding face index fm: Let Vf be the set of 3 vertices of face fm. Let Cv be the color of vertex v. Compute the average color: \mathbf{c}m = \frac{1}{3} \sum{v \in V{fm}} Cv Clamp and cast to 8-bit unsigned integer: \text{colors}[m] = \text{clamp}(\mathbf{c}m, 0, 255).astype(\text{uint8}) Case B: Texture UVs If the mesh has texture UVs, for each surface voxel m with corresponding face index fm: Let UVv be the texture coordinate of vertex v of face fm. Compute the average UV: \mathbf{uv}{avg} = \frac{1}{3} \sum{v \in V{fm}} UVv Map to texture pixel coordinates (tx, ty) using texture dimensions Tw \times Th: tx = \text{clip}(\mathbf{uv}{avg}[0] \times Tw, 0, Tw - 1) ty = \text{clip}((1 - \mathbf{uv}{avg}[1]) \times Th, 0, Th - 1) Note: The y-coordinate is inverted to match typical image coordinate systems. Sample the texture at (tx, ty) to get \mathbf{c}m. Case C: No Visual Data If the mesh has no vertex colors or textures, assign a default gray color: \mathbf{c}m = (180, 180, 180) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def surfacebasedvoxelcolorsampling(filledmask, mesh, pitch, voxelorigins, resolution): """ Assign colors to surface voxels by sampling the nearest point on the mesh surface. Args: filledmask: Boolean array (N, N, N) indicating occupied voxels. mesh: Object with method nearest.onsurface(points) returning (closestpoints,, faceindices). Also has attributes faces, vertexcolors (optional), vertexuvs (optional), textureimage (optional), texturewidth, textureheight. pitch: Float, size of one voxel. voxelorigins: Array (3,), world coordinates of the grid origin (min corner). resolution: Int, N (grid is NxNxN). Returns: colors: Array (N, N, N, 3), RGB values for all voxels. Empty voxels are (0,0,0). """ N = resolution colors = np.zeros((N, N, N, 3), dtype=np.uint8) # Step 1: Identify surface voxels # Standard scipy erosion; kernel checks 3x3x3 neighborhood from scipy.ndimage import binaryerosion erodedmask = binaryerosion(filledmask, structure=np.ones((3, 3, 3))) surfacemask = filledmask & ~erodedmask surfaceindices = np.argwhere(surfacemask) # Shape (K, 3) if len(surfaceindices) == 0: return colors # Step 2: Convert voxel indices to world coordinates worldpoints = (surfaceindices pitch) + voxelorigins + (pitch / 2.0) # Step 3: Find closest point on mesh surface closestpoints,, faceindices = mesh.nearest.onsurface(worldpoints) # Step 4: Assign colors if hasattr(mesh, 'vertexcolors') and mesh.vertexcolors is not None: # Vertex colors case facevertexindices = mesh.faces[faceindices] vertexcolorsforfaces = mesh.vertexcolors[facevertexindices] avgcolors = vertexcolorsforfaces.mean(axis=1) colors[tuple(surfaceindices.T)] = np.clip(avgcolors, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8) elif hasattr(mesh, 'vertexuvs') and mesh.vertexuvs is not None and hasattr(mesh, 'textureimage'): # Texture UV case facevertexindices = mesh.faces[faceindices] vertexuvsforfaces = mesh.vertexuvs[facevertexindices] avguvs = vertexuvsforfaces.mean(axis=1) tw = mesh.texturewidth th = mesh.textureheight px = np.clip(avguvs[:, 0] tw, 0, tw - 1).astype(int) py = np.clip((1 - avguvs[:, 1]) th, 0, th - 1).astype(int) sampledcolors = mesh.textureimage[py, px] colors[tuple(surfaceindices.T)] = sampledcolors else: # Default gray color defaultcolor = np.array([180, 180, 180], dtype=np.uint8) colors[tuple(surfaceindices.T)] = defaultcolor return colors Parameters: pitch: Voxel size in world units. Not given in the sources. voxelorigins: World coordinate of the minimum corner of the voxel grid. Not given in the sources. Default color: RGB (180, 180, 180) gray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Voxel Centers in Empty Space: If center-based sampling is used, voxel centers may land inside empty space, causing incorrect color sampling. This method avoids that by sampling the nearest surface point. Texture Bounds: UVs should be clamped to [0, 1] before mapping to texture coordinates to avoid out-of-bounds access. Measured Performance: In the context of the source pipeline (M4 Pro, 48 GB RAM), voxelization is Stage 3, running in parallel with GPU inference. Performance is bottlenecked by the overall pipeline throughput (~5 seconds per emoji) rather than this specific sampling step. Strengths: Accurate color assignment for surface voxels; avoids artifacts from empty-space center sampling. Limitations: Requires a mesh with surface geometry; does not handle volume interiors (only surface voxels are colored). This method is part of a pipeline for generating voxel assets from images (e.g., emojis) using neural networks (TripoSR) and subsequent voxelization. It is used in the "image-to-voxel" project to produce Minecraft-like voxel representations with correct surface colors. mohamedmansour/image-to-voxel, https://github.com/mohamedmansour/image-to-voxel, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Triangle-to-Voxel Overlap Test
body: The Adaptive Triangle-to-Voxel Overlap Test is a voxelization algorithm that determines which grid voxels overlap with a mesh triangle by classifying the triangle's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) thickness into three cases (1D, 2D, or 3D) to optimize the overlap test. It builds on Occupancy Grid Voxelization by replacing a naive intersection check with a hierarchical classification that skips geometric tests when the bounding box is thin in multiple dimensions, marking those voxels as fully occupied without further computation. Inputs: triangle: A triangle defined by three vertices v0, v1, v2 in world coordinates. unitlength: The physical size of one voxel side in world units. partitionbounds: The grid coordinate bounds [p{min}, p{max}] of the current processing partition. mortonstart: The minimum Morton code index in the voxel array, used for offsetting array accesses. voxels: An array storing voxel states. In BINARYVOXELIZATION mode, it stores char (1 for FULL, 0 for EMPTY). In non-binary mode, it stores sizet indices into a data array. data: An array of VoxelData structures used in non-binary mode. sparsenesslimit: A threshold to prevent data array overflow. Outputs: Updated voxels array entries for overlapping voxels. Updated data array entries in non-binary mode. Data Structures: AABox: Axis-aligned bounding box defined by min and max vectors. VoxelData: Structure containing voxel attributes (e.g., color, density). Triangle: Structure containing vertices v0, v1, v2. Steps: 1. Compute Bounding Box: Compute the triangle's world bounding box t{bbox\world} using the minimum and maximum of the three vertices' coordinates. Convert t{bbox\world} to grid coordinates t{bbox\grid} by multiplying by unit\div = 1.0 / unitlength and casting to integers: t{bbox\grid.min} = \lfloor t{bbox\world.min \times unit\div} \rfloor t{bbox\grid.max} = \lfloor t{bbox\world.max \times unit\div} \rfloor 2. Clamp to Partition: Clamp t{bbox\grid.min} and t{bbox\grid.max to the partition bounds p{bbox\grid.min} and p{bbox\grid.max} to ensure the triangle is processed only within its assigned grid region: t{bbox\grid.min} = \max(t{bbox\grid.min, p{bbox\grid.min}) t{bbox\grid.max} = \min(t{bbox\grid.max, p{bbox\grid.max}) 3. Determine Thickness: Determine the 'thickness' of the bounding box in each axis. For each axis i \in \{X, Y, Z\}, if t{bbox\grid.min[i] == t{bbox\grid.max[i]}, that axis is 'onethick'. Let N{one} be the sum of onethick axes. 4. Case 1-3 (1D Bounding Boxes): If N{one} \ge 2 (meaning the bbox is 1 voxel thick in at least 2 directions), iterate over all voxels in the bbox defined by t{bbox\grid.min and t{bbox\grid.max. No geometric overlap test is needed; mark all as FULLVOXEL. 5. Compute Triangle Geometry: Compute triangle edges e0 = v1 - v0, e1 = v2 - v1, e2 = v0 - v2. Compute the normalized normal n = \frac{e0 \times e1}{\|e0 \times e1\|}. 6. Case 4-6 (2D Bounding Boxes): If N{one} == 1, perform a 2D projection test on the plane perpendicular to the thin axis. If thin in X (one\thick[X]==1): Project to YZ plane. Compute edge normals n{yz\e0}, n{yz\e1}, n{yz\e2} from the projected edges. If n[X] < 0, negate these normals. Compute distances d{yz\e0}, d{yz\e1}, d{yz\e2} using the formula: d = -\text{dot}(n{edge}, v{proj}) + \max(0, unitlength \cdot n{edge}[0]) + \max(0, unitlength \cdot n{edge}[1]) where v{proj} is the projected vertex coordinate. If thin in Y (one\thick[Y]==1): Project to ZX plane. Compute edge normals n{zx\e0}, n{zx\e1}, n{zx\e2}. If n[Y] < 0, negate these normals. Compute distances d{zx\e0}, d{zx\e1}, d{zx\e2} similarly. If thin in Z (one\thick[Z]==1): Project to XY plane. Compute edge normals n{xy\e0}, n{xy\e1}, n{xy\e2}. If n[Z] < 0, negate these normals. Compute distances d{xy\e0}, d{xy\e1}, d{xy\e2} similarly. Iterate over voxels in the bbox. A voxel is marked FULLVOXEL if it passes the 2D projection tests (i.e., lies inside the projected triangle for all edges). 7. Case 7-9 (3D Bounding Boxes): If N{one} == 0, iterate over all voxels in the 3D bbox. Perform a 3D overlap test: 1. Triangle plane test: Let p be the voxel center. Compute nDOTp = \text{dot}(n, p). Let d1 and d2 be the signed distances of two vertices of the triangle to the plane. The test is: (nDOTp + d1) \cdot (nDOTp + d2) \le 0 2. Projection tests: Perform projection tests on XY, YZ, and ZX planes using the respective edge normals and distances computed as in the 2D cases. A voxel is marked FULLVOXEL if it passes the plane test and all three projection tests. 8. Store Result: For each voxel passing the tests: If BINARYVOXELIZATION is defined, store 1 in voxels and optionally push the index to data. Otherwise, compute barycentric coordinates of the voxel center with respect to the triangle, interpolate color (or other attributes), and store VoxelData in the data array, storing the data index in voxels. Check if a voxel is already FULLVOXEL before processing to avoid duplicate work and data insertion. If the number of voxels exceeds a calculated limit based on sparsenesslimit, revert to non-data mode (usedata = false) to prevent memory issues. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def morton3D64encode(x, y, z): # Standard 3D Morton code interleaving (64-bit) m = 0 for i in range(10): m |= ((x & (1 << i)) << (2i)) | ((y & (1 << i)) << (2i + 1)) | ((z & (1 << i)) << (2i + 2)) return m class VoxelData: def init(self, morton=0, color=(0,0,0), normal=(0,0,1)): self.morton = morton self.color = color self.normal = normal def adaptivetrianglevoxeloverlap(triangle, unitlength, partitionbounds, mortonstart, voxels, data, binarymode, sparsenesslimit): v0, v1, v2 = triangle.v0, triangle.v1, triangle.v2 # 1. Compute Bounding Box tbboxworldmin = (min(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]), min(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]), min(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2])) tbboxworldmax = (max(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]), max(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]), max(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2])) unitdiv = 1.0 / unitlength tbboxgridmin = tuple(math.floor(c unitdiv) for c in tbboxworldmin) tbboxgridmax = tuple(math.floor(c unitdiv) for c in tbboxworldmax) # 2. Clamp to Partition pmin = partitionbounds.min pmax = partitionbounds.max tbboxgridmin = tuple(max(tbboxgridmin[i], pmin[i]) for i in range(3)) tbboxgridmax = tuple(min(tbboxgridmax[i], pmax[i]) for i in range(3)) # 3. Determine Thickness onethick = [1 if tbboxgridmin[i] == tbboxgridmax[i] else 0 for i in range(3)] none = sum(onethick) # 5. Compute Triangle Geometry e0 = (v1[0]-v0[0], v1[1]-v0[1], v1[2]-v0[2]) e1 = (v2[0]-v1[0], v2[1]-v1[1], v2[2]-v1[2]) e2 = (v0[0]-v2[0], v0[1]-v2[1], v0[2]-v2[2]) n = normalize(cross(e0, e1)) # Helper: 2D Projection Test def run2dtest(thinaxis, planeaxes): # Project edges to plane edgesproj = [] for e in [e0, e1, e2]: edgesproj.append((e[planeaxes[0]], e[planeaxes[1]])) # Compute 2D edge normals (perpendicular in projection plane) edgenormals2d = [] for dx, dy in edgesproj: nx, ny = -dy, dx l = math.sqrt(nx2 + ny2) if l > 0: nx, ny = nx/l, ny/l edgenormals2d.append((nx, ny)) # Adjust sign based on triangle normal direction if n[thinaxis] < 0: edgenormals2d = [(-nx, -ny) for nx, ny in edgenormals2d] # Compute distances for each vertex distances = [] for v in [v0, v1, v2]: vproj = (v[planeaxes[0]], v[planeaxes[1]]) nx, ny = edgenormals2d[0] # Use first edge normal for formula indexing d = -dot(edgenormals2d[0], vproj) + max(0, unitlength edgenormals2d[0][0]) + max(0, unitlength edgenormals2d[0][1]) distances.append(d) return edgenormals2d, distances # Helper: Mark voxel def markvoxel(x, y, z): morton = morton3D64encode(x, y, z) idx = morton - mortonstart if binarymode: if voxels[idx] == 1: return voxels[idx] = 1 else: if voxels[idx] != 0: return if len(data) > sparsenesslimit: return # Pitfall: sparsenesslimit check # Compute barycentric coords and interpolate color voxels[idx] = len(data) data.append(VoxelData(morton, (1.0, 1.0, 1.0), n)) # 4. Case 1-3 (1D Bounding Boxes) if none >= 2: for x in range(tbboxgridmin[0], tbboxgridmax[0] + 1): for y in range(tbboxgridmin[1], tbboxgridmax[1] + 1): for z in range(tbboxgridmin[2], tbboxgridmax[2] + 1): markvoxel(x, y, z) return # 6. Case 4-6 (2D Bounding Boxes) if none == 1: if onethick[0] == 1: # Thin in X planeaxes = (1, 2) # YZ edgenormals2d, distances = run2dtest(0, planeaxes) for x in range(tbboxgridmin[0], tbboxgridmax[0] + 1): for y in range(tbboxgridmin[1], tbboxgridmax[1] + 1): for z in range(tbboxgridmin[2], tbboxgridmax[2] + 1): pproj = (y, z) inside = all(dot(edgenormals2d[i], pproj) <= distances[i] for i in range(3)) if inside: markvoxel(x, y, z) elif onethick[1] == 1: # Thin in Y planeaxes = (2, 0) # ZX edgenormals2d, distances = run2dtest(1, planeaxes) for x in range(tbboxgridmin[0], tbboxgridmax[0] + 1): for y in range(tbboxgridmin[1], tbboxgridmax[1] + 1): for z in range(tbboxgridmin[2], tbboxgridmax[2] + 1): pproj = (z, x) inside = all(dot(edgenormals2d[i], pproj) <= distances[i] for i in range(3)) if inside: markvoxel(x, y, z) elif onethick[2] == 1: # Thin in Z planeaxes = (0, 1) # XY edgenormals2d, distances = run2dtest(2, planeaxes) for x in range(tbboxgridmin[0], tbboxgridmax[0] + 1): for y in range(tbboxgridmin[1], tbboxgridmax[1] + 1): for z in range(tbboxgridmin[2], tbboxgridmax[2] + 1): pproj = (x, y) inside = all(dot(edgenormals2d[i], pproj) <= distances[i] for i in range(3)) if inside: markvoxel(x, y, z) # 7. Case 7-9 (3D Bounding Boxes) if none == 0: D = -dot(n, v0) d1 = dot(n, v0) + D d2 = dot(n, v1) + D for x in range(tbboxgridmin[0], tbboxgridmax[0] + 1): for y in range(tbboxgridmin[1], tbboxgridmax[1] + 1): for z in range(tbboxgridmin[2], tbboxgridmax[2] + 1): p = (x, y, z) nDOTp = dot(n, p) # Plane test if (nDOTp + d1) (nDOTp + d2) > 0: continue # Projection tests on XY, YZ, ZX # Reuse logic from 2D case for each plane planes = [((0,1), (x,y)), ((1,2), (y,z)), ((2,0), (z,x))] passes = True for planeaxes, pproj in planes: # Compute normals/distances for this plane (simplified for brevity) edgesproj = [((e[planeaxes[0]], e[planeaxes[1]])) for e in [e0, e1, e2]] normals2d = [] for dx, dy in edgesproj: nx, ny = -dy, dx l = math.sqrt(nx2 + ny2) if l > 0: nx, ny = nx/l, ny/l normals2d.append((nx, ny)) if n[planeaxes[0]] < 0 or n[planeaxes[1]] < 0: # Approximate sign check normals2d = [(-nx, -ny) for nx, ny in normals2d] dists = [-dot(normals2d[0], (v[planeaxes[0]], v[planeaxes[1]])) + max(0, unitlengthnormals2d[0][0]) + max(0, unitlengthnormals2d[0][1]) for v in [v0, v1, v2]] if any(dot(normals2d[i], pproj) > dists[i] for i in range(3)): passes = False break if passes: markvoxel(x, y, z) Time Complexity: Depends on the number of voxels in the triangle's bounding box. The 1D and 2D cases are faster as they skip the 3D plane test. The 3D case requires more computations per voxel. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels in the partition. The voxels array size is determined by the partition bounds. The data array size depends on the number of overlapping voxels and whether BINARYVOXELIZATION is enabled. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The algorithm scales with the number of triangles and the resolution of the voxel grid. The partitioning strategy helps in distributing the workload. Strengths: Optimizes the overlap test by classifying the bounding box thickness, reducing the number of geometric tests required. Limitations: The 3D case can be computationally expensive for large bounding boxes. The source code does not provide a complete implementation of the 3D case, which may lead to gaps in understanding. When to use: When voxelizing meshes with high resolution and when performance is critical. When not to use: When the mesh is very sparse or when the bounding box is very large, as the 3D case may be inefficient. The Adaptive Triangle-to-Voxel Overlap Test is part of the oocsvobuilder project by Forceflow. It is used in the context of building sparse voxel octrees (SVO) for volume rendering. The algorithm is designed to efficiently determine which voxels are occupied by a mesh triangle, which is a crucial step in voxelization. name: Tessellation-based Voxelization
head: VoxelizationByTessellationPass
body: Tessellation-based Voxelization is a GPU-accelerated method for generating 3D voxel grids from triangle meshes by leveraging the hardware tessellation pipeline to subdivide geometry before rasterization. It differs from fixed-function or CPU-based voxelizers by enabling adaptive triangle density and displacement mapping during the generation phase, allowing for higher fidelity in complex regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh defined by index buffers and vertex data. Output: A 3D voxel grid stored in a Unordered Access View (UAV), where each voxel stores occupancy or density information. Data Structures: The method relies on a specific Direct3D 12 pipeline layout named PASSVOXELIZETESS. The descriptor ranges are defined as follows: Range 0: Constant Buffer View (CBV), count 1, offset 0, flags DATASTATIC. Range 1: Constant Buffer View (CBV), count 1, offset 0, flags DATASTATIC. Range 2: Unordered Access View (UAV), count numUAVs, offset 0, flags DATASTATICWHILESETATEXECUTE. Range 3: Constant Buffer View (CBV), count 1, offset 0, flags DATASTATIC [G: This range likely holds projection or camera parameters, though the source does not explicitly define the content]. Shader Stages: The pipeline utilizes five shader stages: 1. Vertex Shader (VS): VSTRIPROJTESS. 2. Hull Shader (HS): HSTRIPROJ. 3. Domain Shader (DS): DSTRIPROJ. 4. Pixel Shader (PS): PSTRIPROJ. 5. Geometry Shader: Not used; the primitive topology is set to CONTROLPOINT3PATCHLIST. Numbered Steps: 1. Bind the pipeline layout PASSVOXELIZETESS with the descriptor ranges specified above. 2. Bind the pipeline state object (PSO) configured with the shader stages listed above. 3. Set the primitive topology type to PATCH (specifically CONTROLPOINT3PATCHLIST). 4. Force the instance count to 1. 5. Execute the draw call: DrawIndexed(mnumIndices, instanceCount, 0, 0, 0). Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode represents the setup and execution sequence derived from the source. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervoxelizationtess(pcommandlist, mvoxelizer, msolid, mvoxmethod, mframeindex, prendertarget, mdepth, mnumindices): # Apply resource barriers if necessary (omitted for brevity, see source context) # Clear render target if not solid if not msolid: clearcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for CLEARCOLOR pcommandlist.clearrendertargetview(prendertarget.getrtv(), clearcolor) # Clear depth stencil pcommandlist.cleardepthstencilview(mdepth.getdsv(), clearflag=ClearFlag.DEPTH, depth=1.0) # Render voxelization mvoxelizer.render( pcommandlist, msolid, mvoxmethod, mframeindex, prendertarget.getrtv(), mdepth.getdsv()) def voxelizerrender(pcommandlist, msolid, mvoxmethod, mframeindex, rtv, dsv): # Bind Pipeline Layout # Range 0: CBV(1), DATASTATIC # Range 1: CBV(1), DATASTATIC # Range 2: UAV(numUAVs), DATASTATICWHILESETATEXECUTE # Range 3: CBV(1), DATASTATIC pcommandlist.setpipelinelayout("PASSVOXELIZETESS") # Bind Pipeline State with Shaders pcommandlist.setshader(ShaderStage.VS, getshader(ShaderStage.VS, "VSTRIPROJTESS")) pcommandlist.setshader(ShaderStage.HS, getshader(ShaderStage.HS, "HSTRIPROJ")) pcommandlist.setshader(ShaderStage.DS, getshader(ShaderStage.DS, "DSTRIPROJ")) pcommandlist.setshader(ShaderStage.PS, getshader(ShaderStage.PS, "PSTRIPROJ")) # Set Primitive Topology pcommandlist.iasetprimitivetopologytype(PrimitiveTopologyType.PATCH) # Draw Call instancecount = 1 pcommandlist.drawindexed( indexcount=mnumindices, instancecount=instancecount, startindexlocation=0, basevertexlocation=0, startinstancelocation=0) Parameters and Edge Cases: mnumIndices: The number of indices in the input mesh. numUAVs: The number of UAVs required for the voxel grid storage. Edge Cases: The method assumes the hardware supports Direct3D 12 and the tessellation stages. Precision issues may arise if the tessellation factor is not appropriately scaled to the voxel grid resolution. A sibling method that classifies triangles against voxels using a simpler, non-tessellation approach. Choose this when hardware tessellation is unavailable or when the mesh is static and low-poly. See Level 1 Triangle-Voxel Classification. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on numUAVs and the voxel grid resolution. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables adaptive density and displacement mapping. Limitations: Requires a GPU with Direct3D 12 support and tessellation capabilities. The method is implemented in the VoxelizerX project, an unofficial Direct3D 12 voxelization sample. It was developed by StarsX and published on GitHub. name: Fake Voxelization via Triangle-Cube Intersection
head: Laine's method implementation, Mesh Voxelization (DGtal), MeshVoxelizer, Triangle Digitization, Triangle Rasterization into Voxels
body: Fake Voxelization via Triangle-Cube Intersection is a surface-only voxelization technique that digitizes a triangulated mesh by independently testing each triangle against a grid of axis-aligned cubes (voxels). Unlike solid voxelization methods that fill the interior volume using Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG), this approach outputs only the voxels intersected by the mesh surface, making it computationally simpler and suitable for generating surface representations. It is distinguished from its siblings by its independence from tessellation depth and its reliance on a template-based intersection test to control topological separability (6- or 26-connectivity). Inputs: A triangulated mesh M consisting of vertices V and triangles T. A 3D domain (grid) defined by an origin O and dimensions Dx, Dy, Dz, representing the voxel grid resolution. A scale factor S (e.g., 15.0) defining the relationship between mesh coordinates and grid units. A separability parameter K \in \{6, 26\} determining the topology of the resulting digital set. Outputs: A digital set (voxel grid) containing the coordinates of all voxels intersected by at least one triangle in M. Data Structures: Mesh: List of triangles, where each triangle is defined by three 3D points (v1, v2, v3). DigitalSet: A collection of integer grid points (i, j, k) representing occupied voxels. Template: A geometric shape centered at a grid point, used to define the intersection criteria. The geometry of the template depends on K: For K=6: The template is a cross-shaped structure (face-connected neighbors). For K=26: The template is a cube-shaped structure (edge and corner-connected neighbors). Note: The exact geometric definition of the templates is implementation-specific (e.g., in DGtal) but serves to ensure topological consistency. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: If the input mesh contains non-triangular faces, triangulate them using a naive fan approach. 2. Initialization: Create an empty digital set for the specified domain. 3. Iteration: For each triangle t in the mesh: a. Determine the bounding box of the triangle in grid coordinates. b. Iterate through all voxels v within this bounding box. c. Perform an intersection test between triangle t and the template centered at voxel v. d. If the intersection is true, add voxel v to the digital set. 4. Parallelization: The iteration over triangles can be parallelized using OpenMP or similar frameworks. Intersection Test: The core operation is determining if a triangle intersects a template centered at a grid point. This is often implemented as a triangle-cube intersection test, potentially refined by the template geometry. A common optimization is to limit the voxel iteration to the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the triangle. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fakevoxelization(mesh, domainorigin, domainsize, scalefactor, separability): """ Voxelize a mesh using fake voxelization via triangle-cube intersection. Args: mesh: List of triangles, each triangle is a list of 3 points (x, y, z). domainorigin: Tuple (ox, oy, oz) representing the grid origin. domainsize: Tuple (dx, dy, dz) representing the grid dimensions. scalefactor: Float scaling mesh coordinates to grid units. separability: Integer, either 6 or 26. Returns: A set of voxel coordinates (ix, iy, iz). """ voxels = set() # Preprocess mesh: ensure all faces are triangles # If non-triangular faces exist, triangulate using fan method. triangles = preprocessmesh(mesh) # Define the template geometry based on separability # The template is a shape centered at (0,0,0) in local grid coordinates. # For 6-separability, it includes face-adjacent neighbors. # For 26-separability, it includes all adjacent neighbors. template = createtemplate(separability) for triangle in triangles: # Calculate bounding box of the triangle in grid coordinates minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz = gettrianglegridbbox( triangle, domainorigin, scalefactor) # Iterate over voxels in the bounding box for ix in range(int(minx), int(maxx) + 1): for iy in range(int(miny), int(maxy) + 1): for iz in range(int(minz), int(maxz) + 1): # Check intersection between triangle and template at (ix, iy, iz) if triangleintersectstemplate(triangle, template, ix, iy, iz, domainorigin, scalefactor): voxels.add((ix, iy, iz)) return voxels def preprocessmesh(mesh): """Convert non-triangular faces to triangles using fan triangulation.""" triangles = [] for face in mesh: if len(face) == 3: triangles.append(face) else: # Naive fan triangulation v0 = face[0] for i in range(1, len(face) - 1): triangles.append([v0, face[i], face[i+1]]) return triangles def gettrianglegridbbox(triangle, origin, scale): """Compute the grid bounding box of a triangle.""" # Transform triangle vertices to grid coordinates gridverts = [( (v[0] - origin[0]) / scale, (v[1] - origin[1]) / scale, (v[2] - origin[2]) / scale) for v in triangle] minx = min(v[0] for v in gridverts) maxx = max(v[0] for v in gridverts) miny = min(v[1] for v in gridverts) maxy = max(v[1] for v in gridverts) minz = min(v[2] for v in gridverts) maxz = max(v[2] for v in gridverts) return minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz def triangleintersectstemplate(triangle, template, ix, iy, iz, origin, scale): """ Check if the triangle intersects the template centered at (ix, iy, iz). This is typically implemented as a triangle-cube intersection test. """ # The template is centered at the voxel center. # The voxel center in world coordinates is: voxelcenter = ( origin[0] + (ix + 0.5) scale, origin[1] + (iy + 0.5) scale, origin[2] + (iz + 0.5) scale) # Perform intersection test between triangle and the template shape. # For a cube template, this is a standard triangle-AABB intersection. # For a cross template, it may involve multiple smaller cubes or a custom test. return triangleintersectscube(triangle, voxelcenter, scale) def triangleintersectscube(triangle, cubecenter, cubesize): """ Check if a triangle intersects a cube centered at cubecenter with side length cubesize. Uses Separating Axis Theorem (SAT) or similar method. """ # Implement SAT for triangle-cube intersection. # Axes to test: # 1. Cube normals (x, y, z axes) # 2. Triangle normal # 3. Cross products of triangle edges and cube axes # This is a standard geometric primitive. # If any separating axis is found, return False. # Otherwise, return True. pass # Implementation details depend on specific SAT library or code. Parameters: Separability (K): Integer, 6 or 26. Determines the connectivity of the output digital set. Scale Factor: Float, e.g., 15.0. Defines the voxel size relative to the mesh coordinate system. Domain: Defined by origin and dimensions. Controls the spatial extent and resolution of the output. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-triangular faces: If the input mesh has non-triangular faces, they are triangulated using a naive fan approach. If the face is not planar or convex, the digitization may be incorrect. Precision: Intersection tests use floating-point arithmetic (double) as an approximation of \mathbb{R}^3. Digitization may not be exact for meshes with integer or rational vertices. Empty Interior: The method does not fill the interior of closed surfaces. Only surface voxels are output. This method determines if a voxel is intersected by a triangle by checking if the voxel's diagonals cross the triangle's plane within the triangle bounds, and handling edge cases where the triangle lies entirely within or touches the voxel faces. It is a specific implementation of Fake Voxelization via Triangle-Cube Intersection that avoids complex Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) operations by treating each triangle independently. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of triangles and M is the number of voxels in the bounding box of each triangle. Optimizations can reduce M by limiting the iteration to the triangle's AABB. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the number of voxels in the output digital set. Performance: The method is generally faster than solid voxelization due to the absence of CSG operations. Parallelization is supported via OpenMP. Strengths: Simple implementation, no CSG required, suitable for surface representation, parallelizable. Limitations: Does not produce solid interiors, precision issues with floating-point arithmetic, incorrect results for non-planar/non-convex faces. When to use: When only surface voxelization is needed, and computational simplicity is prioritized over topological accuracy of the interior. When not to use: When solid interior filling is required, or when high precision is needed for integer/rational meshes. The method is based on the approach described by Laine. It is implemented in the DGtal library as the MeshVoxelizer class, part of the Shapes package. The method is used for digital geometry processing, specifically for digitizing triangulated structures. name: Triangle Voxelization with Diagonal and Edge Checks
head: Line-Plane Collision Voxelization, numpy.stl Voxelization
body: This method determines if a voxel is intersected by a triangle by checking if the voxel's diagonals cross the triangle's plane within the triangle bounds, and handling edge cases where the triangle lies entirely within or touches the voxel faces. It is a specific implementation of Fake Voxelization via Triangle-Cube Intersection that avoids complex Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) operations by treating each triangle independently. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle defined by three vertices P0, P1, P2 in 3D space. Output: A set of voxel coordinates (x, y, z) that are intersected by the triangle. Data Structures: Triangle vertices: Array of 3 vectors, each with 3 floats (x, y, z). Voxel coordinates: Integer triplets (x, y, z). Plane normal: 3D vector \mathbf{n}. Steps: 1. Compute Bounding Box: Calculate the minimum and maximum coordinates of the triangle vertices. \begin{aligned} \text{minx} &= \lfloor \min(P{0x}, P{1x}, P{2x}) \rfloor \\ \text{maxx} &= \lceil \max(P{0x}, P{1x}, P{2x}) \rceil \\ \text{miny} &= \lfloor \min(P{0y}, P{1y}, P{2y}) \rfloor \\ \text{maxy} &= \lceil \max(P{0y}, P{1y}, P{2y}) \rceil \\ \text{minz} &= \lfloor \min(P{0z}, P{1z}, P{2z}) \rfloor \\ \text{maxz} &= \lceil \max(P{0z}, P{1z}, P{2z}) \rceil \end{aligned} Iterate through all integer voxel coordinates (x, y, z) such that \text{minx} \le x \le \text{maxx}, \text{miny} \le y \le \text{maxy}, and \text{minz} \le z \le \text{maxz}. 2. Compute Triangle Plane: Calculate the plane normal \mathbf{n} and a point on the plane (e.g., P0). \begin{aligned} \mathbf{v}0 &= P1 - P0 \\ \mathbf{v}3 &= P2 - P0 \\ \mathbf{n} &= \mathbf{v}0 \times \mathbf{v}3 \end{aligned} 3. Diagonal Intersection Check: For each voxel (x, y, z), check if any of the 4 main diagonals of the voxel cube intersect the triangle plane inside the triangle bounds. The voxel cube is centered at (x, y, z) with side length 1, extending from x-0.5 to x+0.5, etc.. The 4 diagonals connect opposite corners. The specific diagonals checked in the reference implementation are: From (x-0.5, y-0.5, z-0.5) to (x, y, z) with direction (1, 1, 1). From (x+0.5, y+0.5, z-0.5) to (x, y, z) with direction (-1, -1, 1). From (x+0.5, y-0.5, z-0.5) to (x, y, z) with direction (-1, 1, 1). From (x-0.5, y+0.5, z-0.5) to (x, y, z) with direction (1, -1, 1). For each diagonal, perform a line-plane intersection test. If the intersection point lies within the voxel bounds and inside the triangle, the voxel is marked as intersected. 4. Edge Case Check: If all diagonal checks fail, check for edge cases where the triangle might be completely inside the voxel or touch its faces without crossing the main diagonals in a detectable way. This involves: Checking if the triangle intersects the faces of the voxel. Checking if a triangle vertex (origin) is completely inside the voxel bounds. Formulas: Line-Plane Intersection: Given a ray defined by origin \mathbf{r}0 and direction \mathbf{d}, and a plane defined by normal \mathbf{n} and point \mathbf{p}0: \begin{aligned} \mathbf{w} &= \mathbf{r}0 - \mathbf{p}0 \\ \text{ndotu} &= \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d} \\ \text{If } |\text{ndotu}| < \epsilon, & \text{ the ray is parallel to the plane. Return False.} \\ si &= -\frac{\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{w}}{\text{ndotu}} \\ \mathbf{P}{si} &= \mathbf{w} + si \cdot \mathbf{d} + \mathbf{p}0 \end{aligned} Where \epsilon = 10^{-6}. Point-in-Triangle Test: A point \mathbf{p} is inside triangle abc if it is on the same side of each edge as the opposite vertex. \begin{aligned} \text{SameSide}(p1, p2, a, b) &= (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}) \times (\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{a}) \cdot (\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}) \times (\mathbf{p}2 - \mathbf{a}) \ge 0 \\ \text{PointInTriangle}(\mathbf{p}, abc) &= \text{SameSide}(\mathbf{p}, a, b, c) \land \text{SameSide}(\mathbf{p}, b, a, c) \land \text{SameSide}(\mathbf{p}, c, a, b) \end{aligned} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trianglevoxalize(triangle): """ Voxelize a single triangle using diagonal and edge checks. triangle: list of 3 numpy arrays, each shape (3,) representing P0, P1, P2 Returns: list of voxel coordinates (x, y, z) """ p0 = np.array(triangle[0], dtype=float) p1 = np.array(triangle[1], dtype=float) p2 = np.array(triangle[2], dtype=float) # Compute plane normal v0 = p1 - p0 v3 = p2 - p0 planenormal = np.cross(v0, v3) # Compute bounding box trix = [p0[0], p1[0], p2[0]] triy = [p0[1], p1[1], p2[1]] triz = [p0[2], p1[2], p2[2]] minx = int(np.floor(np.min(trix))) maxx = int(np.ceil(np.max(trix))) miny = int(np.floor(np.min(triy))) maxy = int(np.ceil(np.max(triy))) minz = int(np.floor(np.min(triz))) maxz = int(np.ceil(np.max(triz))) points = [] # Iterate through voxels in bounding box for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): # Check 4 diagonals # Diagonal 1: (x-0.5, y-0.5, z-0.5) to (x, y, z) if lineplanecollision(triangle, planenormal, p0, np.array([1, 1, 1]), np.array([x-0.5, y-0.5, z-0.5]), np.array([x, y, z])): points.append([x, y, z]) continue # Diagonal 2: (x+0.5, y+0.5, z-0.5) to (x, y, z) if lineplanecollision(triangle, planenormal, p0, np.array([-1, -1, 1]), np.array([x+0.5, y+0.5, z-0.5]), np.array([x, y, z])): points.append([x, y, z]) continue # Diagonal 3: (x+0.5, y-0.5, z-0.5) to (x, y, z) if lineplanecollision(triangle, planenormal, p0, np.array([-1, 1, 1]), np.array([x+0.5, y-0.5, z-0.5]), np.array([x, y, z])): points.append([x, y, z]) continue # Diagonal 4: (x-0.5, y+0.5, z-0.5) to (x, y, z) if lineplanecollision(triangle, planenormal, p0, np.array([1, -1, 1]), np.array([x-0.5, y+0.5, z-0.5]), np.array([x, y, z])): points.append([x, y, z]) continue # Edge case check if checkedgecases(triangle, planenormal, p0, x, y, z): points.append([x, y, z]) return points def lineplanecollision(triangle, planenormal, planepoint, raydirection, raypoint, voxelcenter, epsilon=1e-6): """ Check if a ray intersects the triangle plane within the triangle bounds and voxel. """ ndotu = np.dot(planenormal, raydirection) if abs(ndotu) < epsilon: return False w = raypoint - planepoint si = -np.dot(planenormal, w) / ndotu psi = w + si raydirection + planepoint # Check if intersection point is within the voxel cube if (abs(psi[0] - voxelcenter[0]) <= 0.5 and abs(psi[1] - voxelcenter[1]) <= 0.5 and abs(psi[2] - voxelcenter[2]) <= 0.5): # Check if point is inside the triangle if pointintriangle(psi, triangle): return True return False def pointintriangle(p, triangle): """ Check if point p is inside triangle defined by 3 vertices. """ a, b, c = triangle return sameside(p, a, b, c) and sameside(p, b, a, c) and sameside(p, c, a, b) def sameside(p1, p2, a, b): """ Check if p1 and p2 are on the same side of edge ab. """ cp1 = np.cross(b - a, p1 - a) cp2 = np.cross(b - a, p2 - a) return np.dot(cp1, cp2) >= 0 def checkedgecases(triangle, planenormal, p0, x, y, z): """ Check edge cases: triangle intersects voxel faces or is completely inside. """ # Check if triangle origin is inside voxel bounds if (x - 0.5 <= p0[0] <= x + 0.5 and y - 0.5 <= p0[1] <= y + 0.5 and z - 0.5 <= p0[2] <= z + 0.5): return True # Check line-plane collisions on voxel faces (x, y, z faces) facenormals = [np.array([1,0,0]), np.array([-1,0,0]), np.array([0,1,0]), np.array([0,-1,0]), np.array([0,0,1]), np.array([0,0,-1])] facecoords = [x+0.5, x-0.5, y+0.5, y-0.5, z+0.5, z-0.5] for normal, coord in zip(facenormals, facecoords): raydir = normal if np.arrayequal(normal, np.array([1,0,0])) or np.arrayequal(normal, np.array([-1,0,0])): raypt = np.array([coord, y, z]) elif np.arrayequal(normal, np.array([0,1,0])) or np.arrayequal(normal, np.array([0,-1,0])): raypt = np.array([x, coord, z]) else: raypt = np.array([x, y, coord]) if lineplanecollision(triangle, planenormal, p0, raydir, raypt, np.array([x,y,z])): return True return False Parameters: Epsilon: 10^{-6}, used to determine if the ray direction is parallel to the plane. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the triangle is completely inside the voxel or touches its faces, diagonal checks might miss it. The checkedgecases function handles this by checking line-plane collisions on the voxel faces (x, y, z faces) and checking if the triangle origin is within the voxel bounds. Precision issues may arise when the triangle is nearly parallel to the voxel faces or diagonals. Hollow Voxel Rasterization is a fast, memory-efficient method for generating a voxel shell (hollow interior) from an arbitrary polyhedron, rather than a solid volume. It is specifically suited for shapes intended to be hollow or meshes with fine structures at low target resolutions. Unlike solid voxelization methods that fill the interior, this approach inverts the containment test: it marks a voxel as part of the mesh if any mesh face lies inside the voxel's bounding box, effectively capturing the surface geometry without occupying internal voxels. Dachille and Kaufman devised a more accurate software method that employs fast incremental arithmetic for rapid voxelization of poly-meshes on a per-triangle basis. The algorithm voxelize a triangle by scanning a bounding box of the triangle in raster order. For each voxel in the bounding box, a filter equation (linear function of distance from triangle) is evaluated and stored. Voxels within the translucent surface are updated with values corresponding to the distance to the triangle surface, using the max operator for storage. The result is stored in a volumetric texture map, enabling hardware-based voxelization. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot V), where N is the number of triangles and V is the number of voxels in the bounding box of each triangle. Memory Complexity: O(V{total}), where V{total} is the total number of voxels in the output volume. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement, avoids complex CSG operations, suitable for surface representation. Limitations: May miss intersections in edge cases if not handled properly, performance degrades with high-resolution meshes and large bounding boxes. When to use: When a surface representation is sufficient and CSG is too complex or expensive. When not to use: When a solid volume fill is required or when high precision is needed for thin structures. This method originates from a Stack Overflow answer by kolenda in 2012, which was used to voxelize STL 3D files using numpy.stl. It is a practical implementation of fake voxelization, focusing on simplicity and correctness for surface meshes.
