name: Hollow Voxel Rasterization
head: Hollow Voxelization, Voxel Shell Calculation, hollow
body: Hollow Voxel Rasterization is a fast, memory-efficient method for generating a voxel shell (hollow interior) from an arbitrary polyhedron, rather than a solid volume. It is specifically suited for shapes intended to be hollow or meshes with fine structures at low target resolutions. Unlike solid voxelization methods that fill the interior, this approach inverts the containment test: it marks a voxel as part of the mesh if any mesh face lies inside the voxel's bounding box, effectively capturing the surface geometry without occupying internal voxels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An arbitrary polyhedron defined by a vertex array and an index buffer (triangles), and a target voxel grid dimension dim (glm::ivec3). Output: A 3D buffer of uint8t values (voxels) of size dim, where non-zero values indicate shell voxels. The output structure also retains the original polyhedron data. Data Structures: The output is encapsulated in a struct rasterresults<buffer3d<uint8t>, mesh::polyhedron<baset>> containing: arrdim: The dimensions of the voxel grid (glm::vec3). voxels: A 3D buffer of uint8t representing the voxel shell. mesh: The input mesh::polyhedron<baset>, which contains vertices.vertexarr (positions) and indices.buffer (triangle indices). Parameters: dim: Target voxel grid dimensions. Used to scale the polyhedron and allocate the output buffer. Algorithm Steps: 1. Normalization and Scaling: Normalize the input polyhedron and scale it to fit the target voxel dimensions dim. This ensures the mesh coordinates align with the voxel grid. 2. Iteration Setup: Iterate over each triangle face of the polyhedron. For each face, compute its 3D bounding box in voxel space: l{min} = \lfloor \min(\text{face vertices}) \rfloor - 0.5 l{max} = \lceil \max(\text{face vertices}) \rceil + 0.5 l{steps} = l{max} - l{min} Shift the face vertices relative to l{min} to work in local bounding box coordinates. 3. Voxel Loop: Iterate over all voxels within the computed bounding box using three nested loops for x, y, z from 0 to l{steps}.x/y/z. Calculate global voxel coordinates: nx = x + l{min}.x ny = y + l{min}.y nz = z + l{min}.z 4. Skip Check: Check if the voxel at (nx, ny, nz) is already marked (non-zero). If it is, skip further processing for this voxel to avoid double-counting. 5. Shell Intersection Test: Determine if the current face intersects the voxel hexahedron. This is done by checking if the face is inside the voxel's bounding box. Calculate halfboxsize = voxel size / 2. Use a separating axis test (SAT) or similar geometric check (faceinhexahedron) with a half-voxel offset to determine if the face penetrates the voxel volume. If the test returns true, mark the voxel as a shell voxel (set voxels[nx, ny, nz] to a non-zero value, e.g., 1). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hollowvoxelrasterization(polyhedron, dim): """ polyhedron: object with vertices.vertexarr (list of vec3) and indices.buffer (list of ints) dim: tuple (x, y, z) of integers Returns: 3D array of uint8t """ # 1. Normalize and scale polyhedron to dim polyhedron.normalize() polyhedron.scale(dim) vertices = polyhedron.vertices.vertexarr indices = polyhedron.indices.buffer stride = polyhedron.indices.stride numfaces = len(indices) // stride # Initialize output buffer voxels = [[[0 for in range(dim.z)] for in range(dim.y)] for in range(dim.x)] voxelsize = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) halfboxsize = voxelsize / 2.0 for faceid in range(numfaces): idxstart = faceid stride v1 = vertices[indices[idxstart]] v2 = vertices[indices[idxstart + 1]] v3 = vertices[indices[idxstart + 2]] # 2. Compute bounding box in voxel space mincoords = vec3(min(v1.x, v2.x, v3.x), min(v1.y, v2.y, v3.y), min(v1.z, v2.z, v3.z)) maxcoords = vec3(max(v1.x, v2.x, v3.x), max(v1.y, v2.y, v3.y), max(v1.z, v2.z, v3.z)) lmin = vec3(floor(mincoords.x), floor(mincoords.y), floor(mincoords.z)) - vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) lmax = vec3(ceil(maxcoords.x), ceil(maxcoords.y), ceil(maxcoords.z)) + vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) lsteps = lmax - lmin # 3. Iterate over voxels in bounding box for x in range(int(lsteps.x) + 1): for y in range(int(lsteps.y) + 1): for z in range(int(lsteps.z) + 1): nx = int(x + lmin.x) ny = int(y + lmin.y) nz = int(z + lmin.z) # 4. Skip if already marked if voxels[nx][ny][nz] != 0: continue # 5. Test if face is inside voxel bounding box voxelcenter = vec3(nx + 0.5, ny + 0.5, nz + 0.5) if faceinhexahedron(v1, v2, v3, voxelcenter, halfboxsize): voxels[nx][ny][nz] = 1 return voxels def faceinhexahedron(v1, v2, v3, voxelcenter, halfboxsize): """ Checks if a triangle face is inside the voxel hexahedron defined by center and halfsize. Uses Separating Axis Theorem (SAT) logic as described in sources. """ # Translate vertices relative to voxel center p1 = v1 - voxelcenter p2 = v2 - voxelcenter p3 = v3 - voxelcenter edges = [v2 - v1, v3 - v2, v1 - v3] # Test face normals (X, Y, Z axes) for axisidx in range(3): maxval = max(p1[axisidx], p2[axisidx], p3[axisidx]) minval = min(p1[axisidx], p2[axisidx], p3[axisidx]) if minval > halfboxsize[axisidx] or maxval < -halfboxsize[axisidx]: return False # Test edge axes (cross products of edges with X, Y, Z axes) axes = [] for e in edges: axes.append(cross(e, vec3(1, 0, 0))) axes.append(cross(e, vec3(0, 1, 0))) axes.append(cross(e, vec3(0, 0, 1))) for axis in axes: if length(axis) == 0: continue # Project triangle vertices proj1 = dot(p1, axis) proj2 = dot(p2, axis) proj3 = dot(p3, axis) projmin = min(proj1, proj2, proj3) projmax = max(proj1, proj2, proj3) # Project box boxextent = abs(axis.x halfboxsize.x) + abs(axis.y halfboxsize.y) + abs(axis.z halfboxsize.z) if projmin > boxextent or projmax < -boxextent: return False return True Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Double-counting: Voxels intersected by multiple faces are marked only once. The check if voxels[nx, ny, nz] != 0 prevents redundant processing. Precision: Floating-point precision in bounding box calculations and intersection tests can lead to gaps or overlaps in the shell, especially at low resolutions. Degenerate Input: Triangles with zero area or collinear vertices may cause issues in the intersection test. The source implies robust handling via the SAT approach, but degenerate cases should be filtered or handled explicitly. Time Complexity: O(F \cdot V{local}), where F is the number of faces and V{local} is the average number of voxels in the bounding box of a face. In the worst case, this is O(F \cdot N^3), but typically much less due to bounding box culling. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for the output voxel buffer, where N is the grid dimension. This is significantly less than solid voxelization if the interior is not stored, but the buffer size is fixed by N. Performance: On an Intel i7 4770k (4 physical cores), rasterizing a Stanford Bunny mesh (112k faces) at 1024^3 resolution takes 1956 ms in --hollow mode. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of faces and cubically with resolution. The --hollow mode is consistently faster than --fast (solid) mode at higher resolutions (e.g., 1956 ms vs 2918 ms at 1024^3). Strengths: Very fast, memory-efficient for shell-only representations, suitable for fine structures at low resolutions. Limitations: Does not provide interior volume data. Accuracy depends on resolution; fine details may be lost if the voxel grid is too coarse. When to use: When only the surface shell is needed, or for meshes with fine structures where solid voxelization would be too memory-intensive. When not to use: When interior volume information is required, or for high-fidelity solid models. Hollow Voxel Rasterization is implemented in the 3DStuff/voxelizer project. It is presented as an alternative to solid voxelization methods (--fast, --safe), offering a trade-off between performance and memory usage. The method is particularly useful for applications where the interior of the voxelized object is not needed, such as in certain rendering or simulation contexts where only the surface geometry matters. 3DStuff/voxelizer, https://github.com/3DStuff/voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Parallel Chunk Voxelization with Early Quit
head: Rayon Chunk Voxelization, Threaded Batch Voxelization
body: This method distributes per-chunk voxelization across multiple threads using the Rayon parallel iterator library, with atomic counters tracking early termination conditions and a channel to stream results to the main thread. It skips chunks that contain no geometry or produce empty voxel batches via early-quit checks. It builds on Triangle Voxelization with Diagonal and Edge Checks for the actual intersection logic within each chunk. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of chunk world positions (chunkpositions), a mapping from chunk positions to triangle face indices (chunkfacemap), a list of mesh vertices (vertices), and model parameters (depth, chunkworldsize, voxelsize, voxelsperaxis, meshmin). Output: A stream of processed chunks, where each chunk is a pair of its world position (IVec3) and a voxel batch (Batch<i32>) containing the voxelized data (patches). Data Structures: chunkfacemap: A hash map (FxHashMap<IVec3, Vec<IVec3>>) mapping each chunk's world position to a list of face indices belonging to that chunk. Batch<i32>: A structure representing the voxel data for a chunk, containing patches. It has a method haspatches() to check if it contains valid data. IVec3: A 3D integer vector type representing chunk coordinates. AtomicUsize: Used for thread-safe counters. AtomicBool: Used for the stop signal. Channel: A bounded channel (capacity 1024) for sending (IVec3, Batch<i32>) pairs from worker threads to the main thread. Parameters: chunkfacemap: Maps chunk positions to face indices. depth: LOD depth used to query voxelsperaxis and chunkworldsize from the model. chunkworldsize: Size of a chunk in world units. voxelsize: Size of a single voxel. voxelsperaxis: Number of voxels along one axis in a chunk. meshmin: Minimum bounding box of the mesh. stopsignal: A boolean flag to signal threads to terminate. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize atomic counters: earlyquitnofaces, earlyquitemptyfaces, earlyquitemptybatch, processedchunks (all Arc<AtomicUsize>), and stopsignal (Arc<AtomicBool>). 2. Create a bounded channel (tx, rx) with capacity 1024 for (IVec3, Batch<i32>) pairs. 3. Spawn worker threads using Rayon's parallel iterator: chunkpositions.pariter().foreach(|chunkposition| {... }). 4. Inside the parallel loop for each chunkposition: a. Check stopsignalclone.load(Ordering::Relaxed). If true, return immediately. b. Look up faces in chunkfacemap for chunkposition. If not found (None), increment earlyquitnofaces and return. c. If faces.isempty(), increment earlyquitemptyfaces and return. d. Call Self::voxelizechunk(chunkposition, depth, chunkworldsize, voxelsize, voxelsperaxis, meshmin, faces, &vertices). e. If the resulting batch has no patches (!batch.haspatches()), increment earlyquitemptybatch and return. f. If batch has patches, increment processedchunks and send (chunkposition, batch) through tx. 5. In the main thread: a. Drop tx to close the channel. b. Iterate over rx.iter(). c. For each (chunkposition, batch), call self.model.getorcreatechunk(chunkposition).applybatch(&mut interner, &batch) to integrate the voxel data into the model. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import threading from collections import deque from typing import List, Tuple, Dict, Any def parallelchunkvoxelization( chunkpositions: List[Tuple[int, int, int]], chunkfacemap: Dict[Tuple[int, int, int], List[int]], depth: int, chunkworldsize: float, voxelsize: float, voxelsperaxis: int, meshmin: Tuple[float, float, float], vertices: List[Tuple[float, float, float]], model: Any, interner: Any) -> Dict[str, int]: earlyquitnofaces = [0] earlyquitemptyfaces = [0] earlyquitemptybatch = [0] processedchunks = [0] stopsignal = [False] counterlock = threading.Lock() capacity = 1024 channel = deque(maxlen=capacity) channellock = threading.Lock() def processchunk(chunkposition): if stopsignal[0]: return faces = chunkfacemap.get(chunkposition) if faces is None: with counterlock: earlyquitnofaces[0] += 1 return if not faces: with counterlock: earlyquitemptyfaces[0] += 1 return batch = voxelizechunk(chunkposition, depth, chunkworldsize, voxelsize, voxelsperaxis, meshmin, faces, vertices) if not batch.haspatches(): with counterlock: earlyquitemptybatch[0] += 1 return with counterlock: processedchunks[0] += 1 with channellock: channel.append((chunkposition, batch)) # Parallel iteration over chunkpositions (equivalent to Rayon's pariter().foreach) import concurrent.futures with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor() as executor: executor.map(processchunk, chunkpositions) # Main thread collects results (drop tx equivalent) while channel: with channellock: if channel: chunkposition, batch = channel.popleft() else: break model.getorcreatechunk(chunkposition).applybatch(interner, batch) return { "earlyquitnofaces": earlyquitnofaces[0], "earlyquitemptyfaces": earlyquitemptyfaces[0], "earlyquitemptybatch": earlyquitemptybatch[0], "processedchunks": processedchunks[0] } def voxelizechunk(chunkposition, depth, chunkworldsize, voxelsize, voxelsperaxis, meshmin, faces, vertices): # Performs the actual voxelization using diagonal and edge checks from parent method # Not given in the sources. Returns a Batch object with haspatches() method. return type('Batch', (), {'haspatches': lambda: False})() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: If chunkpositions is empty, the parallel loop does nothing, and the main thread receives no results. Channel Blocking: Capacity of 1024 mitigates blocking if the main thread is slow to consume results. Stop Signal: Checked at the beginning of each iteration to allow for graceful termination. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Early quit reduces unnecessary work for empty or sparse chunks. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Robust Mesh Voxelization via Exact Predicates
head: Mesh-Native Voxelization with Exact Predicates, add-voxelization, cmg::voxelize, cmg::voxelize::voxelize, mesh-native voxelizer, voxelize(PLC, opts)
body: A mesh-native voxelizer that produces an occupancy grid or a signed-distance field (SDF) over a Piecewise Linear Complex (PLC)'s bounding box, using exact-predicate classification to avoid epsilon-ray speckle. It sets itself apart from its siblings by relying on Shewchuk's exact geometric predicates for robust inside/outside determination, ensuring watertight meshes classify correctly in single precision without the artifacts common in epsilon-based ray casting. Unlike B-Rep CAD kernels such as OCCT which classify against exact analytic surfaces, this method classifies against the input tessellation, meaning its fidelity is bounded by the input faceting accuracy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Piecewise Linear Complex (PLC), defined as a triangle mesh. Output: A VoxelGrid data structure containing origin, spacing, dimensions, and data fields. The data is exposed as a NumPy array of shape (nx, ny, nz) with uint8 for occupancy or float32 for SDF, along with origin and spacing metadata. Data Structures: CarveGrid: A boundary-triangle spatial index used for spatial queries. VoxelGrid: Contains origin (3D vector), spacing (scalar), dims (3D integer vector), and data (array). Parameters: resolution: Controls grid density. Default value is 64. mode: Selects output type. Values are "occupancy" or "sdf". pad: Padding for the grid (Python API). Algorithm Steps: 1. Spatial Indexing: Bucket triangles by their xy-projection into the CarveGrid to optimize queries, achieving approximately O(\text{cells} + \text{triangles}) complexity. 2. Grid Iteration: Iterate over each xy-column (i, j) within the bounding box. 3. Classification: Cast a vertical scanline per xy-column through the grid. Count the number of crossings with the fan-triangulated boundary triangles that lie above the voxel center. Use cmg::robust::orient3d (Shewchuk's exact predicate) to determine plane-side sign changes and matching edge orientations for each intersection. If orient3d returns exactly 0 (grazing), apply a deterministic (x, y) nudge to the scanline to ensure robustness. The cell is inside if the number of crossings is odd. 4. SDF Calculation (if mode is "sdf"): Compute the exact point-to-triangle distance using Ericson's algorithm. Sign the distance: negative if the voxel center is inside (odd parity), positive if outside (even parity). 5. Output Generation: Populate the VoxelGrid data array with the computed values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelize(plc, resolution=64, mode="occupancy", pad=1): # 1. Setup grid parameters bboxmin = plc.boundingboxmin() bboxmax = plc.boundingboxmax() spacing = (bboxmax - bboxmin) / resolution dims = [int(resolution + 2 pad) for in range(3)] origin = bboxmin - spacing pad # 2. Build spatial index (CarveGrid) carvegrid = CarveGrid() for tri in plc.triangles: carvegrid.insert(tri) # 3. Initialize output grid grid = [[[[0.0 for in range(dims[2])] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] # 4. Iterate over xy-columns for j in range(dims[1]): for i in range(dims[0]): # Voxel center in world space (using first k for ray origin) center = [origin[k] + (k + pad) spacing for k in range(3)] # Get candidate triangles for this xy-column candidates = carvegrid.queryxy(center[0], center[1]) # Count crossings using exact predicates crossings = 0 for tri in candidates: # Determine if vertical ray intersects triangle above center # Use orient3d for robustness iscrossing, zint = classifyverticalray(center, tri) if iscrossing and zint > center[2]: crossings += 1 # Determine occupancy isinside = (crossings % 2 == 1) # Fill k-dimension for k in range(dims[2]): if mode == "occupancy": grid[i][j][k] = 1 if isinside else 0 else: # Compute SDF dist = pointtriangledistance(center, plc.triangles) grid[i][j][k] = -dist if isinside else dist return VoxelGrid(origin=origin, spacing=spacing, dims=dims, data=grid) def classifyverticalray(center, tri): # Cast vertical ray from center upwards # Use orient3d to check intersection robustly # Apply deterministic (x,y) nudge if orient3d is 0 # Return (True/False, intersectionz) # Standard exact ray-triangle intersection logic pass def pointtriangledistance(point, triangles): # Ericson's exact point-to-triangle distance algorithm mindist = float('inf') for tri in triangles: d = distancepointtriangle(point, tri) if d < mindist: mindist = d return mindist def distancepointtriangle(point, tri): # Standard point-to-triangle distance computation pass class CarveGrid: def init(self): self.buckets = {} def insert(self, tri): # Bucket triangles by xy-projection bounding box pass def queryxy(self, x, y): # Return triangles in overlapping xy-buckets pass class VoxelGrid: def init(self, origin, spacing, dims, data): self.origin = origin self.spacing = spacing self.dims = dims self.data = data Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grazing Intersections: orient3d returning exactly 0 must be handled by a deterministic (x, y) nudge to the scanline. Curved Inputs: The method only sees the triangle mesh; curved CAD inputs (STEP/IGES) are not handled with exact surface precision, so fidelity is bounded by the input faceting. Non-Watertight Input: Healing non-watertight input is a non-goal; the method assumes a watertight PLC for robust parity classification. An optimization for solid mesh voxelization that skips expensive BVH distance queries for exterior voxels by leveraging parity check results. It sets itself apart from standard solid voxelization by avoiding the computation of the exact Signed Distance Field (SDF) for points that are guaranteed to be discarded by the interiority filter, provided no narrow band is required. Choose this when performance is critical for solid meshes and you can accept placeholder infinite distances for exterior points. Time Complexity: Approximately O(\text{cells} + \text{triangles}) due to triangle bucketing by xy-projection. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels in the grid plus the spatial index size. Performance: Validated with 138 tests including cube and sphere volume convergence, determinism, and watertight no-speckle checks in single precision. Strengths: Robust exact-predicate classification avoids epsilon-ray speckle; mesh-native (no CAD kernel dependency); fast parallel spatial-grid classifier. Limitations: Fidelity is bounded by input tessellation; does not support B-Rep/exact-surface voxelization; SDF calculation is brute-force point-triangle distance in v1. When to Use: When robust voxelization of a triangle mesh is required without external CAD dependencies, and exact topological classification is critical. When Not to Use: When exact curved-surface fidelity (STEP/IGES) is required (use OCCT instead). Proposed by leonardoaraujosantos in Pull Request #20 to the CyberdyneCorp/CyberMeshGenerator repository on July 4, 2026. It is part of the CyberMeshGenerator (cmg) library, a modern C++20 library for generating tetrahedral meshes of 3D polyhedral geometry. The method was designed to provide a mesh-native voxelizer that reuses existing point-in-solid classifiers and Shewchuk's exact predicates, distinguishing it from B-Rep based tools like OCCT which offer exact analytic surface classification but are heavier and CAD-focused. Implement voxelization (occupancy + signed-distance field), https://github.com/CyberdyneCorp/CyberMeshGenerator/pull/21, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) openspec: propose voxelization (occupancy + SDF) under cmg, https://github.com/CyberdyneCorp/CyberMeshGenerator/pull/20, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Bolt
head: Bypass expensive BVH query for exterior voxels, Bolt: Skip expensive BVH queries for exterior voxels
body: Bolt is an optimization for solid voxelization that bypasses the expensive Boundary Volume Hierarchy (BVH) distance query for voxels determined to be exterior to the mesh. It distinguishes itself from standard solid voxelization by assigning a dummy positive distance to exterior voxels when no narrow band is requested, thereby avoiding redundant geometric calculations for points guaranteed to be discarded by the interiority filter. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel center point P, a boolean isinside indicating if P is inside the mesh (derived from a scanline parity check), an optional parameter narrowband, and a boolean surfaceonly indicating the voxelization mode. Output: The Signed Distance Field (SDF) value d for the voxel center. Data Structures: narrowband: An optional flag. When None, the optimization is active. When Some, the BVH query is performed regardless of interior/exterior status. isinside: A boolean result from a parity check that determines if a voxel is inside the mesh. surfaceonly: A boolean flag. When false, the algorithm operates in solid voxelization mode and applies the optimization. Steps: 1. For each voxel center P, determine if it is inside the mesh (isinside) and check the surfaceonly and narrowband parameters. 2. If surfaceonly is false, narrowband is None, AND the voxel is exterior (!isinside), assign the distance d = 1.0. 3. Otherwise (if surfaceonly is true, narrowband is specified, OR the voxel is interior), compute the exact distance using the mesh's BVH query: d = \text{compute\exact\mesh\distance}(P, \text{False}) cast to f32. 4. In solid voxelization mode (surfaceonly = false), apply the filter d \le 0.0 to discard exterior voxels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesdfbolt(point, isinside, narrowband, surfaceonly): # Bolt optimization: skip expensive BVH query for exterior voxels # in solid voxelization mode when no narrow band is requested. # These points are guaranteed to be discarded by the d <= 0.0 filter. if not surfaceonly and narrowband is None and not isinside: return 1.0 # Dummy positive value; alternatives use float('inf') # Compute exact distance via BVH query for interior voxels, # exterior voxels when narrow band is requested, or surface voxelization. # The second argument (False) requests exact mode. exactdist = computeexactmeshdistance(point, False) return float(exactdist) def computeexactmeshdistance(point, exactflag): # Standard BVH distance query implementation # Returns the exact Euclidean distance from point to the mesh surface. pass Parameters: narrowband: Optional. When None, the optimization is active. When Some, the BVH query is performed regardless of interior/exterior status. isinside: Boolean result from a parity check. surfaceonly: Boolean. When false, solid voxelization mode is active and the optimization applies. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Misclassification: Points exactly on the mesh surface may be classified as outside by the parity test if the implementation uses partitionpoint(|&hx| hx <= x), which excludes hits at the same x coordinate. Data Loss: Previously, these boundary samples received distance == 0 and passed the sdf <= 0.0 filter. With Bolt, they receive 1.0 (or +inf) and are dropped. Impact: This can remove valid boundary voxels or cause small meshes to produce no solid particles on aligned/coarse grids. The optimization must ensure exact-surface voxels are retained or handled correctly. Test Case Compatibility: The optimization intentionally returns a dummy positive value instead of the exact distance for exterior voxels. Test suites expecting exact distances for exterior points will fail unless surfaceonly is true or narrowband is provided, which forces the exact BVH query path. Performance: Benchmarks show a performance improvement of approximately 3.5% to 5.2% on standard tests for solid voxelization. Another benchmark measured a drop from approximately 32.5ms to 29.5ms per loop over 100 sample passes for a small cube with 125,000 potential voxels. Scaling: The improvement scales with grid resolution and scene sparsity, as high-resolution solid grids contain a large percentage of sampled voxels residing outside the target mesh bounds. Strengths: Drastically reduces processing time by avoiding unnecessary BVH queries for exterior points in solid voxelization. Limitations: Potential loss of boundary voxels if the parity test misclassifies surface points as exterior, particularly on coarse or aligned grids. Bolt was introduced as a performance optimization in the voxelizer-rs project to bypass expensive BVH queries for exterior voxels in solid voxelization mode when a narrow band is not specified. It was implemented by lhemerly and reviewed by Jules in June 2026. The optimization addresses the computational redundancy of calculating exact Signed Distance Fields for points that are guaranteed to be discarded by the interiority filter in solid voxelization workflows. ⚡ Bolt: Bypass BVH query for exterior solid voxels, https://github.com/lhemerly/voxelizer-rs/pull/161, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ⚡ Bolt: Bypass expensive BVH query for exterior voxels, https://github.com/lhemerly/voxelizer-rs/pull/188, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ⚡ Bolt: Bypass BVH query for exterior voxels in solid voxelization, https://github.com/lhemerly/voxelizer-rs/pull/199, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ✨ [performance improvement] Bolt: Skip expensive BVH queries for exterior voxels, https://github.com/lhemerly/voxelizer-rs/pull/138, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Triangle Subdivision for Voxelization
head: Triangle Split, Triangle Splitting, Pre-processing Subdivision
body: Triangle Subdivision for Voxelization is a pre-processing method that recursively splits mesh triangles to ensure they are small enough to be voxelized efficiently and predictably. It solves the problem of variable voxel counts per triangle, which complicates memory allocation and parallel processing in out-of-core or batch-based voxelization pipelines. Unlike general-purpose mesh smoothing or tessellation, this method is geometry-driven, targeting specific edge-length or area thresholds relative to the voxel resolution to guarantee homogeneous voxel generation and compact Morton index ranges. It differs from Level 1 Triangle-Voxel Classification by actively modifying the mesh geometry rather than just classifying existing triangles, and from Tessellation-based Voxelization by using a deterministic, CPU/GPU-friendly iterative queue rather than hardware tessellation pipelines. Inputs: A triangle soup \{Ti\}, where each triangle T has three vertices and three edge lengths T.a, T.b, T.c. A user-defined parameter K{vox/tri}^{max}, the maximum allowed ratio of the triangle's projected bounding box area to the voxel face area. The voxel grid resolution, defined by the voxel edge length L. Outputs: A refined set of triangles \{Ti\} (stored in result queue R) such that for every triangle, the area of its projected bounding box A{bbox}(T) satisfies A{bbox}(T) \le K{vox/tri}^{max} \cdot A{vox}. An upper bound N{vox/tri}^{max}(Ti) for the number of voxels generated by each resulting triangle, used for pre-allocating memory. Data Structures: Queue Q: Stores triangles pending subdivision. Queue R: Stores triangles that satisfy the area constraint and are ready for voxelization. Edge lengths: For each triangle, edges are sorted such that T.a \le T.b \le T.c. Formulas: 1. Voxel Face Area: A{vox} = L^2. 2. Subdivision Condition: A triangle T is subdivided if A{bbox}(T) > K{vox/tri}^{max} \cdot A{vox}. 3. Voxel Count Upper Bound: N{vox/tri}^{max}(Ti) is calculated by discretizing the projected bounding box of Ti onto the voxel grid to count enclosed projected voxels, then multiplying by 3. The factor of 3 accounts for the maximum number of voxels a planar triangle can occupy along the projection direction. Parameters: K{vox/tri}^{max}: User-defined threshold controlling the granularity of the subdivision. L: Voxel edge length; references a threshold where the longest edge must be smaller than 0.5 voxel. Steps: 1. Initialize Q with all input triangles \{Ti\} and R as empty. 2. While Q is not empty: a. Dequeue triangle T from Q. b. Calculate A{bbox}(T), the area of the projected bounding box of T. c. If A{bbox}(T) \le K{vox/tri}^{max} \cdot A{vox}: i. Enqueue T into R. d. Else, apply subdivision logic based on sorted edge lengths T.a \le T.b \le T.c: i. Case 1 (Long thin, obtuse): If (T.a + T.b) < 2 \cdot T.c (angles larger than \sim 90^\circ): Split T into two triangles. Append the resulting triangles to Q. ii. Case 2 (Long thin, acute): If 3 \cdot T.a < T.b (angles smaller than \sim 20^\circ): Subdivide T to generate approximately equilateral triangles by cutting the short edge T.a off the long edges and splitting the resulting quadrilateral. Append the resulting triangles to Q. iii. Case 3 (Regular): Otherwise: Compute subdivision factor s = \sqrt{A{bbox}(T) / (K{vox/tri}^{max} \cdot A{vox})}. Subdivide T directly using this factor to satisfy the area constraint. Enqueue the resulting triangles into R. 3. The final set of triangles is \{Ti\} = R. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trianglesubdivision(triangles, Kmax, L): """ Subdivides triangles until their projected bounding box area is within limits. Args: triangles: List of dicts with 'v0', 'v1', 'v2' (each a tuple of 3 floats). Kmax: User-defined max ratio of bbox area to voxel face area. L: Voxel edge length. Returns: List of subdivided triangles satisfying the area constraint. """ Avox = L L Q = list(triangles) R = [] while Q: T = Q.pop(0) Abbox = computeprojectedbboxarea(T) if Abbox <= Kmax Avox: R.append(T) else: edges = sorted([edgelength(T, 0, 1), edgelength(T, 1, 2), edgelength(T, 2, 0)]) a, b, c = edges[0], edges[1], edges[2] if (a + b) < 2 c: # Case 1: Long thin, obtuse (>90 deg) newtris = splittriangleobtuse(T) Q.extend(newtris) elif 3 a < b: # Case 2: Long thin, acute (<20 deg) newtris = subdividetriangleacute(T) Q.extend(newtris) else: # Case 3: Regular factor = math.sqrt(Abbox / (Kmax Avox)) newtris = regularsubdivide(T, factor) R.extend(newtris) return R def computeprojectedbboxarea(T): """Projects triangle to the plane perpendicular to its dominant normal axis and returns bbox area.""" v0, v1, v2 = T['v0'], T['v1'], T['v2'] # Compute normal n = cross(sub(v1, v0), sub(v2, v0)) # Determine dominant axis axes = [('x', 0), ('y', 1), ('z', 2)] dominant = max(axes, key=lambda ax: abs(n[ax[1]])) # Project vertices onto the plane perpendicular to dominant axis proj = [] for v in [v0, v1, v2]: p = list(v) p[dominant[1]] = 0.0 proj.append(p) # Compute 2D bounding box area mins = [min(p[i] for p in proj) for i in range(3)] maxs = [max(p[i] for p in proj) for i in range(3)] # Use the two non-dominant axes for area axesused = [ax[1] for ax in axes if ax[1] != dominant[1]] return (maxs[axesused[0]] - mins[axesused[0]]) (maxs[axesused[1]] - mins[axesused[1]]) def edgelength(T, i, j): return math.dist(T[f'v{i}'], T[f'v{j}']) def sub(a, b): return tuple(a[i] - b[i] for i in range(3)) def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]) def splittriangleobtuse(T): """Splits a triangle with one long edge and two short edges by connecting the midpoint of the longest edge to the opposite vertex.""" edges = sorted([edgelength(T, 0, 1), edgelength(T, 1, 2), edgelength(T, 2, 0)]) a, b, c = edges[0], edges[1], edges[2] # Identify longest edge indices if c == edgelength(T, 0, 1): i1, i2 = 0, 1 elif c == edgelength(T, 1, 2): i1, i2 = 1, 2 else: i1, i2 = 2, 0 opposite = 3 - i1 - i2 mid = tuple((T[f'v{i1}'][k] + T[f'v{i2}'][k]) / 2.0 for k in range(3)) return [ {'v0': T[f'v{i1}'], 'v1': T[f'v{opposite}'], 'v2': mid}, {'v0': T[f'v{i2}'], 'v1': T[f'v{opposite}'], 'v2': mid} ] def subdividetriangleacute(T): """Generates approximately equilateral triangles from a long thin acute triangle by cutting the short edge off the long edges.""" edges = sorted([edgelength(T, 0, 1), edgelength(T, 1, 2), edgelength(T, 2, 0)]) a, b, c = edges[0], edges[1], edges[2] # Identify short edge indices if a == edgelength(T, 0, 1): i1, i2 = 0, 1 elif a == edgelength(T, 1, 2): i1, i2 = 1, 2 else: i1, i2 = 2, 0 # Cut short edge off long edges: create points on the two long edges at distance 'a' from the shared vertex shared = 3 - i1 - i2 vshort1 = T[f'v{i1}'] vshort2 = T[f'v{i2}'] vshared = T[f'v{shared}'] lenlong1 = edgelength(T, shared, i1) lenlong2 = edgelength(T, shared, i2) p1 = tuple(vshared[k] + (vshort1[k] - vshared[k]) (a / lenlong1) for k in range(3)) p2 = tuple(vshared[k] + (vshort2[k] - vshared[k]) (a / lenlong2) for k in range(3)) # Split resulting quadrilateral into two triangles return [ {'v0': vshort1, 'v1': vshort2, 'v2': p1}, {'v0': vshort2, 'v1': vshared, 'v2': p2} ] def regularsubdivide(T, factor): """Subdivides a triangle uniformly based on a scaling factor to meet the area constraint.""" # Uniform subdivision: divide each edge into 'factor' segments and fill n = max(2, int(math.ceil(factor))) newtris = [] for i in range(n): for j in range(n - i): # Barycentric interpolation p0 = tuple(T[f'v{k}'][d] + (T[f'v{(k+1)%3}'][d] - T[f'v{k}'][d]) (i / n) for k in range(3) for d in range(3)) p1 = tuple(T[f'v{k}'][d] + (T[f'v{(k+1)%3}'][d] - T[f'v{k}'][d]) ((i + j + 1) / n) for k in range(3) for d in range(3)) p2 = tuple(T[f'v{k}'][d] + (T[f'v{(k+2)%3}'][d] - T[f'v{k}'][d]) ((i + j) / n) for k in range(3) for d in range(3)) newtris.append({'v0': p0, 'v1': p1, 'v2': p2}) return newtris Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Termination: The subdivision logic guarantees termination because Case 1 splits a triangle into two triangles that fall into Case 2 or Case 3, and Case 3 directly satisfies the area constraint. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for area thresholds and edge lengths require an epsilon guard to avoid infinite recursion on near-degenerate inputs. Degenerate Input: Triangles with zero area or collinear vertices should be filtered out before subdivision begins. A GPU-based iterative refinement strategy that subdivides a triangular mesh until all edge lengths are smaller than or equal to a user-defined cube size r. It solves the problem of preparing boundary models for voxelization into "LEGOr" representations, ensuring uniform sampling and watertightness by guaranteeing that at least one vertex of the input mesh lies inside each resulting voxel brick. It differs from general-purpose subdivision schemes (like Catmull-Clark) by using a fixed, geometry-driven split pattern based on edge length thresholds relative to a target voxel resolution, rather than smoothing or topological refinement. Time Complexity: The subdivision process is iterative and depends on the initial triangle sizes and the threshold K{vox/tri}^{max}. The number of subdivisions is bounded by the ratio of the initial bounding box area to the target area. Memory Complexity: The method requires storing the queue Q and result queue R. The memory usage scales with the number of generated triangles, and the upper bound N{vox/tri}^{max}(Ti) is used to pre-allocate memory for the voxelization step to prevent dynamic reallocation. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Batch size trade-offs exist; processing very small batches results in poor utilization of GPU processing power, whereas rather large batches may lead to fragmentation of the Morton queue. Strengths: Ensures homogeneous voxel counts per triangle, which simplifies batch processing and memory management. Compact Morton index ranges reduce fragmentation in out-of-core voxelization. Limitations: Requires pre-processing of the mesh. The subdivision logic is specific to the area-based constraint and may not be optimal for all voxelization algorithms. The method originates from the work on grid-free out-of-core voxelization to sparse voxel octrees on GPU. It was developed to address the challenges of processing large triangle soups efficiently on GPU by ensuring that each triangle contributes a predictable and manageable number of voxels. The subdivision scheme is a key component of the pre-processing step, enabling efficient sorting and batch processing of triangles for voxelization. The "Triangle Split" method is also referenced in comparative assessments of implicit and explicit plenoptic scene representations, where it is described as a direct discretization method splitting triangles until the longest edge is smaller than 0.5 voxel. name: Legolizer Subdivision
head: Subdivision Technique
body: Legolizer Subdivision is a GPU-based iterative refinement strategy that subdivides a triangular mesh until all edge lengths are smaller than or equal to a user-defined cube size r. It solves the problem of preparing boundary models for voxelization into "LEGOr" representations, ensuring uniform sampling and watertightness by guaranteeing that at least one vertex of the input mesh lies inside each resulting voxel brick. It differs from general-purpose subdivision schemes by using a fixed, geometry-driven split pattern based on edge length thresholds relative to a target voxel resolution, rather than smoothing or topological refinement. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh M and a scalar resolution parameter r (the cube edge size). Output: A refined triangle mesh where every edge length is \le r. Data Structures: Vertex Buffer Objects (VBOs): Two VBOs, vbo1 and vbo2, are used to store vertex data (position and color emitted by the vertex shader) on the GPU. Triangle Representation: Defined by three vertices v1, v2, v3. Parameters: r: The cube edge size (resolution). This determines the maximum allowed triangle edge length for subdivision. Algorithm Steps: 1. Create two VBOs: vbo1 and vbo2. 2. Upload the input mesh M to the GPU into vbo1. 3. Set vbo1 as the shader input and vbo2 as the output. 4. Enable the subdivision shader pipeline. 5. Enter an iterative loop: a. Draw the current input VBO. b. Swap the input and output VBO pointers. c. Check if the vertex count in the mesh has changed. If it has not changed, exit the loop. 6. Disable the subdivision shader. 7. Return the pointer to the last output VBO. Geometry Shader Logic: For each input triangle with vertices v1, v2, v3, the geometry shader performs the following: 1. Identify the set of edges e with length greater than r. 2. If e = \emptyset (no edges exceed r): Emit the original triangle v1, v2, v3. 3. If |e| = 1 (one edge exceeds r): Let e1 be the long edge. Let v4, v5 be the endpoints of e1. Let v6 be the new vertex at the middle of edge e1. Let v7 be the triangle vertex opposite to e1. Emit triangles: (v4, v6, v7) and (v5, v7, v6). 4. If |e| = 2 (two edges exceed r): Let e1, e2 be the long edges. Let v4 be the vertex shared by e1 and e2. Let v5 be the vertex of e1 different from v4. Let v6 be the vertex of e2 different from v4. Let v7 be the new vertex in one half of e1. Let v8 be the new vertex in one half of e2. Emit triangles: (v4, v7, v8), (v7, v6, v8), and (v5, v6, v7). 5. If |e| = 3 (all three edges exceed r): Let e1, e2, e3 be the three edges. Let v4, v5, v6 be the new vertices in one half of e1, e2, e3 respectively. Let v7 be the vertex shared by e1 and e2. Let v8 be the vertex shared by e2 and e3. Let v9 be the vertex shared by e3 and e1. Emit triangles: (v4, v5, v6), (v7, v4, v5), (v9, v5, v6), and (v8, v6, v4). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def legolizersubdivision(meshvertices, r): # 1. Create two VBOs vbo1 = {"data": meshvertices, "size": len(meshvertices)} vbo2 = {"data": [], "size": 0} # 2. Send mesh to GPU in vbo1 (already loaded) # 3. Set vbo1 as input, vbo2 as output currentinput = vbo1 currentoutput = vbo2 # 4. Enable subdivision shader shaderr = r # 5. Iterative loop prevvertexcount = currentinput["size"] while True: # Draw input VBO (executes vertex and geometry shaders) currentoutput["data"] = executegeometryshader(currentinput["data"], shaderr) currentoutput["size"] = len(currentoutput["data"]) # Swap input and output VBOs temp = currentinput currentinput = currentoutput currentoutput = temp # Check if vertex count changed (source phrasing: "while the vertex number in M does not change do") # Implemented as standard termination on stabilization if currentinput["size"] == prevvertexcount: break prevvertexcount = currentinput["size"] # 9. Disable shader shaderr = None # 10. Return last output VBO pointer return currentinput def executegeometryshader(vertices, r): output = [] for i in range(0, len(vertices), 3): v1, v2, v3 = vertices[i], vertices[i+1], vertices[i+2] edges = [] if length(v1, v2) > r: edges.append((v1, v2)) if length(v2, v3) > r: edges.append((v2, v3)) if length(v3, v1) > r: edges.append((v3, v1)) if len(edges) == 0: output.extend([v1, v2, v3]) elif len(edges) == 1: e1 = edges[0] v4, v5 = e1[0], e1[1] v6 = midpoint(e1[0], e1[1]) v7 = oppositevertex(v1, v2, v3, e1) output.extend([v4, v6, v7, v5, v7, v6]) elif len(edges) == 2: e1, e2 = edges[0], edges[1] v4 = next(v for v in e1 if v in e2) v5 = next(v for v in e1 if v != v4) v6 = next(v for v in e2 if v != v4) v7 = midpoint(e1[0], e1[1]) v8 = midpoint(e2[0], e2[1]) output.extend([v4, v7, v8, v7, v6, v8, v5, v6, v7]) elif len(edges) == 3: e1, e2, e3 = edges[0], edges[1], edges[2] v4 = midpoint(e1[0], e1[1]) v5 = midpoint(e2[0], e2[1]) v6 = midpoint(e3[0], e3[1]) v7 = next(v for v in e1 if v in e2) v8 = next(v for v in e2 if v in e3) v9 = next(v for v in e3 if v in e1) output.extend([v4, v5, v6, v7, v4, v5, v9, v5, v6, v8, v6, v4]) return output def midpoint(a, b): # Source specifies "new vertex in one half" or "middle" return (a + b) / 2.0 def oppositevertex(v1, v2, v3, edge): return next(v for v in (v1, v2, v3) if v not in edge) def length(a, b): return ((a[0]-b[0])2 + (a[1]-b[1])2 + (a[2]-b[2])2)0.5 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Read-Write Limitations: The inability to read-write textures on the GPU requires swapping between two VBOs to serve as input and output buffers during the iterative process. Termination Condition: The loop must correctly detect when no further subdivision is required (i.e., when the vertex count stabilizes) to avoid infinite loops. Watertightness: The subdivision ensures that at least one vertex of the input mesh lies inside each resulting voxel brick, which is a requirement for the resulting LEGOr surface to be watertight (without holes). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fully GPU-accelerated; ensures uniform sampling for voxelization; guarantees watertightness for the LEGOr representation. Limitations: Requires multiple passes; dependent on GPU memory for VBO swapping; subdivision pattern is fixed and may not be optimal for all mesh types compared to adaptive schemes. When to use: When generating LEGOr representations from boundary models where watertightness and uniform voxel sampling are required. When not to use: When general-purpose mesh smoothing or topological refinement is needed rather than resolution-specific subdivision for voxelization. The Legolizer Subdivision technique was introduced as part of the Legolizer system, a real-time system for modeling and rendering LEGO representations of boundary models. It was developed to address the specific needs of converting 3D boundary models into voxel-based structures that mimic LEGO bricks, requiring a subdivision scheme that respects a fixed brick size r. name: Triangle Subdivision Voxelization
head: Barycentric Rasterization to Voxel Grid, Subdivision-based Voxelization
body: A rasterization technique that subdivides triangle edges based on grid resolution and accuracy, sampling points and interpolated normals across the triangle surface to populate a 3D voxel grid. Inputs: Triangle vertices p1, p2, p3, vertex normals n1, n2, n3, grid dimensions vx, vy, vz, and boolean flag octreerender. Outputs: Voxel coordinates (voxel\x, voxel\y, voxel\z) and optionally quantized normal colors (color\x, color\y, color\z). Data Structures: The voxel grid is addressed by integer coordinates derived from continuous positions; normal storage uses 8-bit signed integers mapped to a specific range when octreerender is true. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trianglesubdivisionvoxelization(p1, p2, p3, n1, n2, n3, vx, vy, vz, octreerender): d1 = p2 - p1 d2 = p3 - p1 temp = cross(d1 10.0, d2 10.0) lengthtemp = length(temp) if lengthtemp > 0: normal = temp (1.0 / lengthtemp) else: return # Skip degenerate triangle vm = max(vx, vy, vz) if vx < 512: accuracy = 4 elif vx < 1024: accuracy = 3 else: accuracy = 2 c = max(length(d1), length(d2)) vm accuracy for i in range(c + 1): a = i / c x1 = p1 + d1 a x2 = p1 + d2 a dx = x2 - x1 xn1 = n1 + (n2 - n1) a xn2 = n1 + (n3 - n1) a dnx = xn2 - xn1 d = length(dx) vm accuracy for j in range(d + 1): b = j / d p = x1 + dx b n = xn1 + dnx b voxelx = p.x vx voxely = (1.0 - p.y) vy voxelz = p.z vz if octreerender: colorx = int(n.x 127 + 128) & 0xfc colory = int(n.y 127 + 128) colorz = int(n.z 127 + 128) # Populate voxel grid at (voxelx, voxely, voxelz) with position p and optional color else: # Populate voxel grid at (voxelx, voxely, voxelz) with position p only Parameters: vx, vy, vz are integer grid dimensions; accuracy is a subdivision multiplier (4 if vx < 512, 3 if 512 \le vx < 1024, 2 otherwise); octreerender controls whether quantized normals are passed to the voxel setter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate triangles (len \le 0) must be skipped to prevent division by zero during normalization. Floating-point interpolation and grid mapping require boundary checks to avoid off-by-one voxel indexing errors. The Y-axis mapping uses (1.0 - p.y), inverting the input Y coordinate relative to the grid space. Not given in the sources. name: Voxel Plane Intersection via Vertex Weights
head: Plane Weight Sum Voxelization, Vertex Weight Voxelization
body:
This method rasterizes a triangle into a voxel grid by testing candidate voxels within the triangle's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) against the triangle's plane and its three edge tangent planes. It is distinguished from sibling methods by using a discrete vertex-weight summation algorithm instead of continuous geometric intersection tests or tessellation, providing a brute-force but highly parallelizable approach suitable for CPU implementation. The method operates on a voxel grid and a single triangle. It assumes the voxel grid uses a data structure with shared vertex indexing to optimize computation. Inputs: A triangle defined by three vertices, a voxel grid with shared vertex indexing, and grid resolution/origin. Outputs: A set of voxel indices marked as intersected by the triangle. Voxel Grid: A 3D array or hash map where each voxel is identified by integer coordinates (i, j, k). Shared Vertices: The grid stores vertex positions indexed by (i, j, k), allowing each voxel to reference its 8 corners via shared indices (i+\deltax, j+\deltay, k+\deltaz) where \delta \in \{0, 1\}. 1. Calculate Triangle AABB and Tangent Planes: Compute the minimum and maximum coordinates of the triangle vertices to define the voxel sub-grid (AABB) to process. Calculate the plane equation for the triangle itself (P{tri}) and the three edge tangent planes (P{e0}, P{e1}, P{e2}). The edge tangent planes are defined by an edge vector and the triangle normal. 2. Filter by Triangle Plane: For each voxel in the AABB sub-grid, determine if the voxel intersects the triangle plane P{tri} using the vertex weight sum method. If the voxel does not intersect P{tri}, skip further checks for this voxel. 3. Check Edge Tangent Planes: For voxels intersecting P{tri}, check intersection with each of the three edge tangent planes. A voxel is considered intersected by the triangle only if it intersects P{tri} AND is not entirely on one side of any edge tangent plane. 4. Vertex Weight Summation: To determine if a voxel intersects a specific plane: Retrieve the 8 vertices of the voxel. If using shared vertices, compute the position for each unique vertex index once per plane. For each vertex Vv, calculate the signed distance to the plane: dv = (Vv - P{pos}) \cdot N{plane}, where P{pos} is a point on the plane and N{plane} is the plane normal. Assign a weight wv to each vertex: wv =  egin{cases} 1 & 	ext{if } dv > 0 \quad (	ext{in front}) \ 0 & 	ext{if } dv = 0 \quad (	ext{on plane}) \ -1 & 	ext{if } dv < 0 \quad (	ext{behind}) \end{cases} Sum the weights: W = \sum{v=0}^{7} wv. 5. Determine Intersection: Standard Case: If W 
eq 8 and W 
eq -8, the voxel intersects the plane. If W = 8 or W = -8, the voxel is entirely on one side and does not intersect. Strict Case (Vertex on Plane): If a vertex lies exactly on the plane (dv=0), it is treated as intersecting by default in the standard case. To exclude voxels where the triangle merely touches a vertex, ignore vertices with dv=0 in the sum. Let N{valid} be the count of vertices with dv 
eq 0. If W = N{valid} or W = -N{valid}, the voxel does not intersect. Otherwise, it does. 6. Optimization: Compute vertex positions and dot products only for unique vertices within the sub-grid. Only perform edge tangent plane checks for voxels that already intersect the triangle plane. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dotproduct(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def crossproduct(a, b): return [a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]] def planefromtriangle(v0, v1, v2): normal = crossproduct([v1[i]-v0[i] for i in range(3)], [v2[i]-v0[i] for i in range(3)]) return normal, v0 def edgetangentplane(edgevertex, edgevec, trinormal): normal = crossproduct(edgevec, trinormal) return normal, edgevertex def weightsum(vertices, planenormal, planepoint): total = 0 for v in vertices: dist = dotproduct([v[i]-planepoint[i] for i in range(3)], planenormal) if dist > 0: total += 1 elif dist < 0: total -= 1 return total def voxelplaneintersection(triangle, gridorigin, voxelsize): v0, v1, v2 = triangle # 1. Calculate AABB bounds minx = min(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]) maxx = max(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]) miny = min(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]) maxy = max(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]) minz = min(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2]) maxz = max(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2]) imin = int((minx - gridorigin[0]) / voxelsize) imax = int((maxx - gridorigin[0]) / voxelsize) jmin = int((miny - gridorigin[1]) / voxelsize) jmax = int((maxy - gridorigin[1]) / voxelsize) kmin = int((minz - gridorigin[2]) / voxelsize) kmax = int((maxz - gridorigin[2]) / voxelsize) trinormal, tripoint = planefromtriangle(v0, v1, v2) e0 = [v1[i]-v0[i] for i in range(3)] e1 = [v2[i]-v1[i] for i in range(3)] e2 = [v0[i]-v2[i] for i in range(3)] edgeplanes = [ edgetangentplane(v0, e0, trinormal), edgetangentplane(v1, e1, trinormal), edgetangentplane(v2, e2, trinormal) ] intersected = [] # 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6: Iterate over sub-grid for i in range(imin, imax + 1): for j in range(jmin, jmax + 1): for k in range(kmin, kmax + 1): # Compute 8 vertices using shared indices verts = [] for dx in (0, 1): for dy in (0, 1): for dz in (0, 1): verts.append([gridorigin[0]+(i+dx)voxelsize, gridorigin[1]+(j+dy)voxelsize, gridorigin[2]+(k+dz)voxelsize]) # Check triangle plane if weightsum(verts, trinormal, tripoint) in (8, -8): continue # Check edge tangent planes intersects = True for epn, epp in edgeplanes: if weightsum(verts, epn, epp) in (8, -8): intersects = False break if intersects: intersected.append((i, j, k)) return intersected Precision: Floating-point comparisons for dv = 0 are sensitive. Use a small epsilon if exact equality is not desired. Degenerate Input: If the triangle is degenerate (area zero), the tangent planes may be undefined. The method assumes a valid triangle. Vertex on Plane: As noted, the standard sum treats vertices on the plane as neutral (weight 0). This means a voxel touching only a vertex will have a sum less than 8 in magnitude and be marked as intersecting. Use the strict case logic if this is undesirable. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the triangle's AABB. Each voxel requires a constant number of dot products (up to 4 planes 	imes 8 vertices). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per voxel, assuming shared vertex access. Performance: Described as "lighting fast on modern day CPU's anyway, even with large voxel grids" due to the simplicity of operations and lack of complex branching. It is highly parallelizable as voxel checks are mutually exclusive. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust against precision issues compared to continuous intersection tests, easily parallelizable. Limitations: Brute-force nature means it processes all voxels in the AABB, even those far from the triangle surface. Less efficient than hierarchical methods for sparse grids. This method is a practical, production-oriented approach to 3D triangle rasterization into voxels. It was popularized in community discussions on computer graphics forums as a robust alternative to more complex geometric algorithms. It relies on the geometric property that a convex polyhedron (the voxel) intersects a plane if and only if its vertices are not all strictly on one side of the plane. 3D triangle rasterization to voxels, https://computergraphics.stackexchange.com/questions/13420/3d-triangle-rasterization-to-voxels, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Mesh Voxelization
head: STL Mesh Voxelization, Raycasting-based Voxelization, VoxelGrid from Mesh (Ray Method)
body: Mesh Voxelization converts a continuous polygon mesh (typically STL or OBJ) into a discrete 3D grid of voxels, determining the occupancy (solid/empty) and optionally the signed distance field (SDF) for each cell. It solves the problem of discretizing surface geometry for volume rendering, simulation, or 3D printing preparation. Unlike Mesh to Voxel Generation via AABB-Triangle Intersection, which relies on bounding box overlap, or Template-based Voxelization, which uses precomputed patterns, this method uses ray casting to robustly determine topological inside/outside status, handling complex concavities and open meshes via multi-directional sampling. Inputs: A triangle mesh (vertices and indices), a target resolution (grid dimensions or voxel size), and optional parameters for interior filling, narrow bands, and double-sided mesh handling. Outputs: A voxel grid (binary occupancy or SDF values), often exported as a point cloud of voxel centers, a binary volume (binvox), or a mesh representation of the voxel surface. 1. Mesh: List of triangles, each defined by 3 vertices (V1, V2, V3) in 3D space. 2. Voxel Grid: A 3D array or hash map indexed by (i, j, k) corresponding to spatial coordinates. Layout: Bounding box (bb{min}, bb{max}) derived from mesh vertices. Spacing s = \max(bbx, bby, bbz) / (dim - 2) for a cubic grid of size dim. Origin shifted by -0.5 \cdot s. 3. Ray: Defined by origin O and direction D. 1. Preprocessing: Load mesh vertices and triangles. Validate that index arrays are multiples of 3. Compute the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the mesh: bb{min}, bb{max}. Calculate grid dimensions: Nx = \lceil (bb{max,x} - bb{min,x}) / resolution \rceil, similarly for Ny, Nz. If a narrowband is specified, expand bounds: bb{min} -= band, bb{max} += band. 2. Surface Voxelization (Ray Casting): For each voxel center P within the grid bounds: Cast one or more rays from P to determine if it is inside the mesh. Single Ray (Closed Mesh): Cast a ray along a fixed axis (e.g., +X). Count intersections with mesh triangles. Use Möller–Trumbore intersection test for each triangle. If the mesh is double-sided (e.g., 2D surfaces with thickness), check if (intersections / 2) \% 2 == 1. Otherwise, use parity: is\inside = (intersections \% 2) != 0. Multi-Directional Sampling (Open/Complex Mesh): If the mesh is not watertight or samples > 1, cast N rays in random directions distributed on a sphere. Generate direction from spherical coordinates (\theta, z): \begin{aligned} dir.x &= \sqrt{1-z^2} \cos(\theta) \\ dir.y &= \sqrt{1-z^2} \sin(\theta) \\ dir.z &= \sqrt{1-z^2} \cos(\theta) \quad \text{(Note: Source uses cos for z, likely intended sin for one component, but implemented as cos)} \end{aligned} Where \theta = u1 \cdot 2\pi, z = 2u2 - 1 for uniform randoms u1, u2 \in [0,1]. Vote for inside/outside status based on the majority of ray results. 3. Interior Filling (Optional): If fillinterior is enabled, fill enclosed empty voxels. The implementation calls voxelgrid.fill() to fill enclosed empty voxels, catching exceptions for problematic meshes. Alternatively, perform 3D scan-filling along all three axes (X, Y, Z) and intersect the results to eliminate singular point errors. 4. Signed Distance Field (SDF) Computation (Optional): For each voxel center P, compute the distance to the nearest mesh surface: d = \text{mesh.distance}(P). Assign SDF value: SDF = -d if is\inside, else SDF = d. Apply narrow band filter: Keep voxel only if |SDF| \le band or if surfaceonly is true. 5. Output Generation: Extract centers of occupied voxels. Export to formats such as.obj (vertices),.binvox (binary volume),.csv/.txt (x, y, z, voxelsize), or.ply. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def voxelizemesh(meshvertices, meshtriangles, resolution, samples=1, fillinterior=False, narrowband=None, doublethick=False): # 1. Preprocessing bbmin = [min(v[i] for v in meshvertices) for i in range(3)] bbmax = [max(v[i] for v in meshvertices) for i in range(3)] if narrowband is not None: bbmin = [bbmin[i] - narrowband for i in range(3)] bbmax = [bbmax[i] + narrowband for i in range(3)] size = [bbmax[i] - bbmin[i] for i in range(3)] nx = math.ceil(size[0] / resolution) ny = math.ceil(size[1] / resolution) nz = math.ceil(size[2] / resolution) occupiedvoxels = [] # 2. Iterate over grid for iy in range(ny): for iz in range(nz): y = bbmin[1] + (iy resolution) + (resolution 0.5) z = bbmin[2] + (iz resolution) + (resolution 0.5) for ix in range(nx): x = bbmin[0] + (ix resolution) + (resolution 0.5) point = [x, y, z] isinside = False if samples == 1: rayorigin = [bbmin[0] - 1.0, y, z] raydir = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] maxdist = (bbmax[0] - rayorigin[0]) + 1.0 intersections = countintersections(meshtriangles, rayorigin, raydir, maxdist) # Handle double-thick meshes if doublethick: isinside = (intersections // 2) % 2 == 1 else: isinside = (intersections % 2) != 0 else: votesinside = 0 for in range(samples): theta = random.uniform(0, 1) 2 math.pi zcoord = 2 random.uniform(0, 1) - 1 dirx = math.sqrt(1 - zcoord2) math.cos(theta) diry = math.sqrt(1 - zcoord2) math.sin(theta) dirz = math.sqrt(1 - zcoord2) math.cos(theta) # Source specific raydir = [dirx, diry, dirz] intersections = countintersections(meshtriangles, point, raydir, 1e6) if (intersections % 2) != 0: votesinside += 1 isinside = votesinside > (samples // 2) if isinside: sdfval = 0.0 if narrowband is not None: # Standard point-to-triangle distance calculation dist = meshdistance(meshtriangles, point) sdfval = -dist if isinside else dist if abs(sdfval) > narrowband: continue occupiedvoxels.append((x, y, z, sdfval)) # 3. Interior Filling (if requested) # Standard flood-fill or scan-fill to enclose empty voxels if fillinterior: occupiedvoxels = fillinteriorvoxels(occupiedvoxels, bbmin, bbmax, resolution) return occupiedvoxels def countintersections(triangles, origin, direction, maxdist): count = 0 currentpos = origin[:] maxhits = 100000 for in range(maxhits): hitpoint, hitdist = findnearestintersection(triangles, currentpos, direction) if hitdist is None or hitdist > maxdist: break count += 1 # Advance ray origin to prevent re-hitting the same face currentpos = [currentpos[i] + direction[i] (hitdist + 1e-4) for i in range(3)] return count def findnearestintersection(triangles, origin, direction): closestdist = float('inf') closestpoint = None for tri in triangles: v1, v2, v3 = tri e1 = [v2[i] - v1[i] for i in range(3)] e2 = [v3[i] - v1[i] for i in range(3)] h = [direction[1]e2[2] - direction[2]e2[1], direction[2]e2[0] - direction[0]e2[2], direction[0]e2[1] - direction[1]e2[0]] a = e1[0]h[0] + e1[1]h[1] + e1[2]h[2] if abs(a) < 1e-8: continue inva = 1.0 / a f = [direction[i] inva for i in range(3)] s = [origin[i] - v1[i] for i in range(3)] u = (s[0]h[0] + s[1]h[1] + s[2]h[2]) inva if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: continue q = [s[1]e1[2] - s[2]e1[1], s[2]e1[0] - s[0]e1[2], s[0]e1[1] - s[1]e1[0]] v = (direction[0]q[0] + direction[1]q[1] + direction[2]q[2]) inva if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: continue t = (e2[0]q[0] + e2[1]q[1] + e2[2]q[2]) inva if t > 1e-8: if t < closestdist: closestdist = t closestpoint = [origin[i] + direction[i] t for i in range(3)] if closestpoint is not None: return closestpoint, closestdist return None, None def meshdistance(triangles, point): # Not given in the sources. return 0.0 def fillinteriorvoxels(voxels, bbmin, bbmax, resolution): # Not given in the sources. return voxels resolution: Voxel grid spacing (float). Must be > 10^{-6} to prevent division by zero or excessive memory. Default varies (e.g., 0.5 in voxelizer-rs, 3.0 in GUI). samples: Number of sample rays per voxel (int). Default 1 (single ray). Higher values handle open meshes. fillinterior: Boolean. If true, fills enclosed empty voxels. Default True. narrowband: Float. Distance threshold for SDF. Expands bounds and filters voxels. Default None. surfaceonly: Boolean. If true, retains only voxels intersecting the surface, ignoring interior. Default False. doublethick: Boolean. Handles double-sided geometry by checking (intersections/2)%2 == 1. Default False. Ray Re-hitting: Floating-point precision can cause a ray to intersect the same face multiple times. Mitigated by advancing the ray origin by a small epsilon (10^{-4}) after each hit. Open Meshes: Single-ray casting fails for non-watertight meshes. Mitigated by multi-directional sampling and voting. Double-Thick Meshes: Standard odd-even rule fails. Requires specific parity check (intersections/2)%2 == 1. Precision Ordering: Intersection points may be returned out of order due to precision errors. Sorting is required if exact distance ordering is needed, though simple counting often suffices for parity. Memory Usage: High resolutions generate massive files. A 256x256x256 resolution can produce >4.7 GB OBJ files. Use binary formats (binvox) for high res. Solid Voxelization based on Octree converts a polygon mesh (specifically OBJ format) into a hierarchical octree representation to determine the solid/empty status and distance to surface for each leaf node. It differs from fixed-grid voxelization by using an octree structure for adaptive resolution and from ray-casting-only methods by combining spatial partitioning with ray casting for sign determination. It builds on Mesh Voxelization by providing the specific octree-based implementation for mesh inputs. An extension of surface voxelization for closed objects that fills the inner region of the object using a 3D scan-filling operation. It traverses the volume slice by slice and line by line, maintaining an inside/outside flag for each scan line that toggles when crossing the object boundary. To eliminate errors from singular points, it performs scan-filling along all three axis directions and intersects the results. Memory Usage: High resolutions generate massive files. A 256x256x256 resolution can produce >4.7 GB OBJ files. Use binary formats (binvox) for high res. Performance: GPU acceleration (CUDA) provides massive speedups (400-2750x) over CPU. On an NVIDIA GTX 970, a 512^3 voxelization of a teapot (2464 triangles) took 15.64 seconds. A 1024^3 sphere (960 triangles) took 49.93 seconds. Strengths: Robust handling of complex geometry; produces watertight volumes; supports SDF generation. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high resolutions without acceleration; sensitive to mesh quality (non-manifold edges, double-sided faces); large output file sizes for dense grids. Implementations often leverage GPU parallelism (CUDA) to handle the massive number of ray-triangle intersection tests required for high-resolution grids. The Möller–Trumbore algorithm is the standard efficient method for ray-triangle intersection in this context. autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, https://github.com/autonomousvision/differentiablevolumetricrendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) kctess5/voxelizer, https://github.com/kctess5/voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Guda108/3D-Voxelization-GUI, https://github.com/Guda108/3D-Voxelization-GUI, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) voxelizer-rs, https://github.com/lhemerly/voxelizer-rs, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) (PDF) Real-time Voxelization for Complex Models, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/252533918Real-timeVoxelizationforComplexModels, fetched 2026-11-03 (unofficial)

name: Solid Voxelization based on Octree
head: Polygon-to-Octree Rasterization, RFVoxelOctreeBuilder, voxelization via bounding box overlap
body: Solid Voxelization based on Octree converts a polygon mesh (specifically OBJ format) into a hierarchical octree representation to determine the solid, empty, and distance-to-surface status of leaf nodes. It differs from fixed-grid voxelization by using adaptive spatial subdivision, allowing for efficient representation of sparse scenes or high-resolution details where a uniform grid would be prohibitively large. Unlike Solid Voxelization via Ray Casting, which casts rays per pixel to find intervals, this method recursively partitions space and assigns triangles to nodes, using ray sampling only for ambiguous internal empty leaves. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangular mesh in OBJ format (vertices, faces). Note: Only supports OBJ files with vertices ordered in triangles [v0,v1,v2]. Output: An octree structure where each leaf node contains a distance to the surface (negative for inside, positive for outside) and type (Empty, Internal, Leaf). Data Structures: 1. Octree Node (RFVoxelOctreeNode): mkWorldAabb: Axis-aligned bounding box in world space (RFAABB3d). mkBuildAabb: Axis-aligned bounding box in build/grid space (RFAABB3d with integer min/max). mpkChildren: Array of 8 pointers to child nodes. meNodeType: Enum indicating NTEMPTYLEAF, NTLEAF, or NTINTERNAL. mfDistanceToSurface: Double precision distance to the closest triangle surface. Alternative Layout (): vxnode uses uint32t childpointers[8], uint8t validmasks, uint8t leafmask, uint16t padding. 2. Octree Container (RFVoxelOctree): muiOctreeDim: Dimension of the voxelization grid (next power of two). mfVoxelSize: Size of a single voxel. mkOctreeOrigin: World space origin of the octree. mkDataDimension: Integer dimensions (RFVector3i). mpkRoot: Pointer to the root node. muiNumberOfLeafs, muiNumberOfEmptyLeafs, muiNumberOfInternalNodes: Counters. 3. Voxel Data (vxvoxel): int8t normals[3]: Normal vector multiplied by 128. uint8t colors[4]: Color (typically white 255,255,255,255). Padding fields. Parameters: kOctreeDim (or detail): The requested dimension of the voxelization grid. Default is 64. In, detail is the logarithmic resolution; typical value is 8. fMinCoverage: Threshold for ray coverage to classify an internal empty leaf as solid. Default is 0.9 (header) or 0.8 (implementation). fBorderSize: Default 0.0, not used in provided logic. Algorithm Steps: 1. Parse Mesh: Read the OBJ file. Count vertices, UVs, normals, and faces. Track the bounding box min/max coordinates. Load vertices and faces into memory arrays. Decrement face indices by 1 to convert from 1-based OBJ indices to 0-based array indices. 2. Calculate Grid Dimensions: Find the longest axis of the mesh AABB: kDim = kMax - kMin. Calculate the next power of two for the octree dimension (m\uiOctreeDim). If input is 0, return 2. Otherwise, decrement, then bitwise OR with right shifts of 16, 8, 4, 2, and 1 bits, then increment. Calculate voxel size: m\fVoxelSize = fMaxDim / m\uiOctreeDim. Calculate world size: fOctreeWorldSize = m\uiOctreeDim \times m\fVoxelSize. Set origin: m\kOctreeOrigin = kMeshAabb.GetCenter() - RFVector3d(fOctreeWorldSize / 2.0f). Alternative Normalization (): Calculate offset and scale to normalize model into unit cube [0,1]^3: offset = -min, scale = 1.0 / max(width, height, depth). Grid step size: step = 1.0 / (1 \ll detail). 3. Initialize Root Node: Create root RFVoxelOctreeNode. Set mkWorldAabb from mkOctreeOrigin to mkOctreeOrigin + RFVector3d(fOctreeWorldSize). Set mkBuildAabb.kMin to (0,0,0) and kMax to (m\uiOctreeDim, m\uiOctreeDim, m\uiOctreeDim). Set mkDataDimension to RFVector3i(muiOctreeDim). Alternative (): Initialize with allocated size 4096, size 1, leafmask and validmasks to 0. 4. Recursive Subdivision and Triangle Assignment: For a parent node, create 8 children (octants x,y,z \in \{0,1\}). Child AABB: Build AABB: kMin = parent.kMin + (iAabbDim \cdot x, iAabbDim \cdot y, iAabbDim \cdot z), kMax = kMin + iAabbDim. World AABB: Calculate using mkOctreeOrigin and mfVoxelSize. Triangle Assignment: For each triangle in the parent's list, check if TriangleAabbIntersects(kTriangleVerts, kWorldAabb). If true, add the triangle index to the child's list. Alternative (): Expand triangle bounding box by one step size. Iterate through grid cells within the expanded box. Check overlap using triBoxOverlap. If overlapping, retrieve or create the voxel. 5. Classify Child Node: If child triangle list is empty: Set type to NTEMPTYLEAF. If iAabbDim == 1 (leaf level): Set type to NTLEAF and call UpdateLeafNodeDistanceValue. Otherwise: Set type to NTINTERNAL and recursively call Subdivide. 6. Update Leaf Distance Value (NTLEAF): Initialize fMinDist to max double. For each triangle in the leaf's list: Compute normal: kNormal = VectorCross(kTriangleVerts[2] - kTriangleVerts[0], kTriangleVerts[1] - kTriangleVerts[0]). Find closest point on triangle to leaf center: kClosestPoint = ClosestPointOnTriangle(kTriangleVerts, leaf\center). Compute delta: kDelta = kClosestPoint - leaf\center. Compute sign: fSign = (VectorDot(kDelta, kNormal) < 0.0f) ? -1.0f: 1.0f. Compute distance: fDist = VectorLength(kDelta). If fDist < |fMinDist|, set fMinDist = fDist \times fSign. Store fMinDist in mfDistanceToSurface. 7. Update Internal Empty Leaf Signs (NTEMPTYLEAF): For NTINTERNAL nodes, recurse to children. For NTEMPTYLEAF nodes: Cast rays from node center using precomputed sample directions (200 directions generated via Hammersley2D and UniformSphericalSampling). Count hits (uiCoverage) and misses (uiMisses). Stopping Heuristic: Stop if uiMisses >= size/4 (25% of total samples). Calculate coverage: fCoverage = uiCoverage / size. If fCoverage \ge fMinCoverage, set mfDistanceToSurface = -1.0f (solid/inside). Else, set mfDistanceToSurface = 1.0f (empty/outside). Pseudocode: Unverified code. Parse and Normalize mincoord = (min(v[0] for v in meshvertices), min(v[1] for v in meshvertices), min(v[2] for v in meshvertices)) maxcoord = (max(v[0] for v in meshvertices), max(v[1] for v in meshvertices), max(v[2] for v in meshvertices)) width = maxcoord[0] - mincoord[0] height = maxcoord[1] - mincoord[1] depth = maxcoord[2] - mincoord[2] maxdim = max(width, height, depth) dim = nextpoweroftwo(octreedim) voxelsize = maxdim / dim worldsize = dim voxelsize origin = ((mincoord[0]+maxcoord[0])/2.0, (mincoord[1]+maxcoord[1])/2.0, (mincoord[2]+maxcoord[2])/2.0) origin = (origin[0] - worldsize/2.0, origin[1] - worldsize/2.0, origin[2] - worldsize/2.0) # 2.
