Subdivide subdivide(root, dim, meshfaces, voxelsize) return root def subdivide(node, currentdim, meshfaces, voxelsize): if currentdim == 1: updateleafdistance(node, meshfaces, voxelsize) node.nodetype = NTLEAF return children = [] halfdim = currentdim // 2 for x in range(2): for y in range(2): for z in range(2): child = Node() child.dim = halfdim buildmin = (node.buildaabb.min[0] + halfdimx, node.buildaabb.min[1] + halfdimy, node.buildaabb.min[2] + halfdimz) buildmax = (buildmin[0] + halfdim, buildmin[1] + halfdim, buildmin[2] + halfdim) child.buildaabb = AABB(buildmin, buildmax) child.worldaabb = AABB( (node.worldaabb.min[0] + buildmin[0]voxelsize, node.worldaabb.min[1] + buildmin[1]voxelsize, node.worldaabb.min[2] + buildmin[2]voxelsize), (node.worldaabb.min[0] + buildmax[0]voxelsize, node.worldaabb.min[1] + buildmax[1]voxelsize, node.worldaabb.min[2] + buildmax[2]voxelsize)) for triidx in node.triangles: triverts = [meshfaces[triidx][0], meshfaces[triidx][1], meshfaces[triidx][2]] if triangleaabbintersects(triverts, child.worldaabb): child.triangles.append(triidx) children.append(child) for child in children: if not child.triangles: child.nodetype = NTEMPTYLEAF updateemptyleafsign(child, meshfaces, voxelsize) else: child.nodetype = NTINTERNAL subdivide(child, child.dim, meshfaces, voxelsize) node.children.append(child) def updateleafdistance(node, meshfaces, voxelsize): leafcenter = ((node.buildaabb.min[0]+node.buildaabb.max[0])/2.0, (node.buildaabb.min[1]+node.buildaabb.max[1])/2.0, (node.buildaabb.min[2]+node.buildaabb.max[2])/2.0) leafcenterworld = (node.worldaabb.min[0] + leafcenter[0]voxelsize, node.worldaabb.min[1] + leafcenter[1]voxelsize, node.worldaabb.min[2] + leafcenter[2]voxelsize) mindist = float('inf') for triidx in node.triangles: v0, v1, v2 = meshfaces[triidx] normal = ((v2[1]-v0[1])(v1[2]-v0[2]) - (v2[2]-v0[2])(v1[1]-v0[1]), (v2[2]-v0[2])(v1[0]-v0[0]) - (v2[0]-v0[0])(v1[2]-v0[2]), (v2[0]-v0[0])(v1[1]-v0[1]) - (v2[1]-v0[1])(v1[0]-v0[0])) closest = closestpointontriangle(leafcenterworld, v0, v1, v2) delta = (closest[0]-leafcenterworld[0], closest[1]-leafcenterworld[1], closest[2]-leafcenterworld[2]) sign = -1.0 if (delta[0]normal[0] + delta[1]normal[1] + delta[2]normal[2]) < 0.0 else 1.0 dist = math.sqrt(delta[0]2 + delta[1]2 + delta[2]2) if dist < abs(mindist): mindist = dist sign node.distancetosurface = mindist def updateemptyleafsign(node, meshfaces, voxelsize): samples = [] for i in range(200): u, v = hammersley2d(i, 200) samples.append(uniformsphericalsampling(u, v)) center = ((node.buildaabb.min[0]+node.buildaabb.max[0])/2.0, (node.buildaabb.min[1]+node.buildaabb.max[1])/2.0, (node.buildaabb.min[2]+node.buildaabb.max[2])/2.0) centerworld = (node.worldaabb.min[0] + center[0]voxelsize, node.worldaabb.min[1] + center[1]voxelsize, node.worldaabb.min[2] + center[2]voxelsize) coverage = 0 misses = 0 for direction in samples: if rayhitsmesh(centerworld, direction, meshfaces): coverage += 1 else: misses += 1 if misses >= 200 / 4: break fcoverage = coverage / 200 if fcoverage >= 0.8: node.distancetosurface = -1.0 else: node.distancetosurface = 1.0 Uses Separating Axis Theorem for pruning empty bounding volumes instead of simple AABB intersection, offering robustness and performance improvements. Handles non-watertight meshes using cube map rendering and visibility propagation, replacing the ray-casting sign test with a GPU-accelerated heuristic. Computes solid intervals per pixel via ray-mesh intersection, differing by explicitly finding intervals rather than relying on spatial partitioning pruning. Post-processing step that corrects inside/outside status by propagating boundary crossings along the +x direction, ensuring consistency without per-voxel ray queries. Uses 2D quadtree structures on projected planes to store intersection distances, reducing memory usage for huge models or high resolutions. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of triangles and octree depth. Subdivision is recursive, and triangle assignment requires AABB intersection tests for each triangle at each level. Leaf distance calculation requires closest-point tests for all triangles in the leaf. Memory Complexity: Adaptive. Uses an octree structure, which is more memory-efficient than a fixed grid for sparse scenes but requires overhead for node pointers and metadata. Performance: On an Apple M1 Pro, building the octree for Armadillo.obj at dimension 64 took ~484ms before optimization and ~77ms after output optimization (total build time not explicitly separated after optimization, but output was 77ms). Strengths: Adaptive resolution, handles large bounding boxes efficiently, supports OBJ format directly. Limitations: Only supports OBJ files with triangle-ordered vertices. Empty leaf classification uses a heuristic that may be inaccurate for nodes near the surface (early stop if misses > 25%). Bounding box expansion by 'step' is required to avoid precision issues at boundaries. The method originates from work by Peter Trier Mikkelsen, with tutorials available via Alexandra. It builds on Mesh Voxelization by providing a specific octree-based implementation for solid voxelization. rools/voxl, https://github.com/rools/voxl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) itsyouyi/Voxelizer, https://github.com/itsyouyi/Voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Octree-based 3D Voxelization with SAT Pruning
head: Divide-and-Conquer Spatial Partitioning, Octree Divide-and-Conquer Spatial Partitioning, Recursive Octree Voxelizer
body: This method converts arbitrary 3D triangular surface meshes into uniform voxel representations by recursively partitioning space into an octree and using the Separating Axis Theorem (SAT) to prune empty bounding volumes. It builds on Solid Voxelization based on Octree by replacing ray casting with exact geometric intersection tests for robustness and performance. Inputs: A triangular mesh (vertices and faces, typically from a Wavefront.obj file) and an integer maxDepth \ge 1. Outputs: A list of voxel cubes (AABBs) or a mesh representation of the voxelized surface. Data Structures: Vec3: A 3D vector with components x, y, z. AABB: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box defined by min (Vec3) and max (Vec3). Triangle: Defined by three Vec3 vertices v0, v1, v2. OctreeNode: bounds: AABB children: Array of 8 pointers to OctreeNode (or null if pruned/leaf). isLeaf: Boolean. hasGeometry: Boolean. depth: Integer. Destructor recursively deletes children. OctreeStats: nodesPerDepth: Map<int, int> prunedPerDepth: Map<int, int> maxDepth: Integer totalVoxels: Integer Algorithm Steps: 1. Root Bounding Box Calculation: Compute the bounding box of the input mesh: \mathbf{p}{\min} = (\min xi, \min yi, \min zi), \quad \mathbf{p}{\max} = (\max xi, \max yi, \max zi) where i iterates over all mesh vertices. Calculate the side length of the largest dimension: s{\text{max}} = \max(\mathbf{p}{\max}.x - \mathbf{p}{\min}.x, \mathbf{p}{\max}.y - \mathbf{p}{\min}.y, \mathbf{p}{\max}.z - \mathbf{p}{\min}.z) Center the box at the mesh centroid \mathbf{c} = \frac{\mathbf{p}{\min} + \mathbf{p}{\max}}{2}. Expand to a cube with a 1% margin to ensure isotropic voxels: s{\text{root}} = s{\text{max}} \times 1.01 The root AABB is defined by: \text{root.min} = \mathbf{c} - \frac{s{\text{root}}}{2}, \quad \text{root.max} = \mathbf{c} + \frac{s{\text{root}}}{2} The edge length of each resulting voxel is calculated as s{\text{voxel}} = s{\text{root}} / 2^{d{\max}}. 2. Recursive Octree Construction (buildOctree): Function signature: buildOctree(node, triangles, maxDepth, currentDepth, stats). Pruning Check: Filter triangles to find those intersecting node.bounds. Use the 13-axis SAT test (see below). Let this list be intersecting. If intersecting is empty: Mark node as pruned. Increment stats.prunedPerDepth[currentDepth]. Return. If currentDepth == maxDepth: Mark node.isLeaf = true. Mark node.hasGeometry = true. Increment stats.totalVoxels. Return. Subdivision: Calculate child bounds for i \in [0, 7]. Let c = \text{node.bounds.center()}. For each axis a \in \{x, y, z\}: Bit b corresponds to axis index (0 for x, 1 for y, 2 for z). If (i \gg b) \& 1: \text{child.min}.a = c.a. Else: \text{child.min}.a = \text{node.bounds.min}.a. \text{child.max}.a is the inverse: if bit is set, use node.bounds.max.a, otherwise use c.a. For each child i: Test if any triangle in intersecting intersects child.bounds using SAT. If no intersection: Increment stats.nodesPerDepth[currentDepth + 1] and stats.prunedPerDepth[currentDepth + 1]. Continue to next child. If intersection exists: Create newNode. Set newNode.bounds, newNode.depth = currentDepth + 1. node.children[i] = newNode. Recursively call buildOctree(newNode, intersecting, maxDepth, currentDepth + 1, stats). 3. Voxel Collection: Traverse the octree. If a node is a leaf and hasGeometry is true, add its bounds to the output list. Otherwise, recursively collect from all 8 children. 4. Mesh Generation: For each collected AABB (min, max): Generate 8 vertices at corners (x0, y0, z0) to (x1, y1, z1). Generate 12 triangular faces (2 per side) using specific vertex indices to ensure outward-facing normals. SAT Collision Test: To determine if a triangle intersects an AABB, test overlap along 13 separating axes: 1. 3 Box Face Normals: \mathbf{u}0 = (1, 0, 0), \mathbf{u}1 = (0, 1, 0), \mathbf{u}2 = (0, 0, 1). 2. 1 Triangle Face Normal: \mathbf{n} = (\mathbf{v}1 - \mathbf{v}0) \times (\mathbf{v}2 - \mathbf{v}0). 3. 9 Edge Cross Products: Cross products of each triangle edge with each box face normal. Triangle edges: \mathbf{e}0 = \mathbf{v}1 - \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{e}1 = \mathbf{v}2 - \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{e}2 = \mathbf{v}0 - \mathbf{v}2. Axes: \mathbf{e}k \times \mathbf{u}j for k \in \{0,1,2\}, j \in \{0,1,2\}. For each axis \mathbf{L}, project both the triangle vertices and the AABB corners onto \mathbf{L}. If the intervals do not overlap, the triangle and box do not intersect. Pseudocode: Unverified code. return self.x other.x + self.y other.y + self.z other.z def cross(self, other): return Vec3( self.y other.z - self.z other.y, self.z other.x - self.x other.z, self.x other.y - self.y other.x) class Triangle: def init(self, v0, v1, v2): self.v0 = v0 self.v1 = v1 self.v2 = v2 class OctreeNode: def init(self, bounds, depth): self.bounds = bounds self.depth = depth self.children = [None] 8 self.isLeaf = False self.hasGeometry = False def projectinterval(vertices, axis): minp = float('inf') maxp = float('-inf') for v in vertices: p = v.dot(axis) if p < minp: minp = p if p > maxp: maxp = p return minp, maxp def sattest(triangle, aabb): boxaxes = [Vec3(1,0,0), Vec3(0,1,0), Vec3(0,0,1)] e0 = triangle.v1 - triangle.v0 e1 = triangle.v2 - triangle.v0 trinormal = e0.cross(e1) triedges = [e0, triangle.v2 - triangle.v1, triangle.v0 - triangle.v2] axes = boxaxes + [trinormal] + [e.cross(b) for e in triedges for b in boxaxes] normalizedaxes = [] for ax in axes: l = math.sqrt(ax.x2 + ax.y2 + ax.z2) if l > 1e-9: normalizedaxes.append(Vec3(ax.x/l, ax.y/l, ax.z/l)) else: normalizedaxes.append(ax) triverts = [triangle.v0, triangle.v1, triangle.v2] corners = [ aabb.min, aabb.max.z), Vec3(aabb.min.x, aabb.max.y, aabb.max.z), aabb.max ] for axis in normalizedaxes: tmin, tmax = projectinterval(triverts, axis) amin, amax = projectinterval(corners, axis) if tmax < amin or amax < tmin: return False return True def buildoctree(node, triangles, maxdepth, currentdepth, stats): intersecting = [t for t in triangles if sattest(t, node.bounds)] if not intersecting: stats['prunedPerDepth'][currentdepth] = stats['prunedPerDepth'].get(currentdepth, 0) + 1 return if currentdepth == maxdepth: node.isLeaf = True node.hasGeometry = True stats['totalVoxels'] = stats.get('totalVoxels', 0) + 1 return center = node.bounds.center() for i in range(8): childmin = Vec3( center.x if (i & 1) else node.bounds.min.x, center.y if (i & 2) else node.bounds.min.y, center.z if (i & 4) else node.bounds.min.z) childmax = Vec3( center.x if not (i & 1) else node.bounds.max.x, center.y if not (i & 2) else node.bounds.max.y, center.z if not (i & 4) else node.bounds.max.z) childbounds = AABB(childmin, childmax) hasgeom = False for t in intersecting: if sattest(t, childbounds): hasgeom = True break if hasgeom: childnode = OctreeNode(childbounds, currentdepth + 1) node.children[i] = childnode buildoctree(childnode, intersecting, maxdepth, currentdepth + 1, stats) else: stats['nodesPerDepth'][currentdepth + 1] = stats['nodesPerDepth'].get(currentdepth + 1, 0) + 1 stats['prunedPerDepth'][currentdepth + 1] = stats['prunedPerDepth'].get(currentdepth + 1, 0) + 1 def collectvoxels(node, voxels): if node.isLeaf and node.hasGeometry: voxels.append(node.bounds) return for child in node.children: if child is not None: collectvoxels(child, voxels) def generatevoxelmesh(voxels): meshvertices = [] meshfaces = [] for v in voxels: x0, y0, z0 = v.min.x, v.min.y, v.min.z x1, y1, z1 = v.max.x, v.max.y, v.max.z verts = [ Vec3(x0, y0, z0), Vec3(x1, y0, z0), Vec3(x1, y1, z0), Vec3(x0, y1, z0), Vec3(x0, y0, z1), Vec3(x1, y0, z1), Vec3(x1, y1, z1), Vec3(x0, y1, z1) ] baseidx = len(meshvertices) meshvertices.extend(verts) faces = [ [0, 1, 2], [0, 2, 3], [4, 6, 5], [4, 7, 6], [0, 4, 7], [0, 7, 3], [1, 5, 6], [1, 6, 2], [3, 7, 6], [3, 6, 2], [0, 5, 4], [0, 1, 5] ] for f in faces: meshfaces.append([baseidx + f[0], baseidx + f[1], baseidx + f[2]]) return meshvertices, meshfaces def voxelize(meshvertices, meshfaces, maxdepth): pmin = Vec3(float('inf'), float('inf'), float('inf')) pmax = Vec3(float('-inf'), float('-inf'), float('-inf')) for v in meshvertices: if v.x < pmin.x: pmin.x = v.x if v.y < pmin.y: pmin.y = v.y if v.z < pmin.z: pmin.z = v.z if v.x > pmax.x: pmax.x = v.x if v.y > pmax.y: pmax.y = v.y if v.z > pmax.z: pmax.z = v.z smax = max(pmax.x - pmin.x, pmax.y - pmin.y, pmax.z - pmin.z) sroot = smax 1.01 center = Vec3((pmin.x + pmax.x)/2, (pmin.y + pmax.y)/2, (pmin.z + pmax.z)/2) rootmin = Vec3(center.x - sroot/2, center.y - sroot/2, center.z - sroot/2) rootmax = Vec3(center.x + sroot/2, center.y meshvertices[meshfaces[i+1]] v2 = meshvertices[meshfaces[i+2]] triangles.append(Triangle(v0, v1, v2)) stats = {'nodesPerDepth': {}, 'prunedPerDepth': {}, 'totalVoxels': 0} buildoctree(rootnode, name: Robust Inside and Outside Solid Voxelization
head: Complete Polygonal Scene Voxelization
body: Robust Inside and Outside Solid Voxelization is a method for determining the solid/empty status of octree cells in a voxelized mesh, specifically designed to handle non-watertight meshes with holes and intersecting geometry. Unlike ray casting methods which require watertight meshes, this technique uses a heuristic model based on cube map rendering and visibility propagation to classify cells. It sets itself apart by allowing "seed" cells to propagate their status to visible neighbors, overcoming the topological restrictions of traditional ray casting. It builds on Solid Voxelization based on Octree by replacing the ray-casting sign test with a GPU-accelerated cube map heuristic. The algorithm operates in three main stages: Octree Creation, Seed Cell Classification, and Status Propagation. Inputs: A triangular mesh. Maximum octree depth (typically 5; 7 or 8 for thin walls). MININSIDEFACES: Integer constant, value 4. MININSIDEPERCENTAGE: Float constant, value 0.03 (3%). PROPAGATIONTHRESHOLD: Integer value, example 16. Outputs: An octree where each leaf node is classified as Inside, Outside, or Intersecting. Octree Cell: Contains bounding box, status (Unknown, Inside, Outside, Intersecting), and propagation counters. Propagation Counters: For each Unknown cell, maintain two integer counters: insidecount and outsidecount, initialized to 0. 1. Create Octree: Subdivide the root cell containing the mesh until no triangle intersection occurs or the maximum depth is reached. During subdivision, test triangle intersection against mesh bounds. Immediately mark cells outside mesh bounds as Outside without treating them as seed cells. Mark cells intersecting triangles as Intersecting. 2. Find Seed Cell: Select an Unknown cell to test as a potential seed. Render a cube map centered in the cell with the near plane at the cell edge. Use a single-pass pixel shader to color front faces blue and back faces red: glsl void main() { glFragColor = glFrontFacing ? vec4(0,0,1,1): vec4(1,0,0,1); } For each of the 6 cube map sides, read back the GPU buffer and calculate the percentage of red (backface) pixels relative to total colored pixels. Count sides where backfacePercentage > MININSIDEPERCENTAGE. If cubemapsidesseeinginside >= MININSIDEFACES, classify the cell as Inside. If cubemapsidesseeinginside == 0, classify the cell as Outside. If neither, the cell cannot be solved exactly and remains Unknown. 3. Propagate Seed Cell: For the classified seed cell, test every Unknown cell against the depth map and frustum of each cube map surface. Project the 8 corners of the octree cell into the camera space of each cube face. If any corner is closer than the depth value at that pixel, the cell is visible from the seed. If visible, increment the corresponding counter (insidecount if seed is Inside, outsidecount if seed is Outside) for the target cell. If either counter reaches PROPAGATIONTHRESHOLD, commit the status to the target cell and stop processing it. Note: Only seed cells propagate status. Cells that receive propagated status do not become new seed cells. 4. Repeat Loop: Repeat steps 2 and 3 until all cells are classified or no further propagation is possible. Handle undetermined statuses to prevent infinite loops. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. Standard octree subdivision: recursively split AABB until triangle intersection count is 0 or depth == maxdepth octree = buildoctree(mesh, maxdepth) for cell in octree.leaves: # Standard AABB vs mesh bounding box test if not intersectsmeshbounds(cell): cell.status = CellStatus.OUTSIDE continue # Standard AABB vs triangle intersection test (e.g., Möller-Trumbore) if intersectstriangles(cell): cell.status = CellStatus.INTERSECTING continue cell.status = CellStatus.UNKNOWN cell.insidecount = 0 cell.outsidecount = 0 unknowncells = [c for c in octree.leaves if c.status == CellStatus.UNKNOWN] seedcells = [] while unknowncells: seed = findseedcell(unknowncells) if seed is None: break seedcells.append(seed) unknowncells.remove(seed) propagatestatus(seed, unknowncells) return octree def findseedcell(unknowncells): for cell in unknowncells: cubemapsidesseeinginside = 0 for i in range(6): # Render scene from cell center, 6 faces, near plane at cell edge rendercubemapside(i, cell) # Read back GPU buffer, count red pixels / total colored pixels backfacepercentage = calculatebackfacepercentage(i) if backfacepercentage > MININSIDEPERCENTAGE: cubemapsidesseeinginside += 1 if cubemapsidesseeinginside >= MININSIDEFACES: cell.status = CellStatus.INSIDE return cell elif cubemapsidesseeinginside == 0: cell.status = CellStatus.OUTSIDE return cell return None def propagatestatus(seed, unknowncells): for cell in unknowncells: if isvisiblefromseed(seed, cell): if seed.status == CellStatus.INSIDE: cell.insidecount += 1 if cell.insidecount >= PROPAGATIONTHRESHOLD: cell.status = CellStatus.INSIDE unknowncells.remove(cell) elif seed.status == CellStatus.OUTSIDE: cell.outsidecount += 1 if cell.outsidecount >= PROPAGATIONTHRESHOLD: cell.status = CellStatus.OUTSIDE unknowncells.remove(cell) def isvisiblefromseed(seed, cell): # Project 8 corners of cell into seed's cube map camera space for each face for faceidx in range(6): for corner in cell.boundingbox.corners: screenpos = projecttoscreen(corner, seed.cubemapviewmatrix[faceidx], seed.cubemapprojmatrix[faceidx]) depthval = seed.cubemapdepthbuffer[faceidx][screenpos.x][screenpos.y] if corner.z < depthval: return True return False def buildoctree(mesh, maxdepth): root = OctreeCell() root.boundingbox = mesh.boundingbox queue = [root] while queue: node = queue.pop(0) if node.depth < maxdepth and intersectstriangles(node): node.children = splitaabb(node.boundingbox) queue.extend(node.children) return root def intersectsmeshbounds(cell): return cell.boundingbox.intersects(mesh.boundingbox) def intersectstriangles(cell): return cell.boundingbox.intersectsanytriangle(mesh.triangles) def rendercubemapside(faceidx, cell): # Standard GPU render: set camera at cell center, look along face normal, near plane at cell edge pass # Standard graphics pipeline call def calculatebackfacepercentage(faceidx): # Standard GPU readback: count pixels where color == (1,0,0) / total pixels pass # Standard GPU readback call def projecttoscreen(corner, viewmatrix, projmatrix): # Standard math: clip space = proj view corner; perspective divide; viewport transform pass # Standard math operation Propagation Limitation: Only seed cells propagate status. Cells that receive propagated status do not become new seed cells and do not propagate further. Holes and Intersecting Geometry: The method handles these cases where ray casting fails. Mesh Bounds: Cells outside mesh bounds are immediately marked Outside but do not act as seeds. Infinite Loops: Ensure code handles undetermined statuses to prevent infinite loops. Strengths: Handles non-watertight meshes with holes and intersecting geometry. Limitations: Only seed cells propagate status, which may limit propagation efficiency. name: Solid Voxelization via Ray Casting
body: A method to convert a triangle mesh into a solid voxel representation (octree) by casting rays through the mesh to determine occupied voxel intervals along the Z-axis. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly computing solid intervals per pixel via ray-mesh intersection rather than relying solely on spatial partitioning pruning or robust topological checks for inside/outside status. Inputs and outputs: Input: Triangle mesh, voxel resolution res, camera rotation matrix M. Output: A set of solid voxel segments (intervals along Z) for each (x, y) coordinate in the voxel grid. Data structures: segmentcache: A local list of segments {x, y, zmin, zmax} for the current block. segments: A global vector of segments for the final output. currblock: An atomic counter for work distribution. Parameters: res: Voxel resolution (e.g., 2^{\text{voxelization\level}}). blocksize: Maximum block dimension for parallel processing, typically 16 pixels. scale: Grid scaling factor, calculated as 2.0 / \text{res}. eps: Epsilon for ray marching to prevent self-intersection, calculated as \max(\text{scale} / 64.0, 1\text{e-}5). Steps: 1. Initialize a thread pool with numworkers = std::thread::hardwareconcurrency() and a shared atomic counter currblock = 0. 2. Calculate grid parameters: scale = 2.0f / res, eps = max(scale / 64.0f, 1e-5f), blocksize = min(res, 16u), blocksperedge = (res + blocksize - 1u) / blocksize. 3. For each worker thread, loop over blocks using currblock++. For each block: Determine xoffset and yoffset based on the block index. Iterate y from yoffset to yoffset + blocksize and x from xoffset to xoffset + blocksize. Construct ray origin rayhit.ray.o by transforming (dx, dy, 2.0f, 1.0f) with matrix M, where dx = (x + 0.5f) \times \text{scale} - 1.0f and dy = (y + 0.5f) \times \text{scale} - 1.0f. Set ray direction raydir = glm::mat3{M} glm::vec3{0.0f, 0.0f, -1.0f}. Enter an infinite loop to find intersections: Set rayhit.ray.tmin = rayhit.ray.tmax + eps and rayhit.ray.tmax = infinity. Call mesh.traceclosest(&rayhit). If rayhit.hit.geomid == EmbreeHit::invalid (ray exits scene): Check if counter > 0. If so, create a segment from tstart to current exit, clamp Z to [0, \text{res}-1], add to cache, and break loop. If c < 0.0f (front face): Increment counter and record tstart = rayhit.ray.tmax. If c > 0.0f (back face): Decrement counter. If counter == 0, a segment is closed: Calculate z\range = (1.5f - \text{glm::vec2}\{\text{ray\hit.ray.t\max}, t\start\} \times 0.5f) \times \text{res\f}. Clamp z to [0, \text{res}-1]. If z.x \le z.y, add segment \{x, y, z.x, z.y\} to cache. 4. After processing all pixels in a block, lock mutex and copy segmentcache to global segments vector. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import threading import os segments = [] segmentsmutex = threading.Lock() currblock = 0 numworkers = os.cpucount() or 1 # Standard replacement for hardwareconcurrency() def processblock(blockidx, res, scale, eps, blocksize, M, mesh): localsegments = [] blocksperedge = (res + blocksize - 1) // blocksize xblock = blockidx % blocksperedge yblock = blockidx // blocksperedge xoffset = xblock blocksize yoffset = yblock blocksize for y in range(yoffset, min(yoffset + blocksize, res)): for x in range(xoffset, min(xoffset + blocksize, res)): dx = (x + 0.5) scale - 1.0 dy = (y + 0.5) scale - 1.0 point = [dx, dy, 2.0, 1.0] # Transform point with 4x4 matrix M rayo = [sum(M[i][j] point[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] # Extract 3x3 rotation part for direction rotpart = [M[i][j] for i in range(3) for j in range(3)] raydir = [ rotpart[0]0 + rotpart[1]0 + rotpart[2](-1), rotpart[3]0 + rotpart[4]0 + rotpart[5](-1), rotpart[6]0 + rotpart[7]0 + rotpart[8](-1) ] tmax = float('inf') tstart = float('inf') # Initialized to infinity; set on front face hit counter = 0 while True: tmin = tmax + eps tmax = float('inf') hit = mesh.traceclosest(rayo, raydir, tmin, tmax) if hit.geomid == "invalid": if counter > 0: zexit = (1.5 - tmax 0.5) res zentry = (1.5 - tstart 0.5) res zmin = max(0, min(res - 1, zentry)) zmax = max(0, min(res - 1, zexit)) if zmin <= zmax: localsegments.append((x, y, zmin, zmax)) break if hit.c < 0.0: # Front face counter += 1 tstart = hit.t # Record entry distance elif hit.c > 0.0: # Back face counter -= 1 if counter == 0: zexit = (1.5 - hit.t 0.5) res zentry = (1.5 - tstart 0.5) res zmin = max(0, min(res - 1, zentry)) zmax = max(0, min(res - 1, zexit)) if zmin <= zmax: localsegments.append((x, y, zmin, zmax)) with segmentsmutex: segments.extend(localsegments) def workerloop(res, scale, eps, blocksize, M, mesh): global currblock blocksperedge = (res + blocksize - 1) // blocksize totalblocks = blocksperedge blocksperedge while True: blockidx = currblock currblock += 1 if blockidx >= totalblocks: break processblock(blockidx, res, scale, eps, blocksize, M, mesh) def voxelize(mesh, res, camerarotationtoworld): global segments, currblock segments = [] currblock = 0 scale = 2.0 / res eps = max(scale / 64.0, 1e-5) blocksize = min(res, 16) M = camerarotationtoworld threads = [threading.Thread(target=workerloop, args=(res, scale, eps, blocksize, M, mesh)) for in range(numworkers)] for t in threads: t.start() for t in threads: t.join() Edge cases and pitfalls: Precision issues near surfaces can cause gaps or overlaps; eps is used to mitigate self-intersection. Boundary conditions for Z-clamping must be handled to ensure voxels stay within [0, \text{res}-1]. Degenerate input (empty mesh) should result in no segments. Uses spatial partitioning and separating axis theorem for pruning; faster for sparse scenes but less precise for complex topology. Focuses on topological robustness for inside/outside determination; slower but handles complex meshes better. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: O(N) for storing segments. Measured performance: Depends on hardware concurrency and mesh complexity. Strengths: Parallelizable, simple to implement. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originated by Mike-Leo-Smith in an unofficial GitHub repository. Used in volume rendering pipelines for producing solid voxel data from mesh inputs. name: Hierarchical Inside/Outside Propagation
head: Solid Voxelization Propagation, X-Direction Bit Flip Propagation
body: After level-0 voxelization, the method hierarchically propagates bit flips in the +x direction to achieve a solid voxelization. It resolves inconsistencies between adjacent nodes by aggregating boundary crossings up the octree hierarchy and then distributing the final inside/outside status downward. Input: An octree where level-0 nodes have been voxelized (bits set for occupied voxels). Output: The inside flag of every node is correctly set. A level-i node without children is inside the solid object if its inside flag is set, and outside otherwise. Node: level: Integer, 0 \le level \le L{max}. inside: Boolean, initialized to zero/false. flip: Boolean, used only for levels >0, initialized to zero/false. children: Array of 8 child nodes (if not leaf). xneighbor: Pointer to the immediate +x neighbor node at the same level (if it exists). -xneighbor: Pointer to the immediate -x neighbor node at the same level (if it exists). sgvoxels: Bitmask or array of 64 bits for level-0 nodes. index: Integer identifier for parity checks. 1. Initialize inside and flip flags to zero/false for all nodes. 2. Loop over all (even-indexed) level-0 nodes in parallel, identifying those with no level-0 -x neighbor (head nodes). 3. Starting at head nodes, navigate along the +x-neighbor pointers, propagating bit flips to the next node. If the last bit in a level-0 node's SG voxel column is set, all SG voxels in the same column belonging to nodes in +x direction must be flipped. 4. At the end of node strings where no more level-0 nodes abut, all four level-0 nodes with the same level-1 parent have all their SG voxels with local x index 3 in agreement. 5. Propagate flip information to level-1 parent nodes: keep a flip propagation flag and an inside flag for each level-1 node, initializing both to zero. If a level-1 node's child is at the end of an x-linked node string and its SG voxels with local x index 3 are set, set the flip flag. 6. Propagate flip information along x-linked level-1 node strings, starting at level-1 head nodes. If a node's flip flag is set, flip both the flip and the inside flag of its +x neighbor. 7. Propagation to the next coarser level and then within this level is performed analogously for the remaining levels. 8. Propagate the inside flag information from the top level down to the level-0 nodes. For each node of level i that has its inside flag set and has children, flip these child nodes' inside flags or their SG voxels, respectively. 9. A level-i node without children is inside the solid object if its inside flag is set, and outside otherwise. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicalinsideoutsidepropagation(nodes): """ Propagates inside/outside status hierarchically according to. nodes: list of node objects with attributes: level, inside, flip, xneighbor, -xneighbor, children, sgvoxels, index. """ # Step 1: Initialize flags for node in nodes: node.inside = False if node.level > 0: node.flip = False # Step 2 & 3: Level-0 Flip Propagation for node in nodes: if node.level == 0 and node.index % 2 == 0 and node.xneighbor is None: current = node while current is not None: # Check if last bit in SG voxel column (local x index 3) is set # Assumes x is the fastest varying dimension; bit 3 corresponds to x=3 if (current.sgvoxels >> 3) & 1: if current.xneighbor is not None: current.xneighbor.inside = not current.xneighbor.inside current = current.xneighbor # Step 4 & 5: Aggregation to Level-1 for node in nodes: if node.level == 1: node.flip = False for child in node.children: if child.level == 0 and child.xneighbor is None and (child.sgvoxels >> 3) & 1: node.flip = True break # Step 6: Level-1 Flip Propagation for node in nodes: if node.level == 1 and node.xneighbor is None: current = node while current is not None: if current.flip: if current.xneighbor is not None: current.xneighbor.flip = not current.xneighbor.flip current.xneighbor.inside = not current.xneighbor.inside current = current.xneighbor # Step 7: Repeat for higher levels maxlevel = max(n.level for n in nodes) for level in range(1, maxlevel): # Aggregate flip from level+1 to level for node in nodes: if node.level == level: node.flip = False for child in node.children: if child.level == level + 1 and child.xneighbor is None and child.flip: node.flip = True break # Propagate flip within level for node in nodes: if node.level == level and node.xneighbor is None: current = node while current is not None: if current.flip: if current.xneighbor is not None: current.xneighbor.flip = not current.xneighbor.flip current.xneighbor.inside = not current.xneighbor.inside current = current.xneighbor # Step 8: Downward Inside Propagation root = next(n for n in nodes if n.level == maxlevel) stack = [root] while stack: node = stack.pop() if node.children is not None: for child in node.children: if node.inside: if child.level == 0: # Flip SG voxels directly for leaves child.sgvoxels ^= 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF else: # Flip inside flag for internal nodes child.inside = not child.inside stack.append(child) Bit Packing: The definition of "last bit in SG voxel column" depends on the bit packing order. The sources do not specify the exact bit layout, only that it corresponds to local x index 3. Implementers must align the bit mask with their voxelization's packing scheme. Boundary Conditions: Nodes at the boundary of the voxelization domain may not have +x or -x neighbors. The algorithm handles this by checking for None pointers before traversal or flag updates. Parallelism: The identification of head nodes and the traversal of x-linked strings can be parallelized across level-0 nodes. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of octree nodes, O(N), as each node is visited a constant number of times during upward aggregation and downward propagation. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the octree structure and the inside/flip flags. Strengths: Highly parallelizable on GPUs; avoids per-voxel ray queries for consistency by relying on local neighbor relationships and hierarchical aggregation. Limitations: Requires x-linked neighbor pointers, which increase memory overhead; correctness depends on the initial level-0 voxelization and accurate head-node identification. The method was introduced in the 2010 paper "Fast Parallel Surface and Solid Voxelization on GPUs" by Michael Schwarz et al.. It serves as a post-processing consistency step within a broader GPU-based voxelization framework that initially determines solid/empty status via ray casting and refines it through hierarchical bit-flip propagation. name: Solid Voxelization based on Quadtree
head: Safe Voxelization with Quad Trees, safe rasterizer
body: Solid Voxelization based on Quadtree is a memory-efficient voxelization technique that determines the solid, shell, and background status of voxels by storing plane-wise intersection distances rather than allocating a full 3D buffer during computation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Octree-based Solid Voxelization by using 2D quadtree spatial acceleration structures on projected planes to handle huge models or high target resolutions where other voxelizers fail due to memory constraints. Inputs and Outputs Input: A mesh defined as mesh::polyhedron<baset>, typically imported from.stl or.obj files. The mesh contains a vertex buffer (vertices) and an index buffer (indices.buffer) representing triangular faces. Output: A rasterresults structure containing arrdim (the voxel grid dimensions), voxels (intersection data), and mesh (the input mesh). The final voxel types (interior, shell, background) are derived from the intersection counts. Data Structures The method utilizes three 2D quadtree structures to accelerate ray casting: 1. xytree: Stores faces projected onto the XY plane. 2. yztree: Stores faces projected onto the YZ plane. 3. xztree: Stores faces projected onto the XZ plane. Each quadtree node contains a buffer of face indices. The quadtree is configured with a constant branchsize of 128 used as the branch size for the quad tree. Coordinates are scaled by a constant treescale of 2.0f for insertion and search. Parameters treescale: 2.0f (float). Scales coordinates for quadtree insertion and search. branchsize: 128 (sizet). The branch size for the quad tree. treesearchsteps: Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization and Normalization Normalize and scale the input polyhedron by the provided scale vector. Calculate the polyhedron dimension: polyhedrondim = glm::ceil(polyhedron.dim()) + 1.0f. The + 1.0f handles the edge case where a face lies exactly on the array boundary, ensuring voxels can be drawn. Calculate half-dimensions: dimhalf = polyhedrondim / 2.0f. Initialize the three quadtrees (xytree, yztree, xztree) with boundaries: xytree: dimhalf.xy() treescale yztree: dimhalf.yz() treescale xztree: dimhalf.xz() treescale. 2. Tree Population Iterate through each face f in polyhedron.indices.buffer. Retrieve the three vertices v1, v2, v3 of the face and scale them by treescale. Calculate the integer bounding box [min, max] of the projected face for each plane. Insert the face index f into the respective quadtrees for all integer coordinates within the bounding box: Insert into xytree for x in [min.x, max.x] and y in [min.y, max.y]. Insert into xztree for x in [min.x, max.x] and z in [min.z, max.z]. Insert into yztree for y in [min.y, max.y] and z in [min.z, max.z]. 3. Plane Rasterization (Intersection Calculation) The method performs parallel loops over each 2D plane to calculate ray intersections. For each pixel in the plane, a ray is cast through the mesh, and intersection distances are stored. YZ Plane Rasterization: Parallel loop over y in [0, polyhedrondim.y) and z in [0, polyhedrondim.z). Calculate 2D position: p = glm::vec2(y, z) treescale. Find the relevant face buffer in yztree using p and treesearchsteps. Get intersections inters by calling getintersectionssafe<yzx>(glm::vec2(y, z), polyhedron.vertices, buffer). Store results in r.yz[y][z]. XZ Plane Rasterization: Parallel loop over x in [0, polyhedrondim.x) and z in [0, polyhedrondim.z). Calculate 2D position: p = glm::vec2(x, z) treescale. Find the relevant face buffer in xztree. Get intersections inters by calling getintersectionssafe<xzy>(glm::vec2(x, z), polyhedron.vertices, buffer). Store results in r.xz[x][z]. XY Plane Rasterization: Parallel loop over x in [0, polyhedrondim.x) and y in [0, polyhedrondim.y). Calculate 2D position: p = glm::vec2(x, y) treescale. Find the relevant face buffer in xytree. Get intersections inters by calling getintersectionssafe<xyz>(glm::vec2(x, y), polyhedron.vertices, buffer). Store results in r.xy[x][y]. 4. Intersection Calculation (Safe Mode) The getintersectionssafe function performs robust ray-triangle intersection checks, including edge collision detection. For a given 2D position p and a set of candidate faces, the implementation follows this logic: python def getintersectionssafe(swizzlemode, p2d, vertices, buffer, raystart): intersdist = set() for f in buffer: v1, v2, v3 = vertices[f[0]], vertices[f[1]], vertices[f[2]] if swizzlemode == 'yzx': dir = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) pos3d = (p2d.x, raystart, p2d.y) elif swizzlemode == 'xzy': dir = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) pos3d = (p2d.x, raystart, p2d.y) elif swizzlemode == 'xyz': dir = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) pos3d = (p2d.x, p2d.y, raystart) barypos, distance = intersectraytriangle(pos3d, dir, v1, v2, v3) if barypos is not None and distance > 0: intersdist.add(round(distance + raystart)) return intersdist The function returns the set of rounded integer intersection distances. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Faces: If a face lies exactly on the end of the array, a voxel cannot be drawn without increasing the dimension. The algorithm adds 1.0f to the calculated dimension to accommodate this. Edge Collisions: The safe mode includes additional checks for edge collisions to ensure accuracy, which makes it slower than the fast mode but more robust. Time Complexity: The method is parallelized and described as one of the fastest CPU rasterizers. However, the safe mode is slower than the fast mode due to edge collision checks and quadtree overhead. Memory Complexity: The primary advantage is memory efficiency. It avoids allocating a huge 3D buffer array by saving plane-wise intersections in 2D structures. This allows it to handle huge models or high target resolutions where other voxelizers fail due to memory issues. Measured Performance: On an Intel i7 4770k CPU with a Stanford Bunny mesh (112k faces): 64³: 118 ms 128³: 298 ms 256³: 1089 ms 512³: 4483 ms 1024³: 17933 ms Strengths: Memory efficiency, robustness (edge checks), ability to handle high resolutions. Limitations: Slower than the --fast mode due to safety checks and quadtree traversal overhead. This method is part of the 3DStuff/voxelizer project, an open-source voxelization tool. It was developed as a solution to memory limitations in existing CPU-based voxelizers, providing a trade-off between performance and memory usage for large-scale 3D models. 3DStuff/voxelizer, https://github.com/3DStuff/voxelizer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Template-based Voxelization
head: DGtal::MeshVoxelizer, MeshVoxelizer
body: Template-based Voxelization computes the digitization of a continuous triangle or mesh by determining if a voxel belongs to the digitization based on whether a geometric template centered at the voxel intersects the triangle. It converts a continuous surface mesh into a discrete set of voxels (DigitalSet). This method is distinguished from sibling methods like AABB-triangle intersection by its reliance on topological separation properties (6- or 26-connectivity) to define the boundary, ensuring that the resulting digital surface separates the interior from the exterior in the specified connectivity sense. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A mesh (collection of vertices and faces) or a single triangle defined by vertices A, B, C. Input: The mesh may contain non-triangular faces. Input: A DigitalSet defining the output domain (a 3D hyperrectangular grid) and the connectivity type (6 or 26). Input: A scaleFactor (double, default 1.0) applied to vertex coordinates before voxelization. Output: A DigitalSet containing the indices of voxels that intersect the mesh geometry. Data Structures: DigitalSet: A container modeling concepts::CDigitalSet with a 3D space dimension. It stores the set of voxel indices belonging to the digitization. Domain: A HyperRectDomain defined by a minimum point (e.g., (0,0,0)) and a maximum point (e.g., (128,128,128)). IntersectionTarget: A type derived from IntersectionTargetTrait<Space, Separation, 1>::Type. This template defines the geometric shape (the "template") used to test for intersection. The shape depends on the Separation parameter (6 or 26). TriangleOrientation: An enum (TRIANGLEOUTSIDE, TRIANGLEINSIDE, TRIANGLEONEDGE, TRIANGLEONVERTEX) used by the 2D containment test. Parameters: Separation: Integer constant, must be 6 or 26. 6: Corresponds to 6-connectivity (face-adjacent voxels). The digitization of a Euclidean plane ensures no 6-path exists from one side to the other. 26: Corresponds to 26-connectivity (vertex/edge/face-adjacent voxels). scaleFactor: Double value applied to mesh vertex coordinates. Default is 1.0. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Instantiate the MeshVoxelizer template class with the DigitalSet type and the chosen Separation connectivity (6 or 26). 2. Preprocessing (Mesh): If the input mesh contains non-triangular faces, naively triangulate them using a triangle fan centered at the first vertex (index 0). Pitfall: If a face is not convex, this triangulation strategy produces incorrect digitization results. 3. Scaling: Apply the scaleFactor to the coordinates of all mesh vertices. 4. Iteration: For each triangle (or triangulated face) in the mesh: a. Extract vertices A, B, C and compute the bounding box bbox of the triangle in voxel space. b. Call voxelizeTriangle with A, B, C, the normal n, and bbox. 5. Voxelization (Triangle): Inside voxelizeTriangle: a. Iterate over all voxel indices v within the bbox. b. Construct the template centered at voxel v based on the Separation parameter. c. Test if the template intersects the triangle. d. If intersection is true, insert voxel v into outputSet. e. Boundary Check: If voxel v is outside the domain of outputSet, skip it. 6. Completion: Return the populated outputSet. Core Formula: A voxel v belongs to the digitization if and only if the template Tv centered at v intersects the triangle T: v \in \text{Digitization} \iff Tv \cap T \neq \emptyset Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Triangle: def init(self, A, B, C): self.A = A self.B = B self.C = C def computeboundingbox(A, B, C): mins = [min(A[i], B[i], C[i]) for i in range(3)] maxs = [max(A[i], B[i], C[i]) for i in range(3)] return mins, maxs class Template: def init(self, voxelidx, separation): self.voxelidx = voxelidx self.separation = separation def intersects(self, tri): # Standard geometric predicate for template-triangle intersection. # In DGtal, this uses IntersectionTargetTrait and OrientationFunctor. return True class MeshVoxelizer: def init(self, DigitalSet, Separation): assert Separation in [6, 26], "Separation must be 6 or 26" self.Separation = Separation self.DigitalSet = DigitalSet def voxelize(self, outputSet, aMesh, scaleFactor=1.0): triangles = [] for face in aMesh.faces: if len(face) == 3: triangles.append(face) else: v0 = face[0] for i in range(1, len(face) - 1): triangles.append([v0, face[i], face[i+1]]) scaledvertices = [v scaleFactor for v in aMesh.vertices] for triindices in triangles: A = scaledvertices[triindices[0]] B = scaledvertices[triindices[1]] C = scaledvertices[triindices[2]] bbox = computeboundingbox(A, B, C) self.voxelizetriangle(outputSet, A, B, C, bbox) def voxelizetriangle(self, outputSet, A, B, C, bbox): tri = Triangle(A, B, C) for x in range(bbox[0][0], bbox[1][0] + 1): for y in range(bbox[0][1], bbox[1][1] + 1): for z in range(bbox[0][2], bbox[1][2] + 1): v = (x, y, z) if not outputSet.domain.contains(v): continue template = Template(v, self.Separation) if template.intersects(tri): outputSet.insert(v) Subtopics: 6-Separating Digitization: Uses 6-connectivity templates. Ensures no 6-path crosses the digitized plane. Choose when strict topological separation in face-adjacent connectivity is required. 26-Separating Digitization: Uses 26-connectivity templates. Allows for thicker boundaries or different topological properties. Choose when 26-connectivity background separation is needed. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of triangles and the volume of their bounding boxes. For each triangle, the algorithm iterates over all voxels in the bounding box and performs a template intersection test. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels in the output DigitalSet. Performance: CPU straightforward implementation. Performance depends heavily on the resolution (scaleFactor) and the surface area of the mesh relative to the voxel grid. Strengths: Guarantees topological separation properties (6- or 26-separability). Simple to implement. Limitations: Incorrect results for non-convex faces due to naive triangulation. Skips voxels outside the defined domain. When to use: When topological correctness (separability) is more important than speed or handling complex non-convex geometry directly. When not to use: For meshes with many non-convex faces, or when high-performance GPU implementation is required (this is a CPU method). Template-based Voxelization is a CPU straightforward implementation of the method described in reference [78] (also cited as [79] in some versions). It is part of the DGtal library, a C++ library for geometric modeling and digital geometry analysis. The method relies on the concept of "separability" in digital topology, where the choice of connectivity (6 or 26) determines the topological properties of the digitized surface. name: Triangle Rendering with Thickness
head: Triangle Thickness Rasterization
body: Triangle Rendering with Thickness renders a triangle as a volumetric shell by voxelizing grid points that lie within a specified distance from the triangle's plane or edges. It differs from solid triangle rasterization by including points outside the triangle boundary up to the thickness limit, and from sphere-based thickness methods by using planar geometry defined by three vertices. This method is a specialized case of mesh rasterization where the primitive is a polygon. Inputs: Triangle vertices v1, v2, v3 (3D vectors), thickness T (scalar), and grid bounds. Outputs: A list of voxel indices or a density field where points within the thickness are marked. Data Structures: Vec3: 3D vector with components x, y, z. Bucket: A subset of the grid defined by integer bounds [mini, maxi] \times [minj, maxj] \times [mink, maxk]. Steps: 1. Bounding Box: Compute the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the triangle vertices v1, v2, v3. 2. Bucket Selection: Calculate the grid indices for the AABB extended by the thickness T in all directions. 3. Geometry Precomputation: Compute edge vectors: e{21} = v2 - v1, e{32} = v3 - v2, e{13} = v1 - v3. Compute squared magnitudes: m{21} = \|e{21}\|^2, m{32} = \|e{32}\|^2, m{13} = \|e{13}\|^2. Compute the triangle normal: n = e{21} \times e{13}. Compute squared normal magnitude: mn = \|n\|^2. Compute cross products for edge orientation checks: c{21} = e{21} \times n, c{32} = e{32} \times n, c{13} = e{13} \times n. 4. Voxel Evaluation: For each voxel center p in the bucket: Compute vectors from vertices: p1 = p - v1, p2 = p - v2, p3 = p - v3. Inside Check: Determine if p projects inside the triangle using barycentric sign checks. The source implementation contains a bug where it repeats the first edge cross product three times; the correct logic uses all three edge cross products. Distance Calculation: If inside: Calculate the squared distance to the closest edge. d^2 = \min \left( \| e{21} \cdot \text{clamp}\left(\frac{e{21} \cdot p1}{m{21}}, 0, 1\right) - p1 \|^2, \| e{32} \cdot \text{clamp}\left(\frac{e{32} \cdot p2}{m{32}}, 0, 1\right) - p2 \|^2, \| e{13} \cdot \text{clamp}\left(\frac{e{13} \cdot p3}{m{13}}, 0, 1\right) - p3 \|^2 \right) If outside: Calculate the squared distance to the triangle's plane. d^2 = \frac{(n \cdot p1)^2}{mn} Thickness Test: If d^2 < T^2, add the voxel to the render list. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendertrianglethickness(v1, v2, v3, thickness, gridcellsize): # 1. Bounding Box minv = [min(v1[0], v2[0], v3[0]), min(v1[1], v2[1], v3[1]), min(v1[2], v2[2], v3[2])] maxv = [max(v1[0], v2[0], v3[0]), max(v1[1], v2[1], v3[1]), max(v1[2], v2[2], v3[2])] # 2. Bucket Indices (extended by thickness) mini = int(math.floor((minv[0] - thickness) / gridcellsize)) maxi = int(math.ceil((maxv[0] + thickness) / gridcellsize)) minj = int(math.floor((minv[1] - thickness) / gridcellsize)) maxj = int(math.ceil((maxv[1] + thickness) / gridcellsize)) mink = int(math.floor((minv[2] - thickness) / gridcellsize)) maxk = int(math.ceil((maxv[2] + thickness) / gridcellsize)) bucketindices = [] for i in range(mini, maxi + 1): for j in range(minj, maxj + 1): for k in range(mink, maxk + 1): bucketindices.append((i, j, k)) # 3. Precompute Geometry e21 = [v2[0]-v1[0], v2[1]-v1[1], v2[2]-v1[2]] e32 = [v3[0]-v2[0], v3[1]-v2[1], v3[2]-v2[2]] e13 = [v1[0]-v3[0], v1[1]-v3[1], v1[2]-v3[2]] m21 = e21[0]2 + e21[1]2 + e21[2]2 m32 = e32[0]2 + e32[1]2 + e32[2]2 m13 = e13[0]2 + e13[1]2 + e13[2]2 normal = [e21[1]e13[2]-e21[2]e13[1], e21[2]e13[0]-e21[0]e13[2], e21[0]e13[1]-e21[1]e13[0]] magnormal = normal[0]2 + normal[1]2 + normal[2]2 c21 = [e21[1]normal[2]-e21[2]normal[1], e21[2]normal[0]-e21[0]normal[2], e21[0]normal[1]-e21[1]normal[0]] c32 = [e32[1]normal[2]-e32[2]normal[1], e32[2]normal[0]-e32[0]normal[2], e32[0]normal[1]-e32[1]normal[0]] c13 = [e13[1]normal[2]-e13[2]normal[1], e13[2]normal[0]-e13[0]normal[2], e13[0]normal[1]-e13[1]normal[0]] thicknesssq = thickness thickness renderlist = [] for pt in bucketindices: # Convert grid index to coordinates (assuming origin at 0,0,0) p = [pt[0]gridcellsize, pt[1]gridcellsize, pt[2]gridcellsize] p1 = [p[0]-v1[0], p[1]-v1[1], p[2]-v1[2]] p2 = [p[0]-v2[0], p[1]-v2[1], p[2]-v2[2]] p3 = [p[0]-v3[0], p[1]-v3[1], p[2]-v3[2]] # Inside Check (Fixed: source repeats c21 three times) s1 = 1 if (c21[0]p1[0]+c21[1]p1[1]+c21[2]p1[2]) > 0 else (-1 if (c21[0]p1[0]+c21[1]p1[1]+c21[2]p1[2]) < 0 else 0) s2 = 1 if (c32[0]p2[0]+c32[1]p2[1]+c32[2]p2[2]) > 0 else (-1 if (c32[0]p2[0]+c32[1]p2[1]+c32[2]p2[2]) < 0 else 0) s3 = 1 if (c13[0]p3[0]+c13[1]p3[1]+c13[2]p3[2]) > 0 else (-1 if (c13[0]p3[0]+c13[1]p3[1]+c13[2]p3[2]) < 0 else 0) inside = (s1 + s2 + s3) < 2.0 distsq = 0.0 if inside: # Distance to edges proj1 = max(0.0, min(1.0, (e21[0]p1[0]+e21[1]p1[1]+e21[2]p1[2]) / m21)) vec1 = [e21[0]proj1-p1[0], e21[1]proj1-p1[1], e21[2]proj1-p1[2]] d1sq = vec1[0]2 + vec1[1]2 + vec1[2]2 proj2 = max(0.0, min(1.0, (e32[0]p2[0]+e32[1]p2[1]+e32[2]p2[2]) / m32)) vec2 = [e32[0]proj2-p2[0], e32[1]proj2-p2[1], e32[2]proj2-p2[2]] d2sq = vec2[0]2 + vec2[1]2 + vec2[2]2 proj3 = max(0.0, min(1.0, (e13[0]p3[0]+e13[1]p3[1]+e13[2]p3[2]) / m13)) vec3 = [e13[0]proj3-p3[0], e13[1]proj3-p3[1], e13[2]proj3-p3[2]] d3sq = vec3[0]2 + vec3[1]2 + vec3[2]2 distsq = min(d1sq, d2sq, d3sq) else: # Distance to plane distsq = (normal[0]p1[0]+normal[1]p1[1]+normal[2]p1[2])2 / magnormal if distsq < thicknesssq: renderlist.append(pt) return renderlist Parameters: thickness: The distance from the triangle surface. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Degenerate Triangle: If mn \approx 0, the normal is zero, causing division by zero in the plane distance calculation. Guard against this by checking mn < \epsilon. Precision: Floating point errors in clamp or dot products may cause jitter at boundaries. Sphere Rendering with Thickness renders a sphere as a hollow shell by voxelizing grid points that lie between an inner and outer radius. It differs from solid sphere rendering by excluding the core volume, and from triangle-based thickness methods by using a spherical coordinate system defined by a center point and a single radius parameter. This method is a specialized case of mesh rasterization where the primitive is a sphere rather than a polygon. A function to display three-dimensional objects composed by triangles and line segments, used for displaying boundary planes of simulations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement; produces smooth volumetric edges; suitable for thin-shell rendering. Limitations: The source implementation contains a bug in the inside/outside test (repeating the same edge check three times). Performance degrades with large thickness values relative to triangle size. When to use: When rendering wireframe-like structures or thin shells from triangle meshes. When not to use: For solid volume rendering where interior density is required; for high-performance applications where the bug in the inside check leads to incorrect geometry. This method is derived from an unofficial volumetric display implementation found in a GitHub repository. It represents a direct rasterization approach to creating volumetric primitives from mesh data, specifically focusing on the "thickness" aspect to create hollow or shell-like structures. The VFIVE visualization software utilizes a minimum function to display boundary planes of simulations using triangles and line segments. quertzuiop/Volumetric-display, https://github.com/quertzuiop/Volumetric-display, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) IMMERSIVE VR VISUALIZATIONS BY VFIVE PART 1: DEVELOPMENT, https://doi.org/10.1142/s1793962313400035, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Sphere Rendering with Thickness
head: Hollow Sphere Rendering with Thickness Clipping, Shell Sphere Voxelization, Shell sphere, Sphere Thickness Rasterization, Thick sphere clipping
body: Sphere Rendering with Thickness renders a sphere with a specified thickness as a hollow shell by checking grid points against the sphere's inner and outer radii. It filters grid points based on a thickness parameter, excluding points that fall within the inner radius. Inputs and Outputs Input: Sphere center position pos (3D vector), sphere radius r, thickness parameter \tau, and a grid of query points (voxel centers). Output: A subset of grid points that fall within the spherical shell, added to a render list. Data Structures SphereGeometry: Contains pos (center) and radius (r). BucketIndices: A list of grid indices covering the bounding box of the sphere to optimize query scope. Steps 1. Compute bounding box indices for the sphere: auto bucketIndices = calculateIndicesFromBB(params, pos, pos, radius);. 2. Compute squared radius: float radius2 = radius radius;. 3. For each point ptCoords in the bucket, calculate squared distance to center: float d2 = dist2(ptCoords, pos);. 4. If thickness > 0 and d2 < (2 radius thickness - radius2), skip the point as it lies inside the hollow core. 5. If d2 < radius2, add the point to the render list with color, dithering, and clipping behavior. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderspherethickness(center, radius, thickness, gridpoints): """ Renders a sphere with thickness by filtering grid points. Args: center: Vec3, sphere center position. radius: float, outer radius of the sphere. thickness: float, thickness of the shell. gridpoints: List[Vec3], voxel centers within the computed bounding box bucket. Returns: List[Vec3], points inside the shell. """ r2 = radius radius innerthreshold = 2 radius thickness - r2 renderedpoints = [] for pt in gridpoints: dx = pt.x - center.x dy = pt.y - center.y dz = pt.z - center.z d2 = dxdx + dydy + dzdz if thickness > 0 and d2 < innerthreshold: continue if d2 < r2: renderedpoints.append(pt) return renderedpoints Parameters radius: Sphere outer radius. thickness: Shell thickness parameter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls The inner radius check formula 2 radius thickness - radius2 is described as "magic math" in the source code comment, implying it approximates the inner radius squared for a thin shell. Renders a triangle with a specified thickness by checking if grid points are within the thickness distance from the triangle plane or edges. Use this for planar surfaces. Triangle Rendering with Thickness The general framework for converting 3D mesh primitives into voxel data. Sphere rendering is a specialized primitive within this framework. Mesh Rasterization and Triangle Intersection Not given in the sources. This method originates from the Volumetric-display project by quartzzuiop, which implements a custom volumetric renderer. The specific implementation for sphere thickness is found in the source code comments and demo applications, where it is used to render moving spheres with a defined thickness. quertzuiop/Volumetric-display, https://github.com/quertzuiop/Volumetric-display, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Mesh Normal Rasterization with Softmax Blending
head: Barycentric Normal Interpolation, GT Normal Rendering, Mesh Normal Rasterization with Barycentric Interpolation and Softmax Blending
body: This method renders ground-truth normal maps by interpolating per-vertex normals across rasterized faces using barycentric coordinates, then blending overlapping faces per pixel via a softmax function. It differs from hard-edge rasterization by providing smooth, differentiable normal fields suitable for gradient-based optimization. Inputs: vertexnormals: Tensor of shape (V, 3) containing per-vertex normal vectors, where V is the number of vertices. facespacked: Tensor of shape (F, 3) containing face indices, where F is the number of triangles. fragments: Rasterization output containing pixtoface (indices of faces overlapping each pixel) and barycentriccoords (barycentric coordinates of each pixel relative to overlapping faces). blendparams: Configuration object containing blurradius, facesperpixel, and perspectivecorrect. Outputs: images: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) containing the blended normal map. Data Structures: Vertex Textures: Stored as RGB values representing the encoded normal vectors. Face Textures: Derived from vertex textures using face indices, with shape (F, 3, 3). Fragments: Contains the mapping from pixel coordinates to triangle indices and the interpolation weights (barycentric coordinates). Steps: 1. Encode and Normalize Vertex Normals: Transform raw normal vectors (nx, ny, nz) by applying n{x,y} \leftarrow (n{x,y} + 1) / 2 and nz \leftarrow (nz + 3) / 4, then L2-normalize across the channel dimension. 2. Map to Face Textures: Index the normalized vertex textures using packed face indices: facestextures = vertextextures[facespacked]. 3. Interpolate Attributes: For each pixel, interpolate the face textures across the overlapping faces using the provided barycentric coordinates. 4. Softmax Blending: Blend the contributions of overlapping faces per pixel using a softmax function over the face dimension. The blurradius parameter in blendparams controls the soft edge blending radius; set to 0.0 for hard edges. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendernormals(vertexnormals, faces, fragments, blendparams): # Step 1: Encode and normalize vertex normals vertextextures = vertexnormals.clone() vertextextures[:, 0] = (vertextextures[:, 0] + 1.0) / 2.0 vertextextures[:, 1] = (vertextextures[:, 1] + 1.0) / 2.0 vertextextures[:, 2] = (vertextextures[:, 2] + 3.0) / 4.0 norms = torch.norm(vertextextures, p=2, dim=-1, keepdim=True) norms = torch.clamp(norms, min=1e-8) vertextextures = vertextextures / norms # Step 2: Map to face textures facestextures = vertextextures[faces] # Step 3: Interpolate face attributes # fragments.pixtoface: (H, W, K), fragments.barycentriccoords: (H, W, K, 3) H, W, K = fragments.pixtoface.shape texels = torch.zeros(H, W, K, 3, device=vertextextures.device) for h in range(H): for w in range(W): for k in range(K): faceidx = fragments.pixtoface[h, w, k] bary = fragments.barycentriccoords[h, w, k] v0, v1, v2 = facestextures[faceidx] texels[h, w, k] = bary[0] v0 + bary[1] v1 + bary[2] v2 # Step 4: Softmax blend # Blend overlapping face contributions per pixel using softmax blending # Map blurradius to a temperature parameter for the softmax function temperature = 1.0 / (blendparams.blurradius + 1e-6) images = softmaxrgbblend(texels, temperature) return images def softmaxrgbblend(texels, temperature): # texels: (H, W, K, 3) # Apply softmax over the face dimension (K) to blend overlapping faces expvals = torch.exp(texels / temperature) sumexp = torch.sum(expvals, dim=-2, keepdim=True) sumexp = torch.clamp(sumexp, min=1e-8) weights = expvals / sumexp images = torch.sum(weights texels, dim=-2) return images Parameters: blurradius: Controls soft edge blending radius. Set to 0.0 for hard edges. facesperpixel: Number of faces considered per pixel. Default is 1. perspectivecorrect: Enables perspective-correct interpolation. Default is True. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Normals: If a vertex normal is zero, the normalization step will result in NaNs. A small epsilon should be added to the norm denominator. Degenerate Triangles: Triangles with zero area may produce undefined barycentric coordinates. The rasterizer should handle or filter these. Precision: The encoding step (n+1)/2 maps [-1, 1] to [0, 1], but the subsequent normalization changes the magnitude. Ensure the downstream renderer expects normalized vectors. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides smooth, differentiable normal maps suitable for training neural rendering models. Limitations: Softmax blending can blur sharp edges if blurradius is large. When to Use: Training differentiable rendering pipelines, normal map generation for neural fields. When Not to Use: Real-time rendering where performance is critical, or when hard edges are required. Uses nearest-face or first-hit logic without blending. Choose when performance is critical and normal continuity is not required. Link to Mesh Rasterization and Triangle Intersection. Computes normals from depth gradients. Choose when mesh geometry is unavailable but depth maps are present. Link to Triangle Rendering with Thickness. This method is used in the dn-splatter project for differentiable normal splatting. name: Rasterization-based Voxelization Shader
head: GVShader, Geometry Volume (GV) Shader
body: A fragment shader that rasterizes geometry into a 3D grid volume by mapping clip-space coordinates to grid indices and writing a value to a structured buffer. It differs from Rasterization-based Voxelization by operating directly on the GPU via fragment shaders to produce volumetric data (binary occupancy or spherical harmonic coefficients) rather than 2D buffers, and from Mesh-to-Voxel Geometry Shader by relying on standard rasterization pipelines rather than explicit geometry shader topology expansion. Inputs: Clip-space vertex positions and vertex normals. Grid resolution parameter: CVCTGridResolutionI for CVCT or LPVGridResolution for LPV. Transformation matrix LPVWorldToLightLocalMatrix for converting world normals to light local space. Boolean flag UNITYREVERSEDZ indicating reversed-Z depth buffer layout. Fixed-point conversion scale SHF2I for spherical harmonic coefficients. Outputs: CVCTgv: A RWStructuredBuffer<int> storing binary occupancy values (1 for a hit). RSMgv: A RWStructuredBuffer<int> storing spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients weighted by normal, used for lighting accumulation. Data Structures: Grid Indexing: 3D integer coordinates (posx, posy, posz) mapped to a 1D linear index. CVCT: index = posx + posy \cdot R + posz \cdot R^2, where R = \CVCT\GridResolutionI. LPV: index = (posx + R \cdot (posy + R \cdot posz)) \cdot 4, storing 4 integer components per voxel. Spherical Harmonic Coefficients: Stored as int4 in RSMgv, representing the first-order SH basis functions for the normal direction. Steps: 1. Vertex Transformation: Transform vertex position to clip space and vertex normal to world space. 2. Clip-Space Extraction: Extract the clip-space position xyz from the vertex shader output. 3. Z-Handling: If UNITYREVERSEDZ is defined, invert the Z component: xyz.z = 1 - xyz.z. 4. Coordinate Scaling: Scale xyz.z by the grid resolution multiplied by 0.99999 (using CVCTGridResolutionI for CVCT or LPVGridResolution for LPV). The factor 0.99999 prevents out-of-bounds writes due to floating-point precision errors at the grid boundary. 5. Integer Conversion: Cast the scaled coordinates to integer grid coordinates int3 pos. 6. Orientation Permutation (LPV only): If ORIENTATION2 is defined, permute pos = pos.yzx and set reduce = normal.y. If ORIENTATION3 is defined, permute pos = pos.zxy and set reduce = normal.x. 7. Index Calculation: Compute the linear buffer index based on the grid resolution and permuted coordinates. 8. Value Computation: CVCT: The value is simply 1 (binary occupancy). LPV: Transform the normal to light local space, then compute spherical harmonic normal coefficients: shNormalScaled = int4(dirToCosineLobe(normal) SHF2I (reduce reduce)). 9. Atomic Write: CVCT: Write 1 to CVCTgv[index]. LPV: Atomically add shNormalScaled components to RSMgv[index], RSMgv[index+1], RSMgv[index+2], and RSMgv[index+3]. Pseudocode (CVCT Variant): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fragcvct(clippos, gridres, reversedz, buffer): xyz = clippos[:3] if reversedz: xyz[2] = 1.0 - xyz[2] xyz[2] = gridres 0.99999 pos = [int(x) for x in xyz] index = pos[0] + pos[1] gridres + pos[2] (gridres gridres) buffer[index] = 1 Pseudocode (LPV Variant): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in v)) return [x/l for x in v] def mul(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j]v[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] def dirtocosinelobe(normal): # First-order SH cosine lobe projection C0 = 0.886226925 C1 = 1.02332671 return [C0, -C1 normal[1], C1 normal[2], -C1 normal[0]] def atomicadd(buffer, index, value): buffer[index] = buffer[index] + value def fraglpv(clippos, worldnormal, gridres, reversedz, orientation, worldtolightmatrix, buffer, SHF2I): xyz = clippos[:3] if reversedz: xyz[2] = 1.0 - xyz[2] xyz[2] = gridres 0.99999 pos = [int(x) for x in xyz] lightnormal = normalize(mul(worldtolightmatrix, worldnormal)) if orientation == 2: pos = [pos[1], pos[2], pos[0]] reduce = lightnormal[1] elif orientation == 3: pos = [pos[2], pos[0], pos[1]] reduce = lightnormal[0] else: reduce = lightnormal[2] baseindex = (pos[0] + gridres (pos[1] + gridres pos[2])) 4 shcoeffs = dirtocosinelobe(lightnormal) shscaled = [int(c SHF2I (reduce reduce)) for c in shcoeffs] atomicadd(buffer, baseindex, shscaled[0]) atomicadd(buffer, baseindex + 1, shscaled[1]) atomicadd(buffer, baseindex + 2, shscaled[2]) atomicadd(buffer, baseindex + 3, shscaled[3]) Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient GPU-based voxelization without CPU-GPU synchronization; supports atomic operations for concurrent writes. Limitations: Precision issues at grid boundaries require the 0.99999 scaling factor; orientation permutations add complexity for LPV. When to use: When real-time voxelization is required for techniques like Cascaded Voxel Cone Tracing (CVCT) or Local Persistent Volumes (LPV). The method originates from implementations of Cascaded Voxel Cone Tracing (CVCT) and Local Persistent Volumes (LPV) in real-time rendering engines. The CVCT variant was introduced by arigo in the "CascatedVoxelConeTracing" repository, while the LPV variant was developed in the "LPVTest" repository. These methods are used in Unity-based projects to provide efficient global illumination and shadowing. arigo/CascatedVoxelConeTracing, https://github.com/arigo/CascatedVoxelConeTracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) arigo/LPVTest, https://github.com/arigo/LPVTest, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Rasterization
body: Rasterization is a rendering technique that exploits the geometric properties of objects (primarily meshes) to quickly create a 2D image from 3D data. It solves the problem of mapping continuous geometric primitives to a discrete pixel buffer by projecting vertices and interpolating face attributes, rather than simulating light transport. It is distinguished from ray tracing by scaling with the number of visible vertices rather than pixel count, making it highly parallelizable and favored for high-performance applications like video games. However, implementing physically-based rendering (PBR) numerical methods atop rasterization is markedly harder or impossible compared to ray-tracing. Inputs: A set of vertices V and faces F (triangles or quads) defining the geometry. An extrinsic camera matrix E (world-to-camera transformation). An intrinsic camera matrix K (projection parameters). A 2D image buffer (framebuffer) with associated depth buffer (z-buffer). Outputs: A discretized 2D image buffer containing color and depth values for each pixel. Data Structures: Vertices: Array of 3D points (x, y, z) in world space. Faces: List of indices referencing vertices, defining surface connectivity. Z-buffer: 2D array storing depth values for occlusion testing. Steps: 1. Transform: Transform each vertex v from world coordinates to camera coordinates using the extrinsic matrix E. 2. Cull: Discard vertices or faces that are outside the view frustum or have incorrect normal orientation (back-face culling) to reduce processing load. 3. Project: Project the remaining camera-space vertices to 2D image coordinates using the intrinsic matrix K. 4. Interpolate and Rasterize: For each visible face, interpolate attributes (such as depth) across the 2D projected triangle. Store the topmost (closest to camera) face values in the z-buffer, overwriting previous values if the new depth is smaller. Formulas: Camera transformation: v{cam} = E \cdot v, where v is a vertex in world space and v{cam} is its position in camera space. Image projection: p{image} = K \cdot v{cam}, where p{image} is the projected 2D image coordinate. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Harder to capture complex lighting effects, shadows, and reflections compared to ray casting. Implementing physically-based rendering (PBR) numerical methods atop rasterization is markedly harder or impossible in some cases compared to ray-tracing. Precision and boundary handling during perspective division and barycentric interpolation require standard graphics safeguards. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rasterize(vertices, faces, E, K, imagewidth, imageheight): # Initialize output buffers colorbuffer = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) zbuffer = np.full((imageheight, imagewidth), np.inf) for face in faces: # 1. Transform vertices to camera space vcam = E @ vertices[face] # 2. Cull: skip if outside view frustum or back-facing if vcam[:, 2] <= 0: continue # 3. Project to 2D image coordinates vproj = K @ vcam # Perspective division vimg = vproj[:,:2] / vproj[:, 2] # 4. Interpolate attributes and rasterize # Determine bounding box of projected triangle minx, maxx = int(np.floor(min(vimg[:, 0]))), int(np.ceil(max(vimg[:, 0]))) miny, maxy = int(np.floor(min(vimg[:, 1]))), int(np.ceil(max(vimg[:, 1]))) minx, maxx = max(0, minx), min(imagewidth - 1, maxx) miny, maxy = max(0, miny), min(imageheight - 1, maxy) for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): # Interpolate depth and color across the 2D projected triangle # Standard barycentric interpolation computes coverage and attributes # If inside triangle and depth < zbuffer[y, x]: # zbuffer[y, x] = interpolateddepth # colorbuffer[y, x] = interpolatedcolor pass return colorbuffer, zbuffer Uses rasterization to generate voxel data from meshes; chosen when GPU-accelerated mesh-to-volume conversion is needed. GPU-based approach using geometry shaders for voxelization; chosen for on-the-fly volume generation during rendering. Algorithmic approach to rasterizing geometric shapes; chosen for CPU-side or legacy pipeline implementations. Focuses on triangle intersection logic within rasterization; chosen when precise primitive clipping and coverage testing are required. Shader implementation of rasterization for voxel generation; chosen for compute-heavy, parallel voxelization workloads. Sampling techniques for Local Persistent Volumes using rasterization; chosen for dynamic lighting in voxel-based engines. Uses proxy geometry and cluster culling for efficient rasterization; chosen for massive scene culling and draw-call reduction. Parent article covering GPU shader integration; links to broader pipeline context. Performance: Scales with the number of visible vertices and primitives, not the number of pixels. This makes it significantly faster than ray casting for scenes with many pixels but manageable geometry. Parallelization: Highly parallelizable on GPUs, favoring its use in real-time applications like video games. Limitations: Struggles with accurate global illumination, shadows, and reflections without additional techniques. PBR implementation is restricted compared to ray tracing. Differentiability: Can be made differentiable through "soft" rasterization techniques, enabling use in optimization and learning-based rendering. Rasterization is an alternative to ray casting, primarily used with meshes described by vertices and faces. It was developed as a method to quickly create images by exploiting geometric properties rather than emulating the physical image formation process. Modern approaches have extended it to be differentiable for neural rendering applications.
