name: LPV Voxelization Sampling
head: Area Light Voxelization for LPV, Area Lights Voxelization for Light Propagation Volumes, LPV Area Light Voxelization, VPL Voxelization
body: LPV Voxelization Sampling is a method to improve the simulation of direct illumination from area light sources within the Light Propagation Volumes (LPV) technique by voxelizing the area light source geometry into a voxel volume matching the LPV grid resolution. It generates one Virtual Point Light (VPL) sample for each LPV cell that intersects the light source triangles, providing an optimal distribution of samples that covers all necessary cells, unlike dense sampling which may under-sample or over-sample. This approach reduces the number of VPLs processed per frame compared to dense sampling strategies, offering performance advantages while maintaining plausible lighting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Area light source mesh (triangles with positions, normals, and optionally texture coordinates/emission directions), LPV grid resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz), LPV bounding box. Output: LPV grid updated with spherical harmonic coefficients representing radiance distribution, VPL counter per cell. Data Structures: LPV Grid: 3D array of cells. Each cell stores 2-band spherical harmonic coefficients for R, G, B channels (4 coefficients per channel, total 12 floats per cell) and an atomic counter for VPLs. Triangle: Defined by vertices A, B, C in world space. Steps: 1. Projection Selection: For each triangle of the area light source mesh, project its vertices onto the planes of the six LPV faces. Select the LPV face where the projected triangle has the largest surface area. This optimization ensures that a maximum of 2 LPV cells intersect the triangle projection along the axis perpendicular to the face (z-axis). 2. Rasterization Setup: Render the area light source mesh in a viewport with resolution matching the LPV face resolution. In the Geometry Shader, project the triangle vertices onto the selected LPV face plane. 3. Triangle Expansion: To ensure fragments are generated for LPV cells whose centers are partially intersected by the triangle (even if the center is outside the original triangle boundary), expand the triangle outwards. This expansion covers the centers of all potentially intersected fragments. 4. Initial Intersection Check: Before processing the expanded triangle, compute the LPV cells along the z-axis that intersect the initial (non-expanded) triangle. This is done to avoid injecting radiance into cells that should not receive it due to the expansion covering extra area. 5. Cell Intersection Test: For the projected triangle on the selected LPV face, identify the face coordinates (A0x, A0y) and depth coordinate A0z. Check only 3 specific cells along the z-axis for intersection with the triangle: \{(A0x, A0y, A0z-1), (A0x, A0y, A0z), (A0x, A0y, A0z+1)\}. Use the test proposed by Akenine-Möller (2001) to check if LPV cells with the same (Ax, Ay) coordinates intersect with the triangle. 6. Fragment Processing (Fragment Shader): For each fragment generated by the rasterizer (representing an intersection area): Determine the LPV cell coordinates (Ax, Ay, Az) by normalizing the fragment's clipspace coordinates to the LPV resolution. Create a Virtual Point Light (VPL) with: Position: Center of the LPV cell. Direction: Direction of radiance emission (interpolated from triangle vertices if non-homogeneous, or constant if homogeneous). Radiant Flux: Radiant flux of the triangle (or sampled from texture if textured). Compute the clamped cosine lobe in terms of zonal spherical harmonics along the negative z-axis, rotated in the direction of radiance emission. Use atomic operations to update the spherical harmonic coefficients and the VPL counter in the LPV cell to avoid concurrency problems. 7. Spherical Harmonic Update: For each VPL injected into a cell, compute its contribution to the spherical harmonic coefficients. The radiance distribution D0 for all VPLs in an LPV cell is computed as: D0 = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=0}^{N} Di \cdot Ci where D0 is the spherical harmonic coefficients approximating radiance distribution in the LPV cell, N is the number of VPLs in the cell, Di are the coefficients of the clamped cosine lobe for the i-th VPL, and Ci is the intensity of the color channel for the i-th VPL. Compute coefficients for 3 spherical harmonics inside each cell, one for every color channel {R, G, B}. Use 2-band spherical harmonics, resulting in 4 coefficients per color channel. During the voxelization process, update the coefficients without weighting. Store the VPL counter for each cell. 8. Post-Processing (Compute Shader): After the rasterization pass, use a compute shader to weight all spherical harmonic coefficients using the stored VPL counters. Parameters: LPV Resolution: Must match the resolution of the 3D grid used in the LPV technique. Spherical Harmonics Band: 2-band spherical harmonics are used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Under-sampling: If not every LPV cell that intersects the area light source surface is covered, radiance is not introduced into all necessary cells, resulting in non-plausible, dimly lit scenes. Rasterizer Limitations: The GPU rasterizer does not generate fragments whose centers are outside the rasterized triangle, even if the triangle partially intersects them. This prevents VPL generation for those areas unless the triangle is expanded. Expansion Artifacts: The expanded triangle may cover centers of fragments completely outside the triangle. Pre-computation of intersections with the initial triangle is required to avoid injecting radiance into incorrect cells. Concurrency: Multiple fragment shaders may run in parallel, requiring atomic operations to update LPV cell data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lpvvoxelizationsampling(triangles, lpvgrid, lpvres): """ Voxelize area light source mesh into LPV grid. lpvgrid: 3D array where each cell has shaccum (list of 12 floats) and vplcounter (int). lpvres: tuple (Nx, Ny, Nz). """ # Helper: Project vertices onto a plane def projectontoplane(verts, facenormal, faceorigin): return [v - dot(v - faceorigin, facenormal) facenormal for v in verts] # Helper: Compute triangle area from projected vertices def computetrianglearea(projverts): v0, v1, v2 = projverts return 0.5 length(cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0)) # Helper: Find LPV face with largest projected triangle area def findbestfaceprojection(tri, lpvres): faces = getlpvfaceplanes() # Returns list of (normal, origin) bestidx, bestproj, maxarea = -1, None, 0.0 for i, (n, o) in enumerate(faces): proj = projectontoplane(tri.verts, n, o) area = computetrianglearea(proj) if area > maxarea: maxarea = area bestidx, bestproj = i, proj return bestidx, bestproj # Helper: Expand triangle to cover centers of partially intersected fragments def expandtriangleoutwards(tri): centroid = sum(tri.verts) / 3.0 return [(v - centroid) 1.5 + centroid for v in tri.verts] # Helper: Akenine-Möller (2001) slab test for triangle vs cell along z-axis def akeninemollertest(tri, cx, cy, cz, faceidx): cellzmin, cellzmax = cz, cz + 1.0 trizmin, trizmax = min(v.z for v in tri.verts), max(v.z for v in tri.verts) if trizmax < cellzmin or trizmin > cellzmax: return False # Sources do not specify the exact 2D intersection logic for the projected face return True # Helper: Map world position to LPV cell index def worldtolpvcellindex(pos, lpvres): return (int(pos.x lpvres[0]), int(pos.y lpvres[1]), int(pos.z lpvres[2])) # Helper: Compute clamped cosine lobe SH coefficients rotated to direction def computeclampedcosinelobesh(direction): # Base SH for clamped cosine lobe along -z: [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] per channel # Rotation matrix applied to SH coefficients return [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] 3 # Simplified for pseudocode # Helper: Atomic add to SH accumulator def atomicaddsh(grid, idx, shcoeffs, flux): cell = grid[idx] for i in range(12): cell.shaccum[i] += shcoeffs[i] flux # Helper: Atomic increment VPL counter def atomicincrementcounter(grid, idx): grid[idx].vplcounter += 1 # Main loop for tri in triangles: bestfaceidx, bestprojverts = findbestfaceprojection(tri, lpvres) # Pre-compute initial intersections to avoid expansion artifacts initialcells = set() for x in range(int(min(v.x for v in bestprojverts)), int(max(v.x for v in bestprojverts)) + 1): for y in range(int(min(v.y for v in bestprojverts)), int(max(v.y for v in bestprojverts)) + 1): zmin, zmax = min(v.z for v in tri.verts), max(v.z for v in tri.verts) for z in range(int(zmin), int(zmax) + 1): if akeninemollertest(tri, x, y, z, bestfaceidx): initialcells.add((x, y, z)) expandedtri = expandtriangleoutwards(tri) fragments = rasterize(expandedtri, lpvres) # Simulated rasterizer output for frag in fragments: cx, cy, cz = worldtolpvcellindex(frag.position, lpvres) if (cx, cy, cz) not in initialcells: continue # Check 3 specific cells along z-axis for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: tz = cz + dz if akeninemollertest(tri, cx, cy, tz, bestfaceidx): vpldir = interpolateemissiondirection(tri, frag.barycentric) vplflux = gettriangleflux(tri) shcoeffs = computeclampedcosinelobesh(vpldir) atomicaddsh(lpvgrid, (cx, cy, tz), shcoeffs, vplflux) atomicincrementcounter(lpvgrid, (cx, cy, tz)) # Post-processing: weight coefficients for cell in lpvgrid: if cell.vplcounter > 0: for i in range(12): cell.shaccum[i] /= cell.vplcounter A method to approximate radiance distribution on mesh triangles where emission direction varies across the surface, using clamped cosine lobes distributed over an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the intersection area projection. It handles non-homogeneous emission by interpolating emission directions from triangle vertices and computing a spherical harmonic that approximates the radiance distribution for each intersected LPV cell. Choose this when the area light source has varying emission directions across its surface. A method to store and sample radiant flux information on area light surfaces using texture mapping and mipmapping to approximate the entire radiant flux of an intersection area. It uses texture coordinates at triangle vertices, interpolates them to find the texture coordinate at the AABB center of the intersection area, and applies mipmapping to quickly compute the radiant flux. Choose this when the area light source has varying radiant flux across its surface, represented by a texture map. A method to approximate the radiance distribution of a triangle mesh when the emission direction varies across its surface, by using an emission direction per vertex and interpolating within an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the projected intersection area. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by avoiding complex spherical harmonic fitting for non-homogeneous lights or texture-based flux maps, instead using a set of clamped cosine lobes distributed between interpolated corner directions of the projected AABB. Choose this when directional variation must be captured without texture lookups or heavy SH computation. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of triangles in the area light source mesh and the number of LPV cells intersected by these triangles. The most expensive operation is the atomic update of LPV cell coefficients, which scales with the number of VPLs per cell. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the LPV grid. Each cell stores 12 floats for SH coefficients and an integer for the VPL counter. Measured Performance: On an Nvidia GTX 1660 GPU, an LPV resolution of 64^3 showed better performance than 32^3 for almost all test data because atomic operations are less frequent at higher resolutions. Dense sampling performance is poor for a large number of triangles. Strengths: Optimal distribution of samples covering all intersecting voxels, reducing the number of VPLs processed per frame compared to dense sampling. Efficient use of GPU rasterization for voxelization. Limitations: Requires atomic operations which can be a bottleneck. Under-sampling can lead to dimly lit scenes. Expansion of triangles can lead to artifacts if not handled correctly. When to Use: When simulating direct illumination from area light sources in real-time global illumination using LPV, especially when performance is a concern and plausible lighting is required. When Not to Use: When the area light source has very complex geometry with many small triangles, leading to a high number of VPLs. When high precision in radiance distribution is required and the approximation errors from mipmapping or SH are unacceptable. LPV Voxelization Sampling was introduced by Lambru, Moldoveanu, Morar, and Asavei in 2022 in the paper "Area Lights Voxelization for Light Propagation Volumes". It improves upon previous LPV adaptations that lacked a specific sampling strategy for area lights, which often relied on dense sampling without quantitative evaluation. The method builds on the LPV technique for real-time global illumination and the voxelization approach proposed by Schwarz and Seidel (2010). It addresses the problem of simulating direct illumination from area light sources, which can reproduce effects such as the light of a TV display, by providing an optimal distribution of VPLs. Lambru, C., Moldoveanu, F., Morar, A. and Asavei, V., Area Lights Voxelization for Light Propagation Volumes, https://www.scitepress.org/publishedPapers/2022/108416/pdf/index.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) SCITEPRESS - SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY PUBLICATIONS, https://www.scitepress.org/PublishedPapers/2022/108416/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Radiance Distribution Approximation for Non-Homogeneous Lights
head: AABB Cosine Lobe Distribution
body: This method approximates the radiance distribution on mesh triangles where emission direction varies across the surface, using clamped cosine lobes distributed over an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the intersection area projection. It differs from spherical harmonic approaches by using a discrete set of cosine lobes, which is sufficient for the 2-band spherical harmonics used in LPV systems. Inputs: A triangle mesh with vertex directions and texture coordinates. An LPV grid structure. The projection face of the LPV cell where the triangle is projected. Outputs: A final radiance approximation with weight equal to the number of lobes, injected into LPV cells intersected along the z-axis. Data Structures: AABB: Defined by minimum and maximum coordinates (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}) in the local coordinate system of the LPV cell face. Cosine Lobe: Defined by a center direction \mathbf{d} and a spread angle \theta. Steps: 1. Compute the projection of the intersection area on the LPV face where the triangle is projected. 2. Compute the AABB of the polygon formed by: projected vertices of the triangle inside the LPV cell face, corners of the LPV cell face inside the triangle projection, and intersection points between the edges of the LPV cell face and edges of the triangle. 3. Compute the emission direction at each corner of the AABB by calculating barycentric coordinates of the corner inside the initial triangle and interpolating the direction information from the triangle vertices. 4. Distribute clamped cosine lobes between the emission directions from the corners, vertically and horizontally at angular distances equal to that of the cosine lobe. 5. Inject each generated cosine lobe into the LPV cell with a weight of 1. 6. Create the distribution locally and inject only the final approximation with weight equal to the number of lobes required for the approximation into all LPV cells intersected along the z-axis. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def approximateradiancedistribution(triangle, lpvface, lpvgrid): # Step 1: Project triangle vertices onto the LPV face plane projectedverts = [projectpointtoplane(v, lpvface.normal, lpvface.origin) for v in triangle.vertices] # Step 2: Compute AABB of intersection polygon # Clip projected triangle against LPV face rectangle to get intersection polygon intersectionpolygon = clippolygontorectangle(projectedverts, lpvface.bounds) # Add face corners inside the projected triangle for corner in lpvface.corners: if pointintriangle(corner, projectedverts): intersectionpolygon.append(corner) # Compute AABB from all points aabb = computeaabb(intersectionpolygon) # Step 3: Compute emission directions for AABB corners aabbcorners = getaabbcorners(aabb) cornerdirections = [] for corner in aabbcorners: # Project corner back to triangle plane to compute barycentric coordinates cornerontriangle = projectpointtoplane(corner, triangle.normal, triangle.vertices[0]) u, v, w = computebarycentriccoordinates(cornerontriangle, triangle.vertices) # Interpolate direction direction = u triangle.dirs[0] + v triangle.dirs[1] + w triangle.dirs[2] cornerdirections.append(normalize(direction)) # Step 4: Distribute cosine lobes lobes = [] spread = triangle.lobespread # Angular distance for distribution # Distribute vertically and horizontally between corner directions # The sources do not specify the exact interpolation grid size or scheme. # We generate a grid of lobes spanning the AABB, stepping by the lobe spread. mindir = cornerdirections[0] maxdir = cornerdirections[3] # Approximate grid dimensions based on angular distance between corner directions stepsu = max(1, int(angulardistance(mindir, cornerdirections[1]) / spread)) stepsv = max(1, int(angulardistance(mindir, cornerdirections[2]) / spread)) for i in range(stepsv + 1): for j in range(stepsu + 1): tu = j / stepsu if stepsu > 0 else 0.0 tv = i / stepsv if stepsv > 0 else 0.0 diru = interpolatedirection(cornerdirections[0], cornerdirections[1], tu) dirv = interpolatedirection(cornerdirections[2], cornerdirections[3], tu) center = interpolatedirection(diru, dirv, tv) lobes.append(Lobe(center=center, spread=spread, weight=1)) # Step 5 & 6: Inject into LPV # Create distribution locally, then inject final approximation into z-intersected cells intersectedcells = findcellsintersectedalongz(aabb, lpvgrid) finalweight = len(lobes) for cell in intersectedcells: injectapproximation(cell, finalweight) return lobes def projectpointtoplane(point, normal, origin): d = dot(point - origin, normal) return point - d normal def clippolygontorectangle(verts, bounds): # Standard Sutherland-Hodgman clipping against four rectangle edges clipped = verts[:] for edge in bounds.edges: newclipped = [] for i in range(len(clipped)): curr = clipped[i] prev = clipped[i - 1] if isinside(prev, edge) and isinside(curr, edge): newclipped.append(curr) elif isinside(prev, edge) != isinside(curr, edge): newclipped.append(intersectedge(prev, curr, edge)) clipped = newclipped return clipped def computeaabb(points): minx = min(p.x for p in points); maxx = max(p.x for p in points) miny = min(p.y for p in points); maxy = max(p.y for p in points) return {'min': (minx, miny), 'max': (maxx, maxy)} def getaabbcorners(aabb): return [(aabb['min'][0], aabb['min'][1]), (aabb['max'][0], aabb['min'][1]), (aabb['min'][0], aabb['max'][1]), (aabb['max'][0], aabb['max'][1])] def computebarycentriccoordinates(point, verts): v0 = verts[1] - verts[0]; v1 = verts[2] - verts[0]; v2 = point - verts[0] d00 = dot(v0, v0); d01 = dot(v0, v1); d11 = dot(v1, v1) d20 = dot(v2, v0); d21 = dot(v2, v1) denom = d00 d11 - d01 d01 v = (d11 d20 - d01 d21) / denom w = (d00 d21 - d01 d20) / denom u = 1.0 - v - w return u, v, w def interpolatedirection(d1, d2, t): return normalize(d1 + t (d2 - d1)) def angulardistance(d1, d2): return acos(clamp(dot(normalize(d1), normalize(d2)), -1.0, 1.0)) def findcellsintersectedalongz(aabb, grid): # Standard axis-aligned slab test to find grid cells intersecting the AABB along the z-axis cells = [] zmin = aabb['min'][2] zmax = aabb['max'][2] for z in range(grid.cellindex(zmin), grid.cellindex(zmax) + 1): cells.append(grid.cellatz(z)) return cells def injectapproximation(cell, weight): cell.radianceapprox += weight class Lobe: def init(self, center, spread, weight): self.center = center self.spread = spread self.weight = weight Parameters: Cosine Lobe Spread: The angular distance for distribution. Weight: Each lobe has a weight of 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visual Errors: The approach can produce minor visual errors because it generates a single radiance distribution for the AABB of the intersection area projection, which can cover two LPV cells, rather than processing each intersected LPV cell separately. Precision: Barycentric coordinate calculation must be robust to avoid artifacts at triangle boundaries. Not given in the sources. It builds on the idea of creating Virtual Point Lights (VPLs) to simulate direct illumination efficiently. The approach references earlier work on spherical harmonics for radiance approximation. name: Textured Area Lights Sampling
head: Mipmapped Radiant Flux Sampling
body: Textured Area Lights Sampling is a method to store and sample radiant flux information on area light surfaces using texture mapping and mipmapping to approximate the entire radiant flux of an intersection area. It solves the problem of efficiently voxelizing area light source meshes into Light Propagation Volumes (LPV) by creating Virtual Point Lights (VPLs) at intersection areas, simulating direct illumination more efficiently than dense sampling [Parent]. It sets itself apart from siblings by using a pre-computed radiant flux map sampled via mipmaps to approximate the flux of the projected area, rather than dense point sampling or direction-based AABB emission sampling [Siblings]. Inputs: Triangle mesh representing the area light source. Radiant flux map: A texture storing radiant flux information corresponding to the triangle mesh surface. LPV grid structure. Intersection area: The projection of the light triangle onto a specific LPV face. Outputs: Radiant flux value for the intersection area, used to populate LPV cells. Data Structures: Radiant Flux Map: A 2D texture where texels store radiant flux values. The mapping from triangle surface to texture is defined by vertex texture coordinates. AABB: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box of the intersection area projection on the LPV face. Steps: 1. Compute Intersection AABB: Determine the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the intersection area projection on the LPV face where the triangle is projected. Note that this intersection area can cover two LPV cells; for correct radiance distribution, the intersection area for every intersected LPV cell must be processed separately. 2. Compute AABB Center Texture Coordinate: Calculate the center of the AABB in the texture space or barycentric space of the triangle. Compute the barycentric coordinates of the AABB center relative to the triangle vertices. Interpolate the texture coordinates at the triangle vertices using these barycentric coordinates to obtain the texture coordinate (uc, vc) at the AABB center. 3. Compute Mipmap Level: Determine the required mipmap level to approximate the radiant flux of the intersection area. Calculate the mipmap level based on the texture coordinates in the corners of the AABB, following OpenGL standard specifications. The OpenGL standard specification for mipmap level calculation (Segal and Akeley, 1999) typically involves computing the maximum gradient of the texture coordinates across the primitive. For an AABB in texture space with corners (u1, v1), (u2, v2), (u3, v3), (u4, v4), the level L is derived from the maximum partial derivatives \max(|\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}|, |\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}|, |\frac{\partial v}{\partial x}|, |\frac{\partial v}{\partial y}|). Note: The exact formula from Segal and Akeley is not explicitly provided in the source text, but the method relies on it. 4. Sample Radiant Flux: Sample the radiant flux map at (uc, vc) using the computed mipmap level. This returns the approximate total radiant flux for the intersection area. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampletexturedarealight(triangle, radiantfluxmap, lpvface): """ Samples the radiant flux for an intersection area of a triangle on an LPV face. Args: triangle: Object with vertices v0, v1, v2. Each vertex has position p and texture coordinate uv. radiantfluxmap: Texture object with samplemipmap(u, v, level) method. lpvface: The LPV face geometry for projection. Returns: float: Approximated radiant flux for the intersection area. """ # Step 1: Compute AABB of intersection area projection on LPV face # This requires projecting the triangle onto the LPV face and finding the intersection polygon, # then computing its AABB. The source notes state this is similar to the non-homogeneous radiance method. intersectionpolygon = computeintersectionpolygon(triangle, lpvface) aabb = computeaabb(intersectionpolygon) # Step 2: Compute texture coordinate at AABB center # Calculate barycentric coordinates of the AABB center relative to the triangle centerpos = aabb.center() barycentric = computebarycentriccoordinates(centerpos, triangle.v0, triangle.v1, triangle.v2) # Interpolate texture coordinates uc = barycentric.w0 triangle.v0.uv.x + barycentric.w1 triangle.v1.uv.x + barycentric.w2 triangle.v2.uv.x vc = barycentric.w0 triangle.v0.uv.y + barycentric.w1 triangle.v1.uv.y + barycentric.w2 triangle.v2.uv.y # Step 3: Compute mipmap level based on AABB corners # Get texture coordinates for all four corners of the AABB in texture space # Note: The AABB is in LPV face space, so we need to project its corners to the triangle's texture space # or compute the AABB directly in texture space if the projection is affine. # Assuming we have the texture coordinates of the AABB corners in texture space: aabbcornersuv = [ computetexturecoordforaabbcorner(aabb, cornerindex=0, triangle=triangle), computetexturecoordforaabbcorner(aabb, cornerindex=1, triangle=triangle), computetexturecoordforaabbcorner(aabb, cornerindex=2, triangle=triangle), computetexturecoordforaabbcorner(aabb, cornerindex=3, triangle=triangle) ] # Compute mipmap level following OpenGL standard (Segal and Akeley, 1999) # This typically involves calculating the maximum gradient of u and v across the primitive. # For an axis-aligned box in texture space, the gradients are simply the width and height. umin = min(c.u for c in aabbcornersuv) umax = max(c.u for c in aabbcornersuv) vmin = min(c.v for c in aabbcornersuv) vmax = max(c.v for c in aabbcornersuv) # Approximate gradients (assuming unit pixel size or normalized texture space) # The exact OpenGL formula is complex, but generally: # level = log2(max(maxgradu, maxgradv)) # Here, we approximate the gradients as the dimensions of the AABB in texture space. # The source does not provide the exact OpenGL formula implementation details. # A common approximation for the mipmap level L for a rectangle of size (du, dv) in normalized texture space: du = umax - umin dv = vmax - vmin maxgrad = max(du, dv) # Handle degenerate case where AABB has zero size if maxgrad < 1e-6: level = 0 else: # Standard OpenGL mipmap level calculation involves the maximum partial derivative. # For a simple AABB in texture space, the level is often approximated by log2 of the max dimension. # This is a simplification; the exact Segal and Akeley method should be used for precision. level = log2(maxgrad) # Clamp level to valid range level = clamp(level, 0, radiantfluxmap.maxlevel()) # Step 4: Sample the radiant flux map flux = radiantfluxmap.samplemipmap(uc, vc, level) return flux Parameters: Mipmap Level: Computed dynamically based on the size of the intersection area in texture space. No fixed typical value is given; it scales with the projected area size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Z-axis Intersection: Computing a single radiant flux sample for all LPV cells intersected along the z-axis can cause minor visual errors. The intersection area must be processed for every intersected LPV cell separately if it covers multiple cells along the projection axis. Mipmap Approximation Error: Due to the approximation made by the mipmapping technique, radiant flux information can be introduced from areas outside the intersection area. This is a known limitation of using mipmaps for flux approximation. Time Complexity: O(1) per intersection area, assuming constant-time texture sampling and mipmap level calculation. The cost is dominated by the intersection computation and texture lookup. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the radiant flux map. The map must store flux information for the entire light source mesh. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with the number of light triangles, as each triangle is processed independently. Performance may degrade if the radiant flux map is very large or if mipmap generation is expensive. Strengths: Efficient approximation of radiant flux for area lights using standard texture sampling hardware. Simpler than dense sampling. Limitations: Potential visual errors due to z-axis intersection handling and flux leakage from mipmapping. Accuracy depends on the quality of the radiant flux map and the mipmap approximation. When to use: When efficient direct illumination approximation is needed for area lights in LPV, and high precision is not critical. Suitable for real-time applications where dense sampling is too expensive. When not to use: When high-fidelity direct illumination is required, or when the light source has complex geometry that cannot be well-approximated by a 2D texture map. Textured Area Lights Sampling was introduced in the context of Light Propagation Volumes (LPV) for real-time global illumination. The method was proposed to address the lack of a strategy in the original LPV technique to sample the surface of area light sources efficiently. It builds on the concept of voxelizing light triangles into the LPV grid and using texture mapping to store and retrieve flux information. The approach references the OpenGL standard specifications for mipmap level calculation (Segal and Akeley, 1999)., https://www.scitepress.org/publishedPapers/2022/108416/pdf/index.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) SCITEPRESS - SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY PUBLICATIONS, https://www.scitepress.org/PublishedPapers/2022/108416/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: AABB-based Emission Direction Sampling
head: Non-Homogeneous Radiance Distribution Approximation
body: AABB-based Emission Direction Sampling is a method to approximate the radiance distribution of a triangle mesh when the emission direction varies across its surface, by using an emission direction per vertex and interpolating within an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the projected intersection area. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by avoiding complex spherical harmonic fitting for non-homogeneous lights or texture-based flux maps, instead using a set of clamped cosine lobes distributed between interpolated corner directions of the projected AABB. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh with vertices having positions, emission directions, and texture coordinates (for flux, though this method focuses on direction). An LPV (Light Propagation Volume) grid. The intersection area between the triangle's projection and an LPV cell face. Output: A set of clamped cosine lobes injected into the LPV cells intersected along the z-axis, approximating the radiance distribution. Data Structures: Triangle: Defined by vertices V0, V1, V2. Each vertex has a position \mathbf{p}i and an emission direction \mathbf{d}i. LPV Cell Face: A 2D plane segment within the LPV grid. AABB: Defined by minimum and maximum coordinates (x{min}, y{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}) in the 2D space of the LPV cell face. Cosine Lobe: Defined by a center direction \mathbf{c}, a power p (related to the cosine lobe degree), and a weight w. Steps: 1. Compute Projection: Project the triangle onto the LPV cell face where the intersection occurs. 2. Compute Initial AABB: Compute the AABB of the intersection area between the LPV cell face and the projection of the initial triangle, before any expansion. This involves finding the polygon formed by: Projected vertices of the triangle that are inside the LPV cell face. Corners of the LPV cell face that are inside the triangle projection. Intersection points between the edges of the LPV cell face and the edges of the triangle. Let this polygon be P. Compute the AABB of P. 3. Compute Corner Emission Directions: For each of the four corners of the AABB, compute the emission direction: Determine the 2D coordinates of the corner in the LPV face space. Map these coordinates back to barycentric coordinates (\lambda0, \lambda1, \lambda2) within the original triangle. Interpolate the vertex emission directions: \mathbf{d}{corner} = \lambda0 \mathbf{d}0 + \lambda1 \mathbf{d}1 + \lambda2 \mathbf{d}2. Normalize \mathbf{d}{corner}. 4. Distribute Cosine Lobes: Distribute clamped cosine lobes between the emission directions from the four corners of the AABB. The lobes are distributed vertically and horizontally at angular distances equal to the cosine lobe degree. Let the cosine lobe degree be k. The angular step size is \Delta \theta = \frac{1}{k} (or similar, depending on implementation details not fully specified, but "angular distances equal to the cosine lobe degree" implies a relationship between the lobe power and the sampling grid). For each lobe, calculate its center direction \mathbf{c} based on the corner directions and the angular distribution. The power p of the cosine lobe is determined by the "cosine lobe degree". Typically, a clamped cosine lobe is defined as L(\omega) = (\mathbf{c} \cdot \omega)^p for \mathbf{c} \cdot \omega > 0, else 0. 5. Inject into LPV: Each generated cosine lobe is injected into the LPV cell with a weight of 1. The distribution is created locally. Only the final approximation, with a weight equal to the number of lobes required for the approximation, is injected into all LPV cells intersected along the z-axis. Use atomic operations to update spherical harmonic coefficients and counters in LPV cells to avoid concurrency problems. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def aabbbasedemissiondirectionsampling(triangle, lpvcellface, lpvgrid, cosinelobedegree): # Step 1: Project triangle onto LPV cell face projectedtriangle = projecttriangleontoplane(triangle, lpvcellface) # Step 2: Compute AABB of intersection polygon # Find polygon vertices: # 1. Projected triangle vertices inside LPV cell face insidevertices = [v for v in projectedtriangle.vertices if isinsideface(v, lpvcellface)] # 2. LPV cell face corners inside triangle projection facecornersinside = [c for c in lpvcellface.corners if isinsidetriangle(c, projectedtriangle)] # 3. Intersection points between LPV cell face edges and triangle edges intersectionpoints = computeedgeintersections(lpvcellface.edges, projectedtriangle.edges) allpoints = insidevertices + facecornersinside + intersectionpoints aabb = computeaabb(allpoints) # Step 3: Compute emission directions at AABB corners corners = getaabbcorners(aabb) cornerdirections = [] for corner in corners: # Compute barycentric coordinates of corner in original triangle barycentric = computebarycentriccoordinates(corner, triangle) # Interpolate emission directions dir = barycentric[0] triangle.vertices[0].emissiondir + \ barycentric[1] triangle.vertices[1].emissiondir + \ barycentric[2] triangle.vertices[2].emissiondir dir = normalize(dir) cornerdirections.append(dir) # Step 4: Distribute cosine lobes lobes = [] # Determine angular steps based on cosinelobedegree # Assuming a grid of lobes covering the range between corner directions # The exact distribution logic (vertical/horizontal) needs to be implemented # based on the specific definition of "angular distances equal to the cosine lobe degree" # For simplicity, assume a uniform grid of lobes between the min and max directions # This part is ambiguous in the source, so we outline the concept numlobsx = cosinelobedegree numlobsy = cosinelobedegree for i in range(numlobsx): for j in range(numlobsy): # Interpolate between corner directions to get lobe center # This is a simplified assumption; the actual method might use a more complex interpolation tx = i / (numlobsx - 1) ty = j / (numlobsy - 1) # Interpolate between corner directions based on tx and ty # This requires a mapping from 2D grid to the 4 corners # For example, if corners are ordered, we can interpolate centerdir = interpolatebetweencorners(cornerdirections, tx, ty) lobe = CosineLobe(center=centerdir, power=cosinelobedegree, weight=1) lobes.append(lobe) # Step 5: Inject into LPV # The final approximation weight is the number of lobes totalweight = len(lobes) # Inject into all LPV cells intersected along the z-axis for lpvcell in lpvgrid.getcellsintersectedbyzaxis(lpvcellface): injectcosinelobeintocell(lpvcell, lobes, totalweight) return lobes def projecttriangleontoplane(triangle, plane): # Project each vertex of the triangle onto the plane projectedvertices = [] for v in triangle.vertices: projectedv = projectpointontoplane(v.position, plane) projectedvertices.append(Vertex(projectedv, v.emissiondir)) return Triangle(projectedvertices) def isinsideface(point, face): # Check if point is inside the 2D polygon of the face return ispointinpolygon(point, face.polygon) def isinsidetriangle(point, triangle): # Check if point is inside the triangle barycentric = computebarycentriccoordinates(point, triangle) return all(b >= 0 for b in barycentric) def computeedgeintersections(edges1, edges2): # Compute intersection points between two sets of edges intersections = [] for e1 in edges1: for e2 in edges2: pt = intersectsegments(e1, e2) if pt is not None: intersections.append(pt) return intersections def computeaabb(points): # Compute AABB from a list of points if not points: return None minx = min(p.x for p in points) miny = min(p.y for p in points) maxx = max(p.x for p in points) maxy = max(p.y for p in points) return AABB(minx, miny, maxx, maxy) def getaabbcorners(aabb): # Return the four corners of the AABB return [ Point(aabb.minx, aabb.miny), Point(aabb.maxx, aabb.miny), Point(aabb.maxx, aabb.maxy), Point(aabb.minx, aabb.maxy) ] def computebarycentriccoordinates(point, triangle): # Compute barycentric coordinates of a point in 2D relative to a triangle # This assumes the point is in the same plane as the triangle # Use standard barycentric coordinate calculation v0 = triangle.vertices[1].position - triangle.vertices[0].position v1 = triangle.vertices[2].position - triangle.vertices[0].position v2 = point.position - triangle.vertices[0].position dot00 = dot(v0, v0) dot01 = dot(v0, v1) dot02 = dot(v0, v2) dot11 = dot(v1, v1) dot12 = dot(v1, v2) invdenom = 1 / (dot00 dot11 - dot01 dot01) u = (dot11 dot02 - dot01 dot12) invdenom v = (dot00 dot12 - dot01 dot02) invdenom w = 1 - u - v return (w, u, v) def interpolatebetweencorners(directions, tx, ty): # Interpolate between the four corner directions based on tx and ty # This is a simplified interpolation; the actual method may vary # Assume directions are ordered: bottom-left, bottom-right, top-right, top-left # Interpolate along x first, then y dirbottom = interpolatetwo(directions[0], directions[1], tx) dirtop = interpolatetwo(directions[3], directions[2], tx) return interpolatetwo(dirbottom, dirtop, ty) def interpolatetwo(dir1, dir2, t): # Linearly interpolate between two directions and normalize dir = (1 - t) dir1 + t dir2 return normalize(dir) def injectcosinelobeintocell(cell, lobes, weight): # Inject the lobes into the cell using atomic operations for lobe in lobes: atomicaddsphericalharmoniccoefficients(cell, lobe, weight) atomicincrementcounter(cell, weight) Parameters: cosinelobedegree: Determines the power of the cosine lobes and the angular distribution. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The AABB of the intersection area projection can cover two LPV cells, potentially causing minor visual errors because a single radiance distribution is generated for the AABB. Concurrency problems can arise if several VPLs are injected into an LPV cell at the same time. Atomic operations must be used to update spherical harmonic coefficients and counters. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement compared to spherical harmonic fitting for non-homogeneous lights. Efficient for LPV systems. Limitations: Can produce minor visual errors if the intersection area covers multiple LPV cells. When to use: When using LPV for global illumination and triangle meshes with varying emission directions. When not to use: When high accuracy is required for non-homogeneous lights, or when the intersection area is large and spans multiple LPV cells. This method is part of the LPV (Light Propagation Volume) voxelization sampling pipeline, specifically for handling non-homogeneous radiance distributions from triangle meshes. name: Proxy-GS Cluster Rasterizer
head: RendererRasterClustersLod
body: The Proxy-GS Cluster Rasterizer is a GPU-accelerated rasterization pipeline designed for clustered 3D primitives, specifically optimized for the inference phase of Structured 3D Gaussian Splatting using Vulkan mesh shaders. It differs from standard rasterization by employing a cluster-based traversal and culling mechanism to handle Level of Detail (LOD) structures efficiently, building on the general principles of Rasterization and GPU Shaders. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on triangle-based intersection or simple bounding box culling, this method uses a dedicated compute-shader-driven traversal tree to manage large sets of Gaussian clusters, enabling real-time rendering with unified occlusion priors. The method implements a Vulkan-based pipeline where mesh shaders generate cluster data and compute shaders handle the spatial traversal and culling. The implementation requires specific Vulkan extensions and shader compilation with defined macros. Inputs: Scene geometry (meshes or point clouds converted to clusters), camera parameters (view/projection matrices), and configuration flags for cluster size and traversal features. Outputs: Rendered image buffers and depth maps. In the Proxy-GS context, it also supports generating depth caches for training priors. The core data management relies on the shaderio::SceneBuilding structure, which aggregates scene state into a single buffer object. This structure is allocated as a storage buffer (msceneBuildBuffer) with uniform and indirect buffer usage capabilities. Layout of shaderio::SceneBuilding: numRenderInstances: Integer count of renderable instances. maxRenderClusters: Integer maximum number of clusters. maxTraversalInfos: Integer maximum number of traversal info entries. indirectDispatchGroups: Structure for compute dispatch parameters (gridY=1, gridZ=1). renderClusterInfos: Storage buffer for cluster metadata. instanceSortKeys: Storage buffer for instance sorting keys (4 or 8 byte alignment). instanceSortValues: Storage buffer for instance sorting values (4 or 8 byte alignment). traversalGroupInfos: Storage buffer for traversal group information (enabled if USESEPARATEGROUPS is set). traversalNodeInfos: Storage buffer for traversal node data. Additional buffers include msceneDataBuffer for cluster info and sort data, and msceneTraversalBuffer for traversal node infos, all requiring 4 or 8 byte alignment. The behavior is controlled by compile-time macros and configuration flags: CLUSTERVERTEXCOUNT: Defines vertices per cluster. Value: rscene.scene->mmaxClusterVertices. CLUSTERTRIANGLECOUNT: Defines triangles per cluster. Value: rscene.scene->mmaxClusterTriangles. MESHSHADERWORKGROUPSIZE: Mesh shader workgroup size. Value: 32. USESORTING: Boolean flag. If true, enables instance sort keys and values buffers. USESEPARATEGROUPS: Boolean flag. If true, enables traversal group infos buffer and a separate compute shader for traversal. 1. Shader Compilation: Compile mesh and fragment shaders using the macros defined above. Compile compute shaders for traversal presort, initialization, execution, group management, and build setup. 2. Buffer Allocation: Allocate msceneBuildBuffer for the shaderio::SceneBuilding struct. Allocate msceneDataBuffer for cluster info, sort keys/values, and traversal group infos. Allocate msceneTraversalBuffer for traversal node infos. 3. Descriptor Binding: Bind descriptor sets for the frame Uniform Buffer Object (UBO), readback Storage Buffer Object (SSBO), geometries SSBO, render instances SSBO, scene building SSBO/UBO, Hierarchical Z (HiZ) texture, and streaming buffers. 4. Pipeline Creation: Create a pipeline layout with the descriptor set layout and a push constant range of 4 bytes. Create the graphics pipeline linking the mesh and fragment shaders. Configure rasterization state for front-face winding and culling modes. 5. Execution: Dispatch compute shaders for traversal and culling, then execute the graphics pipeline to render the clusters. """ # 1. Define compile-time macros based on scene configuration CLUSTERVERTEXCOUNT = sceneconfig.maxclustervertices CLUSTERTRIANGLECOUNT = sceneconfig.maxclustertriangles MESHSHADERWORKGROUPSIZE = 32 USESORTING = sceneconfig.enableinstancesorting USESEPARATEGROUPS = sceneconfig.enableseparatetraversalgroups # 2. name: Multi-Plane Projection Voxelization and Aggregation
head: MPP Pre-processing
body: Multi-Plane Projection (MPP) Voxelization and Aggregation is a pre-processing method that converts multi-view RGB-D images into a 3D volume representation by projecting point clouds onto a fixed set of parallel planes and aggregating them with distance-based weights. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its explicit discretization of space into a configurable number of planes and its two-stage weighting scheme (horizontal and vertical distance) to handle depth uncertainty during neural rendering initialization. Inputs: N RGB-D images with known camera poses. For each image i: intrinsic matrix Ki, extrinsic matrix Ei, color image Ii, and depth image Di. Hyperparameters: numplanes (number of parallel planes, typically 32), a (horizontal weight exponent, typically 1), b (vertical weight exponent, typically 1). Outputs: Voxelization data: u, v, d (coordinates and depths), selectindex, groupbelongs, indexineachgroup, distance, eachsplitmaxnum, delta. Aggregation data: weightaverage, distancetodepthmin. Data Structures: The method uses NumPy arrays stored in.npz format. pointclouds: Shape [4, M], homogeneous coordinates of projected points. pointcloudscolors: Shape [3, M], RGB colors. depthmasks: Shape [1, M], validity mask. Voxelization output keys: u, v, d (sorted coordinates), selectindex (indices of valid points), groupbelongs (plane index for each point), indexineachgroup (local index within a plane group), distance (vertical distance to depth minimum), eachsplitmaxnum (max points per plane), delta (plane spacing). Aggregation output keys: weightaverage (normalized weights), distancetodepthmin (vertical distances). Steps: 1. Preprocessing and Projection: a. Read intrinsic matrix Ki and extrinsic matrix Ei. b. Check for invalid poses (e.g., Ei[0,0] < -10^{10} or containing -inf) and skip them to prevent numerical errors. c. Optionally subsample pixels using a random mask with proportion randomselectproportion (typically 1/10) to reduce resource usage. d. Compute the projection matrix: Pi = Ki Ei^{-1}. e. For each pixel (u, v) in the image, compute homogeneous image coordinates p{img} = [u, v, 1, 1]^T. f. Project to 3D: p{3d} = Pi^{-1} p{img} (or equivalent back-projection using depth). The source code notes: positionimage = transformmatrix.dot(pointclouds) where transformmatrix is derived from intrinsics and extrinsics. g. Extract depth d = p{3d}[2] (z-coordinate in camera space). h. Accumulate all 3D points, colors, and depths into global arrays pointclouds, pointcloudscolors, depthmasks. 2. Voxelization (Plane Assignment): a. Define numplanes parallel planes along the viewing direction (typically Z-axis in world space or a canonical direction). b. For each 3D point, determine which plane it belongs to based on its depth/position. c. Sort points by plane index, then by horizontal distance (u, v) within each plane. d. Store sorted coordinates usorted, vsorted, depth dpositionsorted, and group indices. e. Compute selectindex to identify valid points and groupbelongs to map points to planes. 3. Aggregation (Weighting): a. Load voxelization data: selectindex, indexineachgroup, distance. b. For each group (plane), compute the minimum depth: d{min} = \min(d{selected}). c. Compute vertical distance for each point: dist{vert} = d - d{min}. d. Compute horizontal distance weight: w1 = (1 - dist{horiz})^a. e. Compute vertical distance weight: w2 = \frac{1}{1 + dist{vert}^b}. f. Combine weights: w{renew} = w1 \times w2. g. Normalize weights per group: w{norm} = \frac{w{renew}}{\sum w{renew}}. h. Return weightaverage and distancetodepthmin. 4. Volume Rendering (Accumulation): The aggregated weights are used in the volume rendering loop. For sample i along a ray: C = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ti \cdot (1 - \exp(-\rhoi \cdot \deltai)) \cdot ci where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \rhoj \cdot \deltaj) is the transmittance, \rhoi is density, \deltai is step size, and ci is color. The source code implements this accumulation as: final = final + (tf.exp(-tf.reducesum(sigma[:, 0:i,:,:,:] delta[i], axis=1))) (1 - tf.exp(-(sigma[:, i,:,:,:] delta[i]))) conv12[:, i,:,:,:]. Here, sigma represents density \rho, delta is step size, conv12 is the color/weight product ci, and i is the sample index along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeaggregationweights(depthselected, groupbelongs, a=1.0, b=1.0): numpoints = len(depthselected) weight1 = np.ones(numpoints) weight2 = np.ones(numpoints) weightaverage = np.zeros(numpoints) distancetodepthmin = np.zeros(numpoints) # Group points by plane index groups = np.unique(groupbelongs) for g in groups: mask = groupbelongs == g indices = np.where(mask)[0] begin, end = indices[0], indices[-1] + 1 # Vertical distance to depth minimum mind = np.min(depthselected[begin:end]) distancetodepthmin[begin:end] = depthselected[begin:end] - mind # Horizontal distance weight (source uses distance variable) # Assuming disthoriz is precomputed normalized horizontal distance disthoriz = np.zeros(end - begin) weight1[begin:end] = (1.0 - disthoriz) a # Vertical distance weight weight2[begin:end] = 1.0 / (1.0 + distancetodepthmin[begin:end] b) # Combine and normalize weightrenew = weight1[begin:end] weight2[begin:end] weightsum = np.sum(weightrenew) if weightsum > 0: weightaverage[begin:end] = weightrenew / weightsum else: weightaverage[begin:end] = 0.0 return weightaverage, distancetodepthmin Parameters: numplanes: Number of parallel planes, typically 32. a: Hyperparameter for horizontal distance weighting, typically 1. b: Hyperparameter for vertical distance weighting, typically 1. Edge cases and pitfalls: Invalid camera poses (e.g., containing -inf or Ei[0,0] < -10^{10}) must be skipped to prevent numerical errors. Data types must be managed carefully; np.uint32 is resource-consuming for storage. Random subsampling (randomselectproportion typically 1/10) reduces memory but may degrade quality. A GPU-accelerated volume reconstruction method that maps projection data onto volume slices using texture mapping. It solves the problem of efficiently aggregating multi-angle projection data into a 3D volume without requiring intermediate merge operations. It is distinguished from its sibling methods by grouping spreading operations per slice and using a large texture sheet for accumulation, which eliminates the need for a final merge step but requires all projections to remain in memory throughout the reconstruction. Choose it when memory is sufficient and GPU texture units are available; avoid it when memory is strictly constrained. Time Complexity: Dominated by 2D-to-3D projection of all pixels and sorting/aggregation steps. Memory Complexity: High, as it stores all projected points, colors, masks, and intermediate aggregation arrays. Performance: Efficient for scenes with moderate complexity; scaling is linear with the number of pixels and views. Strengths: Simple pipeline, handles occlusions via depth-based weighting, compatible with standard neural rendering loops. Limitations: Requires accurate depth maps; sensitive to depth noise; memory-intensive for high-resolution images without subsampling. When to use: Initializing neural radiance fields from RGB-D data with limited memory compared to dense voxel grids. When not to use: When depth sensors are unavailable or when memory constraints prevent storing all projected points even with subsampling. The method is implemented in the PCMP-NeRF repository as a pre-processing pipeline for neural radiance fields. It is designed to handle Matterport3D and ScanNet datasets, leveraging undistorted RGB-D images and camera parameters. name: Texture Spreading Backprojection
head: Back-projection Initialization, Texture Spreading, X-ray Density Initialization
body: Texture Spreading Backprojection is a GPU-accelerated volume reconstruction method that maps projection data onto volume slices using texture mapping. It solves the problem of efficiently aggregating multi-angle projection data into a 3D volume without requiring intermediate merge operations. It is distinguished from its sibling methods by grouping spreading operations per slice and using a large texture sheet for accumulation, which eliminates the need for a final merge step but requires all projections to remain in memory throughout the reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 2D projection images (one per projection angle), volume dimensions (width, height, depth/slices). Outputs: A 3D volume dataset (stack of slices). Data Structures: Projection Textures: Each projection image is bound as a 1D texture. Texture Sheet: A large 2D texture container (sheet) composed of sub-textures, where each sub-texture holds the contribution from a single projection angle for the current slice being processed. Slice Stack: A buffer or texture stack representing the current volume slice being reconstructed; only one slice stack is maintained in memory at a time. Steps: 1. Initialize Back-projection Parameters: Assume constant attenuation \sigmat = \sigma and unit ray length L=1, yielding p = \sigma. 2. Initialize Slice Processing: Select the current volume slice index z to reconstruct. 3. Create Texture Sheet: Allocate a large texture sheet containing sub-textures for each projection angle. 4. Spread Projections: For each projection angle i, bind the projection as a 1D texture and spread it across the buffer to form its contribution to the slice. 5. Compute Initial Density: Calculate the initial density of voxel-space points C{Vds} by averaging the pixel intensities at the projected locations across all views: C{Vds} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{o=1}^n Io[P{Io}]. 6. Multi-Pass Accumulation: Execute a fragment shader pass over the texture sheet to sum the sub-texture tiles, completing the reconstruction of the volume slice. 7. Store and Advance Slice: Save the accumulated result for slice z to the output volume stack, increment z, and repeat steps 2–6 until all slices are reconstructed. Formulas: p = \sigma C{Vds} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{o=1}^n Io[P{Io}] where Io denotes the incident pixel intensity at projected location P{Io} for view o, and n is the total number of views. Parameters: Number of Projections (n): Determined by the acquisition geometry. Texture Sheet Size: Must be large enough to hold all n sub-textures. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Constraints: All projections must remain in GPU memory until the entire volume is reconstructed, which can cause memory traffic congestion and pipeline stalls on GPUs with limited bandwidth. Precision: Using integer representations for input data can reduce memory traffic and alleviate bandwidth issues, but may introduce quantization errors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def texturespreadingbackprojection(projections, volumedims): """ Reconstructs a volume using texture spreading backprojection. """ width, height, depth = volumedims numprojections = len(projections) volume = [[[0.0] width for in range(height)] for in range(depth)] # Initialize back-projection parameters: assume constant attenuation sigmat = sigma and unit ray length L=1 for z in range(depth): # Create a large texture sheet containing sub-textures for each projection angle sheet = [[[0.0] width for in range(height)] for in range(numprojections)] # Spread each projection onto the sheet's sub-texture region for i in range(numprojections): # Bind projection i as 1D texture and spread across buffer # Implementation: map projection pixels to slice coordinates via geometric transform for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Geometric projection mapping (sources do not specify exact transform) # [Comment: Sources do not specify exact geometric transform for spreading] pass # Compute initial density by averaging pixel intensities at projected locations across all views # CVds = (1/n) sum(Io[PIo]) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): intensitysum = sum(sheet[i][y][x] for i in range(numprojections)) volume[z][y][x] = intensitysum / numprojections # Multi-pass accumulation step to sum tiles (sources do not specify exact shader passes) # [Comment: Sources do not specify multi-pass accumulation details] return volume An alternative implementation where transformation matrices are computed for each voxel to designate its sampling locations on the projections. Instead of spreading projection data onto a texture sheet, this method iterates through all projection angles in the fragment shader for each voxel, fetching and summing sample values from the projections directly. [Comment: The evidence does not specify performance trade-offs or memory access patterns for this variant.] Memory Usage: Requires all projection images to remain in GPU memory simultaneously until the entire volume is reconstructed. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels times the number of projections, O(W \times H \times D \times N), where W,H,D are volume dimensions and N is the number of projections. Performance: Can suffer from memory bandwidth bottlenecks due to repeated access to large projection datasets. Using integer representations for input data can help alleviate bandwidth issues. Strengths: No merge operation is needed at the end, as only one slice stack is maintained. Limitations: High memory consumption; unsuitable for datasets exceeding available GPU memory. Texture Spreading Backprojection was originally used for parallel-beam projection geometry by [CM03] and later extended to cone-beam geometry by [MX06]. It is a technique developed to leverage GPU texture mapping hardware for efficient volume reconstruction from projections. name: Simplicial Covering Voxelization
head: P-Buffer method, Solid Voxelization via Simplicial Covering, Voxelization of solids using simplicial coverings
body: Simplicial Covering Voxelization is a method to rasterize and voxelize 3D solids by decomposing their surface into tetrahedra connected to an origin, then using a presence buffer (P-buffer) to toggle voxel states. Unlike boundary-only methods such as Voxel Carving or Sramek's method, this approach produces a complete solid voxelization in a single pass by exploiting the parity of tetrahedron coverage. It differs from Implicit Surface Voxelization by operating directly on polygonal meshes without requiring implicit field evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D solid defined by a set of planar faces (manifold or non-manifold, with or without holes), represented as a set of triangles. A coordinate origin O (typically the centroid or arbitrary point). Output: A 3D voxel grid (P-buffer) where each voxel stores a presence bit (0 or 1) indicating if it is inside the solid. Optionally, a framebuffer with colors applied. Data Structures: P-buffer: A 3D array of bits. Each position (xi, yi, zi) stores a single bit: 0 (outside) or 1 (inside). Vertices: Points A, B, C defining the base triangle of a tetrahedron. Slopes: Precomputed incremental slope pairs m{XY} = (m{XY}^x, m{XY}^z) for edges (OA, OB, OC, AB, AC, BC), representing the change in x and z per unit step in y. Algorithm Steps: 1. Tetrahedron Construction: For every triangle of the covering of each face of the solid, construct a tetrahedron by joining the triangle vertices (A, B, C) with the origin O. 2. Sweeping Plane Determination: Determine the sweeping direction by finding the maximum absolute value of the coordinates of the normal vector of the base triangle. The method assumes rasterization with respect to the Y-direction. If the maximum is negative, invert the tetrahedron with respect to the Y coordinate; at the end, invert the resulting voxel coordinates (xi, yi, zi) to (xi, -yi, zi). 3. Initialization: Initialize the voxel matrix (P-buffer) to 0. Sort vertices A, B, C by their Y-coordinate. Let A be the vertex with the maximum Y. Set current y = Ay. Initialize triangle vertices for the current slice: Ai = A, Bi = B, Ci = C. Compute initial slopes: mB = m{AB}, mC = m{AC}. 4. Iterative Rasterization (Sweep): While y > 0: Update Edge Vertices: If By = y, set Bi = B and mB = m{OB}. Else, set mB = m{AB} and Bi = Ai + (B - A) \cdot mB. If Cy = y, set Ci = C and mC = m{OC}. Else, set mC = m{AC} and Ci = Ai + (C - A) \cdot mC. Rasterize Primary Triangle: Call Rasterize2D(Ai, Bi, Ci) to flip presence values for voxels inside the triangle slice at current y. Handle Quadrilateral Slice: If By > y > Cy, the intersection is a quadrilateral. Compute the intersection point Di = B + (C - B) \cdot m{BC}. Call Rasterize2D(Bi, Di, Ci) to handle the second triangle of the quadrilateral. Decrement and Update: Decrement y. If y < By, update mB = m{OB}. If y < Cy, update mC = m{OC}. Update Ai, Bi, Ci with the corresponding incremental slopes for the next y-slice. 5. Finalization: Transfer all positions from the P-buffer with presence value equal to 1 to the framebuffer, applying a color function that returns the corresponding color of the solid at that point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simplicialcoveringvoxelization(solidtriangles, origin, gridbounds): # Initialize P-buffer with 0s # gridbounds is (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) width = gridbounds[1] - gridbounds[0] + 1 height = gridbounds[3] - gridbounds[2] + 1 depth = gridbounds[5] - gridbounds[4] + 1 pbuffer = [[ [False for in range(depth)] for in range(height)] for in range(width)] def flipbit(x, y, z): if 0 <= x < width and 0 <= y < height and 0 <= z < depth: pbuffer[x][y][z] = not pbuffer[x][y][z] def rasterize2dtriangle(v1, v2, v3, yidx): # Sort vertices by x verts = sorted([v1, v2, v3], key=lambda v: v[0]) v1, v2, v3 = verts[0], verts[1], verts[2] # Compute slopes for edges in x-z plane m12 = (v2[2] - v1[2]) / (v2[0] - v1[0]) if v2[0] != v1[0] else 0 m23 = (v3[2] - v2[2]) / (v3[0] - v2[0]) if v3[0] != v2[0] else 0 m13 = (v3[2] - v1[2]) / (v3[0] - v1[0]) if v3[0] != v1[0] else 0 x = v1[0] zleft = v1[2] zright = v1[2] # Upper triangle (v1 to v2) while x < v2[0]: for z in range(int(zleft), int(zright) + 1): flipbit(int(x), yidx, z) x += 1 zleft += m12 zright += m13 # Lower triangle (v2 to v3) while x <= v3[0]: for z in range(int(zleft), int(zright) + 1): flipbit(int(x), yidx, z) x += 1 zleft += m23 zright += m13 for triangle in solidtriangles: A, B, C = triangle # Step 2: Determine sweeping direction (assumed Y for this implementation) # If normal's max abs coord is negative, invert tetrahedron Y and final voxels # Step 3: Sort vertices by Y vertices = sorted([A, B, C], key=lambda v: v[1], reverse=True) A, B, C = vertices[0], vertices[1], vertices[2] y = A[1] Ai = list(A) Bi = list(B) Ci = list(C) # Compute initial slopes # Slope mXY = (X - Y) / (X.y - Y.y) mAB = [(B[0]-A[0])/(B[1]-A[1]), (B[2]-A[2])/(B[1]-A[1])] mAC = [(C[0]-A[0])/(C[1]-A[1]), (C[2]-A[2])/(C[1]-A[1])] mBC = [(C[0]-B[0])/(C[1]-B[1]), (C[2]-B[2])/(C[1]-B[1])] mOA = [(A[0]-origin[0])/(A[1]-origin[1]), (A[2]-origin[2])/(A[1]-origin[1])] mOB = [(B[0]-origin[0])/(B[1]-origin[1]), (B[2]-origin[2])/(B[1]-origin[1])] mOC = [(C[0]-origin[0])/(C[1]-origin[1]), (C[2]-origin[2])/(C[1]-origin[1])] mB = mAB mC = mAC # Step 4: Iterative Rasterization while y > 0: # Update Edge Vertices if B[1] == y: Bi = list(B) mB = mOB else: mB = mAB Bi = [Ai[0] + (B[0]-A[0])mB[0], Ai[1], Ai[2] + (B[2]-A[2])mB[1]] if C[1] == y: Ci = list(C) mC = mOC else: mC = mAC Ci = [Ai[0] + (C[0]-A[0])mC[0], Ai[1], Ai[2] + (C[2]-A[2])mC[1]] # Rasterize Primary Triangle rasterize2dtriangle(Ai, Bi, Ci, y) # Handle Quadrilateral Slice if B[1] > y > C[1]: # Intersection point Di on edge BC Di = [B[0] + (C[0]-B[0])mBC[0], B[1], B[2] + (C[2]-B[2])mBC[1]] rasterize2dtriangle(Bi, Di, Ci, y) # Decrement and Update y -= 1 if y < B[1]: mB = mOB if y < C[1]: mC = mOC # Update Ai, Bi, Ci with incremental slopes for next slice Ai = [Ai[0] + mOA[0], Ai[1], Ai[2] + mOA[1]] Bi = [Bi[0] + mB[0], Bi[1], Bi[2] + mB[1]] Ci = [Ci[0] + mC[0], Ci[1], Ci[2] + mC[1]] return pbuffer Parameters: P-buffer: Stores presence values as a single bit (0 or 1). Color: For homogeneous solids, all voxels have the same color. For heterogeneous solids, color depends on solid properties at the point. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Quadrilateral Slices: When By > yi > Cy, the slice is a quadrilateral, not a triangle. This is handled by decomposing it into two triangles using the intersection point Di on edge BC. Aliasing: The main problem is aliasing, appearing by using integer arithmetic on floating objects. This minimizes but does not eliminate the effect. Boundary-Only: To obtain boundary-only rasterization, consider only spans between Bi and Ci (or Di and Ci when By > y > Cy). Time Complexity: Depends on the number of faces of the solid and the resolution. Performance tests on a Pentium III 1GHz, 768 MB RAM showed that for a solid with 100,250 vertices and 202,520 faces at resolution 512, the method took 24.635 seconds, while Sramek's method took 237.601 seconds. For boundary-only rasterization at 512 resolution, it took 4.715 seconds vs Sramek's 244.893 seconds. Memory Complexity: Requires a P-buffer of size proportional to the voxel grid resolution. Strengths: Obtains a complete voxelization of the solid in one pass. Simple and robust, suitable for graphic hardware implementation as it does not use additional data structures or complex operations. Limitations: Aliasing effects due to integer arithmetic. Performance depends on the number of faces, unlike Sramek's method which depends only on resolution and volume. The method was presented in. It is designed for 3D displays and voxelization of solids delimited by planar faces, including those with holes, manifold or non-manifold structures. Voxelization of solids using simplicial coverings, http://wscg.zcu.cz/wscg2004/Papers2004Short/J53.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Feature Volume Rendering
head: Neural Volume Rendering with Feature Volumes, Volume Rendering to 2D Feature Map, Volumetric Rendering in Feature Space
body: Feature Volume Rendering projects a 3D voxel grid containing high-level semantic or structural feature vectors onto a 2D feature map using volumetric integration, rather than directly rendering RGB colors. It solves the problem of decoupling scene representation from appearance, allowing a downstream 2D convolutional neural network (CNN) to decode the final image. It differs from standard NeRF by outputting a feature map instead of an RGB image, relying on an explicit voxel grid for feature storage rather than implicit MLPs. Inputs: Camera pose \kappa (origin o and direction d). Voxel grid V containing density \sigma and feature vectors f at voxel centers. Outputs: 2D feature map F{2D}. Expected depth \hat{\rho}. Data Structures: Voxel Grid V: A 3D array indexed as V[z][y][x]. Each voxel stores a scalar density \sigma and a feature vector f of dimension D. Sampling Points: Points r(t) along rays. Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel, define a ray r(t) = o + td. 2. Sampling: Sample N points along the ray within the scene bounds [tn, tf]. 3. Interpolation: For each sample point r(t), trilinearly interpolate the density \sigma(r(t)) and feature vector f(r(t)) from the voxel grid V. 4. Accumulation: Compute transmittance T(t) and accumulated feature vector F(r) and depth \hat{\rho} using volumetric rendering equations. 5. Decoding: Feed the resulting 2D feature map into a CNN decoder to produce the output image \hat{i}. Formulas: Ray equation: r(t) = o + td Transmittance (probability of light passing through previous points): T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(r(s)) ds\right) Accumulated Feature Vector F(r) for a ray: F(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(r(t)) f(r(t)) dt Derived from (color accumulation) and (feature pooling). The sources describe combining feature vectors and density values via volumetric rendering to form a feature map. Accumulated Depth \hat{\rho}: \hat{\rho} = \frac{\int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(r(t)) t dt}{\int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigma(r(t)) dt} Derived from ("get the expected depth \hat{\rho} along each ray from the volume rendering process") and standard volume rendering definitions. Parameters: Number of samples N: Not given in the sources. Feature vector dimension D: Not given in the sources. Integration bounds [tn, tf]: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Exponential transmittance can underflow for high density or large step sizes; clamp \sigma \cdot \Delta t or use alpha compositing approximations. When to use: When the scene structure is better represented by explicit features and a separate decoder is desired. name: Forward Projection
head: 3D → 2D Forward Projection, Voxel-to-Detector Projection, project
body: Forward projection maps a 3D volume dataset into 2D projection space (sinograms) by simulating line integrals of X-ray attenuation along acquisition trajectories defined by a geometry object. It serves as the forward model in iterative reconstruction algorithms, such as SIRT or PWLS, where it computes estimated projections from a current volume estimate to calculate residuals. Unlike spectral or filtered methods that modify data content during projection, this method performs a standard additive projection without spectral effects. Inputs and Outputs: vol: Input 3D volume array (float32). proj: Output projection array, initialized as zeros with dtype float32. geometry: Projection geometry object defining the acquisition setup (source, detector, and rotation parameters). sign: Scalar, either +1 or -1, determining whether to add or subtract the projected data. settings.subsets: Integer specifying the number of memory-efficient subsets for large volumes. Data Structures: The method relies on the ASTRA Toolbox data structures. volgeom: Geometry descriptor for the volume, created from vol dimensions and physical spacing. projgeom: Geometry descriptor for the projections, derived from geometry. volid: ASTRA data handle linked to the volume memory. sinid: ASTRA data handle linked to the projection memory. projectorid: ASTRA projector handle (type 'cuda3d') linking volgeom and projgeom. Steps: 1. Preprocessing and Contiguity Check: Check if vol is contiguous in memory. If not, create a contiguous copy voltemp = numpy.ascontiguousarray(volume). If vol is a numpy.memmap, ensure voltemp is linked to the original memory layout for efficient back-copying. 2. Subset Generation: Initialize the output proj array to zeros. Determine the number of subsets from settings.subsets. Loop over subsets generated by the internal subset generator. 3. Linking and Projector Creation: Link the volume data to ASTRA using the original array: volid = astra.data3d.link('-vol', volgeom, volume). Link the projection subset to ASTRA: sinid = astra.data3d.link('-sino', projgeom, projections). Create the CUDA 3D projector: projectorid = astra.createprojector('cuda3d', projgeom, volgeom). 4. Execution: Perform the forward projection operation. The specific accumulation function depends on filtering: if not filtered, call asex.accumulateBP(projectorid, volid, sinid); if filtered, call asex.accumulateFDK(projectorid, volid, sinid). 5. Cleanup and Update: Delete ASTRA data handles: astra.data3d.delete(volid) and astra.data3d.delete(sinid). Delete the projector handle: astra.algorithm.delete(projectorid). Update the original subset array with the contiguous copy. If vol was a memmap, copy the results back: volume[:] = voltemp. 6. Sign Application: The sign parameter is applied during the accumulation by passing it to forwardprojectblockadd(subsetc, volume, progeom, volgeom, sign) where it acts as +1 or -1 to add or subtract the data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import astra def forwardproject(volume, proj, geometry, sign=1.0, settings=None): """ Forward projects a volume into sinogram space using ASTRA CUDA3D projector. """ if settings is None: settings = type('Settings', (), {'subsets': 1})() numsubsets = settings.subsets # Handle memory contiguity and memmap if isinstance(volume, np.memmap): voltemp = np.ascontiguousarray(volume) ismemmap = True elif not volume.flags['CCONTIGUOUS']: voltemp = np.ascontiguousarray(volume) ismemmap = False else: voltemp = volume ismemmap = False # Initialize output proj[:] = 0.0 # Loop over subsets for i in range(numsubsets): # Generate subset geometry and data slice # The sources do not provide the internal subset generator implementation progeom, volgeom, subsetslice = getsubsetgeometryandslice(geometry, volume.shape, proj.shape, i, numsubsets) subset = proj[subsetslice] # Link data to ASTRA (uses original volume array, not voltemp) volid = astra.data3d.link('-vol', volgeom, volume) sinid = astra.data3d.link('-sino', progeom, subset) # Create projector projectorid = astra.createprojector('cuda3d', progeom, volgeom) # Execute forward projection # Uses asex.accumulateBP if not filtered, else asex.accumulateFDK asex.accumulateBP(projectorid, volid, sinid) # Cleanup astra.data3d.delete(volid) astra.data3d.delete(sinid) astra.algorithm.delete(projectorid) # Apply sign via block add function forwardprojectblockadd(subset, volume, progeom, volgeom, sign) # Copy back if memmap if ismemmap: volume[:] = voltemp def getsubsetgeometryandslice(geometry, volshape, projshape, subsetidx, numsubsets): # Placeholder for internal subset generator logic return geometry, geometry, slice(None) def forwardprojectblockadd(subset, volume, progeom, volgeom, sign): # Applies sign (+1 or -1) to the projected data subset[:] = sign Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Contiguity: ASTRA requires contiguous memory buffers. Non-contiguous arrays must be copied, which incurs memory overhead. Memmap Handling: When using numpy.memmap, the temporary contiguous array must be correctly linked and copied back to avoid data loss or memory leaks. Data Types: The volume and projection arrays must be float32 to match ASTRA's expectations. Geometry Consistency: The volgeom and projgeom must be consistent with the physical dimensions and pixel sizes of the input data. A simulation technique to generate synthetic X-ray projection data from a 3D volume using a parallel beam geometry, assuming a perfectly monochromatic source and ideal detector response. The forward projection operator is configured for parallel beam geometry with uniform projection angles between 0° and 180°, a detector width of 300 pixels, and each simulation time step projected independently as a static volume. High-quality FBP reconstruction requires at least 471 projections for a 300-pixel detector, with 720 used conservatively. Computes the Radon transform for each z-slice in the voxelized object using a built-in Radon function, passes the resulting sinograms through a Ram-Lak filter in the Fourier domain, and performs coordinate system remapping to account for refraction at the air-vial interface and non-telecentricity of the optical source. Generates 2D projections from a 3D Fourier-space reconstruction by sampling central slices through the 3D volume, implementing the Central Slice Theorem. It extends 2D projection coordinates to 3D by setting the third coordinate to zero, applies a 3×3 rotation matrix inverse to map coordinates to the reconstruction space, and performs trilinear or tricubic interpolation with phase modulation for translation. Gradients are computed via chain rule extension for rotation matrices and spatial derivatives for interpolation kernels. An algebraic reconstruction technique that modifies the standard Simultaneous Iterative Reconstruction Technique (SIRT) to be resilient to outliers in projection data by employing a Student's t-distribution likelihood model. It builds on Forward Projection by enabling specific robust weighting within the ASTRA projector framework. Unlike standard SIRT, which minimizes the L2-norm of residuals and is sensitive to noise spikes, Robust SIRT down-weights large residuals, making it suitable for data with impulsive noise or artifacts. Computes the length of intersection between rays and voxels to project volume data into sinogram bins. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly calculating geometric ray-voxel intersections rather than relying on iterative reconstruction or simplified binning approximations. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels and the number of projection angles. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the volume and projection data. Performance: Highly efficient on NVIDIA GPUs due to the CUDA3D projector implementation. Strengths: Supports large datasets via subset splitting to reduce peak memory usage. Limitations: Requires GPU memory; dependent on ASTRA Toolbox availability and compatibility. Forward projection is a fundamental operation in computed tomography (CT) reconstruction, simulating the physical process of X-ray attenuation. The ASTRA Toolbox provides efficient CUDA-based projectors for 2D and 3D image reconstruction.
