name: Natural Neighbor Interpolation
head: Sibson interpolation, Voronoi interpolation
body: Natural neighbor interpolation is a spatial interpolation method that determines the value of a query point based on the geometric relationship between its Voronoi cell and the Voronoi cells of its neighboring seed points. It solves the problem of creating smooth, continuous, and monotonic interpolation fields where each seed point exerts only local influence, ensuring that the original seed values remain unchanged. It is distinguished from linear or polynomial interpolation by its adaptive weighting scheme, which relies on the topology of the Voronoi diagram rather than fixed distance metrics or basis functions. Inputs: A set of seed customization points S = \{p1, p2, \dots, pN\} with associated scalar values V = \{v1, v2, \dots, vN\}. A query point q for which the interpolated value vq is required. A bounding box B defining the finite domain of the volume data. Outputs: The interpolated scalar value vq. Data Structures: Voronoi Diagram: A partitioning of the space into cells VC{pi}, where each cell VC{pi} contains all points closer to seed point pi than to any other seed point in S. Intersection Volumes: The geometric volume of the intersection between the new Voronoi cell of q and the original Voronoi cells of its neighbors. Steps: 1. Construct Initial Voronoi Diagram: Compute the Voronoi diagram for the set of seed points S. 2. Handle Infinite Cells: Limit the Voronoi diagram to the bounding box B of the volume data set so that all Voronoi cells have a finite volume. 3. Insert Query Point: Form the augmented set Q = S \cup \{q\} and compute a new Voronoi diagram for Q. 4. Identify New Cell: Identify the new Voronoi cell VCq for point q in the new diagram. 5. Calculate Intersection Volumes: Calculate the volume of the intersection between VCq and each original Voronoi cell VC{pi} of the neighbors. 6. Compute Weights: Compute the weight for each neighbor as the ratio of the intersection volume to the total volume of VCq. 7. Interpolate Value: Sum the products of weights and seed values vi to get vq. Formula: vq = \sum{i=1}^N \frac{vol(VC{pi} \cap VCq)}{vol(VCq)} \cdot vi where vq is the interpolated value for query point q, N is the number of neighbors, vol(VC{pi} \cap VCq) is the volume of the intersection between the original Voronoi cell of seed point pi and the new Voronoi cell of q, vol(VCq) is the volume of the new Voronoi cell of q, and vi is the value associated with seed point pi. Parameters: Default Seed Points: Eight default seed customization points are provided, each corresponding to a corner of the volume's bounding box, to prevent global influence from a single local seed point and allow simple linear gradients. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Infinite Voronoi Cells: A Voronoi cell can have infinite volume if its associated point is not strictly inside the convex hull of the given set of points, making the weight calculation undefined for query points outside the convex hull of seed points. Clipping the diagram to the bounding box resolves this by forcing finite cell volumes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def naturalneighborinterpolation(seedpoints, seedvalues, querypoint, boundingbox): # Step 1: Compute initial Voronoi diagram for seed points S, clipped to boundingbox # Note: The sources do not provide the Voronoi diagram construction algorithm. initialvoronoi = computevoronoidiagram(seedpoints, clipto=boundingbox) # Step 2: Form augmented set Q = S U {q} augmentedpoints = list(seedpoints) + [querypoint] # Step 3: Compute new Voronoi diagram for Q, clipped to boundingbox newvoronoi = computevoronoidiagram(augmentedpoints, clipto=boundingbox) # Step 4: Identify the new Voronoi cell VCq for the query point vcq = newvoronoi.getcell(querypoint) # Step 5: Calculate total volume of VCq volvcq = vcq.volume() # Guard against zero volume (degenerate case) if volvcq == 0: return 0.0 # Fallback for degenerate configuration interpolatedvalue = 0.0 N = len(seedpoints) # Step 6 & 7: Iterate over neighbors and compute weighted sum for i in range(N): pi = seedpoints[i] vcpi = initialvoronoi.getcell(pi) # Note: The sources do not provide the geometric intersection volume calculation. intersectionvol = vcpi.intersectionvolume(vcq) # Calculate weight weight = intersectionvol / volvcq # Accumulate weighted value interpolatedvalue += weight seedvalues[i] return interpolatedvalue Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: It satisfies continuity and monotonicity requirements and ensures local influence (occlusion), meaning only nearby seed points affect the interpolation result. It naturally adapts to the distribution of seed points. Limitations: It is computationally expensive compared to linear interpolation due to the need for Voronoi diagram construction and geometric intersection calculations. It is sensitive to the distribution of seed points and requires careful handling of boundary conditions (infinite cells). Natural neighbor interpolation was proposed by Sibson in 1981. It is also known as Sibson interpolation or Voronoi interpolation. In the context of volume rendering, it is used for the position-dependent customization of transfer function classification parameters, allowing for smooth and intuitive user interaction with volume data. name: Soft Voronoi Decomposition
head: Differentiable Voronoi Diagram, SoftVoronoi
body: Soft Voronoi Decomposition is a differentiable spatial partitioning method that decomposes a scene into N regions (Voronoi cells) defined by a set of N sites \phi \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}. It solves the problem of creating a smooth, differentiable approximation of a hard Voronoi diagram, allowing gradients to flow to the site positions \phi during training while maintaining spatial coherence. Unlike MLP-based decomposition methods which use softmax activations and suffer from random memory access patterns during integration, Soft Voronoi provides cache-friendly memory access and accelerates inference by ensuring that for any query point x, only one rendering head needs to be evaluated in the limit. Inputs: A set of N Voronoi sites \phi = [\phi1, \dots, \phiN], where each \phin \in \mathbb{R}^3. The sites are typically scaled to the range [-1, 1] to prevent optimizer magnitude invariance issues. A temperature parameter \beta \in \mathbb{R}^+, which controls the softness of the approximation. Outputs: A set of weights w{\phi}(x) = [w{\phi1}(x), \dots, w{\phiN}(x)] for a query point x \in \mathbb{R}^3, where \sum{n=1}^N w{\phin}(x) = 1. Data Structures: The sites \phi are stored as a dense array of shape (N, 3). The weights are computed on-the-fly for each query point x. Parameters: \beta: Temperature parameter. Typical value: 10^9. Schedule: \beta is not constant; it is scheduled over the training process. Steps: 1. Initialize \beta: Start training with a sufficiently low value of \beta such that wi(x) \approx wj(x) for all i, j and all x. 2. Schedule \beta: Exponentially increase \beta during training until it reaches a high value (e.g., 10^9). This ensures that as training progresses, the decomposition becomes indistinguishable from a hard Voronoi diagram, where wi(x) \approx 1 or wi(x) \approx 0 for all i. 3. Compute Weights: For a query point x, compute the weight for each site n using the formula below. 4. Select Head: In inference, identify the site n^ with the maximum weight w{\phi{n^}}(x). Evaluate only the rendering head corresponding to n^ for point x. Formula: The weight w{\phin}(x) for site n at query point x is defined as: w{\phin}(x) = \frac{\exp(-\beta \|x - \phin\|^2)}{\sum{j=1}^{N} \exp(-\beta \|x - \phij\|^2)} where \| \cdot \| denotes the Euclidean distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def softvoronoiweights(x, sites, beta): """ Compute Soft Voronoi weights for a single query point x. Args: x: numpy array of shape (3,), query point. sites: numpy array of shape (N, 3), Voronoi sites. beta: float, temperature parameter. Returns: weights: numpy array of shape (N,), weights for each site. """ # Calculate squared Euclidean distances from x to each site # sites shape: (N, 3), x shape: (3,) # diff shape: (N, 3) diff = sites - x # Squared L2 norm for each site # distsq shape: (N,) distsq = np.sum(diff 2, axis=1) # Compute unnormalized weights # exp(-beta distsq) unnormalizedweights = np.exp(-beta distsq) # Normalize weights to sum to 1 sumweights = np.sum(unnormalizedweights) # Avoid division by zero if all weights are extremely small (numerical underflow) if sumweights == 0: return np.ones(len(sites)) / len(sites) weights = unnormalizedweights / sumweights return weights def softvoronoiinference(x, sites, beta): """ Select the rendering head for query point x using Soft Voronoi. Args: x: numpy array of shape (3,), query point. sites: numpy array of shape (N, 3), Voronoi sites. beta: float, temperature parameter. Returns: bestsiteindex: int, index of the site with the highest weight. """ weights = softvoronoiweights(x, sites, beta) bestsiteindex = np.argmax(weights) return bestsiteindex Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \beta is too low, the decomposition is not spatially distinct, leading to poor scene separation. If \beta is too high too early in training, gradients may be zero or unstable because the weights become effectively one-hot, preventing gradient flow to the site positions \phi. The exponential scheduling of \beta resolves this. The magnitude of the scene coordinates must be scaled (e.g., \phi \in [-1, 1]^{N \times 3}) to prevent training instability when using optimizers like Adam. This method modifies the standard Voronoi partitioning within a barycentric simplex (triangle or tetrahedron) by shifting the central "Y-point" or centroid to arbitrary locations. It solves the problem of inaccurate material interface representation in cases where the uniform distribution assumption fails, such as T-intersections or specific material distributions. Unlike standard Soft Voronoi Decomposition which assumes symmetric sector subdivision, this approach allows the center point c to be adjusted to better weigh materials about the junction, ensuring planar separating surfaces remain consistent. Time Complexity: Computing weights for a single point x requires O(N) operations to calculate distances and exponentials. Inference is accelerated because only one rendering head needs to be evaluated per point, unlike MLP-based methods where all heads might be accessed. Memory Complexity: Storage of sites \phi is O(N). No additional large data structures are required for the decomposition itself. Measured Performance: Soft Voronoi decomposition allows for efficient compositing of rendering heads using the Painter’s Algorithm. Compared to MLP-based decomposition, Soft Voronoi runtime cost grows much slower as the number of heads N increases, due to cache-friendly memory access patterns and the ability to skip evaluating most heads. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Differentiable with respect to site positions \phi, spatially coherent, cache-friendly, compatible with Painter’s Algorithm. Limitations: Requires careful scheduling of \beta to balance differentiability and spatial distinctness. When to Use: Use when differentiable scene decomposition is required for training neural radiance fields or similar models, and when spatial coherence and efficient inference are priorities. When Not to Use: Avoid if the scene does not benefit from spatial partitioning or if the overhead of managing N sites is prohibitive for the specific hardware. Soft Voronoi Decomposition was introduced in the context of Decomposed Radiance Fields (DeRF). The method leverages the properties of Voronoi diagrams to create a balanced scene decomposition where all regions represent a similar amount of visual complexity. It was proposed as an alternative to naive decomposition strategies and MLP-based decompositions, which suffer from random memory access and inefficient scaling. The approach builds on the mathematical formulation of soft Voronoi diagrams using exponential weighting. name: Adjustable Center Point for Voronoi Partitioning
body: This method modifies Voronoi partitioning within a barycentric simplex by adjusting the center point to better handle specific material distributions, such as T-intersections. Unlike standard Soft Voronoi Decomposition which assumes symmetric sector subdivision, it allows the center c to be shifted to arbitrary locations within the simplex to correctly weigh materials about the junction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A barycentric simplex (triangle for 3 materials, tetrahedron for 4 materials) containing material fraction data. Input: A target adjustment for the center point c within the simplex. Output: Adjusted intersection edges and vertices defining the material boundaries. Data Structures: Barycentric Coordinates: For an m-material case, each vertex of the grid has an associated barycentric coordinate vector \lambda = (\lambda1, \lambda2, \dots, \lambdam). Center Point c: A point within the simplex, defaulting to c = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3) in the standard 3-material case. Steps: 1. Identify Material Distribution: Determine if the material distribution deviates from the uniform assumption, such as a T-intersection where one material occupies half the volume and others one-quarter each. 2. Sample Neighborhood: Sample in a larger neighborhood of the specific cell to understand how to weigh the materials about the "Y point". 3. Adjust Center Point c: Move the center point c from its default position to an arbitrary location within the barycentric triangle or tetrahedron. 4. Adjust Intersection Edges: Modify the edges that determine the intersections between material sectors to remain consistent with the new position of c. 5. Adjust Face Centers (4+ materials): If the simplex is a tetrahedron or higher-dimensional simplex (m materials), adjusting the center implies that the "center" vertices on the faces must also be adjusted so that the separating surfaces remain planar. Formulas: Standard 3-material center: c = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3). General m-material case: The algorithm generalizes Nielson's and Franke's algorithm. Each vertex has barycentric coordinates \lambda, and restricting material fractions such that exactly one \lambdai = 1 yields the case where each vertex is associated with only one material. Pitfalls: Planarity Constraints: In the four-material case, adjusting the center of the tetrahedron implies that the "center" vertices on the faces must also be adjusted so that the separating surfaces remain planar. Complexity: Similar considerations hold when adjusting the center of the m-simplex as m increases. An acceleration technique for computing Voronoi cell centroids by averaging the positions of projected and un-projected vertices associated with the cell, instead of evaluating the exact centroid. It is chosen when computational speed is prioritized over exact geometric precision, as computing the exact centroid is time-consuming. In practice, no noticeable difference in the final results was observed. Accuracy: Improves material interface representation in non-uniform distributions (e.g., T-intersections) compared to uniform barycentric assumptions. Complexity: Requires neighborhood sampling to determine weights, adding computational overhead compared to static centers. Constraints: Requires careful adjustment of face vertices in 4+ material cases to maintain planar surfaces. Usage: Use when material boundaries cannot be detected from vertex information alone or when uniform sector subdivision fails. Avoid when exact centroid computation is required and performance constraints are strict. The method is a direct generalization of Nielson's and Franke's algorithm. It addresses limitations in isosurface-type algorithms where material boundaries in tetrahedra cannot be detected if the isosurface enters a tetrahedron but only intersects one edge. The standard assumption of three distinct sectors subdividing a triangle in a "Y" fashion with equal material distribution is often invalid in complex scenes. name: Variational Tetrahedral Mesh Generation from Discrete Volume Data
head: Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation (CVT) based meshing, Voronoi-based tetrahedralization
body: This method generates high-quality tetrahedral meshes directly from discrete volumetric data (voxels) without requiring an intermediate polygonal surface mesh. It solves the problem of poor mesh quality and discretization error inherent in voxel-based meshing by using a variational clustering framework to aggregate voxels into cells, replacing each with a vertex, and then triangulating these vertices. Unlike surface-based meshing methods that enrich an input surface with new vertices—often inducing bad aspect ratios at boundaries—this method constrains sites near object boundaries to preserve accuracy and quality. Input: A discrete volume domain \Omega composed of voxels belonging to one or more objects Oi. The domain is defined as \Omega = \cupi Oi. Parameters: n: User-defined number of vertices (cells) in the meshing domain. \rho(x): A density function denoting the local desired vertex density. It can be generated from a medial axis approximation or manually painted by the user. Output: A tetrahedral mesh where each tetrahedron is associated with an object Oi. Voxel Grid: The input domain \Omega represented as a grid of voxels. Each voxel is assigned to an object ID. Sites (zi): A set of n points representing the vertices of the mesh. Each site zi corresponds to a cluster Ci of voxels. Clusters (Ci): A partition of the input voxels into n cells. Each cell Ci is associated with a site zi. Mesh: A set of tetrahedra defined by their vertex indices. Each tetrahedron is tagged with an object ID. 1. Density Map Calculation (Optional but Recommended): Calculate a density map \rho(x) to ensure dense sampling in complex or narrow regions. This is done by computing the medial axis of the shape using a constrained Discrete Voronoi Cell (DVC). The user may modify this map manually. 2. Variational Clustering (Centroidal Voronoi Diagram Approximation): Partition the input space \Omega by clustering input voxels into n cells Ci, approximating a Centroidal Voronoi Diagram (CVD). Each cell Ci is assigned a site zi. The site zi is the barycenter of its cell, weighted by the density function \rho(x): zi = \frac{\int{Ci} x \cdot \rho(x) dx}{\int{Ci} \rho(x) dx} The clustering minimizes the energy term: EV = \sum{i=1}^{n} \int{Ci} \rho(x) \|x - zi\|^2 dx Boundary Constraints: Sites zi located on the boundary of an object Oi are constrained to lie on the boundary subset (e.g., the barycenter of the boundary voxels) to preserve the accuracy of the object surface. 3. Triangulation (Mesh Generation): Triangulate the sites zi using the dual of the generated clustering. Construct a Voronoi Diagram from the point cloud of sites. The geometrical dual is the Delaunay triangulation. Greedy Algorithm: Build the mesh using a set of acceptable tetrahedra \Gamma. 1. Choose two neighbor tetrahedra in an unambiguous region of \Gamma. 2. Create a front from their external faces. 3. Add new tetrahedra to the front until it reaches the domain boundary \partial \Omega. Ambiguity Resolution: Resolve local ambiguities (e.g., co-cyclic sites causing undefined Delaunay triangles) using Constrained Delaunay Triangulation. 4. Object Association: Associate each constructed tetrahedron to an object Oi. Count the voxels contained within each tetrahedron. If voxels belong to two objects, assign the tetrahedron to the dominant class (the object with the majority of voxels). 5. Topological Optimization: Improve mesh quality without inserting or deleting vertices, only modifying connectivity (edge flips). Operations are denoted m-n, where m tetrahedra are removed and n are created. 3-2 Transformation: On three tetrahedra sharing the same edge, the cycle of tetrahedra around this edge forms a polygon which is triangulated. The faces of this triangulation are associated with the vertices of the initial common edge to form new tetrahedra. This deletes one edge and adds one or several faces. 2-3 Transformation: The inverse of 3-2. Deletes one or several faces and builds one edge. Can be extended to neighborhoods where faces are joined by edges of degree four. 5-4 Transformation: Removes slivers. Deletes one sliver and four of its neighbors, creating four new tetrahedra. Can have two different results for a given set. 4-4 Transformation: Used for 3D boundary restoration. Similar to 3-2 but with one more input tetrahedron. Restores boundaries where tetrahedra belong to two regions. Optimization Loop: 1. Fill a priority queue Q(id, qual) with tetrahedra whose quality indicator qual does not meet the criterion. 2. Pick element id with the worst quality. 3. Apply the transformation (3-2, 2-3, 5-4, or 4-4) that provides the best quality improvement. 4. Repeat until the criterion is fulfilled or no new transformation is possible. 6. Boundary Enhancement: Apply transformations that best decrease the number of voxels in non-dominant classes to remove spikes on the object surfaces. This improves the accuracy of the objects' boundaries. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatetetrahedralmesh(voxels, n, densitymap=None): """ Generate a tetrahedral mesh from discrete volume data. Args: voxels: List of voxel objects, each with position (x,y,z), objectid, and volume. n: Number of desired vertices in the mesh. densitymap: Optional function rho(x) returning local density. If None, uniform density is assumed. Returns: mesh: List of tetrahedra, each defined by 4 vertex indices and an objectid. """ # Step 1: Density Map Calculation (if not provided) if densitymap is None: # Compute medial axis from constrained DVC medialaxis = computemedialaxis(voxels) densitymap = generatedensityfrommedialaxis(medialaxis) # Step 2: Variational Clustering # Initialize n sites randomly or via k-means++ within the voxel bounds sites = initializesites(n, voxels) clusters = [[] for in range(n)] # Iterate to minimize Ev (Lloyd's algorithm variant with constraints) for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Assign voxels to nearest site (weighted by density) for voxel in voxels: # Find site zi minimizing integral of rho(x)||x-zi||^2 # Approximated by assigning voxel to site with smallest weighted distance bestsiteidx = argmin([weighteddistance(voxel, sites[i], densitymap) for i in range(n)]) clusters[bestsiteidx].append(voxel) # Update sites (barycenters) for i in range(n): if not clusters[i]: continue # Calculate weighted barycenter numerator = Vector3(0, 0, 0) denominator = 0.0 for voxel in clusters[i]: # Density at voxel position rho = densitymap(voxel.position) numerator += voxel.position rho denominator += rho if denominator > 0: newsite = numerator / denominator # Apply boundary constraints if site is on object boundary if isonboundary(clusters[i], voxelobjects): newsite = constraintoboundary(newsite, clusters[i]) sites[i] = newsite # Step 3: Triangulation # Construct Delaunay triangulation of sites # Use Greedy algorithm with ambiguity resolution meshtetrahedra = [] front = [] # Pick initial unambiguous tetrahedra initialtets = findinitialunambiguoustetrahedra(sites) for tet in initialtets: meshtetrahedra.append(tet) front.extend(tet.externalfaces) while front: face = front.pop() # Find candidate tetrahedron on the other side of the face candidatetet = findcandidatetetrahedron(face, sites, meshtetrahedra) if candidatetet is not None: # Check for ambiguity (co-cyclic sites) if isambiguous(candidatetet, face): # Resolve using Constrained Delaunay Triangulation resolvedtets = constraineddelaunaytriangulate(face, candidatetet, sites) meshtetrahedra.extend(resolvedtets) front.extend(resolvedtets.externalfaces) else: meshtetrahedra.append(candidatetet) front.extend(candidatetet.externalfaces) # Step 4: Object Association for tet in meshtetrahedra: voxelcounts = countvoxelsintetrahedron(tet, voxels) # Assign to dominant object tet.objectid = getdominantobject(voxelcounts) # Step 5 & 6: Topological Optimization and Boundary Enhancement optimizemeshquality(meshtetrahedra, sites, densitymap) enhanceboundaries(meshtetrahedra, voxels) return meshtetrahedra def weighteddistance(voxel, site, densitymap): """ Approximate the contribution to the energy term for a voxel. """ # In practice, this involves integrating rho(x)||x-z||^2 over the voxel volume. # A simple approximation is using the voxel center and density at center. distsq = voxel.position.distancesquared(site) rho = densitymap(voxel.position) return distsq rho def optimizemeshquality(tetrahedra, sites, densitymap): """ Apply topological transformations to improve quality. """ qualitycriteria = ['Q1', 'Q2', 'Q3', 'Q4'] priorityqueue = PriorityQueue() # Fill queue with poor quality tetrahedra for tet in tetrahedra: qual = calculatequality(tet, qualitycriteria) if qual < threshold: priorityqueue.push(tet.id, qual) while not priorityqueue.empty(): worsttetid = priorityqueue.pop() worsttet = tetrahedra[worsttetid] # Try all possible transformations (3-2, 2-3, 5-4, 4-4) besttransformation = None bestimprovement = -infinity for trans in getpossibletransformations(worsttet, tetrahedra): newquality = evaluatetransformationquality(trans, tetrahedra) if newquality > bestimprovement: bestimprovement = newquality besttransformation = trans if besttransformation is not None: applytransformation(besttransformation, tetrahedra, sites) # Update queue with affected tetrahedra updatequeuewithnewtetrahedra(tetrahedra, priorityqueue) def calculatequality(tetrahedron, criteria): """ Calculate quality metrics. Q1: Minimal dihedral angle (normalized 0-1, max 70.5 deg) Q2: Maximal dihedral angle Q3: Radius ratio Q4: Form factor normalized 0-1 """ if 'Q4' in criteria: V = tetrahedron.volume l = tetrahedron.averageedgelength # Q4 = 12 / ((3 V)^(2/3) l) q4 = 12.0 / ((3.0 V)(2.0/3.0) l) return q4 #... other criteria return 0.0 Ambiguities: Co-cyclic sites (in 2D) or co-spherical sites (in 3D) cause undefined Delaunay triangulations. These must be resolved locally using Constrained Delaunay Triangulation. Boundary Accuracy: If sites on boundaries are not constrained, the mesh may deviate from the object surface, leading to spikes and poor boundary representation. Slivers: Poor quality tetrahedra (slivers) can degrade FEM simulation performance. The 5-4 transformation is specifically designed to remove slivers. Precision: The quality criterion Q4 is sensitive to volume and edge length. Small numerical errors in volume calculation can affect quality assessment. Clustering: The clustering step dominates the runtime. For a 50^3 voxel grid, clustering takes 2.42 seconds. The complexity is related to the number of voxels and the number of iterations in the Lloyd's algorithm variant. Meshing: The greedy meshing step is fast. For 50^3 voxels, meshing takes 0.44 seconds. Optimization: Topological optimization is iterative. For 50^3 voxels, optimization takes 0.72 seconds. Total Time: For a 50^3 voxel grid resulting in 55,329 tetrahedra, the total time is approximately 3.58 seconds (2.42 + 0.44 + 0.72). For larger grids (200^3), the time increases significantly (271.96s clustering, 36.11s meshing, 42.26s optimization). Discretization Error: Measured as Hausdorff distance using an isosurface mesh (S1) as reference. AMIRA voxel mesh (S2): 0.31% of bounding box diagonal. Proposed method (S3): 0.17% of bounding box diagonal. The proposed method has approximately half the error of standard voxel meshing. Mesh Quality: Q1 (Min Dihedral Angle): The proposed method (S3) achieves a minimum Q1 of 16.31°, compared to 10.12° for AMIRA voxel mesh (S2) and 13.41° for AMIRA isosurface mesh (S1). Q4 (Form Factor): The proposed method (S3) achieves an average Q4 of 0.911, compared to 0.824 for S2 and 0.843 for S1. Simulation Performance: The high-quality mesh reduces the number of iterations for FEM solvers. EM Simulation: S3 required 121 iterations vs. 171 (S1) and 205 (S2). Thermal Simulation: S3 required 4004 iterations vs. 5002 (S1) and 5004 (S2). Strengths: Directly uses voxel data, avoiding intermediate surface reconstruction. Produces high-quality tetrahedra suitable for FEM simulations. Lower discretization error than standard voxel meshing. Allows user control over vertex density via \rho(x). Limitations: Higher error than isosurface-based meshing (S1) for thermal simulations where surface accuracy is critical. Computation time increases significantly with voxel grid size. Requires careful handling of boundary constraints to avoid spikes. Use when you have discrete volumetric data (voxels) and need a high-quality tetrahedral mesh for FEM simulations (e.g., electromagnetic or thermal). Use when you want to control mesh density in specific regions via a density map. Do not use if you already have a high-quality surface mesh; isosurface-based methods may yield better surface accuracy. The method was proposed by Valette, Siauve, Burais, and Prost. The paper "Variational tetrahedral mesh generation from discrete volume data" was published in The Visual Computer. The method builds on the concept of Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation (CVT) and its discrete approximation. It extends previous work on medial axis-based density maps and topological optimization techniques for mesh quality improvement. The authors implemented the algorithm in C++ using the VTK library. The method has been tested on various models including the Armadillo, Stanford Bunny, Venus body, and the Visible Human Project (VHP) models. It is particularly suited for 3D numerical simulations such as electromagnetic field computation and thermal simulations. name: Voxel Coloring
head: Photorealistic Scene Reconstruction by Voxel Coloring, Voxel Colouring Reconstruction, Voxel-based 3D reconstruction
body: Voxel Coloring is a volumetric reconstruction technique that computes photo-realistic 3D models from multiple color images by assigning colors (radiances) to voxels in a 3D volume, guaranteeing consistency with the input images. It distinguishes itself from other reconstruction methods by using a "carving" approach: it starts with an opaque volume and iteratively removes (carves) voxels that are inconsistent with the observed image colors, rather than building geometry from surface points. Unlike multi-scan methods such as Space Carving, Voxel Coloring relies on an ordinal visibility constraint to allow reconstruction in a single scan. Inputs: A set of N color images V0, \dots, V{N-1}. Camera parameters for each image: position, focal angles (vertical and horizontal), and depth information (or synthesized depth maps). A 3D grid defining the spatial domain with resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz) and a bounding box containing the scene. Outputs: A 3D volume where each voxel stores a color value (RGB) and an alpha value (transparency). Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array of voxels. Each voxel contains: color: A 3-component vector (RGB) representing the assigned radiance. alpha: A scalar value (typically 0–255) representing transparency. 0 indicates transparent (carved), 255 indicates opaque. Pixel Map (\pi): A set or mask tracking which image pixels have been successfully mapped to voxels, used to ensure coverage. Parameters: thresh: The maximum allowable correlation error threshold for color consistency. A low value yields precise but potentially incomplete reconstruction; a larger value yields a more complete reconstruction but may include false voxels. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize a reconstruction volume of voxels as opaque (alpha = 255) to represent the initial volume containing the scene. 2. Camera Space Transformation: For each camera, compute the change of scale matrix M between object space and camera space. The matrix is defined as M = RX \times RY \times T, where: RX and RY are rotation matrices that bring the vision vector to the OZ axis. T is the translation matrix that brings the camera to the center of the scene. 3. Voxel Traversal: Traverse the voxels in a monotonic order (near-to-far relative to the cameras) to ensure correct visibility handling. Constraint: The camera locations must satisfy an ordinal visibility constraint, meaning cameras cannot surround the scene, ensuring voxels can be visited in a single near-to-far scan relative to every camera. 4. Projection and Consistency Test: For each voxel v in the traversal order: Compute the position of the corresponding voxel in the grid and project it to the image plane using the transformation matrix M. Retrieve the color C{img} from the corresponding pixel in each input image Vi. Test for color consistency: Check if the correlation error between the voxel's assigned color and the projected image colors exceeds thresh. 5. Carving: If a voxel is found to be color inconsistent across the input images, carve it by setting its alpha value to 0 (transparent). If consistent, retain its opacity (alpha = 255) and assign the pixel's color to the found voxel. 6. Termination: Stop when all remaining opaque voxels are color consistent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelcoloring(images, cameras, gridresolution, boundingbox, thresh): """ Reconstructs a 3D volume using Voxel Coloring. Args: images: List of N color images. cameras: List of N camera objects with position, rotation, and depth info. gridresolution: Tuple (Nx, Ny, Nz) defining the voxel grid size. boundingbox: Tuple defining the 3D space bounds. thresh: Maximum allowable correlation error threshold. Returns: volume: 3D array of voxels with 'color' and 'alpha' fields. """ # Initialize volume with opaque voxels (alpha = 255) volume = [[[{'color': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'alpha': 255} for in range(gridresolution[2])] for in range(gridresolution[1])] for in range(gridresolution[0])] for x in range(gridresolution[0]): for y in range(gridresolution[1]): for z in range(gridresolution[2]): voxel = volume[x][y][z] if voxel['alpha'] == 0: continue consistentcolors = [] for i, cam in enumerate(cameras): # Compute transformation matrix M = RX RY T # RX, RY rotate vision vector to OZ axis; T translates camera to scene center M = cam.RX @ cam.RY @ cam.T # Project voxel center to image plane # Homogeneous coordinate: ph = M @ [x, y, z, 1]^T ph = M @ [x, y, z, 1.0] # Perspective division to get normalized device coordinates if ph[3] == 0: continue pndc = [ph[0]/ph[3], ph[1]/ph[3], ph[2]/ph[3]] # Map to pixel coordinates (u, v) using image dimensions imgw, imgh = images[i].shape[1], images[i].shape[0] u = int((pndc[0] + 1.0) imgw / 2.0) v = int((1.0 - pndc[1]) imgh / 2.0) # Check bounds if not (0 <= u < imgw and 0 <= v < imgh): continue # Retrieve pixel color pixelcolor = images[i].getcolor(u, v) consistentcolors.append(pixelcolor) if not consistentcolors: voxel['alpha'] = 0 continue # Assign average color from consistent views avgcolor = [sum(c[j] for c in consistentcolors) / len(consistentcolors) for j in range(3)] # Test consistency: max allowable correlation error threshold # Using Euclidean distance as a standard proxy for correlation error maxdeviation = max(sum((c[j] - avgcolor[j])2 for j in range(3))0.5 for c in consistentcolors) if maxdeviation <= thresh: voxel['color'] = avgcolor voxel['alpha'] = 255 else: voxel['alpha'] = 0 return volume Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ordinal Visibility Constraint: If cameras surround the scene, the monotonic traversal order cannot be established, leading to incorrect visibility handling and reconstruction artifacts. Threshold Selection: A low thresh may result in an incomplete reconstruction (holes), while a high thresh may include false voxels (noise). Depth Information: The method relies on depth information or synthesized depth maps to project voxels accurately. Lack of accurate depth can lead to misalignment. Improves upon standard Voxel Coloring by computing visibility exactly using Item Buffers or Layered Depth Images, allowing for more accurate color-consistent models. A post-processing method that refines voxel colors to handle noise and non-Lambertian reflectance, preserving sharp edges. Renders volumetric textures by converting the voxel volume into 2D image layers for real-time rendering on standard graphics hardware. Time Complexity: The algorithm traverses all voxels in the volume and checks consistency against all camera views. Complexity is O(V \times N), where V is the number of voxels and N is the number of cameras. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D volume (O(V)) and the input images (O(N \times I), where I is image size). Performance: The method is computationally intensive due to the voxel traversal and consistency checks. However, it allows for a single scan reconstruction if the ordinal visibility constraint is met, which is faster than multi-scan methods like Space Carving. Strengths: Produces photo-realistic volume models with consistent colors across views. Simple to implement conceptually. Limitations: Restricted by the ordinal visibility constraint; cannot handle scenes surrounded by cameras. Sensitive to the threshold parameter. Voxel Coloring was introduced by Seitz and Dyer in 1997 in the paper "Photorealistic Scene Reconstruction by Voxel Coloring". The method laid the foundation for subsequent voxel-based reconstruction techniques. name: Generalized Voxel Coloring
head: GVC, GVC-IB, GVC-LDI, Voxel Colouring
body: Generalized Voxel Coloring (GVC) is a voxel-based 3D reconstruction technique that computes photo-realistic volume models from multiple color images by assigning colors (radiances) to voxels while guaranteeing consistency with a set of base images. It extends standard Voxel Coloring by computing visibility exactly using Item Buffers (IB) or Layered Depth Images (LDI), yielding models that are numerically more consistent with the input images. Inputs: A set of n+1 calibrated input images I0, \dots, In, camera parameters (position, focal angles), and a 3D volume subdivision into layers. Outputs: A set of colored voxels S representing the reconstructed scene. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: The 3D space is subdivided into layers of voxels at uniform distance d from the camera. The total volume is \nu = \bigcup{i=1}^{r} vdi, where vdi = \{ V \mid V = di \} and d1, \dots, dr is a sequence of increasing numbers. 2. Marked Pixels (\pi): A global set tracking pixels in input images that have already been associated with a colored voxel to ensure each pixel contributes to at most one voxel's color consistency check. 3. Visibility Structure: Either an Item Buffer (IB) or a Layered Depth Image (LDI). IB: Records for every pixel in an image, the single surface voxel that is visible from that pixel. LDI: Records for every pixel in an image, a depth-sorted list of all surface voxels that project to that pixel. LDI contains a superset of IB information but consumes considerably more memory. Parameters: thresh: The maximum allowable correlation error. A low value yields precise but incomplete reconstruction; a larger value yields complete reconstruction with potential false voxels. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the set of colored voxels S \leftarrow \emptyset and the global marked pixel set \pi \leftarrow \emptyset. 2. Iterate through layers i from 1 to r: 3. For each voxel V in layer vdi: 4. For each input image j from 0 to n: 5. Project voxel V onto image Ij and compute its footprint \rho. 6. Identify the subset of pixels \pij within the footprint \rho that are not yet marked: \pij \leftarrow \{ p \in \rho \mid p \notin \pi \}. 7. Compute the consistency metric \lambdaV for voxel V based on the unmarked pixels in the footprints across all images. 8. Let m be the number of consistent pixels found (where consistency is determined by \lambdaV). 9. If m > 0 AND \lambdaV < \text{thresh}: 10. Color the voxel V and add it to S: S \leftarrow S \cup \{V\}. 11. Update the global marked pixel set: \pi \leftarrow \pi \cup \bigcup{j} \pij. 12. Mark the individual pixels in the current footprints \pij as used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generalizedvoxelcoloring(images, cameras, layers, thresh): S = set() pi = set() # Global marked pixel set for i in range(1, len(layers) + 1): d = layers[i - 1] vdi = getvoxelsfordistance(d) # Retrieves voxels at uniform distance d from camera for V in vdi: allpij = [] for j in range(len(images)): Ij = images[j] rho = project3dto2d(V, cameras[j], Ij.resolution) # Standard perspective projection to pixel coordinates pij = [p for p in rho if (j, p) not in pi] allpij.append((j, pij)) lambdaV = computecorrelationerror(V, allpij, images, cameras) # Computes correlation error across projected colors m = sum(len(pij) for, pij in allpij) # Count of unmarked pixels in footprints if m > 0 and lambdaV < thresh: V.color = meancolor(V, allpij, images, cameras) # Averages colors of consistent pixels S.add(V) for j, pij in allpij: for p in pij: pi.add((j, p)) return S An algorithm that attempts to reconstruct semi-transparent voxels, unlike previous algorithms that assumed opaque object voxels. A method for reconstructing time-varying scenes by linking two time-consecutive 3D voxel spaces together to form a 6D space. Time Complexity: The algorithm iterates through all voxels in all layers and all input images. For each voxel, it computes footprints and consistency metrics. Exact visibility computation (via IB/LDI or ray casting) adds overhead compared to approximate methods. The source notes that voxel carving is computationally expensive, typically requiring tens of seconds or more. Memory Complexity: Depends on the visibility structure. LDI consumes considerably more memory than IB because it stores a depth-sorted list of all surface voxels per pixel, whereas IB stores only the single visible voxel. Strengths: Produces numerically more consistent reconstructions with input images compared to approximate visibility methods like Space Carving. Provides photo-realistic volume models. Limitations: Computationally expensive. High memory usage if LDI is used. Sensitive to the thresh parameter; low values yield incomplete reconstructions, high values yield false voxels. Requires accurately calibrated cameras. When to use: When high geometric and photometric consistency is required and computational resources are sufficient. When exact visibility is critical for quality. When not to use: For real-time applications or very large scenes where memory is constrained (prefer IB over LDI, or approximate methods). For scenes with significant calibration errors (use Approximate Space Carving). Generalized Voxel Coloring was introduced by Culbertson et al. in 1999 (cited as [CMS99] in sources) and further detailed in subsequent works. It is an extension of the original Voxel Coloring technique introduced by Seitz in 2000 (cited as [21] in), which itself is based on the Space Carving paradigm. The method was developed to address the shortcomings of approximate visibility in standard voxel coloring by computing visibility exactly using Item Buffers or Layered Depth Images. It is used in volumetric reconstruction from uncalibrated or calibrated camera views, often as a core component in multiresolution carving methods. name: Multi-view Color Consistency and Smoothing
head: Color Consistency with Blur Grouping, Colour Selection, Colour Selection for Voxels, Weighted Average Colour Selection, Weighted Color Selection, Weighted average colour definition
body: Multi-view Color Consistency and Smoothing is a post-processing method for assigning colors to voxels in a fine volumetric reconstruction, designed to compensate for noise arising from camera calibration, imaging artifacts, imperfect light balance, and volume quantization. It distinguishes itself from basic voxel coloring by explicitly handling non-Lambertian reflectance and preventing visual blurring through a "blur group" mechanism that preserves sharp edges. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A fine voxel grid with 3D positions (x, y, z) and visibility status per view. Source view images with known camera centers cv. Output: A color value C for each voxel, using intensity (Y) or color (U,V) components. Data Structures: Voxel: Stores position (x, y, z) and a list of visible view indices. Group Tag: Each voxel is classified as either a Clear Group or Blur Group based on color difference. Steps: 1. Mark Center Line: Approximately mark the line Lc passing through the center of the volume. 2. Identify Visible Views: For a voxel x, determine visible views. If visible in fewer than two views, assign C = C1 from the single visible view and skip to Step 6. Otherwise, identify the two nearest visible views (View 1 and View 2). 3. Define Reference Lines: For each nearest view v \in \{1, 2\}, define line Lv as the intersection of the volume surface and the line connecting Lc to the camera center cv of view v. 4. Calculate Weighted Color: Check if voxel x lies between L1 and L2. If true, compute C = (\alpha1 C2 + \alpha2 C1) / (\alpha1 + \alpha2), where C1, C2 are the Y or U,V components from View 1 and View 2, and \alpha1, \alpha2 are the angles between voxel x and the points in the same layer on L1 and L2 respectively. If false, assign C = C1. 5. Blur Grouping Check: Calculate the difference between C1 and C2. If the difference exceeds a particular threshold, place the voxel in the Blur Group; otherwise, place it in the Clear Group. 6. Sharpness Preservation: For voxels in the Blur Group, let C{old} be the color computed in Step 4. Replace C{old} with the color of a neighboring voxel in the Clear Group that has the closest value to C{old}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computevoxelcolor(voxelpos, visibleviews, cameras, threshold, surface): # Step 1: Visibility check if len(visibleviews) < 2: return getviewcolor(voxelpos, visibleviews[0], cameras, surface) # Identify two nearest visible views by camera distance viewdists = [] for v in visibleviews: camcenter = cameras[v].center dist = math.sqrt(sum((voxelpos[i] - camcenter[i])2 for i in range(3))) viewdists.append((dist, v)) viewdists.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) v1, v2 = viewdists[0][1], viewdists[1][1] # Step 2: Retrieve colors from nearest views C1 = getviewcolor(voxelpos, v1, cameras, surface) C2 = getviewcolor(voxelpos, v2, cameras, surface) # Step 3: Define reference points on L1 and L2 # Lv is the intersection of the volume surface and the line from Lc to camera center cv ref1 = surface.intersectplane(voxelpos, cameras[v1].center) # ref2 = surface.intersectplane(voxelpos, cameras[v2].center) # # Step 4: Calculate angles alpha1 and alpha2 vecv1 = [voxelpos[i] - cameras[v1].center[i] for i in range(3)] vecr1 = [ref1[i] - cameras[v1].center[i] for i in range(3)] alpha1 = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot(vecv1, vecr1) / (norm(vecv1) norm(vecr1))))) vecv2 = [voxelpos[i] - cameras[v2].center[i] for i in range(3)] vecr2 = [ref2[i] - cameras[v2].center[i] for i in range(3)] alpha2 = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot(vecv2, vecr2) / (norm(vecv2) norm(vecr2))))) # Check if voxel lies between L1 and L2 if not isbetweenlines(voxelpos, ref1, ref2): color = C1 else: denom = alpha1 + alpha2 if denom == 0: color = (C1 + C2) / 2.0 # Fallback for degenerate angles else: color = (alpha1 C2 + alpha2 C1) / denom # Step 5: Blur grouping check diff = abs(C1 - C2) isblur = diff > threshold # Step 6: Sharpness preservation if isblur: neighborcolor = findclosestclearneighbor(voxelpos, color) if neighborcolor is not None: color = neighborcolor return color def getviewcolor(pos, viewidx, cameras, surface): cam = cameras[viewidx] u, v = projecttoimage(pos, cam) # return imagebuffer[viewidx].sample(u, v) # def dot(v1, v2): return sum(ab for a,b in zip(v1, v2)) def norm(v): return math.sqrt(sum(aa for a in v)) def isbetweenlines(pos, ref1, ref2): # Geometric containment test for angular sector defined by ref1 and ref2 relative to camera center cam = cameras[0] vec1 = [ref1[i] - cam.center[i] for i in range(3)] vec2 = [ref2[i] - cam.center[i] for i in range(3)] vecp = [pos[i] - cam.center[i] for i in range(3)] # Check if pos is within the cone spanned by ref1 and ref2 return True def findclosestclearneighbor(pos, targetcolor): # Scan 3x3x3 voxel neighborhood for clear-group voxels # Return color with minimum Euclidean distance to targetcolor return None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If \alpha1 + \alpha2 = 0, the weights are undefined; a fallback to a simple average or C1 is required. Non-Lambertian Surfaces: Highly specular or non-Lambertian surfaces cause C1 and C2 to differ significantly, triggering the blur group. Threshold Selection: A particular threshold determines whether a voxel enters the blur or clear group. Visibility: Voxels visible in only one view are assigned C1 directly, which may retain noise. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces smooth colors and brightness, compensating for calibration and quantization noise. The blur group mechanism preserves sharpness better than simple averaging. Limitations: Computationally intensive due to multi-view projection. Sensitive to the threshold parameter. May fail on highly reflective surfaces if the "clear" neighbor is not available or representative. When to Use: Post-processing for fine volumetric reconstructions where visual smoothness is prioritized, and non-Lambertian artifacts are manageable. When Not to Use: Real-time applications requiring low latency, or scenes with extreme specularities where color consistency is fundamentally violated. This method was introduced in the context of volumetric representation for sparse multi-view synthesis. It was proposed to address the limitations of iterative volume refinement, which can produce noisy or inconsistent colors due to non-Lambertian reflectance and calibration errors. The approach was tested on sequences like the "Leo" sequence, composed of five cameras. It is part of a pipeline that includes pre-processing for adaptive resolution, allowing for scalable view synthesis. name: Volumetric Texture Rendering via Image Layers
head: Image layers representation, Rendering by using the new model of volumetric texture, Volumetric Textures Representation Based on Image Layers
body: This method renders volumetric textures by converting a reconstructed voxel volume into a set of 2D transparent image layers, which are then projected and alpha-composited onto the image plane using a Z-buffer. It solves the performance bottleneck of traditional ray-casting volumetric rendering by leveraging standard graphics hardware polygon processing, offering real-time capabilities for complex repetitive scenes. It differs from its parent Voxel Coloring by shifting from a voxel-based storage model to a layered 2D texture model, and from siblings like Generalized Voxel Coloring by explicitly utilizing 2D image layers for rendering rather than direct voxel traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A reference volume generated by voxel coloring, represented as N 2D images of size X \times Y in RGBA format. Output: A final 2D image on the screen. Data Structures: Volume Representation: The volume is treated as a collection of N layers. Each layer is a 2D image (texture) containing precalculated colors (RGB) and transparency (Alpha). No reflectance or lighting information is stored; shading is fixed during construction. Box: The volumetric grid is decomposed into boxes. Each box is defined by 2N points: N points for the base and N points for the top. Each point has 3D space coordinates (X, Y, Z) and 2D texture coordinates (U, V). Texel Directions: Each texel has three orthogonal directions: Normal (NR), Tangent (T), and Bi-normal (B). Algorithm Steps: 1. Layer Conversion: Convert the volumetric texture (reference volume) into a set of N layers, where each layer is a 2D image considered as a transparent texture. 2. View Direction Selection: For each texel, determine the best viewing direction to minimize distortion or occlusion issues. Compute the scalar products between the view axis V and the three texel directions (NR, T, B). Select the direction with the largest absolute scalar product. 3. Coordinate Interpolation: Calculate the spatial coordinates for the intermediate sections of a box. Let A0, B0, C0 be the coordinates of the bottom layer points and A{n-1}, B{n-1}, C{n-1} be the coordinates of the top layer points, where n is the number of layers. The coordinates for section i are calculated as: Ai = A0 + \frac{i}{n} (A{n-1} - A0) Bi = B0 + \frac{i}{n} (B{n-1} - B0) Ci = C0 + \frac{i}{n} (C{n-1} - C0) The source text contains a conflicting definition Ai = A0 alongside the interpolation formula; the interpolation formula is used for rendering. 4. Rendering Loop: Iterate through all boxes and all sections within each box. Load the texture for the current section. Display the section of the box. This involves changing context using a texture identifier binding function and loading the 2D image data into graphics memory. 5. Projection and Composition: Project each layer onto the image plane using a Z-buffer. Successively compose the projected layers. Each projected layer is combined with the preceding result taking into account the density (alpha) of each pixel. 6. Alpha Compositing: Render transparent faces in depth order (back-to-front). For each point: If the point's depth is further than the Z-buffer value AND the Z-buffer point belongs to a completely opaque polygon, reject the point. Otherwise, apply alpha compositing: C{screen} = \alpha{point} \times C{point} + (1 - \alpha{point}) \times C{screen} For opaque semi-polygons, compose colors by displaying faces back-to-front respecting depth order relative to the viewpoint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolumetrictexture(volumelayers, boxes, viewdirection): # Initialize buffers zbuffer = [[float('inf')] for in range(width)] screenbuffer = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)] for in range(width)] for box in boxes: n = len(volumelayers) # Interpolate box vertices for each layer/section for i in range(n): interpolatedvertices = [] for k in range(len(box.basepoints)): p0 = box.basepoints[k].xyz pn = box.toppoints[k].xyz # Source formula: Pi = P0 + (i/n) (P{n-1} - P0) pi = p0 + (i / n) (pn - p0) interpolatedvertices.append(Vertex(pi, box.basepoints[k].uv)) # Bind texture identifier to current context # Load 2D image data into graphics memory currenttexture = volumelayers[i] # Project vertices to screen space screenvertices = [projecttoscreen(v.xyz, viewdirection) for v in interpolatedvertices] # Rasterize polygon for pixel in rasterizepolygon(screenvertices): zpoly = pixel.zdepth uv = pixel.uv # Sample texture at pixel UV texcolor, texalpha = sampletexture(currenttexture, uv) # Z-buffer test zbuf = zbuffer[pixel.x][pixel.y] if zpoly > zbuf and isopaque(zbuf): continue # Alpha compositing currentcolor = screenbuffer[pixel.x][pixel.y] newcolor = texalpha texcolor + (1.0 - texalpha) currentcolor # Update buffers screenbuffer[pixel.x][pixel.y] = newcolor zbuffer[pixel.x][pixel.y] = zpoly def projecttoscreen(point, viewdir): # Standard perspective/orthographic projection return ScreenVertex(point.x, point.y, point.z, point.u, point.v) def rasterizepolygon(vertices): # Bounding box and scanline rasterization for y in range(minv.y, maxv.y + 1): for x in range(minv.x, maxv.x + 1): if pointintriangle(x, y, vertices): z = interpolatedepth(x, y, vertices) uv = interpolateuv(x, y, vertices) yield Pixel(x, y, z, uv) def sampletexture(texture, uv): # Bilinear sampling from RGBA image r, g, b, a = texture[uv.y][uv.x] return (r, g, b), a def isopaque(zval): # Z-buffer point belongs to a completely opaque polygon return zval != float('inf') class Vertex: def init(self, xyz, uv): self.xyz = xyz self.uv = uv Parameters: Level of Detail (LOD): The number of display layers n can be reduced based on the distance d of the observer and the vision angle a. Two criteria are mentioned: 1. H \times \tan(a) < d0, where n is the minimum number of sections to keep constant visual quality. 2. Spacing between layers is defined to balance realism and speed. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opaque Semi-polygons: Must be rendered back-to-front respecting depth order. Z-buffer Rejection: Transparent points behind opaque surfaces must be correctly rejected to avoid visual artifacts. Deformation: Coordinates of box faces are recomputed only when the box becomes deformed. A volumetric reconstruction algorithm that uses color consistency to distinguish object surface voxels from background, starting with an opaque volume and carving inconsistent voxels. It sets itself apart by storing scene data as a 3D voxel grid rather than 2D image layers. Choose it when dynamic lighting, reflectance, or complex volumetric traversal is required. Voxel Coloring An extension of voxel coloring that handles more complex scene structures. It sets itself apart by retaining voxel-based traversal and direct rendering rather than projecting pre-converted 2D layers. Choose it for non-repetitive or highly complex volumetric data where layer approximation would lose detail. Generalized Voxel Coloring Techniques to refine color values across multiple input views. It sets itself apart by focusing on color accuracy and smoothing rather than rendering speed or layer projection. Choose it when input images have significant color variation or lighting inconsistencies that must be resolved before texture generation. Multi-view Color Consistency and Smoothing Time Complexity: Faster than traditional ray casting. The projection of a layer is faster than calculating projection for each voxel along a ray, providing an appreciable time benefit. Memory Complexity: Requires storing N 2D images of size X \times Y in RGBA format. The memory usage is proportional to the number of layers and image resolution. Measured Performance: The method allows for real-time rendering, reducing calculation times from 5-20 minutes (typical for ray casting) to acceptable real-time frames. Strengths: Exploits graphics board capacities effectively; suitable for repetitive complex scenes; supports Level of Detail (LOD) based on viewer distance and angle. Limitations: Fixed shading and lighting (no dynamic reflectance); requires precalculation of colors; relies on Z-buffer for transparency, which can be sensitive to draw order. When to Use: Real-time applications requiring realistic rendering of repetitive complex scenes (e.g., fur, foliage) where dynamic lighting is not required or is baked in. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring dynamic lighting, complex material interactions, or non-repetitive volumetric data. Origin: The method was presented by Hemidi Djallel and Jedi Noureddine in 2006. History: Volumetric textures were initially introduced by Kajiya and Kay in 1989 for fur rendering. This method integrates voxel coloring techniques into volumetric textures to improve rendering speed for real-time applications. Usage: Used in real-time graphics applications for rendering complex repetitive scenes such as fur, grass, or other volumetric textures where traditional ray casting is too slow. name: Reference Reconstruction
head: Brick Merging, Component Reconstruction
body: Reference Reconstruction assembles a complete volumetric dataset from exported component bricks (chunks), resolving spatial overlaps by taking the maximum value of the constituent components. It differs from generative methods like Voxel Coloring by strictly reconstructing an existing discrete grid structure rather than inferring geometry from projections, and from Voronoi-like Segmentation Volume Generation by handling pre-existing discretized data rather than generating segmentation boundaries. Inputs: A list of component records, each containing a path to a raw data file (.raw), a spacing factor per axis, an extent (crop region), and an origin (placement offset). Outputs: A 3D array result of shape (Nz, Ny, Nx) and a boolean coverage array coverage of the same shape. Data Structures: result: uint8 or uint16 array, initialized to zeros. coverage: uint8 array, initialized to zeros, tracking how many bricks contribute to each voxel. block: Temporary buffer for the current brick's data. Steps: 1. Initialize result and coverage arrays with shape (Nz, Ny, Nx) (ZYX order) filled with zeros. 2. For each component record in the input list: a. Read the raw data file into block. b. Upsample block along each axis by repeating values spacing times, where spacing is derived from comp['spacingxyz'][::-1] (ZYX order). c. Crop the upsampled block to the specified extentxyz[::-1] (ZYX order). d. Map the cropped block to the result array at the position defined by originxyz[::-1] (ZYX order) using the operation: \text{result}[target] = \max(\text{result}[target], \text{block}) This is implemented as np.maximum(result[target], block, out=result[target]). e. Update the coverage map: \text{coverage}[target] \leftarrow \text{coverage}[target] + (\text{block} > 0) where (\text{block} > 0) is a boolean mask converted to integer. Pitfalls: Lossy Merging: Overlapping bricks are resolved by np.maximum. If overlapping regions contain different non-zero values, the lower value is discarded, potentially losing information. Precision: Ensure the output array type (uint8/uint16) matches the source data to prevent overflow or truncation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def referencereconstruction(components, shapezyx): """ Reconstructs a volume from component bricks. Args: components: List of dicts with keys: 'path': str, path to.raw file 'spacingxyz': tuple of int, (x, y, z) spacing factors 'extentxyz': tuple of int, (x, y, z) crop extent 'originxyz': tuple of int, (x, y, z) placement origin shapezyx: tuple of int, (Nz, Ny, Nx) Returns: result: np.ndarray, shape (Nz, Ny, Nx) coverage: np.ndarray, shape (Nz, Ny, Nx) """ # Initialize result and coverage arrays result = np.zeros(shapezyx, dtype=np.uint8) coverage = np.zeros(shapezyx, dtype=np.uint8) for comp in components: # Load raw data # Note: In a real implementation, this would read the binary file. # Here we assume 'blockraw' is the loaded data of shape (H, W, D) or similar. # The source code implies reading into a block variable. blockraw = loadrawfile(comp['path']) # Placeholder for actual file I/O # Upsample by repeating values # spacingxyz is (x, y, z), but numpy repeat works on axes 0,1,2 (z,y,x) # So we reverse spacing for axis alignment spacingzyx = comp['spacingxyz'][::-1] # Repeat along axis 0 (z), axis 1 (y), axis 2 (x) block = blockraw for axis, factor in enumerate(spacingzyx): if factor > 1: block = np.repeat(block, factor, axis=axis) # Crop to extent # extentxyz is (x, y, z), reverse to (z, y, x) for slicing extentzyx = comp['extentxyz'][::-1] # Define slice objects for cropping # Assuming extent defines the size of the crop, not start/end. # The source says "Crop block to extentxyz". # If extent is size, we take the first 'extent' elements. # If extent is [start, end], we use that. # Given "crop to extent", it usually implies size. # Let's assume extentzyx is the size of the region to take from the start. # If the source implies a specific region, more context is needed. # Standard interpretation: take block[:extentzyx[0],:extentzyx[1],:extentzyx[2]] blockcropped = block[:extentzyx[0],:extentzyx[1],:extentzyx[2]] # Map to result # originxyz is (x, y, z), reverse to (z, y, x) originzyx = comp['originxyz'][::-1] # Calculate target slice in result # The blockcropped is placed at originzyx zstart, ystart, xstart = originzyx zend = zstart + blockcropped.shape[0] yend = ystart + blockcropped.shape[1] xend = xstart + blockcropped.shape[2] # Ensure we don't go out of bounds zend = min(zend, shapezyx[0]) yend = min(yend, shapezyx[1]) xend = min(xend, shapezyx[2]) # Adjust blockcropped if it exceeds bounds (though source implies valid inputs) # For robustness, we crop the block to fit actualz = zend - zstart actualy = yend - ystart actualx = xend - xstart targetblock = blockcropped[:actualz,:actualy,:actualx] # Update result with maximum np.maximum(result[zstart:zend, ystart:yend, xstart:xend], targetblock, out=result[zstart:zend, ystart:yend, xstart:xend]) # Update coverage # block > 0 creates a boolean array, convert to uint8 mask = (targetblock > 0).astype(np.uint8) coverage[zstart:zend, ystart:yend, xstart:xend] += mask return result, coverage Derives reduced-resolution basis matrices U^{(k)} \in \mathbb{R}^{Jk \times Rk} by subsampling the original bases U^{(k)} at a reduced rate Jk < Ik in the corresponding index dimensions, then reconstructs a lower resolution volume A from these bases. Simple regular subsampling achieves very good results, though other re-sampling and interpolation methods can be considered. This allows for multiresolution hierarchies similar to mipmapping. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the total number of voxels in the output volume and the number of components, dominated by the upsampling and merging operations. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the output volume plus the temporary storage for each component brick. Strengths: Simple, deterministic reconstruction of existing data structures; handles overlapping regions via a clear priority rule (maximum). Limitations: Lossy merging if overlapping bricks have conflicting values; requires precise metadata (spacing, origin, extent) for correct alignment. When to use: When reconstructing a full-resolution volume from pre-computed, exported chunks or bricks. When not to use: When the source data is not already discretized into bricks, or when lossy merging of overlapping values is unacceptable. Reference Reconstruction is a method for assembling volumetric data from component parts, as described in the VolumeSegmenter project. It is designed to handle the reconstruction of voxel grids from exported bricks, particularly in the context of large-scale volumetric datasets. name: 3D Interactive Hierarchy Editor
head: 3D IHE, Region Hierarchy Editor, Semantic Region Selection
body: The 3D Interactive Hierarchy Editor (3D IHE) is a semantic control tool that allows users to define regions of interest by selecting primitive collections of voxels, which are then used to modify volume rendering parameters such as color and opacity. It differs from local syntactic controls (like ramp-based classification) and geometric clipping by using global set-membership of data points to isolate morphological features. Unlike sibling methods that segment voxel-by-voxel or via pure geometric intersection, 3D IHE builds a hierarchy of related voxels to enable efficient, 3D-aware selection via a slice paradigm. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric dataset (e.g., 128^3 with 256 gray levels) and a pre-computed hierarchy of voxel primitives. Output: A selection mask and opcodes sent to a volume renderer via TCP/IP. Data Structures: 1. Hierarchy Tree: A directed acyclic graph where nodes represent primitive regions of voxels with similar characteristics. 2. Selection Mask: A 3D array matching the input dataset resolution, storing binary values (selected/not selected) for each voxel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Hierarchy Generation (Preprocessing): Treat the 3D image as a 3-manifold in 4-space (intensity as the 4th dimension). Analyze ridges and valleys in this 3-fold surface. Compute reverse gravity watersheds to segment the volume into primitive regions. Organize these primitives into a hierarchy where parent nodes encompass child regions. This step is computationally expensive; preprocessing a 128^3 image takes ~15 minutes on a Decstation 3100. 2. Interactive Selection: Display a full-size 2D slice of the current 3D dataset. The user selects or deselects primitive regions within this 2D slice using mouse operations. Selections extend in 3D: selecting a primitive in one slice applies the selection to the entire 3D extent of that primitive. Navigate slices using forward/backward buttons or a slider to view adjacent slices. Preview effects using scaled-down thumbnails of multiple slices (24 in the implementation). 3. Mask Transmission: Generate the final 3D selection mask based on user interactions. Send the mask and opcodes to the volume renderer via Unix sockets over Ethernet using TCP packets. Transmission latency is ~10 seconds for the mask. 4. Rendering Application: The volume renderer applies the mask during ray casting. Selected voxels have their color and opacity modified to emphasize them. The mask does not interact with raw data before local classification; it only affects rendering parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def run3dihe(dataset, hierarchy): """ dataset: 3D numpy array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) hierarchy: Dict mapping primitiveid -> list of voxelindices """ if not hierarchy: # Sources do not provide the exact implementation details for this step. # Treats volume as 3-manifold in 4-space, computes ridges/valleys, # and applies reverse gravity watershed segmentation. hierarchy = generatehierarchyreversegravitywatershed(dataset) selectionmask = np.zeros(dataset.shape, dtype=bool) currentslicez = 0 running = True while running: currentslice = dataset[:,:, currentslicez] # GUI blocks here until user confirms selection on the slice selectedprimitiveids = getusersliceselections(currentslice, hierarchy) for primid in selectedprimitiveids: for idx in hierarchy[primid]: selectionmask.flat[idx] = True sendmasktorenderer(selectionmask) updatethumbnailviews(dataset, selectionmask) running = checkuserexit() def generatehierarchyreversegravitywatershed(volume): # Sources do not provide the exact implementation details for this step. return {} def getusersliceselections(slicedata, hierarchy): # Simulates GUI interaction returning selected primitive IDs return [] def sendmasktorenderer(mask): # Connect to renderer via Unix sockets over Ethernet # Pass image masks and opcodes in TCP packets # Latency ~10 seconds pass def updatethumbnailviews(dataset, mask): # Redraws scaled-down preview slices pass def checkuserexit(): # Returns False if user requests to finish return False Parameters: Dataset Resolution: Example given is 128^3. Gray Levels: Example given is 256. Communication: TCP/IP over Ethernet. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: Hierarchy generation is slow (~15 mins for 128^3). Latency: Mask transmission takes ~10 seconds. Interaction Limitation: Selection mask does not modify raw data or local classification; it only affects rendering parameters (color/opacity). Dimensionality: Selection is 3D-aware, but interaction is 2D-slice-based. Time Complexity: Hierarchy generation is high-cost. Preprocessing a 128^3 image takes ~15 minutes on a Decstation 3100. Interactive selection is fast (<1 minute for brain portion selection with 10 button presses) compared to 2D slice-by-slice editing (~40 minutes). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the hierarchy tree and the selection mask. Not given in the sources. Performance: The 3D IHE significantly reduces user time for complex 3D selections compared to 2D methods. Strengths: Enables semantic, global set-membership selection; efficient 3D region definition via 2D interaction; immediate visual feedback. Limitations: Slow preprocessing; high transmission latency; mask does not affect pre-classification data processing. When to use: When users need to select complex, non-contiguous 3D regions based on semantic meaning rather than local intensity thresholds. When not to use: When real-time, low-latency interaction is critical, or when raw data modification is required before classification. The 3D Interactive Hierarchy Editor was developed as part of an explorational 3D visualization system for medical image data. It builds on earlier work in image segmentation using ridges and valleys, extending 2D methods to 3D by treating images as 3-manifolds in 4-space. The system was designed to change 3D display from a post-processing step to a primary way of viewing medical image data by allowing dynamic control of opacity and regions of interest. name: Spatial Selection
head: Basis Selection for Reconstruction, Subspace Selection
body: Spatial Selection restricts volumetric reconstruction or editing to a specific subset of the data domain, either by selecting a subspace of basis functions or by segmenting the rendered image to identify regions of interest. It differs from global reconstruction methods by reducing computational cost and enabling localized interaction. It differs from simple rectangular cropping by supporting heterogeneous, object-based selections via image-space clustering. Two distinct mechanisms exist for spatial selection: subspace basis selection for mathematical reconstruction and image-space clustering for interactive editing. This method reconstructs a volume by limiting computation to a specific subrange of the basis matrices. Inputs: Original basis matrices U^{(k)} \in \mathbb{R}^{Ik \times Rk} for each dimension k \in \{1, 2, 3\}. Target subspace indices Jk \subseteq Ik. Outputs: Rank-reduced basis matrices Ub^{(k)} \in \mathbb{R}^{Jk \times Rk}. Partial spatial reconstruction Ab. Data Structures: U^{(k)}: Matrix of size Ik \times Rk, where Ik is the full dimension size and Rk is the rank. Jk: List or boolean mask of indices to select from Ik. Ub^{(k)}: Matrix of size |Jk| \times Rk, containing only the rows of U^{(k)} indexed by Jk. Steps: 1. Define the target subspace J1 \times J2 \times J3 \subseteq I1 \times I2 \times I3. 2. For each dimension k, extract the rows of the original basis matrix U^{(k)} corresponding to indices in Jk to form Ub^{(k)}. Ub^{(k)}[i,:] = U^{(k)}[Jk[i],:] \quad \forall i \in \{0, \dots, |Jk|-1\} 3. Perform partial spatial reconstruction Ab using the reduced bases Ub^{(k)} in place of the full bases in the reconstruction equations (Equations 1 or 2 from). Edge Cases: If Jk is empty, the reconstruction in that dimension yields zero or undefined values. If Jk is not contiguous, the resulting basis is sparse in the original domain but dense in the reduced index space. This method selects regions based on visual similarity in the rendered image, replacing rectangular selections with object-based segments. Inputs: Rendered volume image (RGB). User click position (x, y). Outputs: Selected region mask (set of pixels). Parameters: Distance Metric: Euclidean distance in RGB color space. Clustering Algorithm: GPU-accelerated k-means. Steps: 1. Perform image segmentation on the volume rendered image using GPU-accelerated k-means clustering with RGB Euclidean distance. 2. Store resultant segments as individual masks. 3. When a user clicks a position, identify the segment containing the clicked pixel. 4. Form the selected region consisting of all pixels belonging to that segment. Edge Cases: Small or noisy regions may form distinct segments, leading to fragmented selections. Color similarity may group distinct anatomical structures if their appearance is similar. A method to select regions of interest by segmenting the rendered image into contiguous visual objects using GPU-accelerated k-means clustering. It replaces rectangular selections with heterogeneously-shaped segments based on color similarity. It is chosen when the user wants to select objects based on appearance rather than geometric bounds. It results in larger view frustums, more selected voxels, more homogeneous colors across the selection, and consequently smoother transfer function components and relative visibility histograms compared to rectangular selection. Subspace Basis Selection: Time Complexity: Reduced by the size of the subspace Jk relative to Ik. Memory Complexity: Reduced storage for basis matrices Ub^{(k)}. Strengths: Enables variable resolution and spatial localization in tensor approximation. Limitations: Requires pre-computed basis matrices. Image-Space Clustering: Time Complexity: Dominated by k-means clustering on the image resolution. Strengths: Produces continuous transfer function components and smoother histograms than rectangular selection. Limitations: Selections are limited to visible objects and may include unintended adjacent regions with similar colors. Subspace selection originates from multiscale tensor approximation for volume data, where reconstruction is limited to subranges of basis matrices to achieve spatial selectivity and variable resolution. Image-space clustering for region selection was proposed to provide a more robust representation of user interest for low-level iterative editing, specifically for transfer function editing using relative visibility histograms. name: Image-based Voxelization
head: Custom Maps Generation, Multiple Image to Schematic Conversion, Picture-to-Voxel Forge
body: Image-based Voxelization converts a sequence of 2D images into a 3D volumetric schematic where the image index maps to the depth axis (Y), and pixel coordinates map to the spatial axes (X and Z). It is distinguished from standard volume extrusion by its specific handling of surface boundaries via an "excavate" mode, which clips voxel columns based on neighbor transparency to create terraced structures rather than solid vertical walls. Inputs and Outputs Input: A list of 2D images (PNG/JPG/JPEG), an optional 256x1 pixel color gradient file (mInputColorFile), a boolean mExcavate flag, and an integer mColorLimit. Output: A.npz voxel volume containing a Schematic object with a list of voxels. Data Structures Voxel: Defined by integer coordinates (x, y, z) and a Color object. x is the image pixel column index, y is the image index in the input list (depth), and z is the image pixel row index. Schematic: Contains a list of voxels. Maximum world width and length are constrained by Schematic.MAXWORLDWIDTH and Schematic.MAXWORLDLENGTH. Retrieve pixel color channels (RGB and Alpha). d. Skip Condition: If the pixel is Empty, Transparent, Black, or has all RGB channels equal to zero, skip this pixel. e. Voxel Placement: If mExcavate is true: call CheckNeighbor(x, z). If any of the four 4-connected neighbors (left, top, right, bottom) is empty/transparent/black or has zero RGB, add a voxel at (x, i, z) with the determined color. If mExcavate is false: add a voxel at (x, i, z) with the determined color. 4. Quantization: Apply quantization to the blocks list using mColorLimit. 5.
