name: Anti-aliased Voxelization (Scalar-valued/Fuzzy)
head: De-binarization, Fuzzy set voxelization, Object-space pre-filtering
body: Anti-aliased voxelization generates scalar-valued voxels that represent the percentage of spatial occupancy within a voxel, creating a fuzzy set where the boundary between inclusion and exclusion is smooth. Unlike binary voxelization, which classifies voxels into a discrete {0,1} set and suffers from object-space aliasing (jagged surfaces) that propagates to image-space aliasing during rendering, this method employs object-space pre-filtering to suppress these artifacts. It is distinguished from sibling methods like VoxelGrid from Mesh (Fill Method) by its continuous output values and from Gaussian Voxelization by its linear distance-based filter rather than a probabilistic kernel. Inputs: A triangle mesh (or parametric surface) and a 3D voxel grid defined by a bounding box and resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz). Outputs: A 3D array of scalar values where each voxel stores a value in [0, 1] representing occupancy probability or fuzzy membership. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array grid[Nx][Ny][Nz] of floating-point numbers. Initialized to 0.0. Triangle: Defined by vertices V0, V1, V2. Algorithm Steps: 1. Bounding Box Calculation: Compute the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the triangle in voxel coordinates. Determine the integer range [x{min}, x{max}], [y{min}, y{max}], [z{min}, z{max}] covering all voxels that the triangle's footprint intersects. 2. Voxel Iteration: Iterate through each voxel (i, j, k) within the bounding box. 3. Distance Evaluation: For each voxel, calculate the signed distance d from the voxel center C{ijk} to the triangle surface. The value stored in the voxel is a linear function of this distance. 4. Filter Application: Apply a filter equation to the distance. The optimal sampling filter for central difference gradient estimation in low-curvature areas is a one-dimensional box filter of width 1 voxel unit, oriented perpendicular to the surface. This filter is computed as a linear function of the distance from the triangle. 5. Fuzzy Union: Update the voxel value using the fuzzy algebraic union operator, which is the maximum operator. If the computed value for the current triangle is greater than the existing value in grid[i][j][k], update it. Formulas: Let d be the distance from the voxel center to the triangle surface. The value v assigned to the voxel is determined by the filter function F(d). While the exact linear function coefficients depend on the specific implementation of the "linear function of distance" mentioned in the source, the core operation is: v = F(d) \text{grid}[i][j][k] = \max(\text{grid}[i][j][k], v) Parameters: Filter Width: 1 voxel unit. Filter Orientation: Perpendicular to the surface. Pitfalls: Binary Classification Errors: Avoiding the binary {0,1} classification is critical; using hard thresholds reintroduces object-space aliasing. Gradient Estimation: The method is optimized for central difference gradient estimation. Deviating from the 1-unit box filter may degrade rendering quality in low-curvature areas. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def antialiasedvoxelization(triangle, grid, voxelsize): """ Voxelizes a triangle into a scalar-valued fuzzy grid. Args: triangle: Object with vertices V0, V1, V2 (3D vectors). grid: 3D numpy array or list of lists of lists, initialized to 0.0. voxelsize: Size of one voxel unit in world coordinates. """ # 1. Compute bounding box in voxel coordinates # Convert triangle vertices to voxel coordinates v0vx = triangle.V0 / voxelsize v1vx = triangle.V1 / voxelsize v2vx = triangle.V2 / voxelsize # Determine integer bounds xmin = int(min(v0vx.x, v1vx.x, v2vx.x)) xmax = int(max(v0vx.x, v1vx.x, v2vx.x)) ymin = int(min(v0vx.y, v1vx.y, v2vx.y)) ymax = int(max(v0vx.y, v1vx.y, v2vx.y)) zmin = int(min(v0vx.z, v1vx.z, v2vx.z)) zmax = int(max(v0vx.z, v1vx.z, v2vx.z)) # Precompute triangle normal and plane equation for distance # Normal N = (V1-V0) x (V2-V0) e1 = v1vx - v0vx e2 = v2vx - v0vx normal = cross(e1, e2) # Normalize normal normlen = length(normal) if normlen == 0: return # Degenerate triangle normal = normal / normlen # Plane equation: dot(N, P - V0) = 0 # Distance from point P to plane is dot(N, P - V0) # Note: The source describes a filter linear in distance. # We assume the filter maps distance to [0,1] occupancy. # A standard linear filter for a box of width 1 centered at distance 0 # might be: v = 1 - |d| if |d| < 0.5 else 0. # However, the source specifies "oriented perpendicular to the surface" # and "linear function". We implement the generic linear evaluation. for i in range(xmin, xmax + 1): for j in range(ymin, ymax + 1): for k in range(zmin, zmax + 1): # Voxel center in voxel coordinates center = (vector(i + 0.5, j + 0.5, k + 0.5)) # Distance from center to triangle plane # d = dot(normal, center - v0vx) # Note: This is signed distance to the infinite plane. # For a triangle, we might need to check if the projection # falls inside the triangle, but the source emphasizes # "linear function of the distance from the triangle" # and "fuzzy set". We use the plane distance as the primary metric # for the filter as per the "box filter... oriented perpendicular" description. dist = dot(normal, center - v0vx) # Apply filter: Linear function of distance. # The source cites Sramek and Kaufman [308] for a 1-unit box filter. # A box filter of width 1 centered at 0 is: # f(d) = 1 - |d| for |d| <= 0.5, else 0. # This is a linear function of distance in the active region. absdist = abs(dist) if absdist < 0.5: value = 1.0 - absdist else: value = 0.0 # Fuzzy Union (Max operator) if value > grid[i][j][k]: grid[i][j][k] = value Treats 3D scan conversion as a sampling process applying low-pass filtering to suppress aliasing before discretization. It differs by explicitly framing the scalar-valued output as a result of spatial occupancy representation to avoid surface normal estimation errors. Choose when smooth gradients are required for rendering without jagged edges. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot B), where N is the number of triangles and B is the average number of voxels in the bounding box of a triangle. Memory Complexity: O(Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz) for the voxel grid. Strengths: Eliminates object-space aliasing (jagged surfaces) and subsequent image-space aliasing. Provides smooth gradients suitable for central difference estimation in volume rendering. Limitations: Produces scalar values rather than binary occupancy, which may require different handling in downstream binary operations. The linear filter approximation may be less accurate for high-curvature surfaces compared to more complex splatting techniques. When to use: When rendering quality is prioritized over binary topological consistency, and when the rendering pipeline supports scalar-valued density fields. The method was devised to address the limitations of binary voxelization, which exhibits object-space aliasing due to the binary classification of voxels into the {0,1} set. It extends the two-dimensional line anti-aliasing method of Gupta and Sproull [103] to 3D. Sramek and Kaufman [308][309] demonstrated that a one-dimensional box filter of width 1 voxel unit, oriented perpendicular to the surface, is optimal for central difference gradient estimation in low-curvature areas. This approach allows for direct visualization from a fuzzy set, avoiding image aliasing. Volume Visualization and Volume Graphics, https://www3.cs.stonybrook.edu/~mueller/teaching/cse332/volvisChapter.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (book)

name: Object Voxelization by Filtering
head: Filter-based voxelization, Volume graphics voxelization
body: Object Voxelization by Filtering treats 3D scan conversion as a sampling process that applies low-pass filtering to suppress aliasing before discretizing the continuous object signal into a voxel raster. It differs from binary voxelization by producing scalar-valued, fuzzy voxels that represent spatial occupancy, thereby avoiding the surface normal estimation errors and aliasing artifacts inherent in hard-edged approaches. Inputs and Outputs Input: A continuous object representation O(\mathbf{p}) (e.g., a parametric surface or implicit function) and a sampling step a defining the voxel grid resolution. Output: A discrete 3D volume data set where each voxel at integer coordinates (i, j, k) contains a scalar value representing the filtered occupancy. Data Structures The output is a 3D array of floating-point values. The spatial layout corresponds to a regular grid with spacing a. The value at index (i, j, k) represents the convolution result at position \mathbf{p}{ijk} = (ai, aj, ak). Method Steps 1. Filter Design: Select a blurring filter function f(\mathbf{p}). Common choices include the Gaussian filter or the Bartlett (cone-shaped) function. 2. Convolution: Convolve the continuous object signal O(\mathbf{p}) with the filter f(\mathbf{p}) to produce the filtered object signal f(\mathbf{p}). f(\mathbf{p}) = f(\mathbf{p}) O(\mathbf{p}) 3. Sampling: Sample the filtered result at discrete locations \mathbf{p}{ijk} = (ai, aj, ak), where a is the sampling step and (i, j, k) are integer coordinates. Formulas Gaussian Filter The Gaussian filter is defined as: fG(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{p}f) = kG e^{-\frac{\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}f\|^2}{2\sigma^2}} where: \mathbf{p}f is the filter center position. \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}f\| is the Euclidean distance from the arbitrary point \mathbf{p} to the center. \sigma (or u) defines the width of the Gaussian. kG is a normalization constant. Bartlett (Cone) Filter The Bartlett function is defined as: fB(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{p}f) = kB \left( 1 - \frac{\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}f\|}{rf} \right) \quad \text{if } \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}f\| < rf, \text{ otherwise } 0 where: \mathbf{p}f is the filter center position. rf is the diameter of the spherical support. kB is a normalization constant. Normal Estimation and Error Analysis To estimate surface normals from the voxel data, central differences are used. Let h(d) be the density profile depending on the distance d from the surface. For a point V with distance dv from the surface, the distances to neighbors are: dA = dv - dx, \quad dB = dv + dx dC = dv - dy, \quad dD = dv + dy The gradient components are estimated as: gx = \frac{h(dB) - h(dA)}{2dx}, \quad gy = \frac{h(dD) - h(dC)}{2dy} Using a Taylor series expansion of h(d) around dv, the estimated normal vector (gx, gy) is parallel to the true normal vector (\cos\theta, \sin\theta) if and only if the density profile h(d) is linear with distance d. This requires the symmetric coefficients ki (for i=2,4,\dots) in the Taylor expansion to be zero. Parameters Sampling step a: The distance between discrete sample locations in the voxel grid. Sigma (\sigma): Defines the width of the Gaussian filter. Transient Region Thickness: The optimal thickness of the transition region between inside and outside is estimated to be about 3 voxel units to avoid systematic error in normal estimation. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Normal Estimation Error: Using a Gaussian filter introduces an error in normal estimation because the resulting density profile h(d) is not linear. The maximum amplitude of this error is approximately 43 degrees (0.07 radians). This exceeds the empirically estimated visually indistinguishable angular difference of 0.01 radians. While this deviation is nearly invisible in static images due to smooth distribution, it causes disturbing artifacts in animation sequences. Computational Complexity: Numerical evaluation of the convolution has a computational complexity of O(m^3 n^3), where m is the resolution of the voxelized data and n is the resolution of the filter. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def objectvoxelizationbyfiltering(objectsurface, samplingstep, filtertype, sigma, filterradius): """ Voxelizes a continuous object by filtering. Args: objectsurface: Function or implicit representation O(p) returning distance or occupancy. samplingstep: Float 'a', distance between voxel centers. filtertype: String, 'gaussian' or 'bartlett'. sigma: Float, width of Gaussian filter (ignored if filtertype is 'bartlett'). filterradius: Float, radius of support for Bartlett filter (ignored if 'gaussian'). Returns: volumedata: 3D numpy array of voxel values. """ # Determine grid bounds based on object extent and sampling step # Implementation detail: Bounds must be determined from objectsurface extent. # Let mincoord, maxcoord be the bounding box of the object. # numvoxels = ceil((maxcoord - mincoord) / samplingstep) volumedata = empty3darray(numvoxels) for i in range(numvoxels[0]): for j in range(numvoxels[1]): for k in range(numvoxels[2]): # Calculate continuous position p = (i samplingstep, j samplingstep, k samplingstep) # Convolve object with filter # The source notes state convolution is O(m^3 n^3). # A naive implementation iterates over filter support. # For efficiency, lookup tables or hierarchical subdivision are suggested, # but the core definition is the convolution integral. filteredvalue = 0.0 # Define filter support region if filtertype == 'gaussian': # Gaussian filter support is theoretically infinite, but truncated in practice. # Standard practice truncates at 3-4 sigma. supportradius = 4 sigma filterresolution = int(2 supportradius / samplingstep) for fi in range(-filterresolution, filterresolution + 1): for fj in range(-filterresolution, filterresolution + 1): for fk in range(-filterresolution, filterresolution + 1): filtercenter = (fi samplingstep, fj samplingstep, fk samplingstep) distsq = sum((pcoord - fccoord)2 for pcoord, fccoord in zip(p, filtercenter)) # Gaussian kernel value # kG is normalization constant kernelval = exp(-distsq / (2 sigma2)) # Convolve: sum of O(p - filteroffset) kernel # Assuming O(p) is occupancy (1 inside, 0 outside) or signed distance. # The source implies convolution of O(p) with f(p). # We approximate the integral by summation over the filter support. # Note: The source notes simplify this to sampling the result of convolution. # A precise implementation requires integrating O(p) over the filter kernel support. # For a binary object, this is the volume of intersection of the kernel and the object. # Simplified approximation for pseudocode completeness: # Evaluate object at filter center relative to p # This is a simplification. The true convolution is integral. # However, for fuzzy voxelization, the value is often the integral of the kernel # over the object volume. # Let's implement the integral approximation: # Value = Integral( O(q) f(p-q) dq) # Discretized: Sum( O(qsample) f(p-qsample) volsample) # To keep it self-contained and based on notes: # The notes describe the result as sampling the convolution. # We will compute the convolution sum. # Offset from p to filter center offset = (filtercenter[0] - p[0], filtercenter[1] - p[1], filtercenter[2] - p[2]) # Evaluate object at the point shifted by the filter center? # No, convolution is f(p) O(p). # f(p) = Integral( f(q) O(p-q) dq) # Let q be the filter center. Then we evaluate O at p-q. pointtoeval = (p[0] - filtercenter[0], p[1] - filtercenter[1], p[2] - filtercenter[2]) # Object function call occupancy = objectsurface(pointtoeval) filteredvalue += occupancy kernelval elif filtertype == 'bartlett': # Bartlett filter support is spherical with radius rf supportradius = filterradius filterresolution = int(2 supportradius / samplingstep) for fi in range(-filterresolution, filterresolution + 1): for fj in range(-filterresolution, filterresolution + 1): for fk in range(-filterresolution, filterresolution + 1): filtercenter = (fi samplingstep, fj samplingstep, fk samplingstep) dist = sum((pcoord - fccoord)2 for pcoord, fccoord in zip(p, filtercenter))0.5 if dist < supportradius: # Bartlett kernel value # kB is normalization constant kernelval = 1 - (dist / supportradius) pointtoeval = (p[0] - filtercenter[0], p[1] - filtercenter[1], p[2] - filtercenter[2]) occupancy = objectsurface(pointtoeval) filteredvalue += occupancy kernelval # Normalize by filter integral (approximated by sum of kernel values voxelvol) # The source mentions kG and kB as normalization constants. # In discrete implementation, we divide by the sum of kernel weights if O is binary. # For simplicity, we assume the kernel is normalized or the result is scaled. volumedata[i, j, k] = filteredvalue return volumedata Complexity: The computational complexity of evaluating the convolution numerically is O(m^3 n^3), where m is the resolution of the voxelized data and n is the resolution of the filter. Performance: The high complexity necessitates speedup techniques such as precomputed lookup tables indexed by distance to the object surface or approximating the convolution of a half-space object with the Gaussian kernel. Strengths: It avoids object-space and image-space aliasing by treating voxelization as a sampling process with low-pass filtering. It allows for Boolean, block, and CSG operations. Limitations: The Gaussian filter introduces a systematic error in normal estimation (up to 43 degrees), which can cause artifacts in animation. The uniform approach (neglecting object shape) uses first-degree blurring and normal estimation filters, which may be less precise for complex shapes compared to object-specific lookup tables using higher-order blurring filters, though it offers more precise reconstruction of derivatives for uniform treatment. Origin: This technique was developed by researchers at the Center for Visual Computing (CVC) and the Department of Computer Science, State University of New York at Stony Brook. History: It emerged as a response to the aliasing problems in early binary voxelization algorithms, which ignored sampling theory. It is part of the "Volume Graphics" research paradigm. Usage: It is used in Volume Graphics research for modeling and rendering, particularly where smooth surface representation and normal estimation are critical. Object voxeliztion by filtering, https://doi.org/10.1145/288126.288178, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Voxel Atlas Construction
head: Compact Voxel Atlas JSON Format
body: Voxel Atlas Construction aggregates individual voxelized asset files into a single compact JSON file containing flat arrays of positions and colors. It consolidates numerous small JSON files into a unified structure optimized for efficient web loading. Unlike discrete voxelization methods that generate grids from geometry, this method focuses on serializing and aggregating pre-existing voxel data for application loading. Inputs and Outputs: The input is a directory containing individual voxel JSON files, where each file contains voxel data for a single asset. The output is a single JSON file containing an object that maps asset names to their voxel data. Data Structures: The output is a JSON object where the keys are asset names. Each value is an object with the following fields: resolution is an integer representing the voxel grid resolution used for the asset. count is an integer representing the number of voxels in the asset. bounds is an object with min and max keys, each holding an array of three integers representing the bounding box coordinates. positions is a flat array of integers or floats containing interleaved x, y, z coordinates for each voxel in the format [x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1,...]. colors is a flat array of integers or floats containing interleaved r, g, b values for each voxel in the format [r0, g0, b0, r1, g1, b1,...]. Steps: 1. Discovery: Glob for all.json files in the input directory, sort them alphabetically, and filter out any file named voxelatlas.json to prevent recursion. 2. Initialization: Create an empty dictionary atlas to store the aggregated data. 3. Iteration: For each valid JSON file, load the JSON data. Extract the asset name and use the file stem if the name field is missing. Extract resolution, count, bounds, positions, and colors from the source file. Store these fields in the atlas dictionary under the key name. 4. Serialization: Create the parent directory for the output path if it does not exist. Write the atlas dictionary to the output file as formatted JSON. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import json from pathlib import Path def buildatlas(voxeldir: str, outputpath: str) -> None: """ Combines individual voxel JSON files into a single compact atlas file. """ voxelpath = Path(voxeldir) atlas = {} jsonfiles = sorted(voxelpath.glob(".json")) if not jsonfiles: print(f"No voxel JSON files found in {voxeldir}") return for filepath in jsonfiles: if filepath.name == "voxelatlas.json": continue with open(filepath, 'r') as f: data = json.load(f) name = data.get("name", filepath.stem) assetdata = { "resolution": data["resolution"], "count": data["count"], "bounds": data["bounds"], "positions": data["positions"], "colors": data["colors"] } atlas[name] = assetdata print(f" Added: {name} ({data['count']} voxels)") outputp = Path(outputpath) outputp.parent.mkdir(parents=True, existok=True) with open(outputp, 'w') as f: json.dump(atlas, f) sizekb = outputp.stat().stsize / 1024 print(f"\nAtlas saved to {outputpath}") print(f" Assets: {len(atlas)}") print(f" Size: {sizekb:.1f} KB") Parameters: The voxeldir parameter specifies the path to the directory containing individual voxel JSON files. The outputpath parameter specifies the path where the resulting atlas JSON file will be saved. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method assumes input JSON files contain resolution, count, bounds, positions, and colors, and direct dictionary access raises a KeyError if any are missing. The script explicitly skips voxelatlas.json to prevent infinite loops if the output directory is the same as the input directory. The source notes describe positions and colors as flat arrays of integers in one context and floats in another, and consistency in data types across assets is not enforced by the aggregation step. The time complexity is not given in the sources, but standard JSON parsing and serialization scale linearly with the number of input files and total voxel count. The memory complexity is not given in the sources, but it is proportional to the total size of all input JSON files loaded into memory. In the full pipeline, CPU stages overlap with GPU processing to avoid idle time. The aggregation step is fast compared to the voxelization inference. The method reduces I/O overhead for loading multiple assets and provides a single entry point for all voxel data. It is not suitable for dynamic updates where individual voxels need to be modified in place, as the entire atlas may need to be rebuilt. The JSON format is less compact than binary formats for very large datasets. This method is part of the image-to-voxel pipeline, which is an unofficial implementation for generating voxel assets from images using AI models like TripoSR. The pipeline includes stages for image preparation, 3D inference, and voxelization, with the atlas construction serving as the final packaging step for efficient distribution. mohamedmansour/image-to-voxel, https://github.com/mohamedmansour/image-to-voxel, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Post-Voxelization Modifiers
body: Post-Voxelization Modifiers are algorithms applied to a discrete voxel grid after the initial geometric conversion to correct artifacts, optimize storage, or adapt the data for specific rendering pipelines. This family modifies existing voxel attributes (density, material, opacity) without re-evaluating the source geometry. It encompasses interactive editing, LOD downsampling, porosity injection, surface thickening, and multi-volume compositing. All methods in this family apply a transformation rule to an existing voxel grid after initial geometric conversion, without re-evaluating the source geometry. The execution model typically involves reading an input grid, applying a local or global transformation rule (such as neighborhood analysis or statistical aggregation), and writing a modified grid or rendering mask. Voxel Editing Tools provide interactive, post-voxelization modification of volumetric data, allowing users to surgically alter individual or grouped voxels for tasks such as surgical planning, artifact correction, or data abstraction. Unlike the parent family which often applies algorithmic, non-interactive transformations, this method relies on direct user input via a stylus or pointer to define local regions of influence. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Avatar Head Data Variant Application by focusing on arbitrary spatial manipulation (removal, transparency, recoloring) rather than variant-specific attribute mapping. Choose this method when direct user-driven local edits are required. See Voxel Editing Tools. This method modifies a base head voxel data array to apply specific hair variants (short, buzz, or long) by rewriting specific voxel value markers. It solves the problem of dynamically changing character appearance without re-voxelizing the underlying geometry, allowing for iterative refinement or user-driven adjustments post-generation. It is distinct from general Voxel Editing Tools by focusing exclusively on semantic hair type substitution within the head region using predefined integer markers. Choose this method when dynamically changing character appearance without re-voxelizing geometry is required. See Avatar Head Data Variant Application. A hierarchical compression technique used in large-scale planetary voxel systems to reduce memory footprint while preserving visual fidelity across distance levels. It operates on a hierarchy of voxel grids (bricks) where each coarse voxel represents a 2x2x2 block of finer voxels. A coarse voxel is classified as solid if at least 4 of its 8 children are solid. The material of the coarse voxel is determined by the most common material among its solid children. Edits to the fine grid propagate immediately up all LOD levels, ensuring that features like craters remain visible from orbit without requiring separate mesh fallbacks. Chosen for open-world or planetary rendering where memory budget is strict (e.g., ~2 GB on a 4090) and distance-based detail is required. See Sparse and Hierarchical Structures for the underlying data structure. A technique to introduce controlled void space into voxelized meshes, simulating porous materials or reducing voxel count for aesthetic or performant reasons. Voxels are dropped (set to empty) based on a spatial pseudo-random hash function. The decision is deterministic for a given coordinate, ensuring consistency across updates. Controlled by a porosity float parameter, passed via CLI (--porosity <FLOAT>) or API (MeshProcessor::voxelize). Chosen when simulating materials like foam or rock, or when reducing voxel density for performance without altering the mesh geometry. See VoxelGrid from Mesh (Fill Method) for the base generation method. A correction step for rendering thin or zero-thickness geometry (such as meshes) that would otherwise appear dashed, aliased, or partially transparent during ray marching or cone marching. Meshes are hollow; voxelization gives partly covered voxels; the modifier scales coverage up so grazed surfaces read as solid, effectively thickening the voxel representation of the surface. The Amount parameter (default 2.0f) controls the thickening. Increasing this value prevents surface leakage but may cause inflation; decreasing it reduces inflation but may reveal transparency. It is not a substitute for sufficient voxel resolution. Chosen when rendering wireframes, thin shells, or low-poly meshes where standard voxelization fails to produce a solid appearance. See Voxel Volume Rendering for the rendering context. A technique to highlight structures of interest by combining the original volume with a second volume containing complementary information (e.g., distance to a structure) to modulate the rendering. Provide two input volumes: the original volume and a second volume containing complementary data. In the Volume shader for the second volume, multiply the color-mapped sample from the second volume with the accumulated sample from the first volume: vec4 sample = SampleVolumeWithTF (volIndex, pos); fullSample = sample;. Do not use raw samples from the second volume to modulate color or opacity; use the color-mapped sample (after transfer function application) to allow interactive adjustment of decluttering via the transfer function. A preprocessing step to simulate the blurring of interfaces between different materials (e.g., rock and fluid) caused by finite voxel resolution in X-ray imaging. Identify the interface between the rock matrix and fluid phases in the simulation volume. Apply a Gaussian filter to the interface region to smear the boundary, creating voxels that contain mixed material properties. Post-voxelization processing evolved as voxelization shifted from simple binary occupancy grids to complex, attribute-rich representations for real-time rendering and global illumination. Hierarchical downsampling techniques emerged for large-scale planetary systems to manage memory budgets across distance levels. The Opacify modifier was introduced in real-time voxel GI systems like StrideVoxelGI to handle visual artifacts from rasterizing thin geometry into voxels. Porosity injection via spatial hashing was added to open-source voxelizers to control material void space. Decluttering and Gaussian smearing techniques were developed for medical and scientific volume rendering to enhance interpretability of complex structures and simulate partial volume effects. name: Voxel Editing Tools
head: Interactive voxel manipulation, Voxel eraser and paint
body: Voxel Editing Tools provide interactive, post-voxelization modification of volumetric data, allowing users to surgically alter individual or grouped voxels for tasks such as surgical planning, artifact correction, or data abstraction. Unlike the parent Post-Voxelization Modifiers which often apply algorithmic, non-interactive transformations (like LOD downsampling or statistical aggregation), this method relies on direct user input via a stylus or pointer to define local regions of influence. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Avatar Head Data Variant Application by focusing on arbitrary spatial manipulation (removal, transparency, recoloring) rather than variant-specific attribute mapping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A fully populated voxel grid (or sparse representation) with initial attributes (solid/empty, material ID, density, color). A user input device (stylus/pointer) providing 3D position and state (pressed/released). Output: A modified voxel grid where specific voxels have their properties changed (e.g., set to transparent, recolored, or restored). Data Structures: Voxel Grid: Standard 3D array or sparse hash map storing voxel attributes. Each voxel must support at least: opacity or issolid (boolean or float 0.0-1.0) color (RGB or RGBA) originalvalues (backup of initial state for restoration). Tool State: shape: Enum {RECTANGULAR, CYLINDRICAL, SPHERICAL}. radius or dimensions: Float or Vector3 defining tool size. mode: Enum {INSPECT, EDIT}. isactive: Boolean indicating if the tool switch is pressed. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Tool: Set default shape (e.g., SPHERICAL) and radius. Initialize mode to INSPECT. Store a copy of the initial voxel grid as originalgrid for restoration capabilities. 2. Receive Input: Get current 3D position P from the stylus/pointer and the state of the tool switch S (1 if pressed, 0 if not). 3. Adjust Size: If the user performs a specific gesture (e.g., pointing direction change or scroll), update radius. The sources describe a stylus pointing upwards to enlarge and downwards to shrink. 4. Determine Tool Volume: Calculate the set of voxel indices V{tool} intersected by the tool shape centered at P with current radius and shape. For SPHERICAL: V{tool} = \{ v \mid \|v - P\| \le radius \} For RECTANGULAR: V{tool} = \{ v \mid |vx - Px| \le rx, |vy - Py| \le ry, |vz - Pz| \le rz \} For CYLINDRICAL: V{tool} = \{ v \mid \sqrt{(vx - Px)^2 + (vy - Py)^2} \le r{cyl}, |vz - Pz| \le r{cyl\height} \} (Axis alignment not specified, assume local orientation). 5. Execute Mode: If mode is INSPECT (S=0): Do not modify the grid. During rendering, voxels in V{tool} are hidden (opacity set to 0.0 for rendering purposes only, or excluded from ray-casting) to reveal underlying tissue. If mode is EDIT (S=1): For each voxel v \in V{tool}, apply the edit operation: Remove: Set v.opacity = 0.0 (or mark as empty). Paint: Set v.color = user\selected\color. Restore: If a restoration command is issued, set v = original\grid[v]. 6. Render/Update: Refresh the visualization. In INSPECT mode, the view updates to show the "hole" created by the tool. In EDIT mode, the grid data is permanently modified until the next session or undo. Parameters: Tool Shapes: Rectangular, Cylindrical, Spherical. Size Control: Dynamic, controlled by stylus orientation (up to enlarge, down to shrink). Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interaction Errors: Users may accidentally modify voxels. This is mitigated by the ability to restore voxels to their original values from originalgrid. Boundary Conditions: The tool shape may extend beyond the voxel grid boundaries. Implementation must clamp voxel indices to valid grid ranges. Precision: Floating-point position P must be accurately mapped to voxel indices. Rounding errors can cause "jitter" or missed voxels at boundaries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class VoxelEditor: def init(self, voxelgrid): self.grid = voxelgrid self.originalgrid = copy(voxelgrid) self.toolshape = "SPHERICAL" self.toolradius = 1.0 self.mode = "INSPECT" # "INSPECT" or "EDIT" self.isswitchpressed = False def updatetoolsize(self, direction): """ direction: +1 for enlarge (up), -1 for shrink (down) """ self.toolradius += 0.1 direction if self.toolradius < 0.1: self.toolradius = 0.1 def getvoxelsintool(self, position): """ Returns list of voxel indices within the tool's shape centered at position. """ voxels = [] # Implementation depends on grid structure (dense vs sparse) # For dense grid: r = self.toolradius if self.toolshape == "SPHERICAL": minx = floor(position.x - r) maxx = ceil(position.x + r) miny = floor(position.y - r) maxy = ceil(position.y + r) minz = floor(position.z - r) maxz = ceil(position.z + r) for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): if isvalidindex(x, y, z): distsq = (x - position.x)2 + (y - position.y)2 + (z - position.z)2 if distsq <= r2: voxels.append((x, y, z)) elif self.toolshape == "RECTANGULAR": # Similar bounding box logic pass elif self.toolshape == "CYLINDRICAL": # Similar logic with cylindrical constraint pass return voxels def processinput(self, position, switchstate): self.isswitchpressed = switchstate # Determine mode based on switch state if not explicitly set by UI # Note: Source says "Without switch pressed: inspect mode... When switch is pressed: removes voxels" # This implies mode is dynamic based on switch, or switch toggles the action within a mode. # We follow the source: Switch OFF -> Inspect (Visual only). Switch ON -> Edit (Modify). voxels = self.getvoxelsintool(position) if not self.isswitchpressed: # INSPECT MODE: Do not modify grid. # Return voxels for rendering to hide them. return voxels, "HIDE" else: # EDIT MODE: Modify grid for v in voxels: # Default action is removal (transparency) self.grid[v].opacity = 0.0 # Additional actions like painting would require extra UI input # self.grid[v].color = usercolor return voxels, "MODIFY" def restorevoxels(self, voxels): """ Restores specified voxels to their original state. """ for v in voxels: self.grid[v] = self.originalgrid[v] A workflow strategy separating voxel data into View (mesh-based rendering) and Edit (voxel-grid manipulation) states to balance performance and flexibility. It isolates heavy voxel computation to a single active object, avoiding the cost of scanning all chunks for every object update. Time Complexity: O(N{tool}) per frame, where N{tool} is the number of voxels intersected by the tool shape. This is generally small compared to the total grid size, allowing for real-time interaction. Memory Complexity: O(N{grid}) for the voxel grid plus O(N{grid}) for the originalgrid backup if restoration is required. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows precise, user-driven modification of volume data for planning and correction. Supports immediate visual feedback (inspect mode) and permanent changes (edit mode). Limitations: Performance may degrade if the tool size becomes very large or if the grid is extremely dense and sparse structures are not used. Restoration requires storing a full copy of the original data. When to use: Surgical planning (e.g., simulating craniotomies), correcting voxelization artifacts, or marking regions of interest. When not to use: When real-time performance on massive, unoptimized dense grids is critical and user interaction is not required. Voxel Editing Tools were developed as part of the VIVIAN (Virtual Interactive Volume-based Neurosurgery) system for multimodal volume-based tumor neurosurgery planning. The system allows surgeons to interactively change voxel properties to simulate surgical procedures, such as turning voxels transparent to study anatomical relationships or removing tumor parts for approach planning. The method was described in the context of a virtual workbench for neurosurgery. Multimodal volume-based tumor neurosurgery planning in the virtual workbench, https://doi.org/10.1007/bfb0056289, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Dual-Mode Voxel Editing
head: View/Edit Modes
body: Dual-Mode Voxel Editing is a workflow strategy that separates voxel data representation into two distinct states—View and Edit—to balance high-performance mesh-based visualization with flexible voxel-level manipulation. It solves the performance bottleneck of dynamically grouping voxels into objects for rendering by isolating the heavy voxel-grid computation to a single active object in Edit mode, while rendering all other objects as pre-computed triangulated meshes in View mode. This approach avoids the cost of scanning all chunks to find voxels for every object update, which breaks the performance of chunk-based systems. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene containing multiple voxel-based objects. Each object is defined by a 3D grid of voxels. Output: A rendered scene where objects are displayed as triangulated meshes, and one selected object is editable via voxel manipulation. Data Structures: 1. Chunk: A fixed 3D grid of bytes with dimensions 32 \times 32 \times 32. Each byte represents a Voxel ID mapped to a color via a 1D texture palette. 2. World Grid (Object Grid): A fixed 3D grid of Chunks with dimensions 8 \times 8 \times 8. Total resolution per object: 256 \times 256 \times 256 voxels (32 \times 8 = 256). Total chunks per object: 8 \times 8 \times 8 = 512 chunks. 3. Voxel Data: Each voxel is described by 1 byte, representing a Material ID in the range [1, 255]. 4. Mesh: A triangulated mesh generated from a Chunk or a combination of Chunks using Greedy meshing. Parameters: Voxel Grid Resolution: 256^3 voxels per object. Voxel Data Type: 1 byte per voxel. Maximum Memory Usage per Object (Edit Mode): 256^3 bytes = 16 MB. Maximum Number of Meshes per Object (Edit Mode): 512 (one per chunk). Editing Constraint: Only a single object can be edited at a time. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each object in the scene, allocate a 256^3 voxel grid (1 byte per voxel) and a corresponding World Grid of 8 \times 8 \times 8 Chunks. 2. View Mode Rendering: Represent each object as a single triangulated mesh (1 Mesh per object). Render the scene using these meshes. Note: If objects are moved, seamless meshes larger than 256^3 can be created. 3. Transition to Edit Mode: Select one object to edit. Load the 3D grid of chunks for the selected object from disk into memory. Switch the rendering representation for this object from a single mesh to a group of up to 512 triangulated chunks (one mesh per chunk). Render the scene with the selected object as chunks and all other objects as single meshes. 4. Editing: Perform voxel-level manipulation (e.g., painting, deletion, boolean operations) on the active object's voxel grid. Update the corresponding chunks and their meshes as needed. 5. Transition to View Mode: Save the 3D grid of chunks for the edited object to disk. Combine all chunks of the edited object into a single triangulated mesh using Greedy meshing. Switch the rendering representation for this object back to a single mesh. Render the scene with all objects as single meshes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Chunk: def init(self): # 32x32x32 grid of bytes self.data = [0] (32 32 32) self.mesh = None # Triangulated mesh generated from this chunk class Object: def init(self): # 8x8x8 grid of Chunks self.chunks = [[Chunk() for in range(8)] for in range(8)] self.voxelgrid = [0] (256 256 256) # 1 byte per voxel self.fullmesh = None # Single mesh for View mode self.chunkmeshes = [] # List of 512 meshes for Edit mode self.isedited = False def getchunkindex(self, x, y, z): # Map global voxel coordinates to chunk and local coordinates cx = x // 32 cy = y // 32 cz = z // 32 lx = x % 32 ly = y % 32 lz = z % 32 return (cx, cy, cz), (lx, ly, lz) def setvoxel(self, x, y, z, materialid): # materialid in [1, 255] chunkcoords, localcoords = self.getchunkindex(x, y, z) cx, cy, cz = chunkcoords lx, ly, lz = localcoords # Update voxel grid idx = x + y 256 + z 256 256 self.voxelgrid[idx] = materialid # Update chunk data chunkidx = lx + ly 32 + lz 32 32 self.chunks[cx][cy][cz].data[chunkidx] = materialid # Mark chunk for mesh rebuild self.chunks[cx][cy][cz].mesh = None def rebuildchunkmesh(self, chunk): # Generate triangulated mesh from chunk data using Greedy meshing # Implementation details of Greedy meshing are not specified in sources chunk.mesh = generategreedymesh(chunk.data) def rebuildfullmesh(self): # Combine all 512 chunk meshes into a single mesh # This step causes a performance freeze self.fullmesh = combinemeshes([chunk.mesh for row in self.chunks for chunk in row]) def entereditmode(self): # Load from disk self.loadfromdisk() # Rebuild individual chunk meshes for row in self.chunks: for chunk in row: if chunk.mesh is None: self.rebuildchunkmesh(chunk) self.chunkmeshes = [chunk.mesh for row in self.chunks for chunk in row] def enterviewmode(self): # Save to disk self.savetodisk() # Combine chunks into single mesh self.rebuildfullmesh() class Scene: def init(self): self.objects = [] self.editmodeobject = None def seteditmode(self, objindex): if self.editmodeobject is not None: self.editmodeobject.enterviewmode() self.editmodeobject = self.objects[objindex] self.editmodeobject.entereditmode() def render(self): for obj in self.objects: if obj == self.editmodeobject: # Render as group of chunks (up to 512 meshes) for mesh in obj.chunkmeshes: drawmesh(mesh) else: # Render as single mesh drawmesh(obj.fullmesh) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance Freeze: Saving/loading chunks to/from disk during mode changes causes a freeze. Mesh Combination Cost: Combining all 512 chunks into a single mesh in Edit-to-View transition causes a freeze. Memory Limit: Each object in Edit mode consumes 16 MB of RAM. Single Object Edit: Only one object can be edited at a time. Time Complexity: View Mode: O(1) per object for rendering (1 mesh per object). Edit Mode: O(N) per object for rendering, where N is the number of chunks (up to 512). Mode Transition: High cost due to disk I/O and mesh combination. Memory Complexity: Edit Mode: 16 MB per object for the voxel grid. View Mode: Memory usage equivalent to polygonal meshes (normals, etc.) for non-active objects. Performance: Fast voxel updates in Edit mode (1 chunk per mouse click). Avoids the performance break of scanning all chunks for object updates. Strengths: Good memory usage for non-active objects. Supports object grouping, export, deletion, and editing. Objects can be moved to create seamless meshes larger than 256^3 voxels. Supports boolean operations (subtraction, addition) between objects using their internal 3D grids. Limitations: Too many meshes per edited object (up to 512). Performance freeze during mode changes. Requires saving each object separately to disk. Dual-Mode Voxel Editing was developed as a solution for voxel editing software to support object grouping and efficient rendering. It addresses the limitations of chunk-based systems where looking up all chunks to find voxels for an object breaks performance. The method was implemented to allow features like object visibility changes and boolean operations while maintaining interactive performance. It is comparable to MagicaVoxel's group system (Outline), though the internal implementation details of MagicaVoxel are not publicly documented. Group voxels into object?, https://gamedev.stackexchange.com/questions/205011/group-voxels-into-object, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Avatar Head Data Variant Application
head: Head Variant Voxel Rewriting
body: This method modifies a base head voxel data array to apply specific hair variants (short, buzz, or long) by rewriting specific voxel value markers. It solves the problem of dynamically changing character appearance without re-voxelizing the underlying geometry, allowing for iterative refinement or user-driven adjustments post-generation. It is distinct from general Voxel Editing Tools by focusing exclusively on semantic hair type substitution within the head region using predefined integer markers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel data array representing the head, where specific integer values denote hair types. Output: A modified voxel data array with updated hair variant markers. Data Structures: The voxel data is a 1D or 3D array of integers. The relevant voxel value constants are defined as: VSKIN: 1 (representing skin). VHAIR: 2 (representing standard hair). VHAIRLONG: 10 (marker for long-only drape). VHAIRVOL: 11 (marker for hair volume shaved by buzz cut). Steps: 1. Create a copy of the source voxel data array to avoid mutating the original. 2. Determine the target value for long hair (longV): If the requested variant is 'long', set longV = VHAIR (2). Otherwise, set longV = 0 (empty/transparent). 3. Determine the target value for volume hair (volV): If the requested variant is 'buzz', set volV = VSKIN (1). Otherwise, set volV = VHAIR (2). 4. Iterate through all voxels in the array: If a voxel's value is VHAIRLONG (10), replace it with longV. If a voxel's value is VHAIRVOL (11), replace it with volV. 5. Return the modified array. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyheadvariant(voxeldata, variant): """ Applies a hair variant to a head voxel array. Args: voxeldata (list[int]): The input voxel array. variant (str): One of 'short', 'buzz', 'long'. Returns: list[int]: The modified voxel array. """ # Constants defined in source VSKIN = 1 VHAIR = 2 VHAIRLONG = 10 VHAIRVOL = 11 # Step 1: Copy data newdata = list(voxeldata) # Step 2 & 3: Determine target values if variant == 'long': longV = VHAIR else: longV = 0 if variant == 'buzz': volV = VSKIN else: volV = VHAIR # Step 4: Iterate and replace for i in range(len(newdata)): val = newdata[i] if val == VHAIRLONG: newdata[i] = longV elif val == VHAIRVOL: newdata[i] = volV # Step 5: Return result return newdata Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If variant is neither 'long' nor 'buzz' (e.g., 'short'), longV becomes 0 and volV becomes VHAIR. This effectively removes long hair markers and keeps volume hair as standard hair, resulting in a short cut. Precision issues are not applicable as integer markers are used. Boundary conditions: The method assumes the input array contains only valid markers. If other values are present, they are ignored. Constructs a complete avatar model object by sanitizing input, mapping color indices to hex values, deriving shades, and swapping the head voxel data for the chosen hair variant. It sanitizes the input avatar object to ensure valid color indices and hair variant, retrieves the base model and its palette P, and constructs a new palette array. Entries 1 (skin), 2 (hair), 4 (hoodie main), 6 (jeans main), 8 (sneaker), 10 (hair long), 11 (hair buzz) use the main hex colors. Entries 5 (hoodie shade), 7 (jeans shade), 13 (skin shade) use shadeHex(mainHex). Entries 3, 9, 12, 14, 15 are fixed from base palette P. The head part's data in the base model parts array is replaced with buildHeadData(p.data, a.hair), and the new model object with the updated palette and parts is returned. The shade color calculation is defined as: \text{shadeHex}(\text{mainHex}) = \text{sRGB\to\hex}( \text{linear\to\sRGB}( \text{linear}(\text{mainHex}) \times \text{shadeFactor})). Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of voxels in the head array, O(N), where N is the total voxel count. Memory complexity is O(N) for the copy of the voxel data. The method is efficient as it avoids re-computing geometric intersections. It is suitable for real-time applications where character appearance changes frequently. Limitations include the assumption of predefined voxel markers; if the voxelization process does not produce these specific markers, the method will not work as intended. Originated in the context of voxel-based avatar systems, specifically within the voxel-demolition project. It allows for dynamic character customization without the computational cost of re-voxelization. The method relies on a pre-defined set of integer markers for hair types, which are established during the initial voxelization phase. JerzySukiennik/voxel-demolition, https://github.com/JerzySukiennik/voxel-demolition, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Detached Re-voxelize
head: detached re-voxelize P3, re-voxelize, round-to-cell re-voxelization
body: Detached re-voxelize is a rendering technique for detached solids that re-voxelizes geometry into a grid, resolves occlusion via a distance buffer, and projects to trixels. It differs from standard voxelization by using a round-to-cell mapping for grid placement and an exposed-face mask to gate emission, specifically addressing defects in prior iterations such as coverage holes and stale-mask artifacts. The method operates on a pool of detached solids, flagging them for re-voxelization and recomputing their spatial occupancy every frame to match the GPU scatter cells. Inputs and Outputs Input: Model-space geometry of detached solids; current frame transformation (rotation/translation); voxel grid resolution and bounding box. Output: A voxel grid with density/color values and an exposed-face mask used during the voxel-to-trixel projection stage. Data Structures Voxel Data Structure: Contains visibleFaceIds. The.w lane of visibleFaceIds is repurposed as a free marker lane to flag solids requiring re-voxelization. Face Occupancy Mask: A per-voxel boolean or bitmask indicating if a face is exposed to the camera. Steps 1. Flagging: Identify solids in the detached pool that require re-voxelization. Set the visibleFaceIds.w lane to a non-zero marker value. 2. World Cell Mapping: Map model-space voxel coordinates to world-space grid cells. Use roundHalfUp rounding to ensure byte-for-byte matching with the GPU scatter cells. Formula: C{world} = \text{roundHalfUp}(C{model}), where C{world} is the world cell coordinate and C{model} is the model-space voxel coordinate. 3. Mask Recomputation: Recompute the per-voxel exposed face mask every frame against the rotated destination cells. This is performed by faceoccupancy::recomputeFaceOccupancyOnCells. This step replaces the stale model-space mask with a mask derived from the current rotated grid position. 4. Occlusion Resolution: In the cvoxeltotrixelstage{1,2} (GLSL+Metal), drop the model-space faceIsExposed gate. Instead, rely on the distance buffer to resolve occlusion. 5. Projection: Project the voxel data to trixels (2D screen pixels) using the recomputed exposed mask and distance buffer for depth testing. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def roundhalfup(x): return int(x + 0.5) if x >= 0 else int(x - 0.5) def detachedrevoxelizestep(solids, voxelgrid): # Step 1: Flag re-voxelize solids using the free visibleFaceIds.w lane for solid in solids: if solid.requiresrevoxelize: solid.visibleFaceIds.w = 1 # Step 2: Map model-space voxels to world cells using roundHalfUp rounding # Step 3: Recompute the per-voxel exposed mask every frame against rotated destination cells for voxel in voxelgrid: worldcell = (roundhalfup(voxel.modelspacecoords.x), roundhalfup(voxel.modelspacecoords.y), roundhalfup(voxel.modelspacecoords.z)) # The sources do not provide the exact occupancy algorithm; it recomputes face visibility against the rotated destination grid to match GPU scatter cells voxel.exposedmask = True return voxelgrid def voxeltotrixelstage(voxelgrid, distancebuffer): # Step 4: In cvoxeltotrixelstage{1,2} (GLSL+Metal), drop the model-space faceIsExposed gate # Let the distance buffer resolve occlusion for voxel in voxelgrid: if voxel.exposedmask: color = voxel.color depth = voxel.depth screencoords = voxel.screencoords if depth < distancebuffer.get(screencoords): distancebuffer.set(screencoords, depth) # Standard fragment output operation pass Parameters Rounding Mode: roundHalfUp is required for consistency with GPU scatter. Marker Lane: visibleFaceIds.w. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sub-cell Gaps: Round-to-cell re-voxelization of a rotated solid leaves sub-cell surface gaps, causing coverage holes. Stale Mask Artifacts: Using a stale model-space exposed mask causes over-emission of interior faces. This accidentally fills coverage holes but results in wrong-face colors on multi-color or sparse content. Color vs. Coverage Tension: Recomputing the mask fixes colors but re-exposes holes. Keeping the stale mask preserves coverage but causes color artifacts. A coverage fix that dilates the re-voxelize face footprint so adjacent surface faces overlap and fill gaps with the correct color, resolving the tension between correct colors and zero holes. It is fully correct but requires a raster/shader change gated to re-voxelize canvases, needing new infrastructure and Metal parity. A coverage fix that increases the detached pool density to push sub-cell gaps below the sub-cell tolerance, though it does not fully eliminate them. Performance: The method introduces a tension between performance and visual fidelity. Keeping the stale mask (over-emission) is cheaper but causes color artifacts. Recomputing the mask is more expensive and re-exposes holes. Accuracy: On a uniform teal cube, the method shows 0.30% of frame with maxdelta 231 when recomputing the mask. On an L-prism surface, it shows +1.9% black-pixel holes. Limitations: The method struggles with multi-color content where wrong-face colors are visible. It is less effective for high-contrast neighbors. When to Use: Suitable for dense, uniform-color solids where coverage is prioritized over per-face color accuracy. For multi-color content, conservative coverage dilation or supersampling may be required. Detached re-voxelize was introduced in the Irreden Engine as part of the detached re-voxelize pipeline (P3), addressing defects observed in P1 screenshots: round-to-cell coverage holes and stale-mask flag trixels. It evolved from P1 and P2 iterations, where P2 rendered demo solids cleanly but relied on side-effect over-emission for coverage. render: detached re-voxelize — round-to-cell occlusion + aliasing (P3) (#1557), https://github.com/jakildev/IrredenEngine/pull/1566, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Manifold Voxel Repair
head: Manifold Voxelization Repair
body: Manifold Voxel Repair is a post-processing step for voxelized meshes that resolves non-manifold contacts by filling empty cells between touching voxels, ensuring the resulting structure is watertight. It specifically targets edge-only and corner-only contacts where voxels share an edge or vertex but no face, which are invalid for manifold mesh generation. Unlike sibling methods that focus on generation or carving, this method operates on an existing voxel set to enforce topological validity, growing the set only to fill gaps. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of occupied voxel coordinates (or keys) representing a voxelized object. Output: A modified set of voxel coordinates where all non-manifold contacts are resolved. Data Structures: keys: A list or array of voxel coordinates (e.g., (x, y, z) tuples or integer indices). present(offset): A helper function that returns a boolean mask indicating which voxels in the current set have a neighbor at the specified relative offset. CONTACTS: A predefined list of tuples (delta, first, between) defining the geometric patterns of non-manifold contacts. delta is the offset to check for existing voxels, first is the offset of the voxel to add, and between is a list of offsets representing the gap cells that must be empty for the contact to be considered non-manifold. Parameters: maxiter: Integer, optional safety cap on repair rounds. Default is 8. Iteration is required because sealing one contact can create another. Algorithm Steps: 1. Margin Expansion: Convert input voxels to keys with a 1-voxel margin to account for neighbors. This ensures that contacts involving voxels adjacent to the input set are detected. \text{keys}{\text{expanded}} = \text{to\keys}(\text{voxels}, \text{margin}=1) 2. Empty Check: If the expanded keys are empty, return an empty result. python if len(keys) == 0: return fromkeys(keys, shift, voxels.dtype) 3. Initialization: Initialize rounds = 0 and add = contactfixes(keys) if maxiter is non-zero, else add is empty. 4. Iterative Repair: While add is not empty and rounds < maxiter: Update keys by adding add. Recompute add = contactfixes(keys). Increment rounds. If contacts remain after the loop, emit a warning. 5. Return: Convert final keys back to voxels. Helper Function contactfixes(keys): 1. Initialize add as an empty list. 2. Iterate through each tuple (delta, first, between) in CONTACTS: Select voxels at delta: sel = present(delta). For each gap in between: If sel is not empty, update sel to exclude voxels where the gap is present: \text{sel} = \text{sel} \ \& \ \sim \text{present}(\text{gap}) If sel has any elements, add keys[sel] + first to the add list. 3. Return unique concatenated additions, or empty array if none. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Topology Change: Filling a cell between offending voxels changes topology: it can close a tunnel or merge two components that previously met at a single edge. The set only grows, never shrinking. Corner to Edge Resolution: Corner contacts resolve to edge contacts first, requiring iteration to reach a fixed point. If maxiter is hit with outstanding contacts, the result may not be manifold. Precision: The method relies on discrete grid offsets, so precision issues are minimal, but the margin expansion must be handled correctly to avoid boundary errors. Time Complexity: The method optimizes ~46 sorted lookups into 17 by memoizing membership tests for distinct offsets. Each iteration involves checking contacts and updating the voxel set. The number of iterations is bounded by maxiter (default 8). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels and the margin expansion. The memoization of membership tests reduces overhead. Strengths: Ensures manifold validity for voxelized meshes; simple and effective for resolving common non-manifold artifacts; iterative approach handles cascading contacts. Limitations: Can alter topology (e.g., closing tunnels); may not fully resolve all non-manifold contacts if maxiter is insufficient; only adds voxels, never removes them. When to Use: After voxelization when a manifold mesh is required for rendering or simulation; when edge-only or corner-only contacts are present. When Not to Use: When preserving the exact original topology is critical and non-manifold contacts are acceptable; when performance is critical and maxiter is large. Manifold Voxel Repair is part of the sparse-cubes library by navis-org, which provides tools for voxelization and skeletonization of biological structures. The method addresses the common issue of non-manifold contacts in voxelized meshes, which are problematic for downstream applications like mesh generation and simulation. The iterative approach and contact definitions are designed to be efficient and robust for large-scale voxel data. navis-org/sparse-cubes, https://github.com/navis-org/sparse-cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Build Process
head: BuildNodeVoxels
body: The Voxel Build Process is a procedural method for constructing a voxel representation of a specific SceneNode into a persistent "built voxels" container, managing state transitions for undo/redo operations. It distinguishes itself from static voxelization methods by maintaining a history of voxel states, allowing the system to detach old representations and atomically swap in newly computed voxel data while preserving spatial origin consistency. Inputs and Outputs Input: A SceneNode to be voxelized, a buildContext containing build parameters, and a reference to the global generatedVoxels collection. Output: A new voxel group labeled BUILTVOXELSGROUPNAME attached to the voxelRoot, replacing any previous built voxels for this node. Data Structures BlockStorageDelegate: Wraps a ChunkedStorage3D structure for efficient voxel storage. RootBuilder: The core algorithmic engine that processes the SceneNode into voxel data. Vec3: A 3D vector type used for coordinate transformations. generatedVoxels: A collection storing the active voxel groups. Steps 1. Initialization Check: Determine if this is the first invocation (firstTime=true). 2. Locate Existing State: Search generatedVoxels for an existing group with the label BUILTVOXELSGROUPNAME. Let this be oldBuiltVoxels. 3. Prepare New Storage: Create a new BlockStorageDelegate initialized with ChunkedStorage3D(). Create a new voxel group with label BUILTVOXELSGROUPNAME, the new storage, the current renderMode, and a visibility flag set to true. Let this be newBuiltVoxels. 4. Origin Handling: If oldBuiltVoxels exists: Copy its voxel data into the new storage using copyTo(). Set newBuiltVoxels.origin to oldBuiltVoxels.origin. If oldBuiltVoxels does not exist: Set newBuiltVoxels.origin to the rounded global position of the SceneNode. 5. Coordinate Transformation: Create a translation transform T that shifts coordinates by -newBuiltVoxels.origin. Apply T to the world coordinates, converting them to local space relative to the voxel group's origin. 6. Voxel Generation: Instantiate a RootBuilder. If verboseBuild is enabled, attach a VerboseLogger listener to the builder. Invoke the builder to generate voxels for the SceneNode, passing the transformed world coordinates, the offsetWorld, and the buildContext. 7. State Swap: Add newBuiltVoxels to voxelRoot. Detach newBuiltVoxels from the root temporarily and store it in a variable newVoxels. Detach oldBuiltVoxels (if it exists) from generatedVoxels. Reattach newVoxels to generatedVoxels. 8. Finalization: Trigger a redraw of the voxel display. Revert Operation Detach newVoxels. If oldVoxels (the state before the current build) exists, reattach it to generatedVoxels. Trigger a redraw. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildnodevoxels(scenenode, buildcontext, generatedvoxels, voxelroot, firsttime, verbosebuild): # Step 1: Locate existing built voxels oldbuiltvoxels = None for group in generatedvoxels: if group.label == "BUILTVOXELSGROUPNAME": oldbuiltvoxels = group break # Step 2: Create new storage and group newstorage = BlockStorageDelegate(ChunkedStorage3D()) newbuiltvoxels = VoxelGroup( label="BUILTVOXELSGROUPNAME", storage=newstorage, rendermode=currentrendermode, visible=True) # Step 3: Handle origin and data copy if oldbuiltvoxels is not None: oldbuiltvoxels.storage.copyto(newbuiltvoxels.storage) newbuiltvoxels.origin = oldbuiltvoxels.origin else: # Round global position to integer grid coordinates newbuiltvoxels.origin = round(scenenode.globalposition) # Step 4: Transform world to local coordinates # Translation vector is negative of the origin translationvector = Vec3(-newbuiltvoxels.origin.x, -newbuiltvoxels.origin.y, -newbuiltvoxels.origin.z) localworld = transformworldcoordinates(translationvector) # Step 5: Build voxels builder = RootBuilder() if verbosebuild: builder.addlistener(VerboseLogger()) # The builder processes the scene node into the new storage # Implementation detail: builder.build(scenenode, localworld, buildcontext, newbuiltvoxels.storage) # Note: Exact signature of builder.build is not fully specified in source, assumed to take node, world, context, storage builder.build(scenenode, localworld, buildcontext, newbuiltvoxels.storage) # Step 6: Swap state voxelroot.add(newbuiltvoxels) # Detach new voxels to store in temporary variable newvoxels = voxelroot.detach(newbuiltvoxels) # Detach old voxels if they exist if oldbuiltvoxels is not None: generatedvoxels.detach(oldbuiltvoxels) # Reattach new voxels to generatedvoxels generatedvoxels.add(newvoxels) # Trigger redraw triggerredraw() def revertbuild(generatedvoxels, oldvoxels, newvoxels): # Detach the newly built voxels generatedvoxels.detach(newvoxels) # Reattach the old voxels if they exist if oldvoxels is not None: generatedvoxels.add(oldvoxels) # Trigger redraw triggerredraw() Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Depends on the ChunkedStorage3D implementation and the density of the voxelized node. Strengths: Supports undo/redo functionality by maintaining state history; handles origin consistency across rebuilds. Limitations: The source code is specific to the VoxelArchitecture library and may not be directly portable without adapting the BlockStorageDelegate and RootBuilder interfaces. The Voxel Build Process is part of the VoxelArchitecture library by Hunternif, a Minecraft modding library for voxel generation. It is designed to handle incremental and reversible voxel building for procedural generation, such as the FlatDungeon generator which creates rooms and corridors. name: Voxel Volume Generation
head: Compute Kernel Voxel Generation, Procedural Voxel Volume Generation
body: Voxel Volume Generation is a procedural method that computes voxel values on-the-fly or via compute shaders by evaluating a generation graph or function at specific world-space coordinates, rather than rasterizing geometry or carving from images. It differs from VoxelGrid from Mesh (Fill Method) and Voxel Carving by decoupling the volume representation from explicit geometric primitives, allowing for infinite or dynamic domains defined by mathematical functions or shader scripts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: numberOfVoxels: uint3 defining the grid dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz). voxelSpacing: float defining the physical size of a single voxel. voxelVolumeToWorldSpaceOffset: float3 defining the translation from the voxel volume's local center to world space. generationGraph: A function or shader script that takes a world position and returns a Voxel structure (containing density, color, material, etc.). Outputs: voxelVolume: A RWStructuredBuffer<PackedVoxel> storing the resulting voxel data. The buffer size is Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Data Structures: PackedVoxel: The specific layout of PackedVoxel is not detailed in the sources, but it is stored in a 1D structured buffer. Indexing: The 3D coordinate (x, y, z) is mapped to a 1D array index using row-major storage where X is the fastest varying dimension: \text{index} = x + y \cdot Nx + z \cdot (Nx \cdot Ny) In vector notation: \text{index} = \text{dot}(\text{coordinate}, \text{uint3}(1, Nx, Nx \cdot Ny)) Coordinate Transformation: The method converts the discrete voxel ID to a continuous world position before evaluation: 1. Voxel to Local Space: The voxel ID (integer coordinate) is converted to a local space position centered at the origin. The formula accounts for the voxel spacing and centers the volume: \text{localPosition} = \text{voxelSpacing} \cdot (\text{voxelID} - 0.5 \cdot (\text{numberOfVoxels} - 1.0)) Note: The source code implies an implicit or explicit position = 0.0f offset in the call VoxelToVoxelVolumeSpace(voxelID) before applying the world offset. 2. Local to World Space: \text{worldPosition} = \text{localPosition} + \text{voxelVolumeToWorldSpaceOffset} Algorithm Steps: 1. Dispatch a compute kernel (e.g., GenerateVoxelVolume) with thread groups of size [4, 4, 4]. 2. Each thread identifies its voxel using SVDispatchThreadID (denoted as voxelID). 3. Check if voxelID is within bounds (0 \le x < Nx, etc.). If out of bounds, return immediately. 4. Calculate worldPosition using the transformation formulas above. 5. Evaluate the procedural generation graph at worldPosition to obtain a Voxel object: voxel = EvaluateGenerationGraph(worldPosition). 6. Store the voxel in the voxelVolume buffer at the index calculated from voxelID. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. NUMTHREADSX = 4 NUMTHREADSY = 4 NUMTHREADSZ = 4 def GenerateVoxelVolume(voxelID: uint3, numberOfVoxels: uint3, voxelSpacing: float, voxelVolumeToWorldSpaceOffset: float3, voxelVolume: RWStructuredBuffer[PackedVoxel]): # 1. Bounds Check if voxelID.x >= numberOfVoxels.x or \ voxelID.y >= numberOfVoxels.y or \ voxelID.z >= numberOfVoxels.z: return # 2. Convert Voxel ID to Local Space (Centered) # Formula: voxelSpacing (voxelID - 0.5 (numberOfVoxels - 1.0)) localPosition = voxelSpacing (voxelID - 0.5 (numberOfVoxels - 1.0)) # 3. Convert to World Space worldPosition = localPosition + voxelVolumeToWorldSpaceOffset # 4. Evaluate Procedural Graph # The graph function is external to this kernel but defined by the user/application voxel = EvaluateGenerationGraph(worldPosition) # 5. Calculate 1D Index (Row-major, X fastest) index = voxelID.x + voxelID.y numberOfVoxels.x + voxelID.z (numberOfVoxels.x numberOfVoxels.y) # 6. Store Result voxelVolume[index] = PackedVoxel(voxel) Parameters and Edge Cases: Thread Group Size: Fixed at [4, 4, 4] in the reference implementation. Precision: Floating-point precision in worldPosition calculation may affect high-resolution volumes or large world offsets. Boundary Conditions: The bounds check prevents out-of-bounds memory access. Generation Graph: The specific implementation of EvaluateGenerationGraph is user-defined. In the MagicaVoxel variant, this is a GLSL script. A GLSL-based scripting system within MagicaVoxel that generates custom voxel volumes through iterative shader execution. It allows for dynamic, procedural generation using a console command interface (xs [shader name] [args...]). Unlike the general compute kernel approach which evaluates a static graph per voxel, Voxel Shader supports iterative refinement and frame-based animation. Parameters: iFrame: Current frame index. iNumFrames: Total number of frames. iIter: Current iteration index. iRand: A vec4 random number updated every iteration and frame. Execution: Iteration count is specified via the -n flag (e.g., xs -n 8 [shaderName]). Frame targeting uses -prev (previous frame) or -cur (current frame) flags, defaulting to -prev. When to choose: Use when dynamic, animated, or interactive procedural generation is required within a voxel editor context, rather than static pre-computed volumes. Time Complexity: O(Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz), as every voxel in the defined domain is evaluated exactly once. Memory Complexity: O(Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz) for the output buffer. Performance: Highly parallelizable on GPU via compute shaders. Performance is limited by the complexity of the EvaluateGenerationGraph function rather than geometric intersection tests. Strengths: Supports infinite or very large domains without explicit mesh storage; easily animatable via shader inputs; no need for rasterization or marching cubes preprocessing. Limitations: Requires a procedural definition (function/shader) for the volume; cannot directly represent arbitrary static mesh geometry without a complex implicit function. When to use: Procedural content generation, animated volumes, or when the volume definition is mathematical rather than geometric. When not to use: When converting existing static mesh assets to voxels (use VoxelGrid from Mesh (Fill Method)) or when reconstructing from images (use Voxel Carving). The method originates from GPU-based procedural voxel generation techniques, specifically implemented in the open-source project "Voxels" by Tantenfisch. It leverages DirectX Compute Shaders ([numthreads(4, 4, 4)]) to map world-space positions to voxel values via a generation graph. A related implementation exists in MagicaVoxel as "Voxel Shader," introduced in version 0.97.1 (Feb 15, 2016), which uses GLSL for iterative volume generation.
