name: Voxel Generation Graph
head: Generation Graph Node Evaluation, GenerationGraph, GenerationGraphStack, Voxel Evaluation Graph
body: The Voxel Generation Graph is a stack-based evaluation system for generating voxel data (value, gradient, and material) at a specific 3D position by executing a sequence of node operations defined in a global buffer. It solves the problem of procedural voxel generation by allowing complex volumetric functions to be composed from atomic primitives (noise, transforms, CSG) in a linear, executable graph. It is distinct from direct shader-based evaluation because it decouples the logical structure of the volume definition (the graph) from the evaluation loop, enabling dynamic modification of voxel properties via CSG operations and material assignment at runtime. The method evaluates a directed acyclic graph of nodes to produce a single Voxel output. The evaluation state is maintained in a fixed-size stack. Input: A global buffer of GenerationGraphNode structures (generationGraphNodes) and an integer numberOfGenerationGraphNodes defining the graph size. The evaluation is triggered for a specific 3D position (typically the world position of a chunk or voxel). Output: A single Voxel structure containing the final value, gradient, and material index. The implementation relies on three primary structures defined in the source: 1. GenerationGraphNode: Defines a single operation in the graph. uint nodeType: Enum value indicating the operation (see NodeType constants below). float4x4 transformMatrix: Used if nodeType is Transform. NoiseParameters noiseParameters: Used if nodeType is Noise or DomainWarp. CSGPrimitive csgPrimitive: Used if nodeType is CSGPrimitive. uint materialIndex: Used if nodeType is Material. CSGOperator csgOperator: Used if nodeType is CSGOperation. 2. GenerationGraphStack: The evaluation stack. Voxel buffer[2]: A fixed buffer holding up to 2 voxels. uint count: The current number of voxels on the stack. Note: The stack size is strictly limited to 2 voxels. 3. Voxel: The data unit pushed/popped from the stack. float4 valueAndGradient: Contains the scalar value and its 3D gradient. Additional gradient/position data may be present depending on the specific Voxel implementation, but the core output is the value/gradient pair. 4. GPUVoxelVolumeCSGOperation: (C# struct, sequential layout) Used to apply CSG operations to existing voxel volumes. GPUCSGOperator CSGOperator GPUCSGPrimitive CSGPrimitive MaterialIndex MaterialIndex Matrix4x4 TransformMatrix The nodeType field in GenerationGraphNode uses the following integer values: Position: 0 Transform: 1 DomainWarp: 2 Noise: 3 CSGPrimitive: 4 Material: 5 CSGOperation: 6 Output: 7 The evaluation iterates through the generationGraphNodes buffer from index 0 to numberOfGenerationGraphNodes - 1. For each node, the corresponding operation is performed on the stack. 1. Initialize Stack: Create an empty GenerationGraphStack with count = 0 and buffer cleared. 2. Iterate Nodes: For i from 0 to numberOfGenerationGraphNodes - 1: Let node be generationGraphNodes[i]. Switch on node.nodeType: Position (0): Push the current evaluation position onto the stack. Implementation Note: The "current evaluation position" is typically the input position passed to the graph evaluation function. If multiple Position nodes exist, they likely refer to the same base position or a context-specific coordinate. Transform (1): Pop pos from the stack. Compute newpos = node.transformMatrix pos. Push newpos onto the stack. DomainWarp (2): Pop pos from the stack. Compute warpedpos = WarpDomain(pos, node.noiseParameters). Push warpedpos onto the stack. Noise (3): Pop pos from the stack. Compute value and gradient using Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise with node.noiseParameters at pos. Create a Voxel with valueAndGradient = float4(value, gradient.x, gradient.y, gradient.z). Push the Voxel onto the stack. CSGPrimitive (4): Pop pos from the stack. Evaluate the signed distance function (SDF) of node.csgPrimitive at pos to get value and gradient. Create a Voxel with valueAndGradient. Push the Voxel onto the stack. Material (5): Pop voxel from the stack. Create a new Voxel with the same valueAndGradient as voxel, but set its material index to node.materialIndex. Push the new Voxel onto the stack. CSGOperation (6): Pop rhs from the stack. Pop lhs from the stack. Note: The right-hand side is popped first to maintain standard left-hand-side operator precedence (lhs op rhs). Compute resultvoxel = ApplyCSG(node.csgOperator, lhs, rhs). Push resultvoxel onto the stack. Output (7): Pop finalvoxel from the stack. Return finalvoxel. 3. Return: If the loop completes without hitting an Output node, the behavior is undefined or returns the top of the stack. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatevoxelgenerationgraph(generationgraphnodes, numberofnodes, initialposition): """ Evaluates a voxel generation graph to produce a single Voxel. Args: generationgraphnodes: List of GenerationGraphNode structs. numberofnodes: Integer count of nodes. initialposition: float3, the starting 3D position for evaluation. Returns: Voxel: The final voxel result. """ # Stack implementation stackbuffer = [None, None] # Fixed size 2 stackcount = 0 def pushvoxel(v): nonlocal stackcount if stackcount >= 2: raise ValueError("Stack overflow: GenerationGraphStack is limited to 2 voxels") stackbuffer[stackcount] = v stackcount += 1 def popvoxel(): nonlocal stackcount if stackcount <= 0: raise ValueError("Stack underflow") stackcount -= 1 return stackbuffer[stackcount] for i in range(numberofnodes): node = generationgraphnodes[i] nodetype = node.nodeType if nodetype == 0: # Position # Push current evaluation position. # In a simple graph, this is the initialposition. # If the graph allows multiple positions, context is needed. # Assuming the graph expects a position input at this stage. # We push a dummy voxel or just the position? # The spec says "Push current evaluation position onto stack". # However, subsequent nodes (Noise, CSG) expect a Voxel or Position? # Noise pops position and pushes Voxel. CSG pops position and pushes Voxel. # Transform pops position and pushes position. # So the stack holds mixed types? Or is it always Voxel? # The spec says GenerationGraphStack has a buffer of 2 Voxels. # This implies Position nodes might push a Voxel with position data? # Or the stack is polymorphic. Given "Voxel buffer[2]", let's assume # Position nodes push a Voxel where valueAndGradient encodes the position? # Or more likely, the "Position" node sets the current position context, # and other nodes read from that context? # Re-reading: "Pop position from stack". This implies the stack holds positions. # But "Push result back" for Transform. # And Noise pushes "result" (Voxel). # This suggests the stack holds heterogeneous data or the "Voxel" struct # can represent a position. # Let's assume the stack holds generic data items, but the struct is named Voxel. # For implementation clarity, we will treat the stack as holding "EvaluationItems". # If the source strictly says "Voxel buffer", we assume a Voxel struct is used # to represent positions (e.g., value=0, gradient=position). # Implementation: Push a Voxel representing the position. # Value=0, Gradient=initialposition (or current context position). # Since Position node is usually at the start, we use initialposition. posvoxel = Voxel(value=0.0, gradient=initialposition) pushvoxel(posvoxel) elif nodetype == 1: # Transform item = popvoxel() # Item is a position (Voxel with value=0) pos = item.gradient newpos = transformmatrixmultiply(node.transformMatrix, pos) newvoxel = Voxel(value=0.0, gradient=newpos) pushvoxel(newvoxel) elif nodetype == 2: # DomainWarp item = popvoxel() pos = item.gradient warpedpos = warpdomain(pos, node.noiseParameters) newvoxel = Voxel(value=0.0, gradient=warpedpos) pushvoxel(newvoxel) elif nodetype == 3: # Noise item = popvoxel() pos = item.gradient value, gradient = generatefbmnoise(pos, node.noiseParameters) newvoxel = Voxel(value=value, gradient=gradient) pushvoxel(newvoxel) elif nodetype == 4: # CSGPrimitive item = popvoxel() pos = item.gradient value, gradient = evaluatecsgprimitive(node.csgPrimitive, pos) newvoxel = Voxel(value=value, gradient=gradient) pushvoxel(newvoxel) elif nodetype == 5: # Material voxel = popvoxel() # Create new voxel with same value/gradient but new material newvoxel = Voxel( value=voxel.value, gradient=voxel.gradient, materialindex=node.materialIndex) pushvoxel(newvoxel) elif nodetype == 6: # CSGOperation rhs = popvoxel() lhs = popvoxel() resultvoxel = applycsgoperation(node.csgOperator, lhs, rhs) pushvoxel(resultvoxel) elif nodetype == 7: # Output finalvoxel = popvoxel() return finalvoxel # If no Output node is reached, return the top of the stack or error if stackcount > 0: return popvoxel() else: raise ValueError("Graph did not produce an output") def transformmatrixmultiply(matrix, position): # Homogeneous coordinate multiplication x, y, z = position w = 1.0 # matrix is float4x4, stored as 4 rows or columns depending on convention # Assuming row-major or standard math library convention # result = matrix float4(x,y,z,1) # Simplified for pseudocode: return float3( matrix[0][0]x + matrix[1][0]y + matrix[2][0]z + matrix[3][0], matrix[0][1]x + matrix[1][1]y + matrix[2][1]z + matrix[3][1], matrix[0][2]x + matrix[1][2]y + matrix[2][2]z + matrix[3][2]) def warpdomain(position, noiseparams): # Apply domain warping using noise # This is a placeholder for the specific warping algorithm # Typically: warped = position + noise(position) scale return position # Placeholder def generatefbmnoise(position, noiseparams): # Generate Fractal Brownian Motion # Returns (value, gradient) return 0.0, float3(0,0,0) # Placeholder def evaluatecsgprimitive(primitive, position): # Evaluate SDF and gradient return 0.0, float3(0,0,0) # Placeholder def applycsgoperation(operator, lhs, rhs): # Apply CSG operator (Union, Intersection, Difference) # Returns new Voxel return lhs # Placeholder class Voxel: def init(self, value, gradient, materialindex=0): self.value = value self.gradient = gradient self.materialindex = materialindex Stack Size: Fixed at 2 voxels. NodeType Enum: Integers 0-7. Noise Parameters: Specific to the noise implementation (octaves, lacunarity, gain, etc.), not detailed in the source. CSG Operators: Standard CSG operations (Union, Intersection, Difference). Stack Overflow: The stack is limited to 2 voxels. Any operation requiring more than 2 operands must be structured as sequential binary operations (e.g., A op B op C must be (A op B) op C). Operand Order: For CSGOperation, the right-hand side (RHS) is popped before the left-hand side (LHS) to ensure correct operator precedence (lhs op rhs). Missing Output: If the graph does not end with an Output node, the result is undefined. The implementation should handle this gracefully, either by returning the top of the stack or raising an error. Type Safety: The stack holds heterogeneous data (positions and voxels). The implementation must ensure that nodes pop the correct type of data. For example, Transform expects a position, while Noise expects a position but produces a voxel. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of nodes in the generation graph. Each node is evaluated exactly once. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the stack (fixed size 2) plus O(N) for the graph node buffer. The memory footprint is dominated by the generationGraphNodes buffer. Performance: Performance depends on the complexity of the individual node operations (e.g., noise generation, CSG evaluation). The stack-based approach is efficient for GPU execution as it minimizes branching and allows for tight loops. Strengths: Dynamic graph construction allows for runtime modification of voxel volumes. Stack-based evaluation is simple to implement and debug. Supports complex compositions of noise, transforms, and CSG. Limitations: Stack size limit of 2 restricts the complexity of single-step operations. Linear evaluation order may not be optimal for all graph structures (e.g., if nodes are independent, parallel evaluation could be faster). When to Use: Suitable for procedural voxel generation in real-time applications where dynamic modification of voxel properties is required, such as in the Tuntenfisch/Voxels project. The Voxel Generation Graph was introduced in the Tuntenfisch/Voxels project, an open-source voxel engine for Unity. It is used to generate procedural voxel volumes by evaluating a graph of nodes that define the volume's properties (noise, CSG, materials) at runtime. The method is part of a larger system that includes dual contouring for mesh generation and chunk-based world management. name: Voxel Volume Configuration
head: VXGI Voxel Volume Configuration & Resolution Management, VoxelVolumeConfig, octant configuration, volume octant, volume octant / volume ~octant
body: Voxel Volume Configuration defines the spatial domain, resolution, and data layout of a voxel grid, serving as the foundational step before geometry is mapped into voxels. It establishes the bounding box, voxel spacing, and resolution hierarchy (mipmaps) required for efficient rendering and storage. Unlike raw voxelization methods that focus on filling cells, this method manages the structure of the volume, including dynamic resolution scaling and octant-based data masking. It is distinct from Sparse and Hierarchical Structures by often employing fixed-resolution 3D textures for the base layer, and from Scene Geometry and Scalar Range Initialization by explicitly handling the geometric bounds and coordinate transforms. The method configures the voxel volume through three main phases: domain definition, buffer/texture allocation, and runtime resolution management. It supports both static configuration (e.g., scientific visualization octants) and dynamic runtime configuration (e.g., VXGI mipmap chains). Inputs: bound: World-space size of the volume (float, default 10.0). center: World-space center of the volume (Vector3). resolution: Base resolution (int or enum: Low=32, Medium=64, High=128, VeryHigh=256). voxelSpacing: Physical spacing between voxels (float, min 0.25, default 1.0). numberOfVoxelsAlongAxis: Number of voxels per axis (int, range 67–131, default 67). octantCenter: Center for octant masking (physical units or grid indices). fillValue: Value assigned to erased octant regions (float, default 0). Outputs: resolution: Active resolution (int). voxelBuffer: Compute buffer containing voxel data. radiances: Array of 3D textures for mipmap levels. voxelSize: Computed physical size of a single voxel. 1. Voxel Buffer Layout (voxelBuffer) Type: ComputeBuffer (Append type). Element Size: VoxelData.size (implementation-specific, typically 16–32 bytes per voxel). Total Size: bufferScale volume elements. bufferScale: Scaling factor for memory alignment or padding. \text{bufferScale} = \frac{64}{\text{resolution} - (\text{resolution} \pmod 2)} volume: Total voxel count. \text{volume} = \text{resolution}^3 2. Radiance Mipmap Array (radiances) Type: Array of RenderTexture (3D, Tex3D). Length: \log2(\text{resolution}). Format: ARGBHalf (16-bit floating point per channel). Flags: enableRandomWrite=true, msaaSamples=1, sRGB=false. Resolution per Level i: Let R0 = \text{resolution}. For i > 0: Ri = \left\lfloor \frac{R{i-1} - \text{resolutionModifier}}{2} \right\rfloor + \text{resolutionModifier} Where resolutionModifier is typically 1 or 2 depending on the anti-aliasing mode. 3. Octant Masking Data (Scientific Visualization) Used in commands like volume octant. Defines a sub-region of the volume where values are either kept or erased based on a center point. 1. Initialize Domain Parameters Set bound (world size) and center (world position). Set numberOfVoxelsAlongAxis or resolution. If numberOfVoxelsAlongAxis is used, adjust it to the closest power of two plus 3: N{adj} = \text{round\to\pow2}(N) + 3. 2. Calculate Voxel Size and Grid Dimensions Compute voxelSize: \text{voxelSize} = \frac{\text{bound}}{\text{resolution} - (\text{resolution} \pmod 2)}. Alternatively, if using mvoxelSpacing: \text{voxelSize} = \text{m\voxelSpacing}. Calculate NumberOfCellsAlongAxis: N{cells} = N{voxels} - 1. Calculate VoxelVolumeDimensions: D = \text{voxelSize} \times N{cells}. 3. Allocate Buffers and Textures Compute bufferScale: \text{bufferScale} = \frac{64}{\text{resolution} - (\text{resolution} \pmod 2)}. Create voxelBuffer with size (int)(bufferScale resolution^3). Create radiances array of length \log2(\text{resolution}). For each level i in radiances: Set width/height/depth to Ri (calculated in Data Structures). Set format to ARGBHalf, enableRandomWrite=true. Assign to shader global ShaderIDs.Radiance[i]. 4. Configure Octant Masking (Optional) If using octant configuration: Define center (physical) or iCenter (grid indices, 0-based). iCenter overrides center if both provided. Set fillValue for erased regions (default 0). Apply mask: Erase values inside/outside the positive octant relative to the center. 5. Runtime Resolution Management (VXGI Specific) Check limitRefreshRate and refreshRate (default 30 Hz). If time since last refresh > 1/\text{refreshRate}: Call UpdateResolution(). If mipmapFilterMode is Gaussian3x3x3, increment newResolution by 1. If newResolution != resolution: Update resolution. Call ResizeBuffers() and ResizeTextures(). If followCamera is true: Set volume center to camera position. Calculate displacement in voxel space: \text{displacement} = \frac{\text{voxelSpaceCenter} - \text{lastVoxelSpaceCenter}}{\text{voxelSize}}. If displacement.sqrMagnitude > 0: Call mipmapper.Shift() to handle grid alignment. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def configurevoxelvolume(bound, center, resolution, followcamera=False, mipmapfiltermode='Box', resolutionmodifier=1): """ Configures the voxel volume structure, buffers, and runtime parameters. """ # 1. Validate and Adjust Resolution # Ensure resolution is even for buffer scaling if resolution % 2 != 0: resolution += 1 # 2. Calculate Derived Dimensions voxelsize = bound / (resolution - (resolution % 2)) volumecount = resolution 3 # Buffer scaling factor for memory alignment bufferscale = 64.0 / (resolution - (resolution % 2)) bufferelementcount = int(bufferscale volumecount) # 3. Allocate Data Structures # voxelBuffer: ComputeBuffer of size bufferelementcount, type Append voxelbuffer = allocatecomputebuffer(bufferelementcount) # radiances: Array of 3D textures mipmaplevels = int(log2(resolution)) radiances = [] currentres = resolution for i in range(mipmaplevels): # Calculate resolution for this mipmap level # Formula: (current - modifier) / 2 + modifier nextres = (currentres - resolutionmodifier) // 2 + resolutionmodifier # Create 3D texture tex = create3dtexture( width=nextres, height=nextres, depth=nextres, format='ARGBHalf', enablerandomwrite=True, msaasamples=1, srgb=False) radiances.append(tex) # Prepare for next level currentres = nextres # 4. Setup Shader Globals setshaderglobal('Resolution', resolution) setshaderglobal('WorldToVoxel', computeworldtovoxelmatrix(center, voxelsize)) setshaderglobal('Radiance', radiances) return { 'voxelbuffer': voxelbuffer, 'radiances': radiances, 'voxelsize': voxelsize, 'resolution': resolution } def updateresolution(currentresolution, mipmapfiltermode, resolutionmodifier): """ Determines if resolution needs to change based on filter mode. """ newresolution = currentresolution # Gaussian 3x3x3 filter requires odd dimensions for symmetry if mipmapfiltermode == 'Gaussian3x3x3': newresolution += 1 return newresolution def computevoxelspacecenter(worldcenter, voxelsize): """ Converts world center to voxel grid coordinates. """ pos = worldcenter / voxelsize # Floor to nearest grid index posx = floor(pos.x) posy = floor(pos.y) posz = floor(pos.z) # Convert back to world space for displacement calculation voxelspacecenter = Vector3(posx, posy, posz) voxelsize return voxelspacecenter resolution: Low=32, Medium=64, High=128, VeryHigh=256. bound: 10.0 (World Space units). center: (0, 0, 0) or Camera Position if followCamera is true. voxelSpacing: 1.0 (min 0.25). refreshRate: 30 Hz. antiAliasing: X1=1, X2=2, X4=4, X8=8. mipmapFilterMode: Box, Gaussian 3x3x3, Gaussian 4x4x4. fillValue: 0 (for octant erasure). Resolution Parity: Buffer scaling and mipmap generation assume even resolutions or specific odd adjustments (e.g., +1 for Gaussian 3x3x3). Failure to adjust causes misalignment. Octant Center Precision: iCenter (integer grid indices) overrides center (float physical units). Using fractional center values requires careful floor/ceil handling to avoid off-by-one errors in masking. Large Negative Fill Values: Using large negative values for fillValue in octant erasure can flatten contour surfaces if the surrounding data is positive. Memory Scaling: bufferScale grows as resolution decreases (due to the denominator), potentially wasting memory at low resolutions. A dynamic architecture that separates data allocation, attribute definition, and format transformation, allowing multiple voxel formats within a single engine. Choose this when static layouts are too rigid for varying rendering tasks. The rendering stage that consumes the configured volume. Choose this when the volume is fully configured and ready for ray marching or ray casting. Time Complexity: Configuration is O(1) for static setups. Runtime resolution updates are O(\log N) for mipmap texture recreation. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for the base volume, plus O(N^3) for mipmap chain (geometric series sum \approx \frac{1}{7} N^3). The bufferScale factor increases memory usage for lower resolutions. Performance: High-resolution volumes (256³) require significant VRAM (~256MB for half-float RGB). Dynamic updates (followCamera) incur CPU overhead for displacement calculation and buffer resizing. Strengths: Efficient hierarchical access via mipmaps; flexible domain definition via bound and center; supports dynamic resolution scaling. Limitations: Fixed-resolution base layers may waste memory in sparse scenes (unlike Sparse and Hierarchical Structures); octant masking is static per frame unless re-applied. The method originates from voxel-based global illumination systems, specifically the Virtual Voxel Global Illumination (VXGI) architecture. It was adapted for real-time rendering in Unity via SRP (Scriptable Render Pipeline) implementations. The octant configuration syntax is derived from scientific visualization tools like UCSF ChimeraX, which use similar commands for volume data manipulation. name: General Volume Pipeline
head: Allocation, Tagging, and Conversion
body: The General Volume Pipeline is a voxel data management architecture designed to solve the rigidity of monolithic voxel formats by enabling dynamic attribute addition and format conversion. It allows engines to utilize multiple voxel formats tailored to specific tasks, analogous to how graphics engines handle 3D model imports and shader conversions. Unlike systems bound to a single static layout, this pipeline separates data allocation, attribute definition, and format transformation into distinct stages. The pipeline consists of three sequential stages: Allocation, Tagging, and Conversion. Input: A volume allocator context and a target memory location (e.g., CPU or GPU). Output: A volume data structure with defined attributes, converted into a target format suitable for rendering or processing. The volume header contains an array of attributes. Each attribute is defined by the following fields: bitsperelement: Size in bits. type: An enum mirroring GLSL primitives (e.g., U8VEC4, VEC3) or a 'custom' label. totalsizeinbytes: Total memory size for the attribute across the volume. name: A string identifier for the attribute. 1. Allocation: Create a buffer for voxel data using a volume allocator context. The developer specifies the target memory location via the allocator name (e.g., "cpurecycled" for CPU, or a GPU-specific allocator). The allocator manages the buffer lifecycle, and the developer is responsible only for returning it when finished. 2. Tagging: Assign attributes to the allocated volume data. For each attribute, define its name, size, data type, and optional data pointer, storing these in the volume header. The data type must mirror GLSL primitives or be labeled 'custom'. 3. Conversion: Convert voxel data from one format to another. This involves binding a conversion function to specific attribute type combinations. The conversion function is selected at runtime based on the source and target attribute types. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. allocator = getvolumeallocatorfromname("cpurecycled") destvolume = allocator.newvolume() albedoattr = Attribute() albedoattr.setname("albedo") albedoattr.bitsperelement = sizeof(u8vec4) 8 albedoattr.type = VOLUMEATTRIBUTETYPEU8VEC4 albedoattr.totalsizeinbytes = aabbvolume sizeof(u8vec4) destvolume.header.attributes[0] = albedoattr normalattr = Attribute() normalattr.setname("normal") normalattr.bitsperelement = sizeof(vec3) 8 normalattr.type = VOLUMEATTRIBUTETYPEVEC3 normalattr.totalsizeinbytes = aabbvolume sizeof(vec3) destvolume.header.attributes[1] = normalattr if (destvolume.header.attributes[0].type == VOLUMEATTRIBUTETYPEU8VEC4 and destvolume.header.attributes[1].type == VOLUMEATTRIBUTETYPEVEC3): conversionfunc = bind(convertterrainblocktostaticstandard, u8vec4, vec3) for x in range(aabbsize.x): for y in range(aabbsize.y): for z in range(aabbsize.z): srcalbedo = cellreader.readu8vec4() srcnormal = cellreader.readvec3() #... conversion logic... albedowriter.write(srcalbedo) normalwriter.write(srcnormal) Type Combinations: The tagging system requires pre-coding supported type combinations because the compiler must generate template conversion functions at compile time. Runtime Flexibility: While the function pointer can be changed at runtime, the underlying template functions must be declared. Memory Management: The allocator handles lower-level tasks; the developer returns the buffer when finished. Flexibility: High. Allows dynamic attribute addition and format conversion. Complexity: Moderate. Requires managing multiple allocators and conversion functions. Performance: Conversion is performed at compile time for supported types, ensuring efficient runtime execution. Limitations: Limited by the pre-coded type combinations; unsupported types require new template functions. The concept originates from graphics programming practices used with 3D models (e.g., OBJ, PLY, FBX) and shaders, where engines import models into a common format and convert them for GPU rasterization. It extends this philosophy to voxel data, drawing inspiration from physics and ray tracing libraries that rely on triangle data as a core common format. The approach is part of an engine design philosophy centered on Entity Component System (ECS) principles to enable flexibility and expandability. name: CAD Mesh to Voxel Conversion
head: CAD mesh to voxel conversion for FLUKA, FLUKA voxel import method, STL-to-voxel conversion, VGM generation
body: This method converts Computer-Aided Design (CAD) mesh files, specifically Standard Triangle Language (.stl) formats, into Voxelized Geometry Models (VGMs) suitable for import into the FLUKA Monte Carlo simulation code. It solves the problem of directly importing complex, non-primitive CAD geometries into FLUKA, which natively supports only basic geometric shapes via Direct Geometry Models (DGMs). Unlike sibling methods that may use rasterization or ray-casting for general rendering, this pipeline is specifically tailored for Monte Carlo transport accuracy, mapping solid materials to a 3D binary grid where "1" represents entity material and "0" represents empty space. Inputs and Outputs Input: A CAD mesh file in.stl format (e.g., generated from FreeCAD). Output: A FLUKA-readable.golem file, which defines the VGM. Data Structures 1. 3D Matrix Array: A 3D grid of binary integers. Value 1: Voxel contains entity material (solid). Value 0: Voxel is empty space. 2. Text File (.txt): The 3D matrix array serialized into a format accepted by FLUKA's user routine. 3. Golem File (.golem): The compiled binary/structured file generated by writegolem.f containing the voxel data. Parameters Convert Resolution: Controls voxelization accuracy. Defined as the number of voxels in a specific direction. Typical values: Uniform resolution (e.g., Cube, Sphere, Cone): 400 voxels in X, Y, and Z directions. Non-uniform resolution (e.g., 1D-Ripple Filter, Ridge Filter): 1000 voxels in X and Z, 10 voxels in Y to reduce total voxel count and compilation time. Mesh Import Settings: Max Surface Deviation: 0.1 mm. Max Angle Deviation: 30°. Steps 1. Export CAD to STL: Create the geometry in a CAD editor (e.g., FreeCAD v0.20) and export it as an.stl file. 2. Generate Coordinate Points: Run the stl-to-voxel Python library (v0.9.3) on the.stl file to produce a file containing 3D space coordinate points. 3. Map to 3D Matrix: Use a Python script to map the 3D spatial coordinates into a 3D matrix array. Assign 1 to coordinates corresponding to solid material and 0 to empty space. 4. Save as Text: Save the 3D matrix array as a.txt file in the format required by FLUKA. 5. Compile Golem File: Compile the FLUKA user routine writegolem.f together with the.txt file to generate the.golem file. 6. Import to FLUKA: Use a FLUKA "voxel card" in the input deck to import the.golem file, establishing the VGM. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from stl import mesh as stlmesh def convertstltovoxel(stlfilepath, resolutionx, resolutiony, resolutionz, bounds): """ Converts an STL file to a 3D binary voxel matrix. Args: stlfilepath (str): Path to the.stl file. resolutionx, resolutiony, resolutionz (int): Number of voxels in each dimension. bounds (tuple): (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) defining the bounding box. Returns: numpy.ndarray: 3D binary array (1 for solid, 0 for empty). """ # Load STL mesh stldata = stlmesh.Mesh.fromfile(stlfilepath) # Define voxel grid dimensions nx, ny, nz = resolutionx, resolutiony, resolutionz # Initialize empty voxel grid voxelgrid = np.zeros((nz, ny, nx), dtype=np.int8) # Calculate voxel size dx = (bounds[3] - bounds[0]) / nx dy = (bounds[4] - bounds[1]) / ny dz = (bounds[5] - bounds[2]) / nz # Iterate through each triangle in the mesh for triangle in stldata.vectors: # Get vertices of the triangle v0, v1, v2 = triangle # Determine the bounding box of the triangle minx = int(np.floor((min(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]) - bounds[0]) / dx)) maxx = int(np.ceil((max(v0[0], v1[0], v2[0]) - bounds[0]) / dx)) miny = int(np.floor((min(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]) - bounds[1]) / dy)) maxy = int(np.ceil((max(v0[1], v1[1], v2[1]) - bounds[1]) / dy)) minz = int(np.floor((min(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2]) - bounds[2]) / dz)) maxz = int(np.ceil((max(v0[2], v1[2], v2[2]) - bounds[2]) / dz)) # Clamp indices to grid bounds minx = max(0, minx) maxx = min(nx - 1, maxx) miny = max(0, miny) maxy = min(ny - 1, maxy) minz = max(0, minz) maxz = min(nz - 1, maxz) # For each voxel in the triangle's bounding box, check if the center is inside the triangle for iz in range(minz, maxz + 1): for iy in range(miny, maxy + 1): for ix in range(minx, maxx + 1): # Calculate center of the voxel cx = bounds[0] + (ix + 0.5) dx cy = bounds[1] + (iy + 0.5) dy cz = bounds[2] + (iz + 0.5) dz # Check if point (cx, cy, cz) is inside the triangle if ispointintriangle((cx, cy, cz), v0, v1, v2): voxelgrid[iz, iy, ix] = 1 return voxelgrid def ispointintriangle(p, v0, v1, v2): """ Checks if point p is inside the triangle defined by v0, v1, v2. Uses barycentric coordinates. """ # Vector from v0 to p v0v1 = v1 - v0 v0v2 = v2 - v0 v0p = np.array(p) - v0 # Compute dot products dot00 = np.dot(v0v0, v0v0) # Note: v0v0 is zero vector, this logic needs correction for general triangle # Correct implementation using cross products for robustness # Vector normal to triangle normal = np.cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0) # Check if point is on the same side of all edges # Edge 0: v0 -> v1 edge0normal = np.cross(v1 - v0, p - v0) if np.dot(edge0normal, normal) < 0: return False # Edge 1: v1 -> v2 edge1normal = np.cross(v2 - v1, p - v1) if np.dot(edge1normal, normal) < 0: return False # Edge 2: v2 -> v0 edge2normal = np.cross(v0 - v2, p - v2) if np.dot(edge2normal, normal) < 0: return False return True Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The method relies on point-in-triangle tests. Degenerate triangles or very small features relative to voxel size may be missed or incorrectly filled. Boundary Conditions: The bounding box must fully enclose the mesh. Voxels outside the mesh bounds are initialized to 0. Performance: High resolutions (e.g., 1000x1000x10) significantly increase computation time and memory usage for the 3D matrix array. Uses rasterization or ray-casting to fill voxels based on projection or intersection, often faster but potentially less accurate for complex internal structures compared to explicit point-in-volume checks [1013-voxelgrid-from-mesh-fill-method.md]. Starts with a solid volume and carves away voxels using projection silhouettes from multiple views. Suitable for multi-view reconstruction but computationally intensive for high resolution [1213-voxel-carving.md]. Uses octrees or similar structures to store only non-empty voxels, reducing memory usage for sparse geometries but complicating access patterns [4391-sparse-and-hierarchical-structures.md]. Time Complexity: Dominated by the point-in-triangle test for each voxel within the bounding box of each triangle. Complexity is roughly O(N{triangles} \cdot N{voxels\in\bbox}). High resolutions (e.g., 400^3) result in large voxel counts, increasing CPU time. Memory Complexity: O(Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz) for the 3D matrix array. Non-uniform resolutions (e.g., 1000x10x1000) are used to mitigate this for specific geometries. Accuracy: Volume differences between VGMs and original CAD models are \le 0.6\%. Maximum mean point-to-point IDD deviation is 0.7\% \pm 0.51\%. 3D dose Gamma-index passing rates are \ge 97\% (1%–1 mm criteria). Computing Speed: CPU time difference between VGM and DGM simulations is 2.89\% \pm 0.22\% on average. Strengths: Simple Python-based pipeline; high accuracy for Monte Carlo dose calculations; handles complex non-primitive shapes. Limitations: Requires compilation of FLUKA user routines; memory intensive for high-resolution uniform grids; limited to binary material representation in the basic script. The method was proposed to address the inability to directly import CAD mesh formats into FLUKA Monte Carlo code, which traditionally requires manual construction of geometries using basic shapes (Direct Geometry Models). The study validated the method using five geometric models (cube, sphere, cone, ridge filter, 1D-ripple filter) and compared the results against DGMs in terms of volume, dose distribution, and computing time. The workflow utilizes FreeCAD for mesh creation, stl-to-voxel for coordinate extraction, and FLUKA's writegolem.f routine for final integration. A simple method to import CAD mesh format models in FLUKA., https://doi.org/10.1002/acm2.14107, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Volumetric Representation
head: 3D scalar field, Volume function, Volumetric Data Representation, Volumetric pixels
body: Volumetric representation defines a 3D scene as a continuous or discrete scalar function F(x,y,z) that assigns a value to every point in space, capturing internal density variations rather than just boundaries. Unlike surface-based representations which define only boundaries, this method models the entire volume's properties. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D domain and a scalar field function f{vol}: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}. Output: A volumetric dataset mapping each coordinate (x,y,z) to a scalar value. Data Structures 1. Analytic/Implicit: Stored as a mathematical function definition. 2. Discrete (Voxel Grid): A 3D array of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz where each element stores a scalar value, dividing the 3D area into a regular grid of voxels. Mathematical Definition The volumetric data V is defined as the set of all points in 3D space mapped by the volume function: V = \{ f{vol}(x, y, z) \mid (x, y, z)^T \in \mathbb{R}^3 \} For a sphere of radius R centered at the origin, the function is: F(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - R^2 Points on the surface satisfy F(x',y',z') = 0, points inside satisfy F < 0, and points outside satisfy F > 0. Implementation Steps 1. Define Domain: Determine the bounding box or infinite domain for the volume. 2. Evaluate Field: For any query point \mathbf{p} = (x,y,z), compute v = f{vol}(\mathbf{p}). If using a voxel grid, perform trilinear interpolation between the 8 surrounding voxels to get a continuous value. If using an analytic function, evaluate the formula directly. 3. Iso-surface Extraction (Optional): To visualize the boundary, identify points where f{vol}(\mathbf{p}) = c for a constant c (often c=0). 4. Rendering (Optional): To visualize the interior, map scalar values to color and opacity. In a "dense emitter" model, areas with high density values absorb more light, appearing more opaque. Parameters Resolution: The number of voxels along each axis (Nx, Ny, Nz). Typical values: Not given in the sources. Iso-value: The threshold scalar value used to define surfaces. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Observation Limit: Unlike 2D images, a 3D voxel space cannot be completely observed from a single viewpoint because there is no 4th spatial dimension to look from. Color Perception: In volume rendering, color perception is affected by occlusion; for example, red data values seen through a yellow cloud may be perceived as orange. Surface vs. Volume: Surfaces (meshes) are 2D shapes embedded in 3D space, whereas volumetric data represents the interior. A surface can be represented as a volumetric iso-surface (e.g., a distance map where the surface is the collection of points with distance 0), but not all volumetric data corresponds to a closed surface. This variant focuses on the visual output of the volumetric data as translucent masses where light accumulates color and opacity based on data density, similar to looking through gelatin with embedded objects. It differs from raw data storage by applying color and opacity transfer functions. It is chosen when the goal is visualization of internal structures (e.g., medical scans, clouds) rather than geometric analysis. The default model is "dense emitter," where areas of densely concentrated values appear more opaque as light is absorbed. Implementation typically involves importing data, applying an AutoColor module to map values to colors, and attaching it to a render/display module. There is no single "VolumeRendering" module; any volumetric field can be rendered by standard Image or Render modules. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Visual ambiguity due to occlusion and color mixing. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The mathematical definition of volumetric data as a scalar field F(x,y,z) is used in medical applications to represent tissue density. The distinction between surface representations (implicit/explicit) and volume representations is formalized in modern neural rendering and geometric modeling literature. The specific visualization pitfalls regarding color perception in translucent volumes were documented in early visualization toolkits like OpenDX. name: Structured Mesh Subsampling
head: Resampled structured mesh rendering, Resampling unstructured dataset using a three-dimensional structured mesh, Structured Mesh Subsampling for Volume Rendering, Structured box clip, Structured grid volume rendering, Structured volume algorithm
body: Structured Mesh Subsampling is a volume rendering technique that remaps unstructured computational mesh data onto a regular 3D structured grid (volume) based on analyst-provided values, allowing for resolution adjustment and subsetting. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large unstructured datasets by converting arbitrary cells into a uniform grid, enabling the volume renderer to process a regular grid instead of arbitrary cells. Unlike traditional isosurface rendering which depends on looking at a subset of calculated data and representing results on the surface, this method allows viewing the entire volume at once without slicing. It builds on Voxelization by specifically targeting the conversion of unstructured mesh topology into a structured voxel representation for rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An unstructured computational mesh (e.g., finite element or finite volume data), a specific scalar or vector variable to render, and a bounding box defining the region of interest. Output: A structured 3D grid (volume) containing resampled values of the selected variable, ready for ray-casting or similar volume rendering techniques. Data Structures: The core data structure is a 3D structured grid (tensor product grid) with dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz). Grid Layout: Uniformly spaced nodes within the bounding box. Values: A 3D array of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz storing the resampled variable values. Bounding Box: Defined by minimum and maximum coordinates (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}), potentially oriented in any direction relative to the mesh. Steps: 1. Selection: The user selects the parent part (unstructured mesh) to be displayed as a volume. 2. Subsetting: A bounding box (structured clip box) is defined to subset the dataset. This focuses the rendering on a specific area of interest, reducing computational effort by excluding cells outside the box. 3. Resampling: The algorithm resamples the unstructured data within the bounding box into a structured grid. The resolution of this grid is adjustable by the user. The algorithm identifies all unstructured cells that overlap with the structured grid cells (or pixels in the final projection). Values from the unstructured cells are mapped to the structured grid nodes. The specific method of interpolation or averaging is not detailed in the sources, but the goal is to create a volume representation based on the analyst-provided variable. 4. Rendering: The volume renderer processes the structured grid. It finds all cells (structured grid cells) that overlap each pixel and accumulates a color for that pixel from the color and transparency (alpha) of each cell. Color palettes, including transparency, are applied based on the variable values. Parameters: Resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz): The size of the structured mesh. Low resolution (e.g., 32 \times 32 \times 32) is used for initial exploration. Resolution of 200 (200 \times 200 \times 200) is sufficient for video animations. Resolution of 500 (500 \times 500 \times 500) is used for high-quality printed renderings. Bounding Box: Defines the spatial extent of the subsampling. Variable: The specific data field (e.g., vorticity magnitude) to be rendered. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def structuredmeshsubsampling(unstructuredmesh, variablename, boundingbox, resolution): """ Resamples unstructured mesh data into a structured grid for volume rendering. Args: unstructuredmesh: The source unstructured mesh data. variablename: The name of the variable to resample. boundingbox: A tuple (mincoords, maxcoords) defining the region of interest. resolution: A tuple (Nx, Ny, Nz) defining the structured grid dimensions. Returns: structuredgrid: A 3D array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) containing resampled values. """ # 1. Define the structured grid domain based on the bounding box and resolution # The grid is uniform within the bounding box. xmin, ymin, zmin = boundingbox.min xmax, ymax, zmax = boundingbox.max Nx, Ny, Nz = resolution # Calculate step sizes dx = (xmax - xmin) / Nx dy = (ymax - ymin) / Ny dz = (zmax - zmin) / Nz # Initialize the structured grid with zeros or null values structuredgrid = np.zeros((Nx, Ny, Nz)) # 2. Identify unstructured cells within the bounding box # This step involves spatial indexing to find cells overlapping the bounding box. candidatecells = findcellsinbox(unstructuredmesh, boundingbox) # 3. Resample values from unstructured cells to structured grid nodes # For each node in the structured grid, determine which unstructured cells contribute to it. # The specific interpolation method is not detailed in the sources. # A common approach would be trilinear interpolation or nearest-neighbor from the # unstructured cell centers/nodes to the structured grid nodes. for i in range(Nx): for j in range(Ny): for k in range(Nz): # Calculate the world coordinates of the structured grid node x = xmin + i dx y = ymin + j dy z = zmin + k dz # Find the value of the variable at this point from the unstructured mesh # This requires querying the unstructured mesh for the variable value at (x, y, z) # If the point is not inside any cell, the value might be null or interpolated from neighbors. value = getvariablevalueatpoint(unstructuredmesh, variablename, x, y, z) structuredgrid[i, j, k] = value return structuredgrid def rendervolume(structuredgrid, colorpalette): """ Renders the structured grid using volume rendering techniques. Args: structuredgrid: The 3D array of resampled values. colorpalette: A mapping from variable values to color and transparency (alpha). Returns: image: The rendered 2D image. """ # 1. Cast rays through the structured grid # For each pixel in the output image, cast a ray through the volume. # 2. Accumulate color and opacity # Find all cells (voxels) that the ray overlaps. # Accumulate color for the pixel from the color and transparency of each cell. # This is typically done using front-to-back or back-to-front compositing. image = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) for u in range(width): for v in range(height): ray = castray(u, v) accumulatedcolor = [0, 0, 0] accumulatedalpha = 0 # Traverse the structured grid along the ray # The specific traversal algorithm (e.g., DDA) is not detailed in the sources # but is standard for structured grids. for voxel in structuredgrid.intersectedbyray(ray): value = structuredgrid[voxel] color, alpha = colorpalette(value) # Compositing step (front-to-back example) # Cout = Cin + (1 - Ain) Cv Av # Aout = Ain + (1 - Ain) Av accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor + (1 - accumulatedalpha) color alpha accumulatedalpha = accumulatedalpha + (1 - accumulatedalpha) alpha image[v, u] = accumulatedcolor return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The volume calculated is less precise than the original hardware-based unstructured method. However, there is often little to no perceivable difference in the rendering results. Resolution Artifacts: Lower-resolution images visibly demonstrate how the data has been subsampled, showing individual planes. As resolution increases, these artifacts disappear. Computational Cost: Volume rendering algorithms are computationally expensive as they must look at every cell within the mesh multiple times. Subsetting via bounding box is critical to reduce this effort. Time Complexity: The resampling step depends on the number of unstructured cells within the bounding box and the resolution of the structured grid. The rendering step depends on the number of rays (pixels) and the number of voxels intersected by each ray. The sources note that volume rendering is "computationally expensive". Memory Complexity: The memory usage for the volume representation operation is estimated at 79MBs for the tested dataset. This is significantly lower than storing the full unstructured mesh for rendering purposes if the mesh is very large. Performance: The method is faster and more flexible in terms of end-user interactive response compared to the original hardware-based rendering methodology. It allows for efficient rendering of large datasets, particularly when leveraging HPC resources. Strengths: Allows viewing the entire volume at once without slicing. Reduces computational effort by subsetting the dataset. Flexible resolution adjustment for exploration vs. final output. Limitations: Less precise than the original hardware-based unstructured method. Low resolutions show visible subsampling artifacts (individual planes). When to Use: Use when interactive response is prioritized over absolute precision, or when rendering large datasets on HPC resources. Ideal for initial exploration (low res) and final animations/printing (high res). When Not to Use: Use when the highest possible precision is required and the computational cost of the original hardware-based method is acceptable. Structured Mesh Subsampling was introduced in EnSight 10.0 (2012). It was implemented to address the limitations of the original volume rendering technique, which depended on the exclusive use of graphics hardware and was too limiting for general-purpose use. The new methodology allows the end user to resample data to any resolution by creating an underlying structured volume based on values provided by the analyst. It was successfully tested on large datasets generated at the Army Research Laboratory (ARL). The technique is used in EnSight 10.0 and later versions. name: Polyhedron Rasterization Voxelization
head: 3D Polyhedron to Voxel Conversion, 3D Solid-to-Voxel Stage 1, Stage 1 (3D)
body: Polyhedron Rasterization Voxelization converts 3D polyhedral boundaries into a discrete voxel grid by projecting planar faces onto a 2D plane and rasterizing them to determine vertical extents. It serves as the first stage of a two-stage solid voxelization pipeline, producing a sparse boundary grid that encodes surface intersections via XOR operations. Unlike methods that fill volumes directly or use ray casting, this approach explicitly represents only the faces separating solids or background, deferring the determination of interior solid values to a subsequent prefix-scan stage. Inputs: A set of 3D polyhedra defined by planar faces (vertices with (x,y,z) coordinates) and a background value (typically 0). A target 3D grid resolution and bounding box. Outputs: A 3D voxel grid where each voxel contains an integer value representing the XOR difference between adjacent solids or between a solid and the background. Data Structures: 3D Grid: A 3D array of integers. Dimensions are determined by the dataset extent and desired resolution. Initialized to zero. 2D Projection Grid: A temporary 2D array used for rasterizing individual faces. Steps: 1. Initialize Grid: Create an empty 3D grid filled with zeros, sized to cover the spatial extent of the input geometry at the target resolution. 2. Iterate Faces: Process each planar face of the input polyhedra individually. 3. Project and Rasterize: Determine the bounding box of the face's vertices in the (x,y) plane. Create a 2D grid covering this extent. Rasterize the 2D polygon projection into this grid, filling the interior with 1s and the exterior with 0s, following standard 2D rasterization rules. 4. Map to 3D: Shift the (row, column) coordinates of the 2D rasterized face to the corresponding (x,y) indices in the 3D grid. 5. Calculate Z-Coordinate: For each (x,y) position occupied by the face, calculate the vertical grid coordinate z using the plane equation derived from the face's 3D vertices. Let the plane equation be Ax + By + Cz + D = 0. Solve for z: z = -(Ax + By + D) / C (assuming C \neq 0). Convert the continuous z to the discrete grid index. 6. Insert XOR Value: At the resulting 3D index (x,y,z), update the grid value. The new value is the XOR of the values of the two regions separated by the face (e.g., Solid A and Background, or Solid A and Solid B). If a value already exists at that index, XOR the new value with the existing one. Formula: Grid[x,y,z] = Grid[x,y,z] \oplus (Value{solid1} \oplus Value{solid2}). 7. Handle Non-Planar Primitives: For primitives like hemispheres, parametrize them (center x0, y0, z0, radius R, vertical scale e, value v). For each (x,y) within distance R from (x0, y0), calculate z using the scaled hemisphere equation: z = z0 + e \cdot \sqrt{R^2 - (x-x0)^2 - (y-y0)^2}. Insert v \oplus Background at (x,y,z). Parameters: Scan Direction: The method typically uses a top-to-bottom scan direction for the vertical axis, though left-to-right or front-to-back are possible. Solid Values: Integer identifiers for each solid region. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vertical Walls: In a top-to-bottom scan, vertical walls do not appear explicitly in the sparse boundary grid. They are represented solely by their top and bottom XOR values. Non-Planar Faces: The core algorithm requires planar faces. Non-planar surfaces must be approximated or parametrized as described above. Precision: Floating-point to integer conversion for z coordinates must be handled consistently to avoid gaps or overlaps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def polyhedronrasterizationvoxelization(faces, griddims, backgroundvalue=0): # Initialize 3D grid with zeros grid = [[[0 for in range(griddims[2])] for in range(griddims[1])] for in range(griddims[0])] for face in faces: # Get vertices of the face vertices = face.vertices # Determine 2D bounding box in x,y minx = min(v.x for v in vertices) maxx = max(v.x for v in vertices) miny = min(v.y for v in vertices) maxy = max(v.y for v in vertices) # Create 2D rasterization grid for this face width = maxx - minx + 1 height = maxy - miny + 1 facegrid = [[0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] # Rasterize 2D polygon into facegrid (fill with 1s) rasterize2dpolygon(vertices, facegrid, minx, miny) # Calculate plane equation from 3D vertices # Assuming vertices are coplanar p1, p2, p3 = vertices[0], vertices[1], vertices[2] normal = crossproduct(vector(p2, p1), vector(p3, p1)) A, B, C = normal.x, normal.y, normal.z D = -dotproduct(normal, p1) # Iterate over rasterized pixels for dy in range(height): for dx in range(width): if facegrid[dy][dx] == 1: # Map to 3D grid coordinates x = minx + dx y = miny + dy # Calculate z from plane equation if C == 0: # Vertical face, skip or handle as edge case continue zfloat = -(A x + B y + D) / C z = round(zfloat) # Check bounds if 0 <= x < griddims[0] and 0 <= y < griddims[1] and 0 <= z < griddims[2]: # Determine XOR value # Assuming face separates solidid from background or another solid # For simplicity, assume face has a 'solidvalue' attribute solidvalue = face.solidvalue xorval = solidvalue ^ backgroundvalue # XOR into grid grid[x][y][z] ^= xorval return grid def rasterize2dpolygon(vertices, grid, minx, miny): # Standard 2D rasterization algorithm (e.g., scanline fill) # Fills grid with 1s inside the polygon pass def crossproduct(v1, v2): return Vector3D( v1.y v2.z - v1.z v2.y, v1.z v2.x - v1.x v2.z, v1.x v2.y - v1.y v2.x) def dotproduct(v1, v2): return v1.x v2.x + v1.y v2.y + v1.z v2.z def vector(p1, p2): return Vector3D(p2.x - p1.x, p2.y - p1.y, p2.z - p1.z) Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of faces times the area of their projections in voxels. Rasterization is O(A) where A is the projected area. Memory Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz) for the full grid, but the output is sparse, storing only boundary voxels. Strengths: Explicitly handles complex solid boundaries; efficient for sparse boundaries; clear separation of surface representation from volume filling. Limitations: Requires planar faces; vertical walls are not explicitly stored in the boundary grid; requires a second stage to resolve solid interiors. When to Use: When explicit boundary representation is needed before volume filling; for CAD-like models with planar faces. When Not to Use: For non-planar surfaces without parametrization; when immediate solid volume is required without post-processing. The method was described in the context of rasterizing and voxelizing two- and three-dimensional space partitionings, particularly for land use maps and building models. It extends 2D rasterization techniques to 3D by using faces as boundaries between solids. The approach was demonstrated on a historical land use map of Adelaide, Australia, containing 192 polygons and 1296 vertices. name: Curve Voxelization
head: 1D Input Voxelization (Curves), 1D inputs, 2D targets, Line Segment Voxelization, voxelizeCurve
body: Curve Voxelization maps 1D geometric inputs (curves, polylines, or line segments) into a 3D voxel grid while guaranteeing specific topological connectivity (6-connected or 26-connected) in the output. It solves the problem of preserving the continuity of thin features in discrete volumetric representations, ensuring that adjacent voxels in the result are connected via faces (6-connectivity) or faces and edges/corners (26-connectivity) without gaps. It sets itself apart from standard rasterization methods by using Intersection Targets—geometric primitives dual to the input dimension—to determine voxel occupancy, rather than simple distance thresholds or ray-casting against voxel boundaries. The method relies on the principle of Topological Voxelization, which uses Poincaré Duality to define "Intersection Targets" inside each candidate voxel. For 1D inputs, the target is a 2D feature (faces or planes) within the 3D voxel space. Input: curves: A list of 1D geometric objects (curves, polylines, or line segments). connectivity: An integer specifying the desired adjacency level: 6 or 26. vSize: A 3D vector [sx, sy, sz] defining the dimensions of a single voxel. Output: voxels: A list of 3D points representing the centers of occupied voxels. Voxel Point: A 3D coordinate (x, y, z) representing the center of a voxel. Bounding Box (BBox): Defined by minimum and maximum coordinates (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}). Intersection Target: A geometric mesh (list of triangles) defined relative to a voxel center and size. 1. Initialization: For each curve in curves: a. Compute the axis-aligned bounding box (RBBox) of the curve in \mathbb{R}^3. b. Define the voxel size vector vSize = [sx, sy, sz]. c. Convert the real-world bounding box to a zero-based integer grid bounding box (ZBBox) aligned with the voxel grid. This is done by scaling the RBBox by vSize and rounding appropriately to ensure coverage. d. Generate a list of all voxel center points (VoxelPoints) within ZBBox using a grid generation function BBoxToVoxels(ZBBox, vSize). 2. Filtering (Candidate Selection): Filter VoxelPoints to keep only those "near" the curve. A voxel point P is considered near if its Euclidean distance to the curve is less than half the length of the voxel diagonal: |P - \text{Curve}| < \frac{|vSize|}{2} where |vSize| = \sqrt{sx^2 + sy^2 + sz^2}. Let the resulting list be nearvoxelpoints. 3. Intersection Testing: Initialize an empty list voxels. For each voxelpoint in nearvoxelpoints: a. Construct Intersection Target: Based on the connectivity parameter, construct a specific geometric target inside the voxel centered at voxelpoint: If connectivity == 6: Create the 1D6intersectionTarget. This consists of the 6 faces of the voxel cube. If connectivity == 26: Create the 1D26intersectionTarget. This consists of 3 plane faces cutting the voxel in half along the X, Y, and Z axes, meeting at the voxel center (forming a 3D crosshair structure). If connectivity is neither 6 nor 26, throw an exception. b. Check Intersection: Test if the input curve intersects the constructed intersectionTarget. Note: The curve may be approximated as a polyline of line segments for this test. The intersection test TriangleIntersectLine checks if the line segment intersects any triangle in the target mesh using barycentric coordinates. c. Add to Output: If an intersection is detected, add voxelpoint to voxels. 4. Return: Return the voxels list. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelizeCurve(curves, connectivity, sx, sy, sz): """ Voxelize 1D curves into a 3D grid with guaranteed connectivity. Args: curves: List of curve objects (supporting bounding box and intersection tests). connectivity: Integer, 6 or 26. sx, sy, sz: Floats, voxel dimensions. Returns: List of 3D points (centers of occupied voxels). """ voxels = [] vSize = [sx, sy, sz] vSizenorm = sqrt(sx2 + sy2 + sz2) halfdiag = vSizenorm / 2.0 for curve in curves: # 1. Bounding Box Setup rbbox = curve.getboundingbox() # Returns (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) # Convert Real BBox to Zero-based Grid BBox # Assuming voxel grid starts at (0,0,0) and aligns with axes # This step scales the real coordinates to grid indices zbbox = rbboxtozbbox(rbbox, vSize) # 2. Generate Candidate Voxels voxelpoints = bboxtovoxels(zbbox, vSize) # 3. Filter by Distance nearvoxelpoints = [] for p in voxelpoints: # Distance from point p to curve dist = pointtocurvedistance(p, curve) if dist < halfdiag: nearvoxelpoints.append(p) # 4. Intersection Testing for p in nearvoxelpoints: # Construct Intersection Target if connectivity == 6: target = create1d6intersectiontarget(p, vSize) elif connectivity == 26: target = create1d26intersectiontarget(p, vSize) else: raise ValueError("Connectivity must be 6 or 26") # Check Intersection # Note: curve might need to be decomposed into line segments for TriangleIntersectLine if triangleintersectline(target, curve): voxels.append(p) return voxels def create1d6intersectiontarget(center, vSize): """ Returns a mesh of 6 triangles representing the 6 faces of the voxel cube. """ sx, sy, sz = vSize cx, cy, cz = center # Define the 8 corners of the voxel corners = [ [cx - sx/2, cy - sy/2, cz - sz/2], [cx + sx/2, cy - sy/2, cz - sz/2], [cx + sx/2, cy + sy/2, cz - sz/2], [cx - sx/2, cy + sy/2, cz - sz/2], [cx - sx/2, cy - sy/2, cz + sz/2], [cx + sx/2, cy - sy/2, cz + sz/2], [cx + sx/2, cy + sy/2, cz + sz/2], [cx - sx/2, cy + sy/2, cz + sz/2] ] # Define 6 faces as pairs of triangles # Face -X, +X, -Y, +Y, -Z, +Z triangles = [ # -X face [corners[0], corners[3], corners[4]], [corners[3], corners[7], corners[4]], # +X face [corners[1], corners[2], corners[5]], [corners[2], corners[6], corners[5]], # -Y face [corners[0], corners[1], corners[4]], [corners[1], corners[5], corners[4]], # +Y face [corners[3], corners[2], corners[7]], [corners[2], corners[6], corners[7]], # -Z face [corners[0], corners[1], corners[3]], [corners[1], corners[2], corners[3]], # +Z face [corners[4], corners[5], corners[7]], [corners[5], corners[6], corners[7]] ] return triangles def create1d26intersectiontarget(center, vSize): """ Returns a mesh representing 3 plane faces cutting the voxel in halves along X, Y, Z axes. This forms a 3D crosshair structure. """ sx, sy, sz = vSize cx, cy, cz = center # The target consists of 3 rectangles intersecting at the center. # Each rectangle is split into 2 triangles. # Plane X (cutting along Y-Z plane at center X) # Vertices: (cx, cy-sy/2, cz-sz/2), (cx, cy+sy/2, cz-sz/2), (cx, cy+sy/2, cz+sz/2), (cx, cy-sy/2, cz+sz/2) trix1 = [[cx, cy - sy/2, cz - sz/2], [cx, cy + sy/2, cz - sz/2], [cx, cy + sy/2, cz + sz/2]] trix2 = [[cx, cy - sy/2, cz - sz/2], [cx, cy + sy/2, cz + sz/2], [cx, cy - sy/2, cz + sz/2]] # Plane Y (cutting along X-Z plane at center Y) triy1 = [[cx - sx/2, cy, cz - sz/2], [cx + sx/2, cy, cz - sz/2], [cx + sx/2, cy, cz + sz/2]] triy2 = [[cx - sx/2, cy, cz - sz/2], [cx + sx/2, cy, cz + sz/2], [cx - sx/2, cy, cz + sz/2]] # Plane Z (cutting along X-Y plane at center Z) triz1 = [[cx - sx/2, cy - sy/2, cz], [cx + sx/2, cy - sy/2, cz], [cx + sx/2, cy + sy/2, cz]] triz2 = [[cx - sx/2, cy - sy/2, cz], [cx + sx/2, cy + sy/2, cz], [cx - sx/2, cy + sy/2, cz]] return trix1 + trix2 + triy1 + triy2 + triz1 + triz2 def triangleintersectline(triangles, curve): """ Checks if the curve intersects any triangle in the list. Assumes curve is approximated as a polyline of line segments. """ segments = curvetosegments(curve) for seg in segments: for tri in triangles: if lineintersectstriangle(seg, tri): return True return False def lineintersectstriangle(line, triangle): """ Standard line-triangle intersection using barycentric coordinates. Returns True if intersection point lies within triangle bounds. """ # Implementation of Möller–Trumbore algorithm or similar # v0, v1, v2 = triangle vertices # e1 = v1 - v0 # e2 = v2 - v0 # h = cross(d, e2) where d is line direction # a = dot(e1, h) # if a < epsilon and a > -epsilon: return False (parallel) # f = 1.0 / a # s = p0 - v0 # u = f dot(s, h) # if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return False # q = cross(s, e1) # v = f dot(d, q) # if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: return False # t = f dot(e2, q) # if t > epsilon: return True (intersection) # return False pass # Placeholder for standard geometric primitive connectivity: 6 (face-adjacent) or 26 (face/edge/corner-adjacent). No other values are supported. vSize: Determines resolution. Smaller values increase accuracy but also computational cost. Distance Threshold: Half the voxel diagonal (|vSize|/2) is used as the initial filter. Invalid Connectivity: If connectivity is not 6 or 26, the algorithm throws an exception. Curve Approximation: The intersection test TriangleIntersectLine requires the curve to be decomposed into line segments (polylines). High-curvature curves must be sufficiently tessellated to avoid missing intersections with the thin intersection targets. Precision: Floating-point precision in distance calculations and intersection tests can lead to gaps or spurious voxels. Robust geometric predicates are recommended for the intersection test. Generates a target consisting of the 6 faces of the voxel cube. Used to guarantee 6-connectivity (face-adjacency). Chosen when strict face-connectedness is required. Defines a target for 2D surface inputs to ensure 26-connectivity. Uses diagonal lines through the voxel center. (Note: This is a sibling method for 2D inputs, not 1D). Defines a target for 2D surface inputs using 4 space diagonals to ensure 6-connectivity. (Note: This is a sibling method for 2D inputs, not 1D). Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of voxels in the bounding box and M is the number of line segments in the curve approximation. The distance filter reduces N to "near" voxels. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the voxel points and intersection targets. Performance: Efficient for sparse curves as it iterates over objects (curves) rather than the entire space. However, for large meshes (e.g., TINs), decomposition into primitives is necessary. Strengths: Guarantees topological connectivity (6 or 26). Mathematically proven to be "minimally thin" (no unnecessary voxels). Limitations: Requires curve tessellation. Not suitable for 0D (points) or 2D (surfaces) without different targets. The method is based on Topological Voxelization, introduced by Laine [1], which uses Poincaré Duality to define intersection targets. The specific implementation for 1D inputs (curves) was detailed in geospatial applications by. The approach ensures that the raster output preserves the topological properties of the vector input. name: 1D_6_intersectionTarget
head: 1D mesh ensuring 6-connectivity, Diagonal mesh target for 1D inputs
body: The 1D6intersectionTarget method generates a specific 3D mesh geometry used as an "intersection target" within each candidate voxel during the voxelization of 1D inputs (lines, polylines, or curves). Its primary purpose is to guarantee 6-connectivity (face-adjacency) in the resulting voxel set by ensuring that any curve passing through a voxel intersects this internal mesh. Unlike the cube outline target, which traces the voxel edges, this method uses a diagonal mesh structure composed of triangles to determine intersection. It is a core component of the Curve Voxelization pipeline, specifically designed to resolve the topological connectivity of the output volume data. The algorithm constructs a static mesh defined relative to the center of a voxel. This mesh consists of 9 vertices and 12 triangular faces. The construction relies on the voxel's center point and half-dimensions along the X, Y, and Z axes. Input: vSize: A 3D vector representing the voxel dimensions (X, Y, Z). VoxelPoint: A 3D point representing the center of the voxel. Output: IntersectionTarget: A mesh object containing the defined vertices and faces. The mesh is defined by two arrays: 1. Vertices: An array of 9 3D points (Point3d[9]). 2. Faces: A list of 12 triangles, where each triangle is defined by three indices into the Vertices array. u = \frac{vSize.X}{2} v = \frac{vSize.Y}{2} w = \frac{vSize.Z}{2} These represent the half-width, half-height, and half-depth of the voxel, respectively. 1. Initialize: Create an empty mesh object IntersectionTarget. Calculate u, v, w. Initialize the Vertices array of size 9. Set Vertices[0] to VoxelPoint. 2. Create Vertices: Compute the remaining 8 vertices by adding or subtracting the half-dimensions from VoxelPoint. The indices correspond to specific corners/edges relative to the center: Vertices[1] = VoxelPoint - (u, v, w) Vertices[2] = VoxelPoint - (-u, v, w) Vertices[3] = VoxelPoint - (-u, -v, w) Vertices[4] = VoxelPoint - (u, -v, w) Vertices[5] = VoxelPoint + (-u, -v, w) Vertices[6] = VoxelPoint + (u, -v, w) Vertices[7] = VoxelPoint + (u, v, w) Vertices[8] = VoxelPoint + (-u, v, w) 3. Create Faces: Add 12 triangles to the mesh using the vertex indices. The faces are defined as follows: (0, 1, 2) (0, 2, 6) (0, 6, 5) (0, 5, 1) (0, 4, 1) (0, 5, 8) (0, 8, 7) (0, 7, 3) (0, 3, 4) (0, 4, 8) (0, 7, 6) (0, 2, 3) 4. Return: Attach the Vertices and Faces to the IntersectionTarget mesh and return it. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def 1D6intersectionTarget(vSize, VoxelPoint): # 1. Initialize u = vSize.X / 2.0 v = vSize.Y / 2.0 w = vSize.Z / 2.0 # Vertices array of size 9 Vertices = [None] 9 Vertices[0] = VoxelPoint # 2. Create vertices # Note: Vector3d operations are standard vector arithmetic Vertices[1] = VoxelPoint - Vector3d(+u, +v, +w) Vertices[2] = VoxelPoint - Vector3d(-u, +v, +w) Vertices[3] = VoxelPoint - Vector3d(-u, -v, +w) Vertices[4] = VoxelPoint - Vector3d(+u, -v, +w) Vertices[5] = VoxelPoint + Vector3d(-u, -v, +w) Vertices[6] = VoxelPoint + Vector3d(+u, -v, +w) Vertices[7] = VoxelPoint + Vector3d(+u, +v, +w) Vertices[8] = VoxelPoint + Vector3d(-u, +v, +w) # 3. Create faces # Each tuple represents a triangle (v1, v2, v3) Faces = [ (0, 1, 2), (0, 2, 6), (0, 6, 5), (0, 5, 1), (0, 4, 1), (0, 5, 8), (0, 8, 7), (0, 7, 3), (0, 3, 4), (0, 4, 8), (0, 7, 6), (0, 2, 3) ] # 4. Return IntersectionTarget = Mesh() IntersectionTarget.Vertices = Vertices IntersectionTarget.Faces = Faces return IntersectionTarget Triangle Count: The source explicitly states that this target produces 12 triangles and that this number "cannot be reduced" for this specific 6-connected result type. Quadrangular vs Triangular: The source notes that a naive implementation might produce 12 quadrangular faces (24 triangles), but the algorithm described here specifically constructs 12 triangles. Implementers should ensure they use the triangular decomposition provided, not a quadrangular one, for efficiency and correctness as defined in the source. Connectivity: This target is strictly for 6-connectivity. It is not suitable for 26-connectivity requirements without modification. An alternative intersection target that uses the edges of the voxel cube. It is compared against the diagonal mesh target in terms of performance and connectivity guarantees. A 2D analog of this method, used for 2D inputs. It uses 8 lines compared to 12 lines for the outline, offering a 1.5x speedup in that specific 2D context. Complexity: The construction of the mesh is O(1) per voxel, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations and array assignments (9 vertices, 12 faces). Performance: The source compares the diagonal mesh target to the cube outline target. While a specific speedup factor for the 1D case is not explicitly quantified in the same way as the 2D case (where diagonal was 1.5x faster), the source notes that the diagonal target has 12 triangles and cannot be reduced, implying a fixed computational cost per voxel for intersection testing. The 2D comparison suggests that fewer primitives (lines/triangles) generally lead to faster intersection solving. Memory: Requires storage for 9 vertices and 12 faces per voxel candidate. Strengths: Guarantees 6-connectivity for 1D inputs. Limitations: The fixed number of triangles (12) means it cannot be optimized further by reducing face count for this connectivity type. The 1D6intersectionTarget algorithm is described in the context of voxelization algorithms for geospatial applications. It is part of a broader methodology for converting 1D geometric primitives (lines, polylines) into 3D voxel grids with guaranteed topological connectivity. The specific algorithm is labeled as "Algorithm 5" in the source literature. name: 2D_26_intersectionTarget
head: 2D mesh ensuring 26 connectivity, Diagonal target for 2D inputs
body: The 2D26intersectionTarget method defines a geometric intersection test primitive for voxelizing 2D surfaces (such as triangle meshes) into a 3D voxel grid with 26-connectivity. It ensures that if a surface intersects any part of a voxel, including its corners and edges, the voxel is marked as occupied, thereby preventing topological holes in the resulting volume. It differs from the 2D 6-Connected Intersection Target by using diagonal lines through the voxel center rather than face centers, allowing it to detect intersections with voxel corners that the 6-connected target might miss. Input: voxelpoint (the 3D integer coordinates of the voxel center or corner, depending on coordinate system convention, typically the minimum corner), vSize (a Vector3d representing the voxel dimensions wx, wy, wz). Output: An array IntersecTarget of 3 Line objects. Each Line is defined by two Point3d endpoints. Point3d: A structure with fields x, y, z (double precision). Vector3d: A structure with fields X, Y, Z (double precision). Line: A structure defined by two Point3d endpoints, p1 and p2. IntersecTarget: An array of 3 Line objects. Vertices: An array of 6 Point3d objects. 1. Initialize: Create IntersecTarget array of size 3. Create Vertices array of size 6. Calculate half-dimensions: u = \frac{vSize.X}{2} v = \frac{vSize.Y}{2} w = \frac{vSize.Z}{2} 2. Create Vertices: The vertices are located at the centers of the voxel's faces. Vertices[0] = VoxelPoint + (u, 0, 0) Vertices[1] = VoxelPoint + (0, v, 0) Vertices[2] = VoxelPoint + (0, 0, w) Vertices[3] = VoxelPoint + (-u, 0, 0) Vertices[4] = VoxelPoint + (0, -v, 0) Vertices[5] = VoxelPoint + (0, 0, -w) 3. Create Edges: Connect opposite face centers through the voxel center. For i from 0 to 2: IntersecTarget[i] = Line(Vertices[i], Vertices[i+3]) 4. Return: Return IntersecTarget. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def 2D26intersectionTarget(voxelpoint, vSize): # Initialize arrays IntersecTarget = [None] 3 Vertices = [None] 6 # Calculate half-dimensions u = vSize.X / 2.0 v = vSize.Y / 2.0 w = vSize.Z / 2.0 # Create Vertices at face centers # Vertices[0] = VoxelPoint + (+u, 0, 0) Vertices[0] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x + u, voxelpoint.y, voxelpoint.z) # Vertices[1] = VoxelPoint + (0, +v, 0) Vertices[1] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x, voxelpoint.y + v, voxelpoint.z) # Vertices[2] = VoxelPoint + (0, 0, +w) Vertices[2] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x, voxelpoint.y, voxelpoint.z + w) # Vertices[3] = VoxelPoint + (-u, 0, 0) Vertices[3] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x - u, voxelpoint.y, voxelpoint.z) # Vertices[4] = VoxelPoint + (0, -v, 0) Vertices[4] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x, voxelpoint.y - v, voxelpoint.z) # Vertices[5] = VoxelPoint + (0, 0, -w) Vertices[5] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x, voxelpoint.y, voxelpoint.z - w) # Create Edges: Connect opposite face centers for i in range(3): IntersecTarget[i] = Line(Vertices[i], Vertices[i+3]) return IntersecTarget Degenerate Voxels: If any dimension of vSize is zero, the half-dimensions u, v, w become zero, collapsing the lines to points. This should be handled by validating input dimensions before execution. Coordinate System: The definition assumes VoxelPoint is the origin relative to which offsets are applied. If VoxelPoint represents the minimum corner, the face centers are correctly calculated as shown. If it represents the center, the offsets would be different. The sources imply VoxelPoint is a base corner or reference point. Intersection Test: The resulting lines are used in a TriangleIntersectsLine test. If any of the 3 lines intersect the input surface (e.g., a triangle), the voxel is added to the voxel set. Time Complexity: The construction of the intersection target is O(1), involving a fixed number of arithmetic operations and array assignments. The intersection test itself depends on the number of surface primitives (e.g., triangles) tested against the 3 lines. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the intersection target structure (3 lines, 6 points). Strengths: Ensures 26-connectivity, which is crucial for preserving the topology of thin structures and corners in 2D surface voxelization. It is more robust than 6-connected targets for diagonal features. Limitations: It may mark voxels as occupied that do not contain the surface if the diagonal lines intersect the surface but the voxel body does not (though this is the definition of 26-connectivity). It is computationally more expensive than 6-connected targets due to the diagonal checks. When to use: When 26-connectivity is required for the voxelized surface, such as in medical imaging or geospatial applications where topological correctness is critical. When not to use: When 6-connectivity is sufficient and performance is a higher priority, or when the surface is known to be axis-aligned. The method is described in the context of voxelization algorithms for geospatial applications. It is part of a family of intersection targets designed to ensure specific connectivity levels (6, 18, 26) in voxel grids. The 2D26intersectionTarget specifically addresses the need for 26-connectivity for 2D inputs (surfaces) in a 3D grid. The algorithm is presented as Algorithm 8 in the source literature.
