name: 2D 6-Connected Intersection Target
head: 2D mesh ensuring 6 connectivity with diagonal target, Diagonal target for 2D 6-connectivity
body: The 2D 6-Connected Intersection Target (Diagonal) defines a set of line segments within a single voxel that serves as the geometric target for ray-casting or curve-voxelization algorithms to ensure 6-connectivity in the resulting voxel grid. It consists of the four space diagonals of the voxel cube, connecting opposite corners. Unlike the 2D6intersectionTarget which uses the 12 edges of the cube, this method uses only 4 internal diagonals. It is chosen when a minimal set of intersection lines is required to guarantee that a 2D input (such as a curve or line segment) intersects the voxel in a manner consistent with 6-connectivity (face-adjacency), while reducing the number of intersection tests compared to the outline target. Input: VoxelPoint: The 3D coordinates of the voxel's center or a reference corner (typically the minimum corner, depending on implementation convention; the sources define vertices relative to a center-like offset, but the formula VoxelPoint + offset implies VoxelPoint is the center if offsets are \pm u, \pm v, \pm w. However, standard voxelization often uses the minimum corner. Let's look at the offsets: +u, +v, +w and -u, -v, -w. If VoxelPoint is the center, these are the corners. If VoxelPoint is the min corner, u,v,w would be half-dimensions, and +u,+v,+w would be the max corner. The code VX[0] = VoxelPoint + (+u, +v, +w) and VX[4] = VoxelPoint + (-u, -v, -w) suggests VoxelPoint is the center of the voxel, because VX[0] and VX[4] are opposite corners. Wait, VX[0] is (+u,+v,+w) and VX[4] is (-u,-v,-w). These are opposite. VX[1] is (-u,+v,+w) and VX[5] is (+u,-v,-w). These are opposite. So VoxelPoint is the center of the voxel. vSize: A 3D vector (Sx, Sy, Sz) representing the dimensions of the voxel. Output: IT: An array of 4 Line objects, where each Line is defined by two 3D points (endpoints). Point3d: A structure with fields x, y, z of type double. Line: A structure with fields p1, p2 of type Point3d. VoxelPoint: Point3d. vSize: Vector3d (or Point3d used as vector). 1. Initialize: Create an array IT of size 4. Create an array VX of size 8. Calculate half-dimensions: u = Sx / 2 v = Sy / 2 w = Sz / 2 2. Create Vertices: Define the 8 corners of the voxel relative to VoxelPoint (the center): VX[0] = (VoxelPoint.x + u, VoxelPoint.y + v, VoxelPoint.z + w) VX[1] = (VoxelPoint.x - u, VoxelPoint.y + v, VoxelPoint.z + w) VX[2] = (VoxelPoint.x - u, VoxelPoint.y - v, VoxelPoint.z + w) VX[3] = (VoxelPoint.x + u, VoxelPoint.y - v, VoxelPoint.z + w) VX[4] = (VoxelPoint.x - u, VoxelPoint.y - v, VoxelPoint.z - w) VX[5] = (VoxelPoint.x + u, VoxelPoint.y - v, VoxelPoint.z - w) VX[6] = (VoxelPoint.x + u, VoxelPoint.y + v, VoxelPoint.z - w) VX[7] = (VoxelPoint.x - u, VoxelPoint.y + v, VoxelPoint.z - w) 3. Create Edges (Diagonals): Connect opposite corners to form the 4 space diagonals: IT[0] = \text{Line}(VX[0], VX[4]) IT[1] = \text{Line}(VX[1], VX[5]) IT[2] = \text{Line}(VX[2], VX[6]) IT[3] = \text{Line}(VX[3], VX[7]) 4. Return IT. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compute2d6connectedintersectiontargetdiagonal(voxelpoint, vsize): """ Computes the 4 space diagonals of a voxel for 6-connectivity intersection testing. Args: voxelpoint: Point3d, the center of the voxel. vsize: Vector3d, the dimensions (width, height, depth) of the voxel. Returns: List[Line]: A list of 4 Line objects representing the space diagonals. """ # 1. Initialize # u, v, w are half-dimensions u = vsize.x / 2.0 v = vsize.y / 2.0 w = vsize.z / 2.0 # 2. Create Vertices (8 corners) # VX indices: # 0: +u, +v, +w # 1: -u, +v, +w # 2: -u, -v, +w # 3: +u, -v, +w # 4: -u, -v, -w # 5: +u, -v, -w # 6: +u, +v, -w # 7: -u, +v, -w vx = [None] 8 vx[0] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x + u, voxelpoint.y + v, voxelpoint.z + w) vx[1] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x - u, voxelpoint.y + v, voxelpoint.z + w) vx[2] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x - u, voxelpoint.y - v, voxelpoint.z + w) vx[3] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x + u, voxelpoint.y - v, voxelpoint.z + w) vx[4] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x - u, voxelpoint.y - v, voxelpoint.z - w) vx[5] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x + u, voxelpoint.y - v, voxelpoint.z - w) vx[6] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x + u, voxelpoint.y + v, voxelpoint.z - w) vx[7] = Point3d(voxelpoint.x - u, voxelpoint.y + v, voxelpoint.z - w) # 3. Create Edges (4 space diagonals) # IT[0]: 0 -> 4 # IT[1]: 1 -> 5 # IT[2]: 2 -> 6 # IT[3]: 3 -> 7 it = [None] 4 it[0] = Line(vx[0], vx[4]) it[1] = Line(vx[1], vx[5]) it[2] = Line(vx[2], vx[6]) it[3] = Line(vx[3], vx[7]) return it Parameters: The voxel size vSize must be positive. If any dimension is zero, the voxel is degenerate, and the diagonals collapse to points or lines. Precision: Using floating-point arithmetic for u, v, w and vertex coordinates may introduce small errors. For exact intersection tests, consider using robust geometric predicates. Connectivity: This target ensures 6-connectivity. A ray intersecting any of these 4 diagonals is guaranteed to pass through the voxel in a way that respects face-adjacency constraints for the connected component. Note that 4 diagonals are sufficient to cover the "interior" connectivity paths between opposite corners, whereas the outline target uses 12 edges. Time Complexity: O(1) to construct the target for a single voxel. The number of intersection tests per voxel is 4 (one for each diagonal). Memory Complexity: O(1) per voxel (stores 4 lines, 8 points). Strengths: Minimal number of intersection lines (4) compared to the outline target (12). This reduces computational cost during the intersection phase. Limitations: Only ensures 6-connectivity. It does not provide the same level of boundary definition as the outline target. It may miss intersections that only touch the voxel faces but not the space diagonals if the ray path is tangent to the voxel interior in a specific way, although for 6-connectivity purposes, this is the intended minimal set. When to use: When 6-connectivity is sufficient and performance is critical. When not to use: When 26-connectivity is required (use 2D26intersectionTarget) or when boundary accuracy is more important than connectivity speed (use 2D6intersectionTarget outline). This method is part of the voxelization algorithms for geospatial applications, specifically designed for curve voxelization. It was introduced in the context of ensuring topological correctness (connectivity) in voxelized representations of curves and lines. The distinction between "diagonal target" and "outline target" highlights the trade-off between the number of intersection tests and the connectivity guarantee. The diagonal target is a subset of the full set of lines that could be used, optimized for 6-connectivity. Voxelization algorithms for geospatial applications, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.mex.2016.01.001, fetched 2026-10-26 Voxelization algorithms for geospatial applications, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2215016116000029, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Procedural and implicit volumes
body: Procedural and implicit volumes generate volumetric data on-the-fly using mathematical functions rather than storing discrete voxel arrays or acquiring physical scans. This family solves the problem of infinite resolution and compact storage by evaluating scalar fields f(\mathbf{x}) at query points, enabling seamless zooming, dynamic deformation, and complex boolean compositions without explicit mesh or grid storage. It differs from Voxelization and Acquisition by being analytic rather than sampled, and from Simulation output by being deterministic and stateless rather than derived from physical time-stepping. See Producing volume data for shared principles. Populates voxel data when a new spatial chunk is created or accessed, establishing a deterministic initial state (e.g., a flat platform) before higher-level features are applied. It sets itself apart by focusing on structural chunk initialization rather than surface noise variation, and from Cloud Mesh Generation by generating solid terrain blocks rather than volumetric fluid meshes. Choose it when initializing procedural worlds with discrete block-based terrain. Enhances coarse volumetric data by superimposing high-frequency details using procedural noise, creating wispy, cloud-like filaments suitable for real-time clouds, smoke, and fire. It sets itself apart by avoiding the computational cost of increasing voxel resolution or recomputing geometric gradients; instead, it warps the sampling domain or modulates optical properties at render time. It differs from Procedural Noise Functions by specifically targeting volume access coordinates or transfer function outputs rather than generating the base field itself. Choose it when adding high-frequency detail to low-resolution volumes without re-sampling. Generates continuous or discrete scalar fields from spatial coordinates to produce organic, structured, or cellular volumetric detail without storing explicit geometry. This family is distinct from Gradient-based Noise (Perlin/Simplex) and Value Noise by encompassing distance-based cellular patterns, flow-advection techniques, and specific application-driven post-processing. Choose it when generating base volumetric fields or textures on-the-fly. Represents 3D geometry as the zero-level set of a scalar field function f(\mathbf{x}), solving the problem of representing complex, smooth, or dynamic geometry without polygonal meshes. It is distinguished from polygonal representations by its continuity and from procedural noise volumes by its focus on sharp or smoothly blended boundaries rather than volumetric density gradients. Choose it for boolean blending, smooth deformation, and efficient ray marching of implicit shapes. Defines the global physical and visual configuration for volumetric cloud rendering, controlling parameters such as coverage, density, cloud type, geometry bounds, lighting angles, and noise interaction weights. It differs from its siblings by providing the input data structures and global constants rather than the algorithmic implementation of density field generation or light integration. Choose it to decouple high-level atmospheric state from low-level procedural noise generation and raymarching integration. Constructs a discrete 3D mesh representation of volumetric cloud data by identifying contiguous regions of non-zero density within a procedural voxel grid. It solves the problem of rendering large-scale, procedurally generated cloud fields efficiently by converting sparse voxel data into a compact triangle or quad mesh, rather than ray-marching the volume directly. It differs from Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation by outputting geometry (mesh) instead of a shader-based volume texture, and from Chunk Generation with Base Terrain by focusing on horizontal planar structures rather than vertical terrain topology. Choose it when converting procedural voxel clouds into renderable mesh geometry. Covers methods for generating, processing, and utilizing Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) as volumetric data for rendering and geometry representation. Unlike standard volume rendering which takes density directly, this approach derives density from the distance to the implicit surface, enabling the representation of open surfaces and varying thickness through an exponential falloff. Choose it when representing continuous 3D surfaces without explicit mesh extraction or requiring resolution-independent thickness. A procedural method for creating stylized, cartoon-like volumetric cloud densities by combining independent noise sets for macro structure, body puffs, edge details, and flow, combined with geometric envelopes for specific cloud types. It differs from realistic cloud generation by enforcing discrete density levels and specific geometric profiles (e.g., anvil shapes for cumulonimbus) to achieve a non-photorealistic aesthetic. Choose it for stylized, non-photorealistic cloud rendering. Resolution: Potentially infinite, but floating point precision limits zoom to 2^{19}, capping maximum virtual resolution at 8.4 \times 10^6 voxels. Performance: Often reaches 90 Hz, and usually stays around 60 Hz. Usage: Uses one unique brick of size 81^3. Naturally chooses N = 3 to rely on one unique instantiation for all non-empty children. Definition: A procedural density function for cloud geometry defined by the union of ellipsoids with Perlin noise perturbation, replacing meteorological simulations for test rendering. Step: Define density as the maximum of several ellipsoidal functions with different parameters to create a union of ellipsoidal clouds. Add Ken Perlin's 3D noise function to roughen and randomize the edges of the cloud density. If the resulting volume function is negative, set opacity kt = 0 (complete transparency). Formula: Ellipsoidal density function: d = a \left( \frac{(X - X0)^2}{b^2} + \frac{(Y - Y0)^2}{c^2} + \frac{(Z - Z0)^2}{c^2} \right) (Note: Source text garbled, likely standard ellipsoid equation form). Contours are ellipsoids. The specific application of procedural noise to volumetric rendering was pioneered by Kajiya and Von Herzen, and later refined by Gardner using pseudo-fractal trigonometric series for cloud surfaces. Modern implementations leverage GPU parallelism for on-the-fly evaluation, as seen in Ray-Guided Streaming techniques. [PDF] Ray-Guided Streaming for Efficient and Detailed Voxel Rendering, https://www-sop.inria.fr/reves/Basilic/2009/CNLE09/CNLE09.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Efficient Light Propagation for Multiple Anisotropic Volume Scattering, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-87825-17, fetched 2026-10-26 (book)

name: Chunk Generation with Base Terrain
head: Procedural Chunk Generation
body: Chunk Generation with Base Terrain is a method for automatically populating voxel data when a new spatial chunk is created or accessed in a procedural world. It solves the problem of empty or undefined space by establishing a deterministic initial state for each chunk, typically a flat platform at a specific Y-level, before higher-level features are applied. Inputs and Outputs Input: The 3D integer position of the chunk (Cx, Cy, Cz), derived from the world coordinate system and chunk dimensions. Output: A populated 3D voxel array representing the chunk's initial geometry. Data Structures Chunk: Contains a mesh handle and a voxel data structure. Voxel Data: A 3D array of dimensions 32 \times 32 \times 32, indexed as voxels[y][z][x]. Each element holds a voxel type (e.g., Air, Dirt). World: A map or dictionary mapping chunk positions (IVec3) to Chunk objects. Steps 1. Retrieve or Create: When a chunk at position P is requested, check if it exists in the world map. 2. Initialize: If the chunk does not exist, allocate a new 3D voxel array initialized to Air. 3. Apply Base Terrain: Determine the base geometry based on the chunk's Y-coordinate. If the chunk's Y-coordinate is 0, iterate through all x \in [0, 32) and z \in [0, 32) indices. Set voxels[0][z][x] to Dirt. For other Y-coordinates, the chunk remains empty unless extended by other methods. 4. Store: Insert the new chunk into the world map. 5. Render Distance Loop: To ensure the world is populated around the viewer, calculate the camera's current chunk position using floor division of the camera's world position by the chunk size. Iterate through a radius R around this chunk position, calling the retrieve/create function for each neighbor. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class VoxelKind: Air = 0 Dirt = 1 class Chunk: def init(self, mesh, voxels): self.mesh = mesh self.voxels = voxels def getorcreatechunk(world: dict, chunkposition: tuple[int, int, int]) -> Chunk: if chunkposition not in world: voxels = [[[VoxelKind.Air for in range(32)] for in range(32)] for in range(32)] if chunkposition[1] == 0: for z in range(32): for x in range(32): voxels[0][z][x] = VoxelKind.Dirt world[chunkposition] = Chunk(mesh=None, voxels=voxels) return world[chunkposition] def generateworldaroundcamera(world: dict, camerapos: tuple[float, float, float], chunksize: int = 32, renderradius: int = 4): camerachunkx = camerapos[0] // chunksize camerachunky = camerapos[1] // chunksize camerachunkz = camerapos[2] // chunksize for dy in range(-renderradius, renderradius + 1): for dz in range(-renderradius, renderradius + 1): for dx in range(-renderradius, renderradius + 1): neighborpos = (camerachunkx + dx, camerachunky + dy, camerachunkz + dz) getorcreatechunk(world, neighborpos) Parameters Chunk Size: Typically 32 units in world coordinates, resulting in a 32^3 voxel grid per chunk. Render Radius: The number of chunks to generate around the camera. A value of 4 is used in the reference implementation. Base Y-Level: The Y-coordinate where the base terrain is applied. Set to 0 in the reference. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Chunk position calculation must use floor division (or equivalent integer truncation towards negative infinity) to ensure consistent chunk boundaries across the world. Boundaries: The base terrain logic only applies to the specific Y-level (e.g., Y=0). Chunks at other Y-levels will be empty unless combined with vertical generation logic. Performance: Generating all chunks in the render radius every frame is inefficient. Caching and lazy loading are implied best practices, though the basic implementation regenerates or checks existence every frame. Negative Coordinates: The modulo operation for local coordinates adds the chunk size before taking the modulo again to ensure positive indices for negative world coordinates. Procedural Terrain Heightmap Generation creates voxel terrain chunks by sampling a 2D noise function to determine column heights, then filling solid blocks from a base level up to the computed height for each (x,z) position within the chunk. It solves the problem of creating deterministic, pseudo-random terrain geometry by leveraging the property that a fixed input yields the same output, allowing terrain data to be preserved across frames without change. It sets itself apart from Procedural Terrain Feature Generation by focusing on continuous height variation rather than discrete feature placement, and from Heightmap generation via circular displacements by using gradient-based noise functions rather than radial displacement patterns. Choose it when deterministic, pseudo-random terrain geometry is required without volumetric complexity. Voxel Evaluation with AABB Culling is a GPU-accelerated technique for computing Signed Distance Function (SDF) values for a chunk's voxel grid by restricting computation to voxels intersecting active SDF primitives. It solves the problem of unnecessary GPU computation for voxels far from any terrain geometry. Choose it when optimizing SDF evaluation for large, sparse voxel grids. Procedural Cave Generation creates subsurface voids in voxel terrain using subtractive particle tracing or threshold-based noise filtering. It operates as a post-processing feature layered on existing terrain data to carve organic underground structures. Choose it when adding complex, erosion-like voids to pre-generated terrain. Procedural Voxel World Generation determines the block type at a given 3D integer coordinate based on height, noise functions, and quality settings, supporting terrain, caves, trees, clouds, and emissive blocks. It differs from Procedural Terrain Heightmap Generation by assigning specific block IDs and handling volumetric features like caves and trees within the same evaluation logic. Choose it when managing diverse block types and volumetric features in a unified system. Chunk-Based Voxel Terrain Generation is a procedural method that divides a 3D world into fixed-size cubic chunks, populating each with voxel data via 3D noise sampling and biome logic. It differs from heightmap-based approaches by explicitly generating a dense 3D voxel grid per chunk before mesh extraction, allowing for overhangs and caves, while differing from raymarching methods by computing the discrete volume explicitly. This method builds on Chunk Generation with Base Terrain by defining the specific procedural noise sampling and block placement rules used within each chunk. Choose it when overhangs and volumetric terrain are required. Spiral Chunk Generation produces a queue of 3D chunk positions in a spiral pattern or vertical columns to drive procedural octree and mesh generation. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly decoupling the spatial traversal order from the chunk processing pipeline via a thread-safe queue. Choose it when progressive loading and memory management are prioritized. Simplex Noise Chunk Generation generates a voxel chunk's geometry and data using a 3D simplex noise function to determine voxel presence, allocating vertex and index buffers for rendering. It differs from heightmap-based siblings by evaluating noise in full 3D space to create volumetric terrain rather than surface-only heightmaps, and from cave generation by using a single scalar threshold for solid vs. empty space rather than complex noise blending. Choose it when volumetric noise-based terrain is needed without heightmap constraints. Procedural Object Generation constructs a basic rectangular house with a floor, roof, walls, a door on a specified side, and supporting legs extending down to solid ground. It sets itself apart by placing discrete, structured architectural primitives rather than continuous terrain surfaces. Choose it when populating worlds with man-made structures. Procedural Arch Generation is a method to generate arches by sweeping a sphere along a cubic Bézier spline, using tapering parameters to simulate greater erosion towards the middle of the arch. It sets itself apart by creating specific structural features via geometric sweeping rather than noise-based volume filling. Choose it when generating natural-looking arched structures with controlled erosion profiles. Steps 1. Define a cubic Bézier spline using four control points. 2. For each step t of the sweep, calculate the radius using tapering parameters Ti at each end of the arch. Formulas Calculate the tapering parameter Ti for each end i: Ti = r \cdot Mi \cdot (1 - Ii^{Ei}) where Mi is the radius multiplier, Ei is the exponent, and Ii is the interpolant defining where tapering occurs. Calculate the total radius: \text{radius} = r + T0 + T1 Compute the delta value D{Arch}(V, P) for voxel V and position P (voxel position after radius application): D{Arch}(V, P) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } \|P - V\| < \text{radius} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Parameters Mi: Radius multipliers for optional tapering at each end of the arch. Ei: Exponents for optional tapering at each end of the arch. Ii: Interpolants defining where the tapering occurs at each end of the arch. r: Base radius of the sphere being swept. Height Query retrieves the height of the terrain at a given world coordinate (x, z) by finding the containing chunk and querying its local height table. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping continuous world coordinates to discrete chunk-local height data. Steps 1. Calculate chunk world position: XChunkPos = floor(x / Chunk::mXSize), ZChunkPos = floor(z / Chunk::mZSize). 2. Create ChunkPosition key and check if the chunk exists in mChunks. If not, return -1. 3. Calculate local coordinates within the chunk: localX = (x % Chunk::mXSize + Chunk::mXSize) % Chunk::mXSize, localZ = (z % Chunk::mZSize + Chunk::mZSize) % Chunk::mZSize. This handles negative modulo correctly. 4. Retrieve the chunk and call chunk->GetHeight(localX, localZ). Pitfalls Negative Coordinates: The modulo operation for local coordinates adds the chunk size before taking the modulo again to ensure positive indices for negative world coordinates. Time Complexity: O(C \cdot R^3 \cdot V), where C is the number of chunks in the render radius, R is the render radius, and V is the number of voxels per chunk (32^3). The base terrain generation is O(V) per chunk. Memory Complexity: O(C \cdot V), storing the voxel data for all generated chunks. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides a deterministic, stable base for further procedural generation; low computational overhead for the base layer. Limitations: Produces flat, featureless terrain; requires additional methods for complex geometry; naive render distance loop may be inefficient for large radii. When to use: As a foundational step in voxel world generation where a flat starting plane is desired, or as a placeholder before applying more complex terrain algorithms. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Chunk Generation with Base Terrain is a fundamental technique in voxel engine development, introduced in popular weekend tutorials on building voxel engines from scratch. It serves as the entry point for procedural world generation, establishing the concept of chunk-based spatial partitioning and lazy loading. Make yourself a Voxel Engine THIS weekend, https://daymare.net/blogs/voxel-engine-in-a-weekend/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Procedural feature generation for volumetric terrains, https://doi.org/10.1145/3102163.3102216, fetched 2026-10-26 adrienlabayle/VoxelEngine, https://github.com/adrienlabayle/VoxelEngine, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Procedural Terrain Heightmap Generation
head: FBM Heightmap Chunk Generation, Procedural World Generation
body: Procedural Terrain Heightmap Generation creates a 3D voxel terrain chunk by sampling a 2D noise function to determine column heights, then filling solid blocks from a base level up to the computed height for each (x,z) position within the chunk. It sets itself apart from Procedural Terrain Feature Generation by focusing on continuous height variation rather than discrete feature placement, and from Heightmap generation via circular displacements by using gradient-based noise functions rather than radial displacement patterns. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Chunk coordinates (cx, cz), chunk dimensions (CX, CZ, CY), and noise generator state (seed, frequency, type). Output: A 3D voxel array blockdata of size [CX][CY][CZ] where each cell contains an integer material ID. Data Structures: blockdata: A 3D array of integers. The standard layout is [16][64][16] for (x, y, z). Index 0 represents air, index 1 represents solid terrain block, and higher indices represent specific materials (dirt, stone, water). noisestate: Configuration for the noise function, including seed, frequency, and noisetype (e.g., OpenSimplex2). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Data: Initialize all blockdata[x][y][z] to 0 (air). 2. Configure Noise: Create the noise state with a fixed seed and set parameters such as frequency (e.g., 0.025) and noisetype (e.g., OPENSIMPLEX2). 3. Iterate Chunk Grid: Loop through each column (x, z) within the chunk boundaries (0 \le x < CX, 0 \le z < CZ). 4. Calculate World Coordinates: Compute the world coordinates for the current column: wx = cx \cdot CX + x wz = cz \cdot CZ + z. 5. Sample Noise for Height: Sample the 2D noise function at (wx, wz) (optionally scaled by frequency). Variant (FBM): Use a Fractional Brownian Motion (FBM) function. Calculate height as: h = \lfloor \text{fbm}(wx / 80, wz / 80) \cdot 60 \rfloor + 60. Variant (Simple Noise): Sample noise, scale by a factor (e.g., 4), add an offset (e.g., 5), and cast to integer: h = \lfloor \text{noise}(wx, wz) \cdot 4 + 5 \rfloor. 6. Fill Terrain Layers: For each y from 0 to h: If y == h: Set blockdata[x][y][z] to Grass (1). If y > h - 4 (and y < h): Set blockdata[x][y][z] to Dirt (2). Otherwise: Set blockdata[x][y][z] to Stone (3). Note: The depth of the dirt layer (4 blocks) is a typical parameter. Source uses a simpler logic, filling all blocks from y=0 to h-1 with solid block (1). 7. Fill Water/Background: For y from h + 1 to a maximum height (e.g., 70 or chunk top): Set blockdata[x][y][z] to Water (4) or Air, depending on the desired sea level logic. Note: If the noise-based height h exceeds the chunk's vertical bounds, clamp or handle overflow appropriately. Parameters with Typical Values: chunkmaxsizex, chunkmaxsizez: 16. chunkmaxsizey: 64. noise.frequency: 0.025. noise.noisetype: FNLNOISEOPENSIMPLEX2. FBM Scale: 80. FBM Height Multiplier: 60. FBM Height Offset: 60. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Casting noise output to integer can cause "stepping" artifacts if the noise scale is too high relative to chunk size. Boundaries: Ensure world coordinate calculation correctly maps chunk-local indices to global space to maintain continuity between adjacent chunks. Degenerate Input: If noise returns values that result in negative heights, clamp h to 0. CORS: When using image sampling variants, local file access may fail due to CORS restrictions, requiring a fallback to mathematical generation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatechunk(cx, cz, chunksizex=16, chunksizez=16, chunksizey=64): # Initialize block data with air (0) blockdata = [[[0 for z in range(chunksizez)] for y in range(chunksizey)] for x in range(chunksizex)] # Noise parameters from seed = 12345 frequency = 0.025 noisetype = "OPENSIMPLEX2" for x in range(chunksizex): for z in range(chunksizez): # Calculate world coordinates wx = cx chunksizex + x wz = cz chunksizez + z # Sample noise for height # Using FBM variant: h = floor(fbm(wx/80, wz/80) 60) + 60 # fbm is a standard Fractional Brownian Motion function noiseval = fbm(wx / 80.0, wz / 80.0) h = int(noiseval 60) + 60 # Clamp height to chunk bounds if h >= chunksizey: h = chunksizey - 1 if h < 0: h = 0 # Fill terrain layers for y in range(h + 1): if y == h: blockdata[x][y][z] = 1 # Grass elif y > h - 4: blockdata[x][y][z] = 2 # Dirt else: blockdata[x][y][z] = 3 # Stone # Fill water below height for y in range(h + 1, chunksizey): if y <= 70: blockdata[x][y][z] = 4 # Water else: blockdata[x][y][z] = 0 # Air return blockdata def fbm(x, y): # Simplified FBM implementation return (noise(x, y) + noise(x 2, y 2) 0.5) / 1.5 def noise(x, y): # Placeholder for OpenSimplex2 or Perlin noise import math return math.sin(x 12.9898 + y 78.233) 43758.5453 % 1 2 - 1 Terrain Generation via Noise generates a 3D voxel volume from a 2D noise heightmap, extruding terrain-like structures into voxel space by filling blocks from a base level up to a calculated height. It solves the problem of creating deterministic, pseudo-random terrain landscapes suitable for voxel engines. It relies on 2D spatial noise functions (typically Perlin or gradient noise) to define surface elevation. Procedural Terrain Feature Generation is a method for creating specific volumetric structures, primarily cliffs and overhangs, by approximating their topology as a bicubic Bézier surface combined with a parabolic plateau function. It produces local delta values (additive blending) applied directly to volumetric data, allowing for nondestructive editing where parameters can be adjusted and transformations applied before surface extraction. It differs from general noise-based terrain generation by focusing on explicit geometric primitives for sharp features rather than stochastic displacement. Smooth Terrain Grid is a smoothing technique for voxel terrain that replaces flat voxel faces with interpolated planes by computing corner heights from neighboring voxel values. It generates a terrain grid with smoothed heights using interpolation between random sample points. This method generates a procedural terrain heightmap by iteratively applying overlapping circular displacement functions to a flat vertex grid. It constructs height by accumulating discrete, localized perturbations defined by random centers, radii, and signs. Terrain Skinning via Perturbation Function represents complex terrain as a simple base surface (e.g., a plane) perturbed by a scalar altitude map, eliminating the need for polygonal triangulation. Unlike voxel-based methods that require mesh extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes) or traditional heightmap rendering that suffers from LOD cracking and high depth complexity, this method uses recursive voxel subdivision and direct texture-sampling of the altitude map to modulate the base surface equation, resulting in low depth complexity and seamless rendering. This method generates macroscopic terrain by stitching together multiple pre-existing heightmaps into a single seamless composite, using simplex noise to guide the selection and blending of regions. It differs from pure procedural noise generation by leveraging real-world or high-fidelity source data, optimizing memory bandwidth by packing multiple heightmaps into a single RGB/RGBA texture for simultaneous retrieval. Far-Terrain Grid Generation produces a coarse, linear-space RGBA vertex grid and height lattice for rendering distant terrain features using analytic heightfield sampling. It differs from sibling methods like Terrain Generation via Noise by explicitly calculating local slope to drive surface color selection and hill shading, and by providing a dedicated map image generation path that includes underwater depth fading and contour banding. Not given in the sources. An algorithm to generate island heightmaps using flares, noise, erosion simulation, and slope-based coloring. A procedural terrain generation algorithm that recursively subdivides a grid, calculating new vertex heights based on the average of surrounding vertices plus a random offset. A method to dictate voxel Y-axis height and vertex colors by extracting raw pixel arrays from 2D.png files (grayscale heightmap and RGB colormap) using getImageData(). Steps: 1. Load heightmap.png and colormap.png images. 2. Extract pixel data using ctx.getImageData(0, 0, gridSize, gridSize).data. 3. Iterate x from 0 to gridSize-1 and z from 0 to gridSize-1. 4. Calculate world position: posX = (x \cdot spacing) - offset, posZ = (z \cdot spacing) - offset, where offset = (gridSize \cdot spacing) / 2. 5. Calculate pixel index: pixelIndex = (z \cdot gridSize + x) \cdot 4. 6. Calculate Y scale from heightmap: yScale = 1 + (heightData[pixelIndex] / 255.0) \cdot 100. 7. Calculate color from colormap: r = colorData[pixelIndex] / 255.0, g = colorData[pixelIndex + 1] / 255.0, b = colorData[pixelIndex + 2] / 255.0. 8. Store instance data: instancePositions[i3] = posX, instancePositions[i3+1] = yScale - 1, instancePositions[i3+2] = posZ; instanceScales[i1] = yScale; instanceColors[i3] = r, instanceColors[i3+1] = g, instanceColors[i3+2] = b. Pitfall: If local image sampling fails due to CORS restrictions, the engine falls back to a mathematical terrain generation using Math.sin and Math.cos. A terrain layer that creates escarpments by stepping into terraces of a specific height, joined by cliffs over the last portion of each step. Steps: 1. Implementation uses integer terracing in 32 bits, identical on CPU (landform::terrace) and GPU (landformterrace). 2. The riser share rides in the stack layer's kind bits. Pitfall: Boundary: A terrace moves a height by less than a step and is not Lipschitz, so each level's margin grows by two steps to contain it. Biome-specific height generation functions using 2D noise or sine/cosine waves to create distinct terrain profiles for different biomes. Formulas: Plains height: h = (1 \cdot N1(x,y) + 0.25 \cdot N2(x,y)) \cdot 8 + 15, where N1 is noise at scale 0.005 and N2 at scale 0.02. Mountain height (ridged noise): n1 = 1 - |2N1 - 1|, n2 = 1 - |2N2 - 1|, h = (n1^2 + 0.5 \cdot n2^2) \cdot 35 + 15, where N1 is noise at scale 0.008 and N2 at scale 0.02. Desert height (dunes): h = |\sin(x \cdot 0.02 + N1(x,y) \cdot 2) \cdot \cos(z \cdot 0.02)| \cdot 10 + 14, where N1 is noise at scale 0.01. Time Complexity: O(CX \cdot CZ \cdot CY) per chunk, where CX, CZ are horizontal chunk dimensions and CY is vertical height. The noise sampling is O(1) per column, making the dominant factor the voxel filling loop. Memory Complexity: O(CX \cdot CZ \cdot CY) for the voxel array. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with chunk size. Strengths: Deterministic output, simple implementation, low memory overhead for simple terrain, easy to integrate with streaming systems. Limitations: Limited to vertical extrusion (no overhangs/caves without additional logic), noise artifacts at chunk boundaries if not carefully managed, fixed layer structure. Procedural terrain generation using noise functions is a foundational technique in computer graphics and game development, popularized by games like Minecraft. The use of FBM (Fractional Brownian Motion) and simplex noise allows for efficient, infinite terrain generation with natural-looking variations. The specific implementation of layering (grass, dirt, stone) is a common heuristic to add visual variety to otherwise uniform noise-based heights. name: Terrain Generation via Noise
head: Perlin Noise Terrain Generation, Perlin Noise Heightmap Generation, Perlin Noise for Terrain, Noise Terrain, Heightmap Terrain Generation, Heightmap Terrain
body:
Terrain Generation via Noise generates a 3D voxel volume from a 2D noise heightmap, extruding terrain-like structures into voxel space by filling blocks from a base level up to a calculated height. It solves the problem of creating deterministic, pseudo-random terrain landscapes suitable for voxel engines. It relies on 2D spatial noise functions (typically Perlin or gradient noise) to define surface elevation. Inputs: Chunk dimensions: width W, height H, depth D. Chunk origin coordinates (Ox, Oz). Noise parameters: Seed, Frequency (f), Octaves (N), Lacunarity (L), Gain (G). Scaling parameters: Height Multiplier, Sea Level (S). Block type definitions (integer IDs). Outputs: A 3D array of block IDs with dimensions W 	imes H 	imes D. Data Structures: BlockType: Integer ID mapping to material (0=Grass, 1=Dirt, 2=Stone, 3=Snow, 255=Air). ChunkBuffer: 3D array of size W 	imes H 	imes D. NoiseState: Object encapsulating the permutation table and gradient vectors for the noise function. Algorithm: 1. Initialize Noise: Create a Perlin noise instance with a fixed seed to ensure deterministic output for the same coordinates. The permutation table typically contains 512 entries, where indices 0-255 are a random permutation of 0-255, repeated to allow tiling. 2. Iterate Chunk Grid: For each local coordinate (x, z) where x \in [0, W-1] and z \in [0, D-1]: a. Calculate Global Coordinates: gx = Ox + x gz = Oz + z b. Sample Noise (Fractal Brownian Motion): Compute the base height using multiple octaves of 2D noise. total
oise = 0 current\amplitude = 1.0 current requency = f For i from 0 to N-1: n = 	ext{Perlin2D}(gx \cdot current requency, gz \cdot current requency) total
oise += n \cdot current\amplitude current\amplitude = current\amplitude \cdot G current requency = current requency \cdot L c. Normalize and Scale Height: Normalize the accumulated noise to [0, 1] range: normalized = (total
oise + 1.0) \cdot 0.5 Apply non-linear shaping if required (e.g., cubic falloff): shaped = 	ext{pow}(normalized, 3) Calculate final terrain height in voxels using the standard scaling formula: h = 	ext{clamp}((shaped \cdot H \cdot 0.6 + H \cdot 0.15), 0, H - 1) (Alternative implementations use h = 	ext{RoundToInt}(shaped \cdot 	ext{HeightMultiplier} + S).) d. Apply Island Mask (Optional): If generating an island, apply a falloff based on distance from center (Cx, Cz): dist = \sqrt{(gx - Cx)^2 + (gz - Cz)^2} mask =  rac{1}{	ext{pow}(0.0025 \cdot dist, 20) + 0.0001} h = 	ext{RoundToInt}(h \cdot 	ext{clamp}(mask, 0, 1)) (Parameters vary; e.g., k=0.0025, p=20.) e. Fill Voxels: For each y from 0 to H-1: i. If y < h: Set block type based on depth layers: If y == 0: Bedrock. If y > h - 3: Dirt. Else: Stone. ii. If y == h: Determine surface type: If y > 	ext{SnowThreshold} + 	ext{Variance}: Snow. Else: Grass. iii. If y > h: Set block type to Air (ID 255). 3. Post-Processing: Apply player edits or saved block states. Generate trees or features if a tree generation pass is integrated. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. BLOCKAIR = 255 BLOCKGRASS = 0 BLOCKDIRT = 1 BLOCKSTONE = 2 BLOCKSNOW = 3 BEDROCK = 0 # Reuses grass ID for base layer in some implementations CHUNKHEIGHT = 64 SEALEVEL = 4 SNOWTHRESHOLD = 20 def generateterrainchunk(chunkoriginx, chunkoriginz, chunkwidth, chunkheight, chunkdepth, noiseseed, frequency, octaves, lacunarity, gain): # Initialize noise generator with seed # Note: PerlinNoise implementation details (permutation table, gradient interpolation) are standard noisegen = PerlinNoise(seed=noiseseed) # 3D array layout: [x][y][z] chunkdata = [[[BLOCKAIR for in range(chunkdepth)] for in range(chunkheight)] for in range(chunkwidth)] for x in range(chunkwidth): for z in range(chunkdepth): # Global coordinates gx = chunkoriginx + x gz = chunkoriginz + z # Fractal Brownian Motion totalnoise = 0.0 currentamp = 1.0 currentfreq = frequency for o in range(octaves): # Sample 2D Perlin noise (returns value in [-1, 1]) n = noisegen.noise2d(gx currentfreq, gz currentfreq) totalnoise += n currentamp currentamp = gain currentfreq = lacunarity # Normalize to [0, 1] normalized = (totalnoise + 1.0) 0.5 # Apply non-linearity (cubic falloff) shaped = pow(normalized, 3) # Calculate height using standard formula h = int(round((shaped chunkheight 0.6 + chunkheight 0.15))) # Clamp height to chunk bounds h = max(0, min(h, chunkheight - 1)) # Fill column for y in range(chunkheight): if y < h: if y == 0: block = BEDROCK elif y > h - 3: block = BLOCKDIRT else: block = BLOCKSTONE elif y == h: # Surface type if h > SNOWTHRESHOLD: block = BLOCKSNOW else: block = BLOCKGRASS else: block = BLOCKAIR chunkdata[x][y][z] = block return chunkdata Parameters & Typical Values: Seed: 123. Frequency: 0.05. Amplitude: 10.0. Octaves: 4. Lacunarity: 2.0. Gain: 0.5. Height Multiplier: 70. Sea Level: 4. Snow Threshold: 20 + variance. Edge Cases & Pitfalls: Repetition: Without a large permutation table or unique seeds per chunk, terrain may tile visibly. Variance Consistency: Using global random number generators for surface details (like snow variance) without seeding per-chunk causes identical patterns across chunks. Sharp Peaks: Non-linear functions like pow(noise, 3) can create flat plateaus or sharp peaks depending on the noise distribution. Boundary Conditions: Ensure height clamping prevents out-of-bounds memory access in the voxel array. Modifies voxel density to create a horizontal cave layer with variable height, stalactites, and Perlin noise displacement. It builds on Terrain Generation via Noise by applying a Z-axis dependent noise profile to carve a specific elevation band. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot D \cdot N) for noise sampling and O(W \cdot H \cdot D) for voxel filling, where N is octaves. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot D) for the voxel buffer. Performance: Fast for simple heightmaps; chunk-based updates triggered by camera movement optimize generation. Caching heightmaps can optimize repeated access. Strengths: Deterministic (same input yields same output), preserves terrain data across frames. Limitations: Blocky appearance without smoothing; limited geological realism. When to Use: Voxel games, Minecraft-like engines. When Not to Use: High-fidelity terrain rendering requiring smooth meshes. The method uses Perlin noise for procedural terrain generation. The permutation table contains 512 numbers (0-255 repeated) to allow tiling without recognition. Improved noise functions use quintic interpolation for smoother gradients. The method leverages the pseudo-random property to preserve terrain data across frames without change. name: Procedural Cave Height and Layer Generation
head: Cave Height and Layer Generation, Cave layer generation, FunctionMakeCaveLayer, Procedural Cave Layer Generation
body: Modifies voxel density to create a horizontal cave layer with variable height, stalactites, and Perlin noise displacement. It builds on Terrain Generation via Noise by applying a Z-axis dependent noise profile to carve a specific elevation band. Inputs: Density: Initial voxel density (float). WorldPos: 3D world position (X, Y, Z) of the voxel center. Outputs: Result: Modified density value (float, clamped to [0, 1]). Parameters: BaseCaveLevel: 7000.0f. The central Z-coordinate offset for the cave layer. BaseCaveHeight: 400.0f. Fixed vertical thickness of the cave layer. ExtraCaveHeightMultiplier: 490.0f. Amplitude for height variation noise. ExtraCaveLevelMultiplier: 1000.0f. Amplitude for Z-level displacement noise. ScaleStalactite: 0.005f. Spatial frequency for stalactite noise. ScaleGeneral: 0.001f. Spatial frequency for general cave noise. Data Structures: No persistent data structures. The method is stateless and evaluates per-voxel. Steps: 1. Initialize Result: \text{Result} = \text{Density} 2. Calculate Base Cave Height Variation: Compute a 3D Perlin noise value using scaled X and Y coordinates, ignoring Z for the base height variation: v3 = (X \cdot 0.001, Y \cdot 0.001, 0) \text{Noise3} = \text{PerlinNoise}(v3) \text{ExtraCaveHeight} = 490 \cdot \text{Noise3} \text{CaveHeight} = \max(0, 400 + \text{ExtraCaveHeight}) 3. Calculate Cave Level Displacement: Compute a 3D Perlin noise value using scaled X and Y coordinates with a fixed Z offset: v4 = (X \cdot 0.00025, Y \cdot 0.00025, 10) \text{Noise4} = \text{PerlinNoise}(v4) \text{ExtraCaveLevel} = 1000 \cdot \text{Noise4} \text{CaveLevel} = 7000 + \text{ExtraCaveLevel} 4. Calculate Cave Layer Falloff: Compute a Gaussian-like falloff based on the distance from the voxel's Z position to the calculated CaveLevel, normalized by CaveHeight: \text{CaveHeightF} = \text{CaveHeight} \cdot 160 \text{CaveLayer} = 1 - \exp\left( -\frac{(Z + \text{CaveLevel})^2}{\text{CaveHeightF}} \right) 5. Calculate Stalactite Noise: v0 = (X \cdot 0.005, Y \cdot 0.005, Z \cdot 0.0002) \text{Noise0} = \text{PerlinNoise}(v0) 6. Calculate General Noise: v1 = (X \cdot 0.001, Y \cdot 0.001, Z \cdot 0.001) \text{Noise1} = \text{PerlinNoise}(v1) 7. Blend Density in Cave Zone: If the voxel's Z coordinate is within the range [-(7000 - 1200), -(7000 + 1200)], i.e., [-8200, -5800], blend the result: \text{CaveLayerN} = 1 - \text{CaveLayer} \text{Result} = \text{Result} \cdot (\text{CaveLayer} + \text{CaveLayerN} \cdot \text{Noise0} \cdot 0.5 + \text{Noise1} \cdot 0.75) 8. Clamp Result: \text{Result} = \max(0, \min(1, \text{Result})) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def perlinnoise(x: float, y: float, z: float) -> float: """Evaluates standard 3D Perlin noise at the given coordinates.""" # Implementation depends on the chosen Perlin noise variant. # Returns a value typically in [-1, 1] or [0, 1]. pass def makecavelayer(density: float, worldpos: tuple) -> float: x, y, z = worldpos # Parameters basecavelevel = 7000.0 basecaveheight = 400.0 extraheightmult = 490.0 extralevelmult = 1000.0 # Step 2: Base Cave Height Variation v3 = (x 0.001, y 0.001, 0.0) noise3 = perlinnoise(v3) extracaveheight = extraheightmult noise3 caveheight = max(0.0, basecaveheight + extracaveheight) # Step 3: Cave Level Displacement v4 = (x 0.00025, y 0.00025, 10.0) noise4 = perlinnoise(v4) extracavelevel = extralevelmult noise4 cavelevel = basecavelevel + extracavelevel # Step 4: Cave Layer Falloff caveheightf = caveheight 160.0 # Guard against division by zero if caveheight is exactly 0 if caveheightf < 1e-6: caveheightf = 1e-6 distsq = (z + cavelevel) 2 cavelayer = 1.0 - math.exp(-distsq / caveheightf) # Step 5: Stalactite Noise v0 = (x 0.005, y 0.005, z 0.0002) noise0 = perlinnoise(v0) # Step 6: General Noise v1 = (x 0.001, y 0.001, z 0.001) noise1 = perlinnoise(v1) # Step 7: Blend Density in Cave Zone result = density # Range is [-8200, -5800] if -8200.0 <= z <= -5800.0: cavelayern = 1.0 - cavelayer result = result (cavelayer + cavelayern noise0 0.5 + noise1 0.75) # Step 8: Clamp result = max(0.0, min(1.0, result)) return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The Z-coordinates involved (around -7000 to -8200) are large. Ensure floating-point precision is sufficient for the noise sampling at these scales. Degenerate Input: If CaveHeight is 0, CaveHeightF becomes 0, leading to division by zero in the exponential term. The max(0,...) in Step 2 ensures CaveHeight is non-negative, but if it is exactly 0, the division by zero must be handled (e.g., by capping CaveHeightF to a small epsilon or skipping the blend). Generates a voxel chunk using two layers of fractal Brownian motion (fBm) noise: one for surface height and one for cave depth. It assigns materials based on vertical distance from the surface and absolute Y position. This method builds on Procedural Cave Height and Layer Generation for procedural terrain implementation. A real-time, customizable method to generate volumetric terrains with layered materials, mineral veins, underground caves, and material mixtures. It uses probabilistic generation to ensure unpredictability and allows designers to specify terrain characteristics via intuitive parameters. The process divides into three steps: read input data and index materials, generate layers/veins/caves, and construct the final volumetric data using a stacked column representation. Sharp limits between materials are avoided by generating underground layers formed with material mixtures, connecting materials with realistic progressive changes. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel. The method involves a constant number of noise evaluations (3) and basic arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is required beyond local variables. Performance: The method is computationally lightweight, suitable for real-time voxel generation. The primary cost is the Perlin noise evaluation. Limitations: The cave layer is strictly horizontal and centered around a fixed Z-coordinate band, which may not suit all terrain types. When to use: When a distinct, horizontal cave layer is desired in a voxel terrain. When not to use: When the terrain uses a different coordinate convention or requires complex, non-horizontal cave structures. Originating from the UE4VoxelTerrain project, this method is part of a procedural terrain generation pipeline. It is designed to create underground cave systems by modifying the density field based on noise-driven height and level variations. bw2012/UE4VoxelTerrain, https://github.com/bw2012/UE4VoxelTerrain, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Procedural approach to volumetric terrain generation, https://zenodo.org/records/18429902, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Terrain Chunk Generation
head: FBM Terrain Synthesis, terrainChunk
body: Generates a voxel chunk using two layers of fractal Brownian motion (fBm) noise: one for surface height and one for cave depth. It assigns materials based on vertical distance from the surface and absolute Y position. Builds on Procedural Cave Height and Layer Generation for procedural terrain implementation. Inputs: seed: number (default 1337). Deterministic seed for noise generation. size: number (default CHUNKSIZE). Dimensions of the cubic chunk (size \times size \times size). materials: number (default 4). Number of material layers. When set to 1, forces single-material output for benchmarking sensitivity. Outputs: A VoxelChunk data structure filled with material IDs. Data Structures: VoxelChunk: A 3D array or flat buffer of size size^3 storing integer material IDs. Noise Generators: Two independent fBm noise functions, surface and cave. Steps: 1. Initialize surface noise generator with seed. 2. Initialize cave noise generator with seed ^ 0x9e3779b9 (XOR with the golden ratio constant). 3. Set cave noise to 3 octaves. 4. Iterate z from 0 to size-1. 5. Iterate x from 0 to size-1. 6. Compute surface height: height = \lfloor (0.55 + surface(\frac{x}{size} \cdot 3.5, \frac{z}{size} \cdot 3.5) \cdot 0.32) \cdot size \rfloor where surface is the fBm noise function. 7. Iterate y from 0 to \min(height, size)-1. 8. Check for cave occlusion: Compute cave value: c = cave(\frac{x}{size} \cdot 5, \frac{z}{size} \cdot 5 + y \cdot 0.21). If y > 2 AND c > 0.45, skip this voxel (it is inside a cave). 9. Compute depth: depth = height - y. 10. Assign material based on materials count and depth: If materials == 1: material = 1. Else if depth \le 1: material = 1. Else if depth \le 4: material = 2. Else if y < 4: material = 4. Else: material = 3. 11. Set voxel at (x, y, z) to the assigned material. Pitfalls: Cave noise uses a different seed and 3 octaves to drill into the chunk, creating inner surfaces. The y-offset in cave sampling (y \cdot 0.21) ensures caves are not perfectly vertical columns, allowing culling tests to distinguish between outer and inner faces. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateterrainchunk(seed=1337, size=64, materials=4): # Standard 2D fBm noise using hash-based base def fbm(x, y, octaves, seed): val = 0.0 amp = 1.0 freq = 1.0 for in range(octaves): val += amp ((seed + int(x 12.9898) + int(y 78.233)) % 10000 / 10000.0 - 0.5) amp = 0.5 freq = 2.0 return val surfacenoise = lambda x, y: fbm(x, y, 3, seed) cavenoise = lambda x, y: fbm(x, y, 3, seed ^ 0x9e3779b9) class VoxelChunk: def init(self, size): self.size = size self.data = [[[0] size for in range(size)] for in range(size)] def set(self, x, y, z, val): self.data[x][y][z] = val chunk = VoxelChunk(size) for z in range(size): for x in range(size): nx, nz = x / size, z / size sval = surfacenoise(nx 3.5, nz 3.5) height = int((0.55 + sval 0.32) size) if height >= size: height = size - 1 if height < 0: height = 0 for y in range(min(height, size)): if y > 2: cval = cavenoise(nx 5, nz 5 + y 0.21) if cval > 0.45: continue depth = height - y if materials == 1: mat = 1 elif depth <= 1: mat = 1 elif depth <= 4: mat = 2 elif y < 4: mat = 4 else: mat = 3 chunk.set(x, y, z, mat) return chunk Not given in the sources. name: Terrain Chunk Voxel Generation
head: Perlin Noise Heightmap Generation, Voxel Chunk Generation
body: Terrain Chunk Voxel Generation populates a 3D voxel grid with solid or air blocks based on a 2D Perlin noise heightmap. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly handling both surface terrain (for y \ge 0) and subsurface layers (for y < 0) within the same chunk generation pass, whereas alternatives like Procedural Cave Height and Layer Generation focus on internal void structures rather than surface elevation. Inputs and Outputs Input: Chunk position (Cx, Cy, Cz) in chunk coordinates; chunk dimensions WIDTH (x/z) and HEIGHT (y); noise parameters (frequency, octaves, dilation, big number); colorist/texture map for subsurface layers. Output: A 3D array voxels[WIDTH][HEIGHT][WIDTH] where each cell contains a Voxel type (e.g., Solid or Air) and associated data (color, density). Data Structures voxels: 3D array of size WIDTH \times HEIGHT \times WIDTH. Voxel: Struct containing type enum (Solid, Air), position, and metadata (e.g., color). dilation: Vector3 (dx, dy, dz) scaling noise coordinates and height. BIGNUMBER: Constant offset for noise domain shifting. Parameters WIDTH: Chunk width in blocks (e.g., 16, 32). HEIGHT: Chunk height in blocks (e.g., 64, 128). m\frequency: Noise frequency constant, typically 0.01. nbOctaves: Number of noise octaves, typically 3. dilation: Scaling factors for noise (x, z) and height (y). BIG\NUMBER: Constant added to noise coordinates to shift sampling domain. Steps 1. Iterate Chunk Coordinates: Loop over local chunk coordinates i (x-axis) and k (z-axis) from 0 to WIDTH-1. 2. Calculate World Coordinates: Compute world coordinates for the current column: x = Cx \cdot WIDTH + i z = Cz \cdot WIDTH + k 3. Determine Surface Height: Calculate the surface height y{surf} using the Perlin noise function: y{surf} = \lfloor dy \cdot \frac{Perlin2D(x \cdot dx + BIG\NUMBER, z \cdot dz + BIG\NUMBER) + 1}{2} \rfloor + 1 Where Perlin2D returns a value in [-1, 1]. 4. Fill Surface Terrain (y \ge 0): If the chunk's vertical position Cy \ge 0 and is within the surface range: For each vertical level j from 0 to HEIGHT-1: If j \le y{surf}, set voxels[i][j][k] to Solid with color from colorist. Else, set voxels[i][j][k] to Air. 5. Fill Subsurface Terrain (y < 0): If the chunk's vertical position Cy < 0: Iterate over all i (x), j (y), and k (z) within the chunk. Compute world coordinates: xw = Cx \cdot WIDTH + i, yw = Cy \cdot HEIGHT + j, zw = Cz \cdot WIDTH + k. Set voxels[i][j][k] to the result of getGroundAt(voxels.cubicsize(), xw, yw, zw). This function likely uses noise to determine subsurface material type. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateterrainchunk(chunkpos, width, height, dilation, bignumber, frequency, octaves, colorist): """ Generates a voxel chunk based on Perlin noise heightmap. Time Complexity: O(WIDTH^2 \cdot HEIGHT) per chunk, as every voxel is visited and potentially computed. Memory Complexity: O(WIDTH^2 \cdot HEIGHT) to store the voxel grid. Performance: Performance is dominated by noise generation and voxel assignment. Efficient noise implementations (e.g., using precomputed gradients) are critical. name: Procedural Terrain Feature Generation
head: Overhang Generation
body: Procedural Terrain Feature Generation is a method for creating specific volumetric structures, primarily cliffs and overhangs, by approximating their topology as a bicubic Bézier surface combined with a parabolic plateau function. It produces local delta values (additive blending) applied directly to volumetric data, allowing for nondestructive editing where parameters can be adjusted and transformations applied before surface extraction. It differs from general noise-based terrain generation by focusing on explicit geometric primitives for sharp features rather than stochastic displacement. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Fdim: User-defined dimensions in voxels for the feature's bounding box. G: A 4x4 geometry matrix of vectors containing the control points of the surface; the second and third rows act as erosion parameters. k: User-defined exponent for the parabolic function to emulate realistic plateaus. Vindex: The unit cube coordinates of the current voxel within the feature's bounding box. Optional transformation matrix (translation and rotation) applied to the feature before voxel submission. Outputs: DCliff(u, v): A delta value (0 or 1) for the voxel, representing the presence of the feature. Data Structures: Geometry Matrix G: A 4x4 matrix of vectors containing the control points of the surface. The second and third rows act as erosion parameters. Bézier Basis Matrix B: A constant 4x4 matrix defined as: B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -6 & 3 & 0 \\ -1 & 3 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} Steps: 1. Calculate Voxel Index: Compute the normalized voxel index I within the feature's bounding box using the unit cube coordinates Vindex and feature dimensions Fdim: I = \frac{Vindex}{Fdim} 2. Compute Parameters: Derive parameters u and v from the normalized index I: u = Iz v = 1 - Iy 3. Compute Bézier Surface: Calculate the surface value S(u, v) using the Bézier basis matrix B, the geometry matrix G, and the parameter vectors U and V: U = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & u & u^2 & u^3 \end{bmatrix} V = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & v & v^2 & v^3 \end{bmatrix} S(u, v) = U \cdot B \cdot G \cdot B^T \cdot V^T 4. Compute Parabolic Function: Calculate the plateau function P(u) using the exponent k: P(u) = (4u \cdot (1-u))^k 5. Compute Delta Value: Determine the final delta value DCliff(u, v) for the voxel based on the x-component of the normalized index Ix: D{Cliff}(u, v) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } Ix < \min(S(u, v), P(u)) \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateclifffeature(Vindex, Fdim, G, k): # Step 1: Calculate normalized index I (component-wise division) Ix = Vindex[0] / Fdim[0] Iy = Vindex[1] / Fdim[1] Iz = Vindex[2] / Fdim[2] # Step 2: Compute parameters u and v u = Iz v = 1.0 - Iy # Step 3: Compute Bézier Surface S(u, v) B = [ [1, 0, 0, 0], [-3, 3, 0, 0], [3, -6, 3, 0], [-1, 3, -3, 1] ] U = [1.0, u, u2, u3] V = [1.0, v, v2, v3] # Matrix multiplication: S(u,v) = U B G B^T V^T # Temp1 = U B (1x4) Temp1 = [0.0] 4 for j in range(4): for idx in range(4): Temp1[j] += U[idx] B[idx][j] # Temp2 = Temp1 G (1x4) Temp2 = [0.0] 4 for j in range(4): for idx in range(4): Temp2[j] += Temp1[idx] G[idx][j] # B^T V^T (4x1) BTV = [0.0] 4 for i in range(4): for idx in range(4): BTV[i] += B[idx][i] V[idx] # Suv = Temp2 BTV (scalar) Suv = 0.0 for idx in range(4): Suv += Temp2[idx] BTV[idx] # Step 4: Compute Parabolic Function P(u) Pu = (4.0 u (1.0 - u)) k # Step 5: Compute Delta Value minval = Suv if Suv < Pu else Pu return 1 if Ix < minval else 0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. name: Smooth Terrain Grid
body: Smooth Terrain Grid is a smoothing technique for voxel terrain that replaces flat voxel faces with interpolated planes by computing corner heights from neighboring voxel values. It generates a terrain grid with smoothed heights using interpolation between random sample points. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A 2D grid of voxel height or volume values. Outputs: A terrain grid storing computed vertex heights and mesh geometry. Data Structures Voxel Grid: A 2D array storing height or volume values for each voxel cell. Vertex Grid: A 2D array storing the computed height Y for each grid corner (x, z). Algorithm Two distinct algorithmic approaches are documented in the sources: a deterministic corner-averaging method and a stochastic interpolation method. 1. Deterministic Corner Averaging: For each voxel corner, sum the height or volume values of the four adjacent voxels surrounding that corner, then divide the sum by four to compute the final corner height. Use the computed corner heights to tilt the terrain geometry, then apply the center voxel value to elevate or lower the surface, creating non-flat shapes. 2. Stochastic Interpolation with Interval: Validate the interval parameter; if interval \le 0 or odd, set interval = 2. Generate sample vertices at indices where (iZ % interval == 0 && iX % interval == 0) || (iZ % interval == interval/2 && iX % interval == interval/2). Assign a random height to each sample vertex. Generate in-between vertices by averaging heights of existing neighbors (Left, Right, Up, Down). For same-parity vertices (both even or both odd), split quad with diagonal from top-left to bottom-right. For opposite-parity vertices, split quad with diagonal from top-right to bottom-left. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def computecornerheights(voxelgrid, width, height): """Method 1: Deterministic corner averaging """ # Vertex grid is (height+1) x (width+1) to store corners cornergrid = [[0.0] (width + 1) for in range(height + 1)] for z in range(height + 1): for x in range(width + 1): # Sum four adjacent voxels surrounding corner (x, z) h1 = voxelgrid[z-1][x-1] if z > 0 and x > 0 else 0.0 h2 = voxelgrid[z-1][x] if z > 0 else 0.0 h3 = voxelgrid[z][x-1] if x > 0 else 0.0 h4 = voxelgrid[z][x] cornergrid[z][x] = (h1 + h2 + h3 + h4) / 4.0 return cornergrid def generatestochasticgrid(gridwidth, gridheight, interval): """Method 2: Stochastic interpolation with interval """ if interval <= 0 or interval % 2 != 0: interval = 2 vertexgrid = [[None] gridwidth for in range(gridheight)] # Generate sample vertices for z in range(gridheight): for x in range(gridwidth): if (z % interval == 0 and x % interval == 0) or \ (z % interval == interval // 2 and x % interval == interval // 2): vertexgrid[z][x] = random.random() # Interpolate in-between vertices by averaging existing neighbors for z in range(gridheight): for x in range(gridwidth): if vertexgrid[z][x] is None: neighbors = [] if x > 0 and vertexgrid[z][x-1] is not None: neighbors.append(vertexgrid[z][x-1]) if x < gridwidth - 1 and vertexgrid[z][x+1] is not None: neighbors.append(vertexgrid[z][x+1]) if z > 0 and vertexgrid[z-1][x] is not None: neighbors.append(vertexgrid[z-1][x]) if z < gridheight - 1 and vertexgrid[z+1][x] is not None: neighbors.append(vertexgrid[z+1][x]) vertexgrid[z][x] = sum(neighbors) / len(neighbors) if neighbors else 0.0 return vertexgrid, interval def splitquads(vertexgrid): """Quad splitting logic based on vertex parity """ triangles = [] for z in range(len(vertexgrid) - 1): for x in range(len(vertexgrid[0]) - 1): # Check parity of grid coordinates (both even or both odd) sameparity = (x % 2) == (z % 2) if sameparity: # Top-left to bottom-right diagonal triangles.append(((z, x), (z, x+1), (z+1, x+1))) triangles.append(((z, x), (z+1, x+1), (z+1, x))) else: # Top-right to bottom-left diagonal triangles.append(((z, x), (z, x+1), (z+1, x))) triangles.append(((z, x+1), (z+1, x+1), (z+1, x))) return triangles Parameters interval: Spacing between random sample points; must be even and positive. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Conditions: Corners on the grid boundary lack four surrounding voxels for Method 1, and sample points near boundaries may lack neighbors for averaging in Method 2. These require clamping, mirroring, or edge-specific handling. Precision: Floating-point precision may cause artifacts in large terrains, and integer heights may limit smoothness. Degenerate Input: Empty or uniform height grids may result in flat or invalid meshes if not handled. Not given in the sources. The deterministic corner-averaging approach was discussed in the context of voxel DDA raymarching. The stochastic interpolation approach with interval-based sampling was implemented in the "bad-minecraft" project. name: Heightmap generation via circular displacements
body: This method generates a procedural terrain heightmap by iteratively applying overlapping circular displacement functions to a flat vertex grid. It constructs height by accumulating discrete, localized perturbations defined by random centers, radii, and signs. Inputs: Grid dimensions MAPSIZE and MAPNUMVERTICES, displacement parameters MAXCIRCLESIZE, MAXDISPLACEMENT, DISPLACEMENTSIGNLIMIT, MAXITER, NUMITERATATIME, and a random number generator. Outputs: A vertex grid mapvertices and a list of triangle indices. The vertex buffer uses a layout mapvertices[component][vertexindex] where component 0 stores the x-coordinate, component 1 stores the y-coordinate (height), and component 2 stores the z-coordinate. The total number of vertices is MAPNUMTOTALVERTICES = MAPNUMVERTICES MAPNUMVERTICES. Typical values from the reference implementation are MAPSIZE = 10.0f, MAPNUMVERTICES = 80, MAXCIRCLESIZE = 5.0f, MAXDISPLACEMENT = 1.0f, DISPLACEMENTSIGNLIMIT = 0.3f, MAXITER = 200, and NUMITERATATIME = 1. 1. Initialize Grid: Create a flat grid of MAPNUMTOTALVERTICES vertices with x and z coordinates spaced by MAPSIZE / (MAPNUMVERTICES - 1), and y = 0.0f. 2. Generate Indices: Generate line indices for a grid fan: close top edge, close right edge, then for each cell (i, j) with ref = i MAPNUMVERTICES + j, add indices for (ref, ref+1), (ref, ref+MAPNUMVERTICES), (ref, ref+MAPNUMVERTICES+1). 3. Iterative Displacement: Repeat MAXITER times: a. Generate random circle parameters: centerx and centerz uniformly in [0, MAPSIZE], circlesize in [0, MAXCIRCLESIZE], sign = -1.0f if rand()/RANDMAX < DISPLACEMENTSIGNLIMIT else 1.0f, disp = sign (MAXDISPLACEMENT rand()/RANDMAX). b. For each vertex ii, compute dx = centerx - mapvertices[0][ii] and dz = centerz - mapvertices[2][ii]. c. Compute pd = (2.0f sqrt(dxdx + dzdz)) / circlesize. d. If fabs(pd) <= 1.0f, compute newheight = disp + cos(pd 3.14f) disp, and update mapvertices[1][ii] += newheight. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def generateheightmap(mapsize, mapnumvertices, maxcirclesize, maxdisplacement, displacementsignlimit, maxiter): numvertices = mapnumvertices mapnumvertices spacing = mapsize / (mapnumvertices - 1) # mapvertices layout: [component][vertexindex] verticesx = [0.0] numvertices verticesy = [0.0] numvertices verticesz = [0.0] numvertices for i in range(mapnumvertices): for j in range(mapnumvertices): idx = i mapnumvertices + j verticesx[idx] = j spacing verticesz[idx] = i spacing verticesy[idx] = 0.0 indices = [] # "close top edge, close right edge" is not specified in the sources for i in range(mapnumvertices - 1): for j in range(mapnumvertices - 1): ref = i mapnumvertices + j indices.append(ref) indices.append(ref + 1) indices.append(ref + mapnumvertices) indices.append(ref) indices.append(ref + mapnumvertices) indices.append(ref + mapnumvertices + 1) for in range(maxiter): centerx = random.uniform(0, mapsize) centerz = random.uniform(0, mapsize) circlesize = random.uniform(0, maxcirclesize) if circlesize == 0: continue randval = random.random() sign = -1.0 if randval < displacementsignlimit else 1.0 disp = sign (maxdisplacement random.random()) for ii in range(numvertices): dx = centerx - verticesx[ii] dz = centerz - verticesz[ii] pd = (2.0 math.sqrt(dx dx + dz dz)) / circlesize if abs(pd) <= 1.0: newheight = disp + math.cos(pd math.pi) disp verticesy[ii] += newheight return verticesx, verticesy, verticesz, indices A zero circlesize causes division by zero in the pd calculation; the implementation must skip such iterations. Not given in the sources for other edge cases. Time complexity is O(MAX\ITER \cdot MAP\NUM\TOTAL\VERTICES). Memory complexity is O(MAP\NUM\TOTAL\VERTICES) for vertex storage and indices.
