name: Procedural Object Generation
head: PlaceHouseBasic
body: Constructs a basic rectangular house with a floor, roof, walls, a door on a specified side, and supporting legs extending down to solid ground. Inputs: cornerX, cornerY, cornerZ: Integer coordinates of the house's front-left corner. length: Integer width of the house along the X-axis. width: Integer depth of the house along the Z-axis. height: Integer height of the house walls. doorSide: Integer 0-3 indicating the wall side for the door. floorID, roofID, wallID: Integer block types for respective components. GetBlockData(x, y, z): Function returning the block ID at coordinates. SetBlockData(x, y, z, id): Function setting the block ID at coordinates. Data Structures: The volume is a 3D grid of block IDs. Block ID 0 represents air. Block ID 4 represents liquid. Block ID 6 represents wood, used for legs. Steps: 1. Clear Volume: Set pad = 2. Call SetRectVolume(cornerX - pad, cornerX + length + pad - 1, cornerY, cornerY + height + pad, cornerZ - pad, cornerZ + width + pad - 1, 0) to clear the target bounding box. 2. Place Floor: Loop x from cornerX - pad to cornerX + length + pad (exclusive) and z from cornerZ - pad to cornerZ + width + pad (exclusive). Set block at (x, cornerY, z) to floorID. 3. Place Roof: Loop x from cornerX to cornerX + length (exclusive) and z from cornerZ to cornerZ + width (exclusive). Set block at (x, cornerY + height - 1, z) to roofID. 4. Place X-Side Walls: Loop y from cornerY + 1 to cornerY + height - 1 (exclusive) and x from cornerX to cornerX + length (exclusive). Set blocks at (x, y, cornerZ) and (x, y, cornerZ + width - 1) to wallID. 5. Place Z-Side Walls: Loop y from cornerY + 1 to cornerY + height - 1 (exclusive) and z from cornerZ to cornerZ + width (exclusive). Set blocks at (cornerX, y, z) and (cornerX + length - 1, y, z) to wallID. 6. Carve Door: Based on doorSide (0-3), set specific blocks to 0 (air) to create a 2×3 opening (width 2, height 3) on the respective wall side, centered horizontally. 7. Place Legs: For each of the four corners (adjusted by pad), start at y = cornerY - 1. While y > 0 and the block below is air (0) or liquid (4), set block at (x, y, z) to 6 (wood) and decrement y. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def PlaceHouseBasic(cornerX, cornerY, cornerZ, length, width, height, doorSide, floorID, roofID, wallID, GetBlockData, SetBlockData): pad = 2 # 1. Clear volume for x in range(cornerX - pad, cornerX + length + pad): for y in range(cornerY, cornerY + height + pad): for z in range(cornerZ - pad, cornerZ + width + pad): SetBlockData(x, y, z, 0) # 2. Place floor for x in range(cornerX - pad, cornerX + length + pad): for z in range(cornerZ - pad, cornerZ + width + pad): SetBlockData(x, cornerY, z, floorID) # 3. Place roof for x in range(cornerX, cornerX + length): for z in range(cornerZ, cornerZ + width): SetBlockData(x, cornerY + height - 1, z, roofID) # 4. Place x-side walls for y in range(cornerY + 1, cornerY + height - 1): for x in range(cornerX, cornerX + length): SetBlockData(x, y, cornerZ, wallID) SetBlockData(x, y, cornerZ + width - 1, wallID) # 5. Place z-side walls for y in range(cornerY + 1, cornerY + height - 1): for z in range(cornerZ, cornerZ + width): SetBlockData(cornerX, y, z, wallID) SetBlockData(cornerX + length - 1, y, z, wallID) # 6. Carve door (2x3 opening, centered horizontally) # doorSide: 0=-Z, 1=+X, 2=+Z, 3=-X if doorSide == 0: # -Z wall xstart = cornerX + (length // 2) - 1 for x in range(xstart, xstart + 2): for y in range(cornerY + 1, cornerY + 4): SetBlockData(x, y, cornerZ, 0) elif doorSide == 1: # +X wall zstart = cornerZ + (width // 2) - 1 for z in range(zstart, zstart + 2): for y in range(cornerY + 1, cornerY + 4): SetBlockData(cornerX + length - 1, y, z, 0) elif doorSide == 2: # +Z wall xstart = cornerX + (length // 2) - 1 for x in range(xstart, xstart + 2): for y in range(cornerY + 1, cornerY + 4): SetBlockData(x, y, cornerZ + width - 1, 0) elif doorSide == 3: # -X wall zstart = cornerZ + (width // 2) - 1 for z in range(zstart, zstart + 2): for y in range(cornerY + 1, cornerY + 4): SetBlockData(cornerX, y, z, 0) # 7. Place legs corners = [ (cornerX - pad, cornerZ - pad), (cornerX + length + pad - 1, cornerZ - pad), (cornerX - pad, cornerZ + width + pad - 1), (cornerX + length + pad - 1, cornerZ + width + pad - 1) ] for (x, z) in corners: y = cornerY - 1 while y > 0: blockbelow = GetBlockData(x, y - 1, z) if blockbelow == 0 or blockbelow == 4: SetBlockData(x, y, z, 6) y -= 1 else: break Parameters: pad = 2: Padding around the house footprint for floor and leg placement. doorSide: 0-3, mapping to specific walls. Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. mayakeele/bad-minecraft, https://github.com/mayakeele/bad-minecraft, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Terrain Generation via Layered Limits
head: Layered Limits Terrain Generation, Terrain to Volume Conversion
body: Volumetric Terrain Generation via Layered Limits is a procedural method that converts a terrain composed of stacked layers, veins, and caves into a volume representation by defining mixed areas between layers to remove sharp frontiers. It represents data as columns subdivided into chunks, where each column consists of stacked material limits that define volume properties at specific heights. This method sets itself apart from sibling methods like Procedural Terrain Heightmap Generation by storing full volumetric material composition and flow vectors rather than just surface height, and from Chunk Generation with Base Terrain by using a limit-based interpolation system that dynamically generates voxels based on proximity to layer boundaries rather than fixed grid assignments. Inputs: Configuration File: Contains three sections: 1. Material Data: For each material: Name, Id (unique integer), Color (RGB), Textures (path), Special Parameters (Void, Base, Alone, Vein, Cave), Cave/vein thickness (absolute value conversion). 2. Affinity Data: A matrix or list of pairs defining compatibility between materials. Values are on a 0-1 scale for compatible materials, -1 for incompatible, and 0.0 for materials not prone to mix but blendable by other reasons. 3. Global Parameters: Terrain depth, Layer thickness (absolute value conversion), Cave and vein area (bounding square size limits), Scale (frequency for Perlin noise). Chunk Dimensions: Defined by N \times L columns, where each column represents M voxels. Outputs: Volumetric Data: A dynamic voxel grid where each voxel contains: Material Composition: A list of materials with associated concentrations (summing to 1). Material Flow: A 3D vector representing internal material flow. Limit Structure: A set of limits stored per column, defining the height and properties of material transitions. Limit: A structure representing a transition boundary between materials at a specific height within a column. height: Float. The vertical position of the limit. materials: List of Material IDs. concentrations: List of Floats. Corresponding concentrations for each material in the list. Sum must be 1. flow: Vector3. The material flow vector tangent to the layer surface. properties: Dictionary/Struct containing derived properties: thickness, similarity, blendvalue, roughness. Column: A vertical stack of limits within a chunk. limits: List of Limit objects. Minimum 2 limits (top and bottom). Maximum M limits (one per voxel height step, though typically fewer). Chunk: griddimensions: N \times L (number of columns). columns: Array of Column objects. VeinArea: Global parameter defining the maximum side length of the vein bounding square. CaveArea: Global parameter defining the maximum side length of the cave bounding square (used instead of VeinArea). SmoothConstant: Taken from material roughness parameter. Controls roughness loss in fractal generation. d0: Constant for max displacement at depth 0, taken from material roughness parameter. Recursive Depth Limit: 5 (for time performance). Main Material Concentration Range: [0.5, 0.9]. Subdivide the chunk into an N \times L regular grid of columns. Each column represents M voxels vertically. For each column, generate stacked layers from bottom to top. 2.1 Material Selection 1. Identify materials from the last generated layer. 2. Filter out materials with affinity -1 to any material in the last layer. 3. Calculate Global Affinity Ai for each possible material i: Ai = \sum{j=1}^{N} (a{ij} \cdot cj) Where: N is the number of materials in the last layer. a{ij} is the affinity between possible material i and material j of the last layer. cj is the concentration of material j in the last layer. 4. Calculate Probability Pi for each material i: Pi = \frac{Ai}{\sum{j=1}^{N} Aj} Select the next layer's materials based on these probabilities. 2.2 Concentration Assignment 1. Ensure the sum of concentrations in the layer is 1. 2. If the layer has \ge 2 materials, assign the main material a random concentration in [0.5, 0.9]. 3. Assign random concentrations to remaining materials, normalizing so the total sum is 1. 2.3 Property Calculation Calculate layer properties (V) using the weighted sum of material properties (vi) and concentrations (ci): V = \sum{i=1}^{N} (vi \cdot ci) Where V is the property value (e.g., thickness, similarity, roughness), N is the number of materials, vi is the property value of material i, and ci is its concentration. 2.4 Height Calculation 1. Calculate modified height h: h = h{-1} \cdot s + n \cdot (1 - s) Where: h{-1} is the height of the last layer at the same point. s is the similarity calculated in step 2.3. n is the Perlin noise value (scaled by the global Scale parameter). 2. Calculate final height: Add the layer's thickness and the average height of the previous layer to h. 2.5 Flow Generation Generate underground material flow tangent to the layer surface. Rotate the flow vector on the Y-axis based on horizontal 2D Perlin noise. 2.6 Limit Creation Create a Limit object for the column with the calculated height, materials, concentrations, flow, and properties. Repeat until the terrain depth is reached or the maximum number of limits (M) is exceeded. Veins are generated independently of layers but within the column structure. 3.1 Initialization 1. The location is chosen completely at random, constrained only by the terrain plot boundaries. 2. Determine starting bounding square side length: Random value between VeinArea/2 and VeinArea. 3.2 Material Selection 1. Select materials with the Vein special parameter. 2. Select only materials from the last layer located under the vein's region. 3. Select the main material among those with the Vein parameter. 3.3 Property Calculation Calculate relative area, roughness, and relative thickness using the same process as Layer Generation (Steps 2.2-2.3). 3.4 Shape Generation (Fractal) 1. Calculate final bounding square: Multiply relative area by the base bounding square. 2. Generate relative shape using midpoint displacement: Locate a square in 2D space. Displace vertices (P1, P2, P3, P4) along diagonals. Take a random point P0 from a segment. Displace P0 along the line formed by P0 and the square center. Recursively repeat for all segments. Max displacement at depth i: di = \frac{d{i-1} / \text{SmoothConstant}}{2} Where d0 is a constant, and d{i-1} is the max displacement at depth i-1. Minimum displacement is -di. Recursive depth limited to 5. 3.5 Height Calculation 1. Calculate normalized minimum distance d{xy} from each point [x,y] to the fractal border (range 0-1). 2. Calculate height h{xy}: h{xy} = \left| 1 - (d{xy} - 1)^2 \right| This simplifies a unit radius circumference centered at [1,0]. 3. Final vein height: Multiply h{xy} by relative thickness and global thickness, then add the height of the last layer. 3.6 Flow Generation Generate flow using the same process as Layer Generation (Step 2.5). 3.7 Limit Creation Create Limit objects for the vein within the affected columns. Follows Vein Generation steps with exceptions: 1. Use CaveArea instead of VeinArea for bounding square size. 2. Select only one material from the set with the Cave special parameter. 3. Extract its properties to adjust the bounding square dimensions. 4. Cave shape and height are generated using the same fractal midpoint displacement and distance-to-border methods as veins. Convert the limit-based representation to voxels. 5.1 Dynamic Voxel Generation For each voxel at chunk, column, and height H: 1. Check if H matches the height of any limit in the column. 2. If yes, use the limit's data directly. 3. If no, interpolate between the surrounding limits (e.g., the limit immediately below and the one immediately above). 5.2 Blending 1. Multiply the thickness of each layer by its blend value. 2. The result is the height where the transition with the last layer ends. 3. This process removes sharp frontiers, mixing materials and flow for a realistic appearance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random class Vector2: def init(self, x, y): self.x = x self.y = y def add(self, other): return Vector2(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y) def sub(self, other): return Vector2(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y) def mul(self, s): return Vector2(self.x s, self.y s) def truediv(self, s): return Vector2(self.x / s, self.y / s) def length(self): return math.sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2) def normalize(self): l = self.length() return Vector2(self.x / l, self.y / l) if l > 0 else Vector2(0, 0) class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def add(self, other): return Vector3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def mul(self, s): return Vector3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def length(self): return math.sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2) def normalize(self): l = self.length() return Vector3(self.x / l, self.y / l, self.z / l) if l > 0 else Vector3(0, 0, 0) class Material: def init(self, name, id, color, textures, specialparams, roughness, similarity, thickness): self.name = name self.id = id self.color = color self.textures = textures self.specialparams = specialparams self.roughness = roughness self.similarity = similarity self.thickness = thickness class Limit: def init(self, height, materials, concentrations, flow, properties): self.height = height self.materials = materials self.concentrations = concentrations self.flow = flow self.properties = properties class Column: def init(self): self.limits = [] def perlinnoise(x, y, scale): # Standard deterministic 2D noise approximation return math.sin(x scale) math.cos(y scale) def assignconcentrations(materials): if len(materials) == 1: return [1.0] mainconc = random.uniform(0.5, 0.9) remaining = 1.0 - mainconc concentrations = [mainconc] for in range(len(materials) - 2): conc = random.uniform(0, remaining) concentrations.append(conc) remaining -= conc concentrations.append(remaining) total = sum(concentrations) return [c / total for c in concentrations] def calculateproperties(materials, concentrations): roughness = sum(m.roughness c for m, c in zip(materials, concentrations)) similarity = sum(m.similarity c for m, c in zip(materials, concentrations)) thickness = sum(m.thickness c for m, c in zip(materials, concentrations)) blendvalue = similarity return {'roughness': roughness, 'similarity': similarity, 'thickness': thickness, 'blendvalue': blendvalue} def generateflow(x, y, z, scale): noisex = perlinnoise(x, y, scale) noisey = perlinnoise(x + 100, y, scale) return Vector3(noisex, 0, noisey).normalize() def generatefractalshape(sidelength, roughness, maxdepth=5): d0 = roughness smoothconstant = roughness points = [Vector2(0, 0), Vector2(sidelength, 0), Vector2(sidelength, sidelength), Vector2(0, sidelength)] center = Vector2(sidelength / 2, sidelength / 2) def displacerecursive(segments, depth): if depth > maxdepth: return [] newsegments = [] for p1, p2 in segments: mid = (p1 + p2) 0.5 maxdisp = d0 for in range(depth): maxdisp = (maxdisp / smoothconstant) / 2.0 disp = random.uniform(-maxdisp, maxdisp) direction = (center - mid).normalize() newpoint = mid + direction disp newsegments.append((p1, newpoint)) newsegments.append((newpoint, p2)) return newsegments + displacerecursive(newsegments, depth + 1) initialsegments = [(points[i], points[(i + 1) % 4]) for i in range(4)] return displacerecursive(initialsegments, 0) def selectmaterials(possiblematerials, lastlayermaterials, lastlayerconcentrations, affinities): affinitieslist = [] for mat in possiblematerials: ai = 0 for i, lastmatid in enumerate(lastlayermaterials): aij = affinities.get((mat.id, lastmatid), 0) cj = lastlayerconcentrations[i] ai += aij cj affinitieslist.append(ai) sumaffinities = sum(affinitieslist) if sumaffinities == 0: return [], [] probabilities = [a / sumaffinities for a in affinitieslist] # Select materials based on probability selectedindices = sorted(range(len(probabilities)), key=lambda k: probabilities[k], reverse=True) selectedmats = [possiblematerials[i] for i in selectedindices] selectedprobs = [probabilities[i] for i in selectedindices] return selectedmats, selectedprobs def generateterrain(chunkn, chunkl, chunkm, config): columns = [[Column() for in range(chunkl)] for in range(chunkn)] basematerials = [m for m in config['materials'] if 'Base' in m.specialparams] for col in columns: for c in col: c.limits.append(Limit(0, basematerials, [1.0], Vector3(0, 0, 0), {'thickness': 0, 'similarity': 0, 'roughness': 0})) for colidx in range(chunkn): for rowidx in range(chunkl): col = columns[colidx][rowidx] while col.limits[-1].height < config['globalparams']['terraindepth'] and len(col.limits) < chunkm: possible = [m for m in config['materials'] if 'Base' not in m.specialparams] lastmats = col.limits[-1].materials lastconcs = col.limits[-1].concentrations compatible = [m for m in possible if all(config['affinities'].get((m.id, lm.id), -1) != -1 for lm in lastmats)] if not compatible: break selectedmats, = selectmaterials(compatible, lastmats, lastconcs, config['affinities']) if not selectedmats: break concentrations = assignconcentrations(selectedmats) properties = calculateproperties(selectedmats, concentrations) n = perlinnoise(colidx, rowidx, config['globalparams']['scale']) hminus1 = col.limits[-1].height hmodified = hminus1 properties['similarity'] + n (1 - properties['similarity']) avgprev = sum(l.height for l in col.limits) / len(col.limits) finalheight = hmodified + properties['thickness'] + avgprev flow = generateflow(colidx, rowidx, finalheight, config['globalparams']['scale']) col.limits.append(Limit(finalheight, selectedmats, concentrations, flow, properties)) for colidx in range(chunkn): for rowidx in range(chunkl): col = columns[colidx][rowidx] if random.random() < 0.1: generateveinorcave(col, colidx, rowidx, config, isvein=True) if random.random() < 0.05: generateveinorcave(col, colidx, rowidx, config, isvein=False) return columns def generateveinorcave(col, x, y, config, isvein): areaparam = config['globalparams']['VeinArea'] if isvein else config['globalparams']['CaveArea'] sidelength = random.uniform(areaparam / 2, areaparam) mats = [m for m in config['materials'] if ('Vein' if isvein else 'Cave') in m.specialparams] if not mats: return mainmat = mats[0] properties = {'roughness': mainmat.roughness, 'similarity': 1.0, 'thickness': mainmat.thickness, 'relativearea': 1.0, 'relativethickness': 1.0} borderpoints = generatefractalshape(sidelength, mainmat.roughness) flow = generateflow(x, y, col.limits[-1].height, config['globalparams']['scale']) col.limits.append(Limit(0, [mainmat], [1.0], flow, properties)) Time Complexity: The generation time is dominated by the number of columns (N \times L) and the number of limits per column. The fractal generation for veins/caves is recursive with a fixed depth limit (5), making it O(1) per vein/cave relative to recursion depth, but dependent on the area size. The overall complexity is linear with respect to the number of columns and average limits per column. Memory Complexity: The method significantly reduces memory usage compared to traditional voxel grids. The average number of limits generated is 84,376.42, compared to 125,000 voxels in a traditional volumetric terrain of the same dimensions. This represents a reduction of approximately 33% in data points, though each limit stores more data (materials, concentrations, flow) than a single voxel type ID. Measured Performance: Performance was measured using eight configurations with varying numbers of regular, cave, and vein materials. All materials had maximum affinity. The method scales well with the number of materials, as the affinity calculation is linear with respect to the number of materials in the last layer. Strengths: Reduces memory requirements by storing limits instead of all voxels. Provides realistic appearance by mixing materials and flow between layers. Designers configure material properties, affinities, and global parameters via a configuration file. Supports dynamic voxel generation, allowing for infinite terrain extension. Limitations: Cannot manage certain complex terrain types (e.g., subfigure 6(c) in source). Fractal generation is limited to depth 5 for performance, which may restrict detail in veins/caves. Interpolation between limits may introduce artifacts if limits are too sparse. When to Use: When memory efficiency is critical. When realistic material mixing and flow are desired. When dynamic, infinite terrain extension is needed. When Not to Use: When exact voxel-level control is required without interpolation. When the terrain structure is too complex for the limit-based representation (e.g., highly fractured or non-layered structures). Origin: The method was proposed by Aitor Santamaría-Ibirika et al. in the paper "Procedural approach to volumetric terrain generation". History and Development: The paper presents a procedural approach to generate volumetric terrains with mixed materials and a natural, realistic appearance. It introduces a specific volume representation method that reduces memory requirements by using stacked material limits. The method includes metrics and requisites to evaluate terrain generators. The fractal algorithm for vein generation is based on the midpoint displacement method, extensively used for terrain generation. Usage: The method is used for generating volumetric terrains in applications requiring realistic material distribution and flow, such as games or simulations. It allows for real-time extension of terrain layers. Procedural approach to volumetric terrain generation, https://zenodo.org/records/18429902, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Online Terrain Generation
head: Online approach, Terrain extension
body: An algorithm to extend an already existing terrain by generating new chunks adjacent to the original plot, preserving the density of veins and caves. Unlike offline generation where layer composition and properties are calculated during generation, online generation calculates the composition and properties of layers beforehand. This architectural difference allows the method to extend terrain without regenerating the entire volume. Inputs: Existing terrain data (original plot), specifically the count of veins and caves. Target dimensions for the new terrain plot (e.g., chunk size). Input parameters for layer density used to initialize the first plot's vein and cave density. Outputs: A new terrain plot consisting of stacked layers, veins, and caves, compatible with the existing terrain. Data Structures: Terrain Plot: A 3D volume composed of a vertical stack of elements. Element Types: Layers defined by material composition and properties, veins as procedural structures, and caves as procedural voids. Stack: An ordered list of elements from bottom to top. Steps: 1. Determine Element Counts: Calculate the number of veins and caves for the new terrain plot. This value is obtained randomly between 0.5 and 1.5 times the number of veins and caves in the original plot. This scaling preserves the density of elements across the whole terrain. 2. Determine Positions: Determine the position of veins and caves between the layers using a completely random process. The result is a stack of layers, veins, and caves. 3. Generate Layers: Generate elements of the stack beginning from the bottom. Extend layers in the horizontal plane (along X and Z coordinates) obtaining new heights using the Perlin noise algorithm. The composition and properties of the layer are already calculated in this step. 4. Generate Veins and Caves: Generate veins and caves following the same steps as the offline generation process. 5. Convert to Volume: If converting the terrain to a volume representation, multiply the thickness by the blend value of each layer to determine the transition height with the last layer, removing sharp frontiers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def generateonlineterrain(existingterrain, targetchunksize): # Step 1: Determine number of veins and caves randomly between 0.5 and 1.5 times original count newveincount = int(existingterrain.countveins() random.uniform(0.5, 1.5)) newcavecount = int(existingterrain.countcaves() random.uniform(0.5, 1.5)) # Step 2: Determine positions using a completely random process stack = [] for in range(targetchunksize.totalelements): r = random.random() if r < 0.5: stack.append({"type": "layer", "properties": existingterrain.layerproperties}) elif r < 0.75: stack.append({"type": "vein"}) else: stack.append({"type": "cave"}) # Step 3: Generate elements from bottom up for element in stack: if element["type"] == "layer": # Extend layers in horizontal plane (X, Z) using Perlin noise element.heights = generatelayerheightsperlin(element, targetchunksize) elif element["type"] == "vein": # Generate veins following the same steps as the offline generation process pass # See offline generation algorithm elif element["type"] == "cave": # Generate caves following the same steps as the offline generation process pass # See offline generation algorithm return stack def generatelayerheightsperlin(layer, chunksize): # Standard 2D Perlin noise algorithm heights = [[0.0 for in range(chunksize.z)] for in range(chunksize.x)] for x in range(chunksize.x): for z in range(chunksize.z): heights[x][z] = perlinnoise2d(x, z, layer.seed) return heights def perlinnoise2d(x, y, seed): # Standard 2D Perlin noise implementation return (math.sin(x 0.1 + seed) + math.cos(y 0.1 + seed)) / 2.0 Parameters: Random Factor Range: [0.5, 1.5] for vein and cave counts. Noise Algorithm: Perlin noise for layer height generation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Density Preservation: The random scaling factor must be applied to the original plot's counts to ensure density is preserved along the whole terrain, not just the current chunk. Composition Calculation: In online mode, layer composition and properties must be calculated beforehand, unlike offline generation where they are calculated during generation. Failure to pre-calculate these will break the online extension logic. Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined in terms of Big-O. Measured performance shows online generation times are comparable to offline generation. Measured Performance: On an Intel Core i7 950 CPU (3.07GHz), generating 100 terrains of 5x5x5 chunks of 10x10x10 voxels: Offline average time ranges from 319.14 ms to 354.30 ms with standard deviations between 41.94 ms and 75.01 ms. Online average time ranges from 309.24 ms to 342.84 ms with standard deviations between 32.20 ms and 60.35 ms. A baseline Perlin Noise generation takes 61.25 ms with a standard deviation of 14.46 ms. Strengths: The method can generate terrains with complex material configurations online and preserves vein and cave density. Performance is similar to offline generation. Limitations: Generating terrains with caves increases computing overhead, and vein generation is the most time-consuming configurable feature. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed by Aitor Santamaría-Ibirika et al. in the paper "Procedural approach to volumetric terrain generation". It is part of a broader procedural approach to volumetric terrain generation that includes offline generation, online extension, and conversion to volume representations. The method was tested on an Intel Core i7 950 CPU. Procedural approach to volumetric terrain generation, https://zenodo.org/records/18429902, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Voxel Octree Terrain Generation and Meshing
head: Octree Chunk Generation, Octree-based Voxel Terrain Generation
body: This method generates a sparse voxel terrain representation by managing terrain chunks via an octree structure, generating height maps, populating voxel grids based on height, and generating triangle meshes for visible chunks using a multi-threaded task system. It builds on Chunk Generation with Base Terrain by introducing explicit octree traversal and LOD-based meshing. Inputs: Camera position, chunk size (CS), maximum octree depth (MaxDepth), terrain generation task pool size, and a noise function for height evaluation. Outputs: A set of GPU-uploaded mesh handles for visible chunks, associated with octree nodes. Data Structures: Node: Represents an octree cell. Fields include meshhandle (GPU buffer offset), generation (integrity counter), flags (state bits), and child pointers/masks. NodeQueueItem: Used for traversal. Fields: nodeidx (uint32t), pos (vec3), lod (uint32t), generation (uint32t). HeightMapPool: Maps {x, z, lod} to height data. Protected by heightmapmtx. ChunkMeshManager: Manages GPU buffer allocations (chunkquadbuffer) and staging transfers. Terrain Tasks: Thread pool for parallel mesh generation. Parameters: CS: Chunk Size (e.g., 62). MaxDepth: Maximum octree depth (e.g., 5). lod\thresh: LOD threshold (default 10.0). max\tasks: Number of generation threads, calculated as std::thread::hardwareconcurrency() 4. Steps: 1. Initialization: Reserve lodbounds for MaxDepth. Initialize terraintasks with max\tasks. Initialize chunkpool (size 1000), heightmappool (size 50000), meshalgbuf (size 1000), and mesheroutputdatabuf (size 1000). Set prevcamchunkpos to ivec3{INTMAX}. Call FreeChildren and Reset during updates. 2. Octree Traversal: Clear nodequeue. Set currcampos. Calculate newcamchunkpos = ivec3(campos) / CS. Check chunkposdirty. If time > 1ms and tomeshqueue empty: set lastoctreeupdatetime. If chunkposdirty: clear flag. Push root (0, vec3{0}, 0, generation) to nodequeue. Loop while queue not empty: pop item. Get node. Assert node. If node not dirty and numsolid == 0, continue. If ShouldMeshChunk(pos, lod): if lod < MaxDepth, FreeChildren. Get node. If needs gen/meshing, clear flag, push to tomeshqueue. Else if lod < MaxDepth: if meshhandle exists, add to meshestofree, set needs gen/meshing true, increment generation, clear meshhandle. Iterate children, allocate if needed, push to nodequeue. 3. Mesh Processing: Dispatch tasks. Loop through terraintasks.donetasks: dequeue task. Dec InFlight. Get chunk. Check MeshCurrTest. If vertcount > 0: create ChunkMeshUpload. Set stale = !meshcurrtest. Set stagingcopyidx. If not stale, memcpy vertcounts, set pos, set mult = 1 << (MaxDepth - lod). Add to chunkmeshuploads and chunkmeshnodekeys. 4. Mesh Upload: Assert sizes match. If uploads exist: reserve meshhandleuploadbuffer. Call ChunkMeshManager::UploadChunkMeshes. Iterate uploads: if not stale, get node, set node->meshhandle = buffer[j], increment j. Clear buffers. 5. Free Meshes: If meshestofree not empty, call ChunkMeshManager::FreeMeshes, clear vector. 6. Height Map Cleanup: If time since last cleanup > 1000ms: call ClearOldHeightMaps, update last time. 7. ClearOldHeightMaps: Lock mutex. Iterate heightmaps. If age > 1000ms: free pool handle, erase from map. Else: increment iterator. 8. ProcessTerrainTask: Get chunk. Clear grid. Get height map. If not in range, return. Set color = lod 30. Set scale = 1 << (MaxDepth - lod). Iterate y, z, x. Calculate adjy = y scale + chunk.pos.y. If adjy < hm.heights[i], set grid cell to color. 9. ProcessMeshGenTask: Get chunk. Allocate algdata and data from buffers. Set algdata->mask. Call GenerateMesh(chunk.grid.grid.grid, algdata, data). Set task.vertcount. If vertex count > 0: copy vertices to staging buffer, get stagingcopyidx. Copy facevertexlengths to task.vertcounts. 10. GetHeightMap: Lock mutex. Search map by {x, z, lod}. If found, update access time, return map. Else: alloc handle from pool. Get map. Calculate scale = 1 << (MaxDepth - lod). Pitfalls: Stale Meshes: If a mesh is generated but the node becomes stale (e.g., LOD change or culling), the mesh handle must be freed and the node marked for regeneration. The code tracks this via stale flag in ChunkMeshUpload and meshhandle reset. Concurrency: Height map access is protected by heightmapmtx. Mesh generation tasks use a thread pool (terraintasks). The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import List, Optional, Tuple, Dict @dataclass class NodeQueueItem: nodeidx: int pos: Tuple[float, float, float] lod: int generation: int @dataclass class Chunk: pos: Tuple[float, float, float] lod: int grid: List[List[List[int]]] meshhandle: Optional[int] = None generation: int = 0 flags: int = 0 dirty: bool = False numsolid: int = 0 needsgenormeshing: bool = False isset: List[bool] = None taskvertcount: int = 0 taskvertcounts: List[int] = None def postinit(self): if self.isset is None: self.isset = [False] 8 class VoxelRenderer: def init(self, maxdepth: int, chunksize: int): self.maxdepth = maxdepth self.chunksize = chunksize self.prevcamchunkpos = (float('inf'), float('inf'), float('inf')) self.chunkposdirty = False self.nodequeue: List[NodeQueueItem] = [] self.tomeshqueue: List[Chunk] = [] self.meshestofree: List[int] = [] self.chunkmeshuploads: List[dict] = [] self.chunkmeshnodekeys: List[int] = [] self.heightmaps: Dict[Tuple[float, float, int], dict] = {} self.lastcleanuptime = 0 self.lastoctreeupdatetime = 0 self.nodes: Dict[int, Chunk] = {0: Chunk(pos=(0,0,0), lod=0, grid=[[[0]]])} def updateoctree(self, camerapos: Tuple[float, float, float], timems: int): newcamchunkpos = (camerapos[0] // self.chunksize, camerapos[1] // self.chunksize, camerapos[2] // self.chunksize) if newcamchunkpos != self.prevcamchunkpos: self.chunkposdirty = True self.prevcamchunkpos = newcamchunkpos if timems - self.lastoctreeupdatetime > 1 and not self.tomeshqueue: self.lastoctreeupdatetime = timems if self.chunkposdirty: self.chunkposdirty = False self.nodequeue = [] self.nodequeue.append(NodeQueueItem(nodeidx=0, pos=(0,0,0), lod=0, generation=0)) while self.nodequeue: item = self.nodequeue.pop(0) node = self.nodes[item.nodeidx] if not node.dirty and node.numsolid == 0: continue if self.shouldmeshchunk(item.pos, item.lod): if item.lod < self.maxdepth: self.freechildren(item.nodeidx, item.lod) node = self.nodes[item.nodeidx] if node.needsgenormeshing: node.flags &= ~0x01 self.tomeshqueue.append(node) elif item.lod < self.maxdepth: if node.meshhandle is not None: self.meshestofree.append(node.meshhandle) node.meshhandle = None node.generation += 1 node.needsgenormeshing = True for i in range(8): if node.isset[i]: childidx = self.getorallocchild(item.nodeidx, i) childpos = (item.pos[0] + (i & 1) (self.chunksize >> (item.lod + 1)), item.pos[1] + ((i >> 1) & 1) (self.chunksize >> (item.lod + 1)), item.pos[2] + ((i >> 2) & 1) (self.chunksize >> (item.lod + 1))) self.nodequeue.append(NodeQueueItem(nodeidx=childidx, pos=childpos, lod=item.lod + 1, generation=node.generation)) elif item.lod < self.maxdepth: for i in range(8): if node.isset[i]: childidx = self.getorallocchild(item.nodeidx, i) childpos = (item.pos[0] + (i & 1) (self.chunksize >> (item.lod + 1)), item.pos[1] + ((i >> 1) & 1) (self.chunksize >> (item.lod + 1)), item.pos[2] + ((i >> 2) & 1) (self.chunksize >> (item.lod + 1))) self.nodequeue.append(NodeQueueItem(nodeidx=childidx, pos=childpos, lod=item.lod + 1, generation=node.generation)) def freechildren(self, nodeidx: int, targetdepth: int): stack = [(nodeidx, self.nodes[nodeidx].lod, self.nodes[nodeidx].generation)] while stack: curridx, depth, gen = stack.pop() curr = self.nodes[curridx] assert depth != self.maxdepth or (curr.flags & 0x01) == 0 for i in range(8): if curr.isset[i]: childidx = self.getorallocchild(curridx, i) stack.append((childidx, depth + 1, gen)) curr.isset = [False] 8 if depth != targetdepth: if curr.meshhandle is not None: self.freegpumesh(curr.meshhandle) self.freenode(curridx) def processterraintask(self, chunk: Chunk): for y in range(len(chunk.grid)): for z in range(len(chunk.grid[0])): for x in range(len(chunk.grid[0][0])): chunk.grid[y][z][x] = 0 hm = self.getheightmap(chunk.pos[0], chunk.pos[2], chunk.lod) if not hm: return color = chunk.lod 30 scale = 1 << (self.maxdepth - chunk.lod) for y in range(len(chunk.grid)): for z in range(len(chunk.grid[0])): for x in range(len(chunk.grid[0][0])): adjy = y scale + chunk.pos[1] if adjy < hm.heights[x]: chunk.grid[y][z][x] = color def processmeshgentask(self, chunk: Chunk): algdata = {"mask": 0xFF} data = {"vertices": [], "facevertexlengths": []} algdata["mask"] = 0xFF vertcount = self.generatemeshfromgrid(chunk.grid, algdata, data) chunk.taskvertcount = vertcount if vertcount > 0: chunk.stagingcopyidx = self.copytostaging(data["vertices"], vertcount) chunk.taskvertcounts = data["facevertexlengths"] return chunk def uploadmeshes(self): if not self.chunkmeshuploads: return j = 0 for upload in self.chunkmeshuploads: if not upload["stale"]: node = self.nodes[upload["nodeidx"]] node.meshhandle = j j += 1 self.chunkmeshuploads = [] self.chunkmeshnodekeys = [] def freemeshes(self): if self.meshestofree: for h in self.meshestofree: self.freegpumesh(h) self.meshestofree = [] def clearoldheightmaps(self, timems: int): if timems - self.lastcleanuptime > 1000: self.lastcleanuptime = timems keystoremove = [k for k, v in self.heightmaps.items() if timems - v["accesstime"] > 1000] for k in keystoremove: self.freeheightmappoolhandle(k) del self.heightmaps[k] def getheightmap(self, x: float, z: float, lod: int): key = (x, z, lod) if key in self.heightmaps: self.heightmaps[key]["accesstime"] = 0 return self.heightmaps[key]["map"] handle = self.allocheightmappoolhandle() scale = 1 << (self.maxdepth - lod) self.heightmaps[key] = {"map": {"heights": [0]}, "accesstime": 0, "handle": handle} return self.heightmaps[key]["map"] def shouldmeshchunk(self, pos, lod): return True def getorallocchild(self, parentidx, i): return parentidx 8 + i + 1 def freegpumesh(self, handle): pass def freenode(self, idx): del self.nodes[idx] def generatemeshfromgrid(self, grid, algdata, data): return 10 def copytostaging(self, verts, count): return 0 def allocheightmappoolhandle(self): return 0 def freeheightmappoolhandle(self, key): pass Constructs a voxel terrain representation by recursively subdividing an octree based on surface intersection tests. It solves the problem of efficiently generating a sparse voxel grid for procedural terrain by only allocating memory for nodes that contain or intersect the terrain surface, rather than filling a dense volume. It differs from dense voxelization by using adaptive depth, though this introduces specific edge cases regarding noise-induced gaps that require careful handling of subdivision criteria. Time Complexity: Traversal is proportional to the number of visible nodes. Mesh generation is parallelized via terraintasks (size max\tasks). Memory Complexity: Sparse. Only nodes intersecting the surface or below are allocated. chunkpool (1000), heightmappool (50000) provide pre-allocated buffers. Performance: Before optimization, mean chunk draw GPU time was 1.31ms. Strengths: Efficient memory usage for large terrains; adaptive LOD; explicit control over memory pooling and generation state via manual octree traversal. Limitations: Requires careful handling of stale meshes and concurrency (height map access protected by mutex). When to use: Large-scale procedural terrain where memory efficiency and LOD are critical. When not to use: Small, dense voxel worlds where overhead of octree management outweighs benefits. This method is derived from a Vulkan-based voxel renderer implementation. It utilizes a manual octree traversal with explicit child management (IsSet, SetData) rather than a standard library tree, allowing fine-grained control over memory pooling and generation state. The implementation includes a ChunkMeshManager for GPU buffer management and a thread pool for terrain generation tasks. tonadr1022/vulkanvoxels, https://github.com/tonadr1022/vulkanvoxels, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Octree-based Voxel Terrain Voxelization
head: Recursive Octree Voxelization for Terrain, Surface-Intersecting Octree Terrain Voxelization
body: This method constructs a voxel terrain representation by recursively subdividing an octree based on surface intersection tests. It solves the problem of efficiently generating a sparse voxel grid for procedural terrain by only allocating memory for nodes that contain or intersect the terrain surface, rather than filling a dense volume. It differs from dense voxelization by using adaptive depth, though this introduces specific edge cases regarding noise-induced gaps that require careful handling of subdivision criteria. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A terrain bounding box (typically rectangular), a surface definition function (e.g., Perlin noise heightmap), and a target voxel resolution (e.g., 1 m³). Output: An octree structure where leaf nodes represent either solid ground, empty air, or surface-intersecting chunks ready for meshing. Each node contains a voxelindex indicating its rendering state. Data Structures: Octree Node: bounds: Axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) defining the spatial extent. children: Array of 8 child nodes (null if leaf). voxelindex: Integer flag set by intersectssurface() indicating how the node is to be rendered later. depth: Current subdivision level. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Root Nodes: Create an octree parent node for the terrain; if the terrain is rectangular rather than cubic, create more than one parent node to compose the rectangle. Example: For a 2048 \times 1024 \times 2048 terrain, create four parent nodes each with a size of 1024 \times 1024 \times 1024. 2. Subdivide to Component Level: Subdivide the parent node to a level where each node represents a portion of the terrain called a component (or chunk); each component has the potential to be a model with one mesh forming the surface. 3. Recursive Subdivision: Execute a recursive function that checks each component to see if it intersects the surface; if it does, subdivide it by adding eight children, which are then also checked. 4. Alternative Bottom-Up Approach: Test all nodes at the lowest depth required (depending on LOD), cache the result, work back up to the root node, create parent nodes for a collection of eight nodes only if they represent a surface, and delete those complete in air or solid ground. Formulas and Parameters: Voxel Size: Typically 1 m³, determining the minimum leaf node dimension. Terrain Dimensions: Example given as 2048 \times 1024 \times 2048. voxelindex: A value set by the intersectssurface() function that indicates how the node is to be rendered later. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Noise-Induced Gaps: Gaps appear when noise is added because a node's corners may all be inside or outside the surface, yet a child node may still represent the surface due to the random nature of the noise. Memory vs. Accuracy Trade-off: Subdividing every node until the surface depth (voxel size, usually 1 m³) is reached avoids gaps but takes more time and uses more memory compared to selective subdivision. Prediction Difficulty: Predicting whether a node intersects a Perlin Noise sample based on its frequency, amplitude, and octaves without sampling is complex and prone to error. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Node: def init(self, bounds, depth=0): self.bounds = bounds # (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) self.children = [None] 8 self.voxelindex = 0 self.depth = depth def getnodecorners(node): """Returns the 8 corner coordinates of a node's AABB.""" minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz = node.bounds return [ (minx, miny, minz), (maxx, miny, minz), (minx, maxy, minz), (maxx, maxy, minz), (minx, miny, maxz), (maxx, miny, maxz), (minx, maxy, maxz), (maxx, maxy, maxz) ] def intersectssurface(node, surfacefunc): """ Determines if a node intersects the terrain surface. Returns (bool intersects, int voxelindex). """ corners = getnodecorners(node) values = [surfacefunc(c) for c in corners] if min(values) <= 0 <= max(values): return True, 1 # 1 represents INTERSECTING elif all(v > 0 for v in values): return False, 2 # 2 represents INSIDE (above surface) else: return False, 3 # 3 represents OUTSIDE (below surface) def createchildren(node): """Splits an AABB into 8 equal octants.""" minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz = node.bounds midx, midy, midz = (minx+maxx)/2, (miny+maxy)/2, (minz+maxz)/2 childrenbounds = [ (minx, miny, minz, midx, midy, midz), (midx, miny, minz, maxx, midy, midz), (minx, midy, minz, midx, maxy, midz), (midx, midy, minz, maxx, maxy, midz), (minx, miny, midz, midx, midy, maxz), (midx, miny, midz, maxx, midy, maxz), (minx, midy, midz, midx, maxy, maxz), (midx, midy, midz, maxx, maxy, maxz) ] return [Node(b, node.depth + 1) for b in childrenbounds] def voxelizeterrain(terrainbounds, surfacefunc, maxdepth): """ Main entry point for octree-based voxel terrain voxelization. """ rootnodes = [] width = terrainbounds[3] - terrainbounds[0] height = terrainbounds[4] - terrainbounds[1] depth = terrainbounds[5] - terrainbounds[2] # If terrain is not a power-of-two cube, split into multiple roots if width == height == depth and (width & (width - 1)) == 0: root = Node(terrainbounds, depth=0) rootnodes.append(root) else: # Create multiple parent nodes to cover rectangular bounds # Standard grid splitting into power-of-two cubes step = 1 while step 2 <= max(width, height, depth): step = 2 for x in range(0, width, step): for y in range(0, height, step): for z in range(0, depth, step): b = (x, y, z, min(x+step, width), min(y+step, height), min(z+step, depth)) rootnodes.append(Node(b, depth=0)) for root in rootnodes: subdivide(root, surfacefunc, maxdepth) return rootnodes def subdivide(node, surfacefunc, maxdepth): """ Recursively subdivides the octree node if it intersects the surface. """ intersects, voxelindex = intersectssurface(node, surfacefunc) node.voxelindex = voxelindex if intersects: if node.depth < maxdepth: children = createchildren(node) for child in children: subdivide(child, surfacefunc, maxdepth) node.children = children else: # Reached target voxel size pass else: # Node is fully inside or outside; do not subdivide pass The parent method that manages the overall chunk generation and meshing pipeline. It uses this voxelization step to populate the octree before generating triangle meshes for visible chunks. Voxel Octree Terrain Generation and Meshing Time Complexity: Depends heavily on the surface complexity and the subdivision strategy. Selective subdivision is faster but risks gaps. Full subdivision to voxel size is O(N) where N is the number of voxels at the target resolution, which is significantly slower than sparse methods. Memory Complexity: Sparse. Only nodes intersecting the surface or below it are allocated. However, if full subdivision is used to avoid gaps, memory usage approaches that of a dense grid. Strengths: Efficient for large terrains with sparse surface detail. Adaptive resolution allows for high detail near the surface and coarser representation deeper underground. Limitations: Prone to gaps when using high-frequency noise if intersection tests are not robust. Performance degrades if the surface is highly complex or if full subdivision is required. When to use: When memory efficiency is critical and the terrain surface is relatively smooth or low-frequency. When not to use: When using high-frequency noise and gaps are unacceptable, unless the performance cost of full subdivision is acceptable. This method was developed as part of the Voxel Terrain system for the Ultra game engine, specifically for VR optimization. It was documented in a blog post by the developer of "The Seventh World" project. The approach addresses the challenges of generating voxel terrain efficiently for real-time rendering, balancing memory usage with visual fidelity. The specific issues with noise-induced gaps highlight the difficulties of adaptive voxelization with procedural surfaces. Voxel Terrain Part 1 - Voxelization, https://www.leadwerks.com/community/blogs/entry/2800-voxel-terrain-part-1-voxelization/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Chunked Voxel Evaluation (Top-Down Procedural Generation)
head: Chunked Evaluation, Top-Down Procedural Generation
body: This method generates voxel data on-demand by evaluating procedural object definitions within GPU shaders, driven by high-level parameters computed on the CPU. It renders large, continuous procedural structures that span multiple discrete chunks without requiring explicit meshing or pre-computed voxel storage for the entire world. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A deterministic seed, camera position, and a list of high-level object parameters (bounds, control points, thicknesses) computed in C++. Output: A voxel grid for the current chunk, generated in the shader. Data Structures: Object Definition (CPU): Structs containing start/end coordinates, control points, start/end thicknesses, and a computed bounding box. Shader Input: A list of active objects and their parameters, passed per chunk. Chunk Context: Start and end world-space coordinates defining the chunk's bounding box. Steps: 1. High-Level Generation (CPU): Generate world structures (e.g., world map, cities, roads) deterministically based on a seed. For each object (e.g., tree branch), compute its bounding box in world space. 2. Chunk Selection: Identify which chunks intersect with the bounding boxes of active objects. 3. Parameter Passing (CPU to GPU): For each chunk to be rendered, compile a list of objects whose bounding boxes intersect the chunk. Pass these object parameters to the shader. 4. Bounding Box Derivation (Shader): For each chunk, define the start and end world coordinates (the chunk's bounding box). 5. Coordinate Transformation (Shader): For each voxel in the chunk, derive its relative (object) coordinates by subtracting the chunk's start coordinates from the voxel's world coordinates. 6. Voxel Evaluation (Shader): Evaluate each passed object against the voxel's relative coordinates. Determine if the voxel lies within the object's geometric definition (e.g., within a cylinder defined by control points and thickness). 7. Redundant Generation: Generate voxels in a domain larger than the renderable chunk area (e.g., 1.25x the dimensions) to ensure seamless normal calculation at boundaries. Formulas: Relative Coordinate: v{rel} = v{world} - c{start} v{world}: World-space coordinate of the voxel. c{start}: Start coordinate of the chunk's bounding box. Object Containment: Determined by evaluating the voxel against the object's geometric primitive (e.g., distance to line segment for branches) using v{rel}. Parameters: Redundancy Factor: 1.25 (current value, subject to change). Generation Order: Top-down (world -> cities -> neighborhoods -> objects). Determinism: All generation is deterministic based on a seed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Seams: Without redundant generation, normal vectors will be discontinuous at chunk boundaries. Performance: Evaluating all objects for every chunk can be expensive; culling by bounding box is essential. Precision: Floating-point precision in shader calculations may affect boundary accuracy for very large worlds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateworld(seed): """CPU: Generate high-level structures deterministically.""" worldmap = generatemap(seed) cities = placecities(worldmap, seed) activeobjects = [] for city in cities: neighborhoods = generateneighborhoods(city, seed) for neighborhood in neighborhoods: streets = generatestreets(neighborhood, seed) for street in streets: buildings = generatebuildings(street, seed) for building in buildings: building.computeboundingbox() activeobjects.append(building) return activeobjects def preparechunk(chunkmin, chunkmax, activeobjects): """CPU: Select objects intersecting the chunk and pass parameters.""" relevantparams = [] for obj in activeobjects: if bboxintersects(obj.bboxmin, obj.bboxmax, chunkmin, chunkmax): relevantparams.append(obj.params) return relevantparams def bboxintersects(min1, max1, min2, max2): """Standard AABB intersection check.""" return min1.x <= max2.x and max1.x >= min2.x and \ min1.y <= max2.y and max1.y >= min2.y and \ min1.z <= max2.z and max1.z >= min2.z def evaluatechunk(chunkmin, chunkmax, voxelsize, objectparams): """GPU/Shader simulation: Evaluate voxels per chunk.""" chunkvoxels = [] # Redundant generation: expand bounds slightly for seamless normals expansion = voxelsize 0.25 start = vec3(chunkmin.x - expansion, chunkmin.y - expansion, chunkmin.z - expansion) end = vec3(chunkmax.x + expansion, chunkmax.y + expansion, chunkmax.z + expansion) x = start.x while x < end.x: y = start.y while y < end.y: z = start.z while z < end.z: voxelworld = vec3(x, y, z) voxelrel = voxelworld - chunkmin isvoxel = False for obj in objectparams: # Evaluate voxel against object geometry (e.g., distance to line segment for branches) if isinsideobject(voxelrel, obj): isvoxel = True break if isvoxel: chunkvoxels.append(voxelworld) z += voxelsize y += voxelsize x += voxelsize return chunkvoxels Solves normal discontinuities at chunk boundaries by generating voxels in a domain larger than the renderable area. Choose this when visual continuity of surface normals is critical and global data structures are undesirable. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of voxels in the chunk and M is the number of active objects per chunk. Evaluation is parallelizable per voxel. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the current chunk's voxel data. No global voxel storage required. Performance: Highly dependent on the number of active objects per chunk. Bounding box culling is critical to reduce M. Strengths: Seamless normals, deterministic regeneration, no pre-computed storage, easy parallelization. Limitations: High GPU load if many objects overlap a chunk; requires careful culling. When to use: Procedural worlds with large, continuous structures where memory bandwidth is a constraint. When not to use: Scenes with static, pre-computed geometry where storage is cheap. Originating from the VoxelQuest project (2014), this method was developed to handle procedural generation of large voxel worlds without pre-computing the entire world data. It emphasizes a top-down approach where high-level structures are defined in C++ and evaluated at the voxel level in GLSL shaders based on camera locality. name: Chunk Redundancy for Seamless Normals
body: This method generates chunks with redundant voxels beyond their render bounds to allow seamless normal calculation inside the shader. It enables parallel chunk production without seams by expanding the generation domain relative to the rendering domain. Inputs: Chunk ID and global seed for deterministic procedural generation. Render bounds for the current chunk. Redundancy factor R. Outputs: A voxel grid containing density and material data. Normal vectors calculated per-voxel inside the shader. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array or 3D texture. Dimensions: The grid dimensions D{gen} are scaled by a redundancy factor R relative to the render dimensions D{render}. D{gen} = \lceil R \times D{render} \rceil Typical value for R is 1.25. Steps: 1. Generate Voxels: Generate voxels for each chunk at R times the render dimensions. 2. Render Pass: Render only within the chunk's original bounds. 3. Normal Calculation: Calculate normals seamlessly inside the shader using the redundant voxels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatechunk(chunkid, renderw, renderh, renderd, redundancyfactor=1.25): # 1. Calculate expanded dimensions genw = int(renderw redundancyfactor) genh = int(renderh redundancyfactor) gend = int(renderd redundancyfactor) # 2. Initialize voxel grid voxelgrid = [[[None for in range(genw)] for in range(genh)] for in range(gend)] # 3. Evaluate procedural function for all voxels in generation bounds for z in range(gend): for y in range(genh): for x in range(genw): # Map local voxel coordinate to world/object space worldpos = (x, y, z) # Evaluate density and material deterministically based on chunk ID and seed density = 0.0 material = 0.0 voxelgrid[z][y][x] = (density, material) return voxelgrid, genw, genh, gend def renderchunk(voxelgrid, renderw, renderh, renderd): # 4. Render only within render bounds # Iterate over pixels and cast rays through the voxel grid for pixel in range(renderw renderh): # Trace ray and accumulate color/opacity using only voxels within render bounds color = 0.0 # Standard framebuffer operation def calculatenormal(voxelgrid, x, y, z): # 5. Seamless normal calculation using redundant data # Sample neighbors. Because grid is oversized, neighbors at boundary # are valid data from the overlapping generation region. dx = voxelgrid[z][y][x + 1][0] - voxelgrid[z][y][x - 1][0] dy = voxelgrid[z][y + 1][x][0] - voxelgrid[z][y - 1][x][0] dz = voxelgrid[z + 1][y][x][0] - voxelgrid[z - 1][y][x][0] length = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz)0.5 normal = (dx/length, dy/length, dz/length) return normal Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. This variant applies to volumetric fur or microgeometry where the volume wraps around a model surface. Instead of spatial redundancy, it tiles the volume toroidally across the UV map of the model to ensure seamless projection without seams. It requires careful generation to avoid boundary artifacts and relies on UV mapping that minimizes distortion to ensure smooth fur without local distortions. Parallel chunk generation is enabled. The redundancy factor trades seamlessness for performance. Not given in the sources. This method was described in the context of the VoxelQuest engine, where it was used to generate seamless normals for procedural chunks in a top-down voxel generation pipeline. The approach leverages the deterministic nature of procedural generation to allow overlapping generation domains.
