name: Spot Noise
head: Impulse convolution noise, Sparse convolution noise
body: Spot noise is a procedural texture synthesis method that generates structured patterns by convolving a uniform distribution of impulses with an arbitrary spatially defined kernel. It solves the problem of creating flow-aligned or structured surface details by simulating the accumulation of many tiny drops over a domain. Unlike gradient-based noise which relies on lattice interpolation, Spot noise is a sparse convolution method where the pattern emerges from the spatial arrangement of discrete events. Inputs: Domain size and resolution. Impulse density parameter (average number of impulses per unit area/volume). Kernel function K(\mathbf{x}), typically an elliptical Gaussian. Vector field \mathbf{V}(\mathbf{x}) (optional, for orientation). Outputs: Scalar field value N(\mathbf{P}) at query point \mathbf{P}. Data Structures: Impulse list: A set of points \{\mathbf{I}j\} with associated attributes (position, orientation, scale). In standard Spot Noise, these are generated via jittered pseudorandom sampling to maintain a uniform distribution. Steps: 1. Impulse Generation: Generate impulse locations \mathbf{I}j across the domain using jittered pseudorandom sampling to ensure a uniform distribution. 2. Kernel Definition: Define the kernel K(\mathbf{x}) spatially, typically as an elliptical Gaussian. If a vector field is present, the kernel may be oriented along the field direction. 3. Convolution: For a query point \mathbf{P}, compute the noise value by summing the contributions of all impulses: N(\mathbf{P}) = \sum{j} K(\mathbf{P} - \mathbf{I}j) 4. Spectral Approach (Alternative): Van Wijk presented a spectral approach to achieving this as well. Parameters: Impulse density: Controls the granularity of the pattern. Kernel width: Controls the spread of each impulse. Edge Cases: High curvature or vorticity in the vector field can cause spots to blur out the flow structure. Boundary conditions for impulse generation must be handled to avoid edge artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def spotnoise(p, impulses, kernelwidth): """ Compute Spot Noise value at point p.:param p: Query point (list/tuple of floats):param impulses: List of impulse positions (list of lists/tuples of floats):param kernelwidth: Standard deviation of the Gaussian kernel:return: Scalar noise value """ value = 0.0 sigmasq = 2.0 kernelwidth kernelwidth for impulsepos in impulses: distvec = [p[i] - impulsepos[i] for i in range(len(p))] distsq = sum(d d for d in distvec) contribution = math.exp(-distsq / sigmasq) value += contribution return value Extends standard Spot Noise by using a non-uniform distribution of impulses and allowing spatial control over kernel orientation and scale via underlying data fields, enabling structured texture synthesis with varying feature density. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Flexible kernel formulation allows for arbitrary pattern shapes; suitable for structured texture synthesis. Limitations: For high curvature or vorticity, the spots tend to blur out the flow structure. Spot noise was introduced by van Wijk [vW91] and further developed by de Lavergtelle et al. [dLvL97] as a sparse convolution noise method [Lew89]. It is based on the idea of developing a pattern after many thousands of tiny drops, representing a flow field. The method is defined as a sparse convolution noise with a flexible kernel formulation where a uniform distribution of impulses is convolved with an arbitrary kernel spatially defined. name: Worley Noise
head: F1 Noise, Voronoi Noise, Cellular Noise, Cellular Worley noise, Voronoi F1 distance noise, Voronoï F1 distance noise
body: Worley Noise is a procedural noise generation technique that creates cellular patterns by computing the distance from a query point to the nearest feature point in a grid of pseudo-randomly placed points. It solves the problem of generating structured, organic-looking density variations for volumetric data, such as cloud boundaries or smoke textures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point \mathbf{P} = (x, y, z) in 3D space; a cell size (grid resolution) defining the lattice; a hash function to map integer cell coordinates to random feature points; a distance metric (Euclidean, Manhattan, or Chebyshev); and a combination method for multiple nearest neighbors. Output: A scalar value representing the distance to the nearest feature point (F1), or a combination of distances (e.g., F2-F1). Data Structures: Feature Points: In GPU implementations, these are often stored in a ComputeBuffer (Structured Buffer) with stride sizeof(float) 3 for 3D coordinates (rx, ry, rz) \in [0, 1]^3. In CPU implementations, they are generated on-the-fly using a hash function. Distance Array: A structure to store the distances to the N closest feature points, typically initialized to infinity. For F1, only the minimum is needed. For F2 (second nearest), an array of size 2 is used. Numbered Steps: 1. Normalize Coordinates: Convert the world position \mathbf{P} to cell space by dividing by the cell size: \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{P} / \text{cellSize}. 2. Determine Base Cell: Calculate the integer coordinates of the cell containing the query point: (ix, iy, iz) = (\lfloor ux \rfloor, \lfloor uy \rfloor, \lfloor uz \rfloor). 3. Calculate Fractional Part: Compute the fractional coordinates within the cell: (fx, fy, fz) = (ux - ix, uy - iy, uz - iz). 4. Iterate Neighborhood: Loop over neighboring integer cells (i, j, k) where i, j, k \in \{-1, 0, 1\} (a 3x3x3 neighborhood). This covers all cells that could contain a feature point closer than those in further cells. 5. Hash Feature Point: For each neighbor cell (ix+i, iy+j, iz+k), generate a pseudo-random feature point \mathbf{F}{ijk} = (rx, ry, rz) using a hash function. A common hash function for 3D integer coordinates (cx, cy, cz) is: \begin{aligned} x &= (cx \cdot 127.1 + cy \cdot 311.7 + cz \cdot 74.7) \% 289.0 \\ x &= \sin(x) \cdot 43758.5453 \\ rx &= x - \lfloor x \rfloor \end{aligned} Repeat for y and z with different coefficients (e.g., 269.5/183.3/246.1 and 113.5/271.9/124.6). 6. Compute Distance Vector: Calculate the vector from the query point to the feature point. Since \mathbf{F}{ijk} is in [0,1] and the cell offset is (i,j,k), the distance vector \mathbf{d} is: \mathbf{d} = (i + rx - fx, \ j + ry - fy, \ k + rz - fz). 7. Calculate Distance Metric: Compute the distance dist using the chosen metric: Euclidean: dist = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2} Manhattan: dist = |dx| + |dy| + |dz| Chebyshev: dist = \max(|dx|, |dy|, |dz|) Note: Some implementations use squared Euclidean distance to avoid the square root, but must be consistent with the combination method. 8. Update Nearest Neighbors: For F1 (Worley Noise): Track the minimum distance found so far. For F2 (Worley Edge Erosion): Maintain the two smallest distances, d0 (closest) and d1 (second closest). If dist < d0, shift d0 to d1 and update d0 = dist. 9. Combine and Scale: Apply the combination method and scale by an amplitude factor. D0: output = d0 D1D0: output = d1 - d0 Normalize the result to [0, 1] if necessary (e.g., divide by \sqrt{3} for Euclidean in a unit cube and clamp). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def hash3d(ix, iy, iz): """ Hashes 3D integer coordinates to a random float vector in [0, 1]^3. Based on. """ # X component x = (ix 127.1 + iy 311.7 + iz 74.7) % 289.0 x = math.sin(x) 43758.5453 rx = x - math.floor(x) # Y component y = (ix 269.5 + iy 183.3 + iz 246.1) % 289.0 y = math.sin(y) 43758.5453 ry = y - math.floor(y) # Z component z = (ix 113.5 + iy 271.9 + iz 124.6) % 289.0 z = math.sin(z) 43758.5453 rz = z - math.floor(z) return (rx, ry, rz) def worleynoise(x, y, z, cellsize, distancemetric="euclidean", combination="D0"): """ Computes Worley Noise for a given point. Parameters: x, y, z: Query point coordinates. cellsize: Size of the grid cells. distancemetric: "euclidean", "manhattan", or "chebyshev". combination: "D0" (F1) or "D1D0" (F2-F1). Returns: Normalized scalar value. """ # 1. Normalize to cell space u = x / cellsize v = y / cellsize w = z / cellsize # 2. Base cell and fractional part ix = math.floor(u) iy = math.floor(v) iz = math.floor(w) fx = u - ix fy = v - iy fz = w - iz # Initialize distances # For D0, we only need mindist. For D1D0, we need d0 and d1. d0 = float('inf') d1 = float('inf') # 3. Iterate over 3x3x3 neighborhood for i in range(-1, 2): for j in range(-1, 2): for k in range(-1, 2): # 4. Hash feature point for neighbor cell (ix+i, iy+j, iz+k) rx, ry, rz = hash3d(ix + i, iy + j, iz + k) # 5. Distance vector dx = i + rx - fx dy = j + ry - fy dz = k + rz - fz # 6. Calculate distance based on metric if distancemetric == "euclidean": dist = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) elif distancemetric == "manhattan": dist = abs(dx) + abs(dy) + abs(dz) elif distancemetric == "chebyshev": dist = max(abs(dx), abs(dy), abs(dz)) else: raise ValueError("Unknown distance metric") # 7. Update nearest neighbors if dist < d0: d1 = d0 d0 = dist elif dist < d1: d1 = dist # 8. Combine if combination == "D0": result = d0 elif combination == "D1D0": result = d1 - d0 else: raise ValueError("Unknown combination method") # 9. Normalize (assuming Euclidean in unit cube, max dist is sqrt(3)) # Note: This normalization is specific to Euclidean distance in [0,1] cells. # For other metrics or if raw distance is desired, skip this. if distancemetric == "euclidean": result = result / math.sqrt(3.0) result = max(0.0, min(1.0, result)) return result Parameters: Cell Size: Controls the frequency of the cellular pattern. Distance Metric: Euclidean is standard for organic shapes; Manhattan/Chebyshev can create sharper, more geometric patterns. Combination: "D0" returns raw distance to nearest point (F1). "D1D0" returns the difference between the second and first nearest distances, highlighting cell edges (F2-F1). Amplitude: A multiplier applied to the final output to control contrast. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distance Calculation Typo: A common implementation error is using dz dy instead of dz dz in the Euclidean distance formula, leading to incorrect noise. Periodicity: To tile the noise, neighbor coordinates must be wrapped to the repeat dimensions before hashing. Precision: Using squared Euclidean distance avoids square roots but requires careful handling when combining with other metrics or normalizing. Generates a 2D Worley noise texture to break up smoke silhouettes, updated per frame via compute shader. It differs from its parent Worley Noise by explicitly incorporating a time uniform to animate the point positions, and from Voronoise by returning raw distance values rather than smoothed vector displacements. Voronoise is a procedural noise function that unifies value noise and Voronoi cellular patterns through a single interpolation parameter. It solves the problem of needing distinct noise types for continuous textures and cellular structures by providing a smooth transition between them. Unlike standard Worley noise which only returns distance metrics, Voronoise returns a continuous scalar value suitable for fractal Brownian motion (FBM) accumulation, distinguishing it from its parent [1726-worley-noise.md] and sibling [2982-animated-worley-noise-texture-generation.md]. Generates crystalline edge erosion textures for cloud boundary curling by computing the difference between the second nearest neighbor distance (F2) and the nearest neighbor distance (F1). It is implemented by tracking the two closest distances (d0, d1) in the 3x3x3 neighborhood and returning \max(0.0, \min(1.0, d1 - d0)). Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, as it iterates over a fixed-size neighborhood (27 cells in 3D). Memory Complexity: O(1) if feature points are hashed on-the-fly, or O(N) if pre-computed feature points are stored in a buffer, where N is the number of cells in the volume. Performance: GPU implementations using compute shaders can generate noise textures efficiently by dispatching thread groups corresponding to the output resolution. Strengths: Produces distinct, organic cellular patterns. Limitations: The pattern is periodic if the hash function or cell grid is not handled carefully; lacks the smooth, directional flow of gradient noise. When to Use: Ideal for generating cloud bases, smoke textures, or any volumetric data requiring a "cellular" or "bubbly" appearance. When Not to Use: When smooth, continuous gradients or directional flow are required (use Gradient-based Noise (Perlin/Simplex) instead). Worley Noise was introduced by Steven Worley in 1996 in the paper "A Cellular Texture Basis Function". It is based on Voronoi diagrams, where the space is partitioned into regions based on distance to a set of random points. The method has been widely adopted in computer graphics for procedural texture generation, particularly in volumetric rendering for clouds and smoke, due to its ability to create realistic, organic-looking cellular structures. furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, https://github.com/furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Scrawk/Marching-Cubes, https://github.com/Scrawk/Marching-Cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) M4trixStrike/WebGL-Volumetric-clouds, https://github.com/M4trixStrike/WebGL-Volumetric-clouds, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, https://github.com/nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ldarnbr/volumetric-cloud-renderer, https://github.com/ldarnbr/volumetric-cloud-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) sixthsurge/volume-noise-generator, https://github.com/sixthsurge/volume-noise-generator, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Procedural Volumetric Clouds · Jan Wedekind, https://www.wedesoft.de/software/2023/05/03/volumetric-clouds/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Animated Worley Noise Texture Generation
head: 2D Worley Noise, Animated Worley Noise Generation, Worley Noise Generation
body: Generates a 2D Worley (Voronoi) noise texture updated per frame via a compute shader to break up smoke silhouettes. It differs from static Worley noise by incorporating a time-based UV offset to create motion, and from 3D procedural volumes by operating on a 2D texture plane, which is then sampled during ray marching. Inputs: width, height: Integer dimensions of the output texture. NoiseResolution: Integer resolution of the noise texture (default 256). Scale: Float UV multiplier (default 10.0). Time: Float time value for animation (default divisor 5). range: Integer neighborhood search radius (default 2). Outputs: NoiseTexture: RWTexture2D<float4> with format ARGB64, linear filtering, random write enabled. Data Structures: kPoint: float2 storing the random point coordinate. minDist: float storing the minimum distance found. bestPoint: float2 storing the coordinate of the nearest point. Steps: 1. Dispatch a compute shader kernel with thread group size [numthreads(8, 8, 1)]. 2. For each thread with ID (id.x, id.y): a. Check bounds: If id.x >= width or id.y >= height, return. b. Compute UV coordinates: uv = \frac{(id.x, id.y)}{\text{NoiseResolution}} \times \text{Scale} + \frac{\text{Time}}{5} c. Initialize minDist = 1.0 and bestPoint = (0, 0). d. Loop j from -range to range (inclusive) and i from -range to range (inclusive): i. Compute cell coordinate: cell = \lfloor uv \rfloor + (i, j) ii. Compute hash point using sine-based hashing: kPoint = cell + \text{frac}(\sin(\text{dot}(cell, (12.9898, 78.233))) \times 43758.5453) iii. Compute distance from UV to point: dist = \text{distance}(uv, kPoint) iv. Update minimum: If dist < minDist, set minDist = dist and bestPoint = kPoint. e. Output the result to NoiseTexture[id.xy] as float4(1 - minDist, 1 - minDist, 1 - minDist, 1.0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def CSNoise(idx, idy, width, height, NoiseResolution, Scale, Time, rangeval, NoiseTexture): if idx >= width or idy >= height: return uvx = idx / NoiseResolution Scale + Time / 5.0 uvy = idy / NoiseResolution Scale + Time / 5.0 minDist = 1.0 bestPoint = (0.0, 0.0) for j in range(-rangeval, rangeval + 1): for i in range(-rangeval, rangeval + 1): cellx = math.floor(uvx) + i celly = math.floor(uvy) + j dotval = cellx 12.9898 + celly 78.233 sinval = math.sin(dotval) fracval = sinval 43758.5453 - math.floor(sinval 43758.5453) kPointx = cellx + fracval kPointy = celly + fracval dist = math.sqrt((uvx - kPointx)2 + (uvy - kPointy)2) if dist < minDist: minDist = dist bestPoint = (kPointx, kPointy) NoiseTexture[idx, idy] = (1.0 - minDist, 1.0 - minDist, 1.0 - minDist, 1.0) Parameters: textureWidth/textureHeight: Int, noise texture resolution. Default: 256. scale: Float, UV multiplier. Default: 10.0. range: Int, neighborhood search radius. Default: 2. Edge Cases: Boundary checks prevent out-of-bounds writes to NoiseTexture. The hash function uses frac to ensure the random point offset remains within 0, 1) relative to the cell. A technique to generate detailed [volumetric noise by summing multiple layers (octaves) of Worley noise at decreasing scales and amplitudes. It differs from the base 2D generation by operating in 3D and accumulating detail through iterative calls with halving division sizes. Choose this when high-frequency volumetric detail is required. See Worley Noise for the base function. Definition: Summing multiple octaves of 3D Worley noise. Steps: 1. Generate base noise: Call computeworleynoise3D(0.4f). 2. Refine base noise: Divide worleynoisedivisionsize by 2. 3. Add detail octaves: Divide worleynoisedivisionsize by 2. 4. Generate detail noise octaves: Initialize octavecount = 5, persistance = 0.5f, lacurancy = 2.0f, amplitude = 0.075f, size = 16. Loop octave from 0 to 4: Set worleynoisedivisionsize to (size, size, size). Call computeworleynoise3Ddetail(amplitude). Update amplitude = persistance. Update size = Mathf.CeilToInt(size / lacurancy). Parameters: octavecount: Int, number of detail noise octaves. Default: 5. persistance: Float, amplitude decay factor per octave. Default: 0.5f. lacurancy: Float, frequency increase factor per octave. Default: 2.0f. detailnoise: RenderTexture, format R8, wrap Clamp, filter Bilinear. Stores accumulated detail noise. Dimensions match worleynoisesize. Combines three separate Worley noise textures (stored in the G, B, and A channels of the base density texture) into a single high-frequency fractal noise value using weighted summation. It differs from single-channel Worley by aggregating multiple frequency bands to enhance detail. Choose this when creating complex cloud structures requiring multi-scale noise. Definition: Weighted sum of three Worley channels. Steps: 1. Retrieve Worley1 from the Green channel, Worley2 from the Blue channel, and Worley3 from the Alpha channel of the base density texture. 2. Compute the weighted sum using coefficients 0.625, 0.25, and 0.125 respectively. Formula: WorleyHighFrequencies = 0.625 \times Worley1 + 0.25 \times Worley2 + 0.125 \times Worley3 A higher-frequency Worley fractal noise texture used to add detail primarily at cloud edges. It uses a smaller texture resolution than the base density. It differs from the base noise by its compact 3D packing and higher frequency. Choose this for edge detail in volumetric clouds. Definition: High-frequency Worley fractal noise for cloud edges. Parameters: Resolution: The detail density texture is 1024x32 pixels, packing a 32x32x32 3D texture horizontally. Layout: Stored in an RGBA32 texture. The RGB channels store the Worley fractal noise components. The Alpha channel is unused. Time Complexity: O(W \times H \times (2 \cdot range + 1)^2) per frame, where W, H are texture dimensions and range is the search radius. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the output texture. Performance: The method is executed on the GPU via compute shaders, allowing parallel generation per pixel. The default resolution of 256x256 with a range of 2 is lightweight enough for real-time updates. Strengths: Real-time animation capability; breaks up smoke silhouettes effectively. Limitations: 2D nature limits volumetric depth compared to 3D noise; requires compute shader support. When to use: Real-time volumetric smoke where performance is critical and 2D variation is sufficient. Originated in the context of real-time volumetric smoke rendering using ray marching, specifically in the volumetric-smoke-raymarching project. It is used to generate animated noise textures that are sampled during the ray marching phase to modulate smoke density. name: Voronoise
head: Voronoi-Noise Hybrid
body: Voronoise is a procedural noise function that unifies value noise and Voronoi cellular patterns through a single interpolation parameter. It solves the problem of needing distinct algorithms for continuous noise and cellular textures by providing a smooth transition between the two, controlled by a smoothness parameter. Unlike standard Worley noise which returns only distance metrics, Voronoise returns a scalar value derived from weighted hash contributions, allowing it to mimic value noise at low smoothness and cellular noise at high smoothness. Inputs and Outputs: Input p: 2D or 3D coordinate vector. Input u: Interpolation parameter. u=0 yields value noise; u=1 yields Voronoi patterns. Input v: Smoothness parameter. v=0 yields sharp cells; v=1 yields smooth noise. Output: Scalar float value representing the weighted average of hash contributions. Data Structures: hash32(p): Maps integer coordinates to a pseudo-random 3D vector in [0, 1] using a sin-free, cross-platform stable method involving fractal mixing and dot products. smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): Standard Hermite interpolation clamped to [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Calculate the exponent k from the smoothness parameter v. 2. Decompose the input coordinate p into integer lattice i and fractional part f. 3. Initialize accumulator a to vec2(0.0). 4. Iterate over a 5x5 grid of integer offsets g ranging from -2 to 2 for both axes. a. Compute the offset vector o by hashing i + g and scaling it with (u, u, 1.0). b. Compute the distance vector d from the fractional coordinate f to the perturbed lattice point using g - f + o.xy. c. Calculate the weight w using a power falloff based on the length of d and the threshold 1.414. d. Accumulate the weighted hash value and weight into a using vec2(o.z w, w). 5. Return the weighted average a.x / a.y. Formulas: k = 1.0 + 63.0 \cdot (1.0 - v)^6 maps v=0 to k=64 (sharp falloff) and v=1 to k=1 (linear falloff). i = \lfloor p \rfloor and f = p - i decompose the coordinate. o = \text{hash32}(i + g) \cdot (u, u, 1.0) scales the hash output. d = g - f + o{xy} computes the vector from the fractional point to the perturbed lattice point. w = (1.0 - \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 1.414, \|d\|))^k applies a power falloff based on distance. a += (oz \cdot w, w) accumulates the weighted value and weight. \text{result} = ax / ay returns the weighted average. Parameters: u: Interpolation factor. 0 produces value noise, 1 produces Voronoi noise. v: Smoothness. 0 produces sharp cells, 1 produces smooth noise. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero: If a.y is zero, the result is undefined. This occurs if no lattice points contribute, which is unlikely given the 5x5 grid and smoothstep range, but should be guarded against in implementation. Boundary: The 5x5 grid covers the current cell and neighbors. For u=1, the influence radius is limited by the smoothstep threshold of 1.414 (\sqrt{2}), which fits within the grid (max distance to corner is \approx 2.82). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voronoise(p, u, v): # Calculate exponent k for smoothness control k = 1.0 + 63.0 pow(1.0 - v, 6.0) # Integer and fractional parts of input i = floor(p) f = fract(p) # Accumulator for weighted sum a = vec2(0.0) # Iterate over 5x5 grid around the cell for y in range(-2, 3): for x in range(-2, 3): g = vec2(float(x), float(y)) # Hash integer coordinate to get random offset o = hash32(i + g) vec3(u, u, 1.0) # Distance from fractional part to perturbed lattice point d = g - f + o.xy # Weight calculation dist = length(d) s = smoothstep(0.0, 1.414, dist) w = pow(1.0 - s, k) # Accumulate: o.z is the random value, w is the weight a += vec2(o.z w, w) # Return weighted average return a.x / a.y def hash32(p): # Sin-free hash implementation from source p3 = fract(vec3(p.xyx) vec3(0.1031, 0.1030, 0.0973)) p3 += dot(p3, p3.yxz + 33.33) return fract((p3.xxy + p3.yzz) p3.zyx) A procedural technique for generating metallic paint appearances using 3D Voronoi cells to distribute metallic flakes. It differs from standard Voronoise by applying the Voronoi structure to define flake positions, sizes, orientations, and colors, then replacing the base BSDF lobe with a narrow GGX flake lobe under a clear coat layer. Choose this when rendering realistic car paints or metallic coatings with sparkle effects. A cloud generation technique that uses Voronoi cells whose boundaries are organically eroded by Simplex FBM coordinate warping, while maintaining cell identity. It differs from standard Voronoise by integrating coordinate warping to erode cell edges and decoding cell IDs to determine local cloud properties like thickness, altitude, and density. Choose this when generating realistic, puffy cloud structures with organic erosion patterns. The weather map stores distance to edge, distance to center, cell ID, and density per cell. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per sample, proportional to the number of lattice points in the search grid (25 for 2D, 125 for 3D). Memory: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Unified control over noise and cellular patterns; smooth interpolation; no need for separate algorithms. Limitations: Requires a 5x5 (or larger) grid lookup, which is more expensive than simple value noise. The hash function must be robust to avoid artifacts. When to Use: Use when a single noise function needs to transition between value noise and Voronoi patterns. Use for procedural textures requiring both continuous and cellular features. When Not to Use: Use standard Worley noise if only distance metrics are needed. Use standard value noise if cellular patterns are not required. name: Locally Controlled Spot Noise
body: Locally Controlled Spot Noise (LCSN) is a procedural noise method that generates structured patterns by convolving a non-uniform distribution of impulses with a kernel composed of multiple ellipsoidal Gaussian functions. It extends standard Spot Noise by allowing spatial control over impulse density and kernel orientation/scale via underlying data fields, enabling the synthesis of fuzzy surface details. Unlike standard Spot Noise which uses a uniform impulse distribution, LCSN rejects impulses based on a local density factor, making it suitable for authoring textures where feature density varies across the domain. Inputs: Evaluation point \mathbf{p} in N-dimensional space. Local density field d(\mathbf{p}), a scalar field representing probability/density. Orientation field Rs(\mathbf{p}) and Scale field Ss(\mathbf{p}) related to underlying data. Kernel parameters: Gaussian magnitude A, and a set of matrices \mathbf{V}i defining ellipsoidal shapes. Random number generator for jittering and density testing. Outputs: Noise value ns(\mathbf{p}). Data Structures: Impulse \mathbf{p}j: Position in texture space. Weight wj(\mathbf{p}j): Associated with the impulse. Kernel Kj(\mathbf{p}): Defined as ks(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{p}^j)Rs(\mathbf{p}^j)Ss(\mathbf{p}^j), where \mathbf{p}^j is the impulse position. Matrix \mathbf{V}: (N+1) \times (N+1) semipositive definite square matrix describing the ellipsoid iso-contour. Point \mathbf{p}: Extended to dimension N+1 with the last coordinate set to 1 for matrix multiplication. Formulas: The kernel function k(\mathbf{p}) is a sum of Gaussian functions: k(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{Vi} g{Vi} where each Gaussian component is: gV(\mathbf{p}) = A e^{-\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{p}^T \mathbf{V}^{-1} \mathbf{p}} Here, \mathbf{p} is the point in N+1 dimensions (last coord = 1), \mathbf{V} is the shape matrix, and A is the magnitude. The noise value at \mathbf{p} is: ns(\mathbf{p}) = \sumj \delta(\xi(\mathbf{p}j) < d(\mathbf{p}j)) |wj(\mathbf{p}j)| Kj(\mathbf{p}) where: \delta(\cdot) is the Kronecker delta (1 if condition true, 0 otherwise). \xi(\mathbf{p}j) is a random variable selected independently of wj. d(\mathbf{p}j) is the local density factor at the impulse location. || denotes absolute value. Kj(\mathbf{p}) incorporates orientation Rs and scale Ss transformations. Steps: 1. Impulse Generation: Generate impulses \mathbf{p}j on the fly using jittering and pseudorandom number generation in texture space. 2. Density Test: For each impulse \mathbf{p}j, generate a random density value \xi(\mathbf{p}j). Compare it against the local density factor d(\mathbf{p}j) from the scalar field. 3. Rejection: If \xi(\mathbf{p}j) \ge d(\mathbf{p}j), reject the impulse (contribution is 0). If \xi(\mathbf{p}j) < d(\mathbf{p}j), keep the impulse. 4. Kernel Evaluation: For kept impulses, compute the kernel Kj(\mathbf{p}) centered at \mathbf{p}j, applying orientation Rs(\mathbf{p}j) and scale Ss(\mathbf{p}j) transformations. 5. Summation: Sum the weighted kernel contributions |wj(\mathbf{p}j)| Kj(\mathbf{p}) for all accepted impulses to produce ns(\mathbf{p}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def locallycontrolledspotnoise(p, densityfield, orientationfield, scalefield, kernelmatrices, gaussianmagnitude, randomgen): totalnoise = 0.0 # Generate impulses on the fly using jittering and PRNG # The sources do not specify the exact grid or jittering parameters. for pj, wj in generatejitteredimpulses(randomgen): # Density test: generate random variable xi independently of wj xival = randomgen.uniform(0.0, 1.0) dval = densityfield(pj) # Kronecker delta delta(xi < d) if xival < dval: # Impulse accepted # Compute relative position for kernel: p - pj prel = [p[i] - pj[i] for i in range(len(p))] prelext = prel + [1.0] # Apply orientation Rs and scale Ss transforms R = orientationfield(pj) S = scalefield(pj) ptransformed = matvecmul(S, matvecmul(R, prel)) ptransformedext = ptransformed + [1.0] # Evaluate kernel k(ptransformed) = sum of Gaussians kernelval = 0.0 for V in kernelmatrices: invV = invertmatrix(V) prod = matvecmul(invV, ptransformedext) exponent = -0.5 dotproduct(ptransformedext, prod) gaussianval = gaussianmagnitude math.exp(exponent) kernelval += gaussianval # Add weighted contribution: |wj| Kj(p) totalnoise += abs(wj) kernelval return totalnoise def generatejitteredimpulses(randomgen): # Standard jittered grid generation strategy # The sources do not specify the exact grid or jittering parameters. # For valid Python execution, this yields a single dummy impulse. yield ([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 1.0) def matvecmul(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j] v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(M))] def dotproduct(u, v): return sum(u[i] v[i] for i in range(len(u))) def invertmatrix(M): # Standard matrix inversion algorithm (e.g., Gauss-Jordan or LU decomposition) # For valid Python execution, returns identity for dummy input. return [[1.0 if i == j else 0.0 for j in range(len(M))] for i in range(len(M))] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parameterization Dependence: LCSN is parameterization dependent because impulses are generated in texture space. Changes in texture mapping can alter the noise pattern. Precision: Matrix inversion \mathbf{V}^{-1} must be handled carefully to ensure numerical stability, especially if \mathbf{V} is near-singular. Boundary Conditions: The density field d(\mathbf{p}) must be defined at boundaries; otherwise, impulse rejection behavior is undefined. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of impulses evaluated per evaluation point. Since impulses are generated on the fly and filtered by density, the effective number of impulses contributing to the sum varies spatially. Evaluating the kernel involves matrix operations for each impulse. Memory Complexity: Low, as impulses are generated on the fly and not stored in a large grid. Only the fields d, Rs, Ss and kernel parameters need to be stored. Strengths: Allows spatial control over noise density and structure. Suitable for authoring fuzzy surface details. Limitations: Parameterization dependent. Computationally demanding for direct volume rendering due to hundreds of evaluations per pixel along a ray. When to Use: When spatial control over noise density and orientation is required, and interactive visualization is not the primary constraint or if splatting with analytic filtering is used. When Not to Use: When parameterization independence is critical or when real-time volumetric rendering performance is paramount without optimization. Locally Controlled Spot Noise was introduced by Nicolas Pavie, Guillaume Gilet, Jean-Michel Dischler, Eric Galin, and Djamchid Ghazanfarpour in 2016 in the paper "Volumetric Spot Noise for Procedural 3D Shell Texture Synthesis". It extends the original Spot Noise concept [vW91, dLvL97] to provide better spatial control for procedural texture synthesis, particularly for shell textures. The method addresses limitations of previous procedural noise methods like Gabornoise, which could only produce Gaussian patterns. name: Gabor Noise
head: GPU Gabor Noise (Procedural), Sparse convolution noise using Gabor kernel
body: Gabor noise is a procedural noise function that generates band-limited, anisotropic or isotropic patterns by convolving a sparse set of random impulses with a Gabor kernel. It solves the problem of visible kernel structures common in general sparse convolution noise at low densities, while providing explicit spectral control over orientation, frequency, and bandwidth. Unlike its sibling Locally Controlled Spot Noise, which allows spatial variation of kernel parameters, standard Gabor noise typically uses fixed or globally varied parameters to define a specific power spectrum. Gabor noise builds on the sparse convolution framework defined in Spot Noise. It replaces the generic kernel with a Gabor kernel, which is the product of a circular Gaussian and a 2D cosine wave. Inputs: Query point (x, y) in 2D space. Random point positions \{(xi, yi)\} distributed according to a Poisson impulse process. Random weights \{wi\}. Kernel parameters for each point: magnitude Ki, inverse width ai, frequency F{0,i}, and orientation \omega{0,i}. Output: Noise value N(x, y). The sources describe a procedural implementation where properties are generated on the fly using a pseudo-random number generator to ensure random accessibility. A virtual grid is used where the cell size equals the Gabor kernel radius, requiring only the containing cell and direct neighboring cells for evaluation. The Gabor kernel in the spatial domain g(x, y) is defined as: g(x, y) = K e^{-\pi a^2 (x^2 + y^2)} \cos [2\pi F0 (x \cos \omega0 + y \sin \omega0)] Where: K is the magnitude. a is the inverse width of the Gaussian. F0 is the frequency of the cosine. \omega0 is the orientation of the cosine. The noise value N(x, y) is the sum of weighted kernels centered at random positions: N(x, y) = \sumi wi g(Ki, ai, F{0,i}, \omega{0,i}; x - xi, y - yi) Substituting the kernel definition: N(x, y) = \sumi wi Ki e^{-\pi ai^2 ((x - xi)^2 + (y - yi)^2)} \cos [2\pi F{0,i} ((x - xi) \cos \omega{0,i} + (y - yi) \sin \omega{0,i})] The power spectrum of the Gabor kernel in the frequency domain G(fx, fy) is a pair of circular Gaussians: G(fx, fy) = \frac{K}{2a^2} \exp \left[ -\frac{\pi}{2a^2} ((fx \pm F0 \cos \omega0)^2 + (fy \pm F0 \sin \omega0)^2) \right] This indicates that the energy is concentrated around polar coordinates (F0, \omega0) in the frequency domain, with a width determined by a. Fixed Parameters: When Ki, ai, F{0,i}, \omega{0,i} are constant for all i, the noise is anisotropic and band-limited. \omega0 controls orientation. F0 controls frequency. a controls bandwidth. Varying Parameters: When parameters vary, the power spectrum is the Gabor kernel integrated over the parameter distribution. If \omega{0,i} is uniformly distributed over [0, 2\pi), the noise becomes isotropic band-limited noise. GUI Specification: The original implementation uses graphical user interface widgets to specify how parameters vary to define the power spectrum. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the evaluation of Gabor noise for a single query point. In practice, points are generated procedurally on the fly using a PRNG to ensure random accessibility. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gabornoise(x, y, points): """ Evaluate Gabor noise at (x, y). Args: x (float): X coordinate of the query point. y (float): Y coordinate of the query point. points (list of dict): List of random points. Each dict contains: 'x': xi (float) 'y': yi (float) 'w': wi (float) 'K': Ki (float) 'a': ai (float) 'F0': F{0,i} (float) 'omega0': omega{0,i} (float) Returns: float: The noise value N(x, y). """ result = 0.0 for p in points: # Relative coordinates dx = x - p['x'] dy = y - p['y'] # Gaussian envelope: exp(-pi a^2 (dx^2 + dy^2)) gaussianarg = -math.pi (p['a'] 2) (dx2 + dy2) gaussianval = math.exp(gaussianarg) # Cosine component: cos(2 pi F0 (dx cos(omega0) + dy sin(omega0))) cosomega = math.cos(p['omega0']) sinomega = math.sin(p['omega0']) cosarg = 2 math.pi p['F0'] (dx cosomega + dy sinomega) cosval = math.cos(cosarg) # Kernel value kernelval = p['K'] gaussianval cosval # Weighted sum result += p['w'] kernelval return result Boundary Conditions: As a sparse convolution noise, it does not have inherent periodicity unless the point distribution and parameters are made periodic. A variant where noise parameters are defined in 2D screen space while point distribution is in 3D object space, used for coherent stylization in non-photorealistic rendering. Gabor noise is used to generate noise directly on parametric surfaces without requiring a 3D volume or texture mapping setup. The method supports analytic anisotropic filtering of the noise. Time Complexity: Approximately O(N) per query, where N is the number of random points within the evaluation radius, with about nine contributing kernels needed per point in 2D. Memory Complexity: O(1) storage requirements relative to the resolution, as it is a procedural function relying on a fixed number of random points. Performance: Speed is generally slower than Perlin noise due to the higher computational cost of the kernel evaluation and the need to iterate over random points. Strengths: Provides explicit spectral control (orientation, frequency, bandwidth). Avoids visible kernel structures at low densities compared to general sparse convolution. Supports setup-free surface noise and analytic filtering. Has a Gaussian amplitude distribution. Limitations: Requires more computation per point than lattice noises. When to use: When spectral control is required, or when generating noise on surfaces without setup overhead. When not to use: When performance is critical and precise spectral control is not required, simpler noise functions are preferred. Gabor noise was introduced by Lagae et al. in 2009. It was presented in the paper "A Survey of Procedural Noise Functions" and related works [LLDD09a, LLDD09b, LLD09]. The method extends the framework of sparse convolution noise by introducing the Gabor kernel, which combines a Gaussian envelope with a cosine wave. It is used for setup-free surface noise and analytic anisotropic filtering of noise. name: Random Spots Noise
head: Cellular Noise (Spot variant), Spots Pattern
body: Random Spots Noise is a procedural noise function that generates random spots within a 3D grid cell, supporting multiple shapes (step, linear, quadratic) and jitter. It solves the problem of generating organic, spot-like structures for volume rendering by evaluating a 3x3x3 neighborhood of grid cells and applying a shape function to each spot's distance. Unlike its sibling Worley Noise, which explicitly computes geometric distances to scattered feature points to create distinct cell boundaries, Random Spots Noise generates spots within grid cells using deterministic seeds, creating isolated spot intensities. It builds on Spot Noise by defining a specific sparse convolution kernel where impulses are placed deterministically within grid cells. Inputs: pos: Input 3D position (float3). scale: Frequency multiplier (float). seed: Integer seed (int). size: Spot radius/threshold (float). minNum: Minimum spots per cell (int). maxNum: Maximum spots per cell (int). jitter: Random offset scale (float). shape: Profile shape enum (SHAPESTEP, SHAPELINEAR, SHAPEQUADRATIC). Outputs: val: The computed noise value, typically in the range [-1, 1] or [0, 1] depending on the shape function. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method relies on a deterministic pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) seeded by cell coordinates and a global seed to generate spot positions and counts. Steps: 1. If size < EPSILON, return 0.0f. 2. Compute integer grid coordinates: ix = \lfloor pos.x \cdot scale \rfloor iy = \lfloor pos.y \cdot scale \rfloor iz = \lfloor pos.z \cdot scale \rfloor 3. Compute fractional coordinates: u = pos.x - ix v = pos.y - iy w = pos.z - iz 4. Initialize val to -1.0f. 5. Loop over x, y, z from -1 to 1 (inclusive) to traverse the 3x3x3 neighborhood of grid cells. 6. For each neighbor cell (ix+x, iy+y, iz+z): a. Calculate the number of spots in the current neighbor cell using a deterministic PRNG seeded by the cell coordinates and global seed. The number of spots is typically clamped between minNum and maxNum. b. For each spot i in numSpots: i. Generate a random position for the spot within the local cell coordinates using the PRNG. Apply jitter if jitter > 0. ii. Calculate the distance from the query point to the spot in local coordinates: distU = u - spotUi distV = v - spotVi distW = w - spotWi iii. Compute the squared distance: distSq = distU^2 + distV^2 + distW^2 iv. Update val based on the shape: SHAPESTEP: If distSq < size, set val to 1.0f. Else, val remains -1.0f (or is updated to the maximum of current val and 1.0f if distSq < size). SHAPELINEAR: Use Manhattan distance D = |distU| + |distV| + |distW|. Apply linear falloff: val = \max(val, 1.0 - D / size). SHAPEQUADRATIC: Use Euclidean distance squared. Apply quadratic falloff: val = \max(val, 1.0 - distSq / size^2). 7. Return val. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def randomspotsnoise(pos, scale, seed, size, minnum, maxnum, jitter, shape): if size < 1e-6: return 0.0 ix = math.floor(pos[0] scale) iy = math.floor(pos[1] scale) iz = math.floor(pos[2] scale) u = pos[0] - ix v = pos[1] - iy w = pos[2] - iz val = -1.0 for x in range(-1, 2): for y in range(-1, 2): for z in range(-1, 2): cellx = ix + x celly = iy + y cellz = iz + z # Deterministic PRNG seeded by cell coordinates and global seed rng = PRNG(seed=seed, cellx=cellx, celly=celly, cellz=cellz) # Determine number of spots in this cell numspots = rng.nextint(minnum, maxnum) for i in range(numspots): # Generate spot position within local cell spotu = rng.nextfloat() spotv = rng.nextfloat() spotw = rng.nextfloat() # Apply jitter if jitter > 0: spotu = (spotu - 0.5) jitter + 0.5 spotv = (spotv - 0.5) jitter + 0.5 spotw = (spotw - 0.5) jitter + 0.5 # Calculate distance distu = u - spotu distv = v - spotv distw = w - spotw distsq = distu2 + distv2 + distw2 # Update value based on shape if shape == SHAPESTEP: if distsq < size: val = max(val, 1.0) elif shape == SHAPELINEAR: manhattandist = abs(distu) + abs(distv) + abs(distw) val = max(val, 1.0 - manhattandist / size) elif shape == SHAPEQUADRATIC: val = max(val, 1.0 - distsq / (size2)) return val Parameters: size: The radius/scale of the spots. If size < EPSILON, the function returns 0.0f. Typical values depend on the desired spot density. shape: Enum determining the falloff of the spot value. Options: SHAPESTEP, SHAPELINEAR, SHAPEQUADRATIC. jitter: Random offset scale. Controls the randomness of spot positions within the cell. minNum, maxNum: Control the density of spots per cell. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The function requires traversing the entire 3x3x3 neighborhood to correctly handle spots near cell edges. Precision issues may arise if size is very small or very large relative to the grid scale. Degenerate input (e.g., size = 0) is handled by returning 0.0f. Worley Cellular Noise is a procedural noise function that calculates the distance to the nearest feature point in a 3D grid, returning a value in [-1, 1]. It solves the problem of generating organic, cell-like structures for volume rendering by leveraging the spatial partitioning properties of Voronoi diagrams. Unlike its sibling Random Spots Noise, which generates spots within grid cells using deterministic seeds, Worley noise explicitly computes geometric distances to scattered feature points, creating distinct cell boundaries rather than isolated spot intensities. Time Complexity: O(1) per query, as it always evaluates a fixed 3x3x3 neighborhood (27 cells) and a bounded number of spots per cell. Memory Complexity: O(1), as no data structures are stored. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of spots per cell, which is bounded by maxNum. Strengths: Simple to implement, fast evaluation, supports various spot shapes. Limitations: Limited to spot-like patterns, may not capture complex organic structures as well as other noise functions. When to use: When spot-like patterns are desired, and computational efficiency is important. When not to use: When complex organic structures or cell-like boundaries are required. Origin: Not given in the sources. History and Development: Not given in the sources. Usage: Used in procedural texture generation and volume rendering for creating spot-like patterns. name: Worley Cellular Noise
head: Cellular Noise, Voronoi Noise
body: Worley Cellular Noise is a procedural noise function that calculates the distance to the nearest feature point in a 3D grid, returning a value in [-1, 1]. Inputs and Outputs Input: Query point (x, y, z), feature size size. Output: Scalar value v \in [-1, 1]. Data Structures The function is stateless and computes values on the fly without persistent data structures. Parameters size: Feature size. If size < EPSILON, the function returns 0.0. Algorithm Steps 1. Grid Decomposition: Compute the integer grid coordinates (ix, iy, iz) and the fractional coordinates (u, v, w) of the query point. 2. Initialization: Initialize minDist to a large value, specifically 1000000.0. 3. Neighborhood Search: Iterate through the 3x3x3 neighborhood of grid cells surrounding the query point. The loop indices dx, dy, dz range from -1 to 1. 4. Feature Point Generation: For each neighbor cell (ix+dx, iy+dy, iz+dz), determine the number of feature points contained within that cell using a deterministic random seed derived from the cell coordinates. 5. Distance Calculation: For each feature point in the current neighbor cell, calculate its squared distance from the query point in local coordinates. 6. Minimum Distance Update: Update minDist if the current point's distance is smaller. 7. Normalization: Return the normalized result using the formula v = \text{saturate}(\text{minDist}) \times 2.0 - 1.0, where \text{saturate}(x) clamps x to [0, 1]. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def worleycellularnoise(x, y, z, size): EPSILON = 1e-6 if size < EPSILON: return 0.0 # 1. Grid decomposition ix = math.floor(x) iy = math.floor(y) iz = math.floor(z) u = x - ix v = y - iy w = z - iz # 2. Initialization mindist = 1000000.0 # 3. Neighborhood search (-1 to 1) for dx in range(-1, 2): for dy in range(-1, 2): for dz in range(-1, 2): # 4. Deterministic seed from cell coordinates seed = (ix + dx) 73856093 ^ (iy + dy) 19349663 ^ (iz + dz) 83492791 # Number of points in cell numpoints = (seed & 0xFF) + 1 for p in range(numpoints): # Feature point in local cell coordinates fx = ((seed (p + 1) 2654435761) >> 24) / 256.0 fy = ((seed (p + 2) 2654435761) >> 24) / 256.0 fz = ((seed (p + 3) 2654435761) >> 24) / 256.0 # Global coordinates gx = ix + dx + fx gy = iy + dy + fy gz = iz + dz + fz # 5. Squared distance calculation distsq = (x - gx)2 + (y - gy)2 + (z - gz)2 # 6. Update minimum if distsq < mindist: mindist = distsq # 7. Normalization per source if mindist > 1.0: mindist = 1.0 if mindist < 0.0: mindist = 0.0 return mindist 2.0 - 1.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundaries: The 3x3x3 neighborhood ensures that the nearest feature point is found even if it lies in an adjacent cell. Degenerate Input: If size is less than EPSILON, the function returns 0.0 to avoid undefined behavior. name: Periodic Cellular Structure Replication
head: FRep cellular model, Periodic Cellular Microstructure Replication, Space Mapping Replication, Unit Cell Replication, infinite cellular structure generation
body: Periodic Cellular Structure Replication is a method for generating infinite cellular microstructures by applying a periodic space mapping function to a base unit cell defined on a finite interval. It solves the problem of modeling regular lattices or truss-based microstructures without explicit geometric duplication, allowing for continuous representation of infinite domains. Unlike sibling methods that rely on discrete tiling or voxelization, this approach uses a continuous real function to map coordinates, enabling seamless blending and parametric control over the lattice geometry. The method constructs an infinite structure by transforming input coordinates through a periodic replication function before evaluating a base geometric function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A continuous real function f(x, y, z) defining the unit cell geometry, and a periodic replication function g(t). Output: A scalar field r(x, y, z) representing the infinite cellular structure. Data Structures: Unit Cell Interval I: Defined by bounds x{min}, x{max}, y{min}, y{max}, z{min}, z{max}. Replication Function g(t): A periodic function mapping real numbers to [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Define the unit cell geometry using the continuous real function f on the interval I. 2. Select a periodic replication function g(t), typically constrained to the range [0, 1]. 3. For any input coordinate (x, y, z), compute the mapped coordinates by applying g to each axis, scaled by the interval dimensions, and offset by the minimum bounds. 4. Evaluate the unit cell function f at the mapped coordinates to produce the final value. Formula: The replicated structure is defined by the equation: r(x, y, z) = f \left( x{min} + g(x) \cdot (x{max} - x{min }), \ y{min} + g(y) \cdot (y{max} - y{min }), \ z{min} + g(z) \cdot (z{max} - z{min }) \right) Where: f(x, y, z) is the continuous real function defining the unit cell geometry on interval I. g(t) is the periodic replication function, where g(t) \in [0, 1] for all t. I is the bounding interval of the unit cell, defined as x{min} \le x \le x{max}, y{min} \le y \le y{max}, z{min} \le z \le z{max}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def periodiccellularreplication(x, y, z, f, g, bounds): """ Computes the value of an infinite cellular structure at (x, y, z). Args: x, y, z: Input coordinates. f: Function defining the unit cell geometry. g: Periodic replication function mapping to [0, 1]. bounds: Tuple (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax). Returns: Scalar value r(x, y, z). """ xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax = bounds mappedx = xmin + g(x) (xmax - xmin) mappedy = ymin + g(y) (ymax - ymin) mappedz = zmin + g(z) (zmax - zmin) return f(mappedx, mappedy, mappedz) Parameters and Typical Values: g(t): Common choices include the Sawtooth wave or Triangle wave. The Sawtooth wave is often implemented using Fourier series with a finite number of harmonics (e.g., 20 or 50) to approximate the discontinuity. f: Depends on the specific microstructure (e.g., spherical shell, rods). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuity: Geometric connectivity discontinuities (C^0 discontinuity) can occur at the boundaries of replicated unit cells if the base function f or the replication function g is not continuous. Artifacts: When using Fourier series approximations for the Sawtooth wave, artifacts may appear in the neighborhood of discontinuities (Gibbs phenomenon) if the number of harmonics is insufficient. The fundamental component of this method, resulting in C^0-discontinuous functions on cell faces unless the unit cell possesses full connectivity. A procedure to model irregular microstructures like porous media by replicating basic pore shapes with variable parameters and pseudo-random variations. The procedure selects a basic pore shape such as a sphere or ellipsoid, replicates it in space with variable parameters, introduces pseudo-random variations of pore positions and sizes, and subtracts the pores from a given initial shape. The space mapping for a basic pore with defining function Fp is computed as x0 = px \sin(qx x), y0 = py \sin(qy x), z0 = pz \sin(qz x), yielding Fr = Fp(x0, y0, z0). The final microstructure is obtained via set-theoretic subtraction: Fm(x, y, z) = F \setminus \alpha Fr. Parameters px, py, pz > 0 specify linear scaling for the coordinates, while qx, qy, qz > 0 control the replication frequency along each axis. F defines the initial shape, Fm defines the final microstructure, and \alpha is a parameter in the subtraction operation. Complexity: The computational cost is dominated by the evaluation of the base function f and the replication function g. It is O(1) per sample point. Strengths: Enables the modeling of infinite cellular structures and microstructures without explicit geometric duplication, supporting blending operations and parametric control. Limitations: Discontinuities at cell boundaries can cause visual or geometric artifacts if not handled by the choice of g or f. The method originates from the field of procedural function-based modeling of volumetric microstructures, specifically within the context of FRep (Function Representation) models. It was developed to address the limitations of BRep and voxel models, which require finite bounding boxes and explicit sets of unit cell copies, by providing a continuous space mapping approach for infinite lattices. name: Sawtooth Replication Function
head: FRep Cellular Structure Replication
body: The Sawtooth Replication Function is a basic periodic replication function used to generate infinite cellular structures from a unit cell defined by a continuous real function. It is a core component of the Periodic Cellular Structure Replication method. Due to its nature, the resulting cellular model exhibits geometric discontinuity on cell faces if the unit cell lacks connectivity, and can be C^0-discontinuous even with geometric connectivity; full unit cell connectivity is required to obtain a C^0-continuous function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A real-valued coordinate t. Output: A real-valued periodic coordinate g(t). Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute the shifted normalized position: u = \frac{t}{a} + \frac{1}{2}. 2. Compute the integer part: k = \text{floor}(u). 3. Compute the remainder: r = t - k \cdot a. 4. Compute the output: g(t) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{r}{a}. Formula: The replication function g(t) is defined as: g(t) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{a} \left( t - \text{floor}\left(\frac{t}{a} + \frac{1}{2}\right) \right) where \text{floor}(x) returns the greatest integer less than or equal to x. Parameters: a: The period of the sawtooth wave. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The resulting cellular model has geometric discontinuity on the faces of the cells if the unit cell has no connectivity property. Even if the unit cell has geometric connectivity, the resulting function can be C^0-discontinuous on the faces of each cell. Full unit cell connectivity is required to obtain C^0-continuous functions. The use of floor can introduce precision issues near boundaries where t/a + 1/2 is an integer; standard floating-point arithmetic should be used, but care must be taken with boundary conditions in high-precision rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sawtoothreplication(t: float, a: float) -> float: """ Computes the sawtooth replication function value. Args: t: Input coordinate. a: Period of the sawtooth wave. Returns: The replicated coordinate value. """ shifted = t / a + 0.5 k = math.floor(shifted) remainder = t - k a result = 0.5 + remainder / a return result The Triangle Wave Replication Function is a mathematical tool used to create C^1-continuous cellular structures. It sets itself apart from the Sawtooth Replication Function by ensuring smooth first-derivative continuity, provided the unit cell geometry is symmetric with respect to planes parallel to the cell faces and passing through their centers. It is chosen when higher continuity is required compared to the basic sawtooth function. The formula is not given in the sources. A connectivity criterion for unit cells ensuring that boundary curves at opposite faces are congruent, allowing replicated cells to connect at these curves. It requires the defining function to be continuous across the entire cellular structure by ensuring function values are identical at opposite faces. To verify full connectivity, check if f(x{min}, y, z) = f(x{max}, y, z) for all y, z \in I, f(x, y{min}, z) = f(x, y{max}, z) for all x, z \in I, and f(x, y, z{min}) = f(x, y, z{max}) for all x, y \in I. This ensures C^0-continuity of the resulting cellular structure. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a basis for generating infinite periodic structures. Limitations: Results in geometric discontinuity on cell faces if the unit cell lacks connectivity, and can be C^0-discontinuous even with geometric connectivity. When to use: When generating basic cellular structures where C^0 continuity is acceptable or when full connectivity is present. When not to use: When C^1 continuity is required or when the unit cell lacks connectivity. The Sawtooth Replication Function is described in the context of procedural function-based modelling of volumetric microstructures. It is part of a family of replication functions used to create infinite cellular structures by applying periodic replication to a unit cell. name: Triangle Wave Replication Function
head: Triangle Wave Replication, g(t) = 1 + (2/pi) arcsin
body: The Triangle Wave Replication Function is a mathematical tool used in procedural volume rendering and geometric modeling to create C^1-continuous cellular structures. It solves the continuity issues inherent in standard sawtooth replication functions, which can produce C^0-discontinuous functions or geometric artifacts on cell faces when the unit cell lacks full connectivity. It sets itself apart from its parent, the Sawtooth Replication Function, by ensuring smooth first-derivative continuity, provided the unit cell geometry is symmetric with respect to planes parallel to the cell faces and passing through their centers. The function maps a scalar input t to a periodic triangle wave output g(t) with a period of 2 and an amplitude range of [0, 2]. This mapping replaces the linear ramp of the sawtooth function with a triangular shape, eliminating the sharp corners that cause discontinuities in the derivative. Inputs and Outputs: Input: t \in \mathbb{R}, a scalar coordinate value (typically normalized or scaled by a period parameter a). Output: g(t) \in [0, 2], the replicated value. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The function is stateless and computed per-vertex or per-voxel. Formula: The exact formula for the triangle wave replication function is: g(t) = 1 + \frac{2}{\pi} \arcsin\left[\sin\left(\pi\left(t - \frac{1}{2}\right)\right)\right] Parameters: t: The input coordinate. In the context of cellular structures, this is often the coordinate value divided by the cell size a, i.e., t = x/a. The period is implicitly 2 due to the \pi scaling inside the sine function. Steps: 1. Shift the input t by -0.5. 2. Multiply the shifted value by \pi. 3. Compute the sine of the result. 4. Compute the arcsine of the sine result. 5. Scale the arcsine result by 2/\pi. 6. Add 1 to the result. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trianglewavereplication(t: float) -> float: """ Computes the triangle wave replication function g(t). Returns a value in [0, 2]. """ # Step 1-3: sin(pi (t - 0.5)) inner = math.sin(math.pi (t - 0.5)) # Step 4: arcsin(inner) # Note: inner should be in [-1, 1]. Floating point errors might push it slightly outside. # Clamp to [-1, 1] to prevent NaNs. inner = max(-1.0, min(1.0, inner)) arcsinval = math.asin(inner) # Step 5-6: 1 + (2/pi) arcsinval result = 1.0 + (2.0 / math.pi) arcsinval return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Symmetry Requirement: This function only yields C^1-continuous results if the unit cell geometry is symmetric with respect to planes parallel to the unit cell faces and passing through their center. If this symmetry is not present, the continuity benefits are lost. Precision: The asin function is sensitive to inputs outside [-1, 1]. Due to floating-point arithmetic, sin might return values slightly outside this range (e.g., 1.0000000000000002), which would result in NaN. Clamping is necessary. A variant that uses a Fourier series to approximate a sawtooth wave, allowing for C^1 and higher continuity but introducing artifacts. The formula is g(t) = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{\pi} \sum{k=1}^{n} \frac{\sin(2\pi k a t)}{k}, where n is the number of harmonics. Using this method adds artifacts (projection-type copies of the unit cell geometry) to the neighborhood of cell faces, which is inappropriate in most cases. Even 50 harmonics are not enough for a good approximation of the sawtooth function. While Fourier series allows C^1 continuity, it requires many harmonics and introduces artifacts, whereas the standard triangle wave is simpler and artifact-free for symmetric cells. Time Complexity: O(1) per evaluation. It involves basic trigonometric operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary storage is needed. Strengths: Provides C^1 continuity for symmetric unit cells, avoiding the geometric discontinuities and surface artifacts associated with standard sawtooth replication when full connectivity is absent. Limitations: Requires the unit cell geometry to be symmetric with respect to the cell center planes. If this condition is not met, the continuity guarantee does not hold. When to use: When modeling cellular microstructures with symmetric unit cells and smooth blending operations are required. When not to use: When the unit cell lacks the required symmetry, or when computational cost of trigonometric functions is prohibitive (though usually negligible compared to other rendering steps). The Triangle Wave Replication Function was introduced in the context of procedural function-based modeling of volumetric microstructures. It addresses the limitations of regular lattice models and standard cellular structures regarding geometric continuity. The method is detailed in the paper "Procedural function-based modelling of volumetric microstructures". The approach builds on the idea that while regular lattices have better analytical properties, they are limited in geometry. Cellular structures offer more geometric flexibility but suffer from continuity issues at cell faces. The triangle wave was selected as an alternative to the sawtooth wave to achieve C^1 continuity for symmetric unit cells.
