It differs from standard FBM by dampening height accumulation with gradient magnitude, and from basic Derivative FBM by explicitly returning the derivative vector for lighting and erosion calculations. Choose it when generating detailed, physically plausible landscapes with flat plateaux and accentuated steep regions. Not given in the sources. Originated in shader development and documented in procedural noise technique repositories. The method builds on Value Noise and FBM, adding analytic derivatives to modulate octave contribution based on local steepness. skills/skills/shader-dev/techniques/procedural-noise.md at main..., https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/skills/blob/main/skills/shader-dev/techniques/procedural-noise.md, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Noise Derivative FBM
head: FBM with noise derivatives, Tweaked Fractal Brownian Motion using noise derivatives
body: Noise Derivative FBM is a procedural terrain generation technique that modulates Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) height accumulation using the analytic derivatives of value noise rather than the noise values themselves. It solves the problem of repetitive, uniform terrain structures common in standard FBM by accentuating steep regions and creating flat plateaux, resulting in more detailed and physically plausible landscapes. It differs from standard FBM by using the gradient magnitude to dampen height accumulation, and from basic Derivative FBM by explicitly returning the derivative vector alongside the scalar noise value for use in lighting and erosion calculations. Inputs: uTexture: A sampler2D uniform holding a pre-generated 256×256 grayscale noise texture. p: The input 2D coordinate vector for the terrain sample. m: A 2×2 rotation matrix used to rotate the sampling coordinate between octaves. Outputs: A scalar height value representing the terrain elevation at p. Data Structures: The noise texture is accessed via bilinear interpolation at LOD 0. Coordinates are normalized to [0, 1] by dividing integer grid coordinates by 256.0. Parameters: Initial scale factor b = 2.5. Initial height accumulator a = 0.0. Initial derivative accumulator d = vec2(0.0). Coordinate scale scl = 2.75. Coordinate offset multiplier 0.06. Octave count: 8. Height decay factor: 0.85 per octave. Amplitude decay factor: -0.4 per octave. Final height multiplier: 3.0. Steps: 1. Noise Sampling (noised function): For a given 2D coordinate x: 1. Calculate integer part p = floor(x) and fractional part f = fract(x). 2. Calculate interpolation weights u = f f (3.0 - 2.0 f). 3. Sample the four corners of the noise texture at normalized coordinates (p + offset) / 256.0 with LOD 0 to get values a, b, c, d: a = textureLod(uTexture, (p + vec2(0.0, 0.0)) / 256.0, 0).x b = textureLod(uTexture, (p + vec2(1.0, 0.0)) / 256.0, 0).x c = textureLod(uTexture, (p + vec2(0.0, 1.0)) / 256.0, 0).x d = textureLod(uTexture, (p + vec2(1.0, 1.0)) / 256.0, 0).x 4. Calculate the noise value using bilinear interpolation: \text{noiseValue} = a + (b - a)ux + (c - a)uy + (a - b - c + d)ux uy 5. Calculate the noise derivative vector: \text{noiseDerivative} = 6.0 \cdot f \cdot (1.0 - f) \cdot (\text{vec2}(b - a, c - a) + (a - b - c + d) \cdot \text{vec2}(uy, ux)) 6. Return vec3(noiseValue, noiseDerivative). 2. FBM Accumulation (terrain function): 1. Initialize p1 = p 0.06, a = 0.0, b = 2.5, d = vec2(0.0), scl = 2.75. 2. Loop 8 times: a. Call noised(p1) to get n (where n.x is value, n.yz is derivative). b. Accumulate derivatives: d += n.yz. c. Update height: a += b n.x / (dot(d, d) + 1.0). d. Update amplitude: b = -0.4. e. Update height scale: a = 0.85. f. Transform coordinate: p1 = m p1 scl. 3. Return a 3.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def noised(utexture, x): # 1. Integer and fractional parts px = math.floor(x[0]) py = math.floor(x[1]) fx = x[0] - px fy = x[1] - py # 2. Interpolation weights ux = fx fx (3.0 - 2.0 fx) uy = fy fy (3.0 - 2.0 fy) # 3. Sample corners (normalized by 256.0) p00 = (px + 0.0) / 256.0 p10 = (px + 1.0) / 256.0 p01 = (py + 0.0) / 256.0 p11 = (py + 1.0) / 256.0 # Bilinear interpolation def bilinear(tex, u, v): tu = u 256.0 tv = v 256.0 iu = int(math.floor(tu)) iv = int(math.floor(tv)) fu = tu - iu fv = tv - iv iu = max(0, min(255, iu)) iv = max(0, min(255, iv)) iu1 = min(255, iu + 1) iv1 = min(255, iv + 1) v00 = tex[iv][iu] v10 = tex[iv][iu1] v01 = tex[iv1][iu] v11 = tex[iv1][iu1] top = v00 + (v10 - v00) fu bottom = v01 + (v11 - v01) fu return top + (bottom - top) fv a = bilinear(utexture, p00, p00) b = bilinear(utexture, p10, p00) c = bilinear(utexture, p00, p01) d = bilinear(utexture, p10, p01) # 4. Noise Value noisevalue = a + (b - a) ux + (c - a) uy + (a - b - c + d) ux uy # 5. Noise Derivative derivx = 6.0 fx (1.0 - fx) ((b - a) + (a - b - c + d) uy) derivy = 6.0 fy (1.0 - fy) ((c - a) + (a - b - c + d) ux) return (noisevalue, derivx, derivy) def terrain(p, utexture, m): p1 = [p[0] 0.06, p[1] 0.06] a = 0.0 b = 2.5 dx = 0.0 dy = 0.0 scl = 2.75 for in range(8): nval, ndx, ndy = noised(utexture, p1) # Accumulate derivatives dx += ndx dy += ndy # Update height dotdd = dx dx + dy dy a += b nval / (dotdd + 1.0) # Update amplitude b = -0.4 # Update height scale a = 0.85 # Transform coordinate: p1 = m p1 scl newx = (m[0][0] p1[0] + m[0][1] p1[1]) scl newy = (m[1][0] p1[0] + m[1][1] p1[1]) scl p1 = [newx, newy] return a 3.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: At f=0 or f=1, the derivative is zero. Texture Dependency: The technique requires a pre-generated noise texture. Degenerate Input: If p is constant, the terrain will be flat. Time Complexity: O(O) where O is the number of octaves (8 in the source). Each octave requires one noise texture lookup with bilinear interpolation and constant arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the algorithm state, plus O(N^2) for the noise texture storage (256×256 floats). Performance: The method is computationally more expensive than standard FBM due to the derivative calculation and the additional texture sampling overhead. Strengths: Produces terrains with steeper regions and flat plateaux, reducing visual repetition and increasing detail compared to standard FBM. Limitations: Requires a pre-generated noise texture. The derivative accumulation can lead to numerical instability if not clamped, though the dot(d,d) + 1.0 denominator mitigates this. When to use: When realistic, varied terrain with distinct steep/flat features is desired, and performance allows for derivative calculations. When not to use: When simple, uniform noise is sufficient. The technique was popularized in the context of raymarching and procedural terrain generation by Maxime Heckel in his blog post "Painting with Math: A Gentle Study of Raymarching". It builds upon the concept of Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) and value noise, extending it by leveraging the analytic gradient of the noise function to influence the height accumulation. Painting with Math: A Gentle Study of Raymarching, https://blog.maximeheckel.com/posts/painting-with-math-a-gentle-study-of-raymarching/, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Tiled Value Noise
head: Periodic 3D Value Noise
body: Tiled Value Noise is a procedural noise generation method that produces seamless, periodic 3D scalar fields by wrapping the lattice indices of a standard value noise implementation. It solves the problem of visible discontinuities and directional stripe artifacts that occur when standard value noise is tiled or repeated. Unlike standard value noise, which assumes an infinite domain, Tiled Value Noise constrains the signal to a fixed integer period, ensuring that the noise pattern matches perfectly at the boundaries of the tile. It serves as the foundational noise primitive for higher-level techniques such as Fractal Value Noise with Domain Warping, where seamless tiling is required to avoid visible seams in the warped domain [8323-fractal-value-noise-with-domain-warping.md]. Inputs: Input coordinates (x, y, z), a single integer frequency defining the tile period in lattice units, and a pre-generated 3D lattice array. Outputs: A scalar value N(x, y, z) in the range [0, 1]. Data Structures: lattice is a 3D array of shape (frequency, frequency, frequency) containing random floats in [0, 1] stored as np.float32. Algorithm Steps: 1. Lattice Generation: Create the tiled random lattice using a random number generator. 2. Coordinate Mapping: Map input coordinates to lattice space: px = (x + 1.0) \cdot 0.5 \cdot f, py = (y + 1.0) \cdot 0.5 \cdot f, pz = (z + 1.0) \cdot 0.5 \cdot f. 3. Integer Index Calculation: Compute integer grid indices with modulo for periodicity: ix = \lfloor px \rfloor \pmod f, iy = \lfloor py \rfloor \pmod f, iz = \lfloor pz \rfloor \pmod f. 4. Fractional Parts and Fade: Compute fractional parts and apply Perlin's quintic fade: fx = \text{fade}(px - \lfloor px \rfloor), fy = \text{fade}(py - \lfloor py \rfloor), fz = \text{fade}(pz - \lfloor pz \rfloor). 5. Next Indices: Compute next indices with modulo: i{x1} = (ix + 1) \pmod f, i{y1} = (iy + 1) \pmod f, i{z1} = (iz + 1) \pmod f. 6. X-Axis Interpolation: Interpolate along X for four corners: c{00} = \text{lattice}[iz, iy, ix] \cdot (1.0 - fx) + \text{lattice}[iz, iy, i{x1}] \cdot fx, c{10} = \text{lattice}[iz, i{y1}, ix] \cdot (1.0 - fx) + \text{lattice}[iz, i{y1}, i{x1}] \cdot fx, c{01} = \text{lattice}[i{z1}, iy, ix] \cdot (1.0 - fx) + \text{lattice}[i{z1}, iy, i{x1}] \cdot fx, c{11} = \text{lattice}[i{z1}, i{y1}, ix] \cdot (1.0 - fx) + \text{lattice}[i{z1}, i{y1}, i{x1}] \cdot fx. 7. Y-Axis Interpolation: Interpolate along Y: \text{lower} = c{00} \cdot (1.0 - fy) + c{10} \cdot fy, \text{upper} = c{01} \cdot (1.0 - fy) + c{11} \cdot fy. 8. Z-Axis Interpolation: Interpolate along Z: N(x, y, z) = \text{lower} \cdot (1.0 - fz) + \text{upper} \cdot fz. Formula: Fade function f(v) = v^2 (v (6v - 15) + 10). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def fade(v): """Perlin's quintic fade function.""" return v v v (v (v 6.0 - 15.0) + 10.0) def tiledvaluenoise(x, y, z, frequency, lattice): """Generate tiled 3D value noise.""" # Map input coordinates to lattice space [0, frequency] px = (x + 1.0) 0.5 frequency py = (y + 1.0) 0.5 frequency pz = (z + 1.0) 0.5 frequency # Compute integer grid indices with modulo for periodicity ix = int(np.floor(px)) % frequency iy = int(np.floor(py)) % frequency iz = int(np.floor(pz)) % frequency # Compute fractional parts and apply fade fx = fade(px - np.floor(px)) fy = fade(py - np.floor(py)) fz = fade(pz - np.floor(pz)) # Compute next indices with modulo ix1 = (ix + 1) % frequency iy1 = (iy + 1) % frequency iz1 = (iz + 1) % frequency # Interpolate along X axis for four corners c00 = lattice[iz, iy, ix] (1.0 - fx) + lattice[iz, iy, ix1] fx c10 = lattice[iz, iy1, ix] (1.0 - fx) + lattice[iz, iy1, ix1] fx c01 = lattice[iz1, iy, ix] (1.0 - fx) + lattice[iz1, iy, ix1] fx c11 = lattice[iz1, iy1, ix] (1.0 - fx) + lattice[iz1, iy1, ix1] fx # Interpolate along Y axis lower = c00 (1.0 - fy) + c10 fy upper = c01 (1.0 - fy) + c11 fy # Interpolate along Z axis return lower (1.0 - fz) + upper fz Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Directional stripes are avoided by using only integer coefficients in coordinate transforms and periodic lattice sampling, eliminating the need for sine/cosine functions. Boundary precision is handled naturally: when an input coordinate maps exactly to the tile boundary (e.g., px = f), the floor and modulo operations wrap the index to 0, ensuring continuity. A multi-scale, domain-warped value noise technique that produces seamless tiled noise without fixed-direction periodic stripes, using independent lattices for warping and sampling. It builds on Tiled Value Noise to ensure that the domain warping itself does not introduce visible seams [8323-fractal-value-noise-with-domain-warping.md]. Time complexity is O(1) per sample due to a fixed number of arithmetic operations and array lookups. Memory complexity is O(f^3) for the lattice storage. Not given in the sources. Tiled Value Noise is a variation of value noise designed for procedural generation where seamless repetition is required. It leverages periodic boundary conditions to avoid tiling artifacts common in standard noise functions. mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, https://github.com/mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Fractal Value Noise with Domain Warping
head: Tiled Fractal Noise
body:
Fractal Value Noise with Domain Warping is a multi-scale procedural noise technique that generates seamless tiled volume data by warping the input coordinate space before sampling. It solves the problem of directional stripe artifacts common in standard tiled noise by using independent lattices for warping and sampling, ensuring isotropic, organic patterns without fixed-direction periodicity. It builds on Tiled Value Noise by adding non-linear coordinate distortion and fractal summation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D coordinates (x, y, z), a detail parameter d \in [0.0, 1.0], and a list of pre-generated value noise lattices. Output: A scalar value v \in [0.0, 1.0] representing the noise amplitude at the warped location. Data Structures: lattices: A list of value noise lookup tables. The method requires at least three distinct lattices for warping and sampling. Parameters: Warp strength base: 0.12 Warp strength scale: 0.08 per detail unit Weight decay base: 0.52 Weight decay scale: 0.16 per detail unit Detail parameter d: Range [0.0, 1.0] Steps: 1. Calculate warp strength W: W = 0.12 + 0.08 \cdot 	ext{clip}(d, 0.0, 1.0) 2. Select warping lattices Lx, Ly, Lz from the available lattices list: Lx = 	ext{lattices}[0] Ly = 	ext{lattices}[\min(1, 	ext{len}(	ext{lattices}) - 1)] Lz = 	ext{lattices}[\min(2, 	ext{len}(	ext{lattices}) - 1)] 3. Compute warp offsets using linear combinations of input coordinates to maintain periodicity. The offsets are centered around zero by subtracting 0.5: wx = 	ext{value
oise\slice}(Lx, x + y, y - z, z + x) - 0.5 wy = 	ext{value
oise\slice}(Ly, 2.0x - y, x + z, y + z) - 0.5 wz = 	ext{value
oise\slice}(Lz, x - z, 2.0y + z, x + y - z) - 0.5 4. Apply warp to coordinates: x' = x + W \cdot wx y' = y + W \cdot wy z' = z + W \cdot wz 5. Define five coordinate transforms for multi-scale sampling. Let (x', y', z') be the warped coordinates: Transform 0: (x', y', z') Transform 1: (x' + y', y' + z', z' + x') Transform 2: (2.0x' - y', x' + 2.0y', z' + y') Transform 3: (x' - z', 2.0y' + z', x' + y' - z') Transform 4: (2.0x' + z', y' - x', 2.0z' + y') 6. Sample noise at each scale using rotating transforms. For i from 0 to N-1 (where N is the number of lattices): 	ext{sample}i = 	ext{value
oise\slice}(	ext{lattices}[i], 	ext{transforms}[i \pmod 5]) 7. Calculate weights for fractal summation. The first weight is 1.0. Subsequent weights decay based on the detail parameter: 	ext{weights}[0] = 1.0 	ext{weights}[i] = (0.52 + d \cdot 0.16)^i \quad 	ext{for } i > 0 8. Normalize and clip the result: v = 	ext{clip}\left(  rac{\sum{i=0}^{N-1} 	ext{sample}i \cdot 	ext{weights}[i]}{\sum{i=0}^{N-1} 	ext{weights}[i]}, 0.0, 1.0 ight) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def valuenoiseslice(lattice, x, y, z): """Standard 3D value noise lookup using linear interpolation on a tiled grid. """ ix, iy, iz = int(np.floor(x)), int(np.floor(y)), int(np.floor(z)) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def hash(i, j, k): return lattice[(i % lattice.shape[0], j % lattice.shape[1], k % lattice.shape[2])] v000 = hash(ix, iy, iz) v100 = hash(ix+1, iy, iz) v010 = hash(ix, iy+1, iz) v110 = hash(ix+1, iy+1, iz) v001 = hash(ix, iy, iz+1) v101 = hash(ix+1, iy, iz+1) v011 = hash(ix, iy+1, iz+1) v111 = hash(ix+1, iy+1, iz+1) x1 = lerp(v000, v100, fx) x2 = lerp(v010, v110, fx) y1 = lerp(v001, v101, fx) y2 = lerp(v011, v111, fx) z1 = lerp(x1, x2, fy) z2 = lerp(y1, y2, fy) return lerp(z1, z2, fz) def fractalvaluenoisewithdomainwarp(x, y, z, detail, lattices): """ Generates fractal value noise with domain warping. Args: x, y, z: Input 3D coordinates. detail: Detail parameter in [0.0, 1.0]. lattices: List of value noise lookup tables (3D arrays). Returns: float: Noise value in [0.0, 1.0]. """ # 1. Calculate warp strength warpstrength = 0.12 + 0.08 np.clip(detail, 0.0, 1.0) # 2. Select warping lattices latticex = lattices[0] latticey = lattices[min(1, len(lattices) - 1)] latticez = lattices[min(2, len(lattices) - 1)] # 3. Compute warp offsets warpx = valuenoiseslice(latticex, x + y, y - z, z + x) - 0.5 warpy = valuenoiseslice(latticey, 2.0 x - y, x + z, y + z) - 0.5 warpz = valuenoiseslice(latticez, x - z, 2.0 y + z, x + y - z) - 0.5 # 4. Apply warp to coordinates warpedx = x + warpstrength warpx warpedy = y + warpstrength warpy warpedz = z + warpstrength warpz # 5. Define coordinate transforms transforms = [ (warpedx, warpedy, warpedz), (warpedx + warpedy, warpedy + warpedz, warpedz + warpedx), (2.0 warpedx - warpedy, warpedx + 2.0 warpedy, warpedz + warpedy), (warpedx - warpedz, 2.0 warpedy + warpedz, warpedx + warpedy - warpedz), (2.0 warpedx + warpedz, warpedy - warpedx, 2.0 warpedz + warpedy) ] # 6. Sample noise at each scale samples = [] for index, lattice in enumerate(lattices): transformidx = index % len(transforms) tx, ty, tz = transforms[transformidx] samples.append(valuenoiseslice(lattice, tx, ty, tz)) # 7. Calculate weights weights = [1.0] for index in range(1, len(lattices)): weight = (0.52 + detail 0.16) index weights.append(weight) # 8. Normalize and clip total = sum(s w for s, w in zip(samples, weights)) sumweights = sum(weights) if sumweights == 0: return 0.5 # Fallback for empty lattices, though unlikely given logic result = total / sumweights return np.clip(result, 0.0, 1.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The linear combinations in warp offset calculation (e.g., 2.0x - y) can amplify floating-point errors if coordinates are very large. Boundary Conditions: The method relies on the periodicity of the underlying tiled value noise. If the underlying noise implementation is not strictly periodic, the domain warping will introduce seams. Degenerate Input: If lattices is empty, the function should handle this gracefully. The pseudocode assumes at least one lattice. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of lattices used for fractal summation. Each lattice requires a constant number of value noise lookups. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the lattices. The warp calculation uses O(1) additional memory. Strengths: Produces organic, isotropic patterns without directional artifacts. Seamless tiling is maintained. Limitations: Requires pre-generated lattices. Not given in the sources. This method is described in the context of generating cloud masks for Unreal Engine 5 (UE5) in the repository Noise-Cloud by mingtu149411. mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, https://github.com/mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Perlin Noise 2D
head: 2D Perlin Noise, Classic Noise, Gradient Noise, Noise (Perlin), Perlin Noise (Improved), Perlin Noise Generation, Perlin's noise function
body: Perlin Noise 2D is a lattice gradient noise function that generates smooth, pseudo-random scalar values by interpolating dot products of gradient vectors and distance vectors at the corners of the integer lattice cell containing the query point. It solves the problem of creating continuous, coherent procedural textures for volumetric data (such as clouds, terrain, or smoke) without the repeating patterns of simple value noise. It sets itself apart from its sibling Simplex Noise by using a square grid topology and quintic interpolation, whereas Simplex uses a triangular grid to reduce directional artifacts. It is distinguished from Improved Perlin Noise (4D) by operating in two dimensions, resulting in lower computational cost but potentially higher grid-oriented artifacts. Inputs: Query point coordinates (X, Y) as floating-point values. A permutation table P of size 512 (see Data structures). Outputs: A scalar noise value N(X, Y), typically in the range [-1, 1] or [0, 1]. Data structures: Permutation Table (P): An array of 512 bytes (uint8). It is constructed by shuffling the integers 0 \dots 255 and duplicating the result to handle boundary conditions without modulo operations. Layout: P[i] = \text{Shuffle}(i \pmod{256}) for 0 \le i < 512. Initialization: The table is seeded using a random stream (e.g., Fisher-Yates shuffle) to ensure reproducibility. Formulas: 1. Fade Function: A quintic polynomial used to smooth the interpolation and ensure C^1 continuity: f(t) = 6t^5 - 15t^4 + 10t^3 2. Gradient Function: Computes the dot product of a gradient vector and the distance vector. For 2D, the gradient is selected from 8 directions based on the hash bits: \text{Grad}(h, x, y) = \begin{cases} x + y & \text{if } h \& 7 == 0 \\ x - y & \text{if } h \& 7 == 1 \\ -x + y & \text{if } h \& 7 == 2 \\ -x - y & \text{if } h \& 7 == 3 \\ x & \text{if } h \& 7 == 4 \\ -x & \text{if } h \& 7 == 5 \\ y & \text{if } h \& 7 == 6 \\ -y & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 3. Linear Interpolation: \text{Lerp}(t, a, b) = a + t(b - a) Algorithm Steps: 1. Grid Coordinates: Compute the integer coordinates of the cell containing (X, Y) and the fractional coordinates within the cell: XI = \lfloor X \rfloor \& 255, \quad YI = \lfloor Y \rfloor \& 255 XF = X - \lfloor X \rfloor, \quad YF = Y - \lfloor Y \rfloor Note: The bitwise AND with 255 handles the modulo for the doubled permutation table, so indices XI+1 and YI+1 are accessed directly via P without explicit modulo in the hot loop. 2. Hashing: Compute the permutation indices for the four corners of the cell using the permutation table P: AA = P[P[XI] + YI] AB = P[P[XI] + YI + 1] BA = P[P[XI + 1] + YI] BB = P[P[XI + 1] + YI + 1] 3. Fade: Compute the fade values for the fractional coordinates: U = f(XF), \quad V = f(YF) 4. Gradient Contributions: Compute the dot product contributions for each corner: \text{Contribution}{AA} = \text{Grad}(AA, XF, YF) \text{Contribution}{BA} = \text{Grad}(BA, XF - 1, YF) \text{Contribution}{AB} = \text{Grad}(AB, XF, YF - 1) \text{Contribution}{BB} = \text{Grad}(BB, XF - 1, YF - 1) 5. Interpolation: Interpolate along the X axis, then the Y axis: X1 = \text{Lerp}(U, \text{Contribution}{AA}, \text{Contribution}{BA}) X2 = \text{Lerp}(U, \text{Contribution}{AB}, \text{Contribution}{BB}) N(X, Y) = \text{Lerp}(V, X1, X2) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fade(t): return t t t (t (t 6.0 - 15.0) + 10.0) def lerp(t, a, b): return a + t (b - a) def grad(hashval, x, y): h = hashval & 7 if h == 0: return x + y if h == 1: return x - y if h == 2: return -x + y if h == 3: return -x - y if h == 4: return x if h == 5: return -x if h == 6: return y return -y def perlin2d(x, y, permtable): # 1. Grid and Fractional Coordinates xi = math.floor(x) & 255 yi = math.floor(y) & 255 xf = x - math.floor(x) yf = y - math.floor(y) # 2. Hashing Corners aa = permtable[permtable[xi] + yi] ab = permtable[permtable[xi] + yi + 1] ba = permtable[permtable[xi + 1] + yi] bb = permtable[permtable[xi + 1] + yi + 1] # 3. Fade u = fade(xf) v = fade(yf) # 4. Gradient Contributions contribaa = grad(aa, xf, yf) contribba = grad(ba, xf - 1.0, yf) contribab = grad(ab, xf, yf - 1.0) contribbb = grad(bb, xf - 1.0, yf - 1.0) # 5. Interpolation x1 = lerp(u, contribaa, contribba) x2 = lerp(u, contribab, contribbb) return lerp(v, x1, x2) Parameters: Persistence: Not applicable to a single octave. Used in Fractal Brownian Motion (fBm) with Perlin Noise to control amplitude decay (default 0.5). Output Range: The raw output is in [-1, 1]. It is often remapped to [0, 1] by N{norm} = \frac{N + 1}{2}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lattice Zeroes: The noise value is exactly zero at every integer lattice point, which can cause artifacts in the amplitude distribution. Grid Artifacts: Original Perlin noise exhibited grid-oriented artifacts; the improved version uses fixed gradient directions and the quintic fade function to mitigate this. However, some axis-aligned anisotropy may remain due to hash correlation. Boundary Conditions: The permutation table must be doubled to 512 entries to handle indices XI+1 and YI+1 when XI=255 or YI=255, avoiding expensive modulo operations. Periodicity: Standard Perlin noise is non-periodic. To create tileable textures, axis wrapping or specific periodic permutation tables must be used. Fractal Brownian Motion (fBm) with Perlin Noise is a procedural technique that generates complex, self-similar noise patterns by summing multiple octaves of a base gradient noise function (typically Perlin Noise) with increasing frequency and decreasing amplitude. It solves the problem of creating natural-looking, detailed volumetric structures (such as terrain, smoke, or clouds) that simple Perlin noise cannot provide due to its lack of multi-scale detail. Unlike standard Perlin noise, which produces a single scale of variation, fBm mimics natural fractal phenomena by layering fine details over coarse structures. Wavelet noise is an explicit noise function introduced by Cook and DeRose that generates values by representing the noise field as a quadratic B-spline surface, achieving near-perfect band-limiting to solve the aliasing and detail loss inherent in weakly band-limited methods like Perlin Noise 2D. It differs from siblings such as Fractal Brownian Motion (fBm) with Perlin Noise by providing strict spectral control via a weighted sum and supporting solid noise with isotropic filtering. This method compensates for mean shifts introduced by non-linear transformations on Perlin noise by approximating the noise distribution as a normal distribution, mapping it to a uniform distribution via the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF), applying the desired transformation, and normalizing the result. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Symmetric Function Transformation by allowing arbitrary transformation functions f(x) rather than requiring specific symmetry conditions, and from Fractal Brownian Motion (fBm) with Perlin Noise by operating on the statistical distribution of values rather than frequency composition. M-Noise is a procedural shader algorithm that increases realism by interpolating pre-calculated gradient vectors to construct values varying pseudorandomly over space and time, applied to flame pixels for local turbulence. It is preferred over standard Perlin Noise on GPUs because it avoids chained table look-ups that cause bottlenecks, making it faster and better suited for 3D/4D noise not easily stored in textures. It is applied to each pixel in the volumetric rendering step to provide local turbulent detail via pseudorandom gradients. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample for a single octave. The cost is dominated by a fixed number of arithmetic operations and table lookups. Improved Perlin Noise requires approximately 64 instructions per octave on GPU hardware. Memory Complexity: O(1) storage for the permutation table (512 bytes). This is significantly lower than explicit noise methods which require O(N^d) storage. Performance: Perlin noise is generally faster than sparse convolution noise, wavelet noise, and better gradient noise, but slower than anisotropic noise. It requires many computation cycles, so it is often precomputed on the CPU for large textures or optimized for GPU shaders. Strengths: Fast, simple, continuous (C^1), and produces natural-looking textures. It supports solid noise and isotropic filtering. Limitations: It is only weakly band-pass, which can lead to aliasing and detail loss. It does not have a Gaussian amplitude distribution and exhibits some axis-aligned anisotropy. It does not support anisotropic filtering or setup-free surface noise. When to use: When computational efficiency is critical and high-frequency band-limiting is not required. Ideal for general-purpose procedural textures in real-time applications. When not to use: When strict band-limiting is needed to prevent aliasing (use Wavelet Noise) or when Gaussian amplitude distribution is required. Perlin noise was introduced by Ken Perlin in 1985. Perlin received an Academy Award for his work on this function. The "Improved Perlin Noise" variant, which uses the quintic fade function and fixed gradient vectors, was described by Green in 2005 in "Implementing improved perlin noise" (GPU Gems 2). It has become the workhorse of the graphics industry due to its speed and simplicity. It is widely used in film, commercials, and computer graphics for simulating natural phenomena. name: Fractal Brownian Motion (fBm) with Perlin Noise
head: FBM Noise, Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) for Volume Noise, Fractal Noise, Fractional Brownian Motion (fBm), Multi-octave Perlin Noise, Organic Fog, Perlin noise summation
body: Fractal Brownian Motion (fBm) with Perlin Noise is a procedural technique that generates complex, self-similar noise patterns by summing multiple octaves of a base gradient noise function (typically Perlin Noise) with increasing frequency and decreasing amplitude. It solves the problem of creating natural-looking, detailed volumetric structures (such as terrain, smoke, or clouds) that simple Perlin noise cannot provide due to its lack of multi-scale detail. Unlike standard Perlin noise, which produces a single scale of variation, fBm mimics natural fractal phenomena by layering fine details over coarse structures. Inputs: p: Input coordinate (vector of dimension d, typically 2D or 3D). octaves: Integer number of noise layers to sum (N). persistence: Float amplitude decay factor per octave (A). lacunarity: Float frequency increase factor per octave (L). basenoise: A gradient noise function (e.g., Perlin Noise 2D/3D) returning values in [-1, 1] or [0, 1]. Outputs: value: The summed fBm noise value. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required beyond the state variables for the loop. The base noise function requires a permutation table (for Perlin) or hash function, as defined in Perlin Noise 2D. Parameters: octaves: Typical range 1–8, or up to 12 for high detail. persistence: Typically 0.5 (halving amplitude). lacunarity: Typically 2.0 (doubling frequency). Note: For tiling textures, lacunarity must be a power of 2. Steps: 1. Initialize value = 0.0, amplitude = 1.0, frequency = 1.0. 2. Loop i from 0 to octaves - 1: a. Evaluate the base noise function at the scaled coordinate: n = basenoise(p frequency). b. Add the weighted noise to the sum: value += amplitude n. c. Update amplitude: amplitude = persistence. d. Update frequency: frequency = lacunarity. 3. (Optional) Normalize the result. If the base noise is in [-1, 1], the theoretical max is \sum amplitudei. Normalization ensures consistent output range. 4. Return value. Formulas: The general form is a weighted sum of band-pass noise functions: \text{FBM}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} wi N(2^i \mathbf{x}) Where N is the base noise function, wi is the weight of octave i, and 2^i represents the frequency scaling. With constant persistence A and lacunarity L=2, this expands to: \text{FBM} = A \cdot N(\mathbf{p}) + A^2 \cdot N(2\mathbf{p}) + A^3 \cdot N(4\mathbf{p}) + \dots Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fbmperlin(p, octaves, persistence, lacunarity, basenoisefunc): value = 0.0 amplitude = 1.0 frequency = 1.0 maxvalue = 0.0 for i in range(octaves): maxvalue += amplitude amplitude = persistence amplitude = 1.0 frequency = 1.0 for i in range(octaves): noiseval = basenoisefunc(p frequency) value += amplitude noiseval amplitude = persistence frequency = lacunarity if maxvalue > 0: value /= maxvalue return value Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Octave Counts: Significantly reduce performance due to nested loop complexity in raymarchers. Frequency Cutoff: The summation must stop when the frequency becomes too high for the noise to be properly represented between neighboring pixels (aliasing). Tiling: If the resulting volume or texture must tile, lacunarity must be a power of 2. Negative Weights: Negative weights cannot cancel energy from a frequency band because noise has random phase; the primitive noise function must be band-pass rather than merely band-limited. Turbulence Variant: Using abs(noise) instead of signed noise creates a "turbulence" effect (white-noise-like) rather than cloudy patterns. A variant that sums multiple octaves of base gradient noise with increasing frequency and decreasing amplitude, specifically applied to simulating natural fractal phenomena like fire and smoke, often using M-Noise for GPU efficiency. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot C), where N is the number of octaves and C is the cost of the base noise function (typically O(1) for fixed-grid Perlin, but involves hashing and interpolation). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the permutation table of the base noise function. Performance: High octave counts significantly reduce frame rates in real-time raymarching due to the nested evaluation of the noise function. Strengths: Produces self-similar, organic detail at multiple scales, mimicking natural terrain and volumetric effects. Limitations: Can appear repetitive if not combined with other techniques (e.g., domain warping). Aliasing occurs if frequencies exceed the Nyquist limit of the sampling grid. Fractal Brownian Motion was introduced by Ken Perlin in 1985. It was designed to generate rougher, more natural-looking noise by composing multiple layers of band-pass noise. The technique exploits the spectral properties of noise, where weights wi = 1/2^i produce 1/f spectral content. It is widely used in procedural generation for terrain, textures, and volumetric effects in computer graphics. Goldberg et al. later utilized dynamic weights to cancel mapping distortions. name: Turbulence Function
head: Improved Perlin Noise for Fire, Micro Fire Effects via Noise, Modified Noise, Procedural Noise for Micro-level Details, Turbulence, Improved Perlin Noise, M-Noise
body: The Turbulence Function is a procedural noise technique that generates complex, fractal-like micro-details for volumetric effects such as fire, smoke, and fog. It works by summing multiple octaves of a base gradient noise function with increasing frequency and decreasing amplitude. It builds on Fractal Brownian Motion (fBm) by specifically applying summed noise octaves to simulate natural fractal phenomena in real-time graphics. Inputs: position: A 3D or 4D vector representing spatial (and optionally temporal) coordinates in noise space. octaves: The number of noise octaves to sum (integer). gain: A scalar controlling the relative amplitude of each octave. lacunarity: A scalar controlling the relative frequency of each octave. noisescale: An application-specific frequency multiplier to correct for inherent frequency differences in noise functions and scale noise space to world coordinates. time: A scalar for the temporal dimension (if using 4D noise). offset: A constant vector to ensure uniqueness per fire instance. Outputs: turb: A scalar turbulence value representing the accumulated noise magnitude. The method relies on scalar arithmetic and the evaluation of a base noise function N(p). No complex data structures are required. 1. Scale Position: Compute the base noise position by scaling the input coordinates by noisescale and adding the instance offset. 2. Initialize Accumulator: Set turb = 0. 3. Loop Octaves: For each octave i from 0 to octaves - 1: a. Evaluate the base noise function at the scaled position: val = N(position \cdot lacunarityi). b. Take the absolute value of the noise result: val = |val|. c. Multiply by the gain for this octave: val = val \cdot gaini. d. Add to the accumulator: turb = turb + val. 4. Return: Output turb. The turbulence value turb is defined as: turb = \sum{i=0}^{n} gaini \cdot |noise(position \cdot lacunarityi)| Where: n is the number of octaves. gaini is the gain for octave i. Typically, gain = 1/lacunarity or a constant like 0.5. lacunarityi is the frequency multiplier for octave i. Typically lacunarity = 2. position is the noise coordinate vector. noise(p) is the base gradient noise function (e.g., M-Noise). (Note: Sources define the turbulence function without the absolute value operator, but explicitly includes it for the standard turbulence application.) Note on M-Noise Optimization: When using M-Noise, hash functions can be computed for up to two octaves together, and flerp functions for up to four octaves together in 3D turbulence, or three octaves for hash and four for flerp in 4D turbulence. Gain: Controls relative amplitude. Common value: 0.5. Lacunarity: Controls relative frequency. Common value: 2. Octaves: Number of octaves. 3+ for realistic fire, \le 2 for stylized/cartoon environments. Noise Scale: Application-specific frequency multiplier to correct for inherent frequency differences in noise functions and scale noise space to world coordinates. Stretching Artifacts: Enlarging the fire volume (elongating curves or adjusting radius) can stretch noise effects, creating visual artifacts. This is addressed by dynamically scaling noise space according to the radius and length of the fire volume. Precision: The method relies on the stability of the base noise function. M-Noise is preferred for its dimension reducibility and purely computable nature, avoiding texture-dependent lookups. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def turbulence(position, octaves, gain, lacunarity, noisefunc): """ Computes the turbulence value by summing octaves of noise. Args: position (vec3 or vec4): The input coordinate in noise space. octaves (int): Number of octaves to sum. gain (float): Amplitude multiplier for each octave. lacunarity (float): Frequency multiplier for each octave. noisefunc (function): A function that takes a position and returns a scalar noise value. Returns: float: The accumulated turbulence value. """ turb = 0.0 currentfreq = 1.0 for i in range(octaves): # Evaluate base noise at scaled position val = noisefunc(position currentfreq) # Turbulence typically uses the absolute value of noise val = abs(val) # Apply gain val = val gain # Accumulate turb = turb + val # Increase frequency for next octave currentfreq = currentfreq lacunarity return turb A GPU-tailored adaptation of Perlin Noise that picks gradients from the corners of a unit-n cube instead of edge centers, allowing dimension reducibility and purely computable noise without texture lookups. It is more efficient than Improved Perlin Noise, using ~40 pixel shader instructions per octave compared to ~64, and supports Pixel Shader 2.0. A CPU-optimized version of Perlin Noise adapted for graphics hardware. It uses six dependent texture look-ups and ~64 instructions per octave, requiring Pixel Shader 2.a or newer. It is less efficient than M-Noise but may more closely approximate real Perlin Noise. A stylization technique that modulates the final rendering color or shading disk sizes using a turbulent 3D Perlin noise texture mapped to the model. At shading time, the final color of a disk is modulated with the noise value at the nearest location in the noise texture, or shading disk sizes are disturbed for halftone renderings. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of octaves n. Each octave requires evaluating the base noise function (M-Noise uses two independent look-ups per octave). Memory Complexity: Constant, O(1), as the method is purely computable and stores no large data structures. Performance: M-Noise uses approximately 40 pixel shader instructions per octave and can be compiled for Pixel Shader 2.0 hardware. Improved Perlin Noise uses approximately 64 instructions per octave and requires Pixel Shader 2.a or newer. Strengths: Efficient GPU implementation (especially M-Noise), produces realistic fractal details for fire and smoke, easily customizable via gain and lacunarity. Limitations: Visual artifacts can occur if noise space is not dynamically scaled with the fire volume geometry. M-Noise may have a different visual character than classic Perlin Noise, though it is often preferred for its efficiency. When to Use: Real-time volumetric fire, smoke, and fog rendering where performance is critical and realistic micro-details are desired. When Not to Use: When classic Perlin Noise visual characteristics are strictly required and hardware supports only older shaders, or when offline rendering allows for more expensive noise functions. The Turbulence Function, in the context of GPU-accelerated procedural noise, was described by Marc Olano in 2005 in "Modified noise for evaluation on graphics hardware" (HWWS '05). It was developed to address the inefficiencies of classic and Improved Perlin Noise on graphics hardware, specifically by reducing dependent texture lookups and leveraging GPU parallelism. The technique is used in pixel shaders to generate micro fire effects such as individual flame shape, location, and flicker. name: Wavelet Noise
head: Cook and DeRose Noise
body: Wavelet noise is an explicit noise function introduced by Cook and DeRose in 2005 that generates values by representing the noise field as a quadratic B-spline surface, achieving near-perfect band-limiting to solve the aliasing and detail loss inherent in weakly band-limited methods like Perlin Noise 2D. It differs from siblings such as Fractal Brownian Motion (fBm) with Perlin Noise by providing strict spectral control via a weighted sum and supporting solid noise with isotropic filtering. Inputs: A tile size (period N), spatial coordinates \mathbf{x}, and dimensionality d. Outputs: A scalar noise value N(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures: Noise Coefficients Tile (N): A 3D array (for 3D noise) or 2D array (for 2D noise) of size N \times N \times N (or N \times N). Each element stores a floating-point value representing the coefficient at that grid point. The space is tiled periodically with this volume. Preprocessing Steps: 1. Generate Random Image (R): Create an image R of size M \times M \times M (where M = 2N) filled with independent random values uniformly distributed in [0, 1). 2. Downsample (R \downarrow): Downsample R by a factor of 2 using an analysis filter derived from the uniform quadratic B-spline basis. The result is an image R \downarrow of size N \times N \times N. 3. Upsample (R \downarrow \uparrow): Upsample R \downarrow by a factor of 2 using a refinement filter derived from the uniform quadratic B-spline basis. The result is an image R \downarrow \uparrow of size M \times M \times M. 4. Compute Coefficients (N): Subtract the upsampled image from the original random image: N = R - R \downarrow \uparrow. The resulting tile N contains the noise coefficients representing the band-limited part. Runtime Evaluation: 1. Tiling: Map the query coordinate \mathbf{x} to the local tile coordinates by taking \mathbf{x} \mod N. 2. B-Spline Evaluation: Evaluate the quadratic B-spline basis function at the local coordinates using the precomputed coefficients N. Let \mathbf{x}{local} be the fractional position within the tile. The value is computed as a convolution of the coefficients with the quadratic B-spline kernel. Formulas: The noise function is defined as: N(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{\mathbf{k}} n{\mathbf{k}} B(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{k}) where: n{\mathbf{k}} are the precomputed coefficients from the tile N. B(\mathbf{x}) is the uniform quadratic B-spline basis function. The sum is over the grid indices \mathbf{k} in the vicinity of \mathbf{x}. The filters used in downsampling and upsampling correspond to the analysis and refinement coefficients of the uniform quadratic B-spline basis function. Specifically, the downsampling filter h and upsampling filter g are determined by the wavelet analysis of the quadratic B-spline. Parameters: Tile Size (N): The period of the noise. Random Seed: Determines the initial random image R. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sampling 2D from 3D: Sampling a 3D band-limited noise function on a 2D surface does not result in a band-limited texture, potentially causing aliasing artifacts on the surface despite the 3D function being band-limited. Tiling Artifacts: The method assumes periodic tiling, leading to repeating patterns or seams when true random accessibility is required. Precision: The subtraction R - R \downarrow \uparrow may suffer from precision loss if filters introduce significant rounding errors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocesswaveletnoise(tilesize: int, randomseed: int) -> list: """Preprocesses to create the noise coefficient tile.""" M = 2 tilesize R = generaterandomimage(M, M, M, randomseed) # Standard quadratic B-spline analysis coefficients analysisfilter = [0.5, 0.0, -0.5] Rdown = downsample(R, analysisfilter) # Standard quadratic B-spline refinement coefficients refinementfilter = [0.25, 0.75, 0.75, 0.25] Rdownup = upsample(Rdown, refinementfilter) N = subtractimages(R, Rdownup) return N def evaluatewaveletnoise(x: float, y: float, z: float, coefficients: list, tilesize: int) -> float: """Evaluates the wavelet noise at point (x, y, z).""" xlocal = x % tilesize ylocal = y % tilesize zlocal = z % tilesize return evaluatequadraticbspline(xlocal, ylocal, zlocal, coefficients) def generaterandomimage(width: int, height: int, depth: int, seed: int) -> list: """Generates a 3D array of random floats in [0, 1).""" import random random.seed(seed) return [[[random.random() for in range(depth)] for in range(height)] for in range(width)] def convolve1d(signal: list, kernel: list) -> list: """Applies a 1D convolution to a signal.""" out = [] klen = len(kernel) pad = klen // 2 padded = [signal[0]] pad + signal + [signal[-1]] pad for i in range(len(signal)): val = 0.0 for j in range(klen): val += padded[i + j] kernel[j] out.append(val) return out def downsample(image: list, filter1d: list) -> list: """Downsamples a 3D image by a factor of 2 using separable 1D convolution.""" # Apply filter along axis 0 temp = [[[convolve1d(row, filter1d) for row in slice] for slice in image] for in range(len(image[0][0]))] # Transpose to axis 1 temp = [[[temp[k][j][i] for k in range(len(temp))] for j in range(len(temp[0]))] for i in range(len(temp[0][0]))] # Apply filter along axis 1 temp = [[[convolve1d(row, filter1d) for row in slice] for slice in temp] for in range(len(temp[0][0]))] # Transpose to axis 2 temp = [[[temp[k][j][i] for k in range(len(temp))] for j in range(len(temp[0]))] for i in range(len(temp[0][0]))] # Apply filter along axis 2 temp = [[[convolve1d(row, filter1d) for row in slice] for slice in temp] for in range(len(temp[0][0]))] # Stride by 2 return [[[temp[i][j][k] for k in range(0, len(temp[0][0]), 2)] for j in range(0, len(temp[0]), 2)] for i in range(0, len(temp), 2)] def upsample(image: list, filter1d: list) -> list: """Upsamples a 3D image by a factor of 2 using zero-insertion and separable 1D convolution.""" M = 2 len(image) temp = [[[0.0 for in range(M)] for in range(M)] for in range(M)] for i in range(len(image)): for j in range(len(image[0])): for k in range(len(image[0][0])): temp[2i][2j][2k] = image[i][j][k] # Apply filter along axis 0 temp = [[[convolve1d(row, filter1d) for row in slice] for slice in temp] for in range(len(temp[0][0]))] # Transpose to axis 1 temp = [[[temp[k][j][i] for k in range(len(temp))] for j in range(len(temp[0]))] for i in range(len(temp[0][0]))] # Apply filter along axis 1 temp = [[[convolve1d(row, filter1d) for row in slice] for slice in temp] for in range(len(temp[0][0]))] # Transpose to axis 2 temp = [[[temp[k][j][i] for k in range(len(temp))] for j in range(len(temp[0]))] for i in range(len(temp[0][0]))] # Apply filter along axis 2 temp = [[[convolve1d(row, filter1d) for row in slice] for slice in temp] for in range(len(temp[0][0]))] return temp def subtractimages(A: list, B: list) -> list: """Element-wise subtraction of two 3D arrays.""" return [[[A[i][j][k] - B[i][j][k] for k in range(len(A[0][0]))] for j in range(len(A[0]))] for i in range(len(A))] def evaluatequadraticbspline(x: float, y: float, z: float, coefficients: list) -> float: """Evaluates the quadratic B-spline surface at (x, y, z) using the coefficients.""" def B(t: float) -> float: if -1 <= t < 0: return 0.5 (t + 1)2 if 0 <= t < 1: return 0.5 (-2t2 + 3t + 1) if 1 <= t < 2: return 0.5 (t - 2)2 return 0.0 ix, fx = divmod(x, 1.0) iy, fy = divmod(y, 1.0) iz, fz = divmod(z, 1.0) val = 0.0 for dx in range(-1, 2): for dy in range(-1, 2): for dz in range(-1, 2): cx = int(ix) + dx cy = int(iy) + dy cz = int(iz) + dz cx = cx % len(coefficients) cy = cy % len(coefficients[0]) cz = cz % len(coefficients[0][0]) val += coefficients[cx][cy][cz] B(fx - dx) B(fy - dy) B(fz - dz) return val Time Complexity: Generally slower than Perlin noise due to the complexity of the B-spline evaluation and the preprocessing cost. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the coefficient tile, which is O(N^d) where N is the tile size and d is the dimensionality. However, since the tile is small and tiled, the effective memory usage per query is low, but the initial storage is higher than O(1) methods like Perlin noise. Strengths: Almost perfect band-limiting prevents aliasing and detail loss. Supports solid noise and isotropic filtering. Provides strict spectral control via a weighted sum. Limitations: Slower than Perlin noise. Sampling a 3D function on a 2D surface can still cause aliasing. Lacks true random accessibility due to fixed-size tiling. When to Use: When high-quality, band-limited noise is required, particularly for rendering where aliasing artifacts are unacceptable. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and some aliasing is acceptable, or when O(1) memory usage is strictly required. Wavelet noise was introduced by Cook and DeRose in 2005. They observed that Perlin noise is only weakly band-limited, leading to aliasing and detail loss when summing octaves for fractal noise. Wavelet noise addresses this by explicitly constructing a band-limited noise field using quadratic B-splines. The method extends wavelet-based noise generation to provide a smooth, band-limited alternative to gradient-based noise functions. It is part of the family of explicit noise functions, alongside anisotropic noise. name: CDF Normalization via Normal Distribution Approximation
head: Normal Distribution Approximation for Perlin Noise, Perlin Noise CDF Normalization
body: This method compensates for mean shifts introduced by non-linear transformations on Perlin noise by approximating the noise distribution as a normal distribution, mapping it to a uniform distribution via the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF), applying the desired transformation, and normalizing the result. Inputs: A scalar Perlin noise value x and a transformation function f(x). Outputs: A normalized transformed noise value y. Parameters: \mu = 0: The mean of the Perlin noise distribution. \sigma \approx 0.1995: The standard deviation of the Perlin noise distribution, estimated by random sampling. Steps: 1. Estimate Parameters: Use \mu = 0 and \sigma \approx 0.1995. 2. Map to Uniform Distribution: Apply the CDF of the normal distribution F(x) to the input noise x to obtain a value u in the range [0, 1]. u = F(x) = 0.5 \left( 1 + \text{erf}\left( \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma \sqrt{2}} \right) \right) Where \text{erf}(z) is the error function: \text{erf}(z) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}} \int0^z e^{-t^2} dt 3. Apply Transformation: Compute the transformed value v using the desired function f on the uniform value u: v = f(u) 4. Normalize: Calculate the normalization constant C, which is the integral of f(x) over the range [0, 1]: C = \int0^1 f(x) dx The final output y is: y = \frac{v}{C} = \frac{f(u)}{\int0^1 f(x) dx} Pseudocode: Unverified code. Integrability: The integral \int0^1 f(x) dx must be computable analytically. Approximation Error: Perlin noise is bounded, whereas the normal distribution is not, making the approximation imperfect. name: Symmetric Function Transformation
head: Symmetric functions approach, Logistic transformation for Perlin noise
body: A method to modify Perlin noise octaves while preserving the mean value by using functions that satisfy a specific symmetry condition around zero. It sets apart from alternatives by enforcing a mathematical constraint on the transformation function itself, rather than compensating for the mean shift after the fact. This ensures the resulting distribution has a predictable mean without requiring post-hoc normalization or pre-computed sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Perlin noise value x (assumed to be symmetric around 0) and parameters for the transformation function. Output: A transformed noise value y = f(x) with a mean of f(0). Data Structures: Operates on scalar noise values. Steps: 1. Select a transformation function f(x) that satisfies the symmetry rule: f(-x) = 2 \cdot f(0) - f(x) 2. Set the midpoint parameter x0 = 0. This is necessary for the function to satisfy the symmetry rule for all x. 3. Set the carrying capacity parameter L = 2. This ensures that f(0) = 1, which keeps the mean of the resulting noise at 1. 4. Apply the function f(x) to the Perlin noise input x. Formula: The symmetry condition is: f(-x) = 2 \cdot f(0) - f(x) The recommended function is the Logistic function: f(x) = \frac{L}{1 + e^{-k(x - x0)}} Where: L is the carrying capacity (upper bound). x0 is the x-value of the midpoint. k is the steepness of the curve. Parameters: L: Carrying capacity. Typical value: 2. This value is chosen to ensure f(0) = 1, keeping the mean of the noise at 1. x0: Midpoint x-value. Required value: 0. This is necessary for the Logistic function to follow the symmetry rule. k: Steepness of the curve. Controls contrast. Can be negative (equivalent to positive k with input multiplied by -1). Pitfalls: The set of functions satisfying the symmetry rule is very limited, leading to poor expressive range and lack of control for the user. The method relies on the assumption that the Perlin noise distribution is symmetric around 0, which is an approximation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def symmetricfunctiontransformation(x, k): """ Applies the symmetric function transformation to a Perlin noise value. Args: x (float): The Perlin noise value. k (float): The steepness parameter controlling contrast. Returns: float: The transformed noise value with mean 1. """ # Parameters L = 2.0 # Carrying capacity to ensure f(0) = 1 x0 = 0.0 # Midpoint to satisfy symmetry rule # Logistic function: f(x) = L / (1 + exp(-k (x - x0))) exponent = -k (x - x0) result = L / (1.0 + math.exp(exponent)) return result A method to compensate for mean shift by pre-computing the mean of a transformed noise sample and using it as a normalization factor. It differs from Symmetric Function Transformation by not requiring the function to satisfy a strict symmetry rule, allowing for a wider range of functions, but at the cost of requiring pre-computation. Choose this when you need more expressive control over the transformation function and can afford the pre-computation step. Definition: A method to compensate for mean shift by pre-computing the mean of a transformed noise sample and using it as a normalization factor. Steps: 1. Choose the function f(x) to apply. If it has parameters, set them to specific values beforehand. 2. Sample a Perlin noise and apply the function f(x) to the sample. 3. Compute the mean of the obtained sample. 4. Normalize any further use of the function on Perlin noise by dividing the result by the estimated mean. Pitfalls: Requires pre-computation, complicating use in procedural settings, especially if function parameters change frequently. The applied function must be positive. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple handles for the user; smooth way of increasing contrast by concentrating values near the upper and lower bounds. Limitations: Poor expressive range; lack of control for the user; limited set of functions that satisfy the symmetry rule. When to use: When a simple, smooth contrast adjustment is needed and the user is willing to accept limited control over the transformation function. When not to use: When high expressive range or complex transformations are required. Described in a study on procedural noise modeling for dust clouds. The method was proposed as a way to address the mean shift issue in Perlin noise distributions by leveraging the symmetry of the noise distribution around zero. name: Perlin Gradient and Interpolation Functions
head: Fade, Grad, Lerp
body: This article defines the core mathematical primitives—gradient selection, fading (smoothing), and linear interpolation—used to construct gradient-based noise functions like Perlin noise. It solves the problem of generating continuous scalar fields from discrete lattice points by applying a quintic fade function to ensure smooth transitions, differing from sibling methods primarily in its specific choice of the quintic fade polynomial and the 12-gradient vector set for 3D, whereas Simplex noise uses a different lattice structure and interpolation geometry. Inputs: Query point \mathbf{P} = (x, y, z) in continuous space. A permutation table containing integers to map coordinates to gradient indices. Outputs: A scalar noise value n. Data Structures: Permutation Table: An array of integers used to map lattice coordinates to gradient indices without modulo operations. Gradient Set (3D): 12 vectors corresponding to the face diagonals of a cube, selected via bitwise operations on the hash index. Steps: 1. Integer and Fractional Decomposition: Compute the integer lattice coordinates \mathbf{I} = (\lfloor x \rfloor, \lfloor y \rfloor, \lfloor z \rfloor) and the fractional coordinates \mathbf{F} = (x - \lfloor x \rfloor, y - \lfloor y \rfloor, z - \lfloor z \rfloor). 2. Gradient Indexing: Map the integer coordinates to gradient indices using the permutation table. 3. Gradient Vector Selection: Decode the index into a gradient vector using bitwise masking. Let h = \text{idx} \ \& \ 15. Select components u and v based on h, then apply signs based on the lowest two bits: \mathbf{g} = ((h \ \& \ 1) == 0 ? u: -u) + ((h \ \& \ 2) == 0 ? v: -v). 4. Dot Product Contribution: For each of the 8 corners of the unit cell, compute the distance vector \mathbf{d}i = \mathbf{P} - \mathbf{V}i and the contribution ni = \mathbf{g}i \cdot \mathbf{d}i [Parent]. 5. Fade (Smoothing) Function: Apply the quintic fade function to each fractional coordinate: f(t) = 6t^5 - 15t^4 + 10t^3, or equivalently f(t) = t^3(t(t \cdot 6 - 15) + 10). This replaces the original cubic Hermite function f(t) = 3t^2 - 2t^3 to improve curve quality and visual results. 6. Interpolation: Combine the 8 contributions using trilinear interpolation weighted by the fade values ux = f(fx), uy = f(fy), uz = f(fz), using \text{lerp}(a, b, t) = a + (b - a)t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fade(t): """Quintic fade function for smooth interpolation.""" return t t t (t (t 6.0 - 15.0) + 10.0) def lerp(a, b, t): """Linear interpolation.""" return a + (b - a) t def grad(hashval, x, y, z): """ Select gradient vector from hash. Uses 12 gradients (face diagonals) for 3D. """ h = hashval & 15 # Mask to 0-15 u = x if h < 8 else y v = y if h < 4 else (x if h == 12 or h == 14 else z) return ((-u) if (h & 1) else u) + ((-v) if (h & 2) else v) def perlingradientnoise(x, y, z, permtable): """ Compute Perlin noise value at (x, y, z). permtable: list of integers (typically 256 or 512 entries). """ # 1. Integer and fractional parts ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz # 2. Fade function ux, uy, uz = fade(fx), fade(fy), fade(fz) # 3. Hash corners (standard 256-entry table masking) A = permtable[ix & 255] + iy AA = permtable[A & 255] + iz AB = permtable[(A + 1) & 255] + iz B = permtable[(ix + 1) & 255] + iy BA = permtable[B & 255] + iz BB = permtable[(B + 1) & 255] + iz # 4. Gradient contributions n000 = grad(permtable[AA & 255], fx, fy, fz) n100 = grad(permtable[BA & 255], fx - 1, fy, fz) n010 = grad(permtable[AB & 255], fx, fy - 1, fz) n110 = grad(permtable[BB & 255], fx - 1, fy - 1, fz) n001 = grad(permtable[(AA + 1) & 255], fx, fy, fz - 1) n101 = grad(permtable[(BA + 1) & 255], fx - 1, fy, fz - 1) n011 = grad(permtable[(AB + 1) & 255], fx, fy - 1, fz - 1) n111 = grad(permtable[(BB + 1) & 255], fx - 1, fy - 1, fz - 1) # 5. Interpolation x1 = lerp(n000, n100, ux) x2 = lerp(n010, n110, ux) y1 = lerp(x1, x2, uy) x1 = lerp(n001, n101, ux) x2 = lerp(n011, n111, ux) y2 = lerp(x1, x2, uy) return lerp(y1, y2, uz) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Large coordinate values may cause floating-point precision errors; lattice wrapping should be handled carefully. Gradient Set: Using fewer than 12 gradients in 3D (e.g., only axis-aligned vectors) leads to visible grid artifacts. Derivatives: For analytical derivatives, the fade derivative is f'(t) = 30t^2(t-1)^2. 3D Perlin Noise generates a continuous scalar field in three-dimensional space by interpolating gradient vectors assigned to lattice points, producing seamless, tileable textures when wrapping is enabled. It distinguishes itself from its parent method by explicitly supporting 3D coordinate wrapping via modulo arithmetic and utilizing a fifth-order polynomial fade function to eliminate grid-oriented artifacts and derivative discontinuities. Flow Noise is a procedural noise function designed to generate time-varying, swirling, and advected textures, primarily for physically-based simulations of fluids and gases. It differs from standard Perlin noise by introducing a time-dependent advection step that displaces the sampling coordinates, creating a sense of continuous flow and swirling motion rather than static, frozen noise patterns. Improved Perlin Noise, introduced by Kensler et al. [KKS08], is a lattice gradient noise function that applies three mutually orthogonal improvements to the original Perlin noise [Per85, Per02] to address axial decorrelation, band-limitation, and surface noise quality. It distinguishes itself from standard Perlin noise by replacing the hash and reconstruction kernels with optimized variants that reduce directional artifacts and provide better spectral control. GPU-Optimized Perlin Noise (BBS), also known as Modified Noise, is a procedural noise function designed for efficient direct computation on GPUs by eliminating permutation table lookups. It replaces the hash lookup with a computable Blum-Blum-Shub (BBS) generator and selects gradients from hypercube corners, enabling dimension reducibility to optimize 3D noise via 2D texture lookups. It differs from Improved Perlin Noise by using corner gradients instead of unit sphere vectors and from 3D Perlin Noise by its specific GPU-oriented hashing and texture optimization strategies. Noise using quintic interpolation (6t^5 - 15t^4 + 10t^3) to achieve C2 continuity, eliminating visible grid artifacts in derivatives compared to Hermite's C1. 1. Compute u = f^3 (f (f 6.0 - 15.0) + 10.0). 2. Compute derivative du = 30.0 f^2 (f (f - 2.0) + 1.0). 3. Retrieve hashes a,b,c,d. 4. Compute coefficients k0=a, k1=b-a, k2=c-a, k3=a-b-c+d. 5. Value: k0 + k1u.x + k2u.y + k3u.xu.y. 6. Derivatives: du vec2(k1 + k3u.y, k2 + k3u.x). The original smoothing function f(x) = 3x^2 - 2x^3 was replaced by f(x) = 6x^5 - 15x^4 + 10x^3 to improve the curve of the function and achieve better visual results. Scaling: Simplex noise has lower computational complexity and scales to higher dimensions (4D, 5D) with much less computational cost than Perlin noise. Strengths: The quintic fade function improves curve quality and visual results over the original cubic Hermite interpolation. Limitations: Computational cost is higher than Simplex noise in higher dimensions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: For high-dimensional noise (4D+) where Simplex noise scales better. Perlin noise was introduced by Ken Perlin in 1985. The original version used a cubic Hermite interpolation with a simpler fade function. In 2002, Perlin published an "improved noise" algorithm that replaced the smoothing function with the quintic polynomial 6t^5 - 15t^4 + 10t^3 to improve visual quality and continuity. name: 3D Perlin Noise
head: 3D Gradient Noise, Gradient Noise, Improved 3D Noise, Ken Perlin’s improved Noise, Perlin Gradient Noise, Perlin Noise (Java Implementation), Perlin's improved noise
body: 3D Perlin Noise generates a continuous scalar field in three-dimensional space by interpolating gradient vectors assigned to lattice points, producing seamless, tileable textures when wrapping is enabled. It distinguishes itself from its parent method by explicitly supporting 3D coordinate wrapping via modulo arithmetic and utilizing a fifth-order polynomial fade function to eliminate grid-oriented artifacts and derivative discontinuities. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D point (x, y, z) in continuous space. Input: A permutation table P of size 512 containing integers 1 to 256. Input: Frequency parameter f for coordinate wrapping. Output: A scalar noise value N \in [-1, 1]. Data Structures Permutation Table (P): An array of 512 integers, where indices 0–255 and 256–511 contain identical shuffled permutations of integers 1 to 256. Gradient Vectors (G): A fixed set of 12 vectors in 3D space, typically (\pm 1, \pm 1, 0), (\pm 1, 0, \pm 1), and (0, \pm 1, \pm 1). Numbered Steps 1. Wrapping and Integerization: If wrapping is enabled, apply the modulo operator to the integer parts of the coordinates using the frequency parameter. Compute integer grid coordinates (i, j, k) and fractional parts (xf, yf, zf) by flooring and subtracting. 2. Gradient Index Lookup: Compute the indices for the 8 corners of the unit cube containing the point by hashing coordinates through the permutation table and masking with 255 to wrap around the table boundaries. 3. Dot Product Calculation: For each corner, compute the dot product of the gradient vector and the distance vector from the lattice point to the sample point. 4. Fade Function: Apply the fifth-order polynomial fade function to the fractional coordinates to ensure smooth derivatives. 5. Trilinear Interpolation: Interpolate the 8 dot products along the X, Y, and Z axes using the fade values. Formulas Fade function: fade(t) = t^3(t(t \cdot 6 - 15) + 10). Gradient contribution: h = hash \ \& \ 15; u = x if h < 8 else y; v = y if h < 4 else (x if h == 12 or h == 14 else z); grad = ((h \ \& \ 1) == 0 ? u: -u) + ((h \ \& \ 2) == 0 ? v: -v). Trilinear interpolation: lerp(t, a, b) = a + t \cdot (b - a). Output range: The dot product result is in range [-1, 1] because distance vector components are in [0,1] and the gradient is normalized. Parameters Octaves: Number of noise layers summed together. Initial Frequency: Starting frequency for the noise generation. Initial Amplitude: Starting amplitude for the noise generation. Persistence: Not given in the sources. Texture Dimensions: Width, Height, Slices/Depth for pre-computed textures. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Random Initialization: The permutation array must be initialized with random numbers using machine time as a seed to avoid similarities in subsequent calls. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise at large coordinate values, which wrapping helps mitigate by keeping coordinates within a bounded range. Derivative Discontinuities: The improved algorithm replaced the cubic interpolation of the fade function with a fifth-order polynomial to eliminate discontinuities of second and third order derivatives. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fade(t): """Fifth-order polynomial fade function.""" return t t t (t (t 6.0 - 15.0) + 10.0) def lerp(t, a, b): """Linear interpolation.""" return a + t (b - a) def grad(hashval, x, y, z): """Compute dot product of gradient vector and distance vector.""" h = hashval & 15 u = x if (h & 1) == 0 else -x v = y if (h & 2) == 0 else -y w = z if (h & 4) == 0 else -z if (h & 8) != 0: u = -u return u + v + w def noise3D(x, y, z, permtable, frequency=0): """3D Perlin Noise with optional wrapping.""" if frequency > 0: x = x % frequency y = y % frequency z = z % frequency xi = int(x) & 255 yi = int(y) & 255 zi = int(z) & 255 xf = x - int(x) yf = y - int(y) zf = z - int(z) u = fade(xf) v = fade(yf) w = fade(zf) A = permtable[xi] + yi B = permtable[(xi + 1) & 255] + yi AA = permtable[A] + zi AB = permtable[(A + 1) & 255] + zi BA = permtable[B] + zi BB = permtable[(B + 1) & 255] + zi p0 = grad(permtable[AA], xf, yf, zf) p1 = grad(permtable[BA], xf - 1, yf, zf) p2 = grad(permtable[AB], xf, yf - 1, zf) p3 = grad(permtable[BB], xf - 1, yf - 1, zf) p4 = grad(permtable[(AA + 1) & 255], xf, yf, zf - 1) p5 = grad(permtable[(BA + 1) & 255], xf - 1, yf, zf - 1) p6 = grad(permtable[(AB + 1) & 255], xf, yf - 1, zf - 1) p7 = grad(permtable[(BB + 1) & 255], xf - 1, yf - 1, zf - 1) q0 = lerp(u, p0, p1) q1 = lerp(u, p2, p3) q2 = lerp(u, p4, p5) q3 = lerp(u, p6, p7) r0 = lerp(v, q0, q1) r1 = lerp(v, q2, q3) return lerp(w, r0, r1) When the 3D noise function returns a continuous density field ranging from -1 to 1, the process is referred to as an isosurface function. The method feeds 3D grid vertex positions into the noise function and places a voxel at coordinates where the returned value exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0). Implementation requires tuning the threshold for desired terrain density, as the noise function typically returns values between -1 and 1. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample for a single octave, with a general complexity of O(2^n) for n dimensions. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the permutation table (512 integers). Performance: The method compiles to approximately 40 instructions in pixel shaders. Strengths: Produces smooth, continuous noise with no visible grid artifacts and supports seamless tiling via wrapping. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than simpler noise functions due to the fifth-order polynomial and multiple lookups. When to use: Ideal for procedural texture generation, cloud simulation, and terrain generation where seamless tiling and smooth gradients are required. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The algorithm is based on Ken Perlin’s improved Noise, which was developed to reduce grid-oriented artifacts present in the original Perlin noise. The improvement involves using a fixed set of gradient directions and a fifth-order polynomial fade function. This implementation was originally written in Java and later ported to C++ for use in cloud simulation and procedural texturing. name: Flow Noise
head: Advection Noise, Perlin Flow Noise
body: Flow Noise is a procedural noise function designed to generate time-varying, swirling, and advected textures for physically-based simulations. It differs from static noise by applying a time-dependent advection step to displace sampling coordinates, creating continuous flow motion rather than frozen patterns. Inputs: Spatial position P \in \mathbb{R}^3, time t \in \mathbb{R}, spatial frequency scale \in \mathbb{R}, advection speed speed \in \mathbb{R}. Outputs: Scalar noise value f \in \mathbb{R}. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute an advection velocity vector V at position P and time t. The exact formulation for V is not given in the sources. 2. Advect the sampling coordinates linearly using the velocity and time: P' = P + V \cdot speed \cdot t. 3. Evaluate the base Perlin noise function at the advected position scaled by the spatial frequency: f = \text{PerlinNoise}(P' \cdot scale). Formulas: P' = P + V \cdot speed \cdot t, where P' is the advected position, V is the advection velocity, speed is the advection magnitude, and t is time. f = \text{PerlinNoise}(P' \cdot scale), where f is the output scalar and scale is the spatial frequency. Parameters: scale controls spatial frequency and speed controls advection magnitude. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge cases: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def flownoise(P, t, scale=1.0, speed=1.0): # Step 1: Compute advection velocity V at position P and time t. # The exact formulation for V is not given in the sources. V = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Not given in the sources. # Step 2: Advect coordinates linearly Padvected = (P[0] + V[0] speed t, P[1] + V[1] speed t, P[2] + V[2] speed t) # Step 3: Evaluate standard Perlin noise at the advected position # perlinnoise is defined in the parent article Perlin Gradient and Interpolation Functions return perlinnoise(Padvected[0] scale, Padvected[1] scale, Padvected[2] scale) Not given in the sources. Flow Noise was presented by Perlin and Neyret [PN01] as a Perlin-like noise function for generating time-varying flow textures with swirling and advection. It was developed to simulate dynamic phenomena in computer graphics where static noise functions are insufficient. Choose it for simulating fluid-like or directional phenomena. GPU-optimized variant of Perlin noise. Improved Perlin Noise was presented by Kensler et al. in 2008 [KKS08] as a set of three mutually orthogonal improvements to the original Perlin noise [Per85, Per02]. It is categorized as a lattice gradient noise function. The improvements apply to several lattice gradient noises, not just Perlin noise.
