name: GPU-Optimized Perlin Noise (BBS)
head: Modified Noise, Blum-Blum-Shub Perlin Noise
body: GPU-Optimized Perlin Noise (BBS), also known as Modified Noise, is a procedural noise function designed for efficient direct computation on GPUs by eliminating permutation table lookups. It replaces hash lookups with a computable Blum-Blum-Shub (BBS) generator and selects gradients from hypercube corners, enabling dimension reducibility to optimize 3D noise via 2D texture lookups. It differs from Improved Perlin Noise by using corner gradients instead of unit sphere vectors and from 3D Perlin Noise by its specific GPU-oriented hashing and texture optimization strategies. Inputs: A 3D point p = (px, py, pz). Outputs: A scalar noise value N(p). Data Structures: Modulus M: A composite number M = pq where p and q are large primes. Textures (Optional Optimization): tex2d: Stores 2D noise values N{2D}(x, y). texzgrad: Stores z-gradient values \frac{\partial N}{\partial z} at integer z slices. Alternatively, a single 2-channel texture storing both. Parameters: M: Modulus for BBS generator. Not given in the sources. Precision mode: "Exact" (5-instruction) or "Inexact" (4-instruction) modulo. Steps: 1. Integer and Fractional Parts: Compute integer coordinates i = \lfloor p \rfloor and fractional coordinates f = p - i. Let ix, iy, iz be the integer components and fx, fy, fz be the fractional components. 2. Hash Construction: Define the hash function using the Blum-Blum-Shub generator: \text{hash}(x) = x^2 \bmod M Construct multidimensional hashes for lattice corners recursively: \text{hash3}(x, y, z) = \text{hash}(\text{hash}(\text{hash}(x+1) + y+1) + z+1) The source uses pi + 1 in the hash construction, implying the hash is computed on the integer lattice indices offset by 1. 3. Gradient Selection: Gradients are selected from the 8 corners of the unit hypercube surrounding p. For a corner defined by bits j, k, l \in \{0, 1\}, the gradient vector g{jkl} has components \pm 1: g{jkl} = [(-1)^j, (-1)^k, (-1)^l] The dot product with the fractional offset f = p - i simplifies to additions and subtractions: \text{grad3D}(f) = \pm fx \pm fy \pm fz The signs are determined by the corner's bit indices. 4. Dimension Reducibility Optimization (3D): To reduce texture lookups, 3D noise is computed using 2D noise and z-gradients. Compute the hash for the current and next integer z-slice: h0 = \text{hash}(iz + 1) h1 = \text{hash}(iz + 2) Index the 2D textures using the x, y coordinates and the z-hash: c0 = (ix, iy, h0) c1 = (ix, iy, h1) Retrieve 2D noise values n0 = \text{tex\2d}(c0), n1 = \text{tex\2d}(c1) and z-gradients g0 = \text{tex\zgrad}(c0), g1 = \text{tex\zgrad}(c1). 5. Interpolation: Perform trilinear interpolation. The final 3D noise using separate 2D noise and z-gradient textures is: N(p) = \text{lerp}(fz, n0 + fz \cdot g0, n1 + fz \cdot g1) The source provides this formula (19), noting that the 2D noise and gradient are pre-combined or accessed such that the final step is a linear interpolation between the two z-slices, where each slice value includes the z-gradient contribution. 6. Modulo Implementation: Exact (5-instruction): i \bmod M = i - \lfloor i/M \rfloor \cdot M. Used for 2D noise to ensure periodicity at M. Inexact (4-instruction): i \bmod M = \text{frac}(i/M) \cdot M. Used for 3D+ where precision loss is less critical. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bbsmodexact(x, M): return x - (x // M) M def bbsmodinexact(x, M): return (x / M - (x // M)) M def bbshash(x, M, exact=True): mod = bbsmodexact if exact else bbsmodinexact return mod(x x, M) def hash3(x, y, z, M, exact=True): h = bbshash(x + 1, M, exact) h = bbshash(h + y + 1, M, exact) return bbshash(h + z + 1, M, exact) def fade(t): return t t t (t (t 6 - 15) + 10) # Standard Perlin fade def lerp(t, a, b): return a + t (b - a) def grad3d(fx, fy, fz, cornerbits): sx = 1 if cornerbits[0] == 0 else -1 sy = 1 if cornerbits[1] == 0 else -1 sz = 1 if cornerbits[2] == 0 else -1 return sx fx + sy fy + sz fz def noise3d(p, M, exact=True): ix, iy, iz = int(p[0]), int(p[1]), int(p[2]) fx, fy, fz = p[0] - ix, p[1] - iy, p[2] - iz # Compute hashes for the 8 corners of the unit hypercube h000 = hash3(ix, iy, iz, M, exact) h100 = hash3(ix + 1, iy, iz, M, exact) h010 = hash3(ix, iy + 1, iz, M, exact) h110 = hash3(ix + 1, iy + 1, iz, M, exact) h001 = hash3(ix, iy, iz + 1, M, exact) h101 = hash3(ix + 1, iy, iz + 1, M, exact) h011 = hash3(ix, iy + 1, iz + 1, M, exact) h111 = hash3(ix + 1, iy + 1, iz + 1, M, exact) # Compute gradient dot products for each corner u000 = grad3d(fx, fy, fz, (h000 % 2, (h000 >> 1) % 2, (h000 >> 2) % 2)) u100 = grad3d(fx - 1, fy, fz, (h100 % 2, (h100 >> 1) % 2, (h100 >> 2) % 2)) u010 = grad3d(fx, fy - 1, fz, (h010 % 2, (h010 >> 1) % 2, (h010 >> 2) % 2)) u110 = grad3d(fx - 1, fy - 1, fz, (h110 % 2, (h110 >> 1) % 2, (h110 >> 2) % 2)) u001 = grad3d(fx, fy, fz - 1, (h001 % 2, (h001 >> 1) % 2, (h001 >> 2) % 2)) u101 = grad3d(fx - 1, fy, fz - 1, (h101 % 2, (h101 >> 1) % 2, (h101 >> 2) % 2)) u011 = grad3d(fx, fy - 1, fz - 1, (h011 % 2, (h011 >> 1) % 2, (h011 >> 2) % 2)) u111 = grad3d(fx - 1, fy - 1, fz - 1, (h111 % 2, (h111 >> 1) % 2, (h111 >> 2) % 2)) # Fade and interpolate fx, fy, fz = fade(fx), fade(fy), fade(fz) ux00 = lerp(fx, u000, u100) ux10 = lerp(fx, u010, u110) ux01 = lerp(fx, u001, u101) ux11 = lerp(fx, u011, u111) uy0 = lerp(fy, ux00, ux10) uy1 = lerp(fy, ux01, ux11) return lerp(fz, uy0, uy1) Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. The BBS hash involves squaring and modulo, which is more expensive than a simple table lookup but avoids memory latency. Memory Complexity: O(1) if purely computed. O(1) with texture optimization (storing 2D slices). Performance: The 4-instruction modulo is faster but inexact. The 5-instruction modulo is exact but slower. Texture lookups accelerate 3D noise by reducing dependent lookups. Strengths: No permutation table required; suitable for GPUs with limited constant memory; dimension reducibility reduces texture fetches. Limitations: Axis-aligned clumping is visible in 2D results; the inexact modulo causes non-repeating noise at modulus M in lower dimensions. When to use: When GPU constant memory is constrained and a permutation table cannot be stored; for 3D/4D turbulence where clumping is less noticeable. When not to use: When exact periodicity at a specific modulus is required in 2D; when visual quality in 2D is critical due to clumping. Modified Noise is described in a thesis on real-time volumetric rendering. It modifies Perlin's improved noise to be more suitable for GPU implementation by removing table lookups and using the Blum-Blum-Shub generator. Real-Time Volumetric Rendering of Fire in a Production System, https://clas.iusb.edu/math-compsci/prior-thesis/YVanzinethesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Curl Noise
head: Bridson Curl Noise
body: Curl noise is a procedural noise function designed to generate time-varying, incompressible turbulent velocity fields. It solves the problem of creating visually plausible fluid-like motion by constructing a divergence-free vector field from a scalar potential. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point \mathbf{P} = (x, y), time t, noise scale s. Output: Velocity vector \mathbf{v} = (vx, vy). Data Structures: Permutation table P: Array of size 512 containing integers 0..255 to map coordinates to gradient indices. Gradient vectors \mathbf{g}: For 2D Perlin noise, typically 4 diagonals: (\pm 1, \pm 1). Steps: 1. Generate Scalar Potential: Compute a single scalar noise value at \mathbf{P} to form the potential \psi. \psi = \text{PerlinNoise}(x/s, y/s, t) 2. Compute Curl: Calculate the 2D curl of \psi to obtain the velocity field \mathbf{v}. \mathbf{v} = \nabla \times (0, 0, \psi) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y} \\ -\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} \end{pmatrix} 3. Numerical Derivatives: Since Perlin noise is interpolated, derivatives are computed using central finite differences to approximate the partial derivatives. Parameters: Scale s: Controls the spatial frequency of the turbulence. Typical values range from 0.1 to 10.0 depending on the desired feature size. Time t: Advances the field to create animation. Incremented per frame or per simulation step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tileability: To create seamless looping textures, the noise function must be implemented with periodic boundary conditions or tileable gradient assignments. Precision: Computing derivatives of interpolated noise requires careful handling of the fade function derivatives or finite difference step size to maintain C^1 continuity and avoid numerical noise. Zero Direction: If the query point lies exactly on a lattice line where the gradient contribution is flat, the derivative may be numerically unstable; clamping or adding a small epsilon mitigates this. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec2: def init(self, x, y): self.x = x self.y = y def add(self, other): return Vec2(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y) def sub(self, other): return Vec2(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y) def mul(self, s): return Vec2(self.x s, self.y s) def truediv(self, s): return Vec2(self.x / s, self.y / s) perm = list(range(256)) 2 gradients = [Vec2(1,1), Vec2(-1,1), Vec2(1,-1), Vec2(-1,-1)] def fade(t: float) -> float: return 6 t5 - 15 t4 + 10 t3 def lerp(a: float, b: float, t: float) -> float: return a + t (b - a) def dot(v1: Vec2, v2: Vec2) -> float: return v1.x v2.x + v1.y v2.y def perlinnoise(p: Vec2, time: float) -> float: ix = int(math.floor(p.x)) & 255 iy = int(math.floor(p.y)) & 255 fx = p.x - math.floor(p.x) fy = p.y - math.floor(p.y) ux = fade(fx) uy = fade(fy) A = perm[ix] + iy AA = perm[A] AB = perm[A + 1] B = perm[ix + 1] + iy BA = perm[B] BB = perm[B + 1] g = lambda idx: gradients[idx % len(gradients)] n00 = dot(g(AA), p) n10 = dot(g(BA), p - Vec2(1, 0)) n01 = dot(g(AB), p - Vec2(0, 1)) n11 = dot(g(BB), p - Vec2(1, 1)) return lerp(lerp(n00, n10, ux), lerp(n01, n11, ux), uy) def curlnoise(p: Vec2, time: float, scale: float) -> Vec2: s = Vec2(p.x / scale, p.y / scale) eps = 1e-4 def dNdx(pos): return (perlinnoise(pos + Vec2(eps, 0), time) - perlinnoise(pos - Vec2(eps, 0), time)) / (2 eps) def dNdy(pos): return (perlinnoise(pos + Vec2(0, eps), time) - perlinnoise(pos - Vec2(0, eps), time)) / (2 eps) vx = dNdy(s) vy = -dNdx(s) return Vec2(vx, vy) Time Complexity: O(1) per query, proportional to the number of lattice points in the cell (4 for 2D Perlin) times the number of derivative evaluations (4 for central differences). Memory Complexity: O(1) for the permutation table and gradient set. Strengths: Produces incompressible flow naturally; visually pleasing turbulence; efficient to evaluate; easily animatable via time parameter. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of scale to balance independence and coherence; finite difference derivatives amplify high-frequency noise if step size is too small. Usage: Commonly rendered using geometry shader sprites with accumulate blend to create colored density trails for fluid visualization. Curl noise was presented by Bridson et al.. It is based on the mathematical property that the curl of any vector field is divergence-free. The method extends earlier flow noise techniques by guaranteeing incompressibility without requiring a separate pressure solve. A gradient noise variant with reduced directional artifacts. Use when isotropic noise is required. Uses 4D noise for 3D spatial variation. Use for higher quality 3D textures. Interpolates scalar values at lattice points rather than gradients. Use for simpler implementations. The 2D version of Perlin noise. Use for 2D textures. Details on the fade and gradient functions. Use for implementation details. Optimized for lower dimensions. Use when memory or performance is constrained. Combines multiple octaves of noise. Use for multi-scale detail. name: Modified Noise (Dimension-Reducible)
head: Dimension-reducible noise
body: Modified Noise is a gradient-based procedural noise function designed to optimize 3D noise calculation on GPUs by exploiting dimension reducibility. It differs from standard Perlin noise by selecting gradient vectors from the corners of a unit-n cube rather than the edge centers, a geometric constraint required to decompose 3D evaluation into independent 2D noise and 1D gradient lookups. This allows the noise to be stored in 2D textures (or a single 2-channel texture) and computed with minimal texture fetches, making it suitable for real-time volumetric rendering of effects like fire and smoke. Modified Noise computes a scalar value n(\mathbf{P}) at a query point \mathbf{P} = (x, y, z) by reducing the 3D problem into two 2D hash lookups and a linear interpolation along the z-axis. Input: Query point \mathbf{P} = (x, y, z). Output: Scalar noise value n(\mathbf{P}). The method relies on pre-computed or on-the-fly hash generation. For performance, gradients are typically pre-baked into textures. 1. 2D Noise Texture (T{noise}): Stores the 2D noise contribution for integer z slices. 2. Z-Gradient Texture (T{zgrad}): Stores the gradient contribution along the z-axis for integer z slices. 3. Alternative Single Texture (T{combined}): A 2-channel texture where each texel returns a pair (v, g). The hash function maps integer coordinates to gradient indices. The source specifies a simple modular hash: \text{hash}(i) = i^2 \mod M where M is the size of the hash table/texture dimension. For a query point \mathbf{P}, let px, py, pz be the integer coordinates of the cell corners. The 2D hash terms for the integer z values below (c0) and above (c1) the noise argument are computed as: c0 = (px, py, \text{hash}(pz)) c1 = (px, py, \text{hash}(pz + 1)) The lookup coordinates for the 2D textures are determined by the x, y coordinates and the hashed z index. The final value is interpolated along the fractional z component (p{zf} = z - \lfloor z \rfloor) using a polynomial interpolation function flerp. The flerp function is defined as: \text{flerp}(t, a, b) = (1 - \text{polynomial}(t)) \cdot a + \text{polynomial}(t) \cdot b where \text{polynomial}(t) is either a Cubic Hermite or Quintic Hermite polynomial. 1. Decompose Input: Extract integer parts px, py, pz and fractional part p{zf} from \mathbf{P}. 2. Compute Hash Indices: Calculate h0 = \text{hash}(pz) and h1 = \text{hash}(pz + 1). 3. Define Lookup Coordinates: Set c0 = (px, py, h0) and c1 = (px, py, h1) for the 2D texture lookups. 4. Lookup Values: Retrieve v0, g0 from c0 and v1, g1 from c1. 5. Interpolate: Compute val0 = v0 + p{zf} \cdot g0 and val1 = v1 + p{zf} \cdot g1, then n(\mathbf{P}) = \text{flerp}(p{zf}, val0, val1). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def modifiednoise3d(x, y, z, hashtablesize=256, noisedata=None, zgraddata=None): """ Computes Modified Noise at point (x, y, z). Assumes pre-baked data structures noisedata and zgraddata are accessible. """ # 1. Decompose coordinates px = int(x) if x >= 0 else int(x) - 1 py = int(y) if y >= 0 else int(y) - 1 pz = int(z) if z >= 0 else int(z) - 1 pzf = z - pz # Fractional z component # 2. Compute hash indices for z-slices # Hash function: h(i) = i^2 mod M h0 = (pz pz) % hashtablesize h1 = ((pz + 1) (pz + 1)) % hashtablesize # 3. Determine 2D lookup coordinates c0 = (px, py, h0) c1 = (px, py, h1) # 4. Lookup values from textures v0, g0 = lookupcombinedtexture(c0, noisedata, zgraddata) v1, g1 = lookupcombinedtexture(c1, noisedata, zgraddata) # 5. Interpolate along Z val0 = v0 + pzf g0 val1 = v1 + pzf g1 # 6. Apply polynomial interpolation (flerp) poly = quintichermite(pzf) result = (1 - poly) val0 + poly val1 return result def quintichermite(t): return 6 t5 - 15 t4 + 10 t3 def lookupcombinedtexture(coord, noisedata, zgraddata): """ Retrieves noise and z-gradient values from pre-baked data structures. Returns (noisevalue, zgradientvalue) """ px, py, h = coord # Simple array lookup for demonstration; replaces GPU texture fetch v = noisedata[px % len(noisedata)][py % len(noisedata)][h] g = zgraddata[px % len(zgraddata)][py % len(zgraddata)][h] return v, g Hash Table Size (M): Determines the period of the noise. Typical values are powers of 2 (e.g., 256, 512) for efficient modulo operations. Polynomial Choice: The source mentions both Cubic and Quintic Hermite polynomials for flerp. Precision: Using x^2 mod M can introduce patterns if M is not chosen carefully (e.g., if M shares factors with the coordinate range). Boundary Conditions: The hash function must handle negative integer coordinates correctly. Time Complexity: O(1) per noise evaluation. The cost is dominated by two texture lookups and a few arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) for 2D textures, where N is the resolution of the hash table/texture. This is significantly less than the O(N^3) required for a full 3D texture. Performance: Optimized for GPUs. The source notes that the low-level OpenGL shader code for 2D Modified noise is 45 instructions, which is too many for a function used several times for the same pixel; this is handled by pre-baking the gradient texture using the hash procedure. Strengths: Dimension reducibility allows efficient storage and computation. It produces a "fluid" character with large, solid parts that separate naturally, making it suitable for fire and smoke. Limitations: Requires pre-computation or texture storage for optimal performance. The visual character differs from Perlin noise due to corner-based gradient selection, which may not be desirable for all applications. Modified Noise was introduced in the context of real-time volumetric rendering of fire in a production system. It was developed to address the performance constraints of rendering complex volumetric effects like fire, smoke, and fog on hardware with limited texture bandwidth and instruction count. The method exploits the dimension reducibility property to store 3D noise data in 2D textures, optimizing the calculation process. It is distinct from Perlin noise in its gradient selection strategy, picking gradients from the corners of a unit-n cube to satisfy the dimension reducibility requirement. name: Fractal Brownian Motion
head: 3D Perlin Noise with Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM), 3D Perlin-like Noise, 3D Perlin-like Noise and Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM), Fractional Brownian Motion, Octave Perlin Noise
body: Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) is a procedural noise construction that generates self-similar, multi-scale stochastic patterns by summing multiple octaves of a base noise function with increasing frequency and decreasing amplitude. It solves the problem of creating fractal-like noise with many frequencies by combining variations of a single base noise function whose parameters are scaled differently. Unlike its sibling Simplex Noise or Value Noise, which define the local interpolation behavior, FBM defines the spectral summation strategy across scales [22470-tileable-noise-generation.md]. FBM constructs a fractal noise field by evaluating a base gradient noise function (such as Perlin Noise) at multiple scales and summing the results. The base noise provides smooth, continuous values, while the summation introduces high-frequency detail. Input: A 3D query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, the number of octaves n, the lacunarity parameter \beta (typically 1), and the base noise function noise(\mathbf{p}) which returns values in [-1, 1]. Output: A scalar value Bn(\mathbf{p}) representing the fractal noise at \mathbf{p}. The method requires no persistent data structures beyond those of the underlying base noise function (e.g., a permutation table and gradient vectors as defined in Gradient-based Noise (Perlin/Simplex)). Octaves (n): The number of noise layers to sum. Typical values are 4–7. Lacunarity (\beta): Controls the rate of frequency increase and amplitude decay. \beta=1 corresponds to 1/f noise, common in nature. Persistence: The amplitude decay factor per octave. Typically 0.5 (halving amplitude each octave). Frequency Multiplier: The factor by which the input coordinate is scaled each octave. Typically 2.0. Seed: Used to initialize the base noise permutation table. 1. Initialize: Set sum = 0.0, amplitude = 0.5, and position = p. 2. Loop Octaves: For i from 0 to n-1: a. Evaluate the base noise at the current position: val = noise(position). b. Add the weighted contribution to the sum: sum += amplitude \times val. c. Update the position for the next octave: position = position \times lacunarity. d. Update the amplitude: amplitude = amplitude \times persistence. 3. Return: Return sum. The formal definition of FBM with n octaves is: Bn(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=1}^n oi(\mathbf{p}), \quad \text{with} \quad oi(\mathbf{p}) = \frac{noise(2^{i-1}\mathbf{p})}{2^{\beta(i-1)}} Where: noise(\mathbf{p}) \in [-1, 1] is the base noise function. \beta \in [0, 2] is the lacunarity parameter. n \in \mathbb{N}^+ is the number of octaves. For \beta=1, this simplifies to summing noise(2^{i-1}\mathbf{p}) / 2^{i-1}, which corresponds to halving the amplitude and doubling the frequency each octave. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fbm(p, octaves, basenoisefunc, persistence=0.5, lacunarity=2.0): """ Computes Fractal Brownian Motion. Args: p: vec3, query point. octaves: int, number of octaves. basenoisefunc: function, takes vec3, returns float in [-1, 1]. persistence: float, amplitude decay per octave. lacunarity: float, frequency multiplier per octave. Returns: float, the FBM value. """ total = 0.0 amplitude = 0.5 position = p for in range(octaves): total += amplitude basenoisefunc(position) position = position lacunarity amplitude = amplitude persistence return total Single Octave Limit: A single-octave implementation (e.g., fbm3 returning 0.5 noise3(p)) lacks the multi-scale detail of true FBM. Precision: High octave counts with high lacunarity can lead to floating-point precision issues at large coordinates. Using modulo arithmetic or tiling techniques can mitigate this [22470-tileable-noise-generation.md]. Boundary Conditions: Standard FBM is not periodic [22470-tileable-noise-generation.md]. For tileable volumes, the base noise must be tileable (e.g., using Fourier-domain techniques or coordinate wrapping) [22470-tileable-noise-generation.md]. Division by Zero: If the base noise function involves vector normalization, ensure the gradient vector is not zero to avoid division by zero errors. Creates a 3D scalar field by summing multiple octaves of layered Simplex noise, offset by a linear vertical gradient [1302-noise-field-generator.md]. It distinguishes itself by explicitly incorporating a vertical bias and Simplex variants, rather than generic Perlin noise [1302-noise-field-generator.md]. Generates global cloud patterns by applying procedural noise to volumetric air blocks, creating 2D cloud patterns on a spherical surface by combining octaves of mixed Perlin and Worley noise [1711-global-cloud-cover-with-curl-noise.md]. Generates volumetric density maps by combining low-frequency Perlin noise for broad mass with inverted Worley (cellular) noise to carve hollows, producing a puffy cumulus appearance [2355-3d-perlin-worley-noise-generation.md]. It uses fBm principles to sum multiple noise octaves. Generates 3D voxel worlds by evaluating fBm noise against a threshold to determine voxel existence and material type, creating organic structures like cave systems [2556-voxel-world-generation-with-perlin-noise.md]. Generates sharp, ridge-like structures by applying a non-linear transformation to the absolute value of base noise, combined with inter-octave feedback [4249-ridged-multifractal.md]. It builds on FBM by replacing linear summation with a ridge-specific kernel and multiplicative feedback. Produces procedural noise fields that are spatially periodic, ensuring seamless continuity when repeated [22470-tileable-noise-generation.md]. It differs from FBM by enforcing strict modulo arithmetic or Fourier techniques for periodicity, whereas FBM defines the spectral summation [22470-tileable-noise-generation.md]. A specific application of the Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) method to FBM, where octaves are presorted by range and have analytic bounds, requiring no memory storage for bounds. It uses analytic expressions for \Deltai and s(i,n) to compute bounds, with \beta=1 ensuring all octaves share the same Lipschitz constant. Introduces high-frequency noise on cloud surfaces by remapping the noise value using a range defined by low-frequency noise, used by Guerilla Games. Accumulates derivatives across octaves, dampening amplitude via 1/(1+|grad|^2) to create realistic erosion patterns where steep slopes stay smooth. Erodes the surface of an SDF by adding negative Perlin noise values to the signed distance, effectively pushing the surface outward where noise is negative. Time Complexity: O(n) per query point, where n is the number of octaves. Each octave requires one evaluation of the base noise function. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory beyond the base noise function's storage (e.g., permutation table). Performance: The method is computationally inexpensive per sample but can be costly in raymarching due to the high number of samples required for volumetric rendering. Strengths: Produces natural, multi-scale detail; simple to implement; widely supported. Limitations: Not inherently periodic; high-frequency artifacts may appear if lacunarity is too high; single-octave implementations lack detail. When to Use: Generating stochastic patterns with details at potentially many different scales. When Not to Use: When strict periodicity is required without additional tiling techniques [22470-tileable-noise-generation.md]. FBM has been extensively used in computer graphics to create stochastic patterns with details at potentially many different scales. The method is a standard technique in procedural generation for volume rendering, terrain synthesis, and texture mapping. name: Noise Field Generator
head: Layered Simplex Noise with Gradient, SimplexNoise3D
body: The Noise Field Generator creates a 3D scalar field for volumetric rendering by summing multiple octaves of layered Simplex noise, offset by a linear vertical gradient. It solves the problem of generating organic, multi-scale density distributions (such as soft clouds or terrain) without requiring pre-baked texture data. It distinguishes itself from its parent, 3D Perlin-like Noise and Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM), by explicitly incorporating a vertical gradient bias and specific Simplex noise variants into the layering process, rather than relying solely on generic hash-based Perlin noise. Inputs: Dims: 3D integer vector defining the voxel grid dimensions (Dx, Dy, Dz). Scale: Scalar spatial frequency multiplier for the noise field. Time: Scalar time offset for animated noise. Voxels: Output buffer (e.g., RWStructuredBuffer<float>) of size Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Data Structures: The output is a flat 1D array representing the 3D grid. The index for a voxel at (x, y, z) is calculated as: \text{index} = x + Dx \times (y + Dy \times z). Thread groups are processed in blocks of [8, 8, 8] threads. Algorithm: 1. Thread Identification: Each thread computes its global 3D coordinate id (x, y, z) based on its group ID and local thread ID. 2. Position Calculation: Compute the centered world position p for the voxel: p = \text{Scale} \times \left( \text{id} + 0.5 - \frac{\text{Dims}}{2} \right). This centers the noise field around the origin (0,0,0). 3. Gradient Initialization: Initialize the scalar value with a vertical gradient: \text{value} = -p.y. 4. Octave Summation: Add multiple octaves of Simplex noise. Each octave uses a different frequency scaling, spatial offset, and amplitude. First Octave: \text{value} \leftarrow \text{value} + \text{SimplexNoise}(p \times 0.83 + \mathbf{v}1 \times \text{Time}) \times 0.5 Where \mathbf{v}1 = (-0.37, -0.12, 0). Second Octave: \text{value} \leftarrow \text{value} + \text{SimplexNoise}(p \times 0.72 + \mathbf{v}2 \times \text{Time}) \times 0.5 Where \mathbf{v}2 = (0.21, 0.07, 0). Note: Sources indicate a 2-octave structure for this specific "SimplexNoise3D" variant. Other FBM implementations may loop for more octaves. 5. Output: Write the computed value to the Voxels buffer at the calculated index. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def noisefieldgeneratorkernel(idx, idy, idz, Dimsx, Dimsy, Dimsz, Scale, Time, Voxels): # 1. Calculate centered world position px = Scale (idx + 0.5 - Dimsx / 2.0) py = Scale (idy + 0.5 - Dimsy / 2.0) pz = Scale (idz + 0.5 - Dimsz / 2.0) p = (px, py, pz) # 2. Initialize with vertical gradient value = -py # 3. Add First Octave of Simplex Noise offset1 = (-0.37 Time, -0.12 Time, 0.0) freq1 = 0.83 sample1 = simplexnoise3d((px freq1 + offset1[0], py freq1 + offset1[1], pz freq1 + offset1[2])) value += sample1 0.5 # 4. Add Second Octave of Simplex Noise offset2 = (0.21 Time, 0.07 Time, 0.0) freq2 = 0.72 sample2 = simplexnoise3d((px freq2 + offset2[0], py freq2 + offset2[1], pz freq2 + offset2[2])) value += sample2 0.5 # 5. Write to output buffer index = idx + Dimsx (idy + Dimsy idz) Voxels[index] = value Parameters: Scale: Spatial scaling factor. Typical values depend on the desired world units; uses a generic Scale variable. Time: Animation speed. Multiplies the spatial offset vectors. Octaves: The number of noise layers. The specific "SimplexNoise3D" variant in uses 2 octaves. General FBM implementations use 4–6 octaves. Gain: Amplitude multiplier per octave. In, both octaves use a gain of 0.5. In standard FBM, Gain is typically 0.5. Lacunarity: Frequency multiplier per octave. In, frequencies are hardcoded (0.83, 0.72). In standard FBM, Lacunarity is typically ~2.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Using float for position calculations may lead to precision loss at large world coordinates. Centering the grid around the origin (as done in Step 2) mitigates this. Boundary Artifacts: Without inter-octave rotation or varying lacunarity, axis-aligned artifacts may appear. The specific Simplex variant in avoids this by using distinct spatial offsets for each octave. Gradient Direction: The vertical gradient -p.y assumes Y is up. If Z is up, the gradient should be -p.z. Integrates Fractal Brownian Motion noise fields with rendering techniques such as raymarching, lighting models, and color mapping. It focuses on deriving density, normals, and color from layered noise samples for use in raymarched scenes, building on the raw noise generation of the Noise Field Generator by applying intersection and shading logic. Generates a 2D terrain heightmap by sampling a 3D scalar noise field at a fixed vertical coordinate (e.g., z=0). It projects the layered noise onto the X-Y plane to produce continuous elevation data, differing from the full 3D volume generation by ignoring the vertical gradient offset and returning a single scalar height per X/Y coordinate. A technique where the output of a noise function is fed back as a coordinate offset to distort the sampling domain, creating organic, fluid-like patterns. It differs from standard FBM by introducing non-linear spatial distortion that mimics turbulent flow, using the noise amplitude itself to drive the displacement. A noise basis function that creates the visual impression of Brownian motion by summing the absolute values of noise at decreasing frequencies. It differs from standard FBM by applying the absolute value operator to each octave, introducing discontinuities in the gradient and creating a "carved" or fragmented appearance. A fractal noise variant that sums the absolute values of Perlin noise octaves. It results in a range of 0.0 to 1.0 and creates "cloudy" or "rough" textures. It differs from standard FBM by eliminating negative values before accumulation. A specialized noise function for simulating ocean waves. It computes wave components by adding noise to UV coordinates, calculating sine/cosine components (wv, swv), and mixing them with a "choppy" factor. It supports bidirectional propagation by summing results for time-shifted UVs. A texture class that maps 3D points to RGB colors using Perlin noise, scaled and bounded within a specific region. It stores color, min/max bounds, scale, and a Perlin noise instance, blending the noise result with a base color. Time Complexity: O(N \times O), where N is the number of voxels and O is the number of octaves. Each voxel requires O noise evaluations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output voxel grid. Performance: More computationally intensive than single-layer noise due to multiple noise samples per voxel. Performance can be optimized by reducing the octave count for distant objects or using LOD. Strengths: Produces realistic, organic, multi-scale details suitable for clouds and terrain. The vertical gradient adds physical plausibility to density distributions. Limitations: Requires significant computation for high-resolution volumes. The specific Simplex variant in is limited to 2 octaves, which may lack fine detail compared to higher-octave FBM. The Noise Field Generator is a specific implementation of procedural noise generation for volumetric data, often used in real-time graphics and GPU-based terrain/cloud generation. It builds on the principles of Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) and Simplex Noise. The specific variant with vertical gradient and layered Simplex noise is documented in GPU-based marching cubes and volumetric raymarching tutorials. name: FBM Combinations
head: FBM Application Pipeline, FBM Integration Techniques
body: FBM Combinations integrates Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise fields with rendering techniques such as raymarching, lighting models, and color mapping to produce complex volumetric or surface appearances. It distinguishes itself from raw noise generation by focusing on the application of the scalar field—specifically how density, normals, and color are derived from layered noise samples for use in raymarched scenes. It builds on Noise Field Generator by taking its output and applying intersection, shading, and compositing logic. Inputs: A 3D position vector \mathbf{p} (world or local space). FBM parameters: octaves N, lacunarity L, gain G. Raymarching parameters: max steps, step size function, termination threshold. Lighting parameters: light direction \mathbf{l}, eye direction \mathbf{e}. Outputs: Raymarched distance or density value. Shaded color with normals and lighting. Data Structures: No complex structures; primarily scalar accumulators and vectors. Steps: 1. FBM Evaluation: Compute the base FBM value f(\mathbf{p}) using layered noise. f(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} G^i \cdot \text{noise}(L^i \cdot \mathbf{p}) 2. Raymarching Intersection: Use f(\mathbf{p}) as a density or height field to determine ray termination. Adaptive step size: dt = \max(0.05, 0.02 \cdot t), where t is current ray distance. Early termination: If accumulated alpha/density > 0.99, break loop. LOD selection: Octave count varies by distance: oct = 5 - \lfloor \log2(1.0 + t \cdot 0.5) \rfloor. 3. Normal Calculation: Approximate surface normals using a directional derivative (1 sample) instead of a full gradient. Formula: \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\text{vec3}(f(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon \mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{p}), \epsilon, f(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon \mathbf{y}) - f(\mathbf{p}))). \epsilon is a small offset. 4. Lighting: Apply lighting model using \mathbf{n} and light direction \mathbf{l}. Volumetric lighting: Approximate illumination by density difference along light direction. 5. Color Mapping: Map noise values to RGB using power curves. Example (flame): \text{color} = \text{vec3}(1.5c, 1.5c^3, c^6). Example (inverse): \text{color} = \text{vec3}(k)/r \cdot z. 6. Fresnel (Optional): For water surfaces, blend based on view angle. \text{fresnel} = \text{pow}(1.0 - \text{dot}(\mathbf{n}, -\mathbf{e}), 3.0). 7. Multi-layer Compositing: Combine shape (low freq), ridged (mid freq), and color (high freq) layers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def noise(p): # Minimal procedural noise for self-containment return math.sin(p[0] 12.9898 + p[1] 78.233 + p[2] 45.164) def fbm(p, octaves): val = 0.0 amp = 1.0 freq = 1.0 for in range(octaves): val += amp noise((p[0]freq, p[1]freq, p[2]freq)) amp = 0.5 freq = 2.0 return val def vec3(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) if mag > 1e-8 else (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def mix(a, b, t): return (a[0] + t(b[0]-a[0]), a[1] + t(b[1]-a[1]), a[2] + t(b[2]-a[2])) def fbmcombinations(p, rayorigin, raydirection, maxsteps=100): t = 0.0 accumulateddensity = 0.0 noiseval = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): dt = max(0.05, 0.02 t) pos = (rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0]t, rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1]t, rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2]t) octaves = 5 - int(math.log2(1.0 + t 0.5)) noiseval = fbm(pos, octaves) accumulateddensity += noiseval dt if accumulateddensity > 0.99: break t += dt eps = 0.01 ex = (eps, 0.0, 0.0) ey = (0.0, eps, 0.0) nx = fbm((pos[0]+ex[0], pos[1]+ex[1], pos[2]+ex[2])) - fbm(pos) ny = fbm((pos[0]+ey[0], pos[1]+ey[1], pos[2]+ey[2])) - fbm(pos) normal = normalize(vec3(nx, eps, ny)) lightdir = normalize(vec3(1.0, 1.0, 0.0)) diffuse = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) c = noiseval color = vec3(1.5 c, 1.5 c3, c6) eyedir = normalize(vec3(-raydirection[0], -raydirection[1], -raydirection[2])) fresnel = (1.0 - dot(normal, normalize(vec3(-eyedir[0], -eyedir[1], -eyedir[2])))) 3.0 watercolor = vec3(0.5, 0.8, 1.0) color = mix(color, watercolor, fresnel) return color, accumulateddensity Synthesizes volumetric-like textures from 2D UVs using tiled cell indexing and multiplicative masks. Choose when rendering 2D surfaces with depth-like appearance. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is octaves and S is raymarch steps. Adaptive step size and LOD reduce effective S and N at distance. Memory Complexity: O(1) for procedural noise; no texture storage required. Strengths: High detail at multiple scales; flexible shading and color mapping; no texture memory overhead. Limitations: Computationally expensive per pixel due to raymarching and multiple noise evaluations; sensitive to step size and \epsilon for normals. When to use: Real-time procedural terrain, ocean, or cloud rendering where texture memory is limited or dynamic detail is needed. When not to use: Static scenes where precomputed textures are more efficient; high-performance requirements with many rays. Originated from procedural noise techniques in computer graphics, popularized by Ken Perlin and others. FBM combinations are widely used in real-time shaders for terrain, water, and volumetric effects. The specific techniques cited (adaptive step, directional derivatives, power curve color mapping) are common in shader development communities. skills/skills/shader-dev/techniques/procedural-noise.md at main..., https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/skills/blob/main/skills/shader-dev/techniques/procedural-noise.md, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Pseudo-Volume Noise Compositing
body: Pseudo-Volume Noise Compositing is a procedural noise generation technique that synthesizes volumetric-like textures by compositing four layered noise samples over a pseudo-3D position field derived from 2D UV coordinates. It distinguishes itself from standard 2D noise by introducing a depth-like dimension via tiled cell indexing and applying a multiplicative cell mask to simulate volume boundaries, while using a power-law brightness reduction to control luminance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Fragment UV coordinates (uv), numCells (integer, number of cells in x and y), tilingPerCell (float, repetitions per cell), positionOffset (vec3), totalBrightness (float), cellMask (float, output from position generator), noiseLayerDistortion (vec4), noiseLayerEnabled (vec4), noiseLayerInverted (vec4), and noiseLayerN (vec4 for each layer N=1..4, containing scale, power, angleOffset, type). Output: Final grayscale intensity C with full alpha. Data Structures: noiseLayerData (vec4): Layout is [scale, power, angleOffset, type]. scale (float): Multiplier for noise position. power (float): Exponent for the noise value. angleOffset (float): Parameter for specific noise types (e.g., Voronoi). type (int): 0=Perlin (cnoise), 1=Simplex (snoise), 2=Voronoi, 3=Nebula. noiseLayerDistortion (vec4): Distortion strength for each layer. Steps: 1. Compute Pseudo-Volume Position and Mask: Remap UV to ensure correct stacking order: uv{remapped} = (uv.x, 1.0 - uv.y). Calculate cell coordinates: cells = fract(uv{remapped} \cdot numCells) and coords = uv{remapped} \cdot numCells. Determine 1D frame index: frameIndex1D = coords.y \cdot numCells + coords.x. Calculate depth index: zFrameIndex = (frameIndex1D / (numCells \cdot numCells)) \cdot tilingPerCell. Calculate per-cell UV: uv{perCell} = cells \cdot tilingPerCell. Construct noise position: noisePosition = (uv{perCell}.x, uv{perCell}.y, zFrameIndex) + positionOffset. Compute cellMask based on boundary conditions (e.g., hiding first/last cells to avoid artifacts). 2. Transform Noise Position: Apply additional UV modifications to noisePosition to produce noiseSamplePosition. 3. Sample Four Noise Layers: For each layer i \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}: Extract noiseLayerData for layer i. If noiseLayerEnabled[i] is false, set Pi = 1.0 and continue. Calculate distortion strength: distortionStrength = 0.1 \cdot noiseLayerDistortion[i]. If distortionStrength > 0, compute distortion noise d = cnoise(distortionStrength \cdot noiseSamplePosition) and update noiseSamplePosition \leftarrow noiseSamplePosition + d. Evaluate noise type: Type 0: val = cnoise(noiseSamplePosition \cdot scale). Type 1: val = snoise(noiseSamplePosition \cdot scale). Type 2: val = voronoi(noiseSamplePosition \cdot scale, angleOffset, scale). Type 3: val = nebulaNoise(noiseSamplePosition \cdot scale). Clamp value: val = clamp(val, 0.0, 1.0). Invert if noiseLayerInverted[i] is true: val = 1.0 - val. Apply power: Pi = val^{|power|}. 4. Sum Layers: Sum = P1 + P2 + P3 + P4. 5. Apply Brightness Reduction: Brightness = Sum^2 \cdot totalBrightness. 6. Compute Multiplicative Mask: Product = P1 \cdot P2 \cdot P3 \cdot P4. Mask = Product \cdot cellMask. 7. Final Compositing: C = Brightness \cdot Mask. Formula: C = (P1 + P2 + P3 + P4)^2 \cdot B \cdot (P1 \cdot P2 \cdot P3 \cdot P4 \cdot M) Where Pi are the processed noise layer outputs, B is totalBrightness, and M is cellMask. Parameters: totalBrightness: Scalar uniform. Value not specified in sources. numCells: Integer. Controls the grid density. tilingPerCell: Float. Controls the frequency of noise within each cell. noiseLayerDistortion: vec4. Controls the intensity of positional distortion per layer. noiseLayerEnabled: vec4. Boolean flags (0 or >0) enabling/disabling layers. noiseLayerInverted: vec4. Boolean flags (0 or >0) inverting layer outputs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Artifacts: Engines like Unity may produce artifacts at the edges of stacked noise slices. The implementation includes logic to hide the first and last cells (isFirstCell, isLastCell) to create padding. Precision: The use of fract and large numCells values may introduce floating-point precision issues in the depth index calculation. Division by Zero: If numCells is 0, the depth index calculation will fail. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pseudovolumenoisecompositing(uv, numcells, tilingpercell, positionoffset, totalbrightness, cellmask, noiselayerdistortion, noiselayerenabled, noiselayerinverted, noiselayerdatalist): """ uv: vec2 (fragment UV) numcells: int tilingpercell: float positionoffset: vec3 totalbrightness: float cellmask: float noiselayerdistortion: vec4 noiselayerenabled: vec4 noiselayerinverted: vec4 noiselayerdatalist: list of 4 vec4 [scale, power, angleOffset, type] """ # 1. Compute Pseudo-Volume Position uvremapped = vec2(uv.x, 1.0 - uv.y) cells = fract(uvremapped numcells) coords = uvremapped numcells frameindex1d = coords.y numcells + coords.x zframeindex = (frameindex1d / (numcells numcells)) tilingpercell uvpercell = cells tilingpercell noiseposition = vec3(uvpercell.x, uvpercell.y, zframeindex) + positionoffset # Note: cellmask is assumed to be computed externally or via createPseudoVolumePosition # Logic for hiding first/last cells is embedded in cellmask generation # 2. Transform Noise Position (modifyUVforNoiseSamplePosition) # Standard coordinate space transform noisesampleposition = modifyuvfornoisesampleposition(noiseposition) samplednoises = vec4(1.0) # 3. Sample Four Noise Layers for i in range(4): if not noiselayerenabled[i]: samplednoises[i] = 1.0 continue noisedata = noiselayerdatalist[i] scale = noisedata.x power = noisedata.y angleoffset = noisedata.z noisetype = int(noisedata.w) distortionstrength = 0.1 noiselayerdistortion[i] currentpos = noisesampleposition if distortionstrength > 0: # Standard 3D Perlin noise evaluation distortionnoise = perlinnoise(distortionstrength currentpos) currentpos += distortionnoise # Evaluate noise type if noisetype == 0: val = perlinnoise(currentpos scale) elif noisetype == 1: val = simplexnoise(currentpos scale) elif noisetype == 2: val = voronoinoise(currentpos scale, angleoffset, scale) elif noisetype == 3: val = nebulanoise(currentpos scale) else: val = 0.0 val = clamp(val, 0.0, 1.0) if noiselayerinverted[i]: val = 1.0 - val powerabs = abs(power) samplednoises[i] = pow(val, powerabs) p1, p2, p3, p4 = samplednoises.x, samplednoises.y, samplednoises.z, samplednoises.w # 4. Sum Layers sumval = p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 # 5. Apply Brightness Reduction brightness = pow(sumval, 2.0) totalbrightness # 6. Compute Multiplicative Mask product = p1 p2 p3 p4 mask = product cellmask # 7. Final Compositing c = brightness mask return c def perlinnoise(p): # Standard 3D Perlin noise evaluation return... def simplexnoise(p): # Standard 3D Simplex noise evaluation return... def voronoinoise(p, angleoffset, scale): # Standard 3D Voronoi noise evaluation return... def nebulanoise(p): # Standard 3D Nebula noise evaluation return... def modifyuvfornoisesampleposition(pos): # Standard coordinate space transform return pos Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment, as it involves a fixed number of noise evaluations (4 layers) and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only uniform storage for layer parameters. Strengths: Produces complex, volumetric-like textures from 2D inputs; allows fine-grained control over each layer's type, distortion, and inversion; multiplicative masking allows for organic voids or cell structures. Limitations: The "pseudo-3D" nature is an approximation; true volumetric lighting or ray-marching is not supported. Performance scales linearly with the number of layers, but the current implementation is fixed at 4. When to use: When a 2D shader needs to simulate volumetric noise effects (e.g., smoke, clouds, stone textures) without the computational cost of true 3D noise or ray-marching. When not to use: When true 3D consistency is required across different viewing angles or when dynamic lighting within the volume is needed. Pseudo-Volume Noise Compositing is implemented in the "texturinator" project by MangoButtermilch, an unofficial tool for generating procedural textures. It leverages GLSL noise functions (cnoise, snoise, voronoi, nebulaNoise) to create layered noise patterns. The technique is designed to work within fragment shaders, mapping 2D UVs to a pseudo-3D space to simulate depth. texturinator, https://github.com/MangoButtermilch/texturinator, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Terrain Heightmap Generation via Noise
head: GetHeightAtWorldLocation, Heightmap Generation via Noise, Perlin Noise Height Generation, Procedural terrain heightmap, Terrain Height Generation, World Height Noise
body: This method generates a 2D terrain heightmap by converting 2D world coordinates into a 3D height value using scaled fractal noise, remapped to a specific vertical range. It differs from its parent, the Noise Field Generator, by taking world-space X/Y coordinates and returning a single height value (Z) rather than a full 3D volume. It is distinct from FBM Combinations and Domain Warped FBM by using standard additive fractal summation without domain warping. The method takes 2D world-space coordinates and returns a single height value. The process involves scaling the input coordinates, computing a Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) sum, and remapping the result to a target vertical range. Inputs: WorldX, WorldY: 2D world-space coordinates (float). Settings: A configuration struct containing Seed, Scale, Octaves, Persistence, Lacunarity, BaseHeight, and HeightScale. Outputs: Height: A single float representing the terrain elevation at (WorldX, WorldY). The Settings struct contains: Seed (int32): Random seed for noise generation. Default: 1337. Scale (float): World units per noise cell. Controls smoothness. Typical range: 1000-5000. Default: 2000.0f. Octaves (int32): Number of noise layers summed. Range: 1-8. Default: 4. Persistence (float): Amplitude falloff per octave. Range: 0.0-1.0. Default: 0.5f. Lacunarity (float): Frequency multiplier per octave. Default: 2.0f. BaseHeight (float): Final output offset. Default: 0.0f. HeightScale (float): Final output amplitude. Default: 500.0f. The implementation relies on a permutation table P of 512 integers to handle wrap-around for gradient indices. 1. Calculate Scale Factor: Prevent division by zero. Scale = \max(Settings.Scale, \text{small\positive\constant}) 2. Normalize Coordinates: Convert world coordinates to noise space. NoiseX = \frac{WorldX}{Scale} NoiseY = \frac{WorldY}{Scale} 3. Compute Raw Noise: Calculate the fractal noise value in the range [-1, 1] using the FractalPerlin2D function. Noise = FractalPerlin2D(NoiseX, NoiseY, Settings) 4. Remap to Target Range: Map the noise value to the final height range. Two variations exist in the sources: Linear Offset/Scale (Source 1): Height = BaseHeight + Noise \times HeightScale Min/Max Mapping (Source 2): Height = minHeight + \lfloor (Noise + 1.0) \times 0.5 \times (maxHeight - minHeight) \rfloor Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def initpermutation(seed): """Initialize a 512-entry permutation table from a seed.""" p = list(range(256)) # Standard Fisher-Yates shuffle seeded deterministically state = seed for i in range(255, 0, -1): state = (state 1103515245 + 12345) & 0x7FFFFFFF j = state % (i + 1) p[i], p[j] = p[j], p[i] return p + p # Duplicate for wrap-around def TerrainHeightmapGeneration(WorldX, WorldY, Settings): """Generates terrain height at WorldX, WorldY.""" # Step 1: Calculate Scale Factor scale = max(Settings.Scale, 1e-6) # Step 2: Normalize world coordinates noisex = WorldX / scale noisey = WorldY / scale # Step 3: Compute raw noise value in [-1, 1] noise = FractalPerlin2D(noisex, noisey, Settings) # Step 4: Remap to target range (Source 1 variant) height = Settings.BaseHeight + noise Settings.HeightScale return height def FractalPerlin2D(X, Y, Settings): """Computes Fractal Brownian Motion using 2D Perlin noise.""" total = 0.0 frequency = 1.0 amplitude = 1.0 maxvalue = 0.0 # Clamp octaves to valid range [1, 8] as per octaves = max(1, min(Settings.Octaves, 8)) for in range(octaves): rawnoise = RawPerlin2D(X frequency, Y frequency, Settings.Seed) total += rawnoise amplitude maxvalue += amplitude amplitude = Settings.Persistence frequency = Settings.Lacunarity return total / maxvalue if maxvalue > 0 else 0.0 def RawPerlin2D(X, Y, Seed): """Standard 2D Perlin Noise implementation.""" P = initpermutation(Seed) xi = int(math.floor(X)) & 255 yi = int(math.floor(Y)) & 255 xf = X - math.floor(X) yf = Y - math.floor(Y) u = Fade(xf) v = Fade(yf) aa = P[P[xi] + yi] ab = P[P[xi] + yi + 1] ba = P[P[xi + 1] + yi] bb = P[P[xi + 1] + yi + 1] gaa = Grad(aa, xf, yf) gba = Grad(ba, xf - 1.0, yf) gab = Grad(ab, xf, yf - 1.0) gbb = Grad(bb, xf - 1.0, yf - 1.0) x1 = Lerp(u, gaa, gba) x2 = Lerp(u, gab, gbb) return Lerp(v, x1, x2) def Fade(t): return t t t (t (t 6 - 15) + 10) def Lerp(t, a, b): return a + t (b - a) def Grad(hash, x, y): h = hash & 3 if h == 0: return x + y elif h == 1: return -x + y elif h == 2: return x - y else: return -x - y Division by Zero: If Settings.Scale is 0, coordinate normalization fails. Octave Clamping: Octaves must be clamped to [1, 8] to prevent undefined behavior. Precision: The noise function returns values roughly in [-1, 1]. The normalization step in FractalPerlin2D ensures strict bounding. Coordinate Wrap: The permutation table lookup uses bitwise AND with 255 (& 255) to handle negative coordinates and large values. FBM Combinations extends basic fractal summation by allowing non-standard combinations of noise layers (e.g., multiplication, subtraction) rather than simple additive summation. Choose this when you need specific spectral shapes or non-Gaussian height distributions. Domain Warped FBM applies a secondary noise function to distort the input coordinates of the primary noise. Choose this for creating more complex, organic features like ridges or swirls that standard FBM cannot produce. Time Complexity: O(O), where O is the number of octaves. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the noise generation itself, assuming the permutation table is pre-computed. Strengths: Simple to implement, produces smooth and organic terrain, easily adjustable via parameters. Limitations: The resulting terrain is purely mathematical and may lack geological realism without post-processing. When to use: Procedural terrain generation, placing objects at ground level, and foliage scatter without a physical landscape actor. When not to use: When high-fidelity, geologically accurate terrain is required, or when 3D volumetric details are needed instead of a surface heightmap. This method is derived from procedural noise techniques popularized by Ken Perlin. The specific implementation in the sources is part of an Unreal Engine 5 voxel project. The use of Perlin noise for terrain generation is a standard technique in procedural content generation for games, allowing for infinite, deterministic landscapes. The parent method, Noise Field Generator, suggests an evolution towards 3D volumetric noise, but this heightmap method remains a common 2D projection for surface-level interactions. name: Absolute Noise Sum
head: fractal abs sum
body: Absolute Noise Sum is a fractal noise technique that sums the absolute values of noise function outputs across multiple octaves. Unlike standard Fractal Brownian Motion (fBm) which preserves the signed nature of the noise, this method produces a scalar field with a range of 0.0, \infty). This characteristic creates "cloudy" or "rough" textures, distinguishing it from its siblings like [FBM Combinations and Turbulence by eliminating negative values before accumulation. Inputs: p: 3D input coordinate (vector). N{oct}: Number of octaves (integer). f0: Initial frequency (scalar). g0: Initial amplitude (scalar, typically 1.0). l: Lacunarity (scalar, typically 2.0). gradientnoise: The underlying gradient-based noise function (e.g., Simplex or Perlin) returning a signed value. Outputs: S: The accumulated absolute noise sum (scalar in [0, \infty)). Data Structures: Standard floating-point accumulators suffice. Algorithm: 1. Initialize the sum accumulator S = 0. 2. Initialize the current frequency f = f0. 3. Initialize the current amplitude a = g0. 4. Loop for i from 0 to N{oct} - 1: a. Evaluate the noise function at the scaled coordinate: v = \text{gradient\noise}(p \cdot f). b. Add the weighted absolute noise to the sum: S \leftarrow S + |v| \cdot a. c. Update frequency: f \leftarrow f \cdot l. d. Update amplitude: a \leftarrow a \cdot g. 5. Return S. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def absolutenoisesum(p, octaves, frequency, lacunarity, gain): """ Computes the sum of absolute noise values over multiple octaves. Args: p (tuple): 3D input coordinate (x, y, z). octaves (int): Number of noise octaves to sum. frequency (float): Initial frequency scaling factor. lacunarity (float): Frequency multiplier per octave (typically 2.0). gain (float): Amplitude multiplier per octave. Returns: float: The accumulated absolute noise sum. """ sumval = 0.0 freq = frequency amp = 1.0 # Initial amplitude as per source for in range(octaves): sumval += abs(gradientnoise((p[0] freq, p[1] freq, p[2] freq))) amp freq = lacunarity amp = gain return sumval def gradientnoise(p): # Standard gradient noise evaluation (e.g., Simplex/Perlin) # Implementation provided by parent article [1302-noise-field-generator.md] # Returns a value in [-1, 1] or [0, 1] depending on implementation. x, y, z = p n = x 127.1 + y 311.7 + z 74.7 n = (n & 0x7fffffff) / 2147483647.0 return n 2.0 - 1.0 Parameters and Typical Values: Initial Amplitude: 1.0. This differs from standard fBm where the first octave often has amplitude 0.5 or 1.0 depending on normalization, but the key distinction is the absolute value operation. Lacunarity: 2.0. Gain: Multiplicative factor per octave. In many implementations, this is < 1.0 to ensure convergence, but the source notes only specify the initial amplitude is 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Summing many octaves with high gain can lead to overflow if not normalized. Boundary Conditions: The noise function gradientnoise must handle arbitrary floating-point coordinates. Degenerate Input: If octaves is 0, the sum is 0. A variant of fBm using Perlin noise where the absolute value of each octave is taken before summing, creating a "billowy" or "cloudy" appearance distinct from the smoother signed sums of standard fBm. It builds on Absolute Noise Sum by specifically utilizing Perlin's gradient noise as the base generator. Time Complexity: O(N{oct}) per sample, where N{oct} is the number of octaves. Each octave requires one noise evaluation and basic arithmetic. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: The method is computationally lightweight compared to domain-warped variants [4493-domain-warped-fbm.md] as it does not require secondary noise evaluations for coordinate perturbation. However, it is more expensive than a single octave of noise. Strengths: Produces natural-looking "cloudy" or "rough" textures with a positive range. Simple to implement. Limitations: The output range is unbounded above if gain \ge 1, requiring manual normalization for consistent rendering. It lacks the directional bias of standard fBm, which may be undesirable for terrain [4214-terrain-heightmap-generation-via-noise.md]. When to use: When a positive-only, rough texture is desired, such as for cloud density or surface roughness maps. When not to use: When signed displacement is required (use standard fBm) or when directional features are needed (use Domain Warped FBM). The method is described in the context of GPU-based Marching Cubes implementations for generating procedural voxel data. The specific implementation details are found in open-source repositories. name: Perlin Absolute Noise (Turbulence)
head: Fractal Abs Sum, Ken Perlin’s trick, Perlin Turbulence
body: Perlin Absolute Noise, commonly known as Turbulence, is a procedural noise technique that modifies Fractal Brownian Motion (fBm) by taking the absolute value of the noise function at each octave before summing. This operation creates a range of non-negative values and introduces discontinuities in the derivative, resulting in a 'billowy' or 'cloudy' appearance distinct from the smoother signed sums of standard fBm. It builds on Absolute Noise Sum by specifically utilizing Perlin's gradient noise as the base generator. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D position vector p (float3). Parameters: octaves: Integer number of noise layers to sum. lacunarity: Float multiplier for frequency increase between octaves (typically 2.0). gain: Float multiplier for amplitude decrease between octaves. Output: A scalar float representing the accumulated turbulence value. Data Structures The method relies on a base Perlin gradient noise implementation, which typically uses permutation and gradient lookup tables. No additional data structures are required for the turbulence summation itself. Steps 1. Initialize sum to 0.0 and amp (amplitude) to 1.0. 2. Loop for i from 0 to octaves - 1: a. Evaluate the base Perlin noise function at the current position p: n = \text{noise}(p). b. Take the absolute value of the noise: |n|. c. Add the weighted absolute noise to the sum: \text{sum} \leftarrow \text{sum} + \text{amp} \times |n|. d. Update the position for the next octave: p \leftarrow p \times \text{lacunarity}. e. Update the amplitude for the next octave: \text{amp} \leftarrow \text{amp} \times \text{gain}. 3. Return sum. Formulas The final value T(p) is calculated as: T(p) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} \text{gain}^i \cdot | \text{noise}( \text{lacunarity}^i \cdot p) | Where: N is the number of octaves. \text{noise}(\cdot) is the underlying Perlin gradient noise function. |\cdot| denotes the absolute value operation. Parameters lacunarity: Typically 2.0, causing the frequency to double each octave. gain: Typically 0.5, halving the amplitude each octave to ensure convergence. octaves: Integer controlling the number of frequency layers. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Discontinuities: Taking the absolute value introduces discontinuities in the first derivative at points where the noise crosses zero. This is intentional for the "billowy" effect but may cause artifacts in applications requiring smooth gradients. Range: The output range is [0, \sum \text{gain}^i]. If gain < 1, the sum converges to a finite maximum less than 2.0 (specifically 1/(1-\text{gain}) if amp starts at 1). The sources do not specify a normalization step to map this back to [0, 1] or [-1, 1] within the core turbulence function itself, though one source mentions a mapToSigned function for other contexts. Implementers should be aware that the raw output is not bounded to [-1, 1]. Alternative Scaling: Some implementations scale the amplitude by 1/f instead of using a separate gain parameter, which diminishes higher frequency contributions while keeping values within the original noise range. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def turbulence(p, octaves, lacunarity, gain): """ Calculates Perlin Turbulence. Args: p (Vector3): Input 3D position. octaves (int): Number of noise octaves. lacunarity (float): Frequency multiplier per octave. gain (float): Amplitude multiplier per octave. Returns: float: The accumulated turbulence value. """ sumval = 0.0 amp = 1.0 for i in range(octaves): # Evaluate base Perlin gradient noise at current position # Returns a signed scalar in [-1, 1] n = noise(p) # Take absolute value (Ken Perlin's trick) absn = abs(n) # Add weighted absolute noise to sum sumval += amp absn # Update position and amplitude for next octave p = p lacunarity amp = amp gain return sumval def noise(p): """Standard Perlin gradient noise evaluation. Uses permutation and gradient lookup tables to return a signed scalar in [-1, 1].""" # Implementation details for base Perlin noise are omitted; # this function represents the standard gradient noise operation. pass Sums signed noise values directly without absolute value, resulting in smoother, continuous derivatives. Choose when smooth gradients are required. A broader category including any noise function (not just Perlin) where absolute values are summed. Perlin Turbulence is a specific instance using Perlin noise. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of octaves. Memory Complexity: Auxiliary space is O(1), but the base Perlin noise implementation requires permutation and gradient lookup tables. Performance: The base Perlin noise implementation compiles to approximately 40 instructions in a pixel shader. The turbulence function adds minimal overhead per octave (multiplications and an absolute value). Strengths: Creates visually appealing "cloudy" or "billowy" textures with visibly sharper edges and doubled peaks compared to standard fBm. Limitations: The absolute value operation introduces derivative discontinuities, which may be undesirable for applications requiring smooth shading or physical simulation. The output range is not automatically normalized to [-1, 1]. Perlin Absolute Noise, or Turbulence, was introduced by Ken Perlin as a variant of fractal Brownian motion. Perlin's original algorithm is Academy Award-winning and uses gradient noise over \mathbb{R}^3 with a scalar output. The technique is widely used in procedural texture generation for creating natural-looking surfaces like clouds, smoke, and marble. It differs from standard fBm by the application of the absolute value function, which was described as "Ken Perlin's trick".
