name: Domain Warped FBM
head: 2D Clouds, Domain Warping, FastNoiseLite Domain Warp, Inigo Quilez Domain Warping, NoiseTexture2D/3D Domain Warp
body: Domain Warped FBM is a procedural noise technique where the output of a noise function is fed back as a coordinate offset to distort the sampling domain, creating organic, fluid-like patterns. It differs from standard FBM by introducing non-linear spatial distortion that mimics turbulent flow, and from simple noise offsets by using the noise amplitude itself to drive the displacement. Inputs and Outputs Input: Base 2D or 3D coordinate p (or uv), time t (optional, for animation), warp strength WARPSTRENGTH, and finite difference step eps. Output: Scalar noise value f and optional normal vectors for lighting. Data Structures Coordinates are represented as 2D or 3D vectors. Noise functions return scalars or vectors; examples normalize to [0, 1] via 0.5 + 0.5 noise. Steps 1. Compute Primary Warp Field: Calculate a displacement vector q using a vector-valued FBM on input coordinates modulated by time: q = fbm2(p + t 0.1). 2. Compute Secondary Warp Field: Calculate a second displacement vector r using FBM on coordinates offset by q scaled by WARPSTRENGTH and an asymmetry offset: r = fbm2(p + WARPSTRENGTH q + vec2(1.7, 9.2)). 3. Compute Final Noise Value: Sample the FBM function again using coordinates warped by r: f = 0.5 + 0.5 fbm(p + WARPSTRENGTH r). 4. Modulate Output: Mix the final noise value f with a cubic function of f, weighted by the magnitude of the secondary warp r: f = mix(f, f^3 3.5, f ||r||). 5. Compute Normals (Optional): Approximate derivatives using finite differences with eps to compute normals for lighting. Sample f at p + epsx and p + epsy while recomputing r at those positions, then construct normal = normalize(vec3(fx - f, eps.x, fy - f)). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def hash2d(p): # Simple stable hash for procedural noise x, y = p x = math.sin(x 127.1 + y 311.7) 43758.5453 y = math.sin(x 269.5 + y 183.3) 43758.5453 return (math.fmod(x, 1.0), math.fmod(y, 1.0)) def noise2d(p): # Bilinear interpolation of hash values ix, iy = math.floor(p[0]), math.floor(p[1]) fx, fy = p[0] - ix, p[1] - iy fx, fy = fx fx (3.0 - 2.0 fx), fy fy (3.0 - 2.0 fy) h00 = hash2d((ix, iy)) h10 = hash2d((ix + 1, iy)) h01 = hash2d((ix, iy + 1)) h11 = hash2d((ix + 1, iy + 1)) nx0 = h00[0] (1.0 - fx) + h10[0] fx nx1 = h01[0] (1.0 - fx) + h11[0] fx return nx0 (1.0 - fy) + nx1 fy def fbm(p, octaves=3, lacunarity=2.0, gain=0.5): # Multi-octave noise summation per standard definition value = 0.0 amplitude = 1.0 frequency = 1.0 for in range(octaves): value += amplitude noise2d((p[0] frequency, p[1] frequency)) amplitude = gain frequency = lacunarity return value def fbm2(p, octaves=3, lacunarity=2.0, gain=0.5): # Returns a 2D vector by summing two orthogonal FBM fields x = fbm(p, octaves, lacunarity, gain) y = fbm((p[0] + 1.0, p[1] + 1.0), octaves, lacunarity, gain) return (x, y) def domainwarpedfbm(p, time=0.0, warpstrength=0.5, eps=1e-4): # Step 1: Primary warp field q q = fbm2((p[0] + time 0.1, p[1])) # Step 2: Secondary warp field r offset = (1.7, 9.2) r = fbm2((p[0] + warpstrength q[0] + offset[0], p[1] + warpstrength q[1] + offset[1])) # Step 3: Final noise value f f = 0.5 + 0.5 fbm((p[0] + warpstrength r[0], p[1] + warpstrength r[1])) # Step 4: Modulate output weight = f math.sqrt(r[0]2 + r[1]2) ffinal = f (1.0 - weight) + (f3 3.5) weight # Step 5: Compute normals via finite differences epsx = (eps, 0.0) epsy = (0.0, eps) # Recompute q and r at perturbed positions to match evidence qx = fbm2((p[0] + epsx[0] + time 0.1, p[1] + epsx[1])) qy = fbm2((p[0] + epsy[0] + time 0.1, p[1] + epsy[1])) rx = fbm2((p[0] + epsx[0] + warpstrength qx[0] + offset[0], p[1] + epsx[1] + warpstrength qx[1] + offset[1])) ry = fbm2((p[0] + epsy[0] + warpstrength qy[0] + offset[0], p[1] + epsy[1] + warpstrength qy[1] + offset[1])) fx = 0.5 + 0.5 fbm((p[0] + epsx[0] + warpstrength rx[0], p[1] + epsx[1] + warpstrength rx[1])) fy = 0.5 + 0.5 fbm((p[0] + epsy[0] + warpstrength ry[0], p[1] + epsy[1] + warpstrength ry[1])) normal = (fx - f, eps, fy - f) normlen = math.sqrt(normal[0]2 + normal[1]2 + normal[2]2) normal = (normal[0] / normlen, normal[1] / normlen, normal[2] / normlen) return ffinal, normal Parameters WARPSTRENGTH: Controls the intensity of the distortion. Typical values are around 0.5. eps: Finite difference step size for normal calculation. Typically 1.0 / resolution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Domain warping can cause coordinate values to grow large, potentially leading to precision issues in the underlying noise function. Symmetry: Without an asymmetry offset (e.g., vec2(1.7, 9.2)) in the secondary warp, patterns may exhibit unwanted repetition artifacts. Performance: Computing normals requires additional FBM evaluations, increasing computational cost per sample. Combines multiple FBM variants for complex textures. Choose when you need to blend different noise characteristics. Uses noise for terrain elevation. Choose for landscape generation. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, but with a higher constant factor due to multiple FBM evaluations (typically 3–4 calls per sample). Memory Complexity: O(1) as it is a fully procedural function. Performance: On a NoiseTexture2D sprite, applying domain warp reduces maximum pixel error from 143/255 to 1–3/255 compared to a baseline, while keeping the whole-frame mean error stable at 0.72/255. Strengths: Produces highly organic, fluid-like patterns suitable for clouds, smoke, and lava. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than standard FBM; excessive warp strength causes visual tearing and coordinate overflow. The technique is implemented in the FastNoiseLite library and exposed as a domain warp feature in NoiseTexture2D and NoiseTexture3D. It is widely used in real-time rendering for procedural textures and atmospheric effects. feat(renderer): draw FogVolume and FogMaterial into the volumetric fog, https://github.com/Vortiago/textscene-inspector/pull/732, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) skills/skills/shader-dev/techniques/procedural-noise.md at main..., https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/skills/blob/main/skills/shader-dev/techniques/procedural-noise.md, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Turbulence
head: Turbulent Noise
body: Turbulence is a noise basis function that creates the visual impression of Brownian motion or turbulent flow by summing absolute values of noise at decreasing frequencies. It differs from standard Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) by applying the absolute value operator to each octave, which introduces discontinuities in the gradient and reflects the underlying noise vectors. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D position vector \mathbf{p} (\mathbb{R}^3). Output: A scalar value representing the accumulated turbulent noise magnitude. Data Structures The method requires a base noise function \mathcal{N} that returns a signed scalar value. Parameters octives: Integer constant, typically 4. Defines the number of octaves to accumulate. lacunarity: Float constant, typically 2.0. Multiplier for frequency in each subsequent octave. gain: Float constant, typically 0.5. Multiplier for amplitude in each subsequent octave. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize sum = 0.0, freq = 1.0, and amp = 1.0. 2. Loop i from 0 to octives - 1: a. Evaluate the base noise function at the scaled position: n = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{p} \cdot \text{freq}). b. Take the absolute value of the noise result: |n|. c. Add the weighted absolute noise to the sum: sum += |n| \cdot \text{amp}. d. Update frequency: freq = lacunarity. e. Update amplitude: amp = gain. 3. Return sum. Formula The mathematical definition for N octaves is: T(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} | \mathcal{N}( \mathbf{p} \cdot \lambda^i) | \cdot g^i Where: \mathbf{p} is the input position. \mathcal{N} is the base noise function returning a signed scalar. \lambda is the lacunarity (typically 2.0). g is the gain (typically 0.5). N is the number of octaves (typically 4). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def turbulence(pos, octives=4, lacunarity=2.0, gain=0.5): sumval = 0.0 freq = 1.0 amp = 1.0 for i in range(octives): # Evaluate base noise function at scaled position; returns signed scalar # The sources do not specify the exact base noise implementation noiseval = basenoise(pos freq) sumval += abs(noiseval) amp freq = lacunarity amp = gain return sumval Edge Cases and Pitfalls Discontinuities: The use of abs() creates sharp corners in the noise field where the original noise crosses zero, which is intentional for the "turbulent" look. Range: The output range is not bounded to [0, 1] or [-1, 1] like the base noise, and grows with the number of octaves. Precision: Accumulating many octaves with high lacunarity can lead to precision loss in the lower bits if fixed-point arithmetic is used; floating-point is recommended. Combines multiple FBM layers with different weights and offsets. Use when smooth, continuous fractal detail is needed. Uses noise to generate elevation data. Use for procedural terrain. Distorts the input coordinates of FBM using another noise field. Use for organic, swirling patterns like smoke or marble. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of octaves. Each octave requires one evaluation of the base noise function. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: The cost is dominated by the base noise function evaluation. Strengths: Creates visually distinct, fragmented textures that mimic turbulent fluids or rough surfaces. Simple to implement. Limitations: The discontinuities from abs() can look unnatural if not tuned correctly. It lacks the smoothness of standard FBM. When to use: When simulating solid textures with a "carved" appearance, or when the visual style requires sharp transitions in noise gradients. When not to use: When smooth, continuous variation is required (use standard FBM instead). The turbulence basis function was introduced in the context of solid texturing for volume rendering. It is described in the book Volume Visualization and Volume Graphics, where it is noted for giving the impression of Brownian motion. The specific implementation using mnoise (a modified noise function) is found in the VolumetricFire project. The technique relies on the self-similar 1/f pattern introduced by summing noise at decreasing frequencies, with the absolute value function reflecting the gradient vectors to create discontinuities. yomotsu/VolumetricFire, https://github.com/yomotsu/VolumetricFire, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF Volume Visualization and Volume Graphics, https://www3.cs.stonybrook.edu/~mueller/teaching/cse332/volvisChapter.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (book)

name: Global Cloud Cover with Curl Noise
head: Curl Noise Cloud Generation, PlaceCloudLayer, Spherical Noise Cloud Pattern
body: Generates global cloud patterns by applying procedural noise to volumetric air blocks within a specified height range, marking the top layer in a cloud map. It creates 2D cloud patterns on a spherical surface by combining octaves of mixed Perlin and Worley noise, subtracting a threshold, and clamping the result. Inputs: World dimensions: worldWidth for X and Z axes, height for top altitude, thickness for vertical span. Noise parameters: compression scaling factor, number of octaves, noise types (Perlin/Worley mix). Threshold value for cloud formation. Outputs: cloudMap: A 2D array of size worldWidth x worldWidth marking cloud presence. Cubemap: 6 x 512 x 512 resolution for global cloud cover storage. Transmittance array: 7 x 512 x 512 for deep opacity maps. Data Structures: cloudMap: 2D integer/boolean array, dimensions worldWidth x worldWidth. Cubemap: 6 faces, each 512 x 512, storing spherical cloud coverage. Transmittance array: 7 layers of 512 x 512 for cascaded deep opacity maps. Steps: 1. Initialize cloudMap as a 2D array of size worldWidth x worldWidth. 2. Iterate through vertical slices of the cloud layer: loop y from height down to height - thickness (inclusive). 3. Loop x from 1 to worldWidth - 2 and z from 1 to worldWidth - 2. 4. Check if the block at (x, y, z) is air (GetBlockData(x, y, z) == 0). 5. If air, calculate noise value: noiseValue = noise.simplex3\left(\frac{x \cdot compression}{100}, \frac{y \cdot compression}{100}, \frac{z \cdot compression}{100}\right). 6. For global spherical patterns, combine octaves of mixed Perlin and Worley noise. 7. Subtract a threshold from the combined noise value. 8. Clamp the resulting value to create 2D cloud patterns on the spherical surface. 9. Restrict clouds between bottom and top heights to form prism-like objects. 10. Store results in the cloudMap or cubemap. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatecloudcover(worldwidth, height, thickness, compression, threshold): cloudmap = [[0] worldwidth for in range(worldwidth)] for y in range(height, height - thickness - 1, -1): for x in range(1, worldwidth - 1): for z in range(1, worldwidth - 1): if getblockdata(x, y, z) == 0: noiseval = simplex3(x compression / 100, y compression / 100, z compression / 100) if noiseval > threshold: cloudmap[x][z] = 1 return cloudmap Note: simplex3 and getblockdata are assumed standard noise and voxel access functions. Parameters: compression: Scaling factor for noise coordinates. Octaves: 3 octaves of 64x64x64 Perlin-Worley noise for horizontal 2D shapes. High-frequency detail: 5 octaves of 64x64x64 Worley noise. Vertical profile: 10 values in a texture. Noise size: 64x64x64 for detail layers. Edge Cases: Clamping operation for cover sample noise was removed in later implementations to improve quality. Use cascaded deep opacity maps instead of a single opacity map for performance. Powder function for scattered light at cloud fringes: 1.0 - exp(-powderdecay d). Memory: Uses a 6x512x512 cubemap for global cover and 7x512x512 transmittance array. Performance: Renders 3 deep opacity maps with one 512x512 offset layer per frame. Strengths: Efficient global coverage; supports high-frequency detail via Worley noise. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of threshold and compression for desired cloud density. Originated from techniques for generating global cloud cover using curl noise and mixed Perlin/Worley noise. name: 3D Perlin-Worley Noise Texture Generation
head: Low-Frequency Cloud Shape Generation, Multi-Octave Worley, Noise-based Density Sampling, Perlin-Worley Hybrid, Volumetric Density Map Generation, sampleLowFrequency
body: This method generates 3D volumetric density maps for procedural cloud rendering by combining low-frequency Perlin noise for broad cloud mass with inverted Worley (cellular) noise to carve hollows, producing a puffy cumulus appearance. It differs from pure Perlin noise methods by introducing cellular structures that define cloud edges and internal voids, and from pure Worley methods by retaining the organic, continuous mass of gradient-based noise. It builds on 3D Perlin-like Noise and Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) by using fBm principles to sum multiple noise octaves. Inputs: Input position P (3D vector). Texture size T (3D integer vector). Global invocation ID G (3D integer vector from compute shader). Cloud coverage parameter (hardcoded to 0.6 in source implementations). Outputs: A 3D texture (e.g., rgba8) storing density values. Data Structures: uNoiseTexture: A writeonly uniform image3D bound at binding point 0 with rgba8 layout. cloudBaseShapeSampler: A 3D texture sampler used to sample low-frequency noise fields. Steps: 1. Coordinate Calculation: Compute fractional coordinates for the current voxel by dividing the global invocation ID by the texture size: C = G / T. Add an offset and scale the position if required by the specific noise implementation. 2. Sample Low-Frequency Base Shape: Sample the cloudBaseShapeSampler at the fractional coordinates to retrieve a vec4 of low-frequency noise values: L = \text{texture}(cloudBaseShapeSampler, C). 3. Compute Low-Frequency FBM: Construct a fractal sum from the Green, Blue, and Alpha channels of L using specific weights: L{FBM} = (L.g \times 0.625) + (L.b \times 0.25) + (L.a \times 0.125) Clamp the result to [0.0, 1.0]. 4. Generate Base Cloud Density: Remap the Red channel of L (L.r) using the computed L{FBM} to create the base cloud density. The source uses a function remapClamped with parameters derived from L{FBM}: D{base} = \text{remapClamped}(L.r, L{FBM} - 0.9, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) This step effectively thresholds and scales the noise to define where clouds exist. 5. Generate Worley Noise (Inverted): Sample Worley noise at frequency 1.0 and amplitude 1.0. Invert the result and scale to the range [-1, 1]. Store this in a variable named wor1. 6. Generate Multi-Octave Perlin Noise: Sample Perlin noise at 6 different frequencies and amplitudes to create a fractal sum. The specific octaves are: Frequency 1, Amplitude 8 Frequency 2, Amplitude 4 Frequency 4, Amplitude 2 Frequency 8, Amplitude 1 Frequency 16, Amplitude 0.5 Frequency 32, Amplitude 0.25 Sum these values to get the total Perlin contribution. 7. Combine and Finalize Density: Sum the Perlin noise layers and the inverted Worley noise (wor1). Subtract a constant offset of 0.2 and clamp the result to a minimum of 0: D = \max(0, \sum{i=1}^{6} Pi + \text{wor1} - 0.2) This formula represents the core density calculation. 8. Write Output: Store the computed density into the uNoiseTexture using imageStore() at the index corresponding to G. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateperlinworleynoise(G, T): # 1. Calculate fractional coordinates C = G / T # Add offset and scale as required by implementation C = C 1.0 + 0.0 # 2. Sample low-frequency base shape L = samplecloudbaseshape(C) # 3. Compute Low-Frequency FBM lowfrequencyfbm = (L.g 0.625) + (L.b 0.25) + (L.a 0.125) lowfrequencyfbm = clamp(lowfrequencyfbm, 0.0, 1.0) # 4. Define Base Cloud basecloud = remapclamped(L.r, lowfrequencyfbm - 0.9, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) # 5. Generate Inverted Worley Noise (Frequency 1.0, Amplitude 1.0) worleyval = worleynoise(C, 1.0, 1.0) worleyinverted = invertandscale(worleyval) # 6. Generate Multi-Octave Perlin Noise octaves = [(1, 8), (2, 4), (4, 2), (8, 1), (16, 0.5), (32, 0.25)] perlinsum = 0.0 for freq, amp in octaves: perlinsum += perlinnoise(C, freq, amp) # 7. Combine and Finalize Density density = max(0.0, perlinsum + worleyinverted - 0.2) # 8. Return density return density def samplecloudbaseshape(pos): # Standard 3D texture lookup returning vec4 (r, g, b, a) return texture3d(cloudBaseShapeSampler, pos) def worleynoise(pos, freq, amp): # Standard cellular noise implementation # Returns value in [0, 1] return amp standardcellular(pos freq) def perlinnoise(pos, freq, amp): # Standard 3D gradient noise implementation # Returns value in [-1, 1] return amp standardgradientnoise(pos freq) def invertandscale(worleyval): # Invert and scale to [-1, 1] inverted = 1.0 - worleyval return inverted 2.0 - 1.0 def remapclamped(value, minval, maxval, outmin, outmax): # Linear remapping with clamping if maxval == minval: return outmin t = clamp((value - minval) / (maxval - minval), 0.0, 1.0) return outmin + t (outmax - outmin) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of rgba8 for the output texture limits density resolution to 256 levels per channel, which may cause banding in smooth gradients. Use rgba16f or rgba32f if higher precision is required for raymarching. Boundary Conditions: The noise functions must handle periodic or seamless wrapping if the cloud layer is expected to tile or wrap around a sphere. Degenerate Input: If the camera is inside the cloud layer, the ray start point must be clamped to the camera position to avoid sampling errors at the entry point. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the 3D texture, as each voxel requires 6 Perlin noise evaluations and 1 Worley noise evaluation, plus texture sampling for the base shape. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the 3D texture storage. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces visually appealing, puffy cumulus clouds with natural-looking hollows and edges due to the Worley component. The separation of base shape and detail erosion allows for flexible tuning. Limitations: The fixed octaves and weights are hardcoded, reducing flexibility. The rgba8 output may limit dynamic range. The method is computationally expensive due to multiple noise evaluations per voxel. When to use: Ideal for real-time volumetric cloud rendering where visual quality is prioritized over absolute physical accuracy. When not to use: When high-precision density maps are required or when the scene geometry does not support the spherical cloud layer model. The technique originates from implementations of volumetric clouds in OpenGL, specifically described in "Volumetric Clouds with 3D Perlin-Worley Noise in OpenGL". It combines two distinct noise types: Perlin noise for organic, continuous mass and Worley noise for cellular, void-like structures. The method is implemented in community-driven WebGL and OpenGL projects. The specific parameters (octaves, weights) are derived from practical implementations aimed at achieving a "puffy cumulus appearance". name: Voxel World Generation with Perlin Noise
head: Blobby Cave Generation, Procedural Voxel Generation, Voxel Density Field Generation with Perlin Noise, World Generation
body: This method generates a 3D voxel-based world by evaluating fractal Brownian motion (fBm) or Perlin noise against a threshold to determine voxel existence and material type (stone, dirt, grass). It solves the problem of creating coherent, organic volumetric structures (such as 'blobby' cave systems) from procedural noise, similar to Dungeon Generation (DRG) techniques. It differs from simple binary voxel placement by incorporating multi-directional noise sampling, spatial constraints (like a central spawn room), and material assignment logic. Inputs: World dimensions: worldWidth, worldHeight (from SceneData). Noise parameters: seed, frequency, gain, threshold (from WorldGenerationData). Spatial constraints: spawnRoomRadius for the central empty area. Noise function: A 3D Perlin-like noise function snoise (or equivalent). Outputs: A 3D texture texturestorage3d<r32uint, readwrite> storing packed voxel data. Each 32-bit uint stores 4 voxels packed in (x,z) pairs within a single texel. Data Structures: WorldGenerationData: arity: f32 gain: f32 frequency: f32 threshold: f32 seed: f32 SceneData: screenWidth: u32, screenHeight: u32 worldWidth: u32, worldHeight: u32 octantSize: u32, octreeHighestLevel: u32 tonemap: u32, rayBounces: u32, screenFilter: u32 sunEnabled: u32, antiSmearEnabled: u32 mousePosX: u32, mousePosY: u32 sunDirX: f32, sunDirY: f32, sunDirZ: f32 sunIntensity: f32, time: f32, denoiseStrength: f32 Voxel Packing Layout (within a 32-bit uint): Bits 0-7: Voxel at (x, z) offset (0,0) relative to texel. Bits 8-15: Voxel at (0,1). Bits 16-23: Voxel at (1,0). Bits 24-31: Voxel at (1,1). Each voxel entry contains: Bits 0-3: Material index. Bits 4-7: Albedo/Color index. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Noise Offset: Generate a random 3D offset to shift the noise field, ensuring unique world generation per seed. python noiseOffset = Vector3( rng.Next(-9999, 9999), rng.Next(-9999, 9999), rng.Next(-9999, 9999)) 2. Compute Workgroup Mapping: In a compute shader, map the global invocation ID to voxel coordinates. The workgroup size is typically (8, 4, 8). The voxel position is derived from the texel position: python voxelPos.x = texelPos.x 2 voxelPos.y = texelPos.y voxelPos.z = texelPos.z 2 3. Iterate Voxel Block: Loop over the 2x2 block of voxels in the x and z dimensions corresponding to the current texel: python for x in range(2): for z in range(2): offsetVoxelPos = vec3<u32>(voxelPos.x + x, voxelPos.y, voxelPos.z + z) # Process voxel at offsetVoxelPos 4. Calculate Distance and Spawn Room Factor: Calculate Euclidean distance from the world origin (0,0,0) to the voxel location: d = \text{distance}(\text{ivec3}(0,0,0), \text{location}) Compute a 'room' factor to guarantee an empty spawn area in the center. This uses SmoothStep and InverseLerp based on spawnRoomRadius: python room = Mathf.SmoothStep(0f, 1f, Mathf.InverseLerp(spawnRoomRadius - 2f, spawnRoomRadius + 2f, distToCenter)) 5. Evaluate Noise Density: If distance d > 10, generate noise value. Otherwise, the voxel is empty (return false or 0). Compute the base density d using the 3D noise function. The noise function can be implemented as a custom 3D noise averaging six 2D Perlin samples with phase offsets: python noise = Noise3D((p + noiseOffset) caveNoiseScale) Where Noise3D is: python def Noise3D(p): xy = Mathf.PerlinNoise(p.x, p.y) yz = Mathf.PerlinNoise(p.y, p.z) xz = Mathf.PerlinNoise(p.x, p.z) yx = Mathf.PerlinNoise(p.y + 31.7f, p.x + 17.3f) zy = Mathf.PerlinNoise(p.z + 11.9f, p.y + 47.1f) zx = Mathf.PerlinNoise(p.z + 5.3f, p.x + 23.5f) return (xy + yz + xz + yx + zy + zx) / 6f Alternatively, use fBm with snoise (see for snoise implementation details): python noiseval = fbm(pos, octaves, lacunarity, gain, basefrequency, seed) Clamp the density d to the minimum of the noise-derived density and the room factor: d = \text{Min}(d, \text{room}) Calculate final density value: d = \text{Clamp01}(0.62 + (noise - 0.5) \times 1.6) 6. Determine Voxel Existence and Material: Check if voxel exists: If noise > threshold AND voxelPos.y < worldGenerationData.ceiling, the voxel is occupied. Otherwise, set to 0 (air) and continue. If distance d \le 10, return false (empty). If noise value val > 0.5, return true (occupied). Determine material color: Default voxelColor = 1u (stone). Check 5 voxels above (y+1 to y+5). If any fail the noise/ceiling check, set voxelColor = 3u (dirt). If the immediate voxel above (y+1) fails OR current y is ceiling-1, set voxelColor = 7u (grass). Border Check: If the voxel is on the border (defined by IsBorder), set density to 1.0 to create an indestructible outer shell. 7. Pack and Store Voxel Data: Pack voxel data: python voxelData = (u32(voxelColor) << 4u) | u32(voxelMaterial) Store in the 3D texture using bit manipulation to update the specific 8-bit slot within the 32-bit uint: python def SetVoxel(voxelPos, voxelType): texelPos = vec3<u32>(voxelPos.x >> 1, voxelPos.y, voxelPos.z >> 1) packedVoxel = textureLoad(voxels, texelPos).r mask = 0xFF xOdd = voxelPos.x & 0x1 zOdd = (voxelPos.z & 0x1) << 1 shiftCount = (xOdd | zOdd) 8 mask = mask << shiftCount mask = ~mask packedVoxel &= mask packedVoxel |= voxelType << shiftCount textureStore(voxels, texelPos, vec4<u32>(packedVoxel, 0, 0, 0)) Pseudocode for Noise Functions: The core noise function snoise (3D Perlin-like) is implemented as follows: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mod289(x): return x - math.floor(x (1.0 / 289.0)) 289.0 def permute(x): return mod289(((x 34.0) + 1.0) x) def taylorInvSqrt(r): return 1.79284291400159 - 0.85373472095314 r def snoise(v): C = (1.0 / 6.0, 1.0 / 3.0) D = (0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0) i = floor(v + dot(v, (C[1], C[1], C[1]))) x0 = v - i + dot(i, (C[0], C[0], C[0])) g = step(x0.yzx, x0.xyz) l = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) - g i1 = min(g.xyz, l.zxy) i2 = max(g.xyz, l.zxy) x1 = x0 - i1 + (C[0], C[0], C[0]) x2 = x0 - i2 + (C[1], C[1], C[1]) x3 = x0 - (D[1], D[1], D[1]) i = mod289(i) p = permute(permute(permute(i.z + (0.0, i1.z, i2.z, 1.0)) + i.y + (0.0, i1.y, i2.y, 1.0)) + i.x + (0.0, i1.x, i2.x, 1.0)) n = 0.142857142857 ns = n (D[3], D[2], D[1]) - (D[0], D[1], D[0]) j = p - 49.0 floor(p ns[2] ns[2]) x = floor(j ns[2]) y = floor(j - 7.0 x) x = x ns[0] + ns[1] y = y ns[0] + ns[1] h = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) - abs(x) - abs(y) b0 = (x[0], y[0], x[1], y[1]) b1 = (x[2], y[2], x[3], y[3]) s0 = floor(b0[0:2]) 2.0 + (1.0, 1.0) s1 = floor(b1[0:2]) 2.0 + (1.0, 1.0) sh = -step(h, 0.0) a0 = (b0[0], b0[1], b0[2], b0[3]) + (s0[0], s0[1], s0[0], s0[1]) (sh[0], sh[0], sh[1], sh[1]) a1 = (b1[0], b1[1], b1[2], b1[3]) + (s1[0], s1[1], s1[0], s1[1]) (sh[2], sh[2], sh[3], sh[3]) p0 = (a0[0], a0[1], h[0]) p1 = (a0[2], a0[3], h[1]) p2 = (a1[0], a1[1], h[2]) p3 = (a1[2], a1[3], h[3]) norm = taylorInvSqrt((dot(p0, p0), dot(p1, p1), dot(p2, p2), dot(p3, p3))) p0 = p0 norm[0] p1 = p1 norm[1] p2 = p2 norm[2] p3 = p3 norm[3] m = max(0.5 - (dot(x0, x0), dot(x1, x1), dot(x2, x2), dot(x3, x3)), 0.0) m = m m return 105.0 dot(m, (dot(p0, x0), dot(p1, x1), dot(p2, x2), dot(p3, x3))) The fBm summation is: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fbm(pos, octaves, lacunarity, gain, basefrequency, seed): amplitude = 1.0 frequency = basefrequency sumval = 0.0 p = pos for i in range(octaves): sumval += amplitude snoiseseeded(p frequency, seed) frequency = lacunarity amplitude = gain return sumval Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of mod289 in snoise requires careful handling of floating-point precision for large coordinates. Boundaries: The outer shell border check ensures the world does not leak, but IsBorder must be correctly defined relative to world dimensions. Degenerate Input: If spawnRoomRadius is larger than the world size, the entire world may be empty. Generates static noise fields for texture synthesis; simpler than procedural world generation which includes spatial logic and material assignment. Uses curl noise for fluid-like motion in volumetric clouds; differs by focusing on dynamic flow rather than static voxel density. Combines Perlin and Worley noise for hybrid textures; differs by targeting 2D/3D texture patterns rather than voxel world structures. Uses inverted noise for mountainous terrain; differs by producing sharp, ridged features rather than blobby caves. Time Complexity: O(W \times H \times D) where W, H, D are world dimensions, as each voxel is evaluated once. The noise evaluation is O(1) per voxel. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H \times D / 4) due to packing 4 voxels per 32-bit uint. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with world size. The use of compute shaders allows parallel evaluation of voxels. Strengths: Generates organic, cave-like structures; efficient packing reduces memory usage; flexible material assignment. Limitations: May require post-processing for smooth surfaces (e.g., Marching Cubes); noise artifacts can appear at boundaries if not handled. When to use: When generating voxel-based worlds with organic caves and varied terrain. When not to use: When smooth, continuous surfaces are required without post-processing; when deterministic, non-procedural layouts are needed. This method originates from procedural generation techniques used in voxel-based games and simulations. The use of fBm and Perlin noise for voxel density is a common approach in indie game development, as seen in projects like webgpu-voxel-raymarching and UnityVoxelTerrain. name: Ridged Multifractal
head: Ridged FBM, Ridged Noise, ridgedmf
body: Ridged Multifractal is a fractal noise technique that generates sharp, ridge-like structures by applying a non-linear transformation to the absolute value of base noise, combined with inter-octave feedback. Unlike standard FBM which produces soft, cloud-like volumes, Ridged Multifractal creates high-contrast linear features suitable for terrain ridges or lightning. It builds on 3D Perlin-like Noise and Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) by replacing the linear summation with a ridge-specific kernel and a multiplicative feedback loop. Inputs and Outputs Input: 3D coordinate p, number of octaves N, initial frequency, lacunarity L, gain G, ridge offset O, and a base noise function returning values in [-1, 1] or [0, 1]. Output: Scalar field value representing the ridged structure intensity. Data Structures Standard floating-point accumulators for sum, freq, amp, and prev. Parameters O (Offset): Controls ridge sharpness, typically 1.0. L (Lacunarity): Frequency scaling per octave, typically 2.0. G (Gain): Amplitude scaling per octave, typically 0.5. N (Octaves): Number of summation layers. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize sum = 0, freq = Frequency, amp = 0.5, prev = 1.0. 2. Loop for i from 0 to N-1: a. Compute base noise: h = \text{noise}(p \times \text{freq}). b. Apply ridge transformation: h{\text{abs}} = |h|, h{\text{ridge}} = (O - h{\text{abs}})^2. c. Apply feedback and accumulate: \text{sum} \leftarrow \text{sum} + h{\text{ridge}} \times \text{amp} \times \text{prev}. d. Update feedback: \text{prev} \leftarrow h{\text{ridge}}. e. Update frequency: \text{freq} \leftarrow \text{freq} \times L. f. Update amplitude: \text{amp} \leftarrow \text{amp} \times G. 3. Return sum. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ridgedmultifractal(p, octaves, frequency, lacunarity, gain, offset, noisefunc): sumval = 0.0 freq = frequency amp = 0.5 prev = 1.0 for in range(octaves): h = noisefunc(p freq) habs = abs(h) hridge = (offset - habs) 2 sumval += hridge amp prev prev = hridge freq = lacunarity amp = gain return sumval Edge Cases and Pitfalls When using the output for coloring, divide by \max(\text{value}, 0.05) to prevent division by zero. Time complexity is O(N) per sample, where N is the number of octaves, as each octave requires one noise evaluation and constant-time arithmetic. Memory complexity is O(1) auxiliary space, requiring only standard floating-point accumulators. The method produces highly realistic terrain ridges and lightning effects but is less suitable for soft volumetric features like clouds. Ridged Multifractal was introduced as a variant of Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) to address the need for sharp, linear features in procedural generation. It is widely used in terrain synthesis and visual effects. The technique relies on the absolute value of noise to create V-shaped ridges at zero crossings, distinguishing it from standard FBM which produces soft, isotropic noise. The feedback mechanism, where the output of one octave influences the amplitude of the next, enhances the structural coherence of the ridges. name: Tileable Noise Generation
head: Tiling Noise, Periodic Noise, Wrap-Around Noise
body: Tileable Noise Generation produces procedural noise fields that are spatially periodic, ensuring seamless continuity when the output is repeated in any dimension. It solves the discontinuity artifacts inherent in standard noise functions at texture or volume boundaries. It differs from its siblings by enforcing strict modulo arithmetic on coordinate indices or by using Fourier-domain techniques to guarantee exact periodicity, whereas Fractal Brownian Motion defines the spectral summation strategy rather than the boundary conditions. All tileable noise methods share the requirement that the noise function N(\mathbf{x}) satisfies the periodicity condition for a given period P in each dimension: N(x + P, y, z) = N(x, y, z) N(x, y + P, z) = N(x, y, z) N(x, y, z + P) = N(x, y, z) This is typically achieved by one of two mechanisms: 1. Coordinate Wrapping: Input coordinates are mapped into the fundamental domain 0, P) using modulo operations before evaluation. For integer-grid noise ([Value Noise), this implies the underlying random grid must also be wrapped. 2. Analytic Periodicity: The noise function is constructed from basis functions that are inherently periodic, such as trigonometric functions in Fourier-based noise or specific polynomial blends that match derivatives at boundaries. In discrete implementations, the grid of random values or gradients must be indexed with modulo P to ensure that neighbors across the boundary are consistent. Generates a 3D tiling noise volume by initializing a grid with uniform random values and applying a 3×3×3 box blur to suppress grid artifacts inherent in trilinear interpolation. It differs from gradient-based noise by using value noise with explicit spatial averaging, and from simple value noise by enforcing seamless tiling via modulo wrapping. Choose this when a smooth, low-frequency volumetric base is needed without the computational cost of gradient calculations. Synthesizes procedural volumetric textures, primarily for cloud simulation, by summing multiple octaves of value noise with decreasing amplitude and increasing frequency. It differs from gradient-based noise by using pre-computed random scalar values at grid vertices rather than gradient vectors, resulting in smoother, less detailed textures that are computationally cheaper to interpolate. Choose this for efficient cloud density fields where high-frequency detail is less critical than performance. A compute shader process that generates four specific noise textures used for volumetric cloud rendering, including Perlin-Worley FBM, Worley FBM, Curl Noise, and Weather Data. The noise algorithms are directly ported from sebh/TileableVolumeNoise. PerlinWorleyFBM texture: 128×128×128 resolution, RGBA8 format. WorleyFBM texture: 32×32×32 resolution, RGBA8 format. CurlNoise texture: 128×128 resolution, RGBA8 format. WeatherData texture: 2048×2048 resolution, RGBA8 format. Tileable noise is a fundamental requirement for rendering infinite environments, such as skies, oceans, and terrain, where seamless tiling prevents visible seams. The specific implementation described in is part of a volumetric cloud rendering pipeline, aiming to replicate the behavior of the RenderEngine's noise initializer. The underlying algorithms are sourced from the sebh/TileableVolumeNoise repository, which provides optimized compute shader implementations for generating these periodic fields. name: 3D Noise Generation with Box Filtering
head: Box-blurred random noise, Tiling noise volume generation
body: This method generates a 3D tiling noise volume by initializing a grid with uniform random values and applying a 3×3×3 box blur to hide trilinear interpolation grid artifacts. It enforces seamless tiling via modulo coordinate wrapping before averaging. Inputs and Outputs: Input: dim (integer, noise volume dimension) and seed (uint32t, PRNG seed). Output: A 3D buffer of size dim \times dim \times dim with 4 channels (RGBA), stored as uint8t in [0, 255]. Data Structures: raw: A 1D array of floats of size dim^3 \times 4, storing initial random values in [0, 1]. out: A 1D array of uint8t of size dim^3 \times 4, storing the final blurred values. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a seeded pseudo-random number generator (PRNG) using seed and fill the raw array with uniform random floats in [0, 1]. 2. Box Filtering: For each voxel (x, y, z) and channel c \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}, compute the average of the 27 neighbors in the 3×3×3 neighborhood. 3. Coordinate Wrapping: Wrap coordinates modulo dim to ensure tiling. 4. Quantization: Convert the averaged float value to an 8-bit integer in [0, 255] and store in out. Formula: The value at output coordinate (x, y, z) for channel c is: v{out}(x,y,z,c) = \frac{1}{27} \sum{dx=-1}^{1} \sum{dy=-1}^{1} \sum{dz=-1}^{1} v{in}((x+dx)\%d, (y+dy)\%d, (z+dz)\%d, c) \cdot 255 where d is the noise dimension, c is the RGBA channel index, and \% denotes modulo wrapping. Parameters: seed: uint32t. Typical value: any 32-bit integer for reproducibility. dim: Integer. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatetilingnoise(dim: int, seed: int) -> list: import random if dim <= 0: raise ValueError("dim must be greater than 0") # random.seed(seed) rawsize = dim dim dim 4 raw = [random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) for in range(rawsize)] out = [0] rawsize for z in range(dim): for y in range(dim): for x in range(dim): for c in range(4): total = 0.0 for dx in (-1, 0, 1): for dy in (-1, 0, 1): for dz in (-1, 0, 1): wx = (x + dx + dim) % dim wy = (y + dy + dim) % dim wz = (z + dz + dim) % dim idx = ((wz dim + wy) dim + wx) 4 + c total += raw[idx] avg = total / 27.0 outval = int(avg 255) if outval < 0: outval = 0 elif outval > 255: outval = 255 outidx = ((z dim + y) dim + x) 4 + c out[outidx] = outval return out Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating point accumulation in the sum may introduce minor errors; using float is sufficient for 27 additions. Boundaries: Modulo wrapping is critical for tiling. Degenerate Input: dim must be > 0. If dim is 1, the box filter averages the single value with itself 27 times, resulting in the same value. A variant that pre-computes a 64×64×64 3D texture of random values and pre-filters it to avoid linear interpolation artifacts during runtime. At runtime, it performs 4 lookups into this single texture to produce turbulence. It is chosen when runtime performance is critical and the noise pattern can be pre-computed. Time Complexity: O(dim^3), as each voxel requires 27 lookups and an average. Memory Complexity: O(dim^3) for storing the raw and output buffers. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively hides trilinear interpolation artifacts; supports seamless tiling. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originated from NVIDIA's GDC 2003 presentation on procedural noise techniques, which advocated pre-filtering 3D textures to avoid interpolation artifacts. sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, https://github.com/sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Noise and Procedural Techniques - NVIDIA, https://www.nvidia.com/docs/IO/8228/GDC2003OGLProceduralNoise.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Value-Noise FBM Texture Generation
head: Cloud Texture Generator, Procedural Cloud Noise Texture Generation, Value-Noise FBM
body: Value-Noise FBM Texture Generation synthesizes procedural volumetric textures, primarily for cloud simulation, by summing multiple octaves of value noise with decreasing amplitude and increasing frequency. It differs from gradient-based noise by using pre-computed random scalar values at grid vertices rather than gradient vectors, resulting in smoother textures that are computationally cheaper to interpolate. Inputs: seed: Integer seed for deterministic generation. resolution: Output texture dimensions (e.g., N \times N for 2D, N \times N \times N for 3D). octaves: Number of noise layers to sum. initialfrequency: Starting frequency for the first octave. initialamplitude: Starting amplitude for the first octave. persistence: Amplitude decay factor between octaves. Outputs: A texture data structure (e.g., DataTexture or packed voxel array) containing the generated noise field. Data Structures: Grid: A 2D array of random floats for each octave. Size is C \times C where C is the cell count for that octave. Field: An array of size N \times N (or N^3) accumulating the weighted noise values. Algorithm Steps: 1. PRNG Initialization: Initialize a Linear Congruential Generator (LCG) with the provided seed. \text{seed}{new} = (\text{seed}{old} \times 1103515245 + 12345) \ \& \ 0x7fffffff Return normalized value: \text{rand} = \frac{\text{seed}{new}}{0x7fffffff} 2. Grid Generation: For each octave i from 0 to octaves - 1: Determine cell count Ci. In the standard 2D cloud implementation, start with C0 = 4 and double for each subsequent octave (C{i+1} = 2 Ci) up to a maximum of 64. For 3D volume textures, the cell count is often derived from the resolution and frequency parameters. Generate a grid of Ci \times Ci random floats using the PRNG. 3. Interpolation and Accumulation: Initialize an empty field array field of size N \times N (or N^3) to zero. Initialize currentamplitude = initialamplitude. Initialize currentfrequency = initialfrequency. For each octave i: Calculate step size (grid spacing) in texture coordinates: \text{step} = \frac{N}{Ci} For each pixel/voxel (x, y) (and z for 3D) in the output grid: Compute fractional coordinates: fx = \frac{x}{\text{step}}, \quad fy = \frac{y}{\text{step}} Get integer indices: ix = \lfloor fx \rfloor, \quad iy = \lfloor fy \rfloor Compute interpolation factors: tx = fx - ix, \quad ty = fy - iy Apply smoothstep for continuity: tx = 3tx^2 - 2tx^3 ty = 3ty^2 - 2ty^3 Fetch four corner values from the octave's grid, handling wrap-around with modulo Ci: a = \text{grid}[ix \pmod{Ci}][iy \pmod{Ci}] b = \text{grid}[(ix+1) \pmod{Ci}][iy \pmod{Ci}] c = \text{grid}[ix \pmod{Ci}][(iy+1) \pmod{Ci}] d = \text{grid}[(ix+1) \pmod{Ci}][(iy+1) \pmod{Ci}] Perform bilinear interpolation: \text{val} = (a(1-tx) + b(tx))(1-ty) + (c(1-tx) + d(tx))ty Add weighted contribution to the field: \text{field}[y \cdot N + x] += \text{current\amplitude} \times \text{val} Update amplitude and frequency for the next octave: \text{current\amplitude} = \text{persistence} \text{current\frequency} = 2 4. Normalization and Output: Sum all amplitudes to get totalamplitude. Normalize the field values to the desired range (e.g., 0-255 for 8-bit textures): v = \text{round}\left( \frac{\text{field}[i]}{\text{total\amplitude}} \times 255 \right) Set RGBA to (v, v, v, 255) for 2D textures. For 3D volume textures, store in the ALPHA channel of a DDS format. Configure texture parameters: Wrap mode: RepeatWrapping. Mag filter: LinearFilter. Min filter: LinearMipmapLinearFilter for 2D, or LINEAR for 3D if mipmaps are unsupported. Generate mipmaps if supported. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def valuenoisefbm(resolution, seed, octaves=6, initialamplitude=0.7, persistence=0.5): # 1. PRNG Setup def lcgnext(s): s = (s 1103515245 + 12345) & 0x7fffffff return s, s / 0x7fffffff # 2. Grid Generation grids = [] currentcells = 4 for i in range(octaves): gridsize = currentcells grid = [] for y in range(gridsize): row = [] for x in range(gridsize): seed, val = lcgnext(seed) row.append(val) grid.append(row) grids.append(grid) currentcells = 2 if currentcells > 64: currentcells = 64 # 3. Interpolation field = [0.0] (resolution resolution) totalamplitude = 0.0 currentamp = initialamplitude for i in range(octaves): grid = grids[i] cells = len(grid) step = resolution / cells totalamplitude += currentamp for y in range(resolution): for x in range(resolution): fx = x / step fy = y / step ix = math.floor(fx) iy = math.floor(fy) tx = fx - ix ty = fy - iy # Smoothstep tx = tx tx (3 - 2 tx) ty = ty ty (3 - 2 ty) # Wrap-around modulo ix1 = ix % cells iy1 = iy % cells ix2 = (ix + 1) % cells iy2 = (iy + 1) % cells a = grid[iy1][ix1] b = grid[iy1][ix2] c = grid[iy2][ix1] d = grid[iy2][ix2] # Bilinear Interpolation val = (a (1 - tx) + b tx) (1 - ty) + (c (1 - tx) + d tx) ty field[y resolution + x] += currentamp val currentamp = persistence # 4. Normalization normalizedfield = [] for v in field: normval = round((v / totalamplitude) 255) normalizedfield.append(normval) return normalizedfield Generates 3D terrain density fields by summing multiple octaves of simplex noise, modified by a base surface plane, terracing, and bedrock layers. It differs from standard value-noise FBM by transforming the raw noise output into peaks at zero-crossings and valleys at extrema, creating distinct topological features suitable for voxel-based terrain generation. A dependency-free CPU value-noise FBM generates a per-body heightfield and cave structures, writing directly into the packed voxel array. Generation is derived from a shared BiomeProfile to produce distinct worlds per body, using a deterministic seed. Generates volume noise texture using NoiseGenerator with 6 octaves, initial frequency 6, initial amplitude 0.7, and persistence 0.5 if no valid DDS file is provided. The default resolution is 128, a compromise between memory and visual appearance. The image format is DDS with only the ALPHA channel to keep size small. Texture filtering is set to LINEAR because DDS format does not support volume texture mipmaps, and gluBuild3DMipMapLevels is not fully supported by all drivers. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Value noise is generally faster than gradient noise because it avoids dot products and gradient vector storage, relying only on scalar interpolation. However, it produces smoother, less detailed textures. Strengths: Deterministic, easy to implement, smooth results suitable for clouds, low memory footprint for intermediate grids. Limitations: Less directional detail than Perlin noise; 3D volume textures may suffer from lack of mipmap support in some formats/drivers (DDS). The specific implementation details cited here originate from voxel game development and early GPU-based cloud simulation research. The use of value noise for clouds allows for efficient runtime generation on both CPU and GPU, with the FBM structure providing the necessary fractal detail to mimic natural cloud formations. sh1ftmaker/voxel-wars, https://github.com/sh1ftmaker/voxel-wars, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Phase 9: Voxel Surface Exploration, https://github.com/LundstedtAdam/SolarSystem/pull/4, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) DTIC ADA427539: Simulating Clouds with Procedural Texturing Techniques Using the GPU, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA427539, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) Terrain Density
head: Octave Noise Terrain Generation
body: Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) Terrain Density generates a 3D scalar field representing terrain density by summing multiple octaves of simplex noise, modified by a base surface plane, terracing, and bedrock layers. It differs from standard Value-Noise FBM Texture Generation by explicitly modeling volumetric terrain structure for solid geometry rather than 2D surface texture, using a specific noise transformation (1 - |val| squared) to create sharp peaks suitable for mountainous topography. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A grid of vertex indices, chunk geometry parameters (chunkSize, vertSpacing, center), noise parameters (scale, lacunarity, persistence, weight, weightMultiplier), and structural parameters (surfaceOffset, bedrockHeight, bedrockWeight, terracing, solidifyEdges, mapSize). Outputs: vertexBuffer (position of each vertex) and densityBuffer (density value at each vertex). Data Structures: The method uses a job struct TerrainDensityJob with the following fields: octaveOffsetBuffer: NativeArray<Vector3>, ReadOnly. Stores the offset vector for each octave. vertexBuffer: NativeArray<Vector3>. Stores the 3D position of each vertex. densityBuffer: NativeArray<float>. Stores the computed density for each vertex. numberOfOctaves: int. Number of noise octaves to sum. numVertsPerAxis: int. Number of vertices along one axis of the chunk. chunkSize: float. Size of the terrain chunk. vertSpacing: float. Distance between adjacent vertices. lacunarity: float. Frequency multiplier per octave. persistence: float. Amplitude multiplier per octave. scale: float. Initial frequency multiplier. weight: float. Multiplier for the noise density component before adding to the surface plane. surfaceOffset: float. Vertical offset for the base surface plane. weightMultiplier: float. Controls how quickly octave weight decays based on the previous octave's value. bedrockHeight: float. Y-coordinate threshold below which bedrock weight is added. bedrockWeight: float. Value added to density if vertex is below bedrock height. center: Vector3. Center of the terrain chunk. offset: Vector3. Global offset for noise evaluation. mapSize: Vector3. Dimensions of the map for edge solidification. terracing: Vector3. x = terrace height step, y = terrace weight multiplier, z = enabled flag (1 if enabled). solidifyEdges: bool. If true, vertices outside the map bounds are set to a solid density. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Vertex Position: Calculate the offset from the center: offsetPos = Vector3(1, 1, 1) chunkSize / 2. Calculate the vertex position from its index id: position = center - offsetPos + ToVector3(id) vertSpacing Where ToVector3(id) converts the linear vertex index into 3D coordinates. 2. Initialize FBM Variables: density = 0 frequency = scale / 100 amplitude = 1 octaveWeight = 1 3. Loop Over Octaves: For each octave i from 0 to numberOfOctaves - 1: a. Evaluate Noise: val = SimplexNoise.Evaluate(position \times frequency + octaveOffsetBuffer[i] + offset) b. Transform Value: The value is transformed to create peaks at noise zeros: val = 1 - |val| val = val \times val c. Apply Weight: val = val \times octaveWeight d. Accumulate Density: density = density + val \times amplitude e. Update Octave Weight: The weight for the next octave depends on the current octave's transformed value: octaveWeight = \max(\min(val \times weightMultiplier, 1), 0) f. Update Amplitude: amplitude = amplitude \times persistence g. Update Frequency: frequency = frequency \times lacunarity 4. Combine with Surface Plane: The density is adjusted relative to a base surface plane: density = -(position.y + surfaceOffset) + density \times weight 5. Apply Terracing (Optional): If terracing.z > 0: density = density + (position.y \pmod{terracing.x}) \times terracing.y 6. Apply Bedrock Layer (Optional): If position.y < bedrockHeight: density = density + bedrockWeight 7. Solidify Edges (Optional): If solidifyEdges is true: Calculate the distance from the center in each axis: edgeOffset = Vector3(|position.x|, |position.y|, |position.z|) - mapSize / 2 If any component of edgeOffset is \ge 0: density = -100 8. Store Results: vertexBuffer[id] = position densityBuffer[id] = density Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def mul(self, s): return Vector3(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) def sub(self, other): return Vector3(self.x-other.x, self.y-other.y, self.z-other.z) def add(self, other): return Vector3(self.x+other.x, self.y+other.y, self.z+other.z) def tovector3(id, numvertsperaxis): z = id // (numvertsperaxis numvertsperaxis) y = (id // numvertsperaxis) % numvertsperaxis x = id % numvertsperaxis return Vector3(x, y, z) def simplexnoise(x, y, z): return 0.0 def computeterraindensity(job, id): # 1. Initialize Vertex Position offsetpos = Vector3(1, 1, 1) job.chunksize / 2 position = job.center - offsetpos + tovector3(id, job.numvertsperaxis) job.vertspacing # 2. Initialize FBM Variables density = 0.0 frequency = job.scale / 100.0 amplitude = 1.0 octaveweight = 1.0 # 3. Loop Over Octaves for i in range(job.numberofoctaves): # Evaluate Noise noiseinput = position frequency + job.octaveoffsetbuffer[i] + job.offset val = simplexnoise(noiseinput.x, noiseinput.y, noiseinput.z) # Transform Value val = 1.0 - abs(val) val = val val # Apply Weight val = val octaveweight # Accumulate Density density += val amplitude # Update Octave Weight octaveweight = max(min(val job.weightmultiplier, 1.0), 0.0) # Update Amplitude amplitude = job.persistence # Update Frequency frequency = job.lacunarity # 4. Combine with Surface Plane density = -(position.y + job.surfaceoffset) + density job.weight # 5. Apply Terracing if job.terracing.z > 0: terracestep = job.terracing.x terraceweight = job.terracing.y density += (position.y % terracestep) terraceweight # 6. Apply Bedrock Layer if position.y < job.bedrockheight: density += job.bedrockweight # 7. Solidify Edges if job.solidifyedges: edgeoffset = Vector3(abs(position.x), abs(position.y), abs(position.z)) - (job.mapsize / 2) if edgeoffset.x >= 0 or edgeoffset.y >= 0 or edgeoffset.z >= 0: density = -100.0 # 8. Store Results job.vertexbuffer[id] = position job.densitybuffer[id] = density Parameters: scale: Initial frequency multiplier. Divided by 100 in the job. lacunarity: Frequency multiplier per octave. persistence: Amplitude multiplier per octave. weight: Multiplier for the noise density component before adding to the surface plane. weightMultiplier: Controls how quickly octave weight decays based on the previous octave's value. surfaceOffset: Vertical offset for the base surface plane. bedrockHeight: Y-coordinate threshold below which bedrock weight is added. bedrockWeight: Value added to density if vertex is below bedrock height. terracing: Vector3 where x is terrace height step, y is terrace weight multiplier, z is enabled flag (1 if enabled). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The transformation 1 - |val| followed by squaring creates sharp peaks at noise zeros and valleys at noise extrema. Boundaries: The solidifyEdges check uses absolute position values relative to mapSize. Degenerate Input: If numberOfOctaves is 0, density is determined solely by the surface plane and bedrock/terracing layers. Generates terrain height fields using ridged and hybrid multifractal components with domain warping. Chose when sharper peaks and more realistic geological features are needed compared to standard additive FBM. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This method is described in the unofficial source tcgj/terrain-generator. It represents a specific implementation of FBM for terrain generation, distinct from standard value-noise FBM texture generation by its focus on 3D volumetric density and specific noise transformations for peak formation. tcgj/terrain-generator, https://github.com/tcgj/terrain-generator, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Multifractal Mountain Synthesis
head: Seeded gradient-noise ridged/hybrid multifractal synthesis
body: Multifractal Mountain Synthesis generates terrain height fields by combining seeded gradient noise with ridged and hybrid multifractal components, enhanced by domain warping, a super-elliptical peak mask, and a directional tilt gradient. It differs from standard Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) Terrain Density by explicitly modeling mountainous topography through ridged noise structures and hybrid multifractal weighting rather than simple additive summation. Inputs: Domain size: W \times H \times D (e.g., 100 \times 64 \times 100 meters). Grid resolution: Nx \times Ny \times Nz (up to 288^2-class grids, ~24 M cells). Octave count: Auto-clamped such that every feature is at least 3 voxels in size. Tilt vector: Directional tilt gradient applied to the terrain. Peak mask: Super-elliptical shape parameters. Preset configuration: Sparse parameter overlay defining peak arrangement and weights. Outputs: Signed Distance Field (SDF) representing the terrain surface. Optional OBJ surface export with normals and UVs. Data Structures: The terrain is stored as a 3D voxel grid of signed distances. Presets are stored as sparse parameter overlays mapping to specific peak arrangements (single, twin, ridge, 5-peak). Steps: 1. Initialize Domain: Create a 3D grid of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz and initialize to zero. 2. Apply Tilt: Apply a directional tilt gradient to the coordinate space to introduce asymmetry. 3. Domain Warp: Apply domain warping to the noise coordinates to introduce organic complexity. 4. Generate Base Noise: Compute seeded gradient noise at multiple octaves, auto-clamped to ensure features \ge 3 voxels. 5. Hybrid Multifractional Combination: Combine the noise values using a hybrid multifractal formula. 6. Apply Peak Mask: Apply a super-elliptical peak mask to the resulting height field. 7. Apply Preset Weights: If a preset is selected, apply sparse parameter overlays to adjust weights and offsets for specific peak arrangements. Offsets are rotated according to the tilt bearing. 8. Finalize SDF: The resulting height field is converted into a Signed Distance Field. Narrow-band fast-sweeping Godunov redistancing is applied to ensure |\nabla d| \approx 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def synthesizemultifractalmountain(domainsize, resolution, tiltvector, presetconfig): Nx, Ny, Nz = resolution W, H, D = domainsize cellsize = (W / Nx, H / Ny, D / Nz) # Initialize 3D grid grid = [[[0.0] Nz for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] # Auto-clamp octaves: min feature size >= 3 voxels minfeaturevoxels = 3 maxfreq = 1.0 / (minfeaturevoxels min(cellsize)) octaves = max(1, int(math.floor(math.log2(maxfreq)))) for x in range(Nx): for y in range(Ny): for z in range(Nz): px = x cellsize[0] py = y cellsize[1] pz = z cellsize[2] # Directional tilt gradient tx, ty, tz = tiltvector tiltedx = px + tx pz tiltedy = py + ty pz # Domain warp (standard fractal noise feedback) warpscale = 0.5 nx = tiltedx warpscale ny = tiltedy warpscale dx = tiltedx + gradientnoise(nx, ny, pz) 0.5 dy = tiltedy + gradientnoise(nx + 100, ny + 100, pz) 0.5 # Ridged/hybrid multifractal combination value = 0.0 amp = 1.0 freq = 1.0 for o in range(octaves): n = gradientnoise(dx freq, dy freq, pz freq) value += n amp amp = 0.5 freq = 2.0 grid[x][y][z] = value # Super-elliptical peak mask nsuper = 4.0 for x in range(Nx): for y in range(Ny): for z in range(Nz): nx = (x / Nx) 2 - 1 ny = (y / Ny) 2 - 1 nz = (z / Nz) 2 - 1 mask = 1.0 - (abs(nx)nsuper + abs(ny)nsuper + abs(nz)nsuper)(1.0/nsuper) mask = max(0.0, mask) grid[x][y][z] = mask # Preset peak arrangements if presetconfig: arrangement = presetconfig.get("arrangement", "single") weights = presetconfig.get("weights", [1.0]) offsets = presetconfig.get("offsets", [(0, 0, 0)]) bearing = math.atan2(tiltvector[1], tiltvector[0]) for i, w in enumerate(weights): if i < len(offsets): ox, oy, oz = offsets[i] rx = ox math.cos(bearing) - oy math.sin(bearing) ry = ox math.sin(bearing) + oy math.cos(bearing) for x in range(Nx): for y in range(Ny): for z in range(Nz): dx = x - rx Nx dy = y - ry Ny dist = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy) if dist < Nx 0.2: grid[x][y][z] = w # Convert to SDF and apply Godunov redistancing sdf = grid # Narrow-band fast-sweeping Godunov redistancing ensures |∇d| ≈ 1 # (Standard Eikonal solver implementation omitted for brevity) return sdf def gradientnoise(x, y, z): # Standard seeded gradient noise evaluation return (math.sin(x) math.cos(y) math.sin(z)) / 3.0 Parameters: Octave count: Auto-clamped. Relief: 20-24 meters achieved across all arrangements. Presets: Alpine Horn, Twin Summits, Desert Mesa, Volcanic Cone, Rolling Range. Edge Cases: Precision: SDF redistancing ensures gradient magnitude is approximately 1. Boundaries: Domain warping and tilt must be handled carefully at grid boundaries to avoid artifacts. Configures peak arrangements (single, twin summits, ridge line, 5-peak range) with offsets rotated with the tilt bearing and weights calibrated for full relief. Implemented as sparse param overlays. Five presets are available: Alpine Horn, Twin Summits, Desert Mesa, Volcanic Cone, Rolling Range. Relief validation shows 20-24 m relief achieved across all four arrangements. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Up to ~24 M cells for 288^2-class grids. Performance: Runs in a Web Worker with zero dependencies. Strengths: True 3D SDF voxelisation, SDF-native hydraulic erosion, realistic mountain shapes via ridged/hybrid multifractal synthesis. When to use: When realistic, eroded mountain terrain is needed in a 3D volume rendering context with SDF support. Originated in the "Frontier: SDF terrain generator" project, an unofficial browser-based SDF terrain workstation. name: Noise Layer Evaluation
head: Procedural Noise Layer Evaluation
body: Evaluates a single procedural noise layer for volume or terrain shading, supporting multiple noise primitives, positional distortion, power scaling, and inversion. Builds on Procedural Noise Functions. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: noiseSamplePosition (vec3), noiseLayerData (vec4), positionDistortion (float), invert (bool), enabled (bool). Output: value (float), the final noise layer contribution. Data Structures noiseLayerData: A vec4 encoding layer parameters: x: noiseScale (float) y: noisePower (float) z: angleOffset (float) w: noiseType (int, cast from float). Steps 1. Enable Check: If enabled is false, return 1.0 immediately. 2. Distortion: Compute distortionStrength = 0.1 positionDistortion. If distortionStrength > 0, sample cnoise at distortionStrength noiseSamplePosition, cast the result to vec3, and add it to noiseSamplePosition. 3. Unpack Parameters: Extract noiseScale, noisePower, angleOffset, and noiseType from noiseLayerData. 4. Noise Sampling: Initialize sampledNoiseValue = 0.0. Based on noiseType, sample the corresponding noise function at noiseSamplePosition noiseScale: 0 for cnoise, 1 for snoise, 2 for voronoi(noiseSamplePosition noiseScale, angleOffset, noiseScale), 3 for nebulaNoise. 5. Clamping: Clamp sampledNoiseValue to [0.0, 1.0] and store in value. 6. Inversion: If invert is true, overwrite value with 1.0 - sampledNoiseValue, bypassing the clamp applied in Step 5. 7. Power Scaling: Take the absolute value of noisePower. Compute finalValue = pow(value, noisePower). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatenoiselayer(noisesampleposition, noiselayerdata, positiondistortion, invert, enabled, depth): # Step 1: Enable Check if not enabled: return 1.0 # Step 2: Distortion distortionstrength = 0.1 positiondistortion if distortionstrength > 0: # cnoise is a standard GLSL continuous noise function distortionoffset = cnoise(distortionstrength noisesampleposition) noisesampleposition = noisesampleposition + vec3(distortionoffset) # Step 3: Unpack Parameters noisescale = noiselayerdata.x noisepower = noiselayerdata.y angleoffset = noiselayerdata.z noisetype = int(noiselayerdata.w) # Step 4: Noise Sampling samplednoisevalue = 0.0 if noisetype == 0: samplednoisevalue = cnoise(noisesampleposition noisescale) elif noisetype == 1: samplednoisevalue = snoise(noisesampleposition noisescale) elif noisetype == 2: # voronoi is a standard GLSL cellular noise function samplednoisevalue = voronoi(noisesampleposition noisescale, angleoffset, noisescale) elif noisetype == 3: # nebulaNoise is a standard GLSL noise function samplednoisevalue = nebulaNoise(noisesampleposition noisescale) # Step 5: Clamping value = clamp(samplednoisevalue, 0.0, 1.0) # Step 6: Inversion if invert: # Pitfall: Uses samplednoisevalue (pre-clamp) instead of value, bypassing the clamp value = 1.0 - samplednoisevalue # Step 7: Power Scaling finalvalue = pow(abs(noisepower), value) return finalvalue def cnoise(p): pass def snoise(p): pass def voronoi(p, angleoffset, scale): pass def nebulaNoise(p): pass class vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def mul(self, scalar): return vec3(self.x scalar, self.y scalar, self.z scalar) def add(self, other): return vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(val, maxval)) Parameters noiseLayerData (vec4): Encoded layer parameters. positionDistortion (float): Scales the offset applied to the sample position before noise evaluation. invert (bool): When true, inverts the noise value before power application. enabled (bool): When false, forces the layer output to 1.0 and skips evaluation. densityMult (float): Default 1.0, range [0.0, 1.0], step 0.001. Multiplies volume density in the raymarching loop. maxSteps (int): Default 70, range [40, 256], step 1. Maximum number of raymarching steps per ray. stepSize (float): Default 0.01, range [0.00001, 0.1], step 0.000001. Distance between consecutive sample positions along the ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Inversion Bypass: The inversion branch uses sampledNoiseValue instead of the clamped value, meaning the clamp applied in Step 5 is ignored when inversion is active. Unused Depth Parameter: The depth parameter is declared in the function signature but is never referenced or used in the function body. Degenerate Distortion: If positionDistortion is 0, distortion is skipped, which is the standard behavior. Calculates the 3D or 4D position in noise space for each triangle fragment to apply procedural noise and turbulence functions. It maps spatial coordinates to a noise field supporting animation and instance uniqueness, distinct from standard 2D texture mapping. It prepares the input for turbulence evaluation and subsequent color lookup. The Procedural Terrain JSON Schema defines a data structure for storing the minimal set of parameters required to reproduce a designed procedural terrain in external applications. It serves as an export format that decouples terrain design from rendering, allowing the same terrain to be synthesized using different base noise implementations or rendering engines. Unlike Noise Layer Evaluation, which describes the runtime evaluation of a single layer, this schema defines the persistent storage format for a collection of layers and their global bounds. Determines which parts of a noise layer are active based on the value ranges of underlying reference layers, allowing multiple noise layers to add detail to specific terrain features. Reference height map layers are evaluated from top to bottom; an underlying layer masks a top layer if the top layer does not span the whole value range of the underlying layer. The masked range is continuous, determined by the minimum and maximum value where the top reference layer overlaps the layer under it. The mask range is saved in the processed noise function, and outside this range, the elevation change evaluates to zero. Smoothstepping is used instead of simple clamping near mask range edges to make seams less visible. Binary masking limits control, and a partial mask altering values using learned distributions would be beneficial but is computationally expensive and non-trivial to determine from example data. Estimates the base frequency of a noise layer by matching the average peak values per row of the reference data. The reference height map array is traversed horizontally and vertically, counting points where the value trend changes from increasing to decreasing (peak values); for masked layers, only visible values are considered. A single scalar, the row average of peak counts, is calculated. The noise frequency is iteratively adjusted using a heuristic search until the peak count matches the reference data, relying on the fact that the number of peak values increases with frequency. The implementation is a naive approximation, very sensitive to unwanted high-frequency noise in the reference data, and only works for height maps with intended patterns representable by a single noise layer. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Supports multiple noise primitives, positional distortion, power scaling, and inversion within a single evaluation pass. Limitations: The inversion logic bypasses the clamping step, which may produce unexpected values outside [0.0, 1.0]. The implementation declares a depth parameter that is never used. When to Use: When a single procedural noise layer with configurable distortion and power is needed for volume density or color. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. name: Noise Position Calculation
body: Calculates the 3D or 4D position in noise space for each triangle fragment to apply procedural noise and turbulence functions. It maps spatial coordinates to a noise field supporting animation and instance uniqueness, distinct from standard 2D texture mapping. It prepares the input for turbulence evaluation and subsequent color lookup. Inputs: tex: Unit volume texture coordinates (3D vector). noiseScale: Scalar scaling factor for spatial frequency. time: Current animation time (scalar). instanceOffset: 3D constant vector unique to each fire instance. stabilityFactor: Scalar for turbulence kernel stability. Outputs: noisePos: 4D position vector in noise space (x, y, z, t). finalTex: Adjusted 3D texture coordinates for color lookup. Data Structures: vec3: 3D floating-point vector. vec4: 4D floating-point vector. Steps: 1. Scale Spatial Coordinates: Multiply the unit texture coordinates by noiseScale to set the base spatial frequency. \mathbf{p}{\text{scaled}} = \mathbf{tex} \times \text{noiseScale} 2. Construct 4D Position: Initialize the noise position with the scaled coordinates and set the fourth dimension to time to enable 4D noise evaluation. \mathbf{p}{4d} = (\mathbf{p}{\text{scaled}}.x, \mathbf{p}{\text{scaled}}.y, \mathbf{p}{\text{scaled}}.z, \text{time}) 3. Apply Vertical Flow Offset: Offset the vertical axis (y) by -\text{time} to create an upward flow effect. \mathbf{p}{\text{flow}} = (\mathbf{p}{4d}.x, \mathbf{p}{4d}.y - \text{time}, \mathbf{p}{4d}.z, \mathbf{p}{4d}.w) 4. Add Instance Offset: Add the instanceOffset to the spatial components (x, y, z) to ensure each fire instance has a unique noise pattern. \mathbf{p}{\text{final}} = (\mathbf{p}{\text{flow}}.x + \text{instanceOffset}.x, \mathbf{p}{\text{flow}}.y + \text{instanceOffset}.y, \mathbf{p}{\text{flow}}.z + \text{instanceOffset}.z, \mathbf{p}{\text{flow}}.w) 5. Calculate Turbulence Kernel: Compute a kernel value f(\text{tex}z) using the stability factor and the square root of the height (z). f(\text{tex}z) = \text{stabilityFactor} \times \sqrt{\text{tex}.z} 6. Apply Turbulence to Position: Multiply the turbulence value by the kernel and add it to the vertical component of the texture lookup position. \text{finalTex}.z = \mathbf{p}{\text{final}}.z + f(\text{tex}z) \text{finalTex}.x = \mathbf{p}{\text{final}}.x \text{finalTex}.y = \mathbf{p}{\text{final}}.y Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from math import sqrt from typing import Tuple def calculatenoiseposition(tex: Tuple[float, float, float], noiseScale: float, time: float, instanceOffset: Tuple[float, float, float], stabilityFactor: float) -> Tuple[Tuple[float, float, float, float], Tuple[float, float, float]]: pscaled = (tex[0] noiseScale, tex[1] noiseScale, tex[2] noiseScale) p4d = (pscaled[0], pscaled[1], pscaled[2], time) pflow = (p4d[0], p4d[1] - time, p4d[2], p4d[3]) pfinal = (pflow[0] + instanceOffset[0], pflow[1] + instanceOffset[1], pflow[2] + instanceOffset[2], pflow[3]) kernel = stabilityFactor sqrt(tex[2]) finaltex = (pfinal[0], pfinal[1], pfinal[2] + kernel) return pfinal, finaltex Parameters: noiseScale: Controls spatial frequency. Not given in the sources. stabilityFactor: Controls turbulence magnitude. Not given in the sources. instanceOffset: Unique per instance. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: tex.z < 0: Square root is undefined. Clamp tex.z to \ge 0 or handle as invalid. time large: Potential precision loss in floating-point subtraction. Use modulo or relative time if needed. Applies procedural noise to surfaces/volumes by evaluating 3D noise at spatial coordinates, avoiding 2D mapping seams. Chosen when continuous material appearance is needed across complex topologies. Time and memory complexity per fragment are not given in the sources. Strengths, limitations, and usage guidelines are not given in the sources.
