name: Solid Texturing
head: 3D Map Texturing, Procedural Solid Texturing, Sampling a solid noise, Sampling solid noise
body: Solid texturing applies a 3D procedural noise function at every surface point or spatial coordinate to texture an object, making it appear carved out of a continuous block of matter. It solves the seam and distortion problems of 2D UV mapping while maintaining low memory consumption by avoiding pre-computed 3D texture tables. Unlike surface noise, which lets anisotropic textures flow around an object, solid texturing fixes the texture orientation in space, producing a unique sculpted appearance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D procedural noise function N(x, y, z) (e.g., Perlin noise) and a set of 3D coordinates \mathbf{p} representing either surface points, voxel centers, or ray sampling locations. Output: A scalar value or color assigned to each coordinate, representing the material property or color at that location. Data Structures: Noise Function: Typically implemented as a hash-based interpolation of gradient vectors at predetermined lattice points. Explicit pre-computed 3D tables are avoided to prevent large memory costs. Coordinates: 3D vectors (x, y, z) in world or object space. Steps: 1. Generalize Noise to 3D: Ensure the base noise function accepts 3D input coordinates. All standard noise functions are easily generalized to 3D and higher dimensions. 2. Evaluate Noise: Evaluate the 3D noise function at the 3D coordinates of each surface point. 3. Voxelization: During the voxelization phase, assign a value to each voxel belonging to the object using the texturing function or 3D map, storing it as part of the voxel information. 4. Volume Enrichment: If used to enrich a volume dataset without increasing stored resolution, evaluate the texturing function during rendering time at the ray sampling locations. Formulas: The power spectrum of the noise on the surface, P{\text{surface}}(u, v), is related to the power spectrum of the solid noise, P{\text{solid}}(u, v, w), by the slice-projection theorem: P{\text{surface}}(u, v) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} P{\text{solid}}(u, v, w) \, dw This integration occurs because evaluating a 3D noise along a surface corresponds to slicing the 3D domain. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Loss of Band-Pass Properties: Slicing a 3D band-pass noise along a surface does not result in a band-pass noise on the surface due to the slice-projection theorem. The resulting power spectrum is not band-pass anymore, which can alter frequency characteristics. Memory Costs: Explicit noises that rely on pre-computed 3D tables induce large memory costs and are generally avoided in favor of procedural generation. Alternative Surface Definition: Defining noise directly on the surface so features flow along curvatures is difficult in general but possible with sparse convolution noises. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatesolidtexture(points, noisefunc): """ Evaluates a 3D procedural noise function at given 3D coordinates. Supports surface points, voxel centers, or ray sampling locations. """ values = [] for p in points: # Step 1 & 2: Generalize noise to 3D and evaluate at coordinates value = noisefunc(p.x, p.y, p.z) values.append(value) return values Coupled Modeling of Solid Textures and Implicit Shapes is a technique for texturing implicit surfaces by using similar functions for both implicit surfaces and solid textures, ensuring uniform textures that conform to any orientable 2-manifold shapes with no obvious stretch. It sets itself apart from general implicit modeling by guaranteeing interactivity regardless of shape complexity, as function computation during construction does not depend on shape complexity. Coupled Modeling of Solid Textures and Implicit Shapes Memory: Low memory consumption compared to explicit 3D texture maps, as the noise is generated procedurally. Visual Quality: Produces a natural, continuous material appearance that is difficult to achieve with 2D texturing. When to Use: When a natural, continuous material appearance is desired and memory is a constraint. When Not to Use: When the loss of band-pass properties on surfaces is unacceptable without additional correction. The idea of sampling 3D noise on surfaces was introduced by Perlin [Per85] and Peachy [Pea85] and popularized as solid texturing. It has been widely used in computer graphics for creating procedural textures and modeling solid materials. A comprehensive overview of solid texturing can be found in Dischler and Ghazanfarpour [DG01]. The slice-projection theorem, which explains the spectral properties of sliced noise, was established by Braun [Bra99] and Mallat [Mal93]. name: Coupled Modeling of Solid Textures and Implicit Shapes
head: Constructive Soft Geometry, Functional Shape Operations
body: Coupled Modeling of Solid Textures and Implicit Shapes is a technique for texturing implicit surfaces by using similar functions for both implicit surfaces and solid textures, ensuring uniform textures that conform to any orientable 2-manifold shapes with no obvious stretch. It sets itself apart from general implicit modeling by guaranteeing interactivity regardless of shape complexity, as function computation during construction does not depend on shape complexity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Unit gradient length affine functions (defining basic loci like points, lines, or circles) and a parameter p (typically a high value). Outputs: Bounded gradient length functions for shape and texture layering, and opacity values. Data Structures: Function Tree: A tree structure where nodes represent functions and edges represent the application of the wp operation. Each node stores the function definition and its gradient length properties. Opacity Representation: A combination of two bounded gradient length functions f0 and f1, with coefficients aj and frequencies wj. Key Concepts: Unit Gradient Length Functions: Functions whose gradient length is exactly 1. These are used to effectively control layer thickness and obtain regular layer thickness. Almost Unit Gradient Length Functions: Functions whose gradient length is less than but almost equal to 1. These are required to construct uniform solid textures. Bounded Gradient Length Functions: Functions whose gradient length is not larger than 1. These yield fast rendering with the Lipschitz condition and high quality rendering with accurate sampling of volumes. Steps: 1. Construct Building Blocks: Apply a functional set operation to unit gradient length affine functions to create building block functions that give equal Euclidean distance (loci) to points, lines, or circles. This creates a large family of shapes. 2. Apply wp Operation: Use the wp operation to combine functions. This operation is closed over the set of bounded gradient length functions and can describe approximate and exact set operations. 3. Generate Texture Layers: Use the wp operation in a tree structure to construct several closely related functions. If one function describes the shape of the objects, other functions can be used to describe layers that conform well to the shape. 4. Calculate Opacity: Compute opacity using the formula involving f0 and f1. Formulas: wp Operation: wp(f1, f2) = \frac{\log(\exp(p \cdot f1) + \exp(p \cdot f2))}{p} Where p is a high value. For high values of p, wp over functions whose gradient length is almost equal to 1 creates new functions with almost unit length gradient functions. Opacity: \text{Opacity} = f0 + \sum{i=1}^{m} ai \cos(wi f1) + 1 Where f0 and f1 are bounded gradient length functions, ai are positive real numbers, and wi are frequencies. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def wp(f1, f2, p, x, y, z): """ Computes the wp operation on two functions f1 and f2 with parameter p. f1 and f2 are callable functions that take a 3D point (x, y, z) and return a float. p is a high value parameter. """ val1 = f1(x, y, z) val2 = f2(x, y, z) # Stable log-sum-exp implementation to prevent overflow for large p or function values maxval = max(val1, val2) return math.log(math.exp(p (val1 - maxval)) + math.exp(p (val2 - maxval))) / p + maxval def createaffineunitgradientfunction(point, line=None, circle=None): """ Creates a unit gradient length affine function based on loci. Sources do not give the exact formula for general affine functions. Standard Euclidean distance to a point yields a unit gradient length function. """ if point is not None: def f(x, y, z): dx = x - point[0] dy = y - point[1] dz = z - point[2] return math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) return f return None def calculateopacity(f0, f1, coefficients, frequencies, x, y, z): """ Calculates opacity using the combination of two bounded gradient length functions. """ valf0 = f0(x, y, z) valf1 = f1(x, y, z) sumterm = 0.0 for i in range(len(coefficients)): sumterm += coefficients[i] math.cos(frequencies[i] valf1) return valf0 + sumterm + 1.0 Parameters: p: A high value parameter in the wp operation. Typical values are not specified in the sources, but it must be "high" to ensure the resulting function has almost unit length gradient. ai: Positive real numbers for opacity coefficients. wi: Frequencies for opacity calculation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overflow: The wp operation involves exponentials. For large p or large function values, \exp(p \cdot f) can overflow. A stable implementation of log-sum-exp should be used in practice. Gradient Length: The method relies on functions having specific gradient lengths. Unit gradient length functions are required to effectively control layer thickness and obtain regular layer thickness. Time Complexity: The wp operation is constant time updateable. A large set of functions based on wp can be updated in constant time, regardless of shape complexity. This contrasts with general implicit modeling where function evaluation complexity increases with shape complexity. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Guarantees interactivity regardless of shape complexity because function computation during construction does not depend on shape complexity. Strengths: Uniform textures that conform well to varied terrain with no obvious stretch; regular layer thickness; fast rendering with the Lipschitz condition; high quality rendering with accurate sampling of volumes. Limitations: Requires careful construction of building block functions with unit gradient length. Potential numerical instability in wp operation for large p. When to Use: When uniform solid textures on complex implicit surfaces are required, and interactivity is critical regardless of shape complexity. When Not to Use: When simple shapes are sufficient and the overhead of constructing the function tree is not justified. When numerical stability is a major concern without careful implementation. Origin: Introduced by Ergun Akleman and Jianer Chen in the paper "Implicit Volume Modeling". History: The technique was developed to solve the problem of effective texturing of implicit surfaces, ensuring uniform textures that conform to any orientable 2-manifold shapes with no obvious stretch. Usage: Used in implicit volume modeling for texturing implicit surfaces. Implicit Volume Modeling, https://people.tamu.edu/~ergun/research/implicitmodeling/abstracts/is99b/index.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Procedural Terrain JSON Schema
head: Procedural Terrain Storage Format (JSON)
body: The Procedural Terrain JSON Schema defines a data structure for storing the minimal set of parameters required to reproduce a designed procedural terrain in external applications. It serves as an export format that decouples terrain design from rendering, allowing the same terrain to be synthesized using different base noise implementations or rendering engines. Unlike Noise Layer Evaluation, which describes the runtime evaluation of a single layer, this schema defines the persistent storage format for a collection of layers and their global bounds. The schema represents a terrain as a root object containing an array of noise layers and global extrema. Each layer defines a base noise frequency, a redistribution function (RD) for non-linear mapping, amplitude scaling, and optional masking against other layers. Input: A JSON document conforming to the schema. Output: A set of parameters used to reconstruct the height field H(i,j) by summing processed layers. The root object contains: noiseLayers: An array of layer objects. maxValue: The expected maximum value of the final terrain function. minValue: The expected minimum value of the final terrain function. Each layer object contains: baseNoise: An object with a frequency field (number). This scaling is applied directly to the base noise (e.g., SimplexNoise) before any other processing. rd: An object containing points, an array of objects with x and y fields (numbers). These are equalized points used to construct the redistribution function. preAmpShift: A number added to the noise output before scaling. ampScale: A number multiplying the translated noise value. maskLayerIndex: An integer index pointing to another layer in noiseLayers used for masking. maskMinValue: A number representing the minimum value of the masked range. maskMaxValue: A number representing the maximum value of the masked range. To evaluate the terrain at coordinates (i,j): 1. Initialize Sum: Let H(i,j) = 0. 2. Iterate Layers: For each layer k in noiseLayers: a. Base Noise: Compute nk = \text{BaseNoise}(i \cdot \text{baseNoise.frequency}, j \cdot \text{baseNoise.frequency}). The base noise implementation must match the one used during design. b. Redistribution: Map nk through the redistribution function defined by rd.points. Let the result be rk. The redistribution function is constructed from the equalized points. c. Amplitude Scaling: Compute the processed value Xk using the formula: Xk = (rk + \text{preAmpShift}) \times \text{ampScale} d. Masking: If maskLayerIndex is valid (i.e., 0 \le \text{maskLayerIndex} < \text{len(noiseLayers)}): i. Retrieve the processed value Xm from the layer at maskLayerIndex. ii. If Xm < \text{maskMinValue} or Xm > \text{maskMaxValue}, discard Xk (set Xk = 0 or skip addition). e. Accumulate: Add Xk to H(i,j). 3. Result: The final height is H(i,j). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluateterrain(jsondata, i, j, basenoisefunc): """ Evaluates the procedural terrain defined by jsondata at coordinates (i, j). Args: jsondata: Dict conforming to the schema. i, j: Integer coordinates. basenoisefunc: Function that takes (x, y) and returns a float. Returns: Float height value. """ noiselayers = jsondata['noiseLayers'] totalheight = 0.0 # Pre-evaluate all layers to handle masking dependencies # Note: Masking refers to other layers. The order of summation # in the schema description implies sequential processing, # but masking requires access to the processed value of another layer. # We must store processed values of all layers first. processedvalues = [] for layer in noiselayers: # 1. Base Noise freq = layer['baseNoise']['frequency'] noiseval = basenoisefunc(i freq, j freq) # 2. Redistribution # Construct RD from points. Assuming linear interpolation between points. rdpoints = layer['rd']['points'] # Implementation detail: Interpolate noiseval through the # redistribution function defined by rdpoints. # rdpoints are sorted by x. Map noiseval (x) to y. rdval = interpolateredistribution(rdpoints, noiseval) # 3. Amplitude Scaling preampshift = layer['preAmpShift'] ampscale = layer['ampScale'] xval = (rdval + preampshift) ampscale # 4. Masking maskindex = layer['maskLayerIndex'] if maskindex is not None and 0 <= maskindex < len(noiselayers): # Check if the masked layer's processed value is within range # Note: We need the processed value of the masked layer. # If the masked layer appears later in the array, we might not have it yet. # However, masking is typically against a layer that has already been # processed or is independent. The schema implies the mask layer's # value is used. We assume the mask layer's processed value is # available. If not, this requires a two-pass approach or # dependency resolution. For simplicity, we assume the mask layer # is either already processed or the mask check is against a # static property. # Standard interpretation: Masking is against the final processed # value of the referenced layer. If the referenced layer is later # in the array, the order of summation matters. The schema does not # specify order independence. We assume the mask layer is processed # before or the mask check is against the layer's own processed # value if it were evaluated. # To be safe, we store processed values in a list. maskedval = processedvalues[maskindex] maskmin = layer['maskMinValue'] maskmax = layer['maskMaxValue'] if maskedval < maskmin or maskedval > maskmax: # Discard current layer's contribution processedvalues.append(0.0) continue processedvalues.append(xval) totalheight += xval return totalheight def interpolateredistribution(points, x): """ Interpolates y for a given x using the provided points. Points are sorted by x. """ if not points: return x # Identity if no RD # Find the segment for k in range(len(points) - 1): p1 = points[k] p2 = points[k+1] if p1['x'] <= x <= p2['x']: # Linear interpolation if p2['x'] == p1['x']: return p1['y'] t = (x - p1['x']) / (p2['x'] - p1['x']) return p1['y'] + t (p2['y'] - p1['y']) # Extrapolate or clamp? Schema doesn't specify. # Clamp to the range of the points. if x < points[0]['x']: return points[0]['y'] else: return points[-1]['y'] Base Noise Consistency: The application rendering the terrain must use the same base noise implementation (e.g., Perlin's reference Simplex) as the design tool. Masking Order: If a layer masks another layer that appears later in the array, the evaluation order must respect this dependency. The schema does not explicitly define evaluation order, but masking implies access to the processed value of the target layer. Redistribution Construction: The rd.points are "equalized points." The exact method of constructing the function (e.g., linear interpolation, spline) is not specified in the schema but is implied to be implemented by the application. Time Complexity: O(L \cdot N), where L is the number of layers and N is the number of pixels/voxels. Each layer requires one noise evaluation, one redistribution lookup, and optional masking check. Memory Complexity: O(L) for storing the schema parameters. The terrain height field requires O(N) memory. Strengths: Decouples design from implementation; allows for non-linear height mapping via redistribution; supports complex masking logic. Limitations: Requires the same base noise implementation in the consumer application; masking dependencies may complicate parallel evaluation if not ordered correctly. The schema was introduced in a thesis on terrain synthesis using noise. It was designed to allow procedural terrains to be exported from a design tool and imported into applications for rendering. The approach uses noise layers, redistribution functions, and masking to create varied terrain features. name: Data Structures and Implementation
body: This family covers the storage, generation, and management of procedural noise data structures used in volume rendering. It addresses the problem of efficiently providing high-frequency detail or base fields to shaders without excessive memory bandwidth or CPU overhead. It differs from its siblings, such as Gradient-based Noise (Perlin/Simplex) and Value Noise, by focusing on the mechanics of data creation (CPU/GPU generation, texture formats, struct layouts) rather than the mathematical definition of the noise fields themselves. The family shares the following mechanism, terms, and math: 1. Gradient Assignment: Each integer lattice point (vertex) in the domain is assigned a pseudo-random gradient vector \mathbf{g}. In 3D, common sets include 12 face diagonals of a cube or 12 axis-aligned vectors. 2. Dot Product Contribution: The noise value at a query point \mathbf{P} is derived from the dot product between the gradient vector \mathbf{g}i at a lattice corner i and the distance vector \mathbf{d}i = \mathbf{P} - \mathbf{V}i from that corner to \mathbf{P}: ni = \mathbf{g}i \cdot \mathbf{d}i. 3. Smoothing/Fade Function: To ensure smooth transitions (C^1 continuity), the fractional coordinates of \mathbf{P} within the cell are passed through a fade function f(t) before interpolation. The quintic function f(t) = 6t^5 - 15t^4 + 10t^3 is standard for Perlin variants, while Simplex uses a different geometric approach. 4. Interpolation: The contributions from the cell corners are combined using linear interpolation (lerp) along the axes, weighted by the fade values. 5. Hashing: Integer coordinates are mapped to gradient indices using a permutation table to avoid modulo operations and ensure uniform distribution. This method generates a 2D texture filled with random values (unit vectors or scalar floats) to serve as a source for noise-based effects, such as SSAO variation, volumetric dithering, or fine detail perturbation. It differs from procedural noise functions (like Perlin or Simplex noise) by providing uncorrelated, high-frequency random data rather than smooth, continuous fields. It is typically generated on the CPU and uploaded to the GPU for sampling during rendering. This variant emphasizes on-the-fly computation to optimize memory usage. Normals are computed dynamically rather than stored, trading computation time for memory efficiency. body: This method generates a 2D texture filled with random unit vectors or scalar floats to serve as a source for noise-based effects, such as SSAO variation and volumetric dithering. Inputs: side (integer dimension for square textures); width and height (viewport dimensions for rectangular textures). Outputs: A GPU 2D texture object containing the noise data. The implementation uses different layouts depending on the noise type and precision: 1. Vector Noise: Host memory holds an array of vec3 of size side side. The GPU texture uses internal format GLRGB32F, dimensions side x side, data type GLFLOAT. 2. Scalar Float Noise: Host memory holds a Color array of size 4096 (64×64). The GPU texture uses format R16, dimensions 64×64, with mipmaps disabled. 3. Scalar Byte Noise: Host memory holds an unsigned char array of size width height. The GPU texture uses internal format GLR8, dimensions width × height, pixel format GLLUMINANCE, and type GLUNSIGNEDBYTE. 1. Initialize Random Number Generator (RNG): Create a seeded RNG using std::randomdevice and std::mt19937 with a uniform distribution over [-1.0, 1.0], or std::srand(std::time(NULL)). 2. Generate Noise Data: For vector noise, loop i from 0 to side^2 - 1: generate three independent uniform values x, y, z \in [-1.0, 1.0], construct \mathbf{v} = (x, y, z), normalize to unit length \mathbf{v}{norm} = \mathbf{v} / \|\mathbf{v}\|, and store in the array. For scalar float noise, generate a random float for the r component of each Color element, leaving other components unspecified (likely 0). For scalar byte noise, fill the array with random bytes in the range [0, 255]. 3. Create and Configure Texture: Generate a texture ID and bind it with glBindTexture(GLTEXTURE2D, id). name: Turing Reaction-Diffusion Noise Generation
head: Reaction Diffusion Scheme
body: This method generates initial noise textures with smooth, large 'spots' using Turing's reaction-diffusion equations, replacing standard white noise for better visual representation of tensor fields. It solves the problem that high-frequency noise textures, such as white noise, are not suitable for achieving a proper visual representation of data in certain visualization approaches. It sets itself apart from its sibling 2D White Noise Texture Generation by producing correlated, spatially structured patterns rather than uncorrelated random values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Grid dimensions, diffusion constants Da and Db, scalar s, and initial random values for grids a and b. Output: Two discrete grids a and b representing the reaction-diffusion state. Data Structures: Two 2D arrays (grids) a and b of identical dimensions, indexed by i and j. Values are floating-point numbers. Parameters: Da: Diffusion constant for grid a. Value: 0.125. Db: Diffusion constant for grid b. Value: 0.031. s: Scalar controlling the size of the spots. Smaller s leads to larger spots. Boundary Conditions: Continuous boundary conditions are assumed for grid coordinates i and j to obtain a seamless texture. Steps: 1. Initialize grids a and b with random values. 2. For each cell (i, j), compute the reaction-diffusion deltas: \Delta a{i,j} = s(16 - a{i,j} \cdot b{i,j}) + Da \cdot (a{i+1,j} + a{i-1,j} + a{i,j+1} + a{i,j-1} - 4 \cdot a{i,j}) \Delta b{i,j} = s(a{i,j} \cdot b{i,j} - b{i,j} - \beta{i,j}) + Db \cdot (b{i+1,j} + b{i-1,j} + b{i,j+1} + b{i,j-1} - 4 \cdot b{i,j}) where \beta{i,j} is an input term. 3. Update the grids using the computed deltas: a{i,j} \leftarrow a{i,j} + \Delta a{i,j} b{i,j} \leftarrow b{i,j} + \Delta b{i,j} 4. Repeat steps 2–3 for a fixed number of iterations until pattern stability is reached. 5. Apply continuous boundary conditions (e.g., coordinate wrapping) to ensure seamlessness across grid edges. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatereactiondiffusionnoise(width, height, s, numiterations, betagrid=None): # Initialize grids with random values a = [[randomfloat() for in range(width)] for in range(height)] b = [[randomfloat() for in range(width)] for in range(height)] Da = 0.125 Db = 0.031 for in range(numiterations): newa = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] newb = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for i in range(height): for j in range(width): # Continuous boundary conditions via wrapping iprev = (i - 1) % height inext = (i + 1) % height jprev = (j - 1) % width jnext = (j + 1) % width # Laplacian diffusion terms lapa = a[inext][j] + a[iprev][j] + a[i][jnext] + a[i][jprev] - 4.0 a[i][j] lapb = b[inext][j] + b[iprev][j] + b[i][jnext] + b[i][jprev] - 4.0 b[i][j] # Reaction terms # betaij is an input term from the source beta = betagrid[i][j] if betagrid is not None else 0.0 F = s (16.0 - a[i][j] b[i][j]) G = s (a[i][j] b[i][j] - b[i][j] - beta) # Compute deltas and update newa[i][j] = a[i][j] + F + Da lapa newb[i][j] = b[i][j] + G + Db lapb a = newa b = newb return a, b def randomfloat(): """Returns a uniform random float in 0, 1).""" import random return random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tiling the reaction diffusion texture can cause minor artifacts at boundaries, but these are ignored in practice due to the advection step. The definition of \beta{i,j} is sparse in the text; it is treated as an input term. name: Gray-Scott Reaction-Diffusion
head: Gray-Scott Reaction-Diffusion Simulation, Gray-Scott model implementation, RD simulation, Reaction-Diffusion System, Reaction-Diffusion Volumetric Simulation, Turing Patterns Simulation, Volumetric Reaction-Diffusion
body: The Gray-Scott model is a 3D reaction-diffusion system that simulates the interaction of two chemical species, U and V, to generate organic, self-organizing patterns such as spots, stripes, and coral-like structures. It produces dynamic volumetric textures useful for camouflage or abstract backgrounds. Unlike its sibling Turing Reaction-Diffusion Noise Generation, which focuses on initial noise generation for tensor fields, the Gray-Scott method explicitly implements feed-kill dynamics to produce distinct morphological regimes based on parameter tuning. The method simulates the evolution of two concentration fields, U (substrate) and V (catalyst), on a cubic grid using explicit Euler time integration and a 7-point stencil finite difference approximation for the Laplacian operator. Inputs: size: Integer, the dimension of the cubic grid (N \times N \times N). config: Object containing simulation parameters: feed (f): Feed rate of chemical U. kill (k): Kill rate of chemical V. du (Du): Diffusion coefficient for U. dv (Dv): Diffusion coefficient for V. dt (\Delta t): Time step size. dx (\Delta x): Grid spacing. boundary: String, either 'periodic' or 'neumann' (default). initialstate: Optional initial concentrations for U and V. If not provided, defaults are assumed (typically U=0.5, V=0 with a localized perturbation). Outputs: u: Final concentration field of chemical U (Float32Array). v: Final concentration field of chemical V (Float32Array). bytebuffer: Uint8Array of length size^3, where each element is the 8-bit representation of V scaled to [0, 255]. metrics: Object containing max, avg, active (count where V \ge threshold), and performance data. 1. Field Arrays: Four Float32Array of length count = size^3: u: Current concentration of U. v: Current concentration of V. nextU: Temporary storage for updated U. nextV: Temporary storage for updated V. 2. Neighbor Arrays: Two Int32Array of length size: neighborMinus: Precomputed indices for the negative direction (left/down/back). neighborPlus: Precomputed indices for the positive direction (right/up/front). 3. Output Buffer: Uint8Array of length count for visualization. f (config.feed): Typical usage Number(config.feed). k (config.kill): Typical usage Number(config.kill). Du (config.du): Typical usage Number(config.du). Dv (config.dv): Typical usage Number(config.dv). \Delta t (config.dt): Typical usage Number(config.dt). \Delta x (config.dx): Retrieved via currentDx(), which returns Math.max(1e-6, Number(config?.dx) || LEGACYDX). Boundary: 'periodic' or 'neumann'. Alternative parameter values from a reference implementation: Du = 10, reaction coefficient = 190, feed rate = 2.8, decay rate = 9.0. The Laplacian operator \nabla^2 is approximated using the 7-point stencil: \nabla^2 C = \frac{C{x-\Delta x} + C{x+\Delta x} + C{y-\Delta y} + C{y+\Delta y} + C{z-\Delta z} + C{z+\Delta z} - 6C{x,y,z}}{\Delta x^2} Let invDx2 = 1 / (\Delta x \cdot \Delta x). For a cell at index i corresponding to coordinates (x, y, z): 1. Laplacian of U: lapU = (u[xm, y, z] + u[xp, y, z] + u[x, ym, z] + u[x, yp, z] + u[x, y, zm] + u[x, y, zp] - 6 \cdot uc) \cdot invDx2 2. Laplacian of V: lapV = (v[xm, y, z] + v[xp, y, z] + v[x, ym, z] + v[x, yp, z] + v[x, y, zm] + v[x, y, zp] - 6 \cdot vc) \cdot invDx2 3. Reaction Term: reaction = uc \cdot vc \cdot vc Where uc = u[i] and vc = v[i]. 4. Update Equations: u{next}[i] = \text{clamp01}\left( uc + \Delta t \cdot (Du \cdot lapU - reaction + f \cdot (1 - uc)) \right) v{next}[i] = \text{clamp01}\left( vc + \Delta t \cdot (Dv \cdot lapV + reaction - (f + k) \cdot vc) \right) Where \text{clamp01}(x) = \max(0, \min(1, x)). 1. Initialize Neighbor Arrays: If boundary is 'periodic': neighborMinus[i] = i - 1 if i > 0, else size - 1. neighborPlus[i] = i + 1 if i < size - 1, else 0. If boundary is 'neumann' (default): neighborMinus[i] = i - 1 if i > 0, else i. neighborPlus[i] = i + 1 if i < size - 1, else i. 2. Compute Inverse Squared Spacing: invDx2 = 1.0 / (dx dx). 3. Initialize Fields: Allocate u, v, nextU, nextV as Float32Array of length sizesizesize. Set u=0.5 and v=0 for all cells. If a cell is within a 3x3x3 cube centered at (5,10,5), set v=0.9. 4. Simulation Loop (for each time step): Iterate over all grid coordinates x, y, z from 0 to size-1. Calculate linear index i = x + y \cdot size + z \cdot size \cdot size. Get neighbor indices: xm = neighborMinus[x], xp = neighborPlus[x] ym = neighborMinus[y], yp = neighborPlus[y] zm = neighborMinus[z], zp = neighborPlus[z] Calculate neighbor linear indices: idx{xm} = xm + y \cdot size + z \cdot size \cdot size idx{xp} = xp + y \cdot size + z \cdot size \cdot size idx{ym} = x + ym \cdot size + z \cdot size \cdot size idx{yp} = x + yp \cdot size + z \cdot size \cdot size idx{zm} = x + y \cdot size + zm \cdot size \cdot size idx{zp} = x + y \cdot size + zp \cdot size \cdot size Retrieve current values: uc = u[i], vc = v[i]. Compute Laplacians: lapU = (u[idx{xm}] + u[idx{xp}] + u[idx{ym}] + u[idx{yp}] + u[idx{zm}] + u[idx{zp}] - 6 \cdot uc) \cdot invDx2 lapV = (v[idx{xm}] + v[idx{xp}] + v[idx{ym}] + v[idx{yp}] + v[idx{zm}] + v[idx{zp}] - 6 \cdot vc) \cdot invDx2 Compute Reaction: reaction = uc \cdot vc \cdot vc. Update Next Values: nextU[i] = \text{clamp01}(uc + dt \cdot (du \cdot lapU - reaction + f \cdot (1 - uc))) nextV[i] = \text{clamp01}(vc + dt \cdot (dv \cdot lapV + reaction - (f + k) \cdot vc)) Swap Buffers: u = nextU, v = nextV (or copy values back to u and v and reuse old arrays as nextU/nextV). 5. Post-Frame Processing: Iterate over all cells to compute metrics. Calculate max, sum, and active count (where v[i] \ge threshold). Convert v[i] to 8-bit integer: bytes[i] = Math.max(0, Math.min(255, Math.round(v[i] 255))). Send frame data to main thread (if using Web Workers) with type 'frame', including size, stepCount, bytes.buffer, and metrics. Transfer ownership of bytes.buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def grayscottsimulation(size, config, numsteps): # Parameters f = float(config['feed']) k = float(config['kill']) du = float(config['du']) dv = float(config['dv']) dt = float(config['dt']) dx = max(1e-6, float(config.get('dx', 1.0))) boundary = config.get('boundary', 'neumann') invDx2 = 1.0 / (dx dx) count = size size size # Data Structures u = [0.0] count v = [0.0] count nextU = [0.0] count nextV = [0.0] count # Initialize Fields for z in range(size): for y in range(size): for x in range(size): i = x + y size + z size size u[i] = 0.5 v[i] = 0.0 # 3x3x3 cube centered at (5, 10, 5) if abs(x - 5) <= 1 and abs(y - 10) <= 1 and abs(z - 5) <= 1: v[i] = 0.9 # Neighbor Arrays neighborMinus = [0] size neighborPlus = [0] size for i in range(size): if boundary == 'periodic': neighborMinus[i] = (i - 1) % size neighborPlus[i] = (i + 1) % size else: # neumann neighborMinus[i] = max(0, i - 1) neighborPlus[i] = min(size - 1, i + 1) # Simulation Loop for step in range(numsteps): for z in range(size): zbase = z size size zm = neighborMinus[z] zp = neighborPlus[z] zmbase = zm size size zpbase = zp size size for y in range(size): ybase = y size ym = neighborMinus[y] yp = neighborPlus[y] ymbase = ym size ypbase = yp size for x in range(size): i = x + ybase + zbase xm = neighborMinus[x] xp = neighborPlus[x] # Neighbors idxxm = xm + ybase + zbase idxxp = xp + ybase + zbase idxym = x + ymbase + zbase idxyp = x + ypbase + zbase idxzm = x + ybase + zmbase idxzp = x + ybase + zpbase uc = u[i] vc = v[i] # Laplacians lapU = (u[idxxm] + u[idxxp] + u[idxym] + u[idxyp] + u[idxzm] + u[idxzp] - 6 uc) invDx2 lapV = (v[idxxm] + v[idxxp] + v[idxym] + v[idxyp] + v[idxzm] + v[idxzp] - 6 vc) invDx2 # Reaction reaction = uc vc vc # Update nextU[i] = max(0.0, min(1.0, uc + dt (du lapU - reaction + f (1 - uc)))) nextV[i] = max(0.0, min(1.0, vc + dt (dv lapV + reaction - (f + k) vc))) # Swap buffers u, nextU = nextU, u v, nextV = nextV, v # Post-processing bytebuffer = [0] count maxv = 0.0 sumv = 0.0 activecount = 0 threshold = 0.1 # Not given in the sources. for i in range(count): val = v[i] bytebuffer[i] = max(0, min(255, round(val 255))) if val > maxv: maxv = val sumv += val if val >= threshold: activecount += 1 avgv = sumv / count return u, v, bytebuffer, {'max': maxv, 'avg': avgv, 'active': activecount} Grid Spacing: dx must not be zero or negative. The implementation ensures dx \ge 10^{-6}. Field Bounds: Field values must remain within [0, 1]. The clamp01 function is applied to both U and V updates to prevent numerical instability. Boundary Handling: Neighbors outside the grid bounds are ignored or clamped depending on the boundary mode; periodic boundaries wrap indices. Stability: Explicit Euler integration is conditionally stable. If dt is too large relative to dx and diffusion coefficients, the simulation may diverge. The sources do not specify a stability criterion (e.g., CFL condition). Generates initial noise textures with smooth, large 'spots' using Turing's reaction-diffusion equations, replacing standard white noise for better visual representation of tensor fields. Choose when you need a static or slowly evolving base texture for field visualization rather than dynamic chemical patterns. Link Generates random noise textures used as initial conditions or base layers for procedural generation. Choose when you need a purely stochastic starting state without chemical interaction dynamics. Link Time Complexity: O(N^3) per time step, where N is the grid size. Each cell requires a constant number of operations (6 neighbors, 2 Laplacians, 1 reaction, 2 updates). Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for storing the four field arrays (u, v, nextU, nextV) and neighbor arrays. For a 512^3 grid, this is approximately 4 \times 512^3 \times 4 bytes \approx 2 GB for floats, plus overhead. Measured Performance: On CPU (Processing 4.3): A 512 \times 512 grid updates at 200 fps using optimized arrays. On GPU (Fragment Shader): The same simulation runs at 4K resolution on modern GPUs. Strengths: Produces highly organic, complex patterns suitable for camouflage, biological textures, and abstract backgrounds. Efficient on GPUs due to regular memory access patterns. Limitations: Explicit Euler integration limits the time step size for stability. High resolution requires significant memory and compute power. When to Use: When organic, self-organizing patterns are desired for volumetric textures, especially for biological or naturalistic materials. When Not to Use: When strict physical accuracy of chemical reactions is required (this is a simplified model). When real-time performance on low-end hardware is critical at high resolutions. The Gray-Scott model is a mathematical model of a reaction-diffusion system, first proposed by Peter Gray and Scott M. Scott in 1983. It is a variant of the Turing reaction-diffusion system, which was originally proposed by Alan Turing in 1952 to explain morphogenesis. The Gray-Scott model is particularly notable for its rich variety of patterns, including spots, stripes, and coral-like structures, depending on the feed and kill rates. It has been used in demoscene productions and mathematical art for its visual appeal and computational efficiency. body: This family encompasses specific mathematical formulations and algorithmic patterns used to generate volumetric data, density fields, and geometric structures procedurally without explicit mesh storage. It solves the problem of creating complex, organic, or fractal 3D shapes and density distributions using deterministic functions. Unlike Gradient-based Noise (Perlin/Simplex) which provides raw noise values, or Value Noise which interpolates scalar values, this family applies specific transformations (such as polar exponentiation, spherical ramps, or sine-based occupancy) to define the final volume characteristics directly. The family shares the following mechanism, terms, and math: 1. Gradient Assignment: Each integer lattice point (vertex) in the domain is assigned a pseudo-random gradient vector \mathbf{g}. In 3D, common sets include 12 face diagonals of a cube or 12 axis-aligned vectors. 2. Dot Product Contribution: The noise value at a query point \mathbf{P} is derived from the dot product between the gradient vector \mathbf{g}i at a lattice corner i and the distance vector \mathbf{d}i = \mathbf{P} - \mathbf{V}i from that corner to \mathbf{P}: ni = \mathbf{g}i \cdot \mathbf{d}i. 3. Smoothing/Fade Function: To ensure smooth transitions (C^1 continuity), the fractional coordinates of \mathbf{P} within the cell are passed through a fade function f(t) before interpolation. S1 uses the cubic smoothstep function f(t) = 3t^2 - 2t^3 for interpolation weighting. 4. Interpolation: The contributions from the cell corners are combined using linear interpolation (lerp) along the axes, weighted by the fade values. 5. Hashing: Integer coordinates are mapped to gradient indices using a permutation table or coordinate mixing constants to avoid modulo operations and ensure uniform distribution. Creates volumetric data by evaluating trigonometric functions against spatial coordinates to determine voxel occupancy and color. It solves the problem of generating deterministic, periodic, and smooth geometric structures without storing explicit mesh or voxel grid data. Unlike Simple Heightmap Voxel Generation which focuses on planar terrain, or Procedural Tree Voxel Generation which uses hierarchical branching, this method relies on global periodic wave interference to define shape boundaries and internal density variations. Is a procedural volume density function that confines a gas (such as steam or smoke) to a spherical slab region using a spherical distance ramp and an offset table, simulating steam rising from a source. It differs from its siblings by combining a base turbulence pattern with a specific radial falloff mechanism that uses a precomputed cosine ramp and spatially varying noise offsets to break symmetry, whereas Sine-based procedural voxel generation relies on sinusoidal modulation and Mandelbulb Fractal Generation uses iterative complex number transformations. Generates a 3D fractal by iteratively applying a polar coordinate power transformation to a complex 3D point. It differs from its siblings by using continuous polar coordinate exponentiation rather than discrete modulo arithmetic (Menger Sponge) or simple polynomial mappings (Bristorbrot). Generates a patchy volumetric density field from procedural noise by applying a power function and a threshold to create sparse, organic structures. It differs from its parent Specific Procedural Patterns and Applications by explicitly combining Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) with non-linear remapping and hard cutoffs, rather than relying on raw noise values or simple linear blending. A method to map pre-shaded texture cells onto a terrain or volume surface without visible repetition, using aperiodic boundary conditions and edge-matching constraints. It differs from standard periodic tiling by enforcing specific edge correlations to prevent seams, and from simple noise-based tiling by relying on pre-computed geometric patterns rather than procedural generation at render time. Definition: A noise function designed for 3D volumetric clouds that samples a 2D texture slice based on 3D coordinates to generate organic randomness. Steps: 1. Compute integer part p and fractional part f of the input 3D coordinate x. 2. Compute smooth interpolation factor u using the formula u = f f (3. - 2. f). 3. name: Sine-based procedural voxel generation
head: Trigonometric voxel pattern
body: Sine-based procedural voxel generation determines voxel occupancy and color by evaluating trigonometric functions against integer spatial coordinates. It generates deterministic, periodic structures without storing explicit grid data. Unlike Simple Heightmap Voxel Generation or Procedural Tree Voxel Generation, it relies on global periodic wave interference for shape boundaries. Inputs and Outputs Input: 3D integer voxel coordinates (posx, posy, posz), grid width, and a scaling constant. Output: A voxel state (empty or filled) and an RGBA color value. Data Structures Coordinates: Integer triplets representing voxel indices. Color: 32-bit value with 8-bit channels (R, G, B, A). Parameters mod: The periodicity divisor, calculated as width / 8. scale: A constant multiplier for color channels, set to 0x20 (32). Algorithm Steps 1. Periodicity Calculation: Compute mod = width / 8. 2. Normalization: Convert integer coordinates to a normalized range [-1, 1] within the periodic cell: xx = \frac{(posx \bmod \text{mod}) \cdot 2}{\text{mod}} - 1 yy = \frac{(posy \bmod \text{mod}) \cdot 2}{\text{mod}} - 1 zz = \frac{(posz \bmod \text{mod}) \cdot 2}{\text{mod}} - 1 3. Radius Calculation: Compute a variable radius r defining the shape boundary: r = \left( \sin\left( \frac{posx/\text{mod} + posy/\text{mod} + posz/\text{mod}}{5} \right) + 1 \right) \cdot 0.3 4. Occupancy Test: A voxel is filled if it satisfies both conditions: It lies inside the spherical boundary: xx^2 + yy^2 + zz^2 \le r. It passes a secondary frequency filter: \sin\left( \frac{posx \cdot 16 + posy \cdot 20 + posz \cdot 30}{\text{width}} \right) \ge 0. If either condition fails, the voxel is empty. 5. Color Assignment: If filled, compute RGB values scaled by the position relative to mod: R = \frac{posx}{\text{mod}} \cdot 0x20 G = \frac{posy}{\text{mod}} \cdot 0x20 B = \frac{posz}{\text{mod}} \cdot 0x20 A = 255 Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sinevoxelgeneration(posx: int, posy: int, posz: int, width: int): mod = width / 8 xx = ((posx % mod) 2.0 / mod) - 1.0 yy = ((posy % mod) 2.0 / mod) - 1.0 zz = ((posz % mod) 2.0 / mod) - 1.0 arg = (posx / mod + posy / mod + posz / mod) / 5.0 radius = (math.sin(arg) + 1.0) 0.3 if xxxx + yyyy + zzzz > radius: return None filterarg = (posx 16 + posy 20 + posz 30) / width if math.sin(filterarg) < 0: return None scale = 0x20 r = int((posx / mod) scale) g = int((posy / mod) scale) b = int((posz / mod) scale) a = 255 return (r, g, b, a) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Harmonic trigonometric displacement noise adds organic or porous textures to volumes by modulating density. It applies a multiplicative amplitude factor to the product of sines along each axis. Formula: amp \cdot \sin(freq \cdot x) \cdot \sin(freq \cdot y) \cdot \sin(freq \cdot z). name: Procedural Tree Voxel Generation
head: L-system-like recursion, L-systems, Lindenmayer systems, Recursive Tree Branching, Tree Voxel Generation
body: Procedural Tree Voxel Generation is a method for creating volumetric tree structures by recursively branching segments represented as spheres of varying thickness. It adapts L-system principles to voxel space, where a single recursive rule generates complex, self-similar shapes by spawning sub-branches with random directional offsets and scaling factors. Unlike shape grammars that output basic shapes directly, this method requires interpreting the recursive production rules to draw voxelized primitives. Inputs: root1: Starting 3D position (vector) of the current segment. root2: Ending 3D position (vector) of the current segment. thicknessA: Radius of the sphere at root1. thicknessB: Radius of the sphere at root2. iteration: Current recursion depth (integer). vx, vy, vz: Dimensions of the voxel grid. voxel: Bit-packed array storing occupancy. voxelcol1, voxelcol2: Arrays storing color data. Outputs: Modified voxel array containing the tree geometry. Modified voxelcol1 and voxelcol2 arrays containing color data. The voxel data is stored in a bit-packed format to save memory. voxel: char array of size (vx/8) \times vy \times vz bytes. Each byte stores 8 voxels along the X-axis. Bit k in a byte corresponds to voxel coordinate x where k = x \pmod 8. Offset calculation for voxel (x, y, z): ofs = (x \gg 3) + y \cdot (vx \gg 3) + z \cdot ((vx \gg 3) \cdot vy) voxelcol1, voxelcol2: uchar arrays of size vx \times vy \times vz, storing color indices or values for each voxel. 1. Base Case Check: If iteration > 5 or thicknessA < 2, draw a leaf sphere at root1 with radius 8 and color index 2, then return. 2. Increment Iteration: Increment iteration for the current recursive step. 3. Calculate Midpoint: Compute the midpoint between root1 and root2, offset by a random vector scaled by half the segment length: mid = \frac{root1 + root2}{2} + random\vector \cdot length \cdot 0.1 where length = \|root2 - root1\| \cdot 0.5. 4. Calculate Midpoint Thickness: thicknessM = \frac{thicknessA + thicknessB}{2} Draw a sphere at mid with radius thicknessM. 5. Add Detail Sphere: Calculate an offset vector using sine and cosine of a detail index iM, then draw a smaller sphere at mid + offset with radius thicknessM / 3 and color index 3. 6. Recursive Branching: Loop branches from 0 to 3. Generate a random direction vector rnd and normalize it. Adjust the Y component to bias upward based on iteration: rnd.y += 0.6 \cdot iteration - 0.5 Calculate the delta vector of the current segment: delta = root2 - root1 Scale and offset the branch vector: branch = rnd \cdot length + delta \cdot 0.6 (Note: Since rnd is normalized, \|rnd\|=1, making the division by branch.length() in the source equivalent to 1). Calculate new thickness for the child branch: thicknessNew = thicknessA \cdot 0.4 Recursively call tree with start point root2, end point root2 + branch, thickness thicknessNew, and incremented iteration. 7. Decrement Iteration: After the branching loop completes, decrement iteration if managed as a shared state. To draw a sphere at position pos with radius r: 1. Iterate x from \lfloor pos.x - r \rfloor to \lceil pos.x + r \rceil. 2. Iterate y from \lfloor pos.y - r \rfloor to \lceil pos.y + r \rceil. 3. Iterate z from \lfloor pos.z - r \rfloor to \lceil pos.z + r \rceil. 4. Calculate squared distance: distSq = (x - pos.x)^2 + (y - pos.y)^2 + (z - pos.z)^2 5. If distSq \le r^2: Set the bit in voxel: voxel[ofs] \ |= \ (1 \ll (x \pmod 8)) Set color in voxelcol1 and voxelcol2 at (x, y, z). After the tree is generated, a mipmap level can be created. 1. Iterate over each voxel in the current tree level. 2. Check the 2x2x2 sub-voxels corresponding to the current voxel. 3. If any sub-voxel is set, set the corresponding bit in the mipmap voxel. 4. Copy color bits if present. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def drawsphere(pos, radius, coloridx, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz): """Draws a sphere into the voxel grid according to S1 specifications.""" r = radius xmin = max(0, int(pos.x - r)) xmax = min(vx - 1, int(pos.x + r)) ymin = max(0, int(pos.y - r)) ymax = min(vy - 1, int(pos.y + r)) zmin = max(0, int(pos.z - r)) zmax = min(vz - 1, int(pos.z + r)) rsq = r r vx8 = vx >> 3 vx8vy = vx8 vy for x in range(xmin, xmax + 1): bitmask = 1 << (x & 7) for y in range(ymin, ymax + 1): yoffset = y vx8 for z in range(zmin, zmax + 1): dx = x - pos.x dy = y - pos.y dz = z - pos.z distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz if distsq <= rsq: ofs = (x >> 3) + yoffset + z vx8vy voxel[ofs] |= bitmask voxelcol1[x + y vx + z vx vy] = coloridx voxelcol2[x + y vx + z vx vy] = coloridx def getrnd(): """Generates a random 3D vector.""" return [random.uniform(-1, 1), random.uniform(-1, 1), random.uniform(-1, 1)] def normalize(v): """Normalizes a vector.""" length = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) if length == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return [v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length] def tree(root1, root2, thicknessA, thicknessB, iteration, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz): """ Recursive function to generate tree branches per S1. """ # Base case if iteration > 5 or thicknessA < 2: drawsphere(root1, 8.0, 2, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz) return # Increment iteration for children nextiteration = iteration + 1 # Calculate delta and half-length delta = [root2[i] - root1[i] for i in range(3)] deltalen = math.sqrt(delta[0]2 + delta[1]2 + delta[2]2) length = deltalen 0.5 # Calculate midpoint with random offset rndmid = getrnd() rndmid = normalize(rndmid) mid = [(root1[i] + root2[i]) / 2.0 + rndmid[i] length 0.1 for i in range(3)] thicknessM = (thicknessA + thicknessB) / 2.0 # Draw main segment sphere drawsphere(mid, thicknessM, 2, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz) # Add detail sphere iM = iteration # Deterministic detail index per source context offsetx = math.sin(iM) (thicknessM / 3.0) offsety = math.cos(iM) (thicknessM / 3.0) offsetz = math.sin(iM + 1) (thicknessM / 3.0) detailpos = [mid[i] + [offsetx, offsety, offsetz][i] for i in range(3)] drawsphere(detailpos, thicknessM / 3.0, 3, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz) # Recursive branching for branches in range(4): rnd = getrnd() rnd = normalize(rnd) # Adjust Y component rnd[1] += 0.6 iteration - 0.5 # Scale and offset branch vector branchvec = [rnd[i] length + delta[i] 0.6 for i in range(3)] newroot2 = [root2[i] + branchvec[i] for i in range(3)] thicknessNew = thicknessA 0.4 tree(root2, newroot2, thicknessA, thicknessNew, nextiteration, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz) def generatetree(vx, vy, vz): """ Initializes voxel data and starts tree generation. """ voxelsize = (vx // 8) vy vz voxel = bytearray(voxelsize) voxelcol1 = bytearray(vx vy vz) voxelcol2 = bytearray(vx vy vz) root1 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] root2 = [0.0, 10.0, 0.0] thicknessA = 10.0 thicknessB = 8.0 iteration = 0 tree(root1, root2, thicknessA, thicknessB, iteration, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz) return voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2 iteration: Static counter for recursion depth. Base case triggers if iteration > 5 or thickness < 2. iso: Isolation threshold for loading voxel data from file, default 168. thicknessA: Initial thickness of the trunk. thicknessB: Thickness at the end of the trunk segment. branches: Number of sub-branches spawned per node (fixed at 4 in the source loop). Precision: Floating point errors in distance calculations may cause gaps or overlaps in sphere voxelization. Using squared distance comparisons avoids square roots. Boundary Checks: Voxel coordinates must be clamped to the grid dimensions [0, vx-1] \times [0, vy-1] \times [0, vz-1] to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Degenerate Input: If root1 equals root2, the delta vector is zero, resulting in no branch direction. The normalization of rnd handles this, but the branch vector becomes purely random, potentially causing instability. L-systems use production rules to model plant growth. Unlike shape grammars, L-systems require interpretation of the output string to produce the final result. They are well-suited for self-similar shapes like trees. Used in city layout generation, these L-systems change under local constraints to avoid overlapping streets or parallel roads. This concept can be adapted for tree generation to prevent branch collision. A post-processing step where 2x2x2 sub-voxels are checked to generate lower-resolution levels of the tree voxel data. Time: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the bounding box of the tree. The number of spheres drawn is proportional to the number of branches, which grows exponentially with iteration (base 4). Each sphere voxelization is O(r^3). Memory: O(vx \cdot vy \cdot vz / 8) for the bit-packed voxel array, plus O(vx \cdot vy \cdot vz) for color arrays. Not given in the sources. The tree size scales with the initial thickness and the number of iterations. Increasing iteration exponentially increases the number of branches and voxels. Strengths: Simple implementation, generates organic-looking structures, low memory footprint due to bit-packing. Limitations: Limited to spherical primitives, no internal structure (hollow branches), random variation may lead to non-physical overlaps. Use for background vegetation, low-poly trees, or when procedural generation is required without external assets. The method is based on L-systems, introduced by Aristid Lindenmayer in 1968 to model plant development. L-systems have been widely used in procedural architectural modeling and city layout generation, such as by Parish & Müller (2001). The voxel-based approach adapts these concepts to volumetric rendering, using sphere splatting to represent branches. Procedural vegetation in voxel-based games and simulations. name: Simple Heightmap Voxel Generation
head: Sine Terrain Grid
body: Simple Heightmap Voxel Generation is a procedural method for creating voxel terrain meshes by mapping 2D grid coordinates to heights using deterministic sine and cosine functions. It replaces stochastic noise with deterministic trigonometric waves to ensure spatial continuity and predictable patterns. It differs from its sibling, Random Heightmap Terrain Generation, by using fixed trigonometric evaluation instead of random assignment. It is distinct from its parent, Sine-based procedural voxel generation, by specifically implementing a 2D heightmap approach for terrain meshing rather than general 3D field evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Grid dimensions defined by chunk count (2x2 chunks) and chunk size (16x16 vertices per chunk), resulting in a 32x32 world area. Output: A flat float array buffer containing vertex data for triangle strips representing the terrain surface. Data Structures: Output Buffer: A flat float array where every 6 vertices (3 floats each) represent a quad (2 triangles). The buffer is filled sequentially. Vertex Format: Each vertex consists of 3 floats: (x, y, z). Parameters: Chunk Size: 16 vertices per side. Chunk Grid: 2x2 chunks. Frequency Factor: 0.15 used in trigonometric calculations. Amplitude Multiplier: 2.0 applied to the sum of sine and cosine. Base Height Offset: 0.0. Formulas: The height h for a world coordinate (worldX, worldZ) is calculated as: h = 0.0 + (\sin(worldX \times 0.15) + \cos(worldZ \times 0.15)) \times 2.0 Where worldX and worldZ are integer world coordinates derived from the chunk and local indices. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty output buffer. 2. Iterate over chunk X from 0 to 1. 3. Iterate over chunk Z from 0 to 1. 4. Iterate over local X from 0 to 15. 5. Iterate over local Z from 0 to 15. 6. Calculate world coordinates: worldX = chunkX \times 16 + x and worldZ = chunkZ \times 16 + z. 7. Calculate height: height = (\sin(worldX \times 0.15) + \cos(worldZ \times 0.15)) \times 2.0. 8. Write the first triangle vertices to the buffer: (worldX, height, worldZ), (worldX+1, height, worldZ), (worldX, height, worldZ+1). 9. Write the second triangle vertices to the buffer: (worldX+1, height, worldZ), (worldX+1, height, worldZ+1), (worldX, height, worldZ+1). 10. Repeat until all chunks and vertices are processed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generatesimpleheightmap(chunkxcount=2, chunkzcount=2, chunksize=16): """ Generates a voxel terrain mesh using sine/cosine heightmap. Returns a flat list of floats representing vertices. """ buffer = [] freq = 0.15 amp = 2.0 for chunkx in range(chunkxcount): for chunkz in range(chunkzcount): for x in range(chunksize): for z in range(chunksize): worldx = chunkx chunksize + x worldz = chunkz chunksize + z height = (math.sin(worldx freq) + math.cos(worldz freq)) amp # Triangle 1: (x, z), (x+1, z), (x, z+1) buffer.append(worldx) buffer.append(height) buffer.append(worldz) buffer.append(worldx + 1) buffer.append(height) buffer.append(worldz) buffer.append(worldx) buffer.append(height) buffer.append(worldz + 1) # Triangle 2: (x+1, z), (x+1, z+1), (x, z+1) buffer.append(worldx + 1) buffer.append(height) buffer.append(worldz) buffer.append(worldx + 1) buffer.append(height) buffer.append(worldz + 1) buffer.append(worldx) buffer.append(height) buffer.append(worldz + 1) return buffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flat Quads: The implementation calculates a single height per quad using the bottom-left corner coordinates and applies it to all four vertices, producing flat-topped quads rather than interpolated slopes. Boundary Conditions: The grid is strictly bounded by the chunk dimensions with no wrapping or infinite terrain implied. Random Heightmap Terrain Generation creates a voxel terrain mesh by assigning independent, uniformly distributed random heights to vertices on a 2D grid. It differs from its parent, Simple Heightmap Voxel Generation, by replacing deterministic sine/cosine functions with stochastic noise, and from its child, Midpoint Displacement Fractal, by lacking spatial correlation between adjacent vertices. This method is chosen when a non-smooth, jagged, or purely random terrain surface is desired without the computational overhead of fractal algorithms. Procedural Voxel Map Generation creates a 3D voxel map by applying a procedural color function and randomly placing solid rectangular blocks within defined bounds. It defines a color function with deterministic hashing for veins using ((x \times 17) \oplus (y \times 31) \oplus (z \times 47)) \times 0x45d9f3b, computes pulse = \sin(x^2 + y^2 + z \times 19) and swirl = \sin((x - y) \times 0.11 + z \times 0.27), calculates RGB channels with fade = z / 63.0, and computes shade based on vein bits. It creates a flat map at Z=63, loops 2048 times sampling random booleans for solidity, generates random start/end coordinates clamped to VSID and MAXZDIM, calls map.setrect with bounds and color set, and writes output via map.writecolumns. Parameters include VSID (horizontal dimension size), MAXZDIM (vertical dimension size), 63 (initial flat Z height), and 2048 (number of random blocks). Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the total number of quads, with constant-time trigonometric evaluation per quad. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output buffer, fixed at 6 \times 1600 floats for the default 4-chunk configuration (32x32 grid). Performance: Very fast due to the simplicity of the height calculation without noise lookup tables or complex interpolation. Strengths: Deterministic output, easy to implement, low memory footprint, predictable terrain patterns. Limitations: Limited terrain variety due to periodic patterns, flat-topped quads without interpolation, no 3D internal structure generation. Simple Heightmap Voxel Generation originates from early web-based voxel game implementations, specifically those targeting WebAssembly for real-time performance. It was developed as a straightforward method to generate terrain meshes in browser environments, leveraging the simplicity of trigonometric functions for height calculation. The method is part of a broader family of procedural generation techniques used in voxel-based games and simulations. nilabh25bcs10235-beep/minecraft-wasm, https://github.com/nilabh25bcs10235-beep/minecraft-wasm, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) mayakeele/bad-minecraft, https://github.com/mayakeele/bad-minecraft, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) MuffinTastic/rust-voxlap-vxl, https://github.com/MuffinTastic/rust-voxlap-vxl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Random Heightmap Terrain Generation
head: Random Terrain Grid
body: Random Heightmap Terrain Generation creates a voxel terrain mesh by assigning independent, uniformly distributed random heights to vertices on a 2D grid. Inputs: xWidth: Width of the terrain grid in world units. zWidth: Depth of the terrain grid in world units. xDetail: Number of segments along the X axis. zDetail: Number of segments along the Z axis. height: Maximum absolute height of random vertices. Outputs: A mesh defined by a list of faces. Each face is an object containing vertex indices A, B, C and normal components NX, NY, NZ. Data Structures: vertices: An array of size (xDetail + 1) \times (zDetail + 1). Each element stores the 3D coordinates (x, y, z) of a vertex. faces: An array of face objects. Steps: 1. Initialize the vertices array with size (xDetail + 1) \times (zDetail + 1). 2. Iterate over grid indices iZ from 0 to zDetail and iX from 0 to xDetail. 3. Calculate the linear index currIndex for the current vertex: \text{currIndex} = (iZ \times xVerts) + iX, where xVerts = xDetail + 1. 4. Calculate the world coordinates for the vertex: \text{tempX} = \left(\frac{iX}{xDetail}\right) \times xWidth - \frac{xWidth}{2} \text{tempZ} = \left(\frac{iZ}{zDetail}\right) \times zWidth - \frac{zWidth}{2} \text{tempY} = \text{height} \times (2 \times (\text{Math.random()} - 0.5)) Store the vertex at vertices[currIndex] with coordinates (\text{tempX}, \text{tempY}, \text{tempZ}). 5. Iterate over grid cells iZ from 0 to zDetail-1 and iX from 0 to xDetail-1. 6. For each cell, identify the four corner vertices using the current currIndex (calculated as in Step 3 for the top-left corner of the cell): Upper triangle vertices: A = \text{currIndex}, B = \text{currIndex} + 1, C = \text{currIndex} + xVerts + 1. Lower triangle vertices: A = \text{currIndex}, B = \text{currIndex} + xVerts, C = \text{currIndex} + xVerts + 1. 7. Compute the face normal for each triangle using the cross product of edge vectors \vec{U} and \vec{V}. For a triangle with vertices A, B, C: \vec{U} = \text{vertices}[B] - \text{vertices}[A] \vec{V} = \text{vertices}[C] - \text{vertices}[A] \vec{N} = \vec{U} \times \vec{V} Normalize \vec{N} to get (NX, NY, NZ). 8. Store the face data (indices A, B, C and normal NX, NY, NZ) in the faces array. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random as random class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def sub(self, other): return Vector3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def cross(u, v): return Vector3(u.yv.z - u.zv.y, u.zv.x - u.xv.z, u.xv.y - u.yv.x) def normalize(v): mag = (v.x2 + v.y2 + v.z2)0.5 return Vector3(v.x/mag, v.y/mag, v.z/mag) if mag > 0 else Vector3(0, 0, 0) def generaterandomheightmap(xWidth, zWidth, xDetail, zDetail, height): xVerts = xDetail + 1 zVerts = zDetail + 1 vertices = [None] (xVerts zVerts) for iZ in range(zVerts): for iX in range(xVerts): currIndex = (iZ xVerts) + iX tempX = (iX / xDetail) xWidth - (xWidth / 2) tempZ = (iZ / zDetail) zWidth - (zWidth / 2) tempY = height (2 (random.random() - 0.5)) vertices[currIndex] = Vector3(tempX, tempY, tempZ) faces = [] for iZ in range(zDetail): for iX in range(xDetail): currIndex = (iZ xVerts) + iX # Upper triangle A = vertices[currIndex] B = vertices[currIndex + 1] C = vertices[currIndex + xVerts + 1] U1 = B - A V1 = C - A N1 = cross(U1, V1) N1 = normalize(N1) faces.append({'A': currIndex, 'B': currIndex + 1, 'C': currIndex + xVerts + 1, 'NX': N1.x, 'NY': N1.y, 'NZ': N1.z}) # Lower triangle A2 = vertices[currIndex] B2 = vertices[currIndex + xVerts] C2 = vertices[currIndex + xVerts + 1] U2 = B2 - A2 V2 = C2 - A2 N2 = cross(U2, V2) N2 = normalize(N2) faces.append({'A': currIndex, 'B': currIndex + xVerts, 'C': currIndex + xVerts + 1, 'NX': N2.x, 'NY': N2.y, 'NZ': N2.z}) return faces Parameters: xWidth, zWidth: Define the physical extent of the terrain. xDetail, zDetail: Control the resolution (grid density). height: Controls the vertical amplitude of the noise. Edge Cases: xDetail or zDetail equal to 0 results in no faces. height equal to 0 results in a flat plane. Random number generator seeding is not specified in the source, but reproducibility requires it. name: Midpoint Displacement Fractal
head: Mid-point Displacement, Plasma fractal grid generation, Stochastic subdivision
body: Midpoint Displacement Fractal generates a 2D noise grid using recursive midpoint displacement to create a fractal terrain or noise map. It differs from its parent, Random Heightmap Terrain Generation, by imposing spatial correlation through recursive averaging and roughening, rather than assigning independent random heights to all vertices. Inputs: width (int): Width of the output grid. height (int): Height of the output grid. roughness (float): Controls fractal roughness. Outputs: grid: A 2D float array of size [width][height] containing the generated height values. Data Structures: grid[width][height]: Stores the height value for each cell. roughness: Internal parameter, calculated as roughness / width. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Calculate roughness = roughness / width. Allocate grid[width][height]. Set the random number generator seed. Set the four corner points to random values in the range [-0.5, 0.5]: grid[0][0] grid[0][height-1] grid[width-1][0] grid[width-1][height-1] Call generate(0, 0, width-1, height-1). 2. Recursive Generation (generate(xl, yl, xh, yh)): Compute midpoints: xm = (xl + xh) / 2 ym = (yl + yh) / 2 Base Case: If xl == xm and yl == ym, return. Edge Midpoints: Compute the unroughened midpoints of the four edges by averaging the adjacent corners: grid[xm][yl] = 0.5 (grid[xl][yl] + grid[xh][yl]) grid[xm][yh] = 0.5 (grid[xl][yh] + grid[xh][yh]) grid[xl][ym] = 0.5 (grid[xl][yl] + grid[xl][yh]) grid[xh][ym] = 0.5 (grid[xh][yl] + grid[xh][yh]) Center Point: Compute the center point by averaging the two horizontal edge midpoints: centerval = 0.5 (grid[xm][yl] + grid[xm][yh]) Roughen the center value and assign it to grid[xm][ym]. Roughen Edges: Roughen the four edge midpoints using roughen() with appropriate span parameters: grid[xm][yl] = roughen(grid[xm][yl], xl, xh) grid[xm][yh] = roughen(grid[xm][yh], xl, xh) grid[xl][ym] = roughen(grid[xl][ym], yl, yh) grid[xh][ym] = roughen(grid[xh][ym], yl, yh) Recurse: Call generate() on the four sub-quadrants: generate(xl, yl, xm, ym) generate(xm, yl, xh, ym) generate(xl, ym, xm, yh) generate(xm, ym, xh, yh) 3. Roughening Function (roughen(v, l, h)): Generate Gaussian noise n with mean 0 and standard deviation proportional to the span (h - l) and roughness. Return v + n. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random class MidpointDisplacement: def init(self, width, height, roughness): self.width = width self.height = height self.roughness = roughness / width self.grid = [[0.0 for in range(height)] for in range(width)] self.initialize() def initialize(self): self.grid[0][0] = random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) self.grid[0][self.height - 1] = random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) self.grid[self.width - 1][0] = random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) self.grid[self.width - 1][self.height - 1] = random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5) self.generate(0, 0, self.width - 1, self.height - 1) def generate(self, xl, yl, xh, yh): xm = (xl + xh) // 2 ym = (yl + yh) // 2 if xl == xm and yl == ym: return self.grid[xm][yl] = 0.5 (self.grid[xl][yl] + self.grid[xh][yl]) self.grid[xm][yh] = 0.5 (self.grid[xl][yh] + self.grid[xh][yh]) self.grid[xl][ym] = 0.5 (self.grid[xl][yl] + self.grid[xl][yh]) self.grid[xh][ym] = 0.5 (self.grid[xh][yl] + self.grid[xh][yh]) centerval = 0.5 (self.grid[xm][yl] + self.grid[xm][yh]) self.grid[xm][ym] = self.roughen(centerval, xl, xh) self.grid[xm][yl] = self.roughen(self.grid[xm][yl], xl, xh) self.grid[xm][yh] = self.roughen(self.grid[xm][yh], xl, xh) self.grid[xl][ym] = self.roughen(self.grid[xl][ym], yl, yh) self.grid[xh][ym] = self.roughen(self.grid[xh][ym], yl, yh) self.generate(xl, yl, xm, ym) self.generate(xm, yl, xh, ym) self.generate(xl, ym, xm, yh) self.generate(xm, ym, xh, yh) def roughen(self, v, l, h): span = h - l noise = random.gauss(0, span self.roughness) return v + noise Parameters: roughness: Float controlling fractal roughness. width, height: Integers defining the grid dimensions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Produces directional artifacts and requires a known fixed-size domain, making it unsuitable for random-access batch generation or parallel processing without visible seams. name: Diamond-Square Algorithm (Chunk-based Midpoint Displacement)
head: DSNoise, Midpoint Displacement
body: The Diamond-Square Algorithm (Chunk-based Midpoint Displacement) is a procedural world generation method that recursively subdivides a 2D grid into squares and diamonds to compute new cell values as the average of surrounding cells plus a scaled random perturbation. It operates asynchronously on chunks to generate a continuous world model, distinguishing itself from standard implementations by its spatial partitioning and lazy evaluation strategy. Inputs and Outputs Input: A chunk coordinate (implied by the asynchronous context), a global WorldSeed, and a sampleLevel integer scaling factor. Output: A populated 2D array of DSDataCase instances representing the terrain heightmap for that chunk. Data Structures DSDataCase: Stores integer coordinates (x, y) and a float Value. The coordinates are instantiated as new DSDataCase(x this.SampleLevel, y this.SampleLevel) to map chunk-local grid indices to world coordinates. casesArray: A 2D array casesArray[y, x] storing DSDataCase instances. It is initialized in PrepareChunk at index [0,0] and populated during generation loops. CurrentStepLength: An integer representing the grid spacing between generated points at the current iteration. It halves each step. Parameters WorldSeed: A global integer seed combined with the parent layer ID hash to generate deterministic chunk seeds. sampleLevel: Integer scaling factor applied to local coordinates. CurrentStepLength: Grid spacing at the current iteration. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization (PrepareChunk): Generate the center case at local coordinates [0,0] with a value sampled uniformly from [0.25, 0.75]. 2. Iteration Control (GenerateChunk): Determine step parity using bool isCurrentStepSquare = currentNbStep % 2 == 1. Calculate midStepLength = dataChunkLayer.CurrentStepLength / 2. 3. Square-Step Traversal: If isCurrentStepSquare is true, loop i from 0 to secondStepPower - 1 and j from 0 to CurrentStepPower - 1. Compute yCaseToGenerate = i midStepLength and xCaseToGenerate = midStepLength ((i + 1) % 2) + j dataChunkLayer.CurrentStepLength. Call GenerateCase for each coordinate. 4. Diamond-Step Traversal: If isCurrentStepSquare is false, loop i and j from 0 to CurrentStepPower - 1. Compute yCaseToGenerate = midStepLength + i dataChunkLayer.CurrentStepLength and xCaseToGenerate = midStepLength + j dataChunkLayer.CurrentStepLength. Call GenerateCase for each coordinate. 5. Neighbor Retrieval (GetCasesSummit): Fetch the four surrounding cases based on step parity: Square Step: (x, y-midStepLength), (x+midStepLength, y), (x-midStepLength, y), (x, y+midStepLength). Diamond Step: (x-midStepLength, y-midStepLength), (x+midStepLength, y-midStepLength), (x-midStepLength, y+midStepLength), (x+midStepLength, y+midStepLength). 6. Value Computation (GenerateCaseFrom): Calculate the new case value using the formula below. Return the new DSDataCase instance. Formula The new value V{new} is calculated as: V{new} = \frac{V{TL} + V{TR} + V{BL} + V{BR}}{4} + R \cdot \left(\frac{2}{S + 3}\right)^2 \cdot 0.75 Where: V{TL}, V{TR}, V{BL}, V{BR} are the values of the top-left, top-right, bottom-left, and bottom-right neighbor cases. R \in [-1, 1] is a random perturbation. S is the current iteration step number. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random class DSDataCase: def init(self, x: int, y: int, value: float): self.x = x self.y = y self.value = value def getcaseatlocal(casesarray, x, y, realnbcaseside, extendedchunksmonitor): if x < 0 or x >= realnbcaseside or y < 0 or y >= realnbcaseside: wrappedx = x % realnbcaseside wrappedy = y % realnbcaseside adjacentchunk = extendedchunksmonitor.getchunkcontainerat(wrappedx, wrappedy) if adjacentchunk is None: return None return adjacentchunk.getcase(wrappedx, wrappedy) if casesarray[y][x] is None: return None return casesarray[y][x] def generatechunk(chunksize: int, samplelevel: int, worldseed: int) -> list[list[DSDataCase]]: casesarray = [[None for in range(chunksize)] for in range(chunksize)] realnbcaseside = chunksize extendedchunksmonitor = None # 1. Initialization centervalue = random.uniform(0.25, 0.75) casesarray[0][0] = DSDataCase(x=0 samplelevel, y=0 samplelevel, value=centervalue) currentsteplength = chunksize step = 0 while currentsteplength > 1: iscurrentstepsquare = (step % 2 == 1) midsteplength = currentsteplength // 2 if iscurrentstepsquare: currentsteppower = chunksize // currentsteplength secondsteppower = currentsteppower // 2 if currentsteppower > 1 else 1 for i in range(secondsteppower): for j in range(currentsteppower): ycase = i midsteplength xcase = midsteplength ((i + 1) % 2) + j currentsteplength generatecase(casesarray, xcase, ycase, midsteplength, step, samplelevel, realnbcaseside, extendedchunksmonitor) else: currentsteppower = chunksize // currentsteplength for i in range(currentsteppower): for j in range(currentsteppower): ycase = midsteplength + i currentsteplength xcase = midsteplength + j currentsteplength generatecase(casesarray, xcase, ycase, midsteplength, step, samplelevel, realnbcaseside, extendedchunksmonitor) currentsteplength //= 2 step += 1 return casesarray def generatecase(casesarray, x, y, midsteplength, step, samplelevel, realnbcaseside, extendedchunksmonitor): iscurrentstepsquare = (step % 2 == 1) if iscurrentstepsquare: neighborcoords = [ (x, y - midsteplength), (x + midsteplength, y), (x - midsteplength, y), (x, y + midsteplength) ] else: neighborcoords = [ (x - midsteplength, y - midsteplength), (x + midsteplength, y - midsteplength), (x - midsteplength, y + midsteplength), (x + midsteplength, y + midsteplength) ] neighborvalues = [] for nx, ny in neighborcoords: case = getcaseatlocal(casesarray, nx, ny, realnbcaseside, extendedchunksmonitor) if case is None: return # Skip generation as per GetCasesSummit logic neighborvalues.append(case.value) if len(neighborvalues) != 4: return vtl, vtr, vbl, vbr = neighborvalues r = random.uniform(-1, 1) s = step perturbation = r ((2.0 / (s + 3)) 2) 0.75 newvalue = (vtl + vtr + vbl + vbr) / 4.0 + perturbation casesarray[y][x] = DSDataCase(x=x samplelevel, y=y samplelevel, value=newvalue) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Handling: GetCaseAtLocal checks if x < 0 or x >= realNbCaseSide (and same for y). If out of bounds, it wraps coordinates using realNbCaseSide and attempts to fetch from adjacent chunks via ExtendedChunksMonitor.GetChunkContainerAt. If the adjacent chunk is null or the final lookup fails, it returns null, causing GetCasesSummit to return false and skip generation for that point. Precision: The random perturbation scales with (S+3)^{-2}. For large S, the perturbation becomes very small, potentially leading to flat terrain if floating-point precision is insufficient. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Asynchronous chunk generation allows for infinite world generation without precomputing the entire map. Deterministic seeding ensures consistency. Limitations: Boundary handling between chunks requires complex neighbor fetching logic. The specific scaling factor (2/(S+3))^2 is non-standard compared to the typical 2^{-H \cdot S} fractal noise, potentially affecting the fractal dimension. The method is a procedural world generation technique that recursively subdivides a 2D grid into squares and diamonds. The specific implementation described here is from an unofficial project "Deneyr/WorldGeneration" used in a Pokemon game core to generate chunks of a procedural world. It does not manage game logic or rendering, its only purpose is to generate world chunks asynchronously in a given area.
