name: Asymmetric Wing Stroke
head: Asymmetric Swim Cycle, Non-sinusoidal Flapping
body: The Asymmetric Wing Stroke is a time-dependent function p(t) that generates non-sinusoidal flapping or swimming motions for procedural volume rendering. It avoids the mechanical appearance of symmetric sine waves by mimicking biological "snap and coast" kinematics, where the power stroke is rapid and the recovery stroke is slow. It builds on Sine-based procedural voxel generation and relates to Procedural Tree Voxel Generation and Simple Heightmap Voxel Generation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Normalized cycle time x \in [0, 1). Output: Scalar amplitude p(x) \in [0, 1]. Parameters: Duty cycle threshold \tau: 0.28 for jellyfish contraction/glide; 0.36 for butterfly downstroke/recovery. FLAPHZ: Wingbeat frequency in Hertz. Value: 1.35. TIPLAG: Phase delay per unit of span. Value: 0.135. Algorithm: 1. Normalize absolute time t{\text{abs}} to 0, 1) via x = t{\text{abs}} \pmod 1. 2. If x < \tau, compute u = x / \tau and p(x) = \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 1.0, u). 3. If x \ge \tau, compute u = (x - \tau) / (1.0 - \tau) and p(x) = 1.0 - \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 1.0, u). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def asymmetricstroke(x, threshold): x = x % 1.0 if x < threshold: progress = x / threshold return smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, progress) else: progress = (x - threshold) / (1.0 - threshold) return 1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, progress) Application to Deformation: The jellyfish model drives radius R and height H in opposite directions: R = 1.00 + 0.13\,p(t) and H = 0.80 - 0.22\,p(t). The butterfly model drives the flap angle with a span-dependent phase lag: \text{phase} = t \cdot \text{FLAP\HZ} + \text{phase\offset} - \text{span} \cdot \text{TIP\LAG}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The smoothstep function guarantees C^1 continuity at \tau and the cycle boundaries, but C^2 is discontinuous, which may affect high-order shading derivatives. The modulo operation handles cycle wrap-around safely without division by zero. Not given in the sources. The technique originates from [GLSL shader implementations for procedural animation. The "Asymmetric Swim Cycle" (28% contraction, 72% glide) was documented for jellyfish simulation to contrast with the equal-time symmetry of sine waves. The "Asymmetric Wing Stroke" (36% downstroke, 64% recovery) was applied to butterfly flapping to replicate quick power strokes and slower recoveries. Both methods are used in procedural voxel and raymarched rendering to animate static distance fields through time-dependent coefficient modulation. el-bakkali/manim-glsl-jellyfish, https://github.com/el-bakkali/manim-glsl-jellyfish, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) el-bakkali/manim-glsl-butterflies, https://github.com/el-bakkali/manim-glsl-butterflies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Density Ramp with Noise
head: ramp-confined turbulence gas, steam_slab1 confined gas modeling
body: Spherical Density Ramp with Noise is a procedural volume density function that confines a gas (such as steam or smoke) to a spherical slab region using a spherical distance ramp and an offset table, simulating steam rising from a source. Inputs: pnt: 3D point in solid texture space (used for turbulence evaluation). pntworld: 3D point in world space (used for distance calculation). density: Initial density value (output parameter, modified in place). parms: Array of floating-point parameters. parms[1] is the scaling factor for the power function, parms[2] is the exponent, and parms[3] is the multiplier for the random offset table. vol: Volume structure containing shape information. vol.shape.center is the 3D center point of the volume slab, and vol.shape.invradsq.y is the inverse squared radius of the slab (1/r^2). Outputs: density: The final computed density value. Data Structures: 1. powtable: Array of size POWTABLESIZE containing precomputed values mapping turbulence intensity to base density. 2. ramp: Array of size RAMPSIZE containing precomputed cosine falloff values. 3. offset: Array of size OFFSETSIZE containing precomputed random numbers used to add spatial variation to the density falloff. Initialization (Precomputed once per image): The tables are initialized using a static flag calcd to ensure they are computed only once. 1. Pow Table: For i from POWTABLESIZE - 1 down to 0: \text{pow\table}[i] = \left( \frac{i}{\text{POW\TABLE\SIZE} - 1} \times \text{parms}[1] \times 2.0 \right)^{\text{parms}[2]} 2. Ramp Table: For i from 0 to RAMPSIZE - 1: \text{dist} = \frac{i}{\text{RAMP\SIZE} - 1.0} \text{ramp}[i] = \frac{\cos(\text{dist} \times \pi) + 1.0}{2.0} Algorithm Steps: 1. Evaluate Base Turbulence: Calculate the turbulence value at the texture point: \text{turb} = \text{fast\turbulence}(\text{pnt}). Map this to a base density using the power table. The index is calculated as: \text{idx} = \lfloor \text{turb} \times 0.5 \times (\text{POW\TABLE\SIZE} - 1) \rfloor. The density is set to \text{pow\table}[\text{idx}]. 2. Calculate Spherical Distance Factor: Compute the vector from the volume center to the world point: \text{diff} = \text{pnt\world} - \text{vol.shape.center}. Compute the squared distance: \text{dist\sq} = \text{diff} \cdot \text{diff}. Scale by the inverse squared radius to get a normalized distance factor: \text{density\max} = \text{dist\sq} \times \text{vol.shape.inv\rad\sq.y}. 3. Add Spatial Noise Offset: Calculate an index into the offset table based on the sum of the texture point coordinates: \text{indx} = \lfloor (\text{pnt}.x + \text{pnt}.y + \text{pnt}.z) \times 100 \rfloor \ \& \ (\text{OFFSET\SIZE} - 1). Add the noise offset scaled by parms[3]: \text{density\max} += \text{parms}[3] \times \text{offset}[\text{indx}]. 4. Apply Cosine Ramp Falloff: If densitymax exceeds the threshold 0.25 (25% from center), compute the ramp index: i = \lfloor (\text{density\max} - 0.25) \times \frac{4}{3} \times \text{RAMP\SIZE} \rfloor. Clamp i to the valid range: i = \min(i, \text{RAMP\SIZE} - 1). Retrieve the ramp value: \text{ramp\val} = \text{ramp}[i]. Multiply the density by this factor: \text{density} = \text{ramp\val}. If densitymax is less than 0.25, the ramp is skipped and the base density remains unchanged. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Initialize tables if not done if not initialized: for i in range(POWTABLESIZE - 1, -1, -1): t = (i / (POWTABLESIZE - 1)) parms[1] 2.0 powtable[i] = t parms[2] for i in range(RAMPSIZE): dist = i / (RAMPSIZE - 1.0) ramp[i] = (math.cos(dist math.pi) + 1.0) / 2.0 # offset table must be populated with precomputed random values # Not given in the sources. initialized = True # 2. Evaluate base turbulence # fastturbulence(pnt) is not defined in the sources. turb = 0.0 idx = int(turb 0.5 (POWTABLESIZE - 1)) # Clamp idx to table bounds idx = max(0, min(idx, POWTABLESIZE - 1)) density = powtable[idx] # 3. Calculate spherical distance factor diffx = pntworld.x - vol.shape.center.x diffy = pntworld.y - vol.shape.center.y diffz = pntworld.z - vol.shape.center.z distsq = diffx diffx + diffy diffy + diffz diffz densitymax = distsq vol.shape.invradsq.y # 4. Add spatial noise offset sumcoords = pnt.x + pnt.y + pnt.z indx = int(sumcoords 100) & (OFFSETSIZE - 1) densitymax += parms[3] offset[indx] # 5. Apply cosine ramp falloff if densitymax >= 0.25: i = int((densitymax - 0.25) (4.0 / 3.0) RAMPSIZE) if i >= RAMPSIZE: i = RAMPSIZE - 1 density = ramp[i] return density Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The offset table index uses integer truncation of a scaled coordinate sum, which can cause discontinuities at integer boundaries if the offset table lacks smoothness. The ramp only activates for densitymax >= 0.25. POWTABLESIZE, RAMPSIZE, and OFFSETSIZE must be defined constants. The Vertical Exponential Density Ramp is a procedural density modulation technique used to simulate natural phenomena like rising steam or smoke by attenuating density as a function of vertical height. It builds on Spherical Density Ramp with Noise by adding a vertical falloff, solving the problem of volumetric objects appearing as solid, unnatural columns by ensuring density decays to zero above a certain altitude. It differs from generic noise textures by applying a specific mathematical ramp based on world-space Y coordinates rather than procedural pattern evaluation. NoiseTexture evaluates a volumetric color and density field by combining radial/vertical fading with double-warping via Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) and sinusoidal noise modulation. It differs from simple procedural noise by applying spatial warping to the noise domain and modulating the result with a sine wave, creating structured, organic patterns suitable for volumetric effects like smoke or clouds. If ZoneIndex is (0, 0, -1), calculate radial falloff: r = \sqrt{P.X^2 + P.Y^2 + P.Z^2}. Calculate t = 1 - \exp(-r^2 / (\text{MaxR} \times 100)) where \text{MaxR} = 1000. Return \text{Density} \times t. If IsCaveLayerZone(ZoneIndex.Z) is true, the function currently returns Density (the cave layer call is commented out). Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently confines gas to a specific volume without complex boundary checks. The noise offset breaks radial symmetry, making the gas look more natural than a pure cosine falloff. Limitations: The confinement is spherical/slab-based, not suitable for arbitrary shapes. When to use: Simulating steam, smoke, or gas clouds originating from a central point or slab. When not to use: When the volume shape is not roughly spherical or slab-like, or when complex internal structure requires more than a simple radial falloff. The method originates from David Ebert's work on procedural modeling of gases and fluids, specifically described in "Procedural Modeling, Animation, and Rendering of Gases, Fluids, and Textures". It was designed to correct the unnatural appearance of basic turbulence-based gases by confining them to a slab and adding a rising/falloff characteristic. The "steamslab1" name reflects its specific application to simulating steam rising from a cup. name: Vertical Exponential Density Ramp
body: The Vertical Exponential Density Ramp is a procedural density modulation technique that attenuates volumetric density as a function of vertical height to simulate rising steam or smoke. It builds on Spherical Density Ramp with Noise by adding a vertical falloff, preventing volumetric objects from appearing as solid columns by ensuring density decays to zero above a specific altitude. It differs from generic noise textures by applying a deterministic mathematical ramp based on world-space Y coordinates rather than procedural pattern evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: World-space point pntworld, base density value (from parent noise/ramp), volume shape metadata vol.shape (containing center and invrad), noise offset array offset, and parameter array parms. Output: Modulated density. Data Structures: vol.shape: Contains center (3D vector) and invrad (3D vector representing inverse bounding radius/scale). offset: Array of noise offsets indexed by indx. parms: Array of parameters, specifically parms[1]. Steps: 1. Calculate the vertical distance from the volume center: dist = pnt\world.y - vol.shape.center.y 2. If dist > 0.0, normalize the distance using the noise offset and inverse vertical radius: dist = (dist + offset[indx] \times 0.1) \times vol.shape.inv\rad.y 3. If dist > 0.05, apply the exponential ramp-off: a. Calculate intermediate offset: offset2 = (dist - 0.05) \times 1.111111 b. Apply exponential decay function: offset2 = 1 - \frac{\exp(offset2) - 1.0}{1.718282} c. Scale by parameter: offset2 = offset2 \times parms[1] d. Multiply base density: density = density \times offset2 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def verticalexponentialdensityramp(pntworld, density, volshape, offset, indx, parms): # Step 1: Vertical distance from center dist = pntworld.y - volshape.center.y # Step 2: Normalize if above center if dist > 0.0: dist = (dist + offset[indx] 0.1) volshape.invrad.y # Step 3: Exponential ramp off if above threshold if dist > 0.05: offset2 = (dist - 0.05) 1.111111 offset2 = 1.0 - (math.exp(offset2) - 1.0) / 1.718282 offset2 = parms[1] density = offset2 return density Parameters: vol.shape.invrad.y: Inverse radius related to vertical scaling. parms[1]: Scaling factor for the ramp intensity. offset[indx]: Noise offset value. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If dist <= 0.0, the density remains unchanged (no ramp applied below the center). If 0.0 < dist <= 0.05 (after normalization), the density remains unchanged. The constant 1.718282 approximates e - 1 and serves as the divisor in the exponential term. The constant 1.111111 scales the distance above the 0.05 threshold. The source contains a typo density = offset; which is corrected to density = offset2 in the implementation. A method for analytically integrating density in a medium where particle density decreases exponentially in a normalized direction \mathbf{n}, offset by \mathbf{o}. It is chosen when closed-form integration of participating media is required for real-time rendering. It differs from the Vertical Exponential Density Ramp by providing an integral over a ray segment rather than a point-wise density modulation. Definition: A medium where density \varrho(\mathbf{x}') decreases exponentially along direction \mathbf{n} offset by \mathbf{o}. Formula: \varrho(\mathbf{x}') = \varrho' \cdot \exp(-b \cdot \langle \mathbf{x}' - \mathbf{o}, \mathbf{n} \rangle) where \varrho' \ge 0 is density factor, b > 0 is exponential parameter, \mathbf{n} is normalized direction, \mathbf{o} is offset, and \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle is inner product. Integrated Density: For a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{c} + t \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega} with length D, if \langle \boldsymbol{\omega}, \mathbf{n} \rangle \neq 0: P(\mathbf{x}{2D}) = \frac{\varrho'}{b \cdot \langle \boldsymbol{\omega}, \mathbf{n} \rangle} \cdot \exp(-b \cdot \langle \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{o}, \mathbf{n} \rangle) \cdot (1 - \exp(-b \cdot D \cdot \langle \boldsymbol{\omega}, \mathbf{n} \rangle)) If \langle \boldsymbol{\omega}, \mathbf{n} \rangle = 0, the integral is solved directly (linear accumulation). Parameters: b > 0 (exponential parameter), \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3, \|\mathbf{n}\|=1 (direction), \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (offset). Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, involving basic arithmetic and one exponential function evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only local variables and access to input parameters. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces natural-looking falloff for rising gases/steam; computationally inexpensive. Limitations: Only affects density above the volume center; requires tuning of parms[1] and thresholds for different scales. When to use: Simulating steam, smoke, or atmospheric layers where density naturally decreases with height. When not to use: When uniform density or different falloff shapes (e.g., spherical) are required. The Vertical Exponential Density Ramp was introduced by David Ebert in the context of procedural modeling and animation of gases and fluids. It is part of a suite of procedural techniques designed to create convincing steam and smoke effects without explicit fluid simulation. The method uses an exponential function to ramp off density as the gas rises, enhancing realism. name: NoiseTexture value evaluation
head: NoiseTexture
body:
NoiseTexture evaluates a volumetric color and density field by combining radial/vertical fading with double-warping via Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) and sinusoidal noise modulation. It differs from simple procedural noise by applying spatial warping to the noise domain and modulating the result with a sine wave, creating structured, organic patterns suitable for volumetric effects like smoke or clouds. Inputs: point: The 3D coordinate in world space to evaluate. minbound, maxbound: The bounding box of the volume. scale: A scaling factor for the noise frequency. color: An RGB color structure defining the base color. noise: A noise object providing FBM evaluation. Outputs: RGB: The final color value at the point. If the point is outside the faded volume, returns RGB(0,0,0). Data Structures: RGB: Structure with fields r, g, b (floating point values, typically 0.0–1.0). Vector3: 3D vector with components x, y, z. Steps: 1. Normalize Coordinates: Map the input point to the unit cube [0,1]^3 using the bounding box bounds: u =  rac{point.x - min ound.x}{max ound.x - min ound.x} v =  rac{point.y - min ound.y}{max ound.y - min ound.y} w =  rac{point.z - min ound.z}{max ound.z - min ound.z} 2. Compute Horizontal Distance: Calculate the normalized horizontal distance from the vertical center axis (u=0.5, w=0.5): dist\xz = \sqrt{(u - 0.5)^2 + (w - 0.5)^2} 	imes 2.0 3. Compute Height-Dependent Radius: Determine the radius of the volume at the current height v: radius\at\height = 0.1 + 0.9 	imes v 4. Compute Horizontal Fade: Apply a smoothstep fade based on the horizontal distance relative to the height-dependent radius: horizontal ade = 	ext{smoothstep}(radius\at\height, radius\at\height 	imes 0.4, dist\xz) 5. Compute Vertical Fade: Apply a smoothstep fade based on height v, fading out from the top: vertical ade = 	ext{smoothstep}(1.0, 0.4, v) 6. Combine Fades: Multiply the horizontal and vertical fades. If the combined fade is negligible, return black: fade = horizontal ade 	imes vertical ade If fade < 0.001, return RGB(0,0,0). 7. First Warp: Apply the first layer of FBM warping to the point: warp1 = 	ext{vector bm}(noise, point 	imes scale 	imes 0.5, 2) warped\p1 = point + warp1 	imes 2.0 8. Second Warp: Apply the second layer of FBM warping using the result of the first warp: warp2 = 	ext{vector bm}(noise, warped\p1 	imes scale 	imes 1.5, 2) deeply\warped\p = warped\p1 + warp2 	imes 1.0 9. Compute Noise Value: Evaluate a sinusoidal noise function using the deeply warped point: n = 0.5 	imes (1.0 + \sin(scale 	imes deeply\warped\p.z + 10.0 	imes noise.	ext{fbm}(deeply\warped\p, 3))) 10. Final Output: Apply the fade, clamp the result to [0,1], and scale by the base color: final
 = 	ext{clamp}(n 	imes fade, 0.0, 1.0) Return RGB(color.r 	imes final
, color.g 	imes final
, color.b 	imes final
). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class RGB: def init(self, r, g, b): self.r = r self.g = g self.b = b class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def mul(self, s): return Vector3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def add(self, other): return Vector3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def fbm(noise, p, octaves): value = 0.0 amplitude = 1.0 frequency = 1.0 for in range(octaves): value += amplitude noise.evaluate(p frequency) amplitude = 0.5 frequency = 2.0 return value def vectorfbm(noise, p, octaves): return Vector3(fbm(noise, p, octaves), fbm(noise, p, octaves), fbm(noise, p, octaves)) def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = clamp((x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0), 0.0, 1.0) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def clamp(x, minval, maxval): if x < minval: return minval if x > maxval: return maxval return x def evaluatenoisetexture(point, minbound, maxbound, scale, color, noise): u = (point.x - minbound.x) / (maxbound.x - minbound.x) v = (point.y - minbound.y) / (maxbound.y - minbound.y) w = (point.z - minbound.z) / (maxbound.z - minbound.z) distxz = math.sqrt((u - 0.5)2 + (w - 0.5)2) 2.0 radiusatheight = 0.1 + 0.9 v horizontalfade = smoothstep(radiusatheight, radiusatheight 0.4, distxz) verticalfade = smoothstep(1.0, 0.4, v) fade = horizontalfade verticalfade if fade < 0.001: return RGB(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) warp1 = vectorfbm(noise, point scale 0.5, 2) warpedp1 = point + warp1 2.0 warp2 = vectorfbm(noise, warpedp1 scale 1.5, 2) deeplywarpedp = warpedp1 + warp2 1.0 fbmval = fbm(noise, deeplywarpedp, 3) n = 0.5 (1.0 + math.sin(scale deeplywarpedp.z + 10.0 fbmval)) finaln = clamp(n fade, 0.0, 1.0) return RGB(color.r finaln, color.g finaln, color.b finaln) Parameters: scale: Frequency multiplier. Not given in the sources. noise: Noise implementation providing vectorfbm (3D output, 2 octaves) and fbm (scalar output, 3 octaves). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If maxbound equals minbound in any dimension, normalization fails. Implementers should check for zero-length bounds and return a default value or error. Precision: The use of sin and multiple FBM evaluations can accumulate floating-point errors. Standard double precision is recommended. Boundary Conditions: The normalization assumes the point is within the bounding box. Points outside may produce negative or >1 coordinates, affecting the fade logic. Clamping normalized coordinates to [0,1] before fade calculation may be necessary depending on desired behavior. Time Complexity: O(1) per evaluation, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations and two FBM evaluations with fixed octave counts (2 and 3). Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only local variables. Performance: Fast enough for real-time ray marching or path tracing, provided the underlying noise function is efficient. Strengths: Produces visually complex, organic structures with minimal computational cost compared to higher-octave FBM. The fading ensures smooth transitions at volume boundaries. Limitations: The fixed warping and sine modulation may not adapt to scene-specific features. Performance depends on the efficiency of the vectorfbm and fbm implementations. When to Use: Suitable for procedural volumetric effects like smoke, clouds, or fire where structured noise patterns are desired. When Not to Use: Not suitable for data-driven volumes or when high-frequency detail is required without increasing octave counts. The method originates from the codebase of TakTikFR. It combines standard procedural noise techniques with specific fading and warping strategies for custom volumetric rendering. name: Mandelbulb Fractal Generation
head: Mandelbulb
body: Generates a 3D fractal by iteratively applying a polar coordinate power transformation to a complex 3D point. It differs from its siblings by using continuous polar coordinate exponentiation rather than discrete modulo arithmetic (Menger Sponge) or simple polynomial mappings (Bristorbrot). Inputs: Query point \mathbf{p}, maximum iterations N{max}, power exponent P, escape radius R{max}. Outputs: Boolean indicating if the point is inside the fractal (bounded orbit). Data Structures: \mathbf{z}: Current 3D point (float3). \mathbf{p}{in}: Original query point (float3). r, \theta, \phi: Polar coordinates of \mathbf{z} (float). Steps: 1. Initialize \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{p}{in} and z{dist} = \|\mathbf{z}\|^2. 2. Loop i from 0 to N{max}-1. 3. Convert \mathbf{z} to spherical coordinates (r, \theta, \phi). 4. Apply power transformation: r{new} = r^P, \theta{new} = \theta \times P, \phi{new} = \phi \times P. 5. Convert back to Cartesian coordinates \mathbf{z}{new}: \mathbf{z}{new}.x = r{new} \sin(\theta{new}) \cos(\phi{new}), \mathbf{z}{new}.y = r{new} \sin(\phi{new}) \sin(\theta{new}), \mathbf{z}{new}.z = r{new} \cos(\theta{new}). 6. Update \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{z}{new} + \mathbf{p}{in}. 7. Update z{dist} = \|\mathbf{z}\|^2. If z{dist} > R{max}, break loop (escape). 8. If loop completes all N{max} iterations without escaping, the point is inside the fractal. Parameters: P = 8.0 (default). N{max} = 5 (default). R{max} = 20 (labeled maxdistance in source code). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lengthsq(v): return v.x v.x + v.y v.y + v.z v.z def mandelbulb(pin, maxiterations=5, power=8.0, maxdistance=20.0): z = pin zdistsq = lengthsq(z) for i in range(maxiterations): r = sqrt(zdistsq) theta = acos(z.z / r) if r > 0 else 0.0 phi = atan2(z.y, z.x) zr = pow(r, power) theta = power phi = power znewx = sin(theta) cos(phi) zr znewy = sin(phi) sin(theta) zr znewz = cos(theta) zr z.x = znewx + pin.x z.y = znewy + pin.y z.z = znewz + pin.z zdistsq = lengthsq(z) if zdistsq > maxdistance: return False return True Generates a 3D fractal using a specific iterative polynomial mapping in Cartesian coordinates. It computes an escape-time field for voxel rendering by iterating a fixed 3D polynomial and checking against a distance threshold. Choose it when a discrete algebraic iteration rule without polar transformations is required. Generates a 3D voxel grid or Signed Distance Field (SDF) representing a Menger sponge by iteratively dividing space into 3 \times 3 \times 3 subcubes and removing those where two or more coordinates fall into the middle third. It differs from its parent Mandelbulb Fractal Generation, which uses polar coordinate power transformations, by relying on discrete coordinate modulo arithmetic and axis-aligned box subtraction. Choose it for exact fractal boundaries without iterative escape-time checks. A fractal distance function based on quaternion iteration, similar to Mandelbrot sets but in 3D. Steps: 1. Initialize v = \text{vec4}(p, 0.0) and d = \text{vec4}(1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0). 2. Loop n from 1 to ITERATIONS-1: Update d = 2.0 \times \text{vec4}(v.x \cdot d.x - \text{dot}(v.xzw, d.yzw), v.x \cdot d.yzw + d.x \cdot v.yzw + \text{cross}(v.yzw, d.yzw)). Update v = \text{vec4}(v.x^2 - \text{dot}(v.yzw, v.yzw), \text{vec3}(2.0 \cdot v.x \cdot v.yzw)) + c. 3. Check divergence: if \text{dot}(v, v) > 10.0, break loop. Formula: Final distance: 0.5 \times r \times \log(r) / \|d\| where r = \|v\|. Parameters: ITERATIONS = 5; c = \text{vec4}(0.18, 0.88, 0.24, 0.16). Choose it when a quaternion-based distance estimator for ray marching is needed. Time complexity is O(N{max}) per voxel evaluation, with O(1) memory complexity. Performance scales linearly with iteration count, and the method is computationally intensive due to trigonometric functions and power operations. Measured performance on specific hardware, resolution, and scenes is Not given in the sources. Strengths include precise procedural generation of complex 3D topology. Limitations include high computational cost per voxel and sensitivity to iteration bounds. It is suitable for offline procedural geometry generation and voxel art, but not recommended for real-time ray marching without optimization. The Mandelbulb is a 3D analogue of the Mandelbrot set, constructed using polar coordinate transformations. It is used in procedural geometry generation and voxel art. jtomori/holographicfractals, https://github.com/jtomori/holographicfractals, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, https://github.com/nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Bristorbrot Fractal Generation
head: Bristorbrot
body: Bristorbrot is a 3D fractal generation method that produces a volumetric structure using a specific iterative polynomial mapping in Cartesian coordinates. It differs from the Mandelbulb [3327-mandelbulb-fractal-generation.md] by employing a distinct algebraic iteration rule that does not rely on polar coordinate power transformations. Inputs: A 3D point p (voxel center or ray origin), maxiterations (integer), maxdistance (float). Outputs: An integer indicating the iteration count at which the point escapes, or maxiterations if the point remains inside the set. Data Structures: point3d: A structure containing three floating-point fields: x, y, z. float: Standard 32-bit or 64-bit floating-point number. Parameters: maxiterations: Default 30. maxdistance: Default 200. Steps: 1. Initialize the iteration state z to the input point p{in}: z = p{in}. 2. Initialize the squared distance accumulator z{dist}: z{dist} = z.x^2 + z.y^2 + z.z^2. 3. Loop i from 0 to maxiterations - 1: a. Compute the new coordinates p{new} based on the current z: p{new}.x = z.x^2 - z.y^2 - z.z^2 p{new}.y = z.y \cdot (2.0 \cdot z.x - z.z) p{new}.z = z.z \cdot (2.0 \cdot z.x + z.y). b. Update z by adding the input point p{in} to the new coordinates: z = p{new} + p{in}. c. Update the squared distance: z{dist} = z.x^2 + z.y^2 + z.z^2. d. Check for escape: If z{dist} > \text{max\distance}, break the loop. 4. If the loop completes all maxiterations without breaking, the point is considered part of the fractal set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bristorbrot(pin, maxiterations=30, maxdistance=200): z = pin zdist = z.x2 + z.y2 + z.z2 for i in range(maxiterations): # Compute new coordinates newx = z.x2 - z.y2 - z.z2 newy = z.y (2.0 z.x - z.z) newz = z.z (2.0 z.x + z.y) # Update z = newp + pin z.x = newx + pin.x z.y = newy + pin.y z.z = newz + pin.z # Update distance zdist = z.x2 + z.y2 + z.z2 # Check escape if zdist > maxdistance: return i return maxiterations Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If p{in} is (0,0,0), z remains (0,0,0) and the point is always inside. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. A fractal distance function representing a knot shape, constructed by iterating and transforming a base curve. It differs from Bristorbrot by using iterative angular transformations and vector offsets to compute a distance field rather than a Cartesian polynomial mapping. Choose this when a knotted topology is required. Definition: Generates a distance field for a knot fractal using iterative angular transformations. Steps: 1. Initialize r = length(p.xz), ang = atan(p.z, p.x), y = p.y, d = HUGEVAL. 2. Loop n from 0 to ITERATIONS - 1: a. Create p = vec3(r, y, ang + 2.0 PI float(n)). b. Subtract offset.z from p.x. c. Calculate ra = (p.z + time) clamp.x / clamp.z and raz = p.z clamp.y / clamp.z. d. Update distance d = min(d, length(p.xy - vec2(offset.ycos(ra)+offset.z, offset.ysin(raz)+offset.z)) - offset.x). Parameters: ITERATIONS: 3. offset: vec3(0.07, 0.29, 0.43). clamp: vec3(-2.0, -4.0, 3.0). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. name: Mandelbulb Isosurface Extraction via Marching Cubes
head: Mandelbulb Mesh Generation
body: This method generates a 3D triangular mesh of the Mandelbulb fractal by evaluating a scalar field function on a 3D voxel grid and extracting the isosurface using the marching cubes algorithm. It differs from ray-traced Mandelbulb rendering by producing a static, manipulable polygonal mesh suitable for standard graphics pipelines, rather than a per-pixel ray-marched image. Inputs: Grid domain: Cube [-1.2, 1.2] \times [-1.2, 1.2] \times [-1.2, 1.2]. Isosurface level: 0.005. Iteration count: 24. Grid resolution: Not given in the sources. Outputs: A triangular mesh representing the Mandelbulb surface. Data Structures: A 3D array of scalar values of size (N+1) \times (N+1) \times (N+1), where each vertex stores the result of mandelbulb(x, y, z) for the corresponding grid point. Standard marching cubes lookup tables for vertex interpolation and triangle topology. Scalar Field Function: The scalar field V(x0, y0, z0) is computed by iterating a polynomial mapping in Cartesian coordinates. The function returns a positive value if the point escapes the bounded region, and 0.0 if it remains bounded within the iteration limit. 1. Initialize x = x0, y = y0, z = z0, and derivative accumulator dr = 1.0. 2. For i from 0 to 23: a. Calculate squared radius: r^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2. b. If r^2 > 4: i. Return escape time value: V = 0.25 \cdot \sqrt{r^2} \cdot \log(r^2) / dr. c. Calculate r^6 = (r^2)^3. d. Update derivative: dr = 8.0 \cdot r^6 \cdot \sqrt{r^2} \cdot dr + 1.0. e. Calculate angles: \theta = 8.0 \cdot \text{atan2}(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}, z). \phi = 8.0 \cdot \text{atan2}(y, x). f. Calculate r^8 = r^6 \cdot r^2. g. Update position: x = r^8 \cos(\phi) \sin(\theta) + x0. y = r^8 \sin(\phi) \sin(\theta) + y0. z = r^8 \cos(\theta) + z0. 3. If the loop completes without escaping, return 0.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def mandelbulbscalarfield(x0: float, y0: float, z0: float) -> float: x, y, z = x0, y0, z0 dr = 1.0 for in range(24): r2 = xx + yy + zz if r2 > 4.0: return 0.25 math.sqrt(r2) math.log(r2) / dr r6 = r2 r2 r2 dr = 8.0 r6 math.sqrt(r2) dr + 1.0 theta = 8.0 math.atan2(math.sqrt(xx + yy), z) phi = 8.0 math.atan2(y, x) r8 = r6 r2 x = r8 math.cos(phi) math.sin(theta) + x0 y = r8 math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta) + y0 z = r8 math.cos(theta) + z0 return 0.0 def interpolateedge(p1, p2, v1, v2, isolevel): if abs(v2 - v1) < 1e-10: return (p1 + p2) 0.5 t = (isolevel - v1) / (v2 - v1) return p1 + t (p2 - p1) def marchingcubes(scalarfield: list, isolevel: float) -> list: # Standard Marching Cubes algorithm implementation # 1. Iterate over all voxels in the grid. # 2. For each voxel, determine the cell configuration index from the 8 vertex signs. # 3. Lookup the corresponding triangle edge pairs from the standard MC table. # 4. Interpolate vertex positions on the intersected edges using interpolateedge. # 5. Collect triangles and return the mesh. return [] Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. name: Menger Sponge Fractal Generation
head: Fractal sponge voxelization, Menger Sponge Fractal, Menger sponge procedural generation, SDF Menger Sponge
body: Generates a 3D representation of a Menger sponge, either as a voxel grid or a Signed Distance Field (SDF), by iteratively subdividing space into 3 \times 3 \times 3 subcubes and removing those where two or more coordinates fall into the middle third. It differs from its parent Mandelbulb Fractal Generation, which applies polar coordinate power transformations, by using discrete coordinate modulo arithmetic and axis-aligned box subtraction. Inputs: p: 3D point (x, y, z) in world space. ITERATIONS: Integer number of fractal iterations (typically 3). Outputs: d: Signed distance from p to the Menger sponge surface. filled: Boolean indicating if p is inside the solid material (voxel method). Data Structures: Stateless procedural computation; no persistent data structures are required. Steps: 1. Initialize distance d to the distance of p to the initial bounding box: d = \text{sdBox}(p, \vec{1.0}). 2. Initialize scale factor s = 1.0. 3. Loop m from 0 to ITERATIONS - 1: a. Fold space into the first octant: p \leftarrow |p| - 1.0. b. Calculate local coordinate: a = \text{mod}(p \cdot s, 2.0) - 1.0. c. Update scale: s \leftarrow s \cdot 3.0. d. Calculate absolute local coordinate: r = |1.0 - 3.0 \cdot |a||. e. Calculate corner distances: da = \max(rx, ry), db = \max(ry, rz), dc = \max(rz, rx). f. Calculate distance contribution: c = (\min(da, db, dc) - 1.0) / s. g. Update global distance: d = \max(d, c). 4. For voxel occupancy tracking, initialize filled = true. For each iteration k, evaluate \lfloor px / 3^k \rfloor \bmod 3 = 1 \lor \lfloor py / 3^k \rfloor \bmod 3 = 1 \lor \lfloor pz / 3^k \rfloor \bmod 3 = 1. Sum the boolean results; if sum > 1, set filled = false and break. 5. Return d for SDF ray marching, or filled with color/alpha for voxel traversal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mengerspongesdf(p, iterations=3): """ Computes the Signed Distance Field for a Menger Sponge. p: vec3, point in space iterations: int, number of recursive steps Returns: float, signed distance """ # Initialize distance to the bounding box (half-extent 1.0) d = max(max(abs(p.x) - 1.0, abs(p.y) - 1.0), abs(p.z) - 1.0) s = 1.0 for in range(iterations): # Fold space into the first octant for symmetry p = abs(p) - 1.0 # Calculate local coordinate in the 3x3x3 grid a = ((p s) % 2.0) - 1.0 # Update scale for next iteration s = 3.0 # r = abs(1.0 - 3.0 abs(a)) r = abs(1.0 - 3.0 abs(a)) # Calculate corner distances da = max(r.x, r.y) db = max(r.y, r.z) dc = max(r.z, r.x) # Calculate distance contribution c = (min(da, min(db, dc)) - 1.0) / s # Update distance d = max(d, c) return d Parameters: ITERATIONS: Number of fractal iterations. Typical value: 3. Edge Cases: Precision: Floating point modulo operations can accumulate errors at high iteration counts. Boundaries: Points exactly on the boundary of removed cubes may have distance 0. Degenerate Input: High iteration counts increase computational cost linearly with ITERATIONS. Generates a 3D fractal by iteratively applying a polar coordinate power transformation to a complex 3D point. Generates a 3D fractal using a different iterative formula. Time Complexity: O(ITERATIONS) per evaluation step. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Simple to implement, no pre-computed data structures required, suitable for real-time ray marching. Limitations: High iteration counts lead to visual artifacts due to floating point precision. When to use: When a procedural, infinite-resolution fractal is needed without storing large voxel grids. When not to use: When exact boolean operations or CSG with other primitives are required, as the SDF is an approximation. The Menger sponge is a classic fractal curve first described by Karl Menger in 1926. It is a 3D generalization of the Cantor set and the Sierpinski carpet. name: Volumetric Density Generation
head: Heterogeneous Volume Density Generation, Procedural Density Generation via Noise and Thresholding, getDensity
body: Generates a patchy volumetric density field from procedural noise by applying a power function and a threshold to create sparse structures. It differs from its parent Specific Procedural Patterns and Applications by explicitly combining Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) with non-linear remapping and hard cutoffs. Inputs: pos: 3D query position vector \mathbf{P}. basedensity: Scalar multiplier for the final density (default 0.8). fbmscale: Frequency scale for the noise function (default 3.0). fbmoctaves: Number of octaves for FBM (default 2). powerexponent: Exponent for the power function (default 2.5). threshold: Density cutoff value (default 0.15). Outputs: density: Clamped scalar density value in [0, 1]. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute Noise: Evaluate the FBM noise at the query position with the specified scale and octaves: n = \text{fbm}(\mathbf{P}, \text{fbm\scale}, \text{fbm\octaves}) 2. Remap: Map the noise value from [-1, 1] to [0, 1]: n{\text{remapped}} = n \cdot 0.5 + 0.5 3. Power Function: Apply a power function to suppress low values and create sparse regions near zero: d = n{\text{remapped}}^{\text{power\exponent}} 4. Threshold: If the density is below the threshold, set it to zero: \text{if } d < \text{threshold}: d = 0.0 5. Scale: Multiply by the base density: d = d \cdot \text{base\density} 6. Clamp: Clamp the result to [0, 1]: \text{density} = \max(0.0, \min(1.0, d)) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getdensity(pos, basedensity=0.8, fbmscale=3.0, fbmoctaves=2, powerexponent=2.5, threshold=0.15): # Standard FBM implementation def fbm(p, scale, octaves): value = 0.0 amplitude = 1.0 frequency = 1.0 for in range(octaves): # basenoise uses gradient assignment, dot product, fade, interpolation, and hashing from parent article value += amplitude basenoise(p scale frequency) amplitude = 0.5 frequency = 2.0 return value # 1. Compute FBM noise noise = fbm(pos, fbmscale, fbmoctaves) # 2. Remap to [0, 1] noise = noise 0.5 + 0.5 # 3. Apply power function density = pow(noise, powerexponent) # 4. Threshold if density < threshold: density = 0.0 # 5. Scale density = basedensity # 6. Clamp return max(0.0, min(1.0, density)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Generates 3D volumetric density fields for clouds using multi-scale domain warping and boundary envelopes. It differs from this method by incorporating style-specific shaping and vertical structure control, rather than relying solely on a power function and threshold on a single noise field. name: Volume Cloud Generation Pipeline
body: The Volume Cloud Generation Pipeline generates a patchy, volumetric density field for cloud simulation by applying procedural noise functions with domain warping and edge constraints. It solves the problem of creating large-scale atmospheric phenomena without requiring pre-computed voxel data or external texture maps. It distinguishes itself from its sibling Volumetric Density Generation by incorporating multi-scale domain warping, specific boundary envelope functions, and dual-style (realistic/cartoon) noise lattices to produce organic, non-repeating cloud structures. Inputs: params: Configuration object containing resolution (int), seed (int), cloudtypeid (int), style (enum: 'realistic' or 'cartoon'), disturbancestrength (float), detailstrength (float), resolvedallowboundaryoverlap (bool). cloud: Cloud definition object containing defaultallowboundaryoverlap (bool). Outputs: density: 3D uint8 array of shape (size, size, size) representing density (0-255). disturbance: 3D uint8 array of shape (size, size, size) representing flow/velocity magnitude (0-255). metadata: Dictionary containing encoding version, dimensions, tile layout, axis order, cloud type info, parameters, style, noise profile, channel meanings, and edge profiles. Data Structures: density, disturbance: np.ndarray of shape (size, size, size), dtype uint8. axis: 1D float32 array of length size, values in [-1.0, 1.0]. x, y: 2D float32 arrays of shape (size, size), generated via np.meshgrid. lattices: Tuple of 3D float32 arrays. Each lattice has shape (frequency, frequency, frequency) where frequency matches predefined sets (e.g., 2, 3, 5, 8, 13). Constants: SAFEEMPTYBORDERZ, SAFEFADEWIDTHZ, LAYERCLOUDTYPEIDS, lobez, lobezradius, weight, verticalpresence, lobe, centerz, halfheight, horizontaltaper, sidevariation: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class VolumeMemoryPressureError(MemoryError): pass def volumecloudgenerationpipeline(params, cloud): size = params.resolution seed = params.seed style = params.style detailstrength = params.detailstrength disturbancestrength = params.disturbancestrength cloudtypeid = params.cloudtypeid # 1. Allocate output arrays try: density = np.zeros((size, size, size), dtype=np.uint8) disturbance = np.zeros((size, size, size), dtype=np.uint8) except MemoryError: raise VolumeMemoryPressureError("Insufficient memory for volume cloud generation") # 2. Generate coordinate grids axis = np.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, size, dtype=np.float32) x, y = np.meshgrid(axis, axis, indexing="xy") # 3. Initialize noise lattices densitylattices = makenoiselattices(seed + 101, (2, 3, 5, 8, 13)) flowlattices = makenoiselattices(seed + 7919, (2, 4, 7, 11)) boundarylattices = makenoiselattices(seed + 12113, (1, 2, 3, 5)) cartoonnoiseset = None shapevariation = None if style == 'cartoon': cartoonnoiseset = makecartoonnoiseset(seed) # Generate shapevariation from seed and cloudtypeid: Not given in the sources. # 4. Determine boundary behavior # LAYERCLOUDTYPEIDS: Not given in the sources. usesnaturalfiniteedge = ( not params.resolvedallowboundaryoverlap and cloud.defaultallowboundaryoverlap and cloudtypeid in LAYERCLOUDTYPEIDS) # 5. Generate boundary noise fields for finite edges topsurfacenoise = valuenoiseslice(boundarylattices[0], x, y, -0.61) (detailstrength 0.22) bottomsurfacenoise = valuenoiseslice(boundarylattices[1], x, y, 0.27) (detailstrength 0.26) thicknessnoise = valuenoiseslice(boundarylattices[2], x, y, 0.83) (detailstrength 0.18) # 6. Calculate XY distance to edges xydistance = np.minimum.reduce((x + 1.0, 1.0 - x, y + 1.0, 1.0 - y)) discretecloudedgeguard = safeedgefade(xydistance, 0.0, 0.045) # 7. Loop over Z slices for zindex in range(size): zcoord = axis[zindex] if style == 'cartoon': macro, body, edge, cartoonflow = cartoonnoisefields( cartoonnoiseset, x, y, zcoord, detailstrength, disturbancestrength) # cartoondensityslice to get raw density: Not given in the sources. rawdensity = macro # cartoonflownoise to get flow: Not given in the sources. flow = cartoonflow else: # realistic densitynoise = fractalvaluenoise(densitylattices, x, y, zcoord, detailstrength) flownoise = fractalvaluenoise(flowlattices, x, y, zcoord, disturbancestrength) # densityslice to get raw density: Not given in the sources. rawdensity = densitynoise flow = 0.5 + (flownoise - 0.5) disturbancestrength # 8. Calculate Z fade zdistance = min(float(zcoord + 1.0), float(1.0 - zcoord)) # SAFEEMPTYBORDERZ, SAFEFADEWIDTHZ: Not given in the sources. zfade = safeedgefade(zdistance, 0.0, 0.045) # 9. Apply boundary constraints if usesnaturalfiniteedge: sideedgenoise = valuenoiseslice( boundarylattices[0], x + zcoord 0.16, y - zcoord 0.11, zcoord 1.75 + 0.19) # Calculate naturalxyedge via naturalxyedgeenvelope: Not given in the sources. naturalxyedge = sideedgenoise # Calculate verticalenvelope via finitelayerverticalenvelope: Not given in the sources. verticalenvelope = 1.0 # Calculate fixedvertical via fixedlayerverticalprofile (min 0.075): Not given in the sources. fixedvertical = max(0.075, 1.0) rawdensity = rawdensity naturalxyedge (verticalenvelope / fixedvertical) elif not params.resolvedallowboundaryoverlap: rawdensity = rawdensity discretecloudedgeguard # 10. Apply Z fade and store rawdensity = rawdensity zfade density[zindex] = np.rint(np.clip(rawdensity, 0.0, 1.0) 255.0).astype(np.uint8) disturbance[zindex] = np.rint(np.clip(flow, 0.0, 1.0) 255.0).astype(np.uint8) # 11. Construct metadata metadata = { "encodingversion": 1, "dimensions": (size, size, size), "tilelayout": {"cols": size, "rows": 1}, "axisorder": "Z,Y,X", "cloudtypeid": cloudtypeid, "parameters": params, "style": style, "noiseprofile": { "densitylattices": densitylattices, "flowlattices": flowlattices, "boundarylattices": boundarylattices }, "channelmeanings": { "R": "density", "G": "flow", "B": "0", "A": "255" }, "edgeprofiles": { "usesnaturalfiniteedge": usesnaturalfiniteedge, "discretecloudedgeguard": discretecloudedgeguard } } return density, disturbance, metadata def smoothstep(value): clipped = np.clip(value, 0.0, 1.0) return clipped clipped (3.0 - 2.0 clipped) def safeedgefade(distancetoedge, emptyborder, fadewidth): return smoothstep(np.maximum(distancetoedge - emptyborder, 0.0) / fadewidth) def fade(value): return value value value (value (value 6.0 - 15.0) + 10.0) def valuenoiseslice(lattice, x, y, z): frequency = lattice.shape[0] px = (x + 1.0) 0.5 frequency py = (y + 1.0) 0.5 frequency pz = (z + 1.0) 0.5 frequency ix = np.floor(px).astype(np.intp) % frequency iy = np.floor(py).astype(np.intp) % frequency iz = np.floor(pz).astype(np.intp) % frequency fx, fy, fz = fade(px - np.floor(px)), fade(py - np.floor(py)), fade(pz - np.floor(pz)) ix1, iy1, iz1 = (ix + 1) % frequency, (iy + 1) % frequency, (iz + 1) % frequency c00 = lattice[iz, iy, ix] (1.0 - fx) + lattice[iz, iy, ix1] fx c10 = lattice[iz, iy1, ix] (1.0 - fx) + lattice[iz, iy1, ix1] fx c01 = lattice[iz1, iy, ix] (1.0 - fx) + lattice[iz1, iy, ix1] fx c11 = lattice[iz1, iy1, ix] (1.0 - fx) + lattice[iz1, iy1, ix1] fx lower = c00 (1.0 - fy) + c10 fy upper = c01 (1.0 - fy) + c11 fy return lower (1.0 - fz) + upper fz def fractalvaluenoise(lattices, x, y, z, detail): warpstrength = 0.12 + 0.08 np.clip(detail, 0.0, 1.0) latticex = lattices[0] latticey = lattices[min(1, len(lattices) - 1)] latticez = lattices[min(2, len(lattices) - 1)] warpx = valuenoiseslice(latticex, x + y, y - z, z + x) - 0.5 warpy = valuenoiseslice(latticey, 2.0 x - y, x + z, y + z) - 0.5 warpz = valuenoiseslice(latticez, x - z, 2.0 y + z, x + y - z) - 0.5 warpedx = x + warpstrength warpx warpedy = y + warpstrength warpy warpedz = z + warpstrength warpz transforms = ( (warpedx, warpedy, warpedz), (warpedx + warpedy, warpedy + warpedz, warpedz + warpedx), (2.0 warpedx - warpedy, warpedx + 2.0 warpedy, warpedz + warpedy), (warpedx - warpedz, 2.0 warpedy + warpedz, warpedx + warpedy - warpedz), (2.0 warpedx + warpedz, warpedy - warpedx, 2.0 warpedz + warpedy),) samples = [ valuenoiseslice(lattice, transforms[index % len(transforms)]) for index, lattice in enumerate(lattices) ] weights = [1.0] for index in range(1, len(samples)): weights.append((0.52 + detail 0.16) index) total = sum(weight sample for weight, sample in zip(weights, samples, strict=True)) return np.clip(total / sum(weights), 0.0, 1.0) def makenoiselattices(seed, frequencies): generator = np.random.defaultrng(seed) return tuple(generator.random((frequency, frequency, frequency), dtype=np.float32) for frequency in frequencies) def makecartoonnoiseset(seed): return { "macrolattices": makenoiselattices(seed + 20101, (1, 2, 3)), "bodylattices": makenoiselattices(seed + 20503, (2, 3, 5)), "edgelattices": makenoiselattices(seed + 20907, (3, 5, 7)), "flowlattices": makenoiselattices(seed + 21301, (2, 3, 5, 8)) } def cartoonnoisefields(noiseset, x, y, z, detail, disturbance): macro = fractalvaluenoise(noiseset["macrolattices"], x, y, z, detail 0.10) body = fractalvaluenoise(noiseset["bodylattices"], x, y, z, detail 0.30) edge = fractalvaluenoise(noiseset["edgelattices"], x, y, z, detail 0.55) flow = fractalvaluenoise(noiseset["flowlattices"], x, y, z, disturbance 0.25) return macro, body, edge, flow Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Pressure: The method allocates two large 3D arrays. If resolution is too high, a MemoryError should be caught and re-raised as VolumeMemoryPressureError. Boundary Overlap: The usesnaturalfiniteedge logic depends on specific cloud type IDs and parameter flags. Precision: The use of np.float32 for lattices and coordinates is specified. Degenerate Input: If lobezradius or halfheight is zero, division by zero must be avoided by using max(..., 0.001) as shown in the source snippets. The Redshift Clouds Object is a procedural volume primitive that generates entire procedural skies. It distinguishes itself from other volumetric methods by offering two distinct rendering modes: a "fast mode" that renders the cloud deck as a clever background, and a "fully volumetric mode" that allows geometry such as skyscrapers or aircraft to pierce the cloud layer and be lit by it. Unlike the Redshift Environment Object, which fills the scene with a homogeneous scattering medium for atmospheric haze and god rays, the Clouds Object is designed specifically for sky generation. Time Complexity: O(N^3) where N is the resolution, as every voxel in the 3D grid is computed once per slice. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for the density and disturbance arrays. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Generates organic, non-repeating cloud structures without external textures. Supports both realistic and cartoon styles. Limitations: Requires significant memory for high resolutions. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Volume Cloud Generation Pipeline is based on the implementation found in the Noise-Cloud repository by mingtu149411. It utilizes procedural noise functions, specifically value noise with domain warping, to generate cloud density fields. mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, https://github.com/mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Redshift Clouds Object
head: Redshift Clouds
body: The Redshift Clouds Object generates entire procedural skies. It distinguishes itself by offering two rendering modes: a "fast mode" that renders the cloud deck as a clever background, and a "fully volumetric mode" that allows geometry such as skyscrapers or aircraft to pierce the cloud layer and be lit by it. Unlike the Redshift Environment Object, which fills the scene or a height-limited layer with a homogeneous scattering medium for atmospheric haze and god rays, the Clouds Object is dedicated to procedural sky generation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene parameters defining the sky volume; camera position and orientation. Output: Rendered image with volumetric sky effects. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. The implementation details of the procedural noise functions or density fields are not specified. Steps: 1. Mode Selection: The user selects between "fast mode" and "fully volumetric mode". 2. Fast Mode Execution: The cloud deck is rendered as a clever background. 3. Fully Volumetric Mode Execution: The cloud layer is treated as a full volume, allowing geometry to pierce it and be lit by it. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Specific parameters for controlling cloud density, color, or procedural noise are not detailed in the provided text. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Redshift Environment Object [10721-redshift-environment-object.md]: A procedural volume primitive that fills the entire scene or a height-limited layer with a homogeneous scattering medium, eliminating the need for voxel data. It is primarily used to simulate atmospheric haze, fog, and volumetric lighting effects such as god rays. Unlike the Clouds Object, which generates procedural sky volumes, the Environment Object provides a uniform background medium that interacts with light sources to create visible light shafts. Choose it for atmospheric haze and light shafts rather than sky generation. Performance: The "fast mode" is optimized for speed by rendering the cloud deck as a background. Use Cases: Ideal for simulating procedural skies where camera or geometry may penetrate the cloud layer. Limitations: Specific performance metrics, resolution limits, or computational costs are not provided. name: Redshift Environment Object
head: God Rays
body: The Redshift Environment Object fills the entire scene or a height-limited layer with a homogeneous scattering medium, eliminating the need for voxel data for uniform media such as atmospheric haze and fog. It is primarily used for volumetric lighting, specifically god rays, which are visible light beams created when light passes through a thin scattering medium. Unlike the Redshift Clouds Object, which generates procedural skies, the Environment Object provides a uniform background medium that interacts with light sources to create visible light shafts and volumetric shadows. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry, light sources, and parameter values for scattering. Output: A rendered image with a uniform scattering medium affecting all rays passing through the defined volume. Data Structures: The object implicitly defines the volume based on scene bounds or a height limit without using voxel grids or point clouds. Parameters: Scattering Value: Controls the amount of scattering in the medium; even small values are powerful. Height Limit: Defines whether the volume fills the entire scene or only a specific height layer. Steps: 1. Add a Redshift Environment Object to the scene hierarchy. 2. Configure the object to fill the scene or a height-limited layer. 3. Set the Scattering Value to the desired intensity. 4. For god rays, add a strong, partially blocked light source such as a sun through a window. 5. Render the scene; rays passing through the medium will scatter, making light beams and volumetric shadows appear naturally. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupenvironmentobject(scatteringvalue: float = 0.1, heightlimit: float | None = None) -> dict: """ Configures a Redshift Environment Object for homogeneous scattering. """ config = { "type": "Redshift Environment Object", "scatteringvalue": scatteringvalue, "heightlimit": heightlimit } # Host application integration: add config to scene hierarchy # Host application integration: assign to renderer's volume manager return config def setupgodraysexample() -> dict: """ Example configuration for volumetric lighting (god rays). """ # Host application integration: create a strong, partially blocked light source (e.g., sun through a window) # Host application integration: create obstruction geometry (e.g., window frame) return setupenvironmentobject(scatteringvalue=0.05, heightlimit=None) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: Volumes are expensive because rays are sampled at many points along their path and can scatter many times inside dense media. Density: High density or high scattering values significantly increase render times. Lighting: God rays require a strong, partially blocked light source; without obstruction, the effect may not be visible. Optimization: To speed up rendering, keep simulations as high resolution as needed, use a moderate Volume Trace Depth, leave Extinction Falloff at its default, lower Shadow Density Scale instead of adding bounces, and let the GPU and denoiser handle the rest. Time Complexity: Rendering time increases with volume density and scattering value, as rays are sampled along their path and can scatter multiple times in dense media. Memory Complexity: Low, as no voxel data is stored and the volume is defined procedurally. Strengths: Simple setup for atmospheric effects; no need for external voxel data; effective for god rays. Limitations: Designed for homogeneous volumes; it cannot represent complex, non-uniform density variations natively. When to Use: For atmospheric haze, fog, and volumetric lighting (god rays). When Not to Use: For complex, non-uniform volumes like clouds or smoke, which require procedural or voxel-based approaches. The Redshift Environment Object is part of the Maxon Redshift renderer's volumetric rendering system. It provides a method to simulate atmospheric effects without the complexity of voxel-based volumes. It is used in scenes requiring atmospheric perspective and volumetric lighting. name: Cartoon Noise Lattice Generation
head: Cartoon Noise Set Generation, Macro/Body/Edge/Flow Lattice Generation
body: Cartoon Noise Lattice Generation produces independent, tileable noise lattices for cartoon-style cloud rendering by separating noise into four distinct functional groups: macro (outline), body (fill), edge (detail), and flow (disturbance). The method generates multiple specialized lattices with specific frequency constraints to ensure stability and avoid fixed-direction ripple artifacts, building on Gradient-based Noise (Perlin/Simplex). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A MaskParameters object containing resolution (512, 1024, or 2048), global height bounds (globalmincm, globalmaxcm), weather type, seed, coverage percentage, cloud region count, and optional CloudHeightRule configurations. Outputs: A CartoonNoiseSet dataclass containing four tuples of numpy arrays: macrolattices, bodylattices, edgelattices, and flowlattices. Data Structures: 1. MaskParameters: resolution: int (512, 1024, or 2048). globalmincm, globalmaxcm: int defining the vertical volume bounds. seed: int for deterministic generation. cloudregioncount: int (1–500). cloudheightrules: tuple[CloudHeightRule,...]. 2. CloudHeightRule: typeid: int. centermincm, centermaxcm: int defining the target center height range. heightdeltamincm, heightdeltamaxcm: int defining the minimum and maximum height difference for the volume box. 3. CartoonNoiseSet: macrolattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...]. bodylattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...]. edgelattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...]. flowlattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Validate Parameters: Ensure resolution is in {512, 1024, 2048}, globalmaxcm > globalmincm, and 0 <= coveragepercent <= 100. 2. Generate Height Rules: For each cloud type, determine vertical bounds. If a CloudHeightRule is provided, sample centermincm and centermaxcm via rng.integers. Otherwise, derive bounds from legacy constants: (0.62, 0.92) for typeid == 10, (0.22, 0.58) for others. Calculate deltamin and deltamax using VOLUMEBOXHEIGHTMULTIPLIER applied to the span. 3. Generate Lattices: Call makenoiselattices for each of the four groups (macro, body, edge, flow) with specific frequencies to ensure they are small, stable, and avoid fixed-direction ripple artifacts. 4. Construct Set: Pack the resulting tuples into the CartoonNoiseSet dataclass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass(frozen=True) class CloudHeightRule: typeid: int centermincm: int centermaxcm: int heightdeltamincm: int heightdeltamaxcm: int @dataclass(frozen=True) class MaskParameters: resolution: int = 1024 globalmincm: int = 0 globalmaxcm: int = 1500000 seed: int = 20260826 coveragepercent: int = 45 cloudregioncount: int = 1 cloudheightrules: tuple[CloudHeightRule,...] = () @dataclass(frozen=True) class CartoonNoiseSet: macrolattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...] bodylattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...] edgelattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...] flowlattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...] def makenoiselattices(grouptype: str, params: MaskParameters, rng: np.random.Generator) -> tuple[np.ndarray,...]: """ Generates lattices for a specific group (macro, body, edge, flow). Uses specific frequencies to ensure stability and avoid artifacts. The actual noise lattice generation kernel using group-specific frequencies is not detailed in the sources. """ # The actual noise lattice generation kernel using group-specific frequencies is not detailed in the sources. pass def generatecartoonnoiselattices(params: MaskParameters) -> CartoonNoiseSet: if params.resolution not in (512, 1024, 2048): raise ValueError("Resolution must be 512, 1024, or 2048.") if params.globalmaxcm <= params.globalmincm: raise ValueError("Max height must be greater than min height.") if not (0 <= params.coveragepercent <= 100): raise ValueError("Coverage percent must be between 0 and 100.") rng = np.random.defaultrng(params.seed) macrolattices = makenoiselattices("macro", params, rng) bodylattices = makenoiselattices("body", params, rng) edgelattices = makenoiselattices("edge", params, rng) flowlattices = makenoiselattices("flow", params, rng) return CartoonNoiseSet( macrolattices=macrolattices, bodylattices=bodylattices, edgelattices=edgelattices, flowlattices=flowlattices) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resolution Constraints: Only 512, 1024, and 2048 are supported. Height Bounds: globalmaxcm must be strictly greater than globalmincm. Artifact Avoidance: Frequencies must be carefully selected per group to prevent fixed-direction ripple artifacts. A variant that computes a coherent flow field by combining the generated lattices. It clips the weighted sum of flow, macro, and body noise channels: coherent = np.clip(0.58 flow + 0.27 macro + 0.15 body, 0.0, 1.0). It then modulates this coherent flow around the center value 0.5 by a strength parameter: return np.clip(0.5 + (coherent - 0.5) strength, 0.0, 1.0). This output drives disturbance in the cloud volume. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces stable, tileable noise suitable for cartoon-style rendering by separating concerns into macro, body, edge, and flow groups. Limitations: Requires specific resolution support (512, 1024, 2048) and relies on hardcoded legacy constants for height rules if not explicitly configured. Originated in the open-source project Noise-Cloud by mingtu149411. The method addresses visual artifacts of standard noise in cloud rendering by decomposing the noise field into specialized components. mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, https://github.com/mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Aperiodic Tiling with Edge Matching
head: Aperiodic mapping, Edge-matching triangular patterns
body: A method to avoid repetitivity when mapping pre-shaded texture cells onto a terrain or volume surface by enforcing aperiodic boundary conditions and edge-matching constraints. It differs from standard periodic tiling by correlating twin edges to prevent seams, and from noise-based tiling by relying on pre-computed geometric patterns rather than procedural generation at render time. It builds on Specific Procedural Patterns and Applications and contrasts with Sine-based procedural voxel generation, Spherical Density Ramp with Noise, Mandelbulb Fractal Generation, and Volumetric Density Generation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of pre-shaded triangular tile patterns and a spatial coordinate system. Output: A seamless, non-repeating texture map for terrain or volume rendering. Data Structures: Reference Texture: A 2D image containing the 8 triangular tiles arranged to satisfy edge constraints. Tile Selection Logic: A mapping from spatial coordinates to one of the 8 tile types based on aperiodic triplet selection. Steps: 1. Define Boundary Conditions: Assume 2 different boundary conditions in each of the 3 directions of a triangular tiling, yielding 8 possible triplets and 16 possible triangles (pointing north or south). 2. Select Subset: Choose a subset of 8 triangles (4 north, 4 south) to save memory, ensuring each triplet is used once without breaking aperiodicity. 3. Arrange Reference Texture: Place the 8 tiles in the reference texture such that edge constraints are met, ensuring each edge kind appears twice as "twin edges". 4. Shear and Wrap: Apply a shear transformation to the pattern to convert the natural slanted wrapping (where bottom and top triangles share an edge) into a square wrapping tractable by hardware textures. 5. Build Patterns (Content Placement): Enforce that objects crossing an edge axis are replicated on the twin edge, making neighborhoods correlated but not identical. Ensure objects never cross two edges (e.g., corners) to avoid correlating them and replicating on half the cells. Place trees crossing boundaries first (replicated on twin edges), starting with one tree close to a corner (not crossing 2 edges) to avoid vicinity bias. Freely place other trees, constrained only by not crossing the triangle tile boundary. Formulas: Shear Transformation: \mathbf{v}' = \mathbf{M}{shear} \mathbf{v}, where \mathbf{v} = [x, y]^T is a vertex coordinate, \mathbf{v}' is the transformed coordinate, and \mathbf{M}{shear} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & k \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} with k as the shear factor. Parameters: Number of Tiles: 8 triangles (4 north, 4 south) are sufficient for aperiodicity. 16 triangles can be used for higher variability. Texture Resolution: Not given in the sources, but must support the sheared square wrapping. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Linear Interpolation: At tile borders, hardware linear interpolation blends outside color with inside color, causing artifacts if the reference texture is not arranged to make twin edges coherent. Corner Crossing: Objects crossing two edges (corners) must be avoided, as this correlates edges and causes replication on half the cells. Pre-shading Limitation: Patterns are pre-shaded, so they cannot be rotated at render time. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampleaperiodictiling(u, v, referencetexture): # Map continuous coordinates to one of the 8 triangular tiles # based on aperiodic triplet selection tileidx = computetileindex(u, v) tile = referencetexture.tiles[tileidx] # Apply inverse shear to convert square-wrapped coordinates back to slanted space # for correct coordinate mapping within the triangular tile sheark = 0.5 localu = u - sheark v localv = v # Sample the texture. Hardware linear interpolation handles coherence # between twin edges return referencetexture.sample(localu, localv) def computetileindex(u, v): # Determine which of the 8 tiles covers the point based on # the 3-direction triangular tiling grid # Implementation depends on specific grid layout gridu = int(u) % 8 gridv = int(v) % 8 return (gridu + gridv) % 8 Time Complexity: Constant time per sample, assuming efficient tile lookup. The shearing and wrapping are pre-computed. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of tiles (8 or 16) and their resolution. Strengths: Eliminates visible repetition in large terrains/volumes without requiring complex procedural noise at render time. Compatible with hardware linear filtering if built correctly. Limitations: Requires pre-shading, limiting dynamic lighting. Manual placement of objects in tiles is required to avoid artifacts. Limited variability compared to fully procedural methods. When to Use: Real-time rendering of large, static or semi-static scenes (e.g., forests) where repetition is noticeable and pre-shading is acceptable. When Not to Use: Dynamic lighting scenarios, or when high variability and organic randomness are required without pre-computation. Originated in the context of rendering forest scenes in real-time, specifically to avoid repetitivity when mapping texcells onto a terrain. The method relies on the aperiodic scheme described in [NC99] and is discussed in detail in. It addresses the limitation of pre-shaded textures, which cannot be rotated, by using separate boundary conditions in each direction. Scenes are lit by fixed directional lights with precomputed shading stored in the textures. Rendering Forest Scenes in Real-Time, https://doi.org/10.2312/egwr/egsr04/093-102, fetched 2026-10-26

name: TGorillaVolumetricNoise
head: Volumetric Noise, cloud / smoke / fog body
body: TGorillaVolumetricNoise is a procedural volume component that generates a 3D texture using fractal Brownian motion (FBM) Perlin noise and renders it as a physically based emission-absorption medium. It solves the problem of creating believable, fly-through clouds, smoke, or fog without requiring external data files or custom shader code. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by baking a smooth 0..1 density gradient into the voxel data while applying opacity via a render-time Beer-Lambert blend, thereby avoiding the terracing artifacts common in naive voxel density approaches. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Parent viewport, size (default 1×1×1), resolution (default 64³), and shaping parameters (Frequency, Octaves, Persistence, Lacunarity, Coverage, EdgeFalloff, Billowy, Seed). Outputs: A 3D texture (volume data) uploaded to the GPU and rendered as a volumetric mesh. Data Structures: The core data structure is a 3D texture where each voxel stores a single floating-point value representing a smooth density gradient in the range [0, 1]. This value is not the final opacity; it acts as a shape mask. Parameters: Frequency (Single): Base noise scale. Higher values produce smaller, more numerous noise cycles. Octaves (Integer): Number of FBM octaves summed. More octaves add finer detail but increase generation time. Persistence (Single): Amplitude falloff per octave (range 0–1). Lower values yield smoother noise; higher values yield rougher noise. Lacunarity (Single): Frequency growth per octave (typically ~2.0). Coverage (Single): Soft threshold (0–1). Value 1 keeps the whole body; lower values carve the body into separate puffs. EdgeFalloff (Single): Radial fade (0–1) toward the volume border to create a rounded blob shape instead of a filled cube. Billowy (Boolean): If True, applies abs() to the noise for a puffy cumulus/smoke look; if False, produces smooth haze. Density (Single): Overall opacity/absorption strength. This is not baked into the voxel data but applied at render time. RenderInside (Boolean): Default True. Allows the camera to move inside the cloud with correct compositing. UseLighting (Boolean): Default False. Volumetric noise is an emission-absorption medium, not a lit surface. Offset (Point3D): Used for animation drift. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create the instance, set the parent, size, assign FrontFaceRenderPass and BackFaceRenderPass, allow control, and apply a preset. 2. Noise Generation: For each voxel in the 3D grid, calculate the base Perlin noise value at the voxel's position scaled by Frequency and shifted by Offset. Apply FBM summation: sum the noise values across Octaves, scaling amplitude by Persistence and frequency by Lacunarity per octave. If Billowy is True, apply abs() to the resulting FBM sum. 3. Shaping: Apply Coverage as a soft threshold to carve the noise field into separate puffs. Apply EdgeFalloff as a radial fade toward the volume border to create a rounded blob shape. 4. Storage: Store the resulting smooth 0..1 gradient in the 3D texture; do not bake the final opacity into the voxel data. 5. Rendering: During ray marching, use the stored voxel value as a density mask and apply the Density parameter as the absorption coefficient in the Beer-Lambert emission-absorption blend to compute opacity and color at render time. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generatevolumetricnoise(width, height, depth, frequency, octaves, persistence, lacunarity, coverage, edgefalloff, billowy, seed): # Initialize standard 3D Perlin noise generator with seed perlin = PerlinNoise(seed) volume = [[0.0] depth for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): for z in range(depth): nx = x / width ny = y / height nz = z / depth fbmvalue = 0.0 amplitude = 1.0 currentfreq = 1.0 for i in range(octaves): fbmvalue += amplitude perlin.noise( nx frequency currentfreq, ny frequency currentfreq, nz frequency currentfreq) amplitude = persistence currentfreq = lacunarity if billowy: fbmvalue = abs(fbmvalue) # Coverage as a soft threshold density = max(0.0, fbmvalue - (1.0 - coverage)) # EdgeFalloff radial fade dist = math.sqrt((nx - 0.5)2 + (ny - 0.5)2 + (nz - 0.5)2) maxdist = math.sqrt(0.75) normalizeddist = dist / maxdist edgefactor = max(0.0, 1.0 - normalizeddist edgefalloff) density = edgefactor volume[y][x][z] = min(1.0, max(0.0, density)) return volume Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Terracing Artifacts: Naïve approaches that bake final density/opacity into voxel data and use linear blending produce hard saturation "shells" or step terraces when viewed from inside. This is solved by storing a smooth 0..1 gradient and applying opacity at render time via emission-absorption blend. Performance: Regenerate re-samples the whole volume on the CPU and is expensive. For animation, use a smaller resolution (e.g., 32³) and update on a timer (~100 ms) rather than every frame. Lighting: UseLighting should remain False for standard volumetric noise. Lit clouds require a separate "light-marching" feature. Generation Cost: Generation is CPU-bound and requires re-sampling the entire volume on the CPU when parameters change or animation drifts. Resolution Independence: Density appearance is resolution-independent; a cloud at 32³ looks comparably dense to one at 64³ for the same Density value. Strengths: No external data files or shader code required; fly-through capability with correct compositing; cheap runtime opacity adjustment via Density. Limitations: CPU-bound regeneration makes high-resolution animation expensive; lacks built-in lighting. When to use: For static or slowly drifting clouds, smoke, or fog where performance allows for CPU regeneration or lower resolutions are acceptable. When not to use: For high-frequency animated smoke requiring high resolution, as CPU regeneration becomes too expensive; use a smaller resolution (e.g., 32³) or a different method instead. For lit volumetric clouds, use light-marching instead. TGorillaVolumetricNoise is part of the Gorilla3D framework. It is designed to provide a "ready-to-use" cloud/smoke/fog body with a handful of properties, abstracting away the need for shader code or data files. It builds on the principles of Procedural and implicit volumes and Volumetric Mesh. Volumetric Noise - Gorilla3D Framework - Documentation, https://gorilla3d.de/doc/v3/version/v1.4/page/Core/Volumetric/Volumetric-Noise.md, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Noise-based Density Generation
body: Noise-based Density Generation creates volumetric density fields by evaluating procedural noise functions at query points. It solves the problem of defining complex, organic material distributions (such as fire, clouds, or smoke) without the memory overhead of storing explicit voxel grids. It differs from its siblings by serving as the foundational mathematical primitive for procedural volumes, whereas specific implementations like Perlin-Worley Noise or Cartoon Cloud Density Generation apply specific compositional strategies to these primitives. This family shares the mechanism, terms, and math defined in Procedural Noise Functions. Enhances coarse volumetric data with high-frequency details using a tiled noise volume, solving missing microstructure without increasing voxel resolution. Sets itself apart by applying noise as a displacement field or optical modifier rather than a direct density scalar. When to choose it: Not given in the sources. Generates base density and color texture for volumetric fire using combined Perlin and Voronoi noise mapped to a 2D profile. Distinguishes itself by providing continuous, artifact-free textures supporting dynamic scaling without stretching. When to choose it: Not given in the sources. Generates cloud density by combining Perlin noise with Worley noise, storing multiple frequency levels of Worley noise in separate texture channels for high-frequency detail reconstruction. When to choose it: Not given in the sources. Generates stylized cloud densities using independent noise sets for macro structure, body puffs, edge details, and flow, combined with geometric envelopes. Differs by relying on multi-layered noise composition and explicit geometric shapes for a blocky/stylized appearance. When to choose it: Not given in the sources. Generates 3D volume density along predefined line paths using OpenSimplex noise to create pipe-like structures, restricting the noise evaluation domain to the vicinity of parametric line segments. When to choose it: Not given in the sources. Adds procedural noise to voxel materials, switching between a sampled noise texture and a deterministic checkerboard pattern based on a cell ID. When to choose it: Not given in the sources. Adds statistical noise to projection or volume data using either Poisson or Normal distributions, scaled by a norm factor or standard deviation. When to choose it: Not given in the sources. A noise injection method that ensures multi-view consistency by assigning Gaussian noise to mesh vertices and rasterizing it, avoiding the view-inconsistency of 2D pixel-space noise. Requires marching cubes extraction and rasterization, slower but captures stochastic details. A parallel job that updates noise density values within a spherical region (explosion) in a chunk's noise map. Not given in the sources.
