name: Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation
head: Texture Coordinate Perturbation, Noise-warped volume rendering, Procedural Volumetric Perturbation, Volume Perturbation via Procedural Noise, Volume Perturbation via Texture Coordinate Displacement
body: Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation enhances coarse, low-resolution volumetric data by superimposing high-frequency details using a small, tiled procedural noise volume. It solves the problem of missing microstructure (e.g., wispy clouds, fur, smoke) without increasing the underlying voxel resolution or computational cost of the base volume. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Worley Noise or Gradient-based Noise (Perlin/Simplex) by applying noise not as a direct density scalar, but as a displacement field or optical modifier, effectively warping the sampling domain or material properties. Inputs: 1. Macrostructure Volume: A low-resolution 3D texture (voxel dataset) representing the coarse density or scalar field. 2. Perturbation Volume: A small 3D texture (typically 32 \times 32 \times 32) initialized with random noise. 3. Transfer Function: Maps scalar density to optical properties (color, opacity). 4. Parameters: kNoiseDim: Integer dimension of the cubic noise volume (typically 32). noiseScale: Scaling factor for the perturbation amplitude. coordPerturb: Boolean/weight enabling coordinate perturbation. propPerturb: Boolean/weight enabling optical property perturbation. time: Animation time offset. flowSpeed: Speed of animation. Outputs: A rendered image with high-frequency procedural details superimposed on the coarse volume. Data Structures: Perturbation Volume: Format: 3D texture, 8-bit unsigned normalized integer per channel (RGBA8). Dimensions: kNoiseDim \times kNoiseDim \times kNoiseDim (e.g., 32^3). Content: Each texel stores four random 8-bit numbers. Filtering: Slightly blurred to hide artifacts from trilinear interpolation. Addressing: Repeat (wrap) mode to allow tiling. Push Constants (Vulkan Example): mvp: 4 \times 4 matrix (Model-View-Projection). params: vec4 containing [time, noiseScale, coordPerturb, propPerturb]. params2: vec4 containing [opacityCorrection, flowSpeed,...]. Steps: 1. Generate Perturbation Volume: Create a 3D texture of size kNoiseDim^3. Initialize each voxel with four random 8-bit values (RGBA). Apply a slight blur to the volume to mitigate trilinear interpolation artifacts. 2. Compute Perturbation Field (Pre-pass or Shader): Due to hardware limits on simultaneous textures and dependent texture reads, an additional pass is often required before the main volume shading. For each pixel/fragment, sample multiple copies of the perturbation volume at different scales. Let Ni be the noise sample at scale i. Compute the weighted sum of noise components to form a displacement vector \mathbf{D}: \mathbf{D} = \sumi wi \cdot Ni where wi are weights for each scale. Low Frequency: Achieved by applying the perturbation texture once with large amplitude. High Frequency: Achieved by applying the perturbation texture again with low amplitude, relying on texture repetition (wrapping) to create fine detail. 3. Apply Perturbation (Two Approaches): Approach 1: Coordinate Perturbation (Geometry/Density Warping) 1. Take the original texture coordinates \mathbf{T} for the volume data lookup. 2. Use three components of the noise vector \mathbf{D} (e.g., RGB) as a displacement vector. 3. Compute perturbed coordinates: \mathbf{T}{perturbed} = \mathbf{T} + \mathbf{D} \cdot \text{scale} 4. Perform a dependent texture read on the Macrostructure Volume using \mathbf{T}{perturbed}. 5. Render the result to a pixel buffer (render-to-texture) to be used in subsequent shading steps. 6. Note: This avoids recomputing gradients on a perturbed grid, which is required for surface shading but not for volume raycasting/shading. Approach 2: Optical Property Perturbation 1. Evaluate the transfer function on the original volume data to get base optical properties (color, opacity). 2. Use all four per-pixel noise components (RGBA) to modify these optical properties. 3. The user selects which specific optical properties (e.g., opacity, color channels) are modified. 4. This creates inhomogeneities and subtle iridescence effects. 4. Animate: Add a varying offset vector to the noise texture coordinates in the fragment shader. Update the offset each frame using time and flowSpeed. Different offsets can be added to each noise texture copy to enhance motion complexity. Pseudocode (Fragment Shader Logic): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sample3dtexture(tex, coord): """Simulates 3D texture sampling with repeat addressing and trilinear filtering.""" # Implementation depends on GPU API; returns RGBA tuple pass def sample1dtexture(tex, value): """Simulates 1D texture lookup for transfer function.""" pass def computeperturbationfield(vtexcoord, unoisevolume, time, flowspeed, noisescale): """Computes the weighted displacement vector from multi-scale noise samples.""" perturbation = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Scale 1: Large amplitude, low frequency coord1 = [vtexcoord[0] 0.5 + time flowspeed, vtexcoord[1], vtexcoord[2]] noise1 = sample3dtexture(unoisevolume, coord1) perturbation[0] += noise1[0] 2.0 perturbation[1] += noise1[1] 2.0 perturbation[2] += noise1[2] 2.0 # Scale 2: Small amplitude, high frequency (via wrapping) coord2 = [vtexcoord[0] 2.0 + time flowspeed 0.5, vtexcoord[1], vtexcoord[2]] noise2 = sample3dtexture(unoisevolume, coord2) perturbation[0] += noise2[0] 0.5 perturbation[1] += noise2[1] 0.5 perturbation[2] += noise2[2] 0.5 return perturbation def applyperturbation(vtexcoord, umacrovolume, utransferfunc, uparams, perturbation): """Applies either coordinate or optical perturbation based on flags.""" coordperturb = uparams[2] propperturb = uparams[3] noisescale = uparams[1] if coordperturb > 0.5: # Coordinate Perturbation: warp lookup coordinate perturbedcoord = [vtexcoord[i] + perturbation[i] noisescale for i in range(3)] density = sample3dtexture(umacrovolume, perturbedcoord)[0] tfresult = sample1dtexture(utransferfunc, density) return tfresult else: # Optical Property Perturbation: modify optical properties after transfer function density = sample3dtexture(umacrovolume, vtexcoord)[0] tfresult = sample1dtexture(utransferfunc, density) # Use noise components to modulate color and opacity noisemod = sample3dtexture(unoisevolume, vtexcoord)[0][0] color = [tfresult[i] (1.0 + noisemod 0.2) for i in range(3)] opacity = tfresult[3] (1.0 + noisemod 0.1) return [color[0], color[1], color[2], opacity] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Trilinear Interpolation Artifacts: The perturbation volume must be blurred slightly to prevent visible artifacts caused by linear interpolation of the random noise values. Hardware Limits: Modern GPUs limit the number of simultaneously applied textures and sequential dependent texture reads. This necessitates an additional render-to-texture pass to store the perturbed data before final shading. Gradient Recomputation: If using surface shading on perturbed volumes, gradients must be recomputed based on the perturbed grid. This method avoids that cost by perturbing the data access location directly. Fog Animation generates the appearance of moving gaseous volumes by perturbing the spatial coordinates of the evaluation point before sampling a static turbulence function, effectively moving the point through a "solid space" texture. Unlike methods that animate the noise function itself, this approach creates motion by shifting the sampling domain, producing upward-swirling gas movement suitable for real-time fog and smoke. It builds on Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation [1370-procedural-volume-rendering-with-noise-perturbation.md] by applying coordinate perturbation specifically to transparency-based fog effects. Time Complexity: Adds a constant overhead per fragment for sampling the perturbation volume at multiple scales. The additional render-to-texture pass adds one full-screen pass per frame. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the small perturbation volume (32^3 \times 4 bytes = 128 KB) and potentially an intermediate render target for the perturbed data. Performance: On hardware like NVIDIA GeForce 3 and ATI Radeon 8500, frame rates were only 50-60% slower than volume rendering with no shading, leveraging OpenGL render-to-texture extensions to avoid costly copy operations. Detail Equivalence: The visual detail produced is equivalent to an unperturbed voxel dataset of at least 100 times the resolution. Strengths: Efficiently adds high-frequency detail (clouds, smoke, fur) to coarse volumes without increasing voxel count or simulation cost. Limitations: Requires additional rendering passes due to texture read limits; artifacts can occur if the perturbation volume is not properly filtered. The technique was introduced by Kniss et al. in 2002 as part of "Interactive Translucent Volume Rendering and Procedural Modeling". It adapts Ebert's lattice-based noise approach for clouds and Peachey's vector-based noise simulation to interactive volume rendering. It is detailed in GPU Gems Chapter 39 and implemented in various open-source projects. sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, https://github.com/sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Interactive Translucent Volume Rendering and Procedural Modeling, https://courses.cs.duke.edu/spring03/cps296.8/papers/knissvolumeshading02.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 GPU Gems ch39, Volume rendering techniques, https://developer.nvidia.com/sites/all/modules/custom/gpugems/books/GPUGems/gpugemsch39.html, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Fog Animation
head: Solid Space Animation: Moving Point
body: Fog Animation generates the appearance of moving gaseous volumes by perturbing the spatial coordinates of the evaluation point before sampling a static turbulence function, effectively moving the point through a "solid space" texture. Unlike methods that animate the noise function itself, this approach creates motion by shifting the sampling domain, producing upward-swirling gas movement suitable for real-time fog and smoke. It builds on Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation [1370-procedural-volume-rendering-with-noise-perturbation.md] by applying coordinate perturbation specifically to transparency-based fog effects. Inputs: pnt: 3D point in world space (x, y, z). framenum: Integer current animation frame. transp: Output pointer to a float representing transparency. Parameters: SWIRLFRAMES: Integer controlling the period of the helical swirl. Typical value: 126. SWIRLAMOUNT: Float controlling the speed of the swirling effect. Typical value: 2\pi/126 (implied by modulo arithmetic for a full rotation). RAD1: Float, radius of the helix in the X direction. Typical value: 0.5. RAD2: Float, radius of the helix in the Z direction. Typical value: 2.0. DOWNAMOUNT: Float, downward movement speed per frame. Typical value: 0.01. turbulence(p, scale): Function returning a scalar noise value at point p with frequency scale. noiseit(p): Function returning a scalar noise value at point p. Data Structures: direction: 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the final sampling coordinate. cyl: 3D vector (x, y, z) representing cylindrical helical offset. tmp: Float scalar used for intermediate noise storage. Steps: 1. Perturb Input Point: Modify the input point pnt to introduce local turbulence and drift. pnt.x \leftarrow pnt.x + 2.0 + \text{turbulence}(pnt, 0.1) tmp \leftarrow \text{noise\it}(pnt) pnt.y \leftarrow pnt.y + 4.0 + tmp pnt.z \leftarrow pnt.z - 2.0 - tmp 2. Calculate Helical Path Components: Determine the position on a helix based on the current frame. \theta \leftarrow (\text{frame\num} \pmod{\text{SWIRL\FRAMES}}) \times \text{SWIRL\AMOUNT} cyl.x \leftarrow \text{RAD1} \times \cos(\theta) cyl.z \leftarrow \text{RAD2} \times \sin(\theta) 3. Calculate Direction Vector: Combine the perturbed point with the helical offset and a downward drift. direction.x \leftarrow pnt.x + cyl.x direction.y \leftarrow pnt.y - (\text{frame\num} \times \text{DOWN\AMOUNT}) direction.z \leftarrow pnt.z + cyl.z 4. Calculate Transparency: Sample turbulence at the direction vector and apply non-linear transformations to map the result to a transparency value. t \leftarrow \text{turbulence}(direction, 0.015) t \leftarrow 1.0 - (t \times t \times 0.275) \text{transp} \leftarrow t \times t \times t Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math SWIRLFRAMES = 126 SWIRLAMOUNT = 2.0 math.pi / SWIRLFRAMES RAD1 = 0.5 RAD2 = 2.0 DOWNAMOUNT = 0.01 def turbulence(p, scale): """Returns a scalar turbulence value at point p with frequency scale.""" pass # Implementation depends on available noise library def noiseit(p): """Returns a scalar noise value at point p.""" pass # Implementation depends on available noise library class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def foganimation(pnt, framenum): # Step 1: Perturb input point pntx = pnt.x + 2.0 + turbulence(pnt, 0.1) tmp = noiseit(pnt) pnty = pnt.y + 4.0 + tmp pntz = pnt.z - 2.0 - tmp # Step 2: Calculate helical path components theta = (framenum % SWIRLFRAMES) SWIRLAMOUNT cylx = RAD1 math.cos(theta) cylz = RAD2 math.sin(theta) # Step 3: Calculate direction vector directionx = pntx + cylx directiony = pnty - (framenum DOWNAMOUNT) directionz = pntz + cylz # Step 4: Calculate transparency t = turbulence(Vector3(directionx, directiony, directionz), 0.015) t = 1.0 - (t t 0.275) transp = t t t return transp Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The cubic mapping of transparency (t^3) can result in very low values for small t, potentially causing fog to disappear if the turbulence amplitude is low. Boundary Conditions: The modulo operation on framenum ensures the swirl repeats every SWIRLFRAMES. If framenum is negative, ensure the modulo operator behaves correctly for the target language (e.g., Python's % vs C++'s %). Noise Function Dependency: The method relies on noiseit and turbulence. A variant that animates marble textures by simulating heating and cooling effects. It calculates a glowpercent based on framenum, startframe, endframe, and heatlength. If outside the heat range, glowpercent=0. In the start heating phase, glowpercent = 1.0 - ease(((startframe+heatlength/2-framenum)/heatlength), 0.4, 0.6). In the end cooling phase, glowpercent = ease(((framenum-(endframe-heatlength/2))/heatlength), 0.4, 0.6). Otherwise, glowpercent=1.0. Turbulence is applied with ease-in/ease-out: turbpercent=ease(turbpercent, 0.3, 0.7). The color is computed as marblecolor(sin((pnt.y + turbpercent3.0turbulence(pnt,.0125) - displacement)MPI)) and blended with a glow color (R:1.0, G:0.4, B:0.8) weighted by 0.5glowpercent. A variant that moves the point along a helical path to create a swirling marble effect. It calculates a displacement based on framenum relative to startframe and endframe. A helical path is computed using theta = (framenum%SWIRLFRAMES)SWIRLAMOUNT, with radii RAD1 and RAD2, and downward drift DOWNAMOUNT. Randomness is added via fastnoise(pnt). The final color is marblecolor(sin((pnt.y + 3.0turbulence(direction,.0125))MPI)) where direction is the sum of pnt and the helical path. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, assuming constant-time noise evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1), as it does not require storing volume data or large lookup tables, only static parameters. Performance: Suitable for real-time rendering due to its procedural nature and lack of ray-marching or grid traversal. Strengths: Simple to implement, low memory footprint, produces organic, swirling motion without animating the noise field itself. Limitations: The motion is constrained to the specific helical and drift patterns defined; less flexible than general noise animation. The method originates from procedural modeling research on gases, fluids, and textures. It was introduced as a technique for animating solid space functions to create realistic fog and smoke effects by moving the evaluation point through a static texture space. The approach is similar to Gardner's cloud technique but uses turbulence for transparency control instead of Fourier synthesis. Procedural Modeling, Animation, and Rendering of Gases, Fluids, and Textures, https://www.researchgate.net/profile/David-Ebert-4/publication/2786953ProceduralModelingAnimationandRenderingofGasesFluidsandTextures/links/00b7d51a73e42a3c4e000000/Procedural-Modeling-Animation-and-Rendering-of-Gases-Fluids-and-Textures.pdf, fetched 2026-10-31 (unofficial)

name: Noise-based 2D Fire
head: 2D Fire Texture Generation, Voronoi-Perlin Fire Noise
body: Noise-based 2D Fire is a procedural technique for generating the base density and color texture of volumetric fire, serving as the input for constructing 3D cylindrical fire volumes. It distinguishes itself from sprite-based systems by providing a continuous, artifact-free texture that supports dynamic scaling, and from photo-realistic fluid simulations by offering real-time performance with artist-controllable aesthetics. The method combines multiple noise functions to create turbulent micro-details, which are then mapped onto a 2D profile to drive the visual appearance of the flame. The method generates a 2D texture that defines the fire's shape, color, and intensity, which is subsequently used to map colors onto a 3D lattice surrounding a central curve. The generation involves creating noise fields, combining them, and applying a color gradient. Inputs: Voronoi noise texture, Perlin noise texture, a standard UV texture for interpolation, and a color gradient definition. Outputs: A 2D color texture where pixel values represent the fire's color and intensity. Noise Space: A coordinate system (x, y, t) where x and y are spatial dimensions and t is time. Fire Profile Texture: A 2D image buffer storing RGBA values, where the horizontal axis represents radial distance from the fire center and the vertical axis represents height along the fire. 1. Generate Noise Fields: Generate a Perlin noise field for turbulent detail and a Voronoi noise field for cellular structure. 2. Combine Noise Functions: Multiply the Voronoi noise texture by the Perlin noise texture. 3. Modify UV Coordinates: Interpolate the product of the combined noises with a standard UV texture to create a modified UV coordinate. 4. Sample Fire Profile: Sample a single Gaussian blob using the modified UV coordinates to create fire-like variations. 5. Apply Color Gradient: Apply a color gradient to the result to give the fire its characteristic orange color. Not given in the sources. The exact mathematical expressions for the interpolation weights or Gaussian parameters are not provided. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def generateperlinnoise(width, height): # Standard 2D Perlin noise generation for turbulent detail return [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] def generatevoronoinoise(width, height): # Standard 2D Voronoi noise generation for cellular structure return [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] def generate2dfire(width, height, uvtexture, colorgradient): # Step 1: Generate noise textures perlintex = generateperlinnoise(width, height) voronoitex = generatevoronoinoise(width, height) # Step 2: Multiply the Voronoi noise texture by the Perlin noise texture combinednoise = [[perlintex[y][x] voronoitex[y][x] for x in range(width)] for y in range(height)] # Step 3: Interpolate the product of the combined noises with a standard UV texture # to create a modified UV coordinate. name: Real-Time Procedural Volumetric Fire
head: Hardware-Accelerated Procedural Fire, Procedural Volumetric Fire
body: A method for producing real-time procedural volumetric fire using hardware acceleration, Improved Perlin Noise, and a realistic particle simulation to create vibrant volumetric fire with bi-directional environmental macro-interactivity. It constructs an arbitrarily detailed lattice around a central curve, slicing it into quadrilateral planar polygons rendered into a unit fire volume. Unlike sprite systems, it avoids common artifacts, and unlike true photo-realistic fire simulation, it avoids high computational costs. It builds on Noise-based 2D Fire by extending the 2D noise application into a 3D volumetric lattice structure. Inputs: A central curve defined by control points, deformed by a particle simulation or pre-scripted movements. A two-dimensional fire profile texture defining color and intensity. Particle simulation parameters: movement, wind, high-energy particle dispersion, and thermal buoyancy. Application-specific frequency for noise detail. Perceived burning speed parameter. Unique constant offset for each fire instance. Outputs: Rendered quadrilateral planar polygons forming the volumetric fire. Data Structures: Central Curve: A 4-dimensional curve (3 spatial + 1 time/parameter) defining the fire's macro shape. Lattice: Constructed around the central curve. Four corner splines are generated at a distance of 2 \cdot r(t) units from the center spline, where r(t) is the radius at parameter t. Unit Fire Volume: A normalized texture space representation of the fire cross-section. Steps: 1. Deform Central Curve: The central curve is deformed by either a pre-scripted sequence of movements or a realistic particle simulation. The simulation accounts for movement, wind, high-energy particle dispersion, and thermal buoyancy. 2. Construct Lattice: Generate four corner splines at distance 2 \cdot r(t) from the center spline. Sample the center spline by length to find associated positions on the corner splines, producing positions and texture coordinates for each lattice corner. 3. Slice Lattice: Slice the lattice into quadrilateral planar polygons. 4. Render Polygons: Render these polygons with appropriate texture coordinates into a unit fire volume. 5. Pixel Shader Processing: Calculate noise space position. Scale horizontal and vertical axes of noise space by the radius and length, respectively, to prevent stretching. Multiply noisescale by an application-specific frequency. Correct noise functions to have a base frequency of one, making the frequency factor the spatial frequency of micro-level detail in world space. Set the fourth dimension of noise space to time. Offset the vertical axis by -time to create upward flow. Add a unique constant offset to the noise position for each fire instance. Use 4D Improved Perlin Noise on the calculated noise position to generate micro fire effects (flame shapes, location, flicker). Combine noise output with the 2D fire profile texture to determine final color and intensity. Formulas: Corner Spline Distance: d = 2 \cdot r(t). Noise Space Scaling (Equation 10 in): \mathbf{p}{noise} = \mathbf{p}{unit} \cdot \text{noisescale} \cdot f{app} \cdot \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{offset} Where: \mathbf{p}{unit} is the position in the unit fire volume texture coordinates. \text{noisescale} scales by radius (horizontal) and length (vertical). f{app} is the application-specific frequency. \mathbf{c} is a correction vector ensuring base frequency of one. \mathbf{offset} is the unique constant offset per instance. The fourth dimension (time) is added to \mathbf{p}{noise}. Vertical axis is offset by -time. Parameters: Perceived Burning Speed: Passed as a parameter to the pixel shader. Application-Specific Frequency: Adjusts desired levels of detail. Unique Constant Offset: Ensures each fire instance is unique. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stretching Artifacts: If noise space is not dynamically scaled according to the fire's radius and length, visual artifacts appear when the fire is enlarged. Precision: The level of detail of Improved Perlin Noise must be scaled to world coordinates in the pixel shader to eliminate stretching and scaling artifacts. A method to dynamically scale noise space according to the fire's radius and length to prevent stretching and scaling artifacts when the fire is enlarged. It scales the horizontal and vertical axes of noise space by the radius and length, respectively. It multiplies noisescale by an application-specific frequency to adjust for desired levels of detail. It corrects each noise function to have a base frequency of one, making the frequency factor the spatial frequency of micro-level detail in world space. This ensures that enlarging the fire (via elongating the central curve or adjusting control point radius) does not stretch noise effects. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is achieved through hardware acceleration and efficient lattice construction. Memory Complexity: Depends on the lattice detail and particle simulation state. Performance: Creates visually convincing real-time 3D fire without the artifacts of sprite systems or the computational costs of true photo-realistic simulation. Strengths: Bi-directional environmental macro-interactivity, easy design by content artists via 2D texture manipulation, dynamic interaction support. Limitations: Relies on particle simulation for macro deformation, which may require tuning for specific environments. Originated by A. Fuller, K. Krishnan, K. Mahrous, H. Hamann, and J. Joy from UC Davis. Presented at I3D 2007. The method allows content artists to easily modify fire shape and color by manipulating a 2D fire profile texture. It supports bi-directional interaction between fire and environment through efficient collision detection on the constructed lattice. name: Perlin-Worley Noise for Cloud Density
head: Base Density Noise, Base Density Noise Calculation, Perlin Noise Density Mapping, Perlin-Worley Noise, Procedural 3D Worley and Perlin Noise
body: This method generates the base volumetric density field for cloud rendering by combining the structural continuity of Perlin noise with the billowy, cellular detail of Worley noise. It differs from standard procedural noise by storing multiple frequency levels of Worley noise in separate texture channels to allow for high-frequency detail reconstruction during runtime remapping, rather than baking all detail into a single low-precision channel. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D coordinate \mathbf{P} and a packed RGBA32 noise texture. Output: A scalar density value for the cloud volume at \mathbf{P}. Data Structures The base density is stored in a 3D texture where each channel holds a distinct noise component. The layout is defined as follows: Red (R) Channel: Stores the low-frequency Perlin-Worley noise value. Green (G) Channel: Stores Worley noise at frequency level 1. Blue (B) Channel: Stores Worley noise at frequency level 2. Alpha (A) Channel: Stores Worley noise at frequency level 3. The texture must be tileable to allow sampling at varying frequencies without edge artifacts. A typical implementation uses a 128 \times 128 \times 128 texture, which is small enough for fast loading but large enough to contain 2–3 Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) levels. Algorithm Steps 1. Generate Perlin Fractal: Compute a low-frequency Perlin fractal noise value, PerlinFractal, using standard FBM summation. 2. Generate Worley Fractals: Compute three separate Worley fractal noise values at increasing frequencies: Worley1, Worley2, and Worley3. 3. Pack Noise: Store PerlinFractal in the Red channel and Worley1, Worley2, Worley3 in the Green, Blue, and Alpha channels, respectively. 4. Unpack and Combine Worley: Retrieve the G, B, and A channels from the texture. Compute the high-frequency Worley sum, WorleyHighFrequencies, using weighted summation: WorleyHighFrequencies = 0.625 \cdot Worley1 + 0.25 \cdot Worley2 + 0.125 \cdot Worley3 5. Remap Perlin-Worley: Retrieve the Red channel value, PerlinWorley. Add a configurable density offset, \Delta, to it. 6. Compute Base Noise: Remap the offset value such that its minimum becomes WorleyHighFrequencies and its maximum becomes 1: BaseNoise = \text{Remap}(PerlinWorley + \Delta, WorleyHighFrequencies, 1, 0, 1) Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeclouddensity(texture, p, densityoffset): """ Computes cloud density using Perlin-Worley noise stored in an RGBA texture. Args: texture: A 3D texture object with sample(x, y, z) returning (r, g, b, a). p: 3D vector coordinate. densityoffset: Configurable float added to Perlin-Worley value. Returns: float: The final base density value. """ # 1. Sample the packed noise texture (trilinear interpolation) r, g, b, a = texture.sample(p) # 2. Combine Worley frequencies worleyhighfreq = 0.625 g + 0.25 b + 0.125 a # 3. Get Perlin-Worley base value and add offset perlinworley = r + densityoffset # 4. Remap to [0, 1] using Worley sum as new minimum basenoise = remap(perlinworley, worleyhighfreq, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) return basenoise def remap(value, inmin, inmax, outmin, outmax): """Linear remapping function.""" if inmax == inmin: return outmin t = (value - inmin) / (inmax - inmin) t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) return outmin + t (outmax - outmin) Parameters Texture Size: 128 \times 128 \times 128 is cited as a practical minimum for web performance, though larger sizes allow for more FBM levels. Worley Weights: 0.625 for the lowest frequency, 0.25 for the middle, and 0.125 for the highest. Density Offset: A configurable scalar added to the Perlin-Worley value before remapping. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Storing noise in 8-bit channels limits detail. Using 32-bit floating-point textures (e.g., RFloat) is recommended to preserve the full range of [0, 1] values and avoid banding. Tileability: The texture must be tileable to support sampling at different frequencies without discontinuities. Channel Usage: The Alpha channel is used for Worley noise in the base density texture, whereas the detail density texture may leave the Alpha channel unused. Generates a voxel grid of cloud density using 3D Perlin noise, modulated by distance from the grid center to create a fluffy, rounded cloud shape. For each voxel, it calculates the Perlin noise value, computes the distance to the grid center, subtracts a scaled distance cover, clamps negatives to zero, multiplies by a base density, and applies a sharpness function to control edge fuzziness. Parameters include a noise seed (default 188), base density multiplier (default 5), and sharpness control (default 0.5). A refinement that combines multiple noise evaluations at different scales to produce higher-frequency detail and more defined structures. It selects multiple octave scales, evaluates Perlin noise at each scaled coordinate, sums the outputs, and uses the accumulated sum as the final density value. Memory: Requires storing a 3D texture. A 128 \times 128 \times 128 texture is cited as a practical size for web performance. Performance: Sampling is efficient for real-time rendering, particularly on web platforms where texture load times are constrained. Quality: The combination of Perlin (connectedness) and Worley (billowiness) produces natural-looking cloud structures. This technique originates from the Nubis cloud rendering engine used by Guerrilla Games. It is implemented in the Volumetric Clouds Tutorial, which provides source code for generating and unpacking these noise textures. The approach is also discussed in the context of efficient volumetric clouds for WebGL and three.js. name: Cartoon Cloud Density Generation
head: Procedural Cloud Shape
body: Cartoon Cloud Density Generation is a procedural method for generating stylized, cartoon-style cloud densities by combining independent noise sets for macro structure, body puffs, edge details, and flow, combined with geometric envelopes for specific cloud types. It differs from its sibling Perlin-Worley Noise for Cloud Density by relying on a multi-layered noise composition and explicit geometric shapes (lobes, clusters) rather than a single unified noise field, allowing for distinct stylized appearances consistent with voxel-based games. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D query point \mathbf{P} = (x, y, z), cloud type identifier typeid (integer 1–9), resolution parameters, and strength/detail/disturbance multipliers. Outputs: A scalar density value in [0.0, 1.0]. Data Structures: CartoonNoiseSet: Contains four independent sets of lattice gradient vectors: macrolattices, bodylattices, edgelattices, and flowlattices. These are pre-generated and stored for reuse. VolumeResult: Contains the resulting density and disturbance arrays as 8-bit linear data. Steps: 1. Generate Noise Fields: Compute four fractal value noise fields using the independent lattice sets. The frequencies are scaled by multipliers: macro at 0.10, body at 0.30, edge at 0.55, and flow at 0.25 \times \text{disturbance}. 2. Compute Base Shapes: Apply smoothstep to normalize and threshold the noise fields. smoothstep(t) is defined as 3t^2 - 2t^3 for t \in [0,1], clamped to [0,1]. Broad structure: \text{broad} = \text{smoothstep}\left(\frac{\text{macro} - 0.27}{0.52}\right). Puffs (body + macro mix): \text{puffs} = \text{smoothstep}\left(\frac{0.56 \times \text{macro} + 0.44 \times \text{body} - 0.37}{0.38}\right). Rim/Edge detail: \text{rim} = \text{smoothstep}\left(\frac{\text{edge} - 0.33}{0.48}\right). 3. Compute Fluffy Composite: Combine the base shapes into a unified "fluffy" density field. \text{fluffy} = \text{clip}(0.62 \times \text{puffs} + 0.23 \times \text{broad} + 0.15 \times \text{rim}, 0.0, 1.0). 4. Compute Vertical Profiles: Define Gaussian vertical profiles based on the z coordinate. These determine the thickness and height of different cloud layers. Thin (high altitude): \text{thin} = \exp\left(-\left(\frac{z + 0.04}{0.13}\right)^2\right). Middle: \text{middle} = \exp\left(-\left(\frac{z + 0.10}{0.30}\right)^2\right). Low: \text{low} = \exp\left(-\left(\frac{z + 0.28}{0.23}\right)^2\right). 5. Compute Horizontal Footprint and Clusters: If the cloud has a finite boundary, use broadfootprint(x, y, variation); otherwise, use ones (infinite). Generate 3D lobe clusters using lobecluster(x, y, z, variation) and wisp clusters using wispcluster(x, y, z, variation). These use the Soft Union function. 6. Combine Based on Cloud Type (typeid): The density is assembled differently for each of the 9 cloud types. Type 1 (Cirrus): \text{density} = \text{thin} \times \text{wisps} \times \text{smoothstep}\left(\frac{0.72 \times \text{body} + 0.28 \times \text{edge} - 0.56}{0.30}\right). Type 9 (Cumulus): \text{base} = \text{CumulusBaseShape}(x, y, z), \text{surface} = \text{smoothstep}\left(\frac{0.58 \times \text{fluffy} + 0.42 \times \text{broad} - 0.20}{0.70}\right), \text{density} = \text{SoftUnion}(\text{cluster} \times (0.22 + 0.78 \times \text{fluffy}), 0.68 \times \text{base} \times (0.30 + 0.70 \times \text{surface})). Cumulonimbus (Else branch): \text{anvil} = \text{footprint} \times \exp\left(-\left(\frac{z - 0.48}{0.16}\right)^2\right), \text{density} = \text{SoftUnion}(\text{cluster}, 0.82 \times \text{anvil}) \times (0.40 + 0.60 \times \text{fluffy}). 7. Final Shaping and Quantization: Apply smoothstep to maintain continuous density and avoid concentric shell artifacts. Quantize into 5 discrete cartoon levels (mapped to 0-1 range). Blend stepped and shaped densities, apply strength and rim/detail modulation, then clip to [0.0, 1.0]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def smoothstep(t): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) return 3.0 t2 - 2.0 t3 def softunion(fields): total = max(0.0, min(1.0, sum(fields))) return max(0.0, min(1.0, 1.0 - math.exp(-1.12 total))) def lobecluster(x, y, z, variation): # Computes weighted sum of Gaussian lobes using Soft Union fieldsum = 0.0 for spec in variation.lobes: dx, dy, dz = spec[0] - x, spec[1] - y, spec[2] - z w = spec[6] fieldsum += w math.exp(-(dx2 + dy2 + dz2)) return max(0.0, min(1.0, 1.0 - math.exp(-1.18 fieldsum))) def fractalvaluenoise(x, y, z, lattices, freqmult): # Not given in the sources; uses parent gradient assignment, dot product, smoothing, interpolation, and hashing # Scales lattice frequencies by freqmult and sums octaves return 0.0 def cartoonclouddensity(x, y, z, typeid, strength, detail, disturbance, variation, finiteboundary): # 1. Generate noise fields macro = fractalvaluenoise(x, y, z, variation.macrolattices, detail 0.10) body = fractalvaluenoise(x, y, z, variation.bodylattices, detail 0.30) edge = fractalvaluenoise(x, y, z, variation.edgelattices, detail 0.55) flow = fractalvaluenoise(x, y, z, variation.flowlattices, disturbance 0.25) # 2. Compute base shapes broad = smoothstep((macro - 0.27) / 0.52) puffs = smoothstep((0.56 macro + 0.44 body - 0.37) / 0.38) rim = smoothstep((edge - 0.33) / 0.48) # 3. Compute fluffy composite fluffy = max(0.0, min(1.0, 0.62 puffs + 0.23 broad + 0.15 rim)) # 4. Compute vertical profiles thin = math.exp(-((z + 0.04) / 0.13) 2) middle = math.exp(-((z + 0.10) / 0.30) 2) low = math.exp(-((z + 0.28) / 0.23) 2) # 5. Compute horizontal footprint and clusters footprint = variation.broadfootprint(x, y) if finiteboundary else 1.0 cluster = lobecluster(x, y, z, variation) wisps = lobecluster(x, y, z, variation.wispspecs) # 6. Combine based on cloud type if typeid == 1: # Cirrus density = thin wisps smoothstep((0.72 body + 0.28 edge - 0.56) / 0.30) elif typeid == 9: # Cumulus base = variation.cumulusbaseshape(x, y, z) surface = smoothstep((0.58 fluffy + 0.42 broad - 0.20) / 0.70) density = softunion([cluster (0.22 + 0.78 fluffy), 0.68 base (0.30 + 0.70 surface)]) else: # Cumulonimbus anvil = footprint math.exp(-((z - 0.48) / 0.16) 2) density = softunion([cluster, 0.82 anvil]) (0.40 + 0.60 fluffy) # 7. Final shaping and quantization shaped = smoothstep((density - 0.07) / 0.62) stepped = math.floor(max(0.0, min(1.0, shaped)) 4.0 + 0.20) / 4.0 return max(0.0, min(1.0, (0.12 stepped + 0.88 shaped) strength (0.94 + 0.06 detail rim))) Formulas: Soft Union: Used to merge multiple density fields smoothly. S(F1, F2, \dots) = \text{clip}\left(1 - \exp\left(-1.12 \times \text{clip}\left(\sum Fi, 0, 1\right)\right), 0, 1\right). Lobe Cluster: A specific instance of soft union for geometric lobes. L = \text{clip}\left(1 - \exp\left(-1.18 \times \sum (wi \times \exp(-\text{dist}i^2))\right), 0, 1\right). Parameters: Detail Multiplier: 0.10 (macro), 0.30 (body), 0.55 (edge), 0.25 disturbance (flow). Strength: Typically in range [0.0, 2.0]. Disturbance: Typically in range [0.0, 2.0]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concentric Shells: To avoid artifacts in volume rendering, the texture body must maintain continuous density. Quantization should only be applied in the final shading stage if needed. Boundary Conditions: For finite cloud regions, the footprint function must handle boundaries to prevent infinite column artifacts along the Z-axis. Blocky Volumetric Clouds is a procedural rendering technique that generates cartoon-style cloud densities by sampling a 2D texture at the cloud layer's Y-coordinate, creating a distinct "blocky" appearance compared to noise-based realistic clouds. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric clouds in a style consistent with voxel-based games while providing simplified lighting calculations. It differs from its sibling Cartoon Cloud Density Generation by relying on a static 2D density map rather than multi-octave noise functions for the base structure. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces distinct, stylized cloud shapes suitable for non-photorealistic rendering. The separation of macro, body, and edge noise allows for fine-tuned artistic control. Limitations: More complex to implement than single-noise methods. The geometric clusters require careful tuning of parameters for different cloud types. When to Use: Stylized games, voxel-based environments, or any application requiring non-realistic, cartoon-like clouds. Originated from procedural generation techniques in game development, specifically for creating consistent cloud shapes in voxel-based games like Minecraft. name: Blocky Volumetric Clouds
head: Blocky Cloud Density
body: Blocky Volumetric Clouds is a procedural rendering technique that generates cartoon-style cloud densities by sampling a 2D texture at the cloud layer's Y-coordinate, creating a distinct "blocky" appearance compared to noise-based realistic clouds. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric clouds in a style consistent with voxel-based games while providing simplified lighting calculations. It differs from its sibling Cartoon Cloud Density Generation by relying on a static 2D density map rather than multi-octave noise functions for the base structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: playerPos (ray direction vector), cameraPosition (world position of the camera), frameTimeCounter (time uniform), frameCounter (integer frame counter), fragCoord (fragment screen coordinates), cloudsShadowcasterDir (direction vector for shadow casting). Output: A tuple (invThickness, invBrightness) containing transmittance and lighting contribution. Data Structures: BLOCKYCLOUDTEXTURE: A 2D texture containing the cloud density map. The alpha channel is sampled for density. Constants: CLOUDBOTTOMY, CLOUDTOPY (defined as CLOUDBOTTOMY + 12.0), CLOUDSQUALITY (number of steps). Steps: 1. Sample Density for Ray Limiting: Calculate the player's direction length in the XZ plane: playerLen = length(playerPos.xz). Normalize playerPos by playerLen. Sample the cloud density at a position 20 units ahead of the camera: distSample = sampleBlockyCloud(cameraPosition + normalize(playerPos) 20.0). Compute distLimitAmount = 1.0 - pow3(1.0 - distSample). Scale the ray direction length: playerPos = min(playerLen, mix(128.0 16.0, 20.0 16.0, distLimitAmount)). 2. Normalize Step Vector: Create a step vector stepVec equal to playerPos. Normalize the XZ components relative to the Y component: stepVec.xz /= abs(stepVec.y). Set the Y component to the sign of the original Y: stepVec.y = sign(stepVec.y). This ensures the ray moves exactly ±1 unit in Y per step in the XZ plane. 3. Determine Y Bounds: Start at the camera's Y position. Clamp the start Y to the cloud layer: posStartY = clamp(cameraPosition.y, CLOUDBOTTOMY, CLOUDTOPY). Calculate the end Y by moving 1000 units in the direction of stepVec.y: posEndY = clamp(posStartY + sign(stepVec.y) 1000.0, CLOUDBOTTOMY, CLOUDTOPY). If posStartY == posEndY, return vec2(1.0, 0.0) (no intersection). 4. Clamp to Foreground: Calculate maxY = abs(playerPos.y). Clamp the start and end Y positions relative to the camera to prevent marching through the ground/foreground: posStartY = clamp(posStartY - cameraPosition.y, -maxY, maxY) + cameraPosition.y and posEndY = clamp(posEndY - cameraPosition.y, -maxY, maxY) + cameraPosition.y. If posStartY == posEndY, return vec2(1.0, 0.0). 5. Calculate Step Vector and Density Multiplier: Calculate the 3D start position: pos = cameraPosition + stepVec abs(posStartY - cameraPosition.y). Calculate the 3D end position: endPos = pos + stepVec abs(posEndY - posStartY). Compute the step vector for the loop: stepVec = pos - endPos. Divide by quality: stepVec /= CLOUDSQUALITY. Compute density multiplier: densityMult = length(stepVec) -0.25. Set current position to endPos. 6. Apply Dithering: Calculate Bayer dither: dither = bayer64(glFragCoord.xy). Offset dither for temporal stability: dither = fract(dither + 1.61803398875 mod(float(frameCounter), 3600.0)). Offset position: pos += stepVec (dither - 0.5). 7. Ray March Loop: Initialize invThickness = 1.0 and invBrightness = 0.0. Loop i from 0 to CLOUDSQUALITY - 1: Sample density: density = sampleBlockyCloud(pos). Calculate inverse density factor: invDensity = exp(density densityMult). Update thickness: invThickness = invDensity. Sample shadow/light: sampleUp = sampleBlockyCloud(pos + cloudsShadowcasterDir). Update brightness: invBrightness = mix(invBrightness, sampleUp, 1.0 - sqrt(invDensity)). Advance position: pos += stepVec. 8. Return Results: Return vec2(invThickness, invBrightness). Helper Function: sampleBlockyCloud Input: pos (vec3). 1. If pos.y < CLOUDBOTTOMY or pos.y > CLOUDBOTTOMY + 12.0, return 0.0. 2. Calculate texture coordinates: texPos = pos.xz. 3. Offset X by time: texPos.x -= frameTimeCounter 3. 4. Scale: texPos = 0.00025. 5. Sample texture: return texture2D(BLOCKYCLOUDTEXTURE, texPos, 0).a. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Inverse Brightness: invBrightness = mix(invBrightness, sampleUp, 1.0 - \sqrt{e^{d \cdot L \cdot -0.25}}). Step Vector Y: stepVec.y = \pm 1, stepVec.xz = stepVec.xz / |stepVec.y|. Parameters: CLOUDBOTTOMY: Lower Y-boundary of the cloud layer. CLOUDTOPY: Upper Y-boundary, calculated as CLOUDBOTTOMY + 12.0. BLOCKYCLOUDTEXTURE: 2D texture containing the cloud density map. frameTimeCounter: Time uniform used to animate the cloud texture horizontally. CLOUDSQUALITY: Number of ray-marching steps. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Vanishing: The ray length shrinking mechanism (Step 1) reduces artifacts when inside clouds but relies on a cloud being nearby. If no cloud is nearby, the optimization may fail or behave unexpectedly. No Intersection: If the ray's Y-start and Y-end are identical after clamping (e.g., looking away from clouds or inside a solid block), the function returns vec2(1.0, 0.0). Division by Zero: If stepVec.y is 0, normalization fails. The source implies this is handled by the bail-out conditions or input constraints. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is CLOUDSQUALITY. Each step involves two texture samples and basic arithmetic. Performance: The method is lightweight compared to full volumetric noise generation, relying on a single 2D texture lookup per step. Strengths: Simple implementation, consistent "blocky" aesthetic, low computational cost. Limitations: Lacks the organic detail of noise-based clouds; lighting is simplified; the ray limiting optimization is noted as not working very well for this specific blocky style. name: Line-Based Pipe Volume Generation
body: Generates a 3D volume density field along predefined line paths using OpenSimplex noise to create pipe-like cave structures, which are later meshed via marching cubes. It differs from general noise-based density generation by restricting the noise evaluation domain to the vicinity of parametric line segments, effectively carving volumetric tubes through space rather than filling a bounding box with uniform noise patterns. The method builds on the shared gradient assignment, dot product, fade function, interpolation, and hashing principles of Noise-based Density Generation. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of line segments defined by nodes and properties; voxel grid dimensions (voxel.numVertex); noise parameters (noiseIntensity, noiseScale, smoothingFactor, frequency, lacunarity); boolean isWorldSpaceNoise. Output: A 3D density field stored in pointsBuffer (ComputeBuffer), which is subsequently processed by a marching cubes shader to produce a triangle mesh. Data Structures The method relies on three primary ComputeBuffers: 1. pointsBuffer: Size voxel.totalVertex. Stride 16 bytes. Layout: Vector4 (x, y, z, density). 2. linePropBuffer: Size lineGenerator.line.Count. Stride 52 bytes. Contains properties for each line segment. 3. nodePositionBuffer: Size lineGenerator.node.Count. Stride 20 bytes. Contains node positions. Algorithm Steps 1. Thread Group Calculation: Calculate the number of thread groups per axis based on the voxel vertex count. The dimension is ceil(numVertex / 8) + 1, where 8 is the number of threads per group. 2. Buffer Initialization: Populate linePropBuffer and nodePositionBuffer with current line generator data. 3. Shader Configuration: Set the following shader inputs: Buffers: nodeProps (from nodePositionBuffer), lineProps (from linePropBuffer). Scalars: isWorldSpaceNoise, noiseIntensity, noiseScale, smoothingFactor, frequency, lacunarity. Vector: offset (used for chunked generation). 4. Density Computation: Dispatch the density shader. For each voxel vertex, the shader evaluates OpenSimplex noise. If isWorldSpaceNoise is false, the query point is converted to the local coordinate system of the nearest line segment. 5. Smoothing: Apply the smoothingFactor to the resulting density values to ensure smooth transitions. 6. Meshing: The resulting density field is passed to a marching cubes shader (marchingCubeShader) with an isoLevel to generate triangles. Pseudocode The following pseudocode represents the CPU-side setup and dispatch logic derived from the source. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. Calculate thread groups per axis numgroupsx = math.ceil(voxel.numvertex.x / NUMTHREADSPERGROUP) + 1 numgroupsy = math.ceil(voxel.numvertex.y / NUMTHREADSPERGROUP) + 1 numgroupsz = math.ceil(voxel.numvertex.z / NUMTHREADSPERGROUP) + 1 # 2. Prepare buffers lineprops = linegenerator.getlineprops() nodepositions = linegenerator.getnodes() # 3. Initialize density field densityfield = [0.0] voxel.totalvertex # 4. Evaluate noise and compute density (simulating GPU dispatch) for k in range(numgroupsz): for j in range(numgroupsy): for i in range(numgroupsx): offset = Vector3(i voxel.boundaryworldpos.x, j voxel.boundaryworldpos.y, k voxel.boundaryworldpos.z) # Dispatch density shader with offset and line/node buffers # The shader evaluates OpenSimplex noise for each vertex in the chunk # If isWorldSpaceNoise is False, coordinates convert to line local space for idx in range(voxel.totalvertex): pos = Vector3(voxel.vertexpositions[idx]) querypos = pos + offset # OpenSimplex noise evaluation using parent principles noiseval = simplexnoise(querypos, lineprops, nodepositions) densityfield[idx] = noiseval voxel.noiseintensity # 5. Marching Cubes # Marching cubes algorithm to extract iso-surface triangles = marchingcubes(densityfield, voxel.numvoxel, isolevel) # 6. Retrieve and Construct Mesh numtris = len(triangles) meshvertices = [] meshindices = [] for i in range(numtris): for j in range(3): meshindices.append(i 3 + j) meshvertices.append(triangles[i][j]) mesh = createmesh(meshvertices, meshindices) mesh.recalculatenormals() return mesh Edge Cases and Pitfalls 0th Line Index: A boundary/edge case issue occurs specifically at the 0th line index during pipe volume generation. Coordinate Systems: If isWorldSpaceNoise is disabled, coordinates are automatically converted to the line's local coordinate system. Incorrect implementation of this conversion may lead to artifacts. Complexity: Thread group dimensions are calculated as ceil(numVertex / 8) + 1 per axis. Performance: The source logs indicate performance measurement in seconds, but specific hardware metrics are not provided. Strengths: Efficiently generates tubular structures (caves/pipes) without needing to evaluate noise across the entire volume uniformly. Limitations: Dependent on the quality of the underlying OpenSimplex noise implementation; potential artifacts at line boundaries or index 0. The project, lineBasedCaveSimplex, was developed as a variation of procedural cave generation using line data for paths and OpenSimplex noise for volume data. name: Voxel Noise/Checkerboard Application
head: Checker Pattern, Checkerboard Cell Noise, Procedural Voxel Noise, checker
body: Voxel Noise/Checkerboard Application generates a deterministic, binary 3D checkerboard pattern by evaluating the parity of the integer grid coordinates of the input position. It serves as a high-frequency, low-cost procedural density or material mask, distinct from smooth gradient noise methods like Perlin or Simplex by providing sharp, discontinuous transitions between cells. Unlike Perlin-Worley Noise for Cloud Density which blends distances, this method relies on discrete integer arithmetic to switch between two states. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D query position \mathbf{P} = (x, y, z) and a frequency scale factor s. Output: A scalar value V \in \{-1.0, 1.0\} (or \{0.0, 1.0\} depending on implementation) representing the checkerboard state. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method relies on integer arithmetic on the input coordinates. Steps: 1. Scale and Integerize: Compute the integer grid coordinates (ix, iy, iz) by scaling the input position by the frequency s and truncating to integers. ix = \lfloor x \cdot s \rfloor, \quad iy = \lfloor y \cdot s \rfloor, \quad iz = \lfloor z \cdot s \rfloor Note: Some implementations use casting (int) which truncates toward zero, while others use floor which truncates toward negative infinity. For positive coordinates, these are identical. For negative coordinates, floor preserves the grid alignment relative to the origin, whereas (int) may shift the pattern. 2. Compute Parity: Calculate the sum of the integer coordinates. S = ix + iy + iz 3. Determine State: Return the binary value based on the parity of S. V = \begin{cases} 1.0 & \text{if } S \pmod 2 == 0 \\ -1.0 & \text{if } S \pmod 2 \neq 0 \end{cases} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelcheckerboard(pos: Vector3, scale: float) -> float: # Step 1: Scale and integerize coordinates # Using floor to ensure consistent grid alignment for negative coordinates ix = floor(pos.x scale) iy = floor(pos.y scale) iz = floor(pos.z scale) # Step 2: Compute parity # Sum of integer coordinates coordsum = ix + iy + iz # Step 3: Return binary value based on parity if coordsum % 2 == 0: return 1.0 else: return -1.0 Parameters: scale (float): Frequency multiplier. Typical values depend on the desired voxel size relative to the scene units. Not given in the sources. pos (Vector3): Input 3D position. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Discontinuities: The function is discontinuous at integer boundaries. This is intentional for the checkerboard effect but can cause aliasing if sampled at high frequencies without mipmapping or if used in ray marching without proper step size control. Negative Coordinates: As noted, the choice between floor and truncation (int) affects the pattern's phase for negative coordinates. floor is generally preferred for mathematical consistency in grid-based systems. Zero Scale: Division by zero or infinite scaling if scale is 0. Guard against scale <= 0. A spatial shader implementation that decodes terrain material IDs from vertex colors and renders textured biome materials using Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise for variation. It uses vertex colors to store material IDs instead of separate texture lookups or uniform arrays, allowing per-vertex material variation. Parameters: texturescale (default 0.08), terrainbrightness (default 1.0), texturedetailstrength (default 0.65), slopedarkening (default 0.08), largevariationstrength (default 0.10). Mechanism: It employs a hash function for noise, value noise interpolation, and an FBM loop with 4 octaves to generate variation. Material IDs for Grass, Clay, Stone, Iron, Path, Sand, Sulfur, and Volcanic Stone are decoded from vertex color channels. Comparison: Unlike the pure binary checkerboard, this variant integrates noise for organic variation and uses vertex attributes for material selection, making it suitable for complex terrain rendering rather than simple binary masking. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. The operation involves basic arithmetic (multiplication, floor, addition, modulo) and a conditional branch. It is significantly faster than gradient-based noise functions which require multiple dot products and interpolations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No lookup tables or textures are required for the basic checkerboard pattern. Strengths: Extremely fast evaluation; deterministic; no memory bandwidth overhead; ideal for binary masks or high-frequency detail where smoothness is not required. Limitations: Discontinuous; prone to aliasing at high frequencies; lacks the organic blending characteristics of gradient noise. When to use: When a sharp, grid-aligned binary pattern is needed (e.g., voxel terrain base layers, checkerboard masks). When not to use: When smooth transitions or organic variation are required; use Perlin-Worley Noise for Cloud Density or Noise-based Density Generation instead. The checkerboard pattern is a fundamental concept in computer graphics and procedural generation, often used as a base for voxel-based worlds. The specific implementation described here, evaluating the parity of integer grid coordinates, is a standard technique for generating binary 3D checkerboards efficiently. It appears in various voxel engine implementations and procedural terrain systems, such as those found in open-source voxel games and engines. The integration of such patterns with vertex-colored material decoding represents a modern optimization in shader-based terrain rendering. name: Noise Application
head: Poisson/Normal Noise Injection, Poisson Noise Modeling for Projection Data
body: Noise Application simulates realistic detector noise in projection data, primarily for X-ray computed tomography (CT) and point cloud processing. It differs from its siblings, which often focus on procedural density generation or visual effects, by modeling statistical photon counting statistics (Poisson) or electrical noise (Normal/Gaussian) to validate reconstruction algorithms against realistic artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Projection data (attenuation values on a negative logarithmic scale) or point cloud vertices; noise mode ('poisson' or 'normal'); noise parameter (norm factor or standard deviation). Outputs: Noisy projection data or displaced point cloud; optional noise vector e for error analysis. Data Structures: Projection Data: 2D array of floating-point values representing line integrals. Point Cloud: Tensor of shape (N, 3) representing vertex coordinates. Steps: 1. Mode Selection: Determine if noise is 'poisson' or 'normal'. 2. Poisson Noise Application (X-ray Projections): Convert projection data from the negative logarithmic scale to photon counts. Let p be the projection data. The photon count c is derived via exponentiation: c = \exp(-p). Apply the floor function to ensure integer values: c{int} = \lfloor c \rfloor. Sample a Poisson distribution using each pixel's intensity c{int} as the mean. Let ni be the sampled value for pixel i: ni \sim \text{Poisson}(c{int, i}). Scale the sampled data back to the negative logarithmic scale: p{noisy} = -\ln(ni). Calculate the noise vector e as the difference between the noisy and clean projections in the forward projection space, or directly in the log domain depending on implementation specifics. The relative noise level \rho is calculated as: \rho = \frac{\|e\|2}{\|A\bar{x}\|2} where e is the noise vector added to the forward projection, A is the forward projection operator, and \bar{x} is the ground truth volume. 3. Normal Noise Application (General/Point Cloud): If mode is 'normal', sample from a Normal distribution with the input image/points as mean \mu and parameter \sigma as standard deviation: y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2). For point clouds, calculate the diagonal length d of the oriented bounding box. Generate random offsets bounded by \pm d \times \text{coeff}, where \text{coeff} is sampled uniformly from [0.003, 0.01]. Apply the offset to the point cloud vertices. Parameters: Noise Levels (Poisson): 0.25% (high-quality scan baseline), 1% (moderate), 5% (high). Mode: String, 'poisson' or 'normal'. Parameter: Float, norm factor for Poisson noise or standard deviation for Normal noise. Coeff (Point Cloud): Scaling factor for noise magnitude, typically [0.003, 0.01]. Pitfalls: Poisson noise modeling assumes a single energy spectrum. Real laboratory X-ray sources provide a wider spectrum of energies, leading to multiple Poisson distributions with different means. Additionally, detectors exhibit electrical (Gaussian) noise, making the single Poisson model an approximation. Precision issues may arise when converting between log scale and photon counts for very low intensity values. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.stats import poisson, norm def applynoise(projectiondata, mode='poisson', param=0.01): """ Apply noise to projection data or point cloud. Args: projectiondata: np.ndarray, projection data (log scale) or point cloud (N,3) mode: str, 'poisson' or 'normal' param: float, noise level or standard deviation Returns: noisydata: np.ndarray noisevector: np.ndarray (only for Poisson) """ if mode == 'poisson': # Convert from negative log scale to photon counts photoncounts = np.exp(-projectiondata) # Floor to ensure integers photoncountsint = np.floor(photoncounts) # Sample Poisson distribution noisycounts = poisson.rvs(photoncountsint) # Convert back to negative log scale # Handle zero counts to avoid log(0) noisycounts = np.maximum(noisycounts, 1) noisyprojection = -np.log(noisycounts) # Calculate noise vector e for relative noise calculation # e is the difference in the forward projection space (photon counts) noisevector = noisycounts - photoncountsint return noisyprojection, noisevector elif mode == 'normal': # Sample from Normal distribution noisydata = norm.rvs(loc=projectiondata, scale=param) return noisydata, None else: raise ValueError("Mode must be 'poisson' or 'normal'") A data augmentation technique that adds random displacement noise to point cloud vertices to simulate misalignment, noise, or outliers for training robustness. It differs from X-ray noise by operating in 3D geometric space rather than projection intensity space. Choose this when training point cloud classification or segmentation models to improve robustness to sensor noise. It uses an oriented bounding box diagonal to scale the noise magnitude. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels or points, as each element is processed independently. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the noisy data and noise vector. Measured Performance: Noise levels of 0.25%, 1%, and 5% are used to simulate high-quality, moderate, and high noise respectively, based on qualitative comparison with real CT scanner data. Strengths: Provides realistic noise models for validating reconstruction algorithms; simple to implement. Limitations: Poisson model is an approximation; does not account for multi-energy spectra or electrical noise fully. Originated in the context of X-ray computed tomography (CT) reconstruction, where realistic noise models are essential for evaluating reconstruction algorithms. The Poisson noise model is based on the statistical nature of photon counting in X-ray detectors. The method is implemented in various CT reconstruction frameworks and research papers. name: Amplitude Distribution Estimation
head: Analysis Tools for Noise Quality, Noise Amplitude Distribution Estimation, Noise Quality Analysis Tools, Yoon et al. Noise Quality Metrics
body: Amplitude Distribution Estimation is a statistical method used to evaluate the quality of procedural noise functions by comparing the histogram of sampled noise values against a theoretical Gaussian distribution. It solves the problem of verifying whether a noise generator produces values with the correct statistical spread and shape, which is critical for visual realism in volume rendering and optimization procedures. It is distinguished from spatial analysis methods like the Autocorrelation Periodicity Test and Band-Pass Test for Noise by focusing exclusively on the fidelity of amplitude values rather than spatial frequency characteristics or periodicity. Inputs: A procedural noise function N(\mathbf{P}) capable of evaluating noise at any point \mathbf{P} in the domain. A set of query points \{\mathbf{P}1, \mathbf{P}2, \dots, \mathbf{P}M\} sampled from the domain. The expected variance \sigma^2{expected} of the noise function, if known analytically (e.g., for standard Perlin noise). If unknown, the variance is estimated from the samples. The number of histogram bins B. Outputs: A histogram H representing the frequency distribution of the sampled noise values. A reference Gaussian curve G(x) defined by the mean \mu and variance \sigma^2 (either expected or estimated). Data Structures: Histogram Array: An array of size B storing integer counts for each bin. Sample Array: An array of size M storing the scalar noise values vi = N(\mathbf{P}i). Gaussian Parameters: Scalar values for mean \mu and variance \sigma^2. Steps: 1. Sampling: Evaluate the noise function N(\mathbf{P}) at M distinct points \mathbf{P}i. The points should be distributed uniformly across the domain of interest to avoid bias. vi = N(\mathbf{P}i) \quad \text{for } i = 1 \dots M 2. Variance Estimation (if needed): If \sigma^2{expected} is not provided, calculate the sample variance \sigma^2{est} from the values vi: \mu = \frac{1}{M} \sum{i=1}^{M} vi \sigma^2{est} = \frac{1}{M-1} \sum{i=1}^{M} (vi - \mu)^2 Let \sigma^2 be \sigma^2{expected} if known, otherwise \sigma^2{est}. 3. Histogram Construction: Initialize an array H of size B with zeros. Determine the range [min\v, max\v] of the sampled values vi. Map each value vi to a bin index bi: bi = \left\lfloor \frac{vi - min\v}{max\v - min\v} \times B \right\rfloor Clamp bi to [0, B-1]. Increment H[bi]. 4. Reference Gaussian Calculation: Define the probability density function (PDF) of a Gaussian distribution with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2: G(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} e^{-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}} Evaluate G(x) at the center of each histogram bin to generate the reference curve. 5. Comparison: Plot the normalized histogram (counts divided by M \times \text{bin\width}) alongside the reference Gaussian curve G(x). Visual inspection or a statistical test (such as the Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test) determines the quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def estimateamplitudedistribution(noisefunc, points, numbins, expectedvariance=None): """ Estimates the amplitude distribution of a noise function. Args: noisefunc: Function taking a point P and returning a scalar noise value. points: List of points P to sample. numbins: Number of bins for the histogram. expectedvariance: Optional float. If None, variance is estimated from samples. Returns: histogram: List of counts for each bin. gaussianref: List of Gaussian PDF values for each bin center. bincenters: List of x-coordinates for the bin centers. """ # Step 1: Sampling samples = [noisefunc(p) for p in points] m = len(samples) if m == 0: return [], [], [] # Step 2: Variance Estimation meanval = sum(samples) / m if expectedvariance is not None: variance = expectedvariance else: # Sample variance variance = sum((v - meanval) 2 for v in samples) / (m - 1) # Guard against zero variance (constant noise) if variance == 0: variance = 1e-9 # Step 3: Histogram Construction minval = min(samples) maxval = max(samples) # Handle edge case where all samples are identical if minval == maxval: histogram = [0] numbins histogram[0] = m # Gaussian reference at the constant value gaussianref = [0] numbins gaussianref[0] = 1.0 / math.sqrt(2 math.pi variance) bincenters = [minval] numbins return histogram, gaussianref, bincenters binwidth = (maxval - minval) / numbins histogram = [0] numbins for v in samples: # Map value to bin index binidx = int((v - minval) / binwidth) # Clamp to last bin for maxval if binidx >= numbins: binidx = numbins - 1 histogram[binidx] += 1 # Step 4: Reference Gaussian Calculation gaussianref = [] bincenters = [] for i in range(numbins): # Center of the bin center = minval + (i + 0.5) binwidth bincenters.append(center) # Gaussian PDF exponent = -((center - meanval) 2) / (2 variance) pdfval = (1.0 / math.sqrt(2 math.pi variance)) math.exp(exponent) gaussianref.append(pdfval) return histogram, gaussianref, bincenters Parameters: M (Number of samples): Not given in the sources. Typically large enough to form a smooth histogram (e.g., 10^4 to 10^6). B (Number of bins): Not given in the sources. Typically 32–128 for visual comparison. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Variance: If the noise function is constant, variance is zero. The Gaussian PDF becomes undefined. A guard value or special handling is required. Boundary Bias: If the noise function has hard clamping or non-periodic boundaries, samples near the edges may skew the distribution. Uniform sampling over the interior is preferred. Anisotropy: Some noise functions (e.g., standard Perlin) exhibit axis-aligned anisotropy, which may affect the uniformity of samples if the sampling grid is aligned with the axes. A statistical method that quantifies the deviation between the observed histogram and the expected Gaussian distribution using the Chi-Square statistic. It provides a numerical quality score rather than just a visual plot. A method that analyzes the spatial correlation of noise samples to detect repeating patterns. It complements amplitude estimation by checking for spatial randomness. A method that measures the spectral bandwidth of the noise by comparing the noise to a down-up-sampled version. It ensures the noise has the correct frequency content, which is distinct from amplitude distribution. A frequency-domain method that averages periodograms to estimate the power spectrum. It is used for spectral analysis rather than amplitude distribution. Time Complexity: O(M), where M is the number of samples. Each sample requires one noise evaluation and constant-time histogram binning. Memory Complexity: O(B + M), where B is the number of histogram bins and M is the number of samples (to store the samples if needed for variance calculation). Strengths: Simple to implement; provides immediate visual feedback on the statistical quality of the noise; effective for detecting non-Gaussian artifacts in noise generators. Limitations: Does not detect spatial artifacts (periodicity, anisotropy) on its own; requires a large number of samples for accurate histogram estimation; sensitive to the choice of bin count. When to use: During the development and optimization of new noise functions to ensure they match the expected statistical properties (e.g., Gaussian amplitude distribution). When not to use: When spatial coherence or frequency content is the primary concern; use Band-Pass Test or Autocorrelation Test instead. Amplitude distribution estimation is part of a suite of analysis tools presented by Yoon et al. [YLC04, YL08] for measuring the quality of procedural noise within optimization procedures. These tools include the Chi-Square goodness-of-fit test, autocorrelation periodicity detection, and band-pass tests. The specific method of estimating amplitude distribution via histogram comparison with a Gaussian reference is described in surveys of procedural noise functions. It is used to verify that noise functions like Perlin noise, sparse convolution noise, and wavelet noise exhibit the expected statistical properties. name: Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test for Noise
head: Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test for Noise Quality, Chi-Square Noise Quality Metric
body: The Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test for Noise is a statistical method used to measure the quality of the amplitude distribution of a procedural noise function. It operates by comparing the histogram of sampled noise values against an expected theoretical distribution (typically Gaussian). It is distinguished from sibling methods like the Autocorrelation Periodicity Test and Band-Pass Test by focusing exclusively on the statistical fidelity of the amplitude values rather than spatial frequency characteristics or periodicity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N noise samples \{x1, x2, \dots, xN\} drawn from the noise function. Input: A target probability distribution (typically Gaussian) with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2. Output: A chi-square statistic \chi^2 indicating the deviation between the observed histogram and the expected distribution. Data Structures: Histogram: A binning of the noise samples. Let B be the number of bins. Observed Counts: An array Oi for i=1 \dots B, where Oi is the count of samples falling into bin i. Expected Counts: An array Ei for i=1 \dots B, where Ei is the expected number of samples in bin i based on the target distribution. Steps: 1. Sample: Collect N independent samples from the noise function over the domain of interest. 2. Define Bins: Partition the range of possible noise values into B equal-width bins. 3. Compute Observed Counts: For each sample xj, determine which bin i it falls into and increment Oi. 4. Compute Expected Counts: Calculate the probability pi that a random variable from the target distribution falls into bin i. Set Ei = N \cdot pi. If the variance is known, use it directly. If not, estimate the variance from the samples. 5. Calculate Statistic: Compute the chi-square statistic: \chi^2 = \sum{i=1}^{B} \frac{(Oi - Ei)^2}{Ei} 6. Interpret: A lower \chi^2 value indicates a better fit to the expected distribution. The degrees of freedom are typically B - 1 - k, where k is the number of estimated parameters (e.g., k=2 for mean and variance). Parameters: Number of Bins (B): Not given in the sources. Target Distribution: Typically Gaussian. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Bins: If Ei = 0, the term is undefined. Bins with very low expected counts should be merged or excluded. Sample Size: N must be sufficiently large for the chi-square approximation to be valid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def chisquarenoisequality(samples, numbins, targetmean, targetvariance): """ Computes the chi-square goodness-of-fit statistic for noise amplitude distribution. Args: samples: List of float noise values. numbins: Integer number of histogram bins. targetmean: Float mean of the expected Gaussian distribution. targetvariance: Float variance of the expected Gaussian distribution. Returns: Float chi-square statistic. """ import math n = len(samples) if n == 0: return 0.0 # Determine range for binning minval = min(samples) maxval = max(samples) # Add small epsilon to avoid edge issues minval -= 1e-9 maxval += 1e-9 binwidth = (maxval - minval) / numbins # Initialize observed counts observed = [0] numbins # Populate histogram for x in samples: binindex = int((x - minval) / binwidth) # Clamp to last bin if exactly on boundary if binindex == numbins: binindex = numbins - 1 observed[binindex] += 1 # Calculate expected counts based on Gaussian PDF expected = [0.0] numbins for i in range(numbins): # Probability mass in this bin # Using cumulative distribution function approximation or integration # For simplicity, assume uniform probability if not specified, # but Gaussian is standard. # Lower and upper bounds of the bin lower = minval + i binwidth upper = lower + binwidth # Approximate probability using PDF at center width # This is an approximation; exact integration is better center = (lower + upper) / 2.0 pdfval = (1.0 / math.sqrt(2 math.pi targetvariance)) \ math.exp(-0.5 ((center - targetmean) 2) / targetvariance) expected[i] = n pdfval binwidth # Compute chi-square statistic chi2 = 0.0 for i in range(numbins): if expected[i] > 0: chi2 += ((observed[i] - expected[i]) 2) / expected[i] else: # Handle zero expected count if observed[i] > 0: chi2 += float('inf') return chi2 Detects periodicity in noise using autocorrelation. Choose when spatial repetition is a concern. Autocorrelation Periodicity Test Measures band-pass characteristics using down-up-sampled differences. Choose when frequency bandwidth is critical. Band-Pass Test for Noise Estimates power spectrum by averaging periodograms. Choose when spectral density analysis is required. Bartlett’s Method for Power Spectrum Estimation Time Complexity: O(N + B), where N is the number of samples and B is the number of bins. Memory Complexity: O(B) for storing histogram bins. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides a single scalar metric for distribution fidelity. Limitations: Only assesses amplitude distribution, not spatial coherence or frequency content. Sensitive to binning choices. When to Use: When optimizing noise functions for statistical correctness of amplitude values. When Not to Use: When spatial properties (periodicity, band-pass) are the primary concern. The Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test for Noise was presented by Yoon et al. in [YLC04] and [YL08] as part of a suite of analysis tools for measuring the quality of noise within an optimization procedure. It is cited in surveys of procedural noise functions as a method for evaluating amplitude distribution quality.
