name: Particle Density Field Computation
head: Particle Power Summation, Particle-to-Grid Transfer
body: Particle Density Field Computation generates a 3D scalar density field by evaluating a radial kernel function for every voxel in a 3D grid, summing contributions from a set of particles. Unlike Radial Gaussian Density Field Generation, which uses smooth Gaussian falloffs, this method employs a specific polynomial kernel with a sharp cutoff at a normalized squared distance of 0.5, resulting in a compact support that strictly excludes distant particles. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A structured buffer posBuffer containing N particles, where each particle is a float4 (x, y, z, r) representing position and radius. A 3D grid with dimensions GRIDDIMX, GRIDDIMY, GRIDDIMZ and voxel spacing textureSizeScale. Output: A structured buffer pixels of float4 values storing the computed scalar field as (density, density, density, 1.0). Data Structures: posBuffer: RWStructuredBuffer<float4> storing particle positions and radii as (x, y, z, radius). pixels: RWStructuredBuffer<float4> storing the output density field as (density, density, density, 1.0). gParams: float4 constant buffer where gParams.z holds textureSizeScale (voxel spacing) and gParams.y holds the grid dimension in Y. Algorithm Steps: 1. Dispatch: Launch a compute shader with thread groups of size 8 \times 8 \times 8, where each thread handles one voxel. 2. Voxel Position: Calculate the world position \mathbf{t} of the current voxel using the thread ID (id.x, id.y, id.z) and textureSizeScale: \mathbf{t} = (id.x \cdot \text{textureSizeScale}, \ id.y \cdot \text{textureSizeScale}, \ id.z \cdot \text{textureSizeScale}) 3. Accumulator Initialization: Initialize a scalar accumulator p to 0.0. 4. Particle Iteration: Iterate over all N particles in posBuffer. For each particle i with position \mathbf{p}i and radius ri: a. Compute the normalized squared distance m^2: m^2 = \frac{\|\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{t}\|^2}{ri^2} b. Evaluate the kernel function f(m^2): f(m^2) = \begin{cases} 0.25 - m^2 + (m^2)^2 & \text{if } m^2 < 0.5 \\ 0.0 & \text{if } m^2 \ge 0.5 \end{cases} c. Add the result to the accumulator: p \leftarrow p + f(m^2). 5. Write Output: Store the accumulated density p into the output buffer at the linearized index corresponding to the voxel (id.x, id.y, id.z): \text{pixels}[idx] = (p, p, p, 1.0) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedensityfield(posBuffer, numParticles, gParams, pixels, GRIDDIMX, GRIDDIMY, GRIDDIMZ): textureSizeScale = gParams.z for idz in range(GRIDDIMZ): for idy in range(GRIDDIMY): for idx in range(GRIDDIMX): # 1. Calculate world position of the voxel testPos = (idx textureSizeScale, idy textureSizeScale, idz textureSizeScale) # 2. Initialize accumulator p = 0.0 # 3. Iterate over all particles for i in range(numParticles): particle = posBuffer[i] dx = particle.x - testPos[0] dy = particle.y - testPos[1] dz = particle.z - testPos[2] # 4. Compute normalized squared distance and kernel msqr = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz) / (particle.w particle.w) if msqr < 0.5: p += 0.25 - msqr + msqr msqr # 5. Linearize index for output buffer (standard row-major order) idx = (idz GRIDDIMY + idy) GRIDDIMX + idx # 6. Write result pixels[idx] = (p, p, p, 1.0) Parameters: textureSizeScale: The physical spacing between adjacent grid voxels. numParticles: The total count of particles in posBuffer. Kernel Cutoff: The normalized squared distance threshold is hardcoded to 0.5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sharp Cutoff: The kernel function returns exactly 0.0 for m^2 \ge 0.5, creating a strict boundary rather than a smooth falloff. A technique to prevent higher-order rounding error propagation during the recursive computation of polynomial coefficients used in particle-wise field approximation. It converts floating-point quantities to fixed-point integers to ensure exact arithmetic. Definition: Shifts numbers encoding contribution approximations into integer multiples of quantum values. Knots (tk, \hat{a}{k0}, \dots, \hat{a}{kD}) and localized coefficients a{kd} are quantized such that tk \approx \bar{t}k \tau and \hat{a}{kd} \approx \bar{\hat{a}}{kd} \zetad, a{kd} \approx \bar{a}{kd} \zetad for integers \bar{t}k, \bar{\hat{a}}{kd}, \bar{a}{kd}. Formula: The update rule becomes integer-only: \bar{a}{kd} = \bar{a}{kd} + \sum{j=d}^D \binom{j}{d} \bar{a}{(k-1)j} (\bar{t}k - \bar{t}{k-1})^{j-d} provided \zetad = \frac{\zeta}{\tau^d}. Parameters: \tau is the length quantum value (resolution of knot positions). \zeta is the field value quantum value (resolution of coefficients, where \zeta0 = \zeta). Pitfall: Direct application of the recursive coefficient update using floating-point numbers causes rounding errors to propagate at higher order from front to back along the viewing ray, leading to unstable results and 'sprinkling' artifacts. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot V), where N is the number of particles and V is the number of voxels in the grid, as each voxel iterates over all particles. Memory Complexity: O(N + V) for storing the particle buffer and the output density grid. Not given in the sources: measured performance on specific hardware, scaling behavior, or explicit usage recommendations. The method is implemented in the context of GPU-based marching cubes and particle rendering, specifically within the Unity engine ecosystem using HLSL compute shaders. The specific kernel function 0.25 - m^2 + (m^2)^2 with a cutoff at m^2=0.5 is designed to plot a curve that is 0.25 at r=0 and 0 at r = \sqrt{0.5} \cdot \text{power}, providing a "nice curve" for particle visualization. The quantization variant is discussed in the context of particle-wise higher-order SPH field approximation to avoid rounding errors in recursive coefficient updates. kristofe/UnityGPUMarchingCubes, https://github.com/kristofe/UnityGPUMarchingCubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Particle-Wise Higher-Order SPH Field Approximation for DVR, https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02896v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Synthetic Active Region Generation
head: Mode C, Synthetic Bipole
body: Synthetic Active Region Generation creates a synthetic bipolar active region magnetogram by summing Gaussian flux concentrations, satellite flux, polarity inversion line (PIL) shear, diffuse background, and instrument noise. It generates a 2D scalar field representing magnetic field strength on a grid, which serves as input for subsequent 3D volume rendering methods. Inputs: seed: Integer seed for the random number generator. GRIDSIZE (g): Integer resolution of the output grid. Outputs: bz: A 2D array of shape (g, g) with dtype=np.float32, representing the magnetic field strength. Data Structures: rng: A random number generator instance initialized with seed. XX, YY: 2D arrays of shape (g, g) created via np.meshgrid, containing the x and y coordinates of each grid cell ranging from -4.0 to 4.0. Steps: 1. Initialize RNG and Grid: Create the random number generator and coordinate grids. python rng = np.random.defaultrng(seed) g = GRIDSIZE x = np.linspace(-4.0, 4.0, g) y = np.linspace(-4.0, 4.0, g) XX, YY = np.meshgrid(x, y) 2. Initialize Bz Grid: Create a zero-filled grid for the magnetic field. python bz = np.zeros((g, g), dtype=np.float32) 3. Add Primary Positive Bipole: Sample parameters for the positive flux concentration and add a Gaussian. pospeak: Sampled from uniform distribution [1200, 1800]. possigma: Sampled from uniform distribution [0.60, 0.85]. poscx, poscy: Fixed centers at (-1.35, 0.10). Formula: bz \ += \ pos\peak \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{(XX - pos\cx)^2 + (YY - pos\cy)^2}{2 \cdot pos\sigma^2}\right) 4. Add Primary Negative Bipole: Sample parameters for the negative flux concentration and add a Gaussian. negpeak: Sampled from uniform distribution [-1400, -900] (implemented as -rng.uniform(900, 1400)). negsigma: Sampled from uniform distribution [0.75, 1.00]. negcx, negcy: Fixed centers at (1.50, -0.05). Formula: bz \ += \ neg\peak \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{(XX - neg\cx)^2 + (YY - neg\cy)^2}{2 \cdot neg\sigma^2}\right) 5. Add Satellite Flux: Generate 3 to 6 satellite flux concentrations (inclusive). nsatellites: Sampled from integers [3, 7). For each satellite: scx: Sampled from uniform distribution [-3.0, 3.0]. scy: Sampled from uniform distribution [-2.5, 2.5]. scpeak: Sampled as \pm \text{uniform}(80, 350), where the sign is chosen randomly from \{-1, 1\}. scsig: Sampled from uniform distribution [0.20, 0.50]. Formula: bz \ += \ sc\peak \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{(XX - sc\x)^2 + (YY - sc\y)^2}{2 \cdot sc\sig^2}\right) 6. Add PIL Shear: Add a shear component modulated by a Gaussian envelope. pilshear: Sampled from uniform distribution [0.08, 0.25]. pilwarp: Calculated as \tanh((XX + pil\shear \cdot YY) \cdot 1.5) \cdot \text{uniform}(30, 80). Formula: bz \ += \ pil\warp \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{XX^2 + YY^2}{8.0}\right) 7. Add Diffuse Background: Add a diffuse background noise term. bgval: Sampled from uniform distribution [-40, 40]. Formula: bz \ += \ bg\val \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{XX^2 + YY^2}{12.0}\right) 8. Add Instrument Noise: Add Gaussian noise to simulate instrument error. noise: Sampled from normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 15.0) with shape (g, g), cast to float32. Formula: bz \ += \ noise 9. Apply Boundary Apodisation: Smoothly fade the field to zero at the boundaries to prevent artifacts. r2: Calculated as (XX / 4.2)^2 + (YY / 4.2)^2. apod: Calculated as \sqrt{\max(0, 1.0 - r2)}. Formula: bz \ = \ apod Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generateactiveregion(seed, GRIDSIZE): # 1. Initialize RNG and Grid rng = np.random.defaultrng(seed) g = GRIDSIZE x = np.linspace(-4.0, 4.0, g) y = np.linspace(-4.0, 4.0, g) XX, YY = np.meshgrid(x, y) # 2. Initialize Bz Grid bz = np.zeros((g, g), dtype=np.float32) # 3. Add Primary Positive Bipole pospeak = rng.uniform(1200, 1800) possigma = rng.uniform(0.60, 0.85) poscx, poscy = -1.35, 0.10 bz += pospeak np.exp(-((XX - poscx)2 + (YY - poscy)2) / (2 possigma2)) # 4. Add Primary Negative Bipole negpeak = -rng.uniform(900, 1400) negsigma = rng.uniform(0.75, 1.00) negcx, negcy = 1.50, -0.05 bz += negpeak np.exp(-((XX - negcx)2 + (YY - negcy)2) / (2 negsigma2)) # 5. Add Satellite Flux nsatellites = rng.integers(3, 7) for in range(nsatellites): scx = rng.uniform(-3.0, 3.0) scy = rng.uniform(-2.5, 2.5) scsign = rng.choice([-1, 1]) scpeak = scsign rng.uniform(80, 350) scsig = rng.uniform(0.20, 0.50) bz += scpeak np.exp(-((XX - scx)2 + (YY - scy)2) / (2 scsig2)) # 6. Add PIL Shear pilshear = rng.uniform(0.08, 0.25) pilwarp = np.tanh((XX + pilshear YY) 1.5) rng.uniform(30, 80) bz += pilwarp np.exp(-(XX2 + YY2) / 8.0) # 7. Add Diffuse Background bgval = rng.uniform(-40, 40) bz += bgval np.exp(-(XX2 + YY2) / 12.0) # 8. Add Instrument Noise noise = rng.normal(0, 15.0, (g, g)).astype(np.float32) bz += noise # 9. Apply Boundary Apodisation r2 = (XX / 4.2)2 + (YY / 4.2)2 apod = np.clip(1.0 - r2, 0, 1)0.5 bz = apod return bz Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The source specifies dtype=np.float32 for the grid and noise. Boundaries: The apodisation factor becomes zero when r2 \ge 1, effectively masking the field outside the radius of 4.2 units. Points exactly on the boundary are handled by np.clip. Degenerate Input: If GRIDSIZE is too small, the Gaussian peaks may not be resolved, leading to aliasing. The source does not specify a minimum resolution. Flux Tube Filament Generation is a procedural algorithm that traces sample points along magnetic field lines (filaments) within a synthetic flux tube volume, incorporating radial convergence and stochastic noise to simulate magnetic field line wandering. It solves the problem of generating structured, volumetric magnetic field data for visualization by converting a parametric tube geometry into a discrete set of 3D points with associated vector field values and intensity. It differs from direct field evaluation methods by explicitly tracing a path with a restoring force and random walk, rather than sampling a static analytical field at grid points. Time Complexity: O(g^2) per Gaussian addition, where g is the grid size. With a constant number of Gaussians (2 primary, 3-6 satellites, 1 shear, 1 background), the total time is linear in the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: O(g^2) for the bz grid and coordinate arrays. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fast to generate; produces visually realistic bipolar structures with shear and noise. Limitations: The output is a 2D magnetogram, not a full 3D volume, though it serves as input for 3D generation methods. The parameters are hardcoded ranges, limiting fine control over specific physical properties. When to use: When a quick, realistic synthetic magnetogram is needed for testing or visualization pipelines. When not to use: When precise physical accuracy or 3D volumetric data is required directly from this step. Origin: The method is described in the repository. It is used in the context of astrophysical vector field visualization, specifically for generating synthetic data that mimics solar active regions. name: Flux Tube Filament Generation
head: Dataset Generation and Encoding, Saturn Polar Magnetic Flux Tube Generation, flux tube filament tracing
body: Flux Tube Filament Generation is a procedural algorithm that traces sample points along magnetic field lines (filaments) within a flux tube, incorporating radial convergence and stochastic noise. It generates, constrains, encodes, and saves the flux tube dataset as a discrete set of 3D points with associated vector field values and intensity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Parameters defining the tube geometry (TUBERADIUS, TUBEHEIGHT), filament count (NSTRANDS), sampling density (POINTSPERSTRAND), noise magnitude (NOISESCALE), dipole tilt (DIPOLETILTDEG), dipole scaling (FIELDSTRENGTH), and a global point limit (MAXPOINTS). Outputs: A list of point records, each containing position (x, y, z), magnetic field vector (Bx, By, Bz), intensity, and a derived grayscale value, saved as a compact JSON dataset. Data Structures: Point Record: A dictionary with keys x, y, z (float, 5 decimal precision), Bx, By, Bz (float, 4 decimal precision), and intensity (float, 4 decimal precision). Dataset: A list of point records, serialized to JSON with compact separators (no spaces). Parameters: TUBEHEIGHT: 10.0 [scene units]. TUBERADIUS: 0.6 [scene units]. NSTRANDS: 8. POINTSPERSTRAND: 500. NOISESCALE: 0.08 [standard deviation per step]. DIPOLETILTDEG: 3.0 [degrees]. FIELDSTRENGTH: 20000.0 [arbitrary units]. MAXPOINTS: 5000 [absolute ceiling]. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty list allpoints. 2. Loop filamentidx from 0 to NSTRANDS - 1: a. Initialize a deterministic random number generator rng with seed filamentidx 7919. b. Calculate initial angular position: \phi0 = \frac{2.0 \pi \cdot \text{filament\idx}}{\text{N\STRANDS}}. c. Calculate initial radial offset: r0 = \text{TUBE\RADIUS} \cdot \text{rng.uniform}(0.15, 0.85). d. Initialize position at the lower boundary: cx = r0 \cos(\phi0) cy = r0 \sin(\phi0) cz = -\frac{\text{TUBE\HEIGHT}}{2.0}. e. Calculate vertical step size: \text{step\z} = \frac{\text{TUBE\HEIGHT}}{\text{POINTS\PER\STRAND}}. f. Calculate tilt offset: \text{tilt\rad} = \text{radians}(\text{DIPOLE\TILT\DEG}), \text{tilt\x} = \sin(\text{tilt\rad}). g. Loop i from 0 to POINTSPERSTRAND - 1: i. Calculate normalized height: \text{frac} = \frac{i}{\text{POINTS\PER\STRAND}}. ii. Calculate radial convergence: r{\text{now}} = r0 (1.0 - 0.4 \cdot \text{frac}). iii. Calculate target position: \text{target\x} = r{\text{now}} \cos(\phi0) + \text{tilt\x} \cdot cz \cdot 0.1 \text{target\y} = r{\text{now}} \sin(\phi0). iv. Update position using Euler integration with restoring force and noise: cx \leftarrow cx + (\text{target\x} - cx) \cdot 0.08 + \mathcal{N}(0, \text{NOISE\SCALE}) cy \leftarrow cy + (\text{target\y} - cy) \cdot 0.08 + \mathcal{N}(0, \text{NOISE\SCALE}) cz \leftarrow cz + \text{step\z}. v. Evaluate a dipole field at (cx, cy, cz) to obtain (Bx, By, Bz). The exact dipole orientation and formula are not specified in the source. vi. Calculate magnitude: \text{mag} = \sqrt{Bx^2 + By^2 + Bz^2}. vii. Append point record with rounded coordinates and field values: x, y, z (5 decimals), Bx, By, Bz (4 decimals), intensity (4 decimals). 3. If len(allpoints) > MAXPOINTS, truncate allpoints to the first MAXPOINTS elements. 4. Extract intensities from all points to find i{\min} and i{\max}. 5. For each point, compute a grayscale value from its intensity using min-max normalization. The exact normalization function is not specified in the source. 6. Save dataset to magnetospheredata.json in compact JSON format. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random import json def generatefluxtubefilaments(): # Parameters TUBEHEIGHT = 10.0 TUBERADIUS = 0.6 NSTRANDS = 8 POINTSPERSTRAND = 500 NOISESCALE = 0.08 DIPOLETILTDEG = 3.0 FIELDSTRENGTH = 20000.0 MAXPOINTS = 5000 allpoints = [] for filamentidx in range(NSTRANDS): # Deterministic seeding per filament rng = random.Random(filamentidx 7919) # Initial conditions phi0 = (2.0 math.pi filamentidx) / NSTRANDS r0 = TUBERADIUS rng.uniform(0.15, 0.85) cx = r0 math.cos(phi0) cy = r0 math.sin(phi0) cz = -TUBEHEIGHT / 2.0 stepz = TUBEHEIGHT / POINTSPERSTRAND tiltrad = math.radians(DIPOLETILTDEG) tiltx = math.sin(tiltrad) for i in range(POINTSPERSTRAND): frac = i / POINTSPERSTRAND rnow = r0 (1.0 - 0.4 frac) targetx = rnow math.cos(phi0) + tiltx cz 0.1 targety = rnow math.sin(phi0) # Euler integration with restoring force and noise cx += (targetx - cx) 0.08 + rng.gauss(0, NOISESCALE) cy += (targety - cy) 0.08 + rng.gauss(0, NOISESCALE) cz += stepz # Evaluate dipole field [G: Standard dipole aligned with Z axis, scaled by FIELDSTRENGTH] rmag = math.sqrt(cx2 + cy2 + cz2) if rmag == 0: bx, by, bz = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 else: bx = FIELDSTRENGTH (3 cz cx) / (rmag5) by = FIELDSTRENGTH (3 cz cy) / (rmag5) bz = FIELDSTRENGTH (3 cz2 - rmag2) / (rmag5) mag = math.sqrt(bx2 + by2 + bz2) # Create record record = { 'x': round(cx, 5), 'y': round(cy, 5), 'z': round(cz, 5), 'Bx': round(bx, 4), 'By': round(by, 4), 'Bz': round(bz, 4), 'intensity': round(mag, 4) } allpoints.append(record) # Truncate if exceeding hardware safety constraint if len(allpoints) > MAXPOINTS: allpoints = allpoints[:MAXPOINTS] # Normalize intensity to grayscale [G: Standard min-max normalization] if allpoints: intensities = [p['intensity'] for p in allpoints] imin = min(intensities) imax = max(intensities) for p in allpoints: if imax == imin: p['gray'] = 0.5 else: p['gray'] = (p['intensity'] - imin) / (imax - imin) # Save to JSON with open('magnetospheredata.json', 'w') as f: json.dump(allpoints, f, separators=(',', ':')) return allpoints Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. It is part of a pipeline that generates synthetic active region magnetograms and converts them into splat-based visualizations. The specific algorithm for flux tube filament generation is designed to create sample points along magnetic field lines within a flux tube, incorporating radial convergence and stochastic noise. name: Blob Field Generation
head: Inverse Distance Weighting for Isosurfaces, Inverse Square Blob Field, Metaball Scalar Field Construction, Procedural Blob Field
body: Blob Field Generation is a procedural method for constructing a 3D scalar field by summing inverse-square distance contributions from a set of source points (blobs), creating smooth, organic "metaball" shapes suitable for isosurface extraction via Marching Cubes. It differs from Radial Gaussian Density Field Generation by using 1/r^2 falloff instead of exponential decay, resulting in sharper, more compact isosurfaces with heavier tails, and from Fuzzy Metaballs Hyper-parameters by relying on explicit inverse-distance weighting rather than probabilistic or fuzzy logic blending. Inputs: A set of N source points (blob centers) Pi = (xi, yi, zi) for i \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}. A query point Q = (x, y, z) in 3D space. A time parameter t for animated blob positions. Optional: Boolean flag to enable a floor effect. Outputs: A scalar field value f(x, y, z). Data Structures: sSourcePoint: An array of N structures, each containing three floating-point coordinates (fX, fY, fZ). numBlobs: Integer count of source points. Steps: 1. Normalize Coordinates: Scale the query point coordinates to the range [0, 1]. 2. Calculate Strength: Compute a uniform strength value using the number of blobs: strength = 1.2 / ((\sqrt{numBlobs} - 1) / 4 + 1). 3. Initialize Total: Set the total field value to 0.0. 4. Iterate Blobs: For each blob i from 0 to N-1: a. Compute blob position (bx, by, bz) using sinusoidal functions of time and index i. b. Calculate squared Euclidean distance: distSq = (x - bx)^2 + (y - by)^2 + (z - bz)^2. c. Compute blob value: v = strength / (0.000001 + distSq) - 12.0. d. If v > 0, add v to the total field value. 5. Optional Floor Effect: If enabled, compute floor distance using the normalized y-coordinate: fy = y. Calculate floor value: floorVal = 2.0 / (0.0001 + fy^2) - 12.0. If floorVal > 0, add it to the total field value. 6. Return: Return the total field value. Formulas: General Inverse Square Field: f(x,y,z) = \sum{i} \frac{wi}{(x - xi)^2 + (y - yi)^2 + (z - zi)^2}. Distance Metrics for Non-Spherical Shapes: Euclidean: dist(p1, p2) = \sqrt{(p1.x - p2.x)^2 + (p1.y - p2.y)^2 + (p1.z - p2.z)^2}. Taxicab (Manhattan): dist1(p1, p2) = |p1.x - p2.x| + |p1.y - p2.y| + |p1.z - p2.z|. Max-Metric: distMax(p1, p2) = \max(|p1.x - p2.x|, |p1.y - p2.y|, |p1.z - p2.z|). Parameters: epsilon (\epsilon): Small constant to prevent division by zero. Value 0.000001 is used for blobs, and 0.0001 for the floor effect. offset: Constant subtracted from the field value to control the isovalue threshold. Value 12.0 is used. time (t): Drives sinusoidal animation of blob positions. alpha: Constant for fading effect in cloud variants. Value 0.6 used in tests. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluateblobfield(x, y, z, numblobs, time, usefloor=False): # Normalize coordinates to [0, 1] xn, yn, zn = x, y, z # Calculate uniform strength strength = 1.2 / ((numblobs 0.5 - 1) / 4 + 1) totalfield = 0.0 # Iterate over all blobs for i in range(numblobs): # Compute blob position using sinusoidal functions of time and index i bx, by, bz = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # Placeholder for sinusoidal position calculation dx = xn - bx dy = yn - by dz = zn - bz distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz # Compute blob contribution with epsilon and offset v = strength / (0.000001 + distsq) - 12.0 if v > 0: totalfield += v # Optional floor effect if usefloor: fy = yn floorval = 2.0 / (0.0001 + fyfy) - 12.0 if floorval > 0: totalfield += floorval return totalfield Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If the evaluation point coincides exactly with a source point, the distance term becomes zero, causing the value to approach infinity. A small epsilon must be added to the denominator. Metric Selection: Using standard Euclidean distance creates spherical metaballs. To create cubic or "Minecraft-like" isosurfaces, Taxicab or Max-metric distances should be used instead. Applies Blinn's metaball technique for organic n-dimensional objects to generate cumulus clouds. It differs from other methods by using optimized equations and pre-calculating the mean value on the CPU for high performance. The field is evaluated as f(x) = \sumi \frac{ri^2}{|x - ci|^2}, where ri is the sphere radius and ci is the center. A constant \alpha = 0.6 adjusts the fading effect at the cloud edges. Render quality is sufficient but lower than Algorithm 1, using only six spheres with randomized radii. Time Complexity: O(N) per query point, where N is the number of blobs. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store source points and weights. Performance: High performance, especially when mean values are pre-calculated on the CPU. Strengths: Simple to implement, produces smooth organic shapes, computationally efficient. Limitations: Sharp falloff can lead to aliasing if not sampled finely; singularities require handling. Use Cases: Isosurface generation for organic shapes, cloud rendering. When Not to Use: When exponential falloff (Gaussian) is preferred for softer edges, or when complex procedural noise is needed. Originated from Blinn's metaball technique for creating organic-looking n-dimensional objects. The inverse square distance method is commonly used in conjunction with the Marching Cubes algorithm for isosurface extraction. It has been applied in computer graphics for generating clouds and organic shapes. 3merillon/WebGL2-GPU-Marching-Cubes, https://github.com/3merillon/WebGL2-GPU-Marching-Cubes, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) 2 Isovalue in Marching Cubes Algorithm, https://stackoverflow.com/questions/11177604/isovalue-in-marching-cubes-algorithm?rq=4, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Efficient Algorithms for Real-Time GPU Volumetric Cloud Rendering with Enhanced Geometry, https://doi.org/10.3390/sym10040125, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Fuzzy Metaballs Hyper-parameters
head: Fuzzy Metaballs Parameters, Metaball Field Hyper-parameters
body: This family defines the five scalar hyper-parameters used to tune the algebraic intersection and alpha-mask generation stages of the Fuzzy Metaballs rendering method. It solves the problem of converting raw implicit field evaluations into differentiable depth and alpha masks suitable for gradient-based pose optimization. What sets this apart from sibling methods like Radial Gaussian Density Field Generation or Blob Field Generation is that these parameters are not intrinsic properties of the volume geometry itself, but rather optimization targets for the rendering pipeline's differentiability and silhouette accuracy, specifically tuned for algebraic surface approximation. The Fuzzy Metaballs approach relies on a fully algebraic formulation of ray-surface intersection, allowing gradients to flow through the rendering process. The hyper-parameters are divided into two functional groups: those influencing the geometric intersection logic and those scaling the final output masks. 1. Intersection Weights (\beta1, \beta2, \beta3): These parameters weight different criteria during the computation of ray-surface intersections. 2. Alpha Mask Scaling (\beta4, \beta5): These parameters apply a linear transformation (scale and offset) to the raw intersection results to generate the final alpha masks. Empirical evidence shows that optimal values for these parameters are robust across varying resolutions, mixture component counts, and intersection polynomial degrees (linear, quadratic, cubic). Prioritizes hits that are geometrically close to the ray origin during intersection computation. Prioritizes hits that are closer to the camera viewpoint. Prioritizes hits that lie in front of the camera plane. The scale factor applied to the raw field value to generate the alpha mask. The offset factor applied to the raw field value to generate the alpha mask. The Fuzzy Metaballs hyper-parameters were introduced in the context of "Approximate Differentiable Rendering with Algebraic Surfaces". The method was developed to enable gradient-based pose optimization for 3D reconstruction using algebraic surface approximations. The authors noted that while the algebraic formulation naturally supports gradient descent into these hyper-parameters (via tools like JAX), they did not use this approach in practice. Instead, they optimized the five parameters using standard black-box optimization techniques on a small simulated dataset (the Stanford bunny) to maximize depth and alpha mask accuracy. This pre-optimization step was performed before running the main experiments. The robustness of these parameters was validated by finding similar optimal values across multiple tested resolutions, a wide range of mixture components, and different intersection computation methods (linear, quadratic, and cubic). name: Distance to Hypertextures
head: Fractal noise deformation, Hypertexture, Hypertexture noise
body: Distance to Hypertextures is a technique for adding relief or details to surfaces without increasing geometry cost, using procedural texture synthesis evaluated within a volumetric region around the object rather than only on the surface. It deforms implicit surfaces by adding procedural noise to the function's range instead of the domain, enabling sphere tracing with distance bounds. Unlike standard hypertexturing which may deform the domain, this variant affects the range, allowing the use of signed distance functions (SDFs) for efficient rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A base signed distance function f(\vec{x}), a noise function noise(\vec{x}), and a spectral exponent \alpha. Output: A deformed implicit surface defined by f(\vec{x}) + noise(\vec{x}) = 0. Data Structures: \Gamma: An array of random unit vectors used for solid noise interpolation. Octaves: A finite integer n controlling the number of noise layers. Steps: 1. Define Base Noise: Construct band-limited solid noise using a piecewise cubic Gaussian approximation \phi and random vectors \Gamma: noise(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=-1}^{1} \sum{j=-1}^{1} \sum{k=-1}^{1} \Gamma(i,j,k) \cdot \phi(\mathbf{x} - (i,j,k)) where \phi is a scalar piecewise cubic approximation of a Gaussian distribution. 2. Compute Lipschitz Constant for Base Noise: The Lipschitz constant for the base noise is derived from the composition of \phi and \Gamma. Given Lip{\phi} = 3/2 and Lip{\Gamma} = 2, the composition results in Lip{noise} = 3. 3. Generate Fractal Noise: Sum scaled versions of the base noise over n octaves to create fractal noise with spectral exponent \alpha: noise\alpha(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=0}^{n} \frac{noise(2^i \mathbf{x})}{2^{i\alpha}} 4. Deform Surface: Evaluate the deformed implicit field F(\vec{x}) = f(\vec{x}) + noise\alpha(\vec{x}). 5. Sphere Tracing: Use the Lipschitz constant of the total function to determine safe step sizes for sphere tracing. Parameters: \alpha: Spectral exponent. \alpha=0 is white noise, \alpha=1 is 1/f noise, \alpha=2 is Brownian motion. n: Number of octaves. Must be finite to ensure the function remains Lipschitz. \Gamma: Array of random unit vectors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unbounded 1/f noise is not Lipschitz; it must be band-limited to a finite number of octaves n to remain Lipschitz for sphere tracing. For 1/f noise, the Lipschitz constant equals the sum of individual noise functions, Lip{1/f \ noise} = 3. For Brownian motion (\alpha=2), the Lipschitz constant is Lip{B} = 3(2^{1-n} - 1) \approx 6. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hypertexturedeformation(x, f, alpha, n, Gamma): """ Computes the deformed implicit surface value using Distance to Hypertextures. Args: x: 3D point (list of 3 floats) f: Base signed distance function (callable) alpha: Spectral exponent (float) n: Number of octaves (int) Gamma: 3x3x3 array of random unit vectors (list of lists of lists of lists) Returns: Deformed field value (list of 3 floats) """ noisevalue = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(n + 1): scaledx = [x[j] (2 i) for j in range(3)] currentnoise = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for di in range(-1, 2): for dj in range(-1, 2): for dk in range(-1, 2): vec = Gamma[di + 1][dj + 1][dk + 1] offset = [scaledx[0] - di, scaledx[1] - dj, scaledx[2] - dk] phival = cubicgaussianapprox(offset) currentnoise = [currentnoise[j] + vec[j] phival for j in range(3)] noisevalue = [noisevalue[j] + currentnoise[j] / (2 (i alpha)) for j in range(3)] return [f(x[j]) + noisevalue[j] for j in range(3)] def cubicgaussianapprox(p): """ Piecewise cubic approximation of Gaussian distribution. Based on Wyvill et al. """ r2 = sum(v v for v in p) threshold = 1.5 if r2 < threshold: term = threshold - r2 return (2.0 / 3.0) (term 3) else: return 0.0 A method where a distance field is derived from the mesh on the fly on the GPU, and surface vicinity is used for hypertexture lookups. It uses 20 octaves of Perlin noise for shading and complex materials. Due to complex GPU computations, frame rate is around 20 FPS for a 1024^3 volume. Time Complexity: High computational cost due to multiple noise evaluations and octaves. Frame rates can be low (e.g., 20 FPS for 1024^3 volume). Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of octaves and the size of the Gamma array. In streaming implementations, memory usage can be optimized using node pools and bricks. Strengths: Adds high-frequency detail without increasing geometric complexity; enables sphere tracing for efficient rendering. Limitations: Unbounded 1/f noise is not Lipschitz and must be band-limited to a finite number of octaves to remain Lipschitz for stable sphere tracing. When to use: When high-quality procedural detail is needed on implicit surfaces and performance allows for complex GPU computations. Proposed by Perlin [PH89], hypertextures were inspired by the idea of evaluating procedural texture synthesis within a volumetric region around an object rather than only on the surface. This allows for the modeling of phenomena intermediate between surface and texture. The specific variant affecting the range to enable sphere tracing was detailed in subsequent work. name: Superelliptic Blends
head: Pseudonorm Blend, Ricci blend, Rockwood and Owen blend
body: Superelliptic blends (also known as pseudonorm blends) are a local geometric deformation technique for implicitly defining the union of two or more signed distance functions (SDFs). This method computes a p-norm distance to the blended union, allowing for smooth transitions between surfaces controlled by a tightness parameter p. It differs from global additive field methods by operating directly on distance values and maintaining local support. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two signed distance functions f1(\mathbf{x}) and f2(\mathbf{x}), a blend parameter p > 0 (thumbweight), and support radii d1, d2 defining the local domain of influence for each function. Output: A new implicit function B(\mathbf{x}) representing the blended union. Data Structures: No specific data structures are required beyond the evaluation functions f1, f2 and the scalar parameters p, d1, d2. The method is stateless and evaluates point-wise. Mathematical Definition: The method relies on reformulating the signed distance functions into strictly non-negative functions, following Ricci's original formulation where implicit surfaces are defined by setting non-negative functions equal to one. For a signed distance function fi(\mathbf{x}), we define the non-negative component gi(\mathbf{x}) as: gi(\mathbf{x}) = \max(1 - fi(\mathbf{x}), 0) This ensures that gi(\mathbf{x}) is non-zero only within the support region where fi(\mathbf{x}) < 1. The superelliptic blend of the union of the implicit surface of f1 and f2 is defined by the implicit surface of the blended function B(\mathbf{x}): B(\mathbf{x}) = \left( g1(\mathbf{x})^p + g2(\mathbf{x})^p \right)^{1/p} The parameter p acts as a thumbweight describing how tightly the blend adheres to the original surfaces. The implicit surface corresponds to B(\mathbf{x}) = 1. Numbered Steps: 1. Evaluate f1(\mathbf{x}) and f2(\mathbf{x}) at the query point \mathbf{x}. 2. Compute the non-negative components: g1(\mathbf{x}) = \max(1 - f1(\mathbf{x}), 0) g2(\mathbf{x}) = \max(1 - f2(\mathbf{x}), 0) 3. Check if both g1(\mathbf{x}) and g2(\mathbf{x}) are zero. 4. Compute the blended value using the p-norm: B(\mathbf{x}) = \left( g1(\mathbf{x})^p + g2(\mathbf{x})^p \right)^{1/p} 5. The resulting implicit surface is defined by B(\mathbf{x}) = 1. Parameters: p: The blend exponent. Typical values depend on the desired smoothness. Small p yields smoother, more "blobby" blends; large p yields sharper, more distinct surfaces. d1, d2: Support radii. If fi are SDFs, these are in Euclidean units. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Discontinuities: The pseudonorm blend creases the space surrounding the blend. Outside the domain where both g1 and g2 are non-zero, it is impossible to smoothly combine the results, resulting in a crease and gradient discontinuities. Root Finding: These gradient discontinuities can be disastrous for iterative root finders (e.g., Newton-Raphson). Sphere Tracing: The discontinuities do not impact geometric ray intersection methods like sphere tracing, as sphere tracing relies on the Lipschitz constant (distance to surface) rather than the gradient direction for step sizing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def superellipticblendunion(x, f1, f2, p): """ Computes the superelliptic blend (pseudonorm) of two SDFs. Returns the blended function value B(x). The implicit surface is at B(x) = 1. """ # 1. Evaluate SDFs dist1 = f1(x) dist2 = f2(x) # 2. Reformulate to non-negative components gi = max(1 - fi, 0) g1 = max(1.0 - dist1, 0.0) g2 = max(1.0 - dist2, 0.0) # 3. Handle case where both are outside support if g1 == 0.0 and g2 == 0.0: return max(dist1, dist2) # Fallback to max SDF outside blend domain # 4. Compute p-norm blend blendedg = (g1 p + g2 p) (1.0 / p) # 5. Return blended value; surface is at blendedg == 1.0 return blendedg Uses additive scalar fields rather than distance norms. Choose when smooth, organic merging is needed without strict distance preservation [1017-metaball-field-evaluation.md]. A variant that softens the transition. Choose when anti-aliasing of the blend edge is required without the sharp creases of the standard pseudonorm [2753-soft-metablobby-sdf.md]. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point, assuming f1 and f2 are O(1). Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are stored. Strengths: Local blending allows for efficient culling using bounding volumes. Limitations: The gradient discontinuities at the boundary of the blend domain make it unsuitable for gradient-based optimization or root-finding algorithms. It is primarily designed for sphere tracing (geometric ray intersection). Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of blended primitives if extended to N inputs, but the local nature means only nearby primitives need evaluation. Cost: The cost is dominated by the exponentiation and root operations. The superelliptic blend was introduced by Rockwood and Owen in 1987. It is based on the pioneering work of Antonio Ricci in 1974, who defined implicit surfaces using strictly non-negative functions set to one. The method is also referred to as the "pseudonorm blend" because it computes a p-norm distance to the union of surfaces. It is widely used in sphere tracing for rendering implicit surfaces due to its compatibility with the Lipschitz property required for safe step sizes. name: Soft Metablobby SDF
head: Soft implicit surface, Wyvill blobby model
body: Soft Metablobby SDF is a procedural implicit surface method that approximates Gaussian blobby fields using piecewise cubic polynomials to avoid expensive exponentiation and iterative root finding. It defines a smooth, blended volume from a set of key points, where the surface is the zero-crossing of the summed field. Unlike standard metaballs that use Gaussian kernels, this method localizes the influence of each point to a finite radius, providing a bounded support that simplifies culling and distance estimation. Inputs: n: Number of key points. \{pi\}{i=1}^n: Positions of the key points in \mathbb{R}^3. \{Ri\}{i=1}^n: Radii of influence for each key point. T: Threshold value for the isosurface. Data Structures: Array of structs KeyPoint: p: vec3 position. R: float radius. Field Evaluation: The scalar field f(\vec{x}) is computed by summing the contributions of all key points: f(\vec{x}) = \sum{i=1}^{n} Ci(\|\vec{x} - pi\|) The basis function Ci(r) for a key point with radius Ri at distance r = \|\vec{x} - pi\| is defined as: Ci(r) = \begin{cases} \frac{r^3}{Ri^2} - \frac{3r^2}{Ri} + 1 & \text{if } r < Ri \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The isosurface is extracted where f(\vec{x}) = T. Negative Key Points: If a key point represents a void or negative mass, its contribution is negated: Ci^{\text{neg}}(r) = -Ci(r) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def evaluatesoftmetablobby(x, keypoints, threshold=1.0): """ Evaluates the soft metablobby field at point x. Args: x: tuple(float, float, float), query point. keypoints: list of tuples (p: tuple(float, float, float), R: float). threshold: float, the isovalue to extract. Returns: float: The field value f(x). """ fieldvalue = 0.0 for p, R in keypoints: dx = x[0] - p[0] dy = x[1] - p[1] dz = x[2] - p[2] r = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) if r < R: rnorm = r / R contribution = (rnorm3 - 3.0 rnorm2) R + 1.0 fieldvalue += contribution return fieldvalue def isinside(x, keypoints, threshold=1.0): """ Determines if point x is inside the implicit surface. Inside is defined as f(x) > threshold for blobby models where the center has value 1. """ return evaluatesoftmetablobby(x, keypoints, threshold) > threshold Parameters: Ri: Radius of influence. Typical values depend on scene scale. Threshold T: Typically 1.0 when Ci(0)=1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Key Points: Incorporate voids by negating Ci(r). Precision: The polynomial is continuous and differentiable (C^1) at r=Ri (value 0, derivative 0), ensuring smooth blending. Boundaries: The function has compact support (r < Ri), allowing efficient culling of points outside the radius. Calculates the Lipschitz constant for the blending function Ci(r) to bound the distance to the implicit blend, enabling sphere tracing. Step: Differentiate Ci(r) to find Ci'(r) = \frac{3r^2}{Ri^2} - \frac{6r}{Ri}. Formula: The maximum slope occurs at the midpoint r = Ri/2. The Lipschitz constant is given by: Lip(Ci(r)) = |Ci'(Ri/2)| = \frac{3}{2Ri} The distance to the implicit blend B is bounded by: d(x, B) \le f(x) + \sum{i=1}^{n} \frac{Ri}{3} Time Complexity: O(n) per sample, where n is the number of key points. Sphere tracing can accelerate convergence by using the Lipschitz constant for step sizes. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store key points. Performance: Avoids exponentiation, making it faster than Gaussian blobs on hardware without efficient exp units. Strengths: Smooth blending, compact support (easy culling), analytical distance bounds for sphere tracing. Limitations: Polynomial approximation may not perfectly match Gaussian falloff; requires tuning of radii. The method was introduced by Wyvill et al. (1986) as "Soft" objects to approximate Gaussian distributions with piecewise polynomials, avoiding exponentiation and iterative root finding. It builds on Blinn's (1982) Gaussian blobby model. The specific cubic polynomial and Lipschitz bounds are detailed in "Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces". name: Implicit Surface Definition
head: Implicit Function Definition, Implicit Function Representation
body: Implicit Surface Definition represents 3D geometry as the zero-level set of a scalar field function f(\vec{x}). It defines surfaces by evaluating a function at arbitrary points in space rather than storing discrete topological data. What sets it apart from explicit surface definitions is that the geometry is defined analytically through a filter function f. All methods in this family rely on the evaluation of a scalar field function f over a domain \Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3. The core mechanism identifies the surface as the locus of points where the function output equals a specific constant, typically zero. Mathematical Definition: The implicit surface is defined as the set of points \vec{x} satisfying: \{\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid f(\vec{x}) = 0\} More generally, an isosurface at isovalue v is defined by: f(\vec{x}) - v = 0 Function Properties: 1. Mapping: The function maps any point in N-dimensional space to a real number: \forall \vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, f(\vec{x}) \in \mathbb{R} 2. Filter/Kernel: The function f acts as a filter or form. It can be algebraic or transcendental, and defined globally or as piecewise kernels. 3. Support: The function can be defined globally over the entire domain or as piecewise kernels (local support). 4. Sign Convention: While the zero set defines the surface, the sign of f(\vec{x}) often carries semantic meaning. In Signed Distance Functions (SDFs), f(\vec{x}) > 0 indicates outside, f(\vec{x}) < 0 indicates inside, and f(\vec{x}) = 0 is on the surface. Evaluation: The geometry is not stored as a discrete structure but is computed on-demand. For volume rendering, this means evaluating f(\vec{x}) at sample points along rays or within voxels Implicit Surface Primitives. Defines fields using superpositions of radial basis functions (typically Gaussian or inverse quadratic) centered at control points. Chosen for organic, blobby shapes that merge smoothly. Combines implicit distance fields with procedural texture functions to define surfaces based on texture thresholds. Chosen for detailed surface patterns without geometric complexity. Uses superelliptic equations to blend primitive shapes with adjustable sharpness. Chosen for hard-surface modeling with smooth transitions. Combines multiple implicit functions using set operations (union, intersection, difference) via norms or smooth min/max functions. Chosen for constructing complex scenes from simple primitives. A variant of metaballs using SDFs with soft blending parameters. Chosen for realistic fluid-like interactions with controlled surface tension. Defines volumes using linear inequalities (half-spaces). Chosen for convex polyhedral shapes and collision detection. Focuses on the numerical techniques for sampling the implicit field to generate point clouds or voxels. Chosen when discrete data is required from an analytic definition. Implements standard analytic shapes (spheres, cylinders, cones) as implicit functions. Chosen for basic geometric building blocks. Uses metaball fields to define weight functions for vertex displacement or envelope painting. Chosen for organic deformation and sculpting. The formalization of implicit functions as general filters f: \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R} allows for a wide variety of analytic forms beyond polynomials, including transcendental functions. S1 defines Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) as a specific class of implicit functions where the value represents the distance to the nearest surface, with positive values outside, negative values inside, and zero on the surface. Historical origins and specific terminology adoption in computer graphics are Not given in the sources. name: Half-Space Field Generation
head: Binary Half-Volume, Level Set Domain Definition, Level Set Masking, Step Function Field
body: Half-Space Field Generation creates a binary volume mask by assigning values to voxels based on a spatial or level-set condition, effectively gating simulation or rendering computations. It differs from continuous implicit primitives by discretizing the domain boundary into a hard binary mask rather than evaluating a smooth scalar field for isosurface extraction. This method restricts physical simulation (such as pressure solving or force application) to active regions, ignoring empty space like air. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D grid domain defined by dimensions (xSize, ySize, zSize) and a logical condition defining the active region (e.g., y \ge ySize/2 or \phi < 0). Output: A 3D array of floats with the same dimensions, containing binary values (0 or 1). Data Structures: volume: A 3D array of size (xSize, ySize, zSize). Data type: Typically 32-bit float or 16-bit float for GPU compatibility. Steps: 1. Initialize the 3D float array volume of size (xSize, ySize, zSize) to zero. 2. Iterate through voxel coordinates (x, y, z) where 0 \le x < xSize, 0 \le z < zSize, and 0 \le y < ySize. 3. Apply the half-space condition. In the canonical example, the domain is split by the Y-axis: if y \ge ySize/2, set volume[x, y, z] = 1; otherwise set to 0. 4. For general level-set based generation, evaluate the level set function \phi(\vec{x}). If \phi(\vec{x}) < 0 (inside fluid), mark the cell as active; otherwise mark it as inactive. 5. Use the resulting binary mask in shaders or solvers to gate computations. For example, set pressure to zero outside the liquid (\phi \ge 0) before solving. Formulas: Half-space condition: y \ge \frac{ySize}{2}. Level-set condition: \phi(\vec{x}) < 0. Pressure masking: P{masked}(\vec{x}) = P(\vec{x}) \cdot M(\vec{x}), where M(\vec{x}) \in \{0, 1\}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatehalfspacevolume(xSize, ySize, zSize): """Generates a binary 3D volume mask based on the canonical Y-axis split.""" volume = [[[0.0] xSize for in range(zSize)] for in range(ySize)] for y in range(ySize // 2, ySize): for z in range(zSize): for x in range(xSize): volume[y][z][x] = 1.0 for y in range(ySize // 2): for z in range(zSize): for x in range(xSize): volume[y][z][x] = 0.0 return volume def applymasktopressure(pressurefield, maskfield): """Sets pressure to zero where the mask field is 0.""" ySize = len(pressurefield) zSize = len(pressurefield[0]) xSize = len(pressurefield[0][0]) for y in range(ySize): for z in range(zSize): for x in range(xSize): if maskfield[y][z][x] == 0: pressurefield[y][z][x] = 0.0 return pressurefield Parameters: splitthreshold: The fractional position of the boundary (e.g., 0.5 for the middle). threshold for level sets: A small epsilon value to determine \phi \ge 0 vs \phi < 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Using 32-bit floating-point textures for storage yields roughly half the performance of 16-bit textures due to bandwidth issues. Boundary Conditions: Forces such as gravity must not be applied outside the liquid domain to avoid numerical artifacts. GPU Flow Control: Checking the level set value in shaders requires dynamic flow control. If the GPU lacks this, performance degrades. Time Complexity: O(N) where N = xSize \times ySize \times zSize, as every voxel must be visited to set the binary value. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the 3D array. Performance: Bandwidth is a major factor. Storing the mask in 16-bit textures improves performance compared to 32-bit. Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively culls empty space in simulations (e.g., air). Alternatives: For GPUs without dynamic flow control, use z-culling to eliminate cells or sparse data structures instead of a dense binary mask. The technique is widely used in real-time fluid simulation to define the domain of the solver. It allows the simulation to ignore air (\phi \ge 0) and only compute pressure and forces within the liquid (\phi < 0). The approach is detailed in GPU Gems 3 regarding real-time 3D fluid simulation. millerc3/Marching-Cubes, https://github.com/millerc3/Marching-Cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids, https://wo1fsea.github.io/files/AboutNavMesh/P5GPUGems3Real-TimeSimulationandRenderingof3DFluids.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Implicit Geometry Sampling
head: GenusTwoSurface, PorousSurface, WineGlassSurface
body: Implicit Geometry Sampling is a technique for generating volume data from mathematical implicit functions, providing value and gradient at any point in space without discrete voxel grids. It solves the problem of defining complex, continuous geometry for volume rendering by evaluating a scalar field function f(\vec{x}) on-demand. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on precomputed grids or specific primitive compositions, this method provides an abstract interface for sampling arbitrary implicit geometries, returning position, scalar value, and gradient. It builds on Implicit Surface Primitives by implementing the core evaluation mechanism for specific algebraic and transcendental functions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point \vec{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 in world space. Output: A structure containing the scalar field value f(\vec{p}) and the gradient vector \nabla f(\vec{p}) at that point. Data Structures: The implementation relies on an abstract base class ImplicitGeometry and specific derived classes. ImplicitGeometry: Contains a protected member AABB boundingbox defining the spatial extent of the geometry. Volume (for discrete variants): Contains protected members griddata (pointer to VolumeSampleData), griddimension (Eigen::Vector3i), and cellsize (Eigen::Vector3f). Evaluation Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Translate the input point \vec{p} to local coordinates relative to the bounding box center \vec{c}: \vec{p}{local} = \vec{p} - \vec{c} 2. Domain Check: If the point lies outside the defined domain of the specific implicit function (e.g., logarithmic singularities), return infinity for the value and zero for the gradient. 3. Function Evaluation: Evaluate the specific implicit function f(\vec{x}) and its partial derivatives \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} at \vec{p}{local}. 4. Gradient Computation (Discrete Fallback): If the geometry is stored as a discrete volume and gradients are not precomputed, compute them using central differences. 5. Voxel Retrieval (Discrete Fallback): For discrete volumes, identify the voxel containing the position. Formulas for Specific Primitives: The following formulas define the value f and gradient components (dx, dy, dz) for the named variants: 1. GenusTwoSurface: f(x,y,z) = 2y(y^2 - 3x^2)(1 - z^2) + (x^2 + y^2)^2 - (9z^2 - 1)(1 - z^2) dx = -12(1-z^2)yx + 4x^3 + 4y^2x dy = 6(1-z^2)(y^2-x^2) + 4y^3 + 4x^2y dz = -4(y^2-3x^2)yz - (20z - 36z^3) 2. WineGlassSurface: Defined for z > -3.2: f(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 - \log(z + 3.2)^2 - 0.09 Note: If z + 3.2 \le 0, f returns INFINITY and gradient returns (0,0,0). 3. PorousSurface: f(x,y,z) = -0.02 + (y^2-0.88)^2(2.92(x^3-x)x + 1.7y^2)^2 + (z^2-0.88)^2(2.92(y^3-y)y + 1.7z^2)^2 + (x^2-0.88)^2(1.7x^2 + 2.92(z^3-z)z)^2 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vector3f: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def sub(self, other): return Vector3f(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) class AABB: def init(self, minpt, maxpt): self.min = minpt self.max = maxpt def center(self): return Vector3f((self.min.x + self.max.x) / 2.0, (self.min.y + self.max.y) / 2.0, (self.min.z + self.max.z) / 2.0) class ImplicitGeometry: def init(self, boundingbox): self.boundingbox = boundingbox def sample(self, p): # 1. Translate to local coordinates relative to bounding box center center = self.boundingbox.center() plocal = p - center # 2. Evaluate specific function and gradient value, gradient = self.evaluate(plocal) return value, gradient def evaluate(self, p): raise NotImplementedError("Derived classes must implement evaluate") class GenusTwoSurface(ImplicitGeometry): def evaluate(self, p): x, y, z = p.x, p.y, p.z # Value term1 = 2 y (y2 - 3 x2) (1 - z2) term2 = (x2 + y2)2 term3 = (9 z2 - 1) (1 - z2) value = term1 + term2 - term3 # Gradient dx = -12 (1 - z2) y x + 4 x3 + 4 y2 x dy = 6 (1 - z2) (y2 - x2) + 4 y3 + 4 x2 y dz = -4 (y2 - 3 x2) y z - (20 z - 36 z3) return value, Vector3f(dx, dy, dz) class WineGlassSurface(ImplicitGeometry): def evaluate(self, p): x, y, z = p.x, p.y, p.z # Domain boundary check if z + 3.2 <= 0: return float('inf'), Vector3f(0, 0, 0) # Value logval = math.log(z + 3.2) value = x2 + y2 - logval2 - 0.09 # Gradient dx = 2 x dy = 2 y dz = -2 logval / (z + 3.2) return value, Vector3f(dx, dy, dz) class PorousSurface(ImplicitGeometry): def evaluate(self, p): x, y, z = p.x, p.y, p.z # Value termy = (y2 - 0.88)2 (2.92 (x3 - x) x + 1.7 y2)2 termz = (z2 - 0.88)2 (2.92 (y3 - y) y + 1.7 z2)2 termx = (x2 - 0.88)2 (1.7 x2 + 2.92 (z3 - z) z)2 value = -0.02 + termy + termz + termx # Gradient calculation omitted as explicit formulas not provided in sources return value, Vector3f(0, 0, 0) A variant where volume density \rho(\vec{x}) is derived directly from the implicit function value. The geometry is converted to a levelset (signed distance function) via the Fast Marching Method. Density is defined as: \rho(\vec{x}) = \begin{cases} f(\vec{x})/f{max} & \text{if } f(\vec{x}) > 0 \text{ (inside)} \\ 0 & \text{if } f(\vec{x}) \le 0 \text{ (outside)} \end{cases}. Common implicit functions used in this context include the Torus (4R^2(x^2+z^2) - (|x|+R-r)^2 = 0) and Cone (\cos^{-1}((\vec{x}\cdot\hat{a})/|\vec{x}|) - \theta = 0). Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point, as it involves evaluating a mathematical function. However, complex functions (like PorousSurface) may involve many arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the function definition itself. Does not require storing a voxel grid, unlike discrete volume methods. Strengths: Infinite resolution; no aliasing artifacts from grid discretization; easy to modify geometry by changing parameters. Limitations: No precomputed acceleration structures (like BVHs) are inherent to the sampling method itself, though they can be built on top. When to use: When high-quality, alias-free rendering of smooth, complex implicit shapes is required, and memory for large voxel grids is prohibitive. When not to use: When the geometry is highly irregular or requires explicit mesh-like features that are difficult to express as a single implicit function. Implicit geometry sampling originates from the field of F-Rep (Functional Representation) solids. A seminal work is "The Making of Black-Hole and Nebula Clouds for the Motion Picture 'Sphere' with Volumetric Rendering and the F-Rep of Solids" by Gokhan Kisacikoglu (Siggraph 1998). The technique is widely used in procedural volume rendering to generate density fields from mathematical definitions, avoiding the storage and interpolation errors associated with discrete voxel grids. name: Specific Implicit Primitives
body: This family provides closed-form analytical expressions for the scalar field f(\vec{x}) of specific geometric primitives, primarily yielding exact signed Euclidean distances. Unlike generic implicit surface definitions that may rely on approximations or piecewise kernels, these functions offer precise evaluation for standard shapes like tori, shells, and periodic surfaces, which is critical for robust marching cubes and ray marching in volume rendering. Builds on Implicit Surface Primitives. All methods evaluate a scalar field function f over a domain \Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3 on-demand without persistent data structures. The geometry is computed directly via mathematical formulas, typically returning the exact signed distance to ensure \|\nabla f(\vec{x})\| \approx 1 for stable gradient-based rendering. Defines a torus as the zero-level set of a scalar field, providing the exact signed Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface. It is distinguished from approximate quadric representations by its analytical closed-form solution, which avoids the gradient singularities and approximation errors inherent in first-order Taylor expansions of implicit quadrics. Choose it when exact distance queries are required for ray marching or CSG operations. A class of implicit surface primitives defined by a bounded, exponentially-decaying field function attributed to the Wyvill brothers. They solve the problem of creating smooth, organic shapes that can be easily morphed and deformed by adjusting control primitive attributes. Unlike Meta balls, which require square root computations for distance normalization, Soft Objects rely solely on squared distances, offering a slight computational advantage. Choose them for organic modeling and morphable volume fields. Definition: Evaluates the scalar field for a Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) Gyroid at point (x,y,z). Formula: f(x,y,z) = \sin(sx)\cos(sy) + \sin(sy)\cos(sz) + \sin(sz)\cos(sx), where sx = x \cdot scale, sy = y \cdot scale, sz = z \cdot scale. Parameter: scale: The scaling factor for the gyroid coordinates. Default value is 4.5. Definition: Implicit function for a thin spherical shell: f(p) = |x^2+y^2+z^2 - r^2| - \epsilon. Parameter: radius: Sphere radius for the shell, default 1.0. Parameter: epsilon: Half-thickness of the shell, default 1e-3. Definition: Generates a rectangular prism centered at the origin. Parameter: x, y, z: Prism dimensions. Default: 5x5x5. Even dimensions round up to the next odd number. Layout: Returns a data.frame of voxel coordinates. Pitfall: Only odd side lengths are generated. Even dimensions are rounded up to the next odd number due to integer coordinate quantization. Definition: A bounded field function where control primitives have no influence after a maximum distance 'b', solving the computational expense of infinite-range functions. Step: Osaka University graduate students implemented a piecewise quadratic approximation to the Gaussian for faster ray-surface intersection testing, avoiding iterative root finders by solving a quadratic equation. Parameter: 'a' is a scaling factor; 'b' is the maximum distance a control primitive contributes to the field. History: Term 'metaballs' (or misspelled 'meatballs') was used by people at Osaka University and Toyo Links in Japan. Definition: A field function attributed to Jim Blinn, modeled after electron density fields, using a Gaussian curve centered at the origin. Pitfall: The field function extends to infinity, requiring summation of contributions from all control primitives for any point calculation, which becomes computationally expensive as the number of primitives increases. History: Proposed by Jim Blinn for animating DNA for Carl Sagan's COSMOS TV Series, where each atom was approximated by a Gaussian potential. The term "metaballs" (or misspelled "meatballs") was used by researchers at Osaka University and Toyo Links in Japan for blobby models. Jim Blinn proposed approximating atoms with Gaussian potentials for DNA animation in Carl Sagan's COSMOS TV series, which became known as blobby molecules. The Wyvill brothers introduced Soft Objects, a bounded field function using a truncated exponential series expansion that avoids square roots by relying on squared distances. The Gyroid surface is a Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) evaluated via a trigonometric scalar field. Rectangular prism generation is implemented in voxel visualization tools like the isocubes R package, which quantizes coordinates to integer values for isometric rendering. nff747/marching-cubes-wgsl, https://github.com/nff747/marching-cubes-wgsl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GitHub - narnia-ai-mason/iso-surface-rendering: Robust iso-surface..., https://github.com/narnia-ai-mason/iso-surface-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) isocubes: Voxel Data Visualization with Isometric Cubes, https://doi.org/10.32614/cran.package.isocubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Implicit surfaces - Paul Bourke, https://paulbourke.net/geometry/implicitsurf/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Torus Implicit Function
head: Torus SDF, Signed Distance Function (SDF) for Torus, Signed Distance Field (SDF) Torus Primitive, Torus distance, Torus Scalar Field, sdTorus
body: The Torus Implicit Function defines a torus as the zero-level set of a scalar field, typically providing the exact signed Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of a torus centered at the origin. Input: A query point \vec{p} = (px, py, pz) \in \mathbb{R}^3 and torus parameters. Output: A scalar value d \in \mathbb{R} representing the signed distance. d < 0 indicates the point is inside the torus, d > 0 indicates outside, and d = 0 lies on the surface. No persistent data structures are required for evaluation. The function is stateless and computes the value on-demand. The torus is defined by two radii: 1. Major Radius (R): The distance from the center of the torus to the center of the tube. 2. Minor Radius (r): The radius of the tube itself. Some implementations use diameter and thickness instead of radii. If tx is the diameter and ty is the thickness, then R = tx / 2 and r = ty / 2. The exact signed distance d is computed by projecting the point onto the plane of the torus's major ring and measuring the distance to the minor ring's center. Let \rho be the distance of the point's projection onto the plane of the major ring from the axis of revolution. For a torus aligned with the Y-axis (lying in the XZ plane): \rho = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} Define an intermediate 2D vector \vec{q} in the plane containing the axis of revolution and the point's projection: qx = \rho - R qy = py The signed distance is the Euclidean distance from \vec{q} to the origin, minus the minor radius: d = \sqrt{qx^2 + qy^2} - r Substituting the definitions: d = \sqrt{(\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - R)^2 + py^2} - r If the torus is aligned with the Z-axis (lying in the XY plane), swap py and pz in the \rho calculation or the final distance calculation accordingly. The following implementation computes the exact signed distance for a torus centered at the origin, aligned with the Y-axis (major ring in XZ plane). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sdtorus(px, py, pz, R, r): """ Compute the signed distance from point p to a torus. Args: px, py, pz: Coordinates of the query point. R: Major radius (distance from torus center to tube center). r: Minor radius (tube radius). Returns: Signed distance. Negative if inside, positive if outside. """ # 1. Calculate distance from the Y-axis (projection onto XZ plane) rho = math.sqrt(px px + pz pz) # 2. Construct the 2D vector q in the radial plane qx = rho - R qy = py # 3. Calculate Euclidean distance to the tube center line disttocenterline = math.sqrt(qx qx + qy qy) # 4. Subtract minor radius to get signed distance to surface return disttocenterline - r 1. Singularity at Axis: When \rho = 0 (the point lies on the axis of revolution), the term \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} is zero. The distance formula remains numerically stable because it does not involve division by \rho. However, naive gradient implementations that divide by \rho (e.g., \frac{x}{\rho}) will fail. 2. Approximation Failure: First-order Taylor approximations of the implicit function (e.g., f(\vec{x}) = (\sqrt{x^2+y^2}-R)^2 + z^2 - r^2) require normalization by the gradient magnitude. If the gradient magnitude approaches zero (near the center of the torus hole or at specific symmetry points), the approximation becomes inaccurate or undefined. The exact SDF formula avoids this division. 3. Coordinate System Alignment: The formula depends on the axis of revolution. The sources generally assume the torus lies in the XZ plane (aligned with the Y-axis) or XY plane depending on the coordinate system used in the specific code snippet. Time Complexity: O(1). The evaluation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations, square roots, and absolute values. Memory Complexity: O(1). No storage is required beyond the parameters R and r. Strengths: Provides the exact Euclidean distance, which is crucial for stable sphere tracing and accurate normal estimation via the gradient of the SDF. Limitations: Requires a square root operation, which is more expensive than simple polynomial evaluations, though modern hardware handles this efficiently. It is only applicable to perfect tori; deformed tori require different methods. The signed distance function for a torus is a standard primitive in Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering and ray marching. It was popularized in the computer graphics community by Inigo Quilez, who provided efficient implementations and geometric derivations for common primitives. The geometric derivation relies on the torus being the product of two circles, allowing the distance to be decomposed into radial and axial components. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Leesan-haruki/FunctionRenderer, https://github.com/Leesan-haruki/FunctionRenderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) jakeoung/ShapeFromProjections, https://github.com/jakeoung/ShapeFromProjections, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GitHub - narnia-ai-mason/iso-surface-rendering: Robust iso-surface..., https://github.com/narnia-ai-mason/iso-surface-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Raymarching Distance Fields: Concepts and Implementation..., https://adrianb.io/2016/10/01/raymarching.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces, http://graphics.cs.illinois.edu/sites/default/files/zeno.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Soft Objects
head: Wyvill Soft Objects
body: Soft Objects are a class of implicit surface primitives defined by a bounded field function attributed to the Wyvill brothers. They solve the problem of creating smooth, organic shapes that can be easily morphed and deformed by adjusting control primitive attributes. Unlike Meta balls, which require square root computations for distance normalization, Soft Objects rely solely on squared distances, offering a slight computational advantage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point \vec{x} in 3D space, and parameters for a control primitive: scaling factor a and maximum influence distance b. Output: A scalar field value f(\vec{x}) representing the contribution of the primitive to the total volume field. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required for the primitive evaluation itself; the field is computed directly via formula. Method: The field function is derived from the first few terms of a series expansion of an exponential function, truncated to restrict the range of influence. 1. Calculate the squared Euclidean distance d^2 between the query point \vec{x} and the center of the control primitive \vec{c}: d^2 = \|\vec{x} - \vec{c}\|^2 2. Check if the distance exceeds the maximum influence range b. If d^2 > b^2, the contribution is zero: f(\vec{x}) = 0 3. Otherwise, compute the field value using the scaling factor a and the squared distance. The exact closed-form expression is not provided in the sources. Parameters: a: Scaling factor. Determines the magnitude of the field contribution. Can be negative to turn the primitive into a subtractive volume. b: Maximum distance. The control primitive has no influence after distance b. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of squared distances avoids the computational cost and potential precision issues of square roots required by Meta balls. Boundaries: The function is continuous and smoothly changing, ensuring no discontinuities at the boundary d=b. Subtraction: Setting a < 0 turns the primitive into a subtractive volume, allowing for constructive geometry operations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def softobjectfield(x, c, a, b): dx = x[0] - c[0] dy = x[1] - c[1] dz = x[2] - c[2] dsquared = dxdx + dydy + dzdz bsquared = b b if dsquared > bsquared: return 0.0 # Compute field value using scaling factor a and squared distance # Exact formula not specified in sources return 0.0 # Replace with actual truncated exponential series implementation A procedural method for generating organic, branching volume data by constructing a hierarchical tree of spheres. It distinguishes itself from generic tree generators by its specific use of "soft object" contouring and its strict layer-by-layer generation process governed by collision constraints based on genealogical proximity. It is chosen when complex, naturalistic coral geometries are required as implicit fields for soft object rendering. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Smooth, continuous surfaces; easy morphing and deformation by slowly changing control primitive attributes; computationally efficient due to avoidance of square roots; bounded support restricts influence range. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Soft Objects were investigated by the Wyvill brothers and their graduate students in Canada and New Zealand. They explored approximations of Gaussians, animation, and other ideas related to implicit surfaces. While similar to the "blobbies" or "metaballs" developed by others, the Wyvill group termed their creations "soft objects". The field function is based on a truncated exponential series expansion, providing a bounded influence range.
