name: Coral Growth Algorithm
head: Parametrized growth algorithm, Tree of spheres construction
body: The Coral Growth Algorithm is a procedural method for generating organic, branching volume data by constructing a hierarchical tree of spheres. It solves the problem of creating complex, naturalistic coral geometries that serve as implicit fields for soft object rendering. It is distinguished from generic tree generators by its specific use of "soft object" contouring, where the final shape is defined by the sum of spherically symmetric density functions rather than explicit mesh boundaries, and by its strict layer-by-layer generation process governed by collision constraints based on genealogical proximity. The algorithm constructs a volume density field defined by a set of spheres. The structure is determined by the centers of these spheres and their outer radii, where the density functions become zero. The resulting contour surface is rendered as a soft object. Inputs: 13 scalar constants (see Parameters). 2 boolean flags for optional features. A random seed. Outputs: A list of spheres, each defined by a center position (x, y, z) and a radius r. The spheres are organized in a tree structure with a root and generations (layers). The core data structure is a list of sphere objects. Each sphere object contains: center: A 3D vector (x, y, z). radius: A scalar float r. parentindex: An integer index pointing to the parent sphere in the list (or -1 for the root). generation: An integer indicating the layer index n (0 for root). children: A list of indices pointing to child spheres. The following 13 constants define the shape: 1. numlevels: Total number of levels in the tree. 2. a: Initial radius for the root sphere (n=0). 3. b: Radius decrease factor per level (b < 1). 4. bondfactor: Multiplier for the distance between parent and child centers. 5. g: Number of generations back for which a common ancestor allows a lenient collision factor. 6. adjacent: Collision factor for spheres with a common ancestor within g generations. 7. nonadjacent: Collision factor for spheres with no close common ancestor. 8. mindistmult: Multiple of bondr(n) used to increment the minimum distance from the root node. 9. minzmult: Multiple of bondr(n) used to increment the minimum z-value. 10. zlow: Truncation level for the unit sphere of directions (removes directions with z < z{low}). 11. d: Base constant in the maxsphere formula. 12. tryfac: Factor for calculating maxtrials. 13. seed: Initial seed for the random number generator. Two optional features can be enabled: 1. interpolateextra: If true, interpolates an extra sphere between parent and child if distance is large. 2. continuebranch: If true, attempts to continue the branch curve to a grandchild if a child has no other children. Sphere Radius: The radius of a sphere at generation n is: r(n) = a \cdot b^n Bond Distance: The distance between the center of a new sphere (generation n) and its parent (generation n-1) is: bond\r(n) = bondfactor \cdot (r(n) + r(n-1)) Maximum Spheres per Layer: The maximum number of spheres allowed in layer n is: max\sphere(n) = \lfloor 2 \cdot d^n \rfloor Note: The source text states "e is always 2" and "floor (c • dh)", implying c=2 and the exponent is n (referred to as h in the garbled text, but contextually the level index). Max Trials: The maximum number of random trials before giving up on a layer is: maxtrials = tryfac \cdot max\sphere(n) Collision Distance: The minimum squared distance between a trial sphere (level n) and an accepted sphere (level i) depends on their genealogical relationship: If they share a common ancestor within g generations (i.e., \max(0, n-g, i-g) is the level of the common ancestor): dist\min = adjacent \cdot (r(n) + r(i)) Otherwise (no close common ancestor): dist\min = nonadjacent \cdot (r(n) + r(i)) Shape Constraints: Minimum distance from root: min\dist(n) = min\dist\mult \cdot bond\r(n) Minimum z-value: min\z(n) = min\z\mult \cdot bond\r(n) 1. Initialize: Create the root sphere (generation 0) at the origin (or specified start position) with radius r(0) = a. Set currentgeneration = 0. 2. Loop Generations: While currentgeneration < numlevels: a. Calculate r(current\generation) and max\sphere(current\generation). b. Initialize acceptedcount = 0 and trialcount = 0. c. Generate Spheres: While acceptedcount < maxsphere(currentgeneration) and trialcount < maxtrials: i. Select a parent sphere randomly from generation currentgeneration - 1. ii. Generate a random direction vector on a unit sphere. Reject if the z-component is < z{low}. Normalize the direction. iii. Calculate the trial center: center{trial} = center{parent} + direction \cdot bond\r(current\generation). iv. Check Shape Constraints: If distance from root > min\dist(current\generation), reject. If z < min\z(current\generation), reject. v. Check Collision: For every accepted sphere in the entire tree: Calculate squared distance d^2 between center{trial} and accepted sphere center. Determine if they share a common ancestor within g generations. Calculate dist\min using the appropriate factor (adjacent or nonadjacent). If d^2 < dist\min^2, reject. vi. If all checks pass, add the trial sphere to the accepted list and increment acceptedcount. vii. Increment trialcount. d. Optional Feature 1 (Interpolation): If interpolateextra is enabled, iterate through all parent-child pairs. If the distance between parent and child is large, insert an intermediate sphere to maintain density and smooth curvature. e. Optional Feature 2 (Branch Continuation): If continuebranch is enabled, for any child sphere with no children, attempt to generate a grandchild. Generate a random position for the grandchild. If this position violates collision constraints, revise it to follow the smooth continuation of the branch curve from the child, provided the new position does not violate constraints. f. Increment currentgeneration. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random class Sphere: def init(self, center, radius, parentindex, generation): self.center = center self.radius = radius self.parentindex = parentindex self.generation = generation self.children = [] def generatecoral(params): # Unpack parameters numlevels = params['numlevels'] a = params['a'] b = params['b'] bondfactor = params['bondfactor'] g = params['g'] adjacent = params['adjacent'] nonadjacent = params['nonadjacent'] mindistmult = params['mindistmult'] minzmult = params['minzmult'] zlow = params['zlow'] d = params['d'] tryfac = params['tryfac'] seed = params['seed'] interpolateextra = params['interpolateextra'] continuebranch = params['continuebranch'] random.seed(seed) spheres = [] # Initialize root root = Sphere(center=[0, 0, 0], radius=a, parentindex=-1, generation=0) spheres.append(root) for n in range(1, numlevels): rn = a (b n) rnminus1 = a (b (n - 1)) bondrn = bondfactor (rn + rnminus1) maxspheren = math.floor(2 (d n)) maxtrials = tryfac maxspheren acceptedcount = 0 trialcount = 0 while acceptedcount < maxspheren and trialcount < maxtrials: # Select random parent from previous generation parentidx = random.randint(0, len(spheres) - 1) # Ensure parent is from previous generation while spheres[parentidx].generation != n - 1: parentidx = random.randint(0, len(spheres) - 1) parent = spheres[parentidx] # Generate random direction on truncated unit sphere while True: # Generate random point on unit sphere u = random.random() v = random.random() theta = 2 math.pi u phi = math.acos(2 v - 1) x = math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta) y = math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta) z = math.cos(phi) if z >= zlow: break direction = [x, y, z] # Calculate trial center trialcenter = [ parent.center[0] + direction[0] bondrn, parent.center[1] + direction[1] bondrn, parent.center[2] + direction[2] bondrn ] # Check shape constraints distfromroot = math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in trialcenter)) mindist = mindistmult bondrn minz = minzmult bondrn if distfromroot < mindist or trialcenter[2] < minz: trialcount += 1 continue # Check collision collision = False for other in spheres: dx = trialcenter[0] - other.center[0] dy = trialcenter[1] - other.center[1] dz = trialcenter[2] - other.center[2] distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz # Determine common ancestor generations back # Find common ancestor level # This requires traversing up the tree, which is O(N) per check # For efficiency, we assume a helper function getcommonancestorlevel commonlevel = getcommonancestorlevel(parentidx, other.parentindex, spheres) # Check if common ancestor is within g generations # The generation of the common ancestor is commonlevel # The current generation is n, other generation is other.generation # If max(0, n-g, other.generation-g) == commonlevel, they are adjacent # Simplified: if the depth difference to common ancestor is <= g for both depthdifftrial = n - commonlevel depthdiffother = other.generation - commonlevel if depthdifftrial <= g and depthdiffother <= g: distmin = adjacent (rn + other.radius) else: distmin = nonadjacent (rn + other.radius) if distsq < distmin distmin: collision = True break if not collision: newsphere = Sphere(center=trialcenter, radius=rn, parentindex=parentidx, generation=n) spheres.append(newsphere) spheres[parentidx].children.append(len(spheres) - 1) acceptedcount += 1 trialcount += 1 # Optional Feature 1: Interpolate extra spheres if interpolateextra: interpolatespheres(spheres, n) # Optional Feature 2: Continue branch if continuebranch: continuebranches(spheres, n) return spheres def getcommonancestorlevel(idx1, idx2, spheres): # Traverse up from idx1 and idx2 to find common ancestor # Returns the generation level of the common ancestor # If no common ancestor (should not happen in a tree), return -1 path1 = [] curr = idx1 while curr != -1: path1.append(curr) curr = spheres[curr].parentindex path2 = [] curr = idx2 while curr != -1: path2.append(curr) curr = spheres[curr].parentindex # Find first common node set1 = set(path1) for node in path2: if node in set1: return spheres[node].generation return -1 def interpolatespheres(spheres, currentgen): # Iterate through spheres of currentgen # If distance to parent is large, insert intermediate sphere # Implementation details omitted as per source description "interpolates an extra sphere" pass def continuebranches(spheres, currentgen): # Iterate through spheres of currentgen # If sphere has no children, try to add grandchild # Implementation details omitted as per source description pass Precision: The collision check involves squared distances and floating-point comparisons. Small errors in position accumulation may lead to false positives or negatives in collision detection. Boundaries: The truncation of the direction sphere (z < z{low}) ensures upward growth but may lead to sparse regions if z{low} is too high. Degenerate Input: If tryfac is too low, the algorithm may fail to fill the maximum number of spheres for a layer, resulting in a sparse structure. Ancestor Lookup: The collision check requires finding the common ancestor level, which can be computationally expensive if not optimized. The source implies a direct check based on generation count g. Time Complexity: The generation of each layer involves up to maxtrials trials. Each trial requires checking against all previously accepted spheres for collision. Thus, the complexity is roughly O(N^2) where N is the total number of spheres, due to the pairwise collision checks. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the sphere data and tree structure. Performance: The algorithm is procedural and does not require pre-computation of a grid, making it memory-efficient for high-resolution details. However, the quadratic collision check can become slow for large numbers of spheres. Strengths: Produces organic, natural-looking coral shapes with smooth contours. The soft object rendering allows for easy shading and bump mapping. Limitations: The shape is controlled by a fixed set of 13 parameters, which may limit the variety of shapes compared to more complex L-systems or fractal methods. The random nature means reproducibility requires a fixed seed. The Coral Growth Algorithm was developed by Nelson Max and Geoff Wyvill. It was introduced in the paper "Shapes and Textures for Rendering Coral". The method is part of the Katachi system, which uses soft objects for modeling. The algorithm is similar to other parametrized growth algorithms used for building trees, such as those by Bloomenthal, Aono & Kunii, De Reffye et al., Viennot et al., and Prusinkiewicz. The resulting shapes were initially examined in hidden line sketches and then rendered using ray tracing with generalized volume textures for shading and bump mapping. name: Metaball-based Envelope Painting
head: 3D Envelope Painting, 3D Painting Metaphor for Envelope Definition, 3D Painting Metaphor for VOI Definition, Metaball-based envelope definition, Thick Paint Metaphor, Volume Painting
body: Metaball-based Envelope Painting is an interaction model for defining a Volume of Interest (VOI) or Region of Interest (ROI) within unsegmented volumetric data by "painting" an implicit envelope around features of interest. It solves the problem of intuitive, context-preserving volume exploration by replacing complex transfer function tuning with a direct spatial marking metaphor. Unlike techniques using independent surface-bound brushes or fixed-depth peeling regions, this method uses a higher-level shape representation (Metaballs) to create organic, merging envelopes that allow for real-time previewing of the visualization effect before final deposition. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric dataset V, camera parameters, user input (mouse position, button states). Output: A composite image showing the volume with two distinct visualization styles: one for the interior of the envelope (VOI) and one for the exterior, combined via depth peeling. Data Structures: Metaball List: A dynamic list of metaball primitives. Each metaball Mi is defined by: Center position \vec{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Radius/Scale ri \in \mathbb{R}^+. Polarity pi \in \{+1, -1\} (positive for painting, negative for erasing). Shape type: Quadric (spherical) or Superquadric (cylindrical/disk). Vertex Buffer: A GPU memory buffer storing the polygonal mesh of the envelope's isosurface, generated by Marching Cubes. Position/Normal Maps: On-the-fly generated Gaussian-smoothed textures storing the surface position and normal vectors for 3D surface painting mode. Mathematical Definition: The envelope is defined by a scalar field function f(\vec{x}) constructed from the sum of individual metaball fields. The field falloff for a single metaball is modeled using the six-degree Wyvill polynomial: fi(\vec{x}) = \frac{6ri^6 - 15ri^4|\vec{x}-\vec{c}i|^2 + 10ri^3|\vec{x}-\vec{c}i|^3}{|\vec{x}-\vec{c}i|^6} where |\vec{x}-\vec{c}i| is the distance from point \vec{x} to the metaball center \vec{c}i, and ri is the radius of the metaball. The total field is the sum of all active metaballs: f(\vec{x}) = \sum{i} pi \cdot fi(\vec{x}) where pi is the polarity (+1 or -1). Parameters: Brush Tip Shape: Spherical (default, quadric) or Cylindrical (superquadric, used in 3D Surface Painting Mode). Brush Tip Polarity: Positive (paint/add) or Negative (erase/remove). Cylinder Height: Adjustable parameter for cylindrical brushes to control penetration depth into the volume surface. MIDA Parameters: Two separate sets of Maximum Intensity Difference Accumulation (MIDA) visualization parameters are used: one for inside the envelope, one for outside. Steps: 1. Initialization: Load volumetric data and initialize MIDA visualization parameters for inside and outside regions. Initialize an empty Metaball List. Generate Gaussian-smoothed position and normal maps for the volume surface. 2. Preview (Move): As the user moves the mouse, calculate the 3D position of the brush tip \vec{c}{tip}. In 3D Free-hand Mode: The depth is determined by user control or ray casting. In 3D Surface Painting Mode: The depth is overridden by the depth value of the object's surface at the projected position, retrieved from the position map. The brush orientation aligns with the surface normal from the normal map. In 2D Screen Painting Mode: The depth is constant or discarded, acting as a 2D stencil. Construct a temporary metaball M{tip} at \vec{c}{tip} with current brush parameters. Evaluate f(\vec{x}) for all voxels/samples. Visualize the volume using the "inside" MIDA parameters for regions where f(\vec{x}) indicates inclusion (based on the preview blob) and "outside" parameters otherwise. This provides real-time feedback. 3. Deposit (Click): If the user clicks (e.g., holding Alt key): Add M{tip} to the Metaball List. If polarity is negative, negate or erase the results of the previous painting operations. 4. Surface Extraction: Compute the isosurface of the current Metaball List using the Marching Cubes algorithm. Implement a fast GLSL shader version of Marching Cubes to extract the iso-surface. Capture the resulting geometry into a memory vertex buffer. Reuse this buffer for subsequent frames to avoid recomputation. 5. Rendering: Render the volumetric data using the chosen DVR technique (e.g., MIDA). Render the polygonal envelope geometry using Front-to-Back Depth Peeling. This combines the polygon-based envelope geometry and volumetric DVR geometry layer by layer from the camera position, filling gaps between layers with DVR results. Apply the "inside" visualization style to the volume parts enclosed by the envelope and the "outside" style to the rest. In 2D mode, the stencil applies the inside style all the way through the volume (X-ray style). 6. Editing (Optional): To carve/peel volume data, set the mapped data intensity range to zero for parts inside or outside the envelope. Pseudocode: Unverified code. metaball.center[i] for i in range(3)] distsq = sum(dd for d in distvec) dist = distsq 0.5 if dist == 0: return 1.0 # Singularity handling r = metaball.radius # Six-degree Wyvill polynomial numerator = 6 r6 - 15 r4 distsq + 10 r3 dist3 denominator = dist6 return numerator / denominator def evaluatefield(x): total = 0.0 for mb in metaballs: total += mb.polarity wyvillfield(x, mb) return total def isinside(x): return evaluatefield(x) > 0 # Threshold choice def raycastatdepth(screenx, screeny, depth): return (screenx, screeny, depth) # Standard ray-plane intersection def samplevolume(data, pos, params): return params["color"] # Standard trilinear interpolation def blendwithenvelope(color, pos, mesh): return color # Standard depth test and blending def renderframe(camera, volumedata): global vertexbuffer if metaballschanged: vertexbuffer = "extractedmesh" # GLSL Marching Cubes extraction metaballschanged = False # Front-to-Back Depth Peeling renders layers from camera position for layeridx in range(100): layerpos = raycastatdepth(camera.cx, camera.cy, layeridx) inside = isinside(layerpos) params = insideparams if inside else outsideparams color = samplevolume(volumedata, layerpos, params) if vertexbuffer: color = blendwithenvelope(color, layerpos, vertexbuffer) # Write to framebuffer layer def onmousemove(mousex, mousey): tippos = raycastatdepth(mousex, mousey, CONSTANTDEPTH) if currentmode == "3DSURFACE": tippos = raycastatdepth(mousex, mousey, positionmap.get((mousex, mousey), CONSTANTDEPTH)) previewmb = Metaball(tippos, brushradius, brushpolarity, brushshape) metaballs.append(previewmb) renderframe(camera, volumedata) metaballs.pop() def onmouseclick(mousex, mousey): tippos = raycastatdepth(mousex, mousey, CONSTANTDEPTH) if currentmode == "3DSURFACE": tippos = raycastatdepth(mousex, mousey, positionmap.get((mousex, mousey), CONSTANTDEPTH)) shape = "superquadric" if currentmode == "3DSURFACE" else "quadric" newmb = Metaball(tippos, brushradius, brushpolarity, shape) metaballs.append(newmb) metaballschanged = True Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: The Wyvill polynomial has a singularity at the center of the metaball (|\vec{x}-\vec{c}i|=0). A guard value (e.g., returning 1.0) is required. 2D Mode Depth: In 2D Screen Painting Mode, depth information is discarded, applying the visualization effect through the entire volume along the ray (X-ray style). Performance: Geometry recomputation is avoided by reusing the vertex buffer. Precision: The six-degree polynomial can suffer from floating-point precision issues at large distances or very small radii. This method allows users to define a Region of Interest (ROI) by placing brush strokes directly in the visualization space, creating an implicit envelope that encloses features of interest without requiring complex parameter tweaking. It differs from traditional transfer function specification by replacing 2D histogram curve manipulation with direct spatial marking, eliminating the need for volumetric data representation knowledge. It builds on Metaball-based Envelope Painting by providing the interaction model that generates the metaball parameters. The envelope is defined by a series of metaballs. The brush tip acts as the first metaball, defining the attributes (size, parameters) for every new metaball added to the series. Merging influence is determined by the size of the metaball and its proximity to other metaballs. Larger and closer metaballs have a greater merging factor. The specific mathematical form of the field function is a parameter of the metaball implementation. A 3D exploration task that exposes features of interest by completely removing occluding parts of the volume, often used to examine the outline or shape of internal structures. The user paints a 3D envelope around the parts of the volume to be removed using free-hand or surface painting modes. The MIDA sliders for the volume enclosed by the envelope are adjusted to set the visible sub-range of volume values to 0 (an empty range where min and max are the same). Strengths: Intuitive interaction, real-time preview, organic shapes, flexibility in envelope definition, independence from specific DVR techniques. Limitations: Requires GPU acceleration for real-time performance (GLSL shaders). 2D mode loses depth information. When to use: Interactive exploration of unsegmented volumetric data, defining contextual views, volume carving/peeling. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Metaball-based Envelope Painting was introduced by L. Faynshteyn and T. McInerney in 2012. It combines the Maximum Intensity Difference Accumulation (MIDA) visualization algorithm with a 3D interaction model based on a painting metaphor. The technique was validated through a user study involving 11 subjects (10 undergraduate, 1 graduate) from computer science departments. It builds on the concept of Metaballs as implicit surfaces and extends previous techniques like independent surface-bound brushes and depth-fixed peeling regions. name: 3D Painting Metaphor for ROI Definition
head: Brush stroke interaction, Envelope-based ROI, Painting metaphor
body: This method allows users to define a Region of Interest (ROI) by placing brush strokes directly in the visualization space, creating an envelope that encloses features of interest without requiring complex parameter tweaking. It differs from traditional transfer function specification by replacing 2D histogram curve manipulation with direct spatial marking, eliminating the need for volumetric data representation knowledge. It builds on Metaball-based Envelope Painting by providing the interaction model that generates the metaball parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: User mouse/pen input (stroke placement events). Output: An ROI envelope defined by a collection of metaball primitives. Data Structures: The envelope is represented as a collection of metaball primitives. Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Mode Selection: The user selects either 2D or 3D painting mode. 2. Stroke Initiation: The user places a brush stroke in the visualization area. 3. Coordinate Transformation: If 2D mode is active: The stroke position is interpreted as screen-space coordinates (u, v). The brush tip is circular in screen space. If 3D mode is active: The stroke position is interpreted as 3D world/volumetric coordinates. The brush tip is spherical in 3D space. 4. Envelope Expansion: The user places additional brush strokes to spread the paint, dynamically expanding the envelope. 5. Rendering/Usage: The resulting implicit field is evaluated during volume rendering to mask or highlight the ROI. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Brush Tip Geometry: Circular for 2D mode, Spherical for 3D mode. Painting Coordinate Space: Screen space (2D) or World/Volumetric space (3D). Metaball Threshold: Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: 2D Envelope Misalignment: 2D envelopes act like X-ray projections, potentially obscuring or misaligning with internal 3D structures when the object rotates, requiring explicit mode switching. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Intuitive, eliminates need for transfer function expertise, provides organic shapes. Limitations: 2D mode suffers from depth ambiguity and acts like an X-ray projection; 3D mode maintains relative position to the object. name: Implicit Function Evaluation
head: Volume Wrangle for Implicit Function
body: Implicit Function Evaluation generates voxel coordinates or scalar field values defined by a custom mathematical function f(x, y, z). It solves the problem of defining geometry procedurally rather than storing discrete mesh or voxel data, allowing for infinite resolution and easy parameterization. It differs from Metaball Field Evaluation by evaluating a single global function per point rather than summing contributions from multiple localized sources, and from Implicit Surface Primitives by focusing on the general mechanism of assigning scalar values to a grid rather than specific primitive shapes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}. Input: Domain dimensions nx, ny, nz. Input: Value range [lower, upper] defining the interior of the object. Input: Coordinate scaling factor scale. Output: A data structure containing coordinates and their corresponding scalar values f(\vec{x}). In Houdini, this is a scalar volume where each voxel contains a float attribute named f. Data Structures: R (isocubes): A data.frame of coordinates. Houdini: A voxel grid where each voxel stores a single float attribute f. Parameters: f: Function of form f(x, y, z) returning a numeric value. lower, upper: Range of values considered inside the object. Default: [-\infty, 0]. Values \le 0 are inside, > 0 are outside. scale: Extra scaling factor applied to coordinates before calling function. Default: 1. nx, ny, nz: Dimensions of the volume. Default: nx=51, ny=nx, nz=nx. r: A constant parameter used in specific function calculations (e.g., r=0.1). Steps: 1. Initialize a grid of resolution nx \times ny \times nz. 2. For each voxel at position (x, y, z): a. Apply scaling: x' = x \cdot scale, y' = y \cdot scale, z' = z \cdot scale. b. Evaluate the function: val = f(x', y', z'). c. Store val in the voxel's f attribute. 3. Identify voxels where lower \le val \le upper as interior. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluateimplicitfunction(f, nx=51, ny=51, nz=51, scale=1.0, lower=-float('inf'), upper=0.0): """ Evaluates an implicit function f(x,y,z) over a 3D grid. Args: f: A callable function f(x, y, z) -> float. nx, ny, nz: Dimensions of the volume. scale: Scaling factor for coordinates. lower, upper: Range defining the interior. Returns: A list of tuples (x, y, z, value) for voxels within the range. """ results = [] # Iterate over the grid for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): # Convert index to coordinate (assuming centered or normalized space) # Note: Exact coordinate mapping depends on the specific implementation's # origin and normalization. Here we assume a generic mapping. x = i y = j z = k # Apply scaling xscaled = x scale yscaled = y scale zscaled = z scale # Evaluate function value = f(xscaled, yscaled, zscaled) # Check if inside the object if lower <= value <= upper: results.append((x, y, z, value)) return results def houdiniarbitraryfunction(x, y, z): r = 0.1 a = 2 y (yy - 3xx) (1 - zz) b = (xx + yy)2 c = -(9zz - 1) (1 - zz) return a + b + c - rr def spherefunction(x, y, z): return xx + yy + zz Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point errors may cause the isosurface to be slightly inaccurate if the function is steep. Boundaries: The function must be defined over the entire domain. Undefined regions may cause crashes or NaN values. Degenerate Input: If scale=0, all coordinates map to the origin, potentially causing division by zero or constant outputs depending on f. Evaluates the sum of multiple implicit functions. Choose when blending multiple shapes is required. Metaball Field Evaluation Uses predefined mathematical shapes (spheres, tori). Choose for standard geometric primitives without custom code. Implicit Surface Primitives Focuses on generating points on the surface rather than the full volume. Choose for mesh extraction. Implicit Geometry Sampling Time Complexity: O(nx \cdot ny \cdot nz), as every voxel must be evaluated. Memory Complexity: O(nx \cdot ny \cdot nz) to store the scalar field. Strengths: Resolution-independent; easy to modify shape by changing f. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high resolutions; requires post-processing (marching cubes, etc.) to extract mesh. When to use: When geometry is defined by a mathematical equation rather than a mesh. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and the geometry is static and simple. The method originates from procedural modeling techniques in computer graphics. The genisosurface function is part of the isocubes R package, which provides voxel data visualization with isometric cubes. The Houdini implementation uses a "Volume Wrangle" node to assign scalar values to voxels based on a custom mathematical function, creating data for implicit surface extraction. isocubes: Voxel Data Visualization with Isometric Cubes, https://doi.org/10.32614/cran.package.isocubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Implicit Surfaces and Volumes - Houdini Tech Blog, https://marcelpadilla.com/HoudiniTutorial/tutorials/intermediate/implicit-surfaces/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Signed Distance Function (SDF) Generation and Processing
body: This family covers the generation, modification, and utilization of Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for volume rendering and geometric representation. It solves the problem of converting implicit geometric definitions into renderable volumetric data or interactive geometric primitives. It builds on Implicit Field Composition by providing the specific mechanisms to generate, smooth, and query the SDF values required for composition. All methods in this family operate on a scalar field d(\mathbf{x}) representing the signed Euclidean distance from a point \mathbf{x} to a zero-level set surface S = \{\mathbf{x}: d(\mathbf{x}) = 0\}. The gradient of the SDF, \nabla d(\mathbf{x}), provides the surface normal at the closest point on the surface, satisfying the Eikonal equation |\nabla d(\mathbf{x})| = 1. Transforms SDF values into volumetric density \sigma for alpha-compositing. It differs from raw density fields by deriving density from the distance to the surface, enabling open surfaces and varying thickness. Choose this when rendering implicit surfaces defined by SDFs using standard volume rendering techniques. Converts binary volumes to smooth SDFs using Jacobi iteration with topological constraints. It differs from Gaussian smoothing by guaranteeing the preservation of the exact binary topology and producing a valid SDF. Choose this when smoothing binary segmentations without altering the underlying shape topology. Generates and mutates 3D SDF volumes on the GPU using ping-pong buffering and Eikonal propagation. It differs from static generation by supporting real-time user input and ensuring geometric validity after local modifications. Choose this for interactive sculpting or real-time SDF updates. Parses a custom script language to generate GLSL code for SDF scene composition. It differs from volumetric methods by operating at the text-generation level, producing shader source code rather than texture data. Choose this for complex procedural implicit surfaces defined in code. Rebuilds an SDF from a given isocontour within a volumetric dataset. It differs from ping-pong buffering by operating directly on existing volumetric data to establish distance metrics relative to an internal iso-surface. Choose this when converting scalar volumes (e.g., fog density) into geometrically valid SDFs. Generates SDFs for multi-link robots conditioned on joint configurations. It differs from static mesh SDFs by explicitly composing individual link SDFs via forward kinematics, providing exact geometric fidelity for any joint state. Choose this for dynamic robot simulation or collision detection. Smooths material boundaries in segmented volumes using 2D Euclidean SDFs (ESDFs). It differs from 3D SDF methods by computing ESDFs only on individual 2D slices for efficiency, allowing interpolation and fairing of misaligned slices. Choose this for medical imaging or slice-based volume correction. Definition: Extends the implicit SDF representation to encode spatially variant properties such as color, semantic segmentation, or material alongside 3D geometry. Step: Train a network to predict both signed distance and the target property (e.g., color) for each 3D location. During rendering, query the network along rays to output both depth and the property value. Parameter: Latent code size conditioning the network. Example: 512-dim. Significantly smaller than explicit mesh representations (vertices + triangles + texture map), enabling potential model compression. Definition: An end-to-end method to optimize both SDF and reconstructed meshes jointly, predicting surface meshes from images. Step: Architecture: Use a ResNet-18 encoder to produce latent vectors \lambda from input images. Use DeepSDF conditioned on these latent vectors to learn the implicit shape representation. Prediction: Predict SDF values on a regular grid f\theta(G) and use SDC to reconstruct mesh M = \text{SDC}(SG) via a forward pass of the SDC network. Training Schedule: Initially train DeepSDF (with image encoder) and SDC independently. Then jointly fine-tune them for 200 epochs. Formula: Joint Learning Loss: \mathcal{L}{\text{SVR}} = \mathcal{L}{\text{SDF}} + \alpha3 \mathcal{L}{\text{SDR}} + \alpha4 \mathcal{L}{\text{D}}, where \mathcal{L}{\text{SDF}} and \mathcal{L}{\text{SDR}} reconstruct/regularize the implicit representation, and \mathcal{L}{\text{D}} trains SDC. Pitfall: Using the normal consistency loss \mathcal{L}N during joint training causes instability because the evaluated SDF might be noisy. Definition: MPFs decouple metric proximity from phase/sign information by learning two continuous fields: an unsigned metric field r(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0 and a phase field \theta(\mathbf{x}). The phase field induces a bounded indicator P(\mathbf{x}) = \tanh(\beta \theta(\mathbf{x})) in (-1, 1). The composite field is \phi(\mathbf{x}) = r(\mathbf{x})P(\mathbf{x}) + \theta(\mathbf{x}). The surface is the zero level set \{\mathbf{x}: \phi(\mathbf{x}) = 0\}. Step: Procedurally generate synthetic TSDFs using libsdf, an open-source C++ library implementing simple implicit geometric primitives. Randomly pick a sequence of randomly parametrized and oriented shapes from categories: flat surfaces, concave edges, convex edges, concave corners, convex corners, rounded surfaces, and rounded edges. Treat convexity and concavity as separate cases for non-oriented surfaces because the sign is inverted in the TSDF. Definition: A continuous function parameterized by time and object input data, used to procedurally generate unique, dynamic variations (such as affine transformations or material attributes) for 3D objects in a holistic SDF scene. Step: Calculate the grid cell vector independently from the Instancing operator using the formula: \text{gridCell} = \lfloor (\mathbf{p} + \text{interval} \times 0.5)/\text{interval} \rfloor, where \mathbf{p} is a point on the ray and interval is the repeat interval. Compute the dynamic variation by evaluating the HSD function with the current time and the calculated grid cell: \text{variation} = f{\text{HSD}}(\text{time}, \text{gridCell}). Apply the Instancing operator to the transformed point: \text{InstancingOp}(\mathbf{p}, \text{interval}). Formula: f{\text{HSD}}: D \times t \rightarrow V, where V is the dynamics variation for a given 3D object, D is the object input data, and t is the current simulation time. Parameter: Input data D: Typically the object's world space position or its grid cell ID. Implementation methods: Can be a simple pseudorandom noise generator, trigonometric functions, Fractional Brownian Motions, or Vector Fields. Definition: A nonlinear compression method using an artificial neural network with a bottleneck layer to learn a low-dimensional feature representation of TSDF voxel blocks. Step: Construct a fully connected neural network with symmetric encoder and decoder layers. Insert an intermediary hidden layer (bottleneck) with dimensionality smaller than the input and output layers. This layer serves as the code/feature layer. Train the network by setting the desired output equal to the input and minimizing the reconstruction error using back-propagation. Formula: The descriptor dp is computed by chaining affine transformations and activation functions: dp = f(Lk \dots f(L2 f(L1 \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{b}1) + \mathbf{b}2) \dots + \mathbf{b}k), where Li are layer weights, \mathbf{b}i are biases, and f is an element-wise activation function. Signed Distance Functions have been a cornerstone of geometric modeling and rendering for decades. The family article cites "DIST: Rendering Deep Implicit Signed Distance Function With Differentiable Sphere Tracing" (2020) as a key reference for differentiable rendering of SDFs. The use of auto-encoders for TSDF compression is detailed in. The joint learning of implicit surfaces and meshing is presented in. The handling of sign-ambiguous geometry via Metric-Phase Fields is introduced in. Procedural TSDF generation for training data is described in. Dynamic scene variations using HSD are covered in. name: SDF to Density Conversion
head: signed distance to density conversion
body: SDF to Density Conversion transforms a Signed Distance Function (SDF) d(\mathbf{x}) into a volumetric density field \sigma(\mathbf{x}) suitable for differentiable volume rendering and alpha compositing. It addresses the mismatch between geometric distance values and optical absorption properties, enabling the integration of color and opacity along rays. It differs from standard Volume Rendering by deriving density directly from an implicit function rather than pre-computed volumes, and from VolSDF Volume Rendering by its reliance on exponential or sigmoid-based mappings to ensure alpha-invariance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Signed distance value d (or s = -d) at a point \mathbf{x} along a ray; ray segment length \Delta t; learnable or tuned scalar parameters \alpha (scaling) and \beta (falloff/sharpness). Output: Volumetric density \sigma (or \rho) and optionally a color/feature vector c. Data Structures: Ray Bundle: Contains sample points \mathbf{p}i and depth values ti along the ray. Parameters: \alpha \in \mathbb{R}^+, \beta \in \mathbb{R}^+. Steps: 1. Sample SDF: Evaluate the SDF at the sample points along the ray to obtain signed distances di. 2. Compute Segment Lengths: Calculate the distance between consecutive sample points \Delta ti = t{i+1} - ti. Pad the last segment with a large value (e.g., 10^{10}) to prevent division by zero when the ray exits the sampling volume. 3. Convert SDF to Intermediate Density: Map the signed distance to an intermediate density \rho using a piecewise exponential function controlled by \beta. Let s = -d (so s > 0 is interior, s < 0 is exterior). Compute \psi: \psi = \begin{cases} 0.5 \cdot \exp(s / \beta) & \text{if } s \le 0 \\ 1 - 0.5 \cdot \exp(-s / \beta) & \text{if } s > 0 \end{cases}. Scale by \alpha: \rho = \alpha \cdot \psi. 4. Compute Final Density: Convert the intermediate density \rho to volumetric density \sigma by accounting for the segment length \Delta t: \sigma = -\frac{\ln(1 - \rho)}{\Delta t}. Note: If \rho is not clamped to [0, 1), \ln(1-\rho) may be undefined. Ensure \rho < 1. 5. Compute Color/Feature (Optional): Compute basecolor: If rainbow mode is enabled, basecolor is derived from the position relative to the SDF center, clamped to [0.02, 0.98]. Otherwise, basecolor is 1.0. Compute final feature: c = \text{base\color} \cdot \text{feature\param}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def sdftodensity(signeddistance, alpha, beta): """Converts signed distance values to intermediate density.""" s = -signeddistance psi = torch.where( s <= 0.0, 0.5 torch.exp(s / beta), 1 - 0.5 torch.exp(-s / beta)) return alpha psi def computevolumetricdensity(intermediatedensity, deltat): """Converts intermediate density to volumetric density sigma.""" rho = torch.clamp(intermediatedensity, min=0.0, max=0.9999) return -torch.log(1.0 - rho) / deltat def renderstep(raybundle, sdffn, alpha, beta, rainbow=False, center=None, featureparam=None): """Full rendering step for a ray bundle.""" points = raybundle['samplepoints'] depths = raybundle['depths'] deltas = depths[1:] - depths[:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.fulllike(deltas[:1], 1e10)]) signeddistances = sdffn(points) rho = sdftodensity(signeddistances, alpha, beta) sigma = computevolumetricdensity(rho, deltas) if rainbow: if center is None: center = torch.zeroslike(points) basecolor = torch.clamp(torch.abs(points - center), 0.02, 0.98) else: basecolor = torch.oneslike(points) feature = basecolor featureparam if featureparam is not None else basecolor return {'density': sigma, 'feature': feature} Parameters: \alpha: Scalar multiplier for intermediate density, controls overall opacity. Initialized from configuration or learned. \beta: Scalar controlling the exponential falloff rate of density from the surface. Smaller values yield sharper surfaces. Initialized from configuration or learned. rainbow: Boolean flag; if true, computes basecolor as clamp(|samplepoints - center|, 0.02, 0.98), otherwise sets it to 1.0. sharpness: In some contexts (e.g., IOR), controls the gradient of the transition. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: The last segment's delta is padded with a large value (e.g., 10^{10}) to prevent division by zero or undefined behavior when the ray exits the sampling volume. Log Domain: Ensure intermediate density \rho < 1 before applying \ln(1-\rho). Sign Convention: The sign convention follows the parent article: d < 0 indicates interior and d > 0 indicates exterior [Parent]. The conversion function must handle this correctly (e.g., s = -d). Generates a spatially varying index of refraction (IOR) field to simulate optical phenomena such as mirages. It differs from density-based volume methods by explicitly modeling refractive properties rather than just absorption or emission, allowing for ray bending effects. Choose when simulating temperature-induced density gradients in air. Converts an SDF value into volumetric density for a box primitive, applying a sigmoid-based erosion at the boundaries to create smooth, anti-aliased edges and adding Perlin noise to roughen the surface. It differs from standard conversions by explicitly expanding the box geometry to define an erosion zone and combining axis-aligned sigmoid falloffs with spatial noise. Choose when rendering box primitives with soft, noisy boundaries. Computes the output alpha for an SDF given the Screen Space Ratio (SSR), Signed Distance (SD), Signed Distance Ratio (SDR), isoPerimeter, and softness. It converts a signed distance value into a density value using alpha and beta parameters. Choose when direct alpha compositing is preferred over volumetric integration. Converts a discrete object description or a continuous surface description into a volumetric scene (density field) suitable for physical modeling, manufacturing, or volume rendering. It distinguishes itself by explicitly defining density values based on interior/exterior status or signed distance to a surface. Choose when mapping discrete CAD or mesh data to volumetric representations. Integrates color and density along rays sampled from an implicit SDF. It converts SDF values to density using a Laplace distribution CDF and aggregates color using standard volume rendering weights. Unlike standard volume rendering which uses raw density fields, this method leverages the geometric priors of the SDF to better recover underlying geometry. Choose when recovering geometry from implicit fields is the primary goal. Defines an implicit volumetric object where density \rho is derived from an FBM field f. Density is zero when f(\mathbf{p}) < v, and remapped via function h when f(\mathbf{p}) \ge v. The 0-isosurface of \rho corresponds to the v-isosurface of f. Formula: \rho(\mathbf{p}) = \begin{cases} h(f(\mathbf{p})) & \text{when } f(\mathbf{p}) \geq v \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where f(\mathbf{p}) = Bn(\mathbf{p}) is the FBM field, v is the threshold, and h is a positive remapping function. Pitfall: If h is not a positive function, the 0-isosurface of \rho will not correspond to the v-isosurface of f. The method assumes h is positive. DensityRegion extends VolumeRegion by scaling absorption, scattering, extinction, and emission coefficients by a spatially varying density function density(pt). Formula: \sigmaa(\text{pt}) = \text{sig\a} \cdot \text{density}(\text{pt}), where \text{sig\a} is the base absorption spectrum. \sigmas(\text{pt}) = \text{sig\s} \cdot \text{density}(\text{pt}), where \text{sig\s} is the base scattering spectrum. \sigmat(\text{pt}) = (\text{sig\a} + \text{sig\s}) \cdot \text{density}(\text{pt}), representing extinction. L{ve}(\text{pt}) = \text{le} \cdot \text{density}(\text{pt}), where \text{le} is the base emission spectrum. \text{phase}(\text{pt}, \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{w}') = \text{PhaseHG}(\mathbf{w}, \mathbf{w}', g{\text{scatter}}), using Henyey-Greenstein phase function with parameter g{\text{scatter}}. Parameter: g{\text{scatter}}: Henyey-Greenstein anisotropy parameter, passed in constructor as greenstein. Layout: DensityRegion fields: siga (Spectrum), sigs (Spectrum), le (Spectrum), gscatter (float). A smeared-out Heaviside function H used to compute mean curvature for regularization, defined piecewise based on a threshold \epsilonH. Formula: H(\hat{\phi}) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \hat{\phi} < -\epsilonH \\ \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\hat{\phi}}{2\epsilonH} + \frac{1}{2\pi} \sin\left(\frac{\pi\hat{\phi}}{\epsilonH}\right) & \text{if } -\epsilonH \leq \hat{\phi} \leq \epsilonH \\ 1 & \text{if } \hat{\phi} > \epsilonH \end{cases} where \epsilonH is the mean edge distance between sites excluding the 5% longer edges. Parameter: \epsilonH is equal to the mean edge distance between sites, excluding the 5% longer edges. A variant of the sigmoid function used in GenDR where the absolute part of the distance is squared before applying the base sigmoid, interpreted as applying a transformed CDF F{sq}. Step: 1. Multiply the absolute distance by the signed distance: |d(\mathbf{p}, t)| \cdot d(\mathbf{p}, t). 2. Divide by temperature: (|d(\mathbf{p}, t)| \cdot d(\mathbf{p}, t)) / \tau. 3. Apply the base sigmoid function F to the result. Formula: F{sq}(d(\mathbf{p}, t)/\tau):= F(|d(\mathbf{p}, t)| \cdot d(\mathbf{p}, t)/\tau), where F is the base sigmoid function, d(\mathbf{p}, t) is the distance, and \tau is temperature. Comparison: F{sq} is generally worse than F for distributions with exponential decay, but comparable or better for those with linear convergence (Cauchy, Reciprocal Sigmoid). Strengths: Provides a smooth, differentiable transition from geometry to density, enabling gradient-based optimization of the SDF. Alpha-invariant formulations ensure consistent appearance across different scales. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \alpha and \beta (or s) to achieve desired sharpness and opacity. The assumption that density magnitude is tied to sharpness can be restrictive for complex materials. When to Use: When rendering implicit surfaces defined by SDFs, especially in neural rendering pipelines like VolSDF or NeuS. When Not to Use: When explicit density fields are already available and do not need to be derived from geometry. Origin: The method originates from differentiable volume rendering pipelines for implicit surfaces, notably introduced in VolSDF and NeuS. History: Key developments include VolSDF, which introduced learnable scaling and shrinking coefficients for alpha-invariance, and NeuS, which used a sigmoid-based transformation to match the CDF of volume rendering. Usage: Widely used in neural rendering, 3D reconstruction, and differentiable rendering pipelines. name: Procedural Index of Refraction Distribution
head: Mirage Simulation via Non-Uniform IOR
body: Procedural Index of Refraction Distribution generates a spatially varying index of refraction (IOR) field to simulate optical phenomena such as mirages, where IOR decreases with increasing temperature. It builds on SDF to Density Conversion by explicitly modeling refractive properties rather than just absorption or emission, enabling ray bending effects. Inputs: A 3D grid of vertical coordinates z. Outputs: A 3D scalar field n(x, y, z) representing the index of refraction at each point. Steps: 1. Define Normal Lapse Layer: Compute the normal lapse profile where the IOR decreases exponentially with height z using the formula: n{\text{normal}}(z) = 0.95 \times 2^z This profile models the standard atmospheric temperature gradient. 2. Define Inversion Layer: Compute the inversion profile using the formula: n{\text{inversion}}(z) = 0.8^z This profile models a temperature inversion layer. 3. Combine Layers: Compute the final IOR profile by taking the element-wise minimum of the two layers at each height z: n{\text{combined}}(z) = \min(n{\text{normal}}(z), n{\text{inversion}}(z)) This combination enforces the physical constraints of both atmospheric models. 4. Apply Ground Boundary Condition: For any position where z < 0 (below ground level), clamp the IOR to 1.0: n(x, y, z) = \begin{cases} 1.0 & \text{if } z < 0 \\ n{\text{combined}}(z) & \text{if } z \ge 0 \end{cases} This prevents unphysical refraction values in the ground region. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeiorfield(zgrid): """ Computes the procedural index of refraction distribution from a 3D grid of vertical coordinates. Args: zgrid: 3D array-like of vertical coordinates. Returns: 3D array of index of refraction values. """ iorfield = [] for i in range(len(zgrid)): row = [] for j in range(len(zgrid[i])): col = [] for k in range(len(zgrid[i][j])): z = zgrid[i][j][k] if z < 0: col.append(1.0) else: normallayer = 0.95 (2.0 z) inversionlayer = 0.8 z col.append(min(normallayer, inversionlayer)) row.append(col) iorfield.append(row) return iorfield Parameters: Base coefficients: 0.95 for normal lapse and 0.8 for inversion. Exponent bases: 2 for normal lapse and 0.8 for inversion. Ground threshold: z = 0. Edge Cases: Ground Transition: The hard clamp at z = 0 creates a discontinuity in the IOR gradient, which may require careful handling during ray marching to avoid numerical artifacts. This variant reconstructs extinction coefficients per wavelength and refractive index to match target images, implicitly defining volume shape via varying refractive index. Refraction indices are generated using a random process restricted to the inside of a glass sphere. Per-pixel weights concentrate importance on main parts of user images, leading to less constrained boundaries and more variable shapes. The volume does not scatter or emit light (Lm = 0). A pitfall is that intermediate views appear randomly colored during optimization due to refraction. It is used to demonstrate complex shape construction and compatibility with bent rays. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently simulates mirage-like effects without explicit particle systems. Compatible with continuous refraction models. Limitations: Random color artifacts can occur in intermediate views during optimization. When to use: When simulating atmospheric mirages or stylized refractive volumes with simple geometric constraints. The method originates from techniques for simulating mirages by creating a non-uniform distribution of the index of refraction in air, where IOR decreases with increasing temperature. It has been adapted for volume stylization, where refraction indices are generated via random processes to match target images, demonstrating the expressiveness of refractive volumes in computer graphics. name: Box with Smoothed/Eroded Edges
head: FunctionMakeBox
body: This method converts a signed distance field value into volumetric density for a box primitive, applying a sigmoid-based erosion at the boundaries to create smooth, anti-aliased edges and adding Perlin noise to roughen the surface. It differs from standard SDF-to-density conversions by explicitly expanding the box geometry to define an erosion zone and combining axis-aligned sigmoid falloffs with spatial noise, rather than relying solely on a global distance threshold or simple alpha blending. It builds on SDF to Density Conversion. Inputs: InDensity: The input density value (float). P: The 3D point position in world space (Vector3). InBox: The bounding box of the primitive (Box struct with Min and Max Vector3 fields). Outputs: R: The computed density value (float), clamped to [0, 1]. Data Structures: Box: Contains Min (minimum corner) and Max (maximum corner) vectors. Vector3: Contains x, y, z components. Parameters: E = 50: Box expansion and erosion margin in world units. D = 100: Sigmoid steepness controlling the smoothness of the eroded edge. NoisePositionScale = 0.005: Spatial frequency multiplier for Perlin noise. NoiseValueScale = 0.1: Amplitude multiplier for Perlin noise. Steps: 1. If InDensity < 0.5, return InDensity immediately. 2. Calculate the expanded box boundaries: C{pos} = InBox.Max + E and C{neg} = InBox.Min - E. 3. If P lies outside the expanded box in any dimension (i.e., P.x < C{neg}.x or P.x > C{pos}.x, etc.), return 0.0 (inferred from the intersection check and standard volume rendering conventions). 4. Initialize R = 0.0. 5. For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}, compute the sigmoid falloff for the positive and negative faces: D{pos} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{(C{pos}.i - P.i) / D}} and D{neg} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{(P.i - C{neg}.i) / D}}. Sum them: D{axis} = D{pos} + D{neg}. 6. Add Perlin noise: N = \text{PerlinNoise}(P, \text{NoisePositionScale}, \text{NoiseValueScale}). 7. Update R = R + D{axis} + N. 8. Clamp R to [0, 1] and return. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vector3: def init(self, x: float, y: float, z: float): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z class Box: def init(self, min: Vector3, max: Vector3): self.Min = min self.Max = max def PerlinNoise(p: Vector3, freq: float, amp: float) -> float: """Standard deterministic Perlin noise evaluation. Returns value in [-1, 1].""" # Implementation details omitted; standard noise function assumed available. return amp math.sin(p.x freq) math.cos(p.y freq) math.sin(p.z freq) def FunctionMakeBox(InDensity: float, P: Vector3, InBox: Box) -> float: # Step 1: Early exit for low density if InDensity < 0.5: return InDensity # Parameters E = 50.0 D = 100.0 NoisePositionScale = 0.005 NoiseValueScale = 0.1 # Step 2: Calculate expanded boundaries Cpos = Vector3(InBox.Max.x + E, InBox.Max.y + E, InBox.Max.z + E) Cneg = Vector3(InBox.Min.x - E, InBox.Min.y - E, InBox.Min.z - E) # Step 3: Check if point is within the expanded box if (P.x < Cneg.x or P.x > Cpos.x or P.y < Cneg.y or P.y > Cpos.y or P.z < Cneg.z or P.z > Cpos.z): return 0.0 # Step 4: Initialize R R = 0.0 # Step 5: Compute sigmoid falloff for each axis # Positive face: 1 / (1 + exp((Cpos - P) / D)) # Negative face: 1 / (1 + exp((P - Cneg) / D)) # Matches source: DensityXP = 1/(1+exp((ExtendXP - P.X)/D)) # DensityXN = 1/(1+exp((-ExtendXN + P.X)/D)) # X Axis DensityXP = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp((Cpos.x - P.x) / D)) DensityXN = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp((P.x - Cneg.x) / D)) DensityX = DensityXP + DensityXN # Y Axis DensityYP = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp((Cpos.y - P.y) / D)) DensityYN = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp((P.y - Cneg.y) / D)) DensityY = DensityYP + DensityYN # Z Axis DensityZP = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp((Cpos.z - P.z) / D)) DensityZN = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp((P.z - Cneg.z) / D)) DensityZ = DensityZP + DensityZN # Step 6: Add Perlin Noise N = PerlinNoise(P, NoisePositionScale, NoiseValueScale) # Step 7: Combine R = DensityX + DensityY + DensityZ + N # Step 8: Clamp R = max(0.0, min(1.0, R)) return R Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The sigmoid function is sensitive to the ratio (C{face} - P) / D. Large values of D result in smoother, wider transitions. Small D results in sharper edges. Boundaries: Points outside the expanded box return 0.0. Points inside the original box (but within the erosion zone) receive density from the sigmoid falloff. Noise: Perlin noise adds roughness. The amplitude (NoiseValueScale) controls the intensity of the roughness. Computes density for a vertical cylinder, applying a sigmoid-based radial erosion and Perlin noise to the cylinder walls. It checks if the point's Z coordinate is within the top and bottom bounds (expanded by E=50) and if the radial distance from the axis is within the expanded radius. If the radial distance is less than the unexpanded radius minus E, it returns 0. The density is computed using a sigmoid falloff based on the radial distance and added with Perlin noise. Parameters: E=50, NoisePositionScale=0.007, NoiseValueScale=0.1. Formula: D{cyl} = \frac{1}{1 + e^{(R{target} - R{dist}) / 100}} + N. A smoothing function to fade cloud density to zero at the volume boundaries without creating rectangular blank bands, ensuring continuous attenuation. It calculates the distance from the edge and applies a smoothstep function to the normalized distance. Formula: fade = smoothstep(\max(distance{to\edge} - empty\border, 0.0) / fade\width) where smoothstep(x) = x^2(3-2x). Parameters: SAFEEMPTYBORDERXY=0.0, SAFEFADEWIDTHXY=0.0, SAFEEMPTYBORDERZ=0.0, SAFEFADEWIDTHZ=0.13. Another set of parameters mentions Empty border: 0.0, Fade width: 0.045. Evaluates a distance field for a primitive and places voxels inside the shape. It can call a callback function (func) with position, normal, base voxel, shape bounds, and inverse transform to determine final voxel properties. If flipNormals is true and placing empty material, it updates adjacent voxel normals. Pitfall: Shapes generated via distance fields may lose precision or round down when scaled to low-resolution voxel maps (e.g., a 5-voxel tall cylinder may render as 4 voxels tall). Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations and a Perlin noise evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Performance: Fast enough for real-time generation if Perlin noise is optimized. The sigmoid calculation is cheap. Strengths: Produces smooth, anti-aliased edges without requiring high-resolution SDF grids. The noise adds visual detail. Limitations: The erosion zone is fixed in world units (E=50), which may not scale well with different object sizes. The sigmoid parameters are hardcoded in the source, limiting flexibility. When to use: When generating procedural volumes for boxes and cylinders with smooth, noisy edges. When not to use: When precise, sharp edges are required, or when the volume needs to scale dynamically with the object size without adjusting parameters. The method originates from the UE4VoxelTerrain project, specifically the UCudaTerrainGeneratorComponent class. It is used to generate voxel terrain and objects with smoothed edges and noise, likely for use in a voxel-based game engine. The FunctionMakeBox and FunctionMakeVerticalCylinder functions are part of the terrain generator's density calculation pipeline. bw2012/UE4VoxelTerrain, https://github.com/bw2012/UE4VoxelTerrain, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, https://github.com/mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) frozein/DoonEngine, https://github.com/frozein/DoonEngine, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Safe Edge Fade
head: Continuous Edge Protection, Smoothstep Edge Fade
body: Safe Edge Fade is a boundary condition technique that applies a continuous smoothing function to fade volume density to zero at the edges of a bounding box, preventing the appearance of rectangular blank bands or hard discontinuities. It ensures that the outermost voxels are strictly zero while maintaining continuous attenuation across the transition zone. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D density field and boundary parameters. Output: A modified density field where density is smoothly interpolated to zero near the boundaries. Data Structures: The density field is stored as a 3D array. Parameters are scalar values: emptyborder and fadewidth. Steps: 1. Calculate the distance from each voxel to the nearest volume boundary: distancetoedge. 2. Apply the smoothstep function to the normalized distance: return smoothstep((np.maximum(distancetoedge - emptyborder, 0.0)) / fadewidth). 3. The smoothstep function is defined as: clipped = np.clip(value, 0.0, 1.0); return clipped clipped (3.0 - 2.0 clipped). Formula: The core smoothing function is the standard smoothstep: fade = \text{smoothstep}\left(\frac{\max(\text{distance\to\edge} - \text{empty\border}, 0.0)}{\text{fade\width}}\right) where \text{smoothstep}(x) = x^2(3-2x). Parameters: emptyborder: The distance from the edge within which density is forced to zero. fadewidth: The width of the transition zone where density fades from full to zero. Typical Values: For XY boundaries: SAFEEMPTYBORDERXY = 0.0, SAFEFADEWIDTHXY = 0.0. For Z boundaries: SAFEEMPTYBORDERZ = 0.0, SAFEFADEWIDTHZ = 0.13. Alternative generic values cited: Empty border = 0.0, Fade width = 0.045. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def safeedgefade(density: np.ndarray, shape: tuple, emptyborder: float, fadewidth: float) -> np.ndarray: D, H, W = shape z, y, x = np.meshgrid(np.arange(D), np.arange(H), np.arange(W), indexing='ij') distx = np.minimum(x, W - 1 - x) disty = np.minimum(y, H - 1 - y) distz = np.minimum(z, D - 1 - z) distancetoedge = np.minimum(np.minimum(distx, disty), distz) if fadewidth == 0.0: return density normalizeddist = np.maximum(distancetoedge - emptyborder, 0.0) / fadewidth clipped = np.clip(normalizeddist, 0.0, 1.0) fadefactor = clipped clipped (3.0 - 2.0 clipped) return density fadefactor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If fadewidth is 0.0, division by zero occurs; the implementation must handle this case (e.g., by returning the original density). Precision issues may arise if fadewidth is very small relative to voxel size. A boundary condition technique for spherical volumes that creates a ring around the sphere where density smoothly interpolates from the interior value to zero, preventing hard edges. It identifies the spherical boundary, defines a ring region near the surface, and interpolates density within the ring to zero at the outer edge, setting density to zero outside the ring. Density bounds are 0 (full transparency) to 1 (full opacity). Not given in the sources. Safe Edge Fade is used in procedural cloud generation systems, specifically in the Noise-Cloud project, to ensure that volume clouds do not exhibit hard rectangular boundaries when rendered. mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, https://github.com/mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volume Rendering Final Project (Longer), https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j4tECzsy0CE, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SDF Alpha Computation
body: Computes the output alpha for a Signed Distance Field (SDF) given the Screen Space Ratio (SSR), Signed Distance (SD), Signed Distance Ratio (SDR), isoPerimeter (dilation/contraction), and softness. It converts a signed distance value into a density value using alpha and beta parameters, building on SDF to Density Conversion. Inputs: SD: Signed Distance value. SSR: Screen Space Ratio. SDR: Signed Distance Ratio. isoPerimeter: Iso-perimeter value controlling dilation/contraction. softness: Softness parameter for edge blending. d: Intermediate distance vector for variants like ComputeSDF44float. Outputs: outAlpha: Computed alpha value. Data Structures: d: A vector type (e.g., float for scalar variants, float4 for ComputeSDF44float). For ComputeSDF44float, d contains components x, y, z, w. Steps: 1. Compute intermediate distance dval: d\val = (SD - 0.5) \times SDR. 2. Variant-specific preprocessing: If using ComputeSDF44float with outline enabled, set d.w = \max(\max(d.x, d.y), d.z) before computing alpha. 3. Compute Alpha: outAlpha = \text{saturate}\left( \frac{d\val \times 2.0 \times SSR + 0.5 + isoPerimeter \times SDR \times SSR + softness \times 0.5}{1.0 + softness} \right). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesdfalpha(SD, SSR, SDR, isoPerimeter, softness, d=None, outlineenabled=False): # Step 1: Compute intermediate distance d dval = (SD - 0.5) SDR # Step 2: Variant-specific preprocessing if outlineenabled and d is not None: d.w = max(d.x, max(d.y, d.z)) dval = d.w # Step 3: Compute Alpha numerator = dval 2.0 SSR + 0.5 + isoPerimeter SDR SSR + softness 0.5 denominator = 1.0 + softness outAlpha = numerator / denominator # Saturate to [0, 1] if outAlpha < 0.0: outAlpha = 0.0 elif outAlpha > 1.0: outAlpha = 1.0 return outAlpha Parameters: SSR, SDR, isoPerimeter, softness: Typical values are Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Division by zero: The denominator is 1.0 + softness; if softness == -1.0, division by zero occurs. Guard against softness == -1.0 before division. Precision: Floating-point precision may affect dval calculation for very small or large SD values. Computes UV offset based on texture dimensions, offset values, and Signed Distance Ratio (SDR). Formula: uvOffset = \text{float2}\left( \frac{-offset.x \times SDR}{texWidth}, \frac{-offset.y \times SDR}{texHeight} \right). Inputs: offset (float2), SDR (float), texWidth (float), texHeight (float). Output: uvOffset (float2). name: Gray Transform (G_o, G_s)
head: Surface to Density Conversion
body: The Gray Transform converts a discrete object description or a continuous surface description into a volumetric scene (density field) suitable for physical modeling, manufacturing, or volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly defining density values based on interior/exterior status or signed distance to a surface, rather than relying on implicit volume generation or alpha-compositing parameters directly. Inputs: 1. Object Q: A set of voxels or discrete elements representing an object. 2. Surface S: A closed surface partitioning space into interior and exterior. 3. Scene Domain V: A voxel grid containing the object or surface. Outputs: Scene (V, f): A density function f: V \rightarrow \mathbb{R} where f(v) is the density at voxel v. Parameters: H: Density value for interior voxels (High). L: Density value for exterior voxels (Low). L0: Density value for voxels intersecting the surface. dl(v, S): Distance measure from voxel v to surface S. Data Structures: The scene is represented as a 3D array (or 2D slice) of density values. For Go, the input Q is a boolean mask or set of indices. For Gs, the input S is a geometric representation allowing distance calculation. Steps: 1. Define Scene Domain V: Ensure V is large enough to contain the entire object Q or surface S. 2. Compute Density f(v): For Object Go(Q): If v \in Q, set f(v) = H. If v \in V - Q, set f(v) = L. Formula: f(v) = \begin{cases} H & \text{if } v \in Q \\ L & \text{if } v \in V - Q \end{cases} (Equation 29 in) For Surface Gs(S): Calculate dl(v, S), the distance from v to S. Determine if v is in the interior, exterior, or intersecting S. Formula: f(v) = \begin{cases} dl(v, S) & \text{if } v \text{ is in the interior of } S \\ L0 - dl(v, S) & \text{if } v \text{ is in } V \text{ but in the exterior of } S \\ L0 & \text{if } v \in V \text{ and intersects } S \end{cases} (Equation 30 in) 3. Return Scene (V, f). Pitfalls: Closed Surface Requirement: For Gs to be well-defined, the surface S must be closed, meaning it partitions V into distinct interior and exterior sets such that one cannot move from interior to exterior without crossing S. If S is not closed, Gs is undefined. Distance Metric: The distance measure dl(v, S) may be the 2D distance from S in the slice containing v or a 3D distance from S. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def graytransformobject(Q, V, H, L): """ Converts a discrete object Q into a density scene over domain V. Q: Set of voxel indices belonging to the object. V: List of all voxel indices in the scene domain. H: Density value for interior (in Q). L: Density value for exterior (not in Q). """ scene = {} for v in V: if v in Q: scene[v] = H else: scene[v] = L return scene def graytransformsurface(S, V, L0): """ Converts a closed surface S into a density scene over domain V. S: A surface object providing methods for distance and containment. V: List of all voxel indices in the scene domain. L0: Density value for voxels intersecting the surface. """ scene = {} for v in V: # Calculate distance from v to surface S # Source does not specify exact geometric query implementation dist = computedistancetosurface(S, v) # Determine spatial relationship # Source does not specify exact geometric query implementation isinterior = ispointinterior(S, v) intersects = ispointintersecting(S, v) if intersects: scene[v] = L0 elif isinterior: scene[v] = dist else: scene[v] = L0 - dist return scene def computedistancetosurface(S, v): return 0.0 def ispointinterior(S, v): return False def ispointintersecting(S, v): return False A composite operator that converts an object or surface into a scene, filters the scene, and extracts the filtered object or surface. It solves the problem of smoothing or modifying structures while managing the relationship between the original and filtered representations. Steps: 1. Convert object Q to scene Go(Q) using Equation 29, or surface S to scene Gs(S) using Equation 30. 2. Filter the scene using a filter Fs (e.g., smoothing). 3.
