name: SDF Volume Rendering
head: Volume SDF Rendering, Signed Distance Field Volume Rendering, Volume Rendering from SDF, SDF → density volume rendering
body: SDF Volume Rendering is a technique that integrates color and density along rays sampled from an implicit Signed Distance Function (SDF). It converts SDF values to density using a Laplace distribution CDF and aggregates color using standard volume rendering weights. Unlike standard volume rendering which uses raw density fields, this method leverages the geometric priors of the SDF to better recover underlying geometry. Inputs: Ray bundle containing origins \mathbf{o} and directions \boldsymbol{\omega}. Implicit SDF function f(\mathbf{x}) returning signed distance and optionally color/features. Parameters \alpha (scaling factor) and \beta (scale parameter for Laplace distribution). Small constant \epsilon = 10^{-10} for numerical stability. Outputs: Rendered color tensor of shape (H, W, 3). Data Structures: RayBundle: Contains origins (shape N, 3), directions (shape N, 3), and samplepoints (shape N, D, 3). deltas: Tensor of shape (N, D) representing segment lengths. Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Sample points along rays using a sampler (e.g., StratifiedRaysampler) to get samplepoints and depth values. 2. SDF Evaluation: Query the implicit function for distance and color at sample points: \text{distance}, \text{color} = \text{implicit\fn}(\text{sample\points}) 3. Delta Computation: Compute segment lengths \Delta t from depth values. For D points, concatenate differences between consecutive depth values with a large constant (10^{10}) at the end to handle the last segment. \deltai = t{i+1} - ti \quad \text{for } i < D-1 \delta{D-1} = 10^{10} This large value ensures that if a ray does not hit a surface within the sampled range, the transmittance decays sufficiently, preventing artifacts from the infinite tail of the ray. 4. SDF to Density Conversion: Convert signed distance d to density \rho using the Laplace distribution CDF: \rho = \alpha \cdot \text{CDF}{\text{Laplace}(0, \beta)}(-d) Explicitly: \rho = \begin{cases} 0.5 \alpha e^{-d/\beta} & d > 0 \\ \alpha (1 - 0.5 e^{d/\beta}) & d \le 0 \end{cases} 5. Transmittance and Weight Calculation: Initialize T0 = 1. For i from 1 to D: Ti = T{i-1} \cdot \exp(-\rho{i-1} \cdot \delta{i-1} + \epsilon) Weights are: wi = Ti \cdot (1 - \exp(-\rhoi \cdot \deltai + \epsilon)) 6. Color Aggregation: Aggregate color by summing the product of weights and per-sample colors: C = \sum{i=0}^{D-1} wi \cdot \text{color}i Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def sdfvolumerendering(raybundle, implicitfn, alpha, beta, eps=1e-10): """ raybundle: object with origins (N, 3), directions (N, 3), and samplepoints (N, D, 3) implicitfn: callable returning (distance, color) for points alpha: scaling factor beta: scale parameter for Laplace distribution eps: small constant for stability """ origins = raybundle.origins # (N, 3) directions = raybundle.directions # (N, 3) samplepoints = raybundle.samplepoints # (N, D, 3) # Compute depths along the ray depths = torch.sum((samplepoints - origins[:, None,:]) directions[:, None,:], dim=-1) # (N, D) # Compute segment lengths (deltas) # Concatenate differences with a large constant for the last segment deltas = torch.cat((depths[:, 1:] - depths[:,:-1], 1e10 torch.oneslike(depths[:,:1])), dim=-1) # (N, D) # Evaluate SDF and color distance, color = implicitfn(samplepoints) # distance: (N, D), color: (N, D, 3) # Convert SDF to density using Laplace CDF # CDFLaplace(0, beta)(-d) = 0.5exp(-d/beta) if d>0, else 1 - 0.5exp(d/beta) density = torch.where( distance > 0, 0.5 torch.exp(-distance / beta), 1.0 - 0.5 torch.exp(distance / beta),) alpha # (N, D) # Compute transmittance T and weights w # T[0] = 1. T[i] = T[i-1] exp(-density[i-1] delta[i-1] + eps) # w[i] = T[i] (1 - exp(-density[i] delta[i] + eps)) # Vectorized computation # exponent for transmittance decay exponent = -density deltas + eps # (N, D) # Cumulative sum of exponents for T # T[i] = exp(sum{j=0}^{i-1} exponent[j]) # cumsumexponent[i] = sum{j=0}^{i} exponent[j] # So T[i] = exp(cumsumexponent[i-1]) for i>0, T[0] = 1 cumsumexponent = torch.cumsum(exponent, dim=1) # (N, D) logT = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cumsumexponent[:,:1]), cumsumexponent[:,:-1]], dim=1) # (N, D) T = torch.exp(logT) # (N, D) # Weights weights = T (1.0 - torch.exp(exponent)) # (N, D) # Aggregate color color = torch.sum(weights[:,:, None] color, dim=1) # (N, 3) return color Pitfalls: The last segment delta is set to 10^{10} to ensure that if a ray does not hit a surface within the sampled range, the transmittance decays sufficiently, preventing artifacts from the infinite tail of the ray. The last ray segment delta is set to 10^{10} to prevent division by zero or numerical instability at the end of the ray, effectively making the last segment contribute negligible density change. The last segment length is set to 10^{10} to ensure the final sample point does not contribute significantly to the volume integral if it is outside the object, effectively treating the ray as terminating or transparent beyond the last sample. VolSDF Volume Rendering performs volume integration using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) as the underlying geometric representation instead of raw density fields. It addresses optimization instability by converting SDF values into volumetric densities using learnable scaling and shrinking coefficients before applying standard alpha compositing. Unlike Volume SDF Rendering, VolSDF explicitly learns these coefficients to ensure alpha-invariance, meaning the magnitude of the volume density function is globally tied to its sharpness. NeUDF is a neural rendering framework that reconstructs surfaces with arbitrary topologies, including open surfaces, from multi-view 2D image supervision by leveraging the Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) as the implicit surface representation. Unlike its sibling Volume SDF Rendering, which is limited to closed (watertight) surfaces, NeUDF resolves the ambiguity of surface orientation in open structures by introducing a specialized "Udensity" probability density function and a normal regularization strategy. It differs from naive extensions of SDF-based rendering by avoiding spurious surfaces in void regions through an unbiased, occlusion-aware weighting paradigm tailored for UDFs. SRDF-based Volume Rendering is a neural scene reconstruction technique that models volume density using a Ray-Specific Signed Distance Function (SRDF) rather than a global Signed Distance Function (SDF). It solves the problem of false local maxima in volume density caused by surfaces not intersecting the camera ray, which leads to inaccurate depth and noisy surface reconstruction in multi-object indoor scenes. Unlike standard SDF-based methods where density is derived from a global field, SRDF computes the shortest distance to the surface along the sampled ray direction, ensuring that density peaks only around the actual surface intersection. This method is distinct from NeUDF by explicitly decoupling the ray-specific density modeling from the global surface representation. This method modulates volume density in a Signed Distance Function (SDF) representation using two separate learnable parameters, \alpha and \beta, rather than tying them equal as in prior work. It solves the convergence instability issues found in methods that use a single tied parameter by allowing independent optimization of the density scale and shape. It differs from VolSDF Volume Rendering by decoupling the \alpha and \beta parameters. Chunked VolSDF Rendering processes rays in chunks to manage memory usage during training. It gets the total number of rays N from raybundle.origins.shape[0], initializes an empty list chunkcolors, and loops over chunks. For each chunk, it slices the raybundle, calls the parent forward method to get curcolor, appends it to the list, and finally concatenates all chunk colors along dimension 0. The parameter chunksize defines the maximum number of rays processed in a single forward pass. NeuS Volume Rendering Transformation is a method that transforms Signed Distance Function (SDF) values into volumetric densities for alpha compositing, ensuring the CDF of volume rendering matches a scaled, flipped sigmoid shape. The transmittance T(t) is related to the SDF S(t) by 1 - T(t) = \text{sigmoid}(s \cdot -SDF(t)), where s is a global scaling coefficient. The weighting function w(t) (derivative of CDF) has local maxima at SDF value 0. NeuS ties the magnitude of volume density globally to its sharpness via the sigmoid parameter s, which is an alpha-invariant formulation by default but restrictive. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray and the number of rays. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples and rays, as all distances, colors, and transmittances must be stored for backpropagation. Chunking can reduce peak memory usage. Strengths: Better recovery of underlying geometry compared to direct density encoding. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \alpha and \beta or learning them. When to use: When geometric accuracy is prioritized over appearance flexibility, or when training from multi-view images where surface reconstruction is the goal. When not to use: For open surfaces (use NeUDF) or when ray-specific density modeling is needed to avoid false maxima (use SRDF). Originating from the need to improve geometric reconstruction in neural rendering, SDF Volume Rendering was introduced as an alternative to NeRF's direct density encoding. VolSDF and NeuS demonstrated that modeling density as a transformed function of an implicit SDF enables better recovery of underlying geometry. The method maps the SDF to a volume density function, assigning a value of 1 to points on the zero-level set and 0 to points far from this set. name: VolSDF Volume Rendering
head: VolSDF Density Transformation, VolumeSDFRenderer
body: VolSDF Volume Rendering performs volume integration using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) as the underlying geometric representation instead of raw density fields. It addresses optimization instability by converting SDF values into volumetric densities using learnable scaling and shrinking coefficients before applying standard alpha compositing. Unlike Volume SDF Rendering, VolSDF explicitly learns these coefficients to ensure alpha-invariance, meaning the magnitude of the volume density function is globally tied to its sharpness. Inputs: Ray bundle containing sample points along rays, typically generated by a stratified sampler. Implicit function (neural network) capable of returning distance and color at query points. Configuration parameters: alpha (scaling), beta (sharpness/shrinking), and whitebackground (boolean, default False). Outputs: Aggregated color tensor of shape (N, 3) where N is the number of rays. Optional geometry output (e.g., depth or normals). Data Structures: samplepoints: Tensor of shape (N \times ppr, 3) containing 3D coordinates of samples along N rays with ppr points per ray. distances: Tensor of shape (N \times ppr, 1) containing SDF values. colors: Tensor of shape (N \times ppr, 3) containing RGB colors predicted by the implicit function. depth: Tensor of shape (N, ppr, 1) containing the metric distance from the camera origin to each sample. deltas: Tensor of shape (N, ppr, 1) containing the step size between adjacent samples. density: Tensor of shape (N, ppr, 1) containing the converted volumetric density. weights: Tensor of shape (N, ppr, 1) containing the rendering weights. transmittance: Tensor of shape (N, ppr, 1) containing the accumulated transmittance. Steps: 1. Sampling: Generate sample points along the rays using a stratified sampler. 2. Implicit Query: Query the implicit function for the signed distance and color at each sample point: \text{distance}, \text{color} = \text{implicit\fn.get\distance\color}(\text{sample\points}) The output shapes are (N \times ppr, 1) for distance and (N \times ppr, 3) for color. 3. Depth and Delta Computation: Extract the depth of each sample from the ray bundle: \text{depth} = \text{ray\bundle.sample\lengths}[\dots, 0] with shape (N, ppr, 1). Compute the step size (delta) between adjacent samples along the ray: \text{deltas} = \text{get\deltas\from\depth}(\text{depth}) Shape is (N, ppr, 1). 4. SDF to Density Conversion: Convert the signed distance values to volumetric density using the sdftodensity function with parameters alpha and beta: \text{density} = \text{sdf\to\density}(\text{distance}, \alpha, \beta) The result is reshaped to (N, ppr, 1). 5. Weight and Transmittance Computation: Compute the transmittance T from the deltas and density. Compute the rendering weights W using the formula: W = T \times (1.0 - \exp(-\text{density} \times \text{deltas} + 10^{-10})) Shape is (N, ppr, 1). 6. Color Aggregation: Reshape the color tensor to (N, ppr, C) where C is the number of color channels (typically 3). Aggregate the final color C{\text{final}} using the computed weights and the reshaped colors: C{\text{final}} = \sum{i=1}^{ppr} Wi \times \text{color}i Result shape is (N, 3). 7. Background Handling: If whitebackground is True, add the background color (white) multiplied by the final transmittance to the aggregated color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def volsdfrender(implicitfn, raybundle, alpha, beta, whitebackground=False): """ Renders a scene using VolSDF volume rendering. Args: implicitfn: Object with method getdistancecolor(points) returning (dist, color). raybundle: Object containing samplepoints, samplelengths, nptsperray. alpha: Scaling parameter for SDF to density conversion. beta: Sharpness/shrinking parameter for SDF to density conversion. whitebackground: Boolean flag for background color. Returns: color: Tensor of shape (N, 3) with aggregated RGB colors. """ # 1. Sample points are already provided in raybundle.samplepoints # Shape: (N ppr, 3) samplepoints = raybundle.samplepoints # 2. Query implicit function for distance and color # Shape: (N ppr, 1) for dist, (N ppr, 3) for color distflat, colorflat = implicitfn.getdistancecolor(samplepoints) # 3. Extract depth and compute deltas # samplelengths shape: (N, ppr, 2) or similar, we take the first component as depth depth = raybundle.samplelengths[..., 0] # Shape: (N, ppr, 1) # Compute deltas between adjacent samples deltas = torch.zeroslike(depth) if depth.shape[1] > 1: deltas[:, 1:,:] = depth[:, 1:,:] - depth[:,:-1,:] # deltas[:, 0,:] remains 0, which correctly contributes zero to the first step's alpha accumulation # 4. Reshape flat tensors to (N, ppr, 1) and (N, ppr, 3) dist = distflat.view(-1, raybundle.nptsperray, 1) color = colorflat.view(-1, raybundle.nptsperray, colorflat.shape[-1]) # 5. SDF to Density Conversion # Standard VolSDF conversion formula: sigma = alpha exp(-beta |d|) density = alpha torch.exp(-beta torch.abs(dist)) # Shape: (N, ppr, 1) # 6. Compute Transmittance and Weights # Compute accumulated density delta alphacomp = density deltas # Shape: (N, ppr, 1) # Cumulative sum for transmittance cumalpha = torch.cumsum(alphacomp, dim=1) # Transmittance before each sample: T[i] = exp(-sum{j=0}^{i-1} alphacomp[j]) # Shift cumalpha to the right and prepend 0 shiftedcumalpha = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cumalpha[:,:1,:]), cumalpha[:,:-1,:]], dim=1) transmittance = torch.exp(-shiftedcumalpha) # Shape: (N, ppr, 1) # Weights: W[i] = T[i] (1 - exp(-density[i] deltas[i])) weights = transmittance (1.0 - torch.exp(-alphacomp + 1e-10)) # Shape: (N, ppr, 1) # 7. Color Aggregation # Final color = sum(W[i] color[i]) coloragg = torch.sum(weights color, dim=1) # Shape: (N, 3) # 8. Background Handling if whitebackground: # Total transmittance after all samples finaltransmittance = 1.0 - torch.sum(weights, dim=1) # Shape: (N, 1) backgroundcolor = torch.oneslike(coloragg) # White background coloragg = coloragg + finaltransmittance backgroundcolor return coloragg Parameters: alpha: Scaling parameter for SDF to density conversion. Defined in config as cfg.alpha. beta: Sharpness/shrinking parameter for SDF to density conversion. Defined in config as cfg.beta. whitebackground: Boolean flag for background color, default False if not in cfg. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Add epsilon (10^{-10}) to the exponent in weight computation to avoid numerical instability when density or delta is zero. Boundaries: Ensure deltas are computed correctly for the first sample (typically 0) and last sample. Degenerate Input: If ppr is 1, deltas may be undefined; handle by setting a default step size or skipping integration. The NeuS weight function is a volume rendering technique that derives an unbiased and occlusion-aware weight function w(t) from a Signed Distance Function (SDF) f(\mathbf{x}) to reconstruct surfaces from multi-view images without explicit 3D supervision. It solves the problem of geometric bias inherent in standard volume rendering formulations when applied to SDFs, ensuring that the volume-rendered surface aligns precisely with the geometric SDF zero-crossing. Unlike its sibling U-density Function, which focuses on Unsigned Distance Fields, this method specifically addresses the asymmetry of SDFs to prevent the weight function from peaking before the actual surface intersection. The U-density function is a rendering weight function designed for Unsigned Distance Fields (UDF) to ensure globally unbiased volume rendering. It solves the volume-surface gap inherent in naive extensions of Signed Distance Field (SDF) techniques to UDFs, specifically preventing redundant floating faces and irregular noises caused by improper weight distribution. Unlike the NeuS weight function, which violates the unbiased property for UDFs by allowing weight leakage to invisible surfaces, the U-density function concentrates rendering weight near the first surface intersection, ensuring the final color is derived solely from the visible surface geometry. Adaptive Surfaceness Finetuning is a method for refining the density representation in Signed Distance Function (SDF) based volume rendering by making the sharpness parameter \beta spatially adaptive. It solves the problem where a uniform \beta degrades rendering quality near fine-grained or transparent structures by allowing \beta(\mathbf{x}) to vary across the scene. Unlike siblings that optimize \beta directly or use fixed functions, this method uses the Eikonal loss as an indicator to increase surfaceness only where the SDF constraint is violated, preventing the model from collapsing into arbitrary density predictions. It builds on VolSDF Volume Rendering. SDF-based Voxel Rendering determines voxel visibility by evaluating a Signed Distance Function (SDF) at each voxel center; a voxel is drawn if the SDF value is less than or equal to zero. It differs from ray-marching volume rendering by using a discrete grid traversal with a binary occupancy test based on the implicit field, rather than continuous integration of density along rays. Distance-Adjusted Eikonal Loss is a regularization technique used in Signed Distance Function (SDF) based neural rendering to enforce the geometric validity of the SDF while preventing the regularization from degrading background reconstruction quality. It modifies the standard Eikonal loss by applying per-sample weights inversely proportional to the square of the sample's distance from the camera, thereby downweighting the constraint in far-field regions. This approach allows the model to maintain well-defined surfaces in the foreground while behaving like a standard volume renderer in the background, avoiding the artifacts associated with uniform Eikonal regularization. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and samples per ray, O(N \times ppr), due to the sequential nature of alpha compositing. Memory Complexity: O(N \times ppr) to store intermediate tensors for distance, color, density, transmittance, and weights. VolSDF was introduced as a method to improve the optimization of neural implicit surfaces by leveraging the properties of Signed Distance Functions. It addresses the issue of "fuzzier" volume rendering by learning scaling and shrinking coefficients on the distance-transformed densities. The method is part of a broader family of neural surface rendering techniques that include NeuS and others. It is commonly used in 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis tasks where explicit surface extraction is desired. autonomousvision/sdfstudio, https://github.com/autonomousvision/sdfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Shreyas120/l3dassignment3, https://github.com/Shreyas120/l3dassignment3, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, https://github.com/Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Alpha Invariance: On Inverse Scaling Between Distance and Volume Density in Neural Radiance Fields, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YQhBEXC464w, fetched 2026-10-31

name: NeuS Weight Function
head: NeuS Unbiased Density, NeuS density function, NeuS opaque density, SDF-based volume rendering weight
body: The NeuS weight function is a volume rendering technique that derives an unbiased and occlusion-aware weight function w(t) from a Signed Distance Function (SDF) f(\mathbf{x}) to reconstruct surfaces from multi-view images without explicit 3D supervision. It solves the problem of geometric bias inherent in standard volume rendering formulations when applied to SDFs, ensuring that the volume-rendered surface aligns precisely with the geometric SDF zero-crossing. Unlike its sibling U-density Function, which focuses on Unsigned Distance Fields, this method specifically addresses the asymmetry of SDFs to prevent the weight function from peaking before the actual surface intersection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{v}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera center and \mathbf{v} is the unit direction vector. An SDF network f(\mathbf{x}) that outputs the signed distance at any point \mathbf{x}. A trainable inverse standard deviation parameter s. Output: The rendered color C(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v}) and the accumulated opacity/transmittance for training losses. Data Structures: SDF Network: A neural network mapping 3D coordinates to scalar SDF values. Sigmoid Function \Phis: Defined as \Phis(x) = (1 + e^{-sx})^{-1}, where s is a trainable parameter that approaches 0 as training converges. Sample Points: A set of n points \{ \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{v} \mid i=1,\dots,n \} sampled along the ray. Formulas: 1. Rendering Integral: C(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v}) = \int0^{+\infty} w(t) c(\mathbf{p}(t), \mathbf{v}) dt where c(\mathbf{p}(t), \mathbf{v}) is the color at point \mathbf{p}(t) along viewing direction \mathbf{v}. 2. Weight Function Definition: w(t) = T(t)\rho(t) where T(t) is the accumulated transmittance and \rho(t) is the opaque density. 3. Accumulated Transmittance: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int0^t \rho(u) du\right) 4. Opaque Density \rho(t): The opaque density is derived to ensure the weight function is unbiased (peaks at f(\mathbf{p}(t^))=0) and occlusion-aware (nearer points contribute more). \rho(t) = \max \left( -\frac{d\Phis}{dt}(f(\mathbf{p}(t))), 0 \right) The term -\frac{d\Phis}{dt}(f(\mathbf{p}(t))) represents the rate of change of the sigmoid SDF. It is clipped to 0 to ensure \rho(t) is non-negative, which occurs when the SDF value is increasing (i.e., the ray is leaving the surface). Derivation Note: In the ideal case of a single plane intersection, the transmittance T(t) equals \Phis(f(\mathbf{p}(t))). Differentiating \ln(T(t)) yields the opaque density formula above. 5. Discrete Opacity \alphai: For discrete sampling intervals [ti, t{i+1}], the opacity \alphai is computed as: \alphai = \max \left( \frac{\Phis(f(\mathbf{p}(ti))) - \Phis(f(\mathbf{p}(t{i+1})))}{\Phis(f(\mathbf{p}(ti)))}, 0 \right) This is derived from \alphai = 1 - \exp\left(-\int{ti}^{t{i+1}} \rho(t) dt\right). 6. Discrete Color Accumulation: \hat{C} = \sum{i=1}^n Ti \alphai ci where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1-\alphaj) is the discrete accumulated transmittance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def sigmoidsdf(s: float, fval: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """Computes the sigmoid of the SDF value.""" return 1.0 / (1.0 + torch.exp(-s fval)) def computeneusweight(s: float, fvals: torch.Tensor, dfdt: torch.Tensor, colors: torch.Tensor) -> tuple: """ Renders color using the NeuS weight function. Args: s: Trainable inverse standard deviation parameter. fvals: SDF values f(p(t)) at n sample points along the ray. dfdt: Directional derivative of f along the ray direction v (df/dt). colors: Colors c(p(t)) at n sample points. Returns: renderedcolor: Rendered color for the pixel. accumulatedopacity: Sum of weights (for mask loss). """ # 1. Compute Phis phis = sigmoidsdf(s, fvals) # 2. Compute opaque density rho(t) = max(-d(Phis)/dt, 0) # Chain rule: d(Phis)/dt = d(Phis)/df df/dt = s Phis (1 - Phis) df/dt dphisdf = s phis (1.0 - phis) dphisdt = dphisdf dfdt rho = torch.clamp(-dphisdt, min=0.0) # 3. Compute discrete opacity alphai # alphai = max((Phis(ti) - Phis(t{i+1})) / Phis(ti), 0) phisnext = torch.cat([phis[1:], torch.zeros(1, device=phis.device)]) denom = phis.clone() denom[denom == 0] = 1e-8 alpha = torch.clamp((phis - phisnext) / denom, min=0.0) # 4. Compute transmittance Ti # Ti = product{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj), T1 = 1 oneminusalpha = 1.0 - alpha cumprod = torch.cumprod(oneminusalpha, dim=0) T = torch.cat([torch.ones(1, device=phis.device), cumprod[:-1]]) # 5. Compute rendered color weights = T alpha renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(1) colors, dim=0) accumulatedopacity = torch.sum(weights) return renderedcolor, accumulatedopacity Parameters: n: Number of points sampled along each ray for discretization. s: Trainable inverse standard deviation parameter. It is optimized during training and used in the sigmoid function \Phis and the computation of the opaque density. \lambda: Weight for the Eikonal regularization term. \beta: Weight for the mask loss term. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bias in Naive Solution: Using standard volume density \sigma(t) = \phis(f(\mathbf{p}(t))) results in a weight function that peaks before the surface intersection, causing geometric bias. Occlusion Failure in Straightforward Unbiased Weight: A simple normalized S-density weight w(t) = \phis(f(\mathbf{p}(t))) / \int \phis(f(\mathbf{p}(u))) du is unbiased but not occlusion-aware. If a ray intersects multiple surfaces, it blends their colors equally regardless of depth. Negative Density: The term -\frac{d\Phis}{dt} can be negative when the SDF is increasing (ray leaving the surface). The \max(\cdot, 0) clipping is essential to ensure non-negative density. A two-stage sampling strategy for Unsigned Distance Functions (UDFs) that decouples sampling distribution from rendering distribution to balance Eikonal loss gradients. It modifies the sampling density to handle UDF asymmetry, unlike the NeuS weight function which handles SDF asymmetry directly in the weight definition. A direct extension of the NeuS weight function to UDFs. It uses a fixed, non-adaptive weight formulation derived from NeuS but suffers from geometric errors like redundant surfaces due to inherent bias in color rendering. Time Complexity: Dominated by the evaluation of the SDF network and its gradients for n samples per ray. Hierarchical sampling adds a coarse pass but reduces the number of fine samples needed for convergence. Memory Complexity: Requires storing SDF values, gradients, colors, and intermediate transmittance/opaque values for n samples per ray. Strengths: Provides unbiased surface reconstruction by aligning the rendering weight peak with the SDF zero-crossing. It is occlusion-aware, correctly handling multiple surface intersections. Limitations: Relies on the first-order approximation of the SDF for unbiasedness. Performance depends heavily on the quality of the SDF gradient (Eikonal regularization). When to Use: When reconstructing surfaces from multi-view images using SDFs and requiring high geometric accuracy without explicit 3D supervision. When Not to Use: When using Unsigned Distance Fields (UDFs) directly without modification, as the SDF-specific derivation may not hold. The NeuS weight function was introduced in the paper "NeuS: Learning Neural Implicit Surfaces by Volume Rendering for Multi-view Reconstruction". It addresses the limitations of previous neural implicit surface methods that suffered from geometric bias when using standard volume rendering formulations with SDFs. The method builds on the idea that the weight function in volume rendering should be derived from the SDF to ensure the rendered surface matches the implicit surface defined by the SDF zero-level set. name: NeUDF Hierarchical Importance Sampling
head: NeUDF sampling, ws(t)
body: NeUDF Hierarchical Importance Sampling is a two-stage ray sampling strategy for Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) volume rendering that balances surface reconstruction accuracy with Eikonal loss regularization. Unlike Naive UDF Solution (NeuS-based) which relies on uniform or simple heuristic sampling, this method hierarchically refines point distribution by first establishing a baseline and then concentrating samples where the UDF value indicates proximity to the surface, ensuring well-balanced gradients on both sides of the implicit surface. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a UDF network f(\mathbf{x}); a transformation function \Psi; a monotonic density function \zetas; a position mapping p(t); N{init}=64 initial samples; N{imp}=64 importance samples; and a mask flag indicating background handling. Output: A set of 128 sample points \{ti\}{i=0}^{127} along the ray and their corresponding normalized sampling weights \{ws''(ti)\}. If no masks are provided, 32 additional points are returned. Data Structures: Sample Points: An array of 128 floating-point distances t along the ray. Weights: An array of 128 floating-point values representing the normalized importance weights. Steps: 1. Uniform Initialization: Sample N{init}=64 points uniformly along the ray within the bounding volume. 2. Density Calculation: For each sample point ti, compute the position p(ti) and apply the transformation \Psi to obtain \Psi(p(ti)). Compute the view-invariant sampling density \taus(ti) using the monotonically decreasing function \zetas: \taus(ti) = \zetas(\Psi(p(ti))) The function \zetas satisfies \zetas(d) > 0 and \zeta's(d) < 0 for all d > 0, ensuring higher density for smaller distances. 3. Base Weight Computation: Compute the unnormalized sampling weight ws(ti) for each point using the volume rendering accumulation formula: ws(ti) = \taus(ti) e^{-\int0^{ti} \taus(s) ds} In discrete form, the integral is computed cumulatively from the ray origin. 4. Neighbor Maximization: Modify the weights to prevent local minima from suppressing valid samples. For each i, compute the modified weight w's(ti): w's(ti) = \max\{ws(t{i+k}) \mid k \in \{-1, 0, 1\}\} This takes the maximum of the current weight and its immediate neighbors. 5. Normalization: Normalize the modified weights so they sum to one: ws''(ti) = \frac{w's(ti)}{\sum{j=0}^{N{init}-1} w's(tj)} This yields the importance sampling distribution for the second stage. 6. Importance Sampling: Perform importance sampling using the distribution ws''(ti) to select N{imp}=64 new points. 7. Boundary Handling: If no masks are provided, randomly sample 32 additional points outside the unit sphere to represent the background scene, bringing the total to 160 points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def neudfhierarchicalsampling(rayorigin, raydirection, udfnet, psifunc, zetasfunc, numinit=64, numimp=64, usemask=True): # Step 1: Uniform sampling tuniform = sorted([random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) for in range(numinit)]) # Step 2 & 3: Compute density and base weights densities = [] for t in tuniform: pos = [rayorigin[j] + t raydirection[j] for j in range(3)] transformed = psifunc(pos) tau = zetasfunc(transformed) densities.append(tau) # Compute unnormalized weights ws(t) weightss = [] cumsum = 0.0 for i, tau in enumerate(densities): if i > 0: dt = tuniform[i] - tuniform[i-1] cumsum += densities[i-1] dt ws = tau math.exp(-cumsum) weightss.append(ws) # Step 4: Neighbor maximization weightsprime = [] for i in range(numinit): maxw = weightss[i] if i > 0: maxw = max(maxw, weightss[i-1]) if i < numinit - 1: maxw = max(maxw, weightss[i+1]) weightsprime.append(maxw) # Step 5: Normalization sumweights = sum(weightsprime) weightsnorm = [w / sumweights for w in weightsprime] # Step 6: Importance sampling for additional points # Build cumulative distribution for discrete sampling cdf = [] acc = 0.0 for w in weightsnorm: acc += w cdf.append(acc) timp = [] for in range(numimp): r = random.random() idx = 0 while idx < len(cdf) - 1 and cdf[idx] < r: idx += 1 timp.append(tuniform[idx]) # Combine points allt = tuniform + timp # Step 7: Boundary handling (if no mask) if not usemask: tbg = [] for in range(32): # Sample point outside unit sphere theta = random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) phi = random.uniform(0, math.pi) r = 1.0 + random.uniform(0.1, 0.5) x = r math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta) y = r math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta) z = r math.cos(phi) bgpos = [x, y, z] dist = math.sqrt(sum((bgpos[j] - rayorigin[j])2 for j in range(3))) tbg.append(dist) allt = allt + tbg return allt Parameters: numinit: 64 (initial uniform samples). numimp: 64 (importance samples). zetas: Monotonically decreasing function with \zetas(d) > 0 and \zeta's(d) < 0. Psi: Transformation function applied to position or UDF values. Edge Cases: No Mask: Requires 32 extra random samples outside the unit sphere for background representation. Degenerate UDF: The condition \zeta's(d) < 0 ensures density remains positive and decreases with distance, preventing singularities at large distances. Provides the specific mathematical formulation for the sampling density \taus(t) used in the second stage of the hierarchy. It sets itself apart by distributing weights before intersection points to balance Eikonal loss gradients, unlike the parent method which focuses on the hierarchical refinement structure itself. Complexity: O(N) per ray where N=128 (or 160 with background). Performance: The two-stage approach (64 + 64) provides a balance between computational cost and sampling quality. Strengths: Improves UDF quality by preventing unbalanced gradient magnitudes on either side of the surface, which is a common issue in UDF rendering. View-invariant density reduces sensitivity to camera position. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \zetas and \Psi. NeUDF Hierarchical Importance Sampling was introduced in the NeUDF paper (2023) to address the challenges of training Unsigned Distance Fields with volume rendering. name: Importance Points Sampling
head: sampling weight function
body: Importance Points Sampling is a specialized sampling weight function ws(t) designed to achieve well-balanced Eikonal loss regularization for Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) volume rendering. Unlike standard rendering weights that concentrate points near the surface, this function distributes more sampling weights before the intersection points to prevent unbalanced gradient magnitudes on the two sides of the surface, which would otherwise hamper UDF quality. It provides the specific mathematical formulation for the sampling density \taus(t) used in the second stage of NeUDF Hierarchical Importance Sampling. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes the ray parameter t, the UDF value \Psi(p(t)) at the ray point p(t), and hyperparameters s and b as inputs. It outputs the opaque density \taus(t) and the sampling weight ws(t). Data Structures: The method requires no complex data structures and relies entirely on scalar arithmetic operations on the ray parameter and UDF values. Formulas: The sampling weight is defined as ws(t) = \taus(t) e^{-\int0^t \taus(u) du}. The opaque density is derived from a transformation function \zetas as \taus(t) = \zetas(\Psi(p(t))). The transformation function is defined as \zetas(d) = s \frac{e^{-bd}}{(1 + e^{-bd})^2}. Constraints: The function \zetas(d) must satisfy \zetas(d) > 0 and \zeta's(d) < 0 for all d > 0. Parameters: The parameter s starts at 0.05 and changes every sampling step z with a rate of 2^{z-1}. The parameter b controls the intensity of the weight at d=0. Steps: 1. Evaluate the UDF value d = \Psi(p(t)) at the current ray point. 2. Compute \zetas(d) using the current values of s and b. 3. Set the opaque density \taus(t) = \zetas(d). 4. Compute the cumulative opacity integral A(t) = \int0^t \taus(u) du, which in discrete implementation is the accumulated sum of \taus along the ray. 5. Compute the sampling weight ws(t) = \taus(t) e^{-A(t)}. 6. Use ws(t) to guide the selection of sample points along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computesamplingdensity(t, udfvalue, s, b): """ Computes the opaque density taus(t) for importance sampling. Args: t: Current ray parameter (distance). udfvalue: The Unsigned Distance Function value d at p(t). s: Scaling parameter (dynamic). b: Intensity control parameter. Returns: taus: The opaque density for sampling. """ # Compute zetas(d) = s exp(-bd) / (1 + exp(-bd))^2 expbd = math.exp(-b udfvalue) denominator = (1 + expbd) 2 taus = s expbd / denominator # Note: The integral term exp(-int0^t taus(u) du) is handled by the # renderer's accumulation buffer or ray marching loop. # This function provides the local density taus(t) which is then # combined with the accumulated transmittance T(t) = exp(-int0^t taus(u) du). # The final weight used for sampling probability is taus(t) T(t). # The discrete accumulation of taus along the ray is performed externally. return taus Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the sampling function employs the same weights as the rendering function, the Eikonal loss regularization leads to highly unbalanced gradient magnitudes on the two sides of the surface, significantly hampering UDF quality. A technique to upsample points along a ray for UDF volume rendering, addressing sampling bias inherent in standard importance sampling. It introduces an auxiliary point sampling prior to refine sampling densities and a uniform upsampling strategy. Choose this when rendering efficiency and 3D perception quality are critical for UDFs. The method requires O(1) time per sample point for weight evaluation. It requires O(1) auxiliary memory. Its primary strength is achieving well-balanced regularization across all space, preventing the unbalanced gradient magnitudes that degrade UDF reconstruction quality. Its main limitation is the requirement for careful tuning of parameters s and b. It should be used when performing volume rendering with Neural Unsigned Distance Fields where Eikonal loss regularization is critical for surface accuracy. It should not be used when using Signed Distance Functions, as the specific bias correction for UDFs is not needed and standard rendering weights may suffice. The method was introduced in the paper "NeUDF: Leaning Neural Unsigned Distance Fields with Volume Rendering". It addresses the specific challenges of rendering UDFs, where the lack of a signed distinction causes standard importance sampling to fail in balancing the Eikonal loss. The approach is inspired by NeuS [53] but adapts the weight function specifically for the UDF domain to ensure unbiased rendering and stable gradient propagation. name: Hierarchical Volume Sampling for UDFs
head: UDF importance sampling, VRP-UDF hierarchical sampling
body: Hierarchical Volume Sampling for UDFs upsamples points along a ray for Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) volume rendering to mitigate sampling bias inherent in standard importance sampling methods. Unlike Signed Distance Functions (SDFs), UDFs lack an explicit zero-level set distinction, causing standard sampling weight functions to concentrate points erroneously before the actual ray-surface intersection due to cumulative multiplicative effects. This method mitigates that bias by introducing an auxiliary point sampling prior to refine sampling densities and a uniform upsampling strategy to ensure even point distribution within intervals, thereby improving 3D perception and rendering efficiency. Inputs: Original sampled points along a ray: \{qn\}{n=1}^{N1}. UDF values at these points: fu(qn). Interval lengths: \deltan = \|q{n+1} - qn\|. Fixed standard deviation parameter: s. Number of points to upsample: N2. Auxiliary point sampling prior network: f{wp} (optional, for bias mitigation). Outputs: Set of N2 upsampled points \{q'm\}{m=1}^{N2} distributed along the ray. Data Structures: Array of original points Q = [q1,..., q{N1}]. Array of sampling densities \tau = [\tau1,..., \tau{N1}]. Array of cumulative probabilities \Omega = [\Omega1,..., \Omega{N1}]. Array of uniform random numbers U = [u1,..., u{N2}] where ui \sim \text{Uniform}[0, 1]. Parameters: s: Fixed standard deviation parameter. Steps: 1. Compute Sampling Densities (\taun): For each original point qn, calculate the sampling density \taun using the UDF value fu(qn) and the fixed standard deviation s: \taun = \frac{s \cdot e^{-s \cdot fu(qn)}}{(1 + e^{-s \cdot fu(qn)})^2}. 2. Refine Densities with Auxiliary Prior (Optional): If using the auxiliary point sampling prior f{wp} to mitigate bias, input a window of UDF values around qn into f{wp} to obtain a mask value mn \in [0, 1], representing the probability that the window contains a ray-surface intersection. Multiply the refined sampling densities \{\taun\} by the mask value for subsequent hierarchical sampling. The network is trained separately using mask images as optimizing objectives to produce binary-like outputs, avoiding circular dependency with the volume rendering prior training. 3. Compute Cumulative Probabilities (\Omegan): Calculate the cumulative probability \Omegan that a new point falls between qn and q{n+1}: \Omega(n) = (1 - e^{-\taun \deltan}) \times \prod{n'=1}^{n-1} e^{-\tau{n'} \delta{n'}}. Compute the product term iteratively to avoid numerical underflow. 4. Inverse Transform Sampling: Generate N2 uniform random numbers um \sim \text{Uniform}[0, 1]. Determine the positions of the N2 upsampled points using F^{-1}{\Omega}(um), where F^{-1}{\Omega} is the inverse CDF of the sampling weights \Omega. 5. Uniform Upsampling Strategy: To correct the non-smooth distribution caused by discrete inverse transform sampling, group the upsampled points that fall within the same interval [qn, q{n+1}] into sets \{q'{n,1}, q'{n,2},..., q'{n,m}\}, where m is the number of points in that interval. Re-order these m points to be evenly distributed within the interval such that the distance between consecutive points is \frac{\deltan}{m+1}. Specifically, for j=1 to m: q'{n,j} = qn + \frac{j}{m+1} \deltan. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicalvolumesamplingudf(Q, fu, s, N2, fwp=None): N1 = len(Q) tau = [0.0] N1 # Step 1: Compute sampling densities for n in range(N1): val = exp(-s fu(Q[n])) tau[n] = (s val) / (1 + val)2 # Step 2: Refine densities with auxiliary prior if fwp is not None: for n in range(N1): # Extract local UDF window around qn mask = fwp(extractudfwindow(Q, n)) tau[n] = mask # Step 3: Compute cumulative probabilities Omega = [0.0] (N1 - 1) prodterm = 1.0 for n in range(N1 - 1): deltan = norm(Q[n+1] - Q[n]) Omega[n] = (1 - exp(-tau[n] deltan)) prodterm prodterm = exp(-tau[n] deltan) # Step 4: Inverse transform sampling U = [random.uniform(0, 1) for in range(N2)] upsampledpoints = [] for u in U: cumprob = 0.0 for k in range(N1 - 1): cumprob += Omega[k] if u <= cumprob: # Linear interpolation within interval [Q[k], Q[k+1]] localu = (u - (cumprob - Omega[k])) / Omega[k] point = Q[k] + localu (Q[k+1] - Q[k]) upsampledpoints.append(point) break # Step 5: Uniform upsampling strategy intervals = [[] for in range(N1 - 1)] for p in upsampledpoints: for k in range(N1 - 1): if Q[k] <= p <= Q[k+1]: intervals[k].append(p) break finalpoints = [] for k in range(N1 - 1): m = len(intervals[k]) if m == 0: continue deltak = norm(Q[k+1] - Q[k]) for j in range(1, m + 1): finalpoints.append(Q[k] + (j / (m + 1)) deltak) return finalpoints Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sampling Bias: Standard hierarchical sampling without the auxiliary prior concentrates points erroneously before the intersection due to the cumulative multiplicative effect of high sampling densities in non-intersection regions. Non-Uniform Distribution: Inverse transform sampling on discrete intervals results in a non-smooth step function for the inverse CDF, leading to highly uneven point distribution and perception degeneration. The uniform upsampling strategy addresses this. Circular Dependency: Cannot directly use the trained volume rendering prior for \taun because its training relies on hierarchical sampling, which itself suffers from bias. The auxiliary prior f{wp} is trained independently using mask images. An auxiliary neural network f{wp} that acts as a mask function for sampling densities. It takes a window of UDFs as input and outputs the probability that the window contains a ray-surface intersection. It is trained similarly to the volume rendering prior but uses mask images as optimizing objectives to produce binary outputs. The mask value is multiplied with the refined sampling densities \{\taun\} for subsequent hierarchical sampling. Unlike standard hierarchical sampling which concentrates points erroneously before intersection, this prior effectively concentrates upsampled points near the actual intersection. A post-processing step for inverse transform sampling results. It groups upsampled points falling within the same interval formed by original sampled points and re-orders them to evenly distribute them within the interval. This prevents perception degeneration caused by the non-smooth nature of the inverse CDF in discrete sampling. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method improves 3D perception and rendering efficiency by mitigating sampling bias and ensuring uniform point distribution. Specific numerical performance metrics (FPS, memory usage) are not provided in the sources. Strengths: Mitigates bias in non-intersection regions; ensures uniform distribution of upsampled points; improves 3D perception. Limitations: Requires training an auxiliary network f{wp}; relies on UDF values; standard hierarchical sampling without this method suffers from bias. When to use: When rendering with UDFs and needing to upsample points along rays while avoiding the bias of standard importance sampling. When not to use: When SDFs are available and standard SDF sampling methods are sufficient; when computational resources for training f{wp} are not available. Hierarchical volume sampling for UDFs was introduced in the VRP-UDF paper. It addresses the limitations of NeuS, which uses S-density functions with fixed standard deviations for importance sampling, a method that becomes complex and biased when applied to UDFs due to the lack of an explicit zero-level set. VRP-UDF identified significant bias in prior tailored weight functions and introduced the auxiliary point sampling prior and uniform upsampling strategy to mitigate it. name: Naive UDF Solution (NeuS-based)
head: Naive UDF, Naive UDF solution based on SDF renderer, UDF extension of NeuS
body: The Naive UDF Solution is a direct extension of the NeuS weight function to Unsigned Distance Fields (UDF) for volume rendering. It integrates UDF values into the standard volume rendering integral but suffers from inherent bias in color rendering, leading to geometric errors such as redundant surfaces and floating noise. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin o, view direction v, UDF field \Psi(x), learnable parameter s. Output: Rendered color C(o, v). Data Structures: \Psi(x): Unsigned Distance Field value at position x. s: Scalar learnable parameter controlling the Sigmoid steepness. Formulas: The rendered color is calculated by integrating the product of a weight term wn(t) and the color c(p(t), v) along the ray from t=0 to +\infty: C(o, v) = \int0^{+\infty} wn(t) c(p(t), v) dt \quad (11) where p(t) is the point on the ray at distance t. The rendering weight wn(t) is defined as: wn(t) = \rhos(t) e^{-\int0^t \rhos(u) du} \quad (12) The opaque density \rhos(t) is derived from the UDF \Psi using a Sigmoid function \Phis and an operator \Phi{op}: \rhos(t) = \max\left\{-\frac{\partial(\Phis \circ \Phi{op})}{\partial t}(t), 0\right\} \quad (13) Where: \Phis(d) is the Sigmoid function: \Phis(d) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-s \cdot d}}. \Psi(x) is the UDF value at position x. s is a learnable parameter expected to increase to infinity during training to approximate a step function. Steps: 1. For a given ray (o, v), sample points p(t) along the ray. 2. Evaluate the UDF value \Psi(p(t)) at each sample point. 3. Compute the density \rhos(t) by taking the negative derivative of the Sigmoid-transformed UDF with respect to t, clamped to non-negative values. 4. Compute the accumulated transmittance T(t) = e^{-\int0^t \rhos(u) du}. 5. Compute the weight wn(t) = \rhos(t) T(t). 6. Integrate wn(t) c(p(t), v) over t \in [0, +\infty). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def naiveudfrender(o, v, udffield, s, numsamples, tmax): """ Renders color using the naive UDF extension of NeuS. Args: o: Ray origin (3D vector) v: Ray direction (3D vector) udffield: Function returning UDF value at a 3D point s: Learnable Sigmoid steepness parameter numsamples: Number of discrete samples along the ray tmax: Truncation distance for the integral to +infinity Returns: C: Rendered color (3D vector) """ T = 1.0 C = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] dt = tmax / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): t = i dt p = o + t v # Evaluate UDF and Sigmoid d = udffield(p) sigma = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-s d)) # Compute derivative of Sigmoid w.r.t t via finite difference eps = 1e-5 deps = udffield(o + (t + eps) v) sigmaeps = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-s deps)) dsigmadt = (sigmaeps - sigma) / eps # Density: rhos(t) = max(-dsigmadt, 0) density = max(-dsigmadt, 0.0) # Accumulate transmittance for next step Tnext = T math.exp(-density dt) # Get color at p (scene-dependent evaluation) c = getcolor(p, v) # Contribution: wn(t) c(t) dt = T density c dt C = [C[k] + T density c[k] dt for k in range(3)] # Update transmittance T = Tnext return C def getcolor(p, v): """Returns the color at position p for view direction v.""" return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for scene-specific color evaluation Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bias: The method suffers from inherent bias in color rendering, leading to geometric errors such as redundant surfaces and floating noise. Parameter s: The parameter s is expected to increase to infinity during training. If s is too small, the surface will be blurry; if too large, numerical instability may occur. Derivative Calculation: The density relies on the derivative of the Sigmoid-transformed UDF. Numerical instability can arise if the UDF is not smooth or if the step size for derivative approximation is inappropriate. This variant adapts the learned volume rendering prior to transform signed distance fields (SDF) into rendering weights for alpha blending, replacing the handcrafted differentiable renderer used in methods like NeuS. It differs from the naive UDF solution by using SDF inputs instead of UDF inputs and learning a weight function f{ws} rather than relying on the fixed NeuS weight formulation. It is chosen when superior numerical Chamfer Distance results are required and reconstruction artifacts such as holes and uneven surfaces need to be corrected. Definition: Adapts the learned volume rendering prior to transform signed distance fields into rendering weights for alpha blending, replacing the handcrafted differentiable renderer used in methods like NeuS. Steps: 1. Sample ground truth signed distances f{s{gt}}^h from ground truth meshes \{Sh\}{h=1}^H. 2. Replace the UDF input f{u{gt}}^h in the training equation with the SDF input f{s{gt}}^h. 3. Train the weight function f{ws} with all other settings identical to UDF training. 4. During inference, use the learned f{ws} to estimate signed distance fields fs instead of the differentiable renderer of NeuS. Parameters: f{ws}: Learned weight function that maps signed distance values to rendering weights for alpha blending. Comparison: Differs from NeuS by replacing its handcrafted differentiable renderer with the learned f{ws}, which yields superior numerical Chamfer Distance results and corrects reconstruction artifacts such as holes and uneven surfaces. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources for the naive UDF solution specifically. Strengths: Simple to implement as a direct extension of NeuS. Limitations: Suffers from inherent bias in color rendering, leading to geometric errors such as redundant surfaces and floating noise. When to use: When a baseline UDF-based volume rendering method is needed for comparison or as a starting point. When not to use: When high-quality geometry without floating noise or redundant surfaces is required; consider NeUDF Hierarchical Importance Sampling or SDF Inference with Volume Rendering Prior instead. The Naive UDF Solution was introduced in the context of NeUDF (Neural Unsigned Distance Fields) as a baseline method to demonstrate the bias inherent in directly extending NeuS's weight function to UDFs. name: U-density Function
head: NeUDF rendering weight function, NeUDF weight, U-density, cumulative distribution function of U-density
body: The U-density function is a rendering weight function designed for Unsigned Distance Fields (UDF) to ensure globally unbiased volume rendering. It solves the volume-surface gap inherent in naive extensions of Signed Distance Field (SDF) techniques to UDFs, specifically preventing redundant floating faces and irregular noises caused by improper weight distribution. Unlike the NeuS weight function, which violates the unbiased property for UDFs by allowing weight leakage to invisible surfaces, the U-density function concentrates rendering weight near the first surface intersection, ensuring the final color is derived solely from the visible surface geometry. Input: A ray defined by origin o and direction v, sampled at discrete points ti along the ray. At each point, a UDF network \Psi outputs a distance value d = \Psi(p(t)) where p(t) = o + tv. Output: A rendering weight wr(t) for each sample point, used in alpha-compositing to compute the final pixel color. Ray Samples: A list of distances t along the ray. UDF Values: A list of scalar distances di = \Psi(p(ti)) retrieved from the neural network. Transformation Function: \varsigmar(d), a parametric function mapping distance to cumulative probability. The rendering weight wr(t) is defined as: wr(t) = \taur(t) e^{-\int0^t \taur(u) du} where \taur(t) is the density derived from the UDF. The density \taur(t) is calculated using the derivative of a transformed UDF: \taur(t) = \left| \frac{\frac{\partial(\varsigmar \circ \Psi \circ p)}{\partial t}(t)}{\varsigmar \circ \Psi \circ p(t)} \right| Here, \circ denotes function composition, \Psi is the UDF network, p(t) is the ray position, and \varsigmar is the transformation function. The transformation function \varsigmar(d) must satisfy the following constraints for all d > 0: 1. \varsigmar(0) = 0 2. \lim{d \rightarrow +\infty} \varsigmar(d) = 1 3. \varsigma'r(d) > 0 (strictly increasing) 4. \varsigma''r(d) < 0 (concave) The specific form of \varsigmar(d) used in the source is: \varsigmar(d) = \frac{r d}{1 + r d} where r is a learnable parameter. r: A learnable parameter controlling the distribution of the density. Initial Value: 0.05. 1. Sample Ray: Discretize the ray into N points t1, \dots, tN. 2. Query UDF: For each point ti, compute the unsigned distance di = \Psi(p(ti)). 3. Transform Distance: Compute the transformed value si = \varsigmar(di) = \frac{r di}{1 + r di}. 4. Compute Density: Calculate the density \taur(ti) using the chain rule: \taur(ti) = \left| \frac{\varsigma'r(di) \cdot \frac{\partial di}{\partial ti}}{\varsigmar(di)} \right|. The term \frac{\partial di}{\partial ti} is the gradient of the UDF along the ray direction, computed via automatic differentiation of \Psi with respect to p(ti) projected onto v. 5. Compute Weight: Calculate the weight wr(ti) using the exponential integral approximation. 6. Composite: Accumulate colors using standard alpha compositing with the computed weights. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmar(d, r): """Transformation function: s = rd / (1 + rd)""" return (r d) / (1 + r d) def sigmarprime(d, r): """Derivative: s' = r / (1 + rd)^2""" denom = 1 + r d return r / (denom denom) def computetau(d, gradalongray, r): """Compute density taur(t) = | (d/dt sigma(d)) / sigma(d) |""" s = sigmar(d, r) sprime = sigmarprime(d, r) numerator = abs(sprime gradalongray) # Guard against division by zero at d=0 if s < 1e-8: return 1e6 return numerator / s def udensityrender(rayso, raysv, udfnetwork, r, numsamples, near, far): """ Discretized volume rendering using U-density weight function. Implements alpha compositing: wr(t) = tau(t) exp(-integral0^t tau(u) du). """ results = [] for o, v in zip(rayso, raysv): T = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = 0.0 deltat = (far - near) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): t = near + (far - near) (i + 0.5) / numsamples p = o + t v d = udfnetwork(p) gradd = udfnetwork.gradient(p) @ v tau = computetau(d, abs(gradd), r) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-tau deltat) c = udfnetwork.color(p) accumulatedcolor += alpha T c T = (1.0 - alpha) results.append(accumulatedcolor) return results Division by Zero: \varsigmar(0) = 0. If a sample point lies exactly on the surface (d=0), the denominator in \taur(t) becomes 0, causing the density to concentrate sharply near the surface. Naive Sigmoid Extension: Using a standard Sigmoid function (as in NeuS) violates \varsigmar(0)=0 because \text{Sigmoid}(0) = 0.5, which leads to bias in rendering weights and results in redundant floating faces and irregular noises. Negative Distances: UDFs are non-negative. The constraints apply for d > 0. Time Complexity: Dominated by the neural network inference for \Psi and its gradient computation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray sample. Strengths: Guarantees global unbiased rendering for UDFs and prevents color mixing from invisible surfaces (cm, cn). Limitations: Requires gradient computation of the UDF network, which can be computationally expensive. When to Use: When rendering with Unsigned Distance Fields and unbiased surface reconstruction is required. When Not to Use: When using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) where other methods may be more appropriate. The U-density function was introduced in the paper "NeUDF: Learning Neural Unsigned Distance Fields with Volume Rendering". It was developed to address the limitations of applying SDF-based neural rendering techniques directly to UDFs. The authors observed that naive extensions violate the unbiased property due to the different value domains of SDFs and UDFs. The method builds on the concept of volume rendering but adapts the weight function to the specific properties of UDFs, ensuring that the rendering process converges to the correct surface geometry without artifacts. name: SDF-based Voxel Rendering
body: SDF-based Voxel Rendering determines voxel visibility by evaluating a Signed Distance Function (SDF) at each voxel center and drawing the voxel if the result is less than or equal to zero. It differs from ray-marching volume rendering by using a discrete grid traversal with a binary occupancy test based on the implicit field, rather than continuous integration of density along rays. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An SDF function evaluating a shape, a voxel grid defined by view bounds and step sizes, and a frame buffer context. Output: A rendered image where voxels satisfying the condition are colored. Data Structures: point3d: A tuple or structure containing three floating-point fields x, y, z. voxieframet: The rendering context or frame buffer object. voxiedrawvox: A function that writes a colored voxel to the frame buffer at specified coordinates. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the voxel grid bounds (e.g., -vw.aspx to vw.aspx) and compute voxel step sizes based on view dimensions and resolution. 2. Iterate through the 3D grid using nested loops for the x, y, and z axes. 3. Evaluate the SDF for the current point \mathbf{p} = (p.x, p.y, p.z). 4. Apply the emission condition: SDF(\mathbf{p}) \le 0. 5. If the condition is true, call the drawing function with the point coordinates and a specified color (e.g., 0x00ff00 or 0xffffff). Formulas: The source provides hardcoded implementations for specific shapes rather than general parametric formulas: Sphere: length3d(p) <= 0.3f (radius r = 0.3). Torus: length2d((length2d((p.x, p.z)) - 0.2f, p.y)) <= 0.1f (major radius R = 0.2, minor radius r = 0.1). Box: length3d(max3d(abs3d(p) - (0.3f, 0.4f, 0.1f), 0.0f)) <= 0.0f (half-extents \mathbf{b} = (0.3, 0.4, 0.1)). Parameters: Voxel size: Computed dynamically from view bounds and resolution (e.g., stepx = (2.0 vw.aspx) / vw.xdim 5.0, stepz = (2.0 vw.aspz) / 200.0 2.0). Color: Hardcoded constants like 0x00ff00 (green) or 0xffffff (white). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point comparisons (SDF \le 0) may suffer from precision errors at the surface boundary. Boundaries: The loop bounds must strictly cover the volume of interest; otherwise, voxels may be missed or drawn outside the intended view. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersdfvoxels(viewbounds, resolution, sdffunc, color, framebuffer): # Compute voxel step sizes exactly as in the source stepx = (2.0 viewbounds.maxx) / resolution.x 5.0 stepy = (2.0 viewbounds.maxy) / resolution.x 5.0 stepz = (2.0 viewbounds.maxz) / 200.0 2.0 # Helper to write a voxel to the frame buffer def drawvoxel(p, col): framebuffer[p] = col # Iterate through the 3D grid x = -viewbounds.maxx while x < viewbounds.maxx: y = -viewbounds.maxy while y < viewbounds.maxy: z = -viewbounds.maxz while z < viewbounds.maxz: if sdffunc((x, y, z)) <= 0.0: drawvoxel((x, y, z), color) z += stepz y += stepy x += stepx A technique to jointly evaluate local and contextual radiance consistency for more reliable color predictions by rendering colors of a patch of size k \times k instead of a single pixel. It leverages the local surface assumption and homography transformation to efficiently derive colors from multiple input views. This method is chosen when regions have weak texture or changing intensity, as it produces more informative and consistent shape context by incorporating neighboring geometric information. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the grid, as each voxel is visited once. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space if rendering directly to the frame buffer, or O(N) if storing a voxel grid. Strengths: Simple implementation; efficient for solid objects; no need for ray marching or density integration. Limitations: Aliasing at surfaces; no transparency or subsurface scattering; resolution-dependent quality. When to use: Real-time visualization of solid implicit shapes; voxel-based collision detection. When not to use: Volumetric data with varying density; soft shadows; translucent materials. Originating from early voxel rendering techniques in the "voxie" library ecosystem, this method leverages the mathematical properties of Signed Distance Functions to determine occupancy in a discrete grid. jtomori/holographicfractals, https://github.com/jtomori/holographicfractals, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Patch-based Color Blending
body: Patch-based Color Blending is a technique for jointly evaluating local and contextual radiance consistency to produce more reliable color predictions than single-pixel blending. It renders colors for a local patch of size k \times k instead of a single pixel, leveraging the local surface assumption and homography transformation to efficiently derive colors from multiple input views. This method is chosen when regions have weak texture or changing intensity, as it produces more informative and consistent shape context by incorporating neighboring geometric information. Inputs: A query ray r and a set of sampled points q along the ray. A signed distance function (SDF) network s(\cdot) to estimate normals. N input views \{Ii\}{i=0}^{N-1} with known poses and intrinsic matrices. Blending weights wi for each input view. Patch dimension k. Outputs: Final predicted patch colors for the ray, aggregated via volume rendering. Data Structures: Local Plane Points: A set of 2D coordinates \mathcal{P}q centered at q on the tangent plane defined by normal nq, representing a k \times k grid. Homography Matrix H: A 3 \times 3 matrix mapping points from the rendered view Ir to input view Ii. Steps: 1. Estimate Normal: For a sampled point q on the query ray, compute the spatial gradient of the SDF network to estimate the surface normal direction nq: nq = \nabla s(q) 2. Define Local Plane Points: Select a set of points \mathcal{P}q on the local plane defined by (q, nq). 3. Compute Homography: For each input view Ii (where i \neq r), compute the homography matrix H between the rendered view Ir and Ii, induced by the local plane (q, nq): H = K \left( Ri + \frac{ti nq^T Rr^T}{nq^T (q + Rr^T tr)} \right) K^{-1} where: K is the camera intrinsic matrix. Ri is the 3 \times 3 rotation matrix of Ii relative to Ir. ti is the 3D translation vector of Ii relative to Ir. (Rr, tr) is the pose of the rendered view Ir in the world coordinate system. nq is the normal vector at q. 4. Project and Interpolate Colors: Apply the homography H to the set of points \mathcal{P}q to obtain their projected pixel locations in view Ii. For each point in \mathcal{P}q, obtain its color by interpolation on the input image Ii. Specifically, for the center point q, the projected pixel location Hq on the view Ii is obtained by the matrix product of H and q (in homogeneous coordinates), and its color is interpolated. 5. Assign Blending Weights: Assign the same blending weights wi to all points on the local plane \mathcal{P}q. This requires only one query of the blending weights for the entire patch. 6. Blend Patch Colors: Blend the patch colors interpolated from each of the N-1 input views \{Ii\}{i=0}^{N-1} using the blending weights wi to obtain the final patch colors for point q. Let Ci(p) be the color of point p \in \mathcal{P}q in view Ii. The blended color for point p is: C{patch}(p) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} wi Ci(p) 7. Volume Rendering Aggregation: Use SDF-based volume rendering to aggregate the interpolated patch colors of all points sampled in the query ray r to generate the final predicted patch colors of the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generatepatchgrid(q2d, k): """Generate k x k grid of 2D homogeneous coordinates centered at q2d.""" half = (k - 1) / 2.0 grid = [] for dy in range(k): for dx in range(k): x = q2d[0] + (dx - half) y = q2d[1] + (dy - half) grid.append([x, y, 1.0]) return np.array(grid) def computehomography(K, Ri, ti, nq, q3d, Rr, tr): """Compute plane-induced homography H from rendered view Ir to input view Ii.""" denom = np.dot(nq, q3d + Rr.T @ tr) # ti is (3,), nq^T Rr^T is (3,). Outer product gives (3,3) matrix. numterm = np.outer(ti, nq @ Rr.T) innermatrix = Ri + numterm / denom H = K @ innermatrix @ np.linalg.inv(K) return H def interpolatecolors(image, projectedpoints): """Nearest-neighbor interpolation of image at projectedpoints (N, 2).""" h, w, = image.shape ys = np.clip(projectedpoints[:, 0], 0, h - 1).astype(int) xs = np.clip(projectedpoints[:, 1], 0, w - 1).astype(int) return image[ys, xs] def patchbasedcolorblending(q3d, q2d, nq, K, poses, images, weights, k, Rr, tr): """ q3d: 3D point on the ray q2d: 2D projection of q3d in rendered view Ir (homogeneous) nq: Normal vector at q K: Intrinsic matrix (3x3) poses: List of (Ri, ti) for each input view i images: List of input images Ii weights: Blending weights wi for each view k: Patch dimension (k x k) Rr, tr: Pose of the rendered view Ir """ patchpoints = generatepatchgrid(q2d, k) blendedpatchcolors = np.zeros((k k, 3)) for i, (Ri, ti) in enumerate(poses): # Step 3: Compute Homography H H = computehomography(K, Ri, ti, nq, q3d, Rr, tr) # Step 4: Project and Interpolate Colors projected = patchpoints @ H.T projected2d = projected[:,:2] / projected[:, 2:3] colorsi = interpolatecolors(images[i], projected2d) # Step 5 & 6: Assign Weights and Blend Patch Colors blendedpatchcolors += weights[i] colorsi return blendedpatchcolors Parameters: Patch size k \times k: The dimension of the patch used for blending. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces more reliable color predictions in regions with weak texture or changing intensity by leveraging contextual information. Enforces better geometric consistency. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than pixel-based blending due to processing k^2 points per sample and computing homographies for each view. When to Use: When high-quality color synthesis is needed in textureless or low-texture regions. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Patch-based Color Blending was introduced in the SparseNeuS paper by Xiaoxiao Long, Cheng Lin, Peng Wang, Taku Komura, and Wenping Wang in 2022. It is part of the SparseNeuS framework for fast generalizable neural surface reconstruction from sparse views. The method builds on SDF-based voxel rendering and aims to improve color prediction reliability by considering local context. SparseNeuS: Fast Generalizable Neural Surface Reconstruction from Sparse Views, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-313, fetched 2026-10-26
