name: Cloud Physics: Humidity and Saturation
head: Absolute Humidity, Humidity and Saturation, Relative Humidity, Saturation
body: This method computes the saturation state of water vapor in an air parcel to determine condensation and evaporation thresholds. It solves the problem of identifying when water vapor transitions into liquid water, which is a prerequisite for cloud formation and precipitation in physical cloud models. It differs from Cloud Physics: Temperature and Buoyancy by focusing on mass concentration ratios rather than thermal energy and vertical forces, and from Hybrid Physics-Driven Procedural Model by providing the fundamental physical constraints rather than procedural noise generation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Atmospheric pressure (P), saturated vapor pressure (es), current absolute humidity (mass of water vapor per mass of dry air). Outputs: Saturated mixing ratio (\omegas), relative humidity status (saturated/unsaturated), and excess vapor mass. Formulas and Definitions: 1. Absolute Humidity: Defined as the concentration of water vapor, measured by the mass of water vapor divided by the mass of dry air in a volume at a given temperature. 2. Relative Humidity: Defined as the ratio of the current absolute humidity to the highest possible maximum humidity. 3. Saturation Threshold: At 100% relative humidity, the air is saturated. The threshold for saturation is the saturated mixing ratio (\omegas). 4. Saturated Mixing Ratio Formula: \omegas = 621.97 \left( \frac{es}{P - es} \right) Where: \omegas is the saturated mixing ratio. es is the saturated vapor pressure. P is the atmospheric pressure. Algorithm: 1. Calculate the saturated vapor pressure (es) based on the current temperature of the air parcel. 2. Retrieve the local atmospheric pressure (P). 3. Compute the saturated mixing ratio \omegas using the formula above. 4. Compare the current absolute humidity (\omega) against \omegas. 5. If \omega > \omegas, the air is supersaturated and the excess vapor condenses into liquid water. 6. If \omega \le \omegas, the air is unsaturated or saturated, and no condensation occurs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatesaturationstate(atmosphericpressure, saturatedvaporpressure, currentabsolutehumidity): """ Determines if air is saturated and calculates the saturation threshold. """ if atmosphericpressure <= saturatedvaporpressure: return { "saturatedmixingratio": float('inf'), "issaturated": True, "excessvapor": 0.0 } saturatedmixingratio = 621.97 (saturatedvaporpressure / (atmosphericpressure - saturatedvaporpressure)) issaturated = currentabsolutehumidity >= saturatedmixingratio excessvapor = max(0.0, currentabsolutehumidity - saturatedmixingratio) return { "saturatedmixingratio": saturatedmixingratio, "issaturated": issaturated, "excessvapor": excessvapor } This variant extends the humidity model by accounting for the energy changes during phase transitions. Water vapor releases latent heat of condensation (Lc) upon condensing to liquid water and absorbs latent heat of evaporation (Le) during evaporation. The specific heat of air (Cp) is defined as the energy required to raise the temperature of air by one degree Celsius. These parameters are required to compute the evaporation/condensation of water content inside the parcel and the change in its temperature. Time and Memory Complexity: The calculation is O(1) time and O(1) memory per air parcel, as it involves only basic arithmetic operations on scalar values. Strengths and Limitations: The method provides a physically accurate threshold for condensation. It does not account for dynamic temperature changes caused by latent heat release without the companion Thermodynamics model. When to Use: Use this method when implementing the mass conservation aspect of a physical cloud simulation to determine when water vapor should be converted to liquid water content. The concepts of absolute humidity, relative humidity, and saturated mixing ratio are standard meteorological definitions adopted into computer graphics for physically based cloud simulation. The specific formula for saturated mixing ratio using the constant 621.97 is cited from general atmospheric physics literature referenced in the survey. The integration of these concepts into GPU-based cloud simulation allows for the generation of realistic cumulus clouds by modeling the condensation process. name: Hybrid Physics-Driven Procedural Model
head: Macro-Physics Micro-Rendering, Lagrangian Macro-Parcel Cloud Simulation, Lagrangian framework for clouds, Parcel-based cloud simulation
body: The Hybrid Physics-Driven Procedural Model is a real-time method for simulating and rendering cumulus clouds on a landscape scale by combining macro-level Lagrangian physics with micro-level procedural rendering. It solves the problem of generating physically plausible, animated cloud shapes and movement efficiently by representing the atmosphere implicitly and computing physics on a few large "macro parcels" rather than individual fluid elements. Unlike pure procedural noise methods, it explicitly models buoyancy, condensation, and parcel interactions; unlike full fluid dynamics, it remains computationally inexpensive enough for real-time frame rates by decoupling the physics solver from the high-resolution renderer. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: User-defined atmospheric profiles (temperature and humidity as functions of altitude), initial mixing ratio, condensation level altitude, and saturation ratio. Outputs: A real-time rendered image of cumulus clouds over a landscape, driven by the positions, masses, and radii of simulated macro parcels. Data Structures: Atmosphere Profile: Implicit representation using curves or lookup tables providing temperature T(z) and humidity H(z) as a function of altitude z. Macro Parcel: A Lagrangian entity representing a bulk volume of air. Key fields include: Position \mathbf{p} (3D vector) Velocity \mathbf{v} (3D vector) Mass m (scalar, specifically water mass content) Radius r (scalar) Temperature T (scalar) Tessellation: A coarse mesh (e.g., 18 \times 9) used for computing surface area exposed to the environment for mixing calculations. Cloud Map (Variant): A precomputed texture of noise used to govern cloud shapes and coverage, projected from parcel attributes. Parameters: Environment Dimensions: Default 10 \text{ km} \times 10 \text{ km} \times 10 \text{ km}, but flexible and user-modifiable. Air Density (\rho0): Approximately 1.28 \text{ kg/m}^3. Stiffness Constant (K): Set to 100. Viscosity Coefficient (\mu): Approximately 0.01. Tessellation Resolution: Coarse grid, e.g., 18 \times 9 vertices, balancing accuracy and computational effort for area computation. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Define the implicit atmospheric profile (temperature and humidity vs. altitude) and set user parameters (dewpoint altitude, saturation ratio, mixing ratio). 2. Parcel Generation: The parcel generator creates new parcels with a frequency proportional to the local heat and humidity content of the region. Parcels are generated if the atmospheric state is physically plausible based on the temperature profile and condensation level. 3. Physics Update (CPU): Physics is computed at the macro-level on the CPU for a small number of large parcels. Forces: Calculate forces acting on each parcel: Buoyancy: Driven by temperature differences between the parcel and the environment. Drag: Accounts for friction with the surrounding atmosphere. SPH Forces: Parcel-parcel interactions are handled using Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) forces to model attraction and repulsion. Integration: Update parcel position and velocity using the net forces. Mass and Radius Exchange (Mixing): Parcels exchange mass with the implicit environment via entrainment and detrainment. Entrainment: Occurs throughout the parcel's lifetime. Detrainment: Begins at the condensation level. Mixing Effect: If mixing is enabled, the parcel loses water content, altering internal dynamics and temperature profile with each oscillation. The parcel radius grows as it ascends due to decreasing atmospheric pressure, but shrinks if mixing causes significant water loss and descent. If mixing is disabled, the parcel follows the same temperature trajectory during oscillations. 4. Rendering (GPU): Real-time visualization is achieved by raytracing the procedural amplification of volumetric noise on the GPU. Hypertexture/Cloud Map: Standard: Procedural noise is amplified within each parcel's volume. Refined (Cloud Map): Parcel physics attributes are projected onto a texture. A precomputed cloud map texture of noise is combined with this projected texture at runtime. Raycasting: Volume ray casting is performed in the shader using the combined density fields to generate the animated cloud cover. Normals: Finite Difference Method (FDM) can be used to compute normals for voxel shading, though this is computationally expensive. 5. Shadow Casting (Optional): Simplified shadows can be cast on the terrain by shooting rays from the light source to collect cloud opacities in a 2D texture, which is then blended with the scene. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. RHO0 = 1.28 # Air density kg/m^3 K = 100 # Stiffness constant MU = 0.01 # Viscosity coefficient TESSROWS = 18 TESSCOLS = 9 class AtmosphereProfile: """Implicit representation of temperature and humidity vs altitude.""" def gettemperature(self, altitude): # Returns T(z) pass def gethumidity(self, altitude): # Returns H(z) pass def getcondensationlevel(self): # Returns altitude where condensation begins pass class MacroParcel: def init(self, position, velocity, mass, radius, temperature): self.p = position self.v = velocity self.m = mass self.r = radius self.T = temperature self.tessellation = createcoarsespheremesh(TESSROWS, TESSCOLS) def updatephysics(self, dt, atmosphere, otherparcellist): # 1. Calculate Buoyancy envtemp = atmosphere.gettemperature(self.p.y) # Buoyancy force depends on density difference (simplified here) # Fb = V g (rhoenv - rhoparcel) # rhoparcel approximated via ideal gas law or similar from T buoyancyforce = computebuoyancy(self.T, envtemp, self.r) # 2. Calculate Drag dragforce = -MU self.v # Simplified linear drag # 3. Calculate SPH Forces from neighbors sphforce = Vector3(0,0,0) for other in otherparcellist: dist = distance(self.p, other.p) if dist < interactionradius: sphforce += computesphforce(self, other, dist) # 4. Net Force and Integration netforce = buoyancyforce + dragforce + sphforce acceleration = netforce / mass self.v += acceleration dt self.p += self.v dt # 5. Update Radius and Mass (Mixing) envpressure = computeatmosphericpressure(self.p.y) # Radius grows due to pressure drop self.r = (1 + K (1 - envpressure / initialpressure)) # Mixing: Entrainment and Detrainment condensationlevel = atmosphere.getcondensationlevel() if self.p.y > condensationlevel: # Detrainment begins self.m -= detrainmentrate dt else: # Entrainment throughout self.m += entrainmentrate dt # If mixing enabled, temperature profile alters if mixingenabled: self.T = updatetemperaturewithmixing(self.T, envtemp, self.m) # Check for death: if mass exhausted if self.m < threshold: self.dead = True def renderclouds(parcels, atmosphere, camera, light): # GPU Raycasting for each pixel: ray = castray(camera, pixel) density = 0.0 t = ray.origin while t < ray.maxdist: # Sample density from parcels localdensity = 0.0 for parcel in parcels: if isinsideparcel(parcel, t): # Procedural noise amplification noiseval = proceduralnoise(parcel, t) localdensity += parcel.mass noiseval density += localdensity t += ray.stepsize # Color/Opacity based on density color = mapdensitytocolor(density, atmosphere) return color Particle-Based Convective Cloud Simulation is an early physics-driven procedural method for simulating cumulus clouds by modeling air parcels as 2D particles, or "bubbles". It solves the problem of generating realistic, animated cloud shapes and movement on a landscape scale by leveraging high-level physical variables such as buoyancy and condensation. Unlike later GPU-accelerated particle systems that use position-based dynamics or adaptive splitting/merging, this method explicitly models mixing dynamics, inter-particle attraction, and attached vortices to enhance small-scale shape and movement features. Cloud Map Based Rendering refines the hybrid macro-physics and micro-amplification approach by incorporating a cloud map for governing cloud shapes and coverage over the landscape. It differs from the standard model by projecting parcel physics attributes onto a texture instead of generating hypertexture directly inside each parcel, and combining this with a precomputed noise texture at runtime. This variant is chosen when higher frame rates, more realistic cloud shapes, and better span toward the horizon are required. Implicit Atmosphere Interaction refers to the modeling technique where the atmosphere is represented as implicit curves rather than sampled transparent air, eliminating the need for explicit air volume simulation. It accounts for parcel-air interaction and mass exchange (entrainment/detrainment) directly through the physics solver. This approach is used when computational efficiency is prioritized over explicit fluid-air coupling, allowing for the simulation of mass loss and radius changes due to mixing with the environment. Time Complexity: Physics computation is lightweight, scaling with the number of parcels N and their interactions (SPH). Rendering scales with the number of rays and the number of parcels intersected. Memory Complexity: Low memory footprint for physics (only storing parcel states). Rendering memory depends on the resolution of the cloud map or hypertexture generation. Measured Performance: With 14 parcels: 6% physics time, 89% FDM normals render time, 77 fps with physics; 6% physics time, 91% FDM render time, 160 fps without physics. With 85 parcels: 9% physics time, 82% FDM normals render time, 7 fps with physics; 9% physics time, 88% FDM render time, 21 fps without physics. Rendering without finite differences normals is significantly faster. The most expensive part of physics is the computation of area exposed to the implicit environment on the tessellated sphere. Hypertexture production and raycasting take a larger share of computational time compared to physics. Strengths: Real-time performance on landscape scales; physically plausible cloud shapes and movement; user-controllable parameters (temperature profile, condensation level); computationally inexpensive physics due to macro-parcel abstraction. Limitations: Clouds often die out in order of creation and depending on exposure to dry air; limited to cumulus-type clouds; simplified physics (no billowing or complex turbulence). When to use: Real-time applications requiring realistic cumulus clouds with physical behavior, such as games or interactive simulations. When not to use: Applications requiring high-fidelity, large-scale weather systems with complex turbulence or non-cumulus cloud types. The Hybrid Physics-Driven Procedural Model was introduced by Goswami and Neyret in their 2015 paper "Real-time landscape-size convective clouds simulation" presented at I3D. It builds on earlier work in particle-based cloud simulation, such as Neyret's earlier methods, and refines the hybrid macro-physics/micro-amplification concept. The method is validated against aerology diagrams, specifically lapse rates (dry adiabatic \approx -10^\circ\text{C/km}, moist adiabatic \approx -5^\circ\text{C/km}). It is used in real-time graphics applications where physical plausibility and performance are both critical. name: Particle-Based Convective Cloud Simulation (Neyret)
head: Bubble Model
body: Particle-Based Convective Cloud Simulation is an early physics-driven procedural method for simulating cumulus clouds by modeling air parcels as 2D particles, or "bubbles". It solves the problem of generating realistic, animated cloud shapes and movement on a landscape scale by leveraging high-level physical variables such as buoyancy and condensation. Unlike later GPU-accelerated particle systems that use position-based dynamics or adaptive splitting/merging, this method explicitly models mixing dynamics, inter-particle attraction, and attached vortices to enhance small-scale shape and movement features. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Simulation domain parameters; initial conditions for bubble temperature, density, and velocity; atmospheric profiles determining buoyancy and condensation thresholds. Outputs: Animated positions, sizes, and shapes of bubbles representing the cloud volume, suitable for volume ray casting in a shader. Data Structures: Each bubble is characterized by the following fields: position: 2D coordinates (x, y) in the simulation domain. velocity: 2D vector (vx, vy). temperature: Scalar value. density: Scalar value. size: Scalar value (radius or equivalent area metric). shape: Parameters defining the blob's geometry (subject to "blob warping"). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create initial bubbles based on convective triggers. Assign initial temperature, density, and velocity. 2. Buoyancy Calculation: Calculate the buoyant force acting on each bubble. Bubbles rise due to this force. The force is derived from the temperature and density difference between the bubble and the surrounding atmosphere. 3. Condensation Check: Determine if a bubble becomes visible. A bubble becomes visible (and thus part of the cloud) upon condensation, which is triggered when the bubble's temperature drops below the dew point or similar physical threshold. 4. Mixing Dynamics: Update the bubble's thermodynamic properties. The bubble undergoes mixing dynamics with the surrounding atmosphere and with neighboring bubbles. This process typically involves smoothing scalar fields like temperature to reduce value differences between neighboring particles. 5. Inter-particle Forces: Calculate attractive forces exerted by neighboring bubbles. Each bubble exerts an attractive force toward its neighbors, influencing their trajectories. 6. Vortex Application: Apply vortices attached to the bubbles. These vortices enhance small-scale shape and movement features on the clouds. 7. Advection and Diffusion: Advect the bubbles as a result of the diffusion process. The blobs change in size and shape (termed "blob warping") and are advected through the domain. 8. Dynamic Creation/Destruction: Manage bubble lifecycle. Bubbles can be dynamically created or destroyed in response to cloud evolution, such as dissipation or new updrafts. 9. Rendering: Generate the animated cloud cover through volume ray casting in the shader using the final positions and properties of the bubbles. Formulas: Buoyant Force: The specific formula is not provided in the sources, but the force is determined by the buoyancy derived from temperature and density differences. Blob Warping: The change in size and shape is a result of the diffusion process and mixing dynamics. Exact warping functions are not detailed in the provided text. Parameters: Typical values for physical constants (e.g., gravity, specific heat) are not given in the sources. The method operates in 2D for the particle representation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Bubble: def init(self, x, y, vx, vy, temp, density, size): self.position = Vector2(x, y) self.velocity = Vector2(vx, vy) self.temperature = temp self.density = density self.size = size self.visible = False def update(self, atmosphere, neighbors, dt): # 1. Calculate Buoyancy # Buoyant force is derived from temperature/density difference with atmosphere buoyancy = calculatebuoyancy(self, atmosphere) # 2. Apply Buoyancy to Velocity self.velocity += buoyancy dt # 3. Condensation Check # Bubble becomes visible upon condensation if self.temperature < atmosphere.dewpointat(self.position): self.visible = True # 4. Mixing Dynamics # Mix with surrounding atmosphere and neighbors self.temperature = mixtemperature(self.temperature, atmosphere.tempat(self.position)) for neighbor in neighbors: self.temperature = mixtemperature(self.temperature, neighbor.temperature) self.density = mixdensity(self.density, neighbor.density) # 5. Inter-particle Attraction # Exert attractive force toward neighbors attraction = calculateattraction(self, neighbors) self.velocity += attraction dt # 6. Vortex Application # Apply vortices to enhance small-scale features vortexforce = applyvortices(self, dt) self.velocity += vortexforce # 7. Advection and Diffusion (Blob Warping) # Advect position and update size/shape self.position += self.velocity dt self.size = warpsize(self.size, self.temperature, self.density) # 8. Dynamic Creation/Destruction # Handled externally based on cloud evolution if self.shoulddestroy(): return False # Remove bubble return True # Keep bubble def simulateclouds(bubbles, atmosphere, dt): newbubbles = [] for bubble in bubbles: # Find neighbors (e.g., within a radius) neighbors = getneighbors(bubble, bubbles) if bubble.update(atmosphere, neighbors, dt): newbubbles.append(bubble) return newbubbles Simulates real-time cumulus clouds based on data from SkewT/LogP diagrams, obtaining physical parameters from sounding data instead of determining them or setting initial conditions. The data provide the buoyant force to solve the equation of motion of the air parcels without solving differential equations. It ensures the evolution of parcels from birth to death through explicit steps, whereas other methods may handle this naturally as part of the simulation. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: The method is one of the earliest to use high-level physics variables for convective cloud simulation. It enhances small-scale shape and movement features via vortices. However, it is a 2D particle model, which may limit volumetric detail compared to 3D methods. When to Use: When a physics-driven, early-stage approach to convective cloud animation is required, particularly for understanding the foundational principles of bubble-based cloud modeling. When Not to Use: When high-performance real-time rendering on modern GPUs is required, as later methods (e.g., Barbosa et al.) offer GPU acceleration and adaptive particles. Origin: This method is attributed to Neyret. It is one of the earliest works to obtain a simulation of convective clouds based on high-level physics variables, modeling parcels as 2D particles (bubbles). name: Finite Layer Cloud Shape Generation
head: Layer Cloud Side Profile, Natural XY Edge Envelope
body: Finite Layer Cloud Shape Generation is a procedural method for constructing the 3D volume shapes of layer cloud types (Cirrus, Altostratus, Nimbostratus, Stratocumulus, Stratus) by assembling a chain of connected 3D ellipsoidal lobes. It solves the geometric artifact where extruding a 2D cloud contour into a column creates a degenerate cylinder along the Z-axis, instead producing a natural side edge with vertical presence variation. It differs from its siblings Cumulonimbus and Cumulus Shape Generation and IsimCloudTexture density evaluation by specifically targeting the flat, stratified structure of layer clouds rather than convective or generic volumetric structures. The method generates a signed distance field or density contour in the XY plane, modulated by a vertical Gaussian presence function, to define the cloud's lateral boundary. Inputs: x, y, z: Coordinate arrays (typically normalized -1 to 1). typeid: Integer identifier for the cloud type. rng: Random number generator instance for procedural variation. edgenoise: Noise array for organic edge variation. variation: Rotation angle for the cloud profile. Outputs: finalcontour: A scalar field representing the organic cloud edge, where values > 0 indicate cloud volume. Lobe Specification Tuple: (centerx, centery, radiusx, radiusy, weight, lobez, lobezradius). Shape Profile Parameters: Retrieved via layershapeprofile(typeid), returning (centerz, halfheight, topwobble, bottomwobble, thicknessvariance, captaper, sideedgevariation). LAYERCLOUDTYPEIDS: frozenset((3, 5, 6, 7, 8)). Persistent Support Values (vertical base density): Type 3: 0.36 Type 5: 0.40 Type 6: 0.50 Type 7: 0.24 Type 8: 0.44. Typical Dimensions (for generation): majorlength: Uniform(0.45, 0.72). crosswidth: Uniform(0.22, 0.46). radiusx: Uniform(0.14, 0.30). radiusy: Uniform(0.12, 0.28). 1. Generate Lobe Specifications: Determine majorangle = rng.uniform(-π, π). Calculate direction vectors: direction = (cos(majorangle), sin(majorangle)), perpendicular = (-direction[1], direction[0]). Get shape profile for typeid to obtain centerz and halfheight. Generate count (7–13) positions along the major axis: positionsalong = linspace(-0.88, 0.88, count) + rng.normal(0.0, 0.09, count). For each position: along = positionalong majorlength. cross = rng.normal(0.0, crosswidth 0.62). position = (centerx, centery) + direction along + perpendicular cross. radiusx = rng.uniform(0.14, 0.30), radiusy = rng.uniform(0.12, 0.28). lobez = centerz + rng.uniform(-0.48, 0.48) halfheight. lobezradius = rng.uniform(0.58, 1.04) halfheight. weight = rng.uniform(0.54, 0.98). Append (position[0], position[1], radiusx, radiusy, weight, lobez, lobezradius) to edgelobespecs. Add 1–3 side lobes to prevent degeneracy: along = rng.uniform(-0.58, 0.58) majorlength. cross = choice([-1, 1]) uniform(0.60, 1.18) crosswidth. Generate similar radius/weight parameters and append to edgelobespecs. 2. Evaluate Density Field: Rotate coordinates: localx, localy = rotatedxy(x, y, variation). Initialize lobefield = zeroslike(x, dtype=float32). For each lobe in edgelobespecs (cx, cy, rx, ry, w, lz, lZR): Rotate lobe center: lcx = cos(variation)cx + sin(variation)cy, lcy = -sin(variation)cx + cos(variation)cy. Calculate 2D lobe contribution: lobe = \exp\left( -\left( \frac{localx - lcx}{rx \cdot 1.15} \right)^2 - \left( \frac{localy - lcy}{ry \cdot 1.15} \right)^2 \right) Calculate vertical presence: persistent\support = \text{lookup}(type\id) vertical\presence = persistent\support + (1.0 - persistent\support) \cdot \exp\left( -\left( \frac{z - lz}{\max(lZR, 0.001)} \right)^2 \right) Add to field: lobefield += float32(w verticalpresence) lobe. 3. Apply Horizontal Taper: Get horizontaltaper from shape profile. Calculate normalizedheight = abs(z - centerz) / max(halfheight, 0.001). Calculate taper mask: captapermask = smoothstep((normalizedheight - 0.12) / 0.88). Calculate taper field: captaper = horizontaltaper captapermask. 4. Final Contour Calculation: Calculate contour: contour = lobe\field + (edge\noise - 0.5) \cdot (0.62 + 0.30 \cdot side\variation) - cap\taper Apply organic smoothing: organic = smoothstep\left( \frac{contour - 0.30}{0.48} \right) Apply final edge guard (clears only outermost voxels): screen\distance = \min(x+1, 1-x, y+1, 1-y) final\guard = safe\edge\fade(screen\distance, 0.0, 0.045) Return organic finalguard. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def finitelayercloudshapegeneration(x, y, z, typeid, rng, edgenoise, variation): """ Generates the 3D shape contour for layer clouds. x, y, z: numpy arrays of coordinates. typeid: int, cloud type ID (3, 5, 6, 7, 8). rng: numpy.random.Generator. edgenoise: numpy array of noise values. variation: float, rotation angle. """ # Fallback for typeid if not in layer set if typeid not in {3, 5, 6, 7, 8}: typeid = 5 # Step 1: Generate Lobe Specifications majorangle = rng.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi) direction = np.array([np.cos(majorangle), np.sin(majorangle)]) perpendicular = np.array([-direction[1], direction[0]]) majorlength = rng.uniform(0.45, 0.72) crosswidth = rng.uniform(0.22, 0.46) # Get shape profile parameters centerz, halfheight,,,, horizontaltaper, sideedgevariation = layershapeprofile(typeid) count = rng.integers(7, 14) positionsalong = np.linspace(-0.88, 0.88, count) + rng.normal(0.0, 0.09, size=count) edgelobespecs = [] centerx, centery = 0.0, 0.0 # Main chain lobes for posalong in positionsalong: along = posalong majorlength cross = rng.normal(0.0, crosswidth 0.62) position = np.array([centerx, centery]) + direction along + perpendicular cross radiusx = rng.uniform(0.14, 0.30) radiusy = rng.uniform(0.12, 0.28) lobez = centerz + rng.uniform(-0.48, 0.48) halfheight lobezradius = rng.uniform(0.58, 1.04) halfheight weight = rng.uniform(0.54, 0.98) edgelobespecs.append((position[0], position[1], radiusx, radiusy, weight, lobez, lobezradius)) # Side lobes numsidelobes = rng.integers(1, 4) for in range(numsidelobes): along = rng.uniform(-0.58, 0.58) majorlength crosssign = rng.choice([-1, 1]) cross = crosssign rng.uniform(0.60, 1.18) crosswidth position = np.array([centerx, centery]) + direction along + perpendicular cross radiusx = rng.uniform(0.14, 0.30) radiusy = rng.uniform(0.12, 0.28) lobez = centerz + rng.uniform(-0.48, 0.48) halfheight lobezradius = rng.uniform(0.58, 1.04) halfheight weight = rng.uniform(0.54, 0.98) edgelobespecs.append((position[0], position[1], radiusx, radiusy, weight, lobez, lobezradius)) # Step 2: Evaluate Density Field localx, localy = rotatedxy(x, y, variation) lobefield = np.zeroslike(x, dtype=np.float32) persistentsupports = {3: 0.36, 5: 0.40, 6: 0.50, 7: 0.24, 8: 0.44} persistentsupport = persistentsupports[typeid] for cx, cy, rx, ry, w, lz, lZR in edgelobespecs: # Rotate lobe center cosv = np.cos(variation) sinv = np.sin(variation) lcx = cosv cx + sinv cy lcy = -sinv cx + cosv cy # 2D Lobe dx = (localx - lcx) / (rx 1.15) dy = (localy - lcy) / (ry 1.15) lobe = np.exp(-(dx2 + dy2)) # Vertical Presence zdiff = z - lz lobezradiussafe = max(lZR, 0.001) verticalpresence = persistentsupport + (1.0 - persistentsupport) np.exp(-(zdiff / lobezradiussafe)2) lobefield += np.float32(w verticalpresence) lobe # Step 3: Horizontal Taper normalizedheight = np.abs(z - centerz) / max(halfheight, 0.001) captapermask = smoothstep((normalizedheight - 0.12) / 0.88) captaper = horizontaltaper captapermask # Step 4: Final Contour contour = lobefield + (edgenoise - 0.5) (0.62 + 0.30 sideedgevariation) - captaper organic = smoothstep((contour - 0.30) / 0.48) screendistance = np.minimum.reduce([x + 1.0, 1.0 - x, y + 1.0, 1.0 - y]) finalguard = safeedgefade(screendistance, 0.0, 0.045) return organic finalguard def rotatedxy(x, y, angle): cosa = np.cos(angle) sina = np.sin(angle) return x cosa - y sina, x sina + y cosa def smoothstep(t): t = np.clip(t, 0.0, 1.0) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def safeedgefade(distance, minval, maxval): # Linear fade from 1.0 at maxval to 0.0 at minval return np.clip((distance - minval) / (maxval - minval), 0.0, 1.0) def layershapeprofile(typeid): # Returns (centerz, halfheight, topwobble, bottomwobble, thicknessvariance, captaper, sideedgevariation) # Only type 6 parameters are explicitly given in the sources; others use a standard default. profiles = { 3: (0.0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1, 0.3, 0.3, 1.0), 5: (0.0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1, 0.3, 0.3, 1.0), 6: (-0.03, 0.58, 0.180, 0.285, 0.40, 0.39, 1.10), 7: (0.0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1, 0.3, 0.3, 1.0), 8: (0.0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1, 0.3, 0.3, 1.0), } return profiles.get(typeid, (0.0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1, 0.3, 0.3, 1.0)) Degeneracy: Without side lobes, the cloud may degenerate into a simple cylinder along the Z-axis. The method explicitly adds 1–3 side lobes to prevent this. Boundary Clearing: The final guard clears only the outermost voxels; the main contour naturally goes to zero before reaching this boundary. Division by Zero: lobezradius and halfheight must be clamped to a minimum of 0.001 to avoid division by zero in vertical presence calculations. Generates non-spherical, multi-lobed shapes for convective clouds. Choose when modeling vertical development and irregular tops/bases. Extrudes a 2D sketch into an ellipsoidal volume for database retrieval. Choose when converting artistic sketches to volumetric data for similarity matching. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels and the number of lobes. Evaluation Loop: The evaluation involves a loop over edgelobespecs (typically 8–16 lobes) per voxel. Memory Complexity: Low. Requires storage for the coordinate arrays, noise, and the lobe specifications. Texture Generation: No large 3D textures are generated during the shape definition phase; it outputs a scalar field. Performance: Efficient for procedural generation. The use of Gaussian functions and smoothsteps allows for fast evaluation on GPU or CPU. Strengths: Produces natural, non-degenerate layer cloud shapes with organic edge variation. Avoids the "cylinder" artifact of simple extrusion. Limitations: Specific to layer cloud types. Not suitable for convective clouds (Cumulus/Cumulonimbus) without modification. When to Use: When generating volume data for Cirrus, Altostratus, Nimbostratus, Stratocumulus, or Stratus clouds. When Not to Use: For convective clouds or when a simple cylindrical cloud shape is desired. The method originates from the "Noise-Cloud" project, an unofficial implementation of procedural cloud generation techniques. It is designed to integrate with volume rendering pipelines, specifically for Unreal Engine 5, as indicated by the volume encoding version "ue5-volume-rg-atlas-v7-undulating-finite-layer-clouds". The technique addresses the limitations of earlier procedural cloud methods that relied on simple extrusion, providing a more physically plausible shape for layer clouds. mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, https://github.com/mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Cumulonimbus and Cumulus Shape Generation
head: Cumulus and Cumulonimbus Shape Generation
body: Cumulonimbus and Cumulus Shape Generation is a procedural method for generating non-spherical, multi-lobed cloud shapes for Cumulus (type 9) and Cumulonimbus (type 10) clouds, creating irregular tops and bases rather than simple spheres. It differs from explicit tessellation approaches by using a parametric lobe-generation pipeline that scales with cloud type and style. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Cloud type ID (9 for Cumulus, 10 for Cumulonimbus), style offset (31009 for realistic, 41003 for cartoon), base seed, and a random number generator (RNG). Outputs: A list of 3D ellipsoidal lobes, each defined by a center position (cx, cy, cz) and radii (rx, ry, rz). Data Structures: Each lobe is stored as a tuple or struct containing cx, cy, cz (float coordinates) and rx, ry, rz (float radii). Steps: 1. Initialize RNG: Set the random seed using the formula: \text{seed} = \text{base\seed} + \text{type\id} \times 1009 + \text{style\offset} Where typeid is 9 for Cumulus and 10 for Cumulonimbus. 2. Generate Center: Generate the base center coordinates (center\x, center\y) from a uniform distribution over the interval [-0.12, 0.12]. 3. Generate Lobes based on Type: If Type 9 (Cumulus): Base Lobes: Generate 3 to 6 base lobes. cx, cy: Generated from a uniform distribution around center\x, center\y. cz: Generated from uniform distribution in [-0.42, -0.16]. rx: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.27, 0.42]. ry: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.23, 0.37]. rz: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.14, 0.25]. Tower Lobes: Generate 5 to 10 tower lobes. direction: Generated from uniform distribution in [-\pi, \pi]. radial: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.06, 0.52]. cx, cy: Offset from the center by radial in the direction direction. cz: Generated from uniform distribution in [-0.06, 0.54]. rx: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.17, 0.34]. ry: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.16, 0.32]. rz: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.18, 0.36]. If Type 10 (Cumulonimbus): Generate a sequence of lobes indexed from 0 to lobe\count - 1. Calculate progress: progress = \frac{index}{lobe\count - 1}. cx, cy: Spread increases with progress. The base spread is 0.13 + progress \times 0.08. cz: Rises from -0.58 to 0.56, calculated as -0.58 + progress \times 1.14. rx, ry: Increase with progress, calculated as 0.24 + progress \times 0.10. rz: Not given in the sources. Other Layer Clouds (Types 1, 7): Generate 3 to 10 lobes with radial from uniform [0.03, 0.52], theta from uniform [-\pi, \pi], and cz from uniform [-0.20, 0.20]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def generatecumuluscumulonimbuslobs(typeid, styleoffset, baseseed, lobecount=15): # 1. Initialize RNG seed = baseseed + typeid 1009 + styleoffset rng = random.Random(seed) # 2. Generate Center centerx = rng.uniform(-0.12, 0.12) centery = rng.uniform(-0.12, 0.12) lobes = [] if typeid == 9: # Cumulus # Base Lobes: 3-6 numbase = rng.randint(3, 6) for in range(numbase): cx = rng.uniform(centerx - 0.12, centerx + 0.12) cy = rng.uniform(centery - 0.12, centery + 0.12) cz = rng.uniform(-0.42, -0.16) rx = rng.uniform(0.27, 0.42) ry = rng.uniform(0.23, 0.37) rz = rng.uniform(0.14, 0.25) lobes.append({'cx': cx, 'cy': cy, 'cz': cz, 'rx': rx, 'ry': ry, 'rz': rz}) # Tower Lobes: 5-10 numtower = rng.randint(5, 10) for in range(numtower): direction = rng.uniform(-math.pi, math.pi) radial = rng.uniform(0.06, 0.52) cx = centerx + radial math.cos(direction) cy = centery + radial math.sin(direction) cz = rng.uniform(-0.06, 0.54) rx = rng.uniform(0.17, 0.34) ry = rng.uniform(0.16, 0.32) rz = rng.uniform(0.18, 0.36) lobes.append({'cx': cx, 'cy': cy, 'cz': cz, 'rx': rx, 'ry': ry, 'rz': rz}) elif typeid == 10: # Cumulonimbus # Guard against division by zero lobecount = max(lobecount, 2) for i in range(lobecount): progress = i / (lobecount - 1) # Spread increases with progress spread = 0.13 + progress 0.08 cx = centerx + rng.uniform(-spread, spread) cy = centery + rng.uniform(-spread, spread) # CZ rises from -0.58 to 0.56 cz = -0.58 + progress 1.14 # RX, RY increase with progress rx = 0.24 + progress 0.10 ry = 0.24 + progress 0.10 # RZ not specified in sources rz = 0.20 lobes.append({'cx': cx, 'cy': cy, 'cz': cz, 'rx': rx, 'ry': ry, 'rz': rz}) else: # Other Layer Clouds (Types 1, 7) numother = rng.randint(3, 10) for in range(numother): radial = rng.uniform(0.03, 0.52) theta = rng.uniform(-math.pi, math.pi) cx = centerx + radial math.cos(theta) cy = centery + radial math.sin(theta) cz = rng.uniform(-0.20, 0.20) rx = rng.uniform(0.27, 0.42) ry = rng.uniform(0.23, 0.37) rz = rng.uniform(0.14, 0.25) lobes.append({'cx': cx, 'cy': cy, 'cz': cz, 'rx': rx, 'ry': ry, 'rz': rz}) return lobes Parameters: styleoffset: 31009 for realistic style, 41003 for cartoon style. typeid: 9 for Cumulus, 10 for Cumulonimbus. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: In Cumulonimbus generation, if lobecount is 1, the progress calculation involves division by zero. The implementation must enforce lobecount >= 2. Precision: The source uses floating-point uniform distributions. Deterministic results require consistent RNG state across platforms. Boundary Conditions: The coordinates and radii are normalized values. The rendering pipeline must handle these normalized coordinates correctly. The Hierarchical Implicit Blob Cloud Model is a procedural method for generating the irregular, multi-lobed shapes of Cumulus and Cumulonimbus clouds by recursively layering quasi-spherical particles. It solves the problem of creating realistic cloud tops and bases with continuous furrows, distinguishing itself from explicit tessellation approaches by using a particle system to extract isosurfaces and place subsequent levels. An algorithm for generating Cumulus (type 9) and Cumulonimbus (type 10) clouds using a sparse set of 3D Gaussian-distributed pseudo-spheroid primitives. It differs from particle-based systems by requiring significantly fewer primitives (typically 35) to achieve realistic results, and from hierarchical implicit blobs by using explicit geometric primitives with pre-processing filters to optimize rendering performance. A vertical profile function that sculpts realistic 'water balloon on a table' puffy clouds using a superellipsoid shape. It sculpts voluminous, vertical structures inside getCloud3DProfile / getCloud3DSDF using a superellipsoid profile driven by eccentricity, curvature exponent, and center distance. Eccentricity determines the widest point of the cloud, decoded from the cell ID hash. Curvature exponent is a parameter driving the superellipsoid profile shape. Uses L-systems (Lindenmayer systems) with grammar rules to generate cloud shapes. It differs from Kang et al. by including a proportional random factor in sphere radius and distance between primitives in each recursive call. It uses volumetric rendering and density function from Equation (2). The host-side C++ interpreter runs before GLSL rendering, acting as a tiny interpreter for recursive generation of spheres based on an axiom and rules, generating a string of symbols. A lexical analyser processes the generated string, inserting a sphere with random radius and length for each 'X' or 'Y' item, and applying rotation angles given by '+' and '&' operators. The BNF Grammar for generation is X \rightarrow X+YF++YF-FX-XFXF-YF+/, where '+' means turn left with angle using a rotation matrix, and '&' means pitch down with angle using a different rotation matrix. Example parameters: Iterations = 7, Angle = 10° produces thin/strange spiral shapes; Angle [50°, 100°] with same grammar produces dense cumulus formations. The string produced by Equation (18) generates 128 spheres, ready to transfer to OpenGL shader for real-time animation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Hierarchical Implicit Blob Cloud Model
head: Cloud Shape Model, Implicit Surface Cloud
body: The Hierarchical Implicit Blob Cloud Model is a procedural method for generating the irregular, multi-lobed shapes of Cumulus and Cumulonimbus clouds by recursively layering quasi-spherical particles. It solves the problem of creating realistic cloud tops and bases with continuous furrows, distinguishing itself from explicit tessellation approaches by using a particle system to extract isosurfaces and place subsequent levels. Inputs: Level 0 particle configuration: A set of initial particles P0, either procedurally generated on a horizontal plane or manually placed by a user to define features like turrets. Global parameters: Flattening range, radius reduction factor, blending amounts, and repulsion offsets. Outputs: A hierarchy of implicit surfaces Sl for l = 0, \dots, L, where SL defines the final cloud shape. A mesh representation of the final surface (via isosurface extraction) suitable for rendering with specific shaders. The model relies on a hierarchical list of particles. Each particle pi at level l stores: Position Pi: 3D coordinates on the surface S{l-1}. Radius ri: Scalar value, typically ri \approx \frac{1}{3} r{parent} \times (1 + \delta), where \delta \in [-0.3, 0.3]. Flattening ei: Scalar value, randomly chosen from [0.1, 1.0]. Local Potential Field: Implicit function values used for surface extraction and neighbor interaction. 1. Initialize Level 0 (l=0): If procedural: Generate a small number of particles randomly positioned on a horizontal plane or in a small subspace. If manual: Allow user placement to shape features (e.g., turrets). Define the initial surface S0 as the union of the implicit fields of these particles. 2. Iterate for Levels l = 1 to L: Extract Surface S{l-1}: Use a particle system to extract the isosurface of the previous level S{l-1}. This involves simulating particles that repel each other and grow to populate the available surface area of S{l-1}. Growth Logic: Particles grow until they reach a target radius or energy. If a particle grows too much or an area is uncrowded, split the particle. If an area is overcrowded, remove particles. Target Distance: Maintain a target inter-particle distance (typically twice the target particle radius) to ensure equilibrium. Place Level l Particles: Use the extracted isosurface points from the previous step as the initial positions for new particles at level l. Define Particle Properties: Set radius ri based on the parent radius r{parent}: ri = \frac{1}{3} r{parent} \times (1 + \text{random}(-0.3, 0.3)). Set flattening ei randomly from [0.1, 1.0]. Set blending parameters b and I based on level l (see Parameters). Compute Implicit Field: For each particle i at level l, compute its implicit field fi(P) (see Formulas). Combine Level: The surface Sl is defined by the maximum potential of all particles at level l and the previous level's surface: Sl = \{ P \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid \max(f{l-1}(P), \maxi fi(P)) = 1 \} (Note: The source defines fl(P) as \max(f{l-1}(P), \maxi fi(P)) implicitly by stating the surface is defined from this max.) 3. Render Final Shape (SL): Extract the mesh of SL. Apply a Gardner-like shader for view-dependent transparency near silhouettes. Apply Perlin solid texture for lower-scale details. (Optional) Apply "normal blending" shader to smooth furrows near the base surface S{L-1}. Implicit Surface Definition: Each particle i defines a surface Si: Si = \{ P \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid fi(P) = 1 \} where: fi(P) = gi(P) + hi(P) Base Shape gi(P): A flattened sphere: gi(P) = \exp \left( 1 - \frac{di}{ri (1 - ei d{l-1})} \right) di: Distance from point P to particle center Pi. ri: Radius of particle i. ei: Flattening factor for particle i. d{l-1}: Distance from point P to the previous level surface S{l-1}. Deformation Field hi(P): hi(P) = mi(P) + ni(P) + oi(P) 1. Repulsion Component mi(P): Prevents overlap and creates furrows: mi(P) = \sumj (1 - \epsilon - gj(P)) \min(1, gj^2(P)) Sum is over neighboring particles j. \epsilon: Offset parameter for repulsion strength. 2. Blending Component ni(P): Enlarges the blob near the base surface S{l-1} to prevent "popping". The source does not provide the explicit mathematical formula for ni(P), only its parameters. b: Blending amount parameter. I: Parameter adjusting the fraction of the bubble enlarged. 3. Floor Repulsion Component oi(P): Creates a flat bottom. The source does not provide the explicit mathematical formula for oi(P), only its parameters. h0: Reference height for the cloud floor. \alphah: Stiffness of repulsion for the flat bottom. Rendering Transparency t: Gardner-like shader for fuzzy layer: t = (1 - \alpha \vec{N} \cdot \vec{C})^{\alphas} \vec{N}: Local normal (gradient of the field). \vec{C}: Camera direction. \alpha: Controls thickness of the transparent margin. \alphas: Controls sharpness of the transparent margin. Normal Blending (Optional): Interpolates normals near the base surface S{l-1}: \vec{N}' = (1 - p \alphaN) \vec{N} + p \alphaN \vec{g} p: Normalized distance to the base surface (1 - \text{potential}). \vec{g}: Normalized gradient of S{l-1}. \alphaN: Controls the blending strength. | Parameter | Description | Typical Value / Range | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | \epsilon | Offset for repulsion in mi(P). Controls furrow size. | 0.5 | | b | Blending amount in ni(P). | 0 for levels 0, 1; 1.0 for level 2 | | I | Fraction of bubble enlarged in ni(P). | 10 | | h0 | Reference height for cloud floor. | 100 m | | \alphah | Stiffness of repulsion for flat bottom in oi(P). | 100 m | | ei | Flattening factor for particle i. | Randomly chosen between 0.1 and 1 | | ri | Radius of particles at level l. | \frac{1}{3} r{l-1} \times (1 \pm 0.3) | | \alpha | Transparency thickness control. | Not given in the sources. | | \alphas | Transparency sharpness control. | Not given in the sources. | | \alphaN | Normal blending strength. | Not given in the sources. | Furrows vs. Contact: Blobs should not stick together; real cloud blobs have furrows. The offset parameter \epsilon in mi(P) must be set >0 (e.g., 0.5) to repulse surfaces more than for simple contact. Level 0 Initialization: Level 0 has no previous surface S{-1}. It must be created procedurally or manually. Procedural generation on a horizontal plane may result in flat bases; manual placement allows for complex features like turrets. Particle Splitting/Removal: During the isosurface extraction for level l, particles must be split if they grow too much or if areas are uncrowded, and removed if overcrowded, to maintain a natural, non-uniform distribution. Formula Gaps: The explicit mathematical formulas for ni(P) and oi(P) are not provided in the source snippets, only their parameters and qualitative descriptions. Implementers must infer these from standard implicit blob techniques or the full paper. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def distance(p1, p2): return math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2))) def dot(v1, v2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def getdisttoprevsurface(P): """Returns distance from P to the previous level surface S{l-1}. In practice, this is evaluated using the potential field of level l-1.""" return 0.0 # Placeholder for actual distance field query def computebaseshape(P, particle): """Computes gi(P) = exp(1 - di / (ri (1 - ei d{l-1})))""" di = distance(P, particle['pos']) dlminus1 = getdisttoprevsurface(P) r = particle['radius'] e = particle['flattening'] denom = r (1 - e dlminus1) if abs(denom) < 1e-6: return 0.0 return math.exp(1 - di / denom) def computerepulsion(P, particle, neighbors): """Computes mi(P) = sumj (1 - epsilon - gj(P)) min(1, gj(P)^2).""" epsilon = 0.5 msum = 0.0 for neighbor in neighbors: gj = computebaseshape(P, neighbor) msum += (1 - epsilon - gj) min(1.0, gj 2) return msum def computedeformation(P, particle, neighbors): """Computes hi(P) = mi(P) + ni(P) + oi(P).""" mi = computerepulsion(P, particle, neighbors) # The explicit formulas for ni(P) and oi(P) are not provided in the sources. # ni(P) uses parameters b and I to enlarge the blob near the base surface. # oi(P) uses parameters h0 and alphah to create a flat bottom. ni = 0.0 oi = 0.0 return mi + ni + oi def computeimplicitfield(P, particle, neighbors): """Computes fi(P) = gi(P) + hi(P).""" gi = computebaseshape(P, particle) hi = computedeformation(P, particle, neighbors) return gi + hi def getneighbors(p, particles, radius): return [p2 for p2 in particles if distance(p['pos'], p2['pos']) < radius] def initializeparticlesonsurface(particlesprev): """Generates initial particles on the isosurface of the previous level.""" # In practice, samples points on the implicit surface of level l-1 return [] # Placeholder for surface sampling logic def extractisosurfacelevel(particlesprev, targetradius): """Extracts isosurface of S{l-1} using a particle system simulation.""" currentparticles = initializeparticlesonsurface(particlesprev) maxiterations = 100 for in range(maxiterations): converged = True for p in currentparticles: # Grow particle towards target radius p['radius'] += 0.1 if p['radius'] > targetradius 1.1: p['radius'] = targetradius 1.1 converged = False neighbors = getneighbors(p, currentparticles, radius=targetradius 2) # Simulate repulsion by adjusting radius based on neighbor density repulsion = computerepulsion(p['pos'], p, neighbors) if repulsion > 0.5: p['radius'] -= 0.05 else: p['radius'] += 0.05 # Split if too big or uncrowded if p['radius'] > targetradius 1.05 or len(neighbors) < 2: # Split logic: create new particles at p['pos'] with smaller radius pass # Remove if overcrowded if len(neighbors) > 10: pass # Remove particle logic if converged: break return currentparticles def rendercloud(mesh, cameradir): """Renders the final cloud mesh using Gardner-like shader and Perlin texture.""" for vertex in mesh.vertices: N = vertex.normal C = cameradir dotproduct = dot(N, C) alpha = 1.0 alphas = 2.0 transparency = (1 - alpha dotproduct) alphas textureval = 0.5 # Placeholder for Perlin noise evaluation color = (textureval, textureval, textureval) (1 - transparency) return color Time Complexity: Shape generation is recursive. Each level l requires extracting the isosurface of S{l-1} using a particle system simulation, which is iterative and depends on the number of particles and convergence criteria. The authors state that rendering and animation are fast because the model does not rely on volumetric representation or voxel discretization. Memory Complexity: Stores the hierarchy of particles. The number of particles increases with each level, but radii decrease by a factor of ~3, potentially limiting the total count if surface area coverage is maintained. Measured Performance: The authors state that rendering and animation are fast because the model does not rely on volumetric representation or voxel discretization. Specific hardware or resolution benchmarks are not given in the sources. Strengths: Realistic shapes with continuous furrows. No voxel discretization artifacts. Fast rendering due to explicit mesh/shader approach. Hierarchical structure allows for multi-scale detail. Limitations: Relies on heuristic parameters (e.g., \epsilon, b, I) which may require tuning. The explicit formulas for blending (ni) and floor repulsion (oi) are not fully provided in the source, making implementation ambiguous. Does not include volumetric rendering effects (e.g., light scattering) in the shape model itself, requiring additional shaders for realistic appearance. When to Use: When generating realistic Cumulus/Cumulonimbus cloud shapes for real-time rendering or animation where performance is critical. When explicit mesh output is desired for further processing or animation. When Not to Use: When volumetric light scattering or complex internal cloud structure is required (the model only defines shape). When exact mathematical continuity of blending/floor effects is critical and the missing formulas cannot be inferred. Origin: Proposed by Fabrice Neyret and A. Bouthors from EVASION-GRAVIR/IMAG-INRIA. Published in 2004 in the paper "Modeling Clouds Shape". History and Development: The model draws on and extends several previous approaches, including implicit surfaces [Gas93] and particle-based surface extraction [WH94, CA97]. It contrasts with explicit tessellation methods like [NND96] by using a particle system for level generation. The model is designed to be integrated with particle animation and advanced rendering, though the paper focuses on shape definition. Applications: Procedural generation of cloud shapes for computer graphics, particularly in real-time rendering and animation. name: 3D Gaussian Cloud Generation
head: Gaussian pseudo-spheroid generation
body: An algorithm for generating Cumulus (type 9) and Cumulonimbus (type 10) clouds using a sparse set of 3D Gaussian-distributed pseudo-spheroid primitives. It differs from particle-based systems by requiring significantly fewer primitives (typically 35) to achieve realistic results, and from hierarchical implicit blobs by using explicit geometric primitives with pre-processing filters to optimize rendering performance. Inputs: Cloud center C; number of primitives N (typically 35); scale constants tx, ty, tz; maximum radius R{max}; radius spread \sigmar. Outputs: List of N pseudo-spheroids, each defined by position Pi, orientation (implied by axis scaling), and radius ri. Data Structures: PseudoSpheroid: struct containing position (vec3), radius (float), mean (vec3), stddev (vec3). Parameters: N = 35. R{max}: Maximum possible radius of a sphere in the variant. \sigmar: Radius spread constant. tx, ty, tz: Scale constants for the normal distribution axes. Typical values for means and standard deviations are provided in Table 2 of the source, but exact numerical values are not listed in the text. Steps: 1. Generate Positions: For each primitive i from 1 to N: Sample a random variable \mathcal{N} with normal distribution for each axis x, y, z using the specific means and standard deviations defined for the cloud type. Calculate position Pi relative to cloud center C: Pi = C + \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma) Where \mu and \sigma are the mean and standard deviation vectors for the respective axes. Note: The source mentions using clamping similar to Huang et al. [1], but does not specify the clamp bounds. Implementation typically clamps sampled values to prevent outliers from extending the cloud too far, often within \pm 3\sigma. 2. Calculate Radii: For each primitive i: Calculate distance di from Pi to C: di = \| Pi - C \| Compute radius ri using Equation (16) for real cumulus generation: ri = R{max} \cdot e^{-\frac{di^2}{2\sigmar^2}} Where R{max} is the maximum radius and \sigmar is the radius spread constant. Note: Equation (15) is a variant, but Equation (16) is specified for the experiments shown. 3. Pre-processing Filter 1 (Hollow Cloud Removal): Identify spheroids within a specific range from the center that would create a hollow appearance. Remove approximately 20% of spheroids in the nucleus. Note: The exact range threshold is not given in the text. A direct implementation removes the innermost primitives by distance until approximately 20% are removed. 4. Pre-processing Filter 2 (Containment Removal): For every pair of spheroids A and B: Calculate distance d{AB} between centers PA and PB. Check if sphere A is inside sphere B: d{AB} + rA < rB If true, remove sphere A. Repeat for all pairs to ensure no primitive is fully contained within another. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def generate3dgaussiancloud(center, numprimitives=35, rmax=1.0, sigmar=0.5, means=None, stddevs=None): """ Generates a cloud using 3D Gaussian distributed pseudo-spheroids. Args: center: (x, y, z) tuple for cloud center C. numprimitives: Number of spheroids (typically 35). rmax: Maximum radius constant. sigmar: Radius spread constant. means: List of 3 floats (meanx, meany, meanz). Not given in sources. stddevs: List of 3 floats (stdx, stdy, stdz). Not given in sources. Returns: List of dicts with 'position' and 'radius'. """ # Use standard normal distribution if Table 2 values are not provided if means is None: means = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if stddevs is None: stddevs = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] primitives = [] # Step 1: Generate Positions for in range(numprimitives): x = random.gauss(means[0], stddevs[0]) y = random.gauss(means[1], stddevs[1]) z = random.gauss(means[2], stddevs[2]) # Apply clamping as mentioned in source (similar to Huang et al.) # Clamp bounds not specified; typical implementation uses ±3σ position = (center[0] + x, center[1] + y, center[2] + z) # Step 2: Calculate Radius dx = position[0] - center[0] dy = position[1] - center[1] dz = position[2] - center[2] distance = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) # Equation (16) for real cumulus generation radius = rmax math.exp(-(distance2) / (2 sigmar2)) primitives.append({ 'position': position, 'radius': radius }) # Step 3: Pre-processing Filter 1 (Hollow Cloud Removal) # Source states ~20% of nucleus spheroids are removed. # Exact range threshold is not given. # Implementation removes innermost primitives by distance. primitives.sort(key=lambda p: math.sqrt( (p['position'][0]-center[0])2 + (p['position'][1]-center[1])2 + (p['position'][2]-center[2])2)) primitives = primitives[int(0.2 len(primitives)):] # Step 4: Pre-processing Filter 2 (Containment Removal) finalprimitives = [] for i, pa in enumerate(primitives): iscontained = False for j, pb in enumerate(primitives): if i == j: continue # Check if A is inside B dx = pa['position'][0] - pb['position'][0] dy = pa['position'][1] - pb['position'][1] dz = pa['position'][2] - pb['position'][2] distab = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) # Condition: distance + radiusA < radiusB if distab + pa['radius'] < pb['radius']: iscontained = True break if not iscontained: finalprimitives.append(pa) return finalprimitives Complexity: The pre-processing computation (comparing radii and distances) is not a drawback due to the reduced number of spheres (e.g., 35) required in the Gaussian model. Performance: The pre-processing filter 1 yields a ~30% average improvement in frame rate without affecting the look of the cloud. Strengths: Requires significantly fewer primitives (typically 35) compared to particle systems (thousands). Limitations: Relies on specific parameter tuning (means, standard deviations) which are not fully detailed in the source. The method is part of a procedural volume cloud modeling approach for real-time GPU volumetric rendering. It builds on the concept of using 3D Gaussian distributions to model cumuliform cloud shapes, which naturally resemble normal distributions. The position generation uses clamping similar to the method by Huang et al. [1], but adapts it for explicit pseudo-spheroid primitives rather than particles. name: Query Shape Generation from Vertical Sketch
body: This method generates a 3D query shape for cloud volume retrieval by extruding a user-sketched 2D vertical profile into a volume where every cross-section is an ellipsoid. It solves the problem of converting a simple 2D artistic sketch into a volumetric representation suitable for similarity matching against a pre-simulated database. It differs from its sibling Cumulonimbus and Cumulus Shape Generation by focusing on layer-cloud-like ellipsoidal cross-sections derived from a single vertical curve, rather than complex convective structures. It serves as the geometric foundation for Sketch-based Cloud Volume Retrieval via SVD, which uses this shape for database matching. Inputs: 1. User-specified cloud plane height. 2. User-specified horizontal thickness parameter d. 3. User-sketched 2D curve representing the vertical shape of the desired clouds. Outputs: A 3D query shape defined by its horizontal thickness T(x, z) at any point (x, 0, z) in the local coordinate system. Data Structures: The method does not explicitly store a voxel grid or mesh in this generation phase; it defines the shape analytically via the thickness function T(x, z). The input sketch is treated as a set of points defining the height function h(x). Steps: 1. Generate Cloud Plane: Create a horizontal plane at the user-specified height. 2. Sketch Input: The user sketches the vertical shape of the desired clouds as a single continuous curve on the screen. 3. Project Endpoints: Identify the start and end points of the sketched curve. Project the line segment connecting these two endpoints onto the cloud plane. 4. Create Vertical Plane: Construct a vertical plane that is perpendicular to the cloud plane and contains the projected line segment. 5. Project Sketch: Project the user's sketched curve onto this vertical plane. 6. Define Local Coordinate System: Establish a local coordinate system (x, y, z) with the following properties: Origin: Center of the line segment connecting the endpoints of the sketched curve. x-axis: Coincides with the direction of the line segment. z-axis: Coincides with the normal vector of the cloud plane. y-axis: Completes the right-handed system, perpendicular to both x and z. 7. Extract Height Function: Determine the height of the vertical shape at each x coordinate, denoted as h(x), based on the projected sketch in the local coordinate system. 8. Compute Thickness: For each point (x, 0, z) within the bounds of the shape, compute the horizontal thickness T(x, z) using the formula below. Formula: The horizontal thickness T(x, z) at a point (x, 0, z) is given by: T(x, z) = \pm d \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{z}{h(x)}\right)^2} \quad \text{for } 0 < z < h(x) Where: T(x, z) is the horizontal thickness at position x and height z. d is the user-specified parameter for horizontal thickness. h(x) is the height of the vertical shape at (x, 0, 0). The \pm indicates that the thickness extends symmetrically in the y direction (positive and negative y). Parameters: d: User-specified parameter used to adjust the horizontal thickness of the query shape. Typical values for d are not given in the sources. The source notes an experimental value of \alpha = 0.9 for the SVD approximation step, but not for d. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Height: If h(x) = 0 at any point, the term \frac{z}{h(x)} becomes undefined. Implementers must handle points where the sketch height is zero or negative by excluding them or clamping. Boundary Conditions: The formula applies strictly within the vertical extent of the sketch (0 < z < h(x)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generatequeryshape(sketchpoints, cloudplanenormal, d): """ Generates a query shape from a vertical sketch. Args: sketchpoints: List of 2D tuples (u, v) representing the user's sketch in screen space. cloudplanenormal: 3D vector representing the normal of the cloud plane. d: User-specified horizontal thickness parameter. Returns: A callable function getthickness(x, z) that returns the horizontal thickness. """ if len(sketchpoints) < 2: raise ValueError("Sketch must have at least two points") # Step 1-3: Project endpoints and define line segment start = sketchpoints[0] end = sketchpoints[-1] dx = end[0] - start[0] dz = end[1] - start[1] seglen = math.hypot(dx, dz) if seglen == 0: raise ValueError("Start and end points are identical") # Step 4-6: Define local coordinate system via rotation # Rotate sketch so the segment aligns with the local x-axis theta = math.atan2(dz, dx) cost, sint = math.cos(theta), math.sin(theta) localpoints = [] for p in sketchpoints: px, pz = p[0] - start[0], p[1] - start[1] rx = px cost + pz sint rz = -px sint + pz cost localpoints.append((rx, rz)) # Shift origin to center of segment centerx = seglen / 2.0 finalpoints = [(rx - centerx, rz) for rx, rz in localpoints] # Step 7: Extract height function h(x) finalpoints.sort(key=lambda p: p[0]) xs = [p[0] for p in finalpoints] hs = [p[1] for p in finalpoints] def geth(x): if x < xs[0] or x > xs[-1]: return 0.0 for i in range(len(xs) - 1): if xs[i] <= x <= xs[i+1]: if xs[i+1] == xs[i]: return hs[i] t = (x - xs[i]) / (xs[i+1] - xs[i]) return hs[i] + t (hs[i+1] - hs[i]) return 0.0 # Step 8: Compute thickness T(x, z) def getthickness(x, z): hx = geth(x) if hx <= 0: return 0.0 if z <= 0 or z >= hx: return 0.0 term = 1.0 - (z / hx) 2 if term < 0: return 0.0 return d math.sqrt(term) return getthickness Sketch-based Cloud Volume Retrieval via SVD is a method for retrieving realistic 3D cloud volumes from a pre-simulated database by matching a user-sketched 2D shape to 3D data using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) basis vectors for efficient similarity calculation. It differs from direct voxel comparison by projecting both the query and database volumes into a low-dimensional subspace, reducing the computational cost of similarity search from proportional to the total number of voxels N to proportional to the number of basis vectors K. Choose this method when fast database matching is required for layer clouds. It builds on Query Shape Generation from Vertical Sketch by converting the generated query shape into a volumetric representation suitable for database matching. Time and Memory Complexity: The generation process scales linearly with the number of sketch points N. The generation phase stores the sketch points and parameter d. The retrieval database stores basis vectors uk and coefficients w{nk} instead of full voxel grids to reduce storage. The subsequent retrieval process using SVD has a complexity proportional to the number of basis vectors K, which is much smaller than the total number of voxels N. Measured Performance: Specific performance metrics for the shape generation step are not provided in the sources. However, the SVD-based retrieval process reduces storage cost to 84% of the original and accelerates retrieval. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement; allows intuitive user input via sketching; generates smooth ellipsoidal cross-sections suitable for layer clouds. Limitations: Limited to shapes that can be represented by a single vertical curve; assumes ellipsoidal cross-sections which may not fit all cloud types; requires a pre-simulated database for retrieval. When to Use: Use this method when the user wants to quickly generate a cloud volume shape for layer clouds (e.g., Stratus, Altostratus) using a simple 2D sketch and intends to retrieve a similar volume from a database. When Not to Use: Do not use this method for convective clouds (e.g., Cumulonimbus) which require more complex shapes. Do not use it if a direct volumetric generation without database retrieval is required. This method was introduced in the context of a sketch-based system for cloud volume retrieval from simulated datasets for realistic image synthesis. It is part of a pipeline that allows users to interactively specify cloud shapes and retrieve realistic volumes from a database. The method relies on the assumption that cloud cross-sections can be approximated by ellipsoids. A sketch-based system for cloud volume retrieval from simulated dataset for realistic image synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1145/2817675.2817690, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Sketch-based Cloud Volume Retrieval via SVD
head: SVD-based Cloud Retrieval
body: Sketch-based Cloud Volume Retrieval via SVD is a method for retrieving realistic 3D cloud volumes from a pre-simulated database by matching a user-sketched 2D shape to 3D data using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) basis vectors for efficient similarity calculation. It differs from direct voxel comparison by projecting both the query and database volumes into a low-dimensional subspace, reducing the computational cost of similarity search from proportional to the total number of voxels M to proportional to the number of basis vectors K. The method converts the generated query shape into a volumetric representation suitable for database matching by creating a bounding box and subdividing it into a uniform grid. Inputs: 1. User sketch of the cloud bottom shape on a 2D screen. 2. User-specified height for the cloud bottom. 3. A database of pre-simulated 3D cloud volumes, each normalized to a 20 \times 20 \times 20 grid. 4. Pre-computed SVD basis vectors uk derived from the database volumes. Outputs: 1. The 3D cloud volume data from the database with the smallest similarity score to the query shape. Data Structures: Cloud Plane Grid: A 2D uniform grid representing the cloud bottom plane. Initial Query Volume (D0): A 3D uniform grid (bounding box of the query shape) where each cell contains a binary value: 1 if inside the query shape, 0 otherwise. Query Vector (x0): A 1D vector containing the voxel values of D0. Basis Vectors (uk): Pre-computed vectors representing the principal components of the database volumes. Database Volumes (Dn): Normalized to a 20 \times 20 \times 20 grid. Parameters: K: The number of basis vectors used for SVD approximation. In experiments, K = M/114, where M is the total number of voxels in the volume data. M: The total number of voxels in the volume data (e.g., 20^3 = 8000 for the normalized grid). Steps: 1. Generate Cloud Plane: The user specifies the height of the cloud bottom. The system generates a horizontal plane (cloud plane) at that height. 2. Grid Subdivision: The cloud plane is subdivided into a uniform 2D grid. 3. Project Sketch: The user sketches the shape of the cloud bottom on the screen. This 2D shape is projected onto the cloud plane grid. 4. Binary Mask Creation: For each grid point on the cloud plane, assign a value of 1 if the point is inside the projected shape, and 0 otherwise, creating a binary image. 5. Distance Transform: Apply a distance transform to the binary image to compute the Euclidean distance from each grid point to the boundary of the projected shape. 6. Query Shape Height Generation: Create the 3D query shape by assuming the cloud height at each grid point (x, y) equals the distance value obtained from the distance transform at that point. 7. Bounding Box and Volume Creation: Create a bounding box for the query shape. Subdivide this bounding box into a uniform 3D grid to form the initial query volume D0. Assign 1 to grid points inside the shape and 0 to points outside. 8. Vectorization: Represent the initial query volume D0 as a vector x0 of voxel values. 9. SVD Approximation of Query: Approximate x0 as a linear combination of the K pre-computed SVD basis vectors uk: x0 \approx \sum{k=1}^{K} w{k0} uk where w{k0} are the projection coefficients. 10. Calculate Query Coefficients: Compute the coefficients w{k0} for the query vector: w{k0} = x0 \cdot uk where \cdot denotes the dot product. 11. Retrieve Database Volumes: For each cloud volume Dn in the database: a. Represent Dn as a vector xn. b. Compute the pre-calculated coefficients w{nk} for Dn: w{nk} = xn \cdot uk c. Calculate the approximate similarity score: scoren \approx \sum{k=1}^{K} (w{k0} - w{nk})^2. 12. Select Best Match: Extract the volume data from the database with the smallest similarity score scoren and display it to the user. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def retrievecloudvolume(usersketchpoints, cloudbottomheight, databasevolumes, basisvectors, gridsize=64): # Step 1-2: Cloud plane grid cloudplane = [[0.0] gridsize for in range(gridsize)] # Step 3-4: Project sketch & binary mask binarymask = [[0] gridsize for in range(gridsize)] for y in range(gridsize): for x in range(gridsize): if pointinpolygon(x, y, usersketchpoints): binarymask[y][x] = 1 # Step 5: Distance transform distancemap = computedistancetransform(binarymask, gridsize) # Step 6-7: Query shape & D0 # Find bounding box of non-zero distances minx = miny = gridsize maxx = maxy = -1 for y in range(gridsize): for x in range(gridsize): if distancemap[y][x] > 0: minx, maxx = min(minx, x), max(maxx, x) miny, maxy = min(miny, y), max(maxy, y) if maxx == -1: minx, maxx, miny, maxy = 0, gridsize - 1, 0, gridsize - 1 width = maxx - minx + 1 heightdim = maxy - miny + 1 maxh = int(max(distancemap[y][x] for y in range(gridsize) for x in range(gridsize))) D0 = [[[0] maxh for in range(width)] for in range(heightdim)] for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): h = int(distancemap[y][x]) for z in range(h): D0[y - miny][x - minx][z] = 1 # Step 8: Vectorize D0 x0 = [D0[y][x][z] for y in range(heightdim) for x in range(width) for z in range(maxh)] # Step 9-10: Query coefficients K = len(basisvectors) wk0 = [dotproduct(x0, uk) for uk in basisvectors] # Step 11: Retrieve bestscore = float('inf') bestvolume = None for volume in databasevolumes: xn = [voxel for layer in volume for row in layer for voxel in row] wnk = [dotproduct(xn, uk) for uk in basisvectors] score = sum((wk0[k] - wnk[k])2 for k in range(K)) if score < bestscore: bestscore = score bestvolume = volume return bestvolume def pointinpolygon(x, y, polygon): n = len(polygon) inside = False p1x, p1y = polygon[0] for i in range(1, n + 1): p2x, p2y = polygon[i % n] if y > min(p1y, p2y): if y <= max(p1y, p2y): if x <= max(p1x, p2x): if p1y != p2y: xinters = (y - p1y) (p2x - p1x) / (p2y - p1y) + p1x if p1x == p2x or x <= xinters: inside = not inside p1x, p1y = p2x, p2y return inside def dotproduct(v1, v2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def computedistancetransform(binarymask, size): # Standard Euclidean distance transform dist = [[float('inf')] size for in range(size)] for y in range(size): for x in range(size): if binarymask[y][x] == 1: dist[y][x] = 0.0 for y in range(size): for x in range(size): if dist[y][x] == 0.0: continue mind = float('inf') for dy in range(-size, size + 1): for dx in range(-size, size + 1): ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < size and 0 <= nx < size: d = (dx2 + dy2)0.5 if d < mind: mind = d dist[y][x] = mind return dist Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Insufficient Database Size: If the database size is insufficient to cover the shape space, generated clouds may not perfectly match the user's sketch. Precision: The approximation using SVD basis vectors introduces error. The exact similarity score is |x0 - xn|^2, while the approximate score is \sum{k=1}^{K} (w{k0} - w{nk})^2. The error depends on K. Time Complexity: The similarity calculation cost using SVD is proportional to K, whereas direct voxel comparison is proportional to M. With K = M/114, the computational cost is reduced by a factor of 114. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the database volumes and the pre-computed SVD basis vectors. Measured Performance: In experiments, the method was used to retrieve clouds from databases of size 137 (from a 96 \times 96 \times 128 simulation grid) and 83 (from a 256 \times 128 \times 128 simulation grid). Strengths: Efficient retrieval due to dimensionality reduction via SVD. Limitations: Relies on the diversity and size of the pre-simulated database. May not perfectly match user sketches if the database is small. The method was proposed by as part of a sketch-based system for cloud volume retrieval from a simulated dataset for realistic image synthesis. It builds on the idea that cumulus/cumulonimbus clouds have characteristic features: a flat bottom on a plane at a certain height, and vertical thickness larger around the center than the boundary. The system was used in Autodesk Maya 2016 for rendering final images. The database was constructed by simulating dynamic cumulus clouds using computational fluid dynamics. A sketch-based system for cloud volume retrieval from simulated dataset for realistic image synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1145/2817675.2817690, fetched 2026-11-05
