name: Baked Cloud Density and AO Sampling
head: 3D Worley cell volume rendering, Baked Density and AO Sampling, Direct 3D Weather Volume Rendering with Analytical SDF, Direct 3D weather volume model, Minimal Cloud Density Function Optimization, calculateCloudDensityMinimal
body: This method replaces procedural noise evaluation with precomputed 3D volume textures containing analytical cloud density and Signed Distance Fields (SDF) derived from tileable 3D Worley cells. It solves the performance bottleneck of real-time procedural cloud rendering by baking physical density and local Ambient Occlusion (AO) into a 3D texture, allowing raymarchers to sample data directly. Unlike its siblings Cumulus Cloud Rendering Configuration, IsimCloudTexture density evaluation, Procedural Gas Modeling via Turbulence, Cloud Density Sampling, Physical Cloud Model (Cumulus Convection), and Finite Layer Cloud Shape Generation that rely on procedural noise or 2D heightmaps, this approach uses horizontal tiling and full advection support for efficient space skipping. The method consists of two phases: Baking (precomputation) and Raymarching (runtime sampling). Inputs: Weather map coordinates, world scale (props.worldScale), cellular frequency (freq = 4.0), horizontal tile count (uCloudVolumeTiles = 4.0). Outputs: A 3D volume texture where: Alpha channel (A) stores analytical physical density. Blue channel (B) stores the 3D SDF. During the shadow bake pass, the B channel also stores shadow transmittance and AO. 3D Volume Texture: Stores density and SDF. Properties (props): Contains worldScale. uCloudVolumeTiles = 4.0: Governs 3D horizontal texture coordinate wrapping. freq = 4.0: Cellular frequency used for SDF scaling. SDF Multiplier = 0.4: Conservative multiplier applied to d3d in sphere tracing step size computation. Max Step Cap = 2000.0 props.worldScale: Maximum skip step size per iteration. The baking process evaluates analytical functions and writes them to the 3D texture. 1. Evaluate Analytical Cloud 3D: Call getAnalyticalCloud3D at each voxel position. This function evaluates tileable 3D Worley cells, 3D SDF, and physical density with vertical layer boundaries. 2. Scale SDF: Inside getAnalyticalCloud3D, divide the cellular SDF value (cellsdf) by the cellular frequency (freq = 4.0) to match meters correctly. SDF{scaled} = \frac{cell\sdf}{4.0} 3. Write to Texture: In cloud3dvolumebake.comp: Write the analytical density to the texture's Alpha channel. Write the 3D SDF to the texture's Blue channel. During rendering, the raymarcher queries the precomputed 3D texture. 1. Query SDF: Call getCloud3DSDF to query the precomputed 3D texture SDF with internal advection support. Continuity: Do not apply a distY > 100.0 props.worldScale threshold check. This ensures a mathematically continuous distance field across the entire domain. 2. Compute Step Size: Calculate the sphere tracing step size using the queried SDF (d3d): step = \max(baseStepSize, 0.4 \times d3d) Apply a cap: step = min(step, 2000.0 props.worldScale). 3. Advance Ray: If outside the cloud mass (d3d > 0.0), advance the ray by step. This skips directly to the exact boundary of the cloud mass. If inside the cloud mass, use baseStepSize for standard volumetric stepping. 4. Sample Density: Read the precomputed physical density and local AO directly from the 3D volume texture (Alpha channel). Bypass old multi-octave 2D-based heightmap evaluation in calculateCloudDensity and calculateCloudDensityMinimal. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bakecloudvolume(texture, props): """ Bakes analytical density and SDF into a 3D texture. texture: 3D image buffer (RGBA) props: object containing worldScale """ freq = 4.0 uCloudVolumeTiles = 4.0 for x, y, z in texture.dimensions(): # 1. Evaluate analytical cloud properties density, cellsdf = getanalyticalcloud3d(x, y, z, props, freq, uCloudVolumeTiles) # 2. Scale SDF to match meters sdfscaled = cellsdf / freq # 3. Write to texture # Alpha channel: Density texture[x, y, z].a = density # Blue channel: SDF texture[x, y, z].b = sdfscaled def getanalyticalcloud3d(x, y, z, props, freq, uCloudVolumeTiles): """ Evaluates tileable 3D Worley cells, SDF, and physical density. Returns (density, cellsdf) """ # Evaluate tileable 3D Worley cells, 3D SDF, and physical density with vertical layer boundaries # Sources do not provide the internal Worley noise implementation return 0.0, 0.0 def raymarchcloud(rayorigin, raydirection, texture, props, baseStepSize=0.5, MAXDISTANCE=10000.0, THRESHOLD=0.001): """ Raymarches through the baked cloud volume using SDF space skipping. """ maxStepCap = 2000.0 props.worldScale sdfmultiplier = 0.4 t = 0.0 color = vec3(0.0) transmittance = 1.0 while t < MAXDISTANCE and transmittance > 0.01: # 1. Query SDF from texture (with advection) pos = rayorigin + raydirection t d3d = getcloud3dsdf(pos, texture) # 2. Compute step size # Outside cloud mass (d3d > 0.0): skip using SDF # Inside cloud mass (d3d <= 0.0): use fixed base step if d3d > 0.0: step = max(baseStepSize, sdfmultiplier d3d) else: step = baseStepSize step = min(step, maxStepCap) # 3. Advance ray t += step # 4. Sample density and AO pos = rayorigin + raydirection t density = texture[pos].a ao = texture[pos].b # Accumulate color/transmittance based on density and AO # Sources do not specify the exact accumulation formula alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density step) color += alpha transmittance vec3(1.0) # Simplified color contribution transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if density < THRESHOLD: break return color def getcloud3dsdf(pos, texture): """ Queries the precomputed 3D texture SDF. No distY > 100.0 worldScale check is performed. """ return texture[pos].b Visual Distortion: Caused by missing steps during camera movement. Resolved by succinct stepping that skips directly to the exact boundary of the cloud mass using max(baseStepSize, d3d). Viewpoint-dependent Banding: Caused by non-continuous SDF domains or overshooting boundaries due to noise domain warping and non-linear height gradients. Eliminated by: 1. Removing the distY > 100.0 props.worldScale threshold check in getCloud3DSDF. 2. Using a conservative 0.4 multiplier on d3d and a 2000.0 props.worldScale cap on step size. SDF Scaling: Incorrect meter matching if cellsdf is not divided by freq = 4.0. Performance: Massive performance gains compared to procedural evaluation because it samples precomputed data instead of evaluating noise and density. Memory: Requires storage for a 3D volume texture containing density and SDF. Strengths: Efficient space skipping, continuous SDF domain, elimination of viewpoint-dependent banding. Limitations: Requires baking phase; less flexible than procedural methods for dynamic changes not covered by advection. This method was introduced in a pull request by ricecake (via Jules) in July 2026, transitioning the volumetric cloud rendering system from a 2D weather/SDF-based model to a direct 3D weather volume model. It was further enhanced to include precomputed density, 3D AO, and shadow transmittance. It is used in the boidsish project. name: Atmospheric Height Gradient
head: Cloud Type Vertical Profile, GetDensityHeightGradientForPoint, GetGradientHeightFactor, Height Density Gradient, Vertical Density Profile Gradient
body: The Atmospheric Height Gradient method defines the vertical density profile for volumetric cloud layers based on cloud type (Stratus, Cumulus, Cumulonimbus, Cirrus), creating bell-shaped or plateau-shaped density distributions relative to atmosphere thickness. Inputs: altitude: Vertical position of the evaluation point in kilometers. cloudtype: Identifier for the cloud layer type (integer 0–2 or string literal). layerbounds: bottomAltitudeKm and topAltitudeKm for the specific cloud type. cloudtypeparams: Shape parameters timewidthup, starttimeup, and starttimedown. Outputs: densitygradient: Scalar vertical shape factor (typically 0.0 to 1.2). Data Structures: The method uses a preset structure CloudAltitudeLayer with fields bottomAltitudeKm (number), topAltitudeKm (number), coverage (number), densityMultiplier (number), and precipitationFactor (number). Parameters: Presets define base altitude bounds and shape parameters per cloud type: | Cloud Type | Bottom (km) | Top (km) | timewidthup | starttimeup | starttimedown | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | Stratus | 1.0 | 2.2 | 0.08 | 0.08 | 0.2 | | Cumulus | 1.5 | 4.5 | 0.14 | 0.1 | 0.5 | | Cumulonimbus | 1.2 | 9.0 | 0.2 | 0.10 | 0.7 | | Cirrus | 7.0 | 10.5 | Not given in the sources. | Not given in the sources. | Not given in the sources. | Steps: 1. Boundary Check: If altitude < bottomAltitudeKm or altitude > topAltitudeKm, return 0.0. 2. Normalized Height: Calculate height fraction h = (\text{altitude} - \text{bottomAltitudeKm}) / (\text{topAltitudeKm} - \text{bottomAltitudeKm}). 3. Cloud Type Selection: Determine gradient logic based on cloudtype. In one implementation, cloudtype is derived from weatherdata.z where z < 0.1 yields 0 (Stratus), z > 0.9 yields 2 (Cumulonimbus), otherwise 1 (Cumulus). 4. Gradient Calculation: Compute the density gradient using the selected type-specific formula. Formulas: Two distinct implementations exist in the sources. Implementation A (Sine-based with linear ramps): If altitude < starttimeup, densitygradient = 0.0. If starttimeup <= altitude < starttimeup + timewidthup: \text{factor} = \frac{2.0 \cdot \pi}{2.0 \cdot \text{timewidthup}} \text{density\gradient} = 0.5 \cdot \sin(\text{factor} \cdot \text{altitude} - \frac{\pi}{2.0} - \text{factor} \cdot \text{starttimeup}) + 0.5 If starttimeup + timewidthup <= altitude < starttimedown, densitygradient = 1.0. If starttimedown <= altitude < starttimedown + timewidthup: \text{factor} = \frac{2.0 \cdot \pi}{2.0 \cdot \text{timewidthup}} \text{density\gradient} = 0.5 \cdot \sin(\text{factor} \cdot \text{altitude} - \frac{\pi}{2.0} - \text{factor} \cdot (\text{starttimedown} + \text{timewidthup})) + 0.5 If altitude >= starttimedown + timewidthup, densitygradient = 0.0. Implementation B (Normalized Height Fraction): Stratus: \text{density\gradient} = \sin(h \cdot \pi) \cdot 0.9. Cumulus: \text{density\gradient} = \sin(h^{0.7} \cdot \pi). Cumulonimbus: If h > 0.8, return 1.2; else return 0.6 + 0.4 \cdot \sin(h \cdot \pi). Cirrus: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: The following implements Implementation B, which is self-contained and uses normalized height fraction: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeverticalprofile(altitudekm: float, cloudtype: str) -> float: """Computes the vertical density gradient for a given cloud type and altitude.""" presets = { 'stratus': {'bottom': 1.0, 'top': 2.2}, 'cumulus': {'bottom': 1.5, 'top': 4.5}, 'cumulonimbus': {'bottom': 1.2, 'top': 9.0}, 'cirrus': {'bottom': 7.0, 'top': 10.5} } if cloudtype not in presets: return 0.0 layer = presets[cloudtype] bottom = layer['bottom'] top = layer['top'] if altitudekm < bottom or altitudekm > top: return 0.0 heightfraction = (altitudekm - bottom) / (top - bottom) if cloudtype == 'stratus': return math.sin(heightfraction math.pi) 0.9 elif cloudtype == 'cumulus': return math.sin(math.pow(heightfraction, 0.7) math.pi) elif cloudtype == 'cumulonimbus': if heightfraction > 0.8: return 1.2 else: return 0.6 + 0.4 math.sin(heightfraction math.pi) elif cloudtype == 'cirrus': # Specific formula not provided in the source code snippet return 0.0 else: return 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When altitude is very close to bottom or top, floating-point errors might cause the normalized height to be slightly outside [0, 1]. The boundary check in Step 1 handles this by returning 0.0. Degenerate Input: If bottom equals top, division by zero occurs in the normalized height calculation. Creates a 3D envelope for layer clouds that does not touch boundaries, using independent low-frequency random height fields for top and bottom surfaces to prevent coherent tilting, and local thickness variation for natural dilution. Steps: 1. Get profile parameters: centerz, halfheight, topwobble, bottomwobble, thicknessvariation,, = layershapeprofile(typeid). 2. Calculate local half-height with thickness noise: localhalfheight = halfheight (0.84 + thicknessvariation thicknessnoise). 3. Calculate top surface: top = centerz + localhalfheight + (topsurfacenoise - 0.5) topwobble 2.0. 4. Calculate bottom surface: bottom = centerz - localhalfheight + (bottomsurfacenoise - 0.5) bottomwobble 2.0. 5. Calculate feather width: feather = np.clip(localhalfheight 0.24, 0.045, 0.16). 6. Calculate rise and fall using smoothstep: rise = smoothstep((z - bottom) / feather), fall = 1.0 - smoothstep((z - top) / feather). 7. Return clipped product: return np.clip(rise fall, 0.0, 1.0). Pitfall: Thickness noise amplitude is limited to ensure the top surface remains above the bottom surface everywhere. Time Complexity: O(1) per point evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) for preset lookup. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Analytically defined, allows easy variation of cloud types via parameters. Limitations: Does not account for horizontal variations or noise; vertical profile is static beyond cloud type selection. When to use: When rendering volumetric clouds with distinct vertical structures for different cloud types. When not to use: When horizontal variation or dynamic weather changes are required within a single cloud layer. The Atmospheric Height Gradient method originates from implementations of realtime volumetric cloud rendering, specifically in the context of procedural cloud parameterization. It is used to define the vertical density falloff for different cloud types, ensuring realistic vertical structures such as flat Stratus, fluffy Cumulus, and towering Cumulonimbus. The method is found in open-source projects such as erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes and nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl. erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, https://github.com/erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, https://github.com/nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, https://github.com/mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Cloud Configuration Parameters
head: CloudConfig
body: Cloud Configuration Parameters provide a structured set of inputs to control density generation, spatial bounds, lighting interaction, and rendering quality for procedural volumetric clouds. This method acts as the central data hub, passing configuration to Volumetric Cloud Raymarching for integration and Procedural Volume Cloud Modeling for noise generation. Inputs consist of physical constants, scene geometry bounds, and rendering quality flags. Outputs are validated configuration structures passed to the rendering pipeline or volume generation algorithm. Scheme A: Shader Uniforms (CloudConfig) Defined in, this structure maps directly to GPU uniforms. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. pub struct CloudConfig { pub cloudtype: f32, // 0=stratus, 0.5=stratocumulus, 1=cumulus pub coveragemultiplier: f32, pub winddirection: [f32; 3], pub windspeed: f32, pub cloudcolor: [f32; 3], pub innersphereradius: f32, pub outersphereradius: f32, pub sphereyoffset: f32, pub maxrenderdistance: f32, pub cloudtopoffset: f32, pub weathertexturescale: f32, pub basenoisescale: f32, pub highfrequencynoisescale: f32, pub highfrequencynoiseuvscale: f32, pub highfrequencynoisehscale: f32, pub quality: CloudQuality, // Low / Medium / High } Scheme B: Volume Generation Dataclass Defined in, this frozen dataclass controls the deterministic generation of volume masks. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. @dataclass(frozen=True) class VolumeParameters: cloudtypeid: int = 9 resolution: int = 128 seed: int = 42 shapestrength: float = 1.0 detailstrength: float = 0.55 disturbancestrength: float = 0.65 cartoonstyle: bool = False allowboundaryoverlap: Optional[bool] = None 1. Initialize Parameters: Load default values or user overrides into the respective structure. 2. Validate Constraints (Scheme B): Verify resolution is exactly 64, 128, or 256. Verify shapestrength, detailstrength, and disturbancestrength are within [0.0, 2.0]. If allowboundaryoverlap is None, assign the default value from the cloud type catalog. 3. Configure Spatial Bounds: Define spherical bounds using innersphereradius, outersphereradius, and sphereyoffset. Set the volume box height using a multiplier relative to the weather height layer, with a standard multiplier of 4.0. 4. Set Lighting and Scattering: Apply cloudcolor as the base albedo. Configure wind advection using winddirection and windspeed. 5. Configure Noise: Apply weathertexturescale to the base weather map. Modulate procedural noise using basenoisescale, highfrequencynoisescale, highfrequencynoiseuvscale, and highfrequencynoisehscale. 6. Select Quality: Set quality to Low, Medium, or High, which determines internal resolution and step counts. Cloud Type Interpolation: C{type} \in [0.0, 1.0], where 0.0 is Stratus, 0.5 is Stratocumulus, and 1.0 is Cumulus. Volume Box Height: The volume box height uses a multiplier relative to the weather height layer, with a standard multiplier of 4.0. cloudtype: Float, [0.0, 1.0]. Not given in the sources. coveragemultiplier: Float. Not given in the sources. winddirection: Vector3. Not given in the sources. windspeed: Float. Not given in the sources. cloudcolor: Vector3. Not given in the sources. innersphereradius: Float. Not given in the sources. outersphereradius: Float. Not given in the sources. sphereyoffset: Float. Not given in the sources. maxrenderdistance: Float. Not given in the sources. cloudtopoffset: Float. Not given in the sources. weathertexturescale: Float. Not given in the sources. basenoisescale: Float. Not given in the sources. highfrequencynoisescale: Float. Not given in the sources. highfrequencynoiseuvscale: Float. Not given in the sources. highfrequencynoisehscale: Float. Not given in the sources. quality: Enum {Low, Medium, High}. Not given in the sources. resolution: Int. Default 128. seed: Int. Default 42. shapestrength: Float. Default 1.0. detailstrength: Float. Default 0.55. disturbancestrength: Float. Default 0.65. cartoonstyle: Bool. Default False. allowboundaryoverlap: Bool/None. Default None. Invalid Resolution: If resolution is not 64, 128, or 256, the volume generation fails. Strength Bounds: Strength parameters outside [0.0, 2.0] are invalid. Boundary Overlap: If allowboundaryoverlap is not explicitly set, the system falls back to the cloud type's default behavior. A strict validation step for Scheme B parameters. It ensures resolution is in \{64, 128, 256\} and strength parameters are in [0.0, 2.0]. It also handles the defaulting of allowboundaryoverlap if left undefined. Time Complexity: Parameter validation runs in O(1) time. The computational cost lies in downstream Volumetric Cloud Raymarching and noise generation, which scale with maxrenderdistance and quality settings. Memory Complexity: Memory complexity is O(1) for the configuration structure itself, while actual volume data memory depends on resolution (Scheme B) or texture size (Scheme A). Strengths: Centralized control over cloud physics and visuals, and decoupling parameter definition from rendering logic. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of noise scales and wind vectors, and Scheme B has rigid resolution choices. When to use: Use this method when implementing a procedural cloud system requiring configurable density, shape, and lighting behavior. The concept originates from real-time volumetric cloud rendering techniques, specifically those ported to Rust/wgpu engines like AetherEngine. The validation scheme derives from procedural noise cloud generation libraries like Noise-Cloud. The parameters bridge high-level artistic controls and low-level rendering requirements. name: Procedural Cloud Modeling via Level Set and FBM
head: Analytical Cloud Structure Method, Pyroclastic Noise-based Cloud Modeling
body: This method provides an analytical form for calculating cloud density at any point in space, enabling the procedural generation of various cloud types (e.g., cumulus, stratus) and cloud layers for flight simulators without relying on particle systems or voxelization. It distinguishes itself by using a level set boundary defined by a hollow spherical primitive, deformed by a virtual space point displaced via Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM), allowing for real-time controllability and variability of cloud geometry and density. It builds on Weather & Cloud Parameterization for global physical and visual parameters. Inputs: Point in space x \in \mathbb{R}^3. Cloud layer parameters: A: Height of the cloud layer above sea level. T: Thickness of the cloud layer. C: Coverage degree (sparsity) of the cloud layer. P: Spatial template characterizing the average spatial size of a cloud (high-frequency for cumulus/wavy). \rho0: Base density, determining cloud color and overall contour clarity. F: Flattening of the base, observed primarily in cumulus clouds. H: Height amplitude, determining the sharpness of height differences in the cloud layer and responsible for gaps in the layer. Turbulence parameters: O: Number of octaves. L: Lacunarity. G: Gain. Level set bounds: R{inner} and R{outer} defining the hollow spherical primitive. Outputs: Density \rho(x) at point x. If \rho(x) \le 0, the cloud is considered non-existent at that point. Data Structures: The method is stateless and analytical; no persistent data structures are required for the density calculation itself. Parameters are passed as uniforms or structure members. Steps: 1. Define Level Set Bounds: Establish the radial bounds [R{inner}, R{outer}] for the hollow spherical primitive. The density is non-zero only if the point's distance from the center lies within these bounds. 2. Calculate FBM Turbulence: Compute the Fractal Brownian Motion value fbm at position x using Perlin noise N(x): fbm = N(x) \cdot G^O where N(x) is the Perlin noise function. Note: The source formula is presented as fbm = N(x) G^O, implying standard FBM structure using Perlin noise, gain G, and octaves O. 3. Define Virtual Space Point: Displace the position x by the turbulence scaled by height amplitude H to create a virtual space point p(x): p(x) = x + fbm \cdot H 4. Define Axial Surface: Construct a sphere with a radius equal to the intermediate value of the bounding radii to define the "axial" surface c(x). The source text provides a garbled formula: c(x): = +. | |. Conceptually, this represents the mean radius surface. Let R{mid} = \frac{R{inner} + R{outer}}{2}. The axial surface is defined by the distance from the origin to this mean radius, modulated by flattening F if necessary to adjust the level set boundary relative to the limits. Implementation Note: The exact formula for c(x) is not clearly recoverable from the garbled text = +. | |. However, it serves as the reference surface for distance calculation. For implementation, c(x) is typically the magnitude |x| adjusted by F. We assume c(x) = |x| \cdot (1 - F) or similar, but strictly following the source, it is the "axial surface" defined by the intermediate radius. Let us define the distance to the axial surface as d{axial}(x) = | |x| - R{mid} |. The parameter F modifies this level. 5. Calculate Distance to Axial Surface: Determine the distance d(x) from the point x to the axial surface using the virtual point p(x): d(x) = | p(x) - c(x) | Correction based on source: The source states: "define distance d(x) from point x to 'axial' surface: d(x) = | p(x) - c(x) |". This implies c(x) is a vector or point, but earlier it says "axial surface c(x)". In level set methods, c(x) is often the signed distance function or the implicit surface equation. Given p(x) is a point, c(x) must be a point on the surface closest to p(x), or c(x) is the center. The source text |! − suggests | p(x) - \text{center} |. Let us assume c(x) refers to the center of the sphere (origin) or the radial projection. The most consistent interpretation of "distance from x to axial surface" via virtual point p(x) is: d(x) = | |p(x)| - R{mid} | However, the source explicitly writes d(x) = | p(x) - c(x) |. If c(x) is the axial surface, it is a scalar field in level set terms. Let us stick to the literal variable names: d(x) is the distance derived from p(x) and the axial surface definition. 6. Calculate Deviation: Compute the deviation D(x) of the level set boundary: D(x) = d(x) \cdot (1 + fbm \cdot L + G) The source formula is garbled: D(x) = '()1 + & " +,. Contextually, it links deviation to distance d(x), FBM, lacunarity L, and gain G. 7. Calculate Final Density: Compute the density \rho(x): \rho(x) = \rho0 \cdot D(x) - d(x) This is calculated only when d(x) is within the level set bounds (0, +), meaning the point is within the hollow sphere. This creates spatial inhomogeneity in density. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateclouddensity(x, params): """ Calculate cloud density at point x using the Analytical Cloud Structure Method. Args: x: vec3, position in space. params: dict containing: Rinner: float, inner radius of hollow sphere. Router: float, outer radius of hollow sphere. rho0: float, base density. F: float, flattening of the base. H: float, height amplitude. O: int, number of octaves. L: float, lacunarity. G: float, gain. C: float, coverage degree (used to adjust bounds or threshold). Returns: float, density rho(x). """ # 1. Define Level Set Bounds Rmid = (params['Rinner'] + params['Router']) / 2.0 # Check if point is within the hollow sphere bounds (simplified check) distorigin = length(x) if distorigin < params['Rinner'] or distorigin > params['Router']: return 0.0 # 2. Calculate FBM Turbulence # N(x) is Perlin noise noiseval = perlinnoise(x) fbm = noiseval (params['G'] params['O']) # 3. Define Virtual Space Point # p(x) = x + fbm H # Note: H is a scalar amplitude. fbm is scalar. px = x + (fbm params['H']) # 4 & 5. Distance to Axial Surface # The source defines d(x) = | p(x) - c(x) | where c(x) is the axial surface. # Conceptually, c(x) is the radial projection onto the mean radius sphere. # c(x) = (px / |px|) Rmid (if px is not zero) # Then d(x) = | px - c(x) | pxlen = length(px) if pxlen == 0: dx = Rmid # Distance from center to surface else: # Project px onto the sphere of radius Rmid cx = normalize(px) Rmid dx = length(px - cx) # Apply flattening F to the axial surface definition? # Source: "Changing parameter flattening F, it is possible to change the level of 'axial' surface" # This might modify Rmid or the distance calculation. # Assuming F modifies the effective radius or distance scaling. # Without explicit formula, we apply F as a modifier to the distance or radius. # Let's assume F scales the deviation impact. # 6. Calculate Deviation D(x) # D(x) = d(x) (1 + fbm L + G) Dx = dx (1.0 + fbm params['L'] + params['G']) # 7. Calculate Final Density # rho(x) = rho0 D(x) - d(x) rho = params['rho0'] Dx - dx # Ensure density is non-negative if required by renderer, # though source says rho <= 0 means non-existent. return rho Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-Resolution Maps: High-resolution density maps may be excessive. To add high-precision structural details during visualization, a fractal transformation is applied at render time rather than pre-computing. Garbled Formulas: The source text contains garbled formulas for c(x) and D(x). The implementation above uses the most logical geometric interpretation of "distance to axial surface" and "deviation" based on the surrounding text. Bounds: Density is strictly zero outside [R{inner}, R{outer}]. Time Complexity: O(1) per point evaluation, dominated by the Perlin noise calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1), as no voxel grid or texture maps are required for the core density function. Performance: Suitable for real-time rendering in flight simulators. Strengths: Controllability, variability, and plausibility without particle systems or voxelization. Allows simulation of complex weather conditions with a simple set of parameters. Limitations: Relies on analytical approximations; may lack the fine-grained detail of high-resolution voxel maps without post-processing fractal transformations. Origin: Proposed by V.V. Podlesny in 2013. Paper: "A method for procedural modeling of clouds of various types for a flight simulator". History: Developed for virtual reality systems of flight simulators to provide instructors with a tool for simulating various cloud types and layers. Usage: Applied in aviation training simulators for real-time cloud rendering. A method for procedural modeling of clouds of various types for a flight simulator, https://doi.org/10.15622/sp.28.11, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Cloud Mesh Generation
body: Cloud Mesh Generation constructs a planar mesh from a procedural voxel grid by identifying contiguous regions of cloud data. It differs from Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation by outputting explicit geometry rather than shader-based volume textures, and from Chunk Generation with Base Terrain by targeting horizontal atmospheric layers. Inputs: WORLDAREA: The total spatial extent of the cloud field in world units. CHUNKSIZE: The resolution of the voxel grid per chunk. CLOUDHEIGHT: The fixed Y-coordinate for cloud rendering. worldvoxels: A 3D boolean or integer array representing the world state. Outputs: A list of vertex positions and an index buffer representing the generated cloud mesh. Data Structures: clouddata: A 1D array of size WORLDAREA CHUNKSIZE 2 storing binary cloud presence (1 for cloud, 0 for void). visited: A boolean array of the same size tracking processed cells to prevent duplicate mesh generation. Steps: 1. Voxelization: Initialize clouddata. Iterate x and z over world dimensions. If noise2(0.13 x, 0.13 z) < 0.2, skip. Otherwise, set clouddata[idx] = 1. 2. Mesh Construction: Iterate z and x. If clouddata[idx] is 0 or idx in visited, skip. 3. X-Strip Detection: Find continuous quads along X: increment xcount while clouddata is 1 and not visited. 4. Z-Strip Detection: Find continuous quads along Z for each X in the strip: store zcount in zcountlist. 5. Primitive Generation: Generate geometric primitives (quads or triangles) covering the identified rectangular regions at CLOUDHEIGHT. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatecloudmesh(worldarea, chunksize, cloudheight): griddim = worldarea chunksize totalcells = worldarea chunksize chunksize clouddata = [0] totalcells visited = [False] totalcells vertices = [] indices = [] # 1. Voxelization for x in range(griddim): for z in range(griddim): idx = x griddim + z if noise2(0.13 x, 0.13 z) < 0.2: continue clouddata[idx] = 1 # 2. Mesh Construction for z in range(griddim): for x in range(griddim): idx = x griddim + z if clouddata[idx] == 0 or visited[idx]: continue visited[idx] = True xcount = 0 currx = x while currx < griddim and clouddata[currx griddim + z] == 1 and not visited[currx griddim + z]: visited[currx griddim + z] = True xcount += 1 currx += 1 zcountlist = [] for dx in range(xcount): currz = z zcount = 0 while currz < griddim and clouddata[(x + dx) griddim + currz] == 1 and not visited[(x + dx) griddim + currz]: visited[(x + dx) griddim + currz] = True zcount += 1 currz += 1 zcountlist.append(zcount) # Generate quads for the detected strip for dx in range(xcount): zcount = zcountlist[dx] x1, x2 = x + dx, x + dx + 1 z1, z2 = z, z + zcount v0 = [x1, cloudheight, z1] v1 = [x2, cloudheight, z1] v2 = [x2, cloudheight, z2] v3 = [x1, cloudheight, z2] vertices.extend([v0, v1, v2, v3]) indices.extend([len(vertices)-4, len(vertices)-3, len(vertices)-2]) indices.extend([len(vertices)-4, len(vertices)-2, len(vertices)-1]) return vertices, indices def noise2(x, y): # Simple deterministic hash for procedural noise return (x 12.9898 + y 78.233) % 1.0 Parameters: Noise scale: 0.13. Density threshold: 0.2. Cloud Height: Fixed Y-coordinate. Edge Cases: Precision: Noise function evaluation must be deterministic across voxelization and rendering passes. Boundaries: Loop conditions must clamp to griddim to prevent out-of-bounds array access during strip detection. A technique to 'inflate' a mesh from a point cloud by applying a scalar to the inside/outside values. A pipeline for generating high-quality artifact-free volumetric and surface meshes from random noise or a reference image without postprocessing. It uses a two-level hybrid approach: a diffusion model for global shape synthesis on voxels, and a neural network plus optimization for mesh deformation and quality control. The pipeline consists of three modules: (1) Voxel generation with diffusion models to get an initial synthesis result; (2) Voxel division to convert the voxel representation into a tetrahedral mesh template; (3) Physically correct mesh deformation using a voxel-conditional neural closest point predictor and regularized projection to add details and ensure quality. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) where W, H are grid dimensions, due to single-pass voxelization and linear strip traversal. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the clouddata and visited arrays. Strengths: Reduces overdraw compared to ray-marching; allows standard rasterization pipelines and GPU instancing. Originating from procedural generation techniques in voxel-based games, this method adapts chunk-based terrain meshing for atmospheric effects. The reference implementation uses a noise-based threshold to determine cloud presence, mapping 2D noise to a planar mesh. name: Ellipsoid Fitting and Rotation for Cloud Meshes
head: Cloud Generation from 3D Meshes, Mesh Decimation and Ellipsoid Smoothing, Mesh-to-Ellipsoid conversion, Rodrigues' Rotation Formula for Cloud Geometry, Triangle-based ellipsoid cloud generation
body: This method converts high-resolution 3D meshes (e.g., from Blender or Maya) into volumetric cloud geometry by replacing triangle faces with fitted ellipsoids. It solves the problem of rendering complex, organic shapes in real-time by decimating the input mesh and approximating its surface with smooth primitives. Unlike raw mesh rendering, this approach acts as a real-time filter that produces softer, cumuliform shapes suitable for smoke and cloud simulation. Inputs: A decimated 3D mesh consisting of N triangles, where each triangle has vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3. Outputs: A set of ellipsoid parameters (center, radii, rotation matrix) for each triangle, ready for GPU rendering. Data Structures: Triangle: Struct containing three 3D vertex coordinates \mathbf{v}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Ellipsoid: Struct containing: Center \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Radii (a, b, c) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Rotation Matrix \mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. Steps: 1. Mesh Decimation: Reduce the input mesh to 300–700 triangles (or \le 1000) to ensure real-time performance. A decimation rate of 80–95% is acceptable. 2. Barycenter Calculation: For each triangle, compute the barycenter \mathbf{B}: \mathbf{B} = \frac{\mathbf{v}1 + \mathbf{v}2 + \mathbf{v}3}{3} \quad \text{(Eq. 22)} 3. Scaling: Scale the triangle vertices relative to the barycenter using a scale factor s. The factor s typically falls in the range (0.1, 2]. The scaled vertices \mathbf{v}'i are calculated as: \mathbf{v}'i = \mathbf{B} + s(\mathbf{v}i - \mathbf{B}) \quad \text{(Eq. 23, 24)} 4. Radii Determination: Calculate the maximum distance from the barycenter to any scaled vertex. This distance defines the maximum radius of the circumscribing ellipsoid. The radii (a, b, c) are derived from this maximum extent. 5. Rotation Optimization: Align the ellipsoid's maximum radius with the direction of the maximum distance from the barycenter to the triangle vertices to produce a softer shape. This uses Rodrigues' Rotation Formula: Axis and Angle: Calculate the rotation axis \mathbf{k} and angle \theta using cross and dot products of the relevant direction vectors: \mathbf{k} = \frac{\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}\|}, \quad \theta = \arccos\left(\frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u}\| \|\mathbf{v}\|}\right) \quad \text{(Eq. 27, 28)} where \mathbf{u} is the ellipsoid's initial principal axis and \mathbf{v} is the vector from the barycenter to the furthest scaled vertex. Skew-Symmetric Matrix: Compute matrix \mathbf{A} corresponding to the axis vector \mathbf{x} (where \mathbf{x} is the normalized rotation axis): \mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -xz & xy \\ xz & 0 & -xx \\ -xy & xx & 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{(Eq. 30)} Rotation Matrix: Calculate \mathbf{R} using the exponential map (Rodrigues' formula): \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I} + (\sin \theta)\mathbf{A} + (1 - \cos \theta)\mathbf{A}^2 \quad \text{(Eq. 29)} 6. GPU Transfer: Pre-calculate formulas (1)–(3) on the CPU. Only the final rotation matrix \mathbf{R} is passed to the GPU for rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vecadd(a, b): return (a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1], a[2] + b[2]) def vecsub(a, b): return (a[0] - b[0], a[1] - b[1], a[2] - b[2]) def vecscale(a, s): return (a[0] s, a[1] s, a[2] s) def vecdot(a, b): return a[0] b[0] + a[1] b[1] + a[2] b[2] def veccross(a, b): return (a[1] b[2] - a[2] b[1], a[2] b[0] - a[0] b[2], a[0] b[1] - a[1] b[0]) def vecnorm(a): return math.sqrt(vecdot(a, a)) def vecnormalize(a): n = vecnorm(a) if n < 1e-9: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return (a[0] / n, a[1] / n, a[2] / n) def computebarycenter(v1, v2, v3): return vecscale(vecadd(vecadd(v1, v2), v3), 1.0 / 3.0) def scaletriangle(v1, v2, v3, barycenter, scalefactor): v1s = vecadd(barycenter, vecscale(vecsub(v1, barycenter), scalefactor)) v2s = vecadd(barycenter, vecscale(vecsub(v2, barycenter), scalefactor)) v3s = vecadd(barycenter, vecscale(vecsub(v3, barycenter), scalefactor)) return v1s, v2s, v3s def getmaxradius(barycenter, v1, v2, v3): d1 = vecnorm(vecsub(v1, barycenter)) d2 = vecnorm(vecsub(v2, barycenter)) d3 = vecnorm(vecsub(v3, barycenter)) return max(d1, d2, d3) def computerotationmatrix(u, v): unorm = vecnormalize(u) vnorm = vecnormalize(v) cross = veccross(unorm, vnorm) dot = vecdot(unorm, vnorm) if vecnorm(cross) < 1e-6: if dot > 0: return ((1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1)) else: # Fallback for 180-degree rotation: use arbitrary orthogonal axis axis = (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) if abs(vecdot(axis, unorm)) > 0.9: axis = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) axis = vecsub(axis, vecscale(unorm, vecdot(axis, unorm))) axis = vecnormalize(axis) cross = axis theta = math.pi else: cross = vecnormalize(cross) theta = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot))) x = cross A = ((0.0, -x[2], x[1]), (x[2], 0.0, -x[0]), (-x[1], x[0], 0.0)) # Matrix multiplication A^2 A2 = ((A[0][0]A[0][0] + A[0][1]A[1][0] + A[0][2]A[2][0], A[0][0]A[0][1] + A[0][1]A[1][1] + A[0][2]A[2][1], A[0][0]A[0][2] + A[0][1]A[1][2] + A[0][2]A[2][2]), (A[1][0]A[0][0] + A[1][1]A[1][0] + A[1][2]A[2][0], A[1][0]A[0][1] + A[1][1]A[1][1] + A[1][2]A[2][1], A[1][0]A[0][2] + A[1][1]A[1][2] + A[1][2]A[2][2]), (A[2][0]A[0][0] + A[2][1]A[1][0] + A[2][2]A[2][0], A[2][0]A[0][1] + A[2][1]A[1][1] + A[2][2]A[2][1], A[2][0]A[0][2] + A[2][1]A[1][2] + A[2][2]A[2][2])) I = ((1,0,0), (0,1,0), (0,0,1)) sint = math.sin(theta) cost = math.cos(theta) R = ((I[0][0] + sint A[0][0] + (1 - cost) A2[0][0], I[0][1] + sint A[0][1] + (1 - cost) A2[0][1], I[0][2] + sint A[0][2] + (1 - cost) A2[0][2]), (I[1][0] + sint A[1][0] + (1 - cost) A2[1][0], I[1][1] + sint A[1][1] + (1 - cost) A2[1][1], I[1][2] + sint A[1][2] + (1 - cost) A2[1][2]), (I[2][0] + sint A[2][0] + (1 - cost) A2[2][0], I[2][1] + sint A[2][1] + (1 - cost) A2[2][1], I[2][2] + sint A[2][2] + (1 - cost) A2[2][2])) return R def fitellipsoidtotriangle(v1, v2, v3, scalefactor=1.0): B = computebarycenter(v1, v2, v3) v1s, v2s, v3s = scaletriangle(v1, v2, v3, B, scalefactor) maxr = getmaxradius(B, v1s, v2s, v3s) # Not given in the sources. The evidence states the max distance is used to calculate radii (a, b, c), # but does not specify how the minor radii are derived from the maximum extent. radii = (maxr, maxr, maxr) dists = [vecnorm(vecsub(v1s, B)), vecnorm(vecsub(v2s, B)), vecnorm(vecsub(v3s, B))] maxidx = dists.index(max(dists)) maxvertex = [v1s, v2s, v3s][maxidx] targetdir = vecsub(maxvertex, B) # Source does not specify the initial principal axis; using a default vector. initialaxis = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) R = computerotationmatrix(initialaxis, targetdir) return {'center': B, 'radii': radii, 'rotationmatrix': R} Parameters: Scale Factor (s): Typically in the range (0.1, 2]. Mesh Resolution: 300–700 triangles after decimation. Up to 1000 triangles is the upper limit for standard GPUs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: Without pre-calculation on the CPU and decimation, performance is hindered on lower-speed GPUs. Precision: The rotation calculation relies on stable cross/dot products; parallel vectors require special handling. Boundary: The method assumes the input mesh is already decimated. Fitting to high-poly meshes directly is not supported. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Significantly improves performance on lower-end GPUs by reducing vertex count and simplifying geometry to ellipsoids. Benchmarks confirm no hindrance on lower-speed hardware. Strengths: Real-time capability; produces soft, organic cloud shapes; leverages standard 3D modeling tools. Limitations: Requires manual or automated decimation; approximation error increases with high decimation rates (>95%) though visual quality remains acceptable. This method was introduced in the context of real-time GPU volumetric cloud rendering, specifically for generating "suggestive cumuliforms". It allows artists to use standard 3D modeling software (Blender, Maya) to create cloud shapes, which are then converted into volumetric primitives for rendering. The technique is part of a broader set of geometry innovations for real-time cloud rendering. Efficient Algorithms for Real-Time GPU Volumetric Cloud Rendering with Enhanced Geometry, https://doi.org/10.3390/sym10040125, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Procedural Cloud Generation
head: Gabor and Gaussian Kernel Cloud Generation
body: Procedural Cloud Generation is a method for synthesizing volumetric cloud assets using a hierarchical structure of "cloud chunks" composed of Gaussian and Gabor kernels. It solves the problem of generating realistic, multi-scale cloud formations (cores, splittings, wispy effects) without relying on regression-based training or manual sculpting. It differs from Ellipsoid Fitting and Rotation for Cloud Meshes by explicitly modeling microstructure and wind-induced wisps via orientation-selective Gabor kernels on chunk surfaces, rather than fitting static geometric primitives. Inputs: Random seed, parameters for kernel distributions (uniform for frequency/orientation, Maxwell for scale/radius), grid resolution for chunk surfaces. Outputs: A hierarchical tree of cloud chunks, where each chunk contains a set of 3D kernels (Gaussian core + Gabor surface kernels) with defined positions, orientations, frequencies, and scales. Data Structures: 1. Cloud Chunk: center: vec3 (position in world space). radius: float (base size, drawn from Maxwell distribution for child chunks). surfacegrid: 2D array or list of cells covering the chunk's surface area. kernels: list of Kernel objects. 2. Kernel: type: enum (GAUSSIAN, GABOR). position: vec3 (3D coordinate). orientation: vec3 or float (angle/direction). frequency: float (spatial frequency). scale: float (width/extent). amplitude: float (optional, default 1.0). 3. Chunk Tree: parent: Cloud Chunk or null. children: list of Cloud Chunk. Steps: 1. Define Base Chunk: Create a root cloud chunk. Model its core using a single Gaussian kernel centered at chunk.center with a base radius. 2. Surface Grid Generation: Define a grid on the surface of the cloud chunk. The grid cells partition the surface area. 3. Generate Gabor Kernels: For each grid cell: a. Select a random position p uniformly within the grid cell on the surface. b. Sample orientation o from a uniform distribution. c. Sample frequency f from a uniform distribution. d. Sample scale s from a Maxwell distribution. e. Create a Gabor kernel at p with parameters o, f, s. f. Add the kernel to the chunk's kernel list. 4. Recursive Chunk Placement (Fractal Layers): a. To generate smaller clouds on the surface of a parent chunk (simulating inner pressure breakthrough): b. Sample a radius rchild for the child chunk from a Maxwell distribution. c. Place the child chunk's center uniformly at random on the surface of the parent chunk. d. Recursively apply Steps 2-3 to the child chunk. 5. Merge Formations (Optional): To create complex merged clouds, generate multiple independent multi-layer cloud trees and translate them together in world space. Formulas: Maxwell Distribution for Scale/Radius: The scale s and child radius r are drawn from a Maxwell distribution. The probability density function is: f(x; \sigma) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{x^2}{\sigma^2} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}} where \sigma is the scale parameter controlling the spread. The specific value of \sigma is not given in the sources. Uniform Distribution for Orientation/Frequency: Orientation \theta and frequency \omega are drawn from U(a, b). The bounds a, b are not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math import numpy as np def maxwellsample(sigma): """Sample from Maxwell distribution with scale parameter sigma.""" # Using Box-Muller or similar to generate normal variables # Maxwell distribution is the distribution of the magnitude of a 3D vector with normal components x = random.gauss(0, sigma) y = random.gauss(0, sigma) z = random.gauss(0, sigma) return math.sqrt(xx + yy + zz) def uniformsample(a, b): return random.uniform(a, b) class Kernel: def init(self, pos, orient, freq, scale, ktype): self.position = pos self.orientation = orient self.frequency = freq self.scale = scale self.type = ktype class CloudChunk: def init(self, center, radius): self.center = center self.radius = radius self.kernels = [] self.children = [] def generatesurfacekernels(self, gridresolution, sigmascale, sigmafreq, sigmaorient): """ Generate Gabor kernels on the surface grid. Note: Exact grid definition and surface parameterization are not specified in sources. We assume a simplified surface sampling for implementation completeness. """ # Simplified: Sample points on a sphere surface numpoints = gridresolution gridresolution for in range(numpoints): # Random point on sphere surface theta = random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) phi = random.acos(2 random.random() - 1) x = self.radius math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta) y = self.radius math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta) z = self.radius math.cos(phi) pos = (self.center[0] + x, self.center[1] + y, self.center[2] + z) # Sample parameters orient = uniformsample(0, 2 math.pi) # Orientation angle freq = uniformsample(sigmafreq[0], sigmafreq[1]) # Frequency scale = maxwellsample(sigmascale) # Scale kernel = Kernel(pos, orient, freq, scale, "GABOR") self.kernels.append(kernel) def addchildchunk(self, sigmaradius): """Add a smaller child chunk on the surface.""" radiuschild = maxwellsample(sigmaradius) # Place uniformly on surface theta = random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) phi = random.acos(2 random.random() - 1) x = self.radius math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta) y = self.radius math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta) z = self.radius math.cos(phi) childcenter = (self.center[0] + x, self.center[1] + y, self.center[2] + z) child = CloudChunk(childcenter, radiuschild) self.children.append(child) return child def generatecloud(depth, sigmaradius, sigmascale, sigmafreq, sigmaorient, gridres): """Generate a hierarchical cloud structure.""" root = CloudChunk((0,0,0), 1.0) # Base radius 1.0 root.generatesurfacekernels(gridres, sigmascale, sigmafreq, sigmaorient) if depth > 0: # Add children to root numchildren = 5 # Not given in sources for in range(numchildren): child = root.addchildchunk(sigmaradius) child.generatesurfacekernels(gridres, sigmascale, sigmafreq, sigmaorient) # Recurse generatecloud(depth - 1, sigmaradius, sigmascale, sigmafreq, sigmaorient, gridres) return root Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Gabor kernels are not orthonormal, which may cause artifacts if not handled carefully during rendering or merging. Boundaries: The exact bounds for the uniform distributions of frequency and orientation are not specified. Degenerate Input: If the grid resolution is too low, the wispy effect may be lost; if too high, computational cost increases significantly. Merging: Merging clouds by translation may cause visual artifacts at the boundary if the underlying density fields are not blended smoothly. An interactive pipeline for generating volumetric clouds using a hierarchical structure of procedural chunks, enabling direct rendering without regression. It differs from the fully procedural method by allowing user interaction to place kernels and guide shapes. Choose this when artistic control is required over the final cloud shape. It uses a base cloud chunk modeled as a textured ellipsoid to capture microstructure. Chunks are organized into a tree to model multi-level formations (e.g., smaller clouds forming on surfaces due to inner pressure). Users place kernels in 3D space interactively using mouse input to achieve desired shapes. A real-time tomography image of the generated cloud supports this process. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Regression-based methods take 0.1-2h on a single RTX 4090. Procedural generation is implied to be faster as it is a forward method. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Captures microstructure and wind-induced wisps; allows for complex multi-layer formations; interactive authoring possible. Limitations: Gabor kernels are not orthonormal, which may complicate certain mathematical operations. The method may require fine-tuning between assets of substantially different classes if regression is used in conjunction. When to use: When realistic, multi-scale cloud formations are needed without the cost of regression training. When not to use: When strict orthonormality is required for mathematical stability. Originated from the paper "Gabor Fields: Orientation-Selective Level-of-Detail for Volume Rendering". Inspired by gradient noise density erosion common in industry [Fajardo and Pharr 2023; Wrenninge et al. 2011] and earlier work on cloud modeling [Bouthors and Neyret [2004]; Dobashi et al. [2000]]. The method uses Gabor noise concepts [Galerne et al. 2012; Lagae et al. 2009] and Maxwell distribution for physical intuition [Wu and McFarquhar 2018]. name: Procedural Density Calculation
head: Density Curve Filter, calculateCloudDensity, calculateCloudDensityMinimal
body: Procedural Density Calculation generates volumetric density fields on-the-fly using mathematical functions and noise modulation rather than relying solely on pre-computed voxel grids. It distinguishes itself from pre-baked approaches by computing density values directly during rendering or generation passes, often integrating shape modulation to preserve detail without storage overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin, ray direction, bounding volume parameters, and procedural parameters (e.g., eccentricity, curvature, noise seeds). Output: Density value \rho and optionally albedo \alpha at a given 3D position \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: 3D Volume Texture: A 3D texture array storing density and albedo per voxel. The layout is defined as: R Channel: Noise value. G Channel: Local Ambient Occlusion (AO). B Channel: Noise-driven height-based baseline albedo. A Channel: Procedural cloud physical density. Cell ID Hash: Used to decode eccentricity and curvature parameters for shape modulation. Steps: 1. Shape Modulation: For a given position \mathbf{p}, compute a base shape function (e.g., ellipsoid profile) driven by eccentricity, curvature exponent, and center distance. 2. Noise Integration: Apply on-the-fly procedural 3D noise to modulate the shape, preserving noise details that might be lost in lower-resolution representations. 3. Density Calculation: Combine the modulated shape and noise to produce the physical density \rho, which is stored in the Alpha channel of the 3D volume texture. 4. Albedo Calculation: Compute the height-based baseline albedo based on noise and store it in the Blue channel. 5. Rendering Consistency: During raymarching, retrieve density and albedo directly from the 3D volume texture in cheap and detailed passes to ensure 100% rendering consistency between generation and rendering. 6. Raymarching Stability: Replace unstable backing-up or bifurcated stepping loops with stable, uniform linear marching between bounding bounds to eliminate spots, missing clouds, noise, and banding. Correct empty space skipping using robust positive-step bifurcated step size logic to eliminate coordinate jumping and infinite loops. 7. Edge Filtering: Apply a density curve between two points (in and out) to add, subtract, multiply, or overwrite volume data, smoothly subtracting false signals at the edge of the data. Formulas: Ellipsoid Profile: S(\mathbf{p}) = \exp\left(-\left(\frac{x^2}{ex^2} + \frac{y^2}{ey^2} + \frac{z^2}{ez^2}\right)^c\right) driven by eccentricity e, curvature exponent c, and center distance d. Density Curve Filter: Creates a curve between two points (in and out) to add, subtract, multiply, or overwrite volume data, smoothing false signals at data edges. Density Storage: \rho(\mathbf{p}) = V{3D}(\mathbf{p}).A. Albedo Storage: \alpha{base}(\mathbf{p}) = V{3D}(\mathbf{p}).B. Parameters: Eccentricity: Decoded from cell ID hash. Curvature Exponent: Decoded from cell ID hash. Step Size & Bounds: Uniform linear marching step size and bounding bounds for raymarching. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Low-resolution raymarching can suffer from coordinate jumping and infinite loops if step size logic is not robust. Artifacts: Unstable stepping loops cause spots, banding, and missing clouds. Consistency: Discrepancies between generation and rendering passes occur if density is not retrieved directly from the same texture used for generation. Preview Limitation: The density curve filter works only in preview; filtered data must be exported to new.df3 files for PovRay rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateclouddensity(p, cellidhash, noiseseed): """Calculate procedural cloud density at position p.""" # Decode shape parameters from hash eccentricity = (cellidhash % 100) / 100.0 + 0.5 curvature = (cellidhash % 50) / 50.0 + 1.0 # Compute base shape (ellipsoid profile) dx, dy, dz = p.x, p.y, p.z baseshape = ((dx/eccentricity)2 + (dy/eccentricity)2 + (dz/eccentricity)2) curvature baseshape = max(0.0, 1.0 - baseshape) # Apply procedural 3D noise # Note: Exact noise function not provided in sources noiseval = (hash(p.x 12.9898 + p.y 78.233 + p.z 45.164) % 1000) / 1000.0 2.0 - 1.0 # Modulate shape with noise density = baseshape (1.0 + noiseval 0.5) return max(0.0, min(1.0, density)) def calculatealbedo(p, noiseseed): """Calculate height-based baseline albedo.""" # Height-based baseline albedo logic # Note: Exact formula not provided in sources heightfactor = max(0.0, min(1.0, p.y / 10.0)) noiseval = (hash(p.x 12.9898 + p.y 78.233 + p.z 45.164) % 1000) / 1000.0 return vec3(0.8, 0.85, 0.9) (1.0 - heightfactor 0.5) + noiseval 0.1 def raymarchclouds(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, stepsize, maxdistance): """Stable linear raymarching through cloud volume.""" t = 0.0 densityaccum = 0.0 coloraccum = vec3(0.0) # Uniform linear marching between bounding bounds while t < maxdistance: p = rayorigin + raydirection t # Retrieve density and albedo directly from 3D volume texture density = volumetexture.sample(p).A albedo = volumetexture.sample(p).B # Accumulate density and color # Note: Density is stored per-voxel; stepsize is used only for traversal, not accumulation scaling densityaccum += density coloraccum += albedo density t += stepsize return coloraccum, densityaccum Simulates a dense flat atmospheric volume by blending voxel colors with a height fog color based on a submersion factor and a visibility curve. It is chosen when a uniform, height-dependent atmospheric effect is needed rather than complex cloud structures. See Height Fog. Applies constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations to volume data, procedurally adding and subtracting thousands of spheres from an empty voxel volume using Boolean operations to create complex landscapes. Sphere size and position are random values within a user-defined range. It is used for generating test terrains or complex geometric volumes. See Procedural Volume Data Creation. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples along the ray, as density is computed on-the-fly. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the volume texture size, required for caching and retrieval consistency. Performance: On-the-fly calculation preserves noise details but requires significant computational power per sample. Limitations: Computationally expensive per sample; potential for artifacts if raymarching steps are not stable. The method originates from implementations in cloud rendering optimization, specifically within the boidsish project, which focuses on eroded Voronoi weather maps and stable linear raymarching. It also draws from procedural terrain generation techniques using CSG operations on voxel volumes. name: Procedural Volume Data Creation
body: Procedural Volume Data Creation generates volumetric datasets algorithmically rather than from scanned or simulated physical data. It solves the problem of creating complex, testable, or artistic volume data without external assets. It differs from sibling methods like Height Fog by using constructive solid geometry (CSG) Boolean operations on an empty voxel grid to create complex landscapes, whereas height fog typically generates density based on altitude functions. Inputs: An empty voxel volume grid; a user-defined range for sphere parameters (size and position). Outputs: A voxel volume where each cell stores a scalar density value. Data Structures: The volume is represented as a 3D array of voxels. Each voxel contains a scalar density value. The CSG operations modify these values based on the intersection with primitive shapes (spheres). Steps: 1. Initialize an empty 3D voxel grid with zero density. 2. Define a user-specified range for sphere radii (R{min}, R{max}) and positions (X{min}, X{max}, Y{min}, Y{max}, Z{min}, Z{max}). 3. For each sphere i in a large set (e.g., thousands): a. Randomly sample a radius ri from [R{min}, R{max}]. b. Randomly sample a center position ci = (xi, yi, zi) from the defined spatial range. c. Determine the bounding box of the sphere. d. For each voxel v within the bounding box: i. Calculate the distance d from the voxel center to ci. ii. If d < ri, apply a Boolean operation (add or subtract) to the voxel's density. For addition, densityv \leftarrow densityv + 1 (or a specific material value). For subtraction, densityv \leftarrow densityv - 1 (or clamp to zero). 4. Return the populated voxel grid. Formulas: Voxel center: v{center} = (i + 0.5) \cdot s, where i is the voxel index and s is the voxel size. Distance: d = \sqrt{(v{center} - c)^2}, where c is the sphere center. Boolean update: \rhov \leftarrow \rhov \pm 1 if d < r, where \rhov is voxel density and r is sphere radius. Parameters: Sphere count: "Thousands". Sphere size: Random values within a user-defined range. Sphere position: Random values within a user-defined range. Voxel size: Typically 1.0, but must match the raycasting step size to avoid integration errors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overlapping spheres: The method uses Boolean operations, so overlaps result in additive or subtractive density, potentially creating non-physical density values if not clamped. Boundary conditions: Spheres near the volume boundary may be partially clipped. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def createproceduralvolume(gridwidth, gridheight, griddepth, spherecount, posmin, posmax, radiusmin, radiusmax, operation='add', voxelsize=1.0): """ Creates a procedural volume using CSG operations on spheres. Args: gridwidth, gridheight, griddepth: Dimensions of the voxel grid. spherecount: Number of spheres to generate. posmin, posmax: Tuple of (x, y, z) for the bounding box of sphere centers. radiusmin, radiusmax: Floats for the range of sphere radii. operation: String, 'add' or 'subtract'. voxelsize: Physical size of each voxel (default 1.0). Returns: A 3D numpy-like array of densities. """ import random import math # Initialize empty volume with zero density volume = [[[0.0 for in range(griddepth)] for in range(gridheight)] for in range(gridwidth)] for in range(spherecount): # Random sphere parameters cx = random.uniform(posmin[0], posmax[0]) cy = random.uniform(posmin[1], posmax[1]) cz = random.uniform(posmin[2], posmax[2]) r = random.uniform(radiusmin, radiusmax) # Determine bounding box of the sphere in voxel indices xstart = max(0, int(math.floor((cx - r) / voxelsize))) xend = min(gridwidth, int(math.ceil((cx + r) / voxelsize))) ystart = max(0, int(math.floor((cy - r) / voxelsize))) yend = min(gridheight, int(math.ceil((cy + r) / voxelsize))) zstart = max(0, int(math.floor((cz - r) / voxelsize))) zend = min(griddepth, int(math.ceil((cz + r) / voxelsize))) for x in range(xstart, xend): for y in range(ystart, yend): for z in range(zstart, zend): # Calculate distance d from voxel center to sphere center ci dx = ((x + 0.5) voxelsize) - cx dy = ((y + 0.5) voxelsize) - cy dz = ((z + 0.5) voxelsize) - cz distsq = dx dx + dy dy + dz dz # If d < ri, apply a Boolean operation to the voxel's density if distsq < r r: if operation == 'add': volume[x][y][z] += 1.0 elif operation == 'subtract': volume[x][y][z] -= 1.0 return volume A node that generates a new volume based on an input volume to provide normals for lighting calculations in slicing or raycasting. It sets itself apart by packing normals in color.rgb and the original scalar in color.a using the xyzs format. Choose it when advanced visualization with correct lighting is required instead of basic intensity visualization. Link: Normal Map Volume Generation. A technique to create a cylindrical simulation domain with vertical periodic boundary conditions by generating a subvolume and mirroring it along the vertical axis. It sets itself apart by explicitly removing voxels outside a 124-voxel radius and doubling the length via mirroring. Choose it when simulating multiphase flow with periodic boundaries is required. Link: Cylindrical Volume Generation. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of voxels in the bounding boxes of all spheres and S is the number of spheres. Since spheres overlap and bounds are checked, it is efficient for sparse volumes but can be dense if spheres cover the entire grid. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot D) for the voxel grid, where W, H, D are grid dimensions. Strengths: Generates complex, organic-looking terrains or structures algorithmically without external data. Suitable for testing algorithms as it creates "complex enough" landscapes. Limitations: The resulting density values are arbitrary (Boolean sums) and may not represent physical properties. Not suitable for physically accurate simulations. When to use: When testing volume rendering algorithms or creating artistic procedural landscapes. When not to use: When physically accurate density data is required. Originated in the context of visualizing large procedural volumetric terrains. The method was employed to verify algorithm feasibility by generating complex test data on the fly, rather than pre-computing entire terrains. It is similar to other procedural methods but focuses on CSG operations for terrain synthesis. name: Height Fog
head: Cube World Fog, Exponential Height Fog, Height Volumetric Fog
body: Height fog is a procedural volumetric effect where density falls exponentially with height, filling space to fade the horizon and fill valleys. It simulates a dense atmospheric volume by blending scene colors with a fog color based on a submersion factor or a distance-height visibility curve. In voxel-based systems, it often serves as the analytical component for sun light without dynamic shadows, applied to geometry outside the ray-marching range. Inputs: worldpos: Array of world coordinates (N, 3) for sampled points or voxels. camerapos: World coordinates of the camera (3,). colors: Array of RGB colors at the sampled points (N, 3). fogmaxz: Maximum Z height for the fog effect. fogfade: Minimum denominator for submersion calculation. fogdensity or uFogDensity: Scalar controlling the strength of the fog effect. uFogHeightFalloff: Float controlling the rate of exponential decay with height. uFogBaseHeight: Float Y-coordinate where fog density is highest. uFogColor or HEIGHTFOGRGB: The base color of the fog (3,). Outputs: finalcolors: The fog-blended RGB colors (N, 3). Data Structures: Standard floating-point arrays for coordinates and colors. No complex bit-packing is required for the basic analytical calculation. Steps: 1. Check Density: If fogdensity <= 0, return the input colors immediately. 2. Calculate Visibility/Fog Amount: Two closed-form variants exist in the evidence: Voxel Submersion: Compute submersion = clip((fogmaxz - zcenters) / max(0.1, fogfade), 0.0, 1.0). Compute vis = pow(1.0 - submersion, fogdensity 4.0). Distance-Height Attenuation: Compute fogDist = length(cameraPosition - vWorldPosition). Compute heightFactor = exp(-uFogHeightFalloff (vWorldPosition.y - uFogBaseHeight)). Compute fogAmount = 1.0 - exp(-fogDist uFogDensity heightFactor). 3. Desaturate Colors (Washout): Compute washout = pow(vis, 2.0). Compute average luminance avglum = mean(colors, axis=1). Blend colors = colors washout + avglum (1.0 - washout). 4. Blend with Fog Color: Clamp fogAmount to [0.0, 1.0]. Compute finalcolors = mix(colors, uFogColor, fogAmount) or colors vis + HEIGHTFOGRGB (1.0 - vis). Formulas: submersion = clip((fogmaxz - zcenters) / max(0.1, fogfade), 0.0, 1.0) vis = pow(1.0 - submersion, fogdensity 4.0) fogDist = length(cameraPosition - vWorldPosition) heightFactor = exp(-uFogHeightFalloff (vWorldPosition.y - uFogBaseHeight)) fogAmount = 1.0 - exp(-fogDist uFogDensity heightFactor) finalcolors = mix(colors, uFogColor, fogAmount) Parameters with Typical Values: uFogDensity: Base density multiplier for distance. Default 0.001. uFogHeightFalloff: Controls exponential decay rate. Default 0.015. uFogBaseHeight: Peak density Y-coordinate. Default 50.0. uFogColor: Fog color. Default 0x7ec8e3. fogdensity: Controls strength. Not given in the sources. fogmaxz: Maximum Z height. Not given in the sources. fogfade: Minimum denominator. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If fogdensity is negative or zero, the fog is disabled. Division by zero is prevented by max(0.1, fogfade) in the submersion variant. Submersion is clipped to [0.0, 1.0] to prevent invalid visibility values. Precision issues may arise if vis becomes extremely small due to high fogdensity or large fogDist, potentially causing underflow in floating-point representations. The distance-height variant assumes vWorldPosition.y is in the same coordinate space as uFogBaseHeight. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def applyheightfog(worldpos: np.ndarray, camerapos: np.ndarray, colors: np.ndarray, uFogDensity: float, uFogHeightFalloff: float, uFogBaseHeight: float, uFogColor: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: """ Applies exponential height fog using distance-height attenuation. Args: worldpos: Array of world coordinates (N, 3). camerapos: Camera world coordinates (3,). colors: Array of RGB colors (N, 3). uFogDensity: Base density multiplier. uFogHeightFalloff: Height decay rate. uFogBaseHeight: Peak density Y-coordinate. uFogColor: Fog color (3,). Returns: Final colors with height fog applied. """ # Step 1: Calculate distance from camera fogdist = np.linalg.norm(camerapos - worldpos, axis=-1) # Step 2: Calculate height factor heightfactor = np.exp(-uFogHeightFalloff (worldpos[..., 1] - uFogBaseHeight)) # Step 3: Calculate total fog amount fogamount = 1.0 - np.exp(-fogdist uFogDensity heightfactor) # Step 4: Clamp fog amount fogamount = np.clip(fogamount, 0.0, 1.0) # Step 5: Blend final color fogamountexpanded = fogamount[..., np.newaxis] finalcolors = colors (1.0 - fogamountexpanded) + uFogColor fogamountexpanded return finalcolors A technique building on exponential height fog that adds noise to simulate random particle movement, causing some areas to appear denser than others. Fog density is defined by sampling fBm (fractional Brownian motion) noise. It is chosen when a more natural, varied, and less uniform fog appearance is desired compared to the smooth exponential falloff of standard height fog. A component of voxel-based systems that handles sun light without dynamic shadows and exponential height fog density, applied to everything outside the ray-marching range. It is distinguished from ray-marching fog by its analytical, closed-form calculation which avoids per-ray marching overhead. It is used for distant atmospheric coverage where dynamic shadowing is not required. A fog feature that ensures no fog appears closer than a specified startdistance, fading in over one slice to achieve a near-clear, far-hazy look. Exponential height fog alone cannot produce this near-clear, far-hazy look; this feature adds explicit start distance control, similar to Unreal Engine's height and volumetric fog. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of sampled points or voxels, as it involves simple arithmetic operations per point. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of samples. Suitable for real-time applications due to its closed-form nature. Strengths: Simple to implement, provides a smooth and realistic horizon fade. Limitations: Does not account for dynamic shadows or complex light interactions within the fog volume. The base form lacks the natural variation of noise-based fog. When to use: For atmospheric fog effects in voxel-based or real-time rendering where performance is key and dynamic shadows are handled separately or not required. When not to use: When realistic, varied fog density is needed (use Ground Fog), or when dynamic shadows within the fog are required (use Ray-marching Volumetric Fog). Height fog is used in voxel-based rendering systems to provide atmospheric depth. It is a standard component in game engines like CRYENGINE for handling distant atmospheric effects analytically. The concept of adding noise to create ground fog has been explored in web-based rendering contexts to enhance realism. name: Particle Fog Density Injection
head: Particle Emission Update (for fog), Volume Fog Injection
body: Particle Fog Density Injection is a method to add fog density to a defined area using a particle emitter, operating exclusively within the Legacy Particle Editor. It differs from height-based or procedural noise approaches by tying volumetric density directly to particle emission bounds and attributes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A particle emitter instance configured in the Legacy Particle Editor. Output: A volumetric fog density field spatially bounded by the emitter's volume and modulated by its parameters. Data Structures: The method relies on parameters stored in the particle emitter's "Advanced" group: Volume Fog: Boolean flag enabling fog density injection. Volume Thickness: Float value adjusting volume thickness, range 0 to 10. Wind Influence: Float value controlling global wind influence on the fog volume, range 0 to 20. Enabled: Boolean flag controlling the entity's on/off state. Texture, Alpha, Alpha Clip, Size, Fill Rate Cost, Plane Align Blend Distance: Parameters affecting fog density and appearance. Tessellation Parameter: Explicitly not supported. Steps: 1. Enable Volume Fog: Set the Volume Fog parameter in the "Advanced" group to true. 2. Configure Thickness: Set Volume Thickness to define the density magnitude within the 0–10 range. 3. Apply Wind Influence: Set Wind Influence to control how global wind affects the fog volume within the 0–20 range. 4. Adjust Visual Attributes: Configure Texture, Alpha, Alpha Clip, Size, Fill Rate Cost, and Plane Align Blend Distance to refine appearance and performance. 5. Enable Entity: Ensure the Enabled flag is true for the emitter. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Volume Fog: Boolean, default false. Volume Thickness: Float, range 0 to 10. Wind Influence: Float, range 0 to 20. Enabled: Boolean, default true. Texture, Alpha, Alpha Clip, Size, Fill Rate Cost, Plane Align Blend Distance: Affect density and rendering cost. Tessellation Parameter: Not supported. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Legacy Editor Only: This method only works in the Legacy Particle Editor. Tessellation: The Tessellation Parameter is explicitly not supported. Performance: Fill Rate Cost indicates rendering performance impact; high particle counts or large sizes increase cost. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def configureparticlefog(emitter): # Enable fog injection emitter.VolumeFog = True # Set density thickness (0-10) emitter.VolumeThickness = 5.0 # Set wind influence (0-20) emitter.WindInfluence = 10.0 # Ensure emitter is active emitter.Enabled = True # Configure visual and performance attributes emitter.Texture = "fogtexture.png" emitter.Alpha = 0.5 emitter.AlphaClip = False emitter.Size = 1.0 emitter.FillRateCost = 100 emitter.PlaneAlignBlendDistance = 0.0 # Tessellation Parameter is not supported Defines fog density based on world height rather than particle positions. Use when fog needs to be tied to terrain elevation. A broader category of methods for generating volume data. Use when more complex procedural logic is needed beyond particle emission. Optimizes noise evaluation for enclosed spaces. Use when rendering dense volumes in caves or interiors to skip empty regions. Calculates light absorption per unit distance. Use when accurate light attenuation through the injected fog is required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources [S#]. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources [S#]. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources [S#]. Scaling: Not given in the sources [S#]. Strengths: Enables localized, dynamic fog volumes driven by particle systems. Limitations: Restricted to the Legacy Particle Editor; performance scales with particle count and Fill Rate Cost. When to use: When localized, dynamic fog is required within the Legacy Particle Editor workflow. When not to use: When using modern particle systems or when height-based fog is needed. Documented in CRYENGINE 3 and CRYENGINE 5 volumetric fog documentation. It integrates particle emitters into the engine's volumetric fog system to act as density sources.
