name: Short-circuit Cave Noise Evaluation
head: Deterministic fixed-point cave density field optimization, Lazy cave generation sampling
body: Short-circuit Cave Noise Evaluation is an optimization for procedural cave generation that avoids computing the second trilinear noise field when the first band check fails, reducing per-voxel generation cost. It differs from eager evaluation by deferring fieldb computation until conda passes, leveraging short-circuit logic to skip expensive trilinear sampling in the common case where banda fails. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D chunk of voxels (typically 32 \times 32 \times 32). Output: A boolean tunnel value for each solid voxel indicating if it should be carved. Data Structures Chunk: A 3D array of voxels. Each voxel is processed if it is "solid" (i.e., not already determined to be air or outside the surface-roof/bedrock-floor bounds). Noise Fields: Two trilinear noise fields, fielda and fieldb. Each field requires 8 hash samples for trilinear interpolation. Constants: NOISEMID: Reference value for band checks, relative to the full 0-65535 hash range. hashsamples: Fixed at 8. Steps 1. Iterate over every voxel in the chunk. 2. Check if the voxel is solid (past surface-roof and bedrock-floor checks). If not, skip. 3. Evaluate conda using fielda. conda is a narrow band check around NOISEMID relative to the 0-65535 hash range. 4. If conda fails: Skip computing fieldb. Set tunnel = false. 5. If conda passes: Compute fieldb (8 hash samples). Evaluate condb using fieldb (same narrow band check logic as conda). Set tunnel = conda && condb. Formula tunnel = conda \land condb where conda and condb are narrow band checks around NOISEMID relative to the full 0-65535 hash range. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatecavenoise(chunk, NOISEMID): """ Evaluates cave noise for a chunk using short-circuit evaluation. chunk: 3D array of voxels, each with a 'issolid' flag. NOISEMID: Reference value for band checks. Returns: 3D array of booleans 'tunnel'. """ tunnelmap = [[False for in range(32)] for in range(32)] for x in range(32): for y in range(32): for z in range(32): voxel = chunk[x][y][z] if not voxel.issolid: continue # Evaluate first noise field fielda = computetrilinearnoise(x, y, z, hashsamples=8) conda = isnarrowband(fielda, NOISEMID) if not conda: # Short-circuit: skip fieldb tunnelmap[x][y][z] = False else: # Compute second noise field only if conda passed fieldb = computetrilinearnoise(x, y, z, hashsamples=8) condb = isnarrowband(fieldb, NOISEMID) tunnelmap[x][y][z] = conda and condb return tunnelmap def computetrilinearnoise(x, y, z, hashsamples): """ Computes a trilinear noise field value at (x, y, z) using hashsamples. Returns a value in the 0-65535 range. """ # Implementation detail: Generate hashsamples and interpolate. # This is a placeholder for the actual noise generation logic. # The key is that this is expensive and should be avoided if possible. return 0 # Placeholder def isnarrowband(value, NOISEMID): """ Checks if value is in a narrow band around NOISEMID. """ # Implementation detail: Define the band width. # This is a placeholder for the actual band check logic. return False # Placeholder Parameters NOISEMID: Reference value for band checks, relative to the full 0-65535 hash range. hashsamples: Number of samples per trilinear noise field, fixed at 8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Eager Evaluation: Computing fieldb before the logical AND operator causes unnecessary computation even when conda fails, as seen in the initial Rust implementation. Chunk Generation Cost: Chunk generation runs on every solid voxel past surface-roof and bedrock-floor checks, making the noise evaluation the single largest cost during generation. Time Complexity: Reduced from O(V) with unconditional dual-field evaluation to O(V) with short-circuit evaluation, where V is the number of solid voxels per chunk. The constant factor is significantly reduced because fieldb is often skipped. Memory Complexity: Memory layout remains unchanged. Strengths: Significantly reduces per-voxel generation cost by avoiding expensive trilinear sampling in the common case where banda fails. Limitations: The optimization is specific to the cave generation logic and does not apply to other procedural volume generation methods. When to Use: Use when generating procedural caves in voxel worlds, especially when performance is critical and the majority of voxels do not form tunnels. When Not to Use: Do not use if the cave generation logic requires both noise fields to be computed for other reasons (e.g., visualization, debugging). Short-circuit Cave Noise Evaluation was introduced in the TEKNIK project to address performance issues in procedural cave generation. The optimization was identified as the main cause of lag on both surface and underground chunks, as even surface-area chunks with no visible caves paid the per-voxel cost during generation. The fix was applied to both GDScript and Rust implementations, with GDScript serving as the parity reference. name: Extinction Coefficient Computation
head: Binning surface area density from hierarchical vegetation model, Opacity calculation from atomic cross-sections
body:
Extinction coefficient computation calculates the volumetric opacity \kappa required for radiative transport simulations by aggregating geometric surface densities or atomic cross-sections. It differs from procedural noise methods by deriving opacity from explicit physical geometry (vegetation models) or fundamental atomic physics (X-ray interactions) rather than stochastic field evaluation. This method serves as the foundational step for defining material interaction properties before ray marching or compositing. Two distinct physical regimes define this method: geometric binning for vegetation and atomic cross-section integration for X-ray radiography. Geometric Input: Hierarchical vegetation model with detailed polygonal descriptions; ranges for height z and polar angle 	heta. Atomic Input: Tabulated atomic cross-sections \sigmaE indexed by photon energy E; material composition (mass fractions mi); density ho. Output: Extinction coefficient table indexed by spatial/angle bins (vegetation) or material number and energy group (atomic). Vegetation Bins: A 2D array indexed by (z, 	heta) bins. Stores summed clipped polygon areas. Atomic Table: A 2D table indexed by material number and energy group number g. Stores constant approximation opacities \mathbf{K}{mat,g}. 1. Define a 2D binning grid over the ranges of height z and polar angle 	heta. 2. Traverse the hierarchical vegetation model using its detailed polygonal description. 3. For each polygon, clip it to the (z, 	heta) ranges it overlaps. 4. Sum the clipped areas of the polygon into the appropriate (z, 	heta) bins. 5. Compute the extinction coefficient K(z, \omega) from the surface area density per unit volume in each bin. The specific conversion from bin area to K is detailed in the source appendix. 1. Interpolate Elemental Cross-Sections: For a given photon energy E, interpolate the atomic cross-section \sigmaE from tabulated data. The energy is defined as E = h
u, where h is Planck's constant and 
u is frequency. 2. Compute Elemental Opacity: Calculate the opacity \kappaE for a single element using: \kappaE =  rac{\sigmaE}{uA} where \sigmaE is in barns/atom (1 	ext{ barn} = 10^{-24} 	ext{ cm}^2), u is the atomic mass unit (1 	ext{ amu} = 1.6605402 	imes 10^{-24} 	ext{ g}), and A is the atomic mass in amu. 3. Group Constant Approximation: Divide the energy spectrum into groups g with bounds Eg and E{g+1}. Compute the constant opacity \mathbf{k}g for each group: \mathbf{k}g =  rac{1}{E{g+1} - Eg} \int{Eg}^{E{g+1}} \mathbf{k}{E'} dE' This approximates the varying opacity \mathbf{k}{E'} as a piecewise constant value per group. 4. Mixture Composition: For a material composed of N elements, compute the material opacity \mathbf{K}{mat,g} for group g using atomic mixing: \mathbf{K}{mat,g} = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} mi \mathbf{K}{i,g} where mi is the mass fraction of element i and \mathbf{K}{i,g} is the opacity of element i in group g. 5. Final Extinction Coefficient: Convert the mass opacity \kappa to the volumetric extinction coefficient K
u using the material density ho: K
u = \kappa ho where \kappa is in 	ext{cm}^2/	ext{g} and ho is the density. Planck's constant (h): 6.6263 	imes 10^{-27} 	ext{ erg/s}. Energy Conversion: 1 	ext{ eV} = 1.60206 	imes 10^{-12} 	ext{ erg}. Atomic Mass Unit (u): 1.6605402 	imes 10^{-24} 	ext{ g}. Barn: 10^{-24} 	ext{ cm}^2. Absorption Edges: At energies corresponding to electron shell binding energies, opacity exhibits sharp discontinuities (sawtooth shape). The piecewise constant approximation must resolve these edges sufficiently to avoid significant error. Precision: Cross-sections are interpolated from tabulated data. Interpolation errors at low energies or near edges can propagate into the final radiograph. Geometry Clipping: In the vegetation model, precise clipping of polygons to (z, 	heta) bins is required to avoid double-counting or gaps in the surface area density. Complexity: Geometric binning depends on the number of polygons in the hierarchical model and the resolution of the (z, 	heta) bins. Atomic computation depends on the number of elements in the mixture and the number of energy groups. Performance: The geometric method requires a full traversal of the model hierarchy. The atomic method is a lookup and summation operation, typically fast per material, but requires pre-computed cross-section tables. Scaling: Geometric binning scales with scene complexity (polygon count). Atomic scaling is linear with the number of elements in a mixture. Strengths: Physically accurate for specific geometries and materials. Limitations: Requires detailed input data (polygons or cross-section tables). Not suitable for generic procedural noise-based volumes. Geometric Method: Originated in the context of global illumination in vegetation, specifically for plane-parallel radiance transport. It was used to process hierarchical vegetation models (e.g., maple trees) to compute density of leaf and non-leaf surfaces. Atomic Method: Developed for hardware-accelerated simulated radiography of emissive objects. It utilizes publicly available tabulations of computed atomic cross-sections to define cold opacities for X-ray simulation. name: Example-based Synthesis of Three-dimensional Clouds from Photographs
head: Example-based Cloud Synthesis, Photograph-guided Cloud Volume Synthesis
body: This method synthesizes a three-dimensional cloud volume V storing extinction coefficients \sigmat such that its rendered image resembles an input photograph I{ph}, using an example volume database V{ex} created by physically-based fluid simulation. It differs from purely procedural methods by optimizing the volume density to match photographic statistics and structural patterns found in a database of physically-based cloud simulations, rather than relying solely on noise functions or parametric weather models. Input: An input photograph I{ph} provided by the user. Input: An example cloud volume database V{ex} = \{V1^{ex}, \dots, VN^{ex}\}, where each volume is created by physically-based fluid simulation. Input: User-specified parameters: sun direction, user-specified depth resolution Nz, and pixel block width w. Output: A cloud volume V storing the extinction coefficient \sigmat at each voxel. Grid: An axis-aligned grid with resolution Nx \times Ny \times Nz voxels. Nx and Ny are equal to the resolution of the input photograph I{ph}. Nz is user-specified. Voxel Indexing: Each voxel is indexed by (p, z), where p is the corresponding pixel coordinate in the image plane and z is the depth coordinate. Voxel Size: The length of a voxel is assumed to be 1. Pixel Block B(p): A set of neighborhood pixels centered around pixel p with width w. Voxel Block C(p): A voxel block consisting of w \times w \times Nz voxels, whose projected area onto the image plane is equal to B(p). The method uses parallel projection with the viewing direction parallel to the z-axis and the image plane on the xy-plane. It employs a single scattering model with an isotropic phase function and a uniform ambient term to compensate for multiple scattering effects. Rendering Equation: The radiance L(p) at pixel p is calculated as: L(p) = L{sky} Tr(p, Nz) + \sum{z=1}^{Nz} Ls(p, z) Tr(p, z-1) Where: L{sky} is the sky radiance. Tr(p, z) is the transmittance between voxel (p, z) and (p, 1). Ls(p, z) is the scattered radiance at voxel (p, z). Transmittance: Tr(p, z) = \exp \left( - \sum{z'=1}^{z} \sigmat(p, z') \right) Scattered Radiance: Ls(p, z) = \sigmat(p, z) (\beta fp L{sun} \tau(p, z) + La) Where: \beta is the albedo. fp is the isotropic phase function, with value 1/4\pi. L{sun} is the sun radiance. \tau(p, z) is the sun transmittance, representing the transmittance between the voxel and the sun, affected by other voxels where incident sunlight travels before reaching (p, z). La is the ambient term. Simplified Scattered Radiance: Since \beta, fp, and L{sun} are constant, their product is represented by a single parameter L0 = \beta fp L{sun}. The scattered radiance simplifies to: Ls(p, z) = \sigmat(p, z) (L0 \tau(p, z) + La) Final Rendering Equation: Substituting Ls into the rendering equation yields: L(p) = L{sky} Tr(p, Nz) + L0 \sum{z=1}^{Nz} \tau(p, z) \sigmat(p, z) Tr(p, z) + La \sum{z=1}^{Nz} \sigmat(p, z) Tr(p, z) Sun Direction: Provided by the user. Sky Radiance L{sky}: Assumed to be uniform, determined as the average intensity of the pixels corresponding to the sky in the input photograph I{ph}. Combined Sun Parameter L0: Represents \beta fp L{sun}. Ambient Term La: Constant parameter. Sun Transmittance \tau: Must be computed from other voxel blocks. 1. Preprocess: Prepare a set of voxels C^{ex} from the example volume database V{ex}. Estimate rendering parameters (e.g., L0, La) to match the rendered images of C^{ex} with pixel blocks B{ph}(p) in I{ph}. 2. Synthesis: Minimize an energy function measuring two differences: 1. The difference between pixels of the rendered image of V and the input photograph I{ph}. 2. The difference between voxels of V and those derived from V{ex}. The optimization follows the example-based texture synthesis technique proposed by Kwatra et al.. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from math import exp def synthesizecloudvolume(Iph, Vex, sundirection, Nz, w): """ Synthesize a cloud volume V from photograph Iph and example volumes Vex. """ Nx, Ny = Iph.shape[0], Iph.shape[1] # Step 1: Preprocess Lsky = computeaverageskyradiance(Iph) L0, La = estimaterenderingparameters(Iph, Vex, sundirection, w) # Step 2: Synthesis via Energy Minimization V = initializevolume(Nx, Ny, Nz) V = minimizeenergy(V, Iph, Vex, Lsky, L0, La, sundirection, w) return V def computeaverageskyradiance(Iph): """Average intensity of pixels corresponding to sky in Iph.""" skymask = detectskypixels(Iph) # return sum(Iph[skymask]) / len(skymask) def estimaterenderingparameters(Iph, Vex, sundirection, w): """Estimate L0 and La to match rendered images of Cex with Bph(p).""" # Solves min{L0, La} || Render(Cex) - Bph(p) ||^2 via least-squares L0, La = solvelinearradiancefit(Vex, Iph, sundirection, w) return L0, La def initializevolume(Nx, Ny, Nz): """Create Nx x Ny x Nz grid of zeros.""" return [[[0.0] Nz for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] def minimizeenergy(V, Iph, Vex, Lsky, L0, La, sundirection, w): """ Minimize energy function measuring difference between rendered image of V and Iph, and difference between voxels of V and those derived from Vex. Follows example-based texture synthesis technique. """ Nx, Ny, Nz = len(V), len(V[0]), len(V[0][0]) for iteration in range(100): # for x in range(Nx): for y in range(Ny): # Patch-based optimization step V[x][y] = updatevoxelblock(V[x][y], Iph, Vex, Lsky, L0, La, sundirection, w) return V def updatevoxelblock(block, Iph, Vex, Lsky, L0, La, sundirection, w): """Iteratively adjust block to minimize energy.""" # Standard example-based synthesis update rule return block # [Comment: Exact solver implementation not provided in sources] def rendervoxelblock(sigmatblock, Lsky, L0, La, tausun): """ Render a voxel block C(p) using the single scattering model. sigmatblock: list of sigmat(p, z) for z=1..Nz tausun: list of tau(p, z) for z=1..Nz """ Nz = len(sigmatblock) Tr = [1.0] (Nz + 1) for z in range(1, Nz + 1): Tr[z] = Tr[z-1] exp(-sigmatblock[z-1]) Lval = Lsky Tr[Nz] for z in range(1, Nz + 1): sigmatz = sigmatblock[z-1] tauz = tausun[z-1] Lsz = sigmatz (L0 tauz + La) Lval += Lsz Tr[z-1] return Lval def computesuntransmittance(sigmatblock, sundirection): """Compute tau(p, z) along sun direction.""" Nz = len(sigmatblock) tau = [1.0] Nz for z in range(1, Nz): tau[z] = tau[z-1] exp(-sigmatblock[z-1]) return tau Sun Transmittance: The sun transmittance \tau(p, z) is affected by other voxel blocks. Sky Radiance: L{sky} is assumed uniform. Single Scattering: The method uses a single scattering model. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Can synthesize realistic cloud structures that match the statistical and structural properties of physically-based fluid simulations, guided by a single photograph. Limitations: Relies on the quality and relevance of the example volume database V{ex}. The single scattering approximation may limit realism in certain lighting conditions. When to use: When a user wants to generate a 3D cloud volume that visually matches a specific photograph, and has access to a database of physically-based cloud simulations. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical, or when the input photograph does not contain clear cloud structures, or when the example database does not cover the desired cloud types. Origin: Proposed by Kei Iwasaki, Yoshinori Dobashi, Makoto Okabe from Wakayama University, Hokkaido University, and Shizuoka University. Publication: Published in CGI ’17, June 27-30, 2017, Yokohama, Japan. History: The method builds on example-based texture synthesis techniques, specifically citing Kwatra et al.. It addresses the difficulty of synthesizing realistic clouds from a single photograph, a task that is difficult with purely procedural methods. Example-based synthesis of three-dimensional clouds from photographs, https://doi.org/10.1145/3095140.3095168, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Cloud Fragment Shader (3D Noise Volume Rendering)
head: Procedural Clouds via 3D Noise
body: The Cloud Fragment Shader is a GPU-based technique for rendering volumetric clouds on a dome geometry by sampling a 3D noise volume texture. It solves the problem of generating dynamic, drifting cloud formations with minimal CPU overhead by performing density calculation and color blending entirely within the fragment shader. It differs from its parent Procedural Noise Functions by operating on pre-computed 3D texture lookups rather than evaluating analytical noise functions per-fragment, and from its sibling Alpha-Blended Cloud Rendering with Occlusion by lacking depth-aware occlusion mixing and multi-layer instancing, relying instead on simple alpha blending with the background sky. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: ModelPosition (varying vec3): Scaled vertex position passed from the vertex shader. Noise (uniform sampler3D): 3D texture containing procedural noise data. Offset (uniform vec3): Dynamic offset for cloud drift and formation. Cutoff (uniform float): Threshold for cloud coverage. Exponent (uniform float): Controls dynamic range and edge sharpness. CloudColor (uniform vec3): RGB color of the cloud volume. Bias (uniform float): Intensity multiplier. glColor.a (built-in varying): Vertex alpha value. Output: glFragColor (built-in output): Final fragment color with alpha. Data Structures: 3D Noise Texture: A 3D texture array where the alpha channel (a) stores the noise value. The red, green, and blue channels are unused for density in this specific implementation. Uniforms: Standard OpenGL uniform variables defined in the shader source. Steps: 1. Receive Position: The fragment shader receives the ModelPosition varying from the vertex shader. This position is already scaled by the Scale uniform to match the noise texture dimensions. 2. Sample Noise: Sample the 3D noise texture using coordinates ModelPosition + Offset. Extract the alpha channel value. n{sampled} = \text{texture3D}(\text{Noise}, \text{ModelPosition} + \text{Offset}).a 3. Clamp Noise: Apply a cutoff threshold. If the sampled noise is below Cutoff, set it to 0.0. Otherwise, subtract Cutoff to shift the range. n{clamp} = \begin{cases} 0.0 & \text{if } n{sampled} < \text{Cutoff} \\ n{sampled} - \text{Cutoff} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 4. Exponentiate and Bias: Apply exponential mapping to control density falloff and edge sharpness, then multiply by Bias. n{out} = \text{Bias} \times (1.0 - \text{pow}(\text{Exponent}, n{clamp})) 5. Compute Final Color: Combine CloudColor with the processed noise alpha and the vertex alpha (glColor.a). \text{FinalColor} = \text{vec4}(\text{CloudColor}, n{out} \times \text{gl\Color.a}) 6. Output: Write FinalColor to glFragColor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def main(): # 1. Sample 3D noise texture using scaled model position and dynamic offset # Note: texture3D is a standard GLSL function for 3D texture lookup noisesample = texture3D(Noise, ModelPosition + Offset).a # 2. Clamp noise based on cutoff threshold if noisesample < Cutoff: noiseclamped = 0.0 else: noiseclamped = noisesample - Cutoff # 3. Apply exponential density mapping and bias # Formula: nout = Bias (1.0 - Exponent^nclamped) noisefinal = Bias (1.0 - pow(Exponent, noiseclamped)) # 4. Compute final color # Combine CloudColor with noise alpha and vertex alpha # Note: glColor.a is the vertex alpha passed through the pipeline finalalpha = noisefinal glColor.a finalcolor = vec4(CloudColor, finalalpha) # 5. Output fragment color glFragColor = finalcolor Parameters: Scale (uniform float): Scales the incoming vertex position relative to the noise texture size. Allows finer control of cloud size. Offset (uniform vec3): Adds a per-frame offset to texture coordinates. The x-component simulates cloud drift, and the y-component controls formation. Cutoff (uniform float): Threshold percentage for cloud coverage. Values below this are clamped to zero alpha. Exponent (uniform float): Controls the dynamic range of the noise after clamping. Higher values sharpen edges and reduce density. CloudColor (uniform vec3): RGB color of the cloud volume. Bias (uniform float): Multiplier applied after exponentiation to adjust the final alpha/color intensity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Vertex Alpha Ignored: The fixed-function glFrontColor is ignored when shaders are enabled. The vertex alpha must be preserved via glColor.a and explicitly multiplied with the computed noise alpha in the final output. Blending: The final cloud color is blended with the background sky using SRCALPHA and ONEMINUSSRCALPHA factors. A fragment-based cloud rendering technique that uses 3D noise sampling with alpha clipping to define volume boundaries, combined with a multi-term lighting model (diffuse, subsurface scattering approximation, view brightening, and shadows) for surface shading. It differs from its parent Cloud Fragment Shader (3D Noise Volume Rendering) by replacing simple background blending with a depth-aware occlusion mixing system that allows clouds to interact with opaque scene geometry, and by using instanced rendering to stack multiple cloud layers with varying density thresholds. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment for the noise lookup and post-processing steps, assuming constant-time texture sampling. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the 3D noise texture, where N is the volume resolution. Performance: The method is efficient for real-time rendering as it offloads density calculation to the GPU fragment shader. Strengths: Simple implementation, dynamic cloud movement via offset uniforms, and low CPU overhead. Limitations: Lacks depth-aware occlusion, multi-layer interaction, and complex lighting models found in more advanced techniques. When to Use: Suitable for simple sky dome cloud rendering where performance is critical and complex volumetric interactions are not required. When Not to Use: When realistic volumetric lighting, occlusion against terrain, or multi-layer cloud systems are needed. The Cloud Fragment Shader was implemented in the OpenSceneGraph (OSG) library for the CloudDome class to render volumetric clouds on a dome geometry. It utilizes GLSL (OpenGL Shading Language) and requires specific extensions (GLARBfragmentshader, GLARBvertexshader, GLARBshaderobjects, GLARBshadinglanguage100) to be supported. The technique was described by George Tarantilis in a thesis on simulating clouds with procedural texturing techniques using the GPU. DTIC ADA427539: Simulating Clouds with Procedural Texturing Techniques Using the GPU, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA427539, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Alpha-Blended Cloud Rendering with Occlusion
head: AlphaTest Cloud Shader, Noise-Clipped Cloud Rendering with Approximate SSS, Unity Cloud Rendering Shader
body: A fragment-based cloud rendering technique that uses 3D noise sampling with alpha clipping to define volume boundaries, combined with a multi-term lighting model (diffuse, subsurface scattering approximation, view brightening, and shadows) for surface shading. It differs from its parent Cloud Fragment Shader (3D Noise Volume Rendering) by replacing simple background blending with a depth-aware occlusion mixing system that allows clouds to interact with opaque scene geometry, and by using instanced rendering to stack multiple cloud layers with varying density thresholds. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A base mesh (typically a plane or dome segment), a 3D noise texture (3DNoise), camera depth normals texture (CameraDepthNormalsTexture), and instanced properties for layer-specific parameters. Outputs: A color buffer with alpha-blended clouds and a depth buffer. Data Structures: Vertex Input (appdata): vertex: half4 (POSITION) normal: half3 (NORMAL) uv: float2 (TEXCOORD0) instanceID: UNITYVERTEXINPUTINSTANCEID Vertex Output (v2f): pos: float4 (SVPOSITION) worldPos: float3 (TEXCOORD0) uv: float3 (TEXCOORD1) normalW: half3 (TEXCOORD4) screenPosxywdepth01z: float4 (TEXCOORD5). Layout: x = 0.5(xc+wc), y = 0.5(yc+wc), z = depth01, w = wc. fogCoord: UNITYFOGCOORDS(2) shadowCoord: SHADOWCOORDS(3) instanceID: UNITYVERTEXINPUTINSTANCEID Instanced Properties Buffer (Props): NoiseTiling: half PosOffset: half ClipThres: half Numbered Steps: 1. Vertex Shader: 1. Setup instance ID: UNITYSETUPINSTANCEID(v). 2. Displace vertex: v.vertex.xyz += v.normal UNITYACCESSINSTANCEDPROP(Props, PosOffset). 3. Compute clip position: o.pos = UnityObjectToClipPos(v.vertex). 4. Compute world position: o.worldPos = mul(unityObjectToWorld, v.vertex).xyz. 5. Compute world normal: o.normalW = UnityObjectToWorldNormal(v.normal). 6. Compute screen position and depth: o.screenPosxywdepth01z = ComputeScreenPos(o.pos). Set o.screenPosxywdepth01z.z = COMPUTEDEPTH01. 7. Compute UVs: o.uv.xyz = v.vertex.xyz 0.5 + 0.5. 8. Animate UVs: o.uv = o.uv UNITYACCESSINSTANCEDPROP(Props, NoiseTiling) + Time.y UVSpeed. 9. Transfer fog and shadow coordinates. 2. Fragment Shader - Direction Setup: 1. Setup instance ID: UNITYSETUPINSTANCEID(i). 2. Normalize directions: normalW, lightDirW, viewDirW. 3. Compute backlit direction: backLitDirW = - (lightDirW + (1 - SSSRange) normalW). 4. Compute shadow attenuation: UNITYLIGHTATTENUATION(atten, i, i.worldPos). 3. Fragment Shader - Cosine Terms: 1. nl = saturate((dot(normalW, lightDirW) + 0.5) / 1.5) 2. nv = saturate(dot(normalW, viewDirW)) 3. sss = saturate(dot(normalW, backLitDirW)) 4. Fragment Shader - Noise Sampling and Clipping: 1. Sample 3D noise: noise = tex3D(3DNoise, i.uv).r. 2. Compute rim inverse: rimInv = pow(nv, 0.2). 3. Compute dither: dither = saturate(frac(99999 sin( Time.y (i.worldPos.x + i.worldPos.y)))). 4. Blend noise with dither: noise = lerp(dither, 1, rimInv). 5. Get clip threshold: clipThres = UNITYACCESSINSTANCEDPROP(Props, ClipThres). 6. Clip fragment: clip(noise - clipThres). 5. Fragment Shader - Lighting Terms: 1. Compute layer intensity: layerIntensity = lerp(1, clipThres, DepthContrast). 2. Compute diffuse term: diffuseTerm = pow(nl, DiffuseContrast - max(clipThres, noise)). 3. Compute view term: viewTerm = ViewBrightenIntensity pow(nv, ViewBrightenContrast (1 - clipThres)). 4. Compute SSS term: sssTerm = SSSIntensity pow(sss, SSSContrast + max(clipThres, noise)). 5. Assemble final factor: python finalFactor = 0 if(ApplyDiffuse): finalFactor += diffuseTerm if(ApplySSS): finalFactor += sssTerm if(ApplyShadow): finalFactor = atten if(ApplyViewBrighten): finalFactor = lerp(finalFactor, 1, viewTerm) finalFactor = saturate(layerIntensity finalFactor) 6. Fragment Shader - Occlusion Mixing: 1. Divide screen position xy by w: i.screenPosxywdepth01z.xy /= i.screenPosxywdepth01z.w. 2. Sample depth from depth normals texture: depthOpaque01 = DecodeFloatRG(tex2D(CameraDepthNormalsTexture, i.screenPosxywdepth01z.xy).zw). 3. Get fragment depth: depthFrag01 = i.screenPosxywdepth01z.z. 4. Compute depth difference: depthDiff = saturate(depthOpaque01 - depthFrag01). 5. Smoothstep and power for occlusion: depthDiff = pow(smoothstep(0, OccludeeVisibleRange 0.1, depthDiff), OccludeeVisibility). 6. Compute alpha: alpha = noise depthDiff. 7. Fragment Shader - Final Output: 1. Compute final color: finalColor = fixed4(LightColor0.rgb lerp(ShadowColor, BrightColor, finalFactor), alpha). 2. Apply fog: UNITYAPPLYFOG(i.fogCoord, finalColor). 3. Return color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct appdata { half4 vertex: POSITION; half3 normal: NORMAL; float2 uv: TEXCOORD0; UNITYVERTEXINPUTINSTANCEID }; struct v2f { float4 pos: SVPOSITION; float3 worldPos: TEXCOORD0; float3 uv: TEXCOORD1; UNITYFOGCOORDS(2) SHADOWCOORDS(3) half3 normalW: TEXCOORD4; float4 screenPosxywdepth01z: TEXCOORD5; UNITYVERTEXINPUTINSTANCEID }; v2f vert(appdata v) { v2f o; UNITYSETUPINSTANCEID(v); UNITYTRANSFERINSTANCEID(v, o); // Displace vertex along normal half posOffset = UNITYACCESSINSTANCEDPROP(Props, PosOffset); v.vertex.xyz += v.normal posOffset; // Clip space position o.pos = UnityObjectToClipPos(v.vertex); // World space position and normal o.worldPos = mul(unityObjectToWorld, v.vertex).xyz; o.normalW = UnityObjectToWorldNormal(v.normal); // Screen position and depth o.screenPosxywdepth01z = ComputeScreenPos(o.pos); o.screenPosxywdepth01z.z = COMPUTEDEPTH01; // UVs o.uv.xyz = v.vertex.xyz 0.5 + 0.5; half noiseTiling = UNITYACCESSINSTANCEDPROP(Props, NoiseTiling); o.uv = o.uv noiseTiling + Time.y UVSpeed; UNITYTRANSFERFOG(o, o.pos); TRANSFERSHADOW(o); return o; } fixed4 frag(v2f i): SVTarget { UNITYSETUPINSTANCEID(i); // Directions half3 normalW = normalize(i.normalW); half3 lightDirW = normalize(WorldSpaceLightPos0.xyz); half3 viewDirW = normalize(WorldSpaceCameraPos.xyz - i.worldPos); half3 backLitDirW = -(lightDirW + (1 - SSSRange) normalW); // Shadow UNITYLIGHTATTENUATION(atten, i, i.worldPos); // Cosine terms half nl = saturate((dot(normalW, lightDirW) + 0.5) / 1.5); half nv = saturate(dot(normalW, viewDirW)); half sss = saturate(dot(normalW, backLitDirW)); // Noise and Clipping half noise = tex3D(3DNoise, i.uv).r; half rimInv = pow(nv, 0.2); half dither = saturate(frac(99999 sin(Time.y (i.worldPos.x + i.worldPos.y)))); noise = lerp(dither, 1, rimInv); half clipThres = UNITYACCESSINSTANCEDPROP(Props, ClipThres); clip(noise - clipThres); // Lighting Terms half layerIntensity = lerp(1, clipThres, DepthContrast); half diffuseTerm = pow(nl, DiffuseContrast - max(clipThres, noise)); half viewTerm = ViewBrightenIntensity pow(nv, ViewBrightenContrast (1 - clipThres)); half sssTerm = SSSIntensity pow(sss, SSSContrast + max(clipThres, noise)); half finalFactor = 0; if(ApplyDiffuse) finalFactor += diffuseTerm; if(ApplySSS) finalFactor += sssTerm; if(ApplyShadow) finalFactor = atten; if(ApplyViewBrighten) finalFactor = lerp(finalFactor, 1, viewTerm); finalFactor = saturate(layerIntensity finalFactor); // Occlusion Mixing float2 screenUV = i.screenPosxywdepth01z.xy / i.screenPosxywdepth01z.w; half depthOpaque01 = DecodeFloatRG(tex2D(CameraDepthNormalsTexture, screenUV).zw); half depthFrag01 = i.screenPosxywdepth01z.z; half depthDiff = saturate(depthOpaque01 - depthFrag01); depthDiff = pow(smoothstep(0, OccludeeVisibleRange 0.1, depthDiff), OccludeeVisibility); half alpha = noise depthDiff; // Final Color fixed4 finalColor = fixed4(LightColor0.rgb lerp(ShadowColor, BrightColor, finalFactor), alpha); UNITYAPPLYFOG(i.fogCoord, finalColor); return finalColor; } Parameters: PosOffset: Instanced half, default 0. Normal extrusion amount. NoiseTiling: Instanced half, range [0.1, 10], default 1. UV scaling. UVSpeed: Float, range [0, 1], default 0.1. UV flow speed. ClipThres: Instanced half, range [0, 1], default 0. Alpha clip threshold. DepthContrast: Float, range [0, 1], default 0.4. Layer intensity blending. DiffuseContrast: Float, range [1, 2], default 1.2. Diffuse exponent. SSSRange: Float, range [0, 1], default 1. SSS direction offset. SSSIntensity: Float, range [0, 1], default 0.8. SSS intensity. SSSContrast: Float, range [0, 1], default 0.2. SSS exponent offset. ViewBrightenIntensity: Float, range [0, 1], default 0.2. View brightening intensity. ViewBrightenContrast: Float, range [1, 10], default 2. View brightening exponent. 3DNoise: 3D texture sampler. OccludeeVisibility: Float, range [0.01, 1], default 0. Occlusion visibility strength. OccludeeVisibleRange: Float, range [0, 1], default 0.1. Occlusion visible range. BrightColor: Color, default (1,1,1). Lit albedo. ShadowColor: Color, default (0,0,0). Shadow albedo. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Light Leaking: The modified nl calculation saturate((dot(normalW, lightDirW) + 0.5) / 1.5) prevents light from leaking into the back of the volume by shifting and scaling the cosine term. Depth Precision: SVPOSITION input in the fragment shader cannot be used directly for clip-space Z because xy are screen pixel coordinates and zw meaning is undocumented. ComputeScreenPos and COMPUTEDEPTH01 must be used in the vertex shader instead. Occlusion Requirements: Uses CameraDepthNormalsTexture for occlusion depth, which requires opaque objects (RenderType = "Opaque"). Alternative CameraDepthTexture requires Queue <= 2500 and ShadowCaster pass. Time Complexity: O(N) per fragment, where N is the number of cloud layers. Each layer requires a 3D texture sample, lighting calculations, and depth texture sampling. Memory Complexity: O(L) for instanced properties, where L is the number of layers. Requires CameraDepthNormalsTexture which adds memory bandwidth pressure. Measured Performance: Performance scales linearly with the number of layers and resolution. The use of instanced rendering (DrawMeshInstanced) reduces CPU overhead compared to individual mesh draws. Strengths: Real-time occlusion with scene geometry, visually rich lighting model (SSS, view brightening), efficient instancing. Limitations: Hard edges from alpha clipping (mitigated by dithering), requires opaque geometry for occlusion, potential overdraw if layers are not sorted or culled properly. When to Use: Real-time cloud rendering in games where interaction with scene geometry is desired. When Not to Use: Offline rendering requiring physically accurate volumetric scattering, or scenes with no opaque geometry for occlusion. Originated from the "VolumeCloud" project by Shuchang Xu, an unofficial implementation of procedural cloud rendering in Unity. It builds on the techniques described in Cloud Fragment Shader (3D Noise Volume Rendering) by adding occlusion and instancing. ShuchangXu/VolumeCloud, https://github.com/ShuchangXu/VolumeCloud, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Horizon Zero Dawn Volumetric Cloud System
head: Horizon Clouds, Procedural Volumetric Clouds for Horizon Zero Dawn
body: The Horizon Zero Dawn Volumetric Cloud System is a real-time procedural method for generating realistic, evolving cloudscapes by combining Perlin noise with Worley noise offsets, stored in compressed 3D and 2D textures. It solves the limitations of previous asset-based approaches (billboards, sky domes) which failed to support inter-cloud shadowing, temporal evolution, and overhead cloud movement while incurring high memory usage and overdraw. Unlike standard fractal Brownian motion (fBm) which lacks large governing shapes, this system uses "Perlin-Worley" noise to create packed, billowy, cauliflower-like structures that imply motion and evolution. Inputs and Outputs Input: 3D sample position \mathbf{P} (world or camera space), altitude/height signal, and coverage signal. Output: Cloud density and shape data for volume rendering. Data Structures The system relies on three pre-computed noise textures to minimize runtime computation and texture reads: 1. Noise Texture 1 (Base Shape): Resolution: 128^3 Channels: 4 Layout: Channel 0: Perlin-Worley noise (base shape). Channels 1–3: Layered Worley noise at increasing frequencies. 2. Noise Texture 2 (Detail): Resolution: 32^3 Channels: 3 Layout: Worley noise at increasing frequencies to add detail to the base shape. 3. Noise Texture 3 (Turbulence): Resolution: 128^2 Channels: 3 Layout: Curl noise (non-divergent) used to distort shapes and fake fluid motion. Parameters Height Signal: A mathematical preset representing major low-altitude cloud types. It is used to blend between cloud types at the sample position. Coverage Signal: A scalar value between 0 and 1 indicating the desired cloud coverage at the sample position. Algorithm Steps 1. Base Shape Generation: Sample 3DTexture1 at position \mathbf{P}. The result is multiplied by the Height Signal to build the low-resolution base cloud shape. This combines the connectedness of Perlin noise with the dilated, billowy shapes of Worley noise. 2. Detail and Turbulence: Sample 3DTexture2 for high-frequency Worley detail and 2DTexture3 for curl noise. The curl noise is used to distort the cloud shape, simulating turbulence and fluid motion. 3. Erosion and Coverage: Erode the result from Step 1. Multiply the eroded shape by the Coverage Signal (0 to 1). 4. Base Density Reduction: Reduce density at the base of the cloud to create whispy bottoms. This ensures that density increases naturally with altitude, enhancing realism. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computehorizonclouddensity(P, heightsignal, coveragesignal): # Step 1: Sample Base Shape from 3DTexture1 (128^3, 4 channels) # Channel 0 is Perlin-Worley, Channels 1-3 are layered Worley basenoise = sample3dtexture(3DTexture1, P) # Multiply by height signal to blend cloud types based on altitude baseshape = basenoise heightsignal # Step 2: Sample Detail from 3DTexture2 (32^3, 3 channels) # Adds high-frequency Worley detail detailnoise = sample3dtexture(3DTexture2, P) # Step 3: Sample Turbulence from 2DTexture3 (128^2, 3 channels) # Curl noise for non-divergent distortion turbulence = sample2dtexture(2DTexture3, P.xy) # Apply turbulence to distort the shape distortedshape = baseshape + turbulence # Step 4: Erode the result erodedshape = erode(distortedshape) # Step 5: Multiply by coverage signal coveredshape = erodedshape coveragesignal # Step 6: Reduce density at the base for whispy bottoms # This assumes 'P.y' or a derived altitude metric is available altitudefactor = computealtitudefactor(P) finaldensity = coveredshape altitudefactor return finaldensity Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The system uses compressed textures to save memory, which may introduce quantization artifacts if resolution is too low. The chosen resolutions (128^3 and 32^3) balance quality and performance. Boundaries: The textures are designed to be tiling, ensuring seamless repetition across the sky domain. Degenerate Input: If the coverage signal is 0, the cloud density is 0. If the height signal is not properly normalized, cloud types may not blend correctly. Performance: Renders in approximately 2 milliseconds per frame. Memory Usage: The system consumes 20 MB of RAM. Strengths: Real-time performance suitable for modern games. Supports inter-cloud shadowing and temporal evolution. Generates realistic, billowy cloud shapes that imply motion. Low memory footprint compared to asset-based solutions. Limitations: Relies on pre-computed textures, limiting on-the-fly generation of arbitrary cloud structures. Complexity of the noise combination (Perlin-Worley) may be difficult to tune for specific artistic styles. When to Use: Real-time volumetric cloud rendering where performance and memory are constrained, and realistic, evolving cloud shapes are required. When Not to Use: Offline rendering where quality is paramount and performance is not a constraint, or when simple, static cloud layers are sufficient. The system was developed for Horizon Zero Dawn by Guerrilla Games, with significant contributions from Han Vos. It was presented at the Advances in Real-Time Rendering (ARTR) 2015 conference. The development was driven by the need to replace asset-based cloud solutions (billboards, sky domes) which could not support inter-cloud shadowing, evolution, or overhead clouds, and suffered from high memory usage and overdraw. The core noise technique, Worley noise, was introduced by Steven Worley in 1996, originally for caustics and water effects. The "Perlin-Worley" hybrid was developed to combine the connectedness of Perlin noise with the packed, billowy shapes of inverted Worley noise, addressing the lack of large governing shapes in standard fBm approaches. name: Speckle Correlation Acquisition for Phase Functions
head: Direct Phase Function Acquisition via Speckle Correlation, Direct acquisition, Direct acquisition of volumetric scattering phase function using speckle correlations, Direct material acquisition using speckle correlations, Empirical Speckle Correlation Acquisition, Phase function from speckles, Speckle Correlation Phase Function Measurement
body: This method extracts the volumetric scattering phase function \rho directly from measured speckle correlations, avoiding the computational cost of inverse rendering optimization. It isolates single-scattering light paths by capturing speckle images under two different illumination directions and computing their spatial correlation, allowing accurate phase function estimation even in thick media where ground-truth single-scattering references are unavailable. Unlike naive intensity profiling which assumes thin samples, this correlation-based approach yields higher anisotropy parameters and remains valid for optical depths (OD) up to 7–8. Inputs: Coherent laser source (wavelength \lambda, e.g., 632nm). Scattering sample of known thickness, sandwiched between parallel glass slides. 4f optical system (two lenses, focal length f). 2D sensor (camera) at the focal plane of the second lens. Motorized translation stages for the source and sample. Outputs: Estimated phase function \rho(\tau), typically fitted to a parametric model like Henyey-Greenstein. Data Structures: Image I{\hat{i}}(\hat{v}): 2D array of pixel intensities corresponding to viewing directions \hat{v} for a specific illumination direction \hat{i}. Window W: A local region of pixels (e.g., 100 \times 100) used for spatial averaging. Parameters: Focal length f: 10.5 cm. Beam diameter: 3 mm. Speckle grain size: 1–2 pixels. Window size w: 100 \times 100 pixels (balance between noise reduction and spatial resolution). Max measurable scattering angle: ~8 degrees (limited by lens aperture). Steps: 1. Setup Optical System: Construct a 4f system. Place two lenses of focal length f separated by distance 2f. Place the scattering sample halfway between them (at the Fourier plane of the imaging lens). Place a coherent point source (fibered laser) at the focal plane of the first lens. Place the 2D sensor at the focal plane of the second lens. 2. Sample Preparation: Cast the target material between two microscope glass slides using spacing stickers (e.g., 250\mum thickness) to ensure parallelism and uniform thickness. For optically thick materials requiring thinner samples, use tape layers (~40\mum), noting reduced uniformity. 3. Illumination Variation: Translate the point source laterally on a 2D stage at the first lens's focal plane. This generates collimated beams at different angles \hat{i}. The source translation allows tilting the illumination beam. 4. Image Capture: Capture speckle images I{\hat{i}1}(\hat{v}) and I{\hat{i}2}(\hat{v}) for two distinct illumination directions \hat{i}1 and \hat{i}2. To improve statistics, capture multiple images by shifting the sample on a motorized stage to illuminate different locations on the sample area. 5. Image Filtering: Reject bad images by analyzing the maximal energy of the ballistic term. Reject images where the ballistic term's energy deviates significantly from the median, indicating sample defects (e.g., air bubbles) or non-uniformity. 6. Registration and Global Shift: Detect the strongest pixel in each image to determine the illumination directions \hat{i}1 and \hat{i}2. Compute the global displacement vector \mathbf{\Delta} = \hat{i}2 - \hat{i}1. Globally shift the second image I{\hat{i}2} by \mathbf{\Delta} to align speckle features, resulting in I{\hat{i}2}(\hat{v} + \mathbf{\Delta}). 7. Local Registration (Distortion Correction): Due to optical aberrations, global shift is insufficient. For every local window (e.g., 100 \times 100), locally shift the windows by a few pixels to maximize correlation, accounting for lens distortions. 8. Covariance Estimation: Compute the correlation C(\tau) for a scattering angle displacement \tau using spatial averaging over a local window W around \tau. The estimator is: C(\tau) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{\zeta \in W} \left[ I1(\hat{i}1 + \tau + \zeta) \cdot I2(\hat{i}1 + \tau + \zeta + \mathbf{\Delta}) \right] - \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum{\zeta \in W} I1(\hat{i}1 + \tau + \zeta) \right) \left( \frac{1}{N} \sum{\zeta \in W} I2(\hat{i}1 + \tau + \zeta + \mathbf{\Delta}) \right) where N is the number of pixels in window W. This avoids noisy single-pixel products. 9. Direction Selection (Optional Optimization): For rotationally invariant phase functions, select measurement directions \tau orthogonal to the illuminator displacement \mathbf{\Delta} (i.e., \mathbf{\Delta} \cdot \tau = 0) to maximize correlation strength. 10. Averaging: Average the correlations produced by pairs of images from multiple samples or multiple locations of the same material to further reject noise. 11. Model Fitting: Fit the estimated correlation values (proportional to the phase function) to a parametric model, such as the Henyey-Greenstein model, to extract parameters like the anisotropy factor g. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def specklecorrelationacquisition(images, deltaglobal, windowsize=100): """ Estimate phase function from speckle correlations. Args: images: List of tuples (I1, I2, localshifts). I1, I2 are 2D numpy arrays (images). localshifts is a list of (dx, dy) for each window position to correct distortion. deltaglobal: Global shift vector (dx, dy) to align I2 to I1. windowsize: Size of the local window for correlation estimation. Returns: correlationmap: 2D array of correlation values C(tau). """ # Assume images are pre-registered globally and filtered # I1 and I2 are the primary pair for this calculation I1 = images[0][0] I2 = images[0][1] H, W = I1.shape correlationmap = np.zeros((H, W)) # Define window boundaries halfw = windowsize // 2 for y in range(halfw, H - halfw): for x in range(halfw, W - halfw): # Determine local shift for this window to correct aberrations # In practice, this is found by maximizing correlation locally # Here we assume localshifts provides the correction for the window centered at (x,y) # If not provided, assume 0 for simplicity, but note this is a critical step dxlocal, dylocal = 0, 0 if 'localshifts' in images[0]: # Placeholder for retrieving pre-computed local shifts # In real implementation, this would be a lookup or optimization pass # Define window region in I1 y1, y2 = y - halfw, y + halfw x1, x2 = x - halfw, x + halfw # Define corresponding region in I2 # Apply global shift and local shift y2shift = y2 + int(deltaglobal[1]) + int(dylocal) x2shift = x2 + int(deltaglobal[0]) + int(dxlocal) y1shift = y1 + int(deltaglobal[1]) + int(dylocal) x1shift = x1 + int(deltaglobal[0]) + int(dxlocal) # Extract windows # Handle boundary checks if not (0 <= y1shift < H and 0 <= y2shift <= H and 0 <= x1shift < W and 0 <= x2shift <= W): continue win1 = I1[y1:y2, x1:x2] win2 = I2[y1shift:y2shift, x1shift:x2shift] # Compute correlation C(tau) for tau = (x, y) relative to center # Formula: E[I1I2] - E[I1]E[I2] N = win1.size term1 = np.mean(win1 win2) term2 = np.mean(win1) np.mean(win2) correlationmap[y, x] = term1 - term2 return correlationmap def estimatephasefunction(correlationmap, windowsize=100): """ Fit Henyey-Greenstein model to the correlation map. Note: The correlation is proportional to the phase function. """ # Normalize correlation map #... (normalization steps) # Fit Henyey-Greenstein # rho(theta) = (1-g^2) / (4pi (1 + g^2 - 2gcos(theta))^(3/2)) # This requires mapping pixel coordinates to scattering angles theta. # Given the 4f system, theta is related to pixel position. # This step is implementation-specific based on calibration. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ballistic Light Saturation: Ballistic light focuses on a small number of pixels, causing high saturation that corrupts scattered values. This prevents measurement of small \tau values (small angles). HDR capture and Jinc subtraction are impractical due to sample non-uniformity and optical flare. Angular Range Limit: The lens aperture limits the maximal measurable scattering angle to about 8 degrees. High OD Noise: For very thick samples (e.g., OD > 10), the correlation is too noisy for practical usage. Window Size Trade-off: Smaller windows are noisy; very large windows over-smooth the phase function. Typical value is 100x100 pixels. Quantifies the statistical reliability of estimating the covariance between two complex speckle fields. It derives the expected SNR for the estimator X of the cross-covariance term |C{12}|^2, guiding the selection of window sizes and the number of averaged frames to balance noise reduction against spatial blurring. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of pixels N in the window and the number of windows. The correlation computation is O(N{windows} \cdot N{pixels}). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the input images and the correlation map. Performance: Validated on materials like silica beads, polystyrene, lotion, honey, wax, toothpaste, milk, mustard, conditioner, and clay. Strengths: Directly extracts phase function without inverse rendering optimization. Works for thick samples (OD up to 7-8) where naive intensity profiling fails. Yields higher anisotropy parameters g than intensity profiles (e.g., Lotion: 0.90 vs 0.85). Limitations: Limited angular range (~8 degrees). Ballistic saturation corrupts small angles. High OD samples produce noisy results. Requires precise optical alignment and calibration for distortion correction. When to Use: When direct measurement of phase function is needed for thick, turbid media, and computational inverse rendering is prohibitive or inaccurate. When Not to Use: When full angular range is required, or for very high OD samples where noise dominates. The method was introduced by Marina Alterman, Evgeniia Saiko, and Anat Levin in 2022. It builds on the principle that speckle correlations serve as a gating mechanism to isolate single-scattering light paths. Previous methods relied on inverse rendering optimization [Gkioulekas et al. 2013] or naive intensity profiling which assumed thin samples. This approach allows direct acquisition even in medium-thickness volumes. name: Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) Analysis for Covariance Estimation
head: SNR for Speckle Covariance Estimation
body: This method quantifies the statistical reliability of estimating the covariance between two complex speckle fields from empirical image data, which is the core operation in Speckle Correlation Acquisition for Phase Functions. It derives the expected Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) for the estimator X of the cross-covariance term |C{12}|^2. It sets apart from naive intensity profiling by providing a theoretical bound on noise based on speckle statistics, guiding the selection of window sizes and the number of averaged frames to balance noise reduction against spatial blurring. Inputs: u1, u2: Two complex random variables representing the complex speckle fields scattered from the same medium under two different illumination directions. N: The number of independent speckle measurements (pixels in a spatial window or independent frames) used for averaging. C{11}: The mean intensity of the speckle field, assumed known or estimated from the speckle image. C{12}: The cross-covariance between the two speckle fields. Outputs: SNR(X): The expected signal-to-noise ratio for the covariance estimator. E[X]: The expected value of the estimator, representing the correlation between speckle intensities. Data Structures: The method operates on scalar statistical moments derived from the complex fields. No specific binary layout is defined; values are treated as floating-point numbers. Steps: 1. Define the Estimator: Let X be the empirical estimator for the covariance between the two speckle fields. 2. Calculate Expected Value: The expected value of the estimator is the squared magnitude of the cross-covariance: E[X] = |C{12}|^2 This value corresponds to the correlation between speckle intensities C(\tau) targeted in the parent method. 3. Calculate Variance: The variance of the estimator X is given by the full statistical derivation: Var[X] = \frac{1}{16} \left( \frac{4|C{12}|^2}{C{11}^2} + \frac{6|C{12}|^4}{C{11}^3} + \frac{15C{11}^4}{C{11}^4} \right) Note: The source text presents the third term as 15C{11}^4 / C{11}^4, which simplifies to 15. The denominators for the first two terms are inferred from the structure of speckle statistics normalization. 4. Simplify Variance: Since the correlation between speckle fields is not exact, |C{12}| < C{11}. Consequently, the term 15C{11}^4/C{11}^4 = 15 is the dominant term in the variance equation. The first two terms are neglected to simplify the expression: Var[X] \approx \frac{15}{16} Correction/Clarification: The source text states "the largest term in Eq. (10) is C{11}^4... neglecting the first two terms." However, the final simplified SNR formula provided is |C{12}|^4 / (4 C{11}^4). Let us re-evaluate the simplification based on the final result provided in the source. The source provides the simplified SNR as: SNR(X) = \frac{|C{12}|^4}{4 C{11}^4} Using the definition SNR(X) = \frac{E[X]^2}{Var[X]}, and knowing E[X] = |C{12}|^2, we have: SNR(X) = \frac{|C{12}|^4}{Var[X]} Equating this to the source's simplified result: \frac{|C{12}|^4}{Var[X]} = \frac{|C{12}|^4}{4 C{11}^4} \implies Var[X] = 4 C{11}^4 This implies the source's simplification of the variance term leads to 4 C{11}^4. The text says "largest term... is C{11}^4". It is likely the source simplifies the variance expression differently or there is a normalization factor not explicitly detailed in the snippet. We must follow the source's final formula for implementation. Revised Step 4 (Simplified SNR): SNR(X) = \frac{|C{12}|^4}{4 C{11}^4} 5. Scale by Averaging: If N independent speckle measurements X1, \dots, XN are averaged, the variance of the mean is reduced by N, and the SNR scales linearly with N: E\left[\frac{1}{N} \sum{n=1}^N Xn\right] = E[X] Var\left[\frac{1}{N} \sum{n=1}^N Xn\right] = \frac{Var[X]}{N} SNR{avg}(X) = N \cdot SNR(X) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatesnrcovariance(c12magnitude, c11meanintensity, numsamples): """ Calculate the SNR for covariance estimation from speckle fields. Args: c12magnitude (float): Magnitude of the cross-covariance |C12|. c11meanintensity (float): Mean intensity C11. numsamples (int): Number of independent speckle measurements N. Returns: float: The expected Signal-to-Noise Ratio. """ # Avoid division by zero if c11meanintensity == 0: return 0.0 # Expected value of the estimator X # E[X] = |C12|^2 expectedvalue = c12magnitude 2 # Simplified SNR formula derived from source # SNR(X) = |C12|^4 / (4 C11^4) # Note: This formula assumes the variance simplification described in the source # where the dominant term is retained and others neglected. numerator = c12magnitude 4 denominator = 4.0 (c11meanintensity 4) if denominator == 0: return 0.0 basesnr = numerator / denominator # Scale SNR by the number of independent samples N finalsnr = basesnr numsamples return finalsnr Parameters: C{11}: Mean intensity. In practice, this is estimated from the speckle image. N: Window size (number of pixels) or number of frames. Increasing N reduces noise but blurs the phase function structure if too large. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Approximation Validity: The simplified SNR formula assumes |C{12}| < C{11}. If the fields are perfectly correlated, the approximation may fail. Window Size Trade-off: A larger window increases N, improving SNR, but risks blurring the spatial structure of the phase function. Mean Intensity Estimation: The derivation assumes C{11} is known, but it must be estimated from data in practice, introducing additional uncertainty not captured in the ideal SNR formula. Time Complexity: The calculation of SNR is O(1) per estimation point. However, the acquisition cost depends on N, the number of frames or pixels averaged. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the statistical moments. Storage of raw speckle images is O(N) per frame. Strengths: Provides a theoretical basis for choosing window sizes and frame counts to achieve a desired noise level. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that speckle fields are complex Gaussian random variables (implied by Goodman's work cited). The simplified formula may underestimate noise if |C{12}| is close to C{11}. When to use: When designing the acquisition parameters for speckle correlation phase function measurement. When not to use: When high-fidelity noise modeling is required beyond the simplified approximation, or when the medium is not homogeneous. This analysis originates from the work on direct acquisition of volumetric scattering phase functions using speckle correlations. It builds on the statistical properties of speckle patterns described by Goodman [Goodman 2007]. The method is used to justify the noise performance of the covariance estimation step in the parent method, ensuring that the measured correlations are statistically significant. name: Simulation output
body: This family covers methods that generate volumetric data by simulating physical phenomena (fluids, fire, smoke) or kinematic systems, producing a discrete or analytic representation suitable for rendering. Unlike Voxelization which converts static geometry, or Procedural and implicit volumes which define volume via analytic functions, simulation output methods evolve state over time based on physical laws (e.g., Navier-Stokes, Position-Based Dynamics) or kinematic rules. The core mechanism involves defining a spatial domain (grid or particles), evolving physical quantities (velocity, density, temperature) through time-stepping, and storing the result in a structure (voxel grid, particle list, or Gaussian kernel) that serves as the input for a volume renderer. All methods in this family map a conceptual or physical source into a discrete or analytic volumetric representation suitable for rendering. The core mechanism involves: 1. Domain Definition: Establishing a spatial domain, typically a 3D grid with resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz) and bounding box, or an infinite analytic space. 2. Value Assignment: Determining the value (density, distance, color) for each point in the domain based on the source method (geometric intersection, function evaluation, or physical state). 3. Storage/Access: Either storing the result in a discrete array (voxelization, simulation) or providing an interface to compute it on-the-fly (procedural). Gaussian Splashing combines 3D Gaussian Splatting with Position-Based Dynamics to simulate fluids, deformable bodies, and rigid objects. It distinguishes itself from vanilla 3DGS by enriching Gaussian kernels with material parameters and aligning kernel orientation with surface normals to eliminate spiky noise. Choose this when interactive, physically-based rendering of deformable objects from novel views is required. Position Based Fluids is a Lagrangian particle-based method that enforces incompressibility by iteratively correcting particle positions based on density constraints. It distinguishes itself from Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics by treating fluid dynamics as a constraint satisfaction problem rather than solving Navier-Stokes equations via pressure gradients, offering superior stability for incompressible flows. Choose this for real-time, stable fluid simulation where meshing is undesirable. This component provides the mathematical and algorithmic building blocks for solving the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on a grid. It distinguishes itself by modularizing advection, diffusion, and projection steps, allowing flexible integration into larger simulation pipelines. Choose this when building a custom grid-based fluid solver from scratch. Grid-Based Simulation maps physical sources (fluids, smoke, fire) into a discrete volumetric representation by solving partial differential equations on a structured spatial domain. It differs from particle-based siblings by storing state in fixed voxel arrays, enabling efficient divergence and advection calculations via 3D textures. Choose this for grid-based fire and smoke effects with explicit physical coupling. A method tracking a reaction coordinate to simulate fire, indicating time since ignition and fuel exhaustion. The coordinate Y evolves as \frac{\partial Y}{\partial t} = -(u \cdot \nabla)Y - k, where k is a constant decrement per time step. A value of 1 indicates ignition, and <0 indicates exhaustion. It is advected using PSADVECTMACCORMACK with k added to the result, and a spherical region is set to 1 to continuously generate fuel. Particles are used as tracer elements to visualize flow, droplets for fire suppression, or fuel elements (embers). Positions are determined by \frac{dxp}{dt} = V(xp, t), assuming drag force is large compared to gravity (mg). Particle size is specified via glPointSize(partpointsize) and streak line length in seconds. Velocity field and particle motion are computed by FDS and communicated to Smokeview via data files. A kinematic approach to simulate galaxy time evolution using differential rotation laws and first-order integration, without full dynamic simulation. Gas and stars on the disk rotate according to a typical galaxy rotation curve, while bulge stars rotate with constant velocity balancing gravitational attraction. Equations of motion are integrated using first-order methods; numerical errors amplify, making the simulation meaningful for only a few hundred million years. Double precision is required for geometrical calculations to handle the large dynamic range. Used to render the galaxy component within cosmological simulations. A simulation driving the control points of the deformation curve, accounting for wind, high-energy dispersion, and thermal buoyancy. The velocity \vec{v} combines base fire velocity, wind \vec{w}(x,t), high-energy dispersion \vec{d}(T), and thermal buoyancy \vec{c}(T, \text{age}). Thermal expansion uses \beta = 1/T, gravity g, and ambient temperature T0 \approx 300\text{K}. Simulation-based volume data generation has roots in computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and scientific visualization. Early methods focused on grid-based Eulerian approaches for smoke and fire, such as the MacCormack advection scheme and reaction coordinate tracking described in GPU Gems. Lagrangian methods like Position-Based Fluids emerged to address stability issues in particle-based simulations. In scientific visualization, tools like Smokeview used massless particles and volumetric rendering to visualize Fire Dynamics Simulation (FDS) data. Kinematic simulations have been applied in astrophysics to visualize galaxy evolution within cosmological contexts using double-precision arithmetic. Procedural fire systems also integrate particle simulations for macro-level effects like wind and thermal buoyancy, combined with pixel-shader noise for micro-level flicker. furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, https://github.com/furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids, https://wo1fsea.github.io/files/AboutNavMesh/P5GPUGems3Real-TimeSimulationandRenderingof3DFluids.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Smokeview (Version 6) A Tool for Visualizing Fire Dynamics Simulation Data Volume II: Technical Reference Guide, https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.sp.1017-2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Splotch: visualizing cosmological simulations, https://doi.org/10.1088/1367-2630/10/12/125006, fetched 2026-10-28 Real-time procedural volumetric fire, https://doi.org/10.1145/1230100.1230131, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Gaussian Splashing
body: Gaussian Splashing is a unified framework that combines 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with Position-Based Dynamics (PBD) to enable realistic, interactive simulation and rendering of fluids, deformable bodies, and rigid objects from novel views. It addresses the limitation of vanilla 3DGS, which simplifies light field composition without well-defined appearance properties, making fluid rendering cumbersome. Gaussian Splashing distinguishes itself by enriching Gaussian kernels with material parameters (diffusiveness, specularity, roughness, normals) and aligning kernel orientation with surface normals to eliminate spiky noise from rotational deformation. Gaussian Splashing treats each Gaussian kernel as a discrete physical particle with volume, allowing direct simulation within the rendering pipeline. The method integrates physically based rendering (PBR) to augment dynamic surface reflections on fluids. Inputs: Initial 3DGS scene representation (positions, covariances, opacities, colors); camera poses; scene geometry (meshes for solids); physical parameters for PBD (density, viscosity, surface tension). Outputs: Rendered images from novel viewpoints; simulated particle states over time. The core data structure is the Gaussian kernel, augmented from standard 3DGS with additional fields for physics and material properties: 1. Position (\mathbf{p}): 3D center of the Gaussian. 2. Covariance (\Sigma): Defines the shape and orientation of the Gaussian ellipsoid. 3. Opacity (\alpha): Transparency of the kernel. 4. Spherical Harmonics (\mathbf{c}): View-dependent color coefficients. 5. Normal (\mathbf{n}): Surface normal vector, aligned with the kernel's orientation for solids and approximated for fluids. 6. Material Parameters: Diffusiveness, specularity, roughness. 7. Mass/Volume: Physical properties for PBD integration. 1. Reconstruction and Disentanglement: Reconstruct surfaces from input images using 3DGS and disentangle objects that will be actively simulated (solids, fluids) from static background elements. 2. Mesh-Based Simulation Framework: Attach Gaussians to meshes for solid objects to enable texture rendering and physical interaction. 3. Normal Alignment and Material Enrichment: For solids: Augment each Gaussian kernel with a normal vector and align the kernel’s orientation with this surface normal to refine the PBD simulation. For fluids: Enrich Gaussians with material parameters (diffusiveness, specularity, roughness) to handle specular and reflective objects. 4. Physics Simulation (PBD): Apply Position-Based Dynamics to update particle positions and velocities. Solid Constraint: Use an anisotropy loss during 3DGS training to cap the stretching ratio, mitigating rendering artifacts induced by rotational deformation. Fluid Normal Approximation: For fluid kernels near the surface: Approximate the normal based on surface tension. For scattered fluid droplets: Estimate normal information using a depth volume rendered via the current camera pose. 5. Rendering: Render the scene using the updated Gaussian kernels and integrate PBR to dynamically synthesize specular shading along with fluid movement. 6. Scene Editing (Optional): Augment the system with an image-space segmentation module to select objects of interest from the 3DGS scene, and exploit generative AI to fill missing pixels for physics-based scene editing. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussiansplashinginit(scenedata): """Initialize GSP from input images and scene geometry.""" gaussians = [] # 1. Reconstruct 3DGS scene gaussians.extend(reconstruct3dgs(scenedata.images)) # 2. Disentangle active objects solidmeshes = extractmeshes(scenedata.geometry) fluidparticles = extractfluidparticles(scenedata.geometry) # 3. Attach Gaussians to meshes for solids for mesh in solidmeshes: meshgaussians = [g for g in gaussians if g.onmesh(mesh)] for g in meshgaussians: g.normal = computesurfacenormal(mesh, g.position) g.covariance = aligncovariancetonormal(g.covariance, g.normal) # 4. Initialize fluid Gaussians with material parameters for particle in fluidparticles: g = creategaussian(particle.position) g.material = {'diffusiveness': 0.5, 'specularity': 0.8, 'roughness': 0.2} if isnearsurface(particle.position, fluidparticles): g.normal = computesurfacetensionnormal(particle.position, fluidparticles) else: g.normal = estimatenormalfromdepth(particle.position, scenedata.camerapose) gaussians.append(g) return gaussians def gaussiansplashingstep(gaussians, dt, camerapose): """Perform one step of PBD simulation and render.""" # 1. PBD Simulation updatepbd(gaussians, dt) # 2. Update Normals fluidlist = [g for g in gaussians if g.isfluid] for g in gaussians: if g.isfluid: if isnearsurface(g.position, fluidlist): g.normal = computesurfacetensionnormal(g.position, fluidlist) else: g.normal = estimatenormalfromdepth(g.position, camerapose) # 3. Render return rendergaussianspbr(gaussians, camerapose) def estimatenormalfromdepth(position, camerapose): """Estimate normal for scattered droplets using depth volume.""" depthmap = renderdepth(camerapose) return computenormalfromdepthgradient(depthmap, position) def reconstruct3dgs(images): return [] # Standard 3DGS optimization routine def extractmeshes(geometry): return [] # Mesh extraction routine def extractfluidparticles(geometry): return [] # Fluid region extraction routine def updatepbd(gaussians, dt): for g in gaussians: g.velocity += dt computeforces(g) g.position += dt g.velocity def computesurfacenormal(mesh, pos): return mesh.normalat(pos) def aligncovariancetonormal(cov, n): return rotatematrix(cov, n) def creategaussian(pos): return {'position': pos, 'covariance': identitymatrix(), 'opacity': 1.0, 'normal': [0,0,1], 'issolid': False, 'isfluid': True} def isnearsurface(pos, particles): return any(distance(pos, p) < SURFACETHRESHOLD for p in particles) def computesurfacetensionnormal(pos, particles): return normalize(sum(p.position - pos for p in particles)) def rendergaussianspbr(gaussians, cam): return splatandshade(gaussians, cam) def renderdepth(cam): return depthbufferfromgaussians(cam) def computenormalfromdepthgradient(depthmap, pos): return gradienttonormal(depthmap, pos) Number of solid Gaussian kernels: 334,815. Number of fluid Gaussian kernels: 280,000. Anisotropy Loss Weight: Not given in the sources. Surface Tension Coefficient: Not given in the sources. Rotational Deformation in Solids: Vanilla 3DGS suffers from spiky noises due to rotational deformation. GSP mitigates this by aligning kernel orientation with surface normals and using an anisotropy loss to cap stretching ratio. Fluid Normal Estimation: For scattered fluid droplets, normal information is not directly available from surface tension. GSP resorts to estimating normals using a depth volume rendered via the current camera pose. Vanilla 3DGS Limitations: Vanilla 3DGS simplifies light field composition without well-defined appearance properties, making fluid rendering cumbersome. GSP addresses this by integrating PBR and normal alignment. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Unified framework for solids, fluids, and deformable bodies; realistic surface reflections on dynamic fluids; eliminates spiky noise from rotational deformation; enables novel view synthesis and physics-based scene editing. Limitations: Relies on PBD, which may not capture complex constitutive models as accurately as SPH or FEM; normal estimation for scattered droplets depends on camera pose and depth rendering quality. When to Use: When realistic interaction between solids and fluids is required in a dynamic scene with novel view synthesis. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity fluid physics (e.g., complex viscosity, turbulence) is more important than visual appearance and novel view synthesis. Gaussian Splashing was introduced by Tianjia Shao, Hongzhi Wu, Kun Zhou, Chenfanfu Jiang, and Yin Yang from the University of Utah, Zhejiang University, and UCLA. The paper was published in CVPR 2025. Gaussian Splashing builds upon GaussianShader, which enriches Gaussians with material parameters. It leverages the coherence of 3DGS and PBD to manage rendering, view synthesis, and dynamics in a cohesive manner. The method addresses the limitations of vanilla 3DGS in handling translucent and specular fluids.
