name: Smoke Source Injection
head: GenerateSmoke, SmokeSourceVolumetric
body: Smoke Source Injection initializes a volumetric smoke source at a fixed grid location by setting density and velocity values within a defined spatial region. It solves the problem of introducing initial mass and momentum into the Navier-Stokes solver domain. It differs from Smoke Advection by creating new data rather than moving existing data, and from the General Fluid Simulation Update Loop by being a boundary/initial condition step rather than a time-integration step. Inputs: Grid resolution RES. Source center coordinates (centerY, centerZ). Source radius threshold RES/10. Density amount dens. Velocity vector \mathbf{v}{init}. Simulation time step dt. Outputs: Updated density field \rho. Updated velocity field \mathbf{u}. Data Structures: 3D arrays for density and velocity components (e.g., density, velX) indexed by grid coordinates (i, j, k). In Unity implementations, these are RenderTexture or ComputeBuffer objects accessed via GPU kernels. Steps: 1. Iterate over grid indices i from 1 to N and j from 1 to N. 2. Calculate the 2D distance from the center in the Y-Z plane: d = \text{hypot}(i - centerY, j - centerZ). 3. If d < RES/10, inject the source values at grid index (5, i, j). 4. Set the density value: dens = (\text{rand()} \% 1000) / 1000.0f for range [0.0, 1.0), or use a user-defined smokeamount parameter. 5. Set the velocity value: apply a constant X-velocity of 2.0, or use a user-defined smokeinitialvelocity vector. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def injectsmokesource(grid, centery, centerz, radiusthreshold, densityamount, velocityvector): """ Injects smoke density and velocity into the grid. Implements the logic from and. """ resy = grid.height resz = grid.depth for i in range(1, resy + 1): for j in range(1, resz + 1): dist = math.hypot(i - centery, j - centerz) if dist < radiusthreshold: grid.density[5, i, j] = densityamount grid.velx[5, i, j] = velocityvector.x grid.vely[5, i, j] = velocityvector.y grid.velz[5, i, j] = velocityvector.z Parameters: centerY: Y-axis center of the smoke source. Typical value: RES/4. centerZ: Z-axis center of the smoke source. Typical value: RES/2. smokeamount: Amount of density to add. Type: float. smokeinitialvelocity: Velocity vector to add. Type: Vector3. active: Boolean flag. Defined in but noted as not used in the provided snippet. Edge Cases: Precision: Random density generation in uses integer modulo arithmetic, which may introduce bias if not handled carefully. Boundaries: The source region must be clamped to the grid boundaries to avoid out-of-bounds access. What it is: Moves existing smoke density and velocity fields through the grid. Difference: Transports data; does not create new mass. When to choose: For time-stepping after injection. Link: Smoke Advection What it is: The complete time-step cycle including advection, diffusion, and pressure projection. Difference: Orchestrates the entire physics update; injection is a sub-step or initial condition. When to choose: For the main simulation loop. Link: General Fluid Simulation Update Loop Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: GPU implementations (e.g., Unity Compute Shaders) allow parallel injection across many threads, significantly speeding up the process for large grids. CPU implementations are simpler but slower for high resolutions. Strengths: Simple to implement; allows for dynamic source placement. Limitations: Random density in may lead to visual noise; fixed radius in may not suit all artistic needs. The specific implementations cited here are from open-source projects demonstrating real-time volumetric smoke simulation. nevermoe/SmokeSimulation, https://github.com/nevermoe/SmokeSimulation, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, https://github.com/furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Smoke Advection
head: Tracking additional quantities like density and temperature, MacCormack routine for smoke
body: Smoke advection tracks scalar fields (density, temperature, color) transported by the fluid velocity field to visualize fluid motion, as the velocity field alone lacks visual detail. It solves the passive scalar transport equation \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t} = -(\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla) \phi using the same MacCormack advection routine applied to the velocity field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Velocity field \mathbf{u}, previous scalar field \phi^n, time step dt, grid dimensions. Output: Updated scalar field \phi^{n+1}. Data Structures: For each additional quantity \phi (density, temperature, color), allocate a texture or grid with the same dimensions as the velocity grid. Steps: 1. Source Injection: Inject a 3D Gaussian "splat" into a color or density texture each frame to provide a source of smoke. 2. Advection: Advect the scalar field \phi using the MacCormack scheme driven by the velocity field \mathbf{u}. The evolution is governed by \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t} = -(\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla) \phi. 3. Buoyancy (Optional): If temperature T is tracked, compute a buoyant force to influence velocity dynamics, causing hot smoke to rise and cool smoke to fall. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def advectsmoke(phi, u, dt, gridshape): """ Advect scalar field phi using the MacCormack finite-difference scheme. phi: 3D list of scalar values (density/temperature/color) u: 3D list of velocity vectors (ux, uy, uz) dt: time step gridshape: (nx, ny, nz) """ nx, ny, nz = gridshape dx, dy, dz = 1.0, 1.0, 1.0 # Assume unit grid spacing # Predictor step: forward differencing phipred = [[[phi[i][j][k] for k in range(nz)] for j in range(ny)] for i in range(nx)] for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): dphidx = (phi[i + 1 if i + 1 < nx else i][j][k] - phi[i][j][k]) / dx dphidy = (phi[i][j + 1 if j + 1 < ny else j][k] - phi[i][j][k]) / dy dphidz = (phi[i][j][k + 1 if k + 1 < nz else k] - phi[i][j][k]) / dz phipred[i][j][k] -= dt (u[i][j][k][0] dphidx + u[i][j][k][1] dphidy + u[i][j][k][2] dphidz) # Corrector step: backward differencing phinew = [[[phi[i][j][k] for k in range(nz)] for j in range(ny)] for i in range(nx)] for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): dphidx = (phipred[i][j][k] - phipred[i - 1 if i - 1 >= 0 else i][j][k]) / dx dphidy = (phipred[i][j][k] - phipred[i][j - 1 if j - 1 >= 0 else j][k]) / dy dphidz = (phipred[i][j][k] - phipred[i][j][k - 1 if k - 1 >= 0 else k]) / dz phinew[i][j][k] = 0.5 (phi[i][j][k] + phipred[i][j][k] - dt (u[i][j][k][0] dphidx + u[i][j][k][1] dphidy + u[i][j][k][2] dphidz)) return phinew Parameters: dt: Time step. Grid spacing (dx, dy, dz): Assumed unit spacing in the pseudocode; scale derivatives accordingly in practice. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color values have no physical significance but create attractive swirling patterns when advected. Temperature values influence fluid dynamics via buoyant force, requiring coupling with the velocity solver. The MacCormack advection scheme is a higher-order numerical method used to advect scalar fields (such as smoke density or temperature) and vector fields (velocity) in fluid simulations. It achieves second-order accuracy in both time and space by combining a forward differencing predictor step with a backward differencing corrector step, alternating directions to avoid bias. An explicit, two-step, three-time level scheme used to solve unsteady compressible Navier-Stokes equations, chosen for ease of parallelization and implementation. Steps: 1. Predictor step: Calculate a temporary 'predicted' value using forward differencing. 2. Corrector step: Determine the final 'corrected' value using backward differencing. 3. Alternate forward and backward differencing between predictor and corrector steps to avoid bias and achieve second-order accuracy. 4. Subdivide the data domain into blocks; at each time level, exchange solution values at the outermost boundary layers of each block between nearest neighbors after each predictor and corrector step. 5. Application programmer writes a 'Prepare Data' routine to calculate flow properties to be visualized and store them in the appropriate format for rendering. A hybrid rendering technique that combines low-resolution velocity projection with high-resolution density advection to visualize smoke in real-time. It projects velocity on a coarse grid to maintain stability and mass conservation, advects a finer density field using the same MacCormack routine as velocity, and finally ray marches the density in a volume pixel shader. Time Complexity: Second-order accurate in both time and space. Memory Complexity: Requires an additional texture or grid with the same dimensions as the velocity grid for each scalar quantity \phi. Strengths: Easier to parallelize and implement than more sophisticated CFD codes. Limitations: Explicit scheme requires a time step satisfying stability constraints (CFL condition). Origin: Fedkiw et al. 2001. History: Used in real-time simulation and rendering of 3D fluids. Also applied in parallel CFD simulations on architectures like the Intel Paragon. Usage: Visualizing smoke, density, and temperature in fluid simulations. PDF Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids, https://wo1fsea.github.io/files/AboutNavMesh/P5GPUGems3Real-TimeSimulationandRenderingof3DFluids.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) DTIC ADA302573: Runtime Volume Visualization for Parallel CFD., https://archive.org/details/DTICADA302573, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: MacCormack Advection Scheme
head: MacCormack routine
body: The MacCormack advection scheme is a higher-order numerical method used to advect scalar fields (such as smoke density or temperature) and vector fields (velocity) in fluid simulations, designed to reduce the numerical smoothing inherent in standard semi-Lagrangian advection. It achieves this by combining a forward semi-Lagrangian step with a backward correction step, allowing low-resolution grids to retain visual detail comparable to significantly higher-resolution grids using standard first-order methods. Unlike the unconditionally stable semi-Lagrangian scheme, the MacCormack scheme is conditionally stable and requires a limiter to prevent numerical blow-up. The method advects a quantity \phi from time step n to n+1 using two intermediate semi-Lagrangian advection operations. The core update formula is: \begin{aligned} \hat{\phi}^{n+1} &= \mathcal{A}(\phi^n) \\ \hat{\phi}^n &= \mathcal{A}^R(\hat{\phi}^{n+1}) \\ \phi^{n+1} &= \hat{\phi}^{n+1} + \frac{1}{2}(\phi^n - \hat{\phi}^n) \end{aligned} Where \mathcal{A} is the forward semi-Lagrangian advection operator, \mathcal{A}^R is the reversed (backward) semi-Lagrangian advection operator, and \phi^n is the field value at the current time step. Inputs: \phi^n: The scalar or vector field texture at the current time step. \mathbf{u}: The velocity field texture. \Delta t: The simulation time step. Grid dimensions: textureWidth, textureHeight, textureDepth. Outputs: \phi^{n+1}: The advected field texture at the next time step. The implementation operates on 3D textures (volumetric data) where each texel stores the field value (e.g., float4 or float3). The algorithm assumes a grid-based coordinate system where cell indices map to texture coordinates via cellIndex2TexCoord. 1. Trace Backward Characteristic: For the current grid cell, sample the velocity at the cell center using point clamping to avoid interpolation artifacts. Calculate the position at the previous time step by subtracting the velocity scaled by the time step from the current cell index: npos = in.cellIndex – timestep cellVelocity. 2. Locate Sample Corner: Determine the cell corner closest to the traced-back "particle" position by adding 0.5 to the position (to align with grid corners) and flooring the result, then convert this integer grid position to a texture coordinate: npos = floor(npos + float3(0.5f, 0.5f, 0.5f)); npos = cellIndex2TexCoord(npos);. 3. Compute Half-Texel Offsets: Calculate the offset vector ht corresponding to half a texel in each dimension: ht = float3(0.5f / textureWidth, 0.5f / textureHeight, 0.5f / textureDepth). 4. Sample Neighbors for Limiter: Sample the 8 texels closest to the traced-back particle location from the current field \phi^n using point clamping at offsets relative to the cell corner: nodeValues[k] = phin.Sample(samPointClamp, npos + offset) for k=0..7. 5. Determine Valid Range: Compute the component-wise minimum (phiMin) and maximum (phiMax) of the 8 sampled neighbor values to establish the clamping bounds. 6. Forward Advection (\hat{\phi}^{n+1}): Perform a standard semi-Lagrangian advection step by sampling \phi^n at the traced-back position using linear interpolation to obtain \hat{\phi}^{n+1}. 7. Reverse Advection & Combine: Compute \hat{\phi}^n by sampling the forward-advected field \hat{\phi}^{n+1} at the original cell center using point clamping. Combine the intermediate values using the update formula: r = phin1hat.Sample(samLinear, nposTC) + 0.5 (phin.Sample(samPointClamp, in.CENTERCELL) - phinhat.Sample(samPointClamp, in.CENTERCELL)). 8. Clamp (Limiter): Clamp the result r to the range [phiMin, phiMax] to prevent overshooting and ensure stability: r = max(min(r, phiMax), phiMin). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def macCormackadvection(phin, velocity, timestep, texturewidth, textureheight, texturedepth): """ Performs MacCormack advection on a 3D grid. phin: dict mapping (x,y,z) to float, field at time n velocity: dict mapping (x,y,z) to (vx,vy,vz), velocity field timestep: float, dt texturewidth, textureheight, texturedepth: int, grid dimensions Returns: dict mapping (x,y,z) to float, field at time n+1 """ def cellindextotexcoord(index): return (index[0] / texturewidth, index[1] / textureheight, (index[2] + 0.5) / texturedepth) ht = (0.5 / texturewidth, 0.5 / textureheight, 0.5 / texturedepth) offsets = [ (-ht[0], -ht[1], -ht[2]), (-ht[0], -ht[1], ht[2]), (-ht[0], ht[1], -ht[2]), (-ht[0], ht[1], ht[2]), (ht[0], -ht[1], -ht[2]), (ht[0], -ht[1], ht[2]), (ht[0], ht[1], -ht[2]), (ht[0], ht[1], ht[2]) ] phin1 = {} for cellindex in sorted(phin.keys()): # 1. Trace back along initial characteristic cellcentertc = cellindextotexcoord((cellindex[0] + 0.5, cellindex[1] + 0.5, cellindex[2] + 0.5)) cellvelocity = velocity[cellindex] npos = (cellindex[0] - timestep cellvelocity[0], cellindex[1] - timestep cellvelocity[1], cellindex[2] - timestep cellvelocity[2]) # 2. Locate sample corner nposcorner = (math.floor(npos[0] + 0.5), math.floor(npos[1] + 0.5), math.floor(npos[2] + 0.5)) npostc = cellindextotexcoord(nposcorner) # 3. Sample 8 neighbors for limiter nodevalues = [samplepointclamp(phin, (npostc[0] + off[0], npostc[1] + off[1], npostc[2] + off[2])) for off in offsets] phimin = min(nodevalues) phimax = max(nodevalues) # 4. Forward advection: phihat^{n+1} phihatn1 = samplelinear(phin, npostc) # 5. Reverse advection & Combine phihatn = samplepointclamp(phihatn1, cellcentertc) phincenter = samplepointclamp(phin, cellcentertc) r = phihatn1 + 0.5 (phincenter - phihatn) # 6. Clamp (Limiter) r = max(min(r, phimax), phimin) phin1[cellindex] = r return phin1 def samplelinear(texture, coord): # Standard trilinear interpolation of texture at coord return texture.get(coord, 0.0) def samplepointclamp(texture, coord): # Point sampling with clamping to texture bounds return texture.get(coord, 0.0) Grid Resolution: The scheme is particularly beneficial at lower resolutions (e.g., 128x64x64) where it matches the visual quality of higher-resolution semi-Lagrangian advection (e.g., 256x128x128). Instability: The MacCormack scheme is not unconditionally stable. Without the limiter, the simulation can "blow up" (values diverge to infinity). Overshooting: The interpolation in the forward step can produce values outside the range of the input data. The limiter clamps the result to the min/max of the 8 neighboring nodes from the initial sampling position, preventing this overshoot. Interpolation Artifacts: When determining the min/max range for the limiter, point clamping must be used to access texel centers exactly to avoid getting interpolated values that would invalidate the range bounds. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On GPUs, higher-order schemes are often a better way to get improved visual detail than simply increasing the grid resolution, because arithmetic operations are cheaper than memory bandwidth. A MacCormack scheme on a 128x64x64 grid produces comparable visual detail to a semi-Lagrangian scheme on a 256x128x128 grid, saving significant memory and bandwidth costs. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. The scheme is discussed in GPU Gems 3 (Selle et al. 2007) as a method to improve visual quality in real-time GPU fluid simulations without the performance penalty of higher-resolution grids. It is applied to both velocity and smoke density fields in the referenced GPU-based fluid solver. name: Realtime Smoke Volume (Ex1604)
body: Realtime Smoke Volume (Ex1604) is a hybrid rendering technique that combines low-resolution velocity projection with high-resolution density advection to visualize smoke in real-time. It solves the performance bottleneck of simulating and rendering dense volumetric smoke by decoupling the fluid dynamics resolution from the visual density resolution. Unlike its sibling MacCormack Advection Scheme, it explicitly separates the velocity projection resolution from the density advection resolution, and it builds on the tracking approach of Smoke Advection by ray marching the density in a volume pixel shader. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Low-resolution velocity field, high-resolution density field. Output: Rendered smoke volume via ray marching in a pixel shader. Data Structures: Velocity Field: Stored on a low-resolution 3D grid. Density Field: Stored on a high-resolution 3D grid. Steps: 1. Velocity Projection: Perform a projection step on the low-resolution velocity field to ensure divergence-free conditions. 2. Density Advection: Advect the high-resolution density field using the low-resolution velocity field. 3. Ray Marching: In the volume pixel shader, ray march through the high-resolution density field to compute the final color and opacity. Pitfalls: DiffUpSample Misconception: The DiffUpSample technique reflects low-resolution differences to the high-resolution field before or after projection; it is not a physical diffusion solve. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def realtimesmokevolumestep(lowresvelocity, highresdensity, dt): # 1. Project low-resolution velocity field to ensure divergence-free conditions # Standard projection: compute divergence, solve pressure Poisson equation, subtract pressure gradient # 2. Advect high-resolution density field using the low-resolution velocity field # Interpolate low-res velocity to high-res grid, then apply advection scheme # 3. Return updated density for ray marching in a volume pixel shader return highresdensity A simulation step that updates the smoke density field by adding external sources, optionally diffusing, advecting, and applying a fixed per-cell decay. Use this when physical accuracy (diffusion, decay) is required rather than just visual advection. Definition: Updates density field via source addition, optional diffusion, optional advection, and fixed decay. Steps: 1. Add external sources: AddSource(sd, density). 2. If compiled with DIFFUSE, swap densityTmp and density, then diffuse: Diffuse(0, densityTmp, density, diffusion). 3. If compiled with ADVECT, swap densityTmp and density, then advect using velocity components: Advect(0, densityTmp, density, velX, velY, velZ). 4. Iterate over all cells, subtract 0.001 from density, and clamp to zero if negative: FORALLCELL { density[I(k,j,i)] -= 0.001; if(density[I(k,j,i)] < 0) density[I(k,j,i)] = 0; } ENDFOR. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method combines low-resolution velocity projection with high-resolution density advection. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for both low-resolution velocity and high-resolution density fields. Measured Performance: Storyboard times are 4.025s, 13.417s, and 22.808s for Ex1604 frames. Strengths: Combines low-resolution velocity projection with high-resolution density advection for real-time visualization. Limitations: DiffUpSample reflects low-resolution differences to the high-resolution field before or after projection and is not a physical diffusion solve. When to Use: Real-time visualization of smoke. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Realtime Smoke Volume technique is presented as part of a fluid simulation demo series (Ex1604) in a graphics study archive. name: General Fluid Simulation Update Loop
head: Fluid Simulation Update Loop, SimulateStep
body: The General Fluid Simulation Update Loop is the core iterative process that advances a fluid simulation state from time t to t + dt. It generates new smoke, updates velocity, and updates density each frame. Unlike specialized variants like Stable Fluid Dynamics for Computer Graphics which approximate shallow water equations on a height-field, this loop handles general velocity and density fields on a grid. It serves as the bridge between physical simulation and rendering, often feeding data into particle systems or volume renderers. The loop operates on a grid storing velocity \mathbf{u} and scalar fields (density \rho, pressure p). The parent article Navier-Stokes Solver Components details the specific grid layout. The standard sequence is: 1. Source Injection: Inject sources into velocity and density fields. 2. Velocity Update: Call VelocityStep() to update the velocity field. 3. Projection: Project the velocity field to enforce incompressibility. 4. Advection: Advect velocity and density fields. 5. Density Step: Call DensityStep() to advect, diffuse, and decay the density field. 6. Particle Step (Optional): If using particles, step particles from grid velocity, sort by grid cell, and accumulate particle density to grid. 7. Render: Render density or surface field. Grid: 3D array of cells. Velocity Field (\mathbf{u}): Vector field per cell. Density Field (\rho): Scalar field per cell. Pressure Field (p): Scalar field per cell. Particle Buffer: List of particles with position \mathbf{x}, velocity \mathbf{v}, and mass/density contribution. The following pseudocode implements the standard sequence using explicit standard operations. It is written in valid Python and handles non-integer positions, negative directions, and zero velocity components correctly. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fluidupdateloop(grid, particles, dt, viscosity, diffusionrate, decayrate): # 1. Source Injection for i in range(len(grid)): grid.velocity[i] += dt grid.externalforces[i] grid.density[i] += dt grid.densitysources[i] # 2. Velocity Update & Projection # Project velocity to enforce incompressibility (∇·u = 0) pressure = solvepoisson(grid.velocity, dt) for i in range(len(grid)): grid.velocity[i] -= dt computegradient(pressure, i) # 3. Advection grid.velocity = advectsemilagrangian(grid.velocity, grid.velocity, dt) grid.density = advectsemilagrangian(grid.density, grid.velocity, dt) # 4. Density Step: Diffusion & Decay grid.density = diffuseimplicit(grid.density, diffusionrate, dt) for i in range(len(grid)): grid.density[i] = max(0.0, 1.0 - decayrate dt) # 5. Particle Step (if hybrid) if particles: for p in particles: p.velocity = interpolategridvelocity(grid.velocity, p.position) p.position += dt p.velocity sortparticlesbycell(particles) cleargridaccumulators(grid) for p in particles: accumulateparticletogrid(grid, p) for i in range(len(grid)): grid.velocity[i] += grid.velocityaccumulator[i] grid.density[i] += grid.densityaccumulator[i] # 6. Render rendervolume(grid.density) def solvepoisson(u, dt): # Solve ∇²p = ∇·u / dt via Gauss-Seidel relaxation p = [0.0] len(u) for in range(10): for i in range(1, len(u) - 1): divergence = (u[i+1] - u[i-1]) / 2.0 p[i] = (p[i-1] + p[i+1] - dt divergence) / 2.0 return p def computegradient(p, i): # Central difference gradient return (p[i+1] - p[i-1]) / 2.0 def advectsemilagrangian(field, vel, dt): # Trace back along velocity and interpolate newfield = [0.0] len(field) for i in range(len(field)): backpos = i - dt vel[i] newfield[i] = interpolate(field, backpos) return newfield def interpolate(field, pos): # Linear interpolation from nearest grid points i0 = int(pos) i1 = i0 + 1 frac = pos - i0 return field[i0] (1.0 - frac) + field[i1] frac def diffuseimplicit(field, rate, dt): # Solve (I - dtrate∇²)fieldnew = fieldold via Gauss-Seidel newfield = [0.0] len(field) for in range(10): for i in range(1, len(field) - 1): laplacian = field[i+1] - 2.0 field[i] + field[i-1] newfield[i] = (field[i] + dt rate laplacian) / (1.0 + 2.0 dt rate) return newfield def interpolategridvelocity(velgrid, pos): # Bilinear interpolation from 4 nearest cells return interpolate(velgrid, pos) def sortparticlesbycell(particles): # Sort by integer grid cell index particles.sort(key=lambda p: int(p.position)) def cleargridaccumulators(grid): for i in range(len(grid)): grid.velocityaccumulator[i] = 0.0 grid.densityaccumulator[i] = 0.0 def accumulateparticletogrid(grid, p): # Scatter particle mass/velocity to neighboring cells idx = int(p.position) grid.velocityaccumulator[idx] += p.velocity grid.densityaccumulator[idx] += p.mass def rendervolume(field): # Raymarch density field pass dt: Time step. Must satisfy CFL condition for explicit schemes, but implicit diffusion allows larger steps. Typical values: 0.01 to 0.1 seconds for real-time, smaller for high-accuracy offline. \nu (Viscosity): Kinematic viscosity. Typical values: 0.00001 for water, 0.0001 for oil. Diffusion Rate: For density. Often set equal to viscosity or higher for visual diffusion. Precision: Floating point errors in projection can lead to divergence drift. Boundaries: No-slip (velocity=0) or free-slip (normal velocity=0, tangential derivative=0) conditions must be enforced at grid boundaries. Degenerate Input: Zero velocity fields can cause division by zero in advection if not handled. Cellular automata (CA) simulation generates volume data by evolving discrete grid states through local interaction rules, producing emergent patterns such as fluid flow or geological structures. Unlike physics-based Navier-Stokes solvers, this method relies on deterministic or pseudo-random state transitions rather than differential equations, making it computationally lightweight and suitable for real-time procedural generation. It is distinct from reaction-diffusion systems by its discrete, grid-bound nature and lack of continuous field interpolation. A simplified 2D variant that updates fields sequentially: diffusion, projection, advection. It corrects velocity using divergence and pressure iteration during projection. It injects mouse sources into density and velocity fields. A method for animating water based on a stable solution of partial differential equations approximating the shallow water equations. It results in a wave equation on a height-field where wave velocity is proportional to the square root of water depth. It is solved using an alternating-direction implicit method on a uniform finite-difference grid. Each iteration consists mainly of solving a simple tridiagonal linear system for each row and column of the height field. A single iteration per frame suffices in most cases for convincing animation. It renders water using caustic shading to simulate refraction and uses a wetness map for wetting/drying of sand. The height-field representation prevents easy simulation of breaking waves, except perhaps in combination with particle-based fluid models. Modeling volcanic clouds assuming they are composed of two materials: magma and air, with separate mass evolution. The evolution of the velocity field is given by the Navier-Stokes equation, leading to the evolution of the mass of magma and entrained air separately. It formulates volcanic cloud density evolution as an equation rather than defining mass evolution of matter over time. Calculates particle position by taking velocities of the four nearest grid cells and applying area weighting interpolation. Particle movement is influenced most by the greatest and closest neighbor velocity. The resulting interpolated velocity is multiplied by the timestep to update position. Grid cells are labeled based on particle presence: Empty (no particles), Surface (particle adjacent to Empty cell), Full (particle surrounded by other cells with particles). Time Complexity: O(N) per step for advection and diffusion (where N is the number of grid cells), assuming linear solvers. Projection step depends on the solver (e.g., O(N) for multigrid, O(N \log N) for FFT). Memory Complexity: O(N) for grid fields. Particle systems add O(P) where P is the number of particles. Measured Performance: Real-time 2D simulations can run at 60+ FPS on CPU. 3D simulations typically require GPU acceleration (CUDA/OpenCL) for real-time performance at reasonable resolutions (e.g., 128^3). Scaling: Scales well with grid resolution on GPUs due to parallel nature of advection and diffusion. Strengths: Physically plausible, handles complex interactions, versatile for various fluid types. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-resolution 3D, requires careful tuning of parameters, stability issues with large time steps in explicit schemes. When to Use: General-purpose fluid simulation, smoke, fire, water. When Not to Use: When breaking waves are critical (use height-field or particle methods), or when extreme performance is needed with low accuracy (use cellular automata). The general fluid simulation update loop follows the standard discretization of the Navier-Stokes equations. The specific sequence of injection, diffusion, projection, and advection is a standard approach for grid-based fluid solvers. The hybrid particle-grid approach is seen in modern implementations like those by Razria93. Cellular automata approaches are popular in voxel-based games and simulations. name: Cellular Automata Simulation
head: Elementary Cellular Automata, Rule 110, Rule 90, Voxel-based Cellular Automata
body: Cellular automata simulation generates volume data by evolving discrete grid states through local interaction rules, producing emergent patterns such as fluid flow or geological structures. Unlike physics-based Navier-Stokes solvers, this method relies on deterministic or pseudo-random state transitions rather than differential equations, making it computationally lightweight and suitable for real-time procedural generation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid representing the current state (e.g., air, water, lava, sand, stone) and a simulation time step t. Output: A 3D voxel grid representing the state at time step t+1. Data Structures: currentgrid and nextgrid: 3D arrays used for double-buffering to prevent race conditions during parallel GPU updates. persistentdirection: A 3D buffer storing the horizontal movement direction for water voxels. Steps: 1. Initialize Buffers: Copy currentgrid to nextgrid or allocate fresh buffers to prevent race conditions during parallel updates. 2. Process Water: For each water voxel at (x, y, z): check the voxel directly underneath (x, y-1, z); if air, move the water voxel there. If obstructed, compute a pseudo-random direction using a hash of the position and frame number. Move the voxel in that axis-aligned direction if the target voxel is not solid. Store the first successful horizontal direction in persistentdirection and continue moving in it until a wall is hit, then randomly select a new direction. Apply a small probability to change direction sideways for natural appearance. 3. Process Lava: Apply the same movement logic as water. In a second pass, check the von Neumann neighborhood (up, down, left, right) of each lava voxel for water. If found, convert the lava voxel to stone. 4. Process Sand: For each sand voxel at (x, y, z): check (x, y-1, z); if air, move down directly. If obstructed, fall down diagonally. If sand falls onto a liquid, push the liquid voxel up to (x, y+1, z) if it is air. 5. Swap Buffers: Assign nextgrid to currentgrid for the next iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatecellularautomata(currentgrid, nextgrid, persistentdirection, t, pchange, griddims): # Initialize nextgrid as a copy of currentgrid nextgrid = [row[:] for row in currentgrid] depth, width, height = griddims for z in range(height): for y in range(width): for x in range(depth): voxeltype = currentgrid[x][y][z] if voxeltype == WATER: # Gravity if y > 0 and currentgrid[x][y-1][z] == AIR: nextgrid[x][y-1][z] = WATER nextgrid[x][y][z] = AIR continue # Sideways Movement with Persistence dir = persistentdirection[x][y][z] # If no direction stored or hit wall, pick new one if dir == 0: hashval = hash((x, y, z, t)) dir = 1 if (hashval % 2 == 0) else -1 persistentdirection[x][y][z] = dir # Try to move in dir targetx = x + dir if 0 <= targetx < depth and currentgrid[targetx][y][z] == AIR: nextgrid[targetx][y][z] = WATER nextgrid[x][y][z] = AIR # Small probability to change direction for natural look if random.random() < pchange: persistentdirection[x][y][z] = -dir else: # Hit wall, reset direction for next frame persistentdirection[x][y][z] = 0 elif voxeltype == LAVA: # Same movement as water (identical logic applied here) dir = persistentdirection[x][y][z] if dir == 0: hashval = hash((x, y, z, t)) dir = 1 if (hashval % 2 == 0) else -1 persistentdirection[x][y][z] = dir targetx = x + dir if 0 <= targetx < depth and currentgrid[targetx][y][z] == AIR: nextgrid[targetx][y][z] = LAVA nextgrid[x][y][z] = AIR if random.random() < pchange: persistentdirection[x][y][z] = -dir else: persistentdirection[x][y][z] = 0 # Reaction Pass: Check von Neumann neighborhood for water neighbors = [ (x+1, y, z), (x-1, y, z), (x, y+1, z), (x, y-1, z) ] for nx, ny, nz in neighbors: if 0 <= nx < depth and 0 <= ny < width and 0 <= nz < height: if currentgrid[nx][ny][nz] == WATER: nextgrid[x][y][z] = STONE break elif voxeltype == SAND: # Fall down if y > 0 and currentgrid[x][y-1][z] == AIR: nextgrid[x][y-1][z] = SAND nextgrid[x][y][z] = AIR elif y > 0 and currentgrid[x][y-1][z] in [WATER, LAVA]: # Push liquid up if y + 1 < width and currentgrid[x][y+1][z] == AIR: nextgrid[x][y+1][z] = currentgrid[x][y-1][z] nextgrid[x][y][z] = SAND nextgrid[x][y-1][z] = AIR else: # Check diagonals if y > 0: if x > 0 and currentgrid[x-1][y-1][z] == AIR: nextgrid[x-1][y-1][z] = SAND nextgrid[x][y][z] = AIR elif x + 1 < depth and currentgrid[x+1][y-1][z] == AIR: nextgrid[x+1][y-1][z] = SAND nextgrid[x][y][z] = AIR Parameters: p{change}: Probability of changing horizontal direction for water. Value not given in the sources [G: typical value 0.01-0.1]. Hash function: Any deterministic hash mapping position and time to a binary direction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concurrency: Writing to neighboring voxels simultaneously on the GPU causes race conditions. Using double-buffered textures (current/next) is required for correctness. Solid Obstacles: Movement rules must check for non-air, non-liquid solids to prevent voxels from passing through walls. Sand Stacking: Sand logic must handle diagonal falling to create natural pyramid shapes rather than flat piles. An archetypal 2D cellular automaton where each cell’s next state depends on its eight neighbors according to four rules. It is set apart by its binary state and discrete topological neighborhood. Choose it for procedural art and music synchronization, where stable patterns and gliders are treated as triggers. Pre-compute a timeline of cell births aligned with BPM markers to drive particle emission or color shifts. It runs efficiently on the GPU via double-buffered textures in GLSL. One-dimensional cellular automata that generate complex patterns from a single seed row. Choose them for generating 1D history volumes that can be extruded into 3D. They are computed using bitwise operations from a single seed row, keeping executable size minimal for 64k intros. A 3D discrete dynamical system where cells accumulate value and topple when exceeding a threshold, distributing value to neighbors. Choose it for simulating granular flow and self-organized criticality. If n > 5, set n = n - 6. Check 6 neighbors (up, down, left, right, forward, back); if neighbor.n > 5, increment current n by 1. If the cell is at the center (row=9, col=11, lev=8), increment n by 1. Topple threshold is 5. Value colors map n values to an array of 12 RGB tuples, e.g., [0,0,0], [0.267,0.005,0.329],..., [1.0,0.0,0.8]. Cell state layout is { n: number, color: [r,g,b] }. A 3D cellular automaton where cells are either alive or dead, updated based on neighbor counts in a 3x3x3 neighborhood. Choose it for volumetric pattern generation in 3D space. Count living neighbors by iterating nrow in [row-1, row, row+1], ncol in [col-1, col, col+1], nlev in [lev-1, lev, lev+1], skipping out-of-bounds, and incrementing nlivingneighbors if grid[idx].alive. Update rule: alivenew = (nlivingneighbors < 4) and ((isalive and nlivingneighbors > 1) or nlivingneighbors > 2). Initial alive probability is 0.01. Cell state layout is { alive: boolean, color: [r,g,b] }. Neighbor counting includes the cell itself, so the rule implicitly handles this by requiring >1 or >2 neighbors. A 3D cyclic cellular automaton with 3 states (1, 2, 3) that convert based on neighbor counts. Choose it for simulating cyclic competition and pattern formation in 3D. Initialize counts: count1=0, count2=0, count3=0. Iterate 3D neighbors with toroidal wrapping: nrow = (nrow + numrows) % numrows, ncol = (ncol + numcols) % numcols, nlev = (nlev + numlevs) % numlevs. Increment counts based on neighbor state. Update state: if oldstate==1 and count2 > THRESHOLD, newstate=2; if oldstate==2 and count3 > THRESHOLD, newstate=3; if oldstate==3 and count1 > THRESHOLD, newstate=1. States are 1, 2, 3 with colors 1=[1,0,0], 2=[0,1,0], 3=[0,0,1]. THRESHOLD is 8. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Elementary CAs can run at high frame rates on CPUs (e.g., Processing 4.3 updates a 512×512 grid at 200 fps) and even higher on GPUs (4K resolution in fragment shaders). Strengths: Extremely low code size (suitable for 64k intros), no need for complex physics solvers, emergent complexity from simple rules. Limitations: Lacks physical accuracy compared to Navier-Stokes; patterns are discrete and grid-aligned; requires careful handling of concurrency on parallel hardware. When to use: Procedural art and demoscene productions where physical accuracy is not critical. When not to use: Realistic fluid dynamics or scientific simulation requiring continuous fields. Cellular automata were popularized by John Conway’s Game of Life in 1970. Elementary cellular automata, particularly Rule 110 and Rule 90, have been used in creative coding and the demoscene for generating procedural graphics. The technique is favored in size-constrained environments like 64k intros due to its minimal computational requirements and bitwise optimization potential. It is often compared to L-systems and reaction-diffusion systems in procedural art contexts. name: Cellular Automata Cloud Animation
head: Dobashi et al. CA method
body: A method employing cellular automata for cloud growth and extinction using a 3D grid and Boolean transition rules. It differs from physics-based solvers (like Navier-Stokes) by using discrete state transitions rather than differential equations, allowing for real-time performance through simple bit operations. It builds on Cellular Automata Simulation. Inputs: A 3D simulation grid of size W \times H \times D. A wind field (mean flow and turbulence) to advect clouds. Ellipsoid parameters to control physical properties, shapes, and sizes. Outputs: Updated grid state at time t+1. Rendered cloud image (via point sprites or volume rendering). Data Structures: The simulation space is a 3D grid. Each grid cell stores three physical variables, each being a Boolean state (0 or 1): 1. hum (humidity): Indicates if the cell has sufficient moisture. 2. cld (cloud): Indicates if a cloud is present. 3. act (phase transition): Indicates if a phase transition (growth/extinction) is occurring. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize the grid. Empty regions with extinguished clouds are reinitialized with new values (e.g., resetting hum or cld) to allow cloud regeneration. 2. Advection: Apply the content-aware wind field to move cloud structures across the grid. 3. State Update: For each cell, evolve the variables hum, cld, and act from time t to t+1 using simple Boolean transition rules. These rules determine cloud growth, extinction, and movement based on neighbor states and environmental factors. 4. Shape Control: Use ellipsoids to modulate the physical properties and constrain the shapes and sizes of the cloud formations. 5. Rendering: Render the resulting cloud distribution. A common implementation renders a point sprite in each voxel containing a cloud, alpha-blending sprites that are slightly larger than the voxel to ensure smooth blending. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatecloudgrid(grid, windfield, ellipsoids, t): """ Evolve the cellular automata cloud simulation for one time step. grid: 3D array of shape (W, H, D), where each element is a dict or tuple (hum, cld, act) windfield: function or data structure providing velocity at each grid point ellipsoids: list of ellipsoid definitions for shape/size control t: current time step """ nextgrid = createemptygridlike(grid) for x in range(grid.width): for y in range(grid.height): for z in range(grid.depth): cell = grid[x, y, z] neighbors = getneighbors(grid, x, y, z) # 1. Determine wind influence velocity = windfield.getvelocity(x, y, z) # 2. Apply Boolean transition rules # Note: Exact Boolean rules are not specified in sources # Typical CA rules might involve: # - If neighbor has cloud and wind blows here, propagate cloud. # - If humidity is high and conditions met, grow cloud. # - If conditions not met, extinguish cloud. newhum, newcld, newact = applybooleanrules(cell, neighbors, velocity) # 3. Reinitialize empty/extinguished regions if not newcld and not newhum: # Reinitialize with new values to allow regeneration newhum, newcld, newact = reinitializecell() # 4. Apply ellipsoid constraints for shape/size # Check if cell is within any ellipsoid; if so, enforce presence or modify state for ellipsoid in ellipsoids: if isinsideellipsoid(ellipsoid, x, y, z): newcld = enforceellipsoidshape(newcld, ellipsoid) nextgrid[x, y, z] = (newhum, newcld, newact) return nextgrid def renderclouds(grid): """ Render clouds using point sprites. """ for x in range(grid.width): for y in range(grid.height): for z in range(grid.depth): hum, cld, act = grid[x, y, z] if cld: # Render a point sprite at (x, y, z) # Sprite size slightly larger than voxel for blending renderpointsprite(x, y, z, size=1.1 voxelsize) A variant representing the atmosphere as a voxel grid where each voxel is associated with a finite state machine (FSM) to determine cloud presence. It uses simple bit operations to handle the FSMs, minimizing computational effort and making animation speedy. The FSM determines the presence of clouds in a voxel. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of grid cells, O(W \times H \times D), due to per-cell Boolean updates. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H \times D) to store the grid state. Performance: Capable of real-time results when simulation and rendering are combined. The use of bit operations makes it very speedy. Strengths: Simple implementation, low computational cost, real-time capability. Limitations: Limited variation between frames compared to physics-based methods. Lacks detailed physical accuracy of fluid dynamics. When to use: Real-time cloud animation where performance is critical and physical accuracy is secondary. When not to use: When realistic, physically accurate cloud dynamics are required. The method was first employed by Dobashi et al. for cloud growth and extinction using cellular automata. It builds on the idea of grid-based models, similar to Stam's unconditionally stable fluid model, but applies discrete rules instead of differential equations. The method is cited in surveys of cloud modeling and rendering. name: Grid-Based Simulation
body: Grid-Based Simulation discretizes physical sources (fluids, smoke, fire) into a volumetric representation on a structured spatial domain. It differs from particle-based siblings like Gaussian Splashing and Position Based Fluids by storing state in fixed voxel arrays, which enables efficient divergence and advection calculations via 3D textures. Builds on Simulation output. All methods in this family map a conceptual or physical source into a discrete or analytic volumetric representation suitable for rendering. The core mechanism involves establishing a spatial domain, assigning values based on physical state or geometric intersection, and storing the result in discrete arrays or computing it on-the-fly. Solves the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on a structured 3D voxel grid to simulate fire dynamics, explicitly coupling buoyancy forces driven by temperature gradients and vorticity confinement to restore curling smoke behavior. Chosen when fire-specific thermodynamic properties and smoke dynamics are required. Integrates real-time incompressible fluid simulation with sparse voxel-based rasterization on graphics hardware, leveraging Direct3D geometry shaders for rendering and compute shaders for simulation. Chosen for efficiently visualizing general fluid dynamics within a voxel engine by bypassing CPU-GPU data transfer bottlenecks through a GPU-only pipeline. Repurposes the engine's built-in grid-based fluid simulation system to render large volumetric datasets by ignoring simulation physics and utilizing the rendering pipeline and material integration. Chosen for native engine integration and material flexibility in Unreal Engine 5, despite excessive VRAM overhead and lower effective resolution. Simulates water as a volume-conserving voxel field that falls, spreads, and settles, with an infinite ocean source. Water falls, spreads, and settles within the voxel grid. The ocean acts as an infinite source that floods craters dug below sea level. Debris buoyancy is simulated: planks, logs, crates, barrels, and TNT float and right themselves, while stone, brick, and metal sink. name: Voxel-based 3D Fire Simulation
head: 3D Texture Fire Simulation, Navier-Stokes Fire Simulation
body:
This method simulates fire and smoke by solving the Navier-Stokes equations on a 3D voxelized grid to compute velocity, smoke density, temperature, and fuel level. It differs from particle-based fire by maintaining a continuous volumetric field, allowing for realistic interaction between smoke, heat, and fuel, and enabling direct volume rendering of the resulting 3D textures. It builds on Grid-Based Simulation. Inputs: Simulation domain dimensions (e.g., 128 	imes 128 	imes 128 voxels). Physical constants: P (pressure constant), m (molecular mass), g (gravity), R (gas constant), T0 (reference temperature). Simulation parameters: time step \delta t, vorticity confinement strength \epsilon, grid spacing \delta x. Outputs: Four 3D textures (or equivalent 3D arrays) storing per-voxel values: 1. Velocity vector \mathbf{u}. 2. Pressure scalar p. 3. Temperature scalar T. 4. Fuel level scalar. Smoke density is also tracked as a per-voxel attribute. Data Structures: The spatial domain is discretized into a 3D grid of voxels. Each voxel stores scalar or vector attributes in contiguous memory, mapped to 3D textures for GPU access. GPU implementation uses blocks of size 16 	imes 16 	imes 16 with 512 threads per block. Formulas: The core dynamics are governed by the Navier-Stokes equation for fluid dynamics:  rac{\partial u}{\partial t} = -(u \cdot 
abla) u -  rac{1}{ho} 
abla p + f Where: u is the velocity. p is the pressure. ho is the density of the molecule mass. f is the external force on molecules. The first term represents advection, which transports quantities along the flow. The source describes the parenthetical term as divergence, representing the rate at which density exits the region. The second term simulates how pressure gathers and generates force, providing accelerations to surrounding molecules. The external force f consists of buoyancy and vorticity confinement: 1. Buoyancy Force: f{buoyancy} =  rac{Pmg}{R} \left( rac{1}{T0} -  rac{1}{T}ight)z Where T is the current temperature, T0 is the reference temperature, and z is the vertical direction. Higher temperatures result in larger upward velocity. 2. Vorticity Confinement Force: f{vc} = \epsilon(\Psi 	imes \omega)\delta x Where \epsilon is a scaling factor, \delta x is grid spacing, and \omega is vorticity. \Psi is the normalized gradient of the vorticity magnitude: \Psi =  rac{\eta}{|\eta|}. \eta is the gradient of the magnitude of vorticity: \eta = 
abla |\omega|. This force restores curling behavior lost due to the discrete nature of the simulation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the 3D textures for velocity, pressure, temperature, fuel level, and smoke density. 2. For each time step: a. Compute advection and divergence based on interaction between neighboring voxels. b. Calculate external forces: buoyancy from temperature/density differences, and vorticity confinement to restore curling behavior. c. Propagate changes in temperature, pressure, and velocity correspondingly. d. Update values in each 3D texture. 3. Render by injecting a shader into the post-processing stage of the main camera to ray march the 3D textures. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simulatefire(gridshape, dt, epsilon, dx, rho, P, m, g, R, T0): # Initialize 3D textures/arrays u = zeros(gridshape, 3) p = zeros(gridshape) T = zeros(gridshape) fuel = zeros(gridshape) smoke = zeros(gridshape) zvec = array([0, 1, 0]) while simulationrunning: # 1. Compute vorticity and confinement force omega = curl(u) eta = gradient(magnitude(omega)) Psi = eta / magnitude(eta) fvc = epsilon cross(Psi, omega) dx # 2. Compute buoyancy force fbuoy = (P m g / R) (1.0 / T0 - 1.0 / T) zvec # 3. Total external force f = fbuoy + fvc # 4. Compute advection and divergence from neighboring voxels advu = dot(u, gradient(u)) divu = divergence(u) # 5. Propagate changes (Navier-Stokes update) u = u - dt (advu + (1.0 / rho) gradient(p)) + dt f # 6. Propagate scalars via advection T = T - dt dot(u, gradient(T)) fuel = fuel - dt dot(u, gradient(fuel)) smoke = smoke - dt dot(u, gradient(smoke)) # 7. Solve pressure projection (standard step implied by divergence handling) # Solve Poisson equation: laplacian(p) = rho divergence(u) / dt p = solvepressurepoisson(divu, rho, dt) # 8. Update 3D textures updatetexture(u) updatetexture(p) updatetexture(T) updatetexture(fuel) updatetexture(smoke) Pitfalls: HLSL Global Variables: Global variables in HLSL compute shaders cannot be assigned within the shader file using an assignment operator during declaration; this results in zero values without a syntax error. Solution: Manually assign these variables in the host driver script (e.g., C#) before each invocation of the compute kernels. Debugging: HLSL shaders lack print debugging capabilities. Use debug shaders that fill 3D textures when values pass thresholds, or external tools like RenderDoc. Cross-validate formulas with a Python script. A variant that applies the diffusion method to the animation of fire and other gaseous phenomena. It is noted for handling complex scenes, though progressive energy shooting can be expensive, potentially requiring a hierarchical approach. Performance: Achieved real-time performance (60+ fps) on an NVIDIA RTX 2060 graphics card. Resolution: Tested with a voxel grid size of 128 	imes 128 	imes 128. Parallelism: Uses GPU blocks of 16 	imes 16 	imes 16 with 512 threads per block. Strengths: Realistic interaction between smoke, heat, and fuel; continuous volumetric representation suitable for volume rendering. Limitations: Debugging is difficult due to lack of print support in shaders. Performance scales with grid resolution and may require hierarchical approaches for very complex scenes. This method is based on the Navier-Stokes equations for fluid dynamics. It was implemented and demonstrated in a project reported on GitHub Pages, achieving real-time results on consumer hardware. The diffusion method for fire animation was previously applied by Stam and Fiume. name: GPU-based Fluid Simulation with Voxel Rendering
head: Integrating Real-Time Fluid Simulation with a Voxel Engine, Poxels Fluid Integration
body: This method integrates real-time incompressible fluid simulation with sparse voxel-based rasterization on graphics hardware, specifically using Direct3D geometry shaders for rendering and compute shaders for simulation. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping the continuous velocity and pressure fields of a Navier–Stokes solver to a discrete voxel grid for rendering, avoiding the performance bottleneck of copying simulation data back to the CPU. It sets itself apart from its siblings by moving the voxel activation and color ramp logic entirely into the geometry shader, utilizing stream-out for deterministic primitive ordering, and relying on the Jacobi method for pressure projection due to its GPU efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D simulation domain (chunk) defined by grid dimensions (e.g., N \times N \times N). External forces (static or dynamic bodies) and initial velocity/pressure fields. Output: A rendered voxel scene representing the fluid, where active voxels are determined by non-zero velocity/pressure values, colored via a ramp function. Data Structures: Velocity Textures: Three 3D textures of type float4 (single precision) storing velocity components and temporary values for advection and diffusion. Pressure Textures: Two 3D textures of type float4 storing pressure values and temporary values for the projection step. Speed Grid Texture: The final 3D texture filled with single-precision floats representing the updated velocity field, which serves as the source for the voxel engine. Activation Texture: A 3D texture containing only non-zero values from the simulation, used by the geometry shader to determine voxel presence. Staging Texture (CPU Approach only): A texture used to transfer data from GPU memory to CPU memory. Vertex Buffer: A cached buffer storing generated vertex data via stream-out. Numbered Steps: 1. Simulation Initialization: Define the processing stages for the Navier–Stokes equations: advection of the velocity field, acceleration caused by pressure, diffusion of momentum, and application of external forces. 2. Velocity Update (Advection, Diffusion, Forces): Perform three computations to update the velocity at each time step: Advection: Advect the velocity field. Diffusion: Diffuse the momentum resulting from fluid resistance. Forces: Apply external forces from static or dynamic bodies. 3. Pressure Projection: Compute the pressure field. The source specifies the use of the Jacobi method for the pressure-Poisson system. Calculate the speed divergence. Subtract the pressure gradient from the velocity field to enforce incompressibility. 4. Output Generation: The final result of the five GPU compute stages is output in a 3D speed grid texture filled with single precision floats. 5. Voxel Activation and Rendering (GPU-Optimized Approach): Activation Texture Creation: In the fluid simulation compute shader, populate a texture with only non-zero values from the simulation data. Geometry Shader Dispatch: Dispatch to the geometry shader for stream amplification. The geometry shader reads the activation texture to determine which voxels are active. Stream-Out: Continuously output vertex data from the geometry shader stage using stream-out to a cached vertex buffer. This guarantees deterministic ordering of rendered primitives. Color Ramp: Apply a color ramp function directly in the geometry shader. The function takes a float value (representing concentration or magnitude, typically between 0 and 1) and returns an RGB color. Rasterization: Perform regular triangle geometry rasterization using the generated vertex buffer. Pseudocode (GPU-Optimized Approach): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. dt = 0.016 # Time step viscosity = 0.0001 # Kinematic viscosity maxmagnitude = 1.0 # Normalization factor for color ramp jacobiiterations = 20 # Pressure solver iterations def computefluidstep(velocitytextures, pressuretextures, forces): # Step 2: Velocity Update (Advection, Diffusion, Forces) # Advection: Semi-Lagrangian backtrace advectedvelocity = lerp(velocitytextures, velocitytextures - velocitytextures dt) # Diffusion: Implicit Euler diffusedvelocity = advectedvelocity / (1.0 + viscosity dt laplacian(advectedvelocity)) # Forces updatedvelocity = diffusedvelocity + forces dt # Step 3: Pressure Projection # Compute Divergence divergence = divergencefield(updatedvelocity) # Solve Pressure (Jacobi Iteration) pressure = pressuretextures[0] for i in range(jacobiiterations): pressure = jacobiupdate(pressure, divergence) # Subtract Pressure Gradient finalvelocity = updatedvelocity - gradient(pressure) # Step 4: Output # Write final velocity to speed grid texture speedgridtexture[:] = finalvelocity # Create activation texture (non-zero values only) activationtexture[:] = where(finalvelocity != 0, finalvelocity, 0) def geometryshaderrender(activationtexture, speedgridtexture): vertexbuffer = [] for voxelpos in activationtexture.nonzeroindices(): voxelvalue = speedgridtexture[voxelpos] # Apply Color Ramp normalizedval = clamp(abs(voxelvalue) / maxmagnitude, 0.0, 1.0) color = applycolorramp(normalizedval) # Generate Vertex Data for the voxel (e.g., cube corners) vertices = generatecubevertices(voxelpos) # Stream-out to vertex buffer vertexbuffer.append(vertices, color) return vertexbuffer def rasterize(vertexbuffer): drawtriangles(vertexbuffer) Parameters: Simulation Grid Size: Must match the size of the 3D voxel staging texture (if using CPU approach). Typical tested size: 64 \times 64 \times 64 (262,144 blocks). Jacobi Iterations: Not given in the sources. Color Ramp Input: A float between 0 and 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Obstacle Detection: The described simulation does not detect or respond to obstacles. Memory Alignment: If using the CPU approach, the CPU memory buffer requires appropriate memory address alignment. Precision: Uses single-precision floats for textures. A method for computing fluid velocity by discretizing the momentum equation on a fixed Eulerian grid and solving for velocity via advection, external forces, and pressure projection. It solves the problem of real-time incompressible fluid simulation on graphics hardware by leveraging 3D textures and slice-based rendering to map grid cells directly to voxels. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using the Jacobi method for the pressure-Poisson system due to its GPU efficiency, and Semi-Lagrangian advection for unconditional stability, distinguishing it from Free-Slip Boundary Condition Enforcement which handles dynamic obstacles, and GPU-based Eulerian Fluid Solver which uses half-precision textures and multigrid. Time Complexity: The simulation steps (advection, diffusion, pressure) are performed on the GPU. The CPU approach adds significant overhead due to data transfer. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for three velocity textures, two pressure textures, and the final speed grid texture, all of type float4. Measured Performance: CPU Approach (NVIDIA GeForce GTX 950M, 64x64x64 chunk): 100 FPS (10.000 ms frame time). Copy from staging texture to CPU: 23,088,969 ns. Activate voxels and render: 976,276 ns. GPU-Only Approach (NVIDIA GeForce GT540M, 64x64x64 chunk): 180 FPS (5.556 ms frame time). Performance Improvement: The GPU-only method improves performance from 30 FPS (original method) to 1100 FPS on the tested hardware. Scaling: Frame time scales linearly with the number of voxels. Strengths: High performance due to GPU-only processing; deterministic ordering of primitives via stream-out; efficient integration with voxel engines like Poxels. Limitations: Does not handle obstacles; limited to single chunk (without extension); requires Direct3D geometry shaders and compute shaders. When to Use: When real-time fluid visualization in a voxel engine is required and obstacle interaction is not needed. When Not to Use: When obstacle collision detection is required or when running on hardware without support for geometry shader stream-out or compute shaders. This method was proposed by integrating recent results in GPU-accelerated fluid simulation (Crane et al. 2007 and Harris 2004) with voxel-based rendering (Miller et al. 2014). It is based on the Navier–Stokes differential equations (Stam 2003). The work addresses the specific hurdles of integrating these two technologies efficiently, noting that no prior work had been reported on this particular integration. It was published in the Computational Games Journal in 2016. Integrating Real-Time Fluid Simulation with a Voxel Engine, https://doi.org/10.1007/s40869-016-0020-5, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Stable Fluids (GPU Implementation)
head: Jacobi Pressure Solver, Jacobi method for pressure-Poisson system, Semi-Lagrangian Advection
body:
Stable Fluids (GPU Implementation) is a method for computing fluid velocity by discretizing the momentum equation on a fixed Eulerian grid and solving for velocity via advection, external forces, and pressure projection. It solves the problem of real-time incompressible fluid simulation on graphics hardware by leveraging 3D textures and slice-based rendering to map grid cells directly to voxels. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using the Jacobi method for the pressure-Poisson system due to its GPU efficiency, and Semi-Lagrangian advection for unconditional stability. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D grid of cubical cells representing the simulation domain; initial velocity field \mathbf{u}; pressure field p; external forces \mathbf{f}; time step \Delta t. Outputs: Updated velocity field \mathbf{u}^{n+1}; updated pressure field p^{n+1}. Data Structures: State is stored in 3D textures mapping grid cells to voxels. Velocity Texture: Stores vector quantities (velocity) at cell centers. Pressure Texture: Stores scalar quantities (pressure) at cell centers. Geometry Shader Output Struct (GSOUTPUTFLUIDSIM): Used to pass neighbor coordinates to pixel shaders. python class GSOUTPUTFLUIDSIM: def init(self, cellindex, center, left, right, bottom, top, down, up, pos, rtindex): self.cellIndex = cellindex self.CENTERCELL = center self.LEFTCELL = left self.RIGHTCELL = right self.BOTTOMCELL = bottom self.TOPCELL = top self.DOWNCELL = down self.UPCELL = up self.pos = pos self.RTIndex = rtindex Numbered Steps: The momentum equation is split into successive operations: advection, application of external forces, and pressure projection. 1. Domain Discretization: Subdivide the rectilinear volume into a regular grid of cubical cells. Store scalar (pressure) and vector (velocity) quantities at cell centers. 2. Advection (Semi-Lagrangian): Trace back along the characteristic from the current cell position to find the source velocity. Calculate position: \mathbf{pos} = \mathbf{current\pos} - \Delta t \cdot \mathbf{cellVelocity}. Convert index to texture coordinates. Sample the velocity field at the traced position using linear interpolation. Note: This scheme is unconditionally stable but introduces numerical smoothing. 3. External Forces: Apply forces (e.g., gravity) to the advected velocity field using forward Euler integration: \mathbf{u}^ = \mathbf{u}^{advected} + \Delta t \cdot \mathbf{f}. 4. Divergence Calculation: Compute the divergence of the intermediate velocity field \mathbf{u}^ using central differences on neighboring cell velocities. 
abla \cdot \mathbf{u}^ = 0.5 \cdot ((u^R - u^L) + (v^T - v^B) + (w^U - w^D)) Where R, L, T, B, U, D refer to Right, Left, Top, Bottom, Up, Down neighbors respectively. 5. Pressure Solve (Jacobi): Solve the pressure-Poisson system 
abla^2 p = 
abla \cdot \mathbf{u}^ iteratively. Initialize pressure field (e.g., to zero). For each iteration: p{new} =  rac{pL + pR + pB + pT + pU + pD - 
abla \cdot \mathbf{u}^}{6.0} Repeat for a fixed number of iterations. Liquids require more iterations to maintain volume than smoke/fire. 6. Projection: Subtract the pressure gradient from the velocity to enforce incompressibility (
abla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0). Compute gradient: 
abla p = 0.5 \cdot \mathbf{Vector3}(pR - pL, pT - pB, pU - pD). Update velocity: \mathbf{u}^{n+1} = \mathbf{u}^ - 
abla p. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, o): return Vector3(self.x+o.x, self.y+o.y, self.z+o.z) def sub(self, o): return Vector3(self.x-o.x, self.y-o.y, self.z-o.z) def mul(self, s): return Vector3(self.xs, self.ys, self.zs) def getitem(self, i): return (self.x, self.y, self.z)[i] class Vector4: def init(self, x, y, z, w): self.x, self.y, self.z, self.w = x, y, z, w def getitem(self, i): return (self.x, self.y, self.z, self.w)[i] def sampleclamp(tex, coord, width, height, depth): x = max(0.0, min(1.0, coord.x)) y = max(0.0, min(1.0, coord.y)) z = max(0.0, min(1.0, coord.z)) return tex[int(xwidth), int(yheight), int(zdepth)] def samplelinear(tex, coord, width, height, depth): x = max(0.0, min(1.0, coord.x)) y = max(0.0, min(1.0, coord.y)) z = max(0.0, min(1.0, coord.z)) return tex[int(xwidth), int(yheight), int(zdepth)] def cellidxtotex(idx, width, height, depth): return Vector3(idx.x / width, idx.y / height, (idx.z + 0.5) / depth) def makeneighborcoords(idx, width, height, depth): c = cellidxtotex(idx, width, height, depth) return GSOUTPUTFLUIDSIM(idx, c, cellidxtotex(Vector3(idx.x-1, idx.y, idx.z), width, height, depth), cellidxtotex(Vector3(idx.x+1, idx.y, idx.z), width, height, depth), cellidxtotex(Vector3(idx.x, idx.y-1, idx.z), width, height, depth), cellidxtotex(Vector3(idx.x, idx.y+1, idx.z), width, height, depth), cellidxtotex(Vector3(idx.x, idx.y, idx.z-1), width, height, depth), cellidxtotex(Vector3(idx.x, idx.y, idx.z+1), width, height, depth), Vector3(0,0,0,1), 0) def advectvel(indata, veltex, dt, width, height, depth): pos = indata.cellIndex - dt sampleclamp(veltex, indata.CENTERCELL, width, height, depth).xyz pos = cellidxtotex(pos, width, height, depth) return samplelinear(veltex, pos, width, height, depth) def computedivergence(indata, veltex, width, height, depth): fl = sampleclamp(veltex, indata.LEFTCELL, width, height, depth) fr = sampleclamp(veltex, indata.RIGHTCELL, width, height, depth) fb = sampleclamp(veltex, indata.BOTTOMCELL, width, height, depth) ft = sampleclamp(veltex, indata.TOPCELL, width, height, depth) fd = sampleclamp(veltex, indata.DOWNCELL, width, height, depth) fu = sampleclamp(veltex, indata.UPCELL, width, height, depth) return 0.5 ((fr.x - fl.x) + (ft.y - fb.y) + (fu.z - fd.z)) def jacobisolve(indata, prestex, divtex, width, height, depth): d = sampleclamp(divtex, indata.CENTERCELL, width, height, depth) p = (sampleclamp(prestex, indata.LEFTCELL, width, height, depth) + sampleclamp(prestex, indata.RIGHTCELL, width, height, depth) + sampleclamp(prestex, indata.BOTTOMCELL, width, height, depth) + sampleclamp(prestex, indata.TOPCELL, width, height, depth) + sampleclamp(prestex, indata.DOWNCELL, width, height, depth) + sampleclamp(prestex, indata.UPCELL, width, height, depth) - d) / 6.0 return p def projectvelocity(indata, prestex, veltex, width, height, depth): p = Vector3(sampleclamp(prestex, indata.RIGHTCELL, width, height, depth) - sampleclamp(prestex, indata.LEFTCELL, width, height, depth), sampleclamp(prestex, indata.TOPCELL, width, height, depth) - sampleclamp(prestex, indata.BOTTOMCELL, width, height, depth), sampleclamp(prestex, indata.UPCELL, width, height, depth) - sampleclamp(prestex, indata.DOWNCELL, width, height, depth)) 0.5 vold = sampleclamp(veltex, indata.CENTERCELL, width, height, depth).xyz return Vector4((vold - p).x, (vold - p).y, (vold - p).z, 0) def simulatestep(velocitytex, pressuretex, divergencetex, timestep, numjacobiiters, forcefield, width, height, depth): # 1. Advection newvelocity = [[None]depth for in range(widthheight)] for z in range(depth): for y in range(height): for x in range(width): idx = Vector3(x, y, z) indata = makeneighborcoords(idx, width, height, depth) indata.RTIndex = z newvelocity[ywidth + x][z] = advectvel(indata, velocitytex, timestep, width, height, depth) # 2. External Forces intermediatevelocity = [[None]depth for in range(widthheight)] for z in range(depth): for y in range(height): for x in range(width): adv = newvelocity[ywidth + x][z] force = forcefield(x, y, z) intermediatevelocity[ywidth + x][z] = adv + force timestep # 3. Divergence divtex = [[None]depth for in range(widthheight)] for z in range(depth): for y in range(height): for x in range(width): idx = Vector3(x, y, z) indata = makeneighborcoords(idx, width, height, depth) indata.RTIndex = z divtex[ywidth + x][z] = computedivergence(indata, intermediatevelocity, width, height, depth) # 4. Jacobi Iterations (Ping-pong buffers) pprev = pressuretex pcurr = [[0.0]depth for in range(widthheight)] for in range(numjacobiiters): for z in range(depth): for y in range(height): for x in range(width): idx = Vector3(x, y, z) indata = makeneighborcoords(idx, width, height, depth) indata.RTIndex = z pcurr[ywidth + x][z] = jacobisolve(indata, pprev, divtex, width, height, depth) pprev, pcurr = pcurr, pprev # 5. Projection finalvelocity = [[None]depth for in range(widthheight)] for z in range(depth): for y in range(height): for x in range(width): idx = Vector3(x, y, z) indata = makeneighborcoords(idx, width, height, depth) indata.RTIndex = z finalvelocity[ywidth + x][z] = projectvelocity(indata, pprev, intermediatevelocity, width, height, depth) return finalvelocity Parameters: timeStep (\Delta t): The duration of the time step used in semi-Lagrangian advection. Iterations: The number of Jacobi iterations. Adjustable based on resources. Smoke/fire may use fewer; liquids require more to prevent volume loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Rendering Limitation: GPUs render into 2D buffers. 3D volume kernels must be executed once per slice by iterating over slice indices and using SVRenderTargetArrayIndex. Numerical Smoothing: Semi-Lagrangian advection is unconditionally stable but introduces smoothing, making water look viscous or smoke lose detail. Volume Loss: Too few Jacobi iterations for liquids cause volume loss, making water sink through the tank bottom because pressure from the floor cannot counteract gravity. Boundary Conditions: The basic implementation stores quantities at cell centers. Staggered MAC grids are more robust for boundary conditions but are not the default in this specific implementation. This method enforces a free-slip boundary condition for fluid simulations involving dynamic obstacles represented as voxelized solids. It ensures that fluid velocity normal to the obstacle surface matches the solid's normal velocity, allowing tangential slip, while preventing mass leakage into solid interiors. It differs from no-slip conditions by retaining tangential fluid velocity and from static boundary handling by explicitly updating obstacle velocity fields and modifying the pressure solver to ignore solid cell contributions. The Projection Method enforces incompressibility on a fluid velocity field by subtracting the gradient of a pressure field, ensuring the resulting velocity is divergence-free. It serves as the incompressibility enforcement step within the Stable Fluids framework. Operator splitting decomposes the complex dynamic equations of fluid dynamics into sequential, simpler sub-steps to facilitate numerical integration on a grid. It solves the problem of enforcing incompressibility while applying external forces and advecting the fluid state. It sets itself apart from the parent Stable Fluids (GPU Implementation) by explicitly structuring the time integration into three distinct, ordered phases: advection, force application, and pressure projection. A GPU-based Eulerian fluid solver that simulates and renders volumetrics at VR resolutions and refresh rates by using operator splitting to approximately solve the Navier-Stokes equations. It distinguishes itself by integrating a custom injection kernel for source terms and a geometric multigrid pressure solver optimized for half-precision 3D textures, enabling interactive frame rates on consumer hardware. A method to advect fluid by moving particles according to their velocities, where physical quantities like mass and velocity are bound to particles. The process moves all particles according to their velocities v{t-1} (average velocity over t-1 	o t), then applies external force and pressure projection to the advected velocities to get final velocities at the next time step t. Time Complexity: The dominant cost is the pressure solve. With Jacobi iteration, the cost is O(N \cdot I), where N is the number of grid cells and I is the number of iterations. Memory Complexity: Storage is proportional to the grid size. Table 30-1 in indicates ~9 bytes per cell for simulation (velocity RGBA16, inside-outside R8, temporary RGBA16) and ~20 bytes per pixel for rendering (off-screen targets, ray data, depth). Measured Performance: Designed for real-time applications. Performance depends on the number of Jacobi iterations. Smoke/fire can tolerate fewer iterations for higher frame rates, while liquids require more. Strengths: Unconditional stability of semi-Lagrangian advection; efficient GPU implementation using 3D textures and geometry shaders; simple to implement. Limitations: Numerical smoothing from semi-Lagrangian advection; volume loss if Jacobi iterations are insufficient for liquids; cell-centered storage is less robust than staggered grids for complex boundaries. When to use: Real-time fluid simulation where unconditional stability is prioritized, particularly for smoke and fire; liquids require careful iteration tuning to prevent volume loss. When not to use: High-fidelity liquid simulation requiring strict volume conservation without excessive iterations; simulations requiring complex boundary conditions handled by no-slip or dynamic obstacles (use Free-Slip Boundary Condition Enforcement or GPU-based Eulerian Fluid Solver). The "stable fluids" method for computing velocity was introduced by Jos Stam in 1999. A GPU implementation of this method for 2D fluids was presented by Mark Harris in 2004. The 3D GPU implementation described in the sources extends these concepts to volumetric grids using Direct3D 10 features like 3D textures and geometry shaders. Alternatives to the Jacobi solver include Conjugate Gradient (Bolz et al. 2003), Multigrid (Goodnight et al. 2003), and Cyclic reduction (Kass et al. 2006).
