name: Lamorlette and Foster Fire Model
head: Macro-movement Fire Model, Parametric Curve-Based Fire, Shrek Fire Model
body:
The Lamorlette and Foster Fire Model is a mixed framework for simulating the macro-movement of fire in production systems, originally developed for the motion picture Shrek by DreamWorks. It solves the problem of achieving a holistic visual appearance for fire, distinguishing it from the atomistic look of standard particle systems and the smoke-suited appearance of texture splats. The method sets itself apart by modeling individual flame elements as parametric space curves that evolve over time, coupled with a reduced form of Navier-Stokes equations, rather than relying solely on discrete point particles or static volumetric fields. Inputs: A set of initial points defining the spine of flame elements. Wind field data (velocity and temperature fields). Procedural control parameters for placement, intensity, lifespan, shape, color, size, and behavior. Outputs: A set of rendered particles representing the visible flame (oxidization region). Data Structures: Parametric Curve: Defined by a sequence of control points interpolating the flame spine. Particle: A point sampled near the curve, carrying position, color, and opacity attributes. Implicit Surface: A cylindrical profile defining the oxidization region boundary. Steps: 1. Curve Initialization: Model individual flame elements as parametric space curves. Each curve interpolates a set of points defining the spine of the flame. 2. Curve Evolution: Evolve the curves over time using a combination of physics-based, procedural, and hand-defined wind fields. Physical properties are derived from statistical measurements of natural diffusion flames. The curves are frequently re-sampled to ensure continuity and to model flames generated from moving sources. Wind dynamics are governed by the velocity of the gas rushing into surrounding air and temperature. Drag (shearing forces) causes rotation and mixing, leading to turbulent swirling. Turbulence is exaggerated if gas flows around solid objects, transitioning from smooth flow to chaotic mixing behind the object. 3. Curve Breaking: Allow curves to break, generating independently evolving flames with a limited lifespan. Engineering observations and stochastic assumptions provide heuristics for this process. 4. Implicit Surface & Sampling: Build an implicit surface representing the oxidization region (the visible part of the flame) using a cylindrical profile. Sample particles close to this region using a volumetric falloff function. 5. Buoyancy Noise: Apply procedural noise to the particles in the parameter space of the profile. Animate this noise to follow thermal buoyancy. 6. Turbulence Noise: Transform particles into the parameter space of the flame’s structural curve. Apply a second level of noise with a Kolmogorov frequency spectrum (derived from Navier-Stokes equations for turbulence) to provide turbulent detail. 7. Rendering: Render particles using either a volumetric method or a fast painterly method. The painterly method simulates a painting-like quality with visible brush strokes using height and opacity maps. Adjust particle color based on neighbor properties to allow flame elements to visually merge in a realistic way. 8. Procedural Control: Apply procedural controls to govern placement, intensity, lifespan, and evolution in shape, color, size, and behavior of the flames. Formulas: The change of velocity of gas in an arbitrary wind field is expressed as: w(u) = v 
abla \cdot (
abla u) - (u \cdot 
abla)u - 
abla p where u = (xp, t) is a four-dimensional vector of spatial dimensions and time, v is kinematic viscosity, 
abla p is the pressure gradient, and (u \cdot 
abla)u is convection. Smaller viscosity leads to more rotation in the gas. The macro-movement of flame spines follows:  rac{dxp}{dt} = w(xp, t) + d(Tp) + Vp + c(Tp, t) where w(xp, t) is an arbitrary controlling wind field, d(Tp) is motion due to diffusion of particles modeled as temperature-scaled Brownian motion, Vp is motion due to movement of the source, and c(Tp, t) is motion due to thermal buoyancy. Thermal buoyancy is constant over the lifetime of the particle: c(Tp, t) = - eta g (T0 - Tp) tp^2 where  eta is the thermal coefficient, g is gravity, T0 is ambient temperature, and tp is particle age. Wind dynamics governed by velocity rushing into surrounding air and temperature. # Drag causes rotation and mixing. for pt in self.spine: pt.velocity = pt.velocity + windvel dt pt.position = pt.position + pt.velocity dt def resample(self): # Stage 2: Re-sample curves frequently to ensure continuity. # Sources do not specify the resampling algorithm. pass def shouldbreak(self, controls) -> bool: # Stage 3: Allow curves to break based on engineering observations and stochastic heuristics. # As the flame grows, separate the top or make it flicker; separated parts burn out as they rise away from the main point. Parameters: Wind fields control flame motion indirectly. Direct animator controls govern basic shape, scale, color, flickering, and separation behavior. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The fast painterly method is described as a way to render the image quickly, but specific performance metrics (e.g., frames per second, resolution) are not provided in the sources. Strengths: Provides a holistic look for fire, superior to atomistic particle systems and better suited for fire than texture splats. Offers artistic control through procedural parameters. Limitations: Relies on heuristics and stochastic assumptions for curve breaking, which may require tuning for different fire types. When to use: When a holistic, production-quality fire appearance is needed, particularly in contexts where artistic control is prioritized over strict physical simulation. When not to use: When atomistic particle effects are desired, or when the scene primarily involves smoke or steam where texture splats are more appropriate. The Lamorlette and Foster Fire Model was developed for the motion picture Shrek by DreamWorks. It is described as a "very solid mixed framework for macro-movement of fire in a production system". The model draws on statistical measurements of natural diffusion flames and applies Navier-Stokes equations to turbulence (Kolmogorov frequency spectrum). It is cited as a key reference for realistic fire rendering in production environments. name: Image-order rendering
body: Image-order rendering generates images by iterating over pixels and computing the contribution of volumetric data along rays cast from the camera through each pixel. It sets itself apart from Object-order rendering by processing pixels rather than voxels, ensuring correct depth sorting and occlusion handling without explicit z-buffering of primitives. All image-order methods share the fundamental loop structure: for each pixel, a ray is defined in world space, intersected with the volume domain, and sampled/composited along its path. The ray is parameterized as r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the origin and \mathbf{d} is the direction. The traversal order is determined by the pixel's position in the image plane. Computes the ordered sequence of grid cells intersected by a ray, returning cell indices and entry/exit distances. It solves the problem of efficiently identifying which volumetric data elements a ray passes through without performing expensive per-voxel bounding box intersection tests or fixed-distance sampling. It sets itself apart from Direct volume ray casting by providing the geometric traversal logic (the "where" and "when") rather than the shading/compositing logic (the "what"), and from Acceleration by operating on uniform or structured grids rather than hierarchical spatial partitioning structures like octrees. Choose it when precise voxel access is required for sampling or acceleration structures. Reduces computational cost by minimizing redundant sampling, skipping invisible data, or parallelizing work. It solves the bottleneck of evaluating the volume rendering integral for every ray or voxel. Unlike Image-order rendering which defines the traversal order (eye-space), acceleration methods optimize the content of that traversal—whether by skipping empty space, terminating rays early, or adapting resolution—without changing the fundamental image-order nature of the parent. Choose it when rendering high-resolution datasets or neural fields where per-voxel evaluation is prohibitive. Casts a ray through a 3D volume for every pixel, sampling scalar values, mapping them to RGBA via a transfer function, and compositing samples front-to-back using alpha blending. It differs from Isosurface and first-hit ray casting by allowing all voxels to contribute to the final image rather than stopping at the first opaque surface, and from Distance-field ray marching by using uniform step sizes rather than distance-field-guided steps. It replaces slice-stack methods by providing a solid volume appearance from any angle without edge-on gaps. Choose it for translucent media where internal structures must be visible through outer layers. Renders a volume by tracing rays from the eye and stopping at the first voxel (or interpolated point) where the scalar field crosses a specified threshold (isovalue), treating the volume as an opaque surface. Unlike Direct volume ray casting, which composites the entire ray path to simulate transparency, this method terminates traversal upon the first hit, offering higher performance for opaque structures and avoiding the visual artifacts of volume integration. It differs from Distance-field ray marching by operating on discrete scalar fields with threshold crossing rather than continuous signed distance functions, and from Ray-grid traversal by focusing on the specific intersection logic of the isosurface rather than general grid traversal optimization. Choose it for opaque structures where surface shading and lighting are prioritized over transparency. Finds surfaces by moving along a ray in repeated steps, using a signed distance field (SDF) to choose each step size adaptively, avoiding the tradeoff of fixed-step marching. Unlike naive fixed-step marching which uses a constant increment, sphere tracing uses the SDF value as the step size, ensuring the step is as large as possible without risk of overshooting. Unlike traditional rasterization, the visible shape is defined mathematically by a scene function, not by a triangle mesh. Choose it when rendering implicit geometry or procedural volumes without explicit voxel grids. Not given in the sources. Widely used in medical imaging, scientific visualization, and computer graphics for rendering volumetric datasets such as CT scans and MRI data.

name: Ray-grid traversal
head: Voxel traversal, Grid traversal, DDA traversal, Amanatides-Woo traversal
body: Ray-grid traversal determines the sequence of uniform grid cells (voxels or tiles) intersected by a ray, enabling efficient sampling and compositing in volume rendering. It solves the problem of enumerating grid intersections without missing thin cells or performing redundant work. Unlike hierarchical methods that skip empty space via tree structures, standard ray-grid traversal steps through every cell boundary along the ray path. It differs from Acceleration by focusing on the geometric stepping logic itself, and from Direct volume ray casting by providing the traversal indices required for the sampling phase. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of advancing analytically from one cell boundary to the next, avoiding fixed-distance sampling steps. The algorithm determines the next cell by comparing the distances to the upcoming boundaries on the x, y, and z axes, selecting the minimum distance to advance. Let the ray be defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized or unnormalized). The grid is defined by cell boundaries. For a uniform grid with voxel size v and dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz, the traversal calculates the distances to the next boundaries for each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: 1. Step Direction (\text{step}i): Determines the index increment direction. \text{step}i = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } di > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } di < 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } di = 0 \end{cases} If di = 0, the ray never crosses a boundary in that dimension, and the corresponding distance is treated as infinity. 2. Time/Distance Delta (\Delta ti or s{\Delta i}): The distance along the ray to traverse one voxel width. \Delta ti = \frac{vi}{|di|} \cdot \text{step}i \quad \text{or} \quad s{\Delta i} = \frac{\Delta xi}{|\widehat{d}i|} where vi is the voxel size and \widehat{d}i is the unit direction component. 3. Time/Distance to Next Boundary (t{max, i} or s{max, i}): The distance from the ray origin to the first boundary crossed in axis i. t{max, i} = \frac{\text{boundary}i - oi}{di} The initial boundary is determined by the starting voxel index. If the ray starts inside the grid, the initial boundary is the next one in the direction of travel. The core loop iterates while the ray remains within the grid bounds: 1. Identify the axis k with the minimum boundary distance: t{min} = \min(t{max, x}, t{max, y}, t{max, z}). 2. Record the current cell and the interval [t{entry}, t{min}]. 3. Advance the index in axis k: \text{index}k \leftarrow \text{index}k + \text{step}k. 4. Update the boundary distance for axis k: t{max, k} \leftarrow t{max, k} + \Delta tk. 5. Update t{entry} \leftarrow t{min}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ddatraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelsize, gridbounds): # Initialize current voxel index currentvoxel = [int(rayorigin[i] // voxelsize) for i in range(3)] currentvoxel = [max(gridbounds.min[i], min(gridbounds.max[i], currentvoxel[i])) for i in range(3)] # Step direction per axis step = [1 if raydirection[i] > 0 else (-1 if raydirection[i] < 0 else 0) for i in range(3)] # Distance to next boundary nextboundary = [(currentvoxel[i] + step[i]) voxelsize for i in range(3)] tmax = [(nextboundary[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] if raydirection[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] # Distance delta per axis tdelta = [voxelsize / abs(raydirection[i]) if raydirection[i] != 0 else 0.0 for i in range(3)] tentry = 0.0 while gridbounds.min[0] <= currentvoxel[0] <= gridbounds.max[0] and \ gridbounds.min[1] <= currentvoxel[1] <= gridbounds.max[1] and \ gridbounds.min[2] <= currentvoxel[2] <= gridbounds.max[2]: minidx = tmax.index(min(tmax)) texit = tmax[minidx] yield currentvoxel, tentry, texit currentvoxel[minidx] += step[minidx] tmax[minidx] += tdelta[minidx] tentry = texit Accelerates rendering by traversing a multi-dimensional hierarchy to adaptively select resolution levels based on error tolerance. A stochastic technique for unstructured tetrahedral meshes using coarse mesh hierarchies to bound extinction. Processes Matryoshka layers in front-to-back order to handle occlusion correctly. Generates a manifold mesh by traversing a dual grid constructed from a primal voxel grid. Maps 3D volumetric data to a 2D image plane by traversing rays from pixels into the volume. Accelerates rendering of irregular grids by exploiting spatial coherence via a sweep-plane paradigm. Combines analytical DDA logic with tree-aware node skipping for sparse volume trees. Advances ray origin in discrete steps using a precomputed octant mask to track traversal state. Iterates through levels of a grid mipmap to efficiently visit child voxels. Processes bundles of coherent rays through uniform grids slice-by-slice. Determines the sequence of uniform grid cells intersected by a ray. Traverses a uniform voxel grid in Z-order while compressing identical runs. Guarantees strict 4-connectivity by resolving boundary crossing ambiguities via stable sorting. Determines the sequence of nodes in a sparse voxel octree intersected by a ray. Traverses rays through multiple binary occupancy grids to generate ray intervals. Stores traversal steps as a ray template to accelerate parallel rays [Yagel-1992-DRT]. Accelerates rendering by replacing fixed-distance steps with analytical traversal. Adapts traversal algorithms to exploit GPU/SIMD architectural features. An alternative traversal algorithm that uses barycentric coordinates (u, v, w, x) to determine the child tetrahedron, avoiding explicit plane tests. The loop continues while childCounts[tetID] > 0 and rLevel ≤ maxDepth. Barycentric coordinates are calculated as u = \text{volume}(point,l,r,b)/\text{vol}, v = \text{volume}(point,t,b,r)/\text{vol}, w = \text{volume}(point,t,l,b)/\text{vol}, and x = 1 - (u + v + w). The child index is computed using boolean logic: tet = (RB × 4) + ((RB == TB) × 2) + inner, where RB is (u + v) < 0.5, TB is (v + w) < 0.5, and inner is (u < 0.5) & (v < 0.5) & (w < 0.5) & (x < 0.5). A hybrid CPU-GPU traversal strategy where the CPU traverses the KD-tree of AMR patches back-to-front, and the GPU traverses cells within a patch. Sub-patches are generated to ensure perspective-correct sorting of cells relative to the observer. The vertex shader modifies each index according to the current observer position to generate proper cell ordering. A medium traversal structure using a supergrid to allow empty and thin regions to be crossed in far fewer null collisions than paying for the densest voxel in the volume. The Medium::samplerealinteraction consumes null collisions in one fused C++ walk instead of iterating them in Python, sharing a single loop with the DDA traversal when a supergrid is used. It is faster than the global majorant approach because it avoids paying optixTrace for every null collision. The majorantresolutionfactor controls supergrid resolution (default 8), and majorantfactor is a safety factor (default 1.2). The 'homogeneous' medium type explicitly rejects the supergrid parameter. A CUDA device function that initializes the parameters for stepping through a voxel grid along a ray. A method to determine if a target isosurface lies within a ray segment defined by voxel entry/exit points, and to calculate its relative position for opacity/color contribution. Trilinear interpolation is used to get values at entry (V{in}) and exit (V{out}). Target values are classified into three categories: (1) strictly between V{in} and V{out}, (2) one endpoint within allowable window, (3) neither endpoint within window. For Category 1, the relative distance t is parameterized using linear interpolation. For Category 2, t is set to 0 or 1. Values are sorted by depth and effects calculated. A property defining the set of cells a ray can traverse to from its current cell, inspired by pixel connectivity in image processing. In 2D, there are 4-connectivity (orthogonal neighbors) and 8-connectivity (including diagonal neighbors). The Taxicab metric is |x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2| and the Chebyshev metric is \max(|x1 - x2|, |y1 - y2|). An algorithm that traverses all blocks a ray intersects with, starting from closest to the camera, to measure the direct impact of block-walking on performance by writing to a scalar at each block visit. Block walking reduces the number of queries (acceleration structure accesses) by 5-10x compared to standard ray tracing, translating to a 1.5x average performance improvement in block traversal mode. However, when content becomes too sparse, block walking is not effective and can have a high cost. In blend mode, performance improvements shrink due to costly access to individual voxel values. A dispatcher function that selects the appropriate traversal variant based on the maximum range of the segment. It computes absolute deltas dx = |end.x - start.x| and dy = |end.y - start.y|, then maxRange = max(dx, dy). If maxRange < 256.0f, it calls traverseGridSegment16 (Q8.8 fixed-point); otherwise, it calls traverseGridSegment32 (Q24.8 fixed-point). A renderer for regular grids (rgridb) that separates primitive generation and rendering into two distinct steps, regenerating all primitives if the volume changes. Unlike the hgridf renderer, it does not support partial updates of dirty cells; it regenerates the entire primitive set upon volume change. All processors accumulate interpolated values along a ray independently. Contributions are sorted with respect to visibility order before composing the final image. Frame rate scales linearly with the number of processors. The foundational algorithm, known as the Amanatides-Woo algorithm or 3D DDA, was introduced by J. Amanatides and A. Woo in 'A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing', published in Eurographics '87. It was designed to efficiently list all voxel IDs traversed by a ray in a 3D grid. The method has been widely implemented in various forms, including in real-time procedural voxel renderers like Minecraft-style raycasting, and in scientific computing tools like FIDASIM for collision detection. jw3126/VoxelRayTracers.jl, https://github.com/jw3126/VoxelRayTracers.jl, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) francisengelmann/fastvoxeltraversal, https://github.com/francisengelmann/fastvoxeltraversal, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Victorique-GOSICK/Voxel-3D-DDA, https://github.com/Victorique-GOSICK/Voxel-3D-DDA, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Super Fast Ray Casting in Tiled Worlds using DDA, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NbSee-XM7WA, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) 2026surfacemeshtools/docs/collisiondetection/04raygridtraversal..., https://github.com/canesesmarjf/2026surfacemeshtools/blob/main/docs/collisiondetection/04raygridtraversal.md, fetched 2026-10-25 Grids in Ray Tracing: A Comprehensive Survey, https://www.scribd.com/document/349616186/GG-400, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) cvcGL VolRenNode, CUDA raycast backend, and the volrenbunny demo, https://github.com/transfix/libcvc/pull/323, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Почему Моя Функция Трассировки Лучей Через Воксели С Использованием Dda..., https://otvet.mail.ru/question/240929436, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Minecraft Voxel DDA Raycast - name: Woodcock Tracking with Macrocell Majorant
head: Woodcock tracker, stochastic ray marching with majorant
body: Woodcock Tracking with Macrocell Majorant is a stochastic ray marching technique for volume rendering on unstructured tetrahedral meshes that utilizes a coarse mesh hierarchy to compute a tighter majorant extinction value. It solves the problem of high null-collision rates in heterogeneous volumes by bounding the local extinction with a precomputed macrocell value, thereby reducing the number of rejected samples compared to using a global or loose majorant on most datasets. It differs from standard Woodcock tracking by integrating coarse mesh traversal logic to manage the majorant bounds, and from Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting by relying on stochastic free-path sampling rather than deterministic grid traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, maximum traversal distance t{\text{max}}, current coarse element ID (coarseTetID), macrocell majorant value M{\text{macro}}, and a transfer function \text{tf} mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Output: A color value if a collision occurs within t{\text{max}}, or false (transparent) if the ray exits the volume or exceeds t{\text{max}}. Data Structures: Macrocell Majorant (M{\text{macro}}): A scalar value representing the upper bound of extinction for a coarse mesh element. Tetrahedron Vertices (tetVertices): An array of four 3D coordinates defining the current tetrahedron. Sample Point (samplePoint): The 3D position in space where the scalar value is sampled. Parameters: t{\text{max}}: The maximum distance the ray is allowed to travel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Majorant: Compute the effective majorant M as the product of the transfer function's maximum opacity and the macrocell majorant: M = \text{tf.opacity} \times M{\text{macro}}. 2. Check Validity: If M \le 0, the ray is skipped and false is returned. 3. Set Exit Boundary: Initialize the exit distance for the current coarse element to the smallest representable float less than the current ray distance t to ensure the first sample is processed: t{\text{exit}} = \text{nextafter}(t, -\infty). 4. Initialize State: Set sampleTetID to 0 and tetVertices to an empty set. 5. Stochastic Step: Generate a random number r \in [0, 1). Advance the ray distance t using the Woodcock step formula: t \leftarrow t - \frac{\ln(1 - r)}{M}. 6. Check Max Distance: If t \ge t{\text{max}}, return false. 7. Calculate Sample Point: Compute the 3D position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. 8. Check Element Boundary: If t > t{\text{exit}}, the ray has crossed a coarse element boundary. Traverse the coarse mesh to find the new tetrahedron containing \mathbf{p}: (\text{sampleTetID}, \text{tetVertices}) \leftarrow \text{traverse}(\mathbf{p}, \text{coarseTetID}). Update the exit distance for the new tetrahedron by intersecting the ray with the tetrahedron faces: t{\text{exit}} \leftarrow \text{intersectFaces}(t, \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{d}, \text{tetVertices}). 9. Sample Data: Sample the scalar value s at \mathbf{p} using the current tetrahedron: s \leftarrow \text{sampleData}(\mathbf{p}, \text{sampleTetID}, \text{tetVertices}). 10. Check Transfer Function Range: If s is not within the transfer function's valid range, continue to the next iteration. 11. Get Color: Retrieve the color C and opacity \alpha from the transfer function: (C, \alpha) \leftarrow \text{tf.getColor}(s). 12. Acceptance Test: Perform the analog acceptance test. Generate a new random number r' \in [0, 1). If: \alpha \times \text{tf.opacity} \ge r' \times M return C. Otherwise, continue to the next iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def woodcocktrackingwithmacrocell(rayorigin, raydirection, tmax, coarsetetid, macrocellmajorant, tf): # 1. Initialize majorant majorant = tf.opacity macrocellmajorant if majorant <= 0: return False # 2. Initialize distance along ray t = 0.0 # 3. Set exit boundary texit = math.nextafter(t, -float('inf')) # 4. Initialize state sampletetid = 0 tetvertices = [] while True: # 5. Stochastic step r = random.random() t -= math.log(1.0 - r) / majorant # 6. Check max distance if t >= tmax: return False # 7. Calculate sample point samplepoint = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] # 8. Check element boundary if t > texit: sampletetid, tetvertices = traverse(samplepoint, coarsetetid) texit = intersectfaces(t, samplepoint, raydirection, tetvertices) # 9. Sample data scalar = sampledata(samplepoint, sampletetid, tetvertices) # 10. Check transfer function range if not tf.inrange(scalar): continue # 11. Get color color = tf.getcolor(scalar) # 12. Acceptance test rprime = random.random() if color.opacity tf.opacity >= rprime majorant: return color def traverse(point, coarsetetid): # Standard coarse mesh traversal to find the tetrahedron containing point # Returns (tetid, vertices) return coarsetetid, gettetvertices(coarsetetid) def intersectfaces(t, p, d, vertices): # Computes the exit distance of ray R(s) = p + sd from the tetrahedron # defined by vertices. Returns the smallest positive s > 0 added to t. minexit = float('inf') faces = [(0,1,2), (0,1,3), (0,2,3), (1,2,3)] for i, j, k in faces: v0, v1, v2 = vertices[i], vertices[j], vertices[k] n = cross(sub(v1, v0), sub(v2, v0)) denom = dot(n, d) if abs(denom) > 1e-9: dist = dot(n, sub(v0, p)) / denom if dist > 0: minexit = min(minexit, dist) return t + minexit def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]] def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def sub(a, b): return [a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]] def sampledata(point, tetid, vertices): return 0.0 # Standard point-in-tetrahedron scalar lookup Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overstepping: When using macrocell values, if the ray crosses a boundary into a denser region, the majorant may no longer be valid. The algorithm must restart traversal from the beginning of the next element to avoid missing collisions. Performance Degradation: On datasets with shallow trees or specific structures (e.g., Agulhas), macrocell optimizations can decrease performance due to the overhead of restarting element processing. Extends this method by integrating coarse mesh traversal for AMR data, using macrocell densities to provide tighter majorants than transfer function opacity alone. An alternative acceleration technique that decomposes the medium into homogeneous and heterogeneous components, allowing non-bounding control extinction. Rendering Performance: Tighter majorants reduce the number of null collisions, improving rendering times on most datasets. Memory Complexity: Low, as it primarily stores the coarse mesh structure and transfer function data. Measured Performance: On the Agulhas dataset, macrocell optimizations degraded performance due to traversal overhead. On other datasets, tighter majorants generally improved rendering times. Strengths: Reduces null collisions in heterogeneous volumes by providing tighter bounds than global majorants. Limitations: Performance can degrade on specific dataset structures (e.g., shallow trees) due to the cost of boundary traversal and restart logic. This method is described in the context of direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data. It builds upon the principles of Woodcock tracking (null-collision method) and adapts them for unstructured tetrahedral meshes using a coarse mesh hierarchy to manage majorant values. name: Woodcock Tracking with Coarse Mesh and Macrocells
head: Null-collision Woodcock with macrocell majorant, Woodcock ray casting on AMR
body: This method performs volume rendering using Woodcock tracking (null-collision) within coarse mesh elements, utilizing macrocell densities to determine the majorant extinction value. It builds on Woodcock Tracking with Macrocell Majorant by integrating the traversal of a coarse mesh structure to manage the underlying adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data. Using macrocell majorant values provides a tighter majorant than using only transfer function opacity, reducing null collisions and improving performance. Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, maximum ray length (t{max}), coarse mesh structure, macrocell density values, transfer function (TF), and scalar field data. Outputs: Final pixel color. Data Structures: Coarse Mesh: A hierarchy of coarse tetrahedra. Each coarse element has an associated macrocellMajorant value. Macrocell Values: An array or map where macrocellValues[coarseID] stores the maximum macrocell density for that coarse element. Transfer Function: Provides tf.opacity (scalar to opacity mapping) and tf.getColor(scalar) (scalar to RGBA color). Refinement Tree: Used to locate the specific fine tetrahedron within a coarse element. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coarse Element Traversal: Call TraverseCoarseMesh(ray) to determine the current coarse element ID (coarseID), the back face distance (tBack), and the next face distance (tNextFace). If coarseID is -1, the ray has exited the volume. Return the background color. 2. Majorant Calculation: Retrieve the macrocell majorant: macrocellMajorant = macrocellValues[coarseID]. Call WoodcockElem with this majorant. Inside WoodcockElem, calculate the effective majorant: \sigma{max} = \text{tf.opacity} \times \text{macrocellMajorant} If \sigma{max} \le 0, return false (no emission/absorption possible). 3. Free Path Sampling: Sample a free path length using the majorant \sigma{max}: t{step} = -\frac{\log(1 - \text{rand}())}{\sigma{max}} Update the ray position: t{ray} = t{ray} + t{step} If t{ray} \ge t{max}, return false. 4. Tetrahedron Location: Calculate the sample point: P = \text{ray.org} + t{ray} \times \text{ray.dir} If the sample point is outside the current tetrahedron (checked against tExit), traverse the refinement tree to find the specific fine tetrahedron (sampleTetID) and its vertices (tetVertices). Update tExit to the distance to the exit face of the new tetrahedron. 5. Scalar Sampling and Acceptance: Sample the scalar value at P using sampleTetID and tetVertices. If the scalar is not in the transfer function range, continue the loop (null collision). Get the color: color = tf.getColor(scalar). Perform the null-collision acceptance test: \text{color.opacity} \times \text{tf.opacity} \ge \text{rand}() \times \sigma{max} If accepted, return color. Otherwise, treat as a null collision and continue the loop. 6. Boundary Handling: When stepping over to the next coarse element, if the previous volume was less dense, the free path might overstep the boundary. To fix this, set ray.t to just after the next coarse element's minimum t value in front of the ray, effectively taking a step back to the beginning of the next coarse element. This step is not needed if macrocell majorant values are not used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Traverse coarse mesh coarseid, tback, tnextface = traversecoarsemesh(ray) if coarseid == -1: return backgroundcolor # 2. Get macrocell majorant macrocellmajorant = macrocellvalues[coarseid] # 3. Process element color = woodcockelem(ray, tback, coarseid, macrocellmajorant, tf, tmax) if color is not None: return color # 4. The source code snippet suggests: # majorant <- tf.opacity macrocellMajorant # However, tf.opacity is usually scalar-dependent. # Looking at Algorithm 12 line 2: majorant <- tf.opacity macrocellMajorant # And line 24: color.opacity tf.opacity >= rand() majorant # This implies tf.opacity might be a constant for the element or the source # uses tf.opacity as a global scaling factor. # Let's follow the source literally: majorant is calculated once per element? # No, line 24 uses color.opacity tf.opacity. # If majorant is constant, then the acceptance test compares against it. # Let's assume tf.opacity in line 2 is a constant for the element, # or the source implies the majorant is based on the max opacity. # Given "maximum macrocell density... scaled with the opacity of the transfer function", # it likely means: sigmamax = maxtfopacity maxmacrocelldensity. # Re-reading Algorithm 12: # 2: majorant <- tf.opacity macrocellMajorant # This line is outside the while loop. So majorant is constant for the element. # This implies tf.opacity is a constant for the element (e.g., max opacity). sigmamax = tf.opacity macrocellmajorant if sigmamax <= 0: return None # Initialize tetrahedron info sampletetid = 0 tetvertices = [] while True: # Sample free path ray.t = ray.t - log(1 - rand()) / sigmamax if ray.t >= tmax: return None samplepoint = ray.org + ray.t ray.dir # Check if we are still in the current tetrahedron if ray.t > texit: # Traverse refinement tree to find the fine tetrahedron sampletetid, tetvertices = traverserefinementtree(samplepoint, coarsetetid) # Update texit to the exit face of the new tetrahedron texit = intersectfaces(ray.t, samplepoint, ray.dir, tetvertices) # Sample scalar scalar = sampledata(samplepoint, sampletetid, tetvertices) if not tf.inrange(scalar): continue color = tf.getcolor(scalar) # Acceptance test # Source: color.opacity tf.opacity >= rand() majorant # Note: tf.opacity here is the same constant used for sigmamax? # If so, this simplifies to: color.opacity >= rand() macrocellmajorant # But let's stick to the source formula. if color.opacity tf.opacity >= rand() sigmamax: return color Performance: Using macrocell majorant values reduces null collisions compared to using only transfer function opacity, leading to better performance. Complexity: The complexity depends on the coarse mesh traversal and the refinement tree depth. The method allows for interactive frame rates on tested datasets. Memory: Requires storing coarse mesh structures, macrocell values, and the refinement tree. The transfer function and scalars reside in GPU memory. Limitations: Only emission and absorption are implemented; secondary effects are not supported. This method is part of a volume rendering system for tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data. It was implemented alongside a ray marching method.
