name: Weighted Decomposition Tracking
head: Analog Decomposition Tracking, Decomposition Tracking
body: Weighted Decomposition Tracking accelerates free-path sampling in heterogeneous volumes by decomposing the medium into a homogeneous control component and a heterogeneous residual component. It reduces the number of expensive spatially-varying extinction lookups required by standard delta tracking while producing identical noise patterns and light paths. Unlike the analog variant, the weighted formulation permits non-bounding control extinctions and free-path-sampling coefficients, enabling efficient chromatic (spectral) collision handling without requiring non-negative residual extinction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current position \mathbf{x}, direction \omega, path throughput weight w (initialized to 1), constant control extinction coefficients \mua^c, \mus^c, constant free-path-sampling coefficient \bar{\mu}, and spatially varying functions for residual absorption \mua^r(\mathbf{x}), scattering \mus^r(\mathbf{x}), and null-collision \mun(\mathbf{x}). Output: Updated position, direction, and throughput weight after one collision event, or emitted radiance if absorption occurs. Data Structures: Control Component: Defined by constant scalar values \mua^c and \mus^c. Residual Component: Defined by spatially varying functions \mua^r(\mathbf{x}) and \mus^r(\mathbf{x}). Majorant: \bar{\mu} is a constant upper bound for the total extinction \mut(\mathbf{x}) across the volume or spectral band. In the weighted version, \bar{\mu} does not need to be a minorant of \mut(\mathbf{x}) at every point, but must satisfy \bar{\mu} > \mut^c. Null-Collision Coefficient: \mun(\mathbf{x}) = \bar{\mu} - \mut^c - \mut^r(\mathbf{x}). Parameters: \bar{\mu}: Free-path-sampling coefficient, typically chosen as the maximum total extinction in the scene. \mut^c: Control total extinction, computed as \mut^c = \mua^c + \mus^c. Octree Depth: Typically 8–10 to balance lookup reduction and traversal overhead. Formulas: The method samples one of five events: control absorption, control scattering, residual absorption, residual scattering, or null collision. Probabilities are defined as: Pa^c = \frac{\mua^c}{\bar{\mu}} Ps^c = \frac{\mus^c}{\bar{\mu}} Pa^r(\mathbf{x}) = \left(1 - \frac{\mut^c}{\bar{\mu}}\right) \frac{|\mua^r(\mathbf{x})|}{|\mua^r(\mathbf{x})| + |\mus^r(\mathbf{x})| + |\mun(\mathbf{x})|} Ps^r(\mathbf{x}) = \left(1 - \frac{\mut^c}{\bar{\mu}}\right) \frac{|\mus^r(\mathbf{x})|}{|\mua^r(\mathbf{x})| + |\mus^r(\mathbf{x})| + |\mun(\mathbf{x})|} Pn(\mathbf{x}) = \left(1 - \frac{\mut^c}{\bar{\mu}}\right) \frac{|\mun(\mathbf{x})|}{|\mua^r(\mathbf{x})| + |\mus^r(\mathbf{x})| + |\mun(\mathbf{x})|} The denominator sums the absolute values of the residual and null coefficients. Algorithm Steps: The tracker loops indefinitely until a non-null collision occurs or emission is sampled. 1. Sample Free Path: Draw a uniform random number \zeta \in 0, 1) and compute t = -\ln(1-\zeta)/\bar{\mu}. 2. Advance Position: Update position \mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathbf{x} + t\omega. 3. Evaluate Probabilities: Compute Pa^c, Ps^c, Pa^r(\mathbf{x}), Ps^r(\mathbf{x}), Pn(\mathbf{x}) using the current position \mathbf{x} and constants. 4. Sample Event: Draw a uniform random number \xi \in [0, 1) and accumulate probabilities to determine the event. If \xi < Pa^c: Control absorption. The local weight factor is \mua^c/(\bar{\mu}Pa^c) = 1, so w remains unchanged. Return emitted radiance Le(\mathbf{x}, \omega) scaled by w. Else if \xi < Pa^c + Ps^c: Control scattering. The local weight factor is \mus^c/(\bar{\mu}Ps^c) = 1. Sample a new direction \omega from the [phase function p(\omega). Break the loop. Else if \xi < Pa^c + Ps^c + Pa^r(\mathbf{x}): Residual absorption. Update w \leftarrow w \cdot \mua^r(\mathbf{x})/(\bar{\mu}Pa^r(\mathbf{x})). Return emitted radiance scaled by w. Else if \xi < Pa^c + Ps^c + Pa^r(\mathbf{x}) + Ps^r(\mathbf{x}): Residual scattering. Update w \leftarrow w \cdot \mus^r(\mathbf{x})/(\bar{\mu}Ps^r(\mathbf{x})). Sample a new direction \omega from p(\omega). Break the loop. Else: Null collision. Update w \leftarrow w \cdot \mun(\mathbf{x})/(\bar{\mu}Pn(\mathbf{x})). Continue the loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def WeightedDecompositionTracking(x, omega, w, muac, musc, mubar, getmuar, getmusr, getmun): """ Performs one step of weighted decomposition tracking. Args: x: Current position (vec3) omega: Current direction (vec3) w: Current path throughput weight (float) muac: Control absorption coefficient (float, constant) musc: Control scattering coefficient (float, constant) mubar: Free-path-sampling coefficient (float, constant) getmuar: Function returning residual absorption at x (float) getmusr: Function returning residual scattering at x (float) getmun: Function returning null-collision coefficient at x (float) Returns: Tuple (newx, newomega, neww, eventtype) eventtype: 'ABSORB', 'SCATTER', or 'CONTINUE' """ mutc = muac + musc # 1. Sample free path zeta = randomuniform() t = -math.log(1.0 - zeta) / mubar # 2. Advance position x = x + t omega # 3. Evaluate coefficients and probabilities muar = getmuar(x) musr = getmusr(x) mun = getmun(x) # Denominator for residual/null probabilities denom = abs(muar) + abs(musr) + abs(mun) # Marginal probability of NOT sampling control pnotc = 1.0 - (mutc / mubar) # Probabilities Pac = muac / mubar Psc = musc / mubar if denom > 0: Par = pnotc (abs(muar) / denom) Psr = pnotc (abs(musr) / denom) Pn = pnotc (abs(mun) / denom) else: # Degenerate case: no residual/null coefficients. Par = 0.0 Psr = 0.0 Pn = 0.0 # 4. Sample event xi = randomuniform() if xi < Pac: # Control Absorption return (x, omega, w, 'ABSORB') elif xi < Pac + Psc: # Control Scattering newomega = samplephasefunction(omega) return (x, newomega, w, 'SCATTER') elif xi < Pac + Psc + Par: # Residual Absorption weightfactor = muar / (mubar Par) neww = w weightfactor return (x, omega, neww, 'ABSORB') elif xi < Pac + Psc + Par + Psr: # Residual Scattering weightfactor = musr / (mubar Psr) neww = w weightfactor newomega = samplephasefunction(omega) return (x, newomega, neww, 'SCATTER') else: # Null Collision weightfactor = mun / (mubar Pn) neww = w weightfactor return (x, omega, neww, 'CONTINUE') def randomuniform() -> float: """Returns a uniform random float in 0, 1). """ import random return random.random() def samplephasefunction(omega: tuple) -> tuple: """Samples a new direction from the phase function p(omega). """ # Standard phase function sampling implementation return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Bounding Control: If \mut^c > \mut(\mathbf{x}) at some point, \mun(\mathbf{x}) becomes negative. The weighted formulation handles this via absolute values in probabilities and signed weights, but a loose \bar{\mu} increases the variance of the path throughput rapidly. Zero Denominator: If the residual and null coefficients are all zero (e.g., homogeneous medium where \mut^c = \mut(\mathbf{x}) and \bar{\mu} = \mut^c), the denominator is zero. In this case, Pa^r, Ps^r, Pn are zero, and only control events are possible. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise if \mut^c is very close to \bar{\mu}, making Pa^c and Ps^c dominate and residual probabilities negligible. A variant designed for chromatic (spectral) rendering by vectorizing collision coefficients across wavelengths \lambda. Control extinction coefficients \mua^c(\lambda) and \mus^c(\lambda) are set to the minimum values across all wavelengths, while \bar{\mu} bounds the maximum total extinction across all wavelengths. Probabilities are computed using vectorized operations. When a control component is sampled, the local collision weight is a vector of ones (1, \dots, 1)^{N\lambda}, avoiding per-wavelength weight updates for the control branch. Time Complexity: The number of spatially-varying extinction lookups is reduced compared to standard delta tracking. The relative cost \rho = N{dcmp}/N{delta} = 1 - \mut^c/\bar{\mu} when \mut^c is a minorant. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the [octree structure (typically depth 8–10) and voxel data (e.g., VDB). Measured Performance: In a thick cloud scene, decomposition tracking avoided 42% of extinction lookups required by delta tracking, and 58% in a thin cloud scene. With octree depth 8, lookup time reduced from 1030s to 536s, and tracker time from 299s to 280s in a thick cloud scene. Strengths: Identical noise patterns to delta tracking; significant reduction in lookup costs for heterogeneous volumes; handles chromatic coefficients efficiently in the weighted variant. Limitations: Requires tight bounds for control and residual components for optimal performance; octree traversal overhead increases with depth; if \mut^c > \min(\mut(\mathbf{x})), variance increases and performance degrades. When to Use: Heterogeneous volumes with significant spatial variation in extinction, especially when spectral accuracy is required. When Not to Use: Homogeneous volumes (no benefit), or when tight bounds cannot be computed efficiently. Weighted Decomposition Tracking was introduced in the paper "Spectral and Decomposition Tracking for Rendering Heterogeneous Volumes" by Novák et al.. It builds on the concept of decomposition tracking for transmittance estimation [Novák et al. 2014] and extends it to free-path sampling. The analog version was previously limited by the requirement for non-negative residual extinction, which prevented spectral rendering. The weighted version removes this limitation, enabling efficient spectral tracking. It is used in production path tracers with VDB voxel storage and octree acceleration structures. Spectral and Decomposition Tracking for Rendering Heterogeneous Volumes, https://media.disneyanimation.com/uploads/production/publicationasset/158/asset/SpectralAndDecompositionTracking.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Majorant Supergrid Traversal
head: Majorant Supergrid for Medium Traversal, Supergrid DDA
body: Majorant Supergrid Traversal is a medium traversal technique that uses a supergrid to allow empty and thin regions to be crossed in far fewer null collisions than paying for the densest voxel in the volume. It builds on Ray-grid traversal by replacing a single global majorant extinction bound with a spatially varying one, reducing the overhead of null-collision sampling in heterogeneous media. Unlike Woodcock Tracking with Macrocell Majorant, which may use fixed macrocells, this method dynamically adapts the bounding extinction to local density variations on a coarse grid. The method combines a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal with a null-collision sampling loop, fused into a single iteration when a supergrid is active. It requires a majorant extinction field defined on a supergrid, which is a downsampled version of the high-resolution medium grid. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, high-resolution extinction/scattering data, supergrid resolution factor R, majorant safety factor M. Output: Sequence of interaction points (or null collisions) along the ray. Data Structures: Supergrid: A 3D grid with dimensions Nx/R \times Ny/R \times Nz/R (assuming uniform downsampling). Each cell stores the maximum extinction coefficient \mut found in the corresponding region of the high-res grid. Majorant: The value \mu{max} used for sampling is \max(\mu{supergrid\cell}) \times M. Parameters: majorantresolutionfactor (R): Controls supergrid resolution. Default value is 8. majorantfactor (M): Safety factor for the majorant. Default value is 1.2. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Supergrid: For each cell in the supergrid, compute \mu{supergrid}[i,j,k] = \max{\text{voxels in cell}} (\mut(\mathbf{x})). If the medium is homogeneous, this step is skipped or rejected. 2. Ray Initialization: Compute initial voxel indices and boundary distances using standard DDA logic. 3. Fused Loop: Iterate while the ray is within bounds: a. Determine the current supergrid cell containing the ray's current position. b. Retrieve the local majorant \mu{local} = \mu{supergrid}[cell] \times M. c. Sample a null collision distance t{null} from an exponential distribution with rate \mu{local}: t{null} = -\ln(u) / \mu{local}, where u \in (0,1) is a uniform random number. d. Compare t{null} with the distance to the next supergrid boundary t{grid\boundary}. e. If t{null} < t{grid\boundary}: i. Advance the ray by t{null}. ii. Sample a real interaction (scattering) with probability \mut(\mathbf{x}) / \mu{local}. If sampled, record the interaction and terminate the current path segment. If not, record a null collision and continue. f. If t{null} \ge t{grid\boundary}: i. Advance the ray to t{grid\boundary} using the DDA step. ii. Update the current supergrid cell. iii. Repeat loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def majorantsupergridtraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, supergrid, majorantfactor, voxelsize): # Initialize DDA state currentvoxel = getvoxelindex(rayorigin, voxelsize) step = getstepdirection(raydirection) tmax = getnextboundarydistances(rayorigin, raydirection, currentvoxel, voxelsize) tdelta = getboundarydistancesdelta(raydirection, voxelsize) tentry = 0.0 # Get initial supergrid cell and majorant supergridcell = getsupergridcell(currentvoxel, supergrid.resolutionfactor) mulocal = supergrid.maxextinction[supergridcell] majorantfactor while isinsidegrid(currentvoxel, gridbounds): # Distance to next supergrid boundary # Note: Supergrid boundaries are spaced by R voxelsize supergridstep = R voxelsize tmaxsuper = computesupergridboundarydistance(rayorigin, raydirection, currentvoxel, supergridstep, step) # Sample null collision u = randomuniform() tnull = -log(u) / mulocal if tnull < tmaxsuper: # Interaction or null collision within current supergrid cell texit = tentry + tnull yield nullcollisionorinteraction(texit, mulocal, supergrid) # Update ray position for next step rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection tnull tentry = texit # Re-evaluate supergrid cell if position changed significantly, # or simply keep mulocal if still in same cell. # For simplicity, assume we re-check cell after small steps or use DDA to advance. # In fused loop, we typically advance via DDA to next cell boundary if tnull is large. # Here, if tnull is small, we might stay in same cell. # To keep loop simple, we advance ray and re-calculate supergrid cell. supergridcell = getsupergridcell(getvoxelindex(rayorigin, voxelsize), supergrid.resolutionfactor) mulocal = supergrid.maxextinction[supergridcell] majorantfactor else: # Advance to next supergrid boundary # Find which axis hits the supergrid boundary first minidx = argmin(tmaxsuper) # Logic adapted from DDA texit = tmaxsuper[minidx] yield nullcollision(tentry + texit) # Or just advance # Update DDA state to next supergrid boundary # This requires aligning DDA steps to supergrid resolution currentvoxel[minidx] += step[minidx] tmax[minidx] += tdelta[minidx] tentry = tentry + texit supergridcell = getsupergridcell(currentvoxel, supergrid.resolutionfactor) mulocal = supergrid.maxextinction[supergridcell] majorantfactor Edge Cases: Homogeneous Medium: The 'homogeneous' medium type explicitly rejects the supergrid parameter because it cannot honour the spatially varying majorant. Zero Extinction: If \mut goes to zero, the derivative involving \mus / \mut can go unstable. A variant that progressively estimates and updates spatially varying bounding extinctions during rendering, making null-tracking resilient to non-bounding extinctions. It builds on Majorant Supergrid Traversal by allowing the bounding extinction to adapt to local density variations rather than relying on a single global worst-case bound. Unlike progressive photon mapping or many-light methods, which introduce bias in every iteration (e.g., from blurring or loss of short-range transport), this approach's individual passes become unbiased once a bounding extinction is reached. Performance: Supergrid traversal is faster than the global majorant approach because it avoids paying optixTrace for every null collision, which prbvolpath does in its symbolic-loop iteration. In measurements, rendering the same frame at 64 spp with no AD graph, prbvolpath took 104.5 s while the supergrid plugin took 72.1 s. Memory: The supergrid adds memory overhead proportional to the downsampled grid size. The archived branch notes that a slot per segment costs about 4.6 GB more than prbvolpath at a specific wavefront, while one slot per lane costs 32 MiB more. Limitations: Not applicable to homogeneous media. Stability issues may arise if \mut approaches zero without proper handling of the \mus / \mut ratio. The method was introduced in the context of Mitsuba 3's sample matching for extinction gradients. It was implemented to optimize null-collision sampling in heterogeneous media by fusing the DDA traversal with the null-collision walk in C++. Sample matching for extinction gradients (review branch), https://github.com/AuroraRyan0301/mitsuba3/pull/1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Progressive Null-Tracking with Super-Voxel Grid
head: progressive medium clamping, spatially varying bounding extinctions
body: Progressive Null-Tracking with Super-Voxel Grid is a technique to make null-tracking methods resilient to non-bounding extinctions by progressively estimating and updating spatially varying bounding extinctions (\mut) on a coarse grid during rendering. It builds on Majorant Supergrid Traversal by allowing the bounding extinction to adapt to local density variations rather than relying on a single global worst-case bound. Unlike progressive photon mapping or many-light methods, which introduce bias in every iteration (e.g., from blurring or loss of short-range transport), this approach's individual passes become unbiased once a bounding extinction is reached. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric medium defined by spatially varying extinction \mue(\mathbf{x}), a rendering pass index k, and a coarse grid of super-voxels covering the medium extents. Output: Updated bounding extinction values \mut^{(k+1)} for each super-voxel, used in the subsequent rendering pass. Data Structures: Super-Voxel Grid: A 3D grid of resolution N^3 (typically 80^3) fitting the medium extents. Grid Cell Layout: Each cell stores a single floating-point value representing the estimated bounding extinction \mut for the portion of the medium it spans. Initialization: \mut^{(1)} = 0.01 for all super-voxels to simulate a near-worst-case scenario for prior methods. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Set the bounding extinction for all super-voxels in the grid to \mut^{(1)} = 0.01. 2. Rendering Pass k: Render the scene using the current bounding extinction grid \mut^{(k)}. Rays traverse the medium using null-tracking, where the probability of interaction is determined by \mut^{(k)}. 3. Density Evaluation: For each super-voxel, evaluate the actual extinction \mue(\mathbf{x}) along rays passing through that voxel during pass k. 4. Update Bounding Extinction: Independently for each super-voxel, update the total extinction \mut^{(k+1)} for the next pass based on the density evaluations from pass k. The update formula is not explicitly provided in the sources, but it is described as a "scene-adaptive and spatially-adaptive update formula". 5. Multithreading: Separate threads write updated bounding extinctions into the super-voxel grid independently with no synchronization. The method is resilient to race conditions, though intermediate states are non-deterministic. 6. Iteration: Increment k and repeat steps 2-5 until convergence or a maximum number of passes is reached. Formulas: \mut^{(k+1)}: Bounding extinction for super-voxel i at pass k+1. \mut^{(1)} = 0.01: Initial bounding extinction for all super-voxels. \mue(\mathbf{x}): Actual spatially varying extinction at position \mathbf{x}. Parameters: Grid Resolution: 80^3 super-voxels covering the medium extents. Initial Extinction: \mut^{(1)} = 0.01 for all super-voxels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Race Conditions: The naive multithreading scheme is resilient to race conditions, but intermediate states are non-deterministic. A more sophisticated multithreading scheme is needed if fully deterministic intermediate behavior is desired. Convergence: The method relies on the bounding extinction eventually reaching a value that bounds the actual extinction. If the update formula is not robust, convergence may be slow or fail. Initialization: Initializing with a very low value (0.01) creates a near-worst-case scenario for prior methods, highlighting the robustness of the progressive approach. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. N = 80 mut = [[0.01 for in range(N)] for in range(NN)] def renderpass(k, mut): # Render scene using current bounding extinction grid # Rays traverse medium using null-tracking with mut # Return list of rays and their interactions pass def updatemut(mut, rays, k): # For each super-voxel, update bounding extinction # based on density evaluations along rays passing through it # This step is performed independently for each super-voxel # using separate threads with no synchronization for i in range(NN): # Evaluate actual extinction mue(x) along rays in super-voxel i # Update mut[i] based on scene-adaptive and spatially-adaptive formula # Formula not explicitly provided in sources pass return mut for k in range(1, maxpasses + 1): rays = renderpass(k, mut) mut = updatemut(mut, rays, k) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for the super-voxel grid, where N=80. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Resilient to non-bounding extinctions; individual passes become unbiased once a bounding extinction is reached; robust to race conditions in multithreading. Limitations: Intermediate states are non-deterministic with naive multithreading; requires multiple rendering passes to converge. When to Use: When the medium has significant spatial variation in extinction and a global bounding extinction is inefficient. When Not to Use: When deterministic intermediate behavior is required without sophisticated synchronization. Origin: The technique was introduced by Davidovič et al. in 2012. History and Development: The method is an extension of null-tracking techniques, aiming to improve efficiency in volumetric rendering by adapting bounding extinctions to local density variations. Usage: Implemented in PBRT for testing and comparison, with plans to incorporate it into production renderers. Progressive null-tracking for volumetric rendering, https://www.yiningkarlli.com/projects/progressivenulltracking/progressivenulltracking.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Hierarchical Grid Traversal
head: Hierarchical Grid Intersection, Ray-Mipmap Traversal
body: Hierarchical Grid Traversal is a ray-grid traversal algorithm that accelerates volume rendering by iterating through levels of a grid mipmap (hierarchical grid tree). It solves the problem of expensive fine-grained sampling in large volumes by recursively visiting child voxels only if the ray intersects the parent voxel's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). Unlike flat grid traversal methods such as DDA Traversal which step through every voxel, this method skips empty or inactive regions at coarse levels, descending into finer grids only where necessary. It sets itself apart from Octree and Tree Traversal by using a fixed-depth, array-based mipmap structure with lookup tables rather than pointer-based nodes, optimizing for memory locality and batch processing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a hierarchical grid structure (mipmap) with L levels; a precomputed lookup table (tableslist) mapping coarse voxel indices to child indices and coordinates; maxlevel (the depth of the hierarchy); cubesize (physical size of a voxel at the current level). Output: A list of voxel grid positions at the maximum level (maxlevel) that are intersected by the ray. Data Structures: Lookup Table (tableslist): A list of arrays, one per level. Each row corresponds to a coarse voxel. Columns 0–7: Indices of the 8 child voxels (or -1 if the child is empty/invalid). Columns 8–10: The 3D grid coordinates (x, y, z) of the coarse voxel. Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. State: cubetouchedidx: A list of indices of voxels at the current level that the ray intersects. Parameters: maxlevel: The maximum depth of the mipmap hierarchy. The loop runs from level 0 to maxlevel inclusive. cubesize: The physical size of a voxel at level l. For a base grid resolution of 256 units, cubesize at level l is calculated as 256 / 2^l. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set cubetouchedidx to [0], representing the root voxel index. Initialize newlist as an empty list. Initialize cubeorilist as an empty list to store final hits. 2. Iterate through Levels: For each level l from 0 to maxlevel: Retrieve the lookup table for the current level: table = tableslist[l]. Compute the physical voxel size for this level: currentcubesize = 256.0 / (2 l). For each voxel index i in cubetouchedidx: 1. Retrieve Voxel Bounds: Get the voxel's 3D grid coordinates from the table: gridcoords = table[i, 8:11]. Calculate the physical origin: cubeori = gridcoords currentcubesize. Calculate the physical end: cubeend = cubeori + currentcubesize. 2. Ray-AABB Intersection: Compute the intersection of the ray with the AABB defined by cubeori and cubeend. This yields a near distance tn and a far distance tf. If the ray does not intersect the AABB, tn > tf or the intersection is behind the ray origin. 3. Check Intersection: If tn \le tf (intersection exists and is in front of the ray): If l == maxlevel: Append the voxel's grid position gridcoords to cubeorilist. If l < maxlevel: Extract the 8 child indices from the table: children = table[i, 0:8]. Filter out invalid children (marked as -1): mask = children != -1. Convert valid indices to integers and add them to newlist. Update State: Set cubetouchedidx to newlist. Reset newlist to an empty list for the next level. If cubetouchedidx is empty, terminate early. 3. Return Result: Return cubeorilist containing the grid positions of voxels touched at the maximum level. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicalgridtraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, tableslist, maxlevel): """ Traverses a hierarchical grid mipmap to find intersected voxels at the finest level. Args: rayorigin: (3,) array, ray origin in world space. raydirection: (3,) array, ray direction in world space. tableslist: List of arrays, where tableslist[l] is the lookup table for level l. Each row has shape (11,): [child0,..., child7, x, y, z]. maxlevel: int, the maximum depth of the hierarchy. Returns: cubeorilist: List of (3,) arrays, grid coordinates of intersected voxels at maxlevel. """ cubetouchedidx = [0] # Start with root voxel index cubeorilist = [] for level in range(maxlevel + 1): table = tableslist[level] newlist = [] currentcubesize = 256.0 / (2 level) for i in cubetouchedidx: # Retrieve voxel coordinates and bounds gridcoords = table[i, 8:11] cubeori = gridcoords currentcubesize cubeend = cubeori + currentcubesize # Compute ray-AABB intersection tn, tf = intersectrayaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, cubeori, cubeend) # Check if intersection exists if tn is not None and tn <= tf: if level == maxlevel: # At the finest level, record the voxel position cubeorilist.append(gridcoords) else: # Not at the finest level, collect child indices children = table[i, 0:8] # Filter out invalid children (-1) mask = children != -1 validchildren = children[mask] newlist.extend(validchildren) cubetouchedidx = newlist if not cubetouchedidx: break return cubeorilist def intersectrayaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, aabbmin, aabbmax): """ Computes the intersection of a ray with an AABB using the slab method. Returns (tn, tf) where tn is the near intersection distance and tf is the far intersection distance. Returns (None, None) if no intersection exists. """ tn = -float('inf') tf = float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] == 0.0: # Ray is parallel to axis; check if origin is within slab if rayorigin[i] < aabbmin[i] or rayorigin[i] > aabbmax[i]: return None, None else: t1 = (aabbmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] t2 = (aabbmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tn = max(tn, t1) tf = min(tf, t2) if tn > tf: return None, None return tn, tf Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero-Length Ray: If the ray direction is zero or the ray has no length, the intersection test should return no intersection. Precision Issues: When the ray is far from the grid, floating-point precision errors in the AABB intersection test may cause incorrect culling. A small epsilon may be needed for robustness. Corner Intersections: Using a small epsilon to clip ray spans may clip tiny corner intersections. Empty Voxels: The lookup table must correctly mark empty children with -1 to avoid traversing non-existent nodes. Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting is a volume rendering technique that accelerates ray casting by traversing a multi-dimensional hierarchy (mdh) to adaptively choose the resolution level for evaluating volume data. It solves the problem of expensive ray traversal in large volumes by approximating homogeneous regions with least-squares trilinear coefficients, allowing the renderer to skip fine-grained sampling in unimportant or smooth areas. Unlike sibling methods that rely on simple opacity thresholds or constant-value homogeneity, this method uses a user-defined error tolerance and data importance weighting to control refinement, providing a balance between image quality and performance. A method to avoid computing all scalar values regardless of visibility by partitioning the volume into smaller sub-volumes with similar properties based on the transfer function. The opacity map corresponds to a region of the frame buffer and stores the minimum opacity of the frame buffer pixels found within that region. It groups scalar values within a certain range together based on the transfer function to define sub-volume properties. It uses a kd-tree to render the partitioned volume with correct visibility order, where each node is associated with a sub-volume. It culls and clips each sub-volume against an opacity map. It reported 10 fps for the Engine data set using a 2.5 GHz Pentium-IV and a nVidia GeForce4 graphics adapter. Hierarchical Voxel Traversal is a recursive raycasting algorithm designed to traverse nested voxel structures, such as chunks containing subvoxels, to find intersections. It distinguishes itself from flat traversal methods by transforming rays into local subvoxel space when entering a detail voxel, allowing for efficient handling of nested voxel data. Unlike First Active Voxel Detection which focuses on finding the first non-empty voxel, this method fully traverses the hierarchy to compute precise intersections within detail voxels. XBrickMap is a space-partitioning ray traversal algorithm for 3-level hierarchical voxel grids that uses 4^3 occupancy bitmasks to skip empty regions via bitwise tests. It improves upon simpler skipping methods by using tiled bitmasks to perform hierarchical skips of 4^3, 2^3, and 1^3 cuboids, while left-packing empty bricks within sectors to save memory. It is distinguished from its sibling Hierarchical Grid Traversal by its specific use of compacted bitmasks for random access and its support for arbitrary in-place edits within bricks. A spherical coordinate voxel traversal algorithm that traces a ray with unit direction over a spherical voxel grid, returning a vector of the spherical coordinate voxels traversed. It computes intersections with spherical shells, polar cones, and azimuthal wedges directly, handling the singularity at the origin by starting traversal at the first non-zero radial shell. First Active Voxel Detection determines if a ray intersects an active value at any level of a hierarchical grid and identifies the first such voxel or tile. It solves the problem of efficiently skipping empty space in sparse volume data structures by performing empty-space ray-marching at all tree levels using a Hierarchical DDA (HDDA). Unlike standard linear traversal, it leverages the hierarchical structure to jump over inactive regions, setting the intersection time and index upon the first hit. Hierarchical and block-based data structures organize volumetric data into a multi-resolution hierarchy of uniform blocks (bricks) or spatial subdivisions (octrees) to accelerate ray traversal and rendering. This approach serves as a compromise between the memory overhead of dense grids and the complexity of unstructured meshes, preferred by many practitioners for its balance of performance and implementation simplicity. It enables efficient empty-space skipping, early ray termination, and adaptive resolution sampling by allowing the renderer to skip large empty regions or sample coarse data for distant objects. This method accelerates ray tracing through sparse volumetric data by introducing a two-level occupancy hierarchy (super-bricks and bricks) to skip large empty regions, while maintaining pixel-identical output to the fine per-voxel DDA. It solves the performance bottleneck of traversing empty space by verifying emptiness at a coarser granularity and using an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for early termination, ensuring exactness by only skipping verified empty blocks and terminating only when the ray definitively passes the occupied volume. Octree-based traversal accelerates rendering by recursively navigating a hierarchical spatial subdivision (octree) to skip empty or low-detail regions, thereby reducing the number of intersection tests and sampling operations. It solves the performance bottleneck of dense voxel traversal by allowing rays to take larger steps through empty space. Unlike Hierarchical Grid Traversal which uses fixed-level mipmap grids, this family explicitly uses regular 2x2x2 (or 2x2 in 2D) subdivision to build a sparse hierarchy, distinguishing it from siblings that may focus on hash grids or specific traversal optimizations. Empty Space Skipping via Data Structures is a family of volume rendering optimization techniques that reduce computational cost by identifying and bypassing inactive (transparent or empty) regions of a volume dataset before or during ray sampling. Unlike methods that rely on hardware occlusion culling or ray coherence, this family uses explicit secondary data structures—such as min-max blocks, occupancy grids, BVHs, or hybrid trees—to store metadata about the spatial distribution of active data. This allows rays to determine entry and exit points of active regions analytically or via coarse traversal, skipping large intervals of empty space that would otherwise require expensive texture lookups and compositing operations. Multi-level Grid Structures are a family of hierarchical acceleration techniques for ray tracing and volume rendering that organize spatial data into a hierarchy of uniform grids (often arranged as mipmaps or nested blocks) to efficiently skip empty regions and adapt resolution to local density. Unlike flat uniform grids which suffer from excessive memory usage or traversal overhead in sparse scenes, or octrees which may break SIMD coherence, this family uses fixed-depth or adaptive uniform subdivisions to balance memory locality and traversal speed. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like KD-Tree Partitioned Volume Rendering by maintaining the regular memory access patterns of grid structures while providing hierarchical empty-space skipping. Quadtree Raycasting is a recursive ray-quadtree intersection algorithm that traverses a 2D quadtree to find the first hit node. It solves the problem of efficiently locating the first occupied voxel in a hierarchical 2D grid by handling ray direction flipping via a mask to ensure consistent traversal order regardless of ray direction. Grid Sphere Traversal (GST) is a ray-grid traversal method that performs sphere tracing through a dense grid of Signed Distance Function (SDF) values. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing empty regions in SDF-based rendering by using a hierarchy of SDF grids where lower-resolution levels encode larger SDF values to accelerate step sizes. It is distinguished from its siblings by performing the entire traversal in shader code using dense grids, whereas alternatives like Sparse Voxel Set leverage DXR hardware acceleration for BVH traversal. A CUDA kernel that marches rays through one or more axis-aligned voxel grids using precomputed, sorted entry/exit intersections to generate sample points and interval boundaries. It handles empty cells by skipping them and fills continuous segments, supporting both fixed step sizes and cone-angle-aware adaptive stepping. It sets itself apart from standard DDA by decoupling the grid boundary traversal from the sample generation, allowing for variable step sizes that scale with distance from the camera origin. Constructs a lookup table for hierarchical grid traversal. It maps coarse grid voxels to their fine grid children. The table is built from a fine grid and a coarse grid mask. It identifies occupied voxels in the fine grid and assigns a unique index to each. It extracts the 8 sub-grid regions corresponding to the 8 children of a coarse voxel by striding the fine grid indices. It flattens these sub-grids and filters them using the coarse grid mask to select only the children that belong to occupied coarse voxels. It initializes the table with shape [numcoarsevoxels, 11] (8 child indices + 3 coordinates), filled with -1. It populates columns 0-7 with the filtered child indices and columns 8-10 with the coarse voxel coordinates. A ray-traversal algorithm for volumetric rendering. Its time complexity is O(p \cdot r), where p is the number of pixels and r is the volume's largest dimension in voxels. Its space complexity is dependent on the size of the data volume. It uses a relative distance formula: \text{relative distance} = (\text{target} - \text{value1}) / (\text{value2} - \text{value1}). Performs raycasting in world space by transforming the ray to local voxel space, calling the generic raycast, and transforming results back. It computes the ray end in world space, transforms the ray origin and end to local space, and calculates the local direction and max distance. It handles zero-length rays by returning an empty result when the squared distance is less than 0.000001. On success, it scales the distance back to world space and transforms the normal if enabled. Time Complexity: The time complexity depends on the number of voxels visited. In the worst case (ray passes through all voxels), it is proportional to the number of voxels in the finest level. However, in sparse volumes, it is significantly faster than flat traversal due to early culling at coarse levels. Memory Complexity: The memory complexity is dominated by the storage of the hierarchical grid and the lookup tables. The lookup table size is proportional to the number of coarse voxels per level. Performance: Performance is highly dependent on the sparsity of the volume and the efficiency of the AABB intersection test. For dense volumes, the overhead of the hierarchy may not be justified. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space; suitable for sparse and multi-resolution data; good memory locality due to array-based structure. Limitations: Requires precomputation of the lookup table; less flexible than pointer-based trees for dynamic data; potential precision issues with far-away rays. When to Use: Sparse volumes, multi-resolution data, static scenes where precomputation is feasible. When Not to Use: Dense volumes with little empty space, highly dynamic data where the hierarchy needs frequent updates. Hierarchical Grid Traversal, also known as Ray-Mipmap Traversal, is a technique used in volume rendering to accelerate ray casting through hierarchical grid structures. It builds on the principles of ray-grid traversal, specifically the DDA algorithm, by adding a hierarchical layer to skip empty regions. The method is often implemented using lookup tables to map coarse voxels to fine voxels, allowing for efficient batch processing. szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, https://github.com/szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ZephirFXEC/HNanoSolver, https://github.com/ZephirFXEC/HNanoSolver, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) DTIC ADA202661: Volumetric Rendering Techniques for the Display of Three-Dimensional Aerodynamic Flow Field Data, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA202661, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Zylann/godotvoxel, https://github.com/Zylann/godotvoxel, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting
head: Adaptive ray casting using trilinear basis functions, Hierarchical Data Structures for Ray Casting, Hierarchical Ray Casting with Trilinear Coefficients, Hierarchically Accelerated Ray Casting with Controlled Error, Ray casting with mdh tree
body: Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting is a volume rendering technique that accelerates ray casting by traversing a multi-dimensional hierarchy (mdh) to adaptively choose the resolution level for evaluating volume data. It solves the problem of expensive ray traversal in large volumes by approximating homogeneous regions with least-squares trilinear coefficients, allowing the renderer to skip fine-grained sampling in unimportant or smooth areas. Unlike sibling methods that rely on simple opacity thresholds or constant-value homogeneity, this method uses a user-defined error tolerance and data importance weighting to control refinement, providing a balance between image quality and performance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin and direction; a hierarchical data structure (mdh tree) where each node stores trilinear coefficients, nodal error, and importance; a user-defined error tolerance; a data importance weighting function (transfer function). Output: Accumulated color and opacity for the pixel corresponding to the ray. Data Structures: The hierarchy uses a BON tree structure. Each node contains: 1. Data Model: Trilinear coefficients representing a least-squares fit to the data in the region covered by the node. This provides C^0 continuity at shared faces. 2. Evaluation Information: Nodal Error: The average deviation of the node's trilinear model from the actual data within the region. Importance: A user-defined value derived from a transfer function, indicating the significance of data values in that range. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. Calculate the entry and exit points of the ray with respect to the volume bounds. 2. Recursive Traversal: Call rayCastRegion(ray, region, entryPt, exitPt) starting from the root region. 3. Termination Check: If the current region is at the bottom level (original data) or the nodal error is within the user-defined tolerance (weighted by importance), render the ray segment directly from entryPt to exitPt using the current region's data model. 4. Refinement: If not at the bottom level and error exceeds tolerance: Initialize subEntry to entryPt. Loop while subEntry is not equal to exitPt and rendering is not interrupted: a. Find Subregion: Determine the specific child subregion containing subEntry using findRegion(region, subEntry). For orthographic projection, a single permutation defines the front-to-back topological order. For perspective, the permutation is fixed per ray but may vary between rays. b. Find Exit: Calculate the exit point of the ray from the current subRegion using findExit(ray, subRegion, subEntry). c. Recurse: Call rayCastRegion(ray, subRegion, subEntry, subExit). d. Advance: Update subEntry to subExit. 5. Direct Rendering (Leaf or Tolerated Node): If stopping at a node higher than the bottom level: Evaluate data, color, and opacity at the intersection points of the region's bounding box using the node's trilinear coefficients. If going down to the data level: Look up the eight corner data values of the cell/voxel and compute colors and opacity at the intersection points of the cell boundary. Integration is performed directly from entry to exit point, approximating the volume rendering integral. The method uses an approximation similar to coherent projection, evaluating the "emission" contribution at the thickest point of the cell's projection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EPSILON = 1e-6 class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def mul(self, s): return Vec3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def length(self): return (self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2)0.5 def getitem(self, i): return (self.x, self.y, self.z)[i] class Bounds: def init(self, minpt, maxpt): self.min, self.max = minpt, maxpt @property def center(self): return Vec3((self.min.x + self.max.x)/2, (self.min.y + self.max.y)/2, (self.min.z + self.max.z)/2) def raycastregion(ray, region, entrypt, exitpt): """Recursively compute the contribution of a ray through a specified region.""" if region.isbottomlevel or region.errorwithintolerance(): return renderraydirect(ray, entrypt, exitpt, region) subentry = entrypt while (exitpt - subentry).length() > EPSILON: subregion = findregion(region, subentry) subexit = findexit(ray, subregion, subentry) if subexit is None: break contrib = raycastregion(ray, subregion, subentry, subexit) subentry = subexit return contrib def findregion(region, point): """Determine the child subregion containing the point.""" idx = 0 for axis in range(3): if point[axis] >= region.bounds.center[axis]: idx |= (1 << axis) return region.children[idx] def findexit(ray, subregion, subentry): """Calculate exit point using Snyder and Barr generalization.""" # Maintains tx, ty, tz for imminent intersections with grid planes. # In adaptive case, updates are nondestructive. # Update amount is wx dtx if tx selected, where wx is width in grid points. tmin = float('inf') for axis in range(3): if abs(ray.direction[axis]) > EPSILON: t1 = (subregion.bounds.min[axis] - subentry[axis]) / ray.direction[axis] t2 = (subregion.bounds.max[axis] - subentry[axis]) / ray.direction[axis] t = t1 if t1 > EPSILON else t2 if t > EPSILON and t < tmin: tmin = t if tmin == float('inf'): return None return subentry + ray.direction tmin def renderraydirect(ray, entrypt, exitpt, region): """Render segment directly using region's data model.""" valin = evaluateregion(region, entrypt) valout = evaluateregion(region, exitpt) # Front-to-back compositing approximation (coherent projection style) alpha = 1.0 - (1.0 - valin.opacity) (1.0 - valout.opacity) color = valin.color (1.0 - valout.opacity) + valout.color valout.opacity return color, alpha def evaluateregion(region, point): """Evaluate data at point using trilinear coefficients or corner values.""" if region.isbottomlevel: return trilinearinterpolate(region.corners, point) else: return trilinearevaluate(region.coefficients, point) def trilinearinterpolate(corners, point): # Standard 8-corner trilinear interpolation return (0.5, 0.5) def trilinearevaluate(coeffs, point): # Evaluate trilinear function defined by coeffs at point return (0.5, 0.5) Parameters: Error Tolerance: A user-defined parameter controlling the maximum allowed error in the image. Higher tolerance allows rendering at coarser levels, increasing speed. Data Importance Weighting: A user-supplied function that weights the error metric. It allows small errors in critical data ranges to be considered serious, while substantial errors are acceptable in uninteresting ranges (e.g., air). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Discontinuity: The gradient calculated using the derivative of the trilinear function may not be continuous at shared cell faces, introducing potential error. Perspective Permutations: For perspective projection, rays may require varying permutations for subregion traversal, though the permutation is fixed within an individual ray. Adaptive Volume Ray Casting is a technique that builds on Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting by using an octree structure to determine traversal depth based on camera-defined resolution limits. It produces better image quality than splatting by avoiding splatting artifacts but is more computationally intensive. A single-pass volume rendering method compatible with a hierarchical data structure, extending Scharsach's ray-casting method. It performs traversal and color accumulation in a fragment shader for each pixel using a quad covering the display surface. The vertex shader calculates ray position and direction in data space, which are interpolated to the fragment shader. Entry/exit points are calculated, and rays not intersecting the volume terminate early. Tree traversal alternates horizontal (within node grid) and vertical (between hierarchy levels) passes, using a mini-stack or stack-less algorithm. Time Complexity: Depends on the error tolerance and data importance. In homogeneous regions, traversal stops at higher levels, reducing complexity. In complex regions, it approaches regular grid ray casting. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the hierarchical tree (mdh) with trilinear coefficients and error/importance metadata for each node. Measured Performance: On an SGI Reality Engine II with four 150 MHz processors: Hipip dataset (64^3) with 10% error and no importance: 27.0 seconds (hierarchical) vs. 97.0 seconds (regular grid). CT Head dataset (256 \times 256 \times 113) with 1% error and importance: 56.0 seconds (hierarchical) vs. 205.0 seconds (regular grid). Strengths: Provides error-controlled rendering; handles perspective and orthographic projections; easily parallelizable (each ray is nearly independent). Limitations: Noticeably slower than ray casting a non-hierarchical rectilinear volume, but usually faster than regular grid ray casting on volumes where importance functions can limit traversal. When to Use: When image quality must be controlled by error tolerance and importance weighting, and when volumes have large homogeneous or unimportant regions. When Not to Use: When maximum speed is required and error control is not critical; when hardware 3D textures or coherent projection are available and sufficient. Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting was developed by Gelder, Kim, and Wilhelms at the University of California, Santa Cruz. It was described in the technical report "Hierarchically Accelerated Ray Casting for Volume Rendering with Controlled Error" (UCSC-CRL-95-31) in March 1995. The method generalizes previous work on homogeneity (which relied on nearly constant values) to least-squares fits with trilinear basis functions. It was implemented within a general system for multi-dimensional trees (mdh). name: Adaptive Volume Ray Casting
head: volume ray casting technique
body: Adaptive Volume Ray Casting is a volume rendering technique where one ray is shot through the volume for each pixel, traversing an octree to accumulate physical values along the ray path. It builds on Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting by using the octree structure to determine traversal depth based on camera-defined resolution limits. It produces better image quality than splatting by avoiding splatting artifacts, but is more computationally intensive. Inputs: Ray origin and direction for each pixel. Octree data structure representing the volume. Camera parameters defining the maximum resolution level. Outputs: Accumulated pixel value for each ray. Data Structures: Octree: Hierarchical structure where nodes represent spatial subdivisions. Leaf Definition: Every cell ranked with the maximum level of resolution defined by the camera is considered as a leaf. Highest level of resolution cells are discarded when these cells are too small compared to the image pixel size. The maximum octree depth level read is therefore defined by the camera. Steps: 1. Find Intersections: Determine the intersections between the grid and the ray. Using basic 3D geometry calculation, compute the coordinates (x,y,z) of the entry and exit points of the ray in the cell faces. 2. Traverse Octree: Start from the root of the octree and traverse down the tree. This top-down traversal of the tree stops when a leaf cell is found. 3. Accumulate Contribution: Multiply the cell's observed physical value by the length between the entry and exit points into the cell faces. Add every contribution along the ray to the resulting pixel value, without taking into account any ordering. 4. Post-Processing (Optional): Apply an adaptive Gaussian blur filter as an image post-processing option to avoid aliasing in coarse mesh regions by adjusting filter size to local image resolution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def adaptivevolumeraycasting(rayorigin, raydirection, octreeroot, cameramaxlevel): """ Renders a single pixel by traversing an octree and accumulating physical values. Args: rayorigin: tuple (x, y, z), origin of the ray. raydirection: tuple (dx, dy, dz), direction of the ray. octreeroot: dict, root node of the octree with keys: 'bbox', 'value', 'children', 'level'. cameramaxlevel: int, maximum octree depth level defined by camera. Returns: float, accumulated pixel value. """ # Step 1 & 2: Traverse octree and accumulate contributions # The sources describe a top-down traversal that stops at leaf cells. # We implement a recursive traversal that computes per-cell entry/exit distances. return traversenode(octreeroot, rayorigin, raydirection, 0.0, float('inf'), cameramaxlevel) def traversenode(node, rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, cameramaxlevel): """Recursively traverse octree nodes along the ray.""" # Compute intersection of ray with current node bounding box # The exact 3D geometry calculation is not detailed in the sources. tentry, texit = rayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, node['bbox']) # If ray misses node or intersection is behind current traversal point, return 0 if tentry is None or texit <= tmin: return 0.0 # Clamp tmax to the exit point of this node texit = min(texit, tmax) # Step 2 & 3: Stop traversal at leaf cell (or max camera level) if node['level'] >= cameramaxlevel or node['children'] is None: # Step 3: Multiply cell's observed physical value by the length between # entry and exit points into this cell faces. celllength = texit - tmin contribution = node['value'] celllength # Add every contribution along the ray to the resulting pixel value, # without taking into account any ordering. return contribution # Recurse into children that intersect the ray totalcontribution = 0.0 for child in node['children']: totalcontribution += traversenode(child, rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, texit, cameramaxlevel) return totalcontribution def rayboxintersection(origin, direction, bbox): """ Compute entry and exit distances (t) of a ray intersecting an axis-aligned bounding box. bbox: tuple (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) Returns (tentry, texit) or (None, None) if no intersection. Standard ray-AABB intersection logic. """ tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bbox[i] or origin[i] > bbox[i + 3]: return None, None else: t1 = (bbox[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bbox[i + 3] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return None, None return tmin, tmax Parameters: Camera Max Level: The maximum octree depth level read is defined by the camera. Cells smaller than the image pixel size at this level are discarded. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Aliasing can be seen on coarse mesh resolution areas because low simulation resolution leads to big pixels. An adaptive Gaussian blur filter can be used to mitigate this. Ordering: Contributions are added without taking into account any ordering, which may affect transparency/opacity calculations if not handled by the physical value definition. Precision: Ray-box intersection calculations may suffer from floating-point precision issues near cell boundaries; standard epsilon guards are recommended. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but described as "more computationally intensive" than splatting. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given. Performance: The software implementation is not interactive on large datasets (e.g., Milky Way simulation with ~200 million AMR cells). Strengths: Produces better image quality than splatting (no splatting artifacts). Convenient to process large datasets as the algorithm is embarrassingly parallel. Limitations: More computationally intensive than splatting. Aliasing in coarse mesh regions. When to use: When image quality is prioritized over interactive performance and splatting artifacts are unacceptable. When not to use: When interactive performance on large datasets is required. Origin: Based on volume ray casting explained by Levoy (1990). History: Described in the context of AMR (Adaptive Mesh Refinement) simulations, specifically for visualizing large datasets like Milky Way simulations. Usage: Used in PyMSES software for volume rendering of AMR simulations. Volume Rendering of AMR Simulations, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.1210.8014, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

A technique introduced into the raycasting algorithm by Bruckner and Gröller to display inner occluded objects of interest by employing a force-based model to partition the volume into several segments. The partition manner is controlled by a number of forces and constraints. Reported 10 fps for the Engine data set using a 2.5 GHz Pentium-IV and a nVidia GeForce4 graphics adapter. Not given in the sources. Proposed by Li et al. [Li03] to address the inefficiency of computing all scalar values regardless of visibility. The approach combines volume partitioning with kd-tree traversal and opacity map-based culling. name: Hierarchical Voxel Traversal
head: Recursive Voxel Traversal
body: Hierarchical Voxel Traversal is a recursive raycasting algorithm designed to traverse nested voxel structures, such as chunks containing subvoxels, to find intersections. It distinguishes itself from flat traversal methods by transforming rays into local subvoxel space when entering a detail voxel, allowing for efficient handling of nested voxel data. Unlike First Active Voxel Detection which focuses on finding the first non-empty voxel, this method fully traverses the hierarchy to compute precise intersections within detail voxels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin, direction, transform, and optional length; a hierarchical voxel structure (e.g., VoxelWorldAccess or generic Voxel<T>); maximum iteration limits. Output: An Intersection struct containing the hit position, normal, index, and an optional inner intersection (for detail voxels). Data Structures: Ray: Contains origin (Vec3), direction (Vec3), transform (Mat4), and length (Option<f32>). Voxel: Generic type T with properties WIDTH, DY, DZ, SCALE, and COUNT. Coordinates are mapped to linear indices using i = x + y \cdot DY + z \cdot DZ. Steps: 1. World Access Entry: Calculate the world origin in float3. Compute the current ray position in chunk-local space: current = ray.origin \cdot (1.0 / self.world.scale) - origin Call the core cast function with the world access, ray, current position, direction, and max iterations (30). 2. Voxel Check (World Access): Validate coordinates are within world bounds: coord[i] \ge 0 and coord[i] < self.world.dims[i]. Compute linear index: i = coord[0] + coord[1] \cdot dims[0] + coord[2] \cdot dims[0] \cdot dims[1]. If the voxel exists and is visible: Construct a local ray by applying scaling (sc) and translation (coord sc) to the ray's transform. Recursively cast on the voxel. If the voxel is a detail voxel (has subvoxels): Return an Intersection with inner set to the sub-intersection, index set to the chunk index, and current position/normal. If the voxel does not exist (empty chunk slot): Return an Intersection with inner: None, index: 0, and current position/normal. 3. Generic Voxel Entry: Inverse the ray transform. Scale by SUBDIV (2^{SUBDIV}). Transform ray origin and direction into subvoxel space. Move ray origin to the start of the bounding box (0 to scale) if not already inside. For each axis i: If direction[i] > 0, t = (0.0 - current[i]) / direction[i]. Else if direction[i] < 0, t = (scale - current[i]) / direction[i]. If t > 0, advance current. Call core cast with the voxel, ray, current position, direction, and max iterations 6 \cdot T::WIDTH. 4. Generic Voxel Check: Validate coordinates within T::WIDTH. Compute linear index: i = coord[0] + coord[1] \cdot T::DY + coord[2] \cdot T::DZ. If the voxel is visible and is detail: Construct local ray with scaling T::SCALE and translation coord \cdot T::SCALE. Recursively cast. Return intersection with inner sub-hit. If the voxel is visible and NOT detail: Return intersection with inner: None, index: i, current position/normal. 5. Core Cast Function: Initialize integer coordinates currenti from current floor. Adjust currenti down by 1 if current is very close to an integer boundary and direction is negative. Check starting position first using raycast.check. If hit, return immediately. Loop up to iterations: Calculate distance to next grid plane intersection for each axis using intersect(currenti[i], current[i], direction[i]). Find minimum distance i[d]. Advance current by direction \cdot i[d] where d is the axis with minimum intersection distance. Decrement currenti[d] if direction[d] < 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cast(worldaccess, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 1: World Access Entry # current is already in chunk-local space return castvoxel(worldaccess, ray, current, direction, maxiterations) def castvoxel(worldaccess, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 2: Voxel Check (World Access) # Assuming worldaccess provides dims and scale # Compute linear index from current coordinates # Check bounds and existence if not worldaccess.check(current): return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) voxel = worldaccess.get(current) if not voxel.visible(): return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) if voxel.isdetail(): # Construct local ray sc = worldaccess.scale localray = transformray(ray, sc, current sc) # Recursively cast subhit = cast(worldaccess, localray, vec3(0), localray.direction, 30) return Intersection(inner=subhit, index=worldaccess.index(current), position=current, normal=vec3(0)) else: return Intersection(inner=None, index=worldaccess.index(current), position=current, normal=vec3(0)) def castgeneric(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 3: Generic Voxel Entry # Inverse transform and scale invtransform = inverse(ray.transform) subdiv = 2 voxel.SUBDIV ray.origin = invtransform (ray.origin subdiv) ray.direction = invtransform (ray.direction subdiv) # Move ray origin to start of bounding box scale = voxel.SCALE for i in range(3): if direction[i] > 0: t = (0.0 - current[i]) / direction[i] elif direction[i] < 0: t = (scale - current[i]) / direction[i] else: t = float('inf') if t > 0: current += direction t return castgenericvoxel(voxel, ray, current, direction, 6 voxel.WIDTH) def castgenericvoxel(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 4: Generic Voxel Check # Check bounds if not voxel.check(current): return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) index = voxel.coordtoindex(current) voxeldata = voxel.get(index) if not voxeldata.visible(): return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) if voxeldata.isdetail(): sc = voxel.SCALE localray = transformray(ray, sc, current sc) subhit = castgeneric(voxeldata, localray, vec3(0), localray.direction, 6 voxeldata.WIDTH) return Intersection(inner=subhit, index=index, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) else: return Intersection(inner=None, index=index, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) def corecast(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 5: Core Cast Function # Initialize integer coordinates currenti = floor(current) # Precision fix for negative direction at integer boundaries for i in range(3): if abs(current[i] - currenti[i]) < epsilon and direction[i] < 0: currenti[i] -= 1 # Check starting position if voxel.check(current): return castgenericvoxel(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations) # Traverse grid for in range(maxiterations): # Calculate distance to next grid plane distances = [] for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: distances.append(float('inf')) else: # intersect function calculates distance to next integer plane # assuming currenti[i] is the current voxel index # distance = (currenti[i] + (1 if direction[i] > 0 else 0) - current[i]) / direction[i] # Note: Exact formula depends on intersect implementation details not fully specified # Using standard AET traversal logic nextplane = currenti[i] + (1 if direction[i] > 0 else 0) distances.append((nextplane - current[i]) / direction[i]) d = argmin(distances) mindist = distances[d] if mindist == float('inf'): break # Advance current current += direction mindist currenti[d] += (1 if direction[d] < 0 else -1) # Decrement if direction is negative # Check hit at new position if voxel.check(current): return castgenericvoxel(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations) return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) Parameters: Max iterations for VoxelWorldAccess raycasting: 30. Max iterations for Voxel<T> raycasting: 6 \cdot T::WIDTH. Pitfalls: Precision issues at integer boundaries: If the ray is exactly on an integer coordinate and moving in a negative direction, the integer coordinate index must be decremented to avoid missing the voxel or double-checking. Not given in the sources. The method is implemented in the amethystvoxel project by Kurble, licensed under Apache-2.0. It is used for rendering voxel worlds with nested detail structures. name: XBrickMap
head: eXtendedBrickMap
body: XBrickMap is a space-partitioning ray traversal algorithm for 3-level hierarchical voxel grids that uses 4^3 occupancy bitmasks to skip empty regions via bitwise tests. It improves upon simpler skipping methods by using tiled bitmasks to perform hierarchical skips of 4^3, 2^3, and 1^3 cuboids, while left-packing empty bricks within sectors to save memory. It is distinguished from its sibling Hierarchical Grid Traversal by its specific use of compacted bitmasks for random access and its support for arbitrary in-place edits within bricks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a hierarchical voxel grid consisting of sectors, bricks, and voxels. Output: The intersection point and material properties of the first non-transparent voxel hit by the ray. Data Structures: The hierarchy consists of three levels: 1. Sector: The top-level container holding a list of bricks. Empty bricks are omitted via left-packing. Sector metadata maps indices. 2. Brick: Contains a 4^3 (64-bit) occupancy bitmask and 8^3 voxel data. The bitmask tracks 4^3 sub-cuboids for hierarchical skipping (4^3, 2^3, 1^3). 3. Voxel: 8-bit value (0 is transparent). Memory Layout: 8³ bits per brick + 12 bytes per sector. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Ray Marching: Start at the ray origin. 2. Sector Traversal: Determine which sector the ray is currently in. 3. Brick Skipping (Hierarchical): Query the sector's data structure to find the bricks in the current path. Use the 4^3 occupancy bitmask of each brick. Perform bitwise tests on the bitmask to identify empty sub-cuboids (4^3, 2^3, 1^3). If a sub-cuboid is empty, skip it entirely. Use popcnt (population count) instructions to count preceding entries for random access to the next non-empty brick or voxel. 4. Voxel Traversal: Once a non-empty brick/sub-region is identified, march through the 8^3 voxels. Intersect the ray with the three front-facing cube planes of the current voxel to compute the step size. Query the voxel data. If non-zero, return the hit. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 until the ray exits the grid or hits a surface. Formulas: Ray position at step t: \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. DDA step size along axes: \Delta tx = \frac{V}{|dx|}, \Delta ty = \frac{V}{|dy|}, \Delta tz = \frac{V}{|dz|}, where V is voxel size and di are direction components. Sub-cuboid bitmask index: idx = (z{local} \cdot 4 + \lfloor y{local} / 2 \rfloor) \cdot 4 + \lfloor x{local} / 2 \rfloor. Random access offset via population count: offset = \text{popcnt}(mask \ \& \ (2^{idx} - 1)). Parameters: Sector size: Not explicitly given in units, but contains 4^3 bricks. Brick size: 8^3 voxels. Bitmask size: 4^3 bits per brick. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating-point precision: Can cause infinite backtracking. Workaround: Bias intersection distances. Dynamic Edits: Supports arbitrary edits within a brick. However, insertions and deletions may require reallocations at the sector level to make space for new bricks. Memory Layout: Left-packing of empty bricks requires careful index mapping using popcnt. Voxel Storage: Each voxel in a brick is 8-bit. 0 is transparent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversexbrickmap(rayorigin, raydirection, grid): # Bias intersection distances to avoid floating-point infinite backtracking t = 1e-6 # Precompute inverse direction components for DDA step calculation invdir = [1.0 / d if d != 0 else float('inf') for d in raydirection] voxelsize = grid.voxelsize # Determine initial sector index from ray origin sectoridx = int(rayorigin.x // grid.sectorsize) sector = grid.sectors[sectoridx] while t < grid.maxdistance: # Compute current voxel position by intersecting with ray voxelpos = rayorigin + raydirection t # Determine current brick index within the sector brickidx = int((voxelpos.x - sector.origin.x) // grid.bricksize) # Check bounds and sector/brick emptiness if brickidx < 0 or brickidx >= len(sector.bricks): # Skip to next sector or exit t += (sector.origin.x + (sectoridx + 1) grid.sectorsize - rayorigin.x) invdir[0] sectoridx += 1 if sectoridx < len(grid.sectors): sector = grid.sectors[sectoridx] else: return None continue brick = sector.bricks[brickidx] # Map voxel position to local brick coordinates and bitmask index localx = int((voxelpos.x - brick.origin.x) // voxelsize) localy = int((voxelpos.y - brick.origin.y) // voxelsize) localz = int((voxelpos.z - brick.origin.z) // voxelsize) maskidx = (localz 4 + localy // 2) 4 + localx // 2 # Check occupancy mask for sub-cuboids if (brick.occupancymask >> maskidx) & 1 == 0: # Sub-cuboid empty; skip using bitmask logic # Advance t to exit current sub-cuboid t += 2.0 voxelsize invdir[0] continue # Traverse voxels within the brick # Intersect ray with three front-facing cube planes to compute step size dx = voxelsize invdir[0] dy = voxelsize invdir[1] dz = voxelsize invdir[2] step = min(dx, dy, dz) # Query voxel data voxelval = brick.voxels[localz 64 + localy 8 + localx] if voxelval == 0: t += step else: return {"t": t, "position": rayorigin + raydirection t, "value": voxelval} return None This method tracks which finest-level brick cells have been visited by rays to enable selective streaming and refinement, preventing redundant data transfers when multiple rays share a cell. It differs from XBrickMap by adding a runtime occupancy buffer that complements the static hierarchical skipping with dynamic visitation history. A data structure storing voxels in a two-level hierarchy to optimize ray traversal and memory usage. It consists of a coarse 128^3 top-level grid pointing to 8^3 voxel bricks, resulting in a total world resolution of 1024^3. Layout: Top-level grid cell is a 32-bit value. Bit 0 determines type: 0 indicates solid color (bits 1-31 store color), 1 indicates pointer to brick (bits 1-31 store brick index). Value 0 represents transparent solid color. Voxel Storage: Each voxel in a brick is 8-bit. 0 is transparent. Non-zero is 3-3-2 RGB triplet. Memory: Top-level grid is 8MB (128^3 \times 4 bytes). Max brick memory is 1GB (128^3 unique bricks \times 8^3 voxels \times 1 byte). Pitfall: Initializing the world to empty/transparent is done via memset(0) because 0 is a valid transparent solid color. Time Complexity: Approximately O(1) per step, though dependent on the density of non-empty regions. Memory Complexity: 8³ bits per brick + 12 bytes per sector. Performance: On the Sponza 2k scene, XBrickMap achieves 165.6 Mrays/s for primary rays and 125.1 Mrays/s for primary + 1 diffuse bounce. Strengths: Good performance relative to simplicity; supports arbitrary edits within bricks; efficient space skipping via bitwise operations. Limitations: Insertions/deletions may require sector-level reallocations; floating-point precision issues require biasing; performance on incoherent rays is ~30-50% worse than coherent rays but still worse than other space-partitioning methods. When to use: When random access and in-place editing of voxel data are required, and the scene has significant empty space to skip. When not to use: When the scene is highly dense with no empty space, or when dynamic topology changes are frequent and costly reallocations are unacceptable. XBrickMap was developed as part of the VoxelRT project by Thijs van Wingerden and Stijn Herfst. It is described in the thesis "VoxelRT: Visualization and Editing of Large Voxel Scenes". The method builds on earlier brick map concepts and aims to provide a high-performance realtime CUDA voxel path tracer. It is designed to handle large voxel scenes with efficient space skipping and dynamic editing capabilities. dubiousconst282/VoxelRT, https://github.com/dubiousconst282/VoxelRT, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) A Voxel Renderer for Learning C/C++ – Jacco's Blog, https://jacco.ompf2.com/2021/02/01/a-voxel-renderer-for-learning-c-c/, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Ray-guided streaming with atomic bitfield marking
head: Atomic bitfield marking for streaming, rayVisited atomic buffer technique [S1, unofficial]
body: This method tracks which finest-level brick cells have been visited by rays to enable selective streaming and refinement, preventing redundant data transfers when multiple rays share a cell. It complements the static hierarchical skipping of its parent XBrickMap with dynamic visitation history stored in an atomic bitfield buffer. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Brick index c (converted to a 3D vector), grid dimensions grid (from the indirection texture), and the rayVisited atomic buffer. Output: Updates the rayVisited buffer to mark the corresponding cell as visited. Data Structures: The rayVisited buffer is a storage buffer of type array<atomic<u32>>. Layout: Word 0 is unused. Cell index i corresponds to bit i & 31 of word 1 + (i >> 5). Size: The buffer must accommodate all finest-level bricks. A single-word buffer disables the feature. Steps: 1. Calculate Global Cell Index: Convert the brick index c to a linear cell index: cell = (c.z grid.y + c.y) grid.x + c.x. 2. Map to Buffer: Determine the word and bit within the rayVisited buffer: word = 1u + (cell >> 5u) and bit = 1u << (cell & 31u). 3. Atomic Check and Set: Perform an atomic read-modify-write. If word < words (total words in buffer) and the bit is not set (atomicLoad(&rayVisited[word]) & bit) == 0u, set the bit using atomicOr(&rayVisited[word], bit). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def markbrickvisited(c, grid, rayvisited, words): # c and grid are tuples/lists of 3 integers (x, y, z) cell = (c[2] grid[1] + c[1]) grid[0] + c[0] wordidx = 1 + (cell >> 5) bitmask = 1 << (cell & 31) if wordidx < words: # Simulate atomic load and compare-and-swap for GPU context currentval = rayvisited[wordidx] if (currentval & bitmask) == 0: rayvisited[wordidx] = currentval | bitmask def markisogradientvisited(c, grid, rayvisited, words): # Marks the center brick and its 6 axis-aligned neighbors markbrickvisited(c, grid, rayvisited, words) neighbors = [ (c[0]+1, c[1], c[2]), (c[0]-1, c[1], c[2]), (c[0], c[1]+1, c[2]), (c[0], c[1]-1, c[2]), (c[0], c[1], c[2]+1), (c[0], c[1], c[2]-1) ] for n in neighbors: markbrickvisited(n, grid, rayvisited, words) Parameters: Buffer Size: Must accommodate all finest-level bricks. Word 0: Always unused. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: ISO Gradient Sampling: Gradient calculations may sample cells outside the volume (e.g., beyond clip planes). These cells must be marked as visited to remain eligible for refinement. This is handled by markIsoGradientVisited, which marks the center brick and its 6 axis-aligned neighbors. Single-Word Buffer: If the buffer has only one word, the feature is effectively off. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not: Not given in the sources. This technique is part of the Kiln renderer, a WebGPU-native out-of-core volume rendering system for multi-GB datasets. It was presented in an unofficial GitHub repository in 2026.
