name: Virtual Memory Volume Rendering
head: Multi-Resolution Virtual Memory Scheme, Virtual Memory Architecture for Volume Rendering, Visualization-Driven Virtual Memory Volume Rendering
body: Virtual Memory Volume Rendering is an out-of-core rendering architecture that virtualizes 3D volumes by subdividing them into small 3D blocks and mapping them to a physical block cache using a multi-resolution page table hierarchy. It solves the problem of interactive exploration of petascale microscopy data streams by decoupling the construction of the 3D multi-resolution representation from data acquisition and decoupling sample access time during ray-casting from the size of the multi-resolution hierarchy. Unlike sibling methods such as Octree-based out-of-core volume rendering which require explicit octree traversal and holding the entire path from leaf to root in GPU memory, this method avoids these drawbacks by using a virtual memory scheme with arbitrary packing and no pre-computed 3D hierarchy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A stream of 2D microscope image tiles (raw or processed into 2D mipmaps) and a camera/view state for ray-casting. Output: A rendered image from single-pass ray-casting. Data Structures: 1. Virtual Volume: The logical 3D volume subdivided into small 3D blocks of size B \times B \times B voxels, where B=32. 2. Multi-Resolution Page Directory: A hierarchy of page tables corresponding to resolution levels l, serving as the top-level structure in the virtual memory hierarchy. 3. Page Table Cache: A cache storing page table entries (PTEs), where each PTE maps a virtual block position to a physical position in the Block Cache or is flagged as unmapped. 4. Block Cache: A large 3D texture resident in GPU memory containing the working set of currently required 3D blocks, packed arbitrarily. 5. Cache Miss Hash Table: A structure used to track requested voxel blocks to manage cache updates. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray-Casting in Virtual Space: For each sample along a ray, the algorithm determines the multi-resolution level l and the page table entry p corresponding to the virtual voxel address. 2. Address Translation: The algorithm performs address translation using the Multi-Resolution Page Directory and the Page Table Cache to find the physical location in the Block Cache. 3. Cache Miss Detection: The system checks if the block is unmapped (not resident in the cache). Unmapped blocks produce cache misses. 4. Backward Propagation: Cache misses are propagated backwards to trigger on-demand out-of-core processing. 5. On-Demand Construction: The system fetches the required 2D sub-tiles from the input stream and stitches/resamples them into 3D blocks. 6. Cache Update: The constructed 3D blocks are stored in the Block Cache, and the Page Table Cache is updated to map the virtual address to the new physical location. Formulas: Virtual block coordinates at level l: vx = \lfloor x / (B \cdot 2^l) \rfloor, vy = \lfloor y / (B \cdot 2^l) \rfloor, vz = \lfloor z / (B \cdot 2^l) \rfloor. Ray marching step: P(t) = O + t \cdot D, where O is origin, D is direction, t is distance. Alpha compositing: C{out} = C{in} + (1 - C{in}.a) \cdot C{sample}.a \cdot C{sample}.rgb. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. Determine virtual address components levell = determineresolutionlevel(currentpos) virtualblockid = getvirtualblockid(currentpos, levell) # 2. Address Translation physicalblockindex = translateaddress( pagedirectory, pagetablecache, levell, virtualblockid) # 3. Cache Miss Detection if physicalblockindex is None: # 4. Propagate Cache Miss & 5. On-Demand Construction handlecachemiss(levell, virtualblockid) # Retry translation after miss handling physicalblockindex = translateaddress( pagedirectory, pagetablecache, levell, virtualblockid) # 5. Texture Fetch & Compositing if physicalblockindex is not None: samplecolor = fetchblockcolor( blockcache, physicalblockindex, currentpos) # Standard front-to-back alpha compositing if samplecolor.a > 0.0: accumulatedcolor.rgb += (1.0 - accumulatedcolor.a) samplecolor.a samplecolor.rgb accumulatedcolor.a += (1.0 - accumulatedcolor.a) samplecolor.a if accumulatedcolor.a >= 0.99: break # Advance ray t += stepsize currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t return accumulatedcolor def determineresolutionlevel(pos): # Standard multi-resolution level selection based on ray step or LOD criteria # Not given in sources. Returns 0 for highest resolution. return 0 def getvirtualblockid(pos, levell): # Computes block coordinates in virtual volume space scale = BLOCKSIZE (2 levell) return (int(pos.x // scale), int(pos.y // scale), int(pos.z // scale)) def translateaddress(pagedirectory, pagetablecache, levell, virtualblockid): # Check page table cache first cachekey = (levell, virtualblockid) if cachekey in pagetablecache: return pagetablecache[cachekey] # Traverse page directory hierarchy to find PTE # Standard hierarchical lookup where higher levels coarsen the address pte = lookuppagedirectory(pagedirectory, levell, virtualblockid) if pte is not None: pagetablecache[cachekey] = pte.physicalindex return pte.physicalindex return None # UNMAPPED def lookuppagedirectory(pagedirectory, levell, virtualblockid): # Accesses the page table at the specified level # Not given in sources. Assumes pagedirectory is a list of 3D textures. if levell < len(pagedirectory): return pagedirectory[levell].sample(virtualblockid) return None def handlecachemiss(levell, virtualblockid): # 6. On-Demand Construction required2dtiles = fetch2dsubtiles(virtualblockid) new3dblock = stitchandresample(required2dtiles, BLOCKSIZE) # Allocate space in Block Cache (arbitrary packing) physicalblockindex = allocateblockincache(blockcache, new3dblock) # Update Page Table Cache cachekey = (levell, virtualblockid) pagetablecache[cachekey] = physicalblockindex cachemisstable.add(virtualblockid) def fetch2dsubtiles(virtualblockid): # Retrieves 2D microscope image tiles corresponding to the virtual block # Not given in sources. Returns list of 2D arrays. return [] def stitchandresample(tiles, blocksize): # Combines 2D tiles into a 3D block with resampling # Not given in sources. Returns 3D array of voxels. return [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(blocksize)] for in range(blocksize)] def allocateblockincache(blockcache, new3dblock): # Finds free space in the 3D cache texture and stores the block # Not given in sources. Returns physical index. return 0 def fetchblockcolor(blockcache, physicalindex, pos): # Samples the 3D block cache at the local position within the block # Not given in sources. Returns RGBA color. return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Parameters: Block Size: 32^3 voxels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Data: Missing data are detected during ray-casting as cache misses. Unmapped blocks produce cache misses which must be handled by the backward propagation mechanism. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The system only stores the working set of currently required blocks in the Block Cache, avoiding the storage of the entire hierarchy in GPU memory. Measured Performance: The system is evaluated for scalability and performance on petascale microscopy data streams. Scaling: The architecture handles missing data naturally and does not pre-compute any 3D multi-resolution representation, allowing it to accept a constant stream of 2D image tiles. Strengths: Decouples construction of the 3D multi-resolution representation from data acquisition; decouples sample access time during ray-casting from the size of the multi-resolution hierarchy; avoids explicit octree traversal and holding the entire path from leaf to root in GPU memory; supports arbitrary packing of blocks in the cache. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Interactive exploration of petascale microscopy data streams where data is acquired as a stream of 2D image tiles. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Virtual Memory Volume Rendering was introduced in a paper by Hadwiger et al.. It is designed for real microscopy data from neuroscience, enabling interactive exploration of petascale volume data. The system is visualization-driven, restricting most computations to the visible volume data. It compares favorably to previous best-of-breed systems like Gigavoxels and CERA-TVR, which use explicit octree traversal. name: Residency Octree Update
head: Incremental Construction
body: Residency Octree Update is a fully GPU-implemented parallel method for maintaining the spatial residency state of volumetric data bricks within a hierarchical octree structure. It solves the problem of keeping the residency octree consistent with the dynamic brick cache during both data loading and cache eviction, enabling efficient culling of non-resident volume regions during rendering. It differs from static octree construction by being fully parallel and event-driven, updating nodes only when bricks are added or removed from the cache. It differs from simple flat caches by maintaining a hierarchical bitmap representation of partial residency across multiple resolution levels and channels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of added brick IDs, a list of removed brick IDs, and the current state of the brick cache (residency status of bricks). Output: Updated culling metadata (min/max values) and partially mapped resolution bitmasks for all affected nodes in the residency octree, up to the root. Data Structures: Residency Octree Node: cullingmin: Scalar minimum value of the volume data within this node's spatial extent. cullingmax: Scalar maximum value of the volume data within this node's spatial extent. residencybitmap: A bitmask where each bit represents a specific resolution level and/or channel. A bit is set if at least one brick at that resolution/channel is resident in the cache and overlaps the node's spatial extent. Update-Candidate Buffer: A dynamic buffer storing indices of nodes that require recomputation in the next level up. Parameters: Brick Size: Typically 32^3 voxels. Leaf-Node Size: The approximate spatial extent of leaf nodes in the residency octree. Can be decoupled from brick size (e.g., 32^3, 16^3, 8^3, or 8 \times 8 \times 4). Algorithm Steps: The update process is initiated by the application immediately after the frame's brick-cache update is completed. It proceeds in a breadth-first manner from leaf nodes up to the root, using indirect compute passes to manage workgroup dispatch and enable early termination. 1. Process Removed Bricks: For each brick ID in the "removed" list, determine the corresponding leaf nodes in the residency octree whose spatial extent overlaps the brick's extent. For each such leaf node, check if it is still partially resident in the resolution level of the removed brick. This is done by verifying if any other brick at that resolution level overlapping the node is still resident in the cache. If the node is no longer partially resident in that resolution, update its residencybitmap (clear the corresponding bit). Mark the parent node of the updated leaf node as an update candidate in the update-candidate buffer. 2. Compute Culling Metadata for New Bricks: For each scalar value in each newly added brick, determine the corresponding leaf node in the residency octree. If the scalar value is lower than the node's current cullingmin or greater than its cullingmax, update the node's metadata. Use atomic operations (atomicMin, atomicMax) to ensure concurrent updates from multiple threads are safe. Mark the parent node of the updated leaf node as an update candidate in the update-candidate buffer. 3. Process Added Bricks: For each brick ID in the "added" list, determine all leaf nodes in the residency octree whose spatial extent overlaps the brick's extent. Mark these leaf nodes as partially mapped in the brick's resolution level and channel by setting the corresponding bits in their residencybitmap. If a node's residencybitmap changed due to this operation, mark its parent node as an update candidate in the update-candidate buffer. 4. Compile Update Candidates: Process the update-candidate buffer to compile a unique list of all nodes marked as candidates for the next level up. Clear the update-candidate buffer for subsequent iterations. Use the count of candidates to control the number of workgroups dispatched for the next indirect compute pass. If no candidates remain, terminate the update process. 5. Process Update Candidates: For each candidate node, recompute its cullingmin, cullingmax, and residencybitmap from its child nodes. The residencybitmap is updated via bitwise OR of the child node bitmasks: B{parent} = B{child1} \lor B{child2} \lor \dots \lor B{child8}, where B is the bitmask. The cullingmin and cullingmax are recomputed as the minimum and maximum of the respective values from all child nodes. If any of the node's values (cullingmin, cullingmax, or residencybitmap) changed compared to the previous state, mark the node's parent as an update candidate in the update-candidate buffer. 6. Repeat: Repeat Steps 4 and 5 until the root node is reached or no update candidates remain. Early termination occurs if a node's bitmask remains unchanged by the OR operation during Step 5. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def residencyoctreeupdate(addedbricks, removedbricks, brickcache, octreenodes): # Step 1: Process Removed Bricks for brickid in removedbricks: if brickcache[brickid].isresident: continue leafnodes = getleafnodesoverlappingextent(brickcache[brickid].spatialextent) for nodeidx in leafnodes: node = octreenodes[nodeidx] res = brickcache[brickid].resolution if not checkpartialresidency(nodeidx, res, brickcache): oldbitmap = node.residencybitmap node.residencybitmap = clearbit(node.residencybitmap, res) if oldbitmap != node.residencybitmap: addtocandidates(node.parentid) # Step 2: Compute Culling Metadata for New Bricks for brickid in addedbricks: if not brickcache[brickid].isresident: continue leafnodes = getleafnodesoverlappingextent(brickcache[brickid].spatialextent) for nodeidx in leafnodes: node = octreenodes[nodeidx] valmin = brickcache[brickid].minvalue valmax = brickcache[brickid].maxvalue oldmin = node.cullingmin oldmax = node.cullingmax node.cullingmin = min(node.cullingmin, valmin) node.cullingmax = max(node.cullingmax, valmax) if node.cullingmin != oldmin or node.cullingmax != oldmax: addtocandidates(node.parentid) # Step 3: Process Added Bricks (Residency Bitmap) for brickid in addedbricks: if not brickcache[brickid].isresident: continue leafnodes = getleafnodesoverlappingextent(brickcache[brickid].spatialextent) for nodeidx in leafnodes: node = octreenodes[nodeidx] res = brickcache[brickid].resolution oldbitmap = node.residencybitmap node.residencybitmap = setbit(node.residencybitmap, res) if oldbitmap != node.residencybitmap: addtocandidates(node.parentid) # Step 4 & 5: Iterative Upward Propagation candidates = list(updatecandidates) while candidates: nextcandidates = [] for nodeidx in candidates: node = octreenodes[nodeidx] newmin = float('inf') newmax = float('-inf') newbitmap = 0 for childidx in node.childids: child = octreenodes[childidx] newmin = min(newmin, child.cullingmin) newmax = max(newmax, child.cullingmax) newbitmap = newbitmap | child.residencybitmap changed = False if newmin != node.cullingmin: node.cullingmin = newmin changed = True if newmax != node.cullingmax: node.cullingmax = newmax changed = True if newbitmap != node.residencybitmap: node.residencybitmap = newbitmap changed = True if changed: addtocandidates(node.parentid, nextcandidates) candidates = nextcandidates # Step 4: Buffer cleared by reassigning candidates list # Dispatch controlled by len(candidates) def setbit(bitmap, bitindex): return bitmap | (1 << bitindex) def clearbit(bitmap, bitindex): return bitmap & ~(1 << bitindex) def addtocandidates(nodeidx, targetlist=None): if nodeidx is None: return if targetlist is None: targetlist = updatecandidates if nodeidx not in targetlist: targetlist.append(nodeidx) def checkpartialresidency(nodeidx, resolution, brickcache): # Verify if any other brick at the given resolution overlapping the node is resident bricks = getbricksoverlappingextent(getnodeextent(nodeidx)) for brick in bricks: if brick.isresident and brick.resolution == resolution: return True return False def getleafnodesoverlappingextent(extent): # Traverse octree to find leaves intersecting extent pass def getnodeextent(nodeidx): # Derived from octree structure pass def getbricksoverlappingextent(extent): # Spatial index lookup pass An optimization technique where the spatial subdivision granularity (leaf-node size) of the residency octree is decoupled from the resolution levels of the bricked volume hierarchy. This allows finer empty-space skipping than the bricking granularity. It is beneficial for anisotropic volumes and can achieve higher frame rates. Typical brick size is 32^3 voxels, while leaf-node sizes can be 32^3, 16^3, 8^3, or even 8 \times 8 \times 4. An approach where the octree is edited by a compute pass on the GPU, rather than on the CPU with deltas uploaded every frame. This is required to satisfy the constraint of no CPU readback per frame in the hot loop. Discrete events (player digs, meteor lands, explosion) may synchronise, but terrain streaming, LOD selection, or acceleration structure refits doing readback per frame remain forbidden. An octree edited on the CPU and re-uploaded every frame violates the constraint of no CPU readback per frame in the hot loop. Time Complexity: The update process is proportional to the number of changed bricks and the height of the octree. The use of indirect compute passes and early termination (when bitmasks do not change) optimizes performance by avoiding unnecessary work. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the octree nodes (culling metadata and bitmasks) and the update-candidate buffer. The buffer size is bounded by the number of affected nodes per frame. Performance: Fully GPU-implemented, allowing parallel construction and updates. Decoupling leaf-node size from brick size can improve performance by enabling finer empty-space skipping. Strengths: Efficient handling of dynamic data loading and eviction; parallel execution on GPU; early termination reduces overhead. Limitations: Requires atomic operations for culling metadata updates, which can introduce contention. Performance depends on the spatial distribution of changes and the octree structure. The method is implemented and evaluated within a scalable web-based volume rendering framework for large biomedical datasets. It is part of the Residency Octree framework, which decouples cache residency from spatial subdivision. The method was evaluated on datasets such as CyCIF Small and CyCIF Medium. name: Decoupling Resolution Levels from Spatial Subdivision
body: This method decouples the spatial subdivision granularity (leaf-node size) of the residency octree from the resolution levels of the bricked volume hierarchy. It solves the limitation where empty-space skipping efficiency is constrained by the coarse bricking granularity, allowing for finer traversal precision. Unlike coupled approaches where tree structure mirrors data resolution, this technique enables independent optimization of rendering quality and memory scalability. Inputs: Bricked volume dataset with fixed brick size B. Residency octree structure. Target leaf-node size L for the octree. Outputs: Updated residency octree with leaf nodes sized independently of brick dimensions. Data Structures: Brick: Fixed size B = 32^3 voxels. Octree Leaf Node: Variable size L, approximating 32^3, 16^3, 8^3, or anisotropic 8 \times 8 \times 4. Steps: 1. Initialize Brick Hierarchy: Construct the bricked volume hierarchy with a fixed brick size of 32^3 voxels. 2. Configure Octree Granularity: Select an approximate leaf-node size L for the residency octree that differs from the brick size B. Typical values for L: 32^3, 16^3, 8^3. Anisotropic value: 8 \times 8 \times 4. 3. Map Bricks to Octree Nodes: Traverse the residency octree. When a node corresponds to a region covered by one or more bricks, update the node's residency status based on the cache state. 4. Decouple Traversal: During ray traversal, use the octree's leaf-node size L for empty-space skipping decisions, while accessing data via the brick size B. If a leaf node is empty, skip the entire region defined by L, even if it spans multiple bricks of size B. 5. Handle Anisotropy (Optional): If L is anisotropic (e.g., 8 \times 8 \times 4), adjust the traversal step sizes along axes to match the leaf dimensions, optimizing for anisotropic volume structures. Parameters: Brick size B: 32^3 voxels. Leaf-node size L: 32^3, 16^3, 8^3, or 8 \times 8 \times 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The leaf-node size is "approximate". Implementation must handle boundary mismatches between brick grids and octree leaf boundaries. Anisotropy: Using non-cubic leaf nodes (e.g., 8 \times 8 \times 4) requires careful handling of ray intersection tests to avoid artifacts in anisotropic volumes. Cache Coherence: Since the octree and brick hierarchy are decoupled, cache updates must correctly map brick-level changes to octree leaf-level residency flags. Decouples spatial subdivision from resolution levels using separate page table hierarchies for each resolution level, enabling scalable address translation for extreme-scale data. Choose when rendering quality and memory scalability need independent optimization. Time Complexity: Traversal depth is determined by leaf-node size L. Smaller L increases traversal steps but improves empty-space skipping. Memory Complexity: Octree size depends on L. Finer L increases node count but reduces wasted space in empty regions. Performance: Achieves higher frame rates than coupled methods by enabling efficient empty-space skipping with finer granularity than bricking. Strengths: Arbitrary spatial subdivision benefits anisotropic volumes. Limitations: Requires managing two independent hierarchies (brick and octree), increasing implementation complexity. When to Use: When empty-space skipping efficiency is critical and data has anisotropic structures or varying resolution needs. When Not to Use: When simplicity of implementation is prioritized over performance gains. Originated in research on scalable web-based volume rendering of large biomedical datasets. The technique builds on the observation that efficient empty-space skipping typically requires finer granularity than bricking. It extends the residency octree update mechanism by allowing independent configuration of traversal and data access granularities. name: Multi-level, multi-resolution page table hierarchy
head: Multi-Level, Multi-Resolution Page Tables, Orthogonal page table hierarchy, Separate page tables per resolution, Single-Level
body: This method decouples the down-sampling ratio of volume data from the hierarchy level count for address translation scalability. Unlike single-level page tables or tree structures where traversal depth and data resolution are coupled, it employs a separate page table hierarchy for each resolution level, allowing independent optimization of rendering quality and memory scalability. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray sample position (x, y, z), current ray direction, desired resolution level L (determined by projected screen size), and the multi-resolution page directory structure resident in GPU memory. Output: Physical address of the voxel brick containing the sample, allowing access to the voxel data cache texture. Data Structures: The structure consists of two orthogonal hierarchies: the resolution hierarchy (data resolutions) and the page table hierarchy (page table resolutions). 1. Resolution Hierarchy: A set of discrete resolution levels L \in \{0, 1, \dots, N{res}\}. 2. Page Table Hierarchy: For each resolution level L, a tree of page tables. Multi-Resolution Page Directory: The top-level page table for each resolution level. It is an array of pointers, one entry per resolution level. This is the only structure required to be resident in GPU memory. Page Tables: Virtualized structures below the directory that map virtual page indices to physical brick indices. One or more additional levels of page tables are added to each resolution level. Cache Textures: Voxel Cache Texture: Stores active voxel bricks. All bricks, regardless of resolution level, must have the same physical resolution (number of voxels) to share this single texture. Page Table Cache Texture: Stores active page table bricks (the virtualized page tables). Address Layout: A virtual address is decomposed into fields. Let Bv be the brick size in voxels for data, and Bp be the brick size in entries for page tables. 1. LOD Selection: Determine resolution level L based on sample distance or projected size. 2. Directory Lookup: Access the L-th entry in the Multi-Resolution Page Directory to get the root of the page table hierarchy for level L. 3. Page Table Traversal: Traverse the page table hierarchy for level L. Let the virtual address be A. For each level k in the page table hierarchy (from top to bottom): Extract the page index Pk from A using bit shifts/masks determined by Bp. Look up Pk in the current page table brick. If the entry is valid, proceed to the next level. If invalid, a page fault occurs (handled by CPU/GPU driver to load the page table brick into the Page Table Cache Texture). 4. Voxel Lookup: The final page table entry provides the physical brick index. Combine this with the offset within the brick (derived from the lower bits of A) to index into the Voxel Cache Texture. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. NUMRESLEVELS = 4 PAGETABLEDEPTH = 2 BV = 16 # Brick size in voxels for data bricks BP = 1024 # Brick size in entries for page table bricks multirespagedirectory = [None] NUMRESLEVELS voxelcachetexture = None # Texture storing active voxel bricks pagetablecachetexture = None # Texture storing active page table bricks cachedreslevel = -1 cachedpagetableptrs = [None] PAGETABLEDEPTH def translateaddress(samplepos): # 1. LOD Selection: Determine resolution level L based on projected screen size lod = samplepos.z / 100.0 # Standard operation: compute based on distance/screen size # 2. Look-up Caching: Exploit spatial coherence if lod == cachedreslevel and cachedpagetableptrs[0] is not None: currentptr = cachedpagetableptrs[0] startlevel = 1 else: currentptr = multirespagedirectory[lod] cachedreslevel = lod startlevel = 0 cachedpagetableptrs = [None] PAGETABLEDEPTH # 3. Address Decomposition & Page Table Traversal virtualaddress = samplepos.x 1000000 + samplepos.y 1000 + samplepos.z # Standard linearization for level in range(startlevel, PAGETABLEDEPTH): # Extract page index Pk from virtualaddress using bit shifts/masks determined by BP pageindex = (virtualaddress >> (level 10)) & (BP - 1) # Load page table brick if not in cache pagetablebrick = pagetablecachetexture.lookup(currentptr, pageindex) entry = pagetablebrick[pageindex] if entry.isvalid: if level < PAGETABLEDEPTH - 1: currentptr = entry.pointertonextlevel cachedpagetableptrs[level] = currentptr else: physicalbrickindex = entry.physicalbrickindex break else: # Page fault: Load required page table brick into pagetablecachetexture pagetablecachetexture.fetchandstore(currentptr, pageindex) # Retry logic required in practice raise Exception("PageFaultException") # 4. Voxel Lookup brickoffset = virtualaddress & (BV3 - 1) voxeldata = voxelcachetexture[physicalbrickindex][brickoffset] return voxeldata Parameters: Brick Size (Voxel): All active voxel bricks must have the same physical resolution (e.g., 16 \times 16 \times 16 voxels) to share the single cache texture. Brick Size (Page Table): Can be chosen independently of voxel brick size. Page Table Levels: Two levels support volumes up to several hundred terabytes; three levels are sufficient for exa-scale data. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Virtual address bit-width must be sufficient to address the entire volume space across all resolution levels. Cache Coherence: The page table cache texture must be kept coherent with the resident directory. Degenerate Input: If a ray sample falls outside the volume bounds, address translation should fail gracefully or return a transparent value. The simpler variant where each resolution level has only one page table level. It is easier to implement but scales poorly to very large data compared to the multi-level variant. Use when data size is moderate and implementation simplicity is prioritized. See Single-Level, Multi-Resolution Page Tables. An alternative address translation structure using spatial hashing. Not discussed in detail here but mentioned as an alternative for GPU-based translation. See Hash Tables. Time Complexity: Address translation is O(D) where D is the page table depth (typically 2-3). Due to spatial coherence, the number of actual texture lookups for page tables is very low, as cached pointers are reused across samples along a ray. Memory Complexity: The resident memory is proportional to the number of resolution levels (size of the multi-resolution page directory). Virtualized page tables are loaded on demand. Performance: Scales well to extreme-scale data (hundreds of terabytes to exabytes). The performance difference between single-level and multi-level page tables is negligible due to caching. Strengths: Decouples resolution quality from traversal scalability. Supports very large datasets. Efficient caching due to coherence. Limitations: Requires two cache textures (voxel and page table). More complex implementation than single-level page tables. When to Use: Rendering extreme-scale volume data (e.g., electron microscopy) where single-level page tables or octrees are insufficient for scalability. When Not to Use: Small to moderate datasets where simpler structures suffice. The multi-level, multi-resolution page table hierarchy was described by Hadwiger et al. [HBJP12] and used for rendering extreme-scale electron microscopy data [BHL 11, HBJP12]. It addresses the limitations of single-level page tables and tree structures by completely decoupling the address translation hierarchy from the multi-resolution rendering hierarchy. This allows independent optimization of data down-sampling (for quality) and page table size reduction (for scalability). State-of-the-Art in GPU-Based Large-Scale Volume Visualization, https://vcg.seas.harvard.edu/publications/20150513-stateof-the-art-in-gpu-based-large-scale-volume-visualization/paper, fetched 2026-10-24

name: Residency-Octree Updates
body: Residency-Octree Updates maintains the spatial residency state of volumetric data bricks within a hierarchical octree, ensuring the tree accurately reflects which data is resident in the GPU cache. It solves the consistency problem between the dynamic brick cache and the octree during data loading and cache eviction, enabling efficient culling of non-resident volume regions during rendering. It differs from static octree construction by being fully GPU-parallel and event-driven, updating nodes only when bricks are added or removed from the cache. The method maintains a multi-channel residency octree where each node stores channel-specific metadata and a residency bitmap. Updates are triggered by two events: receiving new metadata for a volume region and receiving a new brick (or evicting one). Residency Octree Node: metadata: Dictionary or array mapping channel IDs to status values (e.g., INVALID, VALID). residencybitmap: Integer bitfield where each bit corresponds to a resolution level. A bit is set to 1 if the node is partially mapped (i.e., at least one brick at that resolution level is resident in the cache). children: List of references to child nodes (for non-leaf nodes). Brick Cache: Fixed-size LRU cache storing resident bricks. Each brick entry stores its spatial extent, resolution level, and channel. Inputs: New metadata for a volume region (channel ID, list of resolution levels, spatial bounds). New brick data (spatial bounds, resolution level, channel). Eviction trigger (brick to remove). Outputs: Updated residency octree with correct metadata and residencybitmap values. 1. Metadata Update: When new metadata for a volume region is received: Check if a node corresponding to the region's spatial extent exists in the octree. If the node is new, create it and add it to the octree. Initialize metadata as INVALID for all channels except the received one. Initialize residencybitmap by checking each resolution level to see if the node is partially mapped. If the node exists, update its metadata for the specific channel. If this is a multi-channel volume and the node already holds metadata for another channel, re-initialize the residencybitmap for the new channel's resolution levels by checking cache residency. 2. Brick Addition: When a new brick is received and stored in the cache: Select an available slot in the brick cache. Determine all residency-octree leaf nodes whose spatial extent overlaps the brick's spatial extent. Mark them as partially mapped in the brick's resolution level and channel by setting the corresponding bit in the node's residencybitmap. Propagate the update up the tree until the root node is reached. 3. Non-Leaf Propagation: Residency information is stored as bitmaps. Update non-leaf nodes by combining child node bitmaps via bit-wise OR. Terminate upwards propagation as soon as a node's bitmap remains unchanged by this operation. 4. LRU Cache Eviction: If no slot is available, evict the least recently accessed brick. Check all leaf nodes overlapping the evicted brick's spatial extent. For each, check if any other brick in that resolution level is resident. If not, the node is no longer partially mapped in that resolution level; set the corresponding bit in the node's bitmap to zero. Update non-leaf nodes by setting their bitmaps to the bit-wise OR of their child nodes' bitmaps. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setbit(bitmap, level): return bitmap | (1 << level) def clearbit(bitmap, level): return bitmap & ~(1 << level) class BrickCache: def init(self, maxsize): self.maxsize = maxsize self.bricks = [] # List of (brick, lastaccesstime) def add(self, brick, currenttime): if len(self.bricks) >= self.maxsize: self.evictlru() self.bricks.append((brick, currenttime)) def remove(self, brick): self.bricks = [(b, t) for b, t in self.bricks if b is not brick] def evictlru(self): if not self.bricks: return self.bricks.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) self.bricks.pop(0) def hasbrickoverlapping(self, nodeextent, level, channel): # Standard spatial query; returns True if any resident brick overlaps nodeextent # at the given level and channel. return any(b.spatialextent.overlaps(nodeextent) and b.level == level and b.channel == channel for b, in self.bricks) def hasbrickatlevel(self, nodeextent, level): # Checks if any resident brick overlaps nodeextent at the given level return any(b.spatialextent.overlaps(nodeextent) and b.level == level for b, in self.bricks) def propagateup(node): current = node while current.parent is not None: parent = current.parent newbitmap = 0 for child in parent.children: newbitmap |= child.residencybitmap if parent.residencybitmap == newbitmap: break parent.residencybitmap = newbitmap current = parent def updateresidencyonmetadata(nodeid, channel, allchannels, resolutionlevels, cache): # Standard tree lookup or allocation node = getorcreatenode(nodeid) if node.isnew: node.metadata = {ch: "INVALID" for ch in allchannels} node.metadata[channel] = "VALID" else: node.metadata[channel] = "VALID" for reslevel in resolutionlevels: if cache.hasbrickoverlapping(node.spatialextent, reslevel, channel): node.residencybitmap = setbit(node.residencybitmap, reslevel) else: node.residencybitmap = clearbit(node.residencybitmap, reslevel) def updateresidencyonbrickadd(brick, cache): cache.add(brick, currenttime=0) # Standard spatial index query for leaf nodes leafnodes = findleafnodesoverlapping(brick.spatialextent) for node in leafnodes: node.residencybitmap = setbit(node.residencybitmap, brick.resolutionlevel) for node in leafnodes: propagateup(node) def updateresidencyoneviction(evictedbrick, cache): cache.remove(evictedbrick) # Standard spatial index query for leaf nodes leafnodes = findleafnodesoverlapping(evictedbrick.spatialextent) for node in leafnodes: if not cache.hasbrickatlevel(node.spatialextent, evictedbrick.resolutionlevel): node.residencybitmap = clearbit(node.residencybitmap, evictedbrick.resolutionlevel) propagateup(node) Bitmap Size: The number of bits in residencybitmap corresponds to the number of resolution levels. Multi-channel Volumes: Residency is tracked per channel. A node may be partially mapped for one channel but not another. Boundaries: Spatial overlap checks must be robust to handle bricks that exactly match node boundaries or are slightly larger/smaller due to discretization. Degenerate Input: If a brick has no overlap with any node, no updates occur. Parameters: Not given in the sources. A technique used in Mega-NeRF to manage octree size by bounding it to available GPU memory and pruning nodes that do not contribute to rendering. It differs from static residency updates by actively growing and shrinking the tree based on rendering visibility rather than just cache residency. The method tracks the number of pixels visible from each node during rendering traversal, subdivides the top k nodes with the most visible pixels, and prunes entries that have not recently contributed to reclaim space when capacity is hit. The maximum tree size is bounded to 20M elements, the top k nodes to subdivide is 16,384, and the maximum tree depth observed in practice is roughly 12. It should be chosen when memory is constrained and the scene has varying levels of detail that can be dynamically adjusted based on camera view, rather than when managing a fixed set of pre-computed volume bricks. See also Decoupling Resolution Levels from Spatial Subdivision. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Propagation terminates early if bitmaps are unchanged, reducing average update cost. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Each node stores a small bitmap and metadata. Strengths: Efficiently maintains hierarchical residency information using bit-wise operations. Early termination in propagation reduces update cost. Supports multi-channel volumes with per-channel residency tracking. Limitations: Requires frequent spatial overlap checks and cache residency queries to maintain bitmap accuracy. When to use: When rendering large volumetric datasets with dynamic caching and hierarchical culling is required. When not to use: For static volumes where the entire dataset is resident, or for scenes where dynamic LOD based on visibility is more important than cache residency. The Residency-Octree Update method was introduced in the context of scalable web-based volume rendering of large biomedicine datasets. It was designed to efficiently manage the residency of volume bricks in a GPU cache while maintaining a hierarchical octree structure for culling. The method builds on earlier work in spatial culling and LRU cache eviction. Dynamic Octree Generation was introduced in the context of Mega-NeRF for scalable construction of large-scale NeRFs. It addresses the challenge of managing octree size in memory-constrained environments by dynamically adjusting the tree based on rendering visibility. name: Mixed-Resolution Multi-Volume Renderer
body: A ray-guided renderer that accesses metadata and cached volume data through the Residency Octree to enable efficient mixing of resolutions across different channels in multi-volume datasets. It is implemented as a WebGPU compute shader that evaluates each visible channel at every sample along a ray, even when channels have different resolutions, to reduce shader divergence. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin, ray direction, current node index in the full octree, channel mapping, maximum visible channels m, and user-defined parameters. Output: Computed color and opacity for the ray segment, updated ray position, and potential data streaming requests. Data Structures: Residency Octree: Provides metadata (for empty-space skipping) and cached volume data (bricks). Full Octree Layout: Nodes are accessed directly via their index without root traversal. Channel Mapping: Maps dataset channels to the m visible channels (m \le n, where n is total channels); this mapping can change at runtime. Parameters: m: Maximum visible channels, user-defined at initialization. stepScale: User-defined scaling factor to increase or decrease the sampling rate at run-time. Channel Importance: Determined by user-defined resolution ranges via UI sliders; a channel with a higher upper bound in its resolution range is considered more important. Step Size Calculation: The sampling rate is determined globally for all channels based on the channel requiring the highest sampling rate (highest resolution). The step size dt{step} is computed as follows: 1. Calculate the step size component for each dimension i \in [0, 1, 2]: dti = \frac{1}{vi \cdot si \cdot di} Where vi is the volume extent in dimension i, si is the voxel spacing in dimension i, and di is the ray direction in dimension i. 2. Compute the global step size: dt{step} = \min(dt0, dt1, dt2) \cdot stepScale Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set the maximum visible channels m and channel mapping. 2. Traversal Start: Start tree traversal at a user-defined subdivision level or the parent level of the previous termination level; never start at the root. 3. Data Check: For the current node, check if metadata and cached volume data are available. If missing, generate a request for the missing data to be streamed from the server. 4. Empty-Space Skipping: Use metadata to skip empty nodes. 5. Sampling: For each sample along the ray: Compute the global step size dt{step} based on the highest-resolution visible channel. Evaluate all m visible channels at the current sample position to reduce diverging branches in the shader. Accumulate color and opacity. 6. Termination: Stop when the ray exits the volume or opacity threshold is reached. 7. Loop: Repeat for subsequent rays or frames. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, currentnodeindex, channelmapping, stepscale, maxresv, maxress): # Compute global step size based on highest-resolution channel dtcomponents = [] for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] == 0.0: dtcomponents.append(float('inf')) # Guard for zero direction component else: dti = 1.0 / (maxresv[i] maxress[i] raydirection[i]) dtcomponents.append(dti) dtstep = min(dtcomponents) stepscale nodeidx = currentnodeindex color = vec3(0.0) opacity = 0.0 while nodeidx is not None: # Check data availability if not hasmetadata(nodeidx) or not hascacheddata(nodeidx): requeststreaming(nodeidx) # Comment: Sources do not specify streaming protocol # Proceed if data is available or wait for async completion # Empty-space skipping if isempty(nodeidx): nodeidx = getnextnode(nodeidx) # Comment: Standard octree traversal logic continue # Sample along ray segment covered by this node # Evaluate all visible channels at each sample to reduce divergence while opacity < 1.0: samplepos = rayorigin + raydirection dtstep for ch in channelmapping: val = samplevolume(ch, samplepos) # Comment: Standard trilinear interpolation tfcolor, tfalpha = transferfunction(ch, val) # Comment: Standard transfer function lookup color += tfcolor tfalpha (1.0 - opacity) opacity += tfalpha (1.0 - opacity) rayorigin = samplepos if opacity >= 1.0: break nodeidx = getnextnode(nodeidx) # Comment: Advance to next node in traversal order return color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Direction Zero: If a ray direction component is zero, dti becomes infinite. Handle this by taking the minimum of non-infinite components or using a large finite value. Missing Data: Streaming requests may stall rendering. Implement asynchronous handling or fallbacks. Channel Mapping Changes: Ensure smooth transitions when channel mapping changes at runtime. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples per ray, which is determined by dt{step}. Evaluating all m channels at each sample adds a factor of m. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of cached bricks in the residency octree. Performance: Reduces shader divergence by evaluating all channels at each sample. Global step size simplifies sampling logic. Strengths: Efficient handling of multi-resolution data, reduced divergence, ray-guided data streaming. Limitations: Potential over-sampling if lower-resolution channels are evaluated at high resolution. Requires careful tuning of stepScale and channel importance. The mixed-resolution multi-volume renderer is part of a system for scalable web-based volume rendering of large biomedical datasets. It leverages the residency octree for data management and is implemented as a WebGPU compute shader. The CPU drives overall rendering, dispatches rendering and memory management commands to the GPU, forwards brick requests to the server, and uploads bricks received from the server to the GPU. name: Multiresolution with Octree Bricking
head: Octree-based multiresolution, Octree-based multiresolution encoding
body: Multiresolution with Octree Bricking encodes volumetric data at varying resolutions into a spatial hierarchy (octree) to enable adaptive rendering. It solves the problem of rendering large datasets efficiently by allowing the renderer to select nodes based on display resolution, distance from the camera, or user-defined importance. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly linking octree depth to resolution levels (halving at each step) and using subsampling of children to generate parent node data, rather than storing independent resolution levels or using wavelet transforms. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A high-resolution volumetric dataset. Output: An octree structure where internal nodes store lower-resolution data derived from their children, and leaves store the original high-resolution data. Data Structures: The structure is an octree. Nodes: Each node represents a cubic spatial region. Resolution: The resolution of data stored in a node is determined by its depth. If the leaf level (depth D) has resolution R, a node at depth d stores data at resolution R / 2^{D-d}. Content: Internal nodes contain subsampled data from their eight children, while leaves contain the original voxel values. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Octree Construction): 1. Define the leaves of the octree as the original high-resolution data blocks. 2. Set the root node as the coarsest resolution level. 3. For each internal node, compute its data by subsampling its eight children. The resolution of the parent is half that of its children. 4. This process is performed in a single preprocessing step. 2. Frame Update (Node Selection): 1. At every frame, traverse the octree to select a subset of nodes. 2. Selection criteria include display resolution, distance from the camera (high resolution for near, low for far), center of attention or areas of interest, and user-specified bias parameters or importance metrics. 3. The selected nodes form the active set for rendering. 3. Rendering: 1. Sort the selected nodes in back-to-front order relative to the camera. 2. Render the nodes using standard volume rendering techniques (e.g., ray-marching). 3. If artifacts appear due to resolution changes, modify transfer functions in lower-resolution nodes to mitigate visual discontinuities. Parameters: Image Quality: Defined as a combination of importance or user-specified bias parameters. Resolution Scaling: Each octree level halves the resolution of the next finer level. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limits: For datasets larger than texture memory, the entire octree cannot reside in memory; an out-of-core approach saves node data on disk and loads nodes on demand depending on the field of view. Artifacts: Abrupt transitions between resolution levels can cause visual artifacts, which are mitigated by modifying transfer functions in lower-resolution nodes. Combines offline tensor-based compression (Tucker decomposition) with an adaptive, view-dependent loader. It differs by using rank-reduced tensors for storage and on-demand reconstruction upon cache misses, enabling stack-less ray-casting. Time Complexity: Construction is a single preprocessing step. Frame time depends on the number of selected nodes and the cost of sorting them back-to-front. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of nodes stored. Strengths: Allows high-fidelity rendering in regions of interest while maintaining context at lower resolutions. Adaptable to display resolution and user focus. Limitations: Requires preprocessing. Out-of-core implementations introduce I/O latency. Artifacts may occur at resolution boundaries if transfer functions are not adjusted. When to use: Large volumetric datasets where adaptive resolution is beneficial for performance or visual clarity. When not to use: When real-time construction is required or when memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck and I/O latency is unacceptable. The technique was introduced by LaMar et al. for large dataset rendering, using an octree to encode hierarchical volume "bricking". A similar approach was presented by Boada and colleagues. It is part of a broader family of multiresolution techniques that encode data into spatial hierarchies like octrees for selective querying. The method is often used in conjunction with out-of-core strategies to handle datasets exceeding texture memory limits. name: Bricked Multiresolution Tensor Approximation
head: Bricked Multiresolution TA, Multiresolution TA octree
body: Bricked Multiresolution Tensor Approximation is a data management and rendering technique for interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets. It solves the problem of limited working memory by dividing the volume into small cubical bricks, approximating each brick using rank-reduced Tucker decomposition, and organizing them into an out-of-core octree structure. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by combining offline tensor-based compression with an adaptive, view-dependent loader that maintains a GPU cache of reconstructed bricks, enabling stack-less ray-casting with on-demand reconstruction only upon cache misses. Inputs: Original volumetric dataset (scalar field); Brick width B; Rank reduction parameter R; Reconstruction rank K (optional, for interactive control). Outputs: Out-of-core octree structure containing quantized tensor decompositions; Rendered image via CUDA ray-caster. Data Structures: 1. Brick: A cubical subvolume of size B^3. Core Tensor (\mathcal{B}): A third-order tensor of size R \times R \times R. Factor Matrices (U^{(1)}, U^{(2)}, U^{(3)}): Three matrices, each of size B \times R. Binary Histogram: A 64-bit integer used for transfer-function-based culling. Quantization: The tensor and factor matrix coefficients are quantized to reduce memory usage. 2. Octree Node: Represents a brick at a specific resolution level. Contains pointers to children (if non-leaf) or the brick data (if leaf). Includes neighbor pointers for spatial indexing. 3. GPU Cache: A 3D texture storing recently used, reconstructed bricks. Parameters: Brick Width (B): Set to 32 voxels. The source formula B = (2^8 + 2 + 2) = 32 contains a typographical error (2^8=256), but the text explicitly defines B=32 with a 2-voxel overlap at each boundary for trilinear interpolation and gradient computation. Rank Reduction (R): Typically R = B/2. For B=32, R=16, resulting in a rank-(R, R, R) Tucker Approximation. Reconstruction Rank (K): User-selectable integer K \in [1, R]. Allows interactive trade-off between detail and performance. Preprocessing (Offline): The preprocessing is performed in a low-memory setting using a bottom-up process on a brick-by-brick basis. 1. Leaf Bricks: Constructed by sampling the original dataset. Each leaf brick A \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times B \times B} is approximated using a rank-reduced Tucker decomposition. 2. Tucker Decomposition: For a brick A, the decomposition is defined as: A \approx \mathcal{B} \times1 U^{(1)} \times2 U^{(2)} \times3 U^{(3)} where \mathcal{B} is the core tensor of size R \times R \times R, and U^{(n)} are the factor matrices of size B \times R. 3. Quantization: The coefficients of \mathcal{B} and U^{(n)} are quantized to reduce storage size. 4. Non-Leaf Bricks: Constructed from their eight previously constructed children. The children are dequantized and reconstructed into full B^3 volumes. These volumes are spatially averaged to form the parent brick. The parent brick is then approximated with a new rank-reduced Tucker decomposition. 5. Histogram: A 64-bit binary histogram is computed for each brick and stored alongside the decomposition. 6. Octree Assembly: Bricks are organized into an octree, where each level represents a coarser resolution. The root represents the coarsest level. Runtime (Adaptive Loading & Rendering): 1. Working Set Maintenance: An adaptive loader updates a view- and transfer-function-dependent working set of bricks. It asynchronously fetches data from the out-of-core structure and maintains the working set on CPU and GPU memory. 2. GPU Cache: The loader maintains a cache of recently used volume bricks on the GPU, stored in a 3D texture. 3. Spatial Index: At each frame, the loader constructs a spatial index for the current working set in the form of an octree with neighbor pointers. 4. Ray-Casting: A CUDA stack-less octree ray-caster traverses the octree. It uses pre-integrated scalar transfer functions and supports various shading modes. 5. Reconstruction on Miss: The ray-caster works on reconstructed bricks. Reconstruction steps occur only upon GPU cache misses. When a cache miss occurs, the quantized tensor decomposition is dequantized and reconstructed on demand by the adaptive loader on the GPU. 6. Interactive Rank Control: The user can change the reconstruction rank K during visualization. The reconstruction uses only the K most significant ranks of the tensor decomposition. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def quantize(tensor): """Quantize tensor coefficients to reduce memory usage.""" # Exact quantization scheme is not provided in the source. # Standard practice rounds to a fixed-point format or clips to a range. return np.round(tensor, decimals=2) def dequantize(quantizedtensor): """Restore quantized tensor coefficients.""" # Inverse of quantization; typically identity or scaling. return quantizedtensor def compute64bithistogram(brickdata): """Compute a 64-bit binary histogram for transfer-function culling.""" # Source does not specify binning strategy. # Standard approach: map scalar values to 64 bins, set bit if occupied. minval, maxval = brickdata.min(), brickdata.max() bins = np.linspace(minval, maxval, 65) hist, = np.histogram(brickdata, bins=bins) return np.packbits(hist > 0).astype(np.uint64) def tuckerdecomposition(brickdata, rank): """ Computes rank-reduced Tucker decomposition for a brick. brickdata: numpy array of shape (B, B, B) rank: int, R Returns: coretensor (R, R, R), factormatrices [U1 (B, R), U2 (B, R), U3 (B, R)] """ # Standard Higher-Order SVD (HOSVD) or iterative ALS method. # Mode-1 unfolding U1,, = np.linalg.svd(brickdata.reshape(B, -1), fullmatrices=False) U1 = U1[:,:rank] core = np.tensordot(U1.T, brickdata, axes=1) # Mode-2 unfolding U2,, = np.linalg.svd(core.reshape(B, -1), fullmatrices=False) U2 = U2[:,:rank] core = np.tensordot(U2.T, core, axes=1) # Mode-3 unfolding U3,, = np.linalg.svd(core.reshape(B, -1), fullmatrices=False) U3 = U3[:,:rank] core = np.tensordot(U3.T, core, axes=1) return core, [U1, U2, U3] def reconstructtucker(core, factors, rankk): """ Reconstructs the brick from Tucker decomposition using only the top K ranks. core: numpy array of shape (R, R, R) factors: list of 3 matrices, each (B, R) rankk: int, K <= R Returns: numpy array of shape (B, B, B) """ # Truncate factors and core to rank K U1 = factors[0][:,:rankk] U2 = factors[1][:,:rankk] U3 = factors[2][:,:rankk] corek = core[:rankk,:rankk,:rankk] # Reconstruct: A = B x1 U1 x2 U2 x3 U3 temp1 = np.tensordot(U1, corek, axes=([1], [0])) # Shape (B, R, R) temp2 = np.tensordot(U2, temp1, axes=([1], [1])) # Shape (B, B, R) result = np.tensordot(U3, temp2, axes=([1], [2])) # Shape (B, B, B) return result def preprocessleaf(leafdata, B, R): """Preprocesses a leaf brick.""" core, factors = tuckerdecomposition(leafdata, R) quantizedcore = quantize(core) quantizedfactors = [quantize(f) for f in factors] histogram = compute64bithistogram(leafdata) return {'core': quantizedcore, 'factors': quantizedfactors, 'histogram': histogram, 'isquantized': True} def preprocessnonleaf(childrenbricks, B, R): """Preprocesses a non-leaf brick from its 8 children.""" childvolumes = [] for child in childrenbricks: core = dequantize(child['core']) factors = [dequantize(f) for f in child['factors']] vol = reconstructtucker(core, factors, R) childvolumes.append(vol) # Source states "spatially averaged". # Implementation assumes element-wise mean of the 8 child volumes. combinedvolume = np.mean(childvolumes, axis=0) core, factors = tuckerdecomposition(combinedvolume, R) quantizedcore = quantize(core) quantizedfactors = [quantize(f) for f in factors] histogram = compute64bithistogram(combinedvolume) return {'core': quantizedcore, 'factors': quantizedfactors, 'histogram': histogram, 'isquantized': True} def renderraycaster(octree, ray, transferfunction, gpucache): """CUDA stack-less octree ray-caster.""" # Traverse octree spatial index # Check GPU cache (3D texture) for current brick # If cache miss: dequantize & reconstruct on GPU # Integrate along ray using pre-integrated scalar transfer function pass Time Complexity: Preprocessing is O(N \cdot B^3) for N bricks, with tensor decomposition overhead. Runtime complexity depends on the number of cache hits. Reconstruction on cache miss is O(B^3 \cdot R^3) or similar, depending on the reconstruction method. Ray-casting is O(\text{ray length} \cdot \text{samples}). Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to raw data due to Tucker decomposition and quantization. The octree structure adds overhead. The adaptive loader maintains a working set on CPU and GPU memory, asynchronously fetching from the out-of-core structure. Performance: Enables interactive visualization of large datasets. Performance scales with the number of cache hits. Higher K values increase reconstruction time and detail. Strengths: Low memory footprint, adaptive loading, interactive rank control. Limitations: Reconstruction latency on cache misses, quantization artifacts. The method was introduced in the paper "Interactive Multiscale Tensor Reconstruction for Multiresolution Volume Visualization". It builds on the MOVR approach for adaptive refinement. It is used for interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets. name: Hierarchical Data Loading and Abstraction
head: AMRHierarchy, GridPatch, StaticOutput, yt Data Loading and Hierarchy Construction
body: This method provides a software architecture for abstracting Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) simulation data into physical objects, separating dataset metadata from geometric structure to allow cross-code comparison. It solves the problem of efficient, on-demand access to hierarchical volumetric data by mediating all I/O through a lazy-loaded hierarchy, ensuring that memory overhead remains negligible until specific data regions are queried. Unlike general-purpose visualization tools, this approach is a lightweight, domain-specific mechanism designed to facilitate reproducible analysis of astrophysical simulation data without reinventing specialized scripts. The method operates in two distinct phases: metadata initialization and lazy geometric construction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A path to a simulation dataset directory containing parameter files and binary data files. Output: A StaticOutput instance (metadata) and an AMRHierarchy instance (geometry) which mediates access to GridPatch objects and DataContainers. Data Structures: 1. StaticOutput: A lightweight class instance. Fields: currenttime (float), currentredshift (float), domainsize (vector), unitconversion (mechanism), filelocations (list of paths). Size: Minimal; contains only metadata required to orient the dataset. 2. AMRHierarchy: The central manager object. Fields: A tree structure of GridPatch objects. Layout: Contains parentage information and spatial orientation for each patch. 3. GridPatch: Represents a single AMR grid block. Fields: Spatial coordinates (bounding box), refinement level, parent pointer, child pointers, and mapping to disk location (file path and byte offset). 4. DataContainer: A query interface object (e.g., Sphere, Box). Fields: Geometric definition (center, radius, etc.), reference to the AMRHierarchy. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: The user calls load(path) to create a StaticOutput instance. 2. Metadata Scan: StaticOutput scans the parameter file to extract simulation time, redshift, domain size, unit conversion factors, and disk file locations. Geometric data is not loaded at this stage. 3. Hierarchy Trigger: The user accesses the.hierarchy (or.h) attribute of the StaticOutput instance. 4. Lazy Construction: The AMRHierarchy object is instantiated. This is an expensive operation. 5. Patch Creation: GridPatch objects are created for all grids defined in the dataset. They are oriented in space, parent-child relationships are established, and mappings to disk locations are set up. 6. Mediation: All subsequent data access is mediated by the AMRHierarchy. When a DataContainer (e.g., a sphere) is queried for a field: a. The hierarchy identifies intersecting GridPatch objects. b. It selects the highest-resolution patches covering the region. c. It reads the data from disk. d. It masks out regions where higher-resolution data is available (coarser patches are ignored where finer patches exist). e. It returns a one-dimensional array of values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. dataset = load("path/to/dataset") print(dataset.currenttime) hierarchy = dataset.hierarchy sphere = hierarchy.sphere([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 100.0 / dataset["pc"]) densitydata = sphere["Density"] Parameters and Edge Cases: Lazy Loading: The hierarchy is not constructed at load() time. Accessing.hierarchy is the trigger. Performance: AMRHierarchy construction is computationally expensive. It should not be performed unnecessarily. Memory: Creating a DataContainer has negligible memory overhead; data is only loaded upon field access. Python objects that provide a consistent interface to a region of selected data, abstracting the underlying simulation structure (grid patches, files). They allow data to be loaded on demand with negligible memory overhead until accessed. When queried, they select appropriate grid patches, read them from disk, mask out regions where higher resolution data is available, and return a one-dimensional array of values. Implemented types include spheres, rectangular prisms, cylinders (disks), arbitrary regions based on logical operations, topologically-connected sets of cells, axis-orthogonal and arbitrary-angle rays, and slices. Time Complexity: load() is O(1) relative to data size (only metadata scan). AMRHierarchy construction is expensive, proportional to the number of grid patches and their complexity. Data retrieval is O(N) where N is the number of cells in the query region, plus I/O latency. Memory Complexity: StaticOutput is minimal. AMRHierarchy scales with the number of grid patches. DataContainer memory is negligible until data access, at which point it holds the requested field array. Strengths: Enables cross-comparison of datasets from different codes by separating metadata from geometry. Lazy loading prevents memory exhaustion for large datasets. Transparent parallelization of spatially decomposable operations. Limitations: Hierarchy construction is a bottleneck if done repeatedly. Domain-specific to astrophysical AMR data; not a general-purpose volume renderer. Originating from the yt project, this method was developed to address the lack of domain-specific quantitative analysis tools for astrophysical data, which previously led to isolated, unshared scripts within research groups. It was designed as a lighter-weight alternative to general multi-code tools like VisIt and ParaView, facilitating reproducibility and collaboration in astrophysics. The core routines are written in C for performance, while the interface is Python-based, utilizing NumPy. name: Hierarchical DDA with Super-brick Skipping
head: Exact shadow trace with super-brick skipping and occupied-box early-out
body: This method accelerates ray tracing through sparse volumetric data by introducing a two-level occupancy hierarchy (super-bricks and bricks) to skip large empty regions, while maintaining pixel-identical output to the fine per-voxel DDA. It solves the performance bottleneck of traversing empty space by verifying emptiness at a coarser granularity and using an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for early termination, ensuring exactness by only skipping verified empty blocks and terminating only when the ray definitively passes the occupied volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, volume header, brick masks, super-brick masks, and voxel data. Output: Boolean indicating if the ray hits any occupied voxel. Data Structures: The buffer layout consists of a header, bricks, brick mask, and super mask. Header: 20 words (HEADERWORDS 20). Words 12-14: Occupied box minimum coordinates (a{min}). Words 16-18: Occupied box maximum coordinates (a{max}). Word 7: Super-mask offset. Super-bricks: A grid of 4^3 bricks, containing 32^3 cells total. Each super-brick has a nonempty bitset appended after the brick mask. Bricks: The intermediate level between super-bricks and voxels. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize DDA state for the ray \mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d} within the volume bounds. 2. Loop while the ray is within the volume bounds and iteration count < 768. 3. Check super-brick occupancy via its nonempty bitset. If empty, call skipbox(32) to advance the ray state by 32 units and continue to the next iteration. 4. If the super-brick is occupied, check the current brick's occupancy mask. If the brick is empty, call skipbox(8) to advance the ray state by 8 units and continue. 5. If the brick is occupied, perform the fine per-voxel DDA traversal. 6. Early-out: if the ray is monotonic per axis and the current cell index has passed the occupied box boundary on an axis it is moving toward (step \ge 0 \land cell > a{max} or step \le 0 \land cell < a{min}), return false immediately. 7. The iteration cap remains 768; skipping reduces iterations per ray but does not change the cap. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traceshadow(o, d, header, brickmasks, supermasks, voxeldata): # Extract occupied box bounds from header amin = header[12:15] amax = header[16:19] # Initialize standard 3D DDA state t, cell, step, tdelta, tmax = initdda(o, d) # Iteration cap unchanged by skipping maxiterations = 768 for in range(maxiterations): # Early-out check against occupied box for axis in range(3): if step[axis] >= 0 and cell[axis] > amax[axis]: return False if step[axis] <= 0 and cell[axis] < amin[axis]: return False # Determine current super-brick index (32^3 cells per super-brick) superidx = tuple(c // 32 for c in cell) # Check super-brick occupancy via nonempty bitset if not issuperbrickoccupied(superidx, supermasks): # Skip entire 32x32x32 super-brick t, cell, step = skipbox(t, d, o, cell, step, 32) continue # Determine current brick index within super-brick (8^3 cells per brick) brickidx = tuple((c // 8) % 4 for c in cell) # Check brick occupancy mask if not isbrickoccupied(brickidx, brickmasks): # Skip 8x8x8 brick t, cell, step = skipbox(t, d, o, cell, step, 8) continue # Fine per-voxel DDA traversal within occupied brick while iswithinbrick(cell): if isvoxeloccupied(cell, voxeldata): return True t, cell, step = advancedda(t, d, cell, step, tdelta, tmax) # Advance to next cell after brick traversal t, cell, step = advancedda(t, d, cell, step, tdelta, tmax) return False def initdda(o, d): # Standard DDA initialization for unit voxel size and origin 0 step = [1 if d[i] > 0 else -1 for i in range(3)] cell = [int(o[i]) for i in range(3)] tdelta = [abs(1.0 / d[i]) if d[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] tmax = [tdelta[i] (cell[i] - o[i] + (0.5 if step[i] > 0 else -0.5)) for i in range(3)] return 0.0, cell, step, tdelta, tmax def advancedda(t, d, cell, step, tdelta, tmax): # Advance to the next voxel boundary along the closest axis axis = 0 if tmax[1] < tmax[axis]: axis = 1 if tmax[2] < tmax[axis]: axis = 2 t = tmax[axis] cell[axis] += step[axis] tmax[axis] += tdelta[axis] return t, cell, step, tdelta, tmax def skipbox(t, d, o, cell, step, size): # Advances ray by 'size' units using the same crossing/tie logic as fine DDA tnew = t + size # Recompute cell index at new t using DDA crossing logic to maintain exactness newcell = [int(o[i] + tnew d[i]) for i in range(3)] return tnew, newcell, step def issuperbrickoccupied(idx, masks): return masks[idx] def isbrickoccupied(idx, masks): return masks[idx] def isvoxeloccupied(cell, data): return data[cell] def iswithinbrick(cell): # Check if cell is within the current 8x8x8 brick return all(0 <= (c % 8) < 8 for c in cell) Parameters: Iteration cap: 768 iterations per ray. Super-brick size: 32^3 cells. Brick size: 8^3 cells (implied by 32/4=8). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dense Scenes: In dense scenes with no empty space (e.g., sponge1m), the extra super-mask read and early-out math can cause regression compared to the fine DDA. Precision: The skipbox function must use the same crossing/tie logic as the fine DDA to ensure visited-cell decisions are identical between skipping and fine traversal. Early-Out Correctness: The early-out condition must be checked carefully to ensure it only triggers when the ray has definitively passed the occupied volume, not just the current brick/super-brick. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is reduced for sparse volumes due to skipping empty regions, while the iteration cap remains 768. Memory complexity increases slightly due to the super-brick and brick masks. Measured Performance: On M2 Metal, for the terrain1m/orbitclose scene, GPU p50 decreased from 73.11 ms to 44.55 ms (-39.1%). On M2 Metal, for the sponge1m/fit scene, GPU p50 increased from 15.16 ms to 15.24 ms (+0.5%), showing neutral performance for dense scenes. Visual regression tests on M2 Metal show 0% differing pixels and max delta 0 for all 9 stills, confirming exactness. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths include significant speedups in sparse scenes (e.g., autumn, terrain) by skipping empty regions. Limitations include regression in dense scenes due to overhead of hierarchy checks. When to Use: Use for sparse volumetric data where large empty regions are common. Do not use for dense volumetric data where empty regions are rare, as the overhead may outweigh the benefits. This method was introduced in a pull request for the voxelite voxel editor project by 0x63616c. It is part of a performance plan to create a faster exact shadow trace. The method builds on the principles of DDA traversal but adds a hierarchical occupancy check to optimize for sparsity.
