name: Octree-based traversal
head: Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) traversal, Octree sphere tracing, Detail-adaptive octree sampling
body: Octree-based traversal accelerates rendering by recursively navigating a hierarchical spatial subdivision to skip empty or low-detail regions, thereby reducing intersection tests and sampling operations. It solves the performance bottleneck of dense voxel traversal by allowing rays to take larger steps through empty space. Unlike Hierarchical Grid Traversal which uses fixed-level mipmap grids, this family explicitly uses regular 2×2×2 subdivision to build a sparse hierarchy, distinguishing it from siblings that focus on hash grids or specific traversal optimizations. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of hierarchical spatial partitioning using octrees (or quadtrees for 2D terrain) to cull empty space. 1. Spatial Subdivision: The domain is divided recursively into 8 sub-cubes (octants). A node is classified as Empty, Leaf, or Branch. 2. Ray-Node Intersection: For each node, the ray is tested against the node's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). If the ray misses, the node is skipped. 3. Traversal Logic: Empty Nodes: Skipped immediately. The exit time (Time of Intersection, TOI) is calculated to determine the next node to visit. Branch Nodes: The ray intersection point is compared to the node's midpoint to determine which of the 8 children to descend into. Leaf Nodes: Processing occurs here. For volume rendering, this involves sampling or checking for active values. For implicit surfaces, this involves sphere tracing or distance evaluation. 4. Exit Calculation: When a node is fully traversed or missed, the exit time t{exit} for side s in dimension dim is calculated as: t{exit} = \frac{B - \mathbf{o}{dim}}{\mathbf{d}{dim}} where B is the world-space bound value and \mathbf{o}{dim} is the ray origin component. 5. Backtracking: If the ray exits a node, the traversal backtracks to the parent or sibling based on the exit side and ray direction. Sparse Voxel Traversal is a hierarchical ray-intersection method that accelerates volume rendering by recursively traversing a sparse voxel octree (SVO) to find intersections with leaf nodes or branches, skipping empty regions to reduce sampling cost. It solves the performance bottleneck of dense voxel traversal by allowing the ray to take larger steps through empty space, significantly reducing the total number of intersection tests and node visits required to reach active data. Unlike Voxel Grid Raycasting which steps through every voxel boundary in a uniform grid, this method uses hierarchical spatial subdivision to find non-empty space faster. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit use of regular 2×2×2 subdivision and mid-plane sorting logic for interior nodes, whereas other methods may focus purely on traversal optimization or specific data structures like hash grids. Choose it when rendering sparse volumetric data with high empty-space ratios. Octree partitioning for sphere tracing accelerates implicit surface rendering by dividing the spatial domain into an octree, allowing the imposition of local Lipschitz bounds on the signed distance function (SDF). This yields tighter distance bounds than global bounds, enabling the culling of octree nodes guaranteed not to intersect the implicit surface, which solves slow convergence in high-gradient regions. Choose it when rendering complex implicit surfaces where global Lipschitz constants cause excessive step sizes. Octree Enhancement replaces expensive distance evaluations in sphere tracing with octree parsing overhead to accelerate convergence. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by using spatial hierarchy to skip empty space, though experiments on simple scenes have shown it may not always outperform other enhancements like convexity or triangle inequality optimizations. Choose it for complex scenes where unenhanced sphere tracing produces a humped step-size distribution and oscillations at high end of the spectrum. This method organizes large-scale terrain data into a block-based quadtree index where node metadata (bounding boxes, hierarchy levels, offsets) is packed into a compact structure array residing entirely in GPU video memory. It solves the CPU traversal and assembly overhead bottleneck by executing frustum culling and occlusion determination in parallel on the GPU via compute shaders, with each thread processing one node to output a list of visible nodes and their Level of Detail (LOD) levels. It differs from CPU-side hierarchical traversal by offloading the culling logic to the GPU, leveraging parallel processing for cache-friendly Z-order storage. Choose it for rendering massive terrain datasets where CPU-GPU synchronization is a bottleneck. Detail-adaptive Octree Sampling is a method for rendering irregular or curvilinear grids by sampling the data into a detail-adaptive octree where the local height (resolution) is determined by the local granularity of the source grid. It solves the problem of fixed-resolution limitations in regular grids, which often require excessive storage and rendering time to capture the smallest cells of an irregular dataset. Unlike its siblings, which may use uniform sparse voxel grids or sphere-tracing partitioning, this method explicitly adapts the octree structure to the varying density of the input data. Choose it when rendering irregular or curvilinear grids where uniform sampling is inefficient. The concept of using octrees for ray tracing was introduced by Williams. The specific application to sparse voxel volumes for rendering was popularized by Laine and Karras. The use of octrees for sphere tracing implicit surfaces was explored by Akenine-Möller et al.. GPU-based frustum culling for quadtree terrain was detailed by.

name: Sparse Voxel Traversal
head: Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) Ray Intersection, Voxel Tree Raycasting
body: Sparse Voxel Traversal is a hierarchical ray-intersection method that accelerates volume rendering by recursively traversing a sparse voxel octree (SVO) to find intersections with leaf nodes or branches, skipping empty regions to reduce sampling cost. It solves the performance bottleneck of dense voxel traversal by allowing the ray to take larger steps through empty space, significantly reducing the total number of intersection tests and node visits required to reach active data. Unlike Voxel Grid Raycasting which steps through every voxel boundary in a uniform grid, this method uses hierarchical spatial subdivision to find non-empty space faster. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse voxel tree structure (e.g., OpenVDB grid, bit-SVO, or custom 5-4-3 node hierarchy), a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and optional parameters such as dilationCount and NodeLevel. Output: A boolean indicating intersection with active values, and optionally entry/exit times (t0, t1) or a list of hits. Data Structures: VoxelBounds: Stores spatial bounds as multiples of 2^{\text{lg\size}} and the log2 of the voxel size. Fields: x: i32, y: i32, z: i32 (coordinates), lgsize: i16 (log2 of voxel size). World size: 2^{\text{lg\size}} if \text{lg\size} \ge 0, else 1.0 / 2^{-\text{lg\size}}. TOI (Time of Intersection): A wrapper around f32 implementing Ord for sorting intersection times. Entry/Exit: Structures tracking the side index (0-5) and TOI of ray entry/exit relative to the current node. Node Hierarchy (5-4-3 Structure): Some implementations use a fixed hierarchy where Node5 (top, 32^3), Node4 (middle, 16^3), and Node3 (bottom, 8^3) contain child pointers and validity bits. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct the intersector with the grid and optional dilation count. Set the ray using setIndexRay (index space) or setWorldRay (world space). Return false if the ray misses the grid's bounding box. 2. Ray-Node Intersection (Branch): If the current node is a Branch: Compute the midpoint \mathbf{mid} = [ (Bx + 0.5)S, (By + 0.5)S, (Bz + 0.5)S ], where B are bounds coordinates and S is the voxel size. Calculate the intersection point \mathbf{intersect} = \mathbf{o} + t{entry} \mathbf{d}, where t{entry} is the entry TOI (0.0 if none). Determine child coordinates: ci = 1 if \mathbf{intersect}i \ge \mathbf{mid}i, else 0. Recursively call traversal on the selected child, updating bounds by shifting and adding coordinates. 3. Leaf Processing: If the current node is a Leaf: Call an action callback act(bounds, leaf). If the callback returns a result, return it immediately. Otherwise, fall through to calculate the exit. 4. Empty Handling: If the current node is Empty, do nothing and fall through to calculate the exit. 5. Exit Calculation: Define sides array [Bx, By, Bz, Bx+1, By+1, Bz+1]. For each side s, compute dimension dim = s \% 3 and bound value B{val} = Bs \times S. If \mathbf{d}{dim} == 0.0, return None for this side. Compute TOI: t = (B{val} - \mathbf{o}{dim}) / \mathbf{d}{dim}. Accept if: if no entry, t \ge 0.0; if entry exists, t{entry} \le t. Find the minimum accepted TOI among valid exits. Exclude the entry side (s \neq \text{entry.side}). Return Err(exit) with the minimum TOI. 6. Coordinate Update (Backtracking): If an exit is returned, determine dimension dim = \text{exit.side} \% 3. If \mathbf{d}{dim} < 0.0: if current coordinate c{dim} == 0, return error (exited tree); else set c{dim} = 0. If \mathbf{d}{dim} \ge 0.0: if current coordinate c{dim} == 1, return error; else set c{dim} = 1. Update entry to Entry::fromexit(exit) (maps exit side to opposite entry side). Loop to process the next node. 7. Hit Resolution: The march() function returns true if the ray intersects active values (active voxels or tiles). t0 and t1 are updated with entry and exit times along the INDEX ray. Note that t0, t1 are resolved at the NodeLevel (e.g., leaf nodes), not individual active voxels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def castray(node, origin, direction, bounds, entry, act): """ node: 'Empty', 'Leaf', or 'Branch' bounds: dict {'x': int, 'y': int, 'z': int, 'lgsize': int} entry: dict {'side': int, 'toi': float} or None act: callable(bounds, leafdata) -> result or None """ if node == 'Empty': pass # Fall through to exit calculation elif node == 'Leaf': result = act(bounds, node.data) if result is not None: return result # Fall through to exit calculation elif node == 'Branch': voxelsize = 2 bounds['lgsize'] mid = [ (bounds['x'] + 0.5) voxelsize, (bounds['y'] + 0.5) voxelsize, (bounds['z'] + 0.5) voxelsize ] entrytoi = entry['toi'] if entry else 0.0 intersect = [ origin[0] + entrytoi direction[0], origin[1] + entrytoi direction[1], origin[2] + entrytoi direction[2] ] coords = [ 1 if intersect[0] >= mid[0] else 0, 1 if intersect[1] >= mid[1] else 0, 1 if intersect[2] >= mid[2] else 0 ] newbounds = { 'x': (bounds['x'] << 1) + coords[0], 'y': (bounds['y'] << 1) + coords[1], 'z': (bounds['z'] << 1) + coords[2], 'lgsize': bounds['lgsize'] - 1 } return castray(node.child, origin, direction, newbounds, entry, act) # Calculate Exit sides = [bounds['x'], bounds['y'], bounds['z'], bounds['x'] + 1, bounds['y'] + 1, bounds['z'] + 1] minexit = None mintoi = float('inf') for sideidx, boundval in enumerate(sides): dim = sideidx % 3 boundworld = boundval (2 bounds['lgsize']) if direction[dim] == 0.0: continue toi = (boundworld - origin[dim]) / direction[dim] if entry is None: if toi < 0.0: continue else: if toi < entry['toi']: continue if toi < mintoi: mintoi = toi minexit = {'side': sideidx, 'toi': toi} if minexit is None: return {'side': 0, 'toi': 0.0} # Fallback return minexit def traversetree(root, origin, direction, act): """ root: Tree object with.get(coords) and.lgsize attributes """ currentcoords = [0, 0, 0] currentbounds = {'x': 0, 'y': 0, 'z': 0, 'lgsize': root.lgsize} entry = None while True: node = root.get(currentcoords[0], currentcoords[1], currentcoords[2]) result = castray(node, origin, direction, currentbounds, entry, act) # If act returns a non-dict, we found a hit if result is not None and not isinstance(result, dict): return result exitinfo = result dim = exitinfo['side'] % 3 if direction[dim] < 0.0: if currentcoords[dim] == 0: return None # Exited tree currentcoords[dim] = 0 else: if currentcoords[dim] == 1: return None # Exited tree currentcoords[dim] = 1 entry = {'side': (exitinfo['side'] + 3) % 6, 'toi': exitinfo['toi']} currentbounds = { 'x': (currentbounds['x'] << 1) + currentcoords[0], 'y': (currentbounds['y'] << 1) + currentcoords[1], 'z': (currentbounds['z'] << 1) + currentcoords[2], 'lgsize': currentbounds['lgsize'] - 1 } Parameters: dilationCount (int, default 0): Number of voxel dilations on a boolean copy of the grid to account for interpolation kernel sizes. NodeLevel (int, default GridT::TreeType::RootNodeType::ChildNodeType::LEVEL): The tree node level at which traversal stops and hit times are resolved. origin (array of 3 f32): Ray origin in world coordinates. direction (array of 3 f32): Ray direction vector. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If \mathbf{d}{dim} == 0.0, the TOI calculation is skipped for that side. Thread Safety: The intersector contains a ValueAccessor that is not thread-safe. A copy constructor must be used to create a separate instance per computational thread. Index vs World Space: t0 and t1 are computed with respect to the index ray, not world space. Client code must use getIndexPos or getWorldPos to convert. Boundary Conditions: If the ray direction is negative and the coordinate is 0, or positive and the coordinate is 1, the ray has exited the tree. Octree Traversal is a hierarchical ray-intersection method that recursively subdivides 3D space into eight equal octants, skipping empty regions to reduce sampling cost. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit use of regular 2x2x2 subdivision and mid-plane sorting logic for interior nodes, whereas other methods may focus purely on traversal optimization or specific data structures like hash grids. Choose this when you need a standard, well-supported hierarchical structure for general volume rendering. Voxel Pruning is a technique to reduce model size and rendering cost by omitting voxels with low importance scores, based on the observation that a small percentage of voxels contribute the majority of rendering importance. It solves the problem of excessive memory usage in volumetric representations (such as 3D Gaussian Splatting or Neural Radiance Fields) by removing non-essential voxels that contain no significant scene content. Unlike standard volume rendering which processes all voxels uniformly, Voxel Pruning dynamically adjusts sparseness based on viewpoint-dependent occlusion and structural importance, ensuring important features remain visible while suppressing less critical ones. It sets itself apart from intensity-only heuristics by incorporating geometric cues (such as fractional anisotropy) or cumulative ray contributions to determine voxel significance. Choose this when memory footprint is a critical constraint and importance metrics are available. DeepBrick is a ray-marching kernel designed for deep volume raytracing within sparse voxel octrees (specifically VDB structures) that utilizes hierarchical "brick" data structures. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering volumetric data by combining empty space skipping with front-to-back alpha blending, while handling variable step sizes and hierarchical resolution differences via a sample ratio. It is distinguished from standard sparse voxel traversal by its explicit support for "deep" rendering (accumulating depth and transmittance for post-processing) and its specific handling of brick-level data loading and evaluation. Choose this when deep accumulation (depth/transmittance) is required for post-processing effects. Voxel Grid Raycasting is a rendering technique that stores scene geometry in a 3D voxel grid and traces rays through the grid by stepping from voxel to voxel to determine intersections and surface normals. It solves the problem of efficiently determining ray-voxel intersections without performing explicit geometric intersection tests against primitives. Unlike Sparse Voxel Traversal which uses hierarchical structures like octrees to skip empty space, this method assumes a uniform grid and steps through every voxel boundary along the ray path. It differs from Regular Grid Traversal in that it typically renders volumetric density or solid occupancy directly, whereas the latter accelerates geometric ray tracing by storing primitive pointers. Choose this for dense, uniform volumes where hierarchical overhead is unjustified. Cap Node Traversal is a specialized ray traversal routine for "cap nodes" in sparse voxel octrees, which are leaf-like structures containing scalar data for a 2 \times 2 \times 2 block of voxels. It solves the problem of efficiently retrieving voxel values and performing isosurface intersection without the overhead of recursive descent into child nodes. It differs from standard interior node traversal by replacing the isovalue range check and recursive child call with direct scalar retrieval and local neighbor finding. Choose this when using cap nodes to optimize leaf-level access in sparse octrees. Sparse Voxel Ray Marching with AABB Exit Planes is a ray traversal algorithm for sparse voxel hierarchies that skips empty space by computing the exit plane of the current empty cell using precomputed Axis-Aligned Distance Fields (AADF). It differs from standard DDA Voxel Grid Raycasting by avoiding per-voxel checks in empty regions, and from pure octree traversal Octree Traversal by using fixed-size hierarchical chunks (chunks, bricks, voxels) with texture-based occupancy masks and distance fields rather than dynamic node pointers. Choose this when using texture-based sparse structures with precomputed distance fields. Voxel Ray Traversal (AABB-optimized) is an iterator that traverses a 3D voxel volume along a ray, returning hits for voxels contained within the volume. It solves the problem of efficiently enumerating voxels by combining a standard 3D DDA traversal with an initial Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) rejection test. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as Octree Traversal or Sparse Voxel Ray Marching with AABB Exit Planes, is its reliance on a flat or chunk-based volume structure where the AABB test serves primarily as a "jump ahead" mechanism to skip empty space before the voxel-by-voxel iteration begins, rather than using hierarchical node structures for traversal. Choose this for flat/chunk-based volumes where simple AABB culling is sufficient. Hierarchical Brick-Map DDA is a ray traversal technique that replaces dense voxel buffers with a sparse, hierarchical structure to skip empty regions in volumetric data. It operates by maintaining a top-level grid of cells (typically stride 8 voxels) that point to allocated "bricks" containing fine-grained voxel data; if a top-level cell is empty, the ray strides over the entire cell volume, descending only into occupied bricks for local DDA. This approach significantly reduces memory footprint and traversal time for sparse volumes, such as drone airspace which is >99% empty, compared to dense voxel storage or non-hierarchical sparse methods. Choose this for extremely sparse volumes where a grid-of-bricks structure is preferred over a full octree. The Sparse Point Cloud (SPC) Tracer is a ray-intersection method for rendering structured point clouds by treating points as cell centers within a sparse voxel hierarchy. It solves the problem of efficiently determining the visible surface of a point cloud by intersecting rays against the sparse grid structure and querying a neural field for color, without performing neural operations during the traversal phase itself. It differs from sibling methods like Octree Traversal and Sparse Voxel Traversal by operating directly on point indices derived from the grid's bottom-level acceleration structure (BLAS) and returning the color of the intersected cell via an external neural field query, rather than accumulating volume density or traversing explicit voxel nodes for shading. Choose this for neural rendering of point clouds using sparse voxel acceleration. A variant of sparse ray marching used for Ray Traced Ambient Occlusion. It marches from a surface point in a hemisphere direction, counting occlusions up to a radius limit. It starts at the floor of the ray origin, initializes local position and distance to 0, and loops up to 3 \times \text{uniforms.grid\ext} times. It checks voxel occupancy using voxelmasks; if occupied, it returns true (occlusion found). It loads the voxel AADF and calculates the exit plane, then calculates side distance and t, adding t to the accumulated distance. If distance > t{max}, it returns false (no occlusion found within range). It advances the ray position, updating ipos and localpos. Unlike the main sparse ray march, this version does not use the hierarchical chunk/brick structure. It only checks voxelmasks and voxelaadf. It also accumulates distance and stops at t{max}. Parameter: t{max} (maximum distance to march). A ray traversal method that uses interval arithmetic with correct rounding modes to guarantee that no octant is missed during traversal, solving precision errors that occur when subdivision levels approach floating-point limits. It performs ray traversal using interval arithmetic with correct rounding modes (using SSE2 instructions) to determine the order of sub-octants. Precision is 30 bits (NL=30), with resolution at Octree level 9 (512^3 resolution). When subdivision levels approach the limits of floating-point precision, standard traversals mismatch. This is handled by using 128-bit precision binary floating-point arithmetic for verification and interval arithmetic with correct rounding modes for the actual algorithm. Unlike Gargantini's method which only partially eliminates errors and requires restricted conditions, this method guarantees correctness for all cases with minimal performance impact. A hybrid rendering technique using the CGC data structure where cell rasterisation handles primary rays and path tracing handles secondary rays for global illumination. Using the CGC data structure for ray tracing or path tracing of isosurfaces, leveraging pre-computed cluster bounds for hierarchical traversal. It uses cell rasterisation for primary rays and path tracing for secondary rays. It traverses and tests blocks, clusters, metacells, and individual voxals hierarchically using the pre-computed cluster bound stored in the last metacell of each cluster. For shadow and ambient occlusion rays, it fetches only metacell data. For additional bounces in path tracing, it fetches grid cell data to compute a normal at each intersection point. Primary rays can be either traced or rasterised (hybrid approach). Parameter: Path tracing bounces: 3. Measured Performance: In tests with 512^3 resolution and NL=30, interval arithmetic traversal with SSE2 showed similar performance to Gargantini's algorithm, with slight overhead for rounding modes. OpenVDB's intersector is optimized for multi-threading by amortizing bounding box computation via copy constructors. Strengths: Efficient empty space skipping, flexible node levels, thread-safe via copy constructor, supports various data structures (OpenVDB, bit-SVO, custom). Limitations: Overhead of tree traversal for very dense volumes; precision issues at high subdivision levels without interval arithmetic; requires careful handling of index vs world space. When to Use: Sparse volumetric data, large scenes with significant empty space, when memory efficiency is important. When Not to Use: Dense, uniform volumes where the overhead of tree traversal outweighs the benefits of empty space skipping; when high-precision traversal at extreme subdivision levels is required without interval arithmetic. Key papers include "Sparse Voxel Octrees" by Laine and Karras (2010) and "Efficient Sparse Voxel Octrees" by Laine et al. (2014). The method has been widely adopted in production renderers and libraries such as OpenVDB (used in film VFX) and various real-time rendering engines. It evolved from earlier octree-based ray tracing methods to handle the specific challenges of volumetric data, including interpolation, density accumulation, and efficient empty space skipping. Recent developments include integration with neural rendering (e.g., NSVF, SPC Tracer) and robust interval arithmetic for precision-critical applications. name: Octree Traversal
head: Hierarchical Octree Traversal, Octree Space Subdivision
body: Octree Traversal is a hierarchical ray-intersection method that accelerates volume rendering by recursively subdividing 3D space into eight equal octants, skipping empty regions to reduce sampling cost. It solves the performance bottleneck of dense voxel traversal by allowing the ray to take larger steps through empty space, significantly reducing the total number of intersection tests and node visits required to reach active data. Unlike Empty-Space Skipping which uses primitive hulls, Octrees use hierarchical spatial subdivision to find non-empty space faster. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit use of regular 2x2x2 subdivision and mid-plane sorting logic for interior nodes, whereas other methods may focus purely on traversal optimization or specific data structures like hash grids. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; the root node of the octree. Output: A sorted list of leaf nodes (voxels or bricks) intersected by the ray, or a traversal path for rendering. Data Structures: The octree is a tree structure where each parent node contains either 0 or 8 children. Interior Node: Contains pointers (or indices) to its 8 children. In some implementations, it may also store min/max bounds for each child to accelerate culling. Leaf Node: Represents the finest level of subdivision (e.g., a single voxel or a brick of voxels). It contains the actual volumetric data or metadata indicating emptiness. Subdivision: Each child octant is an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) exactly half the size of its parent node. The 8 children achieve a 2x2x2 regular subdivision of the parent node. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Start at the octree root. Given a ray, a parent node, t{enter}, and t{exit}. 2. Intersection Test: Test if the ray intersects the current parent node's bounding box. If not, terminate traversal for this branch. 3. Mid-Plane Computation: For an interior node, compute the ray's intersection with the X, Y, and Z mid-planes that divide the parent node into its eight child octants. Let these parameters be t{midX}, t{midY}, and t{midZ}. 4. Ordering: Sort the mid-plane intersection parameters to determine the spatial order in which the ray traverses the child octants. A ray intersects at most 4 octants of a given node. 5. Child Selection: Iterate through the sorted octants. For each octant, determine if the ray enters it within the current [t{enter}, t{exit}] interval. 6. Recursion/Descent: If the octant is an interior node, recurse with updated t{enter} and t{exit} (clamped to the octant's boundaries). If the octant is a leaf node, record the intersection or sample the data. If the octant is empty (no children and no data), skip it. 7. Termination: The search terminates when encountering a block with no data or reaching the smallest blocks (leaf nodes). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseoctree(rayorigin, raydirection, node, tenter, texit): """ Recursively traverse an octree to find intersected leaf nodes. """ results = [] # 1. Check if ray intersects current node's AABB if not rayaabbintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, node.bounds, tenter, texit): return results # 2. If leaf node, process data if node.isleaf(): results.append(node.data) return results # 3. Interior node: Compute mid-plane intersections # The node has 8 children. Mid-planes are at 0.5 of the node's local extent. # Compute t values where ray crosses X, Y, Z mid-planes relative to node origin tmidx = (node.bounds.center.x - rayorigin.x) / raydirection.x tmidy = (node.bounds.center.y - rayorigin.y) / raydirection.y tmidz = (node.bounds.center.z - rayorigin.z) / raydirection.z # 4. Sort mid-planes to determine traversal order # Note: A ray intersects at most 4 octants of a given node midplanes = sorted([tmidx, tmidy, tmidz]) # 5. Iterate through children in spatial order determined by sorted mid-planes for octantindex in range(8): child = node.children[octantindex] if child is None: continue # Empty octant # Update tenter and texit for the child, clamped to child's bounds childtenter = max(tenter, rayaabbentry(rayorigin, raydirection, child.bounds)) childtexit = min(texit, rayaabbexit(rayorigin, raydirection, child.bounds)) if childtenter < childtexit: results.extend(traverseoctree(rayorigin, raydirection, child, childtenter, childtexit)) return results def rayaabbintersect(origin, direction, bounds, tmin, tmax): """Returns true if ray intersects AABB bounds within [tmin, tmax].""" tenter = tmin texit = tmax for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bounds.min[i] or origin[i] > bounds.max[i]: return False else: t1 = (bounds.min[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bounds.max[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tenter = max(tenter, t1) texit = min(texit, t2) return tenter <= texit def rayaabbentry(origin, direction, bounds): """Returns the ray parameter where the ray enters the child's AABB.""" t = -float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] > 0: t = max(t, (bounds.min[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i]) else: t = max(t, (bounds.max[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i]) return t def rayaabbexit(origin, direction, bounds): """Returns the ray parameter where the ray exits the child's AABB.""" t = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] > 0: t = min(t, (bounds.max[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i]) else: t = min(t, (bounds.min[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i]) return t Parameters: Maximum Depth: Limits the recursion depth to prevent excessive memory usage or over-subdivision. Minimum Octant Size: Stops subdivision when the node size reaches a single voxel or a specified minimum. Data Entries Limit: Subdivision may stop if an octant contains fewer than a threshold number of data entries (for sparse optimization). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Implementation: Octrees are difficult to implement on GPUs because GPU programming does not allow recursive algorithms; the required stack must be implemented manually. Irregular Geometry: For meshes and unstructured volumes, octrees conform poorly to irregular geometry, leading to relatively expensive traversal strategies. Node Types: Separate traversal routines are required for interior nodes (child can be interior, cap, or scalar leaf), scalar leaves (child is always the same scalar leaf, only non-empty at forward edges), and cap nodes (child is a voxel, maps to a cell via reconstruction). Accelerates ray-object intersection by navigating a spatial hierarchy where higher-level nodes cover larger extents, skipping entire subtrees that do not intersect the ray. Uses a one-to-one mapping of data bricks to octree nodes for spatial subdivision and empty-space culling, with explicit LOD selection criteria. Determines the 0–7 linear index of a specific child node within a parent’s 2x2x2 subdivision using precomputed bit-depth masks and bitwise operations. Determines the adjacent leaf nodes in six cardinal directions for a given node in a Sparse Voxel Octree, solving traversal between non-contiguous nodes. Traverses an octree by computing and sorting the intersection order of X, Y, and Z mid-planes to determine the exact traversal sequence. A CPU-based ray traversal algorithm for 3D sparse voxel octrees stored in a linear block structure, using an explicit stack. A GPU-based iterative algorithm using bitwise child-slot permutation and t-span calculations to find the first intersection of a ray with a sparse voxel octree. Determines which data bricks to load from a server into a local cache based on the current viewing ray, integrating residency metadata into traversal. Uses a standard 8-way octree with child and solid masks, visited in front-to-back depth-first order, splitting the screen into tiles for multithreaded rendering. A GPU-based technique using an octree to manage brick-level data, performing adaptive LOD selection of lighting and material information. Accelerates ray traversal using a hierarchical sparse voxel grid (e.g., VDB) to skip empty space, returning only sample locations within occupied cells. Traverses a HashDAG structure to find the path of a ray through a sparse voxel volume, treating the structure as implicit geometry for shadow testing. N3-trees are a generalization of octrees where each node is subdivided into N parts instead of 8. They are considered a special case of Kd-Trees. While octrees offer regular subdivision providing identical node size at each level (interesting for storing regular data bricks), no algorithm in available literature proposes to exploit the specific structure of octrees/N3-trees to accelerate ray traversal beyond standard hierarchical methods. Time Complexity: Theoretically optimal in terms of fewest traversal steps for regularly spaced geometry, assuming objects are contained uniformly within cells with no overlap. Memory Complexity: Sparse octrees consume significantly less memory than complete octrees. A complete octree of depth D=10 consists of ~1.2 billion nodes consuming ~9.14 GiB, whereas a sparse octree only stores non-empty octants. Strengths: Efficient empty space skipping; regular structure allows for simple child index computation; suitable for sparse volumetric data like terrain. Limitations: Difficult to implement on GPUs due to lack of native recursion support; poor conformity to irregular geometry/meshes; requires manual stack management on parallel architectures. When to Use: Sparse volumetric datasets (e.g., terrain, medical volumes with large empty regions); regular voxel geometry. When Not to Use: Dense, fully populated volumes; irregular mesh geometry. The octree was originally proposed by Glassner for top-down point location testing along successive octree nodes hit by the ray. Samet modified this marching procedure to incorporate a neighbor-finding algorithm, delivering dramatic speedups. Sung proposed a DDA traversal similar to a hierarchical grid. Gargantini and Atkinson implemented a traversal similar to a kd-tree where the ray intersection with each octant midplane is ordered. Octrees are used in volumetric rendering applications to perform empty space skipping. name: Octree-based Volume Rendering
head: Chamberlain's algorithm, LaMar's algorithm, Octal tree structure for volume rendering, Octree Approach (Baseline), Octree on a GPU, Octree-based Volume Rendering with Adaptive Sampling, Weiler's smoothing
body: Octree-based volume rendering accelerates the visualization of volumetric datasets by using a hierarchical octree structure to skip invisible voxels and reduce sampling in uniform areas. It solves the problem that only a small percentage of voxels contribute to the final image, while the rest remain invisible. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as Hierarchical Traversal and Residency Octree Traversal, by its specific use of a one-to-one mapping of bricks to octree nodes for culling and spatial subdivision, often relying on CPU-side or unified memory traversal logic rather than specialized GPU residency caches. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset (scalar field), a transfer function mapping scalar values to RGBA, and camera parameters (position, orientation, field of view). Output: A 2D image with accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: Octree: A hierarchical tree where each parent node contains 0 or 8 children, achieving a 2x2x2 regular subdivision of the parent node into 8 equal parts or 'leaves' [Parent]. Node Metadata: Each node stores a visibilityratio, defined as the ratio of visible data to the total amount of data in the cube. At the leaf level, a node represents one cell that is either completely filled or empty. For higher levels, visibilityratio is calculated by averaging the ratios of its 8 children. Empty Cell Condition: A cell is considered completely empty only if its eight angular (corner) values are completely transparent after applying the transfer function. Parameters: Adaptive Sampling Threshold: A predefined threshold for projected size or angular difference to trigger additional sampling points. LaMar's FOV Threshold: Nodes are selected if their projected angle is less than half the field-of-view angle. Early Stopping (PlenOctree variant): Accumulated transmittance Ti < \gamma = 0.01. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Perform octree subdivision of the volumetric data. Calculate the visibilityratio for each node. This calculation depends on the transfer function and must be recalculated if the transfer function changes. For multi-channel rendering, this preprocessing is performed per channel or requires ensuring all required subtrees remain cache resident. 2. Traversal Initialization: Start traversal at the third level of the octree (or from the parent node of the last visited sample's node) to optimize performance. For each ray, determine intersections with the octree structure. 3. Node Selection and Culling: Chamberlain's Criterion: Compute the projected size of each octree node on the fly. If the size is smaller than a predefined threshold, consider the node sufficiently accurate to approximate all nodes below it. LaMar's Criterion: Use two criteria: distance (similar to Chamberlain) and field-of-view. Discard nodes that do not intersect the view frustum. Select nodes whose projected angle is less than half the field-of-view angle. Empty Space Skipping: If a node's visibilityratio indicates it is empty (all corners transparent), skip the node entirely. 4. Adaptive Sampling: Perform adaptive sampling along the ray segment within the node. Take a large step between selection points when the beam passes through uniform areas. If there is a large difference in values between two neighboring selection points, select an additional point between them. This reduces sample size in areas where opacity makes a small contribution or where the volume is uniform. 5. Rendering and Blending: Trilinear Interpolation: Define a cell as a cube whose eight corners are adjacent to voxel values. The intensity value for each position inside the cell is defined as a trilinear interpolation of angular values. Sorting: During traversal, sort children of a node in front-to-back order. Rasterization: While a node is to be drawn, slice the cuboid box corresponding to this node. Rasterize the slices and blend them into the previously drawn slices. PlenOctree Variant: For each ray, produce a sequence of segments between voxel boundaries with constant density and color, of lengths \{\deltai\}. Apply NeRF's volume rendering model: C(r) = \sum{i=0}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj). Early Stopping: Stop rendering when the accumulated transmittance Ti is less than \gamma = 0.01. 6. Smoothing (Optional): Apply an extension (Weiler's smoothing) to smooth discontinuity artifacts at LOD boundaries caused by inconsistencies of the view-plane at different levels of detail. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderoctreevolume(rayorigin, raydirection, octreeroot, transferfunction, camera): # Traversal initialization: start at third level or cached parent currentnode = getcachedparentnode(rayorigin, raydirection, octreeroot) or octreeroot accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 nodestack = [currentnode] while nodestack: node = nodestack.pop() # 1. Frustum and Ray Intersection if not intersectsfrustum(node, camera) or not intersectsray(node, rayorigin, raydirection): continue # 2. Empty Space Skipping if isempty(node, transferfunction): continue # 3. Selection Criteria projectedsize = computeprojectedsize(node, camera) if projectedsize > camera.threshold: # Node too large: push children sorted front-to-back children = getchildren(node) children.sortbydepth(rayorigin, raydirection) nodestack.extend(children) continue # 4. Adaptive Sampling & Rendering step = computelargestep(node) t = node.mint prevvalue = None while t <= node.maxt: pos = rayorigin + raydirection t value = samplevoxel(pos, node) rgba = transferfunction(value) if rgba.a > 0: accumulatedcolor[0] += rgba.r rgba.a accumulatedtransmittance accumulatedcolor[1] += rgba.g rgba.a accumulatedtransmittance accumulatedcolor[2] += rgba.b rgba.a accumulatedtransmittance accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - rgba.a) # Adaptive refinement: check difference with previous sample if prevvalue is not None and abs(value - prevvalue) > thresholddiff: midt = t - step / 2.0 midpos = rayorigin + raydirection midt midvalue = samplevoxel(midpos, node) midrgba = transferfunction(midvalue) if midrgba.a > 0: accumulatedcolor[0] += midrgba.r midrgba.a accumulatedtransmittance accumulatedcolor[1] += midrgba.g midrgba.a accumulatedtransmittance accumulatedcolor[2] += midrgba.b midrgba.a accumulatedtransmittance accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - midrgba.a) prevvalue = value t += step # Early stopping if accumulatedtransmittance < 0.01: break return accumulatedcolor def isempty(node, transferfunction): # A cell is completely empty only if its eight angular values are completely transparent corners = getnodecorners(node) for corner in corners: value = samplevoxel(corner, node) if transferfunction(value).a > 0: return False return True def trilinearinterpolate(cellcorners, pos): # cellcorners: list of 8 scalar values at cube corners # pos: local position [0,1]^3 inside cell x, y, z = pos c000, c100, c010, c110, c001, c101, c011, c111 = cellcorners i0 = c000 (1-x) + c100 x i1 = c010 (1-x) + c110 x i2 = c001 (1-x) + c101 x i3 = c011 (1-x) + c111 x j0 = i0 (1-y) + i1 y j1 = i2 (1-y) + i3 y return j0 (1-z) + j1 z def computelargestep(node): # Step size proportional to node spatial extent along ray return node.extentalongray / 4.0 def getcachedparentnode(rayorigin, raydirection, octreeroot): # Returns parent of last visited node or third level root return octreeroot.children[0] if hasattr(octreeroot, 'children') else octreeroot def computeprojectedsize(node, camera): # Project node bounding box to screen space return node.screenarea def intersectsfrustum(node, camera): return camera.frustum.intersects(node.bbox) def intersectsray(node, rayorigin, raydirection): return node.bbox.intersectsray(rayorigin, raydirection) def getchildren(node): return node.children if hasattr(node, 'children') else [] def samplevoxel(pos, node): # Fetch scalar value at pos, using trilinear interpolation if inside a cell if node.isleaf: return node.data[pos] return trilinearinterpolate(node.corners, node.localpos(pos)) def getnodecorners(node): return node.corners if hasattr(node, 'corners') else [0.0]8 Combines an octree for spatial subdivision with 3D non-standard Haar wavelets in leaf nodes. Distinguished by enabling incremental loading and frustum-clipping-based memory management for large-scale datasets on distributed clusters. Renders cloud surfaces using opacities \rho(X)\sigmat and voxel colors I0(X) with view-dependent octree cubes based on projected area-weighted approximation errors. Distinguished by its use of least-squares approximations and hardware cell-projection compositing. Converts a trained NeRF-SH model into a sparse octree representation for real-time rendering. Uses NeRF's volume rendering model with early stopping at transmittance < 0.01. Time Complexity: Depends on the depth of the octree and the sparsity of the data. In sparse volumes, it achieves significant speedups by skipping empty space. In dense volumes, the overhead of tree traversal may not be compensated by empty space skipping. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the octree structure in main memory or cache. For multi-channel rendering, entire subtrees must be resident in cache, leading to higher memory overhead (overhead ratio 1/3 for anisotropic volumes vs 1/7 for others). Measured Performance: On an Intel Core 2 CPU E8400 3.0 GHz and GeForce 8800 GTX with 512^3 scenes, the optimized version achieved 80 frames per second compared to 9 frames per second for the non-optimized version. Strengths: Eliminates rasterization as a bottleneck by skipping invisible data; effective for sparse datasets. Limitations: Substantial visual artifacts at LOD boundaries due to view-plane inconsistencies; inability to reduce volumetric data size in main memory limits rendering of datasets larger than available memory; high computational cost and memory footprint in multi-channel scenarios due to per-channel tree traversal. When to use: Sparse volumetric data where empty space skipping provides significant gains; interactive applications requiring adaptive sampling. When not to use: Dense volumes where traversal overhead dominates; scenarios with limited main memory for large datasets. The octree spatial hierarchy was first proposed by Chamberlain et al. for rendering surface geometry, involving octree subdivision, recursive traversal, and on-the-fly projection size computation. LaMar et al. developed a similar technique with improved selection criteria (distance and field-of-view). Weiler et al. proposed extensions to smooth discontinuity artifacts at LOD boundaries. The method is widely used in GPU-accelerated volume rendering pipelines to optimize performance by leveraging spatial coherence and transfer function-based culling. name: Octree-based Volume Rendering with Wavelet Leaves
head: Octree space subdivision, Octree-wavelet format
body: This method renders volumetric data by combining an octree for spatial subdivision with a multi-resolution wavelet representation stored in leaf nodes. It solves the problem of rendering large-scale datasets (gigabytes) on distributed clusters with limited per-node texture memory by enabling early termination of traversal in empty space and progressive refinement of detail. It is distinguished from its sibling Octree-based Volume Rendering by the specific use of 3D non-standard Haar wavelets in leaves to support incremental loading and frustum-clipping-based memory management. Input: A volumetric dataset (e.g., CT/MRI scans) stored in an octree-wavelet format on disk; user interaction parameters (viewpoint, scale, rotation); a user-specified octree depth parameter. Output: A rendered image on a display node, progressively refined from low to high resolution. 1. Octree Structure Nodes: Internal nodes represent space subdivisions and leaf nodes contain the volume data. Empty Marking: Empty regions are marked during preprocessing to allow traversal skipping. Indexing Scheme: A fast indexing scheme uses file names to represent the octree traversal path, where numbers in the filename indicate the path (0-7) to the leaf node. 2. Brick Files (Leaf Storage) Format: 3D non-standard Haar wavelet decomposition. Layout: Data is organized for incremental loading. Start of File: Low-resolution information (highest wavelet compression). Subsequent Data: Detail coefficients for lower wavelet levels (higher resolution). Brick Size: Brick size is determined by the user-specified octree depth; deeper octrees result in more brick files, each smaller in size. 3. Fallback Texture Content: The entire dataset is loaded once at startup into the fallback texture. Storage: The fallback texture resides permanently in the graphics card’s texture memory. Detail Level: Its detail level is lower than the maximum detail achievable via clipping, chosen to maintain a predefined minimum frame rate. 1. Preprocessing: Construct the octree from the input volume and mark empty branches to enable early termination. Apply 3D non-standard Haar wavelet decomposition to leaf nodes. Organize leaf data in brick files by placing the lowest detail level (approximation coefficients) at the beginning, followed by detail coefficients in order of increasing resolution. Load the fallback texture (entire dataset at reduced detail) into GPU memory. 2. Rendering Loop (Per Frame): Check Interaction: If the user is transforming the volume (translation, rotation, scaling), switch rendering to the Fallback Texture to maintain interactivity. If Static (User Interaction Paused): 1. Frustum Clipping: Determine which parts of the scene each rendering node must display using the octree structure, disregarding parts outside the view frustum to save RAM and texture memory. 2. Traverse Octree: Use the fast file-name indexing scheme to traverse the octree to the relevant leaf nodes. 3. Skip Empty Branches: During traversal, skip branches marked as empty during preprocessing. 4. Incremental Loading: Load the lowest detail level data from the beginning of the brick file. Display the volume at this resolution. Triggered by a timer, sequentially load detail coefficients from the brick file to reconstruct higher resolution levels (i-1, i-2, \dots). 5. Progressive Refinement: Gradually refine the image up to the maximum level of detail each graphics card can display. Wavelet Reduction: The data reduction factor at wavelet level L is given by: \text{Reduction}L = \left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^L L=1: 1/8th of the data remains. L=2: 1/64th of the data remains (less than 2%). Bit Depth and Levels: With 22 bits available for underflow/precision management, the algorithm can be applied 7 times before running out of bits. \left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^7 \approx 4.77 \times 10^{-7} For a typical dataset of 256^3 = 16,777,216 voxels, this reduces to 8 voxels. Parameters: Octree Depth: User-specified. Determines the size of octree bricks; deeper octrees yield more brick files of smaller size. Threshold: Used during preprocessing to determine if wavelet coefficients can be set to zero for compression. Quantization: Real numbers can be quantized (e.g., removing fraction parts), and low-frequency coefficients may be stored at higher precision than high-frequency ones. Frustum Clipping Performance: Frustum clipping involves time-consuming file operations to load new data chunks from disk, making it impossible to perform clipping at interactive rates during volume transformation. Solution to Clipping Latency: Use the fallback texture during transformation to maintain frame rate, switching back to incremental subvolume loading only when interaction pauses. Data Distribution: The method works best for datasets where the object is near the center of the data cube with an empty or nearly empty background (e.g., CT/MRI scans). Memory Constraints: Leaf data blocks may still be too large for the texture buffer depending on octree depth; the wavelet format allows determining a compression level to fit within GPU texture memory. Time Complexity: Traversal is "almost instantaneous" due to the file-name indexing scheme. Preprocessing time is lower than BSP trees. Memory Complexity: Significant savings in disk space and RAM are achieved by not storing empty areas. Per-node memory usage is limited by the texture buffer size, managed via wavelet compression levels. Performance: Octree traversal consistently outperforms Binary Space Partition (BSP) trees in both preprocessing and traversal time for typical CT/MRI datasets. Scalability: The method is designed for distributed display clusters (e.g., 25 nodes, 50 displays, 200 megapixels). Each node allocates resources only for its portion of the scene. Strengths: Early termination in empty space, progressive refinement for immediate visual feedback, and efficient memory usage via wavelet compression. Limitations: Frustum clipping is too slow for interactive transformation, preprocessing is required to build the octree and wavelet structure, and it is best suited for sparse data with empty backgrounds. Origin: Developed for large-scale multiresolution volume rendering on distributed display clusters. Hardware Context: Tested on a cluster of 25 PowerMac G5 computers with nVidia GeForce 6800 and Quadro FX4500 graphics cards, driving a 10x5 grid of 30-inch Apple Cinema Displays (2560x1600 resolution each). Comparison: Statistical analysis showed octree techniques outperform BSP trees for typical medical imaging datasets. name: Hierarchical Volume Rendering for Cloud Surface
head: Least squares volume rendering, Octree volume rendering for surface
body: This method renders cloud surfaces in regimes where the diffusion approximation is invalid, specifically at cloud edges where single scattering and low-order multiple scattering break directional independence. It solves this by using hierarchical volume rendering with opacities \rho(X)\sigmat and voxel colors I0(X), selecting view-dependent octree cubes based on projected area-weighted approximation errors. It is distinguished from standard octree volume rendering by its specific use of least-squares approximations for color and opacity combined with a hardware cell-projection compositing step, differing from Octree-based Volume Rendering with Wavelet Leaves in its approximation basis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Precomputed octree hierarchy of least-squares approximations for color and opacity values at various cube levels, along with the Root Mean Square (RMS) error for each approximation. Output: Compositing of selected cubes in back-to-front order using the hardware cell-projection method. Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains fields for the least-squares approximation coefficients (for color and opacity), the RMS error of that approximation, and spatial bounds. Approximation Functions: Piecewise linear or piecewise constant functions are used within the hierarchy, computed per wavelength band (red, green, blue). Steps: 1. Precomputation: Compute an octree hierarchy of least-squares approximations to the color and opacity values on various level cubes. Calculate the RMS error for each approximation. 2. View-Dependent Selection: Traverse the octree to select appropriate cubes. The selection is view-dependent and weights the approximation error by the projected area of the cube on the image. 3. Compositing: Composite the selected cubes in back-to-front order using the hardware cell-projection method. Formulas: Opacity: \rho(X)\sigmat, where \rho(X) is density and \sigmat is the extinction coefficient. Voxel Color: I0(X), representing the incident radiance solution per wavelength band. Parameters: Approximation Type: Piecewise linear or piecewise constant. Error Weighting: The selection criterion weights the RMS error by the projected area of the cube on the image plane. Pitfalls: Precision/Boundaries: The diffusion approximation (used for the bulk volume solution I0) is invalid at cloud edges where single scattering and low-order multiple scattering are significant. This method is specifically applied to handle these edge cases where the standard approximation fails. This variant integrates the volume rendering step into an iterative loop with a Partial Differential Equation (PDE) solver. It obtains revised values for Q0 and Q1 by propagating incident radiance from the volume rendering results. The sequence of PDE solution, volume rendering, and ray propagation is iterated until I0 stops changing significantly. It also computes ground illumination and shadowing using hardware volume rendering onto hemicubes placed on a ground sample grid, including diffusely reflecting ground as background. Direct sunlight I{sun}(Xe, \omega{sun}) is propagated and attenuated separately, saved as I{risun}(Xe, \omega{sun}) at every voxel, and added separately to Q0 and Q1. A key pitfall is that the sun's radiance exceeds the dynamic range of the fixed-point frame buffer, so it is not added to the sky background. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Relies on hardware cell-projection for compositing, suggesting GPU acceleration. Strengths: Handles cloud edges where diffusion approximation fails; integrates with ground illumination and shadowing. Limitations: Requires precomputation of octree hierarchies and RMS errors. When to use: Rendering cloud surfaces with significant edge effects or single-scattering dominance. Originated in the context of global illumination in clouds, specifically addressing the limitations of the diffusion approximation at cloud boundaries. The method builds on [Schu01] (Schueller, 2001), which was modified to handle color and use piecewise linear or constant functions in the approximation hierarchy. It is part of a broader workflow that includes PDE solutions for radiance transport and final gather ray tracing for single scattering effects. name: Octree-based Volume Rendering with Delta/Residual Tracking
head: Delta/residual tracking with octree, Octree-based Volume Traversal, Ratio tracking for volume rendering
body: This method replaces traditional volume meshes and volume stacks with an octree encoding volume topology and extra data, enabling direct traversal and shading during ray marching. It differs from stack-based volume shading by evaluating all volume shaders in the current leaf node simultaneously at each step, eliminating the need to maintain and update a volume stack during traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of objects with volume geometry and their volume bounding boxes. Output: Rendered image with volume shading, emission, and direct light. Data Structures: Octree Leaf Node: volumes: A list of active volume objects. The source specifies a fixed size of 1024 objects, but notes this consumes excessive memory and suggests a dynamic pointer to a packed list as an alternative. mindensity: Minimum density value for the volumes in this leaf. maxdensity: Maximum density value for the volumes in this leaf. The mindensity and maxdensity values are used to bound the null scattering probability. Numbered Steps: 1. Build Octree: Construct an octree from the list of objects possessing volume geometry, using their volume bounding boxes. 2. Scene Traversal: During scene traversal, execute octree traversal after sceneintersect in integratorintersectclosest. 3. Volume Shading: In shadevolume, traverse the octree and evaluate all volume shaders in the current leaf node at once, without maintaining a volume stack. 4. Null Scattering: Compute min/max density values per leaf node to bound null scattering probability. Formulas: Null scattering probability is bounded by the actual volume density using the leaf node's mindensity and maxdensity values. Specific formulas are not provided in the sources. Parameters: Fixed list size for volumes per leaf node: 1024. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: A fixed list size of 1024 volume objects per leaf node consumes excessive memory. Null Scattering Efficiency: Computing min/max density over the entire domain yields a minimum of always 0, reducing null scattering efficiency. Computation should be done at the OpenVDB tile or leaf level instead. The method was implemented as a work-in-progress patch (D14656) for Blender's Cycles renderer to improve volume motion blur and delta/residual tracking. It was discussed by Kévin Dietrich and Sam Morse-Brown in April 2022. #92570 - Cycles: volume sampling improvements - blender - Blender Projects, https://projects.blender.org/blender/blender/issues/92570, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Octree Child Index Computation
body: Octree Child Index Computation determines the 0–7 octant offset (and thus the child index) of a specific child node relative to its parent, given the parent's current depth and the target destination coordinates. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping a 3D spatial query to a local child slot in a sparse voxel octree without performing expensive arbitrary bit shifts. Unlike Point Location, which finds the absolute leaf node containing a point, this method yields only the relative offset of a child within a specific parent node. It is distinct from Voxel Child Address Calculation by operating on precomputed depth masks rather than geometric bounds, and from Direction-dependent Morton Order Mapping by focusing on local indexing rather than global sorting. Inputs: destination: The 3D coordinate of the target point or ray end. depth: The current depth level of the parent node in the octree. maxdepth: The maximum depth of the octree. Outputs: childindex: An integer in the range [0, 7] representing the octant offset of the child containing the destination relative to the parent. Data Structures: childbitdepth: A precomputed array of integers where childbitdepth[d] = 1 << (maxdepth - d - 1) for each depth d. This array replaces arbitrary left-shifts with constant shifts. Steps: 1. Precompute Masks: Calculate childbitdepth[d] for all relevant depths d. 2. Compute Octant Offset: Determine the target child octant using binary & and integer inequality operations. 3. Mask and Shift: &-mask the precomputed value with the destination coordinates and bit-shift by constants corresponding to the X, Y, and Z components. 4. Return: Return the scalar value when encountering a leaf; either a scalar leaf in an interior node, or a voxel within a cap node. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computechildindex(destination, depth, maxdepth, childbitdepth): """ Computes the 0-7 octant offset of the child containing destination relative to the parent at the given depth. Args: destination: tuple (dx, dy, dz) - Target point coordinates depth: int - Current octree depth maxdepth: int - Maximum octree depth childbitdepth: list[int] - Precomputed array where childbitdepth[d] = 1 << (maxdepth - d - 1) Returns: int: Child index (0-7) """ # Step 1: Retrieve the precomputed mask for the current depth m = childbitdepth[depth] # Step 2 & 3: &-mask destination coordinates and bit-shift by constants # The shift amount corresponds to the bit position of the current subdivision level k = maxdepth - depth - 1 bitx = (destination[0] & m) >> k bity = (destination[1] & m) >> k bitz = (destination[2] & m) >> k # Step 4: Combine bits to form the 0-7 octant offset childindex = bitx | (bity << 1) | (bitz << 2) return childindex Parameters: maxdepth: Typically determined by the volume resolution and minimum voxel size. Not given in the sources. childbitdepth: Precomputed array. Size is maxdepth + 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The algorithm relies on integer coordinate representation and bitwise operations; floating-point coordinates must be quantized to the grid first. Boundaries: The method assumes a regular octree structure aligned to powers of two. Leaf Detection: The method itself only computes the offset; traversal logic must handle leaf termination and payload retrieval (scalar or voxel within a cap node). Point Location is an accelerated hashing scheme that maps a 3D integer coordinate to a specific leaf node in a canonical sparse voxel octree defined on the interval [0, 2^{d{max}}]. It solves the problem of finding the octree cell containing a given point without traversing parent pointers or performing expensive arbitrary bit shifts. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on Morton codes or spatial partitioning bounds, Point Location uses precomputed depth masks to determine the child octant index (0–7) directly from the destination coordinates using constant bitwise operations. It is distinct from Octree Child Index Computation in that it performs the full top-down traversal to the leaf, whereas the sibling method yields only the offset of a child relative to a current node. Fast Projection for Octree Nodes computes the projected center of an octree node from its parent's projected center using a simple 2D translation. It preprocesses eight constant 2D translation vectors for every octree level to quickly determine subdivisions, affected pixels, and recursively update occlusion maps (HOMs). The same translation approach is used to compute the depth component for fast depth cueing. Voxel Child Address Calculation determines the storage index of a child voxel within a parent's child array, given a query point and the parent's spatial bounds. It solves the problem of mapping a 3D geometric position to a specific slot in a potentially sparse or compacted child payload array. Unlike Point Location, which finds the leaf node containing a point, this method operates at the internal node level to identify which of the 8 octants contains the ray intersection or sample point. It differs from Ordered Child Traversal by focusing on the arithmetic mapping of coordinates to indices rather than the sequence of traversal. Direction-dependent Morton Order Mapping is a remapping function that converts a standard Octree Morton code into a sorting order aligned with the near-to-far rendering direction of a specific ray. It solves the problem that standard Morton codes provide a fixed spatial traversal order, which does not guarantee correct alpha blending (back-to-front) for arbitrary viewing angles. It sets itself apart from Ordered Child Traversal by operating on pre-computed global Morton codes via bitwise permutation rather than dynamic tree traversal, and from Voxel Child Address Calculation by focusing on global sorting keys rather than local child indexing. Ordered Child Traversal determines the visitation sequence of a node's eight children during ray traversal, ensuring they are processed in front-to-back order relative to the ray origin. It differs from Point Location by focusing on traversal order rather than spatial indexing, and from Fast Projection for Octree Nodes by explicitly handling the depth-sorting logic required for correct compositing. Octree Child Bounding Box Computation computes the AABB of a child node given its parent bounds and child index (0-7 for octree, 0-63 for wide). It uses Morton/Z-order bit packing for child indexing. The child index bit packing maps bit 0 to x, bit 1 to y, and bit 2 to z. This supports standard 8-way octree (indices 0-7) and extends to 4x4x4 wide nodes (indices 0-63) by reusing the same bit logic for the first 3 dimensions. The child min is computed as (highx ? mid.x: min.x, highy ? mid.y: min.y, highz ? mid.z: min.z) and child max as (highx ? max.x: mid.x, highy ? max.y: mid.y, highz ? max.z: mid.z), where mid = (min + max) 0.5 and high bits are extracted from childindex. Time Complexity: O(1) per node visit, assuming precomputed childbitdepth array. The operations involve constant-time bitwise shifts and comparisons. Performance: Precomputing childbitdepth avoids expensive arbitrary left-shifts, resulting in noticeably better performance on hardware where variable-shift instructions are costly. Strengths: Efficient, branch-minimal computation of child indices; suitable for GPU and CPU implementations. Limitations: Requires precomputation of depth masks. The method is described in the context of octree traversal and neighbor finding for sparse voxel volumes. It addresses the performance bottleneck of arbitrary bit shifts by using precomputed constants. Details are in Appendix B.1 of the source. name: Point Location
head: Coordinate-based hashing, Frisken and Perry hashing, Integer coordinate point location, Octree Hashing and Point Location, Octree Point Location, Point Location via Bitwise Masking
body:
Point Location is an accelerated hashing scheme that maps a 3D integer coordinate to a specific leaf node in a canonical sparse voxel octree defined on the interval [0, 2^{d{max}}]. It solves the problem of finding the octree cell containing a given point without traversing parent pointers or performing expensive arbitrary bit shifts. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on Morton codes or spatial partitioning bounds, Point Location uses precomputed depth masks to determine the child octant index (0–7) directly from the destination coordinates using constant bitwise operations. It is distinct from Octree Child Index Computation in that it performs the full top-down traversal to the leaf, whereas the sibling method yields only the offset of a child relative to a current node. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A destination coordinate vector dest (integer components x, y, z), the current depth (starting at 0 for root), and the current index (starting at 0 for root). The coordinates are constrained to the range [0, 2^{d{max}}]. Output: The scalar value stored in the leaf node containing the point, or the leaf node itself. Data Structures: The method relies on a global or context-specific OctreeData structure containing: 1. nodes: A 2D array nodes[depth][index] storing OctNode objects. 2. caps: An array of OctCap objects, used for leaf-level storage at the maximum depth. 3. childbitdepth: A precomputed 1D array where childbitdepth[d] = 1 << (maxdepth - d - 1). OctNode Layout: childscalars[8]: Scalar values for 8 potential scalar leaves. childstart: An unsigned integer base pointer/index to the children array. childoffset[8]: A signed char array. If childoffset[child] == -1, the child is a leaf (scalar or cap). Otherwise, it is an interior node, and the actual index is childstart + childoffset[child]. OctCap Layout: scalars[8]: Scalar values for the 8 voxels at the maximum depth. Algorithm Steps: 1. Precomputation: Calculate childbitdepth[d] = 1 << (maxdepth - d - 1) for all depths d \in [0, max\depth]. This avoids arbitrary left shifts during traversal. 2. Initialization: Set currentdepth = depth and currentindex = index. 3. Traversal Loop: Iterate indefinitely: a. Retrieve the current node: node = nodes[currentdepth][currentindex]. b. Retrieve the mask: childbit = childbitdepth[currentdepth]. c. Compute Child Octant: Determine the 0–7 octant index child by testing the bits of dest against childbit: child = ((dest.x \ \& \ child it) 
eq 0) \ll 2 \ | \ ((dest.y \ \& \ child it) 
eq 0) \ll 1 \ | \ ((dest.z \ \& \ child it) 
eq 0) This uses constant shifts (0, 1, 2) instead of arbitrary shifts. d. Check Leaf Status: i. If node.childoffset[child] == -1: If currentdepth == maxdepth - 2: The child is a cap node. Calculate the final cap index: capindex = node.childstart + node.childoffset[child]. Return caps[capindex].scalars[child]. Otherwise: The child is a scalar leaf. Return node.childscalars[child]. ii. If node.childoffset[child] != -1: The child is an interior node. Update currentindex = node.childstart + node.childoffset[child] and currentdepth++. Continue loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointlocate(destx, desty, destz, currentdepth, currentindex, maxdepth, nodes, caps, childbitdepth): """ Locates the leaf node containing the integer coordinate (destx, desty, destz). Returns the scalar value stored in that leaf. """ depth = currentdepth index = currentindex while True: # Retrieve current node node = nodes[depth][index] # Retrieve precomputed bit mask for current depth childbit = childbitdepth[depth] # Compute target child octant (0-7) using bitwise AND and constant shifts # (val & mask) != 0 evaluates to 1 if bit is set, 0 otherwise xbit = 1 if (destx & childbit) else 0 ybit = 1 if (desty & childbit) else 0 zbit = 1 if (destz & childbit) else 0 child = (xbit << 2) | (ybit << 1) | zbit # Check if child is a leaf if node.childoffset[child] == -1: # Leaf detected if depth == maxdepth - 2: # Cap node: calculate index into caps array capindex = node.childstart + node.childoffset[child] return caps[capindex].scalars[child] else: # Scalar leaf in interior node return node.childscalars[child] # Child is an interior node: traverse down index = node.childstart + node.childoffset[child] depth += 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate Range: Coordinates must be within [0, 2^{d{max}}]. Out-of-bounds coordinates may access invalid memory or return incorrect nodes. Cap Nodes: The octree typically uses "cap nodes" at depth max\depth - 2 to store 8 voxels directly, reducing pointer overhead. The algorithm must explicitly handle this depth level by switching from nodes to caps and using the lowest bit (& 1) for the final octant selection if the mask logic differs, though the standard mask childbit at max\depth - 2 is 1 << 1 = 2, which correctly isolates the second-to-last bit. However, sources specify that at max\depth - 2, the final child index uses dest & 1. This implies the cap nodes store the final 2 levels of resolution implicitly or the mask logic adapts. The pseudocode above reflects the source's explicit check for maxdepth - 2 and use of & 1 for the final octant calculation in caps. Parent Pointers: Parent pointers are omitted to save memory. Point location alone does not require them, but neighbor finding does. An algorithm to traverse and insert a voxel into an Octree using a pre-computed bitstream to determine child indices. It extracts the child index from the bitstream b using group(b, d, 3) at each depth d. If the child node is null, it creates a new empty node, then recursively inserts the voxel into the child with depth d-1. This variant is used for construction rather than lookup. A ray traversal strategy for the outer band that searches for the octree node containing the current point and computes step length by evaluating the corresponding polynomial. It uses variable error extension with a delta (\delta) of 0.02 to reduce octree memory size. Compared to standard Octree Traversal, it can start at any position on the ray inside the node, generally requiring fewer iterations on average but having a longer tail in iteration count distribution. Computes the cardinal identity (0-7) of an octant based on absolute voxel coordinates and octree depth levels. It calculates a shift amount d = dm - 1 - dc (where dm is max depth and dc is current depth) and extracts the bit at position d from the z, y, and x coordinates using unsigned right shift and bitwise AND. The result is combined into a 3-bit integer: ((zbit << 2) | (ybit << 1) | xbit). This is a direct calculation of the child index without traversal. Time Complexity: O(d{max}) per point location, as it traverses from root to leaf. Each step involves constant-time bitwise operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space for the traversal, excluding the octree storage itself. The childbitdepth array requires O(d{max}) space. Performance: The use of precomputed masks avoids expensive arbitrary left-shift instructions, providing noticeably better performance than naive bitwise shifting. Strengths: Fast lookup without parent pointers; efficient for sparse data due to octree structure; simple bitwise logic. Limitations: Requires integer coordinates; not suitable for floating-point points without prior quantization; cap node handling adds a branch. The method is based on the octree hashing scheme proposed by Frisken and Perry. They observed that octree locational codes could be represented directly by integer coordinates, allowing hashing from integer coordinates to the correct child node. The specific optimization of caching depth masks to avoid arbitrary shifts was introduced in the implementation of Interactive Isosurface Ray Tracing of Large Octree Volumes.
