name: Direction-dependent Morton Order Sorting
head: Direction-Dependent Morton Sorting, MortonSorter, Ray sign bit sorting, Sparse Voxel Rasterization Sorting
body: This method sorts sparse voxels into a near-to-far order for each image tile to ensure correct alpha blending during rasterization. It replaces the primitive z-depth used in Gaussian Splatting with a direction-dependent Morton order, ensuring the rendering order is correct for all ray directions by duplicating voxels for each ray sign bit pattern they cover. Unlike 3DGS, which uses z-depth, this approach uses precomputed Morton codes remapped by ray direction signs to guarantee topological correctness across the entire viewing sphere. Inputs: positions: Array of voxel coordinates (Float32, interleaved x,y,z). cameraPosition: Camera origin [x, y, z]. cameraTarget: Camera look-at point [x, y, z]. octlevels: Optional array of Octree levels per voxel (Uint8). octpaths: Optional array of Octree paths per voxel (Uint32). If absent, bounding box normalization is used. tileSize: Width/height of image tiles in pixels (e.g., 16). Outputs: sortedKeys: Array of 64-bit integers representing the sort key. sortedValues: Array of 32-bit integers representing voxel IDs and ray sign bits. Data Structures: The sort key is packed into 64 bits: Bits 0–15: Tile ID (16 bits). Bits 16–63: Direction-dependent Morton Order (48 bits, derived from L=16 Octree levels). The sort value is packed into 32 bits: Bits 0–2: Ray Sign Bits (3 bits). Bits 3–31: Voxel ID (29 bits). Parameters: L=16: Maximum Octree levels, determining the Morton code width (3L = 48 bits). Max Tiles: 2^{16} = 65,536 (supports 4096 \times 4096 resolution with 16 \times 16 tiles). Max Voxels: 2^{29} \approx 500 million. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Ray Direction and Sign Bits: Calculate the normalized ray direction vector \vec{d} from cameraPosition to cameraTarget. Determine the 3-bit raySignBits integer: \text{raySignBits} = 4 \cdot (\vec{d}x < 0) + 2 \cdot (\vec{d}y < 0) + 1 \cdot (\vec{d}z < 0) where (\cdot) evaluates to 1 if true, 0 if false. This results in an integer from 0 to 7. 2. Compute Base Morton Code: For each voxel, compute its base Morton code (M) based on its spatial position. If octpaths and octlevels are provided, convert the octpath to a Morton code by iterating level l from 0 to octlevel-1, extracting 3 bits from octpath at position 3 \cdot (\text{octlevel} - 1 - l), and accumulating: M = M \mid (\text{levelBits} \ll (3 \cdot l)). If octpaths are not provided, compute the bounding box of all voxels (minx, maxx, \dots). Normalize voxel coordinates to [0, 1] using ranges rangeX = \max(1, maxx - minx), etc.. Scale to [0, 2^B-1], spread bits, and interleave: M = (x' \ll 2) \mid (y' \ll 1) \mid z'. 3. Apply Direction-Dependent Permutation: Remap the base Morton code M into a direction-dependent order M' using the raySignBits. The Morton code consists of 3-bit chunks corresponding to Octree levels. For each 3-bit chunk c in M, apply a permutation table lookup: M' = \sum{i=0}^{L-1} \text{Table}[\text{raySignBits}][ci] \ll (3 \cdot i) The permutation tables are hard-coded 8x8 arrays that reorder the 3-bit indices (0-7) to ensure near-to-far order for the specific ray direction quadrant. 4. Duplicate Voxels: Each voxel is duplicated for every distinct raySignBits pattern (0-7) that its spatial extent covers. In practice, this often means duplicating the voxel 8 times, once for each possible ray direction sign combination, attaching the specific raySignBits to each copy. 5. Assign Tile IDs: For each duplicated voxel instance, determine which image tiles it overlaps and assign the Tile ID to the key. 6. Sort: Perform a GPU Radix Sort (or similar stable sort) on the list of key-value pairs. The primary sort key is the Tile ID (MSB), followed by the Direction-dependent Morton Order (LSB). This groups voxels by tile and orders them near-to-far within each tile. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. ORDERTABLES = [ [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], [1, 0, 3, 2, 5, 4, 7, 6], [2, 3, 0, 1, 6, 7, 4, 5], [3, 2, 1, 0, 7, 6, 5, 4], [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2, 3], [5, 4, 7, 6, 1, 0, 3, 2], [6, 7, 4, 5, 2, 3, 0, 1], [7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0] ] MAXNUMLEVELS = 16 def computeraysignbits(raydirection): """Compute 3-bit sign mask from normalized ray direction. Bit 2: x < 0, Bit 1: y < 0, Bit 0: z < 0""" signbits = 0 if raydirection[0] < 0: signbits |= 4 if raydirection[1] < 0: signbits |= 2 if raydirection[2] < 0: signbits |= 1 return signbits def applydirectionpermutation(mortoncode, signbits): """Remap Morton code chunks based on ray direction signs.""" table = ORDERTABLES[signbits] permutedorder = 0 currentcode = mortoncode for i in range(MAXNUMLEVELS): chunk = currentcode & 0b111 permutedorder |= table[chunk] << (3 i) currentcode >>= 3 return permutedorder def computemortonfromoctpath(octpath, octlevel): """Convert octpath to Morton code if precomputed path is available.""" morton = 0 for level in range(octlevel): shift = 3 (octlevel - 1 - level) chunk = (octpath >> shift) & 0b111 morton |= chunk << (3 level) return morton def spreadbits(n): """Spread bits of n into every other bit position.""" n = (n ^ (n << 16)) & 0x0000FFFF0000FFFF n = (n ^ (n << 8)) & 0x00FF00FF00FF00FF n = (n ^ (n << 4)) & 0x0F0F0F0F0F0F0F0F n = (n ^ (n << 2)) & 0x3333333333333333 n = (n ^ (n << 1)) & 0x5555555555555555 return n def computemortonfromcoords(x, y, z, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz): """Compute Morton code from normalized coordinates.""" rangex = max(1, maxx - minx) rangey = max(1, maxy - miny) rangez = max(1, maxz - minz) xnorm = (x - minx) / rangex ynorm = (y - miny) / rangey znorm = (z - minz) / rangez bits = 16 scale = (1 << bits) - 1 ix = int(xnorm scale) iy = int(ynorm scale) iz = int(znorm scale) mx = spreadbits(ix) my = spreadbits(iy) mz = spreadbits(iz) return (mx << 2) | (my << 1) | mz def sortvoxels(voxels, camerapos, cameratarget, tilesize, octpaths, octlevels): """Main sorting routine.""" raydir = normalize(cameratarget - camerapos) # Standard vector normalization raysignbits = computeraysignbits(raydir) sorteditems = [] useoctpath = octpaths is not None and octlevels is not None if not useoctpath: minx = min(v.x for v in voxels) maxx = max(v.x for v in voxels) miny = min(v.y for v in voxels) maxy = max(v.y for v in voxels) minz = min(v.z for v in voxels) maxz = max(v.z for v in voxels) for voxel in voxels: if useoctpath: basemorton = computemortonfromoctpath(voxel.octpath, voxel.octlevel) else: basemorton = computemortonfromcoords(voxel.x, voxel.y, voxel.z, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) for s in range(8): permutedmorton = applydirectionpermutation(basemorton, s) # Tile ID assignment depends on camera projection and voxel overlap; not detailed in sources. tileid = 0 key = (tileid << 48) | permutedmorton value = (s << 29) | voxel.id sorteditems.append((key, value)) sorteditems.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return sorteditems Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Voxel ID Indexing: The voxel ID in the value field refers to the 1D array index where the voxel is stored, not the grid (i, j, k) index. Bit Packing: The bit field arrangement is designed to squeeze the 16-bit tile ID, 48-bit Morton order, 3-bit ray sign bits, and 29-bit voxel ID into 64-bit and 32-bit unsigned integers for implementation convenience. Degenerate Input: If max - min is zero, the normalization range defaults to 1 using rangeX = max(1, maxX - minX) to avoid division by zero. Non-Functional Code Warning: Some online implementations (e.g., WebGL ports) are noted as non-functional or AI-generated approximations and do not strictly follow the paper's logic. Time Complexity: Sorting complexity depends on the number of duplicated voxels. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the sorted key-value pairs, with each entry using 64 bits for the key and 32 bits for the value. Strengths: Guarantees correct alpha blending for all viewing directions and avoids popping artifacts associated with z-depth sorting in complex geometries. Limitations: Increases memory and compute overhead due to voxel duplication (up to 8x). This method was introduced in the context of Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster) as an alternative to 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the limitation of z-depth sorting, which can fail to maintain correct occlusion order for non-convex or complex voxel structures depending on the view direction. By using direction-dependent Morton orders, it ensures topological correctness for alpha blending in real-time rendering. name: Ordered Child Traversal
head: Sparse Ray-Octree Intersection (SUBDIVIDE)
body: Ordered Child Traversal determines the visitation sequence of a node's eight children during ray traversal, ensuring they are processed in front-to-back order relative to the ray origin. It differs from Point Location by focusing on traversal order rather than spatial indexing, and from Fast Projection for Octree Nodes by explicitly handling the depth-sorting logic required for correct compositing. Inputs: Ray Ri (origin O, direction D); Current voxel/node V (center C, half-extent h). Outputs: An ordered list of child indices (0-7) to be visited. Data Structures: ORDEREDCHILDREN: A precomputed 8 \times 8 lookup table that maps the octant containing the ray origin (0-7) to a permutation of the 8 child indices (0-7) sorted by their distance from the ray origin along the ray direction. Steps: 1. Determine which of the 8 octants the ray origin O lies in relative to the current node center C. 2. Retrieve the child visitation order from the precomputed table: order = ORDEREDCHILDREN[o]. 3. Iterate through order. For each child index c: compute the child's bounding box, perform ray-box intersection test, and if intersected, push child to the next traversal list. Formulas: The octant o is determined by the signs of the vector O - C: o = 4 \cdot \text{sign}(Ox - Cx) + 2 \cdot \text{sign}(Oy - Cy) + 1 \cdot \text{sign}(Oz - Cz) where \text{sign}(v) = 1 if v \ge 0 else 0. Parameters: ORDEREDCHILDREN: Static constant table. Typical values depend on the coordinate system (e.g., Y-up vs Z-up). Edge Cases: Ray Origin Inside Node: If the ray origin is exactly on a face or edge, the octant determination must be robust. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. ORDEREDCHILDRENTABLE = [ [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], # octant 0 (X-, Y-, Z-) [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2, 3], # octant 1 (X+, Y-, Z-) [2, 3, 0, 1, 6, 7, 4, 5], # octant 2 (X-, Y+, Z-) [6, 7, 4, 5, 2, 3, 0, 1], # octant 3 (X+, Y+, Z-) [1, 0, 3, 2, 5, 4, 7, 6], # octant 4 (X-, Y-, Z+) [5, 4, 7, 6, 1, 0, 3, 2], # octant 5 (X+, Y-, Z+) [3, 2, 1, 0, 7, 6, 5, 4], # octant 6 (X-, Y+, Z+) [7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0], # octant 7 (X+, Y+, Z+) ] def getorderedchildren(rayorigin, nodecenter): """ Returns a list of child indices (0-7) ordered front-to-back. """ # 1. Determine octant of ray origin relative to node center sx = 1 if (rayorigin.x - nodecenter.x) >= 0 else 0 sy = 1 if (rayorigin.y - nodecenter.y) >= 0 else 0 sz = 1 if (rayorigin.z - nodecenter.z) >= 0 else 0 # Octant index (X is MSB, Z is LSB) octant = (sx << 2) | (sy << 1) | sz # 2. Lookup precomputed order table childorder = ORDEREDCHILDRENTABLE[octant] return childorder A function that computes a bitmask of children intersected by a ray, handling edge cases near axis planes. It calculates slab radius and t{min}/t{max} for the current node, checks if the root hit is valid (t{min} < t{max}), and identifies the first child using the midpoint of t{min}/t{max} to avoid precision issues. It checks intersections with X, Y, Z planes within the t range, sets bits in masks A-F based on epsilon comparisons with center coordinates, and combines masks using AND operations. Parameter: epsilon (typically 10^{-4}) for robustness. A view-dependent step that computes a visibility-sorted index array referencing occupancy geometry in front-to-back order, required for correct rasterization. It traverses the occupancy histogram tree in depth-first order, visiting children in front-to-back visibility order determined by the octant containing the viewpoint (perspective) or view direction (orthogonal). Each non-leaf node index is emitted twice: before visiting children (front face) and after (back face). Leaf node indices are emitted twice back-to-back (front then back). Time Complexity: O(1) per node, as it involves a constant-time octant lookup and a fixed-size table access. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory for the lookup table (64 integers). Strengths: Ensures correct alpha blending without post-sorting; efficient lookup. Limitations: Requires precomputation of the table; order depends on ray direction and node position. When to use: Always when front-to-back traversal is required for compositing or rasterization. The concept of ordered child traversal is fundamental to hierarchical volume rendering. The term "SUBDIVIDE" and the specific iterator ORDEREDCHILDREN are used in the Neural Geometric Level of Detail (NGLOD) paper. The visibility-ordering for rasterization is detailed in the SparseLeap paper. name: Direct Access Offset Calculation
head: InternalNode offset calculation, LeafNode offset calculation, VDB Direct Access Offset Calculation
body: Direct Access Offset Calculation computes the index of a child node within a parent node's data structure based on global 3D grid coordinates (x, y, z). It solves the problem of mapping spatial positions to hierarchical tree indices without using division, multiplication, or modulus operations, which are computationally expensive. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Point Location by relying on compile-time constant block sizes to perform bitwise arithmetic, and from Voxel Child Address Calculation by specifically targeting the sparse VDB internal node and leaf node structures. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Global grid coordinates (x, y, z); compile-time constants sLog2X, sLog2Y, sLog2Z representing the base-2 logarithm of the child block dimensions in X, Y, and Z; Log2Y and Log2Z (derived constants); mChildMask (bitmask of existing children); mInternalDAT (data array for internal nodes). Outputs: An unsigned integer offset into the child data structure; for InternalNodes, a boolean indicating if the location is a tile (constant value) or a child node. Data Structures: mChildMask: A bitmask where each bit corresponds to a potential child octant. If the bit is 0, the child is a tile; if 1, it is a sub-node. mInternalDAT: An array storing tile values or child node pointers/indices, indexed by the calculated offset. Formulas: The offset is calculated using bitwise operations to extract the relative position within the child block and pack it into a Morton-like index. For an InternalNode, the offset is: \text{internalOffset} = \left( \left( (x \ \& \ ((1 \ll \text{sLog2X}) - 1)) \gg \text{Child::sLog2X} \right) \ll \text{Log2YZ} \right) + \left( \left( (y \ \& \ ((1 \ll \text{sLog2Y}) - 1)) \gg \text{Child::sLog2Y} \right) \ll \text{Log2Z} \right) + \left( (z \ \& \ ((1 \ll \text{sLog2Z}) - 1)) \gg \text{Child::sLog2Z} \right) Where \text{Log2YZ} = \text{Log2Y} + \text{Log2Z}. For a LeafNode, the offset is: \text{leafOffset} = \left( (x \ \& \ ((1 \ll \text{sLog2X}) - 1)) \ll (\text{Log2Y} + \text{Log2Z}) \right) + \left( (y \ \& \ ((1 \ll \text{sLog2Y}) - 1)) \ll \text{Log2Z} \right) + (z \ \& \ ((1 \ll \text{sLog2Z}) - 1)) Steps: 1. Compute Internal Offset: Calculate internalOffset using the formula above. This involves masking the coordinates to the block size, shifting to align bits, and summing them. 2. Check Child Mask: Check if the bit at index internalOffset in mChildMask is 0. 3. Handle Tile: If the bit is 0, the coordinate (x, y, z) lies within a constant tile. Return the tile value from mInternalDAT at index internalOffset and terminate traversal. 4. Handle Child Node: If the bit is 1, extract the child node from mInternalDAT at index internalOffset and continue traversal recursively or iteratively. 5. Compute Leaf Offset (if LeafNode reached): If a LeafNode is reached, calculate leafOffset using the LeafNode formula to index directly into the leaf's data array. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateinternaloffset(x, y, z, sLog2X, sLog2Y, sLog2Z, Log2Y, Log2Z): # Calculate block-local coordinates # Masking: (1 << sLog2N) - 1 creates a mask of sLog2N ones xlocal = x & ((1 << sLog2X) - 1) ylocal = y & ((1 << sLog2Y) - 1) zlocal = z & ((1 << sLog2Z) - 1) # Shift to align bits for Morton-like packing # Note: Child::sLog2X is typically 1 for standard octrees, but generalized here xidx = xlocal >> sLog2X yidx = ylocal >> sLog2Y zidx = zlocal >> sLog2Z # Combine indices Log2YZ = Log2Y + Log2Z offset = (xidx << Log2YZ) + (yidx << Log2Z) + zidx return offset def calculateleafoffset(x, y, z, sLog2X, sLog2Y, sLog2Z, Log2Y, Log2Z): # Calculate block-local coordinates xlocal = x & ((1 << sLog2X) - 1) ylocal = y & ((1 << sLog2Y) - 1) zlocal = z & ((1 << sLog2Z) - 1) # Pack into offset # Note: The source formula uses left shifts for leaf offset, implying # x, y, z are treated as indices within the leaf block directly offset = (xlocal << (Log2Y + Log2Z)) + (ylocal << Log2Z) + zlocal return offset def traverseinternalnode(x, y, z, mChildMask, mInternalDAT, sLog2X, sLog2Y, sLog2Z, Log2Y, Log2Z): offset = calculateinternaloffset(x, y, z, sLog2X, sLog2Y, sLog2Z, Log2Y, Log2Z) # Check if child exists (bit is 1) or is a tile (bit is 0) if not (mChildMask & (1 << offset)): # Tile value return mInternalDAT[offset] else: # Child node exists, continue traversal childnode = mInternalDAT[offset] # Implementation detail: The specific method to pass coordinates # to the child node (e.g., subtracting base coordinates) is not # detailed in the source, but standard octree traversal requires # adjusting x, y, z relative to the child's origin. return traverse(childnode, x, y, z) Parameters: sLog2X, sLog2Y, sLog2Z: Compile-time constants. Typical values depend on the VDB configuration, often corresponding to the log2 of the number of voxels per child block dimension. Log2Y, Log2Z: Derived constants used for bit shifting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Coordinates: Bit-wise AND is well-defined for signed integers in two's complement representation, allowing these operations to work correctly for negative (x, y, z). However, bit-wise shifts must be performed on unsigned integers to ensure defined behavior. Compile-Time Constants: The efficiency relies on sLog2X, sLog2Y, sLog2Z being known at compile time, allowing the compiler to optimize shifts and masks. Time Complexity: InternalNode offset calculation reduces to three bitwise ANDs, five bit shifts, and two additions. LeafNode offset calculation reduces to three bitwise ANDs, two left shifts, and two additions. This is O(1) with very low constant factors. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Extremely fast, avoiding expensive division/multiplication/modulus operations. Works for negative coordinates. Deterministic performance. Limitations: Requires compile-time knowledge of block sizes. Only applicable to regular hierarchical structures like VDB octrees. When to use: When traversing sparse voxel grids with known, fixed block sizes at compile time, such as in VDB-based rendering or simulation. When not to use: For dynamic structures where block sizes are not known at compile time, or for non-hierarchical data structures. Direct Access Offset Calculation was introduced in the VDB (Voxel Database) system by Ken Museth et al.. It is part of the VDB architecture designed for high-resolution sparse volumes with dynamic topology. The method leverages the height-balanced nature of VDB octrees, where the tree depth and branching factors are fixed at runtime, allowing for level-independent, non-recursive lookup logic. name: Octree Neighbor Finding
head: GetNeighbors, Neighbor Retrieval, forward neighbor retrieval
body: Octree Neighbor Finding determines the adjacent leaf nodes in six cardinal directions (±X, ±Y, ±Z) for a given node in a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO). It solves the problem of traversing between non-contiguous or differently-sized nodes during ray casting or pathfinding by locating the nearest shared ancestor and performing point location to retrieve the neighbor. Inputs: currentnode: The index of the starting leaf node. direction: A vector specifying the target direction (e.g., +X, -Y). parenttrace: An array containing the indices of all parent nodes from the root to currentnode, provided by the ray traversal algorithm. depth: The depth level of currentnode. Outputs: neighborindex: The index of the adjacent leaf node, or a sentinel value (INDEXNONE) if no neighbor exists in that direction. Data Structures: Node Struct: Contains depth (7 bits), isleaf (1 bit), position (3 floats), and size (1 float). Parent Trace Array: trace[] stores the indices of parent nodes for the current ray cap, allowing upward traversal without storing explicit parent pointers in the node structure. Algorithm Steps: 1. Validation: Verify currentnode is a leaf. If not, return immediately. 2. Target Position Calculation: Compute the position just outside the current node in the specified direction by moving slightly farther than HalfSize. 3. Upward Traversal (Find Common Ancestor): Iterate up the tree using parenttrace from the origin node's parent depth down to 0. At each level, check if the target position falls within the spatial bounds of the parent node using &-masking of the origin and destination coordinates with the corresponding depth bit, followed by integer equality. 4. Point Location: Once the common ancestor is found, perform a standard point-location search from the common ancestor to the targetpos to find the leaf at the destination. 5. Neighbor Collection: If the search lands on a leaf node, return it. If the search lands on an internal node, the neighbor is one of its children. To find the specific child adjacent to the current node, use AxisMask and AxisBit to filter by the target axis and collect the four face children. Limit the search depth to the current node's depth to ensure only adjacent leaves of equal or larger size are collected, avoiding all descendants. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. INDEXNONE = -1 def getneighbor(originidx, direction, parenttrace, nodedata, maxdepth): # 1. Validation: Verify currentnode is a leaf if not (nodedata[originidx] & 0x80): return INDEXNONE originpos = nodedata[originidx].position originsize = nodedata[originidx].size origindepth = nodedata[originidx].depth # 2. Target position: move slightly farther than HalfSize in direction targetpos = originpos + direction (originsize 0.5 + 1e-6) # 3. Upward Traversal: Find common ancestor # Begin at the depth of the origin node's parent commonancestoridx = parenttrace[origindepth - 1] if origindepth > 0 else 0 for d in range(origindepth - 1, -1, -1): depthbit = 1 << (maxdepth - d) if ((targetpos.x & depthbit) == (originpos.x & depthbit)) and \ ((targetpos.y & depthbit) == (originpos.y & depthbit)) and \ ((targetpos.z & depthbit) == (originpos.z & depthbit)): commonancestoridx = parenttrace[d] break # 4. Point Location: Find leaf at destination from common ancestor neighboridx = commonancestoridx startdepth = nodedata[commonancestoridx].depth for d in range(maxdepth - startdepth, -1, -1): shift = d childidx = ((targetpos.x >> shift) & 1) | \ (((targetpos.y >> shift) & 1) << 1) | \ (((targetpos.z >> shift) & 1) << 2) neighboridx = nodedata[neighboridx].children[childidx] if neighboridx == INDEXNONE or (nodedata[neighboridx] & 0x80): break # 5. Neighbor Collection: Handle results if neighboridx != INDEXNONE and (nodedata[neighboridx] & 0x80): # Neighbor is internal. Compute 4 face child indices using AxisMask and AxisBit axismask = 0 if direction.x != 0: axismask = 1 elif direction.y != 0: axismask = 2 else: axismask = 4 # AxisBit: returns AxisMask if Side is -1, returns 0 if Side is +1 side = -1 if (direction.x < 0 or direction.y < 0 or direction.z < 0) else 1 axisbit = axismask if side == -1 else 0 # Filter children on the specific directional face facechildren = [] for c in range(8): if (c & axisbit) == axisbit: facechildren.append(c) # Traverse down to leaf level, collecting only adjacent leaves for c in facechildren: childidx = nodedata[neighboridx].children[c] if childidx == INDEXNONE: continue if nodedata[childidx] & 0x80: return childidx neighboridx = childidx return neighboridx Parameters: AxisMask: Bit mask for axis direction. X returns 001, Y returns 010, Z returns 100. AxisBit: Returns AxisMask if Side is -1, returns 0 if Side is +1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Leaf Input: The algorithm must validate that the input node is a leaf; otherwise, it returns immediately. Depth Limiting: The search must stop at a leaf or when the depth matches the current node's depth to avoid collecting all descendants of a neighbor. Memory Footprint: Parent pointers are omitted from nodes to save memory; the parenttrace array must be maintained by the caller (ray traversal). Optimization: Use static polymorphism via templates for each X, Y, Z dimension to perform only one or two equality tests per iteration. Determines the next cell in a hierarchical spatial structure by backtracing from a start coordinate to the common ancestor with a destination coordinate, then performing point location. It differs from Morton Key Vertex Neighbor Iteration by relying on explicit parent-pointer traversal and coordinate bit-masking rather than Morton key arithmetic. Identifies and processes the eight corner vertices of leaf nodes in a sparse voxel octree by leveraging the spatial locality of Morton (Z-order) keys. It solves the dual-grid traversal problem by operating on a pre-computed or iterated list of vertex keys, using bitwise arithmetic to resolve adjacency and handle level mismatches without tree traversal recursion. Time Complexity: O(D) where D is the depth of the octree, due to the upward traversal and subsequent point location. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per neighbor query, assuming the parenttrace array is provided by the traversal context. Strengths: Efficient for sparse structures where explicit parent pointers are too costly; works with arbitrary node sizes. Limitations: Requires the parenttrace array to be maintained by the caller. When to Use: When memory footprint is critical (no parent pointers in nodes) or when traversing non-contiguous nodes in an SVO. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. The authors rejected Frisken and Perry's exclusive "or" method for immediate neighbors because it was no cheaper than &-masking both source and destination and performing integer equality on the results. To minimize memory footprint, parent pointers were omitted from octree nodes, requiring the ray traversal algorithm to fill an index trace array containing the indices of all parent nodes for a given cap. name: Neighbor Finding
head: Octree Hashing (Neighbor-Finding)
body: Neighbor finding locates the octree node containing a destination coordinate relative to a start coordinate by backtracing up the hierarchy to a common ancestor and performing point location. It differs from sibling methods like Morton Key Vertex Neighbor Iteration by relying on explicit coordinate masking and a parent trace array rather than arithmetic on Morton keys. Inputs: start: The 3D integer coordinates of the origin node. dest: The 3D integer coordinates of the desired neighbor. depth: The integer depth of the start node in the octree. parenttrace[]: An array storing pointers to nodes, allowing the tree to use 1-way pointers and minimizing memory footprint. childbitdepth[]: An array where childbitdepth[up] contains the bitmask for the child index at depth up. Outputs: The index or pointer to the node containing dest. Data Structures: childbitdepth[]: Implementation-specific array of bitmasks. parenttrace[]: Array of node pointers indexed by depth. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate from the current depth down to 0: for up = depth down to 0. 2. Retrieve the child bit mask for the current level: childbit = childbitdepth[up]. 3. Check if start and dest share the same bits at this depth level for all three dimensions. This is done by masking both coordinates with the corresponding depth bit and performing integer equality. Condition: (dest.x & childbit) == (start.x & childbit) AND (dest.y & childbit) == (start.y & childbit) AND (dest.z & childbit) == (start.z & childbit). 4. If the condition is true, a common parent is found at this level. Call pointlocate(dest, up, parenttrace[up]) to retrieve the leaf at dest starting from that parent. Return the result. 5. If the loop completes without returning, check the root level match using the same masking logic with childbit from the final iteration (up=0). 6. If the root check passes, call pointlocate(dest, 0, 0) to find the leaf at the root level. 7. If no match is found, return 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neighborfind(start: Vec3i, dest: Vec3i, depth: int, parenttrace: List[int], childbitdepth: List[int]) -> int: """ Finds the node containing dest starting from start by backtracing to a common ancestor. """ # Iterate from current depth down to 0 for up in range(depth, -1, -1): childbit = childbitdepth[up] # Check if start and dest share the same bits at this depth if ((dest.x & childbit) == (start.x & childbit) and (dest.y & childbit) == (start.y & childbit) and (dest.z & childbit) == (start.z & childbit)): # Common parent found; perform point location from this parent return pointlocate(dest, up, parenttrace[up]) # Root node check (if loop completes without returning) childbit = childbitdepth[0] if ((dest.x & childbit) == (start.x & childbit) and (dest.y & childbit) == (start.y & childbit) and (dest.z & childbit) == (start.z & childbit)): return pointlocate(dest, 0, 0) return 0 def pointlocate(dest: Vec3i, startdepth: int, startnode: Node) -> int: """ Standard downward traversal from startnode to find the leaf at dest. """ node = startnode for d in range(startdepth, -1, -1): childidx = ((dest.x >> d) & 1) << 2 | ((dest.y >> d) & 1) << 1 | ((dest.z >> d) & 1) if node.children[childidx] is None: return 0 node = node.children[childidx] return node.index Parameters: childbitdepth: Implementation-specific bitmask array. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parent Pointers: Explicit parent pointers are omitted from node structures to minimize memory footprint. Parent indices are provided by the ray traversal algorithm filling the parenttrace[] array. Root Handling: The algorithm explicitly handles the case where the common ancestor is the root node. Optimization: Static polymorphism via templates can be used for X, Y, Z dimensions to reduce equality tests to one or two per iteration for neighbors along designated axes. Uses a rational t-value approach to locate the exit point directly, bypassing explicit direction vector calculation. Omits explicit parent pointers, using an index trace[] array and bitwise AND masking with integer equality checks to identify common parents. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the depth of the octree, O(D), where D is the maximum depth. Memory Complexity: O(D) for the parenttrace array, which is reused during traversal. Strengths: Minimizes memory footprint by avoiding explicit parent pointers in node structures. Simple to implement using coordinate masking. Limitations: Requires a valid parenttrace array populated by a prior traversal step. Performance depends on the depth of the common ancestor. When to use: Used during sparse octree ray traversal when a neighbor node is required. Originated in the context of interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. The method was developed to optimize ray traversal by efficiently finding neighboring cells without storing redundant parent pointers. It builds on earlier work by Frisken and Perry, who required foreknowledge of neighbor direction (left/right) on midplanes. This implementation omits that distinction, simplifying the logic by using coordinate masking. name: Wyvill and Kunii's Ray Tracing / Neighbor Finding Algorithm
head: Rational t-value Neighbor Finding, Wyvill-Kunii Neighbor Finding
body: Wyvill and Kunii's algorithm is a ray-tracing method for hierarchical spatial structures (quadtrees and octrees) that determines the next intersected cell by calculating a point guaranteed to lie inside it, rather than computing a direction vector. It sets itself apart from its parent Neighbor Finding by using a spatial search procedure (similar to FIND3DBLOCK) to locate the calculated point, and from Octree Neighbor Finding without Parent Pointers by avoiding the explicit neighbor pointer traversal in favor of geometric point location. The algorithm computes the coordinates of a point (POINT) that is purportedly guaranteed to be in the next cell intersected by the ray, and then locates this point using a spatial search procedure similar to FIND3DBLOCK. It does not compute a direction vector. Inputs: Ray parameters defining the exit from the current cell. Geometric parameters: CORNER[I], WB[I], M[I], B[I] for each coordinate I \in \{X, Y, Z\}. Sign indicators: SIGNM[I] for each coordinate I \in \{X, Y, Z\}. Outputs: POINT: A 3D coordinate vector guaranteed to lie in the next cell. Data Structures: T: A rational array of size 3 (for X, Y, Z). Each element stores a numerator and a denominator. POINT: A 3D vector. axis: Variables I and K to track coordinate indices. Formulas: 1. Rational t-value Numerator: NUM(T[I]) = CORNER[I] - SIGN\M[I] \cdot W\B[I] - SIGN\M[I] 2. Rational t-value Denominator: DEN(T[I]) = M[I] 3. Point Coordinate: POINT[I] = M[I] \cdot \frac{NUM(T[K])}{DEN(T[K])} + B[I] Where K is the coordinate index corresponding to the minimum t-value. Parameters: CORNER[I], WB[I], M[I], B[I]: Geometric parameters used in rational t-value and point coordinate calculations. Exact definitions are not provided in the sources. SIGNM[I]: Sign indicators, typically 0 or 1, representing the direction of motion along axis I. Steps: 1. Initialize a rational array T for coordinates X, Y, Z. 2. For each coordinate I \in \{X, Y, Z\}: a. Compute NUM(T[I]) = CORNER[I] - SIGN\M[I] \cdot W\B[I] - SIGN\M[I]. b. Compute DEN(T[I]) = M[I]. 3. Initialize K = X. 4. For each coordinate I \in \{Y, Z\}: a. If |NUM(T[K]) \cdot DEN(T[I])| > |NUM(T[I]) \cdot DEN(T[K])|, then set K = I. b. This comparison identifies the coordinate K corresponding to the minimum t-value without division. 5. For each coordinate I \in \{X, Y, Z\}: a. Compute POINT[I] = M[I] \cdot \frac{NUM(T[K])}{DEN(T[K])} + B[I]. 6. Locate the computed POINT using a spatial search procedure similar to FIND3DBLOCK to identify the next cell in the hierarchy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def wyvillkuniinextcell(CORNER, WB, M, B, SIGNM): """ Computes the next cell point using Wyvill and Kunii's rational t-value method. Args: CORNER: Array of 3 floats [cx, cy, cz] WB: Array of 3 floats [wx, wy, wz] M: Array of 3 floats [mx, my, mz] B: Array of 3 floats [bx, by, bz] SIGNM: Array of 3 integers [sx, sy, sz] (0 or 1) Returns: POINT: Array of 3 floats [px, py, pz] """ # Step 1 & 2: Initialize rational t-values NUM = [0.0] 3 DEN = [0.0] 3 for i in range(3): # NUM(T[I]) = CORNER[I] - SIGNM[I] WB[I] - SIGNM[I] NUM[i] = CORNER[i] - SIGNM[i] WB[i] - SIGNM[i] # DEN(T[I]) = M[I] DEN[i] = M[i] # Step 3 & 4: Find coordinate K with minimum t-value # K corresponds to the index with the smallest NUM/DEN ratio. # We compare cross-products to avoid division: |NUM[K]DEN[I]| > |NUM[I]DEN[K]| K = 0 # Initialize K to X (index 0) for i in [1, 2]: # Iterate over Y (1) and Z (2) # abs(NUM[T[K]] DEN[T[I]]) > abs(NUM[T[I]] DEN[T[K]]) lhs = abs(NUM[K] DEN[i]) rhs = abs(NUM[i] DEN[K]) if lhs > rhs: K = i # Step 5: Compute POINT coordinates POINT = [0.0] 3 for i in range(3): # POINT[I] = M[I] (NUM(T[K]) / DEN(T[K])) + B[I] # Note: Division by zero in DEN[K] is a potential pitfall if M[K] is 0. # The sources do not specify handling for M[K]=0. tval = NUM[K] / DEN[K] POINT[i] = M[i] tval + B[i] return POINT Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Corner Passing: If a ray passes through a cell corner (e.g., SW corner of cell 5 to cell 11), applying FIND2DBLOCK to (ax-1, ay) may report a false object intersection when cell 4 is fully occupied, whereas (ax, ay-1) avoids it. Subdivision Errors: When a cell is subdivided (e.g., cell 3 subdivided like the SE quadrant of a quadtree), the algorithm may compute POINT = (12, 16) instead of the correct (12, 15), causing FIND2DBLOCK to route to the wrong cell (e.g., cell 10 instead of cell 3). Sign Subtraction Fix: Removing the subtraction of SIGNM[I] from the numerator of t for coordinate I does not always fix the error. Decomposing motion (e.g., SW into S and W) can still cause false intersections due to distinct entry/exit conventions. Simultaneous Boundaries: Wyvill and Kunii claim that exact direction computation is unnecessary and that arbitrarily picking a boundary perpendicular to motion when multiple boundaries are reached simultaneously is sufficient. This claim is shown to be incorrect for certain subdivisions. Neighbour List Octree Traversal is a ray-tracing method for sparse voxel octrees that determines the next intersected cell by consulting precomputed lists of adjacent cells, rather than performing geometric intersection tests or restarting a search from the root. It sets itself apart from the parent Wyvill and Kunii's Ray Tracing / Neighbor Finding Algorithm by replacing the calculation of a guaranteed interior point with a direct lookup of potential neighbours, and from the Top-down Method by avoiding the O(depth) traversal cost for every cell crossing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The algorithm involves a constant number of arithmetic operations per step plus the cost of the spatial search procedure (FIND3DBLOCK), which depends on the octree depth and structure. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The algorithm requires storage for the rational array T and the POINT vector. Strengths: The algorithm is simpler in structure than methods that compute exact direction vectors, as it relies on point location. Limitations: The algorithm is prone to errors in specific subdivision cases (e.g., SE quadrant subdivision) and when rays pass through cell corners, leading to false intersections or wrong cell transitions. The claim that exact direction computation is unnecessary is incorrect for certain cases. When to use: Suitable for hierarchical spatial structures where point location is efficient and the specific subdivision patterns do not trigger the known pitfalls. When not to use: When high precision is required in complex subdivision scenarios or when rays frequently pass through cell corners or edges, as the algorithm may produce incorrect results. The algorithm was proposed by Wyvill and Kunii. It is described in the context of implementing ray tracing with octrees and neighbor finding. The algorithm is noted to be shorter than the author's own RAYTRACER algorithm but has a similar structure, adhering to different conventions. name: Neighbour List Octree Traversal
head: Neighbour List Traversal, Neighbour list search, Neighbour-based traversal, Samet method
body: Neighbour List Octree Traversal is a ray-tracing method for sparse voxel octrees that determines the next intersected cell by consulting precomputed lists of adjacent cells, rather than performing geometric intersection tests or restarting a search from the root. It sets itself apart from the parent Wyvill and Kunii's Ray Tracing / Neighbor Finding Algorithm by replacing the calculation of a guaranteed interior point with a direct lookup of potential neighbours, and from the Top-down Method by avoiding the O(depth) traversal cost for every cell crossing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree structure where each node has associated neighbour lists; the current cell index; the exit face (wall) of the current cell through which the ray exits. Output: The index of the next cell entered by the ray. Data Structures: Each cell in the octree stores six pointer lists, one for each of the six faces (walls) of the cubic cell. Structure: Cell neighbours[6]: An array of six lists. neighbours[i]: A list of pointers to neighbouring cells adjacent to face i. Ordering: The pointers in each list are sorted by decreasing overlap surface area between the current cell and the neighbour. Steps: 1. Identify Exit Face: Determine which of the six faces of the current cell the ray crosses to exit. Let this face index be f \in \{0, \dots, 5\}. 2. Retrieve List: Access the precomputed neighbour list neighbours[f] associated with the current cell. 3. Search Neighbours: Iterate through the pointers in neighbours[f] in order. 4. Return: Return the first candidate found in the list as the next cell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversetonextcell(currentcell, exitfaceindex): """ Finds the next octree cell using precomputed neighbour lists. Args: currentcell: The current octree node. exitfaceindex: Integer 0-5 indicating the face crossed. Returns: The next octree node. """ # Retrieve the list of neighbours for the specific exit face # The list is ordered by decreasing overlap area neighbourlist = currentcell.neighbours[exitfaceindex] # Iterate through neighbours in order of decreasing overlap area for candidate in neighbourlist: return candidate # If the list is empty, the ray has exited the octree domain return None Parameters and Edge Cases: Memory Overhead: Six pointer lists per cell. This is considered negligible for simulations storing many properties per cell. Construction Overhead: Creating neighbour lists during octree construction takes less than 1% of simulation time. Edge Cases: Handling empty neighbour lists or rays exiting the simulation domain is not given in the sources. Time Complexity: The search time is proportional to the number of neighbouring cells tested before finding the correct one. Due to the ordering by decreasing overlap area, the correct neighbour is typically found very early in the list. Memory Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of cells, with a constant factor of 6 pointers per cell. Performance: The method is approximately 20% faster than the top-down and bookkeeping methods. It cuts down grid traversal time by 20% compared to the traditional top-down method. Strengths: Simple to implement; applicable to both regular and barycentric octree grids; very low computational overhead for list construction. Limitations: Requires additional memory for neighbour pointers (though negligible in most contexts). Performance depends on the accuracy of the neighbour list construction. When to use: Preferred for 3D radiative transfer simulations and Monte Carlo ray tracing where traversal speed is critical and memory is not severely constrained. The method was first advocated by Hanan Samet in 1989 and 1990 in the context of computer graphics ray-tracing. It has been widely adopted in Monte Carlo radiative transfer codes for astrophysical simulations, such as those by Kurosawa & Hillier (2001) and Bianchi (2008). name: Octree Neighbor Finding without Parent Pointers
head: Mask-based Neighbor Finding, Neighbor Finding without Parent Pointers
body: This method locates the voxel at a coordinate direction relative to an origin node by traversing up the octree hierarchy to find a common parent, then using point location to find the destination leaf. It is distinguished from parent-pointer-based approaches by omitting explicit parent pointers to minimize memory footprint, instead relying on an index trace[] array populated during ray traversal to provide parent indices. Unlike Frisken and Perry’s method which uses exclusive OR with depth masks, this implementation uses bitwise AND masking on both source and destination coordinates followed by integer equality checks to identify common parents, as it is not more expensive. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Origin node index, origin coordinate, destination coordinate, and the index trace[] array containing indices of all parent nodes for the current cap. Output: Index of the destination leaf node. Data Structures: index trace[]: An array storing the indices of parent nodes encountered during the ray traversal up to the current cap. Coordinates: Spatial coordinates for the origin and destination nodes. Steps: 1. Masking: Apply a bitwise AND mask to both the source (origin) and destination coordinates. 2. Comparison: Perform integer equality comparison on the masked source and destination values. 3. Recursion: If the masked values are not equal, move up the tree using the index trace[] array to access the parent node indices. Repeat the masking and comparison at the parent level. 4. Common Parent: Continue until a common parent is found where the masked coordinates are equal. 5. Point Location: Once the common parent is identified, perform point location from this ancestor to find the specific leaf node at the destination coordinate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def maskcoords(coords, depth): # Masks out bits finer than the current depth level. # Assumes depth 0 is the finest level (leaf). return coords & ~((1 << depth) - 1) def findneighbor(originindex, origincoord, destcoord, indextrace, currentdepth): # Mask both coordinates at the current depth maskedorigin = maskcoords(origincoord, currentdepth) maskeddest = maskcoords(destcoord, currentdepth) # Check for equality to find common parent if maskedorigin == maskeddest: # Common parent found; perform point location from this ancestor return pointlocation(indextrace, currentdepth, destcoord) else: # Move up to the parent using the trace array parentindex = indextrace[currentdepth - 1] # Recurse to the parent level return findneighbor(parentindex, origincoord, destcoord, indextrace, currentdepth - 1) def pointlocation(trace, startdepth, targetcoord): # Traverse down from the common ancestor to find the leaf at targetcoord currentindex = trace[startdepth] for depth in range(startdepth, -1, -1): # Extract octant bits for the current depth level octant = (targetcoord >> (3 depth)) & 7 # Compute child index using standard hash-based octree layout childindex = (currentindex << 3) | octant # Standard hash-table lookup for child existence if childindex not in hashtable: return None currentindex = childindex return currentindex Parameters: currentdepth: The depth level in the octree where the comparison is performed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Integer coordinates must be handled carefully to ensure correct masking. Boundaries: If the destination coordinate is outside the octree bounds, point location should handle this gracefully. Degenerate Input: If the origin and destination are the same, the algorithm should return the origin index immediately. An algorithm to find adjacent nodes in an octree without using locational codes, utilizing case decomposition for edges/vertices and bitwise operations for optimization. It computes the 'reflection' function for the adjacent neighbor by performing a binary exclusive OR (XOR) of the current location and the direction vector in which the neighbor is sought. It then recursively traverses up the tree to find the deepest common ancestor between the current node and the reflected location. Finally, it performs point location from the deepest common ancestor to find the target neighbor node. The average cost to find an adjacent neighbor at the same depth is O(1). Time Complexity: The average cost to find an adjacent neighbor at the same depth is O(1). The general neighbor finding algorithm involves recursion up the tree, which depends on the depth of the octree. Memory Complexity: The index trace[] array requires O(D) memory where D is the depth of the octree. O(1) additional memory is required per traversal step if the array is reused. Strengths: Minimizes memory footprint by omitting parent pointers. Efficient for non-adjacent neighbors. Limitations: Requires the index trace[] array to be maintained during ray traversal. When to Use: When memory is constrained and parent pointers are undesirable. When Not to Use: When random access to parent pointers is needed without maintaining a trace array. Neighbor finding was addressed early on in octree research. Gargantini [Gar82] provided a concise algorithm for finding adjacent nodes in the linear quadtree using Morton’s [Mor66] array-based locational code. Samet [Sam82] proposed a more general scheme for adjacent neighbor-finding using only an original node and a desired direction, with no knowledge of a locational code. The algorithm was later applied to accelerating ray tracing using a pointer octree [Sam89]. Samet [Sam90] conducted rigorous analysis of the neighbor finding technique, decomposing the algorithm into cases for edge, vertex, and aligned neighbors. Frisken and Perry noted that the “reflection” function for adjacent neighbors, implemented by Samet via a switch statement, can be accomplished by a binary exclusive “or” of the current location and the direction in which we seek a neighbor. The method described here, using masking and equality checks, was proposed in as an alternative to Frisken and Perry’s method. name: Morton Key Vertex Neighbor Iteration
head: Vertex Neighbor Iteration via Morton Keys
body:
Morton Key Vertex Neighbor Iteration identifies and processes the eight corner vertices of leaf nodes in a sparse voxel octree by leveraging the spatial locality of Morton (Z-order) keys. It solves the dual-grid traversal problem, ensuring each shared vertex is processed exactly once across up to eight adjacent leaf nodes. It differs from standard recursive neighbor finding by operating on a pre-computed list of vertex keys and using bitwise arithmetic to resolve adjacency and level mismatches without recursive tree traversal. Inputs: A sparse voxel octree implementation providing nodeexists(key), issubdivided(key), and parent() operations. An array of vertexkeys containing MortonKey values for the eight vertices of a leaf node, with invalid vertices marked as MortonKey::none(). The target level of the leaf node (vertexlv). Outputs: An array of eight resolved neighbor keys for the valid vertices of the leaf, where each entry is either a valid MortonKey of an existing node at the same level (or an ancestor if the direct neighbor is missing) or MortonKey::none(). MortonKey: A struct wrapping a u64 integer that represents a single node in a hashed octree. Its internal representation starts with 1 for the root node and appends three bits per level for the child index along the X, Y, and Z axes. MortonKey::none() returns Self(0) and MortonKey::root() returns Self(1). HashedOctree: A concurrent hash map-based storage for the octree values. Defined as pub struct HashedOctree<T: Copy> { values: DashMap<MortonKey, T, RandomState>, }. OctreeIndex: Bitflags for child indices where RIGHT = 1 << 0, TOP = 1 << 1, and FOREMOST = 1 << 2. The method relies on three 64-bit dilation constants to perform bitwise arithmetic on Morton keys. These constants have bits set at positions corresponding to the X, Y, and Z axes in the Morton interleaving. DILX = 0b001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001u64. DILY = 0b010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010u64. DILZ = 0b100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100u64. The core of the method uses dilated integer addition and dilated integer subtraction to move along grid axes in Morton space using standard integer arithmetic masked by the dilation constants. 1. Dilated Integer Addition (computes vertex keys from a leaf key): vertex\key = \left( (key.0 \mid 
eg DIL\X) + (vertex\i \ \& \ DIL\X) ight) \ \& \ DIL\X \ \mid \ \left( (key.0 \mid 
eg DIL\Y) + (vertex\i \ \& \ DIL\Y) ight) \ \& \ DIL\Y \ \mid \ \left( (key.0 \mid 
eg DIL\Z) + (vertex\i \ \& \ DIL\Z) ight) \ \& \ DIL\Z Where key.0 is the Morton key of the leaf node, vertex\i is the vertex index (0–7), \mid is bitwise OR, 
eg is bitwise NOT, \& is bitwise AND, and + is integer addition. 2. Dilated Integer Subtraction (computes neighbor leaf keys from a vertex key): key{node\i} = \left( (dc \ \& \ DIL\X) - (node\i \ \& \ DIL\X) ight) \ \& \ DIL\X \ \mid \ \left( (dc \ \& \ DIL\Y) - (node\i \ \& \ DIL\Y) ight) \ \& \ DIL\Y \ \mid \ \left( (dc \ \& \ DIL\Z) - (node\i \ \& \ DIL\Z) ight) \ \& \ DIL\Z Where dc is the dilated coordinate of the vertex computed as vertex\k.0 \ll (vertex\lv - vertex\k.level()) 	imes 3, and node\i is the neighbor index (0–7). The method processes a list of vertex keys to find unique neighbors. 1. Iterate Vertices: Enumerate over the vertexkeys array and stop when vertexk equals MortonKey::none(). Let the current index be vertexi and the key be vertexk. 2. Compute Neighbor Candidates: Call vert2leaf(vertexk, vertexlv) to obtain an array neighbours of eight candidate MortonKey values for the adjacent nodes. 3. Filter Neighbors: For each neighbor index neighbouri from 0 to 7: skip if neighbouri == vertexi (the node itself). Let neighbourk = neighbours[neighbouri]. If !octree.nodeexists(neighbourk), continue to the next neighbor. If octree.issubdivided(neighbourk) (the neighbor is deeper than the current leaf), mark the entire vertex as skipped because the deeper node will process the shared vertex. If neighbouri < vertexi, mark the entire vertex as skipped to ensure shared vertices between same-level nodes are processed exactly once based on fixed indices rather than iteration order. 4. Resolve Keys: If the vertex passes the filter, initialize an array keys: [MortonKey; 8]. For each neighbouri from 0 to 7, let neighbourk = neighbours[neighbouri]. While neighbourk != MortonKey::none() AND !octree.nodeexists(neighbourk), set neighbourk = neighbourk.parent(). Store the resolved neighbourk in keys[neighbouri]. Return keys. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. DILX = 0b001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001 DILY = 0b010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010 DILZ = 0b100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100 class MortonKey: def init(self, val: int): self.0 = val @staticmethod def none(): return MortonKey(0) @staticmethod def root(): return MortonKey(1) def level(self) -> int: if self.0 == 0: raise ValueError("Cannot get level of none key") return (63 - self.0.bitlength() + 1) // 3 def parent(self) -> 'MortonKey': return MortonKey(self.0 >> 3) def leaf2vert(key: MortonKey) -> tuple[int, list[MortonKey]]: level = key.level() levelkey = 1 << (3 level) keys = [None] 8 for vertexi in range(8): vertexkey = ( ((key.0 | ~DILX) + (vertexi & DILX)) & DILX | ((key.0 | ~DILY) + (vertexi & DILY)) & DILY | ((key.0 | ~DILZ) + (vertexi & DILZ)) & DILZ) if (vertexkey >= (levelkey << 1)) or \ ((vertexkey - levelkey) & DILX) == 0 or \ ((vertexkey - levelkey) & DILY) == 0 or \ ((vertexkey - levelkey) & DILZ) == 0: keys[vertexi] = MortonKey.none() else: keys[vertexi] = MortonKey(vertexkey) return level, keys def vert2leaf(vertexk: MortonKey, vertexlv: int) -> list[MortonKey]: dc = vertexk.0 << ((vertexlv - vertexk.level()) 3) keys = [None] 8 for nodei in range(8): keys[nodei] = MortonKey( ((dc & DILX) - (nodei & DILX)) & DILX | ((dc & DILY) - (nodei & DILY)) & DILY | ((dc & DILZ) - (nodei & DILZ)) & DILZ) return keys def processvertexneighbors(vertexkeys: list[MortonKey], octree) -> list[list[MortonKey]]: results = [] for vertexi, vertexk in enumerate(vertexkeys): if vertexk == MortonKey.none(): break neighbours = vert2leaf(vertexk, vertexk.level()) shouldprocess = True for neighbouri in range(8): if neighbouri == vertexi: continue neighbourk = neighbours[neighbouri] if not octree.nodeexists(neighbourk): continue if octree.issubdivided(neighbourk): shouldprocess = False break if neighbouri < vertexi: shouldprocess = False break if not shouldprocess: continue keys = [None] 8 for neighbouri in range(8): neighbourk = neighbours[neighbouri] while neighbourk != MortonKey.none() and not octree.nodeexists(neighbourk): neighbourk = neighbourk.parent() keys[neighbouri] = neighbourk results.append(keys) return results Invalid Vertex Keys: A vertex key is invalid if it falls outside the level's range (vertexkey >= levelkey << 1) or if any dilated axis difference is zero. These invalid cases return MortonKey::none(). Concurrency: When using HashedOctree (backed by DashMap), concurrent access may deadlock if a mutable reference is held while calling value(). Tie-Breaking: The condition neighbouri < vertexi ensures that shared vertices between nodes of the same level are processed only once, relying on fixed neighbor and vertex indices rather than iteration order. Time Complexity: O(V) where V is the number of valid vertices, with constant-time bitwise operations per vertex and a bounded parent-traversal loop. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per vertex for storing eight keys, with external octree storage. Strengths: Avoids recursive tree traversal for neighbor finding and uses fast bitwise arithmetic, making it efficient for sparse grids where many neighbors are missing. Limitations: Requires pre-computed or easily derivable vertex keys and relies on the octree implementation providing efficient nodeexists and issubdivided checks. The method is described in the dmc (Dense Marching Cuber) project by aleokdev. It is used for dual-grid traversal in volume rendering, specifically for extracting isosurfaces from sparse voxel octrees. The approach leverages the properties of Morton keys to map spatial adjacency to arithmetic operations. aleokdev/dmc, https://github.com/aleokdev/dmc, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Residency Octree Traversal
head: Author's residency octree traversal, Ray-Guided Volume Rendering with Residency Octree, Single Channel Residency Traversal
body: Residency Octree Traversal is a ray-guided method for sparse voxel volume rendering that determines which data bricks to load from a server into a local cache based on the current viewing ray. It solves the problem of efficient memory management and bandwidth reduction in large-scale volume visualization by skipping empty or homogeneous regions and only requesting bricks that are actually needed for rendering. It sets itself apart from standard octree traversal by integrating residency metadata directly into the traversal logic, allowing the renderer to decide whether to skip a node, use its aggregate value, or request specific voxel data based on cache status and resolution requirements. The method traverses a residency octree for each pixel's viewing ray to determine the sampling strategy and data requirements. It relies on leaf node metadata to identify empty, homogeneous, or unmapped regions, and uses residency information to manage brick caching. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Viewing ray (origin, direction), current pixel coordinates, current sampling step size, desired resolution level (determined by viewing parameters like distance to camera), maximum traversal depth (derived from step size to prevent skipping over samples smaller than the step). Output: A decision for each ray sample: skip (empty), use node value (homogeneous), request brick (needed but not resident), or advance to next sample. Data Structures: Residency Octree: A hierarchical structure where each node contains metadata. Node Metadata: Includes flags for empty, homogeneous, and partially mapped states, as well as residency status of child bricks. The metadata for newly added bricks is set by the bit-wise OR of their child nodes’ bitmasks. Brick Cache: Stores resident voxel data bricks. Page-Table Hierarchy: Maps nodes and resolution levels to cached brick pages. Parameters: Desired Resolution Level (resolutionLevel): Chosen based on viewing parameters (e.g., distance to camera). Maximum Traversal Depth (traversalDepth): Chosen based on the current sampling step size to ensure the ray does not skip a distance smaller than the distance to the next ray sample. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: For each pixel, march along the viewing ray. Determine the desired resolution level and maximum traversal depth. 2. Traverse: Start at the root node (assumed to have metadata). Traverse the tree until the maximum traversal depth is reached or a terminal condition is met. 3. Check Node State: At the current node, check the metadata: Empty: If the node is empty, skip all samples along the ray that would fall into this node. Advance the ray to the next relevant node or sample. Homogeneous: If the node is homogeneous (all voxels hold approximately the same value), use the node's value directly for rendering for all samples falling into the node. Advance the ray to the next node. Not Partially Mapped: If the node is not even partially mapped, stop traversal for this ray segment and report a brick request. Refinement Needed: If the current subtree is not deep enough to reach the target traversal depth AND culling information does not allow skipping the current node, refine the residency octree by requesting a new node. 4. Retrieve Brick: If the target traversal depth is reached and the current node is non-empty and inhomogeneous: Attempt to retrieve the brick of the chosen resolution level from the brick cache. Cache Miss: If the brick is not resident, report a brick request. Try to load a brick from an alternative resolution level where the node is partially mapped. No Brick Found: If no brick is found in alternative resolutions, advance the ray to the next sample. 5. Adjust Sampling: Depending on the resolution level of the retrieved brick, potentially increase the sampling distance along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def residencyoctreetraversal(ray, stepsize, rootnode): resolutionlevel = chooseresolutionlevel(ray.depth) # View-dependent LOD traversaldepth = choosetraversaldepth(stepsize) # Step-to-depth mapping node = rootnode for i in range(traversaldepth + 1): if node.isempty(): ray = skipnode(node, ray) break if node.ishomogeneous(): ray = renderandskipnode(node, ray) break if not node.ispartiallymapped(): reportbrickrequest(node, ray, resolutionlevel) ray = skipnode(node, ray) break if i < traversaldepth: nextnode = getchildnode(node, ray) if nextnode is None or nextnode.cullinginfomissing: reportnoderequest(nextnode) # Child missing culling info implies whole subtree lacks it; # treat as if max depth reached and proceed to page lookup else: node = nextnode continue page = getpage(node, ray, resolutionlevel) if page.isunmapped: reportbrickrequest(node, ray, resolutionlevel) page = getalternativepage(node, ray, resolutionlevel) if page.isunmapped: skipbrick(node, ray) else: renderuntilnextboundary(page.brick, node, ray) break if i == traversaldepth: # Fixed from source typo (i > traversaldepth) reportbrickrequest(node, ray, resolutionlevel) ray = skipnode(node, ray) def chooseresolutionlevel(depth): return max(0, depth) def choosetraversaldepth(stepsize): return max(1, stepsize) def skipnode(node, ray): return ray.advancepastboundingbox(node) def renderandskipnode(node, ray): return ray.advancepastboundingbox(node) def getchildnode(node, ray): return node.children[ray.childindex(node)] def getpage(node, ray, resolution): return pagetable.lookup(node, ray, resolution) def getalternativepage(node, ray, resolution): return pagetable.lookupalternative(node, ray, resolution) def reportbrickrequest(node, ray, resolution): pass def reportnoderequest(node): pass def skipbrick(node, ray): return ray.advancepastboundingbox(node) def renderuntilnextboundary(brick, node, ray): return ray.advancetoboundary(brick, node) Extends the method to handle multiple volume channels simultaneously within a single ray. It solves the problem of efficient empty-space and homogeneous-node skipping in multi-volume rendering by requiring that a node be empty or homogeneous for all active channels before it can be skipped. Unlike single-channel traversal, which skips a node as soon as it is empty for that specific channel, this algorithm continues traversing deeper levels for non-empty channels until they also reach an empty or homogeneous state, ensuring no visible data is skipped. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Traversal stops early for empty or homogeneous nodes, reducing the number of cache lookups and server requests. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory usage depends on the number of resident bricks and stored metadata. Performance: Efficient for large-scale volumes with significant empty or homogeneous regions, as it minimizes data transfer and processing for irrelevant data. Performance degrades if the cache misses are frequent or if the volume is dense and inhomogeneous. Strengths: Reduces bandwidth and memory usage by only loading necessary data. Supports mixed-resolution rendering for different channels. Limitations: Requires maintaining residency metadata. Complex to implement for multi-channel scenarios where traversal must continue until all channels are processed. The method was introduced in the paper "Residency Octree: A Hybrid Approach for Scalable Web Volume Rendering". It is part of a broader effort to enable scalable volume rendering on the web, leveraging ray-guided techniques to manage data residency efficiently. The algorithm shares with SparseLeap the incremental construction of the underlying tree structure. name: Residency-octree traversal for multiple channels
head: Multi-Channel Residency Octree Traversal, Multi-channel octree traversal
body: This method extends residency-based octree traversal to handle multiple volume channels simultaneously within a single ray. It solves the problem of efficient empty-space and homogeneous-node skipping in multi-volume rendering by requiring that a node be empty or homogeneous for all active channels before it can be skipped. Unlike single-channel traversal, which skips a node as soon as it is empty for that specific channel, this algorithm continues traversing deeper levels for non-empty channels until they also reach an empty or homogeneous state, ensuring no visible data is skipped. Inputs: rootNode: The root of the residency octree. ray: The current ray being evaluated. numChannels: The total number of volume channels to render. noCullingInformation(node, channelIndex): Boolean function returning true if culling metadata (empty/homogeneous flags) is unavailable for the current node and channel. isEmpty(node, channelIndex): Boolean function returning true if the node is empty for the given channel. isHomogeneous(node, channelIndex): Boolean function returning true if the node is homogeneous for the given channel. isPartiallyMapped(node, channelIndex): Boolean function returning true if the node contains data that requires further subdivision or detailed rendering. node.depth: Integer, current depth of the node in the octree. node.spatialextent: Object containing the node's bounding box boundaries. next(node, ray): Returns the child node intersected by the ray, or an object with.missing = True if missing. Outputs: Node requests for missing culling information or missing child nodes. Brick requests for rendering, including the chosen resolution level for each channel. Data Structures: traversalDepth: Integer, the maximum depth to traverse. node: Reference to the current octree node. channelIndex: Integer, index of the current channel being processed (0 to numChannels - 1). emptyChannels: Integer, counter of channels found to be empty for the current node. homogeneousChannels: Integer, counter of channels found to be homogeneous for the current node. Parameters: traversalDepth: The maximum depth for traversal, determined by the ray step size. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize traversalDepth based on the ray step size. 2. Set node to rootNode, channelIndex to 0, emptyChannels to 0, and homogeneousChannels to 0. 3. Loop while node.depth is less than or equal to traversalDepth AND channelIndex is less than numChannels. 4. If no culling information is available for the current node and channelIndex, report a node request for that node and channel, increment channelIndex, and continue to the next iteration. 5. If the current node is empty for the current channelIndex: Check if emptyChannels equals numChannels - 1. If so, skip the node by updating the ray based on the node's spatial extent, break the loop, and stop traversal for this ray. If not all channels are empty, increment emptyChannels, increment channelIndex, and continue to the next channel. 6. If the node is homogeneous for the current channel (logic mirrors empty nodes): Check if homogeneousChannels equals numChannels - 1. If so, skip the node using the spatial extent of the last homogeneous node encountered, break the loop, and stop traversal. If not all channels are homogeneous, increment homogeneousChannels, increment channelIndex, and continue. 7. If the node is not partially mapped for the current channel (i.e., it is fully mapped or requires rendering): Choose the resolution level for the current depth and channel. Report a brick request with the chosen resolution level. Increment channelIndex and break the loop to proceed to rendering. 8. If node.depth is less than traversalDepth: Determine the next node along the ray. If the next node is missing, report a node request for it. Otherwise, update the current node to the next node and continue the loop. 9. If the loop continues past the depth check (implying end of traversal or specific condition), choose the resolution level for the current channel, and increment channelIndex. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def residencyoctreetraversalmultichannel(rootNode, ray, numChannels): # 1. Initialize traversal depth based on ray step size traversalDepth = chooseTraversalDepth(stepSize(ray)) # 2. Initialize state node = rootNode channelIndex = 0 emptyChannels = 0 homogeneousChannels = 0 # 3. Main traversal loop while node.depth <= traversalDepth and channelIndex < numChannels: # 4. Check for culling information availability if noCullingInformation(node, channelIndex): reportNodeRequest(node, channelIndex) channelIndex += 1 continue # 5. Handle empty nodes if isEmpty(node, channelIndex): if emptyChannels == numChannels - 1: # All channels are empty; skip this node # Skipped distance determined by spatial extent of last empty node encountered ray = skipNode(node, ray) break else: # Only some channels are empty; continue to next channel emptyChannels += 1 channelIndex += 1 continue # 6. Handle homogeneous nodes (mirrors empty node logic) if isHomogeneous(node, channelIndex): if homogeneousChannels == numChannels - 1: # All channels are homogeneous; skip this node # Skipped distance determined by spatial extent of last homogeneous node encountered ray = skipNode(node, ray) break else: # Only some channels are homogeneous; continue to next channel homogeneousChannels += 1 channelIndex += 1 continue # 7. Handle partially mapped / renderable nodes if not isPartiallyMapped(node, channelIndex): # Node is fully mapped or requires rendering resolutionLevel = chooseResolutionLevel(depth(ray), channelIndex) reportBrickRequest(node, ray, resolutionLevel, channelIndex) channelIndex += 1 break # 8. Move to next level if depth allows if node.depth < traversalDepth: nextNode = next(node, ray) if nextNode.missing: reportNodeRequest(nextNode) else: node = nextNode continue else: # End of traversal depth reached resolutionLevel = chooseResolutionLevel(depth(ray), channelIndex) reportBrickRequest(node, ray, resolutionLevel, channelIndex) channelIndex += 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Node Skipping: Empty nodes can only be skipped if ALL channels are empty for that node. If a node is empty for one channel but not others, traversal must continue for the non-empty channels to find the subdivision level where they are empty. Skipped Distance: The skipped distance is determined by the spatial extent of the last empty (or homogeneous) node encountered during traversal. Since spatial extents of nodes strictly decrease between tree traversal steps, this strategy ensures that non-empty space is not skipped. Homogeneous Nodes: Homogeneous nodes are handled similarly to empty nodes. They are only skipped if all channels are homogeneous for that node. The values of the last homogeneous node encountered are used for rendering the node for each channel. A technique where different channels of a multi-volume dataset are rendered at different resolution levels to save memory and reduce sample evaluation, based on frequency content or importance. Each channel has a function that constrains the range of resolution levels to choose from, based on viewing parameters like distance to the camera. The resolution constraint function can consider frequency content, viewing parameters, and transfer functions. In Figure 7.2, human tissue data with 5 channels is rendered with mixed resolutions: pink channel at l3, orange channel at l5/l4/l0, and rest at l0. Time Complexity: In multi-volume settings, empty-space skipping may require more traversal steps than single-channel settings because multiple channels must be checked for each node. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty and homogeneous regions across multiple volumes without rendering unnecessary data. Limitations: Increased traversal overhead compared to single-channel rendering due to the need to check all channels before skipping. When to use: Multi-volume rendering where channels share spatial structure and empty/homogeneous regions are common. When not to use: Single-channel rendering where simpler traversal suffices. This method is described in the context of scalable web-based volume rendering of large biomedical datasets. It is part of a mixed-resolution multi-volume rendering framework that uses residency-based octrees to manage memory and traversal efficiently.
