name: PND3D Octree Rendering
head: PND3D
body: PND3D is a volume rendering method that uses a standard 8-way octree with non-leaf nodes containing child and solid masks, visited in front-to-back depth-first order to enable occlusion culling. It distinguishes itself by splitting the screen into large rectangular tiles determined by 3 vanishing points of the voxel grid projected to screen coordinates, allowing each tile to be rendered as an independent job starting from the root of the octree. This approach facilitates multithread optimization and specific hardware-accelerated occlusion queries using bit arrays. Inputs and Outputs: Input: a sparse voxel octree where non-leaf nodes are 64-bit structures, screen resolution, and camera parameters. Output: a rendered image. Intermediate Output: a 64-bit pixel buffer containing position and leaf node index. Data Structures: Non-leaf nodes are packed 64-bit structures with the following layout: chi (char): child byte mask (1=has children, 0=pure air/solid). sol (char): solid byte mask (1=pure solid, 0=not pure solid). mrk (char): alignment padding. mrk2 (char): alignment padding. ind (int): index pointer to the first child. Numbered Steps: 1. Tile Division: Divide the screen into large rectangular tiles determined by 3 vanishing points of the voxel grid projected to screen coordinates. 2. Bounding Box Calculation: For each tile, calculate the bounding box of the cubes more quickly by using only 4 of the 8 vertices of a cube, which are known in advance based on the tile's position relative to the vanishing points. 3. Tile Rendering Job: Render each tile as an independent job, clipped to the tile like a viewport, starting from the root of the octree, allowing for multithread optimization. 4. Occlusion Query: For every non-leaf node containing some solid, perform an occlusion query on its projected bounding box. If the width is larger than 32 pixels, assume it is visible and visit its children. If the bounding box width is 32 pixels or less, use a bit array (cover buffer) with 1 bit per pixel to test if the region is fully occluded using an 'and' instruction. If fully occluded, skip the node and its children. 5. Leaf Node Processing: For leaf nodes (solid surface voxels), visit each pixel of the bounding rectangle and perform 6 dot products in the inner loop using 2 'addps' and 2 'movmskps' instructions to determine if the pixel falls inside the projected cube (a 4- or 6-sided convex polygon). 6. First Pass (CPU): Write a 64-bit pixel to the screen containing 12 bits x, 12 bits y, 12 bits z, and a 28-bit index to the leaf node holding surface voxel information. 7. Second Pass (GPU): The GPU receives the voxel position and a pointer to its surface structure, raytraces to the known cube, determines the face, and performs texture mapping with filters like bilinear and mip mapping. Formulas: Pixel packing formula: P = (x \ \& \ 0xFFF) \ | \ ((y \ \& \ 0xFFF) \ll 12) \ | \ ((z \ \& \ 0xFFF) \ll 24) \ | \ ((idx \ \& \ 0xFFFFFFF) \ll 36), where x, y, z are 12-bit coordinates and idx is the 28-bit leaf index. Parameters: Occlusion query threshold: 32 pixels width. Nodes with projected bounding box width larger than this are assumed visible. Tile count: typically 16-48 tiles per screen. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Older ATI or Intel video cards may require overriding the default rendering mode with /arbasm for full GPU acceleration or /cpu for CPU-based emulation, which lacks trilinear filtering. Precision limits are imposed by the 12-bit coordinate storage in the 64-bit pixel format. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertile(tileid, screenwidth, screenheight, rootnode): tilebounds = computetilebounds(tileid, screenwidth, screenheight) bbox = computebbox4vertices(tilebounds) traversenode(rootnode, tilebounds, bbox) def traversenode(node, tilebounds, bbox): if not node.issolid(): return if bbox.width > 32: visitchildren(node, tilebounds) else: if isfullyoccluded(tilebounds): return visitchildren(node, tilebounds) def visitchildren(node, tilebounds): for child in node.children: childbbox = computechildbbox(child, tilebounds) traversenode(child, tilebounds, childbbox) def processleafnode(leaf, tilebounds): for pixel in leaf.boundingrectanglepixels: if ispixelinsidecube(pixel, leaf): writepixel(pixel.x, pixel.y, leaf.x, leaf.y, leaf.z, leaf.index) def isfullyoccluded(tilebounds): coverbuffer = allocatecoverbuffer(tilebounds) return coverbuffer.isfullyzero() def computetilebounds(tileid, screenwidth, screenheight): return {"x": 0, "y": 0, "w": screenwidth, "h": screenheight} def computebbox4vertices(bounds): return {"x": bounds["x"], "y": bounds["y"], "w": bounds["w"], "h": bounds["h"]} def computechildbbox(child, tilebounds): return {"x": 0, "y": 0, "w": 16, "h": 16} def ispixelinsidecube(pixel, leaf): return True def allocatecoverbuffer(bounds): return {"isfullyzero": lambda: False} def writepixel(px, py, x, y, z, index): pixelval = (x & 0xFFF) | ((y & 0xFFF) << 12) | ((z & 0xFFF) << 24) | ((index & 0xFFFFFFF) << 36) return pixelval Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Multithread optimization through independent tile rendering; efficient occlusion culling using bit arrays for small bounding boxes; fast bounding box calculation using 4 vertices. Limitations: Requires specific hardware instructions ('addps', 'movmskps') for leaf node processing; may need override for older ATI or Intel video cards. When to use: When multithread optimization is desired and hardware supports the required instructions. When not to use: When using older ATI or Intel video cards without override, or when highest quality texture-mapping (trilinear filtering) is required on CPU-based emulation. PND3D was developed by Ken Silverman. It is used for volume rendering with sparse voxel octrees. name: GigaVoxels Ray Traversal and Rendering
head: Octree-Based Sparse Voxelization
body: GigaVoxels is a GPU-based volume rendering technique that uses an octree structure to manage brick-level data, performing adaptive level-of-detail (LOD) selection of lighting and material information during ray-marching of a sparse voxelized scene. It solves the problem of rendering large, sparse 3D scenes efficiently by storing only non-empty or non-constant regions in texture memory, using a hierarchical octree to index these "bricks". Unlike dense voxelization which stores the entire volume, GigaVoxels achieves sparsity by skipping empty space and using cone tracing to automatically select appropriate LODs based on camera distance, mimicking quadrilinear interpolation across different octree levels. Inputs: Triangle mesh geometry for voxelization. Camera position and viewing frustum. Octree structure containing node pointers and brick references. Brick pool: a large 3D texture memory region containing color, normal, and light data for voxels. Outputs: Final pixel color with accumulated lighting and material properties. Octree Node Layout: The octree is implemented in a linear buffer. Each node is stored as a 64-bit value (represented as uvec4 in GLSL). The layout is: Bits 0-29 (30 bits): Pointer to the first child node. The other seven children are accessed via offsets from this pointer. Bits 30-59 (30 bits): Pointer to the brick in the brick pool. Bits 60-63 (4 bits): Status flags (e.g., constant value flag, brick loaded flag). Brick Pool: A 3D texture (BrickSampler) storing voxel data. Each brick contains a region of voxels (e.g., 3 \times 3 \times 3 or 8 \times 8 \times 8). Bricks include border voxels (neighbors) to allow hardware texture interpolation, as neighboring bricks are not necessarily adjacent in memory. Parameters: RayStepSize: Step size of the ray in world coordinates. BrickStepVector: Step size of the ray in brick pool coordinates. BrickDimension: Number of texels in a brick. RootVoxelHalfSize: Size of the voxel in the root node. BrickPoolDimension: Dimensions of the brick pool texture. OctTreeDepthMinusOne: Tree depth minus one. MaxTreeTraversals: Maximum number of tree traversals allowed per ray. MaxNodesToPushThisFrame: Maximum nodes to push onto the node usage list per frame. LodScalar: Scalar used for LOD calculations. 1. Voxelization (Preprocessing): Convert triangles to voxels in a two-step process: 1. Check if the triangle's plane intersects the voxel. 2. Rasterize the triangle along its dominant axis (largest projected area) and check if fragments intersect the 2D projection of the voxel. Insert passing voxels into the octree. If a region of space is empty or has a constant value, the node in the octree does not point to a brick or any children. Static objects are voxelized once; dynamic objects every frame, differentiated by a flag preventing overwrites. 2. Octree Filtering (LOD Generation): Initially, only leaf nodes contain material information. Fill higher octree levels by averaging material properties of child bricks. This is done in separate passes for each level. For global illumination, lights rasterize the scene, writing direction/intensity to leaf nodes, which are then filtered up the octree. 3. Ray Traversal and Cone Tracing (Rendering): For each pixel, shoot a ray. The ray performs a top-down traversal of the octree to find the lowest node containing the ray. Cone Tracing: The sampling cone width adapts to distance. Close to the camera, the cone is thin, sampling leaf nodes (high detail). Far away, the cone widens, sampling higher octree levels (blurred/averaged data). LOD Interpolation: Perform linear interpolation between adjacent octree levels to get precise LOD, mimicking quadrilinear interpolation. Brick Sampling: Sample the brick associated with the current octree node. Use border voxels for hardware interpolation. 4. Ray Marching and Blending: Compute minimum ray-box intersection time (t{Min}) by iterating over 6 planes of the node extent. Update plane D values based on nodeExtentMin/Max. Only consider intersections where dirDotN > 0. Calculate numSteps = int(distToNodeBoundary / rayStepSize) + 1. Advance ray position: rayWorldPosition += rayDir (numSteps rayStepSize). Front-to-Back Blending: If the node is constant (constValue.a < 0.005f), advance ray to exit and return. Loop numSteps times: 1. Advance rayWorldPosition by worldRayStep. 2. If dst.a > 0.995f, advance remaining steps and return. 3. Sample source color/alpha (src). 4. Update source alpha: src.a = 1.0 - (1.0 - src.a)^{sampleRatio}. 5. Update source color: src.rgb = sampleRatio. 6. Update destination: dst = (1.0 - dst.a) src + dst. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nodeisconstant(octtreenode): """Check if node type bits indicate a constant value.""" nodetypebits = octtreenode[0] return (nodetypebits & 0x40000000) != 0 def getchildnodepointer(octtreenode): """Extract 30-bit child pointer split into 3 10-bit indices.""" childptrbits = octtreenode[0] return ( ((childptrbits >> 20) & 0x3FF), ((childptrbits >> 10) & 0x3FF), (childptrbits & 0x3FF)) def brickisloaded(octtreenode): """Check if brick loaded flag is set.""" brickloadedbits = octtreenode[0] return (brickloadedbits & 0x80000000) != 0 def getbrickpointer(octtreenode, brickpooldimension): """Extract 30-bit brick pointer and normalize to [0, 1].""" brickptrbits = octtreenode[1] uis = (brickptrbits >> 20) & 0x3FF uit = (brickptrbits >> 10) & 0x3FF uir = brickptrbits & 0x3FF return (uis / brickpooldimension[0], uit / brickpooldimension[1], uir / brickpooldimension[2]) def getconstantvalue(octtreenode): """Extract 32-bit constant color/alpha value.""" constbits = octtreenode[1] red = constbits & 0xFF constbits >>= 8 green = constbits & 0xFF constbits >>= 8 blue = constbits & 0xFF constbits >>= 8 alpha = constbits & 0xFF return (red / 255.0, green / 255.0, blue / 255.0, alpha / 255.0) def rendergigavoxels(rayorigin, raydir, rootocttreenode, brickpooldimension, raystepsize, sampleratio): dst = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) currentraypos = rayorigin currentnode = rootocttreenode # Compute ray-box intersection and step count disttoboundary = computerayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydir, currentnode.bounds) numsteps = int(disttoboundary / raystepsize) + 1 for in range(numsteps): currentraypos = currentraypos + raydir raystepsize if nodeisconstant(currentnode): constval = getconstantvalue(currentnode) if constval[3] < 0.005: break srca = 1.0 - (1.0 - constval[3]) sampleratio srcrgb = (constval[0] sampleratio, constval[1] sampleratio, constval[2] sampleratio) dst = ((1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[0] + dst[0], (1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[1] + dst[1], (1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[2] + dst[2], (1.0 - dst[3]) srca + dst[3]) if dst[3] > 0.995: break continue if not brickisloaded(currentnode): # The sources do not specify the brick loading mechanism. break brickptr = getbrickpointer(currentnode, brickpooldimension) src = sample3dtexture(BrickSampler, brickptr) # Standard 3D texture fetch srca = 1.0 - (1.0 - src[3]) sampleratio srcrgb = (src[0] sampleratio, src[1] sampleratio, src[2] sampleratio) dst = ((1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[0] + dst[0], (1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[1] + dst[1], (1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[2] + dst[2], (1.0 - dst[3]) srca + dst[3]) if dst[3] > 0.995: break # The sources do not specify the exact next-node selection logic for traversal. # currentnode = getnextocttreenode(currentnode, currentraypos) return dst Slow Octree Traversal: The octree is an indirect mechanism. Traversing down to find the correct node before sampling the brick can be slow. Non-automatic LOD Interpolation: Since bricks of different LODs are in the same memory pool, hardware quadrilinear interpolation cannot be used directly. Linear interpolation between levels must be implemented manually. Redundant Memory: Bricks contain neighbor voxels for interpolation, increasing memory usage by ~33% for 8 \times 8 \times 8 bricks. Filtering Complexity: Determining shared neighbors among bricks during the filtering process is encumbered. Time Complexity: Traversal time depends on the depth of the octree and the number of nodes visited per ray. Cone tracing allows for larger step sizes at distance, reducing samples. Global illumination adds cost due to multiple cone bounces (5 for diffuse, 1 for specular). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of non-empty/constant voxels. Brick pool size is determined by BrickPoolDimension and BrickDimension. Overhead from neighbor voxels in bricks. Performance: Enables real-time rendering of large sparse scenes. Performance degrades if the octree traversal is not optimized or if too many bricks are loaded/unloaded. Strengths: Sparsity: Does not store empty space. Adaptive LOD: Automatic detail selection based on distance. Global Illumination: Supports one-bounce GI efficiently. Limitations: Indirect sampling overhead. Manual LOD interpolation. Memory overhead from neighbor voxels. Origin: GigaVoxels was introduced by Cyril Crassin et al. in 2011. It is a key component of the rendering technology behind Unreal Engine 4. History: The technique was developed to address the limitations of dense voxelization and traditional ray tracing for large scenes. It builds on the concept of sparse voxel octrees and brick-based rendering. Usage: Used in real-time rendering engines, particularly for large-scale environments and global illumination effects. apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, https://github.com/apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) http://realtimevoxels.blogspot.fr/2012/09/introduction-to-gigavoxels-and-sparse.html, http://realtimevoxels.blogspot.fr/2012/09/introduction-to-gigavoxels-and-sparse.html, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Sparse Voxel Grid Raycasting with Occupancy Grid
head: Occupancy Grid Culling, empty block skipping
body: A volume rendering estimator that accelerates ray traversal and sampling by using a hierarchical sparse voxel grid (often implemented via VDB/NanoVDB structures) to skip empty space along rays, returning only sample locations within occupied cells. It differs from standard Voxel Grid Raycasting by replacing dense texture lookups with a hierarchical occupancy check that reduces texture reads by a factor of 3, and from Octree Traversal by using a fixed-resolution sparse grid with hierarchical levels rather than a dynamic tree structure for the primary traversal logic. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins tensor of shape (N, 3). raysd: Normalized ray directions tensor of shape (N, 3). estimator: An OccGridEstimator object containing: binaries: Boolean tensor of shape (L, Rx, Ry, Rz) storing occupancy masks for each level L. Must be contiguous on CPU before transfer to GPU. aabbs: Tensor of shape (L, 6) storing the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) for each level, where level i is enlarged by 2^i relative to the base. resolution: 3D resolution (Rx, Ry, Rz), default 128. levels: Number of hierarchical levels L. nearplane, farplane: Scalar distances, defaults 0.0 and 10^{10}. renderstepsize: Step size for marching, default 10^{-3}. coneangle: Cone angle for linearly-increased step size, default 0.0. alphathre: Alpha threshold for skipping empty space, default 0.0. earlystopeps: Early stop threshold, default 10^{-4}. sigmafn or alphafn: Optional callables taking (t{starts}, t{ends}, ray\indices) and returning density or opacity values, used to skip invisible space. Only one should be provided. renderbkgd: Background color tensor. timestamps: Optional tensor for dynamic scenes. Outputs: rgb: Rendered RGB image. opacity: Accumulated opacity. depth: Accumulated depth. nrenderingsamples: Number of samples used. Data Structures: DensityGrid (or OccGridEstimator): Manages the VDB/NanoVDB structure. tree: The underlying VDB grid object. binaries: The occupancy mask. gridcoords: Integer coordinates for voxels. gridindices: Indices for voxels. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create nearplanes and farplanes tensors of shape (N) filled with nearplane and farplane respectively. If tmin is provided, clamp nearplanes to \max(t{min}, near\plane). If tmax is provided, clamp farplanes to \min(t{max}, far\plane). If stratified is True, add uniform random noise in 0, render\step\size) to nearplanes. Update alphathre to \min(alpha\thre, mean\occupancy) if visibility skipping is enabled. 2. Ray-AABB Intersection: Compute intersections for all rays against all level AABBs: t{mins}, t{maxs}, hits = \text{ray\aabb\intersect}(rays\o, rays\d, aabbs) If L > 1, concatenate t{mins} and t{maxs} along the last dimension and sort them to get t{sorted} and t{indices}. If L = 1, use unsorted concatenation and identity indices to maintain kernel compatibility. 3. Iterative [Ray Marching: Initialize raymask as a boolean tensor of shape (N) with all True. Initialize opacity, depth, and rgb tensors of shape (N, 1) and (N, 3) with zeros. Loop while itersamples < maxsamples and raymask.sum() > 0: a. Calculate nalive = raymask.sum(). b. Determine samples per alive ray: n{samples} = \max\left(\min\left(\frac{N}{n{alive}}, 64\right), min\samples\right) where min\samples = 1 if cone\angle == 0 else 4. c. Call traversegrids CUDA kernel with rays, binaries, aabbs, bounds, renderstepsize, coneangle, nsamples, raymask, and pre-computed t{sorted}/t{indices}/hits. This returns intervals, samples, and terminationplanes. The kernel traverses the sparse VDB structure, skipping empty blocks. d. Extract sample intervals: t{starts} = intervals.vals[intervals.is\left] t{ends} = intervals.vals[intervals.is\right] e. Extract valid ray indices: ray\indices = samples.ray\indices[samples.is\valid] f. Visibility Skipping (if sigmafn or alphafn is provided and alphathre > 0 or earlystopeps > 0): If sigmafn is provided, compute sigmas: positions = rays\o[ray\indices] + rays\d[ray\indices] \times \frac{t{starts} + t{ends}}{2} sigmas = \sigma\fn(t{starts}, t{ends}, ray\indices) (Handle dynamic scenes with timestamps if present). If alphafn is provided (and sigmafn is not), compute alphas similarly. Compute masks using rendervisibilityfromdensity or rendervisibilityfromalpha with packedinfo (stacked chunkindices and chunkcounts) and thresholds. Filter rayindices, tstarts, tends using the masks. g. Query radiance field for RGB and sigma: rgbs, sigmas = \text{rgb\sigma\fn}(t{starts}, t{ends}, ray\indices) (Handle dynamic scenes with timestamps if present). h. Compute rendering weights: prefix\trans = 1 - opacity[ray\indices].squeeze(-1) weights = \text{render\weight\from\density}(sigmas, prefix\trans) i. Accumulate results: rgb = rgb + weights \times rgbs opacity = opacity + weights depth = depth + weights \times \frac{t{starts} + t{ends}}{2} j. Update itersamples by adding nsamples. 4. Finalization: Add background color: rgb = rgb + render\bkgd \times (1.0 - opacity) Compute final depth: depth = \frac{depth}{\max(opacity, \epsilon)} where \epsilon is machine epsilon. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersparsevoxelgrid(rayso, raysd, estimator, sigmafn=None, alphafn=None, nearplane=0.0, farplane=1e10, renderstepsize=1e-3, renderbkgd=None, coneangle=0.0, alphathre=0.0, earlystopeps=1e-4, timestamps=None): numrays = rayso.shape[0] device = rayso.device # 1. Initialization nearplanes = torch.full((numrays,), nearplane, device=device) farplanes = torch.full((numrays,), farplane, device=device) # Clamp near/far planes if needed (omitted tmin/tmax for brevity) # Update alphathre with mean occupancy if visibility skipping is active if (alphathre > 0.0 or earlystopeps > 0.0) and (sigmafn is not None or alphafn is not None): alphathre = min(alphathre, estimator.binaries.float().mean().item()) minsamples = 1 if coneangle == 0 else 4 # 2. Ray-AABB Intersection tmins, tmaxs, hits = rayaabbintersect(rayso, raysd, estimator.aabbs) ngrids = estimator.binaries.size(0) if ngrids > 1: tsorted, tindices = torch.sort(torch.cat([tmins, tmaxs], -1), -1) else: tsorted = torch.cat([tmins, tmaxs], -1) tindices = torch.arange(0, ngrids 2, device=device, dtype=torch.int64).expand(numrays, ngrids 2) # 3. Iterative Marching raymask = torch.ones(numrays, device=device).bool() opacity = torch.zeros(numrays, 1, device=device) depth = torch.zeros(numrays, 1, device=device) rgb = torch.zeros(numrays, 3, device=device) itersamples = 0 maxsamples = 10000 # Example limit while itersamples < maxsamples: nalive = raymask.sum().item() if nalive == 0: break nsamples = max(min(numrays // nalive, 64), minsamples) itersamples += nsamples # Traverse sparse grid intervals, samples, terminationplanes = traversegrids( rayso, raysd, estimator.binaries, estimator.aabbs, nearplanes, farplanes, renderstepsize, coneangle, nsamples, raymask, tsorted, tindices, hits) tstarts = intervals.vals[intervals.isleft] tends = intervals.vals[intervals.isright] rayindices = samples.rayindices[samples.isvalid] # Visibility Skipping if (alphathre > 0.0 or earlystopeps > 0.0) and (sigmafn is not None or alphafn is not None): if tstarts.shape[0] == 0: continue if sigmafn is not None: sigmas = sigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices) masks = rendervisibilityfromdensity(tstarts, tends, sigmas, torch.stack([intervals.chunkindices, intervals.chunkcounts], -1), earlystopeps, alphathre) elif alphafn is not None: alphas = alphafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices) masks = rendervisibilityfromalpha(alphas, torch.stack([intervals.chunkindices, intervals.chunkcounts], -1), earlystopeps, alphathre) rayindices = rayindices[masks] tstarts = tstarts[masks] tends = tends[masks] if rayindices.numel() == 0: continue # Query Radiance Field rgbs, sigmas = rgbsigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices, rayso, raysd, timestamps) # Accumulate prefixtrans = 1.0 - opacity[rayindices].squeeze(-1) weights = renderweightfromdensity(sigmas, prefixtrans) rgb = rgb + weights[:, None] rgbs opacity = opacity + weights[:, None] depth = depth + weights[:, None] (tstarts + tends)[:, None] / 2.0 # 4. Finalization if renderbkgd is not None: rgb = rgb + renderbkgd (1.0 - opacity) depth = depth / torch.clampmin(opacity, torch.finfo(rgbs.dtype).eps) return rgb, opacity, depth, itersamples Accelerates the method by decoupling counting of occupied steps from sample generation, solving variable-length buffer issues in batched CUDA kernels. Time Complexity: Depends on the sparsity of the grid and the number of occupied intervals. The hierarchical traversal reduces the number of texture reads significantly compared to dense grids. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the binaries tensor of shape (L, Rx, Ry, Rz) and the VDB structure overhead. For L=4, R=128, this is manageable on modern GPUs. Performance: Reduces texture reads by a factor of 3. In a specific implementation (lava-lamp), texture reads dropped from 17.6M to 5.9M per frame at 1080p in a default view, and from 138M to 46M in a full-screen lamp view. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space; compatible with hierarchical grids; reduces memory bandwidth pressure. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of occupancy grid; sorting of intersection times adds overhead for multi-level grids; precision issues may arise with very small step sizes or large bounding boxes. When to use: When the scene has large empty regions and the occupancy grid can be pre-computed or updated efficiently. When not to use: When the scene is fully dense, or when the overhead of maintaining the occupancy grid outweighs the traversal savings. The method originates from the use of hierarchical VDB (OpenVDB/NanoVDB) grids for volume rendering, specifically adapted for GPU acceleration. It is widely used in neural radiance field (NeRF) rendering pipelines, such as those in the nerfacc library and unofficial implementations like faster-occgrid. The concept of using an occupancy grid to cull empty blocks is also found in traditional volume rendering, such as in the lava-lamp simulation. name: Two-pass chunked ray traversal for occupancy grids
head: Chunked ray traversal with occupancy grid, Two-pass occupancy grid traversal
body: This method accelerates sparse voxel grid raycasting using a two-pass CUDA kernel launch that first counts the number of traversal steps per ray to allocate exact sample buffers, then fills those buffers with sample intervals and ray indices. It solves the problem of variable-length sample buffers per ray in a batched kernel by computing the exact number of occupied intervals each ray intersects, allocating a contiguous buffer, and then populating it with precise sample intervals. The method consists of two sequential CUDA kernel launches. The first pass counts the number of occupied voxel intervals (chunks) each ray traverses to determine buffer sizes. The second pass writes the actual sample data into pre-allocated tensors using the computed offsets. Inputs: grids: int64 array of pointers to nanovdb::MaskGrid (device memory). rayso: float array of shape [nrays, 3], ray origins. raysd: float array of shape [nrays, 3], ray directions. resolution: int32 array of shape [3], grid resolution per axis. aabbs: float array of shape [ngrids, 6], axis-aligned bounding boxes for each grid. hits: bool array of shape [nrays, ngrids], pre-computed ray-grid intersection flags. tsorted: float array of shape [nrays, ngrids2], sorted entry/exit distances per grid. tindices: int64 array of shape [nrays, ngrids2], indices into tsorted. nearplanes: float array of shape [nrays]. farplanes: float array of shape [nrays]. Outputs (allocated before launch): chunkcounts: int64 array of shape [nrays], number of occupied chunks per ray. chunkindices: int64 array of shape [nrays], starting index in the sample buffer for each ray. rayindices: int64 array of shape [nsamples], maps each sample to its originating ray. tleft: float array of shape [nsamples], entry distance of each sample interval. tright: float array of shape [nsamples], exit distance of each sample interval. The core data structure is the occupancy grid (nanovdb::MaskGrid), accessed via pointers in grids. The traversal relies on sorted entry/exit distances (tsorted) and their corresponding grid indices (tindices) to efficiently skip empty regions. The output buffers are flattened 1D arrays where samples from all rays are concatenated. chunkindices acts as an exclusive prefix sum of chunkcounts to determine write offsets. stepsize: float, fixed step length for traversal. coneangle: float, cone angle for frustum traversal. threads: int, threads per block. Typical value: 256. n: int, grid update frequency. Default: 16. 1. First Pass (Counting): Launch traversekernel with firstpass=true to compute ntrav per ray and store in chunkcounts. 2. Prefix Sum: Compute the cumulative sum of chunkcounts to get total sample count nsamples and starting indices for each ray's chunk. 3. Second Pass (Filling): Launch traversekernel with firstpass=false to write chunkindices, rayindices, tleft, and tright into pre-allocated tensors. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversekernel(rayso, raysd, resolution, aabbs, hits, tsorted, tindices, nearplanes, farplanes, chunkcounts, chunkindices, rayindices, tleft, tright, firstpass, nrays, ngrids): # Standard CUDA thread indexing threadidx = (blockIdx.x blockDim.x) + threadIdx.x if threadidx >= nrays: return rayid = threadidx count = 0 offset = 0 if not firstpass: offset = chunkindices[rayid] # Iterate through pre-sorted grid intervals for this ray # The exact occupancy check logic over tsorted/tindices is implementation-specific for i in range(0, ngrids 2, 2): tentry = tsorted[rayid, i] texit = tsorted[rayid, i + 1] gridid = tindices[rayid, i] # Skip grids the ray does not hit if not hits[rayid, gridid]: continue # Clamp interval to camera near/far planes tl = max(tentry, nearplanes[rayid]) tr = min(texit, farplanes[rayid]) if tl < tr: if firstpass: count += 1 else: tleft[offset] = tl tright[offset] = tr rayindices[offset] = rayid offset += 1 if firstpass: chunkcounts[rayid] = count Pre-allocation: The second pass requires pre-allocated output tensors for tleft, tright, and rayindices. Passing nullptr for these pointers in the first pass avoids overwriting or invalid memory access. Precision: Floating-point precision in tsorted and tleft/tright can cause gaps or overlaps if not handled carefully. Ensure consistent clamping to nearplanes and farplanes. Empty Rays: Rays with no hits should result in chunkcounts[rayid] = 0 and no writes in the second pass. Degenerate Input: If nrays is 0 or ngrids is 0, the kernel should handle this gracefully without launching. Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{grids}) for the first pass (counting) and O(N{samples}) for the second pass (filling), where N{samples} is the total number of occupied intervals. The prefix sum is O(N{rays}). Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{grids}) for tsorted and tindices, plus O(N{samples}) for the output buffers. This is more memory-efficient than fixed-step methods if occupancy is sparse. Performance: Measured performance depends on hardware and scene density. The two-pass approach adds overhead for the counting pass but reduces memory bandwidth usage in the second pass by avoiding redundant writes. It is most beneficial when occupancy is highly variable across rays. Strengths: Exact buffer allocation, reduced memory waste, coalesced memory accesses in the second pass. Limitations: Requires two kernel launches and a prefix sum operation. Not suitable for real-time applications with strict latency constraints where the overhead of the first pass is prohibitive. This method is derived from implementations in the faster-occgrid repository, which adapts techniques from neural radiance field (NeRF) rendering to sparse occupancy grids. It addresses the inefficiency of fixed-step ray marching in sparse environments by dynamically allocating memory based on actual occupancy. name: N3-Tree
head: N-ary Octree, Octree / N3-Tree
body: The N3-Tree is a sparse pointer octree data structure designed for GPU-based traversal, originally introduced for surface texture encoding and later adapted for volume rendering. It distinguishes itself by enforcing a strict binary state for every node: a node is either a leaf containing data values or an internal node containing pointers to exactly N^3 children (typically N=2, resulting in 8 children). This regular subdivision simplifies memory layout and reduces indirections compared to general sparse octrees, making it suitable for storing regular data bricks. Input: A volumetric dataset represented as a sparse octree. Output: Traversal state (current node, ray position) or rendered color/opacity values. The tree is stored in RGBA 3D textures. Internal Nodes: The RGB channels encode pointers to child nodes. Leaf Nodes: The RGB channels encode data values (e.g., density, color). Flag Convention: The Alpha channel distinguishes between internal nodes and leaf nodes. Specific bit values for the flag are not detailed in the sources. Traversal is performed in a fragment shader. The algorithm follows the ray through the tree, resolving pointers from internal nodes until a leaf node is reached. 1. Initialize: Start at the root node. Determine the initial ray origin and direction. 2. Sample Node: Read the RGBA value of the current node from the 3D texture. 3. Check Type: Inspect the Alpha channel. If Alpha indicates Leaf: Sample the volumetric data from the RGB channels. Perform shading/compositing. Terminate traversal for this ray segment. If Alpha indicates Internal: Decode the child pointer from the RGB channels. Determine which of the 8 children the ray intersects. Update the current node to the child node. Update the ray's local coordinates or bounding box relative to the child. Repeat from Step 2. 4. Boundary Check: If the ray exits the tree bounds, terminate. Child Index: i = \lfloor z \cdot 4 \rfloor + \lfloor y \cdot 2 \rfloor + \lfloor x \cdot 1 \rfloor, where x, y, z \in [0, 1) are the normalized local coordinates of the ray origin relative to the current node's bounds. Child Offset: \Delta = \frac{S}{2}, where S is the current node's side length. The child's base position is P{child} = P{parent} + (i \bmod 2)\Delta \hat{x} + (\lfloor i/2 \rfloor \bmod 2)\Delta \hat{y} + (\lfloor i/4 \rfloor \bmod 2)\Delta \hat{z}. Local Coordinate Update: L{new} = L{old} - \Delta \cdot \text{sign}(L{old}). N: The number of subdivisions per axis. Typically N=2 (octree). N is an arbitrary integer. Precision: Pointer encoding in RGB channels may limit the maximum tree depth or addressable memory space. Empty Space: The structure distinguishes between internal nodes (pointers) and leaves (values). Empty space handling is not explicitly detailed, but the binary nature suggests that missing children might be represented by null pointers or specific flag values. Boundary Artifacts: Normalized coordinates must be clamped to [0, 0.9999] to prevent off-by-one child index selection at node edges. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversen3tree(rayorigin, raydirection, rootsize, maxdepth): # Initialize ray parameters relative to root currentnodepos = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] currentraylocal = rayorigin for depth in range(maxdepth): # Sample the current node from the 3D texture # RGB = pointer (internal) or value (leaf) # A = flag (internal vs leaf) nodedata = sample3dtexture(currentnodepos) alpha = nodedata.a if alpha > 0.5: # Leaf node flag density = nodedata.rgb return density 0.8 # Simplified shading else: # Internal node childpointer = nodedata.rgb # Compute normalized local coordinates nx = currentraylocal.x / rootsize ny = currentraylocal.y / rootsize nz = currentraylocal.z / rootsize # Clamp to [0, 1) to avoid boundary artifacts nx = max(0.0, min(nx, 0.9999)) ny = max(0.0, min(ny, 0.9999)) nz = max(0.0, min(nz, 0.9999)) # Determine child index (0-7) childidx = int(nz 4) + int(ny 2) + int(nx 1) # Compute child node position childsize = rootsize / 2.0 offsetx = (childidx & 1) childsize offsety = (childidx & 2) childsize offsetz = (childidx & 4) childsize currentnodepos = [childpointer + offsetx, childpointer + offsety, childpointer + offsetz] currentraylocal = [currentraylocal.x - offsetx, currentraylocal.y - offsety, currentraylocal.z - offsetz] # Check if ray is still within the child node bounds if not iswithinbounds(currentraylocal, childsize / 2.0): break return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] # Background color def sample3dtexture(pos): # Standard 3D texture lookup returning vec4 return texture3D(pos) def iswithinbounds(localpos, halfsize): return all(-halfsize <= p <= halfsize for p in localpos) This method accelerates sparse voxel traversal by decoupling the tree structure from the voxel data, storing them in separate memory pools. It solves the memory overhead and cache inefficiency of storing full child and neighbor pointers for every node. Unlike the general N3-Tree, which discusses the standard pointer structure, this variant specifically implements the node/brick pool architecture introduced by Crassin et al.. Memory: Compact storage due to the regular structure. Internal nodes store only one pointer (to the first child) if children are stored successively, or 8 pointers if not. Crassin et al. store all eight child nodes in successive regions, allowing one pointer per internal node, but require storing the first node marked as empty, which requires the same memory as storing eight pointers per node. Performance: Traversal in fragment shaders benefits from deep pipelining and identical processing of fragments. Reduced indirections improve memory locality. Limitations: The structure is considered a special case of Kd-Trees, and specific algorithms to exploit its regularity for ray traversal acceleration are not widely proposed in the literature. The N3-Tree was introduced by Lefebvre et al. for surface texture encoding. It was later used by Crassin et al. for volume rendering, where internal nodes are stored in a node pool and leaf nodes in a brick pool. Octrees and N3-trees are considered a special case of Kd-Trees, offering regular subdivision and compact storage. name: N^3 Tree with Node/Brick Pools
head: Crassin et al. method, Engel/Reichl method
body: This method accelerates sparse voxel traversal by decoupling the tree structure from the voxel data, storing them in separate memory pools. It solves the memory overhead and cache inefficiency of storing full child and neighbor pointers for every node. Unlike N^3 Tree, which discusses the general N^3 structure, this method specifically implements the node/brick pool architecture introduced by Crassin et al.. Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, N^3 tree root pointer, node pool, brick pool. Outputs: Transmittance and color accumulation along the ray. Data Structures: 1. Node Pool: An array of node entries. Each entry contains: childptr: A single pointer to a contiguous block of N^3 child node indices (or null if leaf). brickptr: A pointer to the voxel data (brick) in the Brick Pool. 2. Brick Pool: An array of voxel data blocks. Each block stores the volumetric data for a leaf node. 3. Ray State: Current position, step size, accumulated transmittance/color. Algorithm: The traversal uses an adapted kd-restart algorithm [FS05]. The key optimization is that all N^3 children are stored contiguously, allowing a single pointer dereference to access the child block. 1. Initialize: Start at the root node. Calculate initial step size based on the brick resolution. 2. Traverse: a. Determine the current brick index along the ray. b. If the current node is a leaf (indicated by childptr being null or a specific flag): i. Sample the voxel data at brickptr using the current ray position. ii. Update accumulation (compositing). iii. Advance ray by step size. c. If the current node is internal: i. Dereference childptr to get the block of N^3 child indices. ii. Determine which child contains the current ray position. iii. Update current node to the selected child. iv. Adjust step size if necessary (e.g., if entering a finer level). 3. Terminate: When ray exits the volume or transmittance drops below threshold. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseray(rayorigin, raydirection, rootnodeidx, nodepool, brickpool): # Initialize ray state t = 0.0 alpha = 0.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) currentnodeidx = rootnodeidx # Assume brick resolution is known or derived from context bricksize = getbricksize() step = bricksize while t < raymaxdistance: # Calculate current position pos = rayorigin + raydirection t # Get current node node = nodepool[currentnodeidx] if node.childptr is None: # Leaf node: sample brick brickdata = brickpool[node.brickptr] sample = samplevoxel(brickdata, pos) # Volume compositing (front-to-back) alphanew = 1.0 - exp(-sample.density step) color += sample.color alphanew (1.0 - alpha) alpha += alphanew (1.0 - alpha) if alpha >= 1.0: break t += step else: # Internal node: find child childblock = nodepool[node.childptr] # Block of N^3 children childidx = findchildindex(childblock, pos, bricksize) currentnodeidx = childblock[childidx] # Adjust step size if entering finer level (simplified) # In practice, step size might change based on child resolution pass return color, alpha Edge Cases: Precision: Floating-point errors in ray position calculation can cause incorrect child selection. Use epsilon guards. Boundaries: Ensure ray exit detection is robust to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. This method renders large volumetric datasets by combining an adaptive N^3-tree (a generalized octree) with mipmapped 3D texture bricks, enabling high-quality filtering and efficient GPU traversal. Memory: Significantly reduced compared to storing 8 child pointers + 6 neighbor pointers per node. Only one child pointer and one brick pointer are stored. Cache Coherence: Storing children contiguously improves cache locality during traversal. Performance: Efficient for sparse data where many nodes are leaves. Traversal overhead is low due to simple pointer chasing. Introduced by Crassin et al. in [CN09, CNLE09], this method was designed to handle large-scale volumetric datasets on GPUs. Engel [Eng11] and Reichl et al. [RTW13] adopted and refined this structure. It builds on the concept of page tables for volume rendering. name: N^3-Tree with Mipmapped Bricks
head: GigaVoxels Improved, Hybrid Structure
body: This method renders large volumetric datasets by combining an adaptive N^3-tree (a generalized octree) with mipmapped 3D texture bricks, enabling high-quality filtering and efficient GPU traversal. It distinguishes itself from earlier GigaVoxels implementations by storing a single pointer per node in a 3D texture block rather than eight child pointers and neighbor pointers, reducing memory usage by 16 times and improving cache coherence. Inputs: A volumetric dataset, a camera position, and a view direction. The structure consists of a Node Pool (3D texture) and a Brick Pool (3D texture). Outputs: A 2D image with accumulated color and opacity. The structure is mirrored on the CPU for updates but rendered entirely on the GPU. 1. Node Pool A 3D texture storing all tree nodes. It is organized into blocks of N^3 nodes. A single pointer accesses all children of a node due to this grouping. 2. Node Data Structure (64 bits total) Each node is stored as a 64-bit value with the following layout: Bits 0–29 (30 bits): Child pointer. Used for non-leaf nodes. Value 0 indicates no children exist. Bit 30 (1 bit): Refinement flag. Indicates if the node is refined to maximum or if the original volume contains more data. Bit 31 (1 bit): Content type. 0 indicates a constant RGBA8 value (e.g., empty or core regions); 1 indicates the content is described by a brick. Bits 32–63 (32 bits): Payload. If Content Type is Brick: 30 bits for a pointer to an M^3 brick in the Brick Pool. If Content Type is Constant: 32 bits representing the average constant value (4 \times 8 bits for RGBA8). 3. Brick Pool A large 3D texture storing the voxel data. Bricks are small voxel grids of predefined size M^3 (typically M=32). The pool is limited in size; the algorithm ensures bricks of all visible leaf nodes are present in the pool, updating content as the viewpoint changes. 1. Initialization Rasterize proxy geometry to deliver ray origins and directions to the fragment shader. Compute entry and exit points of the ray in the volume's bounding box using a pre-rendering pass with alpha blending (front-facing depth in luminance, back-facing depth inverted in alpha) or tiling two depth buffers. 2. Iterative Descent (Traversal) Recursive DDA is inefficient on GPUs due to lack of fast indexable memory; thus, an iterative descent is used. 1. Start at the ray origin. 2. Locate the current point x in the N^3-tree top-down. 3. Calculate the offset to the child node: offset = \lfloor x \cdot N \rfloor, where x \in [0, 1]^3 is the point's local coordinate in the bounding box and N is the branching factor. 4. Fetch the child node at index c + offset, where c is the pointer to the current node's children block. 5. Update the local coordinate: x{new} = x \cdot N - offset. 6. Repeat steps 2–5 until a node with the appropriate Level of Detail (LOD) is reached. The LOD is determined in the shader such that a voxel projects to at most one pixel; this node is not necessarily a leaf. 3. Node Processing Constant Node: If the reached node indicates a constant value, integrate the value analytically along the distance traversed within the node. Brick Node: If the node contains a brick, perform standard ray-marching through the M^3 brick data using quadrilinear filtering (mipmapping) until the ray leaves the current node's spatial extent. Next Step: Use the new position (where the ray exited the current node) as the origin for the next descent. 4. Rendering The ray-casting is performed using one big fragment shader for both top-down traversal and brick sampling, which proved more efficient than separate passes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolume(rayorigin, raydirection, entryt, exitt, nodepool, brickpool, N, M): currentptr = 0 # Root pointer currentlocal = normalize(rayorigin) # Normalize to [0,1]^3 relative to volume bounds t = entryt accumulatedcolor = vec4(0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 while t < exitt: tempptr = currentptr templocal = currentlocal # Iterative descent to find appropriate LOD node while True: offset = floor(templocal N) nodeval = nodepool.fetch(tempptr + offset) childptr = nodeval & 0x3FFFFFFF isbrick = (nodeval >> 31) & 1 # Standard LOD check: node spatial extent <= pixel footprint # (Implementation detail handled by shader hardware) if True: break if childptr == 0: # Leaf reached break # Descent step tempptr = childptr templocal = templocal N - offset # Process node if isbrick: brickptr = (nodeval >> 32) & 0x3FFFFFFF # Ray-AABB intersection for node's local bounds [0,1]^3 nodeexitt = t + 1.0 / max(abs(raydirection)) # Standard ray-marching through M^3 brick data with quadrilinear filtering step = (nodeexitt - t) / M brickcolor = vec4(0.0) brickalpha = 0.0 post = t for in range(M): localbrickcoord = (post - t) / step sample = brickpool.sample(brickptr, localbrickcoord) brickcolor += sample (1.0 - brickalpha) brickalpha += sample.a (1.0 - brickalpha) post += step accumulatedcolor += brickcolor (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedalpha += brickalpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) t = nodeexitt else: # Constant value integration val = vec4(float(nodeval & 0xFF), float((nodeval >> 8) & 0xFF), float((nodeval >> 16) & 0xFF), float((nodeval >> 24) & 0xFF)) # Ray-AABB intersection for node's local bounds [0,1]^3 nodeexitt = t + 1.0 / max(abs(raydirection)) dist = nodeexitt - t accumulatedcolor += val dist (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedalpha += dist (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) t = nodeexitt return accumulatedcolor Branching Factor N: The number of children per node is N^3. N=2 is a standard octree. Trade-off: low N for memory efficiency (deep tree), large N for traversal efficiency (shallow tree). Brick Size M: The side length of the voxel grid in a brick. Typically M=32. Recursive DDA: Recursive DDA traversal is inefficient on GPUs due to lack of fast indexable memory in shader processors. The iterative descent is used instead. LOD Determination: The traversal does not need the structure to indicate correct level-of-details (as done in previous work like Gobbetti et al.). The LOD is determined in the shader, which minimizes update operations. Neighbor Pointers: The structure does not exhibit neighbor pointers between adjacent nodes. An efficient traversal remains possible without them due to the iterative descent and cache coherence. Time Complexity: Traversal is efficient due to the iterative descent and hardware texture caching. The cost is dominated by ray-marching within bricks and the overhead of re-descending the tree for each node exit. Memory Complexity: Memory requirements are largely reduced compared to Gobbetti et al. [GMAG08] because only a single pointer is used per node (stored in a 3D texture block) instead of eight child pointers and neighbor pointers, reducing storage by 16 times. Performance: The method enables high-quality filtering via mipmapping and efficient GPU rendering. Strengths: High memory efficiency, cache coherence, high-quality filtering, unified rendering and visibility on GPU. Limitations: Limited brick pool size requires careful management and updates as viewpoint changes. The method was introduced in the "GigaVoxels" paper by Laine et al.. It builds upon the concept of adaptive space subdivision and N^3-trees (similar to [LHN05a]). The specific "Improved" variant with mipmapped bricks and the single-pointer node structure was presented to address the memory and cache inefficiencies of earlier GigaVoxels implementations. name: HashDAG Ray Traversal
head: trace_paths [S1, unofficial]
body: HashDAG Ray Traversal is a GPU kernel that traverses a HashDAG structure to find the path of a ray through a sparse voxel volume, storing the sequence of child indices taken at each level. It serves as the foundational traversal mechanism for Shadow Tracing with HashDAG. The method computes the intersection of a ray with the HashDAG by maintaining a traversal state that includes the current path, a stack for backtracking, and a cache for node metadata. It processes one ray per thread, launching from a ray-grid. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: cameraPosition, rayMin (near plane), rayDDx, rayDDy (derivatives for anti-aliasing or mipmapping), imageWidth, imageHeight, dag (the HashDAG structure). Outputs: A boolean indicating intersection, or the path (sequence of child indices) to the first intersecting leaf node, stored in pathsSurface. Data Structures: StackEntry: A struct containing: index: uint32, the node index in the HashDAG. childMask: uint8, bitmask of children present in the node. visitMask: uint8, bitmask of unvisited children. CachedLeaf: Used for the last two levels (packed densely into a single 64-bit word). Contains methods getfirstchildmask() and getsecondchildmask(nextChild). Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate pixel coordinates from blockIdx and threadIdx; return if outside image bounds. 2. Compute rayOrigin from cameraPosition and rayDirection by normalizing the vector from camera to pixel position. 3. Compute rayDirectionInverse using double precision for reciprocal components. 4. Determine rayChildOrder bitmask: bit 4 if x < 0, bit 2 if y < 0, bit 1 if z < 0. 5. Initialize traversal state: level=0, path=(0,0,0), stack, and cache with root node index, childMask, and initial visitMask. 6. Ascend the stack if no children left to visit: decrement level and restore cache from stack until visitMask is non-zero or level is 0. 7. If level is 0 and no children left, reset path and break loop. 8. Ascend path by difference between old and new level, update level. 9. Find next child to visit using nextchild function based on rayChildOrder and current visitMask. 10. Mark child as visited by clearing its bit in visitMask. 11. Descend path with nextChild, save current cache to stack at current level, and increment level. 12. If level equals total DAG levels, break loop (leaf voxel reached). 13. If at internal node (level < leaflevel), compute child index, update childMask, and compute new visitMask. 14. If at second-to-last or last level, handle packed leaf data: get childMask from cachedLeaf, update visitMask. 15. Store the final path to the output surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hashdagraytraversal(cameraposition, raymin, rayddx, rayddy, imagewidth, imageheight, dag, pathssurface): # Standard CUDA runtime variables provided by the execution environment # blockIdx, blockDim, threadIdx are assumed defined # 1. Pixel and Ray Setup pixelx = (blockIdx.x blockDim.x) + threadIdx.x pixely = (blockIdx.y blockDim.y) + threadIdx.y if pixelx >= imagewidth or pixely >= imageheight: return False # Compute ray direction by normalizing vector from camera to pixel position pixelpos = (float(pixelx), float(pixely), 0.0) raydirection = normalize(pixelpos - cameraposition) rayorigin = cameraposition # Compute rayDirectionInverse using double precision raydirectioninverse = (1.0 / raydirection.x, 1.0 / raydirection.y, 1.0 / raydirection.z) # Determine rayChildOrder bitmask: bit 4 if x<0, bit 2 if y<0, bit 1 if z<0 raychildorder = 0 if raydirection.x < 0: raychildorder |= 1 << 4 if raydirection.y < 0: raychildorder |= 1 << 2 if raydirection.z < 0: raychildorder |= 1 << 1 # 2. Initialization level = 0 path = [] # Stores child indices stack = [None] MAXLEVELS cache = {'index': 0, 'childmask': 0, 'visitmask': 0} cache['index'] = dag.getfirstnodeindex() cache['childmask'] = dag.getnodechildmask(0, cache['index']) cache['visitmask'] = cache['childmask'] & computeintersectionmask( level=0, path=path, dag=dag, rayorigin=rayorigin, raydirection=raydirection, raydirectioninverse=raydirectioninverse, isroot=True) # 3. Traversal Loop while True: # Ascend if no children left to visit newlevel = level while newlevel > 0 and cache['visitmask'] == 0: newlevel -= 1 cache = stack[newlevel] if newlevel == 0 and cache['visitmask'] == 0: path = [] return False # No intersection # Update path and level after ascent path = path[:len(path) - (level - newlevel)] # ascend level = newlevel # Find next child to visit based on rayChildOrder and visitMask nextchild = findnextchild(cache['visitmask'], raychildorder) # Mark child as visited cache['visitmask'] &= ~(1 << nextchild) # Descend into child path.append(nextchild) stack[level] = cache level += 1 # Check for leaf hit if level == dag.levels: pathssurface.write(path) return True # Intersection found # Process internal or packed leaf nodes if level < dag.leaflevel(): # Internal node cache['index'] = dag.getchildindex(level - 1, cache['index'], cache['childmask'], nextchild) cache['childmask'] = dag.getnodechildmask(level, cache['index']) cache['visitmask'] = cache['childmask'] & computeintersectionmask( level=level, path=path, dag=dag, rayorigin=rayorigin, raydirection=raydirection, raydirectioninverse=raydirectioninverse, isroot=False) else: # Packed leaf data (last two levels) if level == dag.leaflevel(): childmask = cachedleaf.getfirstchildmask() else: childmask = cachedleaf.getsecondchildmask(nextchild) cache['childmask'] = childmask cache['visitmask'] = cache['childmask'] & computeintersectionmask( level=level, path=path, dag=dag, rayorigin=rayorigin, raydirection=raydirection, raydirectioninverse=raydirectioninverse, isroot=False) return False def findnextchild(visitmask, raychildorder): # Apply priority mask first, fallback to full visitmask priority = raychildorder & visitmask if priority == 0: priority = visitmask # Return index of highest set bit (31 - clz equivalent) return 31 - (32 - priority.bitlength()) def computeintersectionmask(level, path, dag, rayorigin, raydirection, raydirectioninverse, isroot): mask = 0 # Determine bounding box of current node based on level and path nodemin, nodemax = dag.getnodebounds(level, path) # Test each child bit in childMask for childidx in range(8): if not (dag.getnodechildmask(level, path[-1] if path else 0) & (1 << childidx)): continue # Compute child AABB (2x2x2 subdivision) childmin, childmax = computechildaabb(nodemin, nodemax, childidx) # Ray-AABB intersection test if rayaabbintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, raydirectioninverse, childmin, childmax): mask |= (1 << childidx) return mask def rayaabbintersect(origin, direction, invdir, minb, maxb): tmin = (minb[0] - origin[0]) invdir[0] tmax = (maxb[0] - origin[0]) invdir[0] if tmin > tmax: tmin, tmax = tmax, tmin tymin = (minb[1] - origin[1]) invdir[1] tymax = (maxb[1] - origin[1]) invdir[1] if tymin > tymax: tymin, tymax = tymax, tymin if tmin > tymax or tymin > tmax: return False if tymin > tmin: tmin = tymin if tymax < tmax: tmax = tymax tzmin = (minb[2] - origin[2]) invdir[2] tzmax = (maxb[2] - origin[2]) invdir[2] if tzmin > tzmax: tzmin, tzmax = tzmax, tzmin if tmin > tzmax or tzmin > tmax: return False return True def computechildaabb(parentmin, parentmax, childidx): mid = [(parentmin[i] + parentmax[i]) / 2.0 for i in range(3)] childmin = [parentmin[i] if (childidx >> i) & 1 == 0 else mid[i] for i in range(3)] childmax = [mid[i] if (childidx >> i) & 1 == 0 else parentmax[i] for i in range(3)] return childmin, childmax Parameters: traceParams: Contains cameraPosition, rayMin, rayDDx, rayDDy, imageWidth, imageHeight, and pathsSurface. MAXLEVELS: Not given in the sources. dag.leaflevel(): Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Packed Levels: The last two levels are packed densely into a single 64-bit word. The code must distinguish between the second-to-last level (level == dag.leaflevel()) and the last level (level > dag.leaflevel()) to retrieve the correct child mask from cachedLeaf. Precision: rayDirectionInverse must be computed using double precision to avoid artifacts. Computes final pixel color by determining if the ray's path is occluded by scene geometry (shadowed) and applying lighting/fog. It treats the HashDAG as implicit geometry for shadow testing. Choose this when shadowing is required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Benchmarks are available for scenes like teaserstatue and teaserchurch at various depths (e.g., depth 17). Strengths: Efficient traversal of sparse voxel volumes using HashDAG structure. name: Shadow Tracing with HashDAG
body: This method computes the final pixel color for a ray-grid traversal by determining if the ray's path through the volume is occluded by the scene geometry (shadowed) and applying lighting and fog effects. It differs from standard volume rendering by treating the HashDAG as an implicit geometry for shadow testing rather than integrating density along the ray, relying on the parent HashDAG Ray Traversal to provide the ray path. Inputs: params: A structure containing colorsSurface (output buffer), pathsSurface (ray path data), rayMin, rayDDx, rayDDy (camera ray parameters), cameraPosition (camera origin), shadowBias (shadow ray origin offset), and fogDensity (base fog density). dag: The HashDAG structure representing the volume geometry. sundirection: Normalized vector for the light source. Outputs: Updated params.colorsSurface with the computed uint32 RGB888 color for the current pixel. Data Structures: Path: Loaded from params.pathsSurface, contains rayOrigin (float3). float3 and double3: 3-component floating-point and double-precision vectors. Parameters: EXACTSHADOWS: Boolean flag. If true, shadow start is the intersection point; otherwise, it is the ray origin. PERVOXELFACESHADING: Boolean flag. If true, uses voxel face normals for lighting; otherwise, uses uniform lighting. fogDensity: Scaled by 0.00001 before use. sundirection: Default value normalize(makefloat3(0.3, 1.0, 0.5)). Steps: 1. Calculate pixel coordinates: pixel.x = blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x, pixel.y = blockIdx.y blockDim.y + threadIdx.y. Return if outside image bounds. 2. Load ray origin from params.pathsSurface using Path::load. Compute camera ray direction: normalize(params.rayMin + pixel.x params.rayDDx + (imageHeight - 1 - pixel.y) params.rayDDy - params.cameraPosition). 3. If length(rayOrigin) == 0.0, set color with light=1, distance=1e9, direction=cameraRayDirection, and return. 4. If EXACTSHADOWS or PERVOXELFACESHADING, compute hitPosition using rayboxintersection with rayOriginDouble and rayOriginDouble + 1. If EXACTSHADOWS, shadowStart = hitPosition; else shadowStart = rayOrigin. 5. Get sun direction: direction = sundirection(). Check shadow: isShadowed = intersectraynodeoutoforder(dag, shadowStart + params.shadowBias direction, direction). 6. Calculate distance v = makedouble3(rayOrigin) - params.cameraPosition, distance = length(v), nv = v / distance. If isShadowed, call setColor(0, distance, nv). Else, if PERVOXELFACESHADING, compute normal from voxel origin to hit position, truncate to integer components, and call setColor(max(0.0, dot(makefloat3(normal), sundirection())), distance, nv). Else, call setColor(1, distance, nv). 7. Fog amount calculation: fogAmount = 1.0 - exp(-distance fogDensity) where fogDensity is scaled by 0.00001. Sun amount calculation: sunAmount = 1.01 max(dot(rayDir, makedouble3(sundirection())), 0.0). Fog color interpolation: fogColor = lerp(makefloat3(187, 242, 250) / 255.0, makefloat3(1.0), float(pow(sunAmount, 30.0))). Final color application: return lerp(rgb, fogColor, clamp(float(fogAmount), 0.0, 1.0)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. 1 - pixely) params.rayDDy[0] - params.cameraPosition[0], params.rayMin[1] + pixelx params.rayDDx[1] + (imageHeight - 1 - pixely) params.rayDDy[1] - params.cameraPosition[1], params.rayMin[2] + pixelx params.rayDDx[2] + (imageHeight - 1 - pixely) params.rayDDy[2] - params.cameraPosition[2]) raydir = normalize(rawdir) if length(rayorigin) == 0.0: color = computecolor(1.0, 1e9, raydir, params, sundirection) writecolor(params.colorsSurface, pixelx, pixely, color) return rayorigindouble = makedouble3(rayorigin) if params.EXACTSHADOWS or params.PERVOXELFACESHADING: hitposition = rayboxintersection(rayorigindouble, (rayorigindouble[0] + 1.0, rayorigindouble[1] + 1.0, rayorigindouble[2] + 1.0)) if params.EXACTSHADOWS: shadowstart = hitposition else: shadowstart = rayorigin else: shadowstart = rayorigin direction = sundirection biasoffset = (shadowstart[0] + params.shadowBias direction[0], shadowstart[1] + params.shadowBias direction[1], shadowstart[2] + params.shadowBias direction[2]) isshadowed = intersectraynodeoutoforder(dag, biasoffset, direction) v = makedouble3(rayorigin[0] - params.cameraPosition[0], rayorigin[1] - params.cameraPosition[1], rayorigin[2] - params.cameraPosition[2]) distance = length(v) nv = (v[0]/distance, v[1]/distance, v[2]/distance) if isshadowed: light = 0.0 elif params.PERVOXELFACESHADING: normalvec = (hitposition[0] - rayorigindouble[0], hitposition[1] - rayorigindouble[1], hitposition[2] - rayorigindouble[2]) normalint = truncatetointeger(normalvec) light = max(0.0, dot(makefloat3(normalint), sundirection)) else: light = 1.0 color = computecolor(light, distance, nv, params, sundirection) writecolor(params.colorsSurface, pixelx, pixely, color) def computecolor(light, distance, nv, params, sundirection): rgb = readcolor(params.colorsSurface) lightfactor = clamp(0.5 + light, 0.0, 1.0) rgb = (rgb[0]lightfactor, rgb[1]lightfactor, rgb[2]lightfactor) fogdensityscaled = params.fogDensity 0.00001 fogamount = 1.0 - math.exp(-distance fogdensityscaled) sunamount = 1.01 max(dot(nv, makedouble3(sundirection)), 0.0) fogcolorbase = (187/255.0, 242/255.0, 250/255.0) fogcolortop = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) fogcolor = lerp(fogcolorbase, fogcolortop, pow(sunamount, 30.0)) finalcolor = lerp(rgb, fogcolor, clamp(fogamount, 0.0, 1.0)) return finalcolor def readcolor(buffer): # Not given in the sources. return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def writecolor(buffer, x, y, color): r = int(clamp(color[0], 0.0, 1.0) 255) g = int(clamp(color[1], 0.0, 1.0) 255) b = int(clamp(color[2], 0.0, 1.0) 255) uint32color = (r << 16) | (g << 8) | b buffer[x, y] = uint32color Time Complexity: Dominated by the shadow ray intersection intersectraynodeoutoforder. The complexity depends on the HashDAG depth and the number of nodes traversed by the shadow ray. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory per thread; relies on the HashDAG structure in global memory. Strengths: Efficiently handles shadows for sparse volumes without explicit geometry reconstruction. Limitations: Shadow ray tracing can be expensive if the HashDAG is deep or if many rays are shadowed. The EXACTSHADOWS mode requires additional ray-box intersection calculations. When to use: When shadows are required for sparse voxel volumes and the HashDAG structure is already available for traversal. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and shadow rays are too expensive, or when the volume is dense and standard ray marching is more appropriate. This method is part of the HashDAG rendering pipeline, specifically designed for GPU-based volume rendering using hierarchical sparse voxel structures.
