name: Ray-AABB Intersection for Octree Traversal
head: Ray-Parameter Function, Revelles, Urena and Lastra Octree Traversal
body: This algorithm determines whether a ray intersects an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) representing an octree node and prepares parameters for traversing its subtrees. It distinguishes itself by normalizing the ray direction to be strictly positive through coordinate flipping, which simplifies the subsequent intersection logic and traversal order determination. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d (3D vectors). Octree node bounds: minimum corner \min, maximum corner \max, and node size \size. Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection. If intersecting, calls processSubtree with entry/exit distances and a bitmask. Data Structures: a: Unsigned integer bitmask (3 bits) indicating which axes were flipped. t0: Vector of entry distances per axis. t1: Vector of exit distances per axis. t: Scalar tracking the maximum entry distance (closest entry point). Steps: 1. Initialize bitmask a = 0. 2. Copy ray origin o and direction d. 3. For each axis i \in \{0, 1, 2\}: If d[i] < 0: Flip origin: o[i] = \size[i] - o[i]. Negate direction: d[i] = -d[i]. Set bit i in a: a \ |= \ (1 \ll (2-i)). Specifically: bit 2 (value 4) for axis 0, bit 1 (value 2) for axis 1, bit 0 (value 1) for axis 2. 4. Compute entry distances: t0 = (\min - o) / d. 5. Compute exit distances: t1 = (\max - o) / d. 6. Initialize t = \infty (maximum double value). 7. Check intersection: If \max(t0) < \min(t1), the ray intersects the box. Call processSubtree(t0, t1, r, t, sd, a). Otherwise, return false. Formulas: Origin flip: o[i] = \size[i] - o[i]. Entry distance: t0[i] = (\min[i] - o[i]) / d[i]. Exit distance: t1[i] = (\max[i] - o[i]) / d[i]. Intersection condition: \max(t0) < \min(t1). Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Incorrect traversal logic or misinterpretation of \size can cause rendering artifacts, such as only the upper-right part of the image being rendered while the rest is rejected. The formula o[i] = \size[i] - o[i] is specific to the implementation cited. Standard implementations often use o[i] = \max[i] - o[i] or similar depending on coordinate space. Sources indicate ambiguity in \size: it is either \size = \max - \min or \size = (\max - \min) / 2. Implementers must verify the definition of \size in their specific octree structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayaabbintersect(octnode, ray): # Inputs: octnode with attributes min, max, size # ray with attributes origin (o), direction (d) a = 0 o = [ray.origin[0], ray.origin[1], ray.origin[2]] d = [ray.direction[0], ray.direction[1], ray.direction[2]] # Normalize ray direction to be positive if d[0] < 0: o[0] = octnode.size[0] - o[0] d[0] = -d[0] a |= 4 # Bit 2 if d[1] < 0: o[1] = octnode.size[1] - o[1] d[1] = -d[1] a |= 2 # Bit 1 if d[2] < 0: o[2] = octnode.size[2] - o[2] d[2] = -d[2] a |= 1 # Bit 0 # Compute intersection distances t0 = [(octnode.min[i] - o[i]) / d[i] for i in range(3)] t1 = [(octnode.max[i] - o[i]) / d[i] for i in range(3)] t = float('inf') # Check for intersection if max(t0) < min(t1): # processsubtree(t0, t1, ray, t, sd, a) is not defined in the sources; # it handles child traversal using bitmask a and distance t. return True else: return False Time Complexity: O(1) per node visit. The intersection test involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Simplifies traversal logic by ensuring positive ray directions, allowing consistent ordering of child node visits based on the bitmask. Limitations: Relies on correct interpretation of node size and bounds. Incorrect implementation can lead to significant rendering errors (e.g., missing image regions). When to use: When traversing an octree where node bounds are axis-aligned and the traversal order needs to be determined by the ray's entry/exit points relative to the node's children. This method is based on the "Efficient Parametric Algorithm for Octree Traversal" by Revelles, Urena, and Lastra. The specific implementation details and pitfalls discussed in the sources stem from a community discussion on Stack Overflow regarding an implementation of this algorithm. The algorithm is a standard technique in volume rendering and ray tracing for efficient spatial subdivision traversal. name: Ray-Octant Traversal (Entry)
head: findEntryOctant, findNextOctant
body: Determines the index of the first octant a ray enters within a local 2×2×2 block of an octree, and the index of the subsequent octant the ray traverses. It maps ray-parametric intersections to discrete octant indices using axis-aligned comparisons. Inputs: tx0, ty0, tz0: Ray projection parameters at the start of the current segment. tx1, ty1, tz1: Ray projection parameters at the end of the current segment. txm, tym, tzm: Ray projection parameters at the midpoint of the current octant along each axis. Outputs: entryIndex: Integer 0–7 representing the octant index the ray enters. nextOctant: Integer 0–7 representing the next octant to visit. Data Structures: octantTable: An 8 \times 3 lookup table where octantTable[currentOctant][exit] returns the next octant index. exit is 0 for the YZ-plane, 1 for the XZ-plane, and 2 for the XY-plane. Formulas: Midpoint parameters: txm = 0.5 \times (tx0 + tx1), tym = 0.5 \times (ty0 + ty1), tzm = 0.5 \times (tz0 + tz1). Steps: 1. Calculate Entry Index: Initialize entry = 0. Compare start parameters to find the largest: If tx0 is the largest (tx0 > ty0 and tx0 > tz0): the ray enters through the YZ-plane (index 0). If tym < tx0, set bit 1: entry |= 2. If tzm < tx0, set bit 0: entry |= 1. Else if ty0 is larger than tz0: the ray enters through the XZ-plane (index 1). If txm < ty0, set bit 2: entry |= 4. If tzm < ty0, set bit 0: entry |= 1. Else (tz0 is largest): the ray enters through the XY-plane (index 2). If txm < tz0, set bit 2: entry |= 4. If tym < tz0, set bit 1: entry |= 2. Return entry. 2. Calculate Next Octant: Compare exit parameters tx1 and ty1. If tx1 < ty1, set mint = tx1 and exit = 0 (YZ-plane). Else, set mint = ty1 and exit = 1 (XZ-plane). If tz1 < mint, set exit = 2 (XY-plane). Return octantTable[currentOctant][exit]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findentryoctant(tx0, ty0, tz0, txm, tym, tzm): entry = 0 if tx0 > ty0 and tx0 > tz0: if tym < tx0: entry |= 2 if tzm < tx0: entry |= 1 elif ty0 > tz0: if txm < ty0: entry |= 4 if tzm < ty0: entry |= 1 else: if txm < tz0: entry |= 4 if tym < tz0: entry |= 2 return entry def findnextoctant(currentoctant, tx1, ty1, tz1, octanttable): if tx1 < ty1: mint = tx1 exitplane = 0 else: mint = ty1 exitplane = 1 if tz1 < mint: exitplane = 2 return octanttable[currentoctant][exitplane] OCTANTTABLE = [ [1, 2, 4], [3, 6, 5], [9, 10, 12], [11, 14, 13], [17, 18, 20], [19, 22, 21], [25, 26, 28], [27, 30, 29] ] Parameters: tx0, ty0, tz0: Start t-values. txm, tym, tzm: Midpoint t-values. tx1, ty1, tz1: End t-values. octantTable: 8 \times 3 integer array. Edge Cases: Ray origin exactly on a plane boundary: The strict comparisons (>, <) determine the entry. Exact equality may lead to arbitrary but consistent selection depending on implementation. Degenerate ray (zero length): tx0 == tx1, etc. The logic still holds but txm == tx0. Outside-in rays: The algorithm assumes tx0, ty0, tz0 represent parametric distances to the current node's faces; negative directions are handled correctly by the midpoint comparisons. Time Complexity: O(1) for both entry and next octant calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the lookup table (24 integers). Strengths: Branch-minimized entry calculation; fast traversal step. Limitations: Requires pre-computed or maintained lookup table; specific to pointer-based octree traversal where children are accessed via flags. Used in efficient raycasting through sparse octrees where nodes are stored in arrays and accessed via bit flags. sparse-octree module, https://github.com/vanruesc/sparse-octree, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Octree Raycasting (Point Intersection)
head: raycast (PointOctant)
body: This method finds points within a pointer-based octree that intersect with a given ray by iterating through intersecting octants and testing the points contained within them. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A raycaster (defining origin and direction) and a PointOctree instance. Output: A list of RayPointIntersection objects representing the intersected points. Data Structures: PointOctree<T>: Extends Octree<PointOctant<T>>. bias: Number. Octant boundary bias. Defaults to 0.0. maxPoints: Number. Maximum distinct points per leaf octant before a split occurs. Defaults to 8. maxDepth: Number. Maximum tree depth level, starting at 0. Defaults to 8. PointOctant<T>: Represents a node in the octree. pointData: Holds the points stored in this octant. Parameters: bias: Default 0.0. Must be \ge 0. maxPoints: Default 8. Must be \ge 1. maxDepth: Default 8. Must be \ge 0. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty list result of type RayPointIntersection. 2. Retrieve the list of octants intersecting the ray by calling the parent traversal method getintersectingnodes(raycaster). 3. If the list of intersecting octants is not empty: a. Iterate through each octant in the list. b. Check if the octant contains point data (pointData is not None). c. If point data exists, call pointData.testPoints(raycaster, result) to identify specific points within the octant that intersect the ray and add them to result. 4. Return the result list. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointoctreeraycast(raycaster, octree): # 1. Initialize result list result = [] # 2. Get intersecting octants using parent traversal logic intersectingoctants = octree.getintersectingnodes(raycaster) # 3. Iterate through octants if intersectingoctants: for octant in intersectingoctants: # 4. Check for point data if octant.pointData is not None: # 5. Test points within this octant against the ray octant.pointData.testPoints(raycaster, result) # 6. Return results return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Allowing maxDepth to be infinite can result in poor performance due to infinitely small octants. The bias parameter must be non-negative and affects the looseness of the octree boundaries. Octants without pointData are skipped, optimizing traversal for sparse data. A GPU-based technique extending this method by adding recursive shading for non-opaque surfaces to simulate transparent and reflective materials. Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. This method originates from the sparse-octree library implementation. It is designed to work with the PointOctant class to provide efficient raycasting against discrete point sets. sparse-octree module, https://github.com/vanruesc/sparse-octree, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Octree Raycasting with Refraction and Reflection
head: CUDA Octree Raycasting with Refraction and Reflection
body: A GPU-based volume rendering technique that traverses an octree using CUDA kernels to compute ray-surface intersections, handling refraction and reflection recursively to simulate transparent and reflective materials. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree data structure representing the volume, camera position, Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix, viewport dimensions (width \times height), and rendering flags (enablereflection, enablerefraction, depth buffer enabled). Output: A color buffer (image) and optionally a depth buffer. Data Structures: The method relies on specific structures to track traversal state and hit information: 1. StackEntry: Used for parent voxel tracking during traversal. parent: const int32t pointer to the parent node. tmax: float maximum t-value for the current voxel. 2. RaycastHit: Stores the result of a raycast intersection. hitt: float distance to the hit. hitpos: glm::vec3 world position of the hit. hitparent: const int32t pointer to the parent node. hitidx: int32t child index. hitposinternal: glm::vec3 internal position within the voxel. hitscale: int32t scale/depth of the hit node. Parameters: MAXSCALE: The maximum depth of the octree, defined as 23, corresponding to the number of bits in a single precision float. THREADSPERBLOCKSQUARE: The number of threads per block in each dimension, set to 32, which is a multiple of the warp size. HALFSQRT2: A constant used for origin offsetting, equal to \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize CUDA Kernel Grid: Calculate block size as dim3(32, 32) and grid size as dim3((width + 31) / 32, (height + 31) / 32) to cover the viewport dimensions. 2. Compute Eye Ray: For each pixel (x, y), normalize coordinates to [0,1], convert to NDC [-1,1], multiply by the MVP matrix, and normalize the resulting vector to get the ray direction. The origin is the camera position. 3. Initial Raycast: Call raycast(tree, &eyeray, stack, &raycastHit) to find the first surface intersection in the octree. 4. Handle Hit: If raycastHit.hitscale < MAXSCALE, calculate NDC depth from hitpos using the MVP matrix, clamp to [-1,1], and write to the depth buffer if enabled. Decompress raw attachment to get shading attributes. 5. Shade Fragment: Call shade<0>(renderingattributes, eyeray, raycastHit, stack, tree) to compute the initial color, which may recursively handle refraction and reflection. 6. Refraction Handling: If enablereflection is false but refraction is active, calculate the surface normal, adjust for the dot product sign, compute the refracted direction using indices of refraction, and offset the origin to avoid self-intersection. 7. Refraction Origin Offset: Set refractionray.origin to hitpos + direction HALFSQRT2 exp2f(hit.hitscale - MAXSCALE) to prevent self-intersection after refraction. 8. Recursive Refraction: If refractionhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE, recursively call shade<recursions+1> and add to output weighted by oneminusalpha. Otherwise, add ambient color weighted by oneminusalpha. 9. Recursive Reflection: If reflectionhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE, recursively call shade<recursions+1> and add to output weighted by reflectivity. Otherwise, add clear color weighted by reflectivity. 10. name: Stack-based traversal
head: Iterative octree traversal, Explicit stack traversal
body: Stack-based traversal is a method for navigating hierarchical spatial structures, such as Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO) or Bounding Volume Hierarchies (BVH), by replacing recursive function calls with an explicit data structure (a stack) to manage the traversal state. It solves the problem of stack overflow in deep trees and improves cache locality by allowing linear memory access patterns for node fetching. Unlike recursive implementations, it explicitly controls visitation order by pushing children onto the stack based on their distance from the ray origin, ensuring closer nodes are processed first. The core mechanism involves maintaining a stack of traversal states, where each state typically contains the node index or pointer, and intersection parameters (t{min}, t{max}) relative to the ray. 1. Initialization: The stack is initialized with the root node and the ray's entry/exit distances for the root bounding volume. 2. Loop: While the stack is not empty: Pop the top state. Perform a ray-node intersection test (e.g., slab method for AABBs). If the node is a leaf, process it (e.g., sample volume) and terminate or continue based on requirements. If the node is internal, compute intersection distances for its children. Push children onto the stack in reverse order of their distance from the ray origin (farthest first) so that the closest child is popped next. 3. Backtracking: Implicitly handled by the stack; when a subtree is exhausted, the algorithm naturally returns to the parent state stored in the stack. Key mathematical operations include the slab intersection test for axis-aligned bounding boxes: t{min} = \maxi \left( \frac{boxMini - oi}{di} \right), \quad t{max} = \mini \left( \frac{boxMaxi - oi}{di} \right) where o is ray origin and d is ray direction. Zero direction components must be handled by clamping di to \epsilon or using infinity for t calculations. Uses a stack to step through a grid hierarchy, prioritizing closer nodes to skip empty regions. Explicitly manages a stack to control visitation order based on eye position, differing from state-machine approaches. Uses an explicit stack on CPU to avoid recursion overhead and leverage cache-friendly memory access. Stack-based traversal is a standard technique in ray tracing and volume rendering, originating from the need to handle deep recursion limits in hardware or constrained environments. It is widely used in CPU-based SVO renderers and GPU implementations where explicit stack management is required for dynamic branching.

name: Hierarchical Traversal
head: SVO Traversal, Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) Traversal
body: Hierarchical traversal accelerates volume rendering by navigating a multi-resolution spatial hierarchy (such as an Octree or Sparse Voxel Octree) where each cell at a higher level covers a 2 \times 2 area of the level below. This allows the renderer to take larger steps at higher levels, reducing the total number of steps compared to non-hierarchical traversal. It sets itself apart from flat grid traversal by using a resolution hierarchy, and from BVH Traversal by maintaining a strict resolution hierarchy coupled to the data structure rather than arbitrary bounding volumes. Hierarchical traversal builds on the stack-based principles of Stack-based traversal, applying them to nodes with variable spatial extents. Input: A ray defined by origin O and direction D; a hierarchical data structure (Octree/SVO) where each node has a bounding box and child pointers. Output: A sequence of leaf nodes intersected by the ray, processed for shading or compositing. The hierarchy is typically stored as a linear array of nodes. A common layout for a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) node packs metadata and child indices, often using bit-masking to distinguish leaves from internal nodes. Cell naming conventions refer to the area covered at Level 0: Level 0 cells are 1\times1, Level 1 are 2\times2, Level 2 are 4\times4. 1. Initialization: Push the root node index and the ray's entry/exit distances [t{min}, t{max}] onto the traversal stack. 2. Loop: While the stack is not empty: Pop the top state (node\idx, t{min}, t{max}, depth). Retrieve the node from the data structure. If depth \ge max\depth or the node is a leaf, record the intersection interval and continue. If the node is empty, continue. Compute intersection intervals [t{child\min}, t{child\max}] for each child using the slab method. Filter children where t{child\max} < t{min} or t{child\min} > t{max}. Sort remaining children by t{child\min} (ascending). Push children onto the stack in reverse order (farthest first) so the closest child is popped next. 3. Termination: Stop when the stack is empty or a termination condition (e.g., opacity threshold) is met. The ray-node intersection uses the slab method for axis-aligned bounding boxes: t{min} = \maxi \left( \frac{boxMini - oi}{di} \right), \quad t{max} = \mini \left( \frac{boxMaxi - oi}{di} \right) where o is the ray origin, d is the ray direction, and boxMin/boxMax define the node's bounds. Zero direction components must be handled by checking if the ray origin lies outside the slab bounds, returning an empty intersection if so. Termination: A termination object (e.g., max depth, opacity threshold) stops traversal early. The termination object must be convex. Precision: Zero direction components in ray-box intersection require explicit handling to avoid division by zero; if di = 0, the ray is parallel to the slab, and intersection fails if oi falls outside [boxMini, boxMaxi]. Stack Depth: Deep hierarchies can cause large stack usage; GPU implementations often use ropes or short-stack techniques to limit memory. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intersectaabb(o, d, boxmin, boxmax): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if d[i] == 0.0: if o[i] < boxmin[i] or o[i] > boxmax[i]: return float('inf'), -float('inf') else: t1 = (boxmin[i] - o[i]) / d[i] t2 = (boxmax[i] - o[i]) / d[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return tmin, tmax def hierarchicaltraverse(rayorigin, raydir, rootnode, maxdepth, tmax): stack = [(rootnode.index, 0.0, tmax, 0)] visited = [] while stack: nodeidx, tmin, tmax, depth = stack.pop() node = rootnode.children[nodeidx] if depth >= maxdepth or node.isleaf: visited.append((nodeidx, tmin, tmax)) continue if node.isempty: continue childrentopush = [] for childidx in node.childrenindices: child = rootnode.children[childidx] tchildmin, tchildmax = intersectaabb(rayorigin, raydir, child.bboxmin, child.bboxmax) if tchildmax > tmin and tchildmin < tmax: childrentopush.append((child.index, tchildmin, tchildmax)) childrentopush.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) for childidx, ctmin, ctmax in reversed(childrentopush): stack.append((childidx, ctmin, ctmax, depth + 1)) return visited Identifies and gathers all terminal nodes intersected by a ray grid, converting sparse traversal into a contiguous list for parallel processing. Locates specific child tetrahedra in TET-AMR trees using geometric half-space tests, avoiding redundant checks. Stores complete models in K-D tree nodes for fast preview and adaptive detail, building on hierarchical traversal. Decouples global search (coarse BVH) from local sampling, skipping empty regions entirely. Optimizes traversal by omitting children from the stack if they are known not to intersect the ray. Combines out-of-core octrees with stackless GPU raycasting for multi-gigabyte volumes. Uses octree traversal to generate screen-space occluders for visibility culling. Uses a tree of bounding volumes for ray-primitive intersection, adapting to geometry distribution. Matches traversal histories to create common sequences for multiple rays, reusing state. Defines algorithmic strategies for navigating hierarchies, optimizing descent/ascent paths. An optimization for isosurface extraction where the traversal checks if a node or its descendants contain a sign change in the scalar field. If the cell is a leaf, it returns whether it has a sign change. If it is a branch, it recursively checks if any of its children have a surface descendant. If it is empty or full, it returns false, allowing the traversal to skip the entire subtree. A GPU optimization that delays intersection tests until enough threads in a warp have stored an intersection child node. When an intersection is found, the voxel intersection data is stored. At the start of every traversal step, the warp checks if enough threads have a stored intersection; if so, they proceed with the test. Otherwise, the warp continues traversing together. Threads that find the next intersection test while already having an intersection stored stop traversing until the next intersection test is performed. Configures CUDA grids and block dimensions as 2D to map threads such that neighboring threads (rays) are spatially coherent (similar direction), causing them to traverse the octree in similar ways and improving cache hit rates. A known pitfall is thread divergence in deep octree subdivisions, causing SIMD stalls on GPU architecture. Binds octree node data to a CUDA texture object and accesses node data using the tex1Dfetch() function, which utilizes the texture cache for random access patterns typical in tree traversal. Texture memory is preferred over constant memory because constant memory is limited in size and optimized for broadcast reads, whereas octree traversal involves random access patterns across different nodes. An octree traversal method inspired by Frisken & Perry (2002), designed to avoid starting the search from the root node for every wall passage. Unlike the top-down method, it does not require starting the search from the root node for every passage through a wall, reducing computational overhead. Time Complexity: O(\log N) for sparse data, where N is the number of voxels, compared to O(N) for dense grids. The number of steps is significantly reduced; e.g., 5 steps for SVO vs. 11 for non-hierarchical in comparable examples. Memory Complexity: Depends on the structure. SVOs store only occupied nodes, offering significant space savings for sparse data. However, pointer overhead exists. Performance: Several times faster than non-hierarchical algorithms. Strengths: Efficient for sparse volumes; adaptive resolution; reduces overdraw. Limitations: Stack depth can be large for deep trees; pointer chasing can cause cache misses on CPU; thread divergence on GPU. When to use: Sparse volumetric data, multi-resolution datasets, isosurface extraction. When not to use: Dense, fully occupied volumes where grid traversal is simpler and faster; hardware with limited stack size (requires stackless variants). Hierarchical traversal originated with the development of ray tracing acceleration structures. Kay and Kajiya (1986) introduced a hierarchy traversal algorithm for ray-object intersection, demonstrating significant speedups. In volume rendering, the concept was adapted to Octrees and Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) to handle large, sparse datasets efficiently. The technique is used for volume rendering octrees or kd-trees, similar to tree traversal in ray tracing. versal algorithm for ray tracing Hur man gör en hierarkisk..., https://kth.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:2069409/FULLTEXT01.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) LCTS: Ray Shooting using Longest Common Traversal Sequences, https://www.slideserve.com/liam/vlastimil-havran, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) mxbrt/svo, https://github.com/mxbrt/svo, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) narnia-ai-mason/isomesh, https://github.com/narnia-ai-mason/isomesh, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) (PDF) Axis‐Normalized Ray‐Box Intersection - ResearchGate, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/390921688Axis-NormalizedRay-BoxIntersection, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) GPU-Based Large-Scale Scientific Visualization, https://johanna-b.github.io/LargeSciVis2018/slides/LargeScaleVisualizationArchitectures.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) GitHub - saurlax/modelvoxelizer: A 3D model voxelization tool that..., https://github.com/saurlax/modelvoxelizer, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Level-of-Detail Independent Voxel-Based Surface..., https://studenttheses.uu.nl/items/a8b8233a-d142-43f1-8f6d-c0b0fe43a767, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Best way of traversing an octree in CUDA? - CUDA Programming and Performance - NVIDIA Developer Forums, https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/best-way-of-traversing-an-octree-in-cuda/9179, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Using hierarchical octrees in Monte Carlo radiative transfer simulations, https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/201220854, fetched 2026-10-24

name: Leaf Collection
body: Leaf Collection identifies and gathers all terminal nodes (leaves) intersected by a ray grid during hierarchical traversal, converting a sparse traversal path into a contiguous list of active volumetric blocks for subsequent ray marching or shading. It separates node identification from radiance computation to enable efficient memory compaction and parallel processing. Inputs: A hierarchical sparse voxel structure (e.g., Octree) with nodes classified as Empty, Full, Branch, or Leaf. A set of rays (ray grid) defined by origin and direction. Traversal state tracking the current node and depth. Outputs: A list (vector) of leaf node identifiers (coordinates, indices, or pointers) intersected by the rays. Data Structures: Node Classification: Each node has a type field: EMPTY, FULL, BRANCH, LEAF. Result Vector: A dynamic array storing tuples of (leafid, depth) or (x, y, z, depth). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize an empty result vector L. 2. For each ray r in the ray grid: a. Start traversal at the root node N. b. While N is not a terminal node (i.e., N is BRANCH): i. Determine which child of N is intersected by r. ii. Let C be the intersected child. iii. Update traversal state (e.g., current coordinates, depth). iv. Set N \leftarrow C. c. If N is LEAF, FULL, or EMPTY: i. Push N's coordinates and depth to L. Formulas: Child coordinate update: xc = 2xp + bx, yc = 2yp + by, zc = 2zp + bz, where (xp, yp, zp) are the parent coordinates, and (bx, by, bz) are the octant bits derived from the child index. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def collectleaves(node, currentcoords, depth, resultlist): """ Recursively collect leaf nodes from a hierarchical structure. Implements the logic from. """ nodetype = node.type if nodetype in ('EMPTY', 'FULL', 'LEAF'): resultlist.append((currentcoords, depth)) elif nodetype == 'BRANCH': for octant in range(8): child = node.children[octant] childcoords = ( currentcoords[0] 2 + (octant & 1), currentcoords[1] 2 + ((octant >> 1) & 1), currentcoords[2] 2 + ((octant >> 2) & 1)) collectleaves(child, childcoords, depth + 1, resultlist) The Leaf Node Representation defines the data structure and logic for terminal nodes in sparse voxel octree traversal. It encapsulates volumetric sample data alongside validity and leaf flags, providing methods for validity checking and color manipulation during ray marching. Leaf Offset Computation calculates the linear memory offsets for each leaf node in an OpenVDB tree to facilitate parallel processing and data copying. It serves as a prerequisite for Leaf Processing, which uses these offsets to copy precomputed voxel data from a contiguous source buffer into leaf node buffers. Unlike Leaf Node Representation, which defines the internal structure of a leaf, this method computes the external indexing required to map leaf nodes to a flat memory space. This variant integrates leaf collection with level-of-detail (LOD) management and feedback mechanisms for streaming. Step: During tree traversal, stop when reaching the node corresponding to the needed level-of-detail. If required data is present, traverse the mipmapped brick and collect the current node index in a node-list. If the appropriate level-of-detail is missing or the node is terminal (no more refined data in the original model), add it to the node-list. If the node needs further subdivision, add it to the node-list and indicate subdivision need via one bit in the node. Push rendered nodes into a FIFO during traversal. Shift the 48-element window over a small set of frames to increase retrievable nodes. Parameter: In the first frame, stop pushing after 48 elements. In the second frame, stop pushing after 96 elements. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of nodes visited during traversal. Memory Complexity: O(L) where L is the number of collected leaves. Strengths: Decouples traversal from shading, allowing for efficient batch processing and memory compaction. Enables adaptive LOD and streaming by identifying exactly which nodes need to be loaded or updated. Limitations: Requires an additional pass or buffer to store the collected leaves. If the volume is dense, the list can become large, potentially causing memory pressure. When to Use: Ideal for sparse voxel octrees where most of the space is empty, and efficient memory access patterns are critical. Also suitable for streaming scenarios where only relevant nodes need to be transferred to the GPU or CPU. When Not to Use: For dense volumes where traversal overhead is negligible compared to shading, or when hardware supports direct hierarchical traversal without intermediate collection. name: Leaf Node Representation
head: Leaf struct
body: The Leaf Node Representation defines the data structure and logic for terminal nodes in sparse voxel octree traversal. It encapsulates volumetric sample data alongside validity and leaf flags, providing methods for validity checking and color manipulation during ray marching. Inputs and Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: The leaf node stores a validity bitmask (valid), a leaf flag bitmask (leaf), and a contiguous array of 4-byte RGBA values (rgba). Each bit in valid and leaf corresponds to a specific octant or voxel within the block. Steps: 1. Validity Check: The valid() method returns true if rgba[3] != 0x00. 2. Leaf Detection: The traversal checks the leaf bitmask to determine if the current octant is a terminal node. 3. Color Application: The setcolor(pixel, lightness) function multiplies the RGB channels of the pixel by the lightness factor while leaving the alpha channel unmodified. 4. Equality Check: Two leaf nodes are compared using a bitwise comparison of their entire 4-byte RGBA blocks rather than element-wise comparison. Formulas: Validity: isvalid = (validmask >> octantindex) & 1. Color update: pixel.rgb = voxel.rgba.rgb lightness. Parameters: lightness: Scalar multiplier for RGB channels. Typical value: Not given in the sources. octantindex: Integer index of the voxel within the leaf block. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero alpha (rgba[3] == 0x00) marks a voxel as invalid. Bitmask indexing requires octantindex to be within the valid range of the bitmask width. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processleaf(voxel, octantindex, pixel, lightness): # Check if the octant is marked as a leaf node isleaf = (voxel.leaf >> octantindex) & 1 if not isleaf: return False # Retrieve RGBA data for the octant rgba = voxel.rgba[octantindex] # Validity check: returns true if alpha channel is non-zero if rgba[3] == 0x00: return False # Apply lighting: multiply RGB by lightness, keep alpha unchanged pixel[0] = rgba[0] lightness pixel[1] = rgba[1] lightness pixel[2] = rgba[2] lightness pixel[3] = rgba[3] return True def checkequality(nodea, nodeb): # Bitwise comparison of the entire 4-byte RGBA block return nodea.rgba == nodeb.rgba This variant stores a histogram of values contained in the spatial region represented by an octree node as a bitfield instead of transfer-function dependent visibility information. The visible value range of a transfer function is also represented as a histogram. To determine if a node is empty, its bitfield is tested against the transfer function's bitfield using a bitwise AND operation. This allows transfer-function changes at run-time without reconstructing the acceleration structure. The approach achieved best results with a leaf-node size of 4^3 and optimized traversal by starting at a subdivision level other than the root node. Memory: Leaf-node size of 4^3 achieved best results. Performance: Bitwise operations are used for validity checks and culling. Limitations: Not given in the sources. The leaf node representation is derived from the Zazen renderer. The bitfield histogram culling variant was proposed by Faludi et al.. gabrielmuller/zazen, https://github.com/gabrielmuller/zazen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Skalierbares Webbasiertes Volume Rendering großer biomedizinischer Datensätze, https://doi.org/10.34726/hss.2023.106203, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Leaf Offset Computation
head: IndexGridBuilder::computeLeafs
body: Leaf Offset Computation calculates the linear memory offsets for each leaf node in an OpenVDB tree to facilitate parallel processing and data copying. It serves as a prerequisite for Leaf Processing, which uses these offsets to copy precomputed voxel data from a contiguous source buffer into leaf node buffers. Inputs: An OpenVDB tree retrieved from a domain grid (mdomainGrid->tree()). Outputs: A vector mleafOffsets containing cumulative offsets, and an integer mtotalVoxels. Data Structures: mleafOffsets: A std::vector<sizet> of size N+1, where N is the number of leaves. mtotalVoxels: A sizet representing the total number of voxels in all leaves. LeafNodeType::SIZE: The constant number of voxels per leaf node. Steps: 1. Retrieve the tree from the domain grid. 2. Create a LeafManager instance wrapping the tree to facilitate leaf counting. 3. Store the leaf count in mnumLeaves. 4. Resize mleafOffsets to hold N+1 elements. 5. Calculate mtotalVoxels as N \times \text{LeafNodeType::SIZE}. 6. Generate a sequence of indices from 0 to N-1. 7. Compute offsets in parallel: for each index i, set mleafOffsets[i] = i LeafNodeType::SIZE. 8. Set the final offset mleafOffsets[N] to mtotalVoxels. This final element acts as a boundary marker for parallel iteration ranges. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeleafoffsets(tree, leafsize): # Step 1: Retrieve tree from domain grid # const auto& tree = mdomainGrid->tree(); # Step 2 & 3: Create LeafManager and store leaf count # const openvdb::tree::LeafManager leafManager{tree}; # mnumLeaves = leafManager.leafCount(); numleaves = tree.leafCount() # Standard OpenVDB API call # Step 4: Resize offset array # mleafOffsets.resize(mnumLeaves + 1); leafoffsets = [0] (numleaves + 1) # Step 5: Calculate total voxels # mtotalVoxels = mnumLeaves LeafNodeType::SIZE; totalvoxels = numleaves leafsize # Step 6: Generate indices # std::vector<sizet> indices(mnumLeaves); std::iota(indices.begin(), indices.end(), 0); indices = list(range(numleaves)) # Step 7: Compute offsets in parallel # std::transform(std::execution::parunseq, indices.begin(), indices.end(), mleafOffsets.begin(), # [](sizet i) { return i LeafNodeType::SIZE; }); for i in indices: leafoffsets[i] = i leafsize # Step 8: Set final offset # mleafOffsets[mnumLeaves] = mtotalVoxels; leafoffsets[numleaves] = totalvoxels return leafoffsets, totalvoxels Parameters: LeafNodeType::SIZE: Typically 512 for 8x8x8 leaves. Not given in the sources for other configurations. Edge Cases: If numleaves is 0, the vector contains two zeros. Precision: Uses sizet (unsigned integer) to prevent overflow for large scenes. Copies precomputed voxel data from a contiguous source buffer into the leaf node buffers of an OpenVDB tree in parallel. It executes the actual memory copy operations using offsets generated by Leaf Offset Computation. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of leaves. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the offset vector. Strengths: Simple, deterministic, and highly parallelizable. Provides a clean boundary marker for subsequent parallel loops. Limitations: Assumes uniform leaf size. Does not handle variable-sized leaves or sparse leaf distributions differently than dense ones (it counts active leaves). name: Leaf Processing
head: IndexGridBuilder::foreach
body: Leaf Processing copies precomputed voxel data from a contiguous source buffer into the leaf node buffers of an OpenVDB tree in parallel. It executes the actual memory copy operations using offsets generated by Leaf Offset Computation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A contiguous source buffer containing voxel values (data), an array of precomputed linear offsets for each leaf (mleafOffsets), and a LeafManager instance iterating over the tree's leaf nodes. Output: The leaf node buffers (leaf.buffer().data()) are populated with the corresponding voxel data from the source buffer. Data Structures: mleafOffsets: An array of sizet where the index corresponds to the leaf node index (leafIdx) and the value is the starting byte offset in the source data buffer. LeafT::SIZE: The number of voxels in a leaf node. ValueT: The data type of the voxel values. Steps: 1. Initialize a parallel iterator over the leaf nodes using LeafManager::foreach. 2. Configure the parallel execution with a chunk size of 12. 3. For each leaf node processed in parallel: a. Retrieve the leaf's global index (leafIdx). b. Look up the base offset for this leaf from mleafOffsets: leafBaseOffset = mleafOffsets[leafIdx]. c. Get the pointer to the leaf's internal buffer: leafData = leaf.buffer().data(). d. Calculate the source pointer: sourcePtr = data + leafBaseOffset. e. Copy the leaf's data from the source to the leaf buffer using std::memcpy. The number of bytes to copy is LeafT::SIZE sizeof(ValueT). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def leafprocessing(data: bytearray, mleafOffsets: list[int], leafmanager: LeafManager, valuesize: int, leafsize: int): """ Copies voxel data from a flat source buffer into OpenVDB leaf nodes in parallel. Args: data: Contiguous source buffer of voxel values (bytes). mleafOffsets: Array mapping leaf index to byte offset in data. leafmanager: Iterator over leaf nodes. valuesize: Size of a single voxel value in bytes. leafsize: Number of voxels in a leaf node. """ chunksize = 12 # Parallel iteration over leaves leafmanager.foreach( lambda leaf: processleaf(leaf, data, mleafOffsets, valuesize, leafsize), parallel=True, chunksize=chunksize) def processleaf(leaf, data, mleafOffsets, valuesize, leafsize): """ Copies data for a single leaf node. """ # Get the index of the current leaf node leafidx = leaf.index() # Retrieve the precomputed base offset for this leaf leafbaseoffset = mleafOffsets[leafidx] # Get pointer to the leaf's internal buffer leafdata = leaf.buffer().data() # Calculate source pointer in the flat data array sourceoffsetinvalues = leafbaseoffset // valuesize # Copy data for i in range(leafsize): leafdata[i] = data[sourceoffsetinvalues + i] Parameters: chunksize: 12. name: IndexGridBuilder::build
body: IndexGridBuilder::build populates a flat output data structure with voxel values from multiple OpenVDB grids (SDF, float, vector) and generates global coordinates for each active voxel, using parallel leaf traversal. Inputs: A collection of OpenVDB grids: SDF grids, float grids, and vector grids. A domain grid tree structure that defines the topology and leaf layout. mleafOffsets: A mapping from leaf index to base offset in the flat output array. mnumLeaves: Total number of leaves in the domain grid. Outputs: moutData: A flat data structure containing: pValues<T>(name): Returns a pointer to the value buffer for grid type T. pCoords(): Returns a pointer to a Coord array storing global coordinates. allocateCoords(totalVoxels): Allocates memory for global coordinates. Data Structures: LeafManager: Manages iteration over leaves of the domain grid tree. TreeType::LeafNodeType::SIZE: Constant integer representing the number of voxels per leaf node. mleafOffsets[i]: Integer offset for leaf i in the flat output buffer. Steps: 1. Create a LeafManager for the domain grid tree. 2. For each SDF grid: get the float tree, create a LeafManager, obtain the output pointer via moutData->pValues<float>(name). Launch a parallel loop over leaf indices i \in [0, m\numLeaves). For each leaf i: get the leaf, compute leafBaseOffset = mleafOffsets[i], get leafPos = leaf.origin(). If the grid leaf exists at leafPos via probeConstLeaf, copy TreeType::LeafNodeType::SIZE floats to outPtr + leafBaseOffset. Else, fill with 1.0f. 3. Repeat step 2 for float grids, filling missing values with 0.0f. 4. Repeat step 2 for vector grids, copying Vec3f data and filling missing values with 0.0f. 5. Launch a parallel loop over leaf indices again. For each leaf i and local index j: compute global coordinate c = \text{leaf.offsetToGlobalCoord}(j), compute outIdx = leafBaseOffset + j, store c in moutData->pCoords()[outIdx]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def IndexGridBuilderbuild(domaintree, sdfgrids, floatgrids, vectorgrids, mleafOffsets, mnumLeaves, moutData): # Step 1: Create LeafManager for the domain grid tree domainleafmanager = LeafManager(domaintree) # Helper to process a single grid type def processgridtype(grids, fillvalue, isvector): for grid in grids: tree = grid.tree leafmanager = LeafManager(tree) outptr = moutData.pValues(grid.name, float if not isvector else Vec3f) # Parallelized over leaf indices for i in range(mnumLeaves): leaf = leafmanager.getleaf(i) leafbaseoffset = mleafOffsets[i] leafpos = leaf.origin() sourceleaf = tree.probeconstleaf(leafpos) if sourceleaf is not None: if isvector: for j in range(3): outptr[leafbaseoffset + j] = sourceleaf.getvoxel(j) else: for j in range(LeafNodeType.SIZE): outptr[leafbaseoffset + j] = sourceleaf.getvoxel(j) else: if isvector: for j in range(3): outptr[leafbaseoffset + j] = fillvalue else: for j in range(LeafNodeType.SIZE): outptr[leafbaseoffset + j] = fillvalue # Step 2: Process SDF grids (fill missing with 1.0f) processgridtype(sdfgrids, 1.0, False) # Step 3: Process float grids (fill missing with 0.0f) processgridtype(floatgrids, 0.0, False) # Step 4: Process vector grids (fill missing with 0.0f) processgridtype(vectorgrids, 0.0, True) # Step 5: Compute global coordinates for i in range(mnumLeaves): leaf = domainleafmanager.getleaf(i) leafbaseoffset = mleafOffsets[i] for j in range(LeafNodeType.SIZE): globalcoord = leaf.offsettoglobalcoord(j) outidx = leafbaseoffset + j moutData.pCoords()[outidx] = globalcoord Parameters: mleafOffsets: Array mapping leaf index to flat buffer offset. Size: mnumLeaves. mnumLeaves: Total number of leaves. TreeType::LeafNodeType::SIZE: Constant leaf voxel count. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Topology Mismatch: The domain grid leaf structure must match all added grids' leaf structures for correct offset mapping; mismatched topology causes incorrect data placement. Missing Leaves: If a leaf exists in the domain grid but not in a source grid, it is filled with a default value (1.0f for SDF, 0.0f for float/vector). Precision: Global coordinates are stored as Coord (typically integer). Creates an OpenVDB grid from the flat output buffer by cloning the domain grid's topology and copying voxel data back into leaf nodes. It differs from build by reconstructing a hierarchical OpenVDB grid structure from the flat buffer, rather than producing a flat array. Choose this when the output needs to be saved as or further processed as an OpenVDB grid. Parameters: voxelSize (float, linear transform scale factor for the output grid). Pitfalls: Topology cloning copies inactive voxels too; pruning/deactivation is commented out but available if needed. Steps: 1. Create new grid, set name and linear transform with voxelSize. 2. Set grid class to GRIDFOGVOLUME for FloatGrid, or GRIDSTAGGERED with VECCONTRAVARIANTRELATIVE for VectorGrid. 3. Assert mtotalVoxels equals moutData->size() to ensure consistency. 4. Call leafManager.foreach with lambda: for each leaf and leafIdx, get leafBaseOffset from mleafOffsets[leafIdx], get leafData pointer, copy LeafT::SIZE values from data + leafBaseOffset to leafData. name: Point Plane Test Traversal
head: Point-Plane Tests for In-Element Lookup, Tetrahedral Refinement Tree Traversal
body: Point Plane Test Traversal is a method for locating the specific child tetrahedron within a TET-AMR (Tetrahedral Adaptive Mesh Refinement) refinement tree that contains a given query point. It solves the in-element lookup problem by traversing from the coarse root to the leaf (or max depth) using geometric half-space tests against planes defined by edge midpoints, avoiding the redundancy of checking all eight children individually. It is distinguished from Leaf Collection by its on-the-fly vertex computation and from VolumeHDDA by its reliance on explicit geometric plane tests rather than incremental rasterization logic. Inputs: coarseTetID: The element ID of the root tetrahedron. childCounts: An array where childCounts[i] stores the number of children of element i. maxDepth: The maximum traversal depth. point: The 3D query point (x, y, z). GetCoarseVertices(tetID): A function returning the four corner vertices of the coarse tetrahedron. Outputs: tetID: The global element ID of the located child tetrahedron. V: The ordered set of four vertices \{t, l, r, b\} of the located tetrahedron. Data Structures: Vertices are represented as 3D vectors. The order is fixed as Top (t), Left (l), Right (r), Back (b). childCounts is an integer array indexed by element ID. Definitions: halfSpace(P, A, B, C): Returns true if point P is in the "front" half-space of the plane defined by points A, B, C. The normal direction is determined by the right-hand rule applied to vectors (B-A) and (C-A). Specifically, it checks if the dot product of the normal \vec{n} = (B-A) \times (C-A) and the vector (P-A) is positive. RB: Boolean result of the first plane test. TB: Boolean result of the second plane test. inner: Boolean result indicating if the point is in the "inner" child (the central tetrahedron formed by midpoints). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize rLevel to 0. 2. Set tetID to coarseTetID. 3. Retrieve the initial vertex set V using GetCoarseVertices(tetID). 4. Loop while childCounts[tetID] > 0 AND rLevel <= maxDepth: a. Extract vertices t, l, r, b from V. b. Compute RB: Test if point is in the front half-space of the plane passing through midpoints M{TR} = \frac{t+r}{2}, M{LB} = \frac{l+b}{2}, and M{TB} = \frac{t+b}{2}. RB = halfSpace(point, M{TR}, M{LB}, M{TB}) c. Compute TB: Test if point is in the front half-space of the plane passing through midpoints M{TR} = \frac{t+r}{2}, M{LB} = \frac{l+b}{2}, and M{TL} = \frac{t+l}{2}. TB = halfSpace(point, M{TR}, M{LB}, M{TL}) d. Compute inner: Perform four half-space tests and AND the results. The tests check if the point is on the same side of the planes forming the inner tetrahedron as the interior of the parent. inner = halfSpace(point, M{TL}, M{TB}, M{TR}) \ \& \ halfSpace(point, M{LT}, M{LR}, M{LB}) \ \& \ halfSpace(point, M{RT}, M{RB}, M{RL}) \ \& \ halfSpace(point, M{BT}, M{BL}, M{BR}) Note: The source lists specific midpoint combinations for these four tests. To ensure self-containment, the midpoints are defined as: Test 1: Plane through \frac{t+l}{2}, \frac{t+b}{2}, \frac{t+r}{2}. Test 2: Plane through \frac{l+t}{2}, \frac{l+r}{2}, \frac{l+b}{2}. Test 3: Plane through \frac{r+t}{2}, \frac{r+b}{2}, \frac{r+l}{2}. Test 4: Plane through \frac{b+t}{2}, \frac{b+l}{2}, \frac{b+r}{2}. e. Calculate localChildNo using the formula: localChildNo = (RB \times 4) + ((RB == TB) \times 2) + inner Where boolean values are treated as 1 for true and 0 for false. f. Update V to the child vertices using CalculateTetrahedronVertices(V, localChildNo). g. Update tetID to the child ID using CalculateChildID(tetID, localChildNo, childCounts). h. Increment rLevel. 5. Return tetID and V. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def halfSpace(point, A, B, C): """ Returns True if point is in the front half-space of plane ABC. Normal n = (B - A) x (C - A). Returns True if dot(n, point - A) > 0. cross and dot are standard vector operations. """ BA = B - A CA = C - A normal = cross(BA, CA) PA = point - A return dot(normal, PA) > 0 def calculatetetrahedronvertices(V, childNo): """ Computes the vertex coordinates of a child tetrahedron given the parent vertices V and the local child number (0-7). V is a tuple/list of 4 vectors: [t, l, r, b] """ t, l, r, b = V midpoints = { 'tl': (t + l) / 2, 'tr': (t + r) / 2, 'tb': (t + b) / 2, 'lr': (l + r) / 2, 'lb': (l + b) / 2, 'rb': (r + b) / 2 } if childNo == 0: return [t, midpoints['tl'], midpoints['tr'], midpoints['tb']] elif childNo == 1: return [midpoints['lb'], midpoints['tb'], midpoints['tr'], midpoints['tl']] elif childNo == 2: return [l, midpoints['tl'], midpoints['lb'], midpoints['lr']] elif childNo == 3: return [midpoints['tr'], midpoints['lr'], midpoints['lb'], midpoints['tl']] elif childNo == 4: return [r, midpoints['rb'], midpoints['tr'], midpoints['lr']] elif childNo == 5: return [midpoints['lb'], midpoints['lr'], midpoints['tr'], midpoints['rb']] elif childNo == 6: return [b, midpoints['rb'], midpoints['lb'], midpoints['tb']] elif childNo == 7: return [midpoints['tr'], midpoints['tb'], midpoints['lb'], midpoints['rb']] else: raise ValueError("Invalid childNo") def calculatechildid(tetID, childNo, childCounts): """ Calculates the global tetrahedron ID of a child element. """ currentid = tetID + 1 for i in range(childNo + 1): currentid = currentid + childCounts[currentid] + 1 return currentid def pointplanetraversal(coarseTetID, childCounts, maxDepth, point, getcoarsevertices): rLevel = 0 tetID = coarseTetID V = getcoarsevertices(tetID) # Note: Source also mentions terminating if tetrahedron screen size falls below a threshold. while childCounts[tetID] > 0 and rLevel <= maxDepth: t, l, r, b = V # Midpoints mtr = (t + r) / 2 mlb = (l + b) / 2 mtb = (t + b) / 2 mtl = (t + l) / 2 # RB half: Plane through TR, LB, TB RB = halfSpace(point, mtr, mlb, mtb) # TB half: Plane through TR, LB, TL TB = halfSpace(point, mtr, mlb, mtl) # Inner tests inner1 = halfSpace(point, (t+l)/2, (t+b)/2, (t+r)/2) inner2 = halfSpace(point, (l+t)/2, (l+r)/2, (l+b)/2) inner3 = halfSpace(point, (r+t)/2, (r+b)/2, (r+l)/2) inner4 = halfSpace(point, (b+t)/2, (b+l)/2, (b+r)/2) inner = inner1 and inner2 and inner3 and inner4 # Calculate local child number rbint = 1 if RB else 0 tbint = 1 if TB else 0 innerint = 1 if inner else 0 localChildNo = (rbint 4) + ((rbint == tbint) 2) + innerint V = calculatetetrahedronvertices(V, localChildNo) tetID = calculatechildid(tetID, localChildNo, childCounts) rLevel += 1 return tetID, V Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point errors in halfSpace tests can lead to incorrect quadrant identification if the point lies exactly on a plane. A small epsilon tolerance should be considered for robustness, though the source does not specify one. Termination: The loop terminates if a leaf is reached (childCounts[tetID] == 0), maxDepth is exceeded, or (in the broader rendering context) if the tetrahedron size on screen falls below a threshold. The core traversal algorithm returns the ID and vertices of the last traversed level in these cases. Vertex Order: The correctness of the plane tests depends strictly on the consistent ordering of vertices (t, l, r, b). Computes the vertex coordinates of a child tetrahedron given the parent vertices V and the local child number (0-7). It maps the local child index to a specific subset of the parent's vertices and the midpoints of its edges. The mapping is deterministic: child 0 is the top corner; child 7 is the central inner tetrahedron formed by all midpoints. Calculates the global tetrahedron ID of a child element given the parent ID, the local child number, and the childCounts array. It iterates through the siblings of the target child, skipping over their respective subtrees (counted by childCounts) to find the correct global index. A method that uses refinement tree traversal to find the vertices of neighbor elements for accurate cell-centered sampling. It relies only on coarse mesh neighborhood information. It finds which coarse tetrahedron the neighbor is in, then uses the traversal process to find the vertices of the element to sample from, ensuring exact geometric alignment unlike approximate methods. Time Complexity: O(D) per query, where D is the traversal depth. Each level requires a constant number of plane tests (6 total: 2 for quadrants, 4 for inner/outer, though the source notes a single test suffices once the quadrant is known, the algorithm provided uses 4 for conciseness). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per traversal step, as vertex coordinates are computed on-the-fly and not stored for lower levels. The childCounts array is required for ID calculation. Performance: Faster than naive containment tests against all 8 children because it prunes the search space using geometric properties of red-refinement tetrahedra. Strengths: No need to store coordinates for refined elements; efficient lookup for sparse data. Limitations: Requires the childCounts array and a method to retrieve coarse vertices. Precision issues may arise near plane boundaries. The method originates from work on Direct Volume Rendering of Tree-Based Tetrahedral Adaptive Mesh Refinement (TET-AMR) data. It was developed to address the inefficiency of naive in-element lookups in adaptive tetrahedral grids, leveraging the regular geometry of red-refinement tetrahedra to optimize the traversal process. Direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement data, https://repository.bilkent.edu.tr/items/fcbc592a-2646-49af-8b84-67308b6fd3e9, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Multi-Resolution Rendering with K-D Tree
head: Error-controlled approximation, Nodal region rendering
body: Multi-resolution rendering with K-D Tree is a hierarchical volume rendering technique that stores approximations of the underlying data within K-D tree nodes. It solves the performance bottleneck of rendering large datasets by allowing the renderer to skip detailed traversal when the data within a spatial region can be represented by a simple model within a user-specified error threshold. Unlike wavelet-based methods which store only detail coefficients, this method stores a complete model for each region, enabling fast preview images and adaptive detail. It builds on Hierarchical Traversal. Inputs: A K-D tree where each node represents a spatial subregion (nodal region). A restrict box defining the region of interest. A user-defined acceptable error threshold \epsilon. A user-defined polygon count cut-off N{cut}. Ray parameters (origin and direction). Outputs: A set of subranges to be rendered, corresponding to K-D tree nodes that satisfy the error or leaf criteria. Rendered image pixels. Data Structures: Each K-D tree node contains: 1. Spatial Bounds: Defining the nodal region. 2. Error Term (E): A scalar representing the deviation of the nodal model from the actual data. 3. Nodal Model Parameters: Eight data values corresponding to the corners of the nodal region. 4. Polygon Subrange: A contiguous range in a global polygon array (Tid) storing polygon IDs within the node's spatial region. 5. Children References: Pointers to child nodes for non-leaf nodes. Nodal Model Construction: The nodal model is a trilinear function induced by eight data values stored at the corners of the nodal region. To compute the data value at a specific corner of the nodal region, the algorithm locates the grid cell in the original dataset that contains the corner point and interpolates within that grid cell to compute the data value at the corner. These eight values are stored directly in the tree node. The trilinear interpolation at a point (x, y, z) within the nodal region is computed as: V(x,y,z) = \sum{i=0}^{1}\sum{j=0}^{1}\sum{k=0}^{1} wi(x) wj(y) wk(z) V{ijk} where V{ijk} are the eight corner values and wi(t) = 1-t or t depending on the corner index. Traversal Algorithm: Traversal occurs in front-to-back visibility order. The algorithm determines which nodes to render in detail and which to approximate. 1. Initialize: Start traversal at the root node. 2. Check Restrict Box: If the node is entirely outside the restrict box, return immediately. 3. Check Inclusion: If the node is entirely inside the restrict box, add its polygon subrange (Tid) to the set of subranges to be rendered and return without traversing children. 4. Check Leaf/Cut-off: If the node is a leaf, or if the number of polygons in its region is less than the user-specified cut-off N{cut}, add its polygon subrange (Tid) to the set of subranges to be rendered and return. 5. Check Error: If the node's stored error term E is less than the acceptable error \epsilon, or the node is a leaf, traversal stops at this node and the nodal region is drawn using the trilinear approximation model. 6. Recursive Step: If none of the above exceptions apply (node is partially inside restrict box, not a leaf, polygon count \ge N{cut}, and error E \ge \epsilon), add the polygon subrange (Tid) associated with the node itself (but not its descendants) to the set of subranges to be rendered, and recursively traverse the node's children. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinear(v000, v100, v010, v110, v001, v101, v011, v111, x, y, z): ix, iy, iz = 1.0 - x, 1.0 - y, 1.0 - z return (ixiyizv000 + xiyizv100 + ixyizv010 + xyizv110 + ixiyzv001 + xiyzv101 + ixyzv011 + xyzv111) def rayboxintersect(boxmin, boxmax, rayorigin, raydirection): tmin, tmax = 0.0, float('inf') for axis in range(3): if raydirection[axis] == 0: if not (boxmin[axis] <= rayorigin[axis] <= boxmax[axis]): return None else: t1 = (boxmin[axis] - rayorigin[axis]) / raydirection[axis] t2 = (boxmax[axis] - rayorigin[axis]) / raydirection[axis] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return (tmin, tmax) if tmin <= tmax else None def drawnodalregion(node, rayorigin, raydirection): bounds = rayboxintersect(node.boundsmin, node.boundsmax, rayorigin, raydirection) if bounds is None: return tstart, tend = bounds dx = node.boundsmax[0] - node.boundsmin[0] dy = node.boundsmax[1] - node.boundsmin[1] dz = node.boundsmax[2] - node.boundsmin[2] steps = max(1, int((tend - tstart) / max(dx, dy, dz))) for i in range(steps + 1): t = tstart + (tend - tstart) i / steps px = rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0] t py = rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1] t pz = rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2] t x = (px - node.boundsmin[0]) / dx y = (py - node.boundsmin[1]) / dy z = (pz - node.boundsmin[2]) / dz value = trilinear(node.corners, x, y, z) # Composite value into framebuffer pass def traversekdnode(node, restrictboxmin, restrictboxmax, epsilon, ncut, tidarray, renderset, rayorigin, raydirection): # 1. Check Restrict Box: entirely outside if (node.boundsmax[0] < restrictboxmin[0] or node.boundsmin[0] > restrictboxmax[0] or node.boundsmax[1] < restrictboxmin[1] or node.boundsmin[1] > restrictboxmax[1] or node.boundsmax[2] < restrictboxmin[2] or node.boundsmin[2] > restrictboxmax[2]): return # 2. Check Inclusion: entirely inside if (node.boundsmin[0] >= restrictboxmin[0] and node.boundsmax[0] <= restrictboxmax[0] and node.boundsmin[1] >= restrictboxmin[1] and node.boundsmax[1] <= restrictboxmax[1] and node.boundsmin[2] >= restrictboxmin[2] and node.boundsmax[2] <= restrictboxmax[2]): renderset.add(tidarray[node.tidstart: node.tidend]) return # 3. Check Leaf/Cut-off if node.isleaf or node.polygoncount < ncut: renderset.add(tidarray[node.tidstart: node.tidend]) return # 4. Check Error if node.error < epsilon or node.isleaf: drawnodalregion(node, rayorigin, raydirection) return # 5. Recursive Step: partially inside & none above renderset.add(tidarray[node.tidstart: node.tidend]) for child in node.children: traversekdnode(child, restrictboxmin, restrictboxmax, epsilon, ncut, tidarray, renderset, rayorigin, raydirection) Parameters: Acceptable error \epsilon (user-specified). Polygon count cut-off N{cut} (user-specified). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Technical problems exist to avoid visual discontinuities on the boundaries between nodal regions that use different rendering methods (approximation vs. detailed polygon rendering). If standard cell projection methods are used exclusively for nodal regions, discontinuities are avoided and graphics hardware acceleration is possible. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The technique constructs very fast "preview" images to help orient the user in a very large data set. Strengths: It enables adaptive detail based on user-defined error. Limitations: It requires careful handling of boundaries to avoid discontinuities between approximated and detailed regions. When to use: It is suitable for large datasets where interactive preview or adaptive detail is required. When not to use: It should be avoided in scenes requiring strict visual continuity across all spatial boundaries without specialized boundary handling. The technique was proposed for hierarchical and parallelizable direct volume rendering. It departs from wavelet-based approaches by storing a complete model for each region rather than just detail information. Traversal occurs in front-to-back visibility order. Hierarchical and parallelizable direct volume rendering for irregular and multiple grids, https://doi.org/10.1109/visual.1996.567606, fetched 2026-10-24

name: Coarse Mesh Traversal
body: Coarse Mesh Traversal is a hierarchical rendering technique that accelerates volume rendering by decoupling the global search for active data regions from the local sampling of fine-grained geometry. It solves the problem of inefficiently traversing large, sparse, or multi-resolution datasets by first identifying which coarse elements (macrocells) a ray intersects, and then performing detailed rendering only within those specific regions. What sets it apart from its siblings is the explicit construction of a coarse mesh (typically a BVH) from the underlying adaptive or hierarchical data structure, allowing the renderer to skip empty or irrelevant volumes entirely before entering the fine-level traversal loop. The family shares a two-stage traversal mechanism. First, a coarse mesh is constructed from the input data, where each element represents a cluster of fine-level primitives (e.g., tetrahedra or voxels). This mesh is indexed by a spatial acceleration structure, typically a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). Second, for each ray, the algorithm performs a coarse traversal to determine the entry and exit distances (t{entry}, t{exit}) for the current coarse element. If the element is active (non-empty), the ray is then marched through the fine-level data contained within those bounds. Key mathematical constraints include: 1. Boundary Precision: To prevent re-intersection artifacts when moving from one coarse element to the next, the exit distance t{exit} is perturbed to the next representable floating-point number using nextafterf(t, INFINITY). 2. Culling: Coarse elements are associated with scalar statistics (e.g., maximum density) to allow early-out culling before fine-level sampling begins. 3. Nested Structure: The fine-level traversal is bounded by the coarse element's intersection distances, ensuring that the inner loop does not exceed the macrocell's spatial extent. Determines entry and exit distances for a ray traversing a non-convex coarse tetrahedral mesh by tracing two auxiliary rays with opposite face culling settings. It sets itself apart by explicitly using the topological distinction between front-facing and back-facing hits to resolve the ray's state without requiring explicit convexity checks. Choose it when rendering complex, potentially hollow geometries where single-ray intersection tests are ambiguous. Performs front-to-back compositing by traversing a coarse mesh of tetrahedral clusters and then marching through the fine-level tetrahedra contained within each active cluster. It sets itself apart by explicitly using a constant adjustable step size for the inner loop and relying on macrocell density statistics for early-out culling. Choose it for efficiently visualizing sparse, multi-resolution AMR data while maintaining native resolution. Optimizes hierarchical volume rendering by selectively inserting elements from specific depths of the input refinement tree into the coarse mesh, rather than using a fixed depth or only leaf nodes. It sets itself apart by allowing the coarse element granularity to be tuned independently of the finest data resolution. Choose it when balancing BVH traversal efficiency against the overhead of traversing the underlying refinement tree structure. Coarse Mesh Traversal builds on the principles of hierarchical volume rendering, specifically leveraging the spatial coherence of adaptive meshes. It is primarily used in the visualization of scientific simulation data, such as fluid dynamics or astrophysics, where data is naturally structured in adaptive tetrahedral or hexahedral meshes. The method addresses the memory and performance bottlenecks of uniform grid resampling by operating directly on the native hierarchical structure.

name: Coarse Mesh Traversal with Dual-Ray Culling
head: Front/back face culling traversal, Two-ray coarse mesh traversal
body: This method determines the entry and exit distances of a ray through a non-convex coarse tetrahedral mesh by tracing two rays—one with front-face culling and one with back-face culling—into a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). It solves the problem of accurately identifying the current coarse element and the transition point to the next element in complex geometries with holes or non-convex boundaries, which single-ray traversal cannot handle robustly. Unlike standard hierarchical traversal that assumes convexity or simple entry/exit, this approach explicitly distinguishes between entering, exiting, and traversing internal elements using the dual-ray intersection results. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and a BVH containing the coarse tetrahedral mesh. Output: A tuple (\text{coarseID}, t{back}, t{next}), where \text{coarseID} is the identifier of the current coarse tetrahedron, t{back} is the exit distance of the current element, and t{next} is the entry distance for the subsequent coarse element. If the ray is outside the mesh, it returns (-1, 0, 0). Data Structures: BVH: A spatial acceleration structure indexing the faces of the coarse tetrahedra. Each leaf node represents a triangle face belonging to a specific coarse tetrahedron ID. Ray Record: Contains the hit distance t, the hit point, and the coarseTetID of the intersected triangle. Algorithm Steps: 1. Front-Face Trace: Trace the ray against the BVH with front-face culling enabled (ignoring back-facing triangles). If the ray misses, return (-1, 0, 0), indicating the ray is outside the coarse mesh. If it hits, store the hit distance as t{back} and the tetrahedron ID as \text{coarseID}. 2. Back-Face Trace: Trace the same ray against the BVH with back-face culling enabled (ignoring front-facing triangles). Let the result be rayRecordback. 3. Determine Transition Distance (t{next}): If rayRecordback misses: The ray is inside the last element of the mesh. Set t{next} = \text{nextafterf}(t{back}, \infty). If rayRecordback hits: If rayRecordback.coarseTetID equals \text{coarseID}: The ray is inside a single element (Case 2 in source, entering/exiting same element or passing through). Set t{next} = \text{nextafterf}(t{back}, \infty) and update the ray's t for the next iteration to \text{nextafterf}(t{front}, \infty), where t{front} is the hit distance of the back-face ray. If rayRecordback.coarseTetID differs from \text{coarseID}: The ray has exited the current element and entered a new one. Set t{next} = \text{nextafterf}(t{front}, \infty), where t{front} is the hit distance of the back-face ray. 4. Return: Return (\text{coarseID}, t{back}, t{next}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def nextafterf(t, direction): """Returns the next representable floating-point number after t towards direction.""" return math.nextafter(t, direction) def traceray(ray, cullmode): """Standard BVH ray tracing routine. Returns a record with.t,.missed,.coarsetetid. cullmode is 'FRONT' or 'BACK' to enable/disable face culling.""" # Implementation depends on the specific BVH structure. # For this algorithm, it returns the closest hit or a miss flag. pass def traversecoarsemesh(ray): # Step 1: Trace with front-face culling rayrecordfront = traceray(ray, cullmode='FRONT') # If missed, ray is outside the mesh if rayrecordfront.missed: return -1, 0, 0 # Store back-face hit info (which is actually the front-face hit in this context) tback = rayrecordfront.t coarseid = rayrecordfront.coarsetetid # Step 2: Trace with back-face culling rayrecordback = traceray(ray, cullmode='BACK') tnextface = 0.0 # Step 3: Determine tnextface based on back-face hit if rayrecordback.missed: # Case 3: Inside the last element, exiting the volume tnextface = nextafterf(tback, math.inf) else: tfront = rayrecordback.t if rayrecordback.coarsetetid == coarseid: # Case 2: Inside the same element (or entering/exiting same element) # Advance ray t for next iteration to just past the front hit ray.t = nextafterf(tfront, math.inf) # Exit current element just past the back hit tnextface = nextafterf(tback, math.inf) else: # Case 1: Entered a new element # Next face is just past the front hit of the new element tnextface = nextafterf(tfront, math.inf) # Step 4: Return results return coarseid, tback, tnextface Parameters: nextafterf(t, direction): A function that returns the next representable floating-point number after t in the direction of direction (e.g., INFINITY or -INFINITY). This is critical for preventing re-intersection artifacts. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Artifacts: When exiting a face, using the exact hit distance t in the next iteration can cause the ray to re-intersect the same geometry due to floating-point inaccuracies. The nextafterf function must be used to perturb t slightly. Non-Convexity: Standard single-ray traversal fails for non-convex shapes or meshes with holes because a single entry/exit pair is insufficient. The dual-ray approach handles these cases by explicitly checking both face orientations. An optimization that renders the back faces of the volume's bounding box to a texture to determine ray entry/exit points, avoiding analytical ray-cube intersection computations in the shader. It builds on the dual-ray principle by offloading geometry processing to the GPU rasterizer in a two-pass pipeline: the first pass captures back-face depth/position, and the second pass initializes the ray march, skipping empty space outside the volume. A software-based technique for unstructured grids that handles non-convex geometries by projecting boundary faces into screen space to determine ray re-entry points. Unlike hierarchical spatial structures, it exploits the discrete nature of the image plane, making it simpler and more robust to floating-point errors, though it is memory-intensive and unsuitable for large grids. Treats coarse mesh elements as macrocells storing pre-computed minimum and maximum density values of their child elements. Before processing a coarse element, the algorithm checks if the maximum macrocell density is zero; if so, it skips the element entirely. Densities are post-classification values obtained by applying the transfer function to child scalars and are recalculated via a CUDA kernel when the transfer function changes. This enables empty space skipping and tighter majorant estimation for Woodcock tracking, reducing sample rejection rates. An optimization that early-returns from refinement tree traversal based on the normalized screen space area of the tetrahedron. The normalized area is calculated by summing the areas of the four triangles formed by the tetrahedron's vertices. A user-defined threshold controls the refinement criteria; this threshold can be converted to true screen space area by multiplying by the total screen space. Time Complexity: The traversal requires two BVH traces per coarse element step. The dual-ray approach doubles the constant factor of the traversal cost compared to a single-ray method. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the BVH for the coarse mesh and, if macrocells are used, the min/max density values for each coarse element. Strengths: Robustly handles non-convex geometries and holes without analytical intersection logic in the shader. Integrates well with macrocell optimizations for empty space skipping. Limitations: The dual-ray trace increases overhead per coarse element. Precision handling requires careful use of nextafterf. When to Use: Ideal for non-convex volumes or meshes with complex topology where single-ray entry/exit detection fails. The method originates from research on direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data. It was developed to address the challenges of rendering non-convex coarse meshes where traditional hierarchical traversal methods fail due to ambiguous entry/exit points. The approach leverages GPU ray tracing capabilities (BVH traversal) to simplify the geometric logic for complex boundaries.
