name: Adaptive Out-of-Core Single-Pass GPU Raycasting
head: Adaptive out-of-core technique, Single-pass GPU ray casting framework
body: This method enables interactive rendering of multi-gigabyte scalar volumes on desktop hardware by combining an out-of-core octree data structure with a single-pass, stackless GPU raycasting algorithm. It solves the memory capacity and bandwidth bottlenecks of in-core rendering by maintaining a view- and transfer-function-dependent working set of volumetric bricks in GPU memory, while the rest of the dataset remains on disk. Unlike separate block rendering techniques that suffer from boundary artifacts and cannot support refractive or global illumination models, this approach performs the entire volume traversal and compositing in a single fragment shader pass, adapting sampling density to the local brick resolution. Input: A massive scalar volume dataset (e.g., 2 Gvoxels, 16-bit) stored on disk. Output: A rendered 2D image (e.g., 1024 × 1024 pixels) with accumulated color and opacity, updating the frame buffer and depth buffer. The dataset is decomposed into small cubical bricks and organized into a coarse octree structure maintained out-of-core. Leaves: Store the original voxel data for the brick. Inner Nodes: Store a filtered representation of their children (aggregated data). Node Metadata: Each node stores: The range of scalar values present in the node. Optionally, precomputed gradients. Boundary Replication: To support neighbor access for interpolation and gradients, bricks are made self-contained: One layer of neighboring samples is replicated for linear interpolation support. Two layers of neighboring samples are replicated if central differences are used for gradient computation at render time. An adaptive loader on the CPU maintains a subset of bricks in GPU memory. This set is view-dependent and transfer-function-dependent. Content: Only the bricks required for the current view and transfer function are loaded. Management: Maintained via an adaptive refinement method guided by node priorities. At each frame, a compact indexing structure is encoded in a small GPU texture. Purpose: Spatially organizes the current working set into an octree hierarchy for the raycaster. Nature: It is not a multiresolution data representation; it is a spatial index. Layout: Inner Nodes: Contain pointers to children. Leaves: Refer to volume data nodes stored in the GPU memory pool (the working set). Pointers: Include neighbor pointers to facilitate on-the-fly bounding box computation and neighbor access. 1. Preprocessing (Offline): 1. Decompose the original volumetric model into small cubical bricks. 2. Organize bricks into a coarse octree structure maintained out-of-core. 3. Store original data at leaves and filtered representations at inner nodes. 4. Store value ranges and optional precomputed gradients for each node. 5. Replicate boundary samples (1 layer for linear interpolation, 2 layers for central difference gradients) to make bricks self-contained. 2. Adaptive Loading (CPU/GPU Interaction): 1. Initialize a working set of bricks in GPU memory. 2. Compute node priorities based on view and transfer function. 3. Asynchronously fetch data from the out-of-core octree to update the working set. 4. Refine the working set incrementally based on priorities. 5. Receive feedback from the renderer regarding occlusion to avoid loading/refining occluded zones. 3. Indexing (Per Frame): 1. Encode the spatial organization of the current working set into a compact texture. 2. Populate inner nodes with pointers to children and leaves with references to GPU memory locations. 4. Single-Pass Raycasting (GPU Fragment Shader): 1. For each pixel, cast a ray into the volume. 2. Traverse the compact indexing structure (stackless octree traversal). 3. Enumerate non-empty bricks in front-to-back order. 4. Adapt sampling density to the resolution of the current brick. 5. Compute the volume rendering integral (accumulating color and opacity). 6. Stop raycasting when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold. 7. Update the frame buffer and depth buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocessvolume(dataset): # 1. Decompose into bricks bricks = decomposeintocubicalbricks(dataset) # 2. Build out-of-core octree octree = buildoctree(bricks) # 3. Populate node data for node in octree.traverse(): if node.isleaf(): node.data = originalvoxeldata else: node.data = filterchildrendata(node.children) node.valuerange = computevaluerange(node.data) node.gradients = computeprecomputedgradients(node.data) # Optional # 4. Replicate boundaries for self-containment if node.isleaf(): replicateneighbors(node.data, layers=1) # For linear interpolation # replicateneighbors(node.data, layers=2) # If central differences needed def updateworkingset(octree, viewparams, transferfunction): # 1. Compute priorities for nodes priorities = computenodepriorities(octree, viewparams, transferfunction) # 2. Determine working set based on memory budget and priorities workingsetnodes = selectnodesbypriority(octree, priorities) # 3. Asynchronously fetch data from disk to GPU gpumemorypool = allocategpumemory(len(workingsetnodes)) for node in workingsetnodes: gpumemorypool[node.id] = fetchdatafromdisk(node) return gpumemorypool, workingsetnodes def buildindextexture(workingsetnodes, gpumemorypool): # Create a compact texture representing the spatial hierarchy of the working set indextexture = createtexture() for node in workingsetnodes: if node.haschildreninworkingset: # Inner node: pointer to children indextexture.setpointer(node.id, node.childrenids) else: # Leaf node: reference to GPU memory indextexture.setreference(node.id, gpumemorypool[node.id].address) return indextexture def raycastfragment(rayorigin, raydirection, indextexture, gpumemorypool, transferfunction): accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 threshold = 0.95 # Example threshold # Stackless traversal of the compact octree index currentnode = indextexture.root t = rayorigin while currentnode is not None and accumulatedopacity < threshold: # 1. Traverse to next non-empty brick # Compute bounding box on-the-fly using the index structure brickbounds = computeboundingbox(currentnode, indextexture) # Intersect ray with brick bounds tenter, texit = intersectraybrick(rayorigin, raydirection, brickbounds) if tenter is None: # Ray missed this brick, move to next sibling or parent currentnode = nextnodeintraversal(currentnode, indextexture) continue t = max(t, tenter) # 2. Sample within the brick # Adapt sampling density to brick resolution stepsize = computestepsize(brickbounds) while t < texit and accumulatedopacity < threshold: samplepos = rayorigin + raydirection t # 3. Retrieve voxel data # Access GPU memory pool using the leaf reference voxelvalue = samplevoxel(samplepos, gpumemorypool[currentnode.ref]) # 4. Transfer function color, opacity = applytransferfunction(voxelvalue, transferfunction) # 5. Front-to-back compositing alpha = opacity (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor += color alpha accumulatedopacity += alpha t += stepsize # 6. Move to next node in front-to-back order currentnode = nextnodeintraversal(currentnode, indextexture) return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity Hardware: NVIDIA 8800 Ultra graphics board. Resolution: 1024 × 1024 window size. Dataset Size: 2 Gvoxels, 16-bit. Performance: Interactive exploration achieved on a desktop PC. Block Boundaries: Unlike separate block rendering, this method avoids artifacts at block boundaries because it performs a full-volume traversal. Occlusion: Feedback from the renderer is used to avoid refinement and data loading of occluded zones, preventing unnecessary GPU stalls. Neighbor Access: Failure to replicate boundary samples correctly will break linear interpolation or gradient computation if neighbor voxels are accessed. Time Complexity: The traversal is stackless and exploits the regular structure of octrees to reduce costly texture memory accesses by computing bounding boxes on-the-fly. The adaptive refinement ensures that only relevant parts of the volume are processed. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is bounded by the size of the working set in GPU memory, which is dynamically adjusted based on view and transfer function dependencies. The rest of the data remains out-of-core. Performance: Enables interactive exploration of multi-gigabyte datasets (e.g., 2 Gvoxels) on desktop hardware. Strengths: Supports full-volume optical models, including refracting volumes and global illumination, which separate block rendering cannot easily handle. Adapts sampling density to brick resolution, providing visual quality proportional to data availability. Reduces GPU stalls via occlusion query feedback. Limitations: Requires a GPU capable of single-pass fragment shader execution for volume traversal. Performance depends on the efficiency of the adaptive loader and the compact indexing structure construction. Unlike flat multiresolution blocking, it does not have a constant number of blocks, which may complicate certain types of parallelization or fixed-size memory allocation strategies. Origin: The method was presented in the paper "A single-pass GPU ray casting framework for interactive out-of-core rendering of massive volumetric datasets" by E. Gobbetti, F. Marton, and J. Jallet. History: It builds upon earlier work on out-of-core volume octrees and stackless ray traversal methods for kd-trees [7, 16], extending them to GPUs for volume rendering. It addresses the limitations of previous GPU volume rendering techniques that were restricted to moderate-sized volumes fitting entirely in texture memory. Usage: Primarily used for interactive exploration of multi-gigabyte CT datasets in medical visualization and numerical simulation analysis. A single-pass GPU ray casting framework for interactive out-of-core rendering of massive volumetric datasets, https://www.crs4.it/vic/data/papers/cgi2008-movr.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: From-Point Algorithm
head: Implicit Occluder Occlusion Culling, Implicit Occluders
body: The From-Point Algorithm is a visibility culling method for volume rendering that uses an octree of scalar field data to generate screen-space occluders, allowing the culling of invisible octree nodes before isosurface extraction. It identifies regions where the scalar field function does not change sign relative to an isovalue to determine occlusion, exploiting the continuity of the field to define conservative visibility bounds implicitly. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on cached polygonal meshes or complex ray-tree traversals, this approach builds occluders from coarse-to-fine traversal of the multiresolution representation, enabling interactive modification of isovalues with reduced memory consumption. It builds on Hierarchical Traversal. The algorithm divides into three parts: 1) Build screen-space per-pixel occluders, 2) Use hardware occlusion-culling queries to prune invisible parts of the octree, 3) Compute and render the isosurface for remaining visible nodes. Input: An octree representation of a volume where each node stores the minimum (fc{min}) and maximum (fc{max}) values of the scalar field within the corresponding voxels. An isovalue w. Output: A set of visible octree nodes for which the isosurface is computed and rendered. Octree Node: Stores fc{min} and fc{max}. Occlusion Map: Implemented as a depth buffer storing the depth of the 'far envelope' of sign changes. Stencil Buffer: One-bit buffer used to track which pixels were covered by 'below' nodes in Pass 1. Isovalue (w): The scalar field threshold value used to determine if a node is an occluder (above or below) or contains the isosurface. Build Depth: The octree depth level used to generate the implicit occluders. A level above the maximum depth can be chosen to save construction time but may lower coverage area. Cull Depth: The octree depth level up to which nodes are tested for occlusion. In the reported experiments, build depth 7 and cull depth 6 (7/6) yielded optimal results. 1. Classification: Classify octree nodes as fully above (fc{min} > w) or fully below (fc{max} < w) the isosurface query value w. 2. Occluder Generation: During the coarse-to-fine traversal, generate occluders as soon as it is established that a cell A is entirely above w (f(A) > 0) and a cell B is entirely below w (f(B) < 0) (or vice versa). Any ray intersecting both must intersect the isosurface between them. 3. Pass 1 (Below Regions): Render all octree nodes where fc{max} < w. Set depth function to GLLESS to keep closest fragments. Set stencil operation to GLREPLACE on both fail and zpass to flag pixels covered by these 'below' regions. 4. Pass 2 (Above Regions): Render all octree nodes where fc{min} > w. Traverse nodes front-to-back (no actual sorting required, just traversal order). Set depth function to GLGREATER. Set stencil function to GLNOTEQUAL with mask 1, so only pixels not covered in Pass 1 are updated. 5. Reset Incomplete Pixels: Render a polygon lying behind the octree (e.g., a slightly expanded root node) to reset depth values for pixels that were covered by 'below' nodes in Pass 1 but not by any 'above' node in Pass 2. These pixels have no sign change and thus no occluder. 6. Occlusion Query: For each octree node to be rendered, test if its bounding volume is visible using hardware occlusion queries. Only render nodes determined to be visible. 7. Isosurface Extraction: For visible nodes, compute the isosurface using an output-sensitive algorithm. Perform a top-down traversal using min-max info to avoid nodes without the isosurface. Use Marching Cubes on visible nodes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. depthbuffer = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] stencilbuffer = [[0] width for in range(height)] incomplete = [[True] width for in range(height)] for i in range(height): for j in range(width): depthbuffer[i][j] = 0.0 stencilbuffer[i][j] = 0 incomplete[i][j] = True for node in nodesbelow: for pixel in node.screenprojection: z = node.depthatpixel(pixel) if z < depthbuffer[pixel]: depthbuffer[pixel] = z stencilbuffer[pixel] = 1 incomplete[pixel] = False for node in nodesabove: for pixel in node.screenprojection: if stencilbuffer[pixel] != 1: z = node.depthatpixel(pixel) if z > depthbuffer[pixel]: depthbuffer[pixel] = z stencilbuffer[pixel] = 1 for i in range(height): for j in range(width): if incomplete[i][j]: depthbuffer[i][j] = float('inf') incomplete[i][j] = False for node in octree: if isnodevisible(node, depthbuffer): extractandrenderisosurface(node) def isnodevisible(node, depthbuffer): # Tests if node's bounding volume overlaps with finite depth values in depthbuffer # using hardware occlusion query logic. pass def extractandrenderisosurface(node): # Performs top-down traversal using min-max info, then runs Marching Cubes [13]. pass Conservative Estimate: The occluder estimate may be too conservative to provide a practical advantage depending on the input data. Refinement Cost: Excessive refinement of the octree for occluder generation can be more expensive than computing and rendering a few additional invisible isosurface faces. Low Build Depth: If the build depth is too low (e.g., 4), no non-trivial occlusion may be found, resulting in no culling benefit. Time Complexity: The algorithm accelerates isosurface extraction by skipping subtrees where the range [fc{min}, fc{max}] does not contain w. Memory: Reduces memory consumption compared to caching polygonal meshes. Performance: On a synthetic dataset (f(x,y,z) = \sin(xyz/8) + \cos((x-2)(y-2)(z-2)) over [-5,5]^3, zero isosurface, 2,023,877 triangles), average time without occlusion was 7.01 seconds. With Implicit Occluders (depth 7 build, adaptive traversal), it was more than twice as fast. On an MRI Head dataset (493,932 triangles), time reduced from 1.12 seconds to 0.43 seconds (38% of original) with 7/6 build/cull depth, reducing faces to 69,663 (14% of total). On the Neghip dataset (246,194 triangles), the baseline time without visibility computations was 0.63 seconds. Strengths: Allows interactive modification of isovalues; very fast rendering path for occlusion map (disabling lighting/texturing); single triangle fans for octree cells. Limitations: More computationally expensive per frame than caching polygonal meshes; occluder estimate may be too conservative. The From-Point Algorithm was proposed as a new efficient visibility algorithm that exploits visibility queries commonly available on graphics hardware to speed up the extraction and rendering of an isosurface by early elimination of large occluded regions. It explores the framework of Wilhelms and Van Gelder with ideas similar to Livnat and Hansen. The concept of Implicit Occluders was developed independently by Tsai et al.. The prototype implementation was presented in C++ using OpenGL, tested on an Nvidia FX 1000 card, Pentium 4 2.8 GHz, 1.5 GB RAM, RedHat 9. name: Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) Traversal
head: BVH for Triangle Traversal, Bounding Volume Hierarchy, GPU BVH Traversal, Iterative BVH Traversal
body: Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) Traversal is a method for accelerating ray-primitive intersection tests by organizing scene geometry (typically triangles) into a hierarchical tree of bounding volumes. It solves the problem of efficiently skipping empty space during ray traversal, replacing stride-based grid walks or linear primitive checks with a tree walk that prunes large portions of the scene. It sets itself apart from Hierarchical Grid Traversal by abandoning the flat CSR grid layout in favor of a tree structure that adapts to the geometry's spatial distribution, and from Leaf Collection by maintaining explicit parent-child relationships for traversal control rather than collecting leaf primitives into a flat buffer. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of triangles (or other primitives) defining the scene geometry. Output: For each ray, the closest intersection point, the primitive ID, and optionally the normal or material data. Data Structures: The BVH is a binary tree where each node contains a bounding volume (e.g., AABB, OBB, or DOP) that encloses all primitives in its subtree. Interior Node: Contains the bounding volume of the node and indices/pointers to two child nodes (left and right). Leaf Node: Contains the bounding volume of the leaf and a list of primitive indices or pointers to the primitive data. Primitive Buffer: A contiguous array storing the primitive data (e.g., triangle vertices). Steps: 1. Build: Construct the BVH over the scene triangles. Common strategies include Surface Area Heuristic (SAH) based splitting. 2. Initialize: For each ray, initialize an explicit stack in local memory (thread-local storage). Push the root node index onto the stack. 3. Traverse: While the stack is not empty: a. Pop the top node index from the stack. b. Check if the ray intersects the node's bounding volume. If not, continue to the next iteration. c. If the node is a leaf: i. Perform intersection tests (e.g., Möller–Trumbore) for all primitives in the leaf. ii. Update the closest hit if a nearer intersection is found. d. If the node is interior: i. Determine the order of child traversal (e.g., based on ray entry distance to child bounding volumes). ii. Push the farther child's index onto the stack. iii. Push the nearer child's index onto the stack. 4. Terminate: When the stack is empty, the closest hit found is the result for the ray. Formulas: Ray-Box Intersection: For an AABB defined by min and max, the ray O + tD intersects if: t{min} = \maxi \left( \frac{mini - Oi}{Di} \right), \quad t{max} = \mini \left( \frac{maxi - Oi}{Di} \right) Intersection exists if t{min} \le t{max} and t{max} > 0. Möller–Trumbore: For a triangle with vertices v0, v1, v2 and ray O + tD: E1 = v1 - v0, \quad E2 = v2 - v0, \quad H = D \times E2, \quad a = E1 \cdot H, \quad f = 1/a S = O - v0, \quad u = f \cdot (S \cdot H), \quad T = D \times E1, \quad v = f \cdot (S \cdot T) t = f \cdot (E2 \cdot T) Intersection if a \ne 0, u \ge 0, v \ge 0, and u + v \le 1. Parameters: Stack Size: Must be sufficient to hold the maximum depth of the BVH. For a balanced tree with N leaves, depth is \approx \log2 N. Primitive Count per Leaf: Affects the trade-off between traversal depth and leaf intersection cost. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Recursion: Recursive traversal is inefficient on GPUs due to call stack overhead and risk of stack overflows. An explicit stack is required. Precision: Floating-point precision issues in ray-box or ray-triangle tests can lead to missed intersections or artifacts. Degenerate Primitives: Triangles with zero area should be handled or filtered during build/traversal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bvhtraverse(rayorigin, raydirection, bvhroot, primitives): # Stack stores node indices stack = [bvhroot] closestt = infinity closestprimid = -1 while stack: nodeidx = stack.pop() node = bvhroot[nodeidx] # Ray-box intersection test if not rayboxintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, node.bboxmin, node.bboxmax): continue if node.isleaf: for primidx in node.primitiveindices: prim = primitives[primidx] t, u, v = möllertrumbore(rayorigin, raydirection, prim.v0, prim.v1, prim.v2) if t is not None and 0 < t < closestt: closestt = t closestprimid = primidx else: # Determine traversal order t0, t1 = rayboxintersectt(rayorigin, raydirection, node.left.bboxmin, node.left.bboxmax) t2, t3 = rayboxintersectt(rayorigin, raydirection, node.right.bboxmin, node.right.bboxmax) # Push farther child first if t0 < t2: stack.append(node.rightidx) stack.append(node.leftidx) else: stack.append(node.leftidx) stack.append(node.rightidx) return closestt, closestprimid Mesh BVH is a GPU-accelerated BVH designed for triangle meshes to support efficient distance queries, signed distance field (SDF) computation, and ray-triangle intersections. It serves as the primary acceleration structure for methods requiring fast nearest-point lookups on high-resolution geometry, such as the isoext.sdf.TriangleMeshSDF implementation. Unlike general-purpose BVHs that may prioritize ray intersection throughput, this variant is optimized for batched point-to-mesh distance calculations and sign determination, often leveraging hardware ray tracing (e.g., OptiX) for the signing phase. It distinguishes itself from IRIS Ray-Geometry Intersection by focusing on distance metrics rather than pure intersection, and from Multi-Hit BVH Traversal by typically returning the single closest primitive for distance queries. IRIS is an intersection-aware ray-based sampling method for implicit editable scenes that determines samples as the maximum response points of Gaussians intersected by each ray. It solves the problem of efficiently gathering depth samples from 3D Gaussian primitives in a hardware-accelerated ray tracing pipeline. It sets itself apart from standard BVH traversal methods by replacing explicit Gaussian volume checks with proxy geometry (affine-transformed icosahedra) and leveraging OptiX Any-hit shaders to compute sampling parameters directly during intersection tests. Multi-Hit BVH Traversal is a SIMD-friendly clipping algorithm for ray-traced direct volume rendering (DVR) that identifies visible volume regions by intersecting viewing rays with arbitrary geometric surface primitives (planes, quadrics, triangle meshes) organized in a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). It sets itself apart from rasterization-based depth peeling or texture-based slicing approaches by implementing clipping as a simple two-pass algorithm that avoids multiple render passes, dynamic memory reallocation, and the conversion of parametric surfaces to polygon meshes. Initial Upper Bound Estimation computes a tight initial upper bound to prune BVH-tree traversal during distance field computation for isosurface approximation. It differs from standard hierarchical traversal by proactively sampling the approximated surface to establish a pruning threshold before traversal begins, rather than waiting for the first leaf encounter. This allows for more aggressive pruning at the beginning of the traversal, reducing the total number of nodes visited. A rendering method using a PackedBVH over triangles, traversed with ray-box slab tests for pruning, and Möller–Trumbore tests for triangle intersections. It determines if a ray is occluded by any triangle (shadow ray), returning true on the first hit. Unlike sphere tracing, it requires no distance function and is exact for sharp CSG operations by walking primitive crossings along the ray. This method traverses a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to find the triangle closest to a specific query point. It solves the problem of efficient nearest-neighbor search in geometric scenes by pruning branches that cannot contain a closer primitive than the current best. It sets itself apart from Mesh BVH and IRIS Ray-Geometry Intersection by operating on point-to-primitive distance rather than ray-parametric distance, and from Multi-Hit BVH Traversal by returning only the single closest hit. Ray Packet BVH Traversal traverses a Wald-ordered Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) for a packet of rays to find the closest intersection for each active ray in the packet, or to determine which rays are occluded by triangles. It differs from single-ray traversal by processing multiple rays simultaneously, leveraging SIMD-like parallelism within the traversal stack and leaf intersection tests. It builds on Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) Traversal by extending the node visitation logic to handle a range of ray indices (first to first + packetsize) rather than a single ray. Uses a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) built over the coarse tetrahedral mesh to efficiently locate the coarse element containing a sample point. Build a triangle BVH over the coarse mesh by inserting four triangular faces facing outside for every coarse element. Trace rays into the BVH using OptiX Wrapper Library (OWL) hit and miss functions. The hit function returns the hit point and the coarse tetrahedron ID. The miss function reports no intersection with BVH faces. Unlike element marching which uses connectivity, point location querying skips coarse elements not being sampled and allows varying refinement levels in the coarse mesh. Computes the unsigned distance from query points to a triangle mesh using a BVH, and provides an analytic gradient for backpropagation. Flatten input x to [N, 3]. Query BVH for distance udf, triangle ID triid, and barycentric coordinates uvw. Clamp uvw to [1e-9, 1-1e-9]. Interpolate nearest point on triangle using uvw and triangle vertices. Return udf reshaped to input shape. In backward pass, retrieve saved x and nearestpoints. Compute diff = x - nearestpoints. Compute norm = diff.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8. Gradient is gradoutput scaled by diff/norm. Formula: \nablax \text{UDF}(x) = \frac{x - p{\text{nearest}}}{\|x - p{\text{nearest}}\|} where p{\text{nearest}} is the closest point on the mesh. Input x shape [N, 3]. Output udf shape [N, 1]. Saved tensors: xflat, nearestpoints. Pitfall: uvw is clamped to [1e-9, 1-1e-9] to avoid invalid barycentric coordinates at triangle edges/corners. A layout optimization for Discrete Oriented Polytopes (DOP-14) where the 14 bounding planes are split into two separate arrays to improve traversal performance by enabling independent memory access patterns. First check the AABB planes of the bounding volume (planes 0-2) during traversal. Only test planes 3–6 if warranted by the result of the initial AABB plane check. The BVHd type defines an Interior node with two children and a Leaf node with primitive count and data. The layout groups fields lo1, hi1, c0, c1 (planes 0-2) in one array, and lo2, hi2 (planes 3-6) in a separate array. In the layout specification, fields lo1, hi1, c0, and c1 correspond to AABB planes occupying the first array, accessed immediately. Fields lo2 and hi2 reside in a separate array, accessed only when the finer-grain intersection test is needed. Separates the logical bounding volume specification (which planes comprise a DOP-14) from the physical organization (which planes are co-located in memory), facilitating exploration of alternative representations. Time Complexity: O(\log N) average case for balanced trees, O(N) worst case for degenerate trees. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the tree and primitives. Performance: Generally faster than linear traversal for complex scenes. Performance depends on tree balance and build quality. Strengths: Efficient pruning of empty space, flexible geometry representation, good cache locality with flat layouts. Limitations: Build time can be significant, sensitive to scene distribution, stack management overhead on GPUs. When to Use: Complex scenes with many primitives, dynamic scenes with moderate updates (if rebuild is feasible), hardware ray tracing support. When Not to Use: Very simple scenes, scenes with high dynamic update rates where rebuild cost is prohibitive, scenes with strong spatial coherence where grid-based methods may be simpler. BVH traversal was introduced as a standard acceleration structure for ray tracing. It has been widely adopted in both CPU and GPU ray tracers due to its efficiency and flexibility. The method has evolved with hardware support for ray tracing (e.g., NVIDIA OptiX). name: Mesh BVH
head: GPU BVH for Triangle Mesh, MeshBVH, TriangleMeshSDF BVH
body: Mesh BVH is a GPU-accelerated bounding volume hierarchy designed for triangle meshes to support efficient distance queries, signed distance field (SDF) computation, and ray-triangle intersections. It serves as the primary acceleration structure for methods requiring fast nearest-point lookups on high-resolution geometry, such as the isoext.sdf.TriangleMeshSDF implementation. Unlike general-purpose BVHs that may prioritize ray intersection throughput, this variant is optimized for batched point-to-mesh distance calculations and sign determination, often leveraging hardware ray tracing (e.g., OptiX) for the signing phase. It distinguishes itself from IRIS Ray-Geometry Intersection by focusing on distance metrics rather than pure intersection, and from Multi-Hit BVH Traversal by typically returning the single closest primitive for distance queries. The method constructs a hierarchical tree over a triangle mesh to accelerate queries for the closest point, distance, and topological sign (inside/outside) for arbitrary 3D points. Inputs: Vertices V: A CUDA tensor of shape (Nv, 3) with float32 data type, representing mesh vertex positions. Faces F: A CUDA tensor of shape (Nf, 3) with int32 data type, representing vertex indices for each triangle. Outputs: closest: For input points P of shape (N, 3), returns a tuple: Distances D: Tensor of shape (N,) float32. Closest Points C: Tensor of shape (N, 3) float32. Face IDs I: Tensor of shape (N,) identifying the closest triangle. sign: For input points P, returns a tensor of shape (N,) float32 with values +1 (outside) or -1 (inside). windingnumber: For input points P, returns a tensor of shape (N,) float32 with value 1 (inside closed mesh) or 0 (outside). The BVH is a binary tree where each node contains an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). Leaf Nodes: Contain references to the triangle indices stored in the input face tensor F. Internal Nodes: Contain an AABB that encloses the union of the bounding volumes of its children. Storage: The hierarchy is stored in GPU memory (CUDA tensors) to enable parallel traversal. The constructor takes the vertex tensor V and face tensor F. 1. Compute the AABB for each triangle in F using the vertices in V. 2. Build the binary tree hierarchy bottom-up or via a parallel cluster merging strategy on the GPU. 3. Store the resulting node structure in device memory. Given a batch of query points P{query}: 1. Traverse the BVH for each point p \in P{query} to find the closest triangle. 2. For the candidate triangle with vertices a, b, c, compute the closest point on the triangle to p using Voronoi region tests: Let ab = b - a, ac = c - a, ap = p - a. Compute dot products: d1 = ab \cdot ap, d2 = ac \cdot ap. If d1 \le 0 and d2 \le 0, the closest point is a. Let bp = p - b. Compute d3 = ab \cdot bp, d4 = ac \cdot bp. If d3 \ge 0 and d4 \le d3, the closest point is b. Compute vc = d1 d4 - d3 d2. If vc \le 0 and d1 \ge 0 and d3 \le 0, the closest point lies on edge ab at a + ab \frac{d1}{d1 - d3}. Let cp = p - c. Compute d5 = ab \cdot cp, d6 = ac \cdot cp. If d6 \ge 0 and d5 \le d6, the closest point is c. Compute vb = d5 d2 - d1 d6. If vb \le 0 and d2 \ge 0 and d6 \le 0, the closest point lies on edge ac at a + ac \frac{d2}{d2 - d6}. Otherwise, the closest point lies in the triangle interior at a + ab \frac{d1 d4 - d3 d2}{vb} + ac \frac{d5 d2 - d1 d6}{vb} (barycentric interpolation). 3. Return the distance \|p - closest\point\|, the closest point coordinates, and the face ID. To determine if a point is inside or outside: 1. Watertight Check: If the mesh is known to be watertight, the sign can be determined by the dot product of the view direction and the normal of the closest triangle found in step 2. However, this is disabled by default due to incompatibility with non-watertight meshes. 2. Stab Ray Method (General): Trace 32 "stab rays" distributed uniformly over the sphere using a Fibonacci lattice. Each ray is pseudorandomly and independently offset for every training position. Use NVIDIA ray tracing hardware (OptiX 7) for ray-triangle intersections. If any ray reaches infinity (no intersection), the point is marked outside (+1). If all rays intersect the mesh, the point is marked inside (-1). Returns 1 if the point is inside a closed mesh, 0 otherwise. This is typically computed via the same ray casting logic as sign, counting intersections or using the stab ray method. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch class MeshBVH: def init(self, vertices: torch.Tensor, faces: torch.Tensor): """ vertices: (Nv, 3) float32 CUDA tensor faces: (Nf, 3) int32 CUDA tensor """ self.vertices = vertices self.faces = faces # Construct BVH structure on GPU. # Implementation details depend on the specific builder (e.g., cluster merging). self.bvhtree = buildbvhgpu(vertices, faces) def closest(self, points: torch.Tensor) -> tuple: """ points: (N, 3) float32 CUDA tensor Returns: distances (N,), closestpoints (N, 3), faceids (N,) """ # Traverse BVH to find closest triangle for each point. # For each point p, find faceid. faceids = traversebvhforclosestface(self.bvhtree, points) # Fetch triangle vertices triverts = self.vertices[self.faces[faceids]] # (N, 3, 3) # Compute closest point on each triangle a = triverts[:, 0] b = triverts[:, 1] c = triverts[:, 2] ab = b - a ac = c - a ap = points - a d1 = torch.sum(ab ap, dim=1) d2 = torch.sum(ac ap, dim=1) # Region 1: Vertex A maska = (d1 <= 0) & (d2 <= 0) bp = points - b d3 = torch.sum(ab bp, dim=1) d4 = torch.sum(ac bp, dim=1) # Region 2: Vertex B maskb = (d3 >= 0) & (d4 <= d3) vc = d1 d4 - d3 d2 # Region 3: Edge AB maskab = (vc <= 0) & (d1 >= 0) & (d3 <= 0) cp = points - c d5 = torch.sum(ab cp, dim=1) d6 = torch.sum(ac cp, dim=1) # Region 4: Vertex C maskc = (d6 >= 0) & (d5 <= d6) vb = d5 d2 - d1 d6 # Region 5: Edge AC maskac = (vb <= 0) & (d2 >= 0) & (d6 <= 0) # Region 6: Interior maskinterior = ~(maska | maskb | maskab | maskc | maskac) closestpoints = torch.zeroslike(points) # Compute barycentric coordinates for interior and edge cases # Edge AB: t = d1 / (d1 - d3) denomab = d1 - d3 safedenomab = torch.where(denomab == 0, torch.oneslike(denomab), denomab) tab = d1 / safedenomab closestpoints[maskab] = a[maskab] + ab[maskab] tab[maskab, None] # Edge AC: t = d2 / (d2 - d6) denomac = d2 - d6 safedenomac = torch.where(denomac == 0, torch.oneslike(denomac), denomac) tac = d2 / safedenomac closestpoints[maskac] = a[maskac] + ac[maskac] tac[maskac, None] # Interior: barycentric coords # u = (d2d5 - d1d6) / vb # v = (d1d4 - d3d2) / vb # w = 1 - u - v # Note: vb can be zero for degenerate triangles, handled by guard denomvb = vb safedenomvb = torch.where(denomvb == 0, torch.oneslike(denomvb), denomvb) u = (d2 d5 - d1 d6) / safedenomvb v = (d1 d4 - d3 d2) / safedenomvb w = 1.0 - u - v closestpoints[maskinterior] = ( u[maskinterior, None] a[maskinterior] + v[maskinterior, None] b[maskinterior] + w[maskinterior, None] c[maskinterior]) # Vertices A and B are already handled by maska and maskb (closestpoint is a or b) closestpoints[maska] = a[maska] closestpoints[maskb] = b[maskb] closestpoints[maskc] = c[maskc] distances = torch.norm(points - closestpoints, dim=1) return distances, closestpoints, faceids def sign(self, points: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ points: (N, 3) float32 CUDA tensor Returns: (N,) float32 tensor: +1 outside, -1 inside """ # Use OptiX 7 for stab ray tracing if available, otherwise software BVH. # Stab rays: 32 rays distributed via Fibonacci lattice. numstabrays = 32 # Generate stab ray directions and offsets. # If any ray hits infinity, point is outside. # This requires a ray-triangle intersection kernel. # Simplified logic: hits = tracestabraysoptix(points, numstabrays) # Returns boolean tensor (N,) # If any ray misses (hits infinity), it's outside. # Assuming hits[i] is True if ALL rays hit the mesh. inside = torch.all(hits, dim=1) sign = torch.where(inside, -1.0, 1.0) return sign Number of stab rays: 32. Ray distribution: Fibonacci lattice with pseudorandom independent offset per point. Non-watertight meshes: The normal-based signing method is disabled by default because it is incompatible with typical non-watertight meshes found in the wild. The stab ray method is required for correctness in these cases. Degenerate Triangles: The barycentric calculation involves division by vb or vc. If the triangle is degenerate (area zero), these denominators are zero. A guard must handle this, typically by falling back to vertex distances or treating it as a line/point. Precision: Floating-point precision in distance calculations can affect SDF accuracy. Using float32 is standard, but float64 may be needed for high-precision applications. A binary tree hierarchy over a triangle mesh where leaves are triangles and internal nodes contain a 3D axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) over positions and a bounding cone over shading normals for all descendants. It stores position and normal information for boundary triangles to enable hierarchical pruning of refractive path searches. It is distinguished from interval-based refinement by prioritizing speed over guaranteed convergence, typically running 2 to 5 times faster while producing visually equivalent results. Choose this when refractive path tracing requires fast normal-based pruning. Position-Normal Tree A raycasting method for voxel meshes that traverses a grid of oriented sub-cubes to find intersections with voxel geometry using BVH triangle intersection tests. It differs from its parent Mesh BVH by adding a spatial grid traversal layer that maps ray positions to specific voxel meshes before delegating to the mesh's internal BVH. It differs from siblings like Position-Normal Tree by relying on explicit triangle intersection tests within leaf nodes rather than implicit distance fields. Choose this for voxel-based scenes with explicit triangle geometry. Voxel Mesh Ray Intersection via BVH This method constructs a Binary Volume Hierarchy (BVH) on the GPU by iteratively merging clusters of triangles. It solves the problem of building hierarchical acceleration structures for ray tracing without CPU-GPU synchronization bottlenecks by using a fully parallel, double-buffered approach involving neighbor finding, prefix scans, and reallocation. It differs from CPU-based top-down or bottom-up builders by keeping all data on the GPU and using a "merge-compact" loop that reduces the number of active clusters by half (approximately) each iteration until a single root remains. Choose this when BVH construction must be fully GPU-accelerated. GPU BVH Construction via Cluster Merging Uses a BVH to compute the unsigned distance and barycentric coordinates from interpolated UV-space positions back to the original high-resolution mesh, correcting geometric errors from simplification/remeshing. Query the BVH for the closest face and UVW coordinates, fetch the original triangle vertices, and reconstruct the corrected position via barycentric interpolation. Choose this when high-fidelity geometric attributes are needed from a simplified mesh. A bounding volume hierarchy adapted for the management of the blending operation, used for efficient evaluation of field functions on large skeletons. Choose this for skeletal animation blending where field evaluation is the bottleneck. A method to compute the signed distance from a 3D point to a triangle mesh efficiently using a BVH for unsigned distance and ray casting for sign determination. Construct a BVH for O(\log N) unsigned distance queries, then trace 32 stab rays using a Fibonacci lattice to determine sign. Use OptiX 7 for ray-triangle intersections for maximum efficiency. Choose this for high-performance SDF computation on GPUs. Time Complexity: Unsigned distance queries are O(\log N{triangles}) on average. Sign determination using 32 stab rays is O(32 \cdot \log N{triangles}) or O(32 \cdot R) where R is ray traversal cost. Memory Complexity: O(N{triangles}) for storing the BVH nodes and triangle references. Performance: Using OptiX 7 for ray-triangle intersections is over an order of magnitude faster than software triangle BVH for ray-shape intersections on an RTX 3090 GPU. Strengths: High performance on GPU, supports batched queries, handles large meshes efficiently. Limitations: Requires GPU memory for the BVH. Sign determination via stab rays is computationally expensive compared to normal-based signing for watertight meshes. When to use: When fast distance queries and SDF computation are needed for triangle meshes on GPU. When not to use: For CPU-only environments or when the mesh is small enough that linear search is faster. Mesh BVH was developed as part of the isoext library for GPU-based signed distance field computation. It leverages NVIDIA's OptiX 7 framework for hardware-accelerated ray tracing, which was shown to significantly outperform software BVH implementations in the context of Instant Neural Graphics Primitives. The method is used in applications requiring efficient geometric queries for neural rendering and SDF-based modeling. name: Position-Normal Tree
head: Position-Normal Tree Hierarchy, Position-Normal Tree for Hierarchical Pruning
body: A binary tree hierarchy over a triangle mesh where leaves are triangles and internal nodes contain a 3D axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) over positions and a bounding cone over shading normals for all descendants. It stores position and normal information for boundary triangles to enable hierarchical pruning of refractive path searches. It is distinguished from interval-based refinement by prioritizing speed over guaranteed convergence, typically running 2 to 5 times faster while producing visually equivalent results. Inputs: A triangle mesh boundary. Outputs: A binary tree structure for pruning refractive path searches. Data Structures: Each node contains an AABB over positions, a bounding cone over normals, child pointers for internal nodes, and a triangle reference for leaves. Memory usage is approximately 100 bytes per boundary triangle. Steps: 1. Construct the hierarchy using a bottom-up approach. 2. Perform a depth-first traversal of the tree. 3. At each node, test for pruning using the spindle test, sidedness test, and cone overlap test. 4. If any test proves no solution exists, prune the subtree. The exact merging algorithm is not given in the sources. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Refractive index (\eta) is typically 1.5 for homogeneous media in the examples. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The tree only needs to be rebuilt if the geometry is deformed. The pruning tests are heuristic and may miss a few paths near caustic cusps on rare occasions, affecting at most a few pixels per image compared to interval-based refinement. A recursive strategy to find refraction points on triangles with smooth normals by progressively splitting the triangle into smaller sub-triangles and pruning those that cannot contain a solution. It is distinguished from interval-based refinement by prioritizing speed over guaranteed convergence, typically running 2 to 5 times faster while producing visually equivalent results. Choose it when performance is critical and visually equivalent results are acceptable over strict convergence guarantees. Essential for performance on meshes with many triangles. Without hierarchical pruning, the pool scene took 1934.6s versus 59.4s with it, a 32x slowdown. Build time is very fast, taking 6ms for the glass tile model. Memory usage is approximately 100 bytes per boundary triangle. The position-normal tree and hierarchical pruning are essential for getting good performance on boundary meshes with more than a few triangles. The position-normal tree was introduced by Bala et al., building on earlier work by Snyder and Walter et al.. It is used in single scattering in refractive media with triangle mesh boundaries to efficiently compute refractive connection paths. name: Split-and-Prune for Sub-Triangle Search
head: Cone Angles Triangle Subdivision Heuristic
body: A recursive strategy to find refraction points on triangles with smooth normals by progressively splitting the triangle into smaller sub-triangles and pruning those that cannot contain a solution. It enables efficient 2D search for refractive paths where interpolated normals create complex, non-planar solution spaces. It is distinguished from interval-based refinement by prioritizing speed over guaranteed convergence, typically running 2 to 5 times faster while producing visually equivalent results. Inputs: Triangle vertices V0, V1, V2 with positions and shading normals. Light direction \hat{L} and view direction \hat{V} at the incident point P. Refraction index \eta. Outputs: A set of sub-triangles containing potential solutions, ready for 2D Newton-Raphson iteration. Data Structures: Bounding Cone: Defined by an axis vector \hat{A} and a semi-angle \theta. Spherical Triangle Bounding Box: A 3D axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) enclosing a spherical triangle on the unit sphere. Steps: 1. Compute Bounding Cone for Shading Normals (\hat{N}s): Construct the spherical triangle defined by the vertex shading normals \hat{N}0, \hat{N}1, \hat{N}2. Compute the bounding cone for this spherical triangle. All bounding cones have their apex at the origin. 2. Compute Bounding Cone for Half-Vector (\hat{H}): Compute the spherical triangles defined by the directions (\hat{L}-Vi)/\|\hat{L}-Vi\| and (\hat{V}-Vi)/\|\hat{V}-Vi\| for i=0,1,2. Compute 3D AABBs for both spherical triangles. Scale the view direction AABB by \eta. Compute the Minkowski sum of the light AABB and the scaled view AABB by adding corresponding min/max bounds. This yields an AABB for the unnormalized half-vector. Compute the bounding cone for this resulting AABB. 3. Pruning Test: Check if the bounding cone for -\hat{H} and the bounding cone for \hat{N}s overlap. If they do not overlap, prune the triangle (it cannot contain a solution). Two cones overlap if the angle between their axes is less than the sum of their bounding semiangles. 4. Subdivision or Termination: If the triangle is not pruned, check the stopping criterion. Heuristic Stopping Criterion: If the sum of the \hat{H} cone angle and the \hat{N}s cone angle is less than 30 degrees, stop subdividing and proceed to 2D Newton-Raphson iteration. If the criterion is not met, split the triangle into 4 smaller sub-triangles by splitting each edge in half. Recursively apply steps 1-4 to each sub-triangle. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class AABB: def init(self, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz): self.minx, self.maxx = minx, maxx self.miny, self.maxy = miny, maxy self.minz, self.maxz = minz, maxz class Triangle: def init(self, v0, v1, v2, n0, n1, n2): self.v0, self.v1, self.v2 = v0, v1, v2 self.n0, self.n1, self.n2 = n0, n1, n2 def midpoint(p1, p2): return ((p1[0]+p2[0])/2, (p1[1]+p2[1])/2, (p1[2]+p2[2])/2) def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) if mag > 0 else (0,0,0) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def anglebetweenvectors(v1, v2): return math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot(normalize(v1), normalize(v2))))) def computesphericaltriangleboundingcone(n0, n1, n2): # Standard computation: axis is normalized sum, semi-angle is max angle to vertices axis = normalize((n0[0]+n1[0]+n2[0], n0[1]+n1[1]+n2[1], n0[2]+n1[2]+n2[2])) angle = max(anglebetweenvectors(n0, axis), anglebetweenvectors(n1, axis), anglebetweenvectors(n2, axis)) return (axis, angle) def computeaabb(sphtri): xs = [p[0] for p in sphtri] ys = [p[1] for p in sphtri] zs = [p[2] for p in sphtri] return AABB(min(xs), max(xs), min(ys), max(ys), min(zs), max(zs)) def scaleaabb(box, s): return AABB(box.minxs, box.maxxs, box.minys, box.maxys, box.minzs, box.maxzs) def minkowskisum(b1, b2): return AABB(b1.minx+b2.minx, b1.maxx+b2.maxx, b1.miny+b2.miny, b1.maxy+b2.maxy, b1.minz+b2.minz, b1.maxz+b2.maxz) def computeboxboundingcone(box): # Axis is direction to box center, semi-angle is max angle to any corner cx, cy, cz = (box.minx+box.maxx)/2, (box.miny+box.maxy)/2, (box.minz+box.maxz)/2 axis = normalize((cx, cy, cz)) corners = [ (box.minx, box.miny, box.minz), (box.maxx, box.miny, box.minz), (box.minx, box.maxy, box.minz), (box.maxx, box.maxy, box.minz), (box.minx, box.miny, box.maxz), (box.maxx, box.miny, box.maxz), (box.minx, box.maxy, box.maxz), (box.maxx, box.maxy, box.maxz) ] angle = max(anglebetweenvectors(c, axis) for c in corners) return (axis, angle) def conesoverlap(cone1, cone2): # Two cones overlap if the angle between their axes is less than the sum of their bounding semiangles return anglebetweenvectors(cone1[0], cone2[0]) < (cone1[1] + cone2[1]) def splitandprunesearch(triangle, Ldir, Vdir, eta): # Step 1: Compute bounding cone for shading normals (Ns) nscone = computesphericaltriangleboundingcone(triangle.n0, triangle.n1, triangle.n2) # Step 2: Compute bounding cone for half-vector (H) # Spherical triangle for L lsphtri = [normalize((Ldir[0]-v[0], Ldir[1]-v[1], Ldir[2]-v[2])) for v in (triangle.v0, triangle.v1, triangle.v2)] # Spherical triangle for V vsphtri = [normalize((Vdir[0]-v[0], Vdir[1]-v[1], Vdir[2]-v[2])) for v in (triangle.v0, triangle.v1, triangle.v2)] lbox = computeaabb(lsphtri) vbox = computeaabb(vsphtri) vboxscaled = scaleaabb(vbox, eta) hbox = minkowskisum(lbox, vboxscaled) hcone = computeboxboundingcone(hbox) # Step 3: Pruning Test # Check if bounding cone for -H and Ns overlap neghcone = (-hcone[0][0], -hcone[0][1], -hcone[0][2]), hcone[1] if not conesoverlap(neghcone, nscone): return [] # Pruned # Step 4: Subdivision or Termination coneanglesumdeg = math.degrees(hcone[1] + nscone[1]) if coneanglesumdeg < 30.0: return [triangle] # Stop subdividing, proceed to Newton-Raphson else: mid01 = midpoint(triangle.v0, triangle.v1) mid12 = midpoint(triangle.v1, triangle.v2) mid20 = midpoint(triangle.v2, triangle.v0) # Interpolate normals for sub-triangles n01 = normalize((triangle.n0[0]+triangle.n1[0], triangle.n0[1]+triangle.n1[1], triangle.n0[2]+triangle.n1[2])) n12 = normalize((triangle.n1[0]+triangle.n2[0], triangle.n1[1]+triangle.n2[1], triangle.n1[2]+triangle.n2[2])) n20 = normalize((triangle.n2[0]+triangle.n0[0], triangle.n2[1]+triangle.n0[1], triangle.n2[2]+triangle.n0[2])) subtriangles = [ Triangle(triangle.v0, mid01, mid20, triangle.n0, n01, n20), Triangle(mid01, triangle.v1, mid12, n01, triangle.n1, n12), Triangle(mid20, mid12, triangle.v2, n20, n12, triangle.n2), Triangle(mid01, mid12, mid20, n01, n12, n20) ] results = [] for subt in subtriangles: results.extend(splitandprunesearch(subt, Ldir, Vdir, eta)) return results Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The heuristic is not guaranteed to find all solutions. It may miss a few paths near caustic cusps on rare occasions, affecting at most a few pixels. Normal-mapped triangles are not supported in the original description, though bounding cones could be precomputed. A heuristic for triangle subdivision used to find refractive paths, preferred over interval-based refinement for speed in the reported results. It is typically 2 to 5 times faster than interval-based refinement test, producing visually equivalent images. It may miss a few paths near caustic cusps on rare occasions, affecting at most a few pixels. Time Complexity: Faster than interval-based refinement, typically 2 to 5 times faster depending on the scene. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Speed; produces visually good results. Limitations: Not guaranteed to find all solutions; may miss paths near caustic cusps. When to use: When visual equivalence is acceptable and speed is prioritized over guaranteed convergence. When not to use: When guaranteed convergence is required, in which case the interval-based refinement test should be used. Originated in the paper "Single Scattering in Refractive Media with Triangle Mesh Boundaries". The method addresses the difficulty of finding refraction points on triangles with interpolated normals, where the problem is 2D rather than 1D due to the potential for multiple solutions not lying within a single incidence plane. name: Voxel Mesh Ray Intersection via BVH
head: Voxel Mesh Raycasting (BVH Triangle Intersection), VoxelGeometryIntersect, VoxelMeshIntersect
body: A raycasting method for voxel meshes that traverses a grid of oriented sub-cubes to find intersections with voxel geometry using BVH triangle intersection tests. It differs from its parent Mesh BVH by adding a spatial grid traversal layer that maps ray positions to specific voxel meshes before delegating to the mesh's internal BVH. It differs from siblings like Position-Normal Tree by relying on explicit triangle intersection tests within leaf nodes rather than implicit distance fields. Inputs: Ray origin (ro), ray direction (rd), maximum distance (MAX\DISTANCE), voxel mesh data structures (indices, vertices, BVH nodes), and world bounds. Outputs: Intersection result containing hit distance (t), hit position, normal, and triangle ID. Data Structures: VoxelMesh struct (80 bytes, 4-byte aligned): state (vec4f, offset 0, x indicates active), position (vec3f, offset 4), indexOffsets (vec4f, offset 8, x = vertex offset, y = index offset, z = BVH tree offset, w = voxel index offset), minBounds (vec3f, offset 12), maxBounds (vec3f, offset 15). AABB struct: min (vec4f, xyz = position, w = active flag), max (vec4f, xyz = position, w = node type: 1 for inner, 2 for voxel geometry). StackNode struct: { nodeId: u32, t: f32 }. Stack: Fixed-size array of 13 StackNode elements (STACKSIZE = 13). Constants: cubeSize = 16.0, subCubeSize = 8.0, halfSize = 8.0, rayLength = 16.0, VOXELNODEINDEX = 4095u. Algorithm Steps: 1. Inverse Direction Calculation: Compute inverse ray direction components to handle near-zero values and avoid division by zero: invDir.x = \frac{1.0}{\text{sign}(rd.x) \cdot \max(|rd.x|, 10^{-8})} The same formula is applied to the y and z components. 2. Initialization: Set t = \infty, totalDistance = 0.0, and rayPosition = ro. 3. Grid Traversal Loop: Define an oriented bounding cube relative to rayPosition using rd, a right vector, and an up vector with halfSize offset. Iterate through a 3 \times 3 \times 3 grid of sub-cubes (indices i, j, k \in [0, 2]). Calculate sub-cube center: subCubeCenter = cubeMinCorner + rd \cdot (i \cdot subCubeSize) + right \cdot (j \cdot subCubeSize) + up \cdot (k \cdot subCubeSize) Calculate sub-cube min corner: subCubeMin = subCubeCenter - rd \cdot \frac{subCubeSize}{2} - right \cdot \frac{subCubeSize}{2} - up \cdot \frac{subCubeSize}{2} Lookup world mesh at subCubeMin using getWorldMesh, which checks bounds and returns the mesh index if found. Perform bounding box intersection test between ray and voxel mesh bounds using BoundingBoxIntersect, storing result in chunkT. If mesh found, chunkT < t, and chunkT < MAX\DISTANCE, call VoxelMeshIntersect with ro, rd, mesh index, and MAX\DISTANCE. If VoxelMeshIntersect returns a hit and result.t \le t, update finalResult and t. 4. BVH Traversal (VoxelMeshIntersect): Initialize stackIndex = 0, currentNodeIndex = 0, currentNodeT = 0.0. Calculate inverseDir = 1.0 / rd. Get mesh position and offset from mesh.indexOffsets.z. Loop: Fetch current node from voxelbvh[currentNodeIndex + offset]. Leaf Check: If currentNode.max.w == 2.0, it is a leaf. Call VoxelGeometryIntersect(ro, rd, currentNodeIndex - VOXELNODEINDEX, voxelMeshIndex). If hit, set intersectResult.found = true, intersectResult.t = currentNodeT, store geometry result, and break loop. Internal Node: Calculate child IDs: leftChildId = 2 currentNodeIndex + 1, rightChildId = 2 currentNodeIndex + 2. Fetch children from voxelbvh. Test left child: If leftChild.min.w >= 0, compute leftChildT = BoundingBoxIntersect(...). If leftChildT > MAXDISTANCE, set leftChildT = \infty. Test right child: If rightChild.min.w >= 0, compute rightChildT = BoundingBoxIntersect(...). If rightChildT > MAXDISTANCE, set rightChildT = \infty. Traversal Logic: If only left hit (leftChildT < \infty and rightChildT == \infty): currentNodeIndex = leftChildId, currentNodeT = leftChildT. If only right hit (rightChildT < \infty and leftChildT == \infty): currentNodeIndex = rightChildId, currentNodeT = rightChildT. If both hit: Push farther child onto stack. Check stack overflow (stackIndex >= STACKSIZE); if overflow, set intersectResult.error = true and break. Traverse closer child. 5. Triangle Intersection (VoxelGeometryIntersect): If length <= 0 (calculated as indiceOffsets.y - indiceOffsets.x), return immediately. Loop indiceIndex from 0 to length with step 3. Get vertex indices v1, v2, v3 from indices array offset by vertexOffset. Call BVHTriangleIntersect1 with transformed vertex positions (vertices[...] + position). If triResult.t < t and triResult.t != \infty: Update intersectResult.hit = true, t = triResult.t, finalTriResult = triResult, triId = indiceIndex / 3, finalIndex = indiceOffset + indiceIndex. 6. Normal Interpolation: If hit, retrieve vertex normals n1, n2, n3 and UVs uv1, uv2, uv3. Interpolate normal: interpolatedNormal = \text{normalize}(n1 \cdot (1.0 - u - v) + n2 \cdot u + n3 \cdot v) where u, v are from finalTriResult. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class IntersectionResult: def init(self, found=False, t=float('inf'), hit=False, error=False, normal=None, triid=-1): self.found = found self.t = t self.hit = hit self.error = error self.normal = normal self.triid = triid class StackNode: def init(self, nodeid, t): self.nodeid = nodeid self.t = t def getworldmesh(subcubemin, voxelmeshes, worldbounds): # Checks bounds and returns mesh index if found, else -1 # Standard grid lookup implementation return -1 def boundingboxintersect(ro, rd, invrd, minb, maxb): tmin = (minb - ro) invrd tmax = (maxb - ro) invrd t1 = min(tmin, tmax) t2 = max(tmin, tmax) tenter = max(t1.x, t1.y, t1.z) texit = min(t2.x, t2.y, t2.z) if tenter > texit: return float('inf') if texit < 0: return float('inf') return max(tenter, 0.0) def bvhtriangleintersect1(ro, rd, v0, v1, v2): edge1 = v1 - v0 edge2 = v2 - v0 h = cross(rd, edge2) a = dot(edge1, h) if a < 1e-8: return IntersectionResult(t=float('inf')) f = 1.0 / a s = ro - v0 u = f dot(s, h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return IntersectionResult(t=float('inf')) q = cross(s, edge1) v = f dot(rd, q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: return IntersectionResult(t=float('inf')) t = f dot(edge2, q) if t > 1e-8: return IntersectionResult(t=t, u=u, v=v) return IntersectionResult(t=float('inf')) def voxelgeometryintersect(ro, rd, nodeidx, meshindex, voxelmeshes): mesh = voxelmeshes[meshindex] length = mesh.indexoffsets.y - mesh.indexoffsets.x if length <= 0: return IntersectionResult(found=False) t = float('inf') finaltriresult = None triid = -1 vertexoffset = mesh.indexoffsets.x indiceoffset = mesh.indexoffsets.y for indiceindex in range(0, length, 3): v1idx = mesh.indices[indiceindex + vertexoffset] v2idx = mesh.indices[indiceindex + 1 + vertexoffset] v3idx = mesh.indices[indiceindex + 2 + vertexoffset] v1 = mesh.vertices[v1idx] + mesh.position v2 = mesh.vertices[v2idx] + mesh.position v3 = mesh.vertices[v3idx] + mesh.position triresult = bvhtriangleintersect1(ro, rd, v1, v2, v3) if triresult.t < t and triresult.t != float('inf'): t = triresult.t finaltriresult = triresult triid = indiceindex // 3 if finaltriresult is not None: v1idx = mesh.indices[triid 3 + vertexoffset] v2idx = mesh.indices[triid 3 + 1 + vertexoffset] v3idx = mesh.indices[triid 3 + 2 + vertexoffset] n1 = mesh.normals[v1idx] n2 = mesh.normals[v2idx] n3 = mesh.normals[v3idx] u = finaltriresult.u v = finaltriresult.v normal = normalize(n1 (1.0 - u - v) + n2 u + n3 v) return IntersectionResult(found=True, t=t, normal=normal, triid=triid) return IntersectionResult(found=False) def voxelmeshintersect(ro, rd, meshindex, maxdistance, voxelmeshes): stack = [StackNode(0, 0.0)] 13 stackindex = 0 currentnodeindex = 0 currentnodet = 0.0 invrd = vec3(1.0 / max(abs(rd.x), 1e-8), 1.0 / max(abs(rd.y), 1e-8), 1.0 / max(abs(rd.z), 1e-8)) mesh = voxelmeshes[meshindex] bvhoffset = mesh.indexoffsets.z voxelbvh = mesh.bvhnodes while True: node = voxelbvh[currentnodeindex + bvhoffset] if node.max.w == 2.0: georesult = voxelgeometryintersect(ro, rd, currentnodeindex - 4095, meshindex, voxelmeshes) if georesult.found: return georesult break leftid = 2 currentnodeindex + 1 rightid = 2 currentnodeindex + 2 leftchild = voxelbvh[leftid + bvhoffset] rightchild = voxelbvh[rightid + bvhoffset] leftt = float('inf') rightt = float('inf') if leftchild.min.w >= 0: leftt = boundingboxintersect(ro, rd, invrd, leftchild.min.xyz, leftchild.max.xyz) if leftt > maxdistance: leftt = float('inf') if rightchild.min.w >= 0: rightt = boundingboxintersect(ro, rd, invrd, rightchild.min.xyz, rightchild.max.xyz) if rightt > maxdistance: rightt = float('inf') if leftt < float('inf') and rightt == float('inf'): currentnodeindex = leftid currentnodet = leftt elif rightt < float('inf') and leftt == float('inf'): currentnodeindex = rightid currentnodet = rightt elif leftt < float('inf') and rightt < float('inf'): if stackindex >= 13: return IntersectionResult(error=True) if leftt < rightt: stack[stackindex] = StackNode(rightid, rightt) currentnodeindex = leftid currentnodet = leftt else: stack[stackindex] = StackNode(leftid, leftt) currentnodeindex = rightid currentnodet = rightt stackindex += 1 else: if stackindex > 0: stackindex -= 1 currentnodeindex = stack[stackindex].nodeid currentnodet = stack[stackindex].t else: break return IntersectionResult(found=False) def voxelmeshrayintersection(ro, rd, maxdistance, voxelmeshes, worldbounds): invrd = vec3( 1.0 / (sign(rd.x) max(abs(rd.x), 1e-8)), 1.0 / (sign(rd.y) max(abs(rd.y), 1e-8)), 1.0 / (sign(rd.z) max(abs(rd.z), 1e-8))) t = float('inf') rayposition = ro cubesize = 16.0 subcubesize = 8.0 halfsize = cubesize / 2.0 rayright = vec3(0, 1, 0) rayup = vec3(0, 0, 1) cubemincorner = rayposition - rayright halfsize - rayup halfsize for i in range(3): for j in range(3): for k in range(3): subcubecenter = ( cubemincorner + rd (i subcubesize) + rayright (j subcubesize) + rayup (k subcubesize)) subcubemin = ( subcubecenter - rd (subcubesize / 2.0) - rayright (subcubesize / 2.0) - rayup (subcubesize / 2.0)) meshindex = getworldmesh(subcubemin, voxelmeshes, worldbounds) if meshindex != -1: mesh = voxelmeshes[meshindex] chunkt = boundingboxintersect(ro, rd, invrd, mesh.minbounds, mesh.maxbounds) if chunkt < t and chunkt < maxdistance: result = voxelmeshintersect(ro, rd, meshindex, maxdistance, voxelmeshes) if result.found and result.t <= t: t = result.t finalresult = result return finalresult A compute shader-based ray tracing technique for voxel data that uses a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to accelerate ray-mesh intersection tests for lighting and ambient occlusion calculations. It differs from hardware-accelerated approaches like Sparse Voxel Set (SVS) or GPU-based Ray Shooting for Volumetric Mapping by performing the traversal logic entirely within a custom compute shader rather than relying on dedicated DXR hardware pipelines. This method is specifically designed for deferred shading pipelines where position and normal buffers are available, enabling efficient shadow and occlusion queries against sparse voxel meshes. Stack Management: Uses a fixed-size stack of 13 nodes for BVH traversal instead of recursive function calls. Recursion Limits: Avoids recursion depth limits inherent in recursive implementations. Overflow Handling: Explicitly checks for stack overflow (stackIndex >= STACKSIZE) during dual-child traversal and sets an error flag if exceeded. Empty Node Handling: Returns immediately without a hit if the triangle count length is zero or negative. Originated in the Divine Voxel Engine (DVE) by Divine Star Software. It is part of the DVE monorepo, which includes packages for voxel rendering and WASM compilation. The method is used in DVE's PBR and Classic rendering modes. name: Voxel Ray Marching with BVH Acceleration
head: VoxelMeshQuery, VoxelRayRender
body: A compute shader-based ray tracing technique for voxel data that uses a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to accelerate ray-mesh intersection tests for lighting and ambient occlusion calculations. It differs from hardware-accelerated approaches like Sparse Voxel Set (SVS) or GPU-based Ray Shooting for Volumetric Mapping by performing the traversal logic entirely within a custom compute shader rather than relying on dedicated ray-tracing hardware pipelines. This method is specifically designed for deferred shading pipelines where position and normal buffers are available, enabling efficient shadow and occlusion queries against sparse voxel meshes. The method operates on a per-pixel basis in a compute shader, utilizing position and normal textures as input buffers to generate lighting and ambient occlusion (AO) textures. It delegates the heavy lifting of ray-voxel intersection to a software-implemented BVH traversal function (voxelMeshQuery). Inputs: positiontexture: texture2d<f32> storing world position at screen coordinates. normaltexture: texture2d<f32> storing surface normals. sceneprops: Contains sunPosition. camera: Contains right, up, forward vectors and tanHalfFov. voxelbvh: array<AABB> representing the hierarchy nodes. voxelindice: array<vec2u> mapping BVH nodes to mesh indices. voxelmeshes: array<VoxelMesh> containing mesh data. vertices: array<VoxelMeshVertex>. indices: array<u32>. Outputs: lighttexture: texturestorage2d<rgba32float, write> for sun lighting. aotexture: texturestorage2d<rgba16float, write> for ambient occlusion. VoxelMeshVertex: position: vec3f normal: vec3f textureIndex: vec3f uv: vec2f colors: vec3f voxelData: f32 padding: vec4f AABB (implied from BVH usage): Minimum and maximum bounds defining the volume. Sun ray max distance: 300.0. AO ray max distance: 0.99. Epsilon offset for shadow/occlusion ray origin: 0.01. AO sample count: 4. 1. Initialization: Calculate screen coordinates from the global invocation ID multiplied by 2. 2. Position Check: Load the world position from positiontexture using the screen coordinates. If the position's alpha component is \le 0, store 1.0 in the light and AO textures and return. 3. Normal Extraction: Extract the world position and normal from the textures. Convert the normal from the [0, 1] range to the [-1, 1] range using the formula below. Set hitPosition to the position's RGB components. 4. Sun Lighting Calculation: Offset hitPosition along the normal by epsilon (\epsilon = 0.01) to get newHitPosition. Calculate the sun direction vector from newHitPosition to sceneprops.sunPosition. Construct an orthonormal basis for the sun direction. Call voxelMeshQuery with newHitPosition, the sun direction, and a max distance of 300.0. If an intersection is found, set the light value to dark gray (0.25, 0.25, 0.25). If an error occurs, set the light value to red (1, 0, 0). 5. Ambient Occlusion Calculation: Build an orthonormal basis from the surface normal using buildOrthonormalBasis. Initialize a hit counter to 0. Loop 4 times (for the sample count): Generate random numbers using getTwoRandomNumbers with a seed based on fragment coordinates and time. Sample a hemisphere direction using cosineWeightedHemisphereSample. Transform the local sample to world space using hemisphereToWorld. Construct an orthonormal basis for the sample direction. Call voxelMeshQuery with hitPosition, the sample direction, and a max distance of 0.99. If an intersection is found, increment the hit counter. Calculate the occlusion factor using the formula below and apply it to the AO color channels. Normal conversion: \mathbf{n} = 2 \cdot \mathbf{c}{normal} - 1, where \mathbf{c}{normal} is the color value from normaltexture. Occlusion factor: f{occlusion} = 1.0 - \frac{\text{hit}}{4}. Ray direction construction in camera space: \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\text{screenCoord}.x \cdot (-\mathbf{c}{right}) \cdot \tan(\text{halfFov}) \cdot \mathbf{c}{settings}.y + \text{screenCoord}.y \cdot \mathbf{c}{up} \cdot \tan(\text{halfFov}) + \mathbf{c}{forward}). Unverified code. Calculate screen coordinates screencoord = (globalinvocationid[0] 2, globalinvocationid[1] 2) # 2. name: Sparse Voxel Set (SVS)
body: Sparse Voxel Set (SVS) is a ray-tracing acceleration method for Signed Distance Function (SDF) grids that constructs a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) from Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs) representing individual surface-intersecting voxels. It differs from software-based traversal methods (like Grid Sphere Tracing or Sparse Brick Set) by offloading the primary traversal logic to dedicated GPU ray-tracing hardware (DXR), thereby reducing the computational burden of the custom intersection shader. Inputs: A voxel grid containing Signed Distance Field (SDF) values; a threshold defining the surface boundary. Outputs: A BVH structure suitable for DirectX Raytracing (DXR) hardware traversal. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Data: Each voxel in the sparse set stores a 4 \times 4 \times 4 array of signed distance values. This is larger than the standard 2 \times 2 \times 2 neighborhood, providing easy access to neighboring voxel values required for normal evaluation. 2. AABB: An Axis-Aligned Bounding Box is created for each voxel that intersects the surface (i.e., where the SDF crosses the threshold). 3. BVH: A hierarchy of these AABBs is built to accelerate ray intersection tests. Algorithm Steps: 1. Voxel Selection: Identify all voxels in the grid that intersect the implicit surface defined by the SDF threshold. 2. AABB Construction: For each selected voxel, compute the AABB that encloses the voxel's spatial extent. 3. BVH Build: Construct a Bounding Volume Hierarchy from the set of AABBs. 4. Ray Tracing Setup: Configure the DXR pipeline to use the constructed BVH. 5. Traversal: For each ray, perform BVH traversal using the GPU's RTX ray tracing hardware. 6. Intersection Shader: When a leaf node (voxel) is reached, invoke a custom intersection shader. 7. SDF Evaluation: Inside the intersection shader, sample the 4 \times 4 \times 4 SDF data associated with the voxel to determine the precise intersection point and normal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class SparseVoxelSet: def init(self, gridresolution, sdfvalues, threshold): self.threshold = threshold self.voxels = [] self.bvh = None # Step 1 & 2: Identify surface voxels and create AABBs for x in range(gridresolution.x): for y in range(gridresolution.y): for z in range(gridresolution.z): # Check if voxel intersects surface # A voxel intersects if the SDF values at its corners span the threshold if self.voxelintersectssurface(x, y, z, sdfvalues): # Store 4x4x4 SDF values for normal evaluation sdfdata = self.get4x4x4sdf(x, y, z, sdfvalues) aabb = self.computeaabb(x, y, z) self.voxels.append({ 'aabb': aabb, 'sdfdata': sdfdata }) # Step 3: Build BVH self.bvh = BVHBuilder(self.voxels) def voxelintersectssurface(self, x, y, z, sdfvalues): # Determine if the voxel contains the surface # This typically involves checking the 8 corners of the voxel # against the threshold. If signs differ, it intersects. # Implementation detail: Check min/max SDF in voxel vs threshold return True # Placeholder for specific intersection logic def get4x4x4sdf(self, x, y, z, sdfvalues): # Retrieve 4x4x4 signed distance values around the voxel # This allows easy access to neighboring values for normal evaluation return sdfvalues[x-1:x+4, y-1:y+4, z-1:z+4] def computeaabb(self, x, y, z): # Compute AABB for the voxel return AABB(min=(x, y, z), max=(x+1, y+1, z+1)) def traceray(self, rayorigin, raydirection): # Step 5: Perform BVH traversal using RTX hardware # The hardware handles the traversal tree walk hit = self.bvh.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if hit: # Step 6: Invoke custom intersection shader # Step 7: Evaluate SDF for precise hit voxeldata = hit.voxeldata sdfval = self.evaluatesdf(hit.position, voxeldata) normal = self.computenormal(hit.position, voxeldata) return sdfval, normal return None def evaluatesdf(self, position, sdfdata): # Sample the 4x4x4 grid at the hit position # Trilinear interpolation of the 4x4x4 data pass def computenormal(self, position, sdfdata): # Compute normal using neighboring SDF values # Central difference or gradient estimation using the 4x4x4 data pass Parameters: SDF Neighborhood Size: 4 \times 4 \times 4 values per voxel. Threshold: The SDF value defining the surface (typically 0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Overhead: SVS has a "much more significant memory overhead" compared to other methods due to the storage of 4 \times 4 \times 4 SDF values per voxel and the BVH structure itself. Complexity: While simpler to construct than Sparse Voxel Octrees, the memory cost is a primary limitation. Performance: SVS outperformed other methods (grid sphere tracing, sparse brick set, sparse voxel octree) in general scenarios. Hardware Dependency: Performance relies heavily on the efficiency of the GPU's RTX ray-tracing hardware. Shader Workload: Requires less work in the custom software intersection shader compared to software-based traversal methods because the BVH traversal is handled by hardware. Memory: High memory usage due to the 4 \times 4 \times 4 SDF storage per voxel and BVH overhead. Construction: Simpler and faster to construct than Sparse Voxel Octrees. Scene Suitability: Effective in general scenes; however, cache coherency in complex scenes might favor other methods like Sparse Brick Set if hardware acceleration is not fully utilized or if memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. Origin: The method is described in the context of real-time rendering of Signed Distance Fields, leveraging DirectX Raytracing (DXR) hardware. Development: It is presented as an alternative to software-based SDF traversal techniques such as Grid Sphere Tracing (similar to Claybook [Aaltonen 2018]) and Sparse Brick Set (SBS). Usage: Used for real-time rendering of SDF-based geometry, particularly where high performance is required and GPU ray-tracing hardware is available.
