name: GPU-based Ray Shooting for Volumetric Mapping
head: GPU-Accelerated Ray Shooting for Probabilistic Volumetric Mapping, GPU-based ray shooting, RTX-based ray shooting
body: This method accelerates the ray-shooting bottleneck in Probabilistic Volumetric Mapping (PVM) by mapping leaf-level octree voxels to Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs) and performing massively parallel ray shooting on an RTX GPU using the DirectX Raytracing (DXR) API. It replaces the CPU-based DDA ray-shooting procedure used in standard Octomap, which typically consumes about 90% of processing time. Unlike Voxel Ray Marching with BVH Acceleration, which uses BVH for lighting and ambient occlusion calculations in a compute shader, this method uses the dedicated DXR ray-tracing pipeline to determine voxel occupancy (free/occupied) by intersecting rays with a BVH of AABBs. Inputs: sensorOrigin: 3D vector representing the camera/sensor position. rayDirections: Array of 3D vectors or point cloud positions defining ray endpoints. octree: The current probabilistic volumetric map on the CPU, containing leaf-level voxels labeled as occupied, free, or unknown. Outputs: intersectedVoxels: A set of finest-resolution voxels labeled as occupied or free, which are read back to the CPU to update the octree. Data Structures: 1. AABB Set: Each leaf-level voxel in the octree is converted to an individual AABB. The AABB geometry (position and size) matches the voxel exactly. Unknown Voxels: Voxels labeled "unknown" are also converted to AABBs. This ensures the AABBs fill the entire 3D workspace, preventing rays from passing through unrepresented space without intersection. 2. BVH (Bounding Volume Hierarchy): Built on the GPU from the AABB set. Bottom Level Acceleration Structure (BLAS): Contains the geometric primitives (the AABBs). Top Level Acceleration Structure (TLAS): Contains transformation matrices and rendering materials (standard DXR requirement, though materials are unused in this specific logic). Parameters: Finest Resolution Subdivision: When an AABB larger than the finest resolution is intersected, it is subdivided into typically 16 finest-resolution voxels using DDA. Ray Count: Proportional to the point cloud size. In benchmarks, 320×240 rays (76,800 rays) were used per view. Octree Depth: Maximum depth of 16 in benchmarks, corresponding to 25K–34K leaf-level voxels. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (CPU): Scan the environment to generate a point cloud. Convert all leaf-level voxels (occupied, free, unknown) from the octree into individual AABBs. 2. Upload and Build (GPU): Upload the set of AABBs to the GPU. The RTX GPU builds the BVH of these AABBs. 3. Ray Generation (GPU): In the Ray Generation Shader, set up rays. Each ray starts at sensorOrigin and ends at a point in the point cloud. The ray length is set to the distance from the sensor origin to the point cloud point. 4. Ray Shooting (GPU): Execute massively parallel ray shooting. Rays traverse the BVH. If a ray hits an AABB within its extent, the Intersection Shader is executed. If the intersected AABB size is greater than the finest resolution voxel size, subdivide the subspace traversed by the ray into finest resolution voxels (typically 16) using DDA. For all newly generated finest resolution voxels: if the voxel includes the ray's end point, set it as occupied; else if the ray passed through the voxel, set it as free. If ray-AABB intersection no longer occurs, the Miss Shader is executed to terminate the ray shooting (the Closest Hit Shader is not used). 5. Readback (GPU to CPU): Read back the intersected voxel data from the GPU to the CPU. 6. Update (CPU): Update the octree with the new occupancy information. Merge leaf-level nodes with the same occupancy and promote them to higher-level nodes using Octomap. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. blas = buildblas(aabblist) tlas = buildtlas(blas, identitymatrices) for point in pointcloud: rayorigin = sensorOrigin raydirection = normalize(point - sensorOrigin) raylength = length(point - sensorOrigin) rayendpoint = rayorigin + raydirection raylength # 3. BVH Traversal hitaabb = None # Traverse BVH to find first intersecting AABB within ray extent # (Standard BVH traversal logic abstracted for DXR) hitaabb = traversebvh(rayorigin, raydirection, raylength, tlas) if hitaabb is not None: # 4. Intersection Shader Logic if hitaabb.size > finestresolutionsize: # Subdivide AABB into finest resolution voxels using DDA # DDA implementation details not provided in sources finestvoxels = subdivideaabbdda(hitaabb, rayorigin, raydirection, raylength) for voxel in finestvoxels: if voxel.contains(rayendpoint): voxel.label = OCCUPIED else: voxel.label = FREE else: # AABB is already at finest resolution if hitaabb.contains(rayendpoint): hitaabb.label = OCCUPIED else: hitaabb.label = FREE # 5. Miss Shader: If no intersection, ray terminates. No action needed. intersecteddata = readbackgpubuffer() return intersecteddata def cpuupdateoctree(intersecteddata, octree): for voxel in intersecteddata: octree.updatevoxel(voxel.position, voxel.label) octree.restructure() # Merge and promote nodes Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unknown Space Handling: Rays can pass anywhere in the space. If unknown voxels are not converted to AABBs, rays may pass through unrepresented subspace without being labeled. Including unknown voxels as AABBs ensures all traversed subspace is labeled. Readback Bottleneck: Reading back voxel data from GPU to CPU takes significantly longer than the ray shooting itself (e.g., 14.19 ms readback vs 1.42 ms shooting in View a). This creates a bottleneck. The described implementation performs the octree update on the CPU after readback, though GPU-based maintenance is noted as a future possibility. Precision: The method relies on the DXR API's ray-tracing precision. No specific numerical precision constraints are given in the sources. Time Complexity: The ray shooting performance is more than three orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art Octomap CPU implementation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the BVH (BLAS and TLAS) on the GPU. The size depends on the number of leaf-level voxels (25K–34K in benchmarks). Measured Performance: Hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X CPU, NVIDIA RTX 2080 GPU, 16GB RAM, Windows 10, DirectX DXR. Benchmark: 77K points, 25K–34K adaptive voxel grids. View (a) Stats: 25,515 voxels. CPU Ray Shooting: 886.83 ms. GPU Ray Shooting: 1.42 ms. BVH Build: 0.59 ms. Readback: 14.19 ms. With readback included, the GPU method is still two orders of magnitude faster than the CPU version. Strengths: Drastic improvement in ray shooting speed, enabling real-time or near-real-time PVM for autonomous robotics. Limitations: The octree is not maintained on the GPU; readback from GPU to CPU is a significant bottleneck (10x the shooting time). When to use: Autonomous robotic navigational tasks requiring Probabilistic Volumetric Mapping where ray shooting is the bottleneck. When not to use: When GPU memory is insufficient for the BVH, or when the overhead of readback dominates the workflow and GPU-based octree maintenance is not implemented. Probabilistic Volumetric Mapping (PVM) represents a 3D environmental map for autonomous robotic navigational tasks. Octomap is a popular implementation using an octree structure. The main bottleneck in Octomap is the massive ray-shooting required to determine voxel occupancy, which takes up about 90% of processing time. This method was proposed by Heajung Min, Kyung Min Han, and Young J. Kim to leverage RTX GPUs and the DXR API to accelerate this process. The work was presented at ICRA 2021. Accelerating Probabilistic Volumetric Mapping using Ray-Tracing Graphics Hardware, https://doi.org/10.1109/icra48506.2021.9561068, fetched 2026-10-24

name: GPU BVH Construction via Cluster Merging
head: Cluster Merging BVH, GPU-based BVH Construction via Cluster Merging, VoxelFragmentML BVH Build
body: This method constructs a Binary Volume Hierarchy (BVH) on the GPU by iteratively merging clusters of triangles. It solves the problem of building hierarchical acceleration structures for ray tracing without CPU-GPU synchronization bottlenecks by using a fully parallel, double-buffered approach involving neighbor finding, prefix scans, and reallocation. It differs from CPU-based top-down or bottom-up builders by keeping all data on the GPU and using a "merge-compact" loop that reduces the number of active clusters by half (approximately) each iteration until a single root remains. Input: A set of static triangles. The number of input triangles is N (referred to as arraySize or staticData.numTriangles in the source). Output: A BVH stored in a GPU buffer (clusterSSBO) containing 2N - 1 nodes (clusters). The final readback size is explicitly staticData.numTriangles 2 - 1. BVHCluster: The data structure representing a cluster. On the CPU, it is defined as Model3D::BVHCluster. On the GPU, it resides in a Shader Storage Buffer Object (SSBO). The exact internal fields are not specified in the source, but it represents a cluster of triangles with a bounding volume. Current Position Buffers: Two CPU-side arrays of type GLuint, currentPosBuffer and currentPosBufferOut, each of size arraySize (initially N). currentPosBufferOut is initialized with sequential integers: currentPosBufferOut[i] = i for 0 \le i < \text{arraySize}. These buffers track the compacted position of valid clusters during the merge process. GPU Buffers (SSBOs): cinBuffer: Read cluster data for the current iteration. coutBuffer: Write cluster data for the next iteration (double-buffered with cinBuffer). inCurrentPosition: Read position data for the current iteration. outCurrentPosition: Write position data for the next iteration (double-buffered with inCurrentPosition). neighborIndex: Stores the index of the nearest neighbor for each cluster. prefixScan: Temporary buffer for the parallel prefix scan. validCluster: Flag indicating if a cluster remains valid. mergedCluster: Buffer storing details of merged clusters. numNodesCount: Buffer to store the count of remaining nodes. arraySizeCount: Buffer to store the updated arraySize. clusterSSBO: Final BVH storage, sized for N \times 2 - 1 clusters. tempClusterSSBO: Temporary cluster storage, sized for arraySize. sortedFaces: Sorted triangle indices (output of Morton sort). gpuData->tempClusterSSBO: Temporary cluster data. The construction consists of three main phases: Morton Code Sorting, Cluster Building, and Iterative Merging. Triangles are sorted by Morton code to improve spatial locality before clustering. 1. Parameters: numBits = 30 (10 bits per coordinate for 3D Morton codes). 2. Loop: Iterate currentBits from 0 to numBits - 1. 3. Bit Mask: Execute bitMaskShader on mortonCodes and indicesBufferID1 to split into pBitsBufferID (bit=1) and nBitsBufferID (bit=0). 4. Reduce: Perform a prefix scan on nBitsBufferID to count zeros. 5. Reset: Execute resetPositionShader on nBitsBufferID with 1 group to set the last position to zero. 6. Down Sweep: Execute downSweepShader to compute final positions for the zeros. 7. Reallocate: Execute reallocatePositionShader to reorder indicesBufferID1 into indicesBufferID2 based on positions. 1. Execution: Execute buildClusterShader with buffers { staticData.groupTopologySSBO, sortedFaces, staticData->clusterSSBO, gpuData->tempClusterSSBO }. 2. Uniforms: Set arraySize to the number of triangles. 3. Groups: Execute with numGroups groups. 4. Result: Initial leaf clusters are created in tempClusterSSBO. The source notes that buildClusterBuffer creates clusterData of size N \times 2 - 1 and sets up clusterSSBO (write) and tempClusterSSBO (write). The core loop reduces the number of clusters until one root remains. Initialization: 1. Calculate arraySize = number of triangles N. 2. Create input buffer outCluster (CPU side). 3. Initialize currentPosBufferOut with std::iota(..., 0). 4. Set up SSBOs: cinBuffer, coutBuffer, inCurrentPosition, outCurrentPosition, neighborIndex, prefixScan, validCluster, mergedCluster, numNodesCount, arraySizeCount. Main Loop: While arraySize > 1: 1. Buffer Swapping: Swap coutBuffer and cinBuffer, and swap outCurrentPosition and inCurrentPosition to double-buffer the cluster and position data. 2. Group Size Calculation: numGroups = ComputeShader::getNumGroups(arraySize), startThreads = std::ceil(arraySize / 2.0f), numExec = std::ceil(std::log2(arraySize)), numGroups2Log = ComputeShader::getNumGroups(startThreads). 3. Neighbor Finding: Execute findNeighborShader with buffers { cinBuffer, neighborIndex }. Set uniforms arraySize and radius. Execute with numGroups groups. 4. Cluster Merging: Execute clusterMergingShader with buffers { cinBuffer, staticData.clusterSSBO, neighborIndex, validCluster, mergedCluster, prefixScan, inCurrentPosition, numNodesCount }. Set uniform arraySize. Execute with numGroups groups. This step merges clusters based on neighbors and writes valid/merged status and prefix scan data. 5. Prefix Scan - Reduce Phase (First Step): Build a binary tree summatory on prefixScan. Initialize iteration = 0. Loop while (iteration < numExec): get numThreads = threadCount[threadCount.size() - 1], set uniforms iteration and numThreads, execute reduceShader with numGroups2Log groups, then push std::ceil(numThreads / 2.0f) to threadCount. 6. Prefix Scan - Reset Last Position (Second Step): Execute resetPositionShader on prefixScan with 1 group to set the last position to zero. This is noted as faster than CPU modification. 7. Prefix Scan - Down Sweep Phase (Third Step): Build tree back to first level and compute final summatory on prefixScan. Initialize iteration = threadCount.size() - 2. Loop while (iteration >= 0 && iteration < numExec): set uniforms iteration and numThreads = threadCount[iteration], execute downSweepShader with numGroups2Log groups, decrement iteration. 8. Reallocation: Execute reallocClustersShader with buffers { cinBuffer, coutBuffer, validCluster, prefixScan, inCurrentPosition, outCurrentPosition }. Set uniform arraySize. Execute with numGroups groups. This compacts the valid clusters into the output buffer. 9. Update Cluster Size: Execute endLoopCompShader with buffers { arraySizeCount, prefixScan, validCluster }. Set uniform arraySize. Execute with 1 group. Read back the new arraySize from arraySizeCount. Final Readback: 1. After the loop, read the final BVH cluster data from staticData.clusterSSBO into a CPU vector. 2. The size is staticData.numTriangles 2 - 1. Cleanup: 1. Delete GPU buffers (coutBuffer, cinBuffer, inCurrentPosition, outCurrentPosition, neighborIndex, prefixScan, validCluster, mergedCluster, numNodesCount, arraySizeCount) and CPU memory (outCluster, currentPosBuffer, currentPosBufferOut, volatileGPUData). 1).bitlength() if arraysize > 1 else 0 # ceil(log2) numgroups2log = (startthreads + 255) // 256 # GPU shader call: findNeighborShader (not given in the sources) findneighbor(cinbuffer, neighborindex, arraysize) # GPU shader call: clusterMergingShader (not given in the sources) clustermerging(cinbuffer, neighborindex, validcluster, mergedcluster, prefixscan, inpos) iteration = 0 while iteration < numexec: numthreads = threadcount[-1] if threadcount else arraysize # GPU shader call: reduceShader (not given in the sources) reduceshader(prefixscan, iteration, numthreads, numgroups2log) threadcount.append((numthreads + 1) // 2) iteration += 1 # GPU shader call: resetPositionShader (not given in the sources) prefixscan[-1] = 0 iteration = len(threadcount) - 2 while iteration >= 0 and iteration < numexec: numthreads = threadcount[iteration] # GPU shader call: downSweepShader (not given in the sources) downsweepshader(prefixscan, iteration, numthreads, numgroups2log) iteration -= 1 # GPU shader call: reallocClustersShader (not given in the sources) reallocclusters(cinbuffer, coutbuffer, validcluster, prefixscan, inpos, outpos, arraysize) # GPU shader call: endLoopCompShader (not given in the sources) arraysize = endloopcomp(prefixscan, validcluster, arraysize) return cinbuffer[:arraysize] # Not given in the sources. def computemorton(t): pass def buildinitialclusters(indices): pass def findneighbor(cin, neighboridx, size): pass def clustermerging(cin, neighboridx, valid, merged, prefix, pos): pass def reduceshader(prefix, iter, threads, groups): pass def downsweepshader(prefix, iter, threads, groups): pass def reallocclusters(cin, cout, valid, prefix, inpos, outpos, size): pass def endloopcomp(prefix, valid, size): pass radius: The search radius for finding nearest neighbor clusters during the merging phase. Passed as a uniform to findNeighborShader. numBits: The number of bits for the radix sort, set to 30 (10 bits per coordinate for 3D Morton codes). Precision: The use of double for AABB calculations (dAABBCC, dvec3) suggests high precision is required for bounding volume operations. Boundary Conditions: The loop condition arraySize > 1 ensures the process stops at a single root. The prefix scan reset step is critical for correctness in the down-sweep phase. Degenerate Input: If arraySize is 0 or 1, the loop does not execute, and the final readback handles the base case. The source does not specify behavior for empty inputs beyond the loop condition. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method is designed for GPU parallelism, using compute shaders and SSBOs. Strengths: Fully GPU-based, no CPU-GPU synchronization during construction, parallel neighbor finding and merging. Limitations: Requires significant GPU memory for double-buffering and temporary buffers. When to Use: When building BVHs for static triangle meshes on the GPU is required. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: The method is described in the VoxelFragmentML project by AlfonsoLRz. History: The specific implementation details are from the VoxelFragmentML repository, which appears to be an unofficial or experimental project. Usage: Used in the VoxelFragmentML project for GPU-based BVH construction. AlfonsoLRz/VoxelFragmentML, https://github.com/AlfonsoLRz/VoxelFragmentML, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: IRIS Ray-Geometry Intersection
head: OptiX-based Gaussian Intersection, Proxy Geometry Intersection
body: IRIS is an intersection-aware ray-based sampling method for implicit editable scenes that determines samples as the maximum response points of Gaussians intersected by each ray. It solves the problem of efficiently gathering depth samples from 3D Gaussian primitives in a hardware-accelerated ray tracing pipeline. It sets itself apart from standard BVH traversal methods by replacing explicit Gaussian volume checks with proxy geometry (affine-transformed icosahedra) and leveraging OptiX Any-hit shaders to compute sampling parameters directly during intersection tests. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction V in world space; a set of 3D Gaussians defined by mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, and opacity \alpha; target sample quota (hyperparameter). Outputs: A list of samples, where each sample is a 2-tuple (t{\text{sample}}, \text{Gaussian index}). Data Structures: 1. Proxy Geometry: Each Gaussian is bounded by a regular, affine-transformed icosahedron. The size of the icosahedron matches the confidence ellipsoid of the underlying \chi^2 distribution with 3 degrees of freedom. Canonical icosahedron: Triangle vertices and indices are stored once in global memory. Instance Buffer: Populated by a dedicated CUDA kernel. Each entry contains an affine transformation matrix M that maps the reference proxy to the specific Gaussian primitive. 2. Hit Buffer: A fixed-size buffer storing 2-tuples of (t{\text{sample}}, \text{Gaussian index}). Size: 16 entries. Content: t{\text{sample}} is the intersection parameter; the index identifies the Gaussian. 3. Output Buffer: Accumulates final samples transferred from the hit buffer. Parameters: Hit Buffer Capacity: 16 entries. Target Sample Quota (IPR - Intersections Per Ray): Bounded scenes (NeRF Synthetic): 128 IPR. Unbounded scenes (Mip-NeRF 360): 256 IPR. Bounding Proxy Threshold (\lambda): Squared Mahalanobis distance threshold defining the proxy size. Bounded scenes: \lambda = 6.25 (covers ~90% of Gaussian probability mass). Unbounded scenes: \lambda = 11.3449 (covers 99% of Gaussian probability mass). Steps: 1. Proxy Construction: For each Gaussian, compute the affine transformation matrix M that scales and rotates the canonical icosahedron to match the Gaussian's confidence ellipsoid defined by \lambda. Populate the OptiX instance buffer with these matrices. 2. Ray Generation: For each pixel, generate a ray (O, V). 3. Intersection Testing: Perform intersection testing using OptiX Ray Generation and Any-hit shaders. 4. Any-Hit Shader Execution: a. When a ray intersects a proxy icosahedron instance, transform the ray origin O and direction V into the object coordinate frame of the underlying Gaussian: O{\text{obj}} = M^{-1}(O - \mu) V{\text{obj}} = M^{-1}V [Note: The source defines O{\text{obj}} and V{\text{obj}} as the ray origin and direction in the object coordinate frame. The exact transformation depends on the definition of the proxy's local frame relative to the Gaussian. The source formula (4) uses these object-space vectors directly.] b. Compute the intersection parameter t{\text{sample}} using the formula: t{\text{sample}} = -\frac{\langle O{\text{obj}}, V{\text{obj}} \rangle}{\langle V{\text{obj}}, V{\text{obj}} \rangle} where \langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle denotes the dot product. c. Store the tuple (t{\text{sample}}, \text{Gaussian index}) in the 16-entry hit buffer. d. Sort the hit buffer by t{\text{sample}} to maintain order. 5. Buffer Transfer: If the hit buffer reaches capacity (16 entries), transfer the sorted samples from the hit buffer to the output buffer in the Ray Generation shader. 6. Iteration: Repeat steps 3-5 iteratively until the total number of gathered samples in the output buffer reaches the predefined target sample quota (IPR). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def irisraygeometryintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussians, targetipr, buffersize=16): """ Simulates the IRIS ray-geometry intersection logic. Note: This is a high-level simulation. The actual method uses OptiX shaders. """ # 1. Pre-compute proxy geometries (Affine icosahedra) for all Gaussians # In practice, this is done via a CUDA kernel populating the OptiX instance buffer. proxies = [] for i, gaussian in enumerate(gaussians): # Determine lambda based on scene type (bounded vs unbounded) # For this simulation, we assume a generic lambda or pass it as arg lambdaval = gaussian.lambdathreshold # Compute affine transformation matrix M for the icosahedron # M maps canonical icosahedron to Gaussian's confidence ellipsoid M = computeaffinematrix(gaussian.mean, gaussian.covariance, lambdaval) proxies.append({ 'index': i, 'matrix': M, 'inversematrix': invertmatrix(M), 'mean': gaussian.mean }) # 2. Initialize buffers hitbuffer = [] # List of (tsample, gaussianindex) outputbuffer = [] # Final samples samplecount = 0 # 3. Ray Tracing Simulation # In reality, this is handled by OptiX traversal. # We simulate the intersection test for all proxies. # Collect all potential intersections allintersections = [] for proxy in proxies: # Transform ray to object space # Oobj = Minv (O - mean) # Vobj = Minv V # Note: The source formula uses Oobj and Vobj directly. # Assuming M includes translation to mean, or Oobj is relative. # Standard affine transform: Pobj = Minv (Pworld - T) # If M is just rotation/scale, T is separate. # Source says "object coordinate frame of the underlying Gaussian". # Let's assume Minv handles the full inverse transform to Gaussian local space. # Simplified: Assume proxy bounding box check first (hardware accelerated) if rayintersectsproxy(rayorigin, raydirection, proxy): # Compute tsample using formula (4) # Oobj and Vobj are in object frame Oobj = transformpoint(proxy['inversematrix'], rayorigin - proxy['mean']) Vobj = transformvector(proxy['inversematrix'], raydirection) dotOV = dotproduct(Oobj, Vobj) dotVV = dotproduct(Vobj, Vobj) if dotVV != 0: tsample = -dotOV / dotVV allintersections.append((tsample, proxy['index'])) # 4. Sort and Select # Sort by tsample to find closest intersections allintersections.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Select top 'targetipr' samples selectedsamples = allintersections[:targetipr] # 5. Output # The hit buffer logic (16 entries) is an optimization to reduce optixTrace calls. # In simulation, we just output the final selected samples. return selectedsamples def computeaffinematrix(mean, covariance, lambdaval): """ Computes the affine transformation matrix for the proxy icosahedron. The size matches the confidence ellipsoid of the chi-squared distribution. """ # Eigen decomposition of covariance eigenvalues, eigenvectors = eig(covariance) # Scale factors based on lambda (Mahalanobis distance threshold) # The proxy size is proportional to sqrt(lambda eigenvalue) scales = sqrt(lambdaval eigenvalues) # Construct rotation matrix from eigenvectors R = eigenvectors # Construct scaling matrix S = diag(scales) # Affine matrix M = [RS, t; 0, 1] # Assuming the proxy is centered at mean M = identity(4) M[0:3, 0:3] = R @ S M[0:3, 3] = mean return M def rayintersectsproxy(rayorigin, raydirection, proxy): """ Simulates hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection for the icosahedron. """ # In OptiX, this is handled by the RT core. # Here we return True for demonstration if we assume intersection. # Real implementation would check against the canonical icosahedron triangles # transformed by the instance matrix. return True # Placeholder for actual intersection test Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The formula for t{\text{sample}} involves division by \langle V{\text{obj}}, V{\text{obj}} \rangle. If the ray direction is zero or nearly zero in object space, this causes division by zero or numerical instability. Boundary Coverage: The proxy geometry is a conservative bound. Using \lambda = 6.25 covers ~90% of mass, and \lambda = 11.3449 covers 99%. If the target sample quota is not reached, it may be due to Gaussians falling outside the proxy bounds. Buffer Overflow: The 16-entry hit buffer is small. If many Gaussians are intersected, frequent transfers to the output buffer are required, which can be costly if not managed efficiently. Time Complexity: Dominated by the number of ray-proxy intersections and the sorting/transfer operations. The use of OptiX hardware acceleration for ray-triangle intersection reduces CPU/GPU overhead. Memory Complexity: Low memory footprint due to geometry instancing (storing only one canonical icosahedron). Performance: On NeRF Synthetic dataset, increasing IPR from 16 to 128 improves Avg. PSNR from 29.87 to 32.65. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated intersection tests; efficient sample gathering via Any-hit shaders; reduced memory footprint via instancing. Limitations: Proxy geometry is an approximation; may miss samples if Gaussians are not well-covered by the icosahedron bounds. When to Use: Implicit editable scenes requiring efficient ray-based sampling from Gaussians. When Not to Use: Scenes where exact Gaussian volume intersection is critical and proxy approximation leads to significant error. IRIS was introduced in the paper "IRIS: Intersection-aware Ray-based Implicit Editable Scenes". It builds on the 3DGRT OptiX API-based approach. The method is implemented in PyTorch within the Nerfstudio ecosystem. Experiments were conducted on NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. name: Multi-Hit BVH Traversal
head: Multi-Hit BVH Traversal for Volume Clipping, Multi-hit intersection, Multi-hit query, Ray Traced Volume Clipping Using Multi-Hit BVH Traversal
body: Multi-Hit BVH Traversal is a SIMD-friendly clipping algorithm for ray-traced direct volume rendering (DVR) that identifies visible volume regions by intersecting viewing rays with arbitrary geometric surface primitives (planes, quadrics, triangle meshes) organized in a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). It sets itself apart from rasterization-based depth peeling or texture-based slicing approaches by implementing clipping as a simple two-pass algorithm that avoids multiple render passes, dynamic memory reallocation, and the conversion of parametric surfaces to polygon meshes. The method determines the N closest intersections of a viewing ray with compound clip objects to construct clip intervals for volume rendering. It operates in two passes: first, intersecting primary viewing rays with all opaque geometry to identify visible volume regions; second, casting primary rays through the volume density and considering only voxels within those visible regions. Inputs: Primary viewing rays defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Clip geometry primitives (planes, spheres, triangle meshes) stored as Plain Old Data (POD) objects in a C array. A BVH acceleration structure managing the triangle meshes. N: The maximum number of intersections to retrieve, decided a priori. Outputs: A static array of size N containing the N closest intersection distances (or hit records). Clip intervals derived from these intersections, used to mask volume rendering in the second pass. Clip Geometry: Primitives are stored as POD objects in a C array. Triangle meshes are managed by a BVH. Planes and spheres are handled via generic routines. BVH: A hierarchical spatial subdivision structure used to reduce ray/primitive interactions. The BVH is rebuilt completely if triangle meshes change, as dynamic updates are not supported in this implementation. Hit Buffer: A static memory array of size N preallocated to store the result of the multi-hit query. This avoids the costly dynamic memory reallocation associated with "all-hit" queries. 1. Preprocessing: Construct the BVH for the triangle mesh clip geometry. If the mesh changes, rebuild the BVH completely. 2. Pass 1 (Clipping): For each primary viewing ray: a. Execute a multi-hit query on the BVH to find the N closest intersections with the clip geometry. b. Store the results in the preallocated static array of size N. c. Process the hit records to construct clip intervals (visible and invisible regions). 3. Pass 2 (Volume Rendering): For each primary viewing ray: a. Cast the ray through the volume density. b. Integrate color and opacity only for voxels that fall within the visible regions identified in Pass 1. c. Skip voxels that are clipped (i.e., inside the geometry or in occluded regions). Ray-Primitive Intersection: The algorithm uses generic routines that call specific intersect() functions for planes, spheres, and triangles. To avoid dynamic branching in the innermost traversal loop, the primitive type is determined without virtual inheritance or vtable lookups. Parameter N: The maximum number of intersections. This value must be chosen to balance the complexity of the clip geometry and the available register space on the GPU. Clip Intervals: Derived from the sorted intersection distances t1, t2, \dots, tN. The visible regions are typically the intervals between t{2i} and t{2i+1} (assuming the ray starts outside the geometry). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. bvh = buildbvh(trianglemeshes) Dynamic Branching: Switching over primitive types in the innermost traversal loop causes performance degradation. The implementation avoids this by using generic routines that call specific intersect() functions. Register Pressure: Storing clip intervals in on-chip GPU memory increases register demand per thread on the shading multi-processor (SM), which may impact kernel performance. Static Geometry: The implementation does not support dynamic updates to triangle meshes. Changing the mesh requires a complete BVH rebuild. Precision: Sub-voxel accurate clipping is achieved, avoiding artifacts associated with rasterization-based clipping of irregular concavities. A technique to process all intersections along a ray for volume rendering on a tetrahedral mesh by modifying a payload in the anyhit shader and collecting results in the raygen program, avoiding the overhead of multiple optixTrace calls. It sets itself apart from multiple closehit calls by shaving off per-ray-cast overhead at the cost of memory bandwidth for storing hits and explicit sorting. Time Complexity: The time complexity of ray tracing grows with the product of the number of primitives and the number of image pixels. The use of BVH reduces the asymptotic behavior to average logarithmic in the number of geometric primitives. Memory Complexity: Uses a static array of size N for hit storage, avoiding dynamic memory allocation. Performance: Evaluated on a 1024x1024 resolution MRI dataset (MNI152, 0.5mm³ voxel size, 364x436x364 voxels) clipped with Utah teapot models. Level 1: 2,464 triangles, 1,559 BVH nodes. Level 2: 14,784 triangles, 9,771 BVH nodes. Level 3: 59,136 triangles, 39,063 BVH nodes. Level 4: 236,544 triangles, 151,637 BVH nodes. Strengths: Sub-voxel accurate clipping for arbitrary geometry; no multiple render passes; no conversion of parametric surfaces to polygons; real-time capable on GPU. Limitations: Static triangle meshes only (BVH rebuild required for changes); increased register pressure on GPU; requires a priori knowledge of maximum intersections N. When to Use: Neurosurgical visualization, tumor border inspection, vessel detection, and intersection analysis with surgical instrumentation or fiber tracks. When Not to Use: When dynamic mesh deformation is required; when memory bandwidth is severely constrained and N is large; when sub-voxel accuracy is not necessary and rasterization suffices. The method was presented in the paper "Ray Traced Volume Clipping Using Multi-Hit BVH Traversal". It addresses the limitations of traditional rasterization pipelines, which require multiple render passes to peel away depth layers for translucent surfaces or complex clipping, and texture-based approaches that require multiple rendering passes or storing clip intervals in GPU DDR3 memory. The implementation uses Visionaray's multi-hit implementation with a template parameter for the maximum size of the static array. name: Multi-hit Collection via OptiX anyhit
head: Collecting all intersections using anyhit in OptiX, Multiple-hit collection via anyhit, Tetrahedral volume rendering intersection collection
body: A technique to process all intersections along a ray for volume rendering on a tetrahedral mesh by modifying a payload in the anyhit shader and collecting results in the raygen program, avoiding the overhead of multiple optixTrace calls. It sets itself apart from multiple closehit calls by shaving off per-ray-cast overhead at the cost of memory bandwidth for storing hits and explicit sorting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin, direction, tmin, tmax, and a traversable acceleration structure. Output: A sorted list of intersection payloads (e.g., tetrahedron ID, barycentric coordinates, depth) in the raygen program. Data Structures: The payload structure must be passed via optixSetPayload and retrieved via optixGetPayload. A typical structure for tetrahedral volume rendering includes: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Payload { float4 barycentric; // Barycentric coordinate of the intersection int tetID; // ID of the belonging tetrahedron (-1 if boundary/missing side) float depth; // Ray depth (t-value) of the intersection }; The payload is stored in registers during traversal. In the raygen program, a static array or dynamic buffer is used to collect these payloads. Since the number of intersections varies per ray, the raygen program must track the count of collected hits. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Initialize the payload array in the raygen program. Set tmin to a small epsilon (scene-size dependent) and tmax to a large value (e.g., 10^{20}) to trace through the entire volume. 2. Trace: Call optixTrace once with OPTIXRAYFLAGNONE (enabling anyhit processing). 3. Anyhit Shader: For every intersection: Compute the intersection attributes (barycentrics, tetID). Update the payload in registers using optixSetPayload. Continue traversal (do not abort) to find subsequent intersections. 4. Miss Shader: If no hit is found, set the payload to a sentinel value (e.g., depth = 10^{20}) to signal termination in raygen. 5. Ray Generation (Collection): After optixTrace returns, iterate through the collected payloads. 6. Sorting: Sort the collected payloads in increasing order of t (depth). This is required because anyhit programs are not guaranteed to be called in t-order. 7. Processing: Use the sorted intervals for volume rendering (e.g., integration). Formulas: Ray Origin Update (for closehit alternative): O{new} = O{old} + D \cdot (t{hit} + \epsilon) Termination Condition: If payload.depth > Threshold (e.g., 10^{15}), stop processing. Parameters: tmin: Small epsilon (e.g., 10^{-6}). Must be scene-size dependent. tmax: Large value (e.g., 10^{20}). epsilon: Offset added to hit position to avoid self-intersection. Pitfalls: Ordering: Anyhit calls are not ordered by t. Explicit sorting in raygen is mandatory. Performance: Storing hits and sorting them consumes significant memory bandwidth. Epsilon Sensitivity: If tmin epsilon is too small, self-intersections occur. If too large, adjacent tetrahedra at thin corners may be missed. Boundary Handling: For boundary faces linking to only one tetrahedron, tetID may be -1, requiring special handling for barycentric coordinates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raygen(): # Initialize payload collection array hits = [] # Define ray parameters tmin = 1e-6f # Scene-size dependent epsilon tmax = 1e20f # Trace through entire volume # Call trace with anyhit enabled (OPTIXRAYFLAGNONE) optixTrace( traversable, origin, rayDir, tmin, tmax, 0.0f, # rayTime OptixVisibilityMask(255), OPTIXRAYFLAGNONE, # Enables anyhit surfaceSBTIndex, rayTypeCount, missSBTIndex, payloadinit) # Collect results from payload registers if using a single payload variable # Note: In practice, multiple hits require a buffer or atomic operations # if using a single payload variable across multiple anyhit calls. # The OptiX 6 sample optixParticleVolumes uses a specific payload structure # to accumulate hits. Here we assume a mechanism to collect them. # Sort hits by depth (t-value) hits.sort(key=lambda h: h.depth) # Process sorted hits for volume rendering for hit in hits: if hit.depth > 1e15f: break # Render interval between hit and next hit pass def anyhit(): # Compute intersection details tetID = gettetid() barycentric = getbarycentrics() depth = getintersectiont() # Update payload # In OptiX, this modifies the payload passed to the ray optixSetPayload0(floatasuint(depth)) optixSetPayload1(intasint(tetID)) optixSetPayload25(barycentric) # Continue traversal to find more hits def miss(): # Signal no hit with a large depth value optixSetPayload0(floatasuint(1e20f)) The parent technique of collecting N closest intersections. Multi-hit collection via anyhit is a specific implementation using OptiX's anyhit shader for tetrahedral meshes. Multi-Hit BVH Traversal An alternative approach calling optixTrace multiple times, advancing the ray origin after each hit. It avoids sorting but incurs per-ray-cast overhead. Time Complexity: Dominated by the sorting step in raygen, O(K \log K) where K is the number of intersections per ray. Traversal is O(\log N) for BVH. Memory Complexity: O(K) to store hit payloads. Performance: Avoids per-ray-cast overhead of multiple closehit calls but adds memory bandwidth costs for storing and sorting hits. Performance depends on scene complexity and intersection count. Strengths: Single ray cast, reduced API overhead. Limitations: Memory bandwidth bottleneck, sorting overhead, sensitivity to epsilon values. When to Use: When the number of intersections is moderate and the overhead of multiple ray casts is prohibitive. When Not to Use: When memory bandwidth is a bottleneck or when hits can be processed out-of-order. Originating from NVIDIA OptiX forums discussions on tetrahedral volume rendering, this technique was demonstrated in the OptiX 6 sample optixParticleVolumes and later in OptiX 7 samples optixCutouts and optixWhitted. It addresses the limitation of closehit-only approaches in handling complex volumetric meshes with many intersections. name: Initial Upper Bound Estimation
head: Heuristic Sampling for BVH Pruning
body: Initial Upper Bound Estimation is a preprocessing step for Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) traversal used in distance field computation for isosurfaces. It solves the problem of inefficient traversal caused by loose or non-existent initial bounds by computing a tight upper bound before the main traversal begins. It differs from standard BVH traversal Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) Traversal by injecting a heuristic sampling phase that prunes the search space early, and from BVH-Based Distance Field Computation with Heuristic Initialization by specifically focusing on the trade-off between sampling cost and traversal gain. Inputs: A set of N sample points \{p1, p2, \dots, pN\} sampled from the approximated isosurface. A Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) tree representing the voxel grid or geometry. The target voxel or query point q for which the distance field is being computed. Outputs: An initial upper bound d{max}, representing the maximum possible distance to the surface within the BVH structure, used to prune branches during traversal. Data Structures: Sample Points: A list of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). BVH Node: Contains bounding volume (AABB) and child pointers. Steps: 1. Sampling: Sample N points evenly from the approximated isosurface. The points should be distributed to represent the surface geometry. 2. Bound Computation: Compute the initial upper bound d{max} based on the distances from the query point q to the sampled points. Specifically, d{max} is typically set to the maximum distance from q to any sampled point, or a conservative estimate derived from the spatial extent of the samples relative to the BVH root. 3. Traversal with Pruning: Perform BVH traversal starting from the root. For each node, calculate the minimum distance from q to the node's bounding volume. If this minimum distance is greater than d{max}, prune the node (do not traverse its children). 4. Fallback: If N=0 (no samples), the initial upper bound is undefined or infinite. The traversal must examine nodes until the first leaf is reached to establish a baseline bound. Parameters: Number of sample points (N): Recommended range: 1000 to 1500 for reasonable-sized datasets. Specific evaluation value: 1500 was selected to yield swift traversal across all tested datasets. Step size for evaluation: 50 points. Pitfalls: High Point Count Variables: For variables with high point counts and even spatial distribution (e.g., CHI, vorticity), increasing N beyond 1500 causes rapid runtime increases. The estimation time rises linearly, and the traversal time plateaus or increases as the process converges toward brute-force. Convergence to Brute-Force: Excessive sampling leads to diminishing returns in pruning efficiency while incurring high preprocessing costs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeinitialupperbound(samplepoints, querypoint): """ Computes the initial upper bound from sampled points. Returns the maximum distance from querypoint to any sample point. """ if not samplepoints: return float('inf') maxdistsq = 0 for p in samplepoints: distsq = (p.x - querypoint.x)2 + \ (p.y - querypoint.y)2 + \ (p.z - querypoint.z)2 if distsq > maxdistsq: maxdistsq = distsq return math.sqrt(maxdistsq) def bvhtraversalwithinitialbound(root, querypoint, initialbound): """ Traverses the BVH using the initial upper bound for pruning. """ stack = [root] mindist = float('inf') while stack: node = stack.pop() # Calculate minimum distance from querypoint to node's AABB distmin = distancepointaabb(querypoint, node.aabb) # Pruning condition: if the closest point in the node is further # than the current best known distance (initialbound), skip this node. if distmin > initialbound: continue # If leaf node, update mindist and potentially tighten bound if node.isleaf: # Compute exact distance to geometry in leaf d = distancepointgeometry(querypoint, node.geometry) if d < mindist: mindist = d # Note: The initial bound is fixed for the traversal start, # but subsequent traversals might use tighter bounds. # Here we assume the initial bound is used for the first pass. else: # Push children to stack stack.append(node.left) stack.append(node.right) return mindist Computes distance fields by initializing the upper bound with evenly sampled points to allow aggressive pruning at the start of traversal, differing from methods that wait for the first leaf encounter. Time Complexity: Estimation time: Increases linearly with the number of sample points N. Traversal time: Decreases rapidly as N increases from 0, then slowly approaches a minimum. Measured Performance: Without samples (N=0), traversal takes the longest time as the tree is examined until the first leaf. Most datasets reach minimum traversal time between 2000 and 2300 points, fluctuating by 1 ms. For variables with high point counts (CHI, vorticity), minimums are reached earlier (1200 and 1500 points respectively). Beyond these points, running times increase rapidly (e.g., CHI: 94.58 ms to 380.36 ms; vorticity: 69.25 ms to 248.82 ms). Scaling: Performance gained by tighter bounds usually outweighs costs for N < 1500. Strengths: Significantly reduces traversal time for most datasets by providing a tight initial bound. Limitations: Inefficient for variables with very high point counts if N is set too high, leading to brute-force-like behavior. This method was evaluated in the context of efficient GPU-accelerated computation of isosurface similarity maps. It addresses the performance bottleneck in BVH traversal for distance field computation by optimizing the initial pruning condition. The approach was tested on various scientific datasets including combustion (CHI, vorticity), hurricane (water vapor ratio), and ionization (GT) data. name: BVH-Based Distance Field Computation with Heuristic Initialization
head: BVH Distance Field Computation, Heuristic BVH Traversal for Distance Fields
body: This method computes a distance field for an isosurface approximation by finding the closest point of the isosurface for every voxel in the volume using a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) tree. It differs from existing approaches by initializing the upper bound before traversal using evenly sampled points, rather than waiting for the first leaf encounter, which allows for more aggressive pruning at the beginning of the traversal. Inputs: An array of points approximating the isosurface. The voxel grid for which the distance field is computed. Outputs: A distance field volume where each voxel contains the distance from its center to the isosurface. Data Structures: BVH Tree: A binary tree where each internal node consists of a bounding box including all descendants. A leaf consists of a single primitive (a single point). Stack: Used for depth-first traversal. Parameters: Downscaling: The resulting distance field is downscaled to decimate the search space. Construction Algorithm: Karras’s algorithm is used to build BVH-trees in parallel. Bounding Volume: Bounding boxes are used for lower construction time. Formulas: Distance to internal node n: d(v, n) is the minimum distance from voxel v to the bounding box of n. Distance to leaf node n: d(v, n) is the distance between voxel v and the corresponding point of n. Initial upper bound: du = \min{p \in P} d(v, p). Steps: 1. Heuristic Initialization: Estimate the upper bound before traversal. Compute the distance from the voxel v to a set of sample points P evenly sampled from the approximating points array (which is in scanline order). Calculate the initial upper bound du = \min{p \in P} d(v, p). 2. Stack Initialization: Add the root of the BVH tree to a stack. 3. Traversal Loop: Pop the first node n from the stack. If n is an internal node: For each child node nc, compute d(v, nc). If d(v, nc) < du, push nc onto the stack. If n is a leaf: Compute d(v, n) between v and n. Update du with \min(du, d(v, n)). 4. Termination: Repeat Step 3 until the stack becomes empty. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedistancefield(voxelcenters, isosurfacepoints): # Parallel BVH construction is implementation-specific; assume bvhroot is built. bvhroot = None # Downscale voxel grid to decimate search space # Standard grid downsampling; assume voxelcenters is updated. # Pre-compute evenly sampled points for heuristic initialization # Stride for even sampling is not specified in the sources. stride = max(1, len(isosurfacepoints) // 100) samplepoints = isosurfacepoints[::stride] distancefield = {} for v in voxelcenters: # Step 1: Heuristic Initialization du = float('inf') for p in samplepoints: dist = distance(v, p) if dist < du: du = dist # Step 2: Stack Initialization stack = [bvhroot] # Step 3 & 4: Traversal Loop while stack: n = stack.pop() if n.isinternal: for child in n.children: dist = distancetobbox(v, child.bbox) if dist < du: stack.append(child) else: # n is leaf dist = distance(v, n.point) if dist < du: du = dist distancefield[v] = du return distancefield def distance(v, p): return ((v[0] - p[0])2 + (v[1] - p[1])2 + (v[2] - p[2])2)0.5 def distancetobbox(v, bbox): # Minimum distance from point v to axis-aligned bounding box distsq = 0.0 for i in range(3): if v[i] < bbox.min[i]: distsq += (bbox.min[i] - v[i])2 elif v[i] > bbox.max[i]: distsq += (v[i] - bbox.max[i])2 return distsq0.5 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision may affect distance calculations, especially for voxels very close to the surface. Boundaries: Voxels far from the isosurface may have large initial upper bounds, reducing pruning efficiency. Degenerate Input: If the isosurface approximation is empty, the BVH will be empty, and the distance field will remain at infinity or a default value. A heuristic sampling process that computes a tight initial upper bound to prune BVH-tree traversal during distance field computation. It sets itself apart by estimating the bound before traversal rather than upon the first leaf encounter, allowing earlier pruning. Choose it when maximizing early traversal pruning is critical. Initial Upper Bound Estimation. Time Complexity: Depends on the BVH traversal depth and the number of pruned nodes. Heuristic initialization improves pruning efficiency, especially at the beginning of traversal. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the BVH tree and the distance field volume. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Parallelized using CUDA threads, one per voxel. Strengths: Efficient pruning due to heuristic initialization; parallel construction and traversal. Limitations: Requires building a BVH for every isosurface approximation; bounding boxes may not be optimal for all shapes. When to Use: When computing distance fields for isosurface approximations on GPU. When Not to Use: When the isosurface approximation is very small or when memory is constrained. Origin: The method is described in "Efficient GPU-Accelerated Computation of Isosurface...". History and Development: The approach leverages BVH trees for accelerating closest point searches, a common technique in computer graphics. The specific heuristic initialization is a novel contribution to improve pruning efficiency. Usage: Used in similarity map generation by computing mutual information of corresponding distance fields. name: Ray Tracing with BVH and Möller–Trumbore
head: Pure ray tracing, Wald BVH Traversal (Occlusion/Shadow), occluded
body: A rendering method using a PackedBVH over triangles, traversed with ray-box slab tests for pruning, and Möller–Trumbore tests for triangle intersections. It determines if a ray is occluded by any triangle (shadow ray), returning true on the first hit. Unlike sphere tracing, it requires no distance function and is exact for sharp CSG operations by walking primitive crossings along the ray. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray r (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, max distance t{far}), PackedBVH (Wald-ordered, leaves contain TriangleSoA). Output: Boolean indicating occlusion (true if hit), or hit distance/normal if extended. Data Structures: PackedBVH: Array of nodes. Each node has a bounding box (box) and children. TriangleSoA: Structure of Arrays for triangles at leaf nodes. Fields: vertex positions \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, normals \mathbf{n}0, \mathbf{n}1, \mathbf{n}2. Stack: Array of node pointers for traversal. Steps: 1. Initialize: Compute reciprocal direction \mathbf{rdir} = 1/\mathbf{d}. Initialize stack with root: stack[0] = root, stacksz = 1. 2. Loop: While stacksz > 0: a. Pop node: node = stack[--stacksz]. b. Pruning: Perform slab intersection test against node->box using \mathbf{rdir} and t{far}. If no intersection (!res.isec), break loop. c. Non-Leaf: If node is internal: i. Identify near and far children based on entry distance along ray. ii. Push far child to stack: stack[stacksz++] = farchild. iii. Process near child: node = nearchild (continue loop). d. Sub-BVH Leaf: If node is a sub-BVH leaf, traverse the sub-BVH recursively. e. Triangle Leaf: If node is a triangle leaf: i. Iterate triangles i from 0 to n-1. ii. Call Möller–Trumbore test raytriangle(tris[i], r.org, r.dir). iii. If hit returns true, return true immediately. Möller–Trumbore Formula: For triangle vertices \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2 and ray \mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}: \mathbf{E}1 = \mathbf{v}1 - \mathbf{v}0 \mathbf{E}2 = \mathbf{v}2 - \mathbf{v}0 \mathbf{P} = \mathbf{d} \times \mathbf{E}2 \text{det} = \mathbf{E}1 \cdot \mathbf{P} If |\text{det}| < \epsilon, triangle is parallel to ray. \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{o} - \mathbf{v}0 u = \mathbf{T} \cdot \mathbf{P} If u < 0 or u > \text{det}, no hit. \mathbf{Q} = \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{E}1 v = \mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{Q} If v < 0 or u + v > \text{det}, no hit. t = \mathbf{E}2 \cdot \mathbf{Q} If t > \epsilon and t < t{far}, hit at t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytracebvhocclusion(ray, bvhroot): # ray: {org: Vec3, dir: Vec3, tfar: float} # bvhroot: Node object with box, children, isleaf, triangles rdir = 1.0 / ray.dir stack = [bvhroot] stacksz = 1 while stacksz > 0: node = stack.pop() stacksz -= 1 # Slab test if not slabintersect(node.box, ray.org, rdir, ray.tfar): continue if node.isleaf: # Triangle leaf for tri in node.triangles: if raytrianglemollertrumbore(tri, ray.org, ray.dir, ray.tfar): return True else: # Non-leaf: push far child, process near child # Determine near/far based on slab entry times tnearchild, tfarchild = getchildintervals(node, ray.org, rdir) if tnearchild < tfarchild: stack.append(node.farchild) stack.append(node.nearchild) else: stack.append(node.nearchild) stack.append(node.farchild) return False def raytrianglemollertrumbore(tri, org, dir, tfar): v0, v1, v2 = tri.v0, tri.v1, tri.v2 E1 = v1 - v0 E2 = v2 - v0 P = cross(dir, E2) det = dot(E1, P) if abs(det) < 1e-8: return False T = org - v0 u = dot(T, P) if u < 0.0 or u > det: return False Q = cross(T, E1) v = dot(dir, Q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > det: return False t = dot(E2, Q) if t > 1e-8 and t < tfar: return True return False def slabintersect(box, org, rdir, tfar): # Standard AABB slab test tmin = (box.min - org) rdir tmax = (box.max - org) rdir t1 = min(tmin, tmax) t2 = max(tmin, tmax) tenter = max(t1) texit = min(t2) return tenter <= texit and texit > 0.0 Parameters: t{far}: Max ray distance. Typical: scene bounds. \epsilon: Epsilon for parallel check. Typical: 10^{-8}. Edge Cases: Ray parallel to triangle: det near zero. Ray origin inside triangle: handled by t > \epsilon check. Degenerate triangles: det near zero. Time Complexity: O(N \log M) average case for N rays and M triangles, dependent on BVH quality. Memory Complexity: O(M) for BVH storage. Performance: ~1.1 billion primary rays/s and ~1.3 billion rays/s with shadows/AO on RTX 3080 Ti. Strengths: Exact for sharp CSG, no distance function needed, efficient pruning. Limitations: Slower than sphere tracing for smooth shapes, requires BVH construction. When to use: Sharp geometry, CSG operations, shadow rays. When not to use: Smooth organic shapes, real-time sphere tracing preferred. Originated in the context of sphere-traced rendering of shapes and tapes, specifically for "Pure ray tracing" mode in EBGeometry. It leverages existing packed BVHs for mesh SDFs, avoiding new acceleration structure construction. Used in interactive viewers for sharp CSG scenes like the "Tunnel" and "Rod" examples. Visualization: sphere-traced rendering of shapes and tapes, https://github.com/rmrsk/EBGeometry/issues/93, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bsegovia/mini.q, https://github.com/bsegovia/mini.q, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: BVH Traversal for Closest Point
head: Closest Point BVH Traversal
body: This method traverses a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to find the triangle closest to a specific query point. It solves the problem of efficient nearest-neighbor search in geometric scenes by pruning branches that cannot contain a closer primitive than the current best. It sets itself apart from Mesh BVH and IRIS Ray-Geometry Intersection by operating on point-to-primitive distance rather than ray-parametric distance, and from Multi-Hit BVH Traversal by returning only the single closest hit. Inputs: A query point p, a BVH root node, and a mutable best state best initialized to (\infty, \text{null}), where the first element is the squared distance and the second is the closest primitive found so far. Outputs: The updated best tuple containing the squared distance to the closest triangle and the triangle itself. Data Structures: The BVH is defined recursively: AABB(low: f32x3, high: f32x3): Axis-aligned bounding box. Triangle(p0: f32x3, p1: f32x3, p2: f32x3): A triangle defined by three vertices. BVH: Interior(low: f32x3, high: f32x3, left: BVH, right: BVH): Internal node with bounding box and two children. Leaf(low: f32x3, high: f32x3, nprims: u16, data: Triangle[nprims]): Leaf node with bounding box and an array of triangles. Helper Functions: 1. distmin(pt, a): Returns the squared minimum distance from point pt to AABB a. 2. distmax(pt, a): Returns the squared maximum distance from point pt to AABB a. Formula: Let u = a.low - pt.v, v = pt.v - a.high, d = \min(u, v). Return \text{dot}(d, d). Algorithm Steps: 1. Interior Node: Compute d{min} = \text{distmin}(p, \text{AABB}(low, high)). If d{min} < \text{best}[0]: Compute upper\bound = \text{distmax}(p, \text{AABB}(low, high)). If upper\bound < \text{best}[0], update \text{best} = (upper\bound, \text{best}[1]). Extract AABBs for left child L{aabb} and right child R{aabb}. Compute L = \text{distmin}(p, L{aabb}) and R = \text{distmin}(p, R{aabb}). If L < R, recurse closestpoint(p, left, best) then closestpoint(p, right, best). Else, recurse closestpoint(p, right, best) then closestpoint(p, left, best). 2. Leaf Node: Compute d{min} = \text{distmin}(p, \text{AABB}(low, high)). If d{min} < \text{best}[0]: Iterate through each triangle t in data. Compute dt = \text{distmin}(p, t). If dt < \text{best}[0], update \text{best} = (dt, t). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distmin(pt, aabb): # Returns squared minimum distance from point to AABB # Implementation details for distmin are not provided in source # Standard implementation: clamp point to AABB, return squared distance pass def distmax(pt, aabb): u = aabb.low - pt v = pt - aabb.high d = min(u, v) return dot(d, d) def closestpoint(p, bvh, best): if bvh.type == "Interior": if distmin(p, bvh.aabb) < best[0]: upperbound = distmax(p, bvh.aabb) if upperbound < best[0]: best[0] = upperbound # best[1] remains unchanged as it holds the primitive, not a bound # Note: Source updates best[1] but it is likely a placeholder or error in source logic # as best[1] is the primitive. We assume best[0] is the distance. # Assuming best is (distance, primitive). Updating best[1] with a float is invalid. # Source says: best = (upperbound, best[1]). This implies best[1] is preserved. best[0] = upperbound # Determine child AABBs leftaabb = bvh.left.aabb rightaabb = bvh.right.aabb L = distmin(p, leftaabb) R = distmin(p, rightaabb) if L < R: closestpoint(p, bvh.left, best) closestpoint(p, bvh.right, best) else: closestpoint(p, bvh.right, best) closestpoint(p, bvh.left, best) elif bvh.type == "Leaf": if distmin(p, bvh.aabb) < best[0]: for t in bvh.data: dt = distmin(p, t) if dt < best[0]: best[0] = dt best[1] = t Parameters: best: Initialized to (\infty, \text{null}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The source uses distmax for pruning upper bounds on interior nodes to potentially update best before descending. Precision issues may arise if distmin or distmax calculations are not robust for degenerate AABBs or points on boundaries. BVH Ray Traversal with Stack is an iterative algorithm for traversing a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to find the closest ray-triangle intersection. It solves the problem of efficiently determining the first surface a ray hits within a scene composed of multiple entities, each with its own local BVH. It sets itself apart from BVH Traversal for Closest Point by using an explicit stack to manage traversal order for multiple entities and by returning the closest hit distance rather than just a boolean or closest point to a query. It differs from Stackless BVH Traversal by relying on a fixed-size explicit stack buffer rather than encoding traversal order in the node structure. Not given in the sources.
