name: BVH Ray Traversal with Stack
head: BVH Ray Traversal for Occlusion, IntersectBVHStack, IntersectBVHStackOcclusion, Iterative BVH traversal, Stack-based iterative BVH traversal
body: BVH Ray Traversal with Stack is an iterative algorithm for traversing a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to find the closest ray-triangle intersection. It solves the problem of efficiently determining the first surface a ray hits within a scene composed of multiple entities, each with its own local BVH. It sets itself apart from BVH Traversal for Closest Point by using an explicit stack to manage traversal order for multiple entities and by returning the closest hit distance rather than just a boolean or closest point to a query. It differs from Stackless BVH Traversal by relying on a fixed-size explicit stack buffer rather than encoding traversal order in the node structure. Inputs: RayOrigin: vec3 ray origin in world space. RayDirection: vec3 ray direction in world space. NodeStartIndex: int starting index in BVHNodes for the current entity. NodeCount: int number of nodes in the current entity's BVH. InverseMatrix: mat4 inverse model matrix of the entity. TMax: float maximum traversal distance. BVHNodes: Array of Node structures. BVHTris: Array of Triangle structures. BVHVertices: Array of Vertex structures. uTotalNodes: int total number of nodes in the global BVH array. Outputs: ClosestTraversal: float distance to the closest intersection, or -1.0f if none. oMesh: int index of the intersected mesh. oTriangleIndex: int index of the intersected triangle. iters: int number of iterations performed. Data Structures: Bounds: Struct with vec4 Min and vec4 Max. For leaf nodes, Min.w contains packed data: StartIdx in the upper 4 bits and Length in the lower 4 bits. Node: Struct with Bounds LeftChildData and Bounds RightChildData. Triangle: Struct with int PackedData[4]. Vertex: Struct with vec4 Position and uvec4 PackedData. Stack: Fixed-size array of int with size 64. Steps: 1. Transform RayOrigin and RayDirection into the entity's local space using InverseMatrix. RayOrigin is treated as a point (w=1.0), RayDirection as a vector (w=0.0). 2. Compute InverseDirection as 1.0 / \text{RayDirection}. 3. Initialize StackPointer = 0, ClosestTraversal = -1.0f, Iterations = 0, and CurrentNodeIndex = NodeStartIndex. 4. Loop while Iterations < 1024: a. Check bounds: If StackPointer >= 64 or StackPointer < 0 or CurrentNodeIndex < NodeStartIndex or CurrentNodeIndex > NodeStartIndex + NodeCount or CurrentNodeIndex < 0 or CurrentNodeIndex > uTotalNodes, break. b. Fetch CurrentNode = BVHNodes[CurrentNodeIndex]. c. Determine if children are leaves: LeftLeaf = IsLeaf(CurrentNode.LeftChildData), RightLeaf = IsLeaf(CurrentNode.RightChildData). d. Calculate traversal distances: i. If LeftLeaf, LeftTraversal = -1.0f. Else, LeftTraversal = RayBounds(RayOrigin, InverseDirection, CurrentNode.LeftChildData.Min, CurrentNode.LeftChildData.Max, TMax). ii. If RightLeaf, RightTraversal = -1.0f. Else, RightTraversal = RayBounds(RayOrigin, InverseDirection, CurrentNode.RightChildData.Min, CurrentNode.RightChildData.Max, TMax). e. If LeftLeaf and IntersectTriangles is true: i. Extract Packed = CurrentNode.LeftChildData.Min.w. ii. StartIdx = Packed >> 4, Length = Packed & 0xF. iii. For Idx from 0 to Length - 1: 1. Fetch Tri = BVHTris[Idx + StartIdx]. 2. Get vertices A, B, C from BVHVertices using Tri.PackedData. 3. Compute Intersect = RayTriangle(RayOrigin, RayDirection, A, B, C). 4. If Intersect.x > 0.0f and Intersect.x < TMax: TMax = Intersect.x ClosestTraversal = Intersect.x oMesh = MeshIndex (from caller context) oTriangleIndex = Idx + StartIdx Return ClosestTraversal. f. If RightLeaf and IntersectTriangles is true, perform the same triangle intersection loop for the right child using CurrentNode.RightChildData. g. If LeftTraversal > 0.0f and RightTraversal > 0.0f: i. Determine closer child. Get child indices from Max.w of the child bounds. ii. If RightTraversal < LeftTraversal, swap CurrentNodeIndex and Postponed indices. iii. If StackPointer >= 63, break. iv. Push Postponed to Stack[StackPointer++]. v. Set CurrentNodeIndex to the closer node index. h. Else if LeftTraversal > 0.0f, set CurrentNodeIndex to the left child's index. i. Else if RightTraversal > 0.0f, set CurrentNodeIndex to the right child's index. j. Else (neither child traversed): i. If StackPointer <= 0, break. ii. CurrentNodeIndex = Stack[--StackPointer]. k. Iterations += 1. 5. Set iters = Iterations and return ClosestTraversal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def IsLeaf(bounds): # Implementation detail: check if bounds indicate a leaf node # Based on source, leaf nodes have specific packed data in Min.w return (bounds.Min.w & 0xF0) != 0 # Placeholder logic based on packing description def RayTriangle(origin, direction, v0, v1, v2): # Möller–Trumbore intersection algorithm edge1 = v1 - v0 edge2 = v2 - v0 h = cross(direction, edge2) a = dot(edge1, h) if a > -0.0000001 and a < 0.0000001: return vec4(-1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) f = 1.0 / a s = origin - v0 u = f dot(s, h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return vec4(-1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) q = cross(s, edge1) v = f dot(direction, q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: return vec4(-1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) t = f dot(edge2, q) if t > 0.0000001: return vec4(t, u, v, 1.0) return vec4(-1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def RayBounds(origin, invdir, minb, maxb, tmax): # Slab intersection test t1 = (minb.x - origin.x) invdir.x t2 = (maxb.x - origin.x) invdir.x tmin = min(t1, t2) tmax = max(t1, t2) t1 = (minb.y - origin.y) invdir.y t2 = (maxb.y - origin.y) invdir.y tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) t1 = (minb.z - origin.z) invdir.z t2 = (maxb.z - origin.z) invdir.z tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < tmin or tmax < 0.0 or tmin > tmax: return -1.0 return tmin def IntersectBVHStack(RayOrigin, RayDirection, NodeStartIndex, NodeCount, InverseMatrix, TMax, BVHNodes, BVHTris, BVHVertices, uTotalNodes, MeshIndex): # 1. Transform ray to local space rayoriginlocal = vec3(InverseMatrix vec4(RayOrigin, 1.0)) raydirlocal = vec3(InverseMatrix vec4(RayDirection, 0.0)) # 2. Compute inverse direction invdir = 1.0 / raydirlocal # 3. Initialize state stack = [0] 64 stackpointer = 0 closesttraversal = -1.0 iterations = 0 currentnodeindex = NodeStartIndex # 4. Traverse while iterations < 1024: # Check bounds if stackpointer >= 64 or stackpointer < 0: break if currentnodeindex < NodeStartIndex or currentnodeindex > NodeStartIndex + NodeCount: break if currentnodeindex < 0 or currentnodeindex > uTotalNodes: break currentnode = BVHNodes[currentnodeindex] # Determine leaves leftleaf = IsLeaf(currentnode.leftchilddata) rightleaf = IsLeaf(currentnode.rightchilddata) # Calculate traversal distances if leftleaf: lefttraversal = -1.0 else: lefttraversal = RayBounds(rayoriginlocal, invdir, currentnode.leftchilddata.min, currentnode.leftchilddata.max, TMax) if rightleaf: righttraversal = -1.0 else: righttraversal = RayBounds(rayoriginlocal, invdir, currentnode.rightchilddata.min, currentnode.rightchilddata.max, TMax) # Intersect triangles if leaf if leftleaf: packed = currentnode.leftchilddata.min.w startidx = packed >> 4 length = packed & 0xF for idx in range(length): tri = BVHTris[idx + startidx] # Get vertices from BVHVertices using tri.packeddata # This is a placeholder for the actual vertex fetching logic v0 = BVHVertices[tri.packeddata[0]] v1 = BVHVertices[tri.packeddata[1]] v2 = BVHVertices[tri.packeddata[2]] intersect = RayTriangle(rayoriginlocal, raydirlocal, v0.position, v1.position, v2.position) if intersect.x > 0.0 and intersect.x < TMax: TMax = intersect.x closesttraversal = intersect.x # Update output parameters return closesttraversal if rightleaf: packed = currentnode.rightchilddata.min.w startidx = packed >> 4 length = packed & 0xF for idx in range(length): tri = BVHTris[idx + startidx] # Get vertices from BVHVertices using tri.packeddata v0 = BVHVertices[tri.packeddata[0]] v1 = BVHVertices[tri.packeddata[1]] v2 = BVHVertices[tri.packeddata[2]] intersect = RayTriangle(rayoriginlocal, raydirlocal, v0.position, v1.position, v2.position) if intersect.x > 0.0 and intersect.x < TMax: TMax = intersect.x closesttraversal = intersect.x # Update output parameters return closesttraversal # Push to stack if both children are valid if lefttraversal > 0.0 and righttraversal > 0.0: # Get child indices from Max.w leftidx = currentnode.leftchilddata.max.w + NodeStartIndex rightidx = currentnode.rightchilddata.max.w + NodeStartIndex if righttraversal < lefttraversal: currentnodeindex = rightidx postponed = leftidx else: currentnodeindex = leftidx postponed = rightidx if stackpointer >= 63: break stack[stackpointer] = postponed stackpointer += 1 elif lefttraversal > 0.0: currentnodeindex = currentnode.leftchilddata.max.w + NodeStartIndex elif righttraversal > 0.0: currentnodeindex = currentnode.rightchilddata.max.w + NodeStartIndex else: if stackpointer <= 0: break stackpointer -= 1 currentnodeindex = stack[stackpointer] iterations += 1 return closesttraversal Parameters: RayOrigin: World space ray origin. RayDirection: World space ray direction. NodeStartIndex: Start index in BVHNodes for the entity. NodeCount: Number of nodes in the entity's BVH. InverseMatrix: Inverse model matrix of the entity. TMax: Maximum traversal distance. oMesh: Output mesh index. oTriangleIndex: Output triangle index. iters: Output iteration count. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stack overflow: The stack size is fixed at 64. If StackPointer reaches 63 during a push, the traversal breaks. Infinite loops: The traversal is limited to 1024 iterations. Invalid node index: Checks ensure CurrentNodeIndex is within NodeStartIndex to NodeStartIndex + NodeCount and 0 to uTotalNodes. Leaf node handling: Leaf nodes have a traversal distance of -1.0f and are intersected directly. Packed data extraction: StartIdx and Length are extracted from Min.w using bit shifting and masking. A high-level wrapper that combines BVH traversal and data retrieval into a single call, returning TUVW, Mesh, TriangleIdx, Albedo, and Normal. It calls IntersectScene (or IntersectSceneIgnoreTransparent) to get TUVW, Mesh, TriangleIdx, and IntersectedEntity, then calls GetData (or GetDataFast) with these values to populate Normal, Albedo, and Alpha. Time Complexity: O(N) in the worst case for a linear BVH, but typically O(\log N) for a balanced BVH, where N is the number of nodes. The fixed iteration limit of 1024 caps the worst-case performance. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space for the stack, with a fixed size of 64 integers. Performance: The fixed stack size and iteration limit make it suitable for environments with limited memory or stack depth, such as GPUs. However, the fixed stack size may lead to early termination on complex scenes with deep BVHs. Strengths: Simple implementation, no dynamic memory allocation, predictable memory usage. Limitations: Fixed stack size may cause incomplete traversal on very deep BVHs. Fixed iteration limit may cause incomplete traversal on degenerate cases. When to use: When memory is constrained, or when a fixed maximum traversal depth is acceptable. When not to use: When the BVH depth is unknown and potentially very large, or when complete traversal is required for correctness. The algorithm is described in the source code of the VolumetricDisplay project by swr06. It is an iterative implementation of BVH traversal, optimized for binary occlusion queries and closest hit queries. The specific implementation details, such as the fixed stack size and iteration limit, are derived from the source code. swr06/VolumetricDisplay, https://github.com/swr06/VolumetricDisplay, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Stackless BVH Traversal
head: GPU BVH traversal without stack, Linear pointer-based BVH traversal
body: Stackless BVH Traversal is a ray traversal algorithm for Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) hierarchies that avoids explicit stack allocation by using a linear pointer-based approach, suitable for GPU execution where stack depth is limited or unavailable. It sets itself apart from BVH Ray Traversal with Stack by eliminating the need for dynamic memory allocation or fixed-size stack buffers, instead relying on a pre-serialized linear array of nodes where traversal order is encoded in the node structure itself. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A linear array of BVHNodes, a ray defined by origin and direction, TMin (near clip), TMax (far clip/current closest hit), and NodeStartIndex (offset for leaf node pointers). Output: The closest intersection distance ClosestTraversal, the associated Mesh ID, and the TriangleIndex. Data Structures: The BVH is stored in a flat array of nodes. Each node is 32 bytes, packed into two vec4 (or equivalent 128-bit) structures: Min and Max. Internal Node: Min.xyz: AABB minimum bounds. Min.w: Unused or reserved. Max.xyz: AABB maximum bounds. Max.w: Unused or reserved. Note: Internal nodes do not store explicit left/right child pointers. The traversal assumes children are stored sequentially in the linear array. Leaf Node: Min.xyz: AABB minimum bounds. Min.w: Packed integer. Upper bits (>> 4): Starting index into the BVHTris array (triangle indices). Lower 4 bits (& 0xF): Triangle count (Length). Max.xyz: AABB maximum bounds. Max.w: Packed integer. Contains the index of the next node to visit in the linear array. If the value is -1 (bit pattern 0xFFFFFFFF interpreted as signed int), it signifies the end of the traversal branch. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Pointer to NodeStartIndex (typically 0 or the root index) and ClosestTraversal to -1.0f. Initialize Iterations to 0. 2. Loop while Pointer >= 0 and Iterations < MaxIterations (1024): a. Fetch CurrentNode = BVHNodes[Pointer]. b. Compute BoxTraversal (ray-AABB intersection test) using RayBounds with tmin = 0.0001f and tmax = TMax. c. If BoxTraversal > 0.0f and BoxTraversal < TMax: i. Check if CurrentNode is a leaf: IsLeaf = (floatBitsToInt(CurrentNode.Min.w) != -1). ii. If Leaf: 1. Decode Packed = floatBitsToInt(CurrentNode.Min.w). 2. StartIndex = Packed >> 4. 3. Length = Packed & 0xF. 4. Iterate i from StartIndex to StartIndex + Length - 1. 5. For each triangle, compute ray-triangle intersection. 6. If hit t < TMax: Update TMax = t. Update ClosestTraversal = t. Update Mesh and TriangleIndex from the triangle data. 7. Set Pointer = floatBitsToInt(CurrentNode.Max.w). 8. If Pointer < 0, break loop. 9. Else, Pointer += NodeStartIndex and continue loop. iii. If Not Leaf: 1. Increment Pointer by 1 (Pointer++). 2. Continue loop. d. Else (Node did not intersect or intersection was beyond TMax): i. Set Pointer = floatBitsToInt(CurrentNode.Max.w). ii. If Pointer < 0, break loop. iii. Else, Pointer += NodeStartIndex and continue loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stacklessbvhtraverse(BVHNodes, rayorigin, raydir, TMin, TMax, NodeStartIndex, BVHTris): Pointer = NodeStartIndex ClosestTraversal = -1.0 Mesh = -1 TriangleIndex = -1 MaxIterations = 1024 Iterations = 0 # TMin for ray-AABB test to avoid precision issues at origin raytmin = 0.0001 while Pointer >= 0 and Iterations < MaxIterations: Iterations += 1 CurrentNode = BVHNodes[Pointer] # Ray-AABB intersection test # Returns thit if ray intersects box within [raytmin, TMax], else <= 0 BoxTraversal = rayboundsintersect(rayorigin, raydir, CurrentNode.Min.xyz, CurrentNode.Max.xyz, raytmin, TMax) if BoxTraversal > 0.0 and BoxTraversal < TMax: # Check if leaf: Min.w != -1 (0xFFFFFFFF) isleaf = (floatbitstoint(CurrentNode.Min.w) != -1) if isleaf: Packed = floatbitstoint(CurrentNode.Min.w) StartIndex = Packed >> 4 Length = Packed & 0xF # Iterate triangles for i in range(StartIndex, StartIndex + Length): tri = BVHTris[i] thit = raytriangleintersect(rayorigin, raydir, tri) if thit is not None and thit < TMax: TMax = thit ClosestTraversal = thit Mesh = tri.meshid TriangleIndex = tri.index # Move to next node NextPointer = floatbitstoint(CurrentNode.Max.w) if NextPointer < 0: break else: Pointer = NextPointer + NodeStartIndex else: # Internal node: children are sequential, just advance Pointer += 1 else: # Node missed or was too far, skip to next node encoded in Max.w NextPointer = floatbitstoint(CurrentNode.Max.w) if NextPointer < 0: break else: Pointer = NextPointer + NodeStartIndex return ClosestTraversal, Mesh, TriangleIndex Parameters: MaxIterations: 1024. Prevents infinite loops in malformed BVHs. TMin: 0.0001f. Used in RayBounds to avoid self-intersection or precision errors at the ray origin. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The traversal assumes a linearized BVH where children are stored sequentially. Non-leaf nodes simply advance to the next index (Pointer++), implying the BVH is built in a specific depth-first or breadth-first order that allows linear traversal without explicit left/right child pointers for internal nodes. If the BVH is not built in the expected linear order, the traversal will fail to visit all nodes or visit incorrect nodes. MaxIterations must be sufficient to cover the maximum possible depth of the BVH. If the BVH is deeper than 1024 nodes, the traversal will terminate prematurely. This variant skips entities marked as transparent during traversal. It checks the entity's alpha value and ignores entities with alpha < 0.99. For opaque entities, it calls the standard IntersectBVHStackless function. If a hit T > 0 and T < TMax is found, it updates TMax, ClosestT, Mesh, TriangleIdx, and Entity. This is useful for visibility checks where transparent objects should not occlude opaque ones. This method performs global scene intersection by iterating over all entities in a scene to find the first entity hit by a ray, effectively serving as an occlusion culling primitive. Unlike standard closest-hit algorithms that search for the minimum distance across all geometry, this approach returns immediately upon finding any valid intersection with an entity's BVH, prioritizing speed for visibility checks over precise depth sorting. It builds on Stackless BVH Traversal by wrapping its traversal logic in a linear entity loop [22324-stackless-bvh-ray-traversal-for-occlusion.md]. Time Complexity: O(N) in the worst case for a linear scan, but typically O(\log N) for balanced BVHs, where N is the number of nodes. The linear pointer approach adds minimal overhead compared to stack-based traversal. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, as no stack is required. The BVH itself is stored in O(N) memory. Performance: Suitable for GPU execution where stack depth is limited or unavailable. It avoids the overhead of stack allocation and management. Strengths: No stack overflow risk, simple implementation, low memory footprint. Limitations: Requires a specific BVH build order (linearized). Less flexible than stack-based traversal for complex traversal strategies (e.g., early termination based on complex criteria). Stackless BVH Traversal is a technique developed for GPU ray tracing to overcome the limitations of stack-based traversal in hardware with limited stack space. It is commonly used in real-time ray tracing applications and global illumination algorithms where performance and memory efficiency are critical. swr06/VolumetricDisplay, https://github.com/swr06/VolumetricDisplay, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Stackless BVH Ray Traversal for Occlusion
head: IntersectBVHStacklessOcclusion, IntersectScene, Scene Intersection for Occlusion, IntersectSceneOcclusion, Scene Intersection with Occlusion Culling
body: This method performs global scene intersection for occlusion culling by iterating over all scene entities and traversing each entity's Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to find the closest hit within a maximum distance. It differs from standard closest-point intersection by returning the first valid hit encountered across the entity list, making it suitable for shadow casting or visibility checks where any obstruction blocks the ray. It builds on Stackless BVH Traversal by incorporating per-entity coordinate space transformations and a global iteration loop. Inputs: RayOrigin: The starting point of the ray in world space. RayDirection: The direction of the ray in world space. uEntityCount: The total number of entities in the scene. BVHEntities: An array of entity descriptors, each containing: NodeOffset: The starting index of the entity's BVH nodes in the global BVHNodes array. NodeCount: The number of nodes in the entity's BVH subtree. InverseMatrix: The inverse model matrix of the entity, used to transform the ray into local space. BVHNodes: An array of BVH nodes. Each node contains: Min: vec3 representing the minimum corner of the AABB. Max: vec3 representing the maximum corner of the AABB. Min.w: Packed data for leaf nodes (see Layout). Max.w: Packed pointer to the next node in the stackless traversal sequence. BVHTris: An array of triangle descriptors. Each triangle contains: PackedData: Indices or packed data to locate vertices. BVHVertices: An array of vertices. Each vertex contains: PackedData: vec4 (normals in xy, UV in w). Position: vec3. TMax: The maximum distance to consider for intersection (default: 1,000,000.0). Output: float: The distance to the closest intersection hit across all entities. Returns -1.0 if no hit is found. BVH Node Layout: Min.xyz: AABB minimum bounds. Min.w: For leaf nodes, packed integer bits: lower 4 bits store triangle count, upper bits store triangle start index. Max.xyz: AABB maximum bounds. Max.w: Packed integer bits representing the pointer to the next node to traverse. If negative, traversal ends. BVH Triangle Layout: PackedData: Used to index into BVHVertices. BVH Vertex Layout: PackedData.xy: Normal components. PackedData.w: UV coordinates. Position: Vertex position. 1. Global Iteration: Loop through each entity i from 0 to u\EntityCount - 1. 2. Ray Transformation: Transform the ray origin and direction into the local space of the current entity using the entity's InverseMatrix. RayOrigin{local} = \text{vec3}(InverseMatrix \cdot \text{vec4}(RayOrigin{world}, 1.0)) RayDirection{local} = \text{vec3}(InverseMatrix \cdot \text{vec4}(RayDirection{world}, 0.0)) 3. Local Traversal: Call the stackless traversal routine for the current entity's BVH subtree using the transformed ray and the entity's NodeOffset and NodeCount. 4. Hit Check: If the local traversal returns a distance T > 0, return T immediately. This ensures the first entity hit in the iteration order is the result. 5. Completion: If the loop completes without a hit, return -1.0. Given a transformed ray, NodeStartIndex, NodeCount, and TMax: 1. Initialization: Pointer = NodeStartIndex Iterations = 0 MaxIterations = 1024 ClosestTraversal = -1.0 2. Traversal Loop: While Pointer \ge 0 and Iterations < MaxIterations: Bounds Check: If Pointer < NodeStartIndex or Pointer > NodeStartIndex + NodeCount or Pointer < 0 or Pointer > u\TotalNodes, break. Increment: Iterations = Iterations + 1 Load Node: CurrentNode = BVHNodes[Pointer] AABB Intersection: Compute BoxTraversal = \text{RayAABB}(CurrentNode.Min.xyz, CurrentNode.Max.xyz, RayOrigin{local}, RayDirection{local}, 0.0001, TMax). If BoxTraversal > 0 and BoxTraversal < TMax: Leaf Check: If CurrentNode is a leaf: Extract Packed = \text{floatBitsToInt}(CurrentNode.Min.w) Length = Packed \ \& \ 0xF StartIdx = Packed \gg 4 For Idx from StartIdx to StartIdx + Length - 1: Triangle = BVHTris[Idx] Extract vertices A, B, C from BVHVertices using Triangle.PackedData and offset 0. Intersect = \text{RayTriangle}(RayOrigin{local}, RayDirection{local}, A, B, C) If Intersect.x > 0 and Intersect.x < TMax: TMax = Intersect.x ClosestTraversal = Intersect.x Return ClosestTraversal Internal Node: If not a leaf, proceed to next node logic. Else: Skip to next node logic. Next Node: NextPointer = \text{floatBitsToInt}(CurrentNode.Max.w) If NextPointer < 0, break. Pointer = NextPointer + NodeStartIndex 3. Return: If loop completes without hit, return -1.0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intersectbvhstacklessocclusion(rayoriginworld, raydirectionworld, entities, bvhnodes, bvhtris, bvhvertices, tmax): """ Iterates over all entities to find the closest occlusion hit. """ for entity in entities: # Transform ray to local space invmatrix = entity.inversematrix rayoriginlocal = vec3(invmatrix vec4(rayoriginworld, 1.0)) raydirectionlocal = vec3(invmatrix vec4(raydirectionworld, 0.0)) # Perform local traversal hitdist = traversebvhstackless(rayoriginlocal, raydirectionlocal, entity.nodeoffset, entity.nodecount, bvhnodes, bvhtris, bvhvertices, tmax) if hitdist > 0.0: return hitdist return -1.0 def traversebvhstackless(rayorigin, raydirection, nodestartindex, nodecount, bvhnodes, bvhtris, bvhvertices, tmax): """ Stackless traversal of a BVH subtree. """ pointer = nodestartindex iterations = 0 maxiterations = 1024 closesttraversal = -1.0 # Precompute inverse direction for slab test invdirection = vec3(1.0 / raydirection) while pointer >= 0 and iterations < maxiterations: # Bounds check if pointer < nodestartindex or pointer > nodestartindex + nodecount or pointer < 0 or pointer > len(bvhnodes): break iterations += 1 currentnode = bvhnodes[pointer] # Ray-AABB intersection boxtraversal = raybounds(currentnode.min.xyz, currentnode.max.xyz, rayorigin, invdirection, 0.0001, tmax) if boxtraversal > 0.0 and boxtraversal < tmax: # Check if leaf if isleafnode(currentnode): packed = floatbitstoint(currentnode.min.w) length = packed & 0xF startidx = packed >> 4 for idx in range(startidx, startidx + length): triangle = bvhtris[idx] # Extract vertices A, B, C from bvhvertices using triangle.packeddata # Note: Exact extraction logic depends on packeddata format, assumed standard here a = getvertex(bvhvertices, triangle.packeddata, 0) b = getvertex(bvhvertices, triangle.packeddata, 1) c = getvertex(bvhvertices, triangle.packeddata, 2) intersect = raytriangle(rayorigin, raydirection, a, b, c) if intersect.x > 0.0 and intersect.x < tmax: tmax = intersect.x closesttraversal = intersect.x return closesttraversal else: # Internal node, continue traversal pass else: # AABB miss, continue traversal pass # Move to next node nextpointer = floatbitstoint(currentnode.max.w) if nextpointer < 0: break pointer = nextpointer + nodestartindex return closesttraversal def raybounds(minval, maxval, rayorigin, invdirection, epsilon, tmax): """ Standard slab-based AABB intersection test. """ tmin = (minval - rayorigin) invdirection tmaxval = (maxval - rayorigin) invdirection tenter = max(max(tmin.x, tmin.y, tmin.z), epsilon) texit = min(min(tmaxval.x, tmaxval.y, tmaxval.z), tmax) if tenter > texit: return -1.0 return tenter def raytriangle(rayorigin, raydirection, v0, v1, v2): """ Möller–Trumbore intersection algorithm. Returns vec3(t, u, v) where t is distance, u,v are barycentric coords. """ edge1 = v1 - v0 edge2 = v2 - v0 h = cross(raydirection, edge2) a = dot(edge1, h) if a > -0.00001 and a < 0.00001: return vec3(-1.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Parallel f = 1.0 / a s = rayorigin - v0 u = f dot(s, h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return vec3(-1.0, 0.0, 0.0) q = cross(s, edge1) v = f dot(raydirection, q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: return vec3(-1.0, 0.0, 0.0) t = f dot(edge2, q) if t > 0.00001: return vec3(t, u, v) return vec3(-1.0, 0.0, 0.0) MaxIterations: Maximum number of traversal steps to prevent infinite loops. Value: 1024. NodeStartIndex: Base index in BVHNodes for the entity's subtree. NodeCount: Number of nodes in the entity's BVH subtree. InverseMatrix: Inverse model matrix of the entity. TMax: Maximum intersection distance. Default: 1,000,000.0. Invalid Pointer: The traversal checks if Pointer is out of bounds (NodeStartIndex, NodeStartIndex + NodeCount, or global uTotalNodes) to prevent accessing invalid memory or entering infinite loops. Infinite Loop Prevention: A hard limit of MaxIterations (1024) is enforced to prevent infinite traversal in case of malformed BVH or logic errors. Precision: A small epsilon (0.0001) is used in ray-AABB intersection to avoid self-intersection artifacts. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H), where N is the number of entities and H is the average height of the BVH. In the worst case (no culling), it checks all entities. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, as it uses a stackless approach. Strengths: No stack allocation required, making it suitable for GPU execution where stack depth is limited. Simple implementation. Limitations: Order-dependent results (first hit wins). Not optimized for finding the global closest hit across all entities simultaneously, which may require sorting or parallel reduction. When to use: Occlusion culling, shadow ray casting where any hit is sufficient. When not to use: When the global closest hit is required regardless of entity order, or for high-performance global illumination where all hits are needed. This method is derived from the IntersectBVHStacklessOcclusion implementation found in the VolumetricDisplay project. It adapts the stackless BVH traversal technique for scene-level occlusion queries. swr06/VolumetricDisplay, https://github.com/swr06/VolumetricDisplay, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray Packet BVH Traversal
head: occluded, closest (packet), shadow ray packet traversal, primary ray packet traversal, Ray Packet Traversal (Closest Hit)
body: Ray Packet BVH Traversal traverses a Wald-ordered Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) for a packet of rays to find the closest intersection for each active ray in the packet, or to determine which rays are occluded by triangles. It differs from single-ray traversal by processing multiple rays simultaneously, leveraging SIMD-like parallelism within the traversal stack and leaf intersection tests. It builds on Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) Traversal by extending the node visitation logic to handle a range of ray indices (first to first + packetsize) rather than a single ray. Inputs: bvhtree: A Wald-ordered BVH structure. p: Ray packet data containing origin, direction, and flags. hit: Output structure for intersection results. flags: Bitwise combination of raypacket::INTERVALARITH, raypacket::SHAREDORG, and others determining optimization paths. Outputs: hit: Intersection data for the closest hit for each ray in the packet. occnum: Count of occluded rays (in shadow ray variants). Data Structures: stack: Array of pair<intersector::node, u32> with fixed size 64. Each element stores a BVH node pointer and the starting ray index (first) for that node in the packet. active: Array of integers (or bitmasks) indicating which rays in the current packet are still active (have not yet hit an object). Size is MAXRAYNUM. signs: Array of 3 integers (0 or 1) indicating the sign of each ray direction component: signs[i] = 1 if dir[i] >= 0, else 0. Parameters: MAXRAYNUM: Maximum number of rays in a packet. Not given in the sources. INTERVALARITH: Flag enabling interval arithmetic optimizations. SHAREDORG: Flag indicating all rays in the packet share the same origin. Steps: 1. Initialize Traversal State: Compute sign bits for ray direction components: python signs[0] = 1 if p.dir().x >= 0 else 0 signs[1] = 1 if p.dir().y >= 0 else 0 signs[2] = 1 if p.dir().z >= 0 else 0 Initialize stack with root node and starting ray index 0: python stack[0] = (bvhtree.root, 0) stacksz = 1 occnum = 0 # For shadow ray variants 2. Traversal Loop: While stacksz > 0: Pop element from stack: elem = stack[--stacksz] Extract node = elem.first and first = elem.second 3. Interval Arithmetic Check (if INTERVALARITH flag set): If SHAREDORG is set: Call slaboneco(node, p). If it returns true, jump to processnode. Call culliaco(node, p). If it returns true, break loop (no rays intersect this node). Else (not SHAREDORG): Call slabone(node, p). If it returns true, jump to processnode. Call cullia(node, p). If it returns true, break loop. 4. First Slab Intersection Check: If SHAREDORG is set: Call slabfirstco(node, p). If it returns false, break loop (no rays intersect this node). Else: Call slabfirst(node, p). If it returns false, break loop. 5. Process Node (processnode label): Get node flag: flag = node.getflag() If flag == NONLEAF: Get split axis and offset: python axis = node.getaxis() offset = node.getoffset() farindex = signs[axis] nearindex = farindex ^ 1 Push far child to stack: python stack[stacksz] = (node + offset + farindex, first) stacksz += 1 Move to near child: python node = node + offset + nearindex Continue loop (process near child) If flag == TRILEAF: Get triangle pointer: tris = node.getptr<waldtriangle>() Get triangle count: n = tris.num Initialize active array: active[first] = 1 (and other rays as needed, typically all 1 initially) Filter active rays within node's box: If SHAREDORG: slabfilterco(active, first, node, p) Else: slabfilter(active, first, node, p) Loop over triangles i from 0 to n-1: Call closest<flags>(tris[i], p, active, first, hit) If shadow ray variant: occnum += result If occnum == p.raynum: return immediately (all rays occluded) Break loop (leaf processed) If flag is neither NONLEAF nor TRILEAF (sub-BVH leaf): Get pointer to child intersector: node = node.getptr<intersector>().root Jump to processnode 6. Dispatch to Specialized Implementation: Initialize extra data: extra = initextra(p, hit) Switch on flags, calling closest<X>(bvhtree, p, extra, hit) for X in {0, 4, 8, 12}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unreachable code path if flags do not match 0, 4, 8, or 12. Handled by assert. Precision issues in slab intersection tests may cause rays to be incorrectly culled. Interval arithmetic flags help mitigate this. Stack overflow if BVH depth exceeds 64 levels. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot \log M) on average, where N is the number of rays in the packet and M is the number of nodes in the BVH. The packet size N provides parallelism, but traversal depth remains logarithmic. Memory Complexity: O(D) for stack depth D, where D is the BVH depth. Fixed stack size of 64 elements. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with packet size up to SIMD width (e.g., 4, 8, 16 rays). Beyond that, diminishing returns due to divergence in ray paths. Strengths: Reduced traversal overhead per ray due to packet processing; efficient culling using slab tests on the entire packet. Limitations: Divergence in ray paths within a packet can lead to wasted work; stack size limit may require dynamic stack for deep BVHs. When to Use: When rendering with many rays (e.g., primary rays, shadow rays) and hardware supports SIMD-like parallelism. When Not to Use: For very small packets (single ray) or highly divergent ray paths where overhead of packet management outweighs benefits. Origin: Implementation details from the mini.q engine. History and development: Part of the mini.q ray tracer's BVH traversal system, optimized for Wald-ordered BVHs. Where it is used: In the mini.q engine for rendering scenes with BVH-accelerated ray tracing. bsegovia/mini.q, https://github.com/bsegovia/mini.q, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical Longest Common Traversal Sequence
body: HLCTS is a hierarchical extension of the Single Longest Common Traversal Sequence (SLCTS) method. It matches traversal histories to create a common traversal history for multiple rays, allowing the incremental construction of common sequences. It sets itself apart from SLCTS by supporting the accumulation of coherence across more than two rays, enabling the reuse of traversal state for a growing group of rays rather than just a pair. Inputs: A set of rays with similar origins or directions; a previously constructed common traversal sequence (HLCTS). Outputs: An updated common traversal sequence that covers the new ray and the existing group. Data Structures: The HLCTS is represented as a sequence of traversal steps. Each step references a node in the acceleration structure (e.g., an octree or BSP tree). The sequence has a head and a tail. Steps: 1. Initial Pair Matching: Match the traversal histories of two rays, R1 and R2, to create the first common traversal history, HLCTS1 = HLCTS(R1, R2). This involves finding the longest common subsequence of nodes visited by both rays. 2. Incremental Extension: To add a new ray R3, match its traversal history against the existing HLCTS1 to construct HLCTS2. The traversal of R3 is compared against the sequence stored in HLCTS1. The result is a new common sequence that is a subsequence of both HLCTS1 and the history of R3. 3. Initial Leaf Handling: When constructing the initial leaf sequence for an HLCTS, the initial leaf nodes need not be matched against each other; they are simply copied into the common sequence. This optimization applies specifically to HLCTS. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def matchtraversalhistories(historya, historyb): """ Finds the longest common subsequence of traversal steps between two histories. Returns a new sequence containing the common steps in order. """ # Implementation details for LCS are not provided in the source. # This function returns the common nodes visited by both rays. pass def buildhlcts(raya, rayb): """ Creates the first HLCTS from two rays. """ historya = raya.gettraversalhistory() historyb = rayb.gettraversalhistory() # Match the two histories commonseq = matchtraversalhistories(historya, historyb) # Apply initial leaf optimization: copy initial leaves without matching # Assuming initial leaves are at the start of the history initialleavesa = getinitialleaves(historya) initialleavesb = getinitialleaves(historyb) # The source states initial leaf nodes are copied only, not matched. # We prepend the common initial leaves to the sequence. # Exact logic for merging initial leaves is not specified, # but they are included in the final HLCTS. commonseq.prepend(initialleavesa) # Or intersection/union as per specific impl return commonseq def extendhlcts(existinghlcts, newray): """ Extends an existing HLCTS with a new ray's traversal history. """ historynew = newray.gettraversalhistory() # Match the existing HLCTS (which is a sequence of nodes) # with the new ray's history. # Note: existinghlcts is a sequence, historynew is a sequence. updatedhlcts = matchtraversalhistories(existinghlcts, historynew) return updatedhlcts Parameters: Ray Similarity: The method assumes rays exhibit similarities in their traversal paths. Initial Leaf Copying: Initial leaf nodes are copied rather than matched. Edge Cases: Degenerate Rays: If rays have no common traversal steps, the common sequence may be empty or minimal. Precision: Not given in the sources. Definition: Application of LCTS (including HLCTS) to Hidden Surface Removal where rays exhibit similarities. Performance: The number of traversal steps decreases typically by more than 60%. Time devoted to ray shooting decreases typically by 20%. Comparison: The speedup achieved is scene and resolution dependent. When to choose: Use when rendering scenes with hidden surface removal where rays are spatially coherent (e.g., scanlines or patches). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In Hidden Surface Removal applications, traversal steps decrease by >60% and ray shooting time decreases by ~20%. Strengths: Reduces redundant traversal steps by exploiting coherence among multiple rays. Limitations: Speedup is dependent on scene content and resolution. Requires rays to exhibit similarities. When to use: When rendering with ray grids or patches where rays are similar. When not: When rays are highly divergent or incoherent. HLCTS was introduced by Vlastimil Havran and Jiří Bittner in their work on "LCTS: Ray Shooting using Longest Common Traversal Sequences". It is part of a broader concept of traversal coherence introduced in that work, which is not restricted to BSP trees only. The method builds upon SLCTS and is designed to handle larger groups of rays hierarchically. name: Traversal Order and Control Flow
body: Traversal Order and Control Flow defines the algorithmic strategies for navigating spatial hierarchies (such as octrees or BVHs) during volume rendering, determining the sequence in which nodes are visited and how transitions between cells are managed. It solves the problem of computational overhead in deep hierarchies by optimizing the descent and ascent paths, reducing redundant intersection tests, and enabling parallel optimizations like tile-sharing. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the control logic of the traversal (e.g., two-pass decoupling, iterative up-down transitions) rather than the specific spatial data structure or the shading model itself. The family operates on a rooted tree \mathcal{H} where each node N has a bounding volume (typically an AABB), pointers to children (if internal), and potentially a pointer to its parent. The core mechanism involves determining the next node to visit based on the ray R(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and the current node's position in the hierarchy. Key shared concepts include: 1. Intersection Testing: Standard ray-AABB intersection tests are used to determine if a ray enters a node's volume. 2. Transition Classification: Transitions between cells are classified based on whether they remain within the bounds of a common ancestor (internal) or leave it (external). 3. Depth Awareness: Many methods require knowledge of the tree's depth or the depth of the current node relative to the leaves to make traversal decisions. 4. State Maintenance: The traversal maintains state such as the current node, entry/exit distances, and potentially a stack or buffer of nodes to process. Two-Pass Hierarchy Traversal is an optimization that reduces computational cost by splitting the descent into a coarse first pass and a detailed second pass. It solves the problem of redundant intersection tests in deep hierarchies by extracting a coarse subtree in the first step and restarting traversal from that subtree in the second step. It sets itself apart from siblings like Iterative Up-Down Tree Traversal by explicitly decoupling the coarse culling phase from the fine traversal phase to enable tile-sharing optimizations for single scattering. See Two-Pass Hierarchy Traversal for algorithm details. Iterative Up-Down Tree Traversal is a hierarchical grid traversal algorithm for octrees that avoids restarting the search from the root node when transitioning between cells. It leverages the current node's position awareness to determine if the next cell is a sibling or child, and if not, it ascends the tree until an internal transition is found, then descends to the leaf. Unlike the standard top-down method which starts the search from the root node for every transition, this method uses local tree structure knowledge to minimize traversal distance, avoiding the overhead of root-to-leaf searches for non-internal transitions. See Iterative Up-Down Tree Traversal for algorithm details. An algorithm to cut a binary tree hierarchy along a certain condition using a breadth-first search (BFS) queue. The procedure initializes a queue with the root of the hierarchy \mathcal{H}. It dequeues nodes one by one; if a node satisfies the condition, it is added to a cut set. Otherwise, its children are enqueued. This allows for efficient pruning or modification of the hierarchy based on specific criteria during training or rendering setup. The specific variants cited here, such as Two-Pass Hierarchy Traversal and Iterative Up-Down Tree Traversal, are discussed in the context of large-scale reconstruction and rendering, particularly in relation to 3D Gaussian Splatting and hierarchical memory management. The BFS Hierarchy Cut algorithm is presented in the context of unified training and rendering for ultra-large scale reconstruction with external memory. These methods address the scalability challenges of rendering massive scenes by optimizing the traversal overhead associated with spatial hierarchies. head: Two-Step Hierarchy Traversal, Two-pass traversal
body: Two-Pass Hierarchy Traversal is an optimization for spatial hierarchy traversal that reduces computational cost by splitting the descent into a coarse first pass and a detailed second pass. It solves the problem of redundant intersection tests in deep hierarchies by extracting a coarse subtree in the first step and restarting traversal from that subtree in the second step. It sets itself apart from siblings like Iterative Up-Down Tree Traversal by explicitly decoupling the coarse culling phase from the fine traversal phase to enable tile-sharing optimizations for single scattering. The method operates on a rooted tree \mathcal{H} where each node N has a bounding volume (AABB) and pointers to children. The traversal is split into two distinct phases based on a configurable stopping depth. Input: Ray R(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, the root of the spatial hierarchy \mathcal{H}, and the stopping depth parameter D{stop} (measured relative to the leaves). Output: A list of leaf nodes intersected by the ray, or the traversal state required to process them. Hierarchy Node: Contains bounding box (AABB), children pointers, and leaf data. Subtree Buffer: A list or stack of nodes identified at the end of Step 1. Stopping Depth (D{stop}): The depth relative to the leaves where the first traversal stops. A value of D{stop}=3 means the first step stops 3 levels above the leaves, producing a set of subtrees of depth 3. 1. Coarse Subtree Extraction (Step 1): Start traversal from the root of \mathcal{H}. Perform standard ray-AABB intersection tests. Descend into children only if the ray intersects the node's bounding box. Termination Condition: Stop descending when the current node's depth relative to the leaves is equal to D{stop}. Collect all such nodes into a Subtree Buffer. These nodes form the roots of the coarse subtrees. 2. Fine Traversal (Step 2): For each node N{sub} in the Subtree Buffer: Restart traversal from N{sub} as the new root. Continue standard ray-AABB intersection tests down to the leaves. Process leaf nodes (e.g., for shading or scattering). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twopasshierarchytraversal(ray, rootnode, stoppingdepth): """ ray: Ray object with origin o and direction d rootnode: Root of the spatial hierarchy stoppingdepth: Integer, depth relative to leaves where pass 1 stops """ # Step 1: Extract coarse subtree subtreebuffer = [] stack = [(rootnode, 0)] # (node, currentdepthfromroot) # Note: To determine stopping condition relative to leaves, # the maxdepth of the tree must be known or precomputed. # Let maxdepth be the depth of the leaves. # Current depth from leaves = maxdepth - currentdepthfromroot while stack: node, depthfromroot = stack.pop() # Check intersection if not rayintersectsaabb(ray, node.bbox): continue # Calculate depth relative to leaves # Assuming maxdepth is available globally or passed in depthfromleaves = maxdepth - depthfromroot if depthfromleaves <= stoppingdepth: # Reached stopping depth, add to buffer for Step 2 subtreebuffer.append(node) else: # Continue descending in Step 1 for child in node.children: stack.append((child, depthfromroot + 1)) # Step 2: Traverse subtrees leafresults = [] for subroot in subtreebuffer: substack = [subroot] while substack: current = substack.pop() # Check intersection (redundant if Step 1 was perfect, but safe) if not rayintersectsaabb(ray, current.bbox): continue if current.isleaf: leafresults.append(current) else: for child in current.children: substack.append(child) return leafresults def rayintersectsaabb(ray, bbox): """Standard slab-based AABB intersection test.""" # Implementation details omitted as per shared principles # Returns True if ray intersects bbox pass Stopping Depth 0: If D{stop}=0, the first step descends through the entire hierarchy. The second step cost is null, and performance equals the direct implementation. Secondary Rays: Do not apply the tile-sharing optimization (sharing Step 1 results) to secondary rays (rays that have bounced at least once). Material Edges: Do not apply tile-sharing when the 2 \times 2 pixel block covers an edge of the material, as the subtree structure may differ significantly between adjacent pixels. In the context of point-based rendering for participating media, the "two-pass" concept extends to the rendering pipeline itself, not just hierarchy traversal. Step 1: Trace rays from the camera. Store rays that encounter translucent material, along with their start and end points, in an auxiliary buffer. Step 2: Process all rays in the buffer to compute single, double, and multiple scattering contributions, adding them to pixel values. Attenuation: After each bounce, compute attenuation from absorption and BRDF reflectance. Stop tracing when attenuation exceeds a threshold. Single Scattering Optimization: Gather single scattering contributions only over a material layer of thickness \ell (one mean-free-path), as it becomes negligible compared to multiple scattering after this distance. Multiple Scattering Optimization: Group neighboring rays using 4 \times 4 downsampling and interpolation, as multiple scattering effects are mostly low frequency. Auxiliary Buffer: Contains all paths through the material, including primary rays (from camera) and secondary rays (after bounces). Performance: Reduces traversal time by up to 30% when combined with tile sharing. The two-pass method alone provides a 15% reduction at optimal stopping depth. Overall, it provides a 20% performance improvement over naive hierarchy traversal. Optimal Stopping Depth: Best performance is achieved when the first step produces a set of trees of depth 3 (i.e., D{stop}=3). Scaling: The gain depends on the stopping depth. Stopping higher in the hierarchy reduces Step 1 cost but increases Step 2 cost. Strengths: Significant speedup for single scattering computations by discarding a large subset of the hierarchy before the second pass. Enables tile sharing for neighboring pixels. Limitations: Not beneficial for secondary rays or at material edges where tile sharing fails. Requires precomputation or knowledge of tree depth to determine stopping condition relative to leaves. Origin: Introduced in the GPU implementation of the point-based rendering algorithm for participating media. Paper: "Point-Based Rendering for Homogeneous Participating Media with Refractive Boundaries". Usage: Used in rendering homogeneous participating media with refractive boundaries, specifically for handling single and multiple scattering. name: Iterative Up-Down Tree Traversal
head: Iterative ascent-descent traversal, Up-Down method
body: Iterative Up-Down Tree Traversal is a hierarchical grid traversal algorithm for octrees that avoids restarting the search from the root node when transitioning between cells. It leverages the current node's position awareness to determine if the next cell is a sibling or child, and if not, it ascends the tree until an internal transition is found, then descends to the leaf. Unlike the standard top-down method which starts the search from the root node for every transition, this method uses local tree structure knowledge to minimize traversal distance, avoiding the overhead of root-to-leaf searches for non-internal transitions. Inputs: Ray R(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Hierarchical octree \mathcal{H} where each node N has a bounding volume (AABB), pointers to children (if internal), and a pointer to its parent. Current node N{curr} (initially the root or the leaf node from the previous ray step). Current entry distance t{entry} and exit distance t{exit} for N{curr}. Outputs: The leaf node N{leaf} intersected by the ray following the transition from N{curr}. Updated t{entry} and t{exit} for N{leaf}. Data Structures: Node structure: Contains AABB bounds, boolean isleaf, array of 8 child pointers (null if leaf), and parent pointer. Ray parameters: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, current interval [t{entry}, t{exit}]. Definitions: Internal Transition: A transition through a cell wall that does not leave the parent cell's bounds. External Transition: A transition through a cell wall that leaves the parent cell's bounds. Algorithm Steps: 1. Check Transition Type: Determine if the transition from N{curr} to the next cell is an internal transition. This is done by checking if the ray exits N{curr} through a face that is shared with a sibling node (i.e., the exit point is still within the parent's AABB). 2. Handle Internal Transition: If the transition is internal: Identify the next cell as one of the current node's siblings. If the sibling is not a leaf node, descend into its children to find the next leaf. Update N{curr} to this new leaf node. 3. Handle External Transition: If the transition is not internal (i.e., the ray leaves the parent's bounds): Ascent: Iteratively move up the tree starting from N{curr} (i.e., set N{curr} = N{curr}.parent) until the transition becomes an internal transition relative to the new current node. This means finding the lowest ancestor where the ray exit from the previous node was an internal transition relative to that ancestor. Descent: Once an internal transition is identified during the ascent, iteratively descend the tree from that node until a leaf node is reached. Update N{curr} to this new leaf node. 4. Process Leaf: Shade or scatter at the identified leaf node. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterativeupdowntraversal(ray, currentnode, tentry, texit): """ Traverses the octree from currentnode to the next leaf node along the ray. Returns the new leaf node and updated tentry, texit. """ node = currentnode while True: # Calculate intersection of ray with current node's AABB # Returns tenternode, texitnode relative to ray origin tin, tout = rayintersectsaabb(ray, node.aabb) # Determine the exit face of the current node exitface = getexitface(ray, node.aabb, tout) # Check if the transition is internal # An internal transition means the exit point is within the parent's bounds isinternal = False if node.parent is not None: # Check if the exit point from node is inside node.parent.aabb if pointinaabb(ray.origin + tout ray.direction, node.parent.aabb): isinternal = True if isinternal: # Internal transition: next node is a sibling or child of sibling sibling = getsibling(node, exitface) if sibling.isleaf: node = sibling break else: # Descend into the sibling's children node = sibling while not node.isleaf: # Find which child of node the ray enters next # This requires checking children's AABBs and tin child = getnextchild(ray, node, tout) node = child break else: # External transition: ascend the tree if node.parent is None: # Reached root and still external? Should not happen if ray is valid break node = node.parent # After moving up, we need to re-evaluate the transition # The "current" exit point is still tout from the previous step # But now we are looking at the parent. # The ascent continues until we find a node where the transition # from the previous node (which is now a child of this node) # was internal relative to this node. # However, the source says "iteratively go up... until the transition # is an internal transition". This implies we check the condition # at the new node level. # Re-check internal status relative to the new node's parent # If we are at root, we might need to restart or handle differently. # Assuming the tree structure allows finding an internal transition. # To implement the "until internal" loop correctly: # We need to check if the exit from the child (old node) was internal # to the parent (new node). # If yes, we break ascent and descend. # If no, we go up again. # Let's refine the loop condition based on: # "iteratively go up the tree starting from the current node until # the transition is an internal transition" # We need to track the previous node to check the transition type # relative to the current node. pass # See refined logic below # Refined Logic for Ascent/Descent # The source implies a single pass: go up until internal, then go down. node = currentnode prevnode = None while True: tin, tout = rayintersectsaabb(ray, node.aabb) exitpoint = ray.origin + tout ray.direction # Determine if transition from prevnode to node was internal # Actually, the source says: "if the path crosses a cell wall that # does not leave the parent cell". # So, when we are at node, we check if the exit from node # is inside node.parent. if node.parent is not None: if pointinaabb(exitpoint, node.parent.aabb): # Internal transition found # Now descend to find the next leaf sibling = getsibling(node, getexitface(ray, node.aabb, tout)) node = sibling while not node.isleaf: node = getnextchild(ray, node, tout) break else: # External transition, go up prevnode = node node = node.parent # If we hit root and it's still external, we might need to # restart from root or handle as a new ray segment. # For now, assume we find an internal transition. if node is None: break else: # Root node, no parent to check against. # If we are at root, we might just descend normally or # treat as internal if we came from a sibling? # The source doesn't specify root handling explicitly for ascent. # Assuming we descend from root if we are here. node = getnextchild(ray, node, tout) while not node.isleaf: node = getnextchild(ray, node, tout) break return node, tin, tout Parameters: Implementation complexity: High. Described as the most complex of the three presented methods in terms of implementation. Memory overhead: None. Additional computations: None. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Root Handling: The source does not specify behavior if the ascent reaches the root without finding an internal transition. In practice, this may require restarting the traversal from the root or treating the root's exit as a special case. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in pointinaabb checks may lead to incorrect classification of internal vs. external transitions. Epsilon comparisons should be used. Degenerate Input: Rays tangent to cell walls may cause ambiguous transition classifications. Robust intersection tests are required. Time Complexity: Depends on the tree depth and the number of ascents/descents. In the best case (internal transitions), it is O(1) per step (sibling lookup). In the worst case, it may require O(D) ascents and O(D) descents, where D is the tree depth. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory, as it uses the existing tree structure and pointers. Strengths: No memory overhead, no additional computations, applicable to regular and barycentric octree grids. Avoids the overhead of root-to-leaf searches for non-internal transitions. Limitations: High implementation complexity. When to use: When memory is constrained and implementation complexity is acceptable. Suitable for regular and barycentric octree grids. When not to use: When implementation simplicity is prioritized over traversal efficiency. Origin: The method is described in the context of Monte Carlo radiative transfer simulations using hierarchical octrees. History: It is presented as an alternative to the standard top-down method and a two-pass hierarchy traversal method. Usage: Used in 3D Monte Carlo radiative transfer simulations. name: Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal
head: GPU Voxel Renderer, OctreeSimple Shader, SVO Ray Tracing, SVO Traversal, Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) Traversal, Sparse Voxel Octree Tracing
body: Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) Ray Traversal is a GPU-based raycasting technique that renders volumetric data stored in a sparse voxel octree by traversing the tree structure along ray paths to find occupied cells. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large, sparse 3D models without the memory overhead of dense voxel grids or the topology complexity of polygon meshes. Unlike sibling methods such as Hierarchical Traversal which may assume in-core data or simpler traversal, SVO Ray Traversal explicitly manages a stack to control visitation order based on eye position, operating directly on the octree structure to skip empty space. It differs from GigaVoxels by not relying on a fixed-resolution texture-based cache, and from Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal (State Machine) by using a standard stack-based backtracking approach rather than a deterministic finite state machine. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin O, ray direction D, SVO data buffer, camera parameters (position, rotation, FOV, viewport size). Outputs: Color C, position P, and optionally normal N for the first occupied leaf node (voxel) hit by the ray. Data Structures: The SVO is stored in a flat array (e.g., std430 buffer or Texture3D). A common layout uses 32-bit integers: Internal Node: The integer contains a pointer to the first child node. In some layouts, bits indicate validity or leaf status. For example, uses bit 31 as a flag: 1 for internal, 0 for leaf. Bits 0-30 store the child address. Leaf Node (Voxel): The integer contains encoded data. store RGBA color in the lower bits (e.g., data[blocki] contains packed RGBA). uses bit 31 to distinguish type (0=Pointer, 1=Voxel) and bits 0-30 for attributes or pointers. Traversal Stack: Stores state for backtracking. defines a stack struct: python struct Stack { uint nodeaddress; uint frontalmask; float tmin; vec3 tcorner; }; uses a ParentElement struct with masks and childPointer. use parallel arrays for child, leaf, valid, corner, and octant. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Compute ray direction from screen coordinates (e.g., glFragCoord) and camera parameters. Handle zero direction components by clamping to epsilon (\epsilon) to avoid division by zero. Typical \epsilon \approx 10^{-4} or 3.55 \times 10^{-15}. If the camera is outside the root bounding box, compute the intersection t{entry} with the root box. If no intersection or t{entry} < 0, return background color. 2. Root Intersection: Compute ray-box intersection for the root node using the slab method: t{min} = \maxi \left( \frac{boxMini - Oi}{Di} \right), \quad t{max} = \mini \left( \frac{boxMaxi - Oi}{Di} \right) If t{min} > t{max}, the ray misses the root. Return background. 3. Traversal Loop: Initialize stack with root node. Set current node address, depth, and scale (root size). Determine the initial octant (child index 0-7) the ray enters. This is done by comparing the ray position to the node center or using direction signs to create a mask.: oct = 0; if (pos.x > corner.x + size/2) oct ^= 4; if (pos.y > corner.y + size/2) oct ^= 2; if (pos.z > corner.z + size/2) oct ^= 1; While stack is not empty (or depth < MAXDEPTH): 1. Fetch Node: Load node data from SVO[nodeaddress]. 2. Check Type: Leaf: If the node is a leaf (e.g., MSB is 0 in, or type bit is 1 in), sample the color/attributes and terminate the ray for this pixel. Internal: If the node is internal (e.g., MSB is 1 in), proceed to children. 3. Descend: Calculate the child address. use addressOf(child, leaf, valid, oct) which accounts for sparse children using bitmasks. uses value & 0x7FFFFFFFu. Push current state (address, mask, t{min}, corner) to stack. Update current node address to child address. Halve the scale (node size). Update the corner position: corner += scale octVec(oct). Recalculate the entry octant for the new child node. 4. Skip Empty Space (if not descending): If the current octant is invalid/empty, compute the exit distance t{exit} from the current child box. Advance ray position: position += direction texit. Pop from stack until a valid sibling or parent is found. If stack empty, ray has exited the SVO. Return background. 4. Normal Calculation (Optional): Normals can be calculated on-the-fly based on the ray exit face from the leaf voxel. Compute vector v = pos - boxPos. The dominant axis of v determines the normal direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. MAXDEPTH = 32 EPSILON = 1e-4 struct StackEntry: nodeaddress: uint frontalmask: uint tmin: float tcorner: vec3 def traceray(O: vec3, D: vec3, svodata: buffer, rootmin: vec3, rootmax: vec3): # 1. Ray Initialization D = clamp(D, -1.0, 1.0) # Normalize # Handle zero components D.x = EPSILON if abs(D.x) < EPSILON else D.x D.y = EPSILON if abs(D.y) < EPSILON else D.y D.z = EPSILON if abs(D.z) < EPSILON else D.z invD = 1.0 / D # 2. Root Intersection tmin = max((rootmin - O) invD) tmax = min((rootmax - O) invD) if tmin > tmax: return vec4(0.0) # Miss tmin = max(tmin, 0.0) O = O + D tmin # 3. Traversal State stack = arrayStackEntry depth = 0 nodeaddress = 0 # Root address scale = length(rootmax - rootmin) / 2.0 corner = rootmin frontalmask = 0 # Bitmask for direction # Determine initial octant # Simplified: check which half of the box the ray is in # This logic varies by implementation (see S3, S6, S10) oct = 0 if O.x > corner.x + scale: oct |= 4 if O.y > corner.y + scale: oct |= 2 if O.z > corner.z + scale: oct |= 1 while depth < MAXDEPTH: # Fetch Node nodeval = svodata[nodeaddress] # Check Leaf/Internal # Assuming MSB (bit 31) indicates Internal Node isinternal = (nodeval & 0x80000000u) != 0 if not isinternal: # Leaf Node: Return Color # Decode color from nodeval or pointer color = decodecolor(nodeval) return vec4(color, 1.0) # Internal Node: Descend # Push state stack[depth].nodeaddress = nodeaddress stack[depth].frontalmask = frontalmask stack[depth].tmin = tmin stack[depth].tcorner = corner depth += 1 # Get Child Address childaddress = nodeval & 0x7FFFFFFFu # Update State for Child scale = 0.5 corner += scale octVec(oct) # Recalculate Octant for new corner # Re-evaluate which sub-cube the ray origin is in relative to new corner newoct = 0 if O.x > corner.x + scale: newoct |= 4 if O.y > corner.y + scale: newoct |= 2 if O.z > corner.z + scale: newoct |= 1 oct = newoct nodeaddress = childaddress # Optimization: If child is empty/invalid, skip # This requires checking validity flags in the SVO layout # If invalid, compute exit t and pop stack # (Implementation detail varies, see S3, S6) return vec4(0.0) # Max depth reached or miss Compresses SVO by merging identical subtrees into a DAG, reducing memory usage while maintaining traversal speed. Extends SVO traversal with GPU caching and ray-guided streaming for out-of-core rendering of billions of voxels. Focuses on the specific routine to map continuous ray coordinates to discrete octree indices. Implements traversal as a deterministic finite state machine using fixed-point arithmetic, suitable for hardware/FPGA. Handles animated SVOs by updating a BVH of rigid octree parts per frame. General term for casting rays into SVOs, often used as a baseline comparison. Adds portal logic to allow rays to jump between disconnected spatial regions. A broader technique for AMR/sparse data, explicitly traversing the octree without grid projection. Time Complexity: O(\log N) on average for sparse data, where N is the number of voxels, but depends on tree depth and branching factor. In the worst case (dense or deep empty space), it can approach O(D) where D is the maximum depth. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the SVO structure, but significantly less than dense grids due to sparsity. DAG variants reduce this further. Performance: Real-time performance (e.g., 20 FPS at 720p) has been demonstrated on AMD 5700 for scenes with >1 billion voxels. Performance is heavily dependent on cache coherence and branch divergence in the shader. Strengths: Efficient memory usage for sparse data; implicit LOD; no polygon mesh overhead; supports complex volumetric data. Limitations: High memory overhead for very dense or deep trees; dynamic updates are expensive (may require full regeneration); stack depth limits (typically 23-32). When to Use: Large, sparse volumetric datasets; real-time rendering on GPU; scenes with high detail but low fill factor. When Not to Use: Dense volumetric data (use ray marching on 3D textures); highly dynamic data requiring frequent tree rebuilds; hardware with limited stack depth or no support for dynamic indexing. Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal originated from the need to render high-resolution volumetric data on GPUs. Key early work includes "Octree Textures on the GPU" in GPU Gems, which introduced the concept of storing octrees in 3D textures. The method has been implemented in various forms, including the mxbrt/svo renderer and Unity-based prototypes. It is often compared to or extended by DAG-based methods and caching systems like GigaVoxels. name: Sparse Voxel DAG Construction with Subtree Caching
head: DAG-based Voxel Grid Compression, Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) and DAG Compression, Subtree Merging Voxel Engine
body: Sparse Voxel DAG Construction with Subtree Caching is a method for compressing a 3D voxel grid into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) by detecting and merging identical subtrees, thereby reducing storage overhead while maintaining real-time decoding capability. It builds on Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal by replacing the explicit octree structure with a shared graph structure where identical spatial configurations are represented by a single node instance. This approach significantly reduces memory usage compared to standard Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) by eliminating redundant node allocations for repeated geometric patterns. The method converts a dense or sparse voxel grid into a DAG through recursive subdivision and subtree hashing. The core mechanism is the use of a cache to store and reuse nodes representing identical subtrees, ensuring that any two spatially identical regions in the voxel grid share the same node object in memory. Input: A 3D voxel grid byte[,,] voxelGrid of size (1 \ll \text{gridDepth}) \times (1 \ll \text{gridDepth}) \times (1 \ll \text{gridDepth}). Output: A root VoxelNode representing the DAG, and a subtreeCache dictionary mapping subtree keys to node instances. VoxelNode: IsLeaf (bool): True if the node represents a leaf voxel; False if it has children. Value (byte): 0 if empty, 1 if filled. Only valid if IsLeaf is true. Children (VoxelNode[8]): Array of 8 child nodes. Only valid if IsLeaf is false. Position (Vector3): World-space position of the voxel/cube center. Size (float): Side length of the voxel/cube. NodeColor (Color): Optional material property. subtreeCache: Dictionary<string, VoxelNode>: Maps a unique string key (hash of subtree content) to a VoxelNode instance. Used to detect and merge identical subtrees. 1. Initialization: Create a voxel grid of size (1 \ll \text{gridDepth})^3 and fill with geometry data. 2. Recursive Construction: Call BuildDAG(voxelGrid, gridDepth) to construct the DAG from the root. 3. Subtree Key Generation: For each recursive call, generate a unique key for the current grid subtree using GenerateSubtreeKey(grid). 4. Cache Lookup: Check if the key exists in subtreeCache. If TryGetValue returns true, return the existing VoxelNode to reuse it. 5. Leaf Detection: If depth == 0 or the grid is homogeneous (all voxels have the same value), create a new leaf node with IsLeaf=true and Value=grid[0,0,0]. 6. Non-Leaf Construction: If not a leaf, create a new non-leaf node with IsLeaf=false. Calculate newDepth = depth - 1 and size = 1 << newDepth. Iterate i from 0 to 7: extract octant using GetOctant(grid, i, size), recursively call BuildDAG(octant, newDepth), and assign result to node.Children[i]. Store the new node in subtreeCache with the key and return it. 7. LOD Generation: For Level of Detail (LOD) generation, downsample the grid by marking a voxel as containing geometry only if any of its composing voxels contain geometry. Unverified code. The concept of Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) was introduced to address the memory inefficiency of dense voxel grids. Kampe et al. realized that merging identical leaves could significantly compact the final level of an SVO. The extension to Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) by merging identical subtrees (not just leaves) further reduces memory usage.
