name: Animated Sparse Voxel Octrees (ASVO)
head: Animated Sparse Voxel Octree Renderer with X-Toon Shading, SVO renderer, XToonVolume
body: ASVO is a GPU-based raycasting method for rendering animated sparse voxel octrees (SVOs) using X-Toon shading. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering voxel-based characters and models that undergo rigid transformations or skinning by animating rigid octree parts via a keyframed skeleton and placing them in a per-frame top-level bounding volume hierarchy (BVH). Unlike static SVO renderers, ASVO dynamically updates the spatial acceleration structure every frame to account for bone-driven deformation, allowing for real-time animation of complex voxel models. The method consists of an octree builder, an animation system, a traversal kernel, and a shading/draw kernel. It is implemented using OpenGL 4.5 compute shaders. Inputs: Sparse Voxel Octree data including inner nodes, leaf nodes (visual data), and animation bone matrices. Scene data including camera position, view and projection matrices, light position, and texture maps (diffuse, illumination, normal, specular). Outputs: Color buffer containing the final rendered image. Depth buffer used for visibility culling. The implementation uses parallel arrays to store the octree and job queue. Inner Nodes (BFSInnerNode): mask: Bitmask indicating which of the 8 children are occupied. childPtr: Index offset to the first child in the inner node array. Leaf Nodes (VisualData): boneWeights: Array of 4 floats representing skinning weights. If boneWeights.x > 0, the leaf is skinned. boneIndex0-3: Indices of the 4 bones influencing this leaf. normal: Surface normal vector. pos: Packed position/size data (used for screen-space checks). tangent, texCoord, eyeVec, originalCenter: Additional visual data. Jobs (BFSJob): index: Index of the node in the inner node array. x, y, z: Subscript within the parent node (0-7). Animation Buffer: animation: Array of float4x4 matrices. Size is mframeCount mboneCount. 1. Octree Building (Pre-processing): Build the octree from Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) or raw volumes using a Morton-sorted, bottom-up approach. Prefilter colour and normal data during construction. Perform size checks on nodes. 2. Animation Update: Update the current animation frame based on elapsed time. Rigid octree parts are animated by a keyframed skeleton. Construct a per-frame top-level BVH containing the animated parts. 3. Traversal Kernel (Job Queue Processing): Each thread processes one job from a shared queue. Grid Cell Calculation: Calculate the dimensions of the voxel at the current octree level: gridCellDim = \frac{dimension}{2^{octreeLevel}} gridCellHalfDim = gridCellDim \times 0.5 Skinning Application: Compute the voxel center in world space. If the leaf node has bone weights (node.vd.boneWeights.x > 0), interpolate the center position using up to 4 bone transformations from the animation buffer based on boneIndex0-3 and boneWeights.x-w. Otherwise, use the original center. Dimension Adjustment: Resize the voxel half-dimension to counteract stretching during skinning: gridCellHalfDim \times= \min(2.0, \text{involvedBones}) Transformation to Clip Space: Transform the center and dimensions into clip space by multiplying by world, view, and projection matrices. Compute the eye vector: eyeVec = \text{normalize}(camPos - center) Culling: Perform frustum culling: The voxel is visible if its clip-space bounds are within [-1, 1]. Perform back-face culling: If the octree level is greater than 8, the voxel is visible only if: \text{dot}(node.vd.normal, eyeVec) \ge -0.4 Screen Projection and Queueing: Project the voxel center to screen coordinates (x, y) and compute depth: depth = center.z \times \text{INT\MAX} If the voxel has children (childCount != 0) and spans more than 1 pixel (dimVec.x > 1.0), add child jobs to the queue using atomicAdd on sharedTravQueuePtr. Otherwise, update the depth buffer: atomicMin(depthBuffer + index, depth) Visual Data Writing: If the voxel was drawn (w==1) and its depth matches the updated depth buffer value, write its visual data (normal, tangent, position, texCoord, eyeVec, originalCenter) to the voxelBuffer at the screen index. 4. Draw Kernel (Shading): For each pixel, scan a 3x3 neighborhood in the depth buffer to find the voxel with the minimum depth that covers the pixel. A voxel covers the pixel if: |vd.pos.x - 0.5 - x| \le vd.pos.z \quad \text{and} \quad |vd.pos.y - 0.5 - y| \le vd.pos.w Lighting: Transform the voxel center to light space. Check shadow mapping against shadowMap. Compute diffuse and specular lighting using textures for diffuse, illumination, normal, and specular maps. Update the color buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. INTMAX = 2147483647 def traversalkernel(jobqueue, innernodes, leaves, animation, worldmatrix, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, campos, depthbuffer, voxelbuffer, sharedtravqueueptr, dimension, octreelevel, dimvec, originalcenter, width): job = jobqueue.pop() node = innernodes[job.index] # Grid cell dimensions gridcelldim = dimension / (2.0 octreelevel) gridcellhalfdim = gridcelldim 0.5 # Get leaf visual data vd = leaves[job.index] # Skinning center = originalcenter if vd.boneweights[0] > 0.0: involvedbones = sum(1 for w in vd.boneweights if w > 0.0) # Interpolate center using up to 4 bone transformations center = (vd.boneweights[0] (animation[job.boneindex0] @ originalcenter) + vd.boneweights[1] (animation[job.boneindex1] @ originalcenter) + vd.boneweights[2] (animation[job.boneindex2] @ originalcenter) + vd.boneweights[3] (animation[job.boneindex3] @ originalcenter)) # Counteract stretching gridcellhalfdim = min(2.0, involvedbones) # Transform to clip space centerworld = center centerclip = projectionmatrix @ viewmatrix @ worldmatrix @ centerworld # Eye vector eyevec = normalize(campos - centerworld) # Culling if not isinfrustum(centerclip): return if octreelevel > 8: if dot(vd.normal, eyevec) < -0.4: return # Project to screen xscreen, yscreen = projecttoscreen(centerclip) depth = centerclip.z INTMAX # Check if leaf or has children childcount = bin(node.mask).count('1') if childcount != 0 and dimvec.x > 1.0: # Add children to queue for i in range(8): if (node.mask & (1 << i)) != 0: newjob = BFSJob(node.childptr + i, (job.x 2) + (i & 1), (job.y 2) + ((i & 2) >> 1), (job.z 2) + ((i & 4) >> 2)) atomicadd(sharedtravqueueptr, 1) jobqueue[atomicadd(sharedtravqueueptr, -1)] = newjob else: # Update depth buffer index = yscreen width + xscreen olddepth = atomicmin(depthbuffer[index], depth) # If we won the depth test (or it was the first write) if depth == depthbuffer[index]: # Write visual data voxelbuffer[index] = VisualData(vd.normal, vd.tangent, centerworld, vd.texcoord, eyevec, vd.originalcenter) def drawkernel(depthbuffer, voxelbuffer, shadowmap, diffusemap, illummap, specmap, normalmap, colorbuffer, width, height): x, y = getpixelcoordinates() # Scan 3x3 neighborhood for min depth mindepth = INTMAX bestvoxel = None for dy in range(-1, 2): for dx in range(-1, 2): idx = (y + dy) width + (x + dx) d = depthbuffer[idx] if d < mindepth: mindepth = d bestvoxel = voxelbuffer[idx] if bestvoxel is None: return # Check coverage if abs(bestvoxel.pos.x - 0.5 - x) <= bestvoxel.pos.z and abs(bestvoxel.pos.y - 0.5 - y) <= bestvoxel.pos.w: # Lighting lightspacepos = transformtolightspace(bestvoxel.originalcenter) shadow = checkshadowmapping(lightspacepos, shadowmap) diffuse = sampletexture(diffusemap, bestvoxel.texcoord) illum = sampletexture(illummap, bestvoxel.texcoord) spec = sampletexture(specmap, bestvoxel.texcoord) normal = sampletexture(normalmap, bestvoxel.texcoord) color = computediffusespecularlighting(normal, bestvoxel.eyevec, lightspacepos, shadow, diffuse, illum, spec) colorbuffer[x, y] = color Graphics API: OpenGL 4.5 compute shaders. Back-face Culling Threshold: dot(normal, eyeVec) >= -0.4 for levels > 8. Skinning Stretch Compensation: min(2.0, involvedBones). Divide by Zero: In the original 2016 shader, a divide by zero error occurred when r = 1 in the X-Toon log formula. This must be guarded against. Light Direction: The original shader incorrectly used the light position as a direction vector. It must be converted to a direction (light position - surface position). Negative Dot Product: Using pow on a negative n.v (normal dot view) caused issues. Ensure the base is non-negative or handle negative results appropriately. Unsigned Gradients: Ensure gradients are handled as signed values if required by the shading model, as unsigned gradients caused artifacts in the original version. GLREPEAT: Issues with GLREPEAT texture wrapping were present in the original shader and must be fixed. Time Complexity: The traversal follows a hierarchical DDA with pixel-footprint LOD. The traversal complexity depends on the depth of the octree and the number of visible voxels. The use of a job queue allows for parallel processing on the GPU. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for inner nodes, leaf nodes, animation matrices, and the per-frame BVH. The per-frame BVH allows for efficient culling of non-visible animated parts. Performance: The implementation includes unit tests for traversal and BVH against brute force, and a --compare mode that checks GPU output against the CPU renderer, ensuring correctness. Strengths: Efficiently handles animated voxel models using skinning and hierarchical culling. Limitations: The per-frame BVH construction adds overhead. The method is specific to OpenGL 4.5 compute shaders in the provided implementation. ASVO originated as a thesis project on animated sparse voxel octrees. The initial high-performance implementation used CUDA/C++ with an XNA/C# prototype for data structure and algorithm design. A later rebuild by Andre Rogers introduced an OpenGL 4.5 compute shader implementation with X-Toon shading, fixing several shader bugs from the original 2016 version. The method is demonstrated with scenes such as a crowd of walkers sharing limb octrees and a bonsai tree. Animates imported voxel scenes using keyed transforms (nTRN) and frame-by-frame model switching (nSHP). Tracks nTRN frame keys for transform animation (rotation and translation) and nSHP model keys for switching. Driven by a root VoxelAnimationPlayback3DComponent clock. Parameter: autoplay boolean in Model3DSource controls automatic playback start. name: Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Tracing
head: SVO Ray Tracing
body: Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) Ray Tracing casts rays from the camera into a world represented as a Sparse Voxel Octree to find the first occupied voxel or leaf node. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large, sparse volumetric datasets without the memory overhead of dense voxel grids. It differs from GigaVoxels by not relying on a fixed-resolution texture-based cache, and from Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal (State Machine) by explicitly managing a stack to control visitation order based on eye position, operating directly on the octree structure without an intermediate bounding volume hierarchy in its pure form. Inputs: SVO node/leaf data stored in GPU buffers, camera parameters (origin, direction, FOV, resolution), and world bounds. Outputs: Hit position, surface normal, traversal status, iteration count, and optionally accumulated color or depth. SVO nodes are stored in flat arrays, typically packed as u32 where the MSB indicates split/leaf status and lower bits store child indices or voxel IDs. Traversal uses a fixed-size stack (e.g., 16 ParentElement structs) containing position, scale, exit distance, node index, and child index for backtracking. Ray state tracks origin, direction, step size, and translation deltas. Hit results are packed into a struct containing status, iterations, position, normal, and voxel data. 1. Ray Generation: Unproject screen coordinates to normalized device coordinates, transform to eye space, and normalize to get world-space direction. 2. Initialization: Set rayPos to floor(rayOrigin), compute rayStep = sign(rayDir), maxTranslation for entry, and deltaTranslation = rayStep / rayDir. Initialize stack with root position and scale. 3. Slab Intersection & Stepping: Compute maxTranslation components. Find the minimum component to determine the next axis to step along. Update maxTranslation and rayPos using advance masks. 4. Node Lookup: Compute chunk coordinates from rayPos, calculate chunk index, and retrieve the root node for that chunk. Traverse down by checking split bits and computing child indices based on position relative to center. 5. Hit Detection: If the current node is a leaf or active at target depth, compute intersection depth with the voxel box using ray-AABB intersection. Set result position and status. 6. Backtracking: If the node is empty or the ray exits the current box, pop the stack, update root position/scale, and continue traversal. 7. Termination: Return on hit, when maxIterations is reached, or when rayPos exceeds world bounds. rayStep = sign(rayDir) maxTranslation = (((0.5 + rayPos) + 0.5 rayStep) - rayOrigin) / rayDir deltaTranslation = rayStep / rayDir rayAdvanceMask = maxTranslation.xyz <= min(maxTranslation.yzx, maxTranslation.zxy) Voxel size at level: q = 1 / (2^level) Pixel error metric: AD2 = q^2 rayScale2, where rayScale2 = 1/(2tan(FOV/2))^2 mRootRadius: Default root radius of the SVO, typically 256.0f. MAXIMUMTREEDEPTH: Maximum depth of the octree, set to 30. MAXSTEPS: Maximum march steps per ray, set to 200. smax: Constant representing maximum scale (float mantissa bits), set to 23. EPS: Epsilon for boundary precision, set to 0.0004. Zero Direction Components: Division by zero occurs if rayDir has a zero component. Clamp near-zero components to 1e-4f or handle via epsilon guards. Boundary Precision: Floating-point errors on voxel boundaries cause incorrect traversal. Nudge ray origin forward by EPS or 0.001 dir to avoid self-intersection. NaN/Inf Handling: If intermediate calculations produce NaN or Inf, coalesce to fposinf and reject null hits. Stack Depth: Deep trees require careful stack management; fixed-size stacks (e.g., 16 elements) may overflow without iterative fallback or loop limits. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tracesvoray(rayorigin, raydirection, maxiterations, worldbounds, getnodeatpos): # Guard against zero direction components EPS = 1e-4 raydirection = vec3( raydirection.x if abs(raydirection.x) > EPS else sign(raydirection.x) EPS, raydirection.y if abs(raydirection.y) > EPS else sign(raydirection.y) EPS, raydirection.z if abs(raydirection.z) > EPS else sign(raydirection.z) EPS) # Initialize traversal state raypos = floor(rayorigin) raystep = sign(raydirection) maxtranslation = (((0.5 + raypos) + 0.5 raystep) - rayorigin) / raydirection deltatranslation = raystep / raydirection stack = [] stackindex = 0 rootpos = vec3(0.0) rootscale = 256.0 # mRootRadius for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Check bounds if not isinsideworld(raypos, worldbounds): return {"status": 3, "iterations": iteration, "position": rayorigin} # Check if octant/voxel is present if getnodeatpos(raypos): # Compute intersection depth with voxel box intersectiondepth = rayboxintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, raypos, raypos + vec3(1.0)) return { "status": 1, "iterations": iteration, "position": rayorigin + raydirection intersectiondepth } # Determine next axis to step along rayadvancemask = maxtranslation.xyz <= min(maxtranslation.yzx, maxtranslation.zxy) maxtranslation = maxtranslation + vec3(rayadvancemask) deltatranslation raypos = raypos + vec3(i32(rayadvancemask)) raystep # Loop completed without hit intersectiondepth = rayboxintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, raypos, raypos + vec3(1.0)) return {"status": 0, "iterations": maxiterations, "position": rayorigin + raydirection intersectiondepth} SVO Ray Marching with Stack-Based Navigation is a ray traversal algorithm for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO) that uses an explicit stack to manage traversal state, enabling efficient navigation through the hierarchical structure to find voxel intersections. It differs from parent methods by decoupling the traversal logic from the ray's parametric distance, using a fixed-point-like scale representation to step through the tree levels, and explicitly managing node validity and corner positions via a stack of nodeinfot elements. This approach allows for robust handling of empty space and early termination based on pixel error thresholds. This method traces rays against a GPU-accessible octree to find the closest intersections with active voxels. It tracks both the nearest active leaf node and the nearest empty space node to support hover interactions. It differs from standard SVO ray tracing [2989-sparse-voxel-octree-ray-tracing.md] by prioritizing closest-hit detection and empty-space fallback for interaction rather than full volume integration. This method performs volume rendering on a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) by traversing the tree structure and sampling data stored in "bricks" (small, fixed-size blocks of voxels) rather than individual leaf voxels. It solves the problem of inefficient memory access and cache thrashing in large-volume rendering by grouping data into bricks, which improves texture cache utilization and reduces traversal overhead compared to single-voxel stepping. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like SVO Ray Marching with Stack-Based Navigation by explicitly handling interpolation between bricks of different resolutions and using early termination based on accumulated opacity to skip empty space, whereas Octree Voxel Raycasting for Hover (Closest Active Voxel) focuses on finding the nearest surface rather than full volume integration. SVO Walk is a depth-first traversal algorithm for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO) that visits nodes in an order determined by the eye position, invoking a callback for each visited node. It differs from pure SVO traversal by explicitly managing a stack to control visitation order based on eye position, and from BVH-based approaches by operating directly on the octree structure without an intermediate bounding volume hierarchy. A rendering method that ray-casts directly against a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) using distance fields to render isosurfaces, avoiding conversion to polygonal geometry. It uses a hybrid octree structure: an octree down to a certain level, then bricks of voxels for the final levels. Unlike Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Tracing which may store down to individual voxel level, this method stores bricks of voxels at the bottom levels, which is more scalable for planetary scales and better suited for GPU application. Time Complexity: Depends on the depth of the tree and the number of nodes visited per ray. In the worst case (dense scene), it is proportional to the number of voxels; in sparse scenes, it is logarithmic with respect to the resolution. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of nodes and leaves in the SVO. The implementation uses parallel arrays, requiring storage for node descriptors, child indices, and leaf data. Performance: The provided implementation uses a GPU-side rendering phase with a single draw call for a fullscreen triangle, avoiding per-chunk draw calls. Measured performance scales with traversal depth and hit density. Strengths: Efficient for sparse data; no need for dense texture memory; flexible resolution; enables real-time path tracing. Limitations: Construction can be slow for very large datasets if not optimized; stack depth can be an issue for deep trees if not managed carefully; precision issues require epsilon nudging. The method originates from GPU-based voxel raymarching implementations, specifically the jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, MasonFeurer/VoxelRayTracing, and Onlinerocker/SVO repositories. name: SVO Ray Marching with Stack-Based Navigation
head: SVO Ray March, SVO Ray Marcher, Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Tracing
body: SVO Ray Marching with Stack-Based Navigation is a ray traversal algorithm for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO) that uses an explicit stack to manage traversal state, enabling efficient navigation through the hierarchical structure to find voxel intersections. It differs from parent methods by decoupling the traversal logic from the ray's parametric distance, using a fixed-point-like scale representation to step through the tree levels, and explicitly managing node validity and corner positions via a stack of nodeinfot elements. This approach allows for robust handling of empty space and early termination based on pixel error thresholds. Inputs: raypos: The origin of the ray (\mathbf{p}). raydir: The direction of the ray (\mathbf{d}), normalized. svotree: The Sparse Voxel Octree data structure. minraylength2: A minimum ray length constant added to the calculated distance. rayScale2: A parameter related to ray step size or resolution, used for pixel error calculation. Outputs: outt: The distance to the hit voxel along the ray. outnormal: The normal of the hit voxel face. bool: True if a hit was found, false otherwise. The algorithm relies on a stack to store traversal state. nodeinfot parent: Index or pointer to the parent node in the SVO. corner: A 3-bit integer (or equivalent) representing the corner of the current node within its parent. lower: A 3D vector (\mathbb{R}^3) representing the absolute lower bound of the current node in world space. Stack A dynamic array or linked list of nodeinfot elements. Operations: push, pop, back (access top element), size (get current depth). rayScale2: Used in svovoxelpixelerror to determine the threshold for pixel error. minraylength2: A minimum ray length constant added to the calculated distance. 1. Initialization: Initialize an empty stack stack. Determine the root node of the SVO. Calculate the initial lower bound for the root node (typically the origin of the SVO space). Push the root node onto the stack. Set rayisoutside = false. 2. Traversal Loop: While stack.size > 0: Let level = stack.size. Calculate scale = 1.0 / (1 << level). Let current = stack.back(). Determine node validity: Check if the node is null using svotreeisnull. Check if the node is a leaf using svotreeisleaff3. Check if the node has children using svotreehaschildren. Check if the node contains a voxel using svotreevoxelexists. If rayisoutside is true: Pop the stack: svostackpop(&stack). If the stack is empty, break and return false. Retrieve the new current from stack.back(). Adjust lower: lower -= cornerincrement0 scale, where cornerincrement0 is the unit vector corresponding to the popped node's corner. Attempt to move to the next corner in the outface direction: nextcorner1 = movecorner(current.corner, outface). If nextcorner1 is valid: Set rayisoutside = false. Update current.parent and current.corner to the popped node's parent and nextcorner1. Adjust lower: lower -= cornerincrement0 scale; lower += cornerincrement1 scale, where cornerincrement1 corresponds to nextcorner1. Continue to the next iteration. If nextcorner1 is invalid (boundary of parent): Set rayisoutside = true. Continue to the next iteration (loop will pop again). If the current node has a voxel (svotreevoxelexists) and the ray intersects the voxel data (svointersectsvoxeldataf3): Calculate direction bounds: dirbounds = svocalculatedirboundsf3(lower, lower + scale, raydir). Check for pixel error: error = svovoxelpixelerror(sdistancef3(raypos, dirlower), rayScale2, level). If error < threshold: Record hit distance: outt = minraylength2 + sdistancef3(raypos, dirlower). Compute normal from the opposite face of outface. Return true. If the node is a leaf (svotreeisleaff3): Record hit distance and normal. Return true. If the node has children (svotreehaschildren): Push the current node onto the stack: svostackpush(&stack, &current). Calculate the next corner for the child node: nextcorner = svopushcalculatenextcornerf3(cubenormalizeddir, dirlower, scale, t1). Update lower for the child node: nextlower = lower + (cornerincrement childscale), where childscale = 1.0 / (1 << (level + 1)). Get the child node descriptor: current = svotreegetchild(addressspace, current, nextcorner). Update lower = nextlower. Continue to the next iteration. 3. Termination: If the stack is empty and no hit was found, return false. Unverified code. level = len(stack) scale = 1.0 / (1 << level) current = stack[-1] isnull = svotreeisnull(svotree, current) isleaf = svotreeisleaff3(svotree, current) haschildren = svotreehaschildren(svotree, current) hasvoxel = svotreevoxelexists(svotree, current) if rayisoutside: stack.pop() if len(stack) == 0: return False, None, None current = stack[-1] cornerincrement0 = getcornerunitvector(current.corner) current.lower -= cornerincrement0 scale outface = getoutface(raydir, current.corner) nextcorner1 = movecorner(current.corner, outface) if nextcorner1 is not None: rayisoutside = False current.corner = nextcorner1 cornerincrement1 = getcornerunitvector(nextcorner1) current.lower -= cornerincrement0 scale current.lower += cornerincrement1 scale continue else: rayisoutside = True continue if hasvoxel rayScale2, level) if error < threshold: outt = minraylength2 + sdistancef3(raypos, dirbounds.dirlower) outnormal = computenormalfromface(oppositeface(outface)) return True, outt, outnormal if isleaf: outt = minraylength2 + sdistancef3(raypos, dirbounds.dirlower) outnormal = computenormalfromface(oppositeface(outface)) return True, outt, outnormal if haschildren: stack.append(current) nextcorner = svopushcalculatenextcornerf3(cubenormalizeddir, dirbounds.dirlower, scale, t1) childscale = 1.0 / (1 << (level + 1)) nextlower = current.lower + (cornerincrement childscale) current = name: Octree Voxel Raycasting for Hover (Closest Active Voxel)
head: Octree Closest Hit Tracing
body: This method traces rays against a GPU-accessible octree to find the closest intersections with active voxels. It tracks both the nearest active leaf node and the nearest empty space node to support hover interactions. It differs from standard SVO ray tracing [2989-sparse-voxel-octree-ray-tracing.md] by prioritizing closest-hit detection and empty-space fallback for interaction rather than full volume integration. Inputs: rays (GPU buffer of Ray structs, size resolution resolution), octree (GPU-accessible sparse voxel octree), resolution (grid width and height). Outputs: hits (GPU buffer of Hit structs, size resolution resolution), hosthits (host std::vector<Hit> of size resolution resolution for downloaded results). Data Structures: Ray: Origin and direction vectors. Hit: Intersection results including distance, position, and normal. OctreeNode: isLeaf (bool), isActive (bool), position (vec3), size (vec3), color (vec3), children (array of 8 pointers). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traceclosestkernel(rays, hits, octree, resolution, currentdepth): for idx in range(resolution resolution): ray = rays[idx] closesthitdistance = float('inf') closestemptydistance = float('inf') foundactivevoxel = False hoverinfo = {"hashit": False, "node": None, "distance": float('inf'), "position": None, "normal": None} node = octree.root depth = 0 while node is not None: hitdistance, hitposition, hitnormal = computeintersection(ray, node) if hitdistance < float('inf'): if node.isActive and node.isLeaf: if hitdistance < closesthitdistance: closesthitdistance = hitdistance foundactivevoxel = True hits[idx].distance = closesthitdistance hits[idx].position = hitposition hits[idx].normal = hitnormal elif not foundactivevoxel and depth >= currentdepth and hitdistance < closestemptydistance: closestemptydistance = hitdistance hoverinfo["hashit"] = True hoverinfo["node"] = node hoverinfo["distance"] = closestemptydistance hoverinfo["position"] = hitposition hoverinfo["normal"] = hitnormal # Advance traversal logic node = getnextnode(node, ray, depth) depth += 1 hits[idx].hoverinfo = hoverinfo Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Reset closestHitDistance to infinity, closestEmptyDistance to infinity, and foundActiveVoxel to false when depth == 1. Reset hoverInfo.hasHit to false. 2. Dispatch: Call octree->traceclosest(rays->data(), hits->data(), resolution, resolution) on the GPU. 3. Traversal: For each ray, traverse the octree. If an active leaf is intersected, update closestHitDistance and record the hit. If an empty/internal node is intersected and !foundActiveVoxel and depth >= currentDepth and hitDistance < closestEmptyDistance, compute position and normal, update hoverInfo to point to the empty space node, set closestEmptyDistance = hitDistance, and set hoverInfo.hasHit = true. 4. Download: Transfer hits to host memory via hits->download(hosthits.data()). Parameters: resolution: Width and height of the ray grid. currentDepth: Maximum traversal depth limit. Edge Cases: No Hit: If no active voxel is intersected, foundActiveVoxel remains false and hoverInfo.hasHit indicates empty-space fallback. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for distance thresholds may require epsilon guards. Boundaries: Ray origins exactly on node boundaries require consistent half-open interval handling. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where N is the number of rays (W \times H) and D is the average octree traversal depth. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the rays and hits GPU buffers. Strengths: Parallel GPU execution efficiently resolves closest-hit queries for interaction. Limitations: Requires host-device synchronization for result downloads and GPU memory allocation. When to Use: Hover interactions, picking, or closest-hit queries in SVO-based renderers. When Not to Use: Full volume integration, ray marching with accumulation, or CPU-only pipelines. The method originates from GPU-based voxelization pipelines that dispatch ray tracing tasks via a stream and thread pool architecture. It builds on Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Tracing by specializing the traversal for closest active voxel detection and empty-space hover feedback. name: Octree Ray Marching with Brick Interpolation and Early Termination
head: GigaVoxels Ray Marching, Brick-Based Octree Traversal
body: This method performs volume rendering by traversing a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) organized into fixed-size cubic "bricks" stored in 3D textures. It solves the problem of inefficient memory access and cache thrashing during ray traversal by combining coarse space-skipping (via brick-level occupancy) with fine-grained interpolation at brick boundaries. Unlike standard SVO traversal which steps voxel-by-voxel or node-by-node, this approach interpolates values across brick borders to maintain visual continuity while minimizing texture fetches. It differs from Two-staged Space-Skipping with Bricking and Octrees by using a fragment shader for post-interpolative RGB\alpha lookup rather than pre-computed textures, and from Stackless GPU Raycasting with Octree Traversal by maintaining an explicit node stack for out-of-core management. Inputs: Ray origin (O), ray direction (D), volume bounding box (VolExtentMin, VolExtentMax), root octree node pointer, brick dimensions (brickDimX, brickDimY, brickDimZ), brick border sizes (brickBorderX, brickBorderY, brickBorderZ), projected voxel size (projVoxelSize), parent voxel size (parentVoxelSize), and texture samplers for the octree structure and brick data (colors/gradients). Outputs: Final color and opacity for the pixel. Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains a pointer to child nodes or a brick. Stores occupancy status. Brick: A fixed-size cubic block of voxels (e.g., 8^3 or 16^3). Stored in a 3D texture. Includes a border region for interpolation. Node Usage List: A circular buffer tracking recently traversed nodes to optimize memory management (pushing nodes to GPU). Parameters: k\ChildNodeSizeScalar: Scalar multiplier for node size on descent (typically 0.5 for octrees). MaxNodesToPushThisFrame: Max nodes added to usage list per frame. maxNodesPerPixelBlock: Threshold for resetting traversal counters. Interpolation threshold: 0.001f. Early termination opacity threshold: 0.995. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set octTreeNode to root. Set extents to VolExtentMin/Max. Set nodeSize to 1.0f (or root voxel size). Set voxelHalfSize to RootVoxelHalfSize. Reset traversal counters: traversalCount = 0, nodeListTraversalCount = 0, pushedNodeCount = 0. 2. Ray Containment Test: Compute test1 = sign(O - VolExtentMin). Compute test2 = sign(VolExtentMax - O). Compute inside = dot(test1, test2). If inside < 0, the ray origin is outside; handle accordingly (e.g., skip or compute entry). 3. Traversal Loop: Increment traversalCount and nodeListTraversalCount. If nodeListTraversalCount \ge maxNodesPerPixelBlock, reset nodeListTraversalCount to 0. Node Management: If nodeListTraversalCount is within startPushingNodes, stopPushingNodes) and pushedNodeCount < MaxNodesToPushThisFrame, increment pushedNodeCount and call AddToNodeUsageList(octTreeNode). 4. Descent and Brick Handling: Check Interpolation Condition: Calculate interpolationFactor. If projVoxelSize > parentVoxelSize and curDepth \neq 0 and interpolationFactor > 0.001f, enable interpolation. Pitfall: Interpolation is disabled at curDepth == 0 (root) to prevent invalid ratios when parentVoxelSize == projVoxelSize. Traverse: If interpolation is enabled, compute prevBrickRayPos and call TraverseBrickInterp. Otherwise, call TraverseBrick. Inside TraverseBrick/TraverseBrickInterp: Compute brick offset: brickOffset = rayBrickPosition \times k\TreeN (where k\TreeN is likely the number of children or a stride factor, context implies mapping to child index). Clamp to child offset: childOffset = clamp(uvec3(brickOffset), 0u, 1u). Update ray position within brick: rayBrickPosition = brickOffset - vec3(childOffset). Update extents: nodeExtentMin += (vec3(childOffset) \times nodeSize) nodeExtentMax -= ((vec3(1.0f) - vec3(childOffset)) \times nodeSize). Fetch next node: octTreeNode = texelFetch(OctTreeSampler, octTreeNodePtr, 0). Update sizes: nodeSize = k\ChildNodeSizeScalar, voxelHalfSize = k\ChildNodeSizeScalar. 5. [Ray Marching within Brick: Sample the brick texture at the current ray position. If interpolation is active, blend values from adjacent bricks or border regions based on interpolationFactor. Accumulate color and opacity using volume rendering integral approximation (e.g., standard front-to-back compositing). 6. Early Termination: Check if accumulated opacity > 0.995. Pitfall: Termination only triggers if the current step actually traversed a brick or constant value, preventing premature cutoff during initialization or empty space traversal. If terminated, return accumulated color. 7. Loop Continuation: If not terminated and ray is within volume, continue to next node/brick. If ray exits volume or node is leaf/empty, handle backtracking or termination. Pseudocode: Unverified code. If node is empty or ray exited, break or backtrack # Update parent voxel size for next level interpolation calc parentvoxelsize = projvoxelsize projvoxelsize = 0.5 # Assuming uniform subdivision return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity def traversebrick(node, origin, direction, brickdim, brickborder, colorsampler, gradsampler, acccolor, accopacity, transmittance): # Sample current brick and neighbor/bricks # Blend based on interpfactor # Update acccolor, accopacity, transmittance # Advance ray pass This method balances GPU bottlenecks by dividing space-skipping into two stages: coarse division using bricking to address bus and texture cache limitations, and fine division using octrees within bricks to address the rasterization bottleneck. It differs from Tong et al.'s bricking technique by storing unmodified scalar values in textures and using a fragment shader for post-interpolative RGB\alpha lookup, avoiding time-consuming texture regeneration when the transfer function changes. Choose this when transfer functions change frequently and texture cache performance is critical. This method performs scalable, out-of-core volume rendering on the GPU by decomposing volumetric data into small cubical bricks organized in an octree structure. It differs from its parent by explicitly managing an out-of-core working set and using a 3D texture spatial index to enable stackless traversal without maintaining a node stack in shader memory. It differs from its sibling by integrating the spatial index construction and neighbor pointer encoding directly into the fragment shader's traversal loop, allowing for on-the-fly bounding box computation. The method solves the problem of rendering very large datasets that exceed GPU texture memory by asynchronously fetching a view-dependent working set of bricks. Choose this for datasets larger than GPU memory. Accelerates rendering by using sparse octrees to store caches, enabling raytracing to skip empty space and terminate rays missing the object. It converts density cache to a signed distance function (SDF) by thresholding at 0.0, optionally downsamples the SDF, generates a collision mesh using marching cubes, and traces rays against the BVH of the mesh to find occupied voxels and skip empty space. For rays hitting occupied voxels, it integrates volume using cached components. It uses BVH/ray-triangle intersection instead of hierarchical DDA to leverage hardware acceleration, allow easy mesh deformation/downsampling, and enable compositing of fake shadows/bouncelight. Cache resolution for NeRF Synthetic 360 is 1024^3 (except ship: 768^3) with 8 components; for LLFF it is 768^3 with 6 components. Volume rendering via ray-casting that traverses the octree hierarchy to skip empty space and march rays near the surface. It uses multi-resolution interpolation to handle variable resolution blocks at boundaries. Steps include: traversing hierarchy to skip empty space and advance ray close to surface, marching ray in steps proportional to distance from zero-crossing in proximity of surface, sampling SDF field via tri-linear interpolation at each step, and computing accurate 3D surface position when ray transitions from positive to negative space. Uses octree to avoid querying empty/occluded voxels. Stops ray when accumulated transmittance is below threshold \taut (set to 0.01). If alpha value of interval after decoding density is below \taut, it does not evaluate color decoder. Storage includes indices and values for features of occupied voxels, binary occupancy mask, and weights for density and color decoders, with parameters stored in half precision. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of visible voxels, but significantly reduced by space-skipping. Brick interpolation reduces the number of texture fetches compared to voxel-by-voxel traversal. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of bricks loaded into GPU memory. The node usage list and brick pool manage memory efficiently, but large scenes may require out-of-core techniques (see Stackless GPU Raycasting with Octree Traversal). Measured Performance: GigaVoxels/GigaVoxelsBrickPool implementation shows efficient memory bandwidth usage due to brick-based texture access. FastNeRF using sparse octrees achieves significant speedups over non-cached methods by reducing grid look-ups, which are expensive on GPU RAM. Strengths: Efficient memory access patterns due to brick coherency; reduced texture cache misses; smooth interpolation at boundaries; early termination improves performance for opaque objects. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of brick structures; interpolation adds complexity; out-of-core management is non-trivial; early termination can cause artifacts if not carefully implemented (e.g., premature cutoff). When to use: Real-time volume rendering of large, sparse datasets where memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. When not to use: Dense volumes where space-skipping provides little benefit; scenes requiring frequent transfer function updates where pre-computed brick textures would need regeneration (though this method mitigates that with fragment shader lookup). The method originates from the GigaVoxels project, which introduced bricking techniques to optimize volume rendering on GPUs. The specific combination of octree traversal, brick interpolation, and early termination is detailed in the VoxViz thesis by Apecoraro. It builds on earlier SVO traversal methods. Variants like FastNeRF apply similar sparse octree concepts to neural radiance fields, using BVH acceleration for mesh-based skipping. Multi-resolution rendering approaches use octrees for adaptive resolution. name: Two-staged Space-Skipping with Bricking and Octrees
head: Bricking with octree refinement, Two-stage space-skipping
body: This method balances GPU bottlenecks by dividing space-skipping into two stages: coarse division using bricking to address bus and texture cache limitations, and fine division using octrees within bricks to address the rasterization bottleneck. It differs from Tong et al.'s bricking technique by storing unmodified scalar values in textures and using a fragment shader for post-interpolative RGB\alpha lookup, avoiding time-consuming texture regeneration when the transfer function changes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar voxel volume dataset; a transfer function mapping scalars to optical properties (RGB\alpha); rendering parameters (brick size b, overlap n, interpolation kernel). Output: A rendered image. Data Structures: 1. Bricks: 3D textures containing unmodified scalar voxel values. Layout: Cubic blocks of size b \times b \times b voxels. Overlap: Adjacent bricks overlap by n voxels in every direction to support interpolation. Memory Overhead: Approximately (3 \cdot n / b) \cdot 100\%. 2. Octrees: Hierarchical structures stored within each brick. Purpose: To skip empty regions at a finer granularity than the brick level. Content: Not explicitly defined in sources, but implied to mark empty/occupied sub-volumes within the brick. Parameters: Brick Size (b): Must be equal to or smaller than the available texture memory size to handle datasets exceeding texture memory. Overlap (n): Depends on the interpolation kernel: Nearest neighbor: n = 0. Trilinear interpolation: n = 1 voxel in every direction. Pre-integrated rendering or on-the-fly gradient calculation: n increased by another voxel in every direction (i.e., n=2 for trilinear with gradients). Texture Format: 3D textures. Many graphics cards require 3D texture sizes to be powers of 2 in every direction. If volume dimensions do not divide evenly, add partially empty bricks or use smaller rest-bricks. Steps: 1. Brick Generation: Divide the volume dataset into chunks called bricks. Ensure adjacent bricks overlap by n voxels. Store unmodified scalar voxel values in these bricks. 2. Octree Construction: For each brick, construct an octree to represent the occupancy of its internal voxels. 3. Memory Management: Load bricks sequentially from main memory into texture memory. If the total data exceeds available texture memory, swap bricks between main and texture memory as needed. 4. Ray Traversal (Stage 1 - Coarse): Traverse the brick structure. Skip entire bricks that are empty or do not intersect the view frustum. This addresses bus and texture cache bottlenecks. 5. Ray Traversal (Stage 2 - Fine): For each active brick, traverse the internal octree. Skip empty sub-volumes within the brick. This addresses the rasterization bottleneck by reducing the number of fragment shader invocations. 6. Early Ray Termination: Apply early ray termination within each brick to alleviate fragment shader load, particularly beneficial for highly-filled datasets. 7. Shading: For each sampled voxel, use a fragment shader program to lookup RGB\alpha values post-interpolatively based on the current transfer function and the scalar value. This allows fast runtime changes to the transfer function without regenerating textures. Pseudocode: Unverified code. alphain) # alphaout = alphain + alphanew (1 - alphain) pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Triangle Throughput Bottleneck: Space-skipping techniques may increase the amount of triangles considerably. name: Quaternary Tree Volume Traversal
head: CPU-GPU Split Volume Rendering, Tile-based Ray Casting
body: Quaternary Tree Volume Traversal is a two-stage rasterization process distributed between a central processor and a graphics processing unit. The CPU divides object space using a quaternary tree to find intersections, and the GPU performs ray casting and shading. Inputs: An implicit function defining the object surface. Camera parameters, with the GPU ray direction fixed along the Z-axis. A target tile size parameter that terminates the CPU subdivision. Outputs: A rendered image with smooth shading and lighting. Z-coordinates and surface normals for each pixel. Data Structures: Quaternary Tree: Each node represents a square region in the XY plane and branches into four children corresponding to the quadrants of the parent region. Fragment List: A list of geometric primitives generated by the CPU, containing the bounding boxes of tiles where the object intersects the volume. Algorithm Steps: 1. CPU: Divide the current cube region into four equal parts in the XY plane. 2. CPU: Test each part for intersection with the object. 3. CPU: If a part does not intersect the object, neglect it; if it intersects, repeat the division procedure on that part. 4. CPU: Stop recursion when the current part corresponds to a tile of the predefined size. 5. CPU: Generate a list of fragments representing the geometric objects intersecting with the tiles. 6. GPU: Feed the fragment list to the GPU input. 7. GPU: For each pixel, test the relevant fragment for intersection with a ray directed along the Z-axis. 8. GPU: Perform a binary search along the ray to find the nearest intersection point, defined as the first point where the object function vanishes. 9. GPU: Determine the z-coordinate and surface normal for each pixel. 10. GPU: Apply a local lighting model using the coordinates and normals to compute the final pixel color. region.xmin < tilesize and region.ymax - region.ymin < tilesize): if intersectsobject(region): fragments.append(Fragment(region)) return fragments midx = (region.xmin + region.xmax) / 2 midy = (region.ymin + region.ymax) / 2 quadrants = [ Region(region.xmin, midx, region.ymin, midy, region.zmin, region.zmax), Region(midx, region.xmax, region.ymin, midy, region.zmin, region.zmax), Region(region.xmin, midx, midy, region.ymax, region.zmin, region.zmax), Region(midx, region.xmax, midy, region.ymax, region.zmin, region.zmax) ] for quad in quadrants: if intersectsobject(quad): fragments.extend(buildquaternarytree(quad, tilesize)) return fragments def evaluatescalarfield(point): # Placeholder for the implicit surface function f(x,y,z) return point.z - 0.5 def binarysearchintersection(origin, direction, fragment): zlow = fragment.region.zmin zhigh = fragment.region.zmax maxiterations = 32 epsilon = 1e-4 for in range(maxiterations): zmid = (zlow + zhigh) / 2 point = (origin[0] + direction[0] zmid, origin[1] + direction[1] zmid, zmid) value = evaluatescalarfield(point) if abs(value) < epsilon: return zmid if value > 0: zhigh = zmid else: zlow = zmid return None def calculatenormal(point): # Approximate normal using central finite differences h = 1e-5 dx = evaluatescalarfield((point[0]+h, point[1], point[2])) - evaluatescalarfield((point[0]-h, point[1], point[2])) dy = evaluatescalarfield((point[0], point[1]+h, point[2])) - evaluatescalarfield((point[0], point[1]-h, point[2])) dz = evaluatescalarfield((point[0], point[1], point[2]+h)) - evaluatescalarfield((point[0], point[1], point[2]-h)) length = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz)0.5 return (dx/length, dy/length, dz/length) def applylighting(point, normal): # Simple diffuse lighting model return (0.5 + 0.5 max(0, normal[2])) def renderfragments(fragments, imagewidth, imageheight, tilesize): image = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): origin = (float(x), float(y), 0.0) direction = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) relevantfragment = None for frag in fragments: if (frag.region.xmin <= x < frag.region.xmax and frag.region.ymin <= y < frag.region.ymax): relevantfragment = frag break if relevantfragment is not None: zintersect = binarysearchintersection(origin, direction, relevantfragment) if zintersect is not None: point = (origin[0], origin[1], zintersect) normal = calculatenormal(point) image[y][x] = applylighting(point, normal) return image Parameters: Tile Size: The size of the fragments generated by the CPU. name: Stackless GPU Raycasting with Octree Traversal
head: Adaptive out-of-core volume rendering, GPU ray-casting with octree, Out-of-Core GPU Volume Ray Casting, Stackless octree traversal on the GPU
body: This method performs scalable, out-of-core volume rendering on the GPU by decomposing volumetric data into small cubical bricks organized in an octree structure. It differs from its parent, Octree Ray Marching with Brick Interpolation and Early Termination, by explicitly managing an out-of-core working set and using a 3D texture spatial index to enable stackless traversal without maintaining a node stack in shader memory. It differs from its sibling, Two-staged Space-Skipping with Bricking and Octrees, by integrating the spatial index construction and neighbor pointer encoding directly into the fragment shader's traversal loop, allowing for on-the-fly bounding box computation. The method solves the problem of rendering very large datasets that exceed GPU texture memory by asynchronously fetching a view-dependent working set of bricks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Large volumetric dataset (16-bit scalars, optionally 32-bit gradients), camera parameters, transfer function. Output: Rendered image (frame-buffer) and depth information (depth-buffer). Data Structures: 1. Out-of-Core Octree: Organizes data into small cubical bricks. Leaves store original data; inner nodes store filtered representations of children, value ranges, and optionally precomputed gradients. Neighboring samples are replicated inside bricks to support interpolation. 2. Spatial Index (3D Texture): A compact indexing structure encoding the current working set's octree hierarchy. Inner Nodes: The RGB components store pointers to children. The W component indicates if the node is inner. Leaf Nodes: The RGB components store a data pointer (if non-empty) and 6 consecutive texels storing pointers to neighbors. Neighbor Pointers: The A component encodes the octree level of the neighbor (same or coarser). Termination: The last leaf data texel always contains a NULL pointer to simplify handling of rays that do not exit the current box. 3. Traversal State (Shader Registers): nodeptr: float3 coordinate in the spatial index texture. octreelevel: Integer, current depth in the octree. boxmin: float3, minimum corner of the current voxel brick in texture coordinates. boxdim: float3, dimensions of the current voxel brick (uniform). color: float4, accumulated color. depth: float, accumulated depth. Parameters: Early Ray Termination Threshold: 0.99 opacity. Data Precision: 16-bit scalars, 32-bit gradients (8 bits per direction, 8 bits norm). Gradient Filter: 5x5x5 Sobel filtering. Algorithm Steps: 1. Working Set Generation: An adaptive loader asynchronously fetches bricks from the out-of-core octree based on the view and transfer function, maintaining a working set on CPU/GPU memory. 2. Spatial Index Construction: At each frame, a compact indexing structure is created from the working set and encoded into a 3D texture acting as the spatial index. Neighbor pointers link leaf nodes via six faces to adjacent nodes or the smallest enclosing node. 3. Initialization: Set fragment.color = float4(0,0,0,0). Set fragment.depth = FAR. Set nodeptr = float3(0,0,0) (root). Set octreelevel = 0. Set boxmin = float3(0,0,0). Set boxdim = float3(1,1,1). 4. Main Traversal Loop: While nodeptr is not null and color.a < 1: 1. Find Leaf: Determine the leaf node containing the current sampling point P = \text{ray.start} + \text{ray.dir} \times t{min}. 2. Down Traversal: While the current node is inner (isinner(node.w)): Subdivide box: boxdim /= 2. Compute center: boxmid = boxmin + boxdim. Compute child offset vector: s = step(P, boxmid) (0 if P < box\mid, 1 otherwise). Update box origin: boxmin += s boxdim. Compute child pointer offset: childoffset = dot3(s, float3(1,2,4)) texelsz. Update nodeptr: nodeptr = node.xyz + float4(childoffset, 0, 0, 0). Fetch node: node = tex3d(spatialindex, nodeptr). Increment octreelevel. 3. Clip Ray: Clip the ray to the current box to find the exit face and t{max}. 4. Accumulate: If the node is not empty (!isempty(node.w)): Access data pointer: dataptr = tex3d(spatialindex, node.xyz). Accumulate color and opacity using adaptive sampling density matching brick resolution. Update fragment.color and fragment.depth. 5. Neighbor Traversal: If the ray exits the current block: Compute neighbor offset based on exit face index. Fetch neighbor node: neighbor = tex3d(spatialindex, node.xyz + neighboroffset). Update nodeptr = neighbor.xyz. Update octreelevel = neighbor.w. If neighbor level is coarser, coarsen box: boxdim = exp2(-octreelevel). boxmin = trunc(boxmin / boxdim) boxdim. Update tmin = boxtmax. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. fragmentcolor = float4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) fragmentdepth = FAR nodeptr = float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) octreelevel = 0 boxmin = float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) boxdim = float3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) while not isnull(nodeptr) and fragmentcolor.a < 1.0: # Find leaf containing current sampling point P = ray.start + ray.dir tmin node = tex3d(spatialindex, nodeptr) # Down Traversal while isinner(node.w): boxdim = boxdim / 2.0 boxmid = boxmin + boxdim s = step(P, boxmid) # Component-wise step function boxmin = boxmin + s boxdim childoffset = dot3(s, float3(1.0, 2.0, 4.0)) texelsz nodeptr = node.xyz + float4(childoffset, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) node = tex3d(spatialindex, nodeptr) octreelevel = octreelevel + 1 # Clip ray to box and find exit face boxtmax, exitfaceidx, exitdir = boxclip(ray, tmin, tmax, boxmin, boxdim) # If non-empty block, access data and accumulate if not isempty(node.w): dataptr = tex3d(spatialindex, node.xyz) fragmentcolor, fragmentdepth = accumulate(fragmentcolor, ray, tmin, boxtmax, dataptr, boxmin, boxmax) # If ray exits from current block, move to neighbor neighboroffset = float3(1 + exitfaceidx, 0.0, 0.0) texelsz neighbor = tex3d(spatialindex, node.xyz + neighboroffset) nodeptr = neighbor.xyz octreelevel = neighbor.w boxdim = exp2(-octreelevel) boxmin = trunc(boxmin / boxdim) boxdim tmin = boxtmax A variant that packs leaf node data into a 3D texture and encodes brick coordinates within the node's color data, allowing for efficient brick-level raymarching. Choose this when memory bandwidth for leaf data access is a bottleneck and brick storage optimization is required. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of non-empty bricks traversed by the ray. The stackless traversal avoids stack push/pop overhead, reducing shader complexity. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the working set and the spatial index texture, which is significantly smaller than the full volume. Performance: Enables interactive real-time visualization of high-resolution anatomical data. Performance scales with the number of leaf nodes in the working set (typically a few thousands). Strengths: Out-of-core capability allows rendering datasets larger than GPU memory; stackless traversal reduces shader register pressure; adaptive sampling and early termination optimize computation. Limitations: Requires on-the-fly construction of the spatial index each frame, which may add CPU/GPU synchronization overhead; occlusion culling is limited to early ray termination, not data loading. When to use: Large volumetric datasets that do not fit in GPU memory; interactive applications requiring view-dependent LOD. When not to use: Small datasets that fit entirely in texture memory (simpler methods may be more efficient); scenes requiring complex lighting or global illumination beyond ray casting. The method was developed by Agus et al. and presented in 2008 as part of a system for advanced volumetric display of the human musculoskeletal system. It builds on the stackless ray traversal method for kd-trees by Havran [HBS98] and its GPU extension for surface rendering by Pfaff et al. [PGSS07]. The approach addresses the limitations of previous GPU ray casting methods that were restricted to moderate size volumes fitting entirely into texture memory. body: A raycasting method that traverses an octree structure stored in a GPU buffer to render voxels, handling both solid nodes and leaf nodes containing 8x8x8 voxel bricks using a 3D texture for brick data storage. It differs from standard sparse voxel octree traversal by packing leaf node data into a 3D texture and encoding brick coordinates within the node's color data, allowing for efficient brick-level raymarching. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin O, ray direction D (normalized), world bounds, octree node buffer, 3D texture voxelBlocks containing 8x8x8 voxel bricks. Output: Accumulated color and opacity for the pixel. Data Structures The octree is stored as a flat array of octreeNode structs in a GPU buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct octreeNode { uint childData; // Encodes leaf/solid flags and child offset uint colorData; // Encodes color for solids or brick coordinates for leaves }; Bit Packing in childData LEAFMASK (0x80000000): Indicates leaf node. SOLIDMASK (0x40000000): Indicates solid node. FINALMASK (0xA0000000): LEAFMASK | SOLIDMASK. If (childData & FINALMASK) == FINALMASK, the node is a leaf or solid. CHILDMASK (0x3FFFFFFF): Stores the index of the first child node if not a leaf. Bit Packing in colorData (Leaf Nodes) For leaf nodes, colorData stores the brick coordinates packed as a uint. COORDMASK (0x000003FF): Extracts 10-bit coordinates. Brick X: Bits 20-29. Calculated as (loc >> 20) & COORDMASK. Brick Y: Bits 10-19. Calculated as (loc >> 10) & COORDMASK. Brick Z: Bits 0-9. Calculated as loc & COORDMASK. Voxel Data Storage Voxel data is stored in a uniform 3D texture voxelBlocks (sampler3D). Each voxel is a vec4 (RGBA). Parameters MAXDEPTH: Maximum octree depth allowed, set to 10. If depth exceeds this, treat as leaf/solid. BRICKSIZE: Size of voxel bricks, defined as 8. MAXSTEPS: Maximum traversal steps, set to 200. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize Ray Traversal: Normalize direction D. Compute inverse direction D{inv} = 1/D. Compute delta T = |D{inv}|. Determine entry/exit parameters s{min}, s{max} based on world bounds and ray origin. 2. Traverse Octree: Initialize current node index to root (0), depth to 0, and bounds (x{min}, dim) to world bounds. Loop with maxSteps = 200. Check if current node is leaf/solid: if ((nodes[node].childData & FINALMASK) == FINALMASK). If true, process leaf/solid logic (Step 3). If false, descend to child node (Step 4). 3. Raymarch through the 8x8x8 brick using DDA-like stepping. Loop through voxels in the brick using stepTmax comparisons to determine which axis to step next. Check voxel alpha; if non-zero, blend color and accumulate alpha. Break if line position goes out of [0, 8) bounds. 4. Compute next node index: python nextNode = (nodes[node].childData & CHILDMASK) + (subNodeLoc.x << 2) + (subNodeLoc.y << 1) + subNodeLoc.z Increment depth, halve dim, update xMin. name: SVO Walk (Traversal)
body: SVO Walk is a depth-first traversal algorithm for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO) that visits nodes in an order determined by the eye position, invoking a callback for each visited node. It differs from pure SVO traversal by explicitly managing a stack to control visitation order based on eye position, and from BVH-based approaches by operating directly on the octree structure without an intermediate bounding volume hierarchy. Inputs: SVO root node, eye position, and a callback function onnode. Outputs: Execution of onnode for each visited node in traversal order. Data Structures: Stack: Stores tuples (noderef, stem, depth). noderef: Pointer or index to the current octree node. stem: A 3D integer vector representing the node's origin coordinates at the current depth. depth: The current octree depth level (integer). Formulas: Offset: The physical size of a voxel at a given depth. \text{offset} = 2^{-\text{depth}} Implemented via bit manipulation for efficiency: python exp = 126 - depth f = exp << 23 offset = struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('I', f))[0] # bit-cast to float Voxel Position: The world-space position of the voxel corner. \text{voxel} = \text{stem} \times \text{offset} Child Origin: For a child at index i (0-7) in the octree: \text{new\origin} = \text{stem} + \text{index\offset}(i, \text{offset}) Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the stack with (ROOTNODE, (0,0,0), 0). 2. While the stack is not empty: a. Pop (noderef, stem, depth) from the stack. b. Retrieve the node from noderef. c. Calculate offset using the bit-manipulation method above. d. Calculate voxel = stem offset. e. Call onnode(isleaf, data, voxel). f. If onnode returns true AND the node is not a leaf: i. Calculate the sorting order of the 8 children based on the eye position and stem. ii. For each child in the sorted order: 1. Determine the child's index i. 2. Calculate neworigin = stem + indexoffset(i, offset). 3. Push (childref, neworigin, depth + 1) to the stack. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct import math def svowalk(rootnode, eyeposition, onnode): stack = [(rootnode, (0, 0, 0), 0)] while stack: noderef, stem, depth = stack.pop() # offset = 2^(-depth) via bit manipulation exp = 126 - depth f = exp << 23 offset = struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('I', f))[0] # bit-cast to float # voxel = stem.extend(offset) voxel = (stem[0] offset, stem[1] offset, stem[2] offset) isleaf = noderef.isleaf() data = noderef.data if onnode(isleaf, data, voxel): if not isleaf: children = noderef.children # Sort children indices 0-7 based on distance to eyeposition def childorigin(i): return (stem[0] + ((i & 1) offset), stem[1] + (((i >> 1) & 1) offset), stem[2] + (((i >> 2) & 1) offset)) sortedchildren = sorted(range(8), key=lambda i: math.dist(eyeposition, childorigin(i))) for i in sortedchildren: neworigin = childorigin(i) stack.append((children[i], neworigin, depth + 1)) Fast Walk Variant: Uses a fixed-size stack array of 256 elements. Uses raw pointers for node access to minimize overhead. Calculates voxel using offset 1.73 (approx \sqrt{3}) in some implementations, though the standard formula is 2^{-\text{depth}}. Edge Cases: Stack Overflow: The fixed-size stack (256 elements) may overflow in deep or complex scenes. Precision: The bit-manipulation method for offset calculation is efficient but limited to specific depth ranges where 126 - \text{depth} yields a valid IEEE 754 exponent. A hybrid variant combining BVH coarse culling with SVO fine-grained evaluation. It reduces visited nodes compared to pure SVO traversal and maintains SVO memory efficiency at the leaves compared to pure BVH traversal. Iterates through all nodes using a PreOrderTraversal to compute global active states. If a node's local state is INACTIVE, it sets activeGlobal to FALSE and marks inactiveAncestors as TRUE; otherwise it inherits inactiveAncestors from the parent. If the node is globally active, it increments the numActiveGlobal counter. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of visited nodes. Memory Complexity: O(D) for the stack, where D is the maximum depth of the tree. The fixed-size stack variant uses constant memory (256 elements). The SVO Walk algorithm is described in the svo-cpu repository by marceline-cramer. marceline-cramer/svo-cpu, https://github.com/marceline-cramer/svo-cpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Lipschitz Pruning: Hierarchical Simplification of Primitive‐Based SDFs, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70057, fetched 2026-10-26
