name: Single-kernel Octree Traversal
head: Iterative Octree Traversal in CUDA, Stack-based Ray Traversal
body: Single-kernel octree traversal is a technique for traversing an octree for ray tracing by performing the entire traversal logic, including recursion simulation, within a single CUDA kernel execution per ray, rather than using multiple kernel launches for each recursion depth. It is preferred over multi-kernel recursion because kernel invocation overhead is high. Although single-kernel traversal may cause thread divergence due to the SIMD nature of GPUs, coherent rays in a warp traverse similarly, mitigating this issue. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin, ray direction, octree node data, and a maximum stack size parameter. Output: Traversal results (e.g., hit node indices) stored in local or shared memory structures. Data Structures: Traversal Stack: A fixed-size array stored in local or shared memory. Fields: Node indices to be visited. Size: Manually defined maximum value because dynamic sizing is not possible in local/shared memory. If too small, overflow occurs; if too large, memory is wasted. Steps: 1. Kernel Launch: Launch a single CUDA kernel where each thread represents a single ray. A 2D grid and 2D block configuration is recommended to help with cache hits. 2. Initialization: Initialize the traversal stack with the root node index. 3. Traversal Loop: While the stack is not empty: a. Pop the top node index from the stack. b. If the node is a leaf, perform the leaf operation (e.g., ray-march or intersection test). c. If the node is internal, compute the child node indices intersected by the ray using explicit ray-box intersection. d. Push the child node indices onto the stack in reverse order of traversal preference. 4. Termination: The kernel completes when all rays have finished their traversal or hit a termination condition. Parameters: Stack Size: A manually defined maximum value for the traversal stack size. Typical values depend on the octree depth and scene complexity, but must be chosen to balance memory waste and overflow risk. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Register Spilling: If the kernel uses too many registers, the compiler spills variables to local memory (which is physically global memory), causing a significant performance penalty. This is determined at compile time, not runtime. Silent Failure: Exceeding register limits or program size limits can cause the kernel to fail silently without error messages, making debugging difficult. Memory Waste: Using a fixed-size stack for all threads can lead to significant memory waste if the actual traversal depth varies greatly among rays. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def singlekerneloctreetraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, octreenodes, maxstacksize): # Local memory stack stack = [0] maxstacksize stacktop = 0 # Push root node index stack[stacktop] = 0 stacktop += 1 while stacktop > 0: # Pop node stacktop -= 1 nodeidx = stack[stacktop] node = octreenodes[nodeidx] # Explicit ray-box intersection (slab method) # Fixes previous bug where undefined helpers caused premature None returns tmin = [(node.minb[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] tmax = [(node.maxb[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] tenter = max(min(tmin), min(tmax)) texit = min(max(tmin), max(tmax)) if tenter > texit or texit <= 0: continue if node.isleaf: return nodeidx # Compute intersected children and push in reverse order for childidx in range(7, -1, -1): # Octree child bounding box calculation halfsize = [(node.maxb[i] - node.minb[i]) / 2.0 for i in range(3)] childmin = [node.minb[i] + ((childidx >> i) & 1) halfsize[i] for i in range(3)] childmax = [childmin[i] + halfsize[i] for i in range(3)] # Reuse intersection logic for child tminc = [(childmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] tmaxc = [(childmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] tenterc = max(min(tminc), min(tmaxc)) texitc = min(max(tminc), max(tmaxc)) if tenterc <= texitc and texitc > 0: if stacktop < maxstacksize: stack[stacktop] = childidx stacktop += 1 else: raise MemoryError("Stack overflow") return None Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of nodes visited per ray. The overhead of kernel invocation is eliminated compared to multi-kernel approaches. Memory Complexity: O(D) per ray, where D is the maximum stack depth, stored in local or shared memory. Performance: Kernel invocation overhead is high, making single-kernel traversal more efficient than multi-kernel recursion. Thread divergence may occur, but coherent rays mitigate this. Strengths: Reduced kernel launch overhead, better cache utilization with coherent rays. Limitations: Risk of register spilling and silent failure if register limits are exceeded. Fixed stack size can lead to memory waste or overflow. When to Use: When kernel invocation overhead is a bottleneck and rays are coherent. When Not to Use: When register pressure is high and cannot be managed, or when stack depth is highly variable and unpredictable. The technique was discussed in the context of CUDA programming for raytracing on the NVIDIA Developer Forums in 2009. It was proposed as an alternative to multi-kernel recursion to avoid the high cost of kernel invocations. References to related work include "GigaVoxels: Ray-Guided Streaming for Efficient and Detailed Voxel Rendering". name: Recursive Octree Traversal
head: Octree Node Traversal (Standard), Raycast Entry Point
body: Recursive octree traversal is a standard algorithm for ray casting against a 3D sparse voxel octree, where the traversal logic is implemented via a recursive function that visits nodes in depth-first order. It solves the problem of efficiently locating and sampling leaf nodes (or specific depth levels) along a ray by recursively descending into child nodes only when the ray intersects their axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs). It differs from its siblings by relying on the call stack for state management rather than an explicit stack or parametric surface equations. Inputs and outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, octree root node, maximum traversal depth, and a branching mode (e.g., Wide4). Outputs: A hit record (closest intersection, leaf ID, depth) or an empty result if no intersection occurs. Data structures: NodeDescriptor: A compact structure stored in a linear array. It contains: childmask: std::uint8t, bitmask of existing children. leafmask: std::uint8t, bitmask of children that are leaves. internalchildmask: std::uint8t, bitmask of children that are internal nodes. payloadbase: Implied offset to leaf data. Morton Code: Used to map spatial position to linear index. Calculated as parentmorton | (i << (3 (depth - 1))) for the i-th child. Algorithm Steps: 1. Validation: Validate that the ray origin is finite and the direction is non-zero. Normalize the direction. 2. Root Check: If the octree is empty, return an empty hit. Get the root AABB and intersect the ray with it. If no intersection, return empty. 3. Depth Check: If maxdepth is 0, treat the root as a leaf with leafid=0 and depth=0, then return. 4. Dispatch: If the branching mode is Wide4, call traversewidenode. Otherwise, call traversenode with the root, origin, normalized direction, and initial t-near/far values. 5. Recursive Traversal (traversenode): Base Case: If nodeindex is out of bounds or depthremaining <= 0, return. Descriptor Load: Retrieve NodeDescriptor for nodeindex. Extract childmask, leafmask, and internalchildmask. Child Iteration: Loop through 8 children (i = 0 to 7). Mask Check: If the bit (1u << i) is not set in childmask, skip. AABB Intersection: Compute the child's AABB using childbounds(bounds, i). Intersect the ray with this AABB. If no intersection, continue. Pruning: If a previous hit exists (best.hit) and the new t{near} > best.t + \epsilon, skip this child. Leaf Handling: If the bit (1u << i) is set in leafmask: Compute leafid using descriptor.payloadbase() and prefixrank(leafmask, i). Compute depth as octree.maxdepth() - depthremaining + 1. Call considerleaf(childaabb, leafid, depth). Internal Node Recursion: If the bit (1u << i) is set in internalchildmask: Calculate the child's Morton code: parentmorton | (i << (3 (depth - 1))). Recursively call traversenode with the child's address/offset and depth + 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverserecursive(nodeindex, depthremaining, rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, octree, besthit): # Base case: out of bounds or depth limit reached if nodeindex >= octree.numnodes or depthremaining <= 0: return # Load node descriptor descriptor = octree.nodes[nodeindex] childmask = descriptor.childmask leafmask = descriptor.leafmask internalchildmask = descriptor.internalchildmask # Iterate over 8 children for i in range(8): childbit = 1 << i # Skip if child does not exist if not (childbit & childmask): continue # Compute child AABB childaabb = computechildaabb(octree.rootbounds, nodeindex, i, depthremaining) # Intersect ray with child AABB tchildnear, tchildfar = intersectrayaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, childaabb) # If no intersection, skip if tchildfar < tnear or tchildnear > tfar: continue # Pruning: if we already have a hit closer than the current node's entry if besthit.hit and tchildnear > besthit.t + EPSILON: continue # Check if leaf if childbit & leafmask: # Calculate leaf ID using prefix rank leafid = descriptor.payloadbase + prefixrank(leafmask, i) depth = octree.maxdepth - depthremaining + 1 # Process leaf (e.g., update besthit if closer) if tchildnear < besthit.t: besthit.t = tchildnear besthit.leafid = leafid besthit.depth = depth besthit.hit = True else: # Recurse into internal node # Calculate child node index or offset childindex = getchildindex(octree, nodeindex, i) traverserecursive(childindex, depthremaining - 1, rayorigin, raydirection, tchildnear, tchildfar, octree, besthit) def raycastone(octree, rayorigin, raydirection): # Validate inputs if not isfinite(rayorigin) or not isfinite(raydirection) or length(raydirection) == 0: raise ValidationError("Invalid ray") normalizeddirection = normalize(raydirection) # Check if octree is empty if octree.numnodes == 0: return EmptyHit() # Check root intersection rootaabb = octree.rootbounds tnear, tfar = intersectrayaabb(rayorigin, normalizeddirection, rootaabb) if tfar < 0 or tnear > tfar: return EmptyHit() # Handle maxdepth == 0 case if octree.maxdepth == 0: return Hit(leafid=0, depth=0, t=tnear) # Dispatch based on branching mode besthit = Hit() besthit.t = infinity if octree.branchingmode == Wide4: traversewidenode(octree.root, rayorigin, normalizeddirection, tnear, tfar, besthit) else: traverserecursive(octree.rootindex, octree.maxdepth, rayorigin, normalizeddirection, tnear, tfar, octree, besthit) return besthit Parameters: BranchingMode::Wide4: Indicates the octree uses wide nodes (4x4x4 cells) for traversal. maxdepth: Maximum depth of the octree. Typically in the range [0, 30]. Edge cases and pitfalls: Precision: Use prefixrank to correctly map child indices to payload indices based on sparse masks. Boundaries: Ensure t{near} is clamped to 0.0 if the ray origin is inside the volume. Degenerate Input: Throw ValidationError if the ray direction is zero or origin is non-finite. Top Level Octree Rendering is a rendering technique that stops octree traversal at a specific depth level determined by the pixel's y-coordinate, then applies lighting. It differs from standard recursive traversal by using the vertical screen position to limit the traversal depth, effectively culling deeper nodes based on their apparent height in the viewport. Time Complexity: O(N) in the worst case where N is the number of nodes visited, but typically much faster for sparse volumes due to early culling of empty space. Memory Complexity: O(D) where D is the maximum depth of the octree, due to the recursion stack. Performance: Efficient for CPU implementation due to simple control flow. Performance degrades if the ray passes through many small, non-empty nodes. Strengths: Simple to implement, handles sparse data well, easy to integrate with other recursive algorithms (e.g., path tracing). Limitations: Stack depth limits maximum octree depth. Not suitable for GPU where explicit stacks or wide traversal are preferred. Recursive octree traversal is a fundamental technique in volume rendering and geometric processing. It is widely used in sparse voxel octree renderers, dual contouring implementations, and procedural generation pipelines. name: Top Level Octree Rendering
head: Depth-dependent Octree Traversal, Y-coordinate based Octree Cutoff
body: Top Level Octree Rendering is a rendering technique that stops octree traversal at a specific depth level determined by the pixel's y-coordinate, then applies lighting. It differs from standard recursive traversal by using the vertical screen position to limit the traversal depth, effectively culling deeper nodes based on their apparent height in the viewport. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree structure (tree) with a known grid length, a ray configuration (rc) containing camera parameters, screen dimensions (ny), and a list of lights. Output: A texture array (texturearray) containing the final RGB color and alpha for each pixel. Data Structures: tree: Contains gridlength, which defines the spatial extent of the voxel grid. rc: Contains ny (screen height in pixels), lights (list of light sources), and camera (containing e, the eye position). TreeTraverser: A helper object initialized with the tree and a specific ray. It maintains a stack representing the current path in the octree. DataPoint: Stored in leaf nodes, containing normal (vector) and color data. Parameters: depth: Calculated as \log2(\text{tree.gridlength}) + 2. step: Calculated as \text{rc.n\y} / \text{depth}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate depth and step using the formulas above. 2. Initialize a parallel loop over the screen height y from 0 to \text{rc.n\y} - 1. 3. For each y, iterate over the screen width x from 0 to \text{rc.n\x} - 1. 4. Initialize a TreeTraverser instance t for the ray corresponding to pixel (x, y). 5. Traverse the octree while the traverser is not terminated: Check if the current stack size is greater than or equal to the cutoff threshold: \lfloor y / \text{step} \rfloor. If the condition is met, break the traversal loop. Otherwise, call t.step() to advance to the next node. 6. After traversal, compute lighting for the current position t.getcurrentposition(). 7. For each active light i: Compute the light vector: \vec{to\light} = \text{lights}[i].\text{position} - \text{current\position}. Compute the half vector for specular reflection: \vec{s} = \text{normalize}(\vec{to\light} + (\text{camera}.e\ - \text{current\position})). Compute distance attenuation: \text{distancecut} = \frac{1.0}{\text{CONSTANT\ATTENUATION} + \text{LINEAR\ATTENUATION} \cdot \|\vec{to\light}\| + \text{QUADRATIC\ATTENUATION} \cdot \|\vec{to\light}\|^2}. Normalize the light vector: \vec{to\light} = \text{normalize}(\vec{to\light}). Compute diffuse factor: \text{diffuse\factor} = \text{data}[\text{current\node}.\text{data}].\text{normal} \cdot \vec{to\light}. Accumulate diffuse color: r += \max(0.0, \text{diffuse\factor}) \cdot \text{distancecut} \cdot \text{lights}[i].\text{diffuse}[0] (similarly for g, b). Compute Phong specular factor: \text{phong\factor} = \text{pow}(\vec{s} \cdot \text{data}[\text{current\node}.\text{data}].\text{normal}, \text{lights}[i].\text{SHININESS}). Accumulate specular color: r += \max(0.0, \text{phong\factor}) \cdot \text{distancecut} \cdot \text{lights}[i].\text{specular}[0] (similarly for g, b). 8. Write the final color to the texture array: \text{texture\array}[\text{index}] = \text{clamp}(255 \cdot r, 0, 255). 9. Set alpha: \text{texture\array}[\text{index}+3] = 1. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalize(v): return [c / math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in v)) for c in v] def length(v): return math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in v)) def dot(a, b): return sum(xy for x, y in zip(a, b)) def clamp(val, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, val)) class TreeTraverser: def init(self, tree, ray): self.tree = tree self.ray = ray self.stack = [] self.currentnode = tree.root self.currentpos = ray.origin self.terminated = False def isterminated(self): return self.terminated def step(self): # Standard octree traversal logic not detailed in sources pass def getcurrentposition(self): return self.currentpos def getcurrentnode(self): return self.currentnode def topleveloctreerendering(tree, rc, texturearray, nx): depth = math.log2(tree.gridlength) + 2 step = rc.ny / depth for y in range(rc.ny): for x in range(nx): ray = rc.getrayforpixel(x, y) t = TreeTraverser(tree, ray) while not t.isterminated(): if len(t.stack) >= (y / step): break t.step() currentpos = t.getcurrentposition() currentnode = t.getcurrentnode() data = currentnode.data r, g, b = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 for light in rc.lights: tolight = [light.position[j] - currentpos[j] for j in range(3)] viewdir = [rc.camera.e[j] - currentpos[j] for j in range(3)] s = normalize([tolight[j] + viewdir[j] for j in range(3)]) dist = length(tolight) distsq = dist dist distancecut = 1.0 / (light.CONSTANTATTENUATION + light.LINEARATTENUATION dist + light.QUADRATICATTENUATION distsq) tolight = normalize(tolight) normal = data.normal diffusefactor = dot(normal, tolight) r += max(0.0, diffusefactor) distancecut light.diffuse[0] g += max(0.0, diffusefactor) distancecut light.diffuse[1] b += max(0.0, diffusefactor) distancecut light.diffuse[2] phongfactor = pow(max(0.0, dot(s, normal)), light.SHININESS) r += max(0.0, phongfactor) distancecut light.specular[0] g += max(0.0, phongfactor) distancecut light.specular[1] b += max(0.0, phongfactor) distancecut light.specular[2] index = (y nx + x) 4 texturearray[index] = clamp(255 r, 0, 255) texturearray[index + 1] = clamp(255 g, 0, 255) texturearray[index + 2] = clamp(255 b, 0, 255) texturearray[index + 3] = 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: The formula \text{depth} = \log2(\text{tree.gridlength}) + 2 ensures depth is at least 2 for any valid gridlength >= 1, preventing division by zero during step calculation. Type Comparison: The cutoff condition len(t.stack) >= (y / step) compares an integer stack size to a floating-point quotient, matching the source's C++ implementation where stack.size() (unsigned int) is compared against y / step (float). Boundary Conditions: The loop bounds for x and y must match the screen resolution provided by rc.ny and rc.nx. Stops traversal at a fixed maxlevel depth regardless of pixel position. name: Fixed-Level Octree Traversal
head: Level Rendering
body: Fixed-Level Octree Traversal is a CPU-based ray casting technique that renders sparse voxel octrees by limiting the traversal depth to a fixed maximum level (maxlevel). It solves the problem of rendering large sparse volumes by avoiding deep recursive traversal, instead processing only the top-level nodes of the octree. It differs from recursive octree traversal by stopping the traversal early at a specific depth, applying lighting directly on the leaf nodes reached, and writing the final color without volumetric integration or alpha blending. Inputs: tree: The sparse voxel octree structure. rc: A rendering context containing rc.ny (image height), rc.lights (array of light sources), rc.camera (camera object with e eye position), and rc.getRayForPixel(x, y) (ray generation function). maxlevel: The fixed maximum depth of the octree to traverse. texturearray: Output buffer of size W \times H \times 4 (RGBA), where W is image width. Outputs: texturearray filled with final RGBA color values. VoxelData: Stored in leaf nodes. Layout: morton (uint64t), color (vec3), normal (vec3). Total size: sizeof(uint64t) + 2 (3 sizeof(float)) bytes. TreeTraverser: Stateful object managing the octree walk. Fields: tree (reference), ray (current ray), stack (list of nodes), isTerminated() (boolean), step() (advance), getCurrentPosition() (3D position), getCurrentNode() (pointer to VoxelData). 1. Initialize Parallelism: Set the number of OpenMP threads to match the number of available CPU cores. 2. Pixel Loop: Iterate over all pixels (x, y) in parallel. 3. Ray Generation: For each pixel, generate the ray using rc.getRayForPixel(x, y). 4. Traversal Initialization: Create a TreeTraverser instance with the tree and the ray. 5. Traversal Loop: While the traverser is not terminated: Check if stack.size() >= maxlevel. If true, break the loop. Otherwise, call t.step() to advance to the next node. 6. Lighting Calculation: If the loop broke due to maxlevel, compute lighting for the current node. Initialize color accumulators r, g, b = 0. For each active light i: Compute light vector: \vec{l} = \text{light}i.\text{position} - \text{current\position}. Compute distance attenuation: \text{distancecut} = \frac{1.0}{C + L \cdot \|\vec{l}\| + Q \cdot \|\vec{l}\|^2} Where C, L, Q are rc.lights[i].CONSTANTATTENUATION, LINEARATTENUATION, and QUADRATICATTENUATION respectively. Normalize light vector: \vec{l} = \frac{\vec{l}}{\|\vec{l}\|}. Compute diffuse factor: \text{diffuse\factor} = \text{normal} \cdot \vec{l} Where normal is data[t.getCurrentNode()->data].normal. Accumulate diffuse color: r += \max(0.0, \text{diffuse\factor}) \cdot \text{distancecut} \cdot \text{light}i.\text{diffuse}[0] (Repeat for g, b using respective light diffuse components). Compute specular vector: \vec{h} = \vec{l} + (\text{camera\eye} - \text{current\position}) \vec{h} = \frac{\vec{h}}{\|\vec{h}\|}. Compute Phong specular factor: \text{phong\factor} = (\vec{h} \cdot \text{normal})^{\text{shininess}} Where shininess is rc.lights[i].SHININESS. Accumulate specular color: r += \max(0.0, \text{phong\factor}) \cdot \text{distancecut} \cdot \text{light}i.\text{specular}[0] (Repeat for g, b using respective light specular components). 7. Output: Write final color: texturearray[index] = clamp(255 r, 0, 255) cast to unsigned char. Set alpha: texturearray[index+3] = 1. Unverified code. Initialize parallelism (reference implementation uses OpenMP) numthreads = os.cpucount() setnumthreads(numthreads) # Configures thread pool size # 2. Parallelize pixel loop for y in range(rc.ny): for x in range(W): # 3. Initialize ray traverser ray = rc.getrayforpixel(x, y) t = TreeTraverser(tree, ray) racc = 0.0 gacc = 0.0 bacc = 0.0 # 4. Traverse tree while not t.isterminated(): if len(t.stack) >= maxlevel: break t.step() # 5. Lighting calculation currentpos = t.getcurrentposition() nodedata = t.getcurrentnode().data normal = nodedata.normal for light in rc.lights: tolight = (light.position[0] - currentpos[0], light.position[1] - currentpos[1], light.position[2] - currentpos[2]) lentolight = length(tolight) len2tolight = lentolight lentolight distancecut = 1.0 / ( light.CONSTANTATTENUATION + light.LINEARATTENUATION lentolight + light.QUADRATICATTENUATION len2tolight) tolight = normalize(tolight) diffusefactor = dot(normal, tolight) diffr = max(0.0, diffusefactor) distancecut light.diffuse[0] diffg = max(0.0, diffusefactor) distancecut light.diffuse[1] diffb = max(0.0, diffusefactor) distancecut light.diffuse[2] racc += diffr gacc += diffg bacc += diffb eye = rc.camera.e s = (tolight[0] + (eye[0] - currentpos[0]), tolight[1] + (eye[1] - currentpos[1]), tolight[2] + (eye[2] - currentpos[2])) s = normalize(s) specfactor = pow(max(0.0, dot(s, normal)), light.SHININESS) specr = specfactor distancecut light.specular[0] specg = specfactor distancecut light.specular[1] specb = specfactor distancecut light.specular[2] racc += specr gacc += specg bacc += specb # 6. Write final color index = (y W + x) 4 texturearray[index] = clamp(int(255 racc), 0, 255) texturearray[index + 1] = clamp(int(255 gacc), 0, 255) texturearray[index + 2] = clamp(int(255 bacc), 0, 255) texturearray[index + 3] = 1 class TreeTraverser: def init(self, tree, ray): self.tree = tree self.ray = ray self.stack = [] # Initialize stack with root node if it intersects ray if self.tree.intersects(ray): self.stack.append(self.tree.root) def isterminated(self): return len(self.stack) == 0 def step(self): if not self.stack: return current = self.stack.pop() # Push children or next sibling based on traversal order children = self.tree.getchildren(current) for child in reversed(children): if child.intersects(self.ray): self.stack.append(child) if not self.stack: self.stack.append(self.tree.getnextsibling(current)) def getcurrentposition(self): return self.stack[-1].center if self.stack else (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def getcurrentnode(self): return self.stack[-1] if self.stack else None maxlevel: The fixed depth limit. Limitations: No volumetric integration, fixed detail level regardless of distance, alpha is always 1. Origin: The method is described in the cpuvoxelraycaster repository by Forceflow. name: Compact Voxel Octree Raycasting
head: Compact Octree Traversal, SVO Workbench Raycasting, Sparse Ray-Octree Intersection
body:
Compact Voxel Octree Raycasting is a CPU-based ray traversal algorithm for Sparse Voxel Octrees that optimizes memory layout and traversal logic by compacting active ray-voxel interactions and decoding node masks on-the-fly. It solves the problem of inefficient traversal in sparse structures by using an explicit stack to manage non-sequential memory layouts and a parallel "COMPACTIFY" step to filter out non-intersecting rays, ensuring that only valid ray-voxel pairs are processed in subsequent levels. Unlike recursive or parametric approaches, it relies on a linear block structure with explicit state management, making it suitable for high-performance CPU implementations where memory bandwidth and cache locality are critical. It builds on CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal and differs from Parametric Octree Traversal, Iterative Octree Traversal, Recursive Octree Traversal, and Sparse Voxel Octree Path Tracing by explicitly managing traversal state and compacting active ray lists between levels. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a ray r=(o,d), a Sparse Voxel Octree ot, a framebuffer fb, screen coordinates (cur\x, cur\y), and a parameter terminLevel as input. It outputs a boolean indicating if a leaf was hit and draws a rendered pixel value to fb at (cur\x, cur\y). Data Structures: The core node structure is CNode, packed to exactly 8 bytes as a union of two layouts. The standard layout contains validmask (UInt8, bit i=1 means child i exists), leafmask (UInt8, bit i=1 means child i is a leaf), and childptr (UInt16, relative offset or far-pointer indicator). The far pointer layout replaces the standard fields with farptr (UInt32) when childptr indicates a far pointer. The traversal stack stores stackitemt entries containing entry t-values (tx0, ty0, tz0), exit t-values (tx1, ty1, tz1), the absolute node address (nodeadr), and the current child index (idx). Numbered Steps and Formulas: 1. Normalize the ray: add epsilon 10^{-10} to zero direction components to prevent division by zero, and flip negative directions by negating origin and direction while setting dirmask bits (x=4, y=2, z=1). 2. Stack underflow occurs when the stack is empty and an exit is requested, resetting t\start to t\exit and restarting initialization to treat the ray as newly entering the octree bounds. Zero direction components must be guarded with epsilon addition to prevent division by zero during t-value calculations. Fixed-point arithmetic uses tnum (SInt32) with clipping at 2^{31}-1000 and -2^{31}+1000 to prevent overflow. The time complexity is O(N) where N is the number of rays, but the COMPACTIFY step reduces active rays as they traverse deeper into the octree. Memory complexity is O(D) for the explicit stack, where D is the maximum octree depth, plus temporary storage for the COMPACTIFY active ray list. The method is optimized for CPU execution, leveraging explicit stack management and parallel reduction to minimize memory bandwidth and cache misses. Strengths include non-recursive traversal avoiding stack overflow, reduced processing load via compaction, and on-the-fly mask decoding minimizing memory accesses. Limitations include a heuristic newnode function that may not be optimal for all ray directions, and fixed-point precision constraints for extreme scene scales. It is best suited for CPU-based ray tracing of sparse voxel octrees where memory efficiency and explicit traversal control are required. It should be avoided for GPU implementations where recursive or parametric methods align better with hardware architecture, and for dense scenes where stack management and compaction overhead outweigh benefits. Compact Voxel Octree Raycasting originates from the SVO Workbench project. The COMPACTIFY technique, which forms the parallel reduction core of this method, was introduced in the context of Neural Geometric Level of Detail (NGLOD) for real-time rendering with implicit 3D shapes. The SVO Workbench provides a concrete CPU implementation of this traversal algorithm for sparse voxel structures. name: Sparse Voxel Octree Path Tracing
head: CPU Sparse Voxel Ray Tracing, CPU-based SVO rendering, Octree path tracing
body: Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) Path Tracing is a CPU-based rendering technique that traverses a sparse voxel octree (or DAG) structure to compute physically based lighting via recursive path tracing. It solves the problem of rendering complex, high-resolution voxel-based scenes efficiently by skipping empty space and only processing occupied nodes, writing the accumulated radiance to a texture for display. Unlike its siblings which focus on specific traversal optimizations (e.g., parametric or iterative steps), this method integrates the traversal directly into a Monte Carlo path tracer with Russian roulette termination, diffuse/specular bounces, and material properties (metalness, roughness, emission) stored in the leaf nodes. Inputs: SVO Data Structure: A flat array tree of uint32t nodes, a root index, and scene metadata (camera position, rotation). Camera: Position (Vector3<f64>), Rotation (Quaternion<f64>), and field of view bounds (fxmin, fxmax, fymin, fymax). Parameters: NumSamples (samples per pixel, 0-250), MaxBounces (0-100), EMISSIVESCALE (15.0), EPSILON (0.000002). Outputs: Image Buffer: An array of Pixel structs (RGBA, scaled to u16::MAX) representing the final rendered image. Node Layout (uint32t): Bits 0-16 (17 bits): Child pointer offset. Used to jump to children in the flat array. Bits 17-31 (15 bits): Mask/Type indicator. Internal Node: Initialized to 0x0000FFFF (binary...1111 1111 1111 1111). Leaf Node: Marker value 0x00004200 (binary...0100 0010 0000 0000). Note: Source uses a separate flags field where flags & 1 != 0 indicates a leaf, suggesting a variation in implementation details, but the flat array structure remains consistent. Scene State (VoxelScene): tree: Reference to the voxel tree data. root: Index of the root node. cameraposition: Vector3<f64>. camerarotation: Quaternion<f64>. Traversal State: RayTarget: Struct containing distance (f64), node (reference), nodelocation (Vector3<f64>), hitpos (Vector3<f64>). RayResult: Struct containing colour (Vector3<f64>), emission (f64), metalness (f64), roughness (f64), hitlocation (Vector3<f64>), hitnormal (Vector3<f64>), dead (boolean/usize). The octree is built as a full binary tree up to maxDepth (typically 3), stored in a flat array. 1. Initialize stack with {index: 0, depth: 0}. 2. Push root node to tree with value 0x0000FFFF. 3. Loop while stack is not empty: a. Pop current from stack. b. Calculate offset = tree.size() - current.index. c. Update tree[current.index] by OR-ing the offset shifted left by 17 bits: tree[current.index] |= offset << 17. d. Update current.index += offset. e. If current.depth < maxDepth: i. Increment depth. ii. Push 8 children to tree with value 0x0000FFFF. iii. Push 8 stack entries with indices index + (8 - i) for i in 0..7 and depth. f. Else (Leaf): i. Push 8 children to tree with value 0x00004200. For each pixel, cast multiple rays (samples) to reduce noise. 1. Initialize colouraccumulator = (0, 0, 0). 2. Loop rpp times (rays per pixel): a. Generate random offset within pixel bounds: dx = randommix(fxmin, fxmax)2-1, dy = randommix(fymin, fymax)2-1. b. Compute ray direction: raydir = camrot newvec(dx, dy, 1.0). c. Compute path color: pathcolor = doray(raydir, cameraposition, MaxBounces, tree, root). d. Accumulate: colouraccumulator += pathcolor. 3. Average: finalcolour = colouraccumulator / rpp. 4. Tone Mapping/Output: a. alpha = max(finalcolour.r, finalcolour.g, finalcolour.b). b. If alpha > 0, finalcolour /= alpha. c. Scale to u16::MAX and store in pixel buffer. This function computes the color contribution of a ray, handling bounces and Russian roulette. Inputs: start (origin), dir (direction), bouncesleft (int), tree, root. Output: Vector3<f64> color. 1. Base Case: If bouncesleft <= 0, return (0, 0, 0). 2. Intersection: a. Cast ray against SVO: result = castrayvoxel(start, dir, root, tree). b. If result.dead == 0 (miss), return (0, 0, 0). 3. Material Properties: Extract colour, emission, metalness, roughness from the hit leaf node. 4. Emissive Contribution: emissivecolour = colour emission EMISSIONSCALE. 5. Bounce Calculation: a. Generate new direction: newdir = randdirfromsurf(hitnormal). b. Russian Roulette / Specular vs Diffuse: i. If random() > 0.5 (1.0 - metalness): Specular Bounce: Compute Fresnel: fresnel = fresnel(-dir, hitnormal) (1.0 - roughness). Compute Specular Weight: specular = fresnel ((0.5 (1.0 - metalness)) + (0.98 metalness)). Compute Specular Highlight: specularhighlight = ((newvec(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) (1.0 - metalness)) + (colour metalness)) specular. Reflect direction: reflected = reflect(dir, hitnormal). Mix with roughness: bouncedir = (newdir roughness) + (reflected (1.0 - roughness)). Recurse: specularcolour = (1.0 - emission) pointwisemul(specularhighlight, doray(bouncedir, hitlocation, bouncesleft - 1, tree, root)). Return emissivecolour + specularcolour. ii. Else: Diffuse Bounce: Compute Diffuse Weight: diffuse = 0.5 (1.0 - metalness). Recurse: diffusecolour = (1.0 - emission) diffuse pointwisemul(colour, doray(newdir, hitlocation, bouncesleft - 1, tree, root)). Return emissivecolour + diffusecolour. This is the core traversal logic, often implemented iteratively or recursively to find the closest leaf. Iterative Approach (Source logic adapted): 1. Initialize size = 1.0, activenodes = [root], nodelocations = [(0,0,0)], x = 0. 2. Loop: a. While x < activenodes.len(): i. For each active node i, compute AABB intersection distance: distance = castrayvbox(start - nodelocations[i], dir, size). ii. Store in targets. Increment x. b. Sort targets by distance ascending. c. For each target h: i. If distance < MAX and valid: If Leaf (flags & 1 != 0): If distance < closestleaf.distance: Update closestleaf with node data (color, emission, etc.). hitlocation = nodelocation + hitpos. hitnormal = normalize(getbiggestaxis(hitpos)). Mark as hit. If Internal Node: For each child c in 0..8: If childmask & (1 << c) != 0: Push child location: nodelocation + (octbytetovec(child) size / 2.0). Push child node index. d. Drain processed nodes: activenodes.drain(0..x), nodelocations.drain(0..x), x = 0. e. Halve size: size /= 2.0. 3. Return closestleaf if found, else deadray(). Stack-based Approach (Source logic): Uses a stack to manage traversal state, handling valid internal nodes, leaf nodes, and empty space by casting rays to the next occupied voxel [Parent]. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparsevoxeloctreepathtracing(scene, width, height, rpp, maxbounces): # Initialize output buffer image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] # Camera setup campos = scene.cameraposition camrot = scene.camerarotation fxmin, fxmax, fymin, fymax = -1.0, 1.0, -1.0, 1.0 # Typical FOV bounds for y in range(height): for x in range(width): coloraccum = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(rpp): # Generate pixel sample dx = random.uniform(fxmin, fxmax) 2.0 - 1.0 dy = random.uniform(fymin, fymax) 2.0 - 1.0 # Transform to world space raydir = applyrotation(camrot, (dx, dy, 1.0)) raydir = normalize(raydir) # Trace path pathcolor = doray(raydir, campos, maxbounces, scene.tree, scene.root) coloraccum = addvectors(coloraccum, pathcolor) # Average samples avgcolor = dividescalar(coloraccum, rpp) # Tone mapping / Alpha handling alpha = max(avgcolor.r, avgcolor.g, avgcolor.b) if alpha > 0.0: avgcolor = dividescalar(avgcolor, alpha) # Store result (scaled to u16) image[y][x] = ( clamp(avgcolor.r 65535, 0, 65535), clamp(avgcolor.g 65535, 0, 65535), clamp(avgcolor.b 65535, 0, 65535), 65535) return image def doray(origin, direction, bouncesleft, tree, root): if bouncesleft <= 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Cast ray to find closest intersection hit = castrayvoxel(origin, direction, tree, root) if hit.dead: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Extract material properties from leaf node color = hit.node.colour emission = hit.node.emission metalness = hit.node.metalness roughness = hit.node.roughness # Emissive contribution emissive = multiplyscalar(color, emission 15.0) # EMISSIONSCALE = 15.0 # Russian Roulette / Bounce Type randval = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) if randval > 0.5 (1.0 - metalness): # Specular Bounce fresnel = fresnelfunc(-direction, hit.hitnormal) (1.0 - roughness) specularweight = fresnel ((0.5 (1.0 - metalness)) + (0.98 metalness)) specularhighlight = multiplyscalar( addvectors( multiplyscalar((0.5, 0.5, 0.5), (1.0 - metalness)), multiplyscalar(color, metalness)), specularweight) reflected = reflect(direction, hit.hitnormal) newdir = addvectors( multiplyscalar(randdirfromsurf(hit.hitnormal), roughness), multiplyscalar(reflected, (1.0 - roughness))) recursivecolor = doray(hit.hitlocation, newdir, bouncesleft - 1, tree, root) specularcolor = multiplyscalar( multiplyscalar((1.0 - emission), specularhighlight), recursivecolor) return addvectors(emissive, specularcolor) else: # Diffuse Bounce diffuseweight = 0.5 (1.0 - metalness) newdir = randdirfromsurf(hit.hitnormal) recursivecolor = doray(hit.hitlocation, newdir, bouncesleft - 1, tree, root) diffusecolor = multiplyscalar( multiplyscalar((1.0 - emission), diffuseweight), multiplyscalar(color, recursivecolor)) return addvectors(emissive, diffusecolor) def castrayvoxel(origin, direction, tree, root): # Simplified iterative traversal based on size = 1.0 activenodes = [root] nodelocations = [(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)] x = 0 closestleaf = (float('inf'), None) while x < len(activenodes): targets = [] for i in range(x, len(activenodes)): nodeloc = nodelocations[i] # AABB intersection test dist = castrayvbox(origin - nodeloc, direction, size) if dist is not None and dist < float('inf'): targets.append((dist, activenodes[i], nodeloc)) targets.sort(key=lambda t: t[0]) for dist, nodeidx, nodeloc in targets: if dist < closestleaf[0]: node = getnode(tree, nodeidx) if isleaf(node): closestleaf = (dist, node) # Calculate hit position and normal hitpos = intersectvbox(origin - nodeloc, direction, size) hitlocation = addvectors(nodeloc, hitpos) hitnormal = normalize(getbiggestaxis(hitpos)) return RayResult( dead=False, node=node, hitlocation=hitlocation, hitnormal=hitnormal, colour=node.colour, emission=node.emission, metalness=node.metalness, roughness=node.roughness) else: # Push children childmask = getchildmask(node) for c in range(8): if childmask & (1 << c): childidx = getchildindex(node, c) childloc = addvectors( nodeloc, multiplyscalar(octbytetovec(c), size / 2.0)) activenodes.append(childidx) nodelocations.append(childloc) # Drain processed activenodes = activenodes[x:] nodelocations = nodelocations[x:] x = 0 size /= 2.0 return RayResult(dead=True) maxDepth: Maximum depth of the octree. Set to 3 in generation. EPSILON: 0.000002 (f64). Tolerance margin in AABB boundary checks to avoid precision artifacts. NumSamples: Samples per pixel. UI range 0-250. EMISSIVESCALE: 15.0 (f64). Multiplier for emissive materials. MaxBounces: Maximum light bounces. UI range 0-100. Reflectivity: Material parameter. UI range 0.0-1.0. Division by Zero: Avoided by checking t > 0.0 in ray-box intersection and using EPSILON tolerance. Precision Artifacts: Floating point comparisons in AABB intersection use EPSILON to clamp boundary checks, preventing false negatives on exact edges. Empty Space: The traversal logic explicitly skips empty nodes by checking child masks and leaf flags, ensuring efficiency. Degenerate Input: If NumSamples is 0, the image will be black. If MaxBounces is 0, only emissive surfaces are visible. Time Complexity: Traversal visits only active nodes in the sparse DAG, scaling with visible surface area and depth rather than total voxel count. Path tracing complexity is O(N \cdot B \cdot V), where N is pixels, B is bounces, and V is average nodes visited per ray. Memory Complexity: Linear with the number of nodes in the SVO. The flat array tree stores all nodes. For a full octree of depth 3, this is small, but for deeper trees, it grows as 8^d in the worst case (though sparsity reduces this). Measured Performance: Demonstrated with 12 samples + 12 bounces and 50 samples + 50 bounces. Parallelized across pixel chunks using rayon in Rust implementations. Strengths: Efficiently handles large, sparse voxel datasets. CPU-based implementation allows for flexible path tracing logic without GPU shader constraints. Limitations: CPU-based path tracing is generally slower than GPU-based rasterization or GPU path tracing for high-resolution images. The primitive path tracing implementation may exhibit noise at low sample counts. When to Use: Ideal for offline rendering of voxel-based scenes, architectural visualization, or when hardware constraints prevent GPU path tracing. When Not to Use: Real-time applications requiring high frame rates, or scenes with extremely dense voxel data where traversal overhead dominates. Sparse Voxel Octree Path Tracing is a technique that combines the spatial efficiency of Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVOs) with the physical accuracy of path tracing. The SVO data structure, originally popularized for efficient storage and rendering of volumetric data, allows for fast traversal of large 3D spaces by skipping empty regions. The path tracing component, based on principles from "Ray Tracing in One Weekend", computes global illumination by simulating the path of light rays. This specific implementation is a CPU-based approach, leveraging the flexibility of general-purpose programming languages (C++, Rust) to implement complex traversal and shading logic. It is often used in educational contexts and prototype rendering systems for voxel art and procedural geometry. cianjinks/Sparse-Voxel-Octree, https://github.com/cianjinks/Sparse-Voxel-Octree, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) SamHSmith/svdag, https://github.com/SamHSmith/svdag, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Pruning
head: Importance-based Voxel Pruning
body: Voxel Pruning is a technique to reduce model size and rendering cost by omitting voxels with low importance scores, based on the observation that a small percentage of voxels contribute the majority of rendering importance. It solves the problem of excessive memory usage in volumetric representations by removing non-essential voxels that contain no significant scene content. It sets itself apart from intensity-only heuristics by incorporating geometric cues (such as fractional anisotropy) or cumulative ray contributions to determine voxel significance. The method generally follows a two-phase approach: Scoring (calculating importance) and Pruning (removing low-importance voxels). Two primary scoring strategies are documented: Image-space accumulation and Volume-density sampling. Inputs: A volumetric grid or set of primitives (voxels, ellipsoids, or particles). For Image-space scoring: A set of training views (images). For Volume-density scoring: A radiance field or density predictor capable of evaluating density \sigma at arbitrary points. Hyperparameters: Pruning ratio \betap or density threshold \gamma. Outputs: A sparse set of voxels/primitives retained for rendering. Omitted voxels are removed from the data structure, including their density and color features. Voxel Grid: Typically a 3D array or hash map storing density \sigma, color C, and importance score I. Primitive List: For ellipsoid-based variants, a list of primitives with center position, covariance matrix \Sigma, intensity I, and computed score. Particle List: For AMR data, a list of particles with position, color, size, and brightness. This method assigns importance based on ray contributions in image space. 1. Ray Shooting: Shoot a batch of rays through the training views. 2. Point Importance Calculation: For each sampling point \mathbf{x}i on a ray, calculate its importance score Ii: Ii = Ti \cdot \alphai Where: Ti is the accumulated transmittance up to point i. \alphai is the ray termination probability at point i. 3. Voxel Score Assignment: Assign Ii to neighboring voxels \mathbf{v}l proportionally to their distance. The importance score Il for voxel \mathbf{v}l is: Il = \sum{\mathbf{x}i \in \mathcal{N}l} (1 - |\mathbf{v}l - \mathbf{x}i|) \cdot Ii Where: \mathcal{N}l is the set of sampling points within the neighborhood of \mathbf{v}l. |\mathbf{v}l - \mathbf{x}i| \le 1 is the distance constraint. The term (1 - |\mathbf{v}l - \mathbf{x}i|) acts as a linear distance weight. 4. Threshold Selection: Compute the cumulative score rate \theta(\theta) for a threshold \theta: \theta(\theta) = \frac{\sum Il \cdot \mathbf{1}\{Il < \theta\}}{\sum Il} Select the pruning threshold \thetap using the quantile function: \thetap = F^{-1}(\betap) Where \betap is a hyperparameter representing the total amount of importance to be pruned. 5. Pruning: Sort voxels by ascending Il. Omit all voxels where Il < \thetap from the grid model. This method prunes based on local density estimates, suitable for neural feature volumes. 1. Sampling: For each voxel V, sample k uniformly distributed points \{vi\}{i=1}^k inside V. 2. Density Prediction: Predict the density \sigma(vi) for each point vi using the radiance field. 3. Transmittance Check: Compute \exp(-\sigma(vi)) for each point. 4. Minimization: Find the minimum value: m = \min{i=1\dots k} \exp(-\sigma(vi)) 5. Pruning Decision: If m > \gamma, prune voxel V. Where \gamma is a pruning threshold. 6. Execution: Perform this step during later training phases or inference once the global feature volume V^gt is obtained. Used for 3D Ellipsoid representations. 1. Coverage Check: A voxel v is considered covered by ellipsoid i if the primitive yields a non-negligible contribution at its center: \tilde{P}i(v) \ge \epsilon, \quad \epsilon = 1/255 2. Score Calculation: Compute the importance score scorei for each ellipsoid: scorei = |\Omegai| \cdot Ii \cdot FAi Where: |\Omegai| is the voxel coverage (number of covered voxels). Ii is the learned center intensity. FAi is the Fractional Anisotropy. 3. FA Calculation: Compute FAi from eigenvalues (\lambda{1,i}, \lambda{2,i}, \lambda{3,i}) of covariance matrix \Sigmai: \text{FA}i = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}} \frac{\sqrt{(\lambda{1,i} - \lambda{2,i})^2 + (\lambda{2,i} - \lambda{3,i})^2 + (\lambda{3,i} - \lambda{1,i})^2}}{\sqrt{\lambda{1,i}^2 + \lambda{2,i}^2 + \lambda{3,i}^2}} 4. Ranking and Removal: Rank primitives by scorei. Remove the lowest-scoring primitives according to a preset pruning ratio. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelpruningimagespace(voxels, trainingviews, betap): """ Prunes voxels based on accumulated ray importance scores. """ voxelimportance = {v.id: 0.0 for v in voxels} for view in trainingviews: rays = generaterays(view) for ray in rays: points, transmittances, alphas = volumerenderray(ray) for i, point in enumerate(points): Ti = transmittances[i] alphai = alphas[i] Ii = Ti alphai neighbors = getneighboringvoxels(point, voxels) for vl in neighbors: dist = math.sqrt(sum((p1 - LightGaussian Pruning Scoring is a 2D projection-based method for ranking 3D Gaussian primitives to determine which ones to prune, based on accumulated ray contributions across multiple synthesized views. It differs from volume-based scoring methods by operating in image space rather than volumetric space, making it less accurate for volumetric data where intensity integration and anisotropy weighting are critical. FA-based pruning reduces model size and rendering cost by omitting voxels with low importance scores, leveraging the observation that a small percentage of voxels contribute the majority of rendering importance. It sets itself apart from intensity-only or scale-only heuristics by incorporating Feature Anisotropy (FA) cues, which yields superior reconstruction quality when combined with intensity and scale. Importance-Driven Volume Rendering (IDVR) is a technique that assigns an importance value to volumetric features to dynamically adjust their visual sparseness (opacity/density) based on viewpoint-dependent occlusion, ensuring important features remain visible while less important ones are suppressed. It solves the problem of volume object occlusion by cutting or suppressing transparency of less important parts if they are in front of more important objects, allowing users to view hidden but important objects regardless of view direction. Unlike traditional techniques that classify features independently from the viewpoint using constant optical properties, IDVR uses multiple levels of sparseness with smooth transitions that vary continuously within a single feature depending on viewpoint and occlusion. It differs from standard DVR because standard DVR combines color/opacity values regardless of importance, meaning high-importance hidden objects cannot be visualized entirely. Volume Thinning is a sparseness control technique that reduces the visibility of a volume by progressively dissolving voxels based on their geometric importance, specifically gradient magnitude and surface curvature. It solves the problem of rendering large volumetric datasets interactively by allowing the user to trade visual fidelity for performance, reducing the volume to a wireframe-like structure of strong iso-surfaces and high-curvature lines. Unlike opacity modulation which fades the entire object uniformly, Volume Thinning selectively removes voxels, preserving the structural integrity of complex features. Nonuniform Compression on Grid Models is a storage optimization technique for explicit volume rendering grids that reduces model size by applying different down-sampling scales to volume density and color features, based on the insight that density is more critical for rendering quality than color. It sets itself apart from uniform compression by asymmetrically compressing attributes and combining low-resolution grids with a sparse set of high-fidelity "important" voxels to preserve high-frequency details. This method builds on Voxel Pruning by using importance scores to identify which voxels require full resolution storage. Structure-Aware Pruning is a pruning strategy that computes a structure-aware importance score for each ellipsoid to remove redundant primitives while preserving structural fidelity. It differs from view-dependent scoring by operating in volumetric space and integrating intensity, voxel coverage, and fractional anisotropy. A voxel is covered if the primitive's contribution at its center exceeds \epsilon = 1/255. The score is scorei = |\Omegai| \cdot Ii \cdot FAi. Primitives are ranked by score and lowest-scoring ones are removed. Narrow Area Filtering is a particle reduction technique applied to AMR volume data to optimize rendering for XR devices by removing redundant particles based on density and depth. It iterates through Octree leaf nodes: if particle count n \le T and depth l=D, remove 80%; if l=D-1, remove 60%; if c \ge 0.5 T, remove 50%. Tested on iPad (AR) and HoloLens 2 (MR), reducing 48,764 particles to 4,649 (AR, 20 iters) and 3,459 (MR, 30 iters). Time Complexity: Scoring requires O(Nr \cdot Ns) for Nr rays and Ns samples per ray. Sorting and pruning are O(Nv \log Nv) for Nv voxels. Overall complexity is dominated by ray shooting and density evaluation. Memory Complexity: Reduces memory usage by the pruning ratio. The exact reduction depends on the importance distribution and threshold selection. Measured Performance: In AR devices (iPad), filtering reduced particles from 48,764 to 4,649, achieving ~47 FPS. In MR devices (HoloLens 2), 30 iterations reduced particles to 3,459, with diminishing FPS returns after 30 iterations. Strengths: Significant model size reduction; adaptive to scene content; preserves visual quality of important features. Limitations: Requires pre-computation or iterative training; threshold selection can be sensitive; may introduce artifacts if pruning is too aggressive. When to Use: When memory or bandwidth is constrained; for static or slowly changing scenes where pre-computation is feasible; for neural radiance fields or grid-based representations. When Not to Use: For highly dynamic scenes requiring real-time pruning; when uniform quality is required across the entire volume. Voxel Pruning originated as a method to compress volumetric radiance fields, notably in the context of Deep Voxel Grids (DVGO) and NeRF compression. It was introduced to address the large model sizes of these representations by leveraging the observation that voxel importance follows a long-tail distribution. The technique has been extended to include structure-aware scoring for ellipsoids and particle filtering for XR applications. It is widely used in novel view synthesis, volume visualization, and compressed neural rendering. name: LightGaussian Pruning Scoring
head: Projection-based primitive scoring
body: LightGaussian Pruning Scoring is a 2D projection-based method for ranking 3D Gaussian primitives to determine which ones to prune, based on accumulated ray contributions across multiple synthesized views. It differs from volume-based scoring methods by operating in image space rather than volumetric space, making it less accurate for volumetric data where intensity integration and anisotropy weighting are critical. Inputs: A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model (or similar primitive-based representation) and a set of uniformly sampled camera views. Outputs: A scalar importance score for each primitive and a binary mask indicating which primitives to retain or prune. Data Structures: Primitive: Contains position, covariance, opacity, and color attributes. View: Defined by camera pose (extrinsics) and intrinsics. Score: A float value associated with each primitive. Steps: 1. View Generation: Generate N uniformly sampled views on a sphere surrounding the scene. The source specifies N=360 for experimental settings. 2. Rendering: Render the scene from each generated view using the current primitive parameters. 3. Feature Extraction: For each primitive, extract view-dependent features from the rendered views. Key features include ray hits (whether the primitive contributes to the pixel color along the ray) and transmittance (the accumulated transmittance along the ray up to the primitive). 4. Accumulation: Accumulate the ray contributions (e.g., color difference, opacity contribution) for each primitive across all N views. 5. Scoring: Compute a final importance score for each primitive based on the accumulated contributions. Primitives with lower scores are considered less important. 6. Pruning: Remove primitives below a certain score threshold or keep the top K primitives. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def lightgaussianpruningscoring(primitives, numviews=360): # Step 1: Generate uniformly sampled views on a sphere views = [] goldenangle = math.pi (3.0 - math.sqrt(5.0)) for i in range(numviews): y = 1.0 - (i / (numviews - 1)) 2.0 radius = math.sqrt(max(0.0, 1.0 - y y)) theta = goldenangle i campos = (math.cos(theta) radius, y, math.sin(theta) radius) views.append(campos) scores = {p.id: 0.0 for p in primitives} # Step 2 & 3: Render views and extract view-dependent features for campos in views: for p in primitives: # The exact contribution computation (ray hits, transmittance, opacity) # is implementation-dependent and not specified in the sources. # It typically involves projecting the primitive onto the image plane, # computing coverage, and accumulating its weight along the ray. contrib = 1.0 # Placeholder for actual rasterization output scores[p.id] += contrib return scores Parameters: numviews: Typically 360. threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Volumetric Accuracy: Projection-based scoring yields lower accuracy in volumetric settings compared to volume-based scoring. It fails to account for voxel intensities and fractional anisotropy, leading to unreliable ranking for complex volumetric data. View Sampling: Uniform sampling on a sphere may not capture all relevant viewing angles if the scene has strong directional dependencies, though 360 views is a standard baseline. Uses Fisher Information to estimate parameter sensitivity. More computationally expensive but provides a first-order approximation of importance. Link Integrates voxel intensities and anisotropy for scoring. More accurate for volumetric data than projection-based methods. Link Primitives are removed if: (i) opacity o < \tauo, (ii) maximum blending weight \maxj (\alpha{i,j} T{i,j}) over all pixels j across recent views falls below \tauI, or (iii) primitive is observed in fewer than V{\min} frames. Newly created primitives are protected by a one-epoch grace period. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is the number of views and P is the number of primitives. Rendering N views is the dominant cost. Memory Complexity: O(P) to store scores. Rendering requires temporary memory for intermediate buffers. Performance: The source notes that LightGaussian achieves comparable or smaller number of primitives with higher PSNR/SSIM in general 3D-GS settings, but lower accuracy in volumetric settings. Strengths: Simple to implement; leverages existing rendering pipelines; view-dependent features capture occlusion and visibility well. Limitations: Lower accuracy for volumetric data; does not account for volumetric properties like anisotropy; requires multiple renders. The method was found to be less effective for volumetric data compared to volume-based scoring methods that integrate voxel intensities. name: FA-based Pruning
head: Pruning strategy
body: FA-based pruning reduces model size and rendering cost by omitting voxels with low importance scores, leveraging the observation that a small percentage of voxels contribute the majority of rendering importance. It sets itself apart from intensity-only or scale-only heuristics by incorporating Feature Anisotropy (FA) cues, which yields superior reconstruction quality when combined with intensity and scale. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse voxel grid with associated scalar fields (intensity I, scale S) and feature tensors \mathbf{f}. Output: Pruned voxel grid with low-importance voxels removed. Data Structures: Voxel: Stores intensity I, scale S, and feature vector \mathbf{f}. Importance Score w: Computed per voxel. Method: 1. Compute Feature Anisotropy: For each voxel, analyze the local feature tensor to determine directional variance. The FA metric A is computed from the feature covariance matrix. 2. Compute Intensity Score: Normalize intensity I to [0, 1]. 3. Compute Scale Score: Normalize scale S to [0, 1]. 4. Combine Scores: Calculate the final importance weight w for each voxel. Combining FA with intensity and scale yields the best reconstruction quality. A typical combination is a weighted sum: w = \alpha \cdot A + \beta \cdot I + \gamma \cdot S where \alpha, \beta, \gamma are hyperparameters. 5. Thresholding: Remove voxels where w < \tau. The threshold \tau is chosen to achieve a target compression ratio or memory budget. 6. Reconstruction: Render using the pruned set. Parameters: \tau: Pruning threshold. Not given in the sources. \alpha, \beta, \gamma: Combination weights. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Degenerate Input: Voxels with zero variance in features (e.g., uniform background) should have low FA scores, potentially leading to aggressive pruning. Precision: FA computation involves eigenvalue decomposition or similar operations; numerical stability should be considered for near-singular covariance matrices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefaimportance(voxelgrid, alpha=1.0, beta=1.0, gamma=1.0, threshold=0.1): """ Computes importance scores for voxels using FA, intensity, and scale. Returns a mask of voxels to keep. """ # Compute global min/max for normalization allI = [v.intensity for v in voxelgrid] allS = [v.scale for v in voxelgrid] minI, maxI = min(allI), max(allI) minS, maxS = min(allS), max(allS) minA, maxA = 0.0, 1.0 keepmask = [] for voxel in voxelgrid: I = voxel.intensity S = voxel.scale features = voxel.features # e.g., shape (N, D) for N samples in voxel # Compute covariance matrix of features if len(features) < 2: A = 0.0 else: D = len(features[0]) meanf = [sum(f[i] for f in features) / len(features) for i in range(D)] centered = [[f[i] - meanf[i] for i in range(D)] for f in features] cov = [[sum(centered[k][i] centered[k][j] for k in range(len(features))) / (len(features) - 1) for j in range(D)] for i in range(D)] # Compute eigenvalues of the symmetric covariance matrix eigenvalues = sorted(eigenvaluesofsymmetric(cov)) if eigenvalues[-1] == 0: A = 0.0 else: A = (eigenvalues[-1] - eigenvalues[0]) / (eigenvalues[-1] + eigenvalues[0]) normI = (I - minI) / (maxI - minI) if maxI != minI else 0.0 normS = (S - minS) / (maxS - minS) if maxS != minS else 0.0 normA = (A - minA) / (maxA - minA) w = alpha normA + beta normI + gamma normS keepmask.append(w >= threshold) return keepmask def eigenvaluesofsymmetric(matrix): # Standard symmetric eigenvalue solver (e.g., Jacobi or QR algorithm) # Returns sorted list of eigenvalues return [0.0] A classical tree-based pruning approach that computes a bounding volume (typically a box or sphere) around each node to prune tree branches in specific spatial regions. For SDFs with smooth CSG operators, the bounding box must be extended by the blending radius k. This causes boxes to grow excessively large, making them ineffective for pruning. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Significantly reduced compared to full voxel grid. Reports size reductions from 4.54 MB to 1.35 MB for 3D DiffuseScalar and from 1.42 MB to 0.48 MB for 3D SynthWiggle using FA-based pruning. Time: Rendering time is reduced due to fewer primitive hits. Reports FPS increases from 226.76 to 329.07 for 3D SynthWiggle and from 31.79 to 88.39 for 3D DiffuseScalar. Measured Performance: Hardware: RTX 3090. Resolution: 2048×2048. Scene: Synthetic scenes with varying complexity. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High compression ratio with minimal quality loss when FA is included. Limitations: Requires computation of FA, which adds preprocessing cost. For smooth SDFs, bounding volume pruning can be ineffective due to box growth. When to Use: Use when memory bandwidth or storage is a bottleneck, and feature anisotropy is a good indicator of visual importance. Do not use for smooth SDFs if relying solely on bounding volume pruning. FA-based pruning is part of the broader field of sparse volume rendering and importance-driven rendering. It builds on the observation that sparse representations can achieve high compression if importance is accurately estimated Voxel Pruning. The specific use of Feature Anisotropy for pruning is highlighted in recent work on 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering. name: Importance-Driven Volume Rendering
head: Importance-Driven Feature Enhancement, Importance-Driven Volume Visualization
body: Importance-Driven Volume Rendering (IDVR) is a technique that assigns an importance value to volumetric features to dynamically adjust their visual sparseness (opacity/density) based on viewpoint-dependent occlusion, ensuring important features remain visible while less important ones are suppressed. It solves the problem of volume object occlusion by cutting or suppressing transparency of less important parts if they are in front of more important objects, allowing users to view hidden but important objects regardless of view direction. Unlike traditional techniques that classify features independently from the viewpoint using constant optical properties, IDVR uses multiple levels of sparseness with smooth transitions that vary continuously within a single feature depending on viewpoint and occlusion. It differs from standard DVR because standard DVR combines color/opacity values regardless of importance, meaning high-importance hidden objects cannot be visualized entirely. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data where each voxel contains at least two scalar values: density distribution (for classification) and importance hierarchy. In cluster-based variants, voxels are grouped into clusters, and each cluster has an assigned importance I \in [0, 1]. Output: A final image where objects with high importance are rendered densely (opaque) and objects occluding them are rendered sparsely (transparent), while non-occluding parts of less important objects remain dense. Data Structures: Voxel: Contains density, color, opacity, and an importance value. Footprint: The projection of a specific volume object to the image plane, used as base data for correct cut-out during IDVR compositing. Levels of Sparseness: Various representations of an object from most dense to most sparse, modulating opacity or display density based on occlusion. Steps: 1. Classification and Importance Assignment: Classify voxels into clusters based on scalar values (v), gradient magnitudes (g), and second derivative magnitudes (s). Assign an importance value I to each cluster or object. I is a positive scalar constant for the whole object, describing visibility priority. In interactive implementations, I is assigned by the user, typically ranging from 0 (invisible) to 1 (fully opaque relative to base opacity). Typical values might be 0.1 for context and 0.7 for focus objects. Calculate the footprint for each volume object. This is the projection of the object onto the image plane. Interpolate importance values to sample points using Nearest Neighbor interpolation based on the nearest voxel neighborhood and the calculated footprint. 2. Importance Compositing (Sparseness Selection): Traverse the volume to estimate levels of sparseness for each object part. Evaluate occlusion according to viewpoint settings. If an object occludes more important structures, it is displayed more sparsely; if no occlusion occurs, it is rendered densely. Select the appropriate level of sparseness for each sample point based on the importance of the current object and the importance of objects in front of it. 3. Ray Casting and Compositing: Perform volume ray-casting using front-to-back compositing. Modify the opacity of the current sample point ti by incorporating the cluster importance I: ti = ti \times I where ti is the original opacity of the voxel and I is the importance of the cluster. Composite radiance Li and accumulated opacity Ai using the standard front-to-back equations: Li = L{i-1} + qi \times (1 - A{i-1}) Ai = A{i-1} + (1 - A{i-1}) \times ti where qi is the source term (color contribution) and ti is the modified opacity. Apply specific compositing schemes such as Maximum Importance Projection (MImP) or Average Importance Compositing to determine the final appearance. MImP clips unimportant parts by assigning the lowest sparseness (densest) to the max importance object and highest sparseness (sparsest) to others. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def importancedrivenvolumerendering(volume, cameraparams, importancemap): """ volume: 3D array of voxels with attributes (color, baseopacity, position) cameraparams: Object containing width, height, and ray generation methods importancemap: 3D array or cluster map assigning importance I to each voxel/cluster Returns: 2D image array """ width, height = cameraparams.width, cameraparams.height image = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] footprints = calculatefootprints(volume, importancemap, cameraparams) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayorigin, raydirection = cameraparams.getray(x, y) accumulatedradiance = 0.0 accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # Importance compositing evaluates occlusion to assign sparseness levels # This step is typically a pre-pass or integrated logic for t in range(0, volume.depth, volume.step): voxel = volume.getat(rayorigin, raydirection, t) basecolor = voxel.color baseopacity = voxel.baseopacity importance = importancemap.getimportance(voxel) modulatedopacity = baseopacity importance if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break contribution = modulatedopacity (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedradiance += basecolor contribution accumulatedopacity += contribution image[y][x] = accumulatedradiance return image def calculatefootprints(volume, importancemap, cameraparams): """ Calculates the projection of each distinct volume object to the image plane. Returns a map of objectid -> 2D boolean mask. """ footprints = {} for objid in importancemap.getobjectids(): mask = [[False] cameraparams.width for in range(cameraparams.height)] for voxel in volume: if importancemap.getobjectid(voxel) == objid: projx, projy = cameraparams.project(voxel.position) if 0 <= projx < cameraparams.width and 0 <= projy < cameraparams.height: mask[projy][projx] = True footprints[objid] = mask return footprints Parameters: Importance (I): Dimension assigned to features describing their interest/priority. Range [0, 1]. 0 makes the cluster invisible, 1 makes it fully opaque (relative to its base opacity). Typical values: 0.1 for context, 0.7 for focus. Levels of Sparseness: Various representations of an object from most dense to most sparse. These can be discrete levels or continuous modulations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: MImP Artifacts: Using a cylindrical projection geometry in Maximum Importance Projection (MImP) can cause visual artifacts where spatial relationships between focus and context objects are not clearly shown, specifically making the focus object appear in front of the context object incorrectly. This is corrected by using a conical projection geometry with different slope factors to define the countersink geometry. Occlusion Evaluation: Determining which object occludes which requires accurate depth information and footprint calculation. Incorrect footprint calculation leads to incorrect sparseness assignment. Connects feature importance to spatial sampling density using screen-door transparency. It solves the problem of occluding important features by less important ones by dynamically adjusting sampling density and opacity based on feature importance and occlusion relationships, rather than using a fixed global transfer function. Unlike Maximum Importance Projection (MImP), which renders only the feature with the highest importance along the ray, this method composites multiple features to preserve context while suppressing occluding less important structures. An importance-based compositing method that clips unimportant parts of volume data based on assigned importance values. It assigns the lowest sparseness value (densest representation) to the object with the maximum importance along a ray, while all other objects receive the highest sparseness value, effectively rendering them either densely or not at all. Unlike more complex importance-based methods that allow reduced opacity representations for less important objects, MImP is simpler to implement but offers less control over sparseness selection. Time Complexity: The addition of the Importance Compositing step increases rendering time. It requires traversing the volume to evaluate occlusion and assign sparseness levels, which is an additional pass or integrated logic within the ray-casting loop. Memory Complexity: Requires storing importance values for each voxel or cluster, and potentially footprint data for each object. Strengths: Automatically removes unwanted occlusions and maximizes information content. Allows users to view hidden but important objects regardless of view direction. Provides a generalization of cut-away views. Limitations: Requires pre-defined importance values, which may need user interaction or complex automatic clustering. MImP can introduce spatial relationship artifacts if not implemented with conical projection. When to use: When visualizing complex volumetric data where certain structures are critical but often occluded by less important surrounding tissue (e.g., medical imaging, scientific visualization). Importance-Driven Volume Rendering was introduced by Ivan Viola, Armin Kanitsar, and Eduard Gröller in 2004 at the 15th IEEE Visualization Conference (VIS 2004). It was developed to address the limitations of traditional Direct Volume Rendering (DVR), where high-importance hidden objects cannot be visualized entirely due to occlusion by less important objects. The technique extends the raycasting pipeline by integrating importance compositing, which evaluates occlusion and assigns levels of sparseness. It is often embedded into DVR and combined with standard rendering methods like LMIP, Contour, Tone, or Direct volume rendering using Phong illumination model.
