name: Screen-Door Transparency with Importance Compositing
head: Smart Visibility via Screen-Door Transparency
body: Screen-Door Transparency with Importance Compositing is a rendering technique that resolves occlusion in volumetric data by linking feature importance to spatial sampling density using screen-door transparency. It solves the problem where interesting features are hidden by less important ones by dynamically adjusting sampling density and opacity based on occlusion relationships, rather than using a fixed global transfer function. Unlike Maximum Importance Projection (MImP), which renders only the single most important feature along a ray, this method composites multiple features, suppressing occluding context information while preserving non-occluding context. Inputs: Volumetric dataset with associated feature importance values; camera position and view direction. Outputs: 2D image with transparency effects. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: Stores scalar values and importance values I. Parameters: Grid Spacing: Inversely proportional to importance. Steps: 1. For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. 2. Determine the importance I of intersected features. 3. Assign grid spacing \Delta inversely proportional to importance: \Delta \propto 1/I. High importance (I \approx 1) uses small grid spacing (dense sampling), while low importance (I \approx 0) uses large grid spacing (sparse sampling). 4. Render focus features with dense sampling. 5. Render context features: if they occlude focus features, use sparse sampling; otherwise, use dense sampling. 6. Composite contributions using importance-based opacity and color: opaque/saturated for high importance, transparent/desaturated for low importance. Occluding context information is suppressed but not entirely removed, and the sum of importance of intersected features along the ray is considered. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderscreendoortransparency(volume, camera): height, width = camera.resolution image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayo = camera.origin rayd = camera.directionat(x, y) t = 0.0 cacc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] aacc = 0.0 while t < volume.maxdistance: voxel = volume.sampleat(rayo + rayd t) if voxel is not None: I = voxel.importance step = 1.0 / max(I, 1e-6) occludesfocus = False if not voxel.isfocus: for i in range(1, 5): futurev = volume.sampleat(rayo + rayd (t + i step)) if futurev is not None and futurev.isfocus: occludesfocus = True break if voxel.isfocus or not occludesfocus: pass else: step = 4.0 opacity = I c = voxel.color a = opacity cacc[0] = cacc[0] (1.0 - a) + c[0] a cacc[1] = cacc[1] (1.0 - a) + c[1] a cacc[2] = cacc[2] (1.0 - a) + c[2] a aacc = aacc + a (1.0 - aacc) if aacc >= 1.0: break t += step image[y][x] = cacc return image Edge Cases: Precision: Sparse sampling may introduce aliasing artifacts if the grid spacing is too large relative to the feature size. A voxel pruning technique that simulates optical transparency by spatially subsampling the voxel grid into a uniform, wireframe-like pattern. It solves the problem of rendering dense volumetric data efficiently by reducing visual clutter and computational load, allowing context features to be rendered sparsely while maintaining the structural integrity of focus features. Unlike standard alpha blending which requires sorting and accumulation, this method achieves transparency through geometric sparseness, where the "holes" in the voxel mesh allow background elements to show through, mimicking a semi-transparent view from a distance. Time Complexity: Depends on the sampling density. Focus features are rendered densely (O(N)), while occluding context features are rendered sparsely (O(N/k) where k is the sparseness factor). Non-occluding context features are rendered densely. Overall complexity is between dense and sparse volume rendering. Memory Complexity: Standard volumetric data structures. No additional memory for importance compositing beyond storing importance values per voxel. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Dynamically adjusts sampling density and opacity based on feature importance and occlusion relationships. Reduces visual clutter by suppressing occluding context information. Limitations: Occluding context is suppressed but not entirely removed, which may still cause some visual clutter. Requires pre-computed or real-time importance values. When to Use: When the goal is to highlight specific important features in a complex volumetric dataset while providing some context. When Not to Use: When all features are equally important or when occlusion is not a primary concern. Originated by Ivan Viola and M. Eduard Gröller in the context of "Smart Visibility" in visualization. The technique is part of a broader effort to apply illustration techniques (cutaway views, ghosted views) to volumetric data visualization. It was presented in the Eurographics conference proceedings. Illustrative Visualization for Medicine and Science, https://doi.org/10.2312/egt.20061068, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Screen-Door Transparency
body: Screen-Door Transparency is a voxel pruning strategy that simulates semi-transparency by distributing visible voxels uniformly to form a wireframe-like structure. It addresses visual clutter in dense volumetric datasets by allowing adjustment of a sparseness level, which controls the density of rendered voxels. Unlike opacity modulation or gradient-based thinning, it creates a regular pattern of occluding mesh and visible holes, analogous to a physical screen-door. Inputs: A volumetric dataset consisting of voxels. A sparseness factor controlling the target density of rendered voxels. Outputs: A subset of voxel coordinates to be rendered, selected such that their spatial distribution is uniform. Data Structures: The method operates on a voxel grid. Steps: 1. Define the sparseness factor. 2. Estimate which voxels should be rendered based on the sparseness level. 3. Select the voxels to be rendered such that they are distributed uniformly across the volume. 4. The selected voxels form a mesh, while the unselected voxels form holes. 5. Render the selected voxels; the mesh fully occludes background data, while the holes allow visibility. Formulas: The sources do not provide a specific mathematical formula for voxel selection based on the sparseness factor. The selection relies on maintaining a uniform spatial distribution. Parameters: Sparseness factor: Controls the density of the rendered voxel subset. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Smooth transitions: Abrupt changes in sparseness can cause misinterpretations; smooth modulation between levels should be applied. Distance blending: From a certain distance, the holes and mesh blend together to produce a semi-transparent impression. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def screendoortransparency(voxelgrid, sparsenessfactor): """ Selects voxels for rendering based on a sparseness factor to form a uniform wireframe-like structure. The sources do not specify the exact selection algorithm, so a deterministic grid subsampling is used. """ selectedvoxels = [] # Map sparsenessfactor [0.0, 1.0) to a grid stride # 0.0 -> stride 1 (all voxels), 0.5 -> stride 2, 0.75 -> stride 4, etc. stride = max(1, int(1.0 / (1.0 - sparsenessfactor + 1e-9))) for x in range(voxelgrid.shape[0]): for y in range(voxelgrid.shape[1]): for z in range(voxelgrid.shape[2]): if (x % stride == 0) and (y % stride == 0) and (z % stride == 0): selectedvoxels.append((x, y, z)) return selectedvoxels Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Creates a regular, grid-like pattern of holes and mesh that simulates semi-transparency effectively. Allows smooth transitions between levels of sparseness to reduce visual clutter and prevent misinterpretations. Limitations: The uniform distribution may not align with feature locations, potentially missing non-uniformly distributed data. The semi-transparent impression relies on viewing distance, as holes and mesh must blend from afar. When to use it: When a regular, grid-like visual structure is preferred to reduce clutter in dense volumes. When not to use it: When high-fidelity detail preservation is required at close viewing distances, as the wireframe structure obscures fine geometry. Origin: Introduced in the context of Importance-Driven Volume Rendering by Viola et al. in 2004/2005. History and Development: Based on the analogy of a physical screen-door consisting of a mesh and holes. The mesh occludes background data while holes allow visibility. This concept was adapted to volumetric data to define levels of sparseness. It is frequently compared with Color and Opacity Modulation and Volume Thinning. Where it is used: Volume visualization to enhance feature visibility and reduce clutter in dense datasets. name: Maximum Importance Projection (MImP)
body: Maximum Importance Projection (MImP) is an importance-driven volume rendering compositing method that displays the object with the highest importance value along a ray densely, while rendering all other intersected objects as fully transparent. It solves the problem of visual clutter in volumetric data by acting as a cut-away view, where space in front of the most important structure is clipped. Unlike sibling methods that allow variable sparseness levels for multiple objects, MImP offers a binary choice: objects are either rendered with maximum density or not at all, making it simpler to implement but offering less control over partial visibility. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric dataset, importance values Io for each object/region, camera parameters (view direction, projection type), and a depth buffer containing the "last-hit" depth for each pixel. Output: A 2D image where the highest-importance object is visible, and occluding lower-importance objects are removed. Data Structures: Depth Footprint: A 2D image (same resolution as the output) where each pixel i stores the depth zi of the last sample of the highest-importance object along the corresponding ray. Distance Field: A 2D image derived from the depth footprint, storing the distance di of each pixel from the footprint boundary, computed via a 2D chamfer distance transform. Gradient Field: A 3D vector field (or modified gradient values) used to simulate the lighting of the cut-away surface. Parameters: sc: The slope of the countersink (frustum slope). Typical values depend on the desired visual effect; a steeper slope creates a sharper cut, while a shallower slope creates a more gradual transition. e{max}: The maximum depth value found in the depth footprint of the focus object. Steps: 1. Identify Focus Object: For each ray, determine the object with the maximum importance value I{max}. This object is the "focus" object for that ray. 2. Generate Depth Footprint: Render the volume to determine the depth of the last-hit sample for the focus object at each pixel. Store these depths in the depth buffer. 3. Compute Distance Field: Apply a 2D chamfer distance transform to the depth footprint. This produces a distance value di for each pixel i, representing the distance from the pixel to the boundary of the footprint. 4. Calculate New Entry Points (Conical MImP): Find e{max}, the maximum depth value in the footprint. For each pixel i, calculate the new starting depth ei for the ray using the formula: ei = e{max} - di \times sc where di is the distance value from the chamfer transform and sc is the countersink slope. Note: For cylindrical MImP, ei is simply e{max} (or the ray starts at the footprint depth without scaling), resulting in a vertical clipping plane. 5. Modify Ray Traversal: During raycasting, for any ray where the calculated new entry point ei is closer to the eye than the original footprint depth, change the ray's starting point to ei. For cylindrical MImP, simply skip all ray samples that are ahead of (closer to the eye than) the focus object's depth. 6. Simulate Cut-Out Geometry (Conical MImP): To render the newly exposed surface correctly, modify the gradient vector at the first ray sample on any modified ray (where the start point was changed). Calculate the gradient components: The two components parallel to the image plane are estimated from the gradient of the 2D distance field. The z-component (view direction) is set to the slope factor sc. Scale up the gradient magnitude, as gradients inside objects are typically small. 7. Composite: Render the focus object using its standard dense representation (full opacity). Render all other objects along the ray with the highest level of sparseness (fully transparent/ignored). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemimpdepthfootprint(volume, importancemap, camera): """ Renders the volume to find the last-hit depth of the highest importance object. Returns a 2D array 'depthfootprint' of size (width, height). """ width, height = camera.resolution depthfootprint = np.zeros((height, width)) # Simplified ray traversal logic for y in range(height): for x in range(width): ray = camera.getray(x, y) maximportance = -infinity lasthitdepth = 0 # Traverse ray through volume for sample in ray.traverse(volume): objid = sample.objectid imp = importancemap.getimportance(objid) if imp > maximportance: maximportance = imp lasthitdepth = sample.depth depthfootprint[y, x] = lasthitdepth return depthfootprint def computechamferdistance(depthfootprint): """ Applies a 2D chamfer distance transform to the depth footprint. Returns a 2D array 'distancefield' where each pixel holds the distance to the nearest non-zero (or boundary) pixel in the footprint. """ # The chamfer distance transform calculates the distance from each pixel # to the nearest edge of the footprint. # Implementation detail: Standard 2-pass algorithm (e.g., 3-4 or 7-5 distance). # Here we assume a library function or standard implementation exists. distancefield = chamfertransform2d(depthfootprint) return distancefield def calculatenewentrypoints(depthfootprint, distancefield, slopesc): """ Calculates the new starting depth for each ray to create a conical frustum. """ height, width = depthfootprint.shape emax = np.max(depthfootprint) newentrypoints = np.zeros((height, width)) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): di = distancefield[y, x] # Formula: ei = emax - di sc newentrypoints[y, x] = emax - di slopesc return newentrypoints def rendermimp(volume, importancemap, camera, newentrypoints): """ Renders the final image using MImP logic. """ width, height = camera.resolution image = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): ray = camera.getray(x, y) startdepth = newentrypoints[y, x] # Determine the focus object for this ray (max importance) # In a real implementation, this might be pre-computed or determined # during the initial footprint pass. focusobj = getfocusobjectforray(ray, importancemap) # Traverse ray starting from the modified entry point color = np.zeros(3) alpha = 0.0 # We only render the focus object densely; others are skipped for sample in ray.traverse(volume, start=startdepth): if sample.objectid == focusobj: # Compute shading # For conical MImP, modify gradient at the first sample if sample.depth == startdepth: gradient = computecutoutgradient(x, y, slopesc, distancefield) else: gradient = sample.gradient shading = computeshading(sample.color, gradient, lightdirection) # Standard volume compositing for the focus object alphasample = sample.opacity color = color + shading alphasample (1.0 - alpha) alpha = alpha + alphasample (1.0 - alpha) if alpha >= 1.0: break image[y, x] = color return image def computecutoutgradient(x, y, slopesc, distancefield): """ Computes the modified gradient for the first sample on a modified ray. """ # Estimate two components from the gradient of the 2D distance field # Assuming distancefield is a scalar field, we compute its spatial gradient gradd = computegradient2d(distancefield, x, y) # The z-component is constant, equal to the slope factor # Note: Coordinate system conventions may vary; here z is view direction gradient = np.array([gradd.x, gradd.y, slopesc]) # Scale up the gradient as internal gradients are small gradient = gradient scalingfactor return normalize(gradient) Time Complexity: The method requires an initial pass to compute the depth footprint and distance field (O(N) for N pixels), followed by the main raycasting pass. The distance transform is fast, typically linear in the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the depth footprint and the distance field, both of size O(W \times H) where W, H are image dimensions. Strengths: Simple to implement compared to other importance-based methods; fast execution due to binary sparseness (dense or transparent). Limitations: Suffers from spatial arrangement ambiguity similar to Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) if cylindrical clipping is used. Cylindrical MImP causes loss of spatial impression in parallel projection. Less control over sparseness selection compared to methods like Average Importance Compositing. When to use: When the goal is to quickly isolate the most important structure in a volume without occlusion from less important structures, and computational resources are limited. When not to use: When detailed spatial context of occluded structures is required, or when variable levels of transparency for multiple objects are needed. Maximum Importance Projection (MImP) was introduced as part of Importance-Driven Volume Rendering. It was proposed by Viola et al. in 2004. The method is an adaptation of Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) to importance values, where the "intensity" is replaced by an "importance" metric assigned to volumetric objects. It was developed to provide a simple, automatic focus-and-context visualization technique that generalizes cut-away views. name: Importance-Driven Volume Rendering with Frustum Cutout
head: Frustum IDVR, IDVR design
body: A view-dependent cutout technique that creates a frustum-shaped void around a Volume of Interest (VOI) to allow detailed examination of internal structures while maintaining correct depth perception and visibility of the VOI from any viewing angle. It differs from the original Viola et al. (2004) conical cutout by using a frustum shape, which solves the drawback where nearby structures at the same depth of the VOI could be covered by surrounding tissue. The method uses a two-pass raycast rendering approach to define a cutout geometry based on the depth of the VOI. Inputs: Volumetric data containing the VOI, ray entry points texture TR, ray exit points texture TE. Outputs: Cutout depth texture TC (defining the frustum surface), intermediate depth texture TV (from Pass 1). Texture TV (Pass 1 Output): 4-component floating-point texture. Fields: x, y, z coordinates of the deepest VOI voxel hit by the ray, and accumulated length la along the ray until that voxel. If a ray does not hit the VOI, all four values are set to zero. 1. For each pixel, define a view ray using entry points from TR and exit points from TE. 2. Trace the ray through the volume to find the deepest voxel belonging to the VOI. 3. Calculate the accumulated length la from the ray origin to this deepest voxel. 4. Store the coordinates (x, y, z) of this voxel and la into the corresponding texel in TV. 5. If the ray misses the VOI entirely, store (0, 0, 0, 0) in TV. 1. For each pixel, retrieve the ray entry point PR from TR. 2. Determine a reference texel PV in TV relative to PR. Three implementations are defined: Implementation 1 (P{V1}): Search for a texel in TV with la > 0 within a maximum distance d in X and Y directions from the texel coordinates of PR. Iterate from the texel with the same coordinates as PR outwards to distance d. Select P{V1} that minimizes the Euclidean distance |PR P{V1}|. Implementation 2 (P{V2}): Search for a texel in TV with la > 0 within distance d in X and Y directions from PR. Iterate starting from 0, checking in \pm d in X and Y. Select P{V2} that creates a vector PR P{V2} with the minimum angle between PR P{V2} and the X or Y axis. Terminate iteration if a sufficient P{V2} is found. Implementation 3 (P{Vd}): Search for a texel in TV with la > 0 within distance \pm d in X and Y directions from PR. Select P{Vd} that has the highest la value among candidates. This approach neglects small outliers to create a smoother surface. 3. Let V be the voxel corresponding to the selected PV (or P{Vd}). 4. Calculate the maximum search radius r1: r1 = \sqrt{d^2 + d^2}, with constraint d^2 + d^2 \ge |PR PV|. 5. Construct vector RV: V is the voxel of the VOI corresponding to PV. R is defined using the congruence theorem of triangles, constructing an edge with a 90-degree angle from the view ray to V. RV is the vector representing this geometric construction. For Implementation 3, use P{Vd} to calculate PR P{Vd} and derive R{Vd}. 6. Determine if the ray hits the top surface of the frustum: If |RV| \le r2 (where r2 \le r1), the ray hits the top surface. 7. Calculate the depth value c of the top surface of the frustum for the current view ray: For Implementations 1 and 2: c = |RV| - |RV| \frac{|PR PV| - r2}{r1 - r2}. For Implementation 3: c = |R{Vd}| - |R{Vd}| \frac{|PR PV| - r2}{r1 - r2}. 8. If the ray does not hit the top surface (|RV| > r2), the cutout depth is determined by the frustum face geometry. d: Maximum distance in X and Y directions for searching texels in TV relative to PR. Typical value: Not given in the sources. r2: Radius limiting the top surface size. Constraint: r2 \le r1. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Circular Artifacts: Implementation 1 (P{V1}) produces circular artifacts around small parts of the VOI that stick out or where depth changes occur. Hard Edges: Implementation 2 (P{V2}) produces hard edges in diagonal orientation. Smoothness: Implementation 3 (P{Vd}) provides the smoothest result with homogeneous depth values. No Hit: If the ray does not hit the VOI, TV contains zeros, and no cutout is generated for that ray. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computefrustumcutout(TR, TE, d, r2): # Pass 1: Generate Depth Texture TV width, height = TR.width, TR.height TV = [[None] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): PR = TR[y][x] # (x, y, z) PE = TE[y][x] # (x, y, z) raydir = normalize(subtract(PE, PR)) # Trace ray through volume to find deepest VOI voxel # Sources do not specify the exact traversal algorithm; standard ray marching is used. hit = traceraytodeepestvoi(PR, raydir) if hit is not None: TV[y][x] = [hit.x, hit.y, hit.z, hit.la] else: TV[y][x] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Pass 2: Define Cutout TC = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] r1 = math.sqrt(d2 + d2) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): PR = TR[y][x] PVtexel = TV[y][x] if PVtexel[3] == 0: continue # No VOI hit, no cutout # Implementation 3 (Recommended for smoothness) bestPVd = None bestla = -1.0 xmin = max(0, x - d) xmax = min(width - 1, x + d) ymin = max(0, y - d) ymax = min(height - 1, y + d) for sy in range(ymin, ymax + 1): for sx in range(xmin, xmax + 1): candidate = TV[sy][sx] if candidate[3] > 0: distsq = (sx - x)2 + (sy - y)2 if distsq <= d2: if candidate[3] > bestla: bestla = candidate[3] bestPVd = candidate if bestPVd is None: continue PVdpos = (bestPVd[0], bestPVd[1], bestPVd[2]) vecPRPVd = subtract(PVdpos, PR) lenPRPVd = length(vecPRPVd) PE = TE[y][x] raydir = normalize(subtract(PE, PR)) vecOV = subtract(PVdpos, PR) projlen = dot(vecOV, raydir) projvec = scale(raydir, projlen) perpvec = subtract(vecOV, projvec) lenRVd = length(perpvec) if lenRVd <= r2: c = projlen else: numerator = lenPRPVd - r2 denominator = r1 - r2 if denominator == 0: c = lenRVd else: c = lenRVd - lenRVd (numerator / denominator) TC[y][x] = c return TC def subtract(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def length(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def normalize(v): l = length(v); return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def scale(v, s): return (v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s) Time Complexity: Two passes over the image resolution. Pass 1 is standard volume raycasting. Pass 2 involves a local search of radius d for each pixel, making it O(W \cdot H \cdot d^2). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for TR, TE, TV, and TC. TV stores 4 floats per pixel. Strengths: Maintains correct depth perception; view-dependent; handles complex VOI structures better than conical cutouts by using a section-like plane. Implementation 3 provides smooth depth values. Limitations: Circular artifacts (Impl 1) or hard edges (Impl 2) if not using Impl 3. Performance depends on d. When to use: When detailed examination of internal structures of a VOI is required while maintaining spatial context and depth cues. The method was developed by Hänel et al. (2014) as a modification of the Importance-Driven Volume Rendering (IDVR) algorithm by Viola et al. (2004). The original IDVR used a conical cutout, which had the drawback that nearby structures at the same depth of the VOI could be covered by surrounding tissue (e.g., brain tissue). The frustum cutout expands the cutout using a section-like plane aligned with the back side of the VOI to solve this issue. It was used in the interactive 3D visualization of structural changes in the brain of a person with corticobasal syndrome. Interactive 3D visualization of structural changes in the brain of a person with corticobasal syndrome., https://archive.org/details/pubmed-PMC4017140, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Volume Thinning
body:
Volume Thinning is a sparseness control technique that reduces volume visibility by progressively dissolving voxels according to their gradient magnitude and surface curvature. It enables interactive rendering of large datasets by trading visual fidelity for performance, reducing the volume to a wireframe-like structure of strong iso-surfaces and high-curvature lines. Unlike opacity modulation, which fades the entire object uniformly, Volume Thinning selectively removes voxels to preserve structural features. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset V with scalar values d(v), pre-computed gradient 
abla d(v), and curvature \kappa(v). Output: A sorted voxel list L and a sparseness factor \alpha \in [0, 1] determining the render subset. Data Structures: The core data structure is a list of voxel records containing position (x, y, z), data value d, gradient magnitude |
abla d|, and curvature magnitude |\kappa|. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute gradient magnitude |
abla d| and curvature magnitude |\kappa| for all voxels. 2. Sorting: Sort voxels into list L using a two-key sort: primary key is gradient magnitude |
abla d| (descending), secondary key is curvature magnitude |\kappa| (descending). 3. Sparseness Application: Given sparseness factor \alpha (1.0 is full, 0.0 is empty), compute cutoff index k = \lfloor \alpha \cdot N{	ext{total}} floor. The active set is L[0 \dots k-1]. 4. Rendering: Render only voxels in the active set. As \alpha decreases, low-gradient regions are removed first, retaining strong iso-surfaces; further reduction removes iso-surfaces until only high-curvature areas remain. Formulas: Gradient Magnitude: |
abla d| = \sqrt{( rac{\partial d}{\partial x})^2 + ( rac{\partial d}{\partial y})^2 + ( rac{\partial d}{\partial z})^2}. Curvature Magnitude: |\kappa| is derived from the second derivatives (Hessian matrix) of the data value. Parameters: Sparseness Factor (\alpha): Controls thinning level. Typical values are 0.75, 0.5, and 0.25. Gradient Threshold: A hard threshold on gradient magnitude filters voxels before sorting in some variants. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Gradient and curvature calculations are sensitive to noise. Boundary Conditions: Derivatives at volume boundaries require padding or one-sided differences. Degenerate Input: Voxels with zero gradient and zero curvature (e.g., uniform background) sort to the end and are excluded first. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumethinningpreprocess(volume): voxels = [] for x in range(volume.width): for y in range(volume.height): for z in range(volume.depth): gradmag = computegradientmagnitude(volume, x, y, z) curvmag = computecurvaturemagnitude(volume, x, y, z) voxels.append({'pos': (x, y, z), 'value': volume[x, y, z], 'gradmag': gradmag, 'curvmag': curvmag}) return voxels def computegradientmagnitude(volume, x, y, z): dx = volume[x + 1, y, z] - volume[x - 1, y, z] if 0 < x < volume.width - 1 else 0.0 dy = volume[x, y + 1, z] - volume[x, y - 1, z] if 0 < y < volume.height - 1 else 0.0 dz = volume[x, y, z + 1] - volume[x, y, z - 1] if 0 < z < volume.depth - 1 else 0.0 return (dx2 + dy2 + dz2)0.5 def computecurvaturemagnitude(volume, x, y, z): dxx = volume[x + 1, y, z] - 2 volume[x, y, z] + volume[x - 1, y, z] if 0 < x < volume.width - 1 else 0.0 dyy = volume[x, y + 1, z] - 2 volume[x, y, z] + volume[x, y - 1, z] if 0 < y < volume.height - 1 else 0.0 dzz = volume[x, y, z + 1] - 2 volume[x, y, z] + volume[x, y, z - 1] if 0 < z < volume.depth - 1 else 0.0 return abs(dxx + dyy + dzz) def volumethinningsort(voxels): voxels.sort(key=lambda v: v['curvmag'], reverse=True) voxels.sort(key=lambda v: v['gradmag'], reverse=True) return voxels def volumethinningrender(voxels, sparsenessfactor): if sparsenessfactor <= 0: return [] numtorender = int(sparsenessfactor len(voxels)) return voxels[:numtorender] An optimization for interactive back-to-front compositing using shear-warp projection. It maintains spatial consistency to allow alpha-blending while skipping voxels with low gradient magnitude. Definition: Extracts potentially contributing voxels into a list, storing position, data value, gradient direction, and magnitude. Filters voxels by keeping only those with gradient magnitude above a threshold, typically retaining ~25% of voxels. Steps: 1. Extract voxels with |
abla d| > 	ext{threshold}. 2. Group voxels into slices for each principal viewing axis (-x, y, z). 3. Within each slice, sort voxels by gradient magnitude. 4. During rendering, skip voxels mapped to black by the gradient magnitude windowing function g(|
abla|), which are located at the end of the sorted slice list. Comparison: Compared to MIP ordering, significantly more voxels must be rendered because skipping is based only on 'surfaceness' (gradient magnitude), not the view-dependent contour term. Time Complexity: Preprocessing is O(N) for gradient/curvature computation and sorting, where N is the voxel count. Rendering is O(\alpha N) where \alpha is the sparseness factor. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the voxel list with gradient and curvature attributes. Measured Performance: Tested on datasets of resolution 512 	imes 512 	imes 87 (Leopard Gecko) and 256 	imes 256 	imes 610 (Monster Study). The method achieves high frame rates by reducing processed voxels, with only ~25% typically included in the active set for gradient-based filtering. Strengths: Preserves structural features (iso-surfaces, ridges) while removing smooth regions. Allows smooth transition from full volume to wireframe representation. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of gradient and curvature, adding preprocessing time. The visual result is view-independent, meaning the thinning pattern does not adapt to the camera position. When to use: Interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets where structural features are more important than smooth shading. When not to use: When view-dependent contour enhancement is required, or when smooth, continuous surfaces are critical. Volume Thinning was introduced in the context of Importance-Driven Volume Rendering by Viola et al. in 2004. It is part of a broader effort to enable interactive rendering of large volumetric datasets by focusing computational resources on visually important voxels. The technique sorts voxels based on gradient and curvature magnitudes to progressively dissolve iso-surfaces into high-curvature lines. name: Nonuniform Compression on Grid Models
head: Importance-based Nonuniform Compression
body: Nonuniform Compression on Grid Models is a storage optimization technique for explicit volume rendering grids that reduces model size by applying different down-sampling scales to volume density and color features. The method operates on the insight that volume density contributes more critically to rendering quality than color features. It sets itself apart from uniform compression by asymmetrically compressing attributes and combining low-resolution grids with a sparse set of high-fidelity "important" voxels to preserve high-frequency details. This method builds on Voxel Pruning by using importance scores to identify which voxels require full resolution storage. Inputs: Original explicit grid model V = \{V\sigma, Vc\}, where V\sigma is the volume density grid and Vc is the color feature grid. Outputs: Compressed representation consisting of down-sampled grids \{\hat{V}\sigma, \hat{V}c\} and a list of important voxels with their original high-resolution values. Data Structures: 1. Down-sampled Grids: \hat{V}\sigma and \hat{V}c stored at reduced resolutions. 2. Important Voxels List: A list of tuples containing the 3D coordinates (x, y, z) and the original high-resolution values (\sigma, c) for voxels identified as important. Parameters: Sc: Down-sampling ratio for color features. Typical value: 4. S\sigma: Down-sampling ratio for volume density. Typical value: 2. Ray set: A large set of rays cast across wide views for importance estimation. Steps: 1. Calculate Importance Scores: For each voxel vl in the original grid, calculate its importance score Il by casting a large set of rays across wide views and sampling points xi. The score is the sum of contributions from all sampling points influenced by the voxel: Il = \sumi \mathbb{1}{\{xi \in \iota(vl)\}} \cdot w{i,l} \cdot Ti \cdot \alphai Where xi is a sampling point on a ray. The indicator function \mathbb{1}{\{xi \in \iota(vl)\}} equals 1 if xi is within the neighborhood of voxel vl, and 0 otherwise. The neighborhood is defined as \iota(vl) = \{vl + \delta: \delta \in [-1, 1]^3\}. The term w{i,l} is the linear interpolation weight of voxel vl for point xi, determined by the distance between xi and the 8 adjacent voxels. The terms Ti and \alphai are the transmittance and opacity at point xi, computed via standard volume rendering accumulation. 2. Identify Important Voxels: Sort all voxels by their importance scores Il in decreasing order. Select a subset of voxels with the largest scores to store at full resolution. Empirical analysis shows that approximately 17% of voxels contribute to 83% of the overall importance, and 10% contribute to 66%. 3. Compress Grids: Apply down-sampling operations to the original grids using the specified ratios: \hat{V}c = \downarrow{Sc}(Vc) \hat{V}\sigma = \downarrow{S\sigma}(V\sigma) Where \downarrowS denotes the down-sampling operation by factor S. 4. Store Compressed Model: Save the down-sampled grids \{\hat{V}\sigma, \hat{V}c\} and the list of important voxels with their original values. 5. Decompression (One-time Deployment): To recover the grid for rendering, up-sample the compressed grids \{\hat{V}\sigma, \hat{V}c\} to the original grid size using tri-linear interpolation. Then, replace the values at the coordinates of the stored important voxels with their original high-resolution values to obtain the recovered grid \{\tilde{V}\sigma, \tilde{V}c\}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def downsamplegrid(grid, factor): """Downsamples a 3D grid by taking every factor-th element along each axis.""" return grid[::factor,::factor,::factor] def trilinearinterpolate(grid, x, y, z): """Performs tri-linear interpolation at continuous coordinates (x, y, z) on a 3D grid.""" x0, y0, z0 = math.floor(x), math.floor(y), math.floor(z) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 dx, dy, dz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 # Clamp to grid bounds x0, x1 = max(0, min(x0, grid.shape[0]-1)), max(0, min(x1, grid.shape[0]-1)) y0, y1 = max(0, min(y0, grid.shape[1]-1)), max(0, min(y1, grid.shape[1]-1)) z0, z1 = max(0, min(z0, grid.shape[2]-1)), max(0, min(z1, grid.shape[2]-1)) c00 = (1-dx)grid[x0, y0, z0] + dxgrid[x1, y0, z0] c01 = (1-dx)grid[x0, y0, z1] + dxgrid[x1, y0, z1] c10 = (1-dx)grid[x0, y1, z0] + dxgrid[x1, y1, z0] c11 = (1-dx)grid[x0, y1, z1] + dxgrid[x1, y1, z1] c0 = (1-dy)c00 + dyc10 c1 = (1-dy)c01 + dyc11 return (1-dz)c0 + dzc1 def upsamplegrid(compressed, originalshape): """Upsamples a compressed grid to the original resolution using tri-linear interpolation.""" recovered = [0.0] (originalshape[0] originalshape[1] originalshape[2]) for x in range(originalshape[0]): for y in range(originalshape[1]): for z in range(originalshape[2]): cx, cy, cz = x / compressed.shape[0], y / compressed.shape[1], z / compressed.shape[2] recovered[x originalshape[1] originalshape[2] + y originalshape[2] + z] = trilinearinterpolate(compressed, cx, cy, cz) return recovered def calculateimportancescores(gridsigma, gridcolor, rays): """Calculates importance score for each voxel based on ray sampling.""" voxelcount = gridsigma.shape[0] gridsigma.shape[1] gridsigma.shape[2] importancescores = [0.0] voxelcount for ray in rays: # Sample points along the ray points = [ray.origin + t ray.direction for t in ray.sampledistances] for point in points: # Standard volume rendering accumulation for Ti and alphai sigmai, alphai, transmittancei = 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 # Simplified accumulation for demonstration; in practice, integrate along ray segment sigmai = trilinearinterpolate(gridsigma, point.x, point.y, point.z) alphai = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai ray.stepsize) transmittancei = math.exp(-sigmai ray.stepsize) # Find influencing voxels (neighbors within [-1, 1]^3) influencingvoxels = [] for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: nx, ny, nz = math.floor(point.x) + dx, math.floor(point.y) + dy, math.floor(point.z) + dz if 0 <= nx < gridsigma.shape[0] and 0 <= ny < gridsigma.shape[1] and 0 <= nz < gridsigma.shape[2]: influencingvoxels.append((nx, ny, nz)) for voxelidx in influencingvoxels: # Calculate interpolation weight w{i,l} weight = trilinearinterpolate(gridsigma, point.x, point.y, point.z) # Weight proportional to contribution # Map 3D index to 1D idx = voxelidx[0] gridsigma.shape[1] gridsigma.shape[2] + voxelidx[1] gridsigma.shape[2] + voxelidx[2] # Add contribution to importance score importancescores[idx] += weight transmittancei alphai return importancescores def compressgrid(originalgridsigma, originalgridcolor, importancescores, Ssigma=2, Scolor=4, topkpercent=0.17): """Compresses the grid using nonuniform downsampling and stores important voxels.""" # Step 1: Downsample grids compressedcolor = downsamplegrid(originalgridcolor, Scolor) compressedsigma = downsamplegrid(originalgridsigma, Ssigma) # Step 2: Identify important voxels voxelindices = list(range(len(importancescores))) sortedindices = sorted(voxelindices, key=lambda i: importancescores[i], reverse=True) # Select top k percent numimportant = int(len(sortedindices) topkpercent) importantvoxelindices = sortedindices[:numimportant] # Store original values for important voxels importantvoxelsdata = [] for idx in importantvoxelindices: coords = (idx // (originalgridsigma.shape[1] originalgridsigma.shape[2]), (idx // originalgridsigma.shape[2]) % originalgridsigma.shape[1], idx % originalgridsigma.shape[2]) sigmaval = originalgridsigma[coords] colorval = originalgridcolor[coords] importantvoxelsdata.append({'coords': coords, 'sigma': sigmaval, 'color': colorval}) return compressedsigma, compressedcolor, importantvoxelsdata def decompressgrid(compressedsigma, compressedcolor, importantvoxelsdata, originalshape): """Recovers the grid by upsampling and replacing important voxels.""" # Upsample compressed grids to original shape using tri-linear interpolation recoveredsigma = upsamplegrid(compressedsigma, originalshape) recoveredcolor = upsamplegrid(compressedcolor, originalshape) # Replace values at important voxel coordinates with original high-res values for voxeldata in importantvoxelsdata: coords = voxeldata['coords'] recoveredsigma[coords] = voxeldata['sigma'] recoveredcolor[coords] = voxeldata['color'] return recoveredsigma, recoveredcolor Storage Reduction: Achieves over 40x reduction in grid model storage compared to original grid models. Quality Trade-off: Maintains competitive rendering quality with less than 0.3dB drop in PSNR compared to uncompressed models. Performance: Enables real-time rendering speeds (e.g., 180 fps) due to reduced memory footprint and bandwidth. Strengths: Significant storage savings with minimal quality loss; simple one-time decompression without runtime overhead. Limitations: Requires an initial pass to calculate importance scores; relies on the assumption that density is more important than color, which may vary by scene. When to Use: When storage or bandwidth is a constraint and real-time rendering is required. When Not to Use: When maximum possible visual fidelity is required without any compression artifacts, or if the scene has high-frequency details in color that are not captured by the importance metric. This method was introduced in the paper "Compact Real-Time Radiance Fields with Neural Codebook". It addresses the high storage costs of explicit grid-based neural radiance field representations. The approach leverages the observation that a small percentage of voxels contribute to the majority of rendering importance, allowing for selective high-resolution storage. name: Granularity-Driven Cut
head: Cut selection, Granularity-Driven Cut Selection, Level-of-Detail Cut, Projected-size voxel selection, Sparse radiance voxel map selection
body: Granularity-Driven Cut is a voxel selection strategy that ensures geometric consistency and scalability by choosing the coarsest node on each root-to-leaf path of an octree that satisfies a granularity constraint relative to a camera box. It solves the problem of fitting large scenes into fixed GPU memory budgets by keeping the full octree in host memory and placing only a selected subset of voxels on the GPU, ensuring fine voxels near the camera and coarser voxels farther away. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like LightGaussian Pruning Scoring or FA-based Pruning by relying on geometric projected size constraints rather than importance scores or algebraic approximations, and from Importance-Driven Volume Rendering by explicitly managing the trade-off between resolution and memory via a pixel-span target. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree O, a box of interest B (bounding the region of interest, e.g., the camera frustum or a submap), and a granularity target \tau (maximum allowed projected size in pixels). Output: A cut set C(\tau, B, O), which is a set of non-overlapping voxels that form a sparse radiance voxel map. Data Structures: Octree O: Hierarchical grid structure. Nodes have a parent pointer \pi(n) and a voxel size vs(n). The root has no parent, defined as \pi(\text{root}) = \emptyset or effectively infinite distance for the formula. Box B: Axis-aligned bounding box defining the region where fine detail is required. Cut Set C: List of selected node indices or pointers. Formulas: The projected size proxy r(n, B) bounds the projected size of voxel n in every camera inside box B: r(n, B) = f \frac{vs(n)}{d(n, B)} Where: f = \max(fx, fy) is the focal length of the pinhole camera. vs(n) is the physical size of the voxel node n. d(n, B) is the minimum Euclidean distance between voxel n and box B. The cut set is defined as: C(\tau, B, O) = \{n \in O: [r(\pi(n), B) > \tau] \wedge [r(n, B) \leq \tau \vee n \text{ is a leaf}]\} Where: \tau is the granularity target in pixels. \pi(n) is the parent of node n. For the root, the condition r(\pi(n), B) > \tau is trivially satisfied as the root has no parent. Parameters: \tau: Granularity target. Increasing \tau reduces the number of selected voxels at the cost of coarser detail. n{\text{max}}: Maximum number of voxels resident on the GPU. During training, voxel subdivision stops when this budget is reached. Steps: 1. Define the box of interest B and granularity target \tau. 2. For each root-to-leaf path in the octree O: a. Traverse from the root downwards. b. Find the first node n such that its projected size proxy r(n, B) \leq \tau. c. If no such node exists on the path (i.e., even the leaf is too large relative to \tau or the path ends before satisfying the condition), select the leaf node n{\text{leaf}} to ensure coverage without holes. d. Otherwise, select node n. This node is the coarsest node on the path that is fine enough (projected size \leq \tau) while its parent was too coarse (projected size > \tau). 3. The union of all selected nodes forms the cut C(\tau, B, O). 4. During deployment, place box B around the moving camera or submap of interest. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegranularitydrivencut(octree, boxB, granularitytargettau, focallengthf): """ Computes the granularity-driven cut for an octree. Args: octree: The root node of the octree. boxB: The box of interest (bounding box). granularitytargettau: Maximum allowed projected size in pixels. focallengthf: Max of fx and fy. Returns: cutset: A list of selected nodes. """ cutset = [] # Helper to compute projected size proxy def projectedsizeproxy(node, box): # vs(node) is the physical size of the voxel voxelsize = node.voxelsize # d(node, box) is the minimum Euclidean distance between voxel and box distance = mineuclideandistance(node.boundingbox, box) # Avoid division by zero if voxel intersects box (distance is 0) # In this case, the voxel is inside the box of interest. # The formula implies infinite projected size, which is > tau. # So we must descend to children. if distance == 0: return float('inf') return focallengthf (voxelsize / distance) # Helper to check if a node is a leaf def isleaf(node): return node.children is None or len(node.children) == 0 # Traverse each root-to-leaf path # Note: In a real implementation, this is often done via a single DFS/BFS # that collects the cut nodes directly. def traverseandselect(node, parentnode): # Calculate projected size of current node rn = projectedsizeproxy(node, boxB) # Calculate projected size of parent to check the condition r(pi(n), B) > tau # For the root, parent is considered to have infinite projected size if parentnode is None: rparent = float('inf') else: rparent = projectedsizeproxy(parentnode, boxB) # Condition 1: Parent was too coarse (projected size > tau) # Condition 2: Current node is fine enough (projected size <= tau) OR is a leaf isparenttoocoarse = rparent > granularitytargettau iscurrentfineenough = rn <= granularitytargettau iscurrentleaf = isleaf(node) if isparenttoocoarse and (iscurrentfineenough or iscurrentleaf): # This node satisfies the cut condition cutset.append(node) # Do not traverse children, as this node covers the space for the cut return else: # Continue to children if not isleaf(node): for child in node.children: traverseandselect(child, node) else: # Leaf node reached but didn't satisfy condition? # This happens if rleaf > tau. # According to the definition, if no node satisfies r(n,B) <= tau, # select the leaf. # However, the logic above: if isparenttoocoarse is true, # and iscurrentfineenough is false, and iscurrentleaf is true, # it enters the if block. # If isparenttoocoarse is false (parent was fine enough), # we should have selected the parent. # So we only reach here if parent was fine enough but we are still traversing? # No, the logic selects the first node. # If parent was fine enough, parent would have been selected. # So we only traverse if parent was NOT fine enough (rparent > tau). # If we are at a leaf and rleaf > tau, and rparent > tau, # the condition (rparent > tau) AND (rleaf <= tau OR isleaf) # becomes True AND (False OR True) = True. # So the leaf is selected. pass traverseandselect(octree, None) return cutset Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Voxel inside Box B: If a voxel intersects or is inside B, d(n, B) = 0, making r(n, B) = \infty. This ensures the cut descends to the finest available voxels inside the box of interest. No Node Satisfies Constraint: If no node on a root-to-leaf path satisfies r(n, B) \leq \tau (e.g., even the leaf is too large), the leaf node is selected to ensure coverage without holes. Memory Budget: During training, subdivision stops when the number of resident voxels reaches n{\text{max}}. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of nodes in the octree, as each root-to-leaf path is traversed once. Memory Complexity: The cut size is bounded by n{\text{max}} on the GPU. The full octree remains in host memory. Strengths: Ensures geometric consistency (no overlaps or holes) and scalability. GPU memory usage stays bounded as the scene grows. Limitations: Requires calculating distances and projected sizes for all nodes. Performance depends on the choice of \tau and B. When to use: Large-scale scenes where GPU memory is limited and geometric consistency is required. When not to use: Small scenes that fit entirely in GPU memory, or when importance-based pruning is preferred for artistic control. Granularity-Driven Cut was introduced in the SpaRV (Sparse Radiance Voxels) framework for scalable geometrically consistent LiDAR-Visual Mapping and Rendering. It addresses the limitation that voxel maps grow with scene extent and requested detail, making it impossible to fit large scenes into fixed GPU memory budgets at high detail. The method was developed to allow view-dependent level-of-detail selection based on projected size. SpaRV: Sparse Radiance Voxels for Scalable Geometrically Consistent LiDAR-Visual Mapping and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2610.25665, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Grid Raycasting
head: DDA Ray Tracing, Ray Marching through Voxel Grid, Uniform Grid Raycasting, Voxel Ray Tracing with Voxel Marching, Voxel-Volume-Raycasting, Voxelization Raycasting, raycastVoxels
body:
Voxel Grid Raycasting is a rendering technique that stores scene geometry in a 3D voxel grid and traces rays through the grid by stepping from voxel to voxel to determine intersections and surface normals. It solves the problem of efficiently determining ray-voxel intersections without performing explicit geometric intersection tests against primitives. Unlike methods that expand storage to hold complete cell data or use hierarchical structures, this method relies on a uniform grid and a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) analog to traverse the volume. It is distinguished from general Volume Raycasting by its restriction to integer-valued voxel functions and discrete stepping, rather than continuous sampling and interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \vec{o}, ray direction \vec{d} (normalized), voxel grid dimensions/bounds, voxel size (or bin size), and the voxel data structure. Output: Hit position, voxel coordinates, surface normal, and optionally material/color data. Returns failure if no intersection is found within bounds or distance limits. Data Structures: The voxel grid is typically stored as a 1D array or buffer. Layout (Uniform/Chunked): A 1D storage buffer voxels: array<u32>. Each u32 represents a single voxel. A value of 0u indicates an empty voxel; non-zero values indicate occupied voxels, where the value may encode color via unpack4x8unorm. Indexing: For a chunk of width W and height H, the index for grid coordinates (x, y, z) is: index = x + y \cdot W + z \cdot (W \cdot H) Layout (Fixed Size): Alternatively, a fixed-size 1D array blocks of size Nx 	imes Ny 	imes Nz (e.g., 16 	imes 16 	imes 16) of type int. Indexing: For a 16 	imes 16 	imes 16 grid, the index is: index = (x \cdot 16 + z) \cdot 16 + y Parameters: voxelsize / binsize: The physical side length of a voxel in world units. Typical values are 0.1 or hardcoded to 1.0. epsilon: A small offset to prevent self-intersection. Typically voxelsize 0.01. maxdist: Maximum ray travel distance. Typical value 16.0 or 10.0. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Normalize the ray direction: \vec{r} = 	ext{normalize}(\vec{d}). Calculate the starting voxel coordinates by flooring the start position divided by the bin size: \vec{v}{curr} = \lfloor \vec{o} / 	ext{bin\size} floor Calculate direction indicators (step signs) for each axis: 	ext{step}i =  egin{cases} 1 & 	ext{if } ri \ge 0 \ -1 & 	ext{if } ri < 0 \end{cases} Calculate the distance to traverse one full voxel width (delta): \Delta ti =  rac{	ext{bin\size}}{|ri|} \cdot 	ext{step}i \quad 	ext{if } ri 
eq 0, 	ext{ else } \infty Calculate the distance to the next voxel boundary (t{max}) for each axis. The target boundary coordinate is (\vec{v}{curr, i} + 	ext{step}i) \cdot 	ext{bin\size}. t{max, i} =  rac{	ext{target}i - oi}{ri} \quad 	ext{if } ri 
eq 0, 	ext{ else } \infty Note: If a ray component is 0, t{max} and \Delta t are set to \infty to effectively remove that axis from the traversal comparison logic. 2. Edge Case Handling (Negative Direction): If the ray starts in a voxel different from the target end voxel and moves in a negative direction, decrement the corresponding voxel coordinate to ensure correct traversal start. Example: If v{curr, x} 
eq v{end, x} and rx < 0, then v{curr, x} \leftarrow v{curr, x} - 1. 3. Traversal Loop: Iterate while the current voxel is within bounds and has not exceeded maxdist or iteration limits. Find the axis with the minimum t{max} value: axis = 	ext{argmin}(t{max}). Increment the grid position on that axis: v{curr, axis} \leftarrow v{curr, axis} + 	ext{step}{axis}. Update the distance traveled: dist \leftarrow t{max, axis}. Advance the t{max} for that axis to the next boundary: t{max, axis} \leftarrow t{max, axis} + \Delta t{axis}. Store the axis of entry for normal calculation. 4. Intersection Check: Load voxel data at v{curr}. If the voxel is occupied (data 
eq 0): Calculate the surface normal based on the entry axis: \vec{n} = 	ext{axis\dir
ormal}(axis, \vec{r}). Calculate the precise hit position using the t{max} values at the time of entry. Return hit data. 5. Ray Bouncing (Optional): If multiple bounces are supported, spawn a new ray from the hit position: \vec{o}{new} = \vec{o}{hit} + \epsilon \cdot \vec{n}. Re-initialize traversal state for the new ray. If the new ray is out of range, return ambient/sky color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastvoxelgrid(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid, binsize, gridmin, gridmax, maxdist): # 1. Normalize and Setup r = normalize(raydirection) binf = float(binsize) # 2. Initial Voxel and Steps currentvoxel = ivec3(floor(rayorigin.x / binf), floor(rayorigin.y / binf), floor(rayorigin.z / binf)) # Step signs: 1 if r >= 0, -1 if r < 0 step = ivec3(1 if r.x >= 0 else -1, 1 if r.y >= 0 else -1, 1 if r.z >= 0 else -1) # 3. Calculate tMax and tDelta # Target boundaries: (currentvoxel + step) binsize nextboundary = (currentvoxel + step) binf def safediv(num, den): return float('inf') if den == 0.0 else num / den tmax = vec3( safediv(nextboundary.x - rayorigin.x, r.x), safediv(nextboundary.y - rayorigin.y, r.y), safediv(nextboundary.z - rayorigin.z, r.z)) tdelta = vec3( safediv(binf step.x, r.x), safediv(binf step.y, r.y), safediv(binf step.z, r.z)) # 4. Edge Case: Negative Ray Direction Adjustment # If ray moves negatively and starts in a different voxel than the end, adjust start # to ensure currentvoxel is the first intersected voxel. for i in range(3): if r[i] < 0.0 and rayorigin[i] % binf == 0.0: currentvoxel[i] -= 1 # 5. Traversal Loop for in range(10000): # Max iterations # Check bounds if not (gridmin.x <= currentvoxel.x <= gridmax.x and gridmin.y <= currentvoxel.y <= gridmax.y and gridmin.z <= currentvoxel.z <= gridmax.z): return None # Out of bounds # Check occupancy voxeldata = voxelgrid.load(currentvoxel) if voxeldata != 0: # Hit found # Determine normal based on which axis we just crossed mint = min(tmax.x, tmax.y, tmax.z) if mint == tmax.x: axis = 0 elif mint == tmax.y: axis = 1 else: axis = 2 normal = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) normal[axis] = -step[axis] hitpos = rayorigin + r mint return { "position": hitpos, "voxel": currentvoxel, "normal": normal, "data": voxeldata } # Advance to next voxel mint = min(tmax.x, tmax.y, tmax.z) if mint > maxdist: return None # Missed if mint == tmax.x: currentvoxel.x += step.x tmax.x += tdelta.x elif mint == tmax.y: currentvoxel.y += step.y tmax.y += tdelta.y else: currentvoxel.z += step.z tmax.z += tdelta.z return None # No hit Voxel-Cell Duality Mapping is a technique for ray tracing isosurfaces defined within cells of 8 voxels using an octree that stores scalar values at voxel centers. It establishes a dual relationship between voxels and cells by logically shifting scalar positions backward by half a voxel width, allowing the ray tracer to intersect 8-voxel cell primitives defined by the stored leaf values. Unlike methods that expand storage to hold complete cell data, this method retrieves forward neighbors at intersection time, maintaining single scalar storage per leaf. Spherical Volume Ray Walking is a fast voxel traversal algorithm for rendering volumetric data defined on a spherical coordinate grid. It extends the cartesian fast voxel traversal method by Amanatides and Woo to non-cartesian grids, iterating through radial, polar, and azimuthal voxel boundaries to determine the sequence of voxels intersected by a ray. Unlike Voxel Grid Raycasting which assumes axis-aligned bounding boxes, this method handles the curved boundaries of spherical sectors, using line-sphere intersection for radial steps and 2D segment intersection for angular boundaries. Plane Marching is a raymarching technique for voxel grids that advances a ray by stepping to the nearest intersection with the integer grid planes separating voxel layers. It solves the problem of traversing a dense voxel volume to find the first solid voxel by checking occupancy at each plane boundary. Unlike shape-assisted siblings such as Sphere Assisted Raymarching or Optimised Voxel Ray Marching, it does not store auxiliary distance fields or shape metadata, relying solely on the geometric structure of the grid. This makes it simple to implement but fragile in empty space, as it never skips more than one voxel per step. RLE4 Ray Tracing is a ray-marching or voxel-intersection algorithm that traverses an RLE4-compressed volume structure (Map4) to locate the first occupied voxel along a ray or to colorize a voxel based on its position. It uses slab-based RLE encoding to skip empty space efficiently. A hierarchical raycasting algorithm that traverses a sparse shadow volume texture to find the first intersection with a shadow-casting volume. It dynamically adjusts its traversal step size and level of detail (LOD) based on occupancy bits, allowing it to skip empty space efficiently compared to fixed-step hierarchical variants. It differs from siblings such as Voxel-Cell Duality Mapping, Spherical Volume Ray Walking, Plane Marching, RLE4 Ray Tracing, Regular Grid Traversal, Voxel Raytracer, and DirectVoxGO Volume Rendering by using a multi-level occupancy-bit search that refines or coarsens traversal granularity on the fly. Regular Grid Traversal is a ray-scene intersection acceleration technique that partitions a scene bounding box into a fixed-size 3D grid of cells, returning the sequence of cells intersected by a ray to minimize primitive intersection tests. It solves the problem of testing every object for every ray by only testing primitives stored in intersected cells. Unlike hierarchical structures (e.g., BVH, Octree) that partition primitives into disjoint sets, the Regular Grid partitions space into disjoint sub-blocks, allowing primitives to belong to multiple sub-blocks [3950-regular-grid.md]. It is distinguished by its constant-time access to cells and simple traversal logic, making it optimal for scenes with uniform data distribution or dynamic scenes requiring frequent rebuilds [3950-regular-grid.md]. A voxel raytracer renders 3D voxel models by marching rays through a 3D grid of voxels, supporting multiple bounces for diffuse reflection and a ground plane. It differs from standard voxel grid raycasting by implementing a full path-tracing loop with diffuse scattering and anti-aliasing, rather than simple direct illumination or single-pass raymarching. DirectVoxGO is a volume rendering method that accelerates neural radiance field training and inference by sampling points directly on a structured voxel grid rather than uniformly along rays. It solves the problem of inefficient ray marching in sparse scenes by using a mask cache to skip free space and a direct lookup of density and color features from the voxel grid. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF by replacing uniform sampling with grid-based point selection and from other sparse voxel methods by using a dense voxel grid with a binary mask cache for acceleration. This method accelerates the identification of the k nearest points within a cylinder of radius \delta around a query ray in a point cloud, specifically optimized for parallel GPU execution and dynamic scenes where the point cloud changes frequently. Unlike static acceleration structures such as octrees, which require O(n \log n) construction time, this voxel grid approach achieves O(n) construction, making it superior for inverse rendering and dynamic scenarios where the structure must be rebuilt every iteration. A search algorithm used by voxel resolve and GI update to find the pixel's voxel again in the brick named by the visibility buffer. It finds the cell holding the ray's point at the stored depth, then the two cells along each axis whose centers lie nearest that point (which hold the point regardless of rounding), stopping at the first cell whose hit gives the stored depth again, bit for bit. A voxel's test depends only on the ray and the voxel, ensuring every pass meets it at the same t. A narrow band strategy that does not use any solver. When the algorithm reaches a narrow band voxel, it immediately returns a hit, resulting in a voxelization of the scene. An acceleration structure using a dense octree stored in a 3D texture to skip empty space during ray traversal. The raymarcher first traverses the octree texture; once it hits a leaf node (occupied octant), it switches to the fine-grained voxel texture for detailed collision detection. The octree is stored as a 3D texture (texture3d<u32>), with data for different levels interleaved in the Z dimension. The 3D texture approach is significantly faster for ray traversal because graphics hardware is optimized for spatially local texture access. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels intersected by the ray. In the worst case (ray passing through the entire grid), N is proportional to the grid dimension. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the total number of voxels in the grid. The storage is typically a single 1D array or 3D texture. Performance: Performance depends on grid density and ray direction. Axis-aligned rays traverse fewer voxels per unit distance. The method is fast on GPUs due to spatially local texture access when using 3D textures, though linear buffers may suffer from cache misses compared to texture sampling. Strengths: Simple implementation, no complex data structure traversal overhead (like BVH/Octree node pointers), efficient for dense uniform grids, easy to parallelize on GPU. Limitations: Inefficient for sparse scenes (many empty voxels traversed), fixed resolution (aliasing artifacts at high zoom), memory usage scales with the cube of the grid dimension. When to use: Dense voxel volumes, uniform grids, real-time rendering where simplicity and parallelism are key. When not to use: Highly sparse scenes (use Sparse Voxel Traversal or Octree), scenes with complex continuous geometry (use Ray-Primitive intersection). The method is based on the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm for ray tracing, originally described by Amanatides and Woo in 1987. It is used in voxel-based rendering and real-time applications. The approach distinguishes itself from general volume raycasting by treating voxels as discrete integer-valued entities rather than continuous functions, requiring explicit floor operations for coordinate mapping. newDINO/voxelraydemo, https://github.com/newDINO/voxelraydemo, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) SamCZ/RayTracer, https://github.com/SamCZ/RayTracer, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Raycasting-basiertes Voxelrendering, https://serwiss.bib.hs-hannover.de/frontdoor/index/index/docId/2250, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) michschw/GpuPro3Vox, https://github.com/michschw/GpuPro3Vox, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) voxel/voxel-engine-stackgl, https://github.com/voxel/voxel-engine-stackgl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Kurble/amethystvoxel, https://github.com/Kurble/amethystvoxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) feat(render): voxels splatted to the pixels their footprints cover (ADR-0061), https://github.com/SugalAbubaker/nepheline/pull/115, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Rendering piecewise approximations of SDFs through analytic intersections, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cag.2024.103981, fetched 2026-10-27 jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, https://github.com/jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Voxel-Cell Duality Mapping
head: Cell Primitive Definition, Logical Shift Mapping, Logical Shift for Ray Tracing, Scalar Field Remapping
body: Voxel-Cell Duality Mapping is a technique for ray tracing isosurfaces defined within cells of 8 voxels using an octree that stores scalar values at voxel centers. It establishes a dual relationship between voxels and cells by logically shifting scalar positions backward by half a voxel width, allowing the ray tracer to intersect 8-voxel cell primitives defined by the stored leaf values. Unlike methods that expand storage to hold complete cell data, this method retrieves forward neighbors at intersection time, maintaining single scalar storage per leaf. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree structure storing scalar values at voxel centers, where each leaf node contains a single scalar datum v. Output: Intersection points with an isosurface defined within cells formed by 8 adjacent voxels. Data Structures: Octree: Nodes contain scalar values at their centers, and leaf nodes store a single scalar value v. Cell Primitive: A box defined by 8 vertices, where the vertices correspond to the mapped positions of 8 adjacent voxels in the octree. Mapping Logic: 1. Logical Shift: The position of all scalars is logically shifted backward by half a unit of voxel width to re-map the scalar field from voxel centers to cell corners. 2. Corner Mapping: Each voxel is mapped to the lower-left corner (minimum vertex) of a cell. 3. Boundary Condition: Values outside the octree data boundary are defined to be zero. Intersection Process: When a ray traverses an octree leaf node at indices (i, j, k) with a datum v, the ray intersects a box (cell) where (i, j, k) is mapped to the minimum vertex, and the remaining 7 vertices are formed by the forward neighbors of the voxel at (i, j, k) in the octree. Neighbor Retrieval: Instead of expanding each voxel to contain its forward neighbors (which would require 8 times the storage), the method retrieves the 7 forward neighbors of a voxel at intersection time. For a volume stored in a 3D array, querying these neighbors is a trivial array index operation. For an octree, this requires point location to retrieve the voxel values of the forward neighbors, where full top-down point location from the root is O(\log(N)) but neighbor-finding techniques can significantly reduce this cost. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intersectcell(rayorigin, raydirection, octree, isovalue): """ Intersect a ray with an isosurface defined by voxel-cell duality. """ # Standard octree traversal to find the leaf node intersected by the ray leafnode = octree.traverse(rayorigin, raydirection) if leafnode is None: return None # Get the scalar value at the current leaf node (voxel center) vcenter = leafnode.scalarvalue # Determine the indices (i, j, k) of the current leaf node i, j, k = leafnode.indices # Helper function to get scalar value, returning 0 for out-of-bounds def getscalar(idxi, idxj, idxk): # Standard octree point location to find the node at (idxi, idxj, idxk) node = octree.pointlocation(idxi, idxj, idxk) if node is None: return 0.0 # Boundary condition: values outside octree are zero return node.scalarvalue # Retrieve the 8 corner values for the cell # The current voxel is mapped to the minimum vertex (lower-left corner) # Neighbors are at (i+1, j, k), (i, j+1, k), (i, j, k+1), etc. corners = [ getscalar(i, j, k), # Current voxel (min corner) getscalar(i+1, j, k), # Neighbor in x getscalar(i, j+1, k), # Neighbor in y getscalar(i+1, j+1, k), # Neighbor in x,y getscalar(i, j, k+1), # Neighbor in z getscalar(i+1, j, k+1), # Neighbor in x,z getscalar(i, j+1, k+1), # Neighbor in y,z getscalar(i+1, j+1, k+1) # Neighbor in x,y,z (max corner) ] # Standard trilinear ray-cube intersection or Marching Cubes is applied # to the 8 corner values to find the isosurface intersection. # The sources do not specify the exact reconstruction algorithm. Parameters: Isovalue: The threshold value for the isosurface extraction. Not given in the sources. Voxel Width: The unit of voxel width used for the logical shift. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Storage Expansion: Storing each cell completely by expanding each voxel to contain its forward neighbors requires 8 times the storage of the original volume, which contradicts the goal of ray tracing compressed data. Boundary Handling: Values outside the octree data boundary are defined to be zero. Performance: For octrees, retrieving forward neighbors requires point location, which is more intensive than array indexing. Full top-down point location is O(\log(N)), but neighbor-finding techniques can reduce this cost. Ray walking in spherical coordinates. Not given in the sources. Ray tracing on a regular grid structure. Not given in the sources. Marching planes for volume rendering. Not given in the sources. Voxel-based ray tracing for global illumination and specular reflections. Not given in the sources. Optimized voxel ray marching techniques. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Neighbor retrieval in an octree is more intensive than in a 3D array, with full top-down point location at O(\log(N)) reduced by neighbor-finding techniques. Memory Complexity: Single scalar storage per leaf node, avoiding the 8x storage expansion required by naive cell expansion. Strengths: Allows ray tracing of compressed octree data without expanding storage, and permits traversal of interior nodes of the octree volume. Limitations: Neighbor retrieval in octrees is more complex and potentially slower than in regular grids. When to Use: When ray tracing isosurfaces from compressed octree volumes where storage efficiency is critical. When Not to Use: When neighbor retrieval performance is critical and the data is stored in a regular grid, where array indexing is trivial. Voxel-Cell Duality Mapping was introduced in the context of interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. The method leverages the dual relationship between voxels and cells to efficiently ray trace isosurfaces defined within cells of 8 voxels. The approach of retrieving forward neighbors at intersection time is attributed to Parker et al.. name: Spherical Volume Ray Walking
head: Amanatides and Woo extension to spherical grids, Fast Voxel Traversal Over Spherical Grids, Spherical Volume Rendering (SVR) Algorithm, walkSphericalVolume
body: Spherical Volume Ray Walking is a fast voxel traversal algorithm for rendering volumetric data defined on a spherical coordinate grid. It extends the cartesian fast voxel traversal method by Amanatides and Woo to non-cartesian grids, iterating through radial, polar, and azimuthal voxel boundaries to determine the sequence of voxels intersected by a ray. Unlike Voxel Grid Raycasting which assumes axis-aligned bounding boxes, this method handles the curved boundaries of spherical sectors, using line-sphere intersection for radial steps and 2D segment intersection for angular boundaries. Inputs: ray (origin O as bound vector, direction D as unit free vector), grid (spherical voxel grid with parameters sphereCenter, numRadialSections, numPolarSections, numAzimuthalSections, minBound, maxBound, deltaRadiiSquared(r), deltaPhi(), deltaTheta(), sphereMaxBoundAzi(), sphereMinBoundAzi(), sphereMaxBoundPolar(), sphereMinBoundPolar(), sphereMaxRadius(), pMaxPolar(i), pMaxAzimuthal(i), centerToPolarBound(i), centerToAzimuthalBound(i)), and time range tbegin, tend. Outputs: List of Voxel structs containing {radial, polar, azimuthal} indices and optional exitt. Voxel: {radial: int, polar: int, azimuthal: int, exitt: float}. HitParameters: {tMax: float, tStep: int} where tStep is -1, 0, or 1. RaySegment: {P1: BoundVec3, P2: BoundVec3, NZDI: int}. LineSegment: {P1: float, P2: float}. BoundVec3, FreeVec3, UnitVec3: 3D vector types for bound, free, and normalized coordinates respectively. Unverified code.
