name: Plane Marching
head: Raymarching Plane Intersections
body: Plane Marching is a raymarching technique for voxel grids that advances a ray by stepping to the nearest intersection with the integer grid planes separating voxel layers. It solves the problem of traversing a dense voxel volume to find the first solid voxel by checking occupancy at each plane boundary. Unlike shape-assisted siblings such as Sphere Assisted Raymarching or Optimised Voxel Ray Marching, it does not store auxiliary distance fields or shape metadata, relying solely on the geometric structure of the grid. This makes it simple to implement but fragile in empty space, as it never skips more than one voxel per step. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin p0 (voxel-unit space), ray direction d (voxel-unit space), voxel grid texture voxels (3D texture containing color/alpha), voxelGridSize (dimensions of the grid in voxels), maxDistToCheck (maximum traversal distance). Output: Color vec4 of the first solid voxel encountered, or transparent black if no solid voxel is found within maxDistToCheck. Data Structures: voxels: A 3D texture where each texel stores the color and alpha of a voxel. The alpha channel determines solidity (c.a > 0). The texture coordinates are normalized to [0, 1] based on voxelGridSize. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize step distance t = 0. 2. Loop while t \le \text{maxDistToCheck}: a. Calculate current position p = p0 + d \cdot t. b. Convert p to texture coordinates by dividing by voxelGridSize. c. If the sampled alpha c.a > 0, return c. d. Calculate the distance to the next integer grid plane along each axis. e. Update t by adding the smallest positive delta plus a small epsilon. Formulas: The distance to the next plane intersection along each axis is computed using the ray direction d and current position p. In voxel-unit-space (where one voxel is 1x1x1 units), the delta for each axis component is: \text{deltas}i = \frac{\text{step}(0, di) - \text{fract}(pi)}{di} Where: i \in \{x, y, z\} \text{step}(0, di) returns 1 if di \ge 0, else 0. This effectively computes \lceil pi \rceil - pi for positive directions and \lfloor pi \rfloor - pi for negative directions. \text{fract}(pi) is the fractional part of pi (pi - \lfloor pi \rfloor). di is the i-th component of the ray direction. The step size to advance is the minimum of these deltas, ensuring the ray moves to the closest plane intersection: t{\text{new}} = t + \max(\min(\text{deltas}x, \text{deltas}y, \text{deltas}z), \epsilon) Where \epsilon is a tiny constant to prevent infinite loops due to floating-point precision errors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def planemarch(p0, d, voxels, voxelgridsize, maxdisttocheck, epsilon=1e-6): # sample3dtexture is a standard trilinear 3D texture lookup returning vec4 t = 0.0 while t <= maxdisttocheck: # Calculate current position p = p0 + d t # Sample voxel color texcoords = p / voxelgridsize c = sample3dtexture(voxels, texcoords) # Check for solidity if c.a > 0: return c # Calculate deltas to next plane boundaries deltas = [] for i in range(3): stepval = 1.0 if d[i] >= 0 else 0.0 fracval = p[i] - math.floor(p[i]) deltas.append((stepval - fracval) / d[i]) # Find the minimum positive delta to step to the closest plane # Add epsilon to guarantee progress and avoid floating point errors t += max(min(deltas), epsilon) return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) Parameters: epsilon: A small constant (e.g., 10^{-6}) added to the step size to guarantee progress and prevent infinite loops caused by floating-point inaccuracies. The exact value is not specified in the sources but must be "tiny". Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating Point Errors: Accumulation of floating-point errors can cause "tunneling" (skipping voxels) and subtle artifacts. The epsilon helps but does not fully eliminate this fragility. Degenerate Performance: In empty space or when the target voxel is far away, the algorithm checks every single voxel along the ray path because it never moves more than one voxel at a time. This leads to poor performance in degenerate cases, such as a single solid voxel in the corner of a large empty grid. Fillrate Limitation: The technique is fragment shader heavy and is likely to be fillrate limited on typical hardware. Stores radius data in empty voxels to skip large distances. Choose when performance in sparse volumes is critical. Optimizes traversal logic with early exits and culling. Choose for better performance in complex scenes. Maps voxels to cells for different traversal strategies. Choose for alternative spatial indexing. Uses spherical stepping for non-axis-aligned volumes. Choose for spherical volume representations. General regular grid traversal. Choose for non-voxel regular structures. Extends ray marching for global illumination. Choose for advanced lighting. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels intersected by the ray. In the worst case (empty space), N is proportional to the distance to the first solid voxel or the grid boundary. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the total number of voxels in the grid, as the entire voxel set must be loaded into a 3D texture. Memory usage is data-independent regarding sparsity; a 32x32x32 grid always consumes the same memory regardless of how many voxels are solid. Measured Performance: In a degenerate case (32x32x32 grid with a single solid voxel in the far corner), Plane Marching shows vastly worse performance compared to shape-assisted techniques. Strengths: Performant in parallelized environments (e.g., GPUs), requires little upfront computation, and is straightforward to implement. Limitations: Fragile due to floating-point errors, fillrate limited, and inefficient in empty space. When to Use: Simple voxel rendering where performance is not critical or the volume is dense. When Not to Use: Sparse volumes, large empty spaces, or when high performance is required. Plane Marching is described as one of the most interesting ways to render voxels, performant and parallelizable. It is based on the concept of raymarching plane intersections, where a ray is advanced along the planes separating voxel layers. The technique is often compared to Inigo Quilez's ray marching work, though Quilez's work primarily focuses on signed distance fields, whereas Plane Marching uses unsigned distance fields (grid planes). The method was popularized in the context of voxel rendering for real-time applications, such as Minecraft-like games, by developers like Caleb Leak. name: RLE4 Ray Tracing
head: Map4 Traversal
body: RLE4 Ray Tracing is a ray-marching or voxel-intersection algorithm that traverses an RLE4-compressed volume structure (Map4) to locate the first occupied voxel along a ray or to colorize a voxel based on its position. It uses slab-based RLE encoding to skip empty space efficiently. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A float position pos (x, y, z), volume dimensions vx, vy, vz, and a pre-compressed RLE4 structure map4 containing a slab pointer array map, a slab data array slabs, and the X-dimension size sx. Output: A packed 16-bit RGB value stored in the texture array if the voxel is found, or a skip indicator if not. Data Structures: The Map4 structure uses map4.map indexed by x + z map4.sx to point into map4.slabs. Each slab entry is a 16-bit integer where bits 0–9 store a Y-coordinate increment and bits 10–15 store the Y-range length. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate Conversion: Convert the float position pos to integer voxel coordinates x, y, z by scaling with volume dimensions vx, vy, vz. 2. Bounds Check: Verify x and z are within bounds. 3. Slab Access: Access the slab pointer for the current XZ coordinate. 4. Read Segment Lengths: Read the lengths of the first and second slab segments to skip header data. 5. Initialize State: Set y1=0, y2=0. Set pointer pt to p+len1. Initialize texture=0. 6. Iterate Slabs: Loop s from 0 to len1-1: a. Read Slab Entry: slab = p[0]; p += 1. b. Decode Y-Range: y1 += slab & 1023; y2 = y1 + (slab >> 10). c. Check Intersection: Check if the target Y coordinate y falls within the current slab range [y1, y2). d. Advance: If not found, advance the texture pointer and Y1: texture += y2 - y1; y1 = y2. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rle4traverse(pos, vx, vy, vz, map4): # 1. Coordinate conversion x = int(pos[0] vx) y = int(pos[1] vy) z = int(pos[2] vz) # 2. Bounds check if x < 0 or x >= vx or z < 0 or z >= vz: return None # 3. Slab access (pointer arithmetic simulated via index offset) p = map4.slabs + map4.map[x + z map4.sx] # 4. Read segment lengths len1 = p[0]; p += 1 len2 = p[0]; p += 1 # 5. Initialize state y1 = 0 y2 = 0 pt = p + len1 texture = 0 # 6. Iterate slabs for s in range(len1): slab = p[0]; p += 1 y1 += slab & 1023 y2 = y1 + (slab >> 10) # 6c. Check intersection if y >= y1 and y < y2: col = readcolorfromtexture(pt, texture + y - y1) r = clamp(col[0] 15 + 16, 0, 31) g = clamp(col[1] 15 + 16, 0, 31) b = clamp(col[2] 15 + 16, 0, 31) packed = int(r + (g << 5) + (b << 10)) pt[texture + y - y1] = packed return packed # 6d. Advance texture += y2 - y1 y1 = y2 return None def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(val, maxval)) def readcolorfromtexture(texturearray, offset): # Standard texture/array lookup return texturearray[offset] Parameters: Color quantization: 5 bits per channel (0–31 range). Y-range decoding: 10 bits for Y-increment, 6 bits for Y-length. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bounds: The algorithm assumes the target Y coordinate is within the volume bounds checked at the start; if the ray passes through multiple slabs, it iterates until the Y range is found. Precision: The color quantization uses 5 bits per channel, which may introduce visible banding in high-dynamic-range scenes. Empty Regions: If the Y coordinate is not found in any slab, the algorithm returns without writing, effectively skipping the voxel. This method performs GPU-based ray casting on volume data compressed using run-length encoding (RLE), storing the compressed structure in 2D textures to facilitate efficient random access. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by avoiding full decompression; instead, it uses a texture-based lookup system to determine if a sample point lies in an uncompressed surface region, an "inside" region, or an "outside" region, returning special markers for the latter two. This approach is particularly suited for scenarios where the volume geometry is sparse or has large uniform interior/exterior regions, allowing the renderer to skip volumetric integration in those areas. Time Complexity: O(k) where k is the number of Y-slabs traversed along the ray. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the compressed RLE4 structure, where N is the number of occupied Y-ranges. Performance: Efficient for sparse volumes with large uniform regions, as it avoids full decompression and skips empty space. Strengths: Low memory footprint for sparse data; fast traversal of empty space; GPU-friendly texture lookups. Limitations: Color quantization limits visual fidelity to 5 bits per channel; requires pre-compression of volume data; not suitable for dense volumes where compression ratio is low. The method is documented in the OpenGL-Voxel-Splatting repository. It is used for efficient ray casting in sparse volumetric data, leveraging RLE compression to skip empty space. sp4cerat/OpenGL-Voxel-Splatting, https://github.com/sp4cerat/OpenGL-Voxel-Splatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: RL-compressed GPU Ray Casting with Texture-Based Lookup
head: Run-Length Encoded GPU Renderer
body: This method performs GPU-based ray casting on volume data compressed using run-length encoding (RLE), storing the compressed structure in 2D textures to facilitate efficient random access. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by avoiding full decompression; instead, it uses a texture-based lookup system to determine if a sample point lies in an uncompressed surface region, an "inside" region, or an "outside" region, returning special markers for the latter two. This approach is particularly suited for scenarios where the volume geometry is sparse or has large uniform interior/exterior regions, allowing the renderer to skip volumetric integration in those areas. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume dataset, compressed into a specific RLE structure. Output: A rendered 2D image generated via fragment shaders. Query: A 3D coordinate (x, y, z) requested by the ray caster to determine the voxel value or classification. Data Structures The compressed data is stored in three 2D textures created by a builder and resident in graphics memory: 1. Index Texture: Stores offsets to the beginnings of each line in the Line Texture. It allows direct access to the RLE data corresponding to a specific (y, z) plane. 2. Line Texture: Contains the run-length encoded data. It stores pairs of values (count, offset) consecutively for each row (line) of the volume. 3. Surface Texture: Stores the actual volumetric values for uncompressed regions. It is accessed via offsets provided in the Line Texture. Encoding Details: Each entry in the Line Texture is a pair: (count, offset). count: The number of voxels in the run. offset: If the run is in an uncompressed area, this is the offset into the Surface Texture where the voxel values begin. If the run is in a compressed area, the offset is fictitiously set to 0 or 1 to distinguish compressed regions from uncompressed ones. Offset 0 typically denotes "Outside" and 1 denotes "Inside" (or vice versa, as they are special markers). The data is organized such that lines of the volume are stored sequentially, with the Index Texture providing the starting position for each (y, z) line. Algorithm: Voxel Lookup When a fragment shader needs the value for a voxel at (x, y, z): 1. Locate Line: Use the Index Texture to retrieve the offset in the Line Texture corresponding to the (y, z) coordinates. 2. Iterate Runs: Read pairs (count, offset) from the Line Texture starting at the located offset. For each pair, check if the requested x coordinate falls within the current run. Let x{start} be the cumulative count of voxels processed so far in this line. The condition is: x{start} \le x < x{start} + count. If the condition is met, the run containing x is found. 3. Determine Region: If the offset of the found pair is 0 or 1 (compressed area): Return a special value: C (Inside) or O (Outside). No further lookup is performed; full decompression is avoided. If the offset is a valid texture address (uncompressed area): Calculate the specific index into the Surface Texture. The index is offset + (x - xstart). Retrieve the actual voxel value from the Surface Texture at this index. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getvoxelvalue(x, y, z, indextexture, linetexture, surfacetexture): """ Retrieves the voxel value or classification for (x, y, z). Returns: A float value if the voxel is in an uncompressed surface region. 'O' if the voxel is in a compressed Outside region. 'I' if the voxel is in a compressed Inside region. """ # Step 1: Get the start offset in the Line Texture for the (y, z) line linestartoffset = indextexture.sample(y, z) # Step 2: Iterate through the run-length pairs in the Line Texture currentoffset = linestartoffset xstart = 0 while True: # Read the next pair (count, offset) from the Line Texture count, offset = linetexture.samplepair(currentoffset) # Check if the requested x falls within this run if xstart <= x < xstart + count: # Step 3: Determine if the region is compressed or uncompressed if offset == 0 or offset == 1: # Compressed region if offset == 0: return 'O' # Outside else: return 'I' # Inside else: # Uncompressed region # Calculate the index in the Surface Texture relativex = x - xstart surfaceindex = offset + relativex return surfacetexture.sample(surfaceindex) # Advance to next pair in the line texture array currentoffset += 1 xstart += count Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The method relies on integer arithmetic for indices. Ensure that the count and offset fields are large enough to represent the volume dimensions and texture sizes without overflow. Compressed Region Semantics: The distinction between "Inside" and "Outside" is binary in compressed regions. The renderer must know which offset value (0 or 1) corresponds to which classification. Time Complexity: Lookup time is proportional to the number of runs in the line segment for the given (y, z) plane. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The memory usage is the sum of the sizes of the Index Texture, Line Texture, and Surface Texture. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient for volumes with large uniform regions (inside/outside). Avoids the computational cost of decompressing the entire volume. Suitable for GPU implementation using texture lookups. Limitations: Random access to uncompressed voxels requires iterating through the Line Texture. Not as efficient as direct indexing for fully dense volumes. The distinction between compressed and uncompressed regions is rigid. This method was implemented in the VRE volume rendering engine. It was designed to illustrate how to develop new plugins requiring special memory representations on the GPU, specifically leveraging OpenGL textures for compressed data storage. The approach was tested with simple command-line interfaces and GUI applications. The VRE volume rendering engine, https://doi.org/10.1145/1925059.1925072, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Sparse Shadow Volume Raycast
head: raycastShadowVolumeSparse
body: A hierarchical raycasting algorithm that traverses a sparse shadow volume texture to find the first intersection with a shadow-casting volume. It dynamically adjusts its traversal step size and level of detail (LOD) based on occupancy bits, allowing it to skip empty space efficiently compared to fixed-step hierarchical variants. It differs from siblings such as Voxel-Cell Duality Mapping, Spherical Volume Ray Walking, Plane Marching, RLE4 Ray Tracing, Regular Grid Traversal, Voxel Raytracer, and DirectVoxGO Volume Rendering by using a multi-level occupancy-bit search that refines or coarsens traversal granularity on the fly. Inputs: origin: Ray origin in world space. dir: Ray direction (normalized). dist: Maximum ray distance. uVolOffset: Offset vector for the shadow volume texture coordinates. uVolTexelSize: Physical size of a texel in the shadow volume. uVolResolution: Resolution of the shadow volume texture (vec3). uShadowVolume: The sparse shadow volume texture. Outputs: d: Distance to the first occupied voxel. Returns dist if no intersection is found within the limit. Data Structures: uShadowVolume: A texture where each texel contains occupancy information. The algorithm samples this texture at different LODs. The exact internal structure is abstracted by the texture fetch, but the algorithm relies on the x component of the sampled value being non-zero to indicate occupancy. Steps: 1. Initialization: Translate origin by uVolOffset. Compute step as uVolTexelSize. Compute stepDir as dir invShadowVolumeResolution. Compute pos as origin invVolumeTexelSize invShadowVolumeResolution. Halve stepDir and step by multiplying by 0.5. Initialize lod to -1 and d to 0.0. 2. Traversal Loop: While d < dist: Sample c = textureLod(uShadowVolume, pos, lod).x. If lod == -1 (Coarse Search): If c != 0, calculate bit index from fractional parts of pos: bit = (fract(pos.x uVolResolution.x) > 0.5 ? 1: 0) + (fract(pos.y uVolResolution.y) > 0.5 ? 2: 0) + (fract(pos.z uVolResolution.z) > 0.5 ? 4: 0). Create mask mask = 1 << bit. If (mask & c) != 0, return d. Else, advance pos += stepDir and d += step. If c == 0, increment lod, double stepDir and step, and advance pos += stepDir and d += step. If lod != -1 (Refinement): If c != 0, halve stepDir and step, decrement lod, and backtrack pos -= stepDir and d -= step. Else (c == 0), if lod < 2, sample c = textureLod(uShadowVolume, pos, lod + 1).x. If that sample is 0, increment lod, double stepDir and step, and advance pos += stepDir and d += step. Formulas: invShadowVolumeResolution = 1.0 / uVolResolution invVolumeTexelSize = 1.0 / uVolTexelSize stepDir = dir invShadowVolumeResolution pos = origin invVolumeTexelSize invShadowVolumeResolution bit = (fract(pos.x uVolResolution.x) > 0.5 ? 1: 0) + (fract(pos.y uVolResolution.y) > 0.5 ? 2: 0) + (fract(pos.z uVolResolution.z) > 0.5 ? 4: 0) Parameters: uVolResolution: vec3, resolution of the shadow volume texture. uVolTexelSize: float, physical size of a texel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The algorithm assumes a maximum LOD of 2. If lod is already 2 and the sample is empty, it does not attempt to go deeper, relying on the coarse search or returning the distance limit. Precision issues may arise when calculating bit indices from fractional parts of pos if pos values are very large or small. The algorithm assumes the shadow volume texture supports textureLod with varying LOD levels. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fract(x): return x - math.floor(x) def textureLod(tex, pos, lod): # Standard GPU texture fetch with explicit LOD bias return tex.sample(pos, lod) def raycastshadowvolumesparse(origin, dir, dist, uVolOffset, uVolTexelSize, uVolResolution, uShadowVolume): invShadowVolumeResolution = 1.0 / uVolResolution invVolumeTexelSize = 1.0 / uVolTexelSize origin = origin + uVolOffset step = uVolTexelSize stepDir = dir invShadowVolumeResolution pos = origin invVolumeTexelSize invShadowVolumeResolution stepDir = stepDir 0.5 step = step 0.5 lod = -1 d = 0.0 while d < dist: c = textureLod(uShadowVolume, pos, lod).x if lod == -1: if c != 0: bit = (1 if fract(pos.x uVolResolution.x) > 0.5 else 0) + \ (2 if fract(pos.y uVolResolution.y) > 0.5 else 0) + \ (4 if fract(pos.z uVolResolution.z) > 0.5 else 0) mask = 1 << bit if (mask & c) != 0: return d else: pos = pos + stepDir d = d + step else: lod = lod + 1 stepDir = stepDir 2.0 step = step 2.0 pos = pos + stepDir d = d + step else: if c != 0: stepDir = stepDir 0.5 step = step 0.5 lod = lod - 1 pos = pos - stepDir d = d - step else: if lod < 2: c = textureLod(uShadowVolume, pos, lod + 1).x if c == 0: lod = lod + 1 stepDir = stepDir 2.0 step = step 2.0 pos = pos + stepDir d = d + step else: # If lod is already 2 and the sample is empty, it does not attempt to go deeper, relying on the coarse search or returning the distance limit pos = pos + stepDir d = d + step return dist A hierarchical raycasting algorithm for shadow volumes that uses fixed step sizes and LODs, traversing from base distance to further distances using specific LOD levels (0, 1, 2). It differs from the sparse variant by not dynamically adjusting step sizes based on occupancy bits, instead using predefined distance thresholds (baseDistance) to switch between LOD levels. It is chosen when the shadow volume is not sparse or when a simpler, fixed-step traversal is preferred. Performs a directional shadow raycast against the sparse shadow volume, including screen-space blocking check and position jittering. It first checks if the ray is blocked in screen space; if so, it returns 0.0. Otherwise, it jitters the position and calls raycastShadowVolumeSparse with the jittered position and direction. It is used to reduce aliasing and improve shadow quality. Not given in the sources. Origin: The method is described in the context of a voxel rendering project, specifically in the mainsv.cpp file of the TTFH/Voxel-Render repository. TTFH/Voxel-Render, https://github.com/TTFH/Voxel-Render, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Regular Grid Traversal
head: Grid Traversal Algorithm, 3D-DDA, Digital Differential Analyzer (for grids)
body: Regular Grid Traversal is a ray-scene intersection acceleration technique that partitions a scene bounding box into a fixed-size 3D grid of cells, returning the sequence of cells intersected by a ray to minimize primitive intersection tests. It solves the problem of testing every object for every ray by only testing primitives stored in intersected cells. Unlike hierarchical structures (e.g., BVH, Octree) that partition primitives into disjoint sets, the Regular Grid partitions space into disjoint sub-blocks, allowing primitives to belong to multiple sub-blocks [3950-regular-grid.md]. It is distinguished by its constant-time access to cells and simple traversal logic, making it optimal for scenes with uniform data distribution or dynamic scenes requiring frequent rebuilds [3950-regular-grid.md]. The method consists of two phases: Grid Construction (building the structure) and Ray Traversal (using the structure). 1. Initialize: Allocate a 1D array of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz and set all entries to NULL. 2. Calculate Dimensions: Compute voxel dimensions and their reciprocals for fast division: dx = \frac{p2.x - p1.x}{Nx}, \quad dx{reci} = \frac{1}{dx} (Similarly for dy, dz and dy{reci}, dz{reci}). 3. Assign Primitives: For each primitive P: Get its Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) [b{min}, b{max}]. Calculate the range of grid cells overlapping this AABB. Clamp coordinates to grid bounds [0, N-1] to handle primitives outside or on the boundary: x1 = \max(0, \lfloor (b{min}.x - p1.x) \cdot dx{reci} \rfloor) x2 = \min(Nx - 1, \lfloor (b{max}.x - p1.x) \cdot dx{reci} \rfloor + 1) (Similarly for y1, y2 and z1, z2). Loop over all cells (x, y, z) in the range x1, x2) \times [y1, y2) \times [z1, z2): Construct the AABB for the current cell. If the primitive intersects the cell AABB, add the primitive to the cell's ObjectList. Note: This mapping must be conservative; it may include more primitives than strictly necessary but never fewer. The traversal identifies the sequence of cells intersected by a ray r(t) = o + t \cdot d. 1. [Ray-Grid Intersection: Intersect the ray with the grid's bounding box [p1, p2] to find entry t{enter} and exit t{exit} parameters. If t{exit} < 0 or t{enter} > t{exit}, the ray misses the grid. If t{enter} < 0, set t{enter} = 0 (ray starts inside). 2. Initialization: Determine the starting point on the ray: start\point = o + d \cdot t{enter}. Calculate the starting cell (X, Y, Z): X = \lfloor \frac{start\point.x - p1.x}{dx} \rfloor (Similarly for Y, Z). Calculate step directions: stepX = \text{sign}(d.x) \quad (\text{1 if } d.x \ge 0, -1 \text{ otherwise}) (Similarly for stepY, stepZ). Calculate delta distances (distance to cross one cell): tDeltaX = \frac{dx}{|d.x|} \text{ if } d.x \neq 0 \text{ else } \infty (Similarly for tDeltaY, tDeltaZ). Calculate initial boundary distances (tMax): If d.x > 0: tMaxX = \frac{(X + 1) \cdot dx + p1.x - start\point.x}{d.x} If d.x < 0: tMaxX = \frac{X \cdot dx + p1.x - start\point.x}{d.x} If d.x = 0: tMaxX = \infty. (Similarly for tMaxY, tMaxZ). 3. Loop: While t{enter} < t{exit}: Process the current cell (X, Y, Z): If the cell is not empty, iterate through the ObjectList. For each primitive, perform intersection test. Deduplication: To avoid testing the same primitive multiple times (if it spans multiple cells), use a "Mailbox" system: assign each ray a unique ID, and store the ray ID in the primitive's intersection cache. Skip tests if the cache already contains the current ray ID. Correctness Check: If an intersection is found but the point is outside the current cell, continue advancing. Advance to the nearest boundary: Find axis A \in \{X, Y, Z\} with minimum tMaxA. Update tMaxA \leftarrow tMaxA + tDeltaA. Update coordinate A \leftarrow A + stepA. If the new coordinate is out of bounds, terminate. A Regular Grid is a spatial acceleration structure that divides a scene bounding box into a fixed-size 3D grid of cells (voxels) to reduce the number of ray-primitive intersection tests. It solves the problem of testing every object for every ray by only testing primitives stored in cells intersected by the ray. Unlike hierarchical structures (e.g., BVH, Octree) that partition primitives into disjoint sets, the Regular Grid partitions space into disjoint sub-blocks, allowing primitives to belong to multiple sub-blocks. It is distinguished by its constant-time access to cells and simple traversal logic, making it optimal for scenes with uniform data distribution or dynamic scenes requiring frequent rebuilds. Voxel-based Ray Tracing is a global illumination (GI) and specular reflection fallback method that performs Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal through a sparse, block-occupancy voxel grid to sample indirect lighting and environment reflections. It serves as a drop-in replacement for Screen-Space Ray Tracing (SSRT) for GI and a fallback for Screen-Space Reflections (SSR) when screen-space coverage is incomplete, combining sky occlusion with Light Propagation Volumes (LPV) colour bleeding. Unlike standard voxel raycasting which often relies on volume density, this method operates on a binary block-occupancy grid to determine surface hits for lighting queries. Optimised Voxel Ray Marching is a ray traversal algorithm for voxel-based scenes that uses fixed-length steps along the ray to traverse a 3D grid of voxels, checking for occupancy at each step. It solves the problem of inefficiently stepping through empty space in large voxel worlds by optimizing memory access patterns, specifically by keeping block lookups within the current working chunk to minimize bitshifts, masks, and multiplication operations. It sets itself apart from Regular Grid Traversal by using a chunked memory layout that reduces boundary calculation overhead, and from Chunked Voxel Traversal by relying on fixed-size inner grids which simplifies implementation and memory layout. The Regular Grid Traversal algorithm is a foundational technique in ray tracing, historically developed to determine the cells traversed by a ray. Algorithms for grid traversal are quite similar to rasterization algorithms (such as Bresenham line draw algorithm [Bre65]), but unlike Bresenham which produces visually acceptable lines in the shortest time without finding all pixels traversed, grid traversal must find all cells traversed by the ray segment. A naive 3D extension of Bresenham is not suitable as a grid traversal algorithm. Traversal time is a critical metric, often modeled by two constants: T{setup} (time to setup traversal algorithm) and T{step} (time spent to advance from a cell to its neighbor without checking intersection). An algorithm with low T{setup} usually performs better for low resolution grids, whereas high T{step} provides bad performance for larger grids. Sources A Survey on Exploiting Grids for Ray Tracing, https://doi.org/10.2312/localchapterevents/italchap/italianchapconf2008/089-096, fetched 2026-10-24

body: A Regular Grid is a spatial acceleration structure that divides the scene bounding box into a fixed-size 3D grid of equal-sized voxels (cells). It solves the problem of testing every object for every ray by only testing primitives stored in cells intersected by the ray, skipping empty cells entirely. Unlike hierarchical structures (e.g., BVH, Octrees) that partition primitives into disjoint sets, the Regular Grid partitions space into disjoint sub-blocks, allowing primitives to belong to multiple sub-blocks. It is distinguished by its linear-time build complexity, making it suitable for dynamic scenes and GPU implementations where repeated construction is feasible. Initialize gridsize = Nx Ny Nz grid = [None] gridsize # 2. Calculate Dimensions dx = (p2.x - p1.x) / Nx dy = (p2.y - p1.y) / Ny dz = (p2.z - p1.z) / Nz dxreci = 1.0 / dx dyreci = 1.0 / dy dzreci = 1.0 / dz # 3. Assign Primitives for prim in primitives: bmin, bmax = prim.getaabb() # Calculate cell range x1 = max(0, int((bmin.x - p1.x) dxreci)) x2 = min(Nx - 1, int((bmax.x - p1.x) dxreci) + 1) y1 = max(0, int((bmin.y - p1.y) dyreci)) y2 = min(Ny - 1, int((bmax.y - p1.y) dyreci) + 1) z1 = max(0, int((bmin.z - p1.z) dzreci)) z2 = min(Nz - 1, int((bmax.z - p1.z) dzreci) + 1) # Loop over candidate cells for x in range(x1, x2 + 1): for y in range(y1, y2 + 1): for z in range(z1, z2 + 1): # Construct cell AABB cellmin = vec3(p1.x + x dx, p1.y + y dy, p1.z + z dz) cellmax = vec3(p1.x + (x + 1) dx, p1.y + (y + 1) dy, p1.z + (z + 1) dz) # Check intersection (conservative) if prim.intersectsaabb(cellmin, cellmax): idx = x + y Nx + z Nx Ny if grid[idx] is None: grid[idx] = ObjectList() grid[idx].add(prim) return grid def traversegrid(ray, grid, p1, p2, Nx, Ny, Nz): # 1. Ray-Grid Intersection tenter, texit = ray.intersectaabb(p1, p2) if texit < 0 or tenter > texit: return None if tenter < 0: tenter = 0 startpoint = ray.origin + ray.direction tenter # 2. Initialization dx = (p2.x - p1.x) / Nx dy = (p2.y - p1.y) / Ny dz = (p2.z - p1.z) / Nz X = int((startpoint.x - p1.x) / dx) Y = int((startpoint.y - p1.y) / dy) Z = int((startpoint.z - p1.z) / dz) # Clamp to grid bounds if ray starts outside but intersects X = max(0, min(Nx - 1, X)) Y = max(0, min(Ny - 1, Y)) Z = max(0, min(Nz - 1, Z)) stepX = 1 if ray.direction.x >= 0 else -1 stepY = 1 if ray.direction.y >= 0 else -1 stepZ = 1 if ray.direction.z >= 0 else -1 tDeltaX = dx / abs(ray.direction.x) if ray.direction.x != 0 else float('inf') tDeltaY = dy / abs(ray.direction.y) if ray.direction.y != 0 else float('inf') tDeltaZ = dz / abs(ray.direction.z) if ray.direction.z != 0 else float('inf') # Calculate tMax if ray.direction.x > 0: tMaxX = ((X + 1) dx + p1.x - startpoint.x) / ray.direction.x elif ray.direction.x < 0: tMaxX = (X dx + p1.x - startpoint.x) / ray.direction.x else: tMaxX = float('inf') if ray.direction.y > 0: tMaxY = ((Y + 1) dy + p1.y - startpoint.y) / ray.direction.y elif ray.direction.y < 0: tMaxY = (Y dy + p1.y - startpoint.y) / ray.direction.y else: tMaxY = float('inf') if ray.direction.z > 0: tMaxZ = ((Z + 1) dz + p1.z - startpoint.z) / ray.direction.z elif ray.direction.z < 0: tMaxZ = (Z dz + p1.z - startpoint.z) / ray.direction.z else: tMaxZ = float('inf') # 3. Loop while tenter < texit: # Process current cell idx = X + Y Nx + Z Nx Ny celllist = grid[idx] if celllist is not None: for prim in celllist: # Deduplication check would go here hit = prim.intersect(ray) if hit is not None: # Correctness check: is hit point within current cell bounds? # If not, continue advancing. # For simplicity, assuming conservative grid ensures # if hit is valid, it's the closest or we handle it. # In strict implementation, verify hit.t is within cell bounds. return hit # Advance to nearest boundary if tMaxX < tMaxY: if tMaxX < tMaxZ: tMaxX += tDeltaX X += stepX else: tMaxZ += tDeltaZ Z += stepZ else: if tMaxY < tMaxZ: tMaxY += tDeltaY Y += stepY else: tMaxZ += tDeltaZ Z += stepZ # Check bounds if X < 0 or X >= Nx or Y < 0 or Y >= Ny or Z < 0 or Z >= Nz: break return None Regular-Grid Mesh Intersection computes intersections between a ray and a regular-grid mesh M of size P \times P \times P with O(P) complexity. It differs from general ray-mesh intersection algorithms by exploiting the structured topology of the regular grid to restrict the search space to a linear number of voxels and faces, enabling efficient quadrature for neural field rendering. The Empty-Space Skipping Grid is a 3D regular grid acceleration structure used in conjunction with the Volumetric Depth Image (VDI) to optimize raycasting by skipping empty regions along a ray's path. It reduces memory accesses by allowing rays to jump over grid cells that contain no supersegments, thereby avoiding unnecessary traversal of empty supersegment lists. Unlike hierarchical grids such as octrees or SparseLeap, this structure is chosen for its ability to be constructed dynamically during VDI generation using atomic operations, trading off some skipping efficiency for simpler, parallelizable build times. Time Complexity: Building time is linear with respect to the number of primitives or grid size, allowing creation from scratch and update at every frame with interactive performance for moderate sized scenes. Traversal time depends on the number of empty cells skipped and the number of primitives per cell. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is high for sparse scenes because the grid is uniform and cannot adapt to primitive density. Many triangles may cluster in a small area but occupy many empty voxels. The total number of cells is Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz. Measured Performance: On Intel Pentium II 350 MHz, for the 'tree' scene (resolution 513x513, recursion depth 4): Uniform Grid with voxel density D=1.0 (voxels = objects) took TB=0.22s (build) and T{TR}=1517.0s (traversal). Uniform Grid Customary with D=20.0 took TB=0.33s and T{TR}=781.3s. Strengths: Simple implementation, constant-time access to elements, good data locality, optimal on GPU for uniform data distribution due to cached texture accesses. Fast build time allows repeated construction for dynamic scenes. Limitations: High memory usage for sparse scenes. Not suitable for dynamic scenes if using Proximity Clouds acceleration as pre-calculating distance information is costly. The rule of thumb D=1.0 is not very good; higher density (D=20.0) is often better for SPD scenes. When to use: Scenes with uniform data distribution, dynamic scenes requiring frequent rebuilds, or as a starting point for learning ray tracing. When not to use: Highly sparse scenes where hierarchical grids (BVH, Octree) would save memory and potentially traversal time. Origin: Grid data structures were introduced by [Gla84]. History: They have been popular for rendering analytical objects, particle-based simulations, and computational fluids dynamics. The 3D-DDA traversal algorithm is heavily based on the paper by Amanatides & Woo. Usage: Used in software ray tracers, recommended for homework assignments, and referenced in Nvidia OptiX contexts. On GPUs, sorting-based construction allows repeated use for each frame and stage, particularly for reflection/refraction rays which lack natural coherence. flipcode - Raytracing Topics & Techniques, https://flipcode.com/archives/RaytracingTopicsTechniques-Part4SpatialSubdivisions.shtml, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) RTNv12n1.txt, https://realtimerendering.com/resources/RTNews/text/RTNv12n1.txt, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) A Survey on Exploiting Grids for Ray Tracing, https://doi.org/10.2312/localchapterevents/italchap/italianchapconf2008/089-096, fetched 2026-10-24 Online Computer Graphics II: Rendering: Raytracing Acceleration: Acceleration Structures and Grids, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c01yvv4WVGs, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Raytracing dynamic scenes on the GPU using grids, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/5728799/, fetched 2026-10-25 光线追踪小记:空间加速结构Regular Grid与3DDDA, https://zhuanlan.zhihu.com/p/415869768, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) PPT - Ray Tracing 2: Acceleration PowerPoint Presentation, free..., https://www.slideserve.com/chaim/ray-tracing-2-acceleration, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Représentation et algorithmes pour l'exploration interactive de volumes procéduraux étendus et détaillés, https://inria.hal.science/inria-00598406v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Regular-Grid Mesh Intersection
head: Ray-Mesh Quadrature
body: Regular-Grid Mesh Intersection computes intersections between a ray and a regular-grid mesh M of size P \times P \times P with O(P) complexity. It differs from general ray-mesh intersection algorithms by exploiting the structured topology of the regular grid to restrict the search space to a linear number of voxels and faces, enabling efficient quadrature for neural field rendering. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Regular-grid mesh M defined on a grid of size P \times P \times P. Acceleration grid G \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times P \times P}, where each element G{i,j,k} is a real number indicating geometry likelihood. Training progress t \in [0, 1] to determine pruning aggressiveness. Scene type flag (e.g., unbounded 360°). Outputs: A set of quadrature points (intersection points) between the ray and the mesh faces. Data Structures: Acceleration Grid G: A 3D array of size P \times P \times P. Each element G{i,j,k} is a real number. The sources do not specify exact bit-packing or normalization range, but it functions as a threshold filter. Mesh M: Implicitly defined by the regular grid vertices, consisting of faces incident to voxel vertices. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Intersected Voxels: Solve 3P ray-plane intersections to determine the set of voxels intersected by the ray. Using these intersection points, identify at most 3P intersected voxels. 2. Prune Empty Voxels (Conditional): Use the acceleration grid G to prune voxels unlikely to contain geometry based on threshold \tauG = 0.1. Training Stage 1 (First Quarter, t < 0.25): Do not use G for pruning. Keep all 3P intersected voxels and all 3P intersection points. Training Stage 2 (Second Quarter, 0.25 \le t < 0.5): Use G to remove empty voxels. Keep at most 3P/2 non-empty voxels and the 3P/2 intersection points closest to the camera. Training Stage 3 (Rest of Training, t \ge 0.5): Use G to remove empty voxels. Keep at most 3P/4 intersection points. Batch Size Adjustment: Double the training batch size each time the number of intersections is halved. 3. Compute Quadrature Points: For each kept voxel, compute intersections between the ray and the faces of M that are incident to the voxel’s vertex. This yields the final set of quadrature points. 4. Special Case for Unbounded 360° Scenes: For concentric boxes in unbounded 360° scenes, compute their intersections and keep all of them, bypassing the pruning steps above. Formulas: Ray-plane intersection parameter: t = \frac{c - \mathbf{o}i}{\mathbf{d}i}, where c is the grid plane coordinate along axis i \in \{x, y, z\}, \mathbf{o}i and \mathbf{d}i are the ray origin and direction components along axis i, and t > 0 ensures forward intersection. Voxel index from intersection point: vi = \lfloor (\mathbf{o}i + t \mathbf{d}i) P \rfloor. Distance to camera for sorting: D(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}\|. Parameters: \tauG = 0.1: Threshold for pruning voxels in the acceleration grid. P: Grid resolution (dimension of the regular grid). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Division by zero occurs when \mathbf{d}i = 0; a small epsilon guard (10^{-8}) is required. Boundaries: Intersection points must be clamped to voxel face bounds to avoid duplicate or out-of-mesh quadrature points. Degenerate Input: Unbounded 360° scenes with concentric boxes require bypassing pruning to retain all intersections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def regulargridmeshintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, accelgrid, P, trainingprogress, isunbounded360): """ Compute intersections between a ray and a regular-grid mesh. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. accelgrid: 3D array of size P x P x P, values indicate geometry likelihood. P: Integer, grid resolution. trainingprogress: Float in [0, 1], normalized training progress. isunbounded360: Boolean, true for unbounded 360 degree scenes. Returns: list of intersection points (quadrature points). """ EPS = 1e-8 intersectedvoxels = [] # Step 1: Solve 3P ray-plane intersections to find intersected voxels for axis in range(3): for i in range(P): planecoord = i / P denom = raydirection[axis] if abs(denom) > EPS: t = (planecoord - rayorigin[axis]) / denom if t > 0: point = rayorigin + t raydirection # Clamp voxel index to valid range [0, P-1] voxelidx = tuple(min(int(point[d] P), P - 1) for d in range(3)) if voxelidx not in intersectedvoxels: intersectedvoxels.append(voxelidx) keptvoxels = [] if isunbounded360 or trainingprogress < 0.25: keptvoxels = intersectedvoxels else: # Filter by acceleration grid threshold filtered = [v for v in intersectedvoxels if accelgrid[v] >= 0.1] # Sort by distance to camera to keep closest points filtered.sort(key=lambda v: sum((rayorigin[d] - v[d] / P) 2 for d in range(3))) # Limit based on training stage limit = int(1.5 P) if trainingprogress < 0.5 else int(0.75 P) keptvoxels = filtered[:limit] # Step 3: Compute quadrature points by intersecting ray with voxel faces quadraturepoints = [] for voxel in keptvoxels: for axis in range(3): for boundary in (0, 1): planecoord = boundary / P denom = raydirection[axis] if abs(denom) > EPS: t = (planecoord - rayorigin[axis]) / denom if t > 0: point = rayorigin + t raydirection # Check if point lies within voxel bounds on other axes valid = True for d in range(3): if d != axis: if not (voxel[d] / P <= point[d] <= (voxel[d] + 1) / P): valid = False break if valid: quadraturepoints.append(point) return quadraturepoints Time Complexity: O(P) for computing intersections. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the acceleration grid G \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times P \times P}. Performance: The method reduces the number of intersection tests, enabling efficient neural field rendering. Strengths: Linear complexity with respect to grid resolution P; efficient pruning via acceleration grid. Limitations: Accuracy of the acceleration grid G is low in the first quarter of training, necessitating full voxel retention initially. The method is described in the context of MobileNeRF, which exploits the polygon rasterization pipeline for efficient neural field rendering. It was introduced to address the computational cost of ray-mesh intersections in neural rendering. MobileNeRF: Exploiting the Polygon Rasterization Pipeline for Efficient Neural Field Rendering on Mobile Architectures, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.01590, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Empty-Space Skipping Grid
head: Grid acceleration data structure
body: The Empty-Space Skipping Grid is a 3D regular grid acceleration structure used in conjunction with the Volumetric Depth Image (VDI) to optimize raycasting by skipping empty regions along a ray's path. It reduces memory accesses by allowing rays to jump over grid cells that contain no supersegments, thereby avoiding unnecessary traversal of empty supersegment lists. Unlike hierarchical grids such as octrees or SparseLeap, this structure is chosen for its ability to be constructed dynamically during VDI generation using atomic operations, trading off some skipping efficiency for simpler, parallelizable build times. Inputs and Outputs Input: A Volumetric Depth Image (VDI) consisting of supersegment lists \mathbb{L}i and supersegments \mathbb{S}j^i; a viewing frustum defined in view space. Output: A 3D regular grid where each cell stores an integer count of overlapping supersegments. Data Structures The grid is a 3D regular grid aligned with the viewing plane. Cell Layout: Each cell stores a single integer value representing the count of supersegments \mathbb{S} overlapping with that cell. Dimensions: Along the viewing plane (width and height), each cell spans an equal number of supersegment lists \mathbb{L}. Along the depth axis (view space), each cell has a constant depth extent. The depth of a cell in view space is larger than its width or height to account for the anisotropic nature of the VDI, where there are fewer supersegments per list than there are lists. Algorithm Steps 1. Grid Construction: During VDI generation, for each generated supersegment \mathbb{S}j^i, determine the grid cell it overlaps. Perform an atomic add operation on that cell to increment its count. 2. Ray Traversal: When a ray traverses the grid: a. Query the grid cell at the current ray position. b. If the cell value is 0, jump the ray to the other end of that cell (skipping the empty region). c. If the cell value is non-zero, proceed to traverse the supersegment lists within that depth range. 3. Query Cost: Querying the grid data structure requires one memory access per cell traversed. Pseudocode Unverified code. Grid Cell Width/Height: Each cell spans an equal number of supersegment lists \mathbb{L} along both dimensions of the viewing plane. Edge Cases and Pitfalls NDC Distortion: In Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) space, grid cells appear larger toward the near plane and smaller toward the far plane due to the constant view-space depth extent. Implementers must account for this non-uniform scaling when mapping ray positions to grid indices in NDC. Empty Region Traversal: Without the grid, a ray must sample each list \mathbb{L}i at least once to determine if it is empty, leading to excessive memory accesses. The grid mitigates this but requires correct atomic operations during construction to ensure accuracy. Construction Time: Low, as it allows construction during VDI generation via atomic adds. This is simpler than building hierarchical structures dynamically. Memory Access: One memory access per grid cell traversed. Performance: Reduces memory accesses in empty regions by allowing rays to jump over cells with zero supersegments. Performance depends on the number of memory accesses and calculations; high frame rates are achieved near the original view direction, but performance reduces with larger viewpoint deviations. Comparison: Chosen over hierarchical grids (octree, SparseLeap) because it allows construction during VDI generation via atomic adds, whereas hierarchical structures are more complex to build dynamically. Hierarchical grids may provide better empty-space skipping performance but at the cost of build complexity. The Empty-Space Skipping Grid was introduced in the context of efficient raycasting of Volumetric Depth Images (VDI) for remote visualization of large volumes at high frame rates. It addresses the limitation of VDI alone, where rays cannot efficiently query empty regions without sampling each supersegment list. The structure was selected over hierarchical alternatives like octrees or SparseLeap to enable parallel construction during VDI generation. name: Voxel-based Ray Tracing for GI and Specular Reflections
head: ApplyVoxelRT, Voxel RT, VoxelDDA, VoxelReflectionFallback
body: Voxel-based Ray Tracing is a global illumination (GI) and specular reflection fallback method that performs Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal through a 128^3 block-occupancy voxel grid to sample indirect lighting and environment reflections. It serves as a drop-in replacement for Screen-Space Ray Tracing (SSRT) for GI and a fallback for Screen-Space Reflections (SSR) when screen-space coverage is incomplete, combining sky occlusion with Light Propagation Volumes (LPV) colour bleeding. Unlike standard voxel raycasting which often relies on volume density, this method operates on a binary block-occupancy grid to determine surface hits for lighting queries. The method consists of a core 3D DDA traversal kernel (VoxelDDA), a lighting sampling function (SampleVoxelLighting), and two high-level application functions: ApplyVoxelRT for GI and VoxelReflectionFallback for specular reflections. Input Grid: A 128^3 block-occupancy grid stored in imgVoxelMask, populated every frame during the shadow pass. Input Lighting: LPV data, accessed via image load/store operations. Input Ray: Origin o, direction d, and maximum traversal steps. Output GI: A blended indirect colour value combining sky occlusion and LPV bounce. Output Reflection: A specular colour sampled from the voxel grid at the hit location. Voxel Grid (imgVoxelMask): A 3D image buffer representing a 128 \times 128 \times 128 grid. Each voxel stores a binary occupancy flag (1 if a block exists, 0 otherwise). LPV Buffer: A 3D texture or image buffer storing propagated light colour and intensity values for each voxel. VOXELGISAMPLES: Number of cosine-weighted hemisphere rays for GI sampling. Default: 4. VOXELGISTEPS: Maximum number of DDA steps for GI ray traversal. VOXELREFLSTEPS: Maximum number of DDA steps for reflection ray traversal. VOXELRTREFLECTIONS: Feature flag (boolean) to enable specular reflection fallback. Default: Disabled (commented out). VOXELGI: Indirect effect mode identifier (value 6). This function performs the 3D DDA traversal to find the first occupied voxel face intersected by a ray. 1. Initialization: Calculate grid dimensions Nx=Ny=Nz=128. Compute step directions: stepX = \text{sign}(d.x), stepY = \text{sign}(d.y), stepZ = \text{sign}(d.z). Compute delta distances: tDeltaX = dx / |d.x| (if d.x \neq 0 else \infty), similarly for Y, Z. Determine starting cell (X, Y, Z) from the ray origin (clamped to entry point). Compute initial boundary distances tMaxX, tMaxY, tMaxZ to the next grid plane in the direction of travel. Apply a small ray bias to the origin to prevent self-intersection and handle near-parallel rays gracefully. 2. Traversal Loop: Iterate up to maxsteps times. Find the axis with the minimum tMax (tMin = \min(tMaxX, tMaxY, tMaxZ)). Check if the current cell (X, Y, Z) is occupied in imgVoxelMask. If occupied, return the hit position (face centre) and the axis-aligned normal of the face crossed. Advance the ray: Increment the coordinate of the minimum axis by its step direction. Update the corresponding tMax by adding its tDelta. If the ray exits the grid bounds or reaches maxsteps without a hit, return a miss status. 1. Given a hit position P and normal N from VoxelDDA: 2. Offset the sampling position by half a block in the direction of the normal to sample the LPV data "in front" of the surface. 3. Read the indirect colour from the LPV buffer at this offset position. 1. Initialize total indirect colour C{indirect} = 0. 2. Generate VOXELGISAMPLES cosine-weighted hemisphere rays. 3. For each ray: Call VoxelDDA with the ray parameters and VOXELGISTEPS. If a hit is found: Call SampleVoxelLighting to get LPV colour C{lpv}. Blend C{lpv} with sky contribution (based on ray direction and sky occlusion). Accumulate into C{indirect}. If no hit, use sky contribution only. 4. Average the results from all samples. 1. Check if VOXELRTREFLECTIONS is enabled and if SSR missed (e.g., environmentReflection.a < 1). 2. Construct a specular reflection ray from the surface normal and view direction. 3. Call VoxelDDA with this ray and VOXELREFLSTEPS. 4. If a hit is found: Call SampleVoxelLighting to get the voxel colour. Scale the voxel lighting to match typical sky-reflection brightness ranges to avoid visual mismatch. Return the scaled colour as the reflection result. 5. If no hit, return the previous screen-space reflection or a default value. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def VoxelDDA(origin, direction, maxsteps, p1, p2, gridsize): """ Performs 3D DDA traversal on the voxel grid. Returns (hitposition, hitnormal) or None if miss. """ # 1. Initialization dx = (p2.x - p1.x) / gridsize dy = (p2.y - p1.y) / gridsize dz = (p2.z - p1.z) / gridsize dxrecip = 1.0 / dx dyrecip = 1.0 / dy dzrecip = 1.0 / dz # Apply small bias to avoid self-intersection bias = 1e-4 startpoint = origin + direction bias # Determine starting cell X = math.floor((startpoint.x - p1.x) dxrecip) Y = math.floor((startpoint.y - p1.y) dyrecip) Z = math.floor((startpoint.z - p1.z) dzrecip) # Clamp to grid bounds X = max(0, min(gridsize - 1, X)) Y = max(0, min(gridsize - 1, Y)) Z = max(0, min(gridsize - 1, Z)) # Step directions stepX = 1 if direction.x > 0 else (-1 if direction.x < 0 else 0) stepY = 1 if direction.y > 0 else (-1 if direction.y < 0 else 0) stepZ = 1 if direction.z > 0 else (-1 if direction.z < 0 else 0) # Delta distances tDeltaX = dx / abs(direction.x) if direction.x != 0 else float('inf') tDeltaY = dy / abs(direction.y) if direction.y != 0 else float('inf') tDeltaZ = dz / abs(direction.z) if direction.z != 0 else float('inf') # Initial tMax if direction.x > 0: tMaxX = ((X + 1) dx + p1.x - startpoint.x) / direction.x elif direction.x < 0: tMaxX = (X dx + p1.x - startpoint.x) / direction.x else: tMaxX = float('inf') if direction.y > 0: tMaxY = ((Y + 1) dy + p1.y - startpoint.y) / direction.y elif direction.y < 0: tMaxY = (Y dy + p1.y - startpoint.y) / direction.y else: tMaxY = float('inf') if direction.z > 0: tMaxZ = ((Z + 1) dz + p1.z - startpoint.z) / direction.z elif direction.z < 0: tMaxZ = (Z dz + p1.z - startpoint.z) / direction.z else: tMaxZ = float('inf') # 2. Traversal Loop for in range(maxsteps): # Check bounds if X < 0 or X >= gridsize or Y < 0 or Y >= gridsize or Z < 0 or Z >= gridsize: return None # Check occupancy in imgVoxelMask if isoccupied(X, Y, Z): # Calculate hit position (face centre) mint = min(tMaxX, tMaxY, tMaxZ) hitpos = startpoint + direction mint # Determine normal if tMaxX <= tMaxY and tMaxX <= tMaxZ: normal = vec3(-stepX, 0, 0) elif tMaxY <= tMaxX and tMaxY <= tMaxZ: normal = vec3(0, -stepY, 0) else: normal = vec3(0, 0, -stepZ) return (hitpos, normal) # Advance to nearest boundary if tMaxX < tMaxY: if tMaxX < tMaxZ: X += stepX tMaxX += tDeltaX else: Z += stepZ tMaxZ += tDeltaZ else: if tMaxY < tMaxZ: Y += stepY tMaxY += tDeltaY else: Z += stepZ tMaxZ += tDeltaZ return None def isoccupied(x, y, z): # Reads binary occupancy flag from imgVoxelMask buffer return True def getLPVColor(pos): # Reads propagated light colour from LPV buffer at pos return vec3(0.0) def cosineweightedhemispheresample(normal): # Standard cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling u1 = random() u2 = random() z = math.sqrt(1.0 - u1) r = math.sqrt(u1) phi = 2.0 math.pi u2 x = math.cos(phi) r y = math.sin(phi) r # Construct orthonormal basis aligned with normal and sample # Simplified return for demonstration return vec3(x, z, y) def getskycontribution(raydir): # Standard sky dome lookup return vec3(0.5) def ApplyVoxelRT(surfacepos, surfacenormal, viewdir): """ Computes GI using cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling. """ totalcolor = vec3(0.0) count = 0 for in range(4): # VOXELGISAMPLES raydir = cosineweightedhemispheresample(surfacenormal) # Trace ray hit = VoxelDDA(surfacepos, raydir, 64, vec3(0,0,0), vec3(1,1,1), 128) # VOXELGISTEPS, grid bounds if hit is not None: hitpos, hitnormal = hit lpvcolor = getLPVColor(hitpos) # Blend sky contribution with LPV bounce skycontrib = getskycontribution(raydir) indirectcolor = mix(skycontrib, lpvcolor, 0.5) # Blending factor is implementation detail totalcolor += indirectcolor count += 1 else: # No hit, use sky contribution skycontrib = getskycontribution(raydir) totalcolor += skycontrib count += 1 if count > 0: return totalcolor / count else: return vec3(0.0) def VoxelReflectionFallback(surfacepos, surfacenormal, viewdir): """ Fallback for specular reflections when SSR misses. """ # Construct reflection ray raydir = reflect(-viewdir, surfacenormal) # Trace ray hit = VoxelDDA(surfacepos, raydir, 32, vec3(0,0,0), vec3(1,1,1), 128) # VOXELREFLSTEPS if hit is not None: hitpos, hitnormal = hit voxelcolor = getLPVColor(hitpos) # Scale to match sky-reflection brightness scaledcolor = voxelcolor 1.5 # brightnessscalefactor return scaledcolor else: return vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Transparent Self-Intersection: A ray bias must be applied to the origin to prevent the ray from immediately hitting the voxel it started in. Near-Parallel Rays: The DDA logic must handle cases where d.x, d.y, or d.z is zero to avoid division by zero in tDelta calculations. Hardware Support: Requires GLARBshaderimageloadstore for reading the voxel mask and LPV data. If unsupported, the system must degrade to SSRT. Visual Mismatch: Voxel lighting for reflections must be scaled to match the brightness of sky reflections to avoid visual discontinuities. Precision Artifacts: On hardware with aggressive FP16 FTZ (Flush To Zero) behaviour (e.g., NVIDIA RTX 5000 series), near-zero values can become exact zeros, causing black flickering artifacts in tonemapping or TAA passes. Epsilon guards are required. A uniform grid in object space used to handle reflection rays, as perspective grids are not useful due to lack of coherence and preferred direction. Rays traverse the uniform grid by walking from one voxel to another using a voxel walk procedure. Each ray independently computes the next voxel starting with the starting point, loads triangles of the encountered voxel, and checks intersection until the first intersection is found. This method is simple but assumes no coherence between rays, which can incur a heavy penalty on older GPUs with large SIMD width and no caching to exploit access locality. Choose this variant when tracing reflection rays in dynamic scenes where perspective grids fail to provide traversal coherence. Time Complexity: O(K \cdot S) per pixel, where K is the number of GI samples (VOXELGISAMPLES) and S is the maximum DDA steps (VOXELGISTEPS or VOXELREFLSTEPS). Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for the voxel grid, where N=128. The grid is stored in imgVoxelMask and LPV buffers. Performance: The method is computationally expensive due to multiple ray traces per pixel for GI. It is intended as a fallback or alternative to SSRT, which is generally cheaper but limited by screen-space coverage. Strengths: Provides global illumination and reflections in areas where screen-space methods fail (e.g., off-screen objects, transparent surfaces). Limitations: Requires LPV data, which adds complexity to the rendering pipeline. Performance scales poorly with high sample counts. Visual quality depends on the accuracy of the LPV propagation. This method was implemented by nyzxor as a pull request to the Eclipse-Shader (an edit of Chocapic13 V9 / Bliss) for Minecraft, integrated via the Iris shader mod. It was added to provide an alternative global illumination method and a specular reflection fallback, leveraging the existing voxel grid infrastructure used for shadowing. The implementation addresses specific hardware issues, such as FP16 precision artifacts on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. name: Optimised Voxel Ray Marching
head: Chunk-based Voxel Traversal, Fixed-step voxel ray marching, Optimised CPU Ray Marching, Sector's Edge, Voxel Volume Ray Tracing, VoxelsRayTracingTutorial
body: Optimised Voxel Ray Marching is a ray traversal algorithm for voxel-based scenes that advances a ray to the next voxel boundary to check for occupancy at each step. It solves the problem of inefficiently stepping through empty space in large voxel worlds by optimizing memory access patterns, specifically by keeping block lookups within the current working chunk to minimize bitshifts, masks, and multiplication operations. It sets itself apart from Regular Grid Traversal by maintaining a reference to the current working chunk and updating it only when the ray crosses a chunk boundary, thereby avoiding repeated chunk index calculations for every voxel step. The method implements a ray marcher optimized for CPU collision detection by maintaining a reference to the current working chunk and updating it only when the ray crosses a chunk boundary. Inputs: start: Ray origin in world/voxel space (Vector3). velocity: Ray direction vector (normalized). max: Maximum ray length in world units. chunks: 3D array of Chunk references indexed by [chunkIndexX, chunkIndexY, chunkIndexZ]. MAPSIZE: World dimensions (e.g., 512 \times 160 \times 512). CHUNKSIZE: Side length of a chunk in blocks (typically 32). Outputs: hit: Boolean indicating if a solid block was intersected. axis: The axis (X, Y, or Z) of the face hit (used for reflection). Chunk: Contains a 1D array data of size CHUNK\SIZE^3 (e.g., 32768 for size 32). data stores Block structs sequentially. Block: Single byte field kind. Value 0 indicates empty; non-zero indicates solid. Map: 3D array chunks[,,] of Chunk references. Chunk indices are derived from world coordinates via bit-shifting: idx = coord \gg SHIFT, where SHIFT = \log2(CHUNK\SIZE). Chunk-relative coordinates are derived via bitmask: rel = coord \& MASK, where MASK = CHUNK\SIZE - 1. EPS: 5 \times 10^{-5}, used to offset ray origins to prevent self-intersection. CHUNKSIZE: 32. SHIFT: 5. MASK: 0x1f (31). MAPSIZEX/Z: 512, MAPSIZEY: 160. 1. Initialization: Convert start to integer voxel coordinates: x = \lfloor start.x \rfloor, y = \lfloor start.y \rfloor, z = \lfloor start.z \rfloor. Check bounds: If (x, y, z) is outside MAPSIZE, return hit = false. Calculate chunk indices: cx = x \gg SHIFT, cy = y \gg SHIFT, cz = z \gg SHIFT. Retrieve current chunk: c = chunks[cx, cy, cz]. Calculate chunk-relative coordinates: i = x \& MASK, j = y \& MASK, k = z \& MASK. Calculate linear access index in chunk: access = j + i \cdot CHUNK\SIZE + k \cdot CHUNK\SIZE^2. Check start block: If c is null or c.data[access].kind == 0, return hit = false (unless start/end are same block, handled separately). 2. Direction Setup: Normalize velocity. Calculate inverted components: invX = |1/velocity.x|, invY = |1/velocity.y|, invZ = |1/velocity.z|. Initialize direction-dependent variables for each axis based on the sign of the velocity component: If velocity.axis > 0: step = 1 comparison = CHUNK\SIZE (boundary exit condition). reset = 0 accessReset = -CHUNK\SIZE (for X/Z) or -1 (for Y). accessIncrement = CHUNK\SIZE (for X) or CHUNK\SIZE^2 (for Z) or 1 (for Y). dist = (coord - start.coord + 1) If velocity.axis < 0: step = -1 comparison = -1 reset = CHUNK\SIZE - 1 accessReset = CHUNK\SIZE (for X/Z) or 1 (for Y). accessIncrement = -CHUNK\SIZE (for X) or -CHUNK\SIZE^2 (for Z) or -1 (for Y). dist = (start.coord - coord) Calculate initial distance to next boundary in t-units: tDist{axis} = velocity.axis == 0 ? \infty: inv{axis} \cdot dist{axis}. 3. Marching Loop: Initialize t = 0.0. While t \le max: Occupancy Check: If c is not null and c.data[access].kind \neq 0, set hit = true, return. Find Closest Boundary: Compare tDistX, tDistY, tDistZ. Advance Axis: Let axis be the axis with the minimum tDist. Update relative coordinate: coord{rel} += step{axis}. Update access index: access += step{axis} (for Y) or access += accessIncrement{axis} (for X/Z). Chunk Boundary Check: If coord{rel} == comparison{axis}: Reset relative coordinate: coord{rel} = reset{axis}. Update access index: access += accessReset{axis}. Update chunk index: chunkIndex{axis} += step{axis}. Check new chunk bounds: If chunkIndex{axis} is out of map bounds, return hit = false. Load new chunk: c = chunks[cx, cy, cz]. Update progress: t = tDist{axis}. Update distance to next boundary: tDist{axis} += inv{axis}. Store hit axis: axis = axis. 4. Termination: If loop completes without hit, return hit = false. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarch(start: Vector3, velocity: Vector3, maxdist: float, chunks: Array3D, mapsize: Vector3i, chunksize: int) -> bool: INF = 1e9 # 1. Initialization x = int(start.x) y = int(start.y) z = int(start.z) # Bounds check if x < 0 or x >= mapsize.x or y < 0 or y >= mapsize.y or z < 0 or z >= mapsize.z: return False shift = 5 # log2(chunksize) mask = 31 # chunksize - 1 cx = x >> shift cy = y >> shift cz = z >> shift c = chunks[cx, cy, cz] if c is None: return False i = x & mask j = y & mask k = z & mask access = j + i chunksize + k (chunksize chunksize) # Handle single-block ray endx = int(start.x + velocity.x maxdist) endy = int(start.y + velocity.y maxdist) endz = int(start.z + velocity.z maxdist) if x == endx and y == endy and z == endz: return c.data[access].kind != 0 # 2. Direction Setup velocity = normalize(velocity) invx = abs(1.0 / velocity.x) if velocity.x != 0 else INF invy = abs(1.0 / velocity.y) if velocity.y != 0 else INF invz = abs(1.0 / velocity.z) if velocity.z != 0 else INF # Setup axis variables for X if velocity.x > 0: xstep, xcomparison, xreset = 1, chunksize, 0 xaccessreset, xaccessinc = -(chunksize chunksize), chunksize xdist = x - start.x + 1 else: xstep, xcomparison, xreset = -1, -1, chunksize - 1 xaccessreset, xaccessinc = chunksize chunksize, -chunksize xdist = start.x - x # Setup axis variables for Y if velocity.y > 0: ystep, ycomparison, yreset = 1, chunksize, 0 yaccessreset, yaccessinc = -chunksize, 1 ydist = y - start.y + 1 else: ystep, ycomparison, yreset = -1, -1, chunksize - 1 yaccessreset, yaccessinc = chunksize, -1 ydist = start.y - y # Setup axis variables for Z if velocity.z > 0: zstep, zcomparison, zreset = 1, chunksize, 0 zaccessreset, zaccessinc = -(chunksize chunksize chunksize), chunksize chunksize zdist = z - start.z + 1 else: zstep, zcomparison, zreset = -1, -1, chunksize - 1 zaccessreset, zaccessinc = chunksize chunksize chunksize, -chunksize chunksize zdist = start.z - z tdistx = invx xdist if velocity.x != 0 else INF tdisty = invy ydist if velocity.y != 0 else INF tdistz = invz zdist if velocity.z != 0 else INF t = 0.0 hitaxis = None # 3. Marching Loop while t <= maxdist: if c is not None and c.data[access].kind != 0: return True # Find closest boundary if tdisty < tdistx: if tdisty < tdistz: # Advance Y j += ystep access += ystep if j == ycomparison: j = yreset access += yaccessreset cy += ystep if cy < 0 or cy >= mapsize.y // chunksize: return False c = chunks[cx, cy, cz] t = tdisty tdisty += invy hitaxis = 'Y' else: # Advance Z k += zstep access += zaccessinc if k == zcomparison: k = zreset access += zaccessreset cz += zstep if cz < 0 or cz >= mapsize.z // chunksize: return False c = chunks[cx, cy, cz] t = tdistz tdistz += invz hitaxis = 'Z' else: if tdistx < tdistz: # Advance X i += xstep access += xaccessinc if i == xcomparison: i = xreset access += xaccessreset cx += xstep if cx < 0 or cx >= mapsize.x // chunksize: return False c = chunks[cx, cy, cz] t = tdistx tdistx += invx hitaxis = 'X' else: # Advance Z k += zstep access += zaccessinc if k == zcomparison: k = zreset access += zaccessreset cz += zstep if cz < 0 or cz >= mapsize.z // chunksize: return False c = chunks[cx, cy, cz] t = tdistz tdistz += invz hitaxis = 'Z' return False Self-Intersection: When computing normals or shadow rays, offset the origin by n \cdot EPS to avoid hitting the surface itself. Null Chunks: Empty chunks may be represented by null references. The algorithm must check for null before accessing data. Boundary Precision: Using floor on the start position is standard, but floating-point inaccuracies at chunk boundaries can cause skipping or double-checking. The EPS offset helps mitigate this. Zero Velocity: If a velocity component is 0, the distance to the next boundary is infinity, preventing advancement on that axis. Optimizes ray marching through a voxel grid by avoiding redundant cell checks when traversing a 2x2x2 block. It steps a 2x2x2 block of grid cells; after stepping along one axis, half of the block was tested in the previous step, so it tests only the 4 cells on the leading side. This reduces the number of grid-walk calls and improves cache locality. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels traversed. The cost per step is very low due to bitwise operations for chunk indexing. Memory Complexity: Depends on the sparse voxel grid implementation. Chunks are allocated on-demand, reducing memory usage for empty worlds. Performance: On a Ryzen 5 1600 CPU, ray marching for 1-10 blocks takes ~250 nanoseconds, allowing 64,000 rays per frame per thread at 60fps. For longer rays (200-400 blocks), it takes ~3400 nanoseconds, allowing 4,700 rays per frame. Strengths: Extremely fast for CPU-based collision detection in voxel games. Minimizes cache misses by keeping access local to the current chunk. Limitations: Fixed-step nature means it may step through empty space if the grid is sparse and chunks are not hierarchical (unlike Octree-based methods). Not suitable for high-precision continuous collision detection without sub-stepping. The method is based on "A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing" by John Amanatides and Andrew Woo. It was specifically optimized for CPU implementation in the game Sector's Edge by Vercidium to handle particle and projectile collisions efficiently. The optimization focuses on reducing the computational overhead of chunk boundary checks by maintaining a "current working chunk" reference. name: Chunked Voxel Traversal
head: Chunk-based Voxel Traversal, Fixed-step voxel ray marching
body: Chunked Voxel Traversal is a hierarchical ray traversal method for sparse voxel grids that accelerates intersection testing by organizing voxels into a 3D grid of smaller 3D sub-grids called "chunks". It solves the problem of inefficiently stepping through empty space in large voxel worlds by allowing the ray to skip entire chunks that contain no geometry. It sets itself apart from pure 3D grid traversal by reducing the number of intersection checks in empty regions, and from octree-based traversal by using fixed-size inner grids which simplifies implementation and memory layout. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, outer grid occupancy data, and chunk data. Output: The first non-empty voxel hit by the ray, or null if the ray exits the world without hitting a voxel. Data Structures: The structure is a two-level hierarchy: 1. Outer Grid: A 3D array representing the world space, divided into chunks. Each entry stores a boolean or bitmask indicating if the chunk is empty. 2. Chunks: Each chunk is a fixed-size 3D array of voxels. Voxel Data: Compressed to 8 bytes per voxel on the GPU to reduce transmission size; material properties are sent separately from voxel data. Bit Packing: Voxel attributes are packed into the 8 bytes. A critical implementation detail is that bitmasks must be applied before shifting data; applying them after results in zeroed-out data. Algorithm Steps: 1. Outer Traversal: Use the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm to traverse the outer 3D grid of chunks along the ray direction \mathbf{d}. 2. Chunk Check: For each chunk visited by the outer DDA, check its occupancy flag. If the chunk is marked as empty, skip it and continue to the next chunk in the outer DDA loop. 3. Inner Traversal: If the chunk is non-empty, use the DDA algorithm to traverse the identified chunk. 4. Voxel Hit Test: If a voxel is hit within the chunk, return that information to the outer DDA loop and terminate traversal. If no voxel is hit in the chunk, continue iterating the outer DDA loop to check the next chunk. Transparency Handling: For transparent voxels, a fraction of the transparent object's color is added to the color behind it. The traversal carries this transparent object information to the next voxel or chunk for final color determination. DDA Step Formula: The traversal advances along the axis with the smallest entry distance: t{next} = t{current} + \Delta t, where \Delta ti = 1/|di| for axis i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Voxel Raytracer
body: A voxel raytracer renders 3D voxel models by marching rays through a 3D grid of voxels, supporting multiple bounces for diffuse reflection and a ground plane. It differs from standard voxel grid raycasting by implementing a full path-tracing loop with diffuse scattering and anti-aliasing, rather than simple direct illumination or single-pass raymarching. Inputs: A 1D array of vec4 (RGBA) representing the voxel grid, stored in row-major order (x, then y, then z). Model metadata: position (vec3) and size (ivec3) for each model in the scene. Camera parameters: resolution (iResolution), number of models, and maximum depth. Outputs: A final color image with gamma correction applied. VoxelModel: position: vec3 (world position of the model). size: ivec3 (dimensions of the voxel grid in voxels). HitRecord: p: vec3 (hit point in world space). t: float (distance from ray origin to hit point). normal: vec3 (surface normal at hit point). albedo: vec3 (diffuse color at hit point). Storage Buffer Object (SSBO): A single array of vec4 bound to binding point 0. Index calculation for voxel (x, y, z) in a model of size (width, height, length): \text{index} = (x + y \cdot \text{width} + z \cdot \text{width} \cdot \text{height}) \cdot 4 This index points to the start of the 4 float components (RGBA) in the flat array. SAMPLESPERPIXEL: 256. MAXDEPTH: 50. MAXMODELS: 10. 1. Random Number Generation: Initialize a PCG state per pixel using iResolution.x glFragCoord.y + glFragCoord.x. The stepRandom function updates state: rngState 747796405 + 1. The random function permutes the state: word = ((rngState >> ((rngState >> 28) + 4)) ^ rngState) 277803737; word = (word >> 22) ^ word; and returns float(word) / 4294967295.0f. 2. Voxel Presence Check: For a given voxel coordinate voxOrigin, check bounds 0 <= x < modelSize.x, 0 <= y < modelSize.y, 0 <= z < modelSize.z. If out of bounds, return false. Otherwise, access data[voxOrigin.x + voxOrigin.y modelSize.x + voxOrigin.z modelSize.x modelSize.y]. Extract albedo from.xyz. Return true if alpha.a > 0. 3. Voxel Marching (DDA): 1. Initialize voxOrigin = ivec3(floor(ray.origin)). 2. Calculate step direction: posStepDir = ivec3(step(0.0, ray.direction)), stepDir = ivec3(posStepDir 2 - 1). 3. Calculate justOut coordinates for boundary exit: posStepDir (models[0].size - 1) + stepDir. 4. Calculate initial tMax: (posStepDir - (ray.origin - voxOrigin)) / ray.direction. 5. Calculate tDelta: stepDir / ray.direction. 6. Loop up to 1000 times: a. Check voxelPresent(voxOrigin). If present, set rec.normal = lastOrigin - voxOrigin, rec.t = tMin, rec.p = ray.origin + tMin ray.direction, return true. b. Update lastOrigin = voxOrigin. c. Compare tMax components to determine which axis to step. d. Increment voxOrigin on that axis. e. If voxOrigin equals justOut on that axis, break loop. f. Update tMin to the tMax of the stepped axis. g. Update tMax for that axis by adding tDelta. 4. Ground Hit: Calculate intersection with plane y=0: t = (0 - ray.origin.y) / ray.direction.y. If t < 0 or t > 50, return false. Set normal: vec3(0.0, float(ray.direction.y < 0) 2.0 - 1.0, 0.0). Set albedo to (0.8, 0.8, 0.0). Set p = ray.origin + ray.direction t. Return true. 5. World Hit: Call groundHit and voxelMarch. If both hit, return the one with smaller t. If only one hits, return that one. If neither, return false. 6. Ray Generation: Camera center is at (models[0].size.x / 2, models[0].size.y / 2, models[0].size.z + 12). Viewport height is 2.0. Viewport width is 2.0 imagewidth / imageheight. Viewport lower left is center - vec3(0, 0, 1.0) - viewportu / 2 - viewportv / 2. Pixel 0,0 location is viewportlowerleft + 0.5 (pixeldeltau + pixeldeltav). Ray direction is normalized vector from center to pixel00loc + (glFragCoord.x - 0.5 + random()) pixeldeltau + (glFragCoord.y - 0.5 + random()) pixeldeltav. 7. Color Calculation (Path Tracing): Initialize outcolor = (1,1,1). Loop d from 0 to MAXDEPTH-1. Generate ray using getray(). Call worldHit(ray, rec). The loop limit of 1000 iterations prevents infinite loops. Boundaries: The voxelPresent function explicitly checks bounds to avoid out-of-bounds memory access.
