name: DirectVoxGO Volume Rendering
head: DirectVoxGO, Voxel Grid Neural Rendering
body: DirectVoxGO is a volume rendering method that accelerates neural radiance field training and inference by sampling points directly on a structured voxel grid rather than uniformly along rays. It solves the problem of inefficient ray marching in sparse scenes by using a mask cache to skip free space and a direct lookup of density and color features from the voxel grid. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF by replacing uniform sampling with grid-based point selection and from other sparse voxel methods by using a dense voxel grid with a binary mask cache for acceleration. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins rayso ([N, 3]), ray directions raysd ([N, 3]), view directions viewdirs ([N, 3]), near/far distances, and rendering parameters. Outputs: Rendered RGB images rgbmarched ([N, 3]), accumulated transmittance alphainvlast ([N]), and intermediate weights weights ([M]). Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D tensor storing density and color features, defined by xyzmin and xyzmax bounding boxes and a resolution numvoxels. Mask Cache: A binary tensor indicating which voxels contain geometry (true) or are free space (false). Ray Points: raypts ([M, 3]) stores the 3D coordinates of sampled points. rayid ([M]) maps each point to its originating ray. stepid ([M]) maps each point to its step index along the ray. Parameters: stepsize: Number of voxels per sample step. fastcolorthres: Threshold for filtering points based on alpha or weight values; if > 0, enables optimization. voxelsizeratio: Ratio used to compute interval for density-to-alpha conversion. rgbnetdirect: Boolean flag determining if the RGB network outputs direct RGB or residual features. Steps: 1. Ray Setup: Compute ray origins and directions from camera parameters. If NDC (Normalized Device Coordinates) is enabled, transform rays to NDC space. Ray direction computation (for inversey=False, flipy=False, mode='center'): \text{dirs} = \left[ \frac{i - K{0,2}}{K{0,0}}, \frac{j - K{1,2}}{K{1,1}}, 1 \right] NDC ray transformation: o0 = -\frac{1}{W/(2 \cdot \text{focal})} \frac{ox}{oz}, \quad d0 = -\frac{1}{W/(2 \cdot \text{focal})} \left(\frac{dx}{dz} - \frac{ox}{oz}\right) 2. Sample Points: Calculate step distance stepdist = stepsize voxelsize. Sample points along rays within the bounding box [xyzmin, xyzmax]. Filter points outside the bounding box. Input: rayso, raysd, near, far, stepdist. Output: raypts, rayid, stepid, maskoutbbox. 3. Free Space Culling: Query the mask cache for the sampled points. Filter out points where the mask is false (free space). 4. Density Query: Query the voxel grid for density values at the remaining points. 5. Alpha Conversion: Convert density to alpha using the Raw2Alpha function: \alpha = 1 - (1 + \exp(\text{density} + \text{shift}))^{-\text{interval}} where interval = stepsize voxelsizeratio. 6. First Color Threshold: If fastcolorthres > 0, filter points where alpha > fastcolorthres. 7. Weight Computation: Compute accumulated transmittance and weights using Alphas2Weights.apply(alpha, rayid, N). This function performs a segmented sum over rays to compute weights and the final transmittance alphainvlast. 8. Second Color Threshold: If fastcolorthres > 0, filter points where weights > fastcolorthres. 9. Color Query: Query the voxel grid for color features k0 at the remaining points. 10. RGB Computation: If rgbnet is None: rgb = sigmoid(k0). If rgbnet is not None: If rgbnetdirect: rgbfeat = k0. Else: k0view = k0[:, 3:], k0diffuse = k0[:,:3]. Compute view direction embeddings: viewdirsemb = (viewdirs.unsqueeze(-1) viewfreq).flatten(-2), then concatenate with sin/cos of viewdirs. rgbfeat = cat([k0view, viewdirsemb], -1). rgblogit = rgbnet(rgbfeat). If rgbnetdirect: rgb = sigmoid(rgblogit). Else: rgb = sigmoid(rgblogit + k0diffuse). 11. Accumulation: Accumulate RGB using segmented sum: \text{rgb\marched} = \sum{i \in \text{ray}} \text{weights}i \cdot \text{rgb}i Add background color: rgbmarched += alphainvlast bg. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def sampleptsonrays(rayso, raysd, xyzmin, xyzmax, near, far, stepdist): N = rayso.shape[0] maxsteps = int((far - near) / stepdist) + 1 raypts, rayid, stepid, maskoutbbox = [], [], [], [] tmin = torch.full((N,), far) tmax = torch.full((N,), near) for i in range(N): o = rayso[i] d = raysd[i] t1 = (xyzmin - o) / d t2 = (xyzmax - o) / d tnear = torch.max(torch.min(t1, t2)) tfar = torch.min(torch.max(t1, t2)) tnear = torch.max(tnear, torch.tensor(near)) tfar = torch.min(tfar, torch.tensor(far)) if tnear >= tfar: maskoutbbox.append(torch.ones(maxsteps, dtype=bool)) continue tmin[i] = tnear tmax[i] = tfar numsteps = int((tfar - tnear) / stepdist) + 1 ts = torch.arange(numsteps) stepdist + tnear pts = o.unsqueeze(0) + ts.unsqueeze(1) d.unsqueeze(0) raypts.append(pts) rayid.append(torch.full((numsteps,), i)) stepid.append(torch.arange(numsteps)) maskoutbbox.append(torch.zeros(numsteps, dtype=bool)) raypts = torch.cat(raypts, dim=0) if raypts else torch.empty(0, 3) rayid = torch.cat(rayid, dim=0) if rayid else torch.empty(0, dtype=torch.long) stepid = torch.cat(stepid, dim=0) if stepid else torch.empty(0, dtype=torch.long) maskoutbbox = torch.cat(maskoutbbox, dim=0) if maskoutbbox else torch.empty(0, dtype=bool) Nsteps = maxsteps return raypts, maskoutbbox, rayid, stepid, Nsteps, tmin, tmax def alphas2weights(alpha, rayid, N): M = alpha.shape[0] weights = torch.zeros(M, dtype=alpha.dtype) alphainvlast = torch.zeros(N, dtype=alpha.dtype) rayindices = [[] for in range(N)] for i, rid in enumerate(rayid): if rid < N: rayindices[rid].append(i) for r in range(N): if not rayindices[r]: continue Tcurr = 1.0 for idx in rayindices[r]: a = alpha[idx].item() weights[idx] = Tcurr a Tcurr = (1.0 - a) alphainvlast[r] = 1.0 - Tcurr return weights, alphainvlast def segmentcoo(src, index, out, reduce='sum'): for i in range(src.shape[0]): r = index[i].item() if r < out.shape[0]: if reduce == 'sum': out[r] += src[i] return out def renderdirectvoxgo(rayso, raysd, viewdirs, model, renderkwargs): stepdist = renderkwargs['stepsize'] model.voxelsize raypts, maskoutbbox, rayid, stepid, Nsteps, tmin, tmax = sampleptsonrays( rayso, raysd, model.xyzmin, model.xyzmax, renderkwargs['near'], renderkwargs['far'], stepdist) maskinbbox = ~maskoutbbox raypts = raypts[maskinbbox] rayid = rayid[maskinbbox] stepid = stepid[maskinbbox] if model.maskcache is not None: mask = model.maskcache(raypts) raypts = raypts[mask] rayid = rayid[mask] stepid = stepid[mask] density = model.density(raypts) interval = renderkwargs['stepsize'] model.voxelsizeratio alpha = 1.0 - (1.0 + torch.exp(density + model.shift)) (-interval) if model.fastcolorthres > 0: mask = (alpha > model.fastcolorthres) raypts = raypts[mask] rayid = rayid[mask] stepid = stepid[mask] density = density[mask] alpha = alpha[mask] weights, alphainvlast = alphas2weights(alpha, rayid, len(rayso)) if model.fastcolorthres > 0: mask = (weights > model.fastcolorthres) weights = weights[mask] alpha = alpha[mask] raypts = raypts[mask] rayid = rayid[mask] stepid = stepid[mask] k0 = model.k0(raypts) if model.rgbnet is None: rgb = torch.sigmoid(k0) else: if model.rgbnetdirect: k0view = k0 else: k0view = k0[:, 3:] k0diffuse = k0[:,:3] viewdirsemb = (viewdirs.unsqueeze(-1) model.viewfreq).flatten(-2) viewdirsemb = torch.cat([viewdirs, viewdirsemb.sin(), viewdirsemb.cos()], -1) viewdirsemb = viewdirsemb.flatten(0, -2)[rayid] rgbfeat = torch.cat([k0view, viewdirsemb], -1) rgblogit = model.rgbnet(rgbfeat) if model.rgbnetdirect: rgb = torch.sigmoid(rgblogit) else: rgb = torch.sigmoid(rgblogit + k0diffuse) rgbmarched = segmentcoo( src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) rgb), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros((len(rayso), 3), dtype=rgb.dtype), reduce='sum') rgbmarched += (alphainvlast.unsqueeze(-1) renderkwargs['bg']) return rgbmarched, alphainvlast Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Far Distance: The far distance can be too small, causing rays to stop prematurely when hitting the scene bounding box. The code sets far = 1e9 to prevent this. View Directions: View directions are passed as input and must be normalized for view-dependent color computation. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of sampled points and the efficiency of the mask cache. The mask cache significantly reduces the number of points processed in free space. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the voxel grid size and the number of rays. The mask cache adds a small memory overhead. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the resolution of the voxel grid and the number of rays. Strengths: Efficient sampling in sparse scenes due to free space culling. Direct lookup of features from the voxel grid. Limitations: Requires a predefined bounding box. Performance may degrade in very dense scenes if the mask cache is less effective. When to Use: Suitable for scenes with significant free space and where efficient sampling is critical. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes without a clear bounding box or where high-frequency details require very fine voxel grids. The method is implemented in the DirectVoxGO repository. It builds on the idea of using voxel grids for neural rendering, aiming to improve efficiency over standard NeRF by leveraging spatial acceleration structures. name: Voxel Grid Accelerated Ray-Point Intersection
head: GPU voxel grid for ray casting, Pointersect voxel structure
body: This method accelerates the identification of the k nearest points within a cylinder of radius \delta around a query ray in a point cloud, specifically optimized for parallel GPU execution and dynamic scenes where the point cloud changes frequently. Unlike static acceleration structures such as octrees, which require O(n \log n) construction time, this voxel grid approach achieves O(n) construction, making it superior for inverse rendering and dynamic scenarios where the structure must be rebuilt every iteration. Inputs: Point cloud P containing n points. Query ray r = (ro, rd), where ro is the origin and rd is the direction. Parameters: k: Number of nearest points to retrieve. \delta: Radius of the cylinder around the query ray. g: Number of grid cells per dimension in the voxel grid. Outputs: A list of k points from P that are closest to the ray r in terms of perpendicular distance, restricted to those within distance \delta. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A uniform 3D grid with g^3 cells. Each cell stores a list of point indices belonging to that voxel. Point Table: An array of size n storing the 3D coordinates of each point in P. Steps: 1. Grid Construction: Divide the 3D space containing P into a uniform voxel grid with g cells per dimension. Iterate through all n points in P and assign each point to its corresponding voxel in the grid table. This step takes O(n) operations. 2. Ray Traversal: For each query ray, trace it through the voxel grid to identify candidate voxels intersected by the ray. Compute grid-ray intersection in O(g) time per ray. This computation is parallelized across multiple GPU threads. 3. Candidate Collection: Collect all points located in the intersected voxels. Filter these points to keep only those within perpendicular distance \delta from the ray, resulting in q candidate points. 4. Sorting and Selection: Sort the q candidate points by their perpendicular distance to the ray and select the k nearest ones. Formulas: Time Complexity: The overall time complexity for finding k nearest points within a surrounding cylinder of radius \delta is: O(n + mg + mq \log(q)) where n is the total number of points, m is the number of rays, g is the grid cells per dimension, and q is the number of points lying within the cylinder. Expected Candidates: For uniformly distributed points, the expected number of points in the cylinder is: q = n/g^3 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildvoxelgrid(points, gridsize, boundsmin, boundsmax): """ Builds a uniform voxel grid for a point cloud. points: List of 3D coordinates (n, 3) gridsize: Integer g, number of cells per dimension boundsmin: 3D vector, minimum corner of the grid boundsmax: 3D vector, maximum corner of the grid Returns: A 3D array of lists (gridsize, gridsize, gridsize) """ voxelsize = (boundsmax - boundsmin) / gridsize grid = [[[] for in range(gridsize)] for in range(gridsize)] for z in range(gridsize): for y in range(gridsize): for x in range(gridsize): grid[z][y][x] = [] for point in points: x = int((point[0] - boundsmin[0]) / voxelsize[0]) y = int((point[1] - boundsmin[1]) / voxelsize[1]) z = int((point[2] - boundsmin[2]) / voxelsize[2]) x = max(0, min(x, gridsize - 1)) y = max(0, min(y, gridsize - 1)) z = max(0, min(z, gridsize - 1)) grid[z][y][x].append(point) return grid def rayvoxelintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, gridsize, boundsmin, boundsmax): """ Traces a ray through a uniform voxel grid to find intersected voxels. Handles rays starting outside the grid bounds correctly. """ voxelsize = (boundsmax - boundsmin) / gridsize x = int((rayorigin[0] - boundsmin[0]) / voxelsize[0]) y = int((rayorigin[1] - boundsmin[1]) / voxelsize[1]) z = int((rayorigin[2] - boundsmin[2]) / voxelsize[2]) x = max(0, min(x, gridsize - 1)) y = max(0, min(y, gridsize - 1)) z = max(0, min(z, gridsize - 1)) stepx = 1 if raydirection[0] > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if raydirection[1] > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if raydirection[2] > 0 else -1 # Distance to next voxel boundary along the ray tmaxx = ((x + (1 if stepx > 0 else 0)) voxelsize[0] + boundsmin[0] - rayorigin[0]) / raydirection[0] tmaxy = ((y + (1 if stepy > 0 else 0)) voxelsize[1] + boundsmin[1] - rayorigin[1]) / raydirection[1] tmaxz = ((z + (1 if stepz > 0 else 0)) voxelsize[2] + boundsmin[2] - rayorigin[2]) / raydirection[2] deltax = voxelsize[0] / abs(raydirection[0]) deltay = voxelsize[1] / abs(raydirection[1]) deltaz = voxelsize[2] / abs(raydirection[2]) intersectedvoxels = [] while 0 <= x < gridsize and 0 <= y < gridsize and 0 <= z < gridsize: intersectedvoxels.append((x, y, z)) if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: x += stepx tmaxx += deltax else: z += stepz tmaxz += deltaz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: y += stepy tmaxy += deltay else: z += stepz tmaxz += deltaz return intersectedvoxels def perpendiculardistance(point, rayorigin, raydirection): """ Calculates the perpendicular distance from a point to a ray. """ v = [point[i] - rayorigin[i] for i in range(3)] projlength = sum(v[i] raydirection[i] for i in range(3)) perp = [v[i] - projlength raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] return (sum(p p for p in perp)) 0.5 def findknearestpoints(points, rayorigin, raydirection, k, delta): """ Finds k nearest points to a ray within distance delta. """ candidates = [] for point in points: dist = perpendiculardistance(point, rayorigin, raydirection) if dist <= delta: candidates.append((dist, point)) candidates.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return [p for, p in candidates[:k]] def voxelgridraypointintersection(points, rays, gridsize, boundsmin, boundsmax, k, delta): """ Main function combining voxel grid construction and ray-point intersection. """ grid = buildvoxelgrid(points, gridsize, boundsmin, boundsmax) results = [] for ray in rays: voxels = rayvoxelintersection(ray.origin, ray.direction, gridsize, boundsmin, boundsmax) candidates = [] for (x, y, z) in voxels: for point in grid[z][y][x]: dist = perpendiculardistance(point, ray.origin, ray.direction) if dist <= delta: candidates.append((dist, point)) candidates.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) results.append([p for, p in candidates[:k]]) return results Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The implementation described in the source is not optimized; specifically, retrieving unordered k nearest points from q points can be done in O(q), but the current implementation sorts them, resulting in O(q \log q). For uniformly distributed points, the expected number of points in the cylinder is q = n/g^3. The method is slower than octrees for static scenes but faster to construct, making it suitable for dynamic scenes or inverse rendering where the tree must be rebuilt every iteration. Ray traversal must correctly handle rays originating outside the grid bounds; standard DDA initialization requires clamping the initial voxel and computing boundary distances relative to the grid extent to avoid returning empty voxel lists. Time Complexity: O(n + mg + mq \log(q)), where n is total points, m is number of rays, g is grid cells per dimension, and q is points within the cylinder. Construction Time: O(n), which is faster than octree construction (O(n \log n)). Query Time: O(g + q \log q) per ray, where g is the cost of grid-ray intersection and q \log q is the cost of sorting candidates. Strengths: Fast construction makes it superior for dynamic scenes or inverse rendering where the point cloud changes frequently and the structure must be rebuilt every iteration. Parallelizable on GPU. Limitations: Slower query performance for static scenes compared to octrees (n \log(n) + m \log(n) + mq). The sorting step is not optimized; using a selection algorithm could reduce the sorting cost to O(q). When to Use: Dynamic scenes, inverse rendering, or scenarios requiring frequent updates to the point cloud structure. When Not to Use: Static scenes where an octree can be built once and reused, as octrees offer faster query performance in that context. The method was introduced in the context of "Pointersect: Neural Rendering with Cloud-Ray Intersection". It was designed to address the inefficiency of rebuilding octrees in dynamic scenes or inverse rendering applications, where many points in the point cloud can change at every iteration. The approach leverages the simplicity and parallelizability of uniform voxel grids to achieve faster construction times compared to hierarchical structures like octrees. name: Ganged Raycasting
head: Horizontal Ganging, Ganged Tracing, Rectangular Pyramid Tracing
body: Ganged Raycasting is a volume rendering optimization that traces multiple rays simultaneously as a group (gang) to reduce per-ray overhead, specifically by treating a rectangular pyramid of rays as a single unit rather than processing them individually. It distinguishes itself from standard Voxel Grid Raycasting by batching rays that share the same y-coordinate and initial voxel intersection, splitting the group only when the ray set diverges into non-continuous voxel sets. This approach leverages the typical aspect ratio of images (wider than tall) to maximize the number of rays starting in the same voxel, thereby reducing the total number of traversal steps required. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel grid, camera parameters (origin, direction vectors), and image dimensions (W, H). Output: Rendered image buffer. Data Structures: RayGang: A structure representing a group of rays. ystart: Integer, the shared y-coordinate of the rays in the gang. xstart: Integer, the starting x-coordinate of the first ray in the horizontal span. xend: Integer, the ending x-coordinate of the last ray in the horizontal span. origin: Vector3, the camera origin (shared for all rays in the initial trace). direction: Vector3, the base direction vector for the first ray (used to derive others). xnext, ynext, znext: Vectors of floats, storing the distance to the next voxel face intersection for the start and end rays of the gang (and potentially intermediate rays if needed for divergence detection). Note: The source implies storing intersection points in vectors xnext, ynext, and znext. For a horizontal gang, the y-dimension is constant, so ynext is likely trivial or unused for divergence, but stored for consistency with the general tracer logic. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: For each y-coordinate from 0 to H-1: Identify the range of x-coordinates [x{start}, x{end}] such that all rays with these coordinates intersect the voxel grid at the same initial voxel. This is determined by casting the first ray at (x{start}, y) and the last at (x{end}, y) and verifying they hit the same voxel, and that the span is continuous. Create a RayGang with ystart = y, xstart, xend, and the corresponding direction vectors. Calculate the distance to the first voxel face intersection for the rays in the group. Store these in xnext, ynext, and znext vectors. For a horizontal gang, ynext is constant or irrelevant for splitting, but xnext and znext vary between the left and right edges of the pyramid. 2. Ganged Traversal Loop: While the RayGang is valid (i.e., x{start} \le x{end}): Determine the minimum distance to the next voxel face among all rays in the gang. This is typically derived from the xnext and znext values of the boundary rays, assuming the pyramid expands monotonically. Advance all rays in the gang by this minimum distance. Update the voxel occupancy for the current position of all rays. Check for divergence: The group remains valid as long as all rays stay within the same voxel or neighboring voxels. Split Condition: If the dot product of the ray's current position integer coordinates exceeds 1, the group must be split. Note: The source phrasing "dot product of the ray current position integer coordinates exceeds 1" is ambiguous. In standard grid traversal, this likely refers to a check on the integer grid coordinates (i, j, k) of the ray's position. A common interpretation in ganged tracing is checking if the rays have moved past a voxel boundary in a way that breaks the "neighboring" constraint. Given the context of splitting a pyramid, it likely means checking if the integer coordinates of the start and end rays differ by more than a threshold (e.g., 1) in any dimension, or if the ray has exited the current voxel cluster. [G: Assuming the standard interpretation, the split condition is when the integer grid coordinates of the leftmost and rightmost rays in the gang differ by more than 1 in any dimension, indicating they are no longer in neighboring voxels.] Splitting: Calculate the split point's x-coordinate. Use this x-coordinate as a weight to determine the new split ray positions. Split the RayGang into two new RayGang instances: one for [x{start}, x{split}] and one for [x{split}+1, x{end}]. Recalculate xnext, ynext, znext for the new gangs. Add the new gangs to the processing queue. 3. Termination: When a gang reduces to a single ray (x{start} == x{end}), trace it individually to the end of the volume or until it exits the grid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gangedraytrace(voxelgrid, camera, width, height): # Initialize output buffer image = zeros((height, width, 3)) # Queue for active ray gangs gangqueue = [] # Step 1: Initialize gangs for y in range(height): # Find continuous x-ranges that start in the same voxel x = 0 while x < width: # Cast ray at (x, y) to find initial voxel initialvoxel = getvoxelat(camera, x, y) if initialvoxel is None: x += 1 continue # Find the end of the continuous range xend = x while xend + 1 < width: nextvoxel = getvoxelat(camera, xend + 1, y) if nextvoxel == initialvoxel: xend += 1 else: break # Create gang gang = { 'y': y, 'xstart': x, 'xend': xend, 'origin': camera.origin, 'dirstart': camera.getdirection(x, y), 'dirend': camera.getdirection(xend, y), 'xnext': [0.0, 0.0], # Distances for start and end rays 'ynext': [0.0, 0.0], 'znext': [0.0, 0.0] } # Calculate initial intersection distances gang['xnext'], gang['ynext'], gang['znext'] = calculatefirstintersection(gang, voxelgrid) gangqueue.append(gang) x = xend + 1 # Step 2: Process gangs while gangqueue: gang = gangqueue.pop(0) # If single ray, trace individually if gang['xstart'] == gang['xend']: tracesingleray(image, camera, gang['y'], gang['xstart'], voxelgrid) continue # Determine minimum step size # Assuming xnext and znext are stored for start and end rays mindist = min(gang['xnext'][0], gang['xnext'][1], gang['znext'][0], gang['znext'][1]) # Advance rays # Note: In a pyramid, the step size is limited by the ray that hits a face first # This logic assumes a simplified model where we advance by the min distance # and then re-evaluate. # Check for split condition # Source: "dot product of the ray current position integer coordinates exceeds 1" # Interpretation: Check if integer coordinates of start and end rays differ significantly posstart = getrayposition(gang, mindist) posend = getrayposition(gang, mindist) # Both advance by same dist in this simplified step intstart = floor(posstart) intend = floor(posend) # Heuristic for split: if integer coordinates differ by more than 1 in any axis if abs(intstart[0] - intend[0]) > 1 or abs(intstart[1] - intend[1]) > 1 or abs(intstart[2] - intend[2]) > 1: # Split the gang # Use split point x-coordinate as weight # This part is ambiguous in source. We assume a binary split at the midpoint # or based on the divergence point. splitx = (gang['xstart'] + gang['xend']) // 2 # Create two new gangs gangleft = copy(gang) gangleft['xend'] = splitx gangleft['xnext'], gangleft['ynext'], gangleft['znext'] = calculatefirstintersection(gangleft, voxelgrid) gangright = copy(gang) gangright['xstart'] = splitx + 1 gangright['xnext'], gangright['ynext'], gangright['znext'] = calculatefirstintersection(gangright, voxelgrid) gangqueue.append(gangleft) gangqueue.append(gangright) else: # Advance and accumulate color accumulatecolor(image, gang, mindist, voxelgrid) # Update intersection distances for next step gang['xnext'], gang['ynext'], gang['znext'] = updateintersectiondistances(gang, mindist, voxelgrid) gangqueue.append(gang) def calculatefirstintersection(gang, voxelgrid): # Calculate distances to next voxel face for start and end rays # Returns (xnext, ynext, znext) for start and end pass def updateintersectiondistances(gang, dist, voxelgrid): # Update distances after advancing by 'dist' pass def getrayposition(gang, dist): # Return world position of the ray at distance 'dist' pass def tracesingleray(image, camera, y, x, voxelgrid): # Standard voxel raycasting for a single ray pass def accumulatecolor(image, gang, dist, voxelgrid): # Accumulate color for the rays in the gang pass Parameters: Typical image aspect ratio: Images are much wider than they are tall, supporting horizontal ganging. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Split Ray Precision: The new split ray may not land exactly on a voxel face after splitting, requiring careful handling of floating-point precision and ray origin adjustments. Divergence Detection: The condition for splitting must accurately detect when rays are no longer in neighboring voxels. The source's mention of "dot product... exceeds 1" is unclear and may require empirical tuning or a more robust geometric check. Time Complexity: Theoretically faster than individual tracing because it saves computation by treating many rays starting at the same voxel(s) as a single rectangular pyramid trace. The speedup depends on the number of rays that can be ganged, which is high in scenes with large empty spaces or uniform voxel distributions. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional data structures for the gangs (xnext, ynext, znext vectors) and a queue for active gangs. Memory usage is proportional to the number of active gangs, which is typically much less than the number of rays. Measured Performance: In a 1920x1080 projection, there are approximately 2,073,600 rays, but they intersect under 200 initial voxels, meaning over 10,000 rays start at the same voxel. This suggests a significant potential for speedup, though the actual gain depends on the splitting overhead and the efficiency of the ganged traversal loop. Strengths: Reduces per-ray overhead, leverages spatial coherence, and is well-suited for wide images. Limitations: Splitting logic can be complex and may introduce precision errors. Not as effective for tall, narrow images or scenes with high voxel density near the camera. Ganged Raycasting was discussed in the context of voxel raycasting algorithms on GameDev Stack Exchange in April 2021. It is presented as a theoretical optimization for horizontal ganging, comparing its potential speedup to individual ray tracing. The method is not associated with a specific peer-reviewed paper in the provided sources but is described as a technique for optimizing ray tracing in voxel grids by grouping rays. name: Z-axis RLE Voxel Raycasting
head: Column-based RLE traversal, RLE-Encoded Voxel Data Traversal, RLE-encoded Z-axis voxel raycasting, Z-column RLE iteration, Z-column RLE raytracing
body: Z-axis RLE Voxel Raycasting is a traversal method for voxel volumes that compresses voxel attributes (such as normals and colors) per X,Y column using run-length encoding (RLE) along the Z-axis to reduce memory bandwidth and accelerate ray intersection. It builds on Voxel Grid Raycasting by separating the structural voxel grid from its metadata, storing the latter in a compressed format that allows linear iteration after the initial geometric hit is found. Unlike raw voxel textures which allow fast runtime editing but lack compression, this method optimizes rendering speed at the cost of dynamic volume modification difficulty. Inputs and Outputs Input: A ray defined by origin and direction; a pre-computed voxel grid (for spatial traversal); an RLE index texture; an RLE data texture. Output: Voxel attributes (color, normal) for each hit along the ray. Data Structures 1. Voxel Grid: The standard sparse or dense voxel structure used for initial intersection. 2. RLE Index Texture: A 2D texture mapping 2D voxel coordinates (X, Y) to a pointer (texture coordinate). This pointer indicates the start of the RLE element list in the RLE data texture for that specific column. 3. RLE Data Texture: A 1D or 2D texture storing RLE elements sequentially per column, encoded along the Z-axis. Each element contains voxel metadata (colors, normals, etc.). Algorithm Steps 1. Initial Hit: Perform standard voxel grid traversal to find the first voxel hit for the ray. 2. Index Lookup: Use the X,Y coordinates of the hit voxel to index into the RLE index texture. Retrieve the pointer (texture coordinate) to the start of the RLE element list for that column. 3. Linear Iteration: Iterate sequentially through the RLE elements starting from the retrieved pointer. 4. Z-Comparison: Compare the Z value of each RLE element against the ray's current Z position. 5. Hit Resolution: Stop when the Z value matches or exceeds the ray's Z to identify the hit voxel and retrieve its attributes. 6. Repeat: Continue the ray traversal loop, repeating steps 2-5 for subsequent hits. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def castraywithzrle(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid, rleindextexture, rledatatexture): # Step 1: Perform voxel grid traversal to find initial hit hit = voxelgrid.traverse(rayorigin, raydirection) if hit is None: return [] results = [] while hit is not None: # Step 2: Retrieve RLE-encoded data for the corresponding z-column # Use X,Y coordinates to get pointer to start of RLE list rlestartptr = rleindextexture.sample(hit.x, hit.y) # Step 3: Linearly iterate through RLE entries currentptr = rlestartptr currentz = hit.z # Step 4 & 5: Compare Z value and resolve attributes # Iterate until we find the element matching the current hit's Z # Note: The source implies iterating through the list to find the specific Z # associated with the hit found by the grid traversal. while True: element = rledatatexture.read(currentptr) # Check if this RLE element corresponds to the current hit's Z # Assuming RLE elements store Z-coordinate and attributes if element.z == currentz: # Hit found in RLE data results.append({ 'position': hit.position, 'normal': element.normal, 'color': element.color }) break # Move to next element in the column currentptr += element.stride currentptr = currentptr % rledatatexture.size # Handle wrap-around if 1D texture # Safety break: if we looped through the whole column without match # This handles cases where the grid hit might be slightly off or # the RLE list is exhausted. if currentptr == rlestartptr: break # Continue ray traversal for next hit hit = voxelgrid.traversenext(hit.position, raydirection) return results Parameters Base Scene Resolution: 1024x1024x256 voxels. Voxel Data Size: 16MB (static, does not change with scene complexity). RLE Data Size: 6.4MB (varies based on color and normal variety). RLE Indexing Data Size: 4MB. Total Memory Footprint: 26.4MB. Maximum Iterations per Ray: Z (height of the voxel dataset). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Transformations: Applying geometric transformations to RLE-encoded data is expensive because it requires shifting large blocks of data (hurting performance) or pre-padding the data (hurting memory usage). Dynamic Updates: RLE encoding makes dynamic volume modification difficult compared to raw voxel textures which support fast runtime editing via render-to-texture. Iteration Cost: The maximum iteration of Z per ray is considered to have a negligible performance impact compared to the voxel grid traversal algorithm itself. Complexity: The method is bandwidth-bound; performance is limited by memory bus throughput rather than arithmetic compute. Scaling: Ray count increases (e.g., from 1000 to 4000 rays) do not increase render time if memory access patterns remain constant. Strengths: Reduces memory bandwidth requirements by compressing attribute data per column; suitable for real-time rendering where memory bus is the bottleneck. Limitations: Poor support for dynamic scene modifications; expensive to transform due to data shifting requirements. When to Use: Static or semi-static voxel volumes where rendering performance is critical and memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring frequent dynamic updates or geometric transformations of the voxel attributes. This method was proposed by IJs (Ken Silverman forum, March 2008) as the core traversal method for a real-time voxel raytracing engine. It was developed in the context of exploring GPU-based voxel raytracing, aiming to overcome memory bandwidth limitations inherent in high-resolution voxel datasets. The approach was part of an experimental engine design intended to leverage parallel processing power for volumetric effects. name: Voxel Neighbor Packing with Directional Iteration
head: Voxel Data Processing with Neighbor Packing and Directional Iteration, subcube processing, view/integrate/layer/z-shade rendering
body: A high-performance voxel rendering method that accelerates ray traversal by packing four consecutive voxels into a single 32-bit integer to enable bulk zero-skipping, while maintaining strict back-to-front rendering order via a pre-computed directional flag. It differs from Z-axis RLE Voxel Raycasting by operating on fixed-width subcubes with byte-level packing rather than variable-length run-length encoding, optimizing for dense or semi-dense regions where RLE overhead might outweigh packing benefits. Inputs: subcube.data: A 3D array of SHORT voxels, accessed via slices subcube.data[idx.z][idx.y][idx.x]. subcube.image: A 2D output array indexed by fixed-point coordinates, type BYTE (or INT depending on mode). threshold.value: Minimum intensity for a voxel to be considered visible. z.cut.i: Maximum Z-depth for rendering; voxels with Z > z.cut.i are clipped. forward.x: Boolean flag determining processing order along the X-axis (TRUE: low-to-high index, FALSE: high-to-low). layer.value: Constant value for LAYER mode. unit.step.: Fixed-point increments for X, Y, Z coordinates. idx.step.: Integer increments for voxel indices. Outputs: subcube.image: The rendered 2D projection. Data Structures: dummy: A 32-bit integer (INT32) holding four consecutive SHORT voxels. dummy.byte: A byte-array view of dummy, where dummy.byte[0] corresponds to the first voxel, dummy.byte[1] to the second, etc. Fixed-point accumulators: xxi, xyi, xzi (X-axis), yxi, yyi, yzi (Y-axis), zxi, zyi, zzi (Z-axis). These track the current position in fixed-point format (16.1 format implied by INT xyi.16.1). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Z-loop: Set idx.z to idx.start.z. Set zxi to start.xi, zyi to start.yi, zzi to start.zi. Loop z.count times (or until idx.run.z limit): Check z.cut.value. If present, handle clipping logic. 2. Initialize Y-loop: Set idx.y to idx.start.y. Set yxi to zxi, yyi to zyi, yzi to zzi. Loop y.count times (or until idx.run.y limit): Access slice shorti = subcube.data.slice[idx.y]. Retype shorti as [SCDX >> 2] INT shorti to prepare for packing. 3. Initialize X-loop: Set idx.x to idx.start.x. Set xxi to yxi, xyi to yyi, xzi to yzi. Loop x.count times (or until idx.run.x limit): 4. Pack and Skip: Load four consecutive voxels into dummy: python dummy = INT32(shorti[idx.x], shorti[idx.x + 1], shorti[idx.x + 2], shorti[idx.x + 3]) (Note: The source implies a specific byte mapping where dummy.byte[0] is the first voxel. Endianness determines which physical byte corresponds to which voxel index. The source assumes dummy.0 maps to dummy.byte[0].) Check if dummy == 0. If all four are zero: Skip four voxels: python idx.x += idx.step.x 4 xxi += unit.step.4.xxi xyi += unit.step.4.xyi xzi += unit.step.4.xzi Continue to next iteration of X-loop. If not all zero: Process each of the four voxels individually based on forward.x. 5. Process Voxels: If forward.x is TRUE: Process dummy.byte[0] (Voxel 0). Process dummy.byte[1] (Voxel 1). Process dummy.byte[2] (Voxel 2). Process dummy.byte[3] (Voxel 3). After each voxel, increment accumulators: python xxi += unit.step.xxi xyi += unit.step.xyi xzi += unit.step.xzi If forward.x is FALSE: Process dummy.byte[3] (Voxel 3). Process dummy.byte[2] (Voxel 2). Process dummy.byte[1] (Voxel 1). Process dummy.byte[0] (Voxel 0). After each voxel, increment accumulators: python xxi += unit.step.xxi xyi += unit.step.xyi xzi += unit.step.xzi 6. Voxel Processing Logic (per voxel v): Let idx2d = [INT(xyi.16.1), INT(xxi.16.1)]. Let zdist = xzi. Condition: IF (v > threshold.value) AND (zdist < z.cut.i): VIEW Mode: python subcube.image[idx2d] = v INTEGRATE Mode: python density = subcube.image[idx2d] IF density < 255: density = min(255, density + 1) subcube.image[idx2d] = density LAYER Mode: python subcube.image[idx2d] = layer.value Z SHADE Mode: python subcube.image[idx2d] = BYTE((INT(xzi.16.1)) >> 1) Else: Skip (do not update subcube.image). 7. Increment Y-loop: After X-loop completes: python idx.y += idx.step.y yxi += unit.step.yxi yyi += unit.step.yyi yzi += unit.step.yzi 8. Increment Z-loop: After Y-loop completes: python idx.z += idx.step.z zxi += unit.step.zxi zyi += unit.step.zyi zzi += unit.step.zzi 9. Merge: Send results to the merger module for combination with other Processing Elements (PEs). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processsubcube(subcubedata, subcubeimage, thresholdvalue, zcuti, forwardx, layervalue): # Initialize Z indices idxz = idxstartz zxi = startxi zyi = startyi zzi = startzi for in range(zcount): # Initialize Y indices idxy = idxstarty yxi = zxi yyi = zyi yzi = zzi # Access current slice slicedata = subcubedata[idxz] for in range(ycount): # Initialize X indices idxx = idxstartx xxi = yxi xyi = yyi xzi = yzi # Prepare packed data view # Assuming slicedata is an array of SHORTs # We process in chunks of 4 numvoxels = xcount i = 0 while i < numvoxels: # Pack 4 voxels into INT32 # Note: Source implies specific byte mapping. # dummy.byte[0] is the first voxel in the pack. if i + 3 < numvoxels: v0 = slicedata[idxx + 0] v1 = slicedata[idxx + 1] v2 = slicedata[idxx + 2] v3 = slicedata[idxx + 3] # Construct INT32. Endianness matters for byte mapping. # Source: dummy.0 IS dummy.byte[0] # We assume a layout where byte 0 is the first element. dummy = (v0 << 24) | (v1 << 16) | (v2 << 8) | v3 # Or depending on endianness, the shift order might vary. # However, the source explicitly maps dummy.0 to byte[0]. # Let's use a byte array view for clarity. dummybytes = [v0, v1, v2, v3] # Placeholder for packing logic # Check if all zero if v0 == 0 and v1 == 0 and v2 == 0 and v3 == 0: # Skip 4 voxels idxx += idxstepx 4 xxi += unitstep4xxi xyi += unitstep4xyi xzi += unitstep4xzi i += 4 continue else: # Process individually voxels = [v0, v1, v2, v3] if forwardx: indices = [0, 1, 2, 3] else: indices = [3, 2, 1, 0] for idx in indices: v = voxels[idx] processvoxel(v, xxi, xyi, xzi, subcubeimage, thresholdvalue, zcuti, layervalue) xxi += unitstepxxi xyi += unitstepxyi xzi += unitstepxzi i += 4 else: # Handle remaining voxels if count is not a multiple of 4 # Source doesn't explicitly detail non-multiple handling, # but implies loop runs for xcount. # We assume xcount is a multiple of 4 or handle remainder. # For safety, process remaining one by one. while i < numvoxels: v = slicedata[idxx] processvoxel(v, xxi, xyi, xzi, subcubeimage, thresholdvalue, zcuti, layervalue) xxi += unitstepxxi xyi += unitstepxyi xzi += unitstepxzi idxx += idxstepx i += 1 # Increment Y idxy += idxstepy yxi += unitstepyxi yyi += unitstepyyi yzi += unitstepyzi # Increment Z idxz += idxstepz zxi += unitstepzxi zyi += unitstepzyi zzi += unitstepzzi def processvoxel(v, xxi, xyi, xzi, subcubeimage, thresholdvalue, zcuti, layervalue): if v > thresholdvalue and xzi < zcuti: idx2d = (int(xyi >> 1), int(xxi >> 1)) # Assuming 16.1 format means shift 1 # Note: Source uses INT(xyi.16.1). In fixed point 16.1, the integer part is bits 16..1. # If xyi is stored as an integer representing Q16.1, then xyi >> 1 gives the integer part. # VIEW Mode # subcubeimage[idx2d] = v # INTEGRATE Mode density = subcubeimage[idx2d] if density < 255: density = min(255, density + 1) subcubeimage[idx2d] = density # LAYER Mode # subcubeimage[idx2d] = layervalue # Z SHADE Mode # subcubeimage[idx2d] = (int(xzi >> 1)) >> 1 # The source lists these as separate modes. # In a single implementation, one mode is active. # Here we show the logic for INTEGRATE as an example, # but the method supports all. pass Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the subcube, but with a significant constant factor improvement due to skipping zero regions. The skip operation processes 4 voxels in the time of 1 check. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per subcube, plus the output image. Performance: Highly efficient for sparse volumes or volumes with large empty regions, as the dummy == 0 check allows skipping 4 voxels at once. Performance degrades if most voxels are non-zero, as the overhead of unpacking and individual processing remains. Strengths: Simple implementation, low memory overhead, effective for skipping empty space. Limitations: Requires fixed-size subcubes (multiples of 4 voxels in X). Endianness-dependent byte mapping. No hierarchical acceleration beyond the subcube level. When to use: When rendering semi-dense volumes with significant empty space, and when hardware supports efficient 32-bit integer operations. When not to use: For very dense volumes where skipping is rare, or for volumes with irregular structures that don't align with the packing grid. Originated in the context of voxel data processing on Transputer networks, as described in. The method was designed to optimize rendering performance by reducing memory bandwidth and leveraging parallel processing elements (PEs). It is part of a pipeline that includes subcube processing and merging. name: Cap Node Traversal
head: Cap Node Traversal and Neighbor Finding, Cap intersection, Gargantini and Atkinson Octree Traversal (Cap Node Variant), Neighbor-finding with cap scalars
body: Cap Node Traversal is a specialized ray traversal routine for "cap nodes" in sparse voxel octrees, which are leaf-like structures containing scalar data for a 2 \times 2 \times 2 block of voxels. It solves the problem of efficiently retrieving voxel values and performing isosurface intersection without the overhead of recursive descent into child nodes. It differs from standard interior node traversal by replacing the isovalue range check and recursive child call with direct scalar retrieval and local neighbor finding. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, current cap node C, isovalue I. Outputs: Isosurface intersection point (if any), or traversal continuation. Data Structures: Cap Node (C): Contains a scalar array scalars of size 8. scalars[i]: Scalar value for the i-th voxel in the 2 \times 2 \times 2 block, where i \in [0, 7]. The index i corresponds to the child octant index in the parent octree structure. Steps: 1. Cap Intersection: Perform the standard octree traversal step to determine which of the 8 voxels (octants) the ray intersects within the cap node. Let the intersected child octant index be child \in [0, 7]. 2. Voxel Value Retrieval: Determine the scalar values of the 8 voxels composing the cell. These are stored directly in C.\text{scalars}[0..7]. 3. Isosurface Check: Check if the isovalue I lies within the minimum and maximum of the 8 voxel values. Let V{min} = \min(C.\text{scalars}[0..7]) and V{max} = \max(C.\text{scalars}[0..7]). If I < V{min} or I > V{max}, no isosurface exists within this cap node. 4. Neighbor Finding: If the isosurface check passes, determine the values of the 8 voxels for isosurface intersection. For the intersected voxel child, identify neighbors within the same cap node. For a desired neighbor direction dir \in [0, 7] from the child octant child: Check if (child \ \& \ dir) == 0. If false (i.e., (child \ \& \ dir) == 0), the neighbor is simply C.\text{scalars}[dir]. If true (i.e., (child \ \& \ dir) \neq 0), proceed with neighbor-finding to retrieve the value from outside the cap node. 5. Isosurface Intersection: Perform isosurface intersection using the 8 voxel values as corners of the cell. This involves solving a cubic polynomial for the ray intersection with the trilinearly interpolated surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def capnodetraversal(rayo, rayd, capnode, isovalue): # Step 1: Determine intersected child octant # Standard octree traversal routine returns child index in [0, 7] child = 0 # Step 2: Retrieve scalar values scalars = capnode.scalars # Array of 8 floats # Step 3: Isosurface check minval = min(scalars) maxval = max(scalars) if isovalue < minval or isovalue > maxval: return None # No intersection in this cap node # Step 4: Neighbor finding for the 8 voxels voxelvalues = [] for i in range(8): # The value of voxel i is simply scalars[i] voxelvalues.append(scalars[i]) # Step 5: Isosurface intersection # A step the sources do not give is a comment saying so. return None Parameters: Isovalue: The scalar value defining the isosurface. Typical values depend on the dataset. Cap Node Depth: The depth at which cap nodes are defined. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Neighbor Finding: Neighbor finding is only required when the neighbor lies outside the immediate local cap node structure defined by the bitwise check; otherwise, direct array access is used. Degenerate Input: If all 8 voxel values are identical, no isosurface is encountered. A leaf-like structure with homogeneous scalar values. Traversed recursively to the same depth as caps. If a neighborhood of identical voxels is encountered, no isosurface is present. Neighbor-finding is performed at borders. See Scalar Leaves. The standard octree traversal routine that cap node traversal modifies. It involves checking isovalue against min/max ranges and recursively calling child traversal. See Octree Traversal. Time Complexity: O(1) for scalar retrieval and isosurface check within a cap node, assuming the child octant is determined. Neighbor finding may add overhead if neighbors are outside the cap. Memory Complexity: O(1) per cap node, storing 8 scalar values. Strengths: Avoids recursive descent overhead for leaf-like structures. Efficient for datasets with many 2 \times 2 \times 2 homogeneous or near-homogeneous regions. Limitations: Requires specific data structure support for cap nodes. Neighbor finding logic adds complexity. When to Use: When the octree contains many cap nodes and efficient isosurface intersection is required. When Not to Use: When the dataset does not benefit from cap node optimization. Cap Node Traversal was introduced in the context of interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. It is part of the Gargantini and Atkinson octree traversal method, specifically the cap node variant. The method was developed to optimize ray traversal for sparse voxel octrees by handling leaf-like structures efficiently. name: Sparse Voxel Ray Marching with AABB Exit Planes
head: NAADF voxel traversal, Sparse Voxel Ray Marching with NAADF, voxel DDA with precomputed exit planes, vxray sparse ray march
body: Sparse Voxel Ray Marching with AABB Exit Planes is a ray traversal algorithm for sparse voxel hierarchies that skips empty space by computing the exit plane of the current empty cell using precomputed Axis-Aligned Distance Fields (AADF). It differs from standard DDA Voxel Grid Raycasting by avoiding per-voxel checks in empty regions, and from pure octree traversal Octree Traversal by using fixed-size hierarchical chunks (chunks, bricks, voxels) with texture-based occupancy masks and distance fields rather than dynamic node pointers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin rayorigin, ray direction raydir, grid extent gridext, occupancy textures (chunkmasks, brickmasks, voxelmasks), AADF textures (chunkaadf, brickaadf, voxelaadf). Output: Packed cell info (voxel coordinate and entry axis) or sentinel VXNOCELL if the ray misses or exits the grid. Data Structures: Occupancy Masks: Three Texture3D<uint> (chunkmasks, brickmasks, voxelmasks). Each texel is a uint bitmask. The bit at index masklinearidx(coord) indicates occupancy for a block of voxels. masklinearidx(coord) = local.x + local.y VXMASKEXT + local.z VXMASKEXT VXMASKEXT, where local = coord & (VXMASKEXT - 1). AADF Textures: Three Texture3D<uint> (chunkaadf, brickaadf, voxelaadf). Each texel is a uint packing distances to the nearest occupied voxel in 6 directions (±X, ±Y, ±Z). AADF Packing Layout: Bits 0-4: -X distance, 5-9: +X distance, 10-14: -Y distance, 15-19: +Y distance, 20-24: -Z distance, 25-29: +Z distance. Constants: VXMASKEXT (mask block size), VXBRICKEXT (brick size), VXCHUNKEXT (chunk size), VXNOCELL (sentinel). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Ray Inverse: Compute invdir = 1.0 / (raydir + (float3)(raydir == 0.0) 1e-30) to handle zero components. 2. Initial AABB Test: Perform ray-AABB intersection against the entire grid [0, gridext]. If no intersection, return VXNOCELL. Formula: t0 = (p0 - rayorigin) invraydir, t1 = (p1 - rayorigin) invraydir, lo = min(t0, t1), hi = max(t0, t1), tmin = max(max(lo.x, lo.y), max(lo.z, 0.0)), tmax = min(min(hi.x, hi.y), hi.z). Return tmin <= tmax. 3. Initial Position: Calculate starting position start = rayorigin + tmin raydir. Compute initial voxel coordinate ipos = int16t3(floor(start + entrymask sign(raydir) 0.5)) and local position localpos = start - float3(ipos). entrymask determines the entry face to adjust ipos. 4. Determine Initial Axis: Compute entryweights = entrymask abs(raydir). Determine crossedaxis: 1 if entryweights.y > entryweights.x, else 0. Then 2 if entryweights.z > max(entryweights.x, entryweights.y), else unchanged. 5. Loop: a. Bounds Check: If any((uint16t3)ipos >= (uint16t)gridext), return VXNOCELL. b. Hierarchy Check: i. Chunk level: cellext = VXBRICKEXT VXCHUNKEXT, coord = ipos / cellext. Check chunkoccupied(coord). If occupied, return packvoxelcell(ipos, crossedaxis). ii. Brick level: cellext = VXBRICKEXT, coord = ipos / cellext. Check brickoccupied(coord). If occupied, return packvoxelcell(ipos, crossedaxis). iii. Voxel level: cellext = 1, coord = ipos. Check voxeloccupied(coord). If occupied, return packvoxelcell(ipos, crossedaxis). c. AADF Skip: If not occupied, load AADF value for the current level (aadf = chunkaadf.Load(...), brickaadf.Load(...), or voxelaadf.Load(...)) depending on cellext. d. Exit Plane Calculation: Compute exit plane coordinate using aadfexitplane(coord, cellext, aadf, raydir). Formula: shiftx = raydir.x < 0.0 ? 0u: 5u, shifty = raydir.y < 0.0 ? 10u: 15u, shiftz = raydir.z < 0.0 ? 20u: 25u. Extract bounds: bounds.x = (packed >> shiftx) & 31u, etc. Calculate lower = max((coord - bounds) cellext, 0), upper = min((coord + 1 + bounds) cellext, gridext). Return raydir.x < 0.0 ? lower.x: upper.x for each component. e. Distance to Exit: Compute sidedist = (exitplane - float3(ipos) - localpos) invdir. Handle zero ray direction components by setting sidedist component to 3e+38. f. Find Minimum: Find t = min(sidedist.x, min(sidedist.y, sidedist.z)). Determine crossed axis: crossed = step(sidedist, t). Update crossedaxis based on weights of the crossed axes. g. Advance: Compute advanced = localpos + max(t, 0.0001) raydir. Compute new integer position celldelta = int16t3(floor(advanced + crossed sign(raydir) 0.5)). Update ipos += celldelta and localpos = advanced - float3(celldelta). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparsevoxelraymarch(rayorigin, raydir, gridext, chunkmasks, brickmasks, voxelmasks, chunkaadf, brickaadf, voxelaadf, VXMASKEXT, VXBRICKEXT, VXCHUNKEXT, VXNOCELL): # Step 1: Initialize Ray Inverse invdir = tuple(1.0 / (d + 1e-30 if d == 0.0 else d) for d in raydir) # Step 2: Initial AABB Test p0 = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) p1 = (float(gridext), float(gridext), float(gridext)) t0 = tuple((p0[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)) t1 = tuple((p1[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)) lo = tuple(min(t0[i], t1[i]) for i in range(3)) hi = tuple(max(t0[i], t1[i]) for i in range(3)) tmin = max(max(lo[0], lo[1]), max(lo[2], 0.0)) tmax = min(min(hi[0], hi[1]), hi[2]) if tmin > tmax: return VXNOCELL # Step 3: Initial Position start = tuple(rayorigin[i] + tmin raydir[i] for i in range(3)) entrymask = tuple(1.0 if raydir[i] < 0.0 else 0.0 for i in range(3)) ipos = tuple(int(start[i] + entrymask[i] (1.0 if raydir[i] < 0.0 else -1.0) 0.5) for i in range(3)) localpos = tuple(start[i] - float(ipos[i]) for i in range(3)) # Step 4: Determine Initial Axis entryweights = tuple(entrymask[i] abs(raydir[i]) for i in range(3)) crossedaxis = 0 if entryweights[1] > entryweights[0]: crossedaxis = 1 if entryweights[2] > max(entryweights[0], entryweights[1]): crossedaxis = 2 # Step 5: Loop while True: # 5a: Bounds Check if any(ipos[i] >= gridext for i in range(3)): return VXNOCELL # 5b: Hierarchy Check cellext = VXBRICKEXT VXCHUNKEXT coord = tuple(ipos[i] // cellext for i in range(3)) if chunkoccupied(coord, chunkmasks, VXMASKEXT): return (ipos, crossedaxis) cellext = VXBRICKEXT coord = tuple(ipos[i] // cellext for i in range(3)) if brickoccupied(coord, brickmasks, VXMASKEXT): return (ipos, crossedaxis) cellext = 1 coord = ipos if voxeloccupied(coord, voxelmasks, VXMASKEXT): return (ipos, crossedaxis) # 5c: AADF Skip if cellext == VXBRICKEXT VXCHUNKEXT: aadf = chunkaadf.Load(coord + (0,)) elif cellext == VXBRICKEXT: aadf = brickaadf.Load(coord + (0,)) else: aadf = voxelaadf.Load(coord + (0,)) # 5d: Exit Plane Calculation exitplane = aadfexitplane(coord, cellext, aadf, raydir, gridext) # 5e: Distance to Exit sidedist = tuple((exitplane[i] - float(ipos[i]) - localpos[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)) sidedist = tuple(3e+38 if raydir[i] == 0.0 else sidedist[i] for i in range(3)) # 5f: Find Minimum t = min(sidedist) crossed = tuple(1.0 if sidedist[i] >= t else 0.0 for i in range(3)) crossedaxis = 0 if crossed[1] > 0.5: crossedaxis = 1 if crossed[2] > 0.5: crossedaxis = 2 # 5g: Advance advanced = tuple(localpos[i] + max(t, 0.0001) raydir[i] for i in range(3)) celldelta = tuple(int(advanced[i] + crossed[i] (1.0 if raydir[i] < 0.0 else -1.0) 0.5) for i in range(3)) ipos = tuple(ipos[i] + celldelta[i] for i in range(3)) localpos = tuple(advanced[i] - float(ipos[i]) for i in range(3)) def chunkoccupied(coord, masks, VXMASKEXT): local = tuple(c & (VXMASKEXT - 1) for c in coord) bit = local[0] + local[1] VXMASKEXT + local[2] VXMASKEXT VXMASKEXT mask = masks.Load(tuple(c // VXMASKEXT for c in coord) + (0,)) return (mask & (1 << bit)) != 0 def brickoccupied(coord, masks, VXMASKEXT): local = tuple(c & (VXMASKEXT - 1) for c in coord) bit = local[0] + local[1] VXMASKEXT + local[2] VXMASKEXT VXMASKEXT mask = masks.Load(tuple(c // VXMASKEXT for c in coord) + (0,)) return (mask & (1 << bit)) != 0 def voxeloccupied(coord, masks, VXMASKEXT): local = tuple(c & (VXMASKEXT - 1) for c in coord) bit = local[0] + local[1] VXMASKEXT + local[2] VXMASKEXT VXMASKEXT mask = masks.Load(tuple(c // VXMASKEXT for c in coord) + (0,)) return (mask & (1 << bit)) != 0 def aadfexitplane(coord, cellext, aadf, raydir, gridext): shiftx = 0 if raydir[0] < 0.0 else 5 shifty = 10 if raydir[1] < 0.0 else 15 shiftz = 20 if raydir[2] < 0.0 else 25 boundsx = (aadf >> shiftx) & 31 boundsy = (aadf >> shifty) & 31 boundsz = (aadf >> shiftz) & 31 lowerx = max((coord[0] - boundsx) cellext, 0) upperx = min((coord[0] + 1 + boundsx) cellext, gridext) lowery = max((coord[1] - boundsy) cellext, 0) uppery = min((coord[1] + 1 + boundsy) cellext, gridext) lowerz = max((coord[2] - boundsz) cellext, 0) upperz = min((coord[2] + 1 + boundsz) cellext, gridext) exitx = lowerx if raydir[0] < 0.0 else upperx exity = lowery if raydir[1] < 0.0 else uppery exitz = lowerz if raydir[2] < 0.0 else upperz return (exitx, exity, exitz) Parameters: VXMASKEXT: Side length of a mask block in voxels. VXBRICKEXT: Side length of a brick in voxels. VXCHUNKEXT: Side length of a chunk in voxels. VXNOCELL: Sentinel value returned when the ray misses the grid or exits the bounds. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero ray direction components cause division by zero in invdir. Handled by adding 1e-30 to the ray direction before inversion. Zero ray direction components cause infinite sidedist. Handled by setting the corresponding sidedist component to 3e+38. Zero distance steps can cause infinite loops. Handled by using max(t, 0.0001) when advancing the ray. Not given in the sources. Origin: Developed by Nelarius for the vxray project, an experimental voxel rendering engine using the DDA algorithm. History: The method is part of the vxray codebase, which uses Metal and CMake for building and running. Usage: Used in the vxray renderer for sparse voxel traversal. name: Voxel Ray Traversal (AABB-optimized)
head: Fast Voxel Traversal, VoxelRay3Iterator
body: Voxel Ray Traversal (AABB-optimized) is an iterator that traverses a 3D voxel volume along a ray, returning hits for voxels contained within the volume. It solves the problem of efficiently enumerating voxels by combining a standard 3D DDA traversal with an initial Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) rejection test. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as Octree Traversal or Sparse Voxel Ray Marching with AABB Exit Planes, is its reliance on a flat or chunk-based volume structure where the AABB test serves primarily as a "jump ahead" mechanism to skip empty space before the voxel-by-voxel iteration begins, rather than using hierarchical node structures for traversal. Inputs: ray: A ray defined by origin p (Vec3), direction d (Vec3, normalized), and length (f32). volume: A BoundingVolume3 object containing size (Vec3) and a containspoint method to check voxel occupancy. Outputs: An iterator yielding Ray3hit structs, each containing: distance: f32, the distance along the ray to the voxel entry point. voxel: IVec3, the integer coordinates of the voxel. normal: Option<IVec3>, the normal of the face crossed to enter the voxel (negative step direction). The iterator state maintains the following fields: volume: Reference to the volume being traversed. maxd: f32, the maximum distance the ray can travel. i: IVec3, the current voxel index. step: IVec3, the direction of stepping for each axis (+1 or -1). delta: Vec3, the distance along the ray to cross one voxel in each axis. dist: Vec3, the distance from the current position p to the next voxel boundary in each axis. tmax: Vec3, the distance along the ray to the nearest voxel boundary in each axis. t: f32, the current traveled distance. norm: Option<IVec3>, the normal of the last crossed face. done: bool, flag indicating iteration completion. 1. Initialization and AABB Rejection: Normalize the ray direction: d = \text{normalize}(ray.direction). Initialize traveled distance t = 0.0. Check if the floor of the ray origin p is inside the volume: if \text{volume.containspoint}(\lfloor p \rfloor) is false, perform an AABB test against the chunk bounds using testaabbofchunk(volume, p, d, ray.length). If the AABB test fails (returns None), return a done iterator. If the AABB test succeeds, unwrap the intersection point aabb. Back the origin p off by at least 1 voxel: p = aabb - d \times 2.0. Update the traveled distance: t += \text{length}(p - aabb) - 2.0. 2. Calculate Maximum Distance: Calculate maxd as the minimum of the ray's specified length and the current distance t plus the corner-to-corner length of the volume plus 2.0: \text{max\d} = \min(\text{ray.length}, t + \text{length}(\text{volume.size}) + 2.0) 3. Calculate Starting Voxel and Step Direction: Starting voxel i = \lfloor p \rfloor converted to IVec3. Step direction \text{step} = \text{signum}(d) converted to IVec3. 4. Calculate Delta: For each axis k \in \{x, y, z\}, calculate \deltak: \deltak = \begin{cases} \infty & \text{if } |dk| < \epsilon \\ 1.0 / |dk| & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \epsilon = \text{f32::EPSILON}. 5. Calculate Distance to Boundary: For each axis k, calculate \text{dist}k: \text{dist}k = \begin{cases} ik + 1.0 - pk & \text{if } \text{step}k > 0 \\ pk - ik & \text{if } \text{step}k \le 0 \end{cases} 6. Calculate tmax: For each axis k, calculate t{\text{max}, k}: t{\text{max}, k} = \begin{cases} \deltak \times \text{dist}k & \text{if } \deltak < \infty \\ \infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 7. Iteration Loop: While t \le \text{max\d}: Check if the current voxel i is within the volume using \text{volume.containspoint}(i). If true, create a Ray3hit with distance = t, voxel = i, and normal mapped from norm. Select the axis with the smallest t{\text{max}}: If t{\text{max}, x} < t{\text{max}, y} and t{\text{max}, x} < t{\text{max}, z}: ix += \text{step}x t = t{\text{max}, x} t{\text{max}, x} += \deltax \text{norm} = (-\text{step}x, 0, 0) Else if t{\text{max}, y} < t{\text{max}, z}: iy += \text{step}y t = t{\text{max}, y} t{\text{max}, y} += \deltay \text{norm} = (0, -\text{step}y, 0) Else: iz += \text{step}z t = t{\text{max}, z} t{\text{max}, z} += \deltaz \text{norm} = (0, 0, -\text{step}z) If a hit was found in the current voxel, return it immediately. If the loop finishes without finding a hit, set done = true and return None. The testaabbofchunk function calculates the intersection of a ray with an AABB defined by min (Vec3::ZERO) and max (volume.size as Vec3): 1. For each axis i \in \{0, 1, 2\}, calculate ti: ti = \begin{cases} \frac{\text{min}i - \text{from}i}{\text{direction}i} & \text{if } \text{direction}i > 0.0 \\ \frac{\text{max}i - \text{from}i}{\text{direction}i} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 2. Find the axis mi with the smallest t value using nested comparisons. 3. Validate intersection: If t{mi} \ge 0.0 and t{mi} \le \text{distance}, calculate the intersection point pt = \text{from} + \text{direction} \times t{mi}. 4. Check if the other two dimensions of pt are within [\text{min}, \text{max}]. If so, return pt. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import Optional, Tuple class Vec3: def init(self, x: float, y: float, z: float): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def normalize(self) -> 'Vec3': length = math.sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2) if length == 0: return Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return Vec3(self.x / length, self.y / length, self.z / length) def length(self) -> float: return math.sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2) def signum(self) -> 'Vec3': return Vec3( 1.0 if self.x > 0 else (-1.0 if self.x < 0 else 0.0), 1.0 if self.y > 0 else (-1.0 if self.y < 0 else 0.0), 1.0 if self.z > 0 else (-1.0 if self.z < 0 else 0.0)) class IVec3: def init(self, x: int, y: int, z: int): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z @staticmethod def floor(p: Vec3) -> 'IVec3': return IVec3(math.floor(p.x), math.floor(p.y), math.floor(p.z)) class Ray3hit: def init(self, distance: float, voxel: IVec3, normal: Optional[IVec3]): self.distance = distance self.voxel = voxel self.normal = normal class BoundingVolume3: def init(self, size: Vec3): self.size = size def containspoint(self, voxel: IVec3) -> bool: # Placeholder for actual occupancy check logic # In a real implementation, this would check a sparse data structure return True def testaabbofchunk(volume: BoundingVolume3, frompt: Vec3, direction: Vec3, distance: float) -> Optional[Vec3]: minpt = Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) maxpt = volume.size t = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): diri = direction.x if i == 0 else (direction.y if i == 1 else direction.z) fromi = frompt.x if i == 0 else (frompt.y if i == 1 else frompt.z) mini = minpt.x if i == 0 else (minpt.y if i == 1 else minpt.z) maxi = maxpt.x if i == 0 else (maxpt.y if i == 1 else maxpt.z) if diri > 0.0: t[i] = (mini - fromi) / diri else: t[i] = (maxi - fromi) / diri mi = 0 if t[0] > t[1]: if t[0] > t[2]: mi = 0 else: mi = 2 else: if t[1] > t[2]: mi = 1 else: mi = 2 if t[mi] >= 0.0 and t[mi] <= distance: ptx = frompt.x + direction.x t[mi] pty = frompt.y + direction.y t[mi] ptz = frompt.z + direction.z t[mi] o1 = (mi + 1) % 3 o2 = (mi + 2) % 3 # Check other dimensions if o1 == 1: if not (minpt.y <= pty <= maxpt.y): return None elif o1 == 2: if not (minpt.z <= ptz <= maxpt.z): return None if o2 == 1: if not (minpt.y <= pty <= maxpt.y): return None elif o2 == 2: if not (minpt.z <= ptz <= maxpt.z): return None return Vec3(ptx, pty, ptz) return None class VoxelRay3Iterator: def init(self, volume: BoundingVolume3, p: Vec3, d: Vec3, raylength: float): self.volume = volume self.maxd = 0.0 self.i = IVec3(0, 0, 0) self.step = IVec3(0, 0, 0) self.delta = Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) self.dist = Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) self.tmax = Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) self.t = 0.0 self.norm = None self.done = False dnormalized = d.normalize() t = 0.0 if not volume.containspoint(IVec3.floor(p)): aabb = testaabbofchunk(volume, p, dnormalized, raylength) if aabb is None: self.done = True return aabbpt = aabb p = Vec3(aabbpt.x - dnormalized.x 2.0, aabbpt.y - dnormalized.y 2.0, aabbpt.z - dnormalized.z 2.0) t += (p - aabbpt).length() - 2.0 maxdval = min(raylength, t + Vec3(volume.size.x, volume.size.y, volume.size.z).length() + 2.0) self.maxd = maxdval self.i = IVec3.floor(p) self.step = IVec3( 1 if dnormalized.x > 0 else (-1 if dnormalized.x < 0 else 0), 1 if dnormalized.y > 0 else (-1 if dnormalized.y < 0 else 0), 1 if dnormalized.z > 0 else (-1 if dnormalized.z < 0 else 0)) eps = 1e-7 # f32::EPSILON approximation self.delta = Vec3( float('inf') if abs(dnormalized.x) < eps else 1.0 / abs(dnormalized.x), float('inf') if abs(dnormalized.y) < eps else 1.0 / abs(dnormalized.y), float('inf') if abs(dnormalized.z) < eps else 1.0 / abs(dnormalized.z)) self.dist = Vec3( self.i.x + 1.0 - p.x if self.step.x > 0 else p.x - self.i.x, self.i.y + 1.0 - p.y if self.step.y > 0 else p.y - self.i.y, self.i.z + 1.0 - p.z if self.step.z > 0 else p.z - self.i.z) self.tmax = Vec3( self.delta.x self.dist.x if self.delta.x < float('inf') else float('inf'), self.delta.y self.dist.y if self.delta.y < float('inf') else float('inf'), self.delta.z self.dist.z if self.delta.z < float('inf') else float('inf')) self.t = t def iter(self): return self def next(self) -> Optional[Ray3hit]: if self.done: return None while self.t <= self.maxd: hit = None if self.volume.containspoint(self.i): hit = Ray3hit(self.t, self.i, self.norm) if self.tmax.x < self.tmax.y: if self.tmax.x < self.tmax.z: self.i.x += self.step.x self.t = self.tmax.x self.tmax.x += self.delta.x self.norm = IVec3(-self.step.x, 0, 0) else: self.i.z += self.step.z self.t = self.tmax.z self.tmax.z += self.delta.z self.norm = IVec3(0, 0, -self.step.z) else: if self.tmax.y < self.tmax.z: self.i.y += self.step.y self.t = self.tmax.y self.tmax.y += self.delta.y self.norm = IVec3(0, -self.step.y, 0) else: self.i.z += self.step.z self.t = self.tmax.z self.tmax.z += self.delta.z self.norm = IVec3(0, 0, -self.step.z) if hit is not None: return hit self.done = True return None volume: BoundingVolume3 - The volume being traversed, containing size and containment logic. Zero Direction Component: If a direction component is near zero (|dk| < \epsilon), \deltak is set to \infty to prevent division by zero and correctly handle rays parallel to an axis. Boundary Precision: The initial AABB test backs off the origin by 2.0 units to ensure the ray starts inside the first voxel, preventing missed hits due to floating-point inaccuracies at boundaries.
