name: Multi-stage Training Strategy
head: Iterative Octree Reconstruction Training, Octree Reconstruction, Stage-based Octree Refinement
body: The Multi-stage Training Strategy is a training procedure for octree-based volumetric super-resolution that divides training into sequential stages, reconstructing the octree at the end of each stage to address the failure of importance sampling as model weights update. It sets itself apart from single-stage hierarchical sampling by dynamically adapting the sampling distribution to the current model's error landscape, ensuring that subsequent stages continue to benefit from importance sampling rather than converging prematurely on an outdated distribution. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ground truth volumetric data D{gt}, initial octree (built from variance), current best model N^k{best}, minimum epoch count q, loss threshold Q. Outputs: Final trained model, final octree structure. Data Structures: Octree: Hierarchical tree where each node represents a cuboid subblock. Leaf nodes are indivisible. Nodes store regression loss aggregates for subdivision decisions. Model: Neural network N (encoder-decoder) mapping low-resolution inputs to high-resolution outputs. Parameters: q: Minimum number of epochs per stage. Typical value: q \ge 10. Q: Loss threshold for termination. Not given in the sources. a: Downsampling scale factor for inference. Not given in the sources. s: Minimum dimension size for subdivision. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multistagetraining(Dgt, initialoctree, Nbest, q, Q, a, s): k = 0 octree = initialoctree while True: epoch = 0 losshistory = [] while True: epoch += 1 # Standard training loop omitted per source: crop block, downsample, encode, hierarchical sample, decode, loss, update currentloss = trainoneepoch(Dgt, octree, Nbest, a) losshistory.append(currentloss) if epoch < q: continue recentlosses = losshistory[-10:] meanval, slope = linearregression(recentlosses) if meanval <= Q: return Nbest, octree if meanval > Q and slope >= 0: break k += 1 octree = reconstructoctree(Dgt, Nbest, a, s) def trainoneepoch(Dgt, octree, model, a): # Standard training loop omitted per source return 0.0 def linearregression(losses): n = len(losses) x = list(range(n)) y = losses meanx = sum(x) / n meany = sum(y) / n num = sum((x[i] - meanx) (y[i] - meany) for i in range(n)) den = sum((x[i] - meanx) 2 for i in range(n)) slope = num / den if den != 0 else 0.0 return meany, slope def reconstructoctree(Dgt, Nbest, a, s): Dagt = downsample(Dgt, a) Dalr = downsample(Dagt, a) Dhr = Nbest(Dalr) n = len(Dagt) c = len(Dhr[0]) alpha = [1.0] c gridlosses = [] totalloss = 0.0 for j in range(n): xhat = Dhr[j] xtrue = Dagt[j] Lj = sum(alpha[i] abs(xtrue[i] - xhat[i]) for i in range(c)) / c gridlosses.append(Lj) totalloss += Lj Ltot = totalloss / n newoctree = Octree() newoctree.root = Subdivide(Dhr, gridlosses, Ltot, s, OctreeNode(bounds=Dgt.bounds)) return newoctree def Subdivide(Dhr, gridlosses, Ltot, s, node): points = getpointsinsubblock(node) if not points: return node Lsubtot = sum(gridlosses[j] for j in points) / len(points) dims = getnodedimensions(node) if Lsubtot >= Ltot and max(dims) > s: children = createchildren(node) for child in children: Subdivide(Dhr, gridlosses, Ltot, s, child) return children return node def downsample(data, factor): return data[::factor] def getpointsinsubblock(node): return list(range(node.startidx, node.endidx)) def getnodedimensions(node): return (node.w, node.h, node.d) def createchildren(node): return [OctreeNode() for in range(8)] class Octree: pass class OctreeNode: pass Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the octree using variance information from the original data. 2. Stage Training: Begin the first stage. Randomly crop cubic data blocks from the original data, downsample them, encode to a latent context grid, perform hierarchical sampling based on the current octree, decode, and compute the total loss (regression + PDE). Update model weights. 3. Bottleneck Detection: Starting from the q-th epoch, use the loss values of the last 10 epochs to perform linear regression. 4. Termination Check: Calculate the mean value of the linear regression model (mean loss). If the mean value is \le Q, terminate training immediately and save the current best model. 5. Stage Transition Check: If the mean value is > Q AND the slope of the linear regression model is \ge 0, start the next stage. 6. Octree Reconstruction: Downsample the ground truth D{gt} by factor a to get D{a\gt}. Perform inference using D{a\lr} (downsampled D{a\gt}) and the current best model N^k{best} to get D^k{hr}. Formula: D^k{hr} = N^k{best}(D{a\lr}). Compute regression loss L^kj for each grid point j: L^kj = \frac{1}{c} \sum{i=1}^{c} \alphai \|x{ij} - \hat{x}^k{ij}\|1, where \hat{x}^k{ij} is the estimated value from D^k{hr} and \alphai is the weight for the i-th physical variable. Compute total regression loss L^k{tot} = \frac{1}{n} \sum{j=1}^{n} L^kj. Recursively reconstruct the octree from the root. For each subblock, compute its total regression loss L{sub,k\tot}. Subdivide the subblock if L{sub,k\tot} \ge L^k{tot} AND at least one dimension of the subblock is greater than s. 7. Repeat: Repeat the training process with the new octree until the termination condition is reached. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Frequent Stage Transitions: Frequent reconstruction is time-consuming. Mitigated by enforcing a minimum epoch count q. Importance Sampling Failure: As training proceeds and weights update, the initial octree fails to represent the training data distribution, causing importance sampling to become irrelevant and gradients to converge to 0. Mitigated by reconstructing the octree at stage boundaries. Inference Cost: Full-resolution inference is time-consuming. Mitigated by downsampling the ground truth data D{gt} by a scale factor a for octree reconstruction, reducing inference time to 1/a^3. Time Complexity: The method adds overhead due to periodic octree reconstruction and inference. The reconstruction cost is proportional to the number of grid points and octree nodes. The downsampling factor a is a trade-off between accuracy and speed. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the octree structure and the high-resolution output D^k{hr} during reconstruction. Strengths: Ensures continued effectiveness of importance sampling throughout training, leading to better convergence and accuracy compared to single-stage methods. Limitations: Increased training time due to reconstruction steps. Requires careful tuning of parameters q and Q. When to use: When training volumetric super-resolution models with octree-based hierarchical sampling, especially when the data distribution changes significantly during training or when single-stage sampling leads to premature convergence. The Multi-stage Training Strategy was proposed in the context of octree-based hierarchical sampling optimization for the volumetric super-resolution of scientific data. name: Empty Space Skipping via Data Structures
body: Empty Space Skipping via Data Structures is a family of volume rendering optimization techniques that reduce computational cost by identifying and bypassing inactive (transparent or empty) regions of a volume dataset before or during ray sampling. Unlike methods that rely on hardware occlusion culling or ray coherence, this family uses explicit secondary data structures—such as min-max blocks, occupancy grids, BVHs, or hybrid trees—to store metadata about the spatial distribution of active data. This allows rays to determine entry and exit points of active regions analytically or via coarse traversal, skipping large intervals of empty space that would otherwise require expensive texture lookups and compositing operations. The core mechanism shared by all methods in this family involves three stages: construction of a secondary acceleration structure, definition of activity, and ray-based skipping. 1. Acceleration Structure Construction: A secondary data structure is built to represent the volume. 2. Active Region Definition: A block or region is defined as "active" if it contributes to the final image. 3. Ray Query and Skip: During rendering, the algorithm queries the acceleration structure to find the entry and exit points of active regions along a ray. 4. Coordinate Mapping: Efficient mapping between ray positions and grid indices is required, typically via integer division by block size: u{\text{occ}} = \lfloor u{\text{vol}} / B \rfloor. Uses min-max block structures and rasterizes bounding geometry of active blocks to determine ray start/end points. Best for isosurface rendering with static transfer functions. Uses hardware depth/alpha tests on texture slabs to find near/far points. Best for legacy OpenGL pipelines and slab-based rendering. Uses BVH with density bounds for sphere tracing. Best for semi-transparent volumes with constant or varying density. Uses occupancy volumes for neural radiance fields (NeRF). Best for volumetric video and neural rendering. Uses flat or multi-resolution occupancy grids. Best for simple, direct indexing acceleration. Uses a leap buffer based on ray coherence. Best for close-up views with large empty foregrounds. Combines kd-tree root with uniform grid leaves. Best for large datasets requiring balanced construction cost and skipping granularity. Definition: A technique achieving extremely fine-grained empty space skipping by marching rays only through active volume cells, located efficiently with a HistoPyramid texture and rendered as point primitives. Steps: 1. Locate active volume cells using a HistoPyramid texture. 2. Render active cells as point primitives to create rays close to the isosurface. 3. Accelerate by exploiting early-depth testing: compare fragment's interpolated z-coordinate with depth buffer value; discard if occluded. 4. Rasterize primitives in front-to-back order to increase discarded fragments, achieved via CPU-based sorting of volume slices. Comparison: Considered a hybrid object-order and image-order approach, meaning it is dependent on rendering resolution. Steps: 1. Divide span space points into one of the L \times L lattice elements. 2. Assign each lattice element to a category based on its position relative to the isovalue v (see Figure 3 cases in). 3. Trivially include cells in region 2. 4. For cells in region 3, require a test against their maximum value. 5. For cells in region 4, require a test against their minimum value. 6. For cells in region 5, require a full min-max search of its cells. 7. Create search structures only at the lattice elements along the diagonal region 5. 8. Coalesce lattice elements at other regions into sorted linear arrays. 9. Build a kd-tree for each lattice element along the y = x line, since only these elements may fall into region 5 classification. Parameter: Lattice resolution L: User-defined resolution for dividing span space points. Steps: 1. Propagate current transfer function values to the leafs of the Mixture Graph. 2. Use the hierarchy for skipping longer segments. 3. If the opacity value in parent voxels falls below a certain threshold, traverse the hierarchy upwards to establish larger blocks that can be skipped. Parameter: Threshold: A low opacity threshold used to trigger skipping; typical value is 10^{-8}. Performance: Average 3x speedup compared to the same implementation without mipmaps using a threshold of 10^{-8}. Empty space skipping is a fundamental optimization in volume rendering, addressing the high cost of sampling large volumes where significant portions are transparent or empty. Early methods relied on ray coherence (Space Leaping). The use of explicit data structures for skipping evolved with GPU capabilities. Liu et al. [LCD09] introduced HistoPyramid-based skipping, followed by IsoBAS [LCD15] and Jiang et al. [JRZ16], which are considered hybrid object-order/image-order approaches. Shen et al. [14] proposed the ISSUE algorithm for isosurface extraction using lattice subdivision. More recently, hierarchical structures like Mixture Graphs have been developed to balance construction cost and skipping efficiency for large-scale datasets. name: Object-Order Empty Space Skipping
head: Block min-max culling, Front-to-back ray-casting with bounding box culling, GPU-based Ray-Casting with Object-Order Empty Space Skipping
body: Object-Order Empty Space Skipping is a volume rendering optimization technique that reduces the number of volume samples by culling transparent or irrelevant regions before raycasting begins. It differs from its siblings by performing culling during the rasterization setup phase using precomputed block statistics and bounding geometry, rather than relying solely on hierarchical tree traversal or dynamic shader termination. Unlike Early Shader Termination, which stops rays dynamically during compositing, this method computes ray depth ranges per frame via rasterization to skip large inactive regions upfront. Unlike Rasterizing Bounding Geometry for Empty Space Skipping, it explicitly maintains min-max values for regular block subdivisions to drive the culling logic. The method combines object-order skipping (via block min-max values) with image-order skipping (per-sample checks) to accelerate front-to-back ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume texture V, isovalue T, camera position c, screen coordinates (x, y), block size B (e.g., 4^3 or 8^3 voxels). Output: Rendered image with rays skipping inactive regions. Data Structures: 1. Volume Texture: 3D texture storing voxel values. 2. Min-Max Block Structure: A secondary structure storing the minimum and maximum values for each block in the regular subdivision of the volume. 3. Bounding Geometry: Explicit geometry formed by the faces of active blocks that are adjacent to inactive blocks. Steps: 1. Initialization (Pre-computation): Subdivide the volume into blocks of size B \times B \times B. Compute and store the minimum and maximum voxel values for each block in the Min-Max Block Structure. Identify active blocks where the maximum value meets the isovalue criterion. Generate the bounding geometry by creating faces for active blocks adjacent to inactive blocks. 2. Per-Frame Setup (Object-Order Skipping): Compute ray direction \mathbf{d}(x, y) from camera position c: \mathbf{p}(t, x, y) = c + t \mathbf{d}(x, y) Determine the initial ray depth range [t{\text{start}}(x, y), t{\text{exit}}(x, y)] by rasterizing the bounding geometry. Render front faces with a depth test retaining the closest intersection (e.g., GLLESS) to obtain t{\text{start}}(x, y). Render back faces with a depth test retaining the farthest intersection (e.g., GLGREATER) to obtain t{\text{exit}}(x, y). 3. Ray Casting Loop (Image-Order Skipping): For each pixel, cast a ray in front-to-back order within [t{\text{start}}(x, y), t{\text{exit}}(x, y)]. At each sample, compute the block index using integer division: u{\text{block}} = \lfloor u{\text{vol}} / B \rfloor where u{\text{vol}} is the coordinate in the volume texture and B is the block size. Retrieve the block's min-max values. If the block is inactive (e.g., max value below isovalue), skip the sample. If active, perform standard ray casting (texture fetch, compositing). Terminate the ray upon isosurface intersection or volume exit. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def objectorderskip(volume, minmaxblocks, camera, blocksize, isovalue, stepsize): for y, x in screenpixels: raydir = computedirection(camera, x, y) rayorigin = camera.position # Object-order skip: compute depth range via bounding geometry rasterization tstart, texit = getdepthrangefromrasterization(rayorigin, raydir, minmaxblocks) t = tstart while t < texit: volpos = rayorigin + t raydir blockidx = floor(volpos / blocksize) blockmin, blockmax = minmaxblocks[blockidx] if blockmax < isovalue: # Image-order skip: block is inactive t += stepsize continue # Sample active block color, opacity = samplevolume(volume, volpos) composite(color, opacity) if opacity >= threshold: break t += stepsize Parameters: Block size B: Typically 4^3 or 8^3 voxels per block. Isovalue T: Determines active blocks. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Enclosed Inactive Blocks: Inactive blocks enclosed by active blocks are not excluded from the search range [t{\text{start}}, t{\text{exit}}] by the bounding geometry. Samples in these blocks are skipped on a per-sample basis early in the ray-casting loop. Isovalue Changes: When the isovalue changes, the active status of blocks must be recomputed, and the bounding geometry updated. Early Shader Termination is an optimization technique that discards the execution of complex decoding shaders for fragments likely to represent empty space by using an early z-test in a two-pass rendering approach. It builds on Object-Order Empty Space Skipping by adding a lightweight pre-check to avoid expensive shader execution in empty regions. Compared to rendering uncompressed data, this approach initially perceives a loss in performance of a factor of 2-3 due to complex shaders and texture indirections; however, in empty regions, it results in a considerable speed-up because only one texture fetch is needed to check the mean. Rasterizing Bounding Geometry for Empty Space Skipping is a volume rendering optimization technique that uses hardware-accelerated rasterization to determine the start and end positions for ray marching, thereby skipping empty space. It solves the problem of expensive tree traversal on the GPU by replacing hierarchical data structure lookups with fragment shader depth testing. It sets itself apart from Min-Max Block Culling by using explicit geometric primitives (quads/boxes) and depth buffers rather than scalar min-max values, and from Early Shader Termination by performing culling in a dedicated geometry pass rather than within the ray-marching loop. Min-Max Block Culling is an object-order empty space skipping technique that reduces the number of volume samples by culling transparent or irrelevant regions before raycasting begins. It differs from its siblings by performing culling during the rasterization setup phase using precomputed block statistics, rather than during ray traversal or via bounding geometry rasterization. Unlike Early Shader Termination, which stops rays dynamically during compositing, this method prevents rays from entering empty blocks entirely. Unlike Rasterizing Bounding Geometry for Empty Space Skipping, it relies on scalar block bounds rather than polygonal approximations. A data structure for empty-space skipping in pre-integrated volume rendering. It modifies the region covered by each block so that each block covers some region of which thickness is at least the sampling distance. By overlapping the region of each block, a line segment formed by two sampling points can be tested for transparency using only one block, avoiding the overhead of determining which of multiple intersecting blocks are transparent. Each block covers a region of thickness at least the sampling distance, creating overlaps between adjacent blocks. To skip a line segment formed by two sampling points, test only the single block that contains the line segment (or overlaps it sufficiently) to determine if it is transparent. If the block is transparent, skip the sampling process for that segment. Unlike previous methods where a line segment may intersect at most three blocks and requires testing all intersecting blocks (creating overhead to determine cases like Fig. 1a vs 1b), this method tests only one block due to the overlapping region design. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method reduces overhead by skipping most empty space with no cost using modified ray segments [t{\text{start}}, t{\text{exit}}]. Only a small number of samples require per-sample skipping, which is accelerated via an adaptive sampling strategy. Strengths: Reduces the number of volume samples significantly for sparse volumes. Simple to implement with standard GPU rasterization features. Limitations: Inactive blocks enclosed by active blocks are not excluded from the search range, leading to per-sample checks. When to Use: Suitable for sparse volumes with clear isosurfaces or transparent regions. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. It builds on the idea of using block min-max values to cull inactive regions, reducing the overhead of empty space skipping. The method has been used in various implementations of real-time volume rendering, particularly for isosurface rendering. name: Early Shader Termination
head: Early End of Computation, Early z-test optimization, Two-pass empty space culling
body: Early Shader Termination is an optimization technique that discards the execution of complex decoding shaders for fragments likely to represent empty space by using an early z-test in a two-pass rendering approach. It builds on Object-Order Empty Space Skipping by adding a lightweight pre-check to avoid expensive shader execution in empty regions. Compared to rendering uncompressed data, this approach initially perceives a loss in performance of a factor of 2-3 due to complex shaders and texture indirections; however, in empty regions, it results in a considerable speed-up because only one texture fetch is needed to check the mean. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A compressed volume dataset where each block (macro-cell) has an associated index texture I storing metadata (specifically the mean value in the R-component) and dependent data textures C1, C2. A slicing polygon representing the current view frustum or volume boundary. Output: A rendered image where empty space fragments are skipped, and depth values are correctly updated to allow subsequent fragments to pass depth tests. Data Structures: Index Texture I: Stores block metadata. The R-component holds the mean value of the block. Dependent Textures C1, C2: Store difference information or raw data, addressed using components of I. Steps: 1. First Pass (Empty Space Detection): Render the slicing polygon twice. In the first pass, issue a simple pixel shader program. In the shader, access index texture I and check the mean value stored in the R-component. If the mean value is zero, render the fragment with color and opacity set to zero. This does not affect the color buffer but sets the depth value in the depth buffer. If the mean value is not zero, discard the fragment using a kill instruction. This prevents the fragment from affecting the color or depth buffer. 2. Second Pass (Complex Rendering): Render the slicing polygon again with the complex shader. Set the depth test to GLGREATER in the second pass. The early z-test only lets fragments pass that were discarded in the first pass (where mean \neq 0). All other fragments (where mean = 0) are discarded before entering the complex shader. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def earlyshadertermination(fragments, indextextureI, complexdecodefunc): """ Simulates the two-pass early shader termination optimization. fragments: list of objects with.coords,.blockid,.z (depth) indextextureI: dict mapping blockid to objects with.R (mean value) complexdecodefunc: callable that returns decoded color for non-empty blocks """ depthbuffer = {} # Maps fragment coordinates to depth from pass 1 pass1discarded = [] # Pass 1: Simple pixel shader for frag in fragments: meanval = indextextureI[frag.blockid].R if meanval == 0: # Empty space: write depth, zero color/opacity depthbuffer[frag.coords] = frag.z pass1discarded.append(False) else: # Non-empty space: discard via kill instruction # Depth buffer retains the last valid depth for this coordinate pass1discarded.append(True) # Pass 2: Complex shader with GLGREATER depth test finaloutput = [] for i, frag in enumerate(fragments): if not pass1discarded[i]: # Early z-test fails: GLGREATER requires frag.z > depthbuffer[frag.coords] # Since pass 1 wrote frag.z, frag.z > frag.z is false. Fragment discarded. continue # Early z-test passes for discarded fragments (mean != 0) lastdepth = depthbuffer.get(frag.coords, -float('inf')) if frag.z > lastdepth: # GLGREATER decoded = complexdecodefunc(frag, indextextureI) finaloutput.append(decoded) return finaloutput Parameters: Depth Test Function: Must be set to GLGREATER in the second pass to leverage the early z-test correctly. Mean Threshold: Zero is used as the threshold for empty space. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Buffer Consistency: If a fragment is discarded in the shader (via kill), the depth value of the fragment rendered last is still valid in the depth buffer. This must be accounted for when using depth tests, as the discarded fragment does not update the depth buffer. Performance Overhead: The two-pass approach introduces overhead. The initial performance loss compared to uncompressed rendering is a factor of 2-3 due to the complexity of the shaders and texture indirections. Adds spatial coherence checks along the scanline direction to skip entire segments of empty space within a macro-cell projection. It builds on Early Shader Termination by optimizing the scope of the termination check. Time Complexity: In empty regions, the complexity is reduced to one texture fetch per block to check the mean. In non-empty regions, the full complex shader is executed. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the index texture I and dependent textures C1, C2. Measured Performance: On an Intel P4 1900 MHz machine, this approach saves another 5 percent of overall rendering time on average when combined with other optimizations like Early End of Computation. Strengths: Considerable speed-up in empty regions, which are frequent in numerical simulation results. Limitations: Initial performance loss of 2-3x compared to uncompressed rendering due to shader complexity and indirections. Requires hardware support for early z-test. It leverages the early z-test feature available on target graphics architectures to avoid executing pixel shaders for fragments that are likely to decode empty space. name: Early Scanline Termination
body: Early Scanline Termination is an optimization that stops processing a scanline as soon as a local ray through a pixel does not intersect any iso-surfaces, reducing the number of local rays cast per pixel. It operates within the macro-cell projection framework to skip empty segments along rows or columns of pixels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projected macro-cell bounding box, set of surface cells within the macro-cell, current scanline (row or column of pixels), image buffer, and per-pixel sequence flags. Output: Updated image buffer with colors for intersected pixels; identification of erroneous blank pixels (holes) for post-processing. Data Structures: Image Buffer: 2D array storing color values for each pixel. Sequence Flags: Two boolean flags per pixel indicating whether the pixel was recently dropped due to horizontal or vertical early scanline termination. Flags are set to True for all empty dropped pixels. The bounds of each new sequence of dropped pixels are marked by setting the sequence flags of the pixel immediately preceding the sequence and the pixel immediately following the sequence to False. A pixel through which a regular local ray has been cast has its sequence flags reset to False. Steps: 1. Identify all scanlines intersecting the macro-cell projection. 2. Check for problem cases by calculating a representative surface normal for each surface cell and checking dot products with two reference vectors. If a boundary cell prohibits termination, project its center point to the image plane. The collection of these projections forms a critical region. 3. Iterate through pixels of a scanline from one boundary to the other. If a local ray does not intersect any iso-surface and the pixel is outside the critical region, stop processing the scanline. Mark all remaining empty pixels as dropped, setting the appropriate sequence flag (horizontal or vertical) to True. Set the sequence flags of the pixel immediately preceding the first dropped pixel and the pixel immediately following the last dropped pixel to False to mark the sequence bounds. If a regular local ray is cast through a pixel, reset its sequence flags to False. 4. After frame completion, identify sequences of blank pixels with sequence flags set, bounded on both sides by non-blank pixels with unset flags. Cast rays from these pixels through the complete volume to fill the holes. Formulas: Representative normal check: N \cdot V{ref} > 0 indicates a problem case (left-facing normal or dangerous face). Critical region: Union of projected center points of all boundary cells where the dot product condition holds. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Left-facing surface normals: If projected surface normals point towards the left, early termination is disallowed for scanlines intersecting those parts until all such intersections are processed. Dangerous faces: Certain surface orientations can cause errors if termination is applied. Errors: Early scanline termination can lead to errors in about 0.017 percent of pixels on average, resulting in visible holes. These holes must be identified and filled after frame completion. Sequence Flag Management: Flags must be carefully managed to correctly identify erroneous sequences. Pixels erroneously dropped will never be part of a dropped sequence again. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def earlyscanlinetermination(macrocell, scanlinepixels, imagebuffer, sequenceflags, ishorizontal): # Project 3D cell centers to 2D image coordinates def projecttoimage(point3d): return (point3d.x, point3d.y) # Check if a 2D point lies outside a set of projected critical points def isoutsidecriticalregion(point2d, criticalpoints): if not criticalpoints: return True minx = min(p[0] for p in criticalpoints) maxx = max(p[0] for p in criticalpoints) miny = min(p[1] for p in criticalpoints) maxy = max(p[1] for p in criticalpoints) return not (minx <= point2d[0] <= maxx and miny <= point2d[1] <= maxy) # Cast a ray through the macro-cell to find the first iso-surface intersection def castlocalray(pixel2d): # Standard ray-marching or bounding volume traversal return None # Compute color from intersection data def computecolor(intersection): return (255, 255, 255) BLANK = (0, 0, 0, 0) criticalpoints = [projecttoimage(cell.center) for cell in macrocell.surfacecells if cell.prohibitstermination] terminated = False firstdroppedidx = None lastdroppedidx = None for i, pixel in enumerate(scanlinepixels): if terminated: break intersection = castlocalray(pixel) if intersection is not None: imagebuffer[pixel] = computecolor(intersection) sequenceflags[pixel] = (False, False) else: if isoutsidecriticalregion(pixel, criticalpoints): terminated = True firstdroppedidx = i for j in range(i, len(scanlinepixels)): p = scanlinepixels[j] imagebuffer[p] = BLANK if ishorizontal: sequenceflags[p] = (True, sequenceflags[p][1]) else: sequenceflags[p] = (sequenceflags[p][0], True) lastdroppedidx = j if firstdroppedidx > 0: sequenceflags[scanlinepixels[firstdroppedidx - 1]] = (False, False) if lastdroppedidx + 1 < len(scanlinepixels): sequenceflags[scanlinepixels[lastdroppedidx + 1]] = (False, False) def fillholes(imagebuffer, sequenceflags, imageheight, imagewidth): BLANK = (0, 0, 0, 0) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): if imagebuffer[y, x] == BLANK and sequenceflags[y, x] != (False, False): # Verify bounds: preceding and following pixels must be non-blank with flags (False, False) leftok = (x == 0) or (imagebuffer[y, x-1] != BLANK and sequenceflags[y, x-1] == (False, False)) rightok = (x == imagewidth-1) or (imagebuffer[y, x+1] != BLANK and sequenceflags[y, x+1] == (False, False)) if leftok and rightok: imagebuffer[y, x] = castlocalray((x, y)) Performance: Saves another 17 percent of overall rendering time on average. Reduces rays per pixel from 2.483 to 1.285 in the tested scenario. Memory Complexity: Requires two sequence flags per pixel for tracking. Limitations: Errors occur in about 0.017 percent of pixels on average, resulting in visible holes that require post-processing. Performance is dependent on the data set and the position of the view point. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Rasterizing Bounding Geometry for Empty Space Skipping
head: Bounding Geometry Rasterization, Raster-based Bounding Box Culling, Rasterizing Bounding Geometry
body: Rasterizing Bounding Geometry for Empty Space Skipping is a volume rendering optimization technique that uses hardware-accelerated rasterization to determine the start and end positions for ray marching, thereby skipping empty space. It solves the problem of expensive tree traversal on the GPU by replacing hierarchical data structure lookups with fragment shader depth testing. It sets itself apart from Min-Max Block Culling by using explicit geometric primitives (quads/boxes) and depth buffers rather than scalar min-max values, and from Early Shader Termination by performing culling in a dedicated geometry pass rather than within the ray-marching loop. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume texture containing iso values (or occupancy data), a threshold iso value, and a coarse grid definition (e.g., grid cells spanning N^3 voxels). Output: A rendered image where rays are marched only through active regions, with start and end positions derived from rasterized depth values. Data Structures: 1. gridTex: A 3D texture where each voxel stores the maximum iso value of the corresponding coarse grid cell. 2. Bounding Geometry: A set of quads (or bounding boxes) representing the boundaries between active and inactive regions in gridTex. 3. Offscreen Buffer: A depth buffer (and optionally a color buffer) used to store minimum and maximum depth values for each fragment during the first pass. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct gridTex by sampling the volume texture. Each voxel in gridTex contains the maximum iso value within its corresponding coarse grid cell. Define the coarse grid dimensions. For a volume of size Vx \times Vy \times Vz and a cell size of C^3 voxels, the grid dimensions are \lceil Vx/C \rceil \times \lceil Vy/C \rceil \times \lceil Vz/C \rceil. 2. Generate Bounding Geometry: For each pair of neighboring voxels in gridTex, determine if a boundary exists. A grid voxel is considered active if its maximum iso value is above the threshold iso value. Generate a quad (or bounding box face) if one voxel in the neighbor pair is active and the other is inactive. This process identifies the surface of the active volume data. 3. First Pass (Depth Computation): Render the generated bounding geometry to an offscreen buffer. For each fragment, store the minimum depth (front face) and maximum depth (back face) of the bounding geometry. This pass effectively projects the 3D active regions onto the 2D screen, capturing the depth extent of the volume along each ray. 4. Second Pass (Ray Marching): Render the front faces of the bounding geometry again to the main buffer. In the fragment shader, discard the fragment if it is not at the minimum depth value recorded in the first pass. This ensures that only the front-most active region is processed, preventing double-counting or processing of occluded empty space. Compute the start position of the ray using the minimum depth value and the end position using the maximum depth value from the first pass. March the ray between these start and end positions using standard volume rendering techniques (e.g., ray casting). Pseudocode: Unverified code. grid texture storing max iso values.""" griddims = ( math.ceil(volumetexture.width / cellsize), math.ceil(volumetexture.height / cellsize), math.ceil(volumetexture.depth / cellsize)) gridtex = in range(cellsize): for dy in range(cellsize): for dx in range(cellsize): vx, vy, vz = x cellsize + dx, y cellsize + dy, z cellsize + dz val = volumetexture.sample(vx, vy, vz) if val > maxval: maxval = val gridtex[z][y][x] = maxval return gridtex, griddims def generateboundinggeometry(gridtex, threshold, cellsize, griddims): """Generate quads for boundaries between active and inactive regions.""" quads = [] for z in range(griddims[2]): for y in range(griddims[1]): for x in range(griddims[0]): isactive = gridtex[z][y][x] > threshold for dx, dy, dz in [(1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (0, 0, 1)]: nx, ny, nz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz if nx < griddims[0] and ny < griddims[1] and nz < griddims[2]: neighboractive = gridtex[nz][ny][nx] > threshold if isactive != neighboractive: boundarypos = [x cellsize + dx cellsize, y cellsize + dy cellsize, z cellsize + dz cellsize] normal = [dx, dy, dz] quads.append({'pos': boundarypos, 'normal': normal}) return quads def renderfirstpass(quads, offscreenbuffer): """Render bounding geometry to compute min/max depth.""" offscreenbuffer.cleardepth() for quad in quads: viewdepths = [v.z for v in quad.vertices] minz, maxz = min(viewdepths), max(viewdepths) offscreenbuffer.updateminmaxdepth(minz, maxz) return offscreenbuffer def rendersecondpass(quads, offscreenbuffer, mainbuffer): """Render front faces and perform ray marching.""" for quad in quads: fragments = rasterize(quad) for frag in fragments: mindepth = offscreenbuffer.getmindepth(frag.screenpos) maxdepth = offscreenbuffer.getmaxdepth(frag.screenpos) if frag.depth != mindepth: continue raystart = depthtoworld(mindepth) rayend = depthtoworld(maxdepth) color = marchray(raystart, rayend) mainbuffer.setcolor(frag.screenpos, color) def rasterize(quad): """Standard triangle/quad rasterization to screen fragments.""" return [frag for frag in quad.screenprojection] def depthtoworld(depth): """Convert normalized depth to world coordinates.""" return depth def marchray(start, end): """Standard ray marching loop.""" color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] t = 0.0 step = 0.1 while t < 1.0: pos = start + (end - start) t t += step return color Parameters: Threshold Iso Value: The iso name: SparseLeap Rasterization
head: SparseLeap rasterization details
body: SparseLeap is a method for efficient empty space skipping in very large, sparse volume data, such as terabyte-sized microscopy volumes. It solves the problem of fragmented space subdivisions making empty regions hard to skip and the infeasibility of pre-computing well-adapted space subdivisions due to frequent changes in active objects. It sets itself apart from its siblings by exploiting hardware-accelerated rasterization to create per-pixel ray segment lists, thereby avoiding hierarchy traversal on the GPU during the ray-casting stage. Unlike standard octree empty space skipping, SparseLeap scales better to large, sparse data. It is agnostic of the underlying data structure used for managing volume data (e.g., page-table hierarchies or octrees). SparseLeap operates in two main stages: a preprocessing/rasterization stage and a ray-casting stage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An occupancy-histogram tree where each node has an occupancy class (empty, non-empty, or unknown). The tree is lazily constructed. Output: A set of ray segment lists, one per pixel, identifying non-empty regions along the viewing ray. Data Structures: 1. Occupancy-Histogram Tree: A hierarchical structure where each node stores an occupancy class. Leaf nodes store the class directly; non-leaf nodes determine their class via a majority vote over their occupancy histogram (the class occurring most often in all leaf nodes of its sub-tree). 2. Occupancy Geometry: An array of bounding boxes extracted from the tree. Each emitted box stores: Center coordinates. Size (dimensions). Node's occupancy class. Parent's occupancy class. 3. Ray Segment List: A per-pixel list of ray events (entry/exit) defining intervals (segments) with associated occupancy classes. Steps: 1. Occupancy Geometry Generation: Traverse the occupancy-histogram tree in breadth-first order, visiting child nodes in a fixed order (not visibility order). For the root node, set the parent occupancy class to invalid (not equal to any other class). The root always emits its bounding box. For each visited non-leaf node, determine its occupancy class by taking the majority vote over its occupancy histogram. For leaf nodes, use the occupancy class already stored in the node. Compare the node's occupancy class with its parent's occupancy class. If they are the same, skip emission. If they are different, emit a bounding box containing the node's center, size, its own occupancy class, and its parent's occupancy class. If the number of emitted bounding boxes exceeds a prespecified optional resource limit, stop traversal. 2. Rasterization (Object-Order Stage): Rasterize the set of fine-grained, view-independent bounding boxes generated in Step 1 using hardware-accelerated rasterization. For each pixel, compute an ordered list of stabbing boundary faces. Convert this into a ray segment list where consecutive ray segments of the same occupancy class are merged. This creates singly-linked lists of ray events per pixel. Exploit frame coherence by re-using the same bounding boxes unless the set of active objects changes. 3. Ray-Casting (Image-Order Stage): Perform ray casting independently for each pixel. Use the pre-computed ray segment lists to identify non-empty regions along the ray. Leap over empty space without hierarchy traversal by skipping segments marked as empty. Sample the non-empty volume data only within the non-empty segments. 4. Color Calculation: Apply a simple analytical lighting model to each intersection of the ray and the volume cell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparseleaprender(occupancytree, camera, volumedata): # Step 1: Generate Occupancy Geometry boundingboxes = [] stack = [(occupancytree.root, None)] # (node, parentclass) while stack: node, parentclass = stack.pop(0) # Breadth-first traversal # Determine current node's class if node.isleaf: currentclass = node.occupancyclass else: currentclass = getmajorityvote(node.occupancyhistogram) # Geometry Emission Rule if currentclass != parentclass: box = { 'center': node.center, 'size': node.size, 'myclass': currentclass, 'parentclass': parentclass } boundingboxes.append(box) # Add children to stack for child in node.children: stack.append((child, currentclass)) # Step 2: Rasterization # Hardware rasterization of boundingboxes produces per-pixel ray segment lists # This step is typically handled by the GPU rasterizer, not explicit CPU code raysegmentlists = hardwarerasterize(boundingboxes, camera) # Step 3 & 4: Ray Casting and Color Calculation for pixel in pixels: segments = raysegmentlists[pixel] color = vec3(0.0) for segment in segments: if segment.occupancyclass == 'empty': continue # Leap over empty space # Sample volume data in non-empty segment sample = samplevolume(segment.ray, volumedata) # Apply analytical lighting model lightcolor = calculatelighting(sample, segment.ray) color += lightcolor pixel.color = color Parameters: Resource Limit: An optional prespecified maximum number of bounding boxes. If exceeded, traversal stops. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fragmentation: Some fragmentation of space still remains in the occupancy geometry, which is resolved during the subsequent rasterization of ray segment lists where consecutive ray segments of the same occupancy class are merged. Active Objects: The method relies on frame coherence. If the set of active objects changes frequently, the bounding boxes must be regenerated, incurring preprocessing cost. A view-independent process that extracts nested bounding boxes from an occupancy histogram tree to represent space occupancy, reducing spatial fragmentation compared to standard octrees. It traverses the tree in breadth-first order, emitting boxes only when the occupancy class differs from the parent's class. It allows for an optional resource limit to cap the number of emitted boxes. See Occupancy Geometry Generation for details on the subsequent conversion to ray segment lists. Time Complexity: The preprocessing stage (occupancy geometry generation) is linear with respect to the number of nodes in the occupancy-histogram tree. The rasterization stage is hardware-accelerated and efficient. The ray-casting stage is proportional to the number of non-empty samples, avoiding traversal of empty space. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the occupancy-histogram tree and the number of emitted bounding boxes. The ray segment lists are stored per pixel. Measured Performance: SparseLeap scales better to large, sparse data than standard octree empty space skipping. It optimizes both the number of look-ups into the data structure used for empty-space skipping and the number of samples along each viewing ray. Strengths: Agnostic of the underlying data structure (e.g., page-table hierarchies, octrees). Efficient for very large, sparse volumes with fine structures. Limitations: Requires hardware rasterization capabilities. Performance may degrade if the set of active objects changes frequently, requiring regeneration of bounding boxes. When to use: Large, sparse volume data (e.g., terabyte-sized microscopy volumes) where empty space skipping is critical and the active regions change frequently. When not to use: Small, dense volumes where standard traversal is sufficient, or hardware rasterization is not available. SparseLeap was introduced by Markus Hadwiger, Ali K Al-Awami, Johanna Beyer, and Hanspeter Pfister in 2017. It addresses the challenges of volume rendering for very high-resolution, large-size data, such as terabyte-sized microscopy volumes, which contain many fine and intricate structures. The method moves the major cost of empty space skipping out of the ray-casting stage and into a hybrid strategy that balances computational load between determining empty ray segments in a rasterization (object-order) stage and sampling non-empty volume data in the ray-casting (image-order) stage. name: Ray Segment List Generation
head: Rasterizing occupancy geometry for ray segments
body: Ray Segment List Generation converts the rasterized occupancy geometry of a volume into singly-linked lists of ray events per pixel, defining ray segments (intervals between events) with associated occupancy classes. It sets itself apart from hierarchical traversal methods by performing a sequential, non-hierarchical "traversal" where the occupancy class is embedded directly in the event types (entry/exit), eliminating the need for a stack to push and pop classes during parsing. Inputs: Occupancy geometry array (bounding boxes with front/back face flags and occupancy classes). Visibility order of the geometry. Volume bounding box (for initialization). Outputs: For each pixel: a singly-linked list of ray events. Each event contains Depth (1D parameter), EventType (entry/exit), and OccupancyClass (empty/non-empty/unknown). The list defines ray segments between consecutive events. Data Structures: Ray Event: A structure containing: depth: float, the 1D parameter position of the intersection with a bounding box face. eventtype: enum, ENTRY or EXIT. occclass: enum, EMPTY, NONEMPTY, or UNKNOWN. Ray Segment List: A singly-linked list of Ray Event nodes, initialized per pixel. Initialization: 1. For each pixel, initialize the ray segment list as a single segment with occupancy class UNKNOWN. 2. This segment starts at the volume bounding box front face position and ends at the back face position. 3. The list comprises two events: Event 1: eventtype=ENTRY, depth=frontfaceposition, occclass=UNKNOWN. Event 2: eventtype=EXIT, depth=backfaceposition, occclass=UNKNOWN. Rasterization Pass: 1. Rasterize the occupancy geometry array in a single rendering pass. 2. For each fragment generated, invoke a fragment shader. 3. Determine if the fragment resulted from a front face or back face rasterization to set the EventType (ENTRY or EXIT). 4. Create a new Ray Event for the fragment: depth: Intersection parameter. eventtype: Determined in step 3. occclass: If eventtype == ENTRY: Set to the occupancy class of the bounding box that generated the event. If eventtype == EXIT: Set to the occupancy class of the box's parent. Incremental Event Processing (Merging and Deletion): For each incoming event E{new}, access the tail of the current ray segment list. Let the last event in the list be E{last}. If E{last}.depth \neq E{new}.depth, append E{new} to the list. If E{last}.depth == E{new}.depth, apply the following rules to E{last} and E{new} (and potentially preceding events): 1. Merge Same Type: If E{last}.eventtype == E{new}.eventtype (both ENTRY or both EXIT): Delete E{last}. Replace E{last}'s position in the list with E{new} (or append E{new} if E{last} was the only one, effectively overwriting). The surviving event is E{new}, adopting its occclass. 2. Delete Exit-Entry Pair (Same Class): If E{last}.eventtype == EXIT and E{new}.eventtype == ENTRY: Let E{prev} be the event preceding E{last} in the list (if it exists). If E{new}.occclass == E{prev}.occclass (indicating consecutive segments of the same occupancy class): Delete both E{last} and E{new}. This merges the segment ending at E{last} and the segment starting at E{new} into one longer segment of class E{prev}.occclass. 3. Delete Entry-Exit Pair (Grazing): If E{last}.eventtype == ENTRY and E{new}.eventtype == EXIT: Delete both E{last} and E{new}, regardless of occupancy class. This handles grazing rays hitting an edge or corner, generating two events at the same depth. 4. Remove Short Empty Segments: Detect very short empty ray segments that cannot be merged because they precede a non-empty segment. Remove these segments to reduce depth complexity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class RayEvent: def init(self, depth, eventtype, occclass): self.depth = depth self.eventtype = eventtype self.occclass = occclass def processevent(raysegmentlist, newevent): """ Incrementally updates the ray segment list with a new event, applying merging and deletion rules for events at the same depth. """ if not raysegmentlist: raysegmentlist.append(newevent) return lastevent = raysegmentlist[-1] # If depths differ, simply append if lastevent.depth != newevent.depth: raysegmentlist.append(newevent) return # Depths are equal, apply rules prevevent = raysegmentlist[-2] if len(raysegmentlist) > 2 else None # Rule 1: Merge same type if lastevent.eventtype == newevent.eventtype: # Overwrite lastevent with newevent raysegmentlist[-1] = newevent return # Rule 2: Exit followed by Entry (same class) if lastevent.eventtype == "EXIT" and newevent.eventtype == "ENTRY": # Check if previous event exists and has same class as new event if prevevent is not None and prevevent.occclass == newevent.occclass: # Delete both lastevent and newevent raysegmentlist.pop() # Remove lastevent # newevent is not added return else: # Cannot merge, append newevent raysegmentlist.append(newevent) return # Rule 3: Entry followed by Exit (grazing) if lastevent.eventtype == "ENTRY" and newevent.eventtype == "EXIT": # Delete both raysegmentlist.pop() # Remove lastevent # newevent is not added return # Fallback: Append if no rule matched raysegmentlist.append(newevent) def generateraysegmentlists(occupancygeometry, volumebbox): """ Main function to generate ray segment lists for all pixels. """ # Initialize ray segment lists for all pixels raysegmentlists = {} for pixel in allpixels: # Default segment: UNKNOWN class, spanning volume bbox frontdepth = volumebbox.frontfacedepth(pixel) backdepth = volumebbox.backfacedepth(pixel) evententry = RayEvent(depth=frontdepth, eventtype="ENTRY", occclass="UNKNOWN") eventexit = RayEvent(depth=backdepth, eventtype="EXIT", occclass="UNKNOWN") raysegmentlists[pixel] = [evententry, eventexit] # Rasterize occupancy geometry # Note: Exact rasterization loop details are not provided in the sources for fragment in rasterize(occupancygeometry): pixel = fragment.pixel raysegmentlist = raysegmentlists[pixel] # Determine event type from face flag if fragment.isfrontface: eventtype = "ENTRY" else: eventtype = "EXIT" # Determine occupancy class if eventtype == "ENTRY": occclass = fragment.boundingbox.occupancyclass else: # EXIT occclass = fragment.boundingbox.parent.occupancyclass newevent = RayEvent(depth=fragment.depth, eventtype=eventtype, occclass=occclass) # Process incrementally processevent(raysegmentlist, newevent) return raysegmentlists Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grazing Rays: Rays hitting box edges/corners generate Entry/Exit pairs at the same depth. These must be deleted to avoid spurious segments. Short Empty Segments: Empty segments preceding non-empty segments that are too short to merge must be explicitly detected and removed to reduce depth complexity. Parent Class for Exit: Correctly identifying the parent box's occupancy class for exit events is critical for the merging logic. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of fragments generated during rasterization, as each fragment triggers an incremental update to the ray segment list tail. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of ray events per pixel. Strengths: Enables sequential, non-hierarchical traversal of the occupancy histogram tree without a stack, simplifying the ray-casting stage. Limitations: Performance depends on the efficiency of the fragment shader and the resulting depth complexity of the lists. Ray Segment List Generation is part of the SparseLeap algorithm for efficient empty space skipping in large-scale volume rendering. It was introduced in the paper "SparseLeap: Efficient Empty Space Skipping for Large-Scale Volume Rendering" (2018). The method builds on the concept of lazy evaluation and occupancy histogram trees, where geometry is generated on-the-fly. name: Texture Box Approximation
head: Li and Kaufman Texture Box Approximation
body: Texture Box Approximation is a volume rendering method that approximates the object with a set of texture boxes to efficiently clip empty space from the rasterization. It differs from level-of-detail approaches by discarding empty regions spatially rather than reducing texture resolution. Inputs: Volume data structure containing leaf nodes and camera parameters. Outputs: Final image with empty space skipped during shading. Data Structures: Texture boxes are 3D axis-aligned bounding boxes that approximate the volume object. Each box stores minimum and maximum coordinates in world space. Steps: 1. Approximate the volume object with a set of texture boxes. 2. Rasterize the bounding geometry of these boxes to clip empty space from the rasterization. 3. Generate a coverage mask indicating which screen pixels fall within at least one projected texture box. 4. Shade only the covered pixels; skip shading for uncovered pixels. name: Min-Max Block Culling
head: Active block culling, Min-Max Bricks, Min-max blocks, Object-Order Empty Space Skipping (Min-Max Bricks)
body: Min-Max Block Culling is an object-order empty space skipping technique that reduces the number of volume samples by culling transparent or irrelevant regions before raycasting begins. It differs from its siblings by performing culling during the rasterization setup phase using precomputed block statistics, rather than during ray traversal or via bounding geometry rasterization. Unlike Early Shader Termination, which stops rays dynamically during compositing, this method prevents rays from entering empty blocks entirely. Unlike Rasterizing Bounding Geometry for Empty Space Skipping, it relies on scalar block bounds rather than polygonal approximations. Inputs: Volume dataset discretized into blocks (bricks) of fixed size. Transfer function or isovalue defining the rendering range. Camera parameters for ray generation. Outputs: A set of active blocks whose front and back faces are rasterized to initiate rays. Final composited image. Data Structures: Block Min-Max Values: For each block Bi, store two scalar values: mini and maxi. These represent the minimum and maximum scalar values contained within the block's voxel grid. Layout: A 1D array or 3D texture where each entry corresponds to a block, containing two floats (or fixed-point values). Size: One entry per block. Steps: 1. Precompute Block Statistics: Calculate mini and maxi for every block in the volume. 2. Cull Blocks: For each block Bi, check if its value range [mini, maxi] intersects the rendering range defined by the transfer function or isovalue. If the block is outside the range (e.g., maxi < \text{isovalue} or mini > \text{isovalue} for isosurface rendering), mark it as culled. If the block intersects the range, mark it as active. 3. Rasterize Active Blocks: For each active block, rasterize its front and back faces against the screen. This generates a coverage mask indicating which screen pixels have rays entering the block. Note: If the viewpoint is inside the volume, near clipping planes may be used to fill holes. 4. Ray Initialization: For each pixel covered by an active block's front face, initialize a ray starting at the intersection point with the front face. 5. Raycasting and Termination: Cast rays through the active blocks. Terminate the ray when full opacity is reached. Terminate the ray when the back face of the block is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeblockbounds(volume, blocksize): bounds = [] nx, ny, nz = len(volume[0][0]), len(volume[0]), len(volume) for z in range(0, nz, blocksize): for y in range(0, ny, blocksize): for x in range(0, nx, blocksize): minv, maxv = float('inf'), float('-inf') for dz in range(blocksize): for dy in range(blocksize): for dx in range(blocksize): if z+dz < nz and y+dy < ny and x+dx < nx: v = volume[z+dz][y+dy][x+dx] if v < minv: minv = v if v > maxv: maxv = v bounds.append((minv, maxv)) return bounds def cullblocks(bounds, isovalue): return [i for i, (minv, maxv) in enumerate(bounds) if minv <= isovalue <= maxv] def renderminmaxculling(volume, blocksize, isovalue, resx, resy): bounds = computeblockbounds(volume, blocksize) activeindices = cullblocks(bounds, isovalue) image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(resy)] # Rasterize active blocks to generate coverage mask coverage = [[False] resx for in range(resy)] for idx in activeindices: # Determine block screen bounds (simplified projection) bx = (idx % (len(volume[0][0]) // blocksize)) blocksize by = ((idx // (len(volume[0][0]) // blocksize)) % (len(volume[0]) // blocksize)) blocksize bz = (idx // ((len(volume[0][0]) // blocksize) (len(volume[0]) // blocksize))) blocksize # Project block to screen coordinates minpx, maxpx = int(bx / len(volume[0][0]) resx), int((bx + blocksize) / len(volume[0][0]) resx) minpy, maxpy = int(by / len(volume[0]) resy), int((by + blocksize) / len(volume[0]) resy) for py in range(minpy, maxpy): for px in range(minpx, maxpx): if 0 <= py < resy and 0 <= px < resx: coverage[py][px] = True for py in range(resy): for px in range(resx): if not coverage[py][px]: continue # Start ray at front face (z=0) currentz = 0.0 opacity = 0.0 step = 1.0 / resy # Terminate when back face (z=1.0) or full opacity reached while currentz < 1.0 and opacity < 1.0: vz = int(currentz len(volume)) if vz < len(volume): sample = volume[vz][int(py)][int(px)] alpha = 1.0 if sample == isovalue else 0.0 opacity += alpha (1.0 - opacity) currentz += step if opacity >= 1.0: image[py][px] = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] return image Parameters: Block Size: Not given in the sources. Isovalue/Transfer Function: Depends on the dataset. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Incomplete Skipping: This method does not skip all empty space, only the empty blocks culled during the rasterization setup phase. Viewpoint Inside Volume: If the camera is inside the volume, near clipping planes must be used to fill holes in the ray coverage. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for min-max values for each block, O(B). Strengths: Reduces sample count by skipping entire blocks that are transparent. Simple to implement as it relies on standard rasterization. Limitations: Does not skip all empty space; internal block emptiness is not exploited. When to Use: When the volume has large transparent regions that can be grouped into blocks. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in GPU-based volume raycasting research, specifically in the work of Markus Hadwiger and others at VRVIS Research Center, Vienna, Austria. The technique is described in the context of advanced illumination techniques for GPU-based volume raycasting. It builds on image-based ray setup and allows for viewpoint inside the volume. body: This method accelerates ray-based volume rendering by using the graphics hardware's depth buffer and alpha test to determine the entry and exit points of the volume along each pixel's ray, thereby skipping sampling in empty space. Unlike its parent method, which relies on a pre-computed or dynamically updated secondary data structure (like an octree) to query occupancy, this technique constructs the acceleration structure (Slab Silhouette Maps) on the fly during the rendering pass using standard OpenGL state. The method operates in three main phases: pre-processing (gradient calculation), acceleration structure generation (Slab Silhouette Maps), and ray casting with skipping. Input: A 3D volume dataset (scalar values), a transfer function mapping scalars to color and opacity, and a camera configuration (view and projection matrices). Output: A 2D image (framebuffer) with the composited volume. 1. Volume Data: Stored in CPU memory or GPU texture memory. 2. Gradient Volume: Pre-computed gradients for each voxel, stored in CPU memory or a GPU texture (typically RGB format for normal vectors). 3. Texture Slabs: The 3D volume is sliced into 2D textures. Slices are grouped into "slabs" to reduce the number of rendering passes. 4. Depth Buffer: Used to store the near and far intersection distances. It is initialized and queried in two separate passes. 5. Slab Silhouette Maps (SSM): Implicitly stored in the depth buffer. These maps identify empty spaces and terminated rays by storing the depth values of the first and last visible fragments of each slab. 1. Pre-compute Gradients and Illumination (CPU): Calculate the gradient for each volume element using central differences. Perform illumination and shading calculations based on the lighting model and store the results in main memory or a texture. This step is performed once on the CPU, unlike methods that compute lighting per-sample on the GPU. 2. Prepare Textures and Display Lists: For each axis (X, Y, Z), create 2D textures for planes parallel to that axis. Load these textures into GPU memory. Create display lists for front-to-back and back-to-front rendering orders. 3. Determine Rendering Axis: Determine the object axis with the smallest angle to the projection plane. Select the farthest texture from the camera in the corresponding set. Rotate the camera and draw the textures starting from the selected one. 4. Generate Slab Silhouette Maps (SSM) via Two Passes: The goal is to find the near (P) and far (Q) intersection points of the ray with the volume. Pass 1 (Find Near Point): Initialize the depth buffer to 1.0 (maximum value). Set depth write criterion to GLLESS. Enable the Alpha Test with GLGREATER and a reference value > 0 (e.g., 0.001) to discard fragments with zero opacity. Render the volume slabs from front to back. The depth buffer now contains the distances of the closest significant fragments to the projection plane for each pixel. Pass 2 (Find Far Point): Initialize the depth buffer to 0.0 (minimum value). Set depth write criterion to GLGREATER. Keep Alpha Test enabled (GLGREATER, ref > 0). Render the volume slabs from back to front. The depth buffer now contains the distances of the farthest significant fragments. 5. Coordinate Transformation: The depth buffer stores values in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC), range [0, 1]. Transform these NDC coordinates to world coordinates to get the ray origin P and ray end Q. For a pixel with screen coordinates (xs, ys, zs), the world coordinates (x, y, z, w) are calculated as: \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ w \end{bmatrix} = (P M)^{-1} V \begin{bmatrix} xs \\ ys \\ zs \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where P is the projection matrix, M is the model matrix, and V is the view matrix. The near point P{world} corresponds to the depth from Pass 1, and the far point Q{world} corresponds to the depth from Pass 2. 6. Ray Casting with Empty Space Skipping: For each pixel, cast a ray between P and Q. Sample the volume only within the interval [P, Q]. Use parametric equations for t \in [0, 1]: \begin{aligned} X(t) &= Px + (Qx - Px)t \\ Y(t) &= Py + (Qy - Py)t \\ Z(t) &= Pz + (Qz - Pz)t \end{aligned} The increment in t is determined by the number of samples n per ray (e.g., \Delta t = 1/n). Composite the samples using the standard volume rendering integral, but restricted to the active segment: L(x) = \int{xA'}^{xB'} \left[ e^{-\int{xA'}^{x00} \phit(x')dx'} \epsilon(x00) dx00 \right] where xA' and xB' are the near and far points, \phit is the extinction coefficient, and \epsilon is the color. Draw the final color to the framebuffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendervolumewithdepthalphaskip(volume, transferfunc, camera, nsamples): """ Renders a volume using Westermann & Sevenich's empty space skipping technique. volume: 3D array [D, H, W] of scalar values transferfunc: callable(scalar) -> (colorrgba, opacityrgba) camera: object with.projectionmatrix,.modelmatrix,.viewmatrix,.width,.height nsamples: int, number of samples per ray segment """ # 1. Pre-compute gradients and illumination on CPU gradients = computecentraldifferencegradients(volume) illuminated = applylightingmodel(volume, gradients, transferfunc) # 2. Prepare texture slabs and determine rendering order slabs = createtextureslabs(illuminated) axis = getaxiswithsmallestangletoprojectionplane(camera) slaborder = getsortedslabs(slabs, axis, camera) # 3. Pass 1: Find Near Points (SSM) neardepthbuffer = [1.0] (camera.height camera.width) for slab in slaborder: neardepthbuffer = applydepthtest(neardepthbuffer, slab, depthfunc='LESS', alphatest=True, alpharef=0.001) # 4. Pass 2: Find Far Points (SSM) fardepthbuffer = [0.0] (camera.height camera.width) for slab in reversed(slaborder): fardepthbuffer = applydepthtest(fardepthbuffer, slab, depthfunc='GREATER', alphatest=True, alpharef=0.001) # 5. Ray Casting with Empty Space Skipping invpm = inversematrix(camera.projectionmatrix camera.modelmatrix) viewmatrix = camera.viewmatrix image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(camera.height)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): znearndc = neardepthbuffer[y camera.width + x] zfarndc = fardepthbuffer[y camera.width + x] if znearndc >= 0.999 or zfarndc <= 0.001: continue ndcx = (2.0 x / camera.width) - 1.0 ndcy = (2.0 y / camera.height) - 1.0 nearworld = unprojectndctoworld(ndcx, ndcy, znearndc, invpm, viewmatrix) farworld = unprojectndctoworld(ndcx, ndcy, zfarndc, invpm, viewmatrix) color = compositeraysegment(nearworld, farworld, illuminated, nsamples, transferfunc) image[y][x] = color return image def computecentraldifferencegradients(volume): D, H, W = volume.shape grad = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(W)] for in range(H)] for d in range(D): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): dx = volume[d][h][min(w+1, W-1)] - volume[d][h][max(w-1, 0)] dy = volume[d][min(h+1, H-1)][w] - volume[d][max(h-1, 0)][w] dz = volume[min(d+1, D-1)][h][w] - volume[max(d-1, 0)][h][w] grad[d][h][w] = [dx, dy, dz] return grad def applylightingmodel(volume, gradients, transferfunc): D, H, W = volume.shape illuminated = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(W)] for in range(D)] for d in range(D): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): scalar = volume[d][h][w] rgba, alpha = transferfunc(scalar) normal = gradients[d][h][w] lightdir = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] dot = max(0.0, sum(nl for n,l in zip(normal, lightdir)) / (math.sqrt(sum(nn for n in normal)) + 1e-6)) color = [c (0.5 + 0.5 dot) for c in rgba] illuminated[d][h][w] = color + [alpha] return illuminated def createtextureslabs(illuminatedvolume): return [illuminatedvolume[d] for d in range(len(illuminatedvolume))] def getaxiswithsmallestangletoprojectionplane(camera): return 'Z' def getsortedslabs(slabs, axis, camera): return sorted(slabs, key=lambda s: 0.0) def applydepthtest(depthbuffer, slab, depthfunc, alphatest, alpharef): """Simulates GPU depth/alpha test per pixel.""" newbuffer = list(depthbuffer) for i in range(len(depthbuffer)): fragdepth = slab[i] if i < len(slab) else depthbuffer[i] fragalpha = 1.0 if alphatest and fragalpha <= alpharef: continue if depthfunc == 'LESS' and fragdepth < newbuffer[i]: newbuffer[i] = fragdepth elif depthfunc == 'GREATER' and fragdepth > newbuffer[i]: newbuffer[i] = fragdepth return newbuffer def unprojectndctoworld(ndcx, ndcy, ndcz, invpm, viewmatrix): clip = [ndcx, ndcy, ndcz, 1.0] view = matvecmul(invpm, clip) if view[3] == 0.0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] view = [v / view[3] for v in view] world = matvecmul(viewmatrix, view) return world def compositeraysegment(origin, end, illuminated, nsamples, transferfunc): alpha = 0.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] raydir = [end[i] - origin[i] for i in range(3)] raylen = math.sqrt(sum(dd for d in raydir)) step = raylen / nsamples for i in range(nsamples): t = (i + 0.5) / nsamples pos = [origin[i] + raydir[i] t for i in range(3)] scalar = samplevolume(pos, illuminated) rgba, alphasample = transferfunc(scalar) alpha += (1.0 - alpha) alphasample color = [color[i] + rgba[i] alphasample (1.0 - (alpha - alphasample)) for i in range(3)] if alpha >= 0.99: break return color def samplevolume(pos, illuminated): """Standard trilinear interpolation or texture fetch.""" return 0.0 def matvecmul(m, v): return [sum(m[i][j] v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(m))] def inversematrix(m): """Matrix inversion.""" return m Alpha Test Reference Value: > 0 (e.g., 0.001) to discard fully transparent fragments. Depth Buffer Initialization: 1.0 for near point pass, 0.0 for far point pass. Number of Samples (n): Determined by desired image quality and ray length. Typical values range from 50 to 200 per ray segment. Coordinate System Mismatch: The depth buffer uses NDC [0, 1], while ray casting requires local/world coordinates. A transformation is necessary. High Data Dispersion: If the volume has high dispersion (many small isolated structures), the technique only skips external empty space. The ray length with skipping may be similar to the naive ray length, reducing effectiveness. Precision: Floating-point precision in the depth buffer can affect the accuracy of the near/far points, especially for thin structures. Uses external polygonal meshes instead of alpha/depth tests to define sampling intervals. Uses camera-facing quads and depth tests to cull occluded primitives before ray marching. Time Complexity: The acceleration structure generation (SSM) is very small compared to total rendering time. The ray casting time is reduced to almost a quarter of a naive ray caster. Measured Performance: 3 to 4 times faster than naive ray casting when using alpha and depth tests. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume, gradients, and 2D texture slabs. No additional hierarchical data structure (like an octree) is needed on the CPU. Strengths: No CPU-side preprocessing required; leverages hardware z-occlusion culling; simple implementation using standard OpenGL features. Limitations: Lighting is pre-computed on the CPU, making dynamic lighting difficult. Effectiveness degrades with high data dispersion. Limited to skipping external empty space; internal holes are not skipped. The method was introduced by Westermann & Sevenich in [WS01]. It is a hybrid volume rendering technique that uses 2D textures and OpenGL alpha/depth tests to discard non-contributing intervals of the volume rendering integral. It differs from Engel, Kraus & Ertl's method by performing illumination calculation on the CPU in the initial phase, whereas Engel's method does it on the GPU. name: Polygon Assisted Ray Casting
head: Empty Space Skipping via Volumetric Clipping, Empty space skipping via the volumetric clipping, Hybrid Space Leaping with Graphics Hardware, PARC, Volumetric clipping
body: Polygon Assisted Ray Casting (PARC) is an acceleration technique for volumetric ray tracing that uses graphics hardware to determine the start and end points of ray segments intersecting the volume, thereby skipping empty space. Unlike its parent method, which relies on the volume's own alpha and depth tests, PARC approximates the volume with an external polygonal mesh to define valid sampling intervals. This approach typically reduces the computation of primary rays by a factor of four. Inputs and Outputs Input: A volumetric dataset, a polygonal mesh that completely encloses all non-transparent or relevant regions of the volume, camera position and orientation, and light source positions for shadow rays. Output: A rendered image where ray sampling is restricted to segments defined by the mesh intersections. Data Structures Bounding Mesh: A polyhedral representation of the volume that must completely contain the actual volumetric objects. It may be non-convex. Distance Buffers: Two OpenGL frame buffers storing distances from the viewpoint to the mesh front and back faces. Closest-Distance Buffer: Stores the nearest intersection distance for each pixel. Farthest-Distance Buffer: Stores the farthest intersection distance for each pixel. Layout: These buffers store up to 4 ray path segments per pixel, allowing the representation of non-convex meshes with multiple entry and exit points. Steps 1. Mesh Creation: Create a polygonal representation that completely contains or encloses all important regions in the volume. 2. Buffer Initialization: Prepare two distance buffers to store the closest and farthest distances. 3. Projection (Closest and Farthest): Render the bounding mesh into the closest-distance buffer using a standard "less than" depth test, and into the farthest-distance buffer using a "greater than" depth test. 4. Shader Execution: During rendering, a specific shader program calculates the distance between the observer and the fragment position on the mesh surface for each pixel. 5. Ray Casting: For each pixel, retrieve the stored distances from the buffers. If no Z-buffer information exists for a pixel, skip intersection calculations for that ray. Use the stored distances to clip the rays, defining the segments of the ray path to be traversed. Perform volumetric ray casting only within these clipped segments. 6. Secondary Rays: For shadow rays from point and directional lights, repeat the projection steps from each light location or direction to determine occlusion. Use uniform space subdivision and bounding boxes to optimize secondary rays. 7. Refinement: The initial PARC image can be refined by continuing to follow PARC rays intersecting data according to a full volumetric ray tracing algorithm to generate shadows, reflections, and transparency. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def polygonassistedraycasting(volume, mesh, camera, lightsources): # Initialize distance buffers: 2D array of lists, max 4 segments per pixel closestbuffer = [[[] for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] farthestbuffer = [[[] for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] # Project mesh to fill buffers using depth tests for face in mesh.faces: for pixel in projectfacetoscreen(face, camera): dist = distance(camera.origin, pixel.position) addtobuffer(closestbuffer, pixel.x, pixel.y, dist, min) addtobuffer(farthestbuffer, pixel.x, pixel.y, dist, max) # Ray Casting image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(camera.height camera.width)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): distsclose = closestbuffer[y][x] distsfar = farthestbuffer[y][x] if not distsclose or not distsfar: continue rayorigin = camera.origin raydirection = normalize(pixel.position - camera.origin) segments = clipraysegments(rayorigin, raydirection, distsclose, distsfar) for seg in segments: # Source does not specify the volumetric ray casting algorithm itself color = volumetricraycastsegment(volume, rayorigin, seg.start, seg.end, raydirection) image[y camera.width + x] = color # Secondary Rays (Shadows) for light in lightsources: shadowclose = [[[] for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] shadowfar = [[[] for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] for face in mesh.faces: for pixel in projectfacetoscreen(face, light): dist = distance(light.origin, pixel.position) addtobuffer(shadowclose, pixel.x, pixel.y, dist, min) addtobuffer(shadowfar, pixel.x, pixel.y, dist, max) # Use shadow buffers to determine occlusion for secondary rays pass return image def addtobuffer(buffer, x, y, dist, op): if len(buffer[y][x]) >= 4: return if op == min: if not buffer[y][x] or dist < min(buffer[y][x]): buffer[y][x].append(dist) elif op == max: if not buffer[y][x] or dist > max(buffer[y][x]): buffer[y][x].append(dist) Parameters Mesh Resolution: Not given in the sources. Must be coarse enough for fast rendering but fine enough to bound the volume accurately. Segments per Pixel: Up to 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Mesh Containment: The polygonal model must completely contain the actual volumetric objects; otherwise, rays may sample empty space or miss data. Non-Convexity: Standard Z-buffering only captures one segment. To handle non-convex meshes, the implementation must support multiple segments per pixel (up to 4). Performance: PARC typically reduces the computation of primary rays by a factor of four. Hardware Dependency: Requires graphics hardware capable of Z-buffering and texture rendering (OpenGL). Memory: Requires additional memory for the distance buffers (two buffers per view/light). Strengths: Significant speedup for primary rays; allows interactive manipulation of the bounding mesh. Limitations: Requires maintaining a separate polygonal representation; less effective if the volume is sparse or the mesh is complex. When to Use: When primary ray computation is the bottleneck and a suitable bounding mesh can be created. When Not to Use: When the volume is dense or the bounding mesh is too complex to render efficiently. Origin: Introduced by Sobierajski in 1995. History: Part of the VolVis volume visualization system, which uses a multi-algorithm progressive refinement approach. Usage: Used in VolVis after user interaction with a polyhedral representation to produce a ray-cast image.
