name: Distance Map Computation (Multi-Stage)
head: Compute Distance Map, Distance Field Compute, Multi-Stage Distance Map Computation, Occupancy Distance Map
body: Distance Map Computation (Multi-Stage) is a GPU compute shader dispatch routine that generates a distance map from an occupancy map, using a swap buffer for iterative or multi-pass distance calculation. It enables ray marching to skip empty regions by providing distances to the nearest occupied blocks, reducing the number of density samples and transfer function evaluations. Unlike sibling methods that may generate mipmaps or recompute bricks independently, this method computes a global distance field across the occupancy grid using a structured multi-stage reduction approach. Inputs and Outputs: Input: textureOccupancyMap, a 3D texture containing binary occupancy data (1 if occupied, 0 if empty). Output: textureDistanceMap, a 3D texture storing the distance to the nearest occupied voxel/block for each location. Auxiliary: textureSwap, a temporary buffer used for intermediate stages of the distance computation. Data Structures: textureOccupancyMap: Bound to image unit 1. Format: GLR8UI (8-bit unsigned integer, single channel). Access: GLREADWRITE. textureDistanceMap: Bound to image unit 0. Format: GLR8UI. Access: GLREADWRITE. textureSwap: Bound to image unit 1 during stages 2 and 3. Format: GLR8UI. Access: GLREADWRITE. Uniform Buffer Object (UBO): Bound to binding point 0. Size: 4 bytes. Contains a single uint value representing the current computation stage (0, 1, or 2). Parameters: sizeOccupancyMap: The dimensions (width, height, depth) of the occupancy map. blockSize: The workgroup size is fixed at 8x8x1 for the dispatch dimensions calculation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Bind textureDistanceMap to image unit 0 and textureOccupancyMap to image unit 1. Create and bind a 4-byte UBO to binding point 0. 2. Work Group Calculation: Calculate the number of work groups required for the 3D grid. The dimensions are derived by dividing sizeOccupancyMap by 8, using ceiling division. Let Nx, Ny, Nz be the dimensions of the occupancy map. The number of work groups is: \text{numWorkGroups}x = \lceil Nx / 8 \rceil, \quad \text{numWorkGroups}y = \lceil Ny / 8 \rceil, \quad \text{numWorkGroups}z = \lceil Nz / 8 \rceil 3. Stage 1 (X-Axis Reduction): Set the UBO stage value to 0. Dispatch compute shader with dimensions (numWorkGroupsx, numWorkGroupsy, 1). Issue a memory barrier to ensure completion. 4. Stage 2 (Y-Axis Reduction): Bind textureSwap to image unit 1. Set the UBO stage value to 1. Dispatch compute shader with dimensions (numWorkGroupsx, numWorkGroupsz, 1). Issue a memory barrier. 5. Stage 3 (Z-Axis Reduction): Set the UBO stage value to 2. Dispatch compute shader with dimensions (numWorkGroupsx, numWorkGroupsy, 1). Issue a memory barrier. 6. Cleanup: Unbind the UBO and delete the buffer object. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedistancemapmultistage(occupancymap, sizeoccupancymap): """ Simulates the multi-stage GPU compute dispatch for distance map generation. Note: This pseudocode describes the host-side dispatch logic. The actual distance calculation logic within the compute shader is not fully detailed in the source. """ # 1. Setup Textures and Buffers texturedistancemap = createtexture3d(sizeoccupancymap, format="GLR8UI", access="GLREADWRITE") textureoccupancymap = occupancymap # Already created textureswap = createtexture3d(sizeoccupancymap, format="GLR8UI", access="GLREADWRITE") ubo = createuniformbuffer(size=4) # 4 bytes for stage index # 2. Calculate Work Groups # Ceiling division: ceil(a / b) = (a + b - 1) // b numworkgroupsx = (sizeoccupancymap[0] + 7) // 8 numworkgroupsy = (sizeoccupancymap[1] + 7) // 8 numworkgroupsz = (sizeoccupancymap[2] + 7) // 8 # 3. Stage 1: X-Axis (and Y-slice processing) bindimageunit(0, texturedistancemap) bindimageunit(1, textureoccupancymap) bindubo(0, ubo) setubovalue(ubo, 0) # Stage 0 dispatchcompute(numworkgroupsx, numworkgroupsy, 1) memorybarrier() # 4. Stage 2: Y-Axis (using Swap buffer) bindimageunit(0, texturedistancemap) # Output remains distance map bindimageunit(1, textureswap) # Input from swap setubovalue(ubo, 1) # Stage 1 dispatchcompute(numworkgroupsx, numworkgroupsz, 1) memorybarrier() # 5. Stage 3: Z-Axis (final reduction) bindimageunit(0, texturedistancemap) bindimageunit(1, textureswap) # Input from swap setubovalue(ubo, 2) # Stage 2 dispatchcompute(numworkgroupsx, numworkgroupsy, 1) memorybarrier() # 6. Cleanup unbindubo(0) deletebuffer(ubo) return texturedistancemap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The distance map uses GLR8UI, limiting distances to 0-255. If the occupancy map dimensions exceed 255 units, distances will saturate. Boundaries: The source does not specify boundary handling (e.g., clamping, wrapping) for the distance calculation within the compute shader. Synchronization: Memory barriers are critical between stages to ensure the output of one stage is visible as input to the next. Empty Space Map Generation is a preprocessing technique that creates a boolean map indicating which voxels in a scalar field contain no visible geometry, allowing ray marching to skip empty regions. It reduces the number of density samples and transfer function evaluations by jumping over contiguous blocks of empty space. Unlike Distance Map Computation (Multi-Stage), which computes distances to occupied blocks, this method uses a binary occupancy check based on a transfer function threshold. Distance Field Precomputation calculates distance fields for scalar fields defining fiber surfaces to enable fast intersection detection via the rule of signs. It builds on Distance Map Computation (Multi-Stage). Unlike Empty Space Map Generation which tracks occupancy, or Distance Transformation (Proximity Clouds) which uses proximity clouds, this method targets geometric boundaries of fiber surfaces for ray-tracing acceleration. Distance Transformation, also known as Proximity Clouds, accelerates ray traversal in regular grids filled with empty zones by pre-calculating distance information to the nearest full element in the grid. It differs from hierarchical structures by storing distance data in a flat 3D volume aligned with the original voxel indices, allowing for O(1) lookup during traversal without tree navigation overhead. AADF Exit Plane Calculation calculates the exit plane of an empty region defined by an Axis-Aligned Distance Field (AADF). The AADF stores distances to the nearest occupied voxel in each of the 6 directions. Steps: 1. Determine the shift for each axis based on the ray direction. If raydir.x < 0, use shift 0 (-X), else use shift 5 (+X). Similarly for Y (10/15) and Z (20/25). 2. Extract the bounds (distances) for each axis from the packed uint. Each distance is 5 bits. 3. Calculate the lower and upper bounds of the empty region in voxel coordinates. The lower bound is coord - bounds, clamped to 0. The upper bound is coord + 1 + bounds, clamped to gridext. 4. Return the exit plane coordinate. For each axis, if raydir is negative, return the lower bound, else return the upper bound. Parameters: cellext: The size of the cell in voxel units. For chunks, this is VXBRICKEXT VXCHUNKEXT. For bricks, VXBRICKEXT. For voxels, 1. Time Complexity: The multi-stage approach suggests a reduction complexity proportional to the number of dimensions (3 stages) plus the grid size, O(N) where N is the number of voxels, assuming constant-time distance updates per voxel per stage. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the occupancy map, distance map, and a swap buffer, totaling 3 \times N bytes (assuming 8-bit unsigned integers). Performance: The method is designed for GPU acceleration using compute shaders, leveraging parallel processing for distance calculation. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space during ray marching, reducing sample count and transfer function evaluations. Limitations: Limited to distances representable in 8-bit unsigned integers (0-255). Requires multiple dispatches and memory barriers, introducing overhead. Distance Map Computation (Multi-Stage) is part of the DVRESSPDM project, an unofficial implementation of volume rendering techniques. It is used in conjunction with other occupancy map generation techniques to accelerate ray traversal in volume rendering. The method is implemented using OpenGL compute shaders. name: Empty Space Map Generation
head: Empty Space Skipping Map, Ray Marching with Empty Space Map, Visibility Map Generation
body: Empty Space Map Generation is a preprocessing technique that creates a boolean map indicating which voxels in a scalar field contain no visible geometry, allowing ray marching to skip empty regions. It reduces the number of density samples and transfer function evaluations by jumping over contiguous blocks of empty space. Unlike Distance Map Computation (Multi-Stage), which computes distances to occupied blocks, this method uses a binary occupancy check based on a transfer function threshold. Inputs: Scalar field data: A 3D array of density values with dimensions W \times H \times D. Transfer function: A function TF(v) that maps a scalar value v to a density or opacity value. Threshold: A tolerance value T. If any vertex of a voxel has a transfer function density > T, the voxel is considered non-empty. Outputs: Empty Space Map: A boolean array of size (W-1) \times (H-1) \times (D-1), where each element indicates if the corresponding voxel is empty. Data Structures: emptyspacemap: A flat boolean array indexed by a field offset function field->Offset(i, j, k). Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Map Generation): 1. Loop over all voxel indices (i, j, k) from 0 to \text{dims}[\text{axis}]-2 for each dimension. 2. For each voxel, evaluate the transfer function at its 8 vertices. 3. Compute the vertex index as v = vi + vj \times 2 + vk \times 4, where vi, vj, vk \in \{0, 1\}. 4. Retrieve the scalar value at (i + vi, j + vj, k + vk) and evaluate its density d = TF(\text{scalar}). 5. Mark the voxel as empty if all 8 vertices have d \le T; otherwise mark it as non-empty. 6. Store the result: emptyspacemap[field->Offset(i, j, k)] = isempty. 2. Ray Marching (Skipping): 1. Compute the current 3D voxel indices (vi, vj, vk) from the current ray position p. 2. Check if the current voxel is marked as empty in emptyspacemap using the computed indices and field offset. 3. If the voxel is empty: a. Compute the voxel minimum V{\min} and maximum V{\max} points in world space. b. Compute the intersection interval [t{\text{enter}}, t{\text{exit}}] of the ray with the voxel bounding box. c. Advance the ray parameter t by the maximum of (t{\text{exit}} - t) and marchingdelta to skip the empty voxel. d. Update the ray position p = O + t \cdot D and recompute voxel indices. e. Repeat the check for the new voxel. 4. If the voxel is not empty, proceed with standard ray marching sampling within the voxel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generateemptyspacemap(field, transferfunction, threshold, width, height, depth): """Generates a boolean map indicating empty voxels based on a transfer function threshold.""" w, h, d = width - 1, height - 1, depth - 1 emptyspacemap = [False] (w h d) for i in range(w): for j in range(h): for k in range(d): isempty = True # Check all 8 vertices of the voxel (i, j, k) for vi in range(2): for vj in range(2): for vk in range(2): # Global coordinates of the vertex x, y, z = i + vi, j + vj, k + vk # Evaluate transfer function density density = transferfunction(field[x][y][z]) # If any vertex exceeds threshold, voxel is not empty if density > threshold: isempty = False break if not isempty: break if not isempty: break # Store using a flat offset (equivalent to field->Offset(i, j, k)) # Implementation of field->Offset depends on memory layout; row-major assumed here. emptyspacemap[i + j w + k w h] = isempty return emptyspacemap def raymarchskip(rayorigin, raydirection, emptyspacemap, voxelorigin, voxelsize, marchingdelta, mapw, maph, mapd): """Advances a ray through empty space using the precomputed map.""" t = 0.0 # Convert ray origin to voxel coordinates vi = math.floor((rayorigin[0] - voxelorigin[0]) / voxelsize) vj = math.floor((rayorigin[1] - voxelorigin[1]) / voxelsize) vk = math.floor((rayorigin[2] - voxelorigin[2]) / voxelsize) while True: # Clamp indices to map bounds vi = max(0, min(vi, mapw - 1)) vj = max(0, min(vj, maph - 1)) vk = max(0, min(vk, mapd - 1)) if emptyspacemap[vi + vj mapw + vk mapw maph]: # Compute voxel bounds in world space vmin = [voxelorigin[0] + vi voxelsize, voxelorigin[1] + vj voxelsize, voxelorigin[2] + vk voxelsize] vmax = [voxelorigin[0] + (vi + 1) voxelsize, voxelorigin[1] + (vj + 1) voxelsize, voxelorigin[2] + (vk + 1) voxelsize] # Compute intersection interval [tenter, texit] of ray with voxel bounding box tenter = -math.inf texit = math.inf for axis in range(3): if raydirection[axis] == 0: if rayorigin[axis] < vmin[axis] or rayorigin[axis] > vmax[axis]: return rayorigin + [raydirection[0]t, raydirection[1]t, raydirection[2]t] else: t1 = (vmin[axis] - rayorigin[axis]) / raydirection[axis] t2 = (vmax[axis] - rayorigin[axis]) / raydirection[axis] tenter = max(tenter, min(t1, t2)) texit = min(texit, max(t1, t2)) if tenter > texit: return rayorigin + [raydirection[0]t, raydirection[1]t, raydirection[2]t] # Advance t: max(texit - t, marchingdelta) to ensure progress (matches FMax clamping) t = t + max(texit - t, marchingdelta) # Update ray position and recompute voxel indices raypos = [rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0]t, rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1]t, rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2]t] vi = math.floor((raypos[0] - voxelorigin[0]) / voxelsize) vj = math.floor((raypos[1] - voxelorigin[1]) / voxelsize) vk = math.floor((raypos[2] - voxelorigin[2]) / voxelsize) else: break return raypos Parameters: threshold: The density threshold for the transfer function. Typical values depend on the specific transfer function and data normalization. Not given in the sources. marchingdelta: The minimum step size to ensure progress. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision problems may occur when computing voxel intersections; the travel value is clamped using FMax to ensure progress. The map size is (W-1) \times (H-1) \times (D-1), so the scalar field must have at least 2 voxels in each dimension. Uses a pre-computed Chebyshev distance map to skip multiple empty voxels in any dimension along a ray. It replaces the binary occupancy check with a metric that quantifies the distance to the nearest occupied block, allowing the ray to jump directly to the next potential intersection. Unlike the occupancy map method, which resumes sampling after a fixed number of empty voxels, this method dynamically calculates the skip distance based on local geometry. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method reduces the number of density samples and transfer function evaluations. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective for volumes with large empty regions. Limitations: Binary check may skip over thin structures if the threshold is not carefully chosen. Precision issues can occur at voxel boundaries. This method is implemented in the SRaimondi/VolumeRender repository as a preprocessing step to accelerate ray marching in volume rendering. name: Chebyshev Distance Map Empty Space Skipping
head: Chebychev distance maps for empty-space skipping, Isotropic Chebyshev distance map
body: Chebyshev distance map empty space skipping is a ray-traversal acceleration technique that uses a pre-computed distance map to skip multiple empty voxels in any dimension along a ray. It builds on Empty Space Map Generation by replacing the binary occupancy check with a metric that quantifies the distance to the nearest occupied block, allowing the ray to jump directly to the next potential intersection. Unlike the occupancy map method, which resumes sampling after a fixed number of empty voxels, this method dynamically calculates the skip distance based on the local geometry, achieving an average speed-up of 5.3 times the baseline frame rate. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An occupancy map (boolean grid indicating visible geometry based on a transfer function threshold). Output: A Chebyshev distance map texture where each voxel stores the Chebyshev distance to the nearest occupied block. Data Structures: Distance Map Texture: A 3D image texture with an unsigned 8-bit integer channel (r8ui). Layout: 3D grid of uint8 values. Constraint: Distances are limited to a maximum of 255 due to the 8-bit storage. Occupancy Map Integration: The distance map can overwrite the occupancy map texture to save memory, but a separate "swap image" of identical dimensions is required during generation. Algorithm: Distance Map Generation The transformation from an occupancy map to a Chebyshev distance map is decomposed into three 1D passes that are trivially parallelized on a GPU. The passes operate on rows (x-axis), columns (y-axis), and slices (z-axis) independently. 1. First Transformation (X-axis): For each column and slice, perform a forward pass and a backward pass along the x-dimension. Forward Pass: Initialize D1 from the occupancy map at x=0. Iterate x from 1 to dim.x-1. Update D = \min(D1 + 1, \text{occ}(x)). Store D in the distance map. Update D1 = D. Backward Pass: Iterate x from dim.x-2 down to 0. Update D = \min(D1 + 1, \text{dist}(x)). Store D in the distance map. Update D1 = D. Note: This pass can read from and write to the same texture if it is the occupancy map. 2. Second Transformation (Y-axis): For each row and slice, perform a single-pass zig-zag search along the y-dimension. Read the current distance D from the output of the first transformation. Iterate n from 1 to D-1. If y \ge n, read Dn = \text{dist}(x, y-n, z). Update D = \min(D, \max(n, Dn)). If y+n < dim.y and n < D, read Dn = \text{dist}(x, y+n, z). Update D = \min(D, \max(n, Dn)). Store the final D in the swap image. 3. Third Transformation (Z-axis): For each row and column, perform a single-pass zig-zag search along the z-dimension. Read from the swap image (output of the second transformation). Perform the same zig-zag logic as the second transformation but on the z-axis. Store the final Chebyshev distance in the distance map. Pseudocode for Generation (Python-like): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def firsttransformation(dist, occ, dim): # Invoked for all columns (y) and slices (z) for y in range(dim[1]): for z in range(dim[2]): pos = (0, y, z) D1 = occ[pos] # Forward pass for x in range(1, dim[0]): currentpos = (x, y, z) D = min(D1 + 1, occ[currentpos]) dist[currentpos] = D D1 = D # Backward pass for x in range(dim[0] - 2, -1, -1): currentpos = (x, y, z) D = min(D1 + 1, dist[currentpos]) dist[currentpos] = D D1 = D def secondtransformation(dist, swap, dim): # Invoked for all rows (x) and slices (z) for x in range(dim[0]): for z in range(dim[2]): pos = (x, 0, z) D = dist[pos] # Zig-zag search along y-axis for n in range(1, D): if pos[1] >= n: Dn = dist[(pos[0], pos[1] - n, pos[2])] D = min(D, max(n, Dn)) if (pos[1] + n) < dim[1] and n < D: Dn = dist[(pos[0], pos[1] + n, pos[2])] D = min(D, max(n, Dn)) swap[pos] = D def thirdtransformation(swap, dist, dim): # Invoked for all rows (x) and columns (y) for x in range(dim[0]): for y in range(dim[1]): pos = (x, y, 0) D = swap[pos] # Zig-zag search along z-axis for n in range(1, D): if pos[2] >= n: Dn = swap[(pos[0], pos[1], pos[2] - n)] D = min(D, max(n, Dn)) if (pos[2] + n) < dim[2] and n < D: Dn = swap[(pos[0], pos[1], pos[2] + n)] D = min(D, max(n, Dn)) dist[pos] = D Ray Traversal Step Calculation: During rendering, the distance D is sampled from the distance map at the current ray position. The number of steps to the next sampling point is calculated to skip D blocks. Chebyshev Distance Definition: D{\text{Chebyshev}}(\mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2) = \max(|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}2|) where \mathbf{p}1 and \mathbf{p}2 are two points. Step Calculation: The number of steps \Delta{ij} to the next sampling point D blocks away on dimension j \in \{x, y, z\} is: \Delta{ij} = \begin{cases} \lceil (D + \lfloor \mathbf{u}j \rfloor - \mathbf{u}j) / \Delta \mathbf{u}j \rceil, & \text{if } \Delta \mathbf{u}j > 0 \\ \lceil (1 - D + \lfloor \mathbf{u}j \rfloor - \mathbf{u}j) / \Delta \mathbf{u}j \rceil, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \mathbf{u} is the current ray position in block coordinates, and \Delta \mathbf{u} is the ray direction in block coordinates. Vectorized Form: \Delta \mathbf{i} = \lceil (\text{step}(-\Delta \mathbf{u}) + \text{sgn}(\Delta \mathbf{u}) \cdot D + \lfloor \mathbf{u} \rfloor - \mathbf{u}) / \Delta \mathbf{u} \rceil This vectorized equation allows skipping multiple blocks with a single sample of the distance map. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Overhead: The generation process requires a swap image, doubling the memory requirements compared to using only an occupancy map. Distance Limit: The use of 8-bit integers limits the maximum skip distance to 255 blocks. Transfer Function Dependency: Since the distance maps are transfer-function dependent, they need to be updated on transfer-function changes. Initial Skip Size: When exiting an occupied region, the initial skip distance D is small. This can be suboptimal if the next occupied region is far away. A variant that uses separate distance maps for each of the 8 directional octants (defined by the sign of the x, y, and z components) to optimize skipping when exiting occupied regions. It is generated by modifying the isotropic transformations to scan in single directions only, requiring a total of 24 transformations (2 for the first pass, 4 for the second, reusing intermediate maps). During traversal, the octant index is computed once based on the fixed ray direction, and the corresponding anisotropic distance map is indexed. Compared to the Extended Anisotropic Chebyshev Distance (Es and Işler [8]), which requires 24x the memory of the isotropic map, this isotropic approach uses significantly less memory while providing sufficient performance gains. Time Complexity: The generation of the distance map involves three 1D passes. The first pass is O(N) where N is the number of voxels. The second and third passes involve a zig-zag search that depends on the current distance value, potentially making them slower than a simple linear pass, but still parallelizable. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the distance map (1 byte per voxel) and a swap image (1 byte per voxel) during generation. Total 2 bytes per voxel for the acceleration structure. Performance: Achieves an average speed-up of 5.3 times the baseline frame rate. Strengths: Allows skipping multiple blocks in any dimension, not constrained by the block size B as in the occupancy map method. Efficiently parallelized on GPU. Limitations: Memory overhead due to the swap image. Limited to 255 block skips due to 8-bit storage. Requires regeneration on transfer function changes. When to Use: When the volume has large empty regions and the transfer function is static or changes infrequently. When memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and the 255-block skip limit is sufficient. When Not to Use: When the transfer function changes frequently, as the regeneration cost may outweigh the rendering benefits. When memory is extremely constrained and the 2x overhead is unacceptable. The technique was introduced by Deakin and Knackstedt. It builds on the work of Saito and Toriwaki [12] for transforming occupancy maps to distance maps, adapted for Chebyshev distance and GPU parallelization. The method was developed to address the limitations of the original occupancy map approach, which resumed sampling after a fixed length of empty voxels, by allowing dynamic skip distances. Deakin and Knackstedt [DK20] further improved the approach by resuming empty-space skipping after a single empty voxel instead of a fixed set length. name: Distance Field Precomputation
head: Distance Field Computation, Precomputed Distance Field Generation
body: Distance Field Precomputation calculates distance fields for scalar fields defining fiber surfaces to enable fast intersection detection via the rule of signs. It builds on Distance Map Computation (Multi-Stage). Unlike Empty Space Map Generation which tracks occupancy, or Distance Transformation (Proximity Clouds) which uses proximity clouds, this method targets geometric boundaries of fiber surfaces for ray-tracing acceleration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar fields defining fiber surfaces (e.g., FSCP). Output: A precomputed 2D distance field array. Data Structures: Distance Field Array: A 2D grid of size 64 \times 64. Steps: 1. Identify the relevant scalar fields defining the fiber surfaces. 2. Compute the distance field for these fields. The computation time is fixed and depends only on the distance field dimensions. 3. Store the result in the 64 \times 64 array for use during ray traversal. Parameters: Distance field array size: 64 \times 64. Typical performance: 1–2 milliseconds for 4 FSCP with 4 segments per polygon. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precomputation time scales linearly with the total number of voxels, but the distance field update itself is fixed time. Smoother data and FSCPs with more empty space allow coarser macrocells, but the distance field size remains fixed at 64 \times 64 for accuracy. Computes the distance field by solving the Eikonal equation to determine the arrival time of a front expanding in the normal direction from a given boundary condition. It respects causality by expanding outwards where the speed function F > 0, ensuring the solution at any grid point depends only on points with earlier arrival times. Time Complexity: Distance field updating time is fixed and depends only on the distance field dimensions. Total precomputation time (including macrocell updates) depends linearly on the total number of voxels. Performance: For 4 FSCP with 4 segments, computation takes 1–2 milliseconds. It is not a bottleneck. Memory: Requires storage for the 64 \times 64 distance field array. Strengths: Facilitates fast intersection detection via the rule of signs. Preserves interactivity when exploring larger datasets with coarser macrocells. Limitations: The source does not specify memory complexity beyond the array size. name: Fast Marching Method
head: Fast Marching SDF
body: The Fast Marching Method (FMM) is a computationally efficient numerical scheme for computing the propagation of an active contour, implicitly handling topological changes. It solves the Eikonal equation to determine the arrival time of a front expanding in the normal direction from a given boundary condition. Unlike standard region growing, FMM respects causality by always expanding outwards where the speed function F > 0, ensuring that the solution at any grid point depends only on points with earlier arrival times. Inputs: A 3D grid of voxels, a strictly positive speed function F(\mathbf{x}) > 0, and a set of boundary voxels defining the initial front. Outputs: An arrival time function T(\mathbf{x}) for all voxels in the grid. Data Structures: 1. Grid T: Stores the arrival time for each voxel, initialized to \infty for non-boundary voxels and to specified boundary values for seeds. 2. Heap H: A min-heap storing voxels in the "Narrow" band (candidates for update), ordered by their current T value. 3. Status Map: Tracks voxel states: Far (T=\infty), Narrow (T<\infty, in heap), and Accepted (T is final, removed from heap). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set T(\mathbf{x}) = \infty for all \mathbf{x}. Set T(\mathbf{x}) = T{init}(\mathbf{x}) for boundary voxels. Insert all boundary voxels into H and mark them as Narrow. 2. Main Loop: While H is not empty: a. Extract \mathbf{x}{min} with the smallest T value from H. b. Mark \mathbf{x}{min} as Accepted. c. For each neighbor \mathbf{x}n of \mathbf{x}{min}: i. If \mathbf{x}n is Accepted, skip. ii. Compute T{new}(\mathbf{x}n) by solving the discretized Eikonal equation using upwind differences from already Accepted neighbors. iii. If T{new}(\mathbf{x}n) < T(\mathbf{x}n), update T(\mathbf{x}n) = T{new}(\mathbf{x}n). If \mathbf{x}n is Far, mark it Narrow and insert into H; if Narrow, update its priority in H. Formula: The core equation is the Eikonal equation: \|\nabla T\| F = 1 where T(\mathbf{x}) is the arrival function and F > 0 is the speed function. In discrete form, the gradient \nabla T uses upwind differences. For a voxel \mathbf{x} with grid spacing h, the new arrival time is computed by taking the minimum over all combinations of upwind neighbors. For a single neighbor \mathbf{x}n along axis i: T(\mathbf{x}) = T(\mathbf{x}n) + \frac{h}{F(\mathbf{x})} When multiple neighbors contribute, the quadratic solution is used: T(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{T1 + T2 - \sqrt{2(h/F(\mathbf{x}))^2 - (T1 - T2)^2}}{2} where T1 and T2 are the smallest arrival times among the accepted neighbors. Parameters: F(\mathbf{x}): Speed function. Must be strictly positive to ensure outward expansion. Boundary conditions: Seeds defining the start of the front. Edge Cases: F=0: Causes division by zero. The speed function must be strictly positive. Disconnected components: FMM propagates from seeds. If the domain is not fully connected to seeds, some voxels remain \infty. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastmarchingmethod(gridshape, speedfunction, boundaryvoxels, h=1.0): import heapq T = [[float('inf')] gridshape[1] for in range(gridshape[0])] status = [[0] gridshape[1] for in range(gridshape[0])] # 0:Far, 1:Narrow, 2:Accepted heap = [] def getneighbors(v, shape): x, y = v for dxi, dyi in [(-1,0),(1,0),(0,-1),(0,1)]: nx, ny = x+dxi, y+dyi if 0 <= nx < shape[0] and 0 <= ny < shape[1]: yield (nx, ny) def computenewT(v, T, F, h): x, y = v acceptedT = [] for nx, ny in getneighbors(v, (len(T), len(T[0]))): if status[nx][ny] == 2: acceptedT.append(T[nx][ny]) if not acceptedT: return float('inf') acceptedT.sort() if len(acceptedT) == 1: return acceptedT[0] + h / F(x, y) else: # Standard 2D FMM quadratic solution T1, T2 = acceptedT[0], acceptedT[1] return (T1 + T2 - (2 (h / F(x, y))2 - (T1 - T2)2)0.5) / 2 for v in boundaryvoxels: T[v[0]][v[1]] = 0.0 status[v[0]][v[1]] = 1 heapq.heappush(heap, (0.0, v)) while heap: tmin, v = heapq.heappop(heap) if status[v[0]][v[1]] == 2: continue status[v[0]][v[1]] = 2 for n in getneighbors(v, gridshape): if status[n[0]][n[1]] == 2: continue newt = computenewT(n, T, speedfunction, h) if newt < T[n[0]][n[1]]: T[n[0]][n[1]] = newt if status[n[0]][n[1]] == 0: status[n[0]][n[1]] = 1 heapq.heappush(heap, (newt, n)) else: heapq.heappush(heap, (newt, n)) return T Uses FMM to precompute distance fields for empty space skipping. Distance Map Acceleration FMM can generate occupancy maps by thresholding the arrival time. Occupancy Map Generation Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles topological changes implicitly; computationally efficient when implemented using heap sort algorithms. Limitations: Requires a well-defined speed function F > 0; sensitive to boundary conditions. When to use: When computing distance fields or propagation times in a grid where the front expands monotonically. When not to use: When the speed function can be zero or negative; when non-causal propagation is required. The Fast Marching Method was proposed first by Tsitsiklis and then by Sethian. It is based on solving the Eikonal equation to compute the arrival time of a front expanding in the normal direction. It is advantageous because it implicitly handles topological changes and is computationally efficient when implemented using heap sort algorithms. It has been used for heart segmentation, where the pericardial cavity acts as a boundary restricting propagation. name: Distance Transformation (Proximity Clouds)
head: Proximity Clouds
body: Distance Transformation, also known as Proximity Clouds, accelerates ray traversal in regular grids filled with empty zones by pre-calculating distance information to the nearest full element in the grid. It differs from hierarchical structures by storing distance data in a flat 3D volume aligned with the original voxel indices, allowing for O(1) lookup during traversal without tree navigation overhead. Inputs and Outputs Input: A binary volume where cells are classified as transparent (empty) or opaque (full). Output: A distance volume (distance map) where each cell contains the distance to the nearest non-empty cell. Data Structures Distance Volume: A 3D grid with the same dimensions as the input binary volume, where each cell stores a scalar value representing the Euclidean distance between the center of the current cell and the center of the nearest non-empty cell. Algorithm Steps 1. Generate Input Binary Volume: Encode the scene geometry into a binary volume, marking cells as transparent or opaque. 2. Compute Distance Map: Calculate the distance from every cell to the nearest non-empty cell using exact metrics (City Block, Euclidean, Chessboard) or approximate methods like Chamfering. Chamfering uses a mask of local distances propagated through the volume, where larger masks yield higher accuracy but increase preprocessing time. 3. Ray Casting with Adaptive Traversal: For each ray, determine the current cell index using fixed-point arithmetic and integer division. Case A (Vicinity of Object): If the current sample is near an object, perform simple incremental ray traversal (step-by-step sampling). Case B (Empty Space): If the current sample is in empty space, use the distance value d stored in the current cell to skip the empty region. 4. Skip Calculation: Calculate the new sample location to jump to the edge of the empty zone using the formula \text{New Sample} = \text{Current Sample} + \text{Unit Ray Direction} \times (d - 1). The stepping distance is d-1 (not d) to avoid skipping beyond the free zone, because the distance is calculated from the center of the current cell. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computedistancemap(binaryvolume): """ Computes the distance map from a binary volume. binaryvolume: 3D list/array where 1 is opaque, 0 is transparent. Returns: 3D array of distances. """ # The sources do not specify the exact distance map generation algorithm. # A standard Chamfering mask pass or BFS would be used here. # Stub implementation for structural completeness. dims = (len(binaryvolume), len(binaryvolume[0]), len(binaryvolume[0][0])) return [[[0.0 for in range(dims[2])] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] def getcellindex(pos, rayorigin, voxelsize): """ Computes the grid cell index containing the given position. Uses floor division as described in the sources. """ return tuple(math.floor((pos[i] - rayorigin[i]) / voxelsize) for i in range(3)) def raycastproximityclouds(rayorigin, raydirection, distancevolume, voxelsize, maxdistance, nearobjectthreshold=1.5): """ Casts a ray using Proximity Clouds acceleration. """ t = 0.0 currentpos = [rayorigin[i] for i in range(3)] # Determine initial cell index currentcell = getcellindex(currentpos, rayorigin, voxelsize) while t < maxdistance: # Bounds check if not (0 <= currentcell[0] < len(distancevolume) and 0 <= currentcell[1] < len(distancevolume[0]) and 0 <= currentcell[2] < len(distancevolume[0][0])): break # Get distance to nearest object from the precomputed map d = distancevolume[currentcell[0]][currentcell[1]][currentcell[2]] # Check if we are in the vicinity of an object if d < nearobjectthreshold: # Simple incremental traversal stepsize = voxelsize currentpos = [currentpos[i] + raydirection[i] stepsize for i in range(3)] t += stepsize currentcell = getcellindex(currentpos, rayorigin, voxelsize) else: # Skip empty region # Formula: New sample = Current + direction (d - 1) skipdistance = max(d - 1.0, 1e-6) # Guard against zero/negative steps # Update position currentpos = [currentpos[i] + raydirection[i] skipdistance for i in range(3)] t += skipdistance # Update cell index currentcell = getcellindex(currentpos, rayorigin, voxelsize) # If we jumped past the object or out of bounds, break if not (0 <= currentcell[0] < len(distancevolume) and 0 <= currentcell[1] < len(distancevolume[0]) and 0 <= currentcell[2] < len(distancevolume[0][0])): break return currentpos, t Parameters Distance Metric: Choice between City Block, Euclidean, Chessboard, or Chamfering approximation, where the applied metric is a compromise between preprocessing and rendering times. Threshold: The value distinguishing "vicinity of an object" from "empty space" is not explicitly defined in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Stepping Distance: The stepping distance must be d-1, not d, to avoid skipping beyond the free zone because the distance is calculated from the center of the current cell. Dynamic Scenes: The method is too costly for dynamic scenes because the distance map must be recomputed for every frame. Preprocessing Time: Depends on the distance metric, where Chamfering is efficient but higher accuracy requires larger masks and longer preprocessing. Rendering Speed: Fast for scenes with large empty regions due to skipping, and the structure is considered optimal on GPUs for scenes with uniform data distribution. Memory: Requires storing an additional 3D volume for distances, in addition to the binary volume. Limitations: Not suitable for dynamic scenes due to high preprocessing cost, and avoids the additional computational cost required for traversing cells at different hierarchy levels found in other methods. Origin: Presented by Cohen and Sheffer in 1994. History: The technique was introduced to accelerate ray traversal in regular grids with empty zones, proving effective for static scenes. Usage: Applied in medical volume rendering and other domains where static scenes with significant empty space are common. name: Occupancy Mipmap Generation
body: Occupancy Mipmap Generation computes a hierarchical occupancy mipmap for a 3D grid using JAX convolutions. It builds on Occupancy Map Generation by extending a single-resolution occupancy mask into a multi-resolution pyramid. Inputs: mat: A 3D array representing the input grid, where non-zero values indicate occupied space. Dimensions are X \times Y \times Z. xdim: The width of the grid (X). Outputs: mipmap: A list of JAX arrays representing the occupancy hierarchy. Data Structures: occupancymat: A 3D binary mask of the same shape as mat, where occupancymat[i,j,k] = 1 if mat[i,j,k] > 0, else 0. data: A 4D JAX tensor with shape (1, X, Y, Z, 1) (batch size 1, channel size 1). kernel: A 5D tensor for convolution, shape (2^i, 2^i, 2^i, 1, 1). mipmap: A Python list of JAX arrays. Steps: 1. Calculate the number of hierarchical levels: L = \lfloor \log2(xdim) \rfloor. 2. Create the binary occupancy mask: occupancymat = (mat > 0).astype(float32). 3. Compute the total number of occupied points: nbofpts = sum(occupancymat). 4. Convert occupancymat to a JAX array and add batch and channel dimensions: data = occupancymat[None,:,:,:, None], resulting in shape (1, X, Y, Z, 1). 5. Initialize an empty list mipmap. 6. For each level i from 0 to L-1: a. Create a convolution kernel of ones with shape (2^i, 2^i, 2^i, 1, 1). b. Define the dimension numbers for lax.convgeneraldilated: input and output dimensions are 'NHWDC' (Batch, Height, Width, Depth, Channel), and kernel dimensions are 'HWDIO' (Kernel Height, Kernel Width, Kernel Depth, Input Channel, Output Channel). c. Apply lax.convgeneraldilated with strides (2^i, 2^i, 2^i) and 'SAME' padding. d. Remove the batch and channel dimensions from the convolution output. e. Append the resulting 3D array to mipmap. f. Update data to the stripped convolution output for the next iteration. 7. Append a final level to mipmap containing nbofpts as a single scalar tensor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp from jax.lax import convgeneraldilated, convdimensionnumbers def generateoccupancymipmap(mat): """ Generates a hierarchical occupancy mipmap from a 3D grid. Args: mat: numpy array, shape (X, Y, Z). Non-zero values indicate occupancy. Returns: mipmap: list of jax arrays. mipmap[i] is the occupancy map at level i. mipmap[-1] is a scalar tensor with the total count of occupied voxels. """ xdim = mat.shape[0] levels = jnp.log2(xdim).astype(int) occupancymat = (mat > 0).astype(jnp.float32) nbofpts = jnp.sum(occupancymat) data = jnp.array(occupancymat) data = data[None,:,:,:, None] # Shape: (1, X, Y, Z, 1) mipmap = [] for i in range(levels): kernelsize = 2i kernel = jnp.ones((kernelsize, kernelsize, kernelsize, 1, 1)) dn = convdimensionnumbers(data.shape, kernel.shape, ('NHWDC', 'HWDIO', 'NHWDC')) # Note: The provided source code snippet only constructs kernels and dimension numbers; # the convolution call and data update are omitted. convout = convgeneraldilated( data, kernel, windowstrides=(kernelsize, kernelsize, kernelsize), padding='SAME', dimensionnumbers=dn) convout = convout[0,:,:,:, 0] # Remove batch and channel dims mipmap.append(convout) data = convout[None,:,:,:, None] # Update for next level mipmap.append(jnp.array(nbofpts)) return mipmap Parameters: mat: Input 3D grid array. xdim: Grid width. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: xdim is truncated to an integer via.astype(int) if not a power of 2, which may truncate the expected level count. The convolution sums occupancy counts, so coarser levels contain values >1 indicating multiple occupied voxels map to a single coarse voxel. Periodically refreshes a 3D occupancy grid by querying a NeRF model for density at voxel centers. It solves stale spatial caching in on-the-fly NeRF training. It differs from this method by using direct density queries rather than convolutional mipmap generation. Generates an occupancy map by counting rays passing through voxels. It differs from this method by using explicit ray traversal statistics rather than JAX convolutions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of JAX-based volumetric rendering, specifically in the Jax-Volumetric-Renderer repository. It leverages JAX's automatic differentiation and convolution capabilities to build occupancy hierarchies for efficient ray marching. szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, https://github.com/szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Occupancy Grid Update
head: Density-Based Grid Update, Grid Density Thresholding, Occupancy Grid Update from Density
body: Occupancy Grid Update is a method to periodically refresh a 3D occupancy grid by querying a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) model for density at grid voxel centers and marking voxels as occupied if the density exceeds a specified threshold. It solves the problem of accelerating ray marching by skipping empty space during training and rendering. It sets itself apart from its sibling, Occupancy Map Generation via Ray Casting, by directly evaluating the neural network's output on a regular lattice rather than casting rays through the scene to infer occupancy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A trained NeRF model, the 3D grid resolution, the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) defining the scene bounds, and a density threshold. Outputs: A 3D boolean occupancy grid indicating which voxels are occupied. Data Structures: Grid: A 3D array of shape (resolution, resolution, resolution) containing boolean values (True/False or 1/0). AABB: Defined by aabbmin and aabbmax (3D vectors). Steps: 1. Generate Grid Coordinates: Create a 3D meshgrid of integer indices from 0 to resolution - 1 for x, y, and z dimensions. \text{grid\coords} = \text{meshgrid}(0, \dots, \text{res}-1, \text{indexing}='ij').\text{reshape}(-1, 3) 2. Convert to World Positions: Map the grid indices to world coordinates using the AABB: \text{positions} = \text{aabb\min} + \left( \frac{\text{grid\indices.float()} + 0.5}{\text{resolution}} \right) \times (\text{aabb\max} - \text{aabb\min}) 3. Query Densities: Pass the world positions to the NeRF model to retrieve volume density \sigma. If the model supports forwardwithdensityonly, use it. Otherwise, call the model with dummy view directions and extract the density component. 4. Update Grid: Compare the queried densities against the threshold: \text{occupied} = \sigma > \text{threshold} Reshape the result back to (resolution, resolution, resolution). Parameters: resolution: Integer, default 128. densitythreshold: Float, default 0.01. updategridevery: Integer, iteration interval for updates, default 500. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateoccupancygrid(model, aabbmin, aabbmax, resolution, threshold, updateevery, step): """ Updates the occupancy grid based on NeRF density predictions. Args: model: NeRF model with a forward method. aabbmin: List/Tensor (3,), minimum bounds of the scene. aabbmax: List/Tensor (3,), maximum bounds of the scene. resolution: int, grid resolution. threshold: float, density threshold for occupancy. updateevery: int, frequency of updates. step: int, current training step. Returns: grid: 3D list/array (resolution, resolution, resolution), boolean occupancy grid. """ # Only update periodically if step % updateevery != 0: return None # 1. Generate grid coordinates gridcoords = [] for x in range(resolution): for y in range(resolution): for z in range(resolution): gridcoords.append([x, y, z]) # 2. Convert to world positions positions = [] for coord in gridcoords: pos = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for d in range(3): pos[d] = aabbmin[d] + ((coord[d] + 0.5) / resolution) (aabbmax[d] - aabbmin[d]) positions.append(pos) # 3. body: This method periodically refreshes a 3D density grid using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of neural network predictions to stabilize training and generate a binary occupancy map for ray-marching acceleration. It sets itself apart from static grid updates by continuously refining the density representation over time, allowing the occupancy threshold to adapt to the evolving scene geometry. It builds on Occupancy Grid Update by providing the specific density estimation and EMA smoothing mechanism required to populate the occupancy grid. Inputs: Neural network density evaluation function f{net}(x) that returns density \sigma at world coordinate x. Grid resolution R (e.g., 256^3). Bounding box bounds [-B, B]^3. EMA decay factor \alpha (typical value: 0.95). Occupancy threshold T{occ} (typical value: 0.01). Warmup steps W (typical value: 256). Current density grid D{old} (initialized to zeros). Outputs: Updated density grid D{new}. Binary occupancy grid O where O{ijk} = 1 if D{new}[ijk] > T{occ}, else 0. Data Structures: densitygrid: 3D tensor of shape (R, R, R) storing EMA-smoothed density values. binaries: 3D boolean tensor of shape (R, R, R) storing occupancy status. Steps: 1. Initialization: If D{old} is not provided, initialize D{new} = \mathbf{0} with shape (R, R, R). Set half-grid size h = B / R. 2. Sampling Strategy: If current training step t < W: Sample all grid cells uniformly. If t \ge W: Sample N = R^3 / 4 cells, mixing uniform samples and cells currently marked as occupied in the occupancy grid. 3. Coordinate Generation: For each sampled cell index (i, j, k), compute normalized grid coordinates g{ijk} = (i, j, k) / R. Add uniform random noise \epsilon \sim \mathcal{U}(-0.5, 0.5) to jitter sampling within the voxel: g'{ijk} = g{ijk} + \epsilon / R. Transform to world coordinates: x{ijk} = (g'{ijk} - 0.5) \times 2B. Alternative Chunked Approach (S4): Generate coordinate lines for X, Y, Z axes using torch.linspace from -B + h to B - h. Construct meshgrid points P = \{x, y, z\}. Add noise \delta \sim \mathcal{U}(-h, h) to each point: P{noisy} = P + \delta. 4. Density Evaluation: Query the neural network for density at each world coordinate: \sigma{ijk} = f{net}(x{ijk}). Detach gradients if only updating the grid for inference/acceleration purposes. 5. EMA Update: Update the density grid using the EMA maximum rule to preserve high-density regions and smooth noise: D{new}[ijk] = \max(D{old}[ijk] \times \alpha, \sigma{ijk}) Note: Some implementations use torch.maximum directly on the tensor slice. 6. Mean Density Calculation: Compute the mean density of the updated grid: \bar{\sigma} = \text{mean}(D{new}). 7. Occupancy Thresholding: Clamp the threshold T{occ} to be no greater than the current mean density to ensure sufficient active cells: T{occ} = \min(T{occ}, \bar{\sigma}) Note: Some sources suggest clamping the mean occupancy itself, but density-based thresholding is standard for density grids. 8. Binary Occupancy Generation: Create the binary occupancy grid: O[ijk] = (D{new}[ijk] > T{occ}) Note: In hierarchical grids, this step may involve enabling/disabling specific IJK indices in a sparse data structure (e.g., OpenVDB) based on O. 9. Tree Reinitialization (Optional): If using a hierarchical structure like OpenVDB, reinitialize the density grid tree with the current resolution and levels, then set values from the binary occupancy grid. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def updatedensitygridwithema( densitynet, resolution: int, bound: float, emadecay: float = 0.95, occthre: float = 0.01, warmupsteps: int = 256, currentstep: int = 0, olddensitygrid: torch.Tensor = None) -> tuple: """ Updates the 3D density grid using EMA and generates binary occupancy. Args: densitynet: Neural network function f(x) -> density. resolution: Grid resolution R (e.g., 256). bound: Half-size of the bounding box [-bound, bound]^3. emadecay: EMA decay factor alpha. occthre: Initial occupancy threshold Tocc. warmupsteps: Number of steps to sample all cells. currentstep: Current training step t. olddensitygrid: Previous density grid (R, R, R). Returns: newdensitygrid: Updated density grid (R, R, R). occupancygrid: Binary occupancy grid (R, R, R). """ device = olddensitygrid.device if olddensitygrid is not None else torch.device('cpu') # Initialize density grid if not provided if olddensitygrid is None: densitygrid = torch.zeros((resolution, resolution, resolution), device=device) else: densitygrid = olddensitygrid.clone() halfgridsize = bound / resolution # Determine sampling strategy if currentstep < warmupsteps: # Sample all cells indices = torch.meshgrid( torch.arange(resolution, device=device), torch.arange(resolution, device=device), torch.arange(resolution, device=device), indexing='ij') indices = torch.stack(indices, dim=-1).reshape(-1, 3) else: # Sample N = R^3 / 4 cells, mixing uniform and occupied # Note: In practice, 'occupied' refers to the previous occupancy grid # For simplicity, we assume a uniform sample if occupancy grid is not passed # or we sample randomly from the volume N = (resolution 3) // 4 # Random uniform sampling within the volume coords = torch.rand(N, 3, device=device) resolution indices = coords.long() % resolution # Wrap around if out of bounds # Generate world coordinates with jitter # Normalize to [0, 1], add noise, then scale to world space # Method 1: Direct from indices gridcoords = indices.float() / resolution # [0, 1] noise = torch.randlike(gridcoords) - 0.5 # [-0.5, 0.5] jitteredcoords = gridcoords + noise / resolution # Jitter within voxel # Transform to world space [-bound, bound] # Centered at 0: (coord - 0.5) 2 bound worldcoords = (jitteredcoords - 0.5) 2 bound # Evaluate density # densitynet expects [N, 3] input densities = densitynet(worldcoords).squeeze(-1).detach() # Update density grid using EMA # Map flat indices back to 3D grid for update # Flatten indices for gathering flatindices = indices[:, 0] (resolution 2) + indices[:, 1] resolution + indices[:, 2] # Gather current values currentvalues = densitygrid.view(-1)[flatindices] # EMA Update: max(old decay, new) newvalues = torch.maximum(currentvalues emadecay, densities) # Scatter back densitygrid.view(-1)[flatindices] = newvalues # Calculate mean density for thresholding meandensity = torch.mean(densitygrid).item() # Clamp threshold effectivethre = min(occthre, meandensity) # Generate binary occupancy occupancygrid = (densitygrid > effectivethre) return densitygrid, occupancygrid This variant applies the EMA principle directly to occupancy values rather than density values, maintaining a dynamic occupancy grid that is continuously refined during training. name: Occupancy Grid Update with EMA
head: Dynamic Space Occupancy Grids
body: This method maintains a dynamic occupancy grid to accelerate ray-marching by skipping empty space during differentiable volume rendering. It updates the occupancy estimator using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of density estimates derived from a 3D scene representation, adaptively guiding point sampling along rays. Unlike static occupancy grids, this approach continuously refines the empty-space map during training, improving efficiency by skipping voxels deemed empty based on the EMA history. It builds on Density Grid Update with EMA by applying similar EMA principles to occupancy rather than density values directly. Inputs: step: Current training step (integer). self.training: Boolean flag indicating training mode. self.resolution: Resolution of the occupancy grid (integer). self.cellsperlvl: Number of cells per level (integer). self.gridcoords: Tensor of grid coordinates (shape: [N, 3], integer). self.binaries: Binary occupancy grid tensor (shape: [m, resx, resy, resz]). self.aabbs: Axis-aligned bounding boxes for grids (shape: [m, 6]). occevalfn: Callable taking sample locations (N, 3) and returning occupancy values (N, 1). occthre: Threshold for binarizing occupancy (float, default: 1e-2). emadecay: Decay rate for EMA (float, default: 0.95). warmupsteps: Steps to sample all cells (integer, default: 256). n: Update interval in steps (integer, default: 16). alpha: EMA smoothing factor (float, default: 0.05 from). Outputs: Updated self.binaries occupancy grid. Data Structures: self.binaries: Binary tensor representing occupancy. 1 indicates occupied, 0 empty. self.gridcoords: Tensor storing 3D coordinates of grid cells. Steps: 1. Check if self.training is False. If so, raise RuntimeError. 2. If step % n == 0 and self.training is True, call update(step, occevalfn, occthre, emadecay, warmupsteps). 3. In update: a. If step < warmupsteps: i. Get all cell indices using self.getallcells(). b. If step >= warmupsteps: i. Set N = self.cellsperlvl // 4. ii. Sample cells using self.sampleuniformandoccupiedcells(N). This samples 1/4 of cells uniformly and 1/4 from occupied regions. c. For each level lvl and indices in lvlindices: i. Get gridcoords = self.gridcoords[indices]. ii. Compute sample positions x = (gridcoords + torch.randlike(gridcoords, dtype=torch.float32)) / self.resolution. This adds uniform noise to sample within the voxel. iii. Evaluate densities at x using occevalfn(x) to get Dg. iv. For each grid g, define point set Xg containing the center and 8 vertices of grid g. v. Get predicted densities Dg = {σig ∈ R+}{i=1}^9 for these 9 points. vi. Calculate density σg as max(Dg). vii. Update occupancy oEMAg using EMA: oEMAg ← max(σg, α(σg - oEMAg) + oEMAg) where α = 0.05. viii. Binarize oEMAg using occthre to update self.binaries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateoccupancygrid(step, self, occevalfn, occthre=1e-2, emadecay=0.95, warmupsteps=256, n=16, alpha=0.05): if not self.training: raise RuntimeError("Occupancy grid update only supported during training") if step % n == 0: update(step, self, occevalfn, occthre, emadecay, warmupsteps, alpha) def update(step, self, occevalfn, occthre, emadecay, warmupsteps, alpha): if step < warmupsteps: indices = self.getallcells() else: N = self.cellsperlvl // 4 indices = self.sampleuniformandoccupiedcells(N) for lvl in self.levels: lvlindices = indices[lvl] gridcoords = self.gridcoords[lvlindices] # Add uniform noise to sample within voxel x = (gridcoords + torch.randlike(gridcoords, dtype=torch.float32)) / self.resolution # Evaluate densities at sample points # occevalfn returns occupancy values (N, 1) densities = occevalfn(x) # For each grid, we need to evaluate 9 points (center + 8 vertices) # This part requires expanding gridcoords to 9 points per grid # Assuming gridcoords is already expanded to 9 points per grid for simplicity # In practice, this involves generating 9 points per grid cell # Calculate max density for each grid # densities shape: [numgrids 9, 1] # Reshape to [numgrids, 9, 1] and take max over 9 points densitiesreshaped = densities.view(-1, 9, 1) sigmag = torch.max(densitiesreshaped, dim=1).values # [numgrids, 1] # Update EMA occupancy # oEMAg is stored in self.occupancyema oEMAg = self.occupancyema[lvlindices] newoEMA = torch.max(sigmag, alpha (sigmag - oEMAg) + oEMAg) self.occupancyema[lvlindices] = newoEMA # Binarize occupancy binaries = (newoEMA > occthre).float() self.binaries[lvlindices] = binaries Parameters: step: Current training step. occevalfn: Callable for occupancy evaluation. occthre: Threshold for binarization, default 1e-2. emadecay: Decay rate for EMA, default 0.95. warmupsteps: Steps to sample all cells, default 256. n: Update interval, default 16. alpha: EMA smoothing factor, default 0.05. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: EMA updates may suffer from precision issues if alpha is very small. Boundaries: Ensure gridcoords are within valid range before sampling. Degenerate Input: If occevalfn returns NaN or Inf, handle gracefully. name: Dynamic Occupancy Grid Sampling
head: occupancy-guided sampling
body: Dynamic Occupancy Grid Sampling is a ray-marching acceleration technique that partitions the 3D scene space into a fixed-resolution grid of occupancy voxels to skip empty space during differentiable volume rendering. It improves training efficiency by adaptively guiding point sampling along rays, skipping voxels deemed empty based on an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of density estimates, whereas ordinary sampling processes all points along the ray regardless of occupancy. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of camera rays R \cup \tilde{R} passing through texture-rich and textureless areas; an inducing Signed Distance Function (SDF) f; a pre-set occupancy threshold \tau{Occu}; a decaying factor \alpha. Output: A set of sampled points along the rays located only within occupied voxels. Data Structures GOccu: A set of occupancy grids with a fixed size of 64^3 voxels. Voxel Indexing: Each voxel is indexed by g \subset GOccu. Voxel State: The occupancy state of voxel g is stored as og, with the EMA version denoted as og^{EMA}. Parameters \alpha: The decaying factor for the EMA update. Typical value: 0.05. \tau{Occu}: The pre-set threshold for determining if a voxel is occupied. If og^{EMA} > \tau{Occu}, the voxel is considered occupied. The exact numerical value is not given in the sources. Grid Size: 64^3 voxels. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize the occupancy grid GOccu with size 64^3. Initialize og^{EMA} for all voxels g (typically to 0.0, exact initialization is not specified). 2. Ray Sampling: During training, randomly sample pixels and define the set of camera rays R \cup \tilde{R}. 3. Voxel Iteration: For each ray, iterate through voxels along the ray path. 4. Density Estimation: Compute the density \sigmag at voxel g using the inducing SDF function f. 5. EMA Update: Update the occupancy value og^{EMA} using the exponential moving average formula: og^{EMA} \leftarrow \max(\sigmag, \alpha(\sigmag - og^{EMA}) + og^{EMA}) where \sigmag is the density at voxel g. 6. Occupancy Check: Compare og^{EMA} against \tau{Occu}. 7. Sampling or Skipping: If og^{EMA} > \tau{Occu}, perform point sampling within that voxel. If og^{EMA} \le \tau{Occu}, skip the voxel entirely. Args: rays: List of ray objects with.origin and.direction attributes. sdffunction: Function f that returns density sigmag at a 3D point. alpha: Decaying factor for EMA (default 0.05). tauoccu: Threshold for occupancy. gridsize: Fixed grid dimension (default 64). boundsmin, boundsmax: World-space bounds for coordinate mapping. Returns: List of sampled points for each ray. """ # Initialize occupancy grid with zeros occupancygrid = [[[0.0 for in range(gridsize)] for in range(gridsize)] for in range(gridsize)] def worldtogridindex(point): # Map world coordinate to grid index idxx = int((point[0] - boundsmin[0]) / (boundsmax[0] - boundsmin[0]) (gridsize - 1)) idxy = int((point[1] - boundsmin[1]) / (boundsmax[1] - boundsmin[1]) (gridsize - 1)) idxz = int((point[2] - boundsmin[2]) / (boundsmax[2] - boundsmin[2]) (gridsize - 1)) idxx = max(0, min(gridsize - 1, idxx)) idxy = max(0, min(gridsize - 1, idxy)) idxz = max(0, min(gridsize - 1, idxz)) return (idxx, idxy, idxz) allsamples = [] for ray in rays: raysamples = [] t = 0.0 tmax = 10.0 # Near/far plane bounds not given in sources step = 0.01 # Voxel traversal step not given in sources while t <= tmax: pos = (ray.origin[0] + t ray.direction[0], ray.origin[1] + t ray.direction[1], ray.origin[2] + t ray.direction[2]) idx = worldtogridindex(pos) # Compute density from SDF sigmag = sdffunction(pos) # Update EMA occupancy oldema = occupancygrid[idx[0]][idx[1]][idx[2]] newema = max(sigmag, alpha (sigmag - oldema) + oldema) occupancygrid[idx[0]][idx[1]][idx[2]] = newema # Check occupancy threshold and sample or skip if newema > tauoccu: # Perform point sampling within that voxel raysamples.append(pos) # Else: skip the voxel entirely t += step allsamples.append(raysamples) return allsamples Edge Cases and Pitfalls Initialization: The exact initialization value for og^{EMA} is not specified in the sources. Threshold Selection: The exact numerical value for \tau{Occu} is not given in the sources. Sampling Strategy: The exact method for point sampling within an occupied voxel is not specified. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for a fixed 64^3 occupancy grid. Strengths: Provides substantial speedup in training by adaptively guiding point sampling along rays. Limitations: Uses a fixed grid resolution of 64^3. Requires careful tuning of \tau{Occu}. name: Voxel Prior Loss
body: Voxel Prior Loss is a regularization term for 3D Gaussian Splatting that aligns learned Gaussian primitives with a precomputed voxel grid occupancy. It solves the problem of floating artifacts in empty space and ensures Gaussians in occupied regions maintain appropriate scale and opacity. It sets itself apart from standard photometric losses by explicitly enforcing geometric priors derived from voxel occupancy, suppressing Gaussians in empty voxels and encouraging dense, correctly scaled Gaussians in occupied ones. Inputs and outputs: Inputs: gaussians: Object containing attributes for N Gaussians. position: Tensor of shape (N, 3), world coordinates. opacity: Tensor of shape (N,), scalar opacity values. scale: Tensor of shape (N, 3), scale factors along principal axes. voxelindices: Tensor of shape (N, 3), integer voxel coordinates (d, h, w) for each Gaussian. voxelgrid: 3D occupancy grid of dimensions gridsize (D, H, W), flattened to 1D for indexing. Values are binary or boolean (occupied vs. empty). voxelcenters: Tensor of shape (D \times H \times W, 3), world coordinates of voxel centers. gridsize: Tuple (D, H, W) representing the dimensions of the voxel grid. voxelsize: Scalar, the physical size of a single voxel edge. penaltyweight: Float, weight for empty voxel opacity suppression. posweight: Float, weight for empty voxel position penalty. scaleweight: Float, weight for occupied voxel scale constraint. encourageweight: Float, weight for occupied voxel opacity encouragement. eps: Small float for numerical stability in normalization. Outputs: totalloss: Scalar, the computed regularization loss. Data structures: flatvoxelgrid: 1D tensor of shape (D \times H \times W), containing occupancy status (1 if occupied, 0 if empty). flatindices: 1D tensor of shape (N), mapping each Gaussian to its corresponding voxel index in the flattened grid. emptymask: Boolean tensor of shape (N), true where flatvoxelgrid indicates empty voxels. occupiedmask: Boolean tensor of shape (N), true where flatvoxelgrid indicates occupied voxels. Steps: 1. Map Gaussians to Voxels: Convert the 3D voxel indices of each Gaussian into a linear index for the flattened grid. 2. Retrieve Voxel Properties: Get occupancy status via isoccupied = flatvoxelgrid[flatindices] and voxel center coordinates via voxelcenter = voxelcenters.view(-1, 3)[flatindices]. 3. Compute Empty Voxel Penalty (Opacity): Identify empty voxels via emptymask = ~isoccupied and calculate the penalty as the weighted sum of opacity for Gaussians in empty voxels. 4. Compute Empty Voxel Position Penalty: Calculate an exponential distance penalty for Gaussians in empty voxels based on their L2 norm. 5. Compute Occupied Voxel Scale Loss: Identify occupied voxels via occupiedmask = isoccupied and penalize Gaussians whose scale exceeds the voxel size, clamping negative differences to zero. 6. Compute Occupied Voxel Opacity Encouragement: Penalize Gaussians in occupied voxels having opacity below 0.1 using a ReLU-like function. 7. Normalize Total Loss: Sum all components and normalize by the number of Gaussians plus a small epsilon. Formulas: Linear index calculation: flat\indices = indices[:,0] \times (grid\size[1] \times grid\size[2]) + indices[:,1] \times grid\size[2] + indices[:,2], where indices is (N, 3) voxel indices and grid\size is (D, H, W). Empty voxel position penalty: penalty\position = pos\weight \times \sum \exp(-5 \times \|position[empty\mask]\|), where \|\cdot\| is the L2 norm. Occupied voxel scale loss: scale\loss = scale\weight \times \sum \max(0, scale[occupied\mask] - voxel\size), summed over all elements of the (N, 3) scale tensor. Occupied voxel opacity encouragement: opacity\loss = encourage\weight \times \sum \max(0, 0.1 - opacity[occupied\mask]). Normalized total loss: total\loss = \frac{penalty\opacity + penalty\position + scale\loss + opacity\loss}{N + eps}. Parameters: penaltyweight: Weight for empty voxel opacity suppression. Default value: 1.0. encourageweight: Weight for occupied voxel opacity encouragement. Default value: 0.5. posweight: Weight for empty voxel position penalty. Default value: 0.2. scaleweight: Weight for occupied voxel scale constraint. Default value: 0.3. Edge cases and pitfalls: Out-of-bounds Indices: If a Gaussian's position falls outside the voxel grid bounds, flatindices may be invalid. Ensure voxelindices are clamped or Gaussians outside the grid are excluded from the loss. Scale Interpretation: The source formula clamp(scale[occupiedmask] - voxelsize, min=0) is ambiguous if scale is a vector (N,3). The implementation sums over all elements of the clamped difference. Empty Mask Logic: Ensure isoccupied is boolean or castable to boolean. If the grid uses 0/1 integers, bitwise inversion ~isoccupied might invert bits incorrectly if not cast to bool first. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def norm(v): return math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) def exp(x): return math.exp(x) def clamp(x, minval): return max(minval, x) def relu(x): return max(0.0, x) def computevoxelpriorloss(gaussians, voxelgrid, voxelcenters, gridsize, voxelsize, penaltyweight=1.0, posweight=0.2, scaleweight=0.3, encourageweight=0.5, eps=1e-8): """ Computes the Voxel Prior Loss for 3D Gaussians. Args: gaussians: Object with attributes.position (N,3),.opacity (N,),.scale (N,3),.voxelindices (N,3) voxelgrid: 1D list/tensor (DHW,) of occupancy (1=occupied, 0=empty) voxelcenters: List/tensor (DHW, 3) of voxel center coordinates gridsize: Tuple (D, H, W) voxelsize: Scalar float, edge length of a voxel penaltyweight: Weight for empty voxel opacity penalty posweight: Weight for empty voxel position penalty scaleweight: Weight for occupied voxel scale penalty encourageweight: Weight for occupied voxel opacity encouragement eps: Small constant for numerical stability Returns: totalloss: Scalar float """ # 1. Map Gaussians to Voxel Indices indices = gaussians.voxelindices # Shape (N, 3) D, H, W = gridsize flatindices = [int(idx[0] (H W) + idx[1] W + idx[2]) for idx in indices] # 2. Retrieve Voxel Properties isoccupied = [bool(voxelgrid[i]) for i in flatindices] voxelcentersflat = [voxelcenters[i] for i in flatindices] # Retrieved per source, unused in loss # Extract Gaussian attributes opacity = gaussians.opacity # Shape (N,) position = gaussians.position # Shape (N, 3) scale = gaussians.scale # Shape (N, 3) # Masks emptymask = [not occ for occ in isoccupied] occupiedmask = [occ for occ in isoccupied] # 3. Empty Voxel Opacity Penalty penaltyopacity = penaltyweight sum(opacity[i] for i in range(len(opacity)) if emptymask[i]) # 4. Empty Voxel Position Penalty penaltyposition = posweight sum(exp(-5 norm(position[i])) for i in range(len(position)) if emptymask[i]) # 5. Occupied Voxel Scale Loss scaleloss = scaleweight sum(clamp(scale[i][j] - voxelsize, 0.0) for i in range(len(scale)) if occupiedmask[i] for j in range(3)) # 6. Occupied Voxel Opacity Encouragement opacityloss = encourageweight sum(relu(0.1 - opacity[i]) for i in range(len(opacity)) if occupiedmask[i]) # 7. Normalize N = len(opacity) totalloss = (penaltyopacity + penaltyposition + scaleloss + opacityloss) / (N + eps) return totalloss Regularizes visible 3D Gaussians by computing their perpendicular distance to voxel plane boundaries, weighting the distance by voxel complexity, and averaging over all voxels. It filters visible Gaussians using a visibility filter, maps positions to voxel grid coordinates via floor division by 2.0, gathers Gaussians per voxel, computes distances as |\mathbf{p}i \cdot \mathbf{n}v + dv| / \|\mathbf{n}v\|, finds the minimum distance per Gaussian, weights by voxel complexity, and divides by the number of voxels. The loss is defined as L{voxel} = \frac{1}{V} \sum{v \in V} \frac{1}{Mv} \sum{i=1}^{Mv} c{v, i} \cdot \min{j} \frac{|\mathbf{p}i \cdot \mathbf{n}v + dv|}{\|\mathbf{n}v\|}, where V is the number of voxels, Mv is Gaussians in voxel v, \mathbf{p}i is Gaussian position, \mathbf{n}v is voxel normal, dv is voxel plane offset, and c{v, i} is voxel complexity. It uses VOXELLOC to convert voxel grid keys to spatial position identifiers for indexing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Occupancy Grid Transition and Update
head: Dynamic Occupancy Grid, HMM-based Occupancy Update, Occ. Grid Transition, Probabilistic Occupancy Grid, Transition and Update of Occupancy Grid
body: This method adapts the occupancy grid for efficient point sampling in dynamic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by treating voxel occupancy as a time-varying probability rather than a static binary state. It solves the problem of maintaining sampling efficiency in on-the-fly training where scene geometry changes, by applying a transition function to predict motion and a Bayesian update to incorporate new density observations. Unlike static NeRFs that cache grids or 4D space-time grids that fail to accelerate per-frame training, this method transitions the 3D grid between frames to preserve occupancy information relevant to the current time step. Inputs and Outputs Input: The final occupancy grid from the previous frame optimization G^J{k-1}, where k is the current frame index and J is the total number of optimization iterations per frame. Input: The volume density output \sigma(x) from the NeRF model during current frame optimization. Input: A 3D convolution kernel S representing motion probability. Output: The updated occupancy grid G^jk for the current frame at iteration j, used to guide point sampling. Data Structures Occupancy Grid (G): A 3D tensor where each element G(x) represents the probability that voxel x contains positive volume density. The values are continuous probabilities in the range [0, 1]. Kernel (S): A 3D kernel used for convolution, defined as a simple 3D Gaussian function. Steps 1. Transition (Prediction): At the start of optimizing frame k, apply a transition function to the previous frame's final grid G^J{k-1} to model potential motion. This is computed by convolving the previous grid with the kernel S: G^0k = S G^J{k-1} Here, G^0k is the initial occupancy probability for frame k before any new observations are processed. The convolution assumes a Markov property where motion is limited and local. 2. Bayesian Update (Correction): During the J optimization iterations for frame k, update the occupancy grid probability G^jk after each iteration j (where j \in [1, J]) using the NeRF's volume density output \sigma(x) at the sampled point x. The update rule is: G^jk = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \sigma(x) < G^{j-1}k \\ \sigma(x) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} This is a simplified Bayesian update P(\sigma(x) | G^{j-1}k). The condition \sigma(x) < G^{j-1}k triggers a certainty of occupancy (probability 1), while otherwise the probability is set to the observed density value. 3. Sampling: Use the updated grid G^jk to sample points only in occupied areas (where probability is significant) during the on-the-fly training process. Parameters Kernel S: A 3D Gaussian function. Its specific width/standard deviation is not given in the sources, but it is chosen to represent the probability of motion based on the Markov assumption of limited historical motion information. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Global Sampling Failure: Using global random sampling (as in Instant-NGP) to update the grid ignores previous occupancy values and transitions. In on-the-fly training with few iterations, this can miss occupied regions that have moved, resulting in "blank cubes" in rendered images. This method avoids that by updating probabilities at occupied points based on transition. Dynamic Scene Assumption: The method is designed for dynamic scenes captured by multi-view forward-facing cameras. It may not be directly applicable to monocular or 360-degree inward-facing setups without modification, as these involve different motion characteristics and hardware constraints. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateoccupancygridtransitionandupdate(Gprev, kernelS, nerfmodel, numiterations): # Gprev: 3D tensor of occupancy probabilities from previous frame (G^J{k-1}) # kernelS: 3D Gaussian kernel for motion transition # nerfmodel: The NeRF model providing volume density sigma(x) # numiterations: J, number of optimization steps per frame # Step 1: Transition (Prediction) # Convolve previous grid with motion kernel # Note: 3D convolution implementation is standard; sources do not specify details. Gcurrent = convolve3d(Gprev, kernelS) # Step 2: Bayesian Update (Correction) for j in range(1, numiterations + 1): # Sample points x based on current occupancy probabilities Gcurrent # Note: Point sampling strategy is standard; sources do not specify details. points = samplepointsfromgrid(Gcurrent) for x in points: # Get volume density from NeRF sigmax = nerfmodel.getvolumedensity(x) # Bayesian update rule from sources if sigmax < Gcurrent[x]: Gcurrent[x] = 1.0 else: Gcurrent[x] = sigmax return Gcurrent def convolve3d(grid, kernel): # Standard 3D convolution implementation # Note: sources do not specify details. return grid def samplepointsfromgrid(grid): # Standard importance sampling from probability distribution # Note: sources do not specify details. return [] Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On the synthetic D-NeRF dataset, the method achieves 6 frames per second (FPS) for training and rendering combined. It significantly accelerates on-the-fly training compared to state-of-the-art algorithms while maintaining comparable rendering quality. Strengths: Maintains occupancy information across frames, avoiding the "blank cube" artifacts caused by global random sampling in dynamic scenes. Efficient for on-the-fly training with limited iterations per frame. Limitations: Relies on the Markov assumption of limited motion, which may not capture complex, long-range movements accurately without tuning the kernel S. Performance may degrade in scenes with rapid, non-local motion. Origin: Proposed in OD-NeRF: Efficient Training of On-the-Fly Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields. History: The method addresses the limitation of static NeRF occupancy grids [13, 1] and 4D space-time grids [16] which do not improve on-the-fly efficiency. It formulates the problem using a Hidden Markov Model approach to transition and update the grid. Usage: Evaluated on synthetic D-NeRF [18], real-world MeetRoom [6], and DyNeRF [8] datasets. It is particularly relevant for streaming scenarios with multi-view forward-facing cameras.
