name: MERF Baking
head: Baking to Discrete Grids, Proposal-MLP-aware baking pipeline
body: MERF Baking is a post-training procedure that converts a trained neural field representation into a block-sparse, texture-based format optimized for real-time web rendering. It solves the problem of storing and transmitting large-scale neural scenes by evaluating the MLP outputs on discrete grids and using a binary occupancy grid to cull empty or occluded voxels. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as Density Grid Update with EMA and Occupancy Grid Transition and Update, by explicitly targeting web-based delivery through texture compression and block-sparse storage, trading higher frame rates for neural field reconstruction capabilities compared to mesh rasterization methods. Unlike existing baking pipelines that do not consider the proposal-MLP and use uniformly-spaced sample points (causing fog-like artifacts and floating blobs), this method uses proposal-MLP sampling and real-time renderer step sizes for visibility culling, resulting in a lossless pipeline. Inputs: Trained Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) parameters. Set of training rays with associated camera poses and ground truth images. Proposal MLP parameters (used during training to sample points near surfaces). Real-time renderer step size parameter \delta (small uniform step size in contracted space). Occupancy threshold \tau = 0.005. Outputs: Binary occupancy grid A at base resolution. Mipmapped occupancy grids for empty space skipping. Baked 2D planes and 3D voxel grid in block-sparse format. Encoded textures (PNGs). Data Structures: 1. Binary Occupancy Grid (A): A 3D grid where each voxel is a binary flag (occupied/unoccupied). The base resolution is typically 4096. 2. Block-Sparse Voxel Grid: Stores the baked density/color data. Only data blocks containing at least one occupied voxel are stored. 3. Mipmapped Occupancy Grids: Lower-resolution versions of A created via max-pooling with filter sizes 16, 32, and 128. For a base resolution of 4096, this results in grids of size 256, 128, and 32. Steps: 1. Render Training Rays and Extract Weighted Points: Render all training rays using the trained Proposal MLP. Extract a set of weighted points \{(xi, wi)\}, where xi is the 3D position of a sample point and wi is the associated volume rendering weight from the volume rendering equation. wi = Ti \cdot (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where Ti is the transmittance up to point i, \sigmai is the density, and \deltai is the distance to the next sample. Note that these points cluster around surfaces because they are sampled by the proposal-MLP. 2. Compute Opacity for Culling: Compute the opacity \alphai for each point xi based on the distance between samples \delta used by the real-time renderer, not the proposal-MLP. The real-time renderer steps through contracted space with a small uniform step size \delta. \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(xi) \cdot \delta) Using the real-time step size \delta ensures aggressive culling while guaranteeing that voxels with significant opacity (\alphai > 0.005) are not culled in the final sampling scheme. The weight wi depends on densities along the entire ray (visibility), while \alphai depends only on the density at xi. 3. Populate Binary Occupancy Grid (A): Initialize grid A to all zeros. For each weighted point (xi, wi): Identify the eight voxels surrounding the position xi. Mark these eight voxels as occupied (set to 1) if both conditions are met: wi > \tau \quad \text{and} \quad \alphai > \tau where \tau = 0.005. Voxels corresponding to occluded content, regions not sampled by any training ray, or low opacity are left unoccupied (0). 4. Generate Mipmapped Occupancy Grids: Create multiple lower-resolution versions of the binary occupancy grid A using max-pooling with filter sizes 16, 32, and 128. These are used for hierarchical empty space skipping during ray traversal. 5. Bake Neural Field Outputs: Evaluate the trained MLP to compute density and color for all occupied voxels in A. Store the resulting 3D voxel grid in a block-sparse format, storing only data blocks that contain occupied voxels. Bake the three high-resolution 2D planes (used in MERF) alongside the 3D voxel grid. 6. Encode Textures: Encode the baked textures as PNGs to reduce storage size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def merfbaking(trainedmlp, proposalmlp, trainingrays, realtimestepsize, threshold=0.005, baseresolution=4096): # Step 1: Render training rays and extract weighted points weightedpoints = [] for ray in trainingrays: samples = proposalmlp.sample(ray) for sample in samples: xi = sample.position sigmai = trainedmlp.density(xi) wi = calculatevolumeweight(ray, sample, trainedmlp) alphai = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai realtimestepsize) weightedpoints.append((xi, wi, alphai)) # Step 2: Populate binary occupancy grid A occupancygrid = [[[0] baseresolution for in range(baseresolution)] for in range(baseresolution)] for (xi, wi, alphai) in weightedpoints: if wi > threshold and alphai > threshold: voxelindices = getsurroundingvoxels(xi, baseresolution) for idx in voxelindices: occupancygrid[idx[0]][idx[1]][idx[2]] = 1 # Step 3: Generate mipmapped occupancy grids mipmaps = [] for filtersize in [16, 32, 128]: mipmap = maxpool3d(occupancygrid, filtersize) mipmaps.append(mipmap) # Step 4: Bake neural field outputs bakedvoxelgrid = {} baked2dplanes = [] for voxel in getoccupiedvoxels(occupancygrid): x = voxel.center sigma = trainedmlp.density(x) color = trainedmlp.color(x) bakedvoxelgrid[voxel.blockid] = (sigma, color) # Note: The exact procedure for baking the three high-resolution 2D planes is not detailed in the sources. # Step 5: Encode textures pngtextures = encodetopng(baked2dplanes) pngvoxeldata = encodetopng(bakedvoxelgrid) return occupancygrid, mipmaps, (bakedvoxelgrid, baked2dplanes), (pngtextures, pngvoxeldata) def calculatevolumeweight(ray, sample, trainedmlp): Ti = 1.0 for prevsample in ray.samplesbefore(sample): sigmaprev = trainedmlp.density(prevsample.position) deltaprev = prevsample.distancetonext() Ti = math.exp(-sigmaprev deltaprev) sigmai = trainedmlp.density(sample.position) deltai = sample.distancetonext() return Ti (1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai deltai)) def getsurroundingvoxels(point, resolution): indices = [] for dx in [-0.5, 0.5]: for dy in [-0.5, 0.5]: for dz in [-0.5, 0.5]: ix = max(0, min(resolution - 1, int(math.floor(point[0] + dx)))) iy = max(0, min(resolution - 1, int(math.floor(point[1] + dy)))) iz = max(0, min(resolution - 1, int(math.floor(point[2] + dz)))) indices.append((ix, iy, iz)) return indices def maxpool3d(grid, filtersize): res = len(grid) newres = res // filtersize newgrid = [[[0] newres for in range(newres)] for in range(newres)] for x in range(newres): for y in range(newres): for z in range(newres): maxval = 0 for dx in range(filtersize): for dy in range(filtersize): for dz in range(filtersize): maxval = max(maxval, grid[xfiltersize+dx][yfiltersize+dy][zfiltersize+dz]) newgrid[x][y][z] = maxval return newgrid def getoccupiedvoxels(grid): occupied = [] res = len(grid) for x in range(res): for y in range(res): for z in range(res): if grid[x][y][z] == 1: occupied.append(type('Voxel', (), {'center': (x + 0.5, y + 0.5, z + 0.5), 'blockid': (x // 16, y // 16, z // 16), 'localindex': (x % 16, y % 16, z % 16)})()) return occupied def encodetopng(data): # Sources do not specify the exact encoding pipeline beyond PNG compression. return data Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The opacity calculation must use the real-time renderer's step size \delta, not the proposal-MLP's step size, to avoid culling voxels that will be sampled in the real-time viewer. Degenerate Input: If the proposal-MLP fails to sample a region, that region will not be marked as occupied, potentially leading to missing geometry if the proposal-MLP is inaccurate. However, the method guarantees that voxels with significant opacity (\alphai > 0.005) are not culled. City-on-Web Baking is a post-training procedure that converts a neural field representation into a block-sparse, texture-based format optimized for real-time web rendering. It solves the problem of storing and transmitting large-scale neural scenes by baking high-resolution 2D planes and low-resolution 3D voxel grids per block, storing only non-empty voxels. It sets itself apart from its parent, MERF Baking, by explicitly targeting web-based delivery through texture compression and block-sparse storage, trading higher frame rates for neural field reconstruction capabilities compared to mesh rasterization methods. Time Complexity: The baking process involves rendering all training rays and evaluating the MLP for occupied voxels. The complexity is proportional to the number of training rays and the number of occupied voxels. Memory Complexity: The memory usage is dominated by the block-sparse voxel grid and the 2D planes. The use of block-sparse storage and PNG compression significantly reduces memory footprint compared to dense grids. Measured Performance: The method achieves real-time rendering speeds in a web browser using three.js. The baking pipeline is almost lossless compared to the pre-baking quality. Strengths: Lossless quality compared to pre-baking; efficient empty space skipping via mipmapped occupancy grids; web-friendly format (PNGs, block-sparse). Limitations: Requires a proposal-MLP for effective sampling; baking time depends on the number of training rays and scene complexity. When to use: Real-time view synthesis in unbounded scenes, particularly for web-based applications. When not to use: Offline rendering where quality is paramount and speed is not a constraint; scenes where the proposal-MLP fails to capture geometry accurately. MERF (Memory-Efficient Radiance Fields) was introduced by Barron et al. in 2022. The baking method is a key component of MERF, enabling real-time rendering of large-scale scenes by converting the neural field into a discrete, sparse format. The method builds on the idea of using occupancy grids for empty space skipping, as seen in Occupancy Grid Update, but extends it with a proposal-MLP-aware pipeline to ensure high fidelity. name: City-on-Web Baking
head: City-on-Web Scene Representation & Baking
body: City-on-Web Baking is a post-training procedure that converts a neural field representation into a block-sparse, texture-based format optimized for real-time web rendering. It solves the problem of storing and transmitting large-scale neural scenes by baking high-resolution 2D planes and low-resolution 3D voxel grids per block, storing only non-empty voxels. It sets itself apart from its parent, MERF Baking, by explicitly targeting web-based delivery through texture compression and block-sparse storage, trading lower frame rates for neural field reconstruction capabilities compared to mesh rasterization methods. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained neural radiance field (NeRF) or neural rendering model, typically using multi-resolution hash encoding and MLPs for density, color, and specular features. Output: A set of compressed PNG texture assets representing baked grid attributes, organized in a block-sparse structure with Level of Detail (LOD) support. Data Structures: Block-Sparse 3D Voxel Grid: Stores only non-empty voxels. Each block has a voxel resolution of 512^3. High-Resolution 2D Planes (Triplanes): Stored as images within each block. Resolution is 2048^2 per plane. Binary Occupancy Grids (\phi^{k,l}): Identifies occupied voxels within each block. Texture Assets: Baked grid attributes stored as images to reduce memory footprint and accelerate web transmission. Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Render all training rays to collect ray samples initially. 2. Thresholding: Retain samples with opacity and weight values above a certain threshold; discard samples below the threshold. 3. Occupancy Marking: Use the preserved samples to mark the adjacent eight grid points as occupied in the binary occupancy grids \phi^{k,l}. 4. Baking: Bake high-resolution 2D planes (triplanes) and a low-resolution 3D voxel grid within each block to derive the attribute function f^{k,l}. 5. Sparse Storage: Store only the non-empty 3D voxels using a block-sparse format. 6. LOD Generation: Downsample the occupancy grid using max-pooling to generate lower-resolution LODs for efficient rendering. 7. Compression: Compress the resulting textures into PNG format to reduce storage footprint. Parameters: Voxel resolution per block: 512^3. Triplane resolution per block: 2048^2. Encoder: 4-layer MLP with 64 hidden dimensions (after multi-resolution hash encoding). Deferred MLP: 3-layer MLP with 16 hidden dimensions for residual view-dependent color. Batch size: 16,384 rays per batch. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Web Performance: The method results in lower frame rates compared to mesh rasterization-based methods due to the use of volume rendering. LOD Management: Resource usage decreases with higher LODs, but the lowest LOD maintains high-fidelity rendering results. This variant emphasizes the specific mechanism of marking occupancy and baking. It renders training rays, retains high-opacity/weight samples, marks adjacent grid points in \phi^{k,l}, and bakes triplanes and voxel grids. It explicitly stores non-empty voxels in a block-sparse format and downsamples occupancy grids via max-pooling for LODs, compressing textures to PNG. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to dense grids due to block-sparse storage and texture compression. The lowest LOD still maintains high-fidelity results, but resource usage increases with higher resolution blocks. Measured Performance: On the Matrix City, Campus, and Rubble datasets, the method achieves competitive PSNR, LPIPS, and SSIM scores (e.g., 25.87 PSNR on Matrix City). Scaling: The method is designed for large-scale scenes (e.g., 1200 × 800 square meters) and supports LODs to manage resource loading on web platforms. Strengths: Enables neural field reconstruction for large-scale scenes on the web; reduces memory and transmission costs via compression and sparse storage. Limitations: Lower frame rates compared to mesh rasterization methods due to volume rendering overhead. When to use: Real-time neural rendering of large-scale scenes on web platforms where neural field quality is prioritized over maximum frame rate. When not to use: Applications requiring mesh rasterization performance or where neural field reconstruction is unnecessary. City-on-Web was introduced in 2024 by F. Author et al. in the paper "City-on-Web: Real-Time Neural Rendering of Large-Scale Scenes on the Web". It builds on MERF Baking and is implemented using the nerfstudio framework with the tiny-cuda-nn extension, targeting JavaScript web applications with GLSL rendering. body: A ray sampling method that fuses occupancy grid-based sparse sampling with importance sampling to generate ray samples efficiently for neural radiance fields, specifically designed for autonomous driving scenes. It builds on Occupancy Grid Update by using the grid to perform an initial coarse pass, then redistributing samples based on the resulting density weights to concentrate computation on opaque regions. Inputs: rayso: Tensor of ray origins, shape (N, 3), contiguous. raysd: Tensor of ray directions, shape (N, 3), contiguous. tmin: Optional near plane distance. If not provided, set to None. tmax: Optional far plane distance. If not provided, set to 10^{10}. densityfn: Callable evaluating density \sigma at positions. If None, density checking is disabled during inference. renderstepsize: Minimum step size for coarse sampling. alphathre: Opacity threshold for skipping samples. Default 0.01. coneangle: Cone angle for adaptive raymarching. 0 for uniform marching. Typical value for real scenes is 1/256 \approx 0.004; 0.0 for Blender scenes. numfinesamples: Number of importance samples to generate per ray for the fine pass. Default 32. self.training: Boolean flag determining if stratified perturbation is applied. occupancygrid: An OccGridEstimator instance used to skip empty space. Outputs: raysamples: Object containing origins, directions, starts, ends, and pixelarea. rayindices: Tensor mapping samples back to original rays. Data Structures: packedinfo: Tensor of shape (R, 2), where R is the number of active rays. Column 0 is the start index in the flattened sample arrays, Column 1 is the count of samples for that ray. rayindices: LongTensor mapping each sample to its source ray ID. starts, ends: 1D Tensors of shape (S,) containing the t-coordinates of sample boundaries, where S is the total number of sample boundaries. Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling via Occupancy Grid: Call self.occupancygrid.sampling() with rayso, raysd, tmin, tmax, sigmafn (derived from densityfn), renderstepsize, nearplane, farplane, stratified (based on self.training), coneangle, and alphathre. This returns rayindices, starts, and ends for the coarse samples. 2. Edge Case Handling: If the number of coarse samples is 0 (i.e., starts.shape[0] == 0), create a single fake sample to prevent empty tensor issues: Set rayindices to torch.zeros((1,)). Set starts and ends to torch.ones((1,)). This effectively represents a single sample on the last ray starting and ending at t=1. 3. Compact Ray Indexing: Transform dilated ray indices to compact indices: Compute uniquerayindices = torch.unique(rayindices). Compute newrayindices = torch.bucketize(rayindices, uniquerayindices, right=False). Compute newnumrays = len(uniquerayindices). 4. Pack Uniform Samples: Create packed info for the coarse samples: packedinfouniform = nerfacc.packinfo(newrayindices, newnumrays). 5. Evaluate Density: Compute positions for coarse samples: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o}{ri} + \mathbf{d}{ri} \cdot \frac{\text{starts}i + \text{ends}i}{2} where \mathbf{o} and \mathbf{d} are indexed by newrayindices. Evaluate density: \sigmai = \text{density\fn}(\mathbf{p}i). Squeeze to 1D. 6. Compute Weights: Compute weights from density using the backend's rendering function: wi = \text{render\weight\from\density}(\text{starts}, \text{ends}, \sigmai, \text{packed\info\uniform}) Add epsilon to prevent zero weights: wi \leftarrow wi + 10^{-2}. 7. Prepare for PDF Sampling: Append Trailing Zeros: Create trailingzeros of shape (\text{new\num\rays}, \dots) (zeros). Use packedappend to append these zeros to weightsuniform to serve as the PDF denominator/normalization tail. weightsuniform, packedinfomerged = packedappend(weightsuniform, trailingzeros, 1, newrayindices, packedinfouniform). Append Trailing Ends: Compute the last sample ID for each ray: \text{last\sample\id}r = \text{packed\info\uniform}[r, 0] + \text{packed\info\uniform}[r, 1] - 1 Get trailingends = ends[lastsampleid]. Use packedappend to append these trailing ends to starts to form the bins for sampling. existingbins, = packedappend(starts, trailingends, 1, newrayindices, packedinfouniform). 8. Importance Sampling (Fine Pass): Perform PDF sampling to get fine sample positions t: t{\text{fine}} = \text{packed\sample\PDF}(\text{bins}=\text{existing\bins}, \text{weights}=\text{weights\uniform}, \text{pack\infos}=\text{packed\info\merged}, \text{num\to\sample}=\text{num\fine\samples} + 1, \text{perturb}=\text{self.training}) Extract the sampled t values. 9. Merge Coarse and Fine Samples: Create Fine Ray Indices: \text{ray\indices\fine} = \text{torch.arange}(\text{new\num\rays}) \cdot \text{repeat\interleave}(\text{num\fine\samples}) packedinfofine = nerfacc.packinfo(rayindicesfine, newnumrays). Merge Starts: starts = mergetwopackssortedaligned(starts, packedinfouniform, samplest[...,:-1].reshape(-1), packedinfofine, bsorted=True, returnval=True)[0]. Merge Ends: ends = mergetwopackssortedaligned(ends, packedinfouniform, samplest[..., 1:].reshape(-1), packedinfofine, bsorted=True, returnval=True)[0]. Update Ray Indices: rayindicescomplete = packedappend(newrayindices, rayindicesfine, numfinesamples, newrayindices, packedinfouniform)[0]. rayindices = uniquerayindices[rayindicescomplete]. 10. Construct Output: Extract origins and directions: \mathbf{o} = \text{rays\o}[\text{ray\indices}], \mathbf{d} = \text{rays\d}[\text{ray\indices}]. If cameraindices exists, index it similarly. Create Frustums with origins, directions, starts[..., None], ends[..., None], and pixelarea = zeros. Return raysamples and rayindices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch from typing import Tuple def occupancygridandimportancesamplingfusion( rayso: torch.Tensor, raysd: torch.Tensor, tmin: float, tmax: float, densityfn, renderstepsize: float, alphathre: float, coneangle: float, numfinesamples: int, training: bool, occupancygrid, nerfacc, nearplane: float, farplane: float) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]: """ Returns: rayindices, starts, ends, origins, directions """ # 1. Coarse Sampling rayindices, starts, ends = occupancygrid.sampling( rayso=rayso, raysd=raysd, tmin=tmin, tmax=tmax, sigmafn=densityfn, # Derived from densityfn renderstepsize=renderstepsize, nearplane=nearplane, farplane=farplane, stratified=training, coneangle=coneangle, alphathre=alphathre) # 2. Edge Case: Empty Samples if starts.shape[0] == 0: rayindices = torch.zeros((1,), dtype=torch.long, device=rayso.device) starts = torch.ones((1,), device=rayso.device) ends = torch.ones((1,), device=rayso.device) origins = rayso[rayindices] directions = raysd[rayindices] return rayindices, starts, ends, origins, directions # 3. Compact Ray Indices uniquerayindices = torch.unique(rayindices) newrayindices = torch.bucketize(rayindices, uniquerayindices, right=False) newnumrays = len(uniquerayindices) # 4. Pack Uniform Samples packedinfouniform = nerfacc.packinfo(newrayindices, newnumrays) # 5. Evaluate Density originscoarse = rayso[newrayindices] dirscoarse = raysd[newrayindices] midt = (starts + ends) / 2.0 positionsuniform = originscoarse + dirscoarse midt[:, None] sigmasuniform = densityfn(positionsuniform).squeeze() # 6. Compute Weights weightsuniform,, = nerfacc.renderweightfromdensity( tstarts=starts, tends=ends, sigmas=sigmasuniform, packedinfo=packedinfouniform) weightsuniform = weightsuniform + 1e-2 # 7. Prepare for PDF Sampling trailingzeros = torch.zeros(newnumrays, device=weightsuniform.device) weightsuniform, packedinfomerged = packedappend( feat=weightsuniform, other=trailingzeros, numappendperpack=1, rayindices=newrayindices, packinfos=packedinfouniform) lastsampleid = packedinfouniform[:, 0] + packedinfouniform[:, 1] - 1 trailingends = ends[lastsampleid] existingbins, = packedappend( feat=starts, other=trailingends, numappendperpack=1, rayindices=newrayindices, packinfos=packedinfouniform) # 8. Importance Sampling samplest = nerfacc.packedsamplepdf( bins=existingbins, weights=weightsuniform, packinfos=packedinfomerged, numtosample=numfinesamples + 1, perturb=training)[0] # 9. Merge Coarse and Fine rayindicesfine = torch.repeatinterleave(torch.arange(newnumrays, device=rayso.device), numfinesamples) packedinfofine = nerfacc.packinfo(rayindicesfine, newnumrays) finestarts = samplest[...,:-1].reshape(-1) starts = mergetwopackssortedaligned( starts, packedinfouniform, finestarts, packedinfofine, bsorted=True, returnval=True)[0] fineends = samplest[..., 1:].reshape(-1) ends = mergetwopackssortedaligned( ends, packedinfouniform, fineends, packedinfofine, bsorted=True, returnval=True)[0] rayindicescomplete = packedappend( feat=newrayindices, other=rayindicesfine, numappendperpack=numfinesamples, rayindices=newrayindices, packinfos=packedinfouniform)[0] rayindices = uniquerayindices[rayindicescomplete] # 10. Construct Output origins = rayso[rayindices] directions = raysd[rayindices] return rayindices, starts, ends, origins, directions def packedappend( feat: torch.Tensor, other: torch.Tensor, numappendperpack: int, rayindices: torch.LongTensor, packinfos: torch.LongTensor) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.LongTensor]: numrays = packinfos.shape[0] newvals = feat.newempty([feat.numel() + numrays numappendperpack]) originalindices = torch.arange(feat.numel(), device=feat.device) originalaranges = torch.arange(numrays numappendperpack, device=feat.device) pidxa = originalindices + (rayindices numappendperpack) expandpackinfos = packinfos.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, numappendperpack, -1).reshape(-1, 2) pidxb = expandpackinfos[:, 0] + expandpackinfos[:, 1] + originalaranges newvals.scatter(0, pidxa, feat) newvals.scatter(0, pidxb, other) newpackedinfos = packinfos.clone() newpackedinfos[:, 0] += originalaranges[::numappendperpack] newpackedinfos[:, 1] += numappendperpack return newvals, newpackedinfos Time Complexity: Dominated by the occupancy grid traversal for coarse sampling and the density evaluation at coarse sample positions. Importance sampling adds overhead proportional to numfinesamples but reduces the total number of samples needed for high-quality rendering by concentrating them in opaque regions. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of active samples. The packedinfo structures and intermediate tensors (weights, bins) scale with the number of rays and samples per ray. Strengths: Significantly accelerates rendering in large-scale autonomous driving scenes by skipping empty space via the occupancy grid and reducing noise/variance via importance sampling. Limitations: Requires maintaining and updating the occupancy grid. The fusion logic adds implementation complexity compared to simple uniform or stratified sampling. Performance depends heavily on the accuracy of the occupancy grid and the density function. When to use: Neural Radiance Fields for large-scale outdoor scenes (e.g., KITTI-360, Argoverse2) where empty space is prevalent and computational efficiency is critical. When not to use: Small-scale indoor scenes with dense geometry where empty space skipping provides little benefit, or when inference speed is prioritized over quality and density checking is disabled. The method is part of the Lightning-NeRF framework, designed for efficient training and inference of neural radiance fields in autonomous driving scenarios. It leverages the nerfacc library for efficient ray marching and packing operations. The approach combines the spatial efficiency of occupancy grids with the statistical efficiency of importance sampling to handle the scale and sparsity of real-world driving data. name: Occupancy Map Generation via Ray Casting
head: DVGO Voxel Count Views
body: This method generates an occupancy map by counting the number of rays passing through each voxel in a 3D grid, identifying regions viewed by training cameras to initialize or refine the geometry mask. Inputs: rays: Tensor of ray origins and directions. worldsize: Dimensions of the 3D grid. stepsize: Distance between sample points along a ray. near, far: Clamping distances for ray segment intersection. downrate: Downsampling factor for rays if irregularshape is false. irregularshape: Boolean flag determining ray batching strategy. Outputs: count: A zero-initialized tensor with the same shape as the density grid, accumulating ray hits. Data Structures: count: 3D tensor, shape (D, H, W), dtype float32. ones: A DenseGrid object representing a 3D grid of ones, used for gradient accumulation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateoccupancymap(rays, worldsize, stepsize, near, far, downrate, irregularshape, worldbounds): count = torch.zeros(worldsize, dtype=torch.float32) if irregularshape: raybatches = [rays[i:i+10000] for i in range(0, len(rays), 10000)] else: raysdownsampled = rays[::downrate,::downrate].reshape(-1, rays.shape[-1]) raybatches = [raysdownsampled[i:i+10000] for i in range(0, len(raysdownsampled), 10000)] for batch in raybatches: ones = DenseGrid(size=1, worldsize=worldsize, bounds=worldbounds) vec = batch.direction.clone() vec[vec == 0] = 1e-6 ratea = (worldbounds.min - batch.origin) / vec rateb = (worldbounds.max - batch.origin) / vec tmin = max(min(ratea), min(rateb)) tmax = min(max(ratea), max(rateb)) tmin = clamp(tmin, near, far) tmax = clamp(tmax, near, far) Nsamples = int(np.linalg.norm(np.array(worldsize) + 1) / stepsize) + 1 interpx = torch.linspace(tmin, tmax, Nsamples) rayspts = batch.origin + interpx.unsqueeze(1) batch.direction ones.query(rayspts).backward() count += (ones.grad > 1).float() return count Formulas: Sample count per ray: N{\text{samples}} = \left\lfloor \frac{\| \text{world\size} + 1 \|}{\text{stepsize}} \right\rfloor + 1. Intersection bounds: t{\min} = \max(\min(\text{rate\a}), \min(\text{rate\b})) and t{\max} = \min(\max(\text{rate\a}), \max(\text{rate\b})), clamped to [\text{near}, \text{far}]. Parameters: far: Set to 10^9 to prevent rays from stopping early due to small bounding box limits. Nsamples: Calculated as above. Edge Cases: Division by zero in ray direction normalization is handled by replacing zeros with 10^{-6}. Small bounding box limits causing premature ray termination are mitigated by setting far to 10^9. Not given in the sources. name: Brick Occupancy Recomputation
head: Brick Occupancy Compute
body: Brick Occupancy Recomputation is a GPU compute shader routine that regenerates the occupancy status of volumetric bricks after dynamic voxel changes, ensuring the hierarchical traversal structure remains consistent with the underlying voxel data. It differs from static generation methods by being designed for frequent, localized updates in interactive simulations, relying on shared memory reduction to avoid atomic operations and global memory contention. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A texture containing voxel data (1-bit solid/air flags) organized into fixed-size bricks. Output: An occupancy map (brickmap) where each entry corresponds to a brick, storing the count of non-air voxels within that brick. Data Structures: Voxel Texture: 1-bit per voxel representation of solid vs. air. Occupancy Map: Array of unsigned integers, one per brick. Shared Memory: Array of 32 unsigned integers, one per thread in the block. Parameters: Thread Block Size: Exactly 32 threads. Voxels per Thread: 16 voxels. Brick Size: Implicitly 32 \times 16 = 512 voxels per brick. Steps: 1. Dispatch: Launch a compute shader where each thread block is assigned to process exactly one brick. 2. Load: Each of the 32 threads reads 16 voxels from its assigned segment of the brick. 3. Count: Each thread counts the number of voxels in its segment that are not air (i.e., are solid). 4. Store: Each thread writes its count to a unique index in a shared memory array of unsigned integers. 5. Sync: Execute a barrier synchronization to ensure all threads have written their partial counts to shared memory. 6. Reduce: The first thread (thread ID 0) sums the values from the shared memory array. 7. Write: Thread 0 writes the total sum to the corresponding entry in the brickmap. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def brickoccupancyrecompute(brickid, voxeltexture, occupancymap): sharedcounts = [0] 32 threadidx = getlocalthreadid() # 0 to 31 brickstart = brickid 512 voxelbase = brickstart + (threadidx 16) count = 0 for i in range(16): voxelval = voxeltexture[voxelbase + i] if voxelval & 1: # 1-bit solid/air flag count += 1 sharedcounts[threadidx] = count threadbarrier() # Synchronize all threads in the block if threadidx == 0: total = sum(sharedcounts) occupancymap[brickid] = total def getlocalthreadid(): return 0 # Thread 0 to 31 within the block def threadbarrier(): pass # Blocks until all threads in the group reach this point Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Uses a 1-bit per voxel solid/air flag; maximum count per brick is 512. Boundaries: Assumes brick boundaries align with the voxel grid and texture sampling coordinates. Degenerate Input: If the voxel texture is not properly bound or aligned, reads may return undefined values. A two-level hierarchical data structure combining an N-ary tree for hierarchy with regular voxel bricks in leaves, generalizing octree-based Brick Maps for efficient GPU traversal and filtering. See N3-tree with regular mipmapped bricks. Time Complexity: O(1) per brick, proportional to the number of voxels in the brick (512 reads, 32 writes). Memory Complexity: O(1) per brick for shared memory (32 integers). Performance: Fast due to avoidance of atomic operations and use of fast shared memory. Strengths: Low latency and no global memory contention. Limitations: Fixed brick size (512 voxels) and thread count (32). When to Use: Interactive voxel simulations where the world changes frequently and collision detection requires up-to-date occupancy data. When Not to Use: Static volumes or scenes where occupancy rarely changes. Originated in the context of voxel-based game development, specifically for the "VoxelPlayground" project by Joris Rijsdijk, to handle dynamic voxel changes in a brick-based rendering and physics system. It addresses the problem of maintaining consistency between the voxel data and the hierarchical occupancy map used for efficient traversal and collision detection. name: N3-tree with regular mipmapped bricks
head: N3-tree with regular voxel bricks, N3-tree+briques de voxels
body: The N3-tree with regular mipmapped bricks is a two-level hierarchical data structure for procedural volume exploration that combines an N-ary tree (N3-tree) for hierarchy with regular voxel bricks stored in the leaves. It links the compactness of a hierarchical structure with the efficient traversal and trilinear/quadrilinear filtering capabilities of regular grids on GPU. It generalizes the original octree-based Brick Maps to allow arbitrary subdivision of nodes (N-ary instead of binary octree) to enable efficient GPU traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A procedural volume defined by a total maximum resolution Rt on each axis, a maximum brick resolution Rb, and a node subdivision resolution N. Output: A GPU-accessible structure consisting of an indirection texture (the tree), a brick storage texture (the data), and a brick indirection storage (mip-level mapping). Data Structures: 1. Indirection Storage (The Tree): Format: 3D texture using an unsigned integer RGBA format with 32 bits per component. Layout: Each node in the N3-tree is stored as a small N^3 grid of indirection cells within this texture. Spatial Locality: The N^3 grids are organized using a Peano curve (Swizzled Walk) layout to maximize cache efficiency during tree traversal. Cell Encoding (Sub-node information): Each cell contains 32 bits packed as follows: Red (R): 3D address (X, Y, Z) of the child node or the regular brick in the brick storage. Green (G): 3D address of the parent node. Blue (B): Reserved for future use. Alpha (A): Average value of all voxels in the node's covered space. Flags: 1 bit identifies the sub-node type (brick or tree node) and 1 bit identifies an empty node flag (no descendants). Addressable Dimension: The 10-bit address per coordinate allows addressing elements in a storage of maximum dimension 1024^3. 2. Brick Storage (The Data): Format: 3D texture storing regular scalar density data or gradients. Layout: Divided into zones grouping bricks of identical resolution. Brick Structure: Each brick includes its data plus a 1-voxel border surrounding the data to allow trilinear filtering without artifacts from adjacent bricks. Filtering: Accessed in the shader by floating-point coordinates; integer coordinates from the indirection storage are transformed on the fly. 3. Brick Indirection Storage: Purpose: Links the hierarchical tree to brick data. Content: A list of addresses for each brick's data for every mip-mapping level in the brick storage. Unloaded Data: Entries marked with a negative value indicate unloaded data. Manual Mip-mapping: Hardware mip-mapping requires duplicating the 1-voxel border 2^n times for a stack of n levels and halving it at each sub-level, which is memory expensive. This method implements 3D mip-mapping manually to achieve identical performance cost but with lower memory overhead. Number of Nodes: In the worst case (full resolution, no empty space skipping), the number of nodes to store in the tree is calculated as: \sum{i=0}^{n} \left( \frac{Nb}{N^i} \right)^3 Where: n = \frac{\log(Nb)}{\log N} Nb = \frac{Rt}{Rb} Rt: Total maximum resolution on each axis. Rb: Maximum resolution of a brick. N: Resolution of each node (e.g., N=2 for octree). Parameters: Example: Rt = 1024^3, N = 4, Rb = 16. Result: An indirection storage of 64^3 is nearly sufficient. Recommended Size: A practical recommended size is 128^3. Degrees of Freedom: Node subdivision resolution (N) and regular brick resolution. These impact traversal performance and update efficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def encodeaddress3d(x, y, z): """Encodes a 3D address into a 30-bit integer (10 bits per coordinate).""" return (x << 20) | (y << 10) | z def packsubnode(childaddr30bit, parentaddr30bit, nodetypebit, emptyflag): """Packs sub-node information into a 32-bit integer for the Red channel. 30 bits address, 1 bit type, 1 bit empty.""" return (childaddr30bit << 2) | (nodetypebit << 1) | emptyflag def generatepeanocoords(dim): """Generates Peano curve coordinates for a dim x dim x dim grid.""" coords = [] def peanorecursive(level, x, y, z, orientation): if level == 0: coords.append((x, y, z)) return step = 1 << (level - 1) if orientation == 0: peanorecursive(level - 1, x, y, z, 1) peanorecursive(level - 1, x + step, y, z, 0) peanorecursive(level - 1, x + step, y + step, z, 0) peanorecursive(level - 1, x, y + step, z, 3) elif orientation == 1: peanorecursive(level - 1, x, y, z, 0) peanorecursive(level - 1, x, y + step, z, 0) peanorecursive(level - 1, x + step, y + step, z, 1) peanorecursive(level - 1, x + step, y, z, 2) elif orientation == 2: peanorecursive(level - 1, x + step, y + step, z, 3) peanorecursive(level - 1, x + step, y, z, 2) peanorecursive(level - 1, x, y, z, 2) peanorecursive(level - 1, x, y + step, z, 1) else: peanorecursive(level - 1, x + step, y + step, z, 2) peanorecursive(level - 1, x, y + step, z, 2) peanorecursive(level - 1, x, y, z, 3) peanorecursive(level - 1, x + step, y, z, 0) peanorecursive(int(math.log2(dim)), 0, 0, 0, 0) return coords def calculatetreesize(Rt, Rb, N): """Calculates the worst-case number of nodes in the N3-tree.""" Nb = Rt / Rb n = math.log(Nb) / math.log(N) totalnodes = 0 for i in range(int(n) + 1): totalnodes += (Nb / (N i)) 3 return totalnodes def buildindirectiontexture(Rt, Rb, N): """Constructs the indirection texture structure.""" nodescount = calculatetreesize(Rt, Rb, N) texdim = 128 # Recommended practical size peanocoords = generatepeanocoords(texdim) # Initialize texture as a flat list of 32-bit integer tuples texture = [None] (texdim 3) # Precompute brick address for root leaf if needed, or use 0 rootbrickaddr = encodeaddress3d(0, 0, 0) # Populate texture using Peano order for idx, (px, py, pz) in enumerate(peanocoords): # For simplicity, assume root node covers the whole volume # In a real traversal, this would be recursive based on data density childaddr = rootbrickaddr parentaddr = 0 nodetype = 1 # Brick emptyflag = 0 rchannel = packsubnode(childaddr, parentaddr, nodetype, emptyflag) gchannel = encodeaddress3d(parentaddr >> 20, (parentaddr >> 10) & 0x3FF, parentaddr & 0x3FF) bchannel = 0 achannel = 0 # Average value placeholder texture[px texdim 2 + py texdim + pz] = (rchannel, gchannel, bchannel, achannel) return texture def buildbrickstorage(Rt, Rb): """Constructs the brick storage texture and brick indirection storage.""" numbricks = Rt / Rb brickindirection = [] for x in range(int(numbricks)): for y in range(int(numbricks)): for z in range(int(numbricks)): brickaddr = encodeaddress3d(x, y, z) miplevels = int(math.log2(Rb)) + 1 brickentry = [-1] miplevels brickentry[0] = brickaddr brickindirection.append(brickentry) return brickindirection The original octree-based structure for global illumination that this method generalizes. Brick Maps The broader category of ray-grid traversal techniques that use hierarchical structures to skip empty space. Hierarchical Grid Traversal Time Complexity: Traversal is efficient on GPU due to the regular grid structure of leaves and the use of 3D textures which exploit hardware cache spatial locality (via Peano curve layout). Memory Complexity: The indirection storage size is determined by the worst-case node count. For Rt=1024^3, N=4, Rb=16, a 64^3 texture is nearly sufficient, but 128^3 is recommended for practical scenes. The manual mip-mapping reduces memory overhead compared to hardware mip-mapping by avoiding border duplication. Strengths: Combines hierarchical compactness with regular grid filtering efficiency. Manual mip-mapping saves memory. Peano curve layout optimizes cache hits. Limitations: Worst-case memory usage can be high if the volume is dense. Update efficiency is secondary to traversal performance but impacted by the choice of N and brick resolution. When to use: Procedural volume exploration on GPU where memory bandwidth and cache efficiency are critical. When not to use: If hardware mip-mapping memory overhead is not a concern and the volume is sparse enough that a simpler octree suffices. The method was developed by Sylvain Lefebvre et al. as an adaptation of the hierarchical volumetric textures model proposed by Sylvain Lefebvre [LHN05] for GPU implementation. It generalizes the Brick Maps proposed by Christensen and Batali [CB04] for global illumination. The work is part of the thesis "Représentation et algorithmes pour l'exploration interactive de volumes procéduraux étendus et détaillés". name: NanoMap GPU-Accelerated Occupancy Mapping
head: GPU-Accelerated OpenVDB-Based Mapping, NanoMap
body: NanoMap is a probabilistic mapping solution that encodes dense point clouds into OpenVDB data structures by off-loading computationally expensive filtering and ray-casting operations to a CUDA-compatible GPU. It solves the bottleneck of processing tens to hundreds of thousands of points on CPUs, which lack sufficient thread counts for meaningful acceleration. Unlike CPU-based predecessors, NanoMap leverages the parallel compute strength of GPUs and the sparse, steep-branching nature of OpenVDB to provide significant speed advantages for real-time updates in dynamic environments. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A point cloud (set of 3D points), an agent/sensor pose, and sensor metadata (used for GPU memory allocation). Outputs: An OpenVDB occupancy grid where cells traversed by rays are marked empty and end-points are marked occupied. Data Structures: The core data structure is the OpenVDB grid, described as a configurable tree structure similar to B+ Trees. Key characteristics include: Steep Branching Factor: Unlike octrees which have 8 children per node, OpenVDB uses a steep branching factor, limiting the maximum number of steps for lookup/insertion. User-Programmable Depth: The depth of the tree is configurable. Caching: The structure implements caching for spatially coherent lookups and insertions, allowing subsequent operations to reference the cache and find target locations in memory immediately. GPU Variant: The GPU implementation uses NanoVDB, a module developed to enable improved rendering and simulation of OpenVDB structures on CUDA GPUs. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Allocate necessary memory for GPU interaction using the user-supplied sensor information. 2. Ray Construction: For each point in the input point cloud, create a ray. The ray's start location is the sensor pose, and the end location is the point coordinate. 3. Ray Casting and Encoding: Step along each ray over a temporary grid. Encode all cells encountered along the ray path as empty. Encode the cell occupied by the end of the ray as occupied. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Ray Marching with Occupancy Grid Skipping
head: grid-based ray marching
body: A GPU-accelerated ray marching algorithm that samples along rays, optionally skipping empty space using a 3D occupancy grid and handling scene contractions. It differs from its parent Distance Map Acceleration by relying on a binary occupancy structure for traversal logic rather than continuous distance fields for step sizing, and from siblings like Partitioned Distance Map Combination by using a single global grid for visibility culling. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origins rayso (CUDA tensor), ray directions raysd, optional scene axis-aligned bounding box sceneaabb, near/far planes nearplane/farplane, base step size renderstepsize, cone angle coneangle, and an optional 3D occupancy grid grid. Outputs: Sample positions tstarts, tends, ray indices rayindices, and packed traversal info packedinfo. Data Structures gridbinary: 3D boolean tensor of shape (resox, resoy, resoz) representing occupied voxels. roi: 1D float32 tensor of shape (6) containing [roimin.x, roimin.y, roimin.z, roimax.x, roimax.y, roimax.z]. packedinfo: 2D int32 tensor of shape (nrays, 2). Column 0 stores the cumulative start index (cumsteps - numsteps), and Column 1 stores the number of steps per ray. rayindices: 1D int64 tensor of shape (totalsteps) mapping each sample to its originating ray. tstarts: 2D float32 tensor of shape (totalsteps, 1) marking the start of each sample interval. tends: 2D float32 tensor of shape (totalsteps, 1) marking the end of each sample interval. Parameters renderstepsize: Base step size for sampling, typically 10^{-3}. coneangle: Used to calculate dynamic step size dt = \text{clamp}(t \cdot \text{cone\angle}, dt{min}, dt{max}). earlystopeps: Epsilon threshold for early stopping in visibility rendering. alphathre: Alpha threshold for filtering invisible samples. Algorithm Steps 1. Input Validation: Raise NotImplementedError if rayso is not on CUDA. Raise ValueError if both alphafn and sigmafn are provided. 2. Determine Bounds: If tmin/tmax are None, compute ray-AABB intersection using sceneaabb if provided; otherwise set tmin = 0.0 and tmax = 10^{10}. 3. Clip Planes: Clip tmin with nearplane and tmax with farplane if provided. 4. Stratified Sampling: If enabled, add uniform random noise to tmin: t{min} = t{min} + \text{torch.rand\like}(t{min}) \cdot \text{render\step\size}. 5. Grid Setup: If grid is None, set gridroiaabb to [-10^{10}, -10^{10}, -10^{10}, 10^{10}, 10^{10}, 10^{10}], gridbinary to [1,1,1] bool, and contractiontype to AABB. 6. Traversal & Filtering: Perform ray marching. If a grid is provided and contraction is AABB, use DDA-based voxel skipping to jump over empty regions. Filter rayindices, tstarts, and tends based on rendervisibility masks and return the filtered arrays. Pitfalls Scene contraction types other than AABB do not work with DDA-based voxel skipping and fall back to regular stepping. If grid is not provided, a dummy 1 \times 1 \times 1 grid is used to ensure the kernel runs without crashing. Complexity: Time complexity depends on the density of the occupancy grid; in sparse scenes, it approaches O(1) per ray for empty space, while dense regions degrade to standard ray marching O(N) where N is the number of samples. Memory complexity is O(V) for the grid volume V. Performance: Accelerates rendering in scenes with large empty volumes by skipping unnecessary samples. Limitations: Ineffective for non-AABB contractions or highly dense scenes where skipping yields minimal benefit. This method is implemented in the RISE-SDF project, a GPU-accelerated framework for implicit surface reconstruction and rendering. It builds on Distance Map Acceleration by replacing distance-based step estimation with binary occupancy checks for traversal efficiency. dehezhang2/RISE-SDF, https://github.com/dehezhang2/RISE-SDF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Two-stage Ray Marching with Empty-Space Skipping
head: Empty Space Compactness, Occupancy Map Empty Space Skipping, Occupancy-based early exit, Simple occupancy map traversal, Two-phase volumetric rendering
body: Two-stage Ray Marching with Empty-Space Skipping is a rendering optimization that accelerates ray traversal in sparse volumetric data by bypassing empty regions using a precomputed occupancy map. It splits ray traversal into two distinct phases: Stage 1 performs cheap lookups in a lower-resolution occupancy grid to locate the entry point into active volume blocks, and Stage 2 performs expensive density sampling only within those active segments. This method sets itself apart from its siblings by decoupling the traversal logic into a coarse "find entry" phase and a fine "integrate" phase, relying on a flat or sparse occupancy grid rather than hierarchical structures like octrees. It builds on the shared principles of Occupancy Grid and Map-Based Empty Space Skipping by utilizing a secondary acceleration structure to define active regions and skip empty space. The method operates by first constructing an occupancy map that indicates which blocks of the primary volume contain data. During rendering, rays traverse this map to skip empty space, then switch to high-resolution sampling upon entering an occupied block. Inputs: Primary volume data (density/opacity field) at resolution N{vol} \times N{vol} \times N{vol}. Occupancy map at resolution N{occ} \times N{occ} \times N{occ}, where N{occ} = N{vol} / B and B is the block size factor. Camera parameters: origin, direction, projection matrix, and world-to-camera transform. Volume bounds: \mathbf{B}{extent} (half-extents) and voxel resolution V{res}. Parameters: RayMaxLength, DensityMult, Smoothing, SmokeOrigin, SmokeRadius. Outputs: Final color buffer (image) with accumulated opacity and color. 1. Primary Volume Buffer: A 3D texture or structured buffer storing density/opacity values. 2. Occupancy Map: A 3D texture or structured buffer storing binary or scalar occupancy status. Layout: Flattened 1D buffer index for voxel (x, y, z) in row-major order: \text{index} = z \cdot (N{vol,x} \cdot N{vol,y}) + y \cdot N{vol,x} + x Values: Typically 0 (empty) or 1 (filled/active). Out-of-bounds queries return -1. 3. Ray State: origin: Camera position in world space. rayVector: Normalized direction vector. length: Current distance along the ray. smokeValue: Current sampled occupancy value (0 for empty, 1 for occupied). A compute shader generates the occupancy map. Each shader invocation evaluates a unique volume block for occupancy and writes the result to the associated occupancy map voxel. For each block in the occupancy grid, sample the corresponding region in the primary volume. Determine occupancy based on a threshold (e.g., max density > 0 or opacity > \epsilon). Write the result to the occupancy map voxel. For each pixel (u, v): 1. Compute ray direction in world space: \mathbf{d}{clip} = (u \cdot 2 - 1, v \cdot 2 - 1, 0) \mathbf{d}{cam} = \text{mul}(\mathbf{M}{invProj}, \mathbf{d}{clip}) \mathbf{rayVector} = \text{normalize}(\text{mul}(\mathbf{M}{camToWorld}, \mathbf{d}{cam})) 2. Set origin to camera position. 3. Initialize length = 0, stepSize = \Delta t{vol} (volume voxel step), smokeValue = 0 (indicating Stage 1 active). Loop until an occupied block is found or the ray exits the volume: 1. Calculate current world position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{origin} + \text{length} \cdot \mathbf{rayVector} 2. Check volume bounds. If \mathbf{p} is outside \mathbf{B}{extent}, return black color (miss). 3. Query occupancy map: Convert \mathbf{p} to occupancy grid coordinates: \mathbf{u}{occ} = \lfloor \mathbf{p} / (B \cdot V{res}) \rfloor (Derived from parent principles and S1 Eq. 10) Sample smokeValue = getSmokeVoxel(p). 4. Skip Logic: If smokeValue == 0 (empty block): Calculate steps to next occupancy voxel boundary. Using the vectorized step calculation: \Delta \mathbf{i} = \lceil (\text{step}(\Delta \mathbf{u}) + \lfloor \mathbf{u} \rfloor - \mathbf{u}) / \Delta \mathbf{u} \rceil where \Delta \mathbf{u} is the ray step in occupancy space: \Delta \mathbf{u}{\text{occ}} = \frac{d{\text{vol}}}{B} \Delta \mathbf{t}{\text{vol}} The scalar step to advance is: \Delta i = \max(\min(\Delta \mathbf{i}), 1) Update length += \Delta i \cdot \Delta t{vol}. If smokeValue == 1 (occupied block): Backward Adjustment: To account for interpolation halos or boundary isosurfaces, decrement the step count to ensure the ray goes back at least one voxel length: \Delta i{\text{backward}} = -\lfloor f \rfloor where f is the sampling factor. \text{length} += \Delta i{\text{backward}} \cdot \Delta t{vol} Switch to Stage 2. Perform high-resolution integration within the occupied block. 1. Initialize stage2StepNum = 0, accumulatedDensity = 0, stage2StepMax = 40 (or until ray exit). 2. Loop while stage2StepNum < stage2StepMax: Calculate samplePoint = origin + length rayVector. Compute density: \text{density} = 1 - \text{smoothstep}(\text{Smoothing}, 1.0, \frac{\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{S}{origin}\|}{\mathbf{S}{radius}}) (Note: Source uses screen UVs for noise, which is a known pitfall; correct implementation uses world position). Accumulate: accumulatedDensity += density DensityMult. Update length += stepSize. Increment stage2StepNum. 3. Resume Skipping: After Stage 2, check if the ray is still within an occupied block. If the occupancy map coordinate u{occ} changes and the previously sampled voxel had zero opacity, resume Stage 1 skipping. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twostageraymarch(origin, rayvector, volumetexture, occupancymap, params): """ params: B: Block size factor (ratio of vol res to occ res) voxelres: Resolution of primary volume voxels (world units per voxel) boundsextent: Half-extents of volume bounds (x, y, z) raymaxlength: Maximum ray length densitymult: Scaling factor for density smoothing: Smoothstep parameter smokeorigin, smokeradius: Sphere parameters for density stage2max: Fixed step limit for Stage 2 (default 40) """ length = 0.0 stepsize = params.voxelres smokevalue = 0 # 0: empty, 1: occupied stage2steps = 0 stage2max = params.stage2max accumulateddensity = 0.0 instage2 = False # Precompute occupancy step delta in world units # From S1 Eq 10: Delta uocc = (dvol / B) Delta tvol. # Here Delta tvol is the step in volume space (voxelres). deltauocc = rayvector (params.voxelres / params.B) while length < params.raymaxlength: pos = origin + length rayvector # Bounds check (fixed asymmetric bug from S2) if (abs(pos.x) > params.boundsextent.x or abs(pos.y) > params.boundsextent.y or abs(pos.z) > params.boundsextent.z): return 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # Miss if not instage2: # Stage 1: Empty Space Skipping occcoord = [int(floor(pos.x / (params.B params.voxelres))), int(floor(pos.y / (params.B params.voxelres))), int(floor(pos.z / (params.B params.voxelres)))] smokevalue = occupancymap.sample(occcoord) if smokevalue == 0: # Empty block: Skip to next occupancy voxel boundary uocc = [pos.x / (params.B params.voxelres), pos.y / (params.B params.voxelres), pos.z / (params.B params.voxelres)] deltaivec = [] for j in range(3): if deltauocc[j] == 0: deltaivec.append(float('inf')) else: stepval = 1.0 if deltauocc[j] >= 0 else 0.0 numerator = stepval + floor(uocc[j]) - uocc[j] deltaivec.append(ceil(numerator / deltauocc[j])) deltai = max(min(deltaivec), 1.0) length += deltai params.voxelres else: # Occupied block found # Backward adjustment for interpolation halos (S1 Eq 11) length -= params.voxelres instage2 = True stage2steps = 0 accumulateddensity = 0.0 else: # Stage 2: Density Sampling samplepoint = pos distfromorigin = sqrt(sum((samplepoint[k] - params.smokeorigin[k])2 for k in range(3))) normalizeddist = distfromorigin / params.smokeradius density = 1.0 - smoothstep(params.smoothing, 1.0, normalizeddist) accumulateddensity += density params.densitymult length += params.voxelres stage2steps += 1 # Check if we exited the occupied block to resume skipping (S1) occcoord = [int(floor(pos.x / (params.B params.voxelres))), int(floor(pos.y / (params.B params.voxelres))), int(floor(pos.z / (params.B params.voxelres)))] currentocc = occupancymap.sample(occcoord) if currentocc == 0 or stage2steps >= params.stage2max: instage2 = False smokevalue = 0 return accumulateddensity, 0.0, 0.0 def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) B (Block Size): Ratio of volume resolution to occupancy map resolution. Larger B skips more empty voxels per sample but reduces precision near occupied regions. Typical values depend on sparsity; e.g., B=4 or B=8. Step Size: Usually equal to the primary volume voxel resolution. Stage 2 Max Steps: Fixed limit (e.g., 40) or until ray exit. Smoothing: Smoothstep edge parameter for density falloff. 1. Stage 2 Bounds Ignorance: The accumulation loop may run for a fixed number of steps regardless of whether the ray has exited the voxel grid, causing smoke to bleed past the volume boundary. 2. Asymmetric Bounds Check: Incorrect bounds checking logic (e.g., position.y < -BoundsExtent.y + BoundsExtent.y) can anchor the volume incorrectly or cause out-of-bounds access. 3. Variable Shadowing: Using length as a variable name can shadow intrinsic functions like length() in HLSL/GLSL. 4. Screen-Space Noise: Sampling noise using screen UVs (uv) pins the noise pattern to the screen, causing it to "swim" as the camera moves. Correct implementation requires sampling noise using world position (samplePoint). 5. Interpolation Halos: Trilinear interpolation can cause a sampling point near the edge of an empty block to map to a non-zero opacity if a neighboring block is occupied. The backward adjustment step is necessary to prevent missing these boundary details. An image-space method that uses detector rays and space leap rays to skip empty space without pre-processing or 3D data structures. Choose when memory is constrained or transfer functions change frequently. Builds on this method by using a preprocessed occupancy map to jump directly from one non-empty voxel to the next. Choose for sparse datasets where a flat occupancy grid offers a better trade-off between memory and traversal simplicity than hierarchical structures. Time Complexity: Stage 1 is O(1) per occupancy voxel visited. Stage 2 is O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the active segment. Total time is proportional to the number of active voxels plus the number of empty blocks skipped. Memory Complexity: O(N{occ}^3) for the occupancy map, where N{occ} = N{vol} / B. This is significantly smaller than the primary volume if B > 1. Performance: Performance scales with the sparsity of the volume. Higher B values improve performance on sparse volumes but may reduce accuracy near boundaries. Strengths: Significantly reduces the number of samples that need to be processed. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of the occupancy map; less effective for dense volumes; fixed step size in Stage 2 may lead to over-sampling or bleeding. The method originates from efficient ray casting techniques for volumetric images, specifically utilizing distance maps and occupancy grids for empty space skipping. It is a foundational technique in GPU-based volume rendering, often implemented using compute shaders to generate the occupancy map and ray marching kernels to perform the traversal. name: PDF Light Weight Space Leaping
head: LWSL, Light Weight Space Leaping, Light Weight Space Leaping using Ray Coherence, Ray Coherence Space Leaping, Space Leaping using Ray Coherence
body: PDF Light Weight Space Leaping (LWSL) is a space-leaping acceleration technique for volume rendering that exploits ray coherence to skip empty space without requiring pre-processing or 3D data structures. It divides image-plane rays into two groups: detector rays, which perform full ray casting to determine the distance to the first non-empty cell, and space leap rays, which are accelerated by skipping empty space based on information propagated from detector rays. Unlike data-structure-based methods (e.g., DFB) or temporal coherence techniques, LWSL is an image-space method with memory and run-time complexity proportional only to the image size, making it independent of dataset complexity and transfer function changes. Inputs: Volume dataset (voxel grid). Camera parameters (eye position, image plane resolution, projection type: parallel or perspective). Sampling distance \delta. Detector pixel configuration (e.g., 1:4 zig-zag pattern). Outputs: Rendered image buffer. Data Structures: Leap Buffer: A 2D array with resolution equal to the image plane. Each element is an 8-bit or 16-bit integer storing the number of samples the ray traverses in empty space before hitting a non-empty cell. For detector pixels: Stores the sample count returned by the detector ray. For space leap pixels: Stores the minimum sample count from neighboring detector rays in their influence area. Initialization: All entries are zero (empty) before Phase 1. Detector Mask: A boolean array indicating which pixels are detector pixels. Definitions: Cell: A cubical region with voxels at all eight corners and no voxels inside. Empty Cell: A cell where the opacity of all eight corner voxels is zero (for tri-linear interpolation). For higher-order interpolation, all contributing neighboring voxels must have zero opacity. Cell Group: The set of 8 cells surrounding a single voxel. Influence Area: The set of neighboring non-detector pixels to which a detector pixel spreads its leap information. It includes all pixels that could potentially project onto the same cell group without intersecting another detector ray. Parameters: Detector Density: 1 detector ray for every 4 pixels (1:4 ratio) using a zig-zag scheme. Leap Buffer Type: 8-bit or 16-bit integer. Algorithm Steps: 1. Phase 1: Detector Ray Casting 1. Initialize the Leap Buffer to zero and the Detector Mask to false. 2. Identify detector pixels using the zig-zag pattern. 3. For each detector pixel: a. Cast a ray from the pixel into the volume. b. Traverse the ray, checking for empty cells. c. To check if a cell is empty, perform a bitwise OR operation on the opacity values of all voxels in the cell (or all contributing voxels for higher-order interpolation). If the result is non-zero, the cell is non-empty; otherwise, it is empty. d. Skip interpolation, shading, and compositing for empty cells to save time. e. Count the number of samples (N{det}) taken until the first non-empty cell is encountered. f. Store N{det} in the Leap Buffer at the detector pixel's location. g. Mark the location in the Detector Mask as true. h. Perform full ray casting (sampling, compositing, shading) for the detector ray and store the result in the image buffer. 2. Phase 2: Leap Buffer Filling (Spreading) 1. For each detector pixel: a. Identify its influence area (neighboring non-detector pixels). b. For each pixel in the influence area: i. If the neighbor's Leap Buffer value is zero (unset), store the detector pixel's N{det} value. ii. If the neighbor's value is already set, compare it with N{det} and store the minimum of the two. This ensures a conservative estimate, preventing the ray from overshooting a non-empty cell. 2. After spreading, the Leap Buffer is fully populated with the minimum empty-space traversal counts for all pixels. 3. Phase 3: Space Leap Ray Casting 1. Sweep the Leap Buffer from top to bottom (or any order) to find non-detector pixels. 2. For each non-detector pixel: a. Retrieve the leap count N{leap} from the Leap Buffer. b. Boundary Check: If N{leap} == 0, do not leap. Start ray casting from the image plane. c. Perspective Clamp (if applicable): If the projected distance exceeds the maximum accuracy distance x1xn (see Formulas), clamp N{leap} to the corresponding sample count for x1xn. d. Leap: Move the ray start point forward by N{leap} \times \delta along the ray direction. e. Backtracking Check: Sample the first point after leaping. If this point is inside a non-empty cell, backtrack the ray origin backwards by sample steps until an empty cell is found. The maximum backtracking distance is bounded by the longest edge of a cell group divided by \delta. f. Perform standard ray casting (sampling, compositing, shading) from the new start point. Early ray termination can be applied. Formulas: Minimum Projection Width (w{min}): w{min} = \sqrt{p^2 + (2p)^2} = p\sqrt{5} where p is the inter-pixel distance on the image plane in world coordinates. Maximum Inter-pixel Distance for Parallel Projection (p{max}): p{max} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \mu{min} where \mu{min} is the length of the smallest edge of the voxel unit size. To guarantee detection of single voxels, p \le p{max}. Maximum Ray Traversal Distance for Perspective Projection (x1xn): x1xn = \left( \frac{\sqrt{2} \times \mu{min}}{\sqrt{5} \times p} - 1 \right) \times ex1 where ex1 is the distance from the eye to the image plane. Rays should not leap beyond this distance to maintain accuracy. Backtracking Limit (M{max}): M{max} = \frac{\max(\mux, \muy, \muz)}{\delta} where \mux, \muy, \muz are the cell group edge lengths (or voxel dimensions along the axes) and \delta is the sampling distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def lightweightspaceleaping(volume, camera, imagewidth, imageheight, delta, bounds): # 1. Initialize Data Structures leapbuffer = [[0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] isdetector = [[False] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] imagebuffer = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight imagewidth)] # 2. Identify Detector Pixels (1:4 Zig-Zag Pattern) detectorpixels = [] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Zig-zag/Checkerboard pattern ensuring 1 detector per 4 pixels if (x % 2 == 0 and y % 2 == 0) or (x % 2 == 1 and y % 2 == 1): detectorpixels.append((x, y)) isdetector[x][y] = True # 3. Phase 1: Cast Detector Rays for (dx, dy) in detectorpixels: rayorigin, raydir = camera.getray(dx, dy) samplescount = 0 currentpos = list(rayorigin) # Traverse until non-empty cell or end of volume while volume.contains(currentpos): cell = volume.getcellat(currentpos) # Check emptiness via bitwise OR of corner opacities cellopacityor = 0 for voxel in cell.corners: cellopacityor |= voxel.opacity if cellopacityor == 0: samplescount += 1 currentpos[0] += raydir[0] delta currentpos[1] += raydir[1] delta currentpos[2] += raydir[2] delta else: break # Store leap info leapbuffer[dx][dy] = samplescount isdetector[dx][dy] = True # Full ray casting for detector pixel color = castray(rayorigin, raydir, volume, delta, samplescount) imagebuffer[dy imagewidth + dx] = color # 4. Phase 2: Fill Leap Buffer (Spreading) # Influence area covers neighbors that could share a cell group projection # Exact radius depends on geometry; a 3x3 window covers immediate neighbors spreadradius = 1 for (dx, dy) in detectorpixels: leapval = leapbuffer[dx][dy] for ny in range(dy - spreadradius, dy + spreadradius + 1): for nx in range(dx - spreadradius, dx + spreadradius + 1): if 0 <= nx < imagewidth and 0 <= ny < imageheight: if not isdetector[nx][ny]: currentval = leapbuffer[nx][ny] if currentval == 0: # Unset leapbuffer[nx][ny] = leapval else: leapbuffer[nx][ny] = min(currentval, leapval) # 5. Phase 3: Cast Space Leap Rays for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): if not isdetector[x][y]: leapval = leapbuffer[x][y] # Boundary check if leapval == 0: rayorigin, raydir = camera.getray(x, y) color = castray(rayorigin, raydir, volume, delta, 0) imagebuffer[y imagewidth + x] = color continue # Perspective clamp maxsamples = calculatemaxsamplesforaccuracy(camera, delta) effectiveleap = min(leapval, maxsamples) rayorigin, raydir = camera.getray(x, y) rayorigin = [rayorigin[i] + raydir[i] effectiveleap delta for i in range(3)] # Backtracking check backtracksteps = 0 maxbacktrack = calculatemaxsamplesforaccuracy(camera, delta) # Upper bound while volume.iscellnonemptyat(rayorigin) and backtracksteps <= maxbacktrack: rayorigin = [rayorigin[i] - raydir[i] delta for i in range(3)] backtracksteps += 1 if not volume.contains(rayorigin): break # Full ray casting from new start color = castray(rayorigin, raydir, volume, delta, 0) imagebuffer[y imagewidth + x] = color return imagebuffer def castray(origin, direction, volume, delta, startsamples): # Inline standard ray casting: sampling, compositing, shading pos = list(origin) for in range(startsamples): pos[0] += direction[0] delta pos[1] += direction[1] delta pos[2] += direction[2] delta color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] while volume.contains(pos): sample = volume.sample(pos) alpha = sample.opacity # Standard front-to-back compositing color = [c (1.0 - alpha) + sample.color[i] alpha for i, c in enumerate(color)] if sum(color) > 0.99: # Early ray termination break pos[0] += direction[0] delta pos[1] += direction[1] delta pos[2] += direction[2] delta return color def calculatemaxsamplesforaccuracy(camera, delta): # x1xn = ((sqrt(2) mumin / (sqrt(5) p)) - 1) ex1 # N = x1xn / delta mumin = camera.mumin p = camera.pixeldistance ex1 = camera.eyetoplanedistance x1xn = ((math.sqrt(2) mumin) / (math.sqrt(5) p) - 1) ex1 return int(x1xn / delta) A correction mechanism applied to space leap rays to ensure that no non-transparent sample points are missed during the leap phase. It is distinguished from standard space leaping by the explicit verification of the first sample's location relative to empty space and the subsequent backward movement of the ray origin if it lands inside a non-empty cell. Time Complexity: Proportional to the image size. The number of detector rays is fixed (e.g., 1/4 of total pixels), and the spreading step is also proportional to the number of detector pixels times the influence area size. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the image size. The Leap Buffer requires 8-bit or 16-bit integers per pixel, independent of the volume dataset size. Performance: Provides significant acceleration for scenes with large empty regions. Performance scales with the amount of empty space; more empty space leads to larger leaps and fewer samples. Strengths: No pre-processing or 3D data structures required. Independent of transfer function (can be changed interactively). Works with both parallel and perspective projection. No temporal coherence required; suitable for out-of-order rendering and mosaics. Easy to implement. Limitations: Accuracy depends on the detector pixel density and the geometric bounds (p{max}). If the pixel distance is too large, small objects may be missed. In perspective projection, accuracy degrades beyond distance x1xn, requiring clamping. Requires backtracking in some cases, adding overhead. Not suitable for scenes with very small, sparse objects if the detector density is too low. PDF Light Weight Space Leaping was introduced by Sarang Lakare and Arie Kaufman at the Center for Visual Computing, Stony Brook University, in 2004. It was presented at the IEEE Visualization 2004 conference. The method was developed to address the limitations of previous space-leaping techniques, which either required complex data structures (like DFB) or depended on temporal coherence. It builds on the concept of ray coherence, where neighboring rays often traverse similar distances in empty space. name: Backtracking Space Leap Rays
head: Backtracking Correction for Space Leap Rays
body: Backtracking Space Leap Rays is a correction mechanism applied to space leap rays in volume rendering to ensure that no non-transparent sample points are missed during the leap phase. It solves the problem where a space leap ray, accelerated by a detector ray, might jump past the boundary of a non-empty cell group, thereby skipping valid data. It is distinguished from standard space leaping by the explicit verification of the first sample's location relative to empty space and the subsequent backward movement of the ray origin if it lands inside a non-empty cell. Inputs and Outputs Input: A space leap ray defined by its origin and direction, a leap buffer containing the number of samples taken by the corresponding detector ray to reach the first non-empty cell, and the volume data structure with cell group boundaries. Output: A corrected ray origin that is guaranteed to be in an empty cell, along with a temporary buffer of sample values collected during backtracking. Data Structures Leap Buffer: An array storing integer values representing the number of samples a detector ray traversed through empty space before hitting a non-empty cell. Temporary Buffer: A small array or stack used to store sample values (color and opacity) collected during the backtracking phase to avoid re-sampling. Parameters \delta: The sampling distance (step size) along the ray. \mux, \muy, \muz: The dimensions (edge lengths) of the current cell group. M{max}: The maximum number of samples to backtrack. Steps 1. Leap Check: Determine the tentative new origin of the space leap ray based on the leap buffer value. 2. Boundary Condition Check: If the leap buffer value is zero, do not leap the ray at all; proceed with standard ray marching from the previous position. 3. Leap Adjustment: When leaping, leap one sample less than the value stored in the leap buffer. This ensures that the sample immediately preceding the leap target is the last sample in an empty cell. 4. Empty Cell Verification: Evaluate the volume data at the first sample point of the (adjusted) space leap ray. 5. Backtracking Decision: If the first sample point is inside an empty cell, the ray is correctly positioned before the cell group. Proceed to standard ray marching from this point. If the first sample point is inside a non-empty cell, the ray has jumped too far and missed the object boundary. Initiate backtracking. 6. Backtracking Execution: Move the ray origin backwards by one sample distance (\delta) at a time. Sample the volume at each backtracked position. Store the resulting sample values in the temporary buffer. Continue backtracking until the sample point is located inside an empty cell. Limit: Do not backtrack beyond the limit defined by the leap buffer value, as this would move the ray behind the image plane. Upper Bound: The maximum number of backtracking steps is bounded by M{max}. 7. Compositing: After backtracking completes, composite the sample values stored in the temporary buffer into the final image buffer before continuing with the forward ray march. Formulas The upper limit for the number of samples a ray needs to backtrack is calculated as: M{max} = 2 \times \frac{\max(\mux, \muy, \muz)}{\delta} Where: \mux, \muy, \muz are the longest edges of the cell group. \delta is the sampling distance. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backtrackingspaceleapray(rayorigin, raydirection, leapbuffervalue, cellgroupdims, samplingdistance, volumedata): """ Corrects a space leap ray to ensure it starts in an empty cell. Args: rayorigin: Initial origin of the space leap ray. raydirection: Unit direction vector of the ray. leapbuffervalue: Number of empty samples from the detector ray. cellgroupdims: Tuple (mux, muy, muz) of the cell group dimensions. samplingdistance: Step size delta. volumedata: Object providing volume access methods. Returns: correctedorigin: The new ray origin guaranteed to be in empty space. tempsamples: List of sample values collected during backtracking. """ # Step 2: Boundary Condition Check if leapbuffervalue == 0: # Do not leap; use original origin or previous position return rayorigin, [] # Step 3: Leap Adjustment # Leap one sample less than the buffer value to land on the last empty sample leapsamples = leapbuffervalue - 1 tentativeorigin = rayorigin + raydirection (leapsamples samplingdistance) # Step 4: Empty Cell Verification # Check if the first sample point is inside a non-empty cell isnonempty = volumedata.isnonempty(tentativeorigin) if not isnonempty: # Step 5a: First sample is in empty cell return tentativeorigin, [] # Step 5b: First sample is in non-empty cell, initiate backtracking correctedorigin = tentativeorigin tempsamples = [] # Calculate upper limit for backtracking maxedge = max(cellgroupdims) mmax = int(2 (maxedge / samplingdistance)) # Step 6: Backtracking Execution # We backtrack until we find an empty cell. # We must not backtrack beyond the leap buffer value to avoid going behind image plane. backtracklimit = min(mmax, leapbuffervalue) for i in range(1, backtracklimit + 1): # Move back one sample correctedorigin = tentativeorigin - raydirection (i samplingdistance) # Sample the volume samplevalue = volumedata.sample(correctedorigin) tempsamples.append(samplevalue) # Check if we are now in an empty cell if not volumedata.isnonempty(correctedorigin): break # Step 7: Compositing is handled by the caller using tempsamples return correctedorigin, tempsamples Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Leap Buffer: If the leap buffer value is zero, the ray must not be leaped at all. Image Plane Boundary: Backtracking must not exceed the leap buffer value, otherwise the ray origin moves behind the image plane. Off-by-One Leap: Leaping exactly the buffer value would land on the first non-empty sample. Leaping one less ensures the first sample checked is the last empty one, but if that is still non-empty (due to interpolation or data structure granularity), backtracking is required. Time Complexity: Backtracking causes no additional overhead because the ray would have been sampled at those missed points anyway. Memory Complexity: Requires a temporary buffer to store sample values during backtracking. Performance: In practice, M{max} is found to be between 1 and 3 samples. Strengths: Guarantees visual correctness by preventing missed objects. Limitations: Requires checking the volume data at the tentative leap position and storing temporary samples. Backtracking Space Leap Rays was introduced in the paper "PDF Light Weight Space Leaping using Ray Coherence" by Lakare et al. (2004). It was implemented in the Vikon system for perspective direct volume rendering, particularly for endoscopy applications such as Virtual Colonoscopy. The method addresses the coherence-based space leaping technique's vulnerability to missing small or distant objects when leap rays jump over cell group boundaries.
