name: Multi-level Grid Structures
body: Multi-level Grid Structures organize spatial data into a hierarchy of uniform grids to efficiently skip empty regions and adapt resolution to local density, solving the memory and traversal overhead problems of flat uniform grids in sparse scenes. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like KD-Tree Partitioned Volume Rendering by maintaining the regular memory access patterns of grid structures while providing hierarchical empty-space skipping. All methods in this family share the following mechanism: 1. Hierarchical Uniform Subdivision: The spatial domain is divided into a coarse grid (Level 0). Occupied cells in the coarse grid point to finer sub-grids (Level 1, Level 2, etc.). Empty cells point to null or are skipped entirely. 2. Ray-Grid Intersection: Rays are tested against the Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs) of the grid cells at each level. If a ray does not intersect a coarse cell, the entire sub-grid is skipped. 3. Traversal Continuity: Traversal typically reuses decision variables (DDA steps) between levels to maintain coherence, or computes new intervals based on sorted intersection events. 4. Memory Layout: Data is often stored in flat arrays or linked lists of cells, with occupancy flags or pointers indicating the presence of child grids. A fixed-depth hierarchical spatial acceleration structure that recursively subdivides the scene bounding box into uniform grids based on item density. It is distinguished from siblings like the Multi-Level Hashed Grid by its use of dense array indexing for child nodes rather than hash tables, making it memory-conservative. Choose it when memory efficiency is prioritized over handling extreme sparsity. Traverses rays through multiple binary occupancy grids to generate ray intervals, sample positions, and termination planes. It explicitly manages intersection events across distinct grid instances rather than hierarchical pointers, handling overlapping bounding boxes where the first grid's occupancy status takes precedence. Choose it for efficiently sampling hierarchical or overlapping volumetric structures. A fixed-depth hierarchical acceleration structure designed to handle non-uniform primitive distributions in dynamic scenes on GPUs. It uses a sparse top-level grid where each occupied cell points to a finer sub-grid of arbitrary resolution. Choose it for GPU-accelerated ray tracing of triangle meshes with sparse regions, avoiding the "teapot in a stadium" problem. A hierarchical acceleration technique that superimposes a coarse grid over a base uniform fine grid to skip empty regions. It uses a fixed, regular downsampling factor to create a simple boolean occupancy map, allowing trivial build times and efficient reuse of frustum setup calculations. Choose it for large, sparse uniform grids where traversal overhead is a concern. A recursive hierarchical subdivision algorithm that integrates regular and adaptive spatial subdivision methods. It uses a top-down build strategy where internal voxels maintain their own local sub-grids, enabling efficient traversal through deep recursion when paired with a hash-table indexing strategy. Choose it for scenes containing both large, regularly distributed objects and small, dense clusters. A volume rendering and projection algorithm for SPH data that assigns particles to a hierarchy of grid levels based on their kernel smoothing length, deposits onto coarser grids, and collapses the hierarchy coarse-to-fine via upsampling to bound per-particle cost. Choose it for SPH data visualization. A preprocessing step to convert unstructured or structured mesh data into a native hypertree grid format for efficient visualization. Choose it when preparing non-grid mesh data for hierarchical traversal. A renderer for hierarchical grids (hgridf) that combines primitive generation and rendering in a single pass, updating only 'dirty' cells to support interactive editing. Traverse the top-level grid and visit each grid-cell unless it is empty. Check if the current grid-cell is 'dirty' (voxels have changed since the last visit). If dirty, use the associated point or polygon engine to regenerate the local isosurface representation for that cell. Mark the cell as 'clean' after regeneration. The hierarchical grid uses a top-level N×N×N grid and sub-grids of size M×M×M, where M=16. The concept of hierarchical grids for volume rendering and ray tracing originated in the early 1990s to address the memory and performance limitations of uniform grids for large datasets. The "hgridf" renderer, described in Hardware Accelerated Point Rendering of Isosurfaces (2003), popularized the use of a top-level N×N×N grid with M×M×M sub-grids (typically M=16) to save space and provide constant-time access compared to octrees. The term "hgrid" refers to this specific two-level structure where empty top-level cells are null, and occupied cells contain sub-grids. Hardware Accelerated Point Rendering of Isosurfaces, http://wscg.zcu.cz/wscg2003/Papers2003/J61.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Multi-Level Array Grid
head: Classic multi-level array grid
body: The Multi-Level Array Grid is a hierarchical spatial acceleration structure for ray tracing that recursively subdivides the scene bounding box into uniform grids based on item density. It solves the problem of efficient ray-primitive intersection by skipping empty regions of space, using a fixed-depth recursion (typically 2 levels) to balance traversal overhead against intersection cost. It is distinguished from sibling methods like the Multi-Level Hashed Grid by its use of dense array indexing for child nodes rather than hash tables, making it memory-conservative but potentially sparse in empty areas. Inputs: A set of scene primitives (items) and their bounding boxes. Outputs: A root GridNode representing the hierarchical grid structure. Data Structures: The structure consists of two main types of nodes, defined in C-like pseudocode below. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. // Inner node: represents a subdivided grid cell struct InnerNode { float min[3]; // Bounding box minimum float max[3]; // Bounding box maximum int dim[3]; // Grid dimensions (Mi for each axis) float delta[3]; // Cell size (width/height/depth) GridNode cells; // Array of pointers to child nodes (size = dim[0]dim[1]dim[2]) }; // Union node: either a leaf containing items or a pointer to an inner node struct GridNode { int index; // High bits: item count (if leaf); Low bit: type flag // Low bit 1 = Inner Node, Low bit 0 = Leaf Node union { struct { int items; // Array of primitive indices } leaf; struct { InnerNode interior; // Pointer to child grid } inner; }; }; Construction Algorithm: 1. Compute Scene Bounding Box: Determine the global minimum and maximum extents of all scene primitives. Let Si be the size of the bounding box in dimension i \in \{x, y, z\}. 2. Initialize Root: Create a root GridNode as a leaf node containing all scene primitives. 3. Recursive Construction: Process each node recursively. Termination Conditions: If the number of items in the current node is less than 8, or if the current grid depth is greater than 2, the node remains a leaf. Recursion stops for this branch. Expansion: If termination conditions are not met, expand the node to an InnerNode. Dimension Calculation: Calculate the grid dimensions Mi for each axis using the heuristic attributed to Woo (1992): Mi = \frac{Si}{\max\{Si\}} \sqrt[3]{\rho N} \quad (i \in \{x, y, z\}) Where: Si is the bounding box size in dimension i. \max\{Si\} is the maximum dimension size among x, y, z. \rho is a density factor, typically 4. N is the number of primitives in the current node. Cell Allocation: Compute delta (cell size) as Si / Mi. Allocate the cells array of size \prod Mi. Item Assignment: Distribute primitives into the grid cells. If a cell contains no primitives, set its pointer to null. If a cell contains primitives, initialize a new GridNode as a leaf, storing the primitive indices in items and the count in the high bits of index. Recurse: For each non-null child leaf node, repeat the construction process (incrementing depth). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class GridNode: def init(self): self.index = 0 self.leafitems = None self.innernode = None class InnerNode: def init(self, minval, maxval, dim, delta, cells): self.min = minval self.max = maxval self.dim = dim self.delta = delta self.cells = cells def computeboundingbox(primitivecenters): minval = [float('inf')] 3 maxval = [float('-inf')] 3 for c in primitivecenters: for i in range(3): if c[i] < minval[i]: minval[i] = c[i] if c[i] > maxval[i]: maxval[i] = c[i] return minval, maxval def buildgrid(primitivecenters, depth=0, maxdepth=2, leafthreshold=8, rho=4): if not primitivecenters: return None bboxmin, bboxmax = computeboundingbox(primitivecenters) S = [bboxmax[i] - bboxmin[i] for i in range(3)] maxS = max(S) N = len(primitivecenters) if depth > maxdepth or N < leafthreshold: node = GridNode() node.index = (N << 1) | 0 # High bits: count, low bit: 0 (leaf) node.leafitems = primitivecenters return node dim = [] for i in range(3): mi = (S[i] / maxS) (rho N) (1/3) dim.append(int(round(mi))) delta = [S[i] / dim[i] for i in range(3)] totalcells = dim[0] dim[1] dim[2] cells = [None] totalcells cellitems = [[] for in range(totalcells)] for c in primitivecenters: cx = int((c[0] - bboxmin[0]) / delta[0]) cy = int((c[1] - bboxmin[1]) / delta[1]) cz = int((c[2] - bboxmin[2]) / delta[2]) cx = min(max(cx, 0), dim[0] - 1) cy = min(max(cy, 0), dim[1] - 1) cz = min(max(cz, 0), dim[2] - 1) cidx = cx + cy dim[0] + cz dim[0] dim[1] cellitems[cidx].append(c) for cidx in range(totalcells): items = cellitems[cidx] if not items: cells[cidx] = None else: leaf = GridNode() leaf.index = (len(items) << 1) | 0 leaf.leafitems = items cells[cidx] = leaf for cidx in range(totalcells): child = cells[cidx] if child is not None: cells[cidx] = buildgrid(child.leafitems, depth + 1, maxdepth, leafthreshold, rho) inner = InnerNode(bboxmin, bboxmax, dim, delta, cells) node = GridNode() node.index = 1 # Low bit: 1 (inner) node.innernode = inner return node Parameters: Leaf Threshold: 8 items. Nodes with fewer items remain leaves. Max Depth: 2. Recursion stops if depth exceeds 2. Density Factor (\rho): 4. Used in the dimension calculation heuristic. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Cells: Represented as null pointers to save memory. Precision: Cell indices are computed using floating-point division. Clamping is required to prevent out-of-bounds access due to floating-point errors at boundaries. Redundant Data: delta is stored in InnerNode but can be computed from max, min, and dim. It is cached for performance. Time Complexity: Construction is O(N) per level using direct assignment. Grid traversal dominates render time, and one-level grids spend twice the time doing ray-triangle intersections than multi-level grids. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of non-empty cells. Empty leaf cells are represented as null pointers to reduce memory requirements. Strengths: The construction uses a memory conservative heuristic. Limitations: The fixed depth limit (2) may not be optimal for all scenes. When to Use: It serves as a baseline for comparison with more advanced structures like hashed grids. The Multi-Level Array Grid was described in a 2010 paper by SCITEPRESS, used as a baseline for comparison against a Multi-Level Hashed Grid implementation. The dimension calculation heuristic is attributed to Woo (1992). It is part of a family of hierarchical grid structures designed to optimize ray tracing performance by reducing the number of intersection tests. SCITEPRESS - SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY PUBLICATIONS, https://www.scitepress.org/PublishedPapers/2010/28153/, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) PDF Multi-level Grid Strategies for Ray Tracing, https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/f922/40132d0d7340ff97ac4074b0a6906fb44c44.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Multi-Grid Ray Traversal
head: Grid Traversal (Multi-Grid), Ray traversal through multiple voxel grids
body: Multi-Grid Ray Traversal traverses rays through multiple binary occupancy grids to generate ray intervals, sample positions, and termination planes. It solves the problem of efficiently sampling hierarchical or overlapping volumetric structures by pre-computing ray-AABB intersections to determine which grids are hit, sorting these entry/exit points, and then performing voxel-level traversal within the valid intervals. Unlike single-grid traversal, this method handles multiple grid levels (mipmaps) and overlapping bounding boxes, where the first grid's occupancy status takes precedence in overlapping regions. It builds on Multi-level Grid Structures by explicitly managing the intersection events across distinct grid instances rather than just hierarchical pointers. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape [nrays, 3]. raysd: Ray directions, shape [nrays, 3]. binaries: Binary occupancy grids, shape [ngrids, resx, resy, resz]. All grids share the same resolution. aabbs: Axis-aligned bounding boxes for the grids, shape [ngrids, 6] storing {xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax}. tsorted (optional): Pre-computed sorted intersection times, shape [nrays, ngrids 2]. tindices (optional): Pre-computed sorted t indices, shape [nrays, ngrids 2] mapping intersections to grid IDs. hits (optional): Pre-computed hit flags, shape [nrays, ngrids]. nearplanes (optional): Per-ray near plane distances, shape [nrays]. farplanes (optional): Per-ray far plane distances, shape [nrays]. stepsize: Step size for ray traversal. Default 1e-3. coneangle: Cone angle for linearly-increased step size. 0.0 means constant step size. Default 0.0. traversestepslimit: Maximum number of samples per ray. Default -1 (unlimited). overallocate: Whether to over-allocate memory for outputs. If True, traversestepslimit must be set > 0. raysmask (optional): Mask for valid rays, shape [nrays]. firstpass: Boolean flag. If false, skips rays with chunkcnts[tid] == 0. continuous: Boolean flag. If false, adjusts tlast to align with interval boundaries. Outputs: intervals: Ray segment intervals. samples: Sample positions within each interval. terminateplanes: Termination t values for each ray, shape [nrays]. Data Structures: PackedRaySegmentsSpec: Stores traversal intervals and sample positions per ray, supporting chunked memory layouts via chunkcnts and chunkstarts. RayIntervals: Object containing traversal intervals. RaySamples: Object containing samples within each interval. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: If raysmask is None, initialize it to all-ones boolean tensor with shape [nrays]. If nearplanes is None, initialize it to zeros with shape [nrays]. If farplanes is None, initialize it to infinity with shape [nrays]. If traversestepslimit is None, set it to -1. If tsorted, tindices, or hits are None, compute ray-AABB intersections to get tmins, tmaxs, and hits. Concatenate tmins and tmaxs along the last dimension and sort them to get tsorted and tindices. 2. Parallel Execution Setup: Parallelize over rays using grid/block indices: tid = blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x. Skip rays where raysmask is false or chunkcnts[tid] == 0 on non-first passes. Initialize ray spec with origins, directions, near/far planes. Set base indices for intersections: basehits = tid ngrids, basetsorted = tid ngrids 2. 3. Interval Processing: Loop over intersection pairs i from basetsorted to basetsorted + ngrids 2 - 1 with step 2. Determine isentering = tindices[i] < ngrids and level = tindices[i] % ngrids. Compute interval bounds: this\tmin = \max(t\sorted[i], near\plane) this\tmax = \min(t\sorted[i + 1], far\plane) Skip if thistmin >= thistmax to prevent degenerate marching. 4. Step Size Adjustment (Discontinuous Traversal): If !continuous, adjust tlast: If stepsize <= 0.0, set tlast = thistmin. Else, march forward using dt = calcdt(tlast, coneangle, stepsize, 1e10) until tlast + dt 0.5 >= thistmin. 5. Voxel Traversal Setup: Setup traversal for the current AABB using setuptraversal(ray, thistmin, thistmax, eps, aabb, resolution, delta, tdist, stepindex, currentindex, finalindex) with eps = 1e-6. 6. Kernel Execution: Call the C++ kernel traversegrids with the prepared inputs, setting computeintervals, computesamples, and computeterminateplanes to True. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Tuple, Optional def rayaabbintersect( rayso: List[List[float]], raysd: List[List[float]], aabbs: List[List[float]]) -> Tuple[List[List[float]], List[List[float]], List[List[bool]]]: """Standard slab method for ray-AABB intersection. Returns tnear, tfar, hit flags.""" nrays = len(rayso) ngrids = len(aabbs) tmins = [[0.0] ngrids for in range(nrays)] tmaxs = [[0.0] ngrids for in range(nrays)] hits = [[False] ngrids for in range(nrays)] for r in range(nrays): ox, oy, oz = rayso[r] dx, dy, dz = raysd[r] for g in range(ngrids): xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax = aabbs[g] t1 = (xmin - ox) / dx if dx != 0 else float('inf') t2 = (xmax - ox) / dx if dx != 0 else float('-inf') t3 = (ymin - oy) / dy if dy != 0 else float('inf') t4 = (ymax - oy) / dy if dy != 0 else float('-inf') t5 = (zmin - oz) / dz if dz != 0 else float('inf') t6 = (zmax - oz) / dz if dz != 0 else float('-inf') tnear = max(min(t1, t2), min(t3, t4), min(t5, t6)) tfar = min(max(t1, t2), max(t3, t4), max(t5, t6)) if tnear <= tfar and tfar >= 0.0: tmins[r][g] = tnear if tnear > 0.0 else 0.0 tmaxs[r][g] = tfar hits[r][g] = True else: tmins[r][g] = float('inf') tmaxs[r][g] = float('inf') hits[r][g] = False return tmins, tmaxs, hits def sortintersections(tmins: List[List[float]], tmaxs: List[List[float]]) -> Tuple[List[List[float]], List[List[int]]]: """Concatenate tmins and tmaxs, sort, and track original grid indices.""" nrays = len(tmins) ngrids = len(tmins[0]) tsorted = [[0.0] (ngrids 2) for in range(nrays)] tindices = [[0] (ngrids 2) for in range(nrays)] for r in range(nrays): # Create pairs: (value, gridid, isentry) events = [] for g in range(ngrids): events.append((tmins[r][g], g, True)) events.append((tmaxs[r][g], g, False)) events.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) for i, (val, gid,) in enumerate(events): tsorted[r][i] = val tindices[r][i] = gid return tsorted, tindices def calcdt(tlast: float, coneangle: float, stepsize: float, maxdt: float) -> float: """Compute adaptive step size based on cone angle and distance.""" if coneangle <= 0.0: return stepsize dt = stepsize (1.0 + coneangle tlast) return min(dt, maxdt) def setuptraversal( rayorigin: List[float], raydir: List[float], tmin: float, tmax: float, eps: float, aabb: List[float], resolution: Tuple[int, int, int], delta: float) -> dict: """Initialize DDA traversal state for a specific grid interval.""" xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax = aabb resx, resy, resz = resolution # Compute voxel step sizes dx = (xmax - xmin) / resx dy = (ymax - ymin) / resy dz = (zmax - zmin) / resz # Initial voxel coordinates ix = int((rayorigin[0] - xmin) / dx) iy = int((rayorigin[1] - ymin) / dy) iz = int((rayorigin[2] - zmin) / dz) # Direction signs stepx = 1 if raydir[0] > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if raydir[1] > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if raydir[2] > 0 else -1 # T-max for crossing planes tmaxx = (xmin + (ix + (1 if stepx > 0 else 0)) dx - rayorigin[0]) / raydir[0] if raydir[0] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = (ymin + (iy + (1 if stepy > 0 else 0)) dy - rayorigin[1]) / raydir[1] if raydir[1] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxz = (zmin + (iz + (1 if stepz > 0 else 0)) dz - rayorigin[2]) / raydir[2] if raydir[2] != 0 else float('inf') return { "ix": ix, "iy": iy, "iz": iz, "stepx": stepx, "stepy": stepy, "stepz": stepz, "tmaxx": tmaxx, "tmaxy": tmaxy, "tmaxz": tmaxz, "dx": dx, "dy": dy, "dz": dz, "tmin": tmin, "tmax": tmax, "eps": eps } def traversegridskernel( rayso: List[List[float]], raysd: List[List[float]], binaries: List, aabbs: List[List[float]], tsorted: Optional[List[List[float]]] = None, tindices: Optional[List[List[int]]] = None, hits: Optional[List[List[bool]]] = None, nearplanes: Optional[List[float]] = None, farplanes: Optional[List[float]] = None, stepsize: float = 1e-3, coneangle: float = 0.0, traversestepslimit: int = -1, overallocate: bool = False, raysmask: Optional[List[bool]] = None, firstpass: bool = True, continuous: bool = True) -> Tuple[List, List, List]: """Multi-Grid Ray Traversal Kernel. Self-contained Python implementation.""" nrays = len(rayso) ngrids = len(aabbs) # 1. Initialization if raysmask is None: raysmask = [True] nrays if nearplanes is None: nearplanes = [0.0] nrays if farplanes is None: farplanes = [float('inf')] nrays if traversestepslimit is None: traversestepslimit = -1 # Compute intersections if not provided if tsorted is None or tindices is None or hits is None: tmins, tmaxs, hits = rayaabbintersect(rayso, raysd, aabbs) tsorted, tindices = sortintersections(tmins, tmaxs) # Output buffers intervals = [] samples = [] terminateplanes = [0.0] nrays # 2. Parallel Execution Setup (simulated sequentially for clarity) for tid in range(nrays): if not raysmask[tid]: continue if not firstpass: # chunkcnts[tid] would be checked here in CUDA pass basetsorted = tid ngrids 2 tlast = 0.0 # 3. Interval Processing for i in range(basetsorted, basetsorted + ngrids 2 - 1, 2): level = tindices[tid][i] % ngrids thistmin = max(tsorted[tid][i], nearplanes[tid]) thistmax = min(tsorted[tid][i + 1], farplanes[tid]) # Skip invalid intervals if thistmin >= thistmax: continue # 4. Step Size Adjustment if not continuous: if stepsize <= 0.0: tlast = thistmin else: dt = calcdt(tlast, coneangle, stepsize, 1e10) while tlast + dt 0.5 < thistmin: tlast += dt dt = calcdt(tlast, coneangle, stepsize, 1e10) # 5. Voxel Traversal Setup state = setuptraversal( rayorigin=rayso[tid], raydir=raysd[tid], tmin=thistmin, tmax=thistmax, eps=1e-6, aabb=aabbs[level], resolution=binaries[level].shape, delta=stepsize) # 6. Perform Voxel Traversal (simplified loop) stepcount = 0 currentt = thistmin while currentt < thistmax and (traversestepslimit <= 0 or stepcount < traversestepslimit): # Advance DDA to next voxel crossing if state["tmaxx"] < state["tmaxy"] and state["tmaxx"] < state["tmaxz"]: currentt = state["tmaxx"] state["ix"] += state["stepx"] state["tmaxx"] += state["dx"] elif state["tmaxy"] < state["tmaxz"]: currentt = state["tmaxy"] state["iy"] += state["stepy"] state["tmaxy"] += state["dy"] else: currentt = state["tmaxz"] state["iz"] += state["stepz"] state["tmaxz"] += state["dz"] # Record sample samplepos = [ rayso[tid][0] + currentt raysd[tid][0], rayso[tid][1] + currentt raysd[tid][1], rayso[tid][2] + currentt raysd[tid][2] ] samples.append(samplepos) intervals.append((thistmin, thistmax)) stepcount += 1 terminateplanes[tid] = thistmax return intervals, samples, terminateplanes A hybrid technique using a low-resolution grid for culling and a high-resolution grid for precise hit testing in dense particle systems. It skips large empty regions by querying a coarser occupancy grid first. A CUDA kernel that handles overlapping grids by priority and outputs traversal intervals with adaptive step sizing based on cone angle. It explicitly manages multiple hierarchical grid levels with sorted intersection events. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and the number of grids, O(N{rays} \cdot N{grids}) for intersection testing, plus O(N{samples}) for voxel traversal within valid intervals. Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{grids}) for storing intersection data (tsorted, tindices, hits). Output buffers scale with the number of samples per ray. Measured Performance: Used in NeRF acceleration libraries like NerfAcc to speed up training on NeRF-Synthetic and Tanks&Temple datasets. Strengths: Efficiently handles multiple grid levels and overlapping regions. Pre-computing intersections reduces per-ray overhead during traversal. Adaptive step sizing allows for coarser sampling in empty space or distant regions. Limitations: Not differentiable to any inputs. Overlapping grids require careful ordering as the first grid's occupancy status overwrites the second's. Requires careful handling of step size alignment when entering new intervals. When to use: When rendering scenes with multiple distinct volumetric grids (e.g., mipmaps, separate objects) or when hierarchical occupancy grids are used for acceleration. When not to use: When differentiability is required for the traversal step. When grids are not axis-aligned or have complex shapes not representable by AABBs. Multi-Grid Ray Traversal is a core component of efficient NeRF acceleration libraries, specifically implemented in nerfacc. It is used in conjunction with occupancy grid estimators to skip empty space during rendering. The method is also referenced in other NeRF-related projects like taylor-nerf and CNC. name: Ray Marching Particle Grid Traversal
head: Hybrid Ray Marching Particle Grid Traversal, Row-Range Particle Lookup
body: Ray Marching Particle Grid Traversal is a hybrid ray-grid traversal technique that traverses a voxel grid to find particle hits, using a low-resolution grid for culling and a high-resolution grid for precise hit testing. It optimizes particle sphere tests by reading contiguous rows of cells as single ranges of sorted particles, reducing memory loads. Unlike standard uniform grid traversal which may visit empty voxels, this method skips large portions of the scene by switching between resolution levels based on occupancy flags. Inputs: Ray origin pos0 and direction rayDirection (normalized). Particle position buffer particlesPositionBuffer: array<vec4f>, stores particle positions. Particle index buffer particlesIndicesBuffer: array<i32>, stores particle IDs. Low-resolution occupancy grid gridBuffer: array<i32>, stores occupancy flags (1 or 0) for low-res grid cells. Scene resolution resolution and inner radius INNER\RADIUS. Outputs: Hit color, hit position, hit velocity, and boolean success flag. Data Structures: 1. particlesPositionBuffer: array<vec4f>, stores particle positions. 2. particlesIndicesBuffer: array<i32>, stores particle IDs. 3. gridBuffer: array<i32>, stores occupancy flags (1 or 0) for low-res grid cells. Parameters: MAX\ITERATIONS = 400. GRID\RATIO = 8. RADIUS = 0.19 (Squared radius threshold for hit check). EPSILON = 1.e-10. acne = 0.05. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Calculate the initial step direction and side distances for slab crossing. Let mapPos = floor(pos0). Let deltaDist = rayDirection / |rayDirection| (normalized direction components). Let rayStep = 1.0 (voxel step size). sideDist = (rayStep \cdot (mapPos - pos0 + 0.5) + 0.5) \cdot deltaDist. Set highResolution = true. Set d = \infty (closest hit distance). Set index = -1000 (hit particle ID). 2. Ray Marching Loop: For i from 0 to MAX\ITERATIONS: a. Determine Step Direction: Calculate the sign of the step for each axis using the step function (returns 1 if a < b, else 0). stepForward = step(sideDist.xyz, sideDist.yxy) \cdot step(sideDist.xyz, sideDist.zzx). Note: This logic determines the next voxel to enter based on which boundary is closest. b. Update Position and Distances: sideDist += stepForward \cdot deltaDist. pos += stepForward \cdot rayStep. mapPos = floor(pos). c. Calculate Distance to Next Boundary: t = \min(sideDist.x, \min(sideDist.y, sideDist.z)). d. Border Check: Check if the ray is outside the inner volume. borders = length(pos.yz / resolution - vec2(0.5)) > INNER\RADIUS. Also check x-bound conditions (implementation specific, typically checking if pos.x is out of bounds). If borders is true, continue to next iteration (skip hit testing). e. Grid Level Selection: Calculate the low-resolution grid index: lowGrid = mapPos / GRID\RATIO \quad (\text{integer division}). indexGrid = lowGrid.x + lowRes \cdot lowGrid.y + lowRes^2 \cdot lowGrid.z. where lowRes = resolution / GRID\RATIO. f. Occupancy Check: resolution\flag = (gridBuffer[indexGrid] == 1). Case 1: High-Res Mode, No Occupancy If highResolution is true and resolution\flag is false: Switch to low-res mode. pos0\l = (pos0\h + t \cdot rayDirection) / GRID\RATIO. pos = pos0\l. mapPos = floor(pos). Recalculate sideDist for the low-res grid. Set highResolution = false. Continue to next iteration. Case 2: High-Res Mode, Occupancy Found If highResolution is true and resolution\flag is true: Perform particle hit test in the current high-res voxel. Calculate linear index in the particle index buffer: index1D = mapPos.x + res \cdot mapPos.y + res^2 \cdot mapPos.z. where res is the high-resolution grid dimension. Iterate z from 0 to 7 (assuming up to 8 particles per voxel slot): particleId = 8 \cdot index1D + z. voxelData = particlesIndicesBuffer[particleId]. If voxelData == 0, break loop (no more particles in this slot). Retrieve particle center: center = particlesPositionBuffer[voxelData].rgb. Check if particle is within valid bounds (e.g., center.x > 0.1 \cdot resolution). Perform sphere intersection test: Calculate distance l from ray to particle center. If checkHit(initPos, center, rayDirection) returns true AND l < d: index = voxelData. d = l. Case 3: Low-Res Mode, Occupancy Found If highResolution is false and resolution\flag is true: Switch back to high-res mode. pos0\h = GRID\RATIO \cdot (pos0\l + 0.9999 \cdot t \cdot rayDirection). pos = pos0\h. mapPos = floor(pos). Recalculate sideDist for the high-res grid. Set highResolution = true. Continue to next iteration. g. Update State: highResolution = resolution\flag. 3. Result: If index > -1000: Set hitColor, hitPosition, hitVelocity from particlesPositionBuffer[index] and other buffers. Return true. Else: Return false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchparticlegrid(pos0, raydirection, particlespositionbuffer, particlesindicesbuffer, gridbuffer, resolution, innerradius): MAXITERATIONS = 400 GRIDRATIO = 8 RADIUS = 0.19 EPSILON = 1e-10 acne = 0.05 pos = pos0 pos0h = pos0 pos0l = pos0 mappos = floor(pos) deltadist = raydirection / length(raydirection) raystep = 1.0 sidedist = (raystep (mappos - pos + 0.5) + 0.5) deltadist highresolution = True d = float('inf') index = -1000 lowres = resolution // GRIDRATIO for i in range(MAXITERATIONS): # stepForward = step(sideDist.xyz, sideDist.yxy) step(sideDist.xyz, sideDist.zzx) stepx = step(sidedist.x, sidedist.y) step(sidedist.x, sidedist.z) stepy = step(sidedist.y, sidedist.z) step(sidedist.y, sidedist.x) stepz = step(sidedist.z, sidedist.x) step(sidedist.z, sidedist.y) stepforward = vec3(stepx, stepy, stepz) sidedist += stepforward deltadist pos += stepforward raystep mappos = floor(pos) t = min(sidedist.x, min(sidedist.y, sidedist.z)) bordercheckyz = length(pos.yz / resolution - vec2(0.5)) > innerradius bordercheckx = (pos.x < 0.0) or (pos.x > resolution) if bordercheckyz or bordercheckx: continue lowgrid = mappos // GRIDRATIO indexgrid = lowgrid.x + lowres lowgrid.y + (lowres lowres) lowgrid.z resolutionflag = (gridbuffer[indexgrid] == 1) if highresolution: if not resolutionflag: pos0l = (pos0h + t raydirection) / GRIDRATIO pos = pos0l mappos = floor(pos) sidedist = (raystep (mappos - pos + 0.5) + 0.5) deltadist highresolution = False continue else: res = resolution index1d = mappos.x + res mappos.y + (res res) mappos.z for z in range(8): particleid = 8 index1d + z voxeldata = particlesindicesbuffer[particleid] if voxeldata == 0: break center = particlespositionbuffer[voxeldata].xyz if center.x > 0.1 resolution: oc = pos0 - center tca = dot(oc, raydirection) d2 = dot(oc, oc) - tca tca if d2 < RADIUS and d2 < d: index = voxeldata d = d2 if index > -1000: return True, index, d else: if resolutionflag: pos0h = GRIDRATIO (pos0l + 0.9999 t raydirection) pos = pos0h mappos = floor(pos) sidedist = (raystep (mappos - pos + 0.5) + 0.5) deltadist highresolution = True continue highresolution = resolutionflag return False, -1, float('inf') def step(edge, x): return 1.0 if edge < x else 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Squared Radius: The checkHit function uses squared radius (RADIUS) to avoid square root calculations. The distance check must be squared as well (d = l^2 - t{CA}^2). Empty Voxels: If particlesIndicesBuffer contains 0s, the loop breaks early, which is efficient but requires careful initialization of the buffer. The 2D Projection 1D Lookup Particle Cache is a spatial data structure that optimizes field value calculations in volume rendering by iterating only over particles within a fixed cutoff radius Rc from a sample point. It solves the inefficiency of retrieving influencing particles for isosurface extraction (e.g., Marching Slices) by combining a 2D projection with a 1D search along the z-axis. Unlike 3D lookup grid approaches (such as those by Wyvill et al., Müller et al., and Triquet) which return approximately 6.5 times more particles due to cubic bounding volumes requiring expensive floating-point distance culling, this method returns exactly the particles within the spherical radius Rc using only integer comparisons. Particle Rendering via Grid Bucketing renders particles as spheres by mapping them to a spatial grid to accelerate ray-sphere intersection tests. It differs from Ray Marching Particle Grid Traversal by explicitly iterating over particle lists stored in grid buckets rather than marching through a voxel grid to find hits, and from 2D Projection 1D Lookup Particle Cache by relying on 3D spatial hashing rather than 2D screen-space caching. Measured Performance: Reading contiguous rows of cells as single ranges of sorted particles reduced memory loads by 14% compared to individual cell access. The method achieved a rendering time of 4.1 ms for a lightbox scene, compared to 4.7 ms for a wall-drawing approach. Strengths: Efficient culling of empty space via low-resolution occupancy flags; reduced memory bandwidth usage due to contiguous memory access patterns; avoids square root calculations for sphere tests by using squared radius thresholds. Limitations: Performance degrades if the scene is densely packed with many particles per voxel, as the inner loop iterates up to 8 particles per cell. Switching between resolution levels adds computational overhead. Ray Marching Particle Grid Traversal was developed as part of a WebGPU-based voxel cone tracing and particle rendering system. The technique was documented in an unofficial GitHub repository by Hector Arellano Dev, which provides a complete implementation of the algorithm in WebGPU shaders. The optimization of reading contiguous rows of cells as ranges was further discussed in a pull request by Siroko for the "kansei" project, which highlighted performance gains in ray-traced lightbox rendering. The method is distinct from traditional grid-based volume rendering as it focuses on discrete particle spheres rather than continuous scalar fields. name: 2D Projection 1D Lookup Particle Cache
head: Field Value Cache, Particle Lookup Cache
body: The 2D Projection 1D Lookup Particle Cache is a spatial data structure that optimizes field value calculations in volume rendering by iterating only over particles within a fixed cutoff radius Rc from a sample point. It solves the inefficiency of retrieving influencing particles for isosurface extraction (e.g., Marching Slices) by combining a 2D projection with a 1D search along the z-axis. Unlike 3D lookup grid approaches (such as those by Wyvill et al., Müller et al., and Triquet) which return approximately 6.5 times more particles due to cubic bounding volumes requiring expensive floating-point distance culling, this method returns exactly the particles within the spherical radius Rc using only integer comparisons. Inputs: A set of particles, each defined by its center position (xp, yp, zp), radius of influence, and a pointer to its data. A cutoff radius Rc defining the maximum distance for influence. A cube size S used for discretization. Grid dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz. Outputs: A projection slice data structure allowing O(1) access to candidate particle lists for any grid corner (x, y). A list of particles influencing a specific field corner (x, y, z) that lie within distance Rc. Data Structures: 1. Projection Slice: A 2D array of dimensions (Nx + 1) \times (Ny + 1). Each element is a pointer to a doubly linked list. 2. List Element: Each node in the linked list contains: minz: Integer, the minimum z-slice index where the particle has influence. maxz: Integer, the maximum z-slice index where the particle has influence. midz: Integer, the z-slice index containing the particle's center. particleptr: Pointer to the particle object. Size: 16 bytes per element (assuming 32-bit integers and pointers). Parameters: Rc: Cutoff radius. Typical value: 3. S: Cube size. Typical value: 0.8. Algorithm Steps: 1. Build the Cache: a. Sort all particles in ascending order of their z-coordinate. b. For each particle, determine the 2D region in the (x, y) plane where it has influence, which forms a disk. c. For each grid column (x, y) intersected by this disk, insert a new list element into the linked list at ProjectionSlice[x][y]. d. Boundary Handling: Do not insert elements into columns on the block boundaries (x=0, x=Nx, y=0, y=Ny). Clamp minz and maxz to the range [1, Nz] to enforce field values of 0 along block boundaries. e. Small Particle Adjustment: If a particle's field of influence is smaller than Rc, shrink the radius used for insertion to ensure an exact lookup with no false positives. 2. Lookup for Corner (x, y, z): a. Access the linked list at ProjectionSlice[x][y]. b. Find Start: Search the list for the bottommost entry where midz \ge \lfloor z - Rc / S \rfloor. (Note: The source formula z − dRc/Se contains typographical artifacts; the intended threshold is Rc/S.) c. Traverse: Traverse the list upwards to the topmost entry where midz \le \lfloor z + Rc / S \rfloor. This traversal identifies all particles within a cylinder of radius Rc and height 2 \cdot Rc centered at z. d. Cull: For each element in the traversed range, perform integer comparisons: check if minz \le z AND maxz \ge z. If true, the particle influences the field at z and is passed to the field calculation routine. e. Optimization: Update the pointer at ProjectionSlice[x][y] to point to the first valid element found in the current lookup to speed up subsequent lookups in the same column. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class ParticleCacheElement: minz: int maxz: int midz: int particle: object next: 'ParticleCacheElement' prev: 'ParticleCacheElement' class ProjectionSlice: # 2D array of pointers to ParticleCacheElement # Dimensions: (Nx + 1) x (Ny + 1) columns: list[list[ParticleCacheElement | None]] # Tail pointers for O(1) insertion while maintaining sorted order by midz tails: list[list[ParticleCacheElement | None]] def buildcache(particles: list[object], Nx: int, Ny: int, Nz: int, Rc: float, S: float) -> ProjectionSlice: # 1. Sort particles by z coordinate ascending sortedparticles = sorted(particles, key=lambda p: p.z) # 2. Initialize Projection Slice projslice = ProjectionSlice() projslice.columns = [[None for in range(Ny + 1)] for in range(Nx + 1)] projslice.tails = [[None for in range(Ny + 1)] for in range(Nx + 1)] # 3. Insert particles into 2D columns for particle in sortedparticles: # Determine 2D disk influence bounding box in grid coordinates xmin = max(1, int(particle.x - Rc)) xmax = min(Nx - 1, int(particle.x + Rc)) ymin = max(1, int(particle.y - Rc)) ymax = min(Ny - 1, int(particle.y + Rc)) for x in range(xmin, xmax + 1): for y in range(ymin, ymax + 1): # Check if (x,y) corner is within the disk of influence distxysq = (x - particle.x)2 + (y - particle.y)2 if distxysq <= Rc2: # Calculate z-range of influence using Pythagorean theorem dzsq = max(0.0, Rc2 - distxysq) dz = dzsq0.5 minzinfluence = particle.z - dz maxzinfluence = particle.z + dz # Clamp to valid slice range [1, Nz] minz = max(1, int(minzinfluence)) maxz = min(Nz, int(maxzinfluence)) # If particle influence is smaller than Rc, shrink radius for exact lookup # Implementation: replace Rc with particle.radius in distxysq check above midz = int(particle.z) # Create new element newelem = ParticleCacheElement() newelem.minz = minz newelem.maxz = maxz newelem.midz = midz newelem.particle = particle newelem.next = None newelem.prev = None # Insert into linked list at (x, y) maintaining sorted order by midz collist = projslice.columns[x][y] tail = projslice.tails[x][y] if tail is None: # Empty list projslice.columns[x][y] = newelem projslice.tails[x][y] = newelem else: # Append to tail (midz is non-decreasing due to sorted input) tail.next = newelem newelem.prev = tail projslice.tails[x][y] = newelem return projslice def lookup(projslice: ProjectionSlice, x: int, y: int, z: float, Rc: float, S: float) -> list[object]: # 1. Access list collist = projslice.columns[x][y] if collist is None: return [] # 2. Find start point startthreshold = int(z - Rc / S) # Search for bottommost entry with midz >= startthreshold current = collist startnode = None while current is not None: if current.midz >= startthreshold: startnode = current break current = current.next if startnode is None: return [] # 3. Traverse upwards endthreshold = int(z + Rc / S) candidates = [] node = startnode while node is not None and node.midz <= endthreshold: # 4. Cull with integer comparisons if node.minz <= z <= node.maxz: candidates.append(node.particle) # Update cache pointer for next lookup in this column projslice.columns[x][y] = node node = node.next return candidates Time Complexity: Building the cache requires sorting particles O(N \log N) and inserting them into 2D columns. Lookup is O(1) for column access plus O(K) for list traversal, where K is the number of particles in the cylindrical volume. The integer culling step is fast. Memory Complexity: Approximately \pi Rc^2 / S^2 elements are inserted per particle. With Rc=3 and S=0.8, this is ~45 elements per particle. At 16 bytes per element, this is 720 bytes per particle. A cache of 1,000 particles consumes 720KB. Performance: On a 3.2GHz Intel Core 2 Duo, this approach is faster than surface-following marching cubes due to improved memory locality (2D accesses vs 3D) and avoids hash map overhead. It uses significantly less memory than hash-based approaches that store all corner values, as it only stores values for active slices. Strengths: Exact particle retrieval within Rc without floating-point distance checks. Reduced memory usage compared to 3D lookup grids. Fast lookup due to integer arithmetic and sorted lists. Limitations: Linked list insertion can be expensive for very large particle counts. Memory usage grows linearly with particle count. Not suitable for unbounded rendering without additional strategies (e.g., keeping only necessary z-ranges). When to use: Real-time particle isosurface extraction (e.g., Marching Slices) where exact particle culling is required and memory is constrained. When not to use: When particle counts are extremely high and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck, or when approximate results are acceptable and 3D grid lookups are preferred for simplicity. The 2D Projection 1D Lookup Particle Cache was introduced in the context of real-time particle isosurface extraction using Marching Slices with block subdivision. It was developed to address the inefficiencies of previous 3D lookup grid approaches used by Wyvill et al. [WMW86b, WMW86a], Müller et al. [MCG03, MST04a, MST04b], and Triquet [TMC01]. These earlier methods used a 3D grid with cube size Rc, resulting in a search volume of (3Rc)^3 which returned 6.5 times more particles than the spherical volume (4/3)\pi Rc^3, necessitating expensive floating-point distance culling. The 2D projection method reduces insertion and lookup costs by leveraging the 2D nature of the slice-based rendering and the sorted order of particles along the z-axis. name: Particle Rendering via Grid Bucketing
head: Grid Bucketing Particle Rendering, Particle Visualization, Sphere Rendering
body: Particle Rendering via Grid Bucketing renders particles as spheres by mapping them to a spatial grid to accelerate ray-sphere intersection tests. It differs from Ray Marching Particle Grid Traversal by explicitly iterating over particle lists stored in grid buckets rather than marching through a voxel grid to find hits, and from 2D Projection 1D Lookup Particle Cache by relying on 3D spatial hashing rather than 2D screen-space caching. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; particle data (positions \mathbf{x}j, radii rj, colors); spatial grid structure mapping cell indices to particle lists; current cell bounds [\mathbf{c}{min}, \mathbf{c}{max}] and index \mathbf{c}. Outputs: Intersection distance \lambdaj, intersection point \mathbf{x}i, normal \mathbf{n}i, and color. Data Structures: The grid maps integer cell indices to lists of particle IDs. Each particle j is assigned to a cell based on its center position \mathbf{x}j. The grid must support retrieval of particles in a cell c and its immediate neighbors. Steps: 1. Ray-Cell Intersection: Calculate the intersection of the current ray with the current grid cell c. This yields the entry distance \lambda{min\c} and exit distance \lambda{max\c}. 2. Neighbor Iteration: Identify all particles that can potentially overlap cell c. This includes all particles contained within cell c and its neighboring cells. 3. Ray-Sphere Intersection: For each candidate particle j: Calculate the ray-sphere intersection distance \lambdaj. If an intersection exists, \lambdaj is the distance from the ray origin to the intersection point. Check if \lambdaj \in [\lambda{min\c}, \lambda{max\c}]. If the condition is met and \lambdaj is smaller than the current closest intersection distance, store j and \lambdaj as the new closest hit. 4. Result Computation: If a particle intersection was found: Compute the intersection point: \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + \lambdaj \mathbf{d}. Compute the normal: \mathbf{n}i = \mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}j. Determine the color using a color mapping of a quantity associated with particle j. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderparticlegridbucketing(rayo, rayd, grid, particles, cellidx, cellmin, cellmax): # 1. Ray-Cell Intersection (Slab method) tmin = [] tmax = [] for i in range(3): if rayd[i] == 0.0: tmin.append(-float('inf')) tmax.append(float('inf')) else: tmin.append((cellmin[i] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i]) tmax.append((cellmax[i] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i]) tenter = max(min(tmin), min(tmax)) texit = min(max(tmin), max(tmax)) lambdaminc, lambdamaxc = tenter, texit closestlambda = float('inf') closestparticleid = -1 # 2. Neighbor Iteration neighborcells = [] for dx in (-1, 0, 1): for dy in (-1, 0, 1): for dz in (-1, 0, 1): neighborcells.append((cellidx[0] + dx, cellidx[1] + dy, cellidx[2] + dz)) candidateparticles = [] for nidx in neighborcells: if nidx in grid: candidateparticles.extend(grid[nidx]) # 3. Ray-Sphere Intersection tests for j in candidateparticles: particle = particles[j] center = particle.position radius = particle.radius # Ray: P(t) = O + tD # Sphere: |P(t) - C|^2 = r^2 # Quadratic: at^2 + bt + c = 0 L = [rayo[k] - center[k] for k in range(3)] a = sum(rayd[k] rayd[k] for k in range(3)) b = 2.0 sum(rayd[k] L[k] for k in range(3)) cval = sum(L[k] L[k] for k in range(3)) - radius radius discriminant = b b - 4 a cval if discriminant >= 0: sqrtdisc = discriminant 0.5 t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) # Select closest positive intersection if t1 > 0: lambdaj = t1 elif t2 > 0: lambdaj = t2 else: continue # Check if intersection is within the cell bounds if lambdaminc <= lambdaj <= lambdamaxc: if lambdaj < closestlambda: closestlambda = lambdaj closestparticleid = j # 4. Result Computation if closestparticleid != -1: particle = particles[closestparticleid] xi = [rayo[k] + closestlambda rayd[k] for k in range(3)] ni = [xi[k] - particle.position[k] for k in range(3)] color = particle.color return closestlambda, xi, ni, color else: return float('inf'), None, None, None Parameters: Grid resolution: Not given in the sources. Particle radius: Defined per particle. Edge Cases: Precision: Ray-sphere intersection discriminant calculation may suffer from precision issues for grazing angles or very small radii. Boundaries: The check \lambdaj \in [\lambda{min\c}, \lambda{max\c}] ensures the intersection is within the current cell's depth range, preventing false positives from particles in the same cell but at different depths if the grid is not perfectly aligned or if particles span multiple cells. Degenerate Input: Particles with zero radius will have no intersection unless the ray origin is exactly at the center. Determines the trade-off between culling efficiency and neighbor list size. Smaller cells reduce neighbor lists but increase grid memory and traversal overhead. Larger cells increase neighbor lists but reduce grid overhead. Not given in the sources. How particle positions, radii, and colors are stored and accessed. Typically a Struct of Arrays (SoA) or Array of Structs (AoS). Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: O(N) in the worst case if all particles are in the same cell or neighbors, but typically O(1) per ray if the grid is well-balanced and particles are uniformly distributed, as only a small constant number of neighbors are checked. Memory Complexity: O(N + G), where N is the number of particles and G is the number of grid cells. Strengths: Efficient culling of non-overlapping particles; simple implementation; supports arbitrary particle shapes (spheres) and sizes. Limitations: Performance degrades with highly clustered particles; requires spatial hashing or grid management overhead. When to use: When rendering large numbers of spherical particles where spatial coherence exists. When not to use: When particles are extremely dense and clustered, leading to large neighbor lists; when non-spherical particles are used without modification. The method is described in the context of Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) simulation and rendering. It was published by The Authors in Computer Graphics Forum published by Eurographics - The European Association for Computer Graphics in 2020. The work is titled Multi‐Level Memory Structures for Simulating and Rendering Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics. name: Multi-Grid Ray Traversal with Adaptive Step Size
body: This method is a CUDA kernel that traverses rays through one or more axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) voxel grids, handling overlapping grids by priority and outputting traversal intervals and sample points with adaptive step sizing based on cone angle. It differs from Ray Marching Particle Grid Traversal by explicitly managing multiple hierarchical grid levels with sorted intersection events, ensuring that the first grid's occupancy status takes precedence in overlapping regions, whereas particle grids typically rely on density accumulation without explicit grid-level priority. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape [nrays, 3]. raysd: Ray directions, shape [nrays, 3]. raysmask: Optional boolean mask, shape [nrays], to skip rays. binaries: Voxel occupancy data, shape [ngrids, resx, resy, resz]. aabbs: AABB bounds for each grid, shape [ngrids, 6] (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz). hits: Pre-computed hit flags, shape [nrays, ngrids]. tsorted: Sorted intersection distances, shape [nrays, ngrids 2]. tindices: Indices indicating which grid and whether the intersection is entering or leaving, shape [nrays, ngrids 2]. nearplanes: Near plane distances, shape [nrays]. farplanes: Far plane distances, shape [nrays]. traversestepslimit: Maximum number of samples per ray (optional). stepsize: Fixed step size. If <= 0.0, variable step mode is used. coneangle: Factor for adaptive step size increase. Must be >= 0.0. Value 0.0 means uniform marching. resolution: Grid resolution [resx, resy, resz]. delta: Voxel size. eps: Epsilon for float comparisons. Outputs: intervals: PackedRaySegmentsSpec structure containing interval endpoints. samples: PackedRaySegmentsSpec structure containing sample points. terminateplanes: Termination planes per ray, shape [nrays]. PackedRaySegmentsSpec: vals: Float array of interval endpoints or sample positions. rayindices: Integer array mapping entries to ray IDs. isleft: Boolean array marking left endpoints of intervals. isright: Boolean array marking right endpoints of intervals. chunkcnts: Integer array, optional, count of segments per ray. chunkstarts: Integer array, optional, start index per ray. MAXGRIDLEVELS: Constant defining the maximum number of grid levels supported. Value is 8. dtmin: Minimum step size. dtmax: Maximum step size. Default value in code is 1e10f. 1. Initialization: Launch a CUDA kernel with a grid-stride loop over rays. 2. Masking: If raysmask is provided and raysmask[tid] is false, skip the ray. 3. Optimization Check: If not the first pass, check intervals.chunkcnts[tid] == 0 or samples.chunkcnts[tid] == 0. If true, skip the ray. 4. Overlapping Grids: The code assumes grid order matters. The first grid's occupancy status overwrites the second if they overlap. This is implemented by iterating through sorted intersections and checking hits and isentering logic to prioritize earlier grids. Invalid Intervals: Intervals where thistmin >= thistmax (e.g., 0.0 to 0.0) are skipped to prevent degenerate rendering. name: Two-Level Grids for Ray Tracing on GPUs
head: Nested Grids, Two-Level Grid, Two-Level Grids for Ray Tracing, Two-Level Nested Grid
body: Two-Level Grids for Ray Tracing on GPUs is a fixed-depth hierarchical acceleration structure designed to handle non-uniform primitive distributions in dynamic scenes on GPUs. It solves the "teapot in a stadium problem" where uniform grids fail to eliminate intersection candidates in sparse regions by using a sparse top-level grid where each occupied cell points to a finer sub-grid (leaf grid) of arbitrary resolution. Unlike Multi-Level Array Grid which may use complex linked structures or varying depths, this method uses a fixed two-level hierarchy with a sort-based construction algorithm optimized for parallel GPU execution, allowing variable resolution sub-grids while consuming less memory than a single high-resolution uniform grid. The method consists of two main phases: construction (building the structure from triangle data) and traversal (ray-grid intersection). This article details the construction and data layout; traversal logic is covered in Two-Level Grid Ray Traversal. Input: Triangle mesh data (position, normal, index), scene bounding box b, top-level grid resolution r. Output: A two-level grid structure consisting of a Top-Level Cells Array, a Leaf Array, and a Reference Array. The structure uses three primary arrays: 1. Top-Level Cells Array: An array where each entry corresponds to a cell in the top-level grid. Each entry is a 64-bit value (or two 32-bit integers) containing: Location (32 bits): The index of the first leaf cell in the Leaf Array. Metadata (32 bits): Lower 24 bits: Cell resolution (limiting sub-grid resolution to 256^3). Upper 8 bits: Flags (e.g., 'is empty', 'has children'). 2. Leaf Array: An array of intervals (start/end indices) into the Reference Array. Each entry corresponds to a leaf cell (sub-grid cell) and stores two 32-bit integers: startindex and endindex. These indices define the contiguous range in the Reference Array where primitives overlapping that specific leaf cell are stored. 3. Reference Array: A flat array storing pairs of (leafcellglobalindex, primitiveid). Each primitive is referenced once for every leaf cell it overlaps. References for the same leaf cell are stored contiguously. The size of this array is determined during construction. The construction is a data-parallel, sort-based algorithm performed on the GPU. It builds the top-level grid first, then computes leaf cell locations, generates and sorts primitive-leaf pairs, and finally extracts the leaf intervals. Parameters: b: Scene bounding box. r: Top-level grid resolution (dimensions rx, ry, rz). t: Input triangle data. G: Grid dimension for leaf counting (typically ry \times rz). B: Block size for leaf counting (typically rx). G{ref}: Grid dimension for reference counting (fixed at 128 in source). B{ref}: Block size for reference counting (fixed at 256 in source). Steps: 1. Compute Bounds and Resolution: Compute the bounding box of all primitives: b \leftarrow \text{COMPUTE BOUNDS}(t). Compute the top-level grid resolution: r \leftarrow \text{COMPUTE TOP LEVEL RESOLUTION}(b). Upload triangle data to GPU memory: t \leftarrow \text{UPLOAD TRIANGLES}(t). 2. Build Top-Level Uniform Grid: Build a temporary uniform grid to initialize top-level cells: \text{data} \leftarrow \text{BUILD UNIFORM GRID}(t, b, r). This uses the sort-based approach by Kalojanov and Slusallek [KS09] to determine triangle-cell overlaps. Get sorted top-level pairs (cell index, primitive ID): \text{Atl}p \leftarrow \text{GET SORTED TOP-LEVEL PAIRS}(\text{data}). Get the number of top-level references: n \leftarrow \text{GET NUMBER OF TOP-LEVEL REFERENCES}(\text{data}). Get top-level cell ranges: \text{tlc} \leftarrow \text{GET TOP-LEVEL CELL RANGES}(\text{data}). 3. Compute Leaf Cell Locations: Initialize accumulator array \text{Acc} of size rx \cdot ry \cdot rz + 1 with zeros. Count leaf cells per top-level cell: \text{Acc} \leftarrow \text{COUNT LEAF CELLS}(b, r, \text{tlc}). This determines how many leaf cells each top-level cell will contain based on its resolution. Perform exclusive scan on \text{Acc}: \text{Acc} \leftarrow \text{EXCLUSIVE SCAN}(\text{Acc}, rx \cdot ry \cdot rz + 1). Initialize top-level cell ranges with scan results: \text{tlc} \leftarrow \text{INITIALIZE}(\text{Acc}, \text{tlc}). This sets the Location field in the Top-Level Cells Array. 4. Compute Reference Array Size: Initialize accumulator array \text{Arc} of size G{ref} + 1 (where G{ref}=128) with zeros. Count leaf references per top-level cell using a fast conservative triangle-cell intersection test (bounding box only): \text{Arc} \leftarrow \text{COUNT LEAF REFS}(t, b, r, n, \text{Atl}p, \text{tlc}). Perform exclusive scan on \text{Arc}: \text{Arc} \leftarrow \text{EXCLUSIVE SCAN}(\text{Arc}, G{ref} + 1). Get total size m \leftarrow \text{Arc}[G{ref}]. Allocate leaf pairs array \text{Ap} of size m. 5. Fill Reference Array: Write pairs (\text{Leaf Location}, \text{Primitive ID}) to \text{Ap}. Leaf Location Key: The global memory location in the leaf array is used as the key. This is computed from the leaf index relative to the top-level cell and the location of the first leaf for that top-level cell (from \text{tlc}). Note: Leaf indices relative to a top-level cell are not unique across the structure, so the global location is required for correct sorting. Intersection Test: Use a more precise test (including plane intersection) when generating the pairs. Invalid intersections are written with a dummy cell index that is discarded during sorting. \text{Ap} \leftarrow \text{WRITE PAIRS}(t, b, r, n, \text{Atl}p, \text{tlc}, \text{Arc}). 6. Sort Reference Array: Sort \text{Ap} using an improved radix sort by Billeter et al. [BOA09] with two- and four-way splits. Sort only on the required bits (up to two bits at a time) based on the known maximum key size. \text{Ap} \leftarrow \text{SORT}(\text{Ap}). 7. Extract Leaf Cells: Extract cell ranges from the sorted reference array to finalize leaf cell intervals. Check for range borders (neighboring pairs with different keys) to determine start and end indices for each leaf cell. \text{leaves} \leftarrow \text{EXTRACT CELL RANGES}(\text{Ap}, m). Populate the Leaf Array with these intervals. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildtwolevelgrid(triangles, scenebounds): """ Constructs a two-level grid for ray tracing on GPU. Returns: toplevelcells, leafarray, referencearray """ # 1. Compute Bounds and Resolution b = computebounds(triangles) r = computetoplevelresolution(b) t = uploadtogpu(triangles) # 2. Build Top-Level Uniform Grid # Uses sort-based approach (Kalojanov and Slusallek) data = builduniformgrid(t, b, r) atlp = getsortedtoplevelpairs(data) n = getnumberoftoplevelreferences(data) tlc = gettoplevelcellranges(data) # 3. Compute Leaf Cell Locations # Acc size: rx ry rz + 1 acc = arrayofzeros(r[0] r[1] r[2] + 1) acc = countleafcells(b, r, tlc) acc = exclusivescan(acc, r[0] r[1] r[2] + 1) tlc = initializetoplevelcellranges(acc, tlc) # 4. Compute Reference Array Size # Gref = 128, Bref = 256 arc = arrayofzeros(129) arc = countleafrefs(t, b, r, n, atlp, tlc) arc = exclusivescan(arc, 129) m = arc[128] ap = allocatearray(m) # 5. Fill Reference Array # Use global leaf location as key ap = writepairs(t, b, r, n, atlp, tlc, arc) # 6. Sort Reference Array # Radix sort (Billeter et al.) ap = radixsort(ap) # 7. Extract Leaf Cells leaves = extractcellranges(ap, m) # Construct final data structures toplevelcells = tlc leafarray = leaves referencearray = ap return toplevelcells, leafarray, referencearray def computebounds(triangles): # Compute min/max of all triangle vertices return minmax(triangles) def computetoplevelresolution(b): # Determine grid dimensions based on scene bounds return (64, 64, 64) # Example, source says compute it def uploadtogpu(triangles): # Copy data to device memory return triangles def builduniformgrid(t, b, r): # Sort-based construction (Kalojanov & Slusallek) # Returns temporary data structure with top-level cell overlaps return sortbaseduniformgrid(t, b, r) def getsortedtoplevelpairs(data): # Extract and sort pairs of (cellindex, primitiveid) return sorted(data.overlaps, key=lambda x: x.cellindex) def getnumberoftoplevelreferences(data): return len(data.overlaps) def gettoplevelcellranges(data): # Compute start/end indices for each top-level cell return computeranges(data) def arrayofzeros(size): return [0] size def countleafcells(b, r, tlc): # Count how many leaf cells each top-level cell contains # Based on resolution stored in tlc acc = [0] (r[0]r[1]r[2] + 1) for i, cell in enumerate(tlc): acc[i] = cell.resolutionx cell.resolutiony cell.resolutionz return acc def exclusivescan(arr, size): # Parallel prefix sum result = [0] size for i in range(1, size): result[i] = result[i-1] + arr[i-1] return result def initializetoplevelcellranges(acc, tlc): # Update tlc with start indices from scan for i, cell in enumerate(tlc): cell.location = acc[i] return tlc def countleafrefs(t, b, r, n, atlp, tlc): # Conservative bounding box test to count primitive-leaf overlaps arc = [0] 129 for cellidx, primid in atlp: # Count leaf cells this primitive overlaps count = countoverlaps(cellidx, primid, b, r, tlc) arc[cellidx] += count return arc def allocatearray(size): return [None] size def writepairs(t, b, r, n, atlp, tlc, arc): # Generate (globalleafindex, primitiveid) pairs pairs = [] for cellidx, primid in atlp: firstleaf = tlc[cellidx].location # Determine overlapping leaf cells for leaflocalidx in getoverlappingleafcells(cellidx, primid, b, r): globalidx = firstleaf + leaflocalidx pairs.append((globalidx, primid)) return pairs def radixsort(pairs): # Improved radix sort (Billeter et al.) return sorted(pairs, key=lambda x: x[0]) def extractcellranges(pairs, m): # Find start/end indices for each unique leaf index leaves = [] if not pairs: return leaves currentkey = pairs[0][0] start = 0 for i in range(1, m): if pairs[i][0] != currentkey: leaves.append((start, i)) currentkey = pairs[i][0] start = i leaves.append((start, m)) return leaves GPU Memory Constraints: Dynamic memory allocation is not supported on older GPUs. The size of the reference array must be computed conservatively (using bounding box tests) before precise generation to ensure sufficient space. Leaf Index Uniqueness: Leaf indices relative to a top-level cell are not unique across the entire structure (e.g., multiple top-level cells may have a leaf index 0). Therefore, the global memory location in the leaf array must be used as the sort key for leaf pairs. Resolution Limit: The 24-bit resolution field limits the sub-grid resolution to 256^3. This is an implementation-specific limitation. A massively parallel, sort-based algorithm for building the structure. It solves the problem of constructing high-quality acceleration structures for non-uniform primitive distributions with linear work complexity and fast build times, overcoming the "teapot in a stadium" problem. It adapts resolution per top-level cell, providing better acceleration for non-uniform distributions while consuming less memory. A ray-grid traversal algorithm designed for two-level hierarchical grid structures. It modifies the standard DDA algorithm to step through top-level cells and then treat each top cell as a uniform grid for leaf traversal. It sets itself apart from uniform grid traversal by handling hierarchical data structures while maintaining SIMD-friendly coherence, and from other hierarchical methods by reusing decision variables between levels to minimize computational overhead. Time Complexity: Construction is O(N \log N) due to sorting, where N is the number of primitive-cell overlaps. Traversal complexity depends on the scene but is generally efficient for non-uniform distributions. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of primitive-cell overlaps. It consumes less memory than a single high-resolution uniform grid for sparse scenes but more than a BVH for highly clustered scenes. Measured Performance: On a GTX 470, the implementation traced 24 million primary rays/sec for the Conference scene and 22 million for the Fairy scene. This is inferior to state-of-the-art approaches for static scenes (e.g., Aila and Laine [AL09]), which reported 142 million and 75 million rays/sec respectively for the same scenes. Strengths: Handles non-uniform primitive distributions robustly; fast construction for dynamic scenes; SIMD-friendly traversal. Limitations: Inferior traversal performance compared to optimized static scene structures; resolution limited to 256^3 per cell; requires conservative pre-allocation of reference array. When to Use: Dynamic scenes with non-uniform primitive distributions where fast construction is critical. When Not to Use: Static scenes where maximum traversal performance is required; scenes with very high-resolution sub-grids needed. The two-level grid is a fixed-depth hierarchical acceleration structure introduced by Kalojanov, Billeter, and Slusallek in 2010. It is a member of a class of hierarchical grids introduced by Jevans and Wyvill [JW89]. The method was developed to address the limitations of uniform grids on GPUs, specifically the "teapot in a stadium problem" where uniform grids fail to eliminate intersection candidates in sparse regions. The construction algorithm generalizes the sort-based uniform grid construction by Kalojanov and Slusallek [KS09] to handle multiple sub-grids of varying resolutions in a single parallel sort. name: Two-Level Grid Construction
head: Two-Level Grids for Ray Tracing on GPUs construction, Two-level nested grids
body: Two-Level Grid Construction is a massively parallel, sort-based algorithm for building a fixed-depth hierarchical acceleration structure for ray tracing dynamic scenes on GPUs. It solves the problem of constructing high-quality acceleration structures for non-uniform primitive distributions with linear work complexity and fast build times, overcoming the "teapot in a stadium" problem where uniform grids fail in sparse regions. Unlike uniform grids, it adapts resolution per top-level cell, providing better acceleration for non-uniform distributions while consuming less memory due to a reduced number of cells. The algorithm constructs a sparse top-level uniform grid where each cell contains a sub-grid (leaf grid) of arbitrary resolution. The construction relies on sorting pairs of (key, primitiveid) to compactly store primitive references. Input: A set of N triangles (primitives) and the scene bounding box. Output: A top-level grid structure containing cell data (leaf location, resolution, flags). A leaf grid structure containing cell data (start/end indices of references). A reference array containing primitive indices, sorted by leaf cell location. Top-Level Cell (32-bit integer for location of first leaf cell, 24-bit integer for cell resolution, 8-bit flags). Resolution is limited to 256^3 due to the 24-bit storage. Flags denote status such as "is empty" or "has children". Leaf Cell (32-bit integer for start of primitive references, 32-bit integer for end of primitive references). Reference Array: 32-bit primitive indices, sorted by leaf cell location. Grid Density (\lambda): A user-defined constant used to determine grid resolution. Global top-level density: \lambda = 1.2. Top-level density for hybrid intersector optimization: \lambda = 16 primitives referenced in the leaves. Resolution Formula: Rx = dx \sqrt{\frac{\lambda N}{V}}, Ry = dy \sqrt{\frac{\lambda N}{V}}, Rz = dz \sqrt{\frac{\lambda N}{V}}, where d is the extent of the box in each dimension, V is the volume of the scene's bounding box, N is the number of primitives, and \lambda is the grid density. Radix Sort: Uses a fast GPU implementation by Billeter et al. [BOA09], sorting by leaf location key. The sort considers only required bits (up to two bits at a time) based on the known size of the largest key. 1. Compute Scene Bounds: Calculate the bounding box b of the scene. 2. Compute Top-Level Resolution: Determine the resolution r of the top-level grid using the density heuristic. 3. Upload Triangles: Upload triangle data to GPU memory. 4. Build Top-Level Uniform Grid: Use a sort-based approach (Kalojanov and Slusallek [KS09]) to build the top-level uniform grid. This yields sorted top-level pairs, the number of top-level references n, and top-level cell ranges tlc. 5. Compute Leaf Cell Locations: Initialize an array Acc of zeros of size rx \times ry \times rz + 1. Count leaf cells for each top-level cell based on bounds, resolution, and top-level cell ranges. Perform an exclusive scan on Acc to determine start positions. Initialize top-level cell data with leaf locations and resolutions using the scanned array. 6. Compute Reference Array Size: Initialize array Arc of size G+1 (where G=128) with zeros. Count leaf references using a fast conservative triangle-cell intersection test (bounding box only). Perform an exclusive scan on Arc. Allocate leaf pairs array Ap of size m, where m is the final value in Arc. 7. Write Pairs to Array: For each primitive, compute its leaf cell location in the leaf array using the leaf index and the first leaf location of the corresponding top-level cell. Use a precise triangle-cell intersection test (including plane intersection) to generate pairs of (leaf location, primitive index). Write these pairs to the allocated array Ap. Atomic increment on shared memory may be used for convenience. 8. Sort Leaf Pairs: Sort the leaf pairs array Ap using radix sort by leaf location key. 9. Extract Leaf Cells: Scan sorted pairs to find range borders (where key changes). Store start and end indices of primitive references for each leaf cell in the leaf array. Extract the reference array out of the pairs array to compact the data and free space after outputting the leaf array. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def constructtwolevelgrid(triangles, scenebounds): # 1. Compute Bounds b = computebounds(triangles) # 2. Compute Top-Level Resolution # R = d sqrt(lambda N / V) r = computetoplevelresolution(b, len(triangles)) # 3. Upload Triangles t = uploadtrianglestogpu(triangles) # 4. Build Top-Level Uniform Grid (Sort-Based) data = builduniformgrid(t, b, r) atlp = getsortedtoplevelpairs(data) n = getnumberoftoplevelreferences(data) tlc = gettoplevelcellranges(data) # 5. Compute Leaf Cell Locations G = (r.y, r.z) B = r.x Acc = arrayofzeros(B G[0] G[1] + 1) Acc = countleafcells(b, r, tlc) Acc = exclusivescan(Acc, B G[0] G[1] + 1) tlc = initializetoplevelcelldata(Acc, tlc) # 6. Compute Reference Array Size Gconst = 128 Bconst = 256 Arc = arrayofzeros(Gconst + 1) Arc = countleafrefs(t, b, r, n, atlp, tlc) Arc = exclusivescan(Arc, Gconst + 1) m = Arc[Gconst] Ap = allocateleafpairsarray(m) # 7. Fill Reference Array Ap = writepairs(t, b, r, n, atlp, tlc, Arc) # 8. Sort Leaf Pairs Ap = sortradix(Ap) # 9. Extract Leaf Cells leaves = extractcellranges(Ap, m) referencearray = extractreferencearray(Ap) return tlc, leaves, referencearray def computebounds(triangles): return min(triangles), max(triangles) def computetoplevelresolution(b, N): d = b.max - b.min V = d.x d.y d.z lam = 1.2 return (d.x (lam N / V)0.5, d.y (lam N / V)0.5, d.z (lam N / V)0.5) def uploadtrianglestogpu(triangles): return triangles # Standard GPU memory upload def builduniformgrid(t, b, r): return {"data": t, "bounds": b, "res": r} # Standard sort-based uniform grid build def getsortedtoplevelpairs(data): return [] # Extracted from sort-based uniform grid build def getnumberoftoplevelreferences(data): return 0 # Extracted from sort-based uniform grid build def gettoplevelcellranges(data): return [] # Extracted from sort-based uniform grid build def arrayofzeros(size): return [0] size def countleafcells(b, r, tlc): return [0] (r.x r.y r.z + 1) # Counts leaves per top cell based on bounds/resolution def exclusivescan(arr, size): result = [0] size acc = 0 for i in range(size): result[i] = acc acc += arr[i] return result def initializetoplevelcelldata(Acc, tlc): for i in range(len(tlc)): tlc[i].loc = Acc[i] tlc[i].res = 256 # Max resolution per top cell return tlc def countleafrefs(t, b, r, n, atlp, tlc): return [0] 129 # Conservative bounding-box intersection count def allocateleafpairsarray(m): return [None] m def writepairs(t, b, r, n, atlp, tlc, Arc): Ap = [None] len(Arc) for prim in t: leafidx = computeleafindex(prim, b, r, tlc) absloc = tlc[leafidx].loc + leafidx Ap.append((absloc, prim.id)) return Ap def sortradix(Ap): return sorted(Ap, key=lambda x: x[0]) # GPU radix sort by leaf location key def extractcellranges(Ap, m): leaves = [] for i in range(len(Ap) - 1): if Ap[i][0] != Ap[i+1][0]: leaves.append({"start": i, "end": i+1}) return leaves def extractreferencearray(Ap): return [pair[1] for pair in Ap] # Compacts data and frees space Leaf Index Uniqueness: Leaf indices relative to a top-level cell are not unique across the entire grid (e.g., multiple top-level cells may have a leaf index 0). To ensure a single sort yields the correct reference array, the key used for sorting must be the absolute memory location of the leaf cell in the global leaf array, not the relative index. GPU Memory Allocation: GPU memory allocation is static. The size of the reference array must be computed in advance using a conservative intersection test (bounding box only) before the precise intersection test is performed during pair generation. Complexity Constraints: The complexity would not be linear if the cell resolution could not be determined in constant time. This requires knowing the number of overlapped primitives and the extent of the bounding box of each top-level cell. Density Selection: Choosing different density or resolution for different top-level cells provides higher quality but makes construction too slow. Time Complexity: Linear work complexity O(N) with respect to the number of primitives and cells, due to the use of radix sort and constant-time resolution computation. Memory Complexity: The main memory bottleneck is the space required to store the references. Two-level grids consume less memory than uniform grids mainly because of the reduced amount of cells. Performance: The runtime is independent of the primitive distribution in the scene, similar to sort-based uniform grid construction. The most time-consuming stages (writing pairs and sorting) are memory bandwidth limited. Strengths: Handles non-uniform primitive distributions more robustly than uniform grids; fast construction on GPUs; linear complexity. Limitations: Static memory allocation requires conservative pre-computation; resolution is limited to 256^3 per top-level cell due to bit packing. When to Use: Dynamic scenes with non-uniform primitive distributions requiring fast build times. When Not to Use: Scenes where uniform distribution is guaranteed and memory bandwidth for references is extremely constrained, or when variable resolution per top-level cell is critical for quality (as it slows construction). The two-level grid is a fixed-depth hierarchical acceleration structure introduced for ray tracing dynamic scenes on GPUs. It is a member of a class of hierarchical grids introduced by Jevans and Wyvill [JW89], but its application to ray tracing on GPUs was not studied before this work. The construction algorithm was proposed by Kalojanov, Billeter, and Slusallek, building on the sort-based uniform grid construction by Kalojanov and Slusallek [KS09] and using radix sort by Billeter et al. [BOA09]. The structure was tested on models such as the Thai Statue (10 million triangles) on a GTX 285 graphics card with 1GB of memory.
