name: Two-Level Grid Ray Traversal
head: Modified DDA Traversal
body: Two-Level Grid Ray Traversal is a ray-grid traversal algorithm designed for two-level hierarchical grid structures, modifying the standard Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm to step through top-level cells and then treat each top cell as a uniform grid for leaf traversal. It sets itself apart from uniform grid traversal by handling hierarchical data structures while maintaining SIMD-friendly coherence, and from other hierarchical methods by reusing decision variables between levels to minimize computational overhead. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of rays Ro, where all rays originate within a given top-level grid cell o. A two-level grid structure consisting of a top-level grid and leaf grids associated with each top-level cell. Output: A sequence of intersected cells (top-level and leaf-level) for each ray in the set. Data Structures The algorithm operates on a two-level grid structure. The top level is treated as a uniform grid. Each top-level cell contains a reference to a leaf grid, which is also treated as a uniform grid. The specific layout of the leaf grids (e.g., dense array, sparse structure) is defined by the construction method [S226-two-level-grid-construction.md], but the traversal logic assumes they behave as uniform grids during the leaf phase. Numbered Steps 1. Top-Level Traversal: Step through the top level of the two-level grid structure using the standard DDA algorithm, identical to traversing a uniform grid. 2. Leaf Initialization: Upon entering a top-level cell, treat that cell as the origin for a new uniform grid traversal. Reuse decision variables from the top-level traversal to spare computations when initializing the decision variables for the leaf level. 3. Leaf Traversal: Advance through the leaf cells within the current top-level cell using the same DDA algorithm used for the top level. 4. Iteration: Repeat steps 2 and 3 for each subsequent top-level cell entered by the rays. Formulas The algorithm relies on the coherence property of DDA traversal. Let Ro be a set of rays, all of which have origin (not necessarily the same) in a given grid cell o. Statement: If a cell c is intersected by any ray r \in Ro and is the n-th cell along r counted from the origin, then c will be the n-th cell along any ray r^ \in Ro that intersects c. Proof Basis: Let o be the 0-th cell along the rays in the set. For each cell c, it holds that it is at distance (x, y, z) from o, where x, y and z are integers denoting the distance (in number of cells) along the coordinate axis with the same name. During traversal, rays advance with exactly one neighbor cell at a time, and the two cells share a side. This means that c will be traversed at x+y+z = n-th step of the traversal algorithm for any ray with origin in o if at all. Parameters Grid Density: A single grid density is determined using the Surface Area Cost Model to work well with the traversal implementation for all test scenes. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Code Divergence: Code divergence occurs only when rays disagree on which level of structure they need to traverse (i.e., whether to stay in the current leaf grid or move to a new top-level cell). Otherwise, the algorithm is SIMD-friendly. Memory Access: A cell along the traversal path, if loaded, will be loaded exactly once from memory. This property transfers to the two-level grid structure when traversing the top level and when rays agree on the first leaf cell when they traverse the leaves. Triangle Intersection: Coherence in computations is lost during the ray-triangle intersection stage as soon as some rays traverse a full cell while others pass through an empty one, due to parallelization by assigning different rays to each thread. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversetwolevelgrid(rays, topgrid, leafgrids): """ Traverses a two-level grid structure for a set of rays. rays: List of Ray objects, each with origin and direction. topgrid: The top-level uniform grid structure. leafgrids: Dictionary mapping top-level cell coordinates to leaf grid structures. """ # Initialize top-level DDA state for all rays # This includes step, tmax, and tdelta for x, y, z axes topddastate = initializedda(rays, topgrid) for step in range(maxsteps): # Determine current top-level cell for each ray currenttopcells = getcurrentcell(rays, topddastate) # Check if rays have moved to a new top-level cell # Divergence occurs here if rays disagree on the next top-level cell newtoplevel = checktopleveltransition(rays, topddastate) if newtoplevel: # Update top-level DDA state topddastate = updatedda(rays, topddastate, topgrid) # Re-initialize leaf DDA state using reused decision variables leafddastate = initializeleafdda(rays, topddastate, leafgrids) # Traverse leaf cells # Reuse decision variables from top-level traversal where possible leafddastate = updateleafdda(rays, leafddastate, leafgrids) # Check for termination (ray exit or intersection) if allterminated(rays): break return rays Note: The specific implementation of initializedda, updatedda, initializeleafdda, and updateleafdda follows the standard Amanatides and Woo DDA algorithm. The reuse of decision variables is a specific optimization mentioned in the sources. Defines how the two-level grid structure is built, including the determination of grid density using the Surface Area Cost Model. Choose this when you need to create the data structure for traversal. Two-Level Grid Construction Provides the broader context of using two-level grids for GPU-based ray tracing, including performance considerations and hardware-specific optimizations. Choose this for understanding the overall system architecture. Two-Level Grids for Ray Tracing on GPUs Time Complexity: The traversal is described as "very inexpensive". The complexity is similar to uniform grid traversal, with the added cost of handling the two-level structure, which is mitigated by reusing decision variables. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The algorithm favors coherent rays. Performance degrades if rays are incoherent, leading to code divergence when rays disagree on which level of structure they need to traverse. Strengths: SIMD (or SIMT) friendly due to lack of code divergence except when rays disagree on level transitions. Efficient memory access as cells are loaded exactly once. Reuse of decision variables reduces computational overhead. Limitations: Code divergence when rays disagree on level transitions. Loss of coherence during ray-triangle intersection if rays traverse different cell types (full vs. empty). When to use: When rendering with two-level hierarchical grids on GPUs, especially with coherent rays. When not to use: When rays are highly incoherent, leading to frequent level transitions and code divergence. Origin: The algorithm is a modification of the DDA traversal algorithm by Amanatides and Woo [AW87]. History: It was developed for use with two-level grids for ray tracing on GPUs. The authors note that they used the Surface Area Cost Model to determine grid density. Usage: Used in GPU-based ray tracing systems employing two-level hierarchical grids. name: Dual-grid Parallel Framework
head: raytheia dual-grid, source-contribution grid
body: The dual-grid parallel framework is a distributed-memory method for evaluating direction-dependent integrals by decoupling ray emission locations from the spatial domain used for accumulation. It improves computational efficiency and methodological generality by allowing the source grid to retain native simulation discretizations (e.g., unstructured or meshless) while using a recursively refined contribution grid for ray walking. Unlike monolithic grid approaches, it enables independent decomposition of source and contribution domains to optimize load balance during parallel execution. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A source grid defining ray emission centers (structured, unstructured, or particles); a direction vector for integration; a contribution grid built from the source grid; domain decomposition parameters. Outputs: The total direction-dependent integral value. Data Structures Source Grid: Stores emission locations. Layout depends on the underlying simulation (e.g., Lagrangian particles or unstructured mesh nodes). Contribution Grid: A uniform or refined mesh used for ray traversal. Built via recursive refinement of the source grid based on problem-specific criteria. Chunks: The computational domain is partitioned into distinct spatial chunks, each assigned to an MPI rank. Each rank stores only data for its local subdomain. Algorithm Steps 1. Grid Construction: Build the contribution grid from the source grid using recursive refinement. 2. Domain Decomposition: Partition the contribution grid into N{\text{ranks}} chunks, one per MPI rank. 3. Parallel Loop (Chunk-to-Chunk): For each contribution chunk c from 0 to N{\text{ranks}}-1: a. Broadcast: Send the data (spatial boundaries and integration variables) of chunk c to all MPI ranks. b. Local Ray Walking: For each source element i local to the current rank: i. Emit a ray from the source element's center along the given direction. ii. Walk the ray through the received chunk c to find intersected cells. iii. For each intersected cell j, compute the local contribution C{i,j} as the product of the cell quantity Qj and the path length L{i,j} within that cell: C{i,j} = Qj \times L{i,j} iv. Accumulate the local contribution for this chunk: I{\text{local}, c} = \sum{j \in \text{intersected}} C{i,j} c. Accumulation: Add I{\text{local}, c} to the rank's total integral accumulator. d. Buffer Reuse: The same communication buffer is reused to receive the next chunk's data, updating the local data after accumulation. 4. Final Result: The total integral is the sum of contributions from all traversed chunks. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. for c in range(Nranks): # (i) Sequential broadcast of chunk c data to all ranks # chunkdata contains: spatial boundaries (min/max coords) and integration variables (cell quantities) chunkdata = receivechunkdata(c) # (ii) Compute local contribution for this chunk localchunkcontribution = 0.0 for source in sourceelements: # Emit ray from source center along direction rayorigin = source.center raydirection = direction # Ray-walk through chunkdata to find intersected cells intersectedcells = raywalk(rayorigin, raydirection, chunkdata) # Accumulate contributions from intersected cells for cell in intersectedcells: # Cell quantity Q and path length L Q = cell.quantity L = cell.pathlengthinchunk # Local contribution: product of cell quantity and path length contribution = Q L localchunkcontribution += contribution # (iii) Accumulate into total integral totalintegral += localchunkcontribution # (iv) Buffer reuse: chunkdata is overwritten in next iteration Parameters and Edge Cases Refinement Criteria: Problem-specific criteria determine the contribution grid's resolution. Memory: The chunk-to-chunk strategy ensures only one chunk is stored in memory at a time, reducing memory requirements. Load Balance: Independent decomposition of source and contribution grids allows for better load balancing. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of source elements and the number of intersected cells per ray. The chunk-to-chunk strategy adds a sequential communication overhead proportional to N{\text{ranks}}. Memory Complexity: O(1) per rank for the contribution grid data, as only one chunk is held in memory at a time. Scalability: Excellent scalability due to coarse-grained, regular communication patterns and reduced memory footprint. Strengths: High efficiency for direction-dependent integrals; supports arbitrary source grid discretizations; flexible load balancing. Limitations: Sequential broadcast of chunks may become a bottleneck if N{\text{ranks}} is very large or if chunk data is large. The framework is implemented in RAYTHEIA, a high-performance ray-tracing algorithm for three-dimensional direction-dependent equations in astronomical simulations. It was developed to handle complex source distributions (e.g., Lagrangian particles) and improve upon traditional grid-based methods by decoupling emission and accumulation domains. name: Direction-Dependent Integration
head: Chunk-wise Direction-Dependent Integration, Raytheia Integration Algorithm
body: Direction-Dependent Integration is a parallel algorithm for computing direction-dependent integrals by decoupling the source locations from the integration domain using a dual-grid structure. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating radiative transfer or similar integrals in large-scale astronomical simulations where the source distribution and the medium properties differ in resolution or topology. Unlike monolithic ray-tracing methods, it partitions the contribution grid into chunks and processes them sequentially across MPI ranks, allowing each rank to accumulate partial contributions from all chunks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A source grid defining ray-emitting elements (cells) and a contribution grid (AMR Cartesian grid) containing the quantity to be integrated fk. Input: N{ranks}: Number of MPI ranks. Input: Ns: Number of source elements within each MPI rank that lie inside the molecular cloud. Input: N{rays}: Number of rays emanated from each source element. Output: The direction-dependent integral I(s, r) for each source element s and ray r. Data Structures: Source Grid: Stores the locations of ray-emitting elements. The algorithm assumes a partitioning where each MPI rank holds a subset of source elements. Contribution Grid: An AMR Cartesian grid built from the source grid, providing a traversal-friendly representation. It is partitioned into N{ranks} chunks. Integration Variable: fk represents the quantity to be integrated for contribution grid cell k. Path Length: r{cell,k} is the path length of the ray through cell k. Algorithm Steps: The algorithm operates on each MPI rank independently, accumulating the integral I(s, r) over all contribution chunks. 1. Chunk Traversal: Iterate over all contribution chunks c from 0 to N{ranks}-1. 2. Data Broadcast: Broadcast the AMR data (spatial boundaries and integration variables) of contribution chunk c to all MPI ranks. 3. Source Iteration: Iterate over all source elements s from 1 to Ns. 4. Validity Check: Check if source element cell s is inside the molecular cloud. If not inside: Set I(s, r) = 0 for all rays r. If inside: Proceed to ray emission. 5. Ray Emission: Iterate over all rays r from 1 to N{rays}. Rays are emitted from the cell center of source element s. 6. Path Determination: Determine the ray-walking path within the current contribution chunk using a parametric traversal method. 7. Path Length Computation: Compute the path length r{cell,k} of the ray through each cell k in the chunk using a slab method. 8. Accumulation: Update the integral: I(s, r) = I(s, r) + fk \cdot r{cell,k} This accumulates the partial contribution of the current chunk. 9. Completion: After traversing all chunks, I(s, r) holds the complete direction-dependent integral. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. for c in range(0, Nranks): # Broadcast AMR data of contribution chunk c to all MPI ranks # Data includes spatial boundaries (min/max coordinates) and integration variables fk chunkdata = MPIBCAST(chunkcdata) # Loop over all source elements in this rank for s in range(1, Ns + 1): # Check if source element cell s is inside the molecular cloud if isinsidemolecularcloud(sourcecell[s]): # Loop over all rays emanated from the cell center for r in range(1, Nrays + 1): # Determine ray-walking path within the contribution chunk # Uses parametric traversal method pathcells = determineraypath(rayorigin[sourcecell[s]], raydirection[r], chunkdata) # Compute path length of the ray through each cell k in the path # Uses slab method for k in pathcells: rcellk = computeslabpathlength(ray, chunkdata.cell[k]) # Accumulate partial contribution # fk is the quantity to be integrated of contribution grid cell k I[s][r] = I[s][r] + chunkdata.f[k] rcellk else: # If cell is not inside the molecular cloud, set integral to 0 for r in range(1, Nrays + 1): I[s][r] = 0 Parameters: N{ranks}: Number of MPI ranks. Ns: Number of source elements within each MPI rank inside the cloud. N{rays}: Number of rays per source element. fk: Quantity to be integrated for cell k. r{cell,k}: Path length through cell k. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Outside Cloud: Source elements outside the molecular cloud must explicitly set I(s, r) = 0 to avoid garbage values. Chunk Boundaries: The parametric traversal must correctly handle rays entering and exiting the contribution chunk boundaries. Precision: Accumulating partial contributions across chunks requires careful handling of floating-point precision if high accuracy is needed, though the algorithm assumes standard accumulation. Time Complexity: The algorithm performs N{ranks} broadcasts and, for each rank, iterates over Ns sources and N{rays} rays. The cost per ray depends on the number of cells traversed in the AMR grid. Total work is proportional to N{ranks} \times Ns \times N{rays} \times (\text{avg cells per ray}). Memory Complexity: Each rank stores the source elements assigned to it and the current contribution chunk data. The AMR data for one chunk is broadcast, so memory usage per rank is dominated by the source grid and the current chunk. Performance: The method is designed for high-performance ray-tracing in astronomical simulations, leveraging MPI for parallelism. Strengths: Decouples source and integration domains; efficient for AMR grids; scalable with MPI. Limitations: Requires broadcasting chunk data; sequential chunk processing per rank may limit parallelism if N{ranks} is large relative to work per chunk. The method is part of the RAYTHEIA algorithm, a high-performance ray-tracing framework for three-dimensional direction-dependent equations in astronomical simulations. It was introduced to handle the complexity of direction-dependent integrals in large-scale simulations where traditional methods struggle with performance and memory. name: Macrocell Grid Traversal
head: Coarse-fine grid, Downscaled Grid Traversal, Macrocell or multigrids, Two-Level Grid (Coarse Macro-Cells), multigrids
body: Macrocell Grid Traversal is a hierarchical acceleration technique for ray-grid traversal that superimposes a coarse grid over a base uniform fine grid to skip empty regions. It solves the problem of excessive traversal overhead in large, sparse uniform grids by allowing rays to bypass blocks of empty fine cells in single steps. Unlike Multi-Level Array Grid which may use complex indexing or variable subdivision, or Multi-Grid Ray Traversal which might involve multiple independent grids, Macrocell Grid Traversal uses a fixed, regular downsampling factor M to create a simple boolean occupancy map. This simplicity allows for trivial build times and efficient reuse of frustum setup calculations, yielding approximately 30% performance improvement over single ray grids for medium-sized animated scenes. Inputs: A base uniform fine grid of resolution N \times N \times N (or W \times H \times D). The ray parameters: origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and inverse direction \mathbf{d}^{-1}. The downsampling factor M (typically 6). Outputs: A traversal sequence of occupied fine grid cells. A boolean occupancy flag for each macrocell indicating if any underlying fine cell is occupied. The structure consists of two grids: 1. Fine Grid: The original voxel data. Cells are indexed by (i, j, k). 2. Macrocell Grid: A coarse grid of resolution \lceil N/M \rceil \times \lceil N/M \rceil \times \lceil N/M \rceil. Layout: Flat array or organized in bricks for locality. Fields: Each macrocell stores a single boolean flag occupied. Definition: A macrocell at coarse index (I, J, K) corresponds to the fine grid block defined by fine indices: i \in [I \cdot M, \min((I+1) \cdot M, N) - 1] j \in [J \cdot M, \min((J+1) \cdot M, N) - 1] k \in [K \cdot M, \min((K+1) \cdot M, N) - 1] Occupancy: macrocell[I][J][K].occupied is true if any fine cell in the corresponding block is occupied, false otherwise. M (Downsampling Factor): The side length of the cubic block of fine cells represented by one macrocell. Typical Value: M = 6. Constraints: Smaller M yields insufficient savings to justify overhead; larger M reduces the probability of finding empty regions, reducing skip benefits. 1. Initialize the macrocell grid with all flags set to false. 2. Iterate through all fine grid cells (i, j, k). 3. If fine cell (i, j, k) is occupied: Compute macrocell coordinates: I = \lfloor i / M \rfloor J = \lfloor j / M \rfloor K = \lfloor k / M \rfloor Set macrocell[I][J][K].occupied = true. 4. Handle boundary conditions where N is not a multiple of M by ensuring array bounds checks during indexing. The traversal reuses the standard ray-grid traversal logic (DDA) but operates on macrocells first to determine skip distances. 1. Frustum Setup (Coarse): Compute the initial intersection interval [t{min}, t{max}] of the ray with the entire scene bounding box. Compute the coarse grid step variables. Since the macrocell grid is a downscaled version, the step sizes in macrocell space are M times larger than in fine cell space. Let \Delta t{x}, \Delta t{y}, \Delta t{z} be the time to cross one fine cell. The time to cross one macrocell is M \cdot \Delta t{x}, etc.. Alternatively, compute the coarse grid traversal parameters by dividing the fine grid setup values by M. 2. Coarse Traversal Loop: Initialize coarse DDA variables (I, J, K) to the macrocell containing the ray origin. While t < t{max}: Check if macrocell[I][J][K].occupied is false. If Empty: Skip the entire macrocell. Advance the coarse DDA to the next macrocell along the ray direction. Update t by adding the time to cross the current macrocell (M \cdot \Delta t). Continue loop. If Occupied: Perform fine grid traversal within this macrocell block. Determine the fine cell indices (i{start}, j{start}, k{start}) corresponding to (I, J, K). Execute standard fine grid DDA steps for cells within the block I \cdot M, (I+1) \cdot M) \times [J \cdot M, (J+1) \cdot M) \times [K \cdot M, (K+1) \cdot M). For each occupied fine cell, perform [ray-volume intersection. Update t and fine DDA variables. If the ray exits the current macrocell block, advance the coarse DDA to the next macrocell (I', J', K') and continue the coarse loop. 3. Edge Cases: Partial Macrocells: At the boundaries of the grid, macrocells may be smaller than M \times M \times M. The traversal must handle these boundary blocks correctly by checking array bounds. Ray Origin Outside: If the ray origin is outside the grid, standard frustum clipping applies before coarse traversal begins. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversemacrocellgrid(rayorigin, raydir, finegrid, macrocellgrid, M, N, scenetmax): """ rayorigin: (ox, oy, oz) raydir: (dx, dy, dz) finegrid: 3D array of booleans, size N x N x N macrocellgrid: 3D array of booleans, size ceil(N/M) x ceil(N/M) x ceil(N/M) M: downsampling factor N: fine grid resolution scenetmax: maximum traversal distance along the ray """ # 1. Fine grid DDA setup deltatx = 1.0 / raydir[0] if raydir[0] != 0 else float('inf') deltaty = 1.0 / raydir[1] if raydir[1] != 0 else float('inf') deltatz = 1.0 / raydir[2] if raydir[2] != 0 else float('inf') i = int(rayorigin[0]) j = int(rayorigin[1]) k = int(rayorigin[2]) tmaxx = (i + 1 - rayorigin[0]) deltatx if raydir[0] > 0 else (i - rayorigin[0]) deltatx tmaxy = (j + 1 - rayorigin[1]) deltaty if raydir[1] > 0 else (j - rayorigin[1]) deltaty tmaxz = (k + 1 - rayorigin[2]) deltatz if raydir[2] > 0 else (k - rayorigin[2]) deltatz stepx = 1 if raydir[0] > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if raydir[1] > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if raydir[2] > 0 else -1 t = 0.0 # 2. Coarse grid DDA setup Ncoarse = (N + M - 1) // M coarsei = i // M coarsej = j // M coarsek = k // M coarsedeltatx = M deltatx coarsedeltaty = M deltaty coarsedeltatz = M deltatz # Distance to next coarse boundary coarsetmaxx = ((coarsei + 1) M - rayorigin[0]) deltatx if raydir[0] > 0 else (coarsei M - rayorigin[0]) deltatx coarsetmaxy = ((coarsej + 1) M - rayorigin[1]) deltaty if raydir[1] > 0 else (coarsej M - rayorigin[1]) deltaty coarsetmaxz = ((coarsek + 1) M - rayorigin[2]) deltatz if raydir[2] > 0 else (coarsek M - rayorigin[2]) deltatz # 3. Traversal loop while t < scenetmax: # Check bounds for coarse indices if not (0 <= coarsei < Ncoarse and 0 <= coarsej < Ncoarse and 0 <= coarsek < Ncoarse): break # Check macrocell occupancy if not macrocellgrid[coarsei][coarsej][coarsek]: # Skip empty macrocell if coarsetmaxx < coarsetmaxy: if coarsetmaxx < coarsetmaxz: coarsei += stepx t = coarsetmaxx coarsetmaxx += coarsedeltatx else: coarsek += stepz t = coarsetmaxz coarsetmaxz += coarsedeltatz else: if coarsetmaxy < coarsetmaxz: coarsej += stepy t = coarsetmaxy coarsetmaxy += coarsedeltaty else: coarsek += stepz t = coarsetmaxz coarsetmaxz += coarsedeltatz else: # Macrocell occupied, traverse fine cells istart = coarsei M jstart = coarsej M kstart = coarsek M iend = min(istart + M, N) jend = min(jstart + M, N) kend = min(kstart + M, N) while t < scenetmax and i < iend and j < jend and k < kend: if finegrid[i][j][k]: # Perform ray-volume intersection pass # Advance fine DDA if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: i += stepx tmaxx += deltatx else: k += stepz tmaxz += deltatz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: j += stepy tmaxy += deltaty else: k += stepz tmaxz += deltatz t = min(tmaxx, tmaxy, tmaxz) # After fine traversal, update coarse DDA to next macrocell coarsei = i // M coarsej = j // M coarsek = k // M # Re-sync coarse tmax values to current fine position coarsetmaxx = ((coarsei + 1) M - rayorigin[0]) deltatx if raydir[0] > 0 else (coarsei M - rayorigin[0]) deltatx coarsetmaxy = ((coarsej + 1) M - rayorigin[1]) deltaty if raydir[1] > 0 else (coarsej M - rayorigin[1]) deltaty coarsetmaxz = ((coarsek + 1) M - rayorigin[2]) deltatz if raydir[2] > 0 else (coarsek M - rayorigin[2]) deltatz An approach based on adopting a coarse grid at the first stage of reconstruction to obtain a rapid, reliable initial volume estimate. It reduces the problem dimension by compressing images while maintaining a 1:1 resolution ratio between voxels and pixels, using a subsampling factor (e.g., fc = 2) to limit noise amplification. An extension of macrocell grid traversal that advances each ray through up to N{Spec} visible blocks instead of just one, recording multiple block IDs to increase GPU utilization and terminate rays in fewer passes. The kernel is run over all w \times h pixels; terminated rays exit early. Calculate offset o = O{Act}[ray] \times N{Spec}. Write up to N{Spec} visible block IDs into R{BID} starting at o. If the ray exits the volume early, fill remaining R{BID} entries with UINT\MAX. Write N{Spec} entries of the ray ID into R{ID} starting at o. Save coarse and fine grid iterator states after N{Spec} visible blocks are found to resume traversal later. Time Complexity: Build time is O(N^3) for the fine grid, but the macrocell build is O((N/M)^3) which is trivial. Traversal time is reduced by skipping empty macrocells. The overhead of checking macrocells is minimal. Memory Complexity: Adds O((N/M)^3) bits (or bytes) for the macrocell grid. For M=6, this is roughly 1/216 of the fine grid size, which is negligible. Measured Performance: Approximately 30% improvement over single ray grids for medium-sized animated scenes. Strengths: Trivial and cheap build process. Simple traversal logic. Low memory overhead. Effective for scenes with large empty regions. Limitations: Fixed block size M may not adapt to varying density. For smaller resolutions, savings are insufficient. For larger resolutions, probability of finding empty regions decreases. Not suitable for scenes with highly varying geometric density without additional robustness. When to Use: Medium-sized animated scenes with significant empty space and uniform fine grid resolution. When Not to Use: Scenes with highly varying density where fixed blocks are inefficient, or very small grids where overhead dominates. Macrocell Grid Traversal was proposed by Parker et al. in 1999. It is a simple hierarchical optimization to a base uniform grid, often used to apply grids to scalar volume fields. The method was designed to formulate a viable grid traversal for medium-size animated scenes, balancing performance and build time. Additional levels of macrocells could further improve performance for more complex models, but were not investigated in the original work. name: Multi-resolution grids
head: Hierarchical voxel grids, JW89, Jevans and Wyvill method, Jevans and Wyvill's approach
body: Multi-resolution grids (JW89) is a recursive hierarchical subdivision algorithm for ray tracing that integrates regular and adaptive spatial subdivision methods. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering scenes containing both large, regularly distributed objects and small, dense clusters by allowing variable resolution across the spatial domain. Unlike fixed-resolution grids or purely octree-based approaches, voxels in recursive grids cannot overlap, so each nested grid along the ray path is tested exactly once. It uses a top-down build strategy where internal voxels maintain their own local sub-grids, enabling efficient traversal through deep recursion when paired with a hash-table indexing strategy. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of geometric primitives and a scene bounding box. Output: A hierarchical grid data structure (root voxel) and a traversal state for ray intersection. Data Structures The structure is a loosely nested recursive grid. Voxel: The fundamental unit. Type: Enum { LEAF, INTERNAL }. Leaf Voxel: Contains a list of primitives intersecting the voxel volume. Internal Voxel: Contains a local voxel grid subdivision (child voxels) and a hash table mapping child coordinates to child voxel pointers. Hash Table: Used to maintain each non-empty internal voxel, allowing direct access to child grids and enabling deep recursion without linear search overhead. Build Process (Top-Down) All primitives are initially inserted into a single root voxel. The build process is top-down. The algorithm recursively subdivides internal voxels based on one of the following criteria: 1. Octree-like: Subdivide into a 2 \times 2 \times 2 grid (8 children). 2. Maximum Depth: Stop subdivision when a predefined tree depth is reached. 3. Constant Resolution: Fix the resolution of voxel subgrids to a specific value regardless of content density. 4. Variable (Adaptive) Resolution: Subdivide based on occupancy or primitive count thresholds. Parameters Coarseness of the initial voxel grid. Depth of adaptive subdivision trees. Maximum number of polygons per voxel (termination criterion for leaf nodes). Maximum depth for grids: typically 2 or 3. Traversal 1. Intersect ray with the root voxel AABB. 2. If intersection fails, terminate. 3. If the current voxel is a Leaf, test the ray against all primitives in the leaf's list. 4. If the current voxel is Internal, use the hash table to locate the specific child voxel corresponding to the ray's current position. 5. Recursively traverse the child voxel. 6. Continue until a primitive intersection is found or the ray exits the structure. Pitfalls Without a good indexing strategy (such as the hash table used in JW89), it is not possible to use deep levels of recursion efficiently due to the cost of locating child nodes. Build cost is generally higher than general bottom-up strategies. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildgrid(primitives, bounds, depth=0, maxdepth=3, threshold=10): # Standard top-down recursive subdivision voxel = Voxel(bounds) if len(primitives) <= threshold or depth >= maxdepth: voxel.type = LEAF voxel.primitives = primitives return voxel voxel.type = INTERNAL # Subdivide bounds into 2x2x2 child cells childcells = splitbounds(bounds) childprimitives = [[] for in range(8)] for prim in primitives: for i, cell in enumerate(childcells): if intersects(prim, cell): childprimitives[i].append(prim) # Recursively build children and populate hash table hashtable = {} for i, cellprims in enumerate(childprimitives): if cellprims: childbounds = childcells[i] childvoxel = buildgrid(childprims, childbounds, depth + 1, maxdepth, threshold) hashtable[i] = childvoxel voxel.children = hashtable return voxel def traverseray(ray, voxel): # Standard ray-voxel traversal if not intersects(ray, voxel.bounds): return None if voxel.type == LEAF: return intersectprimitives(ray, voxel.primitives) # Compute child index from ray position childidx = getchildindex(ray, voxel.bounds) if childidx in voxel.children: return traverseray(ray, voxel.children[childidx]) return None Time Complexity: Build time is higher than bottom-up strategies. Traversal cost depends on recursion depth and hash table lookup. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of internal nodes and the hash table storage for non-empty voxels. Strengths: Efficiently handles mixed-scale scenes (large regular objects + small dense objects). Limitations: High build cost. Not well-suited for GPU computation due to branching and pointer chasing inherent in hash-table-based recursive traversal. When to use: CPU-based ray tracing where scene geometry has significant scale variation. When not to use: GPU ray tracing (due to branching and memory access patterns). The method was proposed by Jevans and Wyvill in 1989. It is described in detail in "A Survey on Exploiting Grids for Ray Tracing" and "Grids in Ray Tracing: A Comprehensive Survey". The approach integrates regular grid traversal with adaptive subdivision, offering a middle ground between uniform grids and octrees. name: Sparse Multi-Scale Grid
head: nested backend, nested multi-resolution backend
body: The Sparse Multi-Scale Grid is a volume rendering and projection algorithm for Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) data that assigns particles to a hierarchy of grid levels based on their kernel smoothing length, deposits contributions onto coarser grids, and collapses the hierarchy coarse-to-fine via upsampling to bound per-particle cost. It sets itself apart from single-resolution backends by providing large speedups for simulations with a wide range of smoothing lengths, such as zoom-ins or cosmological boxes including the intergalactic medium (IGM). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: SPH particle data (positions, masses, smoothing lengths h), target output resolution R, target cells per kernel diameter n{target}, and hierarchy depth n{levels}. Outputs: A rendered volume (3D) or projected image (2D) with density values. Data Structures: The method uses a hierarchical grid structure. Level 0: A coarse grid covering the domain. Levels 1 to n{levels}: Finer sub-grids. Occupancy: Cells in coarser grids point to finer sub-grids if occupied. Empty cells are skipped. Bounding Boxes: Bounding boxes of occupied regions are tracked to skip empty areas during the hierarchy collapse. Parameters: n{target}: Target number of cells per kernel diameter. Default: 6. n{levels}: Depth of the grid hierarchy. Default: 4. R: Output resolution. Must be divisible by 2^{n{levels}}; otherwise, a ValueError is raised. Algorithm Steps: 1. Level Assignment: For each particle, determine the grid level it belongs to based on its smoothing length h. The level is chosen such that the kernel spans approximately n{target} cells at that level. 2. Deposit: Deposit particle contributions (e.g., density) onto the assigned coarser grid level using the appropriate kernel (Wendland-C2). 3. Collapse (Upsampling): Collapse the hierarchy from coarse to fine. For 3D volume rendering, use trilinear interpolation during upsampling. For 2D projection, use bilinear interpolation during upsampling. Only visit cells within the tracked bounding boxes of occupied regions. 4. Periodic Wrapping: Handle periodic boundary conditions per image, but only for images where the kernel overlaps the region. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparsemultiscalegrid(particles, resolution, ntarget=6, nlevels=4): """ Render SPH data using the Sparse Multi-Scale Grid method. Args: particles: List of particle data (pos, mass, h). resolution: Output resolution R. ntarget: Target cells per kernel diameter. nlevels: Hierarchy depth. Returns: Rendered grid (3D) or image (2D). """ # Validate resolution if resolution % (2 nlevels) != 0: raise ValueError("Resolution must be divisible by 2nlevels") # Initialize hierarchy # Level 0 grid covers the domain gridlevels = [creategrid(resolution / (2 (nlevels - i))) for i in range(nlevels)] # Track occupied bounding boxes for each level occupiedbboxes = [None] nlevels # Step 1 & 2: Assign and Deposit for particle in particles: h = particle.smoothinglength # Determine level based on h and ntarget # Level L has cell size CL. We want h / CL approx ntarget # CL = R / 2^(nlevels - 1 - L) ? Or similar scaling. # The source implies assignment based on kernel spanning cells. level = assignlevel(h, resolution, ntarget, nlevels) # Deposit onto gridlevels[level] depositparticle(particle, gridlevels[level]) # Update bounding box for this level updatebbox(occupiedbboxes[level], particle.position) # Step 3: Collapse coarse-to-fine # Start from level 0 (coarsest) up to nlevels-1 (finest) for level in range(nlevels - 1): coarsegrid = gridlevels[level] finegrid = gridlevels[level + 1] # Get bounding box for current level bbox = occupiedbboxes[level] if bbox is None: continue # Upsample coarse grid to fine grid within bbox # 3D uses trilinear, 2D uses bilinear upsamplingfunc = trilinear if is3d else bilinear upsamplingfunc(coarsegrid, finegrid, bbox) # Update bounding box for fine level based on upsampled data updatebbox(occupiedbboxes[level + 1], finegrid) # Final grid is the finest level return gridlevels[nlevels - 1] def assignlevel(h, resolution, ntarget, nlevels): """ Assign particle to grid level based on smoothing length. """ # Cell size at level L: CL = resolution / 2^(nlevels - 1 - L) # We want h / CL approx ntarget => CL approx h / ntarget # resolution / 2^(nlevels - 1 - L) approx h / ntarget # 2^(nlevels - 1 - L) approx resolution ntarget / h # nlevels - 1 - L approx log2(resolution ntarget / h) # L approx nlevels - 1 - log2(resolution ntarget / h) # Clamp L to [0, nlevels - 1] # This is a simplified derivation; actual implementation may vary slightly # but must ensure h spans ~ntarget cells at level L. import math logval = math.log2(resolution ntarget / h) L = nlevels - 1 - logval L = max(0, min(nlevels - 1, int(round(L)))) return L Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If n{target} or n{levels} are set while using a backend other than 'nested', a UserWarning is raised. Periodic wrapping is handled per image, but only for images where the kernel overlaps the region. Resolution must be divisible by 2^{n{levels}}; otherwise, a ValueError is raised. Time Complexity: The per-particle cost is bounded at O(n{target}^3) for 3D volume rendering and O(n{target}^2) for 2D projection, regardless of the smoothing length. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Projecting 200k particles with smoothing lengths spread over ~3 decades at 1024^2 resolution on 32 threads takes 0.12 s with the nested backend versus 1.2 s with the fast backend. Strengths: Large speedups for simulations with a wide range of smoothing lengths (e.g., zoom-ins, cosmological boxes including the IGM) compared to single-resolution backends. Limitations: Requires resolution to be divisible by 2^{n{levels}}. Periodic wrapping is limited to images where the kernel overlaps the region. When to use: Use for SPH data with a wide dynamic range in smoothing lengths. When not to use: Use single-resolution backends if smoothing lengths are uniform or if resolution constraints cannot be met. The Sparse Multi-Scale Grid algorithm was implemented by Benítez-Llambay in 2025 as a new "nested" backend for the swiftsimio library for both 3D volume rendering and 2D projection of SPH data. It builds on the principles of hierarchical uniform subdivision and ray-grid traversal shared by its parent family. name: Hypertree Grid Construction
head: HyperTree Grid Resampling/Conversion, Hypertree Grid Generation
body: Hypertree Grid Construction is a preprocessing method that converts unstructured or structured mesh data into a native hypertree grid format to enable efficient visualization of large-scale Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) simulations. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly building a hierarchical tree structure where coarse cells point to finer sub-grids, allowing full-resolution visualization of datasets with hundreds of millions of cells on consumer hardware, whereas alternatives often require supercomputer nodes for equivalent workloads. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unstructured mesh data (e.g., VTK, Exodus) or structured Cartesian grid data. Output: A native hypertree grid data structure optimized for ray-grid traversal. Data Structures: The hypertree grid consists of a hierarchy of cells. Each cell at level L may have children at level L+1. Root Level: Contains coarse cells covering the domain. Leaf Level: Contains the finest resolution cells. Internal Nodes: Represent intermediate refinement levels. Memory Layout: The structure is stored in a way that minimizes overhead. For unstructured data, the conversion is offline. For structured data, coarser cells are added on top of the final leaves representing the Cartesian grid during streaming/reading. Steps: 1. Data Ingestion: Load the source mesh data. 2. Hierarchy Construction: If the input is unstructured: Perform an offline conversion process to build the hypertree structure from the mesh connectivity and geometry. If the input is structured: During the reading/streaming phase, generate coarser cells that encompass the finest Cartesian grid leaves, effectively wrapping the structured data in a hypertree hierarchy. 3. Optimization: Ensure the tree structure supports efficient ray-grid intersection by maintaining appropriate bounding boxes for each cell level. Parameters: Tree Depth (\delta): The maximum depth of the hypertree. Increasing \delta dilutes the fixed memory costs associated with root-level cells. Conversion Mode: Offline (for unstructured) or Streaming (for structured). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Overhead: Applying rebalancing filters can cause memory overhead as the input mesh must be retained. Load Imbalance: The cost per cell varies depending on execution parameters and algorithm choice, potentially causing load imbalance in parallel execution. A parallelization strategy for hypertree grid visualization using autonomous processes interacting via message passing, distributing the mesh over processes to improve restitution time and handle large-scale HPC data. It differs from sequential construction by requiring a ghost cell mechanism to copy neighbor information for filters like isocontour or gradient computation. Efficiency depends heavily on the quality of mesh distribution and load balancing, as computational cost per cell is variable. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory Footprint: The hypertree grid object shows almost a full order of magnitude improvement (factor of ~7) in memory footprint compared to unstructured grid representation. Execution Time: Linear speedup in execution time is observed when increasing tree depth \delta \in [1; 6] in a synthetic hypertree grid, demonstrating scalability. Measured Performance: Hardware: Tested on a 16 GB laptop and Tera1000-1 supercomputer nodes (128 GB and 1 TB). Dataset: The "asteroid fall" dataset (3x10^8 cells) was visualized at full resolution on a 16 GB laptop, replacing the need for multiple supercomputer nodes. Scalability: Strong scalability demonstrated for a 2D AMR mesh with O(10^8) leaves. It scales almost optimally for memory footprint and super-optimally for execution time until maximum speedup is achieved. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables interactive exploration of massive datasets on consumer hardware; significant memory reduction compared to unstructured grids. Limitations: Parallel efficiency is sensitive to load balancing; rebalancing filters incur memory overhead. The method was developed to address the visualization challenges of large-scale HPC simulations, such as the "asteroid fall" simulation provided by Los Alamos National Laboratory/NASA. It was notably applied to allow the exploitation of a 3x10^8-cell dataset on a 16 GB laptop for the first time, moving away from the requirement of several supercomputer nodes. name: VIPER Ray-Traversal and Surface Intersection Algorithm
head: VIPER, Volume Interactive Picture and Exploration Representation
body: VIPER is a ray-traversal algorithm designed for the interactive volumetric rendering of three-dimensional aerodynamic flow field data. It solves the problem of efficiently identifying surface intersections within large, sparse volumetric datasets by traversing the volume along ray paths. It is distinguished from sibling hierarchical methods by its specific application to fluid fields and its reliance on a traversal efficiency of O(p \cdot r), where p is the pixel count and r is the volume's largest dimension, rather than complex hierarchical mipmap structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric data set representing a flow field (e.g., velocity vectors or scalar values) defined on a grid with dimensions X, Y, Z. Input: A camera view defining a set of rays, one per pixel, cast into the volume. Output: A 2D image displaying superimposed regions on the surface of the object-under-test or vectors/particulates, often rendered as stereo images for depth perception. Data Structures: The data volume is stored as a 3D grid of voxels. The specific bit-packing or memory layout is not given in the sources. The algorithm assumes access to the volume dimensions X, Y, Z. Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel in the output image, initialize a ray origin and direction based on the camera projection. 2. Traversal: Traverse the volume along the ray path. The traversal logic is optimized to achieve an efficiency of O(p \cdot r), where r is the largest dimension of the volume in voxels. The specific traversal step size or boundary checking logic is not detailed in the sources. 3. Intersection Detection: Identify potential surface intersections within the volume. The sources mention "different shells" corresponding to various values, implying isosurface extraction or threshold-based rendering. 4. Relative Distance Calculation: When a candidate intersection point is found, calculate the relative distance to determine its precise position or intensity contribution. The formula is: \text{relative distance} = \frac{\text{target} - \text{value1}}{\text{value2} - \text{value1}} Where: target: The isovalue or threshold being tested. value1: The data value at the first sample point. value2: The data value at the second sample point. 5. Rendering: Render the identified surface regions or vectors onto the 2D display. Stereo rendering may be employed by generating two slightly offset images. Parameters: Isovalues/Thresholds: Used to define the "shells" or surface regions. Volume Dimensions (X, Y, Z): Determine the traversal complexity. Edge Cases: Sparse Data: The algorithm's efficiency depends on the volume size, but handling sparse data specifically is not detailed. Precision: The linear interpolation formula assumes value1 and value2 bracket the target value. If they do not, the relative distance may be outside [0, 1]. A GPU rendering technique that processes one ray per thread, using warp-level parallelism to traverse the simulation domain and calculate ray-fluid surface intersections. Time Complexity: The algorithm operates with an efficiency of O(p \cdot r), where p is the number of pixels and r is the volume's largest dimension in voxels. The data-reading portion operates at a linear efficiency level of O(d), where d is the number of data points to be read in. Space Complexity: Space complexity is dependent on the size of the data volume. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Efficient for interactive rendering of aerodynamic flow fields; supports stereo visualization. Limitations: Complexity scales linearly with the largest volume dimension; specific optimization techniques for sparse data are not described. VIPER was developed for the display of three-dimensional aerodynamic flow field data. It is described in a report from the Defense Technical Information Center (DTIC). The method is used to visualize flow fields around objects, such as frictionless spheres, displaying vectors and particulates. DTIC ADA202661: Volumetric Rendering Techniques for the Display of Three-Dimensional Aerodynamic Flow Field Data, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA202661, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Warp-based Ray-Fluid Surface Intersection
body: A GPU rendering technique that processes one ray per thread, using warp-level parallelism to traverse the simulation domain and calculate ray-fluid surface intersections. It avoids inter-thread communication during traversal and uses intra-warp voting to identify potential intersections. It builds on VIPER Ray-Traversal and Surface Intersection Algorithm. Inputs: A queue of rays, each defined by an origin O and direction D; a simulation data structure containing cells with particles or field values; a warp size w. Outputs: Intersection distances \lambda, normals n, and colors C for each ray. Data Structures: Ray Queue: Stores ray parameters. Processed one ray at a time per thread. Simulation Domain: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) defined by C{min} and C{max}. Cell Data: Cells c contain particles or field quantities \phi(x). Steps: 1. Ray Queue Processing: All rays are stored in a queue. One ray is processed at a time by a single thread. 2. Domain Intersection: Calculate the intersection of the ray with the simulation domain AABB. This yields a close distance \lambda{min} and far distance \lambda{max}. Clamp \lambda{min} to positive values to get \lambda{min}^+ = \max(\lambda{min}, 0). 3. Warp Traversal: Execute simulation domain intersection and data structure traversal independently on all threads in a warp. No inter-thread communication is required during this phase. 4. Synchronization: Synchronize threads in the warp. 5. Potential Intersection Check: Check if any thread found a cell that can potentially contain fluid surfaces. 6. Surface Intersection Calculation: For the potential intersections, calculate the actual ray-fluid intersection and store results if found. This involves evaluating a single intersection of a ray with a found cell \bar{c} in parallel using all threads in a warp. Sequentially process the overall set of potential intersections. Subdivision Formula: To evaluate the intersection within a found cell \bar{c}, the interval [\max\{\lambda{min}^{\bar{c}}, 0\}, \lambda{max}^{\bar{c}}) is subdivided into w-1 segments for a warp size of w. Each segment s \in [0, w-1) is assigned a starting position xs: xs = \text{ray}\left( \max\{\lambda{min}^{\bar{c}}, 0\} + \frac{s}{w-1} \left( \lambda{max}^{\bar{c}} - \max\{\lambda{min}^{\bar{c}}, 0\} \right) \right) \quad (34) Each thread in a warp is assigned one position, with the last thread assigned x = \text{ray}(\lambda{max}^{\bar{c}}). Each ray is assigned an associated distance value \lambdas. Cell Intersection Details: If a cell c is found, calculate the intersection of the ray with the cell to yield \lambda{min}^c and \lambda{max}^c. The point of ray-cell intersection is xi = \text{ray}(\lambda{min}^c). The cell center is xc = D{min} + c \circ C{max}, with half cell size rc = 0.5 C{max}. The normal nc is determined by: nc = \left[ (1 + \epsilon) d \oslash rc \right] \quad (33) where d = xi - xc, \epsilon is a small positive value, [\cdot] denotes rounding to the nearest integer, and \oslash denotes element-wise division. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def warpbasedrayfluidintersection(rays, datastructure, warpsize): results = [] for ray in rays: # Step 2: Domain Intersection lambdamin, lambdamax = intersectrayaabb(ray.origin, ray.direction, datastructure.domain) lambdaminpos = max(lambdamin, 0.0) # Step 3 & 4: Warp Traversal and Sync # Assume warpthreads is a list of thread indices in the current warp # Each thread executes traversal independently potentialcells = [] for tidx in warpthreads: # Independent traversal logic cell = traversedatastructure(ray, lambdaminpos, lambdamax, datastructure) if cell is not None: potentialcells.append((tidx, cell)) syncwarp() # Step 5: Check for potential intersections if potentialcells: # Step 6: Calculate actual intersection for tidx, cell in potentialcells: # Subdivide interval lambdaminc, lambdamaxc = intersectraycell(ray, cell) intervalstart = max(lambdaminc, 0.0) intervalend = lambdamaxc # Assign positions to threads threadpositions = [] for s in range(warpsize - 1): t = s / (warpsize - 1) pos = intervalstart + t (intervalend - intervalstart) threadpositions.append(pos) # Last thread gets the end threadpositions.append(intervalend) # Evaluate intersection in parallel # This part depends on the specific surface representation (particle, cell, or field) # For cell representation: intersectionfound = False for pos in threadpositions: xi = ray.origin + pos ray.direction # Calculate normal and check against cell geometry # See formula 33 for normal calculation # If intersection detected, store result if checkcellintersection(xi, cell): results.append((ray, pos, cell)) intersectionfound = True break Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and the cost of traversal per ray. Warp-level parallelism reduces overhead for potential intersection checks. Memory Complexity: Depends on the simulation data structure size. Rays are stored in a queue. Strengths: Avoids inter-thread communication during traversal, improving efficiency on GPU architectures. Limitations: Requires warp synchronization, which can introduce latency if threads diverge significantly. When to use: Suitable for GPU rendering of fluid simulations where ray-cell or ray-particle intersections are frequent. When not to use: If the simulation domain is sparse and traversal overhead dominates, other methods might be more efficient. Originated in the context of Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) simulation and rendering. The method is described in "Multi‐Level Memory Structures for Simulating and Rendering Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics". Multi‐Level Memory Structures for Simulating and Rendering Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14090, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Quadtree Raycasting
head: raycast2
body: Quadtree Raycasting is a recursive ray-quadtree intersection algorithm that traverses a 2D quadtree to find the first hit node. It solves the problem of efficiently locating the first occupied voxel in a hierarchical 2D grid by handling ray direction flipping via a mask to ensure consistent traversal order regardless of ray direction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: start (Vec2, ray origin in world space), dir (Vec2, ray direction vector), node (QuadtreeNode, the root or current subtree to traverse), tx0, ty0, tx1, ty1 (f32, boundary distances in ray parameter space). Output: Optional[Tuple[QuadtreeNode, float]] representing the first hit node and the hit distance t, or None if no intersection is found within the bounds. Data Structures: The QuadtreeNode structure: isfull: bool, indicates if the node represents a fully occupied volume. children: Optional[List[QuadtreeNode]], a fixed-size array of 4 child nodes (bottom-left, bottom-right, top-left, top-right), or None if leaf. size: f32, the spatial extent (width/height) of the node in world units. position: IVec2, the integer coordinates of the node's bottom-left corner. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization and Masking: Initialize a bitmask mask to 0. If dir.x < 0: Flip start.x using start.x = 2.0 node.position.x + node.size - start.x and set mask bit 0. If dir.y < 0: Flip start.y using start.y = 2.0 node.position.y + node.size - start.y and set mask bit 1. 2. Intersection Check: Calculate intersection distances to the node boundaries: tx0 = (node.position.x - start.x) / |dir.x| ty0 = (node.position.y - start.y) / |dir.y| tx1 = (node.position.x + node.size - start.x) / |dir.x| ty1 = (node.position.y + node.size - start.y) / |dir.y| Determine intersection interval: t{min} = \max(tx0, ty0) t{max} = \min(tx1, ty1) If t{min} \ge t{max}, the ray does not intersect the node bounding box; return None. 3. Recursive Traversal (procsubtree): Call the recursive function with the current node and the calculated boundary distances (tx0, ty0, tx1, ty1). Inside procsubtree(node, tx0, ty0, tx1, ty1, mask): 1. Early Exit: If tx1 < 0 or ty1 < 0, the ray has passed the node's far boundary; return None. 2. Leaf Check: If node.children is None: If node.isfull is true, the ray hits this node. Calculate hit distance t = \max(tx0, ty0). Return (node, t). 3. Internal Node: If the node has children: Calculate midpoints: txm = (tx0 + tx1) / 2 tym = (ty0 + ty1) / 2 Determine the first child index to visit using firstnode(tx0, ty0, txm, tym) which accounts for the ray direction relative to the sub-regions. Iterate through children using a loop variable currnode starting from firstnode(...). For each child, apply the mask to the index: childidx = currnode ^ mask. This ensures the logical child index corresponds to the correct spatial quadrant regardless of ray direction. Child 0 (Bottom-Left): Recurse with bounds (tx0, ty0, txm, tym). If a hit is returned, propagate it up. Else, continue. Child 1 (Bottom-Right): Recurse with bounds (txm, ty0, tx1, tym). If a hit is returned, propagate it up. Else, continue. Child 2 (Top-Left): Recurse with bounds (tx0, tym, txm, ty1). If a hit is returned, propagate it up. Else, continue. Child 3 (Top-Right): Recurse with bounds (txm, tym, tx1, ty1). If a hit is returned, propagate it up. Else, terminate the loop. If no child returns a hit, return None. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from typing import Optional, Tuple, List class QuadtreeNode: def init(self, isfull: bool, children: Optional[List['QuadtreeNode']], size: float, position: Tuple[int, int]): self.isfull = isfull self.children = children self.size = size self.position = position def quadtreeraycast(start: Tuple[float, float], dir: Tuple[float, float], node: QuadtreeNode) -> Optional[Tuple[QuadtreeNode, float]]: # Step 1: Initialization and Masking mask = 0 currentstart = list(start) if dir[0] < 0: currentstart[0] = 2.0 node.position[0] + node.size - name: Hierarchical Data Structure Traversal
head: Ray-Casting with Hierarchical Data Structure (Ma)
body: Hierarchical Data Structure Traversal is a parallel ray-casting method for rendering unstructured volume data, specifically designed to handle complex cell connectivity using a hierarchical data structure (HDS). It solves the problem of efficiently traversing unstructured grids by pre-computing face-node and cell-face relationships, allowing rays to jump between cells based on exterior face intersections rather than dense voxel stepping. Unlike sibling methods that rely on regular grid mips or spatial partitioning trees (e.g., KD-Tree Partitioned Volume Rendering, Octree-based traversal), this approach explicitly manages the topological connectivity of arbitrary unstructured cells to determine ray entry and exit points. Inputs: Unstructured volume dataset (cells, nodes, faces); camera parameters; hierarchical data structure (HDS) containing face-node, cell-face, and cell-node relationships. Outputs: Composite image pixels. Data Structures: The HDS stores topological relationships: 1. facenode: Maps each face to its constituent nodes. 2. cellface: Maps each cell to its constituent faces. 3. cellnode: Maps each cell to its constituent nodes. 4. exteriorfaces: A list of faces that are not shared between two cells (boundary faces). Steps: 1. Connectivity Pre-step: Each processor computes the cell connectivity information and identifies exterior faces. 2. View Frustum Culling: Cells completely outside the camera view are excluded from processing. 3. Ray Casting Application: Each processor applies the ray-casting algorithm to its assigned subset of data. 4. Ray Traversal: a. A ray enters the volume through an exterior face. b. The algorithm uses the HDS connectivity information to determine the next cell intersected by the ray. c. The ray continues traversing cells until it intersects a second exterior face, at which point it exits the volume. 5. Parallel Composition: Image pixels are assigned to different processors. The HDS is used to exchange ray data between processors if necessary. 6. Compositing: Rays are composited (blended) to produce the final pixel color. Formulas: The value of each sample is computed by interpolating cell vertices. The corresponding scalar value is used as a 1D texture coordinate to obtain the color. C = \text{Interpolate}(V{nodes}) \text{Color} = \text{TextureLookup}(C) Slices are rendered in back-to-front order based on distance from the viewing direction. Parameters: Processor Count: Determined by the parallel implementation (many-core sampler). Slicing Strategy: Three slices per cell (perpendicular to X, Y, Z axes) are generated; the camera view determines which slice is used. Edge Cases: Exterior Face Identification: Correctly identifying faces that are not shared between cells is critical for determining ray entry/exit. Parallel Exchange: The HDS must support efficient ray exchange between processors assigned to different image pixels. A structure pointing to a vertex of a hypertree within a hypertree grid, capable of accessing vertex attributes and moving to connected vertices. It solves the problem of navigating tree-based Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) grids by providing a flexible traversal mechanism that does not impose a predetermined scheme, unlike iterators. It sets itself apart from simple iterators by supporting arbitrary displacement operations (such as moving to parents or roots) rather than just sequential iteration. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the HDS (face-node, cell-face, cell-node relationships). Performance: Designed for scalability on many-core architectures using a hybrid scheme. Strengths: Efficient handling of unstructured data via explicit connectivity; parallelizable via processor assignment. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of connectivity; relies on HDS for inter-processor communication. When to use: Rendering unstructured volume data where regular grid traversal is inefficient or impossible. When not to use: Regular structured grids where simpler DDA or grid-based traversal is sufficient. Originated in the work of Max et al. [21] and adapted by the authors of using a many-core sampler (EAVL) implemented by Larsen et al. [22]. The method was developed to address the challenges of rendering unstructured volume data in a parallel environment. name: Hypertree Cursor
head: Hypertree Grid Cursor
body: A hypertree cursor is a structure pointing to a vertex of a hypertree within a hypertree grid, capable of accessing vertex attributes and moving to connected vertices. It solves the problem of navigating tree-based Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) grids by providing a flexible traversal mechanism that does not impose a predetermined scheme, unlike iterators. It sets itself apart from simple iterators by supporting arbitrary displacement operations (such as moving to parents or roots) rather than just sequential iteration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hypertree grid object and a target hypertree index or iterator. Output: A cursor object pointing to a specific vertex, allowing access to attributes and movement to adjacent vertices. Data Structures: The cursor holds at least the following information: 1. A reference to the hypertree being traversed. 2. The identifier of the vertex currently pointed to. From this, the associated Global Index ng can be retrieved. Displacement Operators: The cursor supports the following operations: 1. ToChild(ichild): Descends into the vertex with child index ichild. This respects the depth-limiter and bitmask relative to the current vertex, unless the current vertex is already a leaf. 2. ToParent(): Moves one vertex up in the tree, unless already at the root. 3. ToRoot(): Moves to the root of the tree. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class HypertreeCursor: def init(self, hypertree, vertexid): """ Initialize cursor.:param hypertree: Reference to the hypertree object.:param vertexid: Identifier of the current vertex. """ self.hypertree = hypertree self.vertexid = vertexid def getglobalindex(self): """Retrieve the Global Index ng associated with the current vertex.""" # Implementation depends on hypertree's internal mapping from vertexid to ng return self.hypertree.getglobalindex(self.vertexid) def tochild(self, ichild): """ Descend into the vertex with child index ichild.:param ichild: Index of the child (0 to 7 in 3D, etc.).:raises: If already at a leaf or invalid ichild. """ if self.hypertree.isleaf(self.vertexid): raise ValueError("Cannot descend from leaf") # Check depth-limiter and bitmask constraints if not self.hypertree.isvalidchild(self.vertexid, ichild): raise ValueError("Child index violates depth-limiter or bitmask") self.vertexid = self.hypertree.getchild(self.vertexid, ichild) def toparent(self): """Move one vertex up in the tree.""" if self.hypertree.isroot(self.vertexid): raise ValueError("Already at root") self.vertexid = self.hypertree.getparent(self.vertexid) def toroot(self): """Move to the root of the tree.""" self.vertexid = self.hypertree.getrootid() def getattributes(self): """Access vertex attributes.""" return self.hypertree.getvertexattributes(self.vertexid) Parameters and Constraints: Depth-limiter: A constraint limiting the maximum depth of traversal. Bitmask: A constraint filtering valid children based on refinement status. Edge Cases: Attempting to move to a child of a leaf node. Attempting to move to a parent of the root node. Invalid child indices that violate the bitmask or depth-limiter. A supercursor is a compound structure that extends a standard hypertree cursor by maintaining real-time neighborhood information for the cell it references. It solves the problem of efficiently accessing adjacent cells in an Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) hypertree grid, where neighbors may reside in different hypertrees or exist at varying refinement levels. Unlike a standard cursor that only tracks a single vertex path, the supercursor aggregates references to all immediate neighbors, enabling algorithms like outside boundary extraction that require checking cell adjacency. These are abstractions used to traverse the collection of hypertrees within a hypertree grid. GetTree(nHT): Allows direct access to the n{HT}-th hypertree from a defined hypertree grid. GetNextTree(): Called on a hypertree iterator to iterate through all defined hypertrees, thereby avoiding undefined hypertrees. Oriented vs Non-Oriented: Oriented cursors use only ToChild(ichild) and are more efficient for simple traversal. Non-oriented cursors include ToChild(ichild), ToParent(), and ToRoot(). Two hypertrees H and H' are rectilinearly consecutive for component k (denoted H \preck H' when d \neq 3) if the outside boundary of H \cup H' is a line segment (in d=1), a rectangle (in d=2), or a rectangular prism (in d=3). This boundary must have the same origin, orientation, and size vector as H, except for the k-th component, which is the sum of their k-size vectors. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Oriented cursors are more efficient than non-oriented cursors for simple traversal because they perform fewer operations. Strengths: Richer than iterators by not imposing a predetermined traversal scheme; supports arbitrary navigation within the tree structure. Limitations: Requires careful handling of depth-limiters and bitmasks during traversal. The hypertree cursor was introduced in the context of efficient visualization and analysis of large-scale, tree-based, adaptive mesh refinement simulations with rectilinear geometry. It is part of a broader framework including hypertree grids, accessors, iterators, and supercursors, designed to handle AMR meshes that may not be contiguous or uniform. name: Supercursor
head: Fragrance-based Cursors, Hypertree Grid Cursor System, Hypertree Grid Filters, cursor with neighborhood information [S1, unofficial]
body: A supercursor is a compound structure that extends a standard hypertree cursor by maintaining real-time neighborhood information for the cell it references. It solves the problem of efficiently accessing adjacent cells in an Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) hypertree grid, where neighbors may reside in different hypertrees or exist at varying refinement levels. Unlike a standard cursor that tracks a single vertex path, a supercursor tracks neighborhood information based on the chosen cursor fragrance type (e.g., VonNeumann or Moore), enabling algorithms like outside boundary extraction that require checking cell adjacency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hypertree grid containing multiple hypertrees, and the index of the target hypertree. Output: A supercursor instance pointing to a specific cell and holding a set of references to its neighbors. Data Structures: The supercursor is a compound structure containing: 1. Central Cursor: A standard hypertree cursor that holds a reference to the hypertree and the vertex identifier of the current cell. 2. Neighborhood Information: A collection of references to neighbor cells, which may point to cells within the same hypertree or in adjacent hypertrees. The structure maintains references to neighbors based on the cursor's fragrance type (e.g., VonNeumann uses points in 1D, edges in 2D, faces in 3D; Moore uses points, edges, and faces). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: When created, the central cursor references the cell root of the considered hypertree, and neighborhood information corresponds to the different root cells of the neighbor hypertrees. 2. Traversal (Descending): When the central cursor descends to a child, the supercursor updates its neighborhood information. Neighbors of the new cell can be a mix of cells on the same level (coarse or leaf cells) or from previous levels (which are necessarily leaf cells relative to the current finer grid). 3. Neighbor Reference Management: A neighbor may be referenced multiple times by the same supercursor, which occurs specifically when the neighbor is a leaf cell at the level immediately above (coarser than) the supercursor's current level. Parameters: d: Dimension of the grid (e.g., 1, 2, 3). f: Fan-out factor (number of children per cell, e.g., 2 or 3). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Neighbors may be referenced multiple times by the same supercursor when the neighbor is a leaf cell at the level above the supercursor's current level. When a supercursor cursor points to a coarse cell (not a leaf), it must be descended into the adequate child of the parent cell neighbor, requiring the Child Cursor to Child Index Table. Projective transformations and arbitrary rotations cannot be supported because they do not preserve axis-alignment of rectilinear hypertree grids. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Cursor: def init(self, hypertreeid, vertexid, isleaf): self.hypertreeid = hypertreeid self.vertexid = vertexid self.isleaf = isleaf def descendtochild(self, childindex): # Standard cursor descent logic self.vertexid = self.vertexid 2 + childindex self.isleaf = False class Supercursor: def init(self, grid, targethypertreeid): self.grid = grid self.cursors = [] # Initialization: central cursor references cell root self.cursors.append(Cursor(targethypertreeid, 0, False)) # Neighborhood info corresponds to root cells of neighbor hypertrees for nhid in self.grid.getneighborhypertrees(targethypertreeid): self.cursors.append(Cursor(nhid, 0, False)) def getnumberofcursors(self): return len(self.cursors) def getcursor(self, index): return self.cursors[index] def setcursor(self, index, cursor): self.cursors[index] = cursor def descendtochild(self, childindex): # Update central cursor (index 0) self.cursors[0].descendtochild(childindex) # Algorithm 5.3: SuperCursorToChild(s, i) n = self.getnumberofcursors() c = [self.getcursor(j) for j in range(n)] # Step 2: copy cursors to temp storage # Pre-computed traversal tables for this supercursor type and dimension C = self.grid.getchildcursortochildtable(childindex) P = self.grid.getchildcursortoparentcursortable(childindex) for j in range(n): k = P[j] self.setcursor(j, c[k]) # Step 7: update cursor reference if not c[k].isleaf: # Step 9: descend into adequate child if neighbor is coarse self.getcursor(j).descendtochild(C[j]) Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The supercursor requires additional memory compared to a standard cursor to store the neighborhood references, but the footprint is kept minimal by avoiding dual cell duplication and storing only one virtual dual cell at a time. The size of the neighborhood list depends on the dimensionality and cursor type, but exact neighbor counts are not given in the sources. Time: Initialization is linear in the number of adjacent hypertrees. Traversal updates are linear in the number of cursors maintained by the supercursor, as Algorithm 5.3 iterates over all cursors once. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables efficient implementation of algorithms requiring local topology, such as boundary extraction, without repeatedly querying the global grid structure. Limitations: Must handle cross-hypertree references and varying refinement levels, which requires pre-computed traversal tables. Projective transformations and arbitrary rotations cannot be supported because they do not preserve axis-alignment of rectilinear hypertree grids. When to Use: Use when implementing visualization filters or analysis algorithms that require checking cell adjacency, such as outside boundary extraction. The supercursor was devised and implemented to support visualization algorithms on hypertree grids, which represent AMR simulations with rectilinear geometry. It addresses the gap in hypertree grid-aware filters, which historically had less coverage than unstructured mesh filters. The concept is defined within the Hypertree Grid data structure, where the grid is decomposed into multiple hypertrees to manage large-scale AMR data.
