name: 3DDDA Ray Traversal for Hierarchical Grids
head: 3DDDA for Hierarchical Grids
body: This method performs ray traversal on hierarchical grid structures by combining a top-level grid traversal with 3DDDA (3D Digital Differential Analyzer) steps at each level. It solves the problem of efficiently skipping empty space in sparse volumetric data or hierarchical scene representations. It differs from its parent Hierarchical DDA by explicitly utilizing the 3DDDA algorithm for stepping through voxels within a grid instance, and from its sibling Hierarchical DDA with Chunk Stepping by relying on standard 3DDDA logic rather than chunk-based optimization. Inputs: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a hierarchical grid structure where each node contains a list of objects or children. Outputs: Intersection status and distance, or null if no intersection is found within the grid's bounds. Data Structures: Grid Node: Contains a bounding box, a list of child nodes (or primitives), and a flag indicating if the node has been tested. 3DDDA State: For each grid instance, precomputed constants including step sizes \Delta tx, \Delta ty, \Delta tz and initial t-values t{maxx}, t{maxy}, t{maxz} based on the ray and the grid's bounding box. Algorithm Steps: 1. Cache Check: If the current grid node has already been tested for this ray, return the known result. 2. Initialization: Prepare the 3DDDA constants for the current grid instance based on the ray parameters and the grid's bounding box. 3. Child Intersection Test: Within the current voxel (defined by the 3DDDA position), test all objects or child nodes contained in the list for intersection. If an intersection exists and lies within the current voxel's bounds, return the intersection. 4. Step Forward: If no intersection is found in the current voxel, proceed to the next voxel along the ray path using the 3DDDA algorithm. 5. Termination: If there is no next voxel in the current grid (ray has exited the grid bounds), return no intersection. Otherwise, return to Step 3. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversehierarchicalgrid(ray, gridnode): # Step 1: Cache check if gridnode.tested: return gridnode.result # Step 2: Prepare 3DDDA constants # Calculate tmax and step values for x, y, z axes based on ray and grid bounds tmaxx, tmaxy, tmaxz = compute3dddaconstants(ray, gridnode.bbox) stepx, stepy, stepz = compute3dddasteps(ray) # Initialize current voxel coordinates currx, curry, currz = gridnode.bbox.min tcurrent = 0.0 while True: # Step 3: Test children/objects in current voxel for child in gridnode.children: if intersect(ray, child, tcurrent, tmaxx, tmaxy, tmaxz): gridnode.tested = True gridnode.result = intersection return intersection # Step 4: Proceed to next voxel # Determine which axis to step based on smallest tmax if tmaxx < tmaxy and tmaxx < tmaxz: currx += stepx tmaxx += stepx elif tmaxy < tmaxx and tmaxy < tmaxz: curry += stepy tmaxy += stepy else: currz += stepz tmaxz += stepz # Check if ray has exited the grid if not gridnode.bbox.contains(currx, curry, currz): gridnode.tested = True gridnode.result = None return None # Step 5: Loop back to test children in new voxel Edge Cases: Superfluous Tests: Comparing only object bounding boxes to grid cells can result in objects being added to cells they do not actually overlap, causing unnecessary intersection tests. Pruning by testing primitives against cells can reduce this but may not significantly improve performance for SPD scenes. Precision: Standard 3DDDA precision issues may arise near voxel boundaries; careful handling of floating-point comparisons is required. Complexity: Depends on the sparsity of the grid and the depth of the hierarchy. In the worst case (fully occupied), it degrades to linear traversal. Performance: Pruning bounding box tests against cells can improve performance by at most 10% for SPD scenes. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space using hierarchical structure and 3DDDA stepping. Limitations: Bounding box overlap can lead to redundant intersection tests if not pruned. This method is described in the context of ray tracing for hierarchical grids, where the traversal logic is similar across approaches but differs in how the hierarchy is structured (e.g., BVH vs. grid). The specific 3DDDA steps for hierarchical grids are outlined in early real-time rendering news discussions. name: Octree Traversal (Horizontal and Vertical)
head: 3DDDA Octree Traversal
body: This method defines the traversal logic for hierarchical octree structures using the 3DDDA ray representation. It solves the problem of efficiently navigating a sparse, multi-resolution volume representation by distinguishing between movement within a single node (horizontal traversal) and movement between nodes of different levels (vertical traversal). It sets itself apart from simple cell decomposition by introducing vertical descent and ascent mechanisms that utilize 3DDDA state variables, while reusing the horizontal traversal logic unchanged. The method relies on the 3DDDA ray representation Parent. It operates on an octree where nodes are classified as HETERO-BRANCH, HETERO-LEAF, or HOMO. Node Numbering: Octants within a node are ordered systematically. Each digit of the binary node number corresponds to a cell index in the cell decomposition. For a single node, there are exactly two octants in each principal direction (x, y, z). The indices satisfy 0 \leq i, j, k \leq 1. Pointer Array: An array POINTER stores pointers to child nodes. Working Array: A short working array of length equal to the number of levels in the tree. It stores pointers recorded during descent to facilitate ascent. 3DDDA State Variables: Control terms (typically related to distance to next grid plane). Inverse slopes (reciprocals of ray direction components). Octant size (current voxel size at the current level). 1. Horizontal Traversal (Intra-node): Traverse octants within the current node exactly as in a simple cell-decomposed structure. When moving from one cell to an adjacent cell, update exactly one of the three indices (i, j, k). The new octant number is derived directly from the updated indices. Termination: Horizontal traversal terminates when any index overflows or underflows (i.e., becomes <0 or >1), indicating the ray has left the current node. 2. Vertical Traversal (Descent): Triggered when 3DDDA identifies a HETERO-BRANCH node. Suspend 3DDDA execution. Traverse downwards until a HETERO-LEAF or HOMO node is reached. Determine the child node to enter using the current 3DDDA byproducts: control terms, inverse slopes, and octant size. State Update: On each vertical movement from one level to the next, multiply or divide the relevant state variables by two. This is performed using fixed-point arithmetic (bit shifts). Record the pointer from the POINTER array into the working array at the current level index. 3. Vertical Traversal (Ascent): Triggered when horizontal traversal terminates due to index overflow/underflow. Ascend the tree to identify the adjacent node. Use the working array (populated during descent) to retrieve the correct parent pointers. The pointers are not linked backwards in the tree structure itself, so the working array is essential. Resume 3DDDA execution in the new node. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseoctree(rayorigin, raydirection, rootnode, treelevels): # Initialize 3DDDA state variables based on ray and root node size # These include control terms, inverse slopes, and current octant size ddastate = init3ddda(rayorigin, raydirection, rootnode.size) # Working array to store pointers during descent # Length equals number of levels in the tree pointerstack = [None] treelevels currentlevel = 0 currentnode = rootnode while True: # --- Horizontal Traversal --- # Indices for the 2x2x2 octants within the current node i, j, k = 0, 0, 0 while True: # Process current octant (i, j, k) octantindex = (i << 2) | (j << 1) | k # Example mapping, see Yamaguchi order processvoxel(currentnode, octantindex, ddastate) # Determine next octant in horizontal sequence # Update one index at a time based on systematic order nexti, nextj, nextk = getnextoctantindices(i, j, k) # Check for boundary exit (overflow/underflow) if nexti < 0 or nexti > 1 or nextj < 0 or nextj > 1 or nextk < 0 or nextk > 1: break # Horizontal traversal terminated i, j, k = nexti, nextj, nextk # --- Vertical Traversal (Ascent or Descent Decision) --- # If we exited horizontally, we must ascend to find the adjacent node # If we hit a HETERO-BRANCH during processing, we must descend # Note: The specific trigger for descent vs ascent depends on the # node type encountered at the exit point or during processing. if nodeisheterobranch(currentnode): # --- Descent --- # Suspend 3DDDA suspendedstate = ddastate # Record pointer for ascent later pointerstack[currentlevel] = currentnode.pointertochild # Determine which child to enter using 3DDDA byproducts childindex = determinechild(ddastate) # Move to child currentnode = currentnode.children[childindex] currentlevel += 1 # Update state variables for new level (fixed-point mult/div by 2) ddastate = updatestateforlevel(ddastate, descent=True) # Resume 3DDDA in new node # Loop continues to process horizontal traversal in new node elif horizontalexitoccurred: # --- Ascent --- # Use pointerstack to find parent if currentlevel == 0: break # Reached root, ray is done # Retrieve parent pointer from stack parentpointer = pointerstack[currentlevel - 1] # Move up currentnode = parentpointer.parent currentlevel -= 1 # Update state variables for new level (fixed-point mult/div by 2) ddastate = updatestateforlevel(ddastate, descent=False) # Determine which sibling to enter next # This requires re-evaluating the exit position relative to the parent nextsibling = findadjacentsibling(currentnode, ddastate) currentnode = nextsibling # Resume 3DDDA Fixed-Point Arithmetic: Multiplication/division by two during vertical traversal is implemented as bit shifts to avoid floating-point operations. Precision: The method avoids floating-point division or multiplication during horizontal traversal. Node Types: The algorithm distinguishes between HETERO-BRANCH (requires descent), HETERO-LEAF (leaf with data), and HOMO (uniform) nodes. Complexity: Horizontal traversal is identical to simple cell decomposition, requiring no modifications to 3DDDA. Vertical traversal adds overhead for descent/ascent but avoids expensive floating-point operations by using fixed-point arithmetic. Performance: Initial experiments on a VAX 11/750 showed significant optimization potential by removing subroutine calls and using integer logic. Strengths: Efficient traversal of hierarchical structures; avoids floating-point division/multiplication in the main loop. Limitations: Requires maintaining a working array for ascent; complex logic for determining child nodes during descent. The method was proposed by Yamaguchi et al.. It was implemented in FORTRAN 77 and tested on a Digital Equipment Corporation VAX 11/750. The systematic ordering of octants was adopted from Yamaguchi et al.. name: Differentiable DDA Loop
head: Differentiable DDA
body: A differentiable Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) loop that traverses a grid along a ray, invoking a callback function for each visited cell. It extends standard DDA traversal by maintaining differentiable state variables, allowing gradients to flow back through the ray marching steps. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray direction rayd2, grid resolution gridres, initial ray origin (implicit in p0), and a callback function func. Outputs: The state returned by the final callback invocation. Data Structures: active: Boolean flag indicating whether the ray is still valid. state: User-defined state object passed to the callback. dtv: Array of step sizes to the next grid line for each active ray. p0: Current position of the ray. pi: Current grid index (integer coordinates). trem: Remaining ray length to traverse. absrcpd2: Precomputed absolute reciprocal of the ray direction components. Numbered Steps: 1. Loop Initialization: Initialize active to true. Initialize dtv based on ray direction and grid spacing. Initialize p0 to the ray origin. Initialize pi to the starting grid cell. Initialize trem to the total ray length. Initialize state to the user's initial state. 2. Step Selection: Compute the step size for this iteration: dt = dr.minimum(dr.min(dtv), trem). Identify which grid lines are hit at this step: mask = dtv == dt. 3. Position Update: Compute the new position using the Fused Multiply-Add (FMA) operation: p1 = dr.fma(rayd2, dt, p0). 4. Callback Invocation: Invoke the user callback function: state, cont = func(state, ArrayNu(pi), p0, p1, active & (dt > 0)). 5. Grid Index Update: Update dtv for active rays: dtv[active] = dr.select(mask, absrcpd2, dtv - dt). Update p0 for active rays: p0[active] = dr.fma(rayd2, dt, p0). Reset p0 components for rays that crossed a grid line boundary: p0[mask & active] = dr.select(rayd2 >= 0, Float(0), Float(1)). Increment pi for rays that crossed a grid line boundary: pi[mask & active] += step. Update trem for active rays: trem[active] = trem - dt. 6. Activity Update: Update the active mask for the next iteration: active[active] &= dr.all((pi >= 0) & (pi < ArrayNi(gridres))) & (trem > 0) & cont. Pitfalls: Starting on a grid line: If the ray starts exactly on a grid line, dt can be 0. The code handles this by selecting the minimum of dtv and trem, and checking dt > 0 before invoking the callback. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentiableddaloop(rayd2, gridres, func, initialstate, rayorigin, raylength): # Explicit FMA and select operations to avoid library dependencies def fma(a, b, c): return a b + c def select(cond, t, f): return t if cond else f # Initialization active = True state = initialstate absrcpd2 = [abs(1.0 / d) for d in rayd2] # dtv initialization: distance to next grid boundary dtv = [] for i in range(3): nextgrid = (pi[i] + 1) if rayd2[i] >= 0 else pi[i] dtv.append(abs((nextgrid - rayorigin[i]) / rayd2[i])) p0 = list(rayorigin) pi = [int(rayorigin[i]) for i in range(3)] trem = raylength while active: # Step Selection dt = min(min(dtv), trem) mask = [dtv[i] == dt for i in range(3)] # Position Update p1 = [fma(rayd2[i], dt, p0[i]) for i in range(3)] # Callback Invocation if dt > 0: state, cont = func(state, pi, p0, p1, active and (dt > 0)) else: cont = True # Grid Index Update for i in range(3): if active: dtv[i] = select(mask[i], absrcpd2[i], dtv[i] - dt) p0[i] = fma(rayd2[i], dt, p0[i]) if mask[i]: p0[i] = select(rayd2[i] >= 0, 0.0, 1.0) stepi = 1 if rayd2[i] >= 0 else -1 pi[i] += stepi trem = trem - dt # Activity Update outofbounds = any(pi[i] < 0 or pi[i] >= gridres[i] for i in range(3)) active = active and not outofbounds and (trem > 0) and cont return state Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal
head: Amanatides-Woo, Amanatides and Woo, AW87, Amanatides-Woo traversal
body: Amanatides-Woo is a fast, branch-minimal algorithm for traversing a uniform 3D voxel grid along a ray, visiting only the voxels intersected by the ray in O(nx + ny + nz) time. It solves the problem of efficiently locating geometry in a dense grid without performing expensive per-voxel intersection tests or suffering from the precision errors and missed voxels inherent in naive fixed-step ray marching. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using floating-point parametric distances (t-values) to determine the next voxel boundary crossing based on the minimum time to cross any axis boundary, guaranteeing that the ray stops and tests a voxel index at exactly one of the x, y, or z dividing planes. The algorithm operates in two phases: initialization and incremental traversal. It assumes a uniform grid where voxels are unit cubes (or scaled by a constant voxelsize) aligned with the world axes. Inputs: rayorigin: vec3 (ox, oy, oz), the starting point of the ray in world space. raydirection: vec3 (dx, dy, dz), the direction vector. It is typically normalized, but the algorithm works with any non-zero direction. gridmin, gridmax: vec3 defining the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the voxel grid in world space. voxelsize: float (optional, default 1.0). The side length of a voxel. If the grid is defined by integer indices 0, Nx) \times [0, Ny) \times [0, Nz), voxelsize maps world coordinates to voxel indices. Outputs: A sequence of voxel indices (i, j, k) visited by the ray, in order of increasing distance from the origin. Optionally, the parametric distance t or world position at which each voxel is entered/exited. The algorithm maintains the following state variables, typically stored as 3-component vectors or arrays: 1. currentvoxel: ivec3 (i, j, k), the integer coordinates of the voxel currently being traversed. 2. step: ivec3 (sx, sy, sz), where si \in \{-1, 1\} indicates the direction of traversal along axis i. 3. tmax: vec3 (t{max,x}, t{max,y}, t{max,z}), the parametric distance t along the ray where the ray crosses the next voxel boundary along each axis. 4. tdelta: vec3 (t{\Delta,x}, t{\Delta,y}, t{\Delta,z}), the parametric distance required to traverse one full voxel width along each axis. Compute the inverse direction and signs. Handle degenerate cases where a direction component is zero to avoid division by zero. \text{inv\dir} = \left( \frac{1}{dx}, \frac{1}{dy}, \frac{1}{dz} \right) \text{step}i = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } di \ge 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } di < 0 \end{cases} \text{t\delta}i = \frac{1}{|di|} \quad \text{(or } \frac{\text{voxel\size}}{|di|} \text{ if scaled)} If di = 0, set \text{t\delta}i = \infty and \text{t\max}i = \infty so that axis is never selected for stepping. Determine the voxel containing the ray origin. If the origin is outside the grid, compute the entry point into the grid AABB using [slab intersection. \text{current\voxel}i = \lfloor \frac{oi - \text{grid\min}i}{\text{voxel\size}} \rfloor Calculate the world position of the entry point p{entry} if the origin is outside. Calculate the parametric distance to the first voxel boundary along each axis. Let p{start} be the entry point (or origin if inside). \text{boundary}i = (\text{current\voxel}i + \max(\text{step}i, 0)) \times \text{voxel\size} + \text{grid\min}i \text{t\max}i = \frac{\text{boundary}i - p{\text{start},i}}{di} Note: If di = 0, \text{t\max}i = \infty. Repeat until the ray exits the grid or a hit is found: 1. Visit: Process the voxel at currentvoxel. 2. Select Axis: Find the axis a with the minimum tmax value: a = \arg \min{i \in \{x,y,z\}} (\text{t\max}i) 3. Step: Increment currentvoxel along axis a: \text{current\voxel}a \leftarrow \text{current\voxel}a + \text{step}a 4. Update tmax: Advance the boundary crossing for axis a by one voxel width: \text{t\max}a \leftarrow \text{t\max}a + \text{t\delta}a 5. Check Bounds: If currentvoxel is outside the grid bounds, terminate. import math def amanatideswootraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, gridmin, gridmax, voxelsize=1.0): # 1. Precomputation invdir = [1.0 / d if abs(d) > 1e-10 else float('inf') for d in raydirection] step = [1 if d >= 0 else -1 for d in raydirection] tdelta = [abs(invdir[i]) voxelsize for i in range(3)] # 2. Initial Voxel and Entry Point inside = all(gridmin[i] <= rayorigin[i] < gridmax[i] for i in range(3)) if not inside: tmin = 0.0 tmaxdist = float('inf') for i in range(3): if abs(raydirection[i]) < 1e-10: if rayorigin[i] < gridmin[i] or rayorigin[i] >= gridmax[i]: return [] t1 = (gridmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] t2 = (gridmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] tentry = min(t1, t2) texit = max(t1, t2) tmin = max(tmin, tentry) tmaxdist = min(tmaxdist, texit) if tmin > tmaxdist: return [] entrypos = [rayorigin[i] + (tmin + 1e-9) raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] pstart = entrypos else: pstart = rayorigin currentvoxel = [math.floor((pstart[i] - gridmin[i]) / voxelsize) for i in range(3)] # 3. Initialize tmax tmax = [] for i in range(3): boundary = (currentvoxel[i] + (1 if step[i] > 0 else 0)) voxelsize + gridmin[i] tmax.append((boundary - pstart[i]) invdir[i]) # 4. Traversal Loop visited = [] griddims = [(gridmax[i] - gridmin[i]) / voxelsize for i in range(3)] while all(0 <= currentvoxel[i] < griddims[i] for i in range(3)): visited.append(tuple(currentvoxel)) mint = tmax[0] axis = 0 for i in range(1, 3): if tmax[i] < mint: mint = tmax[i] axis = i currentvoxel[axis] += step[axis] tmax[axis] += tdelta[axis] return visited Zero Direction: If di = 0, the ray is parallel to the grid planes of that axis. It never crosses a boundary in that direction. Set \text{t\delta}i = \infty and \text{t\max}i = \infty so that axis is never selected for stepping. Origin on Boundary: If the ray origin lies exactly on a voxel boundary, floating-point errors may cause the ray to visit the same voxel twice or skip one. A common fix is to nudge the origin slightly in the direction of the ray if it is on the boundary. Grid Bounds: The algorithm must check if currentvoxel is within 0, Nx) \times [0, Ny) \times [0, Nz) after each step. If the ray originates outside, the initial tmax calculation must use the grid entry point, not the origin. The worst-case scenario for the [Amanatides-Woo algorithm occurs when the ray travels along the diagonal of the grid through exclusively empty voxels. In this case, the number of iterations is proportional to the sum of the grid dimensions in each axis (Nx + Ny + Nz), which is O(n) for a grid of size n^3. This makes the algorithm susceptible to false positives (visiting many empty voxels) in sparse grids, motivating the use of hierarchical structures like Octrees or Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO). A vectorized variant simplifies the code by avoiding explicit branching for axis selection using vector operations and operator overloading. It computes steps (distance to next boundary in terms of number of steps) and uses argmin to find the axis. This approach works for arbitrary dimensions but is practically used in 2D and 3D. A variant that checks for a specific 'root' voxel (e.g., (0,0,0)) during traversal to potentially terminate early or signal a specific state. This is useful for debugging or specific game logic where the origin of the world is a significant landmark. The Amanatides-Woo traversal is used to generate single-sample hard shadows by re-tracing a voxel ray from the hit point towards the light source. If a non-empty block is hit during this shadow ray traversal, the point is in shadow. This leverages the same efficient traversal logic for shadow calculations. Time Complexity: O(nx + ny + nz) per ray, where ni is the number of voxels traversed along axis i. This is optimal for uniform grids as it visits each intersected voxel exactly once. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. The algorithm only requires a few scalar/vector variables for state. Performance: The algorithm is extremely fast due to minimal floating-point operations per step (two comparisons and one addition). It is widely used in ray tracing and shadow casting. Strengths: Correctness (no missed voxels), efficiency (no per-voxel intersection tests), simplicity. Limitations: Performance degrades in sparse grids due to traversal of empty space. Not suitable for non-uniform grids without modification (e.g., using hierarchical structures). The algorithm was introduced by Amanatides and Woo in their 1987 paper "A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing". It is an extension of the 2D DDA (Digital Differential Analyzer) line drawing algorithm (Bresenham's algorithm) to 3D. It has become a standard technique in voxel-based rendering, game development, and scientific visualization. name: Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering
head: 3D Raycasting, Vox5
body: A real-time rendering technique for 3D voxel grids that uses a 2D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) to cast rays per screen column, determining the first occupied voxel. It renders the voxel as a vertical stripe (line) rather than a full textured quad, handling depth via a per-column depth buffer to support multiple voxels per column (stacking). Inputs: worldMap: 3D array of ColorRGB values, dimensions [mapWidth][mapHeight][mapDepth]. posX, posY, posZ: Camera position coordinates. dirX, dirY: Camera direction vector components. planeX, planeY: Camera plane vector components controlling FOV. pitch: Vertical offset for centering the view. h: Screen height in pixels. mapWidth, mapHeight, mapDepth: Dimensions of the voxel grid. Outputs: Rendered screen image with vertical stripes representing voxel slices. Updated depth buffers depth[0] and depth[1]. Data Structures: worldMap[mapWidth][mapHeight][mapDepth]: 3D array. mapWidth=96, mapHeight=96, mapDepth=12. ColorRGB is a struct with 3 components (R, G, B). depth[2][384]: Two integer arrays of size 384 (screen height). Initialized to 100000. Used to store Z-depth of the last drawn voxel at each screen row to handle transparency/overdrawing within a column. side: Integer (0 or 1) indicating which side of the voxel was hit (0 for X-side, 1 for Y-side). Steps: 1. Initialize Camera Ray: Calculate ray direction and plane vectors based on camera state. The FOV is controlled by planeY = 0.66. 2. Determine Step Direction and Initial Side Distance: For each screen column x (from 0 to 383): Calculate ray direction: dirX = dirX{base} + planeX \cdot (2x - 384) / 384 dirY = dirY{base} + planeY \cdot (2x - 384) / 384 Calculate initial map position: mapX = \lfloor posX \rfloor mapY = \lfloor posY \rfloor Calculate delta distances (step sizes): deltaDistX = 1.0 / |dirX| \quad \text{if } dirX \neq 0 \text{ else } \infty deltaDistY = 1.0 / |dirY| \quad \text{if } dirY \neq 0 \text{ else } \infty Calculate initial side distances: If dirX < 0: stepX = -1 sideDistX = (posX - mapX) \cdot deltaDistX Else: stepX = 1 sideDistX = (mapX + 1.0 - posX) \cdot deltaDistX If dirY < 0: stepY = -1 sideDistY = (posY - mapY) \cdot deltaDistY Else: stepY = 1 sideDistY = (mapY + 1.0 - posY) \cdot deltaDistY 3. Perform DDA Loop: Initialize hit = 0, count = 0. While mapX < 0 || mapY < 0 || (count < 384 && hit < 900): If sideDistX < sideDistY: sideDistX += deltaDistX mapX += stepX side = 0 Else: sideDistY += deltaDistY mapY += stepY side = 1 Clamp mapX to [0, mapHeight-1] and mapY to [0, mapWidth-1]. Increment hit. If worldMap[mapX][mapY][0] is not empty (or some hit condition is met): Break loop. Increment count. 4. Calculate Perpendicular Wall Distance: If side == 0: perpWallDist = (mapX - posX + (1 - stepX) / 2) / dirX Else: perpWallDist = (mapY - posY + (1 - stepY) / 2) / dirY This corrects for the fisheye effect. 5. Calculate Line Height: lineHeight = \lfloor h / perpWallDist \rfloor Note: The code comments mention dividing by 2 for square voxels but notes it crashes, so it is not divided. 6. Iterate Through Depth Layers: For b from 0 to mapDepth - 1: Calculate drawStart: drawStart = lineHeight \cdot (b - posZ) + pitch Clamp drawStart to [0, h-1]. Calculate drawEnd: drawEnd = lineHeight + lineHeight \cdot (b - posZ) + pitch Clamp drawEnd to [0, h-1]. Get color: color = worldMap[mapX][mapY][b]. Apply shading: If side == 1, color = color / 2. Render voxel slice: If color != RGBBlack, call verLineTriDepth(x, drawStart, drawEnd, color, depth[0], 384, &count, 0, depth[1]). This function draws the vertical line segment, updating the depth buffer depth[0] and depth[1] to handle occlusion within the column. 7. Render Second Pass (Horizontal Fill/Edge): Copy current state to tmapX, tmapY, tside. Advance one step again using the same DDA logic (if(sideDistX < sideDistY)...). Clamp tmapX, tmapY. Calculate tperpWallDist and tlineHeight using the same formulas as above. For b from 0 to mapDepth - 1: Calculate tdrawStart: tdrawStart = tlineHeight \cdot (b - posZ) + pitch Clamp tdrawStart to [0, h-1]. Calculate tdrawEnd: tdrawEnd = tlineHeight + tlineHeight \cdot (b - posZ) + pitch Clamp tdrawEnd to [0, h-1]. Get tcolor = worldMap[mapX][mapY][b]. Apply shading: tcolor = tcolor / 3. Call verLineTriDepth with drawStart or tdrawStart depending on b < posZ, and depth[1] as the primary buffer. 8. Swap Depth Buffers: After processing all depth layers for a voxel hit, swap depth buffers: memcpy(depth[0], depth[1], 384 \cdot sizeof(int)) This prepares depth[1] for the next ray or pass. name: Dual-Layer DDA Raycasting
head: 3D Raycaster, 3D Raycasting with Dual-Layer DDA, DDA Raycasting, DDA impl, Digital Differential Analyzer Raycasting
body: Dual-Layer DDA Raycasting is a real-time rendering technique that extends standard voxel raycasting by supporting two distinct vertical layers (worldMap[0] for ceilings and worldMap[1] for floors) within a single ray traversal pass. Unlike Classic (Column Voxel Space), which typically handles a single layer, this method simultaneously determines the first occupied cell for both layers using a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA). It builds on Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering by adding the capacity to render both top and bottom surfaces of a voxel column in one go. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D voxel grid worldMap with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times 2 (where the third dimension represents the two layers: 0 for top/ceiling, 1 for bottom/floor). Camera position (rayPosX, rayPosY, rayPosZ) and direction (rayDirX, rayDirY, rayDirZ). Screen height h. Outputs: A rendered image where each screen column displays vertical stripes for both the ceiling (layer 0) and floor (layer 1) hits, with correct depth and texture coordinates. Data Structures: worldMap: A 3D array or flattened structure indexed as worldMap[layer][x][y] or equivalent, where layer \in \{0, 1\}. rayPos: 3D vector (rayPosX, rayPosY, rayPosZ). rayDir: 3D vector (rayDirX, rayDirY, rayDirZ). sideDist: 3D vector tracking distance to the next grid boundary for each axis. deltaDist: 3D vector storing the distance the ray travels to cross one cell in each axis. step: 3D vector storing the direction of increment (-1 or 1) for each axis. Parameters: maxdistance: The maximum distance the ray travels before stopping if no wall is found. Typical value: 1000. h: Screen height in pixels. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Initialization: For each screen column x: a. Compute the ray direction vector (rayDirX, rayDirY, rayDirZ) based on the camera position, direction vector, and camera plane. b. Initialize the current map cell coordinates: mapX = \lfloor rayPosX \rfloor, \quad mapY = \lfloor rayPosY \rfloor, \quad mapZ = \lfloor rayPosZ \rfloor c. Calculate the step directions for X, Y, and Z axes: stepX = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } rayDirX < 0 \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \quad stepY = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } rayDirY < 0 \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \quad stepZ = \begin{cases} -1 & \text{if } rayDirZ < 0 \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} d. Compute delta distances for each axis: deltaDistX = \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{rayDirY}{rayDirX}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{rayDirZ}{rayDirX}\right)^2} deltaDistY = \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{rayDirX}{rayDirY}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{rayDirZ}{rayDirY}\right)^2} deltaDistZ = \sqrt{1 + \left(\frac{rayDirX}{rayDirZ}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{rayDirY}{rayDirZ}\right)^2} e. Initialize side distances: sideDistX = \begin{cases} (rayPosX - mapX) \cdot deltaDistX & \text{if } rayDirX < 0 \\ (mapX + 1.0 - rayPosX) \cdot deltaDistX & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} (Similarly for sideDistY and sideDistZ). f. Initialize flags hitA = false (for layer 0) and hitB = false (for layer 1). 2. DDA Loop: Perform the DDA loop while !hitA || !hitB: a. Compare sideDistX, sideDistY, and sideDistZ. b. If sideDistX is the smallest: sideDistX += deltaDistX, \quad mapX += stepX, \quad side = 0 c. Else if sideDistY is the smallest: sideDistY += deltaDistY, \quad mapY += stepY, \quad side = 1 d. Else (if sideDistZ is the smallest): sideDistZ += deltaDistZ, \quad mapZ += stepZ, \quad side = 2 e. Check for wall hit in layer 0 (hitA): If worldMap[0][mapX][mapY] > 0 and !hitA, set hitA = true. Calculate perpendicular wall distance: perpWallDist = \begin{cases} \frac{mapX - rayPosX + (1 - stepX) / 2}{rayDirX} \cdot \frac{1}{2} & \text{if } side == 0 \\ \frac{mapY - rayPosY + (1 - stepY) / 2}{rayDirY} \cdot \frac{1}{2} & \text{if } side == 1 \\ \frac{mapZ - rayPosZ + (1 - stepZ) / 2}{rayDirZ} \cdot \frac{1}{2} & \text{if } side == 2 \end{cases} f. Check for wall hit in layer 1 (hitB): If worldMap[1][mapX][mapY] > 0 and !hitB, set hitB = true. Calculate perpWallDist using the same logic as in step 2e. 3. Rendering: a. Render Layer 0 Stripe (Ceiling): If hitA is true: lineHeight = \left\lfloor \frac{h}{perpWallDist} \right\rfloor drawStart = \max\left(0, \left\lfloor \frac{h}{2} \right\rfloor\right) drawEnd = \min\left(h - 1, \left\lfloor \frac{lineHeight}{2} + \frac{h}{2} \right\rfloor\right) Draw a vertical line from drawStart to drawEnd with color based on worldMap[0][mapX][mapY], halving brightness if side == 1. b. Render Layer 1 Stripe (Floor): If hitB is true: lineHeight = \left\lfloor \frac{h}{perpWallDist} \right\rfloor drawStart = \max\left(0, \left\lfloor -\frac{lineHeight}{2} + \frac{h}{2} \right\rfloor\right) drawEnd = \min\left(h - 1, \left\lfloor \frac{h}{2} \right\rfloor\right) Draw a vertical line from drawStart to drawEnd with color based on worldMap[1][mapX][mapY], halving brightness if side == 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def duallayerddaraycasting(worldmap, camerapos, cameradir, screenheight, maxdistance): """ Renders ceiling (layer 0) and floor (layer 1) stripes for each screen column. worldmap: 3D array [2][Dx][Dy] camerapos: (rayPosX, rayPosY, rayPosZ) cameradir: (rayDirX, rayDirY, rayDirZ) screenheight: int h maxdistance: float """ rayPosX, rayPosY, rayPosZ = camerapos rayDirX, rayDirY, rayDirZ = cameradir # Initialize map coordinates mapX = int(rayPosX) mapY = int(rayPosY) mapZ = int(rayPosZ) # Calculate step directions stepX = -1 if rayDirX < 0 else 1 stepY = -1 if rayDirY < 0 else 1 stepZ = -1 if rayDirZ < 0 else 1 # Guard against division by zero eps = 1e-9 rdx = rayDirX if abs(rayDirX) > eps else eps rdy = rayDirY if abs(rayDirY) > eps else eps rdz = rayDirZ if abs(rayDirZ) > eps else eps # Calculate delta distances deltaDistX = math.sqrt(1 + (rdy / rdx)2 + (rdz / rdx)2) deltaDistY = math.sqrt(1 + (rdx / rdy)2 + (rdz / rdy)2) deltaDistZ = math.sqrt(1 + (rdx / rdz)2 + (rdy / rdz)2) # Calculate initial side distances if rayDirX < 0: sideDistX = (rayPosX - mapX) deltaDistX else: sideDistX = (mapX + 1.0 - rayPosX) deltaDistX if rayDirY < 0: sideDistY = (rayPosY - mapY) deltaDistY else: sideDistY = (mapY + 1.0 - rayPosY) deltaDistY if rayDirZ < 0: sideDistZ = (rayPosZ - mapZ) deltaDistZ else: sideDistZ = (mapZ + 1.0 - rayPosZ) deltaDistZ hitA = False # Layer 0 hit hitB = False # Layer 1 hit side = 0 # 0: vertical face (X), 1: horizontal face (Y), 2: depth face (Z) perpWallDist = 0.0 # DDA Loop while not hitA or not hitB: # Determine which side to step if sideDistX < sideDistY: if sideDistX < sideDistZ: sideDistX += deltaDistX mapX += stepX side = 0 else: sideDistZ += deltaDistZ mapZ += stepZ side = 2 else: if sideDistY < sideDistZ: sideDistY += deltaDistY mapY += stepY side = 1 else: sideDistZ += deltaDistZ mapZ += stepZ side = 2 # Check bounds and hits if 0 <= mapX < worldmap.shape[1] and 0 <= mapY < worldmap.shape[2]: if not hitA and worldmap[0][mapX][mapY] > 0: hitA = True # Calculate perpWallDist for layer 0 if side == 0: perpWallDist = (mapX - rayPosX + (1 - stepX) / 2) / rdx / 2 elif side == 1: perpWallDist = (mapY - rayPosY + (1 - stepY) / 2) / rdy / 2 elif side == 2: perpWallDist = (mapZ - rayPosZ + (1 - stepZ) / 2) / rdz / 2 if not hitB and worldmap[1][mapX][mapY] > 0: hitB = True # Calculate perpWallDist for layer 1 (same logic) if side == 0: perpWallDist = (mapX - rayPosX + (1 - stepX) / 2) / rdx / 2 elif side == 1: perpWallDist = (mapY - rayPosY + (1 - stepY) / 2) / rdy / 2 elif side == 2: perpWallDist = (mapZ - rayPosZ + (1 - stepZ) / 2) / rdz / 2 # Rendering # Layer 0 (Ceiling) if hitA: lineHeight = int(screenheight / perpWallDist) drawStart = max(0, int(screenheight / 2)) drawEnd = min(screenheight - 1, int(lineHeight / 2 + screenheight / 2)) # Draw vertical line from drawStart to drawEnd with color from worldmap[0][mapX][mapY] # Halve brightness if side == 1 # Layer 1 (Floor) if hitB: lineHeight = int(screenheight / perpWallDist) drawStart = max(0, int(-lineHeight / 2 + screenheight / 2)) drawEnd = min(screenheight - 1, int(screenheight / 2)) # Draw vertical line from drawStart to drawEnd with color from worldmap[1][mapX][mapY] # Halve brightness if side == 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If rayDirX, rayDirY, or rayDirZ is zero, the delta distance calculations involve division by zero, resulting in NaN or infinity values. This must be handled by checking for zero direction components and using alternative formulas or clamping. Boundary Conditions: The algorithm must handle cases where the ray exits the map bounds without hitting a wall, potentially requiring a default background color or termination condition. Renders each voxel column as 12 distinct vertical layers, iterating through vertical indices to draw stacked horizontal stripes. Choose when internal voxel structure and thickness visualization are required. Uses a 3D DDA over dual cells for particle rendering with glossy and glass materials. Choose for particle systems requiring refraction and reflection. Computes the horizontal texture coordinate for a raycast hit against a grid-aligned wall. Choose when correct texture mapping on vertical and horizontal faces is required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simultaneous rendering of ceiling and floor layers reduces the number of ray casts per column. Limitations: Limited to two layers. Requires careful handling of zero direction components. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Dual-Layer DDA Raycasting is an extension of classic voxel raycasting techniques, specifically designed to handle both ceiling and floor surfaces in a single pass. The method is commonly used in real-time voxel-based games and simulations where efficient rendering of 3D grids is necessary. The specific implementation details, such as the use of two distinct layers and the rendering of vertical stripes, are documented in various online repositories and tutorials. 3D/ray/casting/dda/main.odin, https://github.com/algo-boyz/odins-raylib/blob/52b8fddb/3D/ray/casting/dda/main.odin, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) JCLemme/voxnine, https://github.com/JCLemme/voxnine, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Raycasting with Vertical Slicing
head: 12-layer vertical raycasting, voxel4.cpp raycaster
body: A raycasting technique that renders a 3D voxel grid by treating each voxel column as 12 distinct vertical layers, drawing them as stacked horizontal stripes centered around the ray's intersection point. Unlike standard 2D raycasting which draws a single vertical line per hit, this method visualizes voxel thickness and internal structure by iterating through all 12 vertical indices of a hit voxel. It builds on Dual-Layer DDA Raycasting by extending the binary floor/ceiling distinction into a continuous 12-layer vertical stack. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 2D camera position (posX, posY), direction vectors (dirX, dirY), camera plane vector (planeX, planeY), screen width w, screen height h, and a 3D voxel map worldMap[mapWidth][mapHeight][12]. Output: A 2D screen buffer where each column x contains up to 12 vertical stripes representing the voxel layers. Data Structures: worldMap: A 3D integer array of size mapWidth \times mapHeight \times 12. Dimensions are typically 96 \times 96. The third dimension (size 12) represents the vertical layers. Values 0-5 have specific color mappings; 6-11 default to Yellow. depth: An integer array of size w (384 in the reference implementation), initialized to 100000. It is reset per ray and used to handle occlusion between vertical slices. Parameters: pitch: A double constant representing the vertical tilt offset for the voxel stack. Default value is 200. cameraPlaneY: The vertical component of the camera plane vector, determining the Field of View (FOV). Value is 0.66. planeX: The horizontal component of the camera plane vector. Value is 0. Steps: 1. Initialize Ray: For each screen column x from 0 to w-1, calculate cameraX = 2 x / w - 1. Calculate rayDirX = dirX + planeX cameraX and rayDirY = dirY + planeY cameraX. Set rayPosX = posX and rayPosY = posY. 2. Initialize DDA State: Determine mapX = int(rayPosX) and mapY = int(rayPosY). Calculate deltaDistX = sqrt(1 + (rayDirY rayDirY) / (rayDirX rayDirX)) and deltaDistY = sqrt(1 + (rayDirX rayDirX) / (rayDirY rayDirY)). Determine stepX and stepY based on ray direction signs. If rayDirX < 0, set stepX = -1 and sideDistX = (rayPosX - mapX) deltaDistX; else set stepX = 1 and sideDistX = (mapX + 1.0 - rayPosX) deltaDistX. Apply the same logic for stepY and sideDistY using rayDirY, rayPosY, and mapY. 3. Perform DDA Loop: Initialize hit = 0. While hit < 100 and map coordinates are within bounds, if sideDistX < sideDistY, add deltaDistX to sideDistX, increment mapX by stepX, and set side = 0; else add deltaDistY to sideDistY, increment mapY by stepY, and set side = 1. Clamp mapX to [0, mapWidth-1] and mapY to [0, mapHeight-1]. If worldMap[mapX][mapY][0] is not empty, set hit = 1 and break the loop. 4. Calculate Perpendicular Distance and Line Height: If side == 0, calculate perpWallDist = (mapX - rayPosX + (1 - stepX) / 2) / rayDirX; else calculate perpWallDist = (mapY - rayPosY + (1 - stepY) / 2) / rayDirY. Calculate lineHeight = int(h / perpWallDist). 5. Render Voxel Layers: Initialize depth array of size w to 100000. Loop b from 0 to 11: calculate drawStart = (lineHeight (b - 6)) + pitch and clamp to [0, h-1]. Calculate drawEnd = lineHeight + (lineHeight (b - 6)) + pitch and clamp to [0, h-1]. Retrieve color = worldMap[mapX][mapY][b]. If side == 1, divide color brightness by 2. If color is not Black, call verLineDepth(x, drawStart, drawEnd, color, depth, w, &count). 1 rayDirX = dirX + planeX cameraX rayDirY = dirY + planeY cameraX rayPosX = posX rayPosY = posY mapX = int(rayPosX) mapY = int(rayPosY) deltaDistX = math.sqrt(1 + (rayDirY rayDirY) / (rayDirX rayDirX)) deltaDistY = math.sqrt(1 + (rayDirX rayDirX) / (rayDirY rayDirY)) if rayDirX < 0: stepX = -1 sideDistX = (rayPosX - mapX) deltaDistX else: stepX = 1 sideDistX = (mapX + 1.0 - rayPosX) deltaDistX if rayDirY < 0: stepY = -1 sideDistY = (rayPosY - mapY) deltaDistY else: stepY = 1 sideDistY = (mapY + 1.0 - rayPosY) deltaDistY hit = 0 side = 0 while hit < 100: if sideDistX < sideDistY: sideDistX += deltaDistX mapX += stepX side = 0 else: sideDistY += deltaDistY mapY += stepY side = 1 # Clamp map coordinates to grid bounds if mapX < 0: mapX = 0 if mapX >= mapWidth: mapX = mapWidth - 1 if mapY < 0: mapY = 0 if mapY >= mapHeight: mapY = mapHeight - 1 # Hit condition from source if worldMap[mapX][mapY][0] != 0: hit = 1 break if hit == 0: continue if side == 0: perpWallDist = (mapX - rayPosX + (1 - stepX) / 2) / rayDirX else: perpWallDist = (mapY - rayPosY + (1 - stepY) / 2) / rayDirY lineHeight = int(h / perpWallDist) # Depth buffer for occlusion within the column, reset per ray depth = [100000] w for b in range(12): drawStart = (lineHeight (b - 6)) + pitch drawEnd = lineHeight + (lineHeight (b - 6)) + pitch # Clamp to screen bounds if drawStart < 0: drawStart = 0 if drawStart >= h: drawStart = h - 1 if drawEnd < 0: drawEnd = 0 if drawEnd >= h: drawEnd = h - 1 color = worldMap[mapX][mapY][b] if side == 1: color = color // 2 # Darken if side hit if color != 0: # Assuming 0 is Black/Empty # verLineDepth is an implementation-specific helper for drawing vertical lines with depth testing # verLineDepth(x, drawStart, drawEnd, color, depth, w, &count) pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The reference implementation notes uncertainty about voxel aspect ratio, using h / perpWallDist without dividing by 2 to correct for non-square voxels, which may cause visual distortion. Division by zero in deltaDistX or deltaDistY occurs if rayDirX or rayDirY is exactly 0; standard DDA guards or epsilon checks are required. Renders a 3D voxel grid by exploiting vertical ray coherence to cut space with multiple planes, determining visible voxel segments in software and projecting them as rectangles onto the screen using an OpenGL stencil buffer. Unlike Voxel Raycasting with Vertical Slicing, which renders and combines lines, VoxlapGL projects rectangles and contains no quadrant distinctions in its traversal code. Time Complexity: O(w \cdot h) for rendering, where w is screen width and h is screen height. The DDA traversal is O(\text{distance}) per ray, and the vertical slicing adds a constant factor of 12 iterations per hit. Memory Complexity: O(\text{mapWidth} \cdot \text{mapHeight} \cdot 12) for the voxel map, plus O(w) for the depth buffer. Strengths: Visualizes voxel thickness and internal structure, providing a more 3D-aware appearance than standard raycasting. Limitations: The aspect ratio of voxels may be distorted if not adjusted (source notes uncertainty about dividing by 2 for square voxels). The fixed 12-layer structure limits flexibility in voxel depth representation. This technique is an unofficial implementation of a 12-layer vertical raycasting method. It extends the concept of dual-layer raycasting to a more granular vertical representation, allowing for the visualization of voxel depth in a 2D screen space. name: VoxlapGL
head: VoxelRenderer
body: VoxlapGL is a raycasting technique that renders a 3D voxel grid by exploiting vertical ray coherence to slice the space with multiple planes. It determines visible voxel segments in software and projects them as rectangles onto the screen using an OpenGL stencil buffer. Unlike its sibling Voxel Raycasting with Vertical Slicing, which renders and combines lines, VoxlapGL projects rectangles and contains no quadrant distinctions in its traversal code. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel array (Voxel Space) and a camera position/orientation. Output: A 2D screen image. Data Structures: The memory layout matches the VXL format. 1. Column Pointers: A 1024x1024 array of pointers, each pointing to the start of a column's data. 2. Column Data: Each column stores a simple array containing the number of visible parts, their length, and the actual voxel data. Memory Note: Storing solid/air information in a simple boolean array for a 1024x1024x256 map requires 32MB of memory without any actual voxel data. Algorithm Steps: 1. Plane Selection: Determine the number of raycast planes based on the view direction: ~300 planes when looking towards the horizon, ~800 when viewing from above, and ~1000 when looking straight up or down. 2. Grid Traversal: For each plane, step through all columns hit by the raycast plane using efficient grid stepping without quadrant distinctions, relying on bitwise operations and incremental updates. 3. Visibility Determination: In software, determine which parts of the columns are visible. 4. Projection: Project all visible parts in the plane onto a virtual projection line that maintains a constant distance to the eye point and is perpendicular to the ground. 5. Rendering: Use OpenGL to project a rectangle onto the screen using a stencil buffer, filling the entire screen with the projected data. Grid Traversal Pseudocode: The core grid stepping logic handles all directional cases in a single loop using incremental operations. Adapted to valid Python syntax: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. k = ((tp[1] - tp[0]) >> 31) & 1 d = tp[k] tp[k] += ti[k] ip += ipi[k] Note: BLOCKSCAN.KC from EVALDRAW provides a working example of this algorithm. Parameters: Field of View: 90 degrees. Viewspace Culling: Provides a 4x speed boost when looking towards the horizon. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: Storing solid/air information in a simple array for a 1024x1024x256 map requires 32MB of memory without any actual voxel data. Performance: Using OpenGL for the second pass (copy & project color data) yields minimal or negative speedup on older graphics hardware, and may cause deceleration on newer hardware. Boundary Calculation: Calculating grid boundaries for "perfect" looking cubes using interpolation requires one multiplication per column. Hardware Requirements: Requires at least a Pentium Pro CPU and a graphics adapter supporting OpenGL. Performance: Viewspace culling is critical for performance, providing a 4x speed boost at a 90-degree FOV when looking towards the horizon. Limitations: The reliance on OpenGL for the second pass can be a bottleneck; software-based projection might be faster on older hardware, while newer hardware may also suffer from deceleration due to this approach. Complexity: The grid traversal is optimized to avoid quadrant distinctions, reducing branching overhead. VoxlapGL was developed by Sebastian Scholz in 2004/2005 as a forum demo. It was created as an alternative to other voxel rendering techniques like VoxLap, aiming to exploit vertical ray coherence more efficiently. The demo was distributed as a ZIP archive with batch files for execution. Forum archive / Ken Silverman / VoxlapGL, https://jonof.id.au/forum/topic-166.html, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Dual-Cell DDA Raycasting for Particles
head: Dual-Cell DDA, Ray-Traced Mirror and Glass Particles
body: A ray-tracing optimization for particle volumes that uses a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) over dual cells to efficiently test for ray-sphere intersections, enabling real-time rendering of glossy mirrors and refractive glass particles. It distinguishes itself from standard voxel raycasting by leveraging a pre-sorted neighbor grid and a 2×2×2 cell expansion strategy to guarantee hit detection within a dual cell without exhaustive search, significantly reducing shading overhead for deep particle piles. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin and direction; particle system data including sortedpositionsbuffer, sortedindicesbuffer, celloffsetsbuffer, cellsize, and gridorigin. Output: Final pixel color, accounting for reflections, refractions, and room geometry intersections. Data Structures: The method relies on additive accessors added to the FluidSimulation structure, requiring no restructuring of existing files: sortedpositionsbuffer: Array of particle positions, sorted spatially. sortedindicesbuffer: Array of indices corresponding to the sorted positions. celloffsetsbuffer: Offsets defining the neighbor grid topology. cellsize: Scalar size of a single grid cell. gridorigin: Origin point of the grid. Parameters: setrtbounces: Integer controlling ray bounce depth. Default is 2. Particle count: Default 8192 larger particles. Particle Radius: Must be less than half a cell size to guarantee the 2×2×2 test coverage. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Cast primary rays from the camera. If rt=on, assign materials: 30% glossy black mirrors, 35% glass (IOR 1.5, Fresnel), and 35% matte grey. 2. DDA Traversal: Perform a 3D DDA over the dual cells of the fluid's neighbor grid. 3. Dual Cell Testing: For each DDA step at a current dual cell, test the 8 surrounding grid cells (forming a 2×2×2 block) for ray-sphere intersections. Geometric Guarantee: Since particle radius r < \frac{1}{2} \times \text{cell\size}, any sphere intersecting the dual cell must intersect at least one of the 8 surrounding grid cells. 4. Material Interaction: If a sphere is hit, compute reflection (for mirrors) or refraction (for glass, exiting the far side). Recursively cast new rays up to setrtbounces. 5. Room Intersection: If a ray misses all spheres during traversal, it intersects the room geometry. Determine color based on the panel's mean irradiance, walls lit by the panel plus one voxel cone, or black for the open front. The sky gradient substitutes for the ceiling and open front. 6. Impostor Depth Optimization: For depth testing, render camera-facing quads at the sphere's nearest point. Do not write fragdepth to avoid running the fragment shader (including ray tracing) before the depth test, which is critical for deep piles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Raycasting Texture Coordinate Calculation
head: u-coordinate derivation, wallX calculation
body: This method computes the horizontal texture coordinate (commonly wallX or the "u" coordinate) for a raycast intersection against an axis-aligned grid wall. It converts the 3D hit point into a normalized 0, 1) texture space value by exploiting the grid's axis alignment: the coordinate depends strictly on the hit face type (vertical or horizontal), using the perpendicular distance and ray direction to determine the position along the wall's local axis. It differs from general [3D texture mapping by avoiding full projection matrices and instead deriving the coordinate directly from DDA traversal state. Inputs: side: Integer indicating the hit face type. 0 for vertical face (constant-X grid line), 1 for horizontal face (constant-Y grid line). px, py: The camera position in world coordinates (x, y). dirX, dirY: The ray direction vector components. perpDist: The perpendicular distance from the camera to the hit wall plane. mapX, mapY: The integer grid coordinates of the cell where the hit occurred. texWidth: The width of the texture image in pixels. Outputs: wallX: The wrapped texture coordinate in 0, 1). texX: The integer column index in the texture image. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the calculation uses scalar values derived from the raycasting traversal. Steps: 1. Determine the varying axis: Identify which world-space coordinate varies along the hit face. If side == 0 (vertical face), the coordinate varies along Y. Use py and dirY. If side == 1 (horizontal face), the coordinate varies along X. Use px and dirX. 2. Compute raw world-space coordinate: Calculate the position along the wall face using the formula: wallX{raw} = \begin{cases} py + perpDist \cdot dirY & \text{if } side == 0 \\ px + perpDist \cdot dirX & \text{if } side == 1 \end{cases} 3. Wrap to [0, 1): Remove the integer part to get the fractional position within the specific wall segment. wallX = wallX{raw} - \lfloor wallX{raw} \rfloor 4. Compute texture column index: Map the normalized coordinate to the texture's pixel width. texX = \lfloor wallX \cdot texWidth \rfloor Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculatetexturecoordinate(side, px, py, dirX, dirY, perpDist, mapX, mapY, texWidth): # Step 1 & 2: Determine axis and compute raw world-space coordinate if side == 0: sideaxisval = py sidedirval = dirY else: sideaxisval = px sidedirval = dirX rawwallx = sideaxisval + perpDist sidedirval # Step 3: Wrap to [0, 1) wallx = rawwallx - math.floor(rawwallx) # Step 4: Compute texture column index texx = math.floor(wallx texWidth) return wallx, texx Parameters: texWidth: Must be positive. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Incorrect Side Logic: If side is misinterpreted (e.g., swapping vertical/horizontal logic), textures will appear sheared or scroll in the wrong direction when rays hit the opposite face type. Negative Coordinates: The wrapping step wallX -= Math.floor(wallX) correctly handles negative rawwallx values, ensuring the result is always in [0, 1). Precision: Floating-point precision errors in perpDist or direction vectors may cause slight jitter in wallX at grazing angles. A variant for handling thin walls recessed to the midline of a cell (tile id 5). Instead of stopping at the cell boundary, the ray advances to the door's centerline (distToMid). The texture coordinate wx is calculated at this midline. If the door is open (slide > 0), rays hitting within the opened gap (wx < slide) pass through without rendering the door. Steps: 1. If tile is 5, calculate distToMid: distToMid = \begin{cases} (sideDistX - deltaDistX) + \frac{deltaDistX}{2} & \text{if } side == 0 \\ (sideDistY - deltaDistY) + \frac{deltaDistY}{2} & \text{if } side == 1 \end{cases} 2. Calculate other (distance to the other side of the cell): other = \begin{cases} sideDistY & \text{if } side == 0 \\ sideDistX & \text{if } side == 1 \end{cases} If distToMid >= other, the ray exits the cell before the midline; continue marching. 3. Calculate texture coordinate wx at midline: wx = \begin{cases} player.y + distToMid \cdot rayDirY - mapY & \text{if } side == 0 \\ player.x + distToMid \cdot rayDirX - mapX & \text{if } side == 1 \end{cases} If wx < 0 or wx >= 1, continue. 4. Get door openness slide. If wx < slide, the ray passes through the open gap; continue. 5. Return hit with wallX: wx and doorShift: -slide. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method is fundamental to early raycasting engines, particularly those used in first-person shooters like Wolfenstein 3D. It leverages the simplicity of [grid-based collision detection to derive texture coordinates without full 3D projection matrices. The technique is often associated with the implementation details of DDA-based ray traversal, where the side of the hit face is known immediately upon intersection. mithraskuipers/InteractiveLearning-Raycasting, https://github.com/mithraskuipers/InteractiveLearning-Raycasting, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) A minimal Wolfenstein 3D raycasting engine, https://4rknova.com/blog/2026/07/06/wolfenstein-3d-raycasting, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Classic (Column Voxel Space)
head: Classic rendering, Column voxel space, Per-pixel 3D column raycast, Scanline voxel rendering
body: Classic rendering is a real-time terrain visualization technique that redraws the camera frustum every frame by marching world-vertical columns from the camera to the horizon. It differs from its sibling Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering by casting one ray per screen column rather than per pixel, and from Dual-Layer DDA Raycasting by using a height-map-based column march instead of a dual-layer DDA approach. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A height map and a color map, both typically 1024 \times 1024 rasters. Camera parameters include position, orientation (yaw/pitch), field of view (FOV), and far clip distance (Distance). Outputs: A 2D image where each screen column is filled by the visible portion of the corresponding world-vertical column. Data Structures: Height Map: A 2D array of height values. Color Map: A 2D array of color values corresponding to the height map. Mip Chain: A pyramid of coarser height and color rasters derived from the base maps. The number of levels (LOD) is configurable, typically ranging from 1 to \log2(\text{map width}). For a 1024 map, this allows stops at 64 \times 64 (5 levels) or 2 \times 2 (10 levels). Parameters: Delta Z: Ray step size for classic and scanline modes. Range: 0.1–2.0. (Note: Unused by voxel mode). Distance: Far clip value. Range: 100–74500 meters. The maximum is approximately 74473 meters at 640 \times 480 resolution with 90^\circ FOV. LOD: Number of mip raster levels used. Range: 1 to \log2(\text{map width}). Default is the middle of the range. LOD Curve: Determines how switch distances fill 0 \dots \text{Distance}. Options: Linear (equal range per level), Doubling (each switch is twice as far as the previous), or Logarithmic (log-spaced from first switch to Distance). LOD Step: Meters to the first LOD switch. Range: 10 m to Distance. Editable only for Logarithmic curve; Linear and Doubling fill 0 \dots \text{Distance} automatically. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Camera: Set up the view matrix based on camera position, yaw, pitch, and FOV. 2. Iterate Screen Columns: For each screen column x from 0 to \text{width}-1: a. Cast Ray: Construct a 3D ray originating from the camera position and passing through the center of the screen pixel at column x. b. March Column: Step along the ray in world-vertical increments until the horizon or far clip is reached. c. Determine LOD: Calculate the distance from the camera. Select the appropriate mip level based on the LOD curve and LOD step. d. Sample Height/Color: i. If LOD is 0: Perform bilinear sampling on the base height/color maps. Refine the sample by snapping to the inner 1/16 \dots 1 m cell grid. Add height noise. ii. If LOD > 0: Perform nearest-neighbor sampling on the coarser mip level to keep coarse blocks flat and avoid interpolation artifacts. e. Render Stripe: Draw the vertical stripe for the column using the sampled color, handling depth via the column's visible height. 3. Repeat: Redraw the entire frustum every frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderclassic(heightmap, colormap, mipchain, camerapos, camerayaw, camerapitch, fov, screenwidth, screenheight, farclip, lodcurve, lodstep, basestep=1.0): # Initialize output buffer image = [[None for in range(screenheight)] for in range(screenwidth)] # Precompute LOD switch distances based on curve lodswitches = computelodswitches(lodcurve, lodstep, farclip) # Camera direction vectors cospitch = math.cos(camerapitch) sinpitch = math.sin(camerapitch) cosyaw = math.cos(camerayaw) sinyaw = math.sin(camerayaw) for x in range(screenwidth): # Cast ray for column x pixelcenterx = (x / screenwidth - 0.5) 2.0 pixelcentery = -((screenheight / 2) / (screenwidth / 2)) (pixelcenterx math.tan(fov / 2)) raydircam = normalize((pixelcenterx math.tan(fov / 2), pixelcentery math.tan(fov / 2), -1.0)) raydir = transformtoworld(raydircam, camerayaw, camerapitch) currentz = 0.0 currentlod = 0 # March column until horizon or far clip while currentz < farclip: # Determine LOD based on distance currentlod = getlodfordistance(currentz, lodswitches) # Step size grows with LOD to skip empty space stepsize = basestep (2 currentlod) # Sample height and color if currentlod == 0: # Bilinear sampling on base map height = samplebilinear(heightmap, camerapos, raydir, currentz) color = samplebilinear(colormap, camerapos, raydir, currentz) # Refine by snapping to 1/16...1 m cell grid cellsize = 1.0 / 16.0 height = math.floor(height / cellsize) cellsize color = math.floor(color / cellsize) cellsize # Add height noise height += math.sin(currentz 0.1) 0.05 # Standard noise function else: # Nearest-neighbor sampling on coarser mip level height = samplenearest(mipchain[currentlod].height, camerapos, raydir, currentz) color = samplenearest(mipchain[currentlod].color, camerapos, raydir, currentz) # Check if voxel is occupied (height < camera height) if height < camerapos.y: # Render the visible part of the column rendercolumnstripe(image, x, currentz, color) break currentz += stepsize return image def computelodswitches(lodcurve, lodstep, farclip): # Implementation depends on curve type if lodcurve == "Linear": # Equal range per level numlevels = int(math.log2(1024)) # Assuming 1024 map width rangeperlevel = farclip / numlevels return [i rangeperlevel for i in range(1, numlevels)] elif lodcurve == "Doubling": # Each switch is twice as far as the previous switches = [] dist = lodstep while dist < farclip: switches.append(dist) dist = 2 return switches elif lodcurve == "Logarithmic": # Log-spaced from first switch to Distance switches = [] numlevels = int(math.log2(1024)) dist = lodstep for i in range(1, numlevels): switches.append(dist) dist = lodstep (farclip / lodstep) (i / (numlevels - 1)) return switches return [] def getlodfordistance(distance, lodswitches): # Find the highest LOD level where distance >= switch distance lod = 0 for i, switch in enumerate(lodswitches): if distance >= switch: lod = i + 1 return lod def samplebilinear(mapdata, origin, direction, distance): # Compute intersection point on map grid mapscale = 1.0 # Assuming 1 unit = 1 meter u = (origin[0] + direction[0] distance) / mapscale v = (origin[2] + direction[2] distance) / mapscale u0, v0 = math.floor(u), math.floor(v) u1, v1 = u0 + 1, v0 + 1 # Bilinear interpolation h00 = mapdata[v0 % mapdata.height][u0 % mapdata.width] h10 = mapdata[v0 % mapdata.height][u1 % mapdata.width] h01 = mapdata[v1 % mapdata.height][u0 % mapdata.width] h11 = mapdata[v1 % mapdata.height][u1 % mapdata.width] fu, fv = u - u0, v - v0 return h00 (1 - fu) (1 - fv) + h10 fu (1 - fv) + h01 (1 - fu) fv + h11 fu fv def samplenearest(mapdata, origin, direction, distance): # Compute intersection point on map grid mapscale = 1.0 u = (origin[0] + direction[0] distance) / mapscale v = (origin[2] + direction[2] distance) / mapscale uidx = int(math.floor(u)) % mapdata.width vidx = int(math.floor(v)) % mapdata.height return mapdata[vidx][uidx] def rendercolumnstripe(image, x, z, color): # Draw vertical stripe for column x starting at z # Rasterization details omitted pass def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def transformtoworld(raydircam, yaw, pitch): # Standard camera-to-world rotation cosy, siny = math.cos(yaw), math.sin(yaw) cosp, sinp = math.cos(pitch), math.sin(pitch) x = raydircam[0] cosy + raydircam[2] siny y = raydircam[0] siny sinp + raydircam[1] cosp - raydircam[2] cosy sinp z = raydircam[0] siny cosp + raydircam[1] sinp + raydircam[2] cosy cosp return (x, y, z) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpolation Artifacts: Higher LODs use nearest-neighbor sampling to keep coarse blocks flat and avoid interpolation artifacts at distance. Precision: LOD 0 uses bilinear sampling and refinement, which may introduce precision issues if not handled correctly. Far Clip: The far clip distance must be set appropriately to avoid performance issues or visual clipping. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot S), where W is screen width, H is screen height, and S is the average number of steps per column. The use of mipmaps and growing step sizes reduces S for distant samples. Scaling: Scales with screen resolution and map size. Mipmaps help maintain performance at distance. Strengths: Simple implementation, real-time performance, effective for terrain visualization. Limitations: Limited to height-map-based terrain, may not handle complex geometry well. Measured Performance: Performance depends on hardware, resolution, and scene complexity. The technique is designed for real-time rendering. Origin: The technique is based on the "Voxel Space" method used in the game Comanche. History: The method has been implemented in various forms, including CPU (JS, WASM) and GPU (WebGPU) backends. varganorbert222/VoxelSpace, https://github.com/varganorbert222/VoxelSpace, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Screen-Space Ray Casting with Layer Traversal
head: Ray Marching through Columns
body: A real-time rendering technique that performs ray casting in screen space by marching pixel by pixel along the projected ray direction to intersect voxel columns and find entry/exit points for volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from its parent Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering by explicitly handling multiple surface layers within a column via a layer index, enabling the tracing of multiple refractions and deep ambient occlusion by leveraging full knowledge of surface layers rather than just the front-most surface. Inputs: A ray origin and direction (potentially perturbed for refraction), a voxel grid with stored surface layers per column, and a starting depth hint. Outputs: A sequence of intersection events (entry/exit) with their depths and layer indices. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin O and direction D. Voxel Column: A vertical stack of surface layers. Layer Index: An integer representing the depth layer within a column. The parity (LSB) of the layer index determines if the ray is entering or exiting the volume material relative to the view direction. Parameters: z\sgn: Sign of the ray direction relative to the view direction. Value is -1 if ray marching against view direction, otherwise 1. Steps: 1. Initialize: Start at the pixel containing the ray origin, using the depth layer from the previous pixel as a starting hint. 2. Column Intersection: Determine the current voxel column intersected by the ray. 3. Depth Bounds: Calculate the entry and exit depths of the ray within the current voxel column: [entry, exit]. 4. Layer Search: Find the first layer index after the entry depth, using the hint as a starting point: layer = first\layer\after(entry, z\sgn, start\hint = layer). 5. Validity Check: Determine if a valid layer exists within the column bounds: layer\found = (z\sgn \times layer \le exit \times z\sgn). 6. State Determination: Determine if the ray is entering the volume at this layer: entering = ((layer \& 1) \neq (z\sgn > 0)) == layer\found. 7. Marching Loop: Iterate through layers within the column bounds, detecting state changes between inside and outside. 8. Hint Update: Use the final layer value as the starthint for the next pixel to optimize the search. 9. Termination: Terminate when the voxel grid boundary is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. layer = initialhint # From previous pixel or initialization wasinside = False # Initial state before first layer column = nextintersected(ray, column) while column: entry, exit = intersectiondepths(ray, column) layer = firstlayerafter(entry, zsgn, starthint=layer) layerfound = (zsgn layer <= exit zsgn) entering = ((layer & 1) != (zsgn > 0)) == layerfound wasinside = entering # Initialize for do-while loop while True: if entering != wasinside: # handleintersection(...) computes contribution and restarts casting with a perturbed ray handleintersection(...) if layerfound: layer += zsgn entering = not entering if not (zsgn layer <= exit zsgn): break column = nextintersected(ray, column) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Hits: Hits may occur on voxel column boundaries in-between stored surface values. These are detected by checking if the ray changes its state between inside and outside when entering a new column (using LSB of layer index). Refraction Restart: When a surface is intersected, marching aborts, the ray's contribution is computed, and ray casting restarts with a new perturbed ray to trace multiple refractions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of surface layers per voxel column. Strengths: Enables deep ambient occlusion by accessing multiple surface layers. Supports multiple refractions by restarting ray casting with perturbed rays. Efficient layer traversal using hints. Limitations: Requires storing multiple layers per voxel column, which increases memory usage compared to single-layer methods. This method is described in the context of memory-efficient on-the-fly voxelization of particle data, where it is used to render complex particle systems as volumetric surfaces. It builds upon the concept of screen-space ray casting and extends it to handle multiple surface layers within a voxel column, facilitating advanced effects like refraction and deep ambient occlusion. name: Voxel Polygon Rendering
body: Voxel Polygon Rendering is a hybrid rendering technique that fills the screen with vertical bars representing heights from a voxel map, effectively projecting a 2D area of the map onto the screen as a flat landscape. It solves the problem of rendering high-detail terrain at constant speed by avoiding traditional 6DOF polygon operations such as rotation matrix calculations and clipping. Unlike its sibling Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering, which casts rays per screen column to find the first occupied voxel, Voxel Polygon Rendering maps screen pixels directly to map locations and draws spans from close to far, using an s-buffer (vertical c-buffer) to handle floating bars and prevent overdraw. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel map (array of height and color per location), screen resolution, camera position, and camera yaw (y-axis rotation). Output: A rendered image with vertical bars representing terrain height. Data Structures: VoxelMap: A 2D array where each cell stores height and color. ColumnHeights: An array of size screenwidth, storing the current drawn height for each screen column to enable clipping. S-Buffer (Vertical C-Buffer): A data structure managing floating voxel bars that do not start at the bottom of the screen, storing depth and height values to handle occlusion for bars with both top and bottom sides. Steps: 1. Map Pixels to Voxel Space: For each pixel on the screen, determine its corresponding location on the voxel map based on the camera's y-axis rotation and position. Calculate the distance of the pixel from the camera to apply perspective correction, ensuring distant "mountains" appear smaller. 2. Retrieve Voxel Data: Fetch the height and color data from the voxel map. To reduce blockiness, apply bilinear filtering by retrieving four adjacent voxels (texels). 3. Calculate Span Height and Color: Compute the weighted average of the heights of the four fetched texels to determine the height of the single one-pixel wide span. Compute the weighted average of the colors of the four fetched texels to determine the span's color. 4. Clip Against Column Height: Compare the calculated span height against the current height stored in ColumnHeights for that column. If the span is behind the existing bar, clip it. If it is in front, update ColumnHeights with the new height. 5. Draw Span: Draw the vertical bar (span) for the pixel. If the bar is floating (not starting at the bottom), use the S-Buffer to manage its visibility and occlusion against other floating bars. 6. Repeat for All Columns: Process all screen columns from the bottom of the screen up to the horizon (approximately halfway up the screen). 7. Fill Backdrop: Fill the screen space above the horizon with a backdrop image. Formulas: Bilinear Height Interpolation: H{span} = \frac{H1 + H2 + H3 + H4}{4} Where H1, H2, H3, H4 are the heights of the four adjacent voxels. Bilinear Color Interpolation: C{span} = \frac{C1 + C2 + C3 + C4}{4} Where C1, C2, C3, C4 are the colors of the four adjacent voxels. Parameters: Rotation Constraint: The scene can only be rotated around the y-axis. Looking up/down (x-axis) is limited to about 10 degrees; looking down by 45 degrees wastes the picture because voxel bars must be perfectly vertical. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flat Floor Performance: Worst-case performance occurs on a completely flat floor. Every column of the screen becomes one higher every time a new line is processed. For the single pixel drawn, significant work is done: comparing to current column height, clipping, drawing, and updating column height. This is likely more expensive than drawing a single perspective-correct texture map. Floating Bars: The usual voxel algorithm assumes bars start at the bottom screen line. Floating bars (e.g., bridges, ceilings) require an s-buffer (vertical c-buffer) to handle correctly, as they have both a top and bottom side. Blockiness: Without bilinear filtering, voxels look blocky. Small details tend to flicker when the camera moves. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervoxelpolygonscreen(voxelmap, screenwidth, screenheight, camerayaw, camerapos): NEGINF = -float('inf') columnheights = [NEGINF] screenwidth horizony = screenheight // 2 for y in range(screenheight - 1, horizony - 1, -1): for x in range(screenwidth): # 1. Map pixel to voxel map location # Standard perspective projection logic not detailed in source voxelx, voxely = mappixeltovoxel(x, y, camerayaw, camerapos) # 2. Retrieve four adjacent voxels for bilinear filtering h1, c1 = getvoxel(voxelmap, voxelx, voxely) h2, c2 = getvoxel(voxelmap, voxelx + 1, voxely) h3, c3 = getvoxel(voxelmap, voxelx, voxely + 1) h4, c4 = getvoxel(voxelmap, voxelx + 1, voxely + 1) # 3. Calculate weighted average height and color spanheight = (h1 + h2 + h3 + h4) / 4.0 spancolor = (c1 + c2 + c3 + c4) / 4.0 # 4. Clip against column height currentcolheight = columnheights[x] if spanheight <= currentcolheight: continue # 5. Draw span bartop = spanheight barbottom = currentcolheight for py in range(int(barbottom), int(bartop) + 1): framebuffer[y][x] = spancolor # Update column height columnheights[x] = bartop # Fill backdrop above horizon for y in range(0, horizony): for x in range(screenwidth): framebuffer[y][x] = backdropcolor def mappixeltovoxel(x, y, camerayaw, camerapos): # Standard perspective projection logic not detailed in source return 0, 0 def getvoxel(voxelmap, x, y): # Standard bounds-checked array access not detailed in source x = max(0, min(x, len(voxelmap[0]) - 1)) y = max(0, min(y, len(voxelmap) - 1)) return voxelmap[y][x].height, voxelmap[y][x].color A hardware-accelerated rendering method for voxel landscapes that replaces software span rendering with triangle strips. It projects voxels onto the screen in columns and constructs geometry based on the visibility of adjacent columns to minimize polygon count and utilize hardware interpolation. Unlike software span rendering which draws spans immediately, this method buffers column projections to construct triangle strips, reducing draw calls and leveraging hardware interpolation for texture coordinates, lightmap colors, and heights. Time Complexity: Virtually constant speed regardless of scene detail, as it processes each screen pixel once. However, worst-case performance occurs on a completely flat floor, where every column's height is updated for every line, leading to significant clipping and drawing overhead per pixel. Memory Complexity: Requires a large voxel map. Memory usage can be mitigated by tiling pre-built tiles of voxels. Strengths: Constant rendering speed; no 6DOF rotation matrix calculations or clipping required; allows for high detail; bilinear filtering reduces blockiness; supports floating structures via s-buffer. Limitations: Limited to y-axis rotation (approx. 10 degrees up/down); cannot handle significant x-axis rotation; blockiness without filtering; flickering of small details; worst-case performance on flat terrain. When to Use: Rendering high-detail terrain at constant speed where y-axis rotation is sufficient. When Not to Use: When full 6DOF rotation is required; when performance on flat terrain is critical; when memory is severely constrained without tiling support. Voxel Polygon Rendering was introduced by Jacco Bikker (a.k.a. "THE PHANTOM") in 1999 on Flipcode. It was developed as an alternative to traditional 6DOF polygon engines, aiming to provide high-detail graphics with constant speed. The technique was considered for inclusion in the "Focus" engine. flipcode - Voxel Polygons, https://www.flipcode.com/archives/VoxelPolygons.shtml, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)
