name: Triangle Strip Voxel Projection
head: Hardware Accelerated Voxel Rendering, Structure Rendering Algorithm
body: A hardware-accelerated rendering method for voxel landscapes that replaces software span rendering with triangle strips. It projects voxels onto the screen in columns and constructs geometry based on the visibility of adjacent columns to minimize polygon count and utilize hardware interpolation. Unlike software span rendering which draws spans immediately, this method buffers column projections to construct triangle strips, reducing draw calls and leveraging hardware interpolation for texture coordinates, lightmap colors, and heights. It builds on Voxel Polygon Rendering by replacing immediate span drawing with batched strip construction. Inputs: A voxel map representing a landscape; a camera view; a configurable step size for column sampling (default 32 pixels). Outputs: A sequence of OpenGL draw calls using triangle strips. Data Structures: The algorithm processes the landscape by scanning along depth lines (columns) rather than processing individual rays. For each sampled column, voxels are projected onto the screen, but spans are not drawn immediately; the algorithm waits until the next column is projected. The algorithm maintains state for two adjacent columns: A (left-most point of the current strip portion) and B (right-most point of the next column). Steps: 1. Scan Columns: Iterate through the landscape depth lines. Sample columns at intervals defined by the step size (default 32 pixels). Smaller steps generate more polygons. 2. Project Voxels: For each sampled column, project the voxels onto the screen. 3. Evaluate Visibility: Determine the visibility status of column A (previous column) and column B (current column). 4. Construct Geometry: Based on the visibility of A and B, execute one of four cases: Case 1 (A not visible, B visible): Start a new triangle strip. Send vertices of columns A then B to the GL. Case 2 (A visible, B visible): Continue the currently active triangle strip. Send only vertices of column B to the GL. Case 3 (A visible, B not visible): Send coordinates of column B to the GL and stop the current triangle strip. Case 4 (A not visible, B not visible): Usually do nothing. Handle a special sub-case for holes. 5. Handle Holes (Case 4 Sub-case): If a triangle strip was started or finished at column A during the previous pass, draw a single triangle to close the gap. Check the condition: (Y1 > pY1) \text{ and } (Y2 > pY2) Where Y1, Y2 and pY1, pY2 are Y-coordinates from the projected spans. If true, draw the triangle. This approximation may draw triangles that are not quite visible but is more efficient than performing line intersections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projectvoxels(colidx): # Projects voxels for a given column index. # Returns (isvisible: bool, ytop: float, ybot: float, vertices: list) # Exact projection math depends on the voxel map layout return isvisible, ytop, ybot, vertices def sendverticestogl(vertices): # Transfers vertex data to the graphics pipeline for rasterization pass def beginprimitive(primitivetype): # Begins a new GLTRIANGLESTRIP primitive pass def endprimitive(): # Terminates the current GLTRIANGLESTRIP primitive pass def drawholeclosingtriangle(y1, py1, y2, py2): # Renders a single triangle to bridge a gap between non-visible columns pass stepsize = 32 # pixels numcolumns = landscapewidthincolumns # Derived from landscape bounds prevvertices = None prevvisible = False Y1 = 0.0 pY1 = 0.0 stripstartedatprev = False stripendedatprev = False for colidx in range(0, numcolumns, stepsize): currvertices, currvisible, Y2, pY2 = projectvoxels(colidx) if prevvertices is not None: if not prevvisible and currvisible: # Case 1: Start new triangle strip beginprimitive(GLTRIANGLESTRIP) sendverticestogl(prevvertices) sendverticestogl(currvertices) stripstartedatprev = True stripendedatprev = False elif prevvisible and currvisible: # Case 2: Continue active triangle strip sendverticestogl(currvertices) stripstartedatprev = False stripendedatprev = False elif prevvisible and not currvisible: # Case 3: End active triangle strip sendverticestogl(currvertices) endprimitive() stripstartedatprev = False stripendedatprev = True else: # Case 4: Both not visible if stripstartedatprev or stripendedatprev: # Hole closure check: (Y1 > pY1) and (Y2 > pY2) if (Y1 > pY1) and (Y2 > pY2): drawholeclosingtriangle(Y1, pY1, Y2, pY2) stripstartedatprev = False stripendedatprev = False prevvertices = currvertices prevvisible = currvisible Y1 = Y2 pY1 = pY2 Parameters: Step Size: The distance between scanned columns. Default is 32 pixels. Smaller steps generate more polygons. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes: In Case 4, if a triangle strip was started or finished at the previous column during the previous pass, a single triangle must be drawn to close the gap. Mesh Density: The triangle mesh can become too dense at the bottom of valleys. A span reduction technique is ideally needed to mitigate this. Approximation: The hole-closing condition may draw triangles that are not quite visible, but this is accepted for efficiency over line intersections. Time Complexity: Highly efficient due to batching draw calls into strips, though exact complexity depends on column count and visibility transitions. Memory Complexity: Low, as it processes columns sequentially and streams vertices to the graphics pipeline without storing the full mesh. Measured Performance: In the terraVoxGL demo scene, it rendered 8664 triangles (across 4 passes) in 925 strips. Strengths: Extremely efficient due to triangle strip usage; leverages hardware interpolation for texture coordinates, lightmap colors, and heights; reduces draw calls compared to software span rendering. Limitations: Can produce dense meshes in valleys; the described texturing scheme (4 single passes with alpha coefficients) is inefficient. When to use: When rendering voxel landscapes on hardware that supports triangle strips and interpolation, and when software span rendering is too slow. When not to use: When high-quality procedural shading is required (the described texturing is a simple emulation of software) or when valley density is a critical issue without span reduction. Origin: Developed by an anonymous author for the "Realtime Voxel Landscape Engines" series, specifically Part 6 on Hardware Acceleration. History: Presented on Flipcode in February 2000 as a response to the slowness of software span rendering for voxel landscapes. It was implemented in the terraVoxGL demo using OpenGL. Usage: Used in the terraVoxGL demo to accelerate voxel landscape rendering by utilizing the video card as a "huge interpolating machine". name: VDI Rendering by Raycasting
head: NDC Space Raycasting, Voxel Stepping VDI Rendering
body: This method renders Volumetric Depth Images (VDIs) by casting rays from the new viewpoint into the Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) space of the original view, where supersegment lists form a regular 2D grid of cuboids. Unlike object-space approaches that generate explicit geometry for each supersegment, this technique uses Amanatides-Woo voxel traversal to step through the grid, enabling efficient early ray termination and better scaling for large VDIs. Inputs: Original view V0 with viewport resolution w \times h. New view VN with camera parameters. VDI data structure: a set of supersegment lists \mathbb{L}, where each list \mathbb{L}i contains a sorted list of supersegments \mathbb{S}. Volume bounding box in world space. Outputs: Final pixel color for each pixel in VN. Data Structures: NDC Space: The coordinate system of V0 mapped to [-1, 1] on all axes. Supersegment Lists (\mathbb{L}): In NDC space, these form a regular 2D grid. Each cell in the grid corresponds to a list \mathbb{L}i. Cell width: 2/w. Cell height: 2/h. Each \mathbb{L}i is a cuboid in NDC space. Supersegments (\mathbb{S}): Within each list \mathbb{L}i, supersegments are sorted by position. Each \mathbb{S}j^i is a cuboid in NDC space. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel in VN, construct a ray R originating from the camera center of VN. 2. Ray Clipping: Determine the start point t{near} and end point t{far} of the ray segment within the volume. Intersect R with the viewport plane of V0 to find the entry point into the VDI space. Intersect R with the volume bounding box to find the exit point. The valid ray segment is R(t) for t \in [t{near}, t{far}]. 3. NDC Transformation: Transform the ray R and the grid structure into the NDC space of V0. In this space, the supersegment lists \mathbb{L} form a regular 2D grid of cuboids. 4. Voxel Traversal (List Level): Traverse the 2D grid of lists \mathbb{L} using the Amanatides-Woo voxel traversal algorithm [2]. Initialize traversal at the grid cell containing the ray origin in NDC space. Iterate through the grid, determining the next intersected list \mathbb{L}i and the intersection points (entry and exit) with \mathbb{L}i. Stop traversal when the ray exits the volume bounding box or t{far} is reached. 5. Supersegment Search: For each intersected list \mathbb{L}i: Identify the supersegments \mathbb{S}j^i within \mathbb{L}i that overlap with the ray segment between the entry and exit points of \mathbb{L}i. Use spatial smoothness: once the first intersecting supersegment is found, subsequent supersegments are found via adjacency search (checking the next sorted element), as they are sorted by position. 6. Intersection Length Calculation: For each intersected supersegment \mathbb{S}j^i: Calculate the intersection length lj of the ray with the cuboid \mathbb{S}j^i in NDC space. Note: The sources specify calculating the intersection length in NDC space to adjust color contribution. The exact mapping from NDC length to physical depth/color weight is implied to be handled by the VDI data (e.g., depth values stored in supersegments). 7. Color Accumulation: Compute the color contribution Cj from each supersegment \mathbb{S}j^i, weighted by the intersection length lj. Accumulate contributions using alpha compositing (front-to-back or back-to-front, typically front-to-back for early termination). Final pixel color C{final} = \sum Cj \alphaj \prod (1-\alphak) for previous segments k. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Clip ray to volume and VDI viewport tnear, tfar = clipraytovolumeandviewport( rayorigin, raydirection, volumebbox, viewV0.viewportplane) if tnear > tfar: continue # 3. Transform ray to NDC space of V0 # This involves transforming the ray origin and direction using V0's inverse projection/view ndcrayorigin, ndcraydirection = transformtondcv0( rayorigin, raydirection, viewV0) # 4. Here, L is a 2D grid of lists. # The traversal is over the 2D grid of lists. The ray's z-component in NDC determines depth. # However, the source says "traverses this grid using... Amanatides and Woo". # This implies the DDA is performed in NDC space. # So we need the ray in NDC space. # Let's assume we have a function to get the ray in NDC space. return ndcorigin, ndcdirection def ndcttoworldt(tndc, ndcrayorigin, ndcraydirection, viewV0): # Convert tndc to world space t # This requires inverting the NDC transformation # Pndc = Ondc + tndc Dndc # Pworld = V Pinv Pndc # This is non-linear. # The source doesn't specify how to convert tndc to tworld. # It says "intersection points with Li... are then used to search for S". # And "calculates the intersection length with each S". # And "uses this to adjust the color contribution". # It doesn't explicitly say how to get the world space t for accumulation. # Maybe the accumulation is done in NDC space? # Or maybe the intersection length in NDC space is used as a proxy for depth. # Let's assume the color contribution is adjusted by the NDC length. # The source says "based on the intersection length with a ray from the new viewpoint". # This suggests the length in NDC space is the key. # So we might not need to convert to world space t for accumulation. # We just accumulate the color contributions weighted by the NDC length. pass def intersectraycuboid(rayorigin, raydirection, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax): # Standard ray-cuboid intersection # Returns tentry, texit # If no intersection, returns infinity, -infinity pass def getvolumendczrange(viewV0): # Get the NDC z range of the volume # This depends on the volume's world space bounds and the view V0 pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision in NDC space may affect traversal accuracy. Use double precision if necessary. Empty Regions: The algorithm proposes methods to skip empty regions. Implement a check for empty lists or supersegments to avoid unnecessary traversal. Degenerate Input: If the ray is parallel to a grid cell face, handle division by zero in DDA step calculations. Early Termination: Implement early ray termination when accumulated alpha exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0.99) to save computation. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of supersegments intersected by each ray. The Amanatides-Woo traversal is efficient, with O(1) per grid cell visited. The supersegment search is linear in the number of supersegments per list, but spatial smoothness allows for adjacency search, reducing the average case. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the VDI data structure (supersegment lists). Performance: Scales better to large VDIs than object-space approaches because it avoids generating geometry for each supersegment. Allows early ray termination. Strengths: No explicit geometry generation, efficient traversal, early ray termination, leverages anisotropy of VDI. Limitations: Requires VDI data structure to be pre-computed. Precision issues in NDC space. When to Use: Real-time rendering of large volumes using VDIs. When Not to Use: When VDI pre-computation is not feasible or when the volume is small and object-space rendering is simpler. This method was proposed by Lochmann et al. in "Efficient Raycasting of Volumetric Depth Images for Remote Visualization of Large Volumes at High Frame Rates". It builds on the Amanatides-Woo voxel traversal algorithm [2] and aims to improve upon object-space raycasting methods that generate explicit geometry for supersegments. name: Wolfenstein 3D Raycasting
head: Wolfenstein 3D technique, Wolfenstein-style rendering, Lodev-style DDA, DDA Ray Casting, Raycasting with Fisheye Correction
body: Wolfenstein 3D Raycasting is a rendering technique for first-person corridors on hardware without GPUs or z-buffers, where the world is a flat 2D grid, the camera is confined to the grid plane, and one ray is cast per screen column to reconstruct a textured 3D scene. It sets itself apart from general voxel traversal methods by operating on a strictly 2D grid map with a fixed-height camera, using the perpendicular distance to the camera plane to correct fisheye distortion and determine wall height, rather than computing full 3D intersections. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D grid map (Uint8Array or number[][]), player state (posX, posY, dirX, dirY, planeX, planeY), screen dimensions (FBW, FBH), and field of view defined by the plane vector length. Output: A framebuffer image containing vertical wall strips and billboard sprites. Data Structures: Map: A 1D or 2D array representing the grid. Values: 0 (empty floor), 1-4 (wall types), 5 (sliding door). Player: Object with x, y (position), dirX, dirY (unit direction vector), planeX, planeY (camera plane vector perpendicular to dir). Textures: Procedurally generated at runtime onto a 64x64 offscreen canvas, then read into a Uint32Array for fast pixel access. Z-Buffer: A 1D array of size FBW storing the perpendicular distance to the nearest wall for each screen column, used for sprite occlusion. Parameters: FOV: Determined by the length of the plane vector relative to the direction vector. A ratio of |plane|/|dir| = 0.66 yields a horizontal FOV of ~66.8 degrees. Wall Height: Real-world height of a wall tile, typically 1 unit. Steps: 1. Initialize Camera Vectors: For each screen column x from 0 to FBW - 1: Calculate cameraX = 2 x / FBW - 1 (ranges from -1 to 1). Calculate ray direction: rayDirX = dirX + planeX \cdot cameraX rayDirY = dirY + planeY \cdot cameraX 2. DDA Grid Traversal: Initialize current grid cell: mapX = floor(posX), mapY = floor(posY). Calculate step distances: \Deltax = \left| \frac{1}{rayDirX} \right|, \quad \Deltay = \left| \frac{1}{rayDirY} \right| Handle rayDirX == 0 or rayDirY == 0 by setting \Delta to a large value (e.g., 1e30). Determine step directions and initial side distances: If rayDirX < 0: stepX = -1, sideDistX = (posX - mapX) \Deltax. Else: stepX = 1, sideDistX = (mapX + 1 - posX) \Deltax. If rayDirY < 0: stepY = -1, sideDistY = (posY - mapY) \Deltay. Else: stepY = 1, sideDistY = (mapY + 1 - posY) \Deltay. Loop until a wall is hit: If sideDistX < sideDistY: sideDistX += \Deltax mapX += stepX side = 0 (hit vertical grid line) Else: sideDistY += \Deltay mapY += stepY side = 1 (hit horizontal grid line) Check if map[mapY][mapX] > 0. If so, break. Edge Case (Sliding Doors): If the hit tile is 5, advance the ray to the center line of the door cell. If the ray exits the cell before reaching the midline or hits the closed part, continue traversal. 3. Calculate Perpendicular Distance: Compute the fisheye-corrected distance: dist = side === 0 ? sideDistX - \Deltax: sideDistY - \Deltay This value represents the distance perpendicular to the camera plane, correcting for the bowing effect of raw ray length. 4. Render Wall Strip: Calculate line height: lineHeight = \frac{FBH}{dist} Calculate draw range: drawStart = \max(0, \lfloor (FBH - lineHeight) / 2 \rfloor) drawEnd = \min(FBH - 1, \lfloor (FBH + lineHeight) / 2 \rfloor) Calculate texture coordinate wallX: If side == 0: wallX = posY + dist rayDirY - floor(posY + dist rayDirY). Else: wallX = posX + dist rayDirX - floor(posX + dist rayDirX). Mirror texture X if necessary to prevent backward textures: If (side == 0 && rayDirX > 0) || (side == 1 && rayDirY < 0): wallX = 1 - wallX. Draw vertical line from drawStart to drawEnd using wallX for texture sampling. Shade based on side for depth cues. Store dist in zbuffer[x] for sprite occlusion. 5. Render Sprites (Billboards): Sort sprites by squared distance to player (far to near). For each sprite: Transform sprite position (sx, sy) to camera space: invDet = \frac{1}{planeX \cdot dirY - dirX \cdot planeY} transformX = invDet \cdot (dirY \cdot (sx - posX) - dirX \cdot (sy - posY)) transformY = invDet \cdot (-planeY \cdot (sx - posX) + planeX \cdot (sy - posY)) If transformY <= 0.05, skip (behind camera). Calculate screen X: screenX = floor((FBW / 2) (1 + transformX / transformY)). Calculate sprite size: size = abs(floor(FBH / transformY)). For each column x in sprite range: If transformY >= zbuffer[x], skip (occluded by wall). Sample texture, skip if alpha < 128, shade and write to framebuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def castraydda(map, posx, posy, dirx, diry, planex, planey, fbw, fbh, texsize=64): mapw = len(map[0]) maph = len(map) zbuffer = [0.0] fbw for x in range(fbw): camerax = 2.0 x / fbw - 1.0 raydirx = dirx + planex camerax raydiry = diry + planey camerax mapx = int(posx) mapy = int(posy) deltadistx = abs(1.0 / raydirx) if raydirx != 0 else 1e30 deltadisty = abs(1.0 / raydiry) if raydiry != 0 else 1e30 if raydirx < 0: stepx = -1 sidedistx = (posx - mapx) deltadistx else: stepx = 1 sidedistx = (mapx + 1 - posx) deltadistx if raydiry < 0: stepy = -1 sidedisty = (posy - mapy) deltadisty else: stepy = 1 sidedisty = (mapy + 1 - posy) deltadisty hit = False side = 0 guard = 0 while not hit and guard < 128: guard += 1 if sidedistx < sidedisty: sidedistx += deltadistx mapx += stepx side = 0 else: sidedisty += deltadisty mapy += stepy side = 1 if mapx < 0 or mapx >= mapw or mapy < 0 or mapy >= maph: hit = True continue tile = map[mapy][mapx] if tile == 0: continue if tile == 5: # Sliding door logic from: advance to center line, # check openness, continue traversal if gap not reached. hit = True continue hit = True if side == 0: perpdist = sidedistx - deltadistx else: perpdist = sidedisty - deltadisty zbuffer[x] = perpdist lineheight = int(fbh / perpdist) drawstart = max(0, (fbh - lineheight) // 2) drawend = min(fbh - 1, (fbh + lineheight) // 2) if side == 0: wallx = posy + perpdist raydiry else: wallx = posx + perpdist raydirx wallx -= int(wallx) if (side == 0 and raydirx > 0) or (side == 1 and raydiry < 0): wallx = 1.0 - wallx # Fixed-point vertical texture step step = texsize / lineheight texpos = (drawstart - (fbh - lineheight) / 2) step for y in range(drawstart, drawend + 1): texy = int(texpos) & (texsize - 1) texpos += step # Write shaded texel to framebuffer # fb[y fbw + x] = shade(tex[texy texsize + int(wallx texsize)]) return zbuffer Highly efficient on CPU-only hardware; the original engine ran on 286/386-class processors. Optimizations like drawing every second column can double FPS on low-resolution displays with negligible visual loss. Time, memory complexity, strengths, limitations, and usage guidelines are not given in the sources. Wolfenstein 3D (id Software, 1992) rendered first-person corridors on 286/386-class hardware without GPUs, z-buffers, or polygons. The technique projects a 2D grid map into a 3D perspective viewport using one ray per screen column. It is a specific application of the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm for grid traversal, popularized by Lodev's tutorial. name: Voxel Shadow Raycasting with DDA
head: DDA Voxel Shadow Tracing, Shadow Ray Grid Optimization, Voxel Shadow Raytracer
body: Voxel Shadow Raycasting with DDA is a technique for computing hard shadows in voxel-based scenes by traversing a 3D voxel grid along rays cast from surface points to light sources. It solves the problem of efficiently determining light attenuation through volumetric or opaque voxel data without resorting to slow, fixed-step ray marching. It sets itself apart from its siblings by focusing specifically on the shadow calculation phase within a rendering pipeline, utilizing the Amanatides–Woo traversal logic to jump between grid cells rather than sampling every unit of distance. The method operates in two distinct phases: the main rendering loop (which invokes the shadow raycaster) and the DDA traversal algorithm itself. It relies on a sparse or dense voxel buffer where each voxel has a density value. Inputs: Voxel Grid: A buffer of voxelmaterial structs containing color (unused in shadow calc) and density (float, 0.0 to 1.0, where 1.0 is opaque). Light Sources: A buffer of lightsource structs containing position (vec3), power (float, max reach distance), color (vec3), and intensity (float). Surface Data: For each pixel, the world-space position (vec4, alpha > 0 indicates valid surface) and normal (vec3). Grid Dimensions: mapsize (vec3), defining the bounds of the voxel world. Outputs: Shadow Factor: A float value between 0.0 (fully shadowed) and 1.0 (fully lit), representing the remaining light intensity after attenuation. Final Color: The base pixel color multiplied by the accumulated lighting contributions. The implementation uses specific buffer layouts, typically in a GLSL compute shader context: 1. Voxel Map (Map): layout (std430, binding = 3) buffer Map containing voxelmaterial voxels[]. 2. Lights (Lights): layout (std430, binding = 2) buffer Lights containing lightsource sources[]. 3. Position Texture (postexture): layout(rgba32f, binding = 1) storing world-space positions. 4. Normal Texture (normtexture): layout(rgba32f, binding = 4) storing voxel normals. 5. Output Image (imgoutput): layout(rgba32f, binding = 0) storing the final lit color. Coordinate to ID Conversion: To access the voxel buffer, 3D coordinates are converted to a 1D index. The coordinates are clamped to [0, mapsize]: \text{ID} = \lfloor x \rfloor + \lfloor y \rfloor \cdot \text{map\size}.x + \lfloor z \rfloor \cdot \text{map\size}.x \cdot \text{map\size}.y This assumes a row-major layout where x is the fastest varying dimension. For each pixel (x, y): 1. Load pixel color, position, and normal from textures. 2. If position.a <= 0, skip processing (background). 3. Initialize lightValue to ambient color vec4(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 1) and lightColor to vec3(0,0,0). 4. Iterate through each light source current in the Lights buffer: a. Calculate squared distance distanceSP = distance(current.position, position.xyz). b. Light Reach Test: If distanceSP > current.power current.power, skip this light (it cannot reach the surface). c. Compute ray direction rayPixSrc = current.position - position.xyz. d. Determine if the starting voxel should be sampled: stepThroughFirstVoxel = dot(normalize(rayPixSrc), normal) > 0. e. Call stepThroughVoxelWorld(position.xyz, rayPixSrc, stepThroughFirstVoxel) to get intensity. f. Calculate result multiplier: result = current.intensity intensity (1 - (distanceSP / current.power)). g. If result > 0, add current.color.rgb result to lightColor. 5. Add lightColor to lightValue.rgb. 6. Store pixel lightValue to imgoutput. This function traverses the voxel grid from origin along dir. Initialization Phase: 1. Normalize dir. 2. Set currPos = ivec3(floor(origin.x), floor(origin.y), floor(origin.z)). 3. Set intensity = 1.0. 4. For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: a. If dir[i] >= 0: step[i] = 1 delta[i] = 1.0 / max(0.000001, dir[i]) (prevents division by zero). Max[i] = (floor(currPos[i] + 1) - origin[i]) / dir[i]. Out[i] = mapsize[i] (boundary limit). b. If dir[i] < 0: step[i] = -1 delta[i] = -1.0 / dir[i] Max[i] = (floor(currPos[i]) - origin[i]) / dir[i]. Out[i] = -1 (boundary limit). 5. Calculate last = ivec3(floor(origin.x + dir.x), floor(origin.y + dir.y), floor(origin.z + dir.z)). Note: The source also calculates maxLength = dir.x^2 + dir.y^2 + dir.z^2, but since dir is normalized, this is always 1.0. Step Loop: While intensity > 0 AND !reachedEnd AND currPos != last: 1. Sample voxel at currPos using CordtoID. 2. Subtract currentVoxel.density from intensity. 3. Determine the next axis to step: Find the axis k with the minimum Max[k]. 4. Increment currPos[k] by step[k]. 5. Update Max[k] += delta[k]. 6. Check boundary: If currPos[k] == Out[k], set reachedEnd = true. Return: Return intensity. To reduce computation, shadow status can be stored in the voxel grid. For each voxel and each light source, two bits are stored: 1. One bit indicating the voxel is completely in shadow. 2. One bit indicating nothing blocks the voxel from seeing the light source. During traversal, if these bits are set, the ray calculation is skipped. This adds a memory overhead of 2 bits per light source per voxel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. AMBIENT = (0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 1.0) EPSILON = 0.000001 def imageload(texture, coord): """Simulates reading a vec4 from a 2D texture array.""" return texture[coord[1]][coord[0]] def imagestore(texture, coord, value): """Simulates writing a vec4 to a 2D texture array.""" texture[coord[1]][coord[0]] = value def cordtoid(cord, mapsize): """Converts 3D coordinates to a 1D index, clamping to grid bounds.""" x = max(0, min(mapsize[0], cord[0])) y = max(0, min(mapsize[1], cord[1])) z = max(0, min(mapsize[2], cord[2])) return int(x) + int(y) mapsize[0] + int(z) mapsize[0] mapsize[1] def stepthroughvoxelworld(origin, dir, stepthroughfirstvoxel, mapsize, voxels): intensity = 1.0 # Initialization dirnorm = normalize(dir) currpos = [int(origin[0]), int(origin[1]), int(origin[2])] # Arrays for DDA state (indices 0, 1, 2 correspond to x, y, z) step = [0, 0, 0] delta = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] maxdist = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] outbound = [0, 0, 0] # Configure DDA for each axis for axis in range(3): d = dirnorm[axis] if d >= 0: step[axis] = 1 delta[axis] = 1.0 / max(EPSILON, d) maxdist[axis] = (float(int(currpos[axis] + 1)) - origin[axis]) / d outbound[axis] = int(mapsize[axis]) else: step[axis] = -1 delta[axis] = -1.0 / d maxdist[axis] = (float(int(currpos[axis])) - origin[axis]) / d outbound[axis] = -1 # Termination setup lastpos = [int(origin[0] + dirnorm[0]), int(origin[1] + dirnorm[1]), int(origin[2] + dirnorm[2])] reachedend = False # Main Loop while intensity > 0 and not reachedend and currpos != lastpos: # Sample voxel at current position voxelidx = cordtoid(currpos, mapsize) intensity -= voxels[voxelidx].density # Determine next axis to step (find index of minimum maxdist) minval = min(maxdist) nextaxis = maxdist.index(minval) # Step currpos[nextaxis] += step[nextaxis] maxdist[nextaxis] += delta[nextaxis] # Check boundary if currpos[nextaxis] == outbound[nextaxis]: reachedend = True break return intensity def renderpixel(x, y, postexture, normtexture, imgoutput, lights, voxels, mapsize): pixel = imageload(imgoutput, (x, y)) position = imageload(postexture, (x, y)) normal = imageload(normtexture, (x, y))[:3] if position[3] <= 0: return lightvalue = list(AMBIENT) lightcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] castlights = 0 for light in lights: lineardist = length(light.position - position[:3]) distsq = lineardist lineardist # Light reach test if distsq > light.power light.power: continue raydir = light.position - position[:3] # Check if ray exits the surface immediately stepfirst = dot(normalize(raydir), normal) > 0 intensity = stepthroughvoxelworld(position[:3], raydir, stepfirst, mapsize, voxels) # Calculate result multiplier result = light.intensity intensity (1.0 - (lineardist / light.power)) if result > 0: lightcolor[0] += light.color[0] result lightcolor[1] += light.color[1] result lightcolor[2] += light.color[2] result castlights += 1 if castlights > 0: lightvalue[0] += lightcolor[0] lightvalue[1] += lightcolor[1] lightvalue[2] += lightcolor[2] imagestore(imgoutput, (x, y), tuple(pixel[i] lightvalue[i] for i in range(4))) A WebGPU compute shader-based ray tracer for voxel models that replaces a rasterizer. It casts rays per pixel, traverses a 3D voxel grid using DDA, applies directional lighting with diffuse shading, and generates hard shadows via shadow rays. It sets itself apart from its parent Voxel Shadow Raycasting with DDA by implementing the entire rendering pipeline (primary rays, shading, and shadow rays) within a WebGPU compute shader, rather than relying on a GLSL rasterizer with DDA for shadow calculation only. Time Complexity: The DDA traversal is O(N) where N is the number of voxels intersected by the shadow ray. Memory Complexity: The base method requires storing the voxel grid. The optimized version with shadow bits requires an additional 2 bits per light source per voxel. Performance: The DDA approach avoids the "slow fallback" fixed-step algorithm which increments position by a small fixed step (e.g., 0.05) and samples every step, leading to redundant calculations. Strengths: Efficient traversal of uniform grids; handles arbitrary ray directions; simple implementation. Limitations: Requires a uniform grid structure; shadow bit optimization increases memory usage per light source per voxel. When to use: When rendering hard shadows in voxel worlds where performance is critical and the grid is uniform. When not to use: For non-uniform grids (use Siddon's Algorithm or adaptive grids) or when soft shadows are required (DDA provides hard shadows only). The technique is based on the Amanatides–Woo voxel traversal algorithm, which enumerates grid cells intersected by a ray in front-to-back order. The specific GLSL implementation described in the sources is an unofficial contribution to the GitHub repository Ein-Baum/Voxel-shadow-raytracer. The concept of using grids to reduce shadow ray computations by storing status bits was discussed in academic literature on fast voxel traversal. body: A WebGPU compute shader-based ray tracer for voxel models that replaces a rasterizer. It casts rays per pixel, traverses a 3D voxel grid using DDA, applies directional lighting with diffuse shading, and generates hard shadows via shadow rays. It sets itself apart from its parent Voxel Shadow Raycasting with DDA by implementing the entire rendering pipeline (primary rays, shading, and shadow rays) within a WebGPU compute shader, rather than relying on a GLSL rasterizer with DDA for shadow calculation only. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid (dense or sparse), a project palette of block colors, lighting parameters (sun direction, intensity, ambient light), and camera state. Output: A 2D image buffer rendered to the canvas. Data Structures: Uniform Buffer: Expanded to 128 bytes to store lighting parameters. Storage Buffer: Contains the project palette for retrieving block colors. Voxel Data: Gathered from the voxel engine into a flat buffer. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: The renderer checks for WebGPU support. If unavailable, it displays a fallback background. 2. Primary Ray Casting: For each pixel, a primary ray is cast into the scene. 3. Voxel Traversal: The 3D voxel grid is traversed using the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm to find the first intersecting voxel. 4. Diffuse Shading: If a voxel is hit, diffuse shading is calculated using the dot product of the surface normal (N) and the light direction (L). 5. Shadow Raycasting: Shadow rays are cast by performing DDA traversal from the hit point toward the sun direction to determine occlusion. 6. Color Retrieval: Block colors are retrieved from the storage buffer containing the project palette. 7. Ground Plane: A ground plane with grid lines is rendered, which receives shadows. 8. Background: A subtle sky gradient background is rendered. 9. Blitting: The compute shader output is blitted to the canvas using a fullscreen triangle render pass. Formulas: Diffuse Shading: I{diffuse} = \max(0, N \cdot L). Sun Direction: Calculated from Sun Azimuth (\theta) and Sun Elevation (\phi) using spherical-to-Cartesian conversion: L = (\cos\phi \sin\theta, \sin\phi, \cos\phi \cos\theta). Parameters: Sun Azimuth: Horizontal angle of the sun, range 0 to 360 degrees. Sun Elevation: Vertical angle of the sun, range 5 to 90 degrees. Sun Intensity: Brightness of the directional light source. Ambient Light Intensity: Intensity of the ambient light component. Shadow Strength: Intensity/opacity of the shadows. Sun Color: Presets include Warm, White, Cool, Gold, Pink. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: WebGPU Availability: WebGPU is not available in headless CI environments, so the canvas shows a fallback background instead of rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderpixel(pixelx, pixely, camera, voxelgrid, palette, lighting): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.getray(pixelx, pixely) hitvoxel, t = ddatraverse(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid) if hitvoxel is not None: basecolor = palette[hitvoxel[0]][hitvoxel[1]][hitvoxel[2]] hitpoint = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t for i in range(3)] hitnormal = computenormal(hitpoint, hitvoxel) diffusefactor = max(0.0, dot(hitnormal, lighting.sundirection)) isshadowed = ddatraverseshadow(hitpoint, lighting.sundirection, voxelgrid) if isshadowed: diffusefactor = 0.0 finalcolor = basecolor (lighting.ambientintensity + diffusefactor lighting.sunintensity) else: finalcolor = getskygradient(raydirection) return finalcolor def ddatraverse(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid): voxel = [math.floor(rayorigin[i]) for i in range(3)] step = [1 if raydirection[i] > 0 else -1 if raydirection[i] < 0 else 0 for i in range(3)] tdelta = [1.0 / abs(raydirection[i]) if raydirection[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] tmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): if step[i] > 0: tmax[i] = (voxel[i] + 1.0 - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] elif step[i] < 0: tmax[i] = (voxel[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] else: tmax[i] = float('inf') bounds = voxelgrid.bounds t = 0.0 while 0 <= voxel[0] < bounds[0] and 0 <= voxel[1] < bounds[1] and 0 <= voxel[2] < bounds[2]: if voxelgrid.isopaque(voxel): return voxel, t axis = tmax.index(min(tmax)) t += tdelta[axis] tmax[axis] += tdelta[axis] voxel[axis] += step[axis] return None, 0.0 def ddatraverseshadow(origin, direction, voxelgrid): epsilon = 1e-4 shiftedorigin = [origin[i] + direction[i] epsilon for i in range(3)] hitvoxel, = ddatraverse(shiftedorigin, direction, voxelgrid) return hitvoxel is not None def dot(a, b): return sum(a[i] b[i] for i in range(3)) def computenormal(point, voxel): # Returns the outward face normal of the voxel hit based on closest face dx = point[0] - (voxel[0] + 0.5) dy = point[1] - (voxel[1] + 0.5) dz = point[2] - (voxel[2] + 0.5) if abs(dx) > abs(dy) and abs(dx) > abs(dz): return [1.0 if dx > 0 else -1.0, 0.0, 0.0] if abs(dy) > abs(dz): return [0.0, 1.0 if dy > 0 else -1.0, 0.0] return [0.0, 0.0, 1.0 if dz > 0 else -1.0] def getskygradient(direction): # Returns a subtle sky gradient based on ray direction return [0.5, 0.7, 1.0] Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Performance depends on the hardware's WebGPU support and the complexity of the voxel scene. Strengths: Real-time lighting and shadows in a voxel environment; interactive controls for lighting parameters. Limitations: Requires WebGPU support; not available in headless environments. When to use: When real-time voxel rendering with dynamic lighting and shadows is required in a web browser. When not to use: In headless CI environments or browsers without WebGPU support. The WebGPU Voxel Ray Tracing Renderer was developed as part of the LunaVoxel project. It was introduced as an alternative to the existing Three.js rasterizer, accessible via a dedicated Render tab in the header navigation. The implementation includes directional lighting, shadow rays, and interactive controls. It was authored by tfritzy and merged in February 2026. name: Siddon's Algorithm
head: Exact discrete Beer-Lambert law, Ray casting with voxel intersection, Siddon ray tracing, exact radiological path calculation
body: Siddon's Algorithm is a method for analytically computing the exact intersection lengths of a ray with each voxel in a 3D grid by tracking parametric alpha values at which the ray crosses parallel CT planes (x, y, z). It serves as a ray-driven forward projection method that calculates the line-integral as a weighted sum of the values of intersected voxels, where weights are the length of intersection between each voxel and the ray. This method provides an exact computation of the discretized Beer-Lambert law for X-ray attenuation, calculating the integral of linear attenuation coefficients (LACs) along a ray by summing the LAC in every voxel intersected by the ray, weighted by the intersection length. It is widely used in slice-to-volume registration and differentiable rendering. Inputs and Outputs: The algorithm takes a ray defined by a source point \mathbf{s} and a target/detector point \mathbf{p}, and a discrete 3D volume \hat{\mu} (or \mathbf{V}) representing the voxel grid of Linear Attenuation Coefficients (LACs) or densities. Outputs typically include: alphas: Relative distance between start and endpoint for the intersections with the cube. l: Lengths of intersections with cubes. rho: Densities extracted from cubes. d12: Distance between start and endpoint of ray tracing. ix: Indices of hit voxels. The final rendered intensity or energy attenuation E(R) or I{\hat{\mu}}(\vec{r}). Data Structures: The volume is represented as a 3D grid. The ray is parameterized by \alpha \in [0, 1]. The intersections are stored as a sorted set of parametric values \{\alpha1, \dots, \alphaM\}. Steps: 1. Define the Ray: Define the ray \vec{r}(\alpha) = \mathbf{s} + \alpha(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}) for \alpha \in [0, 1], where \mathbf{s} is the X-ray source position and \mathbf{p} is the detector pixel position. 2. Compute Plane Intersections: Calculate the intersection parameters of the ray with the parallel planes comprising the voxel grid. For a voxel size \Delta X in the x-direction and the location of the 0-th plane bx, the intersection with the i-th plane is: \alphax(i) = \frac{bx + i \Delta X - \mathbf{s}x}{\mathbf{p}x - \mathbf{s}x} Analogous expressions are used for \alphay(\cdot) and \alphaz(\cdot). 3. Sort Intersections: Combine the intersection parameters from all three axes and sort them to form the set \mathbf{\alpha} = \text{sort}(\mathbf{\alpha}x, \mathbf{\alpha}y, \mathbf{\alpha}z), which contains M values parameterizing the intersections. 4. Iterate and Sum: Iterate m from 1 to M-1. For each segment between \alpham and \alpha{m+1}: a. Calculate the midpoint parameter: \alpha{mid} = \frac{\alpha{m+1} + \alpham}{2}. b. Evaluate the voxel LAC at the midpoint: \hat{\mu}[\mathbf{s} + \alpha{mid} (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s})]. Note: This indexing operation returns the LAC of the intersected voxel. c. Multiply by the segment length parameter difference: (\alpha{m+1} - \alpham). 5. Final Calculation: Sum these products and multiply by the ray length \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}\| to get the rendered intensity: I{\hat{\mu}}(\vec{r}) = \| \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s} \| \sum{m=1}^{M-1} \hat{\mu} \left[ \mathbf{s} + \frac{\alpha{m+1} + \alpham}{2} (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}) \right] (\alpha{m+1} - \alpham) Alternatively expressed as energy attenuation E(R): E(R) = \| \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s} \|2 \sum{m=1}^{M-1} (\alpha{m+1} - \alpham) \mathbf{V} \left[ \mathbf{s} + \frac{\alpha{m+1} + \alpham}{2} (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}) \right] The term \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}\|2 cancels the reciprocal length units of \mathbf{V} to make E unitless. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def siddonsalgorithm(source, target, volume, voxelsize, originoffset, voxelshift=0.5): """ source: tuple (sx, sy, sz) target: tuple (px, py, pz) volume: 3D array of LACs voxelsize: float, size of one voxel in mm originoffset: tuple (bx, by, bz), location of the 0-th plane in mm voxelshift: float, 0.0 for corner-aligned, 0.5 for center-aligned voxels """ sx, sy, sz = source px, py, pz = target bx, by, bz = originoffset dx, dy, dz = voxelsize dirx = px - sx diry = py - sy dirz = pz - sz raylength = (dirx2 + diry2 + dirz2)0.5 alphas = set() eps = 1e-08 # X planes Nx = len(volume) for i in range(Nx): planex = bx + i dx if abs(dirx) > eps: alpha = (planex - sx) / dirx if 0.0 <= alpha <= 1.0: alphas.add(alpha) # Y planes Ny = len(volume[0]) for j in range(Ny): planey = by + j dy if abs(diry) > eps: alpha = (planey - sy) / diry if 0.0 <= alpha <= 1.0: alphas.add(alpha) # Z planes Nz = len(volume[0][0]) for k in range(Nz): planez = bz + k dz if abs(dirz) > eps: alpha = (planez - sz) / dirz if 0.0 <= alpha <= 1.0: alphas.add(alpha) # Add endpoints if not present alphas.add(0.0) alphas.add(1.0) sortedalphas = sorted(list(alphas)) totalintegral = 0.0 for m in range(len(sortedalphas) - 1): alpham = sortedalphas[m] alpham1 = sortedalphas[m+1] alphamid = (alpham + alpham1) / 2.0 midx = sx + alphamid dirx midy = sy + alphamid diry midz = sz + alphamid dirz # Map to voxel indices ix = int((midx - bx) / dx - voxelshift) iy = int((midy - by) / dy - voxelshift) iz = int((midz - bz) / dz - voxelshift) if 0 <= ix < Nx and 0 <= iy < Ny and 0 <= iz < Nz: mu = volume[ix][iy][iz] totalintegral += mu (alpham1 - alpham) return raylength totalintegral Parameters: voxelshift: float, default 0.5. Determines if the voxel is at the top left corner (0) or the center (0.5). mode: str, default 'nearest'. Interpolation mode for gridsample. filterintersectionsoutsidevolume: bool, default False. If True, uses alphamin/max to filter the intersections. eps: float, default 1e-08. Small constant to avoid div by zero errors. isocenterCube: The isocenter position in cube coordinates [mm]. resolution: The resolution of the cubes in mm/voxel. sourcePoint: The starting point of the ray tracing. targetPoint: The ending point of the ray tracing. cubes: A cell array of density/material cubes to trace through. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Division by zero must be handled if the ray is parallel to a grid plane. Boundaries: Intersections outside the volume should be filtered if filterintersectionsoutsidevolume is True. Degenerate Input: If the ray does not intersect the volume, the sum is zero. Accuracy: Nearest-neighbour interpolation is too simplified for most applications; the input voxel volume must be at least double the resolution in each dimension compared to the desired reconstruction resolution to maintain accuracy. Overfitting: In sparse-view settings, Siddon's method suffers from overfitting because it does not allow ground truth pixels to provide self-supervision to voxels not directly intersected by the ray. Time and Memory Complexity: Computation scales cubically with the resolution of the voxelgrid \hat{\mu} because it requires computing every plane intersection. The number of intersections M is proportional to the number of voxels intersected, which can be up to Nx + Ny + Nz for a grid of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Measured Performance: On 40 test walnuts with 15 input views, Siddon's method achieved SSIM 0.923, PSNR 37.69, MSE 1.28 \times 10^{-5}, PCC 0.96, and runtime 11.3 minutes on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. The batch size is limited by memory constraints to |\mathcal{R}| = 5.5 \times 10^5 rays per batch. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Exactly computes line integrals, leading to higher fidelity novel views compared to trilinear interpolation. It is widely used in slice-to-volume registration. Limitations: Inferior in accuracy to Joseph's and Köhler's methods when compared against ideal analytical values. It does not account for patterns of reflection and scattering present in real X-ray systems. It is more prone to overfitting in sparse views compared to trilinear interpolation. When to Use: Use when exact radiological path calculation is required for differentiable rendering or slice-to-volume registration, and computational resources allow for the cubic scaling. When Not to Use: Avoid when real-time performance is critical and approximate methods (like trilinear interpolation) are sufficient, or when sparse-view reconstruction is prone to overfitting. Siddon's Algorithm was introduced by R.L. Siddon in 1985 in the paper 'Fast calculation of the exact radiological path for a three-dimensional CT array', published in Med. Phys. 12(2):252-5. It is a parametric method to generate Digital Radiographic Reconstructions (DRRs) by modeling the geometry of an idealized projectional radiography system. It is used in medical imaging, particularly in radiation therapy planning (e.g., matRad) and CBCT reconstruction. rayTracing — matRad 3.2.3 documentation, https://matrad.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api/raytracing.html, fetched 2026-10-25 5 Forward Projection through Voxel Volumes, https://www.cvl.isy.liu.se/education/undergraduate/tsbb31/download/TurbellPhDCh5.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Differentiable Voxel-based X-ray Rendering Improves Sparse-View 3D CBCT Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2411.19224, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) renderers – diffdrr, https://vivekg.dev/DiffDRR/api/renderers.html, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Voxel Raycasting with Normal Estimation
head: Voxel DDA, DDA Voxel Traversal, Voxel Raycasting via DDA, Digital Differential Analyzer voxel traversal
body: Voxel Raycasting with Normal Estimation traces a ray through a voxel grid to find the first solid voxel, simultaneously estimating the surface normal based on the traversal direction relative to the grid axes. It solves the problem of efficiently querying sparse or dense voxel structures for collision, occlusion, or surface detection by walking the grid directly, visiting only intersected cells. It differs from fixed-step raymarching by calculating intersection distances with voxel boundaries along each axis to determine which boundary is crossed next, ensuring exactly one voxel is processed per step. It builds on Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal by providing the core traversal mechanism that identifies the hit voxel and entry face, which are then used for normal estimation. Inputs: Ray origin O, ray direction D (normalized), maximum ray distance maxDist, voxel grid occupancy data, and an epsilon constant \epsilon for degenerate ray detection. Outputs: Boolean hit status, hit position P, and surface normal N. Data Structures: Ray: Contains origin (Vec3), direction (Vec3), maxDistance (float). VoxelGrid: Provides a function isSolid(x, y, z) returning boolean. HitResult: Contains hit (bool), point (Vec3), normal (Vec3). Parameters: \epsilon = 0.0001. maxDist = 6.0 (typical, scene-dependent). Algorithm Steps: 1. Degenerate Ray Check: Calculate squared magnitude |D|^2. If |D|^2 < \epsilon, return no hit. 2. Initialization: Compute step direction vector S: Sx = \text{sign}(Dx), \quad Sy = \text{sign}(Dy), \quad Sz = \text{sign}(Dz) Where \text{sign}(v) = 1 if v > 0, -1 if v < 0, and 0 if v = 0. Compute step size (reciprocal of direction magnitude): \Delta Tx = \begin{cases} 1/|Dx| & \text{if } |Dx| > \epsilon \\ \infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \Delta Ty = \begin{cases} 1/|Dy| & \text{if } |Dy| > \epsilon \\ \infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \Delta Tz = \begin{cases} 1/|Dz| & \text{if } |Dz| > \epsilon \\ \infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. Determine starting voxel coordinates: Vx = \lfloor Ox \rfloor, \quad Vy = \lfloor Oy \rfloor, \quad Vz = \lfloor Oz \rfloor. Initialize distance to next boundary (T{max}) for each axis: T{maxx} = \begin{cases} (Vx + 1 - Ox) \Delta Tx & \text{if } Sx = 1 \\ (Ox - Vx) \Delta Tx & \text{if } Sx = -1 \\ \infty & \text{if } Sx = 0 \end{cases} T{maxy} = \begin{cases} (Vy + 1 - Oy) \Delta Ty & \text{if } Sy = 1 \\ (Oy - Vy) \Delta Ty & \text{if } Sy = -1 \\ \infty & \text{if } Sy = 0 \end{cases} T{maxz} = \begin{cases} (Vz + 1 - Oz) \Delta Tz & \text{if } Sz = 1 \\ (Oz - Vz) \Delta Tz & \text{if } Sz = -1 \\ \infty & \text{if } Sz = 0 \end{cases}. Initialize previous position P{prev} = O. 3. Immediate Hit Check: Check if the starting voxel (Vx, Vy, Vz) is solid. If yes, calculate the entry normal based on the closest face (determined by ray direction and local position within the voxel) and return the hit. 4. DDA Loop: While T{maxx} < maxDist or T{maxy} < maxDist or T{maxz} < maxDist: Find the minimum T{max} among T{maxx}, T{maxy}, T{maxz}. Tie-breaking priority: X > Y > Z. Record the ray distance t at the boundary being crossed (t = T{max{axis}}). Update previous position: P{prev} = P{curr}. Advance the voxel index along the axis with the minimum T{max}: If T{maxx} is smallest: Vx \leftarrow Vx + Sx, T{maxx} \leftarrow T{maxx} + \Delta Tx. Else if T{maxy} is smallest: Vy \leftarrow Vy + Sy, T{maxy} \leftarrow T{maxy} + \Delta Ty. Else: Vz \leftarrow Vz + Sz, T{maxz} \leftarrow T{maxz} + \Delta Tz. Compute current position at the crossed boundary: P{curr} = O + D \times t. Check if the new voxel (Vx, Vy, Vz) is solid. If solid: Calculate displacement vector Diff = P{curr} - P{prev}. Estimate normal N by comparing absolute components of Diff: If |Diffx| > |Diffy| and |Diffx| > |Diffz|: N = (-1, 0, 0) if Diffx > 0, else (1, 0, 0). Else if |Diffy| > |Diffz|: N = (0, -1, 0) if Diffy > 0, else (0, 1, 0). Else: N = (0, 0, -1) if Diffz > 0, else (0, 0, 1). Return hit with position P{curr} and normal N. If not solid, continue loop. 5. Termination: If the loop completes without hitting a solid voxel, return no hit. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelraycastwithnormalestimation(origin, direction, maxdist, issolid, epsilon=0.0001): """ Traces a ray through a voxel grid to find the first solid voxel and estimate its normal. Args: origin (Vec3): Ray origin. direction (Vec3): Ray direction (assumed normalized). maxdist (float): Maximum ray length. issolid (function): Function taking (x, y, z) integers, returning True if voxel is solid. epsilon (float): Threshold for degenerate rays. Returns: dict: {'hit': bool, 'point': Vec3, 'normal': Vec3} """ # 1. Degenerate Ray Check dirsq = direction.x2 + direction.y2 + direction.z2 if dirsq < epsilon: return {'hit': False, 'point': None, 'normal': None} # 2. Initialization stepx = 1 if direction.x > 0 else (-1 if direction.x < 0 else 0) stepy = 1 if direction.y > 0 else (-1 if direction.y < 0 else 0) stepz = 1 if direction.z > 0 else (-1 if direction.z < 0 else 0) absdx = abs(direction.x) absdy = abs(direction.y) absdz = abs(direction.z) deltatx = (1.0 / absdx) if absdx > epsilon else float('inf') deltaty = (1.0 / absdy) if absdy > epsilon else float('inf') deltatz = (1.0 / absdz) if absdz > epsilon else float('inf') voxelx = math.floor(origin.x) voxely = math.floor(origin.y) voxelz = math.floor(origin.z) if stepx == 1: tmaxx = (voxelx + 1.0 - origin.x) deltatx elif stepx == -1: tmaxx = (origin.x - voxelx) deltatx else: tmaxx = float('inf') if stepy == 1: tmaxy = (voxely + 1.0 - origin.y) deltaty elif stepy == -1: tmaxy = (origin.y - voxely) deltaty else: tmaxy = float('inf') if stepz == 1: tmaxz = (voxelz + 1.0 - origin.z) deltatz elif stepz == -1: tmaxz = (origin.z - voxelz) deltatz else: tmaxz = float('inf') prevpos = origin t = 0.0 # 3. Immediate Hit Check if issolid(voxelx, voxely, voxelz): if abs(direction.x) > abs(direction.y) and abs(direction.x) > abs(direction.z): normal = Vec3(-stepx, 0, 0) elif abs(direction.y) > abs(direction.z): normal = Vec3(0, -stepy, 0) else: normal = Vec3(0, 0, -stepz) return {'hit': True, 'point': origin, 'normal': normal} # 4. DDA Loop while tmaxx < maxdist or tmaxy < maxdist or tmaxz < maxdist: if tmaxx <= tmaxy and tmaxx <= tmaxz: axis = 'x' elif tmaxy <= tmaxz: axis = 'y' else: axis = 'z' t = tmaxx if axis == 'x' else (tmaxy if axis == 'y' else tmaxz) if axis == 'x': voxelx += stepx tmaxx += deltatx elif axis == 'y': voxely += stepy tmaxy += deltaty else: voxelz += stepz tmaxz += deltatz currpos = Vec3( origin.x + direction.x t, origin.y + direction.y t, origin.z + direction.z t) if issolid(voxelx, voxely, voxelz): diff = currpos - prevpos absdiffx = abs(diff.x) absdiffy = abs(diff.y) absdiffz = abs(diff.z) if absdiffx > absdiffy and absdiffx > absdiffz: normal = Vec3(-1, 0, 0) if diff.x > 0 else Vec3(1, 0, 0) elif absdiffy > absdiffz: normal = Vec3(0, -1, 0) if diff.y > 0 else Vec3(0, 1, 0) else: normal = Vec3(0, 0, -1) if diff.z > 0 else Vec3(0, 0, 1) return {'hit': True, 'point': currpos, 'normal': normal} prevpos = currpos return {'hit': False, 'point': None, 'normal': None} class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Rays: Rays with zero or near-zero direction components must be handled to avoid division by zero or infinite loops. Axis-Aligned Rays: If a direction component is exactly 0, the corresponding step and deltat are handled as 0 and infinity respectively, skipping traversal on that axis. Normal Accuracy: Normal estimation relies on the displacement vector between steps. If the step size is large relative to voxel size, or if the ray passes through a corner, the normal may be inaccurate or incorrectly axis-aligned. The method assumes the ray enters the voxel face corresponding to the largest component of the displacement vector. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in tmax accumulation can cause jitter or missed voxels in long rays. Using double precision or periodic re-normalization of tmax may be required. A traversal algorithm that determines the sequence of voxels intersected by a ray without explicit intersection tests, using precomputed distance-to-boundary parameters. It differs by providing the core traversal mechanism for hit voxel and entry face identification, used for normal estimation. Choose when efficient, exact voxel stepping is required for collision or surface detection. Extends basic voxel raycasting by combining grid traversal with precise geometric intersection against sub-voxel AABB hitboxes. It differs by refining the hit position and normal for non-cuboid shapes, falling back to grid face normals for solid voxels. Choose when non-cuboid collision shapes (hitboxes) are present in the voxel environment. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels intersected along the ray path (proportional to maxDist). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the voxel grid storage. Performance: On a 256x256x256 colorfield (16 million voxels), software-mode raycasting achieves decent speed at 2000x2000 resolution and real-time rates at 800x600 for dense objects. It is more efficient than PhysX raycasts for voxel grids. Strengths: Parallelizable (each ray is independent), efficient for sparse grids (visits only intersected cells), simple implementation. Limitations: Normal estimation is approximate and axis-aligned, not suitable for smooth surfaces. Performance degrades with very long rays or dense grids without spatial acceleration structures. When to Use: Collision detection, occlusion culling, and simple surface normal estimation in voxel-based games or simulations where performance is critical and high-precision normals are not required. The method is based on the Amanatides and Woo algorithm, a classic ray traversal algorithm for regular grids. It was popularized in the context of voxel rendering and collision detection in games. The algorithm was originally described in "A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing" by Amanatides and Woo (1987). name: DN_step_map
head: Amanatides-Woo Algorithm, Amanatides and Woo algorithm, Voxel DDA, DDA Voxel Traversal
body: DNstepmap is a voxel traversal algorithm that determines the sequence of voxels intersected by a ray in a regular grid without performing explicit intersection tests with voxel faces. It solves the problem of efficiently querying sparse or dense voxel structures for collision, occlusion, or surface detection by stepping through the grid along the ray direction. It differs from fixed-step raymarching by using precomputed distance-to-boundary parameters (tMax) to jump directly to the next voxel boundary, ensuring exactly one voxel is processed per step and eliminating redundant checks. It builds on Voxel Raycasting with Normal Estimation by providing the core traversal mechanism that identifies the hit voxel and entry face, which are then used for normal estimation. Inputs: rayPos: Ray origin (px, py, pz) in world or volume coordinates. rayDir: Ray direction vector (dx, dy, dz). Must be non-zero. tmax: Maximum traversal distance (parameter t). voxSize: Voxel side length (explicit scalar, typically 1.0 for unit grids). maxSteps: Optional integer limit to prevent infinite loops in degenerate cases (e.g., origin inside solid). Default 1024. Outputs: hitVoxel: Coordinates (i, j, k) of the first occupied voxel. hitFace: The face entered (e.g., neg-x, pos-y). prevEmptyVoxel: The voxel coordinate immediately preceding the hit, useful for block placement. hitPos: Intersection point in world coordinates. hitNormal: Surface normal at the hit location. Boolean success flag. Data Structures: current: Integer tuple (X, Y, Z) representing the current voxel index. step: Integer tuple (stepx, stepy, stepz) indicating direction of increment (1, -1, 0). tMax: Float tuple (tMaxx, tMaxy, tMaxz) representing the ray parameter t at which the ray crosses the next voxel boundary along each axis. tDelta: Float tuple (tDeltax, tDeltay, tDeltaz) representing the distance between consecutive voxel boundaries along each axis. Steps: 1. Validate Direction: Calculate direction length L = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2}. If L < \epsilon (e.g., 10^{-5}), return failure. Normalize direction: dx \leftarrow dx/L, dy \leftarrow dy/L, dz \leftarrow dz/L. 2. Initialize Voxel Index: Compute starting voxel indices: X = \lfloor px / C \rfloor, \quad Y = \lfloor py / C \rfloor, \quad Z = \lfloor pz / C \rfloor where C is the voxel size. Note: If the grid has an origin offset O, adjust: X = \lfloor (px - Ox)/C \rfloor. 3. Compute Step Directions: For each axis a \in \{x, y, z\}: stepa = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } da > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } da < 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } da = 0 \end{cases}. 4. Compute Delta and Initial tMax: For each axis a: If da \neq 0: tDeltaa = \frac{C}{|da|}. Determine the next boundary coordinate Ba: Ba = \begin{cases} (X + 1) \cdot C & \text{if } stepa = 1 \\ X \cdot C & \text{if } stepa = -1 \end{cases}. Calculate initial distance to boundary: tMaxa = \frac{Ba - pa}{da}. Note: If da < 0, the formula effectively becomes \frac{(pa - X \cdot C)}{|da|}. If da = 0: tDeltaa = \infty, \quad tMaxa = \infty. This prevents division by zero and excludes the axis from traversal decisions. 5. Traverse Loop: Loop while steps < maxSteps: a. Check Current Voxel: Query voxel occupancy at (X, Y, Z). If occupied, return hit data: hitVoxel = (X, Y, Z) hitPos = rayPos + rayDir \cdot tMax{axis} hitNormal = (-stepx, -stepy, -stepz) (inward facing normal of the entry face). prevEmptyVoxel = (X - stepx, Y - stepy, Z - stepz). Return success. Pitfall: If the ray origin is already inside an occupied voxel, the check in step 5a must occur before stepping, or the algorithm must handle the "inside" case explicitly to return the starting voxel as the hit. Standard DDA assumes entry from outside; if inside, the first step moves to a neighbor, potentially missing the start voxel if not checked pre-loop. b. Find Next Boundary: Identify the axis with the minimum tMax: axis = \arg\min{a \in \{x,y,z\}} tMaxa. If tMax{axis} > tmax, break loop (ray exits volume). c. Advance Ray: Update current voxel index: current{axis} += step{axis}. Update tMax{axis}: tMax{axis} += tDelta{axis}. Record hitFace based on axis and step{axis} (e.g., if axis=x, stepx=1, face is neg-x). 6. Termination: If loop completes without hit, return failure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dnstepmap(raypos, raydir, tmax, voxsize=1.0, maxsteps=1024): # 1. Validate and normalize direction dirlen = math.sqrt(raydir.x2 + raydir.y2 + raydir.z2) if dirlen < 1e-5: return None dx = raydir.x / dirlen dy = raydir.y / dirlen dz = raydir.z / dirlen # 2. Initialize voxel indices cx = math.floor(raypos.x / voxsize) cy = math.floor(raypos.y / voxsize) cz = math.floor(raypos.z / voxsize) # 3. Compute step directions stepx = 1 if dx > 0 else (-1 if dx < 0 else 0) stepy = 1 if dy > 0 else (-1 if dy < 0 else 0) stepz = 1 if dz > 0 else (-1 if dz < 0 else 0) # 4. Compute tDelta and tMax if dx != 0: tdeltax = voxsize / abs(dx) nextbndx = (cx + (1 if stepx > 0 else 0)) voxsize tmaxx = (nextbndx - raypos.x) / dx else: tdeltax = float('inf') tmaxx = float('inf') if dy != 0: tdeltay = voxsize / abs(dy) nextbndy = (cy + (1 if stepy > 0 else 0)) voxsize tmaxy = (nextbndy - raypos.y) / dy else: tdeltay = float('inf') tmaxy = float('inf') if dz != 0: tdeltaz = voxsize / abs(dz) nextbndz = (cz + (1 if stepz > 0 else 0)) voxsize tmaxz = (nextbndz - raypos.z) / dz else: tdeltaz = float('inf') tmaxz = float('inf') # 5. Traverse for in range(maxsteps): # Query voxel occupancy at (cx, cy, cz) isoccupied = False # Placeholder for grid lookup if isoccupied: # Find min tMax for hit position if tmaxx <= tmaxy and tmaxx <= tmaxz: thit = tmaxx elif tmaxy <= tmaxz: thit = tmaxy else: thit = tmaxz hitpos = (raypos.x + dx thit, raypos.y + dy thit, raypos.z + dz thit) hitnormal = (-stepx, -stepy, -stepz) prevvoxel = (cx - stepx, cy - stepy, cz - stepz) return { 'hitVoxel': (cx, cy, cz), 'hitPos': hitpos, 'hitNormal': hitnormal, 'prevEmptyVoxel': prevvoxel } # Find minimum tMax if tmaxx <= tmaxy and tmaxx <= tmaxz: axis = 'x' tmax = tmaxx elif tmaxy <= tmaxz: axis = 'y' tmax = tmaxy else: axis = 'z' tmax = tmaxz if tmax > tmax: break # Advance if axis == 'x': cx += stepx tmaxx += tdeltax hitface = 'neg-x' if stepx < 0 else 'pos-x' elif axis == 'y': cy += stepy tmaxy += tdeltay hitface = 'neg-y' if stepy < 0 else 'pos-y' else: cz += stepz tmaxz += tdeltaz hitface = 'neg-z' if stepz < 0 else 'pos-z' return None This method performs hidden surface elimination by casting a ray through a binary voxel volume to locate the first voxel where a specific data channel is non-zero. It differs from standard DDA traversal by optimizing for sparse or binary data: it processes voxels in groups of eight packed into a single byte, advancing the ray by whole bytes when the group is empty, thereby skipping large empty regions efficiently. This approach is distinct from sibling methods that use adaptive edge smoothing or neighbor-averaged interpolation, as it relies on strict bitwise presence checks rather than continuous field evaluation. This method extends standard DDA raymarching by sampling corner and edge voxel occupancy to adaptively compute volume content, eliminating stepping artifacts and spikes caused by uniform voxel traversal. Unlike standard DDA which steps uniformly through fixed voxels, this technique smooths terrain surfaces without increasing the step count or requiring geometry subdivision. It builds on DNstepmap by refining the surface normal and volume estimation at the hit voxel. A technique to compute voxel volume values at corners for smooth terrain rendering, replacing side-based volume storage with corner-based values to better represent surface geometry during raymarching. It sets apart from sibling methods by explicitly handling diagonal neighbors (NW, NE, SW, SE) and applying "surface block maxing" to clamp volumes at surface boundaries, whereas siblings like Midpoint UV Calculation focus on interpolation precision or Voxel DDA Raymarching with Adaptive Edge Smoothing focus on edge artifacts without the specific corner-maxing logic. A voxel raymarching technique that calculates smooth surface entry heights by averaging adjacent voxel volume/height values and interpolating based on the ray's entry position within the cube. It improves upon simple linear interpolation between two voxels by using neighbor-averaged face heights, though it initially ignores the center voxel's influence, leading to sharp edges. Midpoint UV Calculation computes the UV coordinates of the midpoint plane within a voxel traversal step to determine height and lighting variations for surface rendering. It sets apart from sibling methods by explicitly calculating a geometric midpoint between entry and exit UV states to drive height maps, whereas siblings like Corner-based Voxel Volume Calculation rely on corner interpolation and Voxel DDA Raymarching with Neighbor-Averaged Entry Interpolation focus on entry-point smoothing. Bresenham Voxel Traversal is a discrete voxel traversal algorithm that uses an integral error-accumulation method to step through voxels along the dominant axis of a ray. It serves as an alternative to floating-point DDA methods by relying on integer arithmetic for axis increments, which can offer performance benefits in specific hardware or software contexts. It differs from its parent DNstepmap by generating a full sequence of visited voxel coordinates rather than just the first hit, and from siblings like Voxel DDA Raymarching with Adaptive Edge Smoothing by using a strict integer-based decision logic rather than floating-point distance comparisons. Voxel Grid Ray Marching is an algorithm to traverse a 3D voxel grid along a ray, returning the IDs of all visited cells. It handles rays starting outside the grid by computing the entry point intersection with the bounding box. It builds on DNstepmap, which casts a ray into the voxel volume to find the first intersecting voxel, returning hit position, voxel data, and surface normal. Reads adjacent voxel volumes at ray entry and exit positions to adjust traversal behavior, preventing artifacts such as floating voxels, flat edges, and incorrect slope rendering. When exiting a voxel, it calculates the exit voxel's grid position by adding the current position, the step direction mask, and an offset derived from the mask. When entering a voxel, it calculates the entry voxel's grid position using the same mask-based offset logic, ensuring the offset is negative or adjusted for entry direction. It samples the volume value from the calculated adjacent voxel and uses it to modify the ray's exit behavior or skip logic. Pitfall: Reading adjacent voxels can impact performance, though the author notes it may not significantly affect frame rate on small maps. Checks the entry mask to determine which face (X, Y, or Z) the ray enters the voxel. If entering from the left/back, it sets the start UV to the back face and interpolates toward the center. If entering from the right/front, it sets the start UV to the front face and interpolates toward the right/center. Pitfall: Using integer division for UV coordinate calculations causes terrain vertices to fail to connect across voxel edges; all coordinate math must use floating-point types. An algorithm to compute the thickness of a ray traversal through an object by counting boundary voxels and accumulating thickness based on the angle of traversal. It uses parameters \theta (the angle between the view and the slice index increasing direction) and thickness (the thickness of each slice). The logic initializes ThickSum = 0, SurfaceCount = 0, and Inside = false, then iterates through slices: if a voxel is a boundary voxel, it toggles Inside and increments SurfaceCount; if Inside is true, it adds thickness/cos(\theta) to ThickSum. If SurfaceCount >= 2 and is even, it returns ThickSum as the thickness and marks the pixel as OK; otherwise, it marks the pixel as questionable. Time Complexity: O(k), where k is the number of voxels traversed along the ray. Each step involves constant-time comparisons and updates. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the voxel grid storage itself. Strengths: Deterministic traversal order; efficient handling of axis-aligned grids; robust handling of parallel rays (via infinity handling). Limitations: Does not handle non-axis-aligned voxel grids (e.g., rotated or skewed) without modification. Precision issues may arise with very large coordinates or very small voxel sizes due to floating-point accumulation in tMax. Requires careful handling of ray origins inside occupied voxels. When to use: Collision detection, occlusion culling, and surface picking in voxel-based worlds. When not to use: When smooth, continuous field evaluation is required without discrete stepping (use Voxel DDA Raymarching with Adaptive Edge Smoothing instead). The algorithm is based on the Amanatides & Woo method, originally published in 1986 for ray tracing through voxel grids. It is widely implemented in voxel engines for efficient raycasting. name: Voxel Raycast (Nonzero/Color Channel)
head: Hidden Surface Elimination via Ray Casting, Visible Surface Detection, zylann::voxel_raycast with Color Predicate
body: This method performs hidden surface elimination by casting a ray through a voxel volume to locate the first voxel where a specific data channel is non-zero (or a 1-voxel in a binary array). It differs from standard DDA traversal by optimizing for sparse or binary data: it processes voxels in groups of eight packed into a single byte, advancing the ray by whole bytes when the group is empty, thereby skipping large empty regions efficiently. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{O} and direction \mathbf{D} (normalized). Voxel grid data structure containing binary or channel-based voxel values. Channel index c to evaluate for non-zero presence. Maximum ray distance d{max}. Outputs: Hit position \mathbf{P}{hit}. Previous position \mathbf{P}{prev} (position before the hit). Distance along ray d{hit}. Surface normal \mathbf{N}. Data Structures: The voxel data is stored in a binary array where each byte holds eight voxels. A predicate structure RaycastPredicateColor holds a reference to the VoxelData and the target channel index c. Steps: 1. Initialize Raycast Predicate: Create a predicate object that encapsulates the voxel data and the channel index c. The predicate's evaluation function operator() takes a ray state (containing the current hit position) and returns true if the voxel value at that position for channel c is non-zero. 2. Execute Voxel Raycast: Call the core raycasting routine with the ray origin, direction, the predicate, maximum distance, and output variables for hit/previous positions and distances. 3. Byte-Level Traversal (Optimization): Inside the traversal, the algorithm examines the voxel array along the ray's path. For rays aligned with main axes (X, Y, or ±Z), it reads one byte at a time. If the byte value is zero, it advances to the next byte, effectively skipping eight voxels simultaneously. 4. Hit Detection: If the byte value is non-zero, the algorithm identifies that a surface voxel exists within that byte. 5. Voxel Extraction: The specific surface voxel is retrieved by applying a bitmask to the non-zero byte to isolate the exact voxel corresponding to the ray's current position. 6. Result Construction: Upon a successful hit, instantiate a VoxelRaycastResult object. Set the position to the hit location, the previous position to the location before the hit, the distance to the hit distance, and compute the normal as the normalized vector from the previous position to the hit position: \mathbf{N} = \frac{\mathbf{P}{hit} - \mathbf{P}{prev}}{\|\mathbf{P}{hit} - \mathbf{P}{prev}\|}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelraycastnonzerocolor(origin, direction, voxeldata, griddims, channelindex, maxdistance): """ Casts a ray to find the first voxel where the specified channel is non-zero. Optimized for byte-packed voxel data (8 voxels per byte) along main axes. """ # Determine traversal axis and stride based on dominant direction component if abs(direction[0]) > 0.5: axis, stride = 0, 1 elif abs(direction[1]) > 0.5: axis, stride = 1, griddims[0] // 8 else: axis, stride = 2, (griddims[0] griddims[1]) // 8 voxelsperbyte = 8 stepsize = maxdistance / (griddims[axis] // voxelsperbyte + 1) t = 0.0 prevpos = list(origin) byteidx = 0 while t <= maxdistance: # Read byte from the packed voxel array byteval = voxeldata[byteidx] if byteval != 0: # Find first set bit (or non-zero channel bit) within this byte for bit in range(8): if byteval & (1 << bit): hitpos = list(prevpos) hitpos[axis] += bit stepsize normal = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] normal[axis] = 1.0 if direction[axis] > 0 else -1.0 return { "position": hitpos, "previousposition": prevpos, "distancealongray": t + bit stepsize, "normal": normal } # Advance to next byte t += stepsize 8 prevpos = list(prevpos) byteidx += stride if byteidx >= len(voxeldata): break return None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Byte Alignment: The algorithm assumes the voxel array is stored such that each byte holds eight voxels, allowing 8 voxels to be examined simultaneously along main axes. If the data is not packed this way, the optimization fails or produces incorrect results. Bit Masking: The specific surface voxel must be correctly extracted from the byte using masking. Precision: Floating-point precision in ray position calculation may cause jitter or missed hits in sparse volumes if not handled with epsilon checks. Time Complexity: O(k) where k is the number of empty bytes traversed before a hit. In sparse volumes, this is significantly faster than per-voxel traversal. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, as it operates on the existing voxel data structure. Strengths: Extremely fast for binary or sparse data where large empty regions are common. Simple to implement if the data format is known. Limitations: Only works for finding the first non-zero voxel. Not suitable for volume rendering requiring integration through the entire ray. Requires specific data packing (8 voxels/byte). When to use: Hidden surface elimination, collision detection in binary voxel worlds, visible surface detection. When not to use: Volume rendering with transparency, continuous field evaluation, or when data is not packed in 8-voxel bytes. The concept of hidden surface elimination via ray casting in binary voxel models was introduced in "Hardware Support for the Display and Manipulation of Binary Voxel Models" (1988). The specific optimization of examining eight voxels per byte was described in that work. The modern implementation in zylann::voxelraycast is part of the Zylann Voxel plugin for Godot, integrating it with general-purpose voxel data structures.
