name: NanoVolumeHDDA
head: Span-merging hierarchical DDA, Zero-allocation callback-based HDDA
body: NanoVolumeHDDA is an iterator that traverses a NanoGrid along a ray to yield merged active spans (t0, t1) without heap allocations, using a callback interface. It merges adjacent active leaves and tiles to eliminate seam artifacts at 8-voxel tile edges. It builds on Hierarchical Digital Differential Analyzer (HDDA) by operating specifically on the NanoGrid structure and optimizing for zero-allocation iteration. Inputs: A NanoGrid (containing the sparse voxel data), a Ray (origin and direction). Outputs: TimeSpan structs representing merged active regions along the ray in front-to-back order, yielded via an iterator protocol that internally invokes a callback. Data Structures: TimeSpan: A struct with fields t0::Float64 and t1::Float64. HDDAState{T}: A mutable struct maintaining traversal state: roots::Vector{Tuple{Float64, Int}}: List of root hits, storing (tmin, offset). rootidx::Int: Current index in the roots list. i2ndda::Union{NodeDDA, Nothing}: The DDA state for the I2 (tile) level. i2off::Int: Offset in the buffer for the current I2 node. i2tentry::Float64: Entry time for the current I2 cell. i1ndda::Union{NodeDDA, Nothing}: The DDA state for the I1 (leaf) level. i1off::Int: Offset in the buffer for the current I1 node. i1tentry::Float64: Entry time for the current I1 cell. spant0::Float64: Start time of the current accumulated span; -1.0 indicates no open span. NodeDDA: A simple state struct for hierarchical DDA stepping, containing fields t, tmax, step, cidx, origin, size. Parameters: MAXROOTS: Maximum number of root nodes to process, set to 8. spant0: -1.0 indicates no open span. Algorithm Steps: 1. Collect Root Hits: Iterate i from 0 to rootcount - 1. Calculate entry pointer ep = rootpos + i entrysz. Load ischild from buffer at ep + 12. If ischild != 0x01, continue to next i. Load i2off from buffer at ep + 13. Load origin from buffer at i2off. Construct an AABB with origin as the center and size 4096.0 (extending to origin + (4096, 4096, 4096)). Intersect ray with this AABB. If the intersection is valid, let hit[1] be the entry time tmin. Store (tmin, i2off) in the roots list. Break if the number of roots exceeds MAXROOTS (8). 2. Sort Roots: Perform an insertion sort on the roots list based on the entry time tmin (first element of the tuple) to ensure front-to-back processing order. 3. Initialize State: If roots is empty, return nothing (no intersection). Initialize HDDAState with the sorted roots, rootidx = 0, i2ndda = nothing, i2off = 0, i2tentry = 0.0, i1ndda = nothing, i1off = 0, i1tentry = 0.0, and spant0 = -1.0. 4. Iterate (Callback Loop): The iteration proceeds by calling an internal advance function hddaadvance which manages two phases. Phase 1: I1 (Leaf) DDA Loop While s.i1ndda is not nothing and nodeddainside(s.i1ndda) is true: Get ndda = s.i1ndda and cidx = nodeddachildindex(ndda). Check haschild by testing if the child mask bit cidx is set at s.i1off + I1CMASKOFF in the buffer. Check hastile: If !haschild, check if the voxel mask bit cidx is set at s.i1off + I1VMASKOFF. If haschild or hastile is true AND s.spant0 < 0.0: Set s.spant0 = s.i1tentry. If !(haschild or hastile) is true AND s.spant0 >= 0.0: Call the callback f(s.spant0, s.i1tentry). Reset s.spant0 = -1.0. Update s.i1tentry = nodeddacelltime(ndda). Step ndda.state. Phase 2: I2 (Tile) DDA Loop After Phase 1 (or if Phase 1 was not entered), loop while s.i2ndda is not nothing and nodeddainside(s.i2ndda) is true: Get ndda = s.i2ndda and cidx = nodeddachildindex(ndda). Check haschild by testing if the child mask bit cidx is set at s.i2off + I2CMASKOFF in the buffer. If haschild is true: Calculate tidx using bufcountonbefore to determine the child index count. Load i1off for the child node. Construct an I1 AABB with size 128.0 centered at the child's origin. Intersect ray with this I1 AABB. If it hits: Initialize s.i1ndda with nodeddainit(ray, tmin, i1origin, Int32(16), Int32(8)). Set s.i1tentry = tmin. Set s.i1off = i1off. continue to the I2 loop (which will re-enter Phase 1 in the next advance call). If I1 AABB misses: If s.spant0 >= 0.0, call f(s.spant0, s.i2tentry) and reset s.spant0 = -1.0. If haschild is false: Check hastile by testing if the voxel mask bit cidx is set at s.i2off + I2VMASKOFF. If hastile is true AND s.spant0 < 0.0: Set s.spant0 = s.i2tentry. If !hastile is true AND s.spant0 >= 0.0: Call f(s.spant0, s.i2tentry) and reset s.spant0 = -1.0. Update s.i2tentry = nodeddacelltime(ndda). Step ndda.state. Finalization: After the I2 loop exhausts, if s.spant0 >= 0.0, call f(s.spant0, s.i2tentry) and reset s.spant0 = -1.0. Return the next span or nothing if traversal is complete. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nanovolumehddaiterate(grid, ray, callback): """ Iterates over a NanoGrid along a ray, yielding merged active spans via callback. """ buf = grid.buffer rootcount = grid.rootcount rootpos = grid.rootbufferptr entrysz = 16 # Based on offsets ep+12, ep+13 roots = [] for i in range(rootcount): ep = rootpos + i entrysz ischild = buf[ep + 12] if ischild != 0x01: continue i2off = int.frombytes(buf[ep+13:ep+17], 'little') origin = readvec3(buf, i2off) aabbmin = origin - vec3(2048.0) aabbmax = origin + vec3(2048.0) hit = intersectbbox(ray, aabbmin, aabbmax) if hit is not None: roots.append((hit.entrytime, i2off)) if len(roots) >= 8: break # Insertion sort for i in range(1, len(roots)): j = i while j > 0 and roots[j][0] < roots[j-1][0]: roots[j], roots[j-1] = roots[j-1], roots[j] j -= 1 if not roots: return state = { 'roots': roots, 'rootidx': 0, 'i2ndda': None, 'i2off': 0, 'i2tentry': 0.0, 'i1ndda': None, 'i1off': 0, 'i1tentry': 0.0, 'spant0': -1.0 } while True: span, state = hddaadvance(buf, ray, state) if span is None: break callback(span[0], span[1]) def hddaadvance(buf, ray, s): # Phase 1: I1 DDA while s['i1ndda'] is not None and nodeddainside(s['i1ndda']): ndda = s['i1ndda'] cidx = ndda['cidx'] haschild = (buf[s['i1off'] + I1CMASKOFF] >> cidx) & 1 hastile = (not haschild) and (buf[s['i1off'] + I1VMASKOFF] >> cidx) & 1 if (haschild or hastile) and s['spant0'] < 0.0: s['spant0'] = s['i1tentry'] if not (haschild or hastile) and s['spant0'] >= 0.0: span = (s['spant0'], s['i1tentry']) s['spant0'] = -1.0 s['i1tentry'] = ndda['t'] stepndda(ndda) return span, s s['i1tentry'] = ndda['t'] stepndda(ndda) s['i1ndda'] = None # Phase 2: I2 DDA while s['i2ndda'] is not None and nodeddainside(s['i2ndda']): ndda = s['i2ndda'] cidx = ndda['cidx'] haschild = (buf[s['i2off'] + I2CMASKOFF] >> cidx) & 1 if haschild: tidx = sum(1 for k in range(cidx) if (buf[s['i2off'] + I2CMASKOFF] >> k) & 1) i1off = s['i2off'] + tidx 4 # childstride assumed 4 bytes per child offset i1origin = readvec3(buf, i1off) aabbmin = i1origin - vec3(64.0) aabbmax = i1origin + vec3(64.0) hit = intersectbbox(ray, aabbmin, aabbmax) if hit is not None: tmin = hit.entrytime s['i1ndda'] = nodeddainit(ray, tmin, i1origin, 16, 8) s['i1tentry'] = tmin s['i1off'] = i1off return None, s # Continue to I2 loop, re-enters Phase 1 next advance else: if s['spant0'] >= 0.0: span = (s['spant0'], s['i2tentry']) s['spant0'] = -1.0 return span, s else: hastile = (buf[s['i2off'] + I2VMASKOFF] >> cidx) & 1 if hastile and s['spant0'] < 0.0: s['spant0'] = s['i2tentry'] elif not hastile and s['spant0'] >= 0.0: span = (s['spant0'], s['i2tentry']) s['spant0'] = -1.0 return span, s s['i2tentry'] = ndda['t'] stepndda(ndda) if s['spant0'] >= 0.0: span = (s['spant0'], s['i2tentry']) s['spant0'] = -1.0 return span, s return None, s I1CMASKOFF = 0 I1VMASKOFF = 4 I2CMASKOFF = 0 I2VMASKOFF = 4 def readvec3(buf, addr): return vec3(int.frombytes(buf[addr:addr+4], 'little'), int.frombytes(buf[addr+4:addr+8], 'little'), int.frombytes(buf[addr+8:addr+12], 'little')) def intersectbbox(ray, min, max): # Standard slab intersection tmin = (min.x - ray.origin.x) / ray.direction.x tmax = (max.x - ray.origin.x) / ray.direction.x if tmin > tmax: tmin, tmax = tmax, tmin tymin = (min.y - ray.origin.y) / ray.direction.y tymax = (max.y - ray.origin.y) / ray.direction.y if tymin > tymax: tymin, tymax = tymax, tymin if tmin > tymax or tymin > tmax: return None if tymin > tmin: tmin = tymin if tymax < tmax: tmax = tymax tzmin = (min.z - ray.origin.z) / ray.direction.z tzmax = (max.z - ray.origin.z) / ray.direction.z if tzmin > tzmax: tzmin, tzmax = tzmax, tzmin if tmin > tzmax or tzmin > tmax: return None if tzmin > tmin: tmin = tzmin return type('Hit', (), {'entrytime': tmin})() def nodeddainit(ray, tentry, origin, cellsize, tilesize): # Simplified DDA state initialization step = vec3(cellsize / abs(ray.direction.x), cellsize / abs(ray.direction.y), cellsize / abs(ray.direction.z)) tstep = vec3(step.x if ray.direction.x > 0 else -step.x, step.y if ray.direction.y > 0 else -step.y, step.z if ray.direction.z > 0 else -step.z) return {'t': tentry, 'tmax': tentry + tilesize, 'step': tstep, 'cidx': 0, 'origin': origin, 'size': cellsize} def nodeddainside(ndda): return ndda['t'] < ndda['tmax'] def nodeddachildindex(ndda): return ndda['cidx'] def nodeddacelltime(ndda): return ndda['t'] def stepndda(ndda): ndda['t'] += ndda['step'].x if ndda['cidx'] == 0 else (ndda['step'].y if ndda['cidx'] == 1 else ndda['step'].z) ndda['cidx'] = (ndda['cidx'] + 1) % 3 Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray traversal instance, as it avoids heap allocations for span lists. Strengths: Zero-allocation iteration makes it suitable for GPU kernels or high-performance CPU loops where memory fragmentation or GC pressure is a concern. Merging spans reduces the number of shader invocations. Limitations: Bounded root count (8) may miss intersections in highly fragmented scenes if not handled by the caller. Specific to NanoGrid structure. When to use: When rendering sparse voxel grids (VDB) with NanoGrid and performance/zero-allocation is critical. NanoVolumeHDDA is part of the Lyr.jl rendering library, developed by Tobias Osborne. It is designed to efficiently traverse sparse voxel data structures (specifically NanoGrid) for volume rendering, leveraging the hierarchical nature of the data to skip empty space and merge active regions. tobiasosborne/Lyr.jl, https://github.com/tobiasosborne/Lyr.jl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: RayMajorantIterator
head: HDDA-based ray traversal for volume majorant
body: The RayMajorantIterator is an iterator that traverses a sparse volume grid using a Hybrid Digital Differential Analyzer (HDDA) to step through voxels or leaves, computing the maximum density (majorant) for each segment where the majorant remains constant. It solves the problem of efficiently determining integration segments for volume path tracing by avoiding per-voxel sampling in empty or uniform regions. It builds on Hierarchical Digital Differential Analyzer (HDDA) by bundling consecutive steps with identical majorants into single segments, reducing overhead compared to standard voxel DDA which cannot skip inactive nodes or handle variable leaf sizes efficiently. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray (RayT), a grid accessor (const GridT::AccessorType&), and an optional debug buffer (std::vector<DDAStep>). Output: A sequence of Segment structs, each containing start time t0, end time t1, and the constant majorant density dmaj for that segment. Data Structures: The iterator maintains the following state fields: float mscale: Inverse of the ray direction length in index space, calculated as 1 / density.worldToIndexDirF(ray.dir()).length(). RayT mray: The ray object (typically nanovdb::math::Ray<float>). float mmajorant: The current segment's majorant density, initialized to std::numericlimits<float>::signalingNaN(). const GridT::AccessorType& macc: Reference to the grid accessor for probing values. nanovdb::math::HDDA<RayT> mdda: The HDDA instance managing the traversal step. std::vector<DDAStep> msteprecorddst: Pointer to a debug buffer for recording step details. The Segment struct returned by the iterator contains: float t0: Start time in voxel units. float t1: End time in voxel units. float dmaj: Majorant density value for the segment. The DDAStep struct (used for debugging) contains: int dim: HDDA dimension stepped. float majorant: Current majorant. float t: Current time. Eigen::Vector3i voxel: Current voxel coordinates. Eigen::Vector3f hit: World position. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Calculate mscale = 1.0f / density.worldToIndexDirF(mray.dir()).length(). Initialize mmajorant to std::numericlimits<float>::signalingNaN(). Initialize mdda with the ray and an initial dimension. The initial dimension is determined by gethddadim, which returns std::max<uint32t>(8, acc.getDim(ijk, ray)). This ensures a minimum step dimension of 8 to avoid skipping active leaves. 2. Iteration (next() method): Termination Check: If mdda.time() >= mdda.maxTime(), the ray has left the bounding box. Return std::nullopt. Start Time: Set ans.t0 = mdda.time(). Majorant Update: If mmajorant is NaN, call updatecurrentmajorant() and recordstep(). Dimension Update: Calculate the new HDDA dimension for the next step using the coordinate mray(mdda.time() + 1.0001f).floor(). The offset 1.0001f ensures the coordinate is slightly ahead of the current step to get the correct dimension for the next step, preventing issues with pessimistic HDDA stepping in empty space. Update mdda with mdda.update(mray, newdim). Loop for Constant Majorant: Call updatecurrentmajorant() and recordstep(). If the new mmajorant equals ans.dmaj (the majorant of the current segment), continue the loop to bundle this step into the current segment. If mmajorant differs, exit the loop. End Time: Set ans.t1 = mdda.time(). Return: Return the Segment struct with t0, t1, and dmaj. 3. Majorant Calculation (updatecurrentmajorant()): Determine the current voxel index ijk from the HDDA state. If the current node is not a leaf, attempt to probe the value using macc.probeValue(ijk, value). If probeValue returns true, set mmajorant = value and return. Otherwise, set mmajorant = 0.0f (empty space). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import Optional, Tuple, List class RayMajorantIterator: def init(self, ray, accessor, debugbuffer: Optional[List] = None): self.mray = ray self.macc = accessor self.msteprecorddst = debugbuffer # mscale = 1 / density.worldToIndexDirF(ray.dir()).length() self.mscale = 1.0 / ray.dir().length() self.mmajorant = float('nan') # Initial dimension calculation ensures minimum step of 8 ijkinitial = ray.time(0).floor().astype(int) initdim = max(8, accessor.getDim(ijkinitial, ray)) # HDDA state management and stepping logic are handled by the parent nanovdb::math::HDDA library. self.mdda = HDDA(ray, initdim) def gethddadim(self, ijk, ray, accessor): return max(8, accessor.getDim(ijk, ray)) def updatecurrentmajorant(self): ijk = self.mdda.getvoxelindex() # probeValue returns (success, value) success, value = self.macc.probeValue(ijk) if success: self.mmajorant = value else: self.mmajorant = 0.0 def recordstep(self): if self.msteprecorddst is not None: step = DDAStep( dim=self.mdda.getdim(), majorant=self.mmajorant, t=self.mdda.time(), voxel=self.mdda.getvoxelindex(), hit=self.mray.time(self.mdda.time())) self.msteprecorddst.append(step) def next(self) -> Optional[Tuple[float, float, float]]: if self.mdda.time() >= self.mdda.maxtime(): return None anst0 = self.mdda.time() if math.isnan(self.mmajorant): self.updatecurrentmajorant() self.recordstep() ansdmaj = self.mmajorant while True: nexttimeapprox = self.mdda.time() + 1.0001 ijknext = self.mray.time(nexttimeapprox).floor().astype(int) newdim = self.gethddadim(ijknext, self.mray, self.macc) self.mdda.update(self.mray, newdim) self.updatecurrentmajorant() self.recordstep() if self.mmajorant != ansdmaj: break if self.mdda.time() >= self.mdda.maxtime(): break anst1 = self.mdda.time() return (anst0, anst1, ansdmaj) class HDDA: def init(self, ray, dim): self.ray = ray self.dim = dim self.currenttime = 0.0 self.maxtime = 1000.0 # Bounding box max time not given in sources def time(self): return self.currenttime def maxtime(self): return self.maxtime def update(self, ray, dim): self.currenttime += 1.0 / ray.dir().length() self.dim = dim def getvoxelindex(self): pos = self.ray.time(self.currenttime) return pos.floor().astype(int) def getdim(self): return self.dim class DDAStep: def init(self, dim, majorant, t, voxel, hit): self.dim = dim self.majorant = majorant self.t = t self.voxel = voxel self.hit = hit Parameters and Typical Values: Minimum HDDA Dimension: 8. This is hardcoded to avoid skipping active leaves in sparse grids. Time Offset for Dimension Update: 1.0001f. This small epsilon ensures the coordinate used for dimension lookup is slightly ahead of the current step, handling pessimistic HDDA stepping in empty space. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pessimistic HDDA Stepping: HDDA stepping can be pessimistic in empty space, potentially stepping more frequently than necessary. The iterator mitigates this by bundling consecutive segments with the same majorant into one, reducing overhead. Boundary Conditions: The termination check mdda.time() >= mdda.maxTime() handles the case where the ray leaves the bounding box. Precision: The use of 1.0001f offset is critical for correct dimension updates. Using 1.0f might result in the same voxel being queried, leading to incorrect dimension updates or infinite loops in degenerate cases. Time Complexity: The iterator steps through the grid using HDDA, which allows skipping inactive nodes. The complexity is proportional to the number of distinct majorant segments along the ray, which is typically much less than the number of voxels intersected, especially in sparse or uniform regions. Memory Complexity: The iterator maintains a small constant amount of state per ray (HDDA state, current majorant, etc.). The debug buffer, if used, scales with the number of steps. Strengths: Efficiently handles sparse voxel grids by skipping empty space and variable leaf sizes. Bundling segments with the same majorant reduces the number of integration steps required for volume path tracing. Limitations: HDDA stepping can be pessimistic in empty space, although this is mitigated by segment bundling. The method relies on the underlying HDDA implementation's correctness and efficiency. When to Use: Ideal for volume path tracing in sparse voxel grids where empty space is common and majorant values are constant over large segments. When Not to Use: If the volume is dense and majorant values change frequently per voxel, the overhead of HDDA and segment bundling might not provide significant benefits over standard voxel DDA. The RayMajorantIterator is part of the volume path tracer developed by Shibodd. It leverages the NanoVDB library's HDDA implementation for efficient hierarchical traversal. The method was designed to optimize volume rendering by reducing the number of samples required for accurate integration, particularly in large, sparse scenes. Shibodd/volumepathtracer, https://github.com/Shibodd/volumepathtracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: HDDA Hybrid
body: HDDA Hybrid is a ray traversal algorithm for sparse voxel grids that combines hierarchical skipping with fine-grained traversal. It uses Hierarchical Digital Differential Analyzer (HDDA) to skip empty tiles at resolutions coarser than the leaf level, and switches to standard Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) to traverse occupied tiles voxel-by-voxel. This approach avoids per-voxel checks in empty space while maintaining sampling accuracy in dense regions. It builds on Hierarchical Digital Differential Analyzer (HDDA). Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, ray bounds t{min}, t{max}, VDB grid accessor acc providing isActive(ijk), getDim(ijk, ray), and root bounding box, leafdim (typically 8), coneangle (default 0.0), stepsize (default 10^{-3}), and firstpass flag. Outputs: A sequence of sample points (t, \mathbf{x}) along the ray within occupied regions. Data Structures: hdda (tile traversal state), dda (voxel traversal state), tlast (last processed time), ntrav (voxel counter). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversehddahybrid(ray, acc, leafdim, coneangle, stepsize, firstpass): t0 = ray.t0() + 1e-6 t1 = ray.t1() - 1e-6 if not ray.clip(acc.root().bbox()) or t0 >= t1: return [] ijk = rounddown(ray(t0)) dim = acc.getdim(ijk, ray) tilemode = dim >= leafdim hdda.init(ray, t0, t1, max(leafdim, dim)) ddaIsValid = True tlast = t0 ntrav = 0 samples = [] while ddaIsValid and hdda.time() <= hdda.next(): if not ddaIsValid: dda.init(ray, hdda.time(), hdda.next()) tlast = advancetime(tlast, coneangle, stepsize, hdda.time()) ddaIsValid = True while ddaIsValid: dt = calcdt(tlast, coneangle, stepsize, 1e10) active = acc.isActive(dda.voxel()) while tlast + dt / 2 < dda.next(): if active: if not firstpass: samples.append((tlast + dt / 2, ray(tlast + dt / 2))) ntrav += 1 tlast += dt dt = calcdt(tlast, coneangle, stepsize, 1e10) else: tlast += dt ddaIsValid = dda.step() ddaIsValid = hdda.step() ijk = hdda.voxel() dim = acc.getdim(ijk, ray) tilemode = dim >= leafdim hdda.update(ray, max(leafdim, dim)) return samples def calcdt(tlast, coneangle, stepsize, maxdt): return min(stepsize (1 + coneangle tlast), maxdt) def advancetime(tlast, coneangle, stepsize, nextt): return max(tlast, nextt) # Parameters: leafdim = 8, coneangle = 0.0, stepsize = 10^{-3}. Edge Cases: Epsilon offset (10^{-6}) in t0, t1 prevents boundary precision errors. Degenerate rays (t0 \ge t1) are skipped immediately. HDDA Skip is a ray traversal algorithm for sparse voxel grids (such as VDB) that uses Hierarchical DDA to skip empty regions in bulk steps, advancing ray time t rather than sampling every voxel. It builds on HDDA Hybrid, which combines HDDA for empty tiles and DDA for occupied tiles; HDDA Skip extends this by allowing density-based skipping of invisible space within occupied regions using optional \sigma or \alpha functions. Optimized for very small volumes or specific hardware constraints. Choose when memory footprint is critical. Uses a majorant function to skip empty space. Choose when a tight majorant is available and HDDA overhead is too high. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Faster than pure DDA in sparse scenes due to skipping empty tiles, but slower than HDDA Skip when sampling is required due to DDA switching overhead. Strengths: Efficient for sparse voxel grids with mixed density. Limitations: Overhead of managing two traversal states. When to use: Sparse voxel NeRF rendering, VDB-based volume visualization. When not to use: Fully dense volumes, or when only occupancy queries are needed (use HDDA Skip). HDDA Hybrid was introduced in the context of accelerating occupancy grid-based NeRF rendering using VDB grids. It was presented by Yoshihiro Kato et al. in "Plug-and-Play Acceleration of Occupancy Grid-based NeRF Rendering using VDB Grid and Hierarchical Ray Traversal" (2024). The method leverages the B+tree structure of VDB to perform multi-resolution leapfrogging, combining the coarse skipping of HDDA with the precision of DDA. name: HDDA Skip
head: Hierarchical DDA (HDDA) Skip
body: HDDA Skip is a ray traversal algorithm for sparse voxel grids (such as VDB) that uses Hierarchical DDA to skip empty regions in bulk steps, advancing ray time t rather than sampling every voxel. It builds on HDDA Hybrid, which combines HDDA for empty tiles and DDA for occupied tiles; HDDA Skip extends this by allowing density-based skipping of invisible space within occupied regions using optional \sigma or \alpha functions. Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o}, normalized directions \mathbf{d}, grid bounds [t0, t1], optional density/opacity functions \sigma(\cdot) or \alpha(\cdot), step size s, cone angle \theta, and grid accessors for voxel activity and dimension. Outputs: Sampled points (t{left}, t{right}), ray indices, and traversal counts. Data Structures: HDDAState: Stores current voxel index \mathbf{ijk}, dimension dim, current time t, and validity flag. Ray: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, bounds t{min}, t{max}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hddaskiptraverse(ray, acc, firstpass=True): # 1. Initialize bounds t0 = ray.t0() + 1e-6 t1 = ray.t1() - 1e-6 if not ray.clip(acc.root().bbox()) or t0 > t1: return # Skip to next grid # 2. Initialize HDDA state ijk = floor(ray(t0)) # nanovdb::RoundDown dim = acc.getDim(ijk, ray) hdda.init(ray, t0, t1, dim) ddaIsValid = True tlast = t0 # tlast initialized to t0 # 3. Outer loop while ddaIsValid: # Inner skip loop while ddaIsValid and not acc.isActive(ijk): ddaIsValid = hdda.step() if not ddaIsValid: break ijk = hdda.voxel() dim = acc.getDim(ijk, ray) hdda.update(ray, dim) # 4. Advance to occupied region if not ddaIsValid: break tlast = advancetime(tlast, ray.coneangle, ray.stepsize, hdda.time()) # 5. Traverse occupied region dt = calcdt(tlast, ray.coneangle, ray.stepsize, 1e10) while tlast + dt / 2 < hdda.next(): if not firstpass: recordsample(rayindices, tlast, tlast + dt) ntrav += 1 tlast += dt dt = calcdt(tlast, ray.coneangle, ray.stepsize, 1e10) # 6. Step HDDA for next iteration ddaIsValid = hdda.step() ijk = hdda.voxel() dim = acc.getDim(ijk, ray) hdda.update(ray, dim) Note: advancetime and calcdt are internal helper functions; their exact implementations are not provided in the sources. Formulas: t0 = \text{ray.t0()} + 10^{-6} t1 = \text{ray.t1()} - 10^{-6} \mathbf{ijk} = \lfloor \mathbf{o} + t0 \mathbf{d} \rfloor dt = \text{calc\dt}(t{last}, \theta, s, 10^{10}) Parameters: renderstepsize: Default 10^{-3}. coneangle: Default 0.0. earlystopeps: Default 10^{-4}. alphathre: Default 0.0. Edge Cases: Ray bounds invalid (t0 > t1): Skip grid. Empty grid: HDDA becomes invalid immediately. Precision: Use \epsilon = 10^{-6} to avoid boundary issues. Time Complexity: Proportional to number of occupied voxels traversed, plus overhead of HDDA steps for empty regions. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray for traversal state. Strengths: Efficiently skips large empty regions; supports density-based early termination. Limitations: Requires active voxel check; density evaluation adds overhead if used. When to Use: Sparse grids with large empty regions; when density-based skipping is beneficial. When Not to Use: Dense grids where overhead of HDDA outweighs benefits; when no density function is available and simple DDA is sufficient. Originated in the faster-occgrid project by Yosshi999, HDDA Skip is an unofficial implementation leveraging Hierarchical DDA for efficient traversal of sparse voxel grids. It extends the HDDA Hybrid approach by integrating density-based skipping capabilities. Yosshi999/faster-occgrid, https://github.com/Yosshi999/faster-occgrid, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: VolumeHDDA
head: Hierarchical DDA for Generic Volumes, Hierarchical Digital Differential Analyzer for Volume, Volume Hierarchical DDA (VolumeHDDA), VolumeHDDA (Hierarchical DDA for Volumes), VolumeHDDA< TreeT, RayT, 0 >, ChildLevel>, ChildNodeLevel>
body: VolumeHDDA is a specialized Hierarchical Digital Differential Analyzer (HDDA) designed for ray intersections against generic volume trees. It traverses from a specified ChildNodeLevel down to the leaf level (specialized at 0), performing hierarchical ray-marching by entering child nodes when present and processing active/inactive tiles at leaf levels. It sets itself apart from its sibling Hierarchical Digital Differential Analyzer (HDDA) by being explicitly templated for volume tree structures (handling TreeT, RayT, and ChildNodeLevel) and managing time spans for active/inactive tile sequences, whereas the generic HDDA focuses on geometric intersection tests. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A RayT object representing the ray with methods valid(), setTimes(t0, t1), invDir(), and operator()(time). An AccessorT object providing probeConstNode<NodeT>(coord) and isValueOn(coord). A TimeSpanT object t tracking the current active segment, initialized to (-1, -1). Outputs: For march, a TimeSpanT representing the first continuous active segment or (-1, -1) if none. For hits, a list of TimeSpanT intervals collected into ListT. Data Structures: The class VolumeHDDA<TreeT, RayT, int ChildNodeLevel> contains private members math::DDA<RayT, NodeT::TOTAL> mDDA and VolumeHDDA<TreeT, RayT, ChildNodeLevel-1> mHDDA. NodeT is defined as typename ChainT::template Get<ChildNodeLevel>, where ChainT is typename TreeT::RootNodeType::NodeChainType. Parameters: TreeT: The tree type being traversed. RayT: The ray type used for traversal. ChildNodeLevel: Template argument specifying the entry upper node level for hierarchical ray-marching; the final lowest level is always the leaf node level (specialized at 0), not the voxel level. LeafT: Defined as typename TreeT::LeafNodeType. TimeSpanT: Defined as typename RayT::TimeSpan. Algorithm Steps: The traversal uses a recursive descent where the general case (ChildNodeLevel > 0) and the base case (ChildNodeLevel == 0) share similar logic but differ in node probing. 1. Initialization: Initialize mDDA with the ray. In the base case specialization, mDDA is initialized with LeafT::TOTAL. 2. Loop: Iterate using mDDA.step(). Child Node Check: General case checks acc.probeConstNode<NodeT>(mDDA.voxel()) for non-null. Base case checks acc.probeConstNode<LeafT>(mDDA.voxel()) or acc.isValueOn(mDDA.voxel()). Action: Set ray times to (mDDA.time(), mDDA.next()) and recursively call mHDDA.march (or hits). If the recursive call returns true (for march) or collects data (for hits), handle termination/collection and continue or return. Active Tile Check: If acc.isValueOn(mDDA.voxel()) is true, set t.t0 = mDDA.time() if t.t0 < 0. Inactive Tile / Segment Closure: If t.t0 >= 0 (an active segment is open) and the current tile is inactive, set t.t1 = mDDA.time(). If t.valid() (both t0 and t1 are set), return true (for march) or push t to times (for hits). Reset t.set(-1, -1). 3. Termination: After the loop, if t.t0 >= 0 (the ray ended while in an active segment), set t.t1 = mDDA.maxTime(). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class TimeSpan: def init(self, t0, t1): self.t0 = t0 self.t1 = t1 def valid(self): return self.t0 >= 0 and self.t1 >= 0 def set(self, t0, t1): self.t0 = t0 self.t1 = t1 class DDA: def init(self, ray, log2dim): self.ray = ray self.log2dim = log2dim self.voxelcoord = None self.currenttime = 0.0 self.nexttime = 0.0 self.maxtime = ray.maxTime() self.initddastate() # Standard DDA initialization for ray and node size 2^log2dim def init(self, ray): self.ray = ray self.initddastate() def voxel(self): return self.voxelcoord def time(self): return self.currenttime def next(self): return self.nexttime def maxTime(self): return self.maxtime def step(self): # Advance DDA state to next voxel along ray; returns False when ray exits bounds pass class VolumeHDDA: def init(self, tree, raytype, childnodelevel): self.childnodelevel = childnodelevel self.mDDA = DDA(raytype, tree.nodesizelog2(childnodelevel)) self.mHDDA = VolumeHDDA(tree, raytype, childnodelevel - 1) if childnodelevel > 0 else None self.NodeT = tree.getnodetype(childnodelevel) def march(self, ray, acc): t = TimeSpan(-1, -1) if ray.valid(): self.marchrecursive(ray, acc, t) return t def marchrecursive(self, ray, acc, t): self.mDDA.init(ray) while True: voxel = self.mDDA.voxel() if acc.probeConstNode(self.NodeT, voxel) is not None: ray.setTimes(self.mDDA.time(), self.mDDA.next()) if self.mHDDA.marchrecursive(ray, acc, t): return True elif acc.isValueOn(voxel): if t.t0 < 0: t.t0 = self.mDDA.time() elif t.t0 >= 0: t.t1 = self.mDDA.time() if t.valid(): return True t.set(-1, -1) if not self.mDDA.step(): break if t.t0 >= 0: t.t1 = self.mDDA.maxTime() return False def hits(self, ray, acc, times, t): self.mDDA.init(ray) while True: voxel = self.mDDA.voxel() if acc.probeConstNode(self.NodeT, voxel) is not None: ray.setTimes(self.mDDA.time(), self.mDDA.next()) self.mHDDA.hits(ray, acc, times, t) elif acc.isValueOn(voxel): if t.t0 < 0: t.t0 = self.mDDA.time() elif t.t0 >= 0: t.t1 = self.mDDA.time() if t.valid(): times.append(t) t.set(-1, -1) if not self.mDDA.step(): break if t.t0 >= 0: t.t1 = self.mDDA.maxTime() class VolumeHDDALeaf: def init(self, tree, raytype): self.mDDA = DDA(raytype, tree.leafsizelog2) self.LeafT = tree.leafnodetype def march(self, ray, acc): t = TimeSpan(-1, -1) if ray.valid(): self.marchrecursive(ray, acc, t) return t def marchrecursive(self, ray, acc, t): self.mDDA.init(ray) while True: voxel = self.mDDA.voxel() if acc.probeConstNode(self.LeafT, voxel) is not None or acc.isValueOn(voxel): if t.t0 < 0: t.t0 = self.mDDA.time() elif t.t0 >= 0: t.t1 = self.mDDA.time() if t.valid(): return True t.set(-1, -1) if not self.mDDA.step(): break if t.t0 >= 0: t.t1 = self.mDDA.maxTime() return False def hits(self, ray, acc, times, t): self.mDDA.init(ray) while True: voxel = self.mDDA.voxel() if acc.probeConstNode(self.LeafT, voxel) is not None or acc.isValueOn(voxel): if t.t0 < 0: t.t0 = self.mDDA.time() elif t.t0 >= 0: t.t1 = self.mDDA.time() if t.valid(): times.append(t) t.set(-1, -1) if not self.mDDA.step(): break if t.t0 >= 0: t.t1 = self.mDDA.maxTime() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Time Span Management: The TimeSpanT t is initialized to (-1, -1). t.t0 marks the start of an active segment, t.t1 marks the end. If an inactive tile is hit after an active segment, the segment is closed. If the ray ends while still in an active segment (t.t0 >= 0 after loop), t.t1 is set to maxTime. Precision: The DDA relies on floating-point arithmetic for ray parameterization. Precision issues may arise with very long rays or small nodes, though the DDA implementation typically handles this via clamping. Boundaries: The ray must be valid (ray.valid()) before traversal. If the ray does not intersect the volume bounds, the loop may not execute or return immediately. A reorganization of Hierarchical Data-Driven Approach (HDDA) iterators that separates the traversal of all active values from the traversal of only leaf voxels, enabling tile-skipping for leaf-specific operations. It sets itself apart from its parent VolumeHDDA by providing a specialized leaf-only traversal path that avoids processing active coarse tiles, addressing the latent mis-indexing bugs that occurred when callers assumed the previous single iterator yielded only leaf voxels. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of nodes visited along the ray path, skipping inactive subtrees. Exact asymptotic bounds are Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Low, as it uses recursion and does not store the entire traversal path. The stack depth is proportional to the tree depth. Exact memory limits are Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient for sparse volumes due to hierarchical skipping. Handles active/inactive tile sequences correctly. Limitations: Overhead of recursive calls and template instantiation. Performance depends on the tree structure and ray direction. When to use: When traversing volume trees for ray-marching or intersection tests, especially when dealing with sparse data or needing to skip inactive regions. When not to use: For dense volumes where linear traversal might be simpler or for non-tree-based volume representations. The class is defined in openvdb/math/DDA.h. name: HDDA Iterator Reorganization
head: HDDAActiveValueIterator, HDDAIterators, HDDALeafVoxelIterator
body: A reorganization of Hierarchical Data-Driven Approach (HDDA) iterators that separates the traversal of all active values from the traversal of only leaf voxels, enabling tile-skipping for leaf-specific operations. It sets itself apart from its parent VolumeHDDA by providing a specialized leaf-only traversal path that avoids processing active coarse tiles, addressing the latent mis-indexing bugs that occurred when callers assumed the previous single iterator yielded only leaf voxels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hierarchical grid structure containing active values at various node levels (coarse tiles and leaf voxels). Output: A sequence of coordinates and values. HDDAActiveValueIterator yields all active values (tiles and leaves); HDDALeafVoxelIterator yields only active leaf voxels. Data Structures: Both iterators are aliases over a single implementation class: HDDAValueIteratorImpl<AccT, ScalarT, bool LeafOnly>. AccT: Accessor type. ScalarT: Scalar value type. LeafOnly: A compile-time boolean gate. When LeafOnly is false, the iterator yields all active values (including coarse tiles). When LeafOnly is true, the iterator skips active tiles. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create an instance of HDDAValueIteratorImpl with LeafOnly set to false for HDDAActiveValueIterator or true for HDDALeafVoxelIterator. 2. Traversal Loop: Iterate using the ++ operator. 3. Level Re-alignment (nextVoxel): Use a bounded for (pass < 3) level-realign loop instead of three unrolled getDim/level-update passes. This collapses to a single descent in the common level-aligned case. 4. Segment Advancement (nextSegment): Use predicated TimeSpan setters instead of an if/else ladder. Only the "active region ended" condition remains a real branch, reducing warp divergence. 5. Yielding: If LeafOnly is true, check if the current node is a leaf (getDim == 1). If it is a coarse tile (getDim > 1), skip it in a single coarse HDDA step. If LeafOnly is false, yield the current active value regardless of node level. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class HDDAValueIteratorImpl: def init(self, grid, leafonly: bool): self.grid = grid self.leafonly = leafonly self.currentnode = grid.beginactivevalue() # Standard iterator initialization self.passcount = 0 def iter(self): return self def next(self): while self.currentnode is not None: # nextVoxel optimization: bounded level-realign loop self.passcount = 0 while self.passcount < 3: if self.currentnode.levelisaligned(): # Checks if current node level matches expected traversal level break self.currentnode.realignlevel() # Moves up or down the tree to align levels self.passcount += 1 currentdim = self.currentnode.getDim() # LeafOnly gate: skips active coarse tiles in a single coarse HDDA step if self.leafonly and currentdim > 1: self.currentnode = self.currentnode.next() # Advances to next active value continue # Yield active value (tile or leaf) yield self.currentnode.getCoord(), self.currentnode.getValue() # nextSegment optimization: predicated TimeSpan setters # Only "active region ended" remains a real branch self.currentnode = self.currentnode.next() # Advances to next segment/voxel Parameters: LeafOnly: Compile-time boolean. true for leaf-only traversal, false for all active values. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mis-indexing on tile-bearing grids: Previously, callers indexing per-leaf-voxel buffers (like gridScalars) walked tiles they never needed, causing latent mis-indexing. The leaf iterator fixes this by skipping tiles entirely. Warp Divergence: The nextSegment optimization reduces divergence by using predicated setters, but the "active region ended" break remains a branch. OpenVDB provides two distinct iterators: one for traversing tree topology nodes (internal and leaf nodes) and one for traversing all value-carrying elements (active/inactive voxels and tiles). The node iterator (cbeginNode) traverses the tree structure, while the value iterator (cbeginValueAll) traverses all values, including implicitly allocated tile nodes. Using cbeginValueAll for visualization can lead to dense point clouds that misrepresent the actual sparse data density because it includes inactive values and tiles. The HDDAActiveValueIterator and HDDALeafVoxelIterator are specialized for active values only, aligning more closely with the value iterator's intent but optimized for ray-marching. Performance: The leaf-only iterator provides a significant performance lever for ray-marching kernels like rayimplicitintersection by skipping active coarse tiles, which are not needed for leaf-specific operations. Strengths: Eliminates latent mis-indexing bugs; reduces warp divergence in nextSegment; simplifies caller code by separating tile and leaf traversal. Limitations: Requires compile-time specialization (LeafOnly); not suitable for operations that need to process coarse tiles. The reorganization was inspired by Efty's 'branchless getValue' work in NanoVDB and aimed to apply similar principles to the ray-marching kernels in OpenVDB. It was introduced in the rayimplicitintersection improvements PR. The change addresses issues where the previous HDDAVoxelIterator yielded active values at any node level, forcing callers to branch on getDim() to distinguish between tiles and leaves, which led to inefficiencies and bugs. rayimplicitintersection improvements, https://github.com/openvdb/fvdb-core/pull/663, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Question/doubt about VDB allocation, https://github.com/fzi-forschungszentrum-informatik/vdbmapping/issues/2, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Multi-level DDA with Adaptive Mip Selection
head: DDA-based volume sampling routine, Multi-level traversal scheme
body: This method is a ray traversal and sampling algorithm for volume rendering that combines Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) brick traversal with delta tracking, using multiple mip levels of a majorant texture to adaptively balance step size and sampling accuracy. It solves the problem of inefficient sampling in sparse or heterogeneous volumes by allowing large steps in empty regions (coarse mip levels) while maintaining precision near density changes (fine mip levels). It sets itself apart from standard DDA by dynamically adjusting the spatial resolution of the majorant lookup per step without branching, and from pure delta tracking by using DDA to skip empty space more efficiently. The algorithm traverses a ray through a volume hierarchy of bricks, using a majorant texture to estimate the probability of interaction. It maintains a target optical thickness (tauToGo) and steps through the volume, dynamically selecting the mip level for the majorant lookup based on a heuristic that increases resolution as the ray progresses and decreases it upon collision detection. Inputs: Ray origin (rayOrigin), ray direction (rayDir), volume data (density texture, majorant texture hierarchy), initial distance t (usually 0 or start of volume). Outputs: Collision point, type of collision (real or null), updated ray state. Majorant Texture Hierarchy: A set of mip levels (0 to 3) of a texture storing the majorant density. The source specifies 3 mip levels are computed. Brick Geometry: Bricks are dilated by 0.5 voxels in the direction of travel to improve numerical stability and reduce step counts. The brick dimension at mip level m is dim = 8 << m. Initial Mip Level: 3.0 (coarsest). Mip Increment: 0.33 per iteration. Mip Decrement on Collision: 2.0. Mip Bounds: Clamped between 0.0 and 3.0. Brick Dilation: 0.5 voxels. 1. Initialize the target optical thickness tauToGo by sampling a uniform random number r and computing tauToGo = -log(1.0 - r). 2. Initialize the mip level mip = 3.0. 3. Enter the volume traversal loop (while inside the volume): a. Calculate the current ray position: pos = rayOrigin + t rayDir. b. Lookup the majorant density at pos using the current mip level, rounded to an integer: majorant = lookupMajorant(pos, round(mip)). c. Compute the next DDA step distance nextt using the stepDDA function with the current mip level. d. Increment the mip level: mip = min(3.0, mip + 0.33). e. Calculate the step distance dt = nextt - t and the optical thickness traversed dtau = majorant dt. f. Update the current distance t = nextt. g. Subtract the traversed optical thickness from the target: tauToGo -= dtau. h. If tauToGo > 0, continue to the next iteration (no collision yet). i. If tauToGo <= 0 (collision detected): i. Decrement the mip level: mip = max(0.0, mip - 2.0). ii. Step back to the exact collision point using linear interpolation: t += dt (tauToGo / dtau). iii. Lookup the actual density at the collision point: density = lookup(rayOrigin + t rayDir). iv. Perform Russian roulette for real vs. null collision: if random() majorant < density, handle a real collision; otherwise, treat as a null collision. v. For a null collision, restart the traversal by sampling a new target optical thickness: tauToGo = -log(1.0 - random()). Target Optical Thickness: tauToGo = -log(1.0 - random()). Brick Dimension: dim = 8 << mip. DDA Offset: ofs = ri (((ri >= 0.0) ? dim + 0.5: -0.5) - ro). Where ri is the ray inverse direction (1.0 / rayDir) and ro is the ray origin. DDA Step Distance: tmax = floor(pos (1.0 / dim)) dim ri + ofs. The final step distance is min(tmax.x, min(tmax.y, tmax.z)). Collision Point Refinement: tcollision = tprev + dt (tauToGoremaining / dtautraversed). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def stepdda(ro, ri, pos, mip): """ Compute the next DDA step distance using dilated brick boundaries. ro: Ray origin (float3) ri: Ray inverse direction (float3) pos: Current ray position (float3) mip: Current mip level (float) """ dim = 8 << int(mip) # Calculate offset component-wise based on direction and dilation ofsx = ri.x ((dim + 0.5 - ro.x) if ri.x >= 0 else (-0.5 - ro.x)) ofsy = ri.y ((dim + 0.5 - ro.y) if ri.y >= 0 else (-0.5 - ro.y)) ofsz = ri.z ((dim + 0.5 - ro.z) if ri.z >= 0 else (-0.5 - ro.z)) # Calculate tmax for each dimension tmaxx = math.floor(pos.x (1.0 / dim)) dim ri.x + ofsx tmaxy = math.floor(pos.y (1.0 / dim)) dim ri.y + ofsy tmaxz = math.floor(pos.z (1.0 / dim)) dim ri.z + ofsz return min(tmaxx, tmaxy, tmaxz) def multilevelddaadaptivemip(rayorigin, raydir, volumedata): """ Main traversal loop. rayorigin: float3 raydir: float3 volumedata: Object containing lookupmajorant and lookup functions """ # Initialize target optical thickness r = random.random() tautogo = -math.log(1.0 - r) # Initialize mip level mip = 3.0 # Assume t starts at 0 or entry point t = 0.0 # Precompute inverse ray direction invraydir = 1.0 / raydir # Loop until collision handled or ray exits volume (volume exit handled externally) while True: # Calculate current position pos = rayorigin + t raydir # Lookup majorant at current mip level majorant = volumedata.lookupmajorant(pos, int(round(mip))) # Compute next DDA step nextt = stepdda(rayorigin, invraydir, pos, int(round(mip))) # Increment mip level mip = min(3.0, mip + 0.33) # Calculate step distance and optical thickness dt = nextt - t dtau = majorant dt # Update current distance t = nextt # Update remaining optical thickness tautogo -= dtau # Check for collision if tautogo > 0: continue # No collision, continue to next step # Collision detected # Decrement mip level mip = max(0.0, mip - 2.0) # Step back to exact collision point t += dt (tautogo / dtau) # Lookup actual density at collision point collisionpos = rayorigin + t raydir density = volumedata.lookup(collisionpos) # Russian roulette for real vs null collision r = random.random() if r majorant < density: # Handle real collision return {"type": "real", "position": collisionpos, "density": density} else: # Null collision # Restart traversal with new target r = random.random() tautogo = -math.log(1.0 - r) # Continue loop to step forward again Numerical Instability on Brick Boundaries: Ray intersections falling exactly on brick boundaries can cause numerical issues. This is mitigated by dilating brick boundaries by 0.5 voxels in the direction of travel, ensuring the DDA oversteps into each brick. Execution Divergence on GPUs: Implementing separate loops for each mip level causes execution divergence on SIMT devices (GPUs). The adaptive mip selection is computed dynamically per step without branching to avoid this. Precision: The mip level is rounded to an integer for texture lookup, but maintained as a float for the heuristic increment/decrement. A sibling method that uses a hierarchical DDA structure. It differs in its specific implementation of the hierarchy and traversal logic. HDDA A sibling method, likely an extension or variant of HDDA for volume rendering. VolumeHDDA Time Complexity: The number of steps is reduced compared to regular DDA due to larger steps in empty space and dilated boundaries. For example, the adaptive DDA achieved 3.9ms on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 for one sample per pixel at 1920x1080 with 3 bounces on the Moana cloud scene. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is 86.7MB for the Moana cloud scene with BC4 compression. Strengths: Reduces the number of volume and majorant lookups, especially in empty space regions. Improves numerical stability. Avoids execution divergence on GPUs. Limitations: Requires computation of multiple mip levels of the majorant texture. When to Use: Suitable for GPU-based unbiased volume path tracing where performance and numerical stability are critical. The method was introduced in "Efficient Unbiased Volume Path Tracing on the GPU". It builds on the principles of Hierarchical DDA Traversal [17026-hierarchical-dda-traversal.md] and adapts them for volume rendering by integrating delta tracking and adaptive mip selection. The approach was inspired by techniques used in screen-space reflections. Efficient Unbiased Volume Path Tracing on the GPU, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4842-7185-843, fetched 2026-10-24 (book)

name: Macro-Cell Optimization
head: Macro-Cell Acceleration, Online Macro-Cell Construction
body: Macro-Cell Optimization is an acceleration technique for volume rendering that partitions the spatial domain into disjoint, closely packed macro-cells to minimize null collisions and reduce the number of expensive neural network inferences. It sets itself apart from standard DDA methods by storing aggregate statistics (value range and maximum opacity \mu{\max}) per macro-cell, allowing for early termination of rays and adaptive step sizing based on local density bounds. Inputs and Outputs The method takes volume dimensions Dx, Dy, Dz, macro-cell size parameter Ng, a neural network representation of the volume, and a transfer function as inputs. It outputs the rendered image and updated macro-cell statistics for online training. Data Structures The acceleration structure is a 3D grid of macro-cells. The grid dimensions are \lceil Dx / Ng \rceil \times \lceil Dy / Ng \rceil \times \lceil Dz / Ng \rceil. Each macro-cell stores the maximum opacity \mu{\max} of all contained voxels and the value range of those voxels. If volume dimensions are not an integer multiple of Ng, the macro-cell grid extends beyond the volume domain, which is acceptable. Parameters Ng is the macro-cell size per dimension, typically set to 64 to balance performance and memory footprint. s1 is the minimum sampling step size, set to 1. s2 is the maximum sampling step size, set to 64. p is the exponent for adaptive step size calculation, set to 2. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: For each primary ray, determine the intersection with the volume; if no intersection is found, invalidate the ray. 2. Target Calculation: Generate a uniform random number \zeta \sim \mathcal{U}{[0,1]} and compute the target optical thickness \tau{\text{target}} = -\log(1 - \zeta). 3. Traversal: Traverse the ray through the macro-cells using a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA). 4. Macro-Cell Check: If a macro-cell is transparent (\mu{\max} = 0), bypass it entirely. Otherwise, calculate the optical thickness contribution of the segment within the cell. 5. Accumulation: Accumulate the optical thickness \taun = \sum{i=0}^n \mu{\max}^i \times si, where si is the length of the ray segment within the i-th macro-cell. 6. Termination: Stop the ray when \taun > \tau{\text{target}} for the first time, then step backward to find the exact hit location. 7. Ray Marching Mode: For regular ray marching within cells, adaptively vary the sampling step size \bar{s} based on density \mu using \bar{s} = \max(s1 + (s2 - s1) \cdot |\min(\mu, 1) - 1|^p, s1). Sample the volume at intervals of \bar{s}. Correct the sampled opacity \alpha to \bar{\alpha} = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^{s / \bar{s}}, where s is the actual step size. 8. Online Update: During online training, update the macro-cell value range fields using training samples generated in each step, as the process is embarrassingly parallelizable. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def macrocelloptimization(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, volumedims, ng, mumaxgrid): # 1. Initialize ray (intersection check handled externally per) t = tmin # 2. Target optical thickness zeta = random.uniform(0, 1) tautarget = -math.log(1 - zeta) # 3. DDA state initialization for macro-cell grid griddims = ( math.ceil(volumedims[0] / ng), math.ceil(volumedims[1] / ng), math.ceil(volumedims[2] / ng)) invdir = (1.0 / raydirection[0], 1.0 / raydirection[1], 1.0 / raydirection[2]) mnext = [ (math.floor(rayorigin[i] / ng) + 1) ng - rayorigin[i] if invdir[i] > 0 else math.floor(rayorigin[i] / ng) ng - rayorigin[i] for i in range(3) ] mdelta = [ng invdir[i] for i in range(3)] mstep = [1 if invdir[i] > 0 else -1 for i in range(3)] cellidx = ( math.floor(rayorigin[0] / ng), math.floor(rayorigin[1] / ng), math.floor(rayorigin[2] / ng)) currenttau = 0.0 # 4. Traverse macro-cells while t < tmax: # Find exit distance from current macro-cell texit = t for dim in range(3): if mnext[dim] > 0: texit = min(texit, t + mnext[dim]) si = texit - t mumax = mumaxgrid[cellidx[0]][cellidx[1]][cellidx[2]] # 5. Bypass transparent cells if mumax == 0: t = texit for dim in range(3): if texit == t + mnext[dim]: cellidx = ( cellidx[0] + mstep[0] if dim == 0 else cellidx[0], cellidx[1] + mstep[1] if dim == 1 else cellidx[1], cellidx[2] + mstep[2] if dim == 2 else cellidx[2]) mnext[dim] += mdelta[dim] continue # 6. Accumulate optical thickness currenttau += mumax si # 7. Termination check if currenttau > tautarget: hitt = findexacthit(t, texit, tautarget, currenttau - mumax si, mumax) return hitt # Advance ray to next macro-cell t = texit for dim in range(3): if texit == t + mnext[dim]: cellidx = ( cellidx[0] + mstep[0] if dim == 0 else cellidx[0], cellidx[1] + mstep[1] if dim == 1 else cellidx[1], cellidx[2] + mstep[2] if dim == 2 else cellidx[2]) mnext[dim] += mdelta[dim] return None def findexacthit(tenter, texit, tautarget, taubefore, mumax): low, high = tenter, texit for in range(32): mid = (low + high) / 2.0 seglen = mid - tenter taumid = taubefore + mumax seglen if taumid < tautarget: low = mid else: high = mid return low Performance shows significant speed improvements, particularly with neural representations, due to reduced null collisions and neural network inferences. The choice of Ng balances performance and memory, with Ng=64 being favorable. Adaptive sampling causes the number of volume samples per ray to fluctuate considerably, but stream compaction of terminated rays prevents performance compromise. The method assumes the neural representation approximates ground truth accurately; small discrepancies in online-constructed value ranges do not significantly impact rendering quality. Macro-Cell Optimization was proposed in the context of interactive volume visualization using multi-resolution hash encoding. It builds upon the work of Hofmann et al. for target optical thickness calculation and Morrical et al. for adaptive step sizing. The technique is particularly relevant for neural volume rendering where inference costs are high. Interactive Volume Visualization via Multi-Resolution Hash Encoding, https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11620, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Exact Grid Traversal
head: Cylindrical Grid Approach, Discrete Grid Point Capture, USCG Intersection Calculation, USCG Scheme, Uniformly Sampled Cylindrical Grid (USCG) Line Tracing
body: Exact Grid Traversal is a method for capturing all discrete grid points that a projection line passes through, primarily used in algebraic image reconstruction. It differs from standard Cartesian DDA methods by employing a Uniformly Sampled Cylindrical Grid (USCG) structure, which consists of cylindrical, radial, and axial planes. This approach is specifically designed to speed up line coefficient calculation by avoiding intersection point calculations for radial planes, leveraging the symmetry of the cylindrical geometry. Inputs: Source point S, Detector point D, Grid parameters (Number of slices N, Number of rings N/2, radial length r, slice thickness h, source angle \thetas). Outputs: List of grid indices traversed by the line segment SD. Data Structures: USCG Grid: Defined by N slices along the z-axis and N/2 rings in the xy-plane. Ring n (n=1 \dots N/2): Contains ng = 4(2n - 1) grids. Intersection List Pt: A list of intersection points sorted by distance from S. Line Segment Info: Stores slice number Sn, ring number Rn, and azimuthal angles \phi{Pk}, \phi{P{k+1}}. Steps: 1. Calculate Intersection Points: Compute the intersection points of the line SD with cylindrical and axial planes. Project line SD onto the XY plane to get SD'. Calculate distance d of SD' from the cylinder center: d = \sqrt{\langle S, S \rangle^2 - t^2 \langle S - D', S - D' \rangle^2} where t = \frac{S \cdot (S - D')}{\langle S - D', S - D' \rangle^2} If d \le R (where R is the cylinder radius), the line intersects the cylinder. The intersection points are: S + (t \pm k)(D - S) where k = \sqrt{\frac{R^2 - d^2}{\langle S - D', S - D' \rangle^2}} Sort all intersection points by their distance to S. 2. Identify Line Segments: Identify consecutive intersection points Pk and P{k+1} from the sorted list. These points reside in the same ring and slice throughout the data collection process. 3. Determine Grid Coordinates for Segment: For each segment Pk P{k+1}: Calculate the midpoint Pm: Pm = \left\{ \frac{P{(k+1)x} + P{kx}}{2}, \frac{P{(k+1)y} + P{ky}}{2}, \frac{P{(k+1)z} + P{kz}}{2} \right\} Calculate Slice Number Sn: Sn = \left\lfloor \frac{P{mz}}{h} \right\rfloor Calculate Radius dm of Pm: dm = \sqrt{P{mx}^2 + P{my}^2} Calculate Ring Number Rn: Rn = \left\lfloor \frac{dm}{r} \right\rfloor Calculate Azimuthal Angles \phi{Pk} and \phi{P{k+1}}: \phi{Pk} = \text{atan2}(P{ky}, P{kx}) \phi{P{k+1}} = \text{atan2}(P{(k+1)y}, P{(k+1)x}) Store (Sn, Rn, \phi{Pk}, \phi{P{k+1}}) for the segment. 4. Trace Grids for a Projection: For each projection with source angle \thetas: Update azimuthal angles: \phi{Pk}^{new} = \phi{Pk} + \thetas \phi{P{k+1}}^{new} = \phi{P{k+1}} + \thetas Keep Sn and Rn constant. Calculate Grid Numbers G{Pk} and G{P{k+1}} for the current ring Rn: Azimuthal step angle for ring Rn: \Delta \phi{Rn} = \frac{360}{4(2n - 1)} Grid number: G{Pk} = \left\lfloor \frac{\phi{Pk}}{\Delta \phi{Rn}} \right\rfloor + Hn where Hn is the head of ring Rn. name: Wide DDA Cell Traversal
body:
Wide DDA Cell Traversal is an algorithm for traversing a fixed 4x4x4 grid of "wide cells" within an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) using a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) approach. It generates bounding boxes and t-intervals for each cell to optimize octree traversal by visiting occupied child cells in ray order. Inputs: boundsmin, boundsmax: AABB defining the 4x4x4 grid region (vec3). origin: Ray origin point (vec3). direction: Ray direction vector (vec3). maxs: Maximum traversal distance parameter (float). baset: Base parameter for t-interval calculation (float). reverse: Boolean flag controlling t-interval sign convention (bool). visitor: Callback function bool visitor(cell) that receives the current cell data. Outputs: Sequence of WideDdaCell structures passed to the visitor, representing occupied cells in traversal order. Data Structures: WideDdaCell: childindex (int): Packed index of the cell within the 4x4x4 grid. Layout: cellx | (celly << 2) | (cellz << 4). boundsmin, boundsmax (vec3): Local bounding box of the cell. tnear (float): Entry distance along the ray. tfar (float): Exit distance along the ray. Constants: kEpsilon: Small floating-point tolerance for boundary comparisons (exact value not given in the sources). cellsize: Dimensions of each wide cell, calculated as (boundsmax - boundsmin) 0.25. Steps: 1. Initialize Cell Indices: Map the ray origin to local cell coordinates (cellx, celly, cellz) using localcellforposition, which handles boundary conditions and rounding with kEpsilon tolerance. Compute local coordinate: local = (origin - bounds\min) / cell\size. Compute rounded value: rounded = round(local). Check boundary: If |local - rounded| \le 8.0 	imes kEpsilon, the position is on a boundary. Clamp boundary to [0, 3]. If boundary \le 0, return 0. If boundary \ge 4, return 3. Otherwise, return boundary - 1 if walk\direction < -kEpsilon, else boundary. Otherwise, return clamp(floor(local), 0, 3). Note: walk\direction is the sign of the ray direction component (-1 or 1). 2. Setup Axis Parameters: For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: Determine step direction: stepi = sign(directioni). If |directioni| \le kEpsilon, set stepi = 0. Calculate delta distance: delta\si = cell\size / |directioni| if |directioni| > kEpsilon, else \infty. Calculate next intersection distance: next\si. If stepi = 0, set next\si = \infty. Otherwise, compute the distance to the next cell boundary along axis i from the current cell index. 3. Iterate: Loop up to 96 times. a. Check Bounds: If cellx 
otin 0, 4) or celly 
otin [0, 4) or cellz 
otin [0, 4) or current\s > max\s + kEpsilon, break loop. b. Determine Next Cell: Calculate next\s = \min(next\sx, next\sy, next\sz, max\s). Determine child\index = cell\x \mid (cell\y \ll 2) \mid (cell\z \ll 4). c. Compute Cell Bounds: child\min = bounds\min + cell\size 	imes vec3(cell\x, cell\y, cell\z). child\max = child\min + cell\size. d. Compute t-intervals: If reverse is true: t
ear = base	 - next\s. t ar = base	 - current\s. Else: t
ear = base	 + current\s. t ar = base	 + next\s. e. Visit Cell: Construct WideDdaCell with childindex, childmin, childmax, tnear, tfar. Call visitor(cell). If it returns false, terminate traversal immediately. f. Check Termination: If next\s \ge max\s - kEpsilon, break loop. g. Advance: Update current\s = next\s. Advance the axis with the smallest next\si. If next\sx \le next\sy + kEpsilon and next\sx \le next\sz + kEpsilon, advance x. Else if next\sy \le next\sz + kEpsilon, advance y. Else, advance z. Use advanceaxis to update the corresponding cell index and next\si. Pseudocode: Unverified code. boundsmin) 0.25 # Initialize cell indices (scalar per axis as walkdirection is per-axis) dirxsign = 1.0 if direction.x > 0 else (-1.0 if direction.x < 0 else 0.0) dirysign = 1.0 if direction.y > 0 else (-1.0 if direction.y < 0 else 0.0) dirzsign = 1.0 if direction.z > 0 else (-1.0 if direction.z < 0 else 0.0) cellx = localcellforposition(origin.x, boundsmin.x, cellsize, dirxsign, kEpsilon) celly = localcellforposition(origin.y, boundsmin.y, cellsize, dirysign, kEpsilon) cellz = localcellforposition(origin.z, boundsmin.z, cellsize, dirzsign, kEpsilon) # Setup axis parameters stepx, nextsx, deltasx = axissetup(direction.x, cellsize, cellx, boundsmin.x, origin.x, kEpsilon) stepy, nextsy, deltasy = axissetup(direction.y, cellsize, celly, boundsmin.y, origin.y, kEpsilon) stepz, nextsz, deltasz = axissetup(direction.z, cellsize, cellz, boundsmin.z, origin.z, kEpsilon) currents = 0.0 for in range(96): if not (0 <= cellx < 4 and 0 <= celly < 4 and 0 <= cellz < 4): break if currents > maxs + kEpsilon: break nexts = min(nextsx, nextsy, nextsz, maxs) childindex = cellx | (celly << 2) | (cellz << 4) childmin = vec3(boundsmin.x + cellsize cellx, boundsmin.y + cellsize celly, boundsmin.z + cellsize cellz) childmax = vec3(childmin.x + cellsize, childmin.y + cellsize, childmin.z + cellsize) if reverse: tnear = baset - nexts tfar = baset - currents else: tnear = baset + currents tfar = baset + nexts cell = WideDdaCell(childindex=childindex, boundsmin=childmin, boundsmax=childmax, tnear=tnear, tfar=tfar) if not visitor(cell): return if nexts >= maxs - kEpsilon: break currents = nexts if nextsx <= nextsy + kEpsilon and nextsx <= nextsz + kEpsilon: cellx, nextsx = advanceaxis(stepx, deltasx, nextsx) elif nextsy <= nextsz + kEpsilon: celly, nextsy = advanceaxis(stepy, deltasy, nextsy) else: cellz, nextsz = advanceaxis(stepz, deltasz, nextsz) def localcellforposition(pos, minbound, cellsize, walkdirection, kEpsilon): local = (pos - minbound) / cellsize rounded = round(local) if abs(local - rounded) <= 8.0 kEpsilon: boundary = max(0, min(3, rounded)) if boundary <= 0: return 0 if boundary >= 4: return 3 if walkdirection < -kEpsilon: return boundary - 1 else: return boundary else: return max(0, min(3, floor(local))) def axissetup(dirval, cellsize, cellidx, minbound, origin, kEpsilon): if abs(dirval) <= kEpsilon: return 0, float('inf'), float('inf') step = 1 if dirval > 0 else -1 deltas = cellsize / abs(dirval) local = (origin - minbound) / cellsize if step > 0: nexts = (cellidx + 1 - local) cellsize / dirval else: nexts = (cellidx - local) cellsize / dirval return step, nexts, deltas def advanceaxis(step, deltas, currentnexts): return currentnexts + step, currentnexts + deltas [Wide Node DDA Cell Calculation is a helper function that maps a continuous position to a discrete cell index (0-3) within a 4x4x4 wide node, handling boundary cases where the position falls exactly on a cell edge. It is used by Wide DDA Cell Traversal to initialize the starting cell indices. It differs from standard floor-based mapping by using an 8kEpsilon tolerance window and the walkdirection parameter to break ties, ensuring consistent DDA stepping. Time Complexity: O(1) per wide cell visited, with a maximum of 96 iterations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, storing only current cell indices and axis parameters. Strengths: Handles near-zero ray directions by setting step to 0 and distances to infinity, preventing division by zero and infinite loops. Handles boundary cases robustly using kEpsilon and walkdirection. Limitations: Limited to 4x4x4 grids. When to use: When traversing wide octree nodes or fixed-size blocks where occupancy is high and ray order is important. When not to use: For sparse grids or when the grid size is not a multiple of 4. Wide DDA Cell Traversal is part of the svo (Sparse Voxel Octree) rendering pipeline, specifically designed for efficient traversal of wide nodes in a GPU-based renderer. hectorpiteau/sparse-voxels, https://github.com/hectorpiteau/sparse-voxels, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

head: Wide Node DDA
body: Wide Node DDA Traversal traverses a 4x4x4 grid of wide cells within an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) using a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) approach to visit occupied child cells in ray order. It generates bounding boxes and t-intervals for each cell to optimize octree traversal. It builds on Wide DDA Cell Traversal by providing a visitor callback mechanism and mask-based filtering required for wide octree nodes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: boundsmin, boundsmax: The AABB of the wide node as 3D vectors. origin, direction: Ray origin and direction vectors. tnear, tfar: The ray segment interval to traverse. reverse: Boolean flag for traversal direction. nodeindex: Index of the wide node in the octree structure. octree: The global octree data structure containing widenodes(), maxdepth(), and payloadbase(). depthremaining: Current recursion depth counter. best: Current best hit record containing hit and t for pruning. Outputs: bool: Indicates traversal success or early termination. Side effects: Calls considerleaf or recursive traversal for valid children. Data Structures: WideNodeDescriptor: childmask: std::uint64t, bitmask of occupied child cells. leafmask: std::uint64t, bitmask of children that are leaves. internalchildmask: std::uint64t, bitmask of children that are internal nodes. payloadbase: Implied offset for leaf payloads. childbase: Implied offset for child nodes. Cell Info: childindex: Index of the cell within the 4x4x4 grid (0-63). boundsmin, boundsmax: Bounding box of the specific wide cell. tnear, tfar: T-interval of the ray intersection with the cell. Helper Functions: countbits(mask): Counts set bits in mask. prefixrank(mask, childindex): Returns the rank (index among set bits) of childindex in mask. childindexfordepth(x, y, z, childdepth): Computes the 3-bit child index from coordinates. containspoint(minbound, maxbound, point): Checks if point is inside bounds. Numbered Steps: 1. Boundary Check: If nodeindex is out of bounds or depthremaining <= 0, return immediately. 2. Descriptor Retrieval: Retrieve WideNodeDescriptor from octree.widenodes()[nodeindex]. 3. DDA Iteration: Call visitwidecellsdda with boundsmin, boundsmax, origin, direction, tnear, tfar, reverse, and a lambda visitor. Note: visitwidecellsdda iterates through the 4x4x4 grid using DDA logic, invoking the visitor for each cell intersected by the ray. 4. Visitor Logic (executed for each cell): a. Get childindex from cell.childindex. b. Compute childbit as 1 << childindex. c. Occupancy Check: If childbit is not in childmask, skip this cell. d. Pruning: If best.hit is true and max(cell.tnear, 0.0) > best.t + kEpsilon, skip this cell. e. Leaf Processing: If childbit is in leafmask: i. Compute leafid using descriptor.payloadbase() and prefixrank(leafmask, childindex). ii. Compute depth as octree.maxdepth() - depthremaining + 2. iii. Call considerleaf(cell.boundsmin, cell.boundsmax, leafid, depth). f. Internal Node Processing: If childbit is in internalchildmask (and not leaf), recursively call traversewidenode with updated depthremaining - 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversewidenode(nodeindex, depthremaining, octree, best, boundsmin, boundsmax, origin, direction, tnear, tfar): # Step 1: Boundary Check if nodeindex >= octree.numwidenodes() or depthremaining <= 0: return False # Step 2: Descriptor Retrieval descriptor = octree.widenodes()[nodeindex] childmask = descriptor.childmask leafmask = descriptor.leafmask internalchildmask = descriptor.internalchildmask # Step 3: DDA Iteration def visitor(cell): # Step 4a: Get childindex childindex = cell.childindex # Step 4b: Compute childbit childbit = 1 << childindex # Step 4c: Occupancy Check if not (childbit & childmask): return # Step 4d: Pruning if best.hit and max(cell.tnear, 0.0) > best.t + kEpsilon: return # Step 4e: Leaf Processing if childbit & leafmask: leafrank = prefixrank(leafmask, childindex) leafid = descriptor.payloadbase() + leafrank depth = octree.maxdepth() - depthremaining + 2 considerleaf(cell.boundsmin, cell.boundsmax, leafid, depth) # Step 4f: Internal Node Processing elif childbit & internalchildmask: childnodeindex = descriptor.childbase + childindex traversewidenode(childnodeindex, depthremaining - 1, octree, best, cell.boundsmin, cell.boundsmax, origin, direction, cell.tnear, cell.tfar) visitwidecellsdda(boundsmin, boundsmax, origin, direction, tnear, tfar, False, visitor) return True def visitwidecellsdda(boundsmin, boundsmax, origin, direction, tnearglobal, tfarglobal, reverse, visitor): # Standard 3D DDA for a 4x4x4 grid invdir = [1.0 / d if d != 0.0 else float('inf') for d in direction] step = [1 if d > 0 else -1 for d in direction] # Clamp origin to bounds to find starting cell t = [(boundsmin[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] tmax = [(boundsmax[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] # Initial cell coordinates ix = int((origin[0] - boundsmin[0]) invdir[0]) if direction[0] != 0 else 0 iy = int((origin[1] - boundsmin[1]) invdir[1]) if direction[1] != 0 else 0 iz = int((origin[2] - boundsmin[2]) invdir[2]) if direction[2] != 0 else 0 ix = max(0, min(3, ix)) iy = max(0, min(3, iy)) iz = max(0, min(3, iz)) # DDA state tmaxx = tmax[0] if direction[0] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = tmax[1] if direction[1] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxz = tmax[2] if direction[2] != 0 else float('inf') tnextx = tmaxx if step[0] == 1 else t[0] tnexty = tmaxy if step[1] == 1 else t[1] tnextz = tmaxz if step[2] == 1 else t[2] # Precompute cell size cellsize = [boundsmax[i] - boundsmin[i] for i in range(3)] cellsize = [s / 4.0 for s in cellsize] # Visit cells in DDA order for in range(64): # Compute t-interval for current cell cellmin = [boundsmin[i] + ix cellsize[i] for i in range(3)] cellmax = [cellmin[i] + cellsize[i] for i in range(3)] tentry = max((cellmin[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)) texit = min((cellmax[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)) tnear = max(tentry, tnearglobal) tfar = min(texit, tfarglobal) if tnear < tfar: childindex = ix + 4 iy + 16 iz visitor({'childindex': childindex, 'boundsmin': cellmin, 'boundsmax': cellmax, 'tnear': float(tnear), 'tfar': float(tfar)}) # Step DDA if tnextx < tnexty: if tnextx < tnextz: ix += step[0] tnextx += tmaxx else: iz += step[2] tnextz += tmaxz else: if tnexty < tnextz: iy += step[1] tnexty += tmaxy else: iz += step[2] tnextz += tmaxz if not (0 <= ix <= 3 and 0 <= iy <= 3 and 0 <= iz <= 3): break def prefixrank(mask, childindex): if childindex <= 0: return 0 lowermask = (1 << childindex) - 1 return countbits(mask & lowermask) def countbits(mask): count = 0 while mask != 0: count += mask & 1 mask = mask >> 1 return count def considerleaf(boundsmin, boundsmax, leafid, depth): # Processes leaf hit; implementation depends on downstream rendering logic pass kEpsilon = 1e-6 Parameters: kEpsilon: Small float value for pruning comparison. maxdepth: Maximum depth of the octree. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point comparisons for t-intervals and pruning require epsilon tolerance. Boundaries: nodeindex out of bounds must be checked to prevent memory access violations. Degenerate Input: depthremaining <= 0 stops recursion to prevent infinite loops or invalid accesses. Zero Direction Components: DDA must handle zero direction components by clamping to inf and skipping steps to avoid division by zero. Traverses a wide octree node by iterating over 4x4x4 wide cells using visitwidecellsdda and processing each cell's children based on masks. It distinguishes itself by handling both leaf and internal node children within the same traversal loop, using childmask, leafmask, and internalchildmask to determine the action for each cell. Choose this when you need to traverse a wide octree node with mixed leaf and internal children efficiently. Link: Octree Node Traversal (Wide). Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Proportional to the number of wide cells intersected by the ray, filtered by occupancy masks. Memory: O(1) additional memory per node traversal, excluding the octree structure itself. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of wide cells and the depth of the octree. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Efficiently visits only occupied cells in ray order, reducing unnecessary checks. Limitations: Requires pre-computed masks and descriptors. When to Use: Use when traversing wide octree nodes with sparse occupancy. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources.
