name: Per-pixel 3D-DDA Renderer
head: Brickmap 3D-DDA, CPU-based 3D-DDA Renderer
body: The Per-pixel 3D-DDA Renderer is a CPU-based volume rendering method that performs a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal per pixel over a brickmap. It serves as a clean-room alternative to column-coherent raycasting, specifically designed for the roxlap engine. Unlike its parent Parallel 3D-DDA which focuses on general parallelization strategies, this method implements a strict per-pixel traversal order that enables correct compositing of transparent voxels without depth sorting or Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) schemes. The method takes a brickmap, camera parameters, and a frame buffer as input, and outputs a rendered image frame buffer. Data Structures: Brickmap: The spatial data structure storing voxel data. It supports runtime editing (carve/fill spans, cubes, rectangles, spheres) via roxlapformats::edit::. Material Palette: A 256-entry palette used to drive per-instance, per-voxel, and world-terrain material properties, supporting mixed opaque-frame and glass models. Color Callbacks: Closure-based functions replacing global state, supporting constant, jittered, position-dependent, and texture-mapped color functions. Steps: 1. Frame Partitioning: The renderer splits the frame into row strips for parallel processing using the rayon library. 2. Ray Initialization: For each pixel in a strip, compute the ray origin and direction from camera parameters. 3. 3D-DDA Traversal: Traverse the brickmap along the ray. The traversal must visit voxels strictly front-to-back. 4. Empty Space Skipping: Skip empty cells to optimize performance. A regression test ensures no leaks occur in empty space handling. 5. Voxel Sampling: Sample the voxel at the current DDA step. Retrieve the material ID and use the closure-based color callback to compute color, avoiding global state management. 6. Compositing: Composite the voxel color into the pixel buffer using front-to-back accumulation. Volumetric opacity is weighted by the ray's path length. 7. Termination: Stop traversal when the ray exits the brickmap bounds or the accumulated transmittance drops below a threshold. Formulas: Volumetric Weighting: Opacity is weighted by the ray's path length, causing filled clouds to appear denser at their core. Front-to-Back Compositing: For a sequence of voxels i with transmittance Ti and color Ci, the final color C{final} is computed as: C{final} = \sum{i} Ci \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the effective opacity of voxel i. Parameters: Material Palette Size: 256 entries. Parallelism: Controlled by RAYONNUMTHREADS environment variable. Pitfalls: Empty Space Leaks: Incorrect implementation of empty space skipping can lead to visual artifacts (leaks). A specific regression test is required to ensure correctness. Global State: Avoid global state for color functions; use closure-based callbacks to prevent state management issues. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderframe(brickmap, camera, framebuffer, materialpalette): # Split frame into row strips for parallel processing stripheight = max(1, framebuffer.height // 4) strips = [(y, min(y + stripheight, framebuffer.height)) for y in range(0, framebuffer.height, stripheight)] for ystart, yend in strips: for y in range(ystart, yend): for x in range(framebuffer.width): # Initialize ray for pixel (x, y) rayorigin, raydir = camera.getray(x, y) raydir = normalize(raydir) # Initialize compositing state acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 # 3D-DDA Initialization brickmin = brickmap.bounds.min brickmax = brickmap.bounds.max step = [1 if raydir[i] > 0 else -1 for i in range(3)] tmax = [(brickmin[i] if step[i] == -1 else brickmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] if raydir[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] tdelta = [step[i] / raydir[i] if raydir[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] voxelpos = [brickmin[i] if step[i] == -1 else brickmax[i] - 1 for i in range(3)] # 3D-DDA Traversal loop while tmax[0] < brickmax[0] and tmax[1] < brickmax[1] and tmax[2] < brickmax[2]: axis = 0 if tmax[1] < tmax[axis]: axis = 1 if tmax[2] < tmax[axis]: axis = 2 tmax[axis] += tdelta[axis] voxelpos[axis] += step[axis] if not brickmap.contains(voxelpos): break # Empty space skipping if not brickmap.isvoxelfilled(voxelpos): continue # Sample voxel properties matid = brickmap.getmaterialid(voxelpos) material = materialpalette[matid] colorfunc = material.getcolorcallback() voxelcolor = colorfunc(voxelpos, matid) voxelalpha = material.alpha # Volumetric weighting by path length cellsize = brickmap.cellsize pathlength = cellsize / max(abs(raydir[0]), abs(raydir[1]), abs(raydir[2])) if any(raydir) else cellsize effectivealpha = voxelalpha (pathlength / cellsize) # Front-to-back compositing for i in range(3): acccolor[i] += voxelcolor[i] effectivealpha transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - effectivealpha) acccolor[3] = 1.0 - (1.0 - acccolor[3]) (1.0 - effectivealpha) if transmittance < 0.01: break framebuffer.setpixel(x, y, acccolor) A compositing strategy for transparent voxels (alpha-blended, additive, Beer–Lambert volumetric) that relies on front-to-back traversal order, eliminating the need for depth sorting or Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) schemes. It supports constant, jittered, position-dependent, and texture-mapped color functions via closure-based callbacks, replacing the global-state dance of the original engine. Volumetric opacity is weighted by the ray's path length, causing filled clouds to appear denser at their core. It uses a 256-entry material palette to drive per-instance and per-voxel material properties, supporting mixed opaque-frame and glass models. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the average number of voxels traversed per ray. Parallelized across CPU cores using rayon. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Feature-complete CPU renderer with per-arch SIMD support (SSE2 / NEON / wasm simd128). Correctness is validated against a dense per-voxel reference walk. Strengths: Clean-room implementation independent of Voxlap C source; deterministic on CPU; supports complex material palettes and closure-based color functions. Limitations: CPU-bound; performance depends on brickmap traversal efficiency; empty space skipping must be carefully implemented to avoid leaks. When to Use: When a deterministic, CPU-based volume renderer is needed for brickmap data, especially for transparent voxels requiring correct front-to-back compositing. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Per-pixel 3D-DDA Renderer is part of the roxlap project, an independent Rust implementation inspired by Ken Silverman's Voxlap engine. It was developed as a clean-room alternative to Voxlap's column-coherent raycaster. The renderer is part of the roxlap-cli crate, published on crates.io. The project includes documentation on porting, multicore performance, and scene graph integration. roxlap-cli 0.32.0, https://docs.rs/crate/roxlap-cli/latest, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Transparent Voxel Compositing
head: Front-to-back voxel compositing, Beer–Lambert voxel rendering, closure-based voxel shading
body: Transparent Voxel Compositing is a rendering strategy for alpha-blended, additive, and Beer–Lambert volumetric voxels that relies on strict front-to-back traversal order to eliminate the need for depth sorting or Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) schemes. It is distinct from general OIT methods because it leverages the spatial coherence of voxel grids and the deterministic traversal of the parent Per-pixel 3D-DDA Renderer to composite samples in a single pass. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a voxel grid containing transparent materials; a material palette defining per-voxel or per-instance properties. Output: The final pixel color \mathbf{C} and accumulated transmittance. Data Structures: Material Palette: A 256-entry lookup table used to drive per-instance, per-voxel, and world-terrain material properties. It supports mixed opaque-frame and glass models (e.g., static sprites, animated clips, glass walls, water). Color Function Callbacks: Closure-based callbacks replace global state to support constant, jittered, position-dependent, and texture-mapped color functions. Algorithm Steps: 1. Traversal: The renderer performs a 3D-DDA traversal over the voxel grid, visiting voxels strictly in front-to-back order relative to the ray origin. 2. Sample Evaluation: For each visited voxel segment, evaluate the material properties and color. If using closure-based callbacks, invoke the specific color function (constant, jittered, position-dependent, or texture-mapped). Compute the volumetric opacity. The opacity is weighted by the ray's path length through the voxel, causing filled clouds or volumes to appear denser at their core. 3. Compositing: Accumulate color and transmittance using front-to-back alpha blending. Update transmittance: T{new} = T{old} \times (1 - \alpha). Update color: \mathbf{C}{new} = \mathbf{C}{old} + T{old} \times \alpha \times \mathbf{c}, where \mathbf{c} is the sample color and \alpha is the sample opacity. 4. Termination: Stop when the ray exits the voxel grid or transmittance falls below a threshold. Formulas: The core compositing equation for a single sample is: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C} + T \cdot \alpha \cdot \mathbf{c} T = T \cdot (1 - \alpha) For volumetric density \sigma and path length \Delta t, the opacity \alpha is typically derived via Beer–Lambert law: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \cdot \Delta t) This weighting ensures that longer path lengths through dense media result in higher opacity. Parameters: Material Palette Size: 256 entries. Color Function Types: Constant, jittered, position-dependent, texture-mapped. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Standard floating-point precision is sufficient for the accumulation, but transmittance decay must be handled carefully to avoid premature termination in very transparent scenes. Boundary Conditions: The DDA traversal must correctly handle voxel boundaries to ensure no gaps or overlaps in the compositing order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def transparentvoxelcompositing(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid, materialpalette): # Initialize compositing state accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) transmittance = 1.0 # Perform front-to-back DDA traversal # This part relies on the parent Per-pixel 3D-DDA Renderer logic # which yields voxels in strict front-to-back order. for voxel in voxelgrid.traversefronttoback(rayorigin, raydirection): if transmittance < 1e-4: break # Get material properties from the 256-entry palette material = materialpalette[voxel.materialid] # Evaluate color and opacity # The color function is a closure-based callback color = material.colorfunction(voxel.position, raydirection) # Compute opacity weighted by ray path length through the voxel pathlength = voxel.segmentlength(rayorigin, raydirection) density = material.density opacity = 1.0 - exp(-density pathlength) # Front-to-back alpha blending accumulatedcolor += transmittance opacity color transmittance = (1.0 - opacity) return accumulatedcolor A method to compute sample opacity and accumulate color/depth/transmittance for a ray passing through sparse voxels, using trilinear interpolation of geometry and exponential-linear activation for density. Unlike NeRF, which stores every sample for back-propagation, SpaRV differentiates the compositing equation in a custom CUDA kernel where memory grows with the number of rays rather than samples. Steps: 1. Query: For a point \mathbf{p} inside a voxel, obtain density by trilinear interpolation \text{interp}(\mathbf{v}{\text{geo}}, \mathbf{p}) followed by exponential-linear activation. 2. Discretization: Each ray–voxel intersection segment is discretized into K midpoint samples. The k-th sample in the i-th intersected voxel is at \mathbf{x}{i,k} with spacing \Delta ti. 3. Color Evaluation: Evaluate view-dependent color \mathbf{c}{i,k} at \mathbf{x}{i,k}. The DC component (\text{SH}0) is trilinearly interpolated from vertex-stored coefficients, while higher-order SH coefficients are shared by the voxel. Combine via spherical harmonic evaluation. 4. Accumulation: Accumulate color using front-to-back alpha blending. Formulas: Sample opacity: \alpha{i,k} = 1 - \exp \left( -\Delta ti \exp \text{lin}(\text{interp}(\mathbf{v}{\text{geo}i}, \mathbf{x}{i,k})) \right) Accumulated color: \mathbf{C} = \sum{i=1}^N \sum{k=1}^K T{i,k} \alpha{i,k} \mathbf{c}{i,k} where T{i,k} = \prod{(j,l) \prec (i,k)} (1 - \alpha{j,l}) and \prec denotes ray-marching sampling order. Parameters: N: Number of intersected voxels along the ray. K: Number of midpoint samples per voxel segment. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels intersected by the ray. The front-to-back traversal ensures that each voxel is visited once. Memory Complexity: Constant per pixel, as only the accumulated color and transmittance are stored. The material palette is a fixed 256-entry structure. Strengths: Eliminates the overhead of depth sorting and OIT buffers. Supports complex volumetric effects (smoke, fire, glass) with a single pass. Closure-based shading allows flexible material definitions without global state. Limitations: Requires strict front-to-back traversal order, which is naturally provided by the DDA but may be complex to implement for non-grid-based transparent objects. Performance depends on the density of the voxel grid and the number of samples per voxel in sparse variants. When to use: Ideal for real-time rendering of volumetric scenes (clouds, fog, fire) and transparent objects (glass, water) where order-independent transparency is not required due to the spatial coherence of the voxel grid. Transparent Voxel Compositing is implemented in the roxlap engine, specifically in the CPU renderer which is feature-complete with voxel terrain, animated sprites, and world-voxel lighting. It builds on the Per-pixel 3D-DDA Renderer to provide a clean-room alternative to column-coherent raycasting. The method supports runtime voxel editing (carve/fill spans, cubes, rectangles, spheres) and is byte-equality validated against voxlap C's setspans. The 256-entry material palette and closure-based color callbacks were introduced to replace the global-state dance of the original engine. roxlap-cli 0.32.0, https://docs.rs/crate/roxlap-cli/latest, fetched 2026-10-29 SpaRV: Sparse Radiance Voxels for Scalable Geometrically Consistent LiDAR-Visual Mapping and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2610.25665, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: GPU Screen-Space Ray Tracing via DDA
head: Efficient GPU Screen-Space Ray Tracing via DDA, Linear 2D Iteration, Perspective-Correct DDA Ray Tracing, Thin-line Rasterization for Ray Casting
body: This method provides an efficient GPU solution for screen-space 3D ray tracing against a depth buffer by adapting the perspective-correct Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) line rasterization algorithm. It solves the inefficiency and missing intersections inherent in linear 3D marching by ensuring that sampled pixels form a contiguous set with no oversampling. Unlike linear 3D ray marching, which projects 3D points to screen space and can skip pixels or oversample the same pixel multiple times, this method places each sampled pixel adjacent (in x, y, or diagonally) to the previous one and samples each pixel at most once. Inputs: csOrig: Camera-space ray origin. csDir: Camera-space ray direction. proj: Projection matrix. nearPlaneZ: Negative near plane Z value. csZBuffer: Depth buffer texture. csZBufferSize: Dimensions of the depth buffer. csZBufferIsHyperbolic: Boolean flag indicating if the depth buffer stores hyperbolic (perspective-correct) depth values. csZThickness: Camera-space z-thickness ascribed to each point in the depth buffer. maxDistance: Maximum trace distance in camera-space. maxSteps: Maximum number of steps allowed during the trace. stride: Controls spacing between samples. stride = 1.0 produces thin-line rasterization. jitter: A value in the range [0, 1] used to bump the ray in pixels to conceal banding artifacts introduced by spaced samples. Outputs: Boolean indicating if a surface was hit. hitPixel: Coordinates of the hit pixel. hitLayer: Index of the hit layer in the depth buffer (if multiple layers are supported). csHitPoint: Camera-space position of the hit. The method operates on a depth buffer (csZBuffer) accessed via texelFetch. The depth buffer stores depth values which may be hyperbolic (perspective-correct) or linear, determined by csZBufferIsHyperbolic. The algorithm assumes a right-handed camera space where +z is out of the screen. 1. Unify DDA Cases: The classic DDA has eight cases (4 quadrants \times 2 iteration directions). These are unified by permuting axes and taking derivatives relative to the sign of \Delta x, ensuring iteration is always performed along the x-axis. A matrix permutation compensates for this in the vertical case, allowing all subsequent code to assume iteration in x. This eliminates divergent execution on GPUs. 2. Clip Far End: Clip only the far end of the ray against the near plane. The caller ensures the ray origin lies within the view frustum, eliminating the need for complex frustum clipping logic. 3. Implicit Viewport Clipping: Structure the test so that a zero value returned by texelFetch for an out-of-bounds depth-buffer sample terminates iteration. 4. Iterate and Sample: Perform the DDA iteration. At each step, calculate the 3D point corresponding to the current 2D screen point and test for intersection with the depth buffer. The 3D point Q' corresponding to a 2D screen point (x, y) is calculated as: Q'(x,y) = \frac{(Q \otimes k)(x,y)}{k(x,y)} where k = 1/(H \otimes (0,0,0,1)) is the reciprocal of the homogeneous w component, and Q \otimes k interpolates linearly in 2D. The following pseudocode implements the core DDA loop. It assumes the axis permutation has already been applied so that iteration proceeds along the x-axis. It uses conditional assignment instead of branches to maintain SIMD efficiency. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traceRay(csOrig, csDir, proj, nearPlaneZ, csZBuffer, csZBufferSize, csZBufferIsHyperbolic, csZThickness, maxDistance, maxSteps, stride, jitter): # Standard math/vector operations def projectToScreen(pos, matrix): # Homogeneous projection followed by perspective division h = matrix pos return (h.x / h.w, h.y / h.w, h.w) def texelFetch(tex, ix, iy): # Returns depth value; returns 0.0 for out-of-bounds coordinates if 0 <= ix < tex.width and 0 <= iy < tex.height: return tex[ix, iy] return 0.0 def sign(v): return 1 if v >= 0 else -1 def length(v): return (v.x2 + v.y2 + v.z2)0.5 # 1. Project ray endpoints to screen space P0 = projectToScreen(csOrig, proj) P1 = projectToScreen(csOrig + csDir maxDistance, proj) # 2. DDA parameters (iteration always along x-axis after permutation) dx = P1[0] - P0[0] dy = P1[1] - P0[1] stepx = sign(dx) stride stepy = (dy / dx) stepx # 3. Initialize position with jitter to conceal banding x = P0[0] + jitter stepx y = P0[1] + jitter stepy # 4. Perspective-correct interpolation setup # k = 1/w. Interpolate k and Qk linearly in 2D. k0 = 1.0 / P0[2] k1 = 1.0 / P1[2] dk = k1 - k0 Qk0 = P0[0] k0 Qk1 = P1[0] k1 dQk = Qk1 - Qk0 # Track camera-space distance along ray camDist = 0.0 stepCamDist = length(csDir) stride # 5. Iterate for step in range(maxSteps): camDist += stepCamDist if camDist > maxDistance: break # Perspective-correct interpolation for current screen point t = (x - P0[0]) / dx k = k0 + t dk Qk = Qk0 + t dQk # Reconstruct 3D point from interpolated values: Q' = Qk / k screenPoint = (Qk / k, 0.0, 0.0) # y,z handled similarly in full impl # Calculate ray depth at this screen point in camera space rayDepth = csOrig.z + csDir.z (camDist / length(csDir)) # Implicit viewport clipping: out-of-bounds texelFetch returns 0 depthSample = texelFetch(csZBuffer, int(x), int(y)) if depthSample == 0.0: break # Intersection test with z-thickness for robustness if rayDepth <= depthSample + csZThickness: return True, (int(x), int(y)), 0, screenPoint # Advance DDA x += stepx y += stepy return False, (0, 0), 0, (0, 0, 0) stride: Controls spacing between samples. stride = 1.0 produces thin-line rasterization. Larger values space samples for efficiency at the cost of quality. jitter: A value in the range [0, 1] used to bump the ray in pixels to conceal banding artifacts introduced by spaced samples (stride > 1.0). csZBufferIsHyperbolic: Boolean encoding flag for the depth buffer. Determines if the depth buffer stores hyperbolic (perspective-correct) depth values. csZThickness: Camera-space z-thickness ascribed to each point in the depth buffer, used for robustness in intersection testing. maxDistance: Maximum trace distance in camera-space. maxSteps: Maximum number of steps allowed during the trace. Branch Divergence: Classic DDA implementations suffer from divergent execution on GPUs due to branching for different quadrants and iteration directions. This method avoids this by unifying cases via axis permutation. Banding Artifacts: Banding artifacts appear when using stride > 1.0 for efficiency. This is handled by applying a jitter value in [0, 1] to the ray. Out-of-Bounds Access: The method relies on implicit clipping to the viewport. If the depth buffer does not return zero for out-of-bounds accesses, the iteration may not terminate correctly. Time Complexity: The method performs a fixed number of steps up to maxSteps or maxDistance. The inner loop contains simple fused multiply-add (FMUL) instructions and a single texture lookup per step. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory is required beyond the depth buffer. The algorithm is designed to minimize peak register count and instruction cache pressure. Measured Performance: Used in production for reflections in ripply water, achieving 2 ms at 1080p on GeForce 650M. Strengths: Ensures sampling at a contiguous set of pixels with no oversampling, addressing the inefficiency and missing intersections of linear 3D marching. Efficient on GPUs due to branch unification and simple arithmetic. Limitations: Quality decreases with larger stride values, requiring jitter to mitigate banding. Relies on the caller to ensure the ray origin is within the view frustum. When to Use: Suitable for screen-space effects like reflections in ripply water where performance is critical and the depth buffer is available. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes requiring global illumination or complex ray-object intersections beyond the depth buffer. The underlying method of 2D iteration is about 20 years old, evolving from Bresenham's algorithm through DDA. Recent games brought details for reflection tracing and GPU optimizations. Wronski [2014a, 80][2014b] and Valient [2014b, 90][2014a] sketched algorithms in presentations. The method has been proven in production of recent major game titles. Efficient GPU screen-space ray tracing, https://jcgt.org/published/0003/04/04/paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: DDA Optimizations (Rejected/Retained)
head: Boundary event counts, DDA region traversal, Explicit zero-event guards, Per-ray subtree caching, Redundant floor removal
body: This family article catalogs algorithmic modifications to Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) ray traversal, evaluating their CPU and GPU performance impact to determine which optimizations are retained in the final implementation. It distinguishes between successful optimizations that reduce computational overhead and rejected variants where added complexity or overhead outweighs benefits. The optimizations operate under the parent family's constraints: branch unification, memory coalescing, occupancy management, and implicit clipping. All retained optimizations preserve exact geometric correctness of surface intersections and image byte accumulation. Rejected optimizations occur when reduced traversal steps (e.g., fewer tree visits or skipped empty regions) are offset by increased per-step overhead, such as complex ownership checks, repeated CPU costs, or negative GPU warp efficiency impacts. Evaluation compares cumulative CPU costs, actual work counters, and complete-frame measurements across CPU and GPU workloads using specific benchmark configurations (CPU1, CPU6, CPU12, GPU fork-seven). This optimization compares upstream world representations to optimize how the DDA crosses compressed uniform regions. It is distinguished by its focus on hierarchical region crossing rather than per-voxel stepping. When to choose it and its link: Not given in the sources. This optimization replaces the baseline binary search for event detection with a bounded estimate followed by an exact plane correction. It is distinguished by its hybrid estimation-and-correction approach. When to choose it and its link: Not given in the sources. This optimization caches subtree information on a per-ray basis to reduce tree visits during traversal. It is distinguished by its per-ray state management. When to choose it and its link: Not given in the sources. This optimization checks for short-circuiting conditions where no events are expected, allowing the traversal to skip calculations. It is distinguished by its conditional early-exit logic. When to choose it and its link: Not given in the sources. This optimization simplifies the retained event estimate by removing redundant floor operations. It is distinguished by its arithmetic simplification of the event estimate. When to choose it and its link: Not given in the sources. It preserves exact surfaces and image bytes. This optimization reuses the known integer limit for axes leaving a region to optimize boundary event detection. It is distinguished by its reuse of fixed integer bounds for region exits. When to choose it and its link: Not given in the sources. The optimizations are derived from the development and profiling of the Bend voxel renderer's DDA traversal component. The work is documented in internal reports within the aivv73/bend-voxel repository, specifically docs/dda-optimization.md, docs/dda-profile.md, docs/dda-estimate.md, docs/dda-cursor.md, docs/dda-zero.md, docs/dda-floor.md, and docs/dda-boundary.md. aivv73/bend-voxel, https://github.com/aivv73/bend-voxel, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Voxel DDA Raymarching with Midpoint Interpolation
head: DDA ray marching, sphere tracing (referenced as alternative), triangular prism method [S1, unofficial]
body: Voxel DDA Raymarching with Midpoint Interpolation is a ray-terrain intersection technique for smooth heightfields represented by voxel corner volumes. It computes surface heights at voxel midpoints from adjacent corner values and linearly interpolates the ray's intersection point along the traversal edge. Unlike standard DDA which steps through discrete cells, this method refines the intersection within a single voxel using midpoint geometry, offering a balance between the speed of coarse traversal and the accuracy of continuous surface tracing. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D. Voxel grid of corner heights H{corner}(i,j,k). Voxel size V{size}. Entry UV coordinates on the voxel face where the ray enters. Outputs: Intersection UV coordinate u{intersect}. Intersection height y{intersect}. Boolean flag indicating hit or miss. Data Structures: midpoints: A vector or struct containing height values at the midpoints of voxel edges. Specifically, midpoints.y represents the height at the midpoint of the edge being traversed. entryuv: The UV coordinate where the ray enters the current voxel face. paralleluv: The UV coordinate parallel to the ray's primary traversal direction along the voxel face. perpendicularuv: The UV coordinate perpendicular to the ray's primary traversal direction, used for logic switching in the upper half of the voxel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Midpoint Height: For the edge being traversed, calculate the height at the midpoint using the two adjacent corner volumes: h{mid} = (h{corner1} + h{corner2}) \times 0.5 2. Determine Traversal Logic Branch: Check the Z-component of the entry UV coordinate (entry\uv.z) to determine the traversal logic branch. If entry\uv.z < 0.5: Use "normal" logic (lower half). If entry\uv.z \ge 0.5: Use "perpendicular" logic (upper half). 3. Calculate Intersection Percentage: Determine how far along the voxel edge the ray intersects the surface by comparing the ray's Y-coordinate (ray\y) against the side value (h{side}) and the midpoint value (h{mid}): p = \frac{ray\y - h{side}}{h{mid} - h{side}} Here, h{side} is the height of the corner at the start of the edge segment being considered. 4. Compute Final Intersection UV: Interpolate between the entry UV and the parallel UV using the calculated percentage p: u{intersect} = entry\uv + p \times (parallel\uv - entry\uv) The source also provides an alternative notation that is mathematically equivalent to the percentage calculation but uses ambiguous notation. 5. Ray Height Comparison: Compare the ray's Y-coordinate at the current step against the intersection height. If ray\y > h{intersect}: The ray is above the surface and marching continues. If ray\y \le h{intersect}: The ray has hit or passed below the surface, and the algorithm returns the color at u{intersect} and breaks. 6. Logic Switching (Upper Half): If the traversal logic branch is "perpendicular" (entry\uv.z \ge 0.5): Switch from using paralleluv to perpendicularuv for the interpolation direction. Adjust the starting point reference to ensure consistent reading direction regardless of ray entry angle. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class UV: def init(self, x, y, z, parallel, perpendicular): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z self.paralleluv = parallel self.perpendicularuv = perpendicular def voxelddamidpointinterpolation(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid, voxelsize): # Standard DDA initialization to find first voxel intersection voxelcoords = (int(rayorigin.x / voxelsize), int(rayorigin.y / voxelsize), int(rayorigin.z / voxelsize)) t = 0.0 entryuv = computeentryuv(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelcoords, voxelsize) while True: # 1. Compute Midpoint Height corner1height = voxelgrid[voxelcoords[0], voxelcoords[1], voxelcoords[2]] corner2height = voxelgrid[voxelcoords[0] + 1, voxelcoords[1], voxelcoords[2]] midpointheight = (corner1height + corner2height) 0.5 # 2. Determine Traversal Logic Branch isupperhalf = entryuv.z >= 0.5 # 3. Calculate Intersection Percentage sideheight = corner1height rayy = rayorigin.y + raydirection.y t denom = midpointheight - sideheight percentage = 0.0 if abs(denom) < 1e-6 else (rayy - sideheight) / denom percentage = max(0.0, min(1.0, percentage)) # 4. Compute Final Intersection UV if isupperhalf: paralleluv = entryuv.perpendicularuv baseuv = entryuv.paralleluv else: paralleluv = entryuv.paralleluv baseuv = entryuv intersectuv = baseuv + percentage (paralleluv - baseuv) # 5. Ray Height Comparison surfaceheight = sideheight + percentage (midpointheight - sideheight) if rayy > surfaceheight: # Standard DDA advance to next voxel boundary t += voxelsize / max(abs(raydirection.x), abs(raydirection.y), abs(raydirection.z)) voxelcoords = (voxelcoords[0] + int(raydirection.x > 0) - int(raydirection.x < 0), voxelcoords[1] + int(raydirection.y > 0) - int(raydirection.y < 0), voxelcoords[2] + int(raydirection.z > 0) - int(raydirection.z < 0)) entryuv = computeentryuv(rayorigin + raydirection t, raydirection, voxelcoords, voxelsize) else: return intersectuv, surfaceheight def computeentryuv(origin, direction, voxelcoords, voxelsize): # Standard DDA entry UV calculation voxelmin = [c voxelsize for c in voxelcoords] tx = (voxelmin[0] - origin.x) / direction.x if direction.x != 0 else float('inf') ty = (voxelmin[1] - origin.y) / direction.y if direction.y != 0 else float('inf') tz = (voxelmin[2] - origin.z) / direction.z if direction.z != 0 else float('inf') tenter = min(tx, ty, tz) entrypos = [origin[i] + direction[i] tenter for i in range(3)] return UV(entrypos[0], entrypos[1], entrypos[2], entrypos, entrypos) Parameters: entryuv: The UV coordinate where the ray enters the voxel face. paralleluv: The UV coordinate parallel to the ray's traversal direction along the voxel face. perpendicularuv: The UV coordinate perpendicular to the ray's traversal direction, used when switching logic for the upper voxel half. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Entry Direction Ambiguity: The algorithm must consistently read from the same starting point to the same ending point regardless of whether the ray enters from above, below, or the side. Failure to fix the start/end reference causes incorrect interpolation. Boundary Threshold at 0.5: The entryuvz < 0.5 check splits the voxel traversal logic. Crossing this threshold requires switching from parallel UV to perpendicular UV and adjusting the entry point reference, otherwise the intersection math breaks. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method is described in an unofficial video tutorial on smooth terrain rendering using voxel DDA raymarching. It references sphere tracing as an alternative approach but focuses on a DDA-based traversal with midpoint interpolation for terrain heightfields. name: Ray Casting via Grid Line Intersection
head: DDA Raycasting, DDA Raycasting with Fish-eye Correction, Horizontal/Vertical Hit Comparison Raycaster, Vertical/Horizontal Collision Casting, Wolfy Style DDA Raycasting
body: This method is a 2D grid-based raycasting algorithm that traces a ray from a player position through a grid of blocks to find the first wall intersection. It distinguishes itself by explicitly calculating vertical and horizontal grid crossings separately, selecting the closest hit between the two traces, and applying a fish-eye correction to the distance for rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 2D grid map (level), player position (player.x, player.y), ray angle (angle), grid cell size (BLOCKSIZE), grid dimensions (MAPSIZEX, MAPSIZEY), small epsilon (EPSILON), and scan mode (scanmode). Output: Hit object containing intersection coordinates (rayx, rayy), direct distance (distancedirect), perpendicular distance (distanceperpendicular), step count, and texture coordinate (texturex). Data Structures: level: A 2D array where level[gridy][gridx] stores wall type or color; a value greater than 0 indicates a wall. shared.wallcolorstextureslist: A dictionary mapping texture IDs to pixel arrays for rendering. Parameters: BLOCKSIZE: The size of each grid cell in world units, used to convert coordinates to grid indices and calculate deltas. MAPSIZEX, MAPSIZEY: The dimensions of the grid in cells, used for boundary checks and loop termination. EPSILON: A small value added to deltayi when ysign is -1 to correctly select the grid index backwards. distanceh: Initial high value (1000000) for horizontal distance to prevent premature selection if no hit occurs. Steps: 1. Initialize horizontal ray parameters: Calculate deltayi as BLOCKSIZE - offsetpy if ysign is 1, else -offsetpy. If deltayi is 0, set distanceh to 1000000. Calculate deltaxi = deltayi (1 / tan(angle)). 2. Adjust deltayi for backward ray direction: If ysign is -1, add -EPSILON to deltayi to ensure correct grid index selection backwards. 3. Compute vertical ray direction: right = abs(floor((angle - π / 2) / π) % 2). 4. Compute first vertical grid line intersection X: firstX = right ? floor(player.x / 1) 1 + 1: floor(player.x / 1) 1. 5. Compute corresponding Y: firstY = player.y + (firstX - player.x) tan(angle). 6. Initialize ray position: rayx = player.x + deltaxi, rayy = player.y + deltayi. 7. Calculate external deltas: deltaye = BLOCKSIZE ysign, deltaxe = abs(1 / tan(angle) BLOCKSIZE) xsign. 8. Set step vectors: xA = right ? 1: -1, yA = xA tan(angle). 9. Loop for horizontal hit detection: Increment stepsh. If stepsh > MAPSIZEX 2, print error and quit. Clamp rayx to [0, MAPSIZEX BLOCKSIZE - 1] and rayy to [0, MAPSIZEY BLOCKSIZE - 1]. 10. Compute grid indices: gridx = int(rayx / BLOCKSIZE), gridy = int(rayy / BLOCKSIZE). Check if gridx or gridy is out of bounds [0, MAPSIZEX) or [0, MAPSIZEY); if so, print error and quit. 11. Advance ray: rayx += deltaxe, rayy += deltaye. 12. Compute horizontal ray direction: up = abs(floor(angle / π) % 2). 13. Compute first horizontal grid line intersection Y: firstY = up ? floor(player.y / 1) 1: floor(player.y / 1) 1 + 1. 14. Compute corresponding X: firstX = player.x + (firstY - player.y) / tan(angle). 15. Set step vectors: yA = up ? -1: 1, xA = yA / tan(angle). 16. Loop stepping: cellX = right ? floor(nextX / 1): floor(nextX / 1) - 1, cellY = floor(nextY / 1). Check bounds. If not a wall, nextX += xA, nextY += yA. 17. Select final hit: Compare distanceh and distancev. If scanmode is 'vertical', use vertical hit. If 'horizontal', use horizontal hit. If 'shortest' (default), use the hit with the smaller distance. Store selected rayx, rayy, distancedirect, steps, and texturex. 18. Return hit object with Euclidean distance: distance = sqrt((player.x - nextX)^2 + (player.y - nextY)^2). Formulas: Fish-eye correction: distanceperpendicular = distancedirect cos(player.viewangle - rayangle). Texture coordinate: texturexh = (nextrayhitxh % BLOCKSIZE) / BLOCKSIZE. Initialize horizontal ray parameters offsetpy = player.y % blocksize ysign = 1 if player.ysign > 0 else -1 deltayi = (blocksize - offsetpy) if ysign == 1 else -offsetpy if deltayi == 0: distanceh = 1000000 deltaxi = deltayi (1.0 / math.tan(angle)) # 2. Adjust deltayi for backward ray direction if ysign == -1: deltayi -= epsilon # 3. Compute vertical ray direction right = abs(math.floor((angle - math.pi / 2) / math.pi) % 2) # 4. Compute first vertical grid line intersection X # Note: Sources use division by 1, adapted here to blocksize for consistency firstx = (math.floor(player.x / blocksize) blocksize + blocksize) if right else (math.floor(player.x / blocksize) blocksize) # 5. Compute corresponding Y firsty = player.y + (firstx - player.x) math.tan(angle) # 6. Initialize ray position rayx = player.x + deltaxi rayy = player.y + deltayi # 7. Calculate external deltas deltaye = blocksize ysign deltaxe = abs(1.0 / math.tan(angle) blocksize) (1 if right else -1) # 8. Set step vectors xstepv = 1 if right else -1 ystepv = xstepv math.tan(angle) # 9-11. Loop for horizontal hit detection stepsh = 0 while stepsh <= mapsizex 2: stepsh += 1 # Advance ray rayx += deltaxe rayy += deltaye # Clamp rayx = max(0.0, min(rayx, mapsizex blocksize - 1)) rayy = max(0.0, min(rayy, mapsizey blocksize - 1)) # Calculate grid indices gridx = int(rayx / blocksize) gridy = int(rayy / blocksize) # Check bounds if not (0 <= gridx < mapsizex and 0 <= gridy < mapsizey): raise ValueError("Out of bounds grid access") if level[gridy][gridx] > 0: break verticalhitdist = math.sqrt((player.x - rayx)2 + (player.y - rayy)2) verticalhit = (0, gridx, gridy, verticalhitdist) # 12. Compute horizontal ray direction up = abs(math.floor(angle / math.pi) % 2) # 13. Compute first horizontal grid line intersection Y firsty = (math.floor(player.y / blocksize) blocksize) if up else (math.floor(player.y / blocksize) blocksize + blocksize) # 14. Compute corresponding X firstx = player.x + (firsty - player.y) / math.tan(angle) # 15. Set step vectors ysteph = -1 if up else 1 xsteph = ysteph / math.tan(angle) # 16. Loop stepping nextx = firstx nexty = firsty while True: cellx = math.floor(nextx / blocksize) celly = (math.floor(nexty / blocksize) - 1) if up else math.floor(nexty / blocksize) if not (0 <= celly < mapsizey and 0 <= cellx < mapsizex): break if level[celly][cellx] == 0: nextx += xsteph nexty += ysteph else: break horizontalhitdist = math.sqrt((player.x - nextx)2 + (player.y - nexty)2) horizontalhit = (1, cellx, celly, horizontalhitdist) # 17. Select final hit if scanmode == 'vertical': selected = verticalhit elif scanmode == 'horizontal': selected = horizontalhit else: selected = verticalhit if verticalhitdist < horizontalhitdist else horizontalhit # 18. Return hit object distancedirect = selected[3] distanceperpendicular = distancedirect math.cos(player.viewangle - angle) # texturexh = (nextrayhitxh % BLOCKSIZE) / BLOCKSIZE hitx = selected[1] blocksize + (selected[0] blocksize) texturex = (hitx % blocksize) / blocksize return { 'side': selected[0], 'gridx': selected[1], 'gridy': selected[2], 'distancedirect': distancedirect, 'distanceperpendicular': distanceperpendicular, 'texturex': texturex } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray direction backward along the Y-axis requires adding -EPSILON to deltayi to ensure correct grid index selection. Out-of-bounds grid access requires clamping coordinates before access and explicit bounds checks, quitting the program if indices fall outside [0, MAPSIZEX) or [0, MAPSIZEY). Infinite loop prevention is enforced by a maximum step count of MAPSIZEX 2 in the horizontal hit detection loop. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Requires computing two separate traces and comparing distances, which may be less efficient than a single unified DDA traversal. name: Fast Voxel Traversal 2D
head: 2D grid traversal, 2D voxel traversal
body:
Fast Voxel Traversal 2D is an algorithm to traverse all 2D grid cells (voxels) that a line segment passes through, used for ray tracing acceleration and line-voxel intersection. It differs from Bresenham's line algorithm, which produces an aesthetic approximation of a line but intentionally omits cells the line passes through to avoid visual 'ugliness'; Fast Voxel Traversal aims to visit all cells intersected by the line. Inputs: Start point (sX, sY), end point (eX, eY), grid origin (x0, y0), cell dimensions (dx, dy). Outputs: List of voxel indices (x, y) visited by the segment. Data Structures: geom: Array of parameters. geom[0] = x0, geom[1] = dx, geom[3] = y0, geom[5] = dy. ptsIndexes: List of integer coordinate pairs. Parameters: MaxDelta: Maximum allowed value for tDelta to prevent division by zero or overflow. Default: 1000000.0. Steps: 1. Initialize Indices: Compute start indices: sXIndex =  rac{sX - x0}{dx} sYIndex =  rac{sY - y0}{dy} Compute end indices: eXIndex =  rac{eX - sXIndex}{dx} + sXIndex eYIndex =  rac{eY - sYIndex}{dy} + sYIndex 2. Compute Deltas and Steps: deltaX = eXIndex - sXIndex stepX =  egin{cases} 1 & 	ext{if } deltaX > 0 \ -1 & 	ext{if } deltaX < 0 \ 0 & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} tDeltaX =  egin{cases} \min\left( rac{stepX}{deltaX}, Max\Deltaight) & 	ext{if } stepX 
eq 0 \ Max\Delta & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} deltaY = eYIndex - sYIndex stepY =  egin{cases} 1 & 	ext{if } deltaY > 0 \ -1 & 	ext{if } deltaY < 0 \ 0 & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} tDeltaY =  egin{cases} \min\left( rac{stepY}{deltaY}, Max\Deltaight) & 	ext{if } stepY 
eq 0 \ Max\Delta & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} 3. Compute Initial Distances to Boundaries: Voxels span from 0.0 to 1.0 (grid-aligned), not -0.5 to 0.5 (center-aligned). maxX =  egin{cases} tDeltaX \cdot (1 - sXIndex + \lfloor sXIndex floor) & 	ext{if } stepX > 0 \ tDeltaX \cdot (sXIndex - \lfloor sXIndex floor) & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} maxY =  egin{cases} tDeltaY \cdot (1 - sYIndex + \lfloor sYIndex floor) & 	ext{if } stepY > 0 \ tDeltaY \cdot (sYIndex - \lfloor sYIndex floor) & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} 4. Traverse: Initialize x = sXIndex, y = sYIndex. Add 	ext{round}(x), 	ext{round}(y) to output. Let prevPt = [	ext{round}(x), 	ext{round}(y)]. Loop: If maxX < maxY: maxX += tDeltaX x += stepX Else: maxY += tDeltaY y += stepY Compute pt = [	ext{round}(x), 	ext{round}(y)]. If pt 
eq prevPt: Append pt to output. prevPt = pt. Break if maxX > 1 and maxY > 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastvoxeltraversal2d(strPt, endPt, geom, MaxDelta=1000000.0): x0 = geom[0] dx = geom[1] y0 = geom[3] dy = geom[5] sX, sY = strPt eX, eY = endPt sXIndex = (sX - x0) / dx sYIndex = (sY - y0) / dy # Note: Formula from source eXIndex = ((eX - sXIndex) / dx) + sXIndex eYIndex = ((eY - sYIndex) / dy) + sYIndex deltaX = float(eXIndex - sXIndex) deltaXSign = 1 if deltaX > 0 else (-1 if deltaX < 0 else 0) stepX = deltaXSign if deltaXSign != 0: tDeltaX = min(deltaXSign / deltaX, MaxDelta) else: tDeltaX = MaxDelta if deltaXSign > 0: maxX = tDeltaX (1 - sXIndex + int(sXIndex)) else: maxX = tDeltaX (sXIndex - int(sXIndex)) deltaY = float(eYIndex - sYIndex) deltaYSign = 1 if deltaY > 0 else (-1 if deltaY < 0 else 0) stepY = deltaYSign if deltaYSign != 0: tDeltaY = min(deltaYSign / deltaY, MaxDelta) else: tDeltaY = MaxDelta if deltaYSign > 0: maxY = tDeltaY (1 - sYIndex + int(sYIndex)) else: maxY = tDeltaY (sYIndex - int(sYIndex)) x = sXIndex y = sYIndex ptsIndexes = [] pt = [round(x), round(y)] ptsIndexes.append(pt) prevPt = pt while True: if maxX < maxY: maxX += tDeltaX x += deltaXSign else: maxY += tDeltaY y += deltaYSign pt = [round(x), round(y)] if pt != prevPt: ptsIndexes.append(pt) prevPt = pt if maxX > 1 and maxY > 1: break return ptsIndexes Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Voxel Coordinate System Mismatch: Voxels span from 0.0 to 1.0 (grid-aligned), not -0.5 to 0.5 (center-aligned). Assuming center-aligned voxels causes incorrect initial maxX and maxY calculations. Diagonal Step Cell Omission: When the traversal makes a diagonal step, it may skip intermediate cells that the line actually passes through. name: Z-order curve traversal with run-length encoding
head: Morton order traversal, Z-curve RLE stream
body: This method traverses a uniform voxel grid in Z-order (Morton) sequence while compressing contiguous runs of identical voxel values into run-length encoded (RLE) records, thereby skipping redundant sampling steps. It uses a flat, stack-based iteration over a padded power-of-two grid structure rather than ray-based advancement or hierarchical tree navigation. Inputs: A uniform voxel grid of dimensions W \times H \times D. Outputs: A stream of IndexedLeaf records, each containing a voxel value and the starting linear index of the run. Data Structures: The traversal state is maintained in a ZStream object and a stack of ZFrame objects. 1. ZFrame struct: size (unsigned int): The side length of the current cube in the Z-order hierarchy. offset (3-component integer vector): Stores the x, y, z coordinates of the cube's origin. i (uint8t): An iterator counter (0–7) tracking which of the 8 children of the current node has been visited. 2. ZStream class fields: model (pointer to voxel data): Reference to the voxel data source. index (unsigned integer): The current linear index in the Z-order stream. open (bool): Flag indicating if the stream has more data. streamleaf (voxel value): The value of the most recently fetched voxel. stack (stack of ZFrame): The traversal stack. power (unsigned int): The exponent such that 2^{power} is the padded grid dimension. streamsize (unsigned integer): The total number of voxels in the padded grid (2^{3 \cdot power}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute power as \lceil \log2(\max(W, H, D)) \rceil and streamsize as 2^{3 \cdot power}. 2. Initialize the stack with a root ZFrame: size = 2^{power}, offset = (0,0,0), i = 0. 3. Initialize index = 0, open = true, and fetch the first voxel using nextcoords() to populate streamleaf. 4. Loop while open is true: call nextcoords() to get the next voxel position and fetch its value from model. 5. If the fetched value equals streamleaf, increment index and repeat the fetch until a different value is found or the stream ends. 6. If the value differs from streamleaf or the stream ends, return an IndexedLeaf containing the previous streamleaf value and the index where that run started, then update streamleaf to the new value and increment index. 7. Coordinate Generation (nextcoords): If frame.size == 1, return frame.offset, pop the frame, backtrack by popping frames where top.i >= 8, set open = false if the stack becomes empty, and increment index. Otherwise, compute childsize = frame.size / 2, determine the child offset by adding childsize to the x, y, or z axis if bits 4, 2, or 1 of frame.i are set, increment frame.i, push a new ZFrame with size = childsize, offset = childoffset, i = 0, and recurse. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nextcoords(stack, indexref): """Generates the next coordinate in Z-order traversal using a stack. Returns the coordinate tuple (x, y, z). Modifies stack and indexref.""" while True: frame = stack[-1] # Base case: leaf node if frame['size'] == 1: coord = frame['offset'] stack.pop() # Backtrack if all 8 children of the parent have been visited while len(stack) > 0 and stack[-1]['i'] >= 8: stack.pop() indexref[0] += 1 return coord # Recursive step: determine child childsize = frame['size'] // 2 childidx = frame['i'] # Calculate child offset based on bits 4, 2, 1 of frame.i offset = list(frame['offset']) # [x, y, z] if childidx & 4: offset[2] += childsize # z-axis if childidx & 2: offset[1] += childsize # y-axis if childidx & 1: offset[0] += childsize # x-axis frame['i'] += 1 # Push new frame for the child newframe = { 'size': childsize, 'offset': tuple(offset), 'i': 0 } stack.append(newframe) # Continue to the next level (simulating recursion) # Loop back to process the new top of the stack def traverserle(model, width, height, depth): """Main traversal function. Returns a list of (value, startindex) tuples.""" power = math.ceil(math.log2(max(width, height, depth))) streamsize = 2 (3 power) stack = [{'size': 2power, 'offset': (0, 0, 0), 'i': 0}] indexref = [0] # Mutable container for index open = True # Fetch first voxel firstcoord = nextcoords(stack, indexref) prevleaf = model.at(firstcoord) results = [] while open: currcoord = nextcoords(stack, indexref) currleaf = model.at(currcoord) if currleaf != prevleaf: results.append((prevleaf, indexref[0])) prevleaf = currleaf # If stack is empty, open becomes false inside nextcoords if not stack: open = False # Append the final run results.append((prevleaf, indexref[0])) return results Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Power-of-Two Dimensions: The grid is padded to the next power of two with implicit empty voxels. Stack Depth: The traversal uses a stack-based iterative approach to simulate recursion, and the stack depth is bounded by the 8-children-per-node limit. Run Compression: If all voxels are identical, the RLE stream contains a single entry; if no runs exist, performance degrades to standard Z-order traversal overhead. Time Complexity: O(N) where N = 2^{3 \cdot power} is the number of voxels in the padded grid. Memory Complexity: O(\log N) for the traversal stack. Performance: Highly efficient for volumes with large homogeneous regions; performance degrades if the volume is noisy or lacks contiguous runs. Strengths: Simple stack-based implementation, predictable cache-friendly traversal pattern, and effective compression for coherent data. Limitations: Requires power-of-two padding which wastes memory for non-aligned dimensions, and is unsuitable for highly sparse data without significant overhead. The method is derived from the Zazen project by Gabriel Müller, which implements a Z-order curve traversal with run-length encoding for volume rendering. It leverages the spatial locality of Morton order to provide a predictable traversal pattern while compressing redundant data. gabrielmuller/zazen, https://github.com/gabrielmuller/zazen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Octree and Tree Traversal
body: Octree and Tree Traversal methods determine which nodes of a hierarchical spatial structure (typically an octree or sparse voxel octree) a ray intersects, enabling efficient rendering of sparse volumetric data by skipping empty space. Unlike uniform grid ray marching which samples every voxel, these methods use the tree hierarchy to jump over empty regions, reducing computational cost. They differ from BVH-based approaches by operating directly on the octree structure without an intermediate bounding volume hierarchy, although some implementations may convert the SVO to a BVH for specific traversal optimizations. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of hierarchical descent and ascent. The traversal begins at the root of the octree and determines which of the eight children (octants) the ray intersects. This is typically done by comparing the ray's position relative to the center of the current node's bounding box. 1. Child Selection: For a node with center \mathbf{c} and half-extent s, the ray position \mathbf{p} determines the child index k \in \{0, \dots, 7\}: k = 4 \cdot \mathbb{I}(px \ge cx) + 2 \cdot \mathbb{I}(py \ge cy) + 1 \cdot \mathbb{I}(pz \ge cz) where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function. 2. Empty Space Skipping: If the selected child is marked as empty (or uniform), the traversal skips the subtree. This is achieved by advancing the ray parameter t to the exit of the current node or using neighbor pointers to jump to the next potentially occupied node. 3. Leaf Handling: Upon reaching a leaf node, the method typically switches to a fixed-step traversal (like DDA) within the leaf's voxel grid to sample the volume data. 4. Backtracking: Because octrees are sparse and irregular, traversal often requires backtracking to the parent node when a ray exits a subtree or encounters an empty branch. This is implemented using an explicit stack (on GPU) or recursion (on CPU). Hermite Data Computation via Bisection precisely locates isosurface intersections on the edges of an adaptive octree's leaf cells and computes surface normals. It solves geometric inaccuracy in dual contouring by refining intersection positions to sub-cell accuracy for Quadratic Error Function (QEF) vertex placement, unlike Octree Path Computation which focuses on traversal efficiency. Stackless Traversal eliminates the explicit stack data structure in hierarchical volume traversal by recalculating Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) parameters at every descent and ascent step. It trades increased computational cost for zero stack memory usage, making it advantageous in memory-constrained environments like early GPU architectures. This method decouples branch-intensive octree traversal from the raycasting loop using a rasterization pass to identify active volume regions and a shadow mapping pass for lighting. It solves performance bottlenecks on sparse data by moving empty-space culling into a graphics pipeline stage, achieving 2 to 4 times faster rendering than state-of-the-art algorithms on large out-of-core datasets. This method extends the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm to N-ary hierarchical trees for GPU shader implementation. It solves efficient traversal of sparse voxel structures by maintaining a small, fixed-size stack of DDA states, allowing descent and ascent without dynamic memory allocation. Compositing Tree Rendering minimizes computational cost for time-varying volume rendering by rendering only modified data subtrees and compositing them with retained partial images of unmodified data. It differs from standard incremental rendering by maintaining a persistent hierarchical structure that mirrors the data's compressed octree, enabling efficient spatial updates without full re-rendering. The Tree Marcher is a hierarchical ray traversal algorithm designed to step a ray through a generic grid structure (such as OpenVDB) to identify intersections with active nodes. It solves efficient navigation of sparse, multi-resolution volumetric data by skipping empty subtrees and returning precise intersection intervals for occupied nodes, bridging coarse hierarchical culling and fine-grained voxel sampling. Camera-Driven Octree Subdivision constructs a spatial hierarchy by recursively splitting nodes based on the proximity of visible camera centers to the node's center. It solves efficient mapping of 3D space into local warp spaces for multi-view rendering by ensuring regions near cameras are represented with higher resolution, using camera-centric distance metrics rather than data density. JIT Type Specialization performs type resolution and function routing at Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation time, inlining traversal, type checks, and address lookups to eliminate switch statements and runtime overhead. It sets itself apart from standard dynamic dispatch by making access time independent of the number of elemental node types, as specialized code paths are baked into the executable. Ray Traversal Algorithms are a family of hierarchical methods that determine the sequence of nodes or cells intersected by a ray within a spatial data structure, primarily to accelerate volume rendering and surface intersection tests. This family is distinguished from Stackless Traversal by its explicit reliance on parent-child pointer relationships and backtracking logic rather than encoding traversal state into a bitstream. Tetrahedralization of Octree Cells generates a manifold isosurface from an adaptive octree by constructing a dual simplicial partition. It solves self-intersections and non-manifold vertices inherent in adaptive octrees by creating a dual structure that ensures convexity and manifold topology, unlike Dual Marching Tetrahedra (DMC) which can produce self-intersecting flaps. Topology-Caching is a GPU-based volume rendering technique for interactive visualization of dynamic particle systems (e.g., SPH) that reconstructs a scalar field via raycasting without preprocessing. It solves the performance bottleneck of gathering particle contributions by using three GPU-managed caches: a node-cache for accelerated tree traversal, an influence-cache for fast particle access, and a slab-cache for intermediate compositing. Budgeted-GS Factoring LOD is a hierarchical level-of-detail method for real-time large-scale Gaussian Splatting that reduces rendering cost by aggregating primitives into equivalent planks based on a pixel-footprint budget. It solves rendering millions of Gaussians in real-time by dynamically selecting between raw primitives, fine equivalent planks, or coarse aggregate planks depending on distance and scale relative to the camera. Hierarchical Tree Node Traversal accelerates ray-volume intersection by traversing a sparse octree structure to identify contiguous segments of active data. It solves inefficiently sampling empty space in large volumetric datasets by skipping inactive nodes and resolving hits at the node level rather than the individual voxel level, providing entry and exit times for line-integration. Frustum and Visibility Culling methods optimize volume rendering by identifying and discarding geometry that does not contribute to the final image, thereby reducing computational load. This family distinguishes itself from sibling traversal methods by decoupling visibility determination from the core sampling loop, often serving as a pre-pass or integrated filter to limit the working set of voxels, splats, or bricks. Data Structure and Indexing defines how hierarchical volume data (typically octrees) is organized in memory and accessed during ray traversal. It solves efficiently mapping spatial coordinates to volume samples while minimizing memory bandwidth and traversal overhead, focusing on storage layout and connectivity required to support traversal algorithms. An Octree Sampled SDF Dataset generates signed-distance function (SDF) samples from a sparse octree acceleration structure constructed from a single mesh shape. It limits sampling to occupied octree cells, supports equal distribution of samples per cell, and allows online resampling via a cached narrowband pool, optionally including RGB data derived from mesh textures. Spatial hierarchies organize volumetric or geometric primitives into a tree structure to accelerate ray intersection tests and point location. They solve the problem of O(N) linear scans by enabling O(\log N) traversal, reducing the number of samples required to render a volume, and adapt to data sparsity by skipping empty regions entirely. Octree-based Entropy Rendering accelerates volume rendering by using hierarchical error metrics stored in non-leaf octree nodes to skip or approximate low-entropy regions. Unlike standard traversal which visits all occupied nodes, this method dynamically adjusts traversal granularity based on a user-defined error tolerance or time budget, trading visual fidelity for performance in smooth or transparent areas. Store incoming radiance from a light source in the octree leaves by rendering the scene from the light's view using standard rasterization to output a world position map (light-view map), where each pixel represents a photon. Photons are splatted using a fragment shader with one thread per light-view-map pixel, storing them as a direction distribution and energy proportional to the subtended solid angle of the pixel as seen from the light. Atomic add operations are used to handle multiple photons ending up in the same voxel, though they are currently only available for integer textures, requiring a 16-bit normalized texture format denormalized upon access. Voxels are repeated for adjacent bricks for fast hardware-supported filtering, but copying photons directly to all required locations in adjacent bricks leads to many thread collisions and bandwidth issues. A rendering strategy that uses the tree representation to perform selective rendering efficiently, reducing I/O costs and enabling distribution of data and calculations to multiple workstations. It examines the encoded data to identify partial images built from subtrees which have not changed, and reuses the identified unchanged partial images in the following time steps. A smaller leaf-node size leads to less overlap of node lists between image tiles, but increases storage and traversal overhead. A storage format where the volume is stored as a flat hierarchy of bricks of size n^3 to improve cache-coherence, derived from fully expanded octrees. It uses an efficient indexing scheme to quickly find the memory address of voxels located in the 8-neighborhood required for trilinear interpolation. The use of octrees for volume rendering originated as a method to handle sparse data efficiently, reducing memory usage and traversal time compared to uniform grids. Early implementations focused on minimizing the number of transparent voxels during accumulation. The concept of using hierarchical structures for time-varying data was explored to reduce I/O costs and enable selective rendering, allowing unchanged subtrees to be reused across time steps. Modern implementations often combine these hierarchical traversal techniques with GPU-specific optimizations, such as stackless traversal or mini-stacks, to handle the parallel nature of volume rendering on graphics hardware. name: Ray Marching with Octant Masking
head: Ray march, Ray struct
body: Ray Marching with Octant Masking advances a ray origin in discrete steps through a voxel grid, using a precomputed octant mask to track traversal direction and state. It builds on standard ray-grid traversal principles by maintaining a fixed-step march loop rather than analytically computing exact boundary crossings. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, and a step amount. Outputs: Updated ray origin, traversal state, and visibility mask. Data Structures: The core data structure is the Ray struct, which contains origin (Vector), direction (Vector), negdir (Vector, unused in the reference implementation), and initorigin (Vector, private). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize initorigin with the starting ray position. 2. Clamp any direction component with magnitude below \epsilon to \pm\epsilon with the same sign to prevent division by zero or degenerate cases. 3. Compute an 8-bit octantmask based on the direction signs: bit 2 (value 4) is set if direction.x >= 0, bit 1 (value 2) if direction.y >= 0, and bit 0 (value 1) if direction.z >= 0. 4. Advance the ray origin by \mathbf{o} \leftarrow \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \times \text{amount} using the march function. 5. Track traversal progress using squaredistance(), which computes (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{init\origin})^2 to check against maximum bounds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin.copy() self.direction = direction.copy() self.negdir = direction.copy() # Unused in reference implementation self.initorigin = origin.copy() self.clampdirection() def clampdirection(self): epsilon = 1e-6 for i in range(3): if abs(self.direction[i]) < epsilon: self.direction[i] = epsilon if self.direction[i] >= 0 else -epsilon def octantmask(self): mask = 0 if self.direction[0] >= 0: mask |= 4 if self.direction[1] >= 0: mask |= 2 if self.direction[2] >= 0: mask |= 1 return mask def march(self, amount): self.origin = self.origin + self.direction amount return self def squaredistance(self): return sum((self.origin[i] - self.initorigin[i]) 2 for i in range(3)) Edge Cases: Zero direction components are clamped to \pm\epsilon to avoid numerical instability. Boundary checks rely on external logic comparing squaredistance() against a maximum squared distance, as the core march function does not inherently validate grid bounds. This method renders dense voxel data by combining geometry shader instancing for component-level bounding boxes with ray marching through dense volume textures for the interior. It sets itself apart from pure instancing or static vertex buffers by using a neighbor-sensitive bitmask to determine voxel visibility based on adjacent components, effectively hiding internal faces without storing dense geometry for every voxel. This hybrid approach allows for dynamic updates without recomputing complex meshes while avoiding the high vertex count of instanced cubes. It is chosen when dynamic voxel updates are required without heavy mesh recomputation, and it builds on Ray Marching with Octant Masking by replacing octant-based traversal with uniform grid ray marching through a 2D array texture. Time complexity is O(N) where N is the number of steps, with O(1) work per step. Memory complexity is O(1) auxiliary space for the ray state. Measured performance with specific hardware, resolution, and scene: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths include simple implementation, low overhead per step, and easy integration with GPU shaders. Limitations include fixed step size potentially causing aliasing or missed features if too large, and lower efficiency than analytical traversal for sparse data since it samples uniformly along the path. When to use: dense voxel rendering where simplicity and uniform sampling are prioritized over precise boundary detection. The method is documented in the open-source project zazen by Gabriel Muller, which implements a voxel ray marcher using this specific octant masking technique. gabrielmuller/zazen, https://github.com/gabrielmuller/zazen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching Voxel Textures with Neighbor-Sensitive Masking
head: Hybrid Geometry-Shader-spawned cubes with ray marched volume textures, Voxel Mask Ray Marching
body: This method renders dense voxel data by combining geometry shader instancing for component-level bounding boxes with ray marching through dense volume textures for the interior. It utilizes a neighbor-sensitive bitmask to determine voxel visibility based on adjacent components, effectively hiding internal faces without storing dense geometry for every voxel. Unlike pure instancing or static vertex buffers, this hybrid approach allows for dynamic updates without recomputing complex meshes while avoiding the high vertex count of instanced cubes. It builds on Ray Marching with Octant Masking by replacing octant-based traversal with uniform grid ray marching through a 2D array texture. Inputs: gsobjectPosition: vec3, the position of the component in world space. gsneighbormaterialmipmap: ivec3, flat input from geometry shader. x: Bits 0-5 are neighbor material flags; bits 24-31 are materialIndex. y: codes.x for neighbor material. z: LOD level index (mipmap level). gstexCoord: vec3, texture coordinates within the component box. ucomponentTex: isampler2DArray, uniform volume texture storing voxel data. Each texel fetch returns a 2D code (ivec2). cmWorldView: mat4x4, world-view matrix. cmInverseWorldView: mat4x4, inverse world-view matrix. cmaxTexRes: int, maximum texture resolution used to calculate LOD-dependent texel size. Outputs: fragColor: vec4, the final color of the fragment. Voxel Mask: An integer bitmask where each bit represents a side of the voxel (bits 0-5) and one bit (bit 6, 0x40) represents non-side-dependent voxels. The mask is computed as: \text{voxelMask} = 0x40 \mid ((\sim \text{gs\neighbor\material\mipmap}.x) \ \& \ 0x3f) Visibility is determined by combining this mask with the texture mask using a logical AND: (codes.y & voxelMask) == 0 indicates the voxel is not visible. Ray Marching State: rayPos: ivec3, current voxel coordinates in the texture. d: vec3, distance to the next plane crossing along each axis. projLength: vec3, projected distance between planes (1 / |\text{dir}|). dirSign: ivec3, sign of the view direction components (1 if \ge 0, -1 if < 0). 1. Compute Component-Space Position: Calculate the position in chunk/component space: \text{chunkSpacePos} = \text{gs\objectPosition} + \text{gs\texCoord} - 0.5 2. Transform View Direction: Transform the view direction to chunk space: \text{viewDir} = \text{normalize}((\text{vec4}(\text{chunkSpacePos}, 1) \times \text{c\mWorldView}).\text{xyz}) \text{chunkSpaceDir} = \text{viewDir} \times \text{mat3x3}(\text{c\mInverseWorldView}) 3. Calculate Texture Resolution: Determine the current texture size based on LOD: \text{texSize} = \text{c\maxTexRes} / (1 \ll \text{gs\neighbor\material\mipmap}.z) 4. Initialize Ray Marching: Compute direction signs: \text{dirSign}.x = (\text{chunkSpaceDir}.x < 0.0) ? -1: 1 \text{dirSign}.y = (\text{chunkSpaceDir}.y < 0.0) ? -1: 1 \text{dirSign}.z = (\text{chunkSpaceDir}.z < 0.0) ? -1: 1 Calculate initial voxel position and ray position: \text{voxelPos} = \text{gs\texCoord} \times (\text{texSize} - 0.00001) \text{rayPos} = \text{ivec3}(\text{voxelPos}) Compute projected lengths and initial distances: \text{absDir} = |\text{chunkSpaceDir}| \text{projLength} = 1.0 / (\text{absDir} + 0.0001) d = \text{voxelPos} - \text{rayPos} Adjust d based on direction signs: If \text{dirSign}.x == 1, d.x = 1 - d.x (same for y, z). d = d \times \text{projLength} 5. Ray March Loop: If materialIndex != 0 and texSize > 1: Fetch initial voxel code: \text{codes} = \text{texelFetch}(\text{u\componentTex}, \text{ivec3}(\text{rayPos}.x + \text{rayPos}.y \times \text{texSize}, \text{rayPos}.z, \text{materialIndex}), \text{gs\voxel\material\mipmap}.z).\text{xy} While (codes.y & voxelMask) == 0: Determine step direction: If d.x < d.y or d.z < d.y: If d.x < d.z: Step in X. \text{rayPos}.x += \text{dirSign}.x d.yz -= d.x d.x = \text{projLength}.x Else: Step in Z. \text{rayPos}.z += \text{dirSign}.z d.xy -= d.z d.z = \text{projLength}.z Else: Step in Y. \text{rayPos}.y += \text{dirSign}.y d.xz -= d.y d.y = \text{projLength}.y Boundary Check: If \text{rayPos} \ge \text{ivec3}(\text{texSize}, \text{texSize}, \text{texSize}) or \text{rayPos} < \text{ivec3}(0, 0, 0), discard fragment. Fetch next voxel code: \text{codes} = \text{texelFetch}(\text{u\componentTex}, \text{ivec3}(\text{rayPos}.x + \text{rayPos}.y \times \text{texSize}, \text{rayPos}.z, \text{materialIndex}), \text{gs\voxel\material\mipmap}.z).\text{xy} 6. Estimate Normal: Calculate distance to plane intersection: d = |d - \text{projLength}| Determine normal based on which axis had the smallest distance (indicating the plane crossed): If d.x < 0.0001: \text{normal} = -\text{dirSign}.x \times \text{vec3}(\text{c\mWorldView}[0][0], \text{c\mWorldView}[1][0], \text{c\mWorldView}[2][0]) Else if d.y < 0.0001: \text{normal} = -\text{dirSign}.y \times \text{vec3}(\text{c\mWorldView}[0][1], \text{c\mWorldView}[1][1], \text{c\mWorldView}[2][1]) Else if d.z < 0.0001: \text{normal} = -\text{dirSign}.z \times \text{vec3}(\text{c\mWorldView}[0][2], \text{c\mWorldView}[1][2], \text{c\mWorldView}[2][2]) Normalize the normal: \text{normal} = \text{normalize}(\text{normal}) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def main(): # 1. Compute Component-Space Position chunkSpacePos = gsobjectPosition + gstexCoord - 0.5 # 2. Transform View Direction viewDir = normalize((vec4(chunkSpacePos, 1) cmWorldView).xyz) chunkSpaceDir = viewDir mat3x3(cmInverseWorldView) # 3. Calculate Texture Resolution texSize = cmaxTexRes / (1 << gsneighbormaterialmipmap.z) # 4. Initialize Ray Marching dirSign = ivec3(1, 1, 1) if chunkSpaceDir.x < 0.0: dirSign.x = -1 if chunkSpaceDir.y < 0.0: dirSign.y = -1 if chunkSpaceDir.z < 0.0: dirSign.z = -1 voxelPos = gstexCoord (texSize - 0.00001) rayPos = ivec3(voxelPos) absDir = abs(chunkSpaceDir) projLength = 1.0 / (absDir + 0.0001) d = voxelPos - rayPos if dirSign.x == 1: d.x = 1.0 - d.x if dirSign.y == 1: d.y = 1.0 - d.y if dirSign.z == 1: d.z = 1.0 - d.z d = d projLength # 5. Ray March Loop materialIndex = gsneighbormaterialmipmap.x >> 24 if materialIndex != 0 and texSize > 1: # Compute voxel mask voxelMask = 0x40 | ((~gsneighbormaterialmipmap.x) & 0x3f) # Fetch initial code texCoord = ivec3(rayPos.x + rayPos.y texSize, rayPos.z, materialIndex) codes = texelFetch(ucomponentTex, texCoord, gsneighbormaterialmipmap.z).xy while (codes.y & voxelMask) == 0: # Determine step direction if d.x < d.y or d.z < d.y: if d.x < d.z: rayPos.x += dirSign.x d.yz -= d.x d.x = projLength.x else: rayPos.z += dirSign.z d.xy -= d.z d.z = projLength.z else: rayPos.y += dirSign.y d.xz -= d.y d.y = projLength.y # Boundary Check if any(rayPos >= ivec3(texSize, texSize, texSize)) or any(rayPos < ivec3(0, 0, 0)): discard() # Fetch next code texCoord = ivec3(rayPos.x + rayPos.y texSize, rayPos.z, materialIndex) codes = texelFetch(ucomponentTex, texCoord, gsneighbormaterialmipmap.z).xy # 6. Estimate Normal d = abs(d - projLength) normal = vec3(0.0) if d.x < 0.0001: normal = -dirSign.x vec3(cmWorldView[0][0], cmWorldView[1][0], cmWorldView[2][0]) elif d.y < 0.0001: normal = -dirSign.y vec3(cmWorldView[0][1], cmWorldView[1][1], cmWorldView[2][1]) elif d.z < 0.0001: normal = -dirSign.z vec3(cmWorldView[0][2], cmWorldView[1][2], cmWorldView[2][2]) normal = normalize(normal) # Output color (implementation specific) fragColor = vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Placeholder for shading cmaxTexRes: The maximum texture resolution. Typical value is not explicitly stated as a number, but used to calculate texSize. Boundary Check: If rayPos exceeds texture bounds (>= texSize or < 0), the fragment must be discarded to prevent out-of-bounds access. LOD Artifacts: Computing LOD in the fragment shader causes artifacts because a LOD seam can run through a single component, creating holes. LOD is computed in the geometry shader instead. The parent method using octant-based traversal. This method replaces it with uniform grid ray marching through volume textures for better performance on dense data. A related technique using octrees for efficient ray-casting of 3D textures. This method differs by using uniform grids and volume textures, avoiding the complexity of octree traversal for dynamic transformations. Time Complexity: The method reduces frame time from over 20ms to 3-4ms on a notebook GTX850M for 62,663 components with 16x16x16 voxels each. Memory Complexity: Uses volume textures for dense internal data, avoiding the high vertex count of instanced cubes. Performance: Renders approximately 256 million theoretical voxels in 4.45ms on a notebook GTX850M. Strengths: Allows dynamic updates without recomputing complex meshes; avoids high vertex count; efficient for dense voxel data. Limitations: More sensitive to screen resolution; LOD artifacts if computed in fragment shader. When to Use: When rendering dense voxel data with dynamic updates and a blocky aesthetic is desired. When Not to Use: When continuous surfaces are required (e.g., marching cubes) or when memory bandwidth is severely constrained. This method was developed by Johannes Jendersie for the project Monolith, addressing the unbearable 20ms frame time of previous approaches. It was introduced in May 2015. The technique leverages the observation that components consist of the same voxel patterns repeatedly, allowing for a hybrid approach of geometry shader instancing and ray marching. It was used to render stone and water components with 16x16x16 voxels each.
