name: Stackless Traversal
head: Algorithme sans pile, Parcours sans pile, Parent-link traversal, Stack-less Tree Traversal
body: Stackless Traversal is a method for traversing hierarchical volume structures (such as N3-trees or octrees) that eliminates the need for an explicit stack data structure by recalculating Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) parameters at every descent and ascent. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like DDA Tree Traversal with Mini-Stack by relying on parent pointers stored within the hierarchy to navigate, trading memory usage for computational cost. This approach is particularly advantageous in memory-constrained environments, such as early GPU architectures where dynamic array indexing forced stack data into slow local memory. The algorithm traverses a hierarchical grid by maintaining the current ray state and navigating the tree structure using explicit parent links. Unlike stack-based methods that push and pop nodes, this method recalculates the ray's entry point and DDA deltas whenever it moves between a parent and child node. Input: Ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; Hierarchical volume structure where each node stores a pointer to its parent and its spatial bounds; Grid resolution and voxel size. Output: A sequence of visited nodes (bricks) and their corresponding traversal intervals [t{entry}, t{exit}] for volume integration. The hierarchical structure must support: 1. Parent Pointer: Each node contains a reference to its immediate parent node. 2. Child Pointer: Each node contains references to its children (if not a leaf). 3. Spatial Bounds: Each node stores its minimum and maximum coordinates (or index ranges) to define its voxel extent. 4. Node Type/Status: Flags indicating if the node is empty, a leaf (brick), or an internal node. For a uniform grid with voxel size v and dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz, the traversal relies on three key precomputed values per axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: 1. Step Direction (\text{step}i): \text{step}i = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } di > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } di < 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } di = 0 \end{cases} 2. Time/Distance Delta (\Delta ti): \Delta ti = \frac{vi}{|di|} \cdot \text{step}i If di = 0, the ray never crosses a boundary in that dimension, and the corresponding distance is treated as infinity. 3. Time/Distance to Next Boundary (t{max, i}): t{max, i} = \frac{\text{boundary}i - oi}{di} The initial boundary is determined by the starting voxel index. 1. Initialization: Compute initial DDA parameters (\text{step}, \Delta t, t{max}) for the ray origin within the root node's bounds. Identify the starting leaf node containing the ray origin. 2. Process Current Node: If the current node is empty, skip it and proceed to the next step (ascent). If the current node is a leaf (brick): Perform ray marching within the brick's volume. If data is unavailable (e.g., dynamic loading failure), use the stored average and accumulate it based on the distance traversed by the ray in that brick (pre-integration). If the current node is an internal node, proceed to navigation. 3. Navigation (Descent/Ascent): Ascent: If the ray exits the current node, use the parent pointer stored in the structure to move to the parent node. This link points directly to the exact sub-node of the parent, allowing extraction of the current cell information in the parent's grid without recalculation. Descent: If the ray enters a child node, recalculate all DDA parameters (\text{step}, \Delta t, t{max}) for the new node. 4. Loop: Repeat steps 2-3 until the ray exits the entire volume hierarchy. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stacklesstraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, rootnode, voxelsize): # DDA initialization step = [1 if d > 0 else (-1 if d < 0 else 0) for d in raydirection] tdelta = [voxelsize / abs(d) if d != 0 else float('inf') for d in raydirection] # Find initial leaf node containing rayorigin currentnode = findleaf(rootnode, rayorigin) currentrayt = 0.0 while currentnode is not None: # Compute distance to next boundary on each axis for current node tmax = computetmax(rayorigin, raydirection, currentnode.bounds, step, tdelta) # Exit time from current node texit = min(tmax) # Process node based on type if currentnode.isempty: # Skip empty node, advance ray to exit currentrayt += texit rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection texit # Ascent: move to parent via stored pointer currentnode = currentnode.parent continue if currentnode.isleaf: # Ray march within brick bounds processbrick(currentnode, rayorigin, raydirection, texit) currentrayt += texit rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection texit # Ascent: move to parent via stored pointer currentnode = currentnode.parent continue # Internal node: descend to child containing ray # Child index from ray position relative to node center center = currentnode.center childidx = 4 (rayorigin.x >= center.x) + 2 (rayorigin.y >= center.y) + (rayorigin.z >= center.z) # Descent: move to child currentnode = currentnode.children[childidx] # Recalculate all DDA parameters for the new child node tmax = computetmax(rayorigin, raydirection, currentnode.bounds, step, tdelta) # Advance ray to child entry point tentry = min(tmax) currentrayt += tentry rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection tentry return def findleaf(root, point): node = root while not node.isleaf: center = node.center idx = 4 (point.x >= center.x) + 2 (point.y >= center.y) + (point.z >= center.z) node = node.children[idx] return node def computetmax(origin, direction, bounds, step, tdelta): tmax = [] for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: tmax.append(float('inf')) else: boundary = bounds.max[i] if step[i] > 0 else bounds.min[i] tmax.append((boundary - origin[i]) / direction[i]) return tmax def processbrick(leaf, origin, direction, texit): # Standard fixed-step sampling within leaf bounds [tentry, texit] pass Conditional Block Size: Limit the size of if...then...else bodies to reduce divergent threads on GPU multiprocessors. Register Usage: Limit the number of registers used to allow multiprocessors to handle more parallel threads, better covering texture access latency. GPU Memory Latency: On architectures like the NVIDIA G80, dynamically indexed arrays are placed in "local" memory (device memory), which is uncached and up to 50x slower than registers. This negatively impacts performance compared to register-based stack access. Local memory accesses incur maximum latency and transfer cost from graphics memory. Zero Direction Components: When di = 0, the ray never crosses a boundary in that dimension, and the corresponding distance is treated as infinity to prevent division by zero. A variant for BVHs that uses a bit-array to track processed subtrees, allowing complete stack exhaustion without state loss. Choose this when memory is extremely constrained and restarts are frequent. Time Complexity: Higher per-node computational cost due to DDA recalculation at every ascent/descent. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary stack space (excluding the tree structure itself). Performance: On the NVIDIA G80 GPU, the stackless algorithm was approximately 50% faster than the mini-stack algorithm. This result is attributed to the G80's shader compiler placing dynamically indexed arrays (used for the stack) in slow, uncached local memory, whereas the stackless method kept data in registers or faster memory spaces. Strengths: No stack overflow risk; minimal memory footprint; efficient on hardware with slow local memory for dynamic arrays. Limitations: Higher arithmetic intensity per node visit; requires parent pointers in the data structure. When to Use: Memory-constrained environments (e.g., embedded systems, early GPUs); scenarios where stack depth is unpredictable or large. When Not to Use: Hardware with fast, cached local memory and efficient stack operations; scenes with very shallow hierarchies where recalculation overhead outweighs stack costs. The Stackless Traversal algorithm was developed and tested for traversing hierarchical volume structures (N3-tree/octree). It was designed to address the limitations of stack-based methods on early GPU architectures (specifically the G80) where dynamic memory indexing was penalized by the hardware compiler. The method leverages parent pointers stored in the hierarchical structure to navigate without a stack, recalculating DDA parameters to maintain correctness. name: Restart Trail
head: Generalized Restart Trail, Restart Trail for Wide BVHs, Short Stack BVH Traversal, Short stack traversal with restart trail, Wide BVH Traversal with Short Stack, Wide BVH Traversal with a Short Stack
body: Restart Trail is a stackless or short-stack traversal algorithm for Bounding Volume Hierarchies (BVHs) that enables traversal restarts from the root by storing one bit of data per hierarchy level to track which parts of the tree have been processed. It sets itself apart from standard short-stack traversal by allowing the stack to be completely exhausted without losing traversal state, using a compact bit-array (the "trail") to resume from the correct point, whereas methods like Stack Culling trade a small increase in traversal steps for reduced primitive intersections using only 1 bit of extra storage per stack entry. It solves the problem of memory-constrained traversal (e.g., in hardware or GPUs) where a full stack is too large, by replacing the stack with a fixed-size short stack and a restart mechanism that avoids re-entering already processed subtrees. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray, an N-wide BVH (where N is the number of children per internal node), and a short stack of fixed size (typically 5 entries). Output: The closest intersection (for closest-hit) or all intersections (for any-hit), traversing the BVH. Data Structures: 1. Restart Trail (trail): An array of bits (for binary BVHs) or counters (for N-wide BVHs) with one entry per hierarchy level. For binary BVHs: trail is a single register (trailReg) of 32 or 64 bits. trail[0] is a sentinel. trail[i] corresponds to the node at level i. For N-wide BVHs: trail[i] is a counter ranging from 0 to N-1. trail[i] stores the number of children at level i already processed. N-1 indicates the current subtree is the last child at that level. 2. Level Register (levelReg): A register with exactly one bit set, corresponding to the bit position in trailReg pointing to the parent of the current node. Initialized to 10000... (1 followed by zeros) for the sentinel. 3. Short Stack: A fixed-size array of node references. Each entry may include a reserved bit to mark if the entry corresponds to the last child of its parent node. 4. Pop Level (popLevel): An integer tracking the level where the last stack pop would have taken the traversal. Initialized to NONE. Parameters: N: The width of the BVH (number of children per internal node). Short Stack Size: A small fixed number of entries (e.g., 5) stored in on-chip memory. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set node to ROOT. Set trail to all zeros (or counters to 0). Set level to 0. Set shortstack to empty. Set popLevel to NONE. 2. Traversal Loop: While the current node is not a leaf: a. Intersect Children: Intersect the ray against all children of node. Let H be the list of intersecting children. b. Sort: Sort H by increasing hit distance to obtain sorted list S. c. Handle Multiple Hits (Binary BVH Logic): If both children are intersected: Identify near child (smaller t{min}) and far child (greater t{min}). Increment level (shift levelReg right by 1). If trail[level] is 1 (bit set): Set node to far. (The near child has been fully processed or skipped). Else: Set node to near. Push far onto the short stack. If only one child is intersected: Increment level. If level \neq popLevel: Set trail[level] to 1. Set node to the intersected child. Else (level == popLevel): Invoke POP(). This handles the case where the far child was culled during the processing of the near child. If no children are intersected: Invoke POP(). d. Handle Multiple Hits (N-wide BVH Logic): Let k = \text{trail}[\text{level}]. If k = N-1: Remove all but the last entry in S to form Q. (Current subtree is the last one). Else: Remove the first k entries in S to form Q. (Skip already processed children). If Q is empty: Call POP(trail, level). Else: Set node to the first entry in Q. Remove the first entry from Q. If Q is empty: Set trail[level] to N-1. Else: Mark the last entry in Q as the "last child" and push remaining entries in Q onto the short stack (back-to-front order). 3. Leaf Processing: Intersect the ray against primitives in the leaf node. If a closer primitive is found, shorten the ray at the end. Invoke POP(). 4. POP() Operation: Find Parent Level: Scan the restart trail upwards from the current level. Skip levels with the max count value (N-1 for wide BVHs, or bit=1 for binary BVHs where it indicates completion). Find the largest i \le \text{level} such that trail[i] is 0 (binary) or < N-1 (wide). If no such level exists (all scanned levels are maxed), the stack is empty and traversal is complete. Update Trail: Increment trail[parentLevel] (wide BVH) or set trail[parentLevel] to 1 (binary BVH). Clear all counters/bits below parentLevel to 0. Update State: If short stack is empty: Set node to ROOT, level to 0. Restart traversal. Else: Pop from short stack. If popped node is tagged as "last child": Set trail[parentLevel] to N-1 (wide BVH). If popped node is tagged as "parent node" (Stack Culling extension): Set level to parentLevel. Else: Set level to parentLevel + 1. Save Pop Level: If a node's near child is marked as fully processed (bit set in trail for binary, or counter incremented for wide), save the level of that node into popLevel. Pseudocode (N-wide BVH, generalizing): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def restarttrailtraverse(ray, root, bvhwidth, maxdepth, shortstacksize=5): # Initialization trail = [0] maxdepth level = 0 node = root shortstack = [] while True: # Traverse down while not node.isleaf(): # Intersect children hits = [] for child in node.children: t = ray.intersect(child.bvhnode) if t is not None: hits.append((t, child)) # Sort by hit distance hits.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Skip already processed children k = trail[level] if k == bvhwidth - 1: # Current subtree is the last one, keep only the last child q = hits[-1:] if hits else [] else: # Skip first k children q = hits[k:] if not q: # Stack underflow, pop node, level, shortstack, done = pop(trail, level, shortstack, bvhwidth, root) if done: return None continue # Proceed to next node node = q[0][1] q.pop(0) if not q: trail[level] = bvhwidth - 1 else: # Mark last child and push to stack q[-1][1].islastchild = True # Push back-to-front for childnode, in reversed(q): if len(shortstack) < shortstacksize: shortstack.append(childnode) # Leaf processing tleaf, primitive = ray.intersectleaf(node) if tleaf is not None and tleaf < ray.tmax: ray.tmax = tleaf # Pop after leaf node, level, shortstack, done = pop(trail, level, shortstack, bvhwidth, root) if done: return None # Check if we restarted to root and finished if level == 0 and node == root and trail[0] == bvhwidth - 1: break def pop(trail, level, shortstack, bvhwidth, root): # Find parent level: scan upwards from level-1, skip levels with max count parentlevel = -1 for i in range(level - 1, -1, -1): if trail[i] < bvhwidth - 1: parentlevel = i break if parentlevel < 0: return root, 0, [], True # Stack empty, traversal complete # Increment counter at parent level trail[parentlevel] += 1 # Clear counters below parent level for i in range(parentlevel + 1, len(trail)): trail[i] = 0 if not shortstack: # Restart from root return root, 0, [], False else: node = shortstack.pop() if node.islastchild: trail[parentlevel] = bvhwidth - 1 level = parentlevel + 1 return node, level, shortstack, False Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Traversal Order: Must be front-to-back (closest first) for closest-hit searches. If a child is culled because a closer hit was found, it must not be counted as 'processed' in the restart trail counter, otherwise the restart will skip it incorrectly. Culled Far Child: When a node has two intersecting children, but the far child becomes culled during the processing of the near child (due to ray shortening), the algorithm must detect this via popLevel to avoid re-entering the near branch. If level equals popLevel in the single-child branch, it indicates the far child was culled, and POP() must be invoked. Precision: Care must be taken to ensure that equal t values after a restart do not cause re-entering already processed branches, leading to infinite loops. A technique that pushes the parent node onto the stack instead of multiple children when multiple children intersect and at least one is a leaf. The parent is re-intersected later to cull children with hit distances greater than the current closest hit. It sets itself apart from standard short-stack traversal by trading a small increase in traversal steps (1-7%) for a reduction in primitive intersections (2-14%), using only 1 bit of extra storage per stack entry instead of storing hit distances for every entry. Time Complexity: Traversal steps increase by 1-10% for closest-hit queries and 0-5% for any-hit queries compared to a full stack. Stackless traversal (no short stack) visits approximately 2.2–2.4 times as many nodes as ordinary traversal with a full stack. A short stack with just one entry reduces this multiplier to 1.3–1.4. Memory Complexity: Uses ~3x less memory than a full stack. For a short stack of 5 entries, storage is < 44 bytes (Root: 64 bits, Current Node: 32 bits, Restart Trail: 3x32 bits, Current Depth: 5 bits, Short Stack: 5x32 bits). A full stack for a max depth of 32 requires 136 bytes. Performance: Preliminary tests on NVIDIA G80 and GT200 hardware indicate that memory bandwidth benefits of short stacks may not outweigh costs of restarts, SIMD divergence, and extra instructions. However, it is well-suited for hardware hierarchy traversal units where registers are limited. Strengths: Compact memory footprint, no need for parent pointers or hash lookups in BVH nodes, simpler implementation than stackless backtracking methods. Limitations: Restart overhead increases with smaller stack sizes. Slightly higher extraneous node visits compared to kd-trees due to BVH child overlap causing more stack pushes. Restart Trail was introduced by Tero Laine in 2010. It generalizes the restart trail algorithm for binary BVHs to BVHs of arbitrary widths, as proposed by Scheuermann et al.. It is used in real-time ray tracing, particularly in hardware acceleration units and GPU ray cast kernels where memory bandwidth and on-chip storage are critical constraints. name: Stack Culling (Parent Node Re-intersection)
head: Short Stack Culling
body: Stack culling is a technique for stackless or short-stack ray traversal that reduces expensive ray-primitive intersection tests by deferring the processing of multiple intersecting children. Instead of pushing all intersecting children onto the stack, the algorithm pushes the parent node itself when multiple children intersect and at least one is a leaf. The parent is re-intersected later to cull children with hit distances greater than the current closest hit. It sets itself apart from standard short-stack traversal by trading a small increase in traversal steps (1-7%) for a reduction in primitive intersections (2-14%), using only 1 bit of extra storage per stack entry instead of storing hit distances for every entry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray, BVH (N-wide), short stack, restart trail. Output: Closest hit distance (for closest-hit) or all hits (for any-hit). Data Structures: Short Stack: Stores node references. Each entry includes a flag bit to mark if the node is a "parent node". Restart Trail: An array of counters, one per hierarchy level, tracking how many children at each level have been processed. Current Depth: Tracks the current level in the tree. Steps: 1. Intersection Check: For an internal N-wide node, compute intersections between the N child bounding boxes and the ray to find a list H of intersecting children. 2. Sorting: Sort H based on increasing hit distance to obtain a sorted list S. 3. Restart Handling: If traversal restarts from the root, remove the first k nodes from S (where k is the count value at the current level in the restart trail) to avoid re-traversing previously processed children. 4. Stack Culling Decision: If the number of intersecting children is greater than 2 AND at least one child is a leaf: Push the parent node onto the short stack, tagged as a "parent node". Continue traversal with the closest child (first in S). Otherwise: Push the intersecting children onto the short stack in back-to-front order (excluding the closest child, which is traversed next). Tag the last child pushed as the "last child" to update the restart trail correctly. 5. Stack Pop (Re-intersection): When popping from the stack, if the node is tagged as a "parent node": Set the current depth to the depth of the parent node. Re-intersect the parent node's children against the ray. Use the restart trail to skip children that were already traversed. Cull any child whose hit distance is greater than the current closest hit distance found so far. If the node is not a parent node, proceed with standard traversal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseray(ray, bvh, shortstack, restarttrail, maxlevel): # Initialize currentnode = bvh.root currentlevel = 0 while True: # Get children intersections children = currentnode.children intersections = [] for child in children: hitdist = rayintersectbvhbox(ray, child.bbox) if hitdist is not None: intersections.append((hitdist, child)) # Sort by distance intersections.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Apply restart trail to skip already processed children k = restarttrail[currentlevel] validintersections = intersections[k:] if not validintersections: # No new children to process, pop from stack if not shortstack: return None # No more hits node, isparent, islast = shortstack.pop() if isparent: # Re-intersect parent node currentlevel = findparentlevel(restarttrail, currentlevel) restarttrail[currentlevel] += 1 resettrail(restarttrail, currentlevel + 1, maxlevel) # Re-evaluate children of this parent # Note: In a real implementation, this might loop back to intersection step # or directly process the re-intersection results. # For simplicity, we assume the loop continues to re-evaluate 'node' currentnode = node continue else: if islast: restarttrail[currentlevel] = len(children) - 1 currentnode = node currentlevel += 1 continue # Stack Culling Logic # If > 2 children intersect and at least one is a leaf if len(validintersections) > 2 and any(child.isleaf for, child in validintersections): # Push parent instead of children shortstack.append((currentnode, isparent=True, islast=False)) # Continue with closest child nextdist, nextnode = validintersections[0] currentnode = nextnode currentlevel += 1 else: # Standard short stack push # Push remaining children in back-to-front order for dist, child in reversed(validintersections[1:]): islast = (child == validintersections[-1][1]) shortstack.append((child, isparent=False, islast=islast)) # Continue with closest child nextdist, nextnode = validintersections[0] currentnode = nextnode currentlevel += 1 # Update restart trail if this is the last child if nextnode == validintersections[-1][1]: restarttrail[currentlevel] = len(children) - 1 def findparentlevel(trail, currentlevel): # Find the highest level with a non-max count to determine parent level # Simplified logic based on for i in range(currentlevel, -1, -1): if trail[i] < len(bvh.childrencount[i]) - 1: return i return -1 def resettrail(trail, startlevel, maxlevel): for i in range(startlevel, maxlevel + 1): trail[i] = 0 Parameters: Short stack size: Typically 5 entries. Additional storage: 1 bit per stack entry. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Front-to-back ordering: Strictly required for closest-hit searches to ensure culling logic remains consistent with restart trail counters. Not required for any-hit searches. Precision: Re-intersection may introduce slight numerical differences, but the culling logic relies on distance comparisons. Degenerate Input: If all children are leaves, the culling condition (>2 children and at least one leaf) may not trigger, falling back to standard behavior. An extension that culls leaf node entries on the stack when a closer intersection has been found, skipping expensive primitive intersection tests for further nodes. During traversal, the current hit distance is updated every time a ray intersects a leaf node. Subsequent child node intersections at a distance greater than the current hit distance are culled. When an internal node is re-visited after a restart, children that previously intersected the ray but are now further than the current hit are also culled. Front-to-back ordering is strictly required for closest-hit searches to ensure culling logic remains consistent with restart trail counters. It is not required for any-hit searches. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Approximately 3x less than a full stack. With a short stack of 5 entries, storage is less than 44 bytes (root 64 bits, current node 32 bits, restart trail 3x32 bits, current depth 5 bits, stack entries 5x32 bits). A full stack with max depth 32 requires 136 bytes. Time: Overhead in traversal steps is 1-10% for closest-hit queries and 0-5% for any-hit queries with a short stack of 5 entries. Quad intersections are reduced by 2-14%. Measured Performance: Evaluated with different path traced scenes. Restart overhead is at most 10% with a short stack of 5 entries. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant memory reduction, reduced primitive intersections. Limitations: Slight increase in traversal steps, requires front-to-back ordering for closest-hit. When to Use: Use when memory is constrained and primitive intersection cost is high. Not recommended when traversal step overhead is unacceptable or when any-hit queries are the primary use case (though it still works, the benefit is less pronounced). Originated in the paper "Wide BVH Traversal with a Short Stack". The technique leverages the generalized restart trail mechanism to cull leaf node entries on the stack for closest-hit searches. It addresses the trade-off between memory usage and traversal efficiency in BVH ray casting. Wide BVH Traversal with a Short Stack, https://doi.org/10.2312/hpg.20191190, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: JIT Type Specialization
head: JIT Member Function Evaluation
body: JIT Type Specialization is a technique where type resolution and function routing are performed at Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation time, inlining the traversal, type check, and address lookup into the final function to eliminate switch statements and runtime type resolving overhead. It sets itself apart from standard dynamic dispatch by making access time independent of the number of different elemental node types, as the specialized code paths are baked directly into the executable. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A key (e.g., coordinate or ray parameter) and a root node reference. Output: The result of the specialized function call for the element found at the key. Data Structures: Compact Array (acomp): Stores type identifiers and pointers (addresses) for elements. Types are encoded as distinct identifiers (e.g., colors like green, orange, blue). Specialized Functions: Individual functions for each element type that operate on the element's data. Numbered Steps: 1. Standard Runtime Dispatch: Perform a tree traversal to locate the element index, look up the element structure in acomp, and use a runtime switch statement to route the call to the specialized function based on the element type. 2. JIT Inlining: The JIT compiler generates a specialized version of the function that inlines the traversal logic, type checks, and address lookups. This eliminates the compact array lookup and switch statements. 3. Execution: The generated code directly compares keys against tree-specific thresholds to determine the path and calls the specific function with a pre-resolved address. Formulas: The method relies on conditional comparisons for traversal rather than closed-form mathematical equations. The logic follows the pattern: if (key < threshold) traverse left; else if (key > threshold) traverse right; else call specialized function. Thresholds are derived from the specific tree structure (e.g., 106, 8, 4, 13 in the source example). Parameters: Element Types: Encoded as distinct identifiers in the compact array. Thresholds: Specific to the tree structure being traversed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: JIT Overhead: JIT compilation overhead is incurred once per function or tree configuration, not per access. Memory Fetches: The technique eliminates memory fetches in the top-level traversal code by inlining the logic, reducing memory-bound performance bottlenecks. Code Specificity: The generated code is specific to the tree structure and element types present at JIT time. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode illustrates the difference between the standard runtime dispatch approach and the JIT-specialized approach. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. ADDR0, ADDR1, ADDR2, ADDR3 = 0x1000, 0x1008, 0x1010, 0x1018 ADDR4, ADDR5, ADDR6, ADDR7 = 0x1020, 0x1028, 0x1030, 0x1038 def foogreen(address): return f"greendataat{address}" def fooorange(address): return f"orangedataat{address}" def fooblue(address): return f"bluedataat{address}" def find(key, root): # Standard recursive or iterative tree traversal logic return 0 def fooruntime(key, root, acomp): index = find(key, root) e = acomp[index] if e.type == "green": return foogreen(e.address) elif e.type == "orange": return fooorange(e.address) elif e.type == "blue": return fooblue(e.address) def foojit(key): # Inlined traversal and type specialization # Compare key to root key if key < 106: # Traverse left subtree if key < 8: # Traverse left-left subtree if key < 4: return foogreen(ADDR0) elif key > 4: return foogreen(ADDR2) else: return foogreen(ADDR1) else: # Traverse left-right subtree if key < 13: return foogreen(ADDR4) elif key > 13: return fooorange(ADDR6) else: return foogreen(ADDR5) else: # Traverse right subtree # Code omitted for brevity in source # Follows same pattern of key comparisons and direct address calls return fooorange(ADDR7) Time Complexity: Access time is independent of the number of different elemental node types. The overhead of resolving types is eliminated. Memory Complexity: Requires a compact array to store types and pointers. Strengths: Eliminates runtime type resolving overhead and switch statements. Reduces memory-bound performance issues during tree traversal. Limitations: Requires a JIT compiler infrastructure. The generated code is specific to the tree structure and element types at JIT time. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. JIT Type Specialization, also known as JIT Member Function Evaluation, is described in the context of the JiTTree, a just-in-time compiled sparse GPU volume data structure. It is designed to improve the performance of data processing algorithms by making access less memory-bound. The technique allows an arbitrary number of different kinds of sparse data structures to improve overall quality without introducing new memory fetches. name: Topology-Caching for Dynamic Particle Volume Raycasting
head: GPU-based volume raycasting for particle systems, Topology-Cached Raycasting, Topology-Caching
body: Topology-Caching is a GPU-based volume rendering technique for the interactive visualization of dynamic particle systems (e.g., SPH) that reconstructs a scalar field via raycasting without preprocessing. It solves the performance bottleneck of gathering particle contributions for field reconstruction by using three GPU-managed caches: a node-cache for accelerated tree traversal, an influence-cache for fast particle access, and a slab-cache for intermediate compositing. Unlike scattering approaches that cause memory collisions or splatting techniques that require sorting, this method uses a gathering principle with coherent ray packets and stackless traversal to achieve interactive frame rates for hundreds of thousands of particles. The method operates on a data-parallel octree that is rebuilt every frame to organize the dynamic particle set. It processes the image plane using ray packets organized into slabs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Dynamic particle set \{\mathbf{p}i, qi\} where \mathbf{p}i is position and qi is scalar quantity; camera parameters; proxy geometry defining the entry point into the particle volume. Output: Composited image with alpha values. Data Structures: 1. Data-Parallel Octree: Hierarchical structure of nodes. Each node stores pointers to children and neighbors. Supports Level-of-Detail (LOD) where particles are merged into larger particles on coarser levels. 2. Node-Cache: Stores a local subset of octree nodes relevant for the current slab's spatial extent. 3. Influence-Cache: A reference array within each node storing pointers to particles whose support radius h overlaps the node. Particles are redundantly assigned to up to 8 neighboring nodes. 4. Slab-Cache: Stores intermediate reconstruction results (weighted field values) for all rays in a packet across all slices of the current slab. Parameters: Support radius h: Finite support of the kernel function. Ray Packet Size: 4 rays per packet. Slices per Slab: 3. Slab Size: 8 \times 8 pixels. Early Ray Termination Threshold: \alpha = 0.99. Octree Depth: 8. Algorithm Steps: 1. Octree Construction: Rebuild the data-parallel octree in each frame using level-order traversals to exploit GPU parallelism. 2. LOD Construction: Perform bottom-up construction of a particle LOD hierarchy. Particles are added to the next coarser tree level and merged into larger particles, accumulating quantities. 3. Influence-Cache Creation: Assign each particle (including LOD particles) to a reference array in up to 8 neighboring nodes if the particle's support radius h overlaps the node. 4. Ray Packet Initialization: Subdivide the viewing plane into 8 \times 8 pixel regions. Define ray packet origins. Use a proxy geometry to determine the entry point (smallest distance t{entry}) for the first slab for all rays in the packet. 5. Main Loop (Slab Traversal): 5.1. Node Fetching (Node-Cache Filling): Calculate the mid-point of the current slab to determine the current leaf-node of interest. Determine the respective node for each point of the slab (border points may need neighboring nodes). Restrict slab spatial extent to be smaller than the size of a leaf-node. Load the current leaf-node and all relevant neighboring nodes into the Node-Cache. 5.2. Field Reconstruction (Slab-Cache Population): For each slice in the slab (3 slices): For each ray in the packet: Determine the evaluation point \mathbf{x} along the ray. Identify the node containing \mathbf{x} from the Node-Cache. Access particles contributing to \mathbf{x} via the Influence-Cache of that node. Compute scalar field q(\mathbf{x}) using kernel interpolation: q(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\sum{\mathbf{p}i \in Ni} qi K(\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}i\|, h)}{\sum{\mathbf{p}i \in Ni} K(\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}i\|, h)} where Ni is the set of particles in the node, K is a radial symmetric kernel, and h is the support radius. Store the result in the Slab-Cache. Optimization: If adjacent points along a ray require the same node, the node's particles contribute directly to multiple points, reducing global memory reads. 5.3. Compositing: Composite the slices of the slab in front-to-back order using the values in the Slab-Cache. 5.4. Traversal Decisions: Empty Space Skipping: If the current node is empty, skip the whole ray packet to the next node intersection. Early Ray Termination: Compare individual compositing results among rays in the packet. If all composited values are above \alpha = 0.99, stop packet traversal. Advance: Advance rays to the next slab. Update t{entry} using the proxy geometry for the new slab. 6. Final Composition: Compute the resulting image by compositing the slices of all slabs in front-to-back order. Stackless Traversal Details (for Node Fetching): When traversing to find the required node for a slab's mid-point: 1. If the previously required node is at leaf-level and a valid pointer to the neighboring node exists, load the neighboring node. 2. If the pointer to the neighboring node is invalid (no neighbor at leaf-level), traverse upward following parent links until a valid neighboring node at another tree-level is found. This node is an empty-node, suitable for empty space skipping. 3. If the previous node is at intermediate-level and a valid pointer to the neighboring node exists, traverse following child-pointers until a node at leaf-level is reached. 4. If there is no node at leaf-level available, load the node closest to the leaf-level, which is also suited for empty space skipping. Gradient Computation (Optional for Isosurface): Compute gradients in eye space using the Slab-Cache. Adjust step-size \Delta x of central differences for each slice because adjacent rays are not parallel: \Delta x = \alpha \cdot w \cdot n with the pixel-size w and the distance to the near plane n. Overlapping slabs by border-rays solves discontinuities at slab borders. Pitfalls: Image Quality Approximation: LOD particles cause approximation error, but it is hardly noticeable (<3% difference in white regions vs dark regions). Shared Memory Constraints: The slab size (8 \times 8) and slices (3) are chosen to fit shared memory (16KB on GTX 280). High register count (45) limits occupancy to 31.3% on older GPUs. Time Complexity: Interactive frame rates for up to several 10^5 particles. Memory Complexity: High shared memory usage (~1900 bytes per packet). Node-cache (~300 bytes), Slab-cache (~1536 bytes for weighted results). Performance: GTX 280, 800x600 resolution: T-Sensor (50k particles, 10k nodes): 25ms. Fountain (60k particles, 6k nodes): 21ms. Dam (130k particles, 25k nodes): 45ms. GTX 480 (48KB shared memory): T-Sensor: 132ms. Fountain: 251ms. Dam: 274ms. Scaling: Occupancy improves on GPUs with larger shared memory (e.g., GTX 480 has 48KB vs 16KB on GTX 280), resulting in better performance as noted in the source. Strengths: No preprocessing required; handles dynamic particle sets; fast neighbor access via influence-cache; reduced memory reads via slab-cache; interactive frame rates. Limitations: Approximation error from LOD (though negligible); high register usage limits occupancy on older GPUs; requires rebuilding octree every frame. The method was presented by Jens Orthmann, Maik Keller, and Andreas Kolb from the University of Siegen, Germany. It builds on data-parallel octrees by Zhou et al. [ZGHG10] and stackless traversal techniques by Popov et al. [PGSS07]. It is designed for ad-hoc visualization of SPH fluid simulations directly after each simulation step. Topology-Caching for Dynamic Particle Volume Raycasting, https://doi.org/10.2312/pe/vmv/vmv10/147-154, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical Tree Node Traversal
head: VolumeRayIntersector
body: Hierarchical Tree Node Traversal accelerates ray-volume intersection by traversing a sparse octree to identify contiguous segments of active data. It solves the problem of inefficiently sampling empty space by skipping inactive nodes and resolving hits at the node level rather than the individual voxel level. Unlike sibling methods that rasterize shadows or compute precise Hermite data, this approach focuses on robust ray marching against a generic grid, providing entry and exit times for line-integration. The method is implemented via the VolumeRayIntersector class template, which encapsulates the logic for intersecting a ray with a generic volume grid using an internal boolean tree. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A GridT (the volume data), an optional dilationCount (integer, default 0), and an optional explicit bounding box CoordBBox. Output: Boolean flags indicating ray validity, and updated time parameters t0 and t1 representing the entry and exit points of active regions along the index ray. Data Structures: TreeT: A boolean tree derived from the input grid's root type, converted to store bool values. This tree is used to accelerate ray marching and may be dilated based on dilationCount. CoordBBox: The axis-aligned bounding box of the active voxels in index space, cached for efficient ray-box intersection tests. ValueAccessor: An internal accessor for the tree, which is not thread-safe and must be copied per thread. Parameters: NodeLevel (template int, default GridT::TreeType::RootNodeType::ChildNodeType::LEVEL): Specifies the tree node level at which traversal and hit resolution occur. dilationCount (int, default 0): The number of voxel dilations performed on a boolean copy of the input grid to account for interpolation kernel sizes. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct the intersector with the grid and optional dilation count or bounding box. The constructor validates that grid voxels are uniform and the grid is not empty, throwing a RuntimeError otherwise. 2. Thread Safety Setup: For multi-threaded execution, create a new instance for each computational thread using the shallow copy constructor. This ensures thread safety by duplicating the non-thread-safe ValueAccessor and cached CoordBBox efficiently. 3. Ray Setup: Call setIndexRay or setWorldRay with the ray to traverse. If the ray misses the grid's bounding box, the method returns false, indicating no further marching is required. 4. Marching Loop: Call march(t0, t1) in a loop. This function performs the hierarchical descent. It returns true if the ray intersects active values (active voxels or tiles). 5. Hit Resolution: Upon a successful march, t0 and t1 are updated with the entry and exit times along the INDEX ray. These times are resolved at the node level (e.g., LeafNode) rather than for individual active voxels. 6. Coordinate Conversion: Convert the index-space hit times to world coordinates using getIndexPos(time), getWorldPos(time), and getWorldTime(time). 7. Hit List Generation: Optionally, call hits(list) to populate a container of RayType::TimeSpan objects with all detected hits along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction class CoordBBox: def init(self, mincoord, maxcoord): self.min = mincoord self.max = maxcoord def rayintersectsbbox(ray, bbox): tmin = (bbox.min[0] - ray.origin[0]) / ray.direction[0] tmax = (bbox.max[0] - ray.origin[0]) / ray.direction[0] if tmin > tmax: tmin, tmax = tmax, tmin ty = (bbox.min[1] - ray.origin[1]) / ray.direction[1] if ty > tmax: return False if ty < tmin: tmin = ty tz = (bbox.min[2] - ray.origin[2]) / ray.direction[2] if tz > tmax: return False if tz < tmin: tmin = tz return tmin <= tmax class VolumeRayIntersector: def init(self, grid, dilationcount=0, bbox=None): # Validates uniform voxels; Using a single instance across threads causes race conditions. Always use the copy constructor for each thread. Coordinate Space: t0 and t1 are computed in index space, not world space. Client code must use getIndexPos or maintain an index ray instance for coordinate conversion. Uniform Voxels: Constructors throw a RuntimeError if the grid voxels are not uniform or the grid is empty. Node-Level Resolution: Hits are resolved at the node level (e.g., LeafNode), not individual active voxels. This means t0 and t1 represent the bounds of a node, not necessarily the exact bounds of every active voxel within it. Time Complexity: Depends on the depth of the octree and the sparsity of the volume. Hierarchical traversal skips empty space, reducing the number of samples compared to fixed-step DDA. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the boolean tree (TreeT) and the bounding box cache. Limitations: Not thread-safe without copying; requires uniform voxels; hit resolution is at the node level, which may be coarser than voxel-level precision. When to Use: When rendering large, sparse volumetric datasets on multi-threaded CPU or GPU systems where thread safety and efficient empty space skipping are critical. When Not to Use: When the grid has non-uniform voxels, as the constructor throws a RuntimeError. name: Frustum and Visibility Culling
head: Frustum Culling, Visibility Culling, Frustum-Occlusion Culling
body: Frustum and Visibility Culling methods optimize volume rendering by identifying and discarding geometry that does not contribute to the final image, thereby reducing computational load. This family distinguishes itself from sibling traversal methods by decoupling visibility determination from the core sampling loop, often serving as a pre-pass or integrated filter to limit the working set of voxels, splats, or bricks. Unlike Octree and Tree Traversal which focuses on hierarchical descent, these methods focus on spatial containment relative to the camera. This method renders hierarchical shell and solid volumetric structures by traversing a bounding-sphere tree and adaptively controlling the frame rate through dynamic adjustment of minimum splat sizes. It distinguishes itself from standard octree traversal by replacing fixed-resolution voxel sampling with screen-space splat rendering, where the granularity of the visual output is directly tied to performance feedback. Unlike sibling methods that rely on geometric bounding boxes for culling, this approach uses bounding spheres and hierarchical normal cones to optimize visibility tests for point-based primitives. Choose when adaptive performance control for point-based primitives is needed. See Bounding-Sphere Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control. Frustum Culling Integration is a visibility optimization technique applied during the progressive loading and rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. It filters out splats that lie outside the user's current viewing frustum to prioritize the transmission and rendering of visible geometry. It differs from its sibling Bounding-Sphere Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control by focusing on spatial visibility rather than frame-rate stability, and from Frustum-Occlusion Culling for Octree Traversal by typically operating on a pre-ordered list of splats rather than a hierarchical tree structure during the culling phase. Choose for optimizing transmission and rendering of visible Gaussian splats. See Frustum Culling Integration. This method identifies a set of visible voxels by traversing an octree hierarchy and culling nodes that do not intersect the camera's view frustum or whose projected screen area is smaller than a single pixel. It serves as a visibility pre-pass for voxel rasterization, automatically determining the Level of Detail (LOD) for rendering. Unlike standard ray-marching which samples volume density, this approach outputs a list of 3D bounding boxes (voxels) to be rasterized as geometry using hardware instancing. It is distinct from Bounding-Sphere Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control by using explicit frustum intersection tests rather than frame-rate driven depth limits, and from Frustum Culling Integration by specifically targeting octree structures for voxel-based rendering pipelines. Choose when targeting octree structures for voxel-based rendering pipelines. See Frustum-Occlusion Culling for Octree Traversal. Frustum culling for octree nodes is a hierarchical visibility test that discards entire octree subtrees if their axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) lies completely outside the view frustum. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which parts of a sparse volumetric or point-cloud structure are visible, avoiding per-element processing for millions of points with a single bounding box test. Unlike sibling methods that may integrate occlusion or frame-rate control, this method focuses purely on geometric containment within the six clipping planes, serving as the primary "existence" decision before traversal begins. Choose as a primary existence decision before traversal begins. See Frustum Culling for Octree Nodes. Visibility is determined during ray traversal, providing implicit view frustum culling without extra steps. The method provides implicit occlusion culling without extra steps or occlusion buffers. Rays determine the working set directly by writing out a list of bricks they require (intersect) in front-to-back order. It uses modern OpenGL extensions such as GLARBshaderstoragebufferobject. Introduced by Crassin et al. in 2009. The concept of culling visible geometry is fundamental to computer graphics. In the context of volume rendering, early approaches relied on explicit pre-passes to determine the "working set" of bricks or voxels. As hardware capabilities evolved, particularly with the advent of shader storage buffer objects, methods like Ray-Guided Volume Rendering integrated culling directly into the rendering pipeline. The specific techniques described in the subtopics represent specialized applications of these principles to different data structures (octrees, splats, bounding-sphere trees) and rendering paradigms (rasterization, ray-casting). name: Bounding-Sphere Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control
head: Adaptive Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control, Visibility Culling Tests
body: This method renders hierarchical shell and solid volumetric structures by traversing a bounding-sphere tree and adaptively controlling the frame rate through dynamic adjustment of minimum splat sizes. It distinguishes itself from standard octree traversal by replacing fixed-resolution voxel sampling with screen-space splat rendering, where the granularity of the visual output is directly tied to performance feedback. Unlike sibling methods such as Frustum Culling Integration, Frustum-Occlusion Culling for Octree Traversal, and Frustum Culling for Octree Nodes that rely on geometric bounding boxes for culling, this approach uses bounding spheres and hierarchical normal cones to optimize visibility tests for point-based primitives. The algorithm traverses a hierarchical tree (Shell or Solid) using a recursive descent. It combines visibility culling tests with a feedback loop that adjusts rendering parameters to maintain a target frame rate. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Root node of the bounding-sphere tree; current camera parameters (view frustum); current frame rate measurement. Output: Rendered image composed of splats. Global Parameters: \deltar (minimum regular splat size in pixels), \deltab (minimum boundary splat size in pixels). Data Structures: The tree nodes store bounding sphere attributes. These attributes are compressed and decompressed on-the-fly using table lookups during traversal to save memory and bandwidth. Shell Nodes: Store hierarchical normal vectors and bounding normal cones. Solid Nodes: Do not store normal information during traversal; normals are derived from a CSG probe at render time. Numbered Steps: 1. Frame-Rate Feedback: Measure the current frame rate. If it is too low, smoothly increase \deltar and \deltab. If the frame rate is too high (after a completed traversal), allow \deltar and \deltab to decrease. In the original implementation, these parameters are only allowed to decrease after a fully completed tree traversal has led to too high frame rates. 2. Traverse Tree: Call TraverseTree on the root node. 3. Culling Tests: For each child of the current node, perform the following tests in order. If a test fails, the child and its subtree are ignored. View-Frustum Culling: If the bounding sphere is completely outside the viewing frustum, ignore the node and all children. If the bounding sphere intersects any plane of the view frustum, traverse to the children. If the bounding sphere is completely inside the view frustum, disable this culling test for all children. Back-Face Culling (Shell): Use the hierarchically encoded normal vectors and bounding normal cones to eliminate branches where all nodes point entirely away from the camera. Back-Face Culling (Solid): Hierarchical culling is not performed during traversal because normals depend on the CSG probe. Instead, back-face culling is performed before rendering individual Solid splats using normals derived from the CSG probe. Occlusion Culling: Hierarchical occlusion culling is considered too hard for point-based primitives. Instead, enable the z-buffer algorithm in the graphics hardware for occlusion culling. 4. Splat Sizing: Calculate the screen size S of the child's bounding sphere in pixels. 5. Leaf/Node Handling: If the child is a leaf node, render it as a splat of size S pixels. If the child is a regular node and S < \deltar, render it as a splat of size \deltar pixels. If the child is a boundary node and S < \deltab, render it as a splat of size \deltab pixels. Otherwise, recursively call TraverseTree(child). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. deltar = 1.0 # Minimum regular splat size in pixels deltab = 1.0 # Minimum boundary splat size in pixels traversalcompleted = True # Flag to permit delta decrease def updateframeratecontrol(currentframerate, targetframerate): """Adjusts deltar and deltab based on frame rate feedback.""" nonlocal deltar, deltab, traversalcompleted if currentframerate < targetframerate: deltar = 1.1 # Increase smoothly deltab = 1.1 elif currentframerate > targetframerate and traversalcompleted: # Only allow decrease after a fully completed traversal deltar = max(1.0, deltar 0.9) deltab = max(1.0, deltab 0.9) traversalcompleted = True def traversetree(node): """Recursively traverses the bounding-sphere tree.""" nonlocal traversalcompleted traversalcompleted = False # Decompress attributes on-the-fly using table lookups # Fast on-the-fly table lookup implementation for child in node.children: # 1. View-Frustum Culling # Standard sphere vs 6-plane frustum test frustumstatus = "OUTSIDE" if sphereoutsidefrustum(child.boundingsphere) else ("INSIDE" if sphereinsidefrustum(child.boundingsphere) else "INTERSECTS") if frustumstatus == "OUTSIDE": continue # Ignore node and children elif frustumstatus == "INTERSECTS": pass # Traverse to children, keep culling active elif frustumstatus == "INSIDE": pass # Disable frustum culling for children # 2. Back-Face Culling (Shell specific) if node.type == "SHELL": # Uses hierarchical normal vectors and bounding normal cones if dot(child.normalcone.axis, cameraposition - child.normalcone.center) < -child.normalcone.radius: continue # Eliminate branch # 3. Calculate screen size # Projects bounding sphere radius to screen space S = 2.0 child.boundingsphere.radius camera.focallength / distance(camera.position, child.boundingsphere.center) # 4. Leaf or Node Handling if child.isleaf: # Rasterizes a point/splat at center with screen size drawpoint(child.center, S) elif child.type == "REGULAR" and S < deltar: drawpoint(child.center, deltar) elif child.type == "BOUNDARY" and S < deltab: drawpoint(child.center, deltab) else: traversetree(child) traversalcompleted = True def drawpoint(center, size): # Rasterizes a point/splat at center with screen size pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parameter Adjustment: \deltar and \deltab are only allowed to decrease after a fully completed tree traversal has led to too high frame rates. This prevents oscillation during partial traversals. Solid Node Normals: Solid nodes lack hierarchical normal information. Back-face culling must be deferred to the splat rendering stage using the CSG probe, which adds overhead compared to Shell nodes. Occlusion: Hierarchical occlusion culling is not implemented due to the point-based nature of the primitives. Relying on the hardware z-buffer is the only option, which may be less efficient for highly overlapping structures. Time Complexity: Depends on the tree depth and the selectivity of the culling tests. The adaptive frame-rate control ensures that the number of rendered splats is bounded by the performance target, effectively capping the rendering cost. Memory: The tree is stored breath-first, allowing progressive loading of only the parts of the data structure actually rendered during traversal. Attributes are compressed and decompressed on-the-fly. Strengths: Real-time performance is guaranteed through adaptive refinement. The use of bounding spheres and normal cones allows for efficient visibility culling. Limitations: Occlusion culling is limited to hardware z-buffering. Solid nodes require additional computation for normal derivation. The method was introduced by Museth and Lombeyna in 2004 as part of the TetSplat system for real-time rendering and volume clipping of large volumetric datasets. It was designed to handle both shell (surface) and solid (volume) representations efficiently by leveraging hierarchical tree structures and adaptive rendering techniques. name: Frustum Culling Integration
head: Base+Frustum culling
body: Frustum Culling Integration is a visibility optimization technique applied during the progressive loading and rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. It filters out splats that lie outside the user's current viewing frustum to prioritize the transmission and rendering of visible geometry. It differs from its sibling Bounding-Sphere Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control by focusing on spatial visibility rather than frame-rate stability, and from Frustum-Occlusion Culling for Octree Traversal by operating on a pre-ordered list of splats rather than a hierarchical tree structure during the culling phase. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of 3D Gaussians (splats) with their mean positions, the current camera view and projection matrices, and a frustum margin parameter. Output: A filtered subset of splats that are considered visible (inside the frustum). Data Structures: Splat List: An array of Gaussian objects containing mean positions and screen-space projections. Steps: 1. Global Ordering (Pre-requisite): Frustum culling is applied after a global ordering of splats has been determined. This means the culling step filters the list rather than re-ordering it. 2. Frustum Margin Application: Define the viewing frustum boundaries (left, right, bottom, top, near, far) and increase them by 30%. 3. Projection and Filtering: Project all splats onto the image plane. Filter the splats that fall outside the expanded frustum boundaries. 4. Selection: Retain only those splats where the projected center lies within the expanded frustum. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def frustumcullsplats(splats, viewmatrix, projmatrix, marginfactor=0.3): """ Filters a list of splats based on the viewing frustum with a margin. Args: splats: List of Gaussian objects with 'mean' (vec3). viewmatrix: 4x4 view matrix. projmatrix: 4x4 projection matrix. marginfactor: Percentage to expand frustum boundaries (e.g., 0.3 for 30%). Returns: List of splats inside the expanded frustum. """ visiblesplats = [] vpmatrix = projmatrix @ viewmatrix margin = marginfactor # Standard NDC frustum bounds are [-1, 1] for x and y. # Increasing boundaries by marginfactor expands the visible region. xmin = -1.0 (1.0 + margin) xmax = 1.0 (1.0 + margin) ymin = -1.0 (1.0 + margin) ymax = 1.0 (1.0 + margin) for gaussian in splats: # Standard perspective projection and NDC conversion poshomogeneous = vec4(gaussian.mean, 1.0) clippos = vpmatrix @ poshomogeneous if clippos.w <= 0.0: continue ndcx = clippos.x / clippos.w ndcy = clippos.y / clippos.w if xmin <= ndcx <= xmax and ymin <= ndcy <= ymax: visiblesplats.append(gaussian) return visiblesplats Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion Ignorance: Frustum culling occurs after global ordering and does not account for occlusions from the current viewpoint. Small Background Splats: If more than 10% of splats are visible within the frustum, small background splats may still not be selected for high-quality loading because the culling happens after the initial priority list is formed. Gaussian Extent: Since Gaussians cover areas rather than points on the image plane, a Gaussian with a mean outside the frustum might still contribute to the image. The margin mitigates this by counting Gaussians inside the expanded frustum. A technique to fine-tune the ordering of splats based on the user's initial pose, selecting a percentage of splats from within the viewing frustum to allow for rapid movement while focusing on visible content. It involves projecting all splats onto the image plane and filtering those outside the frustum. A typical parameter is the frustum margin, set to 30% to increase frustum boundaries. This variant is chosen when user-specific view information is available to improve perceived quality during camera movement. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The complete approach (octree + frustum culling) performs better when user-specific view information is available. However, if more than 10% of splats are visible, the benefit is reduced for background details. Strengths: Reduces the number of splats processed by excluding clearly invisible geometry. Limitations: Does not handle occlusion; relies on pre-computed ordering; margin parameter requires tuning. When to use: When user view direction is known and the scene has significant geometry outside the current view. When not to use: When occlusion is the primary bottleneck or when the view is fully contained within the scene (high visibility percentage). The method originates from the PRoGS (Progressive Rendering of Gaussian Splats) paper. It was developed to address the bandwidth and rendering costs of progressive 3D Gaussian Splatting by leveraging user view information to prioritize visible splats. The approach builds on the base progressive rendering method by adding a visibility filter. name: Frustum-Occlusion Culling for Octree Traversal
head: Frustum-octant traversal, Voxel LOD selection, Voxel LOD selection via Frustum Culling, Voxel Rasterization via Frustum Culling and Instancing
body: This method identifies a set of visible voxels by traversing an octree hierarchy and culling nodes that do not intersect the camera's view frustum or whose projected screen area is smaller than a single pixel. It serves as a visibility pre-pass for voxel rasterization, automatically determining the Level of Detail (LOD) for rendering. Unlike standard ray-marching which samples volume density, this approach outputs a list of 3D bounding boxes to be rasterized as geometry using hardware instancing. Inputs: Camera view frustum, octree hierarchy with axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs), global AABB, screen resolution (W, H). Outputs: Buffer of visible voxels, each containing position and size. Data Structures: Octree node with AABB and 8-bit occupancy mask. Voxel buffer storing {position: vec3, size: float}. Algorithm: 1. Frustum Intersection Test: Approximate octant-AABB intersection as a frustum-sphere intersection for efficiency. The sphere diameter equals the octant's AABB diagonal. If the sphere does not intersect the frustum, cull the branch. 2. Projected Area Test (LOD Selection): Calculate the octant's projected area on the screen. If the area is less than one pixel, halt traversal for this branch. 3. Termination: Halt traversal if the node has no further subdivisions (leaf). 4. Buffer Population: When halted (LOD cutoff, leaf, or frustum exit), append the voxel's position and size to the buffer. These attributes are derived implicitly from the node's AABB within the global coordinate space. 5. Rasterization: After traversal, pass the buffer to a hardware instancing pipeline to rasterize the voxels. Formulas: Sphere center: \mathbf{c} = \frac{\mathbf{aabb}{min} + \mathbf{aabb}{max}}{2} Sphere radius: r = \frac{\|\mathbf{aabb}{max} - \mathbf{aabb}{min}\|}{2} LOD condition: A{screen} < 1.0 pixel Parameters: Canonical voxel template: cube with c{min} = (-1, -1, -1) and c{max} = (+1, +1, +1). LOD threshold: projected area < 1 pixel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numeric precision degrades at extreme subdivision depths. Over-subdivision wastes memory when LOD would naturally halt at coarser levels. Sphere approximation may cause false positives (culling fewer nodes than strict AABB test) but never false negatives. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseoctree(node, frustum, screenwidth, screenheight, voxelbuffer): # 1. Frustum Culling via Sphere Approximation center = (node.aabb.min + node.aabb.max) / 2.0 radius = length(node.aabb.max - node.aabb.min) / 2.0 if not frustum.intersectssphere(center, radius): return # 2. Projected Area / LOD Check projectedarea = calculateprojectedarea(node.aabb, frustum.viewmatrix, frustum.projmatrix, screenwidth, screenheight) if projectedarea < 1.0 or node.isleaf(): voxelbuffer.append({'position': center, 'size': length(node.aabb.max - node.aabb.min)}) return # 3. Recurse into children for child in node.children: if child is not None: traverseoctree(child, frustum, screenwidth, screenheight, voxelbuffer) def calculateprojectedarea(aabb, viewmatrix, projmatrix, w, h): # Transform 8 AABB corners to clip space corners = [] for x in [aabb.min.x, aabb.max.x]: for y in [aabb.min.y, aabb.max.y]: for z in [aabb.min.z, aabb.max.z]: corners.append(vec4(x, y, z, 1.0)) clipcorners = [projmatrix (viewmatrix c) for c in corners] # Convert to NDC [-1, 1] and find screen-space bounding box ndcx = [(c.x / c.w) for c in clipcorners] ndcy = [(c.y / c.w) for c in clipcorners] minx, maxx = min(ndcx), max(ndcx) miny, maxy = min(ndcy), max(ndcy) # Map NDC to screen pixels screenw = max(0.0, (maxx - minx) 0.5 w) screenh = max(0.0, (maxy - miny) 0.5 h) return screenw screenh Time Complexity: Worst-case O(N) for a full octree. Average case visits only visible and LOD-relevant nodes. Memory Complexity: Octree stored breadth-first with 1 byte per node mask. Buffer size scales with visible voxel count. Performance: Profiled at 1920x1280 resolution with 25%–85% pixel coverage on Intel Core i5-2540M / NVIDIA Quadro 3000M / Windows 7 / OpenGL 4.2. Voxel rasterization times (ms) for 'basketball' dataset at depth 10: Geometry Shader 3.454, Uniform Buffer 2.549, Hardware Texture Buffer 2.773, Instancing Vertex Buffer 5.599. Strengths and Limitations: Automatic LOD selection and efficient frustum culling. Geometry Shader is slowest for voxels due to hardware optimization for quads; Uniform Buffer is fastest. Described in the context of hardware-accelerated geometry instancing for surfel and voxel rendering of scanned 4D media. Highlights trade-offs between GPU instancing techniques for voxel data. name: Ray-Guided Volume Rendering
head: Hierarchical grids with bricking accessed via multi-level page tables, Multi-level page table hierarchy, Visualization-driven approaches, Visualization-driven volume rendering
body: Ray-guided volume rendering is a category of volume renderers that incorporate a feedback loop between the ray-caster and the culling mechanism, where the ray-caster itself writes out accurate information on missing bricks and brick usage to determine an accurate working set directly on the GPU. Unlike traditional approaches where the working set is computed on the CPU prior to rendering, ray-guided renderers build up the current working set during ray traversal on the GPU. This method sets itself apart from its siblings, such as Bounding-Sphere Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control and Frustum and Visibility Culling, by eliminating explicit CPU-side culling steps and instead using the ray traversal process itself to implicitly determine visibility and data requirements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hierarchical volume data structure (either an octree or a hierarchical grid with bricking) and a transfer function. Output: A rendered image and a list of required bricks for the current frame. Data Structures: The method relies on one of two primary data structures, accessed via a multi-level page table hierarchy or a tree structure with a node/brick pool: 1. Octree/Tree Structure: Node Pool: Stores active tree nodes. Each node contains pointers to child nodes in the pool and a pointer to an associated texture brick in the brick pool. Brick Pool: A shared cache texture storing the actual voxel data (bricks). 2. Hierarchical Grid with Multi-level Page Tables: Page Tables: Multi-level structures mapping virtual addresses to physical brick locations. Entries are flagged as mapped or unmapped. Brick Pool: Shared cache texture for voxel data. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Traversal: Rays traverse the volume structure (e.g., using the kd-restart algorithm for octrees) from front to back. 2. Working Set Determination: As rays traverse, they determine the required data resolution automatically, either on a per-sample basis [HBJP12] or per-brick basis [FSK13]. 3. Missing Brick Detection: The ray-caster detects if a required brick is missing from GPU memory (e.g., a missing octree node, an unmapped page table entry, or a "missing" subtree flag). 4. Write-out: The ray-caster writes out accurate information on missing bricks and brick usage. This is typically done using multiple render targets or modern OpenGL extensions such as GLARBshaderstoragebufferobject. 5. Implicit Culling: Visibility is determined during ray traversal, providing implicit view frustum culling without extra steps. Rays also determine implicit occlusion culling without extra steps or occlusion buffers. 6. Data Streaming: The written-out information is used to load missing data into the GPU cache. 7. Cache Management: The usage information is used to determine which bricks can be evicted from the GPU cache because they are no longer needed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayguidedvolumerender(rayorigin, raydirection, raylength, bricksize, transferfunction): accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 t = 0.0 missingbricks = [] usedbricks = [] while t < raylength and accumulatedopacity < 1.0: pos = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t for i in range(3)] brickidx = [int(pos[i] // bricksize) for i in range(3)] ispresent = brickidx in gpucache if not ispresent: missingbricks.append(brickidx) t += bricksize continue voxelval = samplevoxelat(pos, brickidx) color, alpha = transferfunction(voxelval) weight = alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[i] + color[i] weight for i in range(3)] accumulatedopacity += weight usedbricks.append(brickidx) t += bricksize writemissingbricks(missingbricks) writeusageinfo(usedbricks) return accumulatedcolor + [accumulatedopacity] def samplevoxelat(pos, brickidx): # Standard trilinear interpolation within the brick return 0.5 def transferfunction(value): # Standard mapping from scalar to RGBA return [value, value, value], value def writemissingbricks(bricks): # Appends brick indices to a Shader Storage Buffer Object or render target pass def writeusageinfo(bricks): # Appends brick indices to a usage buffer for eviction policy pass Parameters and Typical Values: Traversal Algorithm: kd-restart algorithm is commonly used for octree traversal. Resolution Determination: Can be per-sample [HBJP12] or per-brick [FSK13]. OpenGL Extensions: GLARBshaderstoragebufferobject is used for writing out working set information. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Bricks: The renderer must handle missing bricks gracefully, either by skipping them or substituting lower resolution data. Working Set Too Large: If the working set exceeds GPU memory, strategies include switching from single-pass to multi-pass rendering or interrupting rendering. Precision: Not given in the sources. It employs an N^3 tree (octree) and the kd-restart algorithm for traversal, storing active nodes in a node pool and voxel data in a brick pool. It targets entertainment applications and supports real-time transfer function updates. Proposed by Hadwiger et al. in 2012, this approach uses hierarchical grids with bricking accessed via multi-level page tables instead of a tree structure. It scales to petavoxel data and efficiently handles highly anisotropic data common in electron microscopy. It offers advantages in traversal complexity and cache access behavior compared to standard octree traversal for very large data. Time and Memory Complexity: Scales to petavoxel data. Provides implicit view frustum and occlusion culling without extra steps or buffers. Determines the working set directly on the GPU, reducing CPU-GPU synchronization overhead. Automatically determines locally required data resolution. Limitations: Requires handling missing bricks and potential cache eviction policies. If the working set is too large, rendering may need to be interrupted or switched to multi-pass. When to Use: Suitable for large-scale volume visualization, especially with petavoxel data or highly anisotropic data. When Not to Use: Not specified in the sources. [GMG08] were among the first to implement a volume ray-caster with stackless GPU octree traversal using occlusion queries, though it was not fully ray-guided because culling was performed on the CPU. name: Frustum Culling for Octree Nodes
head: AABB-in-frustum test, Positive-vertex test
body: Frustum culling for octree nodes is a hierarchical visibility test that discards entire octree subtrees if their axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) lies completely outside the view frustum. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which parts of a sparse volumetric or point-cloud structure are visible, avoiding per-element processing for millions of points with a single bounding box test. Unlike sibling methods that may integrate occlusion or frame-rate control, this method focuses purely on geometric containment within the six clipping planes, serving as the primary "existence" decision before traversal begins. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree node defined by its axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) and the view frustum defined by six planes. Output: A boolean value indicating whether the node's bounding box intersects the frustum (True) or is completely outside (False). Data Structures: Node: Represented by two 3D vectors: bmin (minimum corner) and bmax (maximum corner). Planes: A list of six plane definitions. Each plane is defined by the equation ax + by + cz + d = 0, where (a, b, c) is the normal vector and d is the distance from the origin. Algorithm Steps: 1. For each of the six frustum planes, identify the corner of the node's bounding box that is farthest along the plane's normal vector. 2. The coordinates of this farthest corner (px, py, pz) are selected as follows: px = \text{bmax}[0] if a \ge 0, else \text{bmin}[0]; py = \text{bmax}[1] if b \ge 0, else \text{bmin}[1]; pz = \text{bmax}[2] if c \ge 0, else \text{bmin}[2]. 3. Evaluate the plane equation for this corner: val = a \cdot px + b \cdot py + c \cdot pz + d. 4. If val < 0 for any of the six planes, the entire bounding box is outside the frustum relative to that plane; return False (cull the node). 5. If the condition is not met for all six planes, the bounding box intersects the frustum; return True. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def aabbinfrustum(node, planes): """True if the node's box is at least partly inside the frustum (positive-vertex test).""" bmin, bmax = node["min"], node["max"] for a, b, c, d in planes: px = bmax[0] if a >= 0 else bmin[0] py = bmax[1] if b >= 0 else bmin[1] pz = bmax[2] if c >= 0 else bmin[2] if a px + b py + c pz + d < 0: # most-positive corner still outside return False return True Parameters: Planes: The six coefficients (a, b, c, d) for the view frustum planes. Node Bounds: bmin and bmax define the spatial extent of the octree node. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Conservatism: The test is conservative; it never hides a point that should be shown, ensuring correctness at the cost of potentially keeping some nodes that are mostly outside but have a corner inside. Precision: Standard floating-point arithmetic is sufficient, but care should be taken with near-zero plane distances or degenerate boxes. Time Complexity: O(1) per node, specifically costing six comparisons (one per frustum plane) to decide the existence of the entire subtree. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, requiring only local variables for the corner selection and plane evaluation. Strengths: Extremely fast hierarchical culling; discards millions of points with a single box test; simple implementation. Limitations: Conservative nature may lead to over-culling (keeping nodes that are mostly outside); does not account for occlusion by other geometry. When to Use: As a first-pass visibility filter for sparse volumes or point clouds where hierarchical structure is available. Frustum culling for octree nodes originates from the need to efficiently render large-scale point clouds and sparse volumes. The technique leverages the hierarchical nature of octrees to perform coarse-grained visibility tests. It is a fundamental component in point cloud level-of-detail systems and out-core rendering pipelines. The method is often referred to as the "positive-vertex test" because it tests the most positive vertex relative to each plane normal.
