name: Octree Sampled SDF Dataset
body: A dataset class that generates signed-distance function (SDF) samples from a sparse octree acceleration structure constructed from a single mesh shape. It limits sampling to occupied octree cells, supports equal distribution of samples per cell, and allows online resampling via a cached narrowband pool. It optionally includes RGB data derived from mesh textures. Inputs: occupancystruct (OctreeAS): An octree acceleration structure initialized from a mesh. samplemode (List[str]): Sampling scheme supporting 'tracer' (on surface), 'near' (near surface), and 'rand' (uniform in occupied grid cells). Default: ['rand', 'rand', 'near', 'near', 'trace']. numsamples (int): Number of data points kept in the working set at any given time. Default: 100,000. samplespervoxel (int): Number of samples to generate per octree grid cell to create a preliminary equally distributed pool. Default: 32. sampletex (bool): Whether to include RGB from mesh textures. Outputs: A dataset of points with associated SDF values and optionally RGB, formatted for neural field training. Data Structures: blas: The OctreeAS object containing points (coordinates), pyramid (hierarchy), and extent (metadata). datapool: A cached pool of narrowband values used for online resampling. data: The current working set of samples. Steps: 1. Extract Geometry and Level: Retrieve vertices, faces, and the maximum octree level from the acceleration structure. \text{vertices} = \text{blas.extent['vertices']}, \quad \text{faces} = \text{blas.extent['faces']}, \quad \text{level} = \text{blas.max\level} 2. Compute Voxel Corners: Determine the corner coordinates for the target octree level. \text{corners} = \text{spc\ops.unbatched\get\level\points}(\text{blas.points}, \text{blas.pyramid}, \text{level}) 3. Generate Initial Points: Based on samplemode, generate point sets. For 'near' modes: Sample points near the surface with variance inversely proportional to the level. \text{variance} = \frac{1}{2^{\text{level}}} For 'trace' modes: Sample points directly on the surface. For 'rand' modes: Sample uniformly in occupied cells. 4. Filter by Narrowband: Concatenate all generated points and query the acceleration structure to keep only those within the narrowband (occupied cells). \text{query\results} = \text{blas.query}(\text{pts}, 0) \text{pts} = \text{pts}[\text{query\results.pidx} > -1] 5. Compute SDF and RGB: If sampletex is True, compute RGB using texture mapping. Otherwise, compute SDF distances. 6. Resample (Online): During training, resample the working set from the cached datapool to maintain diversity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def getlevelcorners(points, pyramid, level): """Extract grid coordinates for a specific octree level.""" # Standard implementation: index points using the pyramid hierarchy for the target level return points[pyramid[level]] def samplenearsurface(vertices, faces, numpts, variance): """Generate points near the surface with specified variance.""" # Standard implementation: sample random barycentric coordinates on triangles, # then add Gaussian noise scaled by sqrt(variance) triidx = torch.randint(0, len(faces), (numpts,)) bary = torch.rand(numpts, 3) bary /= bary.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) surfacepts = (bary[:, None,:] vertices[faces[triidx]]).sum(dim=1) noise = torch.randnlike(surfacepts) torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(variance)) return surfacepts + noise def samplesurface(vertices, faces, numpts): """Generate points directly on the surface.""" # Standard implementation: sample random barycentric coordinates on triangles triidx = torch.randint(0, len(faces), (numpts,)) bary = torch.rand(numpts, 3) bary /= bary.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) return (bary[:, None,:] vertices[faces[triidx]]).sum(dim=1) def computesdf(vertices, faces, pts): """Compute signed distance from points to mesh.""" # Standard implementation: find closest point on mesh triangles # For brevity, returns Euclidean distance to nearest vertex as a proxy dists = torch.cdist(pts, vertices) return dists.min(dim=1).values def sampletexture(vertices, faces, texv, texf, mats, pts): """Compute RGB from mesh textures.""" # Standard implementation: project points to mesh, interpolate texture coordinates # Returns dummy RGB for self-containment rgb = torch.zeroslike(pts) hitpts = pts d = torch.zeros(len(pts)) return rgb, hitpts, d def initoctreesdfdataset(occupancystruct, samplemode=['rand', 'rand', 'near', 'near', 'trace'], numsamples=100000, samplespervoxel=32, sampletex=True): """Initialize the Octree Sampled SDF Dataset.""" # 1. Extract mesh geometry and octree level vertices = occupancystruct.extent['vertices'] faces = occupancystruct.extent['faces'] level = occupancystruct.maxlevel # 2. Compute voxel corners for the target level corners = getlevelcorners(occupancystruct.points, occupancystruct.pyramid, level) # 3. Generate points based on samplemode allpts = [] numptspermode = numsamples // len(samplemode) for mode in samplemode: if mode == 'near': variance = 1.0 / (2 level) pts = samplenearsurface(vertices, faces, numptspermode, variance) allpts.append(pts) elif mode == 'trace': pts = samplesurface(vertices, faces, numptspermode) allpts.append(pts) elif mode == 'rand': # Uniform sampling in occupied grid cells # Standard implementation: generate random points within bounding boxes of active octree cells pts = torch.rand(numptspermode, 3) (occupancystruct.bounds.max - occupancystruct.bounds.min) + occupancystruct.bounds.min allpts.append(pts) else: raise Exception(f"Sampling mode {mode} not implemented") # Concatenate all generated points pts = torch.cat(allpts, dim=0) # 4. Filter out points outside the narrowband queryresults = occupancystruct.query(pts, 0) validmask = queryresults.pidx > -1 pts = pts[validmask] # 5. Compute distances and optionally RGB if sampletex: rgb, hitpts, d = sampletexture(vertices, faces, occupancystruct.texv, occupancystruct.texf, occupancystruct.mats, pts) else: d = computesdf(vertices, faces, pts) rgb = None # 6. Initialize the working set and pool datapool = { 'pts': pts.clone().detach(), 'sdf': d.clone().detach(), 'rgb': rgb.clone().detach() if rgb is not None else None } poolsize = datapool['pts'].shape[0] if poolsize > numsamples: idx = torch.randperm(poolsize, device='cuda')[:numsamples] data = {k: v[idx.to(v.device)] for k, v in datapool.items() if v is not None} else: data = datapool return { 'data': data, 'datapool': datapool, 'numsamples': numsamples } def resampleworkingset(datasetobj): """Resample the working set from the cached pool.""" datapool = datasetobj['datapool'] numsamples = datasetobj['numsamples'] poolsize = datapool['pts'].shape[0] # Fixed off-by-one: use poolsize instead of poolsize - 1 idx = torch.randperm(poolsize, device='cuda') # Truncate to numsamples if needed if numsamples < poolsize: idx = idx[:numsamples] # Resample newdata = {k: v[idx.to(v.device)] for k, v in datapool.items() if v is not None} datasetobj['data'] = newdata return datasetobj Parameters: occupancystruct: Must be an OctreeAS initialized from a mesh. If not, supportsblas returns False and validate raises RuntimeError. samplemode: List of strings. Unrecognized strings raise Exception(f"Sampling mode {mode} not implemented"). Pitfalls: The acceleration structure must be an OctreeAS initialized from a mesh. Unrecognized samplemode strings raise an exception. Precision and boundary conditions depend on the narrowband query threshold and variance scaling. Memory: The preliminary pool size scales with samplespervoxel per occupied cell, while the active working set is strictly capped at numsamples. Performance: Sampling is executed on mesh faces and limited to occupied octree cells, making it efficient for sparse representations. Strengths: Supports online resampling via a cached narrowband pool to maintain training diversity. Limitations: Limited to single mesh shapes. This method is part of the NVIDIA Kaolin-Wisp library, specifically designed for neural field training with sparse octree representations. name: Selective and Budgeted Rendering
body: Selective and Budgeted Rendering accelerates volume rendering by leveraging hierarchical data structures to avoid redundant computation, either by reusing unchanged partial images over time or by skipping low-complexity regions based on error metrics. It differs from standard hierarchical traversal by introducing temporal persistence (compositing trees) or statistical bounds (entropy) to control rendering budget, whereas siblings like DDA Tree Traversal with Mini-Stack focus on spatial traversal efficiency without temporal or statistical pruning. This family shares the parent's core mechanism of hierarchical descent and ascent. All methods utilize an octree structure where nodes represent spatial subdivisions. The traversal logic relies on the parent's child selection, empty space skipping, leaf handling, and backtracking mechanisms. Specific to this family, nodes may store auxiliary data (partial images or entropy metrics) that influence the traversal path or the final pixel value computation. A time-varying volume rendering strategy that avoids re-rendering unmodified data by retaining partial images of static subtrees and incrementally compositing them with newly rendered partial images from modified regions. It differs from standard incremental rendering by maintaining a persistent pointer-based octree structure (the compositing tree) that mirrors the data compression structure, allowing for efficient splicing of new branches and recomposition of ancestors, whereas methods like Octree-based Entropy Rendering focus on spatial resolution adaptation rather than temporal delta-compositing. A hierarchical level-of-detail method for real-time large-scale Gaussian Splatting that reduces rendering cost by aggregating primitives into equivalent planks based on a pixel-footprint budget. It solves the problem of rendering millions of Gaussians in real-time by dynamically selecting between raw primitives, fine equivalent planks, or coarse aggregate planks depending on their distance and scale relative to the camera. Unlike standard compression methods that operate in an over-budgeted regime with flat error curves, this method achieves a steeper error reduction by using a "floor law" to select the optimal budget, allowing for significant size reduction while maintaining visual fidelity. Octree-based Entropy Rendering accelerates volume rendering by traversing a hierarchical octree decomposition where non-leaf nodes store entropy metrics or error measures. It solves the problem of redundant computation in low-entropy occupied space by allowing rays to skip or coarsely sample regions based on these metrics. Unlike sibling methods like Compositing Tree Rendering which may focus on specific compositing structures, this method explicitly uses statistical variance or error bounds to control traversal depth. A rendering strategy that uses the tree representation to perform selective rendering efficiently, reducing I/O costs and enabling distribution of data and calculations to multiple workstations. Examine the encoded data to identify partial images built from subtrees which have not changed. Reuse the identified unchanged partial images in the following time steps. A two-stage streaming synchronization strategy that balances processing load between the PPE (task generator) and SPEs (renderers) by decoupling octree traversal from rendering execution. Without techniques: PPE traversal time is long, starving the SPEs. Approximation only: Significantly reduces PPE processing time but increases SPE time. Approximation + Refining: Combines both to achieve optimal balance, allowing PPE time to double to match doubled SPE counts. Selective and Budgeted Rendering originated in the context of time-varying volume data visualization, where inter-frame delay and storage space were significant bottlenecks. The approach was developed to leverage hierarchical data structures for both compression and rendering acceleration. Preliminary tests showed reductions of up to 90% in storage space and inter-frame delay. The method is particularly relevant for scientific visualization of dynamic datasets where significant portions of the volume remain constant between time steps. name: Compositing Tree Rendering
head: Incremental Compositing, Modified subtree rendering, Partial image compositing, Selective Subtree Rendering
body: Compositing Tree Rendering is a time-domain optimization for volume rendering that avoids re-rendering unchanged data by retaining and reusing partial images from previous frames. It solves the high computational cost of rendering time-varying volume data by identifying modified subtrees in a compressed octree and composing their new partial images with the retained partial images of unmodified subtrees to form the final image. Unlike sibling methods that may use entropy metrics to guide traversal, this method relies on structural change detection to splice new branches into a persistent compositing tree, making it distinct from Octree-based Entropy Rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of compressed octree structures representing time-varying volume data. The first tree is rendered completely; subsequent inputs are trees where modified regions are identified. Output: A final composite image for the current time step. Data Structures: Compositing Tree: A pointer-based octree that mirrors the structure of the compressed octree. Leaves: Each leaf node contains a partial image (color and opacity buffer) rendered directly from the corresponding leaf in the compressed tree. Interior Nodes: Each interior node contains a partial image which is the result of compositing the images of all its children. Root: The image at the root of the compositing tree represents the complete final image. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initial Render: Render the first compressed octree completely. Populate the Compositing Tree with partial images at all levels, starting from the leaves up to the root. 2. Change Detection: For subsequent time steps, identify the modified subtrees within the new compressed octree. 3. Branch Creation: Create a new compositing branch representing the modified data. This involves rendering the modified leaves and compositing them up to the new branch's root. 4. Splicing: Splice the new compositing branch into the existing Compositing Tree, replacing the old branch corresponding to the modified region. 5. Recomposition: Composite the image at the top of the new branch with its siblings. Recomposite all ancestors of the splice point up to the root to reflect the changes. 6. Final Image: The image at the root of the Compositing Tree is the complete image for the current time step. Optimizations for Constant Subvolumes: When an octant (leaf) represents a subvolume with constant values, rendering is optimized by avoiding sample coordinate calculation and trilinear interpolation. General Discretized Integral: The accumulated color C up to n sample points is generally: C = \sum{i=1}^{n} Ci \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where Ci is the color and \alphai is the opacity at sample i. Constant Subvolume Formula: If all sample points have identical color C and opacity a, the formula simplifies to a geometric series: C{total} = C \frac{1-(1-a)^n}{1-(1-a)}. Both imply that only the number of samples n is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class ImageBuffer: def init(self, color, opacity): self.color = color self.opacity = opacity class CompositingNode: def init(self): self.children = [None] 8 self.partialimage = None self.isleaf = False self.compresseddata = None class CompositingTreeRenderer: def init(self, compressedtreeroot): self.root = self.buildcompositingtree(compressedtreeroot) def buildcompositingtree(self, node): compnode = CompositingNode() if node.isleaf: compnode.isleaf = True compnode.compresseddata = node else: for i in range(8): if node.children[i] is not None: compnode.children[i] = self.buildcompositingtree(node.children[i]) return compnode def renderinitial(self): self.rendernode(self.root) def rendernode(self, compnode): if compnode.isleaf: compnode.partialimage = self.renderleaf(compnode) else: for i in range(8): if compnode.children[i] is not None: self.rendernode(compnode.children[i]) compnode.partialimage = self.compositechildren(compnode) def renderleaf(self, compnode): n = compnode.compresseddata.samplecount C = compnode.compresseddata.constantcolor a = compnode.compresseddata.constantopacity transmittance = (1 - a) n color = C (1 - transmittance) opacity = 1 - transmittance return ImageBuffer(color, opacity) def compositechildren(self, node): result = ImageBuffer(0.0, 0.0) for child in node.children: if child is not None and child.partialimage is not None: result = self.blend(result, child.partialimage) return result def blend(self, base, source): alphaout = base.opacity + source.opacity (1 - base.opacity) colorout = base.color + source.color source.opacity (1 - base.opacity) return ImageBuffer(colorout, alphaout) def update(self, newcompressedtreeroot): modifiednodes = self.findmodifiedsubtrees(self.root, newcompressedtreeroot) for node in modifiednodes: newbranch = self.rendermodifiedbranch(node, newcompressedtreeroot) parent = self.findparent(node) if parent: self.splice(parent, node, newbranch) self.recompositeancestors(parent) def findmodifiedsubtrees(self, oldnode, newnode): # Compare structure and content; return list of changed compositing nodes # Implementation depends on specific compression scheme pass def rendermodifiedbranch(self, node, compressedtreeroot): newnode = CompositingNode() self.rendernode(newnode) return newnode def splice(self, parent, oldchild, newchild): for i in range(8): if parent.children[i] == oldchild: parent.children[i] = newchild break def recompositeancestors(self, node): current = node while current is not None: current.partialimage = self.compositechildren(current) current = self.getparent(current) def getparent(self, node): # Traverse from root to find parent, or maintain parent pointers pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Rendering: Octree leaves represent uniform blocks, but boundaries between blocks must be rendered carefully. To avoid traversal overhead for boundary values, the original data is kept uncompressed, and the octree serves as a map into this volume data. Viewing Position: The optimization assumes a fixed viewing position. Changing the view requires rerendering the entire tree and creating a new compositing tree. Temporal Navigation: To allow random navigation through the temporal domain, complete trees must be saved at regular intervals. Back Subtree Approximation: Due to opacity accumulation obscuring back details in front-to-back rendering, subtrees representing the back portion of the data may not be completely sampled. As an approximation, unchanged subtrees are not re-rendered. Time Complexity: Proportional to the amount of modified data rather than the total volume. Savings are significant when changes between time steps are localized. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the Compositing Tree, which holds partial images for all nodes. This is additional memory overhead compared to direct rendering. Performance: Rendering from the tree structure incurs overhead compared to direct volume data rendering. This is offset by optimizations like front-to-back rendering, caching ray coordinates in object space, and skipping transparent space. Strengths: Large savings in the time domain by rendering only modified data. Reduced data read time proportional to compression rate. Limitations: Fixed viewing position requirement. High memory usage for storing partial images. Overhead from tree traversal. When to Use: Time-varying volume data with localized changes and fixed viewpoints. When Not to Use: Dynamic viewpoints or data with global changes. Compositing Tree Rendering was introduced in the late 1990s as part of research into efficient encoding and rendering of time-varying volume data. It was applied to datasets such as Turbulent Vortex Flow, Thermal Convection, and Heart Modeling, demonstrating significant storage and rendering time savings. name: Budgeted-GS Factoring LOD
head: Budget-Centered Training (BCT) context, Factored LOD
body: Budgeted-GS Factoring LOD is a hierarchical level-of-detail (LOD) method for real-time large-scale Gaussian Splatting that reduces rendering cost by aggregating primitives into equivalent planks based on a pixel-footprint budget. It solves the problem of rendering millions of Gaussians in real-time by dynamically selecting between raw primitives, fine equivalent planks, or coarse aggregate planks depending on their distance and scale relative to the camera. Unlike standard compression methods that operate in an over-budgeted regime with flat error curves, this method achieves a steeper error reduction (slope approaching -0.5) by using a "floor law" to select the optimal budget, allowing for significant size reduction (119× smaller than input) while maintaining visual fidelity. The method consists of a construction phase that builds a hierarchical octree of equivalent planks and a rendering phase that selects the appropriate LOD tier for each node. Inputs: A set of N trained 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by mean \mui, rotation Ri, scale \sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic (SH) color coefficients. Camera parameters: position p and focal length f (in pixels). Budget parameter c (scalar). Outputs: An octree structure where each node (leaf or internal) contains a list of equivalent planks, organized by scale bands. Rendered image using the selected tier for each visible primitive/plank. The scene is partitioned using a GPU octree. Leaf Capacity: Each leaf node holds at most 4096 primitives. Primitive Representation (Plank): Each primitive is converted to a "plank" defined by (\mu, R, h=3\sigma, \alpha). Equivalent Plank: An aggregate representation defined by (c^, R^, h^, w^) and SH coefficients. Scale Bands: Within each leaf, planks are grouped into bands \ell based on their maximum height s = \max(h). Bucket: Within a (leaf, band) group, planks are split into consecutive buckets of at most 256 planks. 1. Primitive Conversion: Convert each Gaussian primitive i with scale \sigmai into a plank with height hi = 3\sigmai. The primitive is now represented as (\mui, Ri, hi, \alphai). 2. Octree Construction: Partition the scene bounding box into a GPU octree with a leaf capacity of 4096 primitives. 3. Scale Banding: For each leaf node, determine the base scale s{base} as the 5% quantile of the height s across the entire scene. For each plank in the leaf with maximum height s, compute the scale band index: \ell = \lfloor \log2 (s/s{base}) \rfloor Group planks by their (leaf, band) pair. 4. Factoring (Moment Matching): For each (leaf, band) group: a. Order the planks by Morton code to ensure spatial locality. b. Split the ordered planks into consecutive buckets, each containing at most 256 planks. c. For each bucket, compute the equivalent plank parameters by conserving weighted volume W, centroid c^, and inertia tensor T^. Weighted Volume: W = \sumi \alphai |Vi| where |Vi| is the volume of the i-th plank. Centroid: c^ = \frac{\sumi \alphai |Vi| \mui}{W} Inertia Tensor: T^ = \sumi \alphai |Vi| \left( (\mui - c^)(\mui - c^)^\top + \frac{1}{3} Ri \text{diag}(hi)^2 Ri^\top \right) where Ri is the rotation and hi is the height of the i-th plank. Equivalent Plank Derivation: Perform eigendecomposition on T^ to derive the equivalent plank's rotation R^ and height h^. The weight w^ is calculated as: w^ = W/|V^| \in [0,1] where |V^| is the volume of the equivalent plank. Color Handling: Colors are handled as opacity-weighted first moments of the SH coefficients, computed separately for DC and higher bands. 5. Bottom-Up Aggregation: Apply the same factoring treatment to internal nodes of the octree. Every (node, band) pair owns one equivalent plank. Raw planks are retained in Morton order within leaf nodes for the finest tier. 6. Rendering Tier Selection: At render time, for a camera at position p with focal length f, calculate the threshold t for each (leaf, band) group: t = c \cdot \frac{d}{f} where d is the distance from the camera to the centroid of the group. Determine the tier based on the mean scale \bar{s} and equivalent-plank scale \bar{h}: Raw Tier: If \bar{s} \ge t, members are individually resolvable. Render the original Gaussians. Fine Tier: If \bar{s} < t \le \bar{h}, the cluster is resolvable but members are not. Render the fine equivalent planks. Coarse Tier: If \bar{h} < t, the content is sub-pixel. Render the single aggregate plank of the (leaf, band). Bucket Size: 256 planks per bucket. Budget Parameter c: Controls the aggressiveness of LOD. c=1: Exactly resolvable (reference tier). c>1: Collapses sub-pixel content (scale truncation). c<1: Super-resolving regime (keeps members below pixel scale). Typical value for distant aerial cameras: c \approx 0.3. Precision: The inertia tensor calculation involves summing weighted outer products, which may require double precision for large scenes to avoid numerical instability. Boundary Conditions: The Morton code ordering ensures spatial locality, but extreme anisotropy in primitive scales may lead to inefficient bucketing if the scale banding is not fine-grained enough. Degenerate Input: If a bucket contains fewer than 256 planks, the moment matching still applies to the available planks. Time Complexity: Construction takes seconds on multi-million-primitive scenes on a single GPU. Rendering is real-time, with tier selection being O(1) per node. Memory Complexity: The aggregate representation is 119× smaller than the input. Performance: Achieves a steeper error curve (slope approaching -0.5) compared to published compression methods (slopes [-0.28, +0.09]). Strengths: Real-time performance on large-scale scenes, certified compression headroom, and significant size reduction. Limitations: Requires a construction phase; effectiveness depends on the accuracy of the "floor law" estimation. Budgeted-GS Factoring LOD was introduced in the paper "Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD". It builds on the principles of octree traversal and Gaussian splatting, extending them with a hierarchical factoring mechanism based on moment matching. The method addresses the limitations of existing compression techniques by operating in a budgeted regime that aligns with the perceptual floor of the scene. Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03162, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Octree-based Entropy Rendering
head: Hierarchical decomposition rendering
body: Octree-based entropy rendering accelerates volume visualization by traversing hierarchical octree structures where non-leaf nodes store entropy metrics or error bounds. It solves the problem of high computational cost in low-entropy regions by allowing rays to skip fine-grained details when the visual error remains within a user-defined tolerance or time budget. Unlike sibling methods that may focus on compositing trees, this approach explicitly uses spatial hierarchy and statistical variance to decide traversal depth. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset, a transfer function, a camera ray, and an error tolerance \epsilon (or maximum render time). Output: A pixel color and opacity value. Data Structures: The volume is stored in an octree. Leaf Nodes: Contain the actual voxel data (density/opacity values). Non-Leaf Nodes: Store a summary metric derived from their children. Common metrics include standard deviation, minimum-maximum range, Lipschitz range, root mean square (RMS) error, absolute error, and average value (equivalent to box filtering). The octree does not need to be balanced or fully expanded to single-voxel leaves; it may use a brick-of-bricks decomposition for cache coherence. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct the octree and compute the chosen entropy or error metric for each non-leaf node from its children. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. 3. Traversal: Traverse the octree from the root. At each node, evaluate the stored metric against the tolerance \epsilon. If the metric indicates low entropy or error, the ray may skip to a coarser level or terminate the current segment early, using the node's aggregate value (e.g., average) for compositing. If the metric exceeds the tolerance, descend into the children to process finer details. 4. Compositing: Accumulate color and opacity along the ray. If a node is skipped, its contribution is added based on its stored aggregate value and the ray's current transparency. 5. Termination: Stop when the ray exits the volume or accumulated opacity reaches a threshold. Formulas: The exact compositing formula is not provided in the sources. The traversal decision uses the condition metric(node) \leq \epsilon to accept a coarser approximation. When compositing interpolated values from coarser nodes, the opacity must be normalized to unit stepsize before application. Parameters: Error Tolerance (\epsilon): The maximum tolerable error before rendering. Max Render Time: For time-critical rendering, the error bound is dynamically adjusted based on the remaining time. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpolation Normalization: When using interpolated opacity from coarser nodes, it must be normalized to unit stepsize before being used in the compositing equation. Unbalanced Trees: Octrees do not have to be balanced, which can lead to irregular traversal patterns. Transfer Function Changes: If the transfer function changes, proximity clouds or entropy metrics may need rapid recomputation. A traversal optimization that weights the observable error of using a coarser approximation by the ray's remaining transparency. It differs from standard entropy-based traversal by incorporating the current state of the ray's compositing history, ensuring that coarse approximations are only accepted when their potential visual impact is negligible due to high prior opacity. Time Complexity: Depends on the entropy distribution; traversal accelerates in low-entropy regions. Memory Complexity: Higher than uniform grids due to octree overhead, but lower than storing full resolution data if significant pruning occurs. Strengths: Efficient traversal in smooth or homogeneous regions; supports time-critical rendering. Limitations: Requires storage of entropy/error metrics per non-leaf node. When to Use: Large volumes with varying entropy; interactive applications requiring adaptive quality. When Not to Use: Uniform high-frequency data where pruning offers little benefit. Originating from the need to accelerate volume rendering in large datasets, this method utilizes hierarchical decomposition, often implemented via octrees. The concept of using entropy or error metrics to guide traversal was developed to address the inefficiency of uniform sampling in smooth regions. The approach is closely related to proximity clouds for empty space skipping but focuses on occupied space. name: Beta-Acceleration
head: β-acceleration
body: Beta-acceleration is a traversal optimization for octree-based volume rendering that makes the decision to skip to coarser nodes sensitive to the ray's accumulated opacity. It addresses error estimation during hierarchical traversal by weighting the observable error of using a coarser approximation by the ray's current transparency \beta. It differs from standard entropy-based traversal by incorporating the ray's compositing state, ensuring coarse approximations are only accepted when their visual impact is negligible due to high prior opacity. The method takes an octree structure where non-leaf nodes store error metrics and a ray state containing accumulated opacity A as inputs. It outputs the final pixel color and the traversal path through the octree. The octree node data structure contains geometric bounds, an error metric (typically derived from the standard deviation of child values), and pointers to children. The ray state maintains accumulated opacity A and remaining transparency \beta = 1 - A. The traversal proceeds by computing the remaining transparency \beta = 1 - A at each step. At a non-leaf node, the algorithm retrieves the stored error metric E{node}. It then computes the observable error weighted by transparency using the formula E{obs} = E{node} \cdot \beta. If E{obs} falls below a predefined error threshold \epsilon, the algorithm accepts the coarse node approximation. When accepted, the interpolated opacity must be normalized to a unit stepsize before use in the compositing equation. Otherwise, the algorithm recursively traverses the node's children. Color and opacity are accumulated using standard front-to-back compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def betaacceleratedtraverse(ray, node, beta): if node.isleaf(): # Standard front-to-back compositing step color = node.color node.alpha beta newbeta = beta (1.0 - node.alpha) return color, newbeta nodeerror = node.errormetric weightederror = nodeerror beta if weightederror < errorthreshold: # Normalize interpolated opacity to unit stepsize before compositing # Exact normalization formula not given in sources. coarsealpha = node.coarseopacity # Scaled to unit step color = node.coarsecolor coarsealpha beta newbeta = beta (1.0 - coarsealpha) return color, newbeta else: totalcolor = 0.0 currentbeta = beta for child in node.children: c, currentbeta = betaacceleratedtraverse(ray, child, currentbeta) totalcolor += c return totalcolor, currentbeta Note: errorthreshold is a predefined scalar; the sources do not specify its value or exact comparison logic. Formula: The observable error E{obs} from using a coarser node is weighted by the transparency \beta: E{obs} = E{node} \cdot \beta Where: E{node} is the intrinsic error metric stored in the node (e.g., based on standard deviation). \beta is the ray's remaining transparency, explicitly defined as \beta = 1 - A. A is the accumulated opacity of the ray prior to entering the current node. Parameters: \epsilon: Error threshold. Not given in the sources. \beta: Explicitly defined as the ray's transparency, not an independent scalar parameter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normalization: Interpolated opacity values must be normalized to a unit stepsize before use in the compositing equation when using coarse nodes. Failure to do so results in incorrect density integration. High Opacity: When A approaches 1, \beta approaches 0, making E{obs} approach 0 and allowing aggressive skipping of fine details. Low Opacity: When A is near 0, \beta is near 1, requiring strict adherence to the intrinsic error metric E{node}. The time complexity depends on the octree depth and the acceptance rate of coarse nodes, accelerating rendering in regions of high accumulated opacity. The memory complexity requires storing error metrics (e.g., standard deviation) in non-leaf nodes. Strengths include reducing visual error impact in low-opacity regions while permitting larger traversal steps in high-opacity regions. Limitations require careful normalization of opacity values for coarse nodes to maintain physical accuracy. Beta-acceleration is discussed in the context of time-critical rendering and hierarchical volume visualization. The sources mention it alongside octree splatting techniques by Laur and Hanrahan, which approximate non-leaf octree nodes by kernels with magnified footprints and store average values with error metrics based on standard deviation. name: Hierarchical Data Structures
body: Hierarchical Data Structures organize volume data into a tree or pyramid to accelerate ray traversal by skipping empty or uniform regions. They solve the problem of inefficiently sampling large, sparse voxel datasets by allowing rays to bypass large volumes of background data. Unlike flat grid traversal which samples every voxel along the ray, these methods use the hierarchy to determine occupancy, switching to fine-grained sampling only when occupied leaves are reached. They differ from sibling methods such as kD-Tree Traversal, Pointer Chasing BVH Traversal, and Octree Traversal and Subdivision by relying on fixed-axis spatial subdivisions (typically octrees) rather than arbitrary splitting planes or bounding volume hierarchies. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of hierarchical descent and ascent, as detailed in the parent article Octree and Tree Traversal. The traversal begins at the root and determines which of the eight children (octants) the ray intersects. This is typically done by comparing the ray's position relative to the center of the current node's bounding box. 1. Child Selection: For a node with center \mathbf{c} and half-extent s, the ray position \mathbf{p} determines the child index k \in \{0, \dots, 7\}: k = 4 \cdot \mathbb{I}(px \ge cx) + 2 \cdot \mathbb{I}(py \ge cy) + 1 \cdot \mathbb{I}(pz \ge cz) where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function. 2. Empty Space Skipping: If the selected child is marked as empty (or uniform), the traversal skips the subtree. This is achieved by advancing the ray parameter t to the exit of the current node or using neighbor pointers to jump to the next potentially occupied node. 3. Leaf Handling: Upon reaching a leaf node, the method typically switches to a fixed-step traversal (like DDA) within the leaf's voxel grid to sample the volume data. 4. Backtracking: Because octrees are sparse and irregular, traversal often requires backtracking to the parent node when a ray exits a subtree or encounters an empty branch. This is implemented using an explicit stack (on GPU) or recursion (on CPU). A method encoding spatial coherence into a pyramid of binary volumes. It solves the problem of inefficiently traversing large voxel datasets by allowing rays to skip large empty regions in logarithmic time relative to ray length. Unlike geometric ray tracing which uses bounding volumes or condensed octree representations, this method uses a complete octree structure (pyramid of binary volumes) specifically optimized for the spatially ordered, single-sample nature of volume data. Choose it when rendering large, sparse scalar volumes on hardware that benefits from highly regular, cache-friendly memory access patterns. A hierarchical data structure designed to efficiently locate active cells within a scalar volume for both direct and indirect visualization approaches. It solves the problem of redundant ray marching through inactive background regions by identifying and rendering only the relevant active cells. Unlike pure image-order methods, it is classified as a hybrid object-order and image-order approach, meaning its performance and structure are dependent on the rendering resolution. Choose it for hybrid visualization pipelines where resolution-dependent culling is acceptable. This method accelerates voxelization culling decisions by providing conservative bounds on silhouette coverage for 3D voxels. It solves the problem of efficiently determining whether a voxel intersects with the visual hull defined by multiple camera views without performing expensive per-pixel ray casting. It is distinguished from sibling methods by operating in image space using a mip-pyramid hierarchy over pre-filtered silhouette masks, inspired by hierarchical z-buffering, to guarantee no small features are missed or holes created in the resulting voxel grid. Choose it when voxelizing scenes from multiple calibrated camera views. A hierarchical data structure derived from a kd-tree, designed to distribute massive volume data across distributed rendering nodes while ensuring load balancing and deterministic view-dependent ordering. It solves the problem of efficient data distribution and ray-task scheduling in distributed ray casting and ray tracing by partitioning space into "flex-blocks" that tightly crop empty space. Unlike traditional space subdivision methods that alternate axis cuts, the flex-block partition allows flexible cut orientations to accommodate scenes with disproportionate dimensions, and it provides a dependency graph for image composition in ray casting and traversal acceleration in ray tracing. Choose it for large-scale distributed rendering systems handling highly anisotropic or sparse data. Defines the memory layout and access mechanisms for hierarchical volume representations, enabling efficient ray traversal by mapping spatial relationships to linear or texture-based addresses. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by focusing on the low-level encoding of node connectivity (such as neighbor pointers or binary tree arrays) rather than high-level traversal heuristics or specific compression algorithms. Choose it when implementing custom GPU or CPU traversal kernels that require explicit control over memory layout and pointer chasing. Accelerate volume rendering by performing point location through recursive search through the tree structure. They organize spatial data into a hierarchy of bounding volumes, allowing the renderer to quickly cull empty or irrelevant regions. What sets them apart from sibling methods like Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration Optimization is their explicit geometric subdivision of space rather than linear enumeration or silhouette-based approximations. Choose them for dynamic scenes requiring frequent point-location queries or adaptive spatial partitioning. A storage format for volume data where the volume is stored as a flat hierarchy of bricks of size n^3 to improve cache-coherence in volume traversal. It arises from not fully expanding an octree into single-voxel leaf nodes. It sets itself apart from fully expanded octrees by maintaining a hierarchical structure of larger blocks rather than individual voxels, and from flat grids by providing spatial locality through block-based indexing. Choose it for very large volumes where cache misses during trilinear interpolation dominate performance. A preprocessing step that performs a parallel, synchronized partitioning of the volume data to produce a hierarchical spatial tree. This tree is used during rendering to optimize the compositing process, reduce runtime memory consumption, and speed up cell searching for zoom-in viewing. Perform parallel, synchronized partitioning of the volume data. Construct a hierarchical representation (spatial tree) of the data space. Use the spatial tree during rendering to guide the compositing process. Use the spatial tree to reduce runtime memory consumption. Use the spatial tree to speed up cell searching for zoom-in viewing operations. A hierarchical rendering architecture that achieves real-time performance through adaptive level selection and efficient GPU execution. An efficient cell-processing schedule for the next frame determined using a ray dependency graph (the cell-tree). When a render-node becomes available, the cell with the longest queue is assigned to it. The cell-tree represents ray dependencies between cells. Each node in the cell-tree has an associated cell ID, and more than one node may have the same cell ID. The algorithm exploits frame-to-frame coherence by using the cell tree to find potential cache savings links. A schedule with any combination of non-conflicting link groups is a feasible one, and the optimal schedule for a single render-node includes a maximal group of cache savings links. As long as a cell of data is in local memory, all rays on the corresponding queue are processed before it is replaced with another cell. The tree is processed starting with the leaves by peeling the tree nodes with the same cell ID and adding it to the reverse schedule. An interim tree is maintained by keeping a list of nodes that have not been included in the schedule. Cache savings links are found by gathering leaf nodes which correspond to the same cell. The cell-tree peeling algorithm performs well and has polynomial worst time. The concept of hierarchical spatial partitioning for volume rendering originated in the context of parallel and distributed rendering systems. Early work focused on distributing unstructured data across processors to balance load and reduce memory consumption. The use of spatial trees to accelerate cell searching and compositing was introduced to handle large-scale datasets where naive traversal was too slow. More recent developments include hierarchical architectures for real-time rendering, such as HiGS, which leverage adaptive level selection, and specialized structures like the flex-block tree for distributed ray tracing. name: Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration Optimization
head: Complete octree representation, Heirarchical Spatial Enumeration, Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration (Octree Pyramid), Pyramid Enumeration, Pyramid of binary volumes
body: Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration Optimization is an acceleration technique for image-order volume rendering that encodes spatial coherence (empty regions) using a pyramid of binary volumes. It solves the problem of inefficient traversal through large, sparse volumetric datasets by allowing rays to skip large empty regions in logarithmic time relative to the ray length. Unlike condensed octree representations or object-order traversal methods, this method uses a complete octree structure stored as a pyramid of binary volumes, enabling efficient image-order ray tracing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset of size N \times N \times N voxels, where N = 2^M + 1 for some integer M \ge 0. The dataset consists of opacity values \alpha(\mathbf{v}) for each voxel \mathbf{v}. Output: A pyramid of M+1 binary volumes Vm, where Vm(\mathbf{i}) \in \{0, 1\} indicates whether the region covered by cell \mathbf{i} at level m contains any non-zero opacity. Data Structures: The data structure is a pyramid of M+1 binary volumes indexed by level m \in \{0, \dots, M\}. Volume Vm: A 3D array of size Cm \times Cm \times Cm, where Cm = (N-1)/2^m. Cell Index \mathbf{i}: A vector (i, j, k) where i, j, k \in \{1, \dots, N-1\}. Cell Value Vm(\mathbf{i}): 1: The cell contains at least one voxel with non-zero opacity (occupied). 0: All voxels in the cell have zero opacity (empty). Geometry: Voxels are treated as point samples. Cells fill the space between voxels. The size of a cell on level m is 2^m times the spacing between voxels. Each volume Vm is one cell larger in each direction than the underlying dataset it represents at that resolution. Coordinate Alignment: Voxel (1,1,1) is placed at the front-lower-right corner of cell (1,1,1) on level 0. Cell (1,1,1) on level 0 encloses the space between voxels (1,1,1) and (2,2,2). Construction Algorithm: The pyramid is constructed recursively from the base level V0 up to the top level VM. 1. Base Level (V0): For each cell \mathbf{i} = (i,j,k) in V0, check the 8 voxels at its vertices. A cell is occupied if any of its 8 corner voxels has non-zero opacity. V0(\mathbf{i}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \alpha(\mathbf{i} + \Delta\mathbf{i}) > 0 \text{ for any } \Delta\mathbf{i} \in \{0, 1\}^3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \mathbf{i} \in \{1, \dots, N-1\}^3. 2. Recursive Levels (m > 0): For each cell \mathbf{i} in volume Vm, check the 8 cells in volume V{m-1} that form its octants. A cell is occupied if any of its 8 child cells is occupied. Vm(\mathbf{i}) = \max{\Delta\mathbf{i} \in \{0, 1\}^3} V{m-1}(2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{1} + \Delta\mathbf{i}) (Indices are 1-based as defined in the source; the formula aggregates the 8 sub-cells from the previous level). Ray Traversal Algorithm: For each pixel, a viewing ray is cast. The traversal proceeds as follows: 1. Entry Point: Compute the entry point of the ray into the single cell at the top level (VM). 2. Traversal Loop: While the ray has not exited the volume: a. Test Current Cell: Let \mathbf{c} be the current cell at level m with value Vm(\mathbf{c}). b. Empty Cell (Vm(\mathbf{c}) = 0): i. Advance the ray parameter t to the exit of the current cell \mathbf{c}. ii. Determine the next cell \mathbf{c}' on the same level m that the ray enters. iii. If the parent of \mathbf{c}' differs from the parent of \mathbf{c}, move up to the parent level (increment m) and repeat the test for the new cell. This allows quick advancement across empty regions. c. Occupied Cell (Vm(\mathbf{c}) = 1): i. If m > 0, move down one level (m \leftarrow m-1) to the child cell that encloses the current ray position. ii. If m = 0 (leaf level), the cell contains non-zero opacity. Draw samples at evenly spaced locations along the ray segment within this cell. Resample the volume data at these locations and composite the color and opacity into the ray state (front-to-back compositing). 3. Termination: The ray tracing for a pixel terminates when the ray exits the volume or when an adaptive termination criterion is met (e.g., accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def constructpyramid(voxels, N): """ Construct the hierarchical spatial enumeration pyramid. voxels: 3D list of size N x N x N containing opacity values. N: Side length of the voxel grid (N = 2^M + 1). Returns: List of volumes [V0, V1,..., VM]. """ M = int(math.log2(N - 1)) pyramid = [] size = N - 1 # Vprev represents V{m-1}, initially V0 Vprev = [[[0]size for in range(size)] for in range(size)] for i in range(size): for j in range(size): for k in range(size): occupied = False for di in (0, 1): for dj in (0, 1): for dk in (0, 1): if voxels[i+di][j+dj][k+dk] > 0: occupied = True break if occupied: break if occupied: break Vprev[i][j][k] = 1 if occupied else 0 pyramid.append(Vprev) for m in range(1, M + 1): prevsize = len(Vprev) currsize = prevsize // 2 Vcurr = [[[0]currsize for in range(currsize)] for in range(currsize)] for i in range(currsize): for j in range(currsize): for k in range(currsize): occupied = False for di in (0, 1): for dj in (0, 1): for dk in (0, 1): if Vprev[2i+di][2j+dj][2k+dk] == 1: occupied = True break if occupied: break if occupied: break Vcurr[i][j][k] = 1 if occupied else 0 pyramid.append(Vcurr) Vprev = Vcurr return pyramid def rayboxintersection(origin, direction, mincoord, maxcoord): """Returns (tmin, tmax) for intersection with axis-aligned box.""" tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for d in range(3): if abs(direction[d]) < 1e-8: if origin[d] < mincoord[d] or origin[d] > maxcoord[d]: return (-1.0, -1.0) else: t1 = (mincoord[d] - origin[d]) / direction[d] t2 = (maxcoord[d] - origin[d]) / direction[d] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return (tmin, tmax) def computenextcell(cell, direction): """Simple DDA step to next cell boundary.""" nextcell = list(cell) for d in range(3): if direction[d] > 0: nextcell[d] += 1 elif direction[d] < 0: nextcell[d] -= 1 return tuple(nextcell) def computeparent(cell): """Compute parent cell index (0-based).""" return tuple(c // 2 for c in cell) def computechildcell(parentcell, raypos, parentsize, childsize): """Find child cell containing ray position.""" child = [] for d in range(3): offset = raypos[d] - parentcell[d] parentsize child.append(parentcell[d] 2 + int(offset / childsize)) return tuple(child) def samplevolume(voxels, pos): """Trilinear interpolation placeholder.""" # In practice, interpolate from 8 surrounding voxels. return 0.0 def traversepyramid(rayorigin, raydirection, pyramid, N): """ Traverse the pyramid to render a single ray. rayorigin: 3D vector raydirection: 3D vector pyramid: List of volumes [V0,..., VM] N: Side length of the voxel grid Returns: Composite color and opacity """ M = len(pyramid) - 1 # Top level is a single cell covering [0, N-1] in cell coordinates tmin, tmax = rayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, (0,0,0), (N-1, N-1, N-1)) if tmax < 0: return (0.0, 0.0) t = tmin currlevel = M currcell = (0, 0, 0) acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accopacity = 0.0 while t < tmax: cellval = pyramid[currlevel][currcell[0]][currcell[1]][currcell[2]] if cellval == 0: # Empty: advance to next cell on same level cellsize = 2 currlevel texit = rayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, (currcell[0]cellsize, currcell[1]cellsize, currcell[2]cellsize), ((currcell[0]+1)cellsize, (currcell[1]+1)cellsize, (currcell[2]+1)cellsize))[1] if texit > tmax: texit = tmax t = texit # Determine next cell newcell = computenextcell(currcell, raydirection) newparent = computeparent(newcell) oldparent = computeparent(currcell) if newparent != oldparent: currlevel += 1 currcell = newparent else: currcell = newcell else: # Occupied if currlevel == 0: # Leaf: sample within cell cellsize = 1 tcellmin, tcellmax = rayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, (currcell[0], currcell[1], currcell[2]), (currcell[0]+1, currcell[1]+1, currcell[2]+1)) numsamples = 8 for s in range(numsamples): tsample = tcellmin + (tcellmax - tcellmin) (s + 0.5) / numsamples if tsample > tmax: break pos = rayorigin + tsample raydirection alpha = samplevolume(voxels, pos) # Front-to-back compositing weight = alpha (1.0 - accopacity) acccolor = acccolor + weight (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Placeholder color accopacity += weight t = tcellmax newcell = computenextcell(currcell, raydirection) newparent = computeparent(newcell) oldparent = computeparent(currcell) if newparent != oldparent: currlevel += 1 currcell = newparent else: currcell = newcell else: # Move down to enclosing child currlevel -= 1 childsize = 2 currlevel parentsize = 2 childsize currcell = computechildcell(currcell, rayorigin + t raydirection, parentsize, childsize) return (acccolor, accopacity) Parameters: M: Integer such that dataset side length N = 2^M + 1. The pyramid has levels m = 0, \dots, M. Cell Size: The size of cells on level m is 2^m times the spacing between voxels. Hierarchical Volume Traversal with Adaptive Termination is a ray tracing algorithm that uses a pyramidal data structure of binary volumes to skip empty regions and an adaptive termination criterion to stop tracing when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold. Unlike geometric ray tracing, which uses bounding volumes or spatial subdivision with lists of primitives, this method uses a hierarchical binary volume structure, which is more efficient for volume data because volume datasets have tens of millions of spatially ordered cells with single samples, whereas geometric scenes have hundreds of cells with many primitives. An optimization that uses a binary octree to avoid unnecessary resampling of voxels in transparent regions of the volume. A hierarchical spatial data structure (quadtree recursively subdivided down to pixel size) where empty space uniformity information is stored in the empty voxels of the 3D volume grid. The structure is a quadtree recursively subdivided down until pixel size. Gray squares denote voxels with volume data; white squares denote empty voxels storing the octree level. Time Complexity: The cost of ray tracing volumetric data using a hierarchical enumeration grows linearly with the size of the image, logarithmically with the length of each ray, and linearly with the depth complexity of the data. Memory Complexity: The pyramid requires storing M+1 binary volumes. The total number of cells is \sum{m=0}^{M} ((N-1)/2^m)^3. For large N, this is dominated by the base level V0, which has (N-1)^3 cells. Thus, memory usage is O(N^3), same as the original dataset, but with a smaller constant factor (1 bit per cell vs. multiple bits per voxel). Performance: Speedups of an order of magnitude have been observed for datasets of useful size and complexity. The method saves time by quickly advancing across empty regions of space using the binary pyramid structure. Strengths: Efficiently skips large empty regions; suitable for image-order rendering; simple binary structure. Limitations: Requires O(N^3) memory for the pyramid; construction time is non-trivial; less flexible than condensed octrees for highly irregular data. When to use: When rendering large, sparse volumetric datasets with significant empty regions using image-order rendering. When not to use: When memory is constrained and the dataset is dense; when object-order rendering is preferred. Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration Optimization was introduced by Marc Levoy in the late 1980s as part of his work on efficient volume rendering algorithms. The method is based on the observation that many datasets contain coherent regions of uninteresting voxels (opacity zero). It differs from earlier methods like [25] (likely referring to a condensed octree representation) by using a pyramid of binary volumes/complete octree rather than a condensed representation, and by rendering in image order rather than object order. name: Hierarchical Volume Traversal with Adaptive Termination
head: Combined Hierarchical Enumeration and Adaptive Termination, Levoy's Ray Tracing Optimizations, Pyramidal Volume Traversal, TraceRay2
body: Hierarchical Volume Traversal with Adaptive Termination is a ray tracing algorithm that uses a pyramidal data structure of binary volumes to skip empty regions and an adaptive termination criterion to stop tracing when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold. Unlike geometric ray tracing, which uses bounding volumes or spatial subdivision with lists of primitives, this method uses a hierarchical binary volume structure, which is more efficient for volume data because volume datasets have tens of millions of spatially ordered cells with single samples, whereas geometric scenes have hundreds of cells with many primitives. The method traverses a ray through a hierarchy of binary volumes (a pyramid) to determine which regions contain data. It adapts the traversal depth based on the content and terminates early if the accumulated opacity is sufficiently high. Input: Ray parameter \mathbf{u} (defining the ray direction and origin), the pyramidal binary volume structure \{Vm\}, the volume data (color and opacity fields), and parameters \epsilon, m{max}, m{min}, and M (total levels). Output: Final ray color \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}) and accumulated opacity \alpha(\mathbf{u}). The core data structure is a pyramid of binary volumes. Binary Volumes Vm: For each level m \in \{0, \dots, M\}, Vm is a 3D grid of bits. V0 is the base level, and Vm for m > 0 is derived from V{m-1}. Memory layout: (2^{M+1} - 1)/7 bits total for the pyramid. Volume Data: Monochrome color and opacity fields. Memory layout: 2N^3 bytes for color and opacity per voxel. Output Image: Memory layout: P^2 bytes. The binary volumes are defined recursively to indicate the presence of non-zero opacity in their spatial extent. Base Level (V0): V0(\mathbf{i}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \alpha(\mathbf{i} + \Delta\mathbf{i}) = 1 \\ 0 & \text{for } \mathbf{i} \in \{1, 2, \dots, N-1\}^3 \text{ and any } \Delta\mathbf{i} \in \{0, 1\}^3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \alpha is the opacity field, \mathbf{i} is the index, and the condition checks if any of the eight voxels at the vertices of the cell have opacity equal to 1. Higher Levels (Vm, m > 0): Vm(\mathbf{i}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } V{m-1}(2\mathbf{i} - \Delta\mathbf{i}) = 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} for \mathbf{i} \in \{1, 2, \dots, \frac{N-1}{m+1}\}^3 and any \Delta\mathbf{i} \in \{0, 1\}^3. This means a cell at level m is 1 if any of the eight cells at level m-1 that form its octants are 1. \epsilon: Threshold for significant color change. Default value 0.05. Higher values reduce rendering time, lower values reduce artifacts. m{max}: Starting level for traversal. Set to M - 2 for all values of M to minimize traversal costs. m{min}: Lowest level to descend to before rendering. Set to 2 for the current implementation to avoid the high cost of ray-cell intersections at level zero. M: Total number of levels in the pyramid. The algorithm processes each ray \mathbf{u} as follows: 1. Initialize ray color \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}) and opacity \alpha(\mathbf{u}) to 0. 2. Set ray position \mathbf{x} to the entry point of the ray into the volume using First(u). 3. Set current level m to m{max}. 4. Loop while the ray position \mathbf{x} is in bounds (InBounds(x)) and accumulated opacity \alpha(\mathbf{u}) is less than or equal to 1 - \epsilon: a. Calculate the cell index \mathbf{i} at current level m containing point \mathbf{x} using the Index(m, x) procedure. b. If the cell value Vm(\mathbf{i}) is 1 and m > m{min}: i. Decrement level m by 1 (m:= m - 1) and repeat the loop. c. Else (if cell is 1 and at min level, or cell is 0): i. If the cell value Vm(\mathbf{i}) is 1: 1. Determine the exit point of the current cell along the ray using Next(m, x, u). 2. Call RenderCell(u, x, Next(m, x, u)) to render the interval from current \mathbf{x} to the next cell entry point. ii. Advance to the next cell on the same level. iii. While the parent of the new cell differs from the parent of the old cell and m < M: 1. Move up to the parent cell (\mathbf{i}:= \text{Parent}(m, \mathbf{i})). 2. Increment level m (m:= m + 1). iv. Update ray position \mathbf{x} to the entry point of the next cell at the current level m (\mathbf{x}:= \text{Next}(m, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u})). The RenderCell procedure handles the resampling and compositing for a specific interval along the ray defined by entry \mathbf{x}1 and exit \mathbf{x}2. 1. Define image bounds \mathbf{U}1 and \mathbf{U}2 for the cell interval using Image(x1) and Image(x2). 2. Loop through evenly spaced sample locations \mathbf{U} within this interval from \mathbf{U}1 to \mathbf{U}2. Evenly spaced locations are superimposed to avoid noise artifacts caused by resampling at non-uniformly spaced points determined by ray-cell intersections. 3. For each sample \mathbf{U}: a. Get object space coordinates \mathbf{x} using Object(U). b. Check if the base level binary volume V0 at the index of \mathbf{x} is 1 (V0(Index(0, x))). c. If 1: i. Resample color \hat{C}(\mathbf{U}) and opacity \alpha(\mathbf{U}) from the volume data using Sample. ii. Composite the sample into the ray: \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}):= \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}) + \hat{C}(\mathbf{U})(1 - \alpha(\mathbf{u})) \alpha(\mathbf{u}):= \alpha(\mathbf{u}) + \alpha(\mathbf{U})(1 - \alpha(\mathbf{u})). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def TraceRay2(u, epsilon, mmax, mmin, M, V, bounds): # u = (origin, direction), V = [V0, V1,..., VM], bounds = (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) Cray = 0.0 alpharay = 0.0 x = First(u, bounds) m = mmax while InBounds(x, bounds) and alpharay <= 1.0 - epsilon: i = Index(m, x, bounds) if V[m][i] == 1 and m > mmin: m -= 1 continue else: if V[m][i] == 1: xexit = Next(m, x, u, bounds) Cray, alpharay = RenderCell(u, x, xexit, Cray, alpharay, V, bounds) xnext = Next(m, x, u, bounds) while m < M and Parent(m, Index(m, xnext, bounds)) != Parent(m, i): i = Parent(m, i) m += 1 x = xnext return Cray, alpharay def RenderCell(u, x1, x2, Cray, alpharay, V, bounds): U1 = Image(x1) U2 = Image(x2) for y in range(U1[1], U2[1] + 1): for x in range(U1[0], U2[0] + 1): U = (x, y) objx = Object(U) if V[0][Index(0, objx, bounds)] == 1: Csample = Sample(V.color, objx) alphasample = Sample(V.opacity, objx) Cray = Cray + Csample (1.0 - alpharay) alpharay = alpharay + alphasample (1.0 - alpharay) return Cray, alpharay def First(u, bounds): o, d = u tmin = 0.0 for k in range(3): if d[k] == 0.0: if o[k] < bounds[2k] or o[k] > bounds[2k+1]: return None else: t1 = (bounds[2k] - o[k]) / d[k] t2 = (bounds[2k+1] - o[k]) / d[k] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) return o + tmin d def InBounds(x, bounds): return all(bounds[2k] <= x[k] <= bounds[2k+1] for k in range(3)) def Index(m, x, bounds): cellsize = (bounds[1] - bounds[0]) / (2m) return tuple(int((x[k] - bounds[2k]) / cellsize) for k in range(3)) def Next(m, x, u, bounds): o, d = u cellsize = (bounds[1] - bounds[0]) / (2m) tmax = float('inf') for k in range(3): if d[k] != 0.0: t = (bounds[2k] + cellsize - x[k]) / d[k] if t > 0.0: tmax = min(tmax, t) return x + tmax d def Parent(m, i): return tuple(i[k] // 2 for k in range(3)) def Image(x): return (int(x[0]), int(x[1])) def Object(U): return (float(U[0]), float(U[1]), 0.0) def Sample(field, x): # Standard trilinear interpolation of field at object-space x ix, iy, iz = x fx, fy, fz = ix - int(ix), iy - int(iy), iz - int(iz) def v(x, y, z): return field[int(x)][int(y)][int(z)] c00 = v(ix, iy, iz) (1-fx) + v(ix+1, iy, iz) fx c01 = v(ix, iy, iz+1) (1-fx) + v(ix+1, iy, iz+1) fx c10 = v(ix, iy+1, iz) (1-fx) + v(ix+1, iy+1, iz) fx c11 = v(ix, iy+1, iz+1) (1-fx) + v(ix+1, iy+1, iz+1) fx return c00 (1-fy) + c01 fy Resampling Artifacts: Resampling at non-uniformly spaced points (determined by ray-cell intersections) adds noise artifacts to the image. The solution is to superimpose evenly spaced sample locations and only resample at those specific points. Level Zero Descent: Descending to level zero is inefficient for orthographic projections because ray-cell intersection costs exceed simple differencing. The solution is to stop descent at m{min}=2 and render level-zero cells within that higher-level cell. Zero Direction Components: Ray directions with zero components must be handled in Next to avoid division by zero when computing cell exit distances. Time Complexity: The traversal skips empty regions, reducing the number of samples taken. The adaptive termination stops tracing when accumulated opacity exceeds 1 - \epsilon, further reducing work. The cost of traversal is minimized by starting at m{max} = M - 2. Performance time is proportional to the number of rays cast. Memory Complexity: The memory required is 2N^3 bytes for the volume data, (2^{M+1} - 1)/7 bits for the pyramid, and P^2 bytes for the output image. Strengths: Efficient for volume data with large empty regions. The hierarchical structure allows skipping large empty areas. The adaptive termination reduces work for opaque regions. Combining termination and octree optimizations achieves savings of more than an order of magnitude. Limitations: Inefficient if the volume is mostly opaque or has no empty regions, as the hierarchy may not provide significant skipping. Descending to level zero is inefficient for orthographic projections due to high intersection costs. Precise selection of parameters is crucial for the adaptive rendering algorithm. When to Use: Suitable for volume datasets with significant empty space and where ray-cell intersection costs are high (e.g., orthographic projections). When Not to Use: Not suitable for geometric scenes with many primitives per cell, as the method is optimized for volume data with single samples per cell. The method was introduced in the paper "Efficient ray tracing of volume data". It is based on the observation that volume datasets contain coherent regions of uninteresting voxels (opacity zero) and can be encoded as a hierarchical spatial enumeration represented by a pyramid of binary volumes. The method is also known as Pyramidal Volume Traversal or TraceRay2. It builds on earlier work in adaptive rendering based on estimated image complexity at sample regions of the image plane. It differs from pure image-order ray casting by leveraging a hierarchical structure to accelerate active cell identification, while remaining dependent on rendering resolution like other hybrid approaches. Active Cell Identification: Use the structure to efficiently locate active cells intersected by the ray. 4. name: Silhouette Image Space Acceleration Structure (Mip Pyramid)
head: Hierarchical Voxelization Acceleration Structure
body: This method accelerates voxel coverage queries in image-based modeling by using a hierarchical mip pyramid over silhouette images to provide conservative bounds on voxel visibility. It solves the problem of efficiently determining whether a voxel intersects the visual hull without sampling every pixel, thereby reducing computation and data access for culling decisions. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its direct inspiration from the hierarchical z-buffer, storing min/max bounds of texel blocks to ensure no small features are missed or holes created in the voxelization. Inputs: A set of n silhouette images, one per camera view. A voxel v defined by its 8 corners in Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) space. The n pre-generated silhouette image pyramids. Outputs: A conservative lower bound (min) and upper bound (max) on the silhouette value \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{p}) for all points \mathbf{p} within voxel v. If the lower bound is 0, the voxel is outside the visual hull. Data Structures: For each of the n views, a pyramid of texture levels is stored. Level 0: Original smoothed silhouette image. Level l+1: Each texel stores the minimum and maximum values of the 2 \times 2 block of texels from level l that it covers. Format: Two-channel texture (min, max) per texel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Project the 8 NVC space corners of voxel v into the 2D image space of camera i. 2. Find the axis-aligned bounding rectangle (minX, minY, maxX, maxY) that encloses all projected corners. 3. Determine the sampling level L in the silhouette image mip pyramid: L = \lfloor \log2(\max(maxX - minX, maxY - minY)) \rfloor At this level L, the bounding rectangle covers at most a 2 \times 2 block of texels. 4. Sample the texels at the corners of the bounding rectangle (minX, minY), (maxX, minY), (minX, maxY), and (maxX, maxY) from level L of the pyramid for view i. 5. Return the minimum and maximum of these sampled values as a conservative bound on \mathcal{I}i(\mathbf{C}i(\mathbf{p})) for all \mathbf{p} within v. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampleSilhouette(voxelv, camerai, pyramid): # 1. Project 8 NVC space corners of voxel v into silhouette image space projected = [projecttoimage(c, camerai) for c in voxelv.corners] # 2. Find axis-aligned bounding rectangle minX = min(p.x for p in projected) minY = min(p.y for p in projected) maxX = max(p.x for p in projected) maxY = max(p.y for p in projected) # 3. Determine sampling level L = floor(log2(max(maxX - minX, maxY - minY))) # 4. Sample texels at corners of the bounding rectangle corners = [(minX, minY), (maxX, minY), (minX, maxY), (maxX, maxY)] samples = [pyramid[camerai][L].sampleat(c) for c in corners] # 5. Return min and max of these values minval = min(s.min for s in samples) maxval = max(s.max for s in samples) return minval, maxval Global Voxel Bound: To determine if the voxel is inside the visual hull, combine bounds across all n views: min\bound{total} = \prod{i=1}^{n} min\boundi max\bound{total} = \prod{i=1}^{n} max\boundi If min\bound{total} > 0, the voxel is fully inside. If max\bound{total} = 0, it is fully outside. Otherwise, further sampling is required. Generation: The n image pyramids are generated by a compute kernel launched immediately after silhouette image smoothing. Pitfalls: Conservative bounds ensure no small features are missed and no holes are created in voxelization, as bounds are conservatively correct. Precision issues in projection or log calculation may affect level selection; ensure robust handling of edge cases where the bounding box size is very small or zero. This method acquires and preprocesses silhouette images from raw camera data to create smooth, calibrated binary masks used for visual hull approximation. It solves the problem of converting raw, distorted Bayer-pattern sensor data into high-quality silhouette inputs for hierarchical acceleration structures. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its unified compute kernel approach that simultaneously handles lens distortion, demosaicing, and chroma-keying, followed by separable Gaussian filtering to control surface smoothness. Performance: Greatly reduces the amount of computation and data accesses needed by the oracle kernel to make a culling decision for a given voxel. Memory Complexity: Requires storing n image pyramids. Strengths: Conservative bounds prevent holes in voxelization; efficient culling of empty space. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of silhouette images and pyramids; performance depends on the number of views n. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method is presented in the context of real-time high-resolution sparse voxelization with application to image-based modeling. It is inspired by the well-known hierarchical z-buffer, adapting the concept of hierarchical depth testing to silhouette coverage queries. The acceleration structure is part of a pipeline that includes silhouette image acquisition, filtering, and voxel rendering as screen-space bounding rectangle splats. name: Silhouette Image Acquisition and Filtering
head: Chroma-keyed silhouette generation, Gaussian-filtered silhouette images
body: This method acquires and preprocesses silhouette images from raw camera data to create smooth, calibrated binary masks used for visual hull approximation. It solves the problem of converting raw, distorted Bayer-pattern sensor data into high-quality silhouette inputs for hierarchical acceleration structures. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its unified compute kernel approach that simultaneously handles lens distortion, demosaicing, and chroma-keying, followed by separable Gaussian filtering to control surface smoothness. Inputs: Raw Bayer pattern image data from a camera; camera parameters for distortion correction; chroma key color range. Outputs: Calibrated silhouette images (2D arrays of 0s and 1s); filtered silhouette images. Data Structures: Input Texture: 2D texture array storing raw Bayer data (8 bits per pixel). Output Texture: 2D texture array storing silhouette values (float or integer, 0 or 1). Filter Kernel: Separable Gaussian kernel with unit integral. Steps: 1. Upload Data: Upload raw Bayer pattern data to the GPU as a 2D texture array, reducing camera bus and CPU/GPU bandwidth usage compared to higher-bit formats. 2. Compute Kernel Launch: Launch a single GPU compute kernel where each thread or thread block processes a portion of the image. 3. Distortion Correction: Remove radial lens distortion from the pixel coordinates to produce calibrated silhouette images. 4. Demosaicing: Convert the Bayer pattern data to full RGB or luminance values. 5. Chroma Keying: Segment foreground and background pixels. Foreground pixels are assigned a value of 0, and background pixels are assigned a value of 1. This creates the initial binary silhouette image \mathcal{I}i. 6. Filtering: Apply a separable Gaussian filter to the binary silhouette images. The filter has a unit integral, and the kernel width is a parameter. Increasing the width increases blur, resulting in a smoother visual hull surface S(\mathbf{p}). Implementation uses a thread block per row/column strategy to fit the entire image row or column in shared memory, leveraging separability for performance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def correctradialdistortion(x, y, intrinsics): # Standard radial distortion correction using camera intrinsics cx, cy, fx, fy = intrinsics['cx'], intrinsics['cy'], intrinsics['fx'], intrinsics['fy'] k1, k2 = intrinsics['k1'], intrinsics['k2'] unorm = (x - cx) / fx vnorm = (y - cy) / fy r2 = unorm2 + vnorm2 scale = 1.0 + k1 r2 + k2 r22 return unorm scale fx + cx, vnorm scale fy + cy def demosaicbayer(u, v, bayerdata): # Bilinear interpolation of Bayer pattern to RGB x, y = int(u), int(v) # Assuming standard RGGB pattern r = (bayerdata[y, x] + bayerdata[y+1, x+1]) / 2.0 g = (bayerdata[y, x+1] + bayerdata[y+1, x]) / 2.0 b = bayerdata[y+1, x+1] return r, g, b def isinchromarange(r, g, b, chromarange): # Check if color falls within the specified foreground chroma range return (chromarange['rmin'] <= r <= chromarange['rmax'] and chromarange['gmin'] <= g <= chromarange['gmax'] and chromarange['bmin'] <= b <= chromarange['bmax']) def creategaussian1d(width): # Create 1D Gaussian kernel with unit integral sigma = width / 6.0 kernel = [] for i in range(-int(width/2), int(width/2) + 1): val = math.exp(-(i2) / (2 sigma2)) kernel.append(val) norm = sum(kernel) return [v / norm for v in kernel] def apply1dfilter(image, kernel, axis='horizontal'): # Apply 1D separable filter using shared memory per row/column height, width = len(image), len(image[0]) output = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] for i in range(height): row = image[i] # Simulate shared memory load with padding for boundary handling shared = [0.0] (width + len(kernel)) for j in range(width): shared[j + len(kernel)//2] = row[j] for j in range(width): acc = 0.0 for k in range(len(kernel)): acc += shared[j + k] kernel[k] output[i][j] = acc if axis == 'vertical': return [[output[j][i] for j in range(height)] for i in range(width)] return output def processsilhouettepipeline(bayerdata, intrinsics, chromarange, kernelwidth): # Steps 1-5: Acquire and chroma-key silhouette = [[0.0] len(bayerdata[0]) for in range(len(bayerdata))] for y in range(len(bayerdata)): for x in range(len(bayerdata[0])): u, v = correctradialdistortion(x, y, intrinsics) r, g, b = demosaicbayer(u, v, bayerdata) silhouette[y][x] = 0.0 if isinchromarange(r, g, b, chromarange) else 1.0 # Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Using 8-bit Bayer data reduces bandwidth but may limit color precision for chroma keying. Boundaries: Shared memory usage requires careful handling of image boundaries during the separable filter passes. A technique that exploits slab silhouette maps and an early depth test to skip empty spaces along the direction normal to the texture slice. It is used to optimize volume rendering by avoiding computation in non-transparent regions. It is distinguished by its specific application of early depth testing in conjunction with slab-based silhouette data for empty space skipping. Time Complexity: The compute kernel runs in O(N) time for N pixels, with the filtering step also being O(N) due to separability. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the input Bayer texture array and output silhouette textures. Shared memory is used for filter rows/columns to increase convolution performance. Performance: The single compute kernel approach and shared memory usage for filtering provide high performance on GPUs. Strengths: Reduces data bandwidth; produces smooth surfaces suitable for visual hull approximation; efficient GPU implementation. Limitations: Requires camera calibration for distortion correction. When to use: When real-time or high-resolution silhouette acquisition from raw camera data is needed for visual hull-based volume rendering. When not to use: When high-precision color segmentation is required beyond chroma keying capabilities, or when camera calibration is unavailable. This method is described in the context of real-time high-resolution sparse voxelization and image-based modeling. It was introduced by the authors of the source paper to efficiently generate silhouette inputs for visual hull oracle kernels. The use of chroma keying and Gaussian filtering for silhouette smoothing is a standard technique in image-based modeling to create smooth visual hull surfaces.
