name: Visual Hull Oracle Kernel
body: The Visual Hull Oracle Kernel performs binary culling of voxels to determine if they intersect the visual hull surface S(p) = 0.5. It identifies which voxels in a sparse voxel grid contribute to the final volume by leveraging hierarchical mip pyramids over silhouette images to compute conservative bounds on voxel coverage. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific use of component-wise multiplication of conservative bounds across multiple camera views to make a definitive KEEP or CULL decision, building on the silhouette acquisition and filtering techniques described in Silhouette Image Acquisition and Filtering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of voxels (VoxelListIn), n filtered silhouette images, n corresponding mip pyramids, and coordinate transforms from Novel View Camera (NVC) space to silhouette image space and screen space. Output: A decision array (oracleOutput) where each entry is either CULL or KEEP. Data Structures: VoxelListIn: Array of voxel structures, indexed by threadID. oracleOutput: Array of integers, indexed by threadID. boundsx and boundsy: Scalars storing the lower and upper limits of the conservative bound on the silhouette coverage for a voxel. Parameters: numCameras: The number of input camera views. boundsx: Lower limit of the conservative bound on S(p). boundsy: Upper limit of the conservative bound on S(p). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize DECISION to CULL. 2. Read the current voxel v from VoxelListIn[threadID]. 3. Check if the voxel is outside the viewing frustum of the novel view using outsideFrustum(v). If outsideFrustum(v) is true, skip further processing for this voxel and write CULL to oracleOutput[threadID]. If outsideFrustum(v) is false, proceed to step 4. 4. Initialize boundsx and boundsy to 1.0. 5. Loop through each camera index i from 0 to numCameras - 1: Call sampleSilhouette(v, i) to retrieve the conservative bound of voxel v's projection into silhouette image i. Update boundsx and boundsy by performing component-wise multiplication with the returned values. 6. After the loop, evaluate the final boundsx and boundsy: If boundsx < 0.5 AND boundsy > 0.5, set DECISION to KEEP. Otherwise, DECISION remains CULL. 7. Write DECISION to oracleOutput[threadID]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. CULL = 0 KEEP = 1 def visualhulloraclekernel(threadID, VoxelListIn, oracleOutput, numCameras, outsideFrustum, sampleSilhouette): DECISION = CULL v = VoxelListIn[threadID] if not outsideFrustum(v): boundsx = 1.0 boundsy = 1.0 for i in range(numCameras): cambounds = sampleSilhouette(v, i) boundsx = cambounds[0] boundsy = cambounds[1] if boundsx < 0.5 and boundsy > 0.5: DECISION = KEEP oracleOutput[threadID] = DECISION Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Frustum Culling: Voxels outside the viewing frustum of the novel view are automatically culled via the outsideFrustum(v) check to avoid unnecessary computation. Precision: The method relies on conservative bounds; if the mip pyramid levels are too coarse, the bounds may be inaccurate, potentially leading to false positives (keeping voxels that should be culled) or false negatives (culling voxels that should be kept). Surface Definition: The decision is based on the intersection with the surface S(p) = 0.5, making the thresholds 0.5 specific to this definition. A voxel-based approach that retrieves the photo-hull of a shape using a view-dependent plane-sweeping strategy. It differs from the standard Visual Hull Oracle by combining rendering and reconstruction into a single step, producing no explicit volume. A key pitfall is that it performs photo-consistency checks on each fragment regardless of rejection by silhouette/background tests due to a lack of branching support at the time. Performance achieves rendering frame rates of 2-3 frames per second. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels processed, as each voxel culling decision is independent and assigned to a single thread. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for n silhouette images and n mip pyramids, where n is the number of cameras. Performance: The hierarchical, coarse-to-fine manner of processing accelerates computation. Specific frame rates for the oracle kernel alone are not given, but related GPU-based photo-hull methods achieve 2-3 fps. Strengths: Efficient culling of voxels outside the frustum and those not intersecting the visual hull surface. Limitations: Requires pre-computed mip pyramids and silhouette images. The Visual Hull Oracle Kernel was introduced in the context of real-time high-resolution sparse voxelization for image-based modeling. It builds upon hierarchical z-buffer concepts and uses mip pyramids to accelerate voxel/silhouette coverage queries. The approach is part of a broader shift towards GPU-based processing for volumetric reconstruction, following earlier work on GPU-based visual hull rendering. name: Pixel separation for bright foreground
head: Bright pixel separation, Split scattering image
body: Pixel separation for bright foreground is a technique used in silhouette image acquisition and filtering to correct the incorrect blurring of bright pixels located at low depths (foreground) against dark backgrounds. It solves the problem where standard luminance-weighted blurring causes bright foreground objects to lose intensity or blend incorrectly by splitting the input scattering image into two separate components: one for separated bright pixels (L{\text{ssc}}) and one for the rest (L{\text{sc}}). Inputs: Original scattering image \mathbf{L}. Original depth image \mathbf{D}'. Original luminance image \mathbf{Y}^{[0]} derived from \mathbf{L}. MIP chain depth K. Separation parameters: Ty (min luminance), \varepsilony (luminance width), T{d'} (max depth), \varepsilon{d'} (depth width), k{ssc} (fixed MIP level for fetching). Outputs: Separated blurred scattering image \mathbb{L}'{\text{SSC}}. Remaining blurred scattering image \mathbb{L}'{\text{SC}} (constructed via standard luminance-weighted MIP chain on L{sc}). Data Structures: \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[0...K]}: MIP chain for separated scattering, built using simple Gaussian blurring. \mathbb{D}'{\text{SSC}}^{[0...K]}: Depth MIP chain for separated pixels, built using luminance-weighted averaging. \mathbb{L}{\text{sc}}^{[0...K]}: MIP chain for remaining pixels, built using standard luminance-weighted technique. Steps: 1. Compute Separation Mask M: Calculate the mask based on high luminance and low depth using smoothstep functions: M = \text{smoothstep}(Ty, Ty + \varepsilony, \mathbf{Y}^{[0]}) \cdot \left( 1 - \text{smoothstep}(T{d'} - \varepsilon{d'}, T{d'}, \mathbf{D}'^{[0]}) \right) where \mathbf{Y}^{[0]} is the luminance of the original scattering image and \mathbf{D}'^{[0]} is the original depth image. 2. Split Scattering Image: Divide the original scattering image \mathbf{L} into two images using the mask M: L{\text{ssc}} = e^{-Ca \cdot P} \cdot \left( 1 - e^{-Cs \cdot P} \right) \cdot M \cdot L L{\text{sc}} = e^{-Ca \cdot P} \cdot \left( 1 - e^{-Cs \cdot P} \right) \cdot (1 - M) \cdot L The term e^{-Ca \cdot P} \cdot (1 - e^{-Cs \cdot P}) represents the original weight applied to the scattering image. The sum L{\text{ssc}} + L{\text{sc}} equals the original unmasked scattering image, ensuring no information loss. 3. Build MIP Chain for Separated Pixels (L{ssc}): Construct the MIP chain \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[0...K]} using simple Gaussian blurring without luminance weighting or masking, allowing bright pixels to propagate: \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[k]} = \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[k-1]} \mathcal{G} where \mathcal{G} is the Gaussian kernel and \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[0]} = L{\text{ssc}}. 4. Build Depth MIP Chain for Separated Pixels: Construct the depth MIP chain \mathbb{D}'{\text{SSC}}^{[0...K]} using luminance-weighted averaging to prioritize the depth of bright separated pixels: D{\text{ssc}}^{[k]} = \frac{\left( \gamma{\text{ssc}}^{[k]} \cdot D{\text{ssc}}^{[k-1]} \right) \mathcal{U}}{\gamma{\text{ssc}}^{[k]} \mathcal{U}} where \gamma{\text{ssc}}^{[k]} is the luminance of \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[k]}, \mathcal{U} is the uniform averaging kernel, and D{\text{ssc}}^{[0]} = \mathbf{D}'. 5. Build MIP Chain for Remaining Pixels (L{sc}): Filter L{sc} using the standard luminance-weighted MIP chain technique. 6. Fetch Final Separated Image: Determine the level \ell' from the fixed MIP level k{ssc} using the depth chain \mathbb{D}'{\text{SSC}}: \ell' = \ell \left( \mathbb{D}'{\text{SSC}}^{[k{\text{SSC}}]} \right) \mathbb{L}'{\text{SSC}} = \mathbb{L}^{[\ell']}{\text{SSC}} where \ell(\cdot) denotes the level selection function based on depth values. Parameters: Ty: Minimum luminance threshold for separation. Set experimentally. \varepsilony: Luminance threshold width. Set experimentally. T{d'}: Maximum depth threshold for separation. Set experimentally. \varepsilon{d'}: Depth threshold width. Set experimentally. k{ssc}: Fixed MIP level index for fetching from the separated chain (0 \le k{ssc} \le K). Typical value k{ssc} = 0.7 \cdot K. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parameter values (Ty, \varepsilony, T{d'}, \varepsilon{d'}, k{ssc}) must be carefully set based on experiments for individual scenes and media combinations. Incorrect parameter settings may result in incorrect blurring or loss of bright pixel energy. The choice of k{ssc} heavily depends on the number of pixels actually separated in the scene. Time Complexity: Adds overhead for mask computation, image splitting, and construction of a separate MIP chain for bright pixels. The depth chain construction involves additional luminance-weighted averaging. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the additional MIP chains \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[0...K]} and \mathbb{D}'{\text{SSC}}^{[0...K]}. Strengths: Correctly preserves the intensity and appearance of bright foreground objects that would otherwise be incorrectly blurred or suppressed. Limitations: Requires manual tuning of parameters per scene. The fixed level k{ssc} is arbitrary and may not be optimal for all scenes. When to use: When bright foreground objects are present against dark backgrounds and standard luminance-weighted blurring causes visual artifacts. The technique was introduced by Tomas Davidovic in his 2012 thesis "Real-Time Light Transport in Analytically Integrable Participating Media". name: Flex-block tree
head: Cell-tree, Flex-block partition
body: The flex-block tree is a hierarchical data structure derived from a kd-tree partition, designed primarily for load balancing in distributed volume rendering (both ray casting and ray tracing). It partitions a volume into "flex-blocks," which are cells containing tightly cropped subvolumes that do not necessarily occupy the entire cell volume. Unlike traditional space subdivision methods, the flex-block partition does not restrict partition cuts to alternate between axes, allowing it to handle scenes with disproportionate dimensions effectively. It serves as a dependency graph that determines the deterministic depth order of blocks for image compositing in ray casting and accelerates ray traversal by indicating potential neighbor cells in ray tracing. The method constructs a tree where internal nodes define partition boundaries and leaf nodes represent the data containers (flex-blocks). The construction involves preprocessing the volume to remove empty space, partitioning the remaining data using a modified kd-tree algorithm, and extracting view-dependent ordering information. Inputs: Raw volume data (slices or voxels). Optional mask volume defining regions of interest. Number of render-nodes (for distributed systems). View directions (typically 8 quantized directions). Outputs: A flex-block tree (dependency graph). Cropped volume data (bricks) distributed to render-nodes. Look-up tables mapping view directions to flex-block traversal orders. Flex-block Tree Node Internal nodes in the tree store partitioning information similar to a traditional binary tree: cutplane: The position and normal of the splitting plane. children: Pointers or indices to the left and right child nodes. Flex-block (Leaf Node) Each leaf node represents a cell in the partition: bbox: A tightly cropped axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) enclosing the non-empty data within the cell. dataref: Reference to the subvolume data (brick) stored in memory or on disk. dependencies: Information used for ray-task scheduling and traversal speedup. 1. Empty Space Reduction: If a mask volume is not provided, perform out-of-core region growing on raw data slices to create a mask. Crop each slice to bounding rectangles of non-empty regions defined by the mask. Align a tight AABB around cohesive non-empty areas of the volume to eliminate empty space. 2. Partitioning (Moving Walls): Apply a "moving walls" algorithm to partition the scene. This algorithm moves partition walls to simultaneously accommodate non-empty subvolume boundaries and balance the load across render-nodes. This step generates a partition structure that respects the data distribution requirements. 3. kd-tree Extraction: Extract a kd-tree from the output of the moving walls procedure. Unlike standard kd-trees, this partition does not enforce alternating axis cuts. The cut axis is chosen to optimize load balancing and accommodate disproportionate scene dimensions. 4. Dynamic Programming for Load Balancing: Use a dynamic programming (DP) algorithm to group bricks and solve the Load Balanced Network Distribution (LBND) problem. The DP evaluates a cost function to minimize end-to-end rendering time, which is a function of the slowest render-node, image composition time, and network communication time. This step creates the final flex-blocks within the kd-tree-like partition. 5. Dependency Graph Construction: For each of the eight quantized view directions, extract the image priority order (depth order) of the flex-blocks from the kd-tree. Store these orders in look-up tables. These tables form the dependency graph of flex-blocks. This graph is used for ray casting to determine the order for compositing images from different nodes. This graph is used for ray tracing to accelerate traversal by indicating potential neighbors a ray may enter. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildflexblocktree(volumedata, mask=None, numnodes=1, viewdirections=8): """ Constructs a flex-block tree for distributed volume rendering. Args: volumedata: Raw volume slices or voxels. mask: Optional mask volume. If None, generated via region growing. numnodes: Number of render-nodes for load balancing. viewdirections: Number of quantized view directions (typically 8). Returns: flexblocktree: The constructed tree structure. dependencytables: Look-up tables for view-dependent traversal orders. flexblocks: The final partitioned flex-blocks. """ # Step 1: Empty Space Reduction if mask is None: mask = regiongrowing(volumedata) croppedslices = cropslices(volumedata, mask) volumedatareduced = aligntightbboxes(croppedslices) # Step 2: Partitioning (Moving Walls) partitionstructure = movingwallsalgorithm(volumedatareduced, numnodes) # Step 3: kd-tree Extraction kdtree = extractkdtree(partitionstructure) # Step 4: Dynamic Programming for Load Balancing flexblocks = dynamicprogrammingpartition(kdtree, numnodes) # Step 5: Dependency Graph Construction dependencytables = {} for direction in getquantizedviewdirections(viewdirections): order = getimagepriorityorder(kdtree, flexblocks, direction) dependencytables[direction] = order flexblocktree = buildtreestructure(kdtree, flexblocks) return flexblocktree, dependencytables, flexblocks def regiongrowing(volumedata): # Out-of-core region growing to create a mask for each slice mask = [] for slicedata in volumedata: mask.append(computenonemptyregions(slicedata)) return mask def cropslices(volumedata, mask): # Crop each slice to bounding rectangles of non-empty regions cropped = [] for slicedata, m in zip(volumedata, mask): cropped.append(slicedata.croptorects(m)) return cropped def aligntightbboxes(croppedslices): # Align a tight AABB around cohesive non-empty areas reduced = [] for slicedata in croppedslices: reduced.append(slicedata.alignbbox()) return reduced def movingwallsalgorithm(volumedatareduced, numnodes): # Move partition walls to accommodate non-empty boundaries and balance load return partitionscene(volumedatareduced, numnodes) def extractkdtree(partitionstructure): # Extract kd-tree; does not restrict cuts to alternate axes return buildkdtree(partitionstructure, alternateaxes=False) def dynamicprogrammingpartition(kdtree, numnodes): # DP solves LBND problem to minimize end-to-end render time return solvelbnddp(kdtree, numnodes) def getquantizedviewdirections(count): # Extract 8 quantized view directions return generatequantizeddirections(count) def getimagepriorityorder(kdtree, flexblocks, direction): # Extract depth order for compositing/traversal return computedepthorder(kdtree, flexblocks, direction) def buildtreestructure(kdtree, flexblocks): # Internal nodes: cutplane, children. Leaf nodes: flex-block return assembletree(kdtree, flexblocks) View Directions: Typically 8 quantized directions are used to extract image priority orders. Render-nodes: The number of processing units in the distributed system, used to balance the partition. Disproportionate Scenes: Standard kd-trees may perform poorly on scenes with disproportionate dimensions. The flex-block partition addresses this by not restricting cut axes. NP-Completeness: Determining the optimum order for caching cells in ray tracing is NP-Complete. The method uses dynamic programming approximations. Data Movement: Reducing empty space early in the pipeline reduces run-time for preprocessing and network data movement. Failure to crop empty space effectively can lead to inefficient load balancing. A compact representation of ray dependencies between cells, where a cell is a flex-block. It is used for ray-task scheduling and ray traversal speedup in ray tracing. The underlying data distribution method derived from the flex-block tree. It defines how data is split among render-nodes and how bricks are scheduled. Time Complexity: The construction involves region growing, partitioning, and dynamic programming. The DP solution for LBND is optimized to minimize end-to-end rendering time, which depends on the slowest node, composition time, and network communication. The exact complexity of the DP step is not specified, but the problem of optimal caching order is NP-Complete. Memory Complexity: The cell-tree (dependency graph) is described as being several orders of magnitude smaller than the number of dependencies it represents. Strengths: Effective load balancing for distributed rendering. Handles scenes with disproportionate dimensions. Automates space skipping by using data extents of flex-blocks. Reduces data movement by cropping empty space early. Limitations: Requires preprocessing (region growing, cropping, partitioning). Dynamic task scheduling is complex due to the NP-Complete nature of optimal caching. When to Use: Suitable for distributed volume visualization of massive datasets where load balancing and efficient data distribution are critical. The flex-block tree was introduced in the context of massive data management for distributed volume visualization. It addresses the limitations of traditional space subdivision methods, which do not adequately handle load balancing in distributed rendering environments. The method was developed to support both software ray tracing and hardware ray casting in a distributed cluster setting. It builds upon concepts from kd-trees and dynamic programming for load balanced network distribution (LBND). name: Data Structure and Indexing
body: This family defines the memory layout, pointer encoding, and traversal logic for hierarchical acceleration structures (primarily octrees) used in volume rendering. It differs from siblings like Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration Optimization by focusing on the low-level representation of the tree hierarchy itself (e.g., texture encoding, point storage) rather than high-level traversal optimizations or specific acceleration heuristics. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of hierarchical descent and ascent. The traversal begins at the root of the octree and determines which of the eight children (octants) the ray intersects. This is typically done by comparing the ray's position relative to the center of the current node's bounding box. 1. Child Selection: For a node with center \mathbf{c} and half-extent s, the ray position \mathbf{p} determines the child index k \in \{0, \dots, 7\}: k = 4 \cdot \mathbb{I}(px \ge cx) + 2 \cdot \mathbb{I}(py \ge cy) + 1 \cdot \mathbb{I}(pz \ge cz) where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function. 2. Empty Space Skipping: If the selected child is marked as empty (or uniform), the traversal skips the subtree. This is achieved by advancing the ray parameter t to the exit of the current node or using neighbor pointers to jump to the next potentially occupied node. 3. Leaf Handling: Upon reaching a leaf node, the method typically switches to a fixed-step traversal (like DDA) within the leaf's voxel grid to sample the volume data. 4. Backtracking: Because octrees are sparse and irregular, traversal often requires backtracking to the parent node when a ray exits a subtree or encounters an empty branch. This is implemented using an explicit stack (on GPU) or recursion (on CPU). A spatial index structure that augments a branch-on-need octree with links to allow direct traversal to adjacent nodes, used to accelerate ray traversal in volume rendering. It differs from full 26-neighbor structures by maintaining only x-neighbor pointers, reducing memory overhead while enabling efficient skipping of empty space and boundary crossing. The structure is encoded into an 8-bit RGBA 3D texture. Each octree node is encoded in 8 consecutive texels arranged in the x-direction. The layout uses a tagged pointer scheme where the Alpha (A) component determines the node kind: A=1.0 for inner nodes, A=0.5 for data nodes (leaves with data), and A=0.0 for empty nodes. Inner node RGB components point to the first of 8 children, arranged consecutively in the x-direction. Leaf node RGB components point to leaf info, consisting of a data pointer and 6 consecutive texels storing neighbor pointers for the 6 faces. The last leaf data texel contains a None pointer. Neighbor pointers use their A value to encode the octree level of the neighbor. Construction involves initializing top-level nodes (typically two levels below the root) and establishing x-neighbor pointers, propagating these pointers down to child nodes that share boundaries but have different parents, and finally encoding the structure into a 3D texture. Boundary nodes link to the smallest node enclosing all adjacent nodes if multiple exist. Traversal stops before reaching a single root node at the top level to optimize performance. A Point Octree is a recursive hierarchical data structure designed to manage a dynamic set of 3D points, supporting insertion, removal, movement, and spatial queries such as nearest neighbor and radius search. It differs from voxel-based octrees by storing data only at leaf nodes corresponding to occupied regions, allowing for efficient handling of sparse point clouds without allocating memory for empty space. The tree consists of nodes containing an array of up to 8 child octants and a PointData object at leaves. PointData uses two parallel arrays: points (Vector3[]) and data (T[]). Key parameters include maxPoints (leaf capacity), maxDepth (recursion limit), and bias (padding for boundary checks). Insertion recursively finds the leaf, updates existing points, or splits the node if full, redistributing points to children using a bias for containment checks. Radius search recursively traverses intersecting octants and filters leaves by squared distance. Movement updates positions in place or removes/reinserts if the octant changes. A hybrid CPU-GPU traversal strategy where the CPU traverses the KD-tree of AMR patches back-to-front, and the GPU traverses cells within a patch. Sub-patches are generated to ensure perspective-correct sorting of cells relative to the observer. The CPU traverses the KD-tree hierarchy in back-to-front fashion, choosing the appropriate order at each internal node until a leaf node (patch) is found. The vertex shader modifies each index according to the current observer position to generate proper cell ordering, ensuring perspective-correct sorting. Transfers gradient octrees computed on the server side to a rendering client to reduce network traffic and avoid the need to compute gradients on the client. A simple binary tree indexing scheme to identify and organize patches in a breadth-first manner (coarse to fine). Allows quick identification of cousin patches. View-dependent mesh generation uses recursive traversal over the patch hierarchy by indexing into a fixed-size 1D array of patches, accumulating patch IDs for later decompression and rendering. Hierarchical data structures like octrees and KD-trees are used to index sparse volumetric and multi-resolution data for rendering. AMR patch traversal relies on CPU-GPU hybrid strategies where a KD-tree guides back-to-front patch ordering. Gradient octrees can be transferred from server to client to reduce network traffic. Binary tree indexing organizes patches breadth-first for view-dependent mesh generation and decompression. body: A spatial index structure that augments a branch-on-need octree with links to allow direct traversal to adjacent nodes, used to accelerate ray traversal in volume rendering. It differs from full 26-neighbor structures by maintaining only x-neighbor pointers, reducing memory overhead while enabling efficient skipping of empty space and boundary crossing. Inputs: A view-dependent branch-on-need octree. Outputs: A 3D texture acting as a spatial index, encoded with tagged pointers and neighbor links. Data Structures: The structure is encoded into an 8-bit RGBA 3D texture. Each octree node is encoded in 8 consecutive texels arranged in the x-direction. The layout uses a tagged pointer scheme where the Alpha (A) component determines the node kind: A=1.0: Inner node. A=0.5: Data node (leaf with data). A=0.0: Empty node. Inner Node Layout: The RGB components point to the first of 8 children, which are arranged consecutively in the x-direction. Leaf Node Layout: The RGB components point to leaf info, consisting of: 1. A data pointer (if not empty). 2. 6 consecutive texels storing neighbor pointers for the 6 faces. The last leaf data texel contains a None pointer. Neighbor pointers use their A value to encode the octree level of the neighbor. Construction Steps: 1. Top-Level Initialization: Create all nodes at the top level n (typically two levels below the root to speed up traversal) and establish x-neighbor pointers for all adjacent nodes at this level. 2. Pointer Propagation: Propagate x-neighbor pointers from nodes in level i to their child nodes in level i-1. Specifically, link adjacent level-(i-1) nodes that have different parent nodes. 3. Texture Encoding: Encode the resulting structure into a 3D texture. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildoctreewithneighbors(octree, rootlevel, bboxextent): # n is typically two levels below the root to speed up traversal n = rootlevel - 2 toplevelnodes = octree.getnodesatlevel(n) for node in toplevelnodes: node.neighborsx = computexneighbor(node, toplevelnodes) for level in range(n, 0, -1): parentnodes = octree.getnodesatlevel(level) childnodes = octree.getnodesatlevel(level - 1) for parent in parentnodes: for child in parent.getchildren(): child.neighbors = findcrossparentneighbors(child, childnodes) texturewidth, textureheight, texturedepth = computetexturedimensions(octree) texture = allocatetexture(texturewidth, textureheight, texturedepth) for node in octree.allnodes(): encodenode(node, texture) return texture def computexneighbor(node, levelnodes): # Returns pointer to the node immediately adjacent in the +x direction # at the same level. Sources do not specify the exact adjacency arithmetic. return None def findcrossparentneighbors(child, childnodes): # Identifies adjacent nodes in the same level that share a boundary # but have different parents. Sources do not specify the exact adjacency arithmetic. return [] def computetexturedimensions(octree): # Computes dimensions to hold all nodes in the 3D texture return octree.maxindexx, octree.maxindexy, octree.maxindexz def allocatetexture(w, h, d): # Allocates an 8-bit RGBA 3D texture return [None] (w h d) def encodenode(node, texture): # Maps node to 8 consecutive texels in the x-direction # Sets Alpha: 1.0 for inner, 0.5 for data leaf, 0.0 for empty # Sets RGB: pointer to first child (inner) or data pointer (leaf) # Stores 6 neighbor pointers in subsequent texels for leaves # Standard texture write operations. pass # Standard texture write operations. Edge Cases: Boundary Nodes: Neighbor pointers link to the smallest node enclosing all adjacent nodes if there are multiple ones. Depth Limit: Traversal stops before reaching a single root node at the top level to optimize performance. A variant that replaces explicit neighbor pointers with a primal tree graph Gp and a neighbor graph G3 to accelerate ray traversal. Gp stores only parent and first-child indices per cell, relying on consecutive child numbering, while G3 precomputes three immediate neighbors per cell to avoid expensive tree traversals. It sets itself apart by reducing memory overhead compared to full neighbor storage, making it suitable for high-depth trees where neighbor distance in Gp alone can exceed 48 steps. Choose this structure when memory bandwidth is constrained and tree depth is high. See Tree Graph Gp and Neighbor Graph G3. Memory: Memory requirement increases by ~6x. The structure uses a 3D texture with 8-bit RGBA components where each node occupies 8 texels, potentially addressing 16 \times M nodes. Performance: Traversal complexity drops to ~ O(logx(n)). Enables direct jumps to object space neighbours without backtrack or parent pointers. On-the-fly construction at each frame allows for view-dependent optimization. Strengths and Limitations: Accelerates ray casting by providing direct access to adjacent nodes, avoiding backtracking. Differs from Zhou et al. [2010] by storing different payload (mesh vs point cloud) and maintaining only x-neighbor pointers instead of pointers to all 26 neighbors. When to use: Use when accelerating ray traversal in volume rendering and memory overhead must be balanced against traversal speed. Avoid when full 26-neighbor connectivity is strictly required or when on-the-fly texture updates are too costly for the target hardware. Introduced by Popov (2007) and Gobbetti et al. (2008) in the context of GPU-based volume rendering and voxelization. The structure is based on rope trees [HBZ98] and shares similarities with bottom-up breadth-first construction using Morton ordering. It is used to accelerate ray casting by providing direct access to adjacent nodes, avoiding backtracking. name: Point Octree
body: A Point Octree is a recursive hierarchical data structure designed to manage a dynamic set of 3D points, supporting insertion, removal, retrieval, movement, and spatial queries such as nearest neighbor and radius search. It stores points in parallel arrays within leaf octants and dynamically subdivides nodes when capacity limits are reached. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D points \mathbf{p}i with associated user data Di. Output: A tree structure enabling spatial queries and dynamic updates. Data Structures: The tree consists of nodes (octants). Each node contains: children: An array of up to 8 child octants (or null if leaf). data: A PointData<T> object (or null if internal node). PointData<T> layout: Two parallel arrays: points: Vector3[]: Stores the coordinates of points in this leaf. data: T[]: Stores the associated user data for each point. Parameters: maxPoints: Maximum number of points allowed in a leaf before triggering a split. maxDepth: Hard limit on recursion depth to prevent infinite subdivision. bias: A padding value added to octant boundaries during containment checks to handle points near boundaries or sphere intersections. Algorithm Steps: 1. Insertion (set): Recursively traverse from the root to find the leaf octant containing the point \mathbf{p}. Check if \mathbf{p} already exists in the leaf's points array; if yes, update the corresponding entry in data. If the leaf is full (number of points \ge maxPoints) and current depth < maxDepth, call split() and redistribute(). Otherwise, append \mathbf{p} to points and D to data in the leaf. 2. Splitting and Redistribution: split() creates 8 empty child octants. redistribute(bias) iterates through all points in the current node's data and determines which child octant contains each point using contains(point, bias). The point and its data are moved to the child's PointData, and the current node's data is set to null. 3. Radius Search (findPoints): Recursively traverse child octants that intersect the query sphere (defined by center \mathbf{c} and radius r). Intersection is approximated by checking if the sphere center lies within the octant boundaries expanded by the radius using contains(center, radius). In leaf nodes, compute squared distance d^2 = \|\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{c}\|^2 for each point. Filter points where d^2 \le r^2. 4. Movement (move): If the point and new position are in the same octant, update the position in place or recurse into children. If they diverge, remove the point from the old location and insert it at the new location via set(). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Vector3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def truediv(self, scalar): return Vector3(self.x / scalar, self.y / scalar, self.z / scalar) def equals(self, other): return self.x == other.x and self.y == other.y and self.z == other.z def distancesquared(self, other): dx = self.x - other.x dy = self.y - other.y dz = self.z - other.z return dxdx + dydy + dzdz class PointData: def init(self): self.points = [] self.data = [] class PointOctant: def init(self, minbound, maxbound): self.min = minbound self.max = maxbound self.children = None self.data = None def contains(self, point, bias=0): return (point.x >= self.min.x - bias and point.x <= self.max.x + bias and point.y >= self.min.y - bias and point.y <= self.max.y + bias and point.z >= self.min.z - bias and point.z <= self.max.z + bias) def split(self): mid = (self.min + self.max) / 2.0 self.children = [] for i in range(8): xbit = (i >> 2) & 1 ybit = (i >> 1) & 1 zbit = i & 1 newmin = Vector3( self.min.x if xbit == 0 else mid.x, self.min.y if ybit == 0 else mid.y, self.min.z if zbit == 0 else mid.z) newmax = Vector3( self.max.x if xbit == 0 else mid.x, self.max.y if ybit == 0 else mid.y, self.max.z if zbit == 0 else mid.z) self.children.append(PointOctant(newmin, newmax)) self.data = None def redistribute(self, bias): if self.data is None or self.children is None: return for i in range(len(self.data.points)): p = self.data.points[i] d = self.data.data[i] for child in self.children: if child.contains(p, bias): if child.data is None: child.data = PointData() child.data.points.append(p) child.data.data.append(d) break self.data = None def set(self, point, dataentry, maxpoints, maxdepth, currentdepth, bias): if currentdepth >= maxdepth: if self.data is None: self.data = PointData() self.data.points.append(point) self.data.data.append(dataentry) return if self.children is None: if self.data is None: self.data = PointData() for i in range(len(self.data.points)): if self.data.points[i].equals(point): self.data.data[i] = dataentry return if len(self.data.points) >= maxpoints: self.split() self.redistribute(bias) for child in self.children: if child.contains(point, bias): child.set(point, dataentry, maxpoints, maxdepth, currentdepth + 1, bias) return else: self.data.points.append(point) self.data.data.append(dataentry) else: for child in self.children: if child.contains(point, bias): child.set(point, dataentry, maxpoints, maxdepth, currentdepth + 1, bias) return def findpoints(self, center, radius, results): if self.data is None: return if not self.contains(center, radius): return if self.children is None: for i in range(len(self.data.points)): dsq = self.data.points[i].distancesquared(center) if dsq <= radius radius: results.append((self.data.points[i], self.data.data[i])) else: for child in self.children: child.findpoints(center, radius, results) def remove(self, point, bias): if self.data is None: return for i in range(len(self.data.points)): if self.data.points[i].equals(point): self.data.points.pop(i) self.data.data.pop(i) break def move(oldpoint, newpoint, octant, maxpoints, maxdepth, currentdepth, bias): if octant.contains(oldpoint, bias) and octant.contains(newpoint, bias): if octant.children is not None: for child in octant.children: move(oldpoint, newpoint, child, maxpoints, maxdepth, currentdepth + 1, bias) elif octant.data is not None: for i in range(len(octant.data.points)): if octant.data.points[i].equals(oldpoint): octant.data.points[i] = newpoint return octant.data.data[i] else: octant.remove(oldpoint, bias) for child in octant.children: if child.contains(newpoint, bias): child.set(newpoint, None, maxpoints, maxdepth, currentdepth + 1, bias) break return None Uses an octree (or kDTree) to accelerate spatial queries like nearest neighbor and radius search, avoiding O(N^2) brute-force comparisons. On a 1.42 million point indoor scan, building a cKDTree index took 417 ms. For 300k points, 16-Nearest Neighbor queries took 4.1 ms with the tree vs 5,071 ms brute force (1,224x speedup). Radius search (r=0.15m) took 26 ms vs 3,246 ms (126x speedup). Brute force is faster for single lookups, but the tree amortizes build cost over many queries. Used for normal estimation, segmentation, and ground filtering. Time Complexity: Average-case query and update performance scales logarithmically with point count. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of stored points and tree depth. Performance: On a 1.42M point scan, index build took 417 ms. 16-NN query on 300k points: 4.1 ms (tree) vs 5,071 ms (brute force). Strengths: Supports dynamic updates including insertion, removal, and point movement. Limitations: maxDepth is a hard limit that may prevent perfect balancing for very dense clusters. Build cost is non-trivial for large static datasets if queries are few. The Point Octree is a standard recursive octree implementation for managing 3D points. It is widely used in point cloud processing for tasks requiring spatial indexing, such as normal estimation and segmentation. The specific implementation details (parallel arrays, bias-based containment) are derived from the sparse-octree library. sparse-octree module, https://github.com/vanruesc/sparse-octree, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Point Cloud Level of Detail: Octrees and Out-of-Core..., https://learngeodata.eu/point-cloud-level-of-detail-octree/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Spatial Hierarchies
head: Spatial Tree Structures
body: Spatial Hierarchies organize data into tree structures to accelerate point location via recursive search. They solve the problem of inefficient traversal in sparse scenes by reducing intersection tests. Unlike sibling methods such as Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration Optimization or Jiang et al. Acceleration Structure, they dynamically partition space rather than relying on fixed grids or image-order traversal. For the shared family principles, see Hierarchical Data Structures. Insertion into spatial hierarchies refers to the algorithmic process of adding primitives into an existing or growing hierarchical data structure. Unlike static build methods that analyze the entire scene at once, insertion methods process primitives one by one, allowing for incremental updates. This makes it suitable for dynamic environments, though it is highly sensitive to the order of insertion. It is chosen when scenes require frequent updates or when building from unsorted data. Spatial hierarchies such as octtrees, BSP trees, and KD trees were developed to optimize point location by recursive search. name: Insertion into Spatial Hierarchies
body: Insertion into spatial hierarchies incrementally adds primitives to a hierarchical data structure, processing them one by one rather than analyzing the full scene at once. This approach supports dynamic updates and unsorted data ingestion but produces tree quality that depends heavily on the insertion order. It differs from static partitioning methods like Median-Cut or Surface Area Heuristic (SAH) by avoiding full dataset re-sorting. Inputs and Outputs: Input is a hierarchy node and a primitive (e.g., triangle or bounding box). Output is the modified hierarchy with the primitive integrated. Data Structures: Each node stores a bounding volume (bound), a list of primitives (prims), a primitive count (nprims), a depth level (depth), and child pointers (children). A node is a leaf if children is empty. Parameters: MAXDEPTH limits tree depth, typically 16. MAXPRIMS caps primitives per leaf before subdivision, typically 2 to 8. Steps: 1. Test primitive overlap with node.bound. If no overlap, terminate. 2. If node is a leaf: If nprims > MAXPRIMS and depth < MAXDEPTH: subdivide node, then recursively insert the primitive into all children. Otherwise: append the primitive to node.prims and increment nprims. 3. If node is internal: recursively insert the primitive into all children. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Node: def init(self): self.bound = AABB() self.prims = [] self.nprims = 0 self.depth = 0 self.children = [] def insert(node, primitive): if not overlap(node.bound, primitive): return if isleaf(node): if node.nprims > MAXPRIMS and node.depth < MAXDEPTH: subdivide(node) for child in node.children: insert(child, primitive) else: node.prims.append(primitive) node.nprims += 1 else: for child in node.children: insert(child, primitive) def isleaf(node): return len(node.children) == 0 def overlap(a, b): return a.min.x <= b.max.x and a.max.x >= b.min.x and \ a.min.y <= b.max.y and a.max.y >= b.min.y and \ a.min.z <= b.max.z and a.max.z >= b.min.z def subdivide(node): node.children = [Node() for in range(8)] # Octree split Edge cases and pitfalls: Zero-size primitives or degenerate bounds require explicit overlap checks to avoid false negatives. Depth limits prevent infinite recursion on tightly packed scenes. Initialize an empty root node. Iteratively insert one triangle after another into the BVH, possibly extending it. Let the triangle sift to the bottom of the BVH, potentially enlarging the BV of intermediate nodes. If the triangle arrives at a leaf, replace the leaf with an internal node and attach the new and old triangles as its children. If at an internal node, decide to attach the triangle to the current internal node, or let it sift into the left/right subtree. The order in which objects are inserted has a very large influence on the quality of the tree. A spatial partitioning structure built from a mesh to enable fast point queries or collision detection. It visualizes splitting disks at each node and uses a configurable depth parameter, typically set to 14. Input requires mesh vertices and triangles, with optional diskMaterial, visitedDiskMaterial, and drawNaiveClosestPoint for debug visualization. Construction initializes binarySpacePartition = new BSP(mesh, 14) and computes splitting disk matrices using the average position, plane rotation, and scaled radius. Time Complexity: O(D) per insertion, where D is tree depth, assuming constant-time overlap tests. Frequent subdivisions and bounding volume updates add overhead. Memory Complexity: O(N + C), where N is primitive count and C is node count from dynamic splitting. Performance: Highly dependent on insertion order. Sorted or shuffled insertion orders significantly reduce intersection tests per ray compared to model-load order. Strengths: Supports dynamic scenes without full rebuilds; handles unsorted data naturally. Limitations: Tree quality degrades with poor ordering; may require periodic rebalancing. The recursive subdivision approach is standard in octree implementations for spatial partitioning. The Iterative Insert method was introduced by Goldsmith and Salmon in 1987 for incremental BVH construction. BSP tree construction provides an alternative mesh-based partitioning strategy for collision detection and point queries. name: Brick-of-Bricks Decomposition
head: Flat hierarchy of bricks
body: Brick-of-Bricks Decomposition is a storage format where a volume is stored as a flat hierarchy of bricks of size n^3 to improve cache-coherence in volume traversal. It arises from not fully expanding an octree into single-voxel leaf nodes. It sets itself apart from fully expanded octrees by grouping voxels into contiguous blocks for raycasting very large volumes. Inputs: An octree structure where nodes are not necessarily expanded to single-voxel leaf nodes. Outputs: A flat array of bricks of size n^3, along with an indexing scheme to map hierarchical positions to memory addresses for the 8-neighborhood required for trilinear interpolation. Data Structures: 1. Brick Array: A 1D array storing voxel data grouped into contiguous blocks of n^3. 2. Hierarchy Index: A structure mapping the octree topology to the flat brick array, enabling fast lookup of the 8-neighborhood for trilinear interpolation. Steps: 1. Construct Hierarchy: Build an octree where non-leaf nodes may store aggregate metrics (e.g., average, standard deviation, minimum-maximum range, Lipschitz range, or error measures like root mean square). 2. Flatten to Bricks: Traverse the octree and group nodes into bricks of size n^3 to form a flat hierarchy. 3. Indexing Scheme: Implement an efficient indexing scheme to quickly find the memory address of voxels in the 8-neighborhood required for trilinear interpolation. 4. Raycasting: During traversal, use the indexing scheme to access voxel data for shading and interpolation. Parameters: n: The side length of a brick in voxels. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Handling: The indexing scheme must correctly handle bricks at the boundaries of the volume or irregular octree structures. Interpolation: Trilinear interpolation requires access to 8 neighboring voxels. If a neighbor crosses a brick boundary, the indexing scheme must correctly locate the adjacent brick and the relative offset within it. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getvoxel(brickarray, brickoffsets, brickid, x, y, z, n): """Access a voxel at local coordinates (x, y, z) in brickid.""" # Calculate linear offset within the brick (row-major order) offset = x + n y + n n z # Retrieve base address for the brick from the hierarchy index base = brickoffsets[brickid] return brickarray[base + offset] def getneighbor(brickarray, brickoffsets, brickid, x, y, z, n, dx, dy, dz): """Access a neighbor voxel, handling brick boundaries.""" nx, ny, nz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz # Check if neighbor stays within current brick if 0 <= nx < n and 0 <= ny < n and 0 <= nz < n: return getvoxel(brickarray, brickoffsets, brickid, nx, ny, nz, n) # Sources do not specify the exact algorithm for determining the adjacent brick ID when crossing boundaries # Standard practice computes global coordinates, divides by n to find the neighbor brick ID, then wraps local coordinates modulo n return None Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Improves cache-coherence in volume traversal compared to fully expanded octrees. Strengths: Better cache performance for large volumes due to flat storage. Limitations: Requires an efficient indexing scheme for neighbor access. Brick-of-Bricks Decomposition was introduced by Parker et al. for raycasting very large volumes. It arises from the observation that octrees do not have to be balanced nor fully expanded into single-voxel leaf nodes. name: kD-Tree Traversal
head: K-d Tree Spatial Partitioning, Kd Backtrack Algorithm, Multi-dimensional binary search tree
body: kD-Tree Traversal is a ray traversal algorithm for binary spatial partitioning structures where nodes split space using arbitrary axis-aligned planes, offering more flexible geometry adaptation than fixed-center octrees. It solves the problem of efficiently intersecting rays with complex, non-uniform geometry distributions by recursively descending a binary tree, determining which child node (near or far) the ray intersects relative to the splitting plane, and performing early termination upon finding the first hit. Inputs: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), and a root node of the kD-tree. Outputs: The distance t{hit} to the closest intersection with a primitive in the scene, or \infty if no intersection is found. Data Structures: The kD-tree is a binary tree. Each node contains: 1. Splitting Plane: Defined by an axis index axis \in \{0, 1, 2\} (representing x, y, or z) and a split position s along that axis. 2. Children: Pointers to two child nodes (left and right). 3. Primitives: A list of geometry primitives (e.g., triangles) stored only in leaf nodes. 4. Bounding Box: Implicitly defined by the path from the root. The root encloses the entire scene. Each child's bounding box is the parent's box clipped by the splitting plane. Construction: 1. Given a cell (axis-aligned BBox) and a list of primitives, choose an axis-aligned splitting plane perpendicular to one coordinate axis. 2. Distribute geometry among the two children. Polygons straddling the plane must be assigned to both children. 3. Recurse until a stopping criterion is met (e.g., max depth, number of objects, or cost function threshold). 4. Splitting Plane Selection: To minimize traversal cost, use the Surface-Area-Heuristic (SAH). Try all 3 axes. For each axis, evaluate the cost function at finite points (borders of bounding boxes of primitives) using a plane sweep. Choose the axis and split position with the minimum cost. SAH Cost Function: C(B) = Area(B1) \cdot N(B1) + Area(B2) \cdot N(B2) where Area(Bi) is the surface area of child box i and N(Bi) is the number of triangles in child box i. This assumes rays have a far-away origin and hit the root bounding volume. Cost Ratio: The ratio of time for one ray-primitive test (ti) to one ray-splitting-plane intersection test (tt) is typically 80:1. Approximation: For large scenes (>500,000 polygons), sort polygons into buckets and evaluate SAH only at bucket borders. Traversal Algorithm (Recursive): The traversal determines the intersection of the ray with the splitting plane to identify the "near" child (containing the ray origin) and the "far" child. 1. Leaf Check: If the current node is a leaf, intersect the ray with each primitive in the node's object list. Discard intersections with t > t{max}. Return the closest intersection t{hit} if found, otherwise return \infty. 2. Splitting Plane Intersection: Calculate t{split}, the signed distance along the ray to the splitting plane of the current node. t{split} = \frac{s - o{axis}}{d{axis}} where s is the split position, o{axis} is the ray origin component along the split axis, and d{axis} is the ray direction component along the split axis. If d{axis} = 0, the ray is parallel to the plane; handle as a special case by traversing only the child containing the origin. 3. Child Determination: Let near be the child containing the origin, and far be the other child. The child index is determined by comparing o{axis} to s and the sign of d{axis}. 4. Traversal Logic: If t{split} > t{max}: The splitting plane is beyond the current search range. Traverse only the near child with t{min}, t{max}. If t{split} < t{min}: The splitting plane is before the current search range. Traverse only the far child with t{min}, t{max}. Otherwise (t{min} \le t{split} \le t{max}): The ray intersects the splitting plane within the range. Recursively traverse the near child with t{min}, t{split}. If the result t{hit} < t{split}, return t{hit} (early termination). Else, traverse the far child with t{split}, t{max}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, node, tmin, tmax): # 1. Leaf Handling if node.isleaf: closestt = float('inf') for primitive in node.primitives: t = intersectrayprimitive(rayorigin, raydirection, primitive) if tmin <= t < closestt: closestt = t return closestt # 2. Splitting Plane Intersection axis = node.axis splitpos = node.splitposition oaxis = rayorigin[axis] daxis = raydirection[axis] # Handle parallel ray case if daxis == 0.0: # Ray is parallel to splitting plane; it never crosses it. # Traverse only the child containing the ray origin. if oaxis < splitpos: nearchild = node.left else: nearchild = node.right return traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, nearchild, tmin, tmax) tsplit = (splitpos - oaxis) / daxis # 3. Child Determination # Determine which child contains the ray origin if daxis > 0: nearchild = node.left if oaxis < splitpos else node.right farchild = node.right if oaxis < splitpos else node.left else: # daxis < 0 nearchild = node.right if oaxis < splitpos else node.left farchild = node.left if oaxis < splitpos else node.right # 4. Traversal Logic if tsplit > tmax: return traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, nearchild, tmin, tmax) elif tsplit < tmin: return traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, farchild, tmin, tmax) else: thitnear = traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, nearchild, tmin, tsplit) if thitnear < tsplit: return thitnear return traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, farchild, tsplit, tmax) def intersectrayprimitive(rayorigin, raydirection, primitive): # Standard ray-primitive intersection (e.g., Möller–Trumbore for triangles) return float('inf') Optimized Iterative Traversal (for Shadow Rays): For shadow rays where any hit is sufficient, the tree can be transformed to allow pure Depth-First Search (DFS) using a linear array and skip pointers. 1. Transform the tree into a linear array where nodes are ordered for DFS. 2. Each node has a skipNode pointer to the next node to visit if the current node has no primitives or no hit. 3. Algorithm: python def traverseshadowray(rayorigin, raydirection, root): node = root stopnode = root.skipnode while node < stopnode: if rayintersectsnodebounds(rayorigin, raydirection, node): if node.hasprimitives: thit = intersectrayprimitive(rayorigin, raydirection, node.primitives) if thit is not None: return thit node = node.skipnode return float('inf') def rayintersectsnodebounds(rayorigin, raydirection, node): # Standard AABB-ray intersection (slab method) return True Oversized Object Handling: If objects are very large (e.g., in architectural models), they can hinder the finding of good splitting planes. 1. Before each splitting, filter out "oversized objects". 2. If many oversized objects exist, build a separate kD-tree for them. 3. Otherwise, store them in a simple list attached to the node or scene. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Straddling Polygons: In regular kD-trees, polygons straddling the splitting plane must be stored in both subtrees, leading to 2-3 times more pointers to triangles than triangles exist. This increases memory usage and traversal time. Precision: Floating-point precision issues can arise when calculating t{split}, especially when the ray is nearly parallel to the splitting plane (d{axis} \approx 0). Boundary Conditions: Ensure correct handling of ray origins exactly on the splitting plane by using consistent half-open interval logic or epsilon offsets. Hybrid Kd Tree Traversal is a method for efficiently accessing heterogeneous volume data by organizing distinct brick types (e.g., dense grids, octrees, voxel lists) into a hierarchical Kd tree structure. head: JiTTree traversal, Recursive Kd Tree of Bricks
body: Hybrid Kd Tree Traversal is a method for efficiently accessing heterogeneous volume data by organizing distinct brick types (e.g., dense grids, octrees, voxel lists) into a hierarchical Kd tree structure. It solves the problem of sparse or mixed-format volumes where a single uniform data structure would waste memory or require complex type-checking during ray traversal. Unlike its sibling Adaptive Kd Tree, which adapts subdivision based on data density, this method groups bricks by their storage format to enable specialized, type-specific access routines at the leaves. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset partitioned into bricks of varying types (Dense, Octree, Voxel List, Empty). Output: A Kd tree structure where internal nodes define spatial splits and leaf nodes point to homogeneous brick groups or specific access functions. Data Structures: The tree consists of Node structures. Each node contains: axis: Integer (0, 1, 2) indicating the splitting dimension (x, y, z). key: Integer coordinate value of the splitting plane. type: Enum indicating the node's role. Values include INTERNAL, OCTREE, VLIST, DENSE, and EMPTY. leftChild: Pointer or index to the left child node. rightChild: Pointer or index to the right child node. Algorithm Steps: 1. Construction: Recursively split the volume space to minimize the entropy of brick types in the resulting sub-regions. 2. Traversal: For a query position pos, traverse from the root: If node.type == INTERNAL: Compare pos[node.axis] with node.key. If pos[node.axis] < node.key, recurse on leftChild. Else, recurse on rightChild. If node.type != INTERNAL: Route to the specific handler for the leaf type (e.g., getDense, getOctree, getVList) or return EMPTY. Formulas: The construction uses entropy minimization. The entropy E(S) of a region S with respect to brick types is: E(S) = - \sum{i=1}^{b} pi \log2 pi where b is the number of brick types and pi is the proportion of bricks with type i in region S. The average entropy I(S) for a split creating sub-regions Sj is: I(S) = \sum{j=1}^{2} \frac{vj}{v} E(Sj) where vj is the volume of sub-region Sj and v is the total volume of the parent region. The split that minimizes I(S) is selected. Parameters: Number of brick types (b): Typically 4 (Dense, Octree, Voxel List, Empty) in standard implementations. Pitfalls: OpenCL Compatibility: OpenCL does not support switch statements. Type routing must be implemented using if/else chains, which offer comparable performance to switches in this context. Precision: Splitting planes are defined by integer coordinates. Bricks sharing coordinates must be handled carefully during sorting to ensure balanced splits. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Node: axis: int # 0=x, 1=y, 2=z key: int # Splitting coordinate type: int # INTERNAL, OCTREE, VLIST, DENSE, EMPTY leftChild: Node # Reference to left child rightChild: Node # Reference to right child def get(pos: list, node: Node) -> int: """ pos: list of 3 integers [x, y, z] node: current tree node returns: brick data or EMPTY """ if node.type == INTERNAL: # Compare position along the splitting axis if pos[node.axis] < node.key: return get(pos, node.leftChild) else: return get(pos, node.rightChild) # Leaf node type routing elif node.type == OCTREE: return getOctree(pos, node) elif node.type == VLIST: return getVList(pos, node) elif node.type == DENSE: return getDense(pos, node) else: return EMPTY JiTTree is a data structure optimization that uses just-in-time (JIT) compilation to specialize tree traversal code for a specific dataset, eliminating type-checking overhead and pointer-chasing by unrolling the tree structure into nested conditionals. It builds on Hybrid Kd Tree Traversal by grouping homogeneous brick types into leaf nodes and applying partial evaluation at runtime to inline type-specific logic, thereby shifting the performance bottleneck from memory-bound data fetches to instruction-cache-bound code execution. A kd-tree construction algorithm that splits nodes to minimize the average entropy of brick types in child sub-regions, effectively grouping bricks of the same type together. Steps: 1. Sort bricks with respect to x, y, and z coordinates separately. 2. For each coordinate, find the split candidate where left and right sub-lists are closest to equally sized. 3. Calculate the average entropy I(S) for each possible split using the formula I(S) = \sum{j=1}^{2} \frac{vj}{v} E(Sj). 4. Select the split that minimizes I(S). 5. Recursively apply splitting until each kd-tree leaf contains bricks of only one elemental brick type. Example: Split at x=192 in a 320-volume region. Left sub-volume (weight 3/8) has entropy 0.5436. Right sub-volume (weight 5/8) has entropy 0.6775. Weighted average entropy I(S) = 0.627. Time Complexity: Traversal is O(\log N) where N is the number of bricks, assuming a balanced tree. Construction is more expensive due to sorting and entropy calculation. Memory Complexity: Depends on the tree depth and the number of bricks. The tree structure itself is small compared to the volume data. Strengths: Efficiently handles heterogeneous data; reduces memory overhead for sparse volumes; allows specialized access for each brick type. Limitations: Construction is complex; JIT compilation adds runtime overhead; OpenCL compatibility requires careful coding. When to use: Heterogeneous volumes with mixed brick types (dense, octree, voxel lists) where uniform storage is inefficient. When not to use: Uniform dense volumes where a simple grid or octree suffices. The method originates from research on adaptive, hybrid data structures for volume datasets on GPUs. It builds on the concept of Kd trees for sparse data representation. The entropy-based construction criterion was introduced by Michalski et al. in the context of optimizing decision trees. name: Kd Tree Unrolling (JiTTree)
head: JiTTree, Just-in-Time Compilation Tree, Just-in-Time Compiled Tree, Just-in-time compiled kd tree, Kd Tree of Bricks with Partial Evaluation, Unrolled Kd Tree
body: JiTTree is a data structure optimization that uses just-in-time (JIT) compilation to specialize tree traversal code for a specific dataset, eliminating type-checking overhead and pointer-chasing by unrolling the tree structure into nested conditionals. It builds on Hybrid Kd Tree Traversal by grouping homogeneous brick types into leaf nodes and applying partial evaluation at runtime to inline type-specific logic, thereby shifting the performance bottleneck from memory-bound data fetches to instruction-cache-bound code execution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A loaded 3D volume dataset organized as a Hybrid Kd Tree of bricks (Dense, Octree, Voxel List, or Empty). The dataset is static during traversal. Output: A specialized, unrolled traversal function (code) that maps 3D coordinates (x, y, z) to the appropriate brick data or an empty value. Data Structures: The underlying structure is a Kd Tree where leaf nodes contain sub-volumes of a single brick type (homogeneous regions), rather than single bricks or mixed types. Internal Nodes: Define splitting planes. In the unrolled code, these are represented by literals (splitting axis and coordinate) rather than struct fields. Leaf Nodes: Contain pointers to the specific brick data. In the unrolled code, these are either literal pointers (for single-brick leaves) or local constant arrays (for multi-brick leaves). Numbered Steps: 1. Construct Homogeneous Kd Tree: Build a Kd Tree where splitting planes are chosen to maximize the homogeneity of leaf nodes. Each leaf node contains a sub-volume consisting of bricks of a single type (e.g., all Dense, or all Octree). 2. Partial Evaluation (Tree Unrolling): At runtime, upon data load, feed the static dataset into a partial evaluator. This transforms the general tree traversal algorithm into data-specific code. 3. Apply Optimizations: The partial evaluator applies five specific optimizations to generate the final unrolled code: (i) Traversal Optimization: Encode the splitting axis order directly in the conditional structure. Insert splitting plane positions as literal constants. This requires no memory fetches for traversal data. (ii) Empty Discarding: If a coordinate (x, y, z) does not match any leaf node path, return EMPTY (e.g., 0) as the default value. This discards empty regions without memory fetches. (iii) Implicit Specialization: Inline the specialized access functions (e.g., getDense, getOctree, getVList) directly at the leaf nodes. This removes runtime type checks and switch statements. (iv) Pointer In-baking: For leaf nodes containing multiple bricks, store pointers as a local constant array within the generated function. For leaf nodes containing a single brick, use pointer literals directly in the function call, eliminating one memory fetch. (v) Leaf Node Branch Removal: Reduce Kd Tree branches that contain only a single brick type to a single-type bricking approach, simplifying the conditional logic. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode represents the unrolled traversal for a specific example dataset (512x512x512 volume, 64x64x64 bricks) as described in. The literals (192, 64, 384, etc.) are splitting plane coordinates baked into the code. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def get(x, y, z): # Optimization (i): Traversal with literal splitting planes # Splitting plane at x = 192 if x < 192: # Splitting plane at z = 64 if z < 64: # Leaf: Dense bricks # Optimization (iv): Pointer in-baking (local array or literal) # Optimization (iii): Implicit specialization return getDenseSubVolume0(x, y, z) else: # Splitting plane at z = 384 if z < 384: # Leaf: Octree bricks return getOctreeSubVolume0(x, y, z) else: # Leaf: Voxel List bricks return getVListSubVolume0(x, y, z) else: # Splitting plane at x = 384 if x < 384: # Splitting plane at y = 192 if y < 192: # Leaf: Dense bricks return getDenseSubVolume1(x, y, z) else: # Leaf: Voxel List bricks return getVListSubVolume1(x, y, z) else: # Leaf: Octree bricks return getOctreeSubVolume1(x, y, z) def getDenseSubVolume0(x, y, z): # Access dense brick data using baked-in pointers pass def getOctreeSubVolume0(x, y, z): # Access octree brick data using baked-in pointers pass def getVListSubVolume0(x, y, z): # Access voxel list brick data using baked-in pointers pass Parameters: Brick Size: 64x64x64 voxels (typical example value). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Standard Kd Tree Inefficiency: Standard Kd Trees split homogeneous regions unnecessarily, increasing traversal depth. JiTTree avoids this by grouping same-type bricks into leaves. Instruction Cache Pressure: Unrolling increases program length (instruction count), which may impact instruction cache efficiency or register pressure. Code Size Growth: The access time becomes independent of the number of elemental brick types, but the generated code size grows with the number of type-specific branches. A technique where a binary search tree's data is explicitly compiled into the code (instructions) to eliminate memory fetches during traversal, shifting the caching burden from data cache to instruction cache. Mechanism: Replace recursive function calls and pointer dereferences with explicit nested if-else statements comparing the search key against hardcoded node keys, returning hardcoded values. Pitfall: Increases program length, potentially impacting instruction cache efficiency. Comparison: Unlike standard BSTs requiring memory fetches for node.key and node.value, the unrolled version has no memory fetches for node data, eliminating pointer overhead and cache misses. A technique where type-specific functions are inlined directly into the unrolled tree traversal code, eliminating switch statements and runtime type resolution overhead. Mechanism: Traverse the unrolled tree using hardcoded key comparisons. When a leaf node is reached, directly call the specialized function associated with that node's type, passing the value as an argument. Pitfall: Access time is independent of the number of elemental brick types, but code size grows with the number of type-specific branches. Comparison: Differs from standard type routing (which uses a switch statement on an element's type field after a lookup) by eliminating the lookup of the type field and the switch dispatch. Time Complexity: Traversal time is O(\log N) in terms of tree depth, but with a significantly reduced constant factor due to the elimination of pointer chasing and type checks. The overhead depends on the homogeneity of the dataset rather than the number of elemental types. Memory Complexity: The data structure itself (the Kd Tree) is not stored in memory during traversal; instead, the "structure" is stored in the instruction cache. This reduces memory bandwidth requirements for traversal. Measured Performance: In a 512x512x512 volume with 64x64x64 bricks, JiTTree shifts the algorithm from being memory-bound to being instruction-throughput-bound or compute-bound, improving performance on GPUs where memory fetches are costly. Strengths: Eliminates type-checking overhead; removes pointer chasing; efficient discarding of empty regions; specialized access for homogeneous regions. Limitations: Increases program length (instruction count); code size grows with the number of brick types; requires JIT compilation capability at runtime. When to Use: When the dataset is static and loaded at runtime, and the hardware has a large instruction cache or limited memory bandwidth for traversal data. When Not to Use: When the dataset changes frequently (requiring frequent recompilation) or when instruction cache size is severely constrained. JiTTree was introduced in a thesis by as a just-in-time compiled tree data structure. The idea exploits information not known during earlier compilation stages (i.e., the specific dataset loaded at runtime) to optimize traversal code using partial evaluation. It is an extension of the hybrid volume bricking approach, aiming to improve access performance by incorporating the dataset into the traversal code. name: Adaptive Kd Tree
body: The Adaptive Kd Tree is a hierarchical acceleration structure for volume rendering that stores data values exclusively in the leaves of the tree. It addresses the problem of efficient ray traversal through sparse volumetric data by allowing subdivision in all directions, offering more flexibility than octrees which are restricted to center-based subdivisions. It is distinguished from its sibling, the Hybrid Kd Tree, by its specific leaf-only storage strategy and construction method. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of volumetric data points or voxel values. Output: A balanced kd tree structure where internal nodes contain splitting planes and leaf nodes contain the actual data values. Data Structures: The tree is a binary tree. Internal nodes store the axis and position of the splitting plane. Leaf nodes store the volumetric values associated with the region they cover. The tree is constructed to be balanced. Construction Steps: 1. Collect all data points or voxel centers. 2. Select a split direction (e.g., x, y, or z axis). 3. Sort the points with respect to the chosen split direction. 4. Identify the median element in the sorted list. 5. Split the data at the median, creating two child nodes. 6. Recursively apply steps 2-5 to each child node until a stopping criterion is met (e.g., leaf nodes contain single values or a minimum region size). 7. Store the data values only in the resulting leaf nodes. Formulas: Let P be the set of points. For a split direction d, let P{sorted} be P sorted by coordinate d. The split point s is: s = \text{median}(P{sorted}) The left child contains points p \in P where pd < s, and the right child contains points where pd \ge s. Parameters: Split direction selection: Not specified in sources. Typically chosen to minimize variance or balance node counts. Stopping criterion: Not specified in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Balancing: Unbalanced kd trees are difficult to balance and can degrade performance. The median split method ensures balance. Stack usage: Traditional kd tree traversal requires a stack for recursive traversal. The adaptive kd tree itself does not eliminate the need for a stack during traversal, though related algorithms like the kd restart algorithm do. A variant of BSP using splitting planes aligned with data axes for adaptive partitioning. It constructs shallow hierarchies in real-time for moderately sized volumes, supporting efficient empty space skipping in sparse rendering scenarios. It is particularly beneficial in ray casting where it reduces traversal costs for volumetric data exhibiting high sparsity. Construction involves selecting splitting planes to balance empty and filled regions. Time Complexity: Construction is O(N \log N) due to sorting at each level for median selection. Traversal complexity depends on tree balance and data sparsity. Memory Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of leaf nodes storing values. Strengths: Balanced structure ensures predictable traversal performance. Leaf-only storage can be memory efficient for sparse data if internal nodes are small. Limitations: Construction can be costly for large datasets. Not explicitly stack-less, so traversal may require stack management unless combined with specific traversal algorithms like kd restart. When to use: When data sparsity is high and a balanced tree is desired for consistent traversal performance. When not to use: When real-time construction is required for very large volumes, or when stack-less traversal is a strict requirement without additional algorithmic modifications. The Adaptive Kd Tree was introduced as a variant by Friedman et al.. It is used in volume rendering to accelerate ray traversal through volumetric datasets. The approach contrasts with traditional kd trees that may store data in internal nodes or use different balancing strategies.
