head: SDF Tree Query
body: Nearest Neighbor SDF Tree Traversal is an algorithm for computing the signed distance from a query point to a scene represented by a hierarchical Signed Distance Function (SDF) tree. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating complex, potentially infinite or large-scale SDF scenes by traversing a dual-buffer structure (downtree and uptree) that supports boolean operations and geometric primitives. Unlike standard octree traversal which samples voxel data, this method computes exact or approximate analytical distances using union pruning and continuous axis-aligned (CAA) cloning, making it suitable for ray marching in implicit surface rendering. The algorithm maintains a stack of frames, one per tree level, to track the state of the traversal. It processes the downtree (structural hierarchy) and uptree (operation evaluation) in a single pass, using pruning to skip irrelevant subtrees. Input: A query point \mathbf{p} in world space; a hierarchical SDF tree structure containing downtreebuffer and uptreebuffer. Output: The signed distance d from \mathbf{p} to the scene surface. The core state is held in a LevelStackEntry array (pointstack), indexed by tree level. LevelStackEntry Layout: branchpoints: [Vec4; 2] (or [Point; 2]). Stores the current query point and a secondary point for branching logic. branchdists: [f32; 2] (or [f64; 2]). Stores the computed distance for the left and right branches of the current node. Initialized to \infty. fillidx: usize. Index into branchdists indicating how many valid distance values are stored for the current level. Tree Node Layout (Downtree Block): level: u32. Depth in the tree. len: usize. Number of subsequent uptree blocks associated with this node. parentisunion: bool. Flag indicating if the parent node is a union operation (enables pruning). isprimitive: bool. True if this node represents a geometric primitive (e.g., sphere). opcode: u32. Operation type (e.g., union, intersection, primitive type). opspecific: Struct containing operation parameters (e.g., smooth radius, CAA clone vectors). boundingbox: SdfBoundingBox. Axis-aligned or oriented bounding box of the node. otherbox: SdfBoundingBox. The bounding box of the sibling node in a binary operation (used for pruning). Tree Node Layout (Uptree Block): level: u32. Depth in the tree. opcode: u32. Operation type (e.g., union, intersection). opspecific: Struct containing operation parameters (e.g., smoothradius for smooth unions). 1. Initialization: Set dtindex = 0, utindex = 0, lastdtlevel = 0. Initialize pointstack[1] (root level): branchpoints = [point, Vec4::ZERO] branchdists = [INFINITY, INFINITY] fillidx = 0 Initialize lastutlevel = u32::MAX (or equivalent max value). 2. Main Traversal Loop: While dtindex < sdftree.downtreebufferlen: a. Read Downtree Block: Let dtblock = sdftree.downtreebuffer[dtindex]. Let dtpoint = pointstack[dtblock.level].branchpoints[0]. b. Union Pruning: If dtblock.parentisunion is true: Compute thismindist = mindist(dtblock.boundingbox, dtpoint). Compute maxdistsibling = maxdist(dtblock.otherbox, dtpoint). If thismindist > 0 AND (thismindist > dtutprunecmp OR thismindist > maxdistsibling): Skip this subtree: dtindex += 1 + dtblock.len utindex += 1 + dtblock.len Continue to next iteration. c. Uptree Propagation: If dtblock.level < lastdtlevel: Enter loop to process pending uptree blocks: Let utblock = sdftree.uptreebuffer[utindex]. If utblock.level >= lastutlevel, break loop. Let childframe = pointstack[utblock.level + 1]. Let lbranchdist = childframe.branchdists[0]. Let rbranchdist = childframe.branchdists[1]. Let utframe = pointstack[utblock.level]. Compute result = uptreedispatch(utblock.opcode, utblock.opspecific, lbranchdist, rbranchdist). Store utframe.branchdists[utframe.fillidx] = result. Increment utframe.fillidx. Update lastutlevel = utblock.level. Increment utindex. d. Primitive Case: If dtblock.isprimitive: Let thisframe = pointstack[dtblock.level]. Compute local point: \mathbf{p}{local} = M^{-1} \mathbf{p}, where M is dtblock.boundingbox.transinverse. Compute distance: dist = primdispatch(dtblock.opcode, dtblock.opspecific, plocal). Store thisframe.branchdists[thisframe.fillidx] = dist. Increment thisframe.fillidx. Increment utindex. e. Non-Primitive Case: If not primitive: Let childframe = pointstack[dtblock.level + 1]. Compute child points: childpoints = downtreedispatch(dtblock.opcode, dtblock.opspecific, dtblock.boundingbox.transinverse dtpoint). Store childframe.branchpoints = childpoints. Reset childframe.fillidx = 0. Reset childframe.branchdists = [INFINITY, INFINITY]. f. Increment: Update lastdtlevel = dtblock.level. Increment dtindex. 3. Finish Propagation: While utindex < sdftree.uptreebufferlen: Repeat steps 2c (Uptree Propagation) logic for remaining uptree blocks. 4. Return Result: Return pointstack[1].branchdists[0]. Mindist for Bounding Box: Computes the distance from point \mathbf{p} to bounding box defined by matrix M and scale s. \mathbf{q}{local} = (|M^{-1}\mathbf{p}| - 1.0) \cdot s d = \max(0, \|\mathbf{q}{local}\|) + \max(0, \max(qx, qy, qz)) \cdot \min(0, \dots) \quad \text{(Implementation detail varies)} Specific implementation from source: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. qlocal = (trans.abs() - 1.0) bbox.scale d = qlocal.max(0).length() + qlocal.x.max(qlocal.y.max(qlocal.z)).min(0.0) Note: The second term in the source implementation qlocal.x.max(qlocal.y.max(qlocal.z)).min(0.0) effectively adds 0 if the point is inside the box (since max component is \le 0 in local space relative to center? No, local space is normalized. If inside, components are in [-1, 1]. The formula seems to be a specific optimization for OBBs or specific bounding box types). For a standard AABB centered at 0 with half-extents h, d = \max(0, |x|/hx - 1)hx + \dots. The source formula uses trans.abs() which implies transformation to local space. Sphere Primitive Distance: d = \|\mathbf{p}{local}\| - r where \mathbf{p}{local} is the point in the primitive's local space and r is the radius. CAA Clone Downtree Transform: Used for cloning geometry along a lattice. \mathbf{p}{new} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{d} \cdot \text{round}\left(\frac{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{d}}\right) \cdot \text{clamp}\left(\frac{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{d}}, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{p}\right) where \mathbf{d} is displacement (lattice spacing), \mathbf{n} is neglimit, \mathbf{p} is poslimit. Implementation: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. point - opspecific.vec4s[0] (point / opspecific.vec4s[0]).round().clamp(opspecific.vec4s[1], opspecific.vec4s[2]) SdfUnion smoothradius: Stored in opspecific.floats[0]. Controls the blending radius for smooth unions. SdfCaaClone displacement: Vec3. Defines the lattice spacing for cloning. SdfCaaClone neglimit: Vec3. Defines the negative boundary of the clone region. SdfCaaClone poslimit: Vec3. Defines the positive boundary of the clone region. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise in mindist calculations for points very close to bounding box boundaries. Empty Subtrees: Pruning relies on parentisunion. If this flag is incorrect, pruning may skip valid geometry. Stack Depth: The pointstack must be large enough to accommodate the maximum depth of the tree. Infinity Handling: branchdists initialized to INFINITY. If no valid path is found, the result may be INFINITY. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of nodes visited. Pruning reduces the effective N for sparse scenes. Memory Complexity: O(D) where D is the depth of the tree, for the pointstack. Strengths: Efficient for large-scale scenes with hierarchical structure; supports complex boolean operations and cloning; pruning accelerates traversal. Limitations: Requires pre-computed downtree and uptree buffers; less suitable for dynamic scenes without rebuilding the tree; precision depends on bounding box approximations. The method is described in the holger-kibur/sdf repository. It implements a stack-based traversal for SDF trees, supporting union pruning and CAA cloning. The approach is designed for efficient evaluation of hierarchical SDF representations, likely used in real-time rendering or simulation contexts where implicit surfaces are queried frequently. holger-kibur/sdf, https://github.com/holger-kibur/sdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Pointer Chasing BVH Traversal
body: Pointer Chasing BVH Traversal is a method for traversing Bounding Volume Hierarchies (BVHs) that eliminates index arithmetic operations in favor of explicit pointer dereferences. It solves the problem of computational overhead in the traversal hot loop by replacing index-based child selection with direct memory access. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as PBRTv4 BVH Layout, by using explicit child pointers rather than implicit indexing, which reduces memory-dependent operations on latency-bound architectures but severely underutilizes memory bandwidth on GPUs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A BVH structure where nodes contain explicit pointers to their children, and a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Output: The intersection point or the leaf node containing the hit primitive. Data Structures: The BVH is stored as a tree of nodes. Each node contains: bbox: Bounding volume (e.g., AABB) for the subtree. leftchild: Pointer to the left child node. rightchild: Pointer to the right child node. isleaf: Boolean flag indicating if the node is a leaf. data: Primitive indices or volume data (if leaf). Unlike compact layouts that store nodes in contiguous arrays with implicit indexing (e.g., 2i+1, 2i+2), this layout relies on the hardware's ability to fetch memory locations pointed to by leftchild and rightchild. Steps: 1. Initialize: Start at the root node. Initialize ray parameter t{min} = 0 and t{max} = \infty. 2. Intersection Test: Check if the ray intersects the current node's bounding box. If not, terminate traversal for this ray. 3. Child Selection: If the node is a leaf, process the contained primitives/volume data and terminate. If the node is internal, determine which child(ren) the ray intersects. Unlike index-based methods that compute child indices via arithmetic, this method follows the explicit pointers leftchild and rightchild. Typically, the ray is tested against both children's bounding boxes. If both are intersected, both are pushed to the traversal stack or processed recursively. If only one is intersected, only that child is followed. 4. Traversal: Update the current node pointer to the selected child. Repeat from Step 2. 5. Backtracking: If a path is exhausted (no more children or no intersection), backtrack to the parent node using the traversal stack or recursion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversebvhptrchasing(ray, root): stack = [root] closestt = infinity while stack is not empty: node = stack.pop() # Check if node is within ray's tmax if node.bbox.mint > ray.tmax or node.bbox.maxt < ray.tmin: continue if node.isleaf: # Process leaf primitives/volume hit = intersectleafprimitives(ray, node.data) if hit.t < closestt: closestt = hit.t else: # Explicit pointer chasing # Test left child if ray.intersects(node.leftchild.bbox): stack.push(node.leftchild) # Test right child if ray.intersects(node.rightchild.bbox): stack.push(node.rightchild) return closestt Parameters: Stack size: Depends on tree depth. Not given in the sources. Memory alignment: Not specified, but pointer chasing performance is sensitive to cache behavior. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance Degradation: On GPU architectures, this method exhibits catastrophic performance degradation (over 100x slowdown) compared to compact layouts due to severe underutilization of available memory bandwidth. Memory Latency: On ARM architectures, it may marginally outperform index-based layouts (like pbrt-align16) when the workload is memory latency bound, as it reduces memory-dependent operations in the hot loop. A memory-efficient, cache-friendly representation that replaces explicit child pointers with implicit indexing and unified node structures, enabling more predictable memory access patterns during traversal. Choose this for GPU performance where memory bandwidth is the bottleneck. Time Complexity: O(\log N) on average for balanced trees, but dependent on memory access patterns. Memory Complexity: O(N) nodes, but with higher overhead due to pointer storage and potential fragmentation. Measured Performance: ARM: Marginally outperforms pbrt-align16 when the workload is memory latency bound. GPU: Over 100x slower than compact layouts like sg-eq and pbrt-q16 due to underutilized memory bandwidth. Strengths: Reduces computational overhead (index arithmetic) in the traversal hot loop, beneficial on latency-bound CPUs. Limitations: Poor memory bandwidth utilization on GPUs, leading to significant performance penalties. When to Use: On CPU architectures where memory latency is the primary bottleneck and cache behavior favors pointer chasing. When Not to Use: On GPU architectures or any platform where memory bandwidth is the limiting factor. The method is discussed in the context of comparing BVH layouts for volume rendering and ray tracing. It is presented as a baseline or alternative to compact, index-based layouts like pbrt-align16, sg-eq, and pbrt-q16. The performance characteristics are evaluated across ARM and GPU architectures, highlighting the architectural divergence in layout preferences. name: PBRTv4 BVH Layout
head: Decoupled BVH Layout, LinearBVH, LinearBVHNode, Original PBRTv4 layout, PBRTv4 layout, Scion BVH layout
body: The PBRTv4 BVH Layout is a memory-efficient, cache-friendly representation of a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) used in the PBRTv4 rendering system. It solves the problem of pointer-chasing overhead and memory fragmentation inherent in traditional pointer-based BVHs by storing nodes in a contiguous array and primitives in a separate array. It sets itself apart from its parent Pointer Chasing BVH Traversal by replacing explicit child pointers with implicit indexing and unified node structures, enabling more predictable memory access patterns during traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A logical BVH tree (abstract data type) consisting of Interior and Leaf nodes, where Interior contains bounds and two child BVHs, and Leaf contains bounds, a primitive count, and an array of triangles. Output: A LinearBVH struct containing two contiguous arrays: nodes (BVH nodes) and primitives (triangles). Data Structures: The layout uses two primary C++ structs: 1. LinearBVH: The container for the entire BVH. uint32t P: Total number of primitives. uint32t N: Total number of nodes. Triangle primitives: Pointer to the contiguous array of triangles. LinearBVHNode nodes: Pointer to the contiguous array of nodes. 2. LinearBVHNode: The node structure, aligned to 32 bytes. AABB bounds: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box, containing low (float3) and high (float3). uint16t nprims: Discriminator. Value 0 indicates an Interior node; value > 0 indicates a Leaf node. uint8t S[4]: A 4-byte union field. If nprims > 0 (Leaf): Interpreted as uint32t po, the offset into the primitives array. If nprims == 0 (Interior): Interpreted as uint32t co, the offset to the right child relative to the current node index. Logical to Physical Mapping: Left Child: Implicitly located at currentindex + 1. Right Child: Located at currentindex + co. Primitives: Located at primitives + po for nprims elements. Build Process: The build process consists of two recursive passes: counting and building. 1. Counting (reccount): Traverses the logical BVH to determine the total number of nodes (N) and primitives (P). 2. Allocation: Allocates memory for primitives (size P sizeof(Triangle)) and nodes (size N sizeof(Nodes), aligned to 32 bytes). 3. Building (recbuild): Traverses the logical BVH again, filling the physical arrays. Interior Node: Store bounds. Set nprims = 0. Recursively build left child. Recursively build right child. Calculate co = rightindex - thisindex. Store co in S. Leaf Node: Store bounds. Set nprims to the number of primitives. Store current primitivesindex as po in S. Copy primitives from logical node to physical primitives array. Increment primitivesindex by nprims. Return thisindex. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class AABB: low: Vector3 # float3 high: Vector3 # float3 class Triangle: p0: Vector3 p1: Vector3 p2: Vector3 class LinearBVHNode: # 32-byte aligned bounds: AABB nprims: uint16 # 0 for Interior, >0 for Leaf S: uint8[4] # Union: po (Leaf) or co (Interior) class LinearBVH: P: uint32 # Primitive count N: uint32 # Node count primitives: List[Triangle] nodes: List[LinearBVHNode] def intersectsrayaabb(ray, aabb): # Standard ray-AABB intersection test pass def reccount(logicalnode, bvh): if logicalnode is Interior: reccount(logicalnode.left, bvh) reccount(logicalnode.right, bvh) bvh.N += 1 elif logicalnode is Leaf: bvh.P += logicalnode.nprims def recbuild(logicalnode, bvh, nodesindex, primitivesindex): thisindex = nodesindex[0] nodesindex[0] += 1 if logicalnode is Interior: # Store bounds bvh.nodes[thisindex].bounds = logicalnode.bounds bvh.nodes[thisindex].nprims = 0 # Recurse Left (Implicitly thisindex + 1) recbuild(logicalnode.left, bvh, nodesindex, primitivesindex) # Recurse Right rightindex = recbuild(logicalnode.right, bvh, nodesindex, primitivesindex) # Store offset to right child bvh.nodes[thisindex].S = rightindex - thisindex return thisindex elif logicalnode is Leaf: # Store bounds bvh.nodes[thisindex].bounds = logicalnode.bounds bvh.nodes[thisindex].nprims = logicalnode.nprims # Store primitive offset bvh.nodes[thisindex].S = primitivesindex[0] # Copy primitives for i in range(logicalnode.nprims): bvh.primitives[primitivesindex[0] + i] = logicalnode.data[i] # Update primitive index primitivesindex[0] += logicalnode.nprims return thisindex def buildbvh(logicalbvh): bvh = LinearBVH() bvh.P = 0 bvh.N = 0 # Count reccount(logicalbvh, bvh) # Allocate bvh.primitives = [Triangle() for in range(bvh.P)] bvh.nodes = [LinearBVHNode() for in range(bvh.N)] # Build nodesindex = [0] primitivesindex = [0] recbuild(logicalbvh, bvh, nodesindex, primitivesindex) return bvh def closesthit(ray, bvh, best): # best is a tuple (distance, triangle) # Initialize best with infinity if no hit found yet if best[0] == float('inf'): best = (float('inf'), None) stack = [0] # Start at root node index 0 while stack: i = stack.pop() node = bvh.nodes[i] # Check intersection with node bounds if intersectsrayaabb(ray, node.bounds): # Check if closer than current best if distminrayaabb(ray, node.bounds) < best[0]: if node.nprims > 0: # Leaf Node startprimidx = node.S # po for k in range(node.nprims): prim = bvh.primitives[startprimidx + k] if intersectsraytriangle(ray, prim): dist = distminraytriangle(ray, prim) if dist < best[0]: best = (dist, prim) else: # Interior Node # Left child is implicit: i + 1 # Right child is i + co leftchild = i + 1 rightchild = i + node.S # co # Push children to stack. Order depends on traversal strategy. # For closest hit, order matters for early termination. # Standard approach: push right then left to process left first (LIFO) # Or use distance heuristic to order. # Here we simply push both. stack.append(rightchild) stack.append(leftchild) Parameters: Node alignment: 32 bytes. Primitive storage: Separate contiguous array. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The S field is 4 bytes. For interior nodes, co is an offset. If the tree is very deep or unbalanced, offsets must fit in uint32t. does not specify limits, but uint32t implies a max node count of 2^{32}-1. Boundary Conditions: The left child is always i+1. If i is the last node, i+1 is out of bounds. This implies the tree structure must be valid (no dangling left children). assumes a valid BVH structure. Degenerate Input: Empty BVHs or BVHs with no primitives are not explicitly handled in the pseudocode, but P=0 and N=0 would result in empty arrays. A variant that quantizes leaf bounds to save space. The PBRTv4 layout described here is the "Original" or "Uncompressed" version. The parent method that uses explicit pointers. The PBRTv4 layout replaces this with implicit indexing to improve cache performance. Time Complexity: Build time is O(N) where N is the number of nodes, as it requires two passes over the logical tree. Traversal time is O(K) where K is the number of visited nodes, same as pointer-chasing, but with better cache locality. Memory Complexity: O(N + P) where N is node count and P is primitive count. Nodes are 32 bytes each. Primitives are stored separately. Strengths: Cache-friendly due to contiguous node array. Reduced memory overhead by eliminating explicit child pointers and using implicit indexing. Unified node structure simplifies memory management. Limitations: Less flexible than pointer-based structures for dynamic updates (insertions/deletions) due to contiguous layout. Requires two-pass build process (count then build). When to use: Static scenes where ray tracing performance is critical and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. When not to use: Dynamic scenes requiring frequent BVH updates. The PBRTv4 BVH Layout was introduced in the PBRTv4 rendering system. It is described in the paper "Decoupling Data Layouts from Bounding Volume Hierarchies" (2026) by Christophe Gyurgyik et al.. The layout is designed to combine the clarity of Abstract Data Types (ADTs) with the performance of specialized memory layouts. It is implemented in C++ and is also described using the Scion declarative layout language. name: Octree Traversal and Subdivision
body: Octree Traversal and Subdivision manages the hierarchical navigation and structural refinement of volumetric data, solving the problem of efficiently accessing sparse or multi-resolution datasets during rendering. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the fundamental mechanics of hierarchical descent (traversal) and spatial partitioning refinement (subdivision), whereas siblings like JIT Type Specialization focus on shader optimization, Topology-Caching for Dynamic Particle Volume Raycasting handles dynamic particle updates, and Hierarchical Tree Node Traversal generalizes to other tree structures. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of hierarchical descent and ascent. The traversal begins at the root of the octree and determines which of the eight children (octants) the ray intersects. This is typically done by comparing the ray's position relative to the center of the current node's bounding box. 1. Child Selection: For a node with center \mathbf{c} and half-extent s, the ray position \mathbf{p} determines the child index k \in \{0, \dots, 7\}: k = 4 \cdot \mathbb{I}(px \ge cx) + 2 \cdot \mathbb{I}(py \ge cy) + 1 \cdot \mathbb{I}(pz \ge cz) where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function. 2. Empty Space Skipping: If the selected child is marked as empty (or uniform), the traversal skips the subtree. This is achieved by advancing the ray parameter t to the exit of the current node or using neighbor pointers to jump to the next potentially occupied node. 3. Leaf Handling: Upon reaching a leaf node, the method typically switches to a fixed-step traversal (like DDA) within the leaf's voxel grid to sample the volume data. 4. Backtracking: Because octrees are sparse and irregular, traversal often requires backtracking to the parent node when a ray exits a subtree or encounters an empty branch. This is implemented using an explicit stack (on GPU) or recursion (on CPU). This method implements high-performance GPU volume rendering by decoupling the branch-intensive octree traversal from the raycasting loop, using a rasterization pass to identify active volume regions and a shadow mapping pass for lighting. It solves the performance bottleneck of traditional raycasting on sparse data by moving empty-space culling into a graphics pipeline stage, achieving 2 to 4 times faster rendering speeds than state-of-the-art algorithms on large out-of-core datasets. Unlike sibling methods that rely on pure ray-tracing traversal or fixed-step DDA, this approach uses view-dependent proxy geometry rasterization to generate a per-pixel list of penetrated bricks, ensuring front-to-back processing and tighter ray segments. It builds on Octree and Tree Traversal and relates to Stackless Traversal and DDA Tree Traversal with Mini-Stack. Tile-based Octree Traversal accelerates volume rendering by grouping rays into image tiles and pre-computing the set of octree nodes intersecting each tile. Unlike standard per-ray traversal, it reduces redundant node visits by sharing traversal state across rays within a tile, leveraging spatial coherence. It builds on Octree and Tree Traversal by batching the hierarchical descent. Camera-Driven Octree Subdivision constructs a hierarchical spatial partitioning for scene representation by subdividing space based on camera visibility and distance thresholds. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by driving the octree construction directly from camera positions and view frustums rather than geometric occupancy or traversal. This family extracts manifold isosurfaces from sparse, adaptive octree data structures by leveraging the hierarchy to skip empty space and refine geometry only where necessary. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering or meshing high-resolution implicit fields that would be prohibitive to store or process as dense grids. It differs from its siblings by focusing on the geometric extraction phase (computing intersections, dual vertices, or Hermite data) rather than just traversal efficiency or rasterization. For example, Tree Marcher provides the traversal engine, while Hermite Data Computation via Bisection and Tetrahedralization of Octree Cells define how the geometry is constructed from the visited nodes. Pitfall: occupiedCount() walks the whole tree twice, taking about 1 second each at a resolution of 0.01, and validate() runs three times on the final volume. Definition: Rendering large data using multi-resolution octree structures, often based on texture-slicing, to reduce aliasing artifacts from undersampling and improve rendering speed. Steps: 1. Select Level of Detail (LOD) or scale for bricks using one of the following methods: 1. Focus point oracle based on distance from brick center to user-defined focus point. 2. Estimating screen-space error. 3. Using a combined factor of data homogeneity and importance. 4. Using predicted visual significance of a brick. 5. Estimating projected screen space size of the corresponding voxel/brick. 6. Per-sample LOD selection for finer granularity. 2. Refine data resolution using a 'greedy' approach: iteratively load the next higher-resolution brick until the desired resolution is reached. Alternatively, load the highest resolution directly, skipping intermediate resolutions. Pitfall: Interpolation between bricks of two different resolution levels must be handled correctly. Definition: A rendering technique for point cloud/voxel data that uses an object-order front-to-back octree traversal combined with a non-visible subtree rejection technique. Steps: 1. Traverse the octree in object-order front-to-back. 2. Apply a non-visible subtree rejection technique during traversal, which differs from Meagher's original method and may combine R. Yagel's object-order raycasting with S. Teller's frustum casting. 3. Execute the traversal as a greedy algorithm, processing nodes sequentially without lookahead or parallel scheduling. Complexity: Inherently non-parallel due to its greedy sequential nature; typically implemented on the CPU. Comparison: Contrasted with image-order approaches like raycasting, which are deemed impractical except on parallel hardware. The concept of octrees for spatial partitioning was introduced by Meagher in the early 1980s. Early methods focused on object-order traversal and visibility culling. With the advent of GPUs, research shifted towards image-order raycasting and hierarchical traversal optimizations to handle large-scale volumetric data. Multi-resolution rendering techniques based on texture-slicing became prominent for handling large datasets. More recently, GPU-specific optimizations like rasterization-based traversal and tile-based processing have been developed to address the branch divergence and memory access patterns inherent in traditional octree raycasting. Camera-driven subdivision methods have also emerged for specific applications like view-dependent level-of-detail. feat(collision): add compact GPU voxelization and pair export, https://github.com/MrNeRF/LichtFeld-Studio/pull/3789, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) State-of-the-Art in GPU-Based Large-Scale Volume Visualization, https://vcg.seas.harvard.edu/publications/20150513-stateof-the-art-in-gpu-based-large-scale-volume-visualization/paper, fetched 2026-10-24 Procedural World: Euclideon Geoverse 2013, https://procworld.blogspot.com/2013/05/euclideon-geoverse-2013.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

head: asvo renderer, voxel-based octree traversal
body: This method implements high-performance GPU volume rendering by decoupling the branch-intensive octree traversal from the raycasting loop, using a rasterization pass to identify active volume regions and a shadow mapping pass for lighting. It solves the performance bottleneck of traditional raycasting on sparse data by moving empty-space culling into a graphics pipeline stage, achieving 2 to 4 times faster rendering speeds than state-of-the-art algorithms on large out-of-core datasets. Unlike sibling methods that rely on pure ray-tracing traversal or fixed-step DDA, this approach uses view-dependent proxy geometry rasterization to generate a per-pixel list of penetrated bricks, ensuring front-to-back processing and tighter ray segments. It builds on Octree and Tree Traversal and relates to Stackless Traversal and DDA Tree Traversal with Mini-Stack. The method operates in two main phases: a traversal/rasterization phase to identify active volume regions, and a rendering phase that may include a shadow map pass. Inputs: Octree structure composed of bricks, where each brick is split into regular macrocells. Frame dimensions: mwindowWidth, mwindowHeight. Camera and light parameters. Job queue for parallel traversal managed via a device pointer. Outputs: Final color buffer (via PBO/Texture). Shadow map (if shadow pass is enabled). Traversal Queue: A device pointer dTravQueuePtr used to manage parallel traversal jobs. It is initialized to hEndIndex before traversal begins. Depth Buffer Texture: Configured with cudaTextureDesc: addressMode[0] = cudaAddressModeClamp. filterMode = cudaFilterModePoint. normalizedCoords = false. readMode = cudaReadModeElementType. Shadow Map: Stores minimum depth values. Initialized with minDepth = 2147483647. 1. Initialization: Set hStartIndex = 0 and hEndIndex = obj.data()->jobs().size(). Initialize dTravQueuePtr[0] = hEndIndex. Initialize octreeLevel to 0. 2. Traversal Loop: While hEndIndex - hStartIndex > 0: 1. Launch the traverse kernel with job range [hStartIndex, hEndIndex) and current octreeLevel. 2. Update hStartIndex = hEndIndex. 3. Update hEndIndex = dTravQueuePtr[0]. 4. Increment octreeLevel. Pitfall: If dTravQueuePtr[0] is not updated correctly by the kernel, the loop may infinite loop or terminate prematurely. 3. Rendering Pass: If shadowPass is true: 1. Launch drawShadowMap kernel. 2. Pitfall: If no voxels are found, minDepth remains 2147483647 and shadowMap[index] is not written. Else: 1. Launch draw kernel. Unverified code. Initialize traversal state hstartindex = 0 hendindex = model.jobs().size() dtravqueueptr[0] = hendindex octreelevel = 0 # 2. Parallel Traversal Loop while hendindex - hstartindex > 0: # Launch traverse kernel for current job range and depth traversekernel( jobstart=hstartindex, jobend=hendindex, level=octreelevel, camera=camera, model=model, queueptr=dtravqueueptr) # Update indices based on device queue pointer hstartindex = hendindex hendindex = dtravqueueptr[0] octreelevel += 1 # 3. Rendering Pass shadowpassenabled = True # Controlled by application state if shadowpassenabled: # Shadow map generation drawshadowmapkernel( camera=camera, light=light, model=model, mindepthinit=2147483647) else: # Direct volume rendering drawkernel( camera=camera, light=light, model=model) def traversekernel(jobstart, jobend, level, camera, model, queueptr): # Standard GPU kernel launch pattern # Processes jobs in [jobstart, jobend) at given octree depth # Updates queueptr[0] with next batch index upon completion pass def drawshadowmapkernel(camera, light, model, mindepthinit): # Standard GPU kernel launch pattern # Renders shadow map using mindepthinit as initial depth value pass def drawkernel(camera, light, model): # Standard GPU kernel launch pattern # Renders final color buffer pass A GPU-based high-quality volume rendering approach for large out-of-core volume data that reduces rendering time by moving branch-intensive accelerating structure traversal out of the GPU raycasting loop and introducing efficient empty-space culling via rasterization. It stores the volume in an octree of bricks, further splitting every brick into regular macrocells. The method rasterizes proxy geometry of a view-dependent cut of octree nodes to capture penetrated bricks in a per-pixel list in front-to-back order. This allows raycasting to occur only inside tighter ray segments, achieving two levels of empty space skipping (brick and macrocell). It achieved 2 to 4 times faster rendering speed than current state-of-the-art algorithms across various datasets. Performance: Achieves 2 to 4 times faster rendering speed than state-of-the-art algorithms on large out-of-core datasets. Complexity: Reduces branch divergence by moving traversal out of the raycasting loop. Memory: Requires storage for octree bricks and macrocells. Strengths: Efficient empty-space culling, suitability for large out-of-core data, reduced GPU branch intensity. Limitations: Complexity of managing rasterization-based culling and proxy geometry generation. When to use: Large out-of-core volume datasets where traditional raycasting traversal is a bottleneck. The method originates from research on GPU-based high-quality volume rendering of large out-of-core volume data, focusing on reducing rendering time by optimizing ray traversal costs. name: Tile-based Octree Traversal
head: Tile-based rendering with octree
body: Tile-based Octree Traversal accelerates volume rendering by grouping rays into image tiles and pre-computing per-tile node lists of intersecting octree nodes. It addresses scalability for web-based rendering of large biomedical datasets by combining tile-based rendering with hierarchical data structures. It builds on Octree Traversal and Subdivision by batching hierarchical descent across rays sharing a tile frustum. Inputs: Octree structure, volume data, camera parameters, image resolution, tile dimensions. Outputs: Rendered image buffer. Data Structures: 1. Octree Node: Contains a bounding box (center \mathbf{c} and half-extent s), an empty/uniform flag, pointers to children, and leaf data. 2. Tile Node List: A list of pointers to octree nodes intersecting the tile's frustum. Steps: 1. Tile Node List Generation: Traverse the octree to collect nodes intersecting each tile's frustum. Sources do not specify the exact generation algorithm. 2. Ray Generation: For each pixel in a tile, generate a ray from the camera origin through the pixel center. 3. Tile-Aware Traversal: For each ray, traverse the octree using the tile node list as a constraint or starting point. Child Selection: For a node with center \mathbf{c} and half-extent s, the ray position \mathbf{p} determines the child index k \in \{0, \dots, 7\}: k = 4 \cdot \mathbb{I}(px \ge cx) + 2 \cdot \mathbb{I}(py \ge cy) + 1 \cdot \mathbb{I}(pz \ge cz) where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function. Empty-Space Skipping: If the selected child is empty, advance the ray parameter t to the exit of the current node and backtrack to the parent. Leaf Handling: Upon reaching a leaf, switch to fixed-step DDA traversal within the leaf's voxel grid to sample volume data. Backtracking: Use an explicit stack to return to the parent node when a ray exits a subtree or encounters an empty branch. 4. Compositing: Accumulate color and opacity along the ray using front-to-back compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertile(tile, octreeroot, volumedata, maxt): # Tile node list generation is not specified in the sources. tilenodelist = [] for pixel in tile.pixels: rayo = tile.camera.origin rayd = normalize(tile.camera.rayforpixel(pixel)) color = vec3(0.0) alpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 stack = [(octreeroot, t)] while stack: node, tentry = stack.pop() if tentry >= maxt: continue p = rayo + rayd tentry c = node.center s = node.halfextent # Child selection k = 4 int(p.x >= c.x) + 2 int(p.y >= c.y) + 1 int(p.z >= c.z) if node.isempty: # Empty-space skipping: advance t to node exit invd = 1.0 / rayd texit = max(min((c.x - s.x - rayo.x) invd.x, (c.x + s.x - rayo.x) invd.x), min((c.y - s.y - rayo.y) invd.y, (c.y + s.y - rayo.y) invd.y), min((c.z - s.z - rayo.z) invd.z, (c.z + s.z - rayo.z) invd.z)) if node.parent is not None: stack.append((node.parent, texit)) continue if node.isleaf: # Leaf handling: fixed-step DDA step = s / node.leafresolution tstep = max(step / abs(rayd.x), step / abs(rayd.y), step / abs(rayd.z)) while t < maxt: val = samplevolume(rayo + rayd t, node) color, alpha = composite(color, alpha, val, tstep) t += tstep continue # Descent: push children for i in range(7, -1, -1): child = node.children[i] if child is not None: invd = 1.0 / rayd bmin = vec3(c.x - s.x, c.y - s.y, c.z - s.z) bmax = vec3(c.x + s.x, c.y + s.y, c.z + s.z) if i & 4: bmin.x = c.x + s.x if i & 2: bmin.y = c.y + s.y if i & 1: bmin.z = c.z + s.z if not (i & 4): bmax.x = c.x - s.x if not (i & 2): bmax.y = c.y - s.y if not (i & 1): bmax.z = c.z - s.z tchild = max((bmin - rayo) invd) stack.append((child, max(tentry, tchild))) tile.imagebuffer[pixel.coords] = color def samplevolume(pos, node): return 1.0 # Standard volume sampling def composite(c, a, val, dt): return c + val (1.0 - a) dt, a + (1.0 - a) dt # Front-to-back compositing Parameters: Leaf Node Size: A smaller leaf-node size leads to less overlap of node lists between image tiles, but increases storage and traversal overhead. Tile Size: Common sizes are 8 \times 8 or 16 \times 16 pixels. Larger tiles increase coherence but may lead to larger node lists and cache misses. Edge Cases: Precision: Floating-point precision issues in ray-node intersection tests can lead to missed nodes or double-counting. Use epsilon values for comparisons. Degenerate Tiles: Tiles with no intersecting nodes should be skipped entirely. TileTree Rendering is a method for storing and accessing high-resolution texture data on octree-structured volumes, enabling seamless interpolation and adaptive resolution. It differs from standard octree texturing by storing separate tile maps for each face of the octree leaves and using a weighted blending scheme based on surface normal direction to eliminate visible seams at tile boundaries. Choose when scene complexity varies significantly across the image. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot L), where N is the number of rays and L is the average number of nodes visited per ray. Tile-based traversal reduces L by sharing traversal work, but adds overhead for node list generation. Memory Complexity: O(N{nodes} + N{tiles} \cdot L{avg}), where N{nodes} is the number of octree nodes and L{avg} is the average tile node list size. Performance: Generally faster than per-ray traversal for large, sparse volumes due to reduced redundant node visits. Performance degrades if tile node lists are large or if the scene is highly uniform. Strengths: Efficient for sparse volumes, reduces overdraw, leverages spatial coherence. Limitations: Increased memory usage for node lists, complexity in dynamic scenes where the tree changes frequently. When to Use: Large, static, sparse volumes where spatial coherence is high. When Not to Use: Highly dynamic scenes, very dense volumes, or when memory is constrained. Tile-based rendering with octrees was popularized by Wang et al. [WBD+ 21] for scalable web-based volume rendering of large biomedical datasets. It addresses the scalability issues of traditional raycasting by combining tile-based rendering techniques with hierarchical data structures. name: TileTree Rendering
head: TileTree
body: TileTree Rendering is a method for storing and accessing high-resolution texture data on octree-structured volumes, enabling seamless interpolation and adaptive resolution. It differs from standard octree texturing by storing separate tile maps for each face of the octree leaves and using a weighted blending scheme based on surface normal direction to eliminate visible seams at tile boundaries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D position p and a surface normal IN.Nrm. Output: A 4D color value (RGBA) representing the texture at p. Data Structures: Each octree leaf node stores: 1. A 6-bit bit vector marking tile presence on each of the 6 faces (positive/negative X, Y, Z). 2. Two 16-bit integers storing the coordinates of the top-left corner of the tiles within the global tile map. 3. An 8-bit integer storing the resolution of the tiles tileres. Algorithm Steps: 1. Octree Lookup: Perform an octree lookup at position p to retrieve the leaf node data. 2. Decode Face Presence: Decode the 6-bit presence vector into two 3D vectors: facep (positive X, Y, Z) and facen (negative X, Y, Z), where components are 1 if the tile is present and 0 otherwise. 3. Local Coordinates: Compute local coordinates within the node by scaling p by the node's level size (lvlsize) and taking the fractional part: local = \text{frac}(p \times lvlsize) 4. UVW Alignment: Decode the tile resolution tileres from the leaf. Compute UVW coordinates aligned on leaf boundaries to ensure seamless interpolation: uvw = local \times \frac{tileres - 1.0}{tileres} + \frac{0.5}{tileres} 5. Face Selection: Normalize the input normal IN.Nrm to get nrm. Compute view vectors for positive and negative faces: vp = facep \times nrm vn = facen \times (-nrm) Select the active face ID based on the view direction. If vp > 0, use idp = (XP, YP, ZP); otherwise, if vn > 0, use idn = (XN, YN, ZN); otherwise, the ID is -1. Store the result in faceid. 6. Tile Access: Initialize colors clr0, clr1, clr2 to 0. Access tile data for present tiles using the tileLkup function: If faceid.x > -1, clr0 = \text{tileLkup}(leaf, faceid.x, uvw.yz). If faceid.y > -1, clr1 = \text{tileLkup}(leaf, faceid.y, uvw.xz). If faceid.z > -1, clr2 = \text{tileLkup}(leaf, faceid.z, uvw.xy). 7. Sample Usage Vector: Compute the alpha usage vector \alpha{xyz} from the alpha channels (w component) of the sampled colors, adding a small epsilon (10^{-6}) for robustness: \alpha{xyz} = 10^{-6} + \text{float3}(clr0.w, clr1.w, clr2.w) 8. Damping Factor: Compute the damping factor for seamless interpolation. Calculate anrm = |nrm|. Compute: damp = \frac{anrm}{\max(anrm.x, \max(anrm.y, anrm.z))} Multiply \alpha{xyz} by damp. 9. Weight Computation: Compute weights w for blending. Calculate inv = 1 - \alpha{xyz}. Compute: w = \alpha{xyz} \times inv.yzx \times inv.zxy 10. Final Color: Compute the final color by the weighted sum of clr0, clr1, clr2 using weights w.x, w.y, w.z, divided by the dot product of w and 1: \text{return } \frac{clr0 \times w.x + clr1 \times w.y + clr2 \times w.z}{\text{dot}(w, 1)} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tileTreeLookup(p, INNrm, octreelookup, decodeposfacepresence, decodenegfacepresence, decodetileresolution, tileLkup, lvlsize): # 1. Octree Lookup leaf = octreelookup(p) # 2. Decode Face Presence facep = decodeposfacepresence(leaf) facen = decodenegfacepresence(leaf) # 3. Local Coordinates local = [p[i] - int(p[i] lvlsize) for i in range(3)] # 4. UVW Alignment tileres = decodetileresolution(leaf) uvw = [(local[i] (tileres - 1.0) / tileres + 0.5 / tileres) for i in range(3)] # 5. Face Selection nrm = normalize(INNrm) vp = [facep[i] nrm[i] for i in range(3)] vn = [facen[i] (-nrm[i]) for i in range(3)] # Face indices for positive and negative axes XP, YP, ZP = 0, 1, 2 XN, YN, ZN = 3, 4, 5 # Component-wise selection: if vp[i] > 0 use idp[i], else -1 faceid = [-1.0, -1.0, -1.0] for i in range(3): faceid[i] = XP if i == 0 else (YP if i == 1 else ZP) if vp[i] > 0 else -1.0 if vn[i] > 0: faceid[i] = XN if i == 0 else (YN if i == 1 else ZN) # 6. Tile Access clr0 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] clr1 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] clr2 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if faceid[0] > -1: clr0 = tileLkup(leaf, faceid[0], [uvw[1], uvw[2]]) if faceid[1] > -1: clr1 = tileLkup(leaf, faceid[1], [uvw[0], uvw[2]]) if faceid[2] > -1: clr2 = tileLkup(leaf, faceid[2], [uvw[0], uvw[1]]) # 7. Sample Usage Vector alphaxyz = [1e-6 + clr0[3], 1e-6 + clr1[3], 1e-6 + clr2[3]] # 8. Damping Factor anrm = [abs(nrm[i]) for i in range(3)] maxanrm = max(anrm[0], max(anrm[1], anrm[2])) damp = [anrm[i] / maxanrm for i in range(3)] alphaxyz = [alphaxyz[i] damp[i] for i in range(3)] # 9. Weight Computation inv = [1.0 - alphaxyz[i] for i in range(3)] # inv.yzx -> [inv[1], inv[2], inv[0]] # inv.zxy -> [inv[2], inv[0], inv[1]] w = [alphaxyz[i] inv[(i+1)%3] inv[(i+2)%3] for i in range(3)] # 10. Final Color dotw1 = sum(w) finalcolor = [ (clr0[0]w[0] + clr1[0]w[1] + clr2[0]w[2]) / dotw1, (clr0[1]w[0] + clr1[1]w[1] + clr2[1]w[2]) / dotw1, (clr0[2]w[0] + clr1[2]w[1] + clr2[2]w[2]) / dotw1, (clr0[3]w[0] + clr1[3]w[1] + clr2[3]w[2]) / dotw1 ] return finalcolor def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return [v[i] / mag for i in range(3)] This variant refers to the core shader logic described in the main method, specifically focusing on the octree traversal, face selection, UV calculation, and tile access steps. It emphasizes the extraction of sample usage flags (alpha) from tile colors with epsilon addition for robustness. Due to the tile resolution being 2k+1, standard MIP-mapping cannot be directly applied to the tile map. This variant uses a strategy where a separate tile map is computed for each resolution level. One tile coordinate per level is stored in the octree leaves. During rendering, the appropriate MIP level is computed and the color is fetched from the corresponding tile map; two levels may be accessed for linear interpolation between MIP levels. Additionally, the tree itself may be MIP-mapped in cases of extreme undersampling. Time and Memory Complexity: The method requires an octree lookup and a fixed number of tile lookups (up to 3) per sample. The memory footprint is efficient; for example, an Armadillo model textured at 1024^3 resolution fits in 11.4 MB, and a Dragon model fits in 11.3 MB. Strengths and Limitations: The primary strength is seamless interpolation and adaptive resolution, eliminating visible seams at tile boundaries. The limitation is the complexity of handling non-power-of-two tile resolutions (2k+1) for MIP-mapping, requiring separate tile maps per level. When to Use: Use when high-resolution texture storage is required on sparse volumes with the need for seamless interpolation and adaptive resolution. TileTree Rendering was introduced in the paper "TileTrees". It builds on hardware implementations of octree traversal. The method allows for interactive painting and conversion between TileTrees and other texture representations. TileTrees, https://doi.org/10.1145/1230100.1230104, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Camera-Driven Octree Subdivision
head: Adaptive Subdivision, Frustum-Based Octree Subdivision, Leaf Node Construction, Octree Space Subdivision
body: Camera-Driven Octree Subdivision constructs a hierarchical spatial partitioning for scene representation by subdividing space based on camera visibility and distance thresholds. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by driving the octree construction directly from camera positions and view frustums rather than geometric occupancy or traversal. Inputs: Set of camera centers \mathcal{C} = \{c1, \dots, cN\}. Set of camera view frustums \mathcal{F} = \{f1, \dots, fN\}. Parameters: \lambda = 3 (subdivision threshold multiplier), nc = 4 (maximum cameras per leaf). Outputs: An octree structure with leaf nodes \{Si\}. For each leaf node Si, a subset of selected cameras \mathcal{C}{Si} \subseteq \mathcal{C} with |\mathcal{C}{Si}| \le nc. Data Structures: Octree Node: center: \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (world coordinates). sidelength: s \in \mathbb{R} (scalar). children: Array of 8 child nodes (or None if leaf). selectedcameras: List of camera indices (populated only for leaves). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Root: Compute the bounding box size W of all camera centers \mathcal{C}. Create a root node with side length s{\text{root}} = 512 \cdot W. 2. Recursive Subdivision: Starting from the root, for each node with side length s and center \mathbf{c}: Retrieve all visible cameras whose view frustums intersect the node's bounding box. If any visible camera center cj satisfies \|cj - \mathbf{c}\| \le \lambda \cdot s (with \lambda=3), subdivide the node into 8 children with side length s/2 and recurse on each child. Otherwise, mark the node as a leaf and stop subdividing. 3. Camera Selection: For each leaf node visible by more than nc=4 cameras, select exactly nc cameras such that the minimal pairwise distance between the selected cameras is maximized. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildoctree(cameracenters, camerafrustums, lambdaval=3, nc=4): # Compute bounding box size of all camera centers bboxsize = computeaabbsize(cameracenters) rootside = 512.0 bboxsize rootcenter = computeaabbcenter(cameracenters) root = Node(center=rootcenter, sidelength=rootside) subdivide(root, cameracenters, camerafrustums, lambdaval, nc) return root def subdivide(node, centers, frustums, lambdaval, nc): s = node.sidelength c = node.center # Retrieve visible cameras whose frustums intersect the node visindices = [i for i, f in enumerate(frustums) if intersects(f, node.bbox)] if not visindices: node.children = None node.selectedcameras = [] return # Check if any visible camera center is within lambda s of node center shouldsubdivide = any(distance(centers[i], c) <= lambdaval s for i in visindices) if shouldsubdivide: # Subdivide into 8 children with side length s/2 node.children = [None] 8 childside = s / 2.0 for i in range(8): childcenter = computechildcenter(c, i, childside) child = Node(center=childcenter, sidelength=childside) node.children[i] = child subdivide(child, centers, frustums, lambdaval, nc) else: # Mark as leaf node node.children = None node.selectedcameras = visindices if len(visindices) > nc: # Select nc cameras maximizing minimal pairwise distance node.selectedcameras = selectmaxmindistcameras(visindices, centers, nc) Parameters: \lambda = 3: Threshold for subdivision. If a camera is within 3s of the node center, subdivide. nc = 4: Maximum number of cameras associated with a single leaf node for warping function construction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Root Size: The root must be sufficiently large (512 \times camera bounding box) to contain far-away objects like sky. Camera Selection: The exact optimization algorithm for selecting cameras is not provided in the main text and is deferred to supplementary material. Octree Texture Subdivision is a method that subdivides the texture space into an octree to skip empty regions and use lower-resolution textures for distant or low-interest regions. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by operating directly on the texture coordinate space rather than the geometric voxel grid, allowing hardware texture interpolation to handle the hierarchical sampling. Distance-Based Octree LOD Management optimizes rendering load by dynamically subdividing or merging octree chunks based on the camera's distance to the chunk center. It splits chunks into eight children when the camera is close and merges them back when the camera is far, serving as the core subdivision logic for Camera-Driven Octree Subdivision. Unlike Octree Texture Subdivision, which manages LOD via texture mipmaps, this method explicitly creates and destroys geometric child nodes. Not given in the sources. The method originates from F2-NeRF, a technique for fast Neural Radiance Field training with free camera trajectories. It was introduced to organize space based on camera visibility rather than static geometry for scene representation. name: Octree Texture Subdivision
body: Octree Texture Subdivision subdivides the texture space into an octree to skip empty regions and use lower-resolution textures for regions far from the viewpoint or of lower interest. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by applying hierarchical subdivision directly to the texture coordinate space, enabling hardware texture interpolation to handle multi-resolution sampling. Inputs: A 3D scalar field volume, a camera view, and an octree structure defined over the texture coordinate space [0,1]^3. Outputs: A rendered image. Data Structures: The method maintains an octree where each node corresponds to a sub-volume in texture space. Node fields: level: Integer depth of the node (0 is root). resolution: The side length of the voxel grid represented by this node's texture. texturehandle: Reference to a 3D texture object of size 2^{\text{level}} \times 2^{\text{level}} \times 2^{\text{level}}. empty: Boolean flag indicating if the node contains no significant data. Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct the octree over the texture space and populate leaf nodes with 3D textures sampled from the original volume data. 2. Traversal: For each pixel, cast a ray and traverse the octree from the root. 3. Culling: If a node is marked empty, skip it entirely. 4. Subdivision: If the ray intersects a node and the node is not a leaf, or if the node is a leaf but the ray requires higher precision (e.g., near the camera or in high-interest regions), subdivide the node. 5. Sampling: If the current node is a leaf, sample the associated 3D texture using hardware interpolation. 6. Adaptation: Dynamically adjust the octree depth based on view distance and interest, using lower-resolution textures (shallower nodes) for regions far from the viewpoint or of lower interest. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderoctreetexturevolume(volumedata, camera, octreeroot): # Construct octree over texture space; populate leaves with 3D textures octree = buildoctree(volumedata) for x, y in camera.pixelgrid(): ray = camera.castray(x, y) color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) node = octreeroot t = ray.origin while node is not None and t < ray.maxdistance: if node.isempty: break if node.isleaf or shouldsubdivide(node, ray): # Map ray intersection to texture coordinates within node bounds texcoords = mapraytotexturecoords(ray, node.bounds) # Sample using hardware 3D texture interpolation value = hardware3dtexturesample(node.texturehandle, texcoords) # Standard volume classification and compositing alpha, rgb = classifyandcomposite(value, color) color = (rgb, alpha) if alpha >= 1.0: break t += ray.stepsize else: # Advance to next octree node along ray node = getnextnode(node, ray) setpixelcolor(x, y, color) Parameters: Empty threshold: Not given in the sources. Interest metric: Not given in the sources. Edge cases: Boundaries: Texture coordinates must be clamped to [0,1] to avoid out-of-bounds access. It solves the problem of interactive visualization of massive datasets by rendering high-resolution detail near a point-of-interest and lower-resolution data in distant or low-importance regions, blending between levels to reduce artifacts. Unlike prior algorithms that assume data is uniformly complex or uniformly important, this method treats quality as a tunable parameter based on visual importance, such as distance from the viewer. It builds on Octree Texture Subdivision by introducing a specific high/low tile blending mechanism to smooth transitions between the octree levels during cutting plane extraction. Time and memory complexity: Depends on the octree depth and the sparsity of the volume. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Skips empty regions and uses lower-resolution textures for less important areas. Limitations: Relies on hardware 3D texture support. When to use: When hardware supports 3D texture interpolation and the volume has significant empty or low-interest regions. When not: When high precision is required everywhere or hardware support is lacking. Origin: Proposed by Boada et al. and LaMar et al.. History: Emerged with the advent of programmable vertex shaders and advanced PC graphics hardware (NVIDIA, ATI, 3DLabs), making texture-mapped volume rendering accessible to a broader community at less than 2% of the cost of previous workstations. name: Multiresolution Texture-Based Cutting Plane Rendering
head: Adaptive Octree Cutting Plane Rendering, High/Low Texture Tile Blending
body: Multiresolution Texture-Based Cutting Plane Rendering is an adaptive scheme for rendering arbitrarily oriented cutting planes through large volumetric data sets at varying resolutions. It solves the problem of interactive visualization of massive datasets by rendering high-resolution detail near a point-of-interest and lower-resolution data in distant or low-importance regions, blending between levels to reduce artifacts. Unlike prior algorithms that assume data is uniformly complex or uniformly important, this method treats quality as a tunable parameter based on visual importance, such as distance from the viewer. It builds on Octree Texture Subdivision by introducing a specific high/low tile blending mechanism to smooth transitions between the octree levels during cutting plane extraction. Inputs: A volumetric data set. A cutting plane defined by its position and orientation. A point-of-interest (or viewer location) to determine visual importance. Outputs: A blended 2D image of the cutting plane intersection with the volume. The core data structure is an octree decomposing texture space. Octree Nodes: Each node contains two texture tiles: High Tile: Stores the node's copy of the data at its specific resolution level. Low Tile: Stores the portion of the parent's high tile that covers the same area as the current node. Tile Sizes: The size relationship between the high and low tiles is defined by the formula: |high| = |low| 2 - 1 where |high| is the size (number of elements) of the high tile and |low| is the size of the low tile. This implies one tile must have an odd size. If power-of-two sizes are required for hardware compatibility, the low tile is set to a power-of-two size, and the high tile size is calculated accordingly, incurring memory overhead. Selected Node Tree: An incomplete octree formed during traversal, containing only nodes selected for rendering. 1. Construct the Texture Hierarchy: Decompose texture space into an octree. Each level of the octree corresponds to a resolution level, where each level is half the resolution of the next finer level. Leaf nodes are associated with the original data resolution. The root node is associated with the coarsest resolution. Interior nodes are created by subsampling the eight child nodes. For each node, generate the High Tile (the node's own data) and the Low Tile (the subset of the parent's High Tile covering the node's area). 2. Traverse and Select Nodes: Traverse the octree and apply a selection filter to each node based on visual importance (e.g., distance from point-of-interest). Build a 'selected node tree'. For each node, one of three outcomes occurs: 1. The node and its children are skipped entirely. 2. The node is skipped, but its children are visited. 3. The node is rendered, and its children are skipped. 3. Balance the Selected Node Tree: Ensure that all adjacent nodes in the selected tree differ by no more than one level of resolution in the octree. Pitfall: Blending is only possible between nodes differing by exactly one level of resolution. Nodes differing by two or more levels do not share textures and cannot be blended directly. This balancing step is necessary to ensure valid blending pairs exist. 4. Determine Corner Blend Ratios: Examine the neighbors of all selected nodes. For each corner of a given selected node, check the seven adjacent nodes (across faces, edges, and corners). If any adjacent node exists and has a lower resolution than the current node, set the corner's blend ratio to 1 (selecting the low tile). Otherwise, set the corner's blend ratio to 0 (selecting the high tile). 5. Calculate Edge Blend Ratios: For each edge of the selected node, calculate the blend ratio for points along the edge. The value is a linear combination of the ratios at the ends of that edge, proportional to the position of the point along the edge. 6. Render First Weighted Image (Low Tile): Download the Low texture tile for the selected node. For each vertex of the clipped cutting plane polygon intersecting the node, define the RGB color value to be equal to the calculated blend ratio at that vertex. Draw the polygon. The hardware interpolates the color values across the polygon, effectively multiplying the texture by the blend ratio. This produces the first weighted image. 7. Render Second Weighted Image (High Tile): Download the High texture tile for the selected node. For each vertex of the clipped cutting plane polygon, define the RGB color value to be 1 minus the blend ratio. Draw the polygon. This produces the second weighted image. 8. Produce Final Blended Result: Add the first weighted image and the second weighted image together. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiresolutioncuttingplanerendering(volumedata, cuttingplane, pointofinterest): """ Renders a cutting plane through a volume using multiresolution octree blending. """ # Step 1: Construct Texture Hierarchy octree = buildoctree(volumedata) for node in octree.allnodes: node.hightile = node.generatehightile() node.lowtile = node.parent.hightile.getsubset(node.boundingbox) # Step 2: Traverse and Select Nodes selectednodes = [] def traverseandselect(node): importance = calculateimportance(node, pointofinterest) if importance < threshold: # Case 1: Skip node and children return elif importance < highthreshold: # Case 2: Skip node, visit children for child in node.children: traverseandselect(child) else: # Case 3: Render node, skip children selectednodes.append(node) traverseandselect(octree.root) # Step 3: Balance Selected Node Tree # Ensure adjacent selected nodes differ by at most 1 level balancetree(selectednodes) # Step 4 & 5: Determine Blend Ratios # Pre-calculate corner ratios for all selected nodes for node in selectednodes: for corner in node.corners: adjacentnodes = get26neighbors(node, corner) # Check if any adjacent node has lower resolution haslowerneighbor = any( n in selectednodes and n.resolutionlevel > node.resolutionlevel for n in adjacentnodes) corner.ratio = 1.0 if haslowerneighbor else 0.0 # Calculate edge ratios based on corner ratios for edge in node.edges: edge.ratio = linearinterpolate(edge.start.ratio, edge.end.ratio, edge.position) # Step 6, 7, 8: Render Blended Image finalimage = zeroslike(cuttingplanescreencoords) for node in selectednodes: # Clip cutting plane to node's bounding box clippedpolygon = clippolygontonode(cuttingplane, node) if not clippedpolygon: continue # Get blend ratios for clipped polygon vertices vertexratios = [] for vertex in clippedpolygon.vertices: # Interpolate ratio from node edges/corners to vertex position ratio = interpolateratiofromnode(node, vertex) vertexratios.append(ratio) # Render Low Tile Image lowimage = renderpolygon(clippedpolygon, node.lowtile, vertexratios) # Render High Tile Image highratios = [1.0 - r for r in vertexratios] highimage = renderpolygon(clippedpolygon, node.hightile, highratios) # Add to final image finalimage += lowimage + highimage return finalimage def renderpolygon(polygon, texture, ratios): """ Renders a polygon with texture multiplied by vertex ratios. Hardware interpolation handles the per-pixel multiplication. """ # Pseudocode representing the GPU operation described in # 1. Set texture to 'texture' # 2. For each vertex v in polygon: # v.color = (ratios[v.index], ratios[v.index], ratios[v.index]) # 3. Draw polygon # 4. Return resulting image buffer pass Time Complexity: Rendering time is significantly reduced compared to fixed-resolution rendering. On an SGI Onyx2 with a 195MHz R10K processor, rendering the 'Visible Female' data set (256^3 RGB) reduced rendering time from 12.0 seconds (fixed resolution) to 0.37 seconds (multiresolution). Memory/Transfer Complexity: The method reduces the amount of data accessed and transmitted. For the 'Visible Female' data set, bytes transmitted were reduced from 56MB to 7MB. The number of rendered nodes dropped from 443 (fixed) to 50 (multiresolution). Strengths: Allows adaptive rendering where quality is a tunable parameter based on visual importance. Reduces artifacts introduced by resolution changes through blending. Suitable for data mining or visual steering applications where the point-of-interest is unknown or changes frequently. Limitations: Requires balancing the octree to ensure adjacent nodes differ by at most one level, adding preprocessing complexity. If power-of-two tile sizes are required, the high tile size calculation incurs memory overhead. Blending is limited to adjacent nodes differing by exactly one resolution level; larger gaps cannot be blended directly. When to use: When rendering large volumetric datasets interactively, especially when the viewer's focus or point-of-interest varies, or when bandwidth/memory is constrained. When not to use: When uniform high resolution is required across the entire volume, or when the hardware does not support the required texture blending operations. Origin: The method was presented by researchers from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and the University of California, Davis. Paper: "Multiresolution Techniques for Interactive Texture-Based Rendering of Arbitrarily Oriented Cutting Planes". History: The technique was developed to address the limitations of prior algorithms that assumed data was "uniformly complex" or "uniformly important". It was designed for immersive environments where data closer to the viewer has more visual importance. Applications: Data mining, visual steering, and progressive visualization where data sets are too large for a single system and portions are distributed across a network. name: Distance-Based Octree LOD Management
head: Chunk Splitting and Merging
body: Distance-Based Octree LOD Management optimizes rendering load by dynamically subdividing or merging octree chunks based on the camera's distance to the chunk center. It splits chunks into eight children when the camera is close and merges them back when the camera is far, serving as the core subdivision logic for Camera-Driven Octree Subdivision. Unlike Octree Texture Subdivision, which manages LOD via texture mipmaps, this method explicitly creates and destroys geometric child nodes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera position, chunk center position, chunk edge size, current LOD level, and a global semaphore state. Output: Creation of 8 child chunks (splitting) or restoration of the parent chunk (merging). Data Structures: Chunk: Contains edgeSize (float), lodLevel (int), isSplitting (bool), isRestoringParent (bool), mesh (reference), and childrenReady (int, count of active children). DCManager: Contains greenLight (bool semaphore), maxLodLevel (int), and diagonal (float, derived from edge size). Child Naming: Suffixes |DBR, |DBL, |DTR, |DTL, |UBR, |UBL, |UTR, |UTL are appended to chunk names to identify orientation (Down/Up, Back/Front, Right/Left). Formulas: Diagonal: The face diagonal length of the chunk, used as the primary distance threshold. \text{diagonal} = \sqrt{2 \cdot (\text{edgeSize}^2)} Parameters: maxLodLevel: The maximum depth of subdivision allowed. Split Threshold: distance < diagonal Merge Threshold: distance > diagonal 3.0 Steps: 1. Calculate Distance: Compute the Euclidean distance from the camera position to the chunk center. 2. Evaluate Split Condition: If distance < diagonal AND lodLevel < maxLodLevel AND childrenReady < 8 AND !isSplitting AND !isRestoringParent AND mesh != null: Check global semaphore DCManager.greenLight. If false, abort. Set DCManager.greenLight = false. Set isSplitting = true. Call splitCube(). 3. Evaluate Merge Condition: If lodLevel > 0 AND distance > diagonal 3.0 AND mesh != null AND !parent.isRestoringParent: If the chunk name ends with |DBR (indicating it is a specific child type requiring parent restoration): Set parent.isRestoringParent = true. Call restoreParentCube(). 4. Split Cube (splitCube): Calculate delta = edgeSize / 4. Create 8 child chunks. Position each child at the parent's position offset by ±delta in x, y, and z axes. Assign appropriate suffixes (|DBR, etc.) to child names. Increment childrenReady on the parent. 5. Restore Parent Cube (restoreParentCube): Calculate delta = edgeSize / 2. Create the parent cube at transform.position + delta with size edgeSize 2 and lodLevel - 1. Clear edgeDictionary and edgeDictionaryOrphans on the parent. Reset isRestoringParent to false. 1 restoredchunk = createchunk( position=newpos, size=newsize, lodlevel=newlod, name=parentchunk.name, manager=parentchunk.manager) # Clear edge data structures restoredchunk.edgedictionary.clear() restoredchunk.edgedictionaryorphans.clear() parentchunk.isrestoringparent = False Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Race Conditions: Splitting and merging are blocked by isSplitting and isRestoringParent flags to prevent concurrent modification. Serialization: A global DCManager.greenLight semaphore serializes split operations across all chunks to prevent resource contention. Merge Trigger: Merging is only triggered by chunks ending in |DBR, implying a specific traversal or ownership model for parent restoration. Time Complexity: Splitting and merging are O(1) relative to the chunk count, but involve O(1) object creation/destruction. The global semaphore introduces potential contention under high concurrency. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of visible chunks. Splitting increases memory by 8x for the affected region; merging decreases it. Strengths: Simple distance-based heuristic; effective for reducing draw calls in distant areas. Limitations: The global semaphore can bottleneck performance in highly parallel scenes. The merge condition is rigid (diagonal 3.0) and may cause popping if not smoothed. When to use: Suitable for static or slowly changing scenes where camera distance is the primary LOD factor. When not to use: High-frequency camera movement may cause excessive split/merge churn.
