name: Octree Path Computation
body: Octree Path Computation determines the sequence of child nodes traversed by a ray or frustum as it descends from the root of an octree to a target node. It identifies spatial subdivisions without redundant geometric intersection tests at every level. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal by focusing on the explicit encoding and decoding of the traversal sequence for neighbor finding, path caching, or coordinate reconstruction. Inputs: Target grid coordinates (rx, ry, rz) or ray parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}). Octree metadata: maximum depth D, current level lv, and bounding box. Optional: Pre-computed path from root to a reference node (e.g., u,v-minimal ray). Outputs: A path vector or integer representing the sequence of octant indices from root to leaf. Voxel coordinates (i, j, k) at a specific level. Path Vector: A list or array of integers, where each element pl \in \{0, \dots, 7\} represents the octant index at level l. Bit-Path Integer: A single integer where 3 bits are allocated per level, totaling 3 \times D bits. Voxel Coordinates: 3D integer vector (i, j, k) representing the position within the voxel grid at level lv. 1. Path Encoding (Forward Computation): To compute the path for a point or ray: a. Initialize an empty path vector P and a scale variable s = 2^{D-1}. b. For each depth level l from 0 to D-1: i. Determine the octant bits by comparing the current grid coordinates (rx, ry, rz) against the scale s. ii. Calculate the octant index k using the child selection formula: k = 4 \cdot \mathbb{I}(rx \ge s) + 2 \cdot \mathbb{I}(ry \ge s) + 1 \cdot \mathbb{I}(rz \ge s). iii. Subtract s from the coordinate if the bit is set: rx \leftarrow rx - s \cdot \mathbb{I}(rx \ge s), ry \leftarrow ry - s \cdot \mathbb{I}(ry \ge s), rz \leftarrow rz - s \cdot \mathbb{I}(rz \ge s). iv. Append k to P. v. Right-shift the scale: s \leftarrow s / 2. 2. Path Decoding (Coordinate Reconstruction): To reconstruct voxel coordinates from a stored path integer or vector: a. Let lv be the target level and MAX\NUM\LEVELS be the maximum depth. b. Shift the octpath right by 3 \times (MAX\NUM\LEVELS - lv) bits to remove irrelevant higher-level bits. c. Iterate l from 0 to lv-1: i. Extract the lowest 3 bits of the current path to get the octant index. ii. Decode the octant into local coordinates (dx, dy, dz) using bit masks: dx = (idx \gg 2) \& 1, dy = (idx \gg 1) \& 1, dz = idx \& 1. iii. Accumulate the global coordinates: i = (i \ll 1) + dx, j = (j \ll 1) + dy, k = (k \ll 1) + dz. iv. Shift the path right by 3 bits. Voxel Size: The physical size of a voxel at level lv is computed as: s = \text{scene\extent} \times 2^{-lv}. MAX\NUM\LEVELS: Maximum depth of the octree, typically 16. D: The depth of the current node or target leaf. Not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeoctreepath(rx, ry, rz, maxdepth): """ Computes the octree path for a given grid coordinate. rx, ry, rz: Integer grid coordinates. maxdepth: Maximum depth of the octree. Returns: List of octant indices [k0, k1,..., k{maxdepth-1}] """ path = [] scale = 1 << (maxdepth - 1) # 2^(maxdepth - 1) for in range(maxdepth): k = 0 if rx >= scale: k += 4 rx -= scale if ry >= scale: k += 2 ry -= scale if rz >= scale: k += 1 rz -= scale path.append(k) scale >>= 1 # Right shift by 1 return path def decodevoxelfrompath(pathint, lv, maxnumlevels=16): """ Decodes voxel coordinates from a bit-packed path integer. pathint: Integer containing the path bits. lv: Target level to decode to. maxnumlevels: Maximum depth of the octree. Returns: Tuple (i, j, k) """ shift = 3 (maxnumlevels - lv) pathint >>= shift i, j, k = 0, 0, 0 for in range(lv): idx = pathint & 0x7 pathint >>= 3 dx = (idx >> 2) & 1 dy = (idx >> 1) & 1 dz = idx & 1 i = (i << 1) + dx j = (j << 1) + dy k = (k << 1) + dz return (i, j, k) An algorithm to find the adjacent cell a sharing a specific face f with a given cell c in a generalized octree, handling cases where the neighbor might be at a different subdivision level. This method performs 3D pathfinding on a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) by combining A search with Lazy Theta logic, where line-of-sight (LOS) checks are performed optimistically during neighbor expansion to allow straight-line shortcuts, with a recovery step if LOS fails. It differs from standard A on octrees by reducing path length and node visits through direct parent-to-current-node connections when possible, and differs from pure ray-casting pathfinding by caching collision results to avoid expensive per-step ray-marching. It builds on Octree Path Computation and operates alongside Octree Neighbor Search and Access Path Predictor. The Access Path Predictor (APP) is a knowledge-based out-of-core data management algorithm designed to predict and pre-cache the next octree node required for sampling. It solves the problem of inefficient random access patterns in large datasets by learning local access traffic, specifically the frequent appearance of predecessor-current-successor node sequences. Unlike the Ray Driven Predictor (RDP), which assumes spatial continuity along a ray, APP does not require nodes to be on the same line or in the same neighborhood, allowing it to accommodate diverse rendering features such as refraction and space leaping. A method to map implicit macrocell coordinates to the deepest corresponding octree child node to perform isovalue culling using the parent's min/max pair. 1. Store the path from the octree root to the current node along the u,v-minimal ray of the frustum to avoid costly lookups. 2. Use neighbor-finding to traverse inexpensively from one node to the next. 3. Hierarchically recurse from a parent node to a child with a single lookup step in the octree. 1. Shift the octpath right by 3 \times (MAX\NUM\LEVELS - lv) to remove irrelevant higher-level bits. 2. Iterate l from 0 to lv-1: extract the lowest 3 bits of the current path, decode them into i, j, k coordinates using bit masks and shifts, then shift the path right by 3 bits. Voxel size at level lv is computed as: s = \text{scene\extent} \times 2^{-lv}. MAX\NUM\LEVELS = 16, the maximum depth of the octree used for bit shifting and coordinate scaling. An octree constructed over a set of rays (point + direction = 5D object) to precompute visibility, where each node represents a beam in 3D. 1. Construct a bijective mapping between directions and the direction cube S^2 \times D:= [-1, +1]^2 \times \{\pm x, \pm y, \pm z\}. 2. Define the universe of rays R = U \times D where U = [0, 1]^3. 3. Associate an object with an octree node if the object intersects the beam represented by that node. 4. Start with root U \times [-1, +1]^2 and the set of all objects. 5. Subdivide a node into 32 children if too many objects are associated with it or the cell is too large. Associate objects with one or more children. 6. To test a ray: map the ray to a 5D point, find the leaf in the 5D octree, and intersect the ray with its associated objects. Not given in the sources. name: Octree Neighbor Search
head: Get Neighbour Algorithm
body: An algorithm to find the adjacent cell a sharing a specific face f with a given cell c in a generalized octree, handling cases where the neighbor might be at a different subdivision level. Inputs: A cell c and a face f for which the neighbor is sought. Outputs: The adjacent cell a sharing face f with c, or null if no valid neighbor exists. Data Structures: Cell Representation: Defined by spatial coordinates and a Morton code (Z-order curve). Level: The subdivision depth of the cell. Offset: An integer variable tracking the search depth relative to the cell's level. Steps: 1. Determine the level of cell c, denoted as Lc. 2. Identify the coincident face f' corresponding to the input face f. 3. Initialize an offset variable k = 1. 4. Loop while k \le Lc: a. Compute the candidate neighbor using GetAdjacentCellByFace(c, f, k). b. Check if the candidate cell a exists in the octree structure. c. If a exists: i. Retrieve the geometric limit of cell c in the direction of face f, denoted Limitc. ii. Retrieve the geometric limit of cell a in the direction of the coincident face f', denoted Limita. iii. If Limitc == Limita, the cells share the exact same boundary plane. Return a. iv. Else, the limits do not match. Increment k by 1 and continue the loop. d. If a does not exist, increment k by 1 and continue the loop. 5. If the loop completes without returning a cell, no valid neighbor exists. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def GetNeighbor(c, f, storage): level = c.level coincidentFace = (f + 3) % 6 # Opposite face mapping offset = 1 while offset <= level: candidatemorton = GetAdjacentCellByFace(c, f, offset, storage) if candidatemorton is not None: a = storage.get(candidatemorton) if a is not None: cellLimitC = GetCellLimitByFace(c, f) cellLimitA = GetCellLimitByFace(a, coincidentFace) if cellLimitC == cellLimitA: return a offset += 1 return None def GetAdjacentCellByFace(cell, face, offset, storage): # Obtain spatial coordinates, add offset in direction, convert to Morton code coords = list(cell.coords) if face == 0: coords[0] += offset elif face == 1: coords[0] -= offset elif face == 2: coords[1] += offset elif face == 3: coords[1] -= offset elif face == 4: coords[2] += offset elif face == 5: coords[2] -= offset morton = coordstomorton(coords) # If no neighbouring cell exists, look at parent by shifting 3 LSBs if morton not in storage: morton = cell.morton >> 3 return morton def GetCellLimitByFace(cell, face): # Return boundary coordinate along face axis if face < 2: return cell.coords[0] if face < 4: return cell.coords[1] return cell.coords[2] def coordstomorton(coords): # Standard Morton/Z-order encoding x, y, z = coords return (x << 2) | (y << 1) | z Parameters: offset: Starts at 1. The maximum value is bounded by the depth of the octree, as anisotropic subdivision usually occurs at the deepest levels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Anisotropic Subdivision: The algorithm is designed for generalized octrees where cells may have different sizes. The offset loop handles cases where the neighbor is at a different subdivision level. Precision: Geometric limit comparison must use exact equality. Floating-point errors in limit calculation could cause false negatives. Boundary Conditions: If the cell is on the boundary of the domain, Exists will return false for external neighbors, and the loop will terminate correctly. Indirect Neighbor Search computes the set of neighbors for the three faces of a cell c that are not covered by direct neighbors. These neighbors are separated from c by splitting planes located deeper in the octree hierarchy. While Direct Neighbor Search handles the immediate vicinity resulting from the last three splitting steps, Indirect Neighbor Search handles the remaining faces by traversing the tree structure to find cells or planes on the opposite side of bounding splitting planes. It is the second phase of the complete neighborhood computation in generalized octrees. Generates fragments corresponding to rays intersecting the cell. This approach is used for efficient classification of cells in volume rendering contexts, where sub-volumes are projected onto the image plane and fragments are generated for rays intersecting the cell. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles generalized (anisotropic) octrees efficiently without requiring regular grid structures. Limitations: Performance degrades if the octree has very deep levels and neighbors are sparse, requiring many offset increments. The algorithm was introduced by Ricardo Uribe Lobello, Florence Denis, and Florent Dupont in their work on adaptive surface extraction from anisotropic volumetric data using generalized octrees. It addresses the need for efficient neighbor access in non-uniform octrees where standard bitwise neighbor calculations fail due to varying cell sizes. name: Indirect Neighbor Search
body: Indirect Neighbor Search computes the set of neighbors for the three faces of a cell c that are not covered by direct neighbors. These neighbors are separated from c by splitting planes located deeper in the octree hierarchy. While Direct Neighbor Search handles the immediate vicinity resulting from the last three splitting steps, Indirect Neighbor Search handles the remaining faces by traversing the tree structure to find cells or planes on the opposite side of bounding splitting planes. It is the second phase of the complete neighborhood computation in generalized octrees. Inputs: Cell index bd (binary representation). The set of direct neighbors N{direct}(c) computed in the previous step. Cell coordinates (x, y, z) for geometric tests. Outputs: The set of indirect neighbors N{indirect}(c). The complete neighborhood N(c) = N{direct}(c) \cup N{indirect}(c). Data Structures: Cell index bd: A binary integer where every third bit corresponds to a dimension (x0, x1, x2). The least significant bits correspond to the root level, and higher bits to deeper levels. N(c): A set of indices (integers) representing splitting planes and leaf cells. Algorithm Steps: 1. Identify Bounding Splitting Planes: For each dimension d \in \{0, 1, 2\}, determine the splitting plane that bounds cell c on the face not covered by direct neighbors. Extract the bits of bd corresponding to dimension d by considering every third bit starting from the least significant bit (LSB) for that dimension. Scan these bits from LSB to MSB (root to leaf). Find the first bit swap (transition from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0) in this sequence. If the first swap occurs at subsequence index j (where j=0 is the LSB), the index of the bounding splitting plane is b{dj} = bd \gg (3j) (right shift by 3j). If no bit swap occurs in a dimension, the cell lies entirely on one side of all division planes in that dimension relative to the root, and there is no bounding plane in that direction for indirect neighbors. 2. Recursive Search for Indirect Neighbors: For each identified bounding plane p found in Step 1: Perform a recursive search in the subtree starting from p to find cells or planes on the opposite side of p relative to c. The recursion logic for a currentnode (which is a splitting plane) is as follows: 1. If currentnode splits in the same dimension as p: Continue with the subtree of currentnode that is adjacent to c (the side containing c). 2. Else (if currentnode splits in a different dimension): Check if currentnode has a common point with c. This check requires comparing the coordinates of c against the pivot value of the splitting plane. If they have a common point: Add currentnode to N(c). Continue with both subtrees of currentnode. If they do not have a common point: Continue with the subtree of currentnode that is adjacent to c. The recursion stops when leaf nodes (cells) are reached. These leaf cells are added to N(c). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findindirectneighbors(cellindex, cellcoords, directneighbors): """ Computes indirect neighbors for cell c with binary index b. Assumes directneighbors N(c) is already computed. """ indirectneighbors = set() # Dimensions are interleaved in Morton code: bits 0,3,6... for dim 0; 1,4,7... for dim 1; 2,5,8... for dim 2 for dim in range(3): # Extract bits for this dimension bits = [] temp = cellindex while temp > 0: bits.append((temp >> dim) & 1) temp >>= 3 # Scan from LSB (index 0) to MSB to find first swap firstswapidx = -1 for k in range(1, len(bits)): if bits[k] != bits[k-1]: firstswapidx = k break if firstswapidx != -1: # The plane index is the cell index right-shifted by 3j planeindex = cellindex >> (3 firstswapidx) # Step 2: Recursive search searchsubtree(planeindex, cellindex, cellcoords, indirectneighbors, dim) return indirectneighbors def searchsubtree(currentplane, cellindex, cellcoords, neighborset, dimp): """ Recursive search for indirect neighbors. currentplane: index of a splitting plane. cellindex: binary index of the target cell c. cellcoords: (x, y, z) coordinates of c. neighborset: set to add found neighbors to. dimp: split dimension of the initial bounding plane p. """ # Leaf detection: check tree-specific flag or mask indicating a leaf node if isleaf(currentplane): neighborset.add(currentplane) return # Determine split dimension of currentplane (Morton code: dim 0 at bit 0, dim 1 at bit 1, dim 2 at bit 2) dimcurrent = currentplane & 3 if dimcurrent == dimp: # Continue with subtree next to c nextnode = getchildtowardsc(currentplane, cellcoords) if nextnode is not None: searchsubtree(nextnode, cellindex, cellcoords, neighborset, dimp) else: # Different dimension: check if current plane has a common point with c if hascommonpoint(currentplane, cellcoords): neighborset.add(currentplane) # Continue with both subtrees leftchild = currentplane << 1 rightchild = (currentplane << 1) | 1 searchsubtree(leftchild, cellindex, cellcoords, neighborset, dimp) searchsubtree(rightchild, cellindex, cellcoords, neighborset, dimp) else: # Continue with subtree next to c nextnode = getchildtowardsc(currentplane, cellcoords) if nextnode is not None: searchsubtree(nextnode, cellindex, cellcoords, neighborset, dimp) def getchildtowardsc(nodeindex, cellcoords): """ Returns the child node of 'nodeindex' that is on the same side as cell c. Uses coordinate comparison as specified by the source. """ dim = nodeindex & 3 coord = cellcoords[dim] # Retrieve pivot value for the splitting plane; implementation depends on tree storage pivot = getpivot(nodeindex) if coord < pivot: return nodeindex << 1 else: return (nodeindex << 1) | 1 def hascommonpoint(planeindex, cellcoords): """ Checks if the cell c has a common point with the splitting plane. This test uses the coordinates of c when comparing it to the pivot value of the splitting plane. """ dim = planeindex & 3 coord = cellcoords[dim] pivot = getpivot(planeindex) # Exact boundary check return abs(coord - pivot) < 1e-9 Parameters: None explicitly defined. The algorithm is deterministic based on the tree structure. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Bit Swap: If no bit swap is found in a dimension during Step 1, there is no bounding plane in that direction, and no indirect neighbors are searched for that face. Coordinate Dependency: Only the test for whether a plane has a common point with c uses the coordinates of c. All other operations (bit scanning, XOR, recursion path selection) use the binary representation of indices for speed. Worst Case Complexity: The worst-case number of indirect neighbors is O(\sqrt[3]{n^2}), where n is the number of cells. This occurs only for a small number of cells. Average Case: In 3D, the average case has up to 9 neighbors per face, leading to 27 indirect neighbors per cell. Computes the set of direct neighbors N(c) for a cell c with index bd. Direct neighbors include splitting planes and cells resulting from the last three splitting steps. It identifies direct splitting planes at indices b{d1}, b{d2}, b{d3} (right shifts by 1, 2, 3 bits) and adjacent cells using bitwise XOR with 1d, 10d, 100d. It also checks four additional splitting planes beyond the direct ones using specific criteria to complete the neighborhood. This method covers half of the faces of c and includes at least three and at most seven cells plus the respective splitting planes in between. Time Complexity: The search performance is similar to nearest-neighbor search in kd-trees due to the heavy use of binary operations. The worst-case complexity for indirect neighbors is O(\sqrt[3]{n^2}). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fast execution due to bitwise operations; avoids coordinate comparisons except for the final geometric test. Limitations: Worst-case complexity can be high for specific cell configurations, though rare. When to use: When a complete neighborhood of a cell in a generalized octree is required for isosurface extraction or other volume rendering techniques. The method was introduced by P. Rosenthal and L. Linsen in their 2006 paper "Direct Isosurface Extraction from Scattered Volume Data". It is part of a two-step process for computing the neighborhood of a cell in a generalized octree, which is used for direct isosurface extraction from scattered volume data. name: SVO Pathfinder with Lazy Theta* and LOS Recovery
head: Lazy Theta* Pathfinding on SVO
body: This method performs 3D pathfinding on a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) by combining A search with Lazy Theta logic, where line-of-sight (LOS) checks are performed optimistically during neighbor expansion to allow straight-line shortcuts, with a recovery step if LOS fails. It differs from standard A on octrees by reducing path length and node visits through direct parent-to-current-node connections when possible, and differs from pure ray-casting pathfinding by caching collision results to avoid expensive per-step ray-marching. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Start and End world positions, Agent Radius, SVO structure (node array, depth, traversal data). Output: Sequence of nodes forming the path, or failure if no path exists. Data Structures: Node Array: Flat array of SVO nodes. Collision Test Cache: Stores result per node: 0 (no test performed), -1 (collision detected), +1 (no collision). Cost Array: Stores cumulative cost g(n) for each node index. Parent Array: Stores parent node index for each node. Open Array: Priority queue of nodes to expand, ordered by f(n) = g(n) + h(n). Closed Array: Boolean flag array indicating if a node has been expanded. InlineAllocator: Used for neighbor collection; behaves like a fixed allocator but switches to heap allocation if the set capacity is exceeded. Parameters: AgentRadius: Radius of the agent. Clamped to prevent invalid access. MaxDepth: Maximum depth of the SVO. Typical values: 6 or 8. AxisBit: Bit mask for neighbor calculation. Points to 1 when Side is negative, because when the current node faces the positive direction, the neighboring node is adjacent in the negative direction. Steps: 1. Initialize and Validate: Clamp AgentRadius. Get nodes at Start and End positions by accessing the node Array. Verify traversability using cached collision test results. If Start or End nodes are not traversable (result \neq +1), return failure. If Start and End are the same node, return immediately. 2. Neighbor Collection: Iterate from 0 to 7 to collect neighbor indices based on target axis (0 or 1). Traverse the tree using DFS to collect all leaf nodes. Keep only passable nodes (collision test result +1). 3. Pathfinding (Lazy Theta): Initialize Cost, Parent, Open, and Closed arrays. While Open is not empty, pop node u with lowest f(u). If u is End, reconstruct path and return. For each neighbor v, calculate tentative g(v). Perform LOS check between parent of u (or u if u is Start) and v. If LOS is clear, set parent of v to parent of u (or u) and update g(v) using direct distance. Else, set parent of v to u and update g(v) using distance from u to v. 4. LOS Method: Perform a simple collision test between two points. Can be implemented with ray-marching using SVO, but simple collision test is used for lower code complexity with negligible performance loss. Pitfalls: Agent Radius vs Node Size: Simple comparison of octree node size with AgentRadius is insufficient. Example: AgentRadius 700, octree alley sizes 200, 400, 200. It cannot pass through the 400-sized node despite the gap, requiring explicit collision testing. Collision Test Cache: Running a collision test every time is expensive. Only run it when AgentRadius is larger than the node size, and cache the result for each node. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import heapq import math def findpath(svonodes, startpos, endpos, agentradius, maxdepth): # 1. Initialize and Validate agentradius = max(0.0, agentradius) # Clamp to non-negative startidx = getnodeatposition(svonodes, startpos, maxdepth) endidx = getnodeatposition(svonodes, endpos, maxdepth) if startidx is None or endidx is None: return None if svonodes[startidx].collisioncache != 1 or svonodes[endidx].collisioncache != 1: return None if startidx == endidx: return [startidx] numnodes = len(svonodes) cost = [float('inf')] numnodes parent = [-1] numnodes closed = [False] numnodes openset = [] # (fscore, nodeidx) cost[startidx] = 0.0 heapq.heappush(openset, (heuristic(startpos, endpos), startidx)) while openset: fu, u = heapq.heappop(openset) if u == endidx: return reconstructpath(parent, u) if closed[u]: continue closed[u] = True # 2. Neighbor Collection neighbors = collectneighbors(svonodes, u, agentradius, maxdepth) for v in neighbors: if closed[v] or svonodes[v].collisioncache != 1: continue tentativeg = cost[u] + distance(svonodes[u].pos, svonodes[v].pos) # 3. Pathfinding (Lazy Theta) parentu = parent[u] if parent[u] != -1 else u if lineofsight(svonodes, parentu, v): newparent = parentu newg = cost[parentu] + distance(svonodes[parentu].pos, svonodes[v].pos) else: newparent = u newg = tentativeg if newg < cost[v]: cost[v] = newg parent[v] = newparent heapq.heappush(openset, (newg + heuristic(svonodes[v].pos, endpos), v)) return None def getnodeatposition(nodes, pos, maxdepth): # Accesses the node Array to find the leaf containing pos for i, node in enumerate(nodes): if node.containspoint(pos): return i return None def collectneighbors(nodes, nodeidx, agentradius, maxdepth): # Uses InlineAllocator behavior: starts fixed, switches to heap if exceeded neighbors = [] for i in range(8): neighboridx = calculateneighborindex(nodeidx, i) if neighboridx is not None and neighboridx < len(nodes): leaves = traversetree(nodes, neighboridx) for leaf in leaves: if nodes[leaf].collisioncache == 1: neighbors.append(leaf) return neighbors def calculateneighborindex(nodeidx, i): # AxisBit points to 1 when Side is negative return nodeidx + (1 << i) def traversetree(nodes, startidx): # DFS to collect all leaf nodes stack = [startidx] leaves = [] while stack: curr = stack.pop() if nodes[curr].isleaf: leaves.append(curr) else: stack.extend(nodes[curr].children) return leaves def lineofsight(nodes, startidx, endidx): # Perform a simple collision test between two points # Exact implementation details are not provided in the sources return True def heuristic(posa, posb): return math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(posa, posb))) def distance(posa, posb): return math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(posa, posb))) def reconstructpath(parent, endidx): path = [] curr = endidx while curr != -1: path.append(curr) curr = parent[curr] return path[::-1] Time Complexity: Depends on SVO depth and branching factor. At MaxDepth 6, BuildSVO takes 700 microseconds, FindPath takes 300 microseconds. At MaxDepth 8, BuildSVO takes 14 milliseconds, FindPath takes 4 milliseconds. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of nodes in the SVO. Performance: Parallelization improves performance for simple repetitive tasks like BuildSVO. At MaxDepth 6, ParallelFor took 0.7ms, while a regular loop took 1.9ms. Strengths: Reduces path length and node visits through LOS checks. Caching collision results avoids expensive per-step ray-marching. Limitations: Code complexity increases with parallelization. Simple collision test may not be optimal for all scenarios. This method was developed for Unreal Engine 5 (UE5) as a simple SVO pathfinder for 3D pathfinding. It was presented in a tutorial video by an unofficial source. The method leverages the SVO structure for efficient spatial queries and combines A with Lazy Theta for optimal pathfinding. name: Access Path Predictor
head: APP
body: The Access Path Predictor (APP) is a knowledge-based out-of-core data management algorithm designed to predict and pre-cache the next octree node required for sampling. It solves the problem of inefficient random access patterns in large datasets by learning local access traffic, specifically the frequent appearance of predecessor-current-successor node sequences. Unlike the Ray Driven Predictor (RDP), which assumes spatial continuity along a ray, APP does not require nodes to be on the same line or in the same neighborhood, allowing it to accommodate diverse rendering features such as refraction and space leaping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A new sample point s; two recent octree nodes N{last} (the node accessed before N{cur}) and N{cur} (the node currently being accessed). Output: The predicted next node N{new} and cache precaching instructions. Data Structures: Octree Node Metadata: Each octree node stores four pairs of predecessor-successor records, where each record consists of a predecessor node identifier (N{p,i}) and a successor node identifier (N{s,i}). Storage Constraint: Knowledge acquisition and storage are limited to leaf nodes only, which reduces computational costs and utilizes the eight unused child addresses in each leaf node. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set N{new} \leftarrow \text{NULL}. 2. Check Current Node: If s is in N{cur}, set N{new} \leftarrow N{cur} and terminate prediction. 3. Phase I: Access Path Prediction: If N{new} is NULL, iterate through each recorded predecessor N{p,i} of N{cur}. If N{last} == N{p,i} and s is in N{p,i}, set N{new} \leftarrow N{p,i}. 4. Phase II: Historical Successor Prediction: If N{new} is NULL, iterate through each recorded successor N{s,i} of N{cur}. If s is in N{s,i}, set N{new} \leftarrow N{s,i} and return N{new}. 5. Phase III: Fallback Navigation: If N{new} is NULL, set N{new} \leftarrow \text{OctreeNavigation}(N{cur}, s). 6. Update Knowledge: Replace the oldest (N{p,i}, N{s,i}) pair in N{cur} with (N{last}, N{new}). 7. Precaching: If N{cur} is a recorded predecessor of N{new}, set N{next} to the corresponding successor in N{new} and precache N{next} with high priority. Otherwise, precache all four successors in N{new} with low priority. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def AccessPathPredictor(s, Nlast, Ncur): """Predicts the next octree node to access based on learned access patterns.""" Nnew = None # Step 2: Check if sample point is already in the current node if contains(Ncur, s): Nnew = Ncur return Nnew # Step 3: Phase I - Prediction using Access Path for i in range(4): pred = Ncur.predecessors[i] if pred is not None and Nlast == pred and contains(pred, s): Nnew = pred break # Step 4: Phase II - Prediction using Historical Successors if Nnew is None: for i in range(4): succ = Ncur.successors[i] if succ is not None and contains(succ, s): Nnew = succ return Nnew # Step 5: Phase III - Fallback to standard octree navigation if Nnew is None: Nnew = OctreeNavigation(Ncur, s) # Step 6: Update knowledge in Ncur (shift oldest pair out, insert new pair) for i in range(3): Ncur.predecessors[i] = Ncur.predecessors[i+1] Ncur.successors[i] = Ncur.successors[i+1] Ncur.predecessors[3] = Nlast Ncur.successors[3] = Nnew # Step 7: Precaching if Ncur in Nnew.predecessors: idx = Nnew.predecessors.index(Ncur) Nnext = Nnew.successors[idx] # Instruct cache manager to load Nnext with high priority else: for child in Nnew.children: # Instruct cache manager to load child with low priority return Nnew def contains(node, point): """Returns True if point is within the spatial bounds of the node.""" return all(node.min[k] <= point[k] < node.max[k] for k in range(3)) def OctreeNavigation(currentnode, targetpoint): """Standard octree traversal to find the leaf node containing targetpoint.""" if currentnode.isleaf(): return currentnode childindex = getchildindex(currentnode, targetpoint) if currentnode.children[childindex] is not None: return OctreeNavigation(currentnode.children[childindex], targetpoint) return currentnode def getchildindex(node, point): """Determines the index (0-7) of the child containing the point.""" mid = node.center index = 0 if point.x >= mid.x: index |= 1 if point.y >= mid.y: index |= 2 if point.z >= mid.z: index |= 4 return index Parameters: History Depth: Each node stores four predecessor-successor pairs. Storage Scope: Leaf nodes only. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Leaf Node Limitation: Knowledge is restricted to leaf nodes to reduce computational costs and utilize the eight unused child addresses in each leaf node. A knowledge-based algorithm that removes the assumption of specific predecessor-current-successor patterns, relying entirely on historic records of nodes required immediately after a visit. It utilizes the eight unused child addresses in each leaf node to store up to eight potential successors. When visiting a node, it pre-caches all known potential successors. If more than eight successors are identified, the oldest is replaced. A key pitfall is that pre-caching up to eight nodes to load one may generate excessive disk traffic. A prediction-based algorithm closely coupled with a discrete ray-tracing engine. It assumes that octree nodes following the ray and along its path will likely be accessed subsequently. Given a ray and current sampling position sc, it determines a predicted sampling point sp on the ray just outside the current octree node. It then navigates the octree to reach the node containing sp, instructing the lower layer to prefetch any nodes not already in the cache during this navigation. This process repeats for each sampling point. Time Complexity: Prediction phases run in O(1) time relative to the fixed history size of four pairs. Octree navigation complexity is not given in the sources. Memory Overhead: Four predecessor-successor pairs per leaf node. Performance: Effective for applications with regular access patterns such as ray tracing, marching cubes, and feature tracking. Limitations: Less effective for highly irregular or random access patterns where historical patterns do not repeat. Comparison: Unlike RDP, APP does not assume spatial continuity, making it more robust for refraction and space leaping. Unlike HAP, APP uses specific path patterns rather than immediate successors, potentially reducing unnecessary pre-caching. The Access Path Predictor was introduced by D. Chisnall, M. Chen, and C. Hansen in 2006 as part of their work on knowledge-based out-of-core algorithms for data management in visualization. It is part of a suite of predictors including the Ray Driven Predictor and History-based Access Predictor, designed to work within a discrete ray-tracing engine. name: Rational Ray Parameterization for Octree Traversal
head: Integer Ray Tracing, Rational Arithmetic Ray Tracing
body: Rational Ray Parameterization for Octree Traversal is a method for tracing rays through an octree using exact rational arithmetic to avoid floating-point precision errors during cell boundary crossing and neighbor finding. It solves the problem of determining the next cell intersected by a ray when the ray parameters are not integers, which typically occurs when the viewplane is in an arbitrary position in space. Unlike sibling methods that rely on floating-point comparisons or pre-computed structures, this method guarantees robustness by representing ray parameters as rational numbers (numerator/denominator pairs) and using integer arithmetic for all comparisons and boundary tests. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray defined by viewpoint B = (bx, by, bz) with integer coordinates, and direction coefficients mx, my, mz which are rational numbers. Octree root pointer. Scene width W{scene} (assumed power of 2). Output: Sequence of octree nodes visited by the ray, or intersection points with objects within those nodes. Data Structures: Rational Number: Represented as a pair (num, den) where den > 0. Comparisons are performed via cross-multiplication: \frac{a}{b} < \frac{c}{d} \iff a \cdot d < c \cdot b. Cell Record: Contains 6 fields: TIN: Rational number, entry parameter t. TOUT: Rational number, exit parameter t. SIZ: Integer, cell width W. PTR: Pointer to the octree node. CORNER: Array of 3 integers, coordinates of the furthest corner from the origin (cx, cy, cz). DIRECT: Enum/Direction code for the next cell relative to the current one (e.g., 'L', 'R', 'U', 'D', 'F', 'B', or combinations like 'LUB'). Algorithm Steps: 1. Rational Parameterization: Convert the ray direction coefficients mx, my, mz to integers by finding the lowest common denominator c of the three rational coefficients. Define a new parameter t' = t/c. The parametric equations become: x = m'x \cdot t' + bx y = m'y \cdot t' + by z = m'z \cdot t' + bz where m'x, m'y, m'z are integers (numerators) and bx, by, bz are integers (viewpoint coordinates). In the remainder of the algorithm, we use mi and t to refer to these integer numerators and the scaled parameter t' respectively. 2. Initial Entry Point (FIRSTPOINT): Determine the entry point of the ray into the entire scene (bounding box of width W{scene} starting at origin). Clip the ray against the scene boundaries. Compute t^{in} and t^{out} for each coordinate axis i \in \{x, y, z\} against the planes 0 and W{scene}. If mi < 0, t^{in} corresponds to the plane at W{scene} and t^{out} to 0. If mi > 0, t^{in} corresponds to 0 and t^{out} to W{scene}. The valid range for t inside the scene is [\max(t^{in}i), \min(t^{out}i)] over all i. If \max(t^{in}i) > \min(t^{out}i), the ray misses the scene; terminate. Identify the exit point P of the ray from the scene boundary to determine the initial direction of traversal relative to the first cell. 3. Locate First Cell (FIND3DBLOCK): Use a point location algorithm (descend from root) to find the octree node containing the entry point P. Create the initial Cell record with TIN, TOUT, SIZ, PTR, CORNER, and DIRECT. 4. Main Traversal Loop: For each current cell C: a. Process Cell: Intersect the ray with objects in C using RAYINTERSECTSOBJECTINCELL. If an intersection is found, handle reflection/refraction or return the hit. b. Determine Exit: The ray exits C at parameter t^{out} = \min(t^{out}x, t^{out}y, t^{out}z). Let P = (Px, Py, Pz) be the 3D coordinates of the exit point. c. Classify Exit Point: Determine the type of exit point P on the boundary of C: Vertex: t^{out} is equal for all three coordinates. Edge: t^{out} is equal for exactly two coordinates. Face: t^{out} is different for all three coordinates. d. Determine Direction L: Calculate the direction vector L = (lx, ly, lz) to the next cell C' based on the exit type and which boundaries were crossed. e. Find Neighbor: Call OTGTEQNEIGHBOR to find the neighbor N of C in direction L such that width(N) \ge width(C). If no such neighbor exists, the ray has exited the scene; terminate. If N is a leaf (not gray), set C' = N. If N is gray, calculate a point Q guaranteed to be inside C' (see below) and use point location to find the specific descendant C' of N. f. Update State: Create a new Cell record for C' with updated TIN, TOUT, etc., and repeat. 5. Point Q Calculation (for Gray Neighbors): To locate C' when the neighbor N is gray, compute a point Q strictly inside C'. Let P = (Px, Py, Pz) be the exit point from C. Let L = (lx, ly, lz) be the direction to C'. Convention: Left, Down, and Back faces are closed. If a point lies on these faces, it is considered inside the cell bounded by them. For each coordinate j where lj is negative (decreasing direction), subtract a small integer value A from Pj to ensure Q is inside C'. A must be > 1 (width of smallest cell) and compatible with integer arithmetic. The text suggests A=1 is sufficient if coordinates are integers, but notes A must be small enough not to jump over cells. Example: If L = \text{'LUB'} (Left, Up, Back), lx < 0 and lz < 0. Then Q = (Px - 1, Py, Pz - 1). Example: If L = \text{'RD'} (Right, Down), ly < 0. Then Q = (Px, Py - 1, Pz). Note that Px and Pz are already integers because P lies on an edge or vertex. 6. Neighbor Finding Implementation: Pointer-based: Use FATHER links in the octree to traverse up and down to find the neighbor. Pointer-less (Locational Codes): Represent nodes by locational codes (depth + concatenated base-8 digits). Manipulate bits of the code based on direction L to find the neighbor's code, then search for it. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Rational Parameterization c = lcm(raydirectionrational.x.denom, raydirectionrational.y.denom, raydirectionrational.z.denom) mx = raydirectionrational.x.num (c // raydirectionrational.x.denom) my = raydirectionrational.y.num (c // raydirectionrational.y.denom) mz = raydirectionrational.z.num (c // raydirectionrational.z.denom) bx, by, bz = rayviewpoint.x, rayviewpoint.y, rayviewpoint.z # 2. Initial Entry tmin, tmax, exitpoint, exittype = cliprayagainstbox( bx, by, bz, mx, my, mz, 0, scenewidth) if tmin > tmax: return [] # 3. Locate First Cell currentcell = find3dblock(octreeroot, exitpoint, scenewidth) results = [] while currentcell is not None: hit = rayintersectsobjectincell(currentcell, bx, by, bz, mx, my, mz, tmin, tmax) if hit: results.append(hit) break texit = currentcell.tout px = mx texit + bx py = my texit + by pz = mz texit + bz toutx = rationaldiv(currentcell.corner.x - bx, mx) if mx != 0 else None touty = rationaldiv(currentcell.corner.y - by, my) if my != 0 else None toutz = rationaldiv(currentcell.corner.z - bz, mz) if mz != 0 else None exittype = classifyexitpoint(toutx, touty, toutz) l = determinedirection(exittype, px, py, pz, currentcell) neighborptr = otgteqneighbor(currentcell.ptr, l) if neighborptr is None: break if isleaf(neighborptr): nextcellptr = neighborptr nextcellsize = getleafsize(neighborptr) else: q = calculatepointq(px, py, pz, l) nextcellptr = find3dblock(octreeroot, q, scenewidth) nextcellsize = getnodesize(nextcellptr) currentcell = createcellrecord(nextcellptr, nextcellsize, texit) return results def lcm(a, b): return (a b) // gcd(a, b) def gcd(a, b): while b: a, b = b, a % b return a def rationaldiv(num, den): return (num, den) def rationallt(r1, r2): return r1[0] r2[1] < r2[0] r1[1] def rationaleq(r1, r2): return r1[0] r2[1] == r2[0] r1[1] def cliprayagainstbox(bx, by, bz, mx, my, mz, minval, maxval): tcandidates = [] for m, b, pmin, pmax in [(mx, bx, minval, maxval), (my, by, minval, maxval), (mz, bz, minval, maxval)]: if m != 0: t1 = rationaldiv(pmin - b, m) t2 = rationaldiv(pmax - b, m) if m > 0: tcandidates.append((t1, 'in')) tcandidates.append((t2, 'out')) else: tcandidates.append((t2, 'in')) tcandidates.append((t1, 'out')) tin = tcandidates[0][0] tout = tcandidates[0][0] for t, type in tcandidates: if type == 'in' and not rationallt(tin, t): tin = t if type == 'out' and not rationallt(t, tout): tout = t return tin, tout, None, None def classifyexitpoint(toutx, touty, toutz): if toutx is None or touty is None or toutz is None: return 'face' if rationaleq(toutx, touty) and rationaleq(touty, toutz): return 'vertex' elif rationaleq(toutx, touty) or rationaleq(toutx, toutz) or rationaleq(touty, toutz): return 'edge' else: return 'face' def calculatepointq(px, py, pz, l): qx = px - 1 if l.x < 0 else px qy = py - 1 if l.y < 0 else py qz = pz - 1 if l.z < 0 else pz return (qx, qy, qz) def find3dblock(root, point, scenewidth): # Stub for point location from root return None def rayintersectsobjectincell(cell, bx, by, bz, mx, my, mz, tmin, tmax): # Stub for intersection test return None def determinedirection(exittype, px, py, pz, cell): # Stub for direction calculation return type('obj', (object,), {'x': 0, 'y': 0, 'z': 0})() def otgteqneighbor(ptr, l): # Stub for neighbor finding return None def isleaf(ptr): return True def createcellrecord(ptr, size, texit): return type('Cell', (), {'ptr': ptr, 'size': size, 'tout': texit, 'corner': (0,0,0)})() def getleafsize(ptr): return 1 def getnodesize(ptr): return 1 Arbitrary 3D Resolution Discrete Ray Traversal is a method for tracing rays through implicit surfaces by voxelizing both the scene and the rays using interval arithmetic within a recursive octree subdivision. It eliminates explicit intersection calculations by ensuring the discrete ray matches the continuous ray down to the resolution of floating-point numbers, guaranteeing robustness against rounding errors. Unlike sibling methods that calculate explicit intersections or rely on pre-computed structures, this method performs on-the-fly subdivision and uses BSP ordering to determine traversal sequence without geometric intersection tests. Single-ray octree traversal is a method for rendering implicit surfaces by ray tracing an octree-encapsulated volume directly, using the octree as an acceleration structure to locate cell primitives. It solves the problem of efficiently finding the intersection between a ray and a piecewise C^0 isosurface defined by trilinear interpolant patches within octree cells. Unlike coherent traversal techniques that process packets of rays or frustums, this method processes one ray at a time, prioritizing optimized single-ray performance over the modest speedups gained from coherence in highly variant scenes. Time Complexity: The traversal time depends on the number of nodes visited. Neighbor finding is cheaper than point location from the root, but still requires tree traversal. The use of exact arithmetic (rational numbers) increases the cost of basic operations (addition, multiplication, comparison) compared to floating-point arithmetic. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the octree and the rational number representations (two integers per parameter). The cell record structure is small (6 fields). Performance: Exact arithmetic avoids precision errors but is computationally expensive. The method is robust but slower than floating-point counterparts due to the overhead of rational arithmetic and neighbor finding. Strengths: Guaranteed robustness against floating-point errors in boundary crossing and neighbor finding. No tolerance parameters needed for equality tests. Limitations: High computational cost of rational arithmetic. Assumes integer viewpoints and power-of-2 scene widths. The described implementation does not support rational viewpoints, though the solution can be modified to permit them. When to Use: When exact geometric predicates are critical and floating-point errors lead to incorrect traversal or missed intersections. When Not to Use: For real-time applications where performance is paramount and approximate floating-point methods are sufficient. The method was introduced by Wyvill and Kunii in 1989. It addresses the limitations of floating-point arithmetic in ray tracing through octrees, particularly in neighbor finding and boundary crossing. The approach is based on the Cyrus-Beck clipping algorithm and builds on earlier work by Glassner and Wyvill and Kunii. It is used in contexts requiring high precision in ray-triangle or ray-object intersection tests within hierarchical structures. name: Arbitrary 3D Resolution Discrete Ray Traversal
head: Discrete Ray Tracing of Implicit Surfaces, Interval Arithmetic Ray Traversal, Recursive Octree Traversal with BSP Ordering, Robust Octree Ray Traversal
body:
Arbitrary 3D Resolution Discrete Ray Traversal is a method for tracing rays through implicit surfaces by voxelizing both the scene and the rays using interval arithmetic within a recursive octree subdivision. It eliminates explicit intersection calculations by ensuring the discrete ray matches the continuous ray down to the resolution of floating-point numbers, guaranteeing robustness against rounding errors. Unlike sibling methods that calculate explicit intersections or rely on pre-computed structures, this method performs on-the-fly subdivision and uses BSP ordering to determine traversal sequence without geometric intersection tests. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray defined by origin (x0, y0, z0) and direction (dx, dy, dz); an octree representing the voxelized implicit surface up to a maximum level NL; the implicit function f(x,y,z) defining the surface. Output: Boolean indicating if an intersection was found; the intersection point (xm, ym, zm) if found. Data Structures Octant: Defined by three intervals [xc, Xc], [yc, Yc], [zc, Zc], where (xc, yc, zc) is the vertex with lowest coordinates and (Xc, Yc, Zc) is the vertex with highest coordinates. Sub-octant Index: An integer from 0 to 7. Each bit corresponds to an axis (x, y, z). A bit is 1 if the sub-octant lies on the positive side of the splitting plane, 0 otherwise. Parameters NL: Maximum subdivision level (leaf node level). Default value in code is 30. For IEEE 754 double precision, the maximum is 53. Formulas Ray Equation: x = x0 + t \cdot dx, \quad y = y0 + t \cdot dy, \quad z = z0 + t \cdot dz \quad (1) Splitting Planes: For an octant of size l with lowest vertex (xc, yc, zc), the middle point is (xm, ym, zm) = (xc + l/2, yc + l/2, zc + l/2). Implicit Ray Coefficients: cx = sign(dx) \cdot |dy| \cdot |dz| cy = sign(dy) \cdot |dz| \cdot |dx| cz = sign(dz) \cdot |dx| \cdot |dy| \quad (3) Ray Inclusion Test: The ray passes through an octant if the intervals derived from the implicit ray equation overlap:  egin{bmatrix} fx(xc) & fx(Xc) \ fy(yc) & fy(Yc) \ fz(zc) & fz(Zc) \end{bmatrix} =  egin{bmatrix} cx \cdot (xc - x0) & cx \cdot (Xc - x0) \ cy \cdot (yc - y0) & cy \cdot (Yc - y0) \ cz \cdot (zc - z0) & cz \cdot (zc - z0) \end{bmatrix} \quad (4) Overlap is defined such that if a lower bound equals an upper bound, there is no overlap. Algorithm Steps 1. Calculate Traversal Direction Sign: Compute signDir as a 3-bit integer: signDir = (dz<0)2 + (dy<0)1 + (dx<0). 2. Base Case Check: If intersectionFound is true, return true. If level == NL, check if the octant contains a surface using IsoValueTest. If false, apply PartialDifferentialTest. If both fail, return false. If surface is confirmed, set intersectionFound = true, intersectedPoint = mid, and return true. 3. Octant Containment Check: Test if the ray passes through the current octant using the ray voxelization algorithm (Eq. 4). If not, return false. 4. Calculate Traversal Order Mask: Determine the relative position of the ray start point (x0, y0, z0) to the octant middle point (xm, ym, zm). Compute izyx = ((z0 > zm) << 2) + ((y0 > ym) << 1) + (x0 > xm). Compute iaux = izyx XOR signDir. 5. Iterate Through Sub-octants: Loop i from 0 to 7. If (iaux AND i) is non-zero, skip this sub-octant (Octant elimination). Calculate the index for the sub-octant in BSP order: idx = izyx XOR i. Retrieve the sub-octant: suboct = octant[idx]. Check if the ray passes through suboct. If not, continue. If suboct contains a part of a surface, recursively call Traversal(suboct, level+1). If true, break the loop and return true. 6. Return: If the loop completes without finding an intersection, return intersectionFound. Optimized Interval Calculation To avoid branching and frequent rounding mode changes, bounds are calculated using two FPUs (e.g., SSE2 and x87) with independent rounding modes (towards -\infty for lower bounds, +\infty for upper bounds). For the x-axis, an array tx[4] stores bounds. The selection of rounding modes depends on dx. For dx > 0, intervals are [fx^-(xc), fx^+(Xc)], [fx^-(xc), fx^+(xm)], [fx^-(xm), fx^+(Xc)]. For dx < 0, intervals are [fx^-(Xc), fx^+(xc)], [fx^-(Xc), fx^+(xm)], [fx^-(xm), fx^+(xc)]. Partial Differential Test Applied at leaf nodes to reduce overestimations. It calculates inclusion functions for partial derivatives DX = DFX(X), DY = DFY(Y), DZ = DFZ(Z). If 0 
otin DX AND 0 
otin DY AND 0 
otin DZ, the function is monotonic and has no zeroes, so the octant is ignored. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fxminus(val): """Evaluate implicit function at val with rounding towards -inf.""" return math.floor(f(val)) # Standard interval lower bound rounding def fxplus(val): """Evaluate implicit function at val with rounding towards +inf.""" return math.ceil(f(val)) # Standard interval upper bound rounding def intervalsoverlap(int1, int2, int3): """Check if three intervals overlap. Equality is no overlap.""" lower = max(int1[0], int2[0], int3[0]) upper = min(int1[1], int2[1], int3[1]) return lower < upper # Equality considered no overlap def IsoValueTest(octant): """Check for sign changes at the 8 corners of the octant.""" corners = octant.getcorners() # Standard corner enumeration signs = [math.copysign(1, f(c)) for c in corners] return any(s1 != s2 for s1, s2 in zip(signs, signs[1:])) # Sign change detection def PartialDifferentialTest(octant): """Check monotonicity via inclusion functions of partial derivatives.""" X, Y, Z = octant.intervals DX = DFX(X) # Inclusion function for ∂f/∂x DY = DFY(Y) # Inclusion function for ∂f/∂y DZ = DFZ(Z) # Inclusion function for ∂f/∂z # Returns true if 0 is NOT in DX, DY, and DZ (monotonic, no zero) return (0 not in DX) and (0 not in DY) and (0 not in DZ) # def RayPassesThroughOctant(octant, x0, y0, z0, dx, dy, dz, signDir): """Test if ray passes through octant using interval arithmetic.""" cx = (1 if dx >= 0 else -1) abs(dy) abs(dz) cy = (1 if dy >= 0 else -1) abs(dz) abs(dx) cz = (1 if dz >= 0 else -1) abs(dx) abs(dy) xc, Xc = octant.xmin, octant.xmax xm = octant.xmid yc, Yc = octant.ymin, octant.ymax ym = octant.ymid zc, Zc = octant.zmin, octant.zmax zm = octant.zmid # Optimized interval bounds selection based on dx if dx > 0: int1 = (cx fxminus(xc - x0), cx fxplus(Xc - x0)) int2 = (cx fxminus(xc - x0), cx fxplus(xm - x0)) int3 = (cx fxminus(xm - x0), cx fxplus(Xc - x0)) else: int1 = (cx fxminus(Xc - x0), cx fxplus(xc - x0)) int2 = (cx fxminus(Xc - x0), cx fxplus(xm - x0)) int3 = (cx fxminus(xm - x0), cx fxplus(xc - x0)) # Repeat for y and z axes with corresponding intervals if dy > 0: int4 = (cy fxminus(yc - y0), cy fxplus(Yc - y0)) int5 = (cy fxminus(yc - y0), cy fxplus(ym - y0)) int6 = (cy fxminus(ym - y0), cy fxplus(Yc - y0)) else: int4 = (cy fxminus(Yc - y0), cy fxplus(yc - y0)) int5 = (cy fxminus(Yc - y0), cy fxplus(ym - y0)) int6 = (cy fxminus(ym - y0), cy fxplus(yc - y0)) if dz > 0: int7 = (cz fxminus(zc - z0), cz fxplus(Zc - z0)) int8 = (cz fxminus(zc - z0), cz fxplus(zm - z0)) int9 = (cz fxminus(zm - z0), cz fxplus(Zc - z0)) else: int7 = (cz fxminus(Zc - z0), cz fxplus(zc - z0)) int8 = (cz fxminus(Zc - z0), cz fxplus(zm - z0)) int9 = (cz fxminus(zm - z0), cz fxplus(zc - z0)) return intervalsoverlap(int1, int4, int7) def Traversal(octant, level, x0, y0, z0, dx, dy, dz, signDir, NL, foundstate, pointstate): # Base case: intersection already found if foundstate[0]: return True # Base case: leaf node if level == NL: if not IsoValueTest(octant): if not PartialDifferentialTest(octant): return False foundstate[0] = True pointstate[0] = octant.mid return True # Check if ray passes through current octant if not RayPassesThroughOctant(octant, x0, y0, z0, dx, dy, dz, signDir): return False # Calculate traversal order mask xm, ym, zm = octant.mid izyx = ((z0 > zm) << 2) + ((y0 > ym) << 1) + (x0 > xm) iaux = izyx ^ signDir # Iterate through sub-octants in BSP order for i in range(8): # Octant elimination if iaux & i: continue # BSP ordering index idx = izyx ^ i suboct = octant[idx] # Check if ray passes through sub-octant if not RayPassesThroughOctant(suboct, x0, y0, z0, dx, dy, dz, signDir): continue # Check if sub-octant contains surface part if suboct.containssurface(): if Traversal(suboct, level + 1, x0, y0, z0, dx, dy, dz, signDir, NL, foundstate, pointstate): return True return foundstate[0] Edge Cases and Pitfalls Rounding Errors in Midpoint: The midpoint calculation (xc + l/2) must be exact. This is guaranteed if the half-length of the octant is not smaller than 1 ULP. Partial Differential Test False Negatives: In very special cases, the test may return false (indicating non-monotonicity) even if the octant does not contain a surface part. Precision: The intersection point is (xm, ym, zm). The maximum distance to the real intersection is \sqrt{3} \cdot 2^{-NL-1}. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. The method involves recursive traversal down to level NL. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. The octree is stored, but subdivision is done on-the-fly. Measured Performance: Slightly slower than Gargantini's algorithm when using robust interval arithmetic with different rounding modes, but faster otherwise. Gargantini's algorithm eliminates all non-traversed sub-octants, while this method uses BSP ordering and ray voxelization which only partially eliminate them. Strengths: Robustness against rounding errors; eliminates explicit intersection calculations; guarantees that the discrete ray matches the continuous ray. Limitations: Slightly slower than Gargantini's algorithm in non-robust mode; Partial Differential Test may have false negatives in special cases. When to Use: When robustness is critical and explicit intersection calculations are undesirable or prone to errors. Suitable for implicit surfaces where interval arithmetic is applicable. When Not to Use: When performance is the primary concern and Gargantini's algorithm is acceptable; when the scene is not represented by implicit functions suitable for interval arithmetic. Origin: Proposed by Nilo Stolte in the paper "Arbitrary 3D Resolution Discrete Ray Tracing of Implicit Surfaces". History: The method is the first complete solution of an interval arithmetic-based ray tracing with 3D space subdivision using discrete ray traversal. It builds upon previous work using interval arithmetic for ray casting (e.g., Duff) and Lipschitz conditions for voxelization (e.g., Kalra and Barr), but extends it to 3D space subdivision without explicit intersections. Usage: Used for ray tracing implicit surfaces with guaranteed robustness. name: Single-Ray Octree Traversal
head: Octree Traversal Strategy
body: Single-ray octree traversal is a method for rendering implicit surfaces by ray tracing an octree-encapsulated volume directly, using the octree as an acceleration structure to locate cell primitives. It solves the problem of efficiently finding the intersection between a ray and a piecewise C^0 isosurface defined by trilinear interpolant patches within octree cells. Unlike coherent traversal techniques that process packets of rays or frustums, this method processes one ray at a time, prioritizing optimized single-ray performance over the modest speedups gained from coherence in highly variant scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; an octree volume where scalar values are stored at leaf nodes and interior nodes maintain pointers. Output: Intersection point, normal, and depth of the isosurface, or null if no intersection is found. Data Structures: The octree is an adaptive-resolution, hierarchically compressed scalar field. Leaf Nodes: Store scalar values. At maximum depth d{max}, these correspond to the finest available data resolution. Scalars at less than maximum depth store coarser resolutions by factors of 8 per depth level. Interior Nodes: Maintain pointers to children. To avoid explicitly storing a full node for each leaf, the implementation stores nodes corresponding to the parent. Cap Structure: At depth d{max} - 1, a separate structure called a "cap" is employed, consisting simply of 8 scalar values at d{max}. All children at d{max} are guaranteed to be leaves. Cell Primitive: A cell is composed of 8 voxels. Values outside the octree data are defined to be zero. The implicit surface inside each cell is a trilinear interpolant patch. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Traversal: The ray traverses the interior nodes of the octree. This involves determining which child node the ray enters next. 2. Cell Retrieval: When the ray reaches a leaf node (or a node where the primitive is defined), the algorithm retrieves the cell primitive. This primitive is composed of 8 voxels. 3. Neighbor Finding: To construct the cell of 8 voxels, the algorithm performs neighbor-finding on the octree structure to retrieve the forward-neighboring voxels relative to the current leaf. This yields a complete cell of 8 scalar values. 4. Intersection: The ray intersects the well-defined cell primitive (trilinear interpolant patch) composed of the 8 retrieved voxels. The global surface is piecewise C^0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def singlerayoctreetraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, octree): """ Traces a single ray through an octree volume to find an isosurface intersection. Assumes the octree uses the 'cap' structure at max depth - 1. """ # Start traversal from the root node = octree.root while node is not None: # Determine which child the ray enters # This requires ray-box intersection tests against the 8 children # If the ray does not intersect the current node's bounding box, return None if not rayintersectsnode(rayorigin, raydirection, node.bbox): return None # Check if this is a leaf node or a node requiring cell primitive evaluation if node.isleaf or node.iscaplevel: # Retrieve the 8 voxels forming the cell primitive # This involves neighbor-finding to get forward neighbors voxelvalues = getcellvoxels(node, octree) # Intersect ray with the trilinear interpolant patch defined by these 8 voxels intersection = intersecttrilinearpatch(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelvalues) if intersection is not None: return intersection else: # No intersection in this cell, continue traversal if there are deeper leaves # In a pure leaf representation, we might stop or check neighbors # For this specific method, we assume the cell primitive covers the intersection break else: # Interior node: descend into the child that the ray intersects childindex = getraychildindex(rayorigin, raydirection, node) node = node.children[childindex] return None def getcellvoxels(node, octree): """ Retrieves the 8 voxels forming the cell primitive for a leaf node. Uses neighbor-finding to get forward neighbors. """ # Get the scalar value at the current leaf node currentvalue = node.scalarvalue # Perform neighbor-finding to retrieve the 7 forward-neighboring voxels # The exact neighbor-finding algorithm is complex and depends on the octree layout # mentions details in appendices, but the concept is retrieving # the neighborhood to form a 2x2x2 block of voxels. neighbors = findforwardneighbors(node, octree) # Combine current value and neighbors to form the 8-voxel cell # The mapping associates each voxel to the lower-left corner of a cell cellvoxels = [currentvalue] + neighbors return cellvoxels Parameters: Isosurface Value: Implicitly zero for the trilinear patch intersection check in the context of the cell primitive construction. Max Depth: Determines the finest resolution. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Neighbor Finding Complexity: The worst-case complexity of neighbor-finding is O(\dots) (specific bound not given in the sources). Coherence Trade-offs: Aggressively coherent techniques (e.g., frustum-based) entail unnecessary work when a pixel covers multiple voxels, potentially decreasing performance over single-ray techniques. Scene Variance: Highly variant scenes and large data volumes result in modest speedups from coherent techniques, making single-ray traversal competitive. An octree structure where polynomial coefficients are stored only at leaves containing the field isosurface, with empty nodes collapsed to be as large as possible to reduce memory requirements. During ray traversal, a basic octree traversal algorithm (instead of sphere marching) is used to find if the ray intersects any leaf containing the isosurface. To determine if a node contains the isosurface, the algorithm inspects polynomial coefficients using the convex property of Bézier polynomials. The range of control points (convex hull) must contain zero for the surface to be present. For tricubic polynomials, coefficients are computed from field values and derivatives at 8 vertices and transformed to the 64 control points of the corresponding tricubic Bézier patch via a linear transformation. If the range of these 64 control values does not contain zero, the zero iso-surface is guaranteed not to be inside the node. Time Complexity: The traversal time depends on the depth of the octree and the cost of neighbor-finding. The worst-case complexity of neighbor-finding is not fully specified in the sources. Memory Complexity: The octree is adaptive and hierarchically compressed. Storing nodes corresponding to parents and using a "cap" structure at d{max}-1 reduces memory overhead compared to storing a full node for each leaf. The polynomial coefficient variant further reduces memory by collapsing empty nodes. Performance: The method focuses on optimized single-ray behavior. Coherent techniques (SIMD, packets) are not employed because highly variant scenes and large data volumes offer only modest speedups from coherence, and frustum-based techniques can decrease performance due to unnecessary work on pixels covering multiple voxels. Strengths: Efficient for large data volumes where coherence gains are minimal; reduces memory usage through adaptive resolution and node collapsing. Limitations: Neighbor-finding can be complex; single-ray traversal may not exploit hardware parallelism as effectively as packet traversal in highly coherent scenes. This method originates from research on ray tracing implicit surfaces for interactive rendering, specifically focusing on octree-encapsulated volumes. It builds on the duality between voxels and cells, mapping each voxel to the lower-left corner of a cell. The approach was developed to avoid extracting meshes and sending geometry to the GPU, instead ray tracing the octree directly. The polynomial coefficient variant was proposed to improve intersection search at iterations far from the surface in SDF rendering. name: DDA Tree Traversal with Mini-Stack
head: Mini-stack traversal, Stack-based hierarchical traversal
body: This method extends the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) grid traversal algorithm to N-ary hierarchical trees for GPU shader implementation. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing sparse voxel structures by maintaining a small, fixed-size stack of DDA states, allowing the ray to descend into child nodes and ascend back to parent nodes without dynamic memory allocation. It is distinguished from standard DDA by its hierarchical boundary handling and from other tree traversals by its reliance on a statically allocated mini-stack indexed via Shader Model 4.0 features. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, hierarchical tree structure with N-ary nodes, maximum tree depth D{max}, and node accessors. Output: Sequence of leaf voxels visited by the ray, along with their entry and exit distances. Data Structures: Mini-Stack: A fixed-size array of length D{max} (compile-time constant). Each entry at index level stores: tmax[3]: Distance to the next boundary for each axis (x, y, z) within the current node's local grid. tdelta[3]: Distance increment per voxel step for each axis. step[3]: Direction of index increment (+1 or -1) for each axis. currentindex[3]: Current voxel coordinates (i, j, k) within the current node's local grid. nodeaddr: Memory address or index of the node in the indirection pool. Stack Pointer: An integer variable tracking the current depth in the stack, initially 0. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute DDA parameters for the root node's bounding box. Push the root's DDA state onto the stack at index 0. Set stackptr = 0. 2. Descent Phase: While the current node is not a leaf, identify the child node intersected by the ray using the current DDA state. Compute DDA parameters for the child node's local grid (the entry distance into the child equals the exit distance from the parent's current cell). Update the stack entry at stackptr with the new DDA parameters and the child's node address. Increment stackptr. Repeat until a leaf node is reached. 3. Horizontal Advance: Within the current node (leaf or internal), advance the DDA: find the axis k with the minimum tmax[k]. Record the voxel at currentindex and the interval [t{entry}, t{max}[k]]. Advance currentindex[k] by step[k]. Update tmax[k] += tdelta[k]. Update tentry = tmax[k]. If the new currentindex is within the node's bounds, continue processing the next voxel. If outside, proceed to Vertical Ascent. 4. Vertical Ascent: Decrement stackptr. If stackptr < 0, the ray has exited the entire tree; terminate. Retrieve the DDA state from the stack at the new stackptr. Resume the Horizontal Advance loop from the point where the descent occurred, using the stored DDA parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ddatreetraversalministack(rayorigin, raydirection, rootnode, maxdepth, getnode, isleaf, getbounds, voxelsize=1.0): # Initialize DDA parameters for a bounding box def initdda(origin, direction, bounds): step = [0, 0, 0] tmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tdelta = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] currentindex = [0, 0, 0] for i in range(3): if direction[i] > 0: step[i] = 1 currentindex[i] = int((origin[i] - bounds.min[i]) / voxelsize) nextboundary = (currentindex[i] + 1) voxelsize + bounds.min[i] tmax[i] = (nextboundary - origin[i]) / direction[i] tdelta[i] = voxelsize / direction[i] elif direction[i] < 0: step[i] = -1 currentindex[i] = int((origin[i] - bounds.min[i]) / voxelsize) nextboundary = currentindex[i] voxelsize + bounds.min[i] tmax[i] = (nextboundary - origin[i]) / direction[i] tdelta[i] = -voxelsize / direction[i] else: step[i] = 0 tmax[i] = float('inf') tdelta[i] = 0.0 return step, tmax, tdelta, currentindex stack = [None] maxdepth stackptr = 0 # Initialization: root node bounds = getbounds(rootnode) step, tmax, tdelta, currentindex = initdda(rayorigin, raydirection, bounds) stack[0] = {'step': step, 'tmax': tmax, 'tdelta': tdelta, 'currentindex': currentindex, 'nodeaddr': rootnode.address} tentry = 0.0 while True: state = stack[stackptr] node = getnode(state['nodeaddr']) bounds = getbounds(node) if isleaf(node): # Horizontal Advance for leaf while True: minidx = 0 minval = state['tmax'][0] for i in range(1, 3): if state['tmax'][i] < minval: minval = state['tmax'][i] minidx = i texit = minval yield state['currentindex'], tentry, texit state['currentindex'][minidx] += state['step'][minidx] state['tmax'][minidx] += state['tdelta'][minidx] tentry = texit # Check bounds if not (bounds.min[0] <= state['currentindex'][0] <= bounds.max[0] and bounds.min[1] <= state['currentindex'][1] <= bounds.max[1] and bounds.min[2] <= state['currentindex'][2] <= bounds.max[2]): break else: # Internal node: find child to descend minidx = 0 minval = state['tmax'][0] for i in range(1, 3): if state['tmax'][i] < minval: minval = state['tmax'][i] minidx = i texit = minval # Child indexing depends on tree layout (e.g., octree Morton order) childnode = getchild(node, state['currentindex']) if childnode is None: pass # No child in this direction, proceed to ascent else: # Compute DDA for child node childbounds = getbounds(childnode) childorigin = [rayorigin[i] + texit raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] childstep, childtmax, childtdelta, childcurrentindex = initdda(childorigin, raydirection, childbounds) stackptr += 1 stack[stackptr] = {'step': childstep, 'tmax': childtmax, 'tdelta': childtdelta, 'currentindex': childcurrentindex, 'nodeaddr': childnode.address} tentry = texit continue # Vertical Ascent stackptr -= 1 if stackptr < 0: break Parameters: Stack Size: Fixed at compile time, equal to the maximum depth of the hierarchical structure. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction Components: If a ray direction component is zero, the corresponding tdelta is set to 0.0 and tmax to \infty, ensuring the ray never advances in that axis. Precision Errors: Floating-point precision issues may cause the ray to miss small voxels or re-enter previously visited cells. Using epsilon offsets or robust geometric predicates is recommended. Empty Nodes: If a node has no children in the ray's path, the algorithm must correctly ascend without attempting to access non-existent child nodes. This method extends the DDA Tree Traversal with Mini-Stack to support Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAGs (SSVDAGs), a compression format that exploits geometric symmetries to reduce memory footprint. It solves the problem of correctly traversing a DAG where child nodes and leaf voxels may be mirrored relative to their parent's coordinate system. The key distinction from standard octree DDA is the maintenance of a 3-bit mirrormask that tracks reflection transformations, allowing the algorithm to map logical voxel indices to physical storage locations without decompressing the geometry. Time Complexity: Constant per traversal step, with total time proportional to the number of visited cells plus the number of hierarchical transitions. Memory Complexity: O(D), where D is the maximum tree depth, due to the fixed-size mini-stack. Performance: Highly efficient on GPUs due to the use of statically allocated arrays and minimal branching. The fixed stack size avoids dynamic memory allocation overhead. Strengths: Fast traversal, low memory overhead, suitable for real-time rendering on GPUs. Limitations: Requires compile-time knowledge of maximum tree depth; less flexible for dynamically changing tree structures. The method was proposed for the interactive exploration of procedural volumes. It extends the classic DDA algorithm to N-ary trees, leveraging Shader Model 4.0 features for dynamic indexing of local arrays.
