name: Z-list-buffer Ray Representation
head: Z-list-buffer, Ray-Rep, Array of Rays
body: The Z-list-buffer Ray Representation is a volume data storage format that stores voxel data as an array of rays, where each ray contains a list of sample points (position and normal) defining regions. It replaces traditional scalar fields to reduce storage and preserve sharp features. It supports any cell-based triangulation method. It is distinguished from sibling structures by its specific generation method using orthographic projection and a Z-buffer with a Z-list, which is faster than modified ray tracing for axis-aligned rays. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Hermite data (position and normal) at a fine resolution grid of size nk \times nk \times nk. Output: Three arrays of rays (one for each axis: x, y, z), where each array has a resolution of (nk + 1) \times (nk + 1). Data Structures: 1. Sample: A structure containing: position: 3D point (x, y, z). normal: 3D vector (nx, ny, nz). 2. Ray: A list of Sample objects. Samples are classified as left bounding (marks the left boundary of a region) or right bounding (marks the right boundary of a region). A pair of samples defines a region: the first sample is the left boundary, the second is the right boundary. 3. Ray Array: An array of Ray objects. The resolution is (nk + 1) \times (nk + 1). Three such arrays are maintained, one for each axis. Algorithm Steps: 1. Acquire Hermite data at a uniform nk \times nk \times nk grid resolution. 2. Shoot axis-aligned rays along the x, y, and z axes. 3. For each ray, compute all intersection points with the volume data and their corresponding normals. 4. Store these intersection points as Sample objects in the corresponding Ray list. 5. Classify each sample as left or right bounding based on the region it defines. 6. Use orthographic projection and a Z-buffer with a Z-list for each entry to perform scan conversion, which is faster than modified ray tracing for this specific axis-aligned case. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatezlistbuffer(hermitedata, nk): """ Generates Z-list-buffer Ray Representation from Hermite data. Args: hermitedata: 3D grid of (position, normal) pairs at resolution nk x nk x nk. nk: Integer, finest resolution of the input grid. Returns: raysx, raysy, raysz: Three 2D arrays of Ray objects, each of size (nk + 1) x (nk + 1). """ # Initialize three 2D arrays of rays, each of size (nk + 1) x (nk + 1) raysx = [[[] for in range(nk + 1)] for in range(nk + 1)] raysy = [[[] for in range(nk + 1)] for in range(nk + 1)] raysz = [[[] for in range(nk + 1)] for in range(nk + 1)] # The source specifies using orthographic projection and a Z-buffer with a Z-list # for faster scan conversion than modified ray tracing. # We iterate over the 2D grid for each axis, project rays, and accumulate intersections. # Process X-axis rays (rays parallel to X, indexed by Y, Z) for y in range(nk + 1): for z in range(nk + 1): zbuffer = float('inf') zlist = [] # Scan convert along the ray direction (X-axis) for x in range(nk + 1): # Evaluate Hermite data to find surface crossings along X # The source does not specify the exact intersection routine. point, normal = None, None if point is not None: # Z-buffer check: only keep intersections closer than current depth if x < zbuffer: zbuffer = x # Classify as left or right bounding based on region alternation sampletype = "leftbounding" if len(zlist) % 2 == 0 else "rightbounding" zlist.append({"position": point, "normal": normal, "type": sampletype}) raysx[y][z] = zlist # Repeat for Y and Z axes similarly for y in range(nk + 1): for z in range(nk + 1): zbuffer = float('inf') zlist = [] for x in range(nk + 1): point, normal = None, None if point is not None: if y < zbuffer: zbuffer = y sampletype = "leftbounding" if len(zlist) % 2 == 0 else "rightbounding" zlist.append({"position": point, "normal": normal, "type": sampletype}) raysy[z][x] = zlist for x in range(nk + 1): for y in range(nk + 1): zbuffer = float('inf') zlist = [] for z in range(nk + 1): point, normal = None, None if point is not None: if z < zbuffer: zbuffer = z sampletype = "leftbounding" if len(zlist) % 2 == 0 else "rightbounding" zlist.append({"position": point, "normal": normal, "type": sampletype}) raysz[y][x] = zlist return raysx, raysy, raysz Parameters: nk: The finest resolution of the input Hermite data grid. Typical values are not specified, but the example uses a 512^3 grid for comparison. Average number of samples per ray: ~2.86 for a dragon model, ~2.05 for a fandisk model. This is significantly lower than the 512 samples required for a 512^3 distance field. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Redundancy: The representation is redundant and requires regularization. Regularization: Separate blocks of voxel terrain are best stored as triangular meshes and converted to Ray-Rep and back as needed. Precision: The source notes that the representation is precise, but does not specify numerical precision issues. In practice, floating-point precision may affect intersection calculations, especially for thin features. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in the sources. The generation is faster than modified ray tracing due to the use of orthographic projection and Z-buffer with Z-list. Memory Complexity: Redundant, requiring regularization. However, it reduces storage compared to scalar fields. For a 512^3 distance field, it reduces the number of samples per ray from 512 to approximately 2. Measured Performance: Average of ~2.86 samples per ray for a dragon model and ~2.05 for a fandisk model. Strengths: High speed for triangulation using dual methods, preserves sharp features, reduces storage compared to scalar fields. Limitations: Redundant, requires regularization, higher storage than compressible formats. When to use: When fast rendering from polygonal representation and fast CSG operations are required, such as in virtual world sculpting. When not to use: When storage space is a critical constraint and compression is available for other formats. Origin: The concept was introduced in the paper "Detail sculpting using cubical marching squares". The term "Z-list-buffer" was used in the same paper to describe the generation method. History: The GPU implementation of Ray-Rep with normals is called Layered Depth-Normal Images (LDNI). Before GPGPU, layered depth images (LDI) used texture arrays to store depth and normal. With CUDA, OpenCL, and compute shaders, it became possible to build lists of points for each image fragment on the GPU. Usage: Used in virtual world sculpting, which involves continuous subtraction operations on target objects. It is also used for voxel terrain storage in VR system design. name: Grid Sphere Traversal
body: Grid Sphere Traversal (GST) is a ray-grid traversal method that performs sphere tracing through a dense grid of Signed Distance Function (SDF) values. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing empty regions in SDF-based rendering by using a hierarchy of SDF grids where lower-resolution levels encode larger SDF values to accelerate step sizes. It is distinguished from its siblings by performing the entire traversal in shader code using dense grids, whereas alternatives like Sparse Voxel Set leverage DXR hardware acceleration for BVH traversal. Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, SDF grid hierarchy (mipmap levels), grid resolution per level. Outputs: Intersection distance or null. Data Structures: SDF Grid: A 3D texture or array storing SDF values. Value Encoding: SDF values are clamped to [-1, 1]. A value of 1 encodes a distance of 2.5 interior voxel diagonals. This allows storage as 8-bit signed normalized (snorm) integers. Hierarchy: A set of grid levels L0, L1, \dots, Ln. Level L0 is the highest resolution. Lower-resolution levels (higher index) encode larger SDF values to represent empty space more coarsely. Steps: 1. Initialize: Start at the root level (lowest resolution, highest index) of the SDF hierarchy. 2. Traverse Hierarchy: For the current ray, determine the position in the current grid level. 3. Sample SDF: Sample the SDF value at the current ray position from the current grid level. 4. Adaptive Resolution Selection: Use the sampled SDF value to determine if the ray is in empty space. If the SDF value indicates sufficient empty space (larger distance), the algorithm may step forward by a larger amount or switch to a lower-resolution level to maximize step size safely. If the ray is close to the surface (small SDF value), switch to a higher-resolution level to reduce step size and maintain precision. 5. Sphere Trace: Perform sphere tracing steps. The step size is determined by the SDF value at the current position, scaled appropriately for the grid resolution and encoding. 6. Intersection Check: If the SDF value is below a threshold (surface hit), return the intersection distance. If the ray exits the grid or exceeds max distance, return null. 7. Shader Execution: The entire traversal logic is implemented in shader code (e.g., GLSL/HLSL). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gridspheretraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, sdfgrids, gridbounds, maxsteps, epsilon, levelswitchthreshold): # sdfgrids: list of 3D textures/arrays, index 0 is lowest resolution (coarsest) # gridbounds: (mincorner, maxcorner) defining the world-space extent of the grids # levelswitchthreshold: multiplier for voxelsize to decide when to change resolution t = 0.0 currentlevel = 0 pos = rayorigin for in range(maxsteps): # Check if ray has exited the grid bounds if not isinsidegrid(pos, gridbounds): return None # Compute physical voxel size for current level # Assuming cubic grids with side length L at level 0, scaled by 2^level levelscale = 2 currentlevel gridside = gridbounds[1][0] - gridbounds[0][0] voxelsize = gridside / (sdfgrids[0].shape[0] levelscale) # Sample SDF value at current position # Coordinates normalized to [0, 1] for texture lookup uv = (pos - gridbounds[0]) / (gridbounds[1] - gridbounds[0]) uv = clamp(uv, 0.0, 1.0) sdfsnorm = texturesample(sdfgrids[currentlevel], uv) # Decode 8-bit snorm to physical distance # snorm 1.0 -> 2.5 sqrt(3) voxelsize physicaldist = sdfsnorm 2.5 sqrt(3) voxelsize # Surface intersection check if physicaldist < epsilon: return t # Sphere tracing step step = max(epsilon, physicaldist) t += step pos = rayorigin + raydirection t # Adaptive resolution selection # Large empty space (large SDF) -> coarser level (higher index) # Near surface (small SDF) -> finer level (lower index) if physicaldist > levelswitchthreshold voxelsize and currentlevel < len(sdfgrids) - 1: currentlevel += 1 elif physicaldist < 0.5 levelswitchthreshold voxelsize and currentlevel > 0: currentlevel -= 1 return None def isinsidegrid(point, bounds): return all(bounds[0][i] <= point[i] <= bounds[1][i] for i in range(3)) def clamp(v, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(maxval, v)) def texturesample(grid, uv): # Standard trilinear interpolation of 3D texture at normalized coordinates # Returns value in [-1, 1] return grid[uv] Parameters: SDF Encoding: 8-bit snorm, range [-1, 1], mapping 1.0 to 2.5 interior voxel diagonals. Max Steps: Not given in the sources. Epsilon: Not given in the sources. Level Switch Threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Precision: Using 8-bit snorm may introduce quantization errors. The mapping of 1.0 to 2.5 diagonals is a specific design choice to maximize the range of representable distances. Boundaries: Ray must be clamped to the grid bounds. Degenerate Input: Empty space far from surface may require many steps if the hierarchy is not deep enough or if the adaptive resolution selection is not optimal. A grid traversal algorithm used in Claybook (Aaltonen, 2018) where every voxel is uniquely associated with a raytracing bounding box. It performed best in open and simple scenes compared to sparse brick set and sparse voxel octree. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of steps in sphere tracing and the depth of the hierarchy. Adaptive resolution selection aims to reduce steps in empty space. Memory Complexity: Dense grid storage. All voxels are stored, including those without SDF surface. Performance: Performed best in open and simple scenes. Outperformed by sparse voxel set in general due to DXR hardware acceleration, but GST has better cache coherency due to compact data storage. Strengths: Simple implementation in shader code, good cache coherency, effective in open scenes. Limitations: Dense storage is memory-intensive. Less effective in complex scenes compared to sparse methods. Grid Sphere Traversal was evaluated in the context of ray tracing signed distance function grids. It is similar to the technique used in Claybook by Aaltonen (2018). The method was compared against sparse voxel set, sparse brick set, and sparse voxel octree. name: Uniform Grid Traversal
head: Uniform Grid Acceleration
body: Uniform Grid Traversal accelerates volume rendering by partitioning the scene into a regular, axis-aligned voxel grid, allowing rays to skip empty space and quickly locate occupied voxels. It differs from sibling methods by assuming fixed, uniform spacing between grid cells, which simplifies traversal to incremental index updates, unlike Computational Space Traversal which handles curvilinear grids. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, grid bounds [\minx, \miny, \minz] and [\maxx, \maxy, \maxz], grid resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz). Output: Sequence of visited voxel indices (i, j, k) and corresponding entry/exit distances along the ray. Data Structures: The grid is stored as a 3D array of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz containing particle lists or density values. The traversal state maintains: Current voxel indices: i, j, k (integers). Step directions: sx, sy, sz \in \{-1, 0, 1\}, determined by the sign of \mathbf{d}. Distance to next boundary: t{maxx}, t{maxy}, t{maxz} (floats), representing the ray parameter t at which the ray crosses the next grid plane perpendicular to each axis. Delta distances: t{\Delta x}, t{\Delta y}, t{\Delta z} (floats), representing the distance between consecutive grid planes along the ray. Formulas: 1. Voxel Size: \Delta x = \frac{\maxx - \minx}{Nx}, \Delta y = \frac{\maxy - \miny}{Ny}, \Delta z = \frac{\maxz - \minz}{Nz}. 2. Step Direction: si = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } di > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } di < 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } di = 0 \end{cases} for i \in \{x, y, z\}. 3. Delta Distances: t{\Delta i} = \frac{\Delta i}{|di|} if di \neq 0, else \infty. 4. Initial Voxel Index: i0 = \lfloor \frac{ox - \minx}{\Delta x} \rfloor, clamped to [0, Nx-1] (analogous for j, k). 5. Initial Boundary Distances: t{maxi} = \frac{bi - oi}{di} if di \neq 0, else \infty, where the boundary coordinate bi = (i0 + 1)\Delta i + \mini if di > 0, and bi = i0\Delta i + \mini if di < 0. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute voxel sizes, step directions, delta distances, and initial voxel indices. 2. Compute initial boundary distances t{maxx}, t{maxy}, t{maxz} using the actual ray origin. 3. Initialize t{entry} = 0.0. 4. Loop while the current voxel indices remain within grid bounds: a. Record the current cell and the interval [t{entry}, t{exit}] where t{exit} = \min(t{maxx}, t{maxy}, t{maxz}). b. Identify the axis k with the minimum t{max}. c. Advance the index in axis k: \text{index}k \leftarrow \text{index}k + sk. d. Update the boundary distance for axis k: t{maxk} \leftarrow t{maxk} + t{\Delta k}. e. Update t{entry} \leftarrow t{exit}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def uniformgridtraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, gridmin, gridmax, resolution): # 1. Voxel sizes dx = (gridmax[0] - gridmin[0]) / resolution[0] dy = (gridmax[1] - gridmin[1]) / resolution[1] dz = (gridmax[2] - gridmin[2]) / resolution[2] # 2. Step directions and delta distances stepx = 1 if raydirection[0] > 0 else (-1 if raydirection[0] < 0 else 0) stepy = 1 if raydirection[1] > 0 else (-1 if raydirection[1] < 0 else 0) stepz = 1 if raydirection[2] > 0 else (-1 if raydirection[2] < 0 else 0) tdeltax = dx / abs(raydirection[0]) if raydirection[0] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltay = dy / abs(raydirection[1]) if raydirection[1] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltaz = dz / abs(raydirection[2]) if raydirection[2] != 0 else float('inf') # 3. Initial voxel indices (clamped to grid bounds) i = int((rayorigin[0] - gridmin[0]) / dx) j = int((rayorigin[1] - gridmin[1]) / dy) k = int((rayorigin[2] - gridmin[2]) / dz) i = max(0, min(resolution[0] - 1, i)) j = max(0, min(resolution[1] - 1, j)) k = max(0, min(resolution[2] - 1, k)) # 4. Initial tmax (distance to next boundary from ACTUAL origin) bx = (i + 1) dx + gridmin[0] if stepx == 1 else i dx + gridmin[0] by = (j + 1) dy + gridmin[1] if stepy == 1 else j dy + gridmin[1] bz = (k + 1) dz + gridmin[2] if stepz == 1 else k dz + gridmin[2] tmaxx = (bx - rayorigin[0]) / raydirection[0] if raydirection[0] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = (by - rayorigin[1]) / raydirection[1] if raydirection[1] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxz = (bz - rayorigin[2]) / raydirection[2] if raydirection[2] != 0 else float('inf') tentry = 0.0 visited = [] # 5. Traversal loop while 0 <= i < resolution[0] and 0 <= j < resolution[1] and 0 <= k < resolution[2]: texit = min(tmaxx, tmaxy, tmaxz) visited.append((i, j, k, tentry, texit)) if tmaxx <= tmaxy and tmaxx <= tmaxz: i += stepx tmaxx += tdeltax elif tmaxy <= tmaxx and tmaxy <= tmaxz: j += stepy tmaxy += tdeltay else: k += stepz tmaxz += tdeltaz tentry = texit return visited Parameters: Grid Resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz): No analytical formula exists for the optimal resolution. Empirically, a resolution yielding roughly one particle per voxel achieves optimum performance for uniformly distributed particles. For the Bench scene with 2 \times 10^5 particles, 60 \times 60 \times 60 is optimal. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction: If a ray component is zero, t{\Delta} becomes infinite, and the ray never crosses a grid plane in that dimension; the step direction is set to 0 and t{max} is initialized to \infty. Precision Errors: Intersections exactly on grid boundaries may suffer from floating-point rounding; standard practice is to treat the ray as having just entered the voxel or to apply a small epsilon guard. Low Resolution: If grid resolution is much lower than optimal (e.g., < 60 \times 60 \times 60 for the Bench scene), performance degrades because too many particles reside in each voxel. Computational Space Traversal renders data on curvilinear grids by mapping the irregular physical domain to a regular computational space. It solves the difficulty of resampling scalar values along a ray in distorted geometry by performing the traversal in the regular computational space, where standard incremental grid traversal applies. Unlike Uniform Grid Traversal, which assumes uniform spacing, this method handles arbitrary hexahedral meshes by transforming ray segments and vectors using Jacobian matrices. Grid Traversal Setup (DDA) initializes the parameters required for a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) to traverse a voxel grid along a ray. It computes the initial voxel indices, step directions, and distances to the next voxel boundaries for the ray start and end points within the traversal range. This method sets the stage for the iterative traversal loop, distinguishing itself from computational space traversal by operating directly in grid coordinates and from one-pass over-allocated methods by computing exact boundary distances. It solves the problem of robustly determining where a ray enters a voxel grid and how it progresses through adjacent voxels, handling edge cases such as rays parallel to grid axes. A single-pass algorithm to traverse voxel grids, using pre-allocated maximum memory to avoid a second pass. It differs from Grid Traversal (Two-Pass) by allocating buffers large enough for the worst-case scenario upfront, trading memory for a single kernel launch. Robust Grid Traversal is a grid traversal modification that prevents numerical robustness errors by keeping the closest intersection parameter even if it falls outside the current cell, terminating only when the cell's maximum ray parameter exceeds this closest intersection. A compact 64-way full tree that summarizes the occupancy of an underlying uniform grid in a hierarchy, designed to speed up grid traversals on a GPU. Each node in the tree represents a voxel, with its occupancy represented by a single bit. Each node is subdivided into a 64-subgrid, which is stored in a single 64-bit word. The micro 64-tree is built on top of a uniform grid. The GPU grid construction algorithm is improved by computing precise triangle-cell intersections. Non-overlapping triangle-cell pairs are precluded before sorting during the construction phase. The micro 64-tree is built bottom-up from the uniform grid using parallel reductions. The top levels of the micro 64-tree are pre-loaded into the shared memory of a GPU to support on-chip traversals across coarse levels. The traversal algorithm navigates the ray through the 64-subgrids at different levels. A concise context for each level is stored in the GPU's registers to facilitate vertical moves during traversal. The micro 64-tree reduces traversal steps, decreases memory bandwidth consumption, and significantly improves the efficiency of ray tracing on a GPU, with small overheads in memory and building time. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The traversal cost per ray is proportional to the number of voxels visited. In the worst case (ray passing through all voxels), it is O(Nx + Ny + Nz). In practice, it is much faster due to empty space skipping. Memory: The grid requires O(Nx Ny Nz) space to store the voxel data or occupancy flags. Measured Performance: In the Bench scene with 2 \times 10^5 particles, optimal performance is achieved at a grid resolution of 60 \times 60 \times 60. Runtime grows steadily as grid resolution increases due to additional grid traversal costs. A resolution much lower than optimal (e.g., < 60 \times 60 \times 60 for the Bench scene) results in poor performance because too many particles reside in each voxel. Scaling: Performance scales with the number of particles and the efficiency of the grid traversal. Higher resolutions reduce the number of particles per voxel but increase traversal overhead. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Effective for uniformly distributed data. Limitations: Sensitive to resolution choice. When to Use: Use when data is uniformly distributed and the scene is dense enough to benefit from spatial partitioning. When Not to Use: Do not use for non-uniform or curvilinear grids without modification (use Computational Space Traversal instead). Uniform Grid Traversal is commonly used in volume rendering and particle rendering to accelerate ray traversal for uniformly distributed particles. Rendering discrete participating media using geometrical optics approximation, https://doi.org/10.1007/s41095-021-0253-5, fetched 2026-10-26 A micro 64-tree structure for accelerating ray tracing on a GPU, https://openalex.org/W195613556, fetched 2026-10-24 (abstract only, unofficial)

name: Robust Grid Traversal
head: Robust Ray Traversal
body: Robust Grid Traversal is a modification to standard Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) grid traversal designed to prevent numerical robustness errors where valid intersections are missed due to floating-point precision limits. It solves the problem of rejecting valid intersection candidates simply because their computed parameter falls outside the bounds of the currently visited cell due to rounding errors. Unlike traditional methods that discard such intersections, this method retains the closest intersection parameter globally and terminates only when the ray's maximum parameter for the current cell exceeds that retained value. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), grid bounds, cell size, and a list of primitives (e.g., triangles) associated with each cell. Output: The closest intersection point \mathbf{p} and its parameter t{hit}, or null if no intersection is found. Data Structures: Ray State: t{min}: Current cell entry parameter. t{max}: Current cell exit parameter. t{hit}: The parameter of the closest valid intersection found so far. Initialized to \infty. Grid: Uniform grid mapping cells to primitive lists. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute the initial t{min} and t{max} for the first cell entered by the ray. Set t{hit} = \infty. 2. Traversal Loop: While t{min} < t{hit}: a. Process Cell: For each primitive in the current cell, compute the intersection parameter t{prim}. b. Update Hit: If t{prim} < t{hit}, update t{hit} = t{prim}. Note: Standard intersection tests should be used here. c. Advance Ray: Compute the next cell boundaries. Update t{min} and t{max} for the next cell. d. Check Termination: If t{max} \ge t{hit}, terminate and return the intersection corresponding to t{hit}. 3. Return: If the loop completes without finding an intersection, return null. Key Modification: The critical distinction from standard DDA is the termination condition and the handling of intersection candidates. In standard DDA, an intersection computed for a primitive in cell Ci is often discarded if its parameter t is not within the spatial bounds of Ci (i.e., t < t{min}^{Ci} or t > t{max}^{Ci}). Robust Grid Traversal retains t{hit} regardless of whether it falls within the current cell's spatial bounds. The traversal continues until the ray's exit parameter from the current cell (t{max}) exceeds the closest hit found so far (t{hit}). This ensures that even if precision errors place a valid intersection slightly outside the current cell's computed bounds, it is not discarded prematurely. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def robustgridtraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, grid, primitives): # Initialize ray state tmin, tmax = computefirstcellbounds(rayorigin, raydirection, grid) thit = float('inf') # Traverse cells while tmin < thit: # Get primitives in the current cell cellprimitives = grid.getprimitivesatcurrentcell() # Check intersections with primitives for prim in cellprimitives: tprim = intersect(rayorigin, raydirection, prim) if tprim is not None and tprim < thit: thit = tprim # Advance to next cell tmin, tmax = computenextcellbounds(rayorigin, raydirection, grid) # Termination check: if the ray has passed the closest hit, stop if tmax >= thit: break if thit == float('inf'): return None else: return computeintersectionpoint(rayorigin, raydirection, thit) Parameters: No specific epsilon parameters are required, as the method avoids scene-dependent epsilon tests. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Errors: Standard DDA may reject intersections on grid bounding boxes or implied planes if they fall outside the current cell due to numerical errors. This method mitigates that by keeping the closest intersection parameter even if it falls outside the current cell. Termination: The loop must terminate when t{max} \ge t{hit} to avoid infinite loops or unnecessary traversal. Cell-Local Ray Traversal is a ray-grid traversal method that computes cell-exit points and traversal distances using a normalized coordinate system local to each cell, preventing numerical drift and angle errors that accumulate when using global or canvas coordinates. Time Complexity: Same as standard DDA, O(N) where N is the number of cells traversed, plus intersection tests for primitives in visited cells. Memory Complexity: Same as standard DDA. Performance: No significant performance overhead compared to standard DDA, as it avoids the need for complex epsilon tuning. Strengths: Eliminates the need for scene-dependent epsilon tests, which are hard to choose correctly. Prevents missed intersections due to numerical robustness errors. Limitations: Requires storing and comparing t{hit} against t{max}, but this is minimal overhead. When to Use: When high numerical precision is critical, or when working with low-precision floating-point formats on mobile hardware. When standard DDA misses intersections due to precision errors. Robust Grid Traversal was introduced to address numerical robustness issues in grid-based ray tracing. While traditional methods like those by Cleary and Wyvill [CW88] are susceptible to these errors, Robust Grid Traversal provides a simple modification to existing methods. It is used by some researchers in the field [PH04], although many sources still discard intersections [Shi00, Suf07]. The method is particularly relevant in contexts where numerical stability is paramount, such as in mobile hardware or high-precision rendering applications. name: Cell-Local Ray Traversal
head: Accurate Ray Traversal
body: Cell-Local Ray Traversal is a ray-grid traversal method that computes cell-exit points and traversal distances using a normalized coordinate system local to each cell, preventing numerical drift and angle errors that accumulate when using global or canvas coordinates. It sets itself apart from Uniform Grid Traversal and Robust Grid Traversal by decoupling the precision of the intersection calculation from the global scale of the scene, allowing accurate traversal even with low-precision floating-point formats on mobile hardware. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray direction d, current cell-entry point pi in global coordinates, current cell geometry (center, size), and a neighbor texture mapping exit faces to neighbor indices. Output: Next cell-entry point p{i+1}^0 in the neighbor's local coordinate system, and the neighbor cell index. Data Structures: Cell-Local Coordinate System: Origin at cell center, cell size normalized to 1, coordinates range from [-0.5, 0.5] along each axis. Neighbor Texture: A lookup structure mapping the exit face of the current cell to the index of the adjacent neighbor cell. Steps: 1. Transform the global cell-entry point pi into the cell-local coordinate system, yielding pi^{local} = (px, py, pz). 2. Compute the cell-traversal distance ti and the cell-exit point pi^0 in local coordinates, and identify the neighboring cell N containing pi^0. 3. Find the face containing pi^0 with respect to the cell coordinate system. 4. Use the intersecting face and the neighbor texture to choose the neighbor cell (the i+1-th cell) to visit. 5. Update pi^0 to p{i+1}^0, the entry point for the next cell in its local coordinate system. 6. Repeat until the ray accumulates full opacity or exits the canvas. Formulas: Cell-traversal distance for the top surface (positive y-direction): ti = (0.5 - py) / dy, where py is the y-component of pi^{local} and dy is the y-component of d. Floating-point representation error model: f(x + y) = (x + y)(1 + \epsilon+), with \epsilon+ \le \epsilon. Error in computed exit point: f(pi^0) = (pi + ti)(1 + 3\epsilonp), for some \epsilonp \le \epsilon. Error in next cell entry point: p{i+1} = ((pi + ti)s + c)(1 + 5\epsiloni), where s and c are scale and shift factors depending on depth and location, and \epsiloni \le \epsilon. Total error bound: e{total} \le e0 + 7.5 \epsilon L, where e0 is the initial eye location error and L is ray length. Ray angle error bound: \sin^{-1}(\sqrt{2(e0/L + 7.5\epsilon)}), which does not increase as a function of L. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def celllocaltraversal(raydirection, piglobal, cellcenter, cellsize, neighbortexture): # Step 1: Transform to local coordinates (origin at center, size normalized to 1) plocal = (piglobal - cellcenter) / cellsize # Step 2 & 3: Compute traversal distance and exit point, identify exit face # Compute t for each axis, handle zero direction components tx = (0.5 - plocal.x) / raydirection.x if raydirection.x != 0 else float('inf') txneg = (-0.5 - plocal.x) / raydirection.x if raydirection.x != 0 else float('inf') ty = (0.5 - plocal.y) / raydirection.y if raydirection.y != 0 else float('inf') tyneg = (-0.5 - plocal.y) / raydirection.y if raydirection.y != 0 else float('inf') tz = (0.5 - plocal.z) / raydirection.z if raydirection.z != 0 else float('inf') tzneg = (-0.5 - plocal.z) / raydirection.z if raydirection.z != 0 else float('inf') # Find minimum positive t and corresponding face tcandidates = [ (tx, 'X'), (txneg, '-X'), (ty, 'Y'), (tyneg, '-Y'), (tz, 'Z'), (tzneg, '-Z') ] ti, face = min((t, f) for t, f in tcandidates if t >= 0) pexitlocal = plocal + ti raydirection # Step 4: Lookup neighbor using face nextcellindex = neighbortexture[face] # Step 5: Transform exit point to next cell's local system # Convert exit point to global, then to next cell's local coordinates pexitglobal = cellcenter + cellsize pexitlocal # Neighbor geometry (center, size) must be fetched from the hierarchy; # exact scale/shift depends on depth and location # pnextlocal = (pexitglobal - neighborcenter) / neighborsize # For self-contained pseudocode, we assume neighbor geometry is available: neighborcenter, neighborsize = getneighborgeometry(nextcellindex) pnextlocal = (pexitglobal - neighborcenter) / neighborsize return nextcellindex, pnextlocal Parameters: Machine epsilon \epsilon: 2^{-23} for single precision, 1/1024 for half precision. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Global coordinates cause high inaccuracy and ray drift due to large cell size variations and space coverage. Parallel rays (dx=0, etc.) require skipping the division for that axis and checking other axes. Precision limits: The angle error bound remains constant regardless of ray length L, preventing cumulative drift. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Maximum ray-angle error of 7.5 \times 10^{-9} degrees and position error of 2.5 \times 10^{-7} in L2 norm. Enables ray-casting on mobile GPUs with half-precision floats (\epsilon = 1/1024). Strengths: Eliminates ray drift and large angle errors from global coordinates; accuracy is independent of zoom level or global coordinate magnitude. Limitations: Requires coordinate transformations and neighbor texture lookups per cell. When to use: Large volumetric scenes with varying cell sizes (e.g., deep octrees) where global coordinates cause precision loss, or on mobile/low-precision hardware. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Cell-Local Ray Traversal was introduced in the CanvoX system for high-resolution VR painting in large volumetric canvases. It addresses floating-point precision issues in deep octree structures where cell sizes vary significantly and global coordinates span large ranges. The method was demonstrated on an Nvidia GTX 980Ti GPU and HTC Vive, showing that accurate ray-casting is feasible even with half-precision floats on mobile GPUs. name: Computational Space Traversal
head: Frühauf's Curvilinear Grid Traversal, Frühauf's method
body: Computational Space Traversal renders data on curvilinear grids by mapping the irregular physical domain to a regular computational space. It solves the difficulty of resampling scalar values along a ray in distorted geometry by performing the traversal in the regular computational space, where standard incremental grid traversal applies. Unlike Uniform Grid Traversal, which assumes uniform spacing, this method handles arbitrary hexahedral meshes by transforming ray segments and vectors using Jacobian matrices. Inputs: A curvilinear grid defined by vertex positions in physical space and their connectivity; a ray defined by origin and direction in physical space; a viewpoint. Outputs: Sampled scalar values along the ray path in physical space. Data Structures: Grid: Vertices with physical coordinates and computational coordinates following integer indices (i, j, k). Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are Not given in the sources. Jacobian: Pre-computed or on-the-fly approximations at vertices or cell centers. Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are Not given in the sources. Bending Vectors: Pre-computed vectors used to adjust the ray direction at cell boundaries. Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Locate Initial Cell: Determine the starting hexahedral cell containing the ray origin by extracting unshared boundary faces and building a spatial index over them. 2. Approximate Jacobian: Approximate the Jacobian matrix using central differences of adjacent vertices in computational and physical space. 3. Transform to Computational Space: Map the ray origin and direction from physical space to computational space using the Jacobian matrix. 4. Incremental Traversal: Perform standard incremental grid traversal in the regular computational space to determine the sequence of cells and face intersections. 5. Bend Ray at Intersections: At each face intersection in computational space, transform the intersection point and the ray direction back to physical space. The ray direction is bent according to pre-computed bending vectors using bilinear interpolation. 6. Resample Values: Sample the scalar field values at the transformed physical positions. 7. Optimization (Viewpoint Update): Store and update bending vectors along a ray only when the viewpoint changes. If mapping parameters change but the viewpoint remains the same, pre-computed ray paths can be reused directly. Formulas: The exact transformation equations for mapping vertices, vectors, and rays between physical and computational space are Not given in the sources. The exact formula for central differences is Not given in the sources. Parameters: Interpolation: Bilinear interpolation is specified for determining bending vectors at face intersections. Jacobian Approximation: Central differences are used for adjacent vertices. Typical values are Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: Degenerate cells causing singular Jacobians are not discussed in the sources. Precision: Floating-point errors from coordinate transformations are not discussed in the sources. Initial Cell Location: Finding the initial cell in a complex curvilinear mesh requires extracting boundary faces and building a spatial index, which can be expensive. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computationalspacetraversal(grid, rayorigin, raydirection, viewpoint): # 1. Locate initial cell containing ray origin currentcell = findcellcontainingpoint(grid, rayorigin) # 2. Approximate Jacobian using central differences of adjacent vertices # in computational and physical space # Exact formula not given in the sources. J = centraldifferencejacobian(currentcell, grid) # 3. Transform ray origin and direction to computational space comporigin = applyjacobianinverse(J, rayorigin) compdir = applyjacobianinversevector(J, raydirection) # 4. Incremental grid traversal in regular computational space while not rayexitsgrid(comporigin, compdir): # Find next face intersection in computational space t, faceidx = nextregulargridintersection(comporigin, compdir) comphit = comporigin + t compdir # 5. Transform intersection point back to physical space physhit = applyjacobian(J, comphit) # Bend ray direction using pre-computed bending vectors # via bilinear interpolation at the face bendvec = bilinearinterpolatebendingvectors(faceidx, grid) physdir = applybendingvector(physdir, bendvec) # 6. Resample scalar values at physical position yield resamplescalarat(grid, physhit) # Advance traversal comporigin = comphit currentcell = getadjacentcell(currentcell, faceidx) J = centraldifferencejacobian(currentcell, grid) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: No performance measurements were reported in the original source. Strengths: Greatly reduces the difficulties of resampling along the ray since the computational space is regular. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of Jacobians and bending vectors. When to use: When rendering data on curvilinear grids where resampling in physical space is complex. When not to use: When performance measurements are critical and not available, or for uniform grids where Uniform Grid Traversal is simpler. Origin: Introduced by Frühauf in [Frü94]. History: Described in the context of interactive volume rendering with ray tracing. Usage: Used for rendering data on curvilinear grids, particularly hexahedral meshes. name: Grid Traversal Setup (DDA)
head: DDA Ray Casting for Voxel Grids, Digital Differential Analyzer ray casting, Ray marching grid setup, Voxel Traversal Algorithm, Voxel traversal initialization
body: Grid Traversal Setup (DDA) initializes the parameters required for a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) to traverse a voxel grid along a ray. It computes the initial voxel indices, step directions, and distances to the next voxel boundaries for the ray start and end points within the traversal range. The method solves the problem of robustly determining where a ray enters a voxel grid and how it progresses through adjacent voxels, handling edge cases such as rays parallel to grid axes. Inputs: ray.origin: 3D vector, ray origin in world space. ray.dir: 3D vector, ray direction in world space (normalized). ray.invdir: 3D vector, inverse of ray direction (1.0 / ray.dir). tmin: float, near plane distance along the ray. tmax: float, far plane distance along the ray. aabb.min: 3D vector, minimum corner of the grid's axis-aligned bounding box in world space. aabb.max: 3D vector, maximum corner of the grid's axis-aligned bounding box in world space. resolution: 3D integer vector, number of voxels along each axis (Nx, Ny, Nz). eps: float, small epsilon value for numerical stability (e.g., 10^{-6}). Outputs: currentindex: 3D integer vector, the voxel index containing the ray start point. finalindex: 3D integer vector, the voxel index containing the ray end point. tdist: 3D float vector, distance along the ray to the next voxel boundary in each axis direction. delta: 3D float vector, distance along the ray to traverse one voxel in each axis direction. stepindex: 3D integer vector, direction of increment for each axis (+1 or 0). Data Structures: float3: 3-component floating-point vector. int3: 3-component integer vector. makefloat3(x, y, z): Constructs a float3. makeint3(x, y, z): Constructs an int3. clamp(v, minval, maxval): Clamps value v to [minval, maxval]. applycontraction(point, aabbmin, aabbmax): Maps a world-space point to the range [0, 1] along each axis relative to the AABB. Specifically, for each component i, it computes \frac{pointi - aabb\mini}{aabb\maxi - aabb\mini}. Steps: 1. Compute Voxel Size: Calculate the physical size of a single voxel. voxel\size = \frac{aabb.max - aabb.min}{resolution} 2. Compute Ray Start and End Points: Determine the world-space positions of the ray at tmin and tmax, adjusted by epsilon to avoid boundary precision issues. ray\start = ray.origin + ray.dir \times (tmin + eps) ray\end = ray.origin + ray.dir \times (tmax - eps) 3. Compute Current and Final Voxel Indices: Map the start and end points to voxel indices. First, apply contraction to map world coordinates to [0, 1] range relative to the AABB. contracted\start = apply\contraction(ray\start, aabb.min, aabb.max) contracted\end = apply\contraction(ray\end, aabb.min, aabb.max) Then, scale by resolution and clamp to valid voxel indices [0, resolution - 1]. current\index = clamp(contracted\start \times resolution, 0, resolution - 1) final\index = clamp(contracted\end \times resolution, 0, resolution - 1) 4. Compute Step Direction (stepindex): Determine the direction of traversal for each axis based on the ray direction. step\index = make\int3( \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } ray.dir.x > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } ray.dir.y > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } ray.dir.z > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}) 5. Compute Distance to Next Boundary (tdist): Calculate the distance along the ray to the next voxel boundary for each axis. First, compute the start index for boundary calculation: start\index = current\index + step\index Calculate the intermediate distance to the boundary plane: tmax\xyz = \left( \left( aabb.min + (start\index \times voxel\size) - ray\start \right) \times ray.inv\dir \right) + tmin Handle rays parallel to axes (where ray.dir component is 0) to avoid division by zero or invalid distances. If the ray direction component is 0, set the corresponding tdist component to tmax. Otherwise, use the calculated tmaxxyz component. tdist.x = \begin{cases} tmax & \text{if } ray.dir.x == 0.0f \\ tmax\xyz.x & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} tdist.y = \begin{cases} tmax & \text{if } ray.dir.y == 0.0f \\ tmax\xyz.y & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} tdist.z = \begin{cases} tmax & \text{if } ray.dir.z == 0.0f \\ tmax\xyz.z & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 6. Compute Step Distance (delta): Calculate the distance along the ray to traverse one voxel in each axis direction. First, compute the step float vector: step\float.x = \begin{cases} 0.0f & \text{if } ray.dir.x == 0.0f \\ 1.0f & \text{if } ray.dir.x > 0.0f \\ -1.0f & \text{if } ray.dir.x < 0.0f \end{cases} (Similarly for y and z) Calculate the raw delta: delta\temp = voxel\size \times ray.inv\dir \times step\float Handle rays parallel to axes. If the ray direction component is 0, set the corresponding delta component to 0. delta.x = \begin{cases} 0.0f & \text{if } ray.dir.x == 0.0f \\ delta\temp.x & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} (Similarly for y and z) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clamp(v, lo, hi): return lo if v < lo else (hi if v > hi else v) def gridtraversalsetup(rayorigin, raydir, rayinvdir, tmin, tmax, aabbmin, aabbmax, resolution, eps): # 1. Compute Voxel Size voxelsize = (aabbmax - aabbmin) / resolution # 2. Compute Ray Start and End Points raystart = rayorigin + raydir (tmin + eps) rayend = rayorigin + raydir (tmax - eps) # 3. Compute Current and Final Voxel Indices # Contraction: map world point to [0, 1] relative to AABB contractedstart = (raystart - aabbmin) / (aabbmax - aabbmin) contractedend = (rayend - aabbmin) / (aabbmax - aabbmin) # Scale by resolution and clamp currentindex = clamp(contractedstart resolution, 0, resolution - 1) finalindex = clamp(contractedend resolution, 0, resolution - 1) # 4. Compute Step Direction (stepindex) stepindexx = 1 if raydir.x > 0 else 0 stepindexy = 1 if raydir.y > 0 else 0 stepindexz = 1 if raydir.z > 0 else 0 stepindex = (stepindexx, stepindexy, stepindexz) # 5. Compute Distance to Next Boundary (tdist) startindex = currentindex + stepindex # Intermediate distance to boundary plane boundaryplanepos = aabbmin + (startindex voxelsize) tmaxxyz = ((boundaryplanepos - raystart) rayinvdir) + tmin # Handle zero direction components tdistx = tmax if raydir.x == 0.0 else tmaxxyz.x tdisty = tmax if raydir.y == 0.0 else tmaxxyz.y tdistz = tmax if raydir.z == 0.0 else tmaxxyz.z tdist = (tdistx, tdisty, tdistz) # 6. Compute Step Distance (delta) # Step float for direction magnitude stepfloatx = 0.0 if raydir.x == 0.0 else (1.0 if raydir.x > 0.0 else -1.0) stepfloaty = 0.0 if raydir.y == 0.0 else (1.0 if raydir.y > 0.0 else -1.0) stepfloatz = 0.0 if raydir.z == 0.0 else (1.0 if raydir.z > 0.0 else -1.0) stepfloat = (stepfloatx, stepfloaty, stepfloatz) # Raw delta deltatemp = voxelsize rayinvdir stepfloat # Handle zero direction components deltax = 0.0 if raydir.x == 0.0 else deltatemp.x deltay = 0.0 if raydir.y == 0.0 else deltatemp.y deltaz = 0.0 if raydir.z == 0.0 else deltatemp.z delta = (deltax, deltay, deltaz) return currentindex, finalindex, tdist, delta, stepindex Binary Grid Ray Traversal Initialization computes the initial distances to the next voxel boundaries (tdist) and the distance steps between adjacent voxels (delta) for a ray traversing a binary occupancy grid. It handles rays parallel to grid axes by clamping distances to tmax and setting steps to zero, ensuring robust traversal without division by zero. It differs from continuous volume rendering methods by operating on discrete binary occupancy, making it suitable for sparse or binary voxel representations where only presence/absence matters. Precomputes a 3D ray traversal pattern (DDA-like) for light rays to avoid per-ray floating-point division during rendering. It sets up a fixed-size lookup table of integer voxel offsets, allowing the renderer to step through a uniform grid using only integer arithmetic and addition, significantly reducing the computational cost of ray traversal. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, storing only a few vectors. Strengths: Robust handling of edge cases (parallel rays, boundary conditions); efficient setup for subsequent DDA traversal. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of invdir and careful epsilon handling to avoid precision errors at boundaries. When to use: When traversing uniform voxel grids for ray marching or volume rendering. When not to use: For non-uniform grids or hierarchical structures (e.g., octrees) where different traversal logic is required. The Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) for grid traversal is a classic algorithm in computer graphics that leverages the orthogonality of the grid to determine the next neighboring voxel the ray intersects. It initializes parameters for a 3D DDA to traverse a voxel grid along a ray, computing step directions, initial indices, and distances to voxel boundaries. name: - `step_index`: Integer step direction $(s_x, s_y, s_z)$ for index updates [S1, unofficial].
body: Data Structures: Vectors are 3-component floats. stepindex is a 3-component integer vector. Steps: 1. Calculate Start Index: Compute the index of the next voxel to enter: \text{start\index} = \text{current\index} + \text{index\delta} 2. Calculate Distance to Next Voxel Start (tmaxxyz): Compute the distance from the ray origin to the start of the next voxel in each dimension. The formula accounts for the grid origin (aabbmin), the voxel size, and the current ray position relative to tmin: \text{tmax\xyz} = \left( (\text{aabb\min} + (\text{start\index} \times \text{voxel\size}) - \text{ray\start}) \times \text{ray\inv\dir} \right) + \text{tmin} Note: Multiplication is component-wise. 3. Initialize tdist (Distance to Next Boundary): For each axis c \in \{x, y, z\}: If \text{ray\inv\dir}c = 0 (ray parallel to axis): \text{tdist}c = \text{tmax} Else: \text{tdist}c = \text{tmax\xyz}c 4. Initialize stepfloat (Direction Vector): For each axis c \in \{x, y, z\}: If \text{ray\inv\dir}c = 0: \text{step\float}c = 0.0 Else if \text{ray\inv\dir}c > 0 (equivalent to direction > 0): \text{step\float}c = 1.0 Else: \text{step\float}c = -1.0 5. Convert to Integer Step: \text{step\index} = \text{round}(\text{step\float}) 6. Calculate deltatemp (Voxel Crossing Distance): Compute the distance traveled along the ray to cross one voxel in each dimension: \text{delta\temp} = \text{voxel\size} \times \text{ray\inv\dir} \times \text{step\float} Note: Multiplication is component-wise. 7. Initialize delta (Step Size): For each axis c \in \{x, y, z\}: If \text{ray\inv\dir}c = 0: \text{delta}c = \text{tmax} Else: \text{delta}c = \text{delta\temp}c Pseudocode: python def binarygridraytraversalinitialization( raystart, rayinvdir, voxelsize, aabbmin, currentindex, indexdelta, tmin, tmax): # Step 1: Calculate start index startindex = currentindex + indexdelta # Step 2: Calculate tmaxxyz # Component-wise operations voxeloffset = aabbmin + (startindex voxelsize) diff = voxeloffset - raystart tmaxxyz = (diff rayinvdir) + tmin # Step 3: Initialize tdist tdist = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in range(3): if rayinvdir[c] == 0.0: tdist[c] = tmax else: tdist[c] = tmaxxyz[c] # Step 4: Initialize stepfloat stepfloat = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in range(3): if rayinvdir[c] == 0.0: stepfloat[c] = 0.0 elif rayinvdir[c] > 0.0: stepfloat[c] = 1.0 else: stepfloat[c] = -1.0 # Step 5: Convert to integer step stepindex = [int(round(s)) for s in stepfloat] # Step 6: Calculate deltatemp deltatemp = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in range(3): deltatemp[c] = voxelsize rayinvdir[c] stepfloat[c] # Step 7: Initialize delta delta = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in range(3): if rayinvdir[c] == 0.0: delta[c] = tmax else: delta[c] = deltatemp[c] return tdist, delta, stepindex Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Rays: If rayinvdir is 0 for any axis, the ray never crosses a boundary in that dimension. The code clamps tdist and delta to tmax and sets steps to 0 to avoid division by zero and infinite loops. ## Subtopics ### Binary Grid Ray Traversal (Single Voxel Step) Advances the ray through a single voxel by updating the index and checking boundaries. It is the core iterative step following initialization. It differs from parent methods by performing the actual index update and boundary check rather than just setting up initial parameters. Choose it when traversing a binary occupancy grid where only presence/absence matters. ## Operating characteristics Not given in the sources. ## Background This method is part of the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal technique for uniform grids. It is implemented in the CNC (Compressed Neural Fields) project, which uses binary voxel mix encoding for efficient neural field representation. ## Sources YihangChen-ee/CNC, https://github.com/YihangChen-ee/CNC, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Binary Grid Ray Traversal (Single Voxel Step)
head: AABB traversal step
body: This method advances a ray through a single voxel in a binary occupancy grid by determining the exit axis, updating the voxel index, and checking for grid boundary overflow. It is the core iterative step of the Binary Grid Ray Traversal algorithm, following initialization. Unlike continuous volume rendering which samples density, this method operates on discrete binary occupancy, making it suitable for sparse or binary voxel representations where only presence/absence matters. It differs from parent methods by performing the actual index update and boundary check rather than just setting up initial parameters. Inputs and Outputs: currentindex: A 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the current voxel coordinates. tdist: A 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the distance from the ray origin to the next voxel boundary along each axis. delta: A 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the distance between adjacent voxel boundaries along each axis (pre-computed by initialization). stepindex: A 3D vector (x, y, z) containing +1 or -1 indicating the traversal direction along each axis. overflowindex: A 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the grid dimensions (or boundary indices) where traversal must stop. Output: A boolean indicating whether the ray remains within the valid grid bounds (true) or has exited (false). Data Structures: The algorithm assumes currentindex, tdist, delta, stepindex, and overflowindex are 3-component vectors (e.g., vec3 in GLSL or numpy.array in Python). No specific bit-packing is required for the traversal step itself, as it operates on floating-point distances and integer indices. Steps: 1. Determine Exit Axis: Compare tdist.x, tdist.y, and tdist.z to find the minimum distance to the next boundary. If tdist.x < tdist.y and tdist.x < tdist.z, the ray exits through the X-axis. Else, if tdist.y < tdist.z, the ray exits through the Y-axis. Else, the ray exits through the Z-axis. 2. Update Index and Distance: Based on the selected axis, update the currentindex and tdist. X-axis: currentindex.x += stepindex.x and tdist.x += delta.x. Y-axis: currentindex.y += stepindex.y and tdist.y += delta.y. Z-axis: currentindex.z += stepindex.z and tdist.z += delta.z. 3. Check Overflow: Verify if the updated index has exceeded the grid boundaries. If the updated index component equals the corresponding overflowindex component, the ray has exited the valid grid. Return false. Otherwise, return true. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def singlevoxelstep(currentindex, tdist, delta, stepindex, overflowindex): """ Advances ray through one voxel in a binary grid. Args: currentindex: vec3, current voxel coordinates tdist: vec3, distance to next boundary on each axis delta: vec3, distance between adjacent boundaries on each axis stepindex: vec3, direction (+1 or -1) for each axis overflowindex: vec3, grid boundary indices Returns: bool: True if ray is still within grid, False if out of bounds """ # Determine which axis has the minimum distance to the next boundary if tdist.x < tdist.y and tdist.x < tdist.z: # Exit through X-axis currentindex.x += stepindex.x tdist.x += delta.x if currentindex.x == overflowindex.x: return False elif tdist.y < tdist.z: # Exit through Y-axis currentindex.y += stepindex.y tdist.y += delta.y if currentindex.y == overflowindex.y: return False else: # Exit through Z-axis currentindex.z += stepindex.z tdist.z += delta.z if currentindex.z == overflowindex.z: return False return True Parameters and Edge Cases: Precision: Floating-point comparisons (<) are used. If tdist values are equal, the order of checks (X, then Y, then Z) determines the axis, providing a deterministic tie-breaking rule. Parallel Rays: The parent initialization step handles rays parallel to axes by setting delta to 0 and tdist to tmax. This step assumes valid non-zero delta for the active axis, or that the ray has already terminated. If delta is 0 for the selected axis, tdist will not increase, potentially causing an infinite loop if not handled by the caller. However, the parent initialization ensures that for parallel rays, the traversal logic is adjusted or terminated. Overflow: The check currentindex == overflowindex assumes overflowindex represents the exclusive upper bound (or lower bound for negative directions). The exact meaning of overflowindex depends on the initialization step, but typically it is the grid dimension size for positive traversal. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel step. The comparison and update operations are constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. No additional data structures are allocated. Strengths: Extremely fast per-voxel update. Minimal branching compared to more complex traversal methods. Suitable for binary occupancy grids where density integration is not required. Limitations: Only advances one voxel at a time. Requires careful handling of parallel rays and boundary conditions, which are delegated to the initialization step. Not suitable for continuous volume rendering without additional sampling logic. When to Use: When rendering binary occupancy grids (e.g., sparse voxel octrees converted to uniform grids, or simple binary masks) where only the presence of geometry matters. When Not to Use: For continuous volume rendering requiring density integration, or for non-uniform grids where delta varies per voxel. This method is part of the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) ray traversal technique adapted for binary grids. It is commonly used in GPU-based volume rendering and ray marching for binary occupancy data. The implementation originates from the CNC repository. name: Anisotropic Grid Resolution for Ray Traversal
head: Anisotropic Grid Resolution for Radiation Walk, Anisotropic Voxel Grid Traversal, Directional Grid Optimization
body: Anisotropic Grid Resolution is a technique to optimize the cost of grid-based ray traversal by aligning voxel dimensions with the primary direction of ray travel, reducing the number of voxel steps required to traverse empty space. Unlike uniform grids where every voxel is the same size, anisotropic grids allow empty space to be crossed in fewer steps along the travel axis, directly reducing the walk cost which is proportional to distance travelled divided by voxel size. It sets itself apart from siblings like Binary Grid Ray Traversal Initialization by modifying the grid's geometric definition rather than the traversal algorithm's step logic. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The bounding volume of the scene, the distribution of ray origins and directions (or a representative sample), and the target total number of voxels (or memory budget). Output: A grid definition with anisotropic voxel dimensions (dx, dy, dz). Data Structures: The grid is defined by its dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz) and physical extents (Lx, Ly, Lz). The voxel sizes are: dx = \frac{Lx}{Nx}, \quad dy = \frac{Ly}{Ny}, \quad dz = \frac{Lz}{Nz} Unlike a uniform grid where dx \approx dy \approx dz, here the dimensions are optimized based on ray statistics. Steps: 1. Analyze Ray Distribution: Determine the dominant axis of travel for the ray population. For example, in a chamber with pipe cells, rays may travel primarily along the axial direction. 2. Determine Dominant Axis: Identify the axis along which rays travel the longest distance or have the highest density. Let this be the "axial" direction (e.g., x) and the others be "perpendicular" (e.g., y, z). 3. Size Grid Anisotropically: Use coarser voxels along the dominant travel axis. This reduces the number of steps required to traverse the length of the scene for rays aligned with that axis. Use finer voxels along perpendicular axes to maintain sufficient spatial resolution for geometry intersection or density sampling in those directions. 4. Calculate Voxel Dimensions: Set dx to be larger than dy and dz if x is the dominant axis. The total number of voxels N{total} = Nx Ny Nz should remain within the memory budget. Formulas: The cost of traversal is proportional to the number of steps. For a ray traveling distance D along axis i, the number of steps is N{steps} \approx D / vi, where vi is the voxel size along that axis. By increasing v{dominant}, N{steps} decreases. Parameters: Target voxel count: Determined by memory constraints. Anisotropy ratio: The ratio of coarse to fine voxel sizes. In the cited example, a 128³ grid over a long box resulted in 13.6 mm along x and much finer values across, compared to a default near-cubic grid of 8.2 mm. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Near-Cubic Default: The "near-cubic" rule is a shipped default that may be wrong for long thin vessels (like reactors). Scene Geometry: Assuming anisotropy is always better is risky; cube-ish scenes may prefer the current uniform rule. Ray Distribution: If rays are isotropic (random directions), anisotropic resolution may not provide significant benefits and could even degrade performance for non-dominant directions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeanisotropicgrid(scenebounds, raysample, targetvoxelcount): """ Compute anisotropic grid dimensions based on ray distribution. Args: scenebounds: Tuple (Lx, Ly, Lz) representing the physical extents of the scene. raysample: List of ray directions or a statistical summary of ray travel distances per axis. targetvoxelcount: Total number of voxels in the grid. Returns: Tuple (Nx, Ny, Nz) for the grid dimensions. """ Lx, Ly, Lz = scenebounds # Step 1: Analyze ray distribution to find dominant axis # Calculate average travel distance or ray density per axis # For simplicity, assume we have pre-computed weights wx, wy, wz # representing the importance or length of travel along each axis. # In the example, pipe cells have strong axial (x) travel. # Example heuristic: weight by inverse of expected step count # If rays travel mostly along X, we want fewer steps along X, so larger dx. # This implies Nx should be smaller relative to Ly/Lz if we keep total voxels constant. # Let's assume we have a metric 'travelweight' for each axis # travelweight[i] = sum of ray lengths projected on axis i travelweights = computetravelweights(raysample) # Helper to aggregate ray stats # Step 2: Determine dominant axis # The axis with the highest travel weight should have the coarsest voxels (fewest divisions) # However, to minimize total steps, we want voxel size proportional to travel distance? # Actually, the goal is to reduce steps. Steps = Distance / VoxelSize. # To reduce steps for long distances, we need LARGE voxel size. # So, VoxelSize[i] should be proportional to TravelDistance[i]? # But we are constrained by total voxel count. # Let's use the principle: VoxelSize[i] ~ TravelDistance[i]^(1/3) ? # Or simpler: Allocate more voxels to axes where geometry is complex or rays are dense? # The source says: "coarser voxels along the dominant travel axis". # This means if X is dominant, Nx is SMALLER. # Heuristic: Inverse proportionality between voxel count and travel weight? # If travel weight is high, we want fewer voxels (coarser grid) to skip empty space faster. # Normalize weights totalweight = sum(travelweights) weights = [w / totalweight for w in travelweights] # Allocate voxel counts inversely proportional to travel weight? # If X has high weight, we want small Nx. # Let's try: Nx ~ 1 / weightx # But we need to satisfy Nx Ny Nz = targetvoxelcount # Let's use a power law allocation # Nx = targetvoxelcount^(1/3) (1/weightx)^alpha # This is a guess. The source doesn't give a specific formula, just the concept. # Alternative: The source mentions a 128^3 grid vs 212x11x114. # The 212x11x114 grid is anisotropic. # It seems the grid dimensions are chosen to match the aspect ratio of the scene or ray paths. # Let's assume a simple approach: # 1. Identify dominant axis (max travel weight). # 2. Set voxel size along dominant axis to be larger. # 3. Keep voxel sizes along other axes smaller to maintain resolution. # Since no exact formula is given, we use a heuristic based on aspect ratio of travel. # Let's assume the scene bounds are fixed. # We want to minimize sum(Di / vi) subject to product(vi) = constant? # No, the cost is sum of steps. Stepsi = Di / vi. # Total steps = Dx/vx + Dy/vy + Dz/vz. # We want to minimize this sum subject to (Lx/vx) (Ly/vy) (Lz/vz) = Ntotal. # Let vx = Lx/Nx, etc. # Minimize Dx Nx / Lx + Dy Ny / Ly + Dz Nz / Lz # Subject to Nx Ny Nz = Ntotal. # Using Lagrange multipliers, the optimal Ni is proportional to sqrt(Di / Li). # But Di is the ray length, Li is the scene extent. # If rays span the whole scene, Di ~ Li. Then Ni ~ sqrt(1) = constant? # This suggests uniform grid is optimal if rays are isotropic and span the scene. # However, if rays are directional, e.g., Dx >> Dy, Dz. # Then Nx should be larger? No, wait. # Cost = Dx/vx. If Dx is large, we want vx to be large to reduce cost. # Large vx means small Nx. # So Nx should be SMALL if Dx is large. # Let's re-evaluate the Lagrange result. # Minimize sum(Ci Ni) where Ci = Di / Li. # Subject to product(Ni) = K. # Ni = K^(1/3) (1/Ci)^(1/3) ? # No, for sum(Ci Ni) with product(Ni)=K, the minimum is when Ci Ni are equal? # No, that's for sum(Ni) with product fixed? # Let's check: Nx = Ny = Nz -> Cost = sum(Ci) N. # If we vary Nx, Ny, Nz. # The optimal solution for minimizing sum(ai xi) subject to prod(xi)=C is xi proportional to 1/ai? # No, that's for sum(xi) with prod fixed? # Actually, for sum(ai xi) with prod(xi)=C, the minimum is when ai xi are all equal? # Let ax xx = ay xy = az xz = k. # Then xx = k/ax, xy = k/ay, xz = k/az. # prod(xi) = k^3 / (ax ay az) = C. # k = (C ax ay az)^(1/3). # So xi = (C ax ay az)^(1/3) / ai = C^(1/3) (ay az / ax)^(1/3). # So Ni is proportional to (aj ak / ai)^(1/3). # Since ai = Di / Li, Ni is proportional to ( (Dj/Lj)(Dk/Lk) / (Di/Li))^(1/3). # If Di ~ Li (rays span the scene), then ai ~ 1. # Then Ni ~ (11/1)^(1/3) = 1. So Nx = Ny = Nz. Uniform grid. # But if rays are directional, e.g., Dx is large, Dy, Dz small. # Then ax is large, ay, az small. # Nx ~ (small small / large)^(1/3) = small. # Ny ~ (large small / small)^(1/3) = large. # Nz ~ (large small / small)^(1/3) = large. # So Nx is small, Ny and Nz are large. # This means coarse voxels along X, fine voxels along Y and Z. # This matches the source: "coarser voxels along the dominant travel axis". # So the formula is: # Ni = round( Ntotal^(1/3) ( (aj ak) / ai)^(1/3)) # where ai = Di / Li. # We need to estimate Di. If we don't have ray data, we might use Li. # But the source implies we analyze ray distribution. # Let's implement this heuristic. a = [travelweights[i] / scenebounds[i] for i in range(3)] # Calculate Ni N = [0, 0, 0] for i in range(3): j = (i + 1) % 3 k = (i + 2) % 3 # Ni proportional to (aj ak / ai)^(1/3) factor = (a[j] a[k] / a[i]) (1/3) N[i] = factor # Normalize to targetvoxelcount totalfactor = sum([n3 for n in N]) # Wait, Ni are not normalized yet. # We need product(Ni) = targetvoxelcount. # Let Ni = k factori. # prod(Ni) = k^3 prod(factori) = targetvoxelcount. # k = (targetvoxelcount / prod(factori))^(1/3). prodfactors = N[0] N[1] N[2] k = (targetvoxelcount / prodfactors) (1/3) N = [round(k n) for n in N] # Ensure minimum 1 voxel per axis N = [max(1, n) for n in N] return tuple(N) Time Complexity: The grid setup is O(1) after ray analysis. The traversal cost is reduced by a factor proportional to the improvement in voxel size along the dominant axis. In the cited example, a coarser axial voxel provided a 3.26x speedup for pipe-cell rays. Memory Complexity: Depends on the total number of voxels. Anisotropic grids use the same memory budget as uniform grids but distribute it differently. Measured Performance: In a test with 300,000 rays per corner, switching from a default area-sized grid (212, 11, 114) to a 128³ grid for pipe cells resulted in a performance drop? No, the text states: 'a coarser axial voxel is worth 3.26x to them'. Specifically, the default grid (near cubic at 8.2 mm) vs 128³ grid (13.6 mm along x) showed that pipe-cell rays (axial) benefited from the coarser axial voxel size. Strengths: Significant speedup for directional ray distributions (e.g., pipe flows, reactors). Simple to implement by adjusting grid dimensions. Limitations: May degrade performance for isotropic or cube-ish scenes. Requires analysis of ray distribution. When to Use: When rays have a strong dominant direction and the scene is elongated along that direction. When Not to Use: When rays are isotropic or the scene is cube-like. This technique was discussed in the context of optimizing ray traversal for radiation transport simulations in the aquaflux project. It addresses the observation that the grid walk's cost is dominated by the distance travelled, not the number of triangles tested, and that skipping empty space is key. The issue highlights that sizing the grid anisotropically to the ray distribution is a simpler and potentially bigger win than optimizing the walk direction itself. name: Ray Traversal Template Generation
head: Precomputed Ray Traversal Pattern, Ray Template Generation
body: Precomputes a 3D ray traversal pattern (DDA-like) for light rays to avoid per-ray floating-point division during rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Grid resolution (edgeLen or RES), maximum traversal length (maxlen), and ray direction vector (lx, ly, lz). Output: rayTemplate, a lookup table of integer voxel offsets. Data Structures: rayTemplate[4096][3]: Stores integer voxel offsets for up to 4096 steps. Parameters: maxlen: Maximum number of steps, calculated as 3 \times edgeLen \times edgeLen. epsilon: Small value added to direction components to prevent division by zero. ALMOSTEQUALTHRESHOLD: Threshold for float comparison, set to 0.00001f. Steps: 1. Initialize ray direction components lx, ly, lz by adding epsilon. 2. Determine increments xinc, yinc, zinc based on the signs of the direction components. 3. Initialize the fractional position and initial distances to the next voxel boundary tx, ty, tz. Not given in the sources. 4. Loop until maxlen is reached: a. Compute t values to the next voxel boundary. b. Advance the coordinate along the axis with the smallest t. c. Update the fractional position. d. Store the integer voxel coordinates in rayTemplate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateraytemplate(edgelen, maxlen, lx, ly, lz): epsilon = 1e-6 lx += epsilon ly += epsilon lz += epsilon xinc = 1 if lx > 0 else -1 yinc = 1 if ly > 0 else -1 zinc = 1 if lz > 0 else -1 # Not given in the sources: initialization of fractional position and initial t values. fracx, fracy, fracz = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 invlx = 1.0 / lx invly = 1.0 / ly invlz = 1.0 / lz tx = (1.0 - fracx) invlx if xinc > 0 else (0.0 - fracx) invlx ty = (1.0 - fracy) invly if yinc > 0 else (0.0 - fracy) invly tz = (1.0 - fracz) invlz if zinc > 0 else (0.0 - fracz) invlz raytemplate = [[0, 0, 0] for in range(maxlen)] voxelx, voxely, voxelz = 0, 0, 0 for i in range(maxlen): # Compute t values to next voxel boundary (maintained incrementally) # Advance coordinate with smallest t if tx <= ty and tx <= tz: voxelx += xinc tx += invlx raytemplate[i] = [xinc, 0, 0] elif ty <= tx and ty <= tz: voxely += yinc ty += invly raytemplate[i] = [0, yinc, 0] else: voxelz += zinc tz += invlz raytemplate[i] = [0, 0, zinc] # Update fractional position fracx = fracx + xinc fracy = fracy + yinc fracz = fracz + zinc return raytemplate Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The ALMOSTEQUAL macro uses a threshold of 0.00001f for float comparison, which may cause jitter or missed steps in degenerate cases. Adding epsilon to zero direction components prevents division by zero during traversal. Sets the light position, computes the light direction vector, and triggers ray template generation for volume ray casting. It assigns the input position to lightPos, computes lightDir as the negation of lightPos, and calls GenerateRayTemplate with the grid resolution RES to prepare ray casting parameters. Time Complexity: O(maxlen) for template generation, where maxlen = 3 \times edgeLen \times edgeLen. Memory Complexity: O(maxlen \times 3) integers for the template storage, capped at 4096 steps. Performance: Avoids per-ray floating-point division during rendering. Limitations: Fixed template size (4096 steps) may not be sufficient for very large grids or long rays. Precision issues with the ALMOSTEQUAL threshold can lead to artifacts. Originated in the nevermoe/SmokeSimulation project for real-time volume rendering and smoke simulation. nevermoe/SmokeSimulation, https://github.com/nevermoe/SmokeSimulation, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Grid Traversal (One-Pass Over-Allocated)
head: traverse_grids (over-allocate)
body: A single-pass algorithm to traverse voxel grids, using pre-allocated maximum memory to avoid a second pass. It differs from Grid Traversal (Two-Pass) by allocating buffers large enough for the worst-case scenario upfront, trading memory for a single kernel launch. Inputs: Ray origins, ray directions, grid dimensions, traversestepslimit, and raysmask. Outputs: Over-allocated interval and sample buffers, chunkcnts tensors with actual counts per ray, and chunkstarts pointers. Data Structures: 1. intervals.chunkcnts: Tensor of size [numrays] storing the allocated capacity and actual count of intervals per ray. 2. intervals.data: Over-allocated buffer of size [numrays, traversestepslimit 2]. 3. samples.chunkcnts: Tensor of size [numrays] storing the allocated capacity and actual count of samples per ray. 4. samples.data: Over-allocated buffer of size [numrays, traversestepslimit]. Numbered Steps: 1. Allocate intervals.chunkcnts initialized to traversestepslimit 2 for each ray, multiplied by raysmask. 2. Allocate samples.chunkcnts initialized to traversestepslimit for each ray, multiplied by raysmask. 3. Call traversegridskernel once with the over-allocated buffers. 4. Update chunk starts for intervals and samples based on actual counts returned from traversal. Parameters: traversestepslimit: Maximum number of steps allowed per ray. Must be > 0 if overallocate is true. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues near grid boundaries may cause rays to miss voxels or double-count; standard DDA epsilon handling is required. If traversestepslimit is too small, rays may be truncated prematurely. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversegridsonepass(origins, viewdirs, griddims, traversestepslimit, raysmask): numrays = len(origins) # Step 1: Allocate intervals.chunkcnts initialized to traversestepslimit 2 for each ray, multiplied by raysmask intervalschunkcnts = [(traversestepslimit 2) m for m in raysmask] # Step 2: Allocate samples.chunkcnts initialized to traversestepslimit for each ray, multiplied by raysmask sampleschunkcnts = [traversestepslimit m for m in raysmask] # Allocate over-allocated data buffers intervalsdata = [[0.0] (traversestepslimit 2) for in range(numrays)] samplesdata = [[0.0] traversestepslimit for in range(numrays)] # Step 3: Call traversegridskernel once with over-allocated buffers traversegridskernel( origins=origins, viewdirs=viewdirs, griddims=griddims, intervalsdata=intervalsdata, samplesdata=samplesdata, intervalschunkcnts=intervalschunkcnts, sampleschunkcnts=sampleschunkcnts, maxsteps=traversestepslimit) # Step 4: Update chunk starts for intervals and samples based on actual counts returned from traversal intervalschunkstarts = [0] numrays sampleschunkstarts = [0] numrays ioffset, soffset = 0, 0 for i in range(numrays): intervalschunkstarts[i] = ioffset ioffset += intervalschunkcnts[i] sampleschunkstarts[i] = soffset soffset += sampleschunkcnts[i] return intervalsdata, samplesdata, intervalschunkcnts, sampleschunkcnts, intervalschunkstarts, sampleschunkstarts A two-pass algorithm to traverse voxel grids along rays, first counting segments to allocate exact memory, then filling them. First pass: Call traversegridskernel with computeintervals=true (implied by first pass logic) and allocate intervals.chunkcnts and samples.chunkcnts tensors of size [nrays]. Second pass: Allocate data buffers for intervals and samples based on the counts from the first pass using memallocdatafromchunk.
