name: Coherent Grid Traversal with Branch-Hinted Single Loop
head: Branch-Hinted Single Loop Traversal, Single-Loop Coherent Grid Traversal
body: This method is a traversal algorithm for uniform grids optimized for the CELL SPU architecture, which replaces standard nested loops with a single loop to avoid branch misprediction penalties. It differs from Robust Grid Traversal by prioritizing branch hint compatibility over robustness, and from Computational Space Traversal by maintaining the logical slice-by-slice order of Uniform Grid Traversal while flattening the control flow. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A bounding frustum of rays, a uniform grid, and the axis most parallel to the frustum direction (primary axis). Output: A sequence of grid cells intersecting the frustum, traversed outwardly from the camera. Data Structures: The grid is stored as a uniform structure. The traversal maintains state variables for the current cell coordinates (x, y, z) and the boundaries of the frustum in grid space. Specific bit-packing or cell layout details are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Initialization: Determine the primary axis (the axis most parallel to the frustum direction). Initialize the starting cell coordinates at the camera side of the frustum. 2. Single Loop Iteration: Execute a single loop that iterates through grid cells in the same logical order as the standard 3-nested-loop structure: slice-by-slice along the primary axis, then square regions within each slice. 3. Branchless Condition Evaluation: For every iteration, compute the solutions for all three potential if/else clauses that would normally determine the next step (e.g., moving to the next slice, moving to the next region, or terminating). 4. Bitwise Selection: Use bitwise operations to discard incorrect clause results. This avoids branching and allows the hardware to issue branch hints effectively. 5. Update State: Apply the selected result to update the current cell coordinates. 6. Termination: The loop continues until the final iteration is reached. The "always predicting branch" strategy is used, expecting misprediction only on the final iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coherentsinglelooptraversal(frustum, grid, primaryaxis): # Initialize state based on frustum and grid boundaries # Determine start cell (x, y, z) at the camera side x, y, z = getstartcell(frustum, grid, primaryaxis) # Determine loop bounds based on frustum extent # The loop runs for the total number of cells intersecting the frustum totalcells = countintersectingcells(frustum, grid, primaryaxis) for i in range(totalcells): # Compute potential next states for all three logical branches # Branch 1: Move to next cell in current slice/region nextx1, nexty1, nextz1 = computenextcellinregion(x, y, z, primaryaxis) # Branch 2: Move to next slice (if primary axis is x, this changes x) nextx2, nexty2, nextz2 = computenextslice(x, y, z, primaryaxis) # Branch 3: Termination condition check (returns current or sentinel) nextx3, nexty3, nextz3 = computetermination(x, y, z, frustum) # Determine which branch is valid for the current state # This logic replaces if/else with bitwise operations # mask1, mask2, mask3 are 1 if the branch is valid, 0 otherwise mask1 = isvalidbranch1(x, y, z, primaryaxis) mask2 = isvalidbranch2(x, y, z, primaryaxis) mask3 = isvalidbranch3(x, y, z, frustum) # Select the correct next state using bitwise operations # Example: nextx = (nextx1 & mask1) | (nextx2 & mask2) | (nextx3 & mask3) # Note: The exact bitwise implementation depends on how masks are encoded # Assuming masks are 0 or -1 (all bits set) for valid/invalid validmask1 = mask1 -1 validmask2 = mask2 -1 validmask3 = mask3 -1 x = (nextx1 & validmask1) | (nextx2 & validmask2) | (nextx3 & validmask3) y = (nexty1 & validmask1) | (nexty2 & validmask2) | (nexty3 & validmask3) z = (nextz1 & validmask1) | (nextz2 & validmask2) | (nextz3 & validmask3) # Process the current cell (x, y, z) processcell(x, y, z, frustum, grid) return Parameters: Branch Hint Strategy: "Always predicting branch". Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Branch Misprediction: Standard nested loops cause pipeline stalls due to misprediction. The outer loop cannot be predicted because it calls inner loops, and the inner loop executes 1-3 iterations, making prediction strategies frequently mis-predict. Complexity: The single-loop approach is more complex to code than nested loops. Performance: The method is theorized to be faster on CELL architecture due to avoided misprediction, but was not tested or benchmarked in the source. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The code was written but not tested or benchmarked, so performance is only theorized to be faster than 3 nested loops on CELL architecture. Strengths: Maps well to the CELL architecture by allowing branch hinting and avoiding misprediction stalls. Limitations: More complex to code; relies on specific hardware branch hint capabilities. When to use: When targeting the CELL SPU architecture and branch prediction is limited. When not to use: On hardware with powerful branch prediction or when code simplicity is prioritized. Origin: The algorithm was described in a paper by D. Chapman regarding high definition interactive animated ray tracing on the CELL processor. History: It was developed to address the limitations of the CELL SPU's branch prediction unit, which struggled with the irregular control flow of standard nested grid traversal loops. Usage: It is used in the context of efficient voxelization and ray tracing on the CELL processor. High Definition Interactive Animated Ray Tracing on CELL Processor using Coherent Grid Traversal, https://userpages.cs.umbc.edu/olano/class/635-07-2/dchapm2.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Nishita et al. Ray Casting Method
head: Nishita Ray Casting
body: A ray casting technique for rendering participating media that integrates radiance only over segments of a ray that are illuminated by light sources, utilizing precomputed shadow and illumination volumes. It distinguishes itself from standard ray marching by avoiding integration in shadowed regions and from Max’s original scan-line approach by operating in ray space, while extending support to spotlights with angular distributions beyond parallel light sources. Builds on Ray-grid traversal. The method computes the radiance along a ray by intersecting it with shadow volumes generated by occluding geometry and illumination volumes generated by light sources, integrating only where these volumes overlap (lit segments). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry (polygons), light sources (parallel or spotlights), participating medium properties (density, phase function). Output: Pixel color/intensity. Data Structures: Shadow Volumes: Constructed from scene polygons relative to light sources. Illumination Volumes: Constructed from light source geometry. Ray Data: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}. Steps: 1. Volume Construction: Generate shadow volumes for all occluders relative to each light source, and illumination volumes for each light source. 2. Ray Intersection: For each pixel, cast a ray from the camera and intersect it with the shadow and illumination volumes to determine intervals of shadow and light. 3. Segment Identification: Identify "lit segments" where the ray is inside an illumination volume but outside any shadow volume. 4. Integration: For each lit segment, integrate the radiance transfer equation along the ray interval. For a point light source and constant density medium with isotropic scattering, this yields an analytical function of distance. For parallel light and layered density, numerical integration is used. 5. Accumulation: Sum the contributions from all lit segments. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Light type: Parallel or Spotlight. Medium density: Constant or layered. Edge Cases: Spotlights with angular distributions require specific volume construction compared to parallel lights. Degenerate cases where shadow and illumination boundaries coincide must be handled to avoid double counting or gaps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nishitaraycasting(rayorigin, raydirection, shadowintervals, illumintervals, medium): # 1. Intersect ray with shadow and illumination volumes to get t-intervals shadowt = list(shadowintervals) illumt = list(illumintervals) # 2. Determine lit segments (illumination minus shadow) litsegments = [] for istart, iend in illumt: currentstart = istart for sstart, send in shadowt: if sstart < iend and send > istart: if sstart > currentstart: litsegments.append((currentstart, sstart)) currentstart = max(currentstart, send) if currentstart < iend: litsegments.append((currentstart, iend)) totalradiance = 0.0 # 3. Integrate over lit segments for start, end in litsegments: # Integration logic depends on light type and medium density # For point light and constant density: analytical function of distance # For parallel light and layered density: numerical integration # Not given in the sources. segmentradiance = 0.0 totalradiance += segmentradiance return totalradiance Applies Nishita’s method to consider light/water interaction in a two-pass backward beam tracing method to display underwater shafts of light. It is chosen when rendering complex light/water interactions in underwater scenes. A volumetric rendering approach for gaseous phenomena that models non-uniformly modified density blobs convected by wind fields and diffusion processes. It differs from standard particle systems by treating blobs as spherical particles with normally distributed gas volumes, rendered using diffusion equations. It applies a front-to-back strategy to handle turbulent fields. The method avoids integration in shadowed regions, potentially reducing computation compared to full ray marching. However, it requires the construction of shadow and illumination volumes, which adds preprocessing complexity. Originated from Nishita et al. [62], building on Max’s ideas of shadow and illumination volumes but shifting from scan-line to ray casting. Extended to handle spotlights with angular distributions. Used in computer graphics for rendering participating media, particularly for effects like shafts of light in fog or water. A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Stam and Fiume Blob Renderer
head: Blob Renderer, Blob-Warping, Volumetric Blob Rendering
body: A volumetric rendering approach for gaseous phenomena that models non-uniformly modified density blobs convected by wind fields and diffusion processes. It differs from standard particle systems by treating blobs as spherical particles with normally distributed gas volumes, rendered using diffusion equations. It applies a front-to-back strategy specifically for turbulent wind fields in gaseous phenomena. Inputs: A set of spherical blobs (each with position, velocity, radius, and density parameters), a wind field, and diffusion parameters. Outputs: A rendered image of the gaseous phenomenon. Data Structures: Blob: A structure containing position vector \mathbf{p}, velocity vector \mathbf{v}, radius r, and density distribution parameters. Wind Field: A function or grid returning velocity \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}, t) at position \mathbf{x} and time t. Steps: 1. Initialize blob positions and velocities based on physical properties (convection, pressure, drag). 2. For each frame, update blob positions using Newton’s Laws of Motion, accounting for convection, drag, and thermal buoyancy. 3. Model the gas density within each blob as normally distributed over its spherical volume. 4. Apply diffusion equations to modify the density distribution over time. 5. Render turbulent gaseous fields using a front-to-back ray casting strategy. 6. For each pixel, cast a ray and integrate the density contributions of intersecting blobs, considering the normally distributed gas volume. Formulas: Gas density distribution: \rho(\mathbf{x}) = \rho0 \exp\left(-\frac{|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), where \rho0 is peak density, \mathbf{p} is blob center, and \sigma is spread parameter. Parameters: \sigma: Spread parameter for density distribution. Not given in the sources. \rho0: Peak density. Not given in the sources. Clamp or interpolate wind velocities at domain boundaries. Degenerate input: Blobs with zero radius or density. Skip such blobs during rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Cell integration rendering
body: Cell integration rendering is a volume visualization technique that renders data by integrating optical properties over each individual cell and then processing every pixel covered by the cell's projection onto the viewing plane. It is distinguished from its parent method, Cell Projection with Scan-line Conversion, by performing explicit integration within the cell volume rather than simple projection, resulting in significantly higher image quality. However, this approach is computationally prohibitive compared to ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset defined by a grid of cells; camera parameters defining the viewing plane; optical properties (density, color, opacity) associated with the cells. Output: A 2D image where pixel values represent accumulated intensity. Data Structures: Grid: A structured or unstructured set of cells. The specific layout depends on the underlying data representation (e.g., rectangular grid). Pixel Buffer: An image plane storing accumulated intensity and opacity for each pixel. Steps: 1. Projection: For each cell in the volume, project the cell geometry onto the viewing plane to determine the set of pixels covered by the cell's footprint. 2. Integration: For each pixel covered by the cell's projection, determine the specific integration volume within the cell that corresponds to that pixel. 3. Intensity Calculation: Perform an intensity calculation over the bounds of the integration volume. The intensity I is calculated by integrating the contribution of density emitters within the volume. The formula is: I(u) = \int \frac{x}{y} \frac{z}{d} \rho(d) O(s) \left[ Ka(u)Ia + Kd(u, S, M)(N \cdot Lj)Ij \right] + (1 - \rho(d)bc(u)) \, dxdydz Where: u represents spatial coordinates or parameters within the integration volume. x, y, z, d are geometric factors related to the projection and depth. \rho(d) is the density as a function of depth d. O(s) is the opacity as a function of scalar value s. Ka(u) is the ambient color coefficient. Ia is the ambient light intensity. Kd(u, S, M) is the diffuse color coefficient, dependent on position u, scalar S, and material M. N is the surface normal. Lj is the light direction vector for light source j. Ij is the intensity of light source j. bc(u) is a term related to back-scattering or attenuation that modifies the density contribution. The integration is performed over the volume element dxdydz. 4. Accumulation: Add the calculated intensity to the corresponding pixel values in the image buffer. 5. Termination Check: If a pixel's accumulated opacity reaches unity (1.0), set a flag for that pixel to skip further processing. Parameters: Grid Size: The resolution of the input data. Image Size: The resolution of the output image. Transfer Functions: Mapping from scalar values to density \rho(d) and opacity O(s). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: The method is extremely slow. On a Sun 4 workstation, rendering a single image required between two and twelve CPU hours, depending on grid and image size. Incremental Display: While the front-to-back processing order allows for incremental display, stopping early may result in images that are not representative of the final result. Sampling Artifacts: While cell integration reduces sampling artifacts compared to image-order methods, the computational cost makes it impractical for interactive exploration. A hybrid technique where an image-order ray-casting method is used within each cell. Cells are processed in a front-to-back order: first by plane (closest to viewpoint first), then by cell within the plane (closest to viewpoint first). For each cell, the algorithm determines which pixels are affected by the cell's scan lines and defines an integration volume for each pixel. Intensity is accumulated into pixel values, and if a pixel's opacity reaches unity, it is flagged and skipped. This allows for incremental display, though early termination yields non-representative results. Time Complexity: Extremely high. Rendering times of 2–12 CPU hours per image were observed on a Sun 4 workstation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Produces far superior image quality compared to simpler projection methods. Strengths: High visual fidelity; reduction of sampling artifacts inherent in image-order rendering. Limitations: Prohibitively slow for most applications; not recommended for research projects requiring parameter tuning due to excessive processing time. When to use: Only when image quality is the absolute priority and computational time is not a constraint. When not to use: For interactive visualization, large datasets, or when rapid iteration is needed; ray casting is much faster and preferred. The cell integration method was discussed in the context of volume visualization research in the late 1980s and early 1990s. It was identified as an alternative to reduce sampling artifacts but was ultimately deemed impractical due to its computational cost compared to ray casting. The concept of treating volumetric data as a field of density emitters, which underpins the intensity calculation in cell-by-cell processing, was also explored during this period. name: TomoSphero Raytracer
head: Spherical Grid Raytracer, TomoSphero
body: TomoSphero is a differentiable raytracer designed for tomographic reconstruction on spherical grids, specifically targeting planetary and solar atmospheric modeling where spherical symmetry is prevalent. Unlike Cartesian ray-grid traversal methods that assume uniform voxel sizes and axis-aligned boundaries, TomoSphero explicitly computes intersections with spherical (radial), conical (elevational), and planar (azimuthal) boundaries to handle non-uniform and partial spherical domains. It solves the problem of efficiently computing line integrals (Fredholm integrals of the first kind) for optically thin media by precomputing voxel indices and intersection lengths, enabling fast GPU-accelerated forward and backward passes for gradient-based optimization. The method discretizes the continuous line integral of an object \rho along a ray into a weighted sum of voxel values, where weights are the intersection lengths of the ray with each voxel. The algorithm operates in four distinct phases: intersection computation, region indexing, sorting/length calculation, and integration. Inputs: Ray: Origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Grid: Defined by shape (Nr, Ne, Na) representing radial, elevational, and azimuthal dimensions. Radial boundaries: Nr + 1 spheres. Elevational boundaries: Ne + 1 cones. Azimuthal boundaries: Na + 1 planes. Object: 3D volume \rho defined on the spherical grid. Outputs: Measurements: Scalar projection values for each ray. Operator Data: Arrays of voxel indices (regs) and intersection lengths (lens) for use in reconstruction. The core data structure is a table (list of rows) where each row corresponds to a segment of the ray intersecting a specific voxel. For a single ray, the table has N rows, where N = 2(Nr + 1) + 2(Ne + 1) + (Na + 1). Each row contains: 1. Voxel Indices: A tuple (ri, ei, ai) representing the radial, elevational, and azimuthal indices of the voxel. 2. Intersection Length: \Delta li, the distance along the ray within that voxel. The implementation stores these as parallel arrays accessible via.regs (indices) and.lens (lengths). Step 1: Compute Ray-Boundary Intersections For each boundary type, compute the intersection points of the ray with all boundaries and their distances l from the ray origin \mathbf{o}. Radial (Spheres) and Elevational (Cones): Assume an upper bound of 2(Nr + 1) intersections for spheres/cones and Na + 1 for planes. Azimuthal (Planes): Each ray intersects each of the Na + 1 planar boundaries at most once. No Intersection Handling: If a boundary does not intersect the ray, store the coordinate but set the distance l to \infty. Step 2: Determine Crossing Direction and Region Indices For each intersection point, determine if the ray crosses the boundary in a "positive" (increasing index) or "negative" (decreasing index) direction. The direction depends on the crossing point coordinate and the ray direction \mathbf{d}. Convert boundary indices to region indices: If the crossing direction is negative, decrement the boundary index to get the region index. Step 3: Sort and Compute Intersection Lengths 1. Collect all region indices from Step 2 into a single list. 2. Sort all intersection points by their distance l from the ray start. 3. Compute the intersection length \Delta li for each segment as the difference between adjacent sorted distances: \Delta li = l{i+1} - li. Note: If li = \infty, \Delta li becomes \infty or \text{NaN}. 4. Construct the 3D voxel index table: Start with the voxel index of the ray origin. Insert the sorted region indices into the table. Fill in missing indices from the previous row to form complete 3D tuples (r, e, a). The total number of rows is N = 2(Nr + 1) + 2(Ne + 1) + (Na + 1). 5. Invalid Row Handling: Set \Delta li = 0 for any row where: The region index is invalid (less than 0 or \ge the grid dimension size). \Delta li is \infty or \text{NaN}. This ensures invalid segments contribute zero to the final sum. Step 4: Line Integration Compute the projection measurement y as the inner product of the object values and the intersection lengths: y = \sum{i=1}^{N} \rho(ri, ei, ai) \cdot \Delta li where \rho(ri, ei, ai) is the value of the object at the voxel indices (ri, ei, ai). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def intersectsphere(o, d, radius): """Standard ray-sphere intersection. Returns list of distances or [inf].""" oc = o b = 2.0 sum(d[i] oc[i] for i in range(3)) c = sum(oc[i]2 for i in range(3)) - radius2 disc = b2 - 4.0 c if disc < 0: return [float('inf')] sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / 2.0 t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / 2.0 return [t for t in (t1, t2) if t >= 0] if t1 >= 0 else ([t2] if t2 >= 0 else [float('inf')]) def intersectcone(o, d, apex, axis, halfangle): """Standard ray-cone intersection. Returns list of distances or [inf].""" # Simplified standard quadratic solver for ray-cone v = [o[i] - apex[i] for i in range(3)] cosa = math.cos(halfangle) a = sum(d[i]axis[i] for i in range(3))2 - cosa2 sum(d[i]2 for i in range(3)) b = 2.0 (sum(d[i]axis[i] for i in range(3)) sum(v[i]axis[i] for i in range(3)) - cosa2 sum(v[i]d[i] for i in range(3))) c = sum(v[i]axis[i] for i in range(3))2 - cosa2 sum(v[i]2 for i in range(3)) disc = b2 - 4.0 a c if disc < 0 or abs(a) < 1e-9: return [float('inf')] sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) return [t for t in (t1, t2) if t >= 0] if t1 >= 0 else ([t2] if t2 >= 0 else [float('inf')]) def intersectplane(o, d, point, normal): """Standard ray-plane intersection. Returns list of distances or [inf].""" denom = sum(d[i] normal[i] for i in range(3)) if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return [float('inf')] t = sum((point[i] - o[i]) normal[i] for i in range(3)) / denom return [t] if t >= 0 else [float('inf')] def getcrossingdirection(dist, raydir, boundarytype, boundaryidx, grid): """Determines if crossing increases or decreases the region index.""" # Standard logic: positive if moving towards higher index, negative otherwise return 'positive' if raydir[0] > 0 else 'negative' def getvoxelindex(origin, grid): """Maps ray origin to initial voxel indices.""" return (0, 0, 0) # Placeholder for coordinate-to-index mapping def raytrace(rayorigin, raydirection, grid, objectvolume): # Step 1: Compute intersections rdists = [] for rbound in grid.radialboundaries: rdists.extend(intersectsphere(rayorigin, raydirection, rbound)) edists = [] for ebound in grid.elevationalboundaries: edists.extend(intersectcone(rayorigin, raydirection, ebound.apex, ebound.axis, ebound.halfangle)) adists = [] for abound in grid.azimuthalboundaries: adists.extend(intersectplane(rayorigin, raydirection, abound.point, abound.normal)) # Step 2: Determine crossing direction and region indices regions = [] for i, dist in enumerate(rdists): if dist == float('inf'): continue direction = getcrossingdirection(dist, raydirection, 'radial', i, grid) regionidx = i if direction == 'positive' else i - 1 regions.append(('r', regionidx, dist)) for i, dist in enumerate(edists): if dist == float('inf'): continue direction = getcrossingdirection(dist, raydirection, 'elevational', i, grid) regionidx = i if direction == 'positive' else i - 1 regions.append(('e', regionidx, dist)) for i, dist in enumerate(adists): if dist == float('inf'): continue direction = getcrossingdirection(dist, raydirection, 'azimuthal', i, grid) regionidx = i if direction == 'positive' else i - 1 regions.append(('a', regionidx, dist)) # Step 3: Sort and compute lengths regions.sort(key=lambda x: x[2]) segments = [] for i in range(len(regions) - 1): distcurr = regions[i][2] distnext = regions[i+1][2] length = distnext - distcurr if distcurr != float('inf') and distnext != float('inf') else float('inf') segments.append({'type': regions[i][0], 'regionidx': regions[i][1], 'length': length}) # Build 3D voxel table by propagating indices currentvoxel = list(getvoxelindex(rayorigin, grid)) voxeltable = [] prevdist = 0.0 for seg in segments: dim = seg['type'] idx = seg['regionidx'] if dim == 'r': currentvoxel[0] = idx elif dim == 'e': currentvoxel[1] = idx elif dim == 'a': currentvoxel[2] = idx voxeltable.append({'voxel': tuple(currentvoxel), 'length': seg['length']}) # Validate and zero invalid rows for entry in voxeltable: r, e, a = entry['voxel'] length = entry['length'] if (r < 0 or r >= grid.Nr or e < 0 or e >= grid.Ne or a < 0 or a >= grid.Na): entry['length'] = 0.0 continue if math.isinf(length) or math.isnan(length): entry['length'] = 0.0 # Step 4: Line Integration total = 0.0 for entry in voxeltable: r, e, a = entry['voxel'] length = entry['length'] rho = objectvolume[r, e, a] total += rho length return total Grid Shape (Nr, Ne, Na): Determines the resolution and number of boundaries. Data Types: The implementation uses int64 for indices and float64 for distances and values to ensure precision. No Intersection: If a boundary does not intersect the ray, the distance is set to \infty, and the corresponding segment is handled in validation. Parallel Boundaries: Numerically degenerate cases, such as a line of sight parallel to an azimuthal boundary plane, must be tested for consistency. Memory Limits: The algorithm does not support out-of-core operation. If the simultaneous computation for all rays exceeds available memory (VRAM), the algorithm fails. Invalid Indices: Rays passing outside the grid or crossing boundaries with no intersection result in invalid region indices, which are zeroed out to prevent contribution to the sum. Time Complexity: The algorithm involves computing intersections for all boundaries (O(Nr + Ne + Na) per ray), sorting them (O(K \log K) where K is the number of intersections), and integrating (O(K)). Since K \approx 2(Nr + 1) + 2(Ne + 1) + (Na + 1), the complexity is dominated by sorting and intersection computation. Memory Complexity: Peak memory usage is approximately (2Nr + 2Ne + Na) \cdot 6 \cdot N{rays} \cdot 8 / 10^9 GB, accounting for 6 arrays per ray (voxel indices for r/e/a, lengths, values, and temporary arrays) using 8-byte types. Performance: Validation tests on a unit sphere with a (50, 50, 50) grid showed measurements within 0.00001\% of the true value, approaching machine epsilon for float32. Strengths: Efficient for spherical symmetries; differentiable via PyTorch; supports arbitrary projection geometries (cone, parallel). Limitations: High memory usage for large grids and many rays; no out-of-core support; requires precomputation of intersections. TomoSphero was introduced to address the limitations of Cartesian discretization in tomographic reconstruction for planetary and solar atmospheres, where spherical symmetry is common. It is implemented in PyTorch to leverage GPU acceleration and automatic differentiation for gradient-based optimization. The method is used in atmospheric tomography, such as modeling the Carruthers Geocorona Observatory surveying Earth's exosphere. TomoSphero: Fast Differentiable Projector for Planetary and Solar Tomography on Spherical Grids, https://doi.org/10.3847/1538-4357/ae6db5, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Parallel Ray-Tracing for Isosurface Rendering
head: Parallel ray-tracing algorithm for isosurface rendering, Rectilinear isosurfacing, Unstructured isosurfacing
body: This method is a parallel, image-order ray-tracing algorithm designed for shared-memory architectures to render isosurfaces from large volume datasets. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which object contributes to each pixel's final color by traversing a spatial hierarchy to skip empty space and analytically computing intersections within cells containing the isosurface. Unlike object-space rendering methods that scale poorly on shared-memory systems beyond 32 processors, this approach achieves high parallel efficiency on distributed clusters and scales well on large parallel systems. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like DDA Traversal by replacing fixed-step voxel traversal with a multi-level min-max hierarchy for early termination, and from Marching Cubes by computing exact cubic intersections rather than approximating surfaces with polygons. Inputs: Volume dataset \rho(x,y,z) with dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz. Isosurface value \rho{iso}. Ray definition for each pixel: origin \mathbf{o} = (xa, ya, za) and direction \mathbf{d} = (xb, yb, zb). Outputs: Color and depth for each pixel, determined by the first isosurface intersection along the ray. 1. Memory Bricking (Cache Optimization) The volume data is reordered into n \times n \times n cells called "bricks" to fit within the processor's primary data cache. Brick Size (n): For 16-bit data on 128-byte cache lines: n=4. For 32-bit float data: n \approx 3. Macrobrick Size (m): Bricks are grouped into m \times m \times m "macrobricks" to improve Translation Look-aside Buffer (TLB) hit rates. For 16-bit data: m=5. For 32-bit data: m=6. Padding: If volume dimensions are not divisible by mn, padding is applied to fill the volume. Offset Calculation: The raw offset q into the data array for any (x, y, z) triple is: q = \left(\left\lfloor \frac{x}{n} \right\rfloor \div m\right)n^3m^3\left(\left\lfloor \frac{Nz}{n} \right\rfloor \div m\right)\left(\left\lfloor \frac{Ny}{n} \right\rfloor \div m\right) + \left(\left\lfloor \frac{y}{n} \right\rfloor \div m\right)n^3m^3\left(\left\lfloor \frac{Nz}{n} \right\rfloor \div m\right) + \left(\left\lfloor \frac{z}{n} \right\rfloor \div m\right)n^3m^3 + \left(\left\lfloor \frac{x}{n} \right\rfloor \bmod m\right)n^3m^2 + \left(\left\lfloor \frac{y}{n} \right\rfloor \bmod m\right)n^3m + \left(\left\lfloor \frac{z}{n} \right\rfloor \bmod m\right)n^3 + (x \bmod n \times n)n^2 + (y \bmod n) \times n + (z \bmod n). 2. Index Lookup Tables To avoid costly division and modulus operations in the offset calculation, three lookup tables Fx, Fy, Fz are precomputed. Size: Fx has Nx elements, Fy has Ny elements, Fz has Nz elements. Layout: The total size fits in the primary data cache. Formula: For a coordinate c \in \{x, y, z\}, the table value is: Fc(c) = \left(\left\lfloor \frac{c}{n} \right\rfloor \div m\right)n^3m^3 + \left(\left\lfloor \frac{c}{n} \right\rfloor \bmod m\right)n^3 + (c \bmod n). The index into the data array is computed as q = Fx(x) + Fy(y) + Fz(z). 3. Multilevel Spatial Hierarchy A trilevel hierarchy is used to accelerate traversal. Levels: One top-level cell, two intermediate macrocell levels, and the leaf data cells. Content: Each macrocell stores the minimum and maximum data values of its children. Storage Overhead: Less than 0.5% of the data size. Indexing: Macrocells are indexed using the same table-lookup technique as the data, requiring three table lookups per macrocell. 4. Unstructured Mesh Support For unstructured tetrahedral meshes, leaf nodes store a list of integer indices referencing overlapping tetrahedra. The hierarchy traversal is identical to the rectilinear case. The algorithm processes each pixel independently. For a given ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}: 1. Hierarchy Traversal: Start at the top-level cell. Check if the isovalue \rho{iso} lies within the cell's [\min, \max] range. If \rho{iso} is outside the range, skip the cell (it contains no isosurface). If \rho{iso} is inside, recurse to the next level or, if at the leaf level, proceed to intersection testing. The typical complexity of this search is O(\sqrt[3]{n}) for a three-level hierarchy. 2. Intersection Computation (Rectilinear): When a leaf cell contains the isosurface, solve for the intersection parameter t. The ray equation is: \begin{aligned} x &= xa + t xb \\ y &= ya + t yb \\ z &= za + t zb \end{aligned}. The isosurface condition is \rho(x,y,z) - \rho{iso} = 0. Using trilinear interpolation for \rho, this expands into a cubic polynomial in t: A t^3 + B t^2 + C t + D = 0. Solve this cubic equation in closed form to find the real roots for t. 3. Intersection Computation (Unstructured): For each tetrahedron in the leaf cell, compute the intersection of the ray with the isoplane defined by the tetrahedron's vertices and the isovalue. Check if the intersection point lies within the tetrahedron by verifying that all barycentric coordinates are positive. 4. Shading: Shade the resulting intersection point. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def parallelisosurfacerendering(volumedata, isovalue, rays, bricksizen, macrobricksizem): # Precompute index lookup tables Fx, Fy, Fz to avoid division/modulus Fx = computelookuptable(volumedata.shape[0], bricksizen, macrobricksizem) Fy = computelookuptable(volumedata.shape[1], bricksizen, macrobricksizem) Fz = computelookuptable(volumedata.shape[2], bricksizen, macrobricksizem) # Build trilevel spatial hierarchy (top-level, two intermediate macrocells, leaf data) # Each macrocell stores min and max data values of its children hierarchy = buildtrilevelhierarchy(volumedata, bricksizen, macrobricksizem) for ray in rays: tmin = float('inf') hitpoint = None # Phase 1: Traverse hierarchy stack = [hierarchy.root] while stack: cell = stack.pop() if cell.minval <= isovalue <= cell.maxval: if cell.isleaf: # Phase 2: Analytic intersection thit = computeanalyticintersection(ray, cell, isovalue, Fx, Fy, Fz, volumedata) if 0 < thit < tmin: tmin = thit hitpoint = ray.origin + thit ray.direction else: stack.extend(cell.children) # Phase 3: Shading if hitpoint is not None: color = computeshading(hitpoint, ray.direction) writepixel(ray.pixelid, color) def computelookuptable(dimsize, n, m): table = [0] dimsize n3 = n3 m3 = m3 for c in range(dimsize): table[c] = ((c // n) // m) n3 m3 + ((c // n) % m) n3 + (c % n) return table def buildtrilevelhierarchy(volumedata, n, m): # Organize data into n x n x n bricks bricks = [] for i in range(0, volumedata.shape[0], n): for j in range(0, volumedata.shape[1], n): for k in range(0, volumedata.shape[2], n): bricks.append(volumedata[i:i+n, j:j+n, k:k+n]) # Group bricks into m x m x m macrobricks macrobricks = [] for i in range(0, len(bricks), m3): macrobricks.append(bricks[i:i+m3]) # Compute min/max for each level (simplified for pseudocode) # Storage overhead < 0.5% return {'root': {'minval': float(volumedata.min()), 'maxval': float(volumedata.max()), 'children': macrobricks}} def computeanalyticintersection(ray, cell, isovalue, Fx, Fy, Fz, volumedata): # Extract 8 corner values of the cell using lookup tables # Requires 6 table lookups per corner: Fx(x), Fx(x+1), Fy(y), Fy(y+1), Fz(z), Fz(z+1) corners = [] for dx in (0, 1): for dy in (0, 1): for dz in (0, 1): idx = Fx[cell.x + dx] + Fy[cell.y + dy] + Fz[cell.z + dz] corners.append(volumedata.flat[idx]) # Trilinear interpolation expands rho(xa + txb, ya + tyb, za + tzb) - rhoiso = 0 # into a cubic polynomial: At^3 + Bt^2 + Ct + D = 0 A, B, C, D = derivecubiccoefficients(corners, ray.origin, ray.direction, isovalue) roots = solvecubicclosedform(A, B, C, D) validt = float('inf') for t in roots: if t > 0: validt = min(validt, t) return validt def derivecubiccoefficients(corners, origin, direction, isovalue): # Standard derivation of cubic coefficients from trilinear interpolation # Coefficients computed from 8 corner values and ray parameters return 1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 def solvecubicclosedform(A, B, C, D): # Closed-form solution for cubic equation (Cardano's formula) # Standard implementation returns real roots return [0.0] def computeshading(point, raydir): # Compute surface normal via finite differences or tri-cubic filtering # Apply Phong-like shading model return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def writepixel(pixelid, color): # Store color in frame buffer pass Brick Size (n): 16-bit data, 128-byte cache lines: n=4. 32-bit float data: n \approx 3. Macrobrick Size (m): 16-bit data: m=5. 32-bit data: m=6. Hierarchy Levels: Empirically determined to be 3 (one top-level, two intermediate, leaf data). Pitfalls: Index Calculation Cost: Equation 1 for offset calculation contains many integer multiplications, divisions, and moduli, which are costly (32+ cycles on MIPS R10000). Non-Power-of-Two Sizes: If n and m are not powers of two, bit shifts cannot be used for optimization. Incremental Indexing: Computing indices incrementally requires tracking nine counters with poor branch prediction performance. Worst-Case Complexity: While typical complexity is O(\sqrt[3]{n}), the worst case is O(n), though difficult to imagine an isosurface approaching this. Time Complexity: Typical hierarchy traversal: O(\sqrt[3]{n}). Worst-case traversal: O(n). Ray tracing is competitive with hardware z-buffers for sufficiently large datasets because its low asymptotic time complexity overcomes its large time constant. Memory Complexity: Storage overhead for the hierarchy is negligible, typically less than 0.5% of the data size. Index lookup tables (Fx, Fy, Fz) fit in the primary data cache. Measured Performance: SGI Origin 2000 (Shared Memory): Does not scale beyond 32 processors. PC Cluster (Sun Ultra 5/60, Fast Ethernet): >63% parallel efficiency up to 128 processors. Cray T3E (Distributed Memory): >75% parallel efficiency up to 512 processors. Explicit Bone Isosurface Extraction (Table 1): 1 CPU: 4838s (Noise Build) / 110s (Extract) / 627s (Marching Cubes) 32 CPUs: 118s / 14s / 26s 64 CPUs: 59s / 12s / 24s. Strengths: High degree of intrinsic parallelism. Exploits texture maps and incremental features (e.g., transparency, shadows) with incremental cost. Front-to-back traversal guarantees correct compositing order. Limitations: Not suitable for shared-memory architectures beyond 32 processors. Costly index calculations if brick sizes are not powers of two. Origin: The method was developed for large-scale volume visualization on parallel systems, specifically addressing the limitations of object-space rendering on shared-memory architectures. History: It was presented as an alternative to conventional ray tracing, which was considered too slow due to high time constants, but is competitive for large datasets due to low asymptotic complexity. The work highlights the importance of cache hierarchy utilization through bricking and multilevel grids. Usage: Used in parallel rendering systems for scientific visualization, such as flow surrounding aircraft wings and explicit bone isosurface extraction. name: Rendering Strategy and Optimization
body: Rendering Strategy and Optimization is a family of techniques that accelerate volume rendering by optimizing the efficiency of ray-grid traversal and determining optimal data structures for a given scene Optimization and Cost Models. It addresses the computational bottleneck of evaluating every voxel or primitive along a ray, which is often redundant due to empty space or coarse sampling Optimization and Cost Models. Unlike sibling methods that define specific traversal algorithms (e.g., Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) Traversal, Octree and Tree Traversal), this family focuses on how to execute traversal more efficiently (via hardware awareness or algorithmic shortcuts) and what resolution to use (via cost models) to minimize total rendering time Optimization and Cost Models. All methods in this family build on Ray-grid traversal, which advances analytically from one cell boundary to the next. The core mechanism determines the next cell by comparing distances to upcoming boundaries on the x, y, and z axes, selecting the minimum distance to advance. Optimization and cost models do not alter this fundamental geometric logic but instead optimize the cost of executing it or the parameters (like grid resolution) under which it runs Optimization and Cost Models. This family accelerates ray-grid traversal by exploiting spatial coherence among ray bundles or by enforcing strict topological connectivity rules to resolve boundary ambiguities Coherent and Connectivity Traversal. It solves the problem of packet divergence in coherent ray tracing and normal inaccuracies in uniform grid traversal Coherent and Connectivity Traversal. Unlike standard cell-by-cell methods like Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) Traversal which process rays individually and may suffer from divergence or diagonal jumps, this family processes rays as coherent frustums or resolves tie-breaking conditions explicitly. Choose this method when rendering coherent ray bundles or when boundary ambiguities cause traversal divergence. Rendering Order and Strategy defines the sequence in which volumetric cells are processed during ray-grid traversal to ensure correct optical compositing and efficient occlusion culling Rendering Order and Strategy. It solves the problem of determining which cells contribute to the final pixel color and in what order, distinguishing itself from sibling methods by decoupling the geometric traversal logic (handled by the parent Ray-grid traversal) from the semantic processing order required for correct alpha blending or visibility determination Rendering Order and Strategy. Choose this method when correct front-to-back alpha compositing or early ray termination is required, or when spatial partitioning can replace per-ray depth sorting. This family encompasses techniques that optimize the computational cost of ray-grid traversal and determine optimal data structure parameters for volume rendering Optimization and Cost Models. It addresses the bottleneck of redundant voxel or primitive evaluations along a ray by focusing on execution efficiency and resolution tuning rather than defining new traversal algorithms Optimization and Cost Models. Unlike sibling methods that specify traversal order or coherence exploitation, this family optimizes the cost of executing traversal and the parameters under which it runs Optimization and Cost Models. Choose this method when redundant voxel evaluations bottleneck rendering performance or when grid resolution needs tuning for hardware-aware cost minimization. Not given in the sources.

name: Coherent and Connectivity Traversal
body: This family accelerates ray-grid traversal by exploiting spatial coherence among ray bundles or by enforcing strict topological connectivity rules to resolve boundary ambiguities. It solves the problem of packet divergence in coherent ray tracing and normal inaccuracies in uniform grid traversal. All methods in this family build on Ray-grid traversal, which advances analytically from one cell boundary to the next [Parent]. Optimization and cost models do not alter this fundamental geometric logic but instead optimize the cost of executing it or the parameters under which it runs [Parent]. Processes bundles of coherent rays as frustums, advancing slice-by-slice along a dominant axis rather than cell-by-cell. It sets itself apart from its sibling Rendering Order and Strategy and standard 3DDDA by avoiding expensive packet splitting and merging operations, allowing the grid to be rebuilt from scratch every frame for dynamic scenes while maintaining performance competitive with kd-trees. Choose it when rendering dynamic scenes with large coherent ray packets where packet divergence would break cell-by-cell traversal. Guarantees strict 4-connectivity by explicitly resolving boundary crossing ambiguities via stable sorting of intersection distances. It sets itself apart from its sibling Coherent Grid Traversal and standard DDA by explicitly testing a 2x2 cell neighborhood and using axis-priority sorting to prevent diagonal jumps, ensuring that rays crossing grid lines do so one axis at a time. Choose it when topological consistency and correct normal calculation are required, particularly for primary rays hitting silhouettes or when diagonal jumps cause artifacts. A property defining the set of cells a ray can traverse to from its current cell, inspired by pixel connectivity in image processing. Taxicab metric distance between P1=(x1, y1) and P2=(x2, y2) is |x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|. Chebyshev metric distance between P1=(x1, y1) and P2=(x2, y2) is \max(|x1 - x2|, |y1 - y2|). In 2D, there are 4-connectivity (orthogonal neighbors) and 8-connectivity (including diagonal neighbors). The concept of connectivity in ray traversal was formalized in a thesis by Hur, which analyzed the behavior of rays crossing voxel corners. The thesis noted that standard DDA methods might traverse through corners, leading to 8-connectivity, whereas specific algorithms aim for 4-connectivity to ensure correct normal calculation and topological consistency. versal algorithm for ray tracing Hur man gör en hierarkisk..., https://kth.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:2069409/FULLTEXT01.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Coherent Grid Traversal
head: CGT (Coherent Grid Traversal), CGT algorithm, Ize et al. traversal, Slice by slice algorithm
body: Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) is a ray tracing acceleration technique for uniform grids that traverses bundles (frustums) of coherent rays slice-by-slice along a dominant axis, abandoning cell-by-cell traversal to avoid expensive packet splitting and merging operations. It sets itself apart from its sibling Hero-like 4-Connectivity (H4T) and standard 3DDDA by processing entire slices of cells as a coherent whole, allowing the grid to be rebuilt from scratch every frame for dynamic scenes while maintaining performance competitive with kd-trees. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A packet of N \times N coherent rays (spanning an angle < \pi/2) defined by origins \mathbf{o} and directions \mathbf{d}; a uniform grid of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz; the grid's bounding box. Output: A sequence of grid cells (or bricks) overlapped by the ray packet frustum, in traversal order along the major axis. Data Structures: Canonical Grid Space: Rays are transformed such that the grid maps to [0, Nx) \times [0, Ny) \times [0, Nz). Cell coordinates are computed by truncating floating-point positions to integers. Frustum Representation: Defined by four bounding planes in the minor axes (\tilde{U}, \tilde{V}) and near/far planes in the major axis (\tilde{K}). For primary rays, these are derived from the four corner rays of the packet. Overlap Box B(i): A 2D axis-aligned box in the \tilde{U}, \tilde{V} plane representing the frustum's intersection with slice i along \tilde{K}. Stored as four floats: [u{min}, v{min}, u{max}, v{max}]. Bricked Volume (Optional): For volume rendering, the volume is stored as "bricks" referenced by 3 maps (one per principal axis). Empty bricks are not stored for compression. Parameters: Packet Size: Typically 4 \times 4 or 8 \times 8 rays. Major Axis \tilde{K}: Determined by the dominant component (\pm X, \pm Y, \pm Z) of the first ray's direction. All rays must have the same sign along \tilde{K} to allow front-to-back traversal. Minor Axes \tilde{U}, \tilde{V}: The remaining two dimensions. Steps: 1. Transform: Convert all rays in the packet to canonical grid space. 2. Select Major Axis: Identify \tilde{K} as the axis with the maximum absolute direction component of the first ray. Verify all rays have the same sign along \tilde{K}. 3. Compute Frustum Planes: Calculate the slopes and offsets of the four bounding planes in \tilde{U} and \tilde{V} based on the extremal rays (or all rays for secondary packets). 4. Clip to Grid: Intersect the frustum with the grid's bounding box to determine the first slice index k{min} and last slice index k{max} along \tilde{K}. If the interval is empty, terminate. 5. Initialize Overlap Box: Compute the initial overlap box B(0) for slice k{min} by finding the min/max \tilde{U} and \tilde{V} coordinates of the frustum's entry and exit points at that slice. 6. Traverse Slices: For each slice k from k{min} to k{max}: a. Convert to Cell IDs: Truncate the min/max coordinates of B(k) to integers to get the cell range [i0..i1] \times [j0..j1] in the \tilde{U}, \tilde{V} plane. b. Intersect: Intersect all rays in the packet with all primitives (triangles or volume data) in the cells defined by the range. c. Increment Overlap Box: Compute B(k+1) = B(k) + \Delta B, where \Delta B = (du{min}, du{max}, dv{min}, dv{max}) are the slopes of the bounding planes in grid space. This requires four floating-point additions. 7. Early Termination: If all rays have intersected their targets, stop traversal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coherentgridtraversal(rays, griddims, gridbounds): # 1. Transform rays to canonical grid space # Assuming rays are transformed such that grid is [0, Nx) x [0, Ny) x [0, Nz) # rays: list of Ray objects with origin (o) and direction (d) # 2. Select major axis K # Pick the axis with the max absolute component of the first ray's direction firstray = rays[0] absd = [abs(firstray.d[i]) for i in range(3)] kaxis = absd.index(max(absd)) # Determine minor axes U and V uaxis = (kaxis + 1) % 3 vaxis = (kaxis + 2) % 3 # Check coherence: all rays must have same sign along K ksign = 1 if firstray.d[kaxis] > 0 else -1 for ray in rays: if ray.d[kaxis] ksign <= 0: raise ValueError("Rays are not coherent along major axis K") # 3. Compute Frustum Planes # For primary rays, use 4 corner rays. For simplicity, assume we have # min/max slopes for U and V planes in grid space. # dumin, dumax, dvmin, dvmax are the slopes of the bounding planes # in grid coordinate space. # These are computed from the corner rays' origins and directions projected # onto the U-V plane relative to K. # Example calculation for a corner ray (o, d): # slopeu = (o[u] + td[u] - o[k]d[u]/d[k]) / (o[k] - o[k])... simplified: # The slope in grid space is d[u]/d[k] and d[v]/d[k]. # We need min/max of these slopes across all corner rays. slopes = [] for ray in rays: if ray.d[kaxis] == 0: continue # Should not happen if coherent slopes.append((ray.d[uaxis] / ray.d[kaxis], ray.d[vaxis] / ray.d[kaxis])) dumin = min(s[0] for s in slopes) dumax = max(s[0] for s in slopes) dvmin = min(s[1] for s in slopes) dvmax = max(s[1] for s in slopes) # 4. Clip to Grid to find kmin and kmax # Intersect frustum with grid bounds along K # Grid bounds in canonical space: [0, Nx), [0, Ny), [0, Nz) # The frustum extends from near to far. We need the intersection of the # frustum's K-extent with [0, Nz). # Assuming rays are already clipped to view volume, we just need to # find the slice indices where the frustum enters and exits the grid. # This is done by clipping the frustum planes against the grid boundaries. # Simplified: find the min/max K coordinate of the frustum intersection # with the grid bounding box. # Let's assume we have pre-computed kmin and kmax from frustum-grid intersection kmin = 0 kmax = griddims[kaxis] - 1 # 5. Initialize Overlap Box B(0) for slice kmin # Compute min/max U, V coordinates at kmin # B(k) = [umin, vmin, umax, vmax] # umin(k) = uorigin + k dumin # umax(k) = uorigin + k dumax #... where uorigin is the U-coordinate of the frustum at K=0? # Actually, the planes are defined by (U - U0) = slope (K - K0). # So U(K) = U0 + slope (K - K0). # We need to determine the offset. # Let's assume the frustum is defined by 4 planes: # U = dumin K + offsetumin # U = dumax K + offsetumax # V = dvmin K + offsetvmin # V = dvmax K + offsetvmax # Compute offsets from the first ray's origin or corner rays # For a corner ray (o, d), U = o[u] + (K - o[k]) d[u]/d[k] # So offset = o[u] - o[k] d[u]/d[k] offsets = [] for ray in rays: if ray.d[kaxis] == 0: continue offsetu = ray.o[uaxis] - ray.o[kaxis] (ray.d[uaxis] / ray.d[kaxis]) offsetv = ray.o[vaxis] - ray.o[kaxis] (ray.d[vaxis] / ray.d[kaxis]) offsets.append((offsetu, offsetv)) offsetumin = min(o[0] for o in offsets) offsetumax = max(o[0] for o in offsets) offsetvmin = min(o[1] for o in offsets) offsetvmax = max(o[1] for o in offsets) # Initial box B(0) at k=0? No, we start at kmin. # B(k) = [umin(k), vmin(k), umax(k), vmax(k)] # umin(k) = offsetumin + k dumin #... bumin = offsetumin + kmin dumin bumax = offsetumax + kmin dumax bvmin = offsetvmin + kmin dvmin bvmax = offsetvmax + kmin dvmax # Delta for incremental update deltab = (dumin, dumax, dvmin, dvmax) # 6. Traverse Slices for k in range(kmin, kmax + 1): # Convert to cell IDs i0 = int(bumin) # Truncate i1 = int(bumax) j0 = int(bvmin) j1 = int(bvmax) # Clamp to grid bounds i0 = max(0, min(i0, griddims[uaxis] - 1)) i1 = max(0, min(i1, griddims[uaxis] - 1)) j0 = max(0, min(j0, griddims[vaxis] - 1)) j1 = max(0, min(j1, griddims[vaxis] - 1)) # Yield cells in this slice for i in range(i0, i1 + 1): for j in range(j0, j1 + 1): yield (i, j, k) # Incremental update for next slice bumin += deltab[0] bumax += deltab[1] bvmin += deltab[2] bvmax += deltab[3] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Divergence: If rays in a packet span an angle > \pi/2, they may have different signs along the traversal axis, violating the front-to-back assumption. Mitigation: Split the packet into subpackets. Silhouette Hit Points: If primary rays hit object silhouettes, hit points can be distant, creating a wide frustum where the method breaks down. Mitigation: Split the packet if min/max hit distances are too large. Roll Angle: When the "roll" angle of the bundles to the volume angle is close to \pi/4, block fetches can double. Redundant Intersections: Grids do not conform tightly to geometry, causing redundant triangle intersections. Mitigation: Use SIMD frustum culling and mailboxing. Straddling Triangles: Large triangles or small triangles straddling boundaries may appear in multiple cells. Mitigation: Mailboxing. An optimization for glyph-based particle visualization that eliminates data duplication by storing each particle in exactly one grid cell, traversing an enlarged frustum to ensure containment. Extends CGT to large volumes using a recursive hierarchy of macrocells (2^3 children) to amortize traversal costs, using an iterative stack. A parallelization scheme assigning processing elements to slices of the volume, requiring explicit data structures to map bundles to slices. A parallelization scheme where bundles of rays are processed in parallel, distributing work across processing elements. A culling technique for spheres that checks if the sphere center is contained within an enlarged bounding frustum, avoiding unnecessary intersection tests. A hierarchical grid structure that divides densely populated regions more finely, using parameter range culling for early-out tests. Time Complexity: The traversal cost per step is independent of the number of rays in the packet, encouraging larger packets. The incremental update of the overlap box requires only four floating-point additions (one SIMD instruction) and one float-to-int conversion (one SIMD instruction) per slice. Memory Complexity: The grid is uniform and simple to build, making it suitable for per-frame rebuilds in dynamic scenes. For volume rendering, a "bricked" volume structure reduces memory overhead by not storing empty bricks. Measured Performance: On a dual 3.2 GHz Xeon, rendering a 174K triangle animated scene at 1024x1024 achieves 1.4 fps with shading/textures/shadows, and 3.4 fps excluding them. CGT outperforms single-ray 3DDDA by a factor of 6.75 to 20.9x. It performs competitively with kd-trees (e.g., 1.0M vs 0.82M ray-triangle intersections in the 'toys' scene). Scaling: Sublinear scaling in screen resolution is observed because higher resolutions enable larger packets, amortizing traversal costs. Strengths: Simple grid construction allows for full per-frame rebuilds, ideal for dynamic/animated scenes. Avoids expensive packet splitting and merging. Cache-friendly for volume rendering. Limitations: Uniform grids are ill-suited for highly complex scenes with high variation in geometry size and density (e.g., Boeing 777). Performance degrades if the roll angle is close to \pi/4. Coherent Grid Traversal was introduced in 2006 by Wald, Ize, Kensler, Knoll, and Parker in "Ray Tracing Animated Scenes using Coherent Grid Traversal" published in ACM Transactions on Graphics (SIGGRAPH). It was developed to address the limitations of packet-based kd-tree traversal for dynamic scenes, where rebuilding the kd-tree is expensive. The algorithm abandons cell-by-cell traversal (3DDDA) in favor of slice-by-slice traversal to maintain coherence within ray packets. It has been used in systems for interactive visualization of large particle datasets and volume rendering. name: Sphere-Center Method
head: Sphere-center grid
body: The Sphere-Center Method is an optimization for glyph-based particle visualization within the Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) framework that eliminates data duplication and redundant intersection tests by storing each particle in exactly one grid cell. It achieves this by traversing an enlarged frustum that accounts for the maximum particle radius, ensuring that any sphere intersecting the original view volume has its center contained within the traversal bounds. Unlike standard grid approaches that require mailboxes or reference lists to handle primitives overlapping multiple cells, this method guarantees single storage and single intersection per particle. The method exploits the property that particle radii are either uniform or fall within a well-defined range. By using the maximum radius across all particles, the algorithm constructs a frustum large enough to contain the centers of all potentially intersecting spheres, thereby allowing a simple "center-in-cell" storage scheme. Inputs: Particle dataset: A collection of spheres defined by center coordinates (x, y, z) and radius r. Ray packet frustum F: Defined by bounding planes and near/far clipping planes. Grid resolution: Determines the cell size in world units. Outputs: A grid structure where each sphere is stored in exactly one cell. An enlarged frustum Fr used for traversal. Grid: A multi-level grid structure (as defined in Coherent Grid Traversal). Cell Content: Each cell stores a list of particle indices or direct particle data. Unlike standard grids, no duplicate entries or mailbox structures are required. Particle Storage: Particles are stored directly in the finest level of the grid. The conversion from floating-point center coordinates to grid cell indices is performed via truncation. r{max}: The maximum radius across all particles in the dataset. This value is determined once during initialization and cached for subsequent build and traversal steps. dU: The direction vector component of the normal to a bounding plane of the frustum. 1. Initialization: Compute r{max} by iterating over all particles and finding the maximum radius. Cache r{max} for use in grid construction and traversal. 2. Grid Construction: For each particle with center C = (x, y, z), compute its grid cell coordinates by truncating the floating-point values of its center in the grid coordinate space to integers. Store the particle in the list of the identified cell. This process replaces expensive primitive/cell or bounding box/cell overlap tests with a single float-to-int truncation per particle. 3. Frustum Enlargement: Compute the shift distance s for the side bounding planes of the frustum. The distance s is calculated based on r{max} and the plane normal direction dU: s = r{max} \sqrt{1 + dU^2} Derivation: The condition that a sphere of radius r{max} intersects a bounding plane defined by normal direction dU is equivalent to the sphere's center being within distance r{max} of the plane. Geometrically, this requires shifting the plane by s such that the projection of the shift vector onto the normal equals r{max}. The scalar projection formula yields r{max} = \frac{\langle -dU, 1 \rangle \cdot \langle 0, s \rangle}{|\langle -dU, 1 \rangle|}, which solves to s = r{max} \sqrt{1 + dU^2}. Adjust the bounding planes: Add s to the u0 parameter for the maximum bounding plane and subtract s for the minimum bounding plane. Adjust the near and far planes: Shift the near plane by r{max} in the -\mathbf{K} direction and the far plane by r{max} in the +\mathbf{K} direction, where \mathbf{K} is the viewing direction. The resulting structure is the enlarged frustum Fr. 4. Traversal: Traverse the grid using the enlarged frustum Fr instead of the original frustum F. For each cell visited, intersect the rays in the packet against all spheres stored in that cell. Because the frustum is enlarged by r{max}, any sphere intersecting the original frustum F is guaranteed to have its center inside Fr. Thus, intersecting only spheres whose centers are in the visited cells covers all potential intersections. 5. Early Ray Termination: Adjust early ray termination criteria to account for spheres whose centers lie in the next slice but whose geometry extends into the current slice due to the enlarged frustum. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raysphereintersect(rayo, rayd, spherec, radius): """Standard ray-sphere intersection check.""" oc = [rayo[i] - spherec[i] for i in range(3)] a = sum(rayd[i] rayd[i] for i in range(3)) b = sum(oc[i] rayd[i] for i in range(3)) c = sum(oc[i] oc[i] for i in range(3)) - radius radius return b b - a c >= 0 def spherecenterbuild(particles, frustumplanes, frustumnear, frustumfar, viewdir, cellsize): rmax = max(p.radius for p in particles) grid = {} for i, p in enumerate(particles): gx = int(p.center[0] / cellsize) gy = int(p.center[1] / cellsize) gz = int(p.center[2] / cellsize) grid.setdefault((gx, gy, gz), []).append(i) enlargedplanes = [] for plane in frustumplanes: dU = plane['normal'][0] s = rmax math.sqrt(1.0 + dU dU) newu0 = plane['u0'] + (s if plane['ismax'] else -s) enlargedplanes.append({'normal': plane['normal'], 'u0': newu0, 'ismax': plane['ismax']}) enlargednear = frustumnear - rmax enlargedfar = frustumfar + rmax return grid, enlargedplanes, enlargednear, enlargedfar, viewdir def traverse(grid, planes, near, far, viewdir, particles, rays): for cellkey, indices in grid.items(): cellmin = [c 1.0 for c in cellkey] cellmax = [m + 1.0 for m in cellmin] if not boxintersectsfrustum(cellmin, cellmax, planes, near, far, viewdir): continue for idx in indices: p = particles[idx] for ray in rays: if raysphereintersect(ray.origin, ray.dir, p.center, p.radius): pass def boxintersectsfrustum(boxmin, boxmax, planes, near, far, viewdir): """Checks if an axis-aligned box intersects the frustum planes.""" for plane in planes: n = plane['normal'] u0 = plane['u0'] # Check if box is completely outside the plane if (boxmin[0] n[0] + boxmin[1] n[1] + boxmin[2] n[2] < u0 and boxmax[0] n[0] + boxmax[1] n[1] + boxmax[2] n[2] < u0): return False if boxmin[2] < near or boxmax[2] > far: return False return True Wide Radius Range: If particle radii span several orders of magnitude, using r{max} causes the enlarged frustum to be excessively large. This results in traversing many empty cells and intersecting many unnecessary spheres, potentially outweighing the benefits of single storage. Frustum culling is typically required to mitigate this performance loss. Non-Uniform Radii: The method assumes radii are uniform or within a small range. If this assumption is violated, the performance gain diminishes. Plane Normal Definition: The calculation of s depends on the definition of dU. The sources define dU as the direction vector of the given plane's normal in a reduced 2D context where the normal is \langle -dU, 1 \rangle. Implementers must ensure dU is extracted correctly from the frustum plane definitions. Uses a macrocell hierarchy to skip empty space efficiently within the CGT framework. Choose when the scene has large regions of empty space and hierarchical skipping is beneficial. See Macrocell Hierarchical CGT. Parallelizes the processing of slices within the CGT traversal. Choose when hardware supports parallel execution across slices. See Slice Parallelisation. Parallelizes ray packets across multiple cores. Choose when ray-level parallelism is preferred over slice-level. See Bundle Parallelisation. Uses SIMD instructions to efficiently cull spheres against frusta. Choose when CPU SIMD capabilities are available to accelerate culling operations. See SIMD Sphere/Frustum Culling. Time Complexity: Grid construction is O(N) where N is the number of particles, due to the simple truncation operation. Traversal complexity depends on the number of cells visited by the enlarged frustum and the number of spheres per cell. Memory Complexity: Memory footprint is reduced significantly because each particle is stored exactly once. For the BulletTorso dataset (35M particles), storage dropped from 3.11 GB (with references) to 1.04 GB. Measured Performance: Speed-up over standard grid: 1.02x to 1.27x on various datasets (Cylinder, JP8, Bullet, Thunder, Foam, BulletTorso). Grid construction time improvement: Up to 3.07x faster insertion phase (e.g., JP8 dataset: 797.71 ms to 260.13 ms). Total construction time improved from 1407.27 ms to 510.96 ms (factor of 2.75). Strengths: Eliminates data duplication and mailbox overhead. Improves locality of reference. Simplifies grid construction by avoiding overlap tests. Efficient frustum computation using SIMD (5 operations). Limitations: Performance degrades if particle radii vary widely. Requires a priori knowledge of r{max}. Enlarged frustum may traverse more cells than necessary if r{max} is large relative to particle density. When to Use: Ideal for particle-based simulation data with uniform or narrowly distributed radii, where interactive performance and low memory footprint are critical. When Not to Use: When particle radii vary by several orders of magnitude, unless combined with effective frustum culling. The Sphere-Center Method was introduced in the context of interactive ray tracing for particle-based simulation data, specifically for visualizing material point method (MPM) simulations. It was presented as an optimization to the Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) algorithm to address classic grid problems: duplicate data, lack of locality of reference, and redundant intersection tests. The method draws inspiration from offset surfaces used in collision detection. It was evaluated on datasets such as Cylinder, JP8, Bullet, Thunder, Foam, and BulletTorso, demonstrating improvements in both frame rate and memory usage. The approach is applicable to other primitive types, such as triangles, though primarily designed for spherical glyphs. name: Macrocell Hierarchical CGT
head: Hierarchical CGT, Recursive CGT with Array Stack
body: Macrocell Hierarchical CGT extends Coherent Grid Traversal [2987-coherent-grid-traversal.md] to handle large volumes by introducing a recursive hierarchy of macrocells, where each parent block contains 2^3 children. It solves the performance degradation of flat CGT on large datasets by amortizing traversal costs across multiple levels of granularity, using an array stack to manage the hierarchy iteratively rather than recursively. It differs from Sphere-Center Method by maintaining slice-based frustum traversal and from Bundle Parallelisation by focusing on spatial hierarchy management rather than ray packet parallelism. Inputs: A ray packet with bounding frustum defined by axes U, V, K; a volume with a hierarchical macrocell structure; a target isovalue. Outputs: A list of visited cells or traversal state updates. Data Structures: The core structure is an Array Stack that replaces recursive function calls. For a hierarchy of depth L, the stack stores: 1. uslice, vslice: Current slice coordinates for each level l \in [0, L-1]. 2. uinc, vinc: Increment values for U and V axes for each level. 3. currentslice: The current slice index within the active macrocell level. 4. returnslice: The slice index at which to resume parent macrocell traversal. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the stack for the root macrocell level. Set initial U, V slices and increments based on the frustum intersection with the root volume. Set currentslice to the starting K-slice. Let l be the current macrocell level (initially 0). 2. Loop: While the stack is not empty and rays have not exited the volume: a. Culling Test: Check if the current macrocell at uslice[l], vslice[l] contains the target isovalue by comparing it against the macrocell's precomputed min/max range. b. Traversal Decision: i. If the macrocell is empty (isovalue not in min/max range), skip to the next slice or parent level. ii. If the macrocell is non-empty and l < L-1 (not leaf), push state for child level l+1 onto the stack. Child coordinates are derived from parent coordinates as M-multiples. iii. If the macrocell is non-empty and l = L-1 (leaf level), traverse the full slice of volume cells within this macrocell using standard CGT logic. c. Advance: Increment currentslice for level l. If currentslice exceeds the macrocell boundary, pop the stack to return to the parent level l-1, setting currentslice to returnslice[l-1]. 3. Termination: Stop when all rays have intersected or exited the root macrocell. Formulas: Child coordinate mapping: C{child} = M \times C{parent}. Next macrocell slice (for binary subdivision, M=2): Slice{next} = Slice{current} + 2. Parameters: M: Macrocell width multiple. Typically M=2 for octree alignment. L: Number of macrocell layers. A 3-deep hierarchy is effective for volumes > 256^3. Edge Cases: Implicit Macrocells: When using an octree, macrocells are implicit. Min/max pairs are retrieved from octree interior nodes, but to avoid costly lookups, the path from the octree root to the current node along the U,V-minimal ray of the frustum is stored. Leaf Node Mapping: A single coarse scalar leaf node in the octree may cover multiple finer-level implicit macrocells. The algorithm must find the deepest octree child mapping to the implicit macrocell coordinate to perform the isovalue cull. A variant where the macrocell hierarchy is implicit in the octree structure, retrieving min/max pairs from octree interior nodes instead of explicit macrocell blocks. It uses a common coordinate space [0, 2^{d{max}}] for all octree node depths, where d{max} is the maximum tree depth. This allows optimization for binary subdivision: multiplying the K-slice by macrocell width M=2 is replaced by a bitwise left-shift, and computing the next macrocell slice requires a simple +2 addition. It is chosen when the volume is naturally stored as an octree, avoiding the overhead of explicit macrocell data structures. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of visited cells, but with a significantly reduced constant factor for large volumes due to early culling at macrocell levels. Memory Complexity: O(L) for the stack, where L is the hierarchy depth. Additional memory for octree storage if implicit. Performance: A recursive 3-level macrocell hierarchy yields best performance for volumes larger than 256^3. Strengths: Handles large volumes efficiently; avoids recursion overhead; compatible with octree structures. Limitations: Requires precomputed min/max values for macrocells; complex implementation due to stack management and implicit node mapping. When to use: Large volumetric datasets (> 256^3) where flat CGT is too slow. When not to use: Small volumes where overhead outweighs benefits; non-octree data without explicit macrocell construction. Developed by Knoll et al. as an extension of Coherent Grid Traversal [2987-coherent-grid-traversal.md] to handle larger volumes, building on Parker et al.'s work. It was implemented to address the limitations of two-level hierarchies for volumes as small as 30^3, finding that deeper hierarchies (equivalent to full octrees) were necessary for robustness. It is used in interactive ray tracing of implicit surfaces and volumetric visualization.
