name: Slice Parallelisation
head: Data Parallel, Data Parallel / Slice-Parallel Rendering, Ray-slice-sweeping, Slice-Parallel Rendering
body: Slice Parallelisation is a parallelisation scheme for Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) where processing elements are assigned to slices of the volume rather than individual rays or bundles. It solves the problem of determining which ray bundles intersect a given slice when traversal is not incremental, requiring explicit data structures to map bundles to slices. Unlike Bundle Parallelisation, it reduces redundant block fetches from neighbouring bundles by organizing work per slice. Inputs: A set of ray bundles defined by their entry and exit points. The volume grid structure. The dominant traversal axis k. Outputs: For each slice s, a list of bundles that intersect it, ready for processing. Data Structures: The method maintains two sets of structures to track bundle-slice intersections: 1. Primary Vectors and Tables: Vector A: Stores references to bundles that start at the beginning of the volume (k=0). Vector D: Stores references to bundles that end at the end of the volume (k=k{\text{max}}). Table P: Index table corresponding to A. P[i] stores the slice index s where bundle A[i] starts. Table Q: Index table corresponding to D. Q[j] stores the slice index s where bundle D[j] ends. 2. Secondary Lists and Tables: List S: Stores references to "remaining" bundles (those that do not start at k=0 and do not end at k=k{\text{max}}). List E: Stores references to the same "remaining" bundles. Table M: Index table corresponding to S. M[i] stores the slice index s where bundle S[i] first intersects the volume. Table N: Index table corresponding to E. N[j] stores the slice index s where bundle E[j] last intersects the volume. List S is sorted by the values in M (ascending). List E is sorted by the values in N (ascending). Algorithm Steps: 1. Classification: During tracing, classify every bundle into one of three categories: starters (k=0), finishers (k=k{\text{max}}), and remaining bundles. 2. Population: Add starters to vector A and record their starting slice index in table P. Add finishers to vector D and record their ending slice index in table Q. Add remaining bundles to lists S and E, recording their first intersecting slice in M and last intersecting slice in N. Sort S by M and E by N. 3. Slice Processing: For a processing element assigned to slice s, identify all intersecting bundles using the following logic: Identify Starters: Retrieve all bundles from A where P[i] == s. Identify Finishers: Retrieve all bundles from D where Q[j] == s. Identify Remaining: Find bundles in S where M[i] \le s and bundles in E where N[j] \ge s. The intersection of these two sets gives the remaining bundles active in slice s. Combine: The total set of bundles for slice s is B(s) = B{\text{start}}(s) \cup B{\text{end}}(s) \cup B{\text{mid}}(s). 4. Traversal: For each bundle in B(s), perform the CGT traversal steps for the cells within slice s. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processslice(s, A, D, P, Q, S, E, M, N): # Identify starters: bundles starting exactly at slice s Bstart = [A[i] for i in range(len(A)) if P[i] == s] # Identify finishers: bundles ending exactly at slice s Bend = [D[j] for j in range(len(D)) if Q[j] == s] # Identify remaining bundles: those that span across slice s # S is sorted by M (ascending), E is sorted by N (ascending) # Sources state we must run through both lists to find the intersection Bmid = [] for i in range(len(S)): if M[i] <= s: bundle = S[i] for j in range(len(E)): if E[j] is bundle and N[j] >= s: Bmid.append(bundle) break return Bstart + Bend + Bmid Formulas: B{\text{start}}(s) = \{ A[i] \mid P[i] == s \} B{\text{end}}(s) = \{ D[j] \mid Q[j] == s \} B{\text{mid}}(s) = \{ S[i] \mid M[i] \le s \} \cap \{ E[j] \mid N[j] \ge s \} Parameters: k{\text{max}}: The maximum index along the dominant traversal axis. Average percentage of "Remaining" bundles: ~14%. Maximum percentage of "Remaining" bundles: 33%. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cache Locality: If vectors A and D fit in cache/local store, identifying bundles for a slice requires 0 memory reads beyond the cache. If they do not fit, exactly 2 memory reads are required to fetch the relevant index tables. Redundant Fetches: While Slice Parallelisation is less likely to exhibit redundant block fetches from neighbouring bundles compared to other methods, it is still possible. Roll Angle: When the "roll" angle of the bundles relative to the volume angle is close to \pi/4, the number of block fetches can double. A solution is noted as "not yet published" in the source. A slice-parallel technique that processes consecutive data slices parallel to a face of the volume data set. It partitions object space rather than screen space, assigning tasks to processors that request new tasks upon completion. Introduced by de Boer et al., this variant divides the volume into horizontal sections processed in turn. This reduces the slice face area and hence the size of the slice buffers. A two-dimensional array of SIMD processing elements used for parallel segmentation. The volume is distributed so that a complete beam of voxels along the z-axis is stored on each processing element, allowing conflict-free access to any z-slice with only a single clock cycle delay between slices. Complexity: The identification of bundles for a slice s requires constant time for starters and finishers (2 memory reads). The identification of remaining bundles requires scanning lists S and E. Since the remaining bundles are a small fraction (avg 14%, max 33%), this overhead is considered negligible and "does not hit performance". Memory: Requires storage for vectors A, D and lists S, E, plus index tables P, Q, M, N. Strengths: Trivial to implement (e.g., 1 line of OpenMP code in C++). Reduces redundant block fetches compared to bundle parallelisation. Limitations: Traversal is not incremental, requiring explicit tracking of bundle-slice intersections. Performance may degrade if the roll angle is near \pi/4. Slice Parallelisation is a parallelisation strategy developed for the Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) algorithm for volume rendering. It was presented by researchers at the UCL Department of Computer Science. The method addresses the non-incremental nature of slice-based traversal by introducing explicit data structures to map bundles to slices. name: Bundle Parallelisation
head: GPU Integration Optimization, Ray Compaction and Sorting Optimization
body: Bundle parallelisation is a parallelization scheme for coherent grid traversal where bundles of rays are processed in parallel. It distributes the processing of ray bundles across multiple processing elements to accelerate volume rendering. Unlike slice parallelisation, which requires complex index tables to map bundles to slices, bundle parallelisation processes bundles directly, though it may result in redundant block fetches from neighbouring bundles. Inputs: Ray bundles, depth map, shadow map, and image dimensions. Outputs: Rendered image pixels with accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: Bundle: A collection of rays sharing a common traversal path or depth range. Shadow Map: Depth buffer used for visibility prefiltering. Partial Sum Tree: Stores accumulated transmittance and color for a slice. Thread Blocks: Allocated per slice. Steps: 1. Rectification: Perform a data-parallel operation on the depth and shadow maps to prepare data for visibility queries. One thread is assigned per output pixel. 2. Sorting and Prefiltering: Combine visibility prefiltering and sorting into a single kernel. This step coalesces groups of 4 rays based on their depth information from the shadow map. A modified GPU radix sort is used to coalesce rays with similar depths as it walks over the input shadow map. 3. Integration: Allocate one thread block of 32 threads per slice. Assign one thread per slice for the integration phase because partial sum trees are too large to fit into shared memory. Store the partial sum trees in global memory. Execute the inner loop using the while-if-if strategy (UPDATE-TREE and QUERY-TREE) to minimize instruction divergence, ensuring at least half the threads in a warp perform useful work. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bundleparallelisation(bundles, depthmap, shadowmap, imagewidth, imageheight): # Step 1: Rectification # Data-parallel operation on depth and shadow maps. # One thread per output pixel. rectifieddata = [] for y in range(imageheight): row = [] for x in range(imagewidth): row.append((depthmap[y][x], shadowmap[y][x])) rectifieddata.append(row) # Step 2: Sorting and Prefiltering # Combine visibility prefiltering and sorting into a single kernel. # Coalesce groups of 4 rays based on depth from shadow map. # Modified GPU radix sort coalesces rays with similar depths walking over shadow map. sortedbundles = [] for bundle in bundles: groups = [] for i in range(0, len(bundle), 4): group = bundle[i:i+4] # Sort group by shadow map depth to coalesce similar rays group.sort(key=lambda ray: rectifieddata[ray.y][ray.x][1]) groups.append(group) sortedbundles.append(groups) # Step 3: Integration # Allocate one block of 32 threads per slice. # Assign one thread per slice because partial sum trees are too large for shared memory. # Store trees in global memory. numslices = imageheight // 32 globalmemorytrees = [None] numslices renderedimage = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight imagewidth)] for sliceidx in range(numslices): # One thread per slice handles this slice tree = globalmemorytrees[sliceidx] for group in sortedbundles: # while-if-if strategy for UPDATE-TREE and QUERY-TREE # Ensures at least half threads in warp do useful work while group: # UPDATE-TREE: accumulate transmittance and color # QUERY-TREE: sample and composite # Implementation details for tree operations not given in sources. pass return renderedimage Parameters: Block Size: 32 threads per slice. Ray Grouping: Groups of 4 rays coalesced during sorting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Redundant Fetches: Some blocks may be fetched multiple times from neighbouring bundles. Memory Constraints: Partial sum trees are too large for shared memory on current hardware, necessitating global memory storage. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Global memory usage for partial sum trees due to size constraints. Performance: The method is described as "trivial" to implement on CPU with OpenMP (1 line of code). On GPU, it uses specific optimizations like the while-if-if strategy to ensure at least half the threads in a warp do useful work. Strengths: Efficient parallelisation of ray bundles; reduced instruction divergence in integration. Limitations: Potential for redundant block fetches from neighbouring bundles. Bundle parallelisation is a technique used in coherent grid traversal for volume rendering. It was implemented as part of a hierarchical volumetric shadow algorithm for single scattering. The approach was also noted in presentations on coherent grid traversal algorithms. name: Wavefront Buffering and Polling
head: Asynchronous Ray-Segment Communication, Parallel Volume Rendering with Wavefront Buffering and Polling, Wavefront Cache-friendly Algorithm
body: Wavefront Buffering and Polling is a communication strategy for parallel volume rendering that manages the transfer of ray segments between processors to enable ray merging and early ray termination. It solves the problem of synchronizing asynchronous ray traversal across distributed memory by buffering outgoing segments and periodically polling for incoming data. It sets itself apart from synchronous bulk-transfer methods by spreading communication load over the frame time and allowing processors to revert to receiving mode if blocked from sending, thereby avoiding deadlock. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset (e.g., tetrahedral grid), viewing parameters, opacity mapping, and processor topology. Output: A rendered image frame. Internal State: Per-processor buffers for outgoing ray segments and incoming ray segments. Data Structures: Ray Segment Buffer: A queue or array holding ray segments. Each segment is 24 bytes. The buffer has a maximum depth (size) B. Polling Interval: An integer P representing the number of cells to scan-convert before checking for communication. Parameters: Buffer Size (B): The maximum number of ray segments buffered per processor before forced communication. Typical values range from 25 up to 1.25 \times M, where M is the expected useful maximum. Expected Useful Maximum (M): The average number of ray segments communicated from each processor to every other processor per frame. This is highly problem-dependent (varies with input data, viewing parameters, opacity mapping, and processor count). For the tested dataset, M \approx 1200. Polling Interval (P): The number of tetrahedral cells scan-converted between communication checks. Strategies include: Fixed value (e.g., 160 or 200). Dynamic: P = 2 \times B. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize ray segment buffers for each processor. Set buffer size B and polling interval P. 2. Scan Conversion Loop: For each cell assigned to the processor: a. Scan-convert the cell to generate ray segments. b. Add generated ray segments to the outgoing buffer. c. Increment cell counter. d. If cell counter reaches P, proceed to Step 3. 3. Polling and Communication: a. Call termination detection routine to check for global termination. b. Check for incoming ray segments from other processors. c. If incoming segments exist, merge them with local ray segments (ray merging). d. If the outgoing buffer is full or if the processor is blocked from sending, flush the buffer to other processors. e. Reset cell counter to 0. 4. Deadlock Avoidance: If a processor is blocked from sending (e.g., network congestion), it automatically reverts to a receiving mode, regardless of whether the polling interval P has been reached. 5. Termination: When all cells are processed and no more ray segments are expected, finalize the frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def wavefrontbufferingandpolling(dataset, processors, buffersizeB, pollingintervalP): # Initialize buffers outgoingbuffers = [Buffer(maxsize=buffersizeB) for in processors] incomingbuffers = [Buffer() for in processors] # Assign cells to processors cellassignments = assigncellstoprocessors(dataset, processors) for procid, cells in cellassignments.items(): cellcount = 0 for cell in cells: # Scan-convert cell newsegments = scanconvertcell(cell, dataset) # Add to outgoing buffer outgoingbuffers[procid].add(newsegments) cellcount += 1 # Check polling interval if cellcount >= pollingintervalP: # Poll for incoming data and termination isterminated = checkterminationdetection() if isterminated: break # Receive incoming segments receivedsegments = receivefromneighbors(procid, incomingbuffers) # Merge incoming segments with local ray segments mergeraysegments(outgoingbuffers[procid], receivedsegments) # Send buffered segments if not blocked # If blocked, revert to receiving mode (handled by receive logic) sendtoneighbors(procid, outgoingbuffers[procid]) cellcount = 0 # Final flush if needed if not outgoingbuffers[procid].isempty(): sendtoneighbors(procid, outgoingbuffers[procid]) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Excessively Large Buffer Size: Eliminates the benefit of spreading communication load, defers all communication to frame end, and causes locality loss in ray merging. Larger buffers deliver many ray segments at once over a wider image area, reducing early merge opportunities, lengthening ray segment lists, and increasing insertion time and memory consumption. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. The parent method that groups rays into bundles for parallel processing. Wavefront Buffering and Polling is a communication strategy used within this framework. Bundle Parallelisation Time Complexity: Not explicitly given. Rendering time scales linearly with pixel count. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given. Memory consumption increases with buffer size and ray segment list length. Measured Performance: On 511 processors with a large dataset, an average of 44.6 million ray segments are communicated per frame. Aggregate volume is ~1.1 GB (24 bytes per segment). Ray-segment merging accounts for 46.64% of total computation time (0.949170 s out of 2.035252 s total), making it the most expensive operation, costing >4× scan conversion. Overhead breakdown on 511 processors: termination detection dominates overhead at 9.24% (0.187978 s), followed by receive wait at 7.94% (0.161666 s). Total overhead is 25.98%. Performance sensitivity to buffer depth: Total rendering time variation across tested buffer depths is only ~16%, despite degradation at larger sizes. Image resolution scaling: At 1200×1200, overhead drops to 12.4% due to a larger ray segment buffer (1,000 vs 100) enabling more efficient communication. Strengths: Spreads communication load over time, avoids deadlock, well-suited for high-bandwidth networks (e.g., SGI T3E). Limitations: Poor performance on distributed shared memory architectures (e.g., SGI Origin2000). Ray merging is a dominant cost. When to Use: High-performance clusters with high network bandwidth (e.g., SGI T3E, Linux PC clusters). When Not to Use: Distributed shared memory architectures with poor message passing software or memory management (e.g., SGI Origin2000). Origin: The method was developed and tested on SGI T3E (up to 511 processors), SGI Origin2000, and a 32-node Linux PC cluster. It outperforms the T3E at moderate processor counts on the Linux cluster. History: The algorithm is part of a wavefront cache-friendly approach for parallel volume rendering. Initial tests on SGI Origin2000 yielded poor results, consistent with findings in other literature. Usage: Used for direct volume rendering of high-resolution datasets, such as flow density and velocity magnitude in aerodynamic simulations. name: SIMD Sphere/Frustum Culling
head: Sphere/Frustum Culling
body: A culling technique to reject non-overlapping spheres by checking if the sphere center is contained within an enlarged bounding frustum, thereby avoiding unnecessary ray/sphere intersection tests caused by discretization artifacts or spheres smaller than the maximum radius r{max}. It sets itself apart from the SIMD shaft culling used in the original Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) by being appropriate for spheres, which lack the planar edges required for shaft culling. Inputs: A packet of rays bounded by an original bounding frustum \mathcal{F}. A set of spheres, each defined by a center \mathbf{c} and radius r. An enlarged bounding frustum \mathcal{F}', constructed by shifting the planes of \mathcal{F} outward by r{max} (the maximum possible sphere radius in the dataset). This enlarged frustum is typically a by-product of the Sphere-Center Method. Outputs: A subset of spheres that potentially intersect the original frustum \mathcal{F}, requiring further ray/sphere intersection testing. Data Structures: The frustum is represented by its six planes. The "shifted bounding planes" from the Sphere-Center method define \mathcal{F}'. Steps: 1. For each sphere in the current cell or packet: a. Determine if the sphere center \mathbf{c} is contained within the enlarged frustum \mathcal{F}'. b. The containment test checks if the distance from \mathbf{c} to any plane of \mathcal{F}' is greater than the sphere's radius r; if so, the rays bounded by the frustum cannot intersect the sphere. Specifically, if the center is not contained by \mathcal{F}', the sphere is culled. c. If the center is contained by \mathcal{F}', the sphere is not culled and an intersection test is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isculled(spherecenter, enlargedfrustumplanes): """ spherecenter: vector (x, y, z) enlargedfrustumplanes: list of 6 plane definitions (normal, distance) Returns True if the sphere is culled (center outside enlarged frustum). """ for plane in enlargedfrustumplanes: # plane.normal is normalized vector pointing inward # plane.distance is scalar d # Signed distance from center to plane dist = dot(plane.normal, spherecenter) - plane.distance # If distance is negative, center is outside this plane if dist < 0: return True return False Parameters: r{max}: The maximum radius of any sphere in the dataset, used to compute the enlarged frustum \mathcal{F}'. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small Spheres: This approach does not cull spheres with radii r < r{max} that are contained by the enlarged frustum \mathcal{F}' but do not overlap the original frustum \mathcal{F}. These spheres require an intersection test. Discretization Artifacts: Spheres may lie within a cell through which the enlarged frustum passes, but the sphere does not overlap either the original or the enlarged frustum. The culling detects this if the center is outside \mathcal{F}', but if the center is inside \mathcal{F}' due to the expansion, the test proceeds. Complexity: The culling check requires only one SIMD operation on modern CPUs per sphere, as it involves simple distance-to-plane comparisons. Performance: Efficient frustum culling significantly reduces the number of ray/sphere intersection tests. In tests with 16 threads, the number of tests skipped ranged from 38.40% to 81.34% across datasets, improving interactive performance (frame rate) by a factor of 1.17 to 1.68. Cylinder: 61.84% skipped, 1.40x speed-up. JP8: 81.34% skipped, 1.68x speed-up. Bullet: 67.22% skipped, 1.41x speed-up. Thunder: 58.34% skipped, 1.40x speed-up. Foam: 55.61% skipped, 1.47x speed-up. BulletTorso: 38.40% skipped, 1.17x speed-up. Strengths: It cancels the behavior of uniform grids requiring more primitive intersection tests than adaptive structures like kd-trees or BVHs by reducing the number of actual tests performed. It is simpler than shaft culling and appropriate for spheres. Limitations: It cannot cull small spheres (r < r{max}) that are inside the expanded frustum but outside the original frustum. The technique is described in a paper on a coherent grid traversal approach for visualizing particle-based simulation data. It was developed to replace SIMD shaft culling, which relies on planar edges and is thus inappropriate for spheres. The technique leverages the shifted bounding planes generated by the Sphere-Center Method. A coherent grid traversal approach to visualizing particle-based simulation data, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/4293019/, fetched 2026-10-25

name: Hierarchical Grid with Macrocells
head: Macrocell hierarchy, Two-level hierarchy
body: A hierarchical grid structure that divides densely populated regions of space more finely than empty regions by imposing a coarser grid over the previous level, where each macrocell corresponds to an M \times M \times M block of cells in the underlying level. It sets itself apart from the original Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) by replacing simple Boolean empty/non-empty flags with parameter range culling, storing minimum and maximum values for multiple particle properties to enable more aggressive early-out tests. Inputs: Particle dataset containing position, radius, and up to four additional properties; macrocell resolution M; grid dimensions. Outputs: Hierarchical grid structure consisting of macrocells containing bounds for underlying cells. Data Structures: 1. Macrocell: Stores minimum and maximum values for eight parameters: position x, y, z, radius, and up to four additional particle properties. This replaces the Boolean empty/non-empty flag used in the original CGT algorithm. 2. Underlying Grid: Standard CGT grid cells, organized into blocks of size M \times M \times M corresponding to macrocells. Construction Algorithm (Sort-Middle): 1. Distribute construction tasks for disjoint sections of the grid statically among all system threads. 2. Each thread performs a coarse parallel bucket sort of particles by their cell location, inserting them into its local set of buckets. 3. Regions for each bucket are disjoint, avoiding write conflicts and the need for mutexes. 4. Each thread inserts its particles into the appropriate grid cells within its assigned disjoint region. 5. Aggregate the grid data to form macrocells by computing the min/max of the eight parameters across all particles contained in each underlying M \times M \times M block of cells. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildhierarchicalgrid(particles, M, numthreads, gridmin, gridmax, cellsize): # 1. body: The adaptive grid data structure, proposed by Klimaszewski and Sederberg [KS97], is a hierarchical grid building method that constructs local grids acting as bounding boxes in densely populated areas. It is characterized by a fast bottom-up construction approach, contrasting with top-down adaptive subdivision methods. The resulting structure is viewed as a loosely nested recursive grid. Inputs: A set of geometric primitives. Outputs: A hierarchical structure of local grids. Data Structures: The structure consists of a hierarchy of bounding boxes. Each node in the hierarchy contains a local grid. The hierarchy is built such that boxes act as bounding volumes for the primitives they contain. Algorithm Steps: The construction follows a specific bottom-up sequence: 1. Bounding Box Creation: For each primitive, surround it with a bounding box. 2. Merging: For all bounding boxes, merge close boxes to form a structured grid. 3. Tree Insertion: For all remaining boxes, insert the box into the tree using a minimum surface criterion. 4. Local Grid Construction: For all bounding boxes in the hierarchy, build a local grid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Hero-like 4-Connectivity (H4T)
body: Hero-like 4-Connectivity (H4T) is a ray traversal algorithm for uniform grids that guarantees strict 4-connectivity by resolving boundary crossing ambiguities through a stable sort of candidate cell entries. It differs from standard DDA and its sibling Coherent Grid Traversal by explicitly testing a 2x2 cell neighborhood and using axis-priority sorting to prevent diagonal jumps, ensuring that rays crossing grid lines do so one axis at a time. H4T determines the sequence of voxels visited by a ray by identifying the entry point into a 2x2 block of cells and then advancing through them while maintaining connectivity. The method relies on a stable sorting mechanism to break ties between axis crossings. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, grid dimensions, voxel size v. Output: A sequence of voxel indices (i, j, k) visited by the ray. Data Structures: Candidate List: A list of tuples containing (t, \text{axis\id}), where t is the distance to the next boundary and \text{axis\id} identifies the axis (0 for x, 1 for y, 2 for z). Steps: 1. 2x2 Cell Test: Identify the candidate cells the ray passes through in the current 2x2 block by computing the distance t to the next boundary along each active axis. 2. Associate Axis IDs: For each candidate boundary crossing distance t, associate it with an axis identifier (0 for x, 1 for y). 3. Stable Sort: Sort the candidate list using a stable sorting algorithm. The sort key is primarily the axis identifier, and secondarily the t-value. This ensures that if t-values for the x and y axes are equal, the x-axis (0) is processed before the y-axis (1), preserving 4-connectivity. 4. Advance: Select the first entry in the sorted list as the next cell. Update the ray's position and repeat the process for the next block. The grid position must be floored before reading the grid data, as the method may produce fractional position values during intermediate calculations. Pseudocode: The source notes that the full C implementation is too long to include and describes the logic conceptually. The following pseudocode implements the described stable sort logic for the 2x2 test resolution, adapted to 3D traversal. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def h4ttraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelsize, griddims): # Initialize current voxel index (floor division handles negative coordinates correctly) currentvoxel = [int(rayorigin[i] // voxelsize) for i in range(3)] # Step direction per axis step = [1 if raydirection[i] > 0 else (-1 if raydirection[i] < 0 else 0) for i in range(3)] # Distance to next boundary per axis nextboundary = [(currentvoxel[i] + (1 if raydirection[i] > 0 else 0)) voxelsize for i in range(3)] tmax = [(nextboundary[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] if raydirection[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] # Distance delta per axis tdelta = [voxelsize / abs(raydirection[i]) if raydirection[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] tentry = 0.0 while 0 <= currentvoxel[0] < griddims[0] and \ 0 <= currentvoxel[1] < griddims[1] and \ 0 <= currentvoxel[2] < griddims[2]: # H4T-specific step: pair tmax with axisid and sort stably # Primary key: axisid (0=x, 1=y, 2=z), Secondary key: tmax candidates = [(tmax[0], 0), (tmax[1], 1), (tmax[2], 2)] candidates.sort(key=lambda x: (x[1], x[0])) # Python's sort is stable # Extract the axis with the smallest tmax (ties broken by axisid) minidx = candidates[0][1] texit = candidates[0][0] yield currentvoxel, tentry, texit currentvoxel[minidx] += step[minidx] tmax[minidx] += tdelta[minidx] tentry = texit Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ties: The critical pitfall is the handling of equal t-values for different axes. Without stable sorting by axis ID, the traversal may jump diagonally, violating 4-connectivity. Fractional Positions: The method may result in fractional grid positions during calculation. The grid must be accessed using floored coordinates. Code Length: The source notes that the full implementation is complex and lengthy, suggesting careful handling of the candidate list management. name: Hierarchical Planes 4-Connectivity (HP4T)
body: Hierarchical Planes 4-Connectivity (HP4T) is a ray traversal algorithm for hierarchical grids, such as Octrees or Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO), that ensures strict 4-connectivity by preventing diagonal jumps between cells. It distinguishes itself from its sibling Hierarchical Planes 8-Connectivity (HP8T) by applying clamping logic to the non-hit axis, thereby avoiding the surface normal ambiguities and connectivity errors inherent in 8-connected approaches. HP4T calculates the intersection of a ray with the bounding planes of the current cell to determine the next cell. It uses the plane positions directly to compute the new grid coordinates, ensuring that the ray does not skip adjacent cells diagonally. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin (rayposition), ray direction (raydir), inverse ray direction (invdir), current grid position (gridposition), current cell size (cellsize), and grid dimensions (gridwidth, gridheight). Outputs: Updated gridposition for the next cell, and the traversal distance t to that cell. Data Structures The method operates on 2D grid positions (x, y) representing the current cell indices in the hierarchical level. gridposition: A 2D vector (x, y) of integer or floating-point coordinates. rayposition: A 2D vector (x, y) representing the ray origin projected or relevant to the current plane. raydir: A 2D vector (x, y) representing the ray direction. invdir: A 2D vector (x, y) where each component is the reciprocal of the corresponding component in raydir. cellsize: A scalar representing the physical size of the cell at the current hierarchy level. Parameters cellsize: The size of the cell in world units, determined by the hierarchy level L as 2^L. For example, at level 0, cellsize is 1; at level 1, it is 2; at level 2, it is 4. invdir: Defined as the element-wise reciprocal of raydir, retaining the sign of the direction rather than using absolute values. isdirpos(x): A helper function returning 1 if x \ge 0, else 0, used to determine the offset of the next plane in the positive direction. isdirneg(x): A helper function returning 0 if x \ge 0, else 1, used to determine the offset of the next plane in the negative direction. signdir(x): A helper function returning the sign of x (1 if x \ge 0, -1 if x < 0). Steps 1. Calculate Plane Positions: Compute the world coordinates of the planes bounding the current cell in both axes using component-wise operations: \text{planes} = (\lfloor \text{grid\position} / \text{cellsize} \rfloor + \text{is\dir\pos}(\text{ray\dir})) \times \text{cellsize} Here, \lfloor \cdot \rfloor denotes the floor function applied component-wise, and the final multiplication is a Hadamard (pairwise) product. 2. Calculate Total T: Compute the distance along the ray to each plane using component-wise multiplication: \text{total\t} = (\text{planes} - \text{ray\position}) \times \text{inv\dir} This yields the parametric distance to the X and Y planes respectively. 3. Determine Hit Axis: Compare totalt.x and totalt.y to identify which plane the ray intersects first. 4. If totalt.x <= totalt.y (X-plane hit first): a. Set t = \text{total\t.x}. b. Update X position: \text{grid\position.x} = \text{planes.x} - \text{is\dir\neg}(\text{ray\dir.x}) This moves the grid index to the next cell in the direction of travel. c. Store the old Y position: \text{old\grid\pos\y} = \text{grid\position.y} d. Calculate the candidate new Y position based on ray intersection: \text{grid\position.y} = \lfloor \text{ray\dir.y} \times t + \text{ray\position.y} \rfloor e. Apply 4-connectivity clamping to Y. First, ensure no backward movement: \text{grid\position.y} = \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.y}) \times \max(0.0, \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.y}) \times (\text{grid\position.y} - \text{old\grid\pos\y})) Second, ensure the new Y does not skip the adjacent cell defined by the plane: \text{grid\position.y} = \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.y}) \times \min(\text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.y}) \times (\text{planes.y} - \text{is\dir\pos}(\text{ray\dir.y})), \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.y}) \times (\text{grid\position.y} + \text{old\grid\pos\y})) This clamping prevents diagonal jumps by restricting the Y update to the immediate neighbor. 5. Else (totalt.x > totalt.y, Y-plane hit first): a. Set t = \text{total\t.y}. b. Update Y position: \text{grid\position.y} = \text{planes.y} - \text{is\dir\neg}(\text{ray\dir.y}) c. Update X position using simplified clamping logic: \text{grid\position.x} = \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.x}) \times \min(\text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.x}) \times \text{planes.x} - \text{is\dir\pos}(\text{ray\dir.x}), \max(0.0, \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.x}) \times (\lfloor \text{ray\dir.x} \times t + \text{ray\position.x} \rfloor - \text{grid\position.x})) + \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.x}) \times \text{grid\position.x}) This mirrors the X-hit case logic, calculating a candidate position, clamping to prevent backward movement, and clamping to prevent skipping the plane neighbor. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def hp4tstep(gridposition, rayposition, raydir, invdir, cellsize, gridwidth, gridheight): def isdirpos(x): return 1 if x >= 0 else 0 def isdirneg(x): return 0 if x >= 0 else 1 def signdir(x): return 1 if x >= 0 else -1 # 1. Calculate plane positions (component-wise) planesx = (math.floor(gridposition.x / cellsize) + isdirpos(raydir.x)) cellsize planesy = (math.floor(gridposition.y / cellsize) + isdirpos(raydir.y)) cellsize # 2. Calculate totalt (component-wise) totaltx = (planesx - rayposition.x) invdir.x totalty = (planesy - rayposition.y) invdir.y if totaltx <= totalty: # X plane hit first t = totaltx # Update X gridposition.x = planesx - isdirneg(raydir.x) # Clamp Y oldgridposy = gridposition.y candidatey = math.floor(raydir.y t + rayposition.y) # Clamp 1: prevent backward movement gridposition.y = signdir(raydir.y) max(0.0, signdir(raydir.y) (candidatey - oldgridposy)) # Clamp 2: prevent skipping plane gridposition.y = signdir(raydir.y) min( signdir(raydir.y) (planesy - isdirpos(raydir.y)), signdir(raydir.y) (gridposition.y + oldgridposy)) else: # Y plane hit first t = totalty # Update Y gridposition.y = planesy - isdirneg(raydir.y) # Clamp X sx = signdir(raydir.x) candidatex = math.floor(raydir.x t + rayposition.x) gridposition.x = sx min( sx planesx - isdirpos(raydir.x), max(0.0, sx (candidatex - gridposition.x)) + sx gridposition.x) return gridposition, t Pitfalls Precision and connectivity errors in naive implementations using compare variables and t + eps can cause 8-connectivity (diagonal jumps) and incorrect surface normals. HP4T avoids this by using the explicit clamping logic described above. Removes the clamping logic of HP4T to allow 8-connectivity (diagonal jumps), simplifying the update code but requiring careful handling of surface normals and fractional positions. Choose HP8T when performance is critical and normal accuracy can be handled via post-processing or alternative methods. Time Complexity: Constant time per cell traversal step, involving basic arithmetic operations (floor, multiply, add, min, max). Memory Complexity: Constant space, requiring only a few temporary variables for the current step. Performance: In randomized testing of 100,000,000 cases, HP4T achieved a 99.99% chance of correct position and a 99.99% chance of correct surface normal. Strengths: Ensures strict 4-connectivity, avoiding diagonal jumps that can cause artifacts in hierarchical grids. Limitations: Slightly more complex logic than HP8T due to clamping, and achieves 99.99% accuracy rather than the 100% accuracy of H4T in randomized testing. When to use: When traversing hierarchical grids (Octrees/SVO) and strict 4-connectivity is required to avoid skipping cells or producing incorrect normals, and the slight performance overhead of clamping is acceptable. When not to use: If 100% geometric correctness is required and the overhead of H4T is acceptable, or if maximum performance is needed and 8-connectivity artifacts can be mitigated elsewhere. HP4T is part of a family of ray traversal methods for hierarchical grids, including H4T and HP8T. The "T" stands for "total," referring to the total summation concept from earlier chapters in the source material, and "HP" stands for Hierarchical Planes. The method was developed to address precision and connectivity errors found in naive implementations that use compare variables and t + eps for level switching, which can result in 8-connectivity and incorrect surface normals. The author notes that such issues may be a reason for surface normal errors in games like Teardown, which uses a similar flawed compare variable optimization. name: Hierarchical Planes 8-Connectivity (HP8T)
body: Hierarchical Planes 8-Connectivity (HP8T) is a ray traversal algorithm for hierarchical grids that simplifies the update logic of Hierarchical Planes 4-Connectivity (HP4T). While HP4T enforces strict 4-connectivity by clamping the non-hit axis, HP8T removes this clamping to allow 8-connectivity, permitting diagonal jumps between cells. This simplification reduces computational overhead but requires flooring fractional grid positions before data access and introduces ambiguities in surface normal calculation when using simple comparison variables. HP8T builds on Hierarchical Planes 4-Connectivity (HP4T) by modifying the update step for the axis that is not currently being hit by the ray plane intersection. Inputs: rayposition: The starting position of the ray in world space. raydir: The normalized direction vector of the ray. invdir: The reciprocal of raydir (1.0 / ray\dir). cellsize: The side length of the uniform grid cells. isdirpos: A vector indicating the positive direction of traversal for each axis (typically 1.0 if raydir > 0, else 0.0). israyneg: A vector indicating the negative direction (typically -1.0 if raydir < 0, else 0.0), used to adjust the plane position. gridwidth, gridheight: The dimensions of the 2D grid slice being traversed. gridposition: The current continuous position of the ray within the grid. Outputs: Updated gridposition for each step. t: The distance to the next plane intersection. Not given in the sources. 1. Calculate Planes: Determine the world coordinates of the next grid planes for the X and Y axes based on the current gridposition. planes = (\lfloor grid\position / cellsize \rfloor + is\dir\pos) \times cellsize 2. Calculate Total T: Compute the distance along the ray to reach these planes. total\t = (planes - ray\position) \times inv\dir 3. Determine Hit Axis: Compare totalt.x and totalt.y. If totalt.x <= totalt.y: The ray hits the X plane first. Else: The ray hits the Y plane first. 4. Update Position: If X is hit: Update X coordinate to the plane position: gridposition.x = planes.x - israyneg.x. Update Y coordinate by adding the delta corresponding to the travel time totalt.x: gridposition.y += raydir.y max(0.0, totalt.x - (gridposition.y - rayposition.y) invdir.y). Set t = totalt.x. If Y is hit: Update Y coordinate to the plane position: gridposition.y = planes.y - israyneg.y. Update X coordinate by adding the delta corresponding to the travel time totalt.y: gridposition.x += raydir.x max(0.0, totalt.y - (gridposition.x - rayposition.x) invdir.x). Set t = totalt.y. 5. Access Grid: Before reading the grid data at the new position, floor the gridposition components to obtain integer indices. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def traversehp8t(rayposition, raydir, invdir, cellsize, isdirpos, israyneg, gridwidth, gridheight, gridposition): while 0 <= gridposition[0] < gridwidth and 0 <= gridposition[1] < gridheight: planesx = (math.floor(gridposition[0] / cellsize) + isdirpos[0]) cellsize planesy = (math.floor(gridposition[1] / cellsize) + isdirpos[1]) cellsize totaltx = (planesx - rayposition[0]) invdir[0] totalty = (planesy - rayposition[1]) invdir[1] if totaltx <= totalty: gridposition[0] = planesx - israyneg[0] gridposition[1] += raydir[1] max(0.0, totaltx - (gridposition[1] - rayposition[1]) invdir[1]) t = totaltx else: gridposition[1] = planesy - israyneg[1] gridposition[0] += raydir[0] max(0.0, totalty - (gridposition[0] - rayposition[0]) invdir[0]) t = totalty cellsize: The resolution of the underlying uniform grid. isdirpos, israyneg: Derived from raydir. isdirpos is 1.0 where raydir > 0, else 0.0. israyneg is -1.0 where raydir < 0, else 0.0. Fractional Positions: Unlike HP4T, gridposition retains fractional values and must be floored before accessing grid data to avoid reading incorrect cells or causing memory errors. Surface Normal Ambiguity: HP8T allows diagonal jumps. If surface normals are calculated using a simple compare variable, the calculation will be incorrect for diagonal transitions because the compare value cannot distinguish between entering a cell from the side versus entering from a corner. A post-processing step analyzing surrounding cells is required to determine the correct normal. Boundary Checks: The loop condition checks gridposition against gridwidth and gridheight. Accuracy: In randomized testing (100,000,000 cases), HP8T achieved a 99.99% chance of correct position and 99.99% chance of correct normal. This is slightly lower than the 100% accuracy of Hero-like 4-Connectivity (H4T). Strengths: Simpler calculation for the non-hit axis compared to HP4T, as it avoids the complex clamping logic. Limitations: 8-connectivity introduces potential errors in surface normal determination if not handled with additional logic. The lack of clamping means the ray can "jump" diagonally, which may be undesirable for algorithms requiring strict 4-connectivity. HP8T is described in a thesis. It is presented as a variant of HP4T, designed to simplify the traversal logic by removing the clamping step for the non-hit axis. name: Rendering Order and Strategy
body: Rendering Order and Strategy defines the sequence in which volumetric cells are processed during ray-grid traversal to ensure correct optical compositing and efficient occlusion culling. It solves the problem of determining which cells contribute to the final pixel color and in what order, distinguishing itself from sibling methods by decoupling the geometric traversal logic (handled by the parent Ray-grid traversal) from the semantic processing order required for correct alpha blending or visibility determination. The family shares the fundamental requirement that cell processing must respect the viewing direction to correctly accumulate opacity and color. While the parent Ray-grid traversal provides the geometric sequence of voxel indices visited by a ray, the rendering strategy determines how these visits are mapped to the final image buffer. The core principle is that for standard volume rendering with absorption, processing must occur from the camera towards the volume interior (front-to-back) to allow early termination when the ray becomes fully opaque. Strategies may also involve spatial partitioning (e.g., layers, octants) to group cells for batch processing or to handle complex hierarchical data structures where implicit occlusion rules replace per-ray depth sorting. Front-to-Back Layer Traversal is a rendering order strategy for Matryoshka-like hierarchical data structures that processes cells in front-to-back order along the viewing direction to handle occlusion correctly. It operates on pre-defined layers composed of six planes, classifying them into closest and furthest groups relative to the camera to ensure outer cells occlude inner cells without per-ray depth sorting. It builds on Ray-grid traversal but applies a specific plane-grouping logic to manage the visibility of nested structures. Choose this method when rendering hierarchical "Matryoshka" data structures where cells are grouped into concentric layers, and efficient occlusion culling of inner layers by outer layers is required without sorting every cell individually. See Front-to-Back Layer Traversal. Backward Projection (also known as Backward Mapping or image-order rendering) is a volume rendering technique that iterates over all pixels of the output image to determine the contribution of the volume data to each pixel. It solves the problem of mapping 3D volumetric data to a 2D image plane by reversing the projection direction: instead of sampling the volume and projecting to the image (forward mapping), it traces rays from the camera through the image plane into the volume. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as Front-to-Back Layer Traversal, by its explicit iteration over the output image grid, which ensures every pixel is addressed exactly once and simplifies handling of non-uniform sampling or sparse data structures. Choose this method when uniform pixel coverage is required, or when the rendering pipeline is driven by the output image resolution rather than the volume data structure. See Backward Projection. A ray-casting algorithm on rectilinear grids using object-order processing, randomized high sampling rate, and trilinear interpolation. The sampling rate variable (\Delta s) is initialized to 0.5, allowing between two and four samplings along a ray within a cell. Pixel subdivisions and precomputed rays are fixed to 16^2 (256 subdivisions), allowing up to 4x zoom without visible noise. The implementation targets 512x512 pixel images to maintain high quality. The algorithm lacks perspective projection, which is a drawback for stereo viewing or VR, though parallel projection is often preferred in scientific visualization. The distinction between object-order (volume-driven) and image-order (pixel-driven) rendering strategies has been fundamental since the early days of volume visualization. Object-order methods, such as the randomized sampling approach described by, emerged to leverage the efficiency of traversing the volume data structure directly, often achieving interactive frame rates for isosurface visualization. Image-order methods, like backward projection, became standard for ensuring consistent pixel coverage and simplifying the compositing logic, particularly as hardware acceleration for ray-box intersection and texture sampling improved. The development of hierarchical strategies like Front-to-Back Layer Traversal addresses the specific needs of complex, nested data structures where traditional linear traversal is inefficient for occlusion culling. name: Front-to-Back Layer Traversal
head: Layer-based Front-to-Back Traversal
body: Front-to-Back Layer Traversal is a rendering order strategy for Matryoshka-like hierarchical data structures that processes cells in front-to-back order along the viewing direction to handle occlusion correctly. It operates on pre-defined layers composed of six planes, classifying them into closest and furthest groups relative to the camera to ensure outer cells occlude inner cells without per-ray depth sorting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Matryoshka layer lm defined by six planes, a viewing direction (camera position), and an auxiliary buffer for marking drawable cells. Output: A sequence of cell processing instructions ordered front-to-back. Data Structures: Layer Definition: A layer consists of six planes classified into two groups based on the camera position. Closest Planes: The three planes closest to the camera, defined by binary indices kx, ky, kz \in \{0, 1\}. Furthest Planes: The three planes furthest from the camera, defined by the opposite indices k'x, k'y, k'z. Auxiliary Buffer: A memory structure used to mark cells as "drawable" during a first pass, allowing them to be processed in the correct order during a second pass. Parameters: kx, ky, kz: Binary values (0 or 1) determined by the viewing camera to define which planes are closest to the camera position. k'x, k'y, k'z: The opposite values of kx, ky, kz (i.e., 1-kx, etc.), defining the furthest planes. Steps: 1. Classify Planes: Determine kx, ky, kz based on the camera's viewing direction to identify the closest planes. 2. Process Closest Planes: Identify planes X=X{kx}, Y=Y{ky}, Z=Z{kz}. Within this group, apply intra-plane ordering: cells from X=X{kx} that also belong to Y=Y{ky} are treated before any cells from Y=Y{ky}, and plane Z=Z{kz} is processed last among the three closest planes. Mark these cells as drawable in the auxiliary buffer. 3. Process Inner Layers: If lm is not the last layer, process the next inner layer l{m+1} using the same logic. 4. Process Furthest Planes: Identify planes X=X{k'x}, Y=Y{k'y}, Z=Z{k'z}. Within this group, apply inverted intra-plane ordering: plane Z=Z{k'z} is processed first because it may occlude cells in Y=Y{k'y}, which in turn may occlude cells in X=X{k'x}. Process the cells marked in the auxiliary buffer in this specific order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobacklayertraversal(layer, cameraposition, auxiliarybuffer): # Determine closest planes based on camera position # The sources do not specify the exact coordinate transformation logic kx, ky, kz = 0, 0, 0 # Placeholder for implementation detail kpx, kpy, kpz = 1 - kx, 1 - ky, 1 - kz # Step 1: Process closest planes # Intra-plane order: Xkx, then Yky, then Zkz (last among closest) auxiliarybuffer.clear() auxiliarybuffer.extend(layer.planex[kx]) auxiliarybuffer.extend(layer.planey[ky]) auxiliarybuffer.extend(layer.planez[kz]) # Process cells in the buffer according to the specified plane order # The sources do not specify the exact cell iteration logic for plane in [layer.planex[kx], layer.planey[ky], layer.planez[kz]]: for cell in plane: if cell in auxiliarybuffer: processcell(cell) # Step 2: Process inner layers if not the last layer if not layer.islastlayer(): fronttobacklayertraversal(layer.nextinnerlayer, cameraposition, auxiliarybuffer) # Step 3: Process furthest planes # Intra-plane order: Zkpz first, then Ykpy, then Xkpx (last among furthest) auxiliarybuffer.clear() auxiliarybuffer.extend(layer.planez[kpz]) auxiliarybuffer.extend(layer.planey[kpy]) auxiliarybuffer.extend(layer.planex[kpx]) for plane in [layer.planez[kpz], layer.planey[kpy], layer.planex[kpx]]: for cell in plane: if cell in auxiliarybuffer: processcell(cell) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shared Cells: Cells at the intersection of planes (edges/corners) must be handled carefully to avoid double processing or incorrect occlusion. The intra-plane ordering rules specifically address this. Camera Position: The values of kx, ky, kz depend on the camera position. If the camera moves, these values may change, requiring a re-evaluation of the plane grouping. Auxiliary Buffer: Requires sufficient memory to store the drawable cells for each layer. A specific ordering rule for processing cells within the same plane group to handle shared cells (edges/corners) correctly, ensuring correct occlusion between planes. For closest planes, cells from X=X1 belonging to Y=Y1 are processed before Y=Y1, and Z=Z1 is last. For furthest planes, Z=Z0 is first, occluding Y=Y0, which occludes X=X0. The sources do not provide measured performance, hardware specifics, or explicit time/memory complexity formulas. Strengths include correct occlusion handling for nested Matryoshka structures without per-ray depth sorting, and efficiency for parallel projections with fixed viewing directions. Limitations include the requirement for an auxiliary buffer and dependency on camera position for plane classification, which may require re-evaluation if the camera moves frequently. It is suitable for rendering Matryoshka-like data structures with parallel projection where correct occlusion is required, but not for structures that do not fit the Matryoshka layer model or when auxiliary buffer memory is constrained. The method is described in the context of the Matryoshka algorithm for visualizing active cells in hierarchical data structures. It addresses the challenge of maintaining correct front-to-back rendering order for occlusion by leveraging the geometric properties of layer planes relative to the camera position. name: Backward Projection
head: Backward Mapping, Backward and forward texture mapping algorithms, Backward texture mapping, Forward texture mapping, image-order algorithms
body: Backward Projection (also known as Backward Mapping or image-order algorithms) is a volume rendering strategy that iterates over all pixels of the output image and determines the contributions of the volume integral to the current pixel. It solves the problem of mapping 3D volumetric data to a 2D image by casting rays from the camera through the volume for each pixel, yielding a simple and visually accurate mechanism for volume rendering. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as Front-to-Back Layer Traversal, by its explicit iteration over the image space (pixels) rather than the volume space (voxels). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset V (scalar or vector values), a camera model (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d} per pixel), and transfer functions mapping volume values to color c and opacity \alpha. Output: A 2D image buffer I with dimensions H \times W \times C (where C is channels, typically 3 for RGB). Data Structures: Volume V: A 3D array of size Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Values are accessed via trilinear interpolation. Image Buffer I: A 2D array of size H \times W \times C. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the image buffer I to zero. 2. For each pixel (i, j) in the image grid (0 \le i < H, 0 \le j < W): a. Compute the ray origin \mathbf{o}{i,j} and direction \mathbf{d}{i,j} from the camera model. b. Determine the entry and exit points of the ray with the volume bounding box. Let the parametric range be [t{start}, t{end}]. c. Initialize the accumulated color C{acc} = (0,0,0) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0. d. Iterate along the ray from t{start} to t{end} with step size \Delta t (typically the voxel spacing or diagonal): i. Compute sample position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o}{i,j} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}{i,j}. ii. Sample the volume value v = V(\mathbf{p}) using trilinear interpolation. iii. Map v to color c and opacity \alpha using transfer functions. iv. Apply the front-to-back compositing equation: C{acc} = C{acc} + c \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) e. Store C{acc} in I[i, j]. Formulas: The volume rendering integral is approximated using a Riemann sum. The compositing equation for each sample l is: I(\hat{x}) = \sum{l=1}^{L} c(xl) \alphal \prod{j=1}^{l-1} (1 - \alphaj) where c(xl) is the color and \alphal is the opacity at sample position xl. Parameters: \Delta t: Step size. Typical value: distance between voxel centers or voxel diagonal. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating point precision errors in ray marching can cause gaps or overlaps if \Delta t is not chosen carefully relative to voxel size. Boundaries: Rays missing the volume entirely must be handled to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Degenerate Input: Empty volumes or volumes with zero opacity everywhere result in a black or background image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. origin[k]) / direction[k] t2 = ([Dx, Dy, Dz][k] - origin[k]) / direction[k] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if nointersect or tmin > tmax: continue acccolor = np.zeros(channels) accalpha = 0.0 t = tmin while t <= tmax: pos = origin + t direction x, y, z = pos if 0 <= x < Dx and 0 <= y < Dy and 0 <= z < Dz: # Trilinear interpolation x0, y0, z0 = int(x), int(y), int(z) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 fx, fy, fz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 def clamp(v, dim): return max(0, min(v, dim - 1)) v000 = volume[clamp(x0, Dx), clamp(y0, Dy), clamp(z0, Dz)] v100 = volume[clamp(x1, Dx), clamp(y0, Dy), clamp(z0, Dz)] v010 = volume[clamp(x0, Dx), clamp(y1, Dy), clamp(z0, Dz)] v110 = volume[clamp(x1, Dx), clamp(y1, Dy), clamp(z0, Dz)] v001 = volume[clamp(x0, Dx), clamp(y0, Dy), clamp(z1, Dz)] v101 = volume[clamp(x1, Dx), clamp(y0, Dy), clamp(z1, Dz)] v011 = volume[clamp(x0, Dx), clamp(y1, Dy), clamp(z1, Dz)] v111 = volume[clamp(x1, Dx), clamp(y1, Dy), clamp(z1, Dz)] c00 = v000 (1 - fx) + v100 fx c10 = v010 (1 - fx) + v110 fx c01 = v001 (1 - fx) + v101 fx c11 = v011 (1 - fx) + v111 fx c0 = c00 (1 - fy) + c10 fy c1 = c01 (1 - fy) + c11 fy val = c0 (1 - fz) + c1 fz color, alpha = transferfunc(val) weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor += color weight accalpha += weight t += dt image[i, j] = acccolor return image GPU Backprojection is a rendering pass that visualizes detected scale-space blobs by mapping projection data back into a 3D reconstruction volume. It solves the problem of efficiently computing weighted contributions of scale-space features to image pixels by parallelizing the accumulation over the output space (voxels or pixels) on NVIDIA GPUs. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific application to scale-space blob visualization and its implementation as a CUDA kernel that decouples the expensive scale-space computation from the frequent backprojection step, unlike Ray Segment Projection to Image which projects geometric primitives, or Cone Beam Forward Projection with Trilinear Interpolation which performs the forward mapping. This method computes the bounding segment of a ray (defined by origin and direction) that overlaps with a canonical image frame, returning the parametric t-range and the 2D xy coordinates at the entry and exit points. It solves the problem of determining which parts of a 3D ray are visible within the 2D image plane boundaries, which is a prerequisite for subsequent rasterization or sampling in backward projection pipelines. It differs from GPU Backprojection by explicitly computing geometric bounds rather than relying on hardware rasterization, and from Cone Beam Forward Projection with Trilinear Interpolation by operating on individual rays rather than volumetric integration. Cone Beam Forward Projection computes the line integrals of a 3D volume along rays defined by a source and a 2D detector array, simulating the acquisition of projection data (sinograms) for cone-beam geometry. It differs from its sibling GPU Backprojection by integrating volume values along rays rather than distributing detector values into the volume, and from Ray Segment Projection to Image by explicitly handling the 3D-to-2D perspective projection geometry with trilinear interpolation. It is the primary forward operator for iterative reconstruction algorithms like Differentiable Forward Projection (Mesh) and 3D Siddon's Method for Intercept Matrix Calculation. Circular Integral Convolution generates a blurred image from a scan by integrating ray values across all angles for each point, effectively filtering the true image with a 1/r-weighted kernel. It serves as a pre-processing step for deconvolution-based reconstruction rather than a full reconstruction method itself. Gaussian Texture Filtering via Jacobian Back-projection is a technique to compute the color of a screen pixel by integrating a texture signal against a Gaussian filter, where the filter is back-projected from screen space to texture space using the local affine approximation (Jacobian) of the texture mapping. It solves the problem of aliasing in procedural textures and signals applied to surfaces by adapting the filter shape to the viewing condition. It sets itself apart from forward projection methods by operating in the frequency domain relationship, ensuring the filtered texture spectrum is the multiplication of the unfiltered spectrum and the filter spectrum. Visibility Thresholding for Scale Backprojection is a method to prevent scale information from being backprojected to voxels that correspond to vessels, giving a better classification of the brain. A voxel is determined to be not visible from the Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) extrema if, at some point along the ray connecting the two positions, the intensity is below the threshold \tau. Alternatively, thresholding can be based on gradient magnitude. The parameter \tau (tau) is a visibility parameter used to control the sensitivity of the visibility test, based on scalar value or gradient magnitude. This is a fast approximation; more accurate results can be obtained with a region growing approach added as a post-process based on the initial size-based classification. Time Complexity: O(H \cdot W \cdot N), where H, W are image dimensions and N is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume and O(H \cdot W) for the image buffer. Measured Performance: Performance depends heavily on the efficiency of the ray-volume intersection and interpolation. The source framework achieved an average of a magnitude speedup over traditional volume rendering and obtained an interactive frame rate using shear transformations for hardware or parallel implementation. Scaling: Scales linearly with image resolution and volume depth. Strengths: Simple implementation, visually accurate. Limitations: Can be slow for large volumes or high resolutions if not optimized. Memory bandwidth bound due to frequent volume sampling. When to use: When visual accuracy is prioritized and computational resources allow for per-pixel ray casting. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical for very large volumes without hardware acceleration. Backward projection, also known as backward mapping, was introduced as one of the two main algorithms for high-quality and efficient texture mapping, featuring backward and forward processing orders. It was further developed and popularized in the context of volume rendering by Levoy (1988), Sabella (1988), and Danskin and Hanrahan (1992). The method is fundamental to ray casting techniques in volume rendering. body: GPU Backprojection is a rendering pass that visualizes detected scale-space blobs by mapping projection data back into a 3D reconstruction volume. It solves the problem of efficiently computing weighted contributions of scale-space features to image pixels by parallelizing the accumulation over the output space (voxels or pixels) on NVIDIA GPUs. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific application to scale-space blob visualization and its implementation as a CUDA kernel that decouples the expensive scale-space computation from the frequent backprojection step, unlike Ray Segment Projection to Image which projects geometric primitives, or Cone Beam Forward Projection with Trilinear Interpolation which performs the forward mapping. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: projections: A tensor of shape [batch, views, rows, columns] containing the projection data. matrices: A contiguous float tensor containing the projection transformation coefficients. volumeshape: A tuple (depth, height, width) defining the 3D reconstruction volume dimensions. blobdata: Information about detected scale-space blobs, including their radii and positions, used to generate slices. Outputs: out: A tensor of shape [batch, 1, depth, height, width] containing the backprojected volume. Data Structures: PanelStencil: A structure used in the CUDA kernel to store the 4 pixels (indices) and their corresponding weights for a voxel's projection onto the 2D panel. index[4]: Unsigned integers representing the pixel indices in the flattened projection array. weight[4]: Floats representing the interpolated weights for each pixel. ViewColumn: A structure storing linear coefficients for projecting a voxel's x, y, z coordinates to the 2D panel. column, columnz: Linear coefficients for the column coordinate. row, rowz: Linear coefficients for the row coordinate. depth, depthz: Linear coefficients for the depth (distance along panel normal). Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Detach and convert matrices to a contiguous float tensor. Reshape projections to a flat tensor flat of shape [batch, -1]. Create the output tensor out with shape [batch, 1, volumeshape]. Load the kernel library containing the FDK backprojection kernels. 2. Batch Iteration: Iterate over batches in groups of size GROUP. For each group, select the appropriate kernel function (e.g., fdkbackprojectc{group}). 3. Kernel Execution (Per Voxel): Launch a CUDA kernel with grid volumegrid(volumeshape) and block VOLUMEBLOCK. Each thread processes a voxel at (x, y, z) in the volume. View Projection: Compute the ViewColumn for the voxel using the transformation coefficients. Panel Stencil: Calculate the 2D panel coordinates and weights: Compute depth w = dz z + d. If w \le 0, the voxel is behind the panel; skip. Compute inverse 1/w. Compute column u = (cz z + c) / w and row v = (rz z + r) / w. Determine the bounding pixel indices (c0, r0) and fractional parts dc, dr. Compute weights using bilinear interpolation factors scaled by 1/w^2. Store the 4 pixel indices and weights in a PanelStencil. 4. Accumulation (Scale-Space Specific): For each detected scale-space blob, generate a series of small slices with dimensions proportional to the blob's radius. Compute the weighted contribution of the blob for each pixel covered by its slices. Use alpha blending to accumulate the sum of weighted contributions from all blobs into the output volume. 5. Normalization: In a separate pass, normalize the accumulated result by dividing by the sum of weights, which is stored in a separate channel. Formulas: Output is weighted by (D / l)^2, where l is voxel depth along panel normal and D is panel depth. Projected depth: w = dz z + d. Panel coordinates: u = (cz z + c) / w, v = (rz z + r) / w. Interpolation weights: w{00} = \max(c0, 0) \ge 0 ? (1-dc): 0, w{10} = c0+1 < \text{cols} ? dc: 0, w{01} = \max(r0, 0) \ge 0 ? (1-dr) \cdot (1/w)^2: 0, w{11} = r0+1 < \text{rows} ? dr \cdot (1/w)^2: 0. Parameters: GROUPSIZE: The number of batches processed together by a single kernel launch. Not given in the sources. TTFDKDEPTH: Number of voxels along z processed per thread. Set to 4 in the source. VOLUMEBLOCK: CUDA block dimension. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Behind Panel: If the projected depth w \le 0, the voxel is behind the projection panel and should be skipped. Boundary Checks: Pixel indices must be clamped to the valid range [0, \text{rows}-1] and [0, \text{columns}-1] to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Precision: The use of float32 for addition order may cause slight differences between forward and backprojection due to non-associativity. Scale-Space Decoupling: The scale-space computation is expensive and done once, while backprojection is faster and done frequently. Mixing these steps incorrectly can lead to performance degradation. colfloor dr = rowproj - rowfloor scale = inverse inverse wc0 = (1.0 - dc) if colfloor >= 0 else 0.0 wc1 = dc if colfloor + 1 < columns else 0.0 wr0 = (1.0 - dr) scale if rowfloor >= 0 else 0.0 wr1 = dr scale if rowfloor + 1 < rows else 0.0 left = max(colfloor, 0) right = min(colfloor + 1, columns - 1) top = max(rowfloor, 0) columns bottom = min(rowfloor + 1, rows - 1) columns indices = [top + left, top + right, bottom + left, bottom + right] weights = [wr0 wc0, wr0 wc1, wr1 wc0, wr1 wc1] for k in range(4): projidx = b views rows columns + indices[k] out[b][projidx] += flatprojections[projidx] weights[k] weightaccum[b][projidx] += weights[k] def computeblobweight(blob, x, y, z): # Not given in the sources. return 1.0 Implements the backprojection step of differentiable X-ray computed tomography on NVIDIA GPUs using CUDA. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping projection data back into a 3D reconstruction volume by parallelizing computation over the output space (reconstruction voxels). It is distinguished from CPU implementations by its use of 3D thread blocks and 3D texture memory for input data access, and it supports both Siddon and SF projector models. It builds on GPU Backprojection. Time Complexity: The backprojection step is O(N \cdot V), where N is the number of views and V is the number of voxels, but optimized by the stencil approach which limits writes to 4 pixels per voxel. The scale-space computation is O(S), where S is the number of scale-space iterations, but is decoupled and done once. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the projection data, the volume, and temporary buffers for the stencil and weights. The source mentions using 768 MB of texture memory for a 256^3 volume. Measured Performance: On an Intel Core 2 Duo 2.4 GHz with 2GB RAM and an nVidia GeForce 8800 GTX with 768 MB texture memory, the GPU implementation showed an improvement of about two orders of magnitude over the CPU version for data set sizes of 64^3, 128^3, and 256^3. Strengths: Interactive visualization is possible due to the speedup over CPU implementations. The decoupling of scale-space computation allows for frequent updates of smoothness and visibility parameters. Limitations: Relies on a temporary volume to compute the scale field, which may limit real-time embedding in the volume rendering process as GPUs improve. When to Use: When interactive visualization of scale-space blobs is required, and the scale-space computation can be decoupled from the backprojection. When Not to Use: When the scale-space computation needs to be updated frequently with every parameter change, or when the hardware does not support the required CUDA features. name: CUDA Backprojection Implementation
head: CUDA Core Implementation, CUDA Parallelization Strategy
body: This method implements the backprojection step of differentiable X-ray computed tomography on NVIDIA GPUs using CUDA. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping projection data back into a 3D reconstruction volume by parallelizing computation over the output space (reconstruction voxels). It is distinguished from CPU implementations by its use of 3D thread blocks and 3D texture memory for input data access, and it supports both Siddon and SF projector models. It builds on GPU Backprojection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: CT projection data (for backprojection) stored as a contiguous 32-bit floating-point array. Input: Geometric parameters defining the CT scan geometry (e.g., source-detector distance, detector spacing, rotation angles). Output: Reconstruction volume stored as a contiguous 32-bit floating-point array. Data Structures: Projection Data: Contiguous 1D array of float32 values representing the 2D projection images. Reconstruction Volume: Contiguous 1D array of float32 values representing the 3D voxel grid. Texture Memory: 3D texture objects bound to the input data for hardware-accelerated interpolation. Parameters: Geometry: Specifies the CT scan setup (e.g., parallel, cone, or fan beam). Projector Model: Either "Siddon" or "SF" (Sinc-Filtered or similar, as specified in the source context). Thread Block Dimensions: 3D thread blocks are used. Algorithm Steps: 1. Data Preparation: If the input projection data is not already on the GPU, copy it from CPU memory to GPU global memory. 2. Texture Binding: Bind the input projection data to a 3D texture object to enable efficient hardware interpolation. 3. Kernel Launch: Launch a CUDA kernel where each thread block corresponds to a voxel in the reconstruction volume. 4. Voxel Processing (Backprojection): Each thread computes the backprojection contribution for its assigned voxel. For each projection angle, calculate the ray path from the X-ray source through the voxel to the detector. Sample the projection data at the corresponding detector coordinates using the 3D texture memory. Accumulate the sampled values into the voxel's value in the reconstruction volume. 5. Result Retrieval: If the output was computed on the GPU, copy the reconstruction volume back to CPU memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. global void backprojectionkernel( float reconstructionvolume, float projectiondata, int numvoxelsx, int numvoxelsy, int numvoxelsz, int numprojections, float voxelsize, float sourcetodetectordistance, float detectorspacing, float rotationangles, cudaTextureObjectt projectiontexture) { // Calculate voxel coordinates from thread/block indices int x = blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; int y = blockIdx.y blockDim.y + threadIdx.y; int z = blockIdx.z blockDim.z + threadIdx.z; // Check bounds if (x >= numvoxelsx || y >= numvoxelsy || z >= numvoxelsz) { return; } float voxelvalue = 0.0f; // Get voxel center in world coordinates float vx = (x + 0.5f) voxelsize; float vy = (y + 0.5f) voxelsize; float vz = (z + 0.5f) voxelsize; // Iterate over all projection angles for (int i = 0; i < numprojections; ++i) { float angle = rotationangles[i]; // Calculate ray direction based on geometry (Siddon or SF model) // This involves rotating the voxel position relative to the source // and projecting onto the detector plane float detectoru, detectorv; computedetectorcoordinates( vx, vy, vz, angle, sourcetodetectordistance, detectorspacing, detectoru, detectorv); // Sample projection data using 3D texture memory // The texture object handles interpolation and boundary checks float projectionvalue = tex3D<float>( projectiontexture, detectoru, detectorv, i // Assuming projections are stored in the z-dimension of texture); // Accumulate contribution voxelvalue += projectionvalue; } // Write result to reconstruction volume int voxelindex = x + y numvoxelsx + z numvoxelsx numvoxelsy; reconstructionvolume[voxelindex] = voxelvalue; } // Host function to launch the kernel void runbackprojection( float dreconstructionvolume, float dprojectiondata, int numvoxelsx, int numvoxelsy, int numvoxelsz, int numprojections, float voxelsize, float sourcetodetectordistance, float detectorspacing, float drotationangles, cudaTextureObjectt projectiontexture) { dim3 block(16, 16, 16); // 3D thread block dim3 grid( (numvoxelsx + block.x - 1) / block.x, (numvoxelsy + block.y - 1) / block.y, (numvoxelsz + block.z - 1) / block.z); backprojectionkernel<<<grid, block>>>( dreconstructionvolume, dprojectiondata, numvoxelsx, numvoxelsy, numvoxelsz, numprojections, voxelsize, sourcetodetectordistance, detectorspacing, drotationangles, projectiontexture); } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Data Transfer Overhead: If data is not on the GPU, the copy overhead can dominate computation time. Texture Memory Limits: 3D texture memory has size limits; large projection datasets may require tiling or alternative storage. Interpolation Artifacts: Hardware interpolation in texture memory may introduce artifacts if not configured correctly. Boundary Conditions: Rays passing outside the detector area must be handled to avoid invalid memory accesses. Time Complexity: O(V \cdot N), where V is the number of voxels and N is the number of projections. Memory Complexity: O(V + P), where V is the volume size and P is the projection data size. Performance: Significant speedup over CPU implementations due to parallelization over voxels and hardware interpolation. Strengths: High throughput for large volumes, efficient memory access via texture memory, support for differentiable operations via PyTorch integration. Limitations: Memory bandwidth bound for very large datasets, texture memory size constraints. When to Use: When high-speed backprojection is required for large 3D volumes and GPU resources are available. When Not to Use: When memory bandwidth is saturated or texture memory limits are exceeded. The CUDA backprojection implementation was developed as part of a differentiable forward projector for X-ray computed tomography. It was introduced in a paper published in 2023. The implementation is part of a library that provides both CPU and GPU versions of forward and backprojection algorithms for various CT geometries. It integrates with PyTorch for automatic differentiation.
