name: Naive PyTorch Baseline Renderer
head: Sequential CPU loop, Standard tensor operations renderer
body:
The Naive PyTorch Baseline Renderer is a reference implementation for differentiable rendering that processes all primitives for every pixel sequentially using standard PyTorch tensor operations. It serves as a performance baseline to demonstrate the efficiency gains of optimized CUDA implementations, which utilize tile-based culling, per-pixel parallelism, and FP16 optimization. Unlike its siblings, it lacks spatial optimization, tile-based binning, or specialized kernels, resulting in significant memory and computational overhead. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a set of N primitives as input, where each primitive i is defined by parameters \{(xi, yi, si, 	hetai, 
ui, ci)\}{i=1}^N. Here, (xi, yi) is the center, si is the scale, 	hetai is the rotation angle, 
ui is a density parameter, and ci is the base color. A mask texture Mi is associated with each primitive. The method outputs a rendered image tensor I of size H{canvas} 	imes W{canvas}. Data Structures: The implementation uses two 2D tensors X and Y of shape (H{canvas}, W{canvas}) to represent the normalized coordinates of each pixel. It maintains two accumulator tensors I (image) and T (transparency), both of shape (H{canvas}, W{canvas}), initialized to zeros and ones respectively. During execution, full-canvas tensors are allocated for \Delta x, \Delta y, u, v, and mask for each primitive. Algorithm Steps: 1. Generate coordinate grids X, Y over the canvas dimensions H{canvas}, W{canvas} using torch.meshgrid. 2. Initialize the output image I to zeros and the transparency mask T to ones. 3. Iterate through each primitive i from 0 to N-1. 4. Compute displacement vectors: \Delta x = X - xi and \Delta y = Y - yi. 5. Transform coordinates to the primitive's local space by rotating and scaling \Delta x, \Delta y by angle 	hetai and scale si to obtain local coordinates u, v. 6. Sample the primitive's mask texture Mi at (u, v) using torch.gridsample to get the mask value. 7. Compute opacity \alphai and color ci using the defined formulas. 8. Update the image and transparency using alpha compositing: I \leftarrow I + T \cdot \alphai \cdot ci and T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai). 9. Return the final image I. Formulas: \alphai = \alpha{max} \cdot \sigma(
ui) \cdot 	ext{mask} ci = \sigma(ci) where \sigma denotes the sigmoid function, \alpha{max} is a maximum opacity constant, and 	ext{mask} is the sampled texture value. Parameters: The parameter \alpha{max} controls the maximum opacity scaling. Typical values for \alpha{max} are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method allocates full-canvas tensors for every primitive in the loop, which causes massive memory allocation. For 1000 primitives on a 512 	imes 512 canvas, this results in approximately 5 GB of memory allocation at FP32 precision due to intermediate tensors \Delta x, \Delta y, u, v, and mask. Every primitive is evaluated at all H 	imes W pixels, even if the primitive contributes nothing to the final image, yielding 262 million wasted evaluations for the 1000-primitive example. The Python for loop prevents primitive-level parallelism and forces repeated kernel launches, significantly slowing down execution compared to GPU-optimized approaches. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def naivepytorchrenderer(primitives, Hcanvas, Wcanvas, alphamax=1.0): # 1. Create meshgrid X, Y over canvas dimensions y, x = torch.meshgrid( torch.linspace(-1, 1, Hcanvas, device=primitives[0]['x'].device), torch.linspace(-1, 1, Wcanvas, device=primitives[0]['x'].device), indexing='ij') # 2. Initialize output image I to zeros and transparency mask T to ones I = torch.zeros((Hcanvas, Wcanvas), device=primitives[0]['x'].device) T = torch.ones((Hcanvas, Wcanvas), device=primitives[0]['x'].device) N = len(primitives) # 3. Loop i from 0 to N-1 for i in range(N): prim = primitives[i] xi, yi = prim['x'], prim['y'] si, thetai = prim['s'], prim['theta'] nui, ci = prim['nu'], prim['c'] Mi = prim['masktexture'] # 4. Compute deltas ∆x = X - xi, ∆y = Y - yi dx = x - xi dy = y - yi # 5. Rotate/scale deltas by primitive angle θi and scale si to get u, v costheta, sintheta = torch.cos(thetai), torch.sin(thetai) u = (dx costheta + dy sintheta) / si v = (-dx sintheta + dy costheta) / si # 6. Sample mask from primitive's mask texture Mi at (u, v) using torch.gridsample grid = torch.stack([u, v], dim=-1).unsqueeze(0) mask = F.gridsample(Mi, grid, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros', aligncorners=True).squeeze() # 7. Compute opacity αi = αmax · σ(νi) · mask and color ci = σ(ci) alphai = alphamax torch.sigmoid(nui) mask ci = torch.sigmoid(ci) # 8. Update image I = I + T · αi · ci and transparency T = T · (1 - αi) I = I + T alphai ci T = T (1 - alphai) # 9. Return I return I The time complexity is O(N 	imes H 	imes W) because every primitive is evaluated at all H 	imes W pixels. The memory complexity is O(N 	imes H 	imes W) per iteration because each primitive creates full-canvas tensors for intermediate calculations. The naive version is 30-50x slower than the optimized CUDA implementation. Its strengths include a simple implementation using standard PyTorch operations and its role as a clear baseline for comparison. Its limitations are massive memory allocation, sequential processing, lack of spatial culling, and generic interpolation operations. It should only be used for small-scale testing or as a reference for correctness against optimized renderers. It should not be used for large scenes, high-resolution images, or any performance-critical application. The Naive PyTorch Baseline Renderer was introduced in the paper "DiffBMP: Differentiable Rendering with Bitmap Primitives". It was designed to demonstrate the efficiency of a custom CUDA implementation by comparing it against a straightforward PyTorch-based renderer that uses standard tensor operations without tile-based culling or specialized kernels. The paper highlights the major bottlenecks of this approach, including no spatial culling, massive memory allocation, sequential loops, and generic operations. name: Volume Ray Marching Optimization
body: Volume Ray Marching Optimization refers to a set of shader-level techniques in the Unreal Engine 5.8 Volumetric Cloud Component designed to reduce the computational cost of evaluating participating media. It distinguishes itself by optimizing per-sample material evaluation (grayscale inputs), limiting scattering approximation octaves, and substituting secondary ray marching with cascaded shadow maps, rather than relying on spatial acceleration structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray parameters (origin, direction, step size), material parameters (density, color, scattering coefficients, conservative density vector), optimization flags, camera and light positions. Output: Accumulated color and opacity per sample. Data Structures: Material Parameters: Struct containing density, color, and scattering coefficients. Conservative Density: X component of a Vector3 used for early-out culling. Numbered Steps: 1. Conservative Density Culling: Check the X component of the conservative density vector. If the value is greater than 0, evaluate the material; otherwise, skip the expensive material evaluation and proceed directly to the next sample. 2. Grayscale Material Evaluation: If the "Gray Scale Material" optimization is enabled, restrict the material's input parameter evaluation to only the Red (R) channel. The resulting material response will be grayscale, but lighting calculations remain colored. 3. Multi-Scattering Approximation: Limit the number of octaves for the Multi-Scattering Approximation to save performance. The default is single scattering (0 octaves), with a maximum of two approximation octaves allowed. 4. Shadowing Strategy Selection: Toggle between secondary ray marching and cascaded shadow maps using the "Ray March Volume Shadow" checkbox. Unchecking the box enables cascaded shadow maps, providing a performance boost and infinite shadow length at the cost of accuracy and color (grayscale shadows). 5. Ground Contribution (Optional): If the frame budget allows, enable Ground Contribution to sample shadowed lighting from the ground onto the bottom layer of the clouds, which adds tracing cost. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatevolumetriccloudsample(raysample, materialparams, optimizationsettings): """ Evaluates a single sample in a volumetric cloud with optimizations. Args: raysample: Current position and accumulated transmittance along the ray. materialparams: Struct containing density, color, scattering coefficients, and conservativedensity (Vector3). optimizationsettings: Dict with keys: usegrayscalematerial: bool maxscatteringoctaves: int (0-2) usecsmshadows: bool (True if Ray March Volume Shadow is unchecked) enablegroundcontribution: bool Returns: color: vec3 opacity: float """ # Step 1: Conservative Density Culling # Evaluate material only if conservative density X component > 0 if materialparams.conservativedensity.x <= 0.0: return vec3(0.0), 0.0 # Skip evaluation, proceed to next sample # Step 2: Grayscale Material Evaluation if optimizationsettings['usegrayscalematerial']: # Only consider the R channel of material input parameters density = materialparams.densityr color = vec3(materialparams.colorr) else: density = materialparams.density color = materialparams.color # Step 3: Multi-Scattering Approximation # Default is single scattering (0 octaves), max two approximation octaves numoctaves = min(materialparams.scatteringoctaves, optimizationsettings['maxscatteringoctaves']) # Compute scattering contribution based on octaves # Step 4: Shadowing Strategy Selection if optimizationsettings['usecsmshadows']: # Uncheck Ray March Volume Shadow to enable Cascaded Shadow Maps # Provides performance boost, infinite length, less accurate, grayscale # Lookup shadow factor from cascaded shadow map textures # Not given in the sources. shadowfactor = texturelookupcsm(raysample.position) shadowcolor = vec3(shadowfactor) else: # Secondary ray marching through cloud volume # Perform secondary ray march through volume to compute shadow density # Not given in the sources. shadowfactor = raymarchshadowvolume(raysample.position, materialparams) shadowcolor = shadowfactor # Step 5: Ground Contribution (Optional) groundlight = vec3(0.0) if optimizationsettings['enablegroundcontribution']: # Sample shadowed lighting from ground to bottom layer of clouds # Sample lighting contribution from ground plane # Not given in the sources. groundlight = samplegroundlighting(raysample.position) # Combine contributions finalcolor = color scatteringcoefficient shadowcolor + groundlight return finalcolor, density Parameters: Conservative Density Threshold: 0.0. Material evaluated if value > 0, otherwise skips to next sample. Max Scattering Octaves: Default 0. Maximum 2. Use Grayscale Material: Boolean. If true, restricts material input evaluation to the Red (R) channel. Use CSM Shadows: Boolean. True enables cascaded shadow maps (uncheck Ray March Volume Shadow); False enables secondary ray marching. Enable Ground Contribution: Boolean. Adds tracing cost for ground lighting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Grayscale shadows with CSM lose color accuracy in shadowed regions. Boundary: Conservative density culling threshold must be tuned to avoid artifacts in low-density edges. Degenerate Input: Zero material parameters should be handled to prevent division by zero in scattering calculations. Octree-based address translation manages multi-resolution volume data during ray-guided rendering by intrinsically coupling the down-sampling ratio between resolution levels with the spatial subdivision of an octree structure. Each octree node corresponds to exactly one brick in the data set. Unlike page-table hierarchies, this approach requires keeping the entire subtree from the root node to the target node in memory to reach a high-resolution brick, which can lead to sub-optimal GPU memory utilization due to the tight coupling of the multi-resolution hierarchy and spatial subdivision. Time Complexity: The optimization reduces the constant factor of the per-sample cost. Conservative density culling provides an O(1) early-out. Grayscale material evaluation reduces texture fetches. Limiting scattering octaves caps complexity to O(1) (max 2). CSM replaces secondary ray marching with a texture lookup. Memory Complexity: No additional memory structures are introduced by the shader optimizations themselves. CSM requires shadow map textures, but memory impact is not quantified in the sources. Measured Performance: Enabling cascaded shadow maps (by unchecking the Ray March Volume Shadow box) provides a performance boost. Limiting scattering octaves saves performance. Enabling ground contribution adds cost. Exact FPS gains are not given in the sources. Strengths: Significant performance gains in complex cloud scenes. Simplifies material evaluation. Infinite shadow length with CSM. Limitations: Grayscale shadows are less accurate. Ground contribution adds cost. Conservative density culling may cause artifacts if not tuned. When to Use: When frame budget is tight and visual fidelity of shadows/scattering can be compromised. When clouds are dense and material evaluation is the bottleneck. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity color shadows are required. When ground lighting is critical for realism. This method originates from the implementation of the Volumetric Cloud Component in Unreal Engine 5.8, as documented by Epic Games. It is part of the engine's toolkit for optimizing real-time volumetric rendering, specific to the cloud material system. Volumetric Cloud Component in Unreal Engine | Unreal Engine 5.8 Documentation | Epic Developer Community, https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/volumetric-cloud-component-in-unreal-engine, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Octree-based Address Translation
body: Octree-based address translation manages multi-resolution volume data during ray-guided rendering by intrinsically coupling the down-sampling ratio between resolution levels with the spatial subdivision of an octree structure. Each octree node corresponds to exactly one brick in the data set. Unlike page-table hierarchies, this approach requires keeping the entire subtree from the root node to the target node in memory to reach a high-resolution brick, which can lead to sub-optimal GPU memory utilization due to the tight coupling of the multi-resolution hierarchy and spatial subdivision. The method takes a multi-resolution volume dataset and ray parameters as input, and produces ray-marched color and transmittance along with a list of missing brick requests for the CPU. Data Structures: 1. Brick Cache: Stores the actual voxel data (bricks) for active nodes. 2. Node Pool: Acts as a cache for octree nodes, where only nodes with corresponding bricks stored in the brick cache are kept in memory. Octree nodes resident in the node pool are considered active. 3. Octree Node Layout: Each entry in the node pool is a group of eight nodes that all share the same parent node. Each individual node stores: (1) a pointer to its corresponding brick-cache entry, (2) a pointer to the node-pool entry storing its children, and (3) metadata on the region represented by the node (e.g., a flag indicating if it only contains zero values). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the root node of the octree into the node pool and its corresponding brick into the brick cache. 2. Ray Traversal: During ray casting, the octree hierarchy is traversed for each sample. 3. Subtree Requirement: To reach a high-resolution brick, the whole subtree from the root node to the node corresponding to the high-resolution brick must be kept in both the node pool and the brick cache. 4. Missing Brick Handling: If a brick is missing, the request is recorded. Crassin et al. [CNLE09] use multiple render targets to record up to one missing brick per ray and report these brick requests to the CPU. 5. Optimization: Nodes use their stored metadata (e.g., zero-value flags) to skip over translucent or empty regions during rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseoctree(rayorigin, raydirection, rootnode, nodepool, brickcache): missingbricks = [] currentnode = rootnode # Ensure root node and brick are resident in cache if currentnode not in nodepool: nodepool[currentnode] = True brickcache[currentnode.brickid] = loadbrickfromstorage(currentnode.brickid) color = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 while currentnode is not None: # Skip empty regions using node metadata if currentnode.metadata.iszero: break # Request missing brick if not in cache if currentnode.brickid not in brickcache: missingbricks.append(currentnode.brickid) if len(missingbricks) > 1: break brickcache[currentnode.brickid] = loadbrickfromstorage(currentnode.brickid) # Perform standard ray-marching step on the loaded brick data color, transmittance = standardraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, brickcache[currentnode.brickid], color, transmittance) # Move to child node if not a leaf if not currentnode.isleaf: childidx = computeraychildindex(raydirection, currentnode) childnode = currentnode.children[childidx] if childnode not in nodepool: nodepool[childnode] = True brickcache[childnode.brickid] = loadbrickfromstorage(childnode.brickid) currentnode = childnode else: break return color, transmittance, missingbricks def loadbrickfromstorage(brickid): # Fetches brick data from persistent storage or CPU memory pass def standardraymarch(origin, direction, brickdata, color, transmittance): # Advances ray through brick, updates color and transmittance pass def computeraychildindex(direction, node): # Determines which of the 8 children the ray enters based on direction pass Parameters: Brick Size: Not given in the sources. Missing Brick Limit: Up to one missing brick per ray is recorded per frame. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Utilization: Because the entire subtree from root to leaf must be kept in memory to reach a high-resolution brick, potentially unused low-resolution bricks are stored in the cache, leading to sub-optimal GPU memory utilization. This is a direct consequence of the tight coupling of the multi-resolution hierarchy and the spatial subdivision of the octree. The original system by Crassin et al. [CNLE09] that introduced this method. It uses multiple render targets to record up to one missing brick per ray and report these brick requests to the CPU. Brix et al. [BPH14] extended the structure to support multi-channel data. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales with the number of active nodes and their entire subtrees, as the full path from root to leaf must remain resident to maintain address translation integrity. Strengths: Straightforward substitution of missing high-resolution data with low-resolution data; efficient skipping of empty regions via node metadata. Limitations: Sub-optimal GPU memory utilization due to the requirement of keeping the full subtree in cache; tight coupling of resolution and spatial subdivision limits flexibility. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced by Crassin et al. in 2009 as part of the GigaVoxels system. It was one of the first methods to use an octree structure for address translation in ray-guided rendering. Brix et al. [BPH14] later extended the structure to multi-channel data. The approach belongs to the broader category of octree-based ray-guided rendering, which contrasts with page-table hierarchies. name: Per-sample LOD selection
head: Adaptive LOD Sampling, Per-sample Level of Detail
body: Per-sample LOD selection is a volume ray marching optimization where the required data resolution is determined on a per-sample basis. It allows rays to automatically select the locally appropriate data resolution, balancing rendering quality against memory bandwidth and computational cost. It differs from per-brick LOD selection [FSK13] by allowing resolution changes within a single brick traversal, and from uniform sampling by adapting to local scene complexity. Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, ray length, volume data hierarchy (e.g., SVO or brick-based structure), transfer function. Outputs: Accumulated color and opacity for the pixel. Data Structures: The method relies on a hierarchical data structure (such as an Octree or Sparse Voxel Octree) where nodes or bricks have associated LOD levels. Each sample point p along the ray is associated with a specific LOD level L(p). Steps: 1. Ray Marching Loop: For each pixel, cast a ray r through the volume. 2. LOD Determination: At each sample step, determine the required LOD level L for the current position. This is typically based on the projected size of the voxel at that depth relative to the pixel size, often derived from the Nyquist sampling theorem to avoid aliasing. 3. Data Fetch: Retrieve the volume data at the determined LOD level L. 4. Interpolation: Discrete LOD: If using discrete LOD levels, perform tri-linear interpolation using the data from the single selected LOD level. Fractional LOD: If using fractional LOD, interpolate between data from two neighboring LOD levels (e.g., L and L+1). This is referred to as "quad-linear" interpolation. 5. Accumulation: Apply the transfer function to get color and opacity, then accumulate using front-to-back or back-to-front compositing. Formulas: Discrete LOD Interpolation: C = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} ci \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Where ci and \alphai are the color and opacity at sample i, obtained via tri-linear interpolation from the selected LOD level. Fractional LOD Interpolation: Let L{int} be the fractional LOD level. Let L{floor} = \lfloor L{int} \rfloor and L{ceil} = \lceil L{int} \rceil. Let w = L{int} - L{floor}. The interpolated value V is: V = (1-w) \cdot V{floor} + w \cdot V{ceil} Where V{floor} is obtained via tri-linear interpolation from LOD L{floor} and V{ceil} from LOD L{ceil}. Parameters: LOD Selection Criterion: Typically based on the Nyquist rate relative to the pixel footprint at the sample depth. Interpolation Type: Discrete (tri-linear) or Fractional (quad-linear). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Fractional LOD requires careful handling of interpolation weights to avoid artifacts at LOD boundaries. Boundaries: If the ray exits the volume or reaches the maximum LOD depth without finding allocated data, the interval is treated as free space. Incomplete Data: If the SVO is still being built and the ray reaches the global maximum depth, a coarser node is returned instead of treating it as free space to ensure continuous sampling. A scene sampling scheme that adapts sampling density to the Level of Detail (LoD) of the Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO). It samples scene models via multiple steps: uninformed stratified sampling, stochastic filtering, and opacity-based filtering. For each ray r, it creates sampling points s{r,i} via stratified sampling, randomly distributing points within each SVO node intersected by r while ensuring sampling density depends on the side length of the intersected node. The ideal tree depth d is inferred using the Nyquist sampling theorem to find the node with the highest LoD still free of aliasing. The constant relative sampling density factor k is set to 8 samples per node edge length. If no tree node is allocated at the inferred depth, the ray depth interval is treated as free space. Special case: if the SVO is still being built up and traversal reaches the global maximum depth, a coarser higher level node is returned for sampling instead of treating it as free space. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples per ray and the cost of LOD determination. Fractional LOD may incur slightly higher computational cost due to dual LOD fetches and interpolation. Memory Complexity: Requires access to multiple LOD levels of the volume data. The working set size depends on the spatial distribution of high-frequency details. Performance: Reduces aliasing and improves quality in high-frequency regions while saving computation in smooth regions. Measured on electron microscopy volumes (90 GB), it allows efficient rendering by skipping empty space and adapting resolution. Strengths: High visual quality, adaptive to local detail, reduces aliasing. Limitations: Increased complexity in LOD management, potential for artifacts if LOD transitions are not smooth. When to use: When visual quality is critical and the volume has varying frequency content. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and uniform low resolution is acceptable. Per-sample LOD selection was introduced as an optimization for GPU-based volume rendering. It builds on earlier work in empty space skipping and brick-based rendering [GMG08, Eng11, HBJP12]. The method was highlighted in the context of large-scale volume visualization, demonstrating its effectiveness on large datasets like electron microscopy volumes. The concept of fractional LOD interpolation was also explored in this context. name: Conservative Density Evaluation
head: Conservative Density
body: Conservative Density Evaluation is a ray marching optimization technique that uses a user-specified, inexpensive-to-evaluate "conservative density" to gate the execution of expensive material graphs (such as Albedo, Emissive Color, and Extinction calculations). It solves the performance bottleneck of evaluating full volumetric material logic for every sample along a ray, particularly in atmospheric cloud rendering, by skipping expensive computations when the conservative density indicates no participating medium exists. Unlike standard material evaluation which runs for every sample, this method uses a cheap scalar/vector check to gate the expensive evaluation, saving performance when cloud density is zero. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Vector3 conservative density value, typically computed via a separate, inexpensive graph (e.g., a top-down 2D texture lookup or simple geometric check). The X component of the float vector (Vector3) represents the participating medium conservative density. Output: The final material properties (Albedo, Emissive Color, Extinction) if density > 0; otherwise, the sample is skipped or treated as empty. Data Structures: Conservative Density Vector: A 3-component floating-point vector (Vector3). X: The scalar conservative density value used for the branching decision. Y, Z: Unused for the branching logic in the standard implementation described. Numbered Steps: 1. Evaluate Conservative Density: Compute the conservative density input graph. This graph must be inexpensive to evaluate. The result is stored in a Vector3 variable. 2. Check Density Threshold: Inspect the X component of the conservative density vector. 3. Conditional Material Evaluation: If ConservativeDensity.X > 0: Proceed to evaluate the expensive material graph plugged into the Main Material node. This graph computes Albedo, Emissive Color, and Extinction. If ConservativeDensity.X <= 0: Skip the expensive material evaluation entirely and proceed to the next ray marching sample. 4. Access Material Values: If the expensive graph was evaluated, access its output values using the Volumetric Advanced Input node. This node retrieves the values computed in Step 3 without recomputing the conservative density. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluateconservativedensitygraph(pos): # User-defined graph; must return Vector3 where X > 0 if cloud exists return vec3(0.0) def evaluateexpensivematerialgraph(pos): # Computes Albedo, Emissive Color, and Extinction return {"albedo": vec3(0.0), "emissivecolor": vec3(0.0), "extinction": 0.0} def evaluatevolumetricsample(raysampleposition): # Step 1: Evaluate the inexpensive conservative density graph conservativedensityvector = evaluateconservativedensitygraph(raysampleposition) # Step 2: Check the X component of the conservative density densityx = conservativedensityvector.x # Step 3: Conditional branching based on density if densityx > 0: # Step 3a: Evaluate the expensive material graph materialoutput = evaluateexpensivematerialgraph(raysampleposition) # Step 4: Access values from the expensive evaluation albedo = materialoutput["albedo"] emissivecolor = materialoutput["emissivecolor"] extinction = materialoutput["extinction"] else: # Step 3b: Skip expensive evaluation albedo = vec3(0.0) emissivecolor = vec3(0.0) extinction = 0.0 return albedo, emissivecolor, extinction Parameters: Conservative Density Threshold: The threshold is implicitly 0.0. If X > 0, the material is evaluated; otherwise, it is skipped. Conservative Density Graph: The specific implementation of the inexpensive graph is user-defined but must satisfy the condition that it is greater than 0 where cloud/participating medium exists. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Alpha Holdout Interaction: Cloud rendering will use the expensive path when r.PostProcessing.PropagateAlpha is enabled and when any features, such as Exponential Height Fog, Volumetric Cloud, and Sky Atmosphere, have alpha holdout enabled. Dynamic Branching Limitation: Unreal Engine material graphs do not support dynamic branching natively. The Conservative Density input is required to enable this skipping behavior; without it, the expensive material graph would be evaluated for every sample. Ray Tracing Limitations: The cloud system does not support Ray Tracing features for volumetric clouds; they are only taken into account as rendered into the Sky Light. Performance: Significantly reduces cost when cloud density is zero by avoiding expensive material graph evaluations. The optimization is effective because the conservative density check is "inexpensively reasonable to evaluate" compared to the full material graph. Limitations: The optimization is automatically bypassed when r.PostProcessing.PropagateAlpha is enabled or when features like Exponential Height Fog, Volumetric Cloud, and Sky Atmosphere have alpha holdout enabled, forcing the expensive material path. It does not apply to ray-traced reflections, as volumetric clouds do not support ray tracing for reflections. When to use: Use when rendering atmospheric clouds or participating media where large portions of the ray march through empty space, and the engine/material system lacks native dynamic branching support. Conservative Density Evaluation was introduced in Unreal Engine as an optimization for the Volumetric Cloud system. It addresses the limitation of Unreal Engine's material graph system, which does not support dynamic branching natively. Because Unreal Engine material graphs do not support dynamic branching natively, the Conservative Density input is required to enable this skipping behavior. It is part of the broader Volumetric Cloud Component in Unreal Engine. name: Epipolar Sampling with 1D Min/Max Binary Tree Optimization
head: 1D min/max tree acceleration, Epipolar light shafts
body: This method accelerates the calculation of the inscattering integral for volumetric light shafts by casting rays through an epipolar plane defined by the camera and light direction. It utilizes 1D min/max binary trees constructed from shadow map slices to skip large lit or shadowed regions during ray marching, significantly reducing the number of shadow tests required. Inputs: Camera position \mathbf{C}, view and projection matrices, light position (spot) or direction (directional), light transform matrix, shadow map resolution, depth buffer, and camera-space z texture. Outputs: Inscaattered light color for each screen pixel. Interpolation Source Texture: An auxiliary two-channel integer texture storing indices of the two closest ray-marching samples from the same slice for inscattered light interpolation. Shared Memory Array: A 1-bit flag array packed as 32-bit unsigned integers indicating discontinuities between adjacent samples in a ray section. 1D Min/Max Binary Tree: For each epipolar slice, a binary tree where leaves store depth values from the shadow map, and internal nodes store the minimum and maximum depth values of their children. 1. Reconstruct Camera-Space Z: Reconstruct the camera-space z coordinate from the non-linear depth buffer because z can be safely interpolated linearly, whereas depth cannot. 2. Compute Epipolar Slice Geometry: For each epipolar slice, determine the slice origin \mathbf{O} and direction \mathbf{D} in shadow map UV coordinates. Define the epipolar plane normal \mathbf{N} using two vectors in the plane: \mathbf{S}0 (direction from camera to light source) and \mathbf{S}1 (vector from camera to the epipolar slice exit point in world space). \mathbf{N} = \text{cross}(\mathbf{S}1, \mathbf{S}0) Compute the slice direction \mathbf{D} as the cross product of \mathbf{N} and the shadow map plane normal \mathbf{N}{\text{shadow}}, since \mathbf{D} lies in both planes. \mathbf{D} = \text{cross}(\mathbf{N}, \mathbf{N}{\text{shadow}}) Directional Light Origin: Transform the camera world position \mathbf{C} with the shadow map transform matrix to get \mathbf{O}. Spot Light Origin: If the camera is outside the light cone, find a point \mathbf{P}0 on the ray, compute intersections with the light cone, and set \mathbf{O} = \mathbf{P}0 + t{\min} \cdot \mathbf{D}. If inside the cone, \mathbf{O} is the projection of the camera position onto the shadow map plane. Transform \mathbf{O} and \mathbf{D} to shadow map UV coordinates using the light transform matrix. 3. Render Epipolar Coordinates: Cast an epipolar line through each screen pixel to compute the location in the epipolar texture. Account for pixel attribute interpolation bias: the outermost visible screen pixels are biased by 0.5 pixel size inwards, so exit points must be located on a shrunk screen boundary. x{\text{exit}} \in \left[-1 + \frac{1}{W}, 1 - \frac{1}{W}\right], \quad y{\text{exit}} \in \left[-1 + \frac{1}{H}, 1 - \frac{1}{H}\right] where W and H are the viewport width and height. Render a 1D texture containing enter and exit points for each epipolar slice, along with camera-space z, into epipolar coordinates, setting up a depth-stencil buffer to mark valid samples. 4. Construct 1D Min/Max Binary Trees: Use a flip/flop rendering approach with two textures alternately as source and destination. Level 0 (Leaves): Initialize the first level using the shadow map. Use a Gather() instruction to load four samples for PCF filtering, computing conservative minimum and maximum values to guarantee identical results to visiting all texels. Higher Levels: Construct coarse tree levels by loading two min/max values from the corresponding nodes at the next finer level. Full binary trees are not constructed because it is very unlikely that coarse levels could be reached. 5. Detect Depth Breaks: Execute a compute shader where each thread group processes one ray section between two neighboring samples, and each thread processes one sample. Populate the shared-memory array with 1-bit flags indicating discontinuities between adjacent samples, packed as 32-bit uints. Identify interpolation source samples using firstbitlow() and firstbithigh() intrinsic functions that return the bit position of the first non-zero bit starting from the lowest and highest order bits, respectively. Mark ray marching samples in the stencil buffer. 6. Ray Marching with 1D Min/Max Optimization: For each epipolar slice, march along the ray direction \mathbf{D} starting from \mathbf{O}. For each ray section: Let d{\max} be the maximum depth at the ends of the current ray section. Let d{\min} be the minimum depth at the ends of the current ray section. Query the 1D min/max binary tree for the current slice. Skip Lit Regions: If d{\max} < \text{tree\min}, the section is completely lit. Skip Shadowed Regions: If d{\min} > \text{tree\max}, the section is fully in shadow and can be skipped. Refine: If neither condition is true, repeat the test at the next finer tree level. If the leaf level is reached, perform a direct shadow test against the raw shadow map. 7. Interpolate Inscaattered Light: Compute initial inscattering for ray-marched samples. For samples marked for interpolation, use the Interpolation Source Texture to linearly interpolate inscattering between the two closest ray-marching samples from the same slice. Transform inscattering from epipolar to rectangular coordinates using epipolar and rectangular camera-space z textures to compute bilateral weights. 8. Fix-up Pass: Pixels marked in the stencil buffer (those that could not be interpolated or had no appropriate samples) undergo an additional ray marching pass using fewer steps and no 1D min/max optimization. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reconstructcameraz(depthbuffer, invprojmatrix): # Reconstruct camera-space z from non-linear depth buffer pass # Inverse projection matrix multiplication def computeslicegeometry(camerapos, lightparams, shadowmaptransform, shadowplanenormal, isdirectional, camerainsidecone): # S0: Camera to Light direction if isdirectional: S0 = normalize([-v for v in lightparams]) else: S0 = normalize([lightparams[i] - camerapos[i] for i in range(3)]) # S1: Camera to Exit Point (precomputed from screen coordinates) N = cross(S1, S0) D = cross(N, shadowplanenormal) # Origin O calculation depends on light type and camera position if camerainsidecone: O = multiplymatrixvector(shadowmaptransform, append1(camerapos)) else: P0 = camerapos tmin = intersectraycone(P0, D, lightparams) # Standard ray-cone intersection logic O = [P0[i] + tmin D[i] for i in range(3)] O = multiplymatrixvector(shadowmaptransform, append1(O)) Duv = multiplymatrixvector(shadowmaptransform, append0(D)) return O[:2], Duv[:2] def buildminmaxtreeflipflop(shadowmap, levels): # Use flip/flop rendering with two textures alternately as source and destination # Level 0 (Leaves): Initialize the first level using the shadow map # Use Gather() instruction to load four samples for PCF filtering, computing conservative min/max # Higher Levels: Construct coarse tree levels by loading two min/max values from the corresponding nodes at the next finer level # Full binary trees are not constructed because it is very unlikely that coarse levels could be reached pass def detectdepthbreakscomputeshader(raysections): # Each thread group processes one ray section between two neighboring samples # Each thread processes one sample # Populate shared-memory array with 1-bit flags indicating discontinuities between adjacent samples, packed as 32-bit uints # Identify interpolation source samples using firstbitlow() and firstbithigh() intrinsic functions # Mark ray marching samples in the stencil buffer pass def raymarchwithminmaxtree(Ouv, Duv, minmaxtree, cameraz): # March along ray direction D starting from O for each ray section: dmax = max(depth at ends of current ray section) dmin = min(depth at ends of current ray section) treemin, treemax = queryminmaxtree(minmaxtree) if dmax < treemin: # Section is completely lit accumulatelight() elif dmin > treemax: # Section is fully in shadow and can be skipped pass else: # Repeat the test at the next finer tree level pass # If leaf level is reached, perform a direct shadow test against the raw shadow map pass def interpolateinscattering(interpolationsourcetexture, epipolarz, rectangularz): # Compute initial inscattering for ray-marched samples # For marked samples, linearly interpolate inscattering between the two closest ray-marching samples from the same slice # Transform inscattering from epipolar to rectangular coordinates using epipolar and rectangular camera-space z textures to compute bilateral weights pass def fixuppass(stencilbuffer): # Pixels marked in the stencil buffer undergo an additional ray marching pass using fewer steps and no 1D min/max optimization pass def normalize(v): length = math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in v)) return [x/length for x in v] def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def multiplymatrixvector(M, v): return [sum(M[i][j]v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for i in range(len(M))] def append1(v): return v + [1.0] def append0(v): return v + [0.0] def intersectraycone(origin, direction, lightparams): # Standard ray-cone intersection logic return 0.0 def accumulatelight(): pass def accumulateshadow(): pass def sampleshadowmap(uv): return 0.5 Viewport Shrinkage: The exit points of epipolar lines must be located on a shrunk screen boundary to account for pixel center interpolation bias. The shrinkage factor is 1/W and 1/H for width and height respectively. Shadow Map Resolution: Affects the granularity of the 1D min/max tree. 4k x 4k is cited as a high-performance setting. Quality Profiles: Trade-offs between sample count and smoothing. High quality uses more samples; high performance uses fewer, potentially causing artifacts near the light source. Pixel Attribute Interpolation Bias: Ignoring the 0.5 pixel size bias causes inefficient sample distribution and inaccurate interpolation, leading to more pixels requiring the fix-up pass. Spot Light Camera Position: If the camera is behind or on the light projection plane, the simple directional light origin method fails. The universal solution involving cone intersection must be used. Colored Light Shafts: The min/max optimization is less efficient because lit regions cannot be skipped; they must be traversed with a fine step. However, performance remains high (>100 fps). No Appropriate Samples: If no appropriate samples exist for bilateral filtering, the pixel is marked in the stencil buffer and processed with a fallback ray marching pass. Time Complexity: The 1D min/max tree allows skipping large regions, reducing shadow test overhead per sample. Depth break detection is up to 6x faster than direct implementation for long steps. Memory Complexity: Requires auxiliary textures for epipolar coordinates, camera-space z, interpolation sources, and the min/max trees. Memory usage is approximately 5.5 MB on mobile GPUs. Performance: Mobile GPU (Nvidia): 5.38 ms with 5.5 MB memory. Integrated GPU (Intel HD): 8.85 ms, maintaining interactive frame rates. Discrete GPU (Nvidia): Less than 3.4 ms total processing time for a specific scene; just above 4 ms for a 4k x 4k shadow map with directional light. Spot Light Acceleration: Without 1D min/max tree, ray marching time is 3.3x higher and total frame time is 2x higher. Strengths: Fully post-processing, suitable for a wide range of hardware, supports colored light shafts, and provides significant speedups over brute force ray marching. Limitations: Less efficient for colored light shafts due to inability to skip lit regions. Requires careful handling of camera positions relative to spot lights. This technique was developed to accelerate inscattering integral calculations for light shafts, building on the observation that all camera rays in an epipolar slice share the same plane. The concept of using 1D min/max binary trees for epipolar slices was first recognized by Chen et al.. The implementation uses a flip/flop rendering approach with two textures for tree construction due to better GPU utilization compared to compute shaders, while depth discontinuity detection is implemented with a compute shader. name: Hardware-Specific Optimization
head: Hardware-Aware Optimization, Platform-Specific Tuning
body: Hardware-Specific Optimization encompasses techniques that adapt volume rendering algorithms to exploit the architectural characteristics of target execution platforms (CPU, GPU, TPU, or specialized accelerators) to maximize throughput and minimize latency. It differs from general optimization methods by directly addressing hardware constraints such as cache hierarchy, memory bandwidth, instruction-level parallelism, and execution models, rather than solely optimizing algorithmic complexity or geometric traversal costs. A GPU-based ray tracer for Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) that accelerates ray traversal by replacing unindexed full-scans of the root universe with a uniform grid index over the universe's cells. It solves the performance bottleneck where rays outside the model traverse infinite surface extensions, causing redundant full-scans of all region tokens. Unlike its siblings, it operates as a direct f32 transcription of CPU plotting logic into a WGSL shader, maintaining exact visual parity while leveraging hardware-specific optimizations like silent voxel stepping. UltraVis is a software-based volume rendering system designed to maximize cache performance on Intel Pentium III processors by addressing cache thrashing through specific memory layout and interleaved addressing. It sets itself apart from general ray-casting methods by enforcing a rigid cache partitioning scheme that guarantees volume data remains in a private cache block, never being swapped out by competing structures like transfer functions or image buffers. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on hardware-specific instruction sets or GPU parallelism, UltraVis focuses on CPU cache architecture constraints, using bricked decomposition and ray flocking to ensure data locality. VIZARD II is a specialized hardware architecture for interactive volume rendering, developed at the University of Tübingen to bring ray casting to desktop computers. It solves the memory bandwidth bottleneck inherent in image-order ray casting by combining early ray termination, 9-bit quantized gradient look-up tables, and a specialized caching mechanism. Unlike its predecessor VIZARD, which used pre-shaded data, VIZARD II computes gradients on-the-fly via a quantized table, and unlike the VolumePro, it supports perspective rendering while using a table-based gradient scheme instead of hardware gradient estimation. Hardware-Aware Hyperparameter Tuning is an automatic process that determines optimal performance parameters (tile size, unroll factor, number of bins, batch divisor) for a specific scene and view set on a target hardware device, ensuring correctness and performance without manual tuning. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like GPU CSG Ray Tracing with Uniform Grid Index by focusing on compile-time configuration of shader batch sizes and bin layouts rather than geometric traversal optimization or cache locality. Evaluate each visible channel at each sample during ray traversal to reduce diverging branches. Start tree traversal at a user-defined subdivision level, or the parent level of the subdivision level where traversal was terminated for the previous sample. Ray traversal and computations (e.g., ray iso-surface intersection test) are significantly speeded up using SIMD instruction sets similar to AltiVec or SSE. SPUs have in-order execution, requiring careful manual arrangement of crucial instructions. The SPU local store has no hardware caching support, requiring software implementation. High memory latency makes waiting for data costly; hand-tuned virtual multi-threading must be exploited to keep rays or ray bundles busy. A process of evaluating performance by sweeping through tunable algorithmic parameters to find the combination resulting in the best performance, without code generation or exhaustive search heuristics. Image tile sizes (block sizes) for CPU tests: width and height vary over {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128}. Thread block sizes for GPU tests: width and height vary over {1, 2, 4, 8, 16}, excluding 1x1, 1x2, and 2x1 blocks. NVIDIA/Fermi requires at least four threads per block to saturate the computational throughput of a warp of execution; blocks with fewer than four threads are excluded. CPU test battery on AMD/MagnyCours: 5120 tests (10 views, 64 block sizes, with/without ERT, two memory layouts, two concurrency levels, dynamic work assignment only). CPU test battery on Intel/Nehalem: 7680 tests (similar to AMD but with three work assignment methods and 8-way concurrency), plus 7680 additional tests at 1-way, 2-way, and 4-way concurrency with dynamic work assignment only. GPU test battery: 880 tests over 22 thread block sizes, two memory layouts, with/without ERT. Experimental determination of computational cost parameters (CIu, CIm, CRu, CRm) using specific algorithms and hardware. C{Ru} = 8.75 \times 10^{-7} N + (6.50 \times 10^{-5} + 4.31 \times 10^{-12} N) NR derived from linear least squares analysis of uniform subsampling timing data. C{Rm} = 3.21 \times 10^{-5} N + (0.87 \times 10^{-5} + 2.5 \times 10^{-10} N) NR derived from linear least squares analysis of octree data reduction timing data. Hardware: SGI Origin with 250 MHz R10000 chips. Timing method: Unix subroutine gettimeofday(). CIu determination: Used vtkContourMarchingFilter with vtkStructuredPoints for uniform structured point sets. CIm determination: Used vtkContourMarchingFilter with vtkUnstructuredGrid for unstructured octree representation. CIu asymptotic value: Approximately 0.0015 ms/cell as N increases. CIm value: Approximately 0.024 ms/cell, a factor of 16 greater than CIu. An architecture optimization of R2L tailored for mobile devices that does not require pre-storing intermediate data. Leads to significant memory issues when handling large ray sizes. Hardware-specific optimization in volume rendering has evolved alongside the diversification of computing architectures. Early work focused on CPU cache optimization, such as the UltraVis system for Intel Pentium III processors, which addressed cache thrashing through memory layout and partitioning. Concurrently, specialized hardware architectures like VIZARD II were designed to minimize memory bandwidth requirements using quantized gradients and parallel memory access. With the rise of GPUs, optimization shifted towards managing memory bandwidth, instruction divergence, and parallel execution units, leading to methods like hardware-aware hyperparameter tuning for ray tracing. Specialized processors, such as the Cell Broadband Engine, introduced challenges like in-order execution and lack of hardware caching, requiring manual instruction arrangement and software-managed memory. Additionally, cost models have been experimentally determined for specific hardware platforms (e.g., SGI Origin) to guide algorithmic choices like subsampling strategies. name: GPU CSG Ray Tracing with Uniform Grid Index
head: GPU CSG Renderer Features, GPU CSG tracer, GpuPlot
body: A GPU-based ray tracer for Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) that accelerates traversal by replacing unindexed full-scans of the root universe with a uniform grid index over the universe's cells. It solves the performance bottleneck where rays outside the model traverse infinite surface extensions, causing redundant full-scans of all region tokens. Unlike its siblings UltraVis Cache Optimization, VIZARD II, and Hardware-Aware Hyperparameter Tuning, it operates as a direct f32 transcription of CPU plotting logic into a WGSL shader, maintaining exact visual parity while leveraging hardware-specific optimizations like silent voxel stepping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A CSG model defined by surfaces, RPN regions, universes, lattices, and translations, flattened into a single u32 buffer (outramblender::csg::gpu::flat). Output: Rendered images (Solid, Wireframe, Slice) via a WGSL shader, or a CPU fallback if GPU constraints are exceeded. Data Structures: 1. Flat Geometry Buffer (outramblender::csg::gpu::flat): A single u32 buffer containing: surfaces definitions; RPN region expressions; universe definitions and graph; rectangular and hexagonal lattices (including maps and outer definitions); translations; static crossing hints (OpenMC-style neighbor lists); and the universe graph used to skip subtrees with no drawn material. Tori are refused. 2. Uniform Grid Index: A 3D voxel grid over the root universe's bounding box. Each voxel stores a list of candidate cells that intersect it. Each cell's region expression is constant-folded to the specific surfaces passing through that voxel. 3. GpuPlot Struct: Contains variants Solid, Wireframe, and Slice, matching the CPU plotter's structs. Algorithm Steps: 1. Grid Construction: Create a voxel grid over the root universe's bounding box. For each voxel, identify intersecting cells. Constant-fold each cell's region expression to reduce it to the specific surfaces intersecting that voxel. Grid resolution is scene-dependent; the HTR-10 root universe uses a 30 \times 30 \times 47 voxel grid. 2. Grid Closing (Bounding Box Enforcement): Ensure no root cell lies outside the grid bounds to allow rays outside the model to jump directly to the grid. For unbounded OpenMC boxes (e.g., absorber-sphere channels, core cell conus), perform vertex enumeration over plane half-spaces. Apply a bound on the cone radius to create tight bounding boxes. 3. Indexing Budgeting: Index universes with token counts above 512, within a 16 MB memory budget. If the geometry buffer exceeds the device's 128 MiB binding limit, setgeometry returns an error, triggering a CPU fallback. Bed tiles (1,500) were not indexed as they cost 29 MB and changed no frame time. 4. Ray Traversal (Shader Execution): When a ray is outside the model, it jumps directly to the uniform grid. Inside the grid, the ray steps through voxels. Voxel faces act as "silent steps" (no surface intersection test required). Upon entering a voxel, test against the pre-computed surfaces for the candidate cells. Sign complex regions from the surface normal to correct a CPU parity bug where complements were not handled via De Morgan's laws. After a silent voxel step, reset the token to ensure the ray can exit a bore/cell correctly, fixing a bug where the tracer retained the token of the last-crossed surface. 5. Rendering Modes: Phong Solid View renders solid geometry with lighting. Slice View renders section planes with cut faces, supporting per-material visibility and x-ray attenuation with outlines. ClipPlane Correction ensures shadow rays are lit once they pass into the cut-away half of a clip plane, fixing a bug where the shadow ray was blocked by the cut-away half. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traceray(origin, direction, grid): # 1. Outside model: jump directly to grid if not grid.contains(origin): tentry = grid.computeentrydistance(origin, direction) currentpos = origin + direction tentry else: currentpos = origin # 2. Traverse grid while grid.contains(currentpos): voxel = grid.getvoxel(currentpos) # Silent step: advance to next voxel boundary without intersection test tnext = grid.computenextvoxelboundary(currentpos, direction) nextpos = currentpos + direction tnext # 3. Intersection test upon entering voxel hitsurface = None hitt = float('inf') for surface in voxel.candidatesurfaces: # Standard ray-surface intersection test thit = computesurfaceintersection(currentpos, direction, surface) if 0 < thit < hitt: hitsurface = surface hitt = thit if hitsurface is not None: # 4. Complex region handling: sign from surface normal normal = computesurfacenormal(hitsurface) regiontoken = hitsurface.getregiontoken() if regiontoken.iscomplement(): # Apply De Morgan's correction by signing from normal regiontoken = signregionfromnormal(regiontoken, normal) # 5. Post-step correction: reset token to allow exit currenttoken = resettoken(regiontoken) # Advance past hit currentpos = hitsurface.hitpoint + direction 1e-6 continue # Silent step completed, move to next voxel currentpos = nextpos return renderoutput(currentpos) def computesurfaceintersection(origin, direction, surface): # Standard analytical ray-surface intersection; returns t or infinity pass def computesurfacenormal(surface): # Returns the geometric normal vector of the surface at the hit point pass def signregionfromnormal(token, normal): # Adjusts token sign based on normal direction to fix complement parity pass def resettoken(token): # Clears retained surface token to permit ray exit from bores/cells pass def renderoutput(pos): # Applies Phong lighting or slice attenuation based on GpuPlot variant pass Parameters: Grid Resolution: Scene-dependent. HTR-10 root universe: 30 \times 30 \times 47. Indexing Threshold: Universes with token counts > 512. Memory Budget: 16 MB for indexing. Buffer Limit: 128 MiB (device binding limit). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complement Handling: The CPU port did not remove complements by De Morgan's laws or sign complex regions from the surface normal. This caused rays entering a reflector core (written as box & ~core) to be re-located incorrectly. The fix signs complex regions from the normal. Silent Step Token Retention: After stepping through a voxel face, the tracer retained the token of the last-crossed surface. This prevented rays inside a bore from exiting. The fix resets the token. ClipPlane Shadow Bug: In the CPU SolidRayTracePlot with a ClipPlane, the shadow ray was blocked by the cut-away half. The fix ensures the ray is lit once it passes into that half. This changes the shade of 2.5% of pixels but no pixel changes material. Buffer Overflow: If the geometry buffer exceeds 128 MiB, the system must fall back to CPU rendering to avoid panics. Time Complexity: Cost per crossing is approximately 90 ns. Memory Complexity: Indexing budget is 16 MB for universes with >512 tokens. Total geometry buffer must fit within 128 MiB. Measured Performance (Şeker bed, half-section, 900x560): GPU Indexed: 24-60 ms (best 17 ms). GPU Unindexed: 0.36-0.39 s. CPU: 6.95 s (from earlier test). Indexed GPU is ~15-30x faster than unindexed GPU. Scaling: Performance varies 2-4x from run to run because the GPU is shared with the desktop. Strengths: Significant speedup over unindexed GPU and CPU methods for large universes; maintains visual parity with CPU renderer. Limitations: Buffer size limited to 128 MiB; unindexed rays still suffer from full scans; X-ray views with dense lattices (e.g., TRISO) remain slow (~0.64 s). When to Use: When rendering large CSG models on GPU with sufficient VRAM (<128 MiB geometry buffer) and when visual parity with CPU is required. When Not to Use: When geometry buffer exceeds 128 MiB or when tori are present (not supported). Originated in the outram-blender crate, specifically the outramblender::csg::gpu module, as part of the dhoby-ghaut project. The implementation was driven by the need to accelerate 3D and 2D views in a reactor physics visualization tool, replacing a slow CPU-based ray tracer with a GPU-accelerated version using WGSL shaders. The method was developed to address the performance bottleneck of unindexed ray traversal in large CSG universes, such as the HTR-10 and Şeker bed models. dhoby-ghaut: GPU rendering for the 3D and 2D views (sphere impostors for pebbles; GPU or accelerated CSG ray tracing), https://github.com/theodoreOnzGit/outram-park-backend/issues/587, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: UltraVis Cache Optimization
head: Knittel's Ray Casting, Optimized CPU Ray-Casting, Pentium III Optimized Ray Casting, ULTRAVIS Cache-Based Optimization, UltraVis, UltraVis Cache Management, UltraVis System
body: UltraVis is a software-based volume rendering system designed to maximize cache performance on Intel Pentium III processors by addressing cache thrashing via memory layout and interleaved addressing. It sets itself apart from general ray-casting methods by enforcing a rigid cache partitioning scheme that guarantees volume data remains in a private cache block, never being swapped out by competing structures like transfer functions or image buffers. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on hardware-specific instruction sets or GPU parallelism, UltraVis focuses on CPU cache architecture constraints, using bricked decomposition and ray flocking to ensure data locality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data, transfer function tables, camera parameters, and image resolution. Output: Rendered 2D image. Data Structures and Layout: 1. Cache Partitioning: The CPU cache is divided into four distinct, non-overlapping blocks: Volume bricks Transfer function tables Image blocks Temporary buffers 2. Volume Memory Layout: Volume data is mapped exclusively into the "Volume bricks" cache block. To prevent mapping conflicts with other data structures, volume data is placed in the first quarter of each memory page. This results in a main memory footprint four times higher than standard contiguous storage because no volume data may be stored in an address space that would map outside the volume's private cache slots. 3. Interleaved Addressing: Voxel values are reordered using a cubic interleaved address function. This function assumes n is a power of two and n^3 is smaller than the cache size. Under these conditions, a cube of n^3 voxels occupies exactly n \times n \times n cache locations. Algorithm Steps: 1. Brick Decomposition: Divide the volume into bricks. 2. Ray Flocking: Group rays into a "flock" that traverses the same brick simultaneously. 3. Cache Loading: Load the entire brick data into the private volume cache block once. 4. Traversal: Trace all rays in the flock through the loaded brick. Because the rays are close together within the brick, the interleaved memory layout ensures that neighboring rays access cached voxel values, increasing the cache hit ratio. 5. Discard: Once all rays in the flock have finished traversing the brick, discard the brick data from the cache. 6. Shading: Apply transfer functions and compositing. The transfer function tables reside in their own private cache block, ensuring they are not evicted by volume data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ultravisrender(volumedata, transferfunction, camera, imagewidth, imageheight): # 1. Setup Cache Blocks # The system implicitly manages four cache blocks: # - volumeblock: for volume bricks # - tfblock: for transfer function tables # - imageblock: for output image tiles # - tempblock: for temporary buffers # Implementation note: On actual hardware, this requires specific # memory allocation strategies (e.g., page alignment) to enforce # the partitioning described in. # 2. Prepare Volume Data # Reorder voxel data using cubic interleaved address function. # Let n be the brick dimension (power of 2). # Ensure n^3 < cachesize. # Map data to first quarter of memory pages. interleavedvolume = applycubicinterleaving(volumedata) # 3. Prepare Transfer Function # Load transfer function into its dedicated cache block. tftable = transferfunction # 4. Ray Flock Traversal # Generate rays from camera. rays = generaterays(camera, imagewidth, imageheight) # Group rays into flocks that share bricks. # This assumes a bricked volume decomposition. brickflocks = groupraysintobricks(rays, interleavedvolume.bricksize) for flock in brickflocks: brickid = flock.brickid # Load brick into private volume cache block. # Ensure this load does not evict data from tfblock, # imageblock, or tempblock. currentbrick = loadbrick(interleavedvolume, brickid) # Trace all rays in the flock through the loaded brick. # The interleaved layout ensures high cache reuse for neighboring rays. for ray in flock.rays: color = traceraythroughbrick(ray, currentbrick, tftable) compositeintoimage(ray, color, flock.outputcoords) # Discard brick data from cache after flock traversal. unloadbrick(currentbrick) def applycubicinterleaving(volumedata): """ Reorders volume data to minimize cache thrashing. Assumes n is power of 2 and n^3 < cachesize. Standard stride-based permutation to map n^3 voxels to n x n x n cache lines. """ n = volumedata.bricksize interleaved = emptyarraylike(volumedata) for z in range(n): for y in range(n): for x in range(n): # Bit-reversal/stride permutation to ensure spatial locality in cache lines newx = bitreverse(x, log2(n)) newy = bitreverse(y, log2(n)) newz = bitreverse(z, log2(n)) interleaved[newz, newy, newx] = volumedata[z, y, x] return interleaved def traceraythroughbrick(ray, brick, tftable): """ Standard front-to-back volume rendering integration within a brick. Uses the interleaved memory layout for efficient access. """ outcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 t = ray.origin step = ray.stepsize epsilon = 1e-4 while t < ray.end and transmittance > epsilon: voxelcoords = ray.origin + t ray.direction voxelvalue = samplevolume(brick, voxelcoords) rgba = tftable[voxelvalue] # Standard front-to-back compositing alpha = 1.0 - exp(-voxelvalue.density step) outcolor[0] += transmittance rgba.r alpha outcolor[1] += transmittance rgba.g alpha outcolor[2] += transmittance rgba.b alpha outcolor[3] = min(1.0, outcolor[3] + transmittance rgba.a alpha) transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) t += step return outcolor def generaterays(camera, imagewidth, imageheight): rays = [] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): direction = normalize(camera.projectpixel(x, y)) rays.append(Ray(camera.origin, direction, camera.stepsize)) return rays def groupraysintobricks(rays, bricksize): flocks = {} for ray in rays: brickid = computebrickid(ray.origin, bricksize) if brickid not in flocks: flocks[brickid] = [] flocks[brickid].append(ray) return flocks def loadbrick(volume, brickid): return volume.extractbrick(brickid) def unloadbrick(brick): del brick def compositeintoimage(ray, color, coords): image[coords.y][coords.x] = color Parameters: Brick Size (n): Must be a power of two. n^3 must be smaller than the L1 cache size to ensure the entire brick fits in the private cache block. Performance: Renders a 256^3 volume at 10 frames/s. Renders UNC MRI-head (256 \times 256 \times 110) at 1.7 to 7.0 fps on a Pentium III 500MHz with 256 \times 256 image resolution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cache Thrashing: If the volume data is not properly interleaved or if the brick size exceeds the cache capacity, cache thrashing occurs, severely degrading performance. Memory Footprint: The main memory footprint is four times higher than standard storage because no volume data may be stored in an address space that would map outside the volume's private cache slots. Hardware Specificity: The optimization relies heavily on the specific cache replacement strategies and page mapping of the Intel Pentium III processor. Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined in terms of Big-O, but performance is measured in frames per second (fps). Memory Complexity: Main memory footprint is four times that of standard contiguous volume storage due to the private cache block requirement. Measured Performance: 256^3 volume at 10 fps. 256 \times 256 \times 110 volume at 1.7–7.0 fps on Pentium III 500MHz. Scaling: Performance is limited by CPU cache size and memory bandwidth. The method is designed for single-PC execution. Strengths: High cache hit ratio for semi-transparent volume rendering on CPUs; prevents cache thrashing through rigid partitioning. Limitations: High memory overhead (4x); hardware-specific (Pentium III); not suitable for very large datasets that exceed cache capacity without out-of-core techniques (though bricking helps). UltraVis was introduced by Knittel in 2000, though one source lists 2011. It was designed as a highly optimized ray casting approach for semi-transparent volume rendering, specifically targeting the Intel Pentium III processor. The system addresses the major obstacle of limited memory bandwidth and cache thrashing in ray tracing-based volume rendering. It was one of the early software-based systems to demonstrate that good cache management is key to achieving fast volume rendering on commodity hardware. name: VIZARD II
head: UVIZARD, VIZARD
body: VIZARD II is a specialized hardware architecture for interactive volume rendering, developed at the University of Tübingen to bring ray casting to desktop computers. It solves the memory bandwidth bottleneck inherent in image-order ray casting by combining early ray termination, 9-bit quantized gradient look-up tables, and a specialized caching mechanism. Unlike its predecessor VIZARD, which used pre-shaded and pre-classified compressed data, VIZARD II computes gradients on-the-fly via a quantized table. Unlike the VolumePro, it supports perspective rendering while using a table-based gradient scheme instead of hardware gradient estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset (voxel values) and a precomputed quantized gradient table. Output: A 2D image rendered via perspective or parallel projection, supporting multiple cut-planes and segmentation. Data Structures: 1. Volume Data: Stored in memory banks. Voxels are four-way interleaved with respect to the YZ-plane to facilitate parallel access. 2. Gradient Table: A look-up table mapping 9-bit gradient indices to 3D gradient vectors (x, y, z components). The index size is not strictly limited to 9 bits, but 9 bits is the standard implementation. 3. Cache Banks: Separate cache banks store recently accessed voxel neighborhoods and gradient components to allow parallel re-use. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute gradient indices for each voxel using central differences. Store these indices in the volume data or a separate structure. This step is performed once per dataset. 2. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, initialize the ray origin and direction. 3. Memory Access (Trilinear Neighborhood): To sample a voxel, the architecture requires a 2 \times 2 \times 2 trilinear interpolation neighborhood. Four voxels (including their gradient indices) are accessed simultaneously in parallel from the memory banks. These voxels correspond to a slice in the YZ-plane. A sequential burst memory access fetches the adjacent voxels in the X-direction from each bank, providing the remaining four values of the 2 \times 2 \times 2 neighborhood. These values are cached in separate cache banks to allow parallel access and re-use. 4. Interpolation: The Interpolation Unit uses the fractional x, y, and z components of the ray position and the cached voxel values to perform trilinear interpolation, yielding the sample value. The gradient index from the accessed voxels addresses the Gradient Look-up Table. The resulting x, y, and z gradient components are interpolated in a similar manner to the voxel values. The quantized central difference gradient ensures that the voxel re-fetch does not exceed the size of the trilinear interpolation neighborhood. 5. Shading and Compositing: The sample value and interpolated gradient are passed to the Shading and Compositing Unit. Classification: A classification index (derived from the sample value) selects a classification table. The architecture supports segmentation and multiple cut-planes. Shading: Phong shading is implemented using a look-up table based on the gradient and view direction. Compositing: The standard 'over' operator is used to composite the sample into the accumulating ray buffer. 6. Early Ray Termination: If the accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold, the ray is terminated early to increase frame rate. 7. Output: Final pixel values are transferred through the PCI bus to the host computer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vizardrender(volume, volumegradidx, gradtable, rayorigins, raydirs, imgh, imgw, maxt, step=0.1, thresh=0.99): """ Simulates VIZARD II hardware pipeline. volume: 3D array (D, H, W) of voxel values. volumegradidx: 3D array (D, H, W) of precomputed 9-bit gradient indices. gradtable: 2D array (256, 3) mapping 9-bit indices to (gx, gy, gz). rayorigins, raydirs: lists of (x, y, z) tuples. """ D, H, W = volume.shape img = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(imgw)] for in range(imgh)] for py in range(imgh): for px in range(imgw): ox, oy, oz = rayorigins[py imgw + px] rdx, rdy, rdz = raydirs[py imgw + px] accr, accg, accb, acca = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < maxt: x, y, z = ox + t rdx, oy + t rdy, oz + t rdz # Boundary check if not (0.0 <= x < W and 0.0 <= y < H and 0.0 <= z < D): break ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz # Hardware Memory Access: 4 parallel YZ-plane accesses + burst X # Fetch 8 voxels and 8 gradient indices for 2x2x2 neighborhood voxels = [] gradidxs = [] for dz in range(2): for dy in range(2): for dx in range(2): voxels.append(volume[min(iz+dz, D-1)][min(iy+dy, H-1)][min(ix+dx, W-1)]) gradidxs.append(volumegradidx[min(iz+dz, D-1)][min(iy+dy, H-1)][min(ix+dx, W-1)]) # Hardware Interpolation Unit: Trilinear interpolation sampleval = ( voxels[0](1-fx)(1-fy)(1-fz) + voxels[1]fx(1-fy)(1-fz) + voxels[2](1-fx)fy(1-fz) + voxels[3]fxfy(1-fz) + voxels[4](1-fx)(1-fy)fz + voxels[5]fx(1-fy)fz + voxels[6](1-fx)fyfz + voxels[7]fxfyfz) # Interpolate gradient components from LUT gradvals = [gradtable[gi] for gi in gradidxs] weights = [ (1-fx)(1-fy)(1-fz), fx(1-fy)(1-fz), (1-fx)fy(1-fz), fxfy(1-fz), (1-fx)(1-fy)fz, fx(1-fy)fz, (1-fx)fyfz, fxfyfz ] gx = sum(v[0] w for v, w in zip(gradvals, weights)) gy = sum(v[1] w for v, w in zip(gradvals, weights)) gz = sum(v[2] w for v, w in zip(gradvals, weights)) # Hardware Shading/Compositing Unit classidx = int(sampleval 255) % 256 alpha = sampleval 0.5 r, g, b = sampleval, sampleval, sampleval # 'over' compositing if alpha > 0.0: accr += (1.0 - acca) r alpha accg += (1.0 - acca) g alpha accb += (1.0 - acca) b alpha acca += (1.0 - acca) alpha # Early Ray Termination if acca >= thresh: break # Advance ray t += step img[py][px] = (accr, accg, accb, acca) return img Parameters: Gradient Quantization: 9-bit indices are standard. Larger tables increase accuracy but consume more memory. Supersampling: 4:1 mapping of samples to voxels is used in best-case performance estimates. Clock Rates: Cache memory and Trilinear Interpolation Units are clocked 4 times faster than the memory system. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Worst-Case Performance: Occurs with 1:1 sampling (no supersampling) and a transparent classification of the dataset, leading to full ray traversal. Gradient Accuracy: Quantized central difference gradients may degrade image quality compared to traditional central difference gradients. Memory Bandwidth: Performance is memory-limited. The architecture relies on cache hits to sustain high throughput. Time Complexity: The algorithmic speedup is assumed to be 3x due to early ray termination. Memory Efficiency: Worst-case (1:1 sampling): Memory efficiency factor is 0.2. Best-case (4:1 supersampling): Memory bandwidth utilization reaches 0.8 due to cache hits. Performance Metrics: Worst-case: ~14 million samples per second (SPPS) using four MHz SDRAM devices. This results in approximately 1 frame per second for a 256^3 dataset. Best-case: ~56 million SPPS assuming 4:1 supersampling. This results in approximately 10 Hz frame rate for a 256^3 dataset. Strengths: Supports perspective rendering, multiple cut-planes, and segmentation. High performance cost ratio. Limitations: Memory bandwidth limited. Quantized gradients may reduce image quality. Research-stage architecture. VIZARD II is the second generation of the VIZARD systems, developed at the University of Tübingen. It was designed to bring interactive ray casting to desktop computers using a PCI board populated with four FPGAs, a DSP, and SDRAM/SRAM memory. It is a research-stage architecture. It differs from the VolumePro by supporting perspective rendering and using a table-based gradient vector lookup scheme.
