name: Hardware-Aware Hyperparameter Tuning
head: Hyperparameter Selection, XPR Hyperparameter Selection, automatic hyperparameter tuning
body: Hardware-Aware Hyperparameter Tuning is an automatic process that determines optimal performance parameters (tile size, unroll factor, number of bins, batch divisor) for a specific scene and view set on a target hardware device, ensuring correctness and performance without manual tuning. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like GPU CSG Ray Tracing with Uniform Grid Index by focusing on compile-time configuration of shader batch sizes and bin layouts rather than geometric traversal optimization or cache locality. The method operates in two distinct phases: profiling to establish safety bounds, and a sequential search to optimize performance parameters. Inputs: The set of target views to be rendered. The trained primitive parameters (e.g., Gaussian splats). The target hardware device (GPU or TPU). Outputs: Optimal tile size. Optimal unroll factor U. Optimal number of bins L. Optimal batch divisor D. Data-aware assignment of tiles to bins. Global bounds M and I sufficient for all target views. The method relies on the following parameters, defined in the search space: | Parameter | Description | Search Space (GPU) | Search Space (TPU) | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | Tile size | Resolution of the tile grid | \{8 \times 8, 16 \times 16\} | \{16 \times 16, 32 \times 32\} | | P{max} | Global accuracy/speed tuning knob | \{4096, 8192\} | \{4096, 8192\} | | L | Number of bins | \{2, 4, 6, 8\} | \{2, 4, 6, 8\} | | D | Batch divisor | \{1, 2, 4, 8\} | \{1, 2, 4, 8\} | | U | XLA unroll factor | \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\} | \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\} | Bin upper bounds are also selected from hardware-specific sets: GPU: \{64, 128, 256, 512, 768, 1024, 2048\} TPU: \{256, 512, 768, 1024, 1280, 1536, 2048\} 1. Render Forward: Render every target view exactly once using a forward-only pass (no gradients). 2. Record Metrics: For each view, record: M: The maximum number of primitives intersecting any tile. I: The maximum number of primitives intersecting any pixel (or relevant intersection count). The number of primitives each tile intersects. 3. Set Global Bounds: Set the global M and I to the observed maxima across all views. This guarantees bounds are sufficient without safety margins. The search proceeds in five sequential phases. Each phase benchmarks candidates and selects the best performer. 1. Phase 1: Tile Size Search space: Two candidates (hardware-specific). Action: Profile each candidate. Different tile sizes change the tile grid topology, requiring separate profiling. 2. Phase 2: Unroll Factor U Search space: \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\}. Action: Benchmark all six candidates exhaustively. 3. Phase 3: Number of Bins L Search space: \{2, 4, 6, 8\}. Action: Benchmark all four candidates exhaustively. Tie-Breaker: If candidates are tied within a 2% noise tolerance, re-benchmark the lowest and highest tied candidates with additional runs to break the tie. 4. Phase 4: Re-search Unroll Factor U Trigger: Executed whenever L shifts the bin layout. Reason: A larger unrolled scan body shifts the tradeoff between instruction-level parallelism and register pressure. Action: Search U again from the six candidates. 5. Phase 5: Batch Divisor D Search space: \{1, 2, 4, 8\}. Action: Search up to four candidates. Preference: Prefer D=4 within noise tolerance. Compute the assignment of tiles to bins based on the worst-case cumulative counts of primitives across all views recorded in Phase 1. This ensures that the bin capacity accommodates the maximum load. The shader batch size bl for a bin with trip count Pl is derived as: bl = \text{round\to\multiple}(\lfloor Pl / D \rfloor, U) where \text{round\to\multiple}(x, m) rounds x to the nearest integer divisible by m. Tile Size: Depends on hardware. GPU: \{8 \times 8, 16 \times 16\}. TPU: \{16 \times 16, 32 \times 32\}. Number of Bins (L): Affects performance significantly. Increasing bins initially increases FPS by reducing redundant computation. Beyond an optimal count, FPS drops due to reduced SM occupancy and increased launch overhead. Batch Divisor (D): Controls the granularity of early exit in the blend loop. Smaller D checks exit conditions less frequently (lower overhead, more wasted work). Larger D enables tighter early termination (higher overhead). Unroll Factor (U): Specifies the XLA unroll factor for the inner loop over primitive entries in each shader batch. Insufficient Bounds: Any view whose M or I values exceed the chosen bounds can produce incorrect rendered images or a drop in accuracy. Profiling all target views is strictly necessary. Noise in Benchmarking: The 2% noise tolerance in Phase 3 is critical to avoid selecting suboptimal parameters due to measurement variance. One-Time Cost: The selection process takes only a few minutes and is a one-time cost, negligible relative to training time. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardwareawarehyperparametertuning(targetviews, primitives, devicetype): # Phase 1: Profiling and Bounds Mglobal = 0 Iglobal = 0 tileprimitives = {} # Maps (viewid, tileid) to list of primitive indices for view in targetviews: # Render forward pass (no gradients) to record metrics renderresult = renderforward(view, primitives) Mview = renderresult.maxprimitivespertile Iview = renderresult.maxprimitivesperpixel tileintersections = renderresult.tileprimitivecounts if Mview > Mglobal: Mglobal = Mview if Iview > Iglobal: Iglobal = Iview for tileid, primindices in tileintersections.items(): tileprimitives[(view.id, tileid)] = primindices # Phase 2: Sequential Parameter Search tilecandidates = [(8, 8), (16, 16)] if devicetype == 'GPU' else [(16, 16), (32, 32)] Ucandidates = [1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32] Lcandidates = [2, 4, 6, 8] Dcandidates = [1, 2, 4, 8] # Phase 1: Tile Size besttile = max(tilecandidates, key=lambda t: benchmarktilesize(t, Mglobal, Iglobal, tileprimitives)) # Phase 2: Unroll Factor U (Initial) bestU = max(Ucandidates, key=lambda u: benchmarkunroll(u, L=4, D=4, tilesize=besttile, M=Mglobal, I=Iglobal)) # Phase 3: Number of Bins L def scoreL(Lval): return benchmarkbins(Lval, bestU, 4, besttile, Mglobal, Iglobal) scoresL = {L: scoreL(L) for L in Lcandidates} maxscore = max(scoresL.values()) tiedL = [L for L, s in scoresL.items() if abs(s - maxscore) / maxscore < 0.02] if len(tiedL) > 1: lowL, highL = min(tiedL), max(tiedL) # Re-benchmark lowest and highest tied candidates with additional runs fpslow = benchmarkbins(lowL, bestU, 4, besttile, Mglobal, Iglobal, runs=10) fpshigh = benchmarkbins(highL, bestU, 4, besttile, Mglobal, Iglobal, runs=10) bestL = lowL if fpslow > fpshigh else highL else: bestL = tiedL[0] # Phase 4: Re-search Unroll Factor U at chosen L bestU = max(Ucandidates, key=lambda u: benchmarkunroll(u, L=bestL, D=4, tilesize=besttile, M=Mglobal, I=Iglobal)) # Phase 5: Batch Divisor D # Prefer D=4 within noise tolerance def scoreD(Dval): return benchmarkbatchdivisor(Dval, bestU, bestL, besttile, Mglobal, Iglobal) scoresD = {D: scoreD(D) for D in Dcandidates} maxscoreD = max(scoresD.values()) tiedD = [D for D, s in scoresD.items() if abs(s - maxscoreD) / maxscoreD < 0.02] bestD = 4 if 4 in tiedD else tiedD[0] # Data-Aware Assignment # Compute assignment of tiles to bins based on worst-case cumulative counts across all views binassignment = computebinassignment(tileprimitives, bestL, Mglobal) return { 'tilesize': besttile, 'U': bestU, 'L': bestL, 'D': bestD, 'binassignment': binassignment, 'M': Mglobal, 'I': Iglobal } def benchmarktilesize(tilesize, M, I, tileprimitives): # Sources do not provide the benchmarking implementation; this would invoke the renderer with the given parameters and measure FPS. pass def benchmarkunroll(U, L, D, tilesize, M, I, runs=1): # Sources do not provide the benchmarking implementation; this would invoke the renderer with the given parameters and measure FPS. pass def benchmarkbins(L, U, D, tilesize, M, I, runs=1): # Sources do not provide the benchmarking implementation; this would invoke the renderer with the given parameters and measure FPS. pass def benchmarkbatchdivisor(D, U, L, tilesize, M, I, runs=1): # Sources do not provide the benchmarking implementation; this would invoke the renderer with the given parameters and measure FPS. pass def computebinassignment(tileprimitives, L, M): # Sources do not provide the implementation; compute assignment based on worst-case cumulative counts across all views. pass def renderforward(view, primitives): # Standard forward rendering pass without gradients. pass This method is a multi-objective optimization process that automatically selects hyperparameters for HKTex UV-texture and multi-view image fitting, minimizing model storage size and mean squared errors across rendered views. It distinguishes itself from manual tuning by using a Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) to navigate a search space of over 30 parameters, balancing the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and memory footprint. Time Complexity: The profiling phase requires one forward render per target view. The search phase involves a small constant number of benchmarks (2 tile sizes, 6 U candidates, 4 L candidates, 6 U candidates again, up to 4 D candidates). The total time is a few minutes, which is negligible relative to training time. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of tile-primitive counts during profiling. The bin assignment is computed from worst-case cumulative counts. Performance: On an L40 GPU with the 360 dataset, XPR-4K achieves SSIM 0.87 and LPIPS 0.182. XPR-8K achieves SSIM 0.87 and LPIPS 0.182. LinPrim achieves SSIM 0.86 and LPIPS 0.190 for 360, and SSIM 0.83 and LPIPS 0.195 for 360 with XPR-8K. Scaling: Increasing the number of bins initially increases FPS by reducing redundant computation. Beyond an optimal count, FPS drops due to reduced SM occupancy and increased launch overheads. Strengths: Automatic configuration eliminates manual tuning. Data-aware bin assignment optimizes for specific scene geometry. Limitations: Requires profiling all target views. Performance is sensitive to the noise tolerance in benchmarking. Hardware-Aware Hyperparameter Tuning was introduced as part of the XPR (Extensible Cross-Platform Point-Based Differentiable Renderer) framework. It addresses the need for efficient rendering on diverse hardware (GPU, TPU) by automatically selecting parameters that balance instruction-level parallelism, register pressure, and early termination granularity. name: Bayesian Hyperparameter Optimization for Volume Rendering
head: Bayesian Hyperparameter Tuning for HKTex, HKTex Hyperparameter Optimization, Optuna-based Hyperparameter Tuning
body: This method is a multi-objective optimization process that automatically selects hyperparameters for HKTex UV-texture and multi-view image fitting, minimizing model storage size and mean squared errors across rendered views. It distinguishes itself from manual tuning by using a Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) to navigate a search space of over 30 parameters, balancing the trade-off between reconstruction fidelity and memory footprint. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 5 tuning meshes from Objaverse (excluded from evaluation sets); ground-truth UV textures or multi-view images; camera poses for multi-view scenarios. Outputs: Optimal hyperparameters for HKTex fitting, including learning rates, density controller thresholds, initialization strategies, loss functions, and schedulers. Data Structures: The search space consists of: Continuous Variables: Sampled from log-uniform distributions (e.g., learning rates, density controller thresholds). Discrete Categorical Variables: Selections for initialization strategies, loss functions (MSE, Smooth L1, L1), and learning rate schedulers (Step, Cosine, none). Steps: 1. Formulate Multi-Objective Problem: Define the optimization goal as minimizing two objectives: final model storage size and mean squared errors (MSE) across 3 rendered views of the tuning meshes. 2. Initialize TPE Optimizer: Configure Optuna with the Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator. 3. Sample Hyperparameters: Draw a candidate set of hyperparameters from the defined search space (continuous log-uniform and discrete categorical). 4. Execute Fitting Task: Run the HKTex fitting process (UV-texture or multi-view) using the sampled hyperparameters. For UV-texture fitting, use importance sampling. For multi-view fitting, sample V camera views and select a random subset of rays for uniform coverage. 5. Evaluate Objectives: Calculate the final model storage size and the MSE across the 3 rendered views. 6. Update Model: Feed the results back to the TPE optimizer to update the probability models for the next iteration. 7. Select Best Hyperparameters: After the tuning sweep, select the hyperparameters that best balance the multi-objective criteria. Formulas: For UV-texture optimization, the loss function is defined as: L = \|C(p) - C{GT}(p)\|2^2 where C(p) is the HKTex color evaluated at point p, and C{GT}(p) is the ground-truth UV texture color at the same location. Parameters: Optimizer: Optuna with Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator. Search Space Size: Over 30 parameters. Distributions: Log-uniform for continuous variables. Loss Functions: MSE, Smooth L1, L1. Schedulers: Step, Cosine, none. Rendering/Tracing: Mitsuba3 with Dr.Jit, path-replay backpropagation (PRB) integrator, ray depth 3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The eigenproperties precomputation (ALBO eigenproperties \Phi^\ddagger{i,j} and \Lambda^\ddagger{i,j}) averages ~370MB per mesh but is deterministically computed and cached once per mesh, so it does not need to be stored as a hyperparameter. Separate tuning sweeps are executed for UV-texture fitting and multi-view image fitting due to differing optimization dynamics. This variant focuses on optimizing HKTex kernels when a ground-truth UV texture is available. It differs from multi-view fitting by sampling points directly on mesh faces and querying ground-truth UV colors, utilizing importance sampling during fitting. It is chosen when high-fidelity texture reconstruction from known UV maps is required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The precomputation of eigenproperties averages ~370MB per mesh, but this is a one-time cost per mesh and not part of the runtime optimization overhead. Measured Performance: The method was tested on 5 meshes from Objaverse. Strengths: Automates the selection of over 30 hyperparameters, balancing storage and accuracy. Limitations: Requires a separate tuning sweep for each task type (UV vs. multi-view). When to use: When manual hyperparameter tuning is infeasible or suboptimal for HKTex fitting. When not to use: When computational resources for the tuning sweep are unavailable. This method was introduced in the context of Heat Kernel Textures (HKTex) for geodesic Gaussians. It was developed to address the complexity of tuning HKTex parameters, which include kernel locations, densities, and texture fitting parameters. The approach uses Optuna and TPE to handle the multi-objective nature of the problem, minimizing both storage and error. name: HKTex UV-texture Optimization
head: Optimise existing UV-textures, UV-texture Optimization
body: HKTex UV-texture Optimization is a method for compressing existing ground-truth UV textures by fitting Heat Kernel Texture (HKTex) parameters to minimize photometric error. It solves the problem of reducing storage footprint for 3D mesh textures while maintaining high perceptual quality. It differs from neural baselines (MLPs, InstantNGP) and explicit 2D baselines (downsampled images, ImageGS) by using intrinsic geometric kernels, achieving superior structural preservation (SSIM, MS-SSIM) and lower storage costs for high-vertex-count meshes where UV-coordinate overhead dominates other methods. Inputs: A mesh M with a ground-truth albedo UV texture. The mesh geometry (vertices, faces) to compute geodesic distances and heat kernels. Hyperparameters for the HKTex model (kernel locations, pruning/densification thresholds) obtained via Bayesian optimization. Outputs: Optimized HKTex parameters (kernel locations and values) that approximate the ground-truth UV texture. Data Structures: HKTex Model: Defined by a set of kernels on the mesh surface. Each kernel is characterized by its location and associated heat kernel weights. Ground-Truth Texture: A 2D image mapped to the mesh via UV coordinates. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize HKTex parameters. Kernel locations are optimized using a geodesic Riemannian-SGD algorithm on the GPU. 2. Sampling: At each optimization step, uniformly sample a dense set of points p directly on the faces of mesh M. 3. Evaluation: Evaluate the HKTex color C(p) at these sampled points using the current HKTex model. 4. Ground-Truth Query: Query the ground-truth UV texture color C{GT}(p) at the same spatial locations p. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the photometric loss: L = \|C(p) - C{GT}(p)\|2^2 where C(p) is the HKTex color and C{GT}(p) is the ground-truth color. 6. Optimization: Update HKTex parameters to minimize L. Use an Adam optimizer with a step-function learning rate scheduler. For kernel locations, use geodesic Riemannian-SGD. Apply importance sampling during fitting. 7. Hyperparameter Tuning: Use Optuna with a Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) to tune hyperparameters (e.g., pruning/densification thresholds) on a validation set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizehktexuvtexture(mesh, gtuvtexture, hyperparameters): """ Optimizes HKTex parameters to fit a ground-truth UV texture. Args: mesh: The 3D mesh object with geometry and UV map. gtuvtexture: The ground-truth albedo UV texture image. hyperparameters: Dict containing HKTex model settings and optimizer configs. Returns: optimizedhktexparams: The optimized HKTex parameters. """ # Initialize HKTex model with hyperparameters hktexmodel = initializehktex(mesh, hyperparameters) # Setup optimizer # Note: Geodesic Riemannian-SGD is used for kernel locations # Adam is used for other parameters optimizer = setupoptimizer(hktexmodel, hyperparameters['optimizerconfig']) # Bayesian Hyperparameter Tuning (Outer Loop) # Uses Optuna with TPE bestparams = bayesiantuning( objectivefunction=lambda params: evaluateloss(mesh, gtuvtexture, params), searchspace=hyperparameters['searchspace'], ntrials=hyperparameters['ntrials']) # Final Optimization with best hyperparameters hktexmodel.setparameters(bestparams) for step in range(hyperparameters['numsteps']): # 1. Sample points on mesh faces points = uniformsamplepointsonmeshfaces(mesh, hyperparameters['numsamples']) # 2. Evaluate HKTex color at points cp = evaluatehktexcolor(hktexmodel, points) # 3. Query ground-truth color at same locations # Requires mapping 3D points to UV coordinates uvcoords = projectpointstouv(mesh, points) cgtp = sampleuvtexture(gtuvtexture, uvcoords) # 4. Compute Loss loss = meansquarederror(cp, cgtp) # 5. Backpropagate and Update # Gradients backpropagated from loss to HKTex parameters optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() # Apply importance sampling if configured if hyperparameters['useimportancesampling']: applyimportancesampling(points, loss, hktexmodel) return hktexmodel.getparameters() Parameters: Optimizer: Adam with step-function learning rate scheduler. Kernel Location Optimizer: Geodesic Riemannian-SGD on GPU. Bayesian Optimization: Optuna with Tree-Structured Parzen Estimator (TPE). Importance Sampling: Used during fitting. Rendering/Differentiation: Mitsuba3 with Dr.Jit, path-replay backpropagation (PRB) integrator, ray depth 3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Vertex Count: For meshes with high vertex counts, the fixed memory overhead of per-vertex UV coordinates can dominate the storage budget, making it difficult for explicit 2D baselines to match HKTex's efficiency. Storage Budget Matching: Neural baselines require grid search over network width, depth, and hash-grid size to exactly match HKTex's storage cost for fair comparison. Degenerate Input: The method assumes a valid UV map is available. If the UV map is missing, this specific optimization path is not applicable (though multi-view optimization exists). This section details the comparative baselines used to evaluate HKTex UV-texture optimization. Neural Baselines: MLP with Fourier Positional Encoding: Standard MLP using traditional Fourier encoding. InstantNGP Adaptation: Uses hash-grid encoding. Intrinsic Neural Fields: Barycentrically interpolates eigenvectors of the Laplace-Beltrami Operator (LBO). Note: Grid search is performed over network width, depth, and hash-grid size to exactly match HKTex's storage cost. Explicit 2D Baselines: Downsampled Ground-Truth Images: Lower resolution versions of the original UV texture. ImageGS: A 2D Gaussian Splatting approach. Note: Both rely on UV-mapping. For high-vertex-count meshes, the UV-coordinate overhead dominates, leading to catastrophic performance penalties if storage is constrained. Vertex Color Baselines: GT VTex: Vertex colors sampled directly from GT UV-textures at native mesh resolution. HR GT VTex: Iteratively subdivided mesh to match HKTex's storage budget. Performance: HKTex achieves the lowest storage footprint after GT VTex, with competitive PSNR, best SSIM/MS-SSIM/MSE, and second-best LPIPS. Neural baselines and HR GT VTex require significantly larger storage for comparable accuracy. Storage Efficiency: HKTex achieves significantly reduced storage footprint compared to neural and explicit 2D baselines while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality. It yields the best SSIM, MS-SSIM, and MSE among compressed methods. Computational Cost: Training involves differentiable ray tracing via Mitsuba3/Dr.Jit, which is computationally intensive. However, inference is fast as the KNN database and heat kernels are pre-computed once. Scalability: Performance degrades for explicit 2D baselines on high-vertex-count meshes due to UV-coordinate overhead, whereas HKTex scales better by leveraging intrinsic geometry. Strengths: High perceptual quality (LPIPS), structural preservation (SSIM), and low storage cost. Effective for meshes with available UV maps. Limitations: Requires a ground-truth UV texture. Computationally expensive training due to differentiable rendering and geodesic optimization. Not applicable if UV map is missing (use multi-view optimization instead). Origin: Heat Kernel Textures (HKTex) was introduced by Foti et al. in "Heat Kernel Textures the Geodesic Gaussians That Do Not Splat" (2025). Development: The method builds on heat kernel theory to represent textures intrinsically on meshes. The UV-texture optimization variant was developed to compress existing UV textures by fitting HKTex parameters to ground-truth albedo. Usage: Used in 3D computer graphics for texture compression and representation, particularly on datasets like Objaverse. name: Grid Resolution Cost Model
head: Cost-based grid resolution model, ISP07 cost model, Ize et al. cost model
body: The Grid Resolution Cost Model determines the optimal subdivision factor m for a uniform grid in volume rendering or ray tracing by minimizing the average ray traversal time. Unlike Ray Marching Optimization which optimizes step size or Image-based Rendering Cost Model which optimizes pixel sampling, this model optimizes the spatial data structure's granularity based on scene complexity. It distinguishes itself from Uniform Subsampling Cost Model by evaluating the cost of the grid resolution m itself, weighted by primitive occupancy, rather than subsampling the final image. Inputs: N: Total number of primitives in the scene. T{setup}: Time to perform the initial intersection with the main voxel bounding box and setup traversal. T{step}: Time spent to advance from a cell to its neighbor (without checking intersection). T{inter}: Time required to check a ray-primitive intersection. Scene model type: Point-based or Line-based. Outputs: M: The optimal subdivision factor m that minimizes average traversal time T. Data Structures: The model assumes a flat uniform grid. The grid is defined by a single integer parameter m, representing the number of divisions along each axis. The total number of cells is m^3. Nm: The number of intersections between primitives and cells for a given subdivision factor m. Formulas: The average traversal time T is defined as: T = T{setup} + m T{step} + \mu T{inter} where \mu is the average number of primitives contained (or partially contained) in the m cells reached by a ray. \mu = \frac{Nm}{m^2} The value of Nm depends on the scene model: 1. Point-based model: Each primitive is contained in exactly one cell. Thus, Nm = N. Consequently, \mu = \frac{N}{m^2}. 2. Line-based model: Each primitive is partially contained in approximately m cells. Thus, Nm = N \cdot m. Consequently, \mu = \frac{N}{m}. To find the optimal M, we minimize T with respect to m. The source provides explicit closed-form expressions for M, which differ from a direct calculus minimization of the stated \mu expressions: For point-based models: M = \sqrt{\frac{2 T{inter}}{T{step}}} \cdot N = O(N). For line-based models: M = \sqrt[3]{\left(\frac{2 T{inter}}{T{step}}\right)^2} \cdot N^{1.5} = O(N^{1.5}). Parameters: Typical example values provided in: T{setup} \approx 1.0 T{step} \approx 0.1 T{inter} \approx 0.5 Using these values, the bounded interval for searching m is: m \in \left( (10N)^{1/3}, 5N^{1/2} \right) Algorithm: 1. Determine the scene model type (Point-based or Line-based). 2. Estimate or measure T{setup}, T{step}, and T{inter}. 3. Obtain the total number of primitives N. 4. Calculate the theoretical optimal M using the appropriate formula for the scene model. 5. Alternatively, sample the cost function T(m) within the bounded interval ((10N)^{1/3}, 5N^{1/2}) to find the m that minimizes T. This approach yields a linear overall building time. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Scene Model Knowledge: The use of theoretical results requires knowledge of the scene model type. Commonly used models behave between the two opposite ones (point and line), so the result is an approximation. Mailboxing: If mailboxing is used, Nm must be redefined as the average number of distinct primitives contained in the cells, which changes the occupancy statistics. Hierarchical Recursion: The cost model can also determine termination criteria for hierarchical grid building. Recursion introduces a benefit if T{setup} + m T{step} + \mu T{inter} > N T{inter}. However, deep recursion requires good indexing strategies (e.g., hash tables). The Guess and Check Building Algorithm determines the optimal grid resolution parameter m by sampling the cost function over a theoretically bounded interval to minimize average traversal time. It distinguishes itself from exhaustive search methods by guaranteeing linear overall building time while leveraging theoretical bounds to restrict the search space. A cost model that suggests a way to build hierarchical grids and determine a termination criteria to stop recursion. Recursion is beneficial if the cost of the current grid traversal (T{setup} + m T{step} + \mu T{inter}) exceeds the cost of a naive traversal without the grid (N T{inter}). Time Complexity: The building time for determining m via sampling is linear overall. The optimal M scales as O(N) for point-based and O(N^{1.5}) for line-based models. Memory Complexity: The grid size scales with m^3. For point-based models, m \propto N, so memory \propto N^3. For line-based models, m \propto N^{1.5}, so memory \propto N^{4.5}. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides a theoretical baseline for grid resolution; adaptable to hierarchical structures. Limitations: Requires knowledge of the scene model (point vs line); assumes uniform distribution; does not account for spatial coherence or empty space skipping directly (unlike Ray Marching Optimization); memory usage grows rapidly with N. When to use: When a uniform grid is required and scene statistics (N, model type) are known or easily estimable. When not to use: For highly non-uniform scenes where adaptive or hierarchical grids are needed, or when memory is constrained. The cost model was introduced by Ize et al. in [ISP07]. It builds on earlier work, with a first complete cost model for grids introduced in [CW88]. The model is part of the broader effort to optimize grid-based ray tracing, contrasting with SAH (Surface Area Heuristic) used in kd-trees, which evaluates split planes rather than grid resolution. name: Guess and Check Building Algorithm
head: Sampling-based building algorithm
body: The Guess and Check Building Algorithm determines the optimal grid subdivision factor m by sampling a cost function over a theoretically bounded interval to minimize average traversal time. It distinguishes itself from exhaustive search methods by guaranteeing linear overall building time while leveraging theoretical bounds to restrict the search space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The number of geometric primitives N in the scene. Output: The optimal subdivision factor m that minimizes the cost function T. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on scalar values for m and the cost function T. Steps: 1. Determine the Search Interval: Calculate the lower and upper bounds for m using theoretical results derived from the cost model assumptions. For typical constants where T{setup} \approx 1.0, T{step} \approx 0.1, and T{inter} \approx 0.5, the interval is m \in ((10N)^{1/3}, 5N^{2/3}). 2. Sample the Cost Function: Select a set of discrete values for m within the bounded interval. For each candidate m, evaluate the cost function T. The cost function T depends on the number of occupied cells Nm, which can be evaluated in linear time for a given m by performing primitive counting during the build. 3. Select the Minimum: Compare the evaluated cost values and select the m that yields the minimum cost T. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def guessandcheckbuild(N, Tsetup, Tstep, Tinter): # Step 1: Determine bounds based on theoretical analysis lowerbound = (10 N) (1/3) upperbound = 5 (N (2/3)) bestm = None mincost = float('inf') # Step 2: Sample the cost function # A naive approach samples a constant number of points in the interval numsamples = 10 # Example constant, not specified in sources stepsize = (upperbound - lowerbound) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples + 1): mcandidate = lowerbound + i stepsize if mcandidate < lowerbound or mcandidate > upperbound: continue # Evaluate cost for this m # Nm can be computed in linear time for this m via primitive counting # The exact cost formula for T is not provided in the sources Nm = 0 # The sources do not give the primitive counting implementation cost = 0.0 # The sources do not give the exact cost function formula if cost < mincost: mincost = cost bestm = mcandidate return bestm Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The theoretical bounds assume specific values for T{setup}, T{step}, and T{inter}. The algorithm assumes that Nm can be evaluated in linear time for any given m. Time Complexity: Linear overall building time O(N). This is achieved because a naive approach samples the interval in a constant number of points, and evaluating the cost for each sample (including primitive counting for Nm) takes linear time. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Guarantees linear build time while finding a near-optimal resolution. Limitations: Relies on theoretical bounds derived from fixed typical constants. The algorithm is described in the context of grid-based ray tracing as a method to optimize grid resolution. It is compared to similar sampling-based approaches used in SAH kd-tree building, such as the conservatively sub-sampling method by Popov et al. [PGSS06] and the adaptive error-bounded heuristic by Hunt et al. [HMS06]. The work is attributed to Biagio Cosenza in "A Survey on Exploiting Grids for Ray Tracing". name: Image-based Rendering Cost Model
head: Model 1, Model 2, Parallel Visualization Server Cost Model
body: The Image-based Rendering Cost Model estimates the total time cost for remote visualization where a parallel server computes isosurfaces and transmits either six depth images per isosurface (Model 1) or mesh geometry (Model 2) to a local workstation for reconstruction. It differs from Grid Resolution Cost Model and Uniform Subsampling Cost Model by assuming the full original dataset is processed on the server, focusing instead on the trade-off between parallel computation time and network transmission overhead. Inputs: Dataset size (N), number of isosurfaces (I), number of processors (P), network bandwidth (R), network latency (L), image resolution (X), and computational cost per element (C{Im}). Outputs: Total cost in seconds (MI for Model 1, MV for Model 2). Not given in the sources. 1. Calculate the parallel computation time: T{comp} = (N \cdot C{Im} \cdot I) / P. 2. Calculate the transmission time based on the chosen model: Model 1: T{trans} = (48 \cdot 6 \cdot X \cdot I) / (10^6 \cdot R). Model 2: T{trans} = (32 \cdot 6 \cdot N^{2/3} \cdot I) / (10^6 \cdot R). 3. Calculate the network latency: T{lat} = 2 \cdot L \cdot I. 4. Sum the components to obtain the total cost: T{total} = T{comp} + T{trans} + T{lat}. The total cost is defined by two distinct equations depending on the transmission strategy. Model 1: Image-based Rendering (Depth Images) This model assumes the server computes isosurfaces and transmits six depth images per isosurface for reconstruction on the client. Each pixel in the depth image contains 48 bits: 24 bits for color, 16 bits for depth, and 8 bits for surface orientation information. MI = \frac{N C{Im} I}{P} + \frac{48 \cdot 6 \cdot X \cdot I}{10^6 R} + 2 L I Where: \frac{N C{Im} I}{P}: Time required to compute isosurfaces in parallel on the original data set. \frac{48 \cdot 6 \cdot X \cdot I}{10^6 R}: Transmission time for depth images. The numerator calculates total bits (48 bits/pixel \times 6 images/isosurface \times X pixels/image \times I isosurfaces). The denominator 10^6 converts bits to Megabits to match bandwidth R. 2 L I: Network latency for new isosurface requests. The factor of 2 accounts for round-trip latency. Model 2: Parallel Visualization Servers (Mesh Geometry) This model assumes the server computes isosurfaces and transmits the resulting mesh geometry (vertices and connectivity) to the local workstation. It assumes each isosurface contains approximately N^{2/3} triangles, and consequently N^{2/3} vertices. Each triangle requires connectivity information, and each vertex requires three spatial coordinates (32-bit values). The source text writes the triangle count as N^2/3 in the formula, but explicitly describes it as N^{2/3} in the accompanying prose. MV = \frac{N C{Im} I}{P} + \frac{32 \cdot 6 \cdot N^{2/3} \cdot I}{10^6 R} + 2 L I Where: \frac{N C{Im} I}{P}: Time required to compute isosurfaces in parallel (identical to Model 1). \frac{32 \cdot 6 \cdot N^{2/3} \cdot I}{10^6 R}: Transmission time for mesh geometry. The factor 32 represents bits per value, 6 is a constant multiplier from the source derivation, and N^{2/3} represents the number of triangles per isosurface. 2 L I: Network latency for new isosurface requests. N: Number of elements in the original computational mesh. I: Number of isosurfaces to be computed and rendered. P: Number of remote processors available for parallel computation. R: Network bandwidth in Megabits per second (Mbs). L: Network latency in seconds. X: Size of the images in pixels (total pixel count per image). C{Im}: Multiresolution Isosurface Cost per Element. Multiple Isosurfaces per Request: The model assumes a new set of reference depth images is required for each new isosurface. However, if multiple isosurfaces are generated during a single request, the number of depth images does not necessarily increase, which may reduce the actual cost compared to the model's prediction. Mesh Geometry Scaling: Model 2 assumes the number of vertices and elements in a triangular mesh are approximately equal and that the number of triangles scales as N^{2/3}. Deviations from this geometric scaling will affect accuracy. Bandwidth Units: Bandwidth R must be specified in Megabits per second (Mbs) to match the 10^6 conversion factor in the transmission term. Local Workstation Overhead: The models do not address the costs associated with loading and processing the resulting data sets on the local graphics workstation. When Not to Use: For local visualization where network costs are zero. For methods involving subsampling or multiresolution data transfer (see Uniform Subsampling Cost Model). Time Complexity: The computation term scales linearly with N and I, and inversely with P (O(N \cdot I / P)). The transmission term scales linearly with I and either X (Model 1) or N^{2/3} (Model 2). The latency term scales linearly with I (O(I)). Memory Complexity: The model does not explicitly account for local memory usage on the workstation, as it excludes the costs of loading and processing data on the local graphics hardware. Strengths: Provides a clear analytical breakdown of computation versus communication costs for remote visualization. Useful for determining the optimal strategy (image-based vs. mesh-based) based on network conditions (R, L) and dataset size (N). Limitations: Assumes ideal parallel scaling (1/P) which may not hold for all algorithms or hardware. Assumes a specific bit-depth for depth images (48 bits) which may vary with different rendering techniques. Does not account for the computational cost of reconstructing the 3D scene from depth images or meshes on the local workstation. When to Use: When designing or analyzing remote visualization systems where network bandwidth and latency are significant constraints, and the choice is between transmitting rendered images or raw geometry. The Image-based Rendering Cost Model was introduced to compare remote visualization strategies for the interactive exploration of large data sets. It forms part of a series of analytical models (Models 1, 2, and 3) designed to evaluate the performance of parallel visualization servers against image-based rendering and subsampling techniques. The model was developed to quantify the trade-offs between parallel computation, network transmission, and latency in distributed visualization architectures. name: Uniform Subsampling Cost Model
head: Model 3
body: The Uniform Subsampling Cost Model estimates the total latency for remote visualization tasks where the original volumetric data is subsampled onto a uniform grid, and the reduced grid data is transmitted to a local workstation for isosurface generation. It differs from its siblings by assuming a fixed grid topology with no additional spatial or coordinate overhead beyond the grid parameters, unlike the Multiresolution Subsampling Cost Model which accounts for variable vertex counts and connectivity in octree structures. It builds on Ray-grid traversal by optimizing the parameters under which the rendering strategy runs, rather than altering the traversal logic itself. The model calculates the total cost (MU) as the sum of four distinct terms: computational cost for data reduction, computational cost for isosurface generation, transmission cost for the subsampled data, and network latency cost. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: N: Total number of elements in the original dataset. I: Number of isosurfaces to be computed and rendered. P: Number of processors available for parallel computation. R: Network bandwidth in Megabits per second (Mbs). L: Network latency in seconds (s). C{Ru}: Uniform grid subsampling cost (system-dependent computational constant). C{Iu}: Uniform grid isosurface cost per element (system-dependent computational constant). NR: Number of subsampled elements in the reduced uniform grid. Outputs: MU: Total cost (latency) for a single request. Data Structures The model assumes a uniform grid structure. The data transmitted consists of: 1. Grid Parameters: Origin, grid spacing, and problem size in each of the three dimensions. 2. Scalar Data: Scalar value and error for each of the NR elements. 3. Bit Depth: All scalar and integer values are assumed to be 32-bit. Formula The total cost MU is defined as: MU = \frac{C{Ru}}{P} + NR C{Iu} I + \frac{32 \cdot (9 + 2NR)}{10^6 R} + 2 L Symbol Definitions C{Ru}: Uniform Grid Subsampling Cost. Represents the computational effort to reduce the original data to the subsampled grid. P: Number of processors. The subsampling cost scales linearly with the number of processors. NR: Number of subsampled elements. This parameter defines the size of the reduced dataset. C{Iu}: Uniform Grid Isosurface Cost/Element. The computational cost to generate isosurface geometry for one element. I: Number of isosurfaces. The model assumes isosurfaces are computed in parallel. R: Network bandwidth in Mbs. Used to calculate transmission time. L: Network latency in seconds. Represents the round-trip time overhead. 32: Bit width of each value (scalar or integer). 9: Number of grid parameter values (origin x,y,z; spacing x,y,z; size x,y,z). 2: Number of values per element (scalar data and error). 10^6: Conversion factor from bits to Megabits. Pseudocode The following Python-like pseudocode implements the calculation of the total cost MU. It assumes all inputs are provided as floating-point or integer values. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateuniformsubsamplingcost( CRu, # Uniform grid subsampling cost P, # Number of processors NR, # Number of subsampled elements CIu, # Uniform grid isosurface cost per element I, # Number of isosurfaces R, # Network bandwidth in Mbs L # Network latency in seconds): # Term 1: Computational cost for data reduction on the reduced uniform grid termreduction = CRu / P # Term 2: Computational cost for isosurface generation on the reduced uniform grid termgeneration = NR CIu I # Term 3: Transmission cost for a single request # Data transmitted: 9 grid parameters + 2 values (scalar + error) per element # All values are 32-bit integers/floats totalbits = 32 (9 + 2 NR) transmissioncost = totalbits / (106 R) # Term 4: Latency cost for a single request latencycost = 2 L # Total cost MU = termreduction + termgeneration + transmissioncost + latencycost return MU Edge Cases and Pitfalls No Additional Spatial Information: The model explicitly states that no additional spatial or coordinate information is required beyond the grid structure parameters (origin, spacing, size). This simplifies the transmission cost compared to multiresolution methods. Parallel Assumption: The model assumes that isosurface computation is performed in parallel across processors. If the hardware does not support this parallelism, the computational cost terms may not scale as expected. Fixed Bit Depth: The model assumes a fixed 32-bit precision for all transmitted values. Using different precisions would alter the transmission cost term. Uniform Grid Topology: The model is only valid for uniform grids. It does not account for the variable connectivity and vertex sharing found in non-uniform or octree-based representations. Estimates latency for octree-based data where variable vertex counts and connectivity overhead are transmitted. Choose this when the data structure is non-uniform and spatial coordinates/connections must be sent. Optimizes the ray marching step size and traversal logic. Choose this to reduce the number of samples per ray. Optimizes for specific GPU/CPU architectures. Choose this when targeting specific hardware features like SIMD or tensor cores. Optimizes the grid resolution itself. Choose this when the grid resolution is a variable to be tuned for performance. Estimates cost for image-based rendering techniques using depth images. Choose this when rendering isosurfaces via depth images rather than geometry. Time Complexity: The computational terms (C{Ru}/P and NR C{Iu} I) do not depend on the original dataset size N, but are linear with respect to the subsampled size NR and the number of isosurfaces I. The transmission term is linear with respect to NR. Memory Complexity: The model does not explicitly define memory complexity, but the transmission size is proportional to NR. Strengths: Simple to implement and calculate. Assumes minimal communication overhead for data reduction due to uniform grid partitioning. No additional spatial or coordinate information is required. Limitations: Does not account for the costs associated with loading and processing the resulting data sets on the local graphics workstation. Assumes ideal parallelism for isosurface generation. Not suitable for non-uniform data structures where connectivity overhead is significant. When to use: When the data can be effectively subsampled onto a uniform grid and the primary bottleneck is network transmission and basic computational costs for isosurface generation. When not to use: When the data structure is non-uniform (e.g., octree) and requires transmission of connectivity information, or when the local workstation's processing capabilities are a significant bottleneck not captured by the model. The Uniform Subsampling Cost Model, also known as Model 3, was introduced in the context of comparing remote visualization strategies for interactive exploration of large data sets. It is part of a family of cost models that include Image-based Rendering (Model 1), Multiresolution Subsampling (Model 4), and others. The model was developed to provide a quantitative comparison of different remote visualization techniques, specifically focusing on the trade-offs between computational cost, transmission cost, and latency. name: Multiresolution Subsampling Cost Model
head: Model 4
body: The Multiresolution Subsampling Cost Model estimates the total latency for remote visualization using an octree-based data representation, where a reduced mesh is transmitted to a local workstation for isosurface generation. It differs from the Uniform Subsampling Cost Model by accounting for the variable vertex counts and connectivity overhead inherent in nonuniform octree structures, rather than assuming a fixed grid topology. Inputs and Outputs Input: Octree leaf node count (NR), system computational costs (C{Rm}, C{Im}), network parameters (P, R, L), and rendering parameters (I). Output: Total cost MM in seconds. Data Structures The model assumes the transmission of a reduced mesh containing: 1. Spatial coordinates: 32-bit floats. 2. Connectivity, scalar, and error data: 32-bit values. Formulas The total cost MM is the sum of four terms: MM = \frac{C{Rm}}{P} + NR C{Im} I + \frac{32 \cdot (22NR)}{10^6 R} + 2 L Symbol Definitions MM: Total cost (seconds). C{Rm}: Multiresolution subsampling cost (computational cost for data reduction on the nonuniform grid). P: Number of processors. NR: Number of subsampled elements (octant leaves). C{Im}: Multiresolution isosurface cost per element (computational cost for isosurface generation on the reduced nonuniform grid). I: Number of isosurfaces. R: Network bandwidth in Megabits per second (Mbs). L: Network latency in seconds. Step-by-Step Calculation 1. Compute Reduction Cost: Calculate the time to subsample the data on the server side: \frac{C{Rm}}{P}. 2. Compute Isosurface Cost: Calculate the time to generate isosurfaces on the client side: NR \cdot C{Im} \cdot I. 3. Compute Transmission Cost: Estimate the number of vertices V. The model uses an average case assumption: V = 4 NR. Calculate bits for spatial coordinates: 3 \text{ coords} \times 4 \text{ vertices/leaf} \times NR \times 32 \text{ bits} = 384 NR bits. Calculate bits for connectivity/scalar/error data: 10 \text{ values} \times NR \times 32 \text{ bits} = 320 NR bits. Total bits: 384 NR + 320 NR = 704 NR bits, which simplifies to 32 \cdot 22 \cdot NR bits. Convert to Megabits: \frac{32 \cdot 22 \cdot NR}{10^6}. Divide by bandwidth R: \frac{32 \cdot 22 \cdot NR}{10^6 R}. 4. Compute Latency Cost: Add the round-trip latency: 2 L. 5. Sum: Add all four terms to get MM. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Vertex Count Assumption: The number of vertices in an octree mesh is not fixed. The upper bound is 8 NR (no shared vertices between octants), and the lower bound is NR (maximally shared/uniform mesh). The model explicitly assumes an average case of 4 NR. Using a different vertex count requires adjusting the transmission term coefficient. Nonuniform Grid Costs: Ensure C{Rm} and C{Im} are used, not the uniform grid equivalents (C{Ru}, C{Iu}), as the data structure is an octree. Complexity: The computational terms are linear with respect to NR and I. The transmission term is linear with respect to NR and inversely proportional to R. Strengths: Accurately models the overhead of transmitting mesh topology and geometry for sparse or complex datasets where uniform subsampling is inefficient. Limitations: Relies on the heuristic average of 4 NR vertices. Performance may deviate if the octree structure is significantly more or less shared than the average case. When to use: When visualizing large datasets with significant empty space or complex internal structures using octree-based compression, and the client has sufficient power to generate isosurfaces from the reduced mesh. The model was introduced in the paper "Comparison of remote visualization strategies for interactive exploration of large data sets". It is part of a series of four models comparing remote visualization strategies, specifically designed for systems using octree data representations. The work analyzes performance regimes for various values of N, P, I, and R to determine breakeven points between uniform and multiresolution subsampling techniques. name: Workload-Centric Analysis Framework
head: 5-count model, N-resident to N-blend pipeline
body: The Workload-Centric Analysis Framework is a methodological tool for connecting individual rendering optimizations to their systemic effects by tracing the forward rendering path through five specific workload counts: N{resident}, N{active}, N{pair}, N{eval}, and N{blend}. It solves the problem of predicting how a specific optimization (e.g., culling or prefiltering) impacts overall performance by accounting for the non-linear ratios between stages, which vary with scene content, viewpoint, resolution, and backend semantics. Unlike sibling methods that focus on hardware-specific instructions or grid resolution costs, this framework provides a backend-agnostic abstraction of the Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline to isolate the cost of algorithmic decisions from hardware execution details. The framework models the rendering pipeline as a sequence of five stages. Each stage produces a count representing a specific subset of work items. The counts are defined as follows: 1. N{resident}: The count of Gaussians stored in the rendering memory pool and directly accessible to the renderer. The memory tier (device-local, unified, or host-mapped) must be reported. In hierarchical or streamed systems, Gaussians outside the measured rendering pool are excluded. 2. N{active}: The count of Gaussians retained after frame selection, visibility culling, and projected-footprint tests. This is the post-projection count of distinct Gaussians producing at least one materialized association. It excludes rejected inputs that still incurred Projection work. 3. N{pair}: The count of Gaussian–tile association records created during the Sorting stage, where projected footprints are expanded. One active Gaussian can generate several records. Depth ordering reorganizes these records without changing their number. 4. N{eval}: The count of Gaussian response or contribution tests executed by pixel threads traversing tile lists. A rejected candidate still counts because its test has already run. 5. N{blend}: The count of contributions that pass the tests and update pixel color and transmittance. Within the same frame and backend, N{blend} \le N{eval}. Formulas and Bounds The theoretical lower bound for evaluation cost is reached when N{eval} = N{blend}, meaning every non-contributing candidate is rejected before evaluation. Ideal lossless prefiltering leaves N{blend} unchanged. Parameters and Pitfalls Memory Tier: The definition of N{resident} depends on the memory tier. If the tier is not reported, the count is ambiguous. Non-Monotonic Ratios: Reducing one count (e.g., N{active}) does not necessarily reduce later counts (e.g., N{eval}) proportionally. The ratios between successive counts vary with scene content, viewpoint, resolution, tile configuration, selection/culling policy, and backend semantics. Prefiltering Cost: Work performed by prefiltering must be accounted for separately from the savings in N{eval} or N{blend}. System Cost: The five counts describe stored Gaussians and rendering operations, but system cost also depends on work per item, transfers, synchronization, temporary buffers, cached results, and optimizer data. Backward computation and parameter updates add further cost. Pseudocode The following pseudocode illustrates the logical flow of the counts. It assumes a standard Gaussian Splatting backend where Gaussians are projected, sorted, and evaluated per pixel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def analyzeworkload(gaussians, camera, resolution, tilesize): # Stage 1: Resident Count # Nresident is the total number of Gaussians in the accessible memory pool. # This is an input parameter, not computed by the renderer loop. Nresident = len(gaussians) # Stage 2: Active Count # Perform frame selection, visibility culling, and projected-footprint tests. activegaussians = [] projectionworkcount = 0 for g in gaussians: projectionworkcount += 1 if isvisible(g, camera) and hasfootprint(g, camera, resolution): activegaussians.append(g) Nactive = len(activegaussians) # Stage 3: Pair Count # Expand active Gaussians into Gaussian-tile association records. # One Gaussian may generate multiple records if it overlaps multiple tiles. associationrecords = [] for g in activegaussians: tiles = getoverlappingtiles(g, camera, resolution, tilesize) for tile in tiles: associationrecords.append((g, tile)) Npair = len(associationrecords) # Sort records by depth (optional, does not change Npair) associationrecords.sort(key=lambda x: x[0].depth) # Stage 4: Evaluation Count # Traverse tile lists and execute contribution tests. Neval = 0 # Iterate over all pixels in the tile for tile in uniquetiles(associationrecords): for pixel in tile.pixels: # Get list of Gaussians associated with this pixel via the tile candidates = getcandidatesforpixel(pixel, associationrecords) for candidate in candidates: Neval += 1 # Execute Gaussian response/contribution test contribution = evaluategaussian(candidate, pixel) # Stage 5: Blend Count # If the contribution passes the test (e.g., alpha > threshold) if iscontributing(contribution): blendpixel(pixel, contribution) # Note: Nblend is implicitly the number of successful blends. # In a real implementation, this would be tracked explicitly. Nblend = countsuccessfulblends() return { "Nresident": Nresident, "Nactive": Nactive, "Npair": Npair, "Neval": Neval, "Nblend": Nblend } Time Complexity: The framework itself has no computational complexity; it is an analytical model. However, it highlights that the cost of the rendering pipeline is dominated by the stage with the highest work-per-item cost multiplied by its count. Since N{eval} can be significantly larger than N{blend}, optimizations targeting N{eval} (like prefiltering) are critical. Memory Complexity: N{resident} determines the memory footprint. The memory tier (device-local, unified, host-mapped) affects access latency and bandwidth, which are not captured by the count alone but are essential for performance modeling. Strengths: It provides a standardized vocabulary for comparing optimizations across different backends and hardware. It exposes the disconnect between culling effectiveness (N{active}) and actual evaluation savings (N{eval}). Limitations: It does not account for work-per-item variations, synchronization overhead, or backward computation costs. It assumes a specific forward path (Splats to Silicon) and may not apply to other volume rendering techniques. When to Use: When analyzing the impact of algorithmic changes (culling, sorting, prefiltering) on overall rendering performance, especially in Gaussian Splatting systems. When Not to Use: When hardware-specific bottlenecks (e.g., memory bandwidth saturation, cache misses) dominate over algorithmic workload, or when analyzing non-Gaussian volume rendering methods. The Workload-Centric Analysis Framework was introduced in the paper "From Splats to Silicon: Rethinking Computational Efficiency of 3DGS". It emerged from the need to systematically evaluate the efficiency of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipelines, which involve complex interactions between projection, sorting, and evaluation stages. The framework addresses the gap in understanding how individual optimizations propagate through the rendering stack, providing a structured way to measure and compare computational efficiency. From Splats to Silicon: Rethinking Computational Efficiency of 3DGS, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.06157, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: 2D Projective Grid Traversal
head: 2D grid walk over depth heightfield, DepthMesh.raycast() optimization
body: 2D Projective Grid Traversal is a raycasting optimization for depth meshes that replaces brute-force triangle intersection checks with a traversal of a 2D projective grid. It exploits the property that vertices of a DepthMesh lie along perspective unprojection rays from the camera origin, causing 3D triangles in a grid cell to project strictly inside that 2D cell under central projection. Unlike standard 3D grid traversal methods which step through volumetric cells, this method projects the ray segment into 2D grid coordinates and visits only the cells crossed by the projected line segment, reducing the number of intersection checks from thousands to approximately 20–40. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A local-space ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a DepthMesh geometry with precomputed rectilinear grid metadata (segments, min/max depth, rectilinear flag); the truncated depth frustum planes (z{min}, z{max}, r{x,min}, r{x,max}, r{y,min}, r{y,max}). Output: A list of intersection points, distances, face indices, and normals for triangles intersected by the ray. Data Structures: Grid Metadata: Per-geometry metadata tracked by DepthGeometryUpdater includes segments (grid dimensions, e.g., 39 \times 39), isRectilinear (boolean), minVertexDepth, maxVertexDepth, and hasDepthData. Vertex Buffer: Flat Float32Array containing vertex positions, accessed directly to avoid overhead. Algorithm Steps: 1. Frustum Clipping: Clip the local-space ray against the 6 planes of the truncated depth frustum (z{min}, z{max}, r{x,min}, r{x,max}, r{y,min}, r{y,max}) to determine the entry and exit points of the ray segment within the valid depth volume. Let the clipped segment be defined by endpoints \mathbf{p}{entry} and \mathbf{p}{exit}. 2. 2D Projection: Project the clipped ray's entry and exit endpoints from 3D local space into 2D grid coordinates (c, r) using the central projection formula: c = \frac{x}{-z}, \quad r = \frac{y}{-z} where (x, y, z) are the coordinates of the endpoint and -z > 0. This results in a 2D line segment in grid space. 3. 2D Grid Traversal: Traverse only the 2D grid cells crossed by the projected 2D line segment. The grid is typically uniform (e.g., 39 \times 39 cells). The traversal visits approximately 20–40 cells instead of all 1,521 cells in the full grid. 4. Intersection Testing: For each visited 2D grid cell, identify the 3D triangles contained within that cell. Read vertex positions directly from the flat Float32Array buffer into reusable scratch THREE.Vector3 instances to avoid the overhead of repeated accessor calls. Perform standard triangle-ray intersection tests for these triangles. 5. Fallback: If depth data has not yet been populated (hasDepthData is false) or if the projection is non-rectilinear (isRectilinear is false), fallback to standard Mesh.prototype.raycast() which tests all triangles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projectivegridtraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, gridmetadata, frustumplanes): """ rayorigin: Vector3 raydirection: Vector3 gridmetadata: Object containing segments (Nx, Ny), isRectilinear, minVertexDepth, maxVertexDepth, hasDepthData frustumplanes: List of 6 planes (zMin, zMax, rxMin, rxMax, ryMin, ryMax) """ # Fallback condition if not gridmetadata.hasDepthData or not gridmetadata.isRectilinear: return standardmeshraycast(rayorigin, raydirection) # 1. Clip ray against frustum planes clippedsegment = clipraytofrustum(rayorigin, raydirection, frustumplanes) if clippedsegment is None: return [] pentry, pexit = clippedsegment # 2. Project endpoints to 2D grid coordinates # Central projection: c = x / -z, r = y / -z centry = pentry.x / -pentry.z rentry = pentry.y / -pentry.z cexit = pexit.x / -pexit.z rexit = pexit.y / -pexit.z # 3. Traverse 2D grid cells crossed by the line segment (centry, rentry) -> (cexit, rexit) visitedcells = traverse2dgrid(centry, rentry, cexit, rexit, gridmetadata.segments) intersections = [] vertexbuffer = gridmetadata.vertexbuffer # Flat Float32Array # 4. For each visited cell, test contained triangles for cell in visitedcells: trianglesincell = gettrianglesincell(cell, gridmetadata) for tri in trianglesincell: # Read vertices from buffer directly v0 = readvertex(vertexbuffer, tri.v0) v1 = readvertex(vertexbuffer, tri.v1) v2 = readvertex(vertexbuffer, tri.v2) hit = raytriangleintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, v0, v1, v2) if hit: intersections.append(hit) return intersections def clipraytofrustum(origin, direction, planes): """ Clips a ray against 6 frustum planes. Returns (pentry, pexit) or None if no intersection. """ # Standard Liang-Barsky or Cohen-Sutherland style clipping for a ray segment # against 6 planes. # For simplicity, assume a helper function exists or implement standard parametric clipping. # Here we outline the logic: tmin = 0.0 tmax = 1.0 for plane in planes: # Plane defined by normal n and point ponplane # Ray: O + tD # Intersection: (Ponplane - O). n / (D. n) denom = dot(direction, plane.normal) if abs(denom) < 1e-8: # Ray parallel to plane if dot(plane.point - origin, plane.normal) < 0: return None # Ray is outside else: t = dot(plane.point - origin, plane.normal) / denom if denom < 0: tmin = max(tmin, t) else: tmax = min(tmax, t) if tmin > tmax: return None pentry = origin + direction tmin pexit = origin + direction tmax return (pentry, pexit) def traverse2dgrid(c1, r1, c2, r2, gridsize): """ Traverses 2D grid cells crossed by a line segment. Uses a 2D DDA-like approach. """ cells = [] # Determine grid bounds minc, maxc = 0, gridsize.x minr, maxr = 0, gridsize.y # Current cell currc = int(c1) currr = int(r1) # Step directions stepc = 1 if c2 > c1 else -1 stepr = 1 if r2 > r1 else -1 # Distances to next boundary # Boundary coordinates are integers nextcboundary = c1 if stepc < 0 else currc + 1 nextrboundary = r1 if stepr < 0 else currr + 1 # Delta distances if c2 != c1: deltac = abs(nextcboundary - c1) / abs(c2 - c1) else: deltac = float('inf') if r2 != r1: deltar = abs(nextrboundary - r1) / abs(r2 - r1) else: deltar = float('inf') tc = deltac tr = deltar # Add first cell cells.append((currc, currr)) # Traverse until we reach the end t = 0.0 while t < 1.0: if tc < tr: currc += stepc tc += deltac else: currr += stepr tr += deltar # Check bounds if 0 <= currc < gridsize.x and 0 <= currr < gridsize.y: cells.append((currc, currr)) else: break return cells def readvertex(buffer, index): """ Reads a vertex from a flat Float32Array. Assumes interleaved x, y, z. """ offset = index 3 x = buffer[offset] y = buffer[offset + 1] z = buffer[offset + 2] return Vector3(x, y, z) Time Complexity: The traversal visits approximately 20–40 grid cells per ray, compared to testing all triangles in the mesh (e.g., 3,042 triangles for a downsampled mesh). This significantly reduces the number of intersection checks. Measured Performance: On Android XR Chrome Trace, DepthMesh.raycast() time decreased from 1.177 ms/frame to 0.072 ms/frame, a 93.9% reduction (16.3x faster). collectIntersections (Scene Raycast) time decreased from 1.292 ms/frame to 0.187 ms/frame, an 85.5% reduction (6.9x faster). Strengths: Drastic reduction in intersection tests for depth meshes with rectilinear projections. Efficient use of GPU/CPU by minimizing memory access overhead through direct buffer reading. Limitations: Only applicable to DepthMesh geometries with rectilinear projections and populated depth data. Requires fallback to brute-force raycasting if these conditions are not met. This method was introduced in the context of optimizing raycasting for DepthMesh in the xrblocks project. It was implemented in src/depth/DepthMeshRaycast.ts and merged into the main branch in October 2026. The optimization addresses the performance bottleneck of testing thousands of triangles per frame for controller rays in XR applications. perf(depth): use 2D projective grid traversal in DepthMesh.raycast(), https://github.com/google/xrblocks/pull/715, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Z-order Ray Generation
head: Z-order Ray Scanning, Z-order curve ray generation, ZORG (Z-order Ray Generation)
body: Z-order Ray Generation (ZORG) is a hardware-oriented ray generation method that produces pixel coordinates and ray directions by traversing the image plane along a Z-order (Morton) curve rather than in row-major order. It clusters four adjacent rays into Ray Packets (RPs) to enhance spatial locality, thereby increasing traversal path similarity and data access overlap for occupancy grids and feature vectors compared to row-order scanning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An external system provides the image dimensions and the current state of the Z-order counter. Output: Four sets of pixel coordinates (X, Y) and their corresponding ray directions (origin and direction vectors) forming a single Ray Packet (RP). Data Structures: Z-order Counter: A 22-bit unsigned integer counter. Pixel Coordinates: Two 11-bit binary values, CX (X-coordinate) and CY (Y-coordinate), derived from the counter. Steps: 1. Increment Counter: The 22-bit counter is incremented to generate the next value in the Z-order sequence. 2. Bit Interleaving (De-interleaving): The counter output, denoted as FC, is partitioned into odd and even bits to form the X and Y coordinates: CX is formed by the even bits of FC (bits 0, 2, 4,..., 20). CY is formed by the odd bits of FC (bits 1, 3, 5,..., 21). This effectively reverses the Morton encoding process to retrieve spatial coordinates from the linear Z-order index. 3. Ray Direction Computation: Using the generated (CX, CY) coordinates, the ray origin and direction are computed for each of the four rays in the packet. The specific geometric mapping depends on the camera model (e.g., pinhole), but the coordinates define the pixel centers or corners. 4. Boundary Handling: If the generated coordinates fall outside the valid image boundaries (e.g., for non-power-of-two resolutions like 800x800), the system detects out-of-bounds positions and preemptively corrects the coordinates to re-enter the valid region. 5. Packet Assembly: The four rays are assembled into an RP and passed to the AABB Tester (ABT) for culling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zorderraygeneration(counterwidth=22, packetsize=4): """ Generates ray coordinates for a packet of rays using Z-order traversal. Note: This is a simplified logical representation. The actual hardware implementation uses bit-parallel de-interleaving. """ # Initialize counter counter = 0 # Precompute valid bounds if known, otherwise assume power-of-two for simplicity # In practice, bounds checking is integrated into the coordinate generation validxmax = None validymax = None rays = [] for in range(packetsize): # 1. Get current Z-order index zindex = counter # 2. De-interleave bits to get X and Y # Extract even bits for X cx = 0 bitpos = 0 tempz = zindex while tempz > 0: if tempz & 1: cx |= (1 << bitpos) tempz >>= 2 bitpos += 1 # Extract odd bits for Y cy = 0 bitpos = 0 tempz = zindex >> 1 while tempz > 0: if tempz & 1: cy |= (1 << bitpos) tempz >>= 2 bitpos += 1 # 3. Boundary Check and Correction # If dimensions are not power-of-two, coordinates may be out of bounds. # The hardware analyzes correlation between out-of-bounds positions # and re-entry points to correct coordinates preemptively. # Here we assume a simple clamp for logical completeness, # though the source describes a specific correction mechanism. if validxmax is not None: cx = min(cx, validxmax) if validymax is not None: cy = min(cy, validymax) # 4. Compute Ray Direction # This step depends on the specific camera projection model. # For a standard pinhole camera with focal length f and image center (cx0, cy0): # directionx = (cx - cx0) / f # directiony = (cy - cy0) / f # directionz = -1.0 # origin = (0, 0, 0) ray = { 'pixelx': cx, 'pixely': cy, 'direction': None # Placeholder for projection math } rays.append(ray) # 5. Increment Counter counter += 1 return rays Parameters: Counter Width: 22 bits. Coordinate Bit Width: 11 bits per axis. Packet Size: 4 rays per Ray Packet (RP). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Power-of-Two Dimensions: For image dimensions that are not powers of two (e.g., 800x800), the Z-order curve extends beyond valid image boundaries, producing out-of-bounds coordinates before re-entering the valid region. The implementation must handle this via preemptive coordinate correction based on the correlation between out-of-bounds positions and re-entry points. Locality: Z-order scanning provides greater traversal path similarity and increased data access overlap to the occupancy grid, feature vectors, and MLP weights compared to row-order scanning. Performance: Z-order ray scanning reduces Estimated Memory Accesses (EMAs) by 65.4% compared to row-order scanning. Hardware Efficiency: The method is designed for microarchitectural implementation, utilizing a simple 22-bit counter and bit-partitioning logic, which is efficient for on-chip data reuse. Limitations: The irregular pattern of Z-order traversal may complicate simple sequential memory access patterns if not carefully managed by the scheduler. Z-order Ray Generation was introduced as part of an energy-efficient edge coprocessor for neural rendering with explicit data reuse strategies. It was developed to address the inefficiencies of row-order scanning in ray packet processing, specifically targeting spatial locality optimization to enhance on-chip data reuse. The method is integrated into a scheduler that clusters rays into Ray Packets (RPs) and processes them using a Hierarchical Ray Marching (HRM) framework.
