name: Voronoi Grid Ray Traversal
head: 3D Voronoi Grid Ray Tracing, Ray casting through Voronoi cells, Straight path calculation through 3D Voronoi grid, Straight path traversal in Voronoi grid, Voronoi ray marching
body: Voronoi Grid Ray Traversal is a method for computing straight-line paths through an unstructured 3D Voronoi tessellation to determine radiation field properties in radiative transfer (RT) simulations. It solves the problem of accurately tracking photon energy absorption and path length within irregular, convex polyhedral cells, avoiding the directional spread errors and "fuzzy" distance concepts inherent in Delaunay edge approximation methods. Unlike uniform grid traversal Uniform Grid Traversal which relies on axis-aligned voxel boundaries, this method calculates precise intersection points with arbitrary planar cell walls defined by the perpendicular bisectors of Delaunay edges. The algorithm advances a ray through a sequence of Voronoi cells by calculating the intersection of the ray line with the planar boundaries of the current cell. It relies on the topological neighbor list of the current cell rather than explicit vertex/edge geometry. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{r}0 and direction unit vector \mathbf{k}. Domain boundaries \mathbf{D}{min} and \mathbf{D}{max} defining the cuboidal spatial extent. Site positions \{\mathbf{p}m\}{m=1}^M defining the Voronoi tessellation. Neighbor indices \{m{n,i}\} for each site n, where positive indices denote neighboring sites and negative indices denote domain walls. Current point \mathbf{r} (initially \mathbf{r}0) and current cell index mr (initially determined by point location). Outputs: A sequence of path segments, each defined by the entry point, exit point, distance traveled within the cell, and the index of the next cell. Site Positions: Array of 3D vectors \mathbf{p}m. Neighbor Lists: For each cell mr, a list of integers \{mi\} representing adjacent cells or walls. Domain Boundaries: Two 3D vectors \mathbf{D}{min}, \mathbf{D}{max}. 1. Initialization: Set current point \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}0. Determine initial cell index mr by finding the site nearest to \mathbf{r}0 using function C(\mathbf{r}). 2. Loop (Exit Point Calculation): Retrieve neighbor indices \{mi\} for current cell mr. For each neighbor mi, calculate the intersection parameter si where the ray line L(s) = \mathbf{r} + s\mathbf{k} intersects the plane separating cell mr and neighbor mi. Case 1: Regular Neighbor (mi > 0): Calculate normal vector: \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{p}(mi) - \mathbf{p}(mr). Calculate point on plane: \mathbf{p}{plane} = \frac{\mathbf{p}(mi) + \mathbf{p}(mr)}{2}. Calculate intersection parameter: si = \frac{\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{p}{plane} - \mathbf{r})}{\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{k}} Case 2: Domain Wall (mi < 0): Use the specific normal \mathbf{n} and point \mathbf{p}{plane} for the domain boundary. For example, for the left wall (x-min): \mathbf{n} = (-1, 0, 0), \quad \mathbf{p}{plane} = (D{min,x}, 0, 0) si = \frac{D{min,x} - rx}{kx} Optimization: Do not accumulate all si. Track only the smallest non-negative value sq = \min \{ si \mid si > 0 \}. Optimization: Skip calculation if \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{k} \le 0. Since \mathbf{p}(mr) and \mathbf{r} are on the same side of the plane, the numerator \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{p}{plane} - \mathbf{r}) is always non-negative. If \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{k} \le 0, the intersection is behind the ray or parallel, so si cannot be the smallest positive exit. 3. Termination Check: If no positive si exists (i.e., no valid exit point found), handle computational inaccuracy: Do not add a path segment. Advance \mathbf{r} by an infinitesimal distance \epsilon = \|\mathbf{D}{max} - \mathbf{D}{min}\| in direction \mathbf{k}. Recalculate mr = C(\mathbf{r}). Continue loop. If sq corresponds to a domain wall, terminate the traversal. 4. Update: Calculate exit point \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{r} + sq \mathbf{k}. Record path segment from \mathbf{r} to \mathbf{q} with length sq. Update current point \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{q}. Update current cell index mr to the neighbor index mq corresponding to sq. Repeat Loop. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voronoiraytraversal(r0, k, domainmin, domainmax, sites, neighbors): """ r0: 3D vector, ray origin k: 3D vector, ray direction (unit vector) domainmin: 3D vector, minimum domain boundary domainmax: 3D vector, maximum domain boundary sites: list of 3D vectors, site positions pm neighbors: list of lists, neighbors[m] contains indices of adjacent cells/walls """ # Helper to find cell containing point r def findcell(r): # Find index m minimizing ||sites[m] - r|| # Implementation detail: use spatial index or brute force for small M mindist = float('inf') bestm = -1 for m, p in enumerate(sites): dist = sum((p[i] - r[i])2 for i in range(3)) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestm = m return bestm # Initialization r = list(r0) mr = findcell(r) pathsegments = [] while True: currentneighbors = neighbors[mr] smin = float('inf') mexit = -1 for mi in currentneighbors: if mi > 0: # Regular neighbor pmr = sites[mr] pmi = sites[mi] # Normal vector n = pmi - pmr n = [pmi[i] - pmr[i] for i in range(3)] # Dot product n. k ndotk = sum(n[i] k[i] for i in range(3)) # Optimization: if n. k <= 0, intersection is behind or parallel if ndotk <= 0: continue # Point on plane pplane = (pmi + pmr) / 2 pplane = [(pmi[i] + pmr[i]) / 2.0 for i in range(3)] # Numerator n. (pplane - r) num = sum(n[i] (pplane[i] - r[i]) for i in range(3)) # si = num / (n. k) si = num / ndotk if si > 0 and si < smin: smin = si mexit = mi else: # Domain wall (mi < 0) # Determine wall based on negative index convention # Assuming specific mapping of negative indices to walls # For example, -1: x-min, -2: x-max, -3: y-min, etc. # This part depends on the specific implementation of 'neighbors' # Here we assume a generic wall calculation function wallresult = calculatewallintersection(mi, r, k, domainmin, domainmax) if wallresult is not None: si, mexit = wallresult if si > 0 and si < smin: smin = si # mexit might be a special wall marker, but for loop logic # we just need to know it's a wall to terminate later # In this pseudocode, we treat wall exit as a valid smin pass if smin == float('inf'): # No exit point found (computational inaccuracy) # Advance by epsilon domainsize = sum((domainmax[i] - domainmin[i])2 for i in range(3)) epsilon = domainsize 0.5 r = [r[i] + epsilon k[i] for i in range(3)] mr = findcell(r) continue # Exit point found q = [r[i] + smin k[i] for i in range(3)] # Record segment pathsegments.append({ 'entry': list(r), 'exit': list(q), 'distance': smin, 'nextcell': mexit }) # Check if exit is a domain wall # Logic to determine if mexit corresponds to a wall if mexit < 0: break # Update state r = q mr = mexit return pathsegments def calculatewallintersection(wallindex, r, k, domainmin, domainmax): """ Calculates intersection with domain walls. Returns (s, wallmarker) or None. """ # Example mapping: -1: x-min, -2: x-max, -3: y-min, -4: y-max, -5: z-min, -6: z-max if wallindex == -1: if k[0] == 0: return None s = (domainmin[0] - r[0]) / k[0] return (s, -1) elif wallindex == -2: if k[0] == 0: return None s = (domainmax[0] - r[0]) / k[0] return (s, -2) elif wallindex == -3: if k[1] == 0: return None s = (domainmin[1] - r[1]) / k[1] return (s, -3) elif wallindex == -4: if k[1] == 0: return None s = (domainmax[1] - r[1]) / k[1] return (s, -4) elif wallindex == -5: if k[2] == 0: return None s = (domainmin[2] - r[2]) / k[2] return (s, -5) elif wallindex == -6: if k[2] == 0: return None s = (domainmax[2] - r[2]) / k[2] return (s, -6) else: return None Epsilon: The infinitesimal advance \epsilon is defined as the diagonal length of the domain \|\mathbf{D}{max} - \mathbf{D}{min}\|. Parallel Planes: If \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{k} = 0, si becomes \pm \infty. In IEEE 754 arithmetic, this value is never selected as the minimum positive sq, so no special test is required. Point Location: The function C(\mathbf{r}) finds the site closest to \mathbf{r}. This is computationally expensive if done naively; optimized implementations use a coarse spatial grid (blocks) to restrict the search to candidate cells. The method for identifying the specific Voronoi cell containing a query point \mathbf{r} by finding the nearest site. It uses a coarse spatial grid to optimize the search, avoiding complex tree structures. Performance: Shooting photon packages through a 3D Voronoi grid is approximately three times slower than an equivalent octree grid with the same number of cells. Topology: For sites chosen randomly from a uniform distribution, the expected number of nearest neighbors (cells sharing a face) is 15.54. This determines the average number of plane intersection calculations per cell traversal. Accuracy: The method calculates high-precision straight path segments inside each cell, ensuring accurate energy absorption tracking and high-resolution image production, unlike Delaunay edge approximation methods which suffer from directional spread. Limitations: The method requires pre-computed neighbor lists and site positions. It is less efficient than structured grid methods due to the irregular geometry and the cost of point location for initialization or error recovery. The method was presented by Camps et al. in 2013 for use in the SKIRT dust radiative transfer code. It addresses challenges in RT simulations using unstructured grids, such as those derived from smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) or adaptive mesh refinement, where regular voxel traversal is not applicable. The implementation relies on the open-source library Voro++ to obtain Voronoi grid cell properties based solely on generating points. name: Point location in Voronoi grid
head: Cell containment query, Nearest neighbor search for Voronoi cells
body: The point location method identifies the specific Voronoi cell containing a given query point \mathbf{r}, which is equivalent to finding the site closest to that point. It serves as the lookup mechanism for Voronoi Grid Ray Traversal, determining which cell a ray currently traverses. It differs from general nearest-neighbor searches by utilizing a coarse spatial grid (blocks) to restrict the search to a small subset of candidate cells, avoiding the overhead of complex tree structures like k-d trees or R-trees. Inputs: Query point \mathbf{r}. Domain boundaries \mathbf{D}{min} and \mathbf{D}{max}. Block cell lists: For each block Bk, a list of indices \{m{k,j} \mid j=1 \dots Jk\} of Voronoi cells that possibly overlap that block. Site positions: \{\mathbf{p}m \mid m=1 \dots M\}. Outputs: The index m of the Voronoi cell containing \mathbf{r}. A special negative index if \mathbf{r} is outside the domain. Data Structures: 1. Domain Partition: The domain D is partitioned into cuboidal blocks \{Bk \mid k=1 \dots K\} arranged on a regular linear grid. 2. Block Cell Lists: An array or list of lists where blocklists[k] contains the integer indices of all Voronoi cells whose bounding boxes intersect block Bk. 3. Site Positions: An array of 3D coordinates for all M sites. Algorithm Steps: 1. Domain Check: Verify if \mathbf{r} lies within the domain boundaries \mathbf{D}{min} and \mathbf{D}{max}. If \mathbf{r} is outside, return a special negative index value. 2. Block Location: Determine which block Bk contains \mathbf{r}. Since blocks form a regular linear grid, this is a direct arithmetic calculation based on \mathbf{r}'s coordinates and the block dimensions. 3. Candidate Retrieval: Retrieve the list of cell indices \{m{k,j}\} associated with block Bk. These are the only cells that can possibly contain \mathbf{r}. 4. Nearest Site Search: For each cell index m in the candidate list, calculate the squared Euclidean distance from \mathbf{r} to the site position \mathbf{p}m: dm^2 = \| \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{p}m \|^2 The cell corresponding to the site \mathbf{p}m with the minimum dm^2 is the containing cell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findcontainingcell(r, Dmin, Dmax, blocklists, sitepositions, blockdims, blockorigin): """ Finds the Voronoi cell containing query point r. Args: r: 3D vector (x, y, z) Dmin: 3D vector, minimum domain bounds Dmax: 3D vector, maximum domain bounds blocklists: List of lists, blocklists[k] contains indices of cells overlapping block k sitepositions: List of 3D vectors, sitepositions[m] is position of site m blockdims: 3D vector, dimensions of each cuboidal block blockorigin: 3D vector, origin of the block grid Returns: int: Index of the containing Voronoi cell, or negative value if out of bounds. """ # Step 1: Verify query point is inside domain if not (all(r[i] >= Dmin[i] for i in range(3)) and all(r[i] <= Dmax[i] for i in range(3))): return -1 # Special negative index value # Step 2: Locate the block containing the query point # Calculate relative position within the grid relpos = [r[i] - blockorigin[i] for i in range(3)] # Determine block indices (integer division/floor) blockidxx = int(relpos[0] // blockdims[0]) blockidxy = int(relpos[1] // blockdims[1]) blockidxz = int(relpos[2] // blockdims[2]) # Flatten 3D block index to 1D index k # Assuming blocklists is indexed by a linear k. # The exact mapping depends on the grid dimensions Kx, Ky, Kz. # For this implementation, we assume blocklists is a flat list or # we compute k based on grid size. Let's assume we have grid dimensions. # Note: The source does not specify the exact flattening formula, # but implies a regular linear grid. We assume blocklists is accessible # via a computed linear index k. # Assuming standard row-major flattening for a Kx x Ky x Kz grid. # k = blockidxz (Kx Ky) + blockidxy Kx + blockidxx # Since K dimensions are not explicitly passed, we assume blocklists # is structured such that we can find k. # To be strictly implementable from text, we assume blocklists is a # 3D array or we compute k. Let's assume a helper to get k. k = computeblockindex(blockidxx, blockidxy, blockidxz) candidates = blocklists[k] # Step 3 & 4: Find closest site among candidates mindistsq = float('inf') closestcellindex = -1 for m in candidates: # Calculate squared distance to site m dx = r[0] - sitepositions[m][0] dy = r[1] - sitepositions[m][1] dz = r[2] - sitepositions[m][2] distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz if distsq < mindistsq: mindistsq = distsq closestcellindex = m return closestcellindex def computeblockindex(ix, iy, iz): # Placeholder for specific grid flattening logic. # In a regular linear grid, this maps (ix, iy, iz) to k. # The source states blocks are on a "regular linear grid". # Without explicit K dimensions, we assume the caller provides k # or this function uses global grid constants. # For the purpose of this article, we assume the block index k # is derived from the coordinates. return ix + iy 10 + iz 100 # Example mapping, actual depends on grid size Setup Requirements: Bounding Boxes: The bounding box for each Voronoi cell must be calculated from the cell's vertices, not from the convex hull of neighboring sites, as the latter does not necessarily fully enclose the cell. Library Usage: The Voro++ library may be used to construct the initial Voronoi geometry and extract cell data, but the runtime data structures (block lists, site positions) must be extracted and stored in custom structures. Time Complexity: O(1) for block lookup (assuming fixed grid dimensions) plus O(Nc) for the candidate search, where Nc is the average number of cells overlapping a block. This is typically small. Memory Complexity: O(K + M + \sum Jk), where K is the number of blocks, M is the number of sites, and \sum Jk is the total number of entries in all block cell lists. Performance: The method is considered simple and sufficiently fast because it is usually invoked only once per photon path. It avoids the overhead of building and maintaining complex acceleration structures like k-d trees or R-trees. Strengths: Simplicity of implementation; low memory overhead compared to tree structures; fast enough for single-lookup-per-path scenarios. Limitations: Performance degrades if the block size is too large (many candidates) or too small (many blocks, high memory overhead). Not suitable if the point location is queried many times per path. This method is used in the SKIRT code for 3D continuum radiative transfer (RT) simulations of dusty astrophysical objects, such as spiral galaxies and active galactic nuclei. The approach was described in a paper detailing the use of 3D Voronoi grids in RT simulations. The implementation relies on the Voro++ library for the initial geometric setup, but custom data structures are used for runtime performance. name: Voronoi Diagram Traversal with Local Adjacency
head: Voronoi Traversal via Local Adjacency
body: This method accelerates ray traversal in 3D Voronoi tessellations by replacing global bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) intersection queries with local cell adjacency lookups. It solves the performance bottleneck of repeated global searches by leveraging the spatial coherence of neighboring cells, significantly reducing the number of cells visited per ray and improving memory coherence across neighboring rays on the GPU. It is distinct from global BVH approaches by relying on precomputed topological connectivity rather than geometric bounding volumes. Inputs: A set of Voronoi sites (points) S = \{s1, s2, \dots, sN\} in 3D space. For each site si, its associated physical properties (e.g., density, temperature) and geometric bounds. A set of rays R defined by origin o and direction d. Data Structures: 1. Site List: Array of site coordinates and properties. 2. Adjacency Map: A sparse structure mapping each cell index i to a list of neighbor indices \mathcal{N}(i). This replaces the BVH tree. 3. Morton Order Array: An array of cell indices sorted by their 3D Morton (Z-order) code to improve spatial locality. 4. Ray Tile Buffer: A buffer storing rays grouped into compact screen-space tiles. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Offline): Compute the Voronoi diagram to determine the adjacency graph where two cells are neighbors if they share a facet. Store the adjacency list for each cell. Compute the 3D Morton code for each site's centroid. Sort the cell indices based on their Morton codes to create a spatially coherent layout. 2. Ray Scheduling (Per Frame): Project ray origins and directions onto the screen. Group rays into compact 2D tiles (e.g., 8 \times 8 or 16 \times 16 pixels) to maximize GPU warp coherence. 3. Traversal (Per Ray): Initialization: Use the parent method Point location in Voronoi grid to find the initial cell c{start} containing the ray origin o. Loop: While the ray is within the domain and has not terminated: Let current cell be c. Culling: Calculate the maximum possible contribution of cell c to the ray (based on opacity, density, and path length). If this value is below a fixed threshold \tau, skip appearance evaluation and jump to the next cell using adjacency. Appearance Evaluation: If not skipped, compute the radiative transfer contribution of cell c along the ray segment inside it. Exit Point: Compute the exit point p{exit} of the ray from cell c. Next Cell: Identify the neighbor cell c{next} that shares the facet containing p{exit}. This is done by checking the adjacency list \mathcal{N}(c) and selecting the cell whose centroid or bounding box best aligns with the ray direction at p{exit}, or by storing facet-to-neighbor mappings explicitly. Update current cell c \leftarrow c{next}. Parameters: \tau: Threshold for skipping appearance evaluation. Value depends on scene opacity and desired precision. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Degenerate Cells: If a cell has no neighbors (isolated), traversal stops. Precision Errors: Floating-point inaccuracies at facet boundaries may cause the ray to miss the correct neighbor. Robust geometric predicates or epsilon offsets are required. Empty Space: If the ray exits the domain of sites, traversal terminates. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversevoronoiray(ray, sites, adjacency, mortonsortedindices, threshold): # 1. Initial Point Location (from parent method) currentcellidx = pointlocation(ray.origin, sites) # 2. Ray Parameters tmin = 0.0 tmax = ray.maxdistance # 3. Traverse while tmin < tmax and currentcellidx is not None: cell = sites[currentcellidx] # 4. Culling maxcontribution = estimatemaxcontribution(cell, ray, tmin, tmax) if maxcontribution < threshold: # Skip appearance, find next cell nextcellidx = findnextcellviaadjacency(currentcellidx, ray, tmin) if nextcellidx is None: break currentcellidx = nextcellidx continue # 5. Appearance Evaluation texit = computeexitpoint(ray, cell) if texit > tmax: texit = tmax contribution = evaluateradiativetransfer(cell, ray, tmin, texit) accumulateresult(contribution) # 6. Advance tmin = texit nextcellidx = findnextcellviaadjacency(currentcellidx, ray, tmin) if nextcellidx is None: break currentcellidx = nextcellidx return result def findnextcellviaadjacency(currentidx, ray, tatexit): # Find the neighbor cell that contains the exit point # This requires checking the adjacency list and determining which neighbor # the ray enters. A robust implementation checks the facet normal or # uses a point-in-cell test for neighbors. neighbors = adjacency[currentidx] for nidx in neighbors: if ispointincell(ray.origin + ray.direction tatexit, sites[nidx]): return nidx return None A Monte Carlo method for astrophysical radiative transfer using Voronoi tessellations. It is uncoupled from the input model's internal code, requiring only site coordinates and physical properties. Choose this when simulating photon transport in non-uniform density fields like SPH particles. Time Complexity: Traversal is proportional to the number of cells visited per ray. Local adjacency reduces the cost of finding the next cell from O(\log N) (BVH) to O(1) (adjacency lookup), but requires precomputing the adjacency graph. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the adjacency graph, which can be large for complex Voronoi diagrams. Morton ordering improves cache coherence. Performance: Improves GPU throughput by enhancing memory coherence across neighboring rays and reducing traversal overhead. Strengths: Faster traversal than global BVH for dense Voronoi grids; better cache locality due to Morton ordering and tile scheduling. Limitations: Requires precomputed adjacency; culling threshold \tau must be tuned; precision issues at cell boundaries. When to use: When rendering large-scale Voronoi tessellations (e.g., astrophysical simulations) where traversal cost dominates. When not to use: For sparse or dynamic Voronoi diagrams where adjacency computation is too costly. This method was introduced in the context of differentiable Voronoi ray tracing, building on the Radiant Foam renderer. It addresses the limitations of global BVH intersection queries for Voronoi diagrams, which are inefficient due to the irregular shape of cells. The approach was demonstrated to support interactive rendering on mobile devices and advanced camera effects like fisheye projection and motion blur. name: Voronoi Grid Radiative Transfer
head: 3D Voronoi grid RT, Voronoi tessellation radiative transfer
body: Voronoi Grid Radiative Transfer is a Monte Carlo method for computing radiative transfer in astrophysical environments using a 3D Voronoi tessellation as the spatial discretization grid. It solves the problem of efficiently tracing photon packages through complex, non-uniform density fields (such as SPH particles or MHD meshes) by adapting cell boundaries to underlying density gradients. Unlike methods that require tight coupling with the input model's internal code (e.g., Sunrise RT invoking Arepo), this approach remains uncoupled, requiring only site coordinates and cell physical properties. It is implemented in the SKIRT code. Inputs: 1. Voronoi Sites: Coordinates of the generating points (sites) defining the grid. 2. Physical Properties: Scalar values (e.g., mass density, opacity) associated with the cell surrounding each site. 3. Light Source Definition: Position and spectral distribution of the emitter. Outputs: 1. Radiation Field: Discretized quantities (e.g., flux density, dust absorption) on the same grid as the dust density. 2. Spectral Energy Distribution (SED): Integrated flux at observer locations. The method relies on data structures built during initialization using a public Voronoi library (e.g., Voro++). For path calculation, the algorithm requires no information about the Voronoi cell geometry other than: 1. Bounding Box: The axis-aligned bounding box of the current cell. 2. Site Location: The 3D coordinates of the cell's own generating site. 3. Neighbor Locations: The 3D coordinates of all neighboring sites. Note: The specific internal layout of the neighbor list or bounding box structure is not detailed in the sources, but the library (Voro++) handles the geometric construction. 1. Initialization: Construct the Voronoi tessellation from the input sites using a library like Voro++. Build the required data structures: bounding boxes and neighbor lists for each cell. Assign physical properties (density/opacity) to each cell based on the input model. 2. Photon Shooting (Monte Carlo Loop): Emit photon packages from the light source. For panchromatic simulations: Emit packages for multiple wavelength bins on a logarithmic grid (e.g., 100 bins). For monochromatic simulations: Emit packages at a fixed wavelength. For each photon package: Determine the starting cell containing the photon's position. Cell Traversal: Calculate the straight-line path from the current position to the next cell boundary. Use the cell's bounding box and neighbor site locations to determine the exit point. Pitfall: Computational inaccuracies may occasionally cause the algorithm to fail to find an exit point. This occurs at most once per 50 million cell crossings. Interaction: Calculate absorption and scattering within the traversed cell segment using the cell's physical properties. Scattering: If a scattering event occurs, create a new photon package with a new direction and wavelength (if applicable). Repeat traversal until the photon escapes the domain or is absorbed. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voronoirt(sites, properties, lightsource, numphotons, wavelengthbins): """ Perform radiative transfer on a 3D Voronoi grid. Args: sites: List of 3D coordinates for Voronoi generating points. properties: Dictionary mapping site index to physical property (e.g., density). lightsource: Object defining position and spectral emission. numphotons: Total number of photon packages to emit. wavelengthbins: Logarithmic array of wavelengths for panchromatic simulation. Returns: radiationfield: Discretized radiation field on the grid. """ # 1. Initialization # Build Voronoi tessellation and extract necessary data structures # Requires external library (e.g., Voro++) voronoigrid = buildvoronoigrid(sites) # Extract bounding boxes and neighbor site locations for each cell # The library provides the topology; we store only what is needed for traversal celldata = {} for cellid in voronoigrid.cells: celldata[cellid] = { 'bbox': voronoigrid.getboundingbox(cellid), 'ownsite': sites[cellid], 'neighborsites': [sites[n] for n in voronoigrid.getneighbors(cellid)] } # Initialize radiation field accumulator radiationfield = initializefield(voronoigrid) # 2. Photon Shooting for i in range(numphotons): # Determine wavelength for this photon if wavelengthbins is not None: wavelength = samplewavelength(wavelengthbins) else: wavelength = lightsource.fixedwavelength # Emit photon package photon = lightsource.emit(wavelength) # Traverse through the grid currentcellid = findcellcontainingpoint(sites, photon.position) while photon.isalive(): # Get cell data for path calculation data = celldata[currentcellid] # Calculate exit point from current cell # Uses bounding box and neighbor sites to determine intersection exitpoint, nextcellid = calculateexitpoint( photon.position, photon.direction, data['bbox'], data['neighborsites']) # Handle potential failure to find exit point (rare, ~1 in 50M) if exitpoint is None: # Fallback or skip; sources indicate this is negligible break # Calculate interaction in the segment [photon.position, exitpoint] segmentlength = distance(photon.position, exitpoint) cellproperty = properties[currentcellid] # Compute absorption and scattering # This step depends on the specific radiative transfer physics model # For simplicity, we assume a standard Monte Carlo interaction absorption, scattering = computeinteraction( segmentlength, cellproperty, wavelength) # Update radiation field updatefield(radiationfield, currentcellid, absorption, scattering) # Move photon to exit point photon.position = exitpoint # Handle scattering if scattering: # Create new photon package with new direction/wavelength photon = createscatteredphoton(photon, cellproperty) # Find the new cell containing the scattered photon's position currentcellid = findcellcontainingpoint(sites, photon.position) else: # Move to next cell currentcellid = nextcellid # Check if photon has left the domain if currentcellid is None: photon.isalive = False Wavelength Bins: For panchromatic simulations, a logarithmic grid is used. Typical values: 100 bins. Photon Count: Torus model (panchromatic): 10^5 photons per bin. Pascucci benchmark (panchromatic): 10^5 photons per bin. Monochromatic simulations: 10^7 photons. Cell Resolution: Pascucci benchmark: 1 million cells, randomly placed according to a 1/r distribution. Cell Crossing Failure: The algorithm may occasionally fail to find an exit point due to computational inaccuracies. In tests, this occurred at most once per 50 million cell crossings, so it does not significantly affect performance. Precision: The method relies on accurate geometric intersection calculations. The use of bounding boxes and neighbor sites simplifies this but requires robust floating-point handling. Time Complexity: The time per cell crossing is higher for Voronoi grids than for octree grids due to geometric complexity. Torus model (panchromatic): Voronoi 1006 ns vs. Octree 400 ns (ratio 2.5). Torus model (monochromatic): Voronoi 693 ns vs. Octree 219 ns (ratio 3.2). Spiral model (panchromatic): Voronoi 1095 ns vs. Octree 442 ns (ratio 2.5). Spiral model (monochromatic): Voronoi 903 ns vs. Octree 309 ns (ratio 2.9). Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of sites and the storage of neighbor lists. The sources do not provide explicit memory usage figures, but note that the interface is thin and data structures are built from input data. Hardware: Tests performed on a typical desktop computer using a single core. Scaling: The method allows for flexible discretization, potentially requiring fewer cells than octree grids to represent certain density fields, which can balance performance. Strengths: Flexible discretization: Cell size and distribution can be fine-tuned by placing sites in appropriate locations (e.g., high-gradient areas). Uncoupled interface: Does not require access to the input model's source code, unlike methods that invoke non-public codes (e.g., Arepo). Supports various input models: SPH particles, MHD Voronoi meshes, or random points from analytical fields. Limitations: Higher per-cell-crossing time compared to octree grids (2.5x to 3.2x slower). Potential for rare geometric failures in cell crossing. Use when the input data is naturally particle-based (SPH) or already in a Voronoi mesh (MHD). Use when the density field has large dynamic ranges and requires adaptive resolution that can be achieved by placing sites according to density/opacity fields. Use when the input model's source code is not available. Use when maximum performance per cell crossing is critical and the density field is well-represented by an octree. Use when the input model is a regular grid and does not benefit from adaptive Voronoi discretization. The method was introduced in the paper "Using 3D Voronoi grids in radiative transfer simulations". It is implemented in the SKIRT code. The method was developed to address the need for flexible discretization in radiative transfer simulations, particularly for astrophysical environments with complex density structures. It was validated against the Pascucci benchmark. Implemented in the SKIRT code. Used for Pascucci benchmark simulations with optical depths \tau = 0.1, 1, 10. Input models can be SPH particles, MHD Voronoi meshes, or random points from analytical density/opacity fields. name: kd-restart algorithm
head: CERA-TVR
body: The kd-restart algorithm is a stackless traversal method for kd-trees that eliminates the need for an explicit recursion stack by restarting traversal from the root after each leaf is processed. It trades increased runtime for reduced memory complexity, making it suitable for GPU implementations with limited stack space. Inputs: ray origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, kd-tree root, and grid bounds. Outputs: sequence of leaf nodes visited with entry and exit distances. Data Structures: Each internal node stores a split axis a \in \{x, y, z\}, split position s, and pointers to left and right children. Leaf nodes store references to voxel data or texture bricks. Steps: 1. Initialize t{entry} = 0 (or the ray's near plane). Set current node to root. 2. While current node is not null and the ray remains within grid bounds: a. If current node is a leaf, process its data for the interval [t{entry}, t{exit}], then reset current node to root and continue. b. Determine split axis a and position s. c. Compute distance to split plane: t{split} = \frac{s - oa}{da}. If da = 0, treat t{split} as \infty and use the ray origin position relative to s to choose the child. d. If t{split} < t{entry}, the ray has already passed the split plane; select the far child. Otherwise, select the near child. e. Advance to the selected child. Update t{entry} \leftarrow \max(t{entry}, t{split}) for the next iteration. 3. Terminate when the ray exits the grid bounds. Formulas: Split plane distance: t{split} = \frac{s - oa}{da}. Parameters: Typical grid resolutions range from 64^3 to 1024^3 voxels; tree depth depends on data distribution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray parallel to split plane (da = 0): handled by treating t{split} as infinity and using origin position. Floating-point precision near split planes: use a small epsilon or robust geometric predicates to avoid oscillation. Infinite loops: ensure t{entry} advances or leaf processing resets context correctly; restart logic must not re-enter the same leaf without progress. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kdrestarttraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, kdtreeroot): currentnode = kdtreeroot tentry = 0.0 while currentnode is not None: if currentnode.isleaf: # Process leaf data for interval [tentry, texit] (Not given in the sources.) currentnode = kdtreeroot # Restart from root tentry = 0.0 continue splitaxis = currentnode.splitaxis splitpos = currentnode.splitposition daxis = raydirection[splitaxis] if daxis == 0.0: tsplit = float('inf') else: tsplit = (splitpos - rayorigin[splitaxis]) / daxis if tsplit < tentry: nextnode = currentnode.right if rayorigin[splitaxis] >= splitpos else currentnode.left else: nextnode = currentnode.left if rayorigin[splitaxis] < splitpos else currentnode.right tentry = max(tentry, tsplit) currentnode = nextnode A variant that maintains a "restart point" pointer instead of always returning to the root. At every descent, it checks if the ray crosses the split plane; if not, it marks the current node as a new restart point and stores a pointer. When a neighbor must be found, it jumps back to the restart point instead of the root, reducing visited nodes in practice while keeping worst-case complexity at O(n \log n). Time Complexity: O(n \log n) average for balanced trees, but with a higher constant factor due to redundant root restarts. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary stack space, as no explicit stack is used. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance degrades with tree depth due to repeated full traversals from the root. Strengths: Eliminates recursion stack overhead, simple implementation logic, fits GPU memory constraints. Limitations: Higher runtime from redundant root traversals, inefficient for very deep trees. When to Use: Memory-constrained environments (e.g., mobile GPUs) and moderate tree depths. When Not to Use: Deep kd-trees or performance-critical paths where stack space is available. Proposed by Foley et al. for rendering triangle meshes on the GPU. Later adopted for volume rendering, notably in the CERA-TVR system which targets scientific visualization with real-time dynamic transfer function updates. The method addresses early GPU architecture limitations regarding stack depth. name: Discrete Ray Casting
head: 3D Bresenham Ray Casting, Line Scan-conversion Ray Casting, Voxelization-based Ray Casting
body: Discrete Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that traverses a discrete, voxelized representation of the ray rather than a continuous mathematical line. It differs from continuous traversal methods (such as DDA Traversal) by generating the ray path using integer arithmetic via a 3D Bresenham-like algorithm or 3D line scan-conversion, effectively treating the ray as a sequence of occupied voxels. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized or unnormalized). Uniform grid with voxel size v and dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz. Volume data array V where V[i,j,k] stores the scalar value (e.g., density or opacity) at voxel indices (i,j,k). Outputs: Accumulated color and opacity for the pixel corresponding to the ray. Data Structures: Voxel Indices: Integer tuple (i, j, k) representing the current voxel. Ray State: Current position in voxel space, updated via integer increments. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Determine the starting voxel index (i0, j0, k0) containing the ray origin \mathbf{o}. 2. Discretization: Generate the sequence of voxels intersected by the ray using a 3D Bresenham line algorithm or 3D line scan-conversion algorithm. This produces a list of integer voxel coordinates (im, jm, km) for m=0 \dots M-1. 3. Sampling: For each voxel in the sequence, retrieve the scalar value sm = V[im, jm, km]. 4. Integration: Apply the volume rendering integral using the sampled values. Typically, this involves compositing the contribution of each voxel along the path. If the voxel size is v, the optical depth contribution is proportional to v \cdot sm. C = \sum{m=0}^{M-1} cm \cdot \alpham \cdot \prod{n=0}^{m-1} (1 - \alphan) where cm is the color and \alpham is the opacity derived from sm. 5. Termination: Stop when the ray exits the grid bounds or a maximum opacity threshold is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def discreteraycasting(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelsize, volumedata, gridbounds): # 1. Determine starting voxel startvoxel = [ int(rayorigin[i] // voxelsize) for i in range(3) ] # 2. Determine end voxel (intersection with grid bounds) # Simplified: assume ray always intersects or use a robust intersection test endvoxel = [ int((gridbounds.max[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] // voxelsize) if raydirection[i] > 0 else int((gridbounds.min[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] // voxelsize) for i in range(3) ] # 3. Generate discrete ray path using 3D Bresenham-like algorithm # This step replaces continuous distance calculations with integer steps voxelpath = bresenham3d(startvoxel, endvoxel) # 4. Traverse and composite accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 for voxel in voxelpath: # Check bounds if not gridbounds.contains(voxel): continue # Get scalar value (zero-order interpolation) scalar = volumedata[voxel[0], voxel[1], voxel[2]] # Map scalar to color and opacity color, opacity = transferfunction(scalar) # Composite weight = opacity (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor = [ accumulatedcolor[i] + color[i] weight for i in range(3) ] accumulatedopacity += weight if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break return accumulatedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Integer arithmetic avoids floating-point accumulation errors in traversal but may introduce aliasing artifacts if the ray direction is not aligned with the grid. Degenerate Input: Rays parallel to grid axes may require special handling in the Bresenham implementation to avoid skipping voxels or double-counting. Boundary Conditions: The Bresenham algorithm must correctly handle the exit condition from the grid volume. Time Complexity: O(L), where L is the number of voxels intersected by the ray, determined by the length of the Bresenham path. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space if the Bresenham generator is iterative; O(L) if the path is stored. Strengths: Simple implementation; no floating-point division in the traversal loop; efficient for uniform grids. Limitations: Aliasing artifacts due to discrete sampling; less accurate than continuous methods for oblique rays. When to use: When computational resources are limited and high precision is not critical; suitable for real-time applications on simple uniform volumes. Discrete Ray Casting was introduced as an alternative to continuous ray casting methods, leveraging classic computer graphics line-drawing algorithms (Bresenham's algorithm) for volume traversal. It is part of the early direct volume rendering techniques that sought to simplify the traversal process by avoiding floating-point arithmetic. name: Run-based ray traversal
head: Intercept sequence traversal, Run-based Ray Traversal for Height Fields, Run-based traversal
body: Run-based ray traversal is a method for efficiently determining the path of a ray through a discrete height field grid by grouping contiguous cells with identical y-coordinates into "runs," thereby reducing the number of traversal steps from O(n) to O(n/r), where n is the total number of cells and r is the average run length. It differs from standard cell-based algorithms (like DDA) by calculating the length of entire segments of the ray path in a single step using an intercept sequence derived from the ray's slope, rather than stepping through individual lattice points. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray parameters \alpha (slope) and \beta (intercept) in the height field's coordinate system, assuming 0 \le \alpha \le 1 and 0 \le \beta < 1. The height field samples are distributed over an integer lattice. Output: A sequence of runs, where each run is defined by its start position (xj, yj) and length rj. Data Structures: Run: A tuple or struct containing startx (integer), starty (integer), and length (integer). Intercept Sequence: A sequence of real numbers \betaj representing the fractional component of the line's intercept at the start of each run. Constants and Derived Values: Short run length: r = \lfloor 1/\alpha \rfloor. Long run length: r + 1 = \lceil 1/\alpha \rceil. Threshold for run type: v = 1 - \alpha r. Ratio of short runs: \mu = \alpha - v = \alpha(r + 1) - 1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Symmetry Handling: If the ray slope \alpha is outside [0, 1], transform the ray coordinates to map the slope into this range using 8-way symmetry, process the runs, and transform the resulting run positions back to the original coordinate system. 2. Initialization: Set current position (x0, y0) to the integer part of the ray's start point. Set initial intercept \beta{curr} = \beta. Check for initial truncation: If \beta \ge \alpha + v, the first run is truncated. This condition only applies if 0 < \alpha < 1/2. 3. Optimization via Translation: To simplify logic, translate the intercept sequence by subtracting v from the initial \beta. Let \beta' = \beta - v. If \beta' < \alpha, the first run is not truncated. Set r0 = 0 and \beta1 = \beta'. If \beta' \ge \alpha, the first run is truncated. Calculate the truncated length r0 = \lceil (1-\beta)/\alpha \rceil = r - \lfloor \beta - v \rfloor. Calculate the next intercept \beta1 = (\beta - v) - \lfloor \beta - v \rfloor \alpha. Update current position x0 \leftarrow x0 + r0. 4. Iterative Run Generation: While the ray has not exited the height field boundary: Determine run type based on current intercept \beta{curr}: If \beta{curr} < v, the run is long (rj = r + 1). If \beta{curr} \ge v, the run is short (rj = r). Note: The decision can be implemented as a sign check against zero if using the translated intercept \beta'. Record the run: Start (xj, yj), Length rj. Update position for the next run: x{j+1} = xj + rj y{j+1} = yj + 1 Update intercept for the next run: If the current run was long: \beta{j+1} = \betaj + \mu. If the current run was short: \beta{j+1} = \betaj - v Note: In the optimized version using \beta', if the run is long, \beta'{next} = \beta'{curr} + \mu. If short, \beta'{next} = \beta'{curr} - v. The threshold for determining long/short becomes 0. 5. Connectivity Correction (4-Connected Path): The algorithm generates an 8-connected path. To convert to a 4-connected path required for ray tracing, extend the beginning of each run by one cell (backwards in x). Exception: Do not extend if a corner intersection occurs. A corner intersection corresponds to an intercept value of exactly 0 (or -v in the translated system). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def runbasedraytraversal(alpha, beta, width, height): """ Traverses a height field grid using run-based ray traversal. Assumes 0 <= alpha <= 1 and 0 <= beta < 1. Returns a list of runs: [(x, y, length),...] """ runs = [] # Derived constants rshort = floor(1.0 / alpha) rlong = rshort + 1 v = 1.0 - alpha rshort mu = alpha - v # Initial position x = 0 y = 0 # Optimization: Translate intercept betaprime = beta - v # Check for initial truncation # Truncation happens if beta >= alpha + v # In translated terms: if betaprime >= alpha if betaprime >= alpha: # Truncated first run # r0 = ceil((1 - beta) / alpha) # Using integer arithmetic: ceil(a/b) = (a + b - 1) // b for positive integers # But beta is real. Formula: r0 = rshort - floor(beta - v) deltar = floor(betaprime) # floor(beta - v) r0 = rshort - deltar # Calculate next intercept beta1 # beta1 = (beta - v) - deltar alpha betaprime = betaprime - deltar alpha # Add the truncated run if length > 0 if r0 > 0: runs.append((x, y, r0)) x += r0 # If r0 was 0, we haven't moved, but we have a valid betaprime for the next step # The loop below will handle the first full run else: # Not truncated # r0 = 0, beta1 = betaprime pass # Iterative traversal while y < height and x < width: # Determine run type based on betaprime # If betaprime < 0 (which corresponds to beta < v in original), it's long # If betaprime >= 0, it's short if betaprime < 0: runlen = rlong # Update betaprime for next run: beta{j+1} = betaj + mu betaprime = betaprime + mu else: runlen = rshort # Update betaprime for next run: beta{j+1} = betaj - v betaprime = betaprime - v # Check bounds for the run # We need to ensure we don't exceed width/height # Since runs are horizontal, we only check x bound if x + runlen > width: runlen = width - x if runlen <= 0: break # Add run runs.append((x, y, runlen)) # Move to next run position x += runlen y += 1 # Check if we've exited the grid vertically if y >= height: break # Note: The 4-connected extension (backwards by 1 cell) is a post-processing step # or applied during rendering, not strictly part of the traversal path generation # unless the path itself must be 4-connected. return runs Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initial Truncation: The first run may be shorter than the standard short run length. This must be calculated separately using r0 = \lceil (1-\beta)/\alpha \rceil. Corner Intersections: When converting to a 4-connected path, runs must not be extended backwards if the intercept is exactly 0 (or -v), as this indicates a corner intersection where the ray passes through a vertex rather than crossing an edge. Slope Range: The algorithm assumes 0 \le \alpha \le 1. Slopes outside this range require coordinate transformation. Precision: The intercept sequence values are real numbers. Accumulation errors in \betaj may occur over long rays. Using the optimized translation method and checking against zero helps mitigate some logic errors, but fixed-point arithmetic or careful floating-point handling is recommended. Time Complexity: O(n/r), where n is the number of cells in the ray path and r is the average run length. Cell-based algorithms (DDA) have O(n) complexity. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space for traversal state (current position, intercept), plus O(k) for storing the output runs, where k is the number of runs. Performance: Measured average acceleration of 125% over all orientations compared to cell-based traversal. Improvement is 110% for average run length 2, and 180% for average run length 25. No improvement is measured when average run length is close to 1. Strengths: Significant reduction in the number of steps for rays with shallow angles relative to the grid axes (long runs). Provides structural information useful for accelerating intersection testing. Limitations: Performance gain diminishes as run length approaches 1 (steep rays). Requires handling of corner intersections and initial truncation. Origin: The method was introduced by Stephenson and Litow in 2001. History: It was developed to accelerate ray tracing of height fields, which are common in geographic information systems, scientific visualization, and terrain rendering. The mathematical foundation relies on properties of digital lines described by Wu (1982) and Rosenfeld (1974). Usage: Primarily used in terrain rendering and height field visualization. Accelerating the ray tracing of height fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/988834.988878, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Block-based Ray Tracing with Shared Memory Reuse
head: CUDA Block-based Ray Tracing with Shared Memory Reuse, Coherent ray tracing, Packet ray tracing
body: This method accelerates volume rendering by grouping primary camera rays into fixed-size screen-space blocks and reusing traversal state from previously processed rays within the same block to reduce redundant memory accesses. It differs from standard Uniform Grid Traversal by exploiting image-space coherence among rays originating from adjacent pixels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Screen divided into blocks (e.g., 8×8 pixels), volume dataset, and ray origins/directions for each pixel. Output: Rendered color/opacity values for each pixel. Data Structures: Shared Memory: A 16 KB region of low-latency shared memory allocated per block, accessible by all threads in the block. Block State: Stores the traversal state (current voxel index, t{max} values) of the previously processed ray in the block for reuse. Occlusion Bits: One bit per pixel in shared memory tracks occlusion state for quick tests during raycasting. Steps: 1. Divide the image into fixed-size blocks (e.g., 8×8 pixels). 2. Generate primary rays for each pixel in the block. 3. For each ray, check shared memory for a valid traversal state from a previously processed ray in the same block. 4. If valid, initialize the current ray's traversal variables (t{max}, current voxel index) using the reused state; otherwise, compute them from the ray origin. 5. Perform the standard Ray-grid traversal (e.g., DDA) starting from the initialized state. 6. After traversal, store the final voxel index and t{max} values back into shared memory for potential reuse by subsequent rays in the block. 7. Integrate the volume along the ray and store the result. 8. Set the occlusion bit for the current pixel in shared memory to skip it in future passes. Formulas: Let the ray be defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. The grid uses uniform voxel size v. For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: 1. Step Direction (\text{step}i): \text{step}i = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } di > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } di < 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } di = 0 \end{cases} If di = 0, the ray never crosses a boundary in that dimension, and the corresponding distance is treated as infinity. 2. Distance Delta (\Delta ti): The distance along the ray to traverse one voxel width. \Delta ti = \frac{v}{|di|} \cdot \text{step}i \quad \text{(or } 0.0 \text{ if } di = 0\text{)} 3. Distance to Next Boundary (t{max, i}): The distance from the ray origin to the first boundary crossed in axis i. t{max, i} = \frac{\text{boundary}i - oi}{di} The initial boundary is determined by the starting voxel index. If the ray starts inside the grid, the initial boundary is the next one in the direction of travel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blockbasedraytracing(blocksize, sharedmemory, volumemin, volumemax, voxelsize, rays): # rays: list of (origin, direction, pixelid) grouped by block # sharedmemory: dict mapping blockid to {'voxel': [x,y,z], 'tmax': [tx,ty,tz], 'step': [sx,sy,sz], 'valid': bool, 'occlusion': int} for blockid, blockrays in enumerate(rays): for origin, direction, pixelid in blockrays: # Check occlusion bit for this pixel occlusionmask = sharedmemory.get(blockid, {}).get('occlusion', 0) if occlusionmask & (1 << pixelid): continue # Compute step direction unconditionally step = [1 if direction[i] > 0 else (-1 if direction[i] < 0 else 0) for i in range(3)] # Initialize or reuse state prevstate = sharedmemory.get(blockid, {}) if prevstate.get('valid', False): currentvoxel = prevstate['voxel'][:] tmax = prevstate['tmax'][:] tentry = 0.0 else: currentvoxel = [int(origin[i] // voxelsize) for i in range(3)] currentvoxel = [max(volumemin[i], min(volumemax[i], currentvoxel[i])) for i in range(3)] nextboundary = [(currentvoxel[i] + step[i]) voxelsize for i in range(3)] tmax = [(nextboundary[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if direction[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] tentry = 0.0 # DDA Traversal Loop while volumemin[0] <= currentvoxel[0] <= volumemax[0] and \ volumemin[1] <= currentvoxel[1] <= volumemax[1] and \ volumemin[2] <= currentvoxel[2] <= volumemax[2]: minidx = tmax.index(min(tmax)) texit = tmax[minidx] # Standard front-to-back volume integration # density = volume[currentvoxel[0], currentvoxel[1], currentvoxel[2]] # alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density (texit - tentry)) # color += (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) alpha density # accumulatedalpha += (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) alpha currentvoxel[minidx] += step[minidx] tmax[minidx] += (voxelsize / abs(direction[minidx]) if direction[minidx] != 0 else 0.0) tentry = texit # Update shared memory for next ray in block sharedmemory[blockid] = { 'voxel': currentvoxel, 'tmax': tmax, 'step': step, 'valid': True, 'occlusion': occlusionmask | (1 << pixelid) } Edge Cases: Invalid Reuse: If the reused state is invalid (e.g., ray started outside the volume), fall back to full initialization. Precision: Reusing floating-point t{max} values may accumulate error; consider re-normalizing or re-computing t{max} periodically. Zero Direction Component: When di = 0, \Delta ti is set to 0.0 and t{max, i} is set to \infty to prevent division by zero and skip boundary crossing in that axis. The Perspective Grid is a ray-specialized spatial acceleration structure designed to provide perfect coherence for primary camera rays by treating them as packets. Unlike hierarchical structures like BVH or Kd-trees, it lacks tree-based culling properties but leverages image-space tiling to maximize shared memory reuse on GPUs. It is distinct from uniform grids because it aligns voxel boundaries with the camera's perspective, making it highly efficient for primary rays but unsuitable for secondary rays. Links one bit in shared memory to one pixel on the screen to track occlusion state. Uses the bits for quick occlusion tests during the raycasting pass. Achieves approximately a 25% rendering speedup. Time Complexity: Depends on the underlying traversal (e.g., DDA is O(N) per ray), with overhead for shared memory synchronization. Memory Complexity: Requires 16 KB of shared memory per block plus one bit per pixel for occlusion tracking. Performance: Achieves approximately a 25% rendering speedup when using shared memory bits for quick occlusion tests. Strengths: High performance for primary rays with strong spatial coherence; reduces redundant memory accesses. Limitations: Less effective for secondary rays (reflections, shadows) which lack coherence; requires careful management of shared memory state. Originated in discussions around real-time voxel raytracing development, specifically by IJs and Ken Silverman in 2008, leveraging CUDA's shared memory capabilities to exploit ray coherence. name: Perspective Grid for Primary Rays
head: Perspective Grid
body: The Perspective Grid is a ray-specialized spatial acceleration structure designed to provide perfect coherence for primary camera rays by treating them as packets. Unlike hierarchical structures like BVH or Kd-trees, it lacks tree-based culling properties but leverages image-space tiling to maximize shared memory reuse on GPUs. It is distinct from uniform grids because it aligns voxel boundaries with the camera's perspective, making it highly efficient for primary rays but unsuitable for secondary rays. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry (triangles), camera parameters (view frustum), image resolution, and tiling parameters (N, k). Output: A grid data structure mapping triangles to voxels, and the resulting image via ray-triangle intersections. Data Structures: The grid is constructed by binning scene geometry into voxels. The construction cost is low, reducing to a sorting of triangle-voxel pairs. The structure does not possess hierarchy. Parameters: N \times N: The number of raytracing tiles dividing the image. k: The scaling factor for sorting tiles. Sorting Tile Size: Triangles are sorted into kN \times kN tiles in image space. Raytracing Tile Size: The image is divided into N \times N tiles, where each raytracing tile contains a k \times k group of sorting tiles. Optimal Configuration: A 2 \times 2 arrangement of sorting tiles within each raytracing tile provides the best results on current GPU hardware. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-filtering: Apply View Frustum Culling (VFC) and Back-Face Culling to eliminate triangles not visible to the camera. This reduces grid construction time and geometry load. 2. Grid Construction: Sort triangles into the perspective grid voxels by binning triangle-voxel pairs. 3. Thread Mapping: Assign each pixel in an N \times N raytracing tile to a thread (or work item) within a CUDA block (or work group). 4. Shared Memory Loading: Load triangle data into shared memory. The available shared memory is partitioned equally among the sorting tiles. 5. Intersection Loop: Threads alternate between loading a portion of triangles into shared memory and computing intersections, with synchronization between these two roles. 6. Front-to-Back Traversal: Process voxels in front-to-back order. If a thread finds an intersection in a current voxel, it stops checking for intersections in later voxels. 7. Optimization (Indirect Mapping): Use indirect mapping to balance coherence and SIMD utilization. Triangles from each sorting tile are brought to the respective area of shared memory and intersected with rays corresponding to those sorting tiles. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def perspectivegridprimaryrays(triangles, camera, imagewidth, imageheight, N, k): # 1. Pre-filtering: VFC and Back-Face Culling visibletriangles = [] for tri in triangles: if isinviewfrustum(tri, camera) and isfrontfacing(tri, camera): visibletriangles.append(tri) # 2. Grid Construction: Sort triangles into kN x kN sorting tiles sortingtilesize = k N sortingtiles = {} for tri in visibletriangles: tx = (tri.centerx // sortingtilesize) % (imagewidth // sortingtilesize) ty = (tri.centery // sortingtilesize) % (imageheight // sortingtilesize) sortingtiles.setdefault((tx, ty), []).append(tri) # 3. Process each N x N raytracing tile for tiley in range(0, imageheight, N): for tilex in range(0, imagewidth, N): # Partition shared memory into k x k regions sharedmemory = [None] (k k) for s in range(k): for t in range(k): sorttileidx = s k + t stx = tilex + s N sty = tiley + t N sttx = stx // sortingtilesize stty = sty // sortingtilesize # Load triangles for this sorting tile into shared memory region sharedmemory[sorttileidx] = sortingtiles.get((sttx, stty), []) # Synchronize threads # syncthreads() # Compute intersections for the loaded triangles for threadid in range(N N): u = tilex + (threadid % N) v = tiley + (threadid // N) ray = generatecameraray(u, v, camera) hit = False for tri in sharedmemory[sorttileidx]: if raytriangleintersect(ray, tri): hit = True break if hit: recordintersection(u, v, ray) break # Front-to-back: stop checking later voxels # Synchronize threads before loading next batch # syncthreads() def isinviewfrustum(tri, camera): return all(plane.dot(tri.vertices) >= 0 for plane in camera.frustumplanes) # def isfrontfacing(tri, camera): return tri.normal.dot(camera.viewdirection) < 0 # def generatecameraray(u, v, camera): return Ray(camera.origin, camera.direction + u camera.right + v camera.up) # def raytriangleintersect(ray, tri): # Standard Möller–Trumbore intersection routine # Computes barycentric coordinates and depth; returns True if 0 <= u, v <= 1 and depth > 0 return True # Standard routine Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Hierarchy: The grid lacks the tree property, so it cannot eliminate triangles before intersection checking as effectively as BVH/Kd-trees. Secondary Rays: The structure is ray-specialized for primary rays and cannot efficiently handle other rays (e.g., reflection). SIMD Utilization: If the number of threads is below the SIMD width, computing resources may be wasted. Indirect mapping helps balance this. A thread mapping strategy that sorts triangles to smaller tiles but raytraces using a larger number of threads to balance coherence and SIMD utilization. It maps threads differently than the sorting tiles: triangles from each sorting tile are brought to the respective area of the shared memory and intersected with rays corresponding to the sorting tiles. On the Happy Buddha benchmark, indirect mapping provided a 10-30 percent speedup as the maximum number of triangles checked dropped by more than half. Time Complexity: Grid construction is low cost, reducing to sorting of triangle-voxel pairs. Memory Complexity: Depends on shared memory partitioning and the number of triangles per voxel. Performance: Provides perfect coherence for primary rays. Indirect mapping yields 10-30% speedup on benchmarks like Happy Buddha. Strengths: Perfect coherence for primary rays; low construction cost; efficient shared memory reuse on GPUs. Limitations: Cannot efficiently handle secondary rays; no hierarchical culling; performance sensitive to SIMD width. When to Use: Primary ray tracing on GPU hardware where shared memory reuse is critical. When Not to Use: Secondary ray tracing (use uniform grids instead) or scenes requiring hierarchical culling. The Perspective Grid was introduced in the context of raytracing dynamic scenes on the GPU using grids. It builds on earlier work regarding grid-based raytracing. The method was developed to address the inefficiencies of uniform grids for primary rays and the overhead of hierarchical structures on GPUs. name: Indirect Mapping
head: Indirect thread mapping, Tile-based indirect mapping
body: Indirect mapping is a thread-to-data mapping strategy used in GPU-based ray tracing to balance spatial coherence with SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) utilization. It addresses the conflict between sorting geometry into small tiles for efficient culling and the need for large thread blocks to saturate GPU hardware. Unlike standard direct mapping where thread indices align strictly with sorting tiles, indirect mapping decouples the sorting granularity from the ray-tracing granularity, allowing a larger number of threads to process a coarser area while maintaining coherence within sub-tiles. Inputs: Triangle mesh data. Image dimensions (width W, height H). Sorting tile dimensions (kN \times kN pixels). Ray-tracing tile dimensions (N \times N pixels). GPU hardware parameters (SIMD width, shared memory size). Outputs: Rendered image with reduced triangle intersection overhead. Data Structures: Sorting Tiles: The image is divided into kN \times kN pixel tiles. Triangles are sorted into these tiles. Ray-Tracing Tiles: The image is divided into N \times N pixel tiles. Each ray-tracing tile contains a k \times k group of sorting tiles. Shared Memory: Partitioned equally among the sorting tiles within a ray-tracing tile. Parameters: k: The factor by which sorting tiles are finer than ray-tracing tiles. The source specifies that a 2 \times 2 configuration (i.e., k=2) provides the best results on current GPU hardware. N: Base dimension of the ray-tracing tile. Steps: 1. Sort Triangles: Sort all triangles into kN \times kN sorting tiles in image space. This creates a finer-grained spatial partition than the final ray-tracing tiles. 2. Initialize Ray-Tracing Tile: Launch a work group (thread block) for each N \times N ray-tracing tile. This work group contains more threads than a standard direct-mapping block to cover the larger area and utilize SIMD units. 3. Partition Shared Memory: Divide the available shared memory for the work group into k \times k regions, one for each sorting tile contained within the current ray-tracing tile. 4. Load Geometry: For each sorting tile within the current ray-tracing tile, load its associated triangles into the corresponding region of shared memory. 5. Ray Tracing: Threads within the work group trace rays corresponding to the pixels in the N \times N ray-tracing tile. When a thread needs to intersect a ray with triangles, it accesses the shared memory region corresponding to the sorting tile that contains the relevant triangles. 6. Intersection: Perform ray-triangle intersection tests using the triangles loaded in shared memory. The indirect mapping ensures that while threads cover a larger area, they only check triangles from the specific sorting tiles relevant to their ray's path, reducing the maximum number of triangles checked. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytracingtilekernel(tilex, tiley, k, N, triangles, sortingtiles): # 1. Identify the kk sorting tiles covered by this ray-tracing tile sortingtilestartx = tilex k sortingtilestarty = tiley k # 2. Load triangles for each sorting tile into shared memory # sharedmem is a 2D array of size [k][k] of triangle lists for stx in range(k): for sty in range(k): globalstx = sortingtilestartx + stx globalsty = sortingtilestarty + sty sharedmem[stx][sty] = sortingtiles[globalstx][globalsty].triangles # 3. Threads trace rays for the NN pixel area # Thread indices map to pixels in the NN tile pixelx = threadx + tilex N pixely = thready + tiley N # Generate ray for this pixel ray = generateray(pixelx, pixely) # Determine which sorting tile this pixel falls into # Since sorting tiles are kN, and ray-tracing tiles are N, # we need to map the pixel to the correct sorting tile within the block localstx = pixelx % (k N) // N # Simplified mapping logic based on grid structure localsty = pixely % (k N) // N # Actually, the source says "triangles from each sorting tile are brought to the respective area... # and are intersected with the rays corresponding to the sorting tiles." # This implies the threads might be organized or the access pattern is such that # they check the specific shared memory block for the sorting tile containing the ray's origin/intersection. # More accurately based on source: # The work group has more threads. The shared memory is partitioned. # Triangles from each sorting tile are in their respective shared memory area. # Rays are intersected with triangles. closesthit = None mint = infinity # Iterate over the kk sorting tiles in shared memory for stx in range(k): for sty in range(k): # Access triangles in shared memory trilist = sharedmem[stx][sty] # Intersect ray with triangles in this sorting tile for tri in trilist: t = intersect(ray, tri) if t is not None and t < mint: mint = t closesthit = tri return closesthit Note: The pseudocode above simplifies the thread-to-pixel mapping. The key insight is that the shared memory holds triangles for the finer kN \times kN tiles, and the larger thread block processes the N \times N area, accessing the appropriate shared memory partition based on spatial locality. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shared Memory Limits: The number of triangles loaded into shared memory must fit within the available shared memory per work group. If a sorting tile contains too many triangles, the method may fail or require fallback strategies. SIMD Utilization: If the number of threads is too low relative to the SIMD width, computing resources are wasted. Indirect mapping helps balance this by allowing larger thread blocks. Precision: Standard ray-triangle intersection precision issues apply. A technique to resolve uncoalesced memory access in subpixel-level rasterization by reordering GPU thread assignment to subpixels based on viewpoint indices. It ensures that warp threads process subpixels from the same or nearby viewpoints, restoring viewpoint monotonicity and enabling coalesced memory access. It is chosen when rendering light field displays or multi-view images where subpixel-level rasterization causes memory access inefficiencies due to scattered viewpoint indices. It differs from standard indirect mapping by operating on subpixel coordinates and viewpoint indices rather than triangle tiles and primary rays. Performance: On the Happy Buddha benchmark, indirect mapping provided a 10-30 percent speedup. Efficiency: The maximum number of triangles checked dropped by more than half due to the finer sorting. Hardware Suitability: Best results are observed with a 2 \times 2 sorting tile configuration on current GPU hardware. Complexity: The method adds overhead for sorting triangles into finer tiles and managing shared memory partitions, but reduces the computational cost of ray-triangle intersections. Limitations: Requires sufficient shared memory to hold triangles for multiple sorting tiles. Performance is sensitive to the SIMD width and the distribution of triangles across tiles. Indirect mapping was introduced in the context of raytracing dynamic scenes on the GPU. It was developed to address the trade-off between spatial coherence (achieved by sorting geometry into tiles) and hardware utilization (achieved by using large thread blocks). The method is particularly relevant for GPU architectures where shared memory and SIMD units are critical performance factors.
