name: Dynamic Frame Rate Adaptation
head: Automatic resolution adoption, Dynamic resolution distribution
body: Dynamic Frame Rate Adaptation is a runtime adjustment system that tracks rendering performance and adjusts the distribution of resolution levels on the fly to maintain a consistently high update rate above a set threshold. It solves the problem of performance instability in volume rendering, where small parametric changes (e.g., transfer function modifications) can cause frame rate dips leading to cybersickness. It sets itself apart from static resolution schemes by continuously shifting the "anchor points" between resolution levels based on the gradient of recent frame times, rather than using fixed blending factors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sliding window of rendering times for the last n frames; current frame rendering time; lower and upper refresh rate thresholds; the current Multi-Anchor Blending (MAB) configuration. Output: Updated blending factors (resolution level distribution) for the next frame. Data Structures: Performance Window: A circular buffer or array storing the rendering time ti for the last n frames. Lookup Texture (fa): A 1D texture used as a fast lookup function to determine the corresponding resolution level of a texel and whether it has to be traversed by the raycaster. Layout: The texture width corresponds to the domain of the blending function. Channels: The four color channels (RGBA) store the blending factors for the corresponding resolution levels of the MAB. Content: Each channel value represents the weight of a specific resolution level, with a smooth-step function applied between adjacent resolution levels to ensure unnoticeable blending. Parameters: n: Size of the sliding window (number of past frames). T{low}: Lower threshold for minimum acceptable refresh rate (e.g., 90 Hz). T{high}: Upper threshold for sufficiently high refresh rate. Steps: 1. Track Performance: Maintain a sliding window of the last n frame rendering times. 2. Compare Thresholds: Compare the previous frame's rendering time against the lower threshold T{low} and upper threshold T{high}. If the frame rate is below T{low} (performance is poor), shift the resolution distribution to emit fewer rays. If the frame rate is above T{high} (performance is good), increase the number of rays. 3. Compute Gradient: Calculate the gradient of the rendering time window to determine the direction and magnitude of the adjustment. 4. Select Anchor Point: Evaluate the change in rendering time over the last n frames to determine which anchor point between two adjacent resolution levels should be moved. 5. Determine Shift Magnitude: Calculate how far the selected anchor point should be shifted in the corresponding direction. 6. Update Lookup Texture: Modify the fa 1D texture by adjusting the values in the RGBA channels to reflect the new blending factors for each resolution level. 7. Raycasting: During the raycast, use the updated fa texture to look up the corresponding resolution level for each texel and determine if it needs to be traversed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateresolutiondistribution(window, currenttime, tlowhz, thighhz, n, numlevels, fatexture): # Convert Hz thresholds to seconds for time comparison tlowsec = 1.0 / tlowhz thighsec = 1.0 / thighhz # 1. Track Performance: Append current time, maintain window size n window.append(currenttime) if len(window) > n: window.pop(0) # 2. Compare Thresholds: Compare previous frame time against thresholds prevtime = window[-1] if prevtime > tlowsec: direction = -1 # Performance below threshold: shift to fewer rays elif prevtime < thighsec: direction = 1 # Performance above threshold: increase rays else: direction = 0 # Within range: no shift # 3. Compute Gradient: Evaluate change in rendering time over the last n-frames timechange = window[-1] - window[0] gradient = timechange / max(n - 1, 1) # 4 & 5. Select Anchor Point & Determine Shift Magnitude # Map gradient magnitude and direction to an anchor index and shift amount anchoridx = max(0, min(numlevels - 2, int(direction abs(gradient) 10))) shiftmagnitude = min(0.1, abs(gradient) 0.5) # 6. Update Lookup Texture: Modify the fa 1D texture newfa = updatefatexture(fatexture, anchoridx, shiftmagnitude, direction) return newfa def updatefatexture(fatexture, anchoridx, shiftmagnitude, direction): # Adjust blending factors around the selected anchor point newtexture = fatexture.copy() if direction != 0: # Shift anchor point towards lower resolution (direction=-1) or higher (direction=1) for i in range(len(newtexture)): if i == anchoridx: newtexture[i] += shiftmagnitude direction elif i == anchoridx + 1: newtexture[i] -= shiftmagnitude direction # Clamp values to valid blending range newtexture = [max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) for v in newtexture] return newtexture Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Minor Variations: Small performance fluctuations primarily adjust higher resolution levels, causing only slight alterations to the overall distribution. High Deviations: Large performance deviations primarily shift lower resolutions to compensate for rendering performance. Precision: The smooth-step function between adjacent resolution levels is critical for unnoticeable blending; discontinuities here may cause visual artifacts. Time Complexity: The adjustment logic involves a sliding window update and a lookup texture modification, which is O(1) per frame relative to the scene complexity, though dependent on n for gradient calculation. The raycasting cost is reduced by shifting to lower resolutions when performance is poor. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the performance window (O(n)) and the fa lookup texture (constant size, typically small 1D texture). Measured Performance: On an RTX 2070, the baseline system maintained average refresh rates above 90 Hz for MRI and CT datasets. With dynamic adaptation, the system maintained rates above 90 Hz on both RTX 2070 and RTX 2060m hardware, whereas the baseline failed on the RTX 2060m for one dataset. The 1% lowest frame rates also improved (e.g., MRI dataset on RTX 2060m: 62.6 Hz baseline vs 91.2 Hz dynamic). Strengths: Guarantees refresh rates above a set threshold, reducing cybersickness. Adapts to runtime parametric changes (e.g., transfer function updates). Limitations: Relies on accurate tracking of frame times. The specific mapping of gradient to anchor shift requires tuning. The method originates from research on embracing raycasting for virtual reality, specifically addressing the need for consistent high update rates to prevent cybersickness. It builds on the Multi-Anchor Blending (MAB) technique, using a 1D lookup texture (fa) similar to transfer functions in direct volume rendering to manage resolution level blending. The system was tested on MRI and CT datasets using RTX 2070 and RTX 2060m hardware. Embracing Raycasting for Virtual Reality, https://doi.org/10.24132/csrn.3201.16, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Time-critical level-of-detail selection
head: automatic level-of-detail selection
body: Time-critical level-of-detail selection is an adaptive rendering technique that dynamically adjusts the visual fidelity of a volume rendering to maintain a target frame rate. It solves the problem of unpredictable rendering times in complex scenes by predicting the cost of the next frame and selecting an appropriate level-of-detail beforehand. Unlike static LOD schemes, this method is driven by real-time performance statistics, allowing it to react to scene complexity changes or hardware load variations. It differs from Dynamic Resolution Adaptation by adjusting the geometric or shader complexity of the volume representation rather than the pixel resolution of the output viewport. The method operates in a feedback loop per frame. Inputs: Current frame render time (T{current}). Desired frame rate (R{target}), which defines the time budget T{budget} = 1/R{target}. Performance statistics history (used for prediction). Outputs: Selected Level-of-Detail (LOD{next}) for the subsequent frame. Data Structures: Performance Buffer: A circular buffer or moving average window storing recent frame times (Ti). LOD Map: A mapping from predicted time budgets to discrete LOD levels (e.g., voxel spacing, transfer function complexity, or proxy geometry type). Steps: 1. Collect Statistics: Measure the actual rendering time T{current} of the current frame. 2. Predict Time: Estimate the rendering time for the next frame, T{pred}, using the collected performance statistics. The sources do not specify the exact prediction algorithm. A standard implementation uses an exponential moving average: T{pred} = \alpha T{current} + (1-\alpha) T{pred}, where \alpha is a smoothing factor. 3. Select LOD: Compare T{pred} against T{budget}. If T{pred} > T{budget}, select a lower LOD (simpler representation) to reduce future render time. If T{pred} \le T{budget}, select a higher LOD (more detailed representation) to improve visual quality. 4. Apply LOD: Configure the renderer for the next frame with the selected LOD{next}. Parameters: Desired Frame Rate (R{target}): The target frames per second. Prediction Smoothing Factor (\alpha): Controls the responsiveness to sudden changes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Oscillation: Rapid switching between LOD levels if T{pred} hovers near T{budget}; mitigated by hysteresis or a minimum dwell time at each LOD level. Artifacts: Switching LODs can cause visual discontinuities; using different proxy geometries other than planes avoids artifacts but incurs a computational price, while modifying transfer functions in lower-resolution nodes limits artifacts. Prediction Error: Inaccurate prediction models may yield inappropriate LOD selections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def timecriticallodselection(frametime, targetfps, history, lodthresholds, alpha): """ frametime: float, time taken to render the current frame in seconds. targetfps: float, desired frames per second. history: list of floats, recent predicted times (used for EMA). lodthresholds: list of floats, sorted ascending time thresholds for each LOD level. alpha: float, exponential moving average smoothing factor (0 < alpha <= 1). Returns: int, the selected LOD index for the next frame. """ # Update exponential moving average prediction if not history: predictedtime = frametime else: predictedtime = alpha frametime + (1 - alpha) history[-1] history.append(predictedtime) # Calculate time budget timebudget = 1.0 / targetfps # Select LOD based on predicted time vs budget # LOD index 0 is highest detail; higher indices are lower detail selectedlod = 0 for i, threshold in enumerate(lodthresholds): if predictedtime > threshold: selectedlod = i + 1 else: break return selectedlod A method for automatic shader simplification that dynamically adjusts the complexity of procedural texture evaluations to match performance constraints. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its focus on algorithmic simplification of the shader code itself rather than pre-filtering or geometric reduction. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Maintains target frame rate in dynamic scenes; allows user-defined quality preferences via parameters. Limitations: Potential for visual artifacts during LOD transitions. When to Use: Interactive volume visualization where frame rate stability is critical. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The algorithm was developed by Li et al. as part of adaptive volume rendering schemes. It is also known as automatic level-of-detail selection. name: Foveated Rendering
head: Foveated Volume Rendering
body: Foveated rendering increases performance on eye-tracked displays by reducing the resolution of the rendered image or hologram outside the user's tracked foveal position. It differs from sibling methods like Dynamic Resolution Adaptation by relying on biological gaze data rather than temporal frame budgets. It is distinct from Dynamic Frame Rate Adaptation as it maintains a constant frame rate by reducing spatial fidelity rather than temporal fidelity. Inputs: Object points or volume data. Eye-tracking data providing the fovea position on the display. Display resolution parameters. Outputs: A composite image with high resolution in the foveal region and lower resolution in the periphery. Data Structures: Object Points: A list of all object points oi. Exact layout and bit packing are not given in the sources. Sub-hologram Width (w): A parameter defining the resolution of the calculation grid. Exact layout and bit packing are not given in the sources. Blending Weights: A transition band mask used to blend high-resolution and low-resolution pixel values. Exact layout and bit packing are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Determine Foveal Region: Identify the center region corresponding to the user's tracked fovea position. 2. Define Resolution Zones: High-Resolution Zone: A tight projection frustum is defined for the center region to maximize culling efficiency. Low-Resolution Zone: For regions outside the fovea, the sub-hologram width w is decreased. This effectively cuts high frequencies. The periphery is sampled at half resolution in evaluations. Transition Band: A band is established between the high-res and low-res zones. 3. Compute Image Data: Calculate pixel values for the high-resolution center using all object points. Calculate pixel values for the low-resolution periphery using all object points but with the reduced width w. 4. Blend: In the transition band, gradually adjust blending weights for high-res and low-res pixel values to avoid noticeable discontinuities. 5. Upscale and Composite: Upscale the low-resolution peripheral data to match the high-resolution center dimensions. Composite the images using NVIDIA Performance Primitives (NPP) and a custom CUDA kernel. Formulas: The performance gain is derived from the quadratic scaling of calculation speed with sub-hologram size w in point-wise integration methods. If T is time and w is width, T \propto w^2. Reducing w outside the fovea reduces T significantly. Parameters: Transition Band Width: Not given in the sources. Resolution Ratio: The periphery is sampled at half resolution in the evaluation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Performance: The method has not been found to run at high video rates on current GPUs. Discontinuities: Abrupt changes in resolution can cause visible artifacts; a transition band is required. Temporal Aliasing: Including all object points in the calculation helps reduce temporal aliasing compared to methods that remove points. A method to increase performance in eye-tracked displays by reducing the resolution of the hologram outside the tracked fovea position. It includes all object points but decreases the sub-hologram width w outside the fovea, cutting high frequencies. It differs from Hong et al. [2016] who reduced the density of object points oi outside the fovea. It has not been found to run at high video rates on current GPUs. Time Complexity: Scales quadratically with the sub-hologram size w in the point-wise integration method. By reducing w in the periphery, total computation time is reduced. Memory Complexity: Requires storing both high-res and low-res buffers plus blending weights. Performance: Evaluated on a Meta Quest 3 (2064×2208 pixels) with an NVIDIA RTX 4090. However, it has not been found to run at high video rates on current GPUs. Strengths: Reduces temporal aliasing by keeping all object points in the calculation. Maximizes culling efficiency in the center via a tight frustum. Limitations: Does not achieve high video rates on current hardware. Requires eye-tracking hardware. Origin: The concept of reducing resolution outside the fovea in eye-tracked displays is attributed to Guenter et al. [2012]. History: Hong et al. [2016] performed foveated rendering by reducing the density of object points oi outside the fovea. The method described here differs by including all object points but decreasing the sub-hologram width w. Recent implementations utilize 3D Gaussian Splatting frameworks, evaluating performance on VR headsets like the Meta Quest 3. Usage: Used in holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality. name: Render State Machine
body: The Render State Machine is a threaded control mechanism that manages rendering resolution and interruption based on camera movement and user actions to maintain a target frame rate. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly handling interruption via Python trace functions to discard incomplete outputs, ensuring viewer consistency. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Camera state, user actions, current render state, target FPS, maximum resolution, visibility ray budget. Outputs: Rendered image (uint8), updated render state, interrupt flags. Data Structures Transitions Table: A dictionary mapping current states to action-based next states. Type: Dict[RenderStates, Dict[RenderActions, RenderStates]]. Layout: Nested dictionaries. Default: All transitions map to the current state (self-transition). Overrides: lowmove + static → lowstatic; lowstatic + static → high; lowstatic + step → high; lowstatic + move → lowmove; high + move → lowmove; high + rerender → lowstatic. RenderStates: Literal type with values 'lowmove', 'lowstatic', 'high'. RenderActions: Literal type with values 'rerender', 'move', 'static', 'step'. Parameters targetfps: Target frames per second for low-resolution rendering. Default: 24. visrayspersec: Visibility rays per second budget. Default: 100,000 if not initialized or not in global buffer. maxres: Maximum resolution height from control panel. Steps 1. Initialize Transitions: Create an empty dictionary for each state. Set all actions to self-transition. Override specific transitions as defined in the Transitions Table. 2. Interrupt Logic: If the current state is 'high' and the next action is 'move' or 'rerender', set interruptrenderflag to True and trigger rendertrigger. 3. Interrupt Check: In a Python trace function, if the event is 'line' and interruptrenderflag is True, reset the flag and raise IOChangeException. 4. Image Resolution Calculation: If aspectratio is 0, set it to 0.001. Get maxres from the control panel. If state is 'high', set height to maxres. Set width to height aspectratio, capped at maxres. If state is 'lowmove' or 'lowstatic', calculate numvisrays as visrayspersec / targetfps. Calculate height as sqrt(numvisrays / aspectratio), rounded to the nearest 10, clamped between 30 and maxres. Set width to height aspectratio, capped at maxres. 5. Rendering: Update render AABB. Calculate image resolution. Get camera. Generate rays. If model is GaussianSplattingModel or DepthGSModel, use getoutputsforcamera; else use getoutputsforcameraraybundle. If cropviewport is true, set background color and use backgroundcoloroverridecontext; otherwise, no background override. Evaluate model, render with torch.nograd(), then set model to train mode. 6. Output Sending: Get output keys. If changed, send output options message and update control panel. Get selected output render. Apply colormap. If split mode, get split output, apply colormap, calculate split index, concatenate selected and split outputs with a divider line at splitindex. Convert to uint8. Send as background image. Pitfalls If IOChangeException is raised during render, the output is discarded and not sent to the viewer. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import torch from contextlib import contextmanager class IOChangeException(Exception): pass class GaussianSplattingModel: pass class DepthGSModel: pass @contextmanager def backgroundcoloroverridecontext(bgcolor): # Standard context manager to override background color during evaluation yield def generaterays(camera, width, height): # Standard ray generation creates a ray bundle for each pixel return {"origin": camera.position, "direction": camera.direction, "width": width, "height": height} def evaluatemodel(model, raybundle): # Standard model forward pass return {"color": torch.zeros(3, dtype=torch.float32), "backgroundcolor": torch.zeros(3, dtype=torch.float32)} def applycolormap(tensor): # Standard colormap application return tensor def converttouint8(tensor): # Standard uint8 conversion return (tensor.clamp(0, 1) 255).to(torch.uint8) def getsplitoutput(): # Retrieves secondary output for split view return torch.zeros(3, dtype=torch.float32) def calculatesplitindex(width, height): # Calculates divider position return width // 2 def concatenatewithdivider(img1, img2, splitindex): # Concatenates images with a vertical divider line divider = torch.zeros(1, img1.shape[1], dtype=torch.uint8) return torch.cat([img1[:,:splitindex], divider, img2], dim=1) class RenderStateMachine: def init(self, targetfps=24, visrayspersec=100000, maxres=1080): self.targetfps = targetfps self.visrayspersec = visrayspersec self.maxres = maxres self.currentstate = 'lowmove' self.interruptrenderflag = False self.transitions = { state: {action: state for action in ['rerender', 'move', 'static', 'step']} for state in ['lowmove', 'lowstatic', 'high'] } self.transitions['lowmove']['static'] = 'lowstatic' self.transitions['lowstatic']['static'] = 'high' self.transitions['lowstatic']['step'] = 'high' self.transitions['lowstatic']['move'] = 'lowmove' self.transitions['high']['move'] = 'lowmove' self.transitions['high']['rerender'] = 'lowstatic' def setaction(self, action): nextstate = self.transitions[self.currentstate][action] if self.currentstate == 'high' and action in ['move', 'rerender']: self.interruptrenderflag = True # rendertrigger() would be called here self.currentstate = nextstate def calculateresolution(self, aspectratio): if aspectratio == 0: aspectratio = 0.001 if self.currentstate == 'high': height = self.maxres width = min(height aspectratio, self.maxres) else: numvisrays = self.visrayspersec / self.targetfps height = math.sqrt(numvisrays / aspectratio) height = round(height / 10) 10 height = max(30, min(height, self.maxres)) width = min(height aspectratio, self.maxres) return int(width), int(height) def render(self, model, camera, cropviewport=False, splitmode=False): # Interrupt check is handled by Python trace function raising IOChangeException if self.interruptrenderflag: # In actual implementation, trace function raises IOChangeException pass width, height = self.calculateresolution(camera.aspectratio) if isinstance(model, (GaussianSplattingModel, DepthGSModel)): outputs = model.getoutputsforcamera(camera) else: raybundle = generaterays(camera, width, height) outputs = model.getoutputsforcameraraybundle(raybundle) if cropviewport: with backgroundcoloroverridecontext(outputs.get("backgroundcolor", torch.zeros(3))): rendered = evaluatemodel(model, outputs) else: rendered = evaluatemodel(model, outputs) with torch.nograd(): finalimage = applycolormap(rendered) if splitmode: splitoutput = getsplitoutput() splitcolormap = applycolormap(splitoutput) splitindex = calculatesplitindex(width, height) finalimage = concatenatewithdivider(finalimage, splitcolormap, splitindex) finalimageuint8 = converttouint8(finalimage) model.train() return finalimageuint8 Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Maintains target FPS (default 24) during low-resolution states by limiting visibility rays. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. It was developed to address the need for responsive interactive rendering in 3D Gaussian Splatting, where high-resolution rendering can be computationally expensive and slow down interaction. name: Adaptive Quality
head: Frame Rate Maintenance via Quality Adjustment, Time-based Quality Control
body: Adaptive Quality is a resolution adaptation technique that dynamically adjusts rendering parameters (such as ray count or sampling distance) to maintain a target frame rate based on measured rendering time. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on computational budget allocation per frame rather than viewport reduction Parent or spatial foveation Foveated Rendering. It is particularly effective on CPUs where execution time is predictable, whereas GPUs may benefit more from fixed quality settings. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current frame rendering time (T{current}), target frame time (T{target} = 1/FPS{target}), and current quality parameters (number of casted rays, sampling distances, iteration counts). Output: Adjusted quality parameters for the subsequent rendering request. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. The method relies on scalar timing measurements and quality control flags. Steps: 1. Measure the time taken to render the current frame (T{current}). 2. Compare T{current} with the target frame time (T{target}). 3. If T{current} > T{target} (rendering is too slow): Reduce quality parameters for the next frame, such as decreasing the number of casted rays or increasing sampling distances. During interactive scenarios (rotation, setting changes), enforce the target FPS by lowering resolution or quality. 4. If T{current} \le T{target} (rendering is within budget): Increase quality parameters for the next frame to improve image fidelity, such as increasing iterations to reduce Monte Carlo noise. Maintain the target frame rate while maximizing visual quality. Parameters: Target FPS: User-defined or system-default value. Quality Metrics: Number of casted rays, sampling distances, or iteration counts. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU vs. CPU: The method works very well for CPUs because computation time is predictable. For GPU volume rendering, fixed quality (“Normal” setting) may be more suitable due to hardware parallelism and scheduling variability. Interaction: Quality reduction is specifically triggered during user interaction to ensure responsiveness. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivequalitystep(targetfps, currentframetime, currentraycount, currentsamplingdistance, currentiterations): """ Adjusts quality parameters for the next frame based on current render time. Args: targetfps (float): Desired frames per second. currentframetime (float): Time taken to render the current frame in seconds. currentraycount (int): Number of rays cast per pixel. currentsamplingdistance (float): Distance between samples along rays. currentiterations (int): Number of Monte Carlo iterations per sample. Returns: tuple: (nextraycount, nextsamplingdistance, nextiterations) """ targetframetime = 1.0 / targetfps if currentframetime > targetframetime: # Rendering exceeded the time budget; reduce quality # Decrease ray count, increase sampling distance (fewer samples) nextraycount = max(1, currentraycount // 2) nextsamplingdistance = currentsamplingdistance 2.0 nextiterations = max(1, currentiterations // 2) else: # Rendering within budget; increase quality # Increase iterations to reduce Monte Carlo noise nextraycount = currentraycount 2 nextsamplingdistance = currentsamplingdistance / 2.0 nextiterations = currentiterations 2 return nextraycount, nextsamplingdistance, nextiterations A variant described in the context of remote volume rendering where a Web server and rendering server coordinate to maintain quality. If the Web server is fast, the rendering server increases the number of iterations per frame to improve image quality (reduce noise in Monte Carlo rendering) while maintaining the target frame rate. This ensures users receive high-quality images quickly across different network environments. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Works very well for CPUs due to predictable computation time. For GPUs, fixed quality may be more suitable, suggesting limitations in GPU-centric pipelines. Strengths: Maintains interactive frame rates during heavy interaction; improves quality when idle. Limitations: Less effective on GPUs due to unpredictable execution times; requires accurate timing measurement. The method is documented in the 3D Slicer volume rendering module, which provides advanced controls for quality adaptation during interaction. It is also referenced in research on optimized interactive remote realistic volume rendering, where coupling algorithms between Web and rendering servers are used to balance quality and speed. name: Resolution and Frame Splitting
head: Performance Optimization: Resolution and Frame Splitting
body: Resolution and Frame Splitting is an image-order volume rendering acceleration technique that reduces computational load by lowering spatial resolution and/or distributing rendering work across multiple frames. It solves the problem of high ray-marching costs in real-time volume rendering, particularly for large-scale effects like volumetric clouds. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Dynamic Resolution Adaptation by applying fixed, coarse-grained resolution reductions or temporal splitting strategies rather than fine-grained, metric-driven per-pixel sampling adjustments. Inputs: Input buffer (Scene Color RT), camera parameters, hardware capability tier (High/Mid/Low), and target frame rate. Outputs: Final rendered image with volumetric effects composited into the Scene Color RT. Data Structures: Resolution Buffer: A render target with dimensions W' \times H', where W' \le W and H' \le H. Frame History Buffer: Stores previous frame's volumetric contribution for temporal accumulation. Steps: 1. Hardware Tier Detection: Determine if the target platform is High-end or Mid/Low-end. 2. Resolution Selection: If High-end: Set resolution to 1/2 \times 1/2 of the original screen resolution (W' = W/2, H' = H/2). If Mid/Low-end: Enable Frame Splitting. This involves rendering only a subset of the volume (e.g., clouds) in the current frame, assuming no intersection with other scene objects to simplify depth handling. 3. Ray Marching: Perform volume integration (ray marching) at the selected resolution. For frame splitting, this may involve interlaced or partial coverage strategies similar to those used in Red Dead Redemption 2. 4. Temporal Filtering: Apply temporal upsampling and filtering to the rendered volumetric buffer. This step combines the current frame's result with history buffers to reduce noise and stabilize the image. 5. Upsampling: Upsample the filtered volumetric buffer back to the original screen resolution (W \times H). Blue noise dithering may be applied during this step to mitigate aliasing artifacts caused by reduced sampling. 6. Compositing: Blend the upsampled volumetric result into the Scene Color Render Target. Parameters: Resolution Scale: 0.5 for High-end. Splitting Factor: Not explicitly defined, but implies a fraction of the volume or time steps rendered per frame. Edge Cases: Cloud-Object Intersection: The frame splitting method assumes clouds do not intersect other objects. If they do, additional depth handling is required, which complicates the simple splitting approach. Temporal Stability: Rapid camera movement or fast cloud motion can cause ghosting artifacts if the temporal history is not properly aligned or weighted. Interlaced Slice Rendering is an image-order volume rendering optimization that halves the per-frame computational workload by rendering only half of the horizontal slices per frame, alternating between odd and even slices. Time Complexity: Reduces ray marching cost by a factor of 4 for 1/2 \times 1/2 resolution. Frame splitting reduces cost by the splitting factor (e.g., 2x if alternating frames). Memory Complexity: Requires additional buffers for history, temporal accumulation, and potentially lower-resolution intermediate targets. Performance: Significant FPS improvement on Mid/Low-end hardware. High-end hardware sees moderate improvement due to lower resolution but higher fill-rate requirements for upsampling. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective for static or slow-moving scenes; leverages temporal coherence. Limitations: Introduces temporal artifacts (ghosting, jitter) if not filtered properly; resolution loss can be noticeable; frame splitting can cause flickering if not handled with care. When to Use: Real-time rendering of large-scale volumetric effects where performance is critical and visual fidelity can be slightly compromised. When Not to Use: Scenes with fast-moving cameras or rapidly changing volumetric structures where temporal stability is hard to maintain. This technique is commonly used in real-time game engines for rendering volumetric clouds. It is mentioned in the context of High Dynamic Range Rendering (HDRP) and similar to techniques used in Red Dead Redemption 2. 体积云效果的实现，游戏世界的云合雾集, https://leihuo.163.com/institution/news/20230719/384231099592.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Interlaced Slice Rendering
head: Odd-Even Slice Rendering
body: Interlaced Slice Rendering is an image-order volume rendering optimization that halves the per-frame computational workload by rendering only half of the horizontal slices per frame, alternating between odd and even slices. It solves the problem of maintaining high frame rates in real-time volume rendering by doubling the effective frame rate perception while maintaining full spatial resolution over two frames, distinguishing itself from simple half-resolution rendering by preserving pixel detail when the camera is static or moving slowly. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset, camera parameters, and a target frame time budget. Output: A rendered frame buffer. Data Structures: Frame Buffer: A 2D array of pixels. The article does not specify bit depth, but notes 4 voxel colors with a brightness component. Render State: A boolean or integer flag indicating the current interlacing phase (odd/even) and a quality reduction factor (reduceQuality). Steps: 1. Determine the rendering mode based on camera velocity and frame time history. 2. If standard interlacing is active: Calculate the set of slices to render. If the current frame index N is even, render odd-numbered slices (1, 3, 5, \dots). If N is odd, render even-numbered slices (2, 4, 6, \dots). Render the selected slices into the frame buffer. Leave the unselected slices untouched from the previous frame. 3. If fast camera movement is detected (or adaptive quality triggers half-resolution mode): Calculate only 120 slices (half the total, e.g., 240 slices). For each calculated slice, copy the pixel data twice to fill the full resolution height, effectively duplicating rows. Apply dithering separately to the duplicated pixels to avoid interlacing artifacts and improve visual quality over simple blitting. 4. Display the frame buffer. Parameters: Total Slices: Example implementation uses 240 slices. Target Frame Time: Hardcoded to 27 ms in the source, but can be dynamic. Reduce Quality Factor: An integer value (e.g., 20) determining the width of edge regions for adaptive quality reduction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fast Camera Movement: Causes visible banding artifacts because only half the pixels update per frame in standard interlacing mode. The method mitigates this by switching to half-resolution duplication with dithering when movement is rapid. Precision: The source does not specify floating-point precision, but notes shading is pre-computed per tile, not per pixel, in the specific implementation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderinterlacedslice(volume, camera, framebuffer, frameindex, reducequality): # Determine if camera is moving fast isfastmovement = checkcameravelocity(camera) # Determine slice indices to render if not isfastmovement: # Standard interlacing: render half the slices if frameindex % 2 == 0: sliceindices = [i for i in range(1, totalslices + 1) if i % 2 != 0] else: sliceindices = [i for i in range(1, totalslices + 1) if i % 2 == 0] # Render selected slices, leave others untouched for sliceidx in sliceindices: renderslice(volume, camera, sliceidx, framebuffer) else: # Fast movement: half-resolution with duplication # Calculate only half the slices halfslices = totalslices // 2 for i in range(halfslices): sliceidx = i + 1 # Render the slice slicedata = renderslicedata(volume, camera, sliceidx) # Copy slice data twice to fill full resolution framebuffer[2i: 2i+2,:] = slicedata return framebuffer A dynamic quality adjustment system that increases the interlacing factor (e.g., from 2-way to 3-way) at the screen edges when rendering time exceeds a target, reducing workload where visual attention is lowest. It measures frame render time using playdate->system->getElapsedTime() and maintains a moving average over multiple frames. Every four frames, it compares the moving average to the desired time (27 ms); if the average is higher, it increases reduceQuality, and if lower, it decreases it. The reduced quality is applied by performing 3-way interlacing (or tripling slices in fast mode) only in the left-most and right-most slices, proportional to reduceQuality (e.g., 20 slices on each side). This mitigates visible banding artifacts by restricting them to screen edges where user attention is lower. Time Complexity: Reduces per-frame rendering work by approximately 50% in standard interlaced mode, as only half the slices are computed. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the full frame buffer, but no additional significant memory for the interlacing logic itself. Measured Performance: In the source implementation, the method allows for a perceived 30 fps frame rate while only computing 120 slices per frame (out of 240). The target frame time is 27 ms. Scaling: The method scales with the number of slices; halving the slices per frame halves the computational load regardless of total slice count. Strengths: Maintains full spatial resolution over two frames; improves perceived frame rate; adaptive quality allows dynamic adjustment to hardware constraints. Limitations: Fast camera movement causes banding artifacts in standard mode; requires dithering in half-resolution mode which is slightly slower than simple blitting. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering where perceived smoothness is prioritized over instantaneous pixel accuracy, and camera movement is generally slow to moderate. When Not to Use: When fast camera movement is frequent and banding artifacts are unacceptable, or when full instantaneous resolution is required. The method was described by Thomas in a devlog post on the Playdate Developer Forum in 2024, as part of a side project building a 3D engine for the Playdate console. The implementation uses a map of 128x128 tiles, where each tile is a voxel block with a base of 32x32 pixels and a maximum height of 28, using four voxel colors with dynamic brightness for shadows. Shading is pre-computed once per tile during startup, not in real-time. name: Mixed-Resolution Multi-Volume Rendering
head: Per-channel resolution selection
body: Mixed-resolution multi-volume rendering is a technique where different channels of a multi-volume dataset are rendered at different resolution levels to save memory and reduce sample evaluation. It addresses the inefficiency of applying a uniform high resolution to all channels when some possess lower frequency content or lower visual importance. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Level-of-detail (LOD) methods by operating on a per-channel basis within a single ray traversal, rather than switching the entire dataset's resolution or using spatial partitioning for the whole volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A multi-volume dataset with N channels, where each channel c has a multi-resolution hierarchy. Viewing parameters including camera position and ray direction. Output: A rendered image where each pixel is composed of contributions from channels sampled at their individually selected resolution levels. Data Structures: Channel Resolution Map: A function Rc(p, t) for each channel c \in \{0, \dots, N-1\} and spatial position p along ray parameter t. This determines the resolution level l to use for channel c at position p. Multi-resolution Hierarchy: Each channel c stores data at discrete resolution levels l. Level l=0 is the highest resolution level (finest grid), and higher l values represent coarser resolutions. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Ray: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. 2. Traverse Hierarchy: Iterate through the spatial structure (e.g., octree or brick hierarchy) along the ray. 3. Determine Resolution per Channel: For the current sample point p and ray parameter t, evaluate the resolution constraint function for each channel c: lc = \text{clamp}(Rc(p, t), l{\min}, l{\max}) The function Rc constrains the range of valid resolution levels. It may consider distance to the camera, frequency content of the channel, user-defined bounds, and transfer function importance. 4. Select Data: For each channel c, retrieve the voxel value from its hierarchy at level lc. 5. Sample: Evaluate the channel value at the sample point using the data from level lc. Note that if channels have different resolutions, the sampling rate along the ray may effectively differ per channel. A high-frequency channel might be sampled at every step, while a low-frequency channel might only need sampling every second step. 6. Composite: Accumulate the color and opacity contributions from all channels using standard volume rendering integration (e.g., front-to-back compositing). 7. Repeat: Continue until the ray exits the volume or a termination condition is met. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendermixedresolutionray(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds, channeldata, channelconfigs): # volumebounds: tuple of (minpoint, maxpoint), each point is (x,y,z) # channeldata: dict mapping channelid -> MultiResolutionHierarchy object # channelconfigs: dict mapping channelid -> function(pos, t, origin, dir) -> resolutionlevel color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 # Compute ray-volume intersection interval tmin = 0.0 tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if abs(raydirection[i]) > 1e-6: t1 = (volumebounds[0][i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] t2 = (volumebounds[1][i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) else: if rayorigin[i] < volumebounds[0][i] or rayorigin[i] > volumebounds[1][i]: return color if tmin > tmax: return color dt = 0.5 # Base step size t = tmin while t < tmax: pos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] channelsamples = {} for cid, hierarchy in channeldata.items(): # Evaluate resolution constraint function for channel cid level = channelconfigscid # Retrieve and interpolate value from hierarchy at selected level value = hierarchy.sample(level, pos) channelsamples[cid] = value # Composite channels using front-to-back blending for cid, value in channelsamples.items(): # Map channel value to color and opacity via transfer function ccolor = [value, value, value] # Standard transfer function mapping calpha = min(value, 1.0) weight = calpha (1.0 - alpha) color[0] += ccolor[0] weight color[1] += ccolor[1] weight color[2] += ccolor[2] weight alpha += weight if alpha >= 1.0: break t += dt return color Parameters: Resolution Constraint Function: The specific logic for Rc. Can be user-defined bounds or a complex function. Typical example values from human tissue data: pink channel at l3, orange channel at l5/l4/l0, and rest at l0. Resolution Levels: Discrete levels l0, \dots, l{max}. l0 is the highest resolution level. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: A channel with high-frequency content may require a higher sampling rate (lower l) to avoid aliasing, while another may only need sampling at every second step. Memory Management: Limiting the range of resolutions uploaded to the GPU on a per-channel basis saves memory. Synchronization: Ensuring that sampling positions for different channels are consistent or appropriately interpolated if their grid spacings differ significantly. Chooses resolution based on the spectral content of each channel. High-frequency channels use higher resolution. Sets itself apart by analyzing channel-specific frequency spectra rather than spatial distance. Choose when channels have distinct frequency characteristics. Link to parent. Chooses resolution based on the distance to the camera or viewing angle. Distant objects/channels use lower resolution. Sets itself apart by using camera-relative metrics instead of intrinsic data properties. Choose when viewpoint significantly affects perceived detail. Link to parent. Chooses resolution based on the visual importance of the channel, often derived from the transfer function. Less important channels use lower resolution. Sets itself apart by weighting channels against user-defined visual priorities. Choose when some channels are secondary or supplementary. Link to parent. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of channels and the average resolution level selected. If N channels are rendered, and the average number of samples per ray is S, the complexity is roughly O(N \cdot S). However, by reducing the resolution for less important channels, S can be reduced for those channels, leading to an overall speedup. Memory Complexity: Reduced by only uploading the necessary resolution levels for each channel to the GPU. The memory footprint is proportional to the sum of the sizes of the selected resolution levels for all channels. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significant memory savings for large multi-volume datasets. Reduced computational cost for less important or low-frequency channels. Limitations: Potential for visual artifacts if resolution selection is not well-tuned. Complexity in managing different sampling rates for different channels. When to Use: Large-scale multi-volume datasets where channels have varying frequency content or importance. Out-of-core rendering scenarios. When Not to Use: Single-channel volumes or when all channels have similar frequency content and importance. This technique is described in the context of scalable web-based volume rendering of large biomedical datasets. It is part of a system that uses out-of-core methods and multi-resolution hierarchies (e.g., OME-Zarr files) to handle large data volumes. The approach allows for flexible resolution selection per channel based on various factors, enabling efficient rendering of complex multi-channel data. name: Volume Level-of-Detail (LOD) Rendering
head: Active Cut Rendering, Adaptive LOD Rendering
body: Volume Level-of-Detail (LOD) Rendering is a method that maximizes image quality within user-specified frame rate and system constraints (RAM, texture memory, bandwidth) by adaptively modifying the set of rendered octree cells. It solves the problem of maintaining interactivity for large datasets by dynamically adjusting the resolution of the volume representation based on viewing parameters and hardware limits. Unlike static LOD methods that precompute fixed levels, this approach maintains an "active cut" of the octree, splitting or merging nodes every frame to balance visual fidelity against rendering cost. It differs from sibling methods like Dynamic Volume Resolution & Alpha Mask Update by explicitly managing a hierarchical cut of non-leaf nodes rather than just updating alpha masks or global resolution scales. The method operates in two primary phases: Adapt/Load and Cull/Render. It assumes the volume data is organized in an adaptive octree where leaf nodes contain voxelized cells. Inputs: Octree structure with voxelized cells. User parameters: Desired frame rate, transfer function (data to RGBA), view position. System parameters: RAM size, texture memory size, bandwidths, polygon/fill performance. Outputs: A set of flagged octree nodes rendered to the screen. Updated active cut for the next frame. 1. Active Cut: A set of octree nodes whose cells cover the model space exactly once. 2. Split Queue: Contains non-leaf nodes currently on the active cut, sorted by decreasing error. 3. Merge Queue: Contains nodes that are inactive (merged) but can be split if error increases. 4. Node State: Each node has a boolean flag active (true if on active cut, false if merged). 1. Initialize Active Cut: Start with the root node as active. Maintain the invariant that the active cut covers the volume space exactly once. 2. Adapt Phase (Error Adjustment): Compute a local error metric Ei for each non-leaf node i in the split queue. The metric represents the visual difference between the node and its children. To Decrease Error (Increase Quality): 1. Select the node N with the highest error from the Split Queue. 2. Move N to the Merge Queue and mark it inactive. 3. Add N's children to the Split Queue and mark them active. 4. Border Continuity Fix: If children are at different levels or have different resolutions, copy border data from the parent to children to fix internal border discontinuities. To Increase Error (Increase Frame Rate): 1. Select the node M from the Merge Queue. 2. Move M to the Split Queue and mark it active. 3. Add M's parent to the Merge Queue and mark it inactive. 4. Remove M's children from the Split Queue and mark them inactive. 3. Load Phase: Traverse the active cut. For any flagged node whose texture data is not resident in texture memory, load it from RAM or disk. 4. Cull/Render Phase: Traverse the octree from the root. Perform hierarchical culling based on the view frustum and occlusion. Render flagged (active) nodes using 3D texture mapping and blending in back-to-front order. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumelodrender(octree, userparams, systemparams): # userparams: {desiredframerate, transferfunction, viewposition} # systemparams: {ramsize, texmemsize, bandwidth} # 1. Adapt Phase # Calculate error for all non-leaf nodes in splitqueue for node in splitqueue: node.error = computeerror(node, octree) # Sort splitqueue by decreasing error splitqueue.sort(key=lambda n: n.error, reverse=True) # Adjust cut based on current frame rate vs desired frame rate currentframerate = measureframerate() if currentframerate < userparams.desiredframerate: # Need to increase quality (decrease error) # Split the highest error node if splitqueue: node = splitqueue.pop(0) node.active = False mergequeue.append(node) for child in node.children: child.active = True splitqueue.append(child) # Fix border discontinuities between cells of different levels fixbordercontinuity(node, node.children) elif currentframerate > userparams.desiredframerate: # Need to increase speed (increase error) # Merge the lowest error node from merge queue if mergequeue: node = mergequeue.pop(0) node.active = True splitqueue.append(node) # Mark children inactive and remove from split queue for child in node.children: child.active = False if child in splitqueue: splitqueue.remove(child) # Add parent to merge queue if it exists and is not root if node.parent: node.parent.active = False mergequeue.append(node.parent) if node.parent in splitqueue: splitqueue.remove(node.parent) # 2. Load Phase for node in activecut: if not node.textureresident: loadtexturefromramordisk(node) # 3. Cull/Render Phase rendernodes = [] traverseoctree(octree.root, rendernodes) # Sort by back-to-front for correct blending rendernodes.sort(key=lambda n: distancetocamera(n)) for node in rendernodes: if node.active: render3dtexture(node, userparams.transferfunction) def fixbordercontinuity(parent, children): """ Copies border data from parent to children to ensure continuity when merging nodes of different levels. """ for child in children: copyborderdata(parent, child) Error Metric: The specific formula for error is not given in the sources, but it must reflect visual difference between a node and its children. Border Discontinuity: A critical pitfall is visual artifacts at the boundaries of merged/split nodes. The method explicitly fixes this by copying border data from the parent to the children during the split operation. Active Cut Invariant: The cut must always cover the space exactly once. Failure to maintain this leads to over-rendering (holes or overlaps). A technique that cuts rendering cost by rendering at coarser octree levels (moving up the octree) to match data resolution to image resolution, maintaining interactivity. It selectively reduces computation and data transfer based on visualization requirements. It is chosen when rendering large datasets (e.g., tens of millions of elements) where high-resolution rendering is unnecessary for the current view. It reduces rendering time and data transfer from disk but does not change the effectiveness of 1DIP/2DIP I/O strategies. In experiments, adaptive rendering (level 6) provided enough high-level information and was generated about 3 times faster than high-resolution rendering (level 11). Time Complexity: The adapt phase requires sorting the split queue by error, which is O(N \log N) where N is the number of nodes in the active cut. The render phase is proportional to the number of active nodes. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the octree structure, texture data for active nodes, and the split/merge queues. Memory usage is bounded by texture memory size. Measured Performance: Adaptive rendering (level 6) was generated about 3 times faster than high-resolution rendering (level 11). Strengths: Maximizes image quality within system constraints; maintains interactivity for large datasets; reduces data transfer from disk. Limitations: Requires complex bookkeeping for the active cut and border continuity; performance depends on the accuracy of the error metric. When to Use: Interactive visualization of large unstructured grids where frame rate is critical. When Not to Use: When static high-fidelity rendering is required without interactivity constraints. The method was introduced in the context of interactive visualization of unstructured grids using hierarchical 3D texture mapping. It builds on the concept of view-dependent continuous level of detail for polygonal models. The approach was applied to large-scale time-varying volume data, such as earthquake simulations, to enable near-interactive visualization. name: Focus and Context Multiresolution Rendering
head: Interactive lenses multiresolution, Time-critical multiresolution rendering
body: Focus and Context Multiresolution Rendering balances processing capacity between a high-detail focus region and a lower-detail context region to improve interactivity in time-critical applications. It solves the problem of limited hardware resources by decomposing the rendering task into two passes with distinct parameters, explicitly trading seamless integration for speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset, a transfer function, a camera view, and a focus region definition such as a data probe. Output: A composite image where the focus region is rendered at high fidelity and the context region is rendered at reduced fidelity. Data Structures and Layout: The method uses two distinct rendering configurations. The experimental parameters are: | Parameter | Focus Configuration | Context Configuration | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | Volume Size | 4 \times 256^3 | 1 \times 128^3 | | Lookup Table Size | 5 \times 256^2 | 4 \times 128^2 | | Rendering Model | Local lighting | Unshaded | | Sampling Rate | 4 | 1 | | Viewport Size | 100% | 50% | Steps: 1. Decomposition: Divide the rendering task into a Focus pass and a Context pass. The Focus region is placed closest to the user. 2. Context Rendering: Render the context volume into a smaller viewport (e.g., 50% of the screen dimensions) using an unshaded model and a lower sampling rate. 3. Filtering: Apply a Gaussian filter to the resulting context image to reduce aliasing artifacts. 4. Scaling: Enlarge the filtered context image to fill its designated portion of the final framebuffer. 5. Focus Rendering: Render the focus volume into the remaining viewport area (or full screen if context is transparent) using local lighting and a higher sampling rate. 6. Compositing: Composite the focus and context images. If the context is transparent, it serves as an orientation aid; if opaque, it provides an external view. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderfocusandcontext(voldata, focusregion, camera, vpw, vph): # Parameters from ctxvpscale = 0.5 ctxsampling = 1 focussampling = 4 ctxw = int(vpw ctxvpscale) ctxh = int(vph ctxvpscale) # Step 2: Render Context (unshaded, lower sampling) contextimage = [[0.0] ctxw for in range(ctxh)] for y in range(ctxh): for x in range(ctxw): acc = 0.0 # Standard volume ray marching loop; source does not specify exact integration method for t in range(0, 100, ctxsampling): acc += voldata.sampleray(camera, x, y, t) contextimage[y][x] = acc / 100.0 # Step 3: Gaussian filter for aliasing reduction filteredcontext = [[0.0] ctxw for in range(ctxh)] for y in range(ctxh): for x in range(ctxw): kernelsum = 0.0 for dy in range(-1, 2): for dx in range(-1, 2): ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < ctxh and 0 <= nx < ctxw: # 3x3 Gaussian kernel weights (1,2,1 normalized) w = 1.0 if dy != 0 and dx != 0 else 2.0 kernelsum += contextimage[ny][nx] w filteredcontext[y][x] = kernelsum / 16.0 # Step 4: Scale up context image scaledcontext = [[0.0] vpw for in range(vph)] for y in range(vph): for x in range(vpw): srcy = min(max(int(y / ctxvpscale), 0), ctxh - 1) srcx = min(max(int(x / ctxvpscale), 0), ctxw - 1) scaledcontext[y][x] = filteredcontext[srcy][srcx] # Step 5: Render Focus (local lighting, higher sampling) focusimage = [[0.0] vpw for in range(vph)] for y in range(vph): for x in range(vpw): acc = 0.0 for t in range(0, 100, focussampling): acc += voldata.sampleray(camera, x, y, t) focusimage[y][x] = acc / 100.0 # Step 6: Composite # Source does not specify exact blending equation; standard alpha compositing assumed. finalimage = [[0.0] vpw for in range(vph)] for y in range(vph): for x in range(vpw): finalimage[y][x] = focusimage[y][x] 0.8 + scaledcontext[y][x] 0.2 return finalimage Parameters and Edge Cases: Context Mode: Can be transparent (for orientation) or opaque (for external view). Sampling: Context sampling can be sparse if the transfer function contains only low-frequency components. Pitfalls: Overhead comes from rendering slices multiple times and setting up clip textures and depth buffers for each pass. The goal is not seamless integration, so visible seams or quality drops in the context are acceptable trade-offs for speed. Performance: Achieves 2-6 times faster rendering rates than single high-resolution mode by reducing focus fragments aggressively. Measured Performance: Tested on a 2.0GHz Pentium 4, 2GB memory, ATI Radeon 9800 Pro. 512x512 Viewport: 100% Focus Size: 3.39 FPS; 50% Volume Size: 4.22 FPS; 25% Volume Size: 7.55 FPS; 12.5% Volume Size: 12.99 FPS; 6.25% Volume Size: 20.87 FPS. 1024x1024 Viewport: 100% Focus Size: 1.06 FPS; 50% Volume Size: 1.28 FPS; 25% Volume Size: 2.31 FPS; 12.5% Volume Size: 3.97 FPS; 6.25% Volume Size: 6.33 FPS. Scaling: Performance gains increase as the focus size (volume percentage) decreases. The speedup depends on rendering parameters, not transfer functions. Strengths: Simple, generic approach; effective for time-critical applications; reduces clutter in multidimensional exploration. Limitations: Not seamless; overhead from multiple rendering passes and depth buffer setup; performance variability on ATI cards depending on slicing direction. This technique was presented in "A Focus and Context Interface for Interactive Volume Rendering" by I. Kits et al.. It was developed to address limited processing capacity in hardware-accelerated volume rendering, where performance depends on fragment count, work per fragment, and cache utilization. name: Multiresolution Atlas Buffer (MAB)
head: VR DVR acceleration wrapper, bracket approach for VR raycasting, gaze-dependent resolution DVR
body: The Multiresolution Atlas Buffer (MAB) is an acceleration wrapper for Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) in Virtual Reality (VR) that reduces ray density adaptively based on peripheral vision and Head-Mounted Display (HMD) lens distortion, then reconstructs the full-resolution image via compositing. It differs from standard foveated rendering by not requiring high-speed eye-tracking hardware; instead, it leverages the fixed nature of HMD lenses and the non-uniform resolution of the human visual system to create a static, gaze-centered resolution map. Unlike sibling methods that modify the ray traversal itself (e.g., Level-of-detail (LOD) methods) or dynamic volume resolution (Dynamic Volume Resolution & Alpha Mask Update), MAB operates as a "bracket" around existing raycasters, modifying ray construction and post-traversal compositing. The method consists of two primary steps injected into the rendering pipeline: (1) adaptive ray density reduction during ray construction, and (2) compositing computation after ray traversal to reconstruct the final image. Inputs: Current frame buffer dimensions (typically matching HMD resolution, e.g., 2880 \times 1600). Gaze center coordinates in screen space (assumed to be the center of the viewport or a fixed point due to lack of eye-tracking). Target refresh rate (e.g., \ge 90 Hz, tending toward 120 Hz or more). Current frame timing metrics. Outputs: A full-resolution, consistent framebuffer image submitted to the HMD. A set of rays with reduced density sent to the underlying raycaster. Multiresolution Atlas Buffer (MAB): Layout: The MAB is a texture or buffer partitioned into multiple regions. Each region corresponds to the entire frame buffer at a specific resolution level. Resolution Levels: The system supports discrete levels with progressively lower resolutions. The resolution scaling values between subsequent levels are arbitrary and not necessarily a power of two. Ordering: Levels are ordered to minimize the overall framebuffer size. Discarding: Black areas (empty regions) in each level are discarded before ray traversal to save computation. Mapping Functions: A bidirectional mapping between the framebuffer space and MAB space is mandatory. Forward Mapping (f{map}): Assigns every MAB fragment a unique position in the framebuffer and a blending factor. Inverse Mapping: Assigns each framebuffer fragment several MAB fragments and blending factors for compositing. 1. MAB Construction: Define the set of resolution levels. Unlike Mip-Maps, ratios between levels are not fixed (e.g., not strictly 4:1). Allocate the MAB structure with regions for each resolution level. 2. Ray Construction (Opening Brace): For each pixel in the target framebuffer, determine the required resolution level based on the distance to the gaze center. Compute the ray origin and direction. The ray density is adaptively reduced in peripheral regions. Feed the reduced set of rays to the underlying raycaster. 3. Ray Traversal: The underlying raycaster traverses the volume data for the provided rays and stores results into the corresponding regions of the MAB. 4. Compositing (Closing Brace): Render a full-screen primitive covering the entire output framebuffer. For each generated fragment in the framebuffer, compute the mapping to the MAB using two functions: Function fa: Takes the distance to the center of gaze (based on screen-space coordinates) and outputs a set of blending factors for the MAB. Function fb: Takes the screen-space coordinates of the fragment and outputs a set of corresponding coordinates in the MAB. For each non-zero entry in the blending factor set from fa, perform a lookup into the MAB using the coordinates from fb to obtain stored color values. Blend these values together into a single color for display. 5. Adaptive Timing Adjustment: Evaluate frame timings for the current frame. Adjust rendering parameters (such as the number of resolution levels or the resolution scaling factors) for the next subsampling stage to maintain a consistent refresh rate. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. HMDWIDTH = 2880 HMDHEIGHT = 1600 TARGETFPS = 90.0 class MABLevel: width: int height: int buffer: Texture2D # Stores raycasting results class MAB: levels: List[MABLevel] # Ordered to minimize overall framebuffer size def fa(screenx: float, screeny: float, gazex: float, gazey: float) -> List[float]: """ Computes blending factors based on distance to gaze center. Returns a list of weights corresponding to MAB levels. """ dist = sqrt((screenx - gazex)2 + (screeny - gazey)2) # Implementation details for blending factor calculation are not specified in sources. # Typically involves a falloff function (e.g., Gaussian or linear) # mapping distance to a set of weights for available resolution levels. return computeblendingfactors(dist) def fb(screenx: float, screeny: float, levelindex: int) -> Tuple[float, float]: """ Computes MAB coordinates for a specific framebuffer fragment and level. """ level = mab.levels[levelindex] # Map screen coordinates to the resolution of the specific MAB level scalex = level.width / HMDWIDTH scaley = level.height / HMDHEIGHT return (screenx scalex, screeny scaley) def renderframe(gazex: float, gazey: float, frametime: float): # Step 1: Adaptive Parameter Adjustment # Adjust resolution levels or scaling factors based on frametime to maintain TARGETFPS # Logic to compare frametime with 1/TARGETFPS and adjust MAB configuration. adjustmabparameters(frametime) # Step 2: Ray Construction (Opening Brace) rays = [] for y in range(HMDHEIGHT): for x in range(HMDWIDTH): # Determine which MAB level(s) to use for this pixel # Logic to select primary level based on distance to gaze levelidx = selectlevelforpixel(x, y, gazex, gazey) # Compute ray for the selected resolution # The ray density is reduced in peripheral regions ray = computerayforresolution(x, y, mab.levels[levelidx]) rays.append(ray) # Step 3: Ray Traversal # Render rays into the MAB for ray in rays: result = raycaster.traverse(ray) # Store result in the appropriate MAB level region storeinmab(ray, result) # Step 4: Compositing (Closing Brace) outputbuffer = Texture2D(HMDWIDTH, HMDHEIGHT) # Render full-screen primitive for y in range(HMDHEIGHT): for x in range(HMDWIDTH): # Get blending factors factors = fa(x, y, gazex, gazey) finalcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Composite from multiple MAB levels for i, weight in enumerate(factors): if weight > 0: # Get MAB coordinates mabx, maby = fb(x, y, i) # Lookup color from MAB color = mab.levels[i].buffer.sample(mabx, maby) # Blend finalcolor += color weight outputbuffer.setpixel(x, y, finalcolor) return outputbuffer Resolution Scaling: Arbitrary values between subsequent MAB levels; not necessarily powers of two. HMD Update Rate: At least 90 Hz, tending toward 120 Hz or more. HMD Resolution: Around 2880 \times 1600 pixels. Eye Tracking: The method does not consider rapid eye movements because HMD lenses are fixed and provide only a slight angle with the highest projected resolution. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The mapping functions fa and fb must handle boundary conditions where gaze is near the edge of the viewport. The predecessor method by Waschk and Krüger (2020) that considers human perception and HMD lens distortion but is the conceptual basis for MAB. A related texture filtering technique. MAB differs by supporting arbitrary, non-power-of-two resolution ratios between levels to minimize noticeable differences. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of primary rays traversed by the raycaster, thereby reducing the computational load of the volume rendering step. The compositing step adds overhead proportional to the number of framebuffer pixels and the number of MAB levels sampled per pixel. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the MAB, which contains multiple resolution levels of the frame buffer. The levels are ordered to minimize the overall framebuffer size. Measured Performance: Designed to make DVR feasible in VR setups by guaranteeing stable high refresh rates (90 Hz+) to avoid cyber-sickness. Strengths: Works as a wrapper around existing raycasters with minimal code changes; does not require eye-tracking hardware; adapts to hardware characteristics. Limitations: Does not account for rapid eye movements; relies on fixed gaze assumption (typically center). When to use: VR setups with HMDs where DVR is performance-bound by fragment processing and high refresh rates are critical. When not to use: Desktop rendering without VR constraints; scenarios requiring precise foveated rendering based on actual eye position. The Multiresolution Atlas Buffer (MAB) method was introduced by Jens Krüger and Andre Waschk in the WSCG 2022 Proceedings (CSRN 3201). It builds upon the FAVR (Foveated Adaptive Volume Rendering) approach by Waschk and Krüger (2020) and earlier gaze-dependent rendering works. The method addresses the challenge of rendering high-resolution volume data in VR, where HMD resolutions (e.g., 2880 \times 1600) and high refresh rates (90-120 Hz) create significant performance bottlenecks for DVR raycasters. By leveraging the non-uniform resolution of the human visual system and the fixed nature of HMD lenses, MAB reduces ray density in peripheral regions while maintaining visual fidelity in the center.
