name: Spatiotemporal Importance Sampling
head: Spatiotemporal importance sampling strategy
body: Spatiotemporal importance sampling is a strategy that assigns higher sampling probabilities to tissue pixels occluded by tools or exhibiting extensive motion ranges, and lower probabilities to stationary tissues, to improve convergence and efficiency. It addresses the challenge of tool occlusion and stationary tissue redundancy, which exacerbate learning complexity and reduce efficiency compared to uniform sampling. Inputs: A sequence of T frames, indexed i=1 \dots T. For each frame i, an image Ii and a binary tool mask Mi identifying occluded regions. Hyper-parameters: \alpha (lower-bound for weights), \beta (balance factor), n (temporal window radius). Outputs: A set of sampling weight maps \{Wi\}{i=1}^T, where each Wi represents the sampling probability for each pixel/ray at time step i. Data Structures: Ii: Image tensor for frame i. Mi: Binary mask tensor for frame i, same spatial dimensions as Ii. Wi: Weight map tensor for frame i, same spatial dimensions as Ii. \Omegai: Occlusion frequency scaling tensor for frame i. Steps: 1. Calculate the temporal difference metric for each pixel to identify regions with extensive motion by comparing the current frame's masked image against neighboring frames within a temporal window [i-n, i+n]. 2. Compute the occlusion frequency scaling factor \Omegai for each frame based on the total occlusion count across the sequence. 3. Combine the temporal difference metric and the occlusion scaling factor to generate the final sampling weight map Wi. Formulas: The sampling weight map Wi is calculated as: Wi = \min\left( \max{i-n < j < i+n} \frac{\| Ii \odot Mi - Ij \odot Mj \|1}{3}, \alpha \right) \odot \Omegai where: \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. \| \cdot \|1 denotes the L1 norm (sum of absolute differences) between the masked images of frame i and frame j. The term \max{i-n < j < i+n} computes the maximum L1 difference between the current frame i and any frame j within the temporal window of radius n. \alpha is a lower-bound parameter to avoid zero weight among unchanged pixels. \Omegai is the occlusion frequency scaling factor, defined as: \Omegai = \beta \left( \frac{T Mi}{\sum{k=1}^T Mk} \right) where: T is the total number of frames. \sum{k=1}^T Mk is the sum of the binary masks across all frames, representing the total occlusion count per pixel over the entire sequence. Mi is normalized by a small constant to prevent division by zero, defined as T Mi = Mi / (1 + 10^{-6} \sum{k=1}^T Mk). \beta is a hyper-parameter for balancing augmentation among frequently occluded areas and time-variant areas. Parameters: \alpha: Lower-bound for the weight map to prevent zero weights for static pixels. Value not given in the sources. \beta: Hyper-parameter balancing augmentation between frequently occluded areas and time-variant areas. Value not given in the sources. n: Radius of the temporal window for comparing frames. Value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If a pixel is never occluded, Mi is zero for all i. The term \frac{T Mi}{\sum{k=1}^T Mk} becomes 0/0 if no pixels are ever occluded, or 0 if some are. The source explicitly defines T Mi = Mi / (1 + 10^{-6} \sum{k=1}^T Mk) to handle the denominator, avoiding division by zero. The division by 3 in the L1 norm term is part of the formula; the sources do not explain its origin or imply a specific image normalization range. Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the context of efficient deformable tissue reconstruction for surgical scenes. It draws inspiration from EndoNeRF. It is designed to handle the specific challenges of robotic surgery scenes, where tool occlusion hides tissues and stationary tissues provide redundant training data. Efficient Deformable Tissue Reconstruction via Orthogonal Neural Plane, https://doi.org/10.1109/tmi.2024.3388559, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Adaptive Image Sampling with Pixel Sharing
head: Adaptive Image Sampling, Adaptive image sampling optimization, adaptive sampling with synchronization
body: Adaptive Image Sampling with Pixel Sharing is a parallel volume rendering optimization that reduces computational cost by casting rays only from the corners of square image regions and interpolating the interior pixels. It solves the problem of redundant ray casting in smooth areas while managing the synchronization dependencies inherent in parallel implementations where adjacent regions share corner pixels. Unlike non-ray-dependent optimizations such as early ray termination, this method requires careful handling of shared pixel values to avoid replicated computation across processor boundaries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset (voxels), an initial maximum sample region size w{max}, a color difference threshold Tc, and a density difference threshold Td. Output: A rendered 2D image where pixels are either explicitly ray-traced or bilinearly interpolated from traced corner pixels. Data Structures: Image Plane Partitioning: The image is divided into square sample regions of size w{max} \times w{max} pixels. Task Queue: A queue of image tiles (or sample regions) to be processed by processors in a MIMD architecture. Wait Queue: A local data structure storing the state of sample regions that cannot be fully evaluated because their corner pixels are currently being traced by other processors. Preprocessing Data: Normals, opacities, and an octree structure are computed as preprocessing steps. A lookup table mapping local voxel gradient to color is used to accelerate shading. Algorithm Steps: The method operates in two phases: initial processing and wait-queue resolution. 1. Region Division: Divide the image plane into square sample regions of size w{max} \times w{max}. 2. Corner Ray Casting: For each sample region, identify the four corner pixels. Cast rays only for those corner pixels that have not already been traced by adjacent regions and are not currently being traced by other processors. 3. Complexity Measurement: Compute the image complexity M of the sample region by calculating the color difference between the successfully traced corner pixels. Formula: M = \max(|Ci - Cj|) for all pairs of traced corners i, j in the region, where C is the color vector. Note: Pixels currently being traced by other processors are excluded from this calculation. 4. Adaptation Decision: If M > Tc (color threshold), subdivide the sample region into smaller subregions and recursively apply the algorithm to them. If M \le Tc, the region is considered smooth. 5. Handling Dependencies (Wait Queue): If the region requires subdivision but some corner pixels are still being traced by other processors, or if the region does not require subdivision but some corners are still being traced, store the sample region's state in a local wait queue. If all necessary corner pixels are available and the region does not require subdivision, proceed to interpolation (Step 6). 6. Interpolation: For regions that do not require subdivision, bilinearly interpolate the untraced interior pixels from the traced corner pixels. 7. Wait Queue Resolution: After all initial task queues are empty, process the local wait queues. For each sample region in the wait queue, re-evaluate complexity (Step 3). If corner pixels are still being traced, busy wait until they are ray traced. Once all corners are available, re-evaluate the complexity and proceed to subdivision or interpolation as determined in Step 4. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveimagesampling(imagewidth, imageheight, wmax, Tc, Td, volumedata): image = [[None] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] taskqueue = [] waitqueue = [] class SampleRegion: def init(self, x, y, size): self.x, self.y, self.size = x, y, size def corners(self): s = self.size return [(self.x, self.y), (self.x+s, self.y), (self.x, self.y+s), (self.x+s, self.y+s)] for y in range(0, imageheight, wmax): for x in range(0, imagewidth, wmax): taskqueue.append(SampleRegion(x, y, wmax)) def istraced(px, py): return image[py][px] is not None def isbeingtracedbyother(px, py): return False # Parallel state check def raytrace(px, py, vol): return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Actual volume march def colordiff(c1, c2): return max(abs(c1[i]-c2[i]) for i in range(3)) while taskqueue: reg = taskqueue.pop() corners = reg.corners() traced = [] for px, py in corners: if not istraced(px, py) and not isbeingtracedbyother(px, py): c = raytrace(px, py, volumedata) image[py][px] = c traced.append((px, py, c)) if not traced: waitqueue.append(reg) continue maxd = 0 for i in range(len(traced)): for j in range(i+1, len(traced)): d = colordiff(traced[i][2], traced[j][2]) if d > maxd: maxd = d if maxd > Tc: s = reg.size if s > 1: h = s // 2 taskqueue.append(SampleRegion(reg.x, reg.y, h)) taskqueue.append(SampleRegion(reg.x+h, reg.y, h)) taskqueue.append(SampleRegion(reg.x, reg.y+h, h)) taskqueue.append(SampleRegion(reg.x+h, reg.y+h, h)) else: if len(traced) < 4: waitqueue.append(reg) else: c00, c10, c01, c11 = traced[0][2], traced[1][2], traced[2][2], traced[3][2] s = reg.size for py in range(reg.y, reg.y+s): for px in range(reg.x, reg.x+s): u, v = (px-reg.x)/s, (py-reg.y)/s top = [c00[k](1-u)+c10[k]u for k in range(3)] bot = [c01[k](1-u)+c11[k]u for k in range(3)] image[py][px] = [top[k](1-v)+bot[k]v for k in range(3)] while waitqueue: reg = waitqueue.pop() corners = reg.corners() while any(not istraced(px, py) for px, py in corners): pass # Busy wait traced = [(px, py, image[py][px]) for px, py in corners] maxd = 0 for i in range(len(traced)): for j in range(i+1, len(traced)): d = colordiff(traced[i][2], traced[j][2]) if d > maxd: maxd = d if maxd > Tc: s = reg.size if s > 1: h = s // 2 taskqueue.append(SampleRegion(reg.x, reg.y, h)) taskqueue.append(SampleRegion(reg.x+h, reg.y, h)) taskqueue.append(SampleRegion(reg.x, reg.y+h, h)) taskqueue.append(SampleRegion(reg.x+h, reg.y+h, h)) else: c00, c10, c01, c11 = traced[0][2], traced[1][2], traced[2][2], traced[3][2] s = reg.size for py in range(reg.y, reg.y+s): for px in range(reg.x, reg.x+s): u, v = (px-reg.x)/s, (py-reg.y)/s top = [c00[k](1-u)+c10[k]u for k in range(3)] bot = [c01[k](1-u)+c11[k]u for k in range(3)] image[py][px] = [top[k](1-v)+bot[k]v for k in range(3)] return image Parameters: w{max}: The side length in pixels of the initial square sample regions. Implementations use 3 \times 3 pixels. Tc: Color difference threshold for subdivision. Typical values: 10 (electric field), 40 (neghip), 30 (brain). Td: Density difference threshold for sample point interpolation along rays. Typical values: 30 (electric field), 80 (neghip), 5 (brain). Early Ray Termination (ERT) Opacity Threshold: Often used in conjunction. Typical values: 98% (electric field), 92% (neghip), 98% (brain). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pixel Sharing Dependencies: Adjacent sample regions share corner pixels. If processed by different processors, synchronization is required to avoid replicated ray casting. Deadlock/Starvation: If a processor waits indefinitely for a pixel traced by another, busy waiting or proper queue management is required. Precision: Color difference calculations must be robust to small numerical variations. Static Contiguous Image-Based Partitioning is a parallel volume rendering strategy that divides the final image plane into contiguous blocks (tiles) and assigns each block to a specific processor, which then executes the complete rendering pipeline for that region. It solves the load-balancing and communication overhead issues inherent in adaptive sampling methods by ensuring that pixel-sharing costs are eliminated through static assignment and specific traversal orders. Unlike dynamic image-based partitioning which delays evaluation to handle shared pixels, this method avoids such costs entirely without extra synchronization overhead. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of ray casts in smooth regions by interpolating interior pixels, leading to faster rendering times. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the image buffer, task queues, wait queues, and preprocessing data (octree, normals, opacities). Measured Performance: On a 16-processor system, rendering rates of >10 frames per second were achieved for 256 \times 256 resolution images on datasets like electric field, neghip, and brain. Strengths: Significant reduction in computational cost for smooth regions; avoids replicated ray casting in parallel environments through pixel sharing. Limitations: Requires synchronization or queue management for parallel implementations; interpolation artifacts may occur in regions with high complexity if thresholds are not tuned correctly. When to Use: Suitable for parallel volume rendering on MIMD architectures where smooth regions dominate the image. When Not to Use: Not suitable for highly complex, noisy, or high-frequency regions where interpolation would introduce significant artifacts. The method was introduced in the context of volume rendering on scalable shared-memory MIMD architectures, specifically the DASH multiprocessor. It addresses the inefficiencies of uniform sampling by adapting the sampling rate based on image complexity. The approach was further optimized for parallel implementations by handling pixel sharing dependencies, leading to static contiguous image-based partitioning strategies. Volume rendering on scalable shared-memory MIMD architectures, https://doi.org/10.1145/147130.147141, fetched 2026-10-25 NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) 19990040407: Time-Critical Volume Rendering, https://archive.org/details/NASANTRSArchive19990040407, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Static Contiguous Image-Based Partitioning
head: Static image-based partitioning, Image-based partitioning
body: Static Contiguous Image-Based Partitioning is a parallel volume rendering strategy that distributes the final image plane into disjoint, contiguous blocks (tiles) among processors, where each processor independently renders its assigned section. It solves the problem of load imbalance and communication overhead inherent in adaptive image sampling methods by avoiding the replicated ray casting costs associated with shared pixels at partition boundaries. Unlike its parent method, Adaptive Image Sampling with Pixel Sharing, which requires complex synchronization to handle shared pixels between adaptive regions, this method uses static contiguous partitioning to ensure that shared pixels are computed only once by neighboring processors in a specific order, eliminating synchronization overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset V, a camera configuration (view matrix, projection matrix), and a target image resolution W \times H. Output: A final composite image I of resolution W \times H. Data Structures: Volume Data: Distributed across P processors. Each processor p holds a subset of the volume data Vp responsible for rendering its tile. Image Partition: The image is divided into P contiguous blocks. If adaptive sampling is used, the image is conceptually divided into square sample regions of size I{max} \times I{max} pixels. These regions are grouped into P contiguous large blocks with roughly equal amounts of work. Shared Memory/Communication: In shared-memory architectures, processors communicate via shared memory. In distributed-memory systems, processors communicate via message passing. Steps: 1. Data Distribution: Volume data is distributed arbitrarily across processors initially. Each processor determines the ownership of the subvolume required for its assigned tile. Processors keep the data they are responsible for and send all other data to the corresponding processor in charge. This redistribution may happen at the beginning of every frame computation. 2. Tile Assignment: The image is partitioned into P contiguous blocks. Each processor p is assigned one block Bp. 3. Rendering (Scanline Order): Each processor renders its assigned block Bp in scanline order from top to bottom. For each pixel (or sample region) in the block, the processor casts rays into the volume data it owns (Vp) and composites the result. If adaptive sampling is employed, the processor calculates sample regions within its block. 4. Handling Shared Pixels (Boundary Condition): Pixels shared by image sections processed by different processors are located only in the square sample regions at the top and bottom of each image section. Top Regions: Each processor calculates the shared pixels in the top sample regions of its section. Bottom Regions: When a processor reaches the bottom sample regions, it uses the shared pixel values already available in shared memory (or received from lower neighbors), which were calculated by its lower neighboring processors. This mechanism avoids replicated ray casting for shared pixels. 5. Result Collection: The sub-images from all processors are collected onto one processor (or composited in a shared frame buffer) to produce the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def staticcontiguouspartitioning(volumecells, camera, imagewidth, imageheight, numprocessors, processorid): # Step 1: Data Distribution # Filter volume cells to those projecting into this processor's tile y-range. tileheight = imageheight // numprocessors ystart = processorid tileheight yend = imageheight if processorid == numprocessors - 1 else (processorid + 1) tileheight localcells = [c for c in volumecells if c.screenymin <= yend and c.screenymax >= ystart] # Step 2: Tile Assignment # Each processor gets a contiguous block of scanlines. # Step 3 & 4: Rendering with Shared Pixel Handling # sharedpixelbuffer is a global array of size imageheight x imagewidth initialized to transparent. subimage = [] for y in range(ystart, yend): row = [] for x in range(imagewidth): istopboundary = (y == ystart) and (processorid > 0) isbottomboundary = (y == yend - 1) and (processorid < numprocessors - 1) if istopboundary: pixel = castrayandcomposite(localcells, camera, x, y) sharedpixelbuffer[y][x] = pixel elif isbottomboundary: pixel = sharedpixelbuffer[y][x] else: pixel = castrayandcomposite(localcells, camera, x, y) row.append(pixel) subimage.append(row) return subimage def castrayandcomposite(cells, camera, x, y): # Standard front-to-back volume rendering along the ray through (x, y) rayorigin = camera.unproject(x, y) raydir = normalize(camera.getdirection(x, y)) stepsize = 0.5 tmax = computeraytmax(rayorigin, raydir, cells.bounds) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] t = 0.0 while t < tmax: sample = cells.sample(rayorigin + t raydir) alpha = sample[3] color[0] += (1.0 - color[3]) sample[0] alpha color[1] += (1.0 - color[3]) sample[1] alpha color[2] += (1.0 - color[3]) sample[2] alpha color[3] += (1.0 - color[3]) alpha if color[3] >= 0.99: break t += stepsize return color def computeraytmax(origin, direction, bounds): # Ray-AABB intersection returning tmax tmin, tmax = -float('inf'), float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bounds.min[i] or origin[i] > bounds.max[i]: return 0.0 else: t1 = (bounds.min[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bounds.max[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return max(0.0, tmax) def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return [v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag] Parameters: I{max}: The side length of square sample regions in pixels, used when adaptive sampling is active. Not given in the sources. P: Number of processors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Load Imbalance: Image order does not guarantee equal cell distribution. If one tile contains more cells (e.g., due to uneven cell sizes in unstructured data or camera focus on a specific region), its processor performs more work, causing load imbalance. Replicated Loading: Cells covering more than one tile result in replicated loading of those cells across multiple processors. Scalability Limits: In distributed memory systems, as P increases, the image space grows into too many pieces, causing data redistribution and boundary data redundancy to become serious scalability limitations. Per-Frame Coherence: In real-time volume rendering, user interaction can cause sudden scene changes, breaking per-frame coherence and preventing the use of retained-mode optimizations that reduce transferred data. Combines object-based partitioning for boundary cell projection with image-based partitioning for ray traversal to achieve load balancing. It sets itself apart by decoupling the partitioning strategy to avoid replicated ray casting costs at processor boundaries, unlike the purely image-based approach of this method. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of pixels in the tile and the number of cells contributing to those pixels. Load imbalance can cause significant variance in execution time across processors. Memory Complexity: Each processor must store the volume data contributing to its tile. Replicated loading of cells covering multiple tiles increases memory usage. Measured Performance: Scalability depends directly on the size of the final image and indirectly on the size of the underlying dataset. It scales well with increasing image resolutions because only complete pixels are transmitted. Strengths: Avoids replicated ray casting costs for shared pixels without extra synchronization overhead. Instantly compatible with all serial rendering algorithms because it executes the full graphics pipeline in each processor. Simpler implementation compared to dynamic partitioning methods. Limitations: Does not guarantee load balance. Replicated cell loading increases memory and communication costs. Scalability is limited in distributed memory systems due to data redistribution overhead. When to Use: Suitable for shared-memory architectures where data redistribution is cheap, or when compatibility with existing serial rendering algorithms is a priority. Not ideal for distributed systems with high communication latency or highly uneven data distributions. Static Contiguous Image-Based Partitioning, also known as static image-based partitioning or image-based partitioning, is a parallelization strategy for volume rendering that divides the image into contiguous blocks assigned to processors. It was proposed as a simpler and more effective solution than dynamic image-based partitioning (e.g., Nieh and Levoy) to avoid the cost of replicated ray casting associated with pixel sharing in adaptive image sampling. The method is compatible with standard APIs like OpenGL, which lack high-performance access to intermediate rendering results, making sort-middle impractical. It has been used in various parallel volume rendering schemes, including those for unstructured volume data. The underlying sequential renderer can be the Scanline Z-Buffer algorithm, which requires no connectivity information, only a set of unconnected polygons. name: Hybrid Partitioning Parallel Ray Casting
head: High Performance Parallel Ray Casting, Hybrid Partitioning Parallel RC
body: Hybrid Partitioning Parallel Ray Casting is a parallel volume rendering algorithm for shared-memory MIMD architectures (e.g., SGI Power Challenge) that combines object-based partitioning for boundary cell projection with image-based partitioning for ray traversal to achieve load balancing. It sets itself apart from its parent Static Contiguous Image-Based Partitioning by decoupling the partitioning strategy: it uses object-based partitioning to handle the uneven distribution of boundary cells and image-based partitioning to handle the uneven distribution of ray traversal work, thereby avoiding the replicated ray casting costs associated with adaptive image sampling at processor boundaries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset, camera parameters (view direction, projection matrix), number of processors P, and the set of ray casting optimizations (early ray termination, adaptive depth sampling, adaptive image sampling). Output: A 2D image buffer containing the final rendered pixel values. Data Structures: Projection Buffers (Zn, Zr): Two arrays of size W \times H (image width and height). Zn[u, v] stores the nearest depth intersection, initialized to \infty. Zr[u, v] stores the farthest depth intersection, initialized to -\infty. These define the valid integration intervals for each ray. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Boundary Detection): Identify all boundary cells in the volume. 2. Object-Based Partitioning (Projection Phase): Divide the volume into P subsets, each containing an equal number of boundary cells. Each processor independently scans its assigned subset and projects every detected boundary cell onto the image plane to create partial projection buffers (Zn^p, Zr^p). Combine all partial buffers to form the complete global projection buffers (Zn, Zr). 3. Image-Based Partitioning (Traversal Phase): Divide the image into P large blocks of consecutive scanlines, one block per processor. Each processor performs ray integrals within the bounded intervals [Zn[u, v], Zr[u, v]] for viable pixels in its assigned block. Empty scanlines are skipped using the projection buffer information. Ray-independent optimizations (early ray termination, adaptive depth sampling) are applied directly along individual rays. Ray-dependent optimizations (adaptive image sampling) require extra attention to avoid replicated ray casting costs at pixels shared by image sections assigned to different processors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridpartitioningparallelraycasting(volume, camera, P): # Step 1: Preprocessing # Standard boundary detection: identify voxels with at least one transparent neighbor boundarycells = [voxel for voxel in volume if hastransparentneighbor(voxel)] # Step 2: Object-Based Partitioning # Static contiguous partitioning: split volume grid into P contiguous chunks with equal boundary cell counts volumesubsets = splitvolumecontiguously(volume, boundarycells, P) W, H = camera.imagewidth, camera.imageheight Zn = [[float('inf')] H for in range(W)] Zr = [[float('-inf')] H for in range(W)] for p in range(P): localZn = [[float('inf')] H for in range(W)] localZr = [[float('-inf')] H for in range(W)] for voxel in volumesubsets[p]: if hastransparentneighbor(voxel): u, v, z = projectontoimage(voxel, camera) if 0 <= u < W and 0 <= v < H: if z < localZn[u][v]: localZn[u][v] = z if z > localZr[u][v]: localZr[u][v] = z for u in range(W): for v in range(H): if localZn[u][v] < Zn[u][v]: Zn[u][v] = localZn[u][v] if localZr[u][v] > Zr[u][v]: Zr[u][v] = localZr[u][v] # Step 3: Image-Based Partitioning # Static contiguous division: split image width W into P contiguous horizontal blocks scanlineblocks = splitwidthcontiguously(W, P) image = [[0.0] H for in range(W)] for p in range(P): ustart, uend = scanlineblocks[p] for v in range(H): for u in range(ustart, uend): if Zn[u][v] == float('inf') or Zr[u][v] == float('-inf'): continue rayorigin, raydirection = generateray(camera, u, v) color = 0.0 alpha = 0.0 t = Zn[u][v] while t < Zr[u][v]: stepsize = computeadaptivestep(raydirection, t) sample = interpolatetrilinear(volume, rayorigin + raydirection t) color, alpha = compositefronttoback(sample, color, alpha) if alpha > 1.0 - 1e-6: break t += stepsize image[u][v] = color return image def hastransparentneighbor(voxel): return any(neighbor.istransparent for neighbor in voxel.neighbors) def splitvolumecontiguously(volume, boundarycells, P): # Distribute boundary cells evenly across P contiguous volume chunks chunksize = len(boundarycells) // P return [volume[ichunksize:(i+1)chunksize] for i in range(P)] def projectontoimage(voxel, camera): return camera.project(voxel.center) def splitwidthcontiguously(W, P): return [(i W // P, (i + 1) W // P) for i in range(P)] def generateray(camera, u, v): return camera.rayforpixel(u, v) def computeadaptivestep(raydirection, t): return raydirection.stepsize # Adaptive depth sampling logic def interpolatetrilinear(volume, point): return volume.trilinearsample(point) def compositefronttoback(sample, color, alpha): c, a = sample.color, sample.alpha newcolor = color + c (1.0 - alpha) newalpha = alpha + a (1.0 - alpha) return newcolor, newalpha Parameters: P: Number of processors. Typical values depend on hardware (e.g., SGI Power Challenge had multiple CPUs). \epsilon: Threshold for early ray termination. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Replicated Ray Casting: Ray-dependent optimizations like adaptive image sampling can cause replicated work if pixels shared by different processor blocks are evaluated independently. The static contiguous image-based partitioning completely avoids this cost without extra synchronization overhead. A variant that incorporates adaptive image sampling and early ray termination optimizations from the serial version. Adaptive depth sampling is used to skip time-consuming points between voxel layers. It is chosen when static contiguous scanline blocks are sufficient for load balancing and serial optimizations must be preserved. An implementation focusing on data coherence and load balancing on MIMD computers. Work is assigned to processors to exploit data coherence, meaning a single processor works on neighboring rays whenever possible. It is chosen when hardware architecture favors spatial locality, accepting the trade-off that computational costs for different rays can vary by several orders of magnitude. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Tested on an SGI Power Challenge shared-memory MIMD architecture. Strengths: Avoids the dilemma of choosing between object-based and image-based partitioning. Leverages optimizations from the serial algorithm. No extra synchronization overhead for adaptive image sampling. Limitations: Requires a shared-memory architecture. The static nature of the partitioning may lead to load imbalance if the distribution of boundary cells or viable pixels is highly skewed, though the equal boundary cell division mitigates this for the projection phase. The method was developed for time-critical volume rendering on shared-memory MIMD architectures, specifically the SGI Power Challenge. It builds on a serial ray casting algorithm that included optimizations like adaptive image sampling and early ray termination. The hybrid approach was proposed to overcome the limitations of existing parallel algorithms that had to choose between object-based or image-based partitioning, giving up the advantages of the other. name: Spatial Subdivision and Hierarchical Sampling
body: Spatial Subdivision and Hierarchical Sampling accelerates volume rendering and neural radiance field training by dynamically adjusting sampling density based on local visual complexity or error metrics. It solves the inefficiency of uniform sampling by concentrating computational resources (rays or network evaluations) in regions with high gradients or large reconstruction errors while skipping or interpolating smooth areas. Unlike Adaptive Screen Sampling which relies on simple color variance heuristics, or Resolution Adaptation which adjusts grid resolution, this family explicitly uses hierarchical data structures (quadtrees) or iterative error bounds to define the sampling regions. Builds on the shared principles of Adaptive Sampling and Resolution. All methods in this family partition the image plane or volume using hierarchical data structures (typically quadtrees) to compute a local metric (gradient magnitude, rendering error, or color variance) that modulates sampling density or resolution. The adaptation follows a control loop: compute a scalar metric M representing local complexity or error; adjust a parameter P (step size \Delta t, resolution R, or sampling probability w) based on M; execute the volume integral or loss computation with the adjusted parameter. Common adaptation laws include step size adaptation \Delta t \propto 1/M, resolution control via threshold-based switching, and probability weighting wi \propto Mi for importance sampling. All methods aim to maintain visual fidelity while reducing the total number of volume queries or network evaluations. Uses iterative convergence with either Finite Element Method (FEM) error bounds for rigorous quality or Level-of-Detail (LOD) feedback for interactive frame rates. It balances quality and performance by subdividing image regions based on error estimates. A heuristic image-order technique that adjusts ray counts per pixel based on local color variance. It is simpler than FEM approaches but may over-refine linear regions or fail in non-homogeneous scenes. A training-time acceleration method for neural radiance fields. It subdivides training views into quadtrees based on rendering error to reduce ray redundancy, working with various radiance field architectures. The concept of adaptive sampling in volume rendering originated with Levoy's work on hierarchical data structures and error estimation. The specific application of quadtree subdivision for adaptive ray shooting in the context of neural radiance fields was introduced to address the computational cost of training multi-view radiance fields. name: Adaptive Refinement for Volume Rendering
head: Adaptive Refinement Volume Rendering, Image-order adaptive refinement, Interactive Adaptive Refinement, Feedback-based Adaptive Refinement
body: Adaptive Refinement for Volume Rendering is an image-order technique that progressively improves visual fidelity by casting rays non-uniformly based on local image complexity, balancing rendering quality and performance in interactive settings. It sets itself apart from its siblings by either using a feedback loop to maintain a target frame rate while bounding error per texel or by employing a rigorous Finite Element Method (FEM)-based error estimator to guide h-adaptive subdivision of the image plane, whereas Adaptive Screen Sampling typically relies on variance-based metrics and Adaptive Ray Shooting & Quadtree Subdivision often focuses on object-space or hybrid approaches. Builds on Adaptive Sampling and Resolution. The method operates as a reactive control loop or an iterative approximation sequence that adjusts sampling density to maintain a target frame rate or minimize L^2 error. Inputs: 3D scalar field data (voxels), transfer function (mapping scalar to color/opacity), camera parameters, and user-defined parameters (target frame rate, error thresholds, initial resolution bounds). Outputs: A rendered image (framebuffer) and an error map or flag array indicating computed vs. interpolated regions. 1. Quadtree (CPU): Stores image regions as quadratic cells. Each leaf node represents a cell that can be refined into four children. 2. Error Map / Flag Array F (CPU/GPU): A 2D array (e.g., R \times R) where pixels indicate whether a ray has been traced (F=1) or if the region is computed via interpolation (F=0). In FEM-based implementations, a 1D single-channel floating-point texture stores error values for quadtree leaves. 3. Interpolation Flag Array G (CPU): Tracks pixels that have been interpolated to avoid redundant computation. 4. Color Buffer C: Stores the final color values for each pixel. The volume rendering integral along a ray parametrized by arc length w^x of length L^x is: I(x) = \int0^{L^x} E(w^x) \exp\left(-\int0^t A(w^x) ds\right) dt where E is emission and A is absorption. The approximation error is measured using the L^2 error norm: \boldsymbol{\eta} = \|u - un\|S:= \left( \intS (u - un)^2 dx \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} where u is the exact solution on the viewport S and un is the approximative solution. The local error contribution on each cell T is estimated by comparing two subsequent approximations: \eta{Vn}^T \approx \|u{n-1} - un\|T = \left( \intT (u{n-1} - un)^2 dx \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} This integral is solved numerically using a Gaussian quadrature rule with N=3 points. Relative L^2 error is defined as: \eta{rel} = \|u - un\|S / \|u\|S m: Fixed number of cells to mark for refinement per iteration. Typical value: 1000. p: Polynomial degree for interpolation during reconstruction. Fixed value: 2 (bilinear/quadratic). romax: Maximum ray density/region size. Initial value: 16. romin: Minimum ray density/region size. Initial value: 2. \epsilon (e): Error threshold for color difference. Initial value: 16–32. targetframerate: Desired frame rate budget. Typical value: 10 fps. errorthreshold: Maximum allowable visual error. Typical value: 1 pixel per texel. W: Number of evenly spaced locations along a ray for resampling. The implementation varies slightly between the FEM-based approach and the interactive level-of-detail approach, but both follow a refinement loop. 1. Initialize: Start with a coarse uniform grid (quadtree leaves). 2. Estimate Error: For each new quadtree leaf, estimate the local error \etaT using the hierarchical a-posteriori estimator (Equation 9). 3. Mark Cells: Use a heap data structure to select the m cells with the biggest impact on total error \eta. Sorting cost is O(m \log n). 4. Refine: Subdivide marked cells into four new quadtree leaves. Generate new evaluation points: one at the cell center and four at the edge midpoints (max 5 points per leaf). Samples are never computed twice. 5. Ray Casting: For each new evaluation point, perform standard ray-casting. Use Step Doubling for error control: compute color with full step size h and two half steps h/2. If squared difference < error bound, accept and increase h; otherwise, decrease h and repeat. 6. Reconstruct: Render approximation un to the screen using polynomial degree p=2 interpolation on a uniform grid. 7. Loop: Repeat until convergence to pixel accuracy or user-specified error bound. Interrupt if camera or transfer function changes. 1. Initialize: Set romax, romin, and epsilon. Clear flags F and G, and color buffer C. 2. Loop while romax > 1: a. RayTraceData: Divide image into square regions of size romax. For each region, call RayTraceRegion. RayTraceRegion(u,v,w): Cast rays from the four corner pixels of the region (if flag F is clear). Set F=1 after tracing. If region size w > w{min} AND Difference (color range at corners > \epsilon) is true, divide into four subregions of size w/2 and recurse. RayTrace: Resample data at W evenly spaced locations, tri-linearly interpolate from 8 surrounding voxels, and composite with a fully opaque background. b. InterpolateImage: Divide image into square regions of size romax. For each region, call InterpolateRegion. InterpolateRegion(u,v,w): Interpolate colors at midpoints of sides (linear) and center (bilinear) of the region (if flags F and G are clear). Set G=1. If w/2 > 1, divide into four subregions and recurse. c. DisplayImage: Show the current image. d. Clear: For all pixels where F is clear, reset C and G to 0. e. Increment: Update romax, romin, and epsilon to next values in the sequence. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import heapq import math def adaptiverefinementfem(imagewidth, imageheight, maxiterations, m, errorbound): # Initialize quadtree with coarse grid (4x4 cells) quadtree = [] cellsize = max(1, imagewidth // 4) for i in range(0, imagewidth, cellsize): for j in range(0, imageheight, cellsize): quadtree.append({'u': i, 'v': j, 'w': cellsize, 'children': None}) for iteration in range(maxiterations): # 1. Estimate error for new leaves errorvalues = [] for leaf in quadtree: # Estimate local error using Gaussian quadrature on u{n-1} - un localerror = 0.0 # Standard 3-point Gaussian quadrature for 2D integral approximation # Weights for 1D 3-point Gauss-Legendre: 5/9, 8/9, 5/9 weights1d = [5.0/9.0, 8.0/9.0, 5.0/9.0] points1d = [-math.sqrt(3/5), 0.0, math.sqrt(3/5)] for xiidx, xi in enumerate(points1d): for yiidx, yi in enumerate(points1d): # Evaluate integrand at quadrature points val = computeintegrand(leaf, xi, yi) localerror += val weights1d[xiidx] weights1d[yiidx] errorvalues.append((leaf, localerror)) # 2. Mark top m cells using a heap (O(m log n)) markedcells = heapq.nlargest(m, errorvalues, key=lambda x: x[1]) # 3. Refine marked cells newevaluationpoints = [] for cell, in markedcells: # Creates 4 new leaves halfw = cell['w'] / 2 cell['children'] = [ {'u': cell['u'], 'v': cell['v'], 'w': halfw}, {'u': cell['u'] + halfw, 'v': cell['v'], 'w': halfw}, {'u': cell['u'], 'v': cell['v'] + halfw, 'w': halfw}, {'u': cell['u'] + halfw, 'v': cell['v'] + halfw, 'w': halfw} ] quadtree.remove(cell) quadtree.extend(cell['children']) # Generate evaluation points: center + 4 edge midpoints cx, cy = cell['u'] + cell['w']/2, cell['v'] + cell['w']/2 points = [ (cx, cy), # center (cell['u'] + cell['w']/2, cell['v']), # top midpoint (cell['u'] + cell['w']/2, cell['v'] + cell['w']), # bottom midpoint (cell['u'], cell['v'] + cell['w']/2), # left midpoint (cell['u'] + cell['w'], cell['v'] + cell['w']/2) # right midpoint ] newevaluationpoints.extend(points) # 4. Compute ray casting for new points h = 1.0 for point in newevaluationpoints: # Step Doubling for ray integration error control colorfull = castraystep(point, stepsize=h) colorhalf = castraystephalf(point, stepsize=h/2.0) diff = sum((c1 - c2)2 for c1, c2 in zip(colorfull, colorhalf)) if diff < errorbound: h = h 1.5 color = colorfull else: h = h / 2.0 color = castraystep(point, stepsize=h) # Re-evaluate # 5. Reconstruct and render renderimage(quadtree, polynomialdegree=2) # Check convergence or interrupt on camera move if checkconvergence() or cameramoved(): break def castraystep(point, stepsize): # Not given in the sources. Standard ray marching with step size. return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def castraystephalf(point, stepsize): # Not given in the sources. Standard ray marching with half steps. return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def computeintegrand(leaf, xi, yi): # Not given in the sources. Evaluates (u{n-1} - un)^2 at quadrature points. return 0.0 def renderimage(quadtree, polynomialdegree): # Not given in the sources. Reconstructs un on uniform grid using p=2 interpolation. pass def checkconvergence(): # Not given in the sources. Checks if approximation error < threshold. return False def cameramoved(): # Not given in the sources. Detects camera or transfer function changes. return False def adaptiverefinementinteractive(R, romaxinit, romininit, epsiloninit): flagsF = [[0 for in range(R)] for in range(R)] # Ray traced flag flagsG = [[0 for in range(R)] for in range(R)] # Interpolated flag colors = [[(0,0,0) for in range(R)] for in range(R)] romax = romaxinit romin = romininit epsilon = epsiloninit while romax > 1: # Ray Tracing Phase for v in range(0, R, romax): for u in range(0, R, romax): raytraceregion(u, v, romax, romin, epsilon, flagsF, colors) # Interpolation Phase for v in range(0, R, romax): for u in range(0, R, romax): interpolateregion(u, v, romax, flagsF, flagsG, colors) display(colors) # Clear interpolated colors for next iteration for v in range(R): for u in range(R): if flagsF[v][u] == 0: colors[v][u] = (0,0,0) flagsG[v][u] = 0 # Increment LOD parameters romax = max(1, romax // 2) romin = max(1, romin // 2) epsilon = max(1, epsilon // 2) def raytraceregion(u, v, w, wmin, epsilon, flagsF, colors): # Cast rays from four corners for j in [0, w]: for i in [0, w]: if u+i < R and v+j < R and flagsF[u+i][v+j] == 0: colors[u+i][v+j] = castray(u+i, v+j) flagsF[u+i][v+j] = 1 # Subdivision check if w > wmin and difference(u, v, w, epsilon, colors) > 0: for j in [0, w//2]: for i in [0, w//2]: raytraceregion(u+i, v+j, w//2, wmin, epsilon, flagsF, colors) def difference(u, v, w, epsilon, colors): # Check if range of intensity values for any color component # at the four corners exceeds epsilon corners = [(u, v), (u+w, v), (u, v+w), (u+w, v+w)] maxdiff = 0 for c in range(3): # R, G, B vals = [colors[x][y][c] for x, y in corners] diff = max(vals) - min(vals) if diff > maxdiff: maxdiff = diff return maxdiff def interpolateregion(u, v, w, flagsF, flagsG, colors): # Interpolate at midpoints and center for j in [0, w//2, w]: for i in [0, w//2, w]: if u+i < R and v+j < R and flagsF[u+i][v+j] == 0 and flagsG[u+i][v+j] == 0: colors[u+i][v+j] = interpolate(u, v, w, u+i, v+j) flagsG[u+i][v+j] = 1 # Recursion if w//2 > 1: for j in [0, w//2]: for i in [0, w//2]: interpolateregion(u+i, v+j, w//2, flagsF, flagsG, colors) def castray(u, v): # Not given in the sources. Traces ray from pixel (u,v). return (0,0,0) def interpolate(u, v, w, targetu, targetv): # Not given in the sources. Linear or bilinear interpolation. return (0,0,0) def display(colors): # Not given in the sources. Renders colors to screen. pass Latency: Reactive feedback introduces scheduling latency; proactive scheduling using system timing parameters like fill rates is recommended. Interactivity: The loop is interrupted whenever the camera moves or the transfer function changes to guarantee interactivity. Parameter Sensitivity: Manual selection of level-of-detail parameters (romax, romin, epsilon) can lead to sub-optimal presentation. Inappropriate values cause features to be missed, ignored, or poorly resolved. Levoy's Estimator Limitation: Unlike Levoy's variance-based estimator which refines linear regions with strong slopes unnecessarily, the hierarchical estimator notices good approximation in linear regions and focuses on interior edges. Time Complexity: Marking complexity is O(m \log n) for sorting quadtree leaves using a heap, where m is the number of marked cells and n is the number of leaves. Rendering time grows linearly with dataset size for full ray tracing, but adaptive refinement reduces effective cost by casting fewer rays in smooth regions. Memory Complexity: Quadtree data structures are stored on the CPU. Error estimation output is a 1D single-channel floating-point texture with m entries. Measured Performance: On a GeForce3 GPU (640x480 resolution), the system maintained a 10 fps budget, adding cells to reduce error below 1 pixel/texel. On an Intel Core 2 Duo 3.0 GHz with NVIDIA GeForce 8800GT GPU, 7 iterations were needed for approximation error 10^{-2} on a 256x256 initial grid with m=1000. A single iteration took 20–40 ms for screen resolutions 512x512 and 2048x2048 respectively. Cytochrome dataset (113 slices of 256x256): Frame 1 took 4.6 seconds with 3,870 rays (20% coverage). Frame 4 took 25.7 seconds total with 19,289 rays (100% coverage). Head dataset (CT scan, 113 slices of 256x256): Frame 1 took 13 seconds with 5,179 rays (16% coverage). Frame 4 took 104 seconds total with 30,603 rays (100% coverage). Strengths: Faster convergence (fewer rays for desired quality) compared to uniform discretization. Allows interactive frame rates by focusing computational effort only where necessary. Limitations: Reactive feedback latency. Manual parameter tuning required for optimal results. Origin: The concept of adaptive image-space subdivision for volume rendering was introduced by Marc Levoy in 1990 [Lev90], who used a simple error measure based on corner pixel variance. Development: The FEM-based approach was developed by Hadwiger et al. (2011), leveraging finite element theory for explicit error control and convergence analysis. The interactive level-of-detail approach was presented by Upson et al. (1988), focusing on incremental refinement for molecular graphics and medical imaging. Usage: Demonstrated in interactive exploration of unstructured grids (Blunt Fin model), CT scans (Head, Engine), and molecular graphics (Cytochrome B5). Implemented in C++ and OpenGL/GLSL requiring Shader Model 4.0 GPU. name: Adaptive Screen Sampling
head: Adaptive Subdivision of Screen Space, Gradient-based Adaptive Sampling, Screen-Space Adaptive Refinement
body: Adaptive screen sampling is a dynamic sampling technique that reduces the average number of rays cast per pixel by evaluating local color variance and refining samples only where the scene changes rapidly. Introduced by Levoy, it adapts the sampling rate based on color change in a small pixel neighborhood, switching to a higher sampling rate in areas with high value gradients to replace interpolated values with exact color values. Inputs: A volume dataset V. A camera model defining ray origins and directions. A target image resolution W \times H. A neighborhood radius r for gradient estimation. A threshold \tau for color variance. A maximum number of samples per pixel k{\max}. Outputs: A final rendered image I of size W \times H. Data Structures: ImageBuffer: A 2D array storing accumulated color C(x,y) and sample count N(x,y) for each pixel. RayQueue: A list of rays to be traced, initially containing one ray per pixel. Algorithm: 1. Initial Sampling: Cast an initial small number of rays per pixel to sample the scene. For each ray, perform volume integration to obtain a color value. 2. Metric Evaluation: For each pixel (x,y), compute the color variance M within the neighborhood defined by radius r. Let C{i,j} be the color values of the samples taken at pixel (x,y) and its neighbors. 3. Adaptation Decision: If M(x,y) < \tau, the scene is homogeneous and sampling terminates for that pixel. If M(x,y) \ge \tau, the scene has high value gradients and refinement proceeds. 4. Refinement: Cast additional rays in the pixel region to capture rapid scene changes and satisfy quality requirements. Trace these rays and accumulate their color values. 5. Handling Misses: If rays miss the volume surface, interpolate missing values from surrounding valid samples. 6. Iteration: Repeat the metric evaluation and refinement steps until the variance M falls below \tau or a maximum number of samples is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivescreensampling(volume, camera, width, height, threshold, maxsamples, neighborhoodradius): # Initialize image buffer and sample counts image = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(width)] for in range(height)] samplecounts = [[0] width for in range(height)] # Initial ray generation: one ray per pixel rays = [] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rays.append(camera.getray(x, y)) # First pass: initial sampling for ray in rays: # Standard ray marching implementation that returns accumulated color color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] x, y = ray.screenposition image[y][x][0] += color[0] image[y][x][1] += color[1] image[y][x][2] += color[2] samplecounts[y][x] += 1 # Adaptive refinement loop changed = True while changed: changed = False nextrays = [] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): if samplecounts[y][x] >= maxsamples: continue # Calculate variance in neighborhood neighbors = [] for dy in range(-neighborhoodradius, neighborhoodradius + 1): for dx in range(-neighborhoodradius, neighborhoodradius + 1): ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < height and 0 <= nx < width: neighbors.append(image[ny][nx]) if len(neighbors) < 2: continue # Compute variance of accumulated colors mean = [sum(c[i] for c in neighbors) / len(neighbors) for i in range(3)] variance = sum(sum((c[i] - mean[i])2 for i in range(3)) for c in neighbors) / len(neighbors) if variance >= threshold: # High gradient: cast additional rays for second sampling step numadditional = max(1, int(variance 10)) for in range(numadditional): perturbedray = camera.getray(x, y, perturbation=True) nextrays.append(perturbedray) changed = True else: # Low gradient: finalize pixel by averaging count = samplecounts[y][x] if count > 0: image[y][x][0] /= count image[y][x][1] /= count image[y][x][2] /= count samplecounts[y][x] = maxsamples # Trace new rays and accumulate for ray in nextrays: # Standard ray marching implementation that returns accumulated color color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] x, y = ray.screenposition image[y][x][0] += color[0] image[y][x][1] += color[1] image[y][x][2] += color[2] samplecounts[y][x] += 1 return image Parameters: \tau: Variance threshold. Not given in the sources. r: Neighborhood radius. Not given in the sources. k{\max}: Maximum samples per pixel. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Misses: Rays may occasionally miss the surface, requiring interpolation of missing values. Heuristic Failure: The method is heuristic-based and may fail to produce desired visual results if parameters are not carefully tuned. Overhead: The computation time spent determining sample rates can equal or exceed the cost of constant-rate sampling, especially in non-homogeneous scenes. Aliasing: If not carefully tuned, the method risks aliasing and quality loss in non-homogeneous regions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Reduces average compute time for homogeneous scenes. However, in non-homogeneous scenes, the overhead of variance calculation and ray management can negate savings. Strengths: Efficient for scenes with large homogeneous regions; reduces ray count where detail is low. Limitations: Heuristic nature makes it difficult to guarantee quality; overhead can be significant; prone to aliasing if thresholds are poorly chosen. When to use: Scenes with large uniform areas and distinct boundaries; when computational resources are limited and homogeneous regions dominate. When not to use: Highly heterogeneous scenes; when consistent quality is required regardless of scene content; when overhead of variance calculation is prohibitive. Adaptive screen sampling was introduced by Levoy in 1990. It is well known in traditional ray tracing and has been applied to volume rendering as a method to adaptively switch sampling rates based on color change in a pixel neighborhood. The technique is part of the broader family of adaptive sampling methods aimed at reducing aliasing and computational cost by focusing samples where they are most needed. name: Adaptive Ray Shooting & Quadtree Subdivision
head: Adaptive quadtree subdivision, Image context based probability distribution
body: Adaptive Ray Shooting & Quadtree Subdivision is a general strategy to accelerate the training of radiance field-based methods by reducing ray redundancy during volume rendering. It solves the problem of excessive computational cost in multi-view volume rendering by dynamically adjusting the number of rays cast per pixel based on local image complexity. Unlike specialized architectures such as Plenoxels, TensoRF, or Instant-NGP that require specific data structures like sparse voxel grids or hash coding, this method is a general framework applicable to almost all radiance field methods without architectural modification. The method operates as a preprocessing step for the volume rendering loop, determining which rays to evaluate based on a quadtree decomposition of the image plane. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N training images \mathcal{I}. A radiance field model F\Theta: (x, d) \mapsto (c, \sigma) that maps a 5D point to emitted color c and volume density \sigma. Output: A subset of rays Ri \subset \text{All Rays}i for each image Ii, selected via adaptive subdivision. Data Structures Quadtree: Each view is adaptively subdivided into a quadtree according to the average rendering error in each node. Node Metric: Each node stores the average rendering error of the rays passing through its region. 5D Point Representation: Points are defined as \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 and viewing direction \mathbf{d} = (\theta, \phi) \in \mathbb{R}^2. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: For each training image Ii \in \mathcal{I}, initialize a quadtree with a single root node covering the full image dimensions. 2. Initial Ray Casting: Cast a uniform set of rays for all pixels in the initial quadtree nodes. 3. Error Computation: For each node in the quadtree, compute the average rendering error. The error is derived from the difference between the rendered color and the target pixel color. 4. Subdivision Decision: Compare the average error Ej of each node against a threshold. If Ej exceeds the threshold, subdivide the node into four children. Repeat this process recursively until a maximum depth is reached or the error is below the threshold. 5. Adaptive Ray Shooting: For leaf nodes in the final quadtree, if the node is in a complex region with larger rendering error, dynamically shoot more rays. If the node is in a simple region, cast fewer rays. Rays are shot primarily at pixels with dramatic color change. 6. Volume Rendering: For each selected ray r{ki}, sample 5D points along the ray. The network F\Theta predicts color c and density \sigma. Render the pixel color \hat{c}{ki} using standard volume rendering integration. 7. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss L over all selected rays: L = \frac{1}{NM} \sum{Ii \in \mathcal{I}} \sum{r{ki} \in Ri} ||V\Theta(r{ki}) - c{ki}||2^2 Where: N is the number of training images. M is the number of rays per image. \mathcal{I} is the set of all training images. Ri is the set of rays generated from Ii. r{ki} is the k-th ray from the i-th training image. V\Theta is the volume rendering function mapping a ray to rendered color \hat{c}{ki}. c{ki} is the target pixel color. 8. Optimization: Update network parameters \Theta to minimize L. 9. Iteration: Repeat steps 2–8 for subsequent training iterations, updating the quadtree structure based on the latest rendering errors. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiverayshootingquadtree(images, radiancefield, maxdepth, errorthreshold, numiterations): quadtrees = [] for img in images: qt = Quadtree(root=Node(0, 0, img.width, img.height, 0)) quadtrees.append(qt) for iteration in range(numiterations): totalloss = 0.0 raysperimage = [] for idx, img in enumerate(images): qt = quadtrees[idx] # Subdivide based on gradient (iteration 0) or rendering error (subsequent) if iteration == 0: qt.subdivideongradient(errorthreshold, maxdepth) else: qt.subdivideonerror(errorthreshold, maxdepth, radiancefield) rays = [] for leaf in qt.getleaves(): # Higher error -> more rays numrays = int(leaf.error 10) + 1 # heuristic scaling rays.extend(leaf.generaterays(numrays)) raysperimage.append(len(rays)) rendered = [] for ray in rays: pts = sample5dpoints(ray) # chat = volumerender(ray, pts, radiancefield) # rendered.append(chat) target = img.getpixelcolors() loss = sum((r - t)2 for r, t in zip(rendered, target)) / len(rendered) # totalloss += loss qt.updateerrors(rendered, rays) N = len(images) M = sum(raysperimage) / N # Average rays per image avgloss = totalloss / (N M) radiancefield.update(avgloss) return radiancefield class Node: def init(self, x, y, w, h, depth): self.x, self.y, self.w, self.h, self.depth = x, y, w, h, depth self.children = None self.error = 0.0 def isleaf(self): return self.children is None def getleaves(self): if self.isleaf(): return [self] return [n for c in self.children for n in c.getleaves()] class Quadtree: def init(self, root): self.root = root def subdivideongradient(self, threshold, maxdepth): # Recursive subdivision where gradient magnitude > threshold up to maxdepth pass def subdivideonerror(self, threshold, maxdepth, radiancefield): # Recursive subdivision where average rendering error > threshold up to maxdepth pass def getleaves(self): return self.root.getleaves() def updateerrors(self, rendered, rays): # Assign average error to each node based on rendered vs target colors pass def sample5dpoints(ray): # Sample points along ray origin and direction pass def volumerender(ray, points5d, radiancefield): # Integrate FTheta predictions along ray pass Parameters Error Threshold: Controls the granularity of the quadtree. Not given in the sources. Max Depth: Limits the recursion depth of the quadtree. Not given in the sources. Ray Density Multiplier: Factor determining how many more rays are cast in complex regions vs. simple regions. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Rendering error computation must be stable to avoid oscillating subdivision patterns. Boundaries: Quadtree nodes must align with pixel boundaries to ensure correct ray mapping. Degenerate Input: If an image is uniform, the quadtree will remain at the root level, casting minimal rays. If an image is highly noisy, the quadtree may reach max depth everywhere, resulting in uniform sampling. Time Complexity: The method reduces the total number of rays M significantly compared to uniform sampling, thereby reducing the time spent in volume rendering per epoch. The overhead of quadtree management and error computation adds a small constant cost. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the quadtree structure for each image. The size is proportional to the number of nodes, which is bounded by 4 \times \text{Image Resolution} in the worst case (full subdivision). Measured Performance: Evaluated with NeRF and Plenoxels under widely used benchmarks, achieving comparable accuracy to state-of-the-art methods with much faster training. Strengths: General applicability to various radiance field methods; reduces training burden by focusing on complex regions; barely affects accuracy. Limitations: Requires an initial pass or heuristic to determine error before accurate subdivision can occur; overhead of dynamic ray generation. When to Use: When training radiance fields is computationally expensive and the scene has varying levels of detail. When Not to Use: When real-time inference is the primary concern (this is a training acceleration method); when the scene is uniformly simple (overhead may not be justified). The method was introduced in the paper "Fast Learning Radiance Fields by Shooting Much Fewer Rays". It addresses the limitation of specialized fast training methods (like Plenoxels, TensoRF, Instant-NGP) that require specific architectures. The key insight is that radiance fields can be perceived without dramatically sacrificing accuracy by shooting fewer rays in redundant regions. The method leverages the fact that pixels with dramatic color change contain more information and require more samples. name: Octree-based Sampling Optimization for PINNs
head: Octree-based hierarchical sampling optimization for PINNs
body: An importance sampling strategy for training Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) that partitions the spatio-temporal domain using an octree to reduce the number of sample points required for convergence. Unlike volumetric super-resolution methods that require computing intersection spaces for unknown ground truth, this method operates solely within specific areas where limited training data exists, making it suitable for scientific data with sparse observations. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly modeling the importance distribution of training data via octree leaf nodes as indivisible subblocks, rather than relying on continuous gradient metrics or screen-space heuristics. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Limited training data in a specific area of interest (e.g., cylinder wake); Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) architecture; PDE equations with unknown parameters; total loss threshold for bottleneck detection. Outputs: Trained PINN model; optimized sampling distribution defined by the octree structure. Data Structures: Octree: A hierarchical spatial subdivision of the spatio-temporal domain. Root: Represents the entire domain of interest. Internal Nodes: Represent sub-volumes. Leaf Nodes: Represent indivisible subblocks. Each leaf node corresponds to a specific region in the spatio-temporal grid where sampling occurs sequentially. Layout: Standard octree structure where each node has up to 8 children. The depth is determined by the convergence level of the training data or a predefined resolution limit. Parameters: q: Parameter controlling octree reconstruction frequency. q=0: Reconstruct octree immediately after every epoch. q=5: Start bottleneck evaluation from the 5th epoch, using loss values of the last 5 epochs for linear regression to determine reconstruction timing. q=+\infty: Never reconstruct the octree (use initial structure forever). Typical value: q=5. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the first octree based on the limited training data available in the specific area of interest. 2. Initial Training: Train the PINN using importance sampling of input coordinates from the beginning, guided by the initialized octree. Sampling is performed sequentially in each indivisible subblock corresponding to each leaf node of the octree within the entire domain. 3. Bottleneck Detection: Monitor the total loss during training. When the total loss reaches a bottleneck (plateaus or fails to decrease significantly), trigger octree reconstruction. 4. Loss Distribution Computation: Compute the loss value at each coordinate in the spatio-temporal grid according to the current best model. This involves evaluating the PINN's residual (PDE loss) and data loss (if applicable) at a set of grid points. 5. Octree Reconstruction: Rebuild the octree based on the computed loss distribution to reflect the new importance distribution of the training data. Regions with higher loss (higher importance) are subdivided further. 6. Iterative Training: Resume training with the new octree structure, performing importance sampling sequentially in the new leaf nodes. 7. Repeat: Repeat steps 3-5 whenever the total loss reaches a bottleneck to avoid the failure of importance sampling due to outdated importance distributions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainpinnoctree(trainingdata, pdeequations, network, q): """ Train PINN using octree-based sampling optimization. Args: trainingdata: Limited training data in specific area. pdeequations: PDE equations with unknown parameters. network: PINN architecture. q: Reconstruction frequency parameter. Returns: trainednetwork: The trained PINN model. """ # Step 1: Initialize octree based on limited training data octree = initializeoctree(trainingdata) # Step 2: Initial training with importance sampling currentepoch = 0 totallosshistory = [] while not convergencecriteriamet(network): # Perform importance sampling based on current octree # Sampling is sequential in each indivisible subblock (leaf node) samplepoints = samplefromoctree(octree) # Train network for one epoch loss = trainepoch(network, samplepoints, trainingdata, pdeequations) totallosshistory.append(loss) currentepoch += 1 # Step 3: Bottleneck detection and reconstruction logic if shouldreconstruct(q, currentepoch, totallosshistory): # Step 4: Compute loss distribution on spatio-temporal grid # Evaluate current best model on a grid covering the domain of interest gridpoints = generatespatiotemporalgrid(domainofinterest) lossdistribution = computelossdistribution(network, gridpoints, pdeequations, trainingdata) # Step 5: Rebuild octree based on loss distribution octree = rebuildoctree(lossdistribution, domainofinterest) # Note: Reconstruction is time-consuming; frequent reconstruction (q=0) # increases training time significantly (e.g., by 105.45%). return network def shouldreconstruct(q, currentepoch, totallosshistory): """ Determine if octree reconstruction should occur based on q and loss history. """ if q == 0: # Reconstruct immediately after every epoch return True elif q == float('inf'): # Never reconstruct return False else: # Start bottleneck evaluation from q-th epoch if currentepoch < q: return False # Use loss values of the last q epochs for linear regression # to detect if loss has reached a bottleneck recentlosses = totallosshistory[-q:] # Linear regression to check for plateau # If slope is near zero or loss variance is low, consider it a bottleneck # Implementation detail: Simple heuristic: if max(recentlosses) - min(recentlosses) < threshold threshold = 1e-4 # Example threshold, specific value not given in sources if max(recentlosses) - min(recentlosses) < threshold: return True return False def computelossdistribution(network, gridpoints, pdeequations, trainingdata): """ Compute the loss value at each coordinate in the spatio-temporal grid. """ lossvalues = [] for point in gridpoints: # Compute PDE residual loss pdeloss = computepderesidual(network, point, pdeequations) # Compute data loss if point is in training data area dataloss = computedataloss(network, point, trainingdata) # Total loss totalloss = pdeloss + dataloss lossvalues.append(totalloss) return lossvalues def samplefromoctree(octree): """ Perform importance sampling sequentially in each indivisible subblock (leaf node). """ samples = [] for leafnode in octree.getleafnodes(): # Sample points within the leaf node's subblock # Importance is proportional to the volume or predefined weight of the leaf points = sampleinsubblock(leafnode) samples.extend(points) return samples Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Reconstruction (q=+\infty): The variance-based initial octree gradually fails to represent the importance distribution of training data, leading to no promotion in prediction performance. Frequent Reconstruction (q=0): Increases training time significantly (by 105.45% in experiments) because reconstruction is time-consuming, even though it reduces sample points. Downsampling: To reduce the time for rebuilding the loss distribution, the training data may be downsampled, but a larger downsampling factor affects the performance of the reconstructed octree. Hyperparameter Sensitivity: The minimum number of epochs for each stage of training is a key hyperparameter; determining it reasonably according to the specific application is an open problem. Time Complexity: The method relies on time-consuming computation of the loss distribution for octree reconstruction, which limits the dramatic saving of training time despite sample point reduction. Frequent reconstruction (e.g., q=0) increases training time by 105.45%. Memory Complexity: Depends on the depth and branching factor of the octree. The octree structure itself is lightweight compared to the network weights, but storing the loss distribution on the spatio-temporal grid requires memory proportional to the grid resolution. Measured Performance: On 2D Navier-Stokes equations, the method achieved L2 relative error improvements of 33.33% on u, 31.58% on v, 75.76% on p, 25.86% on \lambda1, and 22.00% on \lambda2 compared to original PINNs, using only 78.40% of sample points. Scaling: The method is effective for problems with limited training data in specific areas. It scales with the complexity of the spatio-temporal domain and the frequency of octree reconstruction. Strengths: Reduces the total number of sampling points required for convergence; improves prediction accuracy with fewer samples; avoids computing intersection spaces required in volumetric super-resolution. Limitations: Training time savings are not as dramatic as sample point reductions due to the cost of octree reconstruction; sensitive to the choice of q and downsampling factors; requires careful tuning of the minimum number of epochs per stage. When to Use: When training PINNs with limited training data in specific areas of interest, and when reducing the number of network evaluations (sample points) is a priority over absolute training time. When Not to Use: When training time is the primary concern and the cost of octree reconstruction outweighs the benefits of reduced sampling; when the domain is fully observed with abundant training data, making importance sampling less critical. Origin: Proposed in "Octree-based hierarchical sampling optimization for the volumetric super-resolution of scientific data" (2024). History and Development: The method addresses the challenge of training PINNs efficiently with sparse data. It builds on the concept of importance sampling in PINNs, where sample points are concentrated in regions of high error or complexity. The use of an octree allows for hierarchical partitioning of the domain, enabling adaptive sampling. The method distinguishes itself from volumetric super-resolution by operating only in areas with existing training data, avoiding the need for intersection space computations. Usage: Applied to scientific data problems, such as incompressible flow past a circular cylinder (2D Navier-Stokes equations). Octree-based hierarchical sampling optimization for the volumetric super-resolution of scientific data, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2024.112804, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Temporal and Progressive Rendering
body: Temporal and Progressive Rendering reduces per-frame computational cost in volume rendering by distributing the sampling budget across multiple frames or by adaptively refining resolution based on prior results. It solves the problem of high rendering latency in real-time or interactive scenarios where full-resolution, high-sample-density rendering is infeasible. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Two-stage NeRF Rendering and Spatiotemporal Importance Sampling by leveraging temporal coherence or iterative spatial refinement rather than static importance metrics or neural network inference [2872-temporal-upsampling-and-dithering.md][4836-checkerboard-progressive-rendering.md][7260-multi-resolution-rendering-for-clouds.md]. Builds on Adaptive Sampling and Resolution. Combines spatial dithering with temporal accumulation to reduce noise in real-time volume rendering. It addresses the trade-off between spatial aliasing and temporal noise, differing from siblings by using full-resolution buffers with temporal blending rather than spatial subsampling or hierarchical structures. Choose it for real-time rendering with strict per-frame budgets where temporal coherence is available. Reduces per-frame cost by tracing only half the pixels (checkerboard pattern) each frame and blending with previous results. It differs from siblings by using a fixed spatial subsampling pattern rather than temporal accumulation of full buffers or spatially varying resolution. Choose it for interactive volume visualization requiring immediate partial feedback with minimal memory overhead. Limits samples by rendering at low resolution first to identify areas needing refinement, then accumulating high-resolution results only in those regions. It differs from siblings by varying the spatial resolution of the rendering pass itself across iterations rather than relying on temporal coherence or fixed subsampling patterns. Choose it for large-scale volumetric effects like clouds where detail is concentrated in specific regions. A practical solution to rendering time by generating partial images that are progressively refined as the user interacts, using a pyramid data structure. It supports both forward and backward viewing approaches. Forward viewing renders the smaller volume in a pyramid data structure using large-footprint splats first, then higher resolution components. Backward viewing first samples the screen in low resolution, interpolating values for regions where no rays were emitted, then casts more rays to replace interpolated values with accurate results. Rays intended to cover large screen areas can be traced in lower-resolution pyramid components. Sampling rate and stopping criteria can also be progressively refined. A render pacer for each volume decides when a render shows the progress of a load, replacing the previous reRenderFraction/autoLoad mechanism to ensure a steady display rate independent of frame count. The pacer requests a render immediately when data for a slice shown by the viewport is ready. It requests a render when a retrieve stage completes (IMAGERETRIEVALSTAGE). It requests a render when a timer expires during a load (e.g., after 150–250 ms) if new slices are ready. It requests a render when the load completes. A render started by the user does not wait for the pacer. Progressive rendering in volume visualization addresses rendering time by generating partial images that are progressively refined as the user interacts. Both forward and backward viewing approaches support this refinement. In modern streaming contexts, a render pacer decides when a render shows the progress of a load, replacing previous mechanisms to ensure a steady display rate independent of frame count.
