name: Temporal Upsampling and Dithering
head: Temporal Upsampling
body: Temporal Upsampling and Dithering is a technique that combines spatial dithering to mitigate sampling artifacts with temporal accumulation to reduce noise, primarily used in real-time volume rendering (such as volumetric clouds) where computational budget limits per-frame sampling density. It distinguishes itself from its siblings by addressing the specific trade-off between spatial aliasing (slicing artifacts from coarse steps) and temporal noise (stochastic variation from dithering), whereas Checkerboard Progressive Rendering focuses on spatial resolution adaptation and Multi-Resolution Rendering for Clouds focuses on hierarchical data structures [4836-checkerboard-progressive-rendering.md][7260-multi-resolution-rendering-for-clouds.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current frame's color buffer (often at reduced resolution or with coarse sampling), previous frame's accumulated color buffer, and depth/velocity buffers for reprojection. Output: High-resolution, denoised color frame. Data Structures: History Buffer: A texture storing the accumulated color values from previous frames. Depth/Velocity Buffers: Used to reproject the history buffer into the current frame's pixel coordinates. Steps: 1. Blue Noise Dithering: Apply blue noise dithering to the sampling positions or step sizes during the volume integration pass. This breaks up regular aliasing patterns (slicing artifacts) caused by insufficient sampling steps. 2. Temporal Accumulation: Reproject the previous frame's color into the current frame's coordinate space using depth and velocity information. Blend the reprojected color with the current frame's dithered result. This reduces the high-frequency noise introduced by the dithering process. 3. Upsampling: If the rendering was performed at a lower resolution (e.g., 1/2x1/2), upsample the final accumulated result to the full screen resolution. Formulas: Reprojection: C{reprojected}(x, y) = C{history}(x - vx \cdot z, y - vy \cdot z), where (vx, vy) is the pixel velocity and z is the depth. Blending: C{final}(x, y) = \alpha \cdot C{current}(x, y) + (1 - \alpha) \cdot C{reprojected}(x, y), where \alpha is a blending factor (often related to temporal stability or motion speed). Parameters: Dither Pattern: Blue noise texture. Blending Factor \alpha: Typically small (e.g., 0.1-0.3) to favor history, but adjusted based on motion to prevent ghosting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ghosting: If depth or velocity is inaccurate, the reprojected history will misalign, causing ghosting artifacts. Anti-smear techniques (discarding history pixels with large depth differences) may be required [3614-temporal-anti-aliasing-with-anti-smear.md]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def temporalupsamplinganddithering(currentcolor, historybuffer, depthbuffer, velocitybuffer, bluenoisetexture, alpha): H, W = len(velocitybuffer), len(velocitybuffer[0]) # Step 1: Apply blue noise dithering to sampling positions to break slicing artifacts ditheredcolor = [[currentcolor[y][x] + bluenoisetexture[y][x] 0.05 for x in range(W)] for y in range(H)] # Step 2: Reproject previous frame's color using depth and velocity reprojectedcolor = [[0.0]3 for in range(H)] for y in range(H): for x in range(W): velx = velocitybuffer[y][x][0] vely = velocitybuffer[y][x][1] depth = depthbuffer[y][x] # Screen space offset: velocity depth offsetx = velx depth offsety = vely depth srcx = int(clamp(x - offsetx, 0, W - 1)) srcy = int(clamp(y - offsety, 0, H - 1)) reprojectedcolor[y][x] = historybuffer[srcy][srcx] # Step 3: Blend current dithered result with reprojected history to reduce noise blendedcolor = [[mix(ditheredcolor[y][x], reprojectedcolor[y][x], alpha) for x in range(W)] for y in range(H)] # Step 4: Upsample if rendered at lower resolution (e.g., 1/2x1/2) finalcolor = upscalebilinear(blendedcolor) # Step 5: Update history buffer for next frame historybuffer = finalcolor return finalcolor def mix(a, b, t): return [a[i] (1.0 - t) + b[i] t for i in range(len(a))] def clamp(v, mn, mx): return max(mn, min(mx, v)) def upscalebilinear(tex): h, w = len(tex), len(tex[0]) outh, outw = h 2, w 2 out = [[0.0]3 for in range(outh)] for y in range(outh): for x in range(outw): srcy = y / 2.0 srcx = x / 2.0 y0, x0 = int(srcy), int(srcx) y1, x1 = min(y0 + 1, h - 1), min(x0 + 1, w - 1) dy, dx = srcy - y0, srcx - x0 p00 = tex[y0][x0] p10 = tex[y1][x0] p01 = tex[y0][x1] p11 = tex[y1][x1] out[y][x] = [(1-dy)(1-dx)p00[i] + dy(1-dx)p10[i] + (1-dy)dxp01[i] + dydxp11[i] for i in range(3)] return out Temporal Anti-Aliasing with Anti-Smear is a post-processing technique that blends the current frame's color with an accumulated history buffer using pixel velocity for reprojection, with an optional anti-smear feature that discards accumulated pixels with large depth differences to prevent ghosting. It distinguishes itself from standard TAA by explicitly checking depth discontinuities during reprojection to avoid smearing artifacts. An algorithm for quickly generating a pseudo-uniform distribution of points based on a regular 2D grid, originally proposed by Mitchell. Create a regular 2D grid with sixteen times as many grid cells as the desired number of points. Visit each cell in turn in a left-to-right and top-to-bottom fashion. Calculate potential D{i,j} using the function: D{i,j} = (4D{i-1,j} + D{i-1,j-1} + 2D{i,j-1} + D{i+1,j-1}) / 8 + R, where R = \text{random}(). If D{i,j} is greater than the threshold of one-half, select a jittered point at cell (i,j) and reduce the D{i,j} potential by one. Thus, about 1/16th of the data points are selected. Modifying the threshold or random increment to generate weighted point densities produces regular patterns in the splats and causes the number of dots deposited to vary widely from the expected number. A method using spatial dithering to create the perception of more than 3-bit color from single-bit-depth SLM frames. The system uses a 3-SLM projection engine where each SLM has 1-bit depth. Proprietary rasterization and half-toning/dithering methods process the OpenGL pipeline data before projection. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels, dominated by the reprojection and blending steps. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the history buffer, depth buffer, and velocity buffer. Performance: Significantly reduces the need for high per-frame sampling rates, allowing for real-time rendering of complex volumes like clouds. Strengths: Effective at reducing noise and aliasing artifacts with minimal additional computational cost per frame. Limitations: Can introduce ghosting or smearing artifacts if motion estimation is inaccurate or if there are rapid scene changes. Requires careful tuning of the blending factor and anti-smear thresholds. The technique is commonly used in real-time graphics engines for rendering volumetric effects such as clouds and fog, where high sampling rates are computationally prohibitive. It builds on the principles of Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) and blue noise dithering, adapting them to the specific challenges of volume rendering. 体积云效果的实现，游戏世界的云合雾集, https://leihuo.163.com/institution/news/20230719/384231099592.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Multivariate volume rendering, https://www.osti.gov/biblio/495676, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 100-million-voxel volumetric display, https://doi.org/10.1117/12.480930, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Temporal Anti-Aliasing with Anti-Smear
head: Anti-Smear TAA, TAA, Temporal Upscaling
body: Temporal Anti-Aliasing with Anti-Smear is a post-processing technique that blends the current frame's color with an accumulated history buffer using pixel velocity for reprojection, with an optional anti-smear feature that discards accumulated pixels with large depth differences to prevent ghosting. It distinguishes itself from standard TAA by explicitly checking depth discontinuities during reprojection to avoid smearing artifacts. Inputs: srcColorTexture: Current frame color (texture2d<f32>). velocityTexture: Current frame pixel velocity (texture2d<f32>). currentDepthTexture: Current frame depth (texture2d<f32>). previousDepthTexture: Previous frame depth (texture2d<f32>). accumBuffer: History buffer of accumulated colors (texture2d<f32>). sceneData: Uniform struct containing screen dimensions (screenWidth, screenHeight), anti-smear toggle (antiSmearEnabled), and other rendering parameters. cameraData: Uniform struct containing camera position, rotation, FOV, aspect ratio, and their previous frame counterparts. Outputs: dstColorTexture: Final blended color output (texturestorage2d<rgba8unorm, write>). The CameraData struct layout is defined as: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct CameraData { position: vec3f, fov: f32, rotation: vec3f, aspectRatio: f32, prevPosition: vec3f, padding1: f32, prevRotation: vec3f, padding2: f32 }; The SceneData uniform contains screenWidth, screenHeight, antiSmearEnabled, and other rendering parameters. 1. Initialization: The compute shader entry point ComputeMain uses a workgroup size of (16, 16, 1). The pixel position is calculated as pixelPos = id.xy. If pixelPos.x >= sceneData.screenWidth or pixelPos.y >= sceneData.screenHeight, the shader returns immediately. 2. Reprojection Vector Calculation: Load the current pixel velocity, color, and current/previous depth. Calculate the adjusted pixel position: adjustedPixelPos = vec2<f32>(pixelPos) - pixelVelocity.xy. 3. Boundary Check: Check if adjustedPixelPos is within valid bounds. If adjustedPixelPos.x <= 2.0 or adjustedPixelPos.y <= 2.0 or adjustedPixelPos.x >= f32(sceneData.screenWidth) or adjustedPixelPos.y >= f32(sceneData.screenHeight), store pixelColor to dst and return. The threshold 2.0 is used to avoid artifacts that occur with 0 or 1. 4. UV Coordinate Calculation: Convert pixel positions to normalized UV coordinates: uv = vec2<f32>(pixelPos) / vec2<f32>(f32(sceneData.screenWidth - 1u), f32(sceneData.screenHeight - 1u)) and adjustedUV = vec2<f32>(adjustedPixelPos) / vec2<f32>(f32(sceneData.screenWidth - 1u), f32(sceneData.screenHeight - 1u)). Clamp adjustedUV to [0, 1]. 5. Accumulation Sample: Sample the accumulated color from the history buffer at the adjusted UV: accumCol = textureSampleLevel(accumBuffer, textureSampler, adjustedUV, 0.0). 6. Anti-Smear Rejection (Optional): If sceneData.antiSmearEnabled == 1, sample the current depth at uv (currentPixelDepth) and the previous depth at adjustedUV (previousPixelDepth). Calculate the absolute depth difference: depthDiff = abs(previousPixelDepth - currentPixelDepth). If depthDiff > 4.0, calculate brightness bias: brightness = dot(pixelColor.rgb, vec3<f32>(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)). Store mix(pixelColor, accumCol, brightness). The source does not specify the blending logic when anti-smear is disabled or depthDiff <= 4.0. Depth Threshold: The anti-smear feature triggers if depthDiff > 4.0. Boundary Threshold: A threshold of 2.0 is used for adjusted pixel position bounds to prevent artifacts. Using 0 or 1 causes visible artifacts. Brightness Weights: The luminance weights are hardcoded as (0.299, 0.587, 0.114). Precision: 32-bit float storage is required for previous fragment depth to ensure precision in depth-based rejection. Bounds check if pixelpos[0] >= scenedata['screenWidth'] or pixelpos[1] >= scenedata['screenHeight']: return currentcolor # 2. Reprojection pixelvelocity = velocitytex.sample(pixelpos) adjustedpixelpos = (pixelpos[0] - pixelvelocity[0], pixelpos[1] - pixelvelocity[1]) # 3. Boundary Check with 2.0 threshold if (adjustedpixelpos[0] <= 2.0 or adjustedpixelpos[1] <= 2.0 or adjustedpixelpos[0] >= scenedata['screenWidth'] or adjustedpixelpos[1] >= scenedata['screenHeight']): return currentcolor # 4. UV Calculation uv = (pixelpos[0] / (scenedata['screenWidth'] - 1), pixelpos[1] / (scenedata['screenHeight'] - 1)) adjusteduv = (adjustedpixelpos[0] / (scenedata['screenWidth'] - 1), adjustedpixelpos[1] / (scenedata['screenHeight'] - 1)) adjusteduv = (max(0.0, min(1.0, adjusteduv[0])), max(0.0, min(1.0, adjusteduv[1]))) # 5. Sample Accumulated Color accumcol = accumbuffer.sample(adjusteduv) # 6. Anti-Smear Logic if scenedata['antiSmearEnabled']: currentpixeldepth = currentdepthtex.sample(uv)[0] previouspixeldepth = previousdepthtex.sample(adjusteduv)[0] depthdiff = abs(previouspixeldepth - currentpixeldepth) if depthdiff > 4.0: brightness = currentcolor[0] 0.299 + currentcolor[1] 0.587 + currentcolor[2] 0.114 return (currentcolor[0] (1.0 - brightness) + accumcol[0] brightness, currentcolor[1] (1.0 - brightness) + accumcol[1] brightness, currentcolor[2] (1.0 - brightness) + accumcol[2] brightness, currentcolor[3]) # The source does not specify the blending logic when anti-smear is disabled or depthDiff <= 4.0. return accumcol A variant that combines color rejection (implicit via TAA mixing) with explicit depth consistency checks to eliminate ghosting artifacts. It transforms the current fragment position to the previous frame's clip space, converts to screen space, and samples 9 neighboring pixels in the previous frame's memory texture. It linearizes depths and computes the absolute difference against the current linearized depth, tracking the minimum difference. If the mapped previous position is outside [0, 1] or the minimum depth difference exceeds 0.05 linearizedepth(d), the previous frame is rejected by setting mixAmt = 1.0. This approach effectively removes most ghosting artifacts but requires 32-bit float storage for previous fragment depth to ensure precision. It is integrated into RTGI shaders and the main TAA pass. Performance: The method is computationally expensive, with one implementation reporting a cost of 1.1ms on an NVIDIA GTX 980 at 4K resolution, running at full resolution with r11g11b10f and r32f textures. Memory: Requires storage for the accumulated history buffer, velocity textures, and depth textures (current and previous). The use of 32-bit float for depth increases memory bandwidth requirements. Strengths: Effectively removes most ghosting artifacts when combined with color rejection. The anti-smear feature specifically targets depth discontinuities caused by object motion. Limitations: High computational cost at high resolutions. Sensitive to boundary conditions, requiring specific thresholds (2.0) to avoid artifacts. Requires precise depth precision (32-bit float) to function correctly. The method originates from unofficial implementations in WebGPU voxel raymarching and 3D terrain generation projects. The specific "Anti-Smear" technique with the 4.0 depth threshold and 2.0 boundary check is detailed in the WebGPU voxel raymarching repository. The variant using depth and color rejection with a 0.05 depth difference multiplier is described in the 3D Terrain Generation repository. These implementations leverage TAA for both antialiasing and denoising, particularly in conjunction with SSAO and Global Illumination techniques. jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, https://github.com/jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Maxsimuss/3dTerrainGeneration, https://github.com/Maxsimuss/3dTerrainGeneration, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: TAA with Depth and Color Rejection
head: Depth-based TAA Rejection, TAA Ghosting Removal
body: A Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) variant that eliminates ghosting artifacts by discarding the previous frame's contribution when motion or depth consistency fails. It sets the mixing weight to 1.0 (rejecting history) if the reprojected pixel is out of bounds or if the depth difference exceeds a threshold, effectively combining implicit color rejection via TAA mixing with explicit depth consistency checks. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current fragment position (clip space), current fragment depth, previous frame's clip space projection matrix (projectionPrev), previous frame's depth texture (linearized), current frame's linearized depth. Outputs: Mixing amount mixAmt (float in [0, 1]), where 1.0 means full rejection of history. Data Structures: Depth Texture: 32-bit float (r32f) storage for previous fragment depth to ensure precision. Current Depth: Linearized depth value for the current fragment. Steps: 1. Reprojection: Transform the current fragment's clip-space position to the previous frame's clip space using projectionPrev. Convert to normalized device coordinates (NDC) and then to screen space coordinates (u, v) in [0, 1]. 2. Depth Sampling: Sample 9 neighboring pixels in the previous frame's depth texture centered at (u, v). Linearize their depths if they are not already linear. 3. Depth Comparison: Compute the absolute difference between the current linearized depth and each of the 9 sampled previous depths. Track the minimum difference \Delta d{min}. 4. Rejection Check: If (u, v) is outside the [0, 1] range, set mixAmt = 1.0. If \Delta d{min} > 0.05 \times \text{linearize\depth}(d{current}), set mixAmt = 1.0. Otherwise, mixAmt remains 0.0 (or is determined by other TAA factors not detailed in this specific rejection logic). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetaarejection(currentclippos, projectionprev, currentdepth, prevdepthtexture): # Step 1: Reprojection # Transform current clip pos to previous frame's clip space prevclippos = projectionprev currentclippos # Convert to NDC prevndc = prevclippos / prevclippos.w # Convert to screen space [0, 1] u = (prevndc.x + 1.0) 0.5 v = (prevndc.y + 1.0) 0.5 # Check bounds if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0 or v < 0.0 or v > 1.0: return 1.0 # Reject: out of bounds # Step 2 & 3: Depth Sampling and Comparison # Sample 9 neighbors (3x3 grid) around (u, v) # Assuming texel size is 1.0 / resolution mindiff = infinity currentlineardepth = linearizedepth(currentdepth) for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: sampleu = u + dx texelsize samplev = v + dy texelsize # Sample previous depth and linearize prevdepthsample = prevdepthtexture.sample(sampleu, samplev) prevlineardepth = linearizedepth(prevdepthsample) diff = abs(currentlineardepth - prevlineardepth) if diff < mindiff: mindiff = diff # Step 4: Rejection Check # Threshold multiplier is 0.05 threshold = 0.05 currentlineardepth if mindiff > threshold: return 1.0 # Reject: depth inconsistency return 0.0 # Accept: consistent Parameters: 0.05: Depth difference threshold multiplier for rejection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Requires 32-bit float storage for previous fragment depth to ensure precision in depth-based rejection. Boundaries: Pixels reprojected outside the screen bounds must be rejected to prevent sampling invalid memory or wrapping artifacts. A rendering pipeline configuration that combines Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TA) with 4x Multisample Anti-Aliasing (MSAA) to average out Z-fighting flicker across frames and samples. In testing on Ubuntu 23.10 with Godot 4.1.1-4.1.3, TA + MSAA x4 reduced visible flickering to near invisibility, though minor artifacts remain upon close inspection. Performance: TAA is expensive, taking approximately 1.1ms on a GTX 980 at 4K resolution when running at full res with r11g11b10f and r32f textures. Strengths: Effectively removes most ghosting artifacts when combined with color rejection. Limitations: Requires additional memory bandwidth for 32-bit depth textures and neighbor sampling. This method is described in the context of a voxel terrain generation project (3dTerrainGeneration) that relies heavily on TAA for antialiasing and denoising. It was integrated into the RTGI shader (/shaders/rtgi.frag) and likely the main TAA pass. The author notes that while the concept may not have been used before in this specific combination, it effectively addresses ghosting. name: Spatial Dithering for Color Perception
head: Half-toning / dithering methods, SLM Dithering
body: Spatial dithering for color perception is a technique used in volumetric displays with single-bit-depth spatial light modulators (SLMs) to create the illusion of multi-bit color depth. It solves the problem of limited hardware color resolution by distributing quantization error spatially across the projection screen, allowing the human eye to perceive a wider color gamut than the physical device can natively produce. Unlike temporal methods that rely on frame sequencing, this approach operates within the spatial domain of a single frame or slice, often in conjunction with hardware-specific constraints like 1-bit MEMS mirrors. The method is implemented in systems utilizing a multi-SLM projection engine where each SLM has a 1-bit depth. The core process involves processing OpenGL pipeline data through proprietary rasterization and half-toning/dithering algorithms before projection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Standard OpenGL rendering data (e.g., voxel colors, densities). Output: 1-bit depth frames for each SLM channel (Red, Green, Blue). Data Structures: SLM Frame Buffer: A binary array corresponding to the SLM resolution (e.g., 768 \times 768 pixels). Each element is a single bit representing the state of a micro-mirror (on/off). Color Map: A mapping from voxel density/color values to target RGB intensities. Steps: 1. Color Quantization: Map the desired continuous or high-bit-depth color value for each voxel to a target intensity for each of the R, G, and B channels. 2. Dithering Application: Apply a proprietary half-toning or dithering algorithm to the target intensity values. This algorithm distributes the quantization error to neighboring pixels or sub-pixels to preserve the average perceived brightness and color. 3. Binary Conversion: Convert the dithered intensity values into binary states (0 or 1) for the SLM. 4. Projection: Project the 1-bit images from the R, G, and B SLMs onto a rotating omnidirectional diffuser screen using a color-mixing prism. Parameters: SLM Bit Depth: 1-bit per SLM. Native Color Depth: 3-bit per voxel (1-bit per channel). Perceived Color Depth: Full color (via spatial dithering). SLM Resolution: 768 \times 768 pixels. Update Rate: Approximately 5 kHz or 168 µs per frame. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The perceived color quality depends heavily on the dithering algorithm's ability to minimize visible artifacts (e.g., moiré patterns) while maintaining color accuracy. Hardware Constraints: The method is tightly coupled with the specific hardware (e.g., Texas Instruments DLP technology) and optical setup (rotating screen, Lambertian diffuser). The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spatialditheringforcolorperception(voxelcolors, slmwidth, slmheight): """ Converts high-bit-depth voxel colors to 1-bit SLM frames using spatial dithering. Args: voxelcolors: List of (x, y, z, r, g, b) tuples representing voxel data. slmwidth: Width of the SLM in pixels. slmheight: Height of the SLM in pixels. Returns: rframe, gframe, bframe: 2D binary arrays for R, G, B SLMs. """ # Initialize binary frames rframe = [[0 for in range(slmwidth)] for in range(slmheight)] gframe = [[0 for in range(slmwidth)] for in range(slmheight)] bframe = [[0 for in range(slmwidth)] for in range(slmheight)] # Note: The specific proprietary dithering algorithm is not disclosed in the sources. # The following steps represent the logical flow based on the description. for voxel in voxelcolors: x, y, z, r, g, b = voxel # 1. Map voxel color to target intensities for each channel # This step may involve density-to-color mapping and gamma correction targetr = maptointensity(r) targetg = maptointensity(g) targetb = maptointensity(b) # 2. Apply proprietary dithering/halftoning # The error is distributed spatially to create the perception of intermediate colors ditheredr = applydithering(targetr, x, y, rframe) ditheredg = applydithering(targetg, x, y, gframe) ditheredb = applydithering(targetb, x, y, bframe) # 3. Convert to binary states for SLM rframe[y][x] = 1 if ditheredr > 0.5 else 0 gframe[y][x] = 1 if ditheredg > 0.5 else 0 bframe[y][x] = 1 if ditheredb > 0.5 else 0 return rframe, gframe, bframe def applydithering(targetintensity, x, y, frame): """ Placeholder for the proprietary dithering algorithm. In a real implementation, this would handle error diffusion or ordered dithering. """ # Not given in the sources. The specific algorithm is proprietary. return targetintensity A proprietary algorithm used in Perspecta volumetric displays that maps 3-bit color per voxel to full perceived color through dithering and quasi-halftoning on a rotating omnidirectional diffuser screen. It is distinguished by its integration with the Perspecta hardware platform and its use of a rotating screen to achieve volumetric rendering. It is chosen when using Perspecta's DLP-based microdisplay chips with 768x768 resolution and 168 µs update rates. The native color depth is 3-bit per voxel, but the perceived color depth is full color due to the dithering. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The system operates in real-time, supporting OpenGL-based applications. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The SLM resolution is 768 \times 768 pixels. Measured Performance: The system can project approximately 200 slices of 768 \times 768-pixel 2-D images to create a volume-filling 3-D scene at 5 kHz. Scaling: The method scales with the SLM resolution and update rate. Higher resolutions or frame rates may require more powerful processing for the dithering algorithm. Strengths: Enables multi-bit color perception from 1-bit hardware, reducing hardware complexity and cost. Limitations: The perceived color quality is dependent on the dithering algorithm and viewing conditions. The method is specific to certain hardware configurations (e.g., rotating screens, DLP technology). When to use: When using volumetric displays with 1-bit SLMs and needing to render multi-bit color content. When not to use: When high-fidelity, artifact-free color is required without the trade-offs of dithering, or when using hardware with native multi-bit depth. The method was developed for volumetric displays using Texas Instruments Digital Mirror Device (DMD) technology. The first operational system was demonstrated in March 2001, capable of projecting 100 million voxels. The Perspecta system, described in 2005, further refined this approach with proprietary dithering algorithms. The technology is used in medical imaging (e.g., CT, MRI visualization), military imaging, and mathematical modeling. 100-million-voxel volumetric display, https://doi.org/10.1117/12.480930, fetched 2026-11-01 Volumetric 3D displays and application infrastructure, https://doi.org/10.1109/mc.2005.276, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Checkerboard Progressive Rendering
head: Checkerboard sampling
body: Checkerboard Progressive Rendering reduces per-frame computational cost by tracing only half the pixels in a checkerboard pattern each frame, then blending the new results with previous frames to maintain a complete image. It addresses the problem of interactive volume rendering where full-resolution ray tracing per frame is too expensive, trading per-frame noise for temporal stability. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Previous frame's blended color buffer C{prev}, ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, volume grid V. Output: Current frame's blended color buffer C{final}. Data Structures: C{prev} and C{final}: 2D arrays of color vectors (e.g., float3) with dimensions W \times H. V: 3D array of scalar density values with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty buffer C{curr} of size W \times H. 2. For each pixel (x, y), determine if it is active in the current frame f using a checkerboard mask: M(x, y, f) = ((x + y + f) \bmod 2 == 0). 3. If M(x, y, f) is true, trace a ray through the volume to compute C{new}(x, y). If false, copy the previous buffer: C{curr}(x, y) = C{prev}(x, y). 4. Blend C{curr} and C{prev} to produce C{final}. 5. Return C{final} as the output and the new C{prev} for the next frame. Formulas: Checkerboard activation: M(x, y, f) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } (x + y + f) \bmod 2 = 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. Volume rendering integral (discrete slab march): C = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ti \cdot (1 - e^{-\sigmai \Delta t}) \cdot ci, where Ti = e^{-\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \sigmaj \Delta t} is the accumulated transmittance, \sigmai is the density at step i, \Delta t is the step size, and ci is the emitted color. Temporal blend: C{final}(x, y) = \alpha \cdot C{curr}(x, y) + (1 - \alpha) \cdot C{prev}(x, y), where \alpha is the blend weight. Parameters: Frame index f: Integer, increments by 1 each frame. Blend weight \alpha: Not given in the sources. Standard implementations use \alpha = 0.5 for simple averaging. Step size \Delta t: Not given in the sources. Typically set to the grid cell size or a fraction thereof. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction Components: Division by zero occurs when computing inverse direction for slab stepping. Handled by clamping or using a large sentinel value. Boundary Crossing: Rays exiting the volume grid must be clamped to [0, D{max}] to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Motion Artifacts: Rapid camera or object movement breaks temporal coherence, causing ghosting. The method assumes minimal motion between frames. Convergence: Full resolution is achieved after two frames. The first frame after a scene change or reset will show checkerboard artifacts until blending stabilizes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def checkerboardprogressiverender(frameindex, width, height, prevbuffer, grid, griddims, rayorigin, raydir, stepsize): currbuffer = [[None] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): isactive = ((x + y + frameindex) % 2 == 0) if isactive: color = tracevolume(rayorigin, raydir, grid, griddims, stepsize) currbuffer[y][x] = color else: currbuffer[y][x] = prevbuffer[y][x] alpha = 0.5 # Standard simple averaging finalbuffer = [[None] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): finalbuffer[y][x] = alpha currbuffer[y][x] + (1 - alpha) prevbuffer[y][x] return finalbuffer def tracevolume(origin, direction, grid, griddims, stepsize): invdir = [1.0 / d if d != 0.0 else float('inf') for d in direction] tmin = 0.0 tmax = max(griddims) stepsize # Approximate volume extent t = tmin color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 while t < tmax: gx = int((origin[0] + t direction[0]) / stepsize) gy = int((origin[1] + t direction[1]) / stepsize) gz = int((origin[2] + t direction[2]) / stepsize) if 0 <= gx < griddims[0] and 0 <= gy < griddims[1] and 0 <= gz < griddims[2]: density = grid[gz][gy][gx] else: density = 0.0 absorption = density stepsize color[0] += transmittance (1.0 - math.exp(-absorption)) color[1] += transmittance (1.0 - math.exp(-absorption)) color[2] += transmittance (1.0 - math.exp(-absorption)) transmittance = math.exp(-absorption) if transmittance < 1e-4: break t += stepsize return color Computes only a subset of rays during interaction and progressively fills remaining pixels when interaction stops. Chose when interactive latency is critical and full refinement can occur offline; differs from checkerboard rendering by using spatial subsampling with interpolation rather than temporal blending of half-pixel traces. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) per frame, with a constant factor of 0.5 compared to full rendering, as only half the pixels are traced each frame. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) to store the previous frame's buffer and the current frame's buffer. Performance: Reduces per-frame compute by tracing only half the pixels each frame while blending results over time. Strengths: Provides a complete image every frame, reducing latency for interactive applications. Limitations: Ghosting artifacts with motion; requires two frames to converge to the full-resolution result. When to use: Interactive volume rendering where frame rate is critical and motion is minimal. When not to use: High-motion scenes or when high fidelity is required every frame. Checkerboard Progressive Rendering is a technique used in real-time volume rendering to maintain interactive frame rates by deviating from fixed uniform sampling. It was implemented in a voxel raytracer to reduce per-frame compute by tracing only half the pixels each frame while blending results over time. name: Progressive Ray Tracing
head: Progressive Path Tracing with Preview Scaling, Progressive Refinement Ray Casting
body: Progressive ray tracing is a technique for producing lower quality images which are then improved with time. It addresses interactive volume rendering by computing only a subset of rays during user interaction and progressively filling in the remaining pixels when interaction stops. Unlike its parent Checkerboard Progressive Rendering, which reduces per-frame compute by tracing only half the pixels each frame while blending results over time, progressive ray tracing typically uses spatial subsampling (computing every n-th ray) combined with interpolation during interaction, followed by full-resolution refinement. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Image resolution, preview scaling factor (pratio), total sample count (samples), and exposure value. Scene geometry, density, emission, and camera parameters are standard inputs. Outputs: Tonemapped pixel buffers stored in app->display. Data Structures: app->render: 2D array/vector indexed by {i, j} (x, y) storing pixel values before tonemapping. app->display: 2D array/vector indexed by {i, j} storing tonemapped pixel values for display. pprms: Preview state structure containing resolution and samples. pstate: Temporary render state for preview tracing. app->renderstate: Full-resolution render state for progressive refinement. Parameters: pratio: Integer preview scaling factor. Preview resolution is divided by this value. Range: 1 to 64. exposure: Float tonemapping exposure value. Range: -5 to 5. samples: Integer total sample count for progressive rendering. Range: 16 to 4096. Steps: 1. Initialize Preview State: Set the preview resolution by dividing the application resolution by pratio and set preview samples to 1. 2. Trace Preview Samples: During user interaction, trace rays into the temporary preview state using the reduced resolution. 3. Subsample During Interaction: Compute only every n-th ray along each image dimension and use interpolation to fill in the remaining pixels. 4. Downsample Preview to Full Resolution: Iterate over full image coordinates (i, j), map to preview coordinates (pi, pj) using clamped division, copy to the render buffer, and apply tonemapping. 5. Launch Asynchronous Worker Loop: Start a background loop to progressively render full-resolution samples, updating a progress fraction, tracing with a stop flag, and copying/tonemapping the result each iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(val, maxval)) def progressiveraytracing(app, pratio, samples, exposure): # 1. Initialize preview state pprmsresolution = app.resolution // pratio pprmssamples = 1 # 2. Trace preview samples during interaction tracesamples(pstate, app.scene, app.camera, pprmsresolution, pprmssamples) # 3. Subsample during interaction: compute every n-th ray, interpolate rest # 4. Downsample preview to full resolution and display for i in range(app.resolution.x): for j in range(app.resolution.y): pi = clamp(i // pratio, 0, pstate.render.size.x - 1) pj = clamp(j // pratio, 0, pstate.render.size.y - 1) app.render[i, j] = pstate.render[pi, pj] app.display[i, j] = tonemap(app.render[i, j], exposure) # 5. Asynchronous worker loop for progressive refinement for sample in range(samples): app.progress = sample / samples tracesamples(app.renderstate, app.scene, app.camera, app.params, app.renderstop) if app.renderstop: return for i in range(app.resolution.x): for j in range(app.resolution.y): app.render[i, j] = app.renderstate.render[i, j] app.display[i, j] = tonemap(app.render[i, j], exposure) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Clamping indices during downsampling prevents out-of-bounds access but may introduce aliasing if pratio is large. Boundaries: Ensure pratio is within [1, 64] to avoid excessive blur or performance issues. Degenerate Input: If samples is 1, no progressive refinement occurs, and the preview is displayed directly. FBSlabs is a progressive ray casting technique that refines a low-resolution volume rendering into high resolution by splitting each ray into segments of fixed length (slabs) and rendering them in front-to-back order over subsequent frames. It addresses the problem of interactive volume rendering on mobile and low-performance devices by distributing the computational workload of high-resolution ray casting across multiple frames, ensuring a constant frame rate during user interaction. Unlike sibling methods such as STiles, which sort screen-space tiles by cost, FBSlabs distributes work uniformly across all pixels per frame, making it suitable for hardware lacking compute shaders. Time Complexity: Computing only every n-th ray along each image dimension reduces interaction compute by a factor of n^2, yielding a four-times speed-up for n=2. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Computing only every n-th ray during interaction results in a four-times speed-up without noticeable decrease in image quality. Further speed-ups can be achieved with larger reductions, but at the cost of blurry, less detailed images. Strengths: Improves image quality over time. Limitations: High-frequency details tend to get lost. When to Use: Interactive volume rendering where immediate feedback is prioritized over final image quality. Progressive ray tracing was introduced as a technique for producing lower quality images which are then improved with time. It is part of the broader field of adaptive sampling and resolution in volume rendering, aiming to balance interactivity and image quality. name: FBSlabs
head: Fixed Budget Slabs, Front-to-back Slices, Front-to-back Slabs
body: FBSlabs is a progressive ray casting technique that refines a low-resolution volume rendering into high resolution by splitting each ray into segments of fixed length (slabs) and rendering them in front-to-back order over subsequent frames. It addresses the problem of interactive volume rendering on mobile and low-performance devices by distributing the computational workload of high-resolution ray casting across multiple frames, ensuring a constant frame rate during user interaction. Unlike sibling methods such as STiles, which sort screen-space tiles by cost, FBSlabs distributes work uniformly across all pixels per frame, making it suitable for hardware lacking compute shaders. FBSlabs operates by maintaining two render targets: a low-resolution texture (T{low}) for the unrendered or partially rendered volume, and a high-resolution texture (T{high}) for the progressively refined front portion. The method relies on orthographic projection to ensure slabs remain piecewise planar. Input: Volume dataset, proxy geometry bounding the volume, viewport dimensions (Vw \times Vh), camera parameters (orthographic). Output: Composite image displayed to the user, composed of T{high} overlaid on T{low}. 1. T{low}: A 2D texture storing the color of the volume rendered at low resolution. It acts as the background for the high-resolution overlay. 2. T{high}: A 2D texture storing the accumulated color of the high-resolution ray casting. It is cleared at the start of the progressive phase and updated via front-to-back alpha blending. 3. Frame Counter: An integer tracking the number of frames elapsed since the start of the progressive high-resolution rendering. This determines the starting position of the current slab. N: The fixed number of ray casting samples performed per frame per ray. The source specifies N = 40. Projection: Orthographic. Perspective projection causes slabs to become pseudo-spherical as they extend from the proxy geometry, complicating the fixed-thickness assumption. The algorithm proceeds in two phases: Low-Resolution Initialization and Progressive High-Resolution Refinement. 1. Low Resolution Ray Casting (Initialization): During user interaction, perform standard ray casting at low resolution. Store the resulting color in T{low}. 2. Progressive High Resolution Ray Casting - Initialization: When interaction ceases, clear T{high}. Place the first sampling position for each ray at the entry point on the proxy geometry bounding the volume model. 3. Progressive High Resolution Ray Casting - Slab Rendering: For the current frame, iterate over all pixels in the viewport. For each pixel: a. Calculate the starting position of the ray segment based on the current frame counter and N. Since each slab has a fixed thickness defined by N samples, the start position for frame f is offset by f \times N samples from the entry point. b. Perform a loop of N samples along the ray segment. c. Sample the volume and compute the color contribution. d. Composite the resulting color with the previous partial result in T{high} using front-to-back alpha blending. The blending state must be configured to add color in a front-to-back order. 4. Progressive High Resolution Ray Casting - Low Res Remainder: Render the remaining part of the volume (from the end of the high-resolution slab to the exit of the proxy geometry) using low-resolution ray casting. Start this rendering at the sample position where the high-resolution step finished. Store the result in T{low}, overwriting the previous low-res data for the unrendered portion. 5. Progressive High Resolution Ray Casting - Composite: Generate the current image by compositing T{high} on top of T{low} using alpha blending. The blending time is negligible. 6. Iteration: In the next frame, increase the frame counter and resume from Step 3. Continue until sampling positions exceed volume boundaries. The algorithm conservatively approximates the end of ray casting by repeating the iterative process until the computed rays are longer than the diagonal of the volume bounding box. This ensures all rays have exited the proxy geometry. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fbslabsrender(volume, camera, viewportw, viewporth, nsamples=40): # Data structures tlow = [[None for in range(viewportw)] for in range(viewporth)] thigh = [[None for in range(viewportw)] for in range(viewporth)] framecounter = 0 # Constants STEPHIGH = 1.0 # Fixed step size for high-resolution sampling STEPLOW = 2.0 # Fixed step size for low-resolution sampling ZNEAR = camera.znear ZFAR = camera.zfar VOLUMEDIAGONAL = camera.volumediagonal # Step 1: Low Resolution Ray Casting (Initialization) for y in range(viewporth): for x in range(viewportw): rayorigin = vec3(float(x), float(y), ZNEAR) raydir = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) tlow[y][x] = raycastlowres(volume, rayorigin, raydir, ZFAR) # Step 2: Progressive High Resolution Ray Casting - Initialization for y in range(viewporth): for x in range(viewportw): thigh[y][x] = (vec3(0.0), 0.0) # (color, alpha) framecounter = 0 while True: # Step 3: Progressive High Resolution Ray Casting - Slab Rendering startoffsetsamples = framecounter nsamples entrypoint = vec3(0.0, 0.0, ZNEAR) # Orthographic entry plane raydir = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) startposition = entrypoint + startoffsetsamples STEPHIGH raydir for y in range(viewporth): for x in range(viewportw): acccolor, accalpha = thigh[y][x] rayorigin = vec3(float(x), float(y), ZNEAR) for i in range(nsamples): samplepos = startposition + i STEPHIGH raydir if not (ZNEAR <= samplepos.z <= ZFAR): break color, alpha = samplevolume(volume, samplepos) weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = acccolor + color weight accalpha = accalpha + weight if accalpha >= 1.0: break thigh[y][x] = (acccolor, accalpha) # Step 4: Progressive High Resolution Ray Casting - Low Res Remainder endposition = startposition + nsamples STEPHIGH raydir for y in range(viewporth): for x in range(viewportw): acccolor = vec3(0.0) accalpha = 0.0 currentpos = endposition while currentpos.z <= ZFAR and accalpha < 1.0: color, alpha = samplevolumelowres(volume, currentpos) weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = acccolor + color weight accalpha = accalpha + weight currentpos += STEPLOW raydir tlow[y][x] = (acccolor, accalpha) # Step 5: Progressive High Resolution Ray Casting - Composite displaycomposite(thigh, tlow) # Step 6: Iteration framecounter += 1 # Termination Condition if startoffsetsamples STEPHIGH > VOLUMEDIAGONAL: break Global Early Ray Termination (ERT): Implementing global ERT (stopping ray casting for a pixel entirely if it becomes opaque) requires an extra pass to copy accumulated opacity to a queryable texture. This extra pass incurs a time penalty larger than the benefits of ERT. Therefore, only per-slab ERT is effective. Termination Approximation: The termination condition (ray length > bounding box diagonal) is conservative. It may continue rendering for a few frames after the volume is fully traversed to ensure all rays have exited. Time Complexity: The maximum number of samples per frame is O(Vw \times Vh \times N), where Vw \times Vh is the viewport pixel count and N is the fixed samples per ray. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for two 2D textures (T{low} and T{high}) and a frame counter. Performance: Experiments show average completion times under 1 second for tested models. The blending time is negligible. Convergence: FBSlabs shows a less uniform slope in perceptual convergence compared to tile-based methods. It converges quickly because the front part of the model covers most of the image, but continues executing for several frames after approaching ground truth to render the back part, which has smaller visual impact. Strengths: High interactivity rate; good average completion times; simple implementation; no need for compute shaders. Limitations: Perceptual seams between low-resolution and high-resolution models can be more perceivable than in tile-based methods; non-uniform convergence. When to use: Recommended for less powerful devices that do not provide compute shaders (available from OpenGL ES 3.1) or platforms like WebGL that do not support modern features such as compute shaders. When not to use: When uniform perceptual convergence is critical, or when hardware supports compute shaders and tile-based sorting (STiles) which offers faster completion and smoother transitions. FBSlabs (Front-to-back Slabs) was proposed in the context of mobile volume rendering, specifically for medical data visualization on devices with limited computational power. The method was introduced alongside "STiles" (Sorted Tiles) as part of a multiresolution architecture aimed at achieving interactive rendering of volumetric models. The technique leverages the fact that in medical imaging, orthographic projection is commonly used, allowing slabs to remain piecewise planar. name: Multi-Resolution Rendering for Clouds
head: Low-resolution first rendering for clouds, Progressive resolution cloud rendering
body: Multi-resolution rendering for clouds limits the total number of volume samples by initially rendering the cloud field at a low resolution to identify regions requiring fewer samples, then accumulating the final image with higher-resolution passes. Inputs: A volumetric cloud density field, a camera configuration, and a target resolution R{\text{target}}. Outputs: The final accumulated cloud image I. Data Structures: Not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Render the cloud volume at a lower resolution R{\text{low}} (R{\text{low}} \ll R{\text{target}}) to obtain a quick approximation. 2. Analyze the low-resolution result to identify pixels or regions where fewer or no additional samples are necessary. 3. Render the cloud volume at R{\text{target}}, applying full ray marching only where the analysis indicates it is needed, while skipping or using fewer samples elsewhere. 4. Accumulate the low-resolution render with the higher-resolution passes to produce the final image, reducing the overall sample count. Parameters: R{\text{low}}: Initial low resolution. Not given in the sources. R{\text{target}}: Final target resolution. Not given in the sources. Refinement threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Temporal accumulation is noted as very difficult to apply to clouds due to velocity vector computation and coherence issues. Resolution transitions between low and high-resolution regions may cause visible seams if not properly blended. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiresolutioncloudrendering(camera, cloudfield, Rlow, Rtarget): # Step 1: Low-resolution pass Ilow = rendercloudatresolution(camera, cloudfield, Rlow) # Step 2: Analysis to determine mask Mmask = computerefinementmask(Ilow) # Step 3: High-resolution pass Ihigh = rendercloudatresolution(camera, cloudfield, Rtarget) # Step 4: Accumulation Ifinal = blend(Ilow, Ihigh, Mmask) return Ifinal def rendercloudatresolution(camera, cloudfield, resolution): # Standard ray-marching: iterate over pixel grid at given resolution, # step through cloudfield along camera rays, accumulate transmittance and color. # Source does not specify implementation. pass def computerefinementmask(Ilow): # Compute gradient magnitude or variance of Ilow. # Return binary mask where gradient exceeds a threshold. # Source does not specify implementation. pass def blend(Ilow, Ihigh, Mmask): # Linear interpolation: Ilow (1 - Mmask) + Ihigh Mmask return Ilow (1 - Mmask) + Ihigh Mmask A rendering strategy that reduces computation time by starting at a low resolution and gradually increasing it to the target final resolution. It solves the problem of expensive high-resolution ray-surface intersection tests by deferring them until necessary, using cone-tracing to guarantee that no surface points are skipped during the resolution transition. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Origin: The technique was proposed by an author in the three.js forum who considered it for efficient volumetric cloud rendering but did not implement it. History: The author suspected the technique could be very effective but ultimately gave up on temporal accumulation approaches for clouds due to difficulty. Usage: Discussed in the context of optimizing volumetric cloud rendering in web-based 3D graphics. name: Iteratively Increasing Resolution
head: Multi-resolution rendering strategy
body: Iteratively Increasing Resolution is a rendering strategy that reduces computation time by starting at a low resolution and gradually increasing it to the target final resolution. It solves the problem of expensive high-resolution ray-surface intersection tests by deferring them until necessary, using cone-tracing to guarantee that no surface points are skipped during the resolution transition. Inputs: A signed distance function (SDF) or SDF lower estimate (SDFE) f. Camera parameters (position, direction, resolution). Target final resolution (W{final}, H{final}). Initial low resolution (W{start}, H{start}). Outputs: Final rendered image at target resolution. State textures storing intermediate rendering data (e.g., distance traveled). Data Structures: Ping-Pong Textures: Two screen-sized textures are used to store the state for each pixel, such as the distance traveled along the ray (t) or accumulated color. These are swapped (ping-ponged) between passes. State Field: Each pixel stores the current ray parameter t (distance from origin) where the ray currently stands. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Start rendering at the lowest resolution (W{start}, H{start}). Initialize state textures with t=0 (or the ray origin). 2. Cone-Tracing Pass: For each pixel, perform sphere tracing using cone-tracing logic. The ray is advanced by a step size determined by the modified SDFE, bounded by the cone termination condition to ensure no surface is missed when resolution increases. 3. Termination Check: A pixel is considered complete if it intersects the surface (SDF value \le 0) or exceeds a maximum distance. Incomplete pixels retain their current t in the state texture. 4. Resolution Increase: If the target resolution is not reached, increase the resolution (e.g., double width and height). The starting position for each new pixel in the higher resolution is always the closest pixel in the previous resolution. 5. Incremental Continuation: In the next frame (or pass), computation continues from the stored t values. If the camera or scene has not changed, the state is preserved. 6. Repeat: Steps 2-5 are repeated until the target resolution is achieved. Cone-Tracing Formula: To support resolution increase, cone-tracing ensures that no surface point lies inside the cone defined by the pixel's footprint. The terminating condition for the pixel cone, assuming rectangular pixels, is: f(o + tv) < \frac{p^2}{\text{width}^2 \text{height}^2} where: o is the ray origin (pixel center), v is the ray direction, and t is the distance along the ray. p is the pixel size in world units (or 1 for normalized coordinates). \text{width} \cdot \text{height} is the total number of pixels in the current resolution. Let \alpha = \frac{p^2}{\text{width}^2 \text{height}^2}. Modified SDFE for Safe Travel: The condition above can be incorporated into the SDFE to avoid special termination checks. Let \alpha = \frac{p^2}{\text{width}^2 \text{height}^2}. The modified one-dimensional SDFE F(t) is: F(t) = \frac{f(o + tv) - \alpha t}{1 + \alpha} This transformation offsets the surface by a value that increases with distance. The Lipschitz constant of F is bounded by 1 + \alpha, ensuring stability. This allows the algorithm to approximate the safe travel distance without needing a special termination condition for the cone. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterativelyincreasingresolution(sdf, camera, startres, targetres, maxdist): """ Renders a scene using iteratively increasing resolution with cone-tracing. sdf: callable returning SDF value at (x,y,z) camera: callable getray(x, y) -> (origin, direction) startres: (w, h) targetres: (w, h) maxdist: maximum ray length to prevent infinite loops """ currentw, currenth = startres # Initialize state textures: 2D arrays storing distance t for each pixel statetex = [[0.0] currentw for in range(currenth)] nextstatetex = [[0.0] currentw for in range(currenth)] while currentw <= targetres[0] and currenth <= targetres[1]: # Calculate alpha for current resolution pixelsize = 1.0 # Normalized pixel size alpha = (pixelsize 2) / (currentw 2 currenth 2) for y in range(currenth): for x in range(currentw): t = statetex[y][x] # Skip if already completed or exceeded max distance if t >= maxdist: nextstatetex[y][x] = t continue rayo, rayd = camera.getray(x, y) safet = t while safet < maxdist: pos = (rayo[0] + safet rayd[0], rayo[1] + safet rayd[1], rayo[2] + safet rayd[2]) fval = sdf(pos) # Modified SDFE value for cone-tracing step size fmod = (fval - alpha safet) / (1.0 + alpha) if fmod <= 0: # Surface hit or cone boundary reached break # Step size is the safe travel distance approximated by F(t) stepsize = fmod safet += stepsize # Prevent infinite loops on flat/parallel surfaces if stepsize < 1e-6: break nextstatetex[y][x] = safet # Swap textures statetex, nextstatetex = nextstatetex, statetex # Increase resolution currentw = 2 currenth = 2 # Resize state textures to new resolution using nearest-neighbor mapping newstatetex = [[0.0] currentw for in range(currenth)] for y in range(currenth): for x in range(currentw): srcy = min(y // 2, currenth // 2 - 1) srcx = min(x // 2, currentw // 2 - 1) newstatetex[y][x] = statetex[srcy][srcx] statetex = newstatetex if currentw > targetres[0] or currenth > targetres[1]: break Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The transformation F(t) offsets the surface by a value that increases with distance. Floating-point precision errors may accumulate over many steps. Boundaries: The cone-tracing condition assumes rectangular pixels. Non-rectangular pixels or anisotropic scaling may require adjustment of \alpha. Degenerate Input: If the SDF is not a valid lower estimate (Lipschitz constant > 1), the sphere tracing may overstep. The source assumes \text{Lip } f \le 1. A training and evaluation protocol designed to simulate zoom-in effects and test anti-aliasing performance across resolutions. It trains a model at a single downsampled resolution and renders at multiple higher scales. Steps: 1) Define dataset's default resolution (e.g., 1352×1014) as full resolution baseline. 2) Downsample training data by a fixed factor (e.g., 4×) and train exclusively on this lower resolution. 3) Evaluate rendering quality at progressively higher resolutions (1×, 2×, and 4× relative to training resolution). 4) When comparing against baselines like Mip-Splatting, integrate the baseline into the pipeline and ensure consistency in maximum sampling frequency computation between both methods. Time Complexity: Reduces total render time by performing most of the ray-surface intersection work at lower resolutions. The cost is proportional to the sum of pixel counts across all resolution levels, which is less than rendering at full resolution from the start. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for state textures (distance traveled) at the current resolution. Ping-ponging two textures doubles this requirement. Measured Performance: Implemented in GLSL with C++ test application. Used with relaxed and enhanced sphere tracing. Showed reduced render times for 3D fractals and SDF scenes. Strengths: High-quality rendering for stationary scenes; real-time responsiveness when camera/scene changes (by restarting or incrementing). General applicability to any sphere tracing variant. Limitations: Requires multiple passes or frames to complete. Not suitable for highly dynamic scenes where state cannot be preserved. Precision issues with the modified SDFE transformation over long distances. When to Use: Static or slowly changing scenes where high resolution is needed but initial low-res passes can identify complex areas. When Not to Use: Highly dynamic scenes where state preservation is not feasible. Scenes with very thin structures that might be missed by coarse initial passes (though cone-tracing mitigates this). Originated from work on accelerating sphere tracing, introduced by Csaba Bálint and Gábor Valasek in 2018. Sphere tracing was introduced by Hart in 1994. The method builds on improvements by Keinert et al.. It is used in real-time rendering of SDF representations, such as 3D fractals, where traditional triangle-based engines are inefficient.
