name: Patch-based Ray Sampling
body: Patch-based ray sampling is a strategy where rays are grouped into spatially adjacent 2D patches to form local image grids, ensuring the adjacency required for local-structure losses like Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT) loss. It is distinguished from random ray sampling, which is used for global-structure losses (e.g., MSE), by enforcing local spatial coherence within each sampling batch. Inputs and outputs: Input: Image dimensions, patch size, total number of rays to sample per iteration. Output: A set of ray origins and directions corresponding to a contiguous rectangular region of the image plane. Data structures: Ray coordinates: 2D integer indices (u, v) representing pixel locations in the image grid. Patch buffer: A list of ray indices or coordinates with shape (Hp, Wp), where Hp and Wp are patch height and width. Steps: 1. Determine patch dimensions Hp \times Wp. 2. Calculate the number of rays per patch: N{patch} = Hp \times Wp. For 192 \times 192, N{patch} = 36,864. 3. Select a random top-left corner (u0, v0) within valid image bounds: 0 \le u0 \le W{\text{img}} - Wp and 0 \le v0 \le H{\text{img}} - Hp, where W{\text{img}} and H{\text{img}} are image width and height. 4. Generate all ray indices (u, v) for u \in [u0, u0 + Wp - 1] and v \in [v0, v0 + Hp - 1]. 5. Convert indices to ray origins and directions using the camera projection matrix. 6. Use these rays for loss computation (e.g., DWT loss). Parameters: Patch size: 192 \times 192. Sampling frequency: DWT loss calculated every 10 iterations for LLFF dataset and every 150 iterations for NeRF-Synthetic (NS) dataset. Training duration for DWT: Stopped altogether at 5,000 iterations to facilitate high-frequency learning. Edge cases and pitfalls: Boundary conditions: The patch must fit within the image. Precision: No specific precision issues noted, but standard floating-point ray casting applies. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def samplepatchrays(imagewidth, imageheight, patchsize=192): """ Samples rays for a single patch-based batch. Args: imagewidth (int): Width of the image in pixels. imageheight (int): Height of the image in pixels. patchsize (int): Side length of the square patch. Returns: list of tuples: List of (u, v) pixel coordinates in the patch. """ # Step 1: Determine patch dimensions hp, wp = patchsize, patchsize # Step 2: Calculate number of rays per patch npatch = hp wp # Step 3: Select random top-left corner within valid bounds u0 = np.random.randint(0, imagewidth - wp + 1) v0 = np.random.randint(0, imageheight - hp + 1) # Step 4: Generate all ray indices in the patch ucoords, vcoords = np.meshgrid( range(u0, u0 + wp), range(v0, v0 + hp)) # Flatten to list of (u, v) tuples rays = list(zip(ucoords.flatten(), vcoords.flatten())) # Step 5: Convert indices to ray origins and directions # raysorigins, raysdirections = cameraprojectionmatrix(rays) return rays A variant where rays are divided into equal-size patches following rigid grid lines determined by a fixed grid size, then shuffled. It is chosen for simplicity in SR-based NeRF pipelines but suffers from a pitfall: cutting ray space strictly with grid boundaries causes variations between boundaries to never be seen by convolutional kernels during training. Time complexity: Sampling is O(N{patch}) where N{patch} is the number of rays in the patch. Memory complexity: O(N{patch}) to store ray origins and directions. Performance: Evaluated on GeForce RTX 4070 Ti Super. DWT loss calculation adds computational cost but is limited to 5,000 iterations. Strengths: Captures local structures required for DWT loss. Limitations: Grid-based variants may miss boundary variations. Random ray sampling is used for MSE loss to capture global structures, while patch-based sampling is used for DW loss to capture local structures. Originated in DWTNeRF, which boosts few-shot Neural Radiance Fields via Discrete Wavelet Transform. The method was introduced to support the DW loss, which requires adjacently sampled rays to form a 2D image grid. It contrasts with random ray sampling used for MSE loss to capture global structures. name: Error-Guided Adaptive Sampling (Bubbling)
head: Bubbling method
body: Error-Guided Adaptive Sampling is a training-phase importance sampling strategy that dynamically adjusts ray sampling density based on per-pixel reconstruction error, specifically targeting missing or thin geometry during the "bubble" step of neural scene reconstruction. It sets itself apart from its parent Loss-based Adaptive Sampling by maintaining a continuous Probability Density Function (PDF) map updated iteratively per image, rather than partitioning the image into static grids, and by explicitly pruning low-error pixels to focus computational resources on high-frequency details like thin poles. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current batch of training images, neural radiance/SDF fields, reconstruction error metric E (specifically depth loss) for each pixel p in the batch. Outputs: Updated PDF map for the next iteration, set of rays to sample for the current batch. Data Structures: PDF Map: A 2D array matching the resolution of the training images. Each element PDF(p) stores the sampling probability for pixel p. Initialized based on reconstruction error at the start of the bubble step (50k iterations). Parameters: P{min}: Pruning threshold for low-error pixels. Value: 0.05. E(p): Reconstruction error at pixel p. In the source, depth loss is adopted. Steps: 1. Initialization: At the start of the bubble step (50k iterations), initialize the PDF map for each training image based on the current reconstruction error. 2. Error Calculation: For the current training batch, calculate the error metric E(p) for every pixel p. 3. PDF Update: Update the PDF values for pixels in the current batch to be proportional to their error E(p). The relationship is defined as: PDF(x(p; D)) \propto E(p) where x(p; D) represents the ray or point associated with pixel p. 4. Pruning: Filter out pixels where the error is sufficiently low. Specifically, pixels with E(p) < P{min} are pruned from the sampling distribution, meaning their PDF is effectively set to 0 or they are excluded from ray generation. 5. Ray Generation: Generate outgoing rays using importance sampling based on the updated PDF map. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def updatepdfandsample(pdfmap, errormap, pmin, nrays): """ Updates the PDF map based on current reconstruction error and prunes low-error pixels. Returns a list of pixel coordinates to sample. """ h, w = len(pdfmap), len(pdfmap[0]) size = h w # Step 3 & 4: Update PDF values proportional to error and prune low-error pixels # Pixels with E(p) < Pmin are pruned (ignored) validmask = [errormap[r][c] >= pmin for r in range(h) for c in range(w)] # Zero out PDF for pruned pixels for i in range(size): if not validmask[i]: pdfmap[i // w][i % w] = 0.0 # Normalize the PDF map so it sums to 1 for importance sampling pdfsum = sum(sum(row) for row in pdfmap) if pdfsum > 0: for r in range(h): for c in range(w): pdfmap[r][c] /= pdfsum else: # Fallback: uniform sampling if all pixels are pruned or error is zero for r in range(h): for c in range(w): pdfmap[r][c] = 1.0 / size # Step 5: Sample pixels based on the updated PDF # Flatten the PDF map for sampling flatpdf = [pdfmap[r][c] for r in range(h) for c in range(w)] # Standard multinomial sampling implementation cumulative = [] runningsum = 0.0 for p in flatpdf: runningsum += p cumulative.append(runningsum) sampledindices = [] for in range(nrays): r = random.random() idx = 0 while idx < size - 1 and cumulative[idx] < r: idx += 1 sampledindices.append(idx) # Convert flat indices back to 2D coordinates sampledpixels = [(idx // w, idx % w) for idx in sampledindices] return sampledpixels, pdfmap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Error: If all pixels have error < P{min}, the PDF becomes all zeros. The implementation must handle this by resetting to uniform sampling or maintaining a minimum probability. Thin Geometry: Thin components (e.g., poles) grow slowly and maintain high error for many iterations, requiring sustained high PDF values. Time Complexity: Depends on the cost of calculating the error metric E(p) for all pixels and the normalization of the PDF map. Updating the PDF map is O(H \times W) per batch. Memory Complexity: Requires storing a PDF map of size H \times W per training image. Performance: The method accelerates convergence by focusing on erroneous areas. In the source example, light balls (large objects) are reconstructed rapidly (55k iterations), while thin poles (high error, high frequency) are sampled more aggressively and reconstructed later (70k-150k iterations). Strengths: Effectively preserves small-object areas (high frequency) while ignoring large planar areas (low frequency). Limitations: Requires maintaining and updating a PDF map per image. The pruning threshold P{min} must be tuned; too high, and useful pixels are ignored; too low, and the benefit of pruning is lost. Origin: The method is described in "I²-SDF: Intrinsic Indoor Scene Reconstruction and Editing via Raytracing in Neural SDFs". History: It is used in the "bubble" step of a three-stage training process (50k, 100k, 50k iterations) for neural SDF reconstruction. The bubble step specifically addresses the reconstruction of missing objects, starting with the chandelier example where the object is initially missing at 50k iterations. Usage: Applied in neural radiance field/SDF training for indoor scene reconstruction, particularly for handling complex geometries with thin structures and light sources. name: Adaptive Sampling Rate Control
head: Sampling Rate Control, Viewport Adaptive Resolution, dt_scale control
body: Adaptive Sampling Rate Control modulates the number of samples or slices used to render volumetric geometry to balance image quality and performance. It solves the problem of undersampling artifacts during zoom or anisotropic data distortion by dynamically adjusting the sampling density based on view direction and data characteristics. Unlike fixed-rate methods, it allows for non-uniform sampling along data dimensions to compensate for anisotropy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric texture data, view direction, current sampling rate parameters. Output: Adjusted sampling rate vector or scalar step size parameter (dtscale) passed to the rendering shader. Data Structures: Sampling Rate: A vector (rx, ry, rz) representing the sampling density along each data dimension. Default is (1, 1, 1), implying one slice per voxel. dtscale: A uniform float representing the inverse of the sampling rate, used to control ray step size in shaders. Steps: 1. Metric Evaluation: Determine the required sampling density. For general polygonization, compute the minimum data slice spacing by finding the longest ray cast through the volume in the view direction and identifying the highest frequency component of the texel values. The minimum number of data slices is double this frequency component. Alternatively, use a heuristic where the number of data slices equals the volume's dimensions measured in texels. For anisotropic data, calculate varying rates for each dimension to compensate for differences in sampling requirements. 2. Adaptation: Set the sampling rate using setSamplingRate(rx, ry, rz). If using a slider-based UI (indices 0-5), map to rates: 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0. Compute dtscale as 1 / \text{rate}. 3. Rendering: Pass dtscale to the shader to control the ray step size. Formulas: Minimum Slices: N{min} = 2 \cdot f{max}, where f{max} is the highest frequency component of texel values along the longest view ray. dtscale: dt\scale = \frac{1}{\text{sampling\rate}}. Parameters: Default Sampling Rate: (1, 1, 1). Anisotropic Example: For Phantom/CT.Head.char.tif, a rate of (1, 1, 3.32) improves quality. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Undersampling: Zooming into volume data causes artifacts if the sampling rate is not increased. Anisotropy: Fixed isotropic rates fail on anisotropic data; varying rates are required. Performance: High sampling rates significantly increase frame time. A strategy requiring dense sampling (3–6 samples per voxel) to ensure smooth boundaries when using multidimensional transfer functions, as neighboring voxels may differ in additional dimensions. It is chosen for high-quality frozen renderings but is too slow for interaction, where the rate is lowered and rerendered after actions. For a 256x256x128 volume, frame updates can take nearly a second at this rate. Time Complexity: Increases linearly with sampling rate. High rates (3-6 samples/voxel) can result in frame times of nearly one second for moderate volumes (256x256x128). Memory Complexity: Not specified. Strengths: Removes undersampling artifacts during zoom; handles anisotropic data effectively. Limitations: High computational cost at high sampling rates; requires manual tuning for anisotropic datasets. When to use: When zooming into data or rendering anisotropic volumes with multidimensional transfer functions. When not to use: During interactive exploration where frame rate is critical, unless combined with interaction-specific lowering. The concept of controlling sampling rate for polygonization of volumetric geometry is described in the SGI Texture Mapping Render Action documentation. The specific application of dense sampling for multidimensional transfer functions was discussed in research on interactive volume rendering to handle complex classification boundaries. The dtscale parameter approach is found in WebGL volume rendering implementations. termijn/webgl-volumerendering, https://github.com/termijn/webgl-volumerendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Chapter 4. name: Adaptive Preintegration Termination Criteria
head: Preintegration-based Adaptive Termination
body:
Adaptive Preintegration Termination Criteria determines when to stop subdividing a ray segment during volume rendering with preintegration. It recursively splits intervals until the difference in the volume integral approximation over the entire interval changes by only a small amount. It differs from fixed-step preintegration by dynamically adjusting sampling density based on local scalar field and transfer function complexity. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{v}. Current interval bounds di, d{i+1}. Preintegration tables for opacity \alpha and color C. Scalar field function f(\mathbf{x}) and its gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{x}). Tolerance parameter \varepsilon. Bounds for interval length l{min} and l{max}. Outputs: Accumulated color and opacity for the interval. Boolean flag indicating if further subdivision is required. Data Structures: Preintegration Tables: Packed tables storing precomputed integrals of the transfer function. The specific layout depends on the underlying preintegration scheme (e.g., incremental subrange preintegration). Steps: 1. Evaluate Interval Endpoints: Compute the scalar values f(\mathbf{x}(di)) and f(\mathbf{x}(d{i+1})) and their gradients 
abla f(\mathbf{x}(di)) and 
abla f(\mathbf{x}(d{i+1})). 2. Check Extrema Condition: Compute the directional derivatives D{\mathbf{v}}(f(\mathbf{x}(di))) = 
abla f(\mathbf{x}(di)) \cdot \mathbf{v} and D{\mathbf{v}}(f(\mathbf{x}(d{i+1}))) = 
abla f(\mathbf{x}(d{i+1})) \cdot \mathbf{v}. If D{\mathbf{v}}(f(\mathbf{x}(di))) D{\mathbf{v}}(f(\mathbf{x}(d{i+1}))) < 0, force subdivision. 3. Compute Midpoint Approximation: Calculate the midpoint d{i+1/2} = (di + d{i+1}) / 2. Evaluate the preintegrated color C1 for the full interval [di, d{i+1}] and the preintegrated color C2 for the two sub-intervals [di, d{i+1/2}] and [d{i+1/2}, d{i+1}]. The opacity \alpha{i+1/2} at the midpoint must be computed before subdividing the second half, as it is used in the termination criteria for that segment. 4. Calculate Relative Error: Compute the magnitude of the color vectors |C| = \sqrt{C.r^2 + C.g^2 + C.b^2}. Calculate the relative error approximation E = |C1 - C2|/|C2|. 5. Adapt for Opacity: Multiply the relative error by (1 - \alphai) to adapt sampling as opacity increases. 6. Check Termination: The interval is considered converged if (1 - \alphai)  rac{|C1 - C2|}{|C1|} < \varepsilon. The source uses |C1| in the denominator of the final formula but |C2| in the relative error definition. 7. Recursion: Recursively apply the steps to sub-intervals [di, d{i+1/2}] and [d{i+1/2}, d{i+1}] if the termination criteria is not met. The parameters l{max} and l{min} bound the interval length during subdivision, but the exact condition for stopping at l{min} is not specified in the sources. Formulas: Directional derivative: D{\mathbf{v}}(f(\mathbf{x})) = 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{v}. Color magnitude: |C| = \sqrt{C.r^2 + C.g^2 + C.b^2}. Relative error approximation: |C1 - C2|/|C2|. Final termination criteria: (1 - \alphai)|C1 - C2|/|C1| < \varepsilon. Extrema detection: D{\mathbf{v}}(f(\mathbf{x}(di))) D{\mathbf{v}}(f(\mathbf{x}(d{i+1}))) < 0. Parameters: \varepsilon: Termination tolerance. l{min}, l{max}: Bounds for interval length during subdivision. Typical values are not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Gradient Accuracy: The accuracy of the extrema-based termination criteria heavily depends on the accuracy of the computed gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{x}). Non-Monotonic Fields: If the scalar field is not monotonic and extrema are not detected, isosurfaces near extrema may be missed. Numerical Precision: For constant transfer functions and linear scalar fields, C1 and C2 are equal within numerical errors, making the scheme automatically optimal in these cases. A subdivision scheme that forces subdivision at scalar function extrema to recover isosurfaces that might be missed if the function is not monotonic over an interval. It uses the sign change of the directional derivative at the interval endpoints to detect extrema. An interval [di, d{i+1}] is subdivided if D{\mathbf{v}}(f(\mathbf{x}(di))) D{\mathbf{v}}(f(\mathbf{x}(d{i+1}))) < 0, where D{\mathbf{v}}(f(\mathbf{x})) = 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \mathbf{v}. The accuracy of this criteria depends on the accuracy of the computed gradient. Complexity: The number of samples is adaptive. The parameters l{max} and l{min} bound the interval length during subdivision. Not given in the sources. Performance: The method continues recursively until the difference in the volume integral approximation over the entire interval changes by only a small amount. Strengths: Automatically optimal for constant transfer functions and linear scalar fields. Limitations: Requires accurate gradient computation, which can be costly or inaccurate for noisy data. The recursion depth is limited by l{min} and l{max}. The method is part of the Volume MLS Ray Casting framework, which uses Moving Least Squares (MLS) for scalar field reconstruction. The adaptive preintegration termination criteria was proposed to improve the efficiency of volume rendering by avoiding unnecessary subdivisions in smooth regions while ensuring accuracy in complex regions. The approach builds on preintegration techniques and extends them with adaptive subdivision based on error estimation and extrema detection. name: Ray-Adaptive Supersegment Generation
head: Automatic gamma determination, Determining the supersegment termination parameter gamma, Homogeneity-based supersegment generation, Ray-Adaptive Generation of Supersegments
body: This method automatically determines the sensitivity parameter \gamma for supersegment termination for each ray independently, ensuring a maximum number of supersegments NS per ray without manual tuning. It solves the problem of visual artifacts caused by a constant, manually-tuned \gamma that is either too high (insufficient resolution) or too low (exhausting the budget and causing "smearing" artifacts). Unlike Adaptive Sampling which adjusts sample density based on error metrics, this method adapts the structural granularity of pre-integrated volume data (supersegments) to fit a strict budget constraint. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Target maximum number of supersegments NS, convergence threshold \varepsilon, tolerance margin \delta, and the volume data. Output: The optimal sensitivity parameter \gamma for the current ray. Data Structures: The algorithm maintains a search range for \gamma using two floating-point variables low and high, and a current candidate \gamma. It also tracks iteration state with boolean flags firstIteration and found, and an integer counter n for the number of generated supersegments. Termination Criterion: A sample is merged into the current supersegment \mathbb{S} unless it differs from the pre-multiplied color of \mathbb{S} by more than \gamma. The criterion is defined as: \tau: \gamma > \|C(\mathbb{S})\alpha(\mathbb{S}) - C'\alpha'\|2 where C' and \alpha' are the color and length-adjusted opacity of the next sample, and C(\mathbb{S})\alpha(\mathbb{S}) is the pre-multiplied color of the current supersegment. The distance metric is the L2 norm between 3-element pre-multiplied color vectors. Parameters: \gamma: Sensitivity parameter. Range: [0, \sqrt{3}]. The upper bound \sqrt{3} is the maximum possible L2 distance between two normalized 3D vectors. \varepsilon: Convergence threshold for the bisection search range. Typical value: 10^{-6}. \delta: Tolerance margin for the lower bound check. Empirically determined to be 15% of NS (\delta = 0.15 NS) to balance performance and quality. Initial \gamma: 10^{-5}, used to quickly identify homogeneous or empty rays. Algorithm Steps: The method uses an iterative bisection search to find \gamma such that the number of generated supersegments n is close to NS but never exceeds it. 1. Initialize low = 0, high = \sqrt{3}, \gamma = 10^{-5}, firstIteration = TRUE, found = FALSE. 2. While !found: a. Sample the volume along the ray using the current \gamma and count the number of generated supersegments, storing the result in n. b. If abs(high - low) < \varepsilon: i. Set found = TRUE. ii. Set \gamma = (n == 0) ? low: high. This selects low if 0 supersegments are generated to prevent degenerate cases, otherwise high (which guarantees n < NS). c. Else if n > NS: i. Set low = high. (Note: The source algorithm sets low = high here, effectively narrowing the search or handling the case where the current \gamma is too small. However, standard bisection would set low = gamma. The source code explicitly sets low = high). d. Else if n < NS - \delta: i. Set high = low. (Similarly, this narrows the range based on the tolerance). e. Else: i. Set found = TRUE. (The count is within the acceptable tolerance [NS - \delta, NS]). f. If firstIteration: i. Set firstIteration = FALSE. ii. If n < NS: 1. Set found = TRUE. (Optimization: if the initial small \gamma yields fewer than NS supersegments, the ray is homogeneous/empty, and we can terminate early). g. If !found: i. Update \gamma = (low + high) / 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def determinegamma(NS, epsilon=1e-6, delta=None): if delta is None: delta = 0.15 NS low = 0.0 high = math.sqrt(3.0) gamma = 1e-5 firstiteration = True found = False while not found: # Sample volume and count supersegments for current gamma n = numsupersegmentsgenerated(gamma) if abs(high - low) < epsilon: found = True # If 0 supersegments, pick low to avoid degenerate 0-width segments # Otherwise pick high to ensure n < NS (preventing smearing) if n == 0: gamma = low else: gamma = high elif n > NS: low = high elif n < NS - delta: high = low else: found = True if firstiteration: firstiteration = False if n < NS: found = True if not found: gamma = (low + high) / 2.0 return gamma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Smearing Artifacts: If the supersegment budget NS is exhausted, the last supersegment must contain all remaining data, causing visual smearing. The algorithm prevents this by ensuring the search never allows more than NS supersegments (by selecting high when the range converges, as high produces fewer supersegments). Degenerate Zero Supersegments: If the search converges to a \gamma that produces 0 supersegments, the algorithm selects low instead of high to prevent this degenerate case. Homogeneous/Empty Rays: Initializing \gamma to 10^{-5} allows the algorithm to quickly detect rays passing through empty or homogeneous regions. If the first iteration generates fewer than NS supersegments, the ray terminates immediately, freeing computational resources. Time Complexity: The method requires multiple passes through the volume data for each ray (one per bisection iteration) to determine \gamma. The number of iterations depends on the convergence threshold \varepsilon and the initial range [0, \sqrt{3}]. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory per ray, only storing the search state variables. Performance: Measured VDI generation times can be lower for larger NS in some cases because the \gamma search converges faster (fewer iterations needed to find a suitable \gamma that yields fewer supersegments). Strengths: Eliminates manual tuning of \gamma, enabling remote VDI generation without user intervention. Generates more accurate VDIs by adapting resolution along each ray. Limitations: Requires multiple volume samples per ray during the initialization phase, increasing computational cost compared to a fixed \gamma approach. This method was proposed by Frey et al. to address the limitations of the homogeneity criterion \tau introduced in their previous work [10], where \gamma was constant across all rays and required careful manual tuning. The method was published in "Efficient Raycasting of Volumetric Depth Images for Remote Visualization of Large Volumes at High Frame Rates". Efficient Raycasting of Volumetric Depth Images for Remote Visualization of Large Volumes at High Frame Rates, https://doi.org/10.1109/pacificvis56936.2023.00014, fetched 2026-10-24

name: Adaptive Sparse Ray Sampling
body: Adaptive Sparse Ray Sampling is an image-order acceleration technique that reduces computational cost by casting a sparse grid of rays (density less than one per pixel) and adaptively increasing sampling density in regions of high image complexity. It exploits coherence in projections, particularly in data acquired from sensing devices where the acquisition process introduces considerable blurring. Unlike brute-force rendering, it achieves savings of more than two orders of magnitude over many datasets by deferring full-resolution sampling to areas requiring detail. The method operates in an iterative refinement loop, generating successively more refined images over time. Inputs: Volume dataset V. Camera parameters and viewport dimensions W \times H. Initial sampling density \rho0 < 1. Complexity threshold \tau. Outputs: Final image I at display resolution. Data Structures: Sample Array: A list of tuples (u, v, c), where (u, v) are screen coordinates and c is the computed color for that ray. Steps: 1. Initial Sparse Casting: Cast rays at a sparse grid of screen positions. For a density \rho0 = 1/k^2, cast rays at coordinates (i \cdot k, j \cdot k) for i \in [0, W/k), j \in [0, H/k). For each ray, perform volume rendering to compute color c. Store (u, v, c) in the Sample Array. 2. Complexity Measurement: Divide the image space into blocks. Compute the local complexity metric M as the maximum color difference between adjacent samples within or bordering the block. M{block} = \max{(ui, vi), (uj, vj) \in \text{block}} \| ci - cj \| If a block contains only one sample, M{block} = 0. 3. Adaptive Subdivision: Identify blocks where M{block} > \tau. Recursively subdivide these blocks into smaller regions (e.g., halving the block size). For each new sub-region, cast new rays at the center or corners if they are not already present in the Sample Array. Perform volume rendering for new rays and add (u, v, c) to the Sample Array. Repeat subdivision until M{block} \le \tau for all blocks or a maximum depth is reached. 4. Interpolation and Resampling: Construct the final image I by interpolating colors from the nonuniform Sample Array to the regular W \times H display grid. Use bilinear or bicubic interpolation based on the nearest neighbors in the Sample Array. 5. Iterative Refinement: To generate high-quality images over time, repeat steps 2-4 with a lower threshold \tau or higher initial density, adding new rays to the existing Sample Array and re-interpolating. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivesparseraysampling(volume, width, height, initialdensity, threshold, maxdepth): # Step 1: Initial sparse casting samplearray = [] step = int(1.0 / sqrt(initialdensity)) for i in range(0, width, step): for j in range(0, height, step): ray = standardraygeneration(i, j) color = volumerender(volume, ray) samplearray.append((i, j, color)) # Step 2 & 3: Recursive subdivision def subdivide(samples, x, y, w, h, depth): if depth >= maxdepth: return blocksamples = [s for s in samples if x <= s[0] < x + w and y <= s[1] < y + h] maxdiff = 0.0 if len(blocksamples) > 1: for i in range(len(blocksamples)): for j in range(i + 1, len(blocksamples)): diff = norm(blocksamples[i][2] - blocksamples[j][2]) if diff > maxdiff: maxdiff = diff if maxdiff > threshold: halfw, halfh = w / 2, h / 2 subdivide(samples, x, y, halfw, halfh, depth + 1) subdivide(samples, x + halfw, y, halfw, halfh, depth + 1) subdivide(samples, x, y + halfh, halfw, halfh, depth + 1) subdivide(samples, x + halfw, y + halfh, halfw, halfh, depth + 1) centers = [ (x + halfw / 2, y + halfh / 2), (x + halfw + halfw / 2, y + halfh / 2), (x + halfw / 2, y + halfh + halfh / 2), (x + halfw + halfw / 2, y + halfh + halfh / 2) ] for cx, cy in centers: if not any(s[0] == cx and s[1] == cy for s in samples): ray = standardraygeneration(cx, cy) color = volumerender(volume, ray) samples.append((cx, cy, color)) blocksize = int(1.0 / sqrt(initialdensity)) subdivide(samplearray, 0, 0, blocksize, blocksize, 0) # Step 4: Interpolation and resampling image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height)] for u in range(width): for v in range(height): image[v][u] = interpolate(samplearray, u, v) return image def standardraygeneration(x, y): # Standard ray generation from pixel coordinates pass def volumerender(volume, ray): # Performs front-to-back volume integration along the ray pass def norm(vec): return sqrt(sum(x 2 for x in vec)) def interpolate(samples, u, v): # Bilinear interpolation from nearest non-uniform samples pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Interpolation artifacts may occur if the sample density is too low in high-frequency regions before subdivision. Ensure the interpolation kernel supports non-uniform grids. Empty Space: Skipping integration in empty space provides a speedup without affecting image quality. Recursion Depth: Unbounded subdivision in noisy or highly incoherent data can cause excessive computation; a maximum depth parameter is required. An acceleration method exploiting pixel-space coherency by casting rays from a subset of screen pixels and interpolating empty pixels between them. It casts rays from only a subset of screen pixels (e.g., every other pixel). Empty pixels residing between pixels with similar values are assigned interpolated values. In areas of high image gradient, additional rays are cast to resolve ambiguities. This method was originally developed for traditional ray-tracing and later adapted to volume rendering. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method reduces total ray casts significantly in smooth regions, with complexity scaling adaptively based on image complexity. Memory Complexity: O(K), where K is the number of rays cast, which is much smaller than W \times H in sparse regions. Performance: Savings of more than two orders of magnitude over brute-force rendering methods were obtained for many datasets. Crude images can be obtained in a few seconds, with gradually better images at intervals of a few seconds each, culminating in high-quality images in less than a minute. Strengths: Significant speedup for coherent data; allows progressive refinement over time. Limitations: Interpolation artifacts if subdivision is insufficient; overhead of managing non-uniform sample arrays. When to use: When rendering coherent volumetric data where large regions are smooth and exhibit spatial correlation. When not to use: For highly incoherent or noisy data where subdivision depth becomes excessive. The method is applied in clinical visualization contexts such as radiation treatment beam superimposition and medical prosthesis display. It builds on classical ray tracing techniques for non-uniform ray distribution, such as recursive subdivision of image space. The approach is similar to Whitted's method but extended to allow sampling densities of less than one ray per pixel. It exploits the coherence present in projections of data acquired from sensing devices, where blurring introduces spatial correlation. name: Adaptive Image Supersampling
head: Adaptive image sampling optimization, adaptive sampling with synchronization
body: Adaptive Image Supersampling is an acceleration method that exploits pixel-space coherency by casting rays from a sparse subset of screen pixels and interpolating values for empty pixels, while selectively increasing ray density in regions of high image gradient or depth variance. It differs from its parent, Adaptive Sparse Ray Sampling, by explicitly defining the mechanism for handling the "empty" pixels between the sparse grid (interpolation) and the specific criterion for refinement (image gradient/depth discontinuity) rather than just general complexity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset, a camera configuration, and a sparse ray grid (e.g., every other pixel). Output: A rendered image with adaptive resolution. Data Structures: ImageBuffer: A 2D array of color/depth values corresponding to screen pixels. RayGrid: A boolean mask or coordinate list indicating which pixels have been explicitly ray-cast. Steps: 1. Sparse Ray Casting: Cast rays only from a subset of screen pixels. A common pattern is a regular grid, such as every other pixel in both dimensions. 2. Interpolation: For pixels not explicitly cast ("empty pixels"), assign values by interpolating from the nearest cast pixels. This step assumes pixel-space coherency, meaning adjacent pixels with similar values can be approximated without explicit ray casting. 3. Gradient Analysis: Compute the local image gradient (or depth variance) for the interpolated image. Regions with significant gradients indicate edges or depth discontinuities. 4. Adaptive Refinement: In areas where the image gradient exceeds a threshold, cast additional rays to resolve ambiguities. This effectively performs supersampling only where necessary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveimagesupersampling(volume, camera, threshold): # Step 1: Cast rays from a sparse subset (e.g., every other pixel) sparsepixels = getsparsegrid(camera.resolution, stride=2) imagebuffer = initializeimage(camera.resolution) for pixel in sparsepixels: ray = camera.generateray(pixel) color = castray(volume, ray) imagebuffer[pixel] = color # Step 2: Interpolate empty pixels # Note: Specific interpolation kernel (bilinear, nearest) is not detailed in sources interpolateemptypixels(imagebuffer, sparsepixels) # Step 3 & 4: Analyze gradient and refine gradients = computeimagegradients(imagebuffer) for pixel in camera.allpixels(): if gradients[pixel] > threshold: # Cast additional rays for this pixel (supersampling) # Note: Number of additional rays and pattern (jittered/grid) not specified additionalrays = generatesupersamplerays(camera, pixel) refinedcolor = averagecolors([castray(volume, r) for r in additionalrays]) imagebuffer[pixel] = refinedcolor return imagebuffer Parameters: stride: The spacing of the initial sparse grid. Typical value: 2 (every other pixel). threshold: The gradient magnitude above which additional rays are cast. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Uniform Regions: If the volume is homogeneous, interpolation suffices, and no additional rays are cast, maximizing efficiency. High-Frequency Details: If the initial sparse grid undersamples high-frequency details, aliasing may occur before refinement. The threshold must be tuned to detect these early. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is reduced compared to full supersampling because rays are only cast for a subset of pixels initially. The complexity depends on the fraction of pixels requiring refinement. Memory complexity is dominated by the image buffer and the sparse ray grid. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Exploits pixel-space coherency to skip empty space and uniform regions, providing significant speedup without affecting image quality in smooth areas. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of coherency; may fail in highly textured or noisy volumes. Interpolation artifacts may appear if the sparse grid is too coarse. When to Use: Use when the volume has large homogeneous regions or smooth gradients. Use when computational resources are limited and a trade-off between quality and speed is acceptable. When Not to Use: Avoid for volumes with high-frequency noise or complex, non-coherent structures where interpolation is inaccurate. Adaptive image supersampling was originally developed for traditional ray-tracing and later adapted to volume rendering. It extends the concept of supersampling, which casts multiple rays per pixel to approximate integrals, by varying the number of rays based on local depth variance or image gradient. This approach balances quality and efficiency by allocating more samples to regions with significant depth discontinuities (edges) and fewer in uniform areas. ray casting, https://grokipedia.com/page/Raycasting, fetched 2026-10-26 Volume Visualization and Volume Rendering Techniques, https://www.cs.unh.edu/~cs880/visualization/Meissner-VolRenderingEGTutorial-rdb.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hard Sample Mining
head: HSM
body: Hard Sample Mining (HSM) is a training acceleration technique for neural radiance fields that reduces iteration time and memory usage by subsampling a "hard minibatch" of point samples. The algorithm employs propagated pixel loss to rank point samples and subsequently subsamples a hard minibatch, estimated to retain most of the update information. Unlike approaches that simply prune low-weight samples, HSM uses the magnitude of the reconstruction error to prioritize challenging regions and skip well-reconstructed ones. Inputs: A batch of point samples \mathcal{S} associated with training images. Propagated pixel loss values Li for each sample i \in \mathcal{S}. Total batch size B. Outputs: A subsampled set of hard samples \mathcal{S}{\text{hard}} \subset \mathcal{S} used for the backward pass and parameter update. Data Structures: Sample List: A list of tuples containing the sample index, its associated pixel coordinates, and its computed loss value Li. Ranking Array: An array of indices sorted by Li in descending order. Steps: 1. Loss Computation: Compute the pixel-wise loss \elli for each sample i against the ground truth. 2. Ranking: Sort all samples in the batch \mathcal{S} based on their loss values \elli in descending order. 3. Subsampling: Select the top samples from the sorted list to form the hard minibatch \mathcal{S}{\text{hard}}, constrained by the target batch size B. 4. Backward Pass: Compute gradients and update network parameters using only the samples in \mathcal{S}{\text{hard}}. Parameters: B: Total batch size. Typical values: 220 for Instant-NGP, 218 for Nerfacto. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Uniformly Challenging Content: Scenes with unbounded backgrounds or multiple outward-facing objects result in a more uniform pixel loss distribution, limiting computational efficiency gains. Pose Errors: Severe pose mistakes in the dataset can produce "impossible to learn" point samples that consistently have high loss and crowd the hard minibatch, potentially degrading training stability. Mitigation strategies include uncertainty or pose estimation techniques. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hardsampleminingstep(network, samples, groundtruth, batchsize): # 1. Loss Computation # Compute per-sample loss (e.g., Mean Squared Error) lossvalues = [sum((p - g) 2 for p, g in zip(sample, gt)) / len(sample) for sample, gt in zip(samples, groundtruth)] # 2. Ranking # Sort indices by loss value in descending order sortedindices = sorted(range(len(lossvalues)), key=lambda i: lossvalues[i], reverse=True) # 3. Subsampling # Select top indices up to batchsize hardindices = sortedindices[:batchsize] # 4. Backward Pass # Gather predictions and targets for hard samples hardpreds = [samples[i] for i in hardindices] hardgts = [groundtruth[i] for i in hardindices] # Compute loss on the hard minibatch hardloss = sum(sum((p - g) 2 for p, g in zip(pred, gt)) / len(pred) for pred, gt in zip(hardpreds, hardgts)) / len(hardpreds) # Perform gradient update using only the hard samples hardloss.backward() return hardloss Time Complexity: Reduces iteration time by focusing updates on a subsampled hard minibatch rather than the full batch. Memory Complexity: Reduces dynamic memory footprint during training; for example, usage dropped from 300 MB to 160 MB for normal iterations in Nerfacto. Performance: On Mip-NeRF-360 scenes, converges ~2x faster to a given PSNR level and achieves ~1 dB gain per same training time compared to the baseline. Strengths: Effective for scenes with centrally placed objects against easy backgrounds where loss distribution is skewed. Limitations: Less effective in uniformly challenging scenes (e.g., unbounded scenes) where loss distribution is uniform. Sensitive to severe pose errors in the dataset. When to use: When training time and memory are bottlenecks, and the scene has distinct hard/easy regions. When not to use: When the dataset has significant pose errors or the scene is uniformly complex. Hard Sample Mining was introduced by J. Korhonen et al. in the paper "Efficient NeRF Optimization -- Not All Samples Remain Equally Hard". The method was applied to PyTorch reimplimentations of Instant-NGP and Nerfacto on Mip-NeRF-360 and NeRF synthetic datasets. It differs from Nerfacc's approach of pruning low-weight samples by using propagated pixel loss to rank and subsample a hard minibatch. name: Adaptive Volume Sampling
body: Adaptive Volume Sampling is a GPU-based raycasting acceleration technique that modulates the sampling density along a ray to reduce redundant volume queries and shading operations. It solves the performance bottleneck of uniform sampling in homogeneous regions by switching between "Full density" and "Adaptive density" modes. It builds on Adaptive Ray Sampling by adjusting the number of samples per ray segment rather than just step size or termination probability. Inputs: A volumetric dataset, ray origin, and ray direction. Outputs: A final color and opacity value for the pixel. Data Structures: The method utilizes a multi-resolution hierarchy of the volume data, referenced as Level 0 through Level 3. Each level represents a coarser sampling of the volume. Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Cast a primary ray from the camera through the pixel. 2. Metric Evaluation: Evaluate a scalar metric along the ray to determine local complexity or error. 3. Level Selection: Based on the metric, select the appropriate resolution level (or sampling density) for the current segment of the ray. 4. Volume Integration: Perform the volume integration (e.g., front-to-back compositing) using the selected sampling density. 5. Termination: Stop when the ray exits the volume or the accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold. Parameters: Thresholds: Implicit thresholds determine the switch between levels. Hierarchy Levels: The source mentions Levels 0 through 3. Edge Cases: Discontinuities Parallel to Axis: A naive choice of sampling axis can ignore discontinuities parallel to that axis. Precision: GPU-based implementation requires careful handling of floating-point precision during density evaluation to avoid artifacts. This method extends adaptive volume sampling to scenarios involving multiple sampling axes, such as 2D image grids, by using separate 1D kernels for each axis and combining gradient approximations. It solves the problem where a naive choice of a single axis risks ignoring discontinuities parallel to that axis, while multidimensional prefiltering kernels require computationally challenging n-1 dimensional integration. Unlike its siblings, it ensures discontinuities in any orientation can be sampled with nonzero probability by adaptively selecting the axis closest to perpendicular to the discontinuity. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of volume queries in homogeneous regions, leading to a speed-up of 2.6–2.8x compared to full density sampling. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On an ATI X1800 XT, rendering at 1024x1024 resolution achieved 7.1 FPS with adaptive sampling versus 2.6 FPS with full density. On an NV GF7800 GTX, it achieved 3.0 FPS versus 1.2 FPS. Strengths: Significant performance improvement on GPUs with limited bandwidth or compute power; maintains visual quality by focusing samples where needed. Limitations: Overhead of metric evaluation and level selection; potential artifacts if the metric fails to detect subtle discontinuities. The method was presented by Markus Hadwiger from the VRVIS Research Center, Vienna, Austria, in the paper "Advanced Illumination Techniques for GPU-Based Volume Raycasting". It is part of a broader effort to optimize GPU-based volume rendering by managing out-of-core data and leveraging spatial coherence. GPU-Based Volume Ray-Casting with Advanced Illumination, https://www.uni-ulm.de/fileadmin/websiteuniulm/iui.inst.100/institut/Papers/viscom/2008/advancedillumination.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Multi-Axis Sampling Extension
head: Adaptive Multi-Axis Sampling for Discontinuities
body: This method extends adaptive volume sampling to scenarios involving multiple sampling axes, such as 2D image grids, by using separate 1D kernels for each axis and combining gradient approximations. It solves the problem where a naive choice of a single axis risks ignoring discontinuities parallel to that axis, while multidimensional prefiltering kernels require computationally challenging n-1 dimensional integration. Unlike its siblings, it ensures discontinuities in any orientation can be sampled with nonzero probability by adaptively selecting the axis closest to perpendicular to the discontinuity. Inputs: A set of n sampling axes. A discontinuity function d(x). Evaluation locations on the grid. Outputs: Gradient approximations derived from the selected sampling axis. Data Structures: The method does not define complex persistent data structures. It operates on local evaluation locations and draws samples dynamically. For n sampling axes, the compiler draws 2n + 1 samples per location. These samples can be potentially shared between neighboring locations. Steps: 1. Quantify Discontinuity Feature: For a discontinuity d(x), calculate the feature value for each sampling axis. The feature is quantified as: \left| \frac{dx}{d\theta} \right| This term corresponds to the denominator in the gradient approximation formula (Equation 1 in the source). 2. Select Axis: Choose the sampling axis that yields the largest value of \left| \frac{dx}{d\theta} \right|. Rationale: A larger value in the denominator leads to approximate gradients with smaller magnitude and, consequently, smaller variance. Intuition: The chosen axis is ideally the one closest to perpendicular to the discontinuity, allowing fixed-size small steps along that axis to have a larger probability of sampling the discontinuity. 3. Sample: Draw 2n + 1 samples using the selected axis's 1D kernel. 4. Combine: Combine the gradient approximations from the different sampling axes after the sampling step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multiaxissampling(discontinuityfunction, axes, location): """ Selects the best sampling axis for a discontinuity at a given location and returns the gradient approximation. Args: discontinuityfunction: Function d(x) describing the discontinuity. axes: List of available sampling axes (e.g., [axisx, axisy]). location: Current evaluation point. Returns: gradientapprox: The computed gradient approximation. """ bestaxis = None maxfeaturevalue = -infinity # Step 1 & 2: Quantify and Select Axis for axis in axes: # Calculate | dx / dθ | for the current axis # Note: The exact implementation of dx/dθ depends on the specific # discontinuity function and axis definition. # This is a placeholder for the derivative calculation relative to the axis. featurevalue = computediscontinuityfeature(discontinuityfunction, axis, location) if featurevalue > maxfeaturevalue: maxfeaturevalue = featurevalue bestaxis = axis # Step 3: Sample # Draw 2n + 1 samples along the bestaxis. # n is the number of axes. n = len(axes) samples = drawsamples(bestaxis, location, count=2n + 1) # Step 4: Combine # Compute gradient approximation from samples. # This combines the gradient approximations from the selected axis. gradientapprox = computegradient(samples, bestaxis) return gradientapprox def computediscontinuityfeature(discontinuityfunction, axis, location): """ Computes | dx / dθ | for a specific axis. This corresponds to the denominator in the gradient approximation formula. """ # Implementation detail: This requires calculating the derivative of the # discontinuity parameterization with respect to the axis direction. # Assuming a standard parameterization where dx/dθ represents the # rate of change of the discontinuity position along the axis. # In practice, this might be approximated by finite differences or # analytical derivatives if available. return abs(discontinuityfunction.derivative(axis, location)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Discontinuities: Naively choosing one axis risks ignoring discontinuities parallel to that axis, resulting in measure-zero sampling. This method mitigates this by adaptively choosing the perpendicular axis. Precision: The choice of axis depends on the magnitude of \left| \frac{dx}{d\theta} \right|. Small errors in this calculation could lead to suboptimal axis selection. Sample Sharing: The note mentions that samples can be shared between neighboring locations. Implementers must ensure that the sample grid is consistent across neighbors to allow this sharing, which may require careful coordinate management. Time and Memory Complexity: The method draws 2n + 1 samples per location for n axes. This is linear in the number of axes. It avoids the computational burden of n-1 dimensional integration required by multidimensional prefiltering kernels. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Robustly samples discontinuities in any orientation without the complexity of multidimensional integration. Simpler to implement than multidimensional prefiltering. Limitations: Still relies on 1D kernels, which may be less efficient than a single optimal multidimensional kernel if one could be computed cheaply. The adaptive choice requires calculating the discontinuity feature for all axes. When to Use: Use when dealing with multiple sampling axes (e.g., 2D image grids) and discontinuities that may be parallel to any of the axes. Use when multidimensional prefiltering is too computationally expensive. When Not to Use: If only a single sampling axis is available, this extension is not applicable. If the discontinuity is known to be aligned with a specific axis and that axis is always chosen, the adaptive overhead may be unnecessary. Origin: The method is described in the paper "A \delta". It extends the techniques discussed in Section 4.2 of the source to handle multiple sampling axes. History and Development: The problem of handling multiple sampling axes arises in shader applications where the program is evaluated on a multi-dimensional grid. Previous approaches included naively choosing one axis (risking missed discontinuities) or using multidimensional prefiltering kernels (requiring challenging integration). The multi-axis extension was proposed as a simpler alternative to multidimensional prefiltering, using separate 1D kernels and adaptive selection. Usage: Used in volume rendering and shader applications where discontinuities need to be sampled robustly across multiple dimensions. name: Superpixel-guide Efficient Sampling (SES)
body: Superpixel-guide Efficient Sampling (SES) is a training strategy for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and neural fields that uses SLIC superpixels as the smallest processing units to guide ray sampling. It addresses the slow convergence and scattered sampling issues in high-resolution NeRF training by focusing computational resources on complex regions with high rendering errors. Unlike quadtree-based methods which suffer from redundant computations and fragmented information due to fixed geometric shapes, SES resolves inadequate partitioning issues and reduces computational overhead per instance by adapting to image content. The method builds on Adaptive Ray Sampling by replacing fixed hierarchical partitions with content-aware superpixel masks. SES operates in an iterative loop of random sampling, error recording, secondary segmentation, and guided sampling. It integrates a superpixel loss term into the standard optimization process. Inputs: Input RGB images I, initial neural field parameters (e.g., Instant-NGP or DVGO), hyperparameters \beta0, \lambda{mse}, \lambda{sp}, t, \lambda{error}, \lambda{std}. Outputs: Optimized neural field parameters, rendered images. Superpixel Map: A 2D array where each element (u,v) stores the superpixel ID k assigned to that pixel. Error Map: A 2D array storing the per-pixel rendering error rj for the most recent training batch. Sampling Probability Map: A 2D array storing the probability P(u,v) of selecting pixel (u,v) for the next ray batch. \beta0: Weight between RGB image and render error in secondary segmentation. Synthetic datasets: 0.8. Real datasets: 0.65. \lambda{sp}: Coefficient for superpixel loss. Synthetic datasets: 10^{-6}. Real datasets: 10^{-4}. \lambda{mse}: Coefficient for MSE loss. Typically 1. t: Minimum error threshold to exclude negligible errors (blank/well-learned regions). \lambda{error}, \lambda{std}: Coefficients for sampling probabilities to balance weights. 1. Initialization: Apply the SLIC algorithm F to partition the input RGB image I into superpixels L: \elli = F(T{CIE}(I)), \quad \elli \in L where T{CIE} transforms the image from RGB to CIE color space. 2. Initial Training (Random Sampling): Perform standard random ray sampling and training. After each training session/iteration, record the rendering error rj for each sampled pixel j within a superpixel. 3. Superpixel Error Calculation: Calculate the average error \ell{error}^i for each superpixel i: \ell{error}^i = \frac{1}{N} \sum{j \in N} rj where N is the set of sampled pixels within superpixel i. 4. Secondary Segmentation (Re-segmentation): Identify areas with the largest rendering errors and their adjacent regions. Use a masked SLIC algorithm to re-segment these specific regions. This step considers both RGB color and rendering error simultaneously. The render error is replicated three times to meet dimensional requirements for CIE transformation. The combined feature vector Ck for the masked SLIC is: Ck = \beta0 \cdot T{CIE}(I) + (1 - \beta0) \cdot T{CIE}(R) where R is the portion of render error to be recalculated, and \beta0 is the weight. 5. Sampling Probability Calculation: Calculate the sampling probability \ellp^i for each superpixel i based on its error and standard deviation: \ellp^i = \lambda{error} \cdot \ell{std\p}^i + \lambda{std} \cdot \ell{error}^i where \ell{std\p}^i is the standard deviation of errors within the superpixel. The probability is normalized to lie between 0 and 1, and the threshold t is applied to exclude negligible errors. 6. Guided Sampling: Use the calculated sampling probabilities to direct pixel-level ray sampling. Regenerate sampled rays according to the probability map. Accumulate rendering errors during this phase. 7. Loss Computation: Optimize neural field parameters using pixel-level Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss \mathcal{L}{mse} and superpixel loss \mathcal{L}{sp}: \mathcal{L}{sp} = \ell{error}^i + 0.001 \cdot \ell{std\p}^i Total loss: \mathcal{L} = \lambda{mse} \cdot \mathcal{L}{mse} + \lambda{sp} \cdot \mathcal{L}{sp} Due to the strong bias of \mathcal{L}{sp}, \lambda{sp} is set significantly smaller than \lambda{mse} (three to four orders of magnitude). 8. Position Encoding Adjustment: If using frequency-based position encoding, the method may adjust the maximum frequency K based on superpixel complexity: \gammaK'(x) = \gammaK(x) M(i) where gi(x) denotes the position encoding algorithm, K represents the maximum frequency, and \gammaK(x) defines the specific formulation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def trainSES(inputimages, neuralfield, hyperparams): beta0 = hyperparams['beta0'] lambdasp = hyperparams['lambdasp'] lambdamse = hyperparams['lambdamse'] t = hyperparams['t'] lambdaerror = hyperparams['lambdaerror'] lambdastd = hyperparams['lambdastd'] # Step 1: Initial Segmentation cieimages = [rgbtocie(img) for img in inputimages] superpixelmaps = [slicsegment(cieimg) for cieimg in cieimages] # Step 2: Initial Random Sampling Training errormap = np.zeroslike(inputimages[0][..., 0]) for in range(1000): # Initial training iterations rays = generaterandomrays() colors, errors = renderrays(neuralfield, rays) updateparameters(neuralfield, errors, lambdamse) errormap += errors # Step 3: Superpixel Error Calculation superpixelerrors = {} for spid in np.unique(superpixelmaps[0]): mask = (superpixelmaps[0] == spid) superpixelerrors[spid] = np.mean(errormap[mask]) # Step 4: Secondary Segmentation higherrorspids = np.argsort(list(superpixelerrors.values()))[-10:] # Top regions for spid in higherrorspids: regionmask = (superpixelmaps[0] == spid) regionrgb = inputimages[0][regionmask] regionerror = errormap[regionmask] regionerror3d = np.stack([regionerror] 3, axis=-1) cieregionrgb = rgbtocie(regionrgb) cieregionerror = rgbtocie(regionerror3d) combinedfeatures = beta0 cieregionrgb + (1 - beta0) cieregionerror newsp = maskedslic(combinedfeatures, regionmask) superpixelmaps[0][regionmask] = newsp # Step 5: Sampling Probability Calculation samplingprobs = {} for spid in np.unique(superpixelmaps[0]): mask = (superpixelmaps[0] == spid) err = np.mean(errormap[mask]) std = np.std(errormap[mask]) prob = lambdaerror std + lambdastd err samplingprobs[spid] = np.clip(prob - t, 0, 1) # Normalize and apply threshold # Step 6 & 7: Guided Sampling and Loss for in range(5000): # Guided training iterations rays = sampleraysbyprobability(samplingprobs, superpixelmaps[0]) colors, errors = renderrays(neuralfield, rays) mseloss = np.mean((colors - groundtruth) 2) sploss = np.mean(errormap) + 0.001 np.std(errormap) totalloss = lambdamse mseloss + lambdasp sploss updateparameters(neuralfield, totalloss) errormap = errors def rgbtocie(rgb): return rgb # Standard RGB to CIE transform def slicsegment(img): return np.zeroslike(img[..., 0], dtype=int) # Standard SLIC def maskedslic(features, mask): return np.zeroslike(mask, dtype=int) # SLIC restricted to mask def generaterandomrays(): return np.random.rand(1000, 3) # Uniform random ray generation def renderrays(field, rays): return np.random.rand(1000, 3), np.random.rand(1000) # Forward pass def updateparameters(field, loss, lr): pass # Gradient descent step def sampleraysbyprobability(probs, spmap): return np.random.rand(1000, 3) # Weighted sampling Threshold t: If t is too high, well-learned regions may be excluded from sampling entirely, potentially leading to stagnation in those areas. Weight \beta0: Synthetic data prefers a higher RGB weight (0.8), while real data prefers a higher error weight (0.65). Loss Bias: The superpixel loss \mathcal{L}{sp} has a strong bias. If \lambda{sp} is not set sufficiently small (three to four orders of magnitude smaller than \lambda{mse}), it can dominate the gradient and destabilize training. Dimensionality: The render error must be replicated three times to match the RGB channel dimension before CIE transformation. Time Complexity: The method adds overhead for SLIC segmentation and probability calculation. However, it reduces the total number of volume queries by focusing on complex regions, potentially offsetting this cost. The overhead of SLIC is generally lower than quadtree partitioning for large-scale images. Memory Complexity: Requires storing superpixel maps and error maps. The memory footprint is comparable to standard NeRF training with additional storage for segmentation data. Performance: Integrated with Instant-NGP and DVGO baselines, SES improves rendering quality for high-resolution inputs (2k, 4k) compared to standard random sampling. Strengths: Resolves inadequate partitioning issues of quadtrees; reduces computational overhead per instance; effective for large input scales. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \beta0 and \lambda{sp}; dependent on the quality of SLIC segmentation; scaling to extremely large scenes beyond the tested 2k/4k resolutions is not given in the sources. SES was proposed by Zhongwei Xuan et al. in 2024 for the ACM Multimedia (MM '24) conference. It was developed to address the limitations of existing adaptive sampling methods, such as quadtrees, which increase computational cost with input scale and cause fragmented information. The method is implemented on CUDA to leverage hardware performance and has been tested on synthetic and real datasets using NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPUs. It is integrated into popular neural field methods like Instant-NGP (via nerf-template/torch-ngp) and DVGO. name: Coarse-to-Fine Hierarchical Sampling
body: Coarse-to-Fine Hierarchical Sampling is a family of adaptive ray sampling strategies that improve the learning of high-frequency details in Neural Radiance Fields by performing multiple tiers of volume sampling. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling, where most samples fall in empty space, by using a coarse pass to identify opaque or high-complexity regions and then clustering a second set of samples near those regions to train a fine network. It sets itself apart from standard uniform sampling by adaptively concentrating computational effort on visible geometry, and from its sibling TermiNeRF by not explicitly modeling termination probabilities but rather relying on opacity-based importance sampling. The core mechanism shared by all children is the deviation from a fixed, uniform sampling strategy. Uses a coarse MLP to generate weights, then samples fine points from the resulting PDF. It sets itself apart by using a separate fine network trained jointly with the coarse one, relying on density-based heuristics rather than learned proposals. Choose when you need a simple, effective baseline for high-frequency detail recovery without complex architectural changes. Uses a quadtree structure to dynamically adjust ray distribution across input views during training. It sets itself apart by using rendering error to prune redundant blocks and integrating context-based probability density for intra-block sampling. Choose when you want to accelerate training by focusing rays on high-complexity image regions. Trains a dedicated sampling network to predict importance weights for fixed bins, replacing the heuristic coarse-to-fine step. It sets itself apart by using a single evaluation of a sampling network per ray to predict weights, rather than hierarchical refinement. Choose when you want to eliminate the non-differentiable sampling step and optimize the sampling distribution directly. Replaces heuristic sampling with a differentiable 'proposer' module that outputs fine sample locations from coarse features. It sets itself apart by enabling end-to-end training of the entire system (coarse, proposer, fine) to improve view synthesis quality. Choose when you need a fully differentiable pipeline that learns optimal sampling locations rather than relying on opacity-based PDFs. Combines spatial skipping with biased sampling using an occupancy grid and a nonlinear piecewise exponential function. It sets itself apart by skipping empty space and biasing samples toward surfaces within occupied cells. Choose when you need to reduce wasted computation in empty regions while avoiding random scatter near surfaces. A sampling scheme proposed by the authors that preserves rendering quality while significantly increasing runtime efficiency compared to Hierarchical Sampling. Not given in the sources. name: Coarse-to-Fine NeRF
head: Coarse-Fine NeRF, Hierarchical Rendering (Original NeRF), Two-Stage NeRF
body: Coarse-to-Fine NeRF is a hierarchical sampling strategy that improves the learning of high-frequency details in Neural Radiance Fields by performing two tiers of volume sampling. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling, where most samples fall in empty space, by using a coarse network to identify opaque regions and then clustering a second set of samples near those regions to train a fine network. It sets itself apart from standard uniform sampling by adaptively concentrating computational effort on visible geometry, and from its sibling TermiNeRF by not explicitly modeling termination probabilities but rather relying on opacity-based importance sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3, ray directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3, near bound t{near}, far bound t{far}, number of coarse samples Nc, number of fine samples Nf. Outputs: Rendered RGB color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}), depth map, accumulated alpha, and weights for both coarse and fine passes. Data Structures: Networks: Two separate Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), networkcoarse and networkfine. Both share the same architecture (hidden dimensions, layers) but have distinct parameters. Positional Encoding: Input coordinates are encoded using positional encoding with poslevels (default 10) and view directions with dirlevels (default 4). Raw Output Tensor: For each sample, the network outputs a tensor of shape (raycount, samplecount, 4). The first 3 channels are RGB (sigmoided to [0,1]), and the 4th channel is the raw volume density \sigma. Parameters: ncoarse: Number of coarse samples per ray. Default: 64. nfine: Number of fine samples per ray. Default: 128. perturb: Boolean flag to enable perturbation of uniform samples during the coarse pass to break symmetry and reduce aliasing. Default: True. rawnoisestd: Standard deviation of uniform noise added to volume density before ReLU. Default: 0. whitebkgd: Boolean flag. If True, adds unaccounted transmittance to RGB assuming a white background. Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling: Generate Nc depth values tc uniformly spaced between t{near} and t{far}. If perturb is True, apply perturbation to uniform samples to break symmetry and reduce aliasing. 2. Coarse Query: Convert depth values to 3D points \mathbf{p}c = \mathbf{o} + tc \mathbf{d}. Query networkcoarse with \mathbf{p}c to obtain raw outputs \mathbf{raw}c. 3. Coarse Rendering: Convert \mathbf{raw}c to alpha compositing weights wc using volume rendering equations. Compute the coarse RGB color \mathbf{C}c and depth. 4. Hierarchical Sampling: Use the coarse weights wc to define a probability distribution. Sample Nf new depth values tf from this distribution using inverse transform sampling (or samplepdf). Pitfall: The sampling step is non-differentiable. Gradients must not flow back through this step to the coarse network. The coarse samples/weights used for fine sampling must be detached from the computation graph. 5. Fine Sampling Preparation: Concatenate coarse and fine depth values: t{fine\all} = \text{sort}([tc, tf]). Convert these to 3D points \mathbf{p}{fine\all}. 6. Fine Query: Query networkfine with \mathbf{p}{fine\all} to obtain \mathbf{raw}f. 7. Fine Rendering: Convert \mathbf{raw}f to weights wf and compute the final RGB color \mathbf{C}f. Formulas: Distance between samples: \deltai = z{i+1} - zi An infinite distance (10^{10}) is appended to the last column to ensure the opacity of the last segment is 1. Alpha (Opacity): \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \cdot \delta) Where \sigma is the volume density from the network output, optionally perturbed by noise \mathcal{U}[0,1] if rawnoisestd > 0, and passed through ReLU. Transmittance: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) Computed as the cumulative product of (1 - \alpha), prepended with 1. The last column is discarded. Weights: wi = \alphai \cdot Ti RGB Rendering: \mathbf{C} = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \mathbf{c}i If whitebkgd is True: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C} + (1 - \sum wi) \cdot \mathbf{1}. Loss Function: L = L{coarse} + L{fine} L{coarse} = \text{mean}((\mathbf{C}{coarse} - \mathbf{C}{target})^2) L{fine} = \text{mean}((\mathbf{C}{fine} - \mathbf{C}{target})^2) Both networks are supervised against the target pixel color. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def raw2outputs(raw, zvals, raysd, rawnoisestd=0.0, whitebkgd=False): """ Converts raw network outputs to radiance and weights. raw: list of lists [raycount][samplecount][4] -> RGB and sigma zvals: list of lists [raycount][samplecount] raysd: list of lists [raycount][3] """ raycount = len(zvals) samplecount = len(zvals[0]) # Calculate distances between samples dists = [] for r in range(raycount): row = [] for i in range(samplecount - Unlike standard NeRF which requires two distinct MLPs because standard PE only models one scale, this approach allows one MLP to learn a multiscale representation. It addresses the pitfall where standard uniform sampling results in sparse points on small objects relative to the scene, causing missing areas in rendered images due to inaccurate PDF in the fine stage. It treats the classified depth output vector from a single oracle network evaluation as a piecewise-constant Probability Density Function (PDF) and samples from its Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF). Unlike standard NeRF which builds a PDF from opacity outputs of a coarse shading network evaluated at multiple locations, this uses the oracle's direct output. The compute graph must be static; the coarse-to-fine edge is cut via.detach() to prevent cyclic definitions. Performance: Improves detail learning by clustering samples near opaque regions, unlike evenly distributed sampling. It prevents dense sampling at fine scales in empty space, improving computational efficiency compared to uniformly dense sampling. Strengths: Better reconstruction of high-frequency details; efficient use of samples by focusing on geometry. Limitations: Requires two network passes (or two networks); non-differentiable sampling step breaks gradient flow from fine to coarse. name: Hexagonal Multisampling Pattern Derivation
head: Conical frustum multisampling, Cylindrical multisampling pattern
body: This method constructs a multisampling pattern for a conical frustum by first generating a zero-mean, identity-covariance pattern for a cylinder and then warping it to match the frustum's analytical mean and covariance. It ensures uniform distribution along the ray and in angles around the ray while minimizing the number of samples for efficiency. It differs from siblings like DONeRF Depth Oracle Filtering by explicitly matching statistical moments of the conical frustum rather than filtering depth estimates, and from Hierarchical Sampling for Hemispherical Wavefronts by using a fixed hexagonal geometry derived from cylindrical symmetry rather than hemispherical wavefronts. Inputs: n: Number of samples (fixed to 6). \mathbf{c}: Center of the conical frustum (mean position). \mathbf{\Sigma}: Covariance matrix of the conical frustum. \mathbf{R}: Rotation matrix aligning the cylinder's local z-axis with the ray direction. Outputs: \mathbf{x}j \in \mathbb{R}^3: The j-th sample position in world space, for j = 0, \dots, n-1. Data Structures: theta1: Array of 6 angles [0, 2\pi/3, 4\pi/3, \pi, 5\pi/3, \pi/3]. cylsamples: Array of 6 vectors \mathbf{y}j \in \mathbb{R}^3 representing the canonical cylinder pattern. Steps: 1. Construct Canonical Cylinder Pattern: Generate n=6 points \mathbf{y}j in a local coordinate system where the cylinder axis aligns with the z-axis. The coordinates are defined as: \mathbf{y}j = \begin{bmatrix} \cos (\thetaj)/\sqrt {3} \\ \sin (\thetaj)/\sqrt {3} \\ \frac {j - (n-1)/2}{\sqrt {n(n^2-1)/12}} \end{bmatrix} where \thetaj are taken from theta1. This pattern has a mean of \mathbf{0} and a covariance of I3 (identity matrix). 2. Compute Warping Parameters: Determine the scaling and translation required to map the canonical cylinder to the target conical frustum. The target frustum has mean \mathbf{c} and covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}. The canonical cylinder has mean \mathbf{0} and covariance I3. 3. Warp Samples: Transform each canonical sample \mathbf{y}j to the world space sample \mathbf{x}j. The transformation aligns the cylinder's principal axes with the eigenvectors of \mathbf{\Sigma} and scales them by the square roots of the eigenvalues, then translates by \mathbf{c}. Specifically, if \mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{\Lambda} \mathbf{Q}^T is the eigendecomposition, the transformation is: \mathbf{x}j = \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{\Lambda}^{1/2} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{y}j where \mathbf{R} rotates the canonical cylinder's z-axis to align with the primary direction of the frustum (typically the ray direction). In the context of mip-NeRF, the frustum is oriented along the ray, so \mathbf{R} aligns the local z-axis with the ray direction vector. 4. Return Samples: Return the set \{\mathbf{x}0, \dots, \mathbf{x}{n-1}\}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def hexagonalmultisamplingpattern(n=6): """ Generates the canonical hexagonal multisampling pattern for a cylinder. Returns the n sample coordinates in local cylinder space. """ # Angles from theta1 theta1 = np.array([0, 2np.pi/3, 4np.pi/3, np.pi, 5np.pi/3, np.pi/3]) samples = [] for j in range(n): # x component x = np.cos(theta1[j]) / np.sqrt(3) # y component y = np.sin(theta1[j]) / np.sqrt(3) # z component (along the cylinder axis) z = (j - (n - 1) / 2) / np.sqrt(n (n2 - 1) / 12) samples.append([x, y, z]) return np.array(samples) def warptoconicalfrustum(cylsamples, mean, cov, raydirection): """ Warps canonical cylinder samples to match a conical frustum defined by mean and covariance. Args: cylsamples: (n, 3) array of canonical cylinder samples. mean: (3,) array, center of the frustum. cov: (3, 3) array, covariance matrix of the frustum. raydirection: (3,) array, unit vector along the ray. Returns: (n, 3) array of warped samples in world space. """ # Eigendecomposition of the frustum covariance eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) # Square root of eigenvalues for scaling sqrteigenvalues = np.sqrt(eigenvalues) # Construct scaling matrix S = np.diag(sqrteigenvalues) # Rotation matrix to align canonical cylinder z-axis with ray direction canonicalz = np.array([0, 0, 1]) if np.allclose(raydirection, canonicalz): R = np.eye(3) elif np.allclose(raydirection, -canonicalz): # Rotate 180 degrees around x-axis R = np.diag([1, -1, -1]) else: # General case: rotate canonicalz to raydirection using Rodrigues' formula v1 = canonicalz v2 = raydirection cross = np.cross(v1, v2) dot = np.dot(v1, v2) skew = np.array([ [0, -cross[2], cross[1]], [cross[2], 0, -cross[0]], [-cross[1], cross[0], 0] ]) R = np.eye(3) + skew + skew @ skew (1 / (1 + dot)) # Combined transformation matrix: T = Q S R T = eigenvectors @ S @ R # Transform samples: x = mean + T @ y warpedsamples = (cylsamples @ T.T) + mean return warpedsamples Parameters: n=6: The number of samples. This is the smallest number that allows for a zero-mean, identity-covariance pattern with the specified angular distribution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No samples are placed exactly along the ray; they are distributed at a distance proportional to the cone radius. The full covariance matrices of the samples and the frustum are not necessarily identical, but variance along the ray and total variance perpendicular to the ray are equal. The mismatch goes to zero as t \gg \dot{r}. The pattern relies on specific angular choices (\theta1 or \theta2) to maintain the zero-mean and identity-covariance property for n=6. Using other angles or n values will break these properties. Filters depth estimates to improve sampling. Choose when depth uncertainty is high and analytical covariance is less reliable. Samples hemispherical wavefronts. Choose when rendering scenes with significant hemispherical illumination or when the conical frustum approximation is insufficient for large angles. Time Complexity: O(n) where n=6. The warping involves a fixed number of matrix-vector multiplications. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store the samples. Strengths: Efficient (only 6 samples), matches analytical moments of the conical frustum, ensures uniform angular and axial distribution. Limitations: Does not place samples on the ray axis, which may be suboptimal for some scenes. The covariance mismatch, though small, exists. When to use: When rendering with conical frustums and efficiency is critical, and the frustum is not extremely wide (t \gg \dot{r}). When not to use: When high accuracy on the ray axis is required, or when the frustum is very wide and the covariance mismatch becomes significant. The method was introduced in the context of Mip-NeRF to improve the accuracy of volume rendering by better approximating the integral over a conical frustum. It is based on the Unscented Transform, which uses a minimal set of samples to capture the mean and covariance of a random variable. The specific hexagonal pattern was derived to satisfy the criteria of uniform distribution and moment matching with the smallest number of points.
