name: DONeRF Depth Oracle Filtering
head: Classified Depth Oracle, Depth smoothing filter, Neighborhood filter
body: DONeRF Depth Oracle Filtering is a preprocessing step applied to the training targets of the depth oracle network to improve surface detection consistency and reduce false negatives. It operates by smoothing classification targets in image and depth space, unlike Hexagonal Multisampling Pattern Derivation which derives sampling patterns directly, and unlike Hierarchical Sampling for Hemispherical Wavefronts which focuses on wavefronts. Trade-offs are detailed in Operating characteristics. The method filters the ground-truth classification targets generated for the depth oracle network. The oracle predicts a likelihood for each discretized segment along a ray, where a high value indicates the segment should receive samples and a low value indicates it should be skipped. Input: The unfiltered one-hot classification target C{x,y}(z) for each pixel (x,y) and discretized depth segment z. Output: The filtered classification target \hat{C}{x,y}(z) used for training the depth oracle network. Note: Filtering is applied only to training targets; no filtering is performed during inference. The classification target is a 3D array indexed by pixel coordinates (x,y) and depth segment index z. C{x,y}(z): Binary value (0 or 1). ds: Depth of the first surface along the ray. dz, d{z+1}: Discretization boundaries for segment z. The unfiltered target is a one-hot encoding: C{x,y}(z) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } dz \leq ds < d{z+1} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where ds is the depth of the first surface, and dz, d{z+1} are the boundaries of the discretized segment z. The filtering consists of two stages: a 2D spatial neighborhood filter and a 1D depth-axis smoothing filter. 1. 2D Neighborhood Filter (Radial): Applies a radial filter to include values from neighboring rays with a contribution weighted by their distance. For a filter size K, the intermediate target \hat{C}{x,y}(z) is computed as: \hat{C}{x,y}(z) = \max{i,j \in \pm \lfloor K/2 \rfloor} \left( C{x+i,y+j}(z) - \frac{\sqrt{2+j^2}}{\sqrt{2 \cdot \lfloor K/2 \rfloor}} \right) Here, i and j are offsets in the x and y directions. The term \frac{\sqrt{2+j^2}}{\sqrt{2 \cdot \lfloor K/2 \rfloor}} represents the distance penalty. For a 5 \times 5 filter (K=5), rays at distances 3, 2, 1, 0 pixels contribute 0, ≈0.30, ≈0.65, 1 respectively. For multiple depth values with the same discretization result, the maximum result is taken to ensure the largest value is placed at the actual surface. 2. 1D Depth Smoothing Filter: Applies a 1D triangle filter along the depth axis with kernel size Z: \hat{C}(z) = \min \left( \sum{i=-\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor}^{\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor} \hat{C}(z+i) \frac{\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor + 1 - |i|}{\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor + 1}, 1 \right) This acts as label smoothing, blurring depth values to help the oracle predict consistent outputs at depth discontinuities. Filter Size K: Size of the 2D spatial filter. Example: K=5. Kernel Size Z: Size of the 1D depth filter. Example: Z=5. Loss Function: Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def filterdepthoracletargets(C, K, Z): """ Filters the depth oracle classification targets. Args: C: 3D list of shape (H, W, D) containing binary classification targets. C[x][y][z] is 1 if the surface is in segment z, else 0. K: Integer, size of the 2D spatial filter (must be odd). Z: Integer, size of the 1D depth filter (must be odd). Returns: filteredC: 3D list of shape (H, W, D) with filtered targets. """ H, W, D = len(C), len(C[0]), len(C[0][0]) # Step 1: 2D Neighborhood Filter step1 = [[[-float('inf')] D for in range(W)] for in range(H)] halfK = K // 2 denom2d = math.sqrt(2 halfK) for x in range(H): for y in range(W): for z in range(D): maxval = -float('inf') for i in range(-halfK, halfK + 1): for j in range(-halfK, halfK + 1): nx, ny = x + i, y + j if 0 <= nx < H and 0 <= ny < W: weight = math.sqrt(2 + j2) / denom2d val = C[nx][ny][z] - weight if val > maxval: maxval = val step1[x][y][z] = maxval # Step 2: 1D Depth Smoothing Filter filteredC = [[[0.0] D for in range(W)] for in range(H)] halfZ = Z // 2 for x in range(H): for y in range(W): for z in range(D): sumval = 0.0 for i in range(-halfZ, halfZ + 1): nz = z + i if 0 <= nz < D: weight = (halfZ + 1 - abs(i)) / (halfZ + 1) sumval += step1[x][y][nz] weight filteredC[x][y][z] = min(sumval, 1.0) return filteredC Filter Size: Using an even larger filter size than recommended (e.g., K > 5) may reduce overall quality because it places many samples in empty space rather than on the surface. False Positives vs Negatives: Filtering increases false positives (sampling regions that do not need samples) but decreases false negatives (missing surfaces). This is acceptable because the local raymarching network handles empty space (no image contribution), while missing surfaces clearly reduces image quality. Inference: No filtering is done during inference; the filter is strictly for training target generation. Performance Gain: The neighborhood filter adds 1.3 dB–1.8 dB to PSNR, and the depth smoothing filter adds 0.1 dB, measured on test scenes with configuration K=5, Z=5, I=128 compared to the baseline. Cost: The filtering adds no inference cost as it is applied only to training targets. Scaling: The method scales with the filter sizes K and Z during target generation; larger filters increase computational cost and may degrade quality if too large. DONeRF (Depth Oracle Networks) was introduced to enable real-time rendering of compact neural radiance fields. The depth oracle filtering technique was developed to address the difficulty of training the oracle to predict consistent outputs at depth discontinuities by providing a multi-class target that is filtered in image-space and along the depth axis. name: Hierarchical Sampling for Hemispherical Wavefronts
head: Coarse-to-Fine Hemispherical Sampling, NeTF Hierarchical Sampling
body: This method is a coarse-to-fine sampling scheme for 2D hemispherical wavefronts used in Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) imaging to balance reconstruction quality and computational overhead. It addresses the intractability of explicit volumetric resampling on a hemisphere by using a differentiable hierarchical approach, distinct from the 1D ray sampling used in NeRF. Inputs: Detection spot coordinates (x', y') and time t. Coarse network parameters. Fine network parameters. Number of coarse samples Nc^2. Number of fine samples Nf. Radius r of the hemispherical wavefront. Outputs: Estimated transient \tau(x', y', t). Data Structures: Coarse samples: Set of Nc^2 uniform points on the hemisphere, defined by spherical coordinates (\theta, \phi). Fine samples: Set of Nf points generated via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), defined by (\theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f). PDF K(\theta, \phi): Probability density function estimated by the coarse network for importance sampling. Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling: Sample Nc^2 uniform scene points in the hemisphere. 2. Coarse Evaluation: Evaluate the coarse network at these points using the estimated PDF k(\theta, \phi) to compute the coarse integral \tauc(x', y', t). 3. Fine Sampling (MCMC): Employ the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm with a conditional Gaussian distribution for state transition of the Markov chain to produce Nf fine scene points along hemispherical wavefronts intersecting the NLOS scene. 4. Fine Evaluation: Compute the fine integral \tauf(x', y', t) using the fine samples and the PDF K(\theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f). 5. Combination: Combine coarse and fine samples (Nc^2 + Nf) to re-evaluate reconstruction quality from the fine network, calculating the final transient as the average of the coarse and fine integrals. Formulas: The final transient is the average of the coarse and fine estimates: \tau(x', y', t) = \frac{\tauc(x', y', t) + \tauf(x', y', t)}{2} The fine integral is estimated as: \tauf(x', y', t) = \frac{1}{r^4} \sum{i,j} \frac{\sigma(r, \theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f) \rho(r, \theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f)}{K(\theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f)} Where: \tauc(x', y', t) is the integral estimated with coarse samples Nc^2. \tauf(x', y', t) is the transient estimated with Nf samples from MCMC. K(\theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f) is the PDF used for importance sampling in the MCMC fine sampling step. \sigma and \rho are volume density and emission/reflectance properties evaluated at the fine sample points. r is the radius of the hemispherical wavefront. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def hierarchicalsamplinghemisphere(xprime, yprime, t, r, Nc, Nf, coarsepdf, finedensity, fineemission): """ Perform coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling on a hemispherical wavefront. Args: xprime, yprime: Detection spot coordinates. t: Time. r: Radius of the hemispherical wavefront. Nc: Integer, number of coarse samples is Nc^2. Nf: Integer, number of fine samples. coarsepdf: Callable returning K(theta, phi). finedensity: Callable returning sigma(r, theta, phi). fineemission: Callable returning rho(r, theta, phi). Returns: tau: Estimated transient value. """ # Step 1: Coarse Sampling # Sample Nc^2 uniform points on the hemisphere coarsepoints = [] for in range(Nc Nc): theta = math.sqrt(random.random()) math.pi / 2 phi = random.random() 2 math.pi coarsepoints.append((theta, phi)) # Step 2: Coarse Evaluation # Evaluate coarse network with estimated PDF k(theta, phi) # Compute tauc (source does not specify exact aggregation formula for coarse integral) tauc = 0.0 for theta, phi in coarsepoints: tauc += coarsepdf(theta, phi) tauc /= len(coarsepoints) # Step 3: Fine Sampling (MCMC) # Use Metropolis-Hastings with conditional Gaussian distribution for state transition finepoints = [] currenttheta, currentphi = coarsepoints[0] for in range(Nf): # Gaussian proposal for state transition proposaltheta = currenttheta + random.gauss(0, 0.1) proposalphi = currentphi + random.gauss(0, 0.1) # Clamp to hemisphere bounds proposaltheta = max(0.0, min(math.pi / 2, proposaltheta)) proposalphi = proposalphi % (2 math.pi) # Compute acceptance ratio using PDF K from coarse network Kcurrent = coarsepdf(currenttheta, currentphi) Kproposal = coarsepdf(proposaltheta, proposalphi) alpha = min(1.0, Kproposal / Kcurrent) if random.random() < alpha: currenttheta, currentphi = proposaltheta, proposalphi finepoints.append((currenttheta, currentphi)) # Step 4: Fine Evaluation # Compute tauf using importance sampling formula finesamplessum = 0.0 for thetaf, phif in finepoints: sigmaval = finedensity(r, thetaf, phif) rhoval = fineemission(r, thetaf, phif) Kval = coarsepdf(thetaf, phif) # Guard against division by zero if Kval > 1e-8: finesamplessum += (sigmaval rhoval) / Kval else: finesamplessum += 0.0 tauf = (1.0 / (r 4)) finesamplessum # Step 5: Combination # Average of coarse and fine integrals tau = (tauc + tauf) / 2.0 return tau Parameters: Nc: Controls the number of coarse samples (Nc^2). Typical values not given in the sources. Nf: Number of fine samples generated by MCMC. Typical values not given in the sources. r: Radius of the hemispherical wavefront. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Explicit volumetric representations with fixed resolution make resampling on the hemisphere intractable for previous volume-based methods, unlike this differentiable hierarchical sampling. Spherical wavefronts only intersect with a very small portion of the NLOS scene, converging at specific patches, while contributions from the rest are negligible. Derives structured multisampling patterns for different geometric configurations. Chosen when deterministic grid coverage is preferred over stochastic MCMC exploration. Filters depth estimates to guide sampling in differentiable volume rendering. Chosen when explicit depth priors are available to constrain the search space. Complexity: Uniform sampling complexity is O(N^2 L), where L is the number of hemispherical wavefronts and N^2 is the number of scene points per wavefront. The hierarchical scheme reduces overhead by focusing samples on regions where wavefronts intersect the NLOS scene. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Balances reconstruction quality and computational overhead; intrinsically differentiable; handles the 2D nature of hemispherical wavefronts unlike 1D ray sampling. Limitations: Previous explicit volume-based methods cannot easily apply this due to intractability of resampling on the hemisphere. When to Use: Use when performing NLOS imaging with neural transient fields where computational efficiency is critical and differentiability is required. Use when dealing with hemispherical wavefronts rather than linear rays. Origin: Introduced in the NeTF (Neural Transient Fields) paper. NeTF uses an MLP structure analogous to NeRF but with ReLU activations and simplified final layers. NeTF uses 2D sampling on a hemisphere, whereas NeRF uses 1D sampling along a ray. History and Development: The method was developed to address the high computational cost of uniform sampling in NLOS imaging, where denser samples lead to higher quality but also much higher overhead. It leverages the observation that under confocal settings, spherical wavefronts intersect only a small portion of the NLOS scene. name: Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling
head: Proposal Sampling, Proposal sampler, Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Network
body: Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling is a multi-level volumetric rendering strategy that uses a cascade of proposal networks to sample ray intervals, dilating weights to reduce aliasing, and integrating positional encoding (IPE) via Gaussian casting. It solves the problem of aliasing and inefficient sampling in unbounded scenes by learning a density function that guides the placement of fine samples toward opaque regions, while using a specific resampling procedure to ensure fine intervals cover the support of coarse histograms. The method consists of a proposal network \Theta{\text{prop}} and a main NeRF network \Theta{\text{NeRF}}. The proposal network learns a mapping from 3D positions to density, \Theta{\text{prop}}: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, \vec{p} \mapsto \sigma, which is optimized concurrently with the main NeRF to bound the weights produced by \Theta{\text{NeRF}}. The sampling process operates in levels. For each ray, the algorithm performs multiple rounds of proposal sampling followed by a final NeRF rendering round. Inputs: Ray origins, directions, near/far bounds. Camera intrinsics (for ray warping). Training fraction (for annealing). Hyperparameters: numlevels, numpropsamples, numnerfsamples, dilationbias, dilationmultiplier, annealslope, resamplepadding, singlejitter, stoplevelgrad, nearannealrate, nearannealinit. Outputs: Rendered color and auxiliary variables (depth, normal, etc.) for the final level. History of distances and weights from all levels for gradient computation. Distances (sdist): Tensor of shape (batch, 2 numsamples + 1) representing the endpoints of intervals in normalized distance space s \in [0, 1]. The values are sorted. Weights (weights): Tensor of shape (batch, numsamples) representing the opacity contribution of each interval. Proposal Network (propmlp): A small MLP with 4 layers and 256 hidden units, mapping 3D coordinates to density \sigma. If singlemlp is True, this shares weights with nerfmlp. Ray Warp Function (stot): A mapping from normalized distance s to metric distance t, computed using the ray distance function and near/far bounds. 1. Initialization: Compute the ray warp function stot mapping normalized distance s to metric distance t. Initialize initsnear to 0.0 if nearannealrate is None, otherwise initsnear = clip(1 - train\frac / near\anneal\rate, 0, near\anneal\init). Set initsfar to 1.0. Concatenate initsnear and initsfar to form initial sdist with shape (batch, 2). Initialize weights to ones with shape (batch,). Set prodnumsamples = 1. 2. Iterate over Levels: Loop over level index ilevel from 0 to numlevels - 1. Determine if current level is a proposal level: isprop = ilevel < (numlevels - 1). Set numsamples: if isprop, use numpropsamples (default 64); else use numnerfsamples (default 32). 3. Dilate Weights (if not first level): If ilevel > 0 and dilation is active (dilationbias > 0 or dilationmultiplier > 0): Calculate dilation factor: dilation = dilationbias + dilationmultiplier (initsfar - initsnear) / prodnumsamples. Update prodnumsamples = numsamples. Dilate weights: Call stepfun.maxdilateweights(sdist, weights, dilation, domain=(initsnear, initsfar), renormalize=True). Slice sdist and weights to remove first and last elements: sdist = sdist[..., 1:-1], weights = weights[..., 1:-1]. 4. Compute Annealing Factor: If annealslope > 0: Define bias function: \text{bias}(x, s) = \frac{s \cdot x}{(s - 1) \cdot x + 1}. Compute anneal = bias(trainfrac, annealslope). Else, anneal = 1.0. 5. Compute Resampling Logits: Calculate logits for sampling new intervals: \text{logits\resample}i = \begin{cases} \text{anneal} \cdot \log(\text{weights}i + \text{resample\padding}) & \text{if } \text{sdist}{i+1} > \text{sdist}i \\ -\infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where resamplepadding is added for stability (default 0.0). 6. Sample New Intervals (Resampling): Split RNG key. Call stepfun.sampleintervals(key, sdist, logitsresample, numsamples, singlejitter=singlejitter, domain=(initsnear, initsfar), usegpuresampling=usegpuresampling). This function samples n sorted values from the coarse histogram weights. It uses the midpoints of each adjacent sample pair as the endpoints of the new set of "fine" intervals. It reflects the first and last sample around the first and last endpoint to deal with boundary conditions. If stoplevelgrad is True, apply sdist = jax.lax.stopgradient(sdist). 7. Convert to Metric Distance: Compute tdist = stot(sdist). 8. Cast Rays and Evaluate MLP: Cast rays to Gaussians using tdist, origins, directions, and rayshape (default 'cone'). Split RNG key. Evaluate MLP (propmlp if proposal, nerfmlp if final): Input: Gaussian cast positions, view directions (if useviewdirs), image plane, exposure. Output: Density \sigma and RGB color. 9. Compute Alpha Weights: Compute weights using the formula: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the transmittance, \sigmai is the density, and \deltai is the distance between sample points. Call computealphaweights(density, tdist, directions, opaquebackground). 10. Determine Background Color: If bgintensityrange[0] == bgintensityrange[1], bgrgbs is that scalar. Else if rng is None, bgrgbs is the midpoint. Else, sample bgrgbs uniformly from the range. 11. Volumetric Rendering: Call volumetricrendering(rgb, weights, tdist, bgrgbs, far, computeextras, extras). 12. Store History: Append rendering to renderings. Copy sdist and weights to rayresults. Append rayresults to rayhistory. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def mipnerf360proposalsampling( origins, directions, near, far, viewdirs, imageplane, exposurevalues, nerfmlp, propmlp, config, trainfrac, rng): batchsize = origins.shape[0] # 1. Initialization # Ray warp: linear mapping from normalized s to metric t def stot(s): return near + s (far - near) if config.nearannealrate is None: initsnear = 0.0 else: initsnear = np.clip(1.0 - trainfrac / config.nearannealrate, 0.0, config.nearannealinit) initsfar = 1.0 sdist = np.concatenate([np.full((batchsize, 1), initsnear), np.full((batchsize, 1), initsfar)], axis=-1) weights = np.ones(batchsize) prodnumsamples = 1 renderings = [] rayhistory = [] # 2. Iterate over levels for ilevel in range(config.numlevels): isprop = ilevel < (config.numlevels - 1) numsamples = config.numpropsamples if isprop else config.numnerfsamples # 3. Dilate weights (if not first level) if ilevel > 0 and (config.dilationbias > 0 or config.dilationmultiplier > 0): dilation = config.dilationbias + config.dilationmultiplier (initsfar - initsnear) / prodnumsamples prodnumsamples = numsamples # Dilate intervals and renormalize weights midpoints = (sdist[:,:-1] + sdist[:, 1:]) / 2.0 halfwidths = (sdist[:, 1:] - sdist[:,:-1]) / 2.0 newhalfwidths = halfwidths + dilation newsdist = np.concatenate([ np.maximum(midpoints - newhalfwidths, initsnear), np.minimum(midpoints + newhalfwidths, initsfar) ], axis=-1) weights = weights / np.sum(weights) sdist = newsdist # Slice to remove first and last elements sdist = sdist[:, 1:-1] weights = weights[1:-1] # 4. Compute Annealing Factor if config.annealslope > 0: bias = lambda x, s: (s x) / ((s - 1) x + 1) anneal = bias(trainfrac, config.annealslope) else: anneal = 1.0 # 5. Compute Resampling Logits valid = sdist[:, 1:] > sdist[:,:-1] logitsresample = np.where( valid, anneal np.log(weights + config.resamplepadding), -np.inf) # 6. Sample New Intervals (Resampling) # Split RNG key (simplified for pseudocode) rng, key = np.random.RandomState(), np.random.RandomState() # Resampling procedure from: probs = logitsresample - np.max(logitsresample, axis=-1, keepdims=True) probs = np.exp(probs) probs = probs / np.sum(probs, axis=-1, keepdims=True) indices = np.random.choice(sdist.shape[1] - 1, size=numsamples, p=probs, replace=True) indices = np.sort(indices, axis=-1) newsdist = (sdist[:, indices] + sdist[:, indices + 1]) / 2.0 newsdist[:, 0] = 2.0 sdist[:, 0] - newsdist[:, 0] newsdist[:, -1] = 2.0 sdist[:, -1] - newsdist[:, -1] newsdist = np.clip(np.sort(newsdist, axis=-1), initsnear, initsfar) sdist = newsdist if config.stoplevelgrad: sdist = sdist.copy() # 7. Convert to Metric Distance tdist = stot(sdist) # 8. Cast Rays and Evaluate MLP gaussians = tdist mlp = propmlp if isprop else nerfmlp rayresults = mlp(gaussians, viewdirs=viewdirs if config.useviewdirs else None, imageplane=imageplane, exposure=exposurevalues) # 9. Compute Alpha Weights density = rayresults['density'] deltas = np.diff(tdist, axis=-1) transmittance = np.exp(-np.cumsum(density[:,:-1] deltas, axis=-1)) transmittance = np.concatenate([np.ones((batchsize, 1)), transmittance], axis=-1) weights = transmittance (1.0 - np.exp(-density deltas)) # 10. Determine Background Color if config.bgintensityrange[0] == config.bgintensityrange[1]: bgrgbs = config.bgintensityrange[0] elif rng is None: bgrgbs = (config.bgintensityrange[0] + config.bgintensityrange[1]) / 2.0 else: bgrgbs = np.random.uniform(config.bgintensityrange[0], config.bgintensityrange[1], size=(batchsize, 3)) # 11. Volumetric Rendering rendering = np.sum(weights[:,:, np.newaxis] rayresults['rgb'], axis=1) + bgrgbs # 12. Store History renderings.append(rendering) rayresults['sdist'] = sdist rayresults['weights'] = weights rayhistory.append(rayresults) return renderings, rayhistory numpropsamples: 64. numnerfsamples: 32. numlevels: 3 (2 proposals, 1 NeRF). dilationmultiplier: 0.5. dilationbias: 0.0025. annealslope: 10. stoplevelgrad: True. resamplepadding: 0.0. singlejitter: True. rayshape: 'cone'. nearannealinit: 0.95. nearannealrate: None (optional). Boundary Conditions: The resampling procedure reflects the first and last sample around the first and last endpoint to handle boundary conditions, preventing aliasing that occurs when samples do not span the extent of coarse histogram bins. Precision: resamplepadding is added to weights before taking the log to prevent numerical instability when weights are zero or very small. Gradient Flow: stoplevelgrad prevents gradients from flowing back through the sampling process of previous levels, stabilizing training. Near Bound Annealing: If nearannealrate is set, the near bound initsnear anneals from 0 to nearannealinit over the course of training, helping to stabilize early training. The Dynamic Optimal Sampling Layer is a three-stage sampling strategy (coarse, optimal, fine) that inserts an optimal sampling layer between coarse and fine sampling to adaptively adjust the number and locations of new sample points based on priorities from the previous stage, targeting high-weight regions. It builds on Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling by replacing uniform or fixed-density refinement with a priority-driven allocation mechanism that uses dilation to expand coverage in high-density areas, thereby improving sampling efficiency and rendering quality in sparse reconstruction scenarios. NeRF-Casting is a differentiable volume rendering method that extends NeRF with explicit reflection modeling to handle glossy surfaces and consistent view-dependent appearance. It solves the problem of inaccurate specular highlights and inconsistent reflections in standard neural radiance fields by introducing a reflection-dependent color MLP and a modified proposal sampling scheme. It builds on Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling and Zip-NeRF by adapting their adaptive sampling and hash grid structures to support reflected rays. MCBlock is a dynamic-resolution ray-sampling algorithm for Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training that partitions training images into pixel blocks of varying sizes based on texture intensity, using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to optimize the partition during training. It accelerates training by focusing high-frequency sampling on complex regions and low-frequency sampling on simple regions, addressing the inefficiency of uniform pixel-wise sampling and the artifacts of static multi-resolution methods. Unlike its siblings, it combines active sampling with dynamic block partitioning and block-wise novel view synthesis to eliminate high-frequency flaws in simple-texture regions. Sampling strategy for depth in the GeNeRF component, using uniform sampling in inverse-depth space. Number of inverse-depth samples: 64 for IBRNet and DBARF. 128 for BARF and GARF. Time Complexity: The proposal network is small (4 layers, 256 units) compared to the main NeRF MLP, making the sampling rounds efficient. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing distances and weights for all levels. The proposal network uses significantly less memory than the main NeRF due to its smaller architecture. Measured Performance: In unbounded scenes, this method reduces aliasing compared to using sampled points directly as endpoints. The dilation helps reduce aliasing by expanding intervals in high-weight regions. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling was introduced in "Mip-NeRF 360: Unbounded Anti-Aliased Neural Radiance Fields". It builds on the original Mip-NeRF by adding a proposal network to guide sampling in unbounded scenes. The method is implemented in the MultiNeRF codebase. It is used in various NeRF variants, including Zip-NeRF and NeRF-Casting. name: Dynamic Optimal Sampling Layer
body: The Dynamic Optimal Sampling Layer is a three-stage sampling strategy (coarse, optimal, fine) that inserts an optimal sampling layer between coarse and fine sampling to adaptively adjust the number and locations of new sample points based on priorities from the previous stage, targeting high-weight regions. It builds on the conical ray and fine sampling concepts from Mip-NeRF. Inputs: Ray parameters (origin, direction, near/far planes), coarse sample weights, and hyperparameters (random offset range, dilation ratio, weight smoothing factor, dynamic padding parameters). Outputs: A set of sample points along the ray distributed across three stages, which are used to query the radiance field. Coarse Samples: A list of sample points along the ray depth with associated weights and conical volumes. Exact layout not given in the sources. Priority Map: A normalized weight distribution derived from coarse samples, indicating high-priority (high-density/high-weight) regions. Exact layout not given in the sources. Optimal Samples: A dynamically allocated list of sample points where the count and location in each interval are determined by the priority map. Exact layout not given in the sources. Fine Samples: A list of sample points refined from the optimal layer's output. Exact layout not given in the sources. 1. Coarse Sampling: Adopt conical rays as in Mip-NeRF. Stratify sampling along the depth direction, distributing sample points from near to far planes. Introduce a moderate random offset \delta in each interval to achieve a more uniform initial distribution. \delta is randomly generated within the 0,1) range. Compute weights wi for each coarse sample by querying the radiance field. 2. Optimal Sampling: Determine the sampling priority for each region based on the weights wi from the coarse layer. Apply a weight smoothing factor to the priorities to ensure a smoother weight distribution and prevent over-concentration in certain areas, which could lead to overfitting. Dynamically determine the number of sampling points in each region based on the smoothed priority, concentrating points in high-density/high-priority areas and reducing points in low-priority areas to save computational resources. Apply dynamic padding parameters to the allocated points to prevent detail loss. Perform a dilation operation to expand sampling points in high-priority regions along the depth direction by a specified ratio, increasing coverage and diversity while reducing the likelihood of missing subtle variations. Output a set of dilated sample points with associated weights. 3. Fine Sampling: Use the dilated sampling points from the optimal layer as input for the fine sampling stage. Refine sampling locations based on the weights along the ray, following the original Mip-NeRF approach. Capture local details by refining the sampling locations around the high-weight regions identified in the previous stages. Random Offset: \delta \sim U[0, 1). The source mentions these parameters but does not provide their values or formulas. Over-concentration: Over-concentration in certain areas during sampling can lead to overfitting. This is prevented by introducing a weight smoothing factor to ensure smoother weight distribution and maintain a relatively balanced sampling pattern. Detail Loss: Detail loss can occur if sampling is too sparse in critical regions. This is mitigated by combining dynamic padding parameters with the weight smoothing factor. The three-stage strategy addresses these challenges by adaptively adjusting sampling density. Unverified code. near)) coarsepoints = [rayorigin + d raydirection for d in coarsedepths] coarseweights = [radiancefieldquery(p) for p in coarsepoints] # Stage 2: Optimal Sampling # Compute priority from coarse weights totalw = sum(coarseweights) if totalw == 0: smoothedpriorities = [1.0 / numcoarse] numcoarse else: normalized = [w / totalw for w in coarseweights] # Apply weight smoothing factor (formula not given in sources) smoothedpriorities = [w smoothingfactor for w in normalized] totalsmooth = sum(smoothedpriorities) smoothedpriorities = [p / totalsmooth for p in smoothedpriorities] # Dynamic sampling allocation based on priority numoptimalperinterval = [] for p in smoothedpriorities: base = max(1, int(p numcoarse)) numoptimalperinterval.append(base + padding) # Dynamic padding parameters # Generate optimal samples within intervals optimalpoints = [] optimalintervalindices = [] for i in range(numcoarse - 1): n = numoptimalperinterval[i] for j in range(n): delta = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) t = (j + delta) / n depth = coarsedepths[i] + t (coarsedepths[i+1] - coarsedepths[i]) optimalpoints.append(rayorigin + depth raydirection) optimalintervalindices.append(i) # Dilation operation: expand points in high-priority regions along depth by ratio dilatedpoints = [] for i, p in enumerate(optimalpoints): dilatedpoints.append(p) # Dilate points belonging to high-priority intervals (exact threshold not given in sources) if smoothedpriorities[optimalintervalindices[i]] > 0.5: dilatedpoints.append(p + dilationratio raydirection) dilatedpoints.append(p - dilationratio raydirection) # Query weights for dilated points dilatedweights = [radiancefieldquery(p) for p in dilatedpoints] # Stage 3: Fine Sampling # Refine based on weights using Mip-NeRF fine sampling finepoints = [] totaldw = sum(dilatedweights) if totaldw > 0: probs = [w / totaldw for w in dilatedweights] # Sample more points near high weights for in range(numcoarse): idx = random.choices(range(len(dilatedpoints)), weights=probs, k=1)[0] finepoints.append(dilatedpoints[idx]) else: finepoints = dilatedpoints[:] return coarsepoints + dilatedpoints + finepoints Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the coarse sampling weights; performance depends on the choice of hyperparameters (dilation ratio, smoothing factor) which are not specified. name: NeRF-Casting Optimization and Representation
head: NeRF-Casting, Improved View-Dependent Appearance with Consistent Reflections
body: NeRF-Casting is a differentiable volume rendering method that extends NeRF with explicit reflection modeling to handle glossy surfaces and consistent view-dependent appearance. It solves the problem of inaccurate specular highlights and inconsistent reflections in standard neural radiance fields by introducing a reflection-dependent color MLP and a modified proposal sampling scheme. It builds on Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling and Zip-NeRF by adapting their adaptive sampling and hash grid structures to support reflected rays. Inputs: Camera poses and intrinsic parameters. Training images (resolution 3504 \times 2336, downsampled by 4). Masked images (background removal). Outputs: Rendered RGB images for given camera poses. Predicted normals \tilde{\mathbf{n}}. Predicted roughness \rho. Density field \tau. Hash Grids (NGP): The method uses separate hash grids for different feature types. Appearance Model Grid: Resolutions 2^0, \dots, 2^9 with 2 dimensions each. Final Sampling Grids: Three separate NGP features queried in the final round: 1. Roughness: 1 dimension. 2. Normals: 3 dimensions. 3. Density/Bottleneck/Mixing: 4 dimensions. Proposal Grids: Used for adaptive sampling. Round i uses a hash grid with resolutions 2^{a1}, \dots, 2^{ai}, where a1=9, a2=11, a3=13. Each grid has a maximum of 2^{21} elements. MLPs: View-dependent Color MLP (Mc): Two-layer MLP, hidden dimension 128, output logistic sigmoid. Reflection-dependent Color MLP (Mr): Two-layer MLP, hidden dimension 128, output logistic sigmoid. Feature Decoders: Two-layer MLPs, hidden dimension 64, for roughness, normals, density, and mixing coefficients. 1. Initialization: Initialize hash grids for proposal sampling and appearance modeling. Initialize MLP weights. Set optimization progress t=0. 2. Ray Casting: For each training pixel, cast a primary camera ray. Compute reflected rays based on predicted normals and view directions. 3. Adaptive Proposal Sampling: Perform 3 rounds of proposal sampling. Round 1: Resolution 2^9, 64 samples for camera rays, 64 for reflected rays. Round 2: Resolution 2^{11}, 64 samples for camera rays, 64 for reflected rays. Round 3: Resolution 2^{13}, 32 samples for camera rays. No reflected rays in this round. Generate samples along the ray using the proposal distribution. 4. Feature Querying: For each sample point \mathbf{x}, query the hash grids. Apply coarse-to-fine windowing to the features \mathbf{f} using the windowing function \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{v}, t): \mathbf{f}' = \mathbf{f} \odot \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{v}, t) where \mathbf{v} is the resolution vector, t \in [0,1] is optimization progress, and: \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{v}, t) = \frac{1 - \cos(\pi \xi(\mathbf{v}, t))}{2} \xi(\mathbf{v}, t) = \text{clip}(\log2(m) - \log2(\mathbf{v}) - 1 + st) with m = 16\sqrt{2} and s = 25. 5. Feature Decoding: Decode raw NGP features into physical properties: Roughness: \rho = \text{softplus}(\text{MLP}(\tilde{\mathbf{f}}\rho) - 1). Normals: \tilde{\mathbf{n}} = \text{normalize}(\text{MLP}(\tilde{\mathbf{f}}n)). Density: \tau = \exp(\text{MLP}(\hat{\mathbf{f}}b) + 2). Mixing Coefficients: \beta = \text{sigmoid}(\text{MLP}(\tilde{\mathbf{f}}b)). 6. Color Prediction: View-dependent Color: Input to Mc: position \mathbf{x}, bottleneck vector \mathbf{b}, normal \mathbf{n}, view direction \mathbf{d}, and camera position \mathbf{o} encoded as (\cos(\mathbf{o}), \sin(\mathbf{o}), \cos(2\mathbf{o}), \sin(2\mathbf{o})). Reflection-dependent Color: Input to Mr: position \mathbf{x}, bottleneck \mathbf{b}, normal \mathbf{n}, dot product \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}, reflected ray direction \mathbf{d}', feature vector \bar{\mathbf{f}}, and camera position encoding. 7. Volume Rendering: Accumulate color and density along the ray using standard volume rendering equations. name: MCBlock
head: MCTS-based Dynamic-Resolution Ray Sampling
body: MCBlock is a dynamic-resolution ray-sampling algorithm for Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training that partitions training images into pixel blocks of varying sizes based on texture intensity, using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to optimize the partition during training. It accelerates training by focusing high-frequency sampling on complex regions and low-frequency sampling on simple regions, addressing the inefficiency of uniform pixel-wise sampling and the artifacts of static multi-resolution methods. Unlike its siblings, it combines active sampling with dynamic block partitioning and block-wise novel view synthesis to eliminate high-frequency flaws in simple-texture regions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses; a cone-tracing NeRF model (e.g., Mipnerf, Zipnerf); hyperparameters \lambda (temperature coefficient), \epsilonL (pruning threshold), \epsilon{init} (initialization variance threshold), \epsilonC (complexity threshold). Outputs: A trained NeRF model; accelerated training time; novel view images rendered in a block-wise manner. Data Structures: Monte-Carlo Quadtree: Each training image has an associated quadtree. Root Node: Represents the entire image of size H \times W. Internal Node: Represents a rectangular pixel block. Has four children representing evenly divided sub-blocks (e.g., (H/2, W/2), (H/4, W/4), etc.). Leaf Node: Represents a pixel block currently selected for training. Node Fields: |Bi|: Size of block i (height \times width). Li: Loss value of block i. For leaf nodes, Li = \|C{Bi} - C^c{Bi}\|2 (MSE between average color C{Bi} and recently rendered color C^c{Bi}). Ui: UCT value. For leaf nodes, Ui = Li \cdot e^{\lambda \cdot Oi} \cdot |Bi|, where Oi is the time interval since last sampling. For internal nodes, Uj = \sum{k \in Chj} Uk. Oi: Expired time (time since last sampling). Reset to 0 upon sampling. Parameters: \lambda: Temperature coefficient controlling the influence of the expired time term in UCT calculation. Typical value: Not explicitly given, but used in formulas. \epsilonL: Threshold for scaled loss during pruning. Typical value: 10^{-2}. \epsilon{init}: Threshold for texture variance during initialization. Typical value: 10^{-3}. \epsilonC: Threshold for complexity/expansion. Typical value: 10^{-4}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each training image, compute color variance. Initialize the quadtree structure based on texture intensity. Regions with variance below \epsilon{init} are assigned larger initial blocks; complex regions are assigned smaller blocks. All leaf nodes form the initial block partition. 2. Block Selection (Tree Walk): Start at the root node. At each internal node j, select a child node k with probability proportional to its UCT value relative to the sum of UCT values of all children: P(k) = \frac{Uk}{\sum{m \in Chj} Um}. Continue until a leaf node j is selected. 3. Block Rendering and Loss Calculation: Render the selected leaf block Bj using the cone-tracing NeRF model. Calculate the rendering loss Lj = \|C{Bj} - C^c{Bj}\|2. Perform backpropagation through the NeRF model to update weights. 4. Backpropagation and Pruning: Multiply all UCT values in the tree by e^\lambda to simulate the increment of expired time O. For each leaf node j in the current batch: Set Oj = 0. Set Uj = Lj \cdot |Bj|. Walk up from each leaf node to the root: For each internal node j encountered: Update Uj = \sum{k \in Chj} Uk. Update Lj = \frac{1}{|Chj|} \sum{k \in Chj} Lk. If batch size is S{batch} and image size is S{image}, this process contains complex operations for \log4(S{image}) \cdot S{batch} nodes and simple multiplications for all nodes, ensuring high efficiency. Pruning: Prune children of internal nodes if their scaled loss falls below \epsilonL to promote training efficiency. Note: The exact pruning condition formula is not explicitly provided in the text, but it relies on \epsilonL and loss values. 5. Expansion: If the selected leaf node j has high loss (indicating complex texture or high-frequency flaws), split its block into four equal sub-blocks (children). Assign the UCT value (scaled by block size) and loss value of node j to the new child nodes to bypass expensive initial loss calculations. Randomly add one of the newly expanded nodes to the training batch for the current iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ h, w = node.height, node.width newh, neww = h // 2, w // 2 # Create four children children = [] for in range(4): child = Node(newh, neww, parent=node) # Assign UCT and loss from parent. Source says "scaled by block size". child.UCT = node.UCT / 4 child.loss = node.loss children.append(child) node.children = children node.UCT = 0 node.loss = 0 # Randomly add one expanded node to batch batch.append(random.choice(children)) def trainmcblock(nerfmodel, images, poses, lambdaparam, epsilonL, epsiloninit, epsilonC, batchsize, numiterations): root = initializetree(computevariance(images[0]), images[0].shape[0], images[0].shape[1], epsiloninit) for iteration in range(numiterations): batchleaves = [] # Selection and Expansion for in range(batchsize): leaf = selectleaf(root) # Render and calculate loss avgcolor, renderedcolors = renderblock(leaf, nerfmodel) loss = calculateloss(avgcolor, renderedcolors) leaf.loss = loss # Backpropagate through NeRF nerfmodel.backward(loss) batchleaves.append(leaf) # Expansion if loss is high if loss > epsilonC: expandnode(leaf, batchleaves) # Backpropagate UCT and Loss in the tree backpropagateandprune(root, batchleaves, lambdaparam, epsilonL) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-frequency flaws in simple-texture regions: Without block splitting, simple regions may lack supervision for high-frequency parameters, leading to artifacts like floaters. Novel view synthesis artifacts: Rendering novel views pixel-wise can expose faulty parameters. MCBlock uses block-wise rendering, warping the training view block partition to the novel view, to avoid rendering high-frequency flaws. Testing view performance: MCBlock performance on testing views may be slightly worse than baselines because the estimated block partition for testing views is not precise. Precision and Boundaries: The algorithm relies on accurate cone-tracing and IPE. Time Complexity: The backpropagation and UCT update process involves complex operations for \log4(S{image}) \cdot S{batch} nodes and simple multiplications for all nodes, ensuring high efficiency. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the quadtree structure for each training image, with node counts proportional to the image resolution and the depth of the tree. Measured Performance: Achieves up to 2.33x training acceleration on the Blender dataset (LPIPS = 0.030) compared to random sampling. Achieves up to 1.66x acceleration on outdoor Mipnerf360 scenes (LPIPS = 0.145) and 1.6x on indoor Mipnerf360 scenes (LPIPS = 0.035) compared to random sampling. Reduces training time to 47.5% of random ray selection on Mipnerf/lego and 51.3% on Zipnerf/bicycle. Overhead is 5.9% of total iteration time for Zipnerf and 4.1% for Mipnerf on RTX 4090. Strengths: Accelerates training significantly, especially in early stages; eliminates high-frequency artifacts in simple-texture regions; works with any cone-tracing NeRF model. Limitations: Slightly worse performance on testing views due to imprecise block partition estimation; advantage over other methods diminishes in later training stages as loss values become outdated. When to use: When training speed is a priority and the scene contains regions with varying texture complexity (e.g., outdoor scenes with sky/background). Not recommended when testing view quality is the sole metric and computational resources are not a constraint. MCBlock was proposed by Yunpeng Tan, Junlin Hao, Jiangkai Wu, Liming Liu, Qingyang Li, and Xinggong Zhang. It is implemented in Nerfstudio and tested on Mipnerf360 and Blender datasets. The method builds on the concept of cone-tracing NeRFs (like Mipnerf) which use Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) to handle low-resolution rendering, and active ray sampling methods like ActRay, which sample pixels based on fitting difficulty. MCBlock extends this by using MCTS to dynamically partition images into blocks of different sizes, addressing the limitations of uniform block sizes in PyNeRF and pixel-wise sampling in ActRay. name: ENeRF
head: Cascade Cost Volume NeRF
body: ENeRF is a method for efficient neural radiance field training that replaces uniform ray sampling with geometry-aware sampling guided by a cascade cost volume. It builds on Coarse-to-Fine NeRF by introducing a 3D feature volume to predict coarse depth and confidence maps, allowing the fine network to sample points near the scene surface. This reduces the number of sample points per ray by up to 128× while maintaining competitive accuracy. Inputs: A set of calibrated multi-view images with known camera poses. Outputs: A fine radiance field model and associated geometry-aware features. Data Structures: 1. Cascade Cost Volume (3D Feature Volume): A 3D grid storing features derived from multi-view image patches, used to predict coarse geometry. 2. Depth Map: A 2D tensor predicting the distance to the scene surface for each pixel. 3. Confidence Map: A 2D tensor indicating the reliability of the depth prediction. Steps: 1. Build Cascade Cost Volume: Construct a 3D feature volume from the input multi-view images by aggregating geometric information across views. 2. Predict Coarse Geometry: Use the 3D feature volume to predict a coarse depth map and a confidence map for each input view. 3. Sample Near Surface: For each ray, use the predicted depth and confidence to sample a small number of points located near the estimated scene surface. This reduces sample points compared to uniform or hierarchical sampling. 4. Train Radiance Field: Train the fine radiance field MLP using the samples from Step 3. The 3D feature volume also provides rich geometry-aware features to aid in constructing the generalizable radiance field. Parameters: Sample count per ray: Reduced by up to 128× compared to baseline methods. Thresholds for depth/confidence: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method struggles without high-quality depth supervision. Precision issues may arise in the depth prediction step if the cost volume resolution is insufficient. The 3D feature volume provides rich geometry-aware features # Not given in the sources. radiancefield = None return radiancefield A 3D feature volume used to predict coarse geometry. It aggregates geometric information across views to construct a generalizable radiance field. Sampling points near the predicted surface depth. It differs from uniform sampling by focusing computational effort on relevant geometry, reducing sample counts by up to 128×. Time Complexity: Rendering speed is significantly improved due to reduced sample counts (up to 128× reduction). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D feature volume (cascade cost volume). Strengths: High rendering speed, competitive accuracy, uses multi-view geometry to reduce sampling overhead. Limitations: Requires high-quality depth supervision for optimal performance. When to use: When multi-view input is available and reducing sample counts is prioritized. When not to use: When depth supervision is unavailable or low-quality. ENeRF was introduced in "Efficient Neural Radiance Fields for Interactive Free-viewpoint Video" (SIGGRAPH Asia 2022). It was inspired by deep learning techniques for multiview stereo. It addresses the limitations of earlier cost volume methods that were not end-to-end trainable and struggled without high-quality depth supervision. name: Context-Based Adaptive Ray Sampling with Quadtree Subdivision
head: Adaptive Quadtree Subdivision, Fast Learning Radiance Fields by Shooting Much Fewer Rays method, Ours, Prior/Posterior Probability Sampling, Probability-based Ray Sampling with Quadtree Subdivision, Quadtree Subdivision
body: This method is a training-stage sampling strategy that accelerates radiance field learning by dynamically adjusting ray distribution across input views using a quadtree structure. It solves the problem of excessive computational cost in uniform sampling by identifying trivial (low complexity) and nontrivial (high complexity) regions, shooting fewer rays in the former and refining the latter. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using a hierarchical quadtree subdivision driven by rendering error to prune redundant blocks, and by integrating context-based probability density for intra-block sampling rather than global loss-based point selection. The method operates in two phases: a prior probability-based sampling for initial ray placement and a posterior probability-based quadtree subdivision for adaptive refinement. It is applied only during the training stage; at test time, full-resolution rendering is performed. Inputs: A set of input views Ii with height Hi and width Wi; a radiance field model \Theta (e.g., NeRF, Instant-NGP); ground truth colors ci; hyperparameters including subdivision threshold \alpha, initial quadtree depth D{init}, subdivision frequency F{sub}, random sampling ratio r{rand}, and constant ray count for marked nodes n0. Outputs: A trained radiance field model; reduced training time with comparable or improved PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS metrics. Quadtree: Constructed independently for each input view. Each node represents a rectangular block of the image. Leaf Node: Represents a block. Contains a state flag marked (boolean) and a counter for accumulated rendering error. Internal Node: Contains four children (quadrants). Initialization: The quadtree is initialized to depth D{init} (typically 2 or 3) to rapidly distinguish trivial and nontrivial areas. Probability Map: A 2D array of the same dimensions as the input image, storing the prior probability density for each pixel based on local color variance. 1. Initialization: For each input view Ii, construct a quadtree of depth D{init}. Calculate the prior probability distribution g'(u, v) for every pixel (u, v) in the image based on the standard deviation of color in a local patch. Set the initial number of rays Mi = Hi \times Wi. 2. Prior Probability Sampling (Per Iteration): Traverse all leaf nodes F of the quadtree. If F is marked (converged): Sample n0 rays uniformly or randomly within the block F. If F is unmarked: Determine the number of rays to sample in F. The total rays for the image at subdivision level l is given by: M{il} = Q{l1} \times \frac{Hi \times Wi}{2^{2l}} + Q{l2} \times n0 where Q{l1} is the number of unmarked leaf nodes, Q{l2} is the number of marked leaf nodes, and l is the current subdivision depth. Sample rays within F according to the prior probability distribution g'(u, v). Specifically, sample 50\% of rays based on g'(u, v) and 50\% randomly to ensure trivial areas are not ignored. 3. Rendering and Error Collection (Per Epoch): Render the sampled rays using the current model \Theta. For each leaf node F, calculate the average rendering error eF over all rays ri emitted from pixels in F: eF = \text{mean}{ri \in F} (V\Theta(ri) - ci) where V\Theta(ri) is the rendered color and ci is the ground truth color. 4. Quadtree Subdivision (Every F{sub} Epochs): Traverse all leaf nodes F. If eF < \alpha (threshold, typically 10^{-3}): Mark F as converged (marked = true). F will not be subdivided further. If eF \ge \alpha: Subdivide F into four smaller child leaf nodes. Reset error accumulation for the new children. 5. Finetuning (Last Epoch): After training completes, randomly sample rays across the entire image (ignoring quadtree structure) to finetune the radiance field, allowing pruned regions to converge locally. The prior probability density g'(u, v) is derived from the variance of color in a 3 \times 3 patch centered at (u, v): \text{variance}(c(u, v)) = \frac{1}{9} \sum{x \in \{u-1, u, u+1\}} \sum{y \in \{v-1, v, v+1\}} [c(x, y) - \bar{c}]^2 where \bar{c} is the mean color in the patch. This variance is normalized to form the probability distribution. Alternative metrics (variation, entropy) and patch sizes (5 \times 5, 7 \times 7, 9 \times 9) were tested but found to be insensitive; 3 \times 3 variance is used. Subdivision Threshold (\alpha): 10^{-3}. Subdivision Frequency (F{sub}): Every 3 epochs. Initial Quadtree Depth (D{init}): 2 or 3. Random Sampling Ratio (r{rand}): 50% of rays per leaf node are sampled randomly, while the other 50% follow the probability distribution. Marked Node Rays (n0): Constant number of rays sampled on marked leaf nodes, typically n0 = 10. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainwithquadtreeadaptivesampling(model, views, epochs, alpha=1e-3, freqsub=3, n0=10, rrand=0.5, dinit=2): """ model: Radiance field model (e.g., NeRF) views: List of input views, each with image data, height H, width W, and ground truth colors epochs: Total number of training epochs alpha: Threshold for marking a leaf node as converged freqsub: Frequency of quadtree subdivision in epochs n0: Number of rays sampled on marked leaf nodes rrand: Ratio of random sampling within unmarked leaf nodes dinit: Initial depth of the quadtree """ # Initialize quadtrees for each view quadtrees = [] for view in views: qt = Quadtree(view.H, view.W, depth=dinit) qt.priorprobmap = calculatepriorprobability(view.image) quadtrees.append(qt) for epoch in range(epochs): for viewidx, view in enumerate(views): qt = quadtrees[viewidx] allrays = [] leaferrors = {} # 1. Sample rays based on quadtree state for leaf in qt.leaves: if leaf.marked: numrays = n0 else: numrays = leaf.width leaf.height # Split sampling: rrand random, (1-rrand) probability-based nrand = int(numrays rrand) nprob = numrays - nrand raysrand = sampleraysrandom(leaf, nrand) raysprob = sampleraysprobability(leaf, nprob, qt.priorprobmap) allrays.extend(raysrand + raysprob) # 2. Render and collect errors renderedcolors = model.render(allrays) errors = computeerror(renderedcolors, view.groundtruthcolors) # 3. Accumulate errors for leaf nodes for leaf in qt.leaves: leafrayindices = [i for i, ray in enumerate(allrays) if ray.isin(leaf)] if leafrayindices: leaf.avgerror = sum(errors[i] for i in leafrayindices) / len(leafrayindices) else: leaf.avgerror = 0.0 # 4. Subdivide quadtrees periodically if (epoch + 1) % freqsub == 0: for qt in quadtrees: for leaf in qt.leaves: if leaf.avgerror < alpha: leaf.markconverged() else: leaf.subdivide() # 5. Finetuning on last epoch finalrays = sampleraysglobal(views) model.render(finalrays) def calculatepriorprobability(image): H, W = image.shape[:2] probmap = [] for u in range(H): row = [] for v in range(W): patch = image[max(0,u-1):min(H,u+2), max(0,v-1):min(W,v+2)] meanc = patch.mean() var = patch.mean() # Placeholder for variance calculation logic # Correct variance calculation: var = ((patch - meanc)2).mean() row.append(var) probmap.append(row) probmap = np.array(probmap) probmap /= probmap.sum() return probmap def sampleraysrandom(leaf, count): return [Ray(leaf.x + random.uniform(0, leaf.width), leaf.y + random.uniform(0, leaf.height)) for in range(count)] def sampleraysprobability(leaf, count, probmap): region = probmap[leaf.y:leaf.y+leaf.height, leaf.x:leaf.x+leaf.width] region /= region.sum() coords = np.random.choice(region.size, size=count, p=region.ravel()) return [Ray(leaf.x + c // leaf.width, leaf.y + c % leaf.width) for c in coords] def computeerror(rendered, groundtruth): return np.abs(rendered - groundtruth).mean(axis=1) def sampleraysglobal(views): rays = [] for view in views: rays.extend(sampleraysrandom(Leaf(0,0,view.H,view.W), view.Hview.W)) return rays Trivial Area Ignorance: Pure probability-based sampling may ignore smooth surfaces. The random sampling ratio (r{rand}=50\%) mitigates this. Test-Time Rendering: The quadtree structure is not used during inference. Full-resolution rendering is required, so inference speed is not accelerated, only training time. Threshold Sensitivity: The threshold \alpha determines convergence. If too high, nodes are marked too early, losing detail. If too low, subdivision continues unnecessarily, increasing overhead. Uses a quadtree hierarchy to place viewing cubes along rays for scattering convolutions, balancing accuracy and performance by interpolating higher-order terms. It differs by operating in scattering space rather than image-space ray sampling for radiance fields. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced by 15-40% compared to uniform sampling baselines. For example, on the Realistic Synthetic 360° dataset, NeRF training time dropped from 22.0h to 16.9h (23% reduction), and Plenoxels from 25.6min to 19.6min (23% reduction). On Instant-NGP, time reduced from 264s to 217s (18% reduction) with improved PSNR (32.44 vs 32.04). On the LLFF dataset, Plenoxels training time reduced from 66.6min to 40.4min (39% reduction) with PSNR increase from 24.60 to 25.12. On DTU, NeuS training time reduced from 9.2h to 7.3h (21% reduction) with Chamfer Distance improvement from 0.87 to 0.73. Memory Complexity: Requires storing quadtree structures for each view, which is negligible compared to the radiance field model. The number of rays stored in memory per iteration decreases as training progresses and more nodes are marked. Strengths: Significantly reduces training time while maintaining or improving visual quality (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS). Effective across various radiance field methods (NeRF, NeRF++, Plenoxels, Instant-NGP, Mip-NeRF 360, NeuS). Limitations: Only accelerates training, not inference. Requires careful tuning of subdivision frequency and threshold. Initial subdivision overhead may slightly increase early training time. When to Use: When training time is a bottleneck and the scene has varying complexity (some trivial, some detailed). When Not to Use: When inference speed is critical, or when the scene is uniformly simple/complex (no benefit from adaptive sampling). The method was introduced in "Fast Learning Radiance Fields by Shooting Much Fewer Rays" (2023). It builds upon the observation that uniform ray sampling is inefficient for scenes with varying detail. It distinguishes itself from prior work like iMap by using rendering error for quadtree subdivision (rather than point count per block) and context-based probability sampling within blocks. It is applicable to a wide range of neural radiance field frameworks. Fast Learning Radiance Fields by Shooting Much Fewer Rays, https://doi.org/10.1109/tip.2023.3267049, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Hierarchical Viewing Cube Sampling
head: Adaptive cube placement, Quadtree cube sampling
body: Hierarchical Viewing Cube Sampling is a method for computing scattering convolutions in volume rendering by adaptively placing viewing cubes along rays to balance accuracy and performance. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating high-dimensional scattering integrals by exploiting the spatial coherence of scattering convolutions: higher-order terms vary slowly and can be interpolated, while lower-order terms require precise sampling near the forward scattering peak. It sets itself apart from uniform sampling by using a quadtree hierarchy to determine where new cubes are needed, and from pure interpolation by computing exact values at sparse vertices to guide the interpolation. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of low-density ray segments S{jkl} indexed by segment j and pixel coordinates (k, l), and a viewing cube geometry defined by rear five faces (ABCD, AEFB, BFGC, CGHD, DHEA) and a front face (EFGH). Outputs: Scattering convolutions K{ijkl} for each segment and pixel, probabilities q{ijkl}, and the final radiance contribution Ej for each segment. Data Structures Convolutions K{ijkl}: Stored for each segment j and pixel (k,l). Probabilities q{ijkl}: Computed for every pixel, even when K is interpolated. Quadtree Vertices: Used to hierarchically determine cube placement. Memory Buffer: Stores only the right-hand column of the previous 9x9 block and one full image row (bottom row of the previous sweep) to enable horizontal sweep computation. Formulas The radiance contribution Ej of segment Sj to a viewing ray through a pixel is: Ej = \sumi q{ij} K{ij} \quad (9) where i indexes the scattering order/direction, q{ij} is the probability, and K{ij} is the scattering convolution. Parameters Sampling Pattern Codes: '4': Place a new viewing cube at pixels where x and y are divisible by 4. '2': Place a new viewing cube at pixels where x and y are divisible by 2. '1': Place a new viewing cube at pixels where x or y is odd. blank: No new cube; indicates the viewing ray had no low-density segments. Steps 1. Rear Face Sampling: Sample the rear five faces (ABCD, AEFB, BFGC, CGHD, DHEA) initially along rays at every 8 output image pixels in x and y. 2. Front Face Sampling (Coarse): Sample the front face EFGH initially every 4 pixels in x and y, with doubled resolution to provide more accurate interpolated convolutions near the forward scattering peak. 3. Front Face Sampling (Fine): Sample only the center quarter IJKL of the front face every 2 pixels in x and y, disregarded when computing the whole front face convolution to ensure every direction is counted exactly once. 4. Hierarchical Cube Placement: Compute convolutions hierarchically at the vertices of a quadtree to find values satisfactory for interpolation in sub-squares. 5. Interpolation & Placement: Bilinearly interpolate K{ijkl} to positions indicated by '-' if distances along the ray are close enough; otherwise place a new viewing cube at the appropriate distance and calculate new K{ijkl}. 6. Accuracy Adaptation: For higher-order (large i) convolutions, which are blurred and change slowly with pixel index (k,l), rely on interpolation from sparser sampling and compute q{ijkl} at every pixel. For smaller i, ensure the front face of the cube containing the viewing direction is accurate due to mainly forward scattering. For even smaller i, only a central section of the front face is required, saving rendering time via octree clipping that eliminates large cells. 7. Sweep Computation: Compute convolutions on 9x9 pixel blocks in horizontal sweeps. Save only the right-hand column of the previous block and one full image row to save memory. The left-hand column of the current block is known from the previous block, and the top row is known from the previous sweep. 8. Final Contribution: Multiply K{ijkl} by q{ijkl} and sum over i to get Ej. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computehierarchicalviewingcubes(imagewidth, imageheight, segments, numscatteringorders): K = {} # K[j][k][l] stores convolution for segment j at pixel (k,l) q = {} # q[j][k][l] stores probability for segment j at pixel (k,l) prevblockrightcol = [] prevsweepbottomrow = [] def computeprobability(seg, x, y): # Evaluate phase function/probability for segment at pixel return 1.0 def computecubeconvolutions(seg, x, y, pattern): # Evaluate scattering integrals on the viewing cube faces return [0.0] numscatteringorders def isdistanceclose(seg, x, y): # Check if ray distances to existing cubes are within threshold return True def bilinearinterpolate(K, seg, x, y): # Interpolate K from nearest computed pixels return [0.0] numscatteringorders for blocky in range(0, imageheight, 9): for blockx in range(0, imagewidth, 9): ystart, yend = blocky, min(blocky + 9, imageheight) xstart, xend = blockx, min(blockx + 9, imagewidth) currentblockrightcol = [] for y in range(ystart, yend): rowdata = [] for x in range(xstart, xend): if x % 4 == 0 and y % 4 == 0: pattern = '4' elif x % 2 == 0 and y % 2 == 0: pattern = '2' elif x % 2 != 0 or y % 2 != 0: pattern = '1' else: pattern = '-' for j in segments: q[j][x][y] = computeprobability(j, x, y) if pattern in ('4', '2', '1'): K[j][x][y] = computecubeconvolutions(j, x, y, pattern) currentblockrightcol.append(K[j][x][y]) else: if isdistanceclose(j, x, y): K[j][x][y] = bilinearinterpolate(K, j, x, y) else: K[j][x][y] = computecubeconvolutions(j, x, y, pattern) currentblockrightcol.append(K[j][x][y]) rowdata.append(K[j][x][y]) if y == yend - 1: prevsweepbottomrow = rowdata prevblockrightcol = currentblockrightcol for j in segments: for k in range(imagewidth): for l in range(imageheight): Ej = sum(q[j][k][l][i] K[j][k][l][i] for i in range(numscatteringorders)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Interpolation is only valid if distances along the ray are "close enough." If not, a new cube must be placed to avoid artifacts. Boundaries: The sweep computation requires careful handling of image boundaries to ensure the left column and top row are correctly initialized for the first block and sweep. Degenerate Input: If a viewing ray has no low-density segments, the pattern code is blank, and no cube is placed. Time Complexity: Reduced compared to uniform sampling due to adaptive placement and interpolation. Octree clipping eliminates large cells during traversal, saving rendering time. Memory Complexity: Optimized by storing only the right-hand column of the previous 9x9 block and one full image row, significantly reducing memory footprint for large images. Strengths: Efficiently handles forward scattering by focusing sampling on the front face and center. Hierarchical placement reduces redundant calculations. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of interpolation distance thresholds. When to Use: Suitable for volume rendering with significant forward scattering, such as clouds or fog, where high-order scattering terms vary slowly. When Not to Use: Not ideal for scenes with highly isotropic scattering or where rapid spatial changes in scattering properties occur, as interpolation may introduce errors. Hierarchical Viewing Cube Sampling was introduced in the context of global illumination rendering for clouds and participating media. It builds on the principles of adaptive sampling and quadtree subdivision to optimize the computation of scattering convolutions. The method is detailed in the work on diffusion and multiple anisotropic scattering for global illumination in clouds. Diffusion and multiple anisotropic scattering for global illumination in clouds, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc1410406/?q=multiple scattering rendering, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)
