name: View Adapted Stepping Distances
head: Adaptive Stepping Distances, Adaptive Termination with Bilinear Interpolation, Jump Bilinear, View Adapted Stepping
body: View Adapted Stepping Distances is a volume rendering acceleration technique that aligns sample points with voxel cube faces to enable bilinear interpolation instead of trilinear interpolation, while using adaptive termination to skip empty space. It differs from its parent Bilinear Interpolation by dynamically calculating the stepping distance based on the view direction to enforce this alignment, and from Optimized Trilinear Reconstruction by reducing the number of neighbor lookups from 8 to 4. Inputs: Ray origin O, ray direction D, volume data set V, volume bounds. Outputs: Final pixel color and opacity. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin O=(ox, oy, oz) and direction D=(dx, dy, dz). Voxel Data: Scalar field f(x,y,z). Fast Voxel Traversal State: Current voxel coordinates (x,y,z), step sizes (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z), and t-values for next face crossing (tx, ty, tz). Parameters: Epsilon (\epsilon): Adaptive termination threshold, typically 0.1. Stepping Distance: Variable, calculated per ray to ensure samples fall on cube faces. Steps: 1. Determine Fastest Axis: Identify the axis along which the ray travels the furthest for a given length. This is the axis with the largest absolute component in the direction vector D. Let this axis be k \in \{x, y, z\}. 2. Adjust Ray Start: Adjust the ray origin to start on the closest cube face perpendicular to the fastest axis k. This ensures the first sample lies on a face. 3. Scale Stepping Distance: Scale the stepping distance of the fast voxel traversal algorithm so that the stepping distance along the fastest axis k is exactly 1 unit. This is achieved by dividing the standard step size by |dk|. 4. Align Sample Position: Alter the fractional part of the sample point position so that it is zero in the fastest axis k, while retaining the fractional placement in the other two axes. This ensures every subsequent sample remains on a face perpendicular to k. 5. Fast Voxel Traversal: Perform fast voxel traversal as normal using the adjusted step sizes and t-values. Each sample point is guaranteed to lie on a cube face perpendicular to the fastest axis. 6. Adaptive Termination: For each sample, check if the accumulated opacity exceeds the threshold \epsilon. If so, terminate the ray early to skip empty space. 7. Bilinear Interpolation: For each sample, perform bilinear interpolation using the 4 face-neighboring voxels instead of trilinear interpolation using 8 cube vertices. The formula is: t0 = (v1 - v0)ri + v0 t1 = (v3 - v2)ri + v2 v{pj(i)} = (t1 - t0)rj + t0 where ri and rj are the offsets along the two axes on the face perpendicular to the fastest axis. 8. Normal Calculation: Calculate the normal G = (gx, gy, gz) using central differences from the 4 face-neighboring voxels (reducing operations by 50% compared to 8 neighbors): gx = f(x+1, y, z) - f(x-1, y, z) gy = f(x, y+1, z) - f(x, y-1, z) gz = f(x, y, z+1) - f(x, y, z-1) Normalize the normal: l = \sqrt{gx^2 + gy^2 + gz^2} g'x = gx/l, \quad g'y = gy/l, \quad g'z = gz/l 9. Compositing: Apply the compositing formula: o{out} = (1 - oi)o{in} + oi for i = 1, \dots, n, where n is the number of samples, oi is the opacity at sample i, and o{in} and o{out} are the opacities coming into and going out of sample i. Note that the interval length does not appear in this formula. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def viewadaptedstepping(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, volumebounds, epsilon=0.1): # 1. Determine fastest axis (largest absolute direction component) absd = [abs(raydirection[0]), abs(raydirection[1]), abs(raydirection[2])] k = 0 if absd[0] >= absd[1] and absd[0] >= absd[2] else (1 if absd[1] >= absd[2] else 2) # 2 & 3. Scale stepping distance so fastest axis step is 1 unit intervalsize = 1.0 / absd[k] # Initialize Amanatides & Woo fast voxel traversal state minv, maxv = volumebounds step = [1 if raydirection[i] > 0 else -1 for i in range(3)] currentvoxel = [int(minv[i]) for i in range(3)] tmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tdelta = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] > 0: tmax[i] = (currentvoxel[i] + 1.0 - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] else: tmax[i] = (currentvoxel[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] tdelta[i] = step[i] / abs(raydirection[i]) # Scale tmax and tdelta by intervalsize tmax = [t intervalsize for t in tmax] tdelta = [t intervalsize for t in tdelta] # 4. Adjust sample position to align with face on fastest axis tentry = min(tmax[k], tmax[(k + 1) % 3], tmax[(k + 2) % 3]) samplepos = [rayorigin[i] + tentry raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] samplepos[k] = float(int(samplepos[k])) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] while minv[0] <= currentvoxel[0] <= maxv[0] and \ minv[1] <= currentvoxel[1] <= maxv[1] and \ minv[2] <= currentvoxel[2] <= maxv[2] and \ accumulatedopacity < epsilon: # 5. Fast Voxel Traversal continues; 6. Adaptive Termination checked in loop condition # 7. Bilinear Interpolation iaxis = (k + 1) % 3 jaxis = (k + 2) % 3 ri = samplepos[iaxis] - int(samplepos[iaxis]) rj = samplepos[jaxis] - int(samplepos[jaxis]) v0 = volumedata[currentvoxel[0], currentvoxel[1], currentvoxel[2]] v1 = volumedata[currentvoxel[0] + step[iaxis], currentvoxel[1], currentvoxel[2]] v2 = volumedata[currentvoxel[0], currentvoxel[1] + step[jaxis], currentvoxel[2]] v3 = volumedata[currentvoxel[0] + step[iaxis], currentvoxel[1] + step[jaxis], currentvoxel[2]] t0 = (v1 - v0) ri + v0 t1 = (v3 - v2) ri + v2 value = (t1 - t0) rj + t0 # 8. Normal Calculation using 4 face neighbors gx = volumedata[currentvoxel[0] + step[0], currentvoxel[1], currentvoxel[2]] - \ volumedata[currentvoxel[0] - step[0], currentvoxel[1], currentvoxel[2]] gy = volumedata[currentvoxel[0], currentvoxel[1] + step[1], currentvoxel[2]] - \ volumedata[currentvoxel[0], currentvoxel[1] - step[1], currentvoxel[2]] gz = volumedata[currentvoxel[0], currentvoxel[1], currentvoxel[2] + step[2]] - \ volumedata[currentvoxel[0], currentvoxel[1], currentvoxel[2] - step[2]] l = (gx2 + gy2 + gz2)0.5 if l > 0: gx, gy, gz = gx/l, gy/l, gz/l # Compute opacity and color from value and normal (standard volume rendering shading) opacity = value # Simplified transfer function; real implementations use a transfer function mapping value to opacity. color = [value, value, value] # Simplified color mapping # 9. Compositing finalcolor = [(1.0 - opacity) finalcolor[c] + opacity color[c] for c in range(3)] accumulatedopacity += opacity (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) # Advance ray if tmax[k] < tmax[(k + 1) % 3] and tmax[k] < tmax[(k + 2) % 3]: currentvoxel[k] += step[k] tmax[k] += tdelta[k] elif tmax[(k + 1) % 3] < tmax[(k + 2) % 3]: currentvoxel[(k + 1) % 3] += step[(k + 1) % 3] tmax[(k + 1) % 3] += tdelta[(k + 1) % 3] else: currentvoxel[(k + 2) % 3] += step[(k + 2) % 3] tmax[(k + 2) % 3] += tdelta[(k + 2) % 3] samplepos = [rayorigin[i] + tmax[k] raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] samplepos[k] = float(int(samplepos[k])) # Re-align to face return finalcolor A technique to skip empty space by stopping the ray when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold. It reduces computation in transparent regions. The underlying traversal algorithm (Amanatides and Woo) used to efficiently step through voxels. Time Complexity: Reduces computational cost by approximately 50% per sample due to fewer operations (bilinear vs trilinear) and fewer neighbor lookups (4 vs 8). Normal calculation operations are also reduced by 50%. Memory Complexity: Avoids the extra storage required for precomputed normals (e.g., 200MBytes for a 256^3 dataset) by calculating normals on the fly. Measured Performance: On a 133MHz Dec Alpha with Hydrogen data set at angle 45,45,45, Standard Ray Termination time is 113.16, Jump is 69.18, Bilinear is 39.10, Gain is 26.6%. On the CThead data set at angle 45,45,45, Standard Ray Termination time is 365.85, Jump is 276.57, Bilinear is 141.71, Gain is 36.9%. Overall computation time reduction is about 30%-40%. On the CThead dataset, the method achieved a 30%-40% reduction in computation time compared to standard methods, and was over 7 times faster than the method without optimizations. Scaling: The method is scalable, with time increasing with image size, unlike the Template method which is constant time but produces coarse images. Strengths: Excellent balance between image quality and computation time; very little extra computation to initiate; works for arbitrary viewing directions. Limitations: The interval size varies with viewing angle, being 1 for axis-aligned and \sqrt{3} for 45-degree angles, which affects the number of samples taken. Using larger interval sizes (m > 1) makes the volume appear more transparent than with interval size 1, because the compositing formula depends on sample count n, not interval length. When to use: When computational speed is critical and slight transparency changes due to interval size variation are acceptable. When not to use: When strict opacity preservation across all viewing angles is required, or when precomputed normals are already available and memory is not a constraint. The method was presented by Mark W. Jones from the Department of Computer Science, University of Wales Swansea. It addresses the high computational cost of volume rendering, particularly the dominance of normal calculations and trilinear interpolation. The method builds on the fast voxel traversal algorithm of Amanatides and Woo. Volume Rendering Using View Adapted Stepping Distances, https://zenodo.org/records/14186166, fetched 2026-10-26

name: GPU-adaptive Volume Downsampling
head: volumeDownsampling
body: GPU-adaptive Volume Downsampling dynamically adjusts rendering sample distance multipliers based on a one-time GPU performance test to reduce GPU load during volume rendering. It sets apart from sibling methods by decoupling the sampling rate from the scene content or view direction, instead tying it directly to the hardware's measured capability tier. This ensures consistent frame rates across diverse hardware configurations without manual user intervention. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A configuration object defining GPU tiers and thresholds; a GPU performance score (percentage) derived from an initialization benchmark. Output: Two multipliers: rotateSampleDistanceFactor (applied during viewport rotation) and sampleDistanceMultiplier (applied during static rendering). Data Structures: The method relies on a configuration structure nested under customizationService. The layout is defined as follows: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. { "volumeDownsampling": { "highGpu": { "rotateSampleDistanceFactor": <number>, "sampleDistanceMultiplier": <number> }, "midGpu": { "rotateSampleDistanceFactor": <number>, "sampleDistanceMultiplier": <number> }, "lowGpu": { "rotateSampleDistanceFactor": <number>, "sampleDistanceMultiplier": <number> }, "thresholdHighPercent": <number>, "thresholdMidPercent": <number> } } Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Run a GPU performance test once at application initialization to determine the hardware's capability score. 2. Classification: Compare the obtained GPU score against the configured thresholds to assign the GPU to a tier: High Tier: Score \ge thresholdHighPercent (typically 100%). Mid Tier: thresholdMidPercent \le Score < thresholdHighPercent (typically 90% to <100%). Low Tier: Score < thresholdMidPercent (typically <90%). 3. Configuration Retrieval: Select the configuration block corresponding to the assigned tier (highGpu, midGpu, or lowGpu). 4. Multiplier Assignment: Extract rotateSampleDistanceFactor and sampleDistanceMultiplier from the selected block. 5. Application: Apply sampleDistanceMultiplier to the base sample distance during static rendering. Apply rotateSampleDistanceFactor to the base sample distance during viewport rotation. Formulas: Let S be the GPU performance score (0-100). Let TH be thresholdHighPercent. Let TM be thresholdMidPercent. \text{Tier}(S) = \begin{cases} \text{highGpu} & \text{if } S \ge TH \\ \text{midGpu} & \text{if } TM \le S < TH \\ \text{lowGpu} & \text{if } S < TM \end{cases} Let F{rot} be rotateSampleDistanceFactor and M{static} be sampleDistanceMultiplier from the configuration block of \text{Tier}(S). Let D{base} be the base sample distance. D{render} = D{base} \times M{static} \quad \text{(Static)} D{rotate} = D{base} \times F{rot} \quad \text{(Rotation)} Parameters: thresholdHighPercent: Default 100. thresholdMidPercent: Default 90. rotateSampleDistanceFactor: High/Mid GPU: 2. Low GPU: 3. sampleDistanceMultiplier: High GPU: 1. Mid/Low GPU: 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The score comparison is integer-based in the source example (percentages). Ensure the benchmark returns a comparable scale. Initialization: The test runs only once. If the GPU state changes significantly (e.g., thermal throttling, driver updates) after initialization, the multipliers will not update automatically. Configuration: If thresholds are misconfigured (e.g., TH < TM), the classification logic may fail or assign incorrect tiers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializegpuadaptivedownsampling(config): """ Runs the one-time GPU test and sets up the multipliers. """ # 1. Run GPU performance test # The specific benchmark algorithm is not detailed in the source. # This function returns a score between 0 and 100. gpuscore = rungpuperformancetest() # 2. Extract thresholds thresholdhigh = config['volumeDownsampling']['thresholdHighPercent'] thresholdmid = config['volumeDownsampling']['thresholdMidPercent'] # 3. Classify GPU if gpuscore >= thresholdhigh: tierconfig = config['volumeDownsampling']['highGpu'] elif gpuscore >= thresholdmid: tierconfig = config['volumeDownsampling']['midGpu'] else: tierconfig = config['volumeDownsampling']['lowGpu'] # 4. Assign multipliers rotatesampledistancefactor = tierconfig['rotateSampleDistanceFactor'] sampledistancemultiplier = tierconfig['sampleDistanceMultiplier'] return { 'rotatesampledistancefactor': rotatesampledistancefactor, 'sampledistancemultiplier': sampledistancemultiplier } def calculatesampledistance(basedistance, isrotating, multipliers): """ Calculates the final sample distance based on current state. """ if isrotating: factor = multipliers['rotatesampledistancefactor'] else: factor = multipliers['sampledistancemultiplier'] return basedistance factor Time Complexity: O(1) for multiplier lookup after initialization. The initialization benchmark cost is hardware-dependent and not specified. Memory Complexity: O(1), storing only the configuration object and two multiplier values. Performance: Reduces GPU load by increasing sample distances (decreasing resolution) on lower-tier hardware. High-tier GPUs maintain full resolution (multiplier 1). Strengths: Automatic adaptation to hardware; simple configuration; effective for maintaining frame rates on low-end devices. Limitations: Static adaptation; does not account for scene complexity or view direction; relies on a single initial benchmark which may not reflect real-time thermal or power states. When to use: When rendering diverse hardware configurations and consistent frame rates are prioritized over maximum visual fidelity on high-end hardware. When not to use: When visual fidelity is critical and hardware is uniform, or when dynamic scene-dependent sampling is required. This method originates from the OHIF Viewer project, specifically introduced in the feat/decimated loading pull request. It is part of a broader strategy to handle large volume datasets by combining auto-decimation (based on voxel count thresholds) with adaptive sampling based on GPU capability. The approach is used in medical imaging viewers to ensure smooth interaction across a wide range of client hardware. feat/decimated loading, https://github.com/OHIF/Viewers/pull/6034, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Dynamic Subsampling for Preview Rendering
head: Adaptive Preview Rendering, Adaptive sampling adjustment, Adaptive sub-sampling, Adaptive sub-sampling along the ray, Preview rendering, Subsample VDI, VDI Subsampling for Preview Rendering
body: Dynamic Subsampling for Preview Rendering is a technique to maintain high frame rates during interactive remote visualization when the camera viewpoint deviates significantly from the VDI generation viewpoint. It solves the performance degradation caused by the anisotropic shape of Volumetric Depth Images (VDIs) by adaptively subsampling along the view ray and in image space. Unlike standard downsampling which only reduces ray count, this method combines image-space downsampling with adaptive ray-space subsampling to achieve higher frame rates with significantly better structural similarity (SSIM) than image-space subsampling alone. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Volumetric Depth Image (VDI) consisting of supersegment lists \mathbb{L} and supersegments \mathbb{S}, an acceleration grid storing the number of supersegments per cell, the current camera viewpoint, and target frame rate parameters. Output: A rendered image at display resolution (e.g., 1920 \times 1080). Data Structures: Acceleration Grid: A 3D grid where each cell stores the count of supersegments \mathbb{S} intersecting that cell. Supersegment List (\mathbb{L}i): A list of supersegments associated with a specific image coordinate, found using the sample's x- and y-coordinates in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC). Supersegment (\mathbb{S}j^i): A geometric primitive storing color and opacity information. Parameters: DI: Image space downsampling factor. DI=1.0 is full resolution. Values <1.0 decrease the number of rays. DR: Ray space subsampling factor. Used to thin samples uniformly along the ray. Typically manually chosen (e.g., 0.3 during navigation phases). Target Frame Rate: Used by a dynamic PI Controller to modulate DI. Algorithm Steps: 1. Determine Image Resolution: Calculate the number of rays to cast based on DI. If DI < 1.0, cast rays at a lower resolution grid. 2. Iterate Over Rays: For each ray (x, y) in the lower-resolution image grid: a. Traverse Acceleration Grid: March the ray through the acceleration grid cells. b. Calculate Samples per Cell: For each intersected cell, determine the number of samples N{cell} to place within that cell: N{cell} = DR \times L{cell} \times C{cell} Where: DR is the ray subsampling factor. L{cell} is the intersection length of the ray with the cell. C{cell} is the number of supersegments \mathbb{S} stored in that cell. c. Place Samples: Place N{cell} samples at regular intervals along the ray segment within the cell. d. Query Supersegment: For each sample point P: i. Convert P to NDC coordinates (x{ndc}, y{ndc}). ii. Retrieve the supersegment list \mathbb{L}i corresponding to (x{ndc}, y{ndc}). iii. Find the specific supersegment \mathbb{S}j^i containing P using the intersection algorithm defined in the parent article (Section 4.2 of). iv. If a supersegment is found, obtain its color. If not, the sample is transparent. e. Accumulate Color: Perform volume rendering accumulation (e.g., standard front-to-back compositing) using the colors obtained from the samples. Opacity Correction: Approximate length-based opacity correction using the distance from the previous sample instead of calculating exact intersection lengths with the supersegment boundaries. 3. Upsample: If DI < 1.0, upsample the resulting lower-resolution image to the display resolution using bilinear interpolation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervdipreview(vdi, camera, DI, DR, targetfps): # 1. Determine image resolution based on DI displaywidth, displayheight = getdisplayresolution() renderwidth = int(displaywidth DI) renderheight = int(displayheight DI) # 2. Initialize output image outputimage = zeros((renderheight, renderwidth, 3)) # 3. Iterate over lower-resolution image grid for y in range(renderheight): for x in range(renderwidth): # Get ray for this pixel ray = camera.getray(x, y, displaywidth, displayheight) # Initialize accumulation accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 prevsampledist = 0.0 # 4. Traverse acceleration grid for cell in ray.traverse(vdi.accelerationgrid): if cell.supersegmentcount == 0: continue # Calculate number of samples for this cell # Lcell is intersection length of ray with cell # Ccell is number of supersegments in cell numsamples = DR cell.intersectionlength cell.supersegmentcount # Place samples at regular intervals within the cell segment cellstart, cellend = ray.getcellbounds(cell) stepsize = (cellend - cellstart) / max(numsamples, 1) for k in range(numsamples): sampledist = cellstart + k stepsize samplepoint = ray.getpoint(sampledist) # 5. Query supersegment # Find list Li using NDC coordinates of samplepoint ndcx, ndcy = camera.worldtondc(samplepoint) supersegmentlist = vdi.getsupersegmentlist(ndcx, ndcy) # Find specific supersegment Sj^i containing samplepoint supersegment = supersegmentlist.findcontainingsupersegment(samplepoint) if supersegment is not None: color = supersegment.color opacity = supersegment.opacity # Approximate opacity correction using distance from previous sample # Standard front-to-back compositing formula # alpha = opacity exp(-opacity distance) is an approximation # Here we use simple distance delta for correction as per source distdelta = sampledist - prevsampledist # Assuming standard compositing: Cout = Cin + (1 - alphain) Csample alphasample # The source mentions "length-based opacity correction... approximated using distance" # This implies modulating the sample's contribution by the step size or distance # Since exact intersection is skipped, we use the step size as a proxy for path length effectiveopacity = opacity distdelta # Interpretation of "approximation" # Composite weight = (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) effectiveopacity accumulatedcolor += weight color accumulatedopacity += weight prevsampledist = sampledist else: prevsampledist = sampledist outputimage[y, x] = accumulatedcolor # 6. Upsample to display resolution if DI < 1.0 if DI < 1.0: outputimage = bilinearinterpolateupsample(outputimage, displaywidth, displayheight) return outputimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Manual Tuning: DR lacks automatic control and requires manual activation and tuning, which can lead to jerkiness during rapid navigation phases. Precision: The approximation of opacity correction using distance from the previous sample may introduce artifacts if the step size is large or if supersegment boundaries are not aligned with sample points. NDC Lookup: Finding the supersegment list requires accurate conversion to NDC space; errors here may lead to incorrect supersegment retrieval. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of rays cast (DI^2) times the average number of samples per ray. The number of samples per ray is proportional to DR and the density of supersegments in the VDI. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the VDI storage and acceleration grid. The rendering process itself uses minimal additional memory. Measured Performance: On the Richtmyer-Meshkov dataset with a 30^\circ viewpoint deviation: Full resolution (DI=1.0) yields 45 fps with SSIM=1.0. Image subsampling alone (DI=0.2) yields ~150 fps but SSIM=0.88. Combined adaptive ray subsampling (DR=0.14) and image subsampling (DI=0.6) yields ~150 fps with SSIM=0.94. In an interactive session, the method maintained a steady 25 fps through most of the session, with jerkiness during rapid navigation phases. Strengths: Significantly improves SSIM compared to image-space subsampling alone for the same frame rate. Effective for remote visualization where bandwidth or server-side generation latency is a constraint. Limitations: Requires manual tuning of DR. Does not support directional lighting effects like specular highlights because the VDI stores classified color and opacity. When to Use: When rendering large volumes remotely with significant viewpoint deviations and maintaining high frame rates is critical, and some quality loss is acceptable. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity directional lighting is required, or when automatic parameter tuning is necessary without user intervention. Dynamic Subsampling for Preview Rendering was proposed by Gupta and Sbalzarini in 2023 as part of an efficient raycasting method for Volumetric Depth Images (VDIs). It addresses the challenge of interactive direct volume rendering in remote visualization scenarios, where the VDI is generated on a server and streamed to a client. The method builds on the VDI data structure, which uses supersegments to represent volume data efficiently. It is implemented as an extension of the scenery visualization library. name: Orientation-Selective Sampling Strategies
head: Steerable Pyramid Sampling Strategies
body: Orientation-Selective Sampling Strategies optimize steerable pyramid volume rendering by modulating the evaluation of orientation bins based on the alignment between the viewing ray direction and the kernel's frequency modulation direction. Unlike deterministic approaches that evaluate all orientations or uniform sampling that ignores geometric alignment, this method uses the alignment metric to cull or probabilistically select bins, balancing rendering quality against performance. It is specifically designed for steerable pyramid representations where orientation selectivity is governed by the central frequency f0. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray direction vector \vec{v}, set of K orientation bins \{\mathbf{o}1, \dots, \mathbf{o}K\}, central frequency f0, alignment threshold \delta, and power-law parameters a, b, \beta. Output: A subset of orientation bins to evaluate, or a probability distribution for stochastic selection. Data Structures: Orientation Bins: A list of K unit vectors \mathbf{o}i representing the preferred orientations of the steerable pyramid filters. Alignment Metric: A scalar ai for each bin, computed as the absolute dot product ai = |\vec{v} \cdot \mathbf{o}i|. Contribution Weight Formula: The contribution weight wi for each orientation bin is determined by its alignment with the ray and the central frequency: wi = \exp\left(-\frac{f0^2 ai^2}{2}\right) The total weight is W = \sum{i=1}^K wi. Sampling Strategies: The method defines several strategies for selecting which bins to render. Let K be the total number of bins. 1. Deterministic: Action: Evaluate all K bins. Probability: 1 (for the set). Weight: 1. 2. Threshold Culling: Action: Evaluate only bins where ai \leq \delta. Bins with ai > \delta are culled. Probability: Undefined (deterministic subset). Weight: 1. Note: Lower \delta results in more aggressive culling, potentially degrading to evaluating only the single best-aligned bin. 3. Uniform Sampling: Action: Select one bin i uniformly at random. Probability: P(i) = K^{-1}. Weight: K. 4. Importance Sampling: Action: Select one bin i with probability proportional to wi. Probability: P(i) = \frac{wi}{W}. Weight: \frac{W}{wi}. 5. Threshold + Uniform: Action: Deterministically render all bins where ai \leq \delta. For bins where ai > \delta, uniformly sample one bin. Probability: For a selected bin j in the "above-threshold" set, P(j) = N{\text{above}}^{-1}, where N{\text{above}} is the count of bins with ai > \delta. Weight: N{\text{above}}. Control Variate Note: In "Threshold + Control Variate" mode, bins below the threshold (ai \leq \delta) are assigned a fixed weight of 1. 6. Power-law Weighted: Action: Sample bins proportionally to a power-law function of the alignment. Probability: P(x) \propto x^{(1-\beta)^{-1}}, where x is the alignment metric. Weight: \left(b^{(1-\beta)} - a^{(1-\beta)}\right)^{-1}. Parameters: a, b are bounds for the power-law distribution; \beta is the tuning parameter. 7. Uniform + Control Variate: Action: Use Gaussian-based control variates for certain levels; sample remaining levels uniformly. Probability: (\mathcal{P} - 1)^{-1}, where \mathcal{P} is the total number of levels. Weight: \mathcal{P} - 1. 8. Power-law + Control Variate: Action: Use Gaussians as control variates; sample other levels via power-law. Probability: x^{(1-\beta)^{-1}}. Weight: \left(b^{(1-\beta)} - a^{(1-\beta)}\right)^{-1}. 9. Power-law + CV (Accumulative): Action: Sample level k via power-law; render all levels 0 to k. Probability: x^{(1-\beta)^{-1}}. Weight: \left(1 - \left(\frac{j}{\beta}\right)^{1-\beta}\right)^{-1}. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode implements the computation of alignment weights and the selection logic for the primary strategies. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def computealignmentweights(raydirection, orientationbins, f0): """ Computes the contribution weight wi for each orientation bin. Args: raydirection (list): 3D vector [vx, vy, vz] orientationbins (list): List of K 3D vectors [o1, o2,..., oK] f0 (float): Central frequency of the steerable pyramid Returns: list: Weights wi for each bin """ weights = [] for o in orientationbins: # Compute alignment ai = |v. o| dotproduct = raydirection[0]o[0] + raydirection[1]o[1] + raydirection[2]o[2] ai = abs(dotproduct) # Compute weight wi = exp(-f0^2 ai^2 / 2) wi = math.exp(-(f02 ai2) / 2) weights.append(wi) return weights def selectorientationbins(strategy, raydirection, orientationbins, f0, delta, beta=0.5, abound=0.0, bbound=1.0): """ Selects orientation bins based on the specified strategy. Args: strategy (str): One of 'deterministic', 'thresholdculling', 'uniform', 'importance', 'thresholduniform', 'powerlaw', 'uniformcv', 'powerlawcv', 'powerlawcvaccum' raydirection (list): 3D vector orientationbins (list): List of K 3D vectors f0 (float): Central frequency delta (float): Alignment threshold for culling beta (float): Power-law tuning parameter abound (float): Lower bound for power-law bbound (float): Upper bound for power-law Returns: list: Indices of selected bins """ K = len(orientationbins) weights = computealignmentweights(raydirection, orientationbins, f0) W = sum(weights) if strategy == 'deterministic': return list(range(K)) elif strategy == 'thresholdculling': selected = [] for i, o in enumerate(orientationbins): dotproduct = raydirection[0]o[0] + raydirection[1]o[1] + raydirection[2]o[2] ai = abs(dotproduct) if ai <= delta: selected.append(i) return selected elif strategy == 'uniform': idx = random.randint(0, K - 1) return [idx] elif strategy == 'importance': # Sample proportionally to weights idx = random.choices(range(K), weights=weights, k=1)[0] return [idx] elif strategy == 'thresholduniform': selected = [] abovethresholdindices = [] for i, o in enumerate(orientationbins): dotproduct = raydirection[0]o[0] + raydirection[1]o[1] + raydirection[2]o[2] ai = abs(dotproduct) if ai <= delta: selected.append(i) else: abovethresholdindices.append(i) if abovethresholdindices: idx = random.choice(abovethresholdindices) selected.append(idx) return selected elif strategy == 'powerlaw': # Sample based on power-law of alignment # Note: Exact implementation of power-law sampling on alignment metric # requires normalizing the distribution over the range [abound, bbound] # For simplicity, we assume alignment metrics are normalized or mapped. # This is a placeholder for the specific power-law sampling logic. # In practice, one would sample x from the power-law distribution and # find the bin with closest alignment. # Given the complexity, this strategy is often approximated or precomputed. # Here we return an empty list to indicate complexity not fully detailed in sources. return [] elif strategy == 'uniformcv': # Simplified: Return all but one, or handle control variate logic # Sources indicate sampling remaining levels uniformly. # Assuming P is total levels, sample P-1 uniformly. # This requires knowledge of level structure not present in basic bin list. return [] elif strategy == 'powerlawcv': return [] elif strategy == 'powerlawcvaccum': return [] else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown strategy: {strategy}") Parameters: K: Number of orientation bins. \delta: Alignment threshold for culling. Lower values result in more aggressive dropping of orientation bins. \beta: Decay rate parameter for power-law weighting. f0: Central frequency of the steerable pyramid. High f0 increases orientation selectivity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Culling: If \delta is set too low, the threshold culling strategy may degenerate into evaluating only the single highest-contributing bin, potentially losing necessary frequency information. High Frequency Volumes: Volumes with high f0 exhibit high orientation selectivity. For these volumes, threshold culling is particularly effective, but requires careful tuning of \delta to avoid artifacts. Applies importance sampling to angular bins, stochastically selecting orientations proportional to their contribution to reduce traversal time at the cost of increased variance. Time Complexity: Depends on the strategy. Deterministic is O(K). Threshold culling is O(K) to compute alignments but reduces rendering cost by a factor proportional to the culling rate. Importance sampling is O(K) to compute weights and O(1) to sample. Memory Complexity: O(K) to store orientation bins and weights. Performance: Volumes with high f0 benefit significantly from threshold culling due to high orientation selectivity. Strengths: Direct trade-off between quality and performance via \delta; reduces redundant evaluations of misaligned orientations. Limitations: Stochastic strategies introduce variance; deterministic culling introduces bias if \delta is too aggressive. The method originates from the "Gabor Fields: Orientation-Selective Level-of-Detail for Volume Rendering" paper. It is used in steerable pyramid volume rendering to optimize the evaluation of orientation-selective filters. name: Stochastic Orientation-selective Path Tracing
head: Angular selectivity masking
body: Stochastic Orientation-selective Path Tracing accelerates volume rendering by masking Gabor kernels based on the alignment angle between the ray direction and the kernel's frequency modulation direction. It builds on Orientation-Selective Sampling Strategies by applying importance sampling to angular bins, reducing the number of ray-primitive intersections per sample. Unlike deterministic pruning which culls low-contributing orientations at the cost of bias, this method stochastically selects orientations proportional to their contribution, trading increased variance for reduced traversal time. Inputs: Ray direction \vec{v}; pre-binned Gabor kernels (grouped by orientation and frequency); bin representative orientations \vec{k}i and frequencies f{0,i}. Outputs: Set of primitives to intersect for the current ray. Data Structures: Kernel Bins: A list of bins. Each bin i contains: representativeorientation: Unit vector \vec{k}i indicating the frequency modulation direction. frequency: Scalar f{0,i} (carrier frequency). primitives: List of scene primitives associated with kernels in this bin. Steps: 1. Pre-processing: Bin all Gabor kernels by the orientation and frequency of their modulation. Store the representative orientation \vec{k}i and frequency f{0,i} for each bin. 2. Alignment Calculation: For the current ray with direction \vec{v}, compute the alignment factor ai for each bin i: ai = |\cos \thetai| = |\vec{v} \cdot \vec{k}i| where \thetai is the angle between \vec{v} and \vec{k}i. Note that ai \in [0, 1]. 3. Weight Calculation: Compute the sampling weight wi for each bin based on the dampened contribution of the projected frequency: wi = e^{-f{0,i}^2 ai^2 / 2} This weight reflects the magnitude of the cosine modulation along the ray. 4. Stochastic Selection: Sample bins stochastically with probability proportional to wi. Include the primitives in the selected bins in the set to be intersected. Bins with low weights (high alignment ai where destructive interference occurs) are less likely to be sampled. 5. Intersection: Perform ray-primitive intersection tests only against the primitives in the selected bins. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectprimitivesstochastic(raydirection, bins): """ Select primitives to intersect based on stochastic orientation sampling. Args: raydirection: Unit vector v. bins: List of dicts, each with keys 'k' (unit vector), 'f0' (float), 'primitives' (list). Returns: List of primitives to intersect. """ weights = [] for bin in bins: # Compute alignment factor a = |cos(theta)| # dotproduct is the dot product of two vectors costheta = dotproduct(raydirection, bin['k']) a = abs(costheta) # Compute weight w = exp(-f0^2 a^2 / 2) # exp is the exponential function w = exp(- (bin['f0'] 2) (a 2) / 2.0) weights.append(w) # Normalize weights to form a probability distribution totalweight = sum(weights) if totalweight == 0: # Fallback: if all weights are zero (e.g., infinite frequency), # sample uniformly or return empty set depending on implementation. # Assuming uniform selection if all weights are zero. indices = range(len(bins)) probabilities = [1.0 / len(bins)] len(bins) else: probabilities = [w / totalweight for w in weights] indices = range(len(bins)) # Stochastic selection: sample one bin index based on probabilities # Using a standard discrete sampling method. selectedbinindex = samplecategorical(indices, probabilities) # Return primitives from the selected bin return bins[selectedbinindex]['primitives'] Parameters: f{0,i}: Frequency of the Gabor kernel in bin i. Typical values depend on the Gabor Fields asset. Number of bins: Determined by the pre-processing step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Rays (a=1): When the ray is parallel to the frequency direction, destructive interference significantly reduces the contribution. The weight w becomes e^{-f0^2 / 2}, which can be very small for high frequencies, leading to low sampling probability. Perpendicular Rays (a=0): When the ray is perpendicular to the frequency direction, the cosine modulation contributes uniformly. The weight w is 1.0, making these bins highly likely to be sampled. Precision: Computing a = |\cos \theta| requires accurate dot products. For high frequencies, the exponential decay is rapid, so small errors in a can lead to large errors in weight. Extends this method by adding spectral selection (frequency bands) to angular selection, trading variance/bias for reduced traversal time. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of ray-primitive intersections per sample by culling or stochastically selecting bins. The cost of computing weights is O(B) where B is the number of bins, which is typically small compared to the number of primitives. Memory Complexity: Requires storing bins with representative orientations and frequencies. Strengths: Effective for high-frequency content where analytic rendering is expensive, as it reduces the number of intersections. Limitations: Introduces variance due to stochastic selection. Deterministic pruning (not this method) introduces bias. When to use: When rendering Gabor Fields with high-frequency content and performance is critical. When not to use: When low variance is required and performance is not a bottleneck, or when the scene has low-frequency content where angular selectivity is less pronounced. Originated in "Gabor Fields: Orientation-Selective Level-of-Detail for Volume Rendering". The method exploits the angular selectivity of 3D Gabor kernels to accelerate rendering by masking kernels based on ray alignment. name: Stochastic Laplacian Path Tracing
head: Frequency band masking, Spectral selectivity acceleration, Stochastic Laplacian Rendering, Stochastic-analytical estimators
body: Stochastic Laplacian Path Tracing accelerates volume rendering by stochastically selecting which frequency bands (pyramid levels) of a Gabor asset to integrate for each path segment, trading increased variance or bias for substantially reduced traversal time. Unlike deterministic full integration which intersects all primitives, this method reduces the number of ray-primitive intersections per sample, making it particularly effective for high-frequency content where analytic rendering is expensive. It builds on Stochastic Orientation-selective Path Tracing by adding spectral selection to angular selection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Gabor Field asset decomposed into frequency bands (a low-pass Gaussian base and higher-frequency Gabor residuals); a ray segment defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a power law shape parameter \alpha. Output: An unbiased (in tomographic contexts) or biased (in standard stochastic contexts) estimate of the volume integral contribution for the segment. Data Structures: The asset is represented as a set of primitives partitioned into frequency bands. Low-pass band: Contains the Gaussian base component. High-frequency bands: Contain Gabor kernel residuals. Selection Mask: A boolean vector indicating which bands are active for the current sample. Parameters: \alpha: The shape parameter for the power law curve controlling the probability of selecting higher frequency bands. Typical value: \alpha = 0.2. Algorithm: 1. Decomposition: The volume asset is pre-computed into a hierarchy of frequency bands. The lowest level is a smooth Gaussian approximation; higher levels contain Gabor kernels capturing finer details. 2. Stochastic Selection: For each path segment, determine the subset of bands to intersect. Always include the low-pass (Gaussian) band to ensure baseline stability. Stochastically select one or more higher-frequency bands based on a power law distribution governed by \alpha. 3. Integration: Perform ray-primitive intersection tests only against the selected subset of primitives. Accumulate the contribution from these primitives. 4. Estimation: Compute the final pixel value by averaging the contributions from all samples, accounting for the selection probabilities if an unbiased estimator is required, or accepting the bias if using the biased control-variate inspired technique. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stochasticlaplaciantrace(rayorigin, raydirection, assetbands, alpha): """ rayorigin: 3D vector raydirection: 3D vector assetbands: List of primitive sets, where bands[0] is low-pass Gaussian, bands[1..n] are higher-frequency Gabor residuals. alpha: float, power law shape parameter (e.g., 0.2). """ # Step 1: Always include the low-pass band (index 0) selectedindices = [0] # Step 2: Stochastically select higher frequency bands # The probability of selecting a band decreases with its frequency level. # Using a power law distribution P(k) ~ k^(-alpha) for band index k > 0. # Note: Exact normalization constants depend on the number of bands. # For implementation simplicity, we sample from the available higher bands. numhigherbands = len(assetbands) - 1 if numhigherbands > 0: # Generate a random number to decide if we pick a higher band # In a full implementation, this might involve multiple samples or # a specific sampling strategy defined in the source's Appendix (Table 5). # Here we assume a simplified single-band selection for the segment. # Calculate weights for power law distribution weights = [] for k in range(1, len(assetbands)): # k is the band index relative to the start of higher bands # Using (k) as the frequency level proxy weights.append(k (-alpha)) # Normalize weights totalweight = sum(weights) probs = [w / totalweight for w in weights] # Sample one higher band index (relative to assetbands) # Using inverse transform sampling or a library call for discrete distribution r = random.uniform(0, 1) cumulative = 0.0 selectedhigheridx = -1 for i, p in enumerate(probs): cumulative += p if r <= cumulative: selectedhigheridx = i + 1 # +1 because indices start at 1 break if selectedhigheridx != -1: selectedindices.append(selectedhigheridx) # Step 3: Intersect ray with selected primitives totalcontribution = 0.0 for idx in selectedindices: primitives = assetbands[idx] # Perform ray-primitive intersection for all primitives in this band for primitive in primitives: contribution = integrateprimitive(primitive, rayorigin, raydirection) totalcontribution += contribution # Step 4: Return contribution # Note: To be strictly unbiased, one must divide by the probability of selection. # The source notes that this method can be biased depending on the strategy. # The "control-variate inspired technique" implies a specific estimator form. # Without the exact formula from Table 5, we return the raw sum as a biased estimate # or assume the caller handles the weighting if an unbiased variant is chosen. return totalcontribution Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bias vs. Variance: The method introduces bias if the selection probabilities are not correctly accounted for in the estimator. The amount of bias depends on the scene and the parameter \alpha. Parameter Selection: A poor choice of \alpha can lead to excessive bias at high frequencies or insufficient acceleration. Degenerate Input: If the asset has no high-frequency bands, the stochastic selection step is skipped, and the method degrades to deterministic low-pass rendering. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Reduces per-sample cost by decreasing the number of ray-primitive intersections. The runtime scales with the number of selected bands. In the ablation study, removing scale regularization increased runtime from 24.1 ms to 37.7 ms, while removing importance sampling centers increased it to 38.0 ms, indicating that the full method (including stochastic acceleration) is significantly faster than variants without these optimizations. Memory: Storage costs assume 32-bit floating-point precision without compression. The decomposition into bands does not significantly increase memory overhead compared to storing the full asset, as the bands are derived from the same underlying representation. Measured Performance: On an RTX 4090, the full Gabor Fields method renders at 24.1 ms with 48.86 dB PSNR. Removing Scale Regularization increases runtime to 37.7 ms with 48.78 dB PSNR. Removing Importance Sampling Centers increases runtime to 38.0 ms with 46.36 dB PSNR. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Substantially faster traversal time; good compromise between rendering performance and variance when using control-variate inspired techniques. Supports seamless Level-of-Detail (LoD) rendering by masking out high-frequency kernels. Limitations: Introduces bias or variance depending on the scenario; requires careful selection of the power law parameter \alpha to manage the "exactness or quality price". When to Use: Use when rendering high-frequency volume data where analytic integration is too slow. Use when some bias is acceptable for significant performance gains. Use in tomographic rendering contexts where the method remains unbiased. When Not to Use: Use when strict unbiasedness is required in non-tomographic contexts without proper estimator weighting. Use when the asset lacks high-frequency content, as the acceleration benefit is minimal. Origin: Stochastic Laplacian Path Tracing was introduced in the paper "Gabor Fields: Orientation-Selective Level-of-Detail for Volume Rendering" by Fajardo et al.. It builds upon recent work on stochastic texture filtering and procedural noise using Monte Carlo sampling. History and Development: The method was developed to address the performance bottlenecks of analytic rendering in Gaussian Primitive Volumes and Gabor Fields. It leverages the spectral properties of Gabor kernels to allow for stochastic sampling of frequency bands, similar to techniques used in stochastic texture filtering. Applications: Volume rendering of complex scenes with high-frequency details (e.g., smoke, clouds, explosions). Tomographic rendering where unbiasedness is critical. Level-of-Detail (LoD) rendering, where high-frequency bands can be masked out based on viewing distance or resolution. name: Spectral Adaptive Sampling
head: Adaptive GPU Ray Casting Based on Spectral Analysis, Frequency-based adaptive sampling, Spectral adaptive ray casting
body: Spectral Adaptive Sampling is a volume rendering acceleration technique that determines the sampling step size based on the spectral decomposition (maximal frequency) of the composite signal formed by the volume data and the transfer function. Unlike heuristic methods that rely solely on the gradient of the scalar data, this method analyzes the frequency content of the transfer function to prevent aliasing artifacts caused by non-linear opacity mappings. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly incorporating the transfer function's spectral properties into the step size calculation, allowing for dynamic transfer function adjustments without re-computing global frequencies. Inputs: Volume dataset f(x) (scalar field). Transfer function g(s) mapping scalar values to optical properties. Optional affine transformation parameters a\Psi, b\Psi for dynamic transfer function modification. Maximal step size parameter T{max} (typically 8). Oversampling factor (typically 2) to compensate for linear reconstruction filters. Outputs: Adaptive sampling step size T for each ray segment. Rendered image with reduced sample count compared to regular sampling. 1. Importance Volume: A 3D texture with the same dimensions as the input dataset. It stores the max-filtered gradient magnitudes. For each voxel, the gradient f'(x) is computed in all spatial directions, and a max-filter with width 2T{max} is applied to estimate the maximal gradient over the region covered by the next sampling step. 2. Frequency Texture: A 2D texture storing the maximal frequency vg(I) of the transfer function g for specific value intervals I = [s{min}, s{max}]. This is pre-computed via FFT on g. 1. Pre-processing (Offline/Interactive Setup): 1. Compute the gradient f'(x) of the volume data f for every voxel. 2. Apply a max-filter with width 2T{max} to the gradients in the importance volume. 3. Store the result back in the importance volume to ensure the gradient estimate covers the potential range of the next step. 4. Perform a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) on the transfer function g to determine its spectral decomposition. 5. Store the maximal frequency vg(I) for various intervals I in the Frequency Texture. 2. Runtime (Per Ray Step): 1. Let x0 be the current sample position and f(x0) be the scalar value at that position. 2. Fetch the local gradient magnitude |f'(x0)| from the Importance Volume. 3. Estimate the value interval I = [s{min}, s{max}] covered by the next sampling step using a first-order Taylor expansion around x0: s{min} = f(x0) - |f'(x0)| T{max} s{max} = f(x0) + |f'(x0)| T{max} 4. If the transfer function is modified by an affine map \Psi(t) = a\Psi t + b\Psi, adjust the frequency lookup or the step size calculation to account for the scaling factor |a\Psi|. 5. Fetch the local maximal frequency vg(I) from the Frequency Texture corresponding to the interval I. 6. Calculate the sampling period T using the formula: T = \frac{1}{2 \cdot vg(I) \cdot |a\Psi| \cdot \max |f'(x)|} where \max |f'(x)| is the gradient magnitude fetched in step 2. The factor 2 represents the oversampling factor. 7. Advance the ray by T and repeat. Unverified code. 1): for j in range(1, volumedata.shape[1] - 1): for k in range(1, volumedata.shape[2] - 1): dx = volumedata[i+1, j, k] - volumedata[i-1, j, k] dy = volumedata[i, j+1, k] - volumedata[i, j-1, k] dz = volumedata[i, j, k+1] - volumedata[i, j, k-1] grad[i, j, k] = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) return grad def maxfilter(volume, width): """Apply a 3D max-filter with a cubic window of given width.""" halfw = width // 2 result = np.zeroslike(volume) for i in range(volume.shape[0]): for j in range(volume.shape[1]): for k in range(volume.shape[2]): imin, imax = max(0, i - halfw), min(volume.shape[0], i + halfw + 1) jmin, jmax = max(0, j - halfw), min(volume.shape[1], j + halfw + 1) kmin, kmax = max(0, k - halfw), min(volume.shape[2], k + halfw + 1) result[i, j, k] = np.max(volume[imin:imax, jmin:jmax, kmin:kmax]) return result def computetransferfunctionfrequencies(transferfunction, numintervals=256): """Compute maximal frequency vg for value intervals using FFT.""" # Perform FFT on the transfer function fftvals = np.fft.fft(transferfunction) magnitudes = np.abs(fftvals) # Determine max frequency for each interval vglookup = np.zeros(numintervals) intervalstep = 1.0 / numintervals for idx in range(numintervals): smin = idx intervalstep smax = (idx + 1) intervalstep # Find max frequency component active in this interval vglookup[idx] = np.argmax(magnitudes) intervalstep return vglookup def preprocessvolume(volumedata, transferfunction, Tmax): """Offline setup: compute importance volume and frequency texture.""" gradients = computegradientvolume(volumedata) importancevolume = maxfilter(gradients, width=2 Tmax) frequencytexture = computetransferfunctionfrequencies(transferfunction) return importancevolume, frequencytexture def computestepsize(x0, fx0, importancevolume, frequencytexture, aPsi=1.0, bPsi=0.0, Tmax=8.0, oversampling=2.0): """Runtime: calculate adaptive step size for current ray position.""" # Fetch local gradient magnitude from Importance Volume gradmag = importancevolume[x0] # Estimate value interval I using Taylor expansion smin = fx0 - gradmag Tmax smax = fx0 + gradmag Tmax # Fetch maximal frequency vg(I) from Frequency Texture # Map interval to texture index intervalstep = 1.0 / frequencytexture.shape[0] idx = int((smin + smax) / 2.0 / intervalstep) idx = max(0, min(idx, frequencytexture.shape[0] - 1)) vg = frequencytexture[idx] # Calculate step size T denominator = oversampling vg abs(aPsi) gradmag if denominator == 0: return Tmax # Fallback to max step size if no frequency/gradient T = 1.0 / denominator return T T{max}: The maximal step size used for the max-filter width and Taylor expansion bounds. Typical value: 8. Oversampling Factor: 2. This compensates for errors introduced by the linear (tent) filter kernel used in ray casting reconstruction. Dynamic Transfer Functions: If the transfer function is shifted or scaled via \Psi(t) = a\Psi t + b\Psi, the step size must incorporate |a\Psi|. This allows interactive changes without re-running the FFT on the entire dataset. Approximation Error: The estimate vh = vg \max |f'(x)| is not tight; the actual maximal frequency might be higher. However, signal energy decays exponentially above this estimate, so no visible artifacts occur even without additional oversampling beyond the factor of 2. Memory: The Importance Volume requires memory equal to the dataset size. It contains redundancy due to the max-filter and can be compressed. Time Complexity: The pre-processing step involves FFT and gradient computation, which is done once or infrequently. Per step, the cost is two texture fetches (gradient and frequency) and a few floating-point operations. Memory Complexity: Requires an additional 3D texture (Importance Volume) of the same size as the dataset, plus a 2D Frequency Texture. Performance: Reduces sample points by 50-80% compared to non-adaptive methods without quality loss. Hand Dataset (300x300x300): Regular sampling: 430 samples/pixel, 1.2 FPS. Adaptive: 88 samples/pixel, 5.5 FPS. Direct sampling (theoretical optimal): 75 samples/pixel, 6.5 FPS. Abdomen Dataset (512x512x101): Regular sampling: 752 samples/pixel, 5 FPS. Adaptive: 404 samples/pixel, 6.2 FPS. Direct sampling: 197 samples/pixel, 8.1 FPS. Strengths: Handles non-linear transfer functions effectively; supports dynamic TF changes; significant speedup over regular sampling. Limitations: Less efficient than "direct sampling" (which uses global pre-computed frequencies) because it uses local approximations; requires extra memory for the Importance Volume; approximation may underestimate frequency, though artifacts are minimal. The method is based on the spectral analysis of function composition by Bergner et al. (2006). It was implemented as a module for the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) using C++ and OpenGL/GLSL, tested on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 280. It addresses the limitation of heuristic gradient-based methods which fail to account for high-frequency components introduced by non-linear transfer functions. name: Fixed-Resolution Surface Rendering with View Bounds
head: 2 mm however long rendering, Surface Rendering with Adaptive Voxel Sampling and View Bounds, qc_surfaces surface rendering
body: This method renders medical volumes (CT, MR, PET, RT Dose) as surfaces at a fixed spatial resolution of 2 mm, regardless of the volume's length, provided it stays within strict physical bounds. It solves the problem of coarse sampling in long volumes (e.g., whole-body scans), where previous methods limited the voxel count per side to 256, resulting in resolutions as coarse as ~7 mm for a 1,800 mm long scan. This method enforces a uniform 2 mm grid for visual consistency in medical review, specifically ensuring facial features are rendered with the same fidelity in whole-body scans as in head scans. Inputs: A medical volume dataset (voxel grid with physical spacing). Outputs: Six surface render views and associated projection data. Data Structures: Volume: Contains physical dimensions (Lx, Ly, Lz) in mm and voxel spacing (sx, sy, sz). Surface: Boolean flag large. If true, the volume is rejected. Crossings: 16-bit integers representing ray-surface intersections. Batch: A chunk of 64 slices processed simultaneously. Parameters: MINIMUMVOXEL: 2 mm. The target sampling resolution. LONGEST: 2,000 mm. Maximum allowed extent along the head-to-foot axis (Z). WIDEST: 1,000 mm. Maximum allowed extent along the other two axes (X, Y). BATCHSIZE: 64 slices. Steps: 1. Bound Check: Calculate the volume's physical extent along the head-to-foot axis (Ez) and the maximum extent of the other two axes (E{xy} = \max(Ex, Ey)). If Ez > \text{LONGEST} OR E{xy} > \text{WIDEST}: Set Surface.large = true. Return: No mask, no image, no projection. Slices beyond the cine strip are held (not decoded). Ensure the volume orientation is known to identify the head-to-foot axis correctly. 2. Determine Sampling Resolution: Calculate the effective voxel spacing s{eff}: s{eff} = \min(s{min}, \text{MINIMUM\VOXEL}) where s{min} = \min(sx, sy, sz) is the smallest physical spacing of the input volume. If the volume is already finer than 2 mm, use its native spacing to preserve detail, but do not upsample. 3. Generate Views: Define six viewing directions. Five are standard orthogonal views. The sixth is the "From Behind" view. From Behind Configuration: Rotate the view by 180 degrees around the vertical axis. The patient's left remains on the viewer's left. Rays travel along the voxels in the same direction as the frontal view, reusing frontal ray geometry. 4. Render Crossings (Batch Processing): For each of the six views: a. Initialize a row of crossings for the view width. b. Iterate through the volume slices in batches of BATCHSIZE (64 slices). c. For each batch: i. Step rays for the current slice batch alone. ii. Calculate surface intersections (crossings) for the rays. iii. Store crossings as 16-bit integers to save memory. d. Combine results from all batches into the final row. e. For the "From Behind" view, add a tile to each row but do not create new rows of crossings, as its rays are reversed frontal rays. 5. Handle Edge Cases: Edge Marks: The "From Behind" view draws edges facing the back. This ensures that a mark within two voxels of the slice edge is shown face-on rather than edge-on, correcting a previous pitfall where such marks were only visible as edges from front/side views. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersurface(volume, minvoxel=2.0, longest=2000.0, widest=1000.0, batchsize=64): # 1. Bound Check if volume.extentz > longest or max(volume.extentx, volume.extenty) > widest: return None, None, None # Large volume, hold slices # 2. Determine Resolution minspacing = min(volume.spacingx, volume.spacingy, volume.spacingz) stepsize = min(minspacing, minvoxel) # 3. Generate Views (6 total) views = [ {"name": "Front", "dir": (0, 0, 1)}, {"name": "Left", "dir": (1, 0, 0)}, {"name": "Right", "dir": (-1, 0, 0)}, {"name": "Top", "dir": (0, 1, 0)}, {"name": "Bottom", "dir": (0, -1, 0)}, {"name": "FromBehind", "dir": (0, 0, 1), "tile": True} ] results = {} for view in views: crossings = [] numslices = volume.numslices # 4. Batch Processing for start in range(0, numslices, batchsize): end = min(start + batchsize, numslices) batch = volume.getslices(start, end) # Step rays for the current slice batch alone for rayidx in range(volume.width): rayorigin = volume.getrayorigin(rayidx, view["name"]) raydir = view["dir"] for slicedata in batch: # Calculate surface intersection for this ray and slice t = (slicedata.z - rayorigin.z) / raydir.z if 0.0 <= t <= stepsize: intersection = int(t / stepsize) # Build crossings as 16-bit integers from the start to save memory crossings.append(intersection & 0xFFFF) # For the "From Behind" view, add a tile to each row but do not create new rows if view.get("tile"): for i in range(len(crossings)): crossings[i] |= 0x8000 # Mark tile bit results[view["name"]] = crossings return results Renders anatomical structures from five standard orthogonal directions. Sets itself apart by providing conventional diagnostic angles for general overview. Choose when standard DICOM viewer compatibility or routine anatomical review is required. Link: Standard Orthogonal Surface Rendering. Renders anatomical structures from a posterior direction rotated 180 degrees around the vertical axis. Sets itself apart by showing posterior surfaces face-on, resolving edge-case visibility issues where marks near slice edges were previously only visible edge-on. Choose when reviewing posterior features or ensuring consistent facial preview in whole-body scans. Link: From-Behind Surface Rendering. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the volume data itself. The largest rendered volume (1,000x1,000x2,000 mm) peaks at approximately 1.4 GB memory usage. Using 16-bit integers for crossings reduces intermediate memory overhead compared to 64-bit floats. Measured Performance: In a whole-body MR Otsu threshold calculation, memory usage dropped from 911 MB (with float64 copy) to 355 MB (direct comparison/chunked). Strengths: Consistent visual detail for medical review regardless of volume length; prevents coarse sampling artifacts in long volumes; memory efficient through batching and 16-bit integer storage. Limitations: Volumes exceeding 2,000 mm in length or 1,000 mm in width are not rendered at all; fixed resolution may be overkill for small volumes or under-resolving for very high-resolution small volumes (though native spacing is used if finer). When to use: Medical QC packs, contour sheets, and previews where consistent facial/anatomical detail is critical across varying scan lengths. When not to use: Volumes exceeding the physical bounds; real-time interactive rendering where memory is extremely constrained and the volume is very large. This method was introduced in the pymedphys project to address gaps in the QC pack's surface rendering capabilities. Prior to this change, volumes longer than 510 mm were coarsened to maintain a 256-voxel limit per side, leading to resolutions as coarse as ~7 mm for whole-body CTs. The change, documented in pull request #2434, added a "from behind" view and removed the voxel-side limit, enforcing a 2 mm sampling resolution for volumes within strict bounds. It is used in medical physics QC tools for verifying contour accuracy and dose distributions. name: Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) Optimization
body: NeRF Optimization trains a continuous volumetric scene representation, typically parameterized by a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), to predict density and color from 3D coordinates and viewing directions. It solves novel view synthesis by learning a differentiable volume rendering function that maps camera parameters to pixel colors via ray marching. It sets itself apart from discrete mesh-based rendering by modeling geometry as a continuous density field, allowing for high-fidelity reconstruction of complex, unstructured scenes without explicit topology. Builds on Adaptive Sampling and Resolution. Decouples density estimation from color evaluation using a coarse pass to guide importance sampling in a fine pass. Chosen when computational budget is limited but high-frequency detail is required. Uses an importance network to predict sparse sample locations and a reconstruction network to upsample the result. Chosen for interactive applications where end-to-end differentiability and sparse querying are prioritized over raw ray-casting speed. Exploits temporal smoothness in continuous viewpoint trajectories by reprojecting features from previous frames. Chosen for real-time interactive navigation where camera motion is smooth and previous frames are available. Optimizes the NeRF using gradients from a frozen 2D diffusion model rather than ground-truth images. Chosen for 3D generation from text or image priors where explicit 3D training data is unavailable. NeRF was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. The method represents a scene as a continuous 5D function mapping (x, y, z, \theta, \phi) to volume density and view-dependent color. Optimization involves minimizing the photometric loss between rendered images and ground-truth views using stochastic gradient descent. The foundational approach uses uniform sampling along rays, which is computationally expensive. Subsequent works have focused on acceleration through adaptive sampling, hierarchical representations, and alternative optimization objectives like Score Distillation Sampling.

name: Two-stage NeRF Rendering
head: Coarse and Fine Sampling, Proposal Network Sampler, Rendering Sampling Strategy
body: Two-stage NeRF Rendering is an acceleration technique for Neural Radiance Fields that decouples scene density estimation from detailed color evaluation. It reduces computational cost by first using a coarse pass to identify high-density regions, then importance-sampling a fine pass to refine the result. It sets itself apart from uniform sampling by concentrating computational effort on relevant geometry, and from single-stage methods by explicitly separating rough density estimation from detailed evaluation. The method consists of two distinct rendering passes: a coarse pass to estimate the transmittance and density distribution along rays, and a fine pass that refines the color and density estimates using samples concentrated in high-density regions identified by the coarse pass. Inputs: Ray bundle (origin o, direction d), near/far bounds (tn, tf), coarse network Nc, fine network Nf. Outputs: Rendered color C(r), depth, and optionally opacity for each ray r. Ray Samples: A list of 3D points ti along the ray. Network Outputs: For each point, the network returns density \sigma and color c. Weights: Importance weights wi derived from the coarse pass transmittance. 1. Coarse Sampling: Sample Nc points uniformly or stratified along the ray interval [tn, tf]. Query the coarse network Nc at these points to obtain density \sigmac and color cc. Compute transmittance Ti and weights wi for the coarse samples: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmac(tj) \Delta tj\right) wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmac(ti) \Delta ti)) where \Delta tj is the interval length between adjacent samples. Normalize weights if necessary for stability, though standard volume rendering formulas handle this naturally. 2. Fine Sampling: Use the coarse weights wi to define a probability distribution for sampling. Sample Nf points from this distribution (importance sampling). Query the fine network Nf at these points to obtain density \sigmaf and color cf. Compute final color: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{Nf} wi^f cf(ti) where wi^f are the importance weights derived from the fine samples' contribution to the volume integral, often re-weighted by the coarse transmittance to ensure unbiased estimation. Coarse samples per ray (Nc): Typically 64. Fine samples per ray (Nf): Typically 192 (64 initial + 128 additional). Total samples per ray: 256. Initial Sampler: Can be uniform or piecewise; defaults to uniform if specified. Update Schedule: Determines how often proposal networks are updated during training. Base-NeRF Variant: Proposal 1 queries 128 linearly spaced samples, Proposal 2 queries 96 samples using probability density sampling, and the final NeRF model queries 48 samples using probability density sampling (increased to 192 at test time). Precision: Floating-point precision in transmittance calculation can lead to underflow in long rays. Use log-space computations for stability. Boundaries: Ensure near/far planes are tight to avoid sampling empty space. Degenerate Input: If density is zero everywhere, weights become uniform, and the fine pass may waste samples. A fallback to uniform sampling is recommended. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twostagerender(rayorigins, raydirections, tnear, tfar, coarsenet, finenet): # Step 1: Coarse Sampling numcoarse = 64 # Stratified sampling along the ray interval tcoarse = tnear + (tfar - tnear) (torch.rand(numcoarse) + torch.arange(numcoarse)) / numcoarse # Query coarse network sigmac, colorc = coarsenet(tcoarse) # Compute transmittance and weights dt = (tfar - tnear) / numcoarse alphac = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmac dt) Tc = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alphac, dim=0) Tc = torch.cat([torch.ones(1, device=Tc.device, dtype=Tc.dtype), Tc[:-1]], dim=0) # T1 = 1.0 wc = Tc alphac # Normalize weights for sampling wc = wc / wc.sum() # Step 2: Fine Sampling numfine = 192 # Importance sampling from coarse distribution indices = torch.multinomial(wc, numfine, replacement=True) tfine = tcoarse[indices] + torch.rand(numfine) dt # Query fine network sigmaf, colorf = finenet(tfine) # Compute fine weights alphaf = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigmaf dt) Tf = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alphaf, dim=0) Tf = torch.cat([torch.ones(1, device=Tf.device, dtype=Tf.dtype), Tf[:-1]], dim=0) wf = Tf alphaf # Compute final color using fine weights finalcolor = torch.sum(wf colorf, dim=0) return finalcolor Combined sampling stacks an occupancy grid on top of a proposal network to reduce the number of rays processed and shrink the near-far plane for remaining rays. It leverages transmittance estimation from both structures to skip empty space more effectively than either method alone. It differs from VF-NeRF Rendering Pipeline by using a learned proposal network for initial density estimation rather than a fixed grid, and from Coarse-Fine Sampling by explicitly combining a sparse spatial index with a neural density prior to prune rays before the final fine sampling stage. The VF-NeRF rendering pipeline is a two-stage volume rendering method that uses a vector field network to predict surface normals, features, and Jacobians for density estimation and shading. It differs from standard NeRF by deriving density from the directional derivative of the vector field rather than a direct scalar field prediction, enabling explicit surface representation within the implicit volume. It builds on Two-stage NeRF Rendering by integrating vector field-based density computation into the coarse and fine sampling passes. Coarse-Fine Sampling is a two-pass rendering technique for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that improves image quality and sampling efficiency by first estimating the scene's density distribution with a coarse pass, then using that distribution to importance-sample a fine pass. It sets itself apart from uniform sampling by concentrating computational effort on high-density regions identified in the first pass, and from single-stage methods by decoupling the rough density estimation from the detailed color/density evaluation. Semantic Loss Computation computes the cross-entropy loss over coarse and fine semantic predictions for query rays to train a generalizable semantic field. It differs from standard photometric NeRF losses by enforcing semantic consistency across views via ray-based feature projection, allowing the model to learn contextual geometry for semantic information rather than just color. It is a core component of the Two-stage NeRF Rendering pipeline, specifically enabling the training of the semantic head alongside the geometry-aware network. One-Step NeRF Rendering is a volume rendering method that eliminates the multi-stage sampling pipeline by using only stratified sampling for both foreground and background components. It solves the computational overhead of importance sampling and proposal networks by treating the background as an outer volume, similar to the NeRF++ approach. It differs from Two-stage NeRF Rendering by removing the fine-stage refinement and from Coarse-Fine Sampling by using a single uniform depth distribution for all samples. Base-NeRF uses a hierarchical proposal network structure. Proposal 1 queries 128 linearly spaced samples, Proposal 2 queries 96 samples using probability density sampling, and the final NeRF model queries 48 samples using probability density sampling. At test time, final NeRF sampling is increased to 192 points for higher rendering quality. The architecture uses Hash Grids and MLPs: Proposal 1 (Hash Grid 5/17/16/64, MLP 1/16), Proposal 2 (Hash Grid 5/17/16/256, MLP 1/16), NeRF (Hash Grid 5/19/16/2048, MLP 1/64). On the Blender dataset, rays corresponding to background can be heavily pruned, yielding large speedups. NeRF-ID renders views up to 50% faster while achieving better results than NeRF†. HeadNeRF computes a low-resolution 2D feature map IF from ray samples to serve as input for a subsequent 2D neural rendering module. It samples 64 points per ray. The output feature map IF dimensions are R^{256 \times 32 \times 32}. Hierarchical volume sampling is removed to speed up inference, accepting potential quality trade-offs for real-time performance. A method to balance appearance and geometric continuity in NeRF synthesis by searching patches in two phases, significantly enhancing speed. In the first phase, search patches for density only. Speedup comparison: For 100^2 size, Baseline 163.47s vs Two-phase 14.99s (10.90x); for 200^2, 270.70s vs 23.62s (11.46x); for 300^2, 454.41s vs 38.46s (11.82x); for 400^2, 714.64s vs 59.57s (12.00x). NeRSTF combines Signed Distance Fields (SDF) and Texture Fields (TF) or a combined NeRSTF model, using a two-pass rendering approach (coarse stratified, fine importance) to produce backpropagable views. Steps: 1. Query the model (sdf/tf or nerstf) for density, signed distance, and channels at query points. 2. Render rays with coarse, stratified samples using StratifiedRaySampler. 3. Render rays with fine, importance-weighted samples using the sampler from the coarse pass. 4. Scale output channels by channelscale (default 255.0). 5. If separatesharedsamples is true, include coarse results in the output dictionary. Parameters: ncoarsesamples, nfinesamples, separatesharedsamples. Time Complexity: O(Nc + Nf) network queries per ray, where Nc and Nf are the number of coarse and fine samples. Memory Complexity: O(Nc + Nf) to store intermediate densities and colors. Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA V100, rendering a realistic synthetic dataset (640k rays/image) or real scenes (762k rays/image) takes approximately 30 seconds per frame, resulting in 150-200 million network queries per image. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of rays and samples. Strengths: Significant reduction in network queries compared to uniform sampling; improved image quality by focusing on high-density regions. Limitations: Increased implementation complexity; potential for artifacts if coarse sampling is insufficient. When to use: When computational resources are limited but high-quality novel view synthesis is required. When not to use: For real-time applications requiring very low latency without hardware acceleration, or for scenes with uniform density where uniform sampling is sufficient. Two-stage NeRF Rendering was introduced in the original NeRF paper by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It established the coarse-to-fine sampling paradigm that subsequent acceleration methods, proposal networks, and hierarchical sampling strategies have extended and optimized.
