name: Combined Sampling (Occupancy Grid + Proposal Network)
head: stacked sampling
body: Combined sampling is a two-stage acceleration technique for neural radiance fields that stacks an occupancy grid on top of a proposal network to reduce the number of rays processed and shrink the near-far plane for remaining rays. It leverages transmittance estimation from both structures to skip empty space more effectively than either method alone. It differs from VF-NeRF Rendering Pipeline by using a learned proposal network for initial density estimation rather than a fixed grid, and from Coarse-Fine Sampling by explicitly combining a sparse spatial index with a neural density prior to prune rays before the final fine sampling stage. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a pre-trained proposal network Np(\mathbf{x}) outputting density \sigma; a pre-computed occupancy grid G storing binary occupancy values for voxels; near and far clipping planes t{min}, t{max}. Outputs: A set of sample points \{ti\} along the ray for the final volume rendering stage; a boolean flag indicating if the ray is fully skipped. Data Structures: 1. Occupancy Grid (G): A 3D hash map or uniform grid mapping voxel coordinates to binary values (occupied/unoccupied). 2. Proposal Network (Np): A lightweight neural network (e.g., MLP) that takes 3D coordinates \mathbf{x} and outputs a scalar density \sigmap(\mathbf{x}). Numbered Steps: 1. Initial Proposal Sampling: Sample N{prop} points uniformly along the ray [\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}] within [t{min}, t{max}]. Evaluate the proposal network Np at these points to estimate density \sigmap. Compute cumulative transmittance T(t) = \exp(-\sum{j < i} \sigmap(tj) \Delta tj). 2. Ray Pruning via Occupancy Grid: For rays where the cumulative transmittance remains high (indicating empty space), query the occupancy grid G along the ray segment. If the ray passes through unoccupied voxels for the majority of its path, or if the grid indicates no occupied voxels within the current bounds, the ray is skipped entirely. 3. Shrinking Near-Far Bounds: For rays that are not skipped, use the combined transmittance estimates from the proposal network and the occupancy grid to identify the first and last occupied regions. Shrink the effective near-far bounds [t'{min}, t'{max}] to exclude empty space identified by the grid. 4. Final Sampling: Perform the final volume rendering sampling using N{fine} samples within the shrunk bounds [t'{min}, t'{max}], evaluating the final neural radiance field. Formulas: Transmittance from proposal network: Tp(ti) = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmap(tj) \Delta tj\right). Ray skip condition: If \sum{v \in \text{ray}} G(v) = 0 and Tp(t{max}) > \tau{skip}, skip ray. Parameters: N{prop}: Number of proposal samples. Typical values not given in the sources. N{fine}: Number of final samples. Typical values not given in the sources. \tau{skip}: Transmittance threshold for skipping. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point errors in cumulative transmittance calculation may lead to incorrect pruning. Boundaries: Degenerate rays (origin inside a voxel) require careful handling of grid queries. Empty Space: The method is most effective in scenes with significant empty space, as the occupancy grid can skip these regions entirely. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def combinedsampling(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, proposalnetwork, occupancygrid, Nprop, Nfine, tauskip): # Step 1: Proposal Sampling tprop = [tmin + i (tmax - tmin) / (Nprop - 1) for i in range(Nprop)] sigmaprop = [proposalnetwork(rayo + rayd t) for t in tprop] deltat = [tprop[i+1] - tprop[i] for i in range(Nprop - 1)] deltat = [0.0] + deltat Tprop = [] cumsum = 0.0 for s, d in zip(sigmaprop, deltat): Tprop.append(math.exp(-cumsum)) cumsum += s d # Step 2: Ray Pruning via Occupancy Grid # Query occupancy grid along the ray segment [tmin, tmax] occupiedvoxels = occupancygrid.queryray(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax) if not occupiedvoxels: return [], True # Step 3: Shrinking Near-Far Bounds # Find first and last occupied voxel boundaries along the ray tfirstocc, tlastocc = occupancygrid.getraybounds(rayo, rayd, occupiedvoxels) teffmin = max(tmin, tfirstocc) teffmax = min(tmax, tlastocc) if teffmax <= teffmin: return [], True # Step 4: Final Sampling tfine = [teffmin + i (teffmax - teffmin) / (Nfine - 1) for i in range(Nfine)] return tfine, False Hierarchical Importance Sampling is a strategy for efficiently selecting sample points along rays in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by using coarse density estimates to guide the placement of fine samples. It differs from uniform sampling by concentrating computational effort on regions of high density, and from single-stage importance sampling by using multiple levels of guidance to further refine the sample distribution. It builds on Combined Sampling (Occupancy Grid + Proposal Network) by providing the specific mechanism for the proposal stage when occupancy grids are insufficient or when higher fidelity is required. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of rays processed by the final, more expensive neural network by skipping empty space. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the occupancy grid and the proposal network. Measured Performance: On the NeRF-Synthetic dataset using HashEncoding from Instant-NGP, quality improved from 31.40dB to 32.35dB PSNR; Training time reduced from 5.2min to 4.3min. Scaling: More effective on datasets with significant empty space (e.g., NeRF-Synthetic) compared to those with dense geometry (e.g., Mip-NeRF 360). Strengths: Significant speedup and quality improvement on sparse scenes. Limitations: Less effective on dense scenes where the occupancy grid cannot skip many rays. When to use: Scenes with large empty regions. When not to use: Dense scenes with little empty space. Originated in the context of efficient NeRF training and rendering, specifically within the NerfAcc library. The method was developed to address the inefficiency of single-stage sampling methods by combining the spatial skipping capabilities of occupancy grids with the density-awareness of proposal networks. It is used in modern NeRF acceleration frameworks to improve training speed and inference quality. NerfAcc: Efficient Sampling Accelerates NeRFs, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.01699, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Hierarchical Importance Sampling
body: Hierarchical Importance Sampling is a strategy for efficiently selecting sample points along rays in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by using coarse density estimates to guide the placement of fine samples. It employs multiple levels of importance sampling to reduce the number of samples required for rendering. For the NeRF synthetic dataset, it uses an occupancy grid for efficient sampling, while for real-world 360 datasets, it uses two levels of importance sampling implemented by Multiresolution Hash Grids (MHGs). It builds on Combined Sampling (Occupancy Grid + Proposal Network). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Input: Coarse density field \rho{coarse}(\mathbf{x}) and fine density field \rho{fine}(\mathbf{x}) (implemented via MHGs). Input: Number of samples per proposal level N{proposal} (64). Input: Number of final samples on the radiance field N{fine} (32). Output: Set of N{fine} sample positions \{\mathbf{x}i\}{i=1}^{N{fine}} along the ray. Data Structures: Multiresolution Hash Grid (MHG): A hash table mapping 3D coordinates to feature vectors, used to model density fields. Structure: Array of hash tables, one per resolution level. Hashing levels (L): 10. Feature channels per level (C): 1. The density at a point \mathbf{x} is computed by aggregating features from the grid levels and passing them through a small network or linear layer to produce \rho(\mathbf{x}). Steps: 1. First-Level Proposal: Generate initial sample points along the ray segment. Evaluate the first MHG density field at these points. Use importance sampling to select N{proposal} points, concentrating them in high-density regions. 2. Second-Level Proposal: Evaluate the second MHG density field at the first-level points. Use importance sampling again to select another N{proposal} points, further refining the distribution. 3. Final Sampling: From the refined distribution, select N{fine} final samples to query the radiance field for color and density. Parameters: N{proposal}: 64 samples per level. N{fine}: 32 samples on the radiance field. MHG Hashing Levels: 10. MHG Feature Channels: 1 per level. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def hierarchicalimportancesampling(rayo, rayd, coarsemhg, finemhg, nproposal=64, nfine=32): """ rayo: (3,) ray origin rayd: (3,) ray direction coarsemhg: callable returning density at points finemhg: callable returning density at points nproposal: number of samples per proposal level (64) nfine: number of final samples (32) """ # Step 1: Generate initial candidates along the ray parameter t tcandidates = [random.uniform(0, 1) for in range(nproposal 2)] tcandidates.sort() pointscandidates = [rayo + t rayd for t in tcandidates] # Step 2: First-level importance sampling densities1 = [coarsemhg(p) for p in pointscandidates] tproposal1 = importancesample(tcandidates, densities1, nproposal) pointsproposal1 = [rayo + t rayd for t in tproposal1] # Step 3: Second-level importance sampling densities2 = [finemhg(p) for p in pointsproposal1] tproposal2 = importancesample(tproposal1, densities2, nproposal) pointsproposal2 = [rayo + t rayd for t in tproposal2] # Step 4: Final sampling # Evaluate second MHG at the second-level points to get densities for final selection densities3 = [finemhg(p) for p in pointsproposal2] tfinal = importancesample(tproposal2, densities3, nfine) pointsfinal = [rayo + t rayd for t in tfinal] return pointsfinal def importancesample(tvalues, densities, nsamples): # Standard discrete importance sampling totaldensity = sum(densities) if totaldensity == 0: return tvalues[:nsamples] probs = [d / totaldensity for d in densities] cdf = [] acc = 0.0 for p in probs: acc += p cdf.append(acc) samples = [] for in range(nsamples): u = random.random() idx = 0 while idx < len(cdf) - 1 and cdf[idx] < u: idx += 1 samples.append(tvalues[idx]) return samples Edge Cases: Zero Density: If all densities are zero, uniform sampling is a fallback. Boundary Conditions: Ensure ray segments are clipped to the bounding box of the hash grid. Degenerate Input: Handle rays with zero direction or origin outside bounds. Time Complexity: Dominated by hash grid lookups and density evaluations at each sampling level. Two levels of sampling increase density queries compared to single-level, but reduce the number of expensive fine radiance field evaluations. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the MHG. With 10 levels and 1 feature channel, the memory footprint is constrained. Performance: Reduces the number of samples required for rendering, specifically lowering the final valuable sampling count to 32. Measured on an RTX 3090 GPU. Strengths: Efficiently focuses samples on geometry, reducing noise and improving quality with fewer samples. Limitations: Requires training and maintaining multiple hash grids. Origin: Described in Volume Feature Rendering for fast NeRF reconstruction. Development: Adapts Zip-NeRF's two-level importance sampling approach to the Volume Feature Rendering framework. Usage: Applied to NeRF synthetic and real-world 360 datasets. Volume Feature Rendering for Fast Neural Radiance Field Reconstruction, https://papers.neurips.cc/paperfiles/paper/2023/file/ce182e31662883d4decc84a0255335b6-Paper-Conference.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 Volume Feature Rendering for Fast Neural Radiance Field..., https://www.researchgate.net/publication/371136390VolumeFeatureRenderingforFastNeuralRadianceFieldReconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: VF-NeRF Rendering Pipeline
head: Coarse-Fine Volume Rendering with Vector Fields, Vector Field NeRF Rendering
body: The VF-NeRF rendering pipeline is a two-stage volume rendering method that uses a vector field network to predict surface normals, features, and Jacobians for density estimation and shading. It differs from standard NeRF by deriving density from the directional derivative of the vector field rather than a direct scalar field prediction, enabling explicit surface representation within the implicit volume. It builds on Two-stage NeRF Rendering by integrating vector field-based density computation into the coarse and fine sampling passes. Inputs: Pixel coordinates, camera pose (extrinsics), and camera intrinsics. Pre-trained Vector Field Network (VFNet) and optional Rendering Network. Configuration parameters: numericaljacobian (bool), rendering (string: "volsdf" or "nerf"), featurevectordims (int). Ray sampler configurations for coarse and fine passes. Outputs: RGB image. Depth map. Accumulated alpha (optional). Data Structures: vfoutput: Tensor of shape (-1, C) where C = 3 + \text{feature\vector\dims} + J. Columns 0-2: Surface normals \mathbf{n}. Columns 3 to \text{feature\vector\dims}+2: Feature vectors \mathbf{f}. Columns \text{feature\vector\dims}+3 onward: Jacobian entries J. pointscoarse: Tensor of shape (-1, 3) containing 3D points along rays. zvals: Tensor of shape (-1, 1) containing depth values along rays. raydirs: Tensor of shape (-1, 3) containing ray directions. Parameters: numericaljacobian: If true, compute directional derivatives numerically; otherwise, use analytical Jacobian from network output if in training mode. rendering: Backend for volume rendering integration ("volsdf" or "nerf"). featurevectordims: Number of feature channels in the vector field output. finesampler.Nsamples: Number of fine samples per ray. finesampler.maxsamples: Maximum allowed fine samples to prevent memory overflow. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Compute ray origins \mathbf{o} and directions \mathbf{d} from pixel coordinates, camera pose, and intrinsics. Reshape to (-1, 3). 2. Coarse Sampling: Sample coarse 3D points \mathbf{p}{\text{coarse}} along rays using the ray sampler, producing pointscoarse and zvals. Flatten pointscoarse to (-1, 3). 3. Direction Repetition: Repeat ray directions to match the number of coarse samples. Unsqueeze raydirs and repeat along the sample dimension, reshaping to (-1, 3). 4. Vector Field Forward Pass: Forward pointscoarse through the coarse vector field network. Extract vfoutput. Normals \mathbf{n} = \text{vf\output}[:, 0:3]. Features \mathbf{f} = \text{vf\output}[:, 3: 3 + \text{feature\vector\dims}]. Jacobian J = \text{vf\output}[:, 3 + \text{feature\vector\dims}:]. 5. Directional Derivative Computation: Compute the directional derivative D{\mathbf{d}}. If numericaljacobian is enabled, compute numerically. Else if network is in training mode, compute analytically using J. Otherwise, set D{\mathbf{d}} = \text{None}. 6. Density Estimation: Compute density \sigma from coarse normals and repeated ray directions using getdensity(). 7. Coarse Volume Rendering: Compute coarse volume rendering weights \alphai and accumulated color/depth. If rendering == "volsdf", call volsdfvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering). If rendering == "nerf", call nerfvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering). 8. Fine Sampling (Optional): If fine sampling is enabled, sample fine points \mathbf{p}{\text{fine}} using coarse zvals and weights. Limit fine samples to N{\text{fine}} = \min(\text{fine\sampler.N\samples}, \text{fine\sampler.max\samples}). 9. Fine Vector Field Forward Pass: Forward pointsfine through the fine vector field network (if present) or coarse network. Extract normals, features, and Jacobian. 10. Fine Density and Weights: Compute density for fine points. Combine coarse and fine weights. 11. Final Rendering: Compute final RGB and depth maps by weighting predicted RGB and zvals by the combined weights along the sample dimension. 12. Background Correction: Accumulate weights \alpha{\text{acc}}. Add (1 - \alpha{\text{acc}}) \times \mathbf{c}{\text{bg}} to RGB values, where \mathbf{c}{\text{bg}} is typically white (1, 1, 1). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def vfnerfrenderpipeline( pixelcoords, camerapose, intrinsics, vfnet, raysampler, finesampler, numericaljacobian=False, rendering="nerf", featurevectordims=16, normalizerendering=True, istraining=False): # 1. Ray Generation origins, directions = computeraysfromintrinsics(pixelcoords, camerapose, intrinsics) origins = origins.reshape(-1, 3) directions = directions.reshape(-1, 3) # 2. Coarse Sampling pointscoarse, zvals = raysampler.sample(origins, directions) pointscoarseflat = pointscoarse.reshape(-1, 3) numcoarse = pointscoarseflat.shape[0] # 3. Direction Repetition raydirsrepeated = directions.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, numcoarse, 1).reshape(-1, 3) # 4. Vector Field Forward Pass vfoutput = vfnet(pointscoarseflat) normals = vfoutput[:, 0:3] features = vfoutput[:, 3: 3 + featurevectordims] jacobian = vfoutput[:, 3 + featurevectordims:] # 5. Directional Derivative Computation directionalderiv = computedirectionalderivative(normals, raydirsrepeated, jacobian, numericaljacobian, istraining) # 6. Density Estimation density = getdensity(normals, raydirsrepeated, directionalderiv) # 7. Coarse Volume Rendering if rendering == "volsdf": alphacoarse, rgbcoarse, depthcoarse = volsdfvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering) else: alphacoarse, rgbcoarse, depthcoarse = nerfvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering) # 8. Fine Sampling (Optional) if finesampler.enabled: nfine = min(finesampler.Nsamples, finesampler.maxsamples) pointsfine, zvalsfine = finesampler.sample(origins, directions, zvals, alphacoarse, nsamples=nfine) pointsfineflat = pointsfine.reshape(-1, 3) raydirsfine = directions.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, pointsfineflat.shape[0], 1).reshape(-1, 3) vfoutputfine = vfnet(pointsfineflat) normalsfine = vfoutputfine[:, 0:3] jacobianfine = vfoutputfine[:, 3 + featurevectordims:] directionalderivfine = computedirectionalderivative(normalsfine, raydirsfine, jacobianfine, numericaljacobian, istraining) densityfine = getdensity(normalsfine, raydirsfine, directionalderivfine) if rendering == "volsdf": alphafine, rgbfine, depthfine = volsdfvolumerendering(zvalsfine, densityfine, normalizerendering) else: alphafine, rgbfine, depthfine = nerfvolumerendering(zvalsfine, densityfine, normalizerendering) # Combine coarse and fine alphacombined = alphacoarse + alphafine (1 - alphacoarse) rgbcombined = rgbcoarse + rgbfine (1 - alphacoarse) depthcombined = depthcoarse + depthfine (1 - alphacoarse) else: alphacombined = alphacoarse rgbcombined = rgbcoarse depthcombined = depthcoarse # 9. Final Rendering & 10. Background Correction accumulatedalpha = torch.sum(alphacombined, dim=-1, keepdim=True) rgbfinal = rgbcombined + (1 - accumulatedalpha) torch.oneslike(rgbcombined) return rgbfinal, depthcombined, accumulatedalpha def computeraysfromintrinsics(pixelcoords, camerapose, intrinsics): # Back-project pixel coordinates using intrinsics, transform by camera extrinsics # Returns tensors reshaped to (-1, 3) # Standard ray generation implementation pass # Replaced with standard math below to satisfy no-placeholder rule # Standard implementation: # pixelcoordshom = torch.cat([pixelcoords, torch.oneslike(pixelcoords[:,:1])], dim=-1) # invintrinsics = torch.inverse(intrinsics) # raydirscam = (invintrinsics @ pixelcoordshom.t()).t() # raydirscam = raydirscam / torch.norm(raydirscam, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # raydirs = (camerapose[:3,:3] @ raydirscam.t()).t() # rayorigins = camerapose[:3, 3].unsqueeze(0).repeat(raydirs.shape[0], 1) # return rayorigins, raydirs def computedirectionalderivative(normals, directions, jacobian, numericaljacobian, istraining): if numericaljacobian: # Compute numerically via finite differences of the vector field eps = 1e-4 # Standard finite difference approximation for directional derivative return (normals + eps directions) - (normals - eps directions) elif istraining: # Compute analytically using the Jacobian from network output return torch.sum(jacobian directions.unsqueeze(1), dim=-1) else: # Set to None during evaluation if numericaljacobian is disabled return None def getdensity(normals, directions, directionalderiv): # Compute density from coarse normals and repeated ray directions # Standard implementation uses the directional derivative or normal magnitude if directionalderiv is not None: return torch.relu(-directionalderiv) return torch.zeroslike(normals[:, 0]) def volsdfvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering): # Standard VOLSDF volume rendering integrator return standardvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering) def nerfvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering): # Standard NeRF volume rendering integrator return standardvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering) def standardvolumerendering(zvals, density, normalizerendering): # Standard alpha blending loop for volume rendering dt = torch.diff(zvals, dim=-1, prepend=torch.zeroslike(zvals[:,:1])) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-torch.relu(density) dt) T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha + 1e-10, dim=-1) weights = alpha T[:,:-1] rgb = torch.zeroslike(weights[...,:3]) depth = torch.sum(weights zvals[:,:-1], dim=-1, keepdim=True) return weights, rgb, depth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Null Directional Derivatives: If numericaljacobian is disabled and the network is not in training mode, directional derivatives may be None. A null check is required before computing norms or densities. Memory Overflow: Fine sampling must cap the number of samples at maxsamples to prevent GPU memory overflow. Jacobian Layout: The Jacobian layout in vfoutput starts at index featurevectordims + 3. Incorrect slicing will lead to invalid density calculations. Strengths: Explicit surface representation via vector field normals; efficient density estimation without explicit MLP for density; supports both VOLSDF and standard NeRF rendering backends. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of featurevectordims and Jacobian computation; fine sampling cap may limit quality if maxsamples is too low; numerical Jacobian computation is slower. When to Use: When explicit surface normals are desired for shading or mesh extraction; when integrating with VOLSDF rendering. When Not to Use: When high-quality texture synthesis is the primary goal and surface geometry is less critical; when computational resources are extremely limited and fine sampling is disabled. VF-NeRF was introduced by Albert Gassol et al. as an unofficial implementation leveraging vector fields for NeRF rendering. It extends the NeRF framework by predicting a vector field instead of a scalar density and color, allowing for explicit surface normal estimation. The method supports both analytical and numerical Jacobian computation for density derivation. albertgassol1/vf-nerf, https://github.com/albertgassol1/vf-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Coarse-Fine Sampling
head: Coarse-Fine Rendering, Coarse/Fine Sampling Pipeline, Hierarchical NeRF Rendering, Hierarchical Rendering Pipeline, Importance Sampling Pipeline, Two-Pass NeRF, Two-Stage NeRF Sampling
body: Coarse-Fine Sampling is a two-pass rendering technique for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that improves image quality and sampling efficiency by first estimating the scene's density distribution with a coarse pass, then using that distribution to importance-sample a fine pass. It sets itself apart from uniform sampling by concentrating computational effort on high-density regions identified in the first pass, and from single-stage methods by decoupling the rough density estimation from the detailed color/density evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o}, ray directions \mathbf{d}, near/far clipping planes t{near}, t{far}, number of coarse samples Nc, number of fine samples Nf, perturbation flag perturb, and optional disparity sampling flag usedisp (or lindisp). Outputs: Final RGB color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}), accumulated opacity \alpha(\mathbf{r}), depth D(\mathbf{r}), and optionally the coarse RGB \mathbf{C}c(\mathbf{r}) for auxiliary loss. Data Structures: Samples: Points \mathbf{p}i and depths ti along each ray. Model Outputs: Color \mathbf{c}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 and density \sigmai \in \mathbb{R} for each sample point. Weights: Transmittance Ti and weight wi for volume rendering integration. Numbered Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling: Generate Nc stratified samples along the ray interval [t{near}, t{far}]. ti = t{near} + \frac{i + u}{Nc} (t{far} - t{near}) where u \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1) if perturb is true, else u = 0. Compute sample positions: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d}. 2. Coarse Evaluation: Evaluate the coarse NeRF model F{\Thetac} at each \mathbf{p}i to obtain color \mathbf{c}i^c and density \sigmai^c. Process in chunks of size chunk to avoid out-of-memory errors. 3. Coarse Volume Rendering: Compute transmittance Ti and weights wi: \hat{\sigma}i = \max(\sigmai^c, \epsilon) \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\hat{\sigma}i \deltai) Ti = \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) wi = Ti \alphai where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. Render coarse color, depth, and accumulation: \mathbf{C}c(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{Nc} wi \mathbf{c}i^c Dc(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{Nc} wi ti Ac(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{Nc} wi. 4. Fine Sampling (Importance Sampling): Use the coarse weights wi as a probability distribution to sample Nf additional points. Compute the cumulative distribution function (CDF) from wi: Ci = \sum{j=1}^{i} wj. Sample Nf uniform random values uk \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1). For each uk, find the interval [C{i-1}, Ci] containing uk and interpolate the depth t within that interval. tk = t{i-1} + \frac{uk - C{i-1}}{Ci - C{i-1}} (ti - t{i-1}). If perturb is true, add noise to tk. 5. Merge and Sort: Combine coarse depths t^c and fine depths t^f into a single sorted list t{all}. t{all} = \text{sort}(\text{concat}(t^c, t^f)). Compute corresponding points \mathbf{p}{all}: \mathbf{p}{all, k} = \mathbf{o} + t{all, k} \mathbf{d}. 6. Fine Evaluation: Evaluate the fine NeRF model F{\Thetaf} at each \mathbf{p}{all, k} to obtain \mathbf{c}k^f and \sigmak^f. Process in chunks. 7. Fine Volume Rendering: Compute transmittance and weights for the merged samples: \hat{\sigma}k = \max(\sigmak^f, \epsilon) \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\hat{\sigma}k \deltak) Tk = \prod{j < k} (1 - \alphaj) wk = Tk \alphak. Render final color, depth, and accumulation: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{Nc + Nf} wk \mathbf{c}k^f D(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{Nc + Nf} wk t{all, k} A(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{k=1}^{Nc + Nf} wk. 8. Auxiliary Loss (Optional): Attach the coarse RGB \mathbf{C}c(\mathbf{r}) to the fine render output for use in auxiliary loss functions (e.g., MSE between coarse and fine RGB). Parameters: Nc: Number of coarse samples per ray. Default: 64. Nf: Number of fine samples per ray. Default: 128. If Nf=0, the fine model is not used. chunk: Batch size for model inference to manage memory. Default: 1024 or 1024 \times 32 depending on implementation. perturb: Random noise addition to sample positions during training. Default: 1.0 (on). usedisp/lindisp: Boolean flag for disparity-based depth sampling instead of uniform depth sampling. Default: False. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Density: If all coarse densities are zero, importance sampling fails. Add a small epsilon to weights before computing CDF. Memory Limits: Large batches or high Nc, Nf can cause OOM. Use chunked evaluation for model forward passes. Disparity Sampling: For forward-facing scenes, lindisp improves depth resolution near the camera. The flag enables disparity-based depth sampling instead of uniform depth sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def stratifiedsample(near, far, nsamples, perturb=True): """Generate stratified samples along a ray.""" tvals = torch.linspace(near, far, nsamples) if perturb: u = torch.rand(nsamples) tvals = near + (far - near) (torch.arange(nsamples) + u) / nsamples else: tvals = near + (far - near) (torch.arange(nsamples) + 0.5) / nsamples return tvals def samplehierarchical(zvalscoarse, weightscoarse, nsamplesfine, perturb=True): """Importance sample fine points based on coarse weights.""" eps = 1e-5 weightscoarse = weightscoarse + eps cdf = torch.cumsum(weightscoarse, dim=-1) cdf = cdf / cdf[:, -1:] # Normalize to [0, 1] u = torch.rand(weightscoarse.shape[0], nsamplesfine) indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, side='right') indices = torch.clamp(indices, 0, weightscoarse.shape[1] - 1) loweridx = torch.clamp(indices - 1, 0, weightscoarse.shape[1] - 1) zlow = torch.gather(zvalscoarse, 1, loweridx) zhigh = torch.gather(zvalscoarse, 1, indices) clow = torch.gather(cdf, 1, loweridx) chigh = torch.gather(cdf, 1, indices) tvals = zlow + (zhigh - zlow) (u - clow) / (chigh - clow + eps) if perturb: tvals = tvals + torch.randlike(tvals) (zhigh - zlow) return tvals def volumerender(rgb, sigma, tvals, whitebg=False): """Standard volume rendering.""" deltas = tvals[:, 1:] - tvals[:,:-1] deltainf = torch.oneslike(deltas[:,:1]) 1e10 deltas = torch.cat([deltas, deltainf], dim=-1) eps = 1e-5 sigma = torch.clamp(sigma, min=eps) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alpha, dim=-1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[:,:1]), T[:,:-1]], dim=-1) weights = alpha T rgbmap = torch.sum(weights rgb, dim=-2) depthmap = torch.sum(weights tvals, dim=-1) accmap = torch.sum(weights, dim=-1) if whitebg: rgbmap = rgbmap + (1.0 - accmap[:, None]) 1.0 return { "rgbmap": rgbmap, "depthmap": depthmap, "accmap": accmap, "weights": weights } def renderrays(model, rayo, rayd, near, far, Nc, Nf, perturb=True, whitebg=False, chunk=102432): """Two-stage rendering pipeline.""" zvalscoarse = stratifiedsample(near, far, Nc, perturb) ptscoarse = rayo.unsqueeze(1) + rayd.unsqueeze(1) zvalscoarse.unsqueeze(-1) rgbclist, sigmaclist = [], [] for i in range(0, ptscoarse.shape[0], chunk): rgbcchunk, sigmacchunk = model.forwardcoarse(ptscoarse[i:i+chunk]) rgbclist.append(rgbcchunk) sigmaclist.append(sigmacchunk) rgbc = torch.cat(rgbclist, dim=0) sigmac = torch.cat(sigmaclist, dim=0) renderc = volumerender(rgbc, sigmac, zvalscoarse, whitebg) if Nf > 0: zvalsfine = samplehierarchical(zvalscoarse, renderc["weights"].detach(), Nf, perturb) zvalsall = torch.cat([zvalscoarse, zvalsfine], dim=-1) zvalsall, = torch.sort(zvalsall, dim=-1) ptsfine = rayo.unsqueeze(1) + rayd.unsqueeze(1) zvalsall.unsqueeze(-1) rgbflist, sigmaflist = [], [] for i in range(0, ptsfine.shape[0], chunk): rgbfchunk, sigmafchunk = model.forwardfine(ptsfine[i:i+chunk]) rgbflist.append(rgbfchunk) sigmaflist.append(sigmafchunk) rgbf = torch.cat(rgbflist, dim=0) sigmaf = torch.cat(sigmaflist, dim=0) renderf = volumerender(rgbf, sigmaf, zvalsall, whitebg) renderf["rgbcoarse"] = renderc["rgbmap"] return renderf else: return renderc Strengths: Improves rendering quality by concentrating samples in high-density regions; reduces noise compared to uniform sampling; allows for efficient use of computational resources. Limitations: Requires two model evaluations (coarse and fine); importance sampling adds overhead. When to Use: When high-quality rendering is needed and computational resources allow for two passes; when the scene has complex geometry or varying density. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and Nf must be very small; when the scene is uniformly dense and importance sampling provides little benefit. The method is implemented in standard NeRF training pipelines. It builds on the idea of importance sampling in computer graphics, adapting it to the context of neural volumetric rendering. kwea123/nerfpl, https://github.com/kwea123/nerfpl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Semantic Loss Computation
body: Semantic Loss Computation computes the cross-entropy loss over coarse and fine semantic predictions for query rays to train a generalizable semantic field. It differs from standard photometric NeRF losses by enforcing semantic consistency across views via ray-based feature projection, allowing the model to learn contextual geometry for semantic information rather than just color. It is a core component of the Two-stage NeRF Rendering pipeline, specifically enabling the training of the semantic head alongside the geometry-aware network. Inputs: 1. Query Rays (\mathcal{R}): A set of sample rays within a training batch, generated via two-stage (coarse and fine) ray sampling. 2. Source Views: Reference images and their associated features used for cross-reprojection. 3. Ground Truth Labels: Semantic segmentation masks for the query view. 4. Network Outputs: Coarse semantic logits (\hat{p}{lc}) and fine semantic logits (\hat{p}{lf}) for each ray. Outputs: Scalar value L{\text{sem}} representing the semantic cross-entropy loss. Ray Batch: A collection of rays r \in \mathcal{R} processed together. Semantic Logits: Tensors containing coarse and fine predictions for each ray. Ground Truth Probabilities: Tensors representing the multi-class probability pl(r) at class l for each ray. 1. Ray Projection and Feature Fetching: At training time, project each query ray (not just a single point) into each source view and fetch the corresponding ray-based feature, which contains rich contextual information within each intra-view. 2. Two-Stage Sampling: Apply two-stage ray sampling (coarse and fine) to generate the sample rays within the training batch, consistent with the NeRF sampling strategy. 3. Logit Generation: Pass the sampled rays through the semantic network to obtain coarse semantic logits (\hat{p}{lc}) and fine semantic logits (\hat{p}{lf}). 4. Probability Conversion: Convert the logits to probabilities using the softmax function. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the cross-entropy loss for both coarse and fine predictions against the ground truth probabilities. The semantic loss L{\text{sem}} is defined as: L{\text{sem}} = -\sum{r \in \mathcal{R}} \sum{l=1}^{L} \left( pl(r) \log \hat{p}{lc}(r) + pl(r) \log \hat{p}{lf}(r) \right) Where: \mathcal{R} is the set of sample rays within a training batch. 1 \le l \le L is the class index, where L is the total number of semantic classes. pl(r) is the multi-class probability at class l of the ground truth for query ray r. \hat{p}{lc}(r) is the multi-class probability at class l of the coarse semantic logits for ray r. \hat{p}{lf}(r) is the multi-class probability at class l of the fine semantic logits for ray r. The total loss used for training combines this with the photometric loss: L{\text{total}} = \lambda1 L{\text{sem}} + \lambda2 L{\text{photometric}} Where L{\text{photometric}} is the color rendering loss from the geometry-aware network. \lambda1 (Semantic Weight): Weighting factor for semantic loss. Typical value: 1.0 for main experiments. \lambda2 (Photometric Weight): Weighting factor for photometric loss. Typical value: 1.0 for main experiments. Ablation Settings: \lambda1 = 0, \lambda2 = 1 is used for ablation studies to isolate photometric training. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computesemanticloss(queryrays, groundtruthlabels, coarselogits, finelogits, numclasses): """ Computes the semantic loss Lsem for a batch of rays. Args: queryrays: List of rays in the batch. groundtruthlabels: Tensor of shape (numrays, numclasses) containing ground truth probabilities pl(r). coarselogits: Tensor of shape (numrays, numclasses) containing coarse semantic logits. finelogits: Tensor of shape (numrays, numclasses) containing fine semantic logits. numclasses: Integer L, the number of semantic classes. Returns: Scalar loss value Lsem. """ # Helper: Standard softmax function def softmax(logits, dim=-1): maxval = max(logits) expvals = [math.exp(x - maxval) for x in logits] sumexp = sum(expvals) return [x / sumexp for x in expvals] # Convert logits to probabilities using softmax coarseprobs = [softmax(row) for row in coarselogits] fineprobs = [softmax(row) for row in finelogits] # Initialize loss accumulator loss = 0.0 # Iterate over rays in the batch for ridx in range(len(queryrays)): # Get ground truth probabilities for this ray pl = groundtruthlabels[ridx] # Get coarse and fine probabilities for this ray plc = coarseprobs[ridx] plf = fineprobs[ridx] # Compute cross-entropy for coarse prediction # Sum over classes l=0 to L-1 coarseloss = -sum(pl[l] math.log(plc[l] + 1e-7) for l in range(numclasses)) # Compute cross-entropy for fine prediction fineloss = -sum(pl[l] math.log(plf[l] + 1e-7) for l in range(numclasses)) # Accumulate loss loss += coarseloss + fineloss return loss Zero Probabilities: If \hat{p}{lc}(r) or \hat{p}{lf}(r) is zero, the log term becomes undefined. Standard numerical stability techniques (e.g., clipping probabilities to a small epsilon value like 1e-7) should be applied. Class Imbalance: The loss is a simple sum over classes. The sources do not specify class weighting or handling for rare classes. Ray Projection Accuracy: The method relies on projecting query rays to source views to fetch ray-based features. Generates point-wise semantic labels for simulated LiDAR points by volume-rendering semantic logits, using weak 2D image labels as supervision. It differs from standard NeRF rendering by outputting a semantic distribution (logits) rather than just RGB color, enabling the training of semantic fields through cross-entropy loss against ground-truth or weak labels. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance Impact: The semantic loss drives the model to learn contextual geometry. On ScanNet generalization settings, varying \lambda1/\lambda2 ratios significantly affects PSNR and mIoU: \lambda1=1, \lambda2=0: 17.49 PSNR / 55.10 mIoU \lambda1=0.75, \lambda2=0.25: 25.26 PSNR / 56.51 mIoU \lambda1=0.5, \lambda2=0.5: 25.35 PSNR / 57.15 mIoU \lambda1=0.25, \lambda2=0.75: 26.24 PSNR / 58.12 mIoU \lambda1=0, \lambda2=1: 26.57 PSNR / 3.62 mIoU Strengths: Enables generalization to unseen semantic scenarios. Semantic loss alone can drive the model to learn reasonable contextual geometry. Limitations: Requires accurate ray projection and feature fetching. High computational cost and GPU memory usage associated with the cross-reprojection attention module. Semantic Loss Computation was introduced in the paper "Semantic Ray: Learning a Generalizable Semantic Field with Cross-Reprojection Attention" (CVPR 2023). It builds upon the NeRF rendering pipeline and Semantic-NeRF, adapting the loss function to work with ray-based features and two-stage sampling. The method was designed to improve generalization to unseen semantic scenarios by leveraging cross-view attention and ray-based feature projection. name: Semantic Radiance Field Rendering
head: Semantic NeRF Rendering
body: Semantic Radiance Field Rendering generates point-wise semantic labels for simulated LiDAR points by volume-rendering semantic logits, using weak 2D image labels as supervision. It differs from standard NeRF rendering by outputting a semantic distribution (logits) rather than just RGB color, enabling the training of semantic fields through cross-entropy loss against ground-truth or weak labels. Inputs: A trained Semantic Radiance Field (SRF) model, parameterized by a neural network that maps 3D coordinates and viewing directions to density \sigma, color c, and semantic logits s. Ray origins o and directions d corresponding to simulated LiDAR beams or camera rays. Distances \hat{D} from the sensor to objects (for LiDAR simulation). Ground-truth or weak semantic labels \hat{S} for the target rays. Outputs: Rendered semantic logits S(r) for each ray r. Semantic label loss Ll used for backpropagation. Data Structures: Sampled Points: For each ray, N points are sampled along the ray segment [tn, tf]. Each point i has a 3D position xi, a distance from the previous sample \deltai, and accumulated transmittance Ti. Network Output: At each sampled point xi and viewing direction d, the network outputs: Density \sigmai \in \mathbb{R} Semantic logits si \in \mathbb{R}^C, where C is the number of semantic classes. Formulas: 1. Transmittance and Weight: The transmittance Ti at sample i is defined as: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \deltai is the distance between sample i and i+1. 2. Volume Rendering of Semantic Logits: The rendered semantic logits S(r) for a ray r are computed as a weighted sum of the semantic logits at sampled points: S(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) si Here, Ti is the accumulated transmittance, \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the segment length, and si is the semantic logit vector at point i. 3. Semantic Label Loss: The loss is the cross-entropy (CE) between the rendered logits and the ground-truth (or weak) labels \hat{S}(r): Ll = \text{CE}(\hat{S}(r), S(r)) where \hat{S}(r) is the target semantic label for ray r. 4. Total Reconstruction Loss: The total loss combines depth, RGB, and semantic components: L{\text{rec}} = L{\text{depth}} + w{\text{rgb}} L{\text{rgb}} + \hat{w}l \hat{L}l + Ll where w{\text{rgb}} balances RGB geometry reconstruction, and \hat{w}l (or wl) balances LiDAR rendering and semantic label rendering. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For simulated LiDAR, calculate the 3D point p for each beam direction d and distance \hat{D} using p = o + \hat{D}d. Define the ray r{\text{LiDAR}} originating from the LiDAR sensor. 2. Sampling: Sample N points along the ray r within the bounding volume of the scene. 3. Network Query: Query the SRF network at each sampled point xi with direction d to obtain density \sigmai and semantic logits si. 4. Volume Rendering: Compute the accumulated transmittance Ti and the final semantic logits S(r) using the weighted sum formula. 5. Loss Computation: Compute the cross-entropy loss Ll between S(r) and the label \hat{S}(r). 6. Backpropagation: Update the network parameters to minimize L{\text{rec}}. Parameters: N: Number of samples per ray. Not given in the sources. w{\text{rgb}}: Weight for RGB reconstruction loss. Not given in the sources. wl (or \hat{w}l): Weight for semantic label loss. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Raydrop: Real LiDAR sensors drop points based on reflectance and incidence angle. To align generated points with real LiDAR, a "raydrop" processing step is learned using ground-truth LiDAR frames as supervision. Weak Labels: If no annotated labels exist, weak labels are generated using a pre-trained SegFormer model on mixed datasets (Cityscapes, Mapillary, BDD, IDD). Point Cloud Correspondence: Direct point-to-point correspondence between irregular 3D point clouds is difficult. Equirectangular image projection (panorama sparse depth) is used to leverage point-wise correspondence. A technique to produce point clouds of arbitrary resolution by querying the Semantic Radiance Network (SRN) at sampled points, obtaining both RGB and semantic labels, rather than forming an image per pose. It collects points given by the ray marcher across multiple poses instead of forming an image per each pose, then queries the SRN at each point in this set to obtain both RGB and semantic label point clouds. It is chosen when dense 3D semantic point clouds are required directly from the neural representation. In experiments, the method samples 65,165 points for an unseen chair in the test set. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples N per ray and the number of rays. Memory Complexity: Depends on the neural network size and the number of samples stored during forward/backward passes. Performance: The method enables full 3D reconstruction and dense semantic segmentation from posed RGB images or semantic masks. It requires only 30 human-annotated, posed semantic segmentation masks for training in semi-supervised settings. Strengths: Allows joint reconstruction of appearance, geometry, and semantic labels. Can simulate realistic LiDAR point clouds. Limitations: Requires weak label generation if no 3D semantic labels are available. Sensitive to LiDAR raydrop effects. Semantic Radiance Field Rendering originates from the integration of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with semantic segmentation. It builds on Semantic Loss Computation which computes the cross-entropy loss over coarse and fine semantic predictions. The concept of rendering semantic logits through volume rendering was proposed by Semantic NeRF (Zhi et al. 2021). The specific application to LiDAR simulation and weak supervision was detailed in NeRF-LiDAR (Manivasagam et al. 2020; Fang et al. 2020). The point cloud rendering variant was presented in Semantic Implicit Neural Scene Representations (SRN). name: One-Step NeRF Rendering
head: NeRF++ setup, OneStepNeRFRenderer
body: One-Step NeRF Rendering is a volume rendering method that uses only stratified sampling without a fine-stage or importance sampling refinement. It supports background rendering via an outer volume, similar to the NeRF++ setup. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A batch of rays, foreground NeRF model, foreground spatial volume, optional background NeRF model, optional background spatial volume, and configuration options (sample counts, depth modes, channel scale). Outputs: Rendered channels (RGB), distances, transmittance, ray start/end points (t0, t1), intersection flags, and auxiliary losses. Data Structures: The method constructs a list of RayVolumeIntegral parts. Each part contains: model: A callable representing the NeRF model (foreground or background). volume: The spatial volume object defining the domain. sampler: A StratifiedRaySampler instance configured with a specific depth mode. nsamples: Integer count of samples per ray for this part. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Options: Retrieve rendering settings from instance variables or provided options. Key flags include renderbackground (bool), renderwithdirection (bool), nsamples (int), and sampling modes for foreground and background. 2. Create Foreground Part: Instantiate a RayVolumeIntegral object for the foreground. Set model to the foreground NeRF model wrapped in a partial function with necessary parameters. Set volume to the foreground spatial volume. Set sampler to a StratifiedRaySampler initialized with depthmode from options.foregroundstratifieddepthsamplingmode (default: 'linear'). Set nsamples to options.nsamples. 3. Create Background Part (Conditional): If renderbackground is true and an outervolume is provided, instantiate a second RayVolumeIntegral object for the background. Set model to the background NeRF model wrapped in a partial function. Set volume to the outervolume. Set sampler to a StratifiedRaySampler initialized with depthmode from options.backgroundstratifieddepthsamplingmode (default: 'linear'). Set nsamples to options.nsamples. Append this part to the list of parts. 4. Render Rays: Call the renderrays function with the batch of rays, the list of parts, a voidmodel (for rays that do not intersect any volume), and the renderwithdirection flag. 5. Process Results: Multiply the output channels by channelscale (default: 255.0) to convert from normalized float to standard integer range if required. Return the channels, distances, transmittance, t0, t1, intersection status, and auxiliary losses. Formulas: The rendering equation for a ray r is computed by summing the contributions of all parts. For a single part with N samples at depths ti within interval [t0, t1]: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \left( 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) \right) ci Where: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the accumulated transmittance. \sigmai is the volume density predicted by the model at sample i. ci is the color predicted by the model at sample i. \deltai = t{i} - t{i-1} is the distance between samples. Parameters: nsamples: Number of stratified samples per ray per part. voidmodel: NeRFModel used for rays that do not intersect the foreground or background volumes. foregroundmodel: NeRFModel for the primary scene. backgroundmodel: Optional NeRFModel for the background. volume: Foreground spatial volume. outervolume: Optional background spatial volume. foregroundstratifieddepthsamplingmode: String, default 'linear'. backgroundstratifieddepthsamplingmode: String, default 'linear'. channelscale: Float, multiplier for output channels, default 255.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random from typing import List, Dict, Tuple, Callable, Any def stratifiedsample(t0: float, t1: float, nsamples: int, depthmode: str) -> List[float]: """Generate nsamples stratified depths in [t0, t1].""" if depthmode == 'linear': step = (t1 - t0) / nsamples return [t0 + (i + random.random()) step for i in range(nsamples)] # Fallback for unspecified depth modes return [t0 + (t1 - t0) (i + random.random()) / nsamples for i in range(nsamples)] def renderonestep(rayso: List[Tuple[float, float, float]], raysd: List[Tuple[float, float, float]], options: Dict, foregroundmodel: Callable, foregroundvolume: Any, backgroundmodel: Callable, outervolume: Any, voidmodel: Callable) -> Dict: """ Renders rays using a single stratified sampling stage for foreground and background. """ # 1. Initialize options renderbackground = options.get('renderbackground', True) renderwithdirection = options.get('renderwithdirection', True) nsamples = options.get('nsamples', 64) fgdepthmode = options.get('foregroundstratifieddepthsamplingmode', 'linear') bgdepthmode = options.get('backgroundstratifieddepthsamplingmode', 'linear') channelscale = options.get('channelscale', 255.0) R = len(rayso) channels = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(R)] distances = [0.0 for in range(R)] transmittance = [1.0 for in range(R)] t0vals = [0.0 for in range(R)] t1vals = [1.0 for in range(R)] intersected = [False for in range(R)] auxlosses = [] # 2. Create foreground part fgsampler = {'depthmode': fgdepthmode, 'nsamples': nsamples} fgpart = {'model': foregroundmodel, 'volume': foregroundvolume, 'sampler': fgsampler} parts = [fgpart] # 3. Create background part if applicable if renderbackground and outervolume is not None: bgsampler = {'depthmode': bgdepthmode, 'nsamples': nsamples} bgpart = {'model': backgroundmodel, 'volume': outervolume, 'sampler': bgsampler} parts.append(bgpart) # 4. Render rays for r in range(R): ro = rayso[r] rd = raysd[r] T = 1.0 C = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tprev = t0vals[r] for part in parts: depths = stratifiedsample(tprev, t1vals[r], nsamples, part['sampler']['depthmode']) # Query NeRF model for density and color at given depths along rays sigmas, colors = part'model' # Handle batch dimension if model returns lists of lists sigmas = sigmas[0] if isinstance(sigmas, list) else sigmas colors = colors[0] if isinstance(colors, list) else colors for i, t in enumerate(depths): delta = t - tprev alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-max(sigmas[i], 1e-10) delta) weight = T alpha C = [C[j] + weight colors[j] for j in range(3)] T = (1.0 - alpha) tprev = t if T < 1e-4: break if T > 1e-4: voidc = voidmodel(ro, rd) C = [C[j] + T voidc[j] for j in range(3)] intersected[r] = True channels[r] = C distances[r] = tprev transmittance[r] = T # 5. Process and return results channels = [[c channelscale for c in ch] for ch in channels] return { 'channels': channels, 'distances': distances, 'transmittance': transmittance, 't0': t0vals, 't1': t1vals, 'intersected': intersected, 'auxlosses': auxlosses } Uses learned occupancy grids and proposal networks to concentrate samples in occupied space. Choose when high fidelity is needed and computational budget allows for two-stage sampling. Link A specific pipeline implementation for View-Frontier NeRF. Choose when working with the VF-NeRF architecture. Link The standard two-stage approach using a coarse network for importance sampling and a fine network for refinement. Choose for general high-quality NeRF rendering. Link Computes losses based on semantic segmentation maps. Choose when training with semantic supervision. Link Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R), where N is the number of samples per ray and R is the number of rays. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot R) for storing sample positions, densities, and colors. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of the gsgen3d project. The method is described as a "NeRF++ setup" because it handles background rendering via an outer volume. It is implemented in the gsgen3d/gsgen repository. gsgen3d/gsgen, https://github.com/gsgen3d/gsgen, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Multi-stage Proposal Sampling
head: Multi-scale Proposal Sampling, Progressive Sampling, Proposal Network Sampling (nerfstudio)
body: Multi-stage proposal sampling is a hierarchical ray sampling strategy that iteratively refines ray samples using a sequence of proposal networks. It starts with uniform sampling and subsequently uses PDF sampling weighted by the previous stage's density estimates to concentrate samples near surfaces. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray bundle, current training step, configuration parameters (numproposalnetworkiterations, numproposalsamplesperray, numnerfsamplesperray, anneal), list of proposal network density functions, and previous stage weights. Outputs: Final ray samples for the NeRF stage, list of weights from all proposal stages, list of ray samples from all stages. Data Structures: raybundle: Contains ray origins and directions. raysamples: Structured container for sample positions and frustums. weights: Tensor of importance weights from the previous stage, used for PDF sampling. densityfns: List of callable functions, one per proposal stage, mapping ray sample positions to density values. Parameters: numproposalnetworkiterations (n): Number of proposal stages. The loop runs for i{level} \in [0, n]. numproposalsamplesperray[ilevel]: Number of samples at proposal level i{level}. numnerfsamplesperray: Number of samples at the final stage (i{level} == n). anneal (\alpha): Exponent for weight annealing. Default 1.0. updatesched(step): Function determining update frequency. Algorithm Steps: 1. Update Check: Determine if proposal networks need gradient updates. Update occurs if stepssinceupdate > updatesched(step) OR step < 10. 2. Loop: Iterate i{level} from 0 to n (inclusive). If i{level} < n, it is a proposal stage; otherwise, it is the final NeRF stage. 3. PDF Sampling (for i{level} > 0): Compute annealed weights w{\text{annealed}} = w^{\alpha}. Perform PDF sampling using raybundle, previous raysamples, w{\text{annealed}}, and numsamples. 4. Density Evaluation (if proposal stage): If update is required, evaluate density with gradients enabled: d = \text{density\fns}i{level}. If not updated, evaluate density with gradients disabled. 5. Reset: After the loop, if update occurred, reset stepssinceupdate to 0. 6. Return: Final ray samples, list of all weights, list of all ray samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class MultiStageProposalSampler: def init(self, numproposalnetworkiterations, numproposalsamplesperray, numnerfsamplesperray, anneal=1.0): self.numproposalnetworkiterations = numproposalnetworkiterations self.numproposalsamplesperray = numproposalsamplesperray self.numnerfsamplesperray = numnerfsamplesperray self.anneal = anneal self.stepssinceupdate = 0 def forward(self, raybundle, densityfns, step, updatesched): allweights = [] allraysamples = [] currentraysamples = None shouldupdate = (self.stepssinceupdate > updatesched(step)) or (step < 10) for ilevel in range(self.numproposalnetworkiterations + 1): isproposalstage = (ilevel < self.numproposalnetworkiterations) if ilevel == 0: numsamples = self.numproposalsamplesperray[0] currentraysamples = uniformsampleray(raybundle, numsamples) elif ilevel < self.numproposalnetworkiterations: prevweights = allweights[-1] annealedweights = torch.pow(prevweights, self.anneal) numsamples = self.numproposalsamplesperray[ilevel] currentraysamples = pdfsampler(raybundle, allraysamples[-1], annealedweights, numsamples) else: numsamples = self.numnerfsamplesperray currentraysamples = uniformsampleray(raybundle, numsamples) if isproposalstage: positions = currentraysamples.frustums.getpositions() if shouldupdate: densities = densityfnsilevel else: with torch.nograd(): densities = densityfnsilevel weights = computeimportanceweights(densities, currentraysamples) allweights.append(weights) allraysamples.append(currentraysamples) if shouldupdate: self.stepssinceupdate = 0 return currentraysamples, allweights, allraysamples def uniformsampleray(raybundle, numsamples): t = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples) return RaySamples(origin=raybundle.origin, direction=raybundle.direction, t=t) def pdfsampler(raybundle, prevraysamples, weights, numsamples): cdf = torch.cumsum(weights, dim=-1) cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[:,:1]), cdf], dim=-1) u = torch.rand(numsamples) indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u) return prevraysamples.resample(indices) def computeimportanceweights(densities, raysamples): deltas = raysamples.frustums.getdeltas() alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-densities deltas) transmittance = torch.cumprod(1.0 - alphas + 1e-10, dim=-1) weights = alphas torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alphas[:,:1]), transmittance[:,:-1]], dim=-1) return weights Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Scaling Crashes: The first 10 steps must force an update to prevent issues with gradient scaling in mixed precision training. Annealing: If anneal is 1.0, no annealing occurs. Combines spatial acceleration with proposal networks for faster inference. Uses volume features for rendering, often paired with proposal sampling. Simple two-stage sampling without intermediate proposal networks. Loss function that can be applied to samples generated by proposal networks. Eliminates multi-stage sampling entirely for real-time rendering. This method is implemented in the nerfstudio framework. nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive sampling and reconstruction
head: Weiss et al
body: Adaptive sampling and reconstruction is an end-to-end neural pipeline that predicts high-density sampling locations using an importance network, converts these predictions into sparse sample positions via a differentiable sampler, and reconstructs full-resolution images from the sparse data using a reconstruction network. It addresses the inefficiency of uniform sampling by allocating computational resources only to visually important regions, achieving high fidelity with significantly fewer volume queries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Low-resolution view (typically 128×128) or view parameters. Output: Full-resolution rendered image. Intermediate: Sparse set of sample positions and their corresponding volume values. Data Structures: Importance Map: Scalar field predicted by the importance network representing sampling probability density. Sample Positions: Set of 2D coordinates (u, v) and associated 3D ray parameters derived from the importance map. Sparse Samples: List of tuples (ray\id, t, value), where ray\id is the pixel index, t is the sample position along the ray, and value is the accumulated color/opacity or scalar value. Numbered Steps: 1. Importance Prediction: The importance network takes a low-resolution input (e.g., 128×128) and outputs an importance map I(x, y) for each pixel. This network learns to identify silhouettes and high-curvature regions without explicit feature descriptors. 2. Differentiable Sampling: The importance map I(x, y) is converted into a probability distribution. Sample positions are drawn from this distribution using a soft-max approximation with parameter \alpha. 3. Volume Query: For each selected sample position, a ray is cast into the volume, and the value is queried. This results in a sparse set of samples, significantly reducing the number of volume queries compared to uniform sampling. 4. Reconstruction: The reconstruction network takes the sparse samples and the original low-resolution view as input. It combines pull-push inpainting with a residual CNN to predict the missing pixel values and reconstruct the full-resolution image. 5. Training: The entire pipeline is trained end-to-end using image losses (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) computed on the final reconstructed image. The goal is to minimize the difference between the reconstructed image and the ground truth rendered at high sample density. Formulas: Soft-max approximation parameter \alpha \approx 50 controls the sharpness of the sampling distribution. Explicit sampling distribution formulas are not given in the sources. Parameters: Soft-max approximation parameter (\alpha): Controls the sharpness of the sampling distribution. Typical value: \alpha \approx 50. Sample Density: Fraction of total possible samples used. Typical values: 5–10% for isosurface rendering, 10% for Direct Volume Rendering (DVR). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Reconstruction Overhead: The reconstruction network has a fixed overhead of approximately 90ms, regardless of volume size. This makes the method slower than optimized ray casting for volumes smaller than 1024^3 or images smaller than 1024^2. Transfer Function Mismatch: Quality degrades significantly when test transfer functions use color ranges that were absent during training. The network struggles to reconstruct textures if the color distribution is out-of-distribution. Complex Transfer Functions: Networks struggle with small-scale color variations from complex transfer functions, often defaulting to uniform sampling and resulting in poor reconstruction in textured regions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivesamplingandreconstruction(volume, viewparams, importancenet, reconstructionnet, alpha=50, density=0.1): # Step 1: Generate low-resolution view for importance prediction # Not given in the sources. Standard coarse render or learned feature map. lowresview = coarserender(volume, viewparams, resolution=(128, 128)) # Step 2: Predict importance map importancemap = importancenet(lowresview) # Step 3: Convert importance map to sample positions # Soft-max approximation parameter alpha controls distribution sharpness. numpixels = 128 128 numsamples = int(numpixels density) # Differentiable sampler draws samples based on importance distribution. # Implementation uses soft-max approximation with alpha. # Explicit sampling distribution formulas are not given in the sources. samplepositions = softmaxsample(importancemap, numsamples, alpha) # Step 4: Query volume at sample positions sparsesamples = [] for pos in samplepositions: ray = castrayfrompixel(viewparams, pos) value = trilinearinterpolate(volume, ray.origin, ray.direction) sparsesamples.append((pos, value)) # Step 5: Reconstruct full-resolution image fullresimage = reconstructionnet(lowresview, sparsesamples) return fullresimage Performance: Achieves PSNR > 30 dB and SSIM > 0.95 with only 5–10% of the samples used in uniform sampling. Speedup: Demonstrates a 1.5–2× speedup for large volumes (2048^3) at high resolutions (≥1536^2). Strengths: Reduces computational cost by focusing samples on important regions; learns sampling strategy without explicit feature engineering; high visual fidelity with sparse samples. Limitations: High reconstruction overhead for small volumes/images; sensitive to transfer function changes; struggles with complex, small-scale textures; requires training data and joint optimization. When to Use: Large volumes (≥1024^3) and high resolutions (≥1024^2) where the reconstruction overhead is amortized; scenarios where transfer functions are stable and known during training. When Not to Use: Small volumes or low resolutions; dynamic or unknown transfer functions; scenes with highly complex, small-scale textures that were not present in training data. The method was proposed by Weiss et al. [156] as a learned optimization for volume visualization, addressing the inefficiency of uniform sampling. The approach is part of a broader trend in scientific visualization and computer graphics to leverage deep learning for rendering acceleration and quality improvement. name: SteerNeRF
head: SmooTh viEwpoint trajEctoRy
body: SteerNeRF accelerates Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) rendering for interactive applications by exploiting the smoothness of continuous viewpoint trajectories to reduce the computational cost of volume rendering. Unlike methods that rely on high-precision motion vectors from game engines or static geometry, SteerNeRF uses a low-resolution volume-rendered feature map combined with a lightweight 2D neural renderer to reconstruct high-resolution images, achieving near real-time frame rates with significantly lower memory usage than cache-based acceleration methods. SteerNeRF operates in a pipeline consisting of a rendering buffer, neural feature fields, and a 2D neural renderer. The method reduces the number of sampled points along rays by leveraging depth information from preceding frames and recovers high-resolution detail using a convolutional neural network. Inputs: Current camera pose \xit and intrinsics Kh (high resolution) or Kl (low resolution). Rendering buffer containing low-resolution feature maps \{F{t-L}, \dots, F{t-1}\} and depth maps \{D{t-L}, \dots, D{t-1}\} from the previous L frames. Target image resolution H \times W. Outputs: High-resolution color image It \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. 1. Neural Feature Fields (f\theta): Input: 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3, viewing direction d \in S^2. Output: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^+, feature vector f \in \mathbb{R}^K. Implementation: Based on Instant-NGP. Uses multi-resolution hash tables with fixed length 2^{19} per resolution. 2. Rendering Buffer: Stores a queue of L preceding frames. Each frame contains: Low-resolution feature map F \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4} \times K}. Low-resolution depth map D \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}}. 3. 2D Neural Renderer (g\theta): Input: Concatenation of upsampled current feature map \hat{F}t and reprojected high-resolution feature maps \{\hat{F}{t0 \to t}\} for t0 \in \{t-L, \dots, t-1\}. Output: High-resolution image It \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}. Architecture: Lightweight 2D convolutional neural network. Compared to a traditional U-Net, it reduces convolution layers for high-resolution features and increases depth for low-resolution features to minimize inference time. Optimized via NVIDIA TensorRT. K: Number of feature channels. Typical value: 3 (RGB) or higher. L: Number of preceding frames in the buffer. \epsilon: Depth interval margin for sampling range reduction. Resolution: Low-resolution rendering is performed at \frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}. 1. Pre-training Neural Feature Fields: Render a high-resolution feature map \tilde{F} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times K} at target resolution. Apply L2 reconstruction loss on the first 3 channels against the ground truth image. Leave other K-3 channels unsupervised. 2. Low-Resolution Volume Rendering (Current Frame t): For each pixel (u, v) in the low-resolution grid (\frac{H}{4} \times \frac{W}{4}): Cast ray r. Buffer-Guided Sampling Range Reduction: Fetch depth map D{t0} from the buffer (where t0 is a preceding frame, typically t-1). Unproject D{t0} to 3D points p: p = \xi{t0}^{-1} Kl^{-1} d{t0} [u, v, 1]^T where d{t0} is the depth value at (u,v) in D{t0}. Project p to the current high-resolution view to get reprojected depth coordinates: d{t0 \to t} [\hat{u}{t0 \to t}, \hat{v}{t0 \to t}, 1]^T = Kh \xit p The sampling range for the current ray is limited to [d{t0 \to t} - \epsilon, d{t0 \to t} + \epsilon]. Sample points within the reduced range. Query f\theta(x, d) to get \sigma and f. Compute feature vector fr via volume rendering integral: fr = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai fi where \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) and Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Store fr in Ft and depth dr in Dt. Store Ft and Dt in the rendering buffer. 3. Reprojection of Preceding Features: For each preceding frame t0 \in \{t-L, \dots, t-1\}: Unproject D{t0} to 3D points p as in Step 2. Project p to high-resolution coordinates using Kh and \xit. Map the low-resolution feature F{t0}(u, v) to the high-resolution grid \hat{F}{t0 \to t} using rounded coordinates: \hat{F}{t0 \to t}(\lfloor \hat{u}{t0 \to t} \rfloor, \lfloor \hat{v}{t0 \to t} \rfloor) = F{t0}(u, v) Rounding has negligible impact on performance. 4. High-Resolution Reconstruction: Upsample the current low-resolution feature map Ft to high resolution \hat{F}t (e.g., bilinear interpolation). Concatenate \hat{F}t and \{\hat{F}{t0 \to t}\} along the channel dimension. Pass the concatenated tensor through g\theta to generate It. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def steernrfrender(currentpose, currentintrh, currentintrl, prevfeatures, prevdepths, prevposes, featurefields, renderer, buffer, H, W, K, L, epsilon): """ currentpose: (4, 4) camera-to-world matrix for frame t currentintrh: (3, 3) high-res intrinsic matrix Kh currentintrl: (3, 3) low-res intrinsic matrix Kl prevfeatures: List of (Hl, Wl, K) tensors prevdepths: List of (Hl, Wl) tensors prevposes: List of (4, 4) camera-to-world matrices for t-L to t-1 featurefields: Instant-NGP style MLP returning (sigma, f) renderer: 2D CNN returning (H, W, 3) image buffer: RenderingBuffer instance H, W: Target resolution K: Feature channels L: Buffer capacity epsilon: Depth margin """ Hl, Wl = H // 4, W // 4 # 1. Low-Res Volume Rendering # Standard ray generation from camera intrinsics and pose origins, directions = generaterays(currentpose, currentintrl, Hl, Wl) # Buffer-guided sampling range reduction using most recent frame if len(prevdepths) > 0: Dprev = prevdepths[-1] prevpose = prevposes[-1] # Unproject depth to 3D points ul, vl = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(Wl), torch.arange(Hl), indexing='ij') uv1 = torch.stack([ul.float(), vl.float(), torch.oneslike(ul)], dim=-1) # (Hl, Wl, 3) uv1 = uv1.view(-1, 3) depthvals = Dprev.view(-1, 1) uv1scaled = uv1 depthvals # p = inv(Kl) @ uv1scaled, then transform to world: pworld = inv(Pprev) @ [p, 1] pcam = torch.inverse(currentintrl) @ uv1scaled.T # (3, N) pworld = torch.cat([pcam, torch.ones(1, pcam.shape[1])], dim=0) pworld = torch.inverse(prevpose) @ pworld pworld = pworld[:3].T # (N, 3) # Project to current high-res view pcurrcam = currentpose @ torch.cat([pworld, torch.ones(pworld.shape[0], 1)], dim=1).T proj = currentintrh @ pcurrcam[:3] uvhat = proj[:2] / proj[2] # (2, N) # Compute sampling bounds depthproj = proj[2] tmin = depthproj - epsilon tmax = depthproj + epsilon # Apply bounds to ray origins/directions for volume rendering origins = origins.view(-1, 3) directions = directions.view(-1, 3) # Adjust ray segments to [tmin, tmax] else: tmin, tmax = 0.0, 100.0 # Volume rendering integral # Standard alpha compositing loop over N samples Ft, Dt = volumerenderintegral(origins, directions, tmin, tmax, featurefields, K) # 2. Reproject Preceding Features highresfeatures = [] # Upsample current feature map Ftup = F.interpolate(Ft.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0), size=(H, W), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).squeeze(0).permute(1, 2, 0) # (H, W, K) # Reproject previous frames for i in range(len(prevfeatures)): Fprev = prevfeatures[i] Dprev = prevdepths[i] prevposei = prevposes[i] # Unproject Dprev to 3D points uv1 = torch.stack([ul.float(), vl.float(), torch.oneslike(ul)], dim=-1).view(-1, 3) depthvals = Dprev.view(-1, 1) uv1scaled = uv1 depthvals pcam = torch.inverse(currentintrl) @ uv1scaled.T pworld = torch.cat([pcam, torch.ones(1, pcam.shape[1])], dim=0) pworld = torch.inverse(prevposei) @ pworld pworld = pworld[:3].T # Project to current high-res pcurrcam = currentpose @ torch.cat([pworld, torch.ones(pworld.shape[0], 1)], dim=1).T proj = currentintrh @ pcurrcam[:3] uvhat = proj[:2] / proj[2] # Round coordinates and gather features uint = torch.clamp(uvhat[0].long(), 0, W-1) vint = torch.clamp(uvhat[1].long(), 0, H-1) # Map features using rounded coordinates Fhatprev = Fprev.view(-1, K)[vint Wl + uint].view(H, W, K) highresfeatures.append(Fhatprev) # Concatenate features concatinput = torch.cat(highresfeatures + [Ftup], dim=-1) # 3. Neural Rendering concatinputtensor = concatinput.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0) It = renderer(concatinputtensor) # Update Buffer buffer.push(Ft, Dt) return It def volumerenderintegral(origins, directions, tmin, tmax, featurefields, K): # Standard volume rendering with N samples N = 64 tvals = torch.linspace(tmin, tmax, N) deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([1e10], device=tvals.device)]) x = origins.unsqueeze(1) + directions.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(2) sigma, f = featurefields(x.view(-1, 3), directions.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, N, -1).view(-1, 3)) sigma = sigma.view(-1, N) f = f.view(-1, N, K) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) T = torch.cumprod(torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[:,:1]), 1.0 - alpha[:,:-1]], dim=1), dim=1) weights = alpha T F = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(2) f, dim=1) D = torch.sum(weights tvals, dim=1) return F, D def generaterays(pose, intr, H, W): # Standard ray generation from camera pose and intrinsics u, v = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(W), torch.arange(H), indexing='ij') uv1 = torch.stack([u.float(), v.float(), torch.oneslike(u)], dim=-1) uv1 = uv1.view(-1, 3) camdirs = torch.inverse(intr) @ uv1.T camdirs = camdirs / torch.norm(camdirs, dim=0, keepdim=True) worlddirs = pose[:3,:3] @ camdirs origins = pose[:3, 3].unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, HW) return origins.T, worlddirs.T Overfitting: If the number of training views is small, the 2D neural renderer may overfit. This is mitigated by distillation: using a pre-trained NeRF to synthesize pseudo ground truth viewpoints by randomly sampling within the available viewing zone. Coordinate Rounding: Simply rounding the reprojected coordinates (\hat{u}, \hat{v}) has a negligible impact on performance and is used for efficiency. No Perfect Motion Vectors: Unlike game engines, NeRF does not provide high-precision motion vectors. The method relies on noisy depth maps from volume rendering, which requires the joint training of feature fields and the renderer to hallucinate high-fidelity details. Speed: Achieves nearly 100 FPS at 800 \times 800 resolution and 30 FPS at 1920 \times 1080 resolution. On the Tanks & Temples dataset, it achieves 75.19 FPS (FP16). Memory: Memory usage is less than 20% of KiloNeRF and comparable to Instant-NGP (29.4 MB on Tanks & Temples vs 25.2 MB for Instant-NGP). Quality: Competitive with other methods. On NeRF-Synthetic, it achieves 31.60 PSNR, 0.954 SSIM, and 0.058 LPIPS. Scaling: Performance scales with the efficiency of the 2D neural renderer optimization (e.g., TensorRT FP16/INT8). Strengths: Low memory footprint, high frame rates, suitable for smooth viewpoint trajectories. Limitations: Relies on smooth camera motion; performance may degrade with abrupt viewpoint changes or sparse training views without distillation. SteerNeRF was introduced in 2023 by authors exploring the efficiency-memory trade-off in NeRF rendering. It is inspired by super-sampling methods for real-time rendering (e.g., DLSS) but adapts them to the novel view synthesis (NVS) task where perfect geometry and motion vectors are unavailable. It builds on Instant-NGP for efficient feature field representation.
