name: Enforced Coherence
head: EC method
body: The Enforced Coherence (EC) method is a ray traversal technique that brings coherence to secondary rays (such as reflection or refraction rays) by rearranging the ray-to-voxel mapping using sorting, enabling simultaneous intersection checks within a cell. It solves the problem of incoherent secondary rays by reordering rays to process all rays passing through a specific voxel together, allocating a CUDA block to each voxel (or multiple blocks for load balancing) and loading triangle data into shared memory. It sets itself apart from its sibling Marching Caches by explicitly enforcing coherence through global sorting and shared-memory batch processing, whereas Marching Caches typically relies on spatial locality without explicit reordering. It is distinct from the Independent Voxel Walk method, which traces rays independently and relies on hardware caches rather than explicit data reordering. Inputs: Total number of rays (N{rays}). Ray origins and directions. Scene geometry (triangles) organized in a grid (voxels). Grid resolution (e.g., 128 \times 128 \times 128). Outputs: For each ray, the closest intersection distance (or hit status). Data Structures: rayIDArr: Array of size N{rays} storing ray identifiers. tileIDArr (or voxelIDArr): Array of size N{rays} storing the voxel ID that the ray passes through. Note: In the source, this array is initially allocated for N{rays} entries, but the algorithm implies a list of (ray, voxel) pairs. The source pseudocode suggests tileIDArr and rayIDArr are parallel arrays where index i corresponds to a specific ray-voxel pair. The number of pairs is N{pairs} = \sum{r=0}^{N{rays}-1} (\text{voxels traversed by ray } r). pseudoArr: Array of size N{voxels}, initialized to 0. scratchArr: Array of size N{voxels}, initialized to 1. oArr: Array for compaction output. validArr: Array for compaction validity flags. Shared memory: Buffer for triangle data (vertices/indices) loaded from global memory. Parameters: Sorting library: Radixsort from CUDPP is used. CUDA block allocation: One block per voxel, or multiple blocks for voxels with high ray counts (load balancing). Typical scene size: Conference room scene has \approx 10 million (ray, voxel) pairs, assuming 10 voxels per ray. Steps: 1. Voxel Enumeration: For each ray in parallel, determine the voxels it passes through. Store (rayID, voxelID) pairs in rayIDArr and tileIDArr. The length of these arrays equals the total number of ray-voxel intersections. 2. Sorting: Sort tileIDArr and rayIDArr using tileIDArr (voxel ID) as the key. This brings all rays passing through the same voxel together. 3. Boundary Detection: Compute boundaries for segmented processing. Initialize pseudoArr to 0 and scratchArr to 1 for all voxels. 4. Segmented Scan: Perform a segmented scan on pseudoArr using scratchArr to determine chunks/boundaries for each voxel's ray group. 5. Chunk Determination: Use scratchArr and validArr to determine the number of blocks required. Voxels with many rays may require multiple blocks. 6. Compaction: Compact the data to determine the exact number of blocks and valid ray ranges. 7. Intersection Processing: For all blocks: While all rays in the block are not processed: Load triangles to shared memory. Threads in the CUDA block bring data of one triangle from global memory. If a voxel has more triangles than threads, triangles are brought in batches. Each batch is completely used before loading the next batch. Check for intersection between rays and triangles in shared memory. 8. Minimum Finding: For all rays in parallel, get the minimum of all intersections found across all voxels processed for that ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. countArr = [0] Nrays for ray in range(Nrays) in parallel: countArr[ray] = countVoxels(ray) Npairs = sum(countArr) rayIDArr = allocate(Npairs) tileIDArr = allocate(Npairs) offset = 0 for ray in range(Nrays) in parallel: voxels = getVoxelsForRay(ray) for v in voxels: idx = atomicAdd(&offset, 1) # Or use prefix sum for deterministic order rayIDArr[idx] = ray tileIDArr[idx] = v pseudoArr = [0] Nvoxels scratchArr = [1] Nvoxels oArr = allocate(Nvoxels) # For compaction output sort(tileIDArr, rayIDArr) getBoundaries(tileIDArr, pseudoArr) segScan(pseudoArr, scratchArr) getChunks(scratchArr, validArr) numBlocks = compact(validArr, oArr) for blockid in range(numBlocks): # Load triangles for the voxel(s) assigned to this block # Load triangles to shared memory # Threads in the CUDA block bring data of one triangle from global memory # For voxels with more triangles than threads, triangles are brought in batches while all rays in block are not processed: loadTrianglesToSharedMemory() checkIntersection() minIntersections = [infinity] Nrays for ray in range(Nrays) in parallel: minIntersections[ray] = getMinimumIntersection(ray) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Loss of Order: Because rays are reordered by voxel, the start-to-finish ordering of each ray is lost. Rays cannot terminate early upon finding the first intersection; all intersections must be found to determine the closest one. Memory Intensity: Reordering is computationally and memory intensive. The number of (rayID, voxelID) pairs can be large (e.g., 10 million for a typical conference room scene). Empty Spaces: The method performs poorly on models with large empty spaces because the number of ray-voxel pairs is large, requiring more data movement for sorting. Time Complexity: Dominated by sorting O(N \log N) or O(N) for radix sort, where N is the number of ray-voxel pairs, and the intersection checks. The overhead of reordering (sorting, compaction) must be offset by the coherence obtained. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for rayIDArr, tileIDArr, and auxiliary arrays proportional to the number of rays and voxels. The number of pairs can be very large (e.g., 10 million). Measured Performance: Achieves 8 fps on the Conference model with one light source and one reflection bounce on an Nvidia GTX480, rebuilding data structures for each stage. On GTX280 (cache-less), EC is much faster than IVW on Fairy and Happy Buddha models. On GTX480 (cached), EC is slower than IVW (14 fps for IVW vs 8 fps for EC on Conference model). Strengths: Works best on older generation GPUs with no caches, while the IVW method is slow on them. Provides high performance on GPUs with user-managed caches by exploiting shared memory. Limitations: Poor performance on models with large empty spaces due to high sorting overhead. Slower than IVW on modern GPUs with rich cache architectures (GTX480). When to use: When targeting older GPUs without hardware caches or when reflection/refraction rays exhibit high coherence and the overhead of sorting is justified by the reduction in redundant intersection checks. When not to use: On modern GPUs with large L1/L2 caches where IVW performs better, or on scenes with large empty spaces where the number of ray-voxel pairs is excessively large. The Enforced Coherence method was proposed in the paper "Raytracing dynamic scenes on the GPU using grids". It is part of a broader study comparing grid-based raytracing techniques on GPUs, specifically focusing on reflection and refraction rays which typically have little coherence. The method was implemented and tested on NVIDIA 280 GTX and 480 GTX cards. The authors note that ideas presented are likely to give high performance on future GPUs and other manycore architectures. name: Image-Based Rendering for Volume Surfaces
head: Image-based framework, Image-based volume rendering with keyview caching, Keyview IBR, Keyview-based rendering, Surface IBR
body: Image-Based Rendering (IBR) for Volume Surfaces is an acceleration technique that caches a fully volume-rendered view (the keyview) and reuses it for novel views by texture-mapping it to a geometric iso-surface model, only ray-casting newly visible regions. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Temporal Differential Rendering by explicitly constructing an intermediate geometric surface to project the cached image, rather than relying solely on pixel-space reprojection or buffer accumulation. This approach is particularly effective for large static volumes where camera motion is incremental, such as in virtual colon navigation. The method reduces computational cost by reusing a previously rendered image for the majority of the screen, leveraging temporal coherence between adjacent frames. Inputs: V: A 3D volume dataset. T: A transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity. C{key}: The camera pose of the cached keyview. C{novel}: The camera pose of the current novel view. I{key}: The fully volume-rendered image buffer from the keyview. Outputs: I{novel}: The rendered image for the novel view. 1. Iso-Surface Model (M): A geometric mesh representing the iso-surface extracted from V. Iso-value (v{iso}): Derived from the transfer function T. Generation: Extracted using a levels-of-detail algorithm optimized for regular volumes. 2. Keyview Cache: Image (I{key}): A 2D texture buffer containing the color/opacity data from the previous full render. Camera Pose (C{key}): Stored to compute the transformation to the novel view. 1. Iso-Surface Extraction: Construct the geometric model M from volume V using the iso-value v{iso} deduced from T. 2. Keyview Rendering: If no keyview exists, perform a full volume render of V using camera C{key} to generate I{key}. 3. Texture Mapping: Projectively texture-map the image I{key} onto the geometric model M. The source notes the use of backward and forward processing orders for high-quality texture mapping. 4. Novel View Projection: Render the textured model M using the novel camera pose C{novel}. 5. Identify Newly Visible Regions: Determine which pixels in the novel view correspond to volume data that was occluded or hidden in the keyview but is now visible. 6. Ray Casting for New Regions: For each pixel in the newly visible regions, cast a ray through the volume V using the novel camera C{novel}. 7. Composite Image: Initialize I{novel} with the projected image, then replace the pixel values in the newly visible regions with the results from the ray casting step. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rendernovelview(volume, transferfunction, keyviewimage, keyviewcamera, novelcamera, isovalue): """ Renders a novel view using Image-Based Rendering for Volume Surfaces. """ # Step 1: Extract iso-surface model M from volume V using isovalue # Source does not specify the exact extraction algorithm; standard LOD/marching cubes meshvertices, meshfaces = extractisosurface(volume, isovalue) # Step 2: Texture map keyview image onto mesh M # Source mentions backward/forward processing orders but not exact implementation texturedmesh = texturemapmesh(meshvertices, meshfaces, keyviewimage, keyviewcamera) # Step 3: Project textured mesh to novel view camera # Rasterization produces a depth buffer and a color buffer projectedcolor, projecteddepth = rasterizemesh(texturedmesh, novelcamera) # Step 4: Identify newly visible pixels # Compare depth of M in novel view against keyview visibility # Pixels where novel depth < projected depth are newly visible newpixelmask = identifynewlyvisiblepixels(projecteddepth, keyviewcamera, novelcamera) # Step 5: Ray cast only the new pixels newcolors = np.zeroslike(projectedcolor) for u, v in np.argwhere(newpixelmask): rayorigin, raydirection = computeray(novelcamera, u, v) color = volumeraycast(volume, transferfunction, rayorigin, raydirection) newcolors[u, v] = color # Step 6: Composite result novelviewimage = projectedcolor.copy() novelviewimage[newpixelmask] = newcolors[newpixelmask] return novelviewimage def extractisosurface(volume, isovalue): """Returns (vertices, faces) for the iso-surface at isovalue.""" # Standard implementation omitted for brevity; returns mesh data return np.array([]), np.array([]) def texturemapmesh(vertices, faces, keyviewimage, camera): """Projects keyviewimage onto vertices using camera projection.""" # Assigns texture coordinates to vertices based on keyview projection return {"vertices": vertices, "faces": faces, "texcoords": np.zeroslike(vertices)} def rasterizemesh(mesh, camera): """Renders textured mesh to screen, returning color and depth buffers.""" # Standard GPU rasterization logic return np.zeros((100, 100, 3)), np.zeros((100, 100)) def identifynewlyvisiblepixels(depthbuffer, keyviewcamera, novelcamera): """Returns boolean mask of pixels requiring new ray casting.""" # Compares visibility between keyview and novel view return np.ones((100, 100), dtype=bool) def computeray(camera, u, v): """Computes ray origin and direction from camera and pixel coordinates.""" return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) def volumeraycast(volume, transferfunction, origin, direction): """Performs standard volume integration along the ray.""" # Standard ray marching implementation return np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) Volume Size: The method targets large volumes, specifically those over 1024^3 where traditional rendering is too slow. It has been successfully tested on 512^3 datasets. Camera Motion: The method assumes small camera movements between frames. Fallback: If the camera motion is too large, the newly visible region may cover the entire image, negating the speedup. In such cases, fall back to a full volume render and update the keyview cache. Time Complexity: The cost is proportional to the number of pixels in newly visible regions multiplied by the average ray length through the volume. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, the surface model, and the keyview image buffer. Performance: Provides an average speedup of an order of magnitude (10x) over traditional volume rendering. Achieves interactive frame rates for 512^3 datasets in virtual colon navigation. Strengths: Significant reduction in ray casting operations when camera motion is small; leverages existing hardware rasterization for the bulk of the image. Limitations: Requires construction and maintenance of a geometric iso-surface model; quality depends on the accuracy of the iso-surface approximation; not suitable for highly dynamic volumes or large camera jumps. The method was proposed in the context of interactive volume rendering for large biomedical and geoscience datasets. It was introduced by Baoquan Chen in a dissertation and subsequent Eurographics 2001 paper. The work addresses the computational bottleneck of ray casting large volumes by exploiting temporal coherence between adjacent frames in navigation sequences. It extends the concept of image-based rendering from surface models to volumetric data by using an intermediate iso-surface representation. name: Image-Based Rendering for Subvolumes
head: IBR Subvolume Culling, Image-Based Rendering for Virtual Colonoscopy, Slab Image Caching
body: An image-based rendering scheme that accelerates volume visualization by caching and reusing pre-rendered slab images for subvolumes, thereby reducing the computational load for novel frame generation. It distinguishes itself from its parent method, Image-Based Rendering for Volume Surfaces, by operating on volumetric subvolumes (slabs) rather than surface meshes, making it particularly suitable for direct volume rendering of large datasets like CT scans where surface extraction is either expensive or undesirable. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset, a current viewpoint, a set of subvolumes (typically arranged to approximate complex structures like a colon), and a priority threshold mechanism. Output: A composite image for the current frame, composed of re-rendered high-priority subvolumes and reused cached slab images for low-priority subvolumes. Data Structures: Subvolume List: A collection of subvolume objects. Each object contains: id: Unique identifier. bbox: Axis-aligned bounding box defining the spatial extent. priority: A scalar value representing the visual importance. cachedimage: A 2D texture or buffer storing the rendered slab image from the previous frame. valid: A boolean flag indicating if cachedimage contains valid data for the current viewpoint. Priority Value: A scalar derived from the distance of the subvolume's center (or representative point) to the viewpoint. Steps: 1. Visibility and Priority Calculation: For each subvolume i in the scene: Determine if the subvolume is visible from the current viewpoint. This can be done using frustum culling or window-closing algorithms. Compute the priority value Pi. The sources state that priority decreases as the subvolume moves further away from the viewpoint. Let di be the distance from the viewpoint to the subvolume. A typical implementation might use an inverse distance function: Pi = \frac{1}{di + \epsilon} where \epsilon is a small constant to prevent division by zero. If the subvolume is newly visible (not in the previous frame's visible set), set its valid flag to false. 2. Decision Making: For each visible subvolume i: If Pi is high (near the viewpoint) OR the subvolume is newly visible: Mark for Re-rendering. Determine the rendering quality Qi based on Pi. Higher priority implies higher quality. If Pi is low (distant from the viewpoint) AND the subvolume was visible in the previous frame AND valid is true: Mark for Reuse. Retrieve the cached slab image. 3. Rendering: For subvolumes marked for Re-rendering: Perform volume rendering (e.g., ray casting) for the subvolume. The rendering quality Qi influences the parameters passed to the renderer. Specifically, it determines the thickness of the slab to render, as handled by the Cube Toolkit (CTK). Higher quality (higher priority) likely results in thinner slabs or more samples per ray to preserve detail. Store the resulting 2D image into the subvolume's cachedimage buffer. Set valid to true. For subvolumes marked for Reuse: Retrieve the cachedimage from the previous frame. Transform this 2D image to the current viewpoint. This typically involves texture-mapping the cached slab image onto the subvolume's bounding box or a proxy geometry in screen space. Note: The parent method uses surface models; this method uses slab images, implying the reuse might involve simple screen-space projection or assuming minimal parallax for distant objects. 4. Compositing: Composite all rendered and reused subvolume images into the final frame buffer, respecting depth ordering if necessary (though slab images are often composited front-to-back or back-to-front based on the original rendering pass). Parameters: Priority Threshold: A value or function that separates "high" (re-render) from "low" (reuse) priority. Not explicitly defined in sources, but implied by distance. Rendering Quality (Qi): Mapped from priority. Higher priority \rightarrow higher quality. This affects slab thickness in CTK. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Newly Visible Subvolumes: Must always be rendered, as no cache exists. Occlusion Changes: If a previously visible subvolume becomes occluded, it should not be rendered or reused. Visibility detection is critical. Parallax: For distant subvolumes, the assumption is that parallax is negligible, allowing the reuse of a 2D slab image. If parallax is significant, the cached image will appear distorted. The method relies on the principle that eyes attend to near objects more, so distant errors are less perceptible. CTK Integration: The method relies on the Cube Toolkit (CTK) to interpret the quality parameter and adjust slab thickness. This is a specific implementation detail. Time Complexity: Reduces rendering time for distant subvolumes from O(N) (ray casting) to O(1) (texture fetch and projection). The total time depends on the fraction of subvolumes that are high-priority. Memory Complexity: Requires storing a cached slab image for each subvolume. Memory usage is proportional to the number of subvolumes and the resolution of the cached images. Strengths: Significant speedup for interactive visualization of large volumes, especially in virtual colonoscopy where the camera moves along a path. Limitations: Quality degradation for distant objects due to parallax errors. Requires visibility detection and priority management overhead. When to Use: Interactive volume rendering of large datasets where viewpoint changes are frequent, and distant details are less critical. Particularly effective for virtual colonoscopy. When Not to Use: When high fidelity is required for all depths, or when the scene has significant parallax for distant objects. This method was developed in the context of real-time volume rendering for virtual colonoscopy, leveraging commodity volume visualization hardware like Cube-4/VolumePro. It builds on earlier image-based rendering techniques for volume data. The approach is part of a broader effort to make clinical volume visualization interactive on standard PCs. name: Temporal Differential Rendering
head: Dirty-brick partial re-render, Dirty-row flush
body: Temporal differential rendering reduces per-frame computational cost by skipping the rendering of screen regions that have not changed since the previous frame. It solves the problem of redundant ray-marching or shading work in dynamic scenes where only small portions of the volume or camera view update between iterations. Unlike Reprojection with Temporal Accumulation, which blends historical buffers to reduce noise, this method performs a binary check for change and completely bypasses the rendering pipeline for clean regions. The method operates by maintaining a representation of the previous frame's state and comparing it against the current frame to identify "dirty" regions. Two primary implementations exist: tile-based dirty-brick tracking for GPU-accelerated volume rendering and row-based hashing for CPU-based or console rendering. Inputs: Current frame data (volume state, camera parameters, or canvas content), previous frame data (rendered buffers, hash values, or dirty region masks), and change indicators (physics updates, user edits, or camera movement vectors). Outputs: Rendered image for dirty regions only, and updated previous frame buffer or hash state. 1. Dirty Region Map: A tracking structure mapping screen tiles or rows to their dirty status. 2. Previous Frame Buffers: Arrays storing the previous canvas characters, colors, and row hashes for direct comparison. 3. Hash Table (Row-based): An array of hash values, one per row, used to detect changes in console/ASCII rendering. This variant, described in, projects dirty bricks (from physics or edits) into screen tiles. 1. Dirty Brick Projection: On the CPU, identify bricks that have changed due to physics or edits. Project these bricks into 8×8 screen tiles to mark them as "dirty". 2. Tile Check: For each 8×8 tile, determine if it contains any dirty bricks. If a tile is clean, mark it as "unchanged". 3. Early-Out: In the compute shader, check the tile status. If the tile is clean, skip the ray-marching and shading steps for all pixels in that tile. 4. Rendering: For dirty tiles, perform the standard rendering pass (e.g., distance LOD, DDA traversal). 5. Update State: Update the dirty tile map for the next frame based on new changes. This variant, described in, uses per-row hashing to detect changes in a character canvas. 1. Initialization: Initialize the previous canvas buffer and row hash array. Set FNV offset constant H{offset} = 2166136261u and FNV prime constant H{prime} = 16777619u. 2. Dimension Check: If the current canvas dimensions differ from the previous buffer dimensions, reinitialize the previous buffers to match. 3. Row Hashing: For each row y from 0 to H-1: Initialize hash h = H{offset}. For each column x from 0 to W-1: Get character ch = \text{canvas}[y, x]. Update hash: h = (h \oplus \text{ushort}(ch)) \times H{prime}. Get color string col = \text{colors}[y, x]. Get color hash colId = \text{col} \text{ is null } ? 0: \text{RuntimeHelpers.GetHashCode}(col). Update hash: h = (h \oplus \text{uint}(colId)) \times H{prime}. Store h as \text{rowHash}[y]. 4. Change Detection: Compare \text{rowHash}[y] with \text{prevRowHash}[y]. If they are equal, the row is clean; skip rendering for this row. 5. Flush Dirty Rows: If the row is dirty: Initialize a string builder for ANSI escape sequences. Append cursor move sequence: \x1b[{y+1};1H. For each column x from 0 to W-1: Get color col = \text{colors}[y, x]. If col \neq \text{lastColor}, append color code (or reset code if null) to builder. Set \text{lastColor} = col. Get character ch = \text{canvas}[y, x]. Append ch (or space if null) to builder. Write the accumulated string to the console. 6. Update State: Copy current canvas and colors to previous buffers. Update \text{prevRowHash}[y] with the new hash. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. FNVOFFSET = 2166136261 FNVPRIME = 16777619 def computerowhash(canvasrow, colorsrow): """Compute FNV-1a hash for a single row.""" h = FNVOFFSET for x in range(len(canvasrow)): ch = canvasrow[x] chval = ord(ch) if ch else 0 h ^= chval h = FNVPRIME col = colorsrow[x] colid = hash(col) if col is not None else 0 h ^= colid h = FNVPRIME return h def temporaldifferentialrender(canvas, colors, prevcanvas, prevcolors, prevrowhashes, width, height): """ Render only dirty rows using temporal differential rendering. canvas: 2D array of characters [height][width] colors: 2D array of color strings [height][width] prevcanvas: 2D array of previous characters prevcolors: 2D array of previous colors prevrowhashes: 1D array of previous row hashes """ # Check dimensions if len(canvas) != len(prevcanvas) or len(canvas[0]) != len(prevcanvas[0]): prevcanvas = [[None for in range(width)] for in range(height)] prevcolors = [[None for in range(width)] for in range(height)] prevrowhashes = [0] height outputlines = [] anywrites = False for y in range(height): # Compute current row hash currenthash = computerowhash(canvas[y], colors[y]) # Check if row changed if currenthash == prevrowhashes[y]: # Row is clean, skip rendering continue # Row is dirty, render it anywrites = True linebuffer = [] # Move cursor to start of row (1-based indexing for ANSI) linebuffer.append(f"\x1b[{y+1};1H") lastcolor = None for x in range(width): col = colors[y][x] if col != lastcolor: if col is None: linebuffer.append("\x1b[0m") # Reset else: linebuffer.append(col) # Assume col is ANSI code lastcolor = col ch = canvas[y][x] if ch == '\0': ch = ' ' linebuffer.append(ch) outputlines.append("".join(linebuffer)) # Update previous state prevcanvas[y] = canvas[y][:] prevcolors[y] = colors[y][:] prevrowhashes[y] = currenthash if anywrites: print("".join(outputlines)) else: # No changes, could skip entirely or just copy buffers pass Tile Size: 8×8 pixels is used in. Hash Constants: FNV-1a offset 2166136261u and prime 16777619u are used in. Safety Margin: A 16-voxel safety margin is used in the distance LOD pass to prevent popping artifacts when fast-forwarding rays. Precision: Hash collisions are possible but rare with FNV-1a. In high-contrast scenes, false positives (rendering clean rows) are acceptable; false negatives (skipping dirty rows) cause visual artifacts. Boundaries: Dimension mismatches between frames require buffer reinitialization. Degenerate Input: Empty rows or null characters must be handled explicitly to avoid hash mismatches. A variant where a partial volume rendering pass is performed between visibility detection passes to complete the image and refresh occluding data with newly loaded bricks. The frequency of total scene rendering must be chosen carefully because it is particularly expensive. Future work suggests storing ray state (position, direction, hierarchy position, DDA state) in image space buffers alongside color and opacity for progressive rendering resumption. A heuristic to prevent flicker in static regions by freezing primitives whose bounding boxes do not intersect the inter-frame difference mask D. For each primitive i, if Bi \cap \text{support}(D) = \emptyset, set \text{freeze}i = 1. Only primitives with \text{freeze}i = 0 are updated during optimization, preventing spurious updates in static areas that perturb the loss and trigger compensatory updates in neighboring primitives. The specific implementation using per-row FNV hashing to detect changes in console/ASCII rendering, as detailed in the main algorithm. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: When no changes are detected, both compute passes are skipped entirely. Performance scales with the number of changed tiles or rows. Strengths: Eliminates redundant computation; high fidelity (no temporal blending artifacts); simple implementation. Limitations: Requires strict temporal consistency; cannot handle large camera movements or scene changes without full re-render; hash collisions may cause artifacts. When to Use: Dynamic scenes with small, localized changes (e.g., voxel games, fluid simulations). When Not to Use: Scenes with large, global changes or high-frequency noise where temporal accumulation is more appropriate. Temporal differential rendering originated in the context of voxel-based real-time rendering and console-based graphics. The dirty-brick approach was implemented in the voxelG project by mstampfli, leveraging GPU compute shaders for efficient tile-based culling. The dirty-row hashing approach was developed for console canvas rendering in csRaymarching by 0gecco, using FNV hashing for efficient row-level change detection. Partial volume rendering updates between visibility passes were explored in procedural volume exploration to refresh occluding data with newly loaded bricks. Anti-flicker freezing heuristics were later applied in differentiable rendering of bitmap primitives to prevent spurious updates in static regions. mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) 0gecco/csRaymarching, https://github.com/0gecco/csRaymarching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Représentation et algorithmes pour l'exploration interactive de volumes procéduraux étendus et détaillés, https://inria.hal.science/inria-00598406v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) DiffBMP: Differentiable Rendering with Bitmap Primitives, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2602.22625, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Reprojection with Temporal Accumulation
head: Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) via reprojection
body: Reprojection with Temporal Accumulation is a technique to stabilize voxel rendering over time by blending the current frame's color with the accumulated color from the previous frame, using camera motion vectors to align pixels. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by operating directly on the final radiance image in screen space, leveraging temporal coherence to reduce noise and aliasing without requiring per-voxel state caching or complex model coefficient tracking. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current frame color (colourattachment), current frame world position (positionattachment), previous frame accumulated color (accumulationattachment), camera transformation matrices (traceuniforms.lastcamera), and control uniforms (reprojectionfactor, indirectlighting). Outputs: Final output color for the current pixel. Data Structures: colourattachment: texture2d<f32>, binding 3. Stores the current frame's computed color. positionattachment: texturestorage2d<rgba32float, readwrite>, binding 3. Stores the world-space position for each pixel, used for reprojection. accumulationattachment: texturestorage2d<rgba16float, readwrite>, binding 1. Stores the temporally accumulated color from previous frames. Algorithm Steps: 1. Load Current State: Read the current frame's color C{curr} from colourattachment at sample position (u, v) and the world position P{curr} from positionattachment at (u, v). 2. Check Reprojection Conditions: If indirectlighting is zero or reprojectionfactor \le 0.0, skip reprojection and output C{curr} directly. 3. Compute Local Bounds (Edge Detection): To prevent ghosting across edges, compute local color bounds using C{curr} and its 8 immediate neighbors (C0 to C8) in a 3x3 grid. Calculate the 'plus' bounds (cross pattern: center, top, bottom, left, right) and 'square' bounds (full 3x3). Compute C{min} and C{max} as the average of the minimums and maximums of the 'plus' and 'square' bounds respectively. 4. Reproject Position: Transform P{curr} into the previous frame's clip space using traceuniforms.lastcamera. 5. Convert to Texture Coordinates: Convert the clip space coordinates to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) range [-1, 1], then map to texture coordinates (u{prev}, v{prev}) for the accumulationattachment. 6. Validate Projection: If the projected coordinates are outside the NDC range [-1, 1] (indicating the pixel is newly visible or occluded), the history sample is invalid and blending is skipped. 7. Fetch History: Load the accumulated color C{hist} from accumulationattachment at (u{prev}, v{prev}). 8. Blend: Compute the mixed color C{mix} using the reprojectionfactor \alpha: C{mix} = C{curr} \cdot (1.0 - \alpha) + C{hist} \cdot \alpha 9. Clamp: Clamp C{mix} to the local bounds [C{min}, C{max}] to prevent bleeding across high-frequency details or edges. 10. Output: Return the clamped C{mix} as the final color. Accumulation Step: After the reprojection pass, a separate accumulation shader stores the final output color of the current frame into accumulationattachment for use in the next frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reprojectionpass(u, v, colourattachment, positionattachment, accumulationattachment, traceuniforms, reprojectionfactor, indirectlighting): # 1. Load current state Ccurr = colourattachment[u, v] Pcurr = positionattachment[u, v] # 2. Check conditions if indirectlighting == 0 or reprojectionfactor <= 0.0: return Ccurr # 3. Compute local bounds # Get 3x3 neighborhood colors (flattened indices: 0 1 2 / 3 4 5 / 6 7 8) neighbors = [colourattachment[u + du, v + dv] for du in (-1, 0, 1) for dv in (-1, 0, 1)] # Plus pattern indices: center(4), top(1), bottom(7), left(3), right(5) plusindices = (4, 1, 7, 3, 5) squareindices = (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8) plusmin = min(neighbors[i] for i in plusindices) plusmax = max(neighbors[i] for i in plusindices) squaremin = min(neighbors[i] for i in squareindices) squaremax = max(neighbors[i] for i in squareindices) mincol = (plusmin + squaremin) / 2.0 maxcol = (plusmax + squaremax) / 2.0 # 4. Reproject position # Transform Pcurr to previous frame clip space Pclip = traceuniforms.lastcamera.transformpoint(Pcurr) # 5. Convert to NDC and texture coordinates if Pclip.w == 0: return Ccurr ndcx = Pclip.x / Pclip.w ndcy = Pclip.y / Pclip.w # 6. Validate projection if not (-1.0 <= ndcx <= 1.0 and -1.0 <= ndcy <= 1.0): return Ccurr # Map NDC [-1, 1] to texture coordinates [0, 1] uprev = (ndcx + 1.0) / 2.0 vprev = (ndcy + 1.0) / 2.0 # 7. Fetch history Chist = accumulationattachment[uprev, vprev] # 8. Blend alpha = reprojectionfactor Cmix = Ccurr (1.0 - alpha) + Chist alpha # 9. Clamp to local bounds Cfinal = max(min(Cmix, maxcol), mincol) # 10. Output return Cfinal def accumulationpass(u, v, outputcolor, accumulationattachment): accumulationattachment[u, v] = outputcolor Parameters: reprojectionfactor: Float uniform controlling the blend weight between current and accumulated frames. If \le 0.0, reprojection is skipped. indirectlighting: Unsigned integer uniform. Reprojection is only performed if indirectlighting is non-zero and reprojectionfactor > 0.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Projection: If the projected previous position is outside the NDC range [-1, 1], the pixel is considered invalid (e.g., newly visible or occluded) and must not be blended with the accumulation buffer to avoid ghosting. Edge Bleeding: Without local bound clamping, blending across object boundaries causes "ghosting" artifacts where colors from adjacent objects bleed into each other over time. Temporal Reprojection for Linear Models exploits temporal coherence by reprojecting linear model coefficients and features rather than raw pixel colors, allowing the model to react immediately to abrupt changes in camera, light, or transfer functions. Unlike standard temporal reprojection which caches constant values per pixel, this method uses linear regression to predict gradual changes while maintaining robustness against sudden shading variations, thereby avoiding the need for Monte Carlo (MC) integration resets. Temporal Gradient Denoising is a technique that reduces noise in volume rendering by applying temporal reprojection and blending to gradient images rather than the final radiance image. It solves the problem of high noise levels in Monte Carlo volume rendering, particularly in high-order scattering-dominant media, while avoiding the visible bias and artifacts that occur when denoising the original image directly. It sets itself apart from standard temporal accumulation by operating on the derivative of the radiance with respect to a source parameter (albedo), leveraging the fact that denoising artifacts in the gradient domain are not directly visible in the final color. Alpha-Max Quasi-Depth Motion Vector is a method to compute screen-space motion vectors for direct volume rendering (DVR) by using the 3D position of the point with maximum alpha along the ray as a proxy for depth, enabling temporal reprojection despite the lack of a single surface depth value. For each pixel at current frame coordinates (u, v), it identifies the point p in world space where the alpha value is maximum along the ray passing through the volume. It then reprojects p back to the previous frame's coordinate system using previous camera transformation matrices to obtain coordinates (u', v'). The screen-space motion vector is calculated as the difference between (u, v) and (u', v'). This heuristic provides an acceptable approximation for motion vector estimation because the point of maximum alpha has the maximum contribution to the final accumulated sample. Frame Averaging at Rest is a post-processing technique where, when the camera stops, consecutive frames are averaged with tiny sub-pixel offsets so the image settles into a clean still. It involves detecting camera stop and then averaging frames with tiny sub-pixel offsets to refine the image quality during static periods. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the accumulation buffer, where W and H are the screen dimensions. The accumulationattachment typically uses rgba16float to balance precision and memory usage. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces ghosting and bleeding across edges via local bound clamping. Functions as a post-processing pass in the rendering pipeline. Limitations: History samples can be invalid due to disocclusion, causing ghosting if trivially accepted. Requires accurate position buffers for reprojection. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering where temporal stability is desired. When Not to Use: Scenes with rapid movement or significant disocclusions where ghosting is unacceptable. Reprojection with Temporal Accumulation is a technique used in voxel and volume rendering to stabilize images over time. It is closely related to Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) used in rasterization. The method leverages the correlation between consecutive frames to reduce noise and improve visual quality. Variants such as Alpha-Max Quasi-Depth Motion Vector address specific challenges in volume rendering, such as the lack of a single depth value. Frame Averaging at Rest is used in progressive loading scenarios to refine static images. ria8651/bevy-voxel-engine, https://github.com/ria8651/bevy-voxel-engine, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Deep Learning Based Super-Resolution for Medical Volume Visualization with Direct Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-20713-68, fetched 2026-10-26 Volume rendering: progressive multiscale loading, sorted compositing, lighting and more from a histotomography fork (2.8 TB volume @ 16bits) - what, if anything, would be worth upstreaming?, https://github.com/google/neuroglancer/issues/1134, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Temporal Reprojection for Linear Models
body: Temporal Reprojection for Linear Models exploits temporal coherence by reprojecting linear model coefficients and features rather than raw pixel colors, allowing the model to react immediately to abrupt changes in camera, light, or transfer functions. Unlike standard temporal reprojection which caches constant values per pixel, this method uses linear regression to predict gradual changes while maintaining robustness against sudden shading variations, thereby avoiding the need for Monte Carlo (MC) integration resets. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current frame's noisy MC estimates \tilde{I}j(t), camera view matrix, per-pixel world coordinates, and the history buffer from the previous frame. Outputs: Denoised color values derived from the linear model, updated feature vectors zj(t), and linear model coefficients. Data Structures: History Buffer: Stores the feature vector zj \in \mathbb{R}^3 for each pixel j. The vector corresponds to pixel color (RGB) and is constructed using all three channels simultaneously to avoid color-shift effects, even though denoising is performed per channel. Linear Model: Maintains coefficients for linear regression at each pixel. The specific coefficient update logic is handled by Weighted Recursive Least Squares (wRLS), which allocates high weights to samples with lower noise variance. Steps: 1. Estimate Velocities: Calculate per-pixel velocity vectors \upsilonj = (\upsilonx, \upsilony) using the camera view matrix and per-pixel world coordinates. 2. Reproject Coordinates: Define the reprojection operation \pi(\upsilonj) to map the current pixel index j to the corresponding coordinate q in the previous frame: q \leftarrow \pi(\upsilonj) = j + \upsilonj If \upsilonj = 0 (e.g., static camera), q = j. 3. Retrieve History: Access the history feature zq(t-1) from the reprojected coordinate q in the previous frame's history buffer. 4. Rectify History (Clamping): Apply the neighborhood clamping operator \Psi[\cdot] to the reprojected history zq(t-1) using the current noisy estimate \tilde{I}j(t). This rectification reduces artifacts caused by stale history data when the scene content has changed. 5. Update Feature Vector: Construct the new feature vector zj(t) by combining the rectified history and the current estimate. The update uses an exponentially weighted history buffer: zj(t) = \alpha \Psi[zq(t-1), \tilde{I}j(t)] + (1 - \alpha)\tilde{I}j(t) where \alpha is a weight controlling the balance between history and the current estimate. 6. Linear Regression: Use the updated feature vector zj(t) as input to the linear model (specifically Weighted RLS) to predict the denoised output. The wRLS variant handles temporally varying noise inherent in DVR images generated with small sample counts. Parameters: \alpha: Exponential decay weight for the history buffer. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources, but it controls the trade-off between temporal stability and responsiveness. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Abrupt Changes: Standard reprojection of pixel colors fails to adapt to changes in lighting or transfer functions. Linear model reprojection reacts immediately to these changes, avoiding MC integration resets. Color Shifts: Denoising is performed per channel, but the feature zj(t) must be constructed using all three color channels simultaneously to avoid undesired color-shift effects. Stale History: Without the clamping operator \Psi[\cdot], reprojected history can introduce artifacts if the underlying scene has changed significantly between frames. A feature vector zj(t) constructed from an exponentially weighted history buffer of MC estimates, used as input to the linear model to provide temporal stability and reduce noise variance. It updates via zj(t) = \alpha\Psi[zq(t-1), \tilde{I}j(t)] + (1-\alpha)\tilde{I}j(t), where \Psi[\cdot] is a neighborhood clamping operator that relies on the current-frame input estimate \tilde{I}j(t) to reduce artifacts from stale history data. It is chosen when temporal stability is required without sacrificing responsiveness to lighting changes. It differs from simple color accumulation by integrating clamping and multi-channel construction to prevent color shifts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method involves per-pixel velocity estimation, reprojection, clamping, and weighted RLS updates. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the history buffer zj \in \mathbb{R}^3 per pixel, in addition to the linear model coefficients. Strengths: Reacts immediately to abrupt changes in shading, lighting, or transfer functions, avoiding MC integration resets. More robust than caching constant values per pixel. Limitations: Requires estimation of per-pixel velocities (optical flow) and additional storage for history buffers. Performance: Demonstrated on real-time VPT. Specific hardware or resolution metrics are not given in the sources. This method was introduced in the context of real-time volumetric path tracing (VPT) for direct volume rendering. It addresses the limitations of conventional temporal reprojection, which reprojects pixel colors and struggles with dynamic scene changes. The approach builds on exponentially weighted history buffers and weighted recursive least squares (wRLS) to handle heterogeneous noise in DVR images. name: Temporal Gradient Denoising
head: Temporal denoising of gradient image, Temporal denoising on gradients
body: Temporal Gradient Denoising reduces noise in volume rendering by applying temporal reprojection and blending to gradient images rather than the final radiance image. It solves the problem of high noise levels in Monte Carlo volume rendering, particularly in high-order scattering-dominant media, while avoiding the visible bias and artifacts that occur when denoising the original image directly. It sets itself apart from standard temporal accumulation by operating on the derivative of the radiance with respect to a source parameter (albedo), leveraging the fact that denoising artifacts in the gradient domain are not directly visible in the final color. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of rendered gradient images Gk for k \in [0, N-1], where k=0 is the target frame; motion vector d and velocity vd in screen space; smoothing factor wa; number of frames N; time offset t. Outputs: A denoised gradient image G{\text{denoised}} for the target frame. Data Structures: Gradient Image: A 2D array of floating-point values representing the gradient of radiance with respect to albedo at each pixel. Layout is standard screen-space raster format. Motion Vector: A 2D vector (dx, dy) per pixel or globally, derived from camera movement. Steps: 1. Compute Motion Parameters: Determine the motion vector d and velocity vd in screen space based on the camera's moving direction and velocity. 2. Reproject Pixels: For each pixel i in the target frame, calculate the corresponding pixel coordinate in neighboring frames using the inverse reprojection function f{\text{proj}}^{-1}. 3. Blend Gradients: Compute the weighted average of the reprojected gradient values from neighboring frames to produce the denoised gradient. Formulas: The reprojection function maps a pixel i in the target frame to a coordinate in a neighboring frame at distance k: f{\text{proj}}(i) = i + d \cdot vd \cdot t where t is the time offset. The denoised gradient G{\text{denoised}}(i) is calculated as: G{\text{denoised}}(i) = \frac{\sum{k=0}^{N-1} wa^k (1-wa)^{-1} Gk(f{\text{proj}}^{-1}(i))}{1 - (1-wa)^N} where: k is the frame distance (number of frames between the source image and the target image, with k=0 being the target). Gk is the gradient image at distance k. wa is the smoothing factor. N is the number of frames used for denoising. f{\text{proj}}^{-1} is the reciprocal reprojection function, mapping the target pixel i back to the source frame coordinate. Parameters: Smoothing factor (wa): Set to 0.1 in all test scenes. Number of frames (N): Set to 11 in the implementation. Pitfalls: Direct Image Denoising: Denoising the original radiance image directly causes visible bias and artifacts. Denoising the gradient prevents this because such artifacts are not directly visible in the gradient domain. Boundary Handling: Not given in the sources. Implementation requires clamping or zero-padding when f{\text{proj}}^{-1}(i) falls outside image bounds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def temporalgradientdenoise(targetgradient, neighborgradients, motionvector, velocity, smoothingfactor, numframes): # targetgradient: 2D list of floats, G0 # neighborgradients: list of 2D lists, G1 to G{N-1} # motionvector: tuple (dx, dy) for d # velocity: tuple (vx, vy) for vd # smoothingfactor: float wa # numframes: int N # Returns: 2D list of floats Gdenoised h, w = len(targetgradient), len(targetgradient[0]) weightedsum = [[0.0] w for in range(h)] normalizationfactor = 1.0 - (1.0 - smoothingfactor) numframes # Precompute weight scaling factor (1-wa)^{-1} invoneminuswa = 1.0 / (1.0 - smoothingfactor) # Process all frames k from 0 to N-1 for k in range(numframes): if k == 0: gradframe = targetgradient else: if k - 1 < len(neighborgradients): gradframe = neighborgradients[k - 1] else: break # Calculate reprojection offset for frame k # t is implicitly 1 per frame step in the sequence offsetx = motionvector[0] velocity[0] k offsety = motionvector[1] velocity[1] k # Weight for this frame: wa^k (1-wa)^{-1} weight = (smoothingfactor k) invoneminuswa # Accumulate weighted gradient for y in range(h): for x in range(w): # Inverse reprojection: source coordinate = target coordinate - offset srcx = x - offsetx srcy = y - offsety # Sample gradient with bilinear interpolation and boundary clamping val = samplegradient(gradframe, srcx, srcy) weightedsum[y][x] += weight val # Normalize denoisedgradient = [[weightedsum[y][x] / normalizationfactor for x in range(w)] for y in range(h)] return denoisedgradient def samplegradient(image, x, y): h, w = len(image), len(image[0]) # Clamp to valid range x0 = max(0, min(int(x), w - 1)) y0 = max(0, min(int(y), h - 1)) x1 = min(x0 + 1, w - 1) y1 = min(y0 + 1, h - 1) dx = x - x0 dy = y - y0 val00 = image[y0][x0] val01 = image[y0][x1] val10 = image[y1][x0] val11 = image[y1][x1] return (1 - dx) (1 - dy) val00 + dx (1 - dy) val01 + (1 - dx) dy val10 + dx dy val11 This method denoises Monte Carlo volume rendering images by combining temporal reprojection with a learned kernel prediction network and fusing the result with the background using an alpha map. It addresses the specific challenge of preserving semi-transparent structures and sharp edges in volumetric data while maintaining real-time performance. Unlike direct prediction methods (e.g., FDAE) that rely solely on pixel-wise regression, this approach generates weighted combinations of neighboring samples, offering better structural preservation at the cost of struggling with extreme high-intensity outliers. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the number of frames N. Memory Complexity: Requires storing N gradient images and their corresponding motion vectors. Measured Performance: In test scenes (Bunny, Candle, Lucy) with resolution 256x256, the method produced less error than denoised path tracing and path tracing without denoising, both visually and quantitatively. The method was implemented with N=11 and wa=0.1. Strengths: Effectively reduces noise in high-order scattering-dominant media; avoids visible bias/artifacts associated with direct image denoising; improves quality over standard path tracing with equal time. Limitations: Requires a sequence of frames (temporal coherence); performance gain over path tracing is specific to gradient denoising, as temporal denoising on path tracing itself does not perform better than path tracing with equal time. When to use: When rendering sequences of volume data with high noise levels, particularly in participating media with high albedo, and when temporal coherence is available. When not to use: For single-image rendering; when extreme high-intensity outliers are present and structural preservation is critical without learned kernels. The method was proposed in the context of efficient participating media rendering using differentiable volumetric path tracing. It was introduced to address the high noise levels in gradient images computed with respect to albedo, which are used to predict radiance for different albedo values without re-rendering. The approach leverages the common practice of rendering image sequences with moving cameras. The work was published in 2023. name: Spatiotemporal Volume Denoising with Background Fusion
head: Kernel prediction denoising with background fusion, Real-time volume-rendering image denoising based on kernel prediction
body:
This method denoises Monte Carlo volume rendering images by combining temporal reprojection with a learned kernel prediction network and fusing the result with the background using an alpha map. It addresses the specific challenge of preserving semi-transparent structures and sharp edges in volumetric data while maintaining real-time performance. Unlike direct prediction methods (e.g., FDAE) that rely solely on pixel-wise regression, this approach generates weighted combinations of neighboring samples, offering better structural preservation at the cost of struggling with extreme high-intensity outliers. The method operates on image-order rendering outputs. It takes the current noisy frame, the previous frame's denoised data, and the background color as inputs, producing a final denoised radiance image. Input Images: 1024x1024 resolution, 32-bit floating-point format. Alpha Map A(i,j): A single-channel map representing the transparency of the volume data at pixel coordinates (i,j). Background B(i,j): The color/value of the background at pixel coordinates (i,j). Training Patches: 256x256 image patches extracted from the rendered images (four patches per image). 1. Reprojection: Reproject the previous frame's denoised volume data into the current frame's coordinate space using camera motion and depth information. 2. Kernel Prediction: Use a neural network (kernel prediction network) to predict spatial and temporal weight kernels based on the current noisy frame and the reprojected historical data. 3. Weighted Filtering: Perform pixel-wise weighted filtering on the reprojected historical frame and the current noisy frame using the predicted kernels to obtain an intermediate denoised volume data xn'(i,j). 4. Background Fusion: Blend the intermediate denoised data xn'(i,j) with the background B(i,j) using the alpha map A(i,j) to produce the final denoised pixel value xn''(i,j). 5. Failure Handling: If the camera undergoes rapid motion, abrupt illumination changes, or if a ray passes entirely through transparent regions (where historical frame failure rate can reach 70%), copy the current frame's pixel value to replace the historical frame value, effectively degenerating to spatial denoising for that pixel. Background Fusion: The final denoised pixel value xn'' is calculated as: xn''(i,j) = A(i,j) 	imes xn'(i,j) + (1 - A(i,j)) 	imes B(i,j) where A(i,j) is the alpha map and B(i,j) is the background. Training Loss Functions: The model is trained using a weighted sum of gradient loss and Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss. Gradient Loss L{grad}(I,R): L{grad}(I,R) = \|
ablax I - 
ablax R\|2^2 + \|
ablay I - 
ablay R\|2^2 where I is the predicted image, R is the reference image, and 
ablax, 
ablay are the x and y gradients. MSE Loss L{mse}(I,R): L{mse}(I,R) = \|I - R\|2^2 where \| \cdot \|2^2 denotes the squared L2 norm. Total Loss L{total}(I,R): L{total}(I,R) = w{grad} \cdot L{grad}(I,R) + w{mse} \cdot L{mse}(I,R) where w{grad} and w{mse} are the weights for gradient and MSE losses, respectively. Evaluation Metrics: MSE: MSE(I,R) =  rac{1}{mn} \sum{i=0}^{m-1} \sum{j=0}^{n-1} [I(i,j) - R(i,j)]^2 where m,n are image dimensions. PSNR: PSNR(I,R) = 10 	imes \lg  rac{255^2}{MSE(I,R)} where \lg is the base-10 logarithm. SSIM: SSIM(I,R) =  rac{(2\muI\muR+c1)(\delta{IR}+c2)}{(\muI^2+\muR^2+c1)(\deltaI^2+\deltaR^2+c2)} where \muI, \muR are means, \deltaI, \deltaR are standard deviations, and \delta{IR} is the covariance between images I and R. Temporal PSNR (tPSNR): tPSNR(I,R) = PSNR(It - I{t-1}, Rt - R{t-1}) where t is the time index. w{grad}: Weight for gradient loss. Set to 0.4 to improve visual edge preservation. w{mse}: Weight for MSE loss. Set to 0.6. Learning Rate: 0.0001 (Adam optimizer). Batch Size: 4. Training Epochs: Converges after approximately 300 epochs. High Gradient Weight: If w{grad} is set too high (above 0.5), the image exhibits slight color distortion for some data. Transparent Regions: In ray tracing, if a ray passes entirely through transparent regions, the historical frame failure rate can be as high as 70%. The method handles this by copying the current frame's pixel value to replace the historical value, degenerating to spatial denoising. Rapid Motion/Changes: Historical frames become unusable if the camera undergoes rapid motion, illumination changes abruptly, or the transfer function varies quickly. Outliers: The kernel prediction method struggles with highlighted outliers (e.g., channel values > 200 at 800 samples per pixel) that direct prediction methods can suppress. Unverified code. Temporal Gradient Denoising A class of methods that predict filtering kernels rather than direct pixel values. This method uses kernel prediction to produce outputs as weighted combinations of neighboring samples, distinguishing it from direct prediction methods like FDAE. name: Dynamic Cache Depth Scheduling
head: Anchor-based Cache Depth Adjustment, Cache Depth Heuristic
body: Dynamic Cache Depth Scheduling is a heuristic strategy that adjusts the depth of reuse for cached computation results in subsequent frames based on the intensity of decoding calculations in the current frame. It solves the problem of maintaining rendering quality and suppressing rapid appearance changes caused by sudden cache flushing in large-scale Gaussian Splatting models. Unlike static cache reuse, this method dynamically balances performance and visual stability by modulating how many previous frames' results are retained. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera input (pose), current frame anchors (X{k'}), total anchors (X), previous frame cache state. Outputs: Rendered image, updated cache depth, updated computation cache. Data Structures: Computation Cache: Stores derived 3D Gaussians from previous frames. The cache holds results from up to D{max} previous frames. Anchor Set: The set of anchors to be decoded into 3D Gaussians for the current frame. Cache Depth (D): An integer indicating how many previous frames' Gaussians are reused. Parameters: Max Cache Reuse Depth (D{max}): Set to 10 to balance performance and quality. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the rendering pipeline, set the initial cache depth and the guiding function H. 2. While receiving camera input: a. Perform anchors indexing and filtering. b. Check if the current cache reuse depth has reached D{max}. If yes, invalidate those computation cache lines. c. Calculate the Anchor Duplicate Rate (the ratio of anchors that can be reused or are identical to previous frames). d. Based on the Anchor Duplicate Rate: i. If Anchor Duplicate Rate == 0% or it is the first frame: Decode all anchors into 3D Gaussians. ii. If Anchor Duplicate Rate == 100%: Reuse all 3D Gaussians from the cache. iii. Otherwise: Decode new anchors and update the computation cache. e. Compose the new Gaussians with the cached Gaussians. f. Configure the new cache depth D using the guiding function and the duplicate rate. g. Update the render buffer. h. Rasterize the render buffer into an image. Formula: The expected reuse depth D is determined by the guiding function H applied to the ratio of current anchors to total anchors: D = H\left(\frac{|X{k'}|}{|X|}\right) where: H is the guiding function of the heuristic strategy. |X{k'}| is the number of anchors in the current frame. |X| is the total number of anchors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynamiccachedepthscheduling(camerainput, totalanchorsX, maxreusedepth=10): # Initialize state cachedepth = 0 computationcache = {} # Maps frameid to Gaussian parameters # Implementation of H not specified in sources; standard linear scaling shown guidingfunctionH = lambda ratio: max(1, int(ratio maxreusedepth)) firstframe = True while camerainput is not None: # 1. Anchors indexing and filtering currentanchorsXkprime = indexandfilteranchors(camerainput) # 2. Check max cache reuse depth if cachedepth >= maxreusedepth: computationcache.clear() cachedepth = 0 # 3. Calculate Anchor Duplicate Rate anchorduplicaterate = calculateduplicaterate(currentanchorsXkprime, computationcache) # 4. Decode or Reuse based on duplicate rate if anchorduplicaterate == 0.0 or firstframe: newgaussians = decodeanchorstogaussians(currentanchorsXkprime) cachedepth = 0 firstframe = False elif anchorduplicaterate == 1.0: newgaussians = reusecachedgaussians(computationcache) else: newanchors = getnewanchors(currentanchorsXkprime) decodednewgaussians = decodeanchorstogaussians(newanchors) updatecomputationcache(computationcache, decodednewgaussians) newgaussians = composegaussians(decodednewgaussians, computationcache) # 5. Configure cache depth based on guiding function and duplicate rate ratio = len(currentanchorsXkprime) / len(totalanchorsX) cachedepth = guidingfunctionH(ratio) # 6. Update render buffer and rasterize renderbuffer = updaterenderbuffer(newgaussians, camerainput) image = rasterize(renderbuffer) return image def indexandfilteranchors(camerainput): # Standard view frustum culling and spatial indexing return camerainput.getvisibleanchors() def calculateduplicaterate(currentanchors, cache): # Ratio of current anchors matching cached frame's anchors if not cache: return 0.0 cachedanchors = next(iter(cache.values())).anchors matches = sum(1 for a in currentanchors if a in cachedanchors) return matches / len(currentanchors) if currentanchors else 0.0 def decodeanchorstogaussians(anchors): # Standard Gaussian Splatting derivation return [anchor.derivegaussian() for anchor in anchors] def reusecachedgaussians(cache): return next(iter(cache.values())).gaussians def getnewanchors(currentanchors): return [a for a in currentanchors if not a.iscached()] def updatecomputationcache(cache, newgaussians): cache[cache.get('frameid', 0) + 1] = type('obj', (object,), {'anchors': newgaussians, 'gaussians': newgaussians})() def composegaussians(newgaussians, cache): return newgaussians + next(iter(cache.values())).gaussians def updaterenderbuffer(gaussians, camerainput): return {'gaussians': gaussians, 'camera': camerainput} def rasterize(buffer): return buffer['camera'].project(buffer['gaussians']) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stale Appearance: Maintaining the same Gaussian appearance parameters in the cache for too long causes significant rendering errors, particularly on trajectories around a centered target. This is handled by flushing the cache in time via the max reuse depth limit. Rapid Appearance Changes: Static cache reuse depth can cause rapid changes in scene appearance when the cache is flushed. Dynamic scheduling suppresses this by gradually adjusting the depth. Time Complexity: Depends on the anchor decoding stage and Gaussian rasterization stage. By reusing cached Gaussians, the decoding stage is skipped for duplicate anchors, reducing computational load. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the cache depth D{max} and the number of anchors. With D{max}=10, the cache stores results from up to 10 previous frames. Performance: Tested on Scaffold-GS and OctreeGS models. Setting D{max}=10 balances performance and quality. It is effective for both single GPU and multi-GPU resources. Strengths: Maintains image rendering quality without significant decrease or fluctuation. Suppresses rapid appearance changes caused by sudden cache flushing. The method is model-agnostic and independent of the specific pipeline structure. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the guiding function H and duplicate rate calculation. May introduce latency if cache management is inefficient. Dynamic Cache Depth Scheduling was introduced in the paper "A GS-Cache Inference Framework for Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting Models". It was developed to address redundancy in binocular stereo rendering and to optimize the derivation stage in large-scale Gaussian Splatting models like Scaffold-GS and OctreeGS. The method is designed to be independent of the specific model and pipeline structure. name: Temporal Reuse of Voxel Contributions
head: Temporal caching for volume rendering
body: Temporal reuse of voxel contributions is an optimization for animated sequences that caches segment integrals from prior frames to update only changed regions, optimizing performance for time-varying data. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Inter-Ray Coherency by focusing on temporal stability of accumulated radiance rather than spatial ray-path correlation, and differs from Reprojection with Temporal Accumulation by caching volumetric integration results rather than final pixel colors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current volume data Vt, previous frame's cached segment integrals C{t-1}, camera transform Mt, and a change detection mask D identifying regions where Vt differs from V{t-1}. Output: Rendered image It and updated cache Ct. Data Structures: The cache C stores pre-integrated segment contributions. For a given ray, the cache typically holds: entrypos: 3D float vector, the entry point into the volume. exitpos: 3D float vector, the exit point from the volume. accumulatedtransmittance: float, the transmittance at the exit point. accumulatedcolor: 3D float vector, the accumulated color contribution. valid: boolean, indicating if the cache entry is valid for the current frame's ray. Numbered Steps: 1. Change Detection: Identify voxels or subvolumes that have changed between frame t-1 and t. This can be done by comparing scalar field values or using a dirty-region tracking mechanism. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. 3. Cache Lookup: Determine if the ray's path through the volume overlaps with cached segments from C{t-1}. If the ray path is identical and the volume data is unchanged, reuse the cached segment integral. If the volume data has changed in the overlapping region, mark the cached segment as invalid or partially invalid. 4. Integration: For valid cached segments, use the stored accumulatedtransmittance and accumulatedcolor to skip integration over that portion of the ray. For invalid or new segments, perform standard volume integration (e.g., ray marching) to compute new contributions. 5. Cache Update: Store the computed segment integrals for the current frame into Ct for potential reuse in frame t+1. 6. Compositing: Composite the contributions from cached and newly computed segments to form the final pixel color. Formulas: The standard volume rendering integral is: C = \int{t0}^{t1} T(t) \cdot c(t) \cdot \sigma(t) \, dt where T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{t0}^{t} \sigma(\tau) \, d\tau\right) is the transmittance, c(t) is the color, and \sigma(t) is the density. With temporal reuse, if a segment [ta, tb] is cached: C{total} = C{cached} + T(tb) \cdot \int{tb}^{t1} T'(t) \cdot c(t) \cdot \sigma(t) \, dt where C{cached} is the pre-computed contribution from [ta, tb], and T(tb) is the transmittance at the start of the new integration. Parameters: Cache Size: Not given in the sources. Depends on memory constraints and temporal coherence length. Change Threshold: Not given in the sources. Determines when a voxel is considered "changed." Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Reusing cached transmittance can accumulate floating-point errors over many frames. Consider periodically resetting the cache or using higher precision for transmittance accumulation. Boundaries: Ray entry/exit points must be computed with sufficient precision to match cached segments. Use epsilon tolerances when comparing positions. Degenerate Input: If the volume changes drastically (e.g., explosion), the cache becomes invalid. A robust change detection mechanism is required to avoid visual artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderframe(volumet, cacheprev, camerat, changemask): image = zeroslike(screen) cachecurr = {} for pixel in screenpixels: ray = castray(pixel, camerat) # Check for cache hit cachedsegment = cacheprev.get(ray.id) if cachedsegment and isvalid(cachedsegment, volumet, changemask): # Reuse cached contribution color = cachedsegment.accumulatedcolor transmittance = cachedsegment.accumulatedtransmittance startt = cachedsegment.exitpos else: # Compute from scratch or from last valid point color = vec3(0.0) transmittance = 1.0 startt = ray.entrypos # Integrate remaining ray for t in raymarch(startt, ray.exitpos, stepsize): density = samplevolume(volumet, ray.positionat(t)) if density > 0: color += transmittance samplecolor(volumet, t) density stepsize transmittance = exp(-density stepsize) image[pixel] = color cachecurr[ray.id] = CacheEntry(startt, ray.exitpos, transmittance, color) return image, cachecurr A circular buffer mechanism that stores previous volume data and gradients to allow temporal interpolation or reuse without recomputation. It sets itself apart by storing full volume data snapshots rather than just segment integrals, enabling more complex temporal interpolation. Choose this when the volume data changes smoothly over time and interpolation is feasible. Layout: Per subvolume: oldTimeStep[tstepCache] (int), oldData[tstepCache] (pointer to voxel data), oldGrad[tstepCache] (pointer to gradient data), oldTSpos (int, current write index). Pitfall: Circular buffer overwrites oldest entries when full. The code does not implement a replacement policy beyond simple modulo wrapping, meaning older timesteps are permanently lost once the buffer is full. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels, but with a reduced constant factor proportional to the fraction of unchanged voxels. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the number of voxels, for storing the cache. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with temporal coherence. Performance gain is higher when the volume changes slowly. Strengths: Significant speedup for slowly changing volumes. Reduces redundant computation. Limitations: Requires additional memory for caching. Can introduce visual artifacts if change detection is inaccurate. When to use: Animated sequences with slow temporal changes (e.g., fluid simulation, medical imaging over time). When not to use: Highly dynamic scenes with rapid changes, or memory-constrained environments. Temporal reuse of voxel contributions was introduced as an optimization for animated sequences to cache segment integrals from prior frames. It is particularly useful for time-varying data like fluid simulations, where large portions of the volume remain unchanged between frames. This method trades initial precomputation time for real-time rendering speeds, though accuracy depends on silhouette fidelity and may introduce minor boundary errors in highly opaque scenes. volume rendering, https://grokipedia.com/page/Volumerendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ouyting/simian-spacemonkey, https://github.com/ouyting/simian-spacemonkey, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Exploiting Temporal Coherence (C-Buffer)
head: C-Buffer, C-Buffer Temporal Coherence, Coherent Volume Rendering, Coordinates-buffer
body: Exploiting Temporal Coherence via a C-Buffer (Coordinates-buffer) accelerates volume rendering in animations by storing the 3D coordinates of the first non-transparent voxel hit by each ray, allowing subsequent frames to start ray casting closer to the surface rather than from the volume boundary. It estimates the new ray start points by transforming the stored coordinates according to the new viewing parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset, camera/view parameters, and the C-Buffer from the previous frame. Output: Rendered image, updated C-Buffer. Data Structures: C-Buffer (C): A 2D array of size W \times H (image resolution). Each entry stores the 3D coordinates of the first non-transparent voxel hit by the ray corresponding to that pixel. Format: (x, y, z) representing voxel indices or normalized coordinates within the volume grid. Empty State: A special flag or value indicates no hit was recorded for that pixel in the previous frame. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization (First Frame): Perform standard ray casting for all pixels from the volume entry point to the exit point. Identify the first non-transparent voxel hit at coordinates (x{hit}, y{hit}, z{hit}). Store (x{hit}, y{hit}, z{hit}) in the C-Buffer entry for that pixel. Render the image. 2. Subsequent Frames (Ray Start Determination): For each pixel, retrieve the stored coordinates from the C-Buffer. Case A: Empty Entry: If the C-Buffer entry is empty, start the ray at the volume boundary (standard approach). Case B: Valid Entry: Use the stored coordinates as the starting point for ray casting. The stored coordinate serves as an estimate of where the new rays should start their volume traversal. 3. C-Buffer Update (Rotation Handling): If the world space rotates (or camera rotates relative to volume), the voxel coordinates stored in the C-Buffer must be transformed to align with the new view. Let R be the rotation matrix applied to the world space. For each entry containing (x, y, z): 1. Transform the voxel coordinates to world space (if stored in voxel space) or apply rotation directly if stored in world space. Let the transformed coordinates be (x', y', z'). 2. Project (x', y', z') back to screen space (i', j') using the current view and projection matrices. 3. Map the value from the old C-Buffer entry to the new screen coordinate (i', j'). Collision Detection (Hidden Voxels): If multiple previous entries map to the same new screen coordinate (i', j'), it indicates a change in depth ordering (occlusion). Specifically, if the relative order of projected voxels changes, the deeper voxel is potentially hidden. These entries possibly have to be removed. 4. Rendering and Final Update: Render the frame using the updated C-Buffer for ray starts. Update the C-Buffer with the new first-hit coordinates for the current frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Handle C-Buffer transformation if view changed if frameindex > 0: cbuffer = updatecbufferonrotation(cbuffer, viewmatrix, volmin, volmax, H, W) for j in range(H): for i in range(W): rayorigin, raydir = generateray(i, j, viewmatrix, projmatrix, volmin, volmax) prevhit = cbuffer[j][i] if prevhit is not None: hit = traceraystartingat(volume, rayorigin, raydir, prevhit, volmin, volmax) else: hit = tracerayfromboundary(volume, rayorigin, raydir, volmin, volmax) if hit is not None: image[j][i] = samplecolor(volume, rayorigin, raydir, hit) newcbuffer[j][i] = hit else: image[j][i] = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) newcbuffer[j][i] = None return image, newcbuffer def updatecbufferonrotation(cbuffer, viewmatrix, volmin, volmax, H, W): tempmap = {} for j in range(H): for i in range(W): voxel = cbuffer[j][i] if voxel is None: continue # Transform voxel coordinates to world space worldpos = list(voxel) # Apply rotation/view matrix rotatedpos = applymatrix(viewmatrix, worldpos) # Project back to screen screenpos = worldtoscreen(rotatedpos, H, W) inew, jnew = screenpos if 0 <= inew < W and 0 <= jnew < H: if (inew, jnew) not in tempmap: tempmap[(inew, jnew)] = [] tempmap[(inew, jnew)].append(voxel) newcbuffer = [[None] W for in range(H)] for (inew, jnew), voxels in tempmap.items(): if len(voxels) == 1: newcbuffer[jnew][inew] = voxels[0] else: newcbuffer[jnew][inew] = None return newcbuffer def tracerayfromboundary(volume, origin, direction, volmin, volmax): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for k in range(3): if abs(direction[k]) < 1e-6: if origin[k] < volmin[k] or origin[k] > volmax[k]: return None else: t1 = (volmin[k] - origin[k]) / direction[k] t2 = (volmax[k] - origin[k]) / direction[k] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < 0 or tmin > tmax: return None step = [1 if direction[k] > 0 else -1 for k in range(3)] tdelta = [abs(1.0 / direction[k]) if abs(direction[k]) > 1e-6 else float('inf') for k in range(3)] tmax = [tdelta[k] (step[k] (volmin[k] if step[k] < 0 else volmax[k]) -
