name: Intra-ray Parallelism
head: GPU-acceleration through intra-ray parallelism
body: Intra-ray parallelism is a rendering acceleration scheme that partitions each ray into depth bins to enable efficient parallel accumulation of primitive contributions during rendering. Inputs: w, h: Width and height of the image to rasterize. b: Number of depth bins. E: Set of ellipsoid primitives, defined by world-space parameters (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma). TF: Transfer function mapping intensity to color and opacity. View: View configuration of the current camera. Outputs: I: Rendered image. Data Structures: T: Tile grid including depth-wise subdivisions. E{visible}: Culled ellipsoids. L, K: Lists of primitives and their associated 3D keys relative to tiles. R: Ranges defining the start and end indices of primitives assigned to each tile. I{bin}: Per-bin canvas, initialized to 0. Steps: 1. Create tiles T from image dimensions w, h and bin count b. Tiles include depth-wise subdivisions. 2. Cull ellipsoids E based on the current View to produce E{visible}. 3. Duplicate visible ellipsoids with 3D keys relative to tiles T to produce lists L and K. 4. Sort lists K and L by tile keys. Note: No intra-tile depth sorting is performed. 5. Identify ranges R for each tile t, defining the range of primitives assigned to that 3D tile. 6. Initialize per-bin canvas I{bin} to 0. 7. Loop over all tiles t in T: a. Extract primitives Et assigned to tile t from list L using range R[t]. b. For all pixels i in t: i. Compute ray ray[i, tz] intensity sample based on i, E, and E. ii. Blend the partial ray result into the per-bin canvas: I{bin}[i, tz] \leftarrow \text{BlendPartialRay}(ray[i, tz]). 8. After processing all tiles, reset tile grid z=1 by creating new tiles T with bin count 1: T \leftarrow \text{CreateTiles}(w, h, 1). 9. Loop over all pixels i in image I: a. Merge Z-bins by blending across b bins: I[i] \leftarrow \text{MergeZBins}(I{bin}[i, 0:b]). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def RENDER(w, h, b, E, TF, View): TILEW, TILEH = 16, 16 # Standard tile dimensions def CreateTiles(w, h, b): return [{'x': x, 'y': y, 'z': z, 'w': TILEW, 'h': TILEH} for z in range(b) for y in range(0, h, TILEH) for x in range(0, w, TILEW)] def CullEllipsoid(E, View): return [e for e in E if intersectsfrustum(e, View)] def DuplicateWithKeys3D(Evisible, T): L, K = [], [] for e in Evisible: for t in T: if intersectstile(e, t): L.append(e) K.append((t['x'], t['y'], t['z'])) return L, K def SortByTileKeys(K, L): combined = sorted(zip(K, L), key=lambda x: x[0]) return zip(combined) if combined else ([], []) def IdentifyTileRanges(K): R = {} start = 0 for i in range(len(K)): if i == len(K) - 1 or K[i] != K[i+1]: R[K[i]] = (start, i + 1) start = i + 1 return R def InitializeZero(w, h, b): return [[[0.0] b for in range(h)] for in range(w)] def IntensitySample(i, j, Et, TF): return integrateray(i, j, Et, TF) # Standard ray-primitive intersection def BlendPartialRay(val, current): return composite(val, current) # Standard front-to-back compositing def MergeZBins(bins): result = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for b in bins: result = composite(b, result) return result T = CreateTiles(w, h, b) Evisible = CullEllipsoid(E, View) L, K = DuplicateWithKeys3D(Evisible, T) K, L = SortByTileKeys(K, L) R = IdentifyTileRanges(K) Ibin = InitializeZero(w, h, b) for t in T: key = (t['x'], t['y'], t['z']) if key in R: startidx, endidx = R[key] Et = L[startidx:endidx] for i in range(t['x'], min(t['x'] + t['w'], w)): for j in range(t['y'], min(t['y'] + t['h'], h)): rayval = IntensitySample(i, j, Et, TF) Ibin[i][j][t['z']] = BlendPartialRay(rayval, Ibin[i][j][t['z']]) T = CreateTiles(w, h, 1) I = [[[0.0] 3 for in range(h)] for in range(w)] for i in range(w): for j in range(h): I[i][j] = MergeZBins(Ibin[i][j]) return I Parameters: w, h: Image dimensions. b: Number of depth bins. TF: Transfer function. View: Camera view configuration. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method explicitly states that no intra-tile depth sorting is performed. This may lead to incorrect blending order if primitives within a tile overlap significantly in depth, requiring the blending function to handle depth-aware accumulation or the primitives to be pre-sorted by the caller. Precision issues may arise when merging b bins if the blending function is not associative or commutative in the presence of floating-point errors. Not given in the sources. A technique to partition ray space into discrete depth intervals, allowing batched primitive testing. It is chosen when depth coherence is high and primitives are sparse. Link to Temporal Coherence and Caching. Assigning primitives to 3D tiles based on spatial keys. It differs from pixel-based assignment by grouping rays, enabling coarser culling. Link to Inter-Ray Coherency. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for I{bin} of size w \times h \times b, plus lists L and K proportional to the number of visible primitives. Strengths: Enables parallel accumulation of primitive contributions by grouping them into depth bins, potentially improving GPU occupancy. Limitations: Lack of intra-tile depth sorting may compromise visual accuracy for overlapping primitives. When to Use: Suitable for sparse volume rendering with ellipsoid primitives where depth coherence can be exploited. When Not to Use: Not suitable for dense volumes or scenes with high depth complexity within tiles where sorting is critical. The method originates from research on 3D ellipsoid-based sparse volume rendering, specifically leveraging structure-aware primitive learning and per-primitive ray sampling. It was developed to accelerate rendering by partitioning rays into depth bins, allowing for efficient parallel processing on GPUs. ESVR: 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering via Structure-aware Primitive Learning and Per-primitive Ray Sampling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05564v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Octant-based Distributed Volume Rendering
head: Distributed Ray Casting, Distributed Volume Rendering, Octant-based Distributed VR
body: Octant-based Distributed Volume Rendering is a parallel image-order rendering technique that partitions a 3D volume into eight spatial octants, assigns each to an independent worker process (server) for concurrent ray casting, and composites the resulting subvolume images at a central client process to produce the final frame. It differs from single-processor volume rendering by eliminating redundant computation across the entire volume and from other distributed methods by using a fixed, non-recursive octree subdivision rather than adaptive refinement, relying on a specific opacity correction in the compositing stage to handle boundaries between independent renderers. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scalar field volume V with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz, a camera view (position, orientation, field of view), and a target image plane resolution W \times H. Output: A final composited image buffer containing color and opacity for each pixel. Data Structures 1. Volume Partition: The volume V is divided into 8 equal-sized octants. To handle gradient calculations and interpolation at boundaries, each octant is padded with a 1-voxel wide border from its three adjacent octants, resulting in "padded octants". 2. RLE File: Each server generates a Run-Length Encoded (RLE) file. This file stores the final color (C{out}) and opacity (\alpha{out}) of the ray cast through that specific octant for every pixel in the image plane. 3. Client Buffer (alphabuffer): A subclass of the standard BUFFER class. Unlike server buffers which shade pixels via ray casting, this buffer shades pixels by compositing the results received from the servers. 4. Communication: Uses the AFTTCOM library (socket-based message passing) to send RLE file names from servers to the client, and UNIX rsh to launch remote server processes. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: The client process (administrator) spawns eight server processes. Each server is assigned one of the eight octants of the volume. 2. Local Rendering: Each server independently performs volume rendering on its assigned octant. For each pixel in the image plane, a ray is cast through the padded octant. If a sample point lies within the octant's bordering voxels (the pad), the pad is used to provide the eight surrounding voxels for trilinear interpolation; otherwise, the pad is ignored. Central differences are used to approximate the gradient vector for normal calculation at each voxel. When a ray exits an octant on a face bordering another octant, no background color is composited into the ray because the resulting opacity is zero. The server writes the resulting color and opacity values for all pixels into an RLE file. 3. Communication: Each server sends the filename of its RLE file to the client via AFTTCOM message passing. 4. Buffer Loading: The client reads the RLE files into memory buffers. 5. Sorting: The client sorts the eight buffers in front-to-back image order based on the depth of each server's octant in image space. This is achieved using a bubble sort algorithm on the buffers. 6. Compositing: The client composites the sorted buffers to produce the final image. The client loops through the buffers in depth order. For each pixel, it applies the distributed transparency formulas. If a front pixel and a back pixel are both background, or if either is background, no composition is performed and one color is used directly. If a ray begins with no color and exists on a shared face, it may terminate with no color, skipping composition. Formulas The compositing step uses modified transparency formulas to account for the fact that each server renders a subvolume independently. The opacity term in the buffer represents the remaining opacity behind the octant, not the true opacity of the octant itself. Therefore, for all buffers except the first (closest), the opacity term must be subtracted from 1 to get the true opacity. Let C{in} and \alpha{in} be the accumulated color and opacity from the closest octant(s) processed so far. Let Cs and \alphas be the color and opacity of the current octant's buffer being composited. The distributed transparency formulas are: C{out} = C{in} + (\alpha{in})(1 - \alphas)(Cs) \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} - \alpha{in}(1 - \alphas) Where: C{in}, \alpha{in} are initialized to the pixel values of the closest octant's buffer. Cs, \alphas are the pixel values of the next closest octant's buffer. The term (1 - \alphas) represents the true opacity of the octant. Parameters Octant Division: The volume is split into 8 octants, each handled by one server processor (1/8th of the volume per server). View Naming: Numbers represent the Z-height of the eyepoint in object space or X/Y position along top/bottom. Letters: RS (Right Side), 3F (3D Front), LO (Left Side), SP (Single Processor), Distr (Distributed). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def octantdistributedvolumerendering(volume, camera, imagewidth, imageheight): # 1. Partition volume into 8 octants with 1-voxel padding from adjacent octants octants = [] for i in range(2): for j in range(2): for k in range(2): subvol = extractsubvolume(volume, i, j, k) paddedoctant = padoctant(subvol, volume) octants.append(paddedoctant) # 2. Spawn servers and render each octant rledata = [] for idx, octant in enumerate(octants): buffer = renderoctantlocal(octant, camera, imagewidth, imageheight) rledata.append((buffer, octant)) # 3. Client loads RLE data into memory buffers clientbuffers = rledata # 4. Sort buffers front-to-back by octant depth in image space (bubble sort) for i in range(len(clientbuffers)): for j in range(0, len(clientbuffers) - i - 1): if clientbuffers[j][1].depth > clientbuffers[j+1][1].depth: clientbuffers[j], clientbuffers[j+1] = clientbuffers[j+1], clientbuffers[j] # 5. Composite buffers finalbuffer = createzerobuffer(imagewidth, imageheight) # Initialize with closest octant closestbuf, = clientbuffers[0] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): finalbuffer[y, x] = closestbuf[y, x] # Composite remaining octants for k in range(1, len(clientbuffers)): currentbuf, = clientbuffers[k] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): cin, ain = finalbuffer[y, x] cs, as = currentbuf[y, x] # Optimization: background check if isbackground(cin, ain) or isbackground(cs, as): if not isbackground(cs, as): finalbuffer[y, x] = (cs, as) continue # Optimization: zero color termination if ain == 0.0: continue # Distributed transparency formulas trueopacity = 1.0 - as cout = cin + (ain trueopacity cs) aout = ain - (ain trueopacity) finalbuffer[y, x] = (cout, aout) return finalbuffer def renderoctantlocal(octant, camera, width, height): buffer = createzerobuffer(width, height) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): ray = camera.castray(x, y) tmin, tmax = rayintersectbox(ray, octant.bounds) if tmax < tmin: buffer[y, x] = (0.0, 0.0) continue cacc, aacc = 0.0, 0.0 t = tmin step = computestepsize(ray, octant.resolution) while t < tmax: point = ray.origin + t ray.direction # Trilinear interpolation using pad if near boundary color, opacity = trilinearsample(point, octant.data) # Standard local compositing cacc = cacc + (aacc (1.0 - opacity) color) aacc = aacc - (aacc (1.0 - opacity)) t += step buffer[y, x] = (cacc, aacc) return buffer def extractsubvolume(vol, ix, iy, iz): dx, dy, dz = vol.shape sx, ex = ix dx // 2, (ix + 1) dx // 2 sy, ey = iy dy // 2, (iy + 1) dy // 2 sz, ez = iz dz // 2, (iz + 1) dz // 2 return vol[sx:ex, sy:ey, sz:ez] def padoctant(sub, fullvol): # Pad with 1 voxel from adjacent octants in fullvol pad = np.pad(sub, 1, mode='edge') return pad def trilinearsample(point, grid): # Standard trilinear interpolation coords = pointtogridcoords(point, grid) return interpolatetrilinear(coords, grid) def isbackground(color, opacity): return opacity == 0.0 def createzerobuffer(w, h): return np.zeros((h, w, 2)) def computestepsize(ray, resolution): return 1.0 / max(resolution) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sampling Anomalies at Borders: In uniform artificial volumes, incorrect sampling at octant borders produces visible pixel color anomalies. This occurs because the ray's exit point in one octant (on the volume face) does not equal the last sampled point (within the containing voxel). The adjacent octant's entry point is the first sample point. This breaks Levoy's requirement for equally spaced samples along the ray. In non-uniform volumes (e.g., CT chest), these anomalies are masked by tissue differences. Gradient Approximation: Central differencing for normal approximation was investigated as a cause for shading inconsistencies at shared voxels. This was disproved for uniform box volumes because shared voxels had equal colors assigned during the shade/classify step. Ray Exit at Shared Faces: When a ray exits an octant on a face bordering another octant, no background color is composited into the ray because the resulting opacity is zero. A zero opacity from a forward octant allows no color contribution from the octant behind it. Time Complexity: Preprocessing time scales inversely with the number of octants (O(V/P) where V is volume size, P is processor count). Ray casting time depends heavily on view direction and volume dimensions (e.g., views along the greatest height dimension take longer). Total execution time includes communication overhead and client-side composition. Memory Complexity: Each server stores its octant plus padding. The client stores 8 full-resolution image buffers (RLE files loaded into memory) during compositing. Measured Performance: CT Chest (240x164x175): Single Processor (SP) time 10:05, Distributed (Distr) time 4:14. 58% savings in total execution time. Artificial Box (200x200x210): SP time 6:32, Distr time 2:45. 58% savings in total execution time. Strengths: Significant reduction in processing time. Enables cut-away viewing and intermediate subvolume viewing by accessing individual server RLE files. Limitations: Visible sampling anomalies in uniform volumes at octant boundaries. Fixed subdivision (no adaptive refinement) may lead to load imbalance if volume density is non-uniform. Communication overhead for RLE files and compositing logic. When to Use: When rendering large volumes on a distributed system with 8 processors, and visual fidelity in uniform regions is not critical or can be masked by data complexity. When Not to Use: When uniform volumes require high visual fidelity at boundaries, or when adaptive refinement is needed for variable density volumes. Origin: Developed for distributed volume rendering on an eight-server system. History: The method was implemented using the AFTTCOM message passing library and UNIX rsh. It was tested on CT chest, CT dog heart, and artificial box volumes to demonstrate performance savings and cut-away viewing capabilities. Usage: Used to demonstrate the feasibility of distributed volume rendering, specifically highlighting the trade-off between processing time savings and visual artifacts at octant boundaries in uniform data. DTIC ADA248167: Distributed Ray Casting for High-Speed Volume Rendering, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA248167, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Streaming Model for Acceleration
head: PPE-SPE streaming acceleration, Streaming Model Based Volume Ray Casting
body: The Streaming Model for Acceleration is a parallel implementation of volume ray casting designed for the heterogeneous Cell Broadband Engine (Cell B.E.) architecture. It solves the problems of high computational demands, memory bandwidth bottlenecks, and irregular data access patterns inherent in ray casting by overlapping acceleration techniques with rendering. Unlike texture-mapping based volume rendering, which is limited by graphics memory size and lower quality, this method uses system memory to achieve high-quality interactive rendering. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly separating the hierarchical traversal (empty space skipping) to the PowerPC Processor Element (PPE) and the ray integration (early ray termination) to the Synergistic Processing Elements (SPEs), using asynchronous DMA to hide latency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric dataset (e.g., 256^3), a classification table (mapping voxel values to color and opacity), and an image resolution (e.g., 256^2 pixels). Output: A rendered 2D image tile. Data Structures: 1. Octree: A hierarchical data structure used for empty space skipping. Layout: Each node has 8 children. Field: Each node stores the maximum value of any voxel in the subvolume rooted at that node. Leaf Node Size: A trade-off parameter. Smaller sizes increase traversal time and data transfer overhead; larger sizes increase SPE rendering time due to more empty space handling. 2. Ray Segment: Represents a contiguous sequence of voxels along a ray that lies within non-empty subvolumes. Parameters: R: Ray offset from the viewpoint. L: Length of the corresponding segment. 3. Task List: A concatenated list of ray segments for all pixels in a tile, transferred from PPE to SPE. 4. Subvolume Buffer: A buffer in SPE local memory storing 2^3 voxel data (subvolumes) required for interpolation. Numbered Steps: 1. Work Decomposition: The screen is divided into a grid of small tiles. Tiles are assigned to SPEs using a static Z-order based scheme to exploit spatial locality and balance load. 2. Empty Space Skipping (PPE): The PPE traverses the octree along the ray direction for each pixel in the assigned tile. Empty space determination uses either raw voxel values or opacity values after classification. Pitfall: If opacity values are used, the octree must be updated every time the classification table changes. The PPE collects ray segments located only in non-empty subvolumes. Each ray segment is defined by parameters R and L. The PPE concatenates the collected ray segments for all pixels in the tile. 3. Data Transfer: The PPE sends the size of the task list to the SPE (unless the queue is full). The PPE transfers the concatenated task list to the assigned SPE via DMA. 4. Rendering (SPE): The SPE waits for a signal from the PPE indicating all contributing ray segments for the tile have been collected. The SPE renders the tile using four main steps: prefetching, interpolation, shading/classification, and compositing. SIMD Processing: Four ray sampling points are processed together in a loop to exploit SIMD capabilities. Prefetching: Asynchronous DMA and double buffering are used to fetch the next 4 subvolumes required for rendering the next 4 ray sampling points into local memory. The volume in main memory is arranged into a 3-D grid of small subvolumes. Interpolation: If the 4 subvolumes for the current 4 ray sampling points are ready, 4 tri-linear interpolations are performed concurrently using 4-way SIMD instructions to reconstruct signal values. Shading/Classification: Reconstructed values are mapped to color and opacity using shading and classification tables. Compositing: The 4 values are composited sequentially. However, the R, G, and B values are composited concurrently, utilizing 3/4 of the SIMD capability. Early Ray Termination: The final opacity value is tested for early ray termination. If the threshold is reached, the next ray is processed. 5. Result Transfer: After all pixel values for the tile are computed, the tile image is sent back to main memory using asynchronous DMA. 6. Loop: The PPE and SPEs operate asynchronously. The PPE continues generating lists for the next tile while the SPE renders the current one, overlapping empty space skipping with actual rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pperendertile(tileid, octree, classificationtable): """ PPE traverses octree to generate ray segments for a tile. """ tilepixels = gettilepixels(tileid) raysegmentslist = [] for pixel in tilepixels: ray = createrayfromviewpoint(pixel) segments = traverseoctreeforray(ray, octree) # segments is a list of (R, L) tuples raysegmentslist.extend(segments) # Send task list to SPE speid = getspefortile(tileid) sendtasklisttospe(speid, raysegmentslist) # Wait for SPE to finish this tile before moving to next? # No, asynchronous. But we need to ensure queue isn't full. while not isspequeuefull(speid): # Could start next tile generation here if logic allows, # but typically one tile per SPE assignment in this static scheme. break def sperendertile(tasklist, volumedata, classificationtable): """ SPE renders a tile given a list of ray segments. """ # Double buffering for prefetching buffera = allocatelocalmemory() bufferb = allocatelocalmemory() currentbuffer = buffera nextbuffer = bufferb # Pre-fetch initial subvolumes prefetchsubvolumes(tasklist, volumedata, nextbuffer) for segment in tasklist: R = segment.R L = segment.L # Process 4 sampling points at a time for SIMD # Assume we have a loop over chunks of 4 segments or 4 points per segment # Simplified: processing 4 points concurrently # Check if next 4 subvolumes are ready in nextbuffer if not isprefetchready(nextbuffer): waitfordma(nextbuffer) # Swap buffers temp = currentbuffer currentbuffer = nextbuffer nextbuffer = temp # Prefetch next 4 subvolumes asynchronously prefetchsubvolumesfornextpoints(tasklist, volumedata, nextbuffer) # Interpolation: 4-way SIMD values = trilinearinterpolate4points(currentbuffer, R, L) # Shading/Classification colorsopacities = applyclassificationtable(values, classificationtable) # Compositing: Sequential for alpha, Concurrent for RGB # Assuming standard front-to-back compositing resultcolor = (0, 0, 0) resultopacity = 0 for i in range(4): c = colorsopacities[i] # Concurrent RGB compositing resultcolor = compositergb(resultcolor, c.color) # Sequential Alpha compositing resultopacity = compositealpha(resultopacity, c.opacity) # Early Ray Termination if resultopacity >= TERMINATIONTHRESHOLD: break # Send tile image back to main memory sendtiletomainmemory(tileid, resultimage) def traverseoctreeforray(ray, octree): """ Traverses octree to find non-empty segments. Returns list of (R, L) tuples. """ segments = [] currentpos = ray.origin direction = ray.direction node = octree.root while node is not None: # Check if node is empty if node.maxvalue == EMPTYVALUE: # Skip this subvolume # Advance ray past this subvolume currentpos = advanceraypastsubvolume(currentpos, direction, node.bounds) # Move to next relevant node or terminate # Implementation detail: standard octree traversal logic break # Simplified for pseudocode # If leaf or non-empty, collect segment # Determine intersection with current node tstart, tend = intersectraynode(ray, node.bounds) if tstart < tend: # Calculate R (offset) and L (length) R = tstart L = tend - tstart segments.append((R, L)) # Move to children or next node #... (Standard traversal logic) return segments def prefetchsubvolumes(tasklist, volumedata, buffer): """ Uses asynchronous DMA to fetch subvolumes into local memory. """ # Identify subvolumes needed for the next 4 sampling points subvolumeindices = getsubvolumeindices(tasklist, 4) # Issue DMA transfer dmatransfer(volumedata, subvolumeindices, buffer) def prefetchsubvolumesfornextpoints(tasklist, volumedata, buffer): """ Issues async DMA for the next set of points while current ones are processed. """ subvolumeindices = getsubvolumeindicesfornextchunk(tasklist) dmatransferasync(volumedata, subvolumeindices, buffer) def isprefetchready(buffer): return buffer.dmacomplete def trilinearinterpolate4points(buffer, R, L): """ Performs 4 tri-linear interpolations using 4-way SIMD. """ # Extract voxel data from buffer voxels = getvoxeldatafrombuffer(buffer) # Interpolate values = simdtrilinearinterpolate(voxels, R, L) return values def applyclassificationtable(values, table): """ Maps values to color and opacity. """ return [table.lookup(v) for v in values] def compositergb(c1, c2): """ Standard over operator for RGB. """ return c2 + c1 (1 - c2.a) # Simplified, assuming c2 is foreground def compositealpha(a1, a2): """ Standard over operator for Alpha. """ return a1 + a2 (1 - a1) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limitation: The Cell B.E. memory is limited to 1GB, preventing experiments with larger datasets. Leaf Node Size: Choosing the leaf node size is critical. Too small increases traversal/transfer overhead; too large increases SPE rendering time. Classification Updates: If opacity values are used for empty space detection, the octree must be updated whenever the classification table changes. Heterogeneous Speed Gap: If the PPE is slower than the SPE, the SPE will idle waiting for input. If the PPE is faster, the output must be stored to avoid overflow. The streaming model attempts to balance this via asynchronous DMA. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given in terms of Big-O, but performance is measured in frames per second (FPS). Memory Complexity: Limited by the 1GB memory constraint of the Cell B.E.. Measured Performance: 9 to 26 frames/sec on a single Cell B.E. processor (3.2 GHz) for a 256^3 dataset at 256^2 resolution. Comparison: Approximately an order of magnitude faster than an implementation on an Intel Xeon 3GHz processor. Strengths: Removes overhead of traversing hierarchical structures by overlapping it with rendering. Removes memory access latency via prefetching. Achieves better SIMD utilization in SPEs because SPEs know voxels to process in advance. Uses system memory, allowing larger datasets than graphics memory. Limitations: Limited by 1GB system memory. Requires careful tuning of leaf node size. Static assignment may not adapt to highly variable scene complexity, though fine-grain tiling helps balance load. When to use: When rendering high-quality volumetric data on Cell B.E. hardware where interactive frame rates are required and datasets fit within 1GB. When not to use: When datasets exceed 1GB or when hardware lacks the Cell B.E. architecture (PPE/SPE heterogeneity). Origin: Developed by Sony, Toshiba, and IBM (STI) as part of the Cell Broadband Engine (Cell B.E.) initiative. Paper: "Streaming Model Based Volume Ray Casting Implementation". History: The method addresses the limitations of texture-mapping based volume rendering, which suffers from limited data size (graphics memory) and lower quality. It leverages the Cell B.E.'s heterogeneous cores (PPE for control/traversal, SPEs for SIMD compute) and asynchronous DMA features. Usage: Used for interactive visualization of practical datasets (e.g., 256^3) on the Cell B.E. platform. name: Monte Carlo Integration for Rendering
head: MC Integration, Stochastic Integration
body: Monte Carlo Integration solves the recursive rendering equation integral by converting it into a finite sum of stochastic estimates, allowing for the handling of complex light transport phenomena such as soft shadows, depth-of-field, and self-shadowing. It is distinguished from deterministic volume rendering acceleration methods (e.g., Early Ray Termination and Culling) by its reliance on random sampling to approximate integrals rather than spatial culling or structured traversal, making it suitable for general path tracing but computationally intensive due to variance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Image dimensions (width W, height H), camera parameters (thin lens model), scene geometry/materials, and number of iterations N. Output: Estimated radiance C for each pixel. Data Structures: Ray Buffer: A collection of W \times H rays generated per iteration. Accumulator: Per-pixel sum of estimates. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Initialize pixel accumulators to zero. 2. Iteration Loop: For i from 1 to N: a. Ray Generation: Generate W \times H camera rays using a thin lens model. b. Light Transport: Trace rays through the scene, calculating shading and interactions. c. Estimation: Compute the stochastic estimate f(Xi) for each ray, weighted by the probability density function p(Xi). d. Accumulation: Add the weighted estimate to the pixel accumulator. 3. Finalization: Divide the accumulator by N to obtain the final color. Formula: The expected value C is calculated as: C = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{f(Xi)}{p(Xi)} Where: N: Number of iterations (stochastic estimates) per pixel. f(Xi): The integrand value (e.g., radiance contribution) for the i-th sample. p(Xi): The probability density function (PDF) of generating sample Xi. Xi: The i-th stochastic sample (e.g., ray direction, intersection point). Parameters: N: Number of iterations. The sources note that increasing N reduces variance and converges to the true value. A specific implementation mentioned 2000 iterations for high-quality results with soft shadows and depth-of-field. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Variance: Low N results in noisy images. Importance sampling is used to mitigate this. Precision: Floating-point accumulation errors may occur with very large N or high dynamic range scenes. Degenerate Input: If p(Xi) = 0 for a sample where f(Xi) \neq 0, the estimate is undefined. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def montecarlorender(W, H, N, scene, camera): # Initialize accumulators coloraccumulator = zeros((H, W, 3)) for i in range(N): # Generate rays for all pixels rays = generatecamerarays(W, H, camera) for y in range(H): for x in range(W): ray = rays[y, x] # Trace ray and compute integrand value f(Xi) # and its probability density p(Xi) fxi, pxi = traceray(ray, scene) # Avoid division by zero if pxi == 0: contribution = 0.0 else: contribution = fxi / pxi # Accumulate coloraccumulator[y, x] += contribution # Average over N iterations finalcolor = coloraccumulator / N return finalcolor Reservoir resampling and temporal path guiding are orthogonal variance reduction techniques that exploit temporal, screen space, and scene space correlation. Both are unbiased, computationally lightweight, and effective at spatio-temporal information reuse, making them suitable for combination with control variates. They are chosen when spatio-temporal coherence can be leveraged to reduce noise without significant additional computational cost. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot W \cdot H \cdot C), where C is the cost per ray (bounces, shading). Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for pixel buffers. Performance: Convergence is slow (O(1/\sqrt{N})), requiring many samples (e.g., 2000) for high quality. Strengths: Handles complex lighting (soft shadows, DOF) naturally; unbiased. Limitations: High variance; noisy images at low sample counts; computationally expensive. When to Use: Offline rendering or high-quality stills where noise can be tolerated or denoised. When Not to Use: Real-time applications requiring low latency without heavy denoising. Monte Carlo integration for rendering was popularized in the context of global illumination to solve the recursive rendering equation. The approach converts the integral into a finite sum, with each iteration reducing variance. Recent developments include recursive control variates and combinations with temporal path guiding and reservoir resampling for inverse rendering. name: Acceleration Structures and Traversal
body: This family encompasses the algorithmic strategies for navigating volumetric data structures and the spatial metadata used to skip empty or occluded regions during ray casting. It solves the problem of mapping continuous ray paths to discrete data elements while minimizing memory bandwidth and computation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like GL-NeRF and Occlusion Clipping with Orthogonal Opacity Map by focusing on the topology of the data access path and explicit hierarchical culling rather than neural approximation or rasterized proxies. The core mechanism shared by all children is the determination of the sequence of data elements (voxels, cells, or bricks) intersected by a ray, and the retrieval of values from those elements. This involves: 1. Path Parameterization: Representing the ray as \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and computing intersection intervals [t{entry}, t{exit}] with data boundaries. 2. Coordinate Mapping: Transforming the continuous ray parameter t into discrete data indices (e.g., voxel coordinates, cell IDs, or brick IDs). 3. Data Retrieval: Fetching the value at the mapped index from the appropriate memory structure (texture, buffer, or mesh). Mathematically, for a uniform grid, this is often a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) step. For irregular grids, it involves explicit boundary intersection tests. For hierarchical data, it involves Level of Detail (LoD) selection and cache residency checks. Discards the previous frame's acceleration structure and constructs a new one from scratch every frame for animated scenes [3266-acceleration-structure-rebuild.md]. It supports arbitrary, unrestricted animation types by avoiding the complexity and limitations of incremental or hierarchical update schemes [3266-acceleration-structure-rebuild.md]. It differs from siblings like Adaptive Multi-Step Empty Voxel Skipping or Temporal Coherence and Caching by rejecting temporal reuse of the structure itself, relying instead on full reconstruction speed and parallel processing [3266-acceleration-structure-rebuild.md]. Covers the algorithmic strategies for moving a ray through a volume dataset and retrieving scalar values for compositing [13739-traversal-and-data-access.md]. It sets itself apart from siblings like GL-NeRF and Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling by focusing on the topology of the data access path and memory availability [13739-traversal-and-data-access.md]. A volume rendering technique that accelerates image-order rendering by utilizing a Linear Level Octree (LLO) spatial data structure to skip empty space and facilitate early ray termination [16481-llo-based-ray-casting.md]. It differs from brute-force ray-casting by replacing uniform voxel traversal with hierarchical octree traversal, and from other acceleration structures by encoding the octree in a linear array to optimize cache residency and memory access patterns [16481-llo-based-ray-casting.md]. Accelerates volume rendering by identifying and bypassing transparent or empty regions of the volume data before expensive sampling and compositing occur [17387-empty-space-skipping-via-acceleration-structures.md]. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on geometric proxies [16346-progressive-ray-casting-for-volumetric-models-on-mobile-devi.md], this family constructs explicit hierarchical or grid-based metadata structures (e.g., octrees, BVHs, min/max grids) to determine ray visibility [13062-empty-space-skipping-via-acceleration-structure.md]. It sets itself apart from SparseLeap by typically using scalar min/max values or occupancy flags rather than rasterized segment lists, and from Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree for Empty-Space Skipping by employing fixed-grid brick structures or specific tree traversals rather than generic bounding box hierarchies [13062-empty-space-skipping-via-acceleration-structure.md]. A structure for scenes with dynamic parts. Uses a global grid/structure where articulated bodies (rigid parts) are inserted as elementary objects. Each rigid part has its own local grid or data structure. It is a technique for accelerating ray tracing in scenes with articulated bodies (rigid parts connected by joints) by separating static and dynamic components into different acceleration structures. Implementation uses a separate grid or data structure for each self-contained rigid part of the articulated body. It uses a global grid to store the individual parts as elementary objects. When the figure moves, only update the global grid; the local structures for rigid parts do not need updating. Approximate the hash table for a subtile by taking the union of the hash tables at the 4 surrounding corners and send it to the corresponding SPE. The SPE skips a sampling point if it belongs to an empty subvolume by checking the hash table. The hash key is computed as key = (ranX \cdot x + ranY \cdot y + ranZ \cdot z) \pmod{PR}. Parameters: PR is a prime number equal to the hash table size; ranX, ranY, ranZ are random numbers strictly less than PR; x, y, z are the smallest coordinates of the subvolume. Pitfall: False positives are possible (an empty subvolume may be recognized as non-empty), but false negatives never occur. The false alarm rate can be significantly reduced by setting the hash table size large enough. Not given in the sources. name: Acceleration Structure Rebuild
head: Per-Frame Grid Rebuild
body: Acceleration Structure Rebuild discards the previous frame's acceleration structure and constructs a new one from scratch every frame for animated scenes. It supports arbitrary, unrestricted animation types by avoiding the complexity and limitations of incremental or hierarchical update schemes. It differs from siblings like Adaptive Multi-Step Empty Voxel Skipping or Temporal Coherence and Caching by rejecting temporal reuse of the structure itself, relying instead on full reconstruction speed and parallel processing. Inputs: N: Number of triangles in the scene. V: Volume of the grid bounding box. \mathbf{d}: Diagonal vector of the grid bounding box. \lambda: Multiplier parameter for grid resolution. Previous frame's macrocell information (optional, for optimization). Triangle list (positions, normals, etc.). Outputs: A new acceleration grid mapping grid cells to triangle references. Derived data structures for triangle intersection tests. 1. Grid: A sparse array or hash map mapping 3D cell coordinates (i, j, k) to lists of triangle indices. The grid dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz) are calculated per frame. 2. Triangle List: An array of triangle primitives. 3. Derived Data: Precomputed data for fast triangle-ray intersection as described by Wald. 4. Macrocell Map: A coarse grid structure from the previous frame, used to identify which fine cells might contain changed geometry. \lambda: The multiplier determining the total number of cells relative to the number of triangles. Optimal performance is typically achieved around \lambda \approx 5 for most scenes. 1. Calculate Grid Resolution: Determine the number of cells along each axis to approximate cubic cells, which minimize the surface-area-to-volume ratio and thus expected ray-tracing cost. Nx = dx \sqrt[3]{\frac{\lambda N}{V}} Ny = dy \sqrt[3]{\frac{\lambda N}{V}} Nz = dz \sqrt[3]{\frac{\lambda N}{V}} where dx, dy, dz are the components of the grid diagonal \mathbf{d}, and V is the grid volume. 2. Clear Grid: Initialize the new grid. To optimize, use macrocell information from the previous frame to identify only the cells that need to be cleared or updated, rather than clearing the entire grid if it is sparse. 3. Insert Triangles: For each triangle in the scene: a. Compute the triangle's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). b. Determine all grid cells overlapped by this AABB. c. Add a reference to the triangle to each of these cells. A conservative bounding box test is used instead of an exact triangle-in-box test. While the exact test reduces triangle references by more than one third, it increases rebuild cost significantly with only a few percent gain in ray-triangle test reduction. For scenes with dominantly long, skinny, diagonal triangles, an exact test may be preferable. 4. Build Derived Data: Create derived data structures for triangle intersection tests (e.g., as described by Wald). This step is parallelizable and can be executed concurrently with the grid rebuild. Storage-free triangle tests (e.g., Möller-Trumbore) were found to be slightly inferior in overall performance compared to derived data, even when accounting for rebuild time. 5. Memory Management: Use a preallocated pooled-memory scheme for cell lists to prevent per-cell memory allocations and fragmentation during the frame-to-frame transition. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rebuildaccelerationstructure(triangles, gridmin, gridmax, lambdaparam, prevmacrocells=None): # 1. Calculate Grid Resolution diag = [gridmax[i] - gridmin[i] for i in range(3)] volume = diag[0] diag[1] diag[2] numtriangles = len(triangles) cellcountfactor = (lambdaparam numtriangles / volume) (1.0/3.0) nx = max(1, round(diag[0] cellcountfactor)) ny = max(1, round(diag[1] cellcountfactor)) nz = max(1, round(diag[2] cellcountfactor)) # 2. Initialize Grid & Clear newgrid = {} if prevmacrocells is not None: # Use macrocell info to clear only relevant cells for cell in prevmacrocells: newgrid.pop(cell, None) else: newgrid.clear() # 3. Insert Triangles for triidx, tri in enumerate(triangles): aabbmin = [min(v[i] for v in tri.vertices) for i in range(3)] aabbmax = [max(v[i] for v in tri.vertices) for i in range(3)] mincell = [0, 0, 0] maxcell = [0, 0, 0] dims = [nx, ny, nz] for i in range(3): tmin = (aabbmin[i] - gridmin[i]) / diag[i] tmax = (aabbmax[i] - gridmin[i]) / diag[i] mincell[i] = max(0, int(tmin dims[i])) maxcell[i] = min(dims[i] - 1, int(tmax dims[i])) # Clamp to prevent out-of-bounds when tmax is exactly 1.0 if maxcell[i] >= dims[i]: maxcell[i] = dims[i] - 1 for x in range(mincell[0], maxcell[0] + 1): for y in range(mincell[1], maxcell[1] + 1): for z in range(mincell[2], maxcell[2] + 1): if (x, y, z) not in newgrid: newgrid[(x, y, z)] = [] newgrid[(x, y, z)].append(triidx) # 4. Build Derived Data (Parallelizable) # Precompute plane normal and D for fast triangle-ray intersection deriveddata = [] for tri in triangles: v0, v1, v2 = tri.vertices normal = cross(sub(v1, v0), sub(v2, v0)) d = dot(normal, v0) deriveddata.append({"normal": normal, "d": d}) return newgrid, deriveddata, (nx, ny, nz) def sub(a, b): return [a[i] - b[i] for i in range(3)] def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]] def dot(a, b): return sum(a[i]b[i] for i in range(3)) Long, Skinny, Diagonal Triangles: The conservative bounding box test may insert too many references for such triangles. In these specific cases, an exact triangle-in-box test might be justified despite the higher rebuild cost. Large Scenes: The performance characteristics described (e.g., derived data superiority) are based on medium-size scenes. For much larger scenes, storage-free tests or bricking techniques might yield different results. Memory Fragmentation: Without a pooled memory scheme, frequent rebuilds can lead to significant fragmentation and allocation overhead. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Optimal \lambda \approx 5 for most scenes. The triangle rebuild takes less time than the grid rebuild and can be run in parallel. Strengths: Supports any type of animation without restrictions; simple implementation; no need for complex incremental update logic. Limitations: High build cost per frame compared to incremental updates; not suitable for static scenes where incremental or hierarchical updates would be more efficient; conservative bounding box test may lead to more ray-triangle intersections than necessary. The method was introduced in "Ray Tracing Animated Scenes using Coherent Grid Traversal" by Wald et al. (2006). It was chosen over incremental [Reinhard et al. 2000] or hierarchical [Lext and Akenine-Moller 2001] updates to support arbitrary animations without restrictions. The grid resolution formula is based on the work of Cleary et al. (1983). name: Efficient Space Skipping & Adaptive Sampling of Unstructured Volumes Using H.W. Accel. Ray Tracing
head: Space Skipping and Adaptive Sampling for Unstructured Volumes
body: This method enables interactive visualization of large unstructured volumes (e.g., finite element simulations) by leveraging hardware-accelerated ray tracing to accelerate acceleration structure traversal and point-in-element tests. It solves the bottleneck of traditional rasterization, which requires expensive front-to-back sorting of 20–40 GB of elements when the camera moves, and the limitation of existing space-skipping techniques that assume regular grids. It sets itself apart from siblings like Empty Space Skipping via Acceleration Structures by explicitly targeting unstructured meshes via KD-tree partitioning and using hardware ray tracing to handle both transparent element culling and large void region skipping without significant overhead. Inputs: An unstructured mesh (e.g., tetrahedral mesh) with scalar field values and a transfer function mapping scalar values to opacity and color. Outputs: A rendered image with adaptive sampling rates and skipped empty space. Data Structures: 1. KD-Tree: Built over the mesh elements to partition them into a set of convex, disjoint regions (partitions). 2. Partition Metadata: For each region in the KD-tree, the following precomputed values are stored: S{min} (minimum scalar field value), S{max} (maximum scalar field value), O{max} (maximum opacity derived from the transfer function applied to [S{min}, S{max}]), and V{color} (color variance within the region). Numbered Steps: 1. Build KD-Tree: Construct a KD-tree over the input unstructured mesh elements to create convex disjoint regions. 2. Compute Metadata: For each region, compute S{min}, S{max}, O{max}, and V{color}. 3. Ray Traversal: Use hardware-accelerated ray tracing to iterate rays through the active partitions. 4. Empty Space Skipping: During traversal, skip any partition where O{max} = 0 (entirely transparent elements) or where the partition is unoccupied (large void regions due to data sparsity). 5. Adaptive Sampling: For each partition that is not skipped, determine the sampling rate R based on the local color variance V{color}. 6. Interpolation: Interpolate R between R{min} and R{max} based on V{color}, where high variance regions use R{max} and low variance regions use R{min}. 7. Sampling: Take samples along the ray within the partition at rate R. 8. Termination: Iterate steps 3–7 until the ray reaches maximum capacity (maximum number of samples) or exits the bounds of all partitions. Formulas: The adaptive sampling rate is computed via linear interpolation: R = R{min} + \left( \frac{V{color} - V{min}}{V{max} - V{min}} \right) (R{max} - R{min}) where V{min} and V{max} are the global minimum and maximum color variance across all partitions. Parameters: R{min}: User-specified minimum sampling rate. R{max}: User-specified maximum sampling rate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overhead: The overhead introduced by the technique must be low; otherwise, it overshadows the performance benefits gained from reduced sampling. Data Sparsity: Two forms of empty space exist: entirely transparent elements and large void regions due to sparsity, both of which must be handled. Regular Grid Assumption: Existing techniques often assume a regular grid, which does not apply to unstructured data, necessitating this KD-tree approach. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildaccelerationstructure(mesh): # Standard KD-tree construction over mesh elements. # The source does not specify the exact tree-building algorithm. partitions = [] for region in mesh.partitionintoconvexregions(): smin = min(region.scalarvalues) smax = max(region.scalarvalues) # Compute max opacity from transfer function over the scalar range omax = max(transferfunctionopacity(s) for s in [smin, smax]) # Compute color variance over the region's scalar values vcolor = computecolorvariance(region, smin, smax) partitions.append({ 'smin': smin, 'smax': smax, 'omax': omax, 'vcolor': vcolor, 'length': region.lengthalongray() }) return partitions def computecolorvariance(region, smin, smax): # Standard variance calculation over transfer function color outputs. colors = [transferfunctioncolor(s) for s in region.scalarvalues] meanc = sum(colors) / len(colors) return sum((c - meanc)2 for c in colors) / len(colors) def computesamplingrate(vcolor, vmin, vmax, rmin, rmax): if vmax == vmin: return rmin normalizedv = (vcolor - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) return rmin + normalizedv (rmax - rmin) def renderray(ray, partitions, rmin, rmax, maxsamples): vmin = min(p['vcolor'] for p in partitions) vmax = max(p['vcolor'] for p in partitions) samples = [] samplecount = 0 # Hardware ray tracing traversal iterates partitions in front-to-back order. for partition in sorted(partitions, key=lambda p: ray.distancetopartition(p)): # Empty Space Skipping if partition['omax'] == 0: continue # Adaptive Sampling & Interpolation rate = computesamplingrate(partition['vcolor'], vmin, vmax, rmin, rmax) # Estimate number of samples based on partition length and rate numsamples = max(1, int(partition['length'] rate)) for i in range(numsamples): if samplecount >= maxsamples: return samples # Compute sample position along ray within partition t = ray.origin + ray.direction (i partition['length'] / numsamples) val = samplescalarfield(ray, t) samples.append(val) samplecount += 1 return samples def samplescalarfield(ray, t): # Point-in-element query on the unstructured mesh. return ray.queryscalarat(t) Time Complexity: Depends on the KD-tree traversal and the number of samples taken, with adaptive sampling reducing samples in low-variance regions and space skipping eliminating work in transparent/empty regions. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the KD-tree and partition metadata, with tested datasets ranging from 12 million to 366 million tetrahedra requiring up to 37 GB of GPU memory. Measured Performance: On the Segel Haas dataset, the method achieves roughly a 3.5x performance improvement by adaptively sampling and empty space skipping while preserving details in high-variance regions. On the Japan earthquake dataset, it achieves roughly a 7x performance improvement because a large portion of the volume has very similar data values allowing for adaptive sampling. On a small dataset with much empty space, performance goes from 4 to 20 frames per second using space skipping. Hardware: Tested on an RTX 8000 GPU with 48 GB memory using OptiX 6 and CUDA 10. Strengths: Handles large unstructured volumes (up to 37 GB) interactively, preserves details in high-variance regions, and reduces overhead compared to rasterization sorting. Limitations: Performance gain depends on data type; adaptive sampling works better than space skipping alone on datasets with little empty space but high variance. Origin: The method was presented in a talk/video titled "Efficient Space Skipping & Adaptive Sampling of Unstructured Volumes Using H.W. Accel. Ray Tracing". History: Traditional rasterization of unstructured volumes requires sorting elements front-to-back, which becomes a bottleneck for large datasets (20–40 GB). This method leverages prior work on hardware-accelerated ray tracing to address these challenges. Usage: Used for interactive visualization of large unstructured volumes from finite element simulations. Efficient Space Skipping & Adaptive Sampling of Unstructured Volumes Using H.W. Accel. name: Traversal and Data Access
body: Traversal and Data Access covers the algorithmic strategies for moving a ray through a volume dataset and retrieving scalar values for compositing. It solves the problem of mapping continuous ray paths to discrete data structures (uniform grids, unstructured meshes, or hierarchical bricks) while managing memory bandwidth. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like GL-NeRF and Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling by focusing on the topology of the data access path and memory availability. The core mechanism shared by all children is the determination of the sequence of data elements (voxels, cells, or bricks) intersected by a ray, and the retrieval of values from those elements. This involves: 1. Path Parameterization: Representing the ray as \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and computing intersection intervals [t{entry}, t{exit}] with data boundaries. 2. Coordinate Mapping: Transforming the continuous ray parameter t into discrete data indices (e.g., voxel coordinates, cell IDs, or brick IDs). 3. Data Retrieval: Fetching the value at the mapped index from the appropriate memory structure (texture, buffer, or mesh). Mathematically, for a uniform grid, this is often a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) step. For irregular grids, it involves explicit boundary intersection tests. For hierarchical data, it involves Level of Detail (LoD) selection and cache residency checks. A traversal method for irregular, unstructured grids that uses a sweep-plane paradigm to determine visibility order. It is chosen when rendering complex, non-convex, or disconnected topologies where fixed-step traversal fails. It differs from DDA by relying on explicit cell indexing and sorting rather than analytical grid stepping. An out-of-core data access technique for large-scale volume rendering using hierarchical bricks. It dynamically determines the working set during rendering and reports missing bricks to a subsystem for paging. It is chosen when memory bandwidth is the bottleneck and the volume exceeds GPU memory. It differs from static caching by handling data unavailability explicitly via a lock-free hash table. An acceleration technique that reduces interpolation cost by aligning sample points with voxel layers to enable bilinear interpolation, while skipping intermediate samples. It is chosen when trilinear interpolation dominates the rendering time. It differs from standard traversal by exploiting ray direction to maximize samples on grid planes. A rendering algorithm that accelerates image-order rendering by combining hierarchical data structures (octrees) with adaptive sampling and early ray termination. It is chosen for dense volumetric datasets to skip transparent regions and reduce samples where visual detail is low. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on algorithmic efficiency through spatial coherence and opacity thresholds. A GPU-accelerated dataset traversal technique that exploits frame-to-frame coherence during camera rotation to accelerate isosurface volume rendering. It is chosen for interactive rendering of static or slowly moving volumes. It differs from C-buffer techniques by storing depth distances in a prediction buffer for high-performance GPU parallelism. The concept of ray casting traversal originated with the development of volume rendering in the 1980s, with early methods relying on uniform grid traversal. The introduction of unstructured grids required new traversal algorithms, leading to methods like Lazy Sweep Ray Casting. Out-of-core techniques for large-scale volumes were later developed to handle memory bottlenecks. flipcode - Realtime Voxel Landscape Engines, https://www.flipcode.com/archives/RealtimeVoxelLandscapeEngines-Part4LevelofDetailandOptimisation.shtml, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Lazy Sweep Ray Casting
head: Lazy Sweep, Sweep Plane Ray Casting
body: Lazy Sweep Ray Casting is a fast algorithm for rendering general irregular grids, including disconnected and nonconvex domains with holes. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing unstructured meshes by exploiting spatial coherence between scanlines, replacing expensive 3D ray-casting with simpler 2D regular grid ray-casting. It is distinguished from its siblings by its use of a sweep plane orthogonal to the viewing plane to maintain an Active Cell List (ACL), allowing it to handle complex connectivity without explicit storage. Inputs: An unstructured irregular grid (mesh) defined by vertices and cells; a viewing direction (e.g., along the y-axis); image resolution (pixel rows and columns). Outputs: A rendered image. Data Structures: 1. Active Cell List (ACL): A dynamic list storing the set of cells currently intersected by the sweep plane. 2. Regular Grid (Hash Table): A 2D structure mapping pixel columns to the subset of cells in the ACL that are traversed at the current sweep position. Steps: 1. Event Determination: Identify all "events" in the sweep. Events are defined by vertices in the dataset and y-values corresponding to pixel rows in the image. Sort these events by their y-coordinate. 2. Sweep and Update: Iterate through the sorted events. If the event is a vertex: Update the ACL by adding cells that become intersected by the sweep plane as it passes the vertex, and removing cells that are no longer intersected. If the event is a pixel row: 1. Construct the Regular Grid (Hash Table) for the current ACL, storing the ACL elements for traversal. 2. For each pixel column x in the row: cast a ray corresponding to the x-value through the Regular Grid to retrieve the intersecting cells from the ACL. 3. Perform volume rendering (e.g., ray-marching or cell projection) for the ray segment through the retrieved cells. 3. Repeat: Continue until all pixel rows are processed. Formulas: Ray parameterization: \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the origin and \mathbf{d} is the direction. Intersection with cell boundaries: Determined by the geometry of the irregular grid cells. Sweep plane position: y = y{event}. Image resolution: Determines the spacing of pixel row events. Parameters: Sweep direction: Typically orthogonal to the viewing plane (e.g., y-axis). Image resolution: Determines the spacing of pixel row events. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Disconnected/Nonconvex Grids: The method handles these naturally by maintaining the ACL, which tracks all intersecting cells regardless of domain connectivity. Precision: Care must be taken when determining cell intersections with the sweep plane to avoid gaps or overlaps due to floating-point errors. Hash Table Construction: The cost of building the Regular Grid for each row must be balanced against the savings in ray casting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lazysweepraycasting(mesh, imageheight, imagewidth, viewdirection='y'): # 1. Determine events: vertices and pixel row y-coordinates events = [] for vertex in mesh.vertices: events.append(('vertex', vertex.y, vertex.id)) for row in range(imageheight): yrow = (row + 0.5) / imageheight # Standard normalized mapping events.append(('row', yrow, row)) # Sort events by y-coordinate events.sort(key=lambda e: e[1]) acl = [] # Active Cell List image = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] for eventtype, y, id in events: if eventtype == 'vertex': # Update ACL: add cells starting at this vertex, remove cells ending at this vertex acl = updateacl(acl, mesh, id) elif eventtype == 'row': # Build Regular Grid (Hash Table) from ACL regulargrid = buildregulargrid(acl, imagewidth) # Cast rays for each pixel in the row for col in range(imagewidth): cells = regulargrid.get(col, []) rayorigin = getrayorigin(col, row, imagewidth, imageheight) raydirection = getraydirection(viewdirection) color = castraythroughcells(rayorigin, raydirection, cells) image[row][col] = color return image def updateacl(acl, mesh, vertexid): # Standard implementation: identify cells connected to the vertex. # Add cells whose minimum y equals this vertex y. # Remove cells whose maximum y equals this vertex y. newacl = [] for cell in acl: if cell.maxy > vertex.y: # Keep cells still intersected newacl.append(cell) for cell in mesh.getcells(vertexid): if cell.miny == vertex.y: # Add cells starting at this sweep position newacl.append(cell) return newacl def buildregulargrid(acl, imagewidth): # Standard implementation: map cells to pixel columns they span grid = {} for cell in acl: colstart = max(0, int(cell.xmin imagewidth)) colend = min(imagewidth - 1, int(cell.xmax imagewidth)) for col in range(colstart, colend + 1): if col not in grid: grid[col] = [] grid[col].append(cell) return grid def getrayorigin(col, row, width, height): # Standard mapping from pixel indices to world coordinates return (col / width, row / height, 0.0) def getraydirection(viewdirection): # Standard viewing direction vector if viewdirection == 'y': return (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) def castraythroughcells(origin, direction, cells): # Standard volume rendering accumulation color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for cell in cells: # Intersect ray with cell, sample, and composite pass return color Garrity Ray Casting is a method for rendering unstructured meshes by exploiting intrinsic mesh connectivity to optimize ray traversal. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing non-convex domains where rays may exit and re-enter the mesh multiple times. Time Complexity: Substantially faster (by up to two orders of magnitude) than other software-based algorithms for irregular grids. The complexity depends on the number of cells and the spatial coherence. Memory Complexity: Low memory consumption, as it does not require explicit connectivity storage or large resampled volumes. Strengths: Generality, depth-sorting accuracy, simplicity of implementation, portability (no hardware dependencies), and exploitation of spatial coherence. Limitations: Performance may degrade if spatial coherence is low (e.g., highly disconnected grids). The cost of maintaining the ACL and Regular Grid for each row must be managed. When to use: Ideal for rendering general irregular grids, especially when explicit connectivity is not available or when hardware acceleration is not used. When not to use: If the grid is highly structured and a simpler DDA or texture-based method is applicable. Lazy Sweep Ray Casting was introduced by Cláudio T. Silva and Joseph S. B. Mitchell in 1997. It is based on the sweep-plane paradigm, which has been used in other volume rendering methods, often with hardware assistance. The method was developed to address the limitations of resampling irregular grids into regular volumes, which is computationally expensive, memory-intensive, and time-consuming. name: Garrity Ray Casting
head: Garrity, Garrity's Ray Casting
body: Garrity Ray Casting is a method for rendering unstructured meshes by exploiting intrinsic mesh connectivity to optimize ray traversal. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing non-convex domains where rays may exit and re-enter the mesh multiple times. Inputs: An unstructured mesh defined by cells and their connectivity; a set of rays defined by origin and direction. Outputs: A rendered image where each pixel color is accumulated based on the ray's intersection with the mesh cells. Data Structures: 1. Mesh Connectivity: Explicit adjacency lists or pointers linking each cell to its neighboring cells. Exact layouts, fields, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. 2. Hierarchical Spatial Data Structure: A structure storing only the boundary cells of the mesh to accelerate re-entry queries. Exact layouts, fields, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Initialization: Determine the initial entry point of the ray into the mesh. 2. Cell Traversal: Identify the current cell containing the ray and use the mesh connectivity to determine the exit face along the ray's direction. 3. Intersection Calculation: Compute the intersection point P{exit} between the ray and the exit face. 4. Volume Integration: Accumulate optical properties along the segment [P{entry}, P{exit}] using the cell's volume data. 5. Neighbor Selection: Identify the next cell. In convex regions, this is the neighbor sharing the exit face. 6. Re-entry Handling: If the ray exits the mesh domain, query the hierarchical spatial data structure to find the next intersecting boundary cell, avoiding expensive global searches. 7. Iteration: Update P{entry} = P{exit} and repeat from Step 2 until the ray permanently exits the mesh or reaches a maximum depth. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Standard ray-face intersection is used: t = \frac{(P{face} - O) \cdot N}{D \cdot N}, where O is the ray origin, D is the direction, N is the face normal, and P{face} is a point on the face. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Convexity: Rays may exit and re-enter the mesh multiple times, requiring the spatial structure for efficient re-entry. Degenerate Cells: Zero-volume cells or coplanar faces may cause numerical instability in intersection calculations. Boundary Precision: Floating-point errors at cell boundaries may cause rays to miss neighbors or re-enter the same cell. A small epsilon offset is typically applied to the exit point to ensure it lies within the next cell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def garrityraycasting(mesh, rays): boundarytree = buildboundarytree(mesh) # Hierarchical spatial structure for boundary cells for ray in rays: entry = findinitialentry(mesh, ray) # Initial entry point current = mesh.cellcontaining(entry) # Locate starting cell while current is not None: exitface = findexitface(current, ray) # Use mesh connectivity t = rayintersectface(ray, exitface) # Standard ray-face intersection exitpoint = ray.origin + t ray.direction accumulatevolumedata(current, entry, exitpoint) # Integrate optical properties nextcell = current.neighbors[exitface] # Convex neighbor lookup if nextcell is None: # Ray exited mesh domain current = queryboundarytree(boundarytree, ray, exitpoint) # Find next boundary cell if current is None: break entry = exitpoint Renders curvilinear or unstructured data by determining an initial cell and iteratively traversing subsequent cells along a ray. It differs from regular grid traversal by relying on explicit mesh connectivity and acceleration structures over boundary faces rather than implicit coordinate mapping. Choose this when dealing with complex, non-hierarchical unstructured grids where connectivity is the primary traversal aid. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient for meshes with high connectivity; avoids global searches for re-entry. Limitations: Requires explicit connectivity; spatial structure construction overhead; less effective for highly fragmented or disconnected meshes without careful boundary definition. When to Use: Rendering unstructured grids where connectivity is known and rays traverse many cells. When Not to Use: When the mesh is highly non-convex with frequent re-entries and the spatial structure is too large to fit in memory, or when connectivity is not available. Garrity [28] pioneered the use of ray casting for rendering unstructured meshes. The technique was developed to address the inefficiencies of naive ray casting on irregular grids by leveraging the mesh's intrinsic connectivity. It is cited in surveys of GPU-based volume rendering of unstructured grids as a foundational method for connectivity-based traversal. name: Irregular Data Ray Traversal
head: Software Ray Casting for Irregular Grids
body: Irregular Data Ray Traversal renders curvilinear or unstructured data (such as tetrahedral or hexahedral meshes) by determining an initial cell and iteratively traversing subsequent cells along a ray. It differs from regular grid traversal by relying on explicit mesh connectivity and acceleration structures over boundary faces rather than implicit coordinate mapping. The method consists of two primary phases: initial cell location and iterative traversal. 1. Initial Cell Location: The entry point of the ray into the volume is determined by intersecting the ray with an acceleration structure built over the volume's boundary faces. Boundary faces are identified as those not shared between two cells. Standard ray-triangle or ray-face intersection techniques are used to find the closest intersection. 2. Iterative Traversal: Once the initial cell is identified, the ray is traversed through the mesh. The algorithm moves from the current cell to the next adjacent cell along the ray direction. This process repeats until the ray exits the volume or the last cell is reached. Adjacency Requirement: Incremental traversers require explicit adjacency information. Consequently, complete faces must be shared between adjacent cells. This constraint prohibits sliding interfaces or non-conforming meshes where faces do not perfectly align. This family does not have distinct child algorithms listed in the provided tree structure beyond the parent Garrity Ray Casting, which is a specific implementation context. The general technique applies to both tetrahedral and hexahedral meshes. The rendering of irregular data sets using software ray casting was proposed as early as 1990. Early works include [Gar90, Lev90, WCA 90]. Subsequent developments involved various acceleration structures, such as projecting boundary faces onto the image plane. Researchers such as [BKS97, HK98, HK99, KN91] contributed to methods for locating the initial cell. The approach is detailed in "Interactive Volume Rendering with Ray Tracing".
