name: Span-Buffer Ray-Casting
head: SBRC
body: Span-Buffer Ray-Casting (SBRC) is a hybrid volume rendering algorithm for unstructured grids that adopts an image-then-object traversal order to overcome the inability of prior methods to support early ray termination and to eliminate redundant cell processing. Unlike Koyamada’s algorithm, which lacks image-space coherency, and Challinger’s or Lazy Sweep Ray Casting (LSRC), which use object-then-image traversal that prevents early ray termination, SBRC activates cells only when hit by a ray, thereby maintaining full utilization of both image and object space coherencies. Inputs: A tetrahedral (or general irregular) grid, a camera position, and a screen resolution. Outputs: A rendered image. Data Structures: 1. Active Cell List: Stores entries for cells currently being processed. Each entry includes a pointer to the cell and a y-bucket index. 2. Y-Bucket List: An array of size equal to the screen height (H). Each bucket contains a list of pointers to entries in the Active Cell List. Used for efficient deletion of cells whose bottom y-coordinate is less than the current scanline. 3. Active Edge List: A hash table mapping edge identifiers to edge data. Stores edges currently intersecting the current scanline. 4. Span Buffer: A data structure associated with each active cell for the current scanline. Layout: An array indexed by pixel column (x). Fields per pixel: z: The depth (z-coordinate) of the ray exit point from the cell. s: The accumulated sample value (e.g., opacity/intensity) at the exit point. f{id}: The identifier of the exit face used to determine the next cell. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Traversal Initialization: Iterate through pixels in image order (scanline by scanline, top to bottom). For each pixel, shoot a ray into the volume. 2. Cell Hit and Activation: If the ray hits a cell that is not in the Active Cell List: Activate Cell: Allocate an entry in the Active Cell List. Identify Back-Face Edges: Determine the edges of the cell that belong to at least one back-face (back-face edges). For a tetrahedron, there are 6 edges; depending on the viewpoint, between 2 and 6 edges may be back-face edges. Sort Edges: Sort the back-face edges such that their intersection points with a virtual line parallel to the scanline (constant y) appear in increasing order of x coordinates. This sorting is performed once per cell activation. Y-Bucket Insertion: Calculate the bottom y-coordinate of the cell. Insert a pointer to the Active Cell List entry into the Y-Bucket List at the index corresponding to this y-coordinate. Create Span Buffer: Initialize the Span Buffer for the current scanline. 3. Scan Conversion and Span Buffer Update: Edge State Management: For each back-face edge in the Active Edge List (or newly identified): Compare the edge's y-extent with the current scanline y. Update states: If edge y-extent is above current scanline: State = done. If edge intersects current scanline: State = active. If edge y-extent is below current scanline: State = inactive. If an edge transitions from inactive to active, insert it into the Active Edge List via hashing. Compute Intersections: Using the sorted list of active back-face edges, compute the intersection points of the current scanline with these edges. Let the sorted intersection points be (xi, zi, si) for i=0 \dots k. Fill Span Buffer: For the pixels covered by the cell along the current scanline: Interpolate z and s values between successive intersection points. Store the interpolated (z, s) values and the exit-face identifier in the Span Buffer for the respective pixel column. 4. Ray Sampling and Propagation: First Hit (New Span): If the current ray hits the cell for the first time (creating the span buffer): Use the (z, s) values from the first pixel of the Span Buffer (corresponding to the ray's entry point or the first intersection) for sampling. Determine the exit face from the Span Buffer. Use the exit-point (z, s) values as the entry-point values for the neighbor cell. Follow the ray to the neighbor cell using connectivity relations (as in Koyamada’s algorithm). Subsequent Hit (Same Scanline): If a ray from the same scanline hits the cell: Retrieve the (z, s) values and exit-face identifier directly from the Span Buffer at the current pixel's column. Use these values for sampling and to determine the next cell. No new span buffer creation is needed. Subsequent Hit (Next Scanline): If a ray from the next scanline hits the cell for the first time: Create a new Span Buffer for the cell for this new scanline. Proceed with scan conversion for the new scanline. 5. Deletion and Cleanup: Span Buffer Deletion: After processing a scanline, initialize the span buffer list via a pointer operation to overwrite previous span buffers with new ones for the next scanline. This avoids explicit memory deallocation. Edge Deletion: Traverse the Active Edge List after each scanline. Delete edges that are in the done state and will never be accessed again. Rasterize remaining active edges by updating their coordinates for the next scanline. Cell Deletion: After processing a scanline, use the Y-Bucket List. For the current scanline y, access the Y-Bucket at index y. Delete the cell entries in the Active Cell List pointed to by this bucket. This handles the uncertainty caused by early ray termination, as we cannot guarantee that rays from the rightmost pixels will hit the cell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spanbufferraycasting(grid, camera, screenwidth, screenheight): # Data Structures activecelllist = {} # Map: cellid -> {ybottom, spanbuffer, edges} ybucketlist = [ [] for in range(screenheight) ] activeedgelist = {} # Hash Map: edgeid -> edgedata # Pre-compute back-face edges and sort them for each cell upon first hit # This is done inside the cell activation step for y in range(screenheight): for x in range(screenwidth): ray = camera.getray(x, y) # Find first hit cell cellid = findfirsthitcell(grid, ray) if cellid is None: continue # Check if cell is active if cellid not in activecelllist: activatecell(cellid, grid, activecelllist, ybucketlist, y) celldata = activecelllist[cellid] # Check if span buffer is valid for current scanline # (Implicitly handled by creating new span buffer if needed) if celldata['currentscanline'] != y: createspanbufferforscanline(cellid, y, activecelllist, activeedgelist) celldata['currentscanline'] = y spanbuffer = celldata['spanbuffer'] # Get exit info from span buffer for this pixel exitz, exits, exitfaceid = spanbuffer[x] # Sample the volume at the exit point (or use entry point if first hit) # Note: For the very first hit, entry point is ray origin. # Subsequent hits use previous exit point. samplevalue = samplevolume(grid, cellid, exitz, exits) # Determine next cell using connectivity and exitfaceid nextcellid = getneighborcell(cellid, exitfaceid, grid) if nextcellid is not None: # Update ray entry point for next cell ray.entryz = exitz ray.entrys = exits # Follow ray to next cell (recursive or iterative step) # This part re-enters the loop logic for the next cell # In a real implementation, this might be a stack-based traversal pass # Handle Early Ray Termination / Accumulation # (Standard volume rendering accumulation logic) pass # End of Scanline Processing deletedoneedges(activeedgelist) deletecellsforscanline(y, activecelllist, ybucketlist) def activatecell(cellid, grid, activecelllist, ybucketlist, y): cell = grid.getcell(cellid) # 1. Allocate entry activecelllist[cellid] = { 'ybottom': cell.getbottomy(), 'spanbuffer': None, 'currentscanline': -1, 'backfaceedges': [] } # 2. Identify back-face edges backfaceedges = identifybackfaceedges(cell, grid.cameraposition) # 3. Sort back-face edges by x-intersection with horizontal line sortededges = sortedgesbyxintercept(backfaceedges) activecelllist[cellid]['backfaceedges'] = sortededges # 4. Insert into Y-Bucket ybucketlist[cell.getbottomy()].append(cellid) def createspanbufferforscanline(cellid, y, activecelllist, activeedgelist): celldata = activecelllist[cellid] sortededges = celldata['backfaceedges'] # Update edge states and active edge list currentactiveedges = [] for edge in sortededges: if edge.isintersectingscanline(y): if edge.state == 'inactive': edge.state = 'active' activeedgelist[edge.id] = edge currentactiveedges.append(edge) elif edge.state == 'active': if edge.isbelowscanline(y): edge.state = 'inactive' # Remove from activeedgelist if needed, or mark for deletion pass # Compute intersections and fill span buffer # Intersections are sorted by x intersections = computescanlineintersections(currentactiveedges, y) # Create span buffer array for the cell's x-range spanbuffer = createspanbuffer(intersections) celldata['spanbuffer'] = spanbuffer def deletedoneedges(activeedgelist): edgestodelete = [] for edgeid, edge in activeedgelist.items(): if edge.state == 'done': edgestodelete.append(edgeid) for edgeid in edgestodelete: del activeedgelist[edgeid] def deletecellsforscanline(y, activecelllist, ybucketlist): # Delete cells whose bottom y is <= current scanline # Note: The source says "pointers in the respective y-bucket list are used to delete" # Assuming y-bucket at index y contains cells that end at or before y? # Source: "pointer to active cell list entry is inserted into y-bucket list according to bottom y-coordinate" # "After processing a scanline, the pointers in the respective y-bucket list are used to delete" # If bottom y is <= current scanline, the cell is no longer needed for future scanlines # (Assuming scanlines go top to bottom, and y increases downwards or upwards consistently) # Let's assume y increases downwards. If bottom y <= current y, the cell is below the current scanline. cellstodelete = [] for cellid in ybucketlist[y]: cellstodelete.append(cellid) for cellid in cellstodelete: del activecelllist[cellid] # Clear the bucket ybucketlist[y] = [] Time Complexity: The algorithm avoids the extensive sorting operations of Challinger’s algorithm by using connectivity information. However, it requires sorting back-face edges upon cell activation. The scan conversion step involves hashing and linear traversal of active edges. Overall, it is efficient for general irregular grids. Memory Complexity: Requires three additional data structures: Active Cell List, Active Edge List, and Span Buffers. The memory usage is proportional to the number of active cells and edges per scanline. Strengths: Supports early ray termination, which is not possible in object-then-image methods like Challinger’s or LSRC. Utilizes both image-space and object-space coherencies. Limitations: The sorting of back-face edges adds overhead per cell activation. The span buffer management and edge state updates add complexity compared to simpler ray casting methods. When to Use: Suitable for rendering general irregular grids (e.g., tetrahedral meshes) where early ray termination is beneficial and image-space coherency is high. When Not to Use: If the grid is highly convex and simple, or if early ray termination is not a primary concern, simpler methods might be faster due to lower overhead. Span-Buffer Ray-Casting (SBRC) was proposed by H. Berk et al. in 2003. It is a hybrid method that combines aspects of Koyamada’s algorithm, Challinger’s algorithm, and Lazy Sweep Ray Casting (LSRC). It was designed to address the deficiencies of prior hybrid methods, specifically their inability to support early ray termination and their redundant cell processing. name: Ray-guided volume rendering with missing brick reporting
head: Ray-guided methods
body: Ray-guided volume rendering with missing brick reporting is an out-of-core rendering technique where the working set (the minimal subset of volume data required to render an image) is determined dynamically during the ray-casting process rather than in advance. It solves the problem of memory bottlenecks in large-scale volume rendering by streaming only the bricks actually accessed by rays, ensuring optimal accuracy by never loading data that will not be used. Unlike sibling methods that may estimate working sets conservatively or use fixed traversal patterns, this approach minimizes memory utilization by reporting missing bricks on the GPU for subsequent frame loading. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, volume brick hierarchy (multiple resolutions), current brick cache state, and previous frame's resume state (rayResumeColor, rayResumePos). Output: Final accumulated color for the pixel, updated brick request list for the CPU/disk subsystem, and updated resume state for the next frame. Data Structures: 1. Brick Cache: A 3D texture or buffer storing individual bricks of different resolutions in GPU memory in an unordered manner. 2. Residency Map: A data structure storing whether each brick in the global volume is currently resident in the cache. This is used for address translation, mapping sample locations in reference space (e.g., normalized [0, 1]^3) to texture coordinates within the specific brick in the cache. 3. Missing Brick Hash Table: A lock-free, set-based, linearly-probed hash table stored in an image load store buffer (e.g., using GLARBshaderimageloadstore). It records brick identifiers to coordinate disk access. 4. Ray State: rayResumeColor: Accumulated color from previous frames. rayResumePos: The position in the volume where the first missing brick occurred, used to resume rendering. terminated: Boolean flag indicating if a missing brick has been encountered for the current ray. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set color = rayResumeColor and terminated = true (assuming the ray will finish if no missing bricks are found). 2. Ray Loop: Repeat until the ray exits the volume or saturates: a. Compute Level of Detail (LoD): Determine the required LoD based on the current ray depth. b. Get Brick: Call GetBrick(ray) to retrieve the brick and its associated samplingRate. GetBrick always returns some data, potentially at a lower resolution than requested. c. Address Translation: Retrieve the offsets for the brick from the pool using PoolOffsets(brick). d. Check Resolution: If samplingRate is not equal to RequiredSamplingForLOD(LoD), the data is undersampled. i. Report Missing: Call ReportMissingBrick(brick) to add the brick to the hash table. ii. Record Resume Point: If terminated is true (indicating this is the first missing brick encountered for this ray), set terminated = false and store the current ray position in rayResumePos. e. Raycast: Perform the raycasting step using the ray, stepSize, and offsets. 3. Update State: Set rayResumeColor = color. If the ray completed successfully (no missing bricks), set rayResumePos = FINISHED. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayguidedrendering(rayorigin, raydirection, volumeexitt, rayresumecolor, rayresumepos): # Initialize ray parameter t from previous frame's resume position rayt = rayresumepos if rayresumepos != "FINISHED" else 0.0 color = rayresumecolor terminated = True # Assume ray will finish unless a missing brick is found while rayt < volumeexitt: # 1. Compute required Level of Detail based on ray depth lod = computelod(rayt) # 2. Retrieve brick and its actual sampling rate from cache brickid, samplingrate = getbrick(rayorigin, raydirection, rayt, lod) # 3. Get offsets for address translation within the cache offsets = pooloffsets(brickid) # 4. Check if the retrieved brick matches the required LOD requiredsampling = requiredsamplingforlod(lod) if samplingrate != requiredsampling: # Data is undersampled; report missing brick to hash table reportmissingbrick(brickid) # Record the position of the first missing brick for resumption if terminated: terminated = False rayresumepos = rayt # 5. Perform the raycasting step and accumulate color stepsize = offsets["stepsize"] sample = samplevolume(rayorigin, raydirection, rayt, offsets["texoffsets"]) alpha = computealpha(sample) color = color + sample (1.0 - color) # Standard front-to-back accumulation rayt += stepsize if rayt >= volumeexitt or alpha >= 1.0: break # Update resume state for next frame rayresumecolor = color if terminated: rayresumepos = "FINISHED" return color, rayresumecolor, rayresumepos def computelod(depth): return int(depth) % 4 def getbrick(o, d, t, lod): return (hash((o, d, t, lod)), 1.0 / (2 lod)) def pooloffsets(brickid): return {"stepsize": 0.5, "texoffsets": (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)} def requiredsamplingforlod(lod): return 1.0 / (2 lod) def reportmissingbrick(brickid): pass # Atomic insert into lock-free hash table def samplevolume(o, d, t, offsets): return (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) # GPU texture fetch def computealpha(sample): return 0.8 # Transfer function evaluation Parameters: rayResumePos: Stores the position in the volume where the first missing brick occurred. terminated: Boolean flag indicating if a missing brick has been encountered for the current ray. GLARBshaderimageloadstore: OpenGL extension used for atomic operations and independent image buffers in the hash table implementation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Undersampling: If data is undersampled, the renderer displays a coarser version initially but progressively refines regions with finer resolution data until sampled at a single voxel per pixel or the maximum data resolution. Write Hazards: The lock-free hash table must handle concurrent writes from multiple rays requesting the same brick. Linear probing with atomic operations is used to mitigate hazards. Termination: The terminated flag ensures that rayResumePos is only set once per ray per frame, at the first missing brick encountered. The Greedy Brick Request Strategy is a data-loading heuristic in ray-guided volume rendering that requests all intermediate levels of detail (LoD) along a ray's path when a higher-resolution brick is unavailable, rather than waiting for the final required resolution. Unlike the Global strategy, which only requests the final necessary brick, the Greedy strategy floods the request hash table with intermediate bricks. This prioritizes iterative visual refinement and faster convergence of image quality over minimizing the total number of unique brick requests per frame. It produces more responsive, iteratively-refined images and may converge in fewer frames because it allows rays to sample at final resolution quickly, triggering earlier ray termination. The Global Brick Request Strategy is a data-loading heuristic where a ray only requests the bricks absolutely required to satisfy the final rendering request, leaving space in the hash table for other rays. When a brick is missing, it increments the LoD and looks up the brick at the new resolution, continuing until a missing brick is no longer reported. Unlike the 'Greedy' strategy, the Global strategy does not request intermediate bricks. It generates the final correct image quickest in terms of raw completion but may produce less pleasing intermediate progress. A subsystem for recording missing bricks identified during ray-casting on the GPU, using a lock-free hash table stored in an image load store buffer to coordinate disk access and update the volume pool. It uses the GLARBshaderimageloadstore extension (core in OpenGL 4.2) to create an image buffer independent of the current rendering buffer. It implements a set-based linearly-probed lock-free hash table using atomic load/store operations. Hashing is based on the brick identifier so that multiple rays requesting the same brick hash to the same position, keeping the table size small and avoiding duplicate values inherent in multiple render target approaches. Measured Performance: The greedy strategy was found to converge in the fewest number of frames and produce more pleasing progress information, despite flooding the hash table, because it enables earlier ray termination. The global strategy generates the final correct image quickest in raw completion time but offers less responsive intermediate progress. Strengths: Minimizes working-set size by only streaming accessed bricks. Ensures optimal accuracy by never loading unused data. Scales to extremely large data sets. Limitations: Requires complex GPU-side logic for missing brick reporting and hash table management. Previous approaches using conservative working-set estimates led to sub-optimal memory utilization. When to use: Large-scale volume rendering where data exceeds GPU memory capacity and interactive or progressive refinement is desired. Ray-guided volume rendering was introduced to address the limitations of early approaches that produced conservative estimates of the working set, leading to sub-optimal memory utilization. Key early works include [CNLE09], [HBJP12], [FSK13], and [BPH14]. The specific technique of missing brick reporting with GPU-based hash table coordination was detailed by Crassin et al. (PMC4260263). The method builds on the principle of address translation using octrees or page-table hierarchies. The use of GLARBshaderimageloadstore for lock-free hash tables was adopted to overcome the limitations of multiple render targets, which ignore spatial coherency and lead to duplicate values and larger texture reads back. name: Greedy Brick Request Strategy
head: Greedy algorithm
body: The Greedy Brick Request Strategy is a data-loading heuristic in ray-guided volume rendering that requests all intermediate levels of detail (LoD) along a ray's path when a higher-resolution brick is unavailable, rather than waiting for the final required resolution. Unlike the Global strategy, which only requests the final necessary brick, the Greedy strategy floods the request hash table with intermediate bricks. This prioritizes iterative visual refinement and faster convergence of image quality over minimizing the total number of unique brick requests per frame. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current ray state, the current Level of Detail (LoD) index, and a missing brick report function. Output: A sequence of missing brick reports for all intermediate resolutions up to the first available brick. Data Structures: Hash Table: A table used to accumulate brick requests from all active rays, which is read back from the GPU at the end of a frame to fill the volume pool. Level of Detail (LoD): An integer index representing the resolution of the brick, where higher indices indicate finer resolution. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the current LoD to the base resolution required for the current sample or the last known available resolution. 2. Enter a loop that continues as long as a brick is missing. 3. Increment the LoD index. 4. Look up the brick corresponding to the current ray position and the new LoD. 5. Check if the brick is missing (not resident in memory). 6. If the brick is missing: Report the missing brick to the hash table. Continue the loop to request the next higher resolution. 7. If the brick is found (not missing): Terminate the loop. Proceed with rendering using the found brick. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def greedybrickrequest(ray, currentlod, lookupbrick, ismissing, reportmissing): """ Requests all intermediate bricks from currentlod up to the first available brick. """ lod = currentlod while True: lod += 1 brick = lookupbrick(ray, lod) if ismissing(brick): reportmissing(brick) else: return brick Parameters: LoD Increment: Increments by 1 at each step, moving from coarser to finer resolutions. Hash Table Saturation: Because the Greedy strategy requests all intermediate bricks, it can flood the request hash table with many requests per ray. Convergence Behavior: The strategy allows a ray to sample at its final resolution quickly, which can cause earlier ray termination and faster convergence in fewer frames. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Termination: If the ray exits the volume bounds before finding a resident brick, the loop must terminate to prevent infinite execution. Hash Table Contention: Flooding the hash table with intermediate requests per ray may cause contention or overflow if the table size is not sufficiently large. Lookup Precision: The lookup function must correctly map ray positions to brick indices at each LoD to avoid missing bricks or requesting invalid resolutions. An alternative strategy that performs brick lookup once per brick rather than every sample, maintaining a simple ray-marching core. It differs from the Greedy strategy by using an out-of-core, progressive rendering methodology that breaks the GPU-memory-size barrier, whereas Greedy focuses on iterative refinement via intermediate requests. Time Complexity: The number of lookups and potential hash table writes per ray is proportional to the number of missing intermediate levels of detail. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is dominated by the request hash table, which accumulates more requests per frame than the Global strategy. Performance: The Greedy strategy converges in fewer frames to a visually pleasing result compared to the Global strategy. This is because it allows rays to sample at their final resolution more quickly, which can cause earlier ray termination and faster accumulation of high-frequency details. Strengths: Produces more responsive, iteratively-refined images with more densely-packed intermediate progress. Limitations: Higher memory usage for the request table due to flooding the hash table with intermediate requests. When to use: When visual responsiveness and smooth convergence are critical. When not to use: When the goal is to minimize the total number of disk I/O operations regardless of visual convergence speed, as the Global strategy generates the final correct image quickest. The Greedy Brick Request Strategy was introduced in the context of scalable GPU-based ray-guided volume rendering. It was compared against the "Global" strategy, which only requests the final required brick. The authors found that the Greedy approach, despite its higher request volume, converged faster and produced more pleasing progress information, surprising initial expectations that the Global strategy would be more efficient. name: Ray-Guided Grid Leaping
head: Out-of-core ray-guided rendering, Ray-guided volume rendering
body: Ray-Guided Grid Leaping is an out-of-core volume rendering technique that couples the rendering process with the identification of which sub-volumes ('bricks') must be loaded, using ray-sampling characteristics to determine future data requirements in concert with standard ray traversal and accumulation. It differs from Hadwiger et al. by performing brick lookup once per brick rather than every sample, maintaining a simple ray-marching core, and utilizing an out-of-core, progressive rendering methodology that breaks the GPU-memory-size barrier. Inputs: Input volume data existing at a single resolution. Transfer function. Camera parameters. Outputs: Rendered image. Updated GPU texture pool with paged-in bricks. Data Structures: 1. Multiresolution Hierarchy: A preprocess built from the single-resolution input data, consisting of simple multiresolution Cartesian grids (bricks). 2. Lookup Table: Stores the status for each brick index. It has three states: Empty Non-empty and present on the GPU Non-empty and absent 3. GPU Hash Table: A lock-free hash table used to record missing bricks for feedback to the I/O layer. Parameters: Pixel Error Threshold: The level of detail is computed to maintain a pixel error of less than one. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Build a multiresolution hierarchy as a preprocess for input data which exist at only one resolution. 2. Ray Processing (Per Ray): a. Compute the level of detail (LOD) required to maintain a pixel error of less than one. b. Compute a brick index from the LOD and the position in the volume. c. Use the brick index to fetch information from the lookup table to identify the brick's state: i. If the brick is empty, skip the brick and repeat the process at the brick’s exit point. ii. If the brick is non-empty and present on the GPU, ray-cast that brick. iii. If the brick is non-empty and absent from GPU memory, return the finest coarser level available and add the missing entry to the GPU hash table. 3. End of Frame: a. Read back the GPU hash table to host memory. b. Use the read-back data to page in bricks from disk or cache. c. Upload paged-in bricks to a GPU texture pool. 4. Subsequent Frame: Use the portion of the brick pool for sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EMPTY = 0 NONEMPTYPRESENT = 1 NONEMPTYABSENT = 2 def rayguidedgridleapingraykernel(rayorigin, raydirection, volumemaxt, lookuptable, brickpool, missingbrickshashtable): """ Processes a single ray using Ray-Guided Grid Leaping. rayorigin: vec3, start of the ray raydirection: vec3, normalized direction of the ray volumemaxt: float, maximum distance along the ray within the volume bounds lookuptable: dict, maps brickidx to status (EMPTY, NONEMPTYPRESENT, NONEMPTYABSENT) brickpool: dict, maps brickidx to brick data missingbrickshashtable: lock-free hash table, records missing bricks """ t = 0.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 while t < volumemaxt: # 1. Compute Level of Detail (LOD) to maintain pixel error < 1 # Sources do not provide the exact LOD computation formula. lod = computelodforpixelerrorthreshold(t, threshold=1.0) # 2. Compute Brick Index from LOD and position position = rayorigin + raydirection t brickidx = computebrickindex(lod, position) # 3. Lookup Brick Status status = lookuptable.get(brickidx) if status == EMPTY: # Skip empty brick and jump to exit point # Sources do not provide the exact exit point calculation. t = getbrickexitpoint(brickidx, position, raydirection) continue elif status == NONEMPTYPRESENT: # Ray-cast the present brick brickdata = brickpool.get(brickidx) color, alpha, t = raycastbrick(rayorigin, raydirection, t, brickdata, color, alpha) elif status == NONEMPTYABSENT: # Return finest coarser level available # Add missing entry to GPU hash table for I/O feedback missingbrickshashtable.insert(brickidx) # Use coarser level for sampling coarserbrickidx = getcoarserbrick(brickidx) coarserdata = brickpool.get(coarserbrickidx) color, alpha, t = raycastbrick(rayorigin, raydirection, t, coarserdata, color, alpha) return color def endofframeprocessing(missingbrickshashtable, brickpool, diskcache): """ Handles I/O for missing bricks identified during the frame. """ # 1. Read back GPU hash table to host memory missingbricks = missingbrickshashtable.readbacktohost() # 2. Page in bricks from disk or cache pagedbricks = [] for brickidx in missingbricks: data = diskcache.load(brickidx) pagedbricks.append((brickidx, data)) # 3. Upload paged-in bricks to GPU texture pool for brickidx, data in pagedbricks: brickpool.upload(brickidx, data) # 4. Clear hash table for next frame missingbrickshashtable.clear() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The level of detail calculation must ensure pixel error remains below one to maintain visual fidelity while optimizing performance. Boundaries: When skipping empty bricks, the algorithm must correctly calculate the exit point to resume marching. Missing Data: If a brick is non-empty but absent, the system must gracefully degrade to the finest coarser level available rather than failing. A strategy where a ray requests intermediate levels of detail (bricks) along its path when a resolution is missing, flooding the hash table with requests. This produces more responsive, iteratively-refined images and converges in fewer frames. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The renderer is designed to render massive datasets extremely fast on commodity GPU hardware. It breaks the GPU-memory-size barrier that limits data sizes in prior work. Scaling: The methodology allows graceful scaling down to consumer-level graphics cards. Strengths: Performs brick lookup once per brick instead of every sample, maintaining a simple and familiar ray-marching core. Utilizes modern GPU features to implement a lock-free feedback data structure, enabling the implementation to spend more time computing on the GPU and less time pushing data around. Out-of-core, progressive rendering methodology breaks the GPU-memory-size barrier. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When rendering massive datasets on commodity GPU hardware where GPU memory is insufficient to hold the entire volume. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Ray-Guided Grid Leaping is reminiscent of the recent work of Hadwiger et al. [2] and Engel’s CERA-TVR [26], which in turn is based on the Gigavoxels system [3]. It shares with Hadwiger et al. the requirement of a set of simple multiresolution Cartesian grids and an OpenGL-based table to report missing bricks. From the CERA-TVR system, it inherits the idea to only recompute and request grid cells at boundaries. The work provides new depth to discussions of parameters relevant in the development of a ray-guided direct volume renderer, including strategies for loading higher resolution data, issues surrounding bricking and brick sizes, and the effect of brick layout strategies on large volume access times. An Analysis of Scalable GPU-Based Ray-Guided Volume Rendering, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4260263/, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Adaptive Depth Sampling with Voxel Layer Alignment
head: Layered Interpolation, Optimal Interpolation, Optimal Interpolation for Ray Casting
body: Adaptive Depth Sampling with Voxel Layer Alignment is an acceleration technique for ray traversal that reduces the computational cost of trilinear interpolation by aligning sample points with voxel layers to enable bilinear interpolation, while skipping intermediate samples via adaptive depth sampling. It differs from standard trilinear interpolation by exploiting ray direction to align samples with voxel layers, allowing bilinear interpolation for half the points, and skipping intermediate points via adaptive depth sampling. The method operates on a regular 3D grid where voxels are aligned to a uniform spacing. Standard ray casting inputs (ray origin, direction, volume bounds, and voxel spacing) are assumed. The algorithm produces a sequence of sample positions and their interpolated values. No auxiliary data structures are required beyond the volume data and ray parameters. Steps: 1. Determine the reference axis: Identify the axis perpendicular to the parallel voxel layers that are traversed fastest by the current ray. This corresponds to the axis with the largest absolute component in the ray direction vector. Let this axis be k \in \{x, y, z\}. 2. Decide the first sampling position: Set the initial sampling position to the point where the ray enters the volume. 3. Calculate sampling interval l: Compute the interval l along the ray such that every alternate sampling point lies exactly on a voxel layer perpendicular to the reference axis k. The sources specify the condition but do not provide the explicit mathematical formula; the interval is derived from the voxel spacing along k and the ray's direction component along k. 4. Sample and Interpolate: Use bilinear interpolation for each sampling point lying on a voxel layer, and simplified trilinear interpolation for points between layers. Apply adaptive depth sampling to skip the time-consuming points between layers. Specifically, skip every other sample point along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivedepthsamplingraycasting(rayorigin, raydirection, volumemin, volumemax, voxelspacing, refaxis): # Standard slab intersection to find entry/exit t values tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if abs(raydirection[i]) < 1e-9: if rayorigin[i] < volumemin[i] or rayorigin[i] > volumemax[i]: return [] else: t1 = (volumemin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] t2 = (volumemax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return [] # Step 3: Calculate interval l so every alternate point lands on a voxel layer along refaxis deltak = voxelspacing[refaxis] dk = raydirection[refaxis] if abs(dk) < 1e-9: return [] # Ray parallel to voxel layers; fallback required l = 2.0 deltak / abs(dk) # Step 2: First sampling position at volume entry t = tmin samples = [] while t <= tmax: pos = rayorigin + t raydirection # Check if sample lies on a voxel layer along the reference axis gridcoord = pos[refaxis] / deltak isonlayer = abs(gridcoord - round(gridcoord)) < 1e-6 if isonlayer: # Step 4: Bilinear interpolation on aligned layers val = bilinearinterpolation(pos, voxelspacing, refaxis) samples.append((pos, val)) # Points between layers are skipped by adaptive depth sampling # Step 3/4: Advance by l to land on the next aligned layer t += l return samples def bilinearinterpolation(pos, voxelspacing, refaxis): # Standard bilinear interpolation in the two axes perpendicular to refaxis # Implementation depends on specific grid layout and data format. pass Parameters: Sampling interval l: Chosen so every alternate sampling point lies exactly on a voxel layer. Adaptive depth factor: Skip every other sample point along the ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray parallel to a voxel layer: If the direction component along the reference axis is near zero, the ray is parallel to the voxel layers and the interval calculation divides by zero. This requires a fallback to standard traversal or axis selection. Precision: Floating-point accumulation errors may cause points that should be on a layer to drift slightly off; a tolerance threshold is required when checking layer alignment. Boundary conditions: The slab intersection must correctly handle rays originating inside or outside the volume to avoid out-of-bounds sampling. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of interpolation operations by half and lowers the cost of the remaining interpolations from trilinear to bilinear. Experimental results show the algorithm saved about 70% of ray traversal time by skipping over every other sample point along each ray. Memory Complexity: No additional memory structures are required beyond the volume data and ray parameters. Strengths: Significant speedup in ray traversal time by exploiting the regular structure of the voxel grid. Limitations: Only applicable to regular 3D grids. When to use: When rendering regular 3D volumes with high performance requirements and ray traversal is the bottleneck, particularly when combined with boundary cell-based ray casting. The method was proposed in the context of high-performance parallel volume rendering as part of a fast serial ray casting algorithm. It is described in the NASA Technical Reports Server publication "Time-Critical Volume Rendering". The technique is somewhat similar to Levoy's optimization of adaptive image sampling within the image plane. Time-Critical Volume Rendering, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19990040407/downloads/19990040407.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) 19990040407: Time-Critical Volume Rendering, https://archive.org/details/NASANTRSArchive19990040407, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Optimized Ray Casting
head: Adaptive Ray Casting, Boundary cell projection, Fast Ray Casting Algorithm, Octtree Ray Casting
body: Optimized Ray Casting is a volume rendering algorithm that accelerates image-order rendering by combining hierarchical data structures (octrees) with adaptive image sampling and early ray termination. It solves the performance bottleneck of standard ray casting, which processes every voxel along a ray regardless of transparency or redundancy. It sets itself apart from siblings like Lazy Sweep Ray Casting by using explicit octtree traversal to skip transparent regions rather than relying on sweep-line or slab-based accumulation, and from Ray-guided volume rendering with missing brick reporting by focusing on single-volume hierarchical traversal rather than distributed brick management. Inputs: 3D scalar volume dataset on a regular grid, camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), rendering parameters (opacity threshold, sample region size, color/density difference thresholds). Outputs: 2D color image. Data Structures: 1. Octree: Hierarchical representation of the volume, incrementally updated as macros arrive, with nodes tagged as fully transparent if all constituent voxels are transparent. 2. Backstore: Pixel memory storing intermediate results for parallel renderers. Parameters: Alpha Cutoff: Opacity threshold for early ray termination. Typical values: 92% (electric field), 98% (neghip, brain). Sample Region Size: Square grid for adaptive sampling. Typical value: 3 \times 3 pixels. Color Difference Threshold: Max allowed difference for bilinear interpolation of adjacent pixels. Typical values: 10 (electric field), 40 (neghip), 30 (brain). Density Difference Threshold: Max allowed difference for adaptive ray density along a ray. Typical values: 30 (electric field), 80 (neghip), 5 (brain). Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Offline): Incrementally update the octree as macros arrive. Tag macros containing only transparent voxels. Detect boundary cells for traversal optimization. 2. Ray Initialization: For each pixel in the image, define ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. If a cut plane is defined, start the ray at the intersection with the plane instead of the dataset boundary. 3. Adaptive Ray Casting Loop: Coarse Pass: Cast rays on a coarse grid (e.g., every 3rd pixel). Refinement: For each coarse pixel, check adjacent pixels. If the color difference exceeds the threshold, cast additional rays for the intermediate pixels. Final Image Formation: Form the final image by bilinear interpolation of the ray-cast pixels. 4. Ray Traversal and Compositing (Per Ray): Traverse the octree to find the entry and exit points of the ray within the volume. Initialize accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0 and color C{acc} = (0, 0, 0). While \alpha{acc} < \text{Alpha Cutoff} and ray is within volume: Use the octree to skip over transparent regions. If a node is fully transparent, advance t past it. Sample the voxel value V at current t. Check density difference against previous sample. If difference > Threshold, ensure sufficient sampling density (cast additional rays if in adaptive mode). Compute transmittance T = \exp(-\sigma \Delta t) and opacity contribution \alpha = 1 - T. Update accumulated color: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{voxel} \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}). Update accumulated opacity: \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}). Advance t by step size \Delta t. If \alpha{acc} \ge \text{Alpha Cutoff}, terminate ray (Early Ray Termination). 5. Parallel Execution (Optional): Master GPU controls slave GPUs via a finite state automaton. Slaves render image tiles (e.g., 128 \times 128) independently. Macros are fetched asynchronously to slave pixel memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizedraycasting(volumedata, cameraorigin, cameradir, imagewidth, imageheight, params): """ volumedata: 3D array of voxel values cameraorigin: tuple (ox, oy, oz) cameradir: tuple (dx, dy, dz) params: dict with alphacutoff, colorthresh, densitythresh, regionsize """ # Preprocessing helpers (conceptual, based on evidence) octree = buildoctreeincremental(volumedata) tagtransparentmacros(octree) # Adaptive Sampling: Coarse Grid steppixels = params['regionsize'] castpixels = {} for y in range(0, imageheight, steppixels): for x in range(0, imagewidth, steppixels): raydir = normalize((cameradir[0] + (x - imagewidth/2), cameradir[1] + (y - imageheight/2), cameradir[2])) color = castray(volumedata, cameraorigin, raydir, params) castpixels[(x, y)] = color # Refinement: Interpolate missing pixels image = [[None for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): if (x, y) in castpixels: image[y][x] = castpixels[(x, y)] else: # Check neighbors for color difference neighbors = [] for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: ny, nx = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= ny < imageheight and 0 <= nx < imagewidth and (ny, nx) in castpixels: neighbors.append(castpixels[(ny, nx)]) if len(neighbors) >= 2 and any(abs(neighbors[0][i] - neighbors[1][i]) > params['colorthresh'] for i in range(3)): raydir = normalize((cameradir[0] + (x - imagewidth/2), cameradir[1] + (y - imageheight/2), cameradir[2])) image[y][x] = castray(volumedata, cameraorigin, raydir, params) else: image[y][x] = bilinearinterpolate(castpixels, x, y, imagewidth, imageheight) return image def castray(volume, origin, direction, params): alphaacc = 0.0 coloracc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # DDA initialization invdir = (1.0/direction[0], 1.0/direction[1], 1.0/direction[2]) step = min(abs(invdir[0]), abs(invdir[1]), abs(invdir[2])) t = 0.0 prevval = None while alphaacc < params['alphacutoff']: # Octree skip (conceptual) if istransparentnode(volume, origin, direction, t, step): t += step 2 continue # Sample val = samplevolume(volume, origin, direction, t) # Adaptive density check if prevval is not None and abs(val - prevval) > params['densitythresh']: pass # Ensures sufficient sampling density in high-contrast areas # Compositing alpha = 1.0 - exp(-val step) color = mapvoxeltocolor(val) coloracc[0] += color[0] alpha (1.0 - alphaacc) coloracc[1] += color[1] alpha (1.0 - alphaacc) coloracc[2] += color[2] alpha (1.0 - alphaacc) alphaacc += alpha (1.0 - alphaacc) prevval = val t += step return coloracc def buildoctreeincremental(data): return {} # Placeholder for incremental update logic def tagtransparentmacros(octree): pass # Placeholder for tagging logic def istransparentnode(vol, orig, dir, t, step): return False # Placeholder for octree traversal def samplevolume(vol, orig, dir, t): return vol[int(t)] # Placeholder for coordinate mapping def mapvoxeltocolor(val): return (val, val, val) # Placeholder for transfer function def normalize(v): l = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5; return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def bilinearinterpolate(castpixels, x, y, w, h): # Standard bilinear interpolation of adjacent cast pixels return castpixels.get((x, y), [0,0,0]) Accelerates direct illumination in Monte Carlo volume rendering by optimizing extinction estimates along light rays. Unlike the parent method which optimizes camera rays, this handles stochastic scattering vertices, requiring data structure rebuilding per light ray set. Visualizes CFD density/refractive index fields on distributed supercomputers. Converts curilinear grids to rectilinear multi-block voxel fields to avoid integral errors from overlapping grids, distributing voxels for efficient parallel ray-casting. Progressive ray casting that decomposes the image into screen-space tiles, sorts them by cost, and renders them in batches within a time budget. Optimizes GPU cache locality by processing tiles rather than individual rays, avoiding stalls on mobile/low-performance devices. Considers optical effects (caustics, shafts of light) in water modeled as a uniform particle density medium. Uses analytical functions for scattered light intensity based on distance, avoiding numerical integration and ray-tracing in favor of scanline Z-buffer and accumulation buffer techniques. Replaces real-time gradient calculation during raycasting with a pre-computed 3D RGBA texture lookup. Saves 6 extra texture fetches per sample by trading memory for computation speed, advantageous for VR hardware like HTC Vive. Modifies ray casting to reslice a volume along an arbitrary plane ax + by + cz + d = 0. Implemented by starting the ray search at the z-coordinate determined by the plane equation or continuing until the x-coordinate value, effectively removing voxels on one side of the plane. Time Complexity: Depends on the sparsity of the volume and the effectiveness of the octtree. In the worst case (fully opaque), it approaches O(N) where N is the number of voxels along the ray. With transparent regions, it is significantly faster due to skipping. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data plus O(M) for the octree, where M is the number of macro blocks. Measured Performance: On 16-processor SGI Power Challenge: Electric field (50^3) 0.04s, Neghip (68^3) 0.15s, Brain (256 \times 256 \times 124) 0.09s. On 4 processors: Electric field 0.39s, Neghip 1.02s, Brain 0.17s. On 8 processors: Electric field 0.11s, Neghip 0.93s, Brain 0.12s. On 12 processors: Electric field 0.06s, Neghip 0.28s, Brain 0.11s. More than 10 frames per second achieved on 16 processors for all datasets. Slave GPU rendering of 128 \times 128 tile for 128^3 dataset: 100-240 ms. Strengths: High performance on sparse/transparent volumes; interactive frame rates achievable on parallel hardware; adaptive sampling reduces aliasing without uniform high resolution. When to use: Sparse volumetric data (e.g., medical CT, scientific simulations); interactive applications requiring real-time feedback; parallel rendering architectures. When not to use: Dense, fully opaque volumes where octtree skipping provides little benefit; hardware with limited VRAM for octree storage. Originated in the late 1980s and early 1990s with work by Levoy and others on hierarchical volume representation. The specific "Fast Ray Casting Algorithm" with boundary cell projection and adaptive sampling was demonstrated on SGI workstations and parallel clusters in the early 1990s. It builds on Parent by introducing specific optimizations for hierarchical data traversal and adaptive sampling rates. Time-Critical Volume Rendering, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19990040407/downloads/19990040407.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) DTIC ADA236718: Achieving Direct Volume Visualization with Interactive Semantic Region Selection, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA236718, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26 Rendering and Interacting With Volume Models in Immersive Environments, https://doi.org/10.2312/ceig.20181153, fetched 2026-10-26 Hardware Support for the Display and Manipulation of Binary Voxel Models, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh88/103-117, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Light Ray Extinction Optimization
body: Light Ray Extinction Optimization accelerates direct illumination computation in Monte Carlo volume rendering by estimating extinction values between a scatter vertex y and a point on the light source. While Optimized Ray Casting focuses on visibility along camera rays, this method extends the optimization to light transport paths, reducing variance in shadowed or complex volumetric regions. It differs from camera-ray optimization because stochastic scattering locations prevent data structure reuse across frames, requiring a full rebuild for each set of light rays. Inputs: scattering vertex y, light source position, volume density field, and the visibility optimization data structure. Outputs: optimized extinction coefficient \mu'(y) and transmittance estimates between the scattering vertex and the light source. Data Structures: The method reuses the hierarchical data structure from camera-ray visibility optimization. This structure maintains segments representing extinction intervals and supports insert, merge, and evaluate operations. Algorithm Steps: 1. For each scattering vertex y, cast a ray toward the light source. 2. Draw a fixed number of stratified samples along the light ray segment. 3. Insert the stratified samples into the data structure where merging operations take place. The structure is built from scratch for each set of rays because scattering locations change stochastically. Splitting segments or discarding samples is only required for progressive updates and can be omitted for standard per-pass builds. 4. During transmittance estimation, evaluate the data structure to compute the optimized extinction coefficient \mu'(y) at the current position. 5. Use \mu'(y) to compute decision probabilities for the delta tracking algorithm along the light ray. 6. If multiple scattering is supported, sample additional rays at new scattering locations according to the phase function and apply the same optimization. 7. In implementations using ratio tracking [NSJ14], multiple vertices are produced during transmittance estimation, each requiring an optimized extinction query. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildlightraystructure(scatteringvertex, lightsourcepos, numsamples=200): # 1. Define ray from scattering vertex to light source raydir = normalize(lightsourcepos - scatteringvertex) raylen = distance(scatteringvertex, lightsourcepos) # 2. Generate stratified samples along the ray samples = [scatteringvertex + raydir (i + 0.5) raylen / numsamples for i in range(numsamples)] # 3. Evaluate raw extinction at sample positions # Standard volume density query at each sample position # 4. Build data structure from scratch # Note: Splitting or discarding samples is only required for progressive updates # Hierarchical segment structure initialization structure = [] for pos in samples: structure.append((pos, getdensity(pos))) # Merge adjacent segments structure = mergesegments(structure) return structure def queryoptimizedextinction(position, structure): # Evaluate structure to compute optimized extinction coefficient mu'(y) # Standard segment lookup return lookupextinction(position, structure) Parameters: Number of samples: 200 samples per light ray is recommended as a good trade-off between accuracy and speed. Progressive Updates: Splitting of segments or discarding of samples is optional and only required for progressive rendering updates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stochastic Scattering Locations: Because scattering vertices are determined stochastically, the data structure cannot be reused across frames and must be rebuilt from scratch for each set of light rays. Long Transport Paths: Optimizing extinction along very long transport paths (e.g., multiple scattering events far from the camera) is computationally costly and yields no visual improvement. Memory Allocation: The method requires a static allocation for light ray optimization independent of resolution (e.g., 156MB) plus per-pixel allocations for structure sizes and offsets. A method to reduce sampling operations by applying two observations: only visible samples receive illumination, and only samples visible from the light source need to be illuminated. It determines the interval of samples for illumination computation defined by xl (where visibility becomes zero) and xf (first point hit in camera space). It connects xf and xl through line segments and projects them into light space to determine the minimal set of entry points for light view rays. It casts light rays only from these optimized entry points to ensure only samples visible from the camera are illuminated. Time Complexity: The cost is dominated by building the data structure for each light ray. On the HEPTANE dataset with 5000 samples per pixel, render times dropped from 51.7s for the reference to 21.47s, 27.17s, 28.2s, and 37s for varying numbers of optimization samples. Memory Complexity: Requires a static allocation independent of resolution (e.g., 156MB) plus per-pixel allocations for the data structure. Strengths: Significantly reduces variance in direct illumination, especially in shadowed regions or complex volumetric scenes. Limitations: Cannot be easily integrated into progressive rendering due to the stochastic nature of scattering locations, and optimizing for multiple scattering events far from the camera is inefficient. When to Use: When direct illumination variance is high and the scene contains complex shadowing or participating media. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained, or when the scene is optically thin and variance is already low. Light Ray Extinction Optimization was introduced in the context of view-dependent visibility optimization for Monte Carlo volume visualization. It builds upon the idea of optimizing camera-ray visibility by extending the same hierarchical data structure techniques to light rays. The method addresses the challenge of efficiently computing transmittance in participating media, where standard delta tracking can be inefficient due to high variance in dense regions. By optimizing the extinction coefficient estimates, the method allows for more efficient sampling of light transport paths. View‐Dependent Visibility Optimization for Monte Carlo Volume Visualization, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70064, fetched 2026-11-05 Multimodal Volume Illumination, https://www.uni-ulm.de/fileadmin/websiteuniulm/iui.inst.100/institut/Papers/viscom/2015/sunden15multimodal.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Parallel Volume Rendering for Computational Flow Imaging
head: CFI Parallel Volume Rendering, Preprocessed Raytracing for CFI
body: Parallel Volume Rendering for Computational Flow Imaging (CFI) is a method for visualizing refractive index or density fields from Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations on distributed-memory supercomputers. It solves the problem of integral errors caused by intersecting or overlapping curvilinear CFD grids by converting them into rectilinear multi-block voxel fields. Unlike cell projection, which double-counts overlapping segments, or simple resampling, which creates unmanageably large regular grids, this method uses preprocessing to distribute voxels into balanced, regular regions for efficient parallel ray-casting. Inputs: Curvilinear, multi-zone, overlapping CFD grid data (e.g., hexahedral cells) representing flow fields (density, refractive index). Outputs: Rendered images (shadowgraph, schlieren, or interferometric) or field data. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: A set of voxels derived from the continuous CFD geometry. Each voxel stores the physical property value (e.g., density \rho) and its position. 2. Region Block: A regular sub-region of the flow field, defined by equal divisions along the x and y coordinates. Each block is assigned to a specific processor in the distributed system. Parameters: Integration Rule: Trapezoidal rule. Communication: MPI (Message Passing Interface). Hardware: Distributed-memory architecture (e.g., Beowulf cluster with switch-based interconnect). Language: C++. Steps: 1. Voxelization: Convert the continuous geometric representation of the curvilinear CFD grids into a discrete set of voxels. This step maps the irregular grid cells to a voxel representation, avoiding the need for high-rate resampling to a single regular grid. 2. Region Division: Divide the entire flow field into regular regions by equally partitioning the domain along the x and y coordinates. 3. Load Balancing: Distribute the voxels into these regions such that each region contains approximately the same number of voxels. This mitigates load imbalances caused by the varying sizes and shapes of the original CFD cells, which can differ by several orders of magnitude due to adaptive mesh refinement. 4. Distribution: Assign each region (block of voxels) to a different processor in the parallel distributed-memory system using MPI. 5. Rendering (Ray-Casting): For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. The ray traversal is performed locally on the processor holding the relevant blocks. Each line integral process searches through all voxels in its assigned block. Formulas: The optical intensity I is calculated via line-of-sight integration. The algorithm calculates the appropriate integrand values at specific points along the ray, then applies the trapezoidal rule for integration over n segments. For Shadowgraph systems, which respond to the second derivative of flow density \rho, the intensity is proportional to: I \propto \int \left( \frac{\partial^2 \rho}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \rho}{\partial y^2} \right) dz For Schlieren systems, which respond to the first derivative, the intensity depends on the orientation of the knife-edge or color filter: Vertical knife-edge: I \propto \int \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial x} dz Horizontal knife-edge: I \propto \int \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial y} dz For Interferometric systems (e.g., Mach-Zehnder), the light intensity is proportional to the fringe shift, which relates to the line integral of the refractive index (or density). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelcfirendering(cfdgrids, imagewidth, imageheight, numprocessors): # Step 1: Voxelization # Convert continuous curvilinear CFD grids into a set of voxels. # Not given in the sources. voxels = voxelize(cfdgrids) # Step 2 & 3: Region Division & Load Balancing # Divide the flow field into regular regions along x and y. # Distribute voxels to regions such that each region has ~equal voxel count. regions = createbalancedregions(voxels, numprocessors) # Step 4: Distribution # Assign regions to processors. rank = getrank() myvoxels = regions[rank % len(regions)] # Step 5: Rendering # Initialize output image image = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Cast ray for this pixel (assuming z-axis integration for simplicity) raydir = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Perform line-of-sight integration # The ray searches through all voxels in the assigned blocks intensity = integrateray(raydir, myvoxels) image[y][x] = intensity return image def voxelize(cfdgrids): # Not given in the sources. return [] def createbalancedregions(voxels, numprocessors): if not voxels: return [] # Determine bounds of the flow field minx = min(v[0] for v in voxels) maxx = max(v[0] for v in voxels) miny = min(v[1] for v in voxels) maxy = max(v[1] for v in voxels) # Equally divide the field along x and y coordinates divx = int(numprocessors 0.5) divy = divx if divx divy < numprocessors: divy += 1 regions = [] for i in range(divx): for j in range(divy): regions.append({ 'xstart': minx + i (maxx - minx) / divx, 'xend': minx + (i + 1) (maxx - minx) / divx, 'ystart': miny + j (maxy - miny) / divy, 'yend': miny + (j + 1) (maxy - miny) / divy, 'voxels': [] }) # Distribute voxels into regions for v in voxels: for r in regions: if r['xstart'] <= v[0] < r['xend'] and r['ystart'] <= v[1] < r['yend']: r['voxels'].append(v) break # Re-balance to ensure equal voxel counts per region allv = [v for r in regions for v in r['voxels']] allv.sort(key=lambda v: v[0] + v[1]) countper = len(allv) // len(regions) for i, r in enumerate(regions): start = i countper end = start + countper if i < len(regions) - 1 else len(allv) r['voxels'] = allv[start:end] return regions def getrank(): # Mock for MPICOMMWORLD.Getrank() return 0 def integrateray(raydir, voxels): # Sort voxels along the ray direction (z-axis) sortedv = sorted(voxels, key=lambda v: v[2]) # Trapezoidal rule integration integral = 0.0 for i in range(len(sortedv) - 1): v1 = sortedv[i] v2 = sortedv[i+1] # Calculate integrand value (e.g., density derivative for schlieren) val1 = getintegrand(v1) val2 = getintegrand(v2) # Distance between voxels along the ray dz = abs(v2[2] - v1[2]) # Trapezoidal rule: (val1 + val2) / 2 dz integral += (val1 + val2) / 2.0 dz return integral def getintegrand(v): # Not given in the sources. return v[3] Time Complexity: The preprocessing (voxelization and distribution) incurs a cost, but the rendering speed is improved by having fewer voxels to search in each block. The total searching speed increases as more blocks with fewer voxels are created, despite the distribution cost. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of voxels. This method avoids the excessive memory requirements of resampling to a high-resolution regular grid. Performance: Tested on a Beowulf cluster (9 nodes, 800 MHz Pentium III, 100 Mb/s Ethernet) with datasets of ~0.5 million hexahedral cells. The method showed significant performance improvement over cell projection and simple resampling. Strengths: Eliminates integral errors from overlapping grids; balances load across processors; efficient for large-scale distributed systems. Limitations: Requires preprocessing overhead; load imbalances are unavoidable but reduced; performance depends on the efficiency of the voxelization and distribution steps. Computational Flow Imaging (CFI) is a technique for flow visualization that simulates optical wave interaction with flow fields to generate digital images (shadowgraph, schlieren, interferometric). Traditional methods like cell projection suffer from integral errors when dealing with intersecting or overlapping curvilinear CFD grids. Simple resampling to a regular grid is inefficient due to high storage and rendering costs. This parallel volume rendering method was developed to address these issues on distributed-memory supercomputers, specifically implemented in C++ using MPI. name: STiles (Sorted Tiles)
head: Sorted Tiles, Sorting Tiles
body: STiles is a progressive ray casting technique that decomposes the image space into screen-space tiles, sorts them by estimated rendering cost, and renders them in batches across subsequent frames until a fixed time budget is reached. It addresses the problem of interactive volume rendering on mobile and low-performance devices by avoiding the stall caused by rendering high-resolution images in a single frame. Unlike FBSlabs, which renders fixed slabs across the entire image, STiles groups tiles of similar cost to efficiently utilize the GPU within a strict time budget, leveraging 3D texture cache locality by processing tiles rather than individual rays. The method operates in three phases: an interaction phase, a sorting phase, and a progressive rendering phase. Input: High-resolution volume dataset, transfer function, camera parameters, viewport dimensions. Output: Final high-resolution rendered image. Intermediate Data: T{low}: A 2D texture storing low-resolution color (RGB) and ray cost (Alpha). T{high}: A 2D texture storing high-resolution color for rendered tiles. Correlation Maps: Two 2D textures mapping sorted tile indices to unsorted tile coordinates and vice versa. 1. T{low}: A 2D texture where RGB channels store the low-resolution ray casting color and the Alpha channel stores the ray cost, defined as the number of ray samples taken during the low-resolution pass. 2. Correlation Maps: Two textures generated during sorting that allow translation between the sorted order of tiles and their original screen positions. 3. Tile Grid: The viewport is divided into square tiles of fixed size S \times S. Tile Size (S): 8x8 pixels. This size balances 3D texture cache locality against visual blockiness during the transition from low to high resolution. Time Budget (T{budget}): 0.1 seconds per frame. This is the maximum time allowed for rendering high-resolution tiles in a single frame. 1. Low Resolution Ray Casting (Interaction Phase): While the user interacts (rotates/zooms), perform standard low-resolution ray casting in a fragment shader. For each pixel, store the resulting color in the RGB channels of T{low} and the number of ray samples taken in the Alpha channel of T{low}. This alpha value serves as the estimated rendering cost for the corresponding high-resolution tile. 2. Tile Sorting (Sorting Phase): Triggered once user interaction stops. a. Tile Division: Split the viewport into tiles of size S \times S. b. Cost Estimation: For each tile, estimate its cost by querying the Alpha channel of T{low} at the tile's center pixel. c. GPU Radix Sort: Sort the tiles by their estimated cost using a GPU radix sort implemented in three compute shader steps: i. Group Counting: Classify tiles into groups based on cost and count the number of tiles in each group. ii. Group Offset Setting: Scan the counters to establish start offsets for each group in the output texture. iii. Sorting: Place tiles into the output texture according to the offsets. d. Correlation Maps: Generate two coordinate maps during sorting to translate between sorted tile indices and unsorted screen coordinates. 3. Progressive High Resolution Ray Casting (Rendering Phase): Render tiles in the sorted order into T{high}. a. Budget Management: Determine the number of tiles N to render in the current frame. The algorithm uses a decreasing tile budget per frame to compensate for the non-linear increase in accumulated time (as later tiles may be more expensive or cache misses increase). b. Rendering Loop: Render N tiles from the sorted list. After rendering each tile (or batch), measure elapsed time. If the time budget (0.1s) is exceeded, stop rendering for that frame. c. Ray Casting: In the fragment shader for high-resolution tiles, discard rays that do not intersect the proxy geometry. This allows empty or nearly empty tiles to complete instantly, even if their cost estimate was non-zero. 4. Compositing: For each pixel in the final image, if the pixel belongs to a tile that has been rendered in T{high}, use the high-resolution color from T{high}, otherwise use the low-resolution color from T{low}. This compositing is performed every frame, progressively replacing low-resolution pixels with high-resolution ones. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 3 and 4 in successive frames until all tiles are rendered and T{high} contains the complete high-resolution image. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time TILESIZE = 8 TIMEBUDGET = 0.1 # seconds Tlow = None # Texture2D: RGB=low-res color, A=ray cost (sample count) Thigh = None # Texture2D: RGB=high-res color for rendered tiles SortedTiles = [] # List of (x, y) tile coordinates sorted by cost CorrMapSortedToUnsorted = None # Texture2D CorrMapUnsortedToSorted = None # Texture2D currenttileindex = 0 def initialize(): # 1. Low Resolution Ray Casting # Perform during user interaction for y in range(viewportheight): for x in range(viewportwidth): color, samples = lowresraycast(x, y) Tlow.setrgb(x, y, color) Tlow.setalpha(x, y, samples) def oninteractionstops(): # 2. Tile Sorting numtilesx = (viewportwidth + TILESIZE - 1) // TILESIZE numtilesy = (viewportheight + TILESIZE - 1) // TILESIZE # Estimate costs from Tlow alpha at tile centers tilecosts = [] for y in range(numtilesy): for x in range(numtilesx): centerx = x TILESIZE + TILESIZE // 2 centery = y TILESIZE + TILESIZE // 2 cost = Tlow.getalpha(centerx, centery) tilecosts.append((cost, x, y)) # Sort tiles by cost (ascending) tilecosts.sort(key=lambda item: item[0]) # Extract sorted coordinates global SortedTiles SortedTiles = [(item[1], item[2]) for item in tilecosts] # Generate correlation maps using GPU radix sort compute shaders # Step i: Group counting # Step ii: Group offset setting # Step iii: Sorting # Output: CorrMapSortedToUnsorted and CorrMapUnsortedToSorted CorrMapSortedToUnsorted = generatesortedtounsortedmap(tilecosts) CorrMapUnsortedToSorted = generateunsortedtosortedmap(tilecosts) def progressiverenderingloop(): global currenttileindex currenttileindex = 0 while currenttileindex < len(SortedTiles): starttime = time.time() # Determine number of tiles to render this frame # Sources state a decreasing tile budget is used per frame to compensate for non-linear time increase, # but do not provide an exact formula. tilestorender = max(1, len(SortedTiles) // 4) for i in range(tilestorender): if currenttileindex >= len(SortedTiles): break tilecoord = SortedTiles[currenttileindex] # Render fragment shader for this tile region # Fragment shader discards rays not intersecting proxy geometry renderhighrestile(tilecoord, Thigh) currenttileindex += 1 # Check time budget if time.time() - starttime > TIMEBUDGET: break # Composite current image # For each pixel, select high-resolution color from Thigh if available, # otherwise select low-resolution color from Tlow compositeimage(Tlow, Thigh, CorrMapSortedToUnsorted) # Wait for next frame / vsync def renderhighrestile(tilecoord, targettexture): x, y = tilecoord # Render fragment shader for this tile region # Fragment shader discards rays not intersecting proxy geometry for dy in range(TILESIZE): for dx in range(TILESIZE): px = x TILESIZE + dx py = y TILESIZE + dy if rayintersectsproxy(px, py): color = highresraycast(px, py) targettexture.setrgb(px, py, color) def compositeimage(Tlow, Thigh, corrmap): for py in range(viewportheight): for px in range(viewportwidth): # Determine if this pixel is in a rendered high-res tile # Use correlation maps to check if (px, py) is covered by Thigh if ispixelinrenderedtile(px, py, corrmap): color = Thigh.getcolor(px, py) else: color = Tlow.getcolor(px, py) display(color) def lowresraycast(x, y): # Standard low-resolution ray casting return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 10 def rayintersectsproxy(px, py): # Check if ray intersects proxy geometry return True def highresraycast(px, py): # High-resolution ray casting return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) def ispixelinrenderedtile(px, py, corrmap): # Check if pixel tile index is less than currenttileindex using correlation maps return True def generatesortedtounsortedmap(tilecosts): # GPU compute shader implementation return None def generateunsortedtosortedmap(tilecosts): # GPU compute shader implementation return None Empty Tiles: Tiles with zero cost (empty regions) are rendered first. The fragment shader discards rays not intersecting proxy geometry, allowing these tiles to complete instantly. Cost Estimation Accuracy: Tile cost is estimated from a single sample at the tile center in T{low}. This is not perfectly reliable for the entire tile, but the impact is mitigated by the fast completion of empty tiles. Sorting Granularity: Sorting individual rays yields poorer performance than sorting tiles. Packing rays into tiles leverages the 3D texture cache. Visual Transition: The transition from low to high resolution is visible. Tile size 8 \times 8 is a compromise between cache performance and visual blockiness. Time Budget Exceedance: If the time budget is exceeded, rendering stops for that frame. The next frame resumes from where it left off. Time Complexity: The sorting phase is O(N \log N) or O(N) depending on the radix sort implementation, where N is the number of tiles. This is performed once per interaction session. The rendering phase is proportional to the number of tiles rendered per frame, bounded by the time budget. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for T{low}, T{high}, and correlation maps. Memory usage is O(W \times H), where W, H are viewport dimensions. Measured Performance: On Nexus 6, STiles achieved average completion times of 8.84s (Vix), 9.73s (Head), 8.83s (Obelix), 9.75s (Chamaleon), and 8.65s (Melanix). This is approximately half the time of FBSlabs. On Nexus 6P, times were 16.52s (Vix), 16.20s (Head), 17.06s (Obelix), 16.89s (Chamaleon), and 19.73s (Melanix). Strengths: Maintains interactivity by bounding frame time. Efficiently utilizes GPU cache by processing tiles. Faster completion than slab-based methods. Limitations: Requires multiple frames to reach full resolution. Visual transition artifacts. Sorting overhead (though negligible). When to Use: Mobile and low-performance devices where interactive frame rates are critical and full-resolution rendering cannot be completed in a single frame. When Not to Use: High-performance desktops where full-resolution rendering is feasible in one frame, or where visual continuity is more important than interactivity. STiles was introduced in the paper "Progressive Ray Casting for Volumetric Models on Mobile Devices". The work was motivated by the need to render large medical volume datasets (resolutions > 512^3) on mobile devices at full resolution while maintaining interactive frame rates. The method builds on the observation that rendering time increases non-linearly when rendering a fixed number of tiles per frame, necessitating a decreasing tile budget per frame. It was developed as an alternative to Front-to-back Slabs (FBSlabs) and Simple progressive ray casting, offering better performance and cache utilization.
