name: Depth-based Adaptive Raycasting with LOD
head: EA-raycasting, EA-raycasting with LOD and Depth-based Step Size, Front-to-Back Volume Raycasting with Early Termination and LOD, RaycastResult raycast, simpleRaycastLodDepth, simpleRaycastLodDepthOcclusion
body: Depth-based Adaptive Raycasting with LOD is a front-to-back volume rendering method that optimizes performance by varying the sampling step size based on the ray's depth from the camera, combined with early ray termination. It distinguishes itself from fixed-step raycasting by reducing computational cost in distant regions where visual detail is less critical, while maintaining high resolution near the viewer. It builds on Optimized Ray Casting by introducing depth-aware LOD selection. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: passUV: Screen-space UV coordinates of the current fragment. frontuvwmap, backuvwmap: Textures storing the start (startUVW) and end (endUVW) 3D coordinates of the ray in volume space. volumetexture: The 3D volume texture containing scalar values. transferFunction: A function mapping scalar values and step size to RGBA color. stepSize: Base sampling step size in world/view space. uLodBegin: Depth threshold where LOD degradation begins. uLodRange: Depth range over which LOD degrades from 0 to uLodMaxLevel. uLodMaxLevel: Maximum LOD level multiplier. uScreenToTexture: Matrix to convert screen coordinates to texture coordinates. getViewCoord: Function to linearize depth from view space. uProjection, uViewToTexture: Matrices for depth projection. Outputs: fragColor: The final accumulated RGBA color. fragFirstHit: The projected depth of the first opaque sample. glFragDepth: The depth value for the fragment. Data Structures: RaycastResult: Struct containing: color: vec4 (accumulated RGBA). firstHit: vec4 (xyz: position of first hit, a: depth of first hit). lastHit: vec4 (xyz: position of last hit, a: depth of last hit). VolumeSample: Struct containing: value: float (scalar value from texture). uvw: vec3 (sampling position). Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Retrieve startUVW and endUVW from frontuvwmap and backuvwmap using passUV. Edge Case (Invalid Pixel): If endUVW.a == 0.0 (ray does not intersect volume), discard the fragment. Edge Case (Camera Inside Volume): If startUVW.a == 0.0, clamp the start point to the near plane: python uvwStart = uScreenToTexture vec4(passUV, 0.0, 1.0) uvwStart.a = 0.0 startUVW = uvwStart Linearize depths: python startDistance = abs(getViewCoord(vec3(passUV, startUVW.a)).z) endDistance = abs(getViewCoord(vec3(passUV, endUVW.a)).z) startDepth = startDistance endDepth = endDistance Initialize result: python result.color = vec4(0.0) result.firstHit = vec4(startUVW, endDepth) # Placeholder result.lastHit = vec4(endUVW, endDepth) curColor = vec4(0.0) Calculate parametric step size: python rayLength = length(endUVW - startUVW) parameterStepSize = stepSize / rayLength Initialize ray parameter t: python t = 0.01 if RANDOMOFFSET is defined: t = t 2.0 rand(passUV) 2. Ray Marching Loop: Loop while t < 1.0 + (0.5 parameterStepSize): 1. Interpolate Position: python curUVW = mix(startUVW, endUVW, t) curDepth = mix(startDepth, endDepth, t) 2. Calculate LOD Level: python lodFactor = max(0.0, min(1.0, (curDepth - uLodBegin) / uLodRange)) curLod = lodFactor uLodMaxLevel 3. Calculate Adaptive Step Size: python curStepSize = stepSize pow(2.0, curLod) parameterStepSize = curStepSize / rayLength 4. Sample Volume: python rawValue = textureLod(volumetexture, curUVW, curLod).r curSample.value = int(rawValue) curSample.uvw = curUVW 5. Transfer Function: python sampleColor = transferFunction(curSample.value, curStepSize) 6. Record First Hit: If result.firstHit.a is not set (or effectively 0) AND sampleColor.a > 0.001: python result.firstHit.rgb = curSample.uvw result.firstHit.a = curDepth 7. Front-to-Back Blending: python curColor.rgb = (1.0 - curColor.a) sampleColor.rgb + curColor.rgb curColor.a = (1.0 - curColor.a) sampleColor.a + curColor.a 8. Early Ray Termination: If curColor.a > 0.99, break loop. 9. Increment Parameter: python t += parameterStepSize 3. Finalization: Set result.color = curColor. Output fragColor = result.color. Depth Output: If result.firstHit.a > 0.0: python firstHitProjected = uProjection inverse(uViewToTexture) vec4(result.firstHit.xyz, 1.0) fragFirstHit.a = max((firstHitProjected.z / firstHitProjected.w) 0.5 + 0.5, 0.0) glFragDepth = fragFirstHit.a Else: python fragFirstHit = endUVW glFragDepth = 1.0 Parameters: stepSize: Base sampling step size. Typical value: 1.0 / (2.0 volumesizex). uLodBegin: Depth threshold for LOD start. Not given in the sources. uLodRange: Depth range for LOD transition. Not given in the sources. uLodMaxLevel: Maximum LOD multiplier. Not given in the sources. ALPHASCALE: Multiplier for alpha in transfer function, default 20.0. uWindowingRange, uWindowingMinVal: Windowing parameters for transfer function. Pitfalls: Camera Inside Volume: Must clamp start to near plane. Invalid Rays: Discard if endUVW.a == 0.0. Occlusion Culling: If uvwOcclusion.x is between startUVW.a and endUVW.a, update startUVW to the occlusion point. Scene Clipping: If scenedepth < startUVW.a, set glFragDepth to startUVW.a and return. If scenedepth < endUVW.a, update endUVW to scenedepth. Loop Bound: The condition t < 1.0 + (0.5 parameterStepSize) ensures the endpoint is covered despite variable steps. First Hit Logic: result.firstHit.a > curDepth ensures the closest hit is recorded, assuming depth increases away from camera. A GPU-based technique that splits rays into layers based on opacity thresholds, applying Beer-Lambert law and ambient occlusion. It builds on this method by using its LOD and variable step size to optimize sampling density within each layer. Time Complexity: Reduced compared to fixed-step raycasting due to larger step sizes at greater depths (higher LOD). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for frontuvwmap and backuvwmap textures, plus the volume texture. Strengths: Optimizes performance by adapting sampling density to depth; early termination further reduces cost for opaque regions. Limitations: Visual quality may degrade in distant regions if LOD is too aggressive; requires pre-computed UVW maps. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering where performance is critical and depth-based detail variation is acceptable. When Not to Use: Applications requiring uniform high resolution throughout the volume or where depth-based LOD artifacts are unacceptable. This method is implemented in the VRVRVive project by Secumfex. It represents an evolution from simple fixed-step raycasting (simpleRaycast) by introducing depth-based LOD and step size adjustment. name: Multi-layer Beer-Lambert Raycasting with Ambient Occlusion and Shadowing
head: EA-raycasting, Unified Raycasting
body: Multi-layer Beer-Lambert raycasting is a GPU-based volume rendering technique that splits a ray into discrete segments (layers) based on accumulated opacity thresholds, computing color and alpha using Beer-Lambert law parameters (emission/absorption) for each segment. It distinguishes itself from standard front-to-back alpha blending by decoupling the compositing into layers that can be stored in separate buffers, while simultaneously applying ambient occlusion (AO) from neighboring samples and shadow sampling along a specific direction. This method builds on Depth-based Adaptive Raycasting with LOD by utilizing its LOD and variable step size capabilities to optimize the sampling density within each layer. Inputs: volumetexture: 3D texture containing volume data. frontuvwmap, backuvwmap: Textures providing start and end UVW coordinates for rays per pixel. uStepSize: Base step size for ray traversal. uShadowRayDirection: Direction vector for shadow rays. Uniforms: ALPHASCALE, AMBIENTOCCLUSIONSCALE, AMBIENTOCCLUSIONRADIUS, ABSORPTIONSCALE, SHADOWSCALE, CUBEMAPSTRENGTH, ERTTHRESHOLD. Outputs: fragColor1..4: Four vec4 buffers storing layerColor[0..3]. fragDepth.x..w: Four components storing layerDepth[0..3]. result.color: Final accumulated color. Optional: fragColorDebug, fragFirstHit (if FIRSTHIT is defined). RaycastResult: color: vec4 (end color). firstHit: vec4 (position of first non-zero alpha hit). lastHit: vec4 (position of last non-zero alpha hit). Layer State: layerColor[4]: Array of vec4 storing color per layer. layerDepth[4]: Array of float storing depth per layer. segmentColor: vec4 (accumulated color for current layer). segmentAlpha: float (accumulated alpha for current layer). ALPHASCALE: Default 20.0. Scaling factor for alpha in transfer functions. AMBIENTOCCLUSIONSCALE: Default 2.0. Scales accumulated AO. AMBIENTOCCLUSIONRADIUS: Default 2.0. Radius in steps for AO neighbor sampling. ABSORPTIONSCALE: Default 10.0. Scaling factor for absorption in EMISSIONABSORPTIONRAW mode. SHADOWSCALE: Default 1.0. Scales shadow factor. ERTTHRESHOLD: Default 0.99. Threshold for early ray termination (used in defines, logic relies on currentLayerThreshold). 1. Ray Initialization: Get uvwStart from frontuvwmap and uvwEnd from backuvwmap. If uvwEnd.a == 0.0, discard the pixel (back face not visible). If uvwStart.a == 0.0 (camera inside volume), clamp uvwStart to the near plane using uViewToTexture and getViewCoord. Calculate startDistance and endDistance as the length of view-space coordinates corresponding to UVW depths. 2. Ray Traversal Loop: Initialize curUVW = uvwStart, curDistance = startDistance, curAlpha = 0.0, segmentColor = vec4(0.0), currentLayer = 1, currentLayerThreshold = 1.0 / 4.0. While curDistance < endDistance: Sample volumetexture at curUVW to get sampleColor (color/alpha from transfer function). Ambient Occlusion (AO): If AMBIENTOCCLUSION is defined: Initialize aoaccum = 0.0. For each neighbor offset i in X, Y, Z directions within radius AMBIENTOCCLUSIONRADIUS curStepSize: Sample volumetexture at neighbor position (use textureLod if LEVELOFDETAIL is defined) to get aovalue. If EMISSIONABSORPTIONRAW is defined: aocontrib = 1.0 - exp( - (pow(transferFunctionRaw(aovalue).a ABSORPTIONSCALE, 2.0)) curStepSize). Else: aocontrib = transferFunction(aovalue, curStepSize).a. aoaccum += aocontrib. selfocclusion = sampleColor.a. aoaccum = max(0.0, aoaccum - selfocclusion) AMBIENTOCCLUSIONSCALE. sampleColor.rgb = max(0.0, min(1.0, 1.0 - (aoaccum / numsamples))). (Note: numsamples is typically the number of AO neighbors or a constant; if undefined, assume 1.0 or omit modulation if not specified). Cubemap Indirect Lighting: If CUBEMAPSAMPLING is defined: Generate numopacitysamples random directions using rand() = hash(curUVW, seed). For each direction: Cast shadow ray: Sample volumetexture at distances pow(2.0, float(j)) curStepSize for j = 0..numsteps. Calculate shadowalpha using EMISSIONABSORPTIONRAW or standard transfer function. shadow = (1.0 - shadow) shadowalpha + shadow. cubemapcolor = (1.0 - shadow). sampleColor.rgb = mix(sampleColor.rgb, cubemapcolor, CUBEMAPSTRENGTH). Shadow Sampling: If SHADOWSAMPLING is defined: Initialize shadow = 0.0. For k = 0 to uShadowRayNumSteps: shadowstepSize = curStepSize 2.5 (or use LoD if LEVELOFDETAIL is active). shadowsampleUVW = curUVW + k shadowstepSize uShadowRayDirection. Sample volumetexture at shadowsampleUVW to get shadowalpha. shadow = (1.0 - shadow) shadowalpha + shadow. sampleColor.rgb = max(0.25, min(1.0, 1.0 - shadow SHADOWSCALE)). Layer Compositing: segmentColor.rgb = (1.0 - segmentColor.a) sampleColor.rgb + segmentColor.rgb. segmentColor.a = (1.0 - segmentColor.a) sampleColor.a + segmentColor.a. curAlpha = segmentColor.a. curDistance += curStepSize. curUVW += curStepSize raydirection. Layer Threshold Check: If curAlpha >= currentLayerThreshold and currentLayer < 4: Convert segmentColor to Beer-Lambert emission/absorption parameters: emission, absorption = beerLambertColorTransmissionToEmissionAbsorption(segmentColor.rgb, 1.0 - segmentColor.a, distancesegment). Convert back to color transmission for storage: segmentColor = beerLambertEmissionAbsorptionToColorTransmission(emission, absorption, distancesegment). layerColor[currentLayer-1] = segmentColor. layerDepth[currentLayer-1] = curDistance. Reset segmentColor = vec4(0.0), currentLayer++. currentLayerThreshold = float(currentLayer) / 4.0. lastDistance = curDistance. 3. Finalization: Fill the last layer (index 3) with remaining segmentColor and layerDepth[3] = endDistance. Write layerColor[0..3] to fragColor1..4 and layerDepth[0..3] to fragDepth.x..w. Output final curColor (accumulated from all layers) to result.color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multilayerbeerlambertraycasting(uvwstart, uvwend, ustepsize, volumetexture, viewdirection): # 1. Initialization if uvwend.a == 0.0: return discardpixel() if uvwstart.a == 0.0: uvwstart = clamptonearplane(uvwstart) startdistance = length(viewspace(uvwstart)) enddistance = length(viewspace(uvwend)) curuvw = uvwstart curdistance = startdistance segmentcolor = vec4(0.0) currentlayer = 1 currentlayerthreshold = 0.25 # 1/4 layercolor = [vec4(0.0)] 4 layerdepth = [0.0] 4 # 2. Ray Loop while curdistance < enddistance: sample = samplevolume(curuvw, volumetexture) samplecolor = transferfunction(sample, ustepsize) # Ambient Occlusion if AMBIENTOCCLUSION: aoaccum = 0.0 for offset in getaooffsets(AMBIENTOCCLUSIONRADIUS ustepsize): aosample = samplevolume(curuvw + offset, volumetexture) aoval = transferfunction(aosample, ustepsize).a if EMISSIONABSORPTIONRAW: aocontrib = 1.0 - exp(-(pow(aoval ABSORPTIONSCALE, 2.0)) ustepsize) else: aocontrib = aoval aoaccum += aocontrib selfocclusion = samplecolor.a aoaccum = max(0.0, aoaccum - selfocclusion) AMBIENTOCCLUSIONSCALE samplecolor.rgb = max(0.0, min(1.0, 1.0 - aoaccum)) # Assuming numsamples=1 for simplicity if not defined # Shadow Sampling if SHADOWSAMPLING: shadow = 0.0 for k in range(uShadowRayNumSteps): shadowstep = ustepsize 2.5 shadowuvw = curuvw + k shadowstep uShadowRayDirection shadowsample = samplevolume(shadowuvw, volumetexture) shadowalpha = transferfunction(shadowsample, shadowstep).a shadow = (1.0 - shadow) shadowalpha + shadow samplecolor.rgb = max(0.25, min(1.0, 1.0 - shadow SHADOWSCALE)) # Cubemap Sampling if CUBEMAPSAMPLING: shadow = 0.0 for j in range(numopacitysamples): randdir = getrandomdirection(curuvw, j) for m in range(numshadowsteps): dist = pow(2.0, float(m)) ustepsize shadowuvw = curuvw + dist randdir shadowsample = samplevolume(shadowuvw, volumetexture) shadowalpha = transferfunction(shadowsample, dist).a shadow = (1.0 - shadow) shadowalpha + shadow cubemapcolor = samplecubemap(randdir) (1.0 - shadow) samplecolor.rgb = mix(samplecolor.rgb, cubemapcolor, CUBEMAPSTRENGTH) # Compositing segmentcolor.rgb = (1.0 - segmentcolor.a) samplecolor.rgb + segmentcolor.rgb segmentcolor.a = (1.0 - segmentcolor.a) samplecolor.a + segmentcolor.a curdistance += ustepsize curuvw += ustepsize viewdirection # Layer Threshold Check if segmentcolor.a >= currentlayerthreshold and currentlayer < 4: # Convert to Beer-Lambert and back for storage emission, absorption = beerlambertcolortoemissionabsorption(segmentcolor.rgb, 1.0 - segmentcolor.a, ustepsize) segmentcolor = beerlambertemissionabsorptiontocolor(emission, absorption, ustepsize) layercolor[currentlayer - 1] = segmentcolor layerdepth[currentlayer - 1] = curdistance segmentcolor = vec4(0.0) currentlayer += 1 currentlayerthreshold = float(currentlayer) / 4.0 # 3. Final Layer layercolor[3] = segmentcolor layerdepth[3] = enddistance # Output writefbo(fragColor1, layercolor[0]) writefbo(fragColor2, layercolor[1]) writefbo(fragColor3, layercolor[2]) writefbo(fragColor4, layercolor[3]) writefbo(fragDepth, layerdepth) return segmentcolor # Final accumulated color Time Complexity: O(N \cdot L), where N is the number of steps per ray and L is the number of layers (4). Shadow and AO sampling add constant factors per step. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for layer buffers (4 layers). Performance: Optimized for GPU execution due to parallel ray casting. LOD reduces sampling density in distant layers. Strengths: Real-time capable with AO and shadows; Beer-Lambert model provides physically plausible light transport; layer separation allows for post-processing or further compositing. Limitations: Discrete layers may introduce banding if thresholds are not chosen carefully; AO and shadow sampling increase computational cost significantly. This method is described in the context of VR volume rendering, specifically in the GitHub repository Secumfex/VRVRVive. It is an implementation of a unified raycasting approach that integrates Beer-Lambert law, ambient occlusion, and shadowing into a multi-layer framework. name: Prediction Buffer Voxel Traversal
head: Local Traversal, Modified Depth Buffer Traversal, Prediction Buffer, Sparse Traversal
body: Prediction Buffer Voxel Traversal is a GPU-accelerated dataset traversal technique that exploits frame-to-frame coherence during camera rotation to accelerate isosurface volume rendering. It uses a modified depth buffer, called the prediction buffer, to store ray-cast results from the previous frame, allowing the renderer to skip large portions of the volume or refine local searches instead of performing a full traversal for every pixel. Unlike C-buffer or image cache techniques that store coordinates or iso-maps and suffer from aliasing or lack data parallelism on GPUs, the prediction buffer stores depth distances and is designed for high-performance GPU parallelism. Inputs: Ray \mathbf{R} for each pixel, defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Volume dataset with bounding box defined by t{min} and t{max}. Isosurface value \rho{iso}. Prediction buffer from the previous frame. Step size parameter dt (adaptive based on data variance). Outputs: Intersection distance t along the ray where \rho(t) = \rho{iso}. Updated prediction buffer for the current frame. Prediction Buffer: A 2D array (one value per pixel) storing a single floating-point value d{ij} for pixel p{ij}. The value represents the distance from the eye to the interaction point along the ray. The value types are: 1. Positive number (d{ij} > 0): The ray hit the isosurface in the previous frame. 2. Negative flag (d{hitBoxMissSurf}): The ray missed the isosurface but hit the volume bounding box in the previous frame. 3. Negative flag (d{missBox}): The ray missed the volume bounding box completely in the previous frame. 4. No information (d{noInfo}): No data available (e.g., first frame). \kappa{max}, \kappa{min}: Experimentally determined constants for adaptive step size. Typical values are \kappa{max} = 0.3 and \kappa{min} = 0.1. \alpha: Frequency of full traversal to correct errors. Typical value is \alpha = 10 (perform full traversal every 10 frames). dt: Step size for sparse traversal, calculated based on local data variance. 1. Ray Casting: Cast one ray for each pixel in the final rendered image. 2. Prediction Retrieval: Retrieve the prediction buffer value d{ij} for the current pixel from the previous frame. 3. Traversal Mode Selection: If d{ij} = d{missBox} or d{ij} = d{noInfo}, perform Full Traversal (standard DDA or dense sampling). If d{ij} = d{hitBoxMissSurf}, perform Local Traversal (refine search near bounding box entry). If d{ij} > 0, perform Sparse Traversal (skip to predicted depth). Every \alpha frames, force Full Traversal for all pixels to prevent error accumulation. 4. Adaptive Step Size Calculation: Calculate dt using the variance v of the data in the current brick/region, and global min/max variances v{min}, v{max}: dt = \kappa{min} + (\kappa{max} - \kappa{min}) \frac{v - v{min}}{v{max} - v{min}} 5. Traversal Execution: Sparse Traversal: Start at t{start} = t{min} + d{ij}. Use the algorithm below to find the intersection. Local Traversal: Start at t{start} = d{ij}. Search in both forward and backward directions from t{start} until the isosurface is found or volume bounds are exceeded. 6. Prediction Buffer Update: Store the result of the current frame's ray cast into the prediction buffer for the next frame. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. dmissBox = -2.0 dhitBoxMissSurf = -1.0 dnoInfo = 0.0 def predictionbuffertraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso, predictionbuffer, framecount, alpha, v, vmin, vmax): """ Main entry point for prediction buffer voxel traversal. """ pixelid = getpixelidfromray(rayo, rayd) # Force full traversal periodically to correct drift if framecount % alpha == 0: return fulltraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso) # Retrieve prediction dprev = predictionbuffer[pixelid] # Determine traversal mode if dprev == dmissBox or dprev == dnoInfo: return fulltraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso) elif dprev == dhitBoxMissSurf: return localtraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso, dprev) else: # dprev > 0 (hit isosurface) return sparsetraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso, dprev) def sparsetraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso, dprev): """ Sparse traversal starting from predicted depth. """ dt = calculateadaptivedt(v, vmin, vmax) # Start traversal from the predicted hit point tstart = tmin + dprev tstart = max(tmin, min(tmax, tstart)) tprev = tstart tcurr = tstart + dt if tcurr > tmax: tcurr = tmax rhoprev = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tprev) rhocurr = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tcurr) while tcurr <= tmax: if min(rhoprev, rhocurr) <= rhoiso <= max(rhoprev, rhocurr): return bisectionfind(tprev, tcurr, rhoiso) tprev = tcurr tcurr = tprev + dt if tcurr > tmax: tcurr = tmax rhoprev = rhocurr rhocurr = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tcurr) return -1.0 def localtraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso, dprev): """ Local traversal starting from predicted depth, searching both forward and backward. """ dt = calculateadaptivedt(v, vmin, vmax) tstart = dprev tstart = max(tmin, min(tmax, tstart)) # Forward search tprevfwd = tstart tcurrfwd = tstart + dt if tcurrfwd > tmax: tcurrfwd = tmax rhoprevfwd = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tprevfwd) rhocurrfwd = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tcurrfwd) while tcurrfwd <= tmax: if min(rhoprevfwd, rhocurrfwd) <= rhoiso <= max(rhoprevfwd, rhocurrfwd): return bisectionfind(tprevfwd, tcurrfwd, rhoiso) tprevfwd = tcurrfwd tcurrfwd = tprevfwd + dt if tcurrfwd > tmax: tcurrfwd = tmax rhoprevfwd = rhocurrfwd rhocurrfwd = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tcurrfwd) # Backward search (if forward failed) tprevbwd = tstart tcurrbwd = tstart - dt if tcurrbwd < tmin: tcurrbwd = tmin rhoprevbwd = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tprevbwd) rhocurrbwd = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tcurrbwd) while tcurrbwd >= tmin: if min(rhoprevbwd, rhocurrbwd) <= rhoiso <= max(rhoprevbwd, rhocurrbwd): return bisectionfind(tcurrbwd, tprevbwd, rhoiso) tprevbwd = tcurrbwd tcurrbwd = tprevbwd - dt if tcurrbwd < tmin: tcurrbwd = tmin rhoprevbwd = rhocurrbwd rhocurrbwd = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tcurrbwd) return -1.0 def fulltraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso): """ Standard dense traversal (e.g., DDA). """ # Compute ray step per voxel invd = 1.0 / rayd tminvoxel = (tmin - rayo) invd tmaxvoxel = (tmax - rayo) invd tentry = max(tminvoxel) texit = min(tmaxvoxel) if tentry > texit: return -1.0 # Traverse voxels t = tentry while t <= texit: rho = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, t) if rho == rhoiso: return t t += 1.0 / max(abs(invd)) return -1.0 def calculateadaptivedt(v, vmin, vmax): """ Calculate step size based on data variance. """ if vmax == vmin: return 0.1 return 0.1 + (0.3 - 0.1) (v - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) def trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, t): """ Sample volume data at ray position t using trilinear interpolation. """ pos = rayo + rayd t return volumetexturesample(pos) def bisectionfind(ta, tb, rhoiso): """ Find exact intersection using bisection. """ rhoa = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, ta) rhob = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tb) for in range(10): tmid = (ta + tb) / 2 rhomid = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tmid) if abs(rhomid - rhoiso) < 1e-6: return tmid if (rhomid - rhoiso) (rhoa - rhoiso) < 0: tb = tmid rhob = rhomid else: ta = tmid rhoa = rhomid return (ta + tb) / 2 Skipping Isosurface: Sparse traversal may skip an isosurface if dt is too large, introducing artifacts. Local Traversal Failure: Local traversal may fail to find the isosurface if the surface moves significantly between frames or if the local search exits volume bounds before finding the surface, producing incorrect results compared to Full Traversal. Error Accumulation: To remedy the risk of missing surfaces due to coherence errors, the method performs a full traversal every \alpha frames. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than full traversal during camera rotation due to skipped voxels. Memory Complexity: Requires one additional floating-point value per pixel for the prediction buffer. Performance: The method can double the rendering speed compared to standard techniques. Strengths: High parallelism on GPUs; no divergent branching in sparse traversal; effective for interactive rotation. Limitations: Not suitable for large camera movements (coherence breaks); potential for visual artifacts if dt is poorly chosen or if the surface moves rapidly; requires periodic full traversal to correct errors. When to use: Interactive volume rendering with small camera rotations on GPU architectures. When not to use: Large viewpoint changes, static scenes with no coherence, or when strict visual accuracy is required without periodic correction. Origin: The technique was proposed by Braley et al. in "GPU Accelerated Voxel Traversal using the Prediction Buffer". History: It builds upon earlier work on C-buffers and image caches [Yoon et al. 1997], which were not suited for GPU architectures due to lack of data parallelism. It also relates to temporal coherence techniques by Klein et al. [2005]. Usage: Implemented using NVIDIA's CUDA toolkit (version 2.2 in the source) for massively parallel isosurface volume rendering. GPU Accelerated Voxel Traversal using the Prediction Buffer, https://people.cs.vt.edu/yongcao/publication/pdf/Braley10.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Wave Surfing Optimisations
head: 2D raycasting, Wave surfing algorithm
body: Wave Surfing Optimisations is a technique for accelerating the rendering of 3D landscapes (terrains) by reducing computation time in the rendering loop when the landscape is flat, specifically by minimizing time spent in interpolation between drawing operations. It is a simplified variant of ray-based approaches used for real-time visualization of 3D models on low-end hardware. It sets itself apart from general volume rendering acceleration structures by focusing on a 2D height-map traversal strategy that exploits the coherence of terrain geometry, rather than 3D voxel grid traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A height map representing the landscape, a camera position, and a viewing direction. Output: A rendered image of the terrain. Data Structures: Height Map: A 2D array of elevation values. The specific bit-packing or data type is not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Ray Casting Setup: For each pixel (or column of pixels) in the screen space, cast a ray into the scene. In the context of terrain rendering, this often involves projecting the ray against the height map. 2. Traversal with Variable Step Size: Traverse the height map along the ray's path. To optimize performance, the step size through the height map can be increased as the distance from the camera increases. This discards more information for distant voxels, making them "more vague". 3. Interpolation Reduction: The core optimization is to reduce the number of interpolation operations performed between drawing steps. In a naive implementation, every column of voxels might be processed; Wave Surfing aims to skip or batch these operations when the landscape is flat. 4. Rendering: Draw the visible voxels or terrain segments. Formulas: The traversal complexity is stated as O(n), where n is related to the number of steps through the height map. The sources mention that a hierarchical visibility scheme (e.g., quadtree) could achieve O(\log n) discard of invisible voxels, but Wave Surfing itself is described as taking "nearly constant steps" in the best case for flat landscapes. Parameters: Step Size: Can be variable, increasing with distance from the camera. Typical values for step size or terrain resolution are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flat Landscapes: The rendering loop performs very badly if the landscape is completely flat, because every single column of voxels is higher than the previous and must be drawn. Large Mountains: Variable step sizes can cause problems if large mountains are completely skipped or rendered incorrectly due to the increased step size in the distance. Hierarchical Alternative: A simple quadtree could be stored like mipmaps, containing the maximum value of all subpixels, to allow for O(\log n) discard of invisible voxels, which is considered ideal but not part of the basic Wave Surfing technique. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def wavesurfingrender(heightmap, camera, screenwidth, screenheight): # Initialize output image image = emptyimage(screenwidth, screenheight) for y in range(screenheight): for x in range(screenwidth): # Cast ray from camera through pixel (x, y) ray = castray(camera, x, y) # Determine traversal parameters # Step size may vary based on distance from camera stepsize = calculatestepsize(ray.origin, ray.direction) # Traverse height map along ray # This is the "Wave Surfing" part: reducing interpolation currentt = ray.origin.tmin while currentt < ray.origin.tmax: # Get height at current ray position # Interpolation is minimized here height = getheightatrayposition(heightmap, ray, currentt) # Check if voxel is visible if isvisible(height, currentt): # Draw voxel or terrain segment color = computecolor(height, currentt) image.setpixel(x, y, color) # Break or continue based on visibility logic break # Advance along ray # Step size might increase with distance currentt += stepsize distancefactor(currentt) return image def calculatestepsize(origin, direction): # Not given in sources. # Typically based on voxel size or desired resolution return 1.0 def getheightatrayposition(heightmap, ray, t): # Map ray position to height map coordinates # Interpolate height value # Not given in sources. return 0.0 def isvisible(height, t): # Check if the height is within view frustum and not occluded # Not given in sources. return True def computecolor(height, t): # Compute color based on height and distance # Not given in sources. return (0, 0, 0) def distancefactor(t): # Increase step size with distance # Not given in sources. return 1.0 A sub-technique where step size increases with distance, trading accuracy for speed in the distance. It sets itself apart by dynamically adjusting resolution. Choose it when performance is critical and distant details are less important. An alternative optimization mentioned as ideal for O(\log n) performance. It sets itself apart by using a tree structure for culling. Choose it when flat landscapes cause performance issues with basic Wave Surfing. Time Complexity: The basic technique is O(n), where n is the number of steps through the height map. A hierarchical alternative could achieve O(\log n). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Used in early computer games on low-end hardware, enabling real-time visualization of 3D terrains. Scaling: Performance degrades on completely flat landscapes where every column must be drawn. Strengths: Reduces interpolation overhead, suitable for low-end hardware. Limitations: Poor performance on flat landscapes; variable step sizes can cause artifacts with large mountains. When to use: Real-time terrain rendering on hardware with limited processing power. When not to use: When high accuracy in distant terrain is required, or when landscapes are predominantly flat. Origin: The technique is associated with the development of realtime voxel landscape engines, particularly in the context of early 3D games. History: It was used in games such as Comanche (1992), Delta Force (1998), Armored Fist (1994), Blade Runner (1997), and Hexplore (1998). It was also used in early consoles like Amiga, Nintendo, and Gameboy with software rasterization. Usage: Primarily used for terrain visualization in early 3D games and simulations where polygon-based rendering was not yet feasible or efficient on the target hardware. flipcode - Realtime Voxel Landscape Engines, https://www.flipcode.com/archives/RealtimeVoxelLandscapeEngines-Part4LevelofDetailandOptimisation.shtml, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Simplified voxel based visualization, https://ojs.uni-miskolc.hu/index.php/psaie/article/view/3824, fetched 2026-10-31

name: LLO-based Ray-casting
head: LLO ray-casting, Linear Level Octree ray-casting
body: LLO-based ray-casting is a volume rendering technique that accelerates image-order rendering by utilizing a Linear Level Octree (LLO) spatial data structure to skip empty space and facilitate early ray termination. It differs from brute-force ray-casting by replacing uniform voxel traversal with hierarchical octree traversal, and from other acceleration structures by encoding the octree in a linear array to optimize memory access patterns. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset (voxel grid), camera parameters (origin and direction per pixel), and a homogeneous threshold for LLO generation. Output: A 2D rendered image. Data Structures: The core data structure is the Linear Level Octree (LLO), a hierarchical representation where each node represents an octant (a sub-volume). Nodes are stored in a linear array. Each octant is classified as empty, opaque, or semi-transparent based on voxel values within it. Exact bit-packing and field layouts are Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Generate the LLO by recursively subdividing the volume into octants and classifying each based on a homogeneous threshold. 2. For each pixel, compute the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. 3. Traverse the LLO along the ray: if an octant is empty, skip it and advance the ray parameter t to the octant's exit boundary. 4. If the octant is opaque or semi-transparent, sample voxels within it using front-to-back compositing. 5. Accumulate color and opacity; if accumulated opacity reaches 1.0, apply early ray termination and stop processing the ray. 6. Perform boundary checks during compositing to ensure integrated sample values do not exceed permitted maximums. Formulas: Ray parameterization: \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the ray origin, \mathbf{d} is the normalized direction vector, and t is the distance along the ray. Front-to-back compositing: C{\text{out}} = C{\text{in}} + c \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{\text{in}}), where C{\text{out}} is the output color, C{\text{in}} is the accumulated color, c is the sample color, \alpha is the sample opacity, and \alpha{\text{in}} is the accumulated opacity. Parameters: Homogeneous Threshold: 10, used to classify voxels during LLO generation. Resolution: 256 \times 256 pixels in the cited implementation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise: Noisy blocks in the volume data prevent the LLO from encoding large empty spaces, significantly reducing performance; filtering noise improves speedup by allowing larger empty octants. Semi-transparent Data: Datasets with scattered non-transparent voxels (e.g., brain vessels) result in smaller octants and lower speedup compared to opaque data with clustered non-transparent voxels. Boundary Checks: Integrated sample values may exceed permitted maximums, requiring explicit boundary checks during compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lloraycasting(volumedata, camera, llostructure, threshold=10): """ Renders a volume using LLO-based ray-casting. Args: volumedata: 3D array of voxel values. camera: Object with getray(x, y) returning (origin, direction). llostructure: Linear array of octree nodes. threshold: Homogeneous threshold for LLO generation. Returns: 2D image array. """ height, width = camera.imagedimensions image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height)] voxelsize = 1.0 # Assumes unit spacing tentry, texit = 0.0, 100.0 # Assumes volume bounds for y in range(height): for x in range(width): o, d = camera.getray(x, y) t = tentry acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 # Sources do not specify exact LLO traversal indexing. # Standard DDA traversal computes step sizes and advances t # through octant boundaries, skipping empty nodes. step = voxelsize / max(abs(d[0]), abs(d[1]), abs(d[2])) while t < texit and accalpha < 1.0: # LLO traversal would check node type here and skip empty octants. # For implementation, we sample the current voxel. idx = (int((o[0] + t d[0]) / voxelsize), int((o[1] + t d[1]) / voxelsize), int((o[2] + t d[2]) / voxelsize)) # Boundary check to prevent out-of-bounds access if not (0 <= idx[0] < volumedata.shape[0] and 0 <= idx[1] < volumedata.shape[1] and 0 <= idx[2] < volumedata.shape[2]): t += step continue val = volumedata[idx[0]][idx[1]][idx[2]] alpha = min(val / 255.0, 1.0) # Simple opacity mapping color = [val / 255.0, val / 255.0, val / 255.0] # Grayscale transfer contrib = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor[0] += color[0] contrib acccolor[1] += color[1] contrib acccolor[2] += color[2] contrib accalpha += contrib # Check integrated value against permitted maximum t += step image[y][x] = acccolor return image Time and Memory Complexity: The method achieves an average speedup of 3.8x compared to brute-force ray-casting. Performance is dataset-dependent. Speedups ranged from 2.9x to 4.9x in the cited study. Memory usage is determined by the size of the LLO structure, which is generally smaller than the full voxel grid if significant empty space is encoded. Measured Performance: Hardware: PC with 1.4GHz Pentium III CPU and 512MB RAM. Datasets: Brain Vasculature (128x128x128): 3.2x speedup. CT Head-Face (256x256x113): 2.9x speedup. CT Head-Skull (256x256x113): 4.9x speedup. MR Brain (256x256x109): 4.2x speedup. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant speedup with comparable image quality to brute-force ray-casting. Effective for datasets with opaque surfaces and large empty octants. Limitations: Performance degrades with semi-transparent data and scattered non-transparent voxels. Noise in the data can negatively impact performance. When to Use: Use for volume rendering where significant empty space exists and early ray termination is effective. Suitable for medical imaging datasets (CT, MRI) with opaque structures. When Not to Use: Avoid for datasets with high noise levels unless pre-filtered. Less effective for highly semi-transparent datasets with scattered features. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Shear-Warp Volume Rendering Algorithms Using Linear Level Octree for PC-Based Medical Simulation". History and Development: The technique was developed to accelerate volume rendering on PC-based systems for medical simulation. The cited implementation notes that the shear-warp algorithm was under implementation at the time of publication. Usage: Primarily used in medical imaging for rendering CT, MRI, and rotational angiography datasets. Shear-Warp Volume Rendering Algorithms Using Linear Level Octree for PC-Based Medical Simulation, https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-45787-976, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Empty Space Skipping via Acceleration Structures
body: Empty space skipping via acceleration structures accelerates volume rendering by identifying and bypassing transparent or empty regions of the volume data before expensive sampling and compositing occur. It sets itself apart from SparseLeap by typically using scalar min/max values or occupancy flags rather than rasterized segment lists, and from Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree for Empty-Space Skipping by employing fixed-grid brick structures or specific tree traversals rather than generic bounding box hierarchies. The core mechanism shared by all children is the reduction of work units (samples, voxels, or pixels) processed per frame while maintaining acceptable visual fidelity. This is achieved through three primary strategies: 1. Culling/Skipping: Identifying regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image (e.g., empty space, occluded voxels) and bypassing their evaluation. 2. Termination: Halting the integration loop when the accumulated contribution becomes negligible (e.g., high opacity, low transmittance). 3. Adaptation: Varying the computational effort based on local scene complexity or global performance budgets. Mathematically, these methods modify the standard front-to-back compositing loop: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) by introducing conditions that break the loop early, skip iterations, or reduce the number of C{sample} queries. SparseLeap is a hybrid object-order (rasterization) and image-order (ray-casting) method for efficient empty space skipping in large, sparse volumes with fine structures. It decouples empty space skipping data structures from the underlying volume representation, avoiding the space fragmentation and hierarchy traversal overhead typical of standard octree-based approaches. By rasterizing view-independent occupancy geometry into per-pixel linked lists of ray segments, it moves the major cost of empty space skipping from the ray-casting shader to GPU hardware rasterization. Choose when rendering highly sparse volumes where traditional hierarchical traversal overhead dominates. This method accelerates traditional front-to-back ray casting for large-scale volumetric data (specifically aerosols like smoke, fog, and dust) by combining a Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree (BVH) for empty-space culling, early termination of the compositing loop, and adaptive sampling with grouped linear interpolation. It addresses the low efficiency and high resource consumption of standard ray casting when processing large scalar fields. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on octrees or sparse grids, this approach uses a BVH to avoid recording numerous empty nodes, thereby reducing computational complexity and allowing for dynamic updates when the dataset changes. Choose when rendering large-scale dynamic aerosols where BVH construction overhead is amortized over many frames. SparseLeap is a volume rendering technique that separates meta-data for empty space skipping from the volume data itself, using a ray-guided framework where ray segments are processed in a list. It extends standard ray-casting by adding an outer loop over ray segments and handling 'occupancy misses' to delay the determination of whether a brick is empty or non-empty until it is actually needed. Unlike octree-based skipping which incurs high depth complexity due to fragmented space subdivision, SparseLeap limits depth complexity significantly by substituting homogeneous sub-trees in the occupancy histogram tree on-the-fly. Choose when memory bandwidth is the bottleneck and lazy evaluation of occupancy can be leveraged. Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling refers to a family of acceleration techniques in volume rendering that reduce computational load by identifying and excluding primitives, voxels, or ray segments that do not contribute to the final image. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree for Empty-Space Skipping by encompassing a broader range of strategies, including geometric bounding volumes, visibility masks, and parallel segment lists, rather than relying solely on hierarchical tree traversal. It differs from Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control by focusing on pre-computed or geometrically derived exclusion zones rather than just dynamic ray state termination. Choose when a flexible, geometry-agnostic culling strategy is needed across diverse rendering pipelines. This method accelerates direct volume rendering by using a hierarchical min/max acceleration structure to skip transparent regions of the volume data. It reduces the number of samples taken per ray by jumping over blocks that contain no visible data, distinct from sibling methods that may use sparse voxel grids or hierarchical bounding box trees. Choose when working with uniform or regularly structured volumes where a fixed-grid min/max acceleration structure can be efficiently pre-computed and traversed. This method addresses the computational constraints of interactive volume rendering on mobile devices by combining multiresolution data structures with acceleration techniques. It solves the trade-off between frame rate and visual fidelity by using a lower-resolution dataset for exploration and progressively refining high-resolution details in regions of interest. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly targeting mobile hardware limitations and integrating Empty Space Skipping (ESS) and Early Ray Termination (ERT) within a progressive refinement framework. Choose when rendering on mobile GPUs with strict memory and compute budgets. A method to skip empty space using a hierarchical formulation to reduce computational impact, and a quadratic term on visibility to mitigate smoke-like artifacts in real scenes. For each hierarchical level above the first, the voxel grid of the previous level is stored; if the density value for a voxel in that grid is smaller than a threshold \lambdav = 1.0, the voxel is skipped and treated as empty. An auxiliary loss Ls = \lambdas (-4(T - 0.5)^2 + 1) is applied, where T is the total visibility for each ray and \lambdas = 0.1, to mitigate smoke-like artifacts and keep real scenes sparse. The concept of empty space skipping is fundamental to efficient volume rendering, particularly for large-scale datasets where most of the volume is transparent or empty. The auxiliary terms for smoke mitigation were introduced in the context of view-dependent radiance fields to address shape-radiance ambiguity. Addressing the Shape-Radiance Ambiguity in View-Dependent Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2203.01553, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: SparseLeap
head: Empty Space Skipping via Rasterized Ray Segment Lists, SparseLeap-an effective empty space skipping technique
body: SparseLeap is a hybrid object-order (rasterization) and image-order (ray-casting) method for efficient empty space skipping in large, sparse volumes with fine structures. It decouples empty space skipping data structures from the underlying volume representation, avoiding the space fragmentation and hierarchy traversal overhead typical of standard octree-based approaches. By rasterizing view-independent occupancy geometry into per-pixel linked lists of ray segments, it moves the major cost of empty space skipping from the ray-casting shader to GPU hardware rasterization. SparseLeap operates in four main stages: building an occupancy histogram tree, generating occupancy geometry, rasterizing ray segment lists, and performing ray-casting with linear list traversal. Inputs: Volume data (grid, octree, etc.) and segmentation labels. Current transfer function and set of active (enabled) objects. Camera view parameters (position, orientation). Outputs: Rendered image with empty space skipped. Updated occupancy histogram tree (if grown or pruned). Occupancy Histogram Tree Node (CPU): Child pointers (standard tree structure). Histogram: Three integer counts representing the number of leaf nodes in the sub-tree for each occupancy class: countempty, countnonempty, countunknown. Leaf nodes may store metadata (min/max scalar value, contained objects) for culling. Occupancy Geometry (GPU): A set of nested bounding boxes. Each box has an associated occupancy class (empty, non-empty, unknown). Boxes are emitted only when the occupancy class changes during a top-down tree traversal. Ray Segment List Buffer (GPU): Two arrays per pixel resolution: 1. Linked List Elements: Array of size screenwidth screenheight maxdepthcomplexity. Each element is 12 bytes. Layout: start (float, ray parameter), end (float, ray parameter), class (uint8, occupancy class) [G: inferred from 12-byte size and segment definition]. 2. Linked List Heads: Array of size screenwidth screenheight. Each head is 16 bytes. Layout: headindex (int32, index into elements array), count (uint32, number of segments) [G: inferred from 16-byte size and linked list header definition]. 1. Build/Update Occupancy Histogram Tree: Traverse the tree recursively in depth-first order starting at the root. name: Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree for Empty-Space Skipping
head: Accelerated Ray Casting with BVH and Early Termination, Large-Scale Aerosols Visualization via Accelerated Ray Casting, Large-scale Aerosols Visualization Method, Ray Casting Acceleration Algorithm
body: This method accelerates traditional front-to-back ray casting for large-scale volumetric data (specifically aerosols like smoke, fog, and dust) by combining a Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree (BVH) for empty-space culling, early termination of the compositing loop, and adaptive sampling with grouped linear interpolation. It addresses the low efficiency and high resource consumption of standard ray casting when processing large scalar fields. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on octrees or sparse grids, this approach uses a BVH to avoid recording numerous empty nodes, thereby reducing computational complexity and allowing for dynamic updates when the dataset changes. Input: A 3D scalar field representing volume data (e.g., density/opacity values for aerosols); camera parameters (viewpoint, direction, field of view); rendering parameters (early termination threshold, sampling intervals). Output: A 2D image where each pixel color is computed via front-to-back compositing, skipping empty regions and terminating rays that are sufficiently opaque. An AABB is defined by two 3D vectors: min and max, representing the minimum and maximum coordinates along the x, y, and z axes. The six faces are parallel to the xy, xz, and yz planes. The BVH is a binary tree used to store the shape of bounding boxes. Root Node: Represents the largest bounding box encompassing the entire volume data. Internal Nodes: Each internal node has exactly two child nodes, representing two sub-bounding boxes that partition the parent's space. Leaf Nodes: Each leaf node corresponds to a sub-block of the volume data. Node Attributes: Empty: The sub-block contains no valid data (or values below a significance threshold). Non-Empty: The sub-block contains valid data. Unknown: The status is not yet determined or requires further traversal (used during construction). Proportion: For non-leaf nodes, an attribute representing the proportion of child nodes that are non-empty, used to assign the node's primary attribute. 1. Subdivision: The volume data is subdivided into blocks. Each leaf node corresponds to one such block. 2. Boundary Expansion: To avoid interpolation errors at block boundaries (where interpolated values might exceed the original block's min/max), each sub-data block is expanded by one voxel in all directions during the construction phase. 3. Min/Max Storage: The minimum and maximum values of each sub-data block are counted and stored in the bounding box structure to facilitate 3D texture generation and culling decisions. 4. Octree Pre-processing: The data is recursively divided into eight parts to form an octree. Leaf nodes of this octree are marked as Empty, Non-Empty, or Unknown. Non-leaf nodes are assigned the attribute of their children that has the highest proportion. 5. BVH Generation: A breadth-first search is performed on the octree. Bounding boxes are constructed for volume data blocks whose attributes differ from their parent nodes. These boxes form the BVH. 1. Divide the volume data into initial blocks. 2. For each block, expand the data by one voxel to handle boundary interpolation safety. 3. Compute the minimum and maximum scalar values for each expanded block. 4. Build an underlying octree by recursively dividing blocks into eight children. 5. Label octree leaves as Empty, Non-Empty, or Unknown based on data presence. 6. For each octree internal node, calculate the proportion of Non-Empty children. Assign the node's attribute to the majority label (e.g., if >50% children are Non-Empty, label the parent Non-Empty). 7. Traverse the octree (BFS). Identify blocks where the attribute differs from the parent. 8. Construct AABBs for these differing blocks. 9. Organize these AABBs into a binary BVH structure, where internal nodes represent the union of their children's AABBs, and leaves represent the specific data blocks. For each pixel, cast a ray from the camera through the pixel into the volume. 1. Ray-BVH Intersection: Determine the entry and exit points of the ray into the BVH. 2. Traversal: Traverse the BVH from the root. If the ray does not intersect a node's AABB, skip the entire subtree. If the ray intersects a leaf node's AABB: Check the leaf's attribute. If Empty, skip sampling within this block. If Non-Empty, proceed to sample. 3. Merging and Deletion: As the ray passes through multiple bounding boxes, merge overlapping valid ranges and delete empty ranges to determine the final valid sampling intervals. Standard ray casting uses a fixed sampling interval. This method adapts the interval and interpolation based on the ray's position and data validity. 1. Adaptive Interval: Initialize a base sampling interval \Delta. As the ray traverses the volume: If an invalid (empty) sampling point is encountered, increase the sampling interval (reduce resampling frequency). If a valid (non-empty) sampling point is encountered, restore the interval to the base value. 2. Grouped Linear Interpolation: Divide all resampling points on the ray into three levels based on their distance from the viewpoint: Level 1: Closest to the viewpoint. Level 2: Intermediate distance. Level 3: Farthest from the viewpoint. Apply different linear interpolation complexities for each level. The amount of interpolation calculation decreases from Level 1 to Level 3. This reduces computational load without significantly reducing image authenticity. During the front-to-back compositing loop, check the cumulative opacity \alpha{acc} after each sample. 1. Condition: If \alpha{acc} > T{term}, where T{term} is the early termination threshold, terminate the ray calculation. 2. Rationale: As \alpha{acc} approaches 1, the pixel value becomes saturated, and further sampling has minimal effect on the final color. 3. Threshold: The specific numerical value for T{term} is not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. TTERM = 0.95 # Early termination threshold BASEINTERVAL = 0.5 # Initial sampling step size LEVEL1MAX = 10.0 # Distance threshold for Level 1 LEVEL2MAX = 20.0 # Distance threshold for Level 2 INVALIDTHRESHOLD = 0.0 # Scalar value below which a sample is considered empty BACKGROUNDCOLOR = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Default background def rayaabbintersection(rayorigin, raydir, aabbmin, aabbmax): """Returns (tmin, tmax) of ray intersection with AABB, or None.""" tmin = float('-inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] == 0: if rayorigin[i] < aabbmin[i] or rayorigin[i] > aabbmax[i]: return None else: t1 = (aabbmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] t2 = (aabbmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 if t1 > tmin: tmin = t1 if t2 < tmax: tmax = t2 if tmin > tmax: return None if tmax < 0: return None return (tmin if tmin > 0 else 0, tmax) def mergeranges(ranges): """Merges overlapping intervals.""" if not ranges: return [] ranges.sort(key=lambda r: r[0]) merged = [ranges[0]] for start, end in ranges[1:]: if start <= merged[-1][1]: merged[-1] = (merged[-1][0], max(merged[-1][1], end)) else: merged.append((start, end)) return merged def getvalidrangesbvh(rayorigin, raydir, bvhroot): """Traverses BVH to find valid sampling intervals.""" validranges = [] stack = [bvhroot] while stack: node = stack.pop() tmin, tmax = rayaabbintersection(rayorigin, raydir, node.aabbmin, node.aabbmax) if tmin is None: continue if node.isleaf: if node.attribute == "nonempty": validranges.append((tmin, tmax)) else: stack.append(node.right) stack.append(node.left) return mergeranges(validranges) def getinterpolationlevel(distance): """Divides resampling points into 3 levels based on distance from viewpoint.""" if distance < LEVEL1MAX: return 1 elif distance < LEVEL2MAX: return 2 else: return 3 def samplevolume(pos): """Returns raw scalar value at pos. Returns INVALIDTHRESHOLD if out of bounds or empty.""" # Implementation depends on specific volume storage; returns scalar pass def transferfunction(val): """Maps scalar value to opacity [0,1]. Returns 0 for empty/invalid values.""" # Standard transfer function implementation pass def illuminationmodel(val, pos, raydir): """Computes color contribution for a sample.""" # Simplified illumination model return [val 0.8, val 0.8, val 0.8] def castray(rayorigin, raydir, bvhroot): """Casts a single ray, using BVH for skipping and early termination.""" validranges = getvalidrangesbvh(rayorigin, raydir, bvhroot) if not validranges: return BACKGROUNDCOLOR alphaacc = 0.0 coloracc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] stepsize = BASEINTERVAL for startt, endt in validranges: t = startt while t < endt: samplepos = [rayorigin[i] + raydir[i] t for i in range(3)] sample = samplevolume(samplepos) alphasample = transferfunction(sample) colorsample = illuminationmodel(sample, samplepos, raydir) weight = alphasample (1.0 - alphaacc) coloracc = [coloracc[i] + colorsample[i] weight for i in range(3)] alphaacc += weight if alphaacc > TTERM: break # Adaptive sampling: increase step on invalid points, restore on valid if sample <= INVALIDTHRESHOLD: stepsize = 2.0 else: stepsize = BASEINTERVAL distance = sum((samplepos[i] - rayorigin[i])2 for i in range(3))0.5 level = getinterpolationlevel(distance) # Interpolation complexity handled internally by samplevolume(level) t += stepsize if alphaacc > TTERM: break return coloracc Early Termination Threshold (T{term}): A value for cumulative opacity \alpha{acc} above which the ray calculation is terminated. The sources state "a threshold can be set" but do not specify a numerical value. Sampling Interval: Base interval for resampling. Increased when invalid points are encountered, restored when valid points are found. Boundary Interpolation Errors: Interpolating values at the edges of sub-data blocks can result in values greater than the maximum or smaller than the minimum of the original block. This is mitigated by expanding each sub-data block by one voxel during BVH construction. Empty Node Overhead: Unlike octrees, the BVH construction avoids recording many empty nodes, which reduces computational complexity. However, if the BVH is not constructed efficiently, traversal overhead may negate benefits. Dynamic Data: The BVH can be dynamically updated if the dataset changes frequently, unlike some static structures. Construction: The method involves an octree pre-processing step and BVH construction. The complexity depends on the volume size and the subdivision strategy. The sources note that compared to octree-based methods, this BVH method avoids recording many empty nodes, which increases computational complexity in those alternative methods. Rendering: The time complexity per ray is reduced by skipping empty spaces and early termination. The adaptive sampling and grouped interpolation further reduce the cost of interpolation calculations. Hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 5600H with Radeon Graphics 3.30 GHz, Windows 10 64-bit, 16GB memory. Software: Visual Studio 2019, Unity3D, C#, HLSL. Results: The method reduces unnecessary space debris, lowering hardware load and improving rendering speed, meeting real-time rendering requirements for large-scale aerosols. It significantly shortens total interpolation calculation time compared to traditional algorithms. Strengths: Avoids recording many empty nodes compared to octree-based methods. Not heavily dependent on the spatial position of non-empty voxels. Can be dynamically updated if the dataset changes frequently. Reduces hardware load and improves rendering speed for large-scale aerosols. Limitations: The specific numerical values for parameters (like T{term} and interpolation level ranges) are not provided, requiring empirical tuning. The method is tailored for large-scale aerosols; performance on other types of volumetric data is not explicitly detailed. The method was proposed in the paper "Large-scale Aerosols Visualization Based on the Accelerated Ray Casting Algorithm". It was developed to address the disadvantages of traditional ray casting algorithms, such as low efficiency, slow speed, and large resource consumption when rendering aerosol data (smoke, fog, dust) in 3D scenes. The method combines several optimization techniques: 1. BVH for Empty-Space Skipping: Uses a hierarchical bounding box tree to cull empty voxels. 2. Early Termination: Stops compositing when cumulative opacity exceeds a threshold. 3. Adaptive Sampling: Adjusts sampling intervals based on data validity. 4. Grouped Linear Interpolation: Reduces interpolation cost by varying complexity based on distance from the viewpoint. The method is used for visualizing large-scale aerosols, including smoke, fog, and dust, in 3D scenes. It is implemented using C# and HLSL in Unity3D. name: SparseLeap Ray-Casting with Occupancy Misses
head: Ray-guided volume rendering with empty space skipping [S1, unofficial]
body: SparseLeap is a volume rendering technique that separates meta-data for empty space skipping from volume data, using a ray-guided framework where ray segments are processed in a list. It extends standard ray-casting by adding an outer loop over ray segments and handling 'occupancy misses' to delay the determination of whether a brick is empty or non-empty until it is actually needed. Unlike octree-based skipping which incurs high depth complexity due to fragmented space subdivision, SparseLeap limits depth complexity significantly by substituting homogeneous sub-trees in the occupancy histogram tree on-the-fly. See SparseLeap, Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree for Empty-Space Skipping, Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling, Empty-space skipping via Acceleration Structure, and Progressive Ray Casting for Volumetric Models on Mobile Devices for related methods. SparseLeap operates within a ray-guided volume rendering framework that relies on lazy evaluation. The method augments the standard front-to-back compositing loop with an outer loop that iterates over a list of ray segments. These segments are derived from an occupancy histogram tree, which tracks the empty/non-empty status of volume bricks. Inputs: Ray segment list: A list of segments along each view ray, each tagged with an occupancy class (empty, nonempty, or unknown). Volume data: Stored in bricks, managed by an out-of-core memory system. Occupancy Histogram Tree: A hierarchical structure representing the occupancy status of volume bricks. Outputs: Rendered image pixel colors. Updated occupancy histogram tree (with homogeneous sub-trees substituted and unused nodes retired). Ray Segment Each entry in the ray segment list represents a contiguous portion of a ray. start: Ray parameter t{start} (float). end: Ray parameter t{end} (float). occupancyclass: Enum or integer code. 0: Empty, 1: Nonempty, 2: Unknown. brickid: Identifier for the underlying volume brick. Occupancy Histogram Tree Node occupancyclass: The dominant occupancy class of the sub-tree. ishomogeneous: Boolean flag indicating if all children share the same occupancy class. children: References to child nodes (if not a leaf). usagecount: Integer for LRU eviction tracking. 1. Initialization: For each pixel, cast a view ray. Generate an initial ray segment list covering the ray's path through the volume. Initially, segments may be marked as unknown if their occupancy is not yet determined. 2. Outer Loop (Segment Iteration): Iterate through the ray segment list linearly. Process consecutive overlapping pairs of ray events to define segments. 3. Segment Classification: If occupancyclass is empty: Skip the segment. Advance the ray position to t{end} of the current segment. Continue to the next segment. If occupancyclass is nonempty: Proceed to sampling. If occupancyclass is unknown: Generate an occupancy miss. 4. Occupancy Miss Resolution: When an occupancy miss occurs, trigger culling to determine the actual occupancy class of the underlying volume brick. If the brick is determined to be empty: Update the segment's class to empty and skip. If the brick is determined to be nonempty: Update the segment's class to nonempty and proceed to sampling. Delayed Update: Bricks never intersected by view rays (occluded or outside frustum) do not have their occupancy class determined, saving computation and memory bandwidth. 5. Sampling: If the segment is nonempty, perform standard ray-casting sampling within the segment bounds. Data Cache Miss Handling: If the volume data for the current brick is not in cache, generate a data cache miss to load it. If the class is unknown, do not generate a data cache miss immediately. Resolve the occupancy miss first. Only load data if the resolution confirms the brick is nonempty. If the class is empty or unknown (and resolved as empty), no data cache miss is generated. 6. Homogeneous Sub-tree Substitution: After occupancy updates, check the occupancy histogram tree for sub-trees where all nodes have the same occupancy class. Substitute these homogeneous sub-trees with a single node of that class. This is determined efficiently using occupancy histograms. 7. Memory Management (LRU): The ray-caster reports usage of volume bricks to the out-of-core memory management system. Unused nodes in the occupancy histogram tree are retired regularly using a Least-Recently Used (LRU) scheme based on this usage information. This scales the tree size to the current working set rather than the whole volume. The method modifies the standard front-to-back compositing loop: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) where C{acc} is the accumulated color, \alpha{acc} is the accumulated opacity, C{sample} is the sampled color, and \alpha{sample} is the sampled opacity. The outer loop skips iterations or reduces C{sample} queries based on occupancy classes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EMPTY = 0 NONEMPTY = 1 UNKNOWN = 2 EPSILON = 1e-4 def sparseleapraycast(ray, segmentlist, occupancytree, volumecache): color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 for segment in segmentlist: tstart = segment.start tend = segment.end occclass = segment.occupancyclass if occclass == EMPTY: continue elif occclass == UNKNOWN: actualclass = resolveoccupancymiss(segment.brickid, occupancytree) if actualclass == EMPTY: continue elif actualclass == NONEMPTY: occclass = NONEMPTY else: continue if occclass == NONEMPTY: if not volumecache.contains(segment.brickid): volumecache.load(segment.brickid) samplecolor, samplealpha = integratesegment(ray, tstart, tend, volumecache, segment.brickid) alphacontribution = samplealpha transmittance color[0] += samplecolor[0] alphacontribution color[1] += samplecolor[1] alphacontribution color[2] += samplecolor[2] alphacontribution color[3] += samplealpha alphacontribution transmittance = (1.0 - samplealpha) if transmittance < EPSILON: break return color def resolveoccupancymiss(brickid, occupancytree): if occupancytree.isclassified(brickid): return occupancytree.getclass(brickid) isempty = computeoccupancy(brickid) newclass = EMPTY if isempty else NONEMPTY occupancytree.setclass(brickid, newclass) occupancytree.substitutehomogeneoussubtrees(brickid) return newclass def integratesegment(ray, tstart, tend, volumecache, brickid): samplecolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] samplealpha = 0.0 stepsize = 0.01 t = tstart while t < tend: voxel = volumecache.sample(ray, t, brickid) c, a = voxel.color, voxel.alpha samplecolor[0] += c[0] a (1.0 - samplealpha) samplecolor[1] += c[1] a (1.0 - samplealpha) samplecolor[2] += c[2] a (1.0 - samplealpha) samplealpha += a (1.0 - samplealpha) t += stepsize return samplecolor, samplealpha def computeoccupancy(brickid): return querycullingmetadata(brickid) Empty Space Skipping Granularity: Can be as small as 4^3 blocks for terabyte-sized volumes. This allows finer granularity than the brick size used for memory management (e.g., 32^3 blocks). Block Sizes for Culling: Evaluated sizes include 4^3, 8^3, 16^3, and 32^3 blocks. Order-Dependent Rasterization: The rasterization of occupancy geometry into ray segment lists must process fragments in the same order as they are submitted to OpenGL. This is handled using the ARBfragmentshaderinterlock capability. Short Empty Segments: Very short empty ray segments that cannot be merged into a longer empty segment because they precede a non-empty segment are detected and removed to reduce depth complexity. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of samples processed by skipping empty space. The complexity depends on the depth complexity of the ray segment list. Memory Complexity: The occupancy histogram tree scales with the current output size (working set) rather than the whole volume, thanks to LRU retirement of unused nodes. Measured Performance: On the SEM Mouse Cortex dataset, SparseLeap had an average of 3.84 segments per ray (min 1, max 31), while octree traversal had an average of 13.44 intersected nodes (min 4, max 45). Scaling: The approach scales better to finely detailed, sparse data. Strengths: Limits depth complexity significantly compared to octree-based skipping. Scales better to finely detailed, sparse data. Output-sensitive culling avoids processing occluded regions. Limitations: Requires implementation of fragment shader interlock for correct rasterization order. Culling computation is deferred, which may cause latency spikes if many misses occur simultaneously. When to Use: Large-scale, sparse volume datasets where empty space skipping is critical for performance. When Not to Use: Dense volumes where empty space skipping provides little benefit, or hardware lacking ARBfragmentshaderinterlock. SparseLeap was introduced in the paper "SparseLeap: Efficient Empty Space Skipping for Large-Scale Volume Rendering". It is implemented using OpenGL with GLSL shaders and integrated with a large-scale out-of-core raycasting system. Evaluation was performed on an NVIDIA GeForce Titan X (Pascal) GPU with 12 GB RAM. name: Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling
body: Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling is a family of acceleration techniques in volume rendering that reduces computational load by identifying and bypassing regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image. It encompasses strategies ranging from geometric bounding volumes and visibility masks to parallel segment lists, distinguishing itself from Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control by focusing on pre-computed or geometrically derived exclusion zones rather than dynamic ray state termination. Builds on Empty Space Skipping via Acceleration Structures. Parallel Ray Casting with Segment Lists is a distributed-memory and shared-memory parallel volume rendering algorithm that accelerates ray casting by precomputing lists of occupied volume segments to skip empty space. It distributes image rows across MPI ranks and OpenMP threads, calculating sampling points based on a derived step length. It sets itself apart from siblings like SparseLeap by using explicit segment lists derived from volume geometry rather than sparse voxel octree traversal or occupancy misses, and from Visibility Culling by operating at the ray-segment level rather than tile or view-frustum level. Choose it when rendering large, block-structured volumes on distributed systems. Parallel Ray Casting with Segment Lists. Visibility Culling is a family of acceleration techniques in volume rendering that reduces computational load by identifying and excluding primitives, voxels, or ray segments that do not contribute to the final image. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Bounding Volume Empty-Space Culling by focusing on optical or geometric visibility relative to the camera, rather than purely on geometric emptiness, and from Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control by often operating on pre-computed or screen-space visibility masks rather than just dynamic ray state. Choose it when fragment-level occlusion or screen-space coverage can be leveraged. Visibility Culling. Bounding Volume Empty-Space Culling restricts volume reconstruction computation to the "effective" reconstruction area by calculating an initial bounding volume and slicing it according to the viewing direction, using these slices as a depth buffer to guide reconstruction. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree for Empty-Space Skipping by using a simple geometric approximation (truncated shapes) rather than a hierarchical tree structure, and from Visibility Culling by focusing on the validity of the reconstruction domain itself rather than fragment-level occlusion. Choose it for parallel beam reconstruction pipelines where a geometric bounding volume can serve as a depth buffer. Bounding Volume Empty-Space Culling. A rendering optimization that infers ray-BBox intersection to sample query points only within the scene bounding box, applicable only to bounded scenes. It fuses approximately ten point-wise operations for the forward and backward pass of the density-to-alpha function conversion. In the volume rendering accumulation, it halts tracking a ray once the accumulated transmittance falls below 10^{-3}. Acceleration methods that localize the surface interface and concentrate samples only in relevant regions, effectively skipping empty space, because only 10-20% of evaluated samples have non-zero density. It refines the sampling strategy to focus solely on the localized surface. Standard volumetric rendering is inefficient because it samples the entire ray; surface localization reduces the number of required MLP evaluations by skipping empty space. Choose it when rendering neural radiance fields or implicit representations where surface geometry occupies a small fraction of 3D space. Optimization to avoid visiting every volume at every step. Previously, the march visited every volume at every step just to ask cellindex whether it was inside, and almost always was not. The new method builds an active list up front, so a step only visits volumes whose t-range contains it. It differs from the previous approach which visited every volume at every step. The new approach is pure work elimination and produces byte-identical output. The concept of skipping empty space in volume rendering dates back to the early days of ray casting, where the primary goal was to avoid sampling voxels with zero density. Early methods relied on simple bounding boxes or grid-based occupancy flags. The rise of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and implicit representations has renewed interest in these techniques, leading to methods like parsimonious ray sampling and surface localization acceleration that integrate culling directly into the learning and rendering pipeline.
