name: Visibility Culling
body: Visibility Culling is a family of acceleration techniques in volume rendering that reduces computational load by identifying and bypassing data or primitives that do not contribute to the final image. It sets itself apart from its siblings by encompassing a broad range of strategies—from geometric frustum tests to optical termination and screen-space feedback—unlike Bounding Volume Empty-Space Culling which focuses strictly on geometric emptiness, or Parallel Ray Casting with Segment Lists which focuses on parallelization efficiency. The core mechanism shared by all children is the reduction of work units (samples, voxels, or pixels) processed per frame while maintaining acceptable visual fidelity. This is achieved through three primary strategies: 1. Culling/Skipping: Identifying regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image (e.g., empty space, occluded voxels) and bypassing their evaluation. 2. Termination: Halting the integration loop when the accumulated contribution becomes negligible (e.g., high opacity, low transmittance). 3. Adaptation: Varying computational effort based on local coverage (e.g., skipping full screen regions) or global completion (e.g., terminating when all pixels are covered). Mathematically, these methods modify the standard front-to-back compositing loop: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) by introducing conditions that break the loop early, skip iterations, or reduce the number of C{sample} queries. Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control are acceleration techniques that reduce the computational cost of volume rendering by halting the ray-marching integration loop when the remaining contribution to the pixel is deemed negligible. Unlike Occlusion Clipping with Orthogonal Opacity Map which culls based on pre-computed opacity maps, or Empty-space skipping which skips geometrically empty regions, these methods operate on the accumulated state of the ray during traversal. They set themselves apart from Bounding Volume Culling by relying on optical properties (opacity/transmittance) rather than geometric bounds, and from Adaptive Multi-Step Empty Voxel Skipping by focusing on the termination of the integration path rather than the step size. Probabilistic Culling is a rendering optimization that intentionally allows false-negatives in intersection tests to reduce duplicated fragments and rendering time, particularly in virtual reality (VR) and high-resolution contexts. It sets itself apart from conservative culling methods by trading strict geometric accuracy for performance, relying on the fact that resulting visual artifacts are imperceptible. Visibility Feedback with Screen Space Subdivision is an out-of-core volume rendering optimization that uses visibility information gathered during the current frame to prevent the loading and refinement of occluded data in subsequent frames. Unlike standard early ray termination, which only skips computation after data has already been loaded into the GPU working set, this method feeds visibility results back to the loader to reduce GPU memory usage and bandwidth. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by combining occlusion queries with a screen-space subdivision strategy to interleave query processing with rasterization, thereby hiding the latency inherent in asynchronous occlusion query results. Adaptive Multi-Step Empty Voxel Skipping is an acceleration technique for direct volume rendering that combines space leaping (empty voxel skipping) with adaptive variable step-size sampling. It solves the problem of redundant computation in large datasets containing significant empty space, such as medical CT scans, by bypassing empty regions entirely and adjusting sampling density based on local voxel occupancy. Unlike traditional equidistant ray casting, this method reduces computational overhead without altering the input data structure. A preprocessing technique that decomposes the domain of viewing directions into 24 regions on a directional cube to extract a lower number of potentially visible voxels compared to the standard 6-region decomposition, improving extraction rate and rendering speed. Frustum culling is a visibility culling technique that reduces rendering load by filtering out faces, chunks, or primitives that lie outside the camera's viewing frustum. It solves the problem of unnecessary computation for geometry that does not contribute to the final image by performing a conservative intersection test between bounding volumes and the six planes defining the view frustum. It operates on spatial extent relative to the camera orientation and projection, distinguishing it from depth-based occlusion or transmittance-termination methods. This method prevents infinite rendering loops in interactive volume visualization by detecting when the rendering pipeline exceeds the frame budget and forcing a quality reduction on the subsequent frame. It acts as a safety mechanism distinct from standard early termination, which stops individual rays based on opacity Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control. The Visible Zone Algorithm is a conservative visibility computation method that determines which primitives are potentially visible from a set of viewpoints by projecting them into screen space and retaining only those within a specified depth thickness. It sets itself apart from approximate visibility methods by guaranteeing correct visibility with less than one pixel of screen-space deviation. The Occlusion-Aware Visibility Filter replaces the standard view-frustum test in 3D Gaussian Splatting densification with a rendering-based signal that restricts statistical updates to Gaussians that actually contribute to the final image. Unlike sibling methods that rely on binary flags or pixel counts, this method uses the sum of blending weights to determine visibility, ensuring that occluded Gaussians do not accumulate densification statistics. Definition: An optimization dividing image space into equal-sized squares of n \times n pixels to reduce overhead from per-pixel visibility testing. If a screen region is full, rasterization skips to the next boundary. Performance: Screen regions save another 3 percent of overall rendering time on average. Definition: A GPU-based visibility test using a 2^D Boolean lookup table to cull cells that do not intersect the transfer function's opacity range, reducing load on the rendering stage. Steps: Geometry shader computes the minimum and maximum of the 8 cell corner values. These two values are used as table lookup indices to fetch a visibility value. If the cell is deemed visible, the geometry shader instantiates its 6 faces. Parameters: Visibility Lookup Table: A 2^D table where D is the number of scalar value bins. For each pair of values s1 and s2, the table holds 1 if there exists at least an opacity which is non-zero for scalar values in [s1, s2], otherwise 0. Performance: On a PC with two Xeon E5345 processors, 4GB memory, GeForce 8800 GTX (768MB), using the 'meteorite' dataset (2,377,878 cells), removing the look-up table drops performance to <1 fps (specifically 0.76 fps). Adding the look-up table increases framerate to ~3.48 fps. Adding the hybrid CPU-GPU mesh traversal mechanism to the look-up table optimization increases the framerate to 3.62 fps. Visibility culling in volume rendering has evolved from simple geometric checks to complex, view-dependent, and feedback-driven mechanisms. Early implementations focused on reducing overhead in ray casting by dividing image space into screen regions to skip full areas. As rendering moved to GPU-based pipelines, techniques like scalar range lookup tables were introduced to cull cells based on transfer function opacity ranges, significantly improving performance for AMR datasets. The family also includes safety mechanisms like Interactive Render Quality Estimation & Cancellation to prevent infinite loops in real-time applications, and view-dependent preprocessing such as 24-Region View-Dependent Visibility Preprocessing and feedback loops like Visibility Feedback with Screen Space Subdivision to manage out-of-core data loading. body: Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control are acceleration techniques that reduce the computational cost of volume rendering by halting the ray-marching integration loop when the remaining contribution to the pixel is deemed negligible. Unlike Occlusion Clipping with Orthogonal Opacity Map which culls based on pre-computed opacity maps, or Empty-space skipping which skips geometrically empty regions, these methods operate on the accumulated state of the ray during traversal. They set themselves apart from Bounding Volume Culling by relying on optical properties (opacity/transmittance) rather than geometric bounds, and from Adaptive Multi-Step Empty Voxel Skipping by focusing on the termination of the integration path rather than the step size. The core mechanism shared by all methods in this family is the reduction of work units (samples, voxels, or pixels) processed per frame while maintaining acceptable visual fidelity. This is achieved through three primary strategies: 1. Culling/Skipping: Identifying regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image (e.g., empty space, occluded voxels) and bypassing their evaluation. 2. Termination: Halting the integration loop when the accumulated contribution becomes negligible (e.g., high opacity, low transmittance). 3. Adaptation: Varying the computational effort based on local scene complexity or global performance budgets. Mathematically, these methods modify the standard front-to-back compositing loop: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) by introducing conditions that break the loop early, skip iterations, or reduce the number of C{sample} queries. Proactively skips intervals of the ray path before sampling, often using auxiliary data structures like octrees, bounding volumes, or occupancy grids. It sets itself apart from Early Stop by operating on the internal structure of the volume data rather than accumulated opacity. Limits raymarching to a specific geometric boundary, dropping rays that exceed a certain distance from the eye or miss the volume entirely. It differs from this family's core termination logic by using hard geometric constraints to discard rays before or during traversal. A randomized early-out technique that removes the statistical bias introduced by deterministic early termination. It probabilistically terminates rays with low contribution weights while scaling up the weights of surviving paths to maintain an unbiased expectation of the final pixel color. Limits the computation of noise frequencies in procedural volumes by breaking the evaluation loop as soon as the ray position is determined to be outside the bounding volume of the current frequency level. It builds on this family by applying early loop breaks specifically to hierarchical noise evaluation. A GPU-based technique that combines single-pass fragment shader execution with dynamic branching, transmittance-based early termination, and dithered starting positions to hide staircase effects. Skips fragment shader execution for rays that have already accumulated sufficient opacity by performing a depth test before the main volume rendering pass, deferring the termination decision to the rasterizer's depth buffer. Adjusts the near and far bounds of volumetric ray sampling using a learned depth prior (disparity map) to restrict integration to relevant depth ranges, reducing floating artifacts and unnecessary computation. Halts the front-to-back ray integration loop once the accumulated opacity exceeds a predefined threshold. It differs from Russian Roulette by using a deterministic cutoff rather than a probabilistic one, which introduces a systematic bias in exchange for reduced noise and computational cost. Terminates ray integration early once the accumulated color change between consecutive samples falls below a defined threshold, monitoring the rate of change in the accumulated color rather than just opacity saturation. A mechanism that allows a query coordinate to be finalised early (not processed further) when its predicted uncertainty is less than a certain threshold, avoiding unnecessary calculations. During training, sample points can exit at multiple stages. During inferencing, points exit only once at a specific stage. Points found earlier to be reliable immediately exit and are rendered. Which branch is taken depends on clustering results. The concept of early termination in volume rendering has evolved from simple opacity thresholds to sophisticated probabilistic and uncertainty-aware methods. Early implementations relied on deterministic checks against accumulated opacity or transmittance to skip remaining samples. The introduction of Russian Roulette addressed the bias inherent in deterministic cutoffs by providing an unbiased statistical alternative. More recent developments, such as Recursive-NeRF, incorporate uncertainty prediction to dynamically decide when a query point is reliable enough to terminate processing, enabling efficient rendering of complex scenes by clustering uncertain points into sub-networks. name: Empty-space skipping
head: ESS, Early Ray Termination (ERT), Empty Region Skipping, Empty Space Rendering, Empty space culling
body: Empty-space skipping is an acceleration technique for volume rendering that reduces computational cost by identifying and bypassing regions of the volumetric dataset that are transparent or contain no relevant data. It solves the problem of wasted computation when ray marching through empty space, which constitutes a significant portion of the processing time in standard ray casting. Unlike Early Stop which terminates rays based on accumulated opacity, or Russian Roulette which probabilistically terminates rays, empty-space skipping uses auxiliary data structures (such as octrees, bounding volumes, or occupancy grids) to determine the boundaries of empty regions and "jump" over them. It sets itself apart from Bounding Volume Culling by operating on the internal density distribution of the volume rather than just the external geometric bounds, allowing it to skip holes and transparent interiors. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Volume dataset V (scalar field). Transfer function TF mapping scalar values to color/opacity. Empty-space data structure D (e.g., octree, bounding hull, occupancy grid). Outputs: Final pixel color C{final}. Data Structures: The specific layout depends on the variant, but common structures include: 1. Octree/BSP Tree: Nodes store min/max scalar values or boolean occupancy flags for their sub-volume. 2. Bounding Hull: A set of primitives (triangles/quads) enclosing the non-empty region. 3. Occupancy Grid: A 3D texture or array where each voxel indicates if the region is empty (0) or occupied (1). 4. Distance Map: Stores the distance to the nearest occupied voxel for each cell. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Ray: Determine the entry point into the volume or the bounding hull. If a hull is used, compute the intersection of the ray with the hull to find the start parameter t{start}. If no hull is used, start at the near clipping plane or the first non-empty voxel detected by the acceleration structure. 2. Traversal Loop: While the ray is within the volume bounds and has not reached full opacity (if Early Ray Termination is combined): a. Query Empty Space: Check the current ray segment against the data structure D. If using a Tree: Traverse the tree. If a node is marked empty (e.g., max value below opacity threshold, or occupancy flag false), skip the entire subtree. If using a Hull: The ray is already inside the hull; sample until exit. If using an Occupancy Grid/Distance Map: Sample the grid at the current position. If empty, calculate the skip distance \Delta t{skip} based on the distance map value. b. Advance Ray: If empty space is detected, advance the ray parameter t by \Delta t{skip} (or the size of the empty block). If non-empty space is detected, or if the structure does not support skipping (e.g., standard ray casting without acceleration), advance by the standard step size \Delta t. c. Sample Volume: At the new position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, evaluate the volume density \sigma(\mathbf{p}) and color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}) using the transfer function. d. Composite: Update the accumulated color and opacity using front-to-back compositing: \alpha{sample} = 1 - e^{-\sigma(\mathbf{p}) \Delta t} C{acc} = C{acc} + \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}) \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) e. Check Termination: If \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0.98 or 0.99), terminate the ray. 3. Output: Return C{acc} as the final pixel color. Pseudocode (Generic ESS with Distance Map/Grid): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderraywithess(rayorigin, raydir, volumetexture, essstructure, stepsize, volumebounds): # volumebounds: (mincorner, maxcorner) # Compute ray-box intersection to find tnear and tfar tnear = 0.0 tfar = float('inf') for i in range(3): invdir = 1.0 / raydir[i] t1 = (volumebounds.min[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir t2 = (volumebounds.max[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir tnear = max(tnear, min(t1, t2)) tfar = min(tfar, max(t1, t2)) if tnear > tfar or tfar < 0: return vec3(0.0) # Ray misses volume acccolor = vec3(0.0) accalpha = 0.0 t = tnear while t < tfar and accalpha < 0.98: pos = rayorigin + raydir t # Query distance to nearest occupied region from ESS structure disttooccupied = essstructure.querydistance(pos) # If distance is large, we are in empty space. Skip forward. # Use a threshold to avoid floating point noise if disttooccupied > stepsize 0.5: skipdist = min(disttooccupied, tfar - t) t += skipdist continue # Sample volume value = volumetexture.sample(pos) # Standard transfer function: map scalar to color and opacity color = vec3(value, value, value) 0.5 alpha = min(value 0.1, 1.0) # Front-to-back compositing samplealpha = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor += color samplealpha accalpha += samplealpha # Advance by standard step t += stepsize return acccolor Parameters: stepsize: The base sampling distance. Typical values depend on volume resolution and desired quality. alphathreshold: Threshold for early ray termination. Typical value: 10^{-4} for transmittance or 0.98 for accumulated opacity. emptythreshold: The density/opacity value below which a region is considered empty. Typical value: 10^{-2}. skipmultiplier: In simple implementations, the factor by which step size is increased in empty space. Typical value: 6. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Rays: Rays with infinite length, NaN components, or length > \sqrt{3} (in normalized coordinates) should be terminated immediately to prevent performance regressions. Backtracking: When using distance maps, if the distance to the next occupied voxel is 0 (meaning the ray is exactly on a boundary or the map is coarse), the algorithm may need to backtrack or use a smaller step to ensure no data is missed. Transfer Function Dependency: Empty space is often defined by the transfer function (e.g., low density regions). If the TF changes, the acceleration structure may need to be rebuilt or updated. Load Imbalance: In parallel rendering, tiles with less volume coverage may finish much faster than those with dense data, causing load imbalance if work assignment is static. Intermediate Pass Overhead: In some GPU implementations, an intermediate pass is required to check for empty space and update z-values for early-z testing. This pass cannot be discarded even if Early Ray Termination is active, adding overhead. Uses fixed macrocells with boolean occupancy flags. Best for uniform grids; avoids tree traversal overhead. Uses BSP trees for 3D textures. Handles arbitrary slicing planes; requires complex sorting. Hierarchical min/max storage. Best for sparse volumes; allows large skips. Uses a 3D occupancy grid. Simple to implement; good for dynamic scenes. Classifies bricks as skipped, terminated, or sampled. Good for GPU feedback. Uses coarse/fine voxel grids to skip low-density regions. Good for view-dependent models. Rebuilds acceleration structures on GPU for dynamic TF changes. Stores visibility independent of TF. Avoids reconstruction on TF change. Approximates uniform regions instead of skipping. Good for smooth gradients. A raymarch acceleration technique that skips volume cells provably contributing zero opacity by checking if the cell's stored max deviation is below a cutoff derived from live contrast/trim uniforms. It declares a binding (the max pyramid) in the fragment shader and consults it coarse-to-fine (level 1, then level 0) before paying for a full-res sample. When a skip occurs, it lands back on the fixed step grid defined by t{min} + jitter + k \cdot stepLength to ensure bit-identical results. The cutoff is calculated as cutoff = (deadband - 0.05), where deadband is derived from applyContrastWindow; if the cell's max deviation is less than this cutoff, the cell is skipped. A pitfall is that in dense cosmic-web structures (volume-inside pose), the coarse+fine pyramid check rarely proves a cell empty, adding two textureLoad + slab-test pairs per step with no skip payoff, causing a net regression (+47% volume, +65% scalar-volume per-layer). Time Complexity: Depends on the data structure. Tree traversal requires multiple look-ups per segment, while grid lookup is O(1). The number of samples is reduced by a factor proportional to the empty space ratio. Memory Complexity: Requires additional storage for the acceleration structure. Occupancy grids add O(N) bits per voxel. Measured Performance: In typical real-world examples with opaque structures and empty regions, Empty-Space Skipping (RC-β) significantly outperforms standard Ray Casting (RC). For example, on a Head dataset, RC-β achieved 23.4 fps compared to 4.8 fps for RC and 14.4 fps for RC with only Early Ray Termination. Other implementations report 2.3x to 5x performance gains. In neural rendering contexts, ESS increased rendering speed from 1345 ms to 133 ms for a single shared MLP model. Strengths: Significant speedup for sparse volumes; reduces memory bandwidth usage by skipping texture fetches in empty regions. Limitations: Overhead of building and traversing the acceleration structure; less effective for dense volumes with little empty space; transfer function changes may require structure updates. When to Use: Sparse volumes, large datasets with significant background/empty space, interactive applications requiring high frame rates. When Not to Use: Dense volumes with minimal empty space, where the overhead of traversal outweighs the savings from skipping. Empty-space skipping originated as a fundamental optimization in volume ray casting to address the high computational cost of evaluating hundreds to thousands of samples per ray. Early methods involved rasterizing bounding geometry to skip empty space before and after the object. Later, hierarchical structures like octrees and BSP trees were introduced to allow skipping of internal empty regions. The technique has been widely adopted in GPU-based volume rendering, with implementations by Klein et al. and Lee and Shin exploiting spatial coherence and frame-to-frame estimates. It remains a core component of modern volume rendering pipelines, including neural radiance fields (NeRFs) where occupancy grids are used to prune empty space during training and inference. name: Ray Marcher with Macrocell Empty Space Skipping

body: Ray Marcher with Macrocell Empty Space Skipping is an acceleration technique that divides a volume into coarse macrocells, precomputes a boolean occupancy flag for each, and skips ray marching within macrocells that contain only zero-density data. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Empty Space Skipping with Orthogonal BSP Tree and Empty Space Skipping with Octree by using a fixed, uniform grid hierarchy rather than a dynamic tree structure, and from Spatial Skipping (Occupancy Grid) by operating on precomputed boolean flags derived from transfer-function-dependent densities rather than simple binary occupancy. Inputs: Volume dataset (voxel grid or tetrahedral mesh). Transfer function (TF) mapping density to opacity/color. Ray origin and direction for each pixel. Macrocell size M (number of voxels/elements per side). Outputs: Rendered image. Boolean occupancy grid for macrocells. Data Structures: 1. Volume Data: The underlying voxel or element data. 2. Macrocell Boolean Grid: A 3D array of booleans (or bits) where each entry corresponds to a macrocell. MacrocellGrid[i][j][k] = true if the macrocell contains at least one non-zero density element (according to the current TF). MacrocellGrid[i][j][k] = false if all elements in the macrocell have zero density. 3. Distance Field (Optional, specific to fiber surfaces): A precomputed distance field used to update macrocell booleans when control polygons change. Preprocessing Steps: 1. Divide the volume domain into a 3D grid of macrocells, each of size M \times M \times M. 2. For each macrocell, determine if it contains any non-zero density elements based on the current transfer function. 3. Set the boolean flag for each macrocell: If all elements in the macrocell have zero density, set flag to false (empty). Otherwise, set flag to true (occupied). 4. (Optional) If using fiber surfaces, maintain a distance field and update macrocell booleans when control polygons are modified. Rendering Steps (Ray Marching): 1. For each pixel, cast a ray. 2. Use a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (3DDDA) to traverse the macrocell grid. 3. For each macrocell visited by the ray: a. Fetch the precomputed boolean value for the current macrocell. b. If the boolean value is false (empty): Skip all ray marching steps within this macrocell. Advance the ray to the next macrocell boundary using 3DDDA logic. c. If the boolean value is true (occupied): Perform standard ray marching within the macrocell, sampling the volume data. Accumulate color and opacity according to the volume rendering integral. 4. Composite the accumulated color and opacity into the final pixel value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchwithmacrocell(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, macrocellgrid, macrocellsize, transferfunction): """ Ray marcher with macrocell empty space skipping. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) ray origin in voxel coordinates. raydirection: (dx, dy, dz) normalized ray direction. volumedata: 3D array of voxel densities. macrocellgrid: 3D array of booleans indicating occupied macrocells. macrocellsize: Integer M, number of voxels per macrocell side. transferfunction: Function mapping density to opacity. Returns: color: (r, g, b) final pixel color. opacity: float final pixel opacity. """ accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 tmin = 0.0 tmax = 1000.0 # Scene bounding limit # 3DDDA initialization for macrocell grid currentmcx = int(rayorigin[0] // macrocellsize) currentmcy = int(rayorigin[1] // macrocellsize) currentmcz = int(rayorigin[2] // macrocellsize) stepx = 1 if raydirection[0] > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if raydirection[1] > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if raydirection[2] > 0 else -1 # Distance to next macrocell boundary in t-space nextx = (currentmcx + (1 if stepx > 0 else 0)) macrocellsize nexty = (currentmcy + (1 if stepy > 0 else 0)) macrocellsize nextz = (currentmcz + (1 if stepz > 0 else 0)) macrocellsize tmaxx = (nextx - rayorigin[0]) / raydirection[0] if raydirection[0] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = (nexty - rayorigin[1]) / raydirection[1] if raydirection[1] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxz = (nextz - rayorigin[2]) / raydirection[2] if raydirection[2] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltax = macrocellsize / abs(raydirection[0]) if raydirection[0] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltay = macrocellsize / abs(raydirection[1]) if raydirection[1] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltaz = macrocellsize / abs(raydirection[2]) if raydirection[2] != 0 else float('inf') while tmin < tmax: # Find closest boundary if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: texit = tmaxx currentmcx += stepx tmaxx += tdeltax else: texit = tmaxz currentmcz += stepz tmaxz += tdeltaz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: texit = tmaxy currentmcy += stepy tmaxy += tdeltay else: texit = tmaxz currentmcz += stepz tmaxz += tdeltaz # Bounds check for macrocell grid if not macrocellgrid[currentmcx][currentmcy][currentmcz]: tmin = texit continue # March within occupied macrocell tcurrent = tmin stepsize = 1.0 # Voxel step while tcurrent < texit: voxelpos = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] tcurrent for i in range(3)] voxelcoords = (int(voxelpos[0]), int(voxelpos[1]), int(voxelpos[2])) density = samplevolume(volumedata, voxelcoords) opacity = transferfunction(density) colorcontribution = density opacity # Simplified accumulatedcolor[0] += colorcontribution transmittance accumulatedcolor[1] += colorcontribution transmittance accumulatedcolor[2] += colorcontribution transmittance accumulatedopacity += opacity transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - opacity) tcurrent += stepsize if transmittance < 1e-4: break tmin = texit if transmittance < 1e-4: break return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity def samplevolume(grid, coords): # Clamp to bounds and return density, 0 if out of bounds x, y, z = coords if 0 <= x < grid.shape[0] and 0 <= y < grid.shape[1] and 0 <= z < grid.shape[2]: return grid[x, y, z] return 0.0 Parameters: Voxels per macrocell (M): 23 voxels per macrocell generally give the best rendering performance, but 43 is recommended for the best overall interactive rate. Other tested values include 13, 43, and 83. Larger data sets do not suffer high penalties from 43 or 83 macrocells. Smoother data with more empty space can achieve good performance with coarser macrocells. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Skip Rate: If the number of skipped macrocells is small relative to the total, performance degrades due to the overhead of memory access and condition checks per macrocell. This is observed in the Engine dataset where only 12 macrocells have zero density. Transfer Function Dependency: Performance gains depend heavily on the transfer function, as macrocell values are computed from TF densities. If the TF results in few zero-density macrocells, the overhead may dominate. Agulhas Dataset Anomaly: On the Agulhas dataset, despite a large number of skipped cells (1,395,619), performance was worse with macrocell skipping for the ray marcher due to extra memory access and condition checks per coarse element. Macro-cell trimming is an optimization that reduces the number of local rays by trimming each macro-cell to the smallest cuboid containing its portions of the iso-surfaces, rather than projecting the entire macro-cell. It operates on axis-aligned bounding boxes derived from cell occupancy rather than explicit mesh geometry, and focuses on pre-projection culling of the pixel footprint rather than adaptive step sizing during traversal. A GPU-accelerated space-skipping technique for structured volume rendering that replaces clustered proxy boxes with a triangle mesh bounding the surface between active and inactive macrocells. It differs from Macro-Cell Trimming and Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by generating a boundary mesh entirely on the GPU, avoiding host-to-device transfers and user-defined intersection programs, and leveraging native hardware-accelerated triangle intersection to reduce depth complexity and warp divergence. Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA is an empty-space skipping technique that accelerates volume rendering by dividing the volume into a coarse grid of bricks (macrocells) and traversing them using a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (3DDDA). It solves the problem of excessive sampling in sparse volumes by skipping entire bricks if their opacity upper bound is zero, and adaptively adjusting the sampling step size within non-empty bricks based on local density estimates. It differs from its sibling Macro-Cell Trimming by using a fixed uniform grid with min-max bounds rather than trimming inactive cells, and from Triangulated Active Brick Boundary Mesh for Space Skipping by using a structured grid traversal instead of a boundary mesh. Time and Memory Complexity: Preprocessing time is linear with the total number of voxels. Rendering time scales with the number of non-skipped macrocells, but gains depend on the transfer function and skip fraction. Memory overhead includes the boolean grid for macrocells and distance fields. Measured Performance: Performance without macrocells is 4x-8x slower than with 23-voxel macrocells. On the MRI dataset, increasing skipped macrocells from 0 to 1,190 reduces rendering time from 44.83 ms to 26.05 ms. On the Heptane dataset, macrocell skipping improves time from 51.92 ms to 46.3 ms. On the Advection dataset, macrocell skipping improves time from 58.14 ms to 46.29 ms. On the Engine dataset, macrocell skipping worsens performance due to low skip rate (12 cells). On the Agulhas dataset, macrocell skipping worsens performance for the ray marcher despite high skip count, due to overhead. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple implementation, effective for volumes with large empty regions, interactive performance on mobile GPUs. Limitations: Overhead can negate benefits if skip rate is low, performance is transfer-function dependent. When to Use: Use when the volume has significant empty space and the transfer function results in many zero-density macrocells. Use when interactivity is required and the dataset is large. When Not to Use: Do not use if the volume is dense with few empty regions (e.g., Engine dataset). Do not use if the overhead of checking macrocell flags dominates the cost of marching (e.g., Agulhas dataset for ray marcher). Originating from work on fiber surface volume ray casting, this method was introduced to accelerate interactive exploration of fiber surfaces. It was further analyzed in the context of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement data. The technique leverages the spatial coherence of empty regions in volumes to reduce the number of ray marching steps. name: Macro-Cell Trimming
head: Culling Empty Cap-Level Macrocells
body: Macro-cell trimming is an optimization that reduces the number of local rays by trimming each macro-cell to the smallest cuboid containing its portions of the iso-surfaces, rather than projecting the entire macro-cell. It operates on axis-aligned bounding boxes derived from cell occupancy rather than explicit mesh geometry, and focuses on pre-projection culling of the pixel footprint rather than adaptive step sizing during traversal. Inputs: A macro-cell containing a grid of cells (typically at the finest available octree depth, i.e., cap nodes). An isovalue threshold defining the iso-surface. The spatial bounds of the macro-cell. Outputs: A trimmed bounding cuboid (axis-aligned bounding box) that tightly encloses all cells within the macro-cell intersecting the isovalue. A reduced set of pixels (u,v slice extents) for ray casting. Data Structures: Macro-cell Grid: A 3D array of cells. Each cell contains a scalar value (density or field value). Trimmed Cuboid: Defined by minimum and maximum coordinates (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}). Initialized to an invalid or zero-size state. Steps: 1. Initialize Cuboid: Set the trimmed cuboid to a size of zero or an invalid state. 2. Iterate Cells: Loop through all cells within the macro-cell. 3. Check Iso-surface Intersection: For each cell, determine if it contains the isovalue (i.e., if the cell's value crosses the threshold). 4. Extend Cuboid: If a cell contains the isovalue, calculate its spatial bounds and update the trimmed cuboid's min/max coordinates to include the cell's bounds, maintaining the smallest necessary size. 5. Cull Empty Macro-cells: If the macro-cell is empty (no cells contain the isovalue), omit it from extent computation entirely. 6. Compute Slice Extents: If the macro-cell is not empty, compute the u,v slice extents based on the minimum and maximum u,v coordinates of the macro-cell or trimmed region. 7. Project: Project the resulting trimmed cuboid onto the image plane instead of the full macro-cell. 8. Cast Rays: Cast local rays only for pixels covered by the projected trimmed cuboid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trimmacrocell(cells, isovalue): # Initialize cuboid bounds to None (zero-size state) xmin = None; xmax = None; ymin = None; ymax = None zmin = None; zmax = None # Initialize u,v slice extents umin = None; umax = None; vmin = None; vmax = None # Iterate through all cells in the macro-cell for cell in cells: # Check if cell contains the isovalue if cell['value'] > isovalue: # Standard threshold check # Calculate spatial bounds of the cell cxmin, cxmax, cymin, cymax, czmin, czmax = cell['bounds'] # Get cell u,v coordinates cumin, cumax, cvmin, cvmax = cell['uvbounds'] # Update cuboid min/max to smallest necessary size if xmin is None or cxmin < xmin: xmin = cxmin if xmax is None or cxmax > xmax: xmax = cxmax if ymin is None or cymin < ymin: ymin = cymin if ymax is None or cymax > ymax: ymax = cymax if zmin is None or czmin < zmin: zmin = czmin if zmax is None or czmax > zmax: zmax = czmax # Update u,v slice extents based on minimum and maximum u,v coordinates if umin is None or cumin < umin: umin = cumin if umax is None or cumax > umax: umax = cumax if vmin is None or cvmin < vmin: vmin = cvmin if vmax is None or cvmax > vmax: vmax = cvmax # If no cells contained the isovalue, the macro-cell is empty if xmin is None: return None # Project the resulting cuboid/slice extents onto the image plane # Standard camera projection maps u,v bounds to screen pixel coordinates screenumin, screenvmin, screenumax, screenvmax = projecttoscreen(umin, umax, vmin, vmax) return (screenumin, screenumax, screenvmin, screenvmax) def projecttoscreen(umin, umax, vmin, vmax): """Maps normalized u,v coordinates to screen pixel bounds.""" # Implementation applies viewport transform return umin, vmin, umax, vmax Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Macro-cells: Must be detected and omitted to avoid unnecessary processing. Boundary Conditions: The cuboid must be initialized correctly to handle the first surface cell encountered. Performance: Macro-cell trimming saves about 28 percent of overall rendering time on average. Dependency: The time gain is very much dependent on the data set and the position of the view point. Complexity: The trimming step adds a linear scan over the macro-cell cells, but this is offset by the reduction in ray casting operations. Strengths: Reduces unnecessary calculations and octree lookups by focusing only on relevant pixels. Limitations: Effectiveness varies with data set topology and viewpoint. Macro-cell trimming was introduced as part of cell-based first-hit ray casting techniques to optimize volume rendering performance. It is also referred to as "Culling empty cap-level macrocells" in the context of interactive ray tracing of implicit surfaces. The method leverages the coherence of octree structures to efficiently cull empty regions before ray casting begins. name: Triangulated Active Brick Boundary Mesh for Space Skipping
head: Active Brick Boundary Mesh, Triangulated Active Region Boundary Geometry, Triangulated Active Region Boundary Geometry for RTX Space Skipping
body: A GPU-accelerated space-skipping technique for structured volume rendering that replaces clustered proxy boxes with a triangle mesh bounding the surface between active and inactive macrocells. It differs from sibling methods by generating the boundary mesh entirely on the GPU, avoiding host-to-device transfers and user-defined intersection programs, and leveraging native hardware-accelerated triangle intersection to reduce depth complexity and warp divergence. Inputs: Input volume dimensions Vx \times Vy \times Vz (voxels). Brick size K (default 16, also 8 or 32). Transfer function (TF) defining active/inactive regions. OptiX 7.2 (or equivalent DXR/VKR) runtime. Outputs: Rendering intervals [t0, t1] for volume integration. Final pixel color. Data Structures: 1. Macrocell Grid: 3D grid of size Mx \times My \times Mz, where Mx = \lceil Vx / K \rceil, My = \lceil Vy / K \rceil, Mz = \lceil Vz / K \rceil. Each cell stores \{min\val, max\val\} of all input voxels mapping to it. Computed on host, uploaded to GPU. 2. Active Bricks Mask: Boolean grid of size Mx \times My \times Mz on GPU. active[i][j][k] is true if the macrocell's value range maps to any non-zero alpha in the TF. 3. Vertex Array: Pre-allocated device array of float3 vertices. Size N{vtxMax} = (Mx + 1) \times (My + 1) \times (Mz + 1). Contains all possible macrocell grid vertices. 4. Triangle Index Array: Pre-allocated device array of int3 indices. Size N{triMax} (upper bound derived from boundary geometry on macrocell faces). 5. numTriangles Counter: Single device-side integer, initialized to 0. Used as atomic offset for writing triangles. Steps: 1. Initial Setup: Build macrocell grid on host. Upload to GPU. Allocate GPU memory for Active Bricks Mask, Vertex Array, Triangle Index Array, and numTriangles counter. 2. Active Cell Classification (Rebuild Step 1): Launch CUDA kernel. Each thread maps to one macrocell (i, j, k). Thread checks if macrocellgrid[i][j][k].minval to macrocellgrid[i][j][k].maxval intersects the non-zero alpha range of the current TF. Write result to activecells[i][j][k]. 3. Boundary Triangle Generation (Rebuild Step 2): Reset numTriangles to 0. Launch three templated CUDA kernels (for X, Y, Z orientations). For each orientation, threads map to faces perpendicular to that axis. For a face between curr and prev macrocells: if activecells[prev] == activecells[curr], return. Compute indices of four vertices spanning the face. Atomically increment numTriangles by 2. Write two triangle indices to triangles buffer at offset numTriangles - 2. Winding order points away from active to inactive cell. Download numTriangles to host. 4. BVH Rebuild (Rebuild Step 3): Update OptiX triangle geometry to reference the generated mesh (triangle count and index array pointer). Ask OptiX to rebuild BVH with 'optimize for traversal' flag. Compact BVH to conserve memory. 5. Space Skipping during Rendering: Trace ray against boundary mesh. Closest Hit: Record hit distance t{hit} and hit kind (front/back). No Hit: Terminate ray (no active regions). Back-Facing Hit: Ray is inside volume. Integration interval is [0, t{hit}]. Front-Facing Hit: Ray enters volume at t0 = t{hit}. Trace again with ray.t{min}=t0 to find exit distance t1. Integrate volume over [t0, t1] using gradient shading and early ray termination. If early termination, return. Otherwise, iterate: trace new ray from t1 to find next segment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getquadindices(facecoord, dim, Mx, My, Mz): """Returns 4 vertex indices spanning the macrocell face perpendicular to dim.""" x, y, z = facecoord if dim == 0: # X-face return [x (My + 1) (Mz + 1) + y (Mz + 1) + z, x (My + 1) (Mz + 1) + (y + 1) (Mz + 1) + z, x (My + 1) (Mz + 1) + (y + 1) (Mz + 1) + (z + 1), x (My + 1) (Mz + 1) + y (Mz + 1) + (z + 1)] elif dim == 1: # Y-face return [y (Mx + 1) (Mz + 1) + x (Mz + 1) + z, (y + 1) (Mx + 1) (Mz + 1) + x (Mz + 1) + z, (y + 1) (Mx + 1) (Mz + 1) + (x + 1) (Mz + 1) + z, y (Mx + 1) (Mz + 1) + (x + 1) (Mz + 1) + z] else: # Z-face return [z (Mx + 1) (My + 1) + x (My + 1) + y, (z + 1) (Mx + 1) (My + 1) + x (My + 1) + y, (z + 1) (Mx + 1) (My + 1) + (x + 1) (My + 1) + y, z (Mx + 1) (My + 1) + (x + 1) (My + 1) + y] def generateboundarymesh(activecells, numtriangles, triangles, Mx, My, Mz, dim): """Simulates the CUDA kernel for one dimension.""" for i in range(Mx + 1): for j in range(My + 1): for k in range(Mz + 1): curr = (i, j, k) if dim == 0: prev = (i - 1, j, k) elif dim == 1: prev = (i, j - 1, k) else: prev = (i, j, k - 1) # Boundary check: treat out-of-bounds as inactive if not (0 <= prev[0] < Mx and 0 <= prev[1] < My and 0 <= prev[2] < Mz): prevactive = False else: prevactive = activecells[prev] curractive = activecells[curr] if prevactive == curractive: continue vi = getquadindices(curr, dim, Mx, My, Mz) triid = numtriangles[0] numtriangles[0] += 2 if prevactive: triangles[triid] = (vi[0], vi[1], vi[2]) triangles[triid + 1] = (vi[0], vi[2], vi[3]) else: triangles[triid] = (vi[1], vi[0], vi[2]) triangles[triid + 1] = (vi[2], vi[0], vi[3]) def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, boundarymesh, tf, volumetexture, dt=0.5): """Space skipping and volume integration loop.""" tmin = 0.0 while True: # Hardware BVH trace against boundary mesh hit = None # Hardware BVH trace if hit is None: break thit = hit.distance isbackfacing = hit.kind == 'BACK' if isbackfacing: tend = thit # Volume integration over [tmin, tend] # Early termination check if earlyterminationreached(): return tmin = tend else: tenter = thit # Hardware BVH trace with tmin=tenter to find exit exithit = None # Hardware BVH trace if exithit is None: break texit = exithit.distance # Volume integration over [tenter, texit] # Early termination check if earlyterminationreached(): return tmin = texit Parameters: K: Brick size (8, 16, 32). Default 16. dt: Fixed sampling rate for volume integration (0.5). Interleaved Sampling: Used to reduce aliasing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Faces: Faces on the outside of the volume have indices mapping outside the macrocell grid. These are treated as inactive macrocells to ensure correct boundary detection. Winding Order: Must point away from active to inactive cell for correct front/back face detection. Unused Vertices: Pre-allocating all possible vertices results in unused vertices, accepted as memory cost. Warp Divergence: Reduced by lowering depth complexity to transitions between active/inactive regions. Timings less than 1ms: Should be considered with caution and interpreted as 'less than one millisecond'. Accelerates volume rendering by using RTX-accelerated ray tracing to skip empty space. It constructs a BVH over the boundary surface between active and inactive macrocells, rather than over all active regions, to determine ray integration intervals. It differs from this method by explicitly leveraging hardware-accelerated BVH traversal and triangle intersection via OptiX/OWL to replace costly software intersection tests, and from Ganter and Manzke's method by replacing the BVH over active brick regions with a BVH over only the boundary, resulting in lower depth complexity and fewer rays. Time Complexity: BVH rebuild and triangle generation are GPU-side, avoiding host-GPU transfer bottlenecks. Depth complexity is reduced to transitions between active/inactive regions. Memory Complexity: Upper bounds for vertices and triangles are 3-5 orders of magnitude lower than the number of voxels. Performance: Reduces per-pixel cost by freeing CUDA cores for volume integration. Eliminates warp divergence caused by varying numbers of samples per box. Strengths: No host-GPU transfer for mesh generation. Native hardware acceleration for intersection tests. Lower depth complexity than proxy box methods. Limitations: Requires BVH rebuild on TF change. Pre-allocated vertex array may waste memory. When to Use: Structured volumes with interactive TF editing. When hardware ray tracing is available. When Not to Use: Unstructured volumes (use Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA or unstructured methods). When TF changes are rare and host-side preprocessing is acceptable. Originated from Ganter and Manzke's method [GM19], which used proxy boxes and user-defined intersection programs. This method improves on it by using a GPU-generated boundary mesh and native triangle primitives. The core idea draws motivation from unstructured volume rendering where rays are intersected with outside-facing triangles of boundary tetrahedra [BKS97]. Presented by Ingo Wald, Stefan Zellmann & Nate Morrical in Eurographics Proceedings 2021. Implemented using OptiX 7.2, but maps to DXR and VKR. Used in evaluation datasets including HEPTANE, FLOWER, DNS-4, and LLNL Richtmyer-Meshkov instability. name: RTX-Accelerated Empty Space Skipping using Triangulated Active Bricks
head: Active Brick Classification, Boundary BVH method, Boundary Mesh Method, Ours
body: This method accelerates volume rendering by using RTX-accelerated ray tracing to skip empty space. It constructs a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) over the boundary surface between active and inactive macrocells, rather than over all active regions, to determine ray integration intervals. It differs from Triangulated Active Brick Boundary Mesh for Space Skipping by explicitly leveraging hardware-accelerated BVH traversal and triangle intersection via OptiX/OWL to replace costly software intersection tests, and from Ganter and Manzke's method by replacing the BVH over active brick regions with a BVH over only the boundary, resulting in lower depth complexity and fewer rays. Inputs: 3D volume texture (scalar field). Transfer function (for active brick classification). Macrocell size K (default 16). Sampling rate dt (fixed step size, default 0.5). Ray origin and direction for each pixel. Outputs: Final color for each pixel. Data Structures: Active Brick Mask: A 3D grid indicating which macrocells contain active data. Generated on the GPU. Boundary Triangle Mesh: Vertices and indices representing the surface between active and inactive macrocells. Stored in OWL buffers. Acceleration Structure: OWLTrianglesGeom for the triangle mesh and OWLTrianglesGroup for the BVH. Volume Texture: Created in CUDA, passed to OptiX as OWLUSERTYPE(cudaTextureObjectt). Algorithm Steps: 1. Active Brick Classification: Determine which macrocells are active based on the transfer function. This is performed entirely on the GPU. 2. Boundary Mesh Generation: Extract the boundary geometry (triangles) between active and inactive macrocells. This replaces the clustering step used in prior works. 3. BVH Construction: Build a BVH over the boundary triangle mesh. This is the most expensive part of the update phase. 4. Ray Tracing for Space Skipping: Trace a ray from the camera into the scene against the boundary BVH. Use a closest-hit program to retrieve hit distance t{hit} and triangle orientation (normal vs. ray direction). If no hit is found, the ray does not traverse any active volume; terminate the ray. If a hit is found: If the triangle is facing (ray is inside the volume), the integration interval is [0, t{hit}]. If the triangle is not facing (ray enters the volume), set t0 = t{hit}. Trace the same ray again with ray.tmin = t0 to find the exit distance t1. 5. Volume Integration: Integrate over the interval [t0, t1] using fixed step size dt. Sample the 3D texture, compute gradients, and apply transfer functions. Use interleaved sampling to reduce aliasing. Apply early ray termination if the accumulated opacity reaches a threshold. 6. Iteration: If the ray has not terminated early, trace another ray from t1 to find the next potential segment to integrate. Repeat until the ray terminates or exits the volume bounds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpixel(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, boundarybvh, dt=0.5): """ Renders a single pixel using RTX-accelerated empty space skipping. """ color = vec3(0.0) alpha = 0.0 tcurrent = 0.0 INFINITY = 1e9 while alpha < 1.0: # Trace ray against boundary BVH to find active regions hit = traceray(boundarybvh, rayorigin, raydirection, tcurrent, INFINITY) if hit is None: # No active volume encountered break thit = hit.distance # "facing" triangle indicates the ray is inside the volume isfacing = dot(hit.normal, raydirection) < 0.0 if isfacing: # Ray is inside volume, integrate from current position to hit t0 = tcurrent t1 = thit else: # Ray enters volume at thit t0 = thit # Trace again to find exit hitexit = traceray(boundarybvh, rayorigin, raydirection, t0, INFINITY) if hitexit is None: # Ray exits volume bounds without hitting another boundary t1 = INFINITY else: t1 = hitexit.distance # Integrate over [t0, t1] samplecolor, samplealpha = integratevolume(volumetexture, rayorigin, raydirection, t0, t1, dt) # Composite color = color + samplecolor (1.0 - alpha) alpha = alpha + samplealpha (1.0 - alpha) # Update current position for next segment tcurrent = t1 # Early termination check if alpha >= 1.0: break return color def integratevolume(volumetexture, origin, direction, t0, t1, dt): """ Integrates volume along ray segment [t0, t1] with fixed step dt. """ accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 t = t0 while t < t1: pos = origin + direction t value = sample3dtexture(volumetexture, pos) # Compute gradient and apply transfer function color, alpha = applytransferfunction(value, pos) accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor + color (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedalpha = accumulatedalpha + alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) if accumulatedalpha >= 1.0: break t += dt return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha def traceray(bvh, origin, direction, tmin, tmax): """Standard BVH traversal returning closest hit distance or None.""" # Hardware-accelerated traversal implementation omitted for brevity pass def sample3dtexture(texture, pos): """Trilinear interpolation of the 3D volume texture.""" pass def applytransferfunction(value, pos): """Lookup color and opacity from the transfer function based on the sampled value.""" pass Parameters: Macrocell size K: Grid resolution for active brick classification. Default is 16. Tested values include 8 and 32. Sampling rate dt: Fixed step size for volume integration. Value is 0.5, resulting in an average of two samples per cell. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Timings < 1ms: Timings less than 1ms are considered unreliable and should be interpreted as "less than one millisecond". BVH Build Cost: BVH construction is the biggest cost during data structure update. No Hit: If the space-skipping ray does not hit any geometry, the ray is terminated immediately as it will not traverse any active volume regions. Time and Memory Complexity: The total build time remains within an interactive range, though it varies by dataset; for the LLNL model at K=16 it is 6.0ms. For the LLNL model with K=16, the total build time is 6.0ms, comprising 153µs for active cell classification, 119µs for triangle extraction, and 5.4ms for BVH construction. Measured Performance: Tests were conducted at a resolution of 3840 × 2160 pixels. HEPTANE model: 84 fps (with rebuild) compared to 93 fps for Ganter's method with space skip on. Base off rebuild is 34 fps. FLOWER model: 83 fps (with rebuild) compared to 111 fps for Ganter's method with space skip on. Base off rebuild is 14 fps. DNS (4X) model: 28 fps (with rebuild) compared to 34 fps for Ganter's method with space skip on. Base off rebuild is 13 fps. LLNL model: 32 fps (with rebuild) compared to 41 fps for Ganter's method with space skip on. Base off rebuild is 8 fps. For the LLNL model, the method achieves 40 FPS (render time only, no rebuild) compared to 8 FPS for the base method and 27 FPS for Ganter's method. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Avoids CPU-side clustering, performs active brick classification entirely on the GPU, results in lower depth complexity and fewer/cheaper rays for space skipping. Maintains interactive rates even when data structure rebuilding is forced every frame. Limitations: BVH build time is the dominant cost during data structure updates. When to Use: Use when interactive performance is required and the volume data changes frequently (requiring frequent BVH rebuilds), as the GPU-native classification and boundary mesh generation are more efficient than CPU-side clustering. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: Based on ideas from Ganter and Manzke (2019) 'An Analysis of Region Clustered BVH Volume Rendering on GPU' and Hadwiger et al. (2017) 'SparseLeap'. History and Development: The method modifies prior techniques to reduce overhead. It builds on the macro-cell/active brick mask concept but replaces the BVH over active brick regions with a BVH over only the boundary between active and inactive regions. This reduces depth complexity and the number of rays traced for space skipping. Where it is used: GPU-based large-scale volume rendering. name: Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA
head: Adaptive Macrocell Ray Marching, Macrocell solution
body: Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA is an empty space skipping technique that accelerates volume rendering by dividing the volume into a coarse grid of bricks (macrocells) and using a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (3DDDA) to traverse this grid. It solves the performance bottleneck of sampling empty or low-opacity regions by maintaining minimum and maximum scalar values for each brick; if the accumulated opacity estimate for a brick is zero, the entire brick is skipped, and standard sampling is only invoked for non-empty bricks. It sets itself apart from its parent Ray Marcher with Macrocell Empty Space Skipping by explicitly integrating an adaptive sampling rate within the macrocell traversal loop, adjusting step sizes based on local opacity upper bounds rather than using a fixed step or simple binary skip. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset, a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, a near plane t{min}, and a far plane t{max}. Output: The accumulated color and opacity along the ray segment within [t{min}, t{max}]. Data Structures: The method requires a macrocell grid structure. Each macrocell stores the minimum and maximum scalar values of the voxels contained within it. macrocelldims: The dimensions of the macrocell grid in cells. macrocellspacingsrcp: The reciprocal of the macrocell spacing in world units, used to transform ray parameters into macrocell space. bricksize: The size of each brick is defined as dx^n \times dy^n \times dz^n, where dx, dy, dz are the volume dimensions and n is a scaling parameter. Parameters: n: The exponent for brick size calculation. Tested values range from 0.1 to 0.9, with best performance observed at n=0.3. floatepsilon: A small constant used to determine if a cell is empty. If the opacity upper bound r satisfies |r| \le \text{float\epsilon}, the cell is considered empty. step: The base sampling step size. ADAPTIVESAMPLING: A preprocessor macro that enables or disables the adaptive logic. If defined, adaptive sampling is used; otherwise, fixed-step marching is applied. Algorithm Steps: 1. Macrocell Space Transformation: Transform the ray origin and direction into macrocell space using the reciprocal spacing: \mathbf{m\org} = \mathbf{o} \cdot \text{macrocell\spacings\rcp} \mathbf{m\dir} = \mathbf{d} \cdot \text{macrocell\spacings\rcp} 2. DDA Initialization: Initialize a 3DDDA iterator with \mathbf{m\org}, \mathbf{m\dir}, t{min}, t{max}, and the macrocell dimensions. The 3DDDA algorithm traverses the coarse grid cells. 3. Cell Traversal Loop: For each macrocell (cell, t0, t1) returned by the DDA: a. Opacity Estimate: Calculate the opacity upper bound r for the current cell. This is typically derived from the stored min/max scalar values and the transfer function. b. Empty Check: If |r| \le \text{float\epsilon}, the cell is empty. Skip this cell and continue to the next. c. Step Size Calculation: If the cell is not empty, estimate the adaptive step size ss: ss = \text{sample\size\scaler}(\text{adaptiveSamplingRate}(step, r), t0, t1) d. Interval Initialization: Initialize the sampling interval t = (tx, ty) where tx = t0 and ty = \min(t1, t0 + ss). e. Inner Sampling Loop: While ty > tx: i. Call the rendering body function with the current interval t. ii. Update tx = ty. iii. Update ty = \min(tx + ss, t1). f. If the body function returns a termination signal (e.g., opacity reached 1.0), stop processing. 4. Non-Adaptive Fallback: If ADAPTIVESAMPLING is not defined, use a fixed step size: a. Initialize t = (t{min}, \min(t{max}, t{min} + step)). b. While ty > tx and body returns true: i. Call body(t). ii. tx = ty. iii. ty = \min(tx + step, t{max}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveraymarchingwithmacrocelldda(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, volumedata): # 1. Transform to macrocell space morg = rayorigin volumedata.macrocellspacingsrcp mdir = raydirection volumedata.macrocellspacingsrcp # 2. Initialize 3DDDA for macrocell grid dda = DDA3(morg, mdir, tmin, tmax, volumedata.macrocelldims) # 3. Traverse macrocells for cell, t0, t1 in dda: # 4. Calculate opacity upper bound r = opacityupperbound(volumedata, cell) # 5. Skip empty cells if abs(r) <= floatepsilon: continue # 6. Determine step size if ADAPTIVESAMPLING: ss = samplesizescaler(adaptivesamplingrate(volumedata.step, r), t0, t1) else: ss = volumedata.step # 7. Sample within the cell tx = t0 ty = min(t1, t0 + ss) while ty > tx: # Render segment [tx, ty] color, opacity = rendersegment(tx, ty, rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata) # Update interval tx = ty ty = min(tx + ss, t1) # Check for early termination (e.g., full opacity) if opacity >= 1.0: return color return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dynamic Volumes: For dynamic volumes, the macrocell structure (min/max values) must be updated every frame. This construction can be a major performance bottleneck, especially when the volume image ratio is large. Precision: The use of floatepsilon for empty cell detection requires careful selection to avoid skipping cells with very low but non-zero opacity. Boundary Conditions: The DDA must correctly handle ray entry and exit points relative to the macrocell boundaries to avoid duplicate sampling or gaps. The Resumable Ray Marching Iterator is a GPU-accelerated ray marching algorithm that enables the interruption and subsequent resumption of ray traversal within a single frame or across frames. It solves the problem of limited GPU memory bandwidth and compute time by allowing the ray marcher to pause at a specific spatial coordinate, transfer control to the CPU for data loading or structure adaptation, and resume exactly where it left off. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly exposing the traversal state (macrocell coordinates and ray parameter t) for external interruption, rather than relying solely on pre-loaded hierarchical structures or probabilistic culling. The Network Ray Marching Iterator is a ray marching algorithm designed for distributed or networked rendering environments, typically leveraging GPU ray tracing APIs such as NVIDIA OptiX. It extends the parent Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by introducing block-level divergence control via blockany to manage thread synchronization across macrocell boundaries. This method is distinct from its siblings because it explicitly tracks the "alive" status of rays in a distributed context, ensuring that inactive threads do not waste computation while maintaining adaptive sampling rates based on opacity upper bounds. This method accelerates volumetric path tracing by combining a coarse spatial partition (macrocells) with Delta Tracking (Woodcock tracking) to skip empty or low-opacity regions more efficiently than fixed-step marching. It sets itself apart from its parent Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by explicitly using the alpha component of the transfer function as a majorant extinction coefficient to determine probabilistic free-flight distances, allowing larger steps in homogeneous cells while maintaining unbiased Monte Carlo estimation. Voxel Ray Marching with Cube-Level DDA is a GPU-based fragment shader technique for rendering voxel volumes by casting rays through a hierarchical grid of voxel cubes and individual voxels, using a two-level Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) to skip empty space efficiently. It builds on Adaptive Ray Marching with Macrocell DDA by replacing the adaptive macrocell traversal with a fixed two-level DDA structure: a coarse traversal over 16 \times 16 \times 16 voxel blocks to skip empty regions, followed by a fine traversal over individual voxels within occupied blocks to find the first opaque surface. A mechanism to skip empty regions in sparse volume data using a uniform grid and 3DDDA algorithm. The fragment shader traverses the macrocell grid using 3DDDA in an outer loop. If a macrocell is nonempty, it enters the volume rendering loop with peak finding tests between samples. To begin sampling, it finds the first t to sample when entering a macrocell by solving for the maximum x after T{enter}: x{tenter} = (-b + \sqrt{b^2 + 2aT{enter}})/a. It then computes floor values and samples as in Equation 17 of the source. A uniform grid with 3DDDA is used, where each grid cell stores min-max values of enclosed voxels. Coarse grids (64^3 cells) work best on the GPU. For each ray, this method iterates through spatial steps. It checks occupancy using a bitfield: sitybitfield[ti.u32(idx//8)] & (1 << ti.u32(idx%8)). If occupied, it stores the current position, direction, time, and delta into buffers and marks the ray for network evaluation. If not occupied, it calculates the distance to the next grid boundary and advances time to skip empty space until the next grid boundary is reached. It stores the total number of effective samples and marks rays as dead if no samples were collected. The step size calculation relies on self.expstepfactor, self.gridsize, and self.scale. An extension of RayGauss with optimizations aimed at accelerating ray marching. It implements empty-space skipping, adaptive sampling, and improves ray coherence through Morton-order sorting. It also introduces a regularizer to limit anisotropic Gaussians, as they are highly inefficient since they bound Gaussians by axis-aligned bounding boxes. These additions reduce training time to be comparable with 3DGRT, but frame rates remain approximately 2.5× slower. Time Complexity: The traversal time depends on the number of non-empty macrocells and the adaptive step size within them. In the worst case (fully dense volume), it approaches the complexity of standard ray marching. In sparse volumes, it is proportional to the number of active macrocells. Memory Complexity: Requires additional memory for the macrocell grid storing min/max values. The size depends on the grid resolution, which is determined by the brick size parameter n. Measured Performance: Benchmarked on Jet-Flame simulation volumes (1024×1024×512, ~512 MB per time step). The best performance for brick size parameter n was found at 0.3. Scaling: Performance is highly dependent on the volume image ratio. When rendering large volumes (e.g., 1024×1024×1024) into small resolution images (e.g., 256×256 or 512×512), the construction of the macrocell structure becomes a major performance bottleneck, making Warp Marching a better alternative. Conversely, at higher image resolutions (1024×1024), Macrocell DDA outperforms Warp Marching. Strengths: Significant speedup for sparse volumes; effective empty space skipping; adaptive sampling reduces unnecessary computations in low-opacity regions. Limitations: High overhead for dynamic volumes due to frequent structure updates; poor performance when volume image ratio is large (small image, large volume). When to Use: Static volumes or dynamic volumes rendered at high image resolutions where the structure update cost is amortized over many pixels. When Not to Use: Dynamic volumes with large volume image ratios (small image resolution) where structure update overhead dominates. The Macrocell solution was introduced by Parker et al. (2005) and Parker et al. (1998). It builds upon the 3DDDA algorithm by Amanatides and Woo (1987). The method is part of the broader family of empty space skipping techniques that rely on additional data structures to accelerate volume rendering. It has been used in benchmarks involving dynamic volumetric data, such as the Jet-Flame simulation dataset (Attili et al., 2014).
