name: K-D Tree Hierarchy Construction
head: Polygon distribution in k-d tree, Spatial partitioning with k-d trees
body: K-D Tree Hierarchy Construction builds a binary space-partitioning structure to organize geometric primitives (typically polygons) for efficient spatial queries, such as visibility culling in volume rendering. It sets itself apart from its parent method, Orthogonal BSP Tree Construction, by classifying polygons based on vertex coordinates relative to the splitting hyperplane and retaining spanning polygons at the node, thereby avoiding explicit polygon clipping. Inputs: A set of polygons P, each defined by vertices in 3D space. A user-defined leaf threshold T{leaf}. Outputs: A binary tree where each node v contains a list of polygon IDs and a splitting dimension i (if internal). Data Structures: Tree Node: Contains splitdim (integer, 0-2), splitval (float), leftchild (pointer/index), rightchild (pointer/index), and polyids (list of integers). Polygon ID Array (Tid): A flat array storing polygon IDs in prefix-order traversal sequence, allowing all polygons in a subtree to be passed in one operation without linked lists. Algorithm: 1. Root Initialization: Create the root node. Assign all input polygons to the root's polyids list. 2. Recursive Build Function Build(node, polygons, depth): a. Leaf Check: If len(polygons) <= Tleaf, mark node as a leaf. Return. b. Splitting Dimension Selection: Determine dimension i to split on. The basic implementation uses round-robin selection (e.g., i = depth \mod 3). More sophisticated policies may use variance analysis. c. Split Value Selection: Determine the splitting value Xi. The basic implementation bisects the region along dimension i. d. Polygon Classification: Initialize leftpolys and rightpolys as empty lists. For each polygon p in polygons: i. Check all vertices of p. ii. If all vertices have coordinate xi < Xi, add p to leftpolys. iii. If all vertices have coordinate xi > Xi, add p to rightpolys. iv. Otherwise, retain p in node.polyids. This associates the polygon with the smallest node region that completely contains it, avoiding subdivision. e. Recursive Step: i. If leftpolys is not empty, create node.leftchild and call Build(node.leftchild, leftpolys, depth + 1). ii. If rightpolys is not empty, create node.rightchild and call Build(node.rightchild, rightpolys, depth + 1). iii. If both are empty, the node is a leaf (or contains only overlapping polygons). 3. Serialization: Traverse the tree in prefix order to populate the Tid array. Parameters: T{leaf}: Typical values are not given in the sources. Common practice suggests 1-10 depending on cache size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point comparisons for xi < Xi and xi > Xi must be consistent to avoid polygons being lost or duplicated. Empty Subtrees: If a split results in no polygons on one side, that child should not be created to save space. Degenerate Input: Polygons with zero area or vertices exactly on the split plane are handled by the "retain in node" rule (case iv), ensuring they are not lost. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Node: def init(self): self.splitdim = -1 self.splitval = 0.0 self.leftchild = None self.rightchild = None self.polyids = [] self.isleaf = False def buildkdtree(polygons, depth=0, leafthreshold=4): """ Builds a K-D tree hierarchy. polygons: List of dicts with 'id' and 'vertices' (list of tuples). depth: Current tree depth. leafthreshold: Minimum number of polygons to trigger a split. Returns: Node object. """ node = Node() node.polyids = [p['id'] for p in polygons] # Leaf check if len(polygons) <= leafthreshold: node.isleaf = True return node # Splitting dimension selection (Round-robin as per) splitdim = depth % 3 # Split value selection (Bisection as per) minval = float('inf') maxval = float('-inf') for p in polygons: for v in p['vertices']: val = v[splitdim] if val < minval: minval = val if val > maxval: maxval = val splitval = (minval + maxval) / 2.0 node.splitdim = splitdim node.splitval = splitval node.polyids = [] # Reset to store IDs of polygons retained at this node leftpolys = [] rightpolys = [] for p in polygons: allless = True allgreater = True for v in p['vertices']: val = v[splitdim] if val >= splitval: allless = False if val <= splitval: allgreater = False if allless: leftpolys.append(p) elif allgreater: rightpolys.append(p) else: node.polyids.append(p['id']) # Retain spanning polygons # Recursive step if leftpolys: node.leftchild = buildkdtree(leftpolys, depth + 1, leafthreshold) if rightpolys: node.rightchild = buildkdtree(rightpolys, depth + 1, leafthreshold) node.isleaf = (node.leftchild is None and node.rightchild is None) return node def serializetree(node, tidarray): """Traverses the tree in prefix order to populate the Tid array.""" if node is None: return tidarray.extend(node.polyids) serializetree(node.leftchild, tidarray) serializetree(node.rightchild, tidarray) Real-time KD Tree Construction is a technique for building k-d tree spatial partitioning structures on the GPU to enable immediate use in rendering pipelines. It sets itself apart from its parent method, K-D Tree Hierarchy Construction, by utilizing GPU parallelism and breadth-first search (BFS) to achieve real-time performance. It differs from GPU K-D Tree Ray Traversal by focusing on the construction phase rather than the traversal phase. GPU K-D Tree Ray Traversal accelerates ray tracing on graphics hardware by intersecting rays with a hierarchical spatial partitioning structure (K-D tree). It efficiently skips empty space and identifies intersected primitives, avoiding the computational cost of testing every primitive in the scene. It is distinguished from CPU implementations by its adaptation to GPU architectures: early Shader Model 2.0 hardware used stackless multi-pass streaming kernels, while Shader Model 3.0 introduced single-pass traversal via dynamic branching. It builds on K-D Tree Hierarchy Construction. Parallel k-d tree construction algorithms partition sparse volumetric or unstructured data into spatial regions to enable efficient ray traversal, early termination, and workload distribution in parallel volume rendering. Unlike static partitioning, these methods dynamically determine split planes using occupancy queries or median selection to balance tree depth and node count. They differ from Real-time KD Tree Construction by focusing on distributed-memory or GPU-accelerated top-down recursion rather than single-node heuristic optimization, and from K-D Tree Subdivision by explicitly managing inter-processor communication or GPU kernel synchronization during the build phase. K-D Tree Subdivision partitions a 3D volume into subvolumes using a k-d tree structure with alternating binary subdivision of coordinate planes, enabling unambiguous front-to-back ordering for compositing. Unlike fixed viewpoint partitioning which minimizes overlap by slicing orthogonal to the view, k-D tree partitioning is view-independent and suitable for animation sequences where the viewpoint changes. It determines the front-to-back image compositing order hierarchically by recursive traversal, visiting the 'front' child before the 'back' child. Selects the splitting axis for a K-D tree node by analyzing the variance of the QEF (Quadratic Error Function) solution along each dimension, scaled by the box size. The process involves solving the QEF to get an approximate solution and error, then calculating variance for each axis: variance[i] = qef.getVariance(approximate) \times size[i]. The axis with maximum variance is chosen (dir = maxVarDir). Fallback logic applies if the box size along the selected axis is less than 2, choosing 3 - maxVarDir - minVarDir, and if that is also small, falling back to minVarDir. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Average case is O(N \log N) for balanced trees, where N is the number of polygons; worst case is O(N^2) for degenerate inputs. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing polygons and tree nodes; the flat Tid array avoids overhead of linked lists. Strengths: Avoids explicit polygon clipping, reducing computational cost during rendering. Efficient for static scenes. Limitations: Construction can be slow for very large datasets. Sensitive to the choice of split plane and leaf threshold. When to use: Static scenes with many polygons where visibility culling is critical. When not to use: Highly dynamic scenes where frequent tree rebuilds are prohibitive. The k-d tree was introduced by Jon Bentley. It was originally designed for efficient spatial partitioning in computer graphics, specifically for hidden surface removal and ray tracing. The method described here, which stores polygons in nodes rather than splitting them, is a variation that avoids the need for explicit clipping, as noted in early volume rendering implementations. body: Real-time KD Tree Construction is a technique for building k-d tree spatial partitioning structures on the GPU to enable immediate use in rendering pipelines. It sets itself apart from its parent method, K-D Tree Hierarchy Construction, by utilizing GPU parallelism and breadth-first search (BFS) to achieve real-time performance. It differs from GPU K-D Tree Ray Traversal by focusing on the construction phase rather than the traversal phase. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of primitives or voxel data to be partitioned. Output: A k-d tree structure stored in GPU memory, ready for traversal. Data Structures: The exact memory layout is not detailed in the sources, but the structure follows the standard k-d tree node definition: a split axis, split position, and child node indices. The tree is constructed via breadth-first search rather than the prefix-order traversal used in the parent method. Steps: 1. Load input primitives or voxel data into GPU memory. 2. Perform a breadth-first search (BFS) to determine the tree structure and split planes. 3. Store the resulting node information in GPU texture memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Node: def init(self, bbox=None): self.id = 0 self.axis = 0 self.split = 0.0 self.left = None self.right = None self.bbox = bbox class BBox: def init(self, minval, maxval): self.min = minval self.max = maxval def buildkdtreebfsgpu(data): # 1. Initialize root node with bounding box of all input data rootbbox = computebbox(data) root = Node(bbox=rootbbox) queue = [root] nodecount = 0 # 2. BFS traversal to build tree level by level while queue: current = queue.pop(0) current.id = nodecount nodecount += 1 # Determine split axis and position for current bounding box axis, split = computesplit(current.bbox) # Partition data into left and right subsets based on split leftdata, rightdata = partition(data, current.bbox, axis, split) current.axis = axis current.split = split # Create child nodes if subsets are non-empty if len(leftdata) > 0: current.left = Node(bbox=computebbox(leftdata)) queue.append(current.left) if len(rightdata) > 0: current.right = Node(bbox=computebbox(rightdata)) queue.append(current.right) # Store node in GPU texture memory storetotexture(current) return root def computesplit(bbox): # Standard k-d tree split: choose longest axis, split at midpoint # Not given in the sources axis = maxaxis(bbox) split = (bbox.min[axis] + bbox.max[axis]) / 2.0 return axis, split def partition(data, bbox, axis, split): # Split data into two lists based on axis and split value # Not given in the sources left = [d for d in data if d.pos[axis] < split] right = [d for d in data if d.pos[axis] >= split] return left, right def computebbox(data): # Compute bounding box from data points # Not given in the sources minval = min(d.pos for d in data) maxval = max(d.pos for d in data) return BBox(minval, maxval) def storetotexture(node): # Write node data to GPU texture memory # Not given in the sources pass Parameters: Not given in the sources. name: GPU K-D Tree Ray Traversal
head: K-D Tree GPU Traversal, Kd-Tree Ray Tracing on GPU
body: GPU K-D Tree Ray Traversal accelerates ray tracing on graphics hardware by intersecting rays with a hierarchical spatial partitioning structure (K-D tree). It efficiently skips empty space and identifies intersected primitives, avoiding the computational cost of testing every primitive in the scene. It is distinguished from CPU implementations by its adaptation to GPU architectures: early Shader Model 2.0 hardware used stackless multi-pass streaming kernels, while Shader Model 3.0 introduced single-pass traversal via dynamic branching. It builds on K-D Tree Hierarchy Construction. The K-D tree is a hierarchical spatial partitioning structure where each node is divided into two sub-nodes by a plane orthogonal to an axis, positioned arbitrarily along that axis within the node. It is a special case of a BSP-Tree. Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a K-D tree structure where each node contains a split axis, split position, and references to left/right children or leaf primitives. Output: The closest intersection point or hit primitive along the ray. The tree nodes are typically stored in a flat array. Each node contains: axis: The dimension (0, 1, or 2) along which the split occurs. split: The position of the splitting plane along the specified axis. left: Index of the left child node. right: Index of the right child node. primcount: Number of primitives in the leaf. primoffset: Offset into a global primitive array for leaf nodes. 1. Initialize the ray slab with near and far clip distances. 2. Start traversal at the root node. 3. Calculate the intersection parameter t between the ray and the current node's split plane. 4. Determine traversal order based on the ray origin's position relative to the split plane. 5. Update the slab bounds (t{min}, t{max}) if the split plane is within the current ray segment. 6. Advance to the child node index. 7. If the current node is a leaf, test contained primitives against the ray slab. 8. Terminate when a hit is found, the slab is exhausted, or the maximum depth is reached. The intersection parameter t for the ray to reach the split plane is computed as: t = \frac{s - oa}{da} where s is the split position, oa is the ray origin component along the split axis a, and da is the ray direction component along axis a. The ray-slab bounds t{min} and t{max} are updated by clamping t to the current interval. maxdepth: Maximum traversal depth to prevent infinite loops on degenerate trees; typically set to the tree height or a fixed constant like 32. tmin: Near clip distance; typically 0.0 or the camera's near plane. tmax: Far clip distance; typically 1000.0 or the camera's far plane. Zero direction component: If da = 0, the ray is parallel to the split plane; t is undefined and the ray stays on one side of the plane. Precision errors: Floating-point inaccuracies near split planes can cause rays to miss nodes or traverse incorrectly; epsilon offsets are often applied. Degenerate input: Empty nodes or zero-volume cells can cause infinite loops; handled by maxdepth or node validation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, treenodes, maxdepth): """ Traverses a K-D tree for a single ray using dynamic branching. Assumes treenodes is a flat array of node structures. Returns the closest hit primitive index or -1 if no hit. """ currentnode = 0 # Start at root tmin = 0.0 # Near clip plane tmax = 1e9 # Far clip plane for step in range(maxdepth): node = treenodes[currentnode] # Check if leaf if node.primcount > 0: closestprim = -1 for i in range(node.primcount): primidx = node.primoffset + i thit = intersectprimitive(rayorigin, raydirection, primidx) if thit is not None and tmin <= thit < tmax: tmax = thit closestprim = primidx return closestprim # Determine which child to visit first splitaxis = node.axis splitpos = node.split # Ray parameter to intersection with split plane if raydirection[splitaxis] == 0.0: tsplit = float('inf') if splitpos > rayorigin[splitaxis] else float('-inf') else: tsplit = (splitpos - rayorigin[splitaxis]) / raydirection[splitaxis] # Determine traversal order based on ray origin side if rayorigin[splitaxis] < splitpos: if tsplit < tmin: currentnode = node.right else: currentnode = node.left if tsplit < tmax: tmax = tsplit else: if tsplit < tmin: currentnode = node.left else: currentnode = node.right if tsplit < tmax: tmax = tsplit # If tmax <= tmin, we have passed the region of interest if tmax <= tmin: return -1 return -1 def intersectprimitive(origin, direction, primidx): """Standard primitive intersection routine.""" # Implementation depends on primitive type (triangle, sphere, etc.) return None Time Complexity: O(\log N) on average for balanced trees, where N is the number of primitives; worst case O(N) for degenerate trees. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the tree nodes. Performance: Early GPU implementations (Foley and Sugerman) were slower than CPU counterparts due to streaming limitations. Later implementations (Horn et al.) became competitive with CPU but were limited by SIMD divergence penalties on Shader Model 3.0 hardware. Strengths: Efficient empty-space skipping; flexible for arbitrary scenes. Limitations: Dynamic branching causes divergence penalties on SIMD GPUs; stackless methods require multiple passes or fixed-depth loops. Origin: The K-D tree was shown by Havran [Hav00] to be the most flexible and provide average best results for arbitrary scenes in CPU ray tracing. History: The first GPU ray tracing use of K-D trees was proposed by Ernst et al. [EVG04], using a stack and a heavy multi-pass algorithm, which did not achieve high performance. Foley and Sugerman [FS05] improved this with stackless multi-pass methods for Shader Model 2.0. Horn et al. [HSHH07] proposed the first efficient GPU method competitive with CPU implementations, using Shader Model 3.0 dynamic branching for a single-pass algorithm. name: Parallel K-d Tree Construction
head: Cooperative Spatial Partitioning, GPU k-d tree, Parallel K-d Tree Spatial Partitioning, Parallel Space Partitioning for Volume Rendering, ZSL18/ZSL19 k-d tree, ZSL19 GPU k-d tree
body: Parallel k-d tree construction algorithms partition sparse volumetric or unstructured data into spatial regions to enable efficient ray traversal, early termination, and workload distribution in parallel volume rendering. Unlike static partitioning, these methods dynamically determine split planes using occupancy queries or median selection to balance tree depth and node count. They differ from Real-time KD Tree Construction by focusing on distributed-memory or GPU-accelerated top-down recursion rather than single-node heuristic optimization, and from K-D Tree Subdivision by explicitly managing inter-processor communication or GPU kernel synchronization during the build phase. The method varies based on the target architecture (CPU multi-core, GPU, or MPI distributed). The core logic involves decomposing the volume, determining split planes via occupancy or median finding, and recursively partitioning data. Inputs: Volumetric data (voxels or cells), transfer function (for occupancy), number of processors/threads, halting criteria (target tree height or node count). Outputs: A k-d tree structure (nodes with bounding boxes and split planes), optionally a serialized file (e.g., LODTree) or in-memory hierarchy. Used in CPU/GPU hybrid approaches to query occupancy. Layout: 3D integer array matching brick dimensions (32^3). Content: SVT[x][y][z] stores the sum of non-empty voxels in the box from (0,0,0) to (x,y,z). Bit Packing: Not specified; typically standard integer types. Used in MPI-based LODTree construction. Header (lod-file-header-struct): signature: char[1] source: char[7] width, height, depth: int num-datagoints: int min, max: float size: int (Number of LOD nodes) resolutions: int Min-Max Vertex Coords (char): Format: XlllXlll / mxyzaxyz First 4 bits: Canonical vertex coordinate of cell vertex with minimum data value. Last 4 bits: Canonical vertex coordinate of cell vertex with max value. Cell Dimensions (char + int): First 3 bits: Flags for irregularity in x, y, z. Last 4 bytes: Regular size of cell (max 2^4). Format: Xlllllll / xyzssss Centroids: 3D coordinates (x, y, z) for each cell, used for deterministic region placement. The implementation depends on the specific variant. This method uses the CPU for top-down recursion and plane sweeping, offloading tight bounding box computation to the GPU. 1. Decomposition: Decompose the volume into bricks of size 32^3 voxels. 2. Preclassification: Generate a binary flag for each voxel indicating if it is empty or non-empty based on the current transfer function. 3. SVT Construction: Build a 3D Summed Volume Table (SVT) for each brick in parallel. Brick size 32^3 ensures the SVT fits in the L1 cache of x64 CPUs. 4. Root Bounding Box: Determine the tight bounding box for the root node by shrinking the global AABB to fit non-empty voxels. Perform parallel occupancy queries on SVTs overlapping the global box. Combine local bounding boxes from SVTs to form the global tight box. 5. Recursive Splitting (Top-Down): Plane Selection: Use a cost function to find the optimal splitting plane by sweeping candidate planes and inspecting the volume of the bounding boxes to the left and right. GPU Offload: For each candidate plane, start two GPU kernels (left and right half-spaces). Use a binning approach to reduce kernel calls. Align bin boundaries with SVT macro cells (8^3) to avoid splitting SVTs. Bounding Box Computation: Compute tight bounding boxes for the resulting subregions using parallel reduction (e.g., Thrust) on the GPU. Check if macro cells are within the volumetric region of interest using Morton curve ordering. Recursion: Recursively apply steps 4-5 to the left and right children. 6. Halting: Stop when the targeted tree height or node count is reached. This method uses a recursive "farm-out" strategy across an MPI group. 1. Initialization: Processor 0 initializes MPI, reads the file, and calculates min/max data values for all voxel cells. 2. Median Finding: Processor 0 finds the median cell value to partition the data. 3. Partitioning: Processor 0 schedules the top half of the data array to the next processor in the group. Processor 0 recursively partitions the bottom half locally. Each subsequent processor, upon receiving a message, performs the same partitioning: farms out the top half to the next processor (deterministically predicted by a recursive routine) and partitions the bottom half locally. 4. Message Content: Messages contain only min/max values, Level-of-Detail (LOD), and an index into the full data array on Processor 0. This minimizes communication overhead. 5. Termination: Subcontracting continues until the limit of the processor array is reached. Remaining processors perform recursive partitioning locally. 6. Reconstruction: Processor 0 interrogates each process in the predicted order to retrieve message stubs. The stub order is used to write out the full k-d tree data. Used for unstructured data partitioning in ParaView. 1. Centroid Calculation: Find all centroids for all cells to deterministically place each cell in a region. 2. Axis Selection: Choose the coordinate direction to split the region, typically the longest axis, to prevent elongated regions and minimize plane-cell intersections. 3. Median Selection: Find the index of the median cell such that an equal number of cells lie on either side. Use the Floyd-Rivest selection algorithm, parallelized with prefetching for off-processor tests. 4. Partitioning: Partition cells based on the computed median. 5. Recursion: Apply steps 2-4 recursively until the desired number of regions is reached. Brick Size: 32^3 voxels (CPU/SVT variant). Macro Cell Size: 8^3 (GPU shared memory variant). Targeted Size: Height or number of nodes, influencing construction time and rendering performance. Halting Criteria: Parameters favoring shallow or deep trees. Virtual Voxel Size Increment: Default 1, for LODTree. Virtual Voxel Overlap Factor: Prevents small voxels at grid edges. Number of Processors: Ideally a power of two for efficiency. Identical Values: The Floyd-Rivest algorithm exhibits worst-case behavior with long sequences of identical values (common in aligned volume models), potentially increasing runtime from seconds to hours. A modified algorithm to detect and skip duplicates is required. Memory Limits: In MPI variants, Processor 0 must fit all simulation data in memory to create the initial array, limiting file size by available memory on the initial processor. Tree Balance: The implementation does not guarantee a well-balanced tree, but the extra searching overhead is insignificant compared to rendering calculation time. Java Compatibility: Requires careful consideration of compiler alignment, limiting maximum array size to a 32-bit signed integer, and defining all numeric fields as signed. Load Imbalance: If data cells are distributed as connected components, zooming in on a local region causes severe load imbalances because only a few processors handle rendering while others are idle. KDTreeSamplingPartition is a domain decomposition algorithm for distributing volume rendering samples across multiple compute blocks in a distributed-memory system. It builds a k-d tree structure over spatial data points by recursively splitting blocks along coordinate dimensions using a sampling-based approach to determine split positions. It sets itself apart from static partitioning methods by dynamically determining split planes via random sampling and managing neighbor links via a reduce proxy to handle wrap-around or boundary conditions. CPU/GPU Hybrid: Construction time is dominated by GPU kernel launches for bounding box computation and CPU recursion. The binning approach reduces kernel calls. Memory usage is optimized by fitting SVTs into L1 cache (32^3) and using shared memory for macro cells (8^3). MPI Partitioning: The recursive partitioning is the most time-consuming part (at least 90% of serial run time). Parallelization focuses on this step. Memory is limited by the capacity of Processor 0 to hold the full dataset. Coordinate Bisection: Selection is sub-linear on average (O(n) expected), but worst-case O(n^2) with duplicate values. Specific benchmarks are not provided in the sources, but the GPU variant achieves good utilization due to parallel reductions and smaller macro cell sizes. The MPI variant is most efficient when the number of processors is a power of two. In a test distributing 1 million cells to 128 processors, about 640,000 bytes of data were transferred to and stored at each processor in the worst case of not sharing node information. Strengths: Adaptive partitioning along orthogonal planes; supports early ray merging and culling; efficient for sparse volumes via occupancy queries; scalable to distributed memory. Limitations: Does not guarantee balanced trees; sensitive to data distribution (duplicate values); high memory requirement for root processor in MPI; complex synchronization in GPU hybrid approach. Use for sparse volume rendering where empty space skipping is critical. Use for parallel distributed rendering where spatial locality improves ray merging. Use for unstructured data partitioning in visualization tools like ParaView. K-d trees are preferred over octrees because they support adaptive partitioning along orthogonal coordinate planes and allow straightforward determination of the depth ordering of the resulting regions. Origin: The multi-core CPU variant was first presented in [ZSL18] and refined in [ZSL19], loosely based on work by Vidal et al. [VMD08] using summed area tables. MPI Variant: Developed for the DYNAISOLOD algorithm, targeting SGI and Intel teraflop machines, using a recursive "farm-out" strategy. Coordinate Bisection: Used in ParaView for parallel unstructured volume rendering, employing the Floyd-Rivest algorithm for median selection. History: The methods evolved to address the need for efficient spatial partitioning in large-scale volume rendering, moving from single-node heuristics to distributed and GPU-accelerated constructions. name: KDTreeSamplingPartition
head: DIY2 block sampling, Distributed sample distribution, KDTree Sampling Partitioning
body: KDTreeSamplingPartition is a domain decomposition algorithm for distributing volume rendering samples across multiple compute blocks in a distributed-memory system. It builds a k-d tree structure over spatial data points by recursively splitting blocks along coordinate dimensions using a sampling-based approach to determine split positions. It differs from static partitioning methods by dynamically computing split planes via random sampling and managing neighbor links via a reduce proxy to handle wrap-around or boundary conditions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Spatial points distributed across processing blocks, the spatial dimension dim, the number of samples to draw samples, a Partners object managing communication rounds, dimensions, swap flags, wrap-around, and domain bounds, and an SRP (Splitting Reduce Proxy) object managing communication links, global ID, and current round. Output: A partitioned set of points where each block holds points within its assigned k-d tree leaf region, and updated neighbor links for subsequent communication or rendering steps. Data Structures: dim: Integer representing the spatial dimension. points: Pointer to a member std::vector<Point> inside the Block structure. samples: Sizet specifying the number of samples to draw. Partners: Manages rounds(), dim(round), swapround(round), subround(round), wrap, and domain. SRP: Manages inlink(), outlink(), gid(), and round(). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Assign an equal number of samples to each processing block. Update inter-block links to handle wrap-around or boundary conditions across the domain. 2. Iterative Splitting: For each round r from 0 to partners.rounds() - 1: a. Determine the current splitting dimension dim: if srp.round() < partners.rounds(), dim = partners.dim(srp.round()); else dim = partners.dim(srp.round() - 1). b. If srp.round() == partners.rounds(), call updatelinks(b, srp, dim, partners.subround(srp.round() - 2), partners.swaprounds(), partners.wrap, partners.domain) to finalize links. c. If partners.swapround(srp.round()) is true (and not a link round): receive samples via receivesamples(b, srp, samples), then enqueue exchange via enqueueexchange(b, srp, dim, samples). d. If partners.subround(srp.round()) == 0: if srp.round() > 0, update links for the previous dimension prevdim = (dim - 1 < 0) ? dim + dim - 1: dim - 1 via updatelinks; then compute local samples via computelocalsamples(b, srp, dim). e. Else (final sample aggregation): add local samples via addsamples(b, srp, samples). If samples.size() != 1, find the median using std::nthelement on the samples vector, swap the median to index 0, resize the vector to 1, and forward via forwardsamples(b, srp, samples). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kdtreesamplingpartition(block, srp, partners): # Initialization assignequalsamples(block, partners.numblocks()) updateinterblocklinks(block, srp, partners.wrap, partners.domain) for r in range(partners.rounds()): # Determine splitting dimension if srp.round() < partners.rounds(): dim = partners.dim(srp.round()) else: dim = partners.dim(srp.round() - 1) # Final link update condition if srp.round() == partners.rounds(): updatelinks(block, srp, dim, partners.subround(r - 2), partners.swaprounds(), partners.wrap, partners.domain) # Swap round handling if partners.swapround(r): receivesamples(block, srp, samples) enqueueexchange(block, srp, dim, samples) # Sub-round 0 handling if partners.subround(r) == 0: if r > 0: prevdim = (dim - 1) % dim updatelinks(block, srp, prevdim, partners.subround(r - 2), partners.swaprounds(), partners.wrap, partners.domain) computelocalsamples(block, srp, dim) else: # Final sample aggregation addsamples(block, srp, samples) if len(samples) != 1: samples.sort() median = samples[len(samples) // 2] samples[0] = median samples = samples[:1] forwardsamples(block, srp, samples) def computelocalsamples(block, srp, dim): pointssize = len(block.points) n = min(pointssize, samples) coords = [] for in range(n): idx = rand() % pointssize coord = block.points[idx][dim] coords.append(coord) srp.outlink().target(0).enqueue(coords) def addsamples(block, srp, samples): for nbrgid in range(srp.inlink().size()): neighborsamples = srp.inlink().target(nbrgid).dequeue() samples.extend(neighborsamples) def enqueueexchange(block, srp, dim, samples): if srp.outlink().size() == 0: return split = samples[0] outpoints = [[], []] for p in block.points: if p[dim] < split: outpoints[0].append(p) else: outpoints[1].append(p) # Swap appropriate subset back based on target matching srp.gid() # Enqueue other subsets to respective targets for targetidx in range(srp.outlink().size()): if targetidx == srp.gid(): block.points = outpoints[targetidx] else: srp.outlink().target(targetidx).enqueue(outpoints[targetidx]) # Update link bounds if targetidx == 0: srp.outlink().core.max[dim] = split else: srp.outlink().core.min[dim] = split def dequeueexchange(block, srp, dim): for nbrgid in range(srp.inlink().size()): if nbrgid == srp.gid(): continue inpoints = srp.inlink().target(nbrgid).dequeue() for p in inpoints: if not (srp.inlink().core.min[dim] <= p[dim] <= srp.inlink().core.max[dim]): raise RuntimeError("Point out of bounds") block.points.append(p) def updatelinks(block, srp, dim, prevdim, swaprounds, wrap, domain): linkmap = {target: idx for idx, target in enumerate(srp.inlink())} splits = [] dirs = [] for link in srp.inlink(): data = link.dequeue() splits.append(data.split) dirs.append(-data.dir) # Reverse direction newlink = Link(dim) lower = not (gid & (1 << (rounds - 1 - round))) for entry in linkmap: d = dirs[entry] if d[dim] != 0: if (d[dim] < 0 and lower) or (d[dim] > 0 and not lower): neighborgid = dividegid(gid, lower, rounds, round) updateneighborbounds(newlink.bounds, lower, splits[entry], dim) if wrap: addwrap(newlink, neighborgid) newlink.add(neighborgid) else: for j in range(2): neighborgid = dividegid(gid, lower, rounds, round) updateneighborbounds(newlink.bounds, lower, splits[entry], dim) if intersects(newlink.bounds, domain, wrap, dim): newlink.add(neighborgid) # Add dual block neighbor dualgid = dividegid(gid, not lower, rounds, round) updateneighborbounds(newlink.bounds, not lower, splits[entry], dim) newlink.add(dualgid, direction="right" if lower else "left") link = newlink def dividegid(gid, lower, rounds, round): bit = 1 << (rounds - 1 - round) if lower: return gid & ~bit else: return gid | bit def findsplit(changed, original, dim): for i in range(dim): if changed.min[i] != original.min[i]: return changed.min[i] if changed.max[i] != original.max[i]: return changed.max[i] assert False, "No difference found" def intersects(x, y, wrap, domain, dim): if wrap: return (x.min[dim] == domain.min[dim] and y.max[dim] == domain.max[dim]) or \ (y.min[dim] == domain.min[dim] and x.max[dim] == domain.max[dim]) return x.min[dim] <= y.max[dim] and y.min[dim] <= x.max[dim] def updateneighborbounds(bounds, lower, split, dim): if lower: bounds.max[dim] = split else: bounds.min[dim] = split def forwardsamples(block, srp, samples): for target in srp.outlink(): target.enqueue(samples) def receivesamples(block, srp, samples): samples = srp.inlink().target(0).dequeue() Parameters: samples: Number of samples to draw. Typical value: Not given in the sources. dim: Spatial dimension. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The current implementation does not perform a perfect subsample; it should randomly select samples so the total equals samples nblocks. Random sampling relies on the legacy C rand() function, which must be seeded externally before use. Validation of point coordinates during dequeueexchange throws a std::runtimeerror if a point is outside the expected bounds [link->core().min[dim], link->core().max[dim]]. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: The method dynamically adapts to data distribution via sampling, but relies on legacy rand() and does not guarantee perfect subsampling. When to use it: Not given in the sources. Origin: The algorithm is part of the Rover project, developed at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. History and development: It is integrated into the Rover framework for energy engine rendering. Where it is used: Distributed volume rendering systems. llnl/rover, https://github.com/llnl/rover, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: K-D Tree Subdivision
head: Binary Space Partitioning (BSP) Tree Construction, k-D Tree Volume Subdivision
body: K-D Tree Subdivision partitions a 3D volume into subvolumes using a k-d tree structure with alternating binary subdivision of coordinate planes, enabling unambiguous front-to-back ordering for compositing. Unlike fixed viewpoint partitioning which minimizes overlap by slicing orthogonal to the view, k-D tree partitioning is view-independent and suitable for animation sequences where the viewpoint changes. It determines the front-to-back image compositing order hierarchically by recursive traversal, visiting the 'front' child before the 'back' child. Inputs: A 3D volume grid of points (voxels) or scattered data samples. Outputs: A k-d tree structure defining subvolumes and a traversal order for front-to-back compositing. Data Structures: The volume is represented as a grid of points or an array of samples containing position (x, y, z) and function value. The tree can be stored recursively with node pointers or in a flat array. For array storage, the root is at index 1, and children of node j are at 2j and 2j+1. Steps: 1. Recursive Subdivision: Start with the root node representing the bounding box of all samples. For a node at depth i, determine the split axis d = i \pmod 3. Sort the vector v of samples in the xd direction. Split v into two halves, v1 and v2. If v is odd-sized, store a link to the midpoint and the pivot value in the current node. Recurse on v1 and v2 until the subvector length is 1. Each leaf node contains exactly one sample. 2. Boundary Replication: When a volume is evenly subdivided, ray samples lying in the cut boundary region are lost because each voxel is located at a corner of the grid. To prevent this, replicate one layer of the boundary grid at each subvolume. For example, if splitting into Subvolume 1 and Subvolume 2 at layer k, Subvolume 1 includes layers 1 to k, and Subvolume 2 includes layers k to n, where layer k is replicated in Subvolume 2. 3. Traversal for Compositing: Determine the front-to-back compositing order by recursively traversing the k-d tree. Visit the 'front' child before the 'back' child. The definition of 'front' and 'back' depends on the view direction relative to the split plane. For a split along axis d, if the view direction has a positive component along d, the child with higher coordinate values is 'front'. Formulas: Tree height: \lfloor \log2(n + 1) \rfloor. Worst-case number of nodes (when n = 2^j): 2n - 1. Binary indexing operators: a^0d = ad, a^jd = (a^{j-1}d) 2 (left shift), aj = (a{j-1}) \text{ div } 2 (right shift). Father of node bd is b{d1} (right shift). Children are b{d1} and (b{d1}) \oplus 1d (XOR with 1). Parameters: Alternating axis: x, y, z repeating. Leaf size: 1 sample. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Loss: If boundary replication is not performed, black strips will appear in the composited image when the view vector is parallel to the cut plane. View Dependency: The 'front' and 'back' children must be determined dynamically based on the current view direction during traversal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildkdtree(samples, depth=0): if len(samples) == 1: return LeafNode(pos=samples[0].pos, val=samples[0].val) axis = depth % 3 sortedsamples = sorted(samples, key=lambda s: s.pos[axis]) mid = len(sortedsamples) // 2 leftsamples = sortedsamples[:mid] rightsamples = sortedsamples[mid:] pivot = sortedsamples[mid].pos[axis] return InternalNode(axis=axis, pivot=pivot, left=buildkdtree(leftsamples, depth + 1), right=buildkdtree(rightsamples, depth + 1)) def traversefronttoback(node, viewdir): if node is None: return if node.axis is None: composite(node.val) return frontchild = node.right if viewdir[node.axis] >= 0 else node.left backchild = node.left if viewdir[node.axis] >= 0 else node.right traversefronttoback(frontchild, viewdir) traversefronttoback(backchild, viewdir) A data structure storing n scattered data points in a 3D kd-tree to enable fast neighbor search, avoiding expensive Voronoi diagram computation for natural neighbors. It stores the tree in a single array where the root is at index 1, and children of node j are at 2j and 2j+1. Binary indexing operators are used: a^0d = ad, a^jd = (a^{j-1}d) 2 (left shift), aj = (a{j-1}) \text{ div } 2 (right shift). The father of node bd is b{d1} (right shift). Children are b{d1} and (b{d1}) \oplus 1d (XOR with 1). This method is chosen when fast neighbor search is required for point-based rendering. Time Complexity: Construction is O(n \log n) due to sorting at each level. Traversal is O(N) where N is the number of nodes visited. Memory Complexity: O(n) for storing samples and tree structure. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: View-independent, suitable for animation. Hierarchical structure allows parallel processing of sibling nodes. Limitations: Requires boundary replication to avoid artifacts. Sorting at each level can be costly for large datasets. When to use: When viewpoint is unknown or changes frequently (e.g., animation). When parallel compositing is desired. When not to use: When a fixed orthographic viewpoint is guaranteed and minimal overlap is the primary optimization goal. The method was proposed to handle volume partitioning for distributed rendering where the viewpoint might change or be perspective. It builds on the concept of k-d trees for spatial partitioning. name: Empty Space Skipping with Octree
head: Octree-based Empty Space Skipping, Min-Max Octree Empty Space Skipping, Empty space leaping
body: Empty Space Skipping with Octree is an acceleration technique for semi-transparent volume rendering that skips empty regions using an octree spatial data structure to reduce the number of reconstruction samples. It differs from sibling methods like Brick Classification and Empty Space Skipping by storing conservative min/max scalar ranges at every node of a recursive tree, allowing rays to leap over intervals where the maximum value is below the opacity threshold. Unlike Octree Traversal with Min/Max Pruning which focuses on finer resolution pruning for unclassified volumes, this method provides the foundational hierarchical traversal logic for culling entire empty blocks. Inputs: Volume dataset V with voxel values. Transfer function T(v) mapping voxel values to color and opacity. Ray R(t) = O + tD for each pixel. Precomputed Octree structure. Outputs: Final pixel color and opacity. Reduced number of ray marching steps. Data Structures: The volume is recursively subdivided into an octree. Each node stores the minimum and maximum scalar values of its subtree. Node Layout: isleaf: Boolean. minval: Scalar minimum of the region. maxval: Scalar maximum of the region. children: Array of 8 child nodes (if not leaf). Leaf Node Layout: minval, maxval: Conservative estimates of the min/max values in the leaf's region. data: Pointer to the underlying voxel data or polynomial coefficients. Pre-classification Histograms (Optional but recommended for correctness): To avoid false transparent/opaque classification in pre-classification scenarios, quantized binary histograms are used. histogramv: List of size s (e.g., 255 for 8-bit voxels), quantized into buckets of size 32. Flags are set for every voxel value v present in the brick. histogramo: Similar histogram for opacity values. A brick is classified as fully transparent only if all buckets in both histograms indicate transparency. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Octree Construction): 1. Subdivide the volume recursively into an octree. 2. For leaf nodes, estimate min/max values. If using B-splines, use the convex combination property of the basis functions. If using polynomial pieces (e.g., Bezier-Bernstein), construct BB-forms for tetrahedral pieces and set the cell's min/max to the min/max of these coefficients. 3. Propagate min/max values from leaves to the root. For each internal node, node.minval = min(children.minval) and node.maxval = max(children.maxval). 4. (Optional) For pre-classification, build quantized binary histograms for voxel values and opacities for each brick/leaf to ensure conservative transparency checks. 2. Ray Traversal (Empty Space Skipping): 1. Start traversal at the root of the octree. 2. Intersect the ray with the current node's bounding box. If no intersection, return empty. 3. Check if the node is empty: Min/Max Check: If node.maxval < opacitythreshold (or isovalue), the region is empty. Skip this entire branch. Update the ray's entry point to the exit point of this node's bounding box and return to the parent to continue traversal. Histogram Check (Pre-classification): If histograms indicate all values map to zero opacity, skip the branch. 4. If the node is not empty: If it is a leaf, perform standard ray marching/sampling within this region. If it is an internal node, recursively traverse its 8 children. 5. Update ray entry/exit points as the ray leaps over empty segments. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Returns the accumulated color and opacity, or None if skipped. """ # 1. Intersect ray with node bounding box tmin, tmax = intersectboundingbox(ray, node.bbox) # If ray does not intersect this node's space, skip if tmax < ray.tmin or tmin > ray.tmax: return None # 2. Check for empty space using min/max values # Conservative check: if max value in this region is below threshold, it's transparent if node.maxval < opacitythreshold: # Skip this entire branch # Update ray's tmin to skip past this node's exit point ray.tmin = max(ray.tmin, tmax) return None # 3. If leaf, perform sampling if node.isleaf: return samplevolumeray(ray, node.data, opacitythreshold) # 4. If internal node, traverse children # Note: Order of children traversal can be optimized for coherence accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for child in node.children: # Recursively traverse result = traverseoctree(ray, child, opacitythreshold) # If result is not None, we hit something if result is not None: # Composite result into accumulatedcolor # Standard volume compositing: # Cout = Cin + Cnew alphanew (1 - alphain) # alphaout = alphain + alphanew (1 - alphain) accumulatedcolor = composite(accumulatedcolor, result) # Early ray termination if opaque enough if accumulatedcolor[3] >= 0.99: break return accumulatedcolor def samplevolumeray(ray, data, opacitythreshold): """ Sample the volume data along the ray segment within the leaf node. """ # Intersect ray with leaf bounding box to get precise entry/exit tstart, tend = intersectboundingbox(ray, data.bbox) color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) t = tstart stepsize = data.resolution / 10.0 # Example step size while t < tend: # Sample voxel value at ray position v = samplevoxel(ray, t, data) # Map to opacity alpha = transferfunctionopacity(v) # Composite color = composite(color, (samplecolor(v), alpha)) # Early termination if color[3] >= 0.99: break t += stepsize return color Parameters: opacitythreshold: The minimum opacity value required to consider a region non-empty. Typical value: 0.01 to 0.1 depending on transfer function. bucketsize: Size of quantized histogram buckets. Typical value: 32. b: Trade-off factor for leaf node granularity (group of b^3 polynomials). Higher b reduces tree depth but increases memory and reduces skipping efficiency. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Pre-classification False Positives: In pre-classification, a voxel value might map to zero opacity, but interpolation could yield non-zero color/opacity. Using min/max alone can lead to false transparent classification (skipping visible regions). Use quantized binary histograms to ensure conservative classification (transparent regions may be classified as opaque, but not vice versa). Precision: Min/max values must be conservative estimates. If the estimated max is lower than the true max, empty space skipping will incorrectly skip visible regions. Boundary Conditions: Ensure ray intersection with bounding boxes is robust to avoid gaps between nodes. body: Octree Traversal with Min/Max Pruning is an acceleration technique for volume rendering that uses a hierarchical data structure storing the minimum and maximum scalar values of voxel regions to prune transparent space and determine precise ray entry points. It is specifically designed for unclassified volumes where the opacity transfer function or classification parameters change frequently, avoiding the expensive preprocessing required by pre-classified rendering methods. Unlike block-based entry point determination, it operates at a finer resolution than block granularity, significantly reducing the number of rays intersecting transparent regions. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scalar volume dataset V, a ray R(t) = O + tD defined by origin O and direction D, a target isovalue I, and a transfer function TF(s) mapping scalar s to color/opacity. Output: A boolean hit status and the intersection point t for the isosurface, or null if the ray passes through transparent/empty space. Data Structures The method uses a single structure serving as both data container and acceleration tree. The structure is an octree where each node stores metadata for its children. Node Layout: childmins[8]: Array of 8 floats, storing the minimum scalar value present in each of the 8 child octants. childmaxs[8]: Array of 8 floats, storing the maximum scalar value present in each of the 8 child octants. childoffset: Integer. If negative (typically -1), the node is a leaf. If non-negative, it points to the first child in a contiguous memory block (or hash table entry). Implicit State: During traversal, the algorithm maintains child (current child index 0-7) and childcell (3D integer coordinates of the current cell within the octree level). Leaf Layout: Leaves store the actual scalar values for the voxels in the cell. At the maximum octree depth, leaves may represent "cap geometry" rather than volumetric data, requiring specific traversal logic. Algorithm Steps The traversal is performed in front-to-back visibility order. 1. Initialization: Start at the root node. Initialize ray parameters: tenter (entry time into current node) and texit (exit time from current node). Initialize childcell to the root coordinates. 2. Node Traversal Loop: While tenter < texit: Calculate Child Intersections: Determine the intersection times of the ray with the mid-planes of the 8 child octants. Sort these intersections to process children in front-to-back order. Iterate Valid Children: For each child intersection time tcenter (sorted): Calculate childtexit = min(tcenter, texit). Min/Max Pruning Check: Check if the isovalue I lies within the scalar range of the current child c: I \ge \text{node.child\mins}[c] \quad \text{OR} \quad I \le \text{node.child\maxs}[c] If False: The child does not contain the isovalue. Skip this child. If True: Proceed to traverse the child. Child Traversal: If node.childoffset == -1 (Leaf): Traverse the scalar leaf data. If the isosurface is found, return true. Else if depth == octdata.maxdepth (Cap Geometry): Traverse the cap geometry. If hit, return true. Else (Internal Node): Recursively call the traversal function with updated bounds: tenter becomes childtenter, texit becomes childtexit. If recursive call returns true, return true. Update Bounds: If childtexit == texit, the ray has exited the volume or current bounding region without hitting anything relevant. Return false. Update childtenter = childtexit for the next iteration. Update Child Index: Determine the axis bit from the current axis index using an axis table (e.g., {4, 2, 1} for X, Y, Z). If the current child index has the axis bit set: Clear the bit in child and the corresponding bit in childcell. Else: Set the bit in child and the corresponding bit in childcell. 3. Termination: If the loop completes without a hit, return false. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseminmaxoctree(ray, node, depth, maxdepth, isovalue, tenter, texit): """ Recursively traverse an octree using min/max pruning. ray: Ray object with origin O and direction D. node: Current octree node. depth: Current depth in the octree. maxdepth: Maximum depth of the octree. isovalue: Target scalar value for isosurface. tenter: Entry time of ray into current node. texit: Exit time of ray from current node. """ # Initialize child state for root traversal if needed, # but typically child index and cell are maintained in the loop context. # For this self-contained function, we assume 'child' and 'childcell' # are passed or maintained in a wrapper. Here we iterate children. # Note: The source uses a specific iterative loop over axis intersections. # We replicate that logic. child = 0 # Current child index being processed childcell = Vec3i(0, 0, 0) # Current cell coordinates # Calculate sorted axis intersections for the current node's children # This determines the order in which we visit children (front-to-back) axisisects = calculatesortedaxisintersections(ray, node, tenter, texit) childtenter = tenter for i in range(len(axisisects)): axisidx = axisisects[i] tcenter = ray.intersectplane(axisidx) # Time of intersection with child boundary if tcenter >= texit: break childtexit = min(tcenter, texit) # Determine which child index corresponds to this axis intersection step # In the source, 'child' is updated iteratively. # We need to identify the child index 'c' for the current slab. # The source logic implies 'child' tracks the current child being evaluated. # We assume 'child' is updated at the end of the loop. # For the first iteration, child is 0. c = child # Min/Max Pruning if isovalue >= node.childmins[c] or isovalue <= node.childmaxs[c]: # Child contains isovalue, traverse it if node.childoffset == -1: # Leaf node if traversescalarleaf(ray, node, isovalue, childtenter, childtexit): return True elif depth == maxdepth: # Cap geometry at max depth if traversecap(ray, node, isovalue, childtenter, childtexit): return True else: # Internal node if traverseminmaxoctree(ray, node.children[c], depth + 1, maxdepth, isovalue, childtenter, childtexit): return True # Check if we have exited the current bounding region if childtexit == texit: return False # Update tenter for next child childtenter = childtexit # Update child index and cell coordinates for next iteration axisbit = axistable[axisidx] # e.g., 4 for X, 2 for Y, 1 for Z childbit = 1 << axisidx # Or specific bit mapping if child & axisbit: child &= ~axisbit childcell[axisidx] &= ~childbit else: child |= axisbit childcell[axisidx] |= childbit return False Parameters isovalue: The scalar threshold for the isosurface. octdata.maxdepth: The maximum depth of the octree structure. Transfer Function: The RGB\alpha map used for classification. Changes to this require recomputing local majorants from stored min/max ranges. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Noise Thresholds: If the isolevel is lower than the noise threshold, Octree Max/Min is less affected by low-level noise than Integral Octree because it checks if the max value is below the threshold. Hole Generation: Octree Max/Min must loop through all voxels at the edges of an empty branch to avoid generating holes in the rendered surface. Max Depth Handling: At the maximum octree depth, the algorithm does not traverse further into children but instead calls traversecap, implying leaf nodes at max depth represent cap geometry rather than volumetric data. Precision: Floating-point precision in ray-slab intersection calculations can lead to gaps or overlaps if not handled carefully. A technique to reduce the visited set of cells in marching cubes by embedding a min-max hierarchy in a branch-on-need octree to trivially ignore empty regions of a volume. It enables interactive rendering of data up to 512^3 resolution. Time Complexity: O(N) in the worst case where N is the number of voxels, but typically much faster due to pruning. The complexity depends on the sparsity of the volume and the transfer function. Memory Complexity: The octree structure stores min/max values for each node. For a volume of size V, the memory overhead is proportional to the number of nodes in the octree. Compressed volumes can occupy 10-30% of the original size. Performance: Supports up to 90% reduction in sample computations for sparse data. Strengths: Allows interactive changes to the transfer function without rebuilding the entire acceleration structure, as min/max ranges are stored and used to recompute majorants. Efficient memory order (cache hits) regardless of viewpoint. Suitable for large, time-variant data. Limitations: Requires preprocessing to build the octree and compute min/max values. At max depth, handling cap geometry adds complexity. Less effective for highly dense volumes where most nodes contain the isovalue. The method was introduced by Knoll et al. in 2006. It was developed to address the difficulty of interactive rendering of large volumes, particularly where GPU memory limits and video bus bandwidth restrict real-time rendering of time-variant data. The technique embeds the acceleration tree and scalar data in a single structure, employing optimized octree hash schemes to achieve competitive frame rates on multicore architectures. It is a seminal implementation of min-max octrees for isosurface extraction and direct rendering. body: Min-Max Octree Rendering is an acceleration technique for volume rendering that uses a hierarchical data structure storing the minimum and maximum scalar values of voxel regions to prune transparent space and determine precise ray entry points. It is specifically designed for unclassified volumes where the opacity transfer function or classification parameters change frequently, avoiding the expensive preprocessing required by pre-classified rendering methods. Unlike block-based entry point determination, it operates at a finer resolution than block granularity, significantly reducing the number of rays intersecting transparent regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unclassified volume data (scalar field), rendering context (view, shading, classification tables), and a precomputed min-max octree. Output: Rendered image array. Data Structures: 1. Min-Max Octree: A hierarchical structure where each node stores the minimum and maximum values of the voxel field for its region. Layout: Linearized octree bit encoding using hierarchy compression. Node Content: 2-byte minimum and 2-byte maximum values (4 bytes total per node). Indexing: Nodes are indexed by index(node) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} octanti(node) \cdot 8^{N - i - 1}, where N is the octree depth and octanti(node) is the octant of level i. There are 8^N possible indices for depth N. 2. Entry Point Buffer: Stores the block index and the corresponding octree node index for each ray. 3. Lookup Table: Precomputed relative translational offsets for octree nodes, sized 8^N entries. Parameters: basenodesize: Size in voxels of one side of the smallest node in the octree. Controls resolution vs. memory trade-off. Typical value: 4. range: Range of table indices considered "small" for classification sensitivity. Affects pruning effectiveness. maxopacitythreshold: Threshold for pixel opacity to stop compositing. Typical value: 0.95. intermediateimagesize: Hints for work buffer allocation (VPINTWIDTHHINT, VPINTHEIGHTHINT). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Define the unclassified volume using vpSetVolumeSize(), vpSetVoxelSize(), vpSetVoxelField(), and vpSetRawVoxels(). Initialize volume data. 2. Octree Construction: For each classification table, call vpMinMaxOctreeThreshold(paramnum, range) to define sensitivity. Call vpCreateMinMaxOctree(vpc, rootnodesize, basenodesize) to compute the octree from the raw volume data. Note: If volume data changes, vpCreateMinMaxOctree() must be called again. 3. Rendering Loop: Set view and shading parameters. Choose classification function (opacity transfer function). Call vpRenderRawVolume(). Detailed Rendering Logic (from): 1. Entry Point Determination: Use the min-max octree to find the first non-transparent node along the ray. The entry point buffer stores the block index and octree node index. Calculate the ray entry depth: d{entry} = tz + \text{offset}{node}, where tz is the translation vector component and \text{offset}{node} is retrieved from the lookup table using index(node). 2. Projection: Create a template for every octree level. Recursively traverse the hierarchical classification information in back-to-front order. For each node, if it is non-transparent (based on min/max values vs. classification thresholds), project the appropriate template for that level. 3. Compositing: Compositing proceeds from the determined entry point. Stop compositing when the accumulated opacity reaches maxopacitythreshold. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderminmaxoctree(volumedata, context): # 1. Initialization: Define unclassified volume setvolumesize(context, volumedata.size) setvoxelsize(context, volumedata.voxelsize) setvoxelfield(context, volumedata.field) setrawvoxels(context, volumedata.array) # 2. Octree Construction # Define classification sensitivity for a parameter vpminmaxoctreethreshold(context, paramnum=0, range=10) # Build the octree (rootnodesize is reserved, typically 0) vpcreateminmaxoctree(context, rootnodesize=0, basenodesize=4) # 3. Rendering Loop while renderingneeded(context): setviewandshading(context) setopacitytransferfunction(context, context.currenttransferfunction) # Render using the octree for acceleration vprenderrawvolume(context) def vprenderrawvolume(context): # Get intermediate image buffer size hints if not set if not hasintermediatehints(context): maxdim = 2 max(context.volumedimensions) setstate(context, "VPINTWIDTHHINT", maxdim) setstate(context, "VPINTHEIGHTHINT", maxdim) # Initialize entry point buffer entrypoints = allocateentrypointbuffer() # For each ray in the view: for ray in context.rays: # Traverse min-max octree to find first non-transparent node node = traverseoctreeforentry(ray, context.octree) if node is not None: # Calculate entry depth: tz + relative offset nodeidx = calculatenodeindex(node) offset = lookuprelativeoffset(nodeidx) entrydepth = ray.tz + offset # Store in buffer entrypoints[ray.id] = (node.blockindex, nodeidx, entrydepth) # Compositing from entrydepth opacity = 0.0 finalcolor = 0.0 for sample in ray.samplesfrom(entrydepth): value = sample.value alpha = context.transferfunction(value) opacity += alpha (1.0 - opacity) finalcolor += alpha (1.0 - opacity) sample.color if opacity >= context.maxopacitythreshold: break entrypoints[ray.id].finalcolor = finalcolor def setvolumesize(context, size): context.volumesize = size def setvoxelsize(context, size): context.voxelsize = size def setvoxelfield(context, field): context.voxelfield = field def setrawvoxels(context, data): context.rawvoxels = data def vpminmaxoctreethreshold(context, paramnum, range): context.classificationrange[paramnum] = range def vpcreateminmaxoctree(context, rootnodesize, basenodesize): context.octree = computeminmaxoctree(context.rawvoxels, basenodesize) def renderingneeded(context): return True def setviewandshading(context): pass def setopacitytransferfunction(context, func): context.transferfunction = func def hasintermediatehints(context): return "intermediatehints" in context def setstate(context, key, value): context.state[key] = value def allocateentrypointbuffer(): return {} def traverseoctreeforentry(ray, octree): return octree.findfirstnontransparent(ray) def calculatenodeindex(node): idx = 0 for i, octant in enumerate(node.octants): idx += octant (8 (node.depth - i - 1)) return idx def lookuprelativeoffset(nodeidx): return context.offsettable[nodeidx] Pitfalls and Errors: Shading lookup tables sized incorrectly, invalid voxel fields, or invalid material types cause VPERRORBADSHADER. Singular view transformation matrix causes VPERRORSINGULAR. Volume size not set, invalid, or missing data causes VPERRORBADVOLUME. Opacity transfer function tables have invalid sizes or are incorrectly specified (render raw only) causing VPERRORBADCLASSIFIER. Angle between shadow light vector and viewing direction too large (>45°) causes VPERRORBADSHADOW; fix by changing light direction or disabling shadows. A classification-independent data structure for encoding spatial coherence in unclassified volumes. Unlike standard min-max octrees which may require preprocessing when opacity changes, the rain-max octree allows classification and rendering without an expensive preprocessing step. It enables classifying and rendering a 256^3 voxel volume in three seconds when combined with shear-warp rendering. Time Complexity: Rendering is significantly faster than rendering without an octree, but slower than rendering with pre-classified volumes (vpRenderClassifiedVolume). Memory Complexity: The min-max octree for depth 3 with 4 bytes per node requires at most 2340 bytes; classification information requires 66 bytes. Total memory overhead is approximately 10% for typical datasets (e.g., 32^3 blocks). Strengths: Ideal for interactive exploration where opacity transfer functions or classification parameters change frequently. Provides finer-grained culling than block-based methods. Limitations: Requires preprocessing time to build the octree if the volume data changes. Slower than pre-classified rendering for static classification. When to use: When volume data or opacity transfer function changes between renderings. When not to use: When a single rendering is needed (raw volume rendering is faster due to no octree overhead) or when classification is static (pre-classified rendering is faster). The min-max octree was introduced as part of the VolPack library to accelerate volume rendering of unclassified data. It extends block-based entry point determination by replacing block-level min/max values with an octree structure. The concept was further refined in research on efficient visualization of large medical datasets, where it was combined with shear-warp factorization and cell invisibility caches. The "rain-max" variant was proposed to eliminate preprocessing costs associated with opacity changes. name: Octree Empty Block Culling
head: Octree Leaf Culling, Recursive Status Check
body: Octree Empty Block Culling is a visibility culling technique that recursively traverses an octree to determine if a node contains any non-empty data blocks, returning a status of EMPTY or NONEMPTY to enable early ray termination or skipping. It builds on Empty Space Skipping with Octree by providing the specific recursive logic required to classify nodes based on the presence of underlying data blocks. Unlike Octree Traversal with Min/Max Pruning which uses bounding volume overlaps, this method relies on explicit block existence checks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A linear index to the current octree node (idx), the maximum tree depth (maxdepth), a flat array of octree nodes (nodes), and a memory management unit or block loader interface (mmu). Output: A boolean indicating NONEMPTY (true) or EMPTY (false). Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains a depth field indicating the current hierarchy level and a status field storing EMPTY or NONEMPTY. Block Loader (mmu): Provides a getBlock method that returns a pointer to the data block associated with a leaf node, or nullptr if the block is not loaded or does not exist. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize nodes[idx].status to EMPTY. 2. If nodes[idx].depth == maxdepth (leaf node): Call mmu.getBlock(idx). If the result is nullptr, set nodes[idx].status = EMPTY and return false. Otherwise, set nodes[idx].status = NONEMPTY and return true. 3. If internal node: Iterate i from 0 to 7. Compute child linear index: childidx = (idx << 3) + i + 1. Recursively call the status check on childidx. If any child returns true, set nodes[idx].status = NONEMPTY. Return nodes[idx].status == NONEMPTY. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def checknodestatus(idx, maxdepth, nodes, mmu): """ Recursively determines if an octree node contains non-empty data blocks. Args: idx: Linear index of the current octree node. maxdepth: The maximum depth of the octree. nodes: Flat array of octree node objects. mmu: Memory management unit with a getBlock method. Returns: bool: True if the node or any of its descendants contain non-empty blocks, False otherwise. """ nodes[idx].status = "EMPTY" # Leaf check if nodes[idx].depth == maxdepth: block = mmu.getBlock(idx) if block is None: nodes[idx].status = "EMPTY" return False nodes[idx].status = "NONEMPTY" return True # Internal node: recursively check all 8 children for i in range(8): childidx = (idx << 3) + i + 1 if checknodestatus(childidx, maxdepth, nodes, mmu): nodes[idx].status = "NONEMPTY" return True return nodes[idx].status == "NONEMPTY" Parameters: maxdepth: The depth at which nodes are considered leaves. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Initialization: The leaf check compares node->depth to the maximum depth parameter. If the tree depth is not set correctly during initialization, all nodes may be incorrectly treated as internal or leaf nodes, leading to incorrect culling results. View-dependent visibility culling is an acceleration technique that discards voxels or nodes occluded by previously traversed geometry closer to the camera. It extends empty-space skipping by ordering traversal based on camera position, allowing the renderer to skip nodes hidden behind already-rendered surfaces. Unlike static culling, it leverages the multiresolution nature of hierarchical structures (like octrees or quadtrees) to adaptively decide extraction or rendering resolution based on visibility. In this variant, shells' ranges over a node are computed once per pass for up to 4 tiles of 64 functions (each lane owns a function of every tile) instead of once per tile, only for shells reaching the node. A dropped shell has every AO below 10^{-10} over the node; fntail (2 \times 10^{-10} times the column sum of |C|) is added to every function's bound for them. This method tests whether an octree node collides with obstacles to classify it as Empty or Mixed, avoiding explicit Blocked detection. It runs a collision test using the node size; it returns Empty if no collision is detected, and Mixed if a collision is detected. A pitfall of this single-pass size test is that it may miss internal full occlusion; this is resolved by recursive subdivision in BuildNodeRecursive. Time and Memory Complexity: The time complexity is proportional to the number of nodes visited during the recursive traversal. In the worst case, it visits all nodes; in the best case, it visits only the root and immediate children if they are marked empty. Memory complexity is O(D) auxiliary space per recursive call stack frame, where D is the tree depth. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement; enables early ray termination. Limitations: Requires explicit block existence checks; sensitive to correct depth initialization. When to use it and when not: Use it when the volume data is sparse and stored in an octree with explicit block pointers. Not given in the sources. The method originates from implementations of parallel volume rendering systems using octrees, such as those found in open-source repositories like hopexn/VolumeRenderingParallel. It is used in GPU and CPU-based volume renderers that require efficient culling of empty regions to improve rendering performance. hopexn/VolumeRenderingParallel, https://github.com/hopexn/VolumeRenderingParallel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) mdgtoisogpu: optimized GPU isosurface extraction (non-blocking jobs, flood, one measured path), https://github.com/scanberg/mdlib/pull/15, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) UE5 Tutorial | Simple SVO Pathfinder for 3D Pathfinding, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QmDbXgZSLA, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: View-Dependent Visibility Culling
head: Camera-ordered visibility, Livnat and Hansen culling
body: View-dependent visibility culling is an acceleration technique for volume rendering that orders the traversal of an octree based on the camera position to cull nodes occluded by previously traversed, closer nodes. It extends standard empty-space skipping by ensuring that only visible surface nodes are processed, thereby accelerating both extraction and rasterization. Unlike parent methods that only skip empty space, this method explicitly handles occlusion between non-empty nodes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree structure representing the volume data, and a camera position/orientation. Output: A set of visible nodes (or a traversal order) that excludes occluded subtrees. Data Structures: Octree: The standard octree layout where each node indicates if it contains surface data (non-empty) or is empty. Steps: 1. Camera-Ordered Traversal: Traverse the octree starting from the root, prioritizing nodes closer to the camera. This establishes a depth order for visibility. 2. Empty Subtree Pruning: During traversal, if a node is identified as empty (containing no surface), prune its entire subtree immediately. 3. Occlusion Culling: For each non-empty node reached, check if it is occluded by any previously traversed node that is closer to the camera. If the current node is occluded by a closer, already-processed node, cull it (skip its processing). If it is visible, process it (e.g., extract mesh or render) and mark its spatial extent as "occupied" for subsequent occlusion checks. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Occlusion checks require robust geometric intersection tests or depth buffer comparisons to determine if a node is truly behind a closer node. Dynamic Cameras: If the camera moves significantly, the traversal order and occlusion status must be recomputed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def viewdependentvisibilityculling(octree, camera): # List to keep track of visible bounding boxes for occlusion testing visibleboxes = [] visiblenodes = [] # Helper to check if a box is occluded by any previously visible box def isoccluded(box): for vb in visibleboxes: if boxisbehindcameraandoccluded(box, vb, camera): return True return False # Recursive traversal function def traverse(node): # Base case: leaf node if node.isleaf(): if not node.isempty(): if not isoccluded(node.boundingbox): visiblenodes.append(node) visibleboxes.append(node.boundingbox) return # Recursive case: internal node # Sort children by distance to camera to process closer nodes first children = sorted(node.children, key=lambda c: distancetocamera(c.center, camera)) for child in children: # Prune empty subtrees if child.isempty(): continue # Cull occluded nodes if not isoccluded(child.boundingbox): traverse(child) # If visible, add to occlusion list for children visibleboxes.append(child.boundingbox) traverse(octree.root) return visiblenodes A proposed visibility culling method using a quadtree structure to discard invisible voxels in O(\log n) time in the best cases. The quadtree is stored like mipmaps, containing the maximum value of all the subpixels. It is suitable for heightmap-based terrain rendering where hierarchical visibility can be determined by value thresholds. A culling method for grid-aligned triles (tiles) that finds which triles are visible in the screen or not, and selectively renders them, including handling depth ranges and see-through flags. It traverses to the first visible trile for each screen-space tile and renders this one only. If a trile is flagged as see-through, it continues traversing until a non-seethrough trile or the level’s boundaries are hit. For tilted isometric views, it finds triles with no neighbours on the faces that the camera can see. It is used in games like Fez for efficient 3D tile rendering from an isometric perspective. Time Complexity: Depends on the occlusion test cost. In the best case for quadtree variants, it is O(\log n). For octree variants, it is proportional to the number of visible nodes plus the cost of occlusion checks. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the octree/quadtree and potentially a list of visible bounding boxes for occlusion testing. Strengths: Reduces rendering load by skipping occluded geometry; leverages existing octree structures. Limitations: Requires camera-dependent traversal order; occlusion checks can be expensive if not optimized. Not suitable for perspective views without occlusion queries as noted in Fez development. When to use: Real-time adaptive surface reconstruction where camera position is known and dynamic. When not to use: When occlusion queries are unavailable and perspective views are dominant. The technique was exploited by Livnat and Hansen [LH98] in the context of real-time adaptive surface reconstruction, using the octree structure to order visibility based on the user-specified camera position. It was recognized that the octree could be used not only to speed extraction but also rasterization by culling occluded nodes. Westermann et al. [WKE99] later recognized that speedups could be gained by exploiting the multiresolution nature of the octree structure, adaptively deciding to extract the mesh from fewer, coarser-resolution nodes.
