name: View-Dependent Working Set Generation
head: Incremental refinement procedure
body: This method constructs a view-dependent working set of non-empty octree nodes for out-of-core volume rendering, hiding I/O latency through asynchronous data loading. It differs from static culling methods by dynamically refining a sorted set of visible nodes based on screen-space projection and transfer-function opacity, ensuring only necessary data resides in GPU memory. Inputs: Octree root node, current camera view parameters, isovalue (for isosurface) or transfer function (for volume rendering), GPU cache capacity, CPU cache capacity. Outputs: A set of leaf nodes (the "cut") representing the current view-dependent working set, loaded into GPU texture caches. Data Structures: 1. Working Set: A sorted list of octree nodes. Initially contains only the root. 2. CPU Cache: A pool of blocks stored in system memory, managed via LRU policy. Acts as a level-2 cache to avoid disk I/O for recently used blocks. 3. GPU Texture Cache: A preallocated 3D texture pool. Value Texture: 16-bit single channel. Gradient Texture: RGBA8 format. RGB components store normalized gradients; Alpha component stores gradient norm. Updates are performed incrementally using glTexSubImage calls. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the working set W with the octree root node. 2. Sorting: Sort W by decreasing projected screen-space size of the voxels represented by the nodes. Visibility information (frustum culling) can be incorporated here to exclude occluded zones. 3. Refinement Loop: While termination conditions are not met: a. Select the highest-priority node n from W (top of sorted list). b. Check Availability: Determine if the data for n's children is available in the CPU cache or must be fetched asynchronously from disk. If data is not immediately available, skip refinement for this node and proceed to the next in the sorted list (asynchronous loading hides latency). c. Empty Node Determination: Check if n is empty. Isosurface Rendering: n is non-empty if the isovalue I satisfies: \min(n) \le I \le \max(n) where \min(n) and \max(n) are the minimum and maximum values within the cell. Volume Rendering: Use summed-area tables (SAT) of transfer function opacity. Let T{min} and T{max} be the SAT entries for the minimum and maximum block values. The node is non-empty if: \text{Opacity}(T{max}) - \text{Opacity}(T{min}) > \epsilon where \epsilon is a small threshold. d. Frustum Check: If n is outside the view frustum, mark as terminal (empty for rendering purposes). e. Subdivision: If n is non-empty and inside the frustum: i. Remove n from W. ii. Add n's children to W. iii. Load child data into CPU/GPU caches if not present. 4. Termination: Stop when: All nodes in W are adequately refined (e.g., max depth reached). No data is currently available in-core to perform further refinement (and async load is not ready). No more space is available in the GPU cache for further subdivision. 5. Cache Management: Maintain LRU policy for both CPU and GPU caches to evict least recently used blocks. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateworkingset(root, camera, isovalue, transferfunction, gpucachesize, cpucache): # W is the sorted list of nodes to refine W = [root] while not isterminated(W, gpucachesize, cpucache): # Sort by projected screen size (largest first) W.sort(key=lambda node: node.projectedscreenarea, reverse=True) refinedany = False for i, node in enumerate(W): # Check frustum if not camera.frustumcontains(node.boundingbox): continue # Terminal due to visibility # Check if children data is available if not cpucache.hasdata(node.children): # Data not available; skip this node for now. # Async loader will fetch it. continue # Determine if node is empty isempty = False if isosurfacemode: if not (isovalue >= node.minval and isovalue <= node.maxval): isempty = True else: # Volume rendering with SAT opacitydiff = transferfunctionopacity(node.maxval) - transferfunctionopacity(node.minval) if opacitydiff < EPSILON: isempty = True if isempty: continue # Terminal node # Refine: remove node, add children W.pop(i) for child in node.children: # Ensure child data is in cache cpucache.ensureloaded(child) gpucache.ensureloaded(child) W.append(child) refinedany = True # Note: In a real implementation, one might break or continue # based on cache pressure. The source implies processing the # sorted list until termination conditions hit. # If no refinement happened in this pass due to cache misses, # the loop continues, relying on async data arrival. if not refinedany: # Wait for async data or check termination if not cpucache.haspendingdata(): break return W def isterminated(W, gpucachesize, cpucache): # Condition 1: All nodes adequately refined (e.g., max depth) if all(node.isleaf() for node in W): return True # Condition 2: No data available in-core to perform refinement # AND no pending async data if not any(cpucache.hasdata(node.children) for node in W if not node.isleaf()): if not cpucache.haspendingdata(): return True # Condition 3: No space in GPU cache if gpucachesize.isfull(): return True return False Uses memory mapping to page in active nodes from a static on-disk octree, decoupling refinement and rendering to hide I/O latency. Latency Hiding: Relies on asynchronous data access requests performed by a separate thread to hide out-of-core disk I/O latency. Cache Efficiency: Uses LRU policy for both CPU (system memory) and GPU (texture) caches. The CPU cache acts as a level-2 cache, reducing disk accesses for recently used blocks. Update Frequency: Due to temporal and spatial coherence, the number of updated nodes per frame is generally small, allowing efficient incremental updates via glTexSubImage. Limitations: Performance depends on the effectiveness of the sorting heuristic (screen-space size) and the accuracy of the empty-node determination. If visibility culling is not integrated, occluded zones may be unnecessarily refined. This method was introduced in the context of interactive out-of-core volume rendering frameworks, specifically designed to reduce GPU stalls by exploiting renderer feedback to avoid loading occluded zones. It builds upon earlier work on empty-space skipping and summed-area tables for opacity estimation. name: Out-of-Core View-Dependent Refinement
head: Adaptive octree refinement, Run-time refinement
body: Out-of-core view-dependent refinement is a run-time component of an out-of-core renderer that pages in only the active nodes of a level-of-detail hierarchy using memory mapping, allowing asynchronous refinement and rendering. It solves the problem of rendering large datasets that exceed available memory by dynamically constructing a view-dependent working set (the "front") from a static on-disk octree, hiding I/O latency through asynchronous, breadth-first traversal. Unlike explicit paging systems, it relies on the operating system's memory-mapped file access to fetch data on demand, which is particularly effective when refinement and rendering tasks are decoupled. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A static external octree H stored on disk, a viewpoint e, a view frustum, a screen resolution \lambda (pixels per radian), and an error threshold \tau. Output: A dynamic in-core octree H' (the "front") containing only visible and necessary nodes, and a list of triangles to be rendered. Data Structures: The in-core octree node structure (Table 4 in) contains the following fields: Vertex Data: K: 3 \times 3 curvature matrix. n̂: 3-vector vertex normal. p: 3-vector vertex position. ε: Scalar quadric error (volumetric error mapped to length). r: Scalar bounding sphere radius. Triangle Data: nT: Count of triangles assigned to this node. T: List of triangles (vertex indices). nR: Count of references from child nodes. R: List of references to this node (from children). Octree Data: leaf: Boolean, is this node a leaf in the static on-disk octree H? front: Boolean, is this node a leaf in the dynamic in-core octree H'? l: Index, octree level. s: Pointer to the static external node on disk. C: Array of 8 pointers to children. prev: Pointer to the previous node in the refinement queue Q. next: Pointer to the next node in the refinement queue Q. Refinement Queue: A linear circular queue Q orders active nodes roughly in a breadth-first manner. This ordering allows preemption for paging large data blocks and ensures detail is paged in evenly over the visible surface. A pointer tracks the "tail" of the queue to resume refinement where it left off. Screen Space Error Metric: The screen space error \rho determines if a node requires refinement. It is defined as: \rho = \lambda \eta \frac{\epsilon}{d} = \lambda \epsilon \frac{\sqrt{\mathbf{v}^T \mathbf{K} \mathbf{v}}}{\sqrt{\mathbf{v}^T \mathbf{v}}} Where: \lambda: Screen resolution in pixels per radian. \epsilon: Quadric error (volumetric error converted to length). d = \|\mathbf{v}\|: Distance from the viewpoint e to the node position p. \mathbf{v} = e - p: Vector from node to viewpoint. \mathbf{K}: Curvature matrix. \eta: Directionality factor for silhouette preservation. For efficiency, the active condition \rho > \tau is rearranged to avoid square roots and division: \text{active} \iff \epsilon^2 (\mathbf{v}^T \mathbf{K} \mathbf{v}) > \kappa^2 (\mathbf{v}^T \mathbf{v})^2 Where \kappa = \tau / \lambda is the angular error threshold in radians. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a single node for the root of the dynamic octree H'. Initialize the refinement queue Q with this root. 2. Traversal Loop: While Q is not empty and refinement budget/time permits: a. Dequeue the next node p from Q. b. Frustum Culling: Test p's bounding sphere against the six planes of the view frustum. If not visible, call node-collapse(p) and continue to the next node. c. Error Evaluation: If visible, compute the screen space error metric \rho (or the rearranged active condition). d. Refinement Decision: If \rho > \tau (active) AND front(p) is true (node is a leaf in H'), call node-expand(p). If \rho \le \tau (inactive) AND front(p) is false (node is not a leaf in H'), call node-collapse(p). 3. Rendering Preparation: After refinement, traverse the nodes in H'. Collect triangles from nodes and append vertex positions/normals from proxy nodes to form the final render list. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def outofcorerefinement(rootnode, viewpoint, frustumplanes, lambdaval, tauval): """ Performs out-of-core view-dependent refinement. rootnode: The root node of the dynamic octree H'. viewpoint: The camera position e. frustumplanes: List of 6 plane equations for the view frustum. lambdaval: Screen resolution in pixels per radian. tauval: User-specified screen space error threshold. """ kappa = tauval / lambdaval queue = CircularQueue() queue.enqueue(rootnode) # Track progress for preemption tail = rootnode while not queue.isempty(): node = queue.dequeue() # 1. Frustum Culling if not isvisible(node.boundingsphere, frustumplanes): nodecollapse(node) continue # 2. Error Evaluation # v = e - p v = vectorsub(viewpoint, node.position) dsq = dot(v, v) # Check active condition: epsilon^2 (v^T K v) > kappa^2 (v^T v)^2 # Note: node.quadricerror is epsilon lhs = (node.quadricerror 2) (transpose(v) @ node.curvaturematrix @ v) rhs = (kappa 2) (dsq 2) isactive = lhs > rhs # 3. Refinement Decision if isactive and node.front: nodeexpand(node) elif not isactive and not node.front: nodecollapse(node) # Update tail for preemption/resumption tail = node def nodeexpand(p): """ Expands node p by creating its children. Valid only if p is a leaf in the dynamic octree H'. """ p.front = False for child in p.children: # Initialize child vertex data from static source or computation initializevertexdata(child) # If child is not a leaf in the static octree H, add to queue if not child.leaf: queue.enqueue(child) # Update references: triangles assigned to p are now associated with children # References from proxy nodes need to be updated for triangle in p.triangles: for vertex in triangle.vertices: # Identify proxy node based on vertex octcode proxy = identifyproxynode(vertex.octcode) # Add reference from proxy to this triangle proxy.addreference(triangle) # Transfer references from p to its children for ref in p.references: # Identify which child corresponds to this reference child = getchildforreference(ref) # Transfer ref from p to child child.addreference(ref) # Update proxy pointer for the reference updateproxypointer(ref, child) def nodecollapse(p): """ Collapses node p by removing its descendants. """ for child in p.children: nodecollapse(child) # Transfer references from children back to p for child in p.children: for ref in child.references: p.addreference(ref) # Remove child from queue and H' if it was not a leaf in H if not child.leaf: queue.remove(child) removefromdynamicoctree(child) # Clean up references from proxy nodes for triangle in p.triangles: for vertex in triangle.vertices: proxy = identifyproxynode(vertex.octcode) proxy.removereference(triangle) p.front = True Parameters: \tau: User-specified error threshold for screen space error \rho. \lambda: Screen resolution in pixels per radians. \kappa: Angular error threshold in radians, defined as \tau/\lambda. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Nesting Condition Violation: The direction and length of vector \mathbf{v} vary from node to node. This can potentially violate the property that the parent's projected error is larger than its children's, despite additive quadric errors and increasing curvature. Preemption: The breadth-first queue allows preemption. If refinement is interrupted, the system must track the "tail" of the queue to resume correctly. Memory Mapping Limits: Explicit paging schemes may offer better scalability and cache replacement policies, but memory mapping leverages OS fetching which is attractive for decoupled/asynchronous tasks. Time Complexity: Refinement time depends on the number of visible nodes and the depth of the octree. The breadth-first traversal ensures uniform detail distribution. Memory Complexity: Only active nodes (the "front") are kept in memory. The size of the working set is determined by the error threshold \tau and the view frustum. Performance: Performance is heavily dependent on I/O latency. Memory mapping allows the OS to handle paging, which can be efficient but lacks explicit control over cache replacement. Strengths: Asynchronous refinement and rendering; decoupled tasks; incremental updates; handles very large datasets that do not fit in RAM. Limitations: Potential for frame rate spikes if I/O is slow; memory mapping may be limited by OS addressing space (e.g., 32-bit limits); less control over memory usage compared to explicit paging. When to use: Large-scale out-of-core visualization where the dataset exceeds available memory and asynchronous processing is acceptable. When not to use: Applications requiring strict frame rate control with predictable memory usage (consider explicit paging or priority queues). This method is part of the out-of-core construction and visualization of multiresolution surfaces, described by Lindstrom and Pascucci. It builds on earlier work in out-of-core rendering of large terrain by Hoppe [1998] and Lindstrom and Pascucci [2001]. The approach uses memory mapping to associate the on-disk hierarchy with a logically contiguous address space, letting the OS fetch data on first access. name: Adaptive Empty Node Aggregation into Bounding Volumes
head: Bounding volume merging, Octree empty node clustering
body: This method reduces ray intersection tests in empty space by adaptively clustering empty octree nodes into bounding volumes, allowing rays to skip blank areas faster. It sets itself apart from Octree Traversal with Min/Max Pruning and Octree Empty Block Culling by explicitly merging multiple empty nodes into a single larger bounding volume, rather than just culling individual nodes or using min/max bounds for pruning. It builds on Empty Space Skipping with Octree by optimizing the storage and traversal of those empty regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree structure representing the volume, where nodes are classified as empty, real, or gray. Output: An optimized octree where empty nodes are aggregated into bounding volumes, and leaf nodes store pointers to these volumes or patches. Data Structures: Leaf Nodes: Store either: Pointers to patches (for real and gray nodes). Pointers to the bounding volume of the node (for empty nodes). Constraint: No pointers to child or parent nodes are stored in leaf nodes. Empty Cells: Each empty cell contains a pointer to the empty box (bounding volume) that covers it. Steps: 1. Identify Empty Nodes: Traverse the octree to identify nodes classified as empty. 2. Adaptive Aggregation: Adaptively cluster these empty nodes into bounding volumes. The method uses a simple creation strategy that does not guarantee the minimum number of empty boxes but produces enough to efficiently traverse dynamic scenes. 3. Update Pointers: All nodes participating in the bounding volume merging are updated to point to the new bounding volume. This eliminates redundant storage of empty space information. 4. Constant Update: The bounding volume is constantly updated during the octree merging process to maintain accuracy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def aggregateemptynodes(octree): """ Aggregates empty octree nodes into bounding volumes. Assumes octree has nodes with type (EMPTY, REAL, GRAY) and children. """ # Step 1: Identify all empty nodes emptynodes = findemptynodes(octree) # Step 2: Adaptive aggregation into bounding volumes # The specific clustering algorithm is not detailed, but it groups empty nodes # into larger bounding volumes (empty boxes). # A simple heuristic might be to merge adjacent empty nodes at a certain depth. boundingvolumes = createboundingvolumes(emptynodes) # Step 3: Update leaf nodes to point to bounding volumes for node in emptynodes: if isleaf(node): # Find the bounding volume that covers this node bv = findcoveringboundingvolume(node, boundingvolumes) node.pointer = bv else: # For non-leaf empty nodes, they might be replaced or their children updated # The text says "all nodes participating... point to the bounding volume" # This implies even internal empty nodes might be redirected or their # children are the ones storing the pointer. # Based on "Leaf nodes store pointers...", we focus on leaves. pass # Step 4: Constant update during merging # This is an iterative process. In a static scene, this runs once. # In dynamic scenes, it runs continuously. return octree def findemptynodes(octree): """Returns a list of all nodes classified as EMPTY.""" emptylist = [] queue = [octree.root] while queue: node = queue.pop(0) if node.type == EMPTY: emptylist.append(node) if not isleaf(node): queue.extend(node.children) return emptylist def createboundingvolumes(emptynodes): """ Creates bounding volumes from a list of empty nodes. Uses a simple creation method. """ # Implementation detail not provided. # A simple approach: group nodes by spatial proximity or depth. # Return a list of bounding volume objects. return [] # Placeholder for unspecified algorithm def findcoveringboundingvolume(node, boundingvolumes): """Finds the bounding volume that contains the node's space.""" for bv in boundingvolumes: if bv.contains(node): return bv return None Parameters: Empty Box Count: Fewer empty boxes improve traversal speed. The algorithm aims to minimize this count without guaranteeing the absolute minimum. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dynamic Scenes: The bounding volume must be constantly updated. Failure to do so may lead to incorrect culling in dynamic environments. Precision: The method relies on simple integer operations for speed, which may limit precision in complex geometries. Degenerate Input: The simple creation method may not handle all edge cases of empty space distribution optimally, potentially leading to suboptimal bounding volume counts. This variant focuses on the intersection test phase. During intersection testing, the ray and the merged bounding volume can cross several blank nodes at once without intersecting the boundary of each individual node. This reduces the number of ray intersection tests in empty areas, improving tracking speed. The key parameter is the number of empty boxes; fewer boxes lead to better traversal speed. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but the method claims to increase running speed by about 56.5% compared to existing fastest single-step algorithms. Memory Complexity: Reduces memory usage by eliminating redundant storage of empty space information, as all participating nodes point to a single bounding volume. Measured Performance: In the context of solar ray tracing, the algorithm improved speed by 56.5%. Strengths: Simple integer operations, effective for dynamic scenes, reduces intersection tests. Limitations: Does not guarantee minimum number of empty boxes, potential precision issues with simple integer operations. When to Use: Suitable for ray tracing in large-scale solar energy simulations or other dynamic scenes where empty space skipping is critical. When Not to Use: Not suitable if absolute minimum bounding volume count is required or if high precision floating-point operations are necessary. The method was proposed in the context of improving the speed of ray tracing algorithms for large-scale solar ray tracing. It was published in the Academic Journal of Engineering and Technology Science in 2020. The work is part of a broader effort to optimize solar energy tracking systems using ray tracing. name: Spatial Skipping (Occupancy Grid)
head: Instant-NGP Sampling, Occupancy Grid, Occupancy Grid Pruning
body: Spatial Skipping (Occupancy Grid) is an acceleration technique that improves uniform sampling by identifying empty regions in the volume and skipping them, effectively creating a transmittance estimator based on the ratio of occupied steps. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A radiance field (implicit or explicit), a ray defined by origin o and direction d, and a set of uniformly sampled points ti along the ray interval [tn, tf]. Output: A set of valid samples with associated importance weights (PDF) and transmittance values, allowing the renderer to skip samples in empty space. Data Structures: Occupancy Grid: An explicit voxel grid storing cached density values \sigma(ti) for each spatial location, updated using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) over optimization iterations. Packed Tensors: To handle varying numbers of valid samples per ray, samples are stored in a packed tensor of shape (allsamples,...) rather than a padded (nrays, nsamples,...) tensor, with an associated rayid array mapping each sample to its originating ray. Parameters: Threshold (\tau): A conservative density threshold used to binarize density, where \sigma(ti) > \tau marks a sample as occupied. EMA Decay (\gamma): The decay factor for the Exponential Moving Average update of cached densities. Steps: 1. Uniform Sampling: Generate n uniformly spaced sample points ti along the ray. 2. Density Evaluation: Evaluate the density \sigma(ti) at each sample point using the radiance field. 3. Binarization: Compute the binarized density \hat{\sigma}(ti): \hat{\sigma}(ti) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \sigma(ti) > \tau \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 4. PDF Estimation: Calculate the piece-wise constant probability density function (PDF) for each sample: p(ti) = \frac{\hat{\sigma}(ti)}{\sum{j=1}^{n} \hat{\sigma}(tj)} 5. Transmittance Estimation: Calculate the piece-wise linear transmittance estimator T(ti): T(ti) = 1 - \frac{\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \hat{\sigma}(tj)}{\sum{j=1}^{n} \hat{\sigma}(tj)} 6. EMA Update (Optimization Phase): During training, update the cached density in the occupancy grid using Exponential Moving Average over iteration k: \sigma{\text{cached}}(ti) = \gamma \cdot \sigma{\text{cached}}(ti) + (1 - \gamma) \cdot \sigma{\text{new}}(ti) Note: The source notation uses \sigma(ti)^k = \gamma \cdot \sigma(ti)^{k-1} + (1 - \gamma) \cdot \sigma(ti)^k, where the RHS term denotes the newly evaluated density at iteration k. 7. Sample Filtering (Optional Variant): For samples identified as potentially in empty or occluded spaces, evaluate transmittance without computing gradients and discard those with transmittance below 10^{-4}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from itertools import accumulate def spatialskippingoccupancygrid(rayorigin, raydirection, numsamples, radiancefield, occupancygrid, threshold, gamma): """ Performs spatial skipping using an occupancy grid. Args: rayorigin: (3,) list, ray origin coordinates. raydirection: (3,) list, ray direction vector. numsamples: int, number of uniform samples. radiancefield: callable, returns density sigma at 3D points. occupancygrid: dict mapping (x,y,z) tuples to cached density floats. threshold: float, density threshold for binarization. gamma: float, EMA decay factor. Returns: samplepoints: list of (x,y,z) tuples. pdfs: list of floats, importance weights. transmittances: list of floats, transmittance values. rayids: list of ints, ray index for each sample. """ # 1. Uniform Sampling tvals = [i / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] samplepoints = [(rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) for t in tvals] # 2. Density Evaluation densities = [radiancefield(p) for p in samplepoints] # 3. Binarization occupied = [1.0 if d > threshold else 0.0 for d in densities] # 4. PDF Estimation totaloccupied = sum(occupied) if totaloccupied == 0: return [], [], [], [] pdfs = [o / totaloccupied for o in occupied] # 5. Transmittance Estimation cumsumoccupied = list(accumulate(occupied)) transmittances = [1.0 - (c / totaloccupied) for c in cumsumoccupied] # 6. EMA Update (Optimization Phase) # In practice, coordinates must be quantized to voxel grid indices for i in range(numsamples): pos = samplepoints[i] prevsigma = occupancygrid.get(pos, 0.0) newsigma = gamma prevsigma + (1 - gamma) densities[i] occupancygrid[pos] = newsigma # 7. Return packed data rayids = [0] numsamples return samplepoints, pdfs, transmittances, rayids Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: The voxel-based representation of the transmittance estimator can suffer from aliasing issues. Occluded Areas: The method still samples uniformly within occupied but occluded areas that contribute little to the final rendering. Inaccurate Estimation: Inaccurate transmittance estimations from importance sampling can result in samples lying in empty or occluded spaces, which may require additional filtering. A technique to filter out samples lying in empty or occluded spaces by evaluating their transmittance without computing gradients, detaching the sampling process from the differentiable computational graph to maximize speed. It is chosen when training speed is prioritized over gradient accuracy in empty regions. It is approximately 10x faster than keeping all samples in the computation graph because backward passes are not required for these samples. The process involves: 1. Performing importance sampling (e.g., using Occupancy Grid). 2. Identifying samples potentially in empty or occluded spaces. 3. Evaluating transmittance for these samples using the radiance field with gradients disabled. 4. Disregarding samples with transmittance below 10^{-4}. 5. Including remaining samples in the differentiable computation graph. The transmittance threshold is 10^{-4}. This method is inspired by Instant-NGP's implementation. Time Complexity: Faster than uniform sampling in empty scenes, but slower than PDF-based estimators in complex scenes due to uniform sampling within occupied regions. The "No Gradient Filtering" variant is approximately 10x faster than standard differentiable sampling for filtered samples. Memory Complexity: Uses an explicit voxel grid for the occupancy estimator, which generally consumes more memory than implicit estimators but enables faster lookups. Packed tensors are used to store samples efficiently, avoiding the memory overhead of padded tensors for rays with few valid samples. Strengths: Simple to implement, efficient in empty spaces, and compatible with various radiance field representations such as HashEncoding in Nerfacto. Limitations: Suffers from aliasing, samples uniformly in occluded areas, and may require careful threshold tuning. When to Use: When rendering scenes with large empty spaces and computational efficiency is critical, or in in-the-wild settings when combined with hybrid representations. When Not to Use: When high accuracy in occluded regions is required or when the scene is densely occupied, reducing the benefit of skipping. Spatial Skipping via Occupancy Grid was introduced in Instant-NGP as a method to accelerate neural volume rendering by skipping empty regions during sampling. It is part of a broader class of importance sampling techniques that view sampling through the lens of transmittance estimation. The technique has been adopted and extended in various NeRF-related methods, including NerfAcc and Nerfstudio, often in conjunction with other efficient representations like HashEncoding. name: Brick Classification and Empty Space Skipping
head: Brick-based Empty Space Skipping, Empty space leaping, Shared Array Brick Classification
body: Brick Classification and Empty Space Skipping is an acceleration technique that categorizes volume bricks into three states—skipped (empty), early-terminated (saturated), or sampled—to bypass unnecessary computation for transparent or fully opaque regions. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by maintaining a shared, per-brick classification table on both host and GPU memory, enabling ray-guided feedback where the renderer directly updates brick states during traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset partitioned into bricks; current transfer function; ray-caster traversal state. Output: Classification metadata array; optimized ray traversal that skips or terminates early. Data Structures: The core data structure is a classification array shared between host and GPU memory. Layout: An array of 32-bit integers, one per brick in the dataset. Values: Each integer encodes the brick's state: 1. Skipped: The brick is empty (no valid data or zero opacity). 2. Early Termination: The brick is saturated (ray opacity is 1.0). 3. Sampled: The brick requires dense sampling. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Determine which bricks are completely empty. A brick is defined as empty if it contains no valid data or is mapped to zero opacity by the current transfer function. 2. Classification: Classify each brick into one of the three categories based on the transfer function and data content. 3. Storage: Store the classification state in the shared 32-bit integer array. 4. Ray Casting: a. For each ray, check the classification state of the current brick. b. If the state is Skipped, leap over the brick's spatial extent without sampling. c. If the state is Early Termination, terminate the ray immediately. d. If the state is Sampled, perform dense volume integration within the brick. 5. Feedback (Ray-Guided): The ray-caster writes accurate usage information back to the classification table, updating states for subsequent frames. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def classifybricks(volumedata, transferfunction): """ Classifies bricks based on data content and transfer function. Returns an array of 32-bit integers. """ numbricks = volumedata.numbricks states = [0] numbricks for i in range(numbricks): brick = volumedata.getbrick(i) if isempty(brick, transferfunction): states[i] = 1 # Skipped elif issaturated(brick, transferfunction): states[i] = 2 # Early Termination else: states[i] = 0 # Sampled return states def isempty(brick, transferfunction): """ Returns True if brick has no valid data or maps to zero opacity. """ # Implementation detail: Check if all voxels map to opacity 0 # or if the brick is marked as missing/invalid in the page table. pass def issaturated(brick, transferfunction): """ Returns True if the brick causes ray saturation (opacity 1.0). """ # Implementation detail: Check if integration through brick reaches 1.0 pass def renderray(ray, brickstates, volumedata): """ Renders a single ray using brick classification. """ opacity = 0.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Traverse bricks along the ray for brickid in ray.getbricksequence(): state = brickstates[brickid] if state == 1: # Skipped continue # Leap over this brick elif state == 2: # Early Termination break # Ray is fully opaque, stop processing else: # Sampled # Perform dense sampling and compositing opacity, color = sampleandcomposite(ray, brickid, opacity, color) if opacity >= 1.0: break # Saturated during sampling return color Parameters: Brick Size: Not given in the sources. Update Frequency: Continuous or per-frame, depending on transfer function changes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transfer Function Changes: Changing the transfer function invalidates existing metadata. Recomputing the classification for large datasets causes noticeable delays. Concurrent Updates: To maintain responsiveness, updates are offloaded to a background thread. Unprocessed bricks are treated as 'missing' during the update period, causing the renderer to request and filter them via empty checks. Precision: The method relies on accurate determination of "empty" and "saturated" states, which depends on the transfer function's opacity mapping. Time Complexity: Classification is O(N) where N is the number of bricks. Ray traversal is accelerated by skipping empty bricks, reducing effective sampling count. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the classification array, using 32 bits per brick. Performance: On a test platform (Dual Quad-Core Xeon 2.2 GHz, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 680, 24 GB RAM), the system processes approximately 7.5 million bricks per second for metadata updates. Strengths: Effective for large datasets where most bricks are either empty or saturated, significantly reducing computation. Ray-guided feedback ensures accuracy. Limitations: Transfer function changes require expensive recomputation. Background updates can lead to temporary performance drops or incorrect culling if not managed carefully. When to Use: Large-scale volume rendering with static or slowly changing transfer functions. When Not to Use: When transfer functions change frequently and low latency is critical, or when the dataset has a high proportion of non-saturated, non-empty bricks. Origin: The technique is part of the broader development of ray-guided volume rendering, which incorporates feedback loops between the ray-caster and culling mechanisms. History: It builds on earlier empty space skipping techniques that used BSP trees or octrees. The specific brick-based classification with shared arrays was analyzed in the context of scalable GPU-based rendering. Usage: Used in large-scale volume visualization systems to achieve real-time performance on commodity hardware. name: Free Space Skipping
head: Coarse/Fine Density Threshold Skipping, Training-Time Bounding Box, Two-stage Free Space Skipping
body: Free space skipping is an acceleration technique for volume rendering that avoids computing expensive view-dependent color models for points located in transparent or low-density regions of the scene. It operates by querying a hierarchy of density representations—typically a coarse voxel grid followed by a fine voxel grid—and discarding samples where the activated alpha falls below specific thresholds. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{x}0 and direction \mathbf{d}. Coarse density voxel grid V^{(\text{density})}{(c)}. Fine density voxel grid V^{(\text{density})}{(f)}. Thresholds \tau^{(c)} and \tau^{(f)}. Bounding box (BBox) of the scene. Outputs: A set of valid sample points \{\mathbf{x}i\} for which the view-dependent color model must be evaluated. Data Structures: V^{(\text{density})}{(c)}: A 3D tensor storing density values. Access is performed via trilinear interpolation. V^{(\text{density})}{(f)}: A 3D tensor storing higher-resolution density values. Access is performed via trilinear interpolation. Parameters: \tau^{(c)}: Coarse threshold. Typical value: 10^{-3}. \tau^{(f)}: Fine threshold. Typical value: 10^{-4}. Algorithm: 1. Ray-BBox Intersection: Determine the intersection interval [t{\text{near}}, t{\text{far}}] of the ray with the scene BBox. If the ray origin \mathbf{x}0 is already inside the BBox, t{\text{near}} remains 0 and t{\text{far}} is the exit distance. Otherwise, t{\text{near}} and t{\text{far}} are the entry and exit distances. 2. Ray Filtering: Filter out rays that do not intersect the known free space (the BBox or region defined by the coarse grid). 3. Sampling Loop: For each sample point \mathbf{x} along the ray within [t{\text{near}}, t{\text{far}}]: a. Coarse Check: Query the coarse density grid V^{(\text{density})}{(c)} at \mathbf{x} to obtain density \sigmac. b. Coarse Skip: If the activated alpha derived from \sigmac is less than \tau^{(c)}, skip this point (treat as known free space). c. Fine Check: If the coarse check passes, query the fine density grid V^{(\text{density})}{(f)} at \mathbf{x} to obtain density \sigmaf. d. Fine Skip: If the activated alpha derived from \sigmaf is less than \tau^{(f)}, skip this point (filters unknown space with low activation). e. Color Evaluation: If both checks pass, query the view-dependent color model for the color and opacity at \mathbf{x}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def freespaceskipray(x0, d, bboxmin, bboxmax, Vcoarse, Vfine, Vcolor, tauc, tauf, stepsize): # 1. Ray-BBox Intersection (Slab method) tmin, tmax = 0.0, float('inf') for i in range(3): if d[i] == 0: if x0[i] < bboxmin[i] or x0[i] > bboxmax[i]: return [] else: t1 = (bboxmin[i] - x0[i]) / d[i] t2 = (bboxmax[i] - x0[i]) / d[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax or tmax < 0: return [] # Adjust tnear if origin is inside bbox inside = all(bboxmin[i] <= x0[i] <= bboxmax[i] for i in range(3)) tnear = 0.0 if inside else tmin tfar = tmax validpoints = [] t = tnear while t <= tfar: x = x0 + t d # 2a. Coarse Check sigmac = Vcoarse(x) if sigmac < tauc: t += stepsize continue # 2b. Fine Check sigmaf = Vfine(x) if sigmaf < tauf: t += stepsize continue # 2c. Color Evaluation color = Vcolor(x) validpoints.append((x, color)) t += stepsize return validpoints Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Thresholds: Setting \tau^{(c)} = 0 and \tau^{(f)} = 0 disables skipping, leading to out-of-memory (OOM) errors during the fine stage due to excessive memory usage. Quality Degradation: Setting \tau^{(c)} = 0 while keeping \tau^{(f)} > 0 degrades rendering quality because the coarse stage's priors are ignored. Initialization Conflict: Low-density initialization and free space skipping cannot be applied simultaneously. Precision: The thresholds \tau^{(c)} and \tau^{(f)} must be chosen carefully; too high values may clip valid geometry, while too low values reduce acceleration benefits. The primary implementation using two distinct voxel grids. It applies thresholds to both coarse and fine density grids to filter samples. Refers to the sequential filtering process where points are first checked against the coarse grid and then the fine grid. It improves fine-stage efficiency during training and testing. Adjusts the ray near- and far-bounds to the intersection endpoints with the scene BBox, skipping rays that do not intersect. Time Complexity: The coarse grid query is faster than the fine grid query, which is faster than querying the view-dependent color model. Free space skipping improves fine-stage efficiency in both training and testing. Memory Complexity: Reduces memory consumption by skipping points in free space, preventing out-of-memory errors when thresholds are properly set. Strengths: Removes irrelevant samples in transparent regions; improves training efficiency. Limitations: Requires careful threshold tuning; low-density initialization and free space skipping cannot be applied simultaneously. When to use: Scenes with significant transparent/empty space using voxel-based representations. When not to use: Fully opaque scenes or when memory is unconstrained. Free space skipping was introduced in Direct Voxel Grid Optimization by Sun et al. in 2022. It addresses the computational bottleneck of querying view-dependent color models for every sample point. By leveraging efficient voxel grid lookups, it enables super-fast convergence in radiance field reconstruction. It is primarily used in neural rendering pipelines utilizing multi-resolution voxel grids. name: Parallel Tree-Construction for Empty-Space Skipping
body: Parallel tree-construction algorithms enable the run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures for empty-space skipping, primarily to accommodate dynamic changes in the transfer function. This approach distinguishes itself from static acceleration structures by allowing the hierarchy to be rebuilt on the GPU at interactive frame rates, ensuring that the skipping logic remains consistent with the current visual parameters. The core mechanism involves constructing a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) or similar tree structure in parallel on the GPU. The construction process typically adapts algorithms originally designed for triangle geometry to sparse volumetric data. This adaptation uses the boundaries of non-empty bricks as the bounding geometry for the nodes. The parallel nature of the construction allows for the rapid regeneration of the tree, which is necessary when the transfer function changes, as this alters which regions are considered empty versus occupied. For 1024^3 volumes, the algorithm achieves interactive frame rates. The technique emerged in recent years to address the limitations of static acceleration structures in dynamic volume rendering scenarios. Key contributions include work by Zellmann et al. [ZHL19], who proposed the LBVH adaptation for sparse data, and subsequent works by ZSL18, ZML19, FW20, DK19, DK20, and ZSL21, which further explored parallel tree construction for this purpose. The primary motivation is to support run-time re-construction of acceleration data structures due to changes in the transfer function. name: Transfer-Function Independent Empty-Space Skipping
body: This family of techniques accelerates volume rendering by storing visibility information in the acceleration structure independent of the transfer function, thereby avoiding reconstruction after transfer-function changes. It decouples spatial culling from opacity evaluation, enabling real-time transfer function adjustments without structural overhead, unlike Ray Marcher with Macrocell Empty Space Skipping or Empty Space Skipping with Orthogonal BSP Tree. The method represents the data distribution within a spatial node as a compact, transfer-function-independent descriptor, typically a bitfield encoding the presence of specific data values. The visible value range of the transfer function is similarly represented as a bitfield. To determine if a node is empty for a given transfer function, the system compares the node's descriptor against the transfer function's descriptor using a bitwise AND operation. If the result is zero, the node contains no values that contribute to the final image under the current transfer function, and the node is culled. Mathematically, let B{\text{node}} be the bitfield representing the values present in the node, and B{\text{tf}} be the bitfield representing the values mapped to non-zero opacity by the transfer function. The node is considered empty if: B{\text{node}} \ \& \ B{\text{tf}} = 0 where \& denotes the bitwise AND operation. This allows for efficient runtime changes to the transfer function without modifying the underlying acceleration structure. This variant uses transfer-function independent culling information in residency-octree nodes for empty-space skipping without the need to reconstruct the tree on transfer-function changes. The primary advantage is that cache-residency information also does not have to be redistributed over octree nodes on transfer-function changes. Traditional acceleration structures store transfer-function dependent visibility information and require reconstruction after transfer-function changes. Faludi et al. [FZZ+ 22] proposed storing a histogram of values contained in an octree node as a bitfield instead, allowing a single bitwise AND operation to test for translucency. This concept was extended to residency octrees, which combine empty-space skipping with cache-residency tracking without requiring redistribution on transfer-function changes. name: Homogeneity Acceleration
head: Denskin-Hanrahan acceleration, Range pyramid traversal
body: Homogeneity acceleration is an image-order volume rendering technique that extends empty-space skipping by approximating the contribution of uniform, non-empty regions instead of sampling them voxel-by-voxel. It distinguishes itself from its sibling Empty-space skipping by handling regions that contain data but lack internal variation, thereby reducing computational load where presence acceleration alone would still require per-sample evaluation. Inputs: A scalar volume dataset and a set of rays cast from the image plane into the volume. Outputs: The final color and opacity for each pixel. Data Structures: The method relies on a range pyramid, a hierarchical data structure built over the volume. Unlike the binary pyramids used in presence acceleration, each node in the range pyramid stores two values: the minimum scalar value and the maximum scalar value found in the subvolume covered by the node. The pyramid is constructed such that each level contains the maximum and minimum values of the subvolumes at the level immediately below it. Algorithm Steps: 1. Construct the range pyramid containing the maximum and minimum values of subvolumes at the level below. 2. For each ray, traverse the range pyramid from the root to the leaves. 3. At each node visited, compare the stored minimum and maximum values. 4. If the maximum and minimum values of a cell are nearly the same, the region is considered homogeneous and an approximate evaluation is performed instead of detailed sampling. 5. If the values differ significantly, the region is heterogeneous; descend to its children and repeat the check. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildrangepyramid(levels): # levels is a list of lists; levels[0] is root, levels[-1] is leaves for i in range(len(levels) - 2, -1, -1): for node in levels[i]: node.min = min(c.min for c in node.children) node.max = max(c.max for c in node.children) return levels def renderray(ray, pyramid, epsilon): accumulatedcolor = 0.0 accumulatedopacity = 0.0 t = 0.0 # Traverse cells along the ray while t < ray.length: cell = ray.nextcell(t) # Advances to next grid cell if cell.max - cell.min < epsilon: # Homogeneous region: approximate evaluation value = (cell.min + cell.max) / 2.0 color, opacity = standardtransferfunction(value) # Standard TF evaluation alpha = opacity (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor += color alpha accumulatedopacity += alpha t += cell.stepsize else: # Heterogeneous region: sample directly value = (cell.min + cell.max) / 2.0 color, opacity = standardtransferfunction(value) alpha = opacity (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor += color alpha accumulatedopacity += alpha t += cell.stepsize if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity def standardtransferfunction(value): # Standard volume rendering transfer function lookup and compositing return 0.0, 0.0 Parameters: \epsilon: The homogeneity threshold. Not given in the sources. Typical values depend on the data range and transfer function sensitivity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Comparing floating-point minimum and maximum values requires care. A fixed \epsilon may not scale well across different data ranges. Approximation Error: The approximate evaluation assumes uniformity. If the transfer function is highly non-linear, even small variations within the homogeneous range can cause significant color changes. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of ray-marching steps in homogeneous regions from O(N) to O(1) per region, where N is the number of voxels in the region. The construction time is O(V) where V is the total number of voxels. Memory Complexity: Requires storing two scalar values per node in the pyramid. The size is proportional to the number of nodes in the pyramid, which is O(V) for a full pyramid. Measured Performance: Denskin and Hanrahan reported improvements over presence acceleration, particularly in volumes with large uniform regions. Specific speedup factors are not given in the sources. Strengths: Effective for volumes with large homogeneous areas. Reduces redundant sampling. Limitations: Approximation may reduce visual fidelity if the transfer function is sensitive to small value changes. Requires additional memory for the range pyramid. When to use: When the volume contains significant homogeneous regions and the transfer function is relatively smooth or linear in those regions. When not to use: When the volume is highly heterogeneous or the transfer function is highly non-linear, as the approximation error may be visually unacceptable. Homogeneity acceleration was introduced by Denskin and Hanrahan in 1992. It was an improvement over presence acceleration, which only skipped empty regions. The technique uses a range pyramid instead of a binary pyramid to skip empty ray segments and approximately evaluate homogeneous regions. name: Bounding Volume Culling
head: Distance-based Culling, Ray Termination by Distance
body: Bounding Volume Culling is an optimization that limits raymarching to a specific geometric boundary, dropping rays that exceed a certain distance from the eye or miss the volume entirely to speed up rendering. It differs from its parent, Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control, which relies on accumulated opacity or transmittance to stop integration, by using hard geometric constraints to discard rays before or during traversal. Unlike Empty-space skipping, which skips empty voxels within a defined volume, Bounding Volume Culling often rejects the entire ray if it does not intersect the volume's outer bounds. The method varies by the type of bounding volume used (scalar distance limit, axis-aligned box, or heap-managed collection). The core principle is to compute a distance or intersection test against the bounding geometry before or during the sampling loop. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, bounding volume definition (e.g., max distance D{max}, AABB min/max, or list of bounding volumes), and the volume data structure. Outputs: A color value (or background) if the ray is culled or fully processed; otherwise, the result of the raymarching loop. 1. Scalar Limit: A single floating-point value D{max} representing the maximum travel distance. 2. AABB: Two 3D vectors \mathbf{min} and \mathbf{max} defining the box extents. 3. Heap (for Sphere Tracing): A priority queue (min-heap) storing pairs of (d{bv}, \text{object\id}), where d{bv} is the distance to the bounding volume. This variant tracks the total distance traveled by the ray and terminates if it exceeds a predefined limit. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scalardistanceculling(o, d, Dmax, dt): t = 0.0 while t < Dmax: color = samplevolume(o + t d) # Standard volume sampling t += dt # Standard step advancement return backgroundcolor # Return background or fog color This variant uses the six planar faces of a rectangular grid volume to reject rays that do not intersect the volume. name: Bounding Spheres Optimization
body: Bounding Spheres Optimization reduces the computational cost of sphere tracing by grouping scene objects into larger enclosing spheres, thereby eliminating unnecessary distance calculations during ray traversal. It differs from its parent, Bounding Volume Culling, which typically discards rays entirely based on geometric bounds, by deferring the evaluation of individual object distances until the ray actually penetrates the enclosing volume. Unlike Orthogonal Culling Optimization, which pre-computes object visibility via orthogonal projection to reduce per-step evaluations, Bounding Spheres Optimization dynamically manages the active set of distance fields based on ray proximity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene with objects grouped into enclosing bounding spheres, and a ray defined by origin and direction. Output: The final rendered image with a reduced number of Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluations. Data Structures: Each Bounding Sphere is defined by its location (mean position of enclosed objects), radius (large enough to encompass all enclosed objects), and a list of enclosed objects. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the active set with the top-level enclosing bounding spheres. 2. At each march step, evaluate the distance to all active Bounding Spheres. The distance to a sphere S from a point P on the ray is dS = \max(0, \|P - CS\| - RS). 3. Advance the ray by the minimum distance found among all active spheres. 4. If the ray hits a Bounding Sphere (distance \approx 0), remove it from the active set and add all enclosed objects to the active set. 5. Continue marching until an individual object is hit, a maximum distance is reached, or no active spheres remain. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spheretraceboundingspheres(origin, direction, activespheres, maxsteps, epsilon=1e-4, maxdist=1000.0): t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): if t >= maxdist: return float('inf') mindist = float('inf') hitsphere = None for s in activespheres: tocenter = (origin + t direction) - s.center dist = max(0.0, length(tocenter) - s.radius) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist hitsphere = s if mindist == float('inf'): break t += mindist if hitsphere is not None and mindist <= epsilon: activespheres = [s for s in activespheres if s != hitsphere] activespheres.extend(hitsphere.children) return t Parameters: epsilon: Small threshold for hit detection, typically 10^{-4}. maxdistance: Clipping sphere radius used to terminate ray stepping, e.g., 1000. Edge Cases: Nested Bounding Spheres: The implementation supports nested spheres, but this was not tested. Precision: Large radius spheres may suffer from floating-point precision issues if the scene scale is large. Not given in the sources. Pre-computes object visibility via orthogonal projection to reduce per-step SDF evaluations. Choose when the scene is static and pre-computation is feasible. Discards bounding volumes outside the camera's view frustum. Choose when the camera moves frequently and CPU-side culling is efficient. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of SDF evaluations per step from N (all objects) to K (active bounding spheres), where K \ll N. When a sphere is hit, the number of active objects increases, potentially increasing the cost of subsequent steps until the objects are traversed. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the hierarchy of bounding spheres and their enclosed objects. Measured Performance: For the Zeno logo scene, execution time reduced from 26:29 to 5:28 (21% relative time). For a single sphere, convexity enhancement reduced time from 2:00 to 1:23 (69% relative time). For 9 spheres/plane, triangle inequality reduced time from 2:53 to 1:19 (46% relative time). Strengths: Significantly reduces distance calculations for sparse scenes or scenes with large empty spaces. Limitations: Overhead of managing the active set; nested spheres were not tested. May not benefit simple scenes. Bounding Spheres Optimization was introduced in the context of sphere tracing for antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces. It was developed as part of the Zeno renderer project. The technique is described in detail in a thesis evaluating sphere tracing on GPUs. name: Orthogonal Culling Optimization
head: Orthogonal Culling, Orthogonal Projection Culling
body: Orthogonal Culling is a pre-computation optimization for sphere tracing that reduces the number of signed distance function (SDF) evaluations per ray by determining which scene objects lie within the ray's path before the marching loop begins. It differs from its parent, Bounding Spheres Optimization, which minimizes distance calculations during traversal, and its sibling, Frustum Culling (Sphere vs Frustum), which typically relies on CPU-side broad-phase culling; Orthogonal Culling performs a geometric intersection test between the ray and object bounding volumes using orthogonal projection. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, and a list of scene objects, each defined by a bounding sphere with center \mathbf{c} and radius r. Output: A boolean mask or list of indices indicating which objects intersect the ray, allowing the renderer to skip SDF evaluations for non-intersecting objects. Data Structures Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction vector \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Bounding Sphere: Defined by center \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and scalar radius r \ge 0. Algorithm Steps 1. For each object in the scene, retrieve its bounding sphere center \mathbf{c} and radius r. 2. Project the vector from the ray origin to the sphere center onto the ray direction to find the line's closest point to the object. 3. Calculate the distance between the line and the sphere using the sphere's radius. 4. Compare this distance against zero. 5. If the distance is less than zero, the ray intersects the sphere and the object is considered for distance calculation. Formulas Let \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{o} be the vector from the ray origin to the sphere center. The projection of \mathbf{v} onto the ray direction \mathbf{d} is given by the dot product: t = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{d} This t represents the distance along the ray to the closest point \mathbf{p} on the line: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} The squared distance D^2 from the sphere center \mathbf{c} to the point \mathbf{p} is calculated using the Pythagorean theorem: D^2 = \|\mathbf{v}\|^2 - t^2 = \|\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{o}\|^2 - (\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{d})^2 The distance between the line and the sphere surface is D - r. The intersection condition is D - r < 0, which is equivalent to D^2 < r^2. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def orthogonalcull(rayorigin, raydirection, objects): """ rayorigin: vec3 raydirection: vec3 objects: list of dicts with keys 'center' (vec3) and 'radius' (float) returns: list of indices of objects intersecting the ray """ activeobjects = [] for i, obj in enumerate(objects): c = obj['center'] r = obj['radius'] v = c - rayorigin t = dot(v, raydirection) distsq = dot(v, v) - t t # Source notes check if distance(line, sphere) < 0 if distsq < r r: activeobjects.append(i) return activeobjects Edge Cases and Pitfalls Implementation Efficiency: The described implementation performs this culling check for all objects in the scene for every pixel. This is suboptimal because culling should be done once per object to calculate which rays it intersects, rather than per ray determining which objects it intersects. Time and Memory Complexity Time: O(N \cdot R), where N is the number of objects and R is the number of rays (pixels), because the implementation checks all objects per pixel. Memory: O(1) auxiliary space per ray, assuming the object list is read-only. Measured Performance Tested on a GeForce GTX 1060M at 1920x1080 resolution. Performance gain is significant but varies with object count and scene configuration. Table 5.1 Data (FPS): 1 Object: 600 FPS (optimized) vs 350 FPS (unoptimized) 10 Objects: 500 FPS (optimized) vs 300 FPS (unoptimized) 20 Objects: 40 FPS (optimized) vs 25 FPS (unoptimized) 30 Objects: 29 FPS (optimized) vs 20 FPS (unoptimized) 40 Objects: 6 FPS (optimized) vs 4 FPS (unoptimized) 45 Objects: 4 FPS (optimized) vs 1.5 FPS (unoptimized) Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Provides a consistent performance increase by reducing the number of SDF evaluations per march step. It is particularly effective when objects are not mutually obstructing, such as spheres arranged in a plane, which represents the best-case scenario for the optimization. Limitations: The naive per-pixel, per-object check is computationally expensive for large N. It does not account for occlusion by other objects in the scene, only geometric intersection with the ray. Origin Orthogonal Culling was introduced in the context of GPU-based Sphere Tracing implementations to optimize the evaluation of signed distance functions. It was developed as part of a broader set of optimizations including Bounding Spheres and Ray Grouping. History and Development The method was evaluated using a GLSL software shader and simulated on a GPU architecture (CλaSH simulation). The research highlighted that while the optimization provided high performance gains, the initial implementation was not optimal because it repeated the culling calculation for every ray-object pair per pixel, rather than computing ray-object intersections once per object. The authors suggested that this step could be offloaded to the CPU for better efficiency. Usage The technique is used in real-time ray marching applications, specifically those rendering reflective spheres and mod fields, where reducing the number of distance queries is critical for maintaining high frame rates. name: Frustum Culling (Sphere vs Frustum)
head: Chunk Frustum Culling, Global Frustum Culling, Sphere vs Frustum Culling
body: Frustum culling for spheres is a visibility test that rejects bounding spheres lying outside the camera's view frustum, preventing unnecessary ray-sphere intersection computations during volume rendering traversal. Unlike SIMD shaft culling, which is restricted to primitives with planar edges like triangles, this method works directly for spherical bounding volumes by testing if the signed distance from a sphere's center to any frustum plane exceeds the sphere's radius. Inputs: Camera frustum defined by near/far clipping planes and view direction vectors (right, up, forward). A set of entities or chunks, each represented by a bounding sphere defined by center position C and radius r. Optional chunk parameters if culling is applied to voxel chunks, specifically chunk size CHUNK\SIZE and derived sphere radius CHUNK\SPHERE\RADIUS. Outputs: A boolean visibility flag for each entity or chunk. Data Structures: Sphere: Defined by center coordinates (x, y, z) and radius r. Camera Frustum: Implicitly defined by the camera's position, orientation (quaternion or rotation matrix), and projection parameters (field of view, aspect ratio, near, far). The frustum planes are derived from these parameters. Parameters: r{max}: The maximum radius used to define an "enlarged" frustum for coarse culling. If a sphere's radius is smaller than r{max}, it may overlap the enlarged frustum but not the original one, requiring a more precise test. NEAR, FAR: Clipping plane distances along the forward axis. Typical values: NEAR = 0.1, FAR = 2000.0. CHUNK\SIZE: Grid dimension for voxel chunks. Typical value: 48. H{CHUNK\SIZE} = CHUNK\SIZE // 2. Typical value: 24. CHUNK\SPHERE\RADIUS = H{CHUNK\SIZE} \times \sqrt{3}. Typical value: 24 \times \sqrt{3} \approx 41.57. factor\x, factor\y: Scaling factors for the frustum plane distances, derived from the camera's field of view and aspect ratio. tan\x, tan\y: Tangents of half the horizontal and vertical field of view angles. Steps: 1. Iterate over all entities or chunks in the scene. 2. Calculate Entity Bounding Sphere: Determine the sphere's center C and radius r from the entity's transform and graphics components. 3. Coarse Culling (Optional): If a camera bounding sphere is used, check if the entity's bounding sphere intersects it. If not intersecting, set visibility to false. 4. Frustum Plane Test: For each plane of the view frustum, calculate the signed distance d from the sphere center to the plane normal. If d > r, the sphere is completely outside the frustum on that side. Discard the entity. 5. Refined Culling (for chunks/enlarged frustum): If the sphere passed the coarse test but its radius is smaller than r{max}, or if using chunk-based culling, project the sphere center onto the camera's forward, right, and up axes. Check if the projected position lies within the expanded bounds defined by the near/far planes and the side planes, accounting for the sphere's radius. Specifically for chunks, check if the sphere center's projection on the forward axis is within [NEAR - R{CHUNK}, FAR + R{CHUNK}]. Check if the projections on the right and up axes are within the frustum's width and height at that depth, expanded by the radius. 6. Set Visibility: If the sphere passes all frustum tests, set visibility to true and increment visible object count; otherwise, set it to false. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isonfrustum(spherecenter, sphereradius, camera): """ Checks if a sphere is inside the camera's view frustum. spherecenter: vec3 (x, y, z) sphereradius: float (for chunks, equals CHUNKSPHERERADIUS) camera: object with attributes position, forward, right, up, near, far, tanx, tany, factorx, factory """ # Vector from camera to sphere center spherevec = spherecenter - camera.position # Project onto forward axis (z-axis in camera space) sz = dot(spherevec, camera.forward) # Check near and far planes if not (camera.near - sphereradius <= sz <= camera.far + sphereradius): return False # Project onto up axis (y-axis in camera space) sy = dot(spherevec, camera.up) # Calculate the half-height of the frustum at depth sz, expanded by radius dist = camera.factory sphereradius + sz camera.tany if not (-dist <= sy <= dist): return False # Project onto right axis (x-axis in camera space) sx = dot(spherevec, camera.right) # Calculate the half-width of the frustum at depth sz, expanded by radius dist = camera.factorx sphereradius + sz camera.tanx if not (-dist <= sx <= dist): return False return True def cullentities(entities, camera): visiblecount = 0 for entity in entities: # Get entity's bounding sphere center = entity.position radius = entity.boundingsphereradius entity.scale # Optional coarse culling with camera bounding sphere if not camera.boundingsphere.intersects(center, radius): entity.visible = False continue # Frustum culling if isonfrustum(center, radius, camera): entity.visible = True visiblecount += 1 else: entity.visible = False return visiblecount Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point errors in dot products may cause spheres very close to frustum planes to be incorrectly culled or included. Using a small epsilon tolerance in comparisons can mitigate this. Degenerate Input: If the camera's forward, right, or up vectors are not orthogonal or normalized, the frustum plane calculations will be incorrect. Ensure camera basis vectors are orthonormal. Radius Smaller than r{max}: A sphere with radius r < r{max} might pass an enlarged frustum test but fail the original frustum test. The algorithm must handle this by performing the precise test if the coarse test passes. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of entities or chunks. Performance: Significantly reduces the number of ray-sphere intersection tests, which are computationally expensive. The reduction in visible objects depends on the scene density and camera position. Strengths: Simple to implement, works for any spherical bounding volume, and is efficient for large numbers of objects. Limitations: Only effective for spherical bounding volumes. For non-spherical objects, a bounding sphere approximation may lead to false positives (objects included but not visible). Frustum culling for spheres was introduced as a simpler alternative to SIMD shaft culling for particle visualization. The original CGT algorithm used SIMD shaft culling for triangles, but this technique is not applicable to spheres. The sphere/frustum culling test was proposed to efficiently reject non-overlapping spheres in the Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) approach. It is commonly used in volume rendering and particle systems to optimize ray traversal by eliminating objects outside the view frustum. name: Russian Roulette
head: Monte Carlo termination, Probabilistic Path Termination, RR termination, Russian Roulette Termination, Russian Roulette for Ray Marching Termination, Russian Roulette for Ray Termination, Russian Roulette for Volumetric Paths
body: Russian Roulette is a randomized early-out technique used in Monte Carlo volume rendering to remove the statistical bias introduced by deterministic early termination (such as breaking a ray-marching loop when transmittance drops below a fixed threshold). It probabilistically terminates rays with low contribution weights while scaling up the weights of surviving paths to maintain an unbiased expectation of the final pixel color. Unlike deterministic cutoffs which simply discard remaining contributions, Russian Roulette ensures that the expected value of the rendered image remains correct, albeit at the cost of increased variance (noise). Russian Roulette is applied when the accumulated transmittance (or path throughput) becomes sufficiently small, indicating that the remaining contribution to the pixel is negligible but non-zero. The method replaces a hard cutoff with a probabilistic decision. Inputs: Current accumulated transmittance/throughput T (or weight W). Termination probability parameter p{term} (or continuation probability p{cont}). Random number generator state. Outputs: Boolean: continue or terminate. Updated transmittance/weight T' or W'. No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard scalar variables for transmittance/weight and a random number generator. Threshold (T{thresh}): The minimum transmittance value below which Russian Roulette is considered. Common values are 10^{-3}. Termination Probability (p{term}): The probability of terminating the path. In path tracing, this is often derived from the maximum color channel of the throughput. In ray marching, it is often a constant (e.g., 0.5) or derived from a compensation factor D. Compensation Factor (D): A value > 1 used in some formulations where p{term} = 1 - 1/D and p{cont} = 1/D. 1. Check Threshold: If the current accumulated transmittance T (or weight W) is greater than or equal to the threshold T{thresh}, continue marching/tracing normally. 2. Determine Probability: Set the continuation probability p{cont} (where p{term} = 1 - p{cont}) based on the formulation. Formulation A (Constant/Heuristic): Set p{cont} to a constant (e.g., 0.5). Formulation B (Compensation Factor): Set p{cont} = 1/D where D > 1. Formulation C (Path Tracing): Set p{cont} to the maximum component value of the current throughput vector \beta (or a scaled version thereof). 3. Generate Random Number: Sample a uniform random number \xi from [0, 1]. 4. Probabilistic Decision: If \xi < p{cont} (or \xi > p{term}), continue the path. Otherwise, terminate the path. 5. Weight Compensation: If continuing, scale the transmittance/weight to compensate for the probability of termination: T' = T / p{cont} (or T' = T \cdot D). If terminating, set T' = 0 (or W' = 0). The following pseudocode implements the standard Russian Roulette for volume ray marching, combining the threshold check and probabilistic termination. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def russianroulette(transmittance, threshold=1e-3, pcont=0.5): """ Applies Russian Roulette to the current transmittance. Args: transmittance: Current accumulated transmittance (Spectrum or float). threshold: Minimum transmittance to trigger RR. pcont: Probability of continuing the path (0 < pcont <= 1). Returns: (continuemarching: bool, newtransmittance: float) """ # 1. Check if we are above the threshold if transmittance >= threshold: return True, transmittance # 2. Generate random number r = randomfloat() # 3. Probabilistic decision if r < pcont: # Survive: scale transmittance to compensate for termination probability # Avoid division by zero if pcont > 1e-6: newtransmittance = transmittance / pcont else: newtransmittance = 0.0 return True, newtransmittance else: # Die: terminate path return False, 0.0 def randomfloat(): """Returns a uniform random number in [0, 1].""" import random return random.random() Bias from Simple Cutoff: Simply breaking the loop when transmittance < threshold without compensation introduces significant bias by discarding the remaining volume contribution. Variance Increase: While unbiased, Russian Roulette increases the variance (noise) of the image because it introduces binary outcomes (0 or scaled value) for paths that would have contributed small, deterministic amounts. Division by Zero: Ensure the continuation probability is not zero to avoid division by zero when scaling the weight. A sophisticated variant that probabilistically terminates rays based on accumulated opacity, replacing deterministic threshold-based cutoffs. It differs from standard early termination by allowing rays to continue with scaled weights even when opacity is high, thereby reducing computation while maintaining unbiased expectations through variance masking. Time Complexity: Reduces the average number of samples per ray by terminating low-contribution paths early. Memory Complexity: No additional memory overhead beyond standard scalar variables. Performance: Significant speedup in scenes with high variance or deep paths. For example, rendering with Russian Roulette took 161s (unbiased), compared to 2556s without Russian Roulette (biased, max depth 200) in a cloud example. Strengths: Unbiased results; effective for reducing computation in transparent or deep volumes. Limitations: Increases noise (variance). When to Use: When using Monte Carlo integration for volume rendering, especially with path tracing or when deterministic early termination causes visible bias. When Not to Use: When deterministic bias is acceptable for speed, or when the volume is very dense and transmittance drops to zero quickly anyway. Russian Roulette originated in Monte Carlo particle-tracing methods to avoid simulating particles with low weights without biasing the results. It was adapted for volume rendering to correct the bias introduced by early ray termination (cutoff). The technique is named after the dangerous game of chance, reflecting the probabilistic nature of path survival. It is a standard component of unbiased path tracers and volume integrators. name: Russian Roulette Early Ray Termination
head: Probabilistic Early Termination, Russian Roulette for Ray Termination, Russian Roulette scheme
body: Russian Roulette Early Ray Termination is a sophisticated form of early ray termination in volume rendering where rays probabilistically terminate based on accumulated opacity, capitalizing on the human eye’s tolerance to error masked as noise. It replaces deterministic threshold-based cutoffs with a probabilistic scheme that terminates rays at varying accumulated opacities. Inputs: Accumulated opacity A{acc}, accumulated color C{acc}, remaining transmittance W{acc}, sample color c{sample}, and sample opacity \alpha{sample}. Outputs: Updated C{acc}, W{acc}, and a boolean termination flag. No additional data structures are required beyond the standard ray state variables maintained during the ray marching loop. 1. Calculate Termination Probability: Determine p{term} as a function of the current accumulated opacity A{acc}. 2. Generate Random Number: Draw a uniform random number r \in [0, 1). 3. Decision: If r < p{term}, terminate the ray and discard the remaining contribution. 4. Weight Adjustment: If r \ge p{term}, continue the ray and scale the accumulated weight and current sample contribution by 1 / (1 - p{term}) to maintain unbiased expectation. 5. Accumulation: Update the accumulated color with the scaled sample contribution and update the remaining weight for subsequent steps. Termination condition: r < p{term} where p{term} = A{acc}. Scaling factor: S = \frac{1}{1 - p{term}}. Updated color: C{new} = C{old} + S \cdot W{old} \cdot c{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample}. Updated weight: W{new} = S \cdot W{old} \cdot (1 - \alpha{sample}). A{acc}: Accumulated opacity along the ray, range [0, 1]. p{term}: Termination probability, typically set equal to A{acc}. Precision: When A{acc} approaches 1, 1 - p{term} approaches 0, causing numerical instability in the scaling factor; clamp A{acc} to a maximum value slightly less than 1 (e.g., 0.999) to prevent division by zero. Degenerate Input: If A{acc} = 0, the termination probability is 0 and the ray always continues. If A{acc} = 1, the termination probability is 1 and the ray always terminates. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def russianrouletteearlytermination(Aacc, Cacc, Wacc, csample, alphasample): # Guard against division by zero when opacity is near 1 if Aacc >= 0.999: return Cacc, Wacc, True # Termination probability based on accumulated opacity pterm = Aacc # Generate uniform random number 0, 1) r = random.random() if r < pterm: # Ray terminates; discard remaining contribution return Cacc, Wacc, True else: # Ray continues; scale by inverse survival probability for unbiased expectation scale = 1.0 / (1.0 - pterm) # Update accumulated color with scaled sample contribution Cacc = Cacc + scale Wacc csample alphasample # Update remaining weight for future steps Wacc = scale Wacc (1.0 - alphasample) return Cacc, Wacc, False Terminates rays when accumulated opacity exceeds a fixed threshold. Simpler but introduces bias. Choose when performance is critical and noise is unacceptable. [Deterministic Early Termination Used in path tracing to terminate paths with low throughput. Similar principle but applied to light transport paths rather than volume rays. Choose for general path tracing. Russian Roulette Time and memory complexity, measured performance, scaling, strengths, limitations, and usage guidelines are Not given in the sources. Originated from the application of Russian Roulette sampling techniques to volume rendering, leveraging the human eye's tolerance to noise. It is a refinement of early ray termination, providing a more nuanced approach to ray management in volume rendering pipelines.
