name: Frustum Culling
head: View Frustum Culling, markVisible
body: Frustum culling is a visibility culling technique that reduces rendering load by filtering out faces, chunks, or primitives that lie outside the camera's viewing frustum. It solves the problem of unnecessary computation for geometry that does not contribute to the final image by performing a conservative intersection test between bounding volumes and the six planes defining the view frustum. It operates on spatial extent relative to the camera orientation and projection, distinguishing it from depth-based occlusion or transmittance-termination methods. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Spatial entities (chunks, blocks, segments, or points) defined by bounding volumes (spheres or axis-aligned boxes). Camera parameters: view matrix (V), projection matrix (P), near plane distance (n), and far plane distance (f). Outputs: A boolean tensor or mask indicating which entities are visible within the frustum. Data Structures: Bounding Sphere: Defined by center ck = (xk, yk, zk) and radius rk. Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB): Defined by minimum and maximum corner vectors bmin = (bmin[0], bmin[1], bmin[2]) and bmax = (bmax[0], bmax[1], bmax[2]). Frustum Planes: Six planes derived from the combined projection-view matrix M = P \cdot V, each represented by coefficients (a, b, c, d) for the plane equation ax + by + cz + d = 0. Numbered Steps: 1. Extract the six frustum planes from the combined matrix M = P \cdot V. 2. For each entity, compute its signed distance to every frustum plane. 3. Apply the sphere or AABB intersection test against all six planes. 4. If the entity fails any single plane test, mark it as culled; otherwise, mark it as visible. 5. For hierarchical structures, test the node's bounding volume first; if the node is fully outside, discard the entire subtree; if fully inside, accept all descendants; if intersecting, recurse into children. Formulas: Sphere Frustum Test: For a plane with coefficients (a, b, c, d) and sphere center (xk, yk, zk), the signed distance is dist = a xk + b yk + c zk + d. The sphere is culled if dist < -rk for any plane. AABB Frustum Test (Positive-Vertex Test): For each plane (a, b, c, d), select the box corner farthest along the plane's normal: px = bmax[0] if a \ge 0 else bmin[0], py = bmax[1] if b \ge 0 else bmin[1], pz = bmax[2] if c \ge 0 else bmin[2]. Evaluate val = a \cdot px + b \cdot py + c \cdot pz + d. If val < 0 for any plane, the box is culled. Active Block Set (Two-Level Variant): \mathcal{K}t = \bigcup{c \in \mathcal{B}t} \{k \mid \text{visible}(k, c)\}, where \mathcal{B}t is the camera batch and k is a block. Parameters: Camera Configuration: Typical helper implementations use FOV 20°, aspect ratio 1.77, near plane 0.5, and far plane 5. Depth Tolerance: When combined with depth-based visibility, a relative tolerance \epsilon = 0.15 is used to account for Gaussian mean positions and depth smoothing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Chunk Center Accuracy: Incorrect calculation of chunk centers during map loading can cause valid chunks to disappear erroneously. Boundary Definitions: Using spherical boundaries for frustum culling alongside Euclidean distance for proximity culling can produce visible artifacts or inconsistencies. Mutual Exclusivity: Some implementations cannot run frustum and proximity culling simultaneously due to conflicting state management. Conservatism: The positive-vertex AABB test is conservative; it never hides a point that should be shown, but may retain nodes that are mostly outside the frustum yet have a corner inside. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def multiplymatrices(A, B): """Multiplies two 4x4 matrices (column-major layout).""" C = [[0.0]4 for in range(4)] for i in range(4): for j in range(4): for k in range(4): C[i][j] += A[k][j] B[i][k] return C def normalizeplane(plane): """Normalizes plane coefficients (a,b,c,d) so the normal vector has unit length.""" a, b, c, d = plane length = math.sqrt(aa + bb + cc) if length == 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return (a/length, b/length, c/length, d/length) def extractfrustumplanes(viewmatrix, projmatrix): """Extracts 6 planes from the combined projection-view matrix.""" M = multiplymatrices(projmatrix, viewmatrix) planes = [] # Standard OpenGL extraction (column-major) planes.append(normalizeplane((M[3][0] + M[0][0], M[3][1] + M[0][1], M[3][2] + M[0][2], M[3][3] + M[0][3]))) # Left planes.append(normalizeplane((M[3][0] - M[0][0], M[3][1] - M[0][1], M[3][2] - M[0][2], M[3][3] - M[0][3]))) # Right planes.append(normalizeplane((M[3][0] + M[1][0], M[3][1] + M[1][1], M[3][2] + M[1][2], M[3][3] + M[1][3]))) # Bottom planes.append(normalizeplane((M[3][0] - M[1][0], M[3][1] - M[1][1], M[3][2] - M[1][2], M[3][3] - M[1][3]))) # Top planes.append(normalizeplane((M[3][0] + M[2][0], M[3][1] + M[2][1], M[3][2] + M[2][2], M[3][3] + M[2][3]))) # Near planes.append(normalizeplane((M[3][0] - M[2][0], M[3][1] - M[2][1], M[3][2] - M[2][2], M[3][3] - M[2][3]))) # Far return planes def spherefrustumtest(center, radius, planes): """Tests if a sphere intersects the frustum. Returns True if visible.""" for a, b, c, d in planes: dist = acenter[0] + bcenter[1] + ccenter[2] + d if dist < -radius: return False return True def aabbfrustumtest(bmin, bmax, planes): """Tests if an AABB intersects the frustum using the positive-vertex test.""" for a, b, c, d in planes: px = bmax[0] if a >= 0 else bmin[0] py = bmax[1] if b >= 0 else bmin[1] pz = bmax[2] if c >= 0 else bmin[2] if apx + bpy + cpz + d < 0: return False return True def frustumcullentities(entities, viewmatrix, projmatrix): """ entities: List of dicts with 'type' ('sphere' or 'aabb'), 'center', 'radius', 'bmin', 'bmax'. Returns a boolean list indicating visibility. """ planes = extractfrustumplanes(viewmatrix, projmatrix) visiblemask = [] for entity in entities: if entity["type"] == "sphere": visiblemask.append(spherefrustumtest(entity["center"], entity["radius"], planes)) elif entity["type"] == "aabb": visiblemask.append(aabbfrustumtest(entity["bmin"], entity["bmax"], planes)) else: visiblemask.append(False) # Not given in the sources. return visiblemask An optimization technique specifically for segment-based tetrahedral meshing. It rejects segments lying outside the view frustum early in the rendering pipeline to counteract over-refinement caused by Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) dependencies, thereby reducing mesh size and computational load. A hierarchical approach used in out-of-core 3D Gaussian Splatting (TideGS). Level 1 (CPU) computes an active block set \mathcal{K}t = \bigcup{c \in \mathcal{B}t} \{k \mid \text{visible}(k, c)\} for a camera batch \mathcal{B}t using coarse bounding spheres with center ck and radius rk. It applies a 6-plane frustum test and culls a sphere if its signed distance to any plane satisfies d < -rk. Level 2 (GPU) materializes selected resident blocks Rt in VRAM, runs the standard 3DGS projection/rasterization pipeline, determines the final contributing set It, and restricts the forward/backward pass to only Gaussians in It. Level 1 is conservative and may admit extra blocks, while Level 2 applies exact pipeline semantics. A helper class implementation that uses a camera's frustum to cull an octree and visualizes intersecting octants with an InstancedMesh. It constructs a PerspectiveCamera with FOV 20°, aspect 1.77, near 0.5, and far 5, and initializes camera position using spherical coordinates (radius 5, phi \pi/3, theta \pi \cdot 1.75). It computes the frustum from projectionMatrix matrixWorldInverse, iterates through octree nodes, and updates an InstancedMesh (BoxGeometry 1,1,1, capacity 2500) with the center and dimensions of intersecting octants. A selection method for error feature aggregation that combines frustum and depth tests to ensure only views observing a token's surface are used. The frustum test transforms the token mean position pj into the camera frame to obtain depth d{jn}, projects it to pixel u{jn}, and passes the view if d{jn} > 0 and 0 \le u < W, 0 \le v < H. The depth test samples the expected depth Dn at u{jn} and keeps the view if d{jn} \le (1 + \epsilon) Dn(u{jn}) with \epsilon = 0.15. The tolerance handles Gaussian mean offsets and depth smoothing at discontinuities. Time Complexity: O(N) for flat entity lists, where N is the number of bounding volumes. O(\log N) or better for balanced hierarchical structures, as entire subtrees are discarded with a single box test. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store bounding volumes and visibility masks. Performance: Significantly reduces GPU and PCIe/SSD transfer costs by filtering blocks before data movement. Prevents performance bottlenecks from over-refined meshes outside the view in segment-based rendering. Strengths: Simple to implement, highly effective for large sparse scenes, and conservative (never hides visible geometry). Limitations: Conservative bounding volumes may admit extra geometry; accuracy depends on precise bounding volume generation; some implementations cannot combine it with proximity culling. Frustum culling is a fundamental computer graphics optimization technique originally developed to avoid processing geometry outside the camera's field of view. Møller and Haines discuss several algorithms for volume/frustum intersection. It is widely applied in out-of-core visualization, voxel rendering, and modern 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines to manage memory and processing loads. name: Two-Level Visibility Culling
head: Coarse block visibility, Fine filtering
body: Two-Level Visibility Culling is a hierarchical culling strategy that minimizes data transfer and computation for large-scale out-of-core 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by separating culling into a conservative CPU-side block filter and an exact GPU-side primitive filter. It differs from standard Frustum Culling by operating on aggregated block bounding volumes first to reduce I/O bandwidth, rather than testing every primitive immediately, and builds on Frustum Culling for the geometric tests. Inputs: \mathcal{K} (set of all scene blocks, each summarized by a bounding sphere), \mathcal{B}t (camera batch for the current frame), Rt (set of resident blocks currently materialized in GPU VRAM). Outputs: \mathcal{K}t (active block set intersecting the frustum), It (final contributing Gaussian set for forward/backward passes). Block Metadata: Stored on CPU/SSD, containing ck (3D vector center) and rk (scalar radius). Frustum Planes: 6 planes defining the view volume, each represented by a normal vector \mathbf{n} and distance d, or equivalently by the signed distance function f(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p} + d. 1. Level 1: Coarse Block Culling (CPU) For each camera c \in \mathcal{B}t, iterate over all blocks k \in \mathcal{K}. Perform a 6-plane frustum test against the block's bounding sphere (ck, rk). A sphere is culled if it lies entirely outside any frustum plane. If the sphere intersects the frustum (not culled), add k to the active set \mathcal{K}t. 2. Level 2: Fine Filtering and Rendering (GPU). Transfer blocks in Rt \cap \mathcal{K}t to the GPU if not already resident. Run the standard 3DGS projection and rasterization pipeline on primitives within these blocks. During rasterization, apply standard visibility tests to individual Gaussians. Identify the final contributing set It \subseteq \bigcup{k \in (Rt \cap \mathcal{K}t)} \text{Block}(k). Only Gaussians in It participate in the forward pass and receive non-zero gradients in the backward pass. Active block set: \mathcal{K}t = \mathcal{K}(\mathcal{B}t) = \bigcup{c \in \mathcal{B}t} \{k \mid \text{visible}(k, c)\}. Sphere culling condition: A sphere is culled if its signed distance d to any frustum plane satisfies d < -rk. Bounding Volume: Level 1 uses bounding spheres for culling. Conservatism: Level 1 is conservative and may admit extra blocks, but Level 2 applies the exact 3DGS pipeline, preserving standard rendering and backpropagation semantics. Precision: Signed distance calculations must handle floating-point precision carefully near the boundary d = -rk. Degenerate Input: Empty blocks or blocks with no visible primitives pass Level 1 but are correctly filtered out during Level 2 rasterization. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twolevelvisibilityculling(blocks, cameras, residentblocks): # blocks: list of dicts with 'id', 'center' (vec3), 'radius' (float), 'gaussians' (list) # cameras: list of dicts with 'planes' (list of 6 tuples: (nx, ny, nz, d)) # residentblocks: set of block ids currently in VRAM activeblockids = set() # Level 1: CPU-side coarse culling for cam in cameras: for blk in blocks: visible = True for (nx, ny, nz, d) in cam['planes']: # Signed distance from block center to plane dist = nx blk['center'][0] + ny blk['center'][1] + nz blk['center'][2] + d # Cull if sphere is strictly outside the plane if dist < -blk['radius']: visible = False break if visible: activeblockids.add(blk['id']) # Level 2: GPU-side fine culling (conceptual implementation) contributinggaussians = [] for blk in blocks: if blk['id'] in activeblockids and blk['id'] in residentblocks: for gauss in blk['gaussians']: # Standard 3DGS rasterization visibility test (e.g., projected radius > 0, depth test) contributinggaussians.append(gauss['id']) return activeblockids, contributinggaussians A variant used in hierarchical molecular visualization that employs a simple object-space clipping plane to selectively reveal model parts. It applies trivial reject tests at the lowest primitive of each level of a three-level acceleration structure (µLAS, mLAS, nLAS). At µLAS, if all vertices of a prism/box fall in the invisible region, traversal terminates because mesostructures and nanostructures on it are also invisible. If some vertices are invisible (prism cut in half), traversal continues to finer levels where the clipping test is applied more finely. At mLAS, if all vertices of a molecule's AABB fall in the invisible region, traversal terminates. At nLAS (atom level), clipping is not applied to ensure accurate representation. Time Complexity: Level 1 is O(N \cdot C) where N is the number of blocks and C is the number of cameras, with a very small constant for sphere-plane tests. Level 2 scales with the number of resident visible blocks, not the total scene size. Memory/IO: Reduces SSD/PCIe traffic significantly by only transferring blocks in \mathcal{K}t \cap Rt, preventing traffic from scaling with the full model size N. Strengths: Enables out-of-core rendering of billion-primitive scenes by decoupling culling from rendering and minimizing data movement. Preserves standard 3DGS rendering and backpropagation semantics. Limitations: Level 1 conservatism may transfer more data than strictly necessary if blocks are large relative to visible content. Requires maintaining block metadata on CPU. When to use: Large-scale 3DGS scenes where full scene projection is too expensive and data resides on slower storage. Two-Level Visibility Culling was introduced in TideGS for scalable training of over one billion 3D Gaussian Splatting primitives via out-of-core optimization. It addresses the bottleneck of SSD/PCIe traffic that would otherwise scale with the full model size N. The method leverages the hierarchical nature of 3DGS storage to perform coarse culling on the CPU before engaging the GPU pipeline. name: Frustum Creation and View Culling
head: CheckFrustomView, FrustumFromCamera
body: This method constructs the six planes of a perspective view frustum from camera parameters and performs a strict containment test to determine if an object is visible. It serves as the foundational geometric step for view culling in volume rendering, ensuring that only objects intersecting the view volume are processed for ray casting or traversal. It differs from hierarchical culling methods by operating on individual object bounding volumes without acceleration structures. Inputs: Camera position (P) as a 3D vector. Camera orientation vectors: front (\mathbf{f}), right (\mathbf{r}), and up (\mathbf{u}), assumed to be orthonormal unit vectors. Near plane distance (d{near}). Far plane distance (d{far}). Vertical field of view (\theta) in radians or degrees. Aspect ratio (a). Object bounding volume (typically an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box or Sphere) defined by its center (C) and extent (E). Outputs: Boolean: true if the object is strictly inside the frustum, false otherwise. Data Structures: Plane: Defined by a point Q and a normal vector \mathbf{n}. The plane equation is (X - Q) \cdot \mathbf{n} = 0. For culling, the normal points inward. Steps: 1. Calculate Frustum Extents at Far Plane: Compute the half-height and half-width of the frustum at the far plane distance. h{far} = d{far} \cdot \tan\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right) w{far} = h{far} \cdot a 2. Construct the Six Planes: The frustum is defined by six planes. The normals are oriented to point into the frustum (inward). Near Plane: Point Q{near} = P + d{near} \cdot \mathbf{f} Normal \mathbf{n}{near} = \mathbf{f} Far Plane: Point Q{far} = P + d{far} \cdot \mathbf{f} Normal \mathbf{n}{far} = -\mathbf{f} Right Plane: The right plane passes through the camera position P. Its normal is perpendicular to the vector from the camera to the right edge of the far plane. Vector to right edge of far plane: \mathbf{v}{right} = d{far} \cdot \mathbf{f} - w{far} \cdot \mathbf{r} Normal \mathbf{n}{right} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{v}{right} \times \mathbf{u}) Note: The cross product order ensures the normal points inward (left of the view direction). Left Plane: Vector to left edge of far plane: \mathbf{v}{left} = d{far} \cdot \mathbf{f} + w{far} \cdot \mathbf{r} Normal \mathbf{n}{left} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}{left}) Top Plane: Vector to top edge of far plane: \mathbf{v}{top} = d{far} \cdot \mathbf{f} - h{far} \cdot \mathbf{u} Normal \mathbf{n}{top} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v}{top}) Bottom Plane: Vector to bottom edge of far plane: \mathbf{v}{bot} = d{far} \cdot \mathbf{f} + h{far} \cdot \mathbf{u} Normal \mathbf{n}{bot} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{v}{bot} \times \mathbf{r}) 3. Perform Containment Test: For each plane i \in \{near, far, right, left, top, bottom\}, calculate the signed distance from the object's center C to the plane. di = (C - Qi) \cdot \mathbf{n}i The object is strictly inside the frustum if and only if: di > 0 \quad \forall i If the object is a bounding box, this test is typically performed against the 8 corners of the box, or by expanding the plane distance by the box's radius/extent along the normal. The source notes imply a point-center check or a simplified AABB check where the object's translation is used directly. For a general AABB with center C and half-extents ex, ey, ez, the condition becomes di > -(\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{e}), where \mathbf{e} is the projection of the box extents onto the plane normal. However, the provided source specifies a strict dot product check on objectTranslation, implying a point or sphere test, or a simplified AABB where the extents are pre-subtracted. We follow the source's strict inequality for point-like objects or pre-culled volumes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import Tuple, List class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def add(self, other): return Vector3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Vector3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def scale(self, s): return Vector3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def dot(self, other): return self.x other.x + self.y other.y + self.z other.z def cross(self, other): return Vector3( self.y other.z - self.z other.y, self.z other.x - self.x other.z, self.x other.y - self.y other.x) def normalize(self): mag = math.sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2) if mag == 0: return Vector3(0, 0, 0) return Vector3(self.x / mag, self.y / mag, self.z / mag) class Plane: def init(self, point: Vector3, normal: Vector3): self.point = point self.normal = normal.normalize() def distancefrompoint(self, p: Vector3) -> float: return (p.sub(self.point)).dot(self.normal) def createfrustumplanes(position: Vector3, front: Vector3, right: Vector3, up: Vector3, near: float, far: float, fovdeg: float, aspect: float) -> List[Plane]: # Convert FOV to radians fovrad = math.radians(fovdeg) # 1. Calculate half vertical and horizontal side lengths at far plane halfvside = far math.tan(fovrad / 2.0) halfhside = halfvside aspect # 2. Define planes planes = [] # Near face nearpoint = position.add(front.scale(near)) planes.append(Plane(nearpoint, front)) # Far face farpoint = position.add(front.scale(far)) planes.append(Plane(farpoint, front.scale(-1))) # Right face # Normal = Cross(front far - right halfhside, up) # Note: Source uses Cross(frontMultFar - right halfHSide, up) vecrightfar = front.scale(far).sub(right.scale(halfhside)) rightnormal = vecrightfar.cross(up).normalize() planes.append(Plane(position, rightnormal)) # Left face # Normal = Cross(up, front far + right halfhside) vecleftfar = front.scale(far).add(right.scale(halfhside)) leftnormal = up.cross(vecleftfar).normalize() planes.append(Plane(position, leftnormal)) # Top face # Normal = Cross(right, front far - up halfvside) vectopfar = front.scale(far).sub(up.scale(halfvside)) topnormal = right.cross(vectopfar).normalize() planes.append(Plane(position, topnormal)) # Bottom face # Normal = Cross(front far + up halfvside, right) vecbotfar = front.scale(far).add(up.scale(halfvside)) botnormal = vecbotfar.cross(right).normalize() planes.append(Plane(position, botnormal)) return planes def isobjectinfrustum(planes: List[Plane], objectcenter: Vector3) -> bool: for plane in planes: # Strictly greater than 0 as per source if plane.distancefrompoint(objectcenter) <= 0: return False return True Parameters: fovdeg: Vertical field of view. Default 60 degrees. aspect: Aspect ratio (width/height). Default 1.77. near: Near plane distance. Default 0.1. far: Far plane distance. Default 200. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Camera: If front, right, or up are not orthonormal, the frustum geometry will be skewed. The source assumes valid camera basis vectors. Precision: Floating-point errors may cause objects exactly on the boundary to be culled if the inequality is not handled consistently (e.g., >= vs >). The source uses strict > 0. Zero FOV: If FOV is 0, tan(0) is 0, resulting in a degenerate frustum with no volume. This variant focuses specifically on the derivation of the plane equations from the camera matrix or basis vectors. It sets itself apart by emphasizing the geometric derivation of the normals via cross products of the view direction and the far-plane edges, rather than extracting planes from a projection matrix. It is chosen when explicit control over plane orientation is required for custom culling logic or when the projection matrix is not readily available. It links to Frustum Culling. Time Complexity: O(1) per object. The number of operations is constant (6 planes, 6 dot products). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space for plane storage. Performance: Extremely fast, suitable for per-object culling in real-time engines. The cost is dominated by the trigonometric function (tan) if FOV is not precomputed, but this is typically done once per frame. Strengths: Simple to implement, no preprocessing required, works with any bounding volume type (with appropriate distance calculation). Limitations: Does not account for occlusion. It only checks visibility against the view volume. It may cull too aggressively if the bounding volume is loose. When to use: As a first-pass culling step before more expensive visibility checks. When not to use: When occlusion is significant and needs to be resolved, or when dealing with highly dynamic scenes where hierarchical culling might be more efficient. This method is derived from standard computer graphics techniques for view frustum culling. The specific implementation details, including the plane construction via cross products and the strict inequality check, are documented in the VoxelCoreEngine source code. It is a fundamental technique used in virtually all 3D rendering pipelines, including those for volume rendering, to reduce the number of objects processed by the GPU. name: Interactive Render Quality Estimation & Cancellation
head: Interactive quality fallback, Octree render cancellation
body: This method prevents infinite rendering loops in interactive volume visualization by detecting when the rendering pipeline exceeds the frame budget and forcing a quality reduction on the subsequent frame. It acts as a safety mechanism distinct from standard early termination, which stops individual rays based on opacity Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control. Inputs: Octree structure, camera state, rendering state container. Outputs: Rendered frame data or an early return signal containing reduced quality parameters. Data Structures: renderingRequired: Container holding the boolean flag OCTREERENDERINGCANCELED. OCTREEINTERACTIVERENDERINGPOINTTHRESHOLD: Scalar threshold used to estimate a safe render quality when interactive traversal is canceled. Steps: 1. Check Cancellation Flag: After octree traversal or at frame start, inspect renderingRequired for the OCTREERENDERINGCANCELED flag. 2. Evaluate Condition: If the flag is set, the previous frame exceeded the time budget, risking an infinite loop if the same high-quality parameters are reused. 3. Estimate Lower Quality: Calculate a safe, lower render quality using OCTREEINTERACTIVERENDERINGPOINTTHRESHOLD. This typically involves increasing the step size (coarser sampling) or reducing the number of samples per ray. 4. Unlock and Return: Unlock the rendering API/resources and return early to skip the expensive full-resolution traversal loop. 5. Next Frame Execution: The subsequent frame renders with the reduced quality parameters, ensuring completion and clearing the flag. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderframe(octree, camera, renderingstate): # Check if previous frame exceeded time budget if renderingstate.renderingrequired.OCTREERENDERINGCANCELED: # Estimate lower interactive render quality using the threshold quality = computequality(renderingstate.OCTREEINTERACTIVERENDERINGPOINTTHRESHOLD) # Unlock API to prevent deadlock renderingstate.unlockapi() # Return early to skip expensive traversal return quality try: # Standard high-quality front-to-back traversal result = standardtraversal(octree, camera) renderingstate.renderingrequired.OCTREERENDERINGCANCELED = False return result except TimeLimitExceeded: # Set flag to trigger cancellation on next frame renderingstate.renderingrequired.OCTREERENDERINGCANCELED = True raise def computequality(threshold): # Maps the threshold to a coarser step size or reduced sample count return {"stepsize": threshold 2.0, "samplesperray": max(1, threshold)} def standardtraversal(octree, camera): # Standard front-to-back volume integration loop acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 for ray in camera.rays: for voxel in octree.intersect(ray): C, alpha = samplevoxel(voxel) acccolor = [acccolor[i] + C[i] alpha (1.0 - accalpha) for i in range(3)] accalpha += alpha (1.0 - accalpha) return acccolor def samplevoxel(voxel): # Returns color C and opacity alpha for the voxel return voxel.color, voxel.alpha def unlockapi(): # Releases rendering context locks pass Parameters: OCTREEINTERACTIVERENDERINGPOINTTHRESHOLD: Threshold used to estimate a safe render quality when interactive traversal is canceled. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite Loop: Overestimating render quality when the cancellation flag is set can cause an infinite rendering loop, as the system continues to request more work than the hardware can deliver. The cancellation check and forced quality estimation prevent this by guaranteeing a lower computational load on the next frame. A preprocessing step that computes view-dependent visibility coefficients for each octree leaf, used by the Prioritized-Layered Projection (PLP) algorithm to prioritize visible nodes at runtime. It estimates the likelihood of a node blocking light by rasterizing its contents against its bounding box from multiple sample viewpoints. Steps: 1. For each octree leaf, place an arbitrary number of sample viewpoints around the leaf. 2. Select viewpoints such that the entire node is visible towards its center, maximizing the projected screen area of the node's bounding box. 3. For each sample viewpoint: rasterize the node's bounding box in green; rasterize the node's contents in red over a black background without depth tests; read back the frame buffer; count green pixels (ng) and red pixels (nr). 4. Compute the visibility coefficient as nr / (nr + ng). 5. At runtime, select the coefficient whose corresponding sampling direction is closest to the current viewing direction. Parameters: numcoefficients: The number of visibility coefficients stored per node. Typical value is 20. Time Complexity: The cancellation check is O(1). Quality estimation is O(1). Actual rendering cost is reduced significantly by skipping the full traversal loop. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory for the flag and threshold. Visibility coefficients add constant memory per node. Performance: Guarantees frame completion by degrading quality, preventing hangs. Strengths: Robust against infinite loops; simple to implement. Limitations: Visual quality may fluctuate between frames; does not optimize the current frame's quality, only ensures completion. The method originates from interactive visualization systems for large datasets, specifically those using octree structures for out-of-core rendering. The cancellation mechanism is documented in the iVoxel repository. The visibility coefficient variant is described in Wagner Correa's thesis on out-of-core visualization techniques. larsxschneider/iVoxel, https://github.com/larsxschneider/iVoxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) New Techniques for Out-Of-Core Visualization of Large Datasets, https://ctsilva.github.io/thesis/wagner-correa-thesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Visible Zone Algorithm
head: ComputeVisibilityMask, Hall-Holt and Rusinkiewicz Visible Zone Algorithm, Visibility Mask Computation
body: The Visible Zone Algorithm is a conservative visibility computation method that determines which primitives are potentially visible from a set of viewpoints by projecting them into screen space and retaining only those within a specified depth thickness. It sets itself apart from approximate visibility methods by guaranteeing correct visibility with less than one pixel of screen-space deviation. The algorithm computes a binary visibility matrix O of size N \times K, where N is the number of input points and K is the number of viewpoints. It operates by projecting all points from each viewpoint, grouping them by pixel, sorting by depth, and marking the top \tau points as visible. Inputs: P: Set of N points (e.g., Gaussian centroids or voxel centers). V: Set of K viewpoints. \tau: Thickness parameter, defining the number of visible layers per pixel. Outputs: O: N \times K visibility matrix, where O[i, j] = 1 if point i is visible from viewpoint j, else 0. Data Structures: M: A dictionary mapping pixel coordinates (u, v) to a list of points projected to that pixel. M^: A set of points identified as visible for the current viewpoint. Steps: 1. Initialize O with zeros. 2. For each viewpoint j from 1 to K: a. Let c be the current viewpoint. b. Retrieve extrinsic matrix d and intrinsic matrix K{intr} for c. c. Initialize empty map M. d. For each point i from 1 to N: i. Let p be point P[i]. ii. Compute 2D projection xc = (u, v) using forward projection with d and K{intr}. iii. Add p to the list M{u,v} associated with pixel (u, v) in M. e. Initialize empty set M^. f. For each list M{u,v} in M: i. Sort M{u,v} by depth z (ascending). ii. For i from 1 to \tau: add M{u,v}[i] to M^. g. For each point i from 1 to N: i. If P[i] is in M^, set O[i, j] = 1. 3. Return O. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevisibilitymask(P, V, tau): """ Compute visibility mask for points P from viewpoints V with thickness tau. P: List of N points, each with 3D coordinates (x, y, z). V: List of K viewpoints, each with extrinsic (d) and intrinsic (Kintr) matrices. tau: Integer, number of visible layers per pixel. Returns: N x K matrix O. """ N = len(P) K = len(V) O = [[0] K for in range(N)] for j in range(K): c = V[j] d = c.extrinsicmatrix Kintr = c.intrinsicmatrix M = {} # Project all points for i in range(N): p = P[i] u, v = forwardprojection(p, d, Kintr) if (u, v) not in M: M[(u, v)] = [] M[(u, v)].append(p) Mstar = set() # Determine visible points per pixel for pointlist in M.values(): # Sort by depth z pointlist.sort(key=lambda pt: pt.z) # Pick first tau points (bounds to available points if tau exceeds list length) for k in range(min(tau, len(pointlist))): Mstar.add(pointlist[k]) # Update visibility matrix for i in range(N): if P[i] in Mstar: O[i][j] = 1 return O def forwardprojection(p, d, Kintr): """ Project 3D point p using extrinsic d and intrinsic Kintr. Returns (u, v) pixel coordinates. """ # Transform to camera coordinates pcam = transformpoint(p, d) # Perspective divide and project to pixel coordinates x, y, z = pcam.x, pcam.y, pcam.z if z <= 0: return None u = Kintr.fx (x / z) + Kintr.cx v = Kintr.fy (y / z) + Kintr.cy return int(u), int(v) def transformpoint(p, d): """ Apply 4x4 extrinsic matrix d to 3D point p. Returns transformed Point object. """ wx = d[0][0]p.x + d[0][1]p.y + d[0][2]p.z + d[0][3] wy = d[1][0]p.x + d[1][1]p.y + d[1][2]p.z + d[1][3] wz = d[2][0]p.x + d[2][1]p.y + d[2][2]p.z + d[2][3] return Point(wx, wy, wz) Parameters: \tau: Thickness. Defines the number of visible layers per pixel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \tau exceeds the number of points projected to a pixel, the selection loop bounds to the available points. Precision in projection and sorting affects depth ordering and which points are considered "in front". The algorithm assumes points are distinct; overlapping points at the same depth may require deterministic tie-breaking logic. A method to compute approximate visibility for line drawings from volume data by reducing the number of vertices checked for occlusion, trading accuracy for performance. It sets itself apart from the exact visibility algorithm Visible Zone Algorithm by sacrificing worst-case correctness for a predictable speedup factor, making it suitable for large datasets where interactive frame rates are prioritized over perfect occlusion handling. The algorithm achieves real-time frame rates for 2D and 2.5D datasets. The precomputation cost can be high; for a model with 13 million triangles, the accuracy guarantee costs 128 hours of precomputation on a cluster of 16 PCs. It is suitable for scenarios where conservative visibility is critical and precomputation time is acceptable. It is less suitable for dynamic scenes where viewpoints change frequently, as the mask must be recomputed. The Visible Zone Algorithm was developed by Hall-Holt and Rusinkiewicz. It is designed for conservative visibility computation with incremental updates. It is used to interactively render large datasets with less than one pixel of screen-space deviation. name: Approximate Visibility Algorithm
head: Stride-based Visibility Sampling
body: A method to compute approximate visibility for line drawings from volume data by reducing the number of vertices checked for occlusion, trading accuracy for performance. It sets itself apart from the exact visibility algorithm Visible Zone Algorithm by sacrificing worst-case correctness for a predictable speedup factor, making it suitable for large datasets where interactive frame rates are prioritized over perfect occlusion handling. Input: A loop of vertices V = \{v0, v1, \dots, v{N-1}\} representing a contour or cutting plane intersection, and a stride parameter k. Output: A visibility mask M for each vertex in the loop, where M[i] indicates whether vertex vi is visible or occluded. Visibility Array: An array of boolean values or flags, size N, corresponding to the vertices in the loop. Stride Parameter: Integer k \ge 1. 1. Initialize the visibility status for all vertices in the loop as "unknown". 2. Iterate through the loop indices i with a step size of k (i.e., i = 0, k, 2k, \dots). 3. For each sampled vertex vi: perform the exact visibility test to determine if vi is visible, and store the result in M[i]. 4. For each interval between two consecutive sampled vertices vi and v{i+k}: if M[i] \neq M[i+k] (a transition is detected), iterate through all intervening vertices j where i < j < i+k and perform the exact visibility test for each vj to determine the exact transition point. If M[i] == M[i+k] (no transition detected), assume all intervening vertices j where i < j < i+k have the same visibility as M[i] and set M[j] = M[i] for all such j. 5. Return the visibility mask M. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def approximatevisibility(vertices, k, visibilitytestfunc): """ Compute approximate visibility for a loop of vertices. Args: vertices: List of vertex objects or indices. k: Stride length for sampling. visibilitytestfunc: Function that returns True if vertex is visible, False otherwise. Returns: List of booleans representing visibility status for each vertex. """ n = len(vertices) visibility = [None] n # Step 1: Sample every k-th vertex for i in range(0, n, k): visibility[i] = visibilitytestfunc(vertices[i]) # Step 2: Check intervals between consecutive sampled vertices for i in range(0, n - k, k): start = i end = i + k if visibility[start] != visibility[end]: for j in range(start + 1, end): visibility[j] = visibilitytestfunc(vertices[j]) else: for j in range(start + 1, end): visibility[j] = visibility[start] # Handle remaining vertices if n is not a multiple of k (wrap-around for closed loops) lastsampled = (n - 1) // k k if lastsampled < n - 1: if visibility[lastsampled] != visibility[0]: for j in range(lastsampled + 1, n): visibility[j] = visibilitytestfunc(vertices[j]) else: for j in range(lastsampled + 1, n): visibility[j] = visibility[lastsampled] return visibility k: The stride length for sampling vertices. Typical values tested: 1, 2, 4, 8. k=1 corresponds to the exact visibility algorithm. Narrow occluders: If the stride k is too large, narrow occluders may be missed, causing visible artifacts (mislabeled vertices). Guarantee: The method guarantees that no details larger than k voxels are missed. Precision: The method relies on the visibility test function being consistent. Inconsistent tests may lead to false transitions. Time Complexity: Reduces the algorithm's running time by a factor of at most k compared to checking every vertex. The exact visibility algorithm is O(n^2) for a volume of size n^3. The approximate method is therefore roughly O(n^2/k) in the best case (no transitions), but can degrade to O(n^2) if every interval requires full checking. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On the aneurysm dataset: Stride 1: 590 msec/frame, Stride 2: 370 msec/frame, Stride 4: 280 msec/frame, Stride 8: 244 msec/frame. Strengths: Significant speedup for large datasets where many vertices share the same visibility status. Limitations: May mislabel vertices if narrow occluders are present and k is large. Not suitable for real-time rendering if high accuracy is required for narrow features. When to use: Large datasets where interactive frame rates are needed and narrow occluders are not critical. When not to use: When exact visibility is required, or when the dataset contains many narrow occluders and k must be small. Origin: Developed as part of a system for line drawings from volume data. History: Introduced in the context of line drawings from volume data, specifically for handling visibility of contours and cutting planes. Usage: Used in the aneurysm dataset rendering to handle narrow occluders, though video sequences were created without it. It is part of a system that provides user control over line styles based on visibility. Line drawings from volume data, https://doi.org/10.1145/1073204.1073222, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Window-Closing Visibility Detection
head: ACW algorithm, Aggregate Cull Window, Window Closing for Virtual Colonoscopy
body: Window-Closing Visibility Detection is a conservative visibility culling method designed for perspective navigation within large, tubular datasets, specifically virtual colonoscopy. It solves the problem of efficiently identifying which subvolumes (represented as boxes) lie within the current viewing frustum without performing expensive per-box frustum intersection tests for all candidates. It sets itself apart from its parent, the Visible Zone Algorithm, by utilizing a 2D screen-space projection approach that iteratively shrinks a culling window, and from its sibling, the Approximate Visibility Algorithm, by relying on the geometric "twisted" nature of the colon to guarantee that occlusion is handled via window degeneration rather than approximate distance bounds. The algorithm operates on a preprocessed representation of the volume where the colon shape is approximated by a sequence of piecewise boxes. It determines visibility by projecting these boxes onto the screen and maintaining an Aggregate Cull Window (ACW) that represents the visible portion of the screen through which subsequent boxes can be seen. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of boxes B1, B2, \dots, Bn approximating the colon, ordered by proximity to the viewer (or along the colon path). The current camera view parameters (projection matrix, viewport). Output: A subset of visible boxes to be sent to the volume rendering hardware (e.g., Cube-4/VolumePro). Data Structures: Box: A 3D axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) or a portal defined by its vertices. Current Cull Window (CCW): A 2D axis-aligned bounding rectangle in screen space, defined by (x{min}, y{min}, x{max}, y{max}). Aggregate Cull Window (ACW): A 2D axis-aligned bounding rectangle in screen space, initialized as the CCW of the first box and updated iteratively. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Approximate the colon geometry with a sequence of piecewise boxes. Order these boxes such that the algorithm begins with the closest box to the view point. 2. Initialization: Identify the first box B{start} closest to the view point. 3. Project Initial Portal: Project the vertices of the initial portal (the boundary of B{start} facing the viewer) onto the 2D screen plane. 4. Compute Initial CCW: Calculate the 2D axis-aligned bounding rectangle of the projected vertices. This rectangle is the Current Cull Window (CCW) for the first box. 5. Initialize ACW: Set the Aggregate Cull Window (ACW) equal to the initial CCW. The ACW represents the conservative bound of the visible area through the current box. 6. Iterate Through Boxes: For each subsequent adjacent box B{next} in the sequence: a. Project Next Portal: Project the vertices of B{next}'s portal onto the screen. b. Compute Next CCW: Calculate the 2D axis-aligned bounding rectangle of these projected vertices. c. Update ACW: Compute the intersection of the new CCW and the previous ACW: ACW{new} = ACW{old} \cap CCW{next} Where the intersection of two rectangles R1=(x{1min}, y{1min}, x{1max}, y{1max}) and R2=(x{2min}, y{2min}, x{2max}, y{2max}) is: x{min} = \max(x{1min}, x{2min}) y{min} = \max(y{1min}, y{2min}) x{max} = \min(x{1max}, x{2max}) y{max} = \min(y{1max}, y{2max}) d. Check Degeneration: If the ACW is degenerate (i.e., x{min} \ge x{max} or y{min} \ge y{max}, resulting in an empty or invalid area), stop the iteration. The current box and all subsequent boxes are considered occluded or outside the visible frustum. e. Mark Visible: If the ACW is valid, mark B{next} as visible and continue to the next box. 7. Rendering: Send all marked visible boxes to the volume rendering hardware for perspective rendering. Parameters: Box Approximation: The granularity of the piecewise box approximation affects accuracy and performance. Not given in the sources. Portal Definition: The specific vertices used to define the "portal" of a box. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate ACW: The algorithm relies on the ACW becoming empty to terminate. If the colon geometry is not sufficiently "twisted" or occluded, the ACW may remain valid for many boxes, reducing culling efficiency. Perspective Projection: The method is designed for perspective projection. Ordering: Boxes must be processed in an order that respects occlusion (closest to furthest). Incorrect ordering can lead to incorrect visibility determination. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def windowclosingvisibilitydetection(boxes, camera): """ boxes: List of Box objects, ordered from closest to furthest. camera: Object with projectionmatrix and viewport attributes. Returns: List of visible boxes. """ visibleboxes = [] if not boxes: return visibleboxes # Step 1: Get the first box (closest) currentbox = boxes[0] # Step 2: Project initial portal and compute CCW projectedvertices = applyprojection(currentbox.portalvertices, camera.projectionmatrix, camera.viewport) ccw = compute2daabb(projectedvertices) # Step 3: Initialize ACW acw = ccw # Step 4: Mark first box as visible visibleboxes.append(currentbox) # Step 5: Iterate through remaining boxes for nextbox in boxes[1:]: # Project next portal projectedverticesnext = applyprojection(nextbox.portalvertices, camera.projectionmatrix, camera.viewport) ccwnext = compute2daabb(projectedverticesnext) # Update ACW by intersection acw = intersectrectangles(acw, ccwnext) # Check for degeneration if isdegenerate(acw): break # Mark as visible visibleboxes.append(nextbox) return visibleboxes def applyprojection(vertices, projectionmatrix, viewport): """Standard perspective projection to normalized device coordinates, then to viewport pixels.""" projected = [] for v in vertices: # Homogeneous division and viewport transform (standard graphics pipeline step) x = (v.x projectionmatrix[0][0]) / v.w y = (v.y projectionmatrix[1][1]) / v.w projected.append({'x': x, 'y': y}) return projected def compute2daabb(vertices): """Compute 2D axis-aligned bounding box from a list of 2D points.""" xs = [v['x'] for v in vertices] ys = [v['y'] for v in vertices] return { 'xmin': min(xs), 'ymin': min(ys), 'xmax': max(xs), 'ymax': max(ys) } def intersectrectangles(r1, r2): """Compute intersection of two 2D AABBs.""" return { 'xmin': max(r1['xmin'], r2['xmin']), 'ymin': max(r1['ymin'], r2['ymin']), 'xmax': min(r1['xmax'], r2['xmax']), 'ymax': min(r1['ymax'], r2['ymax']) } def isdegenerate(rect): """Check if a rectangle is empty or invalid.""" return rect['xmin'] >= rect['xmax'] or rect['ymin'] >= rect['ymax'] A technique to decrease the size of the ACW so that rendering terminates earlier. It sets itself apart from standard spatial culling by incorporating image-based feedback and geometric refinement to dynamically shrink the culling bounds. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of boxes until the ACW degenerates. Each box requires projection and a constant-time rectangle intersection. Memory Complexity: Constant space for the ACW and CCW, plus storage for the box sequence. Strengths: Efficient for tubular structures with significant self-occlusion (like the colon). Avoids expensive 3D frustum intersection tests. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that the structure is "twisted" enough to cause occlusion. Performance degrades if the ACW does not degenerate quickly. Limited to perspective projection as described. When to Use: Interactive navigation in large, tubular volume datasets (e.g., virtual colonoscopy) where occlusion is frequent. When Not to Use: Non-tubular structures, parallel projection, or scenes with low self-occlusion. The Window-Closing Visibility Detection algorithm was developed for virtual colonoscopy applications to enable interactive navigation within large human colon datasets. It was presented in the context of real-time volume rendering, leveraging the twisted nature of the colon to optimize visibility culling. name: Aggregate Cull Window (ACW) Reduction
head: ACW Reduction, Dynamic ACW Reduction
body: Aggregate Cull Window (ACW) Reduction is a technique to decrease the size of the Aggregate Cull Window (ACW) so that rendering terminates earlier. It sets itself apart from standard spatial culling by incorporating image-based feedback and geometric refinement to dynamically shrink the culling bounds. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current Aggregate Cull Window (ACW) bounds, subvolume geometry, framebuffer image data. Output: Reduced ACW bounds, visibility status for subvolumes. Data Structures: ACW: A bounding volume (typically a frustum or box) representing the region of interest. Portals: Rectangular intersections between adjacent boxes, used to approximate the shape of the volume (e.g., a colon). Framebuffer: The current image buffer containing rendered pixel data. Steps: 1. Portal Generation: Generate more portals inside each box to better capture the shape of the colon. This improves the accuracy of the spatial culling but increases the number of portals to project. 2. ACW Evaluation: Project the generated portals to determine the initial ACW size. 3. Threshold Check: Determine if the current ACW size is smaller than a predefined threshold. 4. Image-Based Reduction (Conditional): If the ACW size is below the threshold: Access the framebuffer image for each subvolume inside the ACW. Check if the subvolume's image contains rows of opaque pixels. If opaque rows are found, shrink the ACW accordingly. 5. Dynamic Combination: Dynamically combine the portal-based and image-based methods for the most effective ACW reduction. Parameters: Threshold: A specific size value for the ACW. If ACW size < threshold, perform additional pixel checking; otherwise, rely on the standard ACW intersection logic. Pitfalls: Generating more portals increases the expense of ACW evaluation because more portals must be projected. Accessing the framebuffer is expensive; this operation is only performed when the ACW size is smaller than a certain threshold. A dynamic combination method to reduce the cost of Aggregate Cull Window (ACW) calculations by only performing additional pixel checking when the ACW size is smaller than a certain threshold. It relies on a threshold parameter: if ACW size < threshold, perform additional pixel checking; otherwise, rely on the standard ACW intersection logic. Time Complexity: Increases with the number of portals due to projection costs. Framebuffer access is expensive and is conditionally executed. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of portals and framebuffer size. Strengths: Enables earlier termination of rendering by more accurately culling non-visible subvolumes. Limitations: High cost of framebuffer access and portal projection if not managed carefully. When to use: When interactive rendering of complex, twisted volumes (e.g., colon) is required, and standard culling is insufficient. Originated in the context of real-time volume rendering, specifically for medical imaging applications like colon visualization. It builds on the Window-Closing Visibility Detection method [21435-window-closing-visibility-detection.md]. name: Occlusion-Aware Visibility Filter
head: Weight-based Visibility Filter
body: The Occlusion-Aware Visibility Filter replaces the standard view-frustum test in 3D Gaussian Splatting densification with a rendering-based signal that restricts statistical updates to Gaussians that actually contribute to the final image. Unlike sibling methods that rely on binary flags or pixel counts, this method uses the sum of blending weights to determine visibility, ensuring that occluded Gaussians do not accumulate densification statistics. The method operates during the training loop of 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically modifying the Adaptive Density Control (ADC) phase. It ensures that gradient and radius statistics are only accumulated for Gaussians that are not fully occluded by front-facing primitives. Input: The set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, the current camera view parameters, and the rendered image. Output: A boolean visibility mask or accumulated contribution metric for each Gaussian, used to gate densification statistics. Gaussian State: Each Gaussian i maintains a state including its position \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and color ci. Contribution Accumulator: A scalar value Wi per Gaussian, initialized to zero at the start of each view or epoch, accumulating the sum of blending weights. Statistics Buffer: Buffers for positional gradients g{i,v} and other ADC metrics, which are conditionally updated based on the filter's output. 1. Rendering: For each pixel p in the view, render the image using front-to-back compositing. The contribution of Gaussian i to pixel p is determined by its blending weight w{i,p}. 2. Blending Weight Calculation: Calculate the blending weight for Gaussian i at pixel p: w{i,p} = \alpha{i,p} \cdot T{i,p} where \alpha{i,p} is the per-pixel opacity of the Gaussian and T{i,p} is the transmittance (fraction of light reaching the Gaussian from the camera). 3. Accumulation: For each Gaussian i that contributes to any pixel, add its blending weight to its total contribution accumulator Wi: Wi = \sum{p \in \text{pixels}} w{i,p} Rendering typically terminates early when transmittance T{i,p} falls below a threshold (e.g., 10^{-4}), meaning Gaussians behind this point are not rendered and contribute zero. 4. Visibility Determination: After processing all pixels for the view, determine if Gaussian i is visible: If Wi > 0, the Gaussian is considered visible (it participated in rendering). If Wi = 0, the Gaussian is considered occluded (it did not contribute to the image). 5. Statistics Gating: During the Adaptive Density Control (ADC) event: If Gaussian i is visible (Wi > 0), accumulate its positional gradient g{i,v} = \partial L / \partial \mui and other statistics for densification decisions. If Gaussian i is occluded (Wi = 0), exclude it from densification statistics. The raw view count normalizer is replaced by an average-contribution normalizer based on these filtered statistics. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def occlusionawarefilter(gaussians, pixels): """ Filters Gaussians based on their actual contribution to the rendered view. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: id: Unique identifier wtotal: Accumulated blending weight (initialized to 0.0 per view) visible: Boolean visibility flag pixels: List of pixel indices covered by the current view. Returns: gaussians: Updated Gaussian list with visibility flags. """ # Step 1 & 2: Initialize accumulators for g in gaussians: g.wtotal = 0.0 g.visible = False # Step 3: Accumulate blending weights w{i,p} over all pixels p # The rasterizer provides the list of (pixelindex, w{i,p}) pairs for each Gaussian. for g in gaussians: for p, wip in computeblendingweights(g, pixels): g.wtotal += wip # Step 4: Determine visibility for g in gaussians: g.visible = (g.wtotal > 0.0) return gaussians def computeblendingweights(gaussian, pixels): """ Simulates the rasterizer output: returns list of (pixelindex, blendingweight) pairs. """ # Standard front-to-back compositing computes w{i,p} = alpha{i,p} T{i,p} # This function represents the rasterizer's output for Gaussian i. return [(p, gaussian.alpha gaussian.transmittance) for p in pixels] def updateadcstatistics(gaussians, gradients): """ Updates ADC statistics only for visible Gaussians. """ for g in gaussians: if g.visible: # Accumulate gradient and other stats for densification g.gradaccum += gradients[g.id] g.viewcount += 1 else: # Exclude occluded Gaussians from densification statistics g.gradaccum = 0.0 g.viewcount = 0 return gaussians Transmittance Threshold: Rendering terminates when T{i,p} < 10^{-4}. This threshold implicitly defines the occlusion boundary. Zero Contribution: A Gaussian with Wi = 0 is strictly excluded. This handles cases where a Gaussian is within the frustum but completely behind other opaque geometry. Precision: The sum of blending weights Wi is a floating-point accumulation. The binary nature of the filter (zero vs. non-zero) makes it robust to minor numerical noise, provided the threshold is strictly >0. Time Complexity: The visibility filter adds negligible overhead as it reuses data already computed during the forward rendering pass (blending weights). The main cost is the conditional update of statistics, which is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Requires storing one scalar Wi per Gaussian per view or epoch, which is minimal compared to the Gaussian state itself. Performance: In occlusion-heavy scenes, this method reduces the number of Gaussians required by up to 63% compared to occlusion-blind baselines, while improving image quality metrics (e.g., up to 6% lower LPIPS). Strengths: Prevents under-densification in occluded regions by ignoring irrelevant Gaussians. It is more nuanced than binary flags because it uses the magnitude of contribution. Limitations: It is specific to the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework and its densification pipeline. It does not accelerate the forward rendering itself, but rather the training efficiency and final model compactness. The Occlusion-Aware Visibility Filter was introduced in the paper "Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses a limitation in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting where densification statistics are based on view-frustum tests, which count Gaussians that are potentially visible but may be fully occluded in specific views. This leads to inefficient densification in complex, occlusion-heavy scenes. The method replaces the frustum-based filter with a rendering-based signal, specifically the sum of blending weights, which is also used in the proposed "Average Contribution Criterion" for densification decisions. It is integrated into a framework based on StopThePop. name: Bounding Volume Empty-Space Culling
head: Bounding volume strategy
body: Bounding volume empty-space culling restricts volume reconstruction and rendering computation to the "effective" area where voxel values are valid, bypassing empty space outside this region. It builds on Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling by using a geometric bounding volume as a depth buffer to guide the pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projection data, viewing direction, and volume grid dimensions. Output: A depth buffer defining the valid reconstruction bounds for the current view, used to cull invalid voxels during reconstruction and rendering. Data Structures: Bounding Volume: A geometric primitive representing the effective reconstruction area (a truncated circle for 2D square volume slices, or a truncated cylinder for 3D cubic volumes). Depth Buffer: A buffer storing the slice boundaries of the bounding volume, used to restrict computation. Steps: 1. Calculate Initial Bounding Volume: Determine the effective reconstruction area based on the assumption of parallel beam reconstruction. 2. Slice Bounding Volume: Slice the calculated bounding volume according to the current viewing direction. 3. Generate Depth Buffer: Use the resulting bounding volume slices to create a depth buffer. 4. Restrict Computation: Use the depth buffer to guide the reconstruction pipeline, ensuring that computation is restricted to the effective area throughout the entire process. Formulas: The sources do not provide explicit mathematical formulas for the truncation boundaries. The effective area is geometrically defined as a truncated circle for 2D square slices or a truncated cylinder for 3D cubic volumes under parallel beam assumptions. Parameters: Viewing direction: Determines the slicing of the bounding volume. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method assumes parallel beam reconstruction; deviations may affect accuracy. The bounding volume is an approximation; it may include some empty space or exclude valid voxels if the object shape is highly irregular. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateboundingvolume(griddims, projectiontype): """ Calculate the initial bounding volume based on parallel beam assumption. Returns a dictionary representing the geometric primitive. """ if projectiontype == "2D": radius = max(griddims["x"], griddims["y"]) / 2.0 return {"type": "truncatedcircle", "radius": radius} elif projectiontype == "3D": radius = max(griddims["x"], griddims["y"]) / 2.0 height = griddims["z"] return {"type": "truncatedcylinder", "radius": radius, "height": height} else: raise ValueError("Unsupported projection type") def sliceboundingvolume(boundingvolume, viewingdirection): """ Slice the bounding volume according to the viewing direction. Returns a list of slice boundaries (depth buffer). """ # Implementation depends on the specific geometry and viewing direction # This step generates the depth buffer slices # Not given in the sources. return [] def restrictreconstruction(depthbuffer, reconstructionpipeline): """ Use the depth buffer to restrict computation within the effective area. """ processedslices = [] for currentslice in reconstructionpipeline: if currentslice["z"] in depthbuffer: processedslices.append(currentslice) return processedslices A sophisticated preprocessing scheme that reconstructs a volume mask labeling all voxels in the shadow of non-zero projection data, which is then sliced per frame to drive reconstruction more accurately than a bounding sphere. It is equivalent to empty space skipping, with the bounding volume method being a good approximation for many cases, while the occupancy mask is more accurate. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of voxels processed by culling those outside the effective area. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the bounding volume and depth buffer. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective for regular object shapes. Limitations: Approximation may not be accurate for complex or irregular object shapes. The method is described in the paper "GPU-Accelerated D2VR". GPU-Accelerated D2VR, https://doi.org/10.2312/vg/vg06/023-030, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Empty-space skipping via Acceleration Structure
head: Empty space skipping via the acceleration structure
body: This method accelerates direct volume rendering by using a hierarchical min/max acceleration structure to skip transparent regions of the volume data. It reduces the number of samples taken per ray by jumping over blocks that contain no visible data, distinct from sibling methods that may use sparse voxel grids or hierarchical bounding box trees. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A source volumetric dataset (e.g., 512 \times 512 \times 512) and a pre-computed acceleration structure. Output: A rendered image with reduced computational cost. Data Structures: The acceleration structure is a small two-channel volumetric dataset. Dimensions: 16 \times 16 \times 16 cells. Layout: Each cell corresponds to a 32 \times 32 \times 32 block in the source dataset. Content: Each cell stores the minimum and maximum values found within its corresponding source block. Alternative Layout: Some implementations use a per-field min/max structure organized in 32 \times 32 \times 32 bricks. Algorithm Steps: 1. For each ray, determine the intersection with the acceleration structure grid. 2. Traverse the acceleration structure cells along the ray path using a 3D grid traversal algorithm. 3. For each cell, retrieve the stored minimum and maximum values. 4. Check if the space corresponding to the cell is transparent by comparing the maximum value against a visibility threshold. 5. If the cell is transparent, skip the entire 32 \times 32 \times 32 block and advance the ray to the next cell boundary. 6. If the cell is not transparent, sample the source data within that block and perform standard front-to-back compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(o, d, V, A, step=0.5, threshold=0.0): B = 32 # Block size in voxels N = 16 # Acceleration structure dimensions Cacc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphaacc = 0.0 # Initialize DDA for the 16x16x16 acceleration grid ix, iy, iz = int(o[0] // B), int(o[1] // B), int(o[2] // B) if not (0 <= ix < N and 0 <= iy < N and 0 <= iz < N): return Cacc tmaxx = ((ix + 1) B - o[0]) / d[0] if d[0] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = ((iy + 1) B - o[1]) / d[1] if d[1] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxz = ((iz + 1) B - o[2]) / d[2] if d[2] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltax = B / abs(d[0]) if d[0] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltay = B / abs(d[1]) if d[1] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltaz = B / abs(d[2]) if d[2] != 0 else float('inf') stepx = 1 if d[0] > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if d[1] > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if d[2] > 0 else -1 tmin = 0.0 while 0 <= ix < N and 0 <= iy < N and 0 <= iz < N: tnext = min(tmaxx, tmaxy, tmaxz) if tnext < tmin: tnext = tmin minval, maxval = A[ix, iy, iz] if maxval < threshold: tmin = tnext if tnext == tmaxx: ix += stepx; tmaxx += tdeltax if tnext == tmaxy: iy += stepy; tmaxy += tdeltay if tnext == tmaxz: iz += stepz; tmaxz += tdeltaz continue # Process volume block tsample = tmin while tsample < tnext and alphaacc < 1.0: pos = [o[0] + d[0] tsample, o[1] + d[1] tsample, o[2] + d[2] tsample] # Standard volume lookup (e.g., trilinear interpolation or nearest-neighbor) csample, asample = V[pos[0]], V[pos[1]], V[pos[2]] alphaacc += asample (1.0 - alphaacc) Cacc[0] += csample[0] asample (1.0 - alphaacc) Cacc[1] += csample[1] asample (1.0 - alphaacc) Cacc[2] += csample[2] asample (1.0 - alphaacc) tsample += step if alphaacc >= 1.0: break tmin = tnext if tnext == tmaxx: ix += stepx; tmaxx += tdeltax if tnext == tmaxy: iy += stepy; tmaxy += tdeltay if tnext == tmaxz: iz += stepz; tmaxz += tdeltaz return Cacc Parameters: Block Size: 32 \times 32 \times 32 voxels. Acceleration Structure Resolution: 16 \times 16 \times 16 cells. Source Resolution Example: 512 \times 512 \times 512. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Min/max values must accurately represent the range of the source block to avoid false negatives (skipping visible data) or false positives (skipping empty data). Boundary Conditions: Ray traversal must correctly handle entry and exit from the acceleration structure grid. Uses sparse voxel octrees for skipping; chosen for highly sparse data. Uses AABB trees; chosen for complex geometry integration. Extends SparseLeap with occupancy misses; chosen for dynamic scenes. Uses bounding volumes; chosen for static volumes with large empty regions. Adaptive sampling; chosen for mobile performance. Performance: Accelerates visualization by 1.5–2× compared to non-skipping methods. Complexity: Time complexity scales with the number of non-empty cells traversed; measured speedup is 1.5–2×. Memory complexity is dominated by the acceleration structure, which is significantly smaller than the source volume (16^3 vs 512^3). Strengths: Simple to implement on GPU; effective for volumes with large transparent regions. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of the acceleration structure. This technique is an extension of CPU-based empty space skipping methods to GPU implementations. It is used in direct volume rendering to optimize ray casting by avoiding unnecessary sampling of transparent regions. name: Progressive Ray Casting for Volumetric Models on Mobile Devices
body: This method addresses the computational constraints of interactive volume rendering on mobile devices by combining multiresolution data structures with acceleration techniques. It solves the trade-off between frame rate and visual fidelity by using a lower-resolution dataset for exploration and progressively refining high-resolution details in regions of interest. It incorporates Empty Space Skipping (ESS) and Early Ray Termination (ERT) to reduce sampling overhead. The shared principles for this family are inherited from Empty Space Skipping via Acceleration Structures. The provided notes describe a system-level approach rather than distinct algorithmic subtopics. The primary components are: Uses a lower-resolution dataset for interactive exploration and a high-resolution dataset for progressive refinement of regions of interest. Incorporates ESS and ERT to reduce sampling overhead. ESS starts ray sampling at the boundaries of a proxy geometry that roughly adjusts to non-transparent regions of the volume model, discarding transparent regions. ERT finishes ray traversals whenever the computed color is considered opaque. The method was proposed in a paper titled "Progressive Ray Casting for Volumetric Models on Mobile Devices". It addresses GPU horsepower limitations on mobile devices, noting that while models might fit in memory, frame rates can be inefficient for interactivity. It builds upon acceleration techniques described by Krüger and Westermann. It is designed for medical image inspection, where orthographic projections are the standard view.
