name: K-D Tree-Guided Voxels
head: K-D Voxels, K-D tree-guided density-adaptive voxels
body: K-D Tree-Guided Voxels is a density-adaptive rendering method that constructs multi-scale voxels from a K-D tree built on 3D points, allowing the skipping of empty spaces and guiding sampling based on point density as an approximation of volume density. Unlike conventional NeRFs that require explicit empty-space skipping, K-D voxels naturally stick to object surfaces described by the point cloud, automatically focusing rendering on the shape. It sets itself apart from sibling acceleration methods by deriving voxel geometry directly from the spatial partitioning of points rather than a fixed grid or octree, ensuring that voxels in the same tree layer contain the same number of points and thus uniform density. Inputs: A 3D point cloud describing the scene geometry; a querying ray r(t) = o + t \cdot d for each pixel. Outputs: Color and opacity for the pixel. Data Structures: K-D Tree: A binary tree where each node represents a subset of points. Node Layout: bbox: Axis-aligned bounding box (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) with padding margins. points: List of 3D points in the subtree. leftchild, rightchild: References to child nodes. depth: Integer indicating the level in the tree. Properties: Nodes at the same depth have mutually exclusive bounding boxes. Upper-level nodes contain more points (larger voxels); lower-level nodes contain fewer points (smaller voxels). All voxels (bounding boxes) at the same K-D tree layer contain the same number of points, implying uniform density within that layer. Numbered Steps: 1. K-D Tree Construction: Build a K-D tree on the input 3D points (K=3). For each node, compute its bounding box by taking the minimum and maximum x, y, z coordinates of all points in its subtree, applying proper padding margins. Divide points in a top-down manner along one of the x, y, or z axes. Ensure that points are split such that voxels in the same K-D tree layer contain the same number of points. 2. Ray Traversal and Minimal Voxel Identification: For a querying ray, start from the root node. Recursively traverse the tree. A node is "intersected" if the ray intersects its bounding box. Identify "minimal" intersected voxels. A voxel is minimal if the ray intersects the node's bounding box but does not intersect any of its sub-node's bounding boxes. This recursive procedure naturally locates voxels deep enough in the tree that tightly cover the surface. 3. Segmentation: The identified minimal voxels divide the querying ray into segments. Segments covered by a voxel are considered close to the surface and used for rendering. Segments not covered by any minimal voxel are considered empty spaces and skipped. 4. Deterministic Spline Integration: For each intersected voxel i in ray passing order, define the segment interval [li, ri] along the ray. Since points are not necessarily at voxel vertices, trilinear interpolation is not feasible. Instead, use deterministic spline integration. Uniformly select points within the segment [li, ri]. Calculate the average feature fi of the segment: fi = \frac {1}{ri-li} \int {li}^{ri} \textbf {feature}(o+t\cdot d) \mathrm {d}t where \textbf{feature} is obtained from the underlying point cloud (e.g., via KNN-based point features). 5. Color and Density Modeling: For the representative point pi in the i-th voxel, obtain volume density \sigmai and color ci. Use the Phong reflection model to model color, utilizing normal vectors estimated from the point cloud's shape. Composite the results using standard front-to-back compositing over the segments defined by the minimal voxels. Parameters: Pre-set node depth: The maximum depth to which the recursive procedure searches for minimal voxels. This controls the granularity of the rendering. Padding margins: Applied to bounding boxes during construction to ensure coverage. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Spaces: Conventional methods require explicit skipping. K-D voxels avoid this because they stick to object surfaces; only space inside a voxel is considered, and deeper voxels are closer to the surface. Point Distribution: The method assumes the point cloud accurately describes the shape. Noisy or imprecise point clouds may lead to inaccurate voxel placement. Integration Feasibility: Trilinear interpolation cannot be used directly because points are not at voxel vertices; spline integration is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildkdtree(points, depth=0): """ Recursively builds a K-D tree. Ensures that nodes at the same depth have the same number of points. """ if not points: return None # Compute bounding box for current node mincoords = min(points, key=lambda p: p.xyz) maxcoords = max(points, key=lambda p: p.xyz) bbox = BoundingBox(mincoords.xyz, maxcoords.xyz, padding=MARGIN) # Split points if not leaf if depth < MAXDEPTH: # Choose split axis (e.g., based on variance or round-robin) axis = depth % 3 # Split points into two equal-sized parts mid = len(points) // 2 sortedpoints = sorted(points, key=lambda p: p.xyz[axis]) leftpoints = sortedpoints[:mid] rightpoints = sortedpoints[mid:] leftchild = buildkdtree(leftpoints, depth + 1) rightchild = buildkdtree(rightpoints, depth + 1) return Node(bbox=bbox, left=leftchild, right=rightchild, depth=depth) else: return Node(bbox=bbox, left=None, right=None, depth=depth) def findminimalvoxels(node, ray, minimalvoxels): """ Recursively finds minimal intersected voxels. A voxel is minimal if the ray intersects the node's bbox but does not intersect any sub-node's bbox. """ if node is None: return # Check if ray intersects current node's bounding box if not rayintersectsbbox(ray, node.bbox): return # Check children leftintersected = node.left and rayintersectsbbox(ray, node.left.bbox) rightintersected = node.right and rayintersectsbbox(ray, node.right.bbox) if not leftintersected and not rightintersected: # No sub-nodes intersected, so this node's voxel is minimal # Record the intersection interval [l, r] l, r = raybboxintersection(ray, node.bbox) minimalvoxels.append((node, l, r)) else: # Recurse into intersected children if leftintersected: findminimalvoxels(node.left, ray, minimalvoxels) if rightintersected: findminimalvoxels(node.right, ray, minimalvoxels) def integratesegment(ray, l, r, pointcloud): """ Performs deterministic spline integration over segment [l, r]. """ # Uniformly sample points along the segment numsamples = SAMPLESPERSEGMENT features = [] for t in linspace(l, r, numsamples): pointpos = ray.origin + t ray.direction # Get feature from point cloud (e.g., via KNN) feature = getpointcloudfeature(pointpos, pointcloud) features.append(feature) # Average feature avgfeature = sum(features) / len(features) return avgfeature def renderray(ray, kdtreeroot, pointcloud): """ Renders a single ray using K-D tree-guided voxels. """ minimalvoxels = [] findminimalvoxels(kdtreeroot, ray, minimalvoxels) # Sort voxels by distance (l value) minimalvoxels.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) acccolor = Color(0, 0, 0) accalpha = 0.0 for node, l, r in minimalvoxels: # Integrate segment feature = integratesegment(ray, l, r, pointcloud) # Get density and color from representative point # Using Phong reflection with normal vectors from point cloud sigma, c = getphongcoloranddensity(node.representativepoint, pointcloud) # Front-to-back compositing alpha = 1.0 - exp(-sigma (r - l)) weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor += c weight accalpha += weight if accalpha > 1.0 - EPSILON: break return acccolor A deterministic integration method for obtaining segment features within each voxel, used because trilinear interpolation is not feasible when points are not at voxel vertices. It uniformly selects points in the segment defined by interval [li, ri] and integrates their features to obtain the average feature fi. Choose this when the point cloud does not align with voxel vertices, avoiding the artifacts of stochastic integration. Data structures built to accelerate queries of samples for indexing and brushing-and-linking, set up for each layer of parallel coordinates. It constructs one kd-tree for parallel coordinates lines representing original data values (using data domain dimensionality k=m) and 2D kd-trees for continuous indexed points (using downsampled indexed points data from the volume). Choose this for multivariate volume visualization in parallel coordinates views, where it accelerates sample queries. Time Complexity: Construction is O(N \log N) for the K-D tree, where N is the number of points. Rendering traversal is proportional to the number of minimal voxels intersected by the ray, which is typically much smaller than the total number of voxels in a dense grid. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of points and the K-D tree structure. Each node stores a bounding box and references to children. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources for K-D voxels specifically. However, related kd-tree acceleration in parallel coordinates shows significant preprocessing time reductions (38% to 73%) for simulation data and MRI scans, but is not advantageous for noisy CT data where per-voxel computation is recommended. Strengths: Naturally skips empty spaces without explicit culling logic; density-adaptive sampling is inherent in the tree structure; multi-scale representation allows coarse-to-fine rendering. Limitations: Requires a high-quality point cloud; noisy point clouds may degrade performance; trilinear interpolation is not directly applicable, requiring spline integration. When to use: When rendering point-cloud-guided NeRFs or scenes where the geometry is well-described by a point cloud and empty-space skipping is desired without explicit culling. When not to use: When the point cloud is noisy or imprecise, as this affects voxel placement and rendering accuracy. K-D Tree-Guided Voxels were proposed in the context of NeuralEditor, a point cloud-guided NeRF model for novel-view synthesis and shape editing. The method leverages K-D trees to construct density-adaptive voxels, enabling natural and efficient rendering by sticking to object surfaces. It builds on the principles of acceleration structures and traversal and early ray termination and culling, but derives the voxel structure from the point cloud rather than a fixed grid. name: Stereoscopic Projection Constraints
head: Fast Stereoscopic Volume Rendering with Left-to-Right Projection Constraints, Fast stereoscopic images with ray-traced volume rendering, Left-eye projection constraint method
body: Stereoscopic Projection Constraints is a method for generating stereoscopic volume rendering pairs by calculating the left-eye view first and using its results to constrain the right-eye ray traversal, thereby avoiding redundant voxel evaluations in occluded regions. It differs from polygon-based stereo methods by achieving significantly higher time savings (80-90% vs 36%) because it avoids voxel evaluations entirely rather than shading interior polygons. It also differs from standard parallel volume rendering by introducing a global projection boundary that prevents right-eye rays from sampling regions that might be occluded by unknown material beyond the left-eye termination points. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volumetric dataset (e.g., CT scan), left-eye camera parameters, right-eye camera parameters (displaced parallel projection), early termination threshold (opacity = 1.0). Outputs: Left-eye image, Right-eye image. Data Structures: Global Maximum Right-Eye Projection Boundary (B{max}): A scalar value representing the maximum allowable projection coordinate on the right-eye projection plane. Initialized to the minimum possible coordinate (e.g., left edge of the image). Left-Eye Accumulation Buffer: Stores the accumulated color and opacity for each left-eye ray. Right-Eye Accumulation Buffer: Stores the accumulated color and opacity for each right-eye ray. Numbered Steps: 1. Left-Eye Rendering: Calculate all left-eye rays using standard ray-traced volume rendering with early termination. Early termination occurs when the accumulated opacity reaches 1.0. 2. Project Left-Eye Results: For each left-eye ray, project its final accumulation point (or termination point) to the corresponding position in the right-eye projection plane using displaced parallel projection. 3. Update Global Boundary: Maintain a global maximum allowable right-eye projection boundary (B{max}). This boundary is defined as the final right-eye projection coordinate of any left-eye ray already evaluated. No right-eye ray is allowed to project beyond this boundary. 4. Constrain Right-Eye Projections: If a left-eye ray terminates early (opacity=1.0), the corresponding right-eye projection is restricted. Specifically, no right-eye projection is allowed farther to the right (in the direction of increasing parallax/displacement) than the final projection of any previously evaluated left-eye ray. This is because unknown material may exist beyond the termination point of the left-eye ray, which could obscure the right-eye view. 5. Re-examine Right-Eye Rays: After all left-eye rays are processed, re-examine the right-eye rays. Identify any right-eye ray that has not accumulated full opacity AND whose last projection is not on the far side of the volume bounding box. 6. Continue Right-Eye Traversal: For the right-eye rays identified in the previous step, continue the ray traversal from the last projection point into the ray to accumulate the remaining necessary samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stereoscopicprojectionconstraints(volume, leftcamera, rightcamera, opacitythreshold=1.0): """ Generates stereoscopic volume rendering pairs using left-to-right projection constraints. Args: volume: Volumetric dataset (3D array). leftcamera: Camera parameters for the left eye. rightcamera: Camera parameters for the right eye. opacitythreshold: Opacity value at which a ray is considered terminated (default 1.0). Returns: leftimage: Rendered left-eye image. rightimage: Rendered right-eye image. """ width, height = leftcamera.resolution leftimage = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) rightimage = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) # Global maximum allowable right-eye projection boundary # Initialized to the minimum x-coordinate of the right-eye projection plane Bmax = rightcamera.minxprojection # Step 1 & 2: Left-Eye Rendering and Projection for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Generate left-eye ray leftray = leftcamera.generateray(x, y) # Perform ray marching for left eye leftaccumcolor, leftaccumopacity, leftterminationpoint = raymarch( volume, leftray, opacitythreshold) # Store left-eye result leftimage[y, x] = leftaccumcolor # Project the termination point to the right-eye projection plane # Using displaced parallel projection rightprojectionx = projecttorighteye(leftterminationpoint, leftcamera, rightcamera) # Step 3 & 4: Update Global Boundary and Constrain # No right-eye projection is allowed farther to the right than Bmax if rightprojectionx > Bmax: # The projection is constrained to Bmax # This implies that any right-eye ray that would project beyond Bmax # is considered potentially occluded by unknown material beyond the left-eye termination constrainedprojectionx = Bmax else: constrainedprojectionx = rightprojectionx # Update Bmax if this projection is further to the right if constrainedprojectionx > Bmax: Bmax = constrainedprojectionx # Initialize right-eye accumulation for this pixel # Note: The right-eye ray for pixel (x, y) is different from the left-eye ray rightray = rightcamera.generateray(x, y) # We need to accumulate samples for the right-eye ray # However, the constraint applies to the projection of the left-eye termination # onto the right-eye view. The right-eye ray itself must be traversed, # but we can skip samples that project beyond Bmax? # The source states: "No right-eye ray is allowed to project beyond this boundary." # This implies that if the right-eye ray's current sample projects beyond Bmax, # it is skipped? Or does it mean the right-eye ray traversal is limited? # The source says: "continue the ray traversal from the last projection into the ray" # This suggests a two-pass approach or a constrained traversal. # Let's assume a two-pass approach for clarity, as described in steps 5 & 6. # First, accumulate what we can based on the left-eye projection constraint. # Actually, the source implies that the right-eye ray is traversed, but # the projection of the left-eye termination point acts as a mask. # Re-reading: "No right-eye ray is allowed to project beyond this boundary." # This likely means that if the right-eye ray's sample position, when projected # back to the left-eye view (or vice versa), falls beyond the known visible region, # it is skipped. But the source specifically talks about projecting the left-eye # termination to the right-eye view. # Let's implement the constraint as a limit on the right-eye ray traversal depth # or a check on the projected position. # For simplicity, we will accumulate the right-eye ray, but we will track # the projected position of the left-eye termination for this pixel's column? # No, the constraint is global (Bmax). # The source says: "If a left-eye ray terminates early... no right-eye projection # is allowed farther to the right... than the final projection of any previously # evaluated left-eye ray." # This suggests that for a given right-eye ray, if its sample projects to a position # > Bmax, it is skipped? Or is it that the right-eye ray traversal is stopped # when the projected position exceeds Bmax? # Let's assume the latter: The right-eye ray is traversed, but if the current sample's # projection onto the right-eye plane (which is just its x-coordinate in the right-eye view) # is not constrained by Bmax? No, Bmax is a global x-coordinate. # Actually, the constraint is on the projection of the left-eye termination. # The right-eye ray for pixel (x,y) has a specific path. # The source says: "continue the ray traversal from the last projection into the ray." # This implies that the right-eye ray is traversed in segments. # Let's simplify: The right-eye ray is traversed. However, we can skip samples # if they are known to be occluded. The constraint Bmax defines the rightmost # visible x-coordinate in the right-eye view based on the left-eye rendering. # If a right-eye ray's sample projects to an x-coordinate > Bmax, it is skipped. # But the right-eye ray's sample position is in 3D. Its projection is its x-coordinate # in the right-eye image plane. # This seems circular. Let's look at the source again. # "No right-eye ray is allowed to project beyond this boundary." # This likely means that the right-eye ray traversal is limited such that # it does not evaluate voxels that would project beyond Bmax. # For implementation, we can check the projected x-coordinate of the current sample. # If it is > Bmax, skip it. rightaccumcolor, rightaccumopacity, rightterminationpoint = raymarchconstrained( volume, rightray, opacitythreshold, Bmax, rightcamera) rightimage[y, x] = rightaccumcolor # Step 5 & 6: Re-examine and Continue # The source implies that some right-eye rays may not have accumulated full opacity # and whose last projection is not on the far side of the volume bounding box. # These rays need to continue traversal. # This is handled within the raymarchconstrained function by continuing traversal # if the opacity is not 1.0 and the projection is within bounds. return leftimage, rightimage def raymarchconstrained(volume, ray, opacitythreshold, Bmax, camera): """ Performs ray marching with projection constraints. """ accumulatedcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 stepsize = 1.0 # Simplified # Traverse the ray t = 0.0 while t < ray.length: point = ray.origin + t ray.direction # Check if point is within volume bounds if not volume.contains(point): break # Get voxel value voxelvalue = volume.sample(point) # Compute color and opacity for this sample color, opacity = transferfunction(voxelvalue) # Project this point to the right-eye projection plane # In a parallel projection, the x-coordinate in the image plane is proportional # to the x-coordinate of the point in world space (adjusted for camera offset) projectedx = projectpointtoplane(point, camera) # Check constraint if projectedx > Bmax: # Skip this sample and potentially further samples if they are also beyond Bmax # However, the ray might re-enter the visible region? # The source says "No right-eye ray is allowed to project beyond this boundary." # This implies a hard cut-off. t += stepsize continue # Accumulate alpha = opacity (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor += color alpha accumulatedopacity += alpha # Early termination if accumulatedopacity >= opacitythreshold: break t += stepsize return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity, point def projectpointtoplane(point, camera): """ Projects a 3D point to the camera's 2D projection plane. For parallel projection, this is typically just the x-coordinate in the camera's local space. """ # Simplified projection return point.x def projecttorighteye(terminationpoint, leftcamera, rightcamera): """ Projects the left-eye termination point to the right-eye projection plane. """ # Convert termination point to right-eye camera space # Then project to 2D pointinrightspace = rightcamera.worldtocamera(terminationpoint) return pointinrightspace.x Parameters: Early Termination Threshold: Opacity value of 1.0. When opacity reaches this value, the ray is considered terminated, acting as an occluding object. Projection Type: Displaced parallel projection. Voxels are projected using this method to map left-eye samples to right-eye positions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Poor Data Partitioning: Poor partitioning of data across nodes can result in several dense blocks, which slightly lowers the overall savings by increasing the number of terminated rays and thus the number of right-eye voxels that must be evaluated solely for the right-eye. Voxel Count Exceeding 100%: The total percentage of voxels seen in the right-eye view (retained + right-only) can exceed 100% of left-eye voxels. This is due to the volume bounding box being calculated for the left-eye (orthogonal traversal), while right-eye rays pass through at an angle, resulting in a longer traversal path. Unknown Material: If a left-eye ray terminates early, unknown material may exist beyond the termination point. The constraint ensures that right-eye rays do not sample regions that could be obscured by this unknown material. Time Savings: 81.2% time savings on a 128^3 CT scan at 256x256 resolution and 512 nodes. Voxel Retention: 99.4% of left-eye voxels are retained in the right-eye view. Voxel Ratio: The ratio of right-only voxels to left-eye voxels is 0.8%. Comparison to Polygon Methods: Significantly higher time savings (80-90% vs 36%) compared to polygon-based methods like marching cubes. Comparison to Splatting: Achieves similar savings to splatting by using coherence to quickly find affected pixels in the right-eye view. Scaling: As the number of nodes increases, the area of the volume rendered by a given node decreases, lowering the probability that a ray will terminate, thus increasing the retained voxels percentage. However, poor partitioning can lead to dense blocks, lowering savings. Origin: Based on a modified version of Ma, et al.'s parallel volume renderer. History: References include [CLLC88] for dividing cubes, [AdHo93] for non-volumetric ray-tracing stereo techniques, [LOCI87] for marching cubes, [ABCHgl] for polygon coherence, and [West90] for splatting. Usage: Used for generating stereoscopic images for scientific visualization, providing unambiguous depth information without continuous movement. name: Intensity Clipping
head: Range Clipping
body: Intensity clipping is a volume rendering technique that discards or masks voxels whose scalar values fall outside a specified minimum and maximum threshold. By filtering out low-intensity noise or high-intensity outliers, it reduces visual clutter and can accelerate rendering by skipping transfer function lookups for irrelevant samples. Unlike early ray termination, which halts based on accumulated opacity, intensity clipping operates directly on the scalar value domain. Intensity clipping modifies the standard front-to-back compositing loop by applying a filter to the sampled scalar value v before it is used to look up color and opacity in the transfer function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sampled scalar value v from the volume texture. Parameters: minThreshold: The lower bound for visibility. Voxels with v < minThreshold are processed. maxThreshold: The upper bound for visibility. Voxels with v > maxThreshold are processed. DATAMIN and DATAMAX: The lower and upper bounds of the data range, used as replacement values for clipped voxels. In interactive systems, these are often named lower\threshold and upper\threshold with defaults 0.0 and 1.0. Output: A modified scalar value ready for transfer function lookup. Data Structures: The method requires two scalar thresholds and access to the volume's scalar range. In interactive implementations, these are exposed as UI controls with a step size of 0.05 and reset capabilities. Algorithm: The core logic is a simple conditional check performed per sample. 1. Retrieve the scalar value v at the current ray position. 2. If v < minThreshold, set v \leftarrow DATAMIN. 3. If v > maxThreshold, set v \leftarrow DATAMAX. 4. Pass the modified v to the transfer function. In transfer-function-based renderers, values outside the threshold range are mapped to zero opacity, effectively discarding the sample from compositing. Pseudocode: The following Python-like pseudocode implements the filtering logic described in. It assumes the transfer function maps DATAMIN and DATAMAX to zero opacity, which is the standard practice for achieving the clipping effect. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intensityclip(v, minthreshold, maxthreshold, datamin, datamax): """ Apply intensity clipping to a scalar value v. Args: v (float): The sampled scalar value. minthreshold (float): Minimum intensity threshold. maxthreshold (float): Maximum intensity threshold. datamin (float): The minimum value of the dataset range. datamax (float): The maximum value of the dataset range. Returns: float: The clipped scalar value. """ if v < minthreshold: v = datamin if v > maxthreshold: v = datamax return v Interactive Controls: In interactive systems, clipping is toggled and adjusted via keyboard shortcuts: Toggle clipping on/off: 'V' or 'v'. Increase lower threshold: '+'. Decrease lower threshold: '-'. Increase upper threshold: ']'. Decrease upper threshold: '['. Reset to full range: 'R'. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Thresholds must be carefully chosen relative to the data type's precision. Data Range: The DATAMIN parameter must accurately reflect the global minimum of the volume data to avoid artifacts when replacing clipped low values. Degenerate Input: If minThreshold > maxThreshold, the entire volume is clipped. Color clipping is a variant that operates on the RGB color space rather than the scalar intensity domain. It clips (does not render) colors that fall within a defined range across all channels simultaneously. Unlike intensity clipping, which removes values outside a range, color clipping removes values inside a specified box in RGB space. It is controlled by a boolean ClipColorRange and a ColorRangeToClip property defining Min and Max RGB vectors. This is useful for removing specific color artifacts or background hues. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, as it involves only two comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring only two threshold parameters. Performance: Significantly reduces the number of transfer function lookups and compositing operations for voxels outside the range, leading to faster frame rates in noisy or high-dynamic-range data. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective for noise removal, and allows interactive isolation of specific features (e.g., tissue layers in MRI). Limitations: Does not account for spatial context; a noisy voxel with a high intensity might be retained while a valid low-intensity feature is removed if thresholds are not tuned carefully. When to Use: When the volume contains significant noise or outliers that obscure relevant features, or when specific intensity ranges need to be isolated for analysis. When Not to Use: When the full dynamic range of the data is critical for visualization, or when the noise distribution is complex and cannot be separated by simple scalar thresholds. Intensity clipping is implemented in interactive renderers by constructing a piecewise opacity function that maps values outside the threshold range to zero opacity. It is used in medical imaging to isolate tissue layers in MRI volumes. In astronomical data visualization, it masks bright sources like stars or filters noise in spectral cubes. The technique is supported by visualization libraries such as VTK and LightningChart. name: Early Ray Termination and Culling
head: Early Ray Termination, ERT, Culling, Space Skipping
body: Early Ray Termination (ERT) and Culling are acceleration techniques that reduce computational cost by halting ray integration when accumulated opacity reaches a threshold (typically 1.0) or by skipping regions of the volume known to be empty or occluded. Unlike standard ray casting which samples the entire ray length, these methods modify the front-to-back compositing loop to break early, significantly improving performance for opaque or sparse volumes. The core mechanism shared by all acceleration methods is the reduction of work units (samples, voxels, or pixels) processed per frame while maintaining acceptable visual fidelity. This is achieved through three primary strategies: 1. Culling/Skipping: Identifying regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image (e.g., empty space, occluded voxels) and bypassing their evaluation. 2. Termination: Halting the integration loop when the accumulated contribution becomes negligible (e.g., high opacity, low transmittance). 3. Adaptation: Varying the computational effort based on local scene complexity or global performance budgets. Mathematically, these methods modify the standard front-to-back compositing loop: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) by introducing conditions that break the loop early, skip iterations, or reduce the number of C{sample} queries. Uses a 2D opacity map orthogonal to the viewing direction to cull entire sub-volume bounding boxes that are hidden behind opaque surfaces. A GPU-accelerated method for neural volume rendering that uses occupancy grids for empty-space skipping and adaptive step sizing to maximize inference throughput. Accelerates sphere tracing by using a low-resolution pre-pass with scaled SDFs to provide a "head start" for full-resolution rays, reducing the number of steps required for convergence. Targets unstructured meshes by leveraging hardware-accelerated ray tracing to skip transparent elements and adaptively sample based on color variance. A hardware optimization that discards occluded fragments before fragment shader execution, integrating ERT and empty-space skipping into the rasterization pipeline. Extends ERT to stereoscopic rendering by bounding the right-eye projection of subsequent left-eye rays to prevent visual errors caused by terminated rays. Employs an early z-culling technique to cull empty texels, ensuring no computations are wasted on them. Data dependencies are removed (via Equation 4), allowing density computation to be executed in the same pass as force computation. Uses a distribution model instead of the gathering model used in [TH07], avoiding neighborhood searching via texture lookups. A technique that compresses sequences of empty (transparent) voxels into compact representations during ray traversal to allow rays to jump directly to the next non-empty segment, minimizing redundant sampling. Scan the volume to encode runs of transparent voxels into compact representations. During ray casting, use the encoded runs to jump directly to the next non-empty segment along the ray. Achieves speedups of 2 to 5 times on datasets like CT scans when integrated into shear-warp volume rendering. An optimization that determines empty space prior to each traversal pass using a CPU-computed 3D texture map encoding emptiness for blocks of voxels, locking fragments in empty regions via z-buffer writes. Modify intermediate pass: Before each traversal pass, sample coarse grid at current ray position. Determine visibility by a dependent texture lookup. Lock fragments by writing zfar to z-buffer. Data structure: 3D texture map storing minimum and maximum scalar values per block of 3x3x3 cells (8^3 voxels). Parameterized with minimum/maximum values with respect to the current transfer function. Updated on transfer function modification. Early ray termination was introduced as a fundamental optimization for volume rendering to handle opaque surfaces efficiently. The concept of skipping empty space has evolved from simple run-length encoding (RLE) along rays to more complex hierarchical structures like octrees and KD-trees. Hardware-based optimizations, such as early Z-tests, have further integrated these software concepts into the graphics pipeline, allowing for fragment culling before shader execution. The technique is widely used in medical imaging (CT scans), scientific visualization, and modern neural radiance fields (NeRFs) where inference speed is critical. name: Occlusion Clipping with Orthogonal Opacity Map
head: Orthogonal Opacity Map Occlusion Clipping, Orthogonal Opacity Map Occlusion Culling, Opacity Culling and Clipping, Occlusion Culling and Clipping, Empty Space Skipping and Occlusion Clipping
body: Occlusion Clipping with Orthogonal Opacity Map is an acceleration technique for texture-based volume rendering that skips occluded voxels by maintaining a low-resolution 2D opacity map on a plane orthogonal to a major dataset axis. It differs from per-voxel early ray termination by testing occlusion at the sub-volume level, allowing it to cull entire bounding boxes or clip their geometry against the opacity map to avoid rendering thousands of voxels hidden behind opaque surfaces. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D texture dataset, transfer function, viewing parameters, sub-volume bounding boxes (axis-aligned). Output: Final image, updated opacity map. Data Structures: 1. Orthogonal Opacity Map: A 2D map orthogonal to the major axis of the dataset most parallel to the viewing direction. Each pixel represents the minimum opacity accumulated in the corresponding region of the frame buffer. 2. Hierarchical CPU Map: A CPU-side structure built from the GPU-obtained low-resolution opacity map to accelerate culling queries. 3. Sub-volume Bounding Boxes: Axis-aligned boxes defining regions of the volume to be rendered. Parameters: Opacity Threshold (T{op}): Typically 95% of the maximum opacity. Desired Updates (k): Initial empirically determined number of map updates per frame (typically 9). DeltaVoxels (Dv): Number of voxels rendered before an opacity map update. Calculated as Dv = \lfloor \text{Total Voxels in non-empty boxes} / (k + 1) \rfloor. Constant (c): Used in performance function, typically 0.02. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set opacity map to invalid. Render textures as if clipping is not used. Initialize voxel counter V{count} = 0. 2. Rendering Loop (per sub-volume): If opacity map is invalid, render sub-volume normally. Increment V{count} by the number of voxels in the sub-volume. If V{count} \ge Dv: Update Opacity Map (see Step 3). Reset V{count} = 0. If opacity map is valid: 1. Project the front and back faces of the sub-volume's bounding box onto the orthogonal opacity map. Since the box is axis-aligned, projections are rectangles. For perspective projection, apply scaling and translation; for parallel, only translation. 2. Combine the two projections to determine the total projected area. 3. Search for transparent pixels in the map covering the projected rectangle Rp. Pixels with opacity < T{op} are transparent. 4. If Rp falls outside the map border, add that area to visible regions. 5. Compute the bounding rectangle Rv of all visible regions. 6. Back-project: Project Rv back to the front and back faces of the sub-volume (parallel to the opacity map) to get R{vpf} and R{vpb}. 7. Compute union R{vp} = R{vpf} \cup R{vpb}. 8. If R{vp} is empty, cull the sub-volume (skip rendering). 9. Otherwise, use R{vp} as the new front/back faces to create a clipped bounding box and render only the visible portion. 3. Opacity Map Update: Project the current frame buffer onto the object-aligned plane orthogonal to the major axis. Down-sample the result to a low-resolution image to reduce GPU-to-CPU transfer costs and comparison overhead. Each pixel in the map stores the minimum opacity of the corresponding frame buffer region. Note: Opacity values in the map increase monotonically during the rendering of the same frame. Formula: Projection Distance: When projecting a slice parallel to the opacity map, the distance between adjacent voxels d becomes d': d' = d \frac{l1 + l2}{l1} where l1 is the distance from the camera to the slice, and l2 is the slice thickness. Pitfalls: Resolution Trade-off: Low-resolution maps reduce accuracy of occlusion detection but improve efficiency. CPU Bottleneck: Current implementations require CPU involvement and data transfer across the AGP/PCIe bus, limiting performance. This method creates a 2D opacity map on a plane orthogonal to a major axis by projecting the rendered frame buffer onto that plane and downsampling the result. It solves the problem of efficiently generating a low-resolution occlusion mask for volume rendering culling, minimizing data transfer costs between graphics and main memory while preserving sufficient occlusion information. It differs from hierarchical approaches by using a fixed-resolution, multi-pass averaging strategy rather than a tree structure. See Orthogonal Opacity Map Creation. Hidden Volume Removal (HVR) is an occlusion culling optimization for object-order volume rendering that eliminates a large fraction of cells and octree nodes within the opacity range, particularly effective for isosurface visualization. It compensates for the lack of early ray termination inherent in object-order rendering by using Hierarchical Occlusion Maps (HOMs) to skip hidden nodes in the min-max octree. Unlike its sibling Orthogonal Opacity Map Creation, which relies on orthogonal projections and neighbor finding, HVR uses a hierarchical map structure to approximate node visibility, providing superior skipping efficiency at the cost of some artifacts due to approximation. See Hidden Volume Removal using Hierarchical Occlusion Maps. An adaptive system to adjust the number of opacity map updates (k) per frame based on performance history to balance rendering speed and occlusion detection overhead. Polling: Every n-th frame (e.g., n=10), poll performance using the number in range [k-hw, k+hw] that has not been updated for the longest. Increment age of all slots by 1 except the polled one. Update k: When all slots are valid, pick the slot with best performance as the new center. Change k to this new center and shift performance statistics accordingly. Performance function: p = v - c \cdot k, where v is the percentage of voxels culled and clipped, k is the actual number of map updates, and c is a constant (0.02 for tested datasets). Parameter: k: Initial empirically determined number of map updates (typically 9). A technique to save time by culling points that are occluded by opaque volume material in front of their footprint. Require front-to-back rendering to maintain an opacity image (occlusion map). Check if the volume material in front of the point's footprint is opaque; if so, the point is not visible. Mueller '00 method: After compositing, convolve the opacity image with a box filter sized to the projected footprint. If a pixel value in the convolved map is > threshold, the entire footprint neighborhood is > threshold, allowing fast culling by checking only the pixel nearest to the projected point center. Lee '00 method: Keep points in an octree and maintain a visibility map as a quadtree. Check the projection of an octree node against the corresponding level of the visibility map quadtree. Cull occluded octree nodes; subdivide if not occluded; rasterize points that fail the occlusion test. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of sub-volumes and the cost of projecting bounding boxes onto the opacity map. The adaptive update mechanism adjusts the optimal number of opacity map updates to balance accuracy and performance. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the low-resolution opacity map and the CPU-side hierarchical map. Measured Performance: On average, 50-60% of non-empty voxels are excluded from rendering. The average speedup factor for Empty Space Skipping + Occlusion Clipping (ESS+CC) vs conventional is 3.3x. For the 'Knee' dataset, ESS+CC achieves a speedup of 4.7x over Basic, with 63.8% of voxels skipped. Strengths: Highly effective when there are many non-empty voxels and significant occlusion, complementing Empty Space Skipping which is better for large amounts of empty voxels. Limitations: Requires CPU involvement and data transfer across the bus, which limits performance. Low-resolution maps trade off accuracy for efficiency. The technique was introduced by Mueller et al. in 2004. It extends earlier work on empty space skipping and is related to hardware occlusion queries used for visibility culling in opaque surfaces, as described by Govindraju et al. in 2003. It is designed specifically for texture-based volume rendering, where primitives contain thousands of voxels, making per-voxel tests inefficient. name: Orthogonal Opacity Map Creation
body: This method creates a 2D opacity map on a plane orthogonal to a major axis by projecting the rendered frame buffer onto that plane and downsampling the result. It solves the problem of efficiently generating a low-resolution occlusion mask for volume rendering culling, minimizing data transfer costs between graphics and main memory while preserving sufficient occlusion information. It differs from hierarchical approaches by using a fixed-resolution, multi-pass averaging strategy rather than a tree structure. Inputs: Current frame buffer FB containing color/opacity data. Desired low-resolution map dimensions n \times n (typical value: 64 \times 64). Camera projection and view matrices defining the current frame's geometry. High-resolution map side length N (derived from projection geometry so each FB pixel maps to at least one pixel in the high-resolution buffer). Outputs: A low-resolution opacity map of size n \times n in main memory. Data Structures: T{FB}: Texture copy of the frame buffer FB. PB{hm}: High-resolution pixel buffer (optional intermediate; see Optimization). T{hm}: Texture bound to PB{hm}, holding the high-resolution opacity map. PBm: Low-resolution pixel buffer of size n \times n. Steps: 1. Frame Buffer Copy: Copy the current frame buffer FB into a texture T{FB}. 2. Projective Texturing: Imagine a rectangle R parallel to the object-aligned orthogonal plane, oriented orthogonal to the camera. Apply projective texturing: treat T{FB} as a slide projected from the camera position onto R. 3. High-Resolution Projection: Orthogonally project the textured rectangle R onto a high-resolution pixel buffer PB{hm}. The resolution of PB{hm} must be sufficient so that each pixel in FB maps to at least one pixel in PB{hm}. Bind PB{hm} to texture T{hm}. 4. Multi-Pass Downsampling: Initialize PBm (size n \times n). Calculate the number of passes required: P = \left\lceil \frac{(N/n)^2}{4} \right\rceil where N is the side length of the high-resolution map (N \times N) and n is the side length of the low-resolution map (n \times n). For pass k from 0 to P-1: Set the blending function to MIN. Configure texture coordinates so that each pixel in PBm aligns with the center of 4 neighboring texels in T{hm} and uses linear interpolation to fetch their average. Translate the texture coordinates (or view volume) so that each pixel in PBm maps to the center of another 4 uncontributed texels in T{hm}. Render T{hm} to PBm using the configured coordinates and MIN blending. Repeat until all texels in T{hm} have contributed. 5. Readback: Read the contents of PBm to main memory. Optimization: Combine projection and downsampling into a single step by targeting projective texturing directly to PBm (the low-resolution pixel buffer) instead of creating T{hm} explicitly. Since hardware auto-generated texture coordinates (TexGen) cannot be translated for downsampling in this direct path, apply a translation to the view volume using glOrtho() in OpenGL to shift the sampling region for each pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def createorthogonalopacitymap(FBtexture, N, n=64): """ Creates a low-resolution orthogonal opacity map from the frame buffer. FBtexture: 2D list/array of shape (N, N) containing the projected frame buffer data. N: Side length of the high-resolution projected map (N x N). n: Side length of the low-resolution output map (n x n). Returns: 2D list of shape (n, n) containing opacity values. """ # Calculate number of multi-pass rendering steps P = math.ceil((N / n) 2 / 4) # Initialize low-resolution pixel buffer PBm = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] for k in range(P): # Calculate grid offset for this pass. # Shifts the 2x2 sampling window by 0.5 units in x/y to cover # the next set of uncontributed texels per output pixel. dx = (k % 2) 0.5 dy = (k // 2) 0.5 # Simulate GPU projective texturing and downsampling: for i in range(n): for j in range(n): # Map PBm pixel center to projected texture coordinates u = (i + dx) / n v = (j + dy) / n # Sample 4 neighboring texels in the high-res projected image texu = u N texv = v N # Bilinear interpolation of 4 texels x0, y0 = math.floor(texu), math.floor(texv) x1, y1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1 fx, fy = texu - x0, texv - y0 # Fetch texels (clamp to boundaries as standard for opacity) t00 = FBtexture[min(y0, N-1)][min(x0, N-1)] t01 = FBtexture[min(y0, N-1)][min(x1, N-1)] t10 = FBtexture[min(y1, N-1)][min(x0, N-1)] t11 = FBtexture[min(y1, N-1)][min(x1, N-1)] avg = (t00 (1-fx)(1-fy) + t01 fx(1-fy) + t10 (1-fx)fy + t11 fxfy) # MIN blending: keep the smaller opacity value PBm[i][j] = min(PBm[i][j], avg) return PBm Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coverage: The translation step ensures complete coverage of the high-resolution map without gaps or overlaps that would skew the average. Precision: Linear interpolation is used for averaging 4 texels; standard floating-point precision is sufficient for opacity values. Not given in the sources: Degenerate input handling, exact time/memory complexity, and specific boundary conditions beyond the translation coverage. Uses a hierarchical tree structure for occlusion culling, offering better adaptability to varying density but higher complexity. Choose when scene density varies significantly. The parent method that uses this opacity map for culling. Choose this when simple, fast culling along a major axis is sufficient. Performance: Typical low-resolution map size is 64 \times 64. Downsampling reduces the resolution to limit transfer costs from graphics to main memory and reduces the amount of comparisons required for occlusion clipping. Strengths: Simple implementation on GPU; effective for orthogonal views; reduces data transfer overhead. Limitations: Fixed resolution; requires multiple passes for downsampling. Not given in the sources: Exact time and memory complexity, measured performance on specific hardware, or scaling laws. Originated in the context of texture-based volume rendering for empty space skipping and occlusion clipping. The method was proposed by Mueller et al. in "Empty Space Skipping and Occlusion Clipping for Texture-based Volume Rendering". It is used in real-time volume rendering applications where culling occluded voxels improves performance. name: Hidden Volume Removal using Hierarchical Occlusion Maps
head: HOM-based Occlusion Culling, Hidden Volume Removal (HVR), Hierarchical Occlusion Map Occlusion Clipping
body: Hidden Volume Removal (HVR) is an occlusion culling optimization for object-order volume rendering that eliminates a large fraction of cells and octree nodes within the opacity range, particularly effective for isosurface visualization. It compensates for the lack of early ray termination inherent in object-order rendering by using Hierarchical Occlusion Maps (HOMs) to skip hidden nodes in the min-max octree. Unlike its sibling Orthogonal Opacity Map Creation, which relies on orthogonal projections and neighbor finding, HVR uses a hierarchical map structure to approximate node visibility, providing superior skipping efficiency at the cost of some artifacts due to approximation. Inputs: An octree representation of the volume data. A camera view using orthogonal projection. A rendering image plane of width m. Outputs: A rendered image with hidden nodes skipped. Updated HOM structures reflecting current opacity. Data Structures: 1. Hierarchical Occlusion Maps (HOMs): A hierarchy of images where pixels store an integer value in the range [0, 16] and are initialized to 0. Multiple hierarchy levels exist, with the first map size being 1/4 of the image area and the last representing a single pixel. The finest map (Level 0) has a side length of m/2. The coarsest map (Level L) has a side length of 1. A pixel in HOM level k covers a 2^k \times 2^k area of the finest map. 2. Octree: Standard min-max octree structure where each node has a projected center. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize all HOM pixels to 0. Determine the mapping between octree levels and HOM levels. For each octree level, find the finest HOM level such that a single HOM pixel can include the entire projection of the octree node. 2. HOM Update Process: Triggered when a pixel on the image plane becomes opaque during rendering. Identify the corresponding pixel in the finest HOM (Level 0). Increment this pixel and its 3 nearest neighbors in the map (forming a 2 \times 2 block centered on the opaque pixel's projection). Recursive Propagation: If any HOM pixel reaches the maximum value of 16: Increment the corresponding pixel in the superior (coarser) HOM level. Repeat the neighbor incrementation and check for 16 in the superior level. Continue recursively up the hierarchy until no pixel reaches 16 or the top level is reached. 3. Visibility Test: For each octree node to be processed: Project the center of the node onto the image plane. Identify the HOM level associated with the node's octree level (as determined in Step 1). Find the pixel in that HOM level corresponding to the projected center. Test: If the pixel value equals 16, the node is considered hidden and skipped. A value of 16 indicates that an extended square around the pixel (made of 16 quarter-pixels) is opaque. If the value is less than 16, the node is visible and processed. Note: An additional opacity test must be added for every treated ray to handle cases where the HOM approximation is insufficient. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math MAXHOMVALUE = 16 def initializehoms(imagewidth): """Initialize HOM hierarchy with zeros. Finest map (level 0) size is imagewidth/2. Coarsest map (level L) size is 1x1. """ numlevels = int(math.log2(imagewidth)) homs = [] for level in range(numlevels): side = imagewidth // (2 (level + 1)) homs.append([[0] side for in range(side)]) return homs def updatehoms(homs, imagex, imagey): """Update HOMs when an image plane pixel (imagex, imagey) becomes opaque.""" # Map image pixel to finest HOM (level 0) # Finest HOM pixel covers 2x2 image pixels homx = imagex // 2 homy = imagey // 2 propagateupdate(homs, 0, homx, homy) def propagateupdate(homs, level, x, y): """Recursively increment HOM pixels and propagate when MAXHOMVALUE is reached.""" if level >= len(homs): return levelhoms = homs[level] levelh = len(levelhoms) levelw = len(levelhoms[0]) for dx in (0, 1): for dy in (0, 1): nx = x + dx ny = y + dy if 0 <= nx < levelw and 0 <= ny < levelh: levelhoms[ny][nx] += 1 if levelhoms[ny][nx] == MAXHOMVALUE: if level + 1 < len(homs): propagateupdate(homs, level + 1, nx // 2, ny // 2) def computehomlevelforoctreelevel(octreelevel, homlevelmap): """Return the precomputed HOM level for a given octree level.""" return homlevelmap[octreelevel] def isnodehidden(node, homs, homlevelmap): """Check if an octree node is hidden using HOMs.""" homlevel = computehomlevelforoctreelevel(node.octreelevel, homlevelmap) levelhoms = homs[homlevel] levelh = len(levelhoms) levelw = len(levelhoms[0]) # Map projected center to HOM coordinates side = len(levelhoms) homx = int(node.projectedcenterx / side) homy = int(node.projectedcentery / side) if 0 <= homx < levelw and 0 <= homy < levelh: return levelhoms[homy][homx] == MAXHOMVALUE return False Parameters: HOM Max Value: 16. HOM Resolution: Finest map is 1/4 of the image area. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Approximation Artifacts: The visibility test is an approximation, and big block skipping is rare due to the low accuracy of the occlusion maps. Some hidden nodes far beyond the visible surface may still be encountered. Non-Optimal Traversal: The recursive run of the octree does not optimize HVR efficiency optimally, and some hidden nodes are processed unnecessarily. Neighbor Finding: The approach relies on trees that do not allow efficient neighbor finding, which is a limitation compared to other methods. A proposed extension to exploit the hierarchy for accelerating occlusion tests, using the model from [BWPP04] to hierarchically test occlusion of visible nodes without latency from waiting for parent node results. However, the hierarchy is not exploited in the current algorithm to accelerate occlusion tests. Time Complexity: The update complexity is m^2 \cdot \log2(m), where m is the image width. Performance: HVR is more efficient than the method by Lee and Ihm [9]. For similar renderings, Lee and Ihm achieve 25% occluded splats for the head dataset and 67% for the brain dataset, whereas HVR achieves higher occlusion ratios (e.g., 91.70% for Head (a)). Throughput: The algorithm delivers an approximately constant cell throughput (between 1.4 and 2.1 millions cells per second). Strengths: Eliminates a large fraction of cells and octree nodes within the opacity range, particularly effective for isosurface visualization. It is an efficient alternative to the lack of early ray termination in object-order volume rendering. Produces better image quality than some competitors (e.g., Ultravis). Limitations: Big block skipping is rare due to low accuracy of occlusion maps. Some hidden nodes far beyond the visible surface may still be encountered. The recursive run of the octree does not optimize HVR efficiency. When to Use: Effective for isosurface visualization where early ray termination is not available or effective. When Not to Use: When high accuracy in skipping distant hidden nodes is required, or when semi-transparent transfer functions are used (trilinear interpolation becomes predominant, reducing HVR efficiency). Hidden Volume Removal using Hierarchical Occlusion Maps was introduced in the paper "A new object-order ray-casting algorithm". It was developed to address the inefficiencies of previous occlusion culling methods in object-order volume rendering, specifically those that relied on trees without efficient neighbor finding. The method builds on the concept of Hierarchical Occlusion Maps [35] to provide superior skipping of hidden nodes in the octree. A proposed extension to exploit the hierarchy further was discussed in a thesis, but was not implemented in the original algorithm. name: Occlusion Culling for Point Splatting
head: Lee '00 Occlusion Culling, Mueller '00 Occlusion Culling
body: Occlusion culling for point splatting is a technique to accelerate volume rendering by skipping the rasterization of points that are occluded by opaque volume material in front of their screen-space footprint. It builds on Occlusion Clipping with Orthogonal Opacity Map by operating directly on the splatted point primitives rather than voxel sub-volumes. It distinguishes itself from its siblings by using screen-space opacity accumulation (Mueller) or hierarchical spatial structures (Lee) to determine visibility, whereas Hidden Volume Removal using Hierarchical Occlusion Maps and Fine-Scale Occlusion Map Culling operate on voxel hierarchies or finer-scale maps. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of volume points (or octree nodes containing points), camera parameters, and an initial opacity/visibility map. Output: A subset of points to be rasterized (splatted) and an updated opacity/visibility map. Data Structures: Opacity Map: A 2D array of size W \times H (image resolution), storing accumulated opacity values. Octree: A hierarchical structure organizing points in 3D space, where each node has a bounding box and a list of child nodes or leaf points. Visibility Map (Quadtree): A hierarchical structure corresponding to the opacity map, used for fast hierarchical culling. Method Steps: 1. Front-to-Back Rendering Setup: Ensure points are sorted or rendered in front-to-back order to correctly accumulate opacity in the occlusion map. 2. Visibility Test (Mueller '00): After compositing a point, convolve the current opacity image with a box filter. The filter size equals the projected footprint of the point. To check if a new point is occluded, check only the pixel in the convolved opacity map nearest to the projected center of the point's footprint. If the value at this pixel is greater than a threshold (e.g., 1.0 or a specific opacity cutoff), the entire footprint neighborhood is considered occluded, and the point is culled. Otherwise, it is rasterized. 3. Visibility Test (Lee '00): Maintain the points in an octree. Maintain a visibility map in the form of a quadtree, corresponding to the screen space. For each octree node, project its bounding box onto the screen. Check the projection against the corresponding level of the visibility map quadtree. If the node is occluded according to the quadtree, cull the entire node. If not occluded, subdivide the octree node and repeat the test for children. Rasterize (splat) the points that fail the occlusion test (i.e., are visible). Update the visibility map after rasterization. Pseudocode (Mueller '00 Variant): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def occlusioncullingmueller(points, imagewidth, imageheight, footprintradius, opacitythreshold): # Initialize opacity map opacitymap = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) # Pre-convolve kernel for footprint # Box filter of size 2footprintradius + 1 kernel = ones((2 footprintradius + 1, 2 footprintradius + 1)) / (2 footprintradius + 1)2 visiblepoints = [] for point in points: # Project point center to screen coordinates (cx, cy) cx, cy = projecttoscreen(point.position) # Check bounds if not isinbounds(cx, cy, imagewidth, imageheight): continue # Check occlusion using the convolved opacity map # Note: In practice, the convolution is applied to the accumulated opacity map # after each splat or in a post-process step. # For a single pass implementation, we check the current accumulated opacity # at the center pixel, but Mueller's method specifically uses the # convolved map to approximate the footprint coverage. # If the opacity map is not pre-convolved, we approximate by checking # the center pixel. For strict adherence to Mueller '00: # 1. Accumulate splat to opacitymap # 2. Convolve opacitymap with box filter # 3. Check pixel at (cx, cy) in convolved map # Simplified check for implementation clarity: # Check if the center pixel's opacity (or convolved value) exceeds threshold currentopacity = opacitymap[int(cy)][int(cx)] if currentopacity < opacitythreshold: # Point is visible visiblepoints.append(point) # Rasterize point (update opacitymap) rasterizepoint(point, opacitymap, footprintradius) # Re-convolve or update convolved map efficiently # In a full implementation, the convolution would be updated # incrementally or recomputed. Here we assume a simplified check. opacitymap = convolve(opacitymap, kernel) return visiblepoints Pseudocode (Lee '00 Variant): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def occlusioncullinglee(octree, visibilityquadtree, imagewidth, imageheight): visiblepoints = [] def traversenode(node, quadnode): # Project node bounding box to screen screenbbox = projectbbox(node.boundingbox) # Check if screenbbox is fully occluded by quadnode if isfullyoccluded(screenbbox, quadnode): return # Cull entire node if node.isleaf(): # Rasterize points in leaf for point in node.points: visiblepoints.append(point) rasterizepoint(point) # Update visibility map updatevisibilitymap(screenbbox, quadnode) else: # Subdivide for child, childquad in zip(node.children, quadnode.children): traversenode(child, childquad) traversenode(octree.root, visibilityquadtree.root) return visiblepoints Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point errors in projection or opacity accumulation can lead to incorrect culling. Boundaries: Points near the edge of the screen or volume may have partial footprints outside the image bounds. Threshold Selection: The opacity threshold for culling must be chosen carefully to balance performance and visual quality. Too high a threshold may cull visible points; too low may fail to cull occluded ones. Convolution Cost: The Mueller method requires convolution, which can be expensive if not optimized. Hidden Surface Rejection and Hole Filling is a post-processing technique applied to point-splatted volume renderings to improve visual quality by removing occluded points and filling the resulting gaps with surviving data. It distinguishes itself from standard alpha blending by explicitly discarding points deemed occluded by closer neighbors in screen space, followed by a recursive expansion of valid pixels to eliminate holes, thereby creating a solid appearance from sparse point clouds. Z-buffer Occlusion Culling is a visibility approximation technique to avoid updating descriptors of occluded points, reducing computational cost and improving training efficiency. It constructs a Z-buffer using the nearest rasterization scheme, reserving only the points with the lowest Z-value at each pixel position. Time Complexity: Depends on the variant. Mueller's method is O(N) for culling checks if convolution is optimized, but convolution itself is O(W \cdot H \cdot K^2) where K is footprint size. Lee's method is O(N) in the best case (all culled) but can be O(N \log N) or worse depending on tree depth and subdivision. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the opacity map. Lee's method requires additional memory for the octree and quadtree structures. Performance: Significant speedup when a large portion of the volume is occluded. Performance degrades when the volume is sparse or transparent. Strengths: Simple to implement (Mueller), hierarchical culling is efficient for large datasets (Lee). Limitations: Approximate culling may lead to visual artifacts if not handled carefully. Convolution can be costly. The technique was introduced by Mueller et al. in 2000 and Lee et al. in 2000 for accelerating point-based volume rendering. It addresses the computational bottleneck of rasterizing large numbers of points, many of which are occluded. name: Hidden Surface Rejection and Hole Filling
head: Point Rejection and Hole Filling, Screen-space Point Rejection and Hole Filling
body: Hidden Surface Rejection and Hole Filling is a post-processing technique applied to point-splatted volume renderings to improve visual quality by removing occluded points and filling the resulting gaps with surviving data. It distinguishes itself from standard alpha blending by explicitly discarding points deemed occluded by closer neighbors in screen space, followed by a recursive expansion of valid pixels to eliminate holes, thereby creating a solid appearance from dense point clouds. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A buffer of point splats containing color and depth attributes for each pixel, with multiple points per pixel accumulated via atomic operations. Output: A final color buffer where occluded points are removed and empty pixels are filled by expanding surviving points. Data Structures: Attribute Buffer: A texture at backbuffer resolution storing per-pixel color, depth, and a point count. Temporary Texture: An intermediate buffer at backbuffer resolution used to store the result of the rejection and resolve pass. Parameters: Neighbor Grid Size: 7 \times 7 pixels centered on the current pixel. Hole Filling Iterations: 3 iterations. Occlusion Threshold: A defined threshold for the calculated cone size; if the cone is smaller than this, the point is rejected. Steps: 1. Point Rejection and Resolve: For each pixel in the attribute buffer, evaluate a 7 \times 7 grid of neighboring pixels centered on the current pixel. Test each neighbor to determine if it is closer to the camera than the current point. Calculate the largest cone around the current point's center that does not intersect any of the closer points in the grid. If the calculated cone size is smaller than the defined threshold, mark the point as occluded and exclude it from the output. If the point is not occluded, compute its final color by dividing its accumulated color data by the number of points added to the buffer at that pixel. Write the valid color and depth to the temporary texture. 2. Hole Filling (Recursive Expansion): Initialize the working buffer with the output from the Rejection and Resolve step. For 3 iterations, process every empty pixel (no valid color/depth) in the buffer. Identify neighboring pixels that have valid color data. Update the empty pixel's color and depth to the average of these valid neighbors. The expansion continues until the bounds of the 7 \times 7 grid used in rejection are effectively covered. 3. Compositing: Blit the temporary render texture to the framebuffer. Perform a depth comparison to integrate the point cloud pixels with traditional polygon geometry before transparent rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hiddensurfacerejectionandholefilling(attributebuffer, resolution, occlusionthreshold): """ attributebuffer: 2D list of dicts {color: vec3, depth: float, count: int, x: int, y: int} resolution: (width, height) occlusionthreshold: float """ width, height = resolution # Step 1: Point Rejection and Resolve temptexture = [[None] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): current = attributebuffer[y][x] if current['count'] == 0: continue isoccluded = False for dy in range(-3, 4): for dx in range(-3, 4): nx, ny = x + dx, y + dy if 0 <= nx < width and 0 <= ny < height: neighbor = attributebuffer[ny][nx] if neighbor['count'] > 0 and neighbor['depth'] < current['depth']: if calculateconemetric(current, neighbor) < occlusionthreshold: isoccluded = True break if isoccluded: break if not isoccluded: temptexture[y][x] = { 'color': current['color'] / current['count'], 'depth': current['depth'] } # Step 2: Hole Filling workingbuffer = temptexture for in range(3): newbuffer = [[None] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): pixel = workingbuffer[y][x] if pixel is None: valid = [] for dy in range(-1, 2): for dx in range(-1, 2): nx, ny = x + dx, y + dy if 0 <= nx < width and 0 <= ny < height: n = workingbuffer[ny][nx] if n is not None: valid.append(n) if valid: newbuffer[y][x] = { 'color': sum(v['color'] for v in valid) / len(valid), 'depth': sum(v['depth'] for v in valid) / len(valid) } else: newbuffer[y][x] = pixel workingbuffer = newbuffer return workingbuffer def calculateconemetric(current, neighbor): # The exact geometric formula for the cone size is not provided in the sources. # This function implements a standard screen-space occlusion check based on depth difference and radial distance. depthdiff = current['depth'] - name: Fine-Scale Occlusion Map Culling
head: Average occlusion map, Fine-Scale Occlusion Map
body: Fine-Scale Occlusion Map Culling is a visibility culling technique that determines voxel rasterization eligibility using an occlusion map where each pixel represents the average of all pixels within a box-neighborhood footprint. It performs occlusion culling on a finer scale than the box-basis of an octree decomposition, offering an alternative that does not reduce the volume’s frequency content by ways of averaging. Input: Voxel screen-space coordinates and a pre-computed average occlusion map. Output: A rasterization decision for each voxel indicating whether its footprint must be rasterized. Occlusion Map: A 2D grid aligned with the screen where each cell stores a scalar value representing the average of all pixels within the box-neighborhood covered by a footprint. Footprint: A box-shaped neighborhood in screen space corresponding to the projection of a voxel or group of voxels. 1. Construct the Average Occlusion Map: For each pixel in the target resolution, calculate the average of all pixels within the box-neighborhood covered by a footprint. 2. Index the Map for Voxel Culling: For each voxel to be rendered, determine its screen-space coordinate. 3. Evaluate Occlusion: Retrieve the value from the occlusion map at the voxel's screen-space coordinate. 4. Rasterization Decision: Check if the footprint must be rasterized based on the indexed occlusion map value. M(u,v) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i \in \text{footprint}} Pi, where M(u,v) is the occlusion map value at screen coordinate (u,v), N is the number of pixels in the box-neighborhood footprint, and Pi is the opacity of each pixel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def finescaleculling(voxelscreencoords, occlusionmap, threshold=0.99): """ Determine if a voxel should be rasterized based on the fine-scale occlusion map. Args: voxelscreencoords: List of (u, v) tuples representing screen coordinates of voxels. occlusionmap: 2D array where each cell contains the average opacity of its footprint. threshold: Opacity threshold below which a voxel is considered occluded. Returns: List of booleans indicating whether each voxel should be rasterized. """ cullingresults = [] H, W = occlusionmap.shape for u, v in voxelscreencoords: if 0 <= u < W and 0 <= v < H: avgopacity = occlusionmap[v][u] shouldrasterize = avgopacity < threshold cullingresults.append(shouldrasterize) else: cullingresults.append(True) return cullingresults Footprint Size: The size of the box-neighborhood averaged per pixel. Not given in the sources. Threshold: The opacity value used to decide culling. Not given in the sources. Boundary Conditions: Voxels projecting outside the screen bounds must be handled explicitly. Degenerate Input: If the volume has no opacity, the map will be all zeros, and no culling occurs. The prerequisite step that generates the base opacity map. It sets up the orthogonal projection used by this method. Orthogonal Opacity Map Creation A sibling method that uses hierarchical decomposition (octrees) for culling. Fine-Scale Occlusion Map Culling is chosen when preserving high-frequency content is more important than the large-scale culling efficiency of octrees. Hidden Volume Removal using Hierarchical Occlusion Maps Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the occlusion map. The size depends on the screen resolution and footprint size. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Retains volume frequency content better than hierarchical decomposition by using averaging rather than binary culling at node levels. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When fine-scale visibility culling is needed without losing high-frequency details, potentially in combination with octree culling. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was described in the context of volume rendering acceleration, offering an alternative to octree-based space skipping. It was proposed to benefit from both large-scale culling (via octrees) and fine-scale culling (via average occlusion maps).
