name: Inference Ray Marching and Integration
head: CUDA Ray Marching (Inference), Inference Ray Marching, Ray Marching (CUDA Kernel), Ray Marching for Inference, Ray Marching with Sparse Voxel Grid (Test/Inference), Sparse Ray Marching (Inference), iterative ray marching
body: Inference Ray Marching and Integration is a GPU-accelerated method for real-time volume rendering inference that generates sample points, view directions, and integration deltas for active rays by marching through a pre-computed density grid. It solves the performance bottleneck of evaluating volumetric neural fields at inference time by utilizing occupancy grids for empty-space skipping and adaptive step sizing. Unlike training-time marching, which maintains state for backpropagation, this method focuses on throughput by processing rays in batches with strict early-termination logic to maximize frame rates. It modifies the standard front-to-back compositing loop by introducing conditions that break the integration loop early, skip iterations, or reduce the number of neural network queries. The method typically operates as a CUDA kernel or a Python-wrapped backend call that outputs three primary tensors: sampled 3D coordinates (xyzs), view directions (dirs), and step sizes (deltas). These outputs are subsequently used by a neural network to query density and color, and by an integration routine to produce the final pixel color and depth. Inputs: rayso: Float array [N, 3], ray origins for N rays. raysd: Float array [N, 3], ray directions for N rays. near: Float array [N], near plane distances. far: Float array [N], far plane distances. densitybitfield: Uint8 array [CHHH // 8], a hashed grid used for fast occupancy queries. densitygrid: Float array [H, H, H], a pre-computed 3D density grid used for sampling and step estimation. meandensity: Float, average density in the grid, used for step size estimation. bound: Float, spatial boundary limit (scene bounding box size). nalive: Int, number of currently active rays. raysalive: Int array [N], IDs of alive rays (only the first nalive are processed). rayst: Float array [N], current traversal position (t) along each ray. nstep: Int, maximum number of steps per ray. perturb: Bool/Int, enables jittering of sample positions for anti-aliasing. dtgamma: Float, cone angle for adaptive ray marching acceleration. maxsteps: Int, global maximum sampled points per ray. align: Int, padding value to align output tensor size. Outputs: xyzs: Float array [M, 3], 3D coordinates of sampled points. dirs: Float array [M, 3], view directions for each sample. deltas: Float array [M, 2], two delta values per point: one for RGB contribution, one for depth. M is the total output size, calculated as n\alive \times n\step, padded to the next multiple of align if align > 0. The core data structure is the Density Bitfield (or Hash Grid), a compressed representation of the volume occupancy. It allows fast occupancy queries to determine if a ray segment is empty, enabling the skipping of expensive neural network evaluations. The inference process generally follows a batched loop structure to manage GPU memory and handle ray termination dynamically. 1. Initialization: Ensure rayso and raysd are contiguous on the CUDA device. Initialize output tensors xyzs, dirs, deltas with zeros of shape [M, 3], [M, 3], and [M, 2] respectively. If perturbation is enabled, generate random noise for the first step. Initialize ray state: raysalive contains indices 0 \dots n\alive-1, and rayst is set to near distances. 2. Marching Loop: Loop while nalive > 0 and step count < max\steps (typically up to 1024 steps). Step Size Calculation: Determine nstep for the current batch. A common heuristic is n\step = \max(\min(B \cdot N // n\alive, 8), 1), where B is a batch constant and N is total pixels, ensuring balanced work distribution. CUDA Kernel Execution: Call the backend kernel with parameters nalive, nstep, raysalive, rayst, rayso, raysd, bound, densitybitfield, C, H, near, far, align, perturb, dtgamma, maxsteps. Inside the kernel, for each alive ray: Query the densitybitfield or densitygrid at the current t. If the voxel is empty (density below threshold), skip to the next occupied voxel or terminate if far plane is reached. If occupied, compute the step size \Delta t. Adaptive marching uses dt\gamma to accelerate steps in empty space or where density is low. Sample the new position t{new} = t + \Delta t. Store xyz, dir, and \Delta t in the output buffers. Update rayst for the next iteration. Compaction: After the kernel returns, compact the list of raysalive to remove rays that have terminated (reached far or accumulated high opacity). This reduces nalive for the next iteration. 3. Integration (Separate Step): The outputs xyzs, dirs, deltas are passed to a neural network to query density (\sigma) and color (C). An integration routine updates ray colors, transmittance, and termination status using front-to-back compositing. Rays are terminated if transmittance drops below a threshold or opacity accumulates sufficiently. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inferenceraymarching(rayso, raysd, near, far, densitybitfield, densitygrid, meandensity, bound, nalive, raysalive, rayst, nstep, perturb, dtgamma, maxsteps, align): # 1. Ensure inputs are contiguous on the device rayso = contiguous(rayso) raysd = contiguous(raysd) # 2. Calculate output size M and pad to align M = nalive nstep if align > 0: M += align - (M % align) # 3. Initialize output buffers xyzs = zeros((M, 3), dtype=float32) dirs = zeros((M, 3), dtype=float32) deltas = zeros((M, 2), dtype=float32) # 4. Initialize ray state if perturb: noise = randomnoise(nalive) else: noise = zeros(nalive) # 5. Marching loop per ray sampleidx = 0 for r in range(nalive): rayid = raysalive[r] t = rayst[rayid] tfar = far[rayid] raydir = raysd[rayid] rayorigin = rayso[rayid] for step in range(nstep): if t >= tfar: break # Query occupancy at current t occ = querydensitybitfield(densitybitfield, densitygrid, meandensity, t, rayorigin, raydir, bound) if occ: # Compute step size dt dt = computestepsize(t, raydir, bound, dtgamma, meandensity) # Sample new position tnew = t + dt # Store sample data xyzs[sampleidx] = rayorigin + raydir t dirs[sampleidx] = raydir deltas[sampleidx] = [dt, dt] # Update state rayst[rayid] = tnew sampleidx += 1 t = tnew else: # Skip empty space t = skipemptyspace(t, rayorigin, raydir, bound, densitybitfield) return xyzs, dirs, deltas, rayst dtgamma: Default 1/256. Set to 0 to disable adaptive marching. densitythresh: Default 10. Threshold for density grid occupancy. maxsteps: Default 1024. perturb: Default True. align: Default -1 (disabled). Precision: Floating-point errors in t accumulation can cause rays to miss voxels or re-enter them. Empty Space: If densitybitfield is not properly synchronized with densitygrid, rays may march into empty space unnecessarily or terminate prematurely. Boundary Conditions: Not given in the sources. Inference Ray Compositing aggregates per-step volumetric properties into final pixel buffers. It differs from training-time compositing by operating on pre-computed ray samples with strict early-termination logic to maximize throughput during real-time inference. Choose it when bridging sparse ray marching results to final image output with multiple channels. Inference Ray Compositing Sparse Ray Marching (Training) is a GPU-accelerated algorithm that traces rays through a hierarchical sparse voxel grid to collect 3D positions, directions, step sizes, and t-values for training neural radiance fields. It differs from its siblings by explicitly decoupling the counting of occupied samples from the writing of sample data, allowing for dynamic memory allocation based on actual occupancy rather than fixed worst-case bounds. Choose it when training requires efficient memory usage on sparse volumes. Sparse Ray Marching (Training) Chunked Volume Rendering is a memory-efficient inference technique that integrates color and density along rays by processing sampled points in fixed-size batches. It differs from its parent by explicitly batching the forward pass to constrain VRAM, and from its sibling Inference Ray Compositing by focusing on the chunked accumulation of radiance rather than just the compositing logic. Choose it when rendering large scenes or high-resolution implicit fields. Chunked Volume Rendering The BRDF Evaluation Kernel evaluates a Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function for a batch of rays during inference ray marching and integration. It transforms geometric and material inputs into final pixel colors. It is distinct from compositing operations, focusing solely on the local reflection model evaluation. Choose it when rendering reflective surfaces alongside volumetric data. BRDF Evaluation Kernel The Inference Pipeline renders images from a trained dense point cloud (specifically Gaussian Splatting models) and new camera poses without requiring further optimization. It differs from its sibling Inference Ray Compositing by executing the full evaluation loop including rasterization, FPS calculation, and video generation, whereas the sibling focuses specifically on the ray-compositing math. Choose it for full evaluation loops on dense representations. Inference Pipeline DVGO Volume Rendering Forward performs volume rendering for a batch of rays, including sampling, density/alpha computation, transmittance calculation, color estimation, and ray marching. It differs from NeRF Volume Rendering by using a pre-allocated 3D voxel grid for density and color storage, enabling faster training and inference via direct memory access. Choose it when direct memory access to a voxel grid is preferred. DVGO Volume Rendering Forward Light-space opacity precomputation accelerates non-collocated view and light rendering by precomputing the accumulated opacity along light rays, thereby avoiding expensive per-shading-point light-ray marching. It differs from naive non-collocated rendering by precomputing light-transport opacity from the light's point of view and reusing it for any view direction. Choose it for non-collocated light/view scenarios. Light-space opacity precomputation Inference Acceleration Strategies is a set of techniques designed to boost the efficiency of real-time volume rendering inference with minimal quality degradation. It addresses the computational bottleneck of evaluating neural networks and processing rays during the G-Buffer and shading passes. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by combining algorithmic optimizations with hardware-specific acceleration to achieve significant speedups over software-based implementations. Choose it when maximizing throughput on specific hardware. Inference Acceleration Strategies This method replaces the 2.5D point rasterization phase of the original Zellmann et al. remote volume rendering algorithm with an object space ray tracing phase to eliminate rendering artifacts in volumetric and transparent regions. It transmits compacted object space samples and color data from a server to a client, where a software CUDA ray tracer renders them as spheres instead of fixed-size OpenGL points. Choose it for remote volume rendering to eliminate reprojection artifacts. Object Space Ray Tracing for Remote Volume Rendering This method decouples volume rendering computation from display by transmitting object-space samples from a server to a client, where they are rendered as semi-transparent spheres using first-hit ray tracing. It replaces the rasterized point primitives of the base image-warping method to eliminate reprojection artifacts caused by fixed-size point primitives, effectively implementing a distance-aware splatting technique. Choose it for remote rendering requiring distance-aware splatting. Ray Tracing-Based Image Warping for Remote Volume Rendering Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the average number of steps per ray. Adaptive marching reduces S in empty regions. Memory Complexity: O(M) for output buffers, where M is the total number of samples generated. Performance: Capable of real-time rendering on modern GPUs. Performance scales with the sparsity of the volume; denser volumes require more steps and network evaluations. Strengths: High throughput due to CUDA acceleration and occupancy culling; suitable for real-time applications. Limitations: Quality may degrade if dtgamma is too high. Memory usage can be high for very large volumes if not chunked. Inference Ray Marching is a core component of modern neural radiance field (NeRF) rendering pipelines, particularly those based on Instant-NGP. It was developed to address the high computational cost of evaluating dense neural networks along every ray during inference. By leveraging sparse data structures and GPU parallelism, it enables real-time visualization of trained NeRF models. It is used in applications requiring interactive exploration of 3D scenes, such as GUI-based visualization. kwea123/ngppl, https://github.com/kwea123/ngppl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Fictionarry/ER-NeRF, https://github.com/Fictionarry/ER-NeRF, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) megvii-research/cv-master-ex, https://github.com/megvii-research/cv-master-ex, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) blurgyy/jaxngp, https://github.com/blurgyy/jaxngp, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NeRF-Factory/IDDR-NGP, https://github.com/NeRF-Factory/IDDR-NGP, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Implementation of Importance-Driven Volume Rendering, https://www.cg.tuwien.ac.at/research/publications/2005/Thurner-2005-IVR/Thurner-2005-IVR-paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Inference Ray Compositing
head: Ray Compositing for Inference, Ray Compositing with Ambient Light (Inference), Volume Rendering Composite (Inference)
body: Inference Ray Compositing aggregates per-step volumetric properties (density, color, depth, ambient light, uncertainty) into final pixel buffers. It differs from training-time compositing by operating on pre-computed ray samples with strict early-termination logic to maximize throughput during real-time inference. It serves as the bridge between sparse ray marching results and the final image output, handling multiple output channels in parallel. Inputs: nalive: Integer, number of rays currently active. nstep: Integer, maximum number of sampling steps per ray. raysalive: Boolean array [N], mask of active rays. rayst: Integer array [N], current step index for each ray. sigmas: Float array [M], volume densities at sampled points. rgbs: Float array [M, 3], RGB colors at sampled points. deltas: Float array [M, 2], step sizes between samples. weightssum: Float array [N], accumulated opacity for each ray. depth: Float array [N], accumulated depth for each ray. image: Float array [N, 3], accumulated RGB color for each ray. Tthresh: Float, transparency threshold for early termination (default 10^{-2}). ambients: Optional float array for ambient lighting contributions. uncertainties: Optional float array for uncertainty values. uncertaintysum: Optional float array [N], accumulated uncertainty. ambientsum: Optional float array [N], accumulated ambient light. Outputs: weightssum: Updated accumulated opacity. depth: Updated accumulated depth. image: Updated final RGB image. rayst: Updated step indices; set to -1 if terminated early, or final step count if completed. uncertaintysum: Updated accumulated uncertainty (optional). ambientsum: Updated accumulated ambient light (optional). The method operates on contiguous CUDA tensors. The layout follows a flattened structure where M is the total number of samples across all alive rays, and N is the number of alive rays. Exact memory packing details beyond contiguous layout are not given in the sources. The core compositing formula for each step along a ray is: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \cdot \delta) T = 1 - \text{weights\sum} w = \alpha \cdot T \text{weights\sum} \leftarrow \text{weights\sum} + w \text{depth} \leftarrow \text{depth} + w \cdot t \text{image} \leftarrow \text{image} + w \cdot \text{rgb} Where: \sigma is the density (sigmas[i]). \delta is the step size (deltas[i]). t is the distance of the current sample from the camera origin. T is the transmittance up to the current step, calculated as 1 - \text{weights\sum} before adding the current weight. w is the weight contributed by the current sample. For the ambient variant, the color equation includes an ambient term A: \text{image} \leftarrow \text{image} + w \cdot (\text{rgb} + A) And ambientsum accumulates w \cdot A. For the uncertainty variant, uncertainty U is accumulated similarly: \text{uncertainty\sum} \leftarrow \text{uncertainty\sum} + w \cdot U. Tthresh: Float, default 10^{-2}. Rays with transmittance T < T{thresh} are terminated early. 1. Initialization: Initialize weightssum, depth, and image to zero for all rays. Initialize rayst to 0. 2. Loop: While step < nstep: a. Identify active rays using raysalive. b. For each active ray n: i. Retrieve \sigma, \text{rgb}, \delta for the current step. ii. If \delta = 0, mark ray n as terminated (set rayst[n] = -1) and skip further processing for this ray. iii. Compute \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \cdot \delta). iv. Compute T = 1 - \text{weights\sum}[n]. v. Compute w = \alpha \cdot T. vi. Update \text{weights\sum}[n] \leftarrow \text{weights\sum}[n] + w. vii. Update \text{depth}[n] \leftarrow \text{depth}[n] + w \cdot t. viii. Update \text{image}[n] \leftarrow \text{image}[n] + w \cdot \text{rgb}. ix. If using ambient: Update \text{ambient\sum}[n] \leftarrow \text{ambient\sum}[n] + w \cdot \text{ambient} and add ambient to color. x. If using uncertainty: Update \text{uncertainty\sum}[n] \leftarrow \text{uncertainty\sum}[n] + w \cdot \text{uncertainty}. xi. If T < T{thresh}, mark ray n as terminated (set rayst[n] = -1) and skip further steps for this ray. c. If all rays are terminated, break loop. 3. Finalization: For rays that completed all nstep steps without early termination, set rayst[n] to the final step count. Write final weightssum, depth, and image to output buffers. import math def compositerays(nalive, nstep, raysalive, rayst, sigmas, rgbs, deltas, weightssum, depth, image, Tthresh=1e-2): """ Standard ray compositing for inference. Matches CUDA kernel backend.compositerays signature. """ # Initialize accumulators if not already done by caller for n in range(nalive): weightssum[n] = 0.0 depth[n] = 0.0 image[n] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] rayst[n] = 0 # Track distance from camera origin per ray raydist = [0.0] nalive for step in range(nstep): if not any(raysalive): break for n in range(nalive): if not raysalive[n]: continue idx = n nstep + step sigma = sigmas[idx] rgb = rgbs[idx] delta = deltas[idx] # Early termination if delta is zero if delta == 0: rayst[n] = -1 raysalive[n] = False continue # Accumulate distance from camera origin raydist[n] += delta t = raydist[n] # Compute alpha alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) # Compute transmittance T = 1.0 - weightssum[n] # Compute weight w = alpha T # Update accumulators weightssum[n] += w depth[n] += w t image[n][0] += w rgb[0] image[n][1] += w rgb[1] image[n][2] += w rgb[2] # Early termination based on transparency if T < Tthresh: rayst[n] = -1 raysalive[n] = False continue # Finalize rayst for completed rays for n in range(nalive): if raysalive[n]: rayst[n] = nstep Delta Zero: If deltas contains zero, the ray should be terminated immediately to avoid invalid alpha calculations. Precision: Use float32 for compositing to balance speed and accuracy. Boundary Conditions: Ensure rayst is correctly updated to -1 for terminated rays to distinguish them from rays that have completed all steps. Early Termination Logic: The transmittance check T < T{thresh} must occur after weight accumulation to prevent premature termination of visible surfaces. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Highly optimized for GPU execution using CUDA kernels. Strengths: Real-time performance, supports multiple output channels (RGB, depth, ambient, uncertainty), efficient early termination. Limitations: Requires pre-computed ray samples, sensitive to Tthresh parameter. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering inference where latency is critical. When Not to Use: Training phase where gradients are needed through the compositing step (use differentiable compositing instead). Inference Ray Compositing is part of the ER-NeRF (Efficient Real-time Neural Radiance Fields) framework, which focuses on real-time novel view synthesis. It builds on Inference Ray Marching and Integration, which provides the per-ray samples. The method was developed to enable real-time rendering by optimizing the compositing step for GPU execution, leveraging early termination and parallel processing. name: Sparse Ray Marching (Training)
head: Grid-based ray marching, Ray Marching (Training), RayMarcherTaichi, Sparse Ray Marching with Density Bitfield
body: Sparse Ray Marching (Training) is a GPU-accelerated algorithm that traces rays through a hierarchical sparse voxel grid to collect 3D positions, directions, step sizes, and t-values for training neural radiance fields. It solves the inefficiency of uniform sampling by skipping empty regions using a density bitfield, dynamically allocating memory based on actual occupancy rather than fixed worst-case bounds. It differs from its siblings by explicitly decoupling the counting of occupied samples from the writing of sample data, allowing for dynamic memory allocation based on actual occupancy rather than fixed worst-case bounds. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape (N, 3), float32. raysd: Ray directions, shape (N, 3), float32. hitst: Ray segment bounds [t1, t2], shape (N, 2), float32. densitybitfield: Bit-packed occupancy grid, shape (M,), uint8. cascades: Number of mip levels in the density bitfield. scale: Spatial extent (bounding box size) of the scene, used to normalize coordinates. expstepfactor: Factor used in step size calculation. gridsize: Base resolution of the voxel grid. maxsamples: Maximum number of samples allowed per ray. noise: Uniform random perturbation added to the first sample of each ray. perturb: Boolean flag enabling random jittering of the initial sampling position. bound: Spatial extent of the grid. H: Resolution of the cubic density grid (H \times H \times H). densitythresh: Threshold for occupied space. dtmin, dtmax: Minimum and maximum step sizes. dtgamma: Scaling factor for step size calculation. raysalive: List of active ray indices. rayst: Array of current t-values for active rays. counter: Global counter for total samples. Outputs: xyzs: 3D coordinates of occupied samples, shape (TotalSamples, 3), float32. dirs: Ray direction vectors for each sample, shape (TotalSamples, 3), float32. deltas: Step size dt for each sample, shape (TotalSamples,), float32. ts: T-values for each sample, shape (TotalSamples,), float32. raysa: Ray metadata, shape (N, 3), int32. Column 0: original ray index, Column 1: start index in output buffers, Column 2: number of samples. Data Structures: densitybitfield: Bit-packed occupancy grid where each byte stores 8 voxels' occupancy status. raysa: Stores ray index, start index, and sample count for each ray to enable packed output buffers. Parameters: NTHREAD: Number of threads per block in the CUDA kernel launch, set to 256. meandensity: Average density of the grid, used as a fallback density threshold if the specific threshold function returns a lower value. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each active ray, load its index and current t-value. A GPU-accelerated ray marching kernel that samples points along rays using a hashed density grid, supporting adaptive step sizes and perturbation. It differs from standard uniform ray marching by integrating adaptive stepping and perturbation directly into the sampling loop, and from dense voxel tracing by operating on a sparse hashed grid structure. A two-pass GPU algorithm that samples a ray through a sparse voxel grid (density bitfield) to collect 3D positions, directions, step sizes (deltas), and t-values for training neural radiance fields. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly decoupling the counting of occupied samples from the writing of sample data, allowing for dynamic memory allocation based on actual occupancy rather than fixed worst-case bounds. The Sparse Packed Radiance Field Tracer is a differentiable rendering method for sparse, packed radiance fields that generates a variable number of samples per ray, packed into a flat tensor structure. It solves the inefficiency of standard ray marching by using a sparse acceleration structure to sample only within occupied cells, resulting in a custom number of samples per ray rather than a fixed grid. Unlike its siblings, it explicitly manages the "packed" data layout where rays with different intersection counts share a single contiguous buffer, requiring specific reduction operations to handle boundaries between rays. Sparse Grid Volume Rendering (Foreground) is a CUDA-based volume rendering method that traces rays through a sparse voxel grid to compute final color and log-transmittance using volume rendering with spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. It differs from its siblings by explicitly managing warp-level parallelism for SH basis evaluation and accumulation, utilizing shared memory for warp-local data to minimize global memory traffic, and employing early termination based on transmission thresholds. Unlike CUDA Ray Marching (IDDR-NGP Backend) which uses hash encoding, or Sparse Packed Radiance Field Tracer which may use different interpolation schemes, this method relies on trilinear interpolation over a sparse connectivity structure. A technique using LSTM to adaptively sample points along a query ray until it finds the intersection with the scene, then passing this point to a pixel generator network. It employs an LSTM to adaptively sample points along the query ray, continuing sampling until the intersection of the query ray with the scene is found, and then passes the intersection point through a pixel generator network to yield color directly. An approach to avoid suppression of context behind the focus object by suppressing only those samples of the context object that are in front of the focus object. The countersink geometry defines the region of different levels of sparseness, but the starting position of the ray is not changed. During the ray traversal of final image synthesis, each sample location is evaluated whether it belongs to the countersink area or not. Outside the countersink area, the context is represented using a more dense representation, and inside, a more sparse form is chosen. Unlike image-space AImC where the level of sparseness is constant for all samples of one object along a particular ray, object-space AImC has a level of sparseness that is not constant for one object along a particular ray. Time Complexity: Depends on the sparsity of the grid and the distribution of occupied space. In the worst case (fully occupied), it is O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of rays and M is the maximum samples per ray. In practice, it is significantly faster due to skipping empty space. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot M) for output buffers if pre-allocated, or O(\text{total\samples}) if dynamically resized. The density bitfield size depends on the grid resolution and hierarchy. Measured Performance: Tested with RTX 2080 Ti, CUDA 11.3, 32GB RAM. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space, reducing computational waste. Dynamic memory allocation based on occupancy. Limitations: Requires careful management of dynamic memory. Performance depends on the quality of the sparse grid and density threshold. When to Use: Training neural radiance fields where most of the scene is empty or background. When Not to Use: Dense scenes with little empty space, or when real-time inference with fixed latency is required (use Inference Ray Marching instead). body: A GPU-accelerated ray marching kernel that samples points along rays using a hashed density grid, supporting adaptive step sizes and perturbation. It differs from standard uniform ray marching by integrating adaptive stepping and perturbation directly into the sampling loop, and from dense voxel tracing by operating on a sparse hashed grid structure. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: rayso: Origin positions, shape [N, 3], type float32. raysd: Direction vectors, shape [N, 3], type float32. near: Near plane distances, shape [N], type float32. far: Far plane distances, shape [N], type float32. densitybitfield: Hashed density grid lookup table, type uint8. Outputs: xyzs: Sampled 3D coordinates, shape [N, nstep, 3], type float32. dirs: Sampled direction vectors, shape [N, nstep, 3], type float32. deltas: Step sizes, shape [N, nstep, 2] where the first channel stores deltas for RGB integration and the second for depth integration. Data Structures The densitybitfield is a uint8 tensor storing the hashed density grid used for fast lookup during ray marching. The exact hashing scheme (e.g., hash function, grid resolution, bound) is not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: For each ray i \in [0, N), initialize current position p = \text{rays\o}[i], accumulated distance t = \text{near}[i], and step counter k = 0. 2. Marching Loop: While k < n{\text{max\steps}} and t < \text{far}[i]: a. Query Density: Look up density at p using densitybitfield. The exact lookup implementation is not given in the sources. b. Adaptive Step Size: Calculate step size \Delta t based on the queried density and densitythresh. The exact calculation is not given in the sources. c. Perturbation: Apply perturbation to the step or position. The exact perturbation method is not given in the sources. d. Update Position: p \leftarrow p + \Delta t \cdot \text{rays\d}[i] and t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. e. Store Sample: Store p, \text{rays\d}[i], and \Delta t in xyzs[i, k], dirs[i, k], and deltas[i, k] (first channel for RGB, second for depth). f. Increment: k \leftarrow k + 1. 3. Completion: Return xyzs, dirs, and deltas. Pseudocode Unverified code. head: CUDA Ray Tracing Kernel (Backward)
body: The Ray Tracing Kernel is a CUDA compute kernel that performs forward and backward volumetric ray marching through a sparse hashed density grid, handling spherical harmonics (SH) evaluation and ray bounds. It serves as the core inference and training step for the IDDR-NGP backend, computing final pixel colors and log-transmittance in the forward pass, and gradients for SH coefficients and grid outputs in the backward pass. Inputs and Outputs: Forward: Ray origins, directions, grid data, and options. Outputs: pixel color and log-transmittance. Backward: gradoutput, colorcache, logtransmitin, betaloss, sparsityloss, and grads. Outputs: gradients for SH coefficients and grid data. Data Structures: rayspec[TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK]: Shared memory array of SingleRaySpec structs storing ray origin and direction for each ray in the block. sphfuncval[TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK][9]: Shared memory 2D float array storing spherical harmonic function values. tempstorage[TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK]: Shared memory for warp reduction operations. gradsphfuncval[TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK][9]: Shared memory 2D float array storing gradients for spherical harmonic values. Parameters: TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK: Number of rays processed per CUDA block. TRACERAYBKWDCUDATHREADS: Number of threads per block for the backward kernel. grid.basisdim: Number of SH basis functions per color channel. grid.shdatadim: Dimension of SH data, used to mask threads. Algorithm (Forward): 1. Calculate thread indices: rayblkid = threadidx >> 5, laneid = threadidx & 0x1F. 2. If laneid >= grid.shdatadim, return early. 3. Initialize rayspec[rayblkid] with origin and direction from the rays array for the current rayid. 4. Calculate spherical harmonic function values: calcsphfunc(grid, laneid, rayid, rayspec[rayblkid].dir, sphfuncval[rayblkid]). 5. Synchronize warps within the active mask defined by grid.shdatadim to ensure shared memory writes are visible. 6. Find ray bounds within the grid: rayfindbounds(rayspec[rayblkid], grid, opt, rayid). 7. Trace the ray through the volume: traceraycuvol(grid, rayspec, opt, laneid, sphfuncval, tempstorage, output, logtransmit). Algorithm (Backward): 1. Initialize gradient SH values to 0.0f for all lanes less than grid.basisdim. 2. Calculate spherical harmonic function values for the backward pass. 3. Find ray bounds (performed only by lane 0 to avoid redundant computation). 4. Compute gradient output: If gradoutisrgb is true, calculate resid = colorcache - gradoutput, then gradout[i] = resid normfactor where normfactor = 2.0 / (3 Q). Otherwise, gradout[i] = gradoutput[i]. 5. Synchronize warps within the active mask. 6. Trace ray backward: traceraycuvolbackward(grid, gradout, colorcache, rayspec, opt, laneid, sphfuncval, gradsphfuncval, tempstorage, logtransmitin, betaloss, sparsityloss, grads, accumout, logtransmitout). 7. Calculate SH gradients: calcsphfuncbackward(grid, laneid, rayid, vdir, sphfuncval, gradsphfuncval, grads.gradbasisout). Pseudocode (Forward): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def syncwarp(mask): # CUDA intrinsic: syncwarp(mask) pass def renderraykernel(threadidx, rays, grid, opt, out, outlogtransmit): rayblkid = threadidx >> 5 laneid = threadidx & 0x1F if laneid >= grid.shdatadim: return rayid = (blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x) # Standard CUDA indexing rayspec[rayblkid].origin = rays[rayid].origin rayspec[rayblkid].dir = rays[rayid].dir calcsphfunc(grid, laneid, rayid, rayspec[rayblkid].dir, sphfuncval[rayblkid]) syncwarp((1 << grid.shdatadim) - 1) rayfindbounds(rayspec[rayblkid], grid, opt, rayid) traceraycuvol(grid, rayspec, opt, laneid, sphfuncval, tempstorage, out, outlogtransmit) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If laneid >= grid.shdatadim, the thread returns early to handle cases where the number of spherical harmonic basis functions is less than the warp size (32). Ray bounds calculation is performed only by lane 0 in the backward pass to avoid redundant computation. It is designed for the IDDR-NGP backend, where it serves as the core inference step for sparse ray marching, optimizing performance by coarser sampling in distant regions and finer sampling near the center. It differs from standard uniform ray marching by using a logarithmic expansion factor to vary step sizes and cascade levels, and from dense voxel cone tracing by operating on a sparse grid structure with specific boundary handling. name: TracingKernel
body: TracingKernel is a CUDA compute shader that performs volumetric light transport by stepping through a 3D grid, dynamically adjusting step size and cascade resolution based on distance from the center, and accumulating transmittance (alpha). It is designed for the IDDR-NGP backend, where it serves as the core inference step for sparse ray marching, optimizing performance by coarser sampling in distant regions and finer sampling near the center. It differs from standard uniform ray marching by using a logarithmic expansion factor to vary step sizes and cascade levels, and from dense voxel cone tracing by operating on a sparse grid structure with specific boundary handling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: id (uint3), representing the thread's position in the output grid, which also defines the starting X, Y, and initial Z coordinates for a Z-axis ray march. Global Constants: GridResolution (uint, side length of the cubic grid), GridHalfResolution (float, half of GridResolution), GridCascadeBase (uint2, {baselevel, maxlevel}), CVCTtex3d (3D texture/array of pre-processed voxel values), LightTex3d (output texture). Output: LightTex3d[id] (float), the accumulated transmittance (alpha) along the ray. Data Structures: CVCTtex3d: A 3D texture storing pre-processed voxel values. The source preprocessing (RepackAndUpscaleKernel) computes CVCTtex3d[id] = 1 - CVCTgv[srcindex], where srcindex = (z GridResolution + y) GridResolution + x. LightTex3d: A 3D texture storing the final alpha values. Helper Function: SampleGV SampleGV(p) performs trilinear interpolation on CVCTtex3d at position p. The exact mapping of CVCTtex3d to physical density is handled by the preprocessing step, but TracingKernel treats the sampled value a as the per-unit-step transmittance factor. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Convert the thread ID id to a local coordinate system centered at the grid origin. \text{pos} = \text{id} - (\text{GridHalfResolution} - 0.5) 2. Distance Calculation: Compute the Chebyshev distance (max norm) from the center. \text{central\pos} = |\text{pos}| \text{central\distance} = \max(\text{central\pos}.x, \max(\text{central\pos}.y, \text{central\pos}.z)) 3. Normalization and Expansion Factor: Normalize the distance to the range [0, 1] and compute an initial expansion factor. \text{max\distance} = \text{GridHalfResolution} - 0.5 \text{central\distance} \leftarrow \text{central\distance} / \text{max\distance} \text{expand} = \begin{cases} 1.0 & \text{if } \text{central\distance} = 0 \\ \max(\log2(\text{central\distance}) + 2, 1) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} This maps the center (centraldistance \approx 0) to expand = 1 (finest resolution) and the boundary (centraldistance \approx 1) to expand = 2 (coarsest resolution). 4. Initialization: \alpha = 1.0 \text{grid\cascade\base} = \text{GridCascadeBase}.x 5. Ray Marching Loop: While true: a. Cascade Check: If expand >= 2.0, check if the current cascade level is at the maximum. If gridcascadebase >= GridCascadeBase.y, break the loop. Otherwise, advance to the next cascade level: \text{grid\cascade\base} \leftarrow \text{grid\cascade\base} + \text{GridResolution} \text{expand} \leftarrow \text{expand} \times 0.5 \text{pos} \leftarrow \text{pos} \times 0.5 b. Sample Low Position: Calculate the sample position in the current cascade. \text{p} = \text{pos} + (\text{GridHalfResolution} - 0.5) \text{p}.y \leftarrow \text{p}.y + \text{grid\cascade\base} a{\text{low}} = \text{SampleGV}(\text{p}) c. Sample High Position: Calculate the sample position for the next cascade (or boundary). If gridcascadebase >= GridCascadeBase.y: a{\text{high}} = 1.0 Else: \text{q} = \text{pos} \times 0.5 + (\text{GridHalfResolution} - 0.5) \text{q}.y \leftarrow \text{q}.y + \text{grid\cascade\base} + \text{GridResolution} a{\text{high}} = \text{SampleGV}(\text{q}) d. Interpolate Alpha: Blend between the low and high cascade samples based on the expansion factor. a = \text{lerp}(a{\text{low}}, a{\text{high}}, \text{expand} - 1) e. Update Step Size and Accumulate: \text{sample\step} = \text{SAMPLE\STEP\BASE} \times \text{expand} \alpha \leftarrow \alpha \times a^{\text{sample\step}} \text{pos}.z \leftarrow \text{pos}.z - \text{sample\step} \text{expand} \leftarrow \text{expand} \times \text{EXPAND\STEP} f. Termination: The loop continues until expand >= 2.0 and gridcascadebase reaches the limit. 6. Write Result: \text{id}.y \leftarrow \text{id}.y + \text{GridCascadeBase}.x \text{LightTex3d}[\text{id}] = \alpha Parameters: SAMPLESTEPBASE: Base step size for tracing. Typical value: 0.45. EXPANDSTEP: Multiplier for the expansion factor per step. Typical value: 1.21. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Infinite Loop: The loop is guaranteed to terminate because expand increases by EXPANDSTEP (1.21) each iteration, eventually exceeding 2.0, at which point the cascade base is incremented. If the cascade base is already at GridCascadeBase.y, the loop breaks immediately upon the first check. Boundary Conditions: When gridcascadebase reaches GridCascadeBase.y, ahigh is clamped to 1. This assumes that beyond the highest cascade level, the volume is empty or fully transmissive. Precision: The use of log2 and floating-point arithmetic for expand may introduce small precision errors, but the integer-based cascade base ensures robust level switching. Coordinate System: The pos variable is modified in place (scaled and shifted), which requires careful tracking of the coordinate system relative to the grid origin. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def TracingKernel(id: tuple, GridResolution: int, GridHalfResolution: float, GridCascadeBase: tuple, CVCTtex3d: list, LightTex3d: list): # Helper for trilinear interpolation on a 3D array def SampleGV(p: tuple) -> float: # Clamp coordinates to valid range [0, GridResolution-1] x, y, z = p x = max(0, min(GridResolution - 1, x)) y = max(0, min(GridResolution - 1, y)) z = max(0, min(GridResolution - 1, z)) # Get integer and fractional parts ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz # Fetch 8 neighboring voxels v000 = CVCTtex3d[ix, iy, iz] v100 = CVCTtex3d[ix+1, iy, iz] if ix+1 < GridResolution else v000 v010 = CVCTtex3d[ix, iy+1, iz] if iy+1 < GridResolution else v000 v110 = CVCTtex3d[ix+1, iy+1, iz] if (ix+1 < GridResolution and iy+1 < GridResolution) else v010 v001 = CVCTtex3d[ix, iy, iz+1] if iz+1 < GridResolution else v000 v101 = CVCTtex3d[ix+1, iy, iz+1] if (ix+1 < GridResolution and iz+1 < GridResolution) else v001 v011 = CVCTtex3d[ix, iy+1, iz+1] if (iy+1 < GridResolution and iz+1 < GridResolution) else v001 v111 = CVCTtex3d[ix+1, iy+1, iz+1] if (ix+1 < GridResolution and iy+1 < GridResolution and iz+1 < GridResolution) else v011 # Trilinear interpolation c0 = v000 + fx (v100 - name: Training Ray Marching (Forward Only)
head: Ray Marching with Sparse Voxel Grid (Training), two-pass ray marching
body: A two-pass GPU algorithm that samples a ray through a sparse voxel grid (density bitfield) to collect 3D positions, directions, step sizes (deltas), and t-values for training neural radiance fields. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly decoupling the counting of occupied samples from the writing of sample data, allowing for dynamic memory allocation based on actual occupancy rather than fixed worst-case bounds, while supporting an optimization where the maximum allocation size is estimated from previous training epochs. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: rayso: Origin positions, shape [Nrays, 3]. raysd: Direction vectors, shape [Nrays, 3]. hitst: Hit intervals (nears/fars), shape [Nrays, 2]. densitybitfield: Sparse voxel occupancy bitfield, uint8t. noise: Perturbation noise, shape [Nrays, 1]. cascades: Number of MIP cascades, int. scale: Spatial boundary scale, float. expstepfactor: Exponential step factor, float. gridsize: Density grid resolution, int. maxsamples: Hard limit on samples per ray, int. meancount: Estimated max points from previous epoch, int. forceallrays: Boolean flag to ignore meancount and process all rays, bool. perturb: Boolean flag to enable perturbation, bool. align: Alignment padding value, int. stepcounter: Optional int array [2], defaults to zeros if None. Outputs: raysa: Ray metadata, shape [Nrays, 3], dtype int64t. Columns: [rayidx, startidx, Nsamples]. xyzs: Sample positions, shape [M, 3]. dirs: Sample directions, shape [M, 3]. deltas: Step sizes, shape [M]. ts: T-values, shape [M] (or [M, 2] for depth intervals per). counter: Atomic counter, shape [2], dtype int32t. Data Structures: rays: Internal int array [N, 3] storing ray metadata: column 0 is ray ID, column 1 is offset into the xyzs/dirs/deltas arrays, column 2 is number of steps for that ray. densitybitfield: Bit-packed occupancy grid. Index idx corresponds to voxel (nx, ny, nz) via Morton code. Parameters: threads: 256 threads per block. blocks: (Nrays + threads - 1) / threads blocks. bound: Spatial boundary, default 1e-4. densitygrid: Float array [H, H, H]. meandensity: Mean density value. iterdensity: Density value for current iteration. Algorithm Steps: 1. Reshape Inputs: Reshape rayso and raysd to contiguous views of shape [-1, 3]. 2. Initialize Loop Variables: For each ray, set t = t1 (start t from hitst), Nsamples = 0. If perturb is true, add random noise to t. 3. Calculate Position: Compute current 3D position: x = ox + tdx, y = oy + tdy, z = oz + tdz. 4. Calculate Step Size: Compute dt using helper function: dt = calcdt(t, expstepfactor, maxsamples, gridsize, scale). 5. Determine MIP Level: Calculate MIP level mip as the maximum of position-based and dt-based selection: mip = max(mipfrompos(x, y, z, cascades), mipfromdt(dt, gridsize, cascades)). 6. Calculate MIP Bound: Compute MIP bound and its inverse: mipbound = fminf(scalbnf(1.0f, mip-1), scale) and mipboundinv = 1.0f / mipbound. 7. Map to Grid Coordinates: Map position to grid coordinates nx, ny, nz by rounding down to nearest grid position: nx = clamp(0.5f (x mipboundinv + 1.0f) gridsize, 0.0f, gridsize - 1.0f) (similarly for y, z). 8. Compute Morton Index: Compute linear index in the bitfield: idx = mip gridsize^3 + morton3D(nx, ny, nz) where gridsize^3 = gridsize gridsize gridsize. 9. Check Occupancy: Check occupancy: occ = densitybitfield[idx / 8] & (1 << (idx % 8)). 10. Advance Ray: If occupied (occ is true): Increment t by dt (t += dt) and increment sample count (Nsamples++). If not occupied: Calculate target t to skip to next voxel boundary. Compute tx, ty, tz as distances to the next voxel face in each axis: tx = (((nx + 0.5f + 0.5f signf(dx)) gridsizeinv 2 - 1) mipbound - x) dxinv (similarly for ty, tz). Set ttarget = t + fmaxf(0.0f, fminf(tx, fminf(ty, tz))). Advance t in a do-while loop: do { t += calcdt(...) } while (t < ttarget);. 11. Loop Condition: Continue while 0 <= t && t < t2 && Nsamples < maxsamples. 12. First Pass Allocation: After the first pass, allocate output indices using atomic operations on a shared counter: startidx = atomicAdd(counter, Nsamples) and raycount = atomicAdd(counter + 1, 1). 13. Store Ray Metadata: Store ray metadata: raysa[raycount][0] = r, raysa[raycount][1] = startidx, raysa[raycount][2] = Nsamples. 14. Second Pass Initialization: Reset t = t1, samples = 0. 15. Second Pass Loop: Loop condition: while (t < t2 && samples < Nsamples). 16. Second Pass Traversal: Repeat steps 3-11 to re-traverse the ray. 17. Write Sample Data: If occupied: write sample data to global arrays at index s = startidx + samples: xyzs[s] = {x, y, z}, dirs[s] = {dx, dy, dz}, ts[s] = t, deltas[s] = dt. Increment t by dt and samples. 18. Memory Allocation Optimization: Initialize M (max points) to N 1024 as a hardcoded default. If not forceallrays and meancount > 0, use meancount as M. If align > 0, pad M to the next multiple of align. Initialize output tensors xyzs, dirs, deltas with zeros of shape [M, 3], [M, 3], [M] respectively. Initialize rays tensor of shape [N, 3] with dtype int32. If stepcounter is None, initialize it as a zero tensor of shape [2] with dtype int32. If forceallrays or meancount <= 0, retrieve the actual number of points m from stepcounter[0].item() and pad m to the next multiple of align if align > 0. Slice xyzs, dirs, and deltas to size m if the condition in the previous step was met. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Exact formula not given in sources.""" # Standard NGP exponential spacing return expstepfactor (scale / gridsize) (2.0 (t / maxsamples)) def mipfrompos(x, y, z, cascades): """MIP level selection based on position. Exact logic not given in sources.""" return 0 def mipfromdt(dt, gridsize, cascades): """MIP level selection based on step size. Exact logic not given in sources.""" return 0 def morton3D(nx, ny, nz): """Standard 3D Morton code interleaving.""" def interleavebits(v): v = (v | (v << 16)) & 0x00030000FF v = (v | (v << 8)) & 0x0300F00FF v = (v | (v << 4)) & 0x030C30C3 v = (v | (v << 2)) & 0x09249249 return v return interleavebits(nx) | (interleavebits(ny) << 1) | (interleavebits(nz) << 2) def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(val, maxval)) def signf(x): return 1.0 if x > 0 else (-1.0 if x < 0 else 0.0) def scalbnf(x, n): return x (2.0 n) def fminf(a, b): return min(a, b) def fmaxf(a, b): return max(a, b) def trainingraymarching(rayso, raysd, hitst, densitybitfield, noise, cascades, scale, expstepfactor, gridsize, maxsamples, meancount, forceallrays, perturb, align): """ Two-pass GPU algorithm for training ray marching. Args: rayso: Tensor [Nrays, 3] raysd: Tensor [Nrays, 3] hitst: Tensor [Nrays, 2] densitybitfield: uint8t (simulated as tensor for pseudocode) noise: Tensor [Nrays, 1] cascades: int scale: float expstepfactor: float gridsize: int maxsamples: int meancount: int forceallrays: bool perturb: bool align: int Returns: raysa: Tensor [Nrays, 3] xyzs: Tensor [M, 3] dirs: Tensor [M, 3] deltas: Tensor [M] ts: Tensor [M] """ Nrays = rayso.shape[0] # Reshape inputs rayso = rayso.view(-1, 3) raysd = raysd.view(-1, 3) # Determine M (max points) M = Nrays 1024 # Default if not forceallrays and meancount > 0: M = meancount if align > 0: M = ((M + align - 1) // align) align # Initialize output tensors xyzs = torch.zeros((M, 3), dtype=torch.float32) dirs = torch.zeros((M, 3), dtype=torch.float32) deltas = torch.zeros((M,), dtype=torch.float32) ts = torch.zeros((M,), dtype=torch.float32) raysa = torch.zeros((Nrays, 3), dtype=torch.int64) # Counter for atomic operations (simulated) counter = torch.zeros((2,), dtype=torch.int32) gridsizeinv = 1.0 / gridsize for r in range(Nrays): ox, oy, oz = rayso[r] dx, dy, dz = raysd[r] t1, t2 = hitst[r] # Perturbation if perturb: t1 += noise[r].item() # First Pass: Count samples t = t1 Nsamples = 0 while 0 <= t < t2 and Nsamples < maxsamples: # Calculate position x = ox + t dx y = oy + t dy z = oz + t dz # Calculate step size dt = calcdt(t, expstepfactor, maxsamples, gridsize, scale) # Determine MIP level mip = max(mipfrompos(x, y, z, cascades), mipfromdt(dt, gridsize, cascades)) # Calculate MIP bound mipbound = fminf(scalbnf(1.0, mip - 1), scale) mipboundinv = 1.0 / mipbound # Map to grid coordinates nx = clamp(0.5 (x mipboundinv + 1.0) gridsize, 0.0, gridsize - 1.0) ny = clamp(0.5 (y mipboundinv + 1.0) gridsize, 0.0, gridsize - 1.0) nz = clamp(0.5 (z mipboundinv + 1.0) gridsize, 0.0, gridsize - 1.0) # Compute Morton Index gridsize3 = gridsize gridsize gridsize idx = mip gridsize3 + morton3D(int(nx), int(ny), int(nz)) # Check occupancy occ = (densitybitfield[idx // 8] & (1 << (idx % 8))) != 0 if occ: t += dt Nsamples += 1 else: # Skip to next voxel boundary dxinv = 1.0 / dx if dx != 0 else float('inf') dyinv = 1.0 / dy if dy != 0 else float('inf') dzinv = 1.0 / dz if dz != 0 else float('inf') tx = (((nx + 0.5 + 0.5 signf(dx)) gridsizeinv 2 - 1) mipbound - x) dxinv ty = (((ny + 0.5 + 0.5 signf(dy)) gridsizeinv 2 - 1) mipbound - y) dyinv tz = (((nz + 0.5 + 0.5 signf(dz)) gridsizeinv 2 - 1) mipbound - z) dzinv ttarget = t + fmaxf(0.0, fminf(tx, fminf(ty, tz))) while t < ttarget: t += calcdt(t, expstepfactor, maxsamples, gridsize, scale) # Allocate output indices (simulated atomics) startidx = counter[0].item() counter[0] += Nsamples raycount = counter[1].item() counter[1] += 1 raysa[r][0] = r raysa[r][1] = startidx raysa[r][2] = Nsamples # Second Pass: Write samples t = t1 samples = 0 while t < t2 and samples < Nsamples: x = ox + t dx y = oy + t dy z = oz + t dz dt = calcdt(t, expstepfactor, maxsamples, gridsize, scale) mip = max(mipfrompos(x, y, z, cascades), mipfromdt(dt, gridsize, cascades)) mipbound = fminf(scalbnf(1.0, mip - 1), scale) mipboundinv = 1.0 / mipbound nx = clamp(0.5 (x mipboundinv + 1.0) gridsize, 0.0, gridsize - 1.0) ny = clamp(0.5 (y mipboundinv + 1.0) gridsize, 0.0, gridsize - 1.0) nz = clamp(0.5 (z mipboundinv + 1.0) gridsize, 0.0, gridsize - 1.0) gridsize3 = gridsize gridsize gridsize idx = mip gridsize3 + morton3D(int(nx), int(ny), int(nz)) occ = (densitybitfield[idx // 8] & (1 << (idx % 8))) != 0 if occ: s = startidx + samples xyzs[s] = torch.tensor([x, y, z]) dirs[s] = torch.tensor([dx, dy, dz]) ts[s] = t deltas[s] = dt t += dt samples += 1 else: dxinv = 1.0 / dx if dx != 0 else float('inf') dyinv = 1.0 / dy if dy != 0 else float('inf') dzinv = 1.0 / dz if dz != 0 else float('inf') tx = (((nx + 0.5 + 0.5 signf(dx)) gridsizeinv 2 - 1) mipbound - x) dxinv ty = (((ny + 0.5 + 0.5 signf(dy)) gridsizeinv 2 - 1) mipbound - y) dyinv tz = (((nz + 0.5 + 0.5 signf(dz)) gridsizeinv 2 - 1) mipbound - z) dzinv ttarget = t + fmaxf(0.0, fminf(tx, fminf(ty, tz))) while t < ttarget: t += calcdt(t, expstepfactor, maxsamples, gridsize, scale) # Slice outputs to actual size if needed actualsamples = counter[0].item() xyzs = xyzs[:actualsamples] dirs = dirs[:actualsamples] deltas = deltas[:actualsamples] ts = ts[:actualsamples] return raysa, xyzs, dirs, deltas, ts NeuralPointsRayMarching is a PyTorch module that performs ray marching for neural point rendering by aggregating sampled neural point features and blending them along rays. It estimates the maximum number of points to allocate based on mean count from previous epochs, enabling faster training by avoiding over-allocation, while supporting force-all-rays mode for stability. It sets itself apart from standard volume rendering by operating on discrete, learned point entities rather than continuous volumetric fields. Time Complexity: Two passes over the ray space. The first pass counts occupied samples, the second pass writes them. Complexity is proportional to the number of rays and the average number of occupied samples per ray. Memory Complexity: Memory allocation is dynamic based on meancount or maxsamples. The xyzs, dirs, deltas, and ts tensors are allocated up to size M. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of rays Nrays and the density of the voxel grid. Strengths: Avoids over-allocation by using meancount from previous epochs. Supports forceallrays for stability. Limitations: If meancount underestimates the required points, rays may be randomly ignored unless forceallrays is enabled. When to use: Training neural radiance fields with sparse voxel grids where memory efficiency is critical. When not to use: Inference where fixed allocation is preferred for simplicity, or when meancount is not available. body: NeuralPointsRayMarching is a PyTorch module that performs ray marching for neural point rendering by aggregating sampled neural point features and blending them along rays. It estimates the maximum number of points to allocate based on mean count from previous epochs, enabling faster training by avoiding over-allocation, while supporting force-all-rays mode for stability. It sets itself apart from standard volume rendering by operating on discrete, learned point entities rather than continuous volumetric fields. Inputs: pixelidx: Indices of pixels to render. camrotc2w: Camera rotation matrix (C2W). campos: Camera position (C2W). near, far: Near and far clipping planes. focal: Focal length. h, w: Image height and width. intrinsic: Camera intrinsic matrix. gtimage: Ground truth image. raydir: Ray directions. opt: Configuration object containing flags like raydistmodeunit, prob, returncolor, returndepth. neuralpoints: The neural point cloud data structure. numposfreqs, numviewdirfreqs: Number of frequency bands for positional and view-direction encoding. aggregator: Feature aggregation function. renderfunc, blendfunc, tonemap: Rendering, blending, and tone-mapping functions. iscomputedepth: Flag to enable depth computation. Outputs: raycolor: Rendered color per ray. opacity: Opacity per ray. coarsedepth: Depth estimate per ray. coarseisbackground: Background transmission mask. raymask: Valid ray mask. weight, blendweight, confcoefficient: Intermediate blending weights. raymaxshadingopacity, raymaxsamplelocw, raymaxfardist, shadingavgcolor, shadingavgdir, shadingavgconf, shadingavgembedding: Statistics for max-shading opacity mode. The module relies on the neuralpoints structure, which provides sampled features via a forward call. The sampled features include: sampledcolor: RGB color values. sampledRw2c: Rotation matrices (World-to-Camera). sampleddir: View directions. sampledconf: Confidence values. sampledembedding: Feature embeddings. sampledxyzpers: 3D points in perspective space. sampledxyz: 3D points in world space. samplepntmask: Mask for valid points. sampleloc: Sample locations along the ray. samplelocw: Sample locations in world space. sampleraydirs: Ray directions at sample points. raymasktensor: Mask for valid rays. vsize: Voxel size (3D vector). gridvoxsz: Grid voxel size. 1. Initialization: The module is initialized with parameters: tonemapfunc, renderfunc, blendfunc, aggregator, iscomputedepth, neuralpoints, opt, numposfreqs, numviewdirfreqs. 2. Sampling: In the forward pass, call self.neuralpoints with inputs: pixelidx, camrotc2w, campos, near, far, focal, h, w, intrinsic, gtimage, raydir to obtain the sampled features listed above. 3. Aggregation: Aggregate sampled features using self.aggregator to produce decodedfeatures, rayvalid, weight, confcoefficient. 4. Ray Distance Calculation: Compute cumulative maximum of the z-component of sample locations: \text{ray\dist}{\text{cum}} = \text{torch.cummax}(\text{sample\loc}[\dots, 2], \text{dim}=-1)[0] Calculate distances between consecutive samples and the last segment: \text{ray\dist} = \text{torch.cat}([\text{ray\dist}{\text{cum}}[\dots, 1:] - \text{ray\dist}{\text{cum}}[\dots,:-1], \text{torch.full}((\text{ray\dist}{\text{cum}}.\text{shape}[0], \text{ray\dist}{\text{cum}}.\text{shape}[1], 1), \text{vsize}[2], \text{device}=\text{ray\dist}{\text{cum}}.\text{device})], \text{dim}=-1) 5. Invalid Distance Masking: Create a mask for invalid distances: \text{mask} = \text{ray\dist} < 10^{-8} If self.opt.raydistmodeunit > 0, extend the mask: \text{mask} = \text{mask} \lor (\text{ray\dist} > 2 \times \text{vsize}[2]) Convert mask to float32: \text{mask} = \text{mask}.\text{to}(\text{torch.float32}) 6. Distance Correction: Replace invalid distances with vsize[2]: \text{ray\dist} = \text{ray\dist} \times (1.0 - \text{mask}) + \text{mask} \times \text{vsize}[2] Multiply by valid ray mask: \text{ray\dist} = \text{ray\dist} \times \text{ray\valid}.\text{float}() 7. Shading Query Output: Set output['queriedshading'] to a tensor indicating rays with no valid points: \text{output}['\text{queried\shading}'] = \text{torch.logical\not}(\text{torch.any}(\text{ray\valid}, \text{dim}=-1, \text{keepdims}=\text{True})).\text{repeat}(1, 1, 3).\text{to}(\text{torch.float32}) 8. Rendering: If self.returncolor is True: If 'bgray' in kargs, set bgcolor = None. Call raymarch(raydist, rayvalid, decodedfeatures, self.renderfunc, self.blendfunc, bgcolor) to get raycolor, pointcolor, opacity, acctransmission, blendweight, backgroundtransmission,. Apply tone map: \text{ray\color} = \text{self.tone\map}(\text{ray\color}) Store in output. Else (if self.returncolor is False): Call alpharaymarch(raydist, rayvalid, decodedfeatures, self.blendfunc) to get opacity, acctransmission, blendweight, backgroundtransmission,. 9. Depth Computation: If self.returndepth is True: Compute alpha blend weight: \text{alpha\blend\weight} = \text{opacity} \times \text{acc\transmission} Reshape weight to alphablendweight.shape[:3]. Compute average depth: \text{avg\depth} = \frac{\sum (\text{weight} \times \text{ray\ts})}{\sum \text{weight} + 10^{-6}} Store in output['coarsedepth']. 10. Additional Outputs: Store backgroundtransmission in output['coarseisbackground']. Store raymasktensor in output['raymask']. If weight is not None, store weight.detach(), blendweight.detach(), confcoefficient in output. 11. Max Shading Opacity Mode: If self.opt.prob == 1 and output['coarsepointopacity'].shape[1] > 0: Get batch size B and number of rays OR from samplepntmask.shape. If weight is not None: Find max opacity and its index: \text{output}['\text{ray\max\shading\opacity}'], \text{opacity\ind} = \text{torch.max}(\text{output}['\text{coarse\point\opacity}'], \text{dim}=-1, \text{keepdim}=\text{True}) Expand opacityind. name: Sparse Packed Radiance Field Tracer
head: PackedRFTracer
body: The Sparse Packed Radiance Field Tracer is a differentiable rendering method for sparse, packed radiance fields that generates a variable number of samples per ray, packed into a flat tensor structure. It solves the inefficiency of standard ray marching by using a sparse acceleration structure to sample only within occupied cells, resulting in a custom number of samples per ray rather than a fixed grid. Unlike its siblings, it explicitly manages the "packed" data layout where rays with different intersection counts share a single contiguous buffer, requiring specific reduction operations to handle boundaries between rays. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A neural field (nef) with an attached grid/BLAS, a batch of rays (origin, direction), configuration parameters (raymarchtype, numsteps, bgcolor), and optional extra channels. Outputs: Computed RGB color, depth, alpha, and hit status for each ray in the batch. Data Structures: Packed Tensor: A 1D tensor containing samples for all rays concatenated. Pack Info: Metadata indicating the start index and count of samples for each ray in the packed tensor. Boundary: A boolean or integer mask indicating the end of valid samples for each ray in the packed tensor. Parameters: raymarchtype (str): 'voxel' (intersects acceleration structure cells, samples numsteps times per cell) or 'ray' (samples numsteps along ray, culls outside occupied cells). numsteps (int): Number of samples per intersected cell (for 'voxel') or per ray before culling (for 'ray'). stepsize (float): Currently unused. bgcolor (Tuple[float, float, float]): Background color, default (1.0, 1.0, 1.0). Steps: 1. Initialization: Store bgcolor as a float32 tensor. Assert that the neural field has a grid attribute. 2. LOD Selection: If lodidx is None, set it to nef.grid.numlods - 1 (highest detail). 3. Ray Marching: Call nef.grid.raymarch() with rays, activelods[lodidx], numsteps, and raymarchtype. This returns ridx (ray indices), samples (coordinates), deltas (distances), depths, packinfo, and boundary. 4. Preparation: Extract results. Set prevnumsamples to samples.shape[0]. Get hit ray directions using rays.dirs.indexselect(0, ridx). 5. Neural Field Query: Query nef at samples with hitrayd and lodidx for channels ["rgb", "density"]. Reshape density to (numsamples, 1) to prevent squeezing. 6. Buffer Initialization: Initialize output buffers: depth (N, 1), rgb (N, 3) initialized to bgcolor, hit (N, bool), outalpha (N, 1). 7. Optical Thickness: Compute tau = density deltas. Delete density and deltas to free memory. 8. Exponential Integration: Compute raycolors and transmittance using spcrender.exponentialintegration(color, tau, boundary, exclusive=True). 9. Depth Computation (Optional): If 'depth' is requested, compute raydepth = spcrender.sumreduce(depths.reshape(numsamples, 1) transmittance, boundary). Assign depth[ridxhit,:] = raydepth. 10. Alpha and Hit Status: Compute alpha = spcrender.sumreduce(transmittance, boundary). Assign outalpha[ridxhit] = alpha and hit[ridxhit] = alpha[...,0] > 0.0. 11. Color Composition: For hit rays, compute rgb[ridxhit] = (self.bgcolor (1.0-alpha)) + raycolors. 12. Extra Channels: For each extra channel, query nef, perform exponentialintegration, compute compositedfeats = alpha rayfeats, and assign to outfeats[ridxhit]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def trace(self, rays, nef, lodidx=None, channels=None): # 1. Assert grid exists assert hasattr(nef, 'grid') # 2. Determine LOD if lodidx is None: lodidx = nef.grid.numlods - 1 # 3. Ray Marching via Sparse Grid raymarchresults = nef.grid.raymarch( rays=rays, activelods=[lodidx], numsteps=self.numsteps, raymarchtype=self.raymarchtype) ridx, samples, deltas, depths, packinfo, boundary = raymarchresults prevnumsamples = samples.shape[0] # 4. Get directions for hit rays hitrayd = rays.dirs.indexselect(0, ridx) # 5. Query Neural Field color, density = nef( coords=samples, rayd=hitrayd, lodidx=lodidx, channels=["rgb", "density"]) # Protect against squeezed return shape if density.dim() == 1: density = density.unsqueeze(1) # 6. Initialize Output Buffers N = rays.dirs.shape[0] device = rays.dirs.device depthout = torch.zeros((N, 1), device=device) rgbout = torch.tensor(self.bgcolor, dtype=torch.float32, device=device).expand(N, -1).clone() hitout = torch.zeros(N, dtype=torch.bool, device=device) outalpha = torch.zeros((N, 1), device=device) # 7. Compute Optical Thickness tau = density deltas del density, deltas # 8. Exponential Integration raycolors, transmittance = exponentialintegration(color, tau, boundary, exclusive=True) # 9. Depth Computation if 'depth' in channels: depthsreshaped = depths.reshape(prevnumsamples, 1) raydepth = sumreduce(depthsreshaped transmittance, boundary) hitmask = transmittance[:, 0] > 0.0 ridxhit = ridx[hitmask] depthout[ridxhit] = raydepth[hitmask] # 10. Alpha and Hit Status alpha = sumreduce(transmittance, boundary) ridxhit = ridx[transmittance[:, 0] > 0.0] outalpha[ridxhit] = alpha[hitmask] hitout[ridxhit] = alpha[hitmask, 0] > 0.0 # 11. Color Composition if hitmask.any(): bgcontrib = torch.tensor(self.bgcolor, dtype=torch.float32, device=device) (1.0 - alpha[hitmask]) rgbout[ridxhit] = bgcontrib + raycolors[hitmask] # 12. Extra Channels if channels: outfeats = torch.zeros(N, 1, device=device) # Placeholder for channel dimension for ch in channels: if ch in ['rgb', 'density', 'depth']: continue feats, = nef(coords=samples, rayd=hitrayd, lodidx=lodidx, channels=[ch]) rayfeats, = exponentialintegration(feats, tau, boundary, exclusive=True) compositedfeats = alpha rayfeats outfeats = torch.cat([outfeats, compositedfeats], dim=1) # Assign composited features to output buffer (structure depends on extrachannels layout) return rgbout, depthout, outalpha, hitout def sumreduce(arr, boundary): """Sums elements between boundaries, returning per-ray sums.""" out = torch.zeroslike(arr[:,:1]) currentsum = torch.zeroslike(out) for i in range(arr.shape[0]): currentsum += arr[i] if boundary[i]: out[i] = currentsum currentsum = torch.zeroslike(currentsum) return out def exponentialintegration(color, tau, boundary, exclusive=True): """Computes transmittance and ray colors for volume rendering.""" numsamples = tau.shape[0] transmittance = torch.zeroslike(color) raycolors = torch.zeroslike(color) currentT = torch.ones(color.shape[0], device=color.device).unsqueeze(1) for i in range(numsamples): if exclusive: transmittance[i] = currentT sigmadelta = tau[i, 0] Tstep = torch.exp(-sigmadelta) raycolors[i] = currentT (1.0 - Tstep) color[i] currentT = currentT Tstep else: sigmadelta = tau[i, 0] Tstep = torch.exp(-sigmadelta) transmittance[i] = currentT Tstep raycolors[i] = currentT (1.0 - Tstep) color[i] currentT = currentT Tstep if boundary[i]: currentT = torch.ones(color.shape[0], device=color.device).unsqueeze(1) return raycolors, transmittance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: bgcolor must be stored as float32 to ensure consistency during accumulation. Shape Squeezing: Density output from the neural field may be squeezed to 1D if batch size is 1; explicit reshaping to (N, 1) is required. Boundary Handling: The boundary parameter is critical for sumreduce and exponentialintegration to correctly handle rays with varying sample counts in the packed tensor. The parent method that provides the underlying sparse acceleration structure and training-time sampling logic. Sparse Ray Marching (Training) An alternative implementation using CUDA kernels for NGP-style grids, likely offering lower-level performance optimization but potentially less flexibility in packed tensor handling compared to the Python-based tracer. CUDA Ray Marching (IDDR-NGP Backend) A simplified tracer used only for forward passes during training, lacking the full differentiable integration and packed tensor management of the inference tracer. Training Ray Marching (Forward Only) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Differentiable, handles variable sample counts efficiently, integrates with sparse acceleration structures. Limitations: Requires a compatible neural field and grid structure. 'stepsize' is currently unused, limiting control over sampling density in some modes. When to Use: When rendering sparse radiance fields or SDFs where most of the volume is empty, and differentiability is required. When Not to Use: For dense volumes where fixed-step ray marching might be more cache-friendly, or when hardware acceleration for sparse structures is not available. The Sparse Packed Radiance Field Tracer is part of the NVIDIA Kaolin-Wisp framework, introduced in the context of SIGGRAPH 2022 demos for interactive neural rendering. It builds upon the concept of "packed" tensors for variable-length data, a technique popularized in libraries like Kaolin for efficient batched operations on sparse data. The method is designed to work with Neural Geometric LODs and sparse occupancy structures (BLAS) to enable real-time rendering of high-fidelity neural fields.
