name: Sparse Grid Volume Rendering (Foreground)
head: Fused Sparse Voxel Volume Rendering (CuVol), JNeRF volume rendering, Plenoxel Ray Tracing (Forward)
body: Sparse Grid Volume Rendering (Foreground) is a CUDA-based volume rendering method that traces rays through a sparse voxel grid to compute final color and log-transmittance using volume rendering with spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. It differs from its siblings by explicitly managing warp-level parallelism for SH basis evaluation and accumulation, utilizing shared memory for warp-local data to minimize global memory traffic, and employing early termination based on transmission thresholds. Unlike CUDA Ray Marching (IDDR-NGP Backend) which uses hash encoding, or Sparse Packed Radiance Field Tracer which may use different interpolation schemes, this method relies on trilinear interpolation over a sparse connectivity structure. Inputs: rays: Array of ray origins and directions. grid: A PackedSparseGridSpec structure containing sparse voxel data. opt: RenderOptions structure controlling marching parameters. outv: Output buffer for rendered colors. outlogtransmit: Optional output buffer for log-transmittance. Outputs: outv: Rendered color per ray. outlogtransmit: Log-transmittance per ray (if provided). PackedSparseGridSpec: links: Sparse connectivity structure for voxel lookup. stridex: Stride for density data lookup. size[3]: Grid dimensions (width, height, depth). densitydata: Density values (\sigma) stored in a sparse format. shdata: Spherical Harmonics coefficients for color. shdatadim: Number of SH bands/dimensions (typically 9 for 3rd order). basisdim: Number of SH basis functions per color channel. backgroundnlayers: Number of background layers (0 implies simple background). backgroundbrightness: Scalar background color value. SingleRaySpec: origin[3]: Ray origin coordinates. dir[3]: Ray direction vector. tmin: Near bound of the ray segment within the grid. tmax: Far bound of the ray segment within the grid. pos[3]: Current ray position. l[3]: Integer voxel coordinates. worldstep: Step size in world units. RenderOptions: stepsize: Fixed step size for ray marching. sigmathresh: Density threshold below which samples are skipped. stopthresh: Transmission threshold below which ray marching terminates early. lastsampleopaque: Boolean flag; if true, sets worldstep to 10^9 for the last sample. backgroundbrightness: Scalar background color. randomize: Boolean flag for randomization (not used in forward pass logic described). randomsigmastd: Float for randomization (not used in forward pass logic described). The kernel launches with TRACERAYCUDATHREADS = 128 threads per block, processing TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK = 4 rays per block (since WARPSIZE = 32). 1. Initialization: Compute thread ID tid = blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x. Compute rayid = tid // 32 (integer division by 32). Compute laneid = threadIdx.x % 32 (modulo 32). If laneid >= grid.shdatadim, return early. Copy rays.origins[rayid] and rays.dirs[rayid] into shared memory rayspec[rayblkid] where rayblkid = tid // 32. Compute ray bounds tmin and tmax for the ray intersecting the grid. If tmin > tmax, the ray is outside the grid. Output backgroundbrightness if grid.backgroundnlayers == 0, else 0. Set logtransmit to 0 if outlogtransmit is not null. 2. Shared Memory Allocation: shared float sphfuncval[4][9] for SH basis values. shared SingleRaySpec rayspec[4] for ray data. shared WarpReducef::TempStorage tempstorage[4] for warp reductions. 3. Spherical Harmonics Evaluation: Compute SH basis values for the ray direction rayspec[rayblkid].dir using calcsphfunc(grid, laneid, rayid, rayspec[rayblkid].dir, sphfuncval[rayblkid]). This fills sphfuncval[rayblkid] with 9 values (assuming 3rd order SH). Synchronize warp: syncwarp((1 << grid.shdatadim) - 1) to ensure all lanes have computed SH values. 4. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize t = rayspec[rayblkid].tmin. While t <= rayspec[rayblkid].tmax: a. Position Computation: ray.pos[j] = fmaf(t, rayspec[rayblkid].dir[j], rayspec[rayblkid].origin[j]) for j=0,1,2. Clamp ray.pos[j] to [0, grid.size[j] - 1]. Compute integer voxel coordinates: ray.l[j] = min(staticcast<int32t>(ray.pos[j]), grid.size[j] - 2). Compute fractional part: ray.pos[j] -= staticcast<float>(ray.l[j]). b. Density Sampling: Sample density \sigma using trilinear interpolation: \sigma = \text{trilerp\cuvol\one}(grid.links, grid.densitydata, grid.stridex, grid.size[2], 1, ray.l, ray.pos, 0). c. Threshold Check: If \sigma \le opt.sigma\thresh, skip sampling and continue to next step (advance t). d. Color Sampling: Sample SH color coefficients: lane\color = \text{trilerp\cuvol\one}(grid.links, grid.shdata, grid.stridex, grid.size[2], grid.sh\data\dim, ray.l, ray.pos, lane\id). Multiply by SH basis value: lane\color = sphfunc\val[ray\blk\id][lane\id]. e. Weight Computation: Compute optical depth increment: pcnt = ray\spec[ray\blk\id].world\step \times \sigma. Compute weight: weight = \exp(log\transmit) \times (1 - \exp(-pcnt)). Update log-transmittance: log\transmit -= pcnt. f. Accumulation: Reduce lanecolor across the warp using WarpReducef::HeadSegmentedSum with mask lanecolorgrpid == 0 (where lanecolorgrpid groups lanes by SH basis index). Let result be lanecolortotal. Add to output: outv += weight \times \max(lane\color\total + 0.5f, 0.f). This clamps the color to non-negative values. g. Last Sample Handling: If opt.last\sample\opaque is true and t + opt.step\size > ray\spec[ray\blk\id].tmax, set ray\spec[ray\blk\id].world\step = 10^9 to make the last sample fully opaque. h. Step Advancement: t += opt.step\size. i. Early Termination: If \exp(log\transmit) < opt.stop\thresh, set log\transmit = -1000.0f and break the loop. 5. Background Addition: If grid.background\nlayers == 0, add background contribution: outv += \exp(log\transmit) \times opt.background\brightness. 6. Output: If laneid == 0, write out[laneid] = outv and if outlogtransmit is not null, write outlogtransmit = logtransmit. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeraybounds(ray, grid): # Standard AABB ray-box intersection tmin, tmax = -float('inf'), float('inf') for j in range(3): invdir = 1.0 / ray.dir[j] if ray.dir[j] != 0 else float('inf') t0 = (0.0 - ray.origin[j]) invdir t1 = (grid.size[j] - 1.0 - ray.origin[j]) invdir tmin = max(tmin, min(t0, t1)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t0, t1)) return tmin, tmax def renderraykernel(rays, grid, opt, outv, outlogtransmit): tid = blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x rayid = tid // 32 laneid = threadIdx.x % 32 rayblkid = tid // 32 # 0 to 3 if laneid >= grid.shdatadim: return # Shared memory allocation sharedrayspec = shared SingleRaySpec[4] sharedsphfuncval = shared float[4][9] sharedtempstorage = shared WarpReducef::TempStorage[4] # Initialize ray data in shared memory sharedrayspec[rayblkid].origin = rays.origins[rayid] sharedrayspec[rayblkid].dir = rays.dirs[rayid] # Compute ray bounds tmin, tmax = computeraybounds(sharedrayspec[rayblkid], grid) # Handle rays outside grid if tmin > tmax: if grid.backgroundnlayers == 0: outv[rayid] = opt.backgroundbrightness else: outv[rayid] = 0.0 if outlogtransmit is not None: outlogtransmit[rayid] = 0.0 return # Compute SH basis values calcsphfunc(grid, laneid, rayid, sharedrayspec[rayblkid].dir, sharedsphfuncval[rayblkid]) syncwarp((1 << grid.shdatadim) - 1) # Initialize ray marching t = tmin logtransmit = 0.0 outcolor = 0.0 worldstep = opt.stepsize while t <= tmax: # Position computation pos = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for j in range(3): pos[j] = t sharedrayspec[rayblkid].dir[j] + sharedrayspec[rayblkid].origin[j] pos[j] = max(0.0, min(pos[j], grid.size[j] - 1.0)) l = [int(pos[j]) for j in range(3)] for j in range(3): l[j] = min(l[j], grid.size[j] - 2) pos[j] -= l[j] # Density sampling sigma = trilerpcuvolone(grid.links, grid.densitydata, grid.stridex, grid.size[2], 1, l, pos, 0) # Threshold check if sigma <= opt.sigmathresh: t += opt.stepsize continue # Color sampling lanecolor = trilerpcuvolone(grid.links, grid.shdata, grid.stridex, grid.size[2], grid.shdatadim, l, pos, laneid) lanecolor = sharedsphfuncval[rayblkid][laneid] # Weight computation pcnt = worldstep sigma weight = exp(logtransmit) (1.0 - exp(-pcnt)) logtransmit -= pcnt # Warp reduction for color lanecolortotal = WarpReducef(sharedtempstorage[rayblkid]).HeadSegmentedSum(lanecolor, laneid == 0) # Accumulation outcolor += weight max(lanecolortotal + 0.5, 0.0) # Last sample handling if opt.lastsampleopaque and t + opt.stepsize > tmax: worldstep = 1e9 # Step advancement t += opt.stepsize # Early termination if exp(logtransmit) < opt.stopthresh: logtransmit = -1000.0 break # Background addition if grid.backgroundnlayers == 0: outcolor += exp(logtransmit) opt.backgroundbrightness # Output if laneid == 0: outv[rayid] = outcolor if outlogtransmit is not None: outlogtransmit[rayid] = logtransmit grid.basisdim: Number of SH basis functions per color channel. opt.stepsize: Fixed step size for ray marching. opt.sigmathresh: Density threshold below which samples are skipped. opt.stopthresh: Transmission threshold below which ray marching terminates early. opt.lastsampleopaque: Boolean flag; if true, sets worldstep to 10^9 for the last sample. If ray.tmin > ray.tmax, the ray is outside the grid. Output backgroundbrightness if grid.backgroundnlayers == 0, else 0. Set logtransmit to 0 if outlogtransmit is not null. Precision issues may arise from repeated floating-point additions in the ray marching loop; using fmaf helps maintain precision. The SH basis evaluation must be synchronized across the warp before color accumulation to ensure correct reduction. Launches the kernel with blocks = CUDANBLOCKSNEEDED(Q WARPSIZE, cudanthreads), where Q is the number of rays and cudanthreads = TRACERAYCUDATHREADS. Each thread block processes TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK rays. Thread index tid maps to rayid = tid >> 5, rayblkid = threadIdx.x >> 5, laneid = threadIdx.x & 0x1F. Loads ray origin and direction into rayspec[rayblkid], computes direction vector vdir[3]. Evaluates spherical harmonics basis values per lane: calcsphfunc(grid, laneid, rayid, vdir, sphfuncval[rayblkid]). Computes ray traversal bounds: rayfindbounds(rayspec[rayblkid], grid, opt, rayid). Traces ray through grid and accumulates color/transmittance: traceraycuvol(grid, rayspec[rayblkid], opt, laneid, sphfuncval[rayblkid], tempstorage[rayblkid], out + rayid 3, logtransmitout). If grid.backgroundlinks is defined and non-empty, allocates logtransmit tensor and launches renderbackgroundkernel to composite background using logtransmit. Input: PackedSparseGridSpec grid, PackedRaysSpec rays, RenderOptions opt. Output: torch::Tensor results of shape [Q, 3] (float, RGB). Measured Performance: On RTX 3090, Instant-NGP implemented in JNeRF achieves about 133 iterations per second for the lego dataset. Sparse Grid Volume Rendering (Foreground) is derived from Plenoxels, which introduced the use of sparse voxel grids with spherical harmonics for radiance field representation. The implementation in NeRF-Factory and JNeRF adapts this for efficient CUDA execution, leveraging warp-level operations for SH evaluation. kakaobrain/nerf-factory, https://github.com/kakaobrain/nerf-factory, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) OSHMOS/IPRF, https://github.com/OSHMOS/IPRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Jittor/JNeRF, https://github.com/Jittor/JNeRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Tile Warping-based Sparse Rendering
head: Sparse rendering via viewpoint transformation, Tile Warping
body: Tile Warping-based Sparse Rendering (TWSR) is a sparse rendering strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that reuses pixels from a reference frame to a target frame by operating at the tile level rather than the pixel level. It addresses the conflict between standard pixel warping and the 3DGS tile-based architecture, where preprocessing and sorting overheads negate the benefits of pixel-level sparsity. Unlike pixel-based methods that suffer from floating artifacts and high overhead for tiles with even one missing pixel, TWSR interpolates tiles with few missing pixels and re-renders tiles with many missing pixels, bypassing rasterization, preprocessing, and sorting for interpolated tiles. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Reference frame F{ref}, reference scene depth map D{ref}, reference truncated depth map D{ref}^{max}, reference viewpoint V{ref}, target viewpoint V{tgt}, and a re-rendering threshold N0. Outputs: Target frame F{tgt} and a group of tiles T with a tile-level truncated depth map D{tgt}^{max}. Data Structures: Frame (F): Image buffer containing color values for each pixel. Depth Map (D): Per-pixel depth values. Truncated Depth Map (D^{max}): Per-pixel maximum depth bounds used for culling. Point Cloud (P): 3D coordinates (x, y, z) derived from back-projection. Tile (t): A rectangular region of the image. The total number of pixels in a tile is W \times H, where W and H are the tile dimensions. Parameters: N0: The threshold for the number of missing pixels in a tile. If the count of missing pixels N > N0, the tile is re-rendered; otherwise, it is interpolated. The text notes N0 is empirically set to less than one-sixth of the total pixels in the tile for small missing pixel counts, but Algorithm 1 uses N0 as the explicit threshold. Warping Window Size n: Number of frames between every two fully rendered frames. Default value n=5. One frame is fully rendered every n+1 frames. Steps: 1. Initialize: Initialize the target frame F{tgt} and truncated depth map D{tgt}^{max}. 2. Back-project: Project pixels from the reference frame F{ref} into 3D space using D{ref} and D{ref}^{max} to form a reference point cloud P{ref} and truncated point cloud P{ref}^{max}. 3. Transform: Transform the 3D points P{ref} and P{ref}^{max} according to the target frame’s camera pose V{tgt} to obtain target point clouds P{tgt} and P{tgt}^{max}. 4. Reproject: Reproject P{tgt} and P{tgt}^{max} onto the target image plane to generate an initial F{tgt} and D{tgt}^{max}. 5. Iterate Tiles: For each tile t in the target frame: a. Count the number of valid (non-missing) pixels N in F{tgt} for tile t. b. If N > N0: i. Interpolate the missing pixels in F{tgt} for tile t. ii. Mark these interpolated pixels as "blank" (masked) to prevent error accumulation in subsequent frames. c. Else (N \le N0): i. Re-render the entire tile t to ensure visual fidelity. ii. Update D{tgt}^{max} for the tile using the maximum of the current D{tgt}^{max} and the newly rendered depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tilewarpingsparserendering(Fref, Dref, Drefmax, Vref, Vtgt, N0, n): """ Performs Tile Warping-based Sparse Rendering. Args: Fref: Reference frame image buffer. Dref: Reference depth map. Drefmax: Reference truncated depth map. Vref: Reference camera viewpoint. Vtgt: Target camera viewpoint. N0: Threshold for missing pixels. n: Warping window size (frames between full renders). Returns: Ftgt: Target frame image buffer. Dtgtmax: Target truncated depth map. """ # Step 1: Initialize output structures Ftgt = InitializeEmptyFrame() Dtgtmax = InitializeEmptyDepthMap() # Step 2: Back-project reference frame to 3D # ProjectTo3D uses camera intrinsic parameters (implied by Vref) # and depth maps to create 3D points. Pref, Prefmax = ProjectTo3D(Fref, Dref, Drefmax, Vref) # Step 3: Transform 3D points to target view # ViewTransfer applies the transformation from Vref to Vtgt Ptgt, Ptgtmax = ViewTransfer(Pref, Prefmax, Vref, Vtgt) # Step 4: Reproject to target image plane # This creates a preliminary target frame based on warped geometry Ftgt, Dtgt = Reproject(Ptgt, Ptgtmax, Vtgt) # Step 5: Process each tile T = GetTiles(Ftgt) # Get list of all tiles in the image for t in T: # Count valid (non-missing) pixels in the current tile of Ftgt # Missing pixels are those where the reprojection failed or depth was invalid N = CountValidPixels(Ftgt, t) if N > N0: # Too many missing pixels: Re-render the tile # This ensures high visual fidelity for regions with significant occlusion/view change ReRenderTile(Ftgt, t, Vtgt) # Update truncated depth map for this tile # Use max to preserve depth bounds Dtgtmax[t] = Max(Dtgtmax[t], GetDepthForTile(t)) else: # Few missing pixels: Interpolate # Interpolate missing pixels in Ftgt for tile t InterpolateTile(Ftgt, t) # Masking mechanism: Treat interpolated pixels as "blank" # This prevents them from contributing to future warping steps # to mitigate accumulation of interpolation errors MaskInterpolatedPixels(Ftgt, t) return Ftgt, Dtgtmax def ProjectTo3D(F, D, Dmax, V): """ Back-projects pixels from a 2D frame into 3D space. Returns 3D points and truncated 3D points. """ points3d = [] points3dmax = [] for each pixel (u, v) in F: depth = D[u, v] depthmax = Dmax[u, v] if depth is valid: # Convert pixel coordinates and depth to 3D using camera pose V p = InverseProject(u, v, depth, V) points3d.append(p) pmax = InverseProject(u, v, depthmax, V) points3dmax.append(pmax) return points3d, points3dmax def ViewTransfer(Pref, Prefmax, Vref, Vtgt): """ Transforms 3D points from reference view to target view. """ Ptgt = [] Ptgtmax = [] for p in Pref: # Transform point p from Vref coordinate system to Vtgt ptgt = TransformPoint(p, Vref, Vtgt) Ptgt.append(ptgt) for pmax in Prefmax: ptgtmax = TransformPoint(pmax, Vref, Vtgt) Ptgtmax.append(ptgtmax) return Ptgt, Ptgtmax def Reproject(P, Pmax, V): """ Projects 3D points back to 2D image plane. """ Fout = InitializeEmptyFrame() Dout = InitializeEmptyDepthMap() for p in P: u, v = ProjectPoint(p, V) if u, v are within image bounds: Fout[u, v] = GetColorFromPoint(p) # Color from reference frame Dout[u, v] = GetDepthFromPoint(p) # Note: Pmax is used to determine valid depth ranges, # but the primary output is the color frame Ftgt return Fout, Dout def CountValidPixels(F, t): """ Counts pixels in tile t that are not missing/invalid. """ count = 0 for pixel in t: if F[pixel] is not missing: count += 1 return count def ReRenderTile(F, t, V): """ Fully renders tile t using 3DGS rasterization. """ # Standard 3DGS rasterization for the tile RenderTile3DGS(t, V) def InterpolateTile(F, t): """ Interpolates missing pixels in tile t. """ for pixel in t: if F[pixel] is missing: F[pixel] = InterpolateNeighbors(pixel, F) def MaskInterpolatedPixels(F, t): """ Marks interpolated pixels as blank for future warping. """ for pixel in t: if F[pixel] was interpolated: F[pixel] = BLANK def GetDepthForTile(t): """ Returns the depth values for the newly rendered tile. """ return GetCurrentDepth(t) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Accumulation of Interpolation Errors: Repeated viewpoint transformations without re-rendering degrade image quality over time. This is mitigated by the masking mechanism, where interpolated pixels are treated as "blank" in subsequent projections, forcing re-rendering in areas with high error accumulation. Depth Estimation Errors: Unlike NeRF, 3DGS estimates depth in real-time by computing an opacity-weighted sum over the depths of contributing Gaussians. This introduces minor errors that can be amplified in regions with limited pixel reuse, causing projected pixel positions to deviate from actual results. Tile Preprocessing Overhead: In 3DGS, preprocessing and sorting cannot be skipped unless no pixel within a tile requires rendering. TWSR avoids this overhead for tiles with few missing pixels by interpolating them, whereas pixel-based methods still incur this cost if any pixel in the tile is missing. Time Complexity: Reduces computational load by skipping rasterization, preprocessing, and sorting for tiles with few missing pixels. The speedup increases with the warping window size n, but quality degrades. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for reference frames, depth maps, and point clouds. The masking mechanism adds minimal overhead. Measured Performance: On Synthetic-NeRF dataset: TWSR average SSIM loss 0.005, PSNR loss 1.4 dB. Potamoi SSIM loss 0.063, PSNR loss 6.8 dB. On Jetson AGX Orin: LS-Gaussian (using TWSR) achieves 1.85x speedup over AdR-Gaussian and 1.75x over SeeLe. On Deep Blending dataset: LS-Gaussian achieves 5.41x speedup over GPU baseline, satisfying 90 FPS real-time rendering. Scaling: Indoor scenes with flattened structures and uniform color patterns achieve better rendering quality and higher speedups compared to outdoor scenes with more edges and corners. Strengths: Avoids floating pixels and artifacts caused by pixel-based inpainting; bypasses preprocessing and sorting for interpolated tiles; balances efficiency and image quality via masking. Limitations: Quality degrades with larger warping window sizes n; sensitive to depth estimation errors; indoor scenes perform better than outdoor scenes. When to Use: Real-time rendering on edge devices (e.g., Jetson AGX Orin) where computational resources are limited and scene geometry is relatively stable (e.g., indoor environments). When Not to Use: Scenes with high dynamic range, large viewpoint changes, or complex geometry where interpolation errors accumulate rapidly. Tile Warping-based Sparse Rendering (TWSR) was proposed in the paper "No Redundancy, No Stall: Lightweight Streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-time Rendering". It addresses the limitations of existing pixel warping-based sparse rendering (PWSR) methods like Potamoi, which conflict with the 3DGS tile-based architecture. The method was developed to enable real-time rendering on edge devices such as the Jetson AGX Orin. name: Chunked Volume Rendering

body: Chunked Volume Rendering is a memory-efficient inference technique that integrates color and density along rays by processing sampled points in fixed-size batches (chunks). It solves the GPU memory bottleneck associated with rendering large scenes or high-resolution implicit fields by allowing a trade-off between memory usage and computational throughput. It differs from its parent Inference Ray Marching and Integration by explicitly batching the forward pass to constrain VRAM, and from its sibling Inference Ray Compositing by focusing on the chunked accumulation of radiance rather than just the compositing logic. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A raybundle containing origins [B, 3], directions [B, 3], and pre-sampled 3D points [B, N, 3]; an implicit function implicitfn to query density and features; a sampler to generate points; and configuration parameters (chunksize, raymarchingtolerance, whitebackground). Output: A dictionary containing feature (rendered color, shape [B, 3]) and depth (rendered depth, shape [B, 1]). Data Structures: chunkfeatures: List of tensors storing rendered features for each chunk. chunkdepths: List of tensors storing rendered depths for each chunk. accumulatedfreeenergy: Tensor tracking the cumulative free energy (opacity) for early stopping. Parameters: chunksize: Number of rays processed per iteration. Default is 65,536 (1024 64) for training, or chunksize // 1024 for inference. raymarchingtolerance: Threshold for early stopping. If > 0, rays terminate when accumulated free energy exceeds -log(tolerance). whitebackground: Boolean. If True, background is white; otherwise black. Formulas: 1. Segment Lengths (Deltas): \delta = [d2-d1, \dots, dn-d{n-1}, 10^{10}] where di are the distances of sample points from the origin. The last delta is set to a large value to ensure termination. 2. Hit and Empty Probabilities: Let ft be the "free energy" (density \times delta) at step t. at = 1 - \exp(-ft) \quad \text{(Probability of hit at step } t \text{)} bt = \exp\left(-\sum{k=0}^{t-1} fk\right) \quad \text{(Probability of empty space up to step } t \text{)} \text{probs}t = at \times bt 3. Rendering: \text{color} = \sumt \text{texture}t \times \text{probs}t \text{depth} = \sumt \text{sampled\depth}t \times \text{probs}t \text{missed} = 1 - \sumt \text{probs}t Algorithm: 1. Initialize accumulatedfreeenergy to zeros, chunkfeatures and chunkdepths to empty lists. 2. Determine total rays N. Iterate chunkstart from 0 to N with step chunksize. 3. Slice raybundle for the current chunk: curraybundle = raybundle[chunkstart: chunkstart + chunksize]. 4. Call the parent forward method (or forwardonce) with curraybundle to get curfeature and curdepth. Note: If the implementation uses explicit accumulation within the chunk loop (as in), iterate through sample indices i. Compute weights wt = \text{probs}t. Update accumulatedfreeenergy. The logic for early stopping is: if raymarchingtolerance > 0, maintain a running sum of freeenergy. If the sum exceeds -log(raymarchingtolerance), set alpha to 0 for all subsequent steps for that ray. 5. Append curfeature to chunkfeatures and curdepth to chunkdepths. 6. Concatenate all chunks: \text{feature} = \text{cat}(chunk\features, \text{dim}=0) \text{depth} = \text{cat}(chunk\depths, \text{dim}=0) 7. If whitebackground is True, add (1 - missed) 1.0 to color. 8. Return feature and depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def chunkedvolumerender(raybundle, implicitfn, sampler, chunksize=65536, raymarchingtolerance=0.0, whitebackground=False): # raybundle: dict with 'origins' [B, 3], 'directions' [B, 3], 'points' [B, N, 3] # Returns: feature [B, 3], depth [B, 1] B = raybundle['origins'].shape[0] chunkfeatures = [] chunkdepths = [] # Handle edge case: no rays if B == 0: return torch.zeros((0, 3)), torch.zeros((0, 1)) for chunkstart in range(0, B, chunksize): # Slice current chunk endidx = min(chunkstart + chunksize, B) curraybundle = { 'origins': raybundle['origins'][chunkstart:endidx], 'directions': raybundle['directions'][chunkstart:endidx], 'points': raybundle['points'][chunkstart:endidx] } # Sample points if not provided, or use provided points # Assuming sampler returns points [Bchunk, N, 3] points = sampler(curraybundle) # Compute deltas: distances from origin, then differences, then large final delta dists = torch.sqrt(((points - curraybundle['origins'].unsqueeze(1)) 2).sum(dim=-1)) # [Bchunk, N] diffs = dists[:, 1:] - dists[:,:-1] # [Bchunk, N-1] largedelta = torch.oneslike(diffs[:,:1]) 1e10 deltas = torch.cat([diffs, largedelta], dim=1) # [Bchunk, N] # Query implicit function for density and color # density [Bchunk, N, 1], color [Bchunk, N, 3] density, color = implicitfn(points) # Compute probabilities # freeenergy = density deltas freeenergy = density.squeeze(-1) deltas # [Bchunk, N] # Shifted free energy for transmittance # bt = exp(-cumsum(shiftedfreeenergy)) shiftedfreeenergy = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(freeenergy[:,:1]), freeenergy[:,:-1]], dim=1) transmittance = torch.exp(-torch.cumsum(shiftedfreeenergy, dim=1)) # Alpha and weights alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-freeenergy) weights = alpha transmittance # Early stopping logic per if raymarchingtolerance > 0: cumfreeenergy = torch.cumsum(freeenergy, dim=1) earlystopmask = cumfreeenergy > -math.log(raymarchingtolerance) # Zero out weights for steps after early stop weights = weights (~earlystopmask).float() # Render Color and Depth # color = sum(weights color) renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=1) # depth = sum(weights depthsamples) # depthsamples are distances of points from origin depthsamples = dists # [Bchunk, N] rendereddepth = torch.sum(weights depthsamples, dim=1) # Missed probability missed = 1.0 - torch.sum(weights, dim=1) # Apply background if whitebackground: renderedcolor = renderedcolor + (1.0 - missed.unsqueeze(-1)) 1.0 else: renderedcolor = renderedcolor # Black background (0) chunkfeatures.append(renderedcolor) chunkdepths.append(rendereddepth.unsqueeze(-1)) # Concatenate results finalfeature = torch.cat(chunkfeatures, dim=0) finaldepth = torch.cat(chunkdepths, dim=0) return finalfeature, finaldepth The pseudocode above implements the standard NeRF-style integration. The source mentions an accumulatedfreeenergy variable used for early stopping within a loop over samples. The logic for early stopping is: if raymarchingtolerance > 0, maintain a running sum of freeenergy. If the sum exceeds -log(raymarchingtolerance), set alpha to 0 for all subsequent steps for that ray. This is implemented as a vectorized mask in the pseudocode for efficiency, matching the source's intent. This method accelerates volume rendering by combining chunked ray batching with an occupancy grid estimator to sample along rays, query a radiance field for density and color at sample midpoints, and composite the result per chunk. It differs from its parent Chunked Volume Rendering by integrating a hierarchical occupancy grid for adaptive sampling, and from its sibling Block-based Volume Rendering Strategy by using a continuous grid-based estimator rather than discrete block structures. Partitioned Volume Rendering Derivation provides the mathematical foundation for distributing volumetric rendering across multiple disjoint spatial segments (partitions) along a ray. It solves the problem of correctly accumulating color, transmittance, and auxiliary losses (such as distortion) when a ray traverses multiple independent volume tiles, which may be processed by different compute units. It sets itself apart from standard single-volume ray marching by explicitly decomposing global integrals into sums of local segment integrals weighted by upstream transmittance, enabling parallel prefix-scan accumulation. A rendering strategy for large scenes partitioned into blocks, where each block uses a separate shader due to web texture unit limits. It solves the problem where standard volume rendering fails because sampling points across a ray may belong to different blocks loaded by different shaders, breaking 3D consistency and correct occlusion. It differs from Chunked Volume Rendering with Occupancy Grid Estimator by using sequential block rendering with separate shaders rather than occupancy grids to skip empty space, and from Partitioned Volume Rendering Derivation by enforcing strict back-to-front sorting and post-hoc accumulation. Opt-in tricubic B-spline reconstruction fixes texel staircase artifacts but does not remove ringing. It requires a 2-voxel halo. Implementation involves chunking.ts defining LINEARMINHALO / CUBICMINHALO / planSupportsHalo / planSupportsCubic, and NVChunkedVolume.raiseHaloTo() re-planning loaded volumes when the setter fires. Both views gate cubic per draw on halo >= 2 and not-a-label-volume (including coarse-floor cube). The volumeIsCubicInterpolation boolean defaults to off and is available on both backends. The public default halo stays [1,1,1]. Fixes WebGL2 volume blanking when chunk 0 is evicted, caused by draw() early-returning on null volumeTexture/volumeGradientTexture which were best-effort aliases of chunk 0. The fix removes the early-return on null textures for chunked volumes. It fixes swapChunkedVolumePlan to refresh aliases after manager.remap() destroys unmatched chunks. It also fixes switching from chunked to single volume to prevent the single-volume path from deleting textures the chunked cache entry still owns. Hacks the Material of the Heterogeneous Volume Actor (HVA) to extend the single SVT evaluation to select and sample from four different chunks, feeding the internal lighting cache with values from all chunks to create seamless rendering. Uses an SVT of full resolution spanning the volume with values only at min/max corners to trick the HVA into believing it has one volume of a certain resolution, while sampling four payload chunks as if they were one texture. Compensates for heavy performance impact (~1fps) by allowing interactive navigation with fewer samples per ray march (e.g., 32) and rendering with more samples (e.g., 512) when an interesting view is found. Controlled via console command r.HeterogeneousVolumes.MaxStepCount=32. This workaround results in a heavy performance hit, dropping framerates to ~1fps, and requires a complicated chunking/importing setup and custom material. A rendering method that renders at the estimated intersection point of the ray with the surface, rather than integrating along the entire ray. Computes normalized probabilities by clamping min 1e-6 and masking out non-hit voxels. Determines voxel index at intersection by counting how many boundaries are less than or equal to ndepth. Gathers the voxel index at the intersection depth. Calls forwardonce with new samples to get texture and normal at the intersection. Intersection depth: \text{n\depth} = \frac{\sumt \text{sampled\depth}t \times \text{n\probs}t}{\sumt \text{n\probs}t}. Boundary depth: \text{n\bound} = \text{sampled\depth} + \frac{\text{sampled\distance}}{2}. Rendered color: \text{color} = \text{texture} \times (1 - \text{missed}). Eikonal term for surface rendering: \text{eikonal} = (\|\text{normal}\|2 - 1)^2. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot B), where N is the number of samples per ray and B is the number of rays. Chunking does not change the asymptotic complexity but increases overhead due to loop iterations. Memory Complexity: O(B{chunk} \cdot N), where B{chunk} is the chunksize. This allows rendering scenes with B \gg B{chunk} by trading memory for time. Performance: In Unreal Engine, chunking allows rendering datasets >1 gigavoxel, but introduces visual artifacts at chunk borders if lighting is computed independently per chunk. A workaround using a "4-in-1" material can achieve seamless lighting but drops framerates to ~1fps. Strengths: Enables rendering of very large scenes or high-resolution implicit fields on GPUs with limited VRAM. Limitations: Chunking can introduce artifacts if not handled correctly (e.g., lighting discontinuities). Early stopping requires careful tolerance tuning to avoid premature termination. Chunked Volume Rendering is based on the volume rendering equations defined in [Mildenhall et al. 2020] (NeRF). It has been implemented in various contexts, including the TBRayMarcher plugin for Unreal Engine, the NSVF framework by Facebook Research, and web-based viewers like Niivue. The technique is essential for real-time inference of large neural radiance fields and volumetric datasets. head: OccGrid Estimator Rendering Loop, OccGridEstimator Rendering
body: This method accelerates volume rendering by combining chunked ray batching with an OccGridEstimator to sample along rays, query a radiance field for density and color at sample midpoints, and composite the result per chunk. It differs from its parent Chunked Volume Rendering by integrating a hierarchical occupancy grid for adaptive sampling, and from its sibling Block-based Volume Rendering Strategy by using a continuous grid-based estimator rather than discrete block structures. Inputs: Ray origins: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) or (N, 3). View directions: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) or (N, 3). Radiance field: Object with querydensity(positions) and querycolor(positions) methods. OccGridEstimator: Object with sampling(...) method. Parameters: nearplane, farplane, renderstepsize, alphathre, coneangle, testchunksize. Outputs: RGB image: Shape (H, W, 3). Depth image: Shape (H, W). Opacity image: Shape (H, W). Extras: Additional per-sample data. Data Structures: RaySamples: Contains vals (flattened sample data), rayindices (mapping samples to rays), and packedinfo (chunk boundaries). OccGrid: Hierarchical grid storing occupancy probabilities, updated via exponential moving average. Steps: 1. Reshape Rays: If ray origins and directions are 3D tensors of shape (H, W, 3), reshape them to 2D tensors of shape (N, 3) where N = H \times W. Store the original shape for final reshaping. 2. Chunking: Divide the N rays into chunks of size testchunksize. If in training mode, use max(int32) to process all rays at once. 3. Define Density Function: For each chunk, define a function sigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices) that calculates sample midpoints: pos = origins[ray\indices] + dirs[ray\indices] \times \frac{t\starts + t\ends}{2.0}, and queries the radiance field for density: \sigma = radiance\field.query\density(pos). If temporal scenes are supported, pass timestamps to the query. 4. Sampling: Call estimator.sampling(sigmafn, nearplane, farplane, renderstepsize, stratified, coneangle, alphathre). This returns rayindices, tstarts, and tends. 5. Rendering: Call the rendering composite function with tstarts, tends, rayindices, nrays, and a combined function rgbsigmafn (which queries both color and density). This returns rgb, opacity, depth, and extras for the chunk. 6. Concatenation: Concatenate results from all chunks along dimension 0. 7. Reshape: Reshape the concatenated results back to the original image dimensions (H, W, 3) for RGB, (H, W) for depth/opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def renderimagewithoccgridtest( radiancefield, estimator, origins, viewdirs, nearplane=0.0, farplane=1e10, renderstepsize=1e-3, alphathre=0.0, coneangle=0.0, testchunksize=8192, istraining=False): # 1. Reshape rays if origins.dim() == 3: raysshape = origins.shape[:-1] origins = origins.view(-1, 3) viewdirs = viewdirs.view(-1, 3) else: raysshape = (origins.shape[0],) origins = origins.view(-1, 3) viewdirs = viewdirs.view(-1, 3) nrays = origins.shape[0] # 2. Chunking chunksize = 231 - 1 if istraining else testchunksize allrgb = [] alldepth = [] allopacity = [] allextras = [] for i in range(0, nrays, chunksize): chunkend = min(i + chunksize, nrays) chunkorigins = origins[i:chunkend] chunkdirs = viewdirs[i:chunkend] # 3. Define sigmafn for this chunk def sigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices): midpoints = chunkorigins[rayindices] + chunkdirs[rayindices] (tstarts + tends) / 2.0 densities = radiancefield.querydensity(midpoints) return densities # 4. Sampling rayindices, tstarts, tends = estimator.sampling( sigmafn=sigmafn, nearplane=nearplane, farplane=farplane, renderstepsize=renderstepsize, stratified=True, coneangle=coneangle, alphathre=alphathre) # 5. Rendering (explicit front-to-back volume compositing) def rgbsigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices): midpoints = chunkorigins[rayindices] + chunkdirs[rayindices] (tstarts + tends) / 2.0 densities = radiancefield.querydensity(midpoints) colors = radiancefield.querycolor(midpoints) return colors, densities nsamples = len(tstarts) chunkraycount = chunkend - i chunkrgb = torch.zeros(chunkraycount, 3, device=origins.device) chunkopacity = torch.zeros(chunkraycount, device=origins.device) chunkdepth = torch.zeros(chunkraycount, device=origins.device) # Sort samples by tstarts for each ray in the chunk sortedindices = torch.argsort(tstarts) tstartss = tstarts[sortedindices] tendss = tends[sortedindices] rayidxs = rayindices[sortedindices] colorss, densitiess = rgbsigmafn(tstartss, tendss, rayidxs) alphass = 1.0 - torch.exp(-densitiess (tendss - tstartss)) transmittances = torch.ones(chunkraycount, device=origins.device) for k in range(nsamples): r = rayidxs[k] alpha = alphass[k] transmittances[r] = (1.0 - alpha) chunkrgb[r] += colorss[k] alpha transmittances[r] chunkopacity[r] += alpha transmittances[r] chunkdepth[r] += tstartss[k] alpha transmittances[r] chunkdepth = torch.where(chunkopacity > 0, chunkdepth / chunkopacity, chunkdepth) allrgb.append(chunkrgb) alldepth.append(chunkdepth) allopacity.append(chunkopacity) allextras.append({}) # 6. Concatenation finalrgb = torch.cat(allrgb, dim=0) finaldepth = torch.cat(alldepth, dim=0) finalopacity = torch.cat(allopacity, dim=0) # 7. Reshape finalrgb = finalrgb.view(raysshape, 3) finaldepth = finaldepth.view(raysshape) finalopacity = finalopacity.view(raysshape) return finalrgb, finaldepth, finalopacity, allextras Parameters: nearplane: Float, default 0.0. Minimum distance for ray marching. farplane: Float, default 1e10. Maximum distance for ray marching. renderstepsize: Float, default 1e-3. Base step size for sampling. alphathre: Float, default 0.0. Alpha threshold for filtering samples. coneangle: Float, default 0.0. Cone angle for adaptive sampling. testchunksize: Int, default 8192. Number of rays per chunk during inference. name: Partitioned Volume Rendering Derivation
head: Distributed Volume Rendering Equations
body: Partitioned Volume Rendering Derivation provides the mathematical foundation for distributing volumetric rendering across multiple disjoint spatial segments (partitions) along a ray. It solves the problem of correctly accumulating color, transmittance, and auxiliary losses (such as distortion) when a ray traverses multiple independent volume tiles, which may be processed by different compute units. It sets itself apart from standard single-volume ray marching by explicitly decomposing global integrals into sums of local segment integrals weighted by upstream transmittance, enabling parallel prefix-scan accumulation. The method relies on decomposing the continuous volume rendering integral into discrete segments [tk, t{k+1}] defined by the boundaries of spatial partitions. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin o, direction d, and a set of N partition boundaries t1, t2, \dots, t{N+1} along the ray parameter t. For each segment k, the local density \sigma(t) and color c(t) are available. Outputs: Global accumulated color C(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}), global distortion loss \mathcal{L}{dist}(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}), and intermediate terms required for parallel reduction. Data Structures The derivation assumes the ray is divided into N segments. Each segment k corresponds to a spatial tile. The key intermediate values computed per segment are: A(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}): Accumulated weight (alpha) within the segment. D(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}): Accumulated depth-weight within the segment. T(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}): Transmittance through the segment. Formulas Let w(t) = T(t1 \rightarrow t) \sigma(t) be the contribution weight at t. The standard volume rendering equation for color is: C(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}) = \int{t1}^{t{N+1}} w(t) c(t) dt This is decomposed into a sum over N segments: C(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}) = \sum{k=1}^N T(t1 \rightarrow tk) C(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}) where the local segment color is: C(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}) = \int{tk}^{t{k+1}} T(tk \rightarrow t) \sigma(t) c(t) dt Here, T(t1 \rightarrow tk) is the transmittance from the ray origin to the start of segment k, acting as a weight for the local result. For distortion loss, we define the accumulated weight A and accumulated depth D over an interval [ta, tb] as: A(ta \rightarrow tb) = \int{ta}^{tb} w(t) dt D(ta \rightarrow tb) = \int{ta}^{tb} w(t) t dt The global distortion loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{dist}(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}) = 2 \int{t1}^{t{N+1}} w(t) \left( t - \frac{D(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1})}{A(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1})} \right) A(t1 \rightarrow t) dt The derivation shows this global loss can be computed from local segment losses using an intermediate term S: S(t1 \rightarrow tk) = D(tk \rightarrow t{k+1})A(t1 \rightarrow tk) - A(tk \rightarrow t{k+1})D(t1 \rightarrow tk) The final decomposed distortion loss is: \mathcal{L}{dist}(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}) = 2 \sum{k=1}^N T(t1 \rightarrow tk) S(t1 \rightarrow tk) + \sum{k=1}^N T(t1 \rightarrow tk)^2 \mathcal{L}{dist}(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}) where \mathcal{L}{dist}(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}) is the local distortion loss within segment k. Parameters N: The number of segments (partitions) along the ray, corresponding to the number of tiles the ray intersects. It assumes localA[k], localD[k], localC[k], and localLdist[k] are computed independently for each segment k \in [0, N-1]. Unverified code. Accumulate Color globalcolor += Tprefix Clocal # 2. Compute Intermediate Term S S = Dlocal Aprefix - Alocal Dprefix # 3. Accumulate Distortion Loss term1 = 2.0 Tprefix S term2 = (Tprefix 2) Ldistlocal globaldistloss += term1 + term2 # Update prefix sums for next segment Aprefix += Alocal Dprefix += Dlocal Tprefix = Tlocal return globalcolor, globaldistloss Performs volumetric rendering over a partition of possible t values in the union of rendering volumes, combining results from disjoint volume integrals and a void model for empty space. It sets itself apart from standard single-volume ray marching by explicitly handling multiple disjoint volume bounds and accumulating transmittance across partitions, ensuring correct alpha compositing when rays traverse empty space between volumes. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of segments N for the accumulation step, assuming local segment computations are parallelized. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate A, D, C, L{dist} for each segment. The memory footprint scales with N and the number of rays. Strengths: Enables efficient distribution of rendering work across multiple GPUs by minimizing communication (only per-ray aggregates need reduction). Limitations: Requires precise spatial partitioning to ensure correct transmittance accumulation across disjoint volume bounds. When to use: Large-scale NeRF training/inference where a single GPU cannot hold the volume or process all rays efficiently. The derivation originates from NeRF-XL, which scales NeRFs with multiple GPUs. It builds on the spatial partitioning scheme described in Appendix A.3, where space is divided recursively using CDF-based splitting to create nearly cubic partitions. The method allows distributed NeRFs to compute global integrals from local segment results, facilitating batched asynchronous send/receive operations and parallel prefix scans. name: Partitioned Volumetric Rendering with RayVolumeIntegral
head: Partitioned Volumetric Rendering
body: Partitioned Volumetric Rendering with RayVolumeIntegral performs volumetric rendering over a partition of possible t values in the union of rendering volumes, combining results from disjoint volume integrals and a void model for empty space. It sets itself apart from standard single-volume ray marching by explicitly handling multiple disjoint volume bounds and accumulating transmittance across partitions, ensuring correct alpha compositing when rays traverse empty space between volumes. It builds on Partitioned Volume Rendering Derivation. Inputs: rays: Tuple containing ray origins and directions. resultsi: Sequence of RayVolumeIntegralResults objects, each containing volumerange (start/end t), raw (raw network outputs), and transmittance. voidmodel: Function or model that queries background color/transmittance for empty space. importancesamplingoptions: Configuration dictionary for the sampler. Outputs: results: Combined RayVolumeIntegralResults object containing the final rendered channels and transmittance. RayVolumeIntegral: Dataclass holding the rendering configuration. Fields: model (NeRFModel), volume (Volume), sampler (RaySampler), nsamples (int). RayVolumeIntegralResults: Holds the state of integration for a specific volume partition. Fields: volumerange (defines t interval [t0, t1]), raw (raw outputs from the neural network), transmittance (scalar or tensor representing transmittance at the end of the interval), output (rendered channels). 1. Initialization: Initialize origin, direc from rays. Set prevrawoutputs to a list of Nones. Initialize samplers list, rawoutputs list, t0 to None, and results to None. 2. Loop over Volume Partitions: For each resultsi in the sequence of volume results: a. Sampler Creation: Create an ImportanceRaySampler using resultsi.volumerange, resultsi.raw, and importancesamplingoptions. Append this sampler to samplers. b. Raw Output Storage: Append resultsi.raw to rawoutputs. c. Update Start Time: Update t0 to resultsi.volumerange.nextt0(). d. Combine Results: If results is None, set results = resultsi. Otherwise, update results by combining it with resultsi using the partitioned combination rule. 3. Void Background Addition: After the loop, add the void background to the final result: \text{results.output.channels} = \text{results.output.channels} + \text{results.transmittance} \cdot \text{void\model}(\text{Query}(origin, direc)). This method handles the sampling and integration for a single volume partition defined by self.volume. 1. Intersection and Sampling: Intersect rays with the volume: vrange = self.volume.intersect(origin, direction, t0lower=t0). Sample t values: ts = self.sampler.sample(vrange.t0, vrange.t1, self.nsamples). 2. Position and Interval Calculation: Compute sample positions: positions = origin.unsqueeze(-2) + ts[..., None] directions. Compute midpoints: mids = (ts[..., 1:] + ts[...,:-1]) / 2. 3. Model Query: Query the neural network model with positions, optional directions, and interval bounds: python tmin = torch.cat([vrange.t0[..., None,:], mids], dim=-2) tmax = torch.cat([mids, vrange.t1[..., None,:]], dim=-2) raw = Query(position=positions, direction=optionaldirections, tmin=tmin, tmax=tmax). 4. Integration: Call self.integratesamples(vrange, raw) to obtain output and transmittance. 5. Masking Non-Intersected Rays: Mask transmittance: transmittance = torch.where(vrange.intersected, transmittance, torch.oneslike(transmittance)). Mask output tensors: output = output.map(mapfn=maskfn, shouldmap=istensor) where maskfn returns torch.where(vrange.intersected, tensor, torch.zeroslike(tensor)). This method computes the discrete volume integral approximation. 1. Density and Transmittance Calculation: Calculate interval lengths: dt = volumerange.partition(raw.ts). Compute optical depth increments: ddensity = raw.density dt. Compute cumulative optical depth: mass = torch.cumsum(ddensity, dim=-2). Compute final transmittance: transmittance = torch.exp(-mass[..., -1,:]). Compute per-sample alphas: alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-ddensity). Compute per-sample transmittances Ts: Ts = \exp\left(\text{cat}([0, -\text{mass}[...,:-1,:]], \text{dim}=-2)\right). Compute weights: weights = alphas Ts. 2. Weighted Summation: Integrate using integrate(key, samples, weights) which returns torch.sum(samples weights, dim=-2) for keys other than 'density'. Handle auxiliary losses with detached weights if noweightgradauxlosses is enabled: use weights.detach(). When combining results from disjoint volume partitions [t0, t1] and [t1, t2], the integral over [t0, t2] is the sum of the integral over [t0, t1] and the transmittance at t1 times the integral over [t1, t2]: \int{t0}^{t2} = \int{t0}^{t1} + \text{transmittance}(t1) \cdot \int{t1}^{t2} Implemented as: prevval + prevtransmittance curval. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch class RawOutput: def init(self, channels): self.channels = channels class RayVolumeIntegralResults: def init(self, volumerange, raw, transmittance, output): self.volumerange = volumerange self.raw = raw self.transmittance = transmittance self.output = output def combine(self, other): # prevval + prevtransmittance curval combinedchannels = self.output.channels + self.transmittance other.output.channels combinedtransmittance = self.transmittance other.transmittance return RayVolumeIntegralResults( volumerange=other.volumerange, raw=other.raw, transmittance=combinedtransmittance, output=RawOutput(channels=combinedchannels)) class ImportanceRaySampler: def init(self, volumerange, raw, options): self.volumerange = volumerange self.raw = raw self.options = options def sample(self, t0, t1, nsamples): # Standard uniform sampling across the interval ts = torch.linspace(t0, t1, nsamples + 1, device=t0.device) return ts class Query: def init(self, position, direction, tmin, tmax): self.position = position self.direction = direction self.tmin = tmin self.tmax = tmax def QueryModel(position, direction, tmin, tmax): # Standard neural network forward pass for volumetric properties # Returns dict with 'density' and other channels pass def renderpartitionedvolumes(rays, volumeresultslist, voidmodel, cfg): origins, directions = rays prevrawoutputs = [None] len(volumeresultslist) samplers = [] rawoutputs = [] t0 = None results = None for resultsi in volumeresultslist: sampler = ImportanceRaySampler( volumerange=resultsi.volumerange, raw=resultsi.raw, options=cfg.importancesamplingoptions) samplers.append(sampler) rawoutputs.append(resultsi.raw) t0 = resultsi.volumerange.nextt0() if results is None: results = resultsi else: results = results.combine(resultsi) voidcolor = voidmodel(Query(origins, directions, None, None)) results.output.channels = results.output.channels + results.transmittance voidcolor return results def integratesamples(vrange, raw): ts = raw.ts t0 = vrange.t0 t1 = vrange.t1 # Handle non-intersected rays early to prevent shape/dimension errors if not vrange.intersected.any(): transmittance = torch.oneslike(vrange.intersected, dtype=raw.density.dtype) output = RawOutput(channels={k: torch.zeroslike(raw[k]) for k in raw.keys() if k != 'density'}) return output, transmittance # ts are boundaries, shape (..., nsamples + 1) dt = torch.diff(ts, dim=-2) ddensity = raw.density dt mass = torch.cumsum(ddensity, dim=-2) transmittance = torch.exp(-mass[..., -1,:]) alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-ddensity) Ts = torch.exp(torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(mass[...,:1,:]), -mass[...,:-1,:]], dim=-2)) weights = alphas Ts outputchannels = {} for key in raw.keys(): if key == 'density': continue samples = raw[key] integrated = torch.sum(samples weights, dim=-2) outputchannels[key] = integrated output = RawOutput(channels=outputchannels) # Mask non-intersected rays transmittance = torch.where(vrange.intersected, transmittance, torch.oneslike(transmittance)) for key in outputchannels: outputchannels[key] = torch.where(vrange.intersected, outputchannels[key], torch.zeroslike(outputchannels[key])) output = RawOutput(channels=outputchannels) return output, transmittance nsamples: Number of samples per ray segment. Not given in the sources. importancesamplingoptions: Configuration for sampling strategy. Not given in the sources. voidmodel: Background color model. Typically a constant color or a skybox. Not given in the sources. Non-Intersected Rays: Rays that do not intersect the volume must have their transmittance set to 1.0 and output set to 0.0 before combining with the void background. Precision: Cumulative sum of optical depth (mass) can suffer from precision issues for very long rays or high densities. Boundary Conditions: The calculation of dt and Ts requires careful handling of the first and last sample intervals to ensure they align with vrange.t0 and vrange.t1. Time: Linear in the number of samples per ray and the number of volume partitions. Each partition requires a forward pass through the neural network and an integration step. Memory: Proportional to the number of samples and the number of channels stored in raw outputs. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Scales with the number of disjoint volumes. Each volume requires separate intersection, sampling, and integration steps. Strengths: Correctly handles multiple disjoint volumes and empty space between them. Allows for importance sampling within each partition. Limitations: Requires explicit partitioning of the ray space. Performance depends on the number of partitions. Use when rendering scenes with multiple disjoint volumetric objects or when empty space between volumes needs to be explicitly modeled. Use standard ray marching for single, continuous volumes. The method is described in the gsgen repository. The method is part of the gsgen project, which integrates Gaussian Splatting and NeRF-like rendering techniques. The specific implementation of RayVolumeIntegral and partitioned rendering is found in the codebase. Used in the gsgen project for 3D generation from text or images, combining volumetric rendering with other 3D representations. gsgen3d/gsgen, https://github.com/gsgen3d/gsgen, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Block-based Volume Rendering Strategy
head: Multi-shader Block Accumulation, Sequential Block Rendering
body: A rendering strategy for large scenes partitioned into blocks, where each block uses a separate shader due to web texture unit limits. It solves the problem where standard volume rendering fails because sampling points across a ray may belong to different blocks loaded by different shaders, breaking 3D consistency and correct occlusion. It differs from Chunked Volume Rendering with Occupancy Grid Estimator by using sequential block rendering with separate shaders rather than occupancy grids to skip empty space, and from Partitioned Volume Rendering Derivation by enforcing strict back-to-front sorting and post-hoc accumulation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of M scene blocks, each associated with a dedicated shader instance containing its specific texture resources. Output: The final composite color Cr for the pixel. Data Structures: Block List: A list of M blocks, each containing a reference to its shader and its spatial position. Shader State: Each shader instance holds the texture units required to render its specific block. Steps: 1. Depth Sorting: Sort all M scene blocks relative to the camera viewpoint to determine the rendering order from back to front. 2. Sequential Rendering: Iterate through the sorted blocks. For each block k: Activate the dedicated shader for block k. Render the block to obtain its local color ck and opacity \alphak. Store ck and \alphak for accumulation. 3. Accumulation: Combine the results using the volume rendering equation: Cr = \sum{k=1}^{M} \left( \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj) \right) ck Where: Cr is the final composite color. M is the total number of blocks. ck is the color output by the shader for block k. \alphak is the opacity output by the shader for block k. The term \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj) represents the transmittance from all preceding blocks j < k. Parameters: Texture Unit Limit: Typically no more than 16 texture units can be loaded into a single web shader. This constraint necessitates the separation of blocks into different shaders. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Web Platform Limits: Web platforms limit texture units to ~16, preventing loading all block resources into a single shader. 3D Consistency: Using different shaders per block breaks standard volume rendering because sampling points across a ray may belong to different blocks/shaders. This method ensures correctness by rendering sequentially and combining results. Memory Usage: Loading all blocks for rendering is impractical due to excessive memory usage on standard consumer devices. Training Pipeline Consistency is a strategy to minimize the discrepancy between the training and inference phases of block-based volume rendering by enforcing the identical rendering pipeline during both stages. It solves the problem where training with a continuous, global coordinate system leads to artifacts or quality degradation when the model is deployed in a constrained, block-based rendering environment. It sets itself apart from standard neural rendering methods by explicitly simulating the discrete, hardware-bound constraints of the target rendering hardware (such as texture unit limits and quantization) during the optimization process. A memory-saving rendering strategy for high-resolution volumes that splits the spatial dimensions into overlapping patches, renders them independently, and merges the results to scale to arbitrary image resolutions. Unlike full-volume rendering which requires memory proportional to H \times W, the patch-based approach trades redundant computation in overlapping regions for drastically reduced memory footprint, enabling scaling to arbitrary resolutions. Builds on Block-based Volume Rendering Strategy by partitioning the spatial domain into smaller, independently processed regions. A rendering system that divides the volume into blocks, sorts them by distance from the camera, and renders only non-empty blocks using raycasting shaders. Blocks are sorted by distance from the camera eye in descending order (far to near). For each non-empty block with GPU resources, the world matrix is set, the block texture is bound, uniforms are configured, and a cube is drawn. Uniforms include top = b.worldDims(), bot = -top, mv = getViewMatrix() getWorldMatrix(), and normalMatrix = transpose(inverse(mv)). Sampler state is configured with GLTEXTUREMINFILTER = GLLINEAR, GLTEXTUREMAGFILTER = GLLINEAR, and GLTEXTUREWRAPS/T/R = GLCLAMPTOBORDER. The rendered geometry uses 8 vertices at the corners of a unit cube centered at origin: {-0.5,-0.5,0.5}, {0.5,-0.5,0.5}, {0.5,0.5,0.5}, {-0.5,0.5,0.5}, {-0.5,-0.5,-0.5}, {0.5,-0.5,-0.5}, {0.5,0.5,-0.5}, {-0.5,0.5,-0.5}. These are indexed by 36 indices forming 12 triangles (2 per face) for the front, right, back, left, top, and bottom faces. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of blocks M for the sorting and accumulation steps, plus the cost of rendering each block. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of active blocks loaded into shaders, constrained by the texture unit limit (typically 16). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Supports dynamic loading of resources via Level-of-Detail (LOD) generation to handle large scenes on consumer devices. Strengths: Enables rendering of large-scale scenes on web platforms with limited texture unit resources. Ensures correct occlusion and 3D consistency. Limitations: Requires sequential rendering, which may be slower than parallel approaches if not optimized. Limited by the number of texture units available per shader. When to use: When rendering large scenes on web platforms with strict texture unit limits. When not: When the target hardware supports loading all block resources into a single shader, eliminating the need for sequential accumulation. Originated in the "City-on-Web" paper. The method addresses challenges associated with resource-independent block-based rendering on the web, specifically the limitation on the number and resolution of texture units that can be loaded into a shader. It draws inspiration from traditional graphics techniques for Level-of-Detail (LOD) generation. name: Training Pipeline Consistency
head: Simulated finite grid approach, Training-time block rendering
body: Training Pipeline Consistency is a strategy to minimize the discrepancy between the training and inference phases of block-based volume rendering by enforcing the identical rendering pipeline during both stages. It solves the problem where training with a continuous, global coordinate system leads to artifacts or quality degradation when the model is deployed in a constrained, block-based rendering environment. It sets itself apart from standard neural rendering methods by explicitly simulating the discrete, hardware-bound constraints of the target rendering hardware (such as texture unit limits and quantization) during the optimization process. The method ensures that the data flow, sampling logic, and integration order during training are identical to those used in the final web-based rendering stage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray \boldsymbol{r}(t), scene bounding box, block partitioning parameters, proposal MLPs \psi^k, and attribute MLPs f^k for each block k. Output: Final rendered color and opacity for the ray. Data Structures: Blocks (Bk): The scene is partitioned into spatial blocks, each with an associated proposal MLP \psi^k and attribute MLP f^k. Ray Samples: Points sampled along the ray \boldsymbol{r}(t) between near and far boundaries. Numbered Steps: 1. Uniform Sampling: For a given ray \boldsymbol{r}(t), uniformly sample points between the near and far boundaries defined by the scene’s bounding box. 2. Block Determination: For each sample point, determine which block Bk it resides in using an xy-coordinate projection, referred to as Eq. (4) in the source. 3. Proposal Sampling: Query the proposal MLP \psi^k corresponding to the determined block Bk to sample probability distributions along the ray. 4. Attribute Querying: Query the attribute MLP f^k corresponding to block Bk to obtain the rendering attributes for the sample points. 5. Sequential Rendering: Render each block sequentially to obtain the color and opacity for the ray in Bk. 6. Final Composition: Use Eq. (5) to derive the final rendering result by combining the block contributions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderrayconsistent(rayorigin, raydirection, scenebboxmin, scenebboxmax, blocksize, proposalmlps, attributemlps): """ Renders a ray using the same pipeline as the training stage to ensure consistency. Args: rayorigin: 3D array/tuple of ray origin coordinates. raydirection: 3D array/tuple of ray direction vector. scenebboxmin: 3D array/tuple of bounding box minimum coordinates. scenebboxmax: 3D array/tuple of bounding box maximum coordinates. blocksize: Width/height of each spatial block. proposalmlps: Dictionary mapping block index to proposal MLP function. attributemlps: Dictionary mapping block index to attribute MLP function. Returns: finalcolor: Rendered color for the ray. finalopacity: Rendered opacity for the ray. """ # Step 1: Uniform sampling between near and far boundaries tmin = max((scenebboxmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] if raydirection[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)) tmax = min((scenebboxmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] if raydirection[i] != 0 else float('-inf') for i in range(3)) tnear = max(tmin, 0.0) tfar = tmax if tnear >= tfar: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0 numsamples = 128 # Typical value for volume rendering; not explicitly given in S1 tsamples = [tnear + i (tfar - tnear) / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] points = [[rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] for t in tsamples] finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphaaccum = 0.0 # Group points by block blockpoints = {} for i, point in enumerate(points): # Step 2: Determine block Bk using xy-coordinate projection (Eq. 4) blockidx = getblockindexfromxy(point[0], point[1], scenebboxmin, scenebboxmax, blocksize) if blockidx not in blockpoints: blockpoints[blockidx] = [] blockpoints[blockidx].append((i, point)) # Process blocks in order (assuming blocks are ordered along the ray or spatially) # Note: The exact ordering logic for sequential block rendering is not detailed in S1 sortedblockindices = sorted(blockpoints.keys()) for blockidx in sortedblockindices: if blockidx not in blockpoints: continue pointsinblock = blockpoints[blockidx] proposalmlp = proposalmlps[blockidx] attributemlp = attributemlps[blockidx] # Step 3: Query proposal MLP to sample probability distributions proposalweights = proposalmlp(pointsinblock) # Step 4: Query attribute MLP to obtain attributes attributes = attributemlp(pointsinblock) colors = [attr[:3] for attr in attributes] densities = [attr[3] for attr in attributes] # Step 5: Render block sequentially for idxinblock, (globali, point) in enumerate(pointsinblock): # Calculate delta distance if idxinblock == 0: deltat = tsamples[pointsinblock[1][0]] - tsamples[globali] if len(pointsinblock) > 1 else 0.0 elif idxinblock == len(pointsinblock) - 1: deltat = tsamples[globali] - tsamples[pointsinblock[-2][0]] else: deltat = (tsamples[pointsinblock[idxinblock + 1][0]] - tsamples[pointsinblock[idxinblock - 1][0]]) / 2.0 # Convert density to opacity alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-densities[idxinblock] deltat) # Compositing weight = alpha (1.0 - alphaaccum) finalcolor[0] += weight colors[idxinblock][0] finalcolor[1] += weight colors[idxinblock][1] finalcolor[2] += weight colors[idxinblock][2] alphaaccum += weight if alphaaccum >= 1.0: break return finalcolor, alphaaccum def getblockindexfromxy(x, y, bboxmin, bboxmax, blocksize): # Assuming a simple grid-based partitioning based on xy-coordinate projection # as described in the source for Eq. (4). width = bboxmax[0] - bboxmin[0] height = bboxmax[1] - bboxmin[1] cols = int(width / blocksize) rows = int(height / blocksize) col = int((x - bboxmin[0]) / blocksize) row = int((y - bboxmin[1]) / blocksize) return row cols + col Parameters: Number of Samples: Not given in the sources. Loss Weights: The training loss includes \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{\text{s3im}}, \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}, \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}, \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{\text{s}}, and \lambda5 \mathcal{L}{\text{opacity}}. Specific values for \lambdai are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on simulating quantization during training to mimic discrete texture lookups. Failure to accurately simulate this can lead to a gap between training and rendering. Boundaries: The method assumes a well-defined scene bounding box for uniform sampling. Block Assignment: The block determination (Eq. 4) must be consistent between training and rendering. A memory-optimized rendering pipeline that combines a low-resolution sparse voxel representation with high-resolution 2D triplanes, bridging training and rendering by simulating grid and quantization constraints during training. It reduces memory requirements compared to SNeRG by replacing the dense 3D voxel grid with a hybrid sparse voxel and 2D triplane representation. During training, it simulates a finite grid approach by querying MLPs at virtual grid corners instead of continuous coordinates, and simulates quantization to closely mimic the discrete texture lookup behavior of the actual rendering pipeline. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The MERF variant reduces memory requirements compared to SNeRG by using a hybrid sparse voxel and 2D triplane representation. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Minimizes the gap between training and rendering quality by ensuring pipeline consistency. The MERF variant offers significant memory reduction. Limitations: The block-based approach is constrained by web texture unit limits, requiring sequential rendering [Parent]. When to use: When deploying neural radiance fields on web platforms with strict hardware constraints (texture unit limits) and where training-inference consistency is critical for quality. The method originates from the "City-on-Web" project, which focuses on real-time neural rendering of large-scale scenes on the web. It was developed to address the limitations of existing methods like SNeRG, which demand substantial memory. The approach was introduced in the paper "City-on-Web: Real-Time Neural Rendering of Large-Scale Scenes on the Web". name: Patch-based Volume Rendering
head: Image Patching, Patch-based rendering strategy
body: A memory-saving rendering strategy for high-resolution volumes that splits the spatial dimensions into overlapping patches, renders them independently, and merges the results to scale to arbitrary image resolutions. Unlike full-volume rendering which requires memory proportional to H \times W, the patch-based approach trades redundant computation in overlapping regions for drastically reduced memory footprint, enabling scaling to arbitrary resolutions. Partitions the spatial domain into smaller, independently processed regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A target image resolution H \times W, a volume representation (coarse and fine models), and a patch grid configuration P \times P. Output: A rendered image of resolution H \times W. Data Structures: The method relies on the standard volume representation used in MuRF: Coarse Volume: Resolution H/8 \times W/8 \times D1 \times C1. Fine Volume: Resolution H \times W \times D2 \times C2. Patches: The spatial dimensions (H, W) are divided into a grid of P \times P overlapping patches. Parameters: P \times P: Grid size of overlapping patches along the spatial dimensions. Typical value: 4 \times 4 (yielding 16 patches). D1: Number of sampling points per ray for the coarse model. Value: 64. D2: Number of sampling points per ray for the fine model. Value: 16. C1: Feature dimension of the coarse volume representation. Value: 128. C2: Feature dimension of the fine volume representation. Value: 16. Steps: 1. Partition: Split the volume's first two spatial dimensions into a grid of P \times P overlapping patches. 2. name: BRDF Evaluation Kernel
body: The BRDF Evaluation Kernel evaluates a Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) for a batch of rays during inference ray marching and integration. It transforms geometric and material inputs into final pixel colors. It is distinct from compositing operations, focusing solely on the local reflection model evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: rgba: Input RGBA tensor (material color/opacity data). position: Input position tensor (3D coordinates). gradient: Input gradient tensor (normals or density gradients). rayDir: Input ray direction tensor. virtualsize: Dimensions of the virtual batch grid. rgbaOutput: Output RGBA tensor containing the computed color. Data Structures: The kernel operates on flat tensors indexed by a linear batch index b. The layout assumes contiguous memory access for the input tensors and the output tensor. Steps: 1. Initialize the loop over the batch using KERNEL1DLOOP with bounds determined by virtualsize.x virtualsize.y virtualsize.z. 2. For each batch index b: a. Fetch rgba, position, gradient, and rayDir from their respective input tensors at index b. b. Set batch = 0. c. Call brdf.eval(rgba, position, gradient, rayDir, batch) to compute the reflected color. d. Write the resulting color to rgbaOutput at index b. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def brdfevalkernel(rgba, position, gradient, rayDir, virtualsize, rgbaOutput): totalelements = virtualsize[0] virtualsize[1] virtualsize[2] for b in range(totalelements): currentrgba = rgba[b] currentposition = position[b] currentgradient = gradient[b] currentrayDir = rayDir[b] batch = 0 # The source does not provide the internal BRDF formula. color = brdfeval(currentrgba, currentposition, currentgradient, currentrayDir, batch) rgbaOutput[b] = color def brdfeval(rgba, position, gradient, rayDir, batch): # The source does not provide the internal BRDF formula. return rgba Parameters: virtualsize: Defines the batch dimension. Typical values depend on the resolution of the volume and the number of rays processed per frame. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The kernel assumes valid inputs for all tensors. Degenerate inputs (e.g., zero-length gradients) are not explicitly handled in the source description. Precision issues may arise if the evaluation function involves complex trigonometric or normalization operations on the gradient and ray direction vectors. EPBRR is a variant proposed by Poirier-Ginter et al. [2025] as an improvement to 3DGRT's ray tracer. It introduces various optimizations to the ray tracing process. However, it used a crude custom implementation of Depth Importance (DI), summarized as "binning the depth maps". Experiments in EDGS argued against this specific DI approach. Furthermore, EPBRR techniques were not tested against proper dense initialization and were not included in a full ray-tracing solution. They offered only limited comparisons to 3DGRT, which excluded DI and trained at reduced iteration counts without Spherical Harmonics (SH). The method was not validated individually.
