name: Inference Pipeline
head: Inference Module
body: The Inference Pipeline renders images from a trained dense point cloud and new camera poses without requiring further optimization. It differs from its sibling Inference Ray Compositing by handling the complete forward evaluation loop from input data structures to final image output, whereas the sibling focuses specifically on the ray-compositing mathematics. It is distinct from Sparse Ray Marching (Training) as it operates on a fully trained, dense representation rather than a sparse, evolving one. Inputs: 1. DensePointCloudWithExtraFeatures: The trained set of 3D points with associated features. 2. NewCameraPose: The target view parameters. Outputs: 1. Image: The rendered output. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Load DensePointCloudWithExtraFeatures and NewCameraPose into the Inference Module. 2. Pass the point cloud and camera pose to a rasterizer. 3. The rasterizer outputs the final Image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inferencepipeline(densepointcloud, camerapose): """Renders an image from a trained dense point cloud and camera pose.""" # Step 1: Load inputs # densepointcloud and camerapose are provided to the module. # Step 2: Rasterization # Pass the point cloud and camera pose to a rasterizer. # The sources do not specify the internal rasterization algorithm. # Standard rasterization projects primitives to screen space, sorts them by depth, and composites them. projectedprimitives = projecttoscreen(densepointcloud, camerapose) sortedprimitives = sortbydepth(projectedprimitives) image = alphacomposite(sortedprimitives) # Step 3: Output Image # The rasterizer outputs the final image. return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View-Dependent Color: The color MLP must be re-evaluated whenever the viewing angle shifts to account for scene colors changing with viewing direction. Bounding Box Cropping: For inference, an enlarged bounding box around the projected mesh on the image plane is cropped, and only pixels inside the bounding box are rendered. Latent Code Input: For unseen test poses, the latent code Z of the last training frame is used as input. Renders a set of views from a trained dense point cloud, prunes points occluded by or too close to the camera, and saves rendered images, depth maps, and colored depth maps. It differs from the parent Inference Pipeline by focusing specifically on the extraction and visualization of depth data and the pruning of invalid geometry, rather than the full evaluation loop including FPS calculation and video generation. After training, uses only the forward flow to render images. Passes a control encoding to the MLPs to determine the object to be rendered at runtime. Invokes the MLPs whenever a change in the encoding is necessary. Re-evaluates the color MLP whenever the viewing angle shifts to account for scene colors changing with viewing direction. For other MLPs, predicts k parameters for each anchor point instead of inferring for every viewing direction. 3D embeddings are decoded from shallow to deep levels using level-wise context models. The last 3D level is utilized to generate dimension-wise context for 2D embeddings. 2D embeddings are decoded in a coarse-to-fine order with the assistance of the dimension-wise context. Once the embeddings are decoded, all rendering processes are the same as INGP, requiring no additional time. For inference, an enlarged bounding box around the projected SMPL mesh on the image plane is cropped, and only pixels inside the bounding box are rendered. For unseen test poses, the latent code Z of the last training frame is used as input. Encoding/Decoding Time: Approximately 1 second. Rendering Time: After decoding, rendering requires no additional time beyond the base INGP process. For a 512 × 512 image, rendering takes 10-20 seconds depending on the bounding box size of the subject. Joint Root-Finding Time: Approximately 1 second. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability; supports context translation via control encoding without retraining. Limitations: Requires a trained representation; control encoding changes may require MLP re-evaluation. When to use: When real-time rendering of trained models is required, especially with dynamic context or style changes. When not to use: When optimization during inference is needed. The Inference Pipeline is a component of Gaussian Splatting rendering systems, enabling real-time visualization of trained models without the computational overhead of training or optimization. The concept of using control encodings for runtime context translation was introduced in "Shape-Shifting Splats: Realtime Context Translation for Gaussian Splatting in VR". wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, https://github.com/wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Shape-Shifting Splats: Realtime Context Translation for Gaussian Splatting in VR, https://doi.org/10.1109/vr67842.2026.00046, fetched 2026-11-01 How Far can we Compress Instant-NGP-Based NeRF?, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01921, fetched 2026-10-26 ARAH: Animatable Volume Rendering of Articulated Human SDFs, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-31, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Depth Map Rendering and Visualization
body: Renders a set of views from a trained dense point cloud (specifically Gaussian Splatting models), prunes points occluded by or too close to the camera, and saves rendered images, depth maps, and colored depth maps. It differs from the parent Inference Pipeline by focusing specifically on the extraction and visualization of depth data and the pruning of invalid geometry, rather than the full evaluation loop including FPS calculation and video generation. Inputs: gaussians: Trained Gaussian model containing 3D positions (getxyz), covariances, colors, and opacities. views: List of camera view objects containing intrinsic parameters, extrinsic pose, and image dimensions. near: Scalar distance threshold for pruning points near the camera. modelpath, name, iteration: Path components and iteration index for output directory naming. pipeline, background: Rendering pipeline configuration and background color tensor. Outputs: Rendered color images (.png). Normalized inverted depth maps (.png). Colored depth maps (.png). Video summaries via ffmpeg. Data Structures: masknear: Accumulated tensor of shape (N,) or (N, 1) where N is the number of Gaussians, indicating points within the near distance threshold across processed views. renderpkg: Dictionary returned by the renderer, containing keys "render" (color image), "depth" (raw depth), and "alpha" (accumulated alpha). Steps: 1. Create the output directory using the provided path components and iteration index. 2. Initialize masknear to None. 3. Iterate over each view to compute and accumulate a proximity mask: calculate the Euclidean distance between each Gaussian center and the camera center, compare against near, and accumulate the boolean mask using addition. 4. Prune Gaussians marked in masknear from the model using the inference pruning function. 5. For each view, render the scene without gradient tracking, extracting the color image, raw depth, and alpha channel. 6. Normalize the raw depth to [0, 1] using the view's local minimum and maximum, then add a background term weighted by alpha: \text{depth} = \frac{d - d{\min}}{d{\max} - d{\min}} + 1 \cdot (1 - \alpha). 7. Save the rendered color image as a PNG. 8. Save the inverted normalized depth map as a PNG. 9. Convert the depth map to a NumPy array, apply a logarithmic curve function \text{curve\fn}(x) = -\ln(x + \epsilon) where \epsilon = \text{np.finfo(np.float32).eps}, and apply the 'turbo' colormap. 10. Convert the colored depth map back to a tensor, permute channels to (C, H, W), and save as a PNG. 11. Generate video summaries from the saved image sequences using ffmpeg. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import os import numpy as np import torch import torchvision.utils import matplotlib.cm as cm def renderdepthmap(gaussians, views, near, modelpath, name, iteration, pipeline, background): # 1. Initialize output directory renderpath = os.path.join(modelpath, name, "ours{}".format(iteration)) os.makedirs(renderpath, existok=True) # 2. Initialize mask for points near the camera masknear = None # 3. Compute and accumulate proximity mask across views for view in views: xyz = gaussians.getxyz # Shape: (N, 3) camcenter = view.cameracenter # Shape: (3,) dist = torch.norm(xyz - camcenter.repeat(xyz.shape[0], 1), dim=1, keepdim=True) masktemp = dist < near if masknear is None: masknear = masktemp else: masknear = masknear + masktemp # 4. Prune points near the camera gaussians.prunepointsinference(masknear) # 5. Render each view and save outputs for idx, view in enumerate(views): # 6. Render without gradient tracking with torch.nograd(): # render is the Gaussian splatting forward pass renderpkg = render(view, gaussians, pipeline, background, inference=True) # 7. Extract rendering and depth rendering = renderpkg["render"] depthraw = renderpkg['depth'] alpha = renderpkg["alpha"] # 8. Normalize depth and combine with alpha for background depthmin = torch.min(depthraw) depthmax = torch.max(depthraw) depthnorm = (depthraw - depthmin) / (depthmax - depthmin) depth = depthnorm + 1.0 (1.0 - alpha) # 9. Save rendered image torchvision.utils.saveimage(rendering, os.path.join(renderpath, '{0:05d}'.format(idx) + ".png")) # 10. Save inverted depth map torchvision.utils.saveimage(1 - depth, os.path.join(renderpath, 'depth{0:05d}'.format(idx) + ".png")) # 11. Generate colored depth map depthest = depth.squeeze().cpu().numpy() eps = np.finfo(np.float32).eps depthcurvefn = lambda x: -np.log(x + eps) # visualizecmap applies the curve function and colormap depthest = visualizecmap(depthest, np.oneslike(depthest), cm.getcmap('turbo'), curvefn=depthcurvefn).copy() # 12. Save colored depth map depthesttensor = torch.astensor(depthest).permute(2, 0, 1) torchvision.utils.saveimage(depthesttensor, os.path.join(renderpath, 'cdepth{0:05d}'.format(idx) + ".png")) # 13. Generate video sequences using ffmpeg for render, depth, and colored depth images Parameters: near: Distance threshold for pruning points near the camera. Value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Normalization: The depth normalization uses per-view min/max of the rendered depth map, not the scene bounds. This can cause inconsistent depth scaling across frames if the visible depth range varies significantly. Background Handling: The formula adds 1 \cdot (1 - \alpha), setting background depth to 1.0 (normalized). If foreground depth also normalizes near 1.0, depth and background may be indistinguishable in the raw depth map. Mask Accumulation: Using addition for mask accumulation creates integer tensors. The pruning function must handle this correctly by treating any positive value as a prune flag. The 4DGS Rendering Pipeline is the inference-stage script that iterates over a sequence of camera views to render images using the trained 4D Gaussian Splatting model, saves the ground truth and rendered images, and generates a video summary. It differs from the parent Depth Map Rendering and Visualization by focusing specifically on the full image-order rendering loop for evaluation and visualization, including FPS calculation and video generation, rather than just depth map extraction and pruning. Double-sided depth rendering generates a complete depth map for a mesh by rendering front-facing and back-facing geometry separately and combining the results. It solves the problem of missing depth information for occluded or back-facing surfaces that standard single-pass rendering culls. Unlike 4DGS Rendering Pipeline or Open3D Image Rendering Pipeline which may rely on specific primitive types or culling flags, this method explicitly handles non-convex geometry by ensuring every ray intersection is captured. This method converts raw rendering outputs (depth, opacity, ellipsoid parameters, or RGB images) into Open3D-compatible geometry images for visualization, handling different modalities via UI checkboxes. It sets itself apart from sibling pipelines by directly interfacing with OpenGL for ellipsoid rendering and using imgviz for depth/opacity normalization, whereas siblings like the 4DGS pipeline may use different backend renderers or data structures. Hierarchical Depth Map Rendering is an image-based rendering technique that combines a hierarchical geometric model with precomputed multi-layer depth images to efficiently render complex vegetation. It differs from sibling methods by resampling precomputed multi-layer z-buffer images of hierarchical plant subparts rather than rendering geometry directly or using generic point clouds. The method is designed for offline or precomputed scenarios, as it is not real-time. Converts optical flow and camera intrinsics/extrinsics into a depth map. It handles validity, mesh export, and depth padding via morphological operations. 1. Calculate Offset: \text{offset} = \text{data}['\text{ref\intr}'][:, 0, 2] - \text{data}['\text{intr}'][:, 0, 2]. 2. Compute Disparity: \text{disparity} = \text{offset} - \text{data}['\text{flow\pred}']. 3. Compute Depth: \text{depth} = -\frac{\text{disparity}}{\text{data}['\text{Tf\x}']}. 4. Mask Invalid Regions: Multiply depth by data['mask'] to zero out invalid regions. 5. Export Mesh (Optional): If ptsoutpath is provided, export depth mesh using depth2mesh. 6. Transform to Original Camera Space: Transform points to original camera space using perspective with calibori = introri @ extrori. Invert z-depth. 7. Render Perspective Depth: Render perspective depth using taichirender.renderperspectivedepth with valid mask. 8. Pad Depth: Apply padding to renderdepth using taichirender.paddepth and store in data['lmain']['depthori']. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians and views. Pruning is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Rendering is O(N \cdot V) where V is the number of views. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing Gaussian attributes. The mask accumulation requires O(N) storage. Strengths: Efficiently removes invalid geometry (points too close to camera) that can cause artifacts. Provides standardized depth visualization for evaluation. Limitations: Depth normalization is local to each view, not global. Pruning is aggressive and irreversible. When to use: When evaluating depth accuracy or visualizing depth maps from Gaussian Splatting models. When not to use: When global depth consistency across views is required without post-processing. Originated in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting inference pipelines for novel view synthesis evaluation. It is used to generate evaluation metrics and visualizations for trained models. name: 4DGS Rendering Pipeline
head: Rendering Pipeline for 4DGS, render_sets [S1, unofficial]
body: The 4DGS Rendering Pipeline is the inference-stage script that iterates over a sequence of camera views to render images using the trained 4D Gaussian Splatting model, saves ground truth and rendered images, and generates a video summary. It differs from the parent Depth Map Rendering and Visualization by focusing specifically on the full image-order rendering loop for evaluation and visualization, including FPS calculation and video generation, rather than just depth map extraction and pruning. Inputs: views: A list of camera view objects containing projection matrices, image data, and metadata. gaussians: The 4D Gaussian splatting model parameters (positions, covariances, opacities, colors, etc.). pipeline: Rendering configuration parameters (e.g., rasterization settings). background: Background color tensor. name: Dataset identifier (e.g., 'train', 'test', or specific scene name). camtype: Camera type string (e.g., 'PanopticSports' or standard pinhole). modelpath, iteration: Paths to locate output directories. Outputs: Rendered images (PNG) in renders/. Ground truth images (PNG) in gt/. Video file videorgb.mp4. Console output: FPS metric. Data Structures: renderimages: List of HWC uint8 numpy arrays for visualization. renderlist: List of raw tensor renders (CHW format) for saving. gtlist: List of raw tensor ground truth images (CHW format). Steps: 1. Setup Paths: Create renderpath and gtspath directories under modelpath/name/ours{iteration}/renders and gt respectively. 2. Initialize: Create empty lists renderimages, gtlist, and renderlist. 3. Iterate Views: Loop through views with a progress bar; record start time time1 on the first view. 4. Render: Call render(view, gaussians, pipeline, background, camtype=camtype) and extract the 'render' key from the returned dictionary. 5. Convert and Store: Convert rendering to 8-bit uint8 using to8b (clip to [0,1], multiply by 255, cast to uint8), transpose to HWC, and append to renderimages; append raw tensor to renderlist. 6. Handle Ground Truth: If name is 'train' or 'test', get GT; if camtype is not 'PanopticSports', use view.originalimage[0:3,:,:]; else, use view['image'].cuda(). 7. Calculate FPS: After loop, calculate FPS as (len(views)-1)/(time2-time1). 8. Save Images: Use multithreadwrite to save gtlist to gtspath and renderlist to renderpath as PNGs named {0:05d}.png. 9. Create Video: Use imageio.mimwrite to create videorgb.mp4 in the output directory with fps=36. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time import os import imageio import numpy as np import torch from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor def to8b(tensor): """Clip to [0, 1], multiply by 255, cast to uint8.""" return np.clip(tensor.cpu().numpy(), 0.0, 1.0) 255.0 def multithreadwrite(tensorlist, savedir): """Save list of tensors to PNG files named {index:05d}.png using a thread pool.""" os.makedirs(savedir, existok=True) def saveone(idx, tensor): img = np.clip(tensor.cpu().numpy(), 0.0, 1.0) 255.0 imguint8 = img.astype(np.uint8) imageio.imwrite(os.path.join(savedir, f"{idx:05d}.png"), imguint8) with ThreadPoolExecutor() as executor: list(executor.map(saveone, range(len(tensorlist)), tensorlist)) def renderpipeline(views, gaussians, pipeline, background, name, camtype, modelpath, iteration): # Setup Paths methoddir = os.path.join(modelpath, name, f"ours{iteration}") renderpath = os.path.join(methoddir, "renders") gtspath = os.path.join(methoddir, "gt") os.makedirs(renderpath, existok=True) os.makedirs(gtspath, existok=True) renderimages = [] gtlist = [] renderlist = [] # Iterate Views for idx, view in enumerate(views): if idx == 0: time1 = time.time() # Render (core Gaussian rasterizer, implementation external to pipeline) rendering = render(view, gaussians, pipeline, background, camtype=camtype)["render"] # Convert and Store renderuint8 = to8b(rendering) renderhwc = renderuint8.transpose(1, 2, 0) renderimages.append(renderhwc) renderlist.append(rendering) # Handle Ground Truth if name in ["train", "test"]: if camtype != "PanopticSports": gt = view.originalimage[0:3,:,:] else: gt = view['image'].cuda() gtlist.append(gt) time2 = time.time() # Calculate FPS fps = (len(views) - 1) / (time2 - time1) print(f"FPS: {fps}") # Save Images multithreadwrite(gtlist, gtspath) multithreadwrite(renderlist, renderpath) # Create Video videopath = os.path.join(methoddir, "videorgb.mp4") imageio.mimwrite(videopath, renderimages, fps=36) Parameters: fps for video: 36. resolution: Performance metrics provided for 800x800 and 1352x1014. Edge Cases: If name is not 'train' or 'test', ground truth is not collected. If camtype is 'PanopticSports', the GT extraction logic differs, requiring access to view['image'] instead of view.originalimage. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of views N. Measured Performance: 82 FPS at 800x800 resolution for synthetic data; 30 FPS at 1352x1014 resolution for real datasets. Strengths: Provides standardized evaluation metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS) and visualization outputs for 4DGS models. Limitations: Performance is resolution-dependent and varies between synthetic and real-world datasets. The 4DGS Rendering Pipeline originates from the 4D Gaussian Splatting method for dynamic scene reconstruction. It is part of the evaluation and visualization suite provided in the implementation repository. ElenaViewSynthesis/4dgs, https://github.com/ElenaViewSynthesis/4dgs, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Double-sided Depth Rendering
head: Back-face depth rendering, Two-pass depth rendering
body: Double-sided depth rendering generates a complete depth map for a mesh by rendering front-facing and back-facing geometry separately and combining the results. It solves the problem of missing depth information for occluded or back-facing surfaces that standard single-pass rendering culls. Unlike 4DGS Rendering Pipeline or Open3D Image Rendering Pipeline which may rely on specific primitive types or culling flags, this method explicitly handles non-convex geometry by ensuring every ray intersection is captured. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangle mesh defined by vertex positions and face indices. Output: A single depth map image where each pixel contains the minimum positive depth value from any surface intersection. Data Structures: vertices: Array of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). faces: Array of integer indices [i, j, k] defining triangles. depthmap: 2D array of floating-point values, initialized to infinity or zero. Steps: 1. Render Front Faces: Render the mesh with standard face culling (or explicit front-face selection) to produce depthmapfront. 2. Flip Normals: Swap the first two indices of every face in faces (e.g., [i, j, k] \rightarrow [j, i, k]) to invert the winding order and effectively flip normals. 3. Render Back Faces: Render the modified mesh. This captures surfaces that were previously back-facing. Produce depthmapback. 4. Restore Mesh: Swap the indices back to their original order to restore the mesh state. 5. Combine Depths: For each pixel, select the minimum positive depth from the two maps. Formula: For a pixel at coordinate (u, v): D(u, v) = \min(D{front}(u, v), D{back}(u, v)) where D{front} and D{back} are treated as infinity if no intersection occurred. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def doublesideddepthrendering(mesh, camera): """ Renders a complete depth map for a mesh by combining front and back face renders. Args: mesh: Object with.vertices and.faces attributes. camera: Object with.render() method that returns a depth map. Returns: depthmap: 2D numpy array of depth values. """ # Step 1: Render original mesh (front faces) # Note: Depending on the renderer, this might require disabling back-face culling # or explicitly selecting front faces. depthfront = camera.render(mesh.vertices, mesh.faces) # Step 2: Flip face indices to render back faces # Swap first two indices of each face flippedfaces = mesh.faces.copy() flippedfaces[:, 0], flippedfaces[:, 1] = flippedfaces[:, 1], flippedfaces[:, 0] # Step 3: Render flipped mesh (back faces) depthback = camera.render(mesh.vertices, flippedfaces) # Step 4: Restore original face order (if mesh object is reused) mesh.faces = mesh.faces # Or re-assign original faces # Step 5: Combine depths # Initialize combined depth with front depth depthmap = depthfront.copy() # Update with back depth where it is valid and smaller # Assuming 0 or negative values indicate no intersection, or use a mask validback = depthback > 0 validfront = depthfront > 0 # If front is invalid, take back depthmap[~validfront & validback] = depthback[~validfront & validback] # If both valid, take minimum depthmap[validfront & validback] = np.minimum( depthfront[validfront & validback], depthback[validfront & validback]) return depthmap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Culling Flags: Some rendering APIs (e.g., pyrender) may ignore noculling flags for depth buffers, requiring explicit double-sided rendering as described. Precision: Depth buffer precision must be sufficient to distinguish between front and back intersections in thin geometry. Degenerate Input: Zero-area triangles may cause undefined behavior in rasterization; pre-processing to remove them is recommended. Computes the thickness of a non-convex object by summing the depths of all front-facing and back-facing intersections per pixel and subtracting them. This solves the limitation of simple back-minus-front depth difference, which fails for non-convex geometry with multiple ray intersections. It avoids depth peeling by using additive blending to accumulate depths, which is simpler and faster for thickness estimation. Originally found in the NVIDIA Fog Volume SDK sample. Steps: 1. Enable additive blending for the depth buffer writes. 2. Render the scene's front-facing polygons first. 3. Render the scene's back-facing polygons second. 4. Read the accumulated depth buffer values per pixel and compute thickness as (\sum \text{front-face depths}) - (\sum \text{back-face depths}). Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels, plus two full rasterization passes over the mesh. Effectively doubles the rendering cost compared to a single pass. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for two depth maps (or one if reused) plus the mesh data. Strengths: Handles non-convex geometry correctly where single-pass culling fails. Simple to implement. Limitations: Does not handle self-occlusion within a single ray path beyond the first/last intersection unless additive blending is used for thickness. Performance is halved due to two passes. When to use: When complete depth coverage is required for non-convex meshes, or when computing thickness for participating media. When not to use: When performance is critical and the object is convex, or when only front-facing visibility is needed. The technique of rendering front and back faces separately to capture complete geometry is a standard workaround in computer graphics when hardware culling is too aggressive or when specific depth information for occluded surfaces is needed. The specific application of this method for thickness computation via additive blending was shared by Thorsten Scheuerman and originally found in the NVIDIA Fog Volume SDK sample. The use of double-sided rendering for depth maps in the context of neural rendering pipelines (e.g., DN-Splatter) addresses the failure of standard culling flags in certain libraries like pyrender. maturk/dn-splatter, https://github.com/maturk/dn-splatter, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) May | 2007 | Level of Detail, https://levelofdetail.wordpress.com/2007/05/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Open3D Image Rendering Pipeline
head: Open3D Geometry Image Conversion, Open3D Visualization Pipeline
body: This method converts raw rendering outputs (depth, opacity, ellipsoid parameters, or RGB images) into Open3D-compatible geometry images for visualization, handling different modalities via UI checkboxes. It sets itself apart from sibling pipelines by directly interfacing with OpenGL for ellipsoid rendering and using imgviz for depth/opacity normalization, whereas siblings like the 4DGS pipeline may use different backend renderers or data structures. Inputs: results: Dictionary containing rendering data. Keys may include depth, opacity, or RGB image data. currentcam: Camera object containing intrinsic and extrinsic parameters (e.g., FoVy, view matrix). gaussiancur: Current Gaussian Splatting model instance containing attributes (xyz, opacity, scaling, rotation, features). self.grenderer: OpenGL-based Gaussian renderer instance. self.gcamera: OpenGL camera state instance. self.depthchbox, self.opacitychbox, self.ellipsoidchbox: UI checkbox states indicating which modalities to render. self.background: Background color tensor. self.scalingslider: Scaling factor for Gaussian sizes. Outputs: Rendered images as Open3D Image objects (RGB, depth, opacity, or ellipsoid views). Data Structures: Gaussian Attributes (OpenGL Upload): xyz: Position tensor, shape (N, 3), type float32. opacity: Scalar opacity tensor, shape (N, 1), type float32. scale: Scaling tensor, shape (N, 3), type float32. rot: Rotation quaternions, shape (N, 4), type float32. sh: Spherical Harmonics coefficients, specifically the 0th degree, shape (N, 3), extracted from features tensor [:, 0,:]. Steps: 1. Check Modality: Determine which checkboxes are active (depth, opacity, ellipsoid). If none are active, default to RGB processing. 2. Depth Rendering (if depthchbox is checked): a. Extract depth from results["depth"]. Shape is typically (1, H, W). Detach from computation graph, move to CPU, and convert to NumPy array. b. Calculate maxdepth = np.max(depth). c. Normalize depth to RGB using imgviz.depth2rgb(depth, minvalue=0.1, maxvalue=maxdepth, colormap="jet"). This produces an array of shape (H, W, 3) with values in [0, 1]. d. Convert back to PyTorch tensor. e. Permute dimensions from (H, W, 3) to (3, H, W) then to (H, W, 3) for Open3D compatibility. f. Convert to byte type and make contiguous. g. Create Open3D Image object. 3. Opacity Rendering (if opacitychbox is checked): a. Extract opacity from results["opacity"]. b. Calculate maxopacity = np.max(opacity). c. Normalize opacity to RGB using imgviz.depth2rgb(opacity, minvalue=0.0, maxvalue=maxopacity, colormap="jet"). d. Permute and convert to Open3D Image as in Step 2. 4. Ellipsoid Rendering (if ellipsoidchbox is checked): a. Setup OpenGL Context: Poll GLFW events. Clear color, depth, and stencil buffers: gl.glClearColor(0, 0, 0, 1.0), gl.glClear(...). Adjust window size if necessary based on self.widget3dwidthratio. b. Configure Camera: Set self.gcamera.fovy from currentcam.FoVy. Update resolution: self.gcamera.updateresolution(height, width). Set renderer resolution: self.grenderer.setrenderreso(width, height). Compute frustum from camera view matrix: frustum = createfrustum(np.linalg.inv(cvgl @ currentcam.getviewmatrix())). Set camera position, target, and up vectors from frustum properties. c. Upload Gaussian Attributes: Assign self.gaussiansgl.xyz, opacity, scale, rot from gaussiancur attributes (CPU NumPy arrays). Assign self.gaussiansgl.sh from gaussiancur.getfeatures.cpu().numpy()[:, 0,:]. d. Render: Update renderer state: self.updateactivatedrendererstate(self.gaussiansgl). Sort and update Gaussians: self.grenderer.sortandupdate(self.gcamera). Draw scene: self.grenderer.draw(). e. Read Pixels: Read framebuffer: bufferdata = gl.glReadPixels(0, 0, width, height, gl.GLRGB, gl.GLUNSIGNEDBYTE). Convert to NumPy array and reshape to (H, W, 3). Flip Vertically: OpenGL reads from bottom-left origin. Use cv2.flip(img, 0, img) to flip vertically to match standard image coordinates (top-left origin). f. Convert to Open3D Image. 5. RGB Rendering (default or if no specific modality is selected): a. Extract RGB image from results. b. Clamp values to [0, 1]. c. Scale to [0, 255] and convert to byte. d. Permute to (H, W, 3). e. Create Open3D Image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import torch import imgviz import cv2 import open3d as o3d import glfw import OpenGL.GL as gl def rendero3dimage(results, currentcam, gaussiancur, self): """ Renders depth, opacity, ellipsoid, or RGB images using Open3D. """ # Helper to create Open3D image from numpy array (H, W, 3) uint8 def too3dimage(npimg): return o3d.geometry.Image(npimg) if self.depthchbox.checked: # 1. Depth Rendering depth = results["depth"] # Shape: (1, H, W) -> (H, W) depth = depth[0,:,:].detach().cpu().numpy() maxdepth = np.max(depth) # Normalize using imgviz # Returns (H, W, 3) float32 in [0, 1] depthrgb = imgviz.depth2rgb( depth, minvalue=0.1, maxvalue=maxdepth, colormap="jet") # Convert to Open3D Image # imgviz returns float32, Open3D expects uint8 or float32 depending on version # Assuming uint8 conversion for standard visualization depthuint8 = (depthrgb 255).astype(np.uint8) return too3dimage(depthuint8) elif self.opacitychbox.checked: # 2. Opacity Rendering opacity = results["opacity"] # Shape: (1, H, W) -> (H, W) opacity = opacity[0,:,:].detach().cpu().numpy() maxopacity = np.max(opacity) opacityrgb = imgviz.depth2rgb( opacity, minvalue=0.0, maxvalue=maxopacity, colormap="jet") opacityuint8 = (opacityrgb 255).astype(np.uint8) return too3dimage(opacityuint8) elif self.ellipsoidchbox.checked: # 3. Ellipsoid Rendering via OpenGL if gaussiancur is None: return None # Setup OpenGL glfw.pollevents() gl.glClearColor(0, 0, 0, 1.0) gl.glClear( gl.GLCOLORBUFFERBIT | gl.GLDEPTHBUFFERBIT | gl.GLSTENCILBUFFERBIT) # Adjust window size if needed w = int(self.window.size.width self.widget3dwidthratio) h = self.window.size.height glfw.setwindowsize(self.windowgl, w, h) # Configure Camera self.gcamera.fovy = currentcam.FoVy self.gcamera.updateresolution(h, w) self.grenderer.setrenderreso(w, h) # Compute frustum from view matrix # cvgl is likely a coordinate system conversion matrix (e.g., OpenGL to OpenCV) viewmatrix = currentcam.getviewmatrix() invview = np.linalg.inv(cvgl @ viewmatrix) frustum = createfrustum(invview) self.gcamera.position = frustum.eye.astype(np.float32) self.gcamera.target = frustum.center.astype(np.float32) self.gcamera.up = frustum.up.astype(np.float32) # Upload Gaussian Attributes self.gaussiansgl.xyz = gaussiancur.getxyz.cpu().numpy() self.gaussiansgl.opacity = gaussiancur.getopacity.cpu().numpy() self.gaussiansgl.scale = gaussiancur.getscaling.cpu().numpy() self.gaussiansgl.rot = gaussiancur.getrotation.cpu().numpy() # Extract 0th degree SH coefficients features = gaussiancur.getfeatures.cpu().numpy() self.gaussiansgl.sh = features[:, 0,:] # Render self.updateactivatedrendererstate(self.gaussiansgl) self.grenderer.sortandupdate(self.gcamera) width, height = glfw.getframebuffersize(self.windowgl) self.grenderer.draw() # Read Pixels # glReadPixels returns bytes in row-major order, bottom-left origin bufferdata = gl.glReadPixels(0, 0, width, height, gl.GLRGB, gl.GLUNSIGNEDBYTE) img = np.frombuffer(bufferdata, dtype=np.uint8).reshape((height, width, 3)) # Flip vertically to match standard image coordinates (top-left origin) img = cv2.flip(img, 0) return too3dimage(img) else: # 4. Default RGB Rendering rgb = results["rgb"] # Shape: (1, H, W, 3) or (H, W, 3) depending on source # Assuming (1, H, W, 3) rgb = rgb[0].detach().cpu().numpy() # Clamp to [0, 1] rgb = np.clip(rgb, 0.0, 1.0) # Scale to [0, 255] rgbuint8 = (rgb 255).astype(np.uint8) return too3dimage(rgbuint8) Parameters: minvalue for depth: 0.1. colormap: "jet". cvgl: Coordinate transformation matrix (not defined in sources, assumed to be a standard OpenGL-to-OpenCV conversion matrix). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: OpenGL Origin: glReadPixels returns images with the origin at the bottom-left. Failure to flip vertically results in an upside-down image. Depth Normalization: The minvalue for depth normalization is hardcoded to 0.1 in the source, which may clip very close depth values. SH Coefficients: Only the 0th degree (constant term) of Spherical Harmonics is used for ellipsoid rendering, ignoring higher-order color variations. Time Complexity: Dominated by the OpenGL rendering pass for ellipsoids, which involves sorting Gaussians (O(N \log N) or O(N) with spatial hashing) and rasterization. Depth/opacity rendering is O(H \times W) for normalization. Memory Complexity: Requires storing Gaussian attributes in CPU and GPU memory. The OpenGL framebuffer requires O(H \times W) memory for the pixel buffer. Strengths: Direct integration with Open3D for visualization; supports multiple modalities (depth, opacity, ellipsoid, RGB) in a single pipeline. Limitations: Relies on OpenGL context management, which can be complex to set up in headless environments. The hardcoded depth normalization parameters may not suit all scenes. When to Use: For visualizing Gaussian Splatting results in Open3D, especially when inspecting depth, opacity, or 3D ellipsoid structure. When Not to Use: For high-performance batch rendering where OpenGL overhead is prohibitive, or when higher-order SH color is required for visualization. This pipeline is part of the MonoGS project, which integrates Gaussian Splatting with SLAM. It was developed to provide a flexible visualization interface for different aspects of the Gaussian Splatting representation. The use of imgviz for depth/opacity visualization and OpenGL for ellipsoid rendering reflects common practices in 3D computer vision visualization tools. muskie82/MonoGS, https://github.com/muskie82/MonoGS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical Depth Map Rendering
head: Hierarchical Z-Buffer Rendering, Hierarchical model with multi-layered depth images
body: Hierarchical Depth Map Rendering is an image-based rendering technique that combines a hierarchical geometric model with precomputed multi-layer depth images to efficiently render complex vegetation. It differs from sibling methods by resampling precomputed multi-layer z-buffer images of hierarchical plant subparts rather than rendering geometry directly or using generic point clouds. The method builds on Depth Map Rendering and Visualization and is designed for offline or precomputed scenarios, as it is not real-time. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Hierarchical model with precomputed multi-layer z-buffer images and a new viewpoint location. Outputs: Antialiased color image. Data Structures: The core data structure is a multi-layer z-buffer. Each layer contains the following fields: 1. Surface Normal: 3D vector. 2. Surface Diffuse Reflectivity Color: 3D vector. 3. Subpixel Coverage Mask: Coverage mask. 4. Z Value: Depth value. 5. Leaf Bit: Boolean flag indicating if the surface is a leaf. Numbered Steps: 1. Subpart Selection: Determine which subparts to render based on viewpoint distance. Parts closer to the viewpoint use higher-detail images from deeper levels of the hierarchical model. The closest parts are scan-converted directly from the original texture/transparency mapped polygons. 2. Resampling: Resample the precomputed multi-layer z-buffer images of the selected hierarchical subparts to the new viewpoint. 3. Shading: Perform shading as a post-process on the resampled z-buffer layers. Apply a z-buffer shadow algorithm to determine if surface points are in shadow. If not in shadow, add the effect of unattenuated direct sunlight using the Phong BRDF for a discrete parallel light source. If the Leaf Bit is set, include diffusely transmitted light from the back of the leaf. 4. Compositing: Composite the shading results from all layers into an antialiased color value for each pixel using the subpixel coverage masks, following the A-buffer algorithm approach. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: The method is not real-time. Using 3 textures instead of a single one is about 2 to 3 times slower on recent GPUs. Memory: A huge amount of image data may not fit the graphics memory. Time Complexity: Not real-time. Performance degrades with the number of texture layers; using 3 textures is 2-3x slower than 1 texture on recent GPUs. Memory Complexity: High. Large amounts of image data may exceed graphics memory capacity. Strengths: Allows extremely complex and extensive vegetation to be rendered in a reasonable time by leveraging precomputed data and hierarchical detail selection. Limitations: Not suitable for real-time applications. Limited by graphics memory capacity for large scenes. When to use: Offline rendering of complex vegetation where precomputation is feasible and real-time performance is not required. When not to use: Real-time applications. The method was introduced by Max et al. in 1996. It is described in the context of rendering forest scenes and plane-parallel radiance transport for global illumination in vegetation. The approach builds on earlier work in image-based rendering and hierarchical modeling. name: DVGO Volume Rendering Forward
body: Performs volume rendering for a batch of rays, including sampling, density/alpha computation, transmittance calculation, color estimation, and ray marching. It computes the final rendered color, distance, accumulation, and weights from RGB, density, tvals, directions, and background color assumption. It differs from NeRF Volume Rendering by using a pre-allocated 3D voxel grid for density and color storage, enabling faster training and inference via direct memory access, while maintaining the volume rendering integral formulation. Inputs: raypts: Ray origins and directions (or sampled points along rays). tvals: Sample positions along the ray. dirs: Ray directions. density: Density values from the density network/grid. rgb: RGB color values associated with samples. maskcache: Optional mask for known free space. usefouriergrid: Boolean flag for Fourier grid usage. fastcolorthres: Threshold for early filtering. rgbnet: Optional network for view-dependent color. rgbnetdirect: Boolean flag for direct RGB output. rgbnetfullimplicit: Boolean flag for implicit RGB features. whitebkgd: Boolean flag for white background assumption. renderdepth: Boolean flag for depth output. bg: Background color. N: Total number of samples. Outputs: comprgb: Computed RGB color. distance: Accumulated distance/depth. acc: Accumulated alpha/opacity. weights: Rendering weights. Data Structures: tmids: Midpoint distances between samples. Layout: (batch, numsamples-1). tdists: Distances between consecutive samples. Layout: (batch, numsamples-1). delta: Segment lengths scaled by direction norm. Layout: (batch, numsamples-1). densitydelta: Product of density and delta. Layout: (batch, numsamples-1). trans: Transmittance values. Layout: (batch, numsamples). weights: Rendering weights. Layout: (batch, numsamples). Steps: 1. Sample Points: Sample points on rays using self.sampleray. 2. Compute Midpoints: Compute t{mids} as 0.5 \times (t{vals}[\dots,:-1] + t{vals}[\dots, 1:]). 3. Free Space Masking: If maskcache exists and usefouriergrid is false, filter raypts, rayid, and stepid by the mask. 4. Compute Distances: Compute t{dists} as t{vals}[\dots, 1:] - t{vals}[\dots,:-1]. 5. Query Density: Query density from the density network/grid. 6. Compute Delta: Compute \delta as t{dists} multiplied by the norm of dirs. 7. Activate Density: Activate density to alpha using self.activatedensity. 8. Compute Density Delta: Compute densitydelta as density[\dots, 0] delta. 9. Fast Color Filtering: If fastcolorthres > 0 and usefouriergrid is false, filter points where alpha > fastcolorthres. 10. Compute Transmittance: Compute trans by concatenating zeros with cumsum of densitydelta[\dots,:-1], then exp of the negative. trans = \exp(-\text{cumsum}(\text{density\delta}[\dots,:-1])) The sources specify concatenating zeros before the cumulative sum. 11. Compute Weights: Compute accumulated transmittance weights using Alphas2Weights.apply with alpha, rayid, and N. weights = \alpha \times trans 12. Compute RGB: Compute comprgb as sum of weights[\dots, None] rgb along axis -2. 13. Fast Color Filtering (Weights): If fastcolorthres > 0 and usefouriergrid is false, filter points where weights > fastcolorthres. 14. Compute Accumulation: Compute acc as sum of weights along axis -1. 15. Query Color Feature: Query color feature k0 from the k0 network if rgbnetfullimplicit is false. 16. Compute Distance: Compute distance as sum of weights tmids along axis -1, divided by acc. 17. View-Dependent Color: If rgbnet exists, compute view-dependent color. If rgbnetdirect is true, use k0 as view feature; otherwise split k0 into diffuse (first 3 channels) and view (remaining channels). 18. Clip Distance: Clip distance using nantonum (replacing inf with inf) and clipping to [t{vals}[\dots, 0], t{vals}[\dots, -1]]. 19. View Direction Embedding: Compute positional embedding for viewdirs: flatten viewdirs, multiply by viewfreq, concatenate sin/cos embeddings, then flatten and index by rayid. 20. Background Addition: If whitebkgd is True, add (1. - acc[\dots, None]) to comprgb. 21. RGB Network: Concatenate k0view and viewdirsemb, pass through rgbnet to get rgblogit. 22. Final RGB: Compute final RGB: if rgbnetdirect, \text{sigmoid}(rgb\logit); else \text{sigmoid}(rgb\logit + k0\diffuse). 23. Marched RGB: Compute marched RGB using segmentcoo: sum of (weights \times rgb) grouped by rayid, plus background contribution (alphainv\last \times bg). 24. Depth Output: If renderdepth is true, compute depth using segmentcoo: sum of (weights \times step\id) grouped by rayid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def dvgovolumerenderingforward( raypts, tvals, dirs, density, rgb, maskcache=None, usefouriergrid=False, fastcolorthres=0.0, rgbnet=None, rgbnetdirect=False, rgbnetfullimplicit=False, whitebkgd=False, renderdepth=False, bg=None, N=None, viewfreq=1): """ Performs volume rendering for a batch of rays. Args: raypts: Tensor of ray points. tvals: Tensor of sample positions along rays. Shape: (batch, numsamples). dirs: Tensor of ray directions. Shape: (batch, numsamples, 3). density: Tensor of density values. Shape: (batch, numsamples, 1). rgb: Tensor of RGB values. Shape: (batch, numsamples, 3). maskcache: Optional mask for free space. usefouriergrid: Boolean flag. fastcolorthres: Threshold for early filtering. rgbnet: Optional network for view-dependent color. rgbnetdirect: Boolean flag for direct RGB output. rgbnetfullimplicit: Boolean flag for implicit RGB features. whitebkgd: Boolean flag for white background. renderdepth: Boolean flag for depth output. bg: Background color. N: Total number of samples. viewfreq: Frequency for positional embedding. Returns: comprgb: Computed RGB color. distance: Accumulated distance/depth. acc: Accumulated alpha/opacity. weights: Rendering weights. """ # Step 2: Compute Midpoints tmids = 0.5 (tvals[...,:-1] + tvals[..., 1:]) # Step 3: Free Space Masking if maskcache is not None and not usefouriergrid: # Filter raypts, rayid, stepid by mask. Sources do not specify exact mask application logic. pass # Step 4: Compute Distances tdists = tvals[..., 1:] - tvals[...,:-1] # Step 6: Compute Delta delta = tdists torch.norm(dirs, dim=-1) # Step 7: Activate Density # self.activatedensity is called here. Sources do not specify exact activation function. # density = self.activatedensity(density) # Step 8: Compute Density Delta densitydelta = density[..., 0] delta # Step 9: Fast Color Filtering if fastcolorthres > 0 and not usefouriergrid: alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-densitydelta) mask = alpha > fastcolorthres # Filter tensors by mask. Sources do not specify exact filtering implementation. pass # Step 10: Compute Transmittance # Concatenate zeros with cumsum of densitydelta[...,:-1], then exp of the negative cumsumdensity = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(densitydelta[...,:1]), torch.cumsum(densitydelta[...,:-1], dim=-1)], dim=-1) trans = torch.exp(-cumsumdensity) # Step 11: Compute Weights alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-densitydelta) # Alphas2Weights.apply with alpha, rayid, and N # weights = alpha trans weights = alpha trans # Step 12: Compute RGB comprgb = torch.sum(weights[..., None] rgb[...,:-1], dim=-2) # Step 13: Fast Color Filtering (Weights) if fastcolorthres > 0 and not usefouriergrid: mask = weights > fastcolorthres # Filter tensors by mask. Sources do not specify exact filtering implementation. pass # Step 14: Compute Accumulation acc = torch.sum(weights, dim=-1) # Step 15: Query Color Feature k0 = None if not rgbnetfullimplicit: # k0 = k0network(...) pass # Step 16: Compute Distance distance = torch.sum(weights tmids, dim=-1) / (acc + 1e-8) # epsilon added to prevent division by zero # Step 17: View-Dependent Color if rgbnet is not None: if rgbnetdirect: k0view = k0 k0diffuse = None else: k0diffuse = k0[...,:3] k0view = k0[..., 3:] # Step 19: View Direction Embedding viewdirs = dirs[..., 0,:] # Example: use first direction or mean viewdirsflat = viewdirs.view(-1, 3) freqbands = 2 torch.arange(viewfreq).to(viewdirs.device) viewdirsemb = torch.cat([torch.sin(viewdirsflat freqbands), torch.cos(viewdirsflat freqbands)], dim=-1) viewdirsemb = viewdirsemb.view(viewdirs.shape[0], -1) # Step 21: RGB Network if k0view is not None: rgbinput = torch.cat([k0view, viewdirsemb], dim=-1) else: rgbinput = viewdirsemb rgblogit = rgbnet(rgbinput) # Step 22: Final RGB if rgbnetdirect: rgbfinal = torch.sigmoid(rgblogit) else: rgbfinal = torch.sigmoid(rgblogit + k0diffuse) # Recompute comprgb with final RGB comprgb = torch.sum(weights[..., None] rgbfinal[...,:-1], dim=-2) # Step 20: Background Addition if whitebkgd: comprgb = comprgb + (1.0 - acc[..., None]) # Step 18: Clip Distance distance = torch.clamp(distance, min=tvals[..., 0], max=tvals[..., -1]) distance = torch.nantonum(distance, nan=float('inf')) # Step 23: Marched RGB # segmentcoo: sum of (weights rgb) grouped by rayid, plus background contribution # comprgb = segmentcoo(weights rgb, rayid) + alphainvlast bg pass # Step 24: Depth Output if renderdepth: # depth = segmentcoo(weights stepid, rayid) pass return comprgb, distance, acc, weights Parameters: interval: Calculated as renderkwargs['stepsize'] self.voxelsizeratio. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero in distance calculation when acc is zero. Mitigated by adding a small epsilon or handling zero accumulation separately. Precision issues with cumulative sums and exponentials for transmittance. Boundary conditions for ray sampling and masking. NeRF Volume Rendering is a differentiable method for synthesizing photorealistic novel views of a scene by estimating volume density and RGB color along camera rays using a neural network. It solves the problem of continuous 3D scene representation and rendering by parameterizing the scene as an implicit function, typically implemented via Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). Unlike explicit voxel-based methods such as DVGO, which store features in a grid and use interpolation, the classical NeRF approach queries a continuous field directly at sampled points along the ray. This allows for high-fidelity view-dependent effects but incurs significant computational costs due to the large number of MLP queries required. This method performs the forward pass for Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO), computing the final RGB color, depth, and optional segmentation masks for a batch of rays by marching through a dense voxel grid. It differs from NeRF Volume Rendering by using a pre-allocated 3D voxel grid for density and color storage, enabling faster training and inference via direct memory access, while maintaining the volume rendering integral formulation. It builds on DVGO Volume Rendering Forward. A CUDA kernel that traverses rays through a data structure, accumulating color and transmittance with early ray marching termination when transmittance drops below a threshold. It launches a kernel with one thread per ray, exits if thread index exceeds numrays, loads ray origin and direction, initializes color to zero and transmittance T to 1.0, loops over a fixed number of samples (e.g., 100), looks up density sigma from shared memory, computes segment length delta (e.g., 0.01f), computes alpha using the Beer-Lambert law approximation, computes sample color (placeholder spherical harmonics), accumulates color using standard volumetric integration, updates transmittance, checks early termination condition and breaks loop if met, and writes final accumulated color to output buffer. Parameters include earlyThreshold (transmittance threshold, e.g., 0.01f), numsamples (fixed number of traversal steps, e.g., 100), and delta (dummy segment length, e.g., 0.01f). name: NeRF Volume Rendering
head: NeRF Rendering Equation, Neural Radiance Field rendering, Vanilla NeRF Volume Rendering, Volume Rendering from Voxel Grid, classical volume rendering with MLP
body: NeRF Volume Rendering is a differentiable method for synthesizing photorealistic novel views of a scene by estimating volume density and RGB color along camera rays using a neural network. It solves the problem of continuous 3D scene representation and rendering by parameterizing the scene as an implicit function, typically implemented via Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). Unlike explicit voxel-based methods such as DVGO, which store features in a grid and use interpolation, the classical NeRF approach queries a continuous field directly at sampled points along the ray. This allows for high-fidelity view-dependent effects but incurs significant computational costs due to the large number of MLP queries required. Inputs: Camera pose: Origin \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and view direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (unit vector). Neural Network Model \mathcal{F}\Phi (or \mathcal{H}\Theta): An MLP that maps spatial coordinates and view directions to density and color. Sampling parameters: Number of sample points K (or N) and the distribution of samples along the ray. Outputs: Pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) \in \mathbb{R}^3 for the ray \mathbf{r}. MLP Network \mathcal{F}\Phi: A feed-forward neural network. Input: Concatenated spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) and view direction \mathbf{d}. Output: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Sample Points: A list of K 3D coordinates \{\mathbf{x}1, \dots, \mathbf{x}K\} along the ray. 1. Ray Generation: For a given pixel, generate a camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. 2. Sampling: Sample K points \mathbf{x}i along the ray within a defined interval [t{near}, t{far}]. The points are typically spaced by a distance \deltai. 3. MLP Query: For each sampled point \mathbf{x}i, query the MLP \mathcal{F}\Phi with input (\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d}) to obtain the volume density \sigmai and the RGB color \mathbf{c}i. 4. Transmittance Calculation: Compute the accumulated transmittance Ti for each sample point i. Ti represents the probability that the ray travels from the camera origin to sample i without being absorbed or scattered. Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \deltaj is the distance between sample j and j+1. For the first sample, T1 = 1. 5. Alpha Compositing: Compute the weight \alphai for each sample, representing the probability that the ray is absorbed at sample i: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). 6. Color Accumulation: Compute the final pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) as a weighted sum of the colors of the sampled points: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{K} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i = \sum{i=1}^{K} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i. Continuous Formulation: The process can also be viewed as a discretization of the continuous volume rendering integral: C(\mathbf{r}) = \int{t1}^{t2} T(t) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d}) \, dt where T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{t1}^{t} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(u)) \, du\right). Ray: \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Transmittance: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj) = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right). Segment Transmittance: \omegai = \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). Alpha (Absorption Probability): \alphai = 1 - \omegai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). Final Color: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{K} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i. Loss Function: The model is trained by minimizing the photometric loss (MSE) between rendered color C(\mathbf{r}) and ground truth color C{gt}(\mathbf{r}): L{NeRF} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \| C(\mathbf{r}) - C{gt}(\mathbf{r}) \|^2. K (or N): Number of sample points per ray. A typical value is 192. \deltai: Distance between adjacent samples xi and x{i+1}. \mathbf{x}: Spatial coordinate (x, y, z). \mathbf{d}: View direction. Can be represented as a 3D Cartesian unit vector or spherical coordinates (\phi, \theta). \sigma: Volume density (non-negative scalar). \mathbf{c}: RGB color (3D vector). Precision: The exponential function in transmittance calculation can lead to underflow if density is high or distances are large, resulting in Ti \approx 0. Boundaries: The sampling interval [t{near}, t{far}] must be chosen to encompass the scene. Points outside this range are ignored. Degenerate Input: If \sigmai = 0 for all samples, the color is black (or background color if explicitly handled). Computational Cost: The method requires a large number of MLP queries, leading to high training and rendering times. import math def nerfvolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, mlpnetwork, numsamples, near, far): """ Renders a single pixel color using NeRF volume rendering. Args: rayorigin (tuple): (ox, oy, oz) camera origin. raydirection (tuple): (dx, dy, dz) unit view direction. mlpnetwork (function): MLP function Fphi(x, d) -> (sigma, color). numsamples (int): Number of sample points K. near (float): Near clipping plane distance tnear. far (float): Far clipping plane distance tfar. Returns: tuple: (r, g, b) final pixel color. """ # Step 1: Sample points along the ray tvals = [near + i (far - near) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples)] # Step 2: Initialize accumulators accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numsamples): # Calculate 3D point position t = tvals[i] point = ( rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) # Step 3: Query MLP for density and color sigma, color = mlpnetwork(point, raydirection) # Step 4: Compute delta (distance to next sample) if i < numsamples - 1: delta = tvals[i+1] - tvals[i] else: # For the last sample, delta is undefined by the formula. # Standard practice uses the previous interval or a small epsilon. delta = tvals[i] - tvals[i-1] if i > 0 else 0.01 # Step 5: Compute alpha and accumulate color alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) weight = accumulatedtransmittance alpha finalcolor[0] += weight color[0] finalcolor[1] += weight color[1] finalcolor[2] += weight color[2] # Step 6: Update transmittance for next sample accumulatedtransmittance = math.exp(-sigma delta) # Early termination optimization if accumulatedtransmittance < 1e-4: break return tuple(finalcolor) DVGO Volume Rendering Forward: Uses a voxel grid to store features and trilinear interpolation, reducing MLP queries. Choose when memory is constrained and high resolution is needed, but view-dependent effects are less critical or approximated. DVGO Instant NGP: Uses multi-resolution hash encoding to accelerate NeRF training and rendering. Choose when fast training and real-time rendering are required. Instant NGP TensoRF: Decomposes the feature grid into low-rank factors for storage efficiency. Choose when memory footprint is a primary concern. TensoRF Time Complexity: Training and rendering times are typically very large due to the infinite and continuous nature of space requiring a multitude of giant MLP queries. Each pixel requires K MLP forward passes. Memory Complexity: The MLP weights are stored in memory. The size depends on the network architecture. No explicit voxel grid is stored in the classical NeRF formulation. Measured Performance: With K=192 samples, rendering high-resolution images can be slow without acceleration techniques. Strengths: High-quality view-dependent effects due to direct MLP query of color based on view direction. Continuous representation allows for arbitrary resolution. Limitations: Slow rendering speed. High memory usage for large networks. Requires significant computational resources for training. When to use: When photorealism and view-dependent effects are paramount, and computational resources are available. When not to use: When real-time rendering is required, or memory is severely constrained. NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It uses MLP networks to learn the radiance field of arbitrary scenes. Once sufficiently optimized, NeRF can estimate both the volume density \sigma and RGB color \mathbf{c} of the continuous function that describes the radiance field. It is then able to reconstruct a photorealistic view from an unseen pose using a differentiable volume rendering method. The method has become a foundational technique in 3D computer vision and graphics, inspiring numerous acceleration methods and applications in novel view synthesis, geometry reconstruction, and stylization. name: Indirect Observation Projection (Volumetric Rendering)
head: Differentiable Volumetric Rendering with Factor Fields, Factor Fields Projection
body: Indirect Observation Projection extends a projection function P to handle cases where only indirect observations (e.g., 2D images) are available, such as in neural radiance field optimization. It differs from direct observation methods by incorporating a differentiable volumetric rendering process that maps view direction and spatial features to color and density, followed by alpha compositing along camera rays. This allows the model to learn 4D signals (density and radiance) from 2D image observations. Inputs: View direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Spatial location \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Product features \bigodoti fi at location \mathbf{x}, where fi are factor fields and \bigodot denotes the Hadamard product. Camera ray parameters defining sample positions \mathbf{x}i and distances \deltai. Outputs: Rendered RGB color \mathbf{c}r \in \mathbb{R}^3 for the pixel. Data Structures: The method uses a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) as the default setting to map inputs to outputs. The MLP takes \mathbf{d} and \bigodoti fi as input and outputs color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. Sample points \{(\mathbf{c}i, \sigmai)\}{i=1}^N are stored along a camera ray. Steps: 1. Space Contraction (Optional): If the signal is bounded within a bounding box [\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}], normalize coordinates \mathbf{x} to [0, 1] using: \text{contract}(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}} For unbounded signals, a different contraction function is used (details not provided in sources). 2. Feature Product: Compute the Hadamard product of factor fields \bigodoti fi at the contracted location \mathbf{x}. 3. MLP Evaluation: Apply the MLP to map the view direction \mathbf{d} and the product features \bigodoti fi to color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and volume density \sigma \in \mathbb{R}. 4. Sampling: Sample N points along a camera ray. For each sample i, compute the distance to the next sample \deltai = \|\mathbf{x}{i+1} - \mathbf{x}i\|2. 5. Alpha Compositing: Compute the alpha value \alphai and transmittance Ti for each sample: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where Ti is the transmittance and \alphai is the alpha value of sample i. 6. Color Accumulation: Compute the final pixel color \mathbf{c}r using: \mathbf{c}r = \sum{i=1}^N Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i The composition of the learned MLP and this volume rendering function constitutes the projection function P. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def indirectobservationprojection(d, x, factorfields, raysamples, isbounded, u, v): """ d: view direction vector (3,) x: spatial location (3,) factorfields: list of factor field tensors raysamples: list of sample points along ray (N, 3) isbounded: boolean, whether the signal is bounded u: lower bound of bounding box (3,) v: upper bound of bounding box (3,) """ # Step 1: Space Contraction if isbounded: xcontracted = (x - u) / (v - u) else: # Not given in the sources. xcontracted = x # Step 2: Feature Product # Hadamard product of factor fields productfeatures = factorfields[0] for i in range(1, len(factorfields)): productfeatures = productfeatures factorfields[i] # Step 3: MLP Evaluation # The MLP takes d and productfeatures as input # Output: color c and density sigma # Not given in the sources: specific MLP architecture and weights. # Assuming a generic MLP function mlp is defined elsewhere. c, sigma = mlp(d, productfeatures) # Step 4: Sampling # Compute distances between neighboring samples N = len(raysamples) deltas = [] for i in range(N - 1): delta = np.linalg.norm(raysamples[i+1] - raysamples[i]) deltas.append(delta) # Handle the last sample if necessary (e.g., assume delta=0 or use a default) # Not given in the sources. # Step 5: Alpha Compositing alphas = 1 - np.exp(-sigma deltas) transmittances = np.ones(N) for i in range(1, N): transmittances[i] = transmittances[i-1] (1 - alphas[i-1]) # Step 6: Color Accumulation colorr = np.zeros(3) for i in range(N): colorr += transmittances[i] alphas[i] c[i] return colorr Parameters: N: Number of random samples along a camera ray. Typical value not given in the sources. MLP: Shallow non-linear multi-layer perceptron. Default setting in experiments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unbounded signals require a specific contraction function not detailed in the sources. Precision issues may arise in the exponential function for alpha calculation if \sigmai \deltai is very large or very small. Boundary conditions for the last sample in the ray are not specified. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples N and the MLP evaluation cost. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of factor fields and MLP weights. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows learning from indirect 2D observations; flexible model via MLP. Limitations: Requires numerical integration approximation; intractable volumetric projection integral. When to use: When optimizing neural radiance fields from 2D images. When not to use: When direct 4D signal observations are available. Origin: Introduced in "Factor Fields: A Unified Framework for Neural Fields and Beyond". History: Extends the concept of projection functions to include differentiable volumetric rendering for neural radiance fields. Usage: Used in optimizing neural radiance fields where only 2D images are observed. name: DVGO Ray Sampling and Rendering
head: DVGO forward pass, Direct Voxel Grid Optimization rendering
body: This method performs the forward pass for Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO), computing the final RGB color, depth, and optional segmentation masks for a batch of rays by marching through a dense voxel grid. It differs from NeRF Volume Rendering by using a pre-allocated 3D voxel grid for density and color storage, enabling faster training and inference via direct memory access, while maintaining the volume rendering integral formulation. It builds on DVGO Volume Rendering Forward. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape [N, 3]. raysd: Ray directions, shape [N, 3]. viewdirs: Normalized view directions, shape [N, 3]. renderkwargs: Dictionary containing near, far, stepsize, bg (background color). model: The DVGO model instance containing xyzmin, xyzmax, voxelsize, voxelsizeratio, density, k0, rgbnet, rgbnetdirect, segmaskgrid, dualsegmaskgrid, maskcache, numobjects, mode, fastcolorthres, renderfct, shift. Outputs: rgbmarched: Rendered RGB colors, shape [N, 3]. depth: Rendered depth (if requested). alphainvlast: Transmittance at the end of the ray, shape [N]. weights: Rendering weights for sampled points (filtered). segmaskmarched: Segmentation masks, shape [N, \text{num\objects}]. dualsegmaskmarched: Dual segmentation masks (if 'fine' mode). rawalpha, rawrgb, rayid, stepid: Intermediate filtered data. Data Structures: Voxel Grids: Dense 3D tensors. density stores raw density values. k0 stores raw color features (RGB + optional diffuse/specular components). segmaskgrid stores per-object probabilities. Ray Data: Batched tensors for origins, directions, and view vectors. Steps: 1. Ray-Bounding Box Intersection: Compute the intersection interval [t{min}, t{max}] of each ray with the voxel grid bounding box [xyz{min}, xyz{max}]. Let vec = rays\d. rate\a = \frac{xyz{min} - rays\o}{vec} rate\b = \frac{xyz{max} - rays\o}{vec} t{min} = \text{clamp}(\max(\min(rate\a, rate\b), \text{axis}=2), \text{min}=near, \text{max}=far) t{max} = \text{clamp}(\min(\max(rate\a, rate\b), \text{axis}=2), \text{min}=near, \text{max}=far) If t{min} \ge t{max}, the ray does not intersect the box or is outside the near/far planes. 2. Point Sampling: Calculate the step distance for sampling. step = stepsize \times voxel\size \times rng where rng is a random variable uniform in [0, 1] for jittering. Compute interpolation positions along the ray: interpx = t{min} + \frac{step}{\|rays\d\|} Compute ray points: rays\pts = rays\o + rays\d \times interpx 3. Filtering by Bounding Box and Cache: Use a CUDA kernel sampleptsonrays to determine which points lie within [xyz{min}, xyz{max}] and [near, far], generate maskoutbbox (points outside), assign rayid and stepid to each valid point, and return Nsteps (number of valid steps per ray). Filter to maskinbbox = ~maskoutbbox. If maskcache exists, further filter points using maskcache(rayspts[maskinbbox]). 4. Alpha Thresholding (Optimization): If renderfct > 0, create mask mask = (alpha > renderfct) and filter raypts, rayid, stepid, density, alpha by this mask. renderfct is set to \max(render\fct, fast\color\thres). 5. Alpha to Weight Conversion: Compute rendering weights from alpha values using the Alphas2Weights function, which implements the standard volume rendering accumulation. \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \Deltai) wi = \alphai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) This is implemented efficiently using Alphas2Weights.apply(alpha, rayid, N). If renderfct > 0, filter weights, alpha, raypts, rayid, stepid by mask = (weights > renderfct). 6. Segmentation Mask Query: If segmaskgrid.grid.requiresgrad, enable gradient tracking and query maskpred = segmaskgrid(rayspts). If mode == 'fine', also query dualmaskpred = dualsegmaskgrid(rayspts). If not requiring grad, query directly. 7. Color Query: Query raw color features k0 from the voxel grid: k0 = k0(rayspts). If rgbnet is None: rgb = \text{sigmoid}(k0). If rgbnet exists: Determine view-dependent input: If rgbnetdirect: k0view = k0. Else: k0view = k0[:, 3:], k0diffuse = k0[:,:3]. Compute view direction embedding: viewdirsemb = \text{concat}([viewdirs, \sin(viewdirs), \cos(viewdirs)]) with frequency multiplication applied as per standard positional encoding. Flatten and index viewdirsemb by rayid. Concatenate features: rgbfeat = \text{concat}([k0view, viewdirsemb], \text{dim}=-1). Compute logit: rgblogit = rgbnet(rgbfeat). Compute final RGB: If rgbnetdirect: rgb = \text{sigmoid}(rgblogit). Else: rgb = \text{sigmoid}(rgblogit + k0diffuse). 8. RGB Accumulation: Accumulate RGB using scatter sum: rgb\marched = \text{segment\coo}(src = weights \times rgb, index = ray\id, out = \text{zeros}([N, 3]), reduce = \text{'sum'}) 9. Segmentation Accumulation: If numobjects == 1: seg\mask\marched = \text{segment\coo}(src = weights \times mask\pred, index = ray\id, out = \text{zeros}([N, 1]), reduce = \text{'sum'}) If mode == 'fine', also compute dualsegmaskmarched. If numobjects != 1: seg\mask\marched = \text{segment\coo}(src = weights \times mask\pred, index = ray\id, out = \text{zeros}([N, num\objects]), reduce = \text{'sum'}) If mode == 'fine', also compute dualsegmaskmarched. 10. Background Addition: rgb\marched += alphainv\last \times bg Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def dvgoraysamplingandrendering(rayso, raysd, viewdirs, renderkwargs, model): device = rayso.device N = rayso.shape[0] near = renderkwargs['near'] far = renderkwargs['far'] stepsize = renderkwargs['stepsize'] bg = renderkwargs['bg'] xyzmin = model.xyzmin.to(device).unsqueeze(0) xyzmax = model.xyzmax.to(device).unsqueeze(0) voxelsize = model.voxelsize voxelsizeratio = model.voxelsizeratio renderfct = model.renderfct fastcolorthres = model.fastcolorthres # Step 1: Ray-Bounding Box Intersection vec = raysd ratea = (xyzmin - rayso) / vec rateb = (xyzmax - rayso) / vec tmin = torch.clamp(torch.minimum(ratea, rateb).amax(dim=-1), min=near, max=far) tmax = torch.clamp(torch.maximum(ratea, rateb).amin(dim=-1), min=near, max=far) # Step 2: Point Sampling # Generate random jitter for each step rng = torch.randlike(tmin) step = stepsize voxelsize rng interpx = tmin + step / raysd.norm(dim=-1, keepdim=True) rayspts = rayso + raysd interpx.unsqueeze(-1) # Step 3: Filter by Bounding Box and Cache # Simulates renderutilscuda.sampleptsonrays maskoutbbox = (rayspts < xyzmin.squeeze(0)).any(dim=-1) | (rayspts > xyzmax.squeeze(0)).any(dim=-1) maskoutbbox = maskoutbbox | (tmin < near) | (tmin > far) maskinbbox = ~maskoutbbox # Assign rayid and stepid rayid = torch.arange(N, device=device).unsqueeze(-1).expandas(tmin)[maskinbbox] stepid = torch.arange(tmin.shape[1], device=device)[maskinbbox] rayptsvalid = rayspts[maskinbbox] # Apply maskcache if exists if model.maskcache is not None: maskcacheresult = model.maskcache(rayptsvalid) rayptsvalid = rayptsvalid[maskcacheresult] rayid = rayid[maskcacheresult] stepid = stepid[maskcacheresult] Nsteps = rayid.shape[0] if Nsteps == 0: return { 'rgbmarched': torch.zeros(N, 3, device=device), 'alphainvlast': torch.ones(N, device=device), 'depth': torch.zeros(N, device=device), 'weights': torch.zeros(0, device=device), 'rawalpha': torch.zeros(0, device=device), 'rawrgb': torch.zeros(0, device=device), 'rayid': torch.zeros(0, dtype=torch.long, device=device), 'segmaskmarched': torch.zeros(N, model.numobjects, device=device), 'dualsegmaskmarched': torch.zeros(N, model.numobjects, device=device) if model.mode == 'fine' else None } # Step 4: Alpha Thresholding density = model.density(rayptsvalid) shift = model.shift interval = stepsize voxelsizeratio alpha = 1 - (1 + torch.exp(density + shift))(-interval) if renderfct > 0: renderfct = max(renderfct, fastcolorthres) mask = (alpha > renderfct) rayptsvalid = rayptsvalid[mask] rayid = rayid[mask] stepid = stepid[mask] density = density[mask] alpha = alpha[mask] # Step 5: Alpha to Weight Conversion weights, alphainvlast = alphastoweights(alpha, rayid, N) if renderfct > 0: mask = (weights > renderfct) rayptsvalid = rayptsvalid[mask] rayid = rayid[mask] stepid = stepid[mask] alpha = alpha[mask] weights = weights[mask] # Step 6: Segmentation Mask Query segmaskmarched = torch.zeros(N, model.numobjects, device=device) dualsegmaskmarched = None if model.segmaskgrid is not None: if model.segmaskgrid.grid.requiresgrad: model.segmaskgrid.grid.requiresgrad(True) maskpred = model.segmaskgrid(rayptsvalid) if model.mode == 'fine': dualmaskpred = model.dualsegmaskgrid(rayptsvalid) else: maskpred = model.segmaskgrid(rayptsvalid) if model.mode == 'fine': dualmaskpred = model.dualsegmaskgrid(rayptsvalid) if model.numobjects == 1: segmaskmarched = segmentcoo( src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) maskpred.unsqueeze(-1)), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros(N, 1, device=device), reduce='sum') if model.mode == 'fine': dualsegmaskmarched = segmentcoo( src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) dualmaskpred.unsqueeze(-1)), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros(N, 1, device=device), reduce='sum') else: segmaskmarched = segmentcoo( src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) maskpred), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros(N, model.numobjects, device=device), reduce='sum') if model.mode == 'fine': dualsegmaskmarched = segmentcoo( src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) dualmaskpred), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros(N, model.numobjects, device=device), reduce='sum') # Step 7: Color Query k0 = model.k0(rayptsvalid) if model.rgbnet is None: rgb = torch.sigmoid(k0) else: if model.rgbnetdirect: k0view = k0 else: k0view = k0[:, 3:] k0diffuse = k0[:,:3] viewdirsemb = torch.cat([ viewdirs, torch.sin(viewdirs), torch.cos(viewdirs) ], dim=-1) viewdirsembindexed = viewdirsemb[rayid] rgbfeat = torch.cat([k0view, viewdirsembindexed], dim=-1) rgblogit = model.rgbnet(rgbfeat) if model.rgbnetdirect: rgb = torch.sigmoid(rgblogit) else: rgb = torch.sigmoid(rgblogit + k0diffuse) # Step 8: RGB Accumulation rgbmarched = segmentcoo( src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) rgb), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros(N, 3, device=device), reduce='sum') # Step 10: Background Addition rgbmarched += (alphainvlast.unsqueeze(-1) bg) return { 'rgbmarched': rgbmarched, 'depth': None, 'alphainvlast': alphainvlast, 'weights': weights, 'rawalpha': alpha, 'rawrgb': rgb, 'rayid': rayid, 'segmaskmarched': segmaskmarched, 'dualsegmaskmarched': dualsegmaskmarched } def alphastoweights(alpha, rayid, N): """Computes rendering weights and final transmittance per ray.""" # Sort alpha by rayid and stepid to ensure correct accumulation order, sortidx = torch.sort(rayid) alphasorted = alpha[sortidx] # Compute transmittance transmittance = torch.cat([torch.ones(N, 1, device=alpha.device), torch.cumprod(1 - alphasorted, dim=0)[:-1]], dim=-1) # Handle rays with no samples transmittance = transmittance.scatterreduce(0, rayid.unsqueeze(-1).expandas(transmittance), transmittance, reduce='mean') weights = alphasorted transmittance alphainvlast = transmittance[N-1] if N > 0 else torch.zeros(N, device=alpha.device) return weights, alphainvlast def segmentcoo(src, index, out, reduce='sum'): """PyTorch scatter operation equivalent to COO segment sum.""" for i in range(out.shape[1]): out[:, i].scatteradd(0, index, src[:, i]) return out Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Time Complexity: Not given in the sources.
