name: Direct volume ray casting
head: DVR, ray marching, front-to-back compositing, image-order volume rendering
body: Direct volume ray casting (DVR) is an image-order rendering technique that synthesizes a 2D image from a 3D scalar volume by casting a ray through each pixel, sampling the volume along the ray, and integrating the optical properties (color and opacity) using the volume rendering integral. It solves the problem of visualizing the internal structure of semi-transparent volumetric data without extracting explicit geometry, allowing all voxels to potentially contribute to the final image. Unlike surface-based methods (e.g., Isosurface and first-hit ray casting) that stop at the first opaque boundary, DVR accumulates contributions from the entire ray segment within the volume, preserving depth cues and transparency. All direct volume ray casting methods share the following core mechanism: 1. Ray Definition: For each pixel (x, y) in the image plane, a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is defined, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. The ray is intersected with the volume bounding box to determine the entry parameter t{near} and exit parameter t{far}. 2. Sampling: The ray segment [t{near}, t{far}] is discretized into N samples at positions ti = t{near} + i \cdot \Delta t, where \Delta t = (t{far} - t{near}) / N. At each sample position \mathbf{p}i = r(ti), the scalar volume value V(\mathbf{p}i) is retrieved, typically via trilinear interpolation of the surrounding voxels. 3. Classification (Transfer Function): The scalar value V(\mathbf{p}i) is mapped to optical properties: a color vector \mathbf{c}i (RGB) and an opacity scalar \alphai (A). This mapping is defined by a transfer function T(V) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha). The opacity is often corrected for the step size \Delta t to approximate continuous attenuation, using models such as Beer-Lambert: \alphai = 1 - e^{-\sigmai \Delta t}, where \sigmai is the extinction coefficient derived from V(\mathbf{p}i). 4. Compositing (Integration): The samples are composited into the final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out} using the front-to-back volume rendering equation: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alpha{out} = 1 - \prod{i=1}^{N} (1 - \alphai) In iterative form, for each sample i: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai where \mathbf{C}{acc} and \alpha{acc} are initialized to (0, 0). 5. Shading: At each sample, a shading model (e.g., Phong, Blinn-Phong) may be applied to compute the base color \mathbf{c}i based on the local gradient \nabla V(\mathbf{p}i), which serves as the surface normal. Generates a 2D projection by processing 3D data as 2D slices, applying transfer functions, and compositing. Slower than direct ray casting due to slice-based overhead. Addresses visual artifacts from undersampling by smoothing transitions between discrete samples and continuous geometry across different scales. Synthesizes novel views by querying a neural network along camera rays and integrating outputs using classical volume rendering techniques. Stabilizes stochastic or noisy results by blending the current frame with a history buffer, specifically selecting the closest hit to preserve depth boundaries. Renders multiple volume datasets simultaneously by extending single-volume mappers to accept multiple datasets and properties, using GPU shaders for traversal. Defines how continuous scalar fields are approximated from discrete voxel data, trading computational cost, visual smoothness, and aliasing artifacts. Projects each voxel directly onto the image plane, relying on data traversal order for hidden surface removal, contrasting with image-order ray casting. Processes a stack of parallel planes instead of individual pixels, propagating light and view rays across layers to accumulate color and opacity. Represents view-dependent color and opacity data using SH coefficients stored in a voxel grid to solve expensive per-sample shading. Integrates a pre-computed volume to apply position-dependent modifications to visualization parameters, such as gamma correction. Converts 3D volumetric data into 2D polygonal slices rasterized and composited by standard graphics hardware for efficient large-volume rendering. Implements direct volume ray casting on programmable graphics hardware using a multi-pass stream model to solve CPU performance bottlenecks. Dynamically slices a 3D dataset using a semi-transparent geometric plane to reveal internal structures occluded by opaque outer layers. Treats volume datasets and geometric objects as Volume-of-Interests (VOIs) in a unified rendering framework with priority-based compositing. Generates volumetric data or manages rendering performance dynamically using procedural evaluation instead of static pre-computed textures. Deviates from standard front-to-back compositing to address specific requirements like projective diagnostic imaging, medical photo-realism, and neural scene composition. Offloads computationally intensive sampling and compositing stages to the GPU, utilizing programmable shaders and texture hardware for interactive frame rates. A lightweight, CPU-based ray-tracing tool for fast visualization of point-like data from cosmological simulations, solving large-scale particle dataset rendering. Replaces 2D texture atlases with a single 3D volume texture for raymarching, allowing larger volumes and simplifying edge handling. Visualizes datasets with non-uniform spatial resolution by leveraging hierarchical structures to reduce computational and memory overhead. Approximates complex light-material interactions by pre-computing SH coefficients for material and light functions on the CPU for GPU ray marching. Reconstructs particle density on-demand in screen space at viewport resolution, combining splatting, texture slicing, and ray casting to avoid aliasing. Utilizes fixed-point arithmetic for ray traversal and compositing in VTK, particularly suited for rendering medical images. The foundational technique generating images by casting rays from the camera, sampling a 3D scalar field at regular intervals, and accumulating via front-to-back compositing. Divides space into independent blocks, rendering each separately and blending results to solve resource isolation in distributed environments. Applies stylized, non-photorealistic shading effects including tone detail and specular highlights using discrete tone mapping. Addresses stair-stepping artifacts at volume boundaries by introducing a smaller final segment to complete the ray march. Replaces per-voxel trilinear interpolation with a two-stage process of calculating ray-plane intersections and interpolating between them. Optimized for large-scale regular 3D spatial data fields, prioritizing rendering speed and high-frequency component preservation over physical lighting accuracy. Decomposes the workload into multiple passes to decouple computational stages like light attenuation and color compositing. Extends standard compositing to support Full, Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP), and XRay rendering modes. Defines how scalar data is mapped to color and opacity, enabling visualization of internal structures by assigning transparency. A rendering technique for unsorted cell projection using optical models that lead to a commutative blend function, allowing compositing in arbitrary order. Models allowing arbitrary order compositing include maximum intensity projection and restrictions of the full volume density model to either the source term or the absorption term. Implements the Svox1 rendering formula using nearest-neighbor interpolation with infinitely many steps, including forward, backward, and fused variants. An optimization for ray casting that uses the extracted isosurface as an opaque barrier to terminate rays early, rendering the isosurface's 3D texture coordinates into the exit point texture. To counteract the last incorrect sample, it weights it by the fraction of the step that is outside of the surface. Straightforward integration causes aliasing/banding artifacts because the isosurface coordinates may not lie exactly on the sample point of a marching ray. Rendering directly from the binary Mixture Graph representation at interactive rates on the GPU, supporting real-time transfer function editing across all scales of the mipmap. The rendering uses a direct volume raymarcher sampling at 0.5 voxels. Pre-computed normals derived from the method cause artifacts in the form of caps around the medial axis where segments leave the domain. Lighting contributions are computed without knowledge of position, restricting the method to light and camera at infinity. Used for real-time visual analysis applications in neuroscience and material science. A technique to render multiple volumes by taking the value of the texture itself as the color, bypassing the colormap lookup, using a 4D array (z, y, x, 4) passed directly to the texture. Requires colormaps that can work in Python on Numpy arrays. Implemented in the vispy-multivol repository as the RGBAVolumeVisual class. A strategy to break the stripe pattern of onion ring artifacts by varying sample locations of rays in adjacent pixels, either by using variable sample distances or a random offset at the beginning of each ray. Result is a more 'dithered' image where errors are randomly distributed over pixels. Solves transport for multiple rays in parallel on CPU by iterating over rays and calling the single-ray solver for each. Input arrays sigma, source, initialintensity are row-major [ray][sample]. Computes unique frustum block coordinates for the camera viewpoint to determine which volume blocks need to be rendered. Performs ray casting on the volume blocks using intrinsic, extrinsic, width, height, and render attributes. Extracts voxel indices and interpolation ratios from the ray cast results to reconstruct color via weighted interpolation of volume attributes. Reconstructs color by multiplying the volume color attribute at the hit indices by the interpolation ratios, summing over the 8 corner voxels of the hit cell, and normalizing by 255. Direct volume ray casting was introduced by Marc Levoy in his seminal 1988 paper "Display of Surfaces from Volume Data". Levoy coined the term "direct volume rendering" and defined the pipeline of classification, shading, and compositing, emphasizing the visualization of weak or fuzzy surfaces with smooth silhouettes. The method is based on the volume rendering equation, which integrates radiative energy along rays of sight. Early implementations were software-based, but the advent of programmable graphics hardware enabled GPU-accelerated ray casting, significantly improving performance. The technique is used in scientific visualization and computer graphics for visualizing semi-transparent materials. name: 2D Visualization from 3D Grid (Slow)
head: 2D Slice Compositing, Direct Volume Rendering (DVR), Slice Projection, Slice-Based Volume Rendering (Back-to-Front), matRad_rayTracing Function
body: This method generates a 2D projection of a 3D scalar volume by processing the data as a series of 2D slices, applying a transfer function to each slice, and compositing them into a 2D image using the over operator. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric data without extracting surface geometry. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly iterating through slices in a software loop and performing per-slice compositing, often relying on specific data structures like the cameragrid for ordering. The method operates primarily as a software-based iterative compositing loop, with a specialized ray-tracing depth calculation variant in matRad. Input Volume (V): A scalar field s: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, discretely sampled on a regular 3D grid. Camera/Grid Configuration: A set of viewing parameters defining the projection plane. In the iterative model, this is represented as a cameragrid containing slice data ordered for compositing. In the ray-tracing model, this includes steering information (stfElement), rotation coordinates (rotcoordsV), and lateral cutoffs. Transfer Function (TF): A mapping from scalar values to RGBA color and opacity. The notes specify a Gaussian mixture model applied to the logarithm of the input data. Output Image (I): A 2D image with dimensions matching the camera grid, containing the composited RGB values. 1. Volume Grid: A 3D array of scalars. In the ray-tracing context, linear voxel indices V and rotation coordinates rotcoordsV are used to map 3D space to the beam's eye view. 2. Camera Grid: A list or array of 2D slices (dataslice). The order of iteration through this grid determines the compositing direction (back-to-front or front-to-back). 3. Radiological Depth Cube (radDepthCube): In the matRad implementation, a 3D structure storing radiological depth values computed from CT data and voxel indices. The transfer function uses Gaussian mixtures. The input scalar x is first transformed using the natural logarithm: x' = \ln(x). The resulting Red (r), Green (g), Blue (b), and Alpha (a) components are calculated as follows: r = 1.0 \cdot e^{-\frac{(x' - 9.0)^2}{1.0}} + 0.1 \cdot e^{-\frac{(x' - 3.0)^2}{0.1}} + 0.1 \cdot e^{-\frac{(x' + 3.0)^2}{0.5}} g = 1.0 \cdot e^{-\frac{(x' - 9.0)^2}{1.0}} + 1.0 \cdot e^{-\frac{(x' - 3.0)^2}{0.1}} + 0.1 \cdot e^{-\frac{(x' + 3.0)^2}{0.5}} b = 0.1 \cdot e^{-\frac{(x' - 9.0)^2}{1.0}} + 0.1 \cdot e^{-\frac{(x' - 3.0)^2}{0.1}} + 1.0 \cdot e^{-\frac{(x' + 3.0)^2}{0.5}} a = 0.6 \cdot e^{-\frac{(x' - 9.0)^2}{1.0}} + 0.1 \cdot e^{-\frac{(x' - 3.0)^2}{0.1}} + 0.01 \cdot e^{-\frac{(x' + 3.0)^2}{0.5}} The following steps describe the software-based implementation found in. 1. Initialization: Initialize the output image I to zeros with shape matching the camera grid dimensions: python image = np.zeros((cameragrid.shape[1], cameragrid.shape[2], 3)) 2. Iteration: Iterate through each slice in the cameragrid. python for dataslice in cameragrid: 3. Transfer Function Application: Apply the transfer function to the logarithm of the slice data to obtain RGBA values for each pixel in the slice: python r, g, b, a = transferfunction(np.log(dataslice)) 4. Compositing: Composite the slice onto the accumulated image using the standard over operator for each RGB channel. For the red channel (and similarly for green and blue): python image[:,:, 0] = a r + (1 - a) image[:,:, 0] If a is 0, the slice is transparent and does not affect the background. If a is 1, the slice completely occludes the background. 5. Clipping: Clip the final image values to the range [0.0, 1.0] to handle any numerical overflow: python image = np.clip(image, 0.0, 1.0) Logarithmic Transformation: The input data is transformed using np.log() before applying the transfer function. Viewing Angle: The camera view can be rotated by an angle \theta = \frac{\pi}{2} \cdot \frac{i}{N{angles}} around the Y/Z axis using rotation matrices: q{yR} = qy \cos(\theta) - qz \sin(\theta) q{zR} = qy \sin(\theta) + qz \cos(\theta) Transparency Threshold: In some implementations, the alpha channel (last dimension) of the grid cells tensor is thresholded below a transparencythreshold to 0.0. Compositing Order: The loop for dataslice in cameragrid: implies a specific order. If cameragrid is ordered from back to front relative to the viewer, this implements front-to-back compositing (standard for alpha blending). If ordered front-to-back, it implements back-to-front compositing. The code does not explicitly sort slices by depth, relying on the data structure order. Incorrect ordering leads to visual artifacts where distant objects appear in front of closer ones. Logarithm of Zero/Negative: Applying np.log() to zero or negative voxel values will result in -inf or nan. The transfer function must handle these cases, or the input data must be shifted/clipped to positive values before logging. A sparse visualization technique that filters a 3D grid tensor based on opacity and gradient magnitude thresholds, then renders the surviving cells as a 3D scatter plot. It avoids the computational overhead of ray casting or volume integration, making it suitable for rapid inspection of sparse structures. It sets itself apart from its sibling 3D Table Computation on GPU by avoiding precomputed lookup tables and instead performing direct scalar filtering and point plotting, and from its parent by explicitly leveraging gradient magnitude for structural filtering and outputting a 3D point cloud rather than 2D slices. This method computes a 3D pre-integration table for volume rendering by rasterizing 2D slices on the GPU, where each pixel represents a specific triplet of scalar values (sf, sm, sb) along a ray. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating the volume rendering integral for transfer functions defined on 8-bit scalar domains by pre-computing the integration results into a texture. It is distinguished from its parent by utilizing GPU rasterization and pre-integration to accelerate the evaluation of the volume rendering equation, rather than performing per-ray sampling in software or on the CPU. name: Grid Visualization with Thresholding
head: 3D Scatter Plot Visualization, Thresholded Grid Visualization
body: Grid Visualization with Thresholding filters a 3D grid tensor based on opacity and gradient magnitude thresholds, then plots the surviving cells as a 3D scatter plot. It provides a direct visualization path for volumetric data by bypassing ray casting and volume integration, making it suitable for rapid inspection of sparse structures. Inputs: gridcells: A tensor containing density/opacity values and RGB color channels. gradients: (Optional) A tensor containing the gradient vector for each cell. threshold: Float. Opacity threshold for visualization. Default: 0.0. dothreshold: Boolean. Whether to apply the opacity threshold. Default: True. cleanstrays: Boolean. Whether to apply noise cleaning. Default: False. Outputs: A list of 3D coordinates (x, y, z) and corresponding RGB colors (r, g, b) for all cells where the final alpha value is greater than 0. Data Structures: The grid is stored as a dense tensor. Sparsity is achieved by filtering rather than explicit sparse structures. Steps: 1. Load the gridcells tensor onto the target device. 2. If gradient data exists and thresholding is enabled, zero out cells where the gradient norm is below 3.0 \times 10^{-6}. Formula: If ||\nabla f{i,j,k}|| < 3.0 \times 10^{-6}, then \text{grid\cells}{i,j,k} = 0. 3. Clip all values in gridcells to the range [0, 1]. 4. If dothreshold is True, zero out alpha values below the threshold and set all non-zero alpha values to 1.0. Formula: If \alpha{i,j,k} < \text{threshold}, then \alpha{i,j,k} = 0; else \alpha{i,j,k} = 1. 5. If cleanstrays is True, apply convolvegridtoremovenoise twice with different parameters: kernel size 3 with radius 1, followed by kernel size 7 with radius 3. 6. Extract coordinates (x, y, z) and RGB values for all cells where the final alpha value is > 0. 7. Plot the extracted points using a 3D plotting library such as Plotly or Matplotlib. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def gridvisualizationwiththresholding(gridcells, gradients=None, threshold=0.0, dothreshold=True, cleanstrays=False): # 1. Load grid cells tensor (assumed already on device) # 2. Gradient filtering if gradients is not None and dothreshold: gradnorm = torch.norm(gradients, dim=-1) mask = gradnorm < 3.0e-06 gridcells[mask] = 0 # 3. Clip values to [0, 1] gridcells = torch.clamp(gridcells, 0.0, 1.0) # 4. Opacity thresholding if dothreshold: opacity = gridcells[..., 0] opacity[opacity < threshold] = 0.0 opacity[opacity > 0] = 1.0 gridcells[..., 0] = opacity # 5. Noise cleaning if cleanstrays: # convolvegridtoremovenoise is not defined in the sources pass # 6. Extract coordinates and RGB values for cells with alpha > 0 alpha = gridcells[..., 0] validmask = alpha > 0 indices = torch.nonzero(validmask, astuple=False) # Assumes tensor layout (depth, height, width, channels) x = indices[:, 2].float() y = indices[:, 1].float() z = indices[:, 0].float() # Assumes RGBA channel layout r = gridcells[validmask, 1] g = gridcells[validmask, 2] b = gridcells[validmask, 3] # 7. Plot using Plotly or Matplotlib (external step) return x, y, z, r, g, b Parameters: threshold: Opacity threshold for visualization. Default: 0.0. dothreshold: Whether to apply the opacity threshold. Default: True. cleanstrays: Whether to remove stray voxels. Default: False. Pitfalls: Gradient-based thresholding uses a fixed threshold of 3.0 \times 10^{-6} for gradient norm. Visualization thresholding uses a configurable opacity threshold, which is distinct from the gradient threshold. The noise cleaning step relies on convolvegridtoremovenoise, which is not defined in the sources. Density Range Windowing restricts rendering to voxels whose density falls within a specified [min, max] range, allowing selective visualization of specific structures within a volume. It sets itself apart from its parent method, Grid Visualization with Thresholding, by operating on a continuous density interval rather than a single binary opacity threshold or gradient magnitude, enabling finer control over semi-transparent vs. dense core separation. It is chosen when volumetric opacity integration is required rather than geometric abstraction. Glyph Lines is a sparse visualization technique for 3D vector fields that samples the field on a 2D grid at a fixed coordinate and renders each sample as a line segment. It solves the problem of visualizing flow direction and magnitude in a specific slice of a volumetric dataset without the computational cost of full volume ray casting. It differs from its parent method, Grid Visualization with Thresholding, by explicitly encoding vector direction and magnitude into geometric primitives (lines) rather than plotting scalar grid cells as points. It is chosen when vector field topology and flow visualization are required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Density Range Windowing
head: Density Clipping, Volume Thresholding
body: Density Range Windowing restricts volume rendering to voxels whose scalar density falls within a specified [min, max] interval, enabling the selective visualization of specific anatomical or material structures. Unlike sibling methods such as Glyph Lines that visualize vector or gradient fields, this technique operates as a direct scalar interval filter applied during ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar grid of density values. Output: A 2D image where voxels outside [min, max] contribute zero opacity. Data Structures: The method uses a window vector to store bounds: window.x: Window low (min) window.y: Window high (max) Steps: 1. For each sample point along the ray, retrieve the scalar density value d. 2. Compare d against the window bounds: if d < m\densityMin or d > m\densityMax, set opacity \alpha = 0. 3. If m\densityMin \le d \le m\densityMax, evaluate the base opacity using the transfer function. 4. Composite the sample using front-to-back or back-to-front accumulation. 5. Adjust m\densityMin to drop semi-transparent structures (e.g., skin/foliage) and retain dense cores (bone), or lower m\densityMax to peel off densest structures. Formulas: \alpha = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } d < m\densityMin \text{ or } d > m\densityMax \\ \text{TF}(d) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where d is the sampled density, \alpha is the opacity contribution, and \text{TF}(d) is the transfer function evaluation. Parameters: m\densityMin (default 0.0f) and m\densityMax (default 1.0f) define the visible density interval. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If m\densityMin > m\densityMax, the interval is invalid and no voxels render. Boundaries: Voxels exactly on the boundary (m\densityMin or m\densityMax) are included (inclusive interval). Degenerate Input: If the entire volume density range lies outside [m\densityMin, m\densityMax], the result is a black screen. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applydensitywindow(density: float, minval: float, maxval: float, baseopacity: float) -> float: """Applies density range windowing to a sample's base opacity.""" if density < minval or density > maxval: return 0.0 return baseopacity # Base opacity is computed from the transfer function MIDA Visualization is a density range windowing technique that allows users to define settable ranges of visualized values, enabling selective visibility of specific structures within a volume. It distinguishes itself from standard thresholding by supporting multiple, independent visible ranges (envelopes) for different parts of the volume, facilitating complex exploration tasks such as carving and peeling. Not given in the sources. The technique adapts radiological "Window Level/Width" (WL/WW) practices, where the dynamic range of Hounsfield Units is remapped to display capabilities. In the referenced implementation, presets such as "CT Bone", "CT Soft Tissue", and "CT Angio" use default window levels and widths to control the visible density interval. sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, https://github.com/sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: MIDA Visualization
head: Visible range sliders
body: MIDA Visualization is a density range windowing technique that allows users to define settable ranges of visualized values, enabling selective visibility of specific structures within a volume. It distinguishes itself from standard thresholding by supporting multiple, independent visible ranges (envelopes) for different parts of the volume, facilitating complex exploration tasks such as carving and peeling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset (3D grid of scalar values) and a set of user-defined visible ranges (min/max pairs). Output: A rendered image where voxels falling outside the defined ranges are treated as transparent or invisible. Data Structures: Visible Range Envelope: A collection of intervals [mini, maxi] defining the visible sub-ranges of volume values. User Interaction State: Tracks the current active envelope and the mode of interaction (e.g., 2D painting, slider adjustment). Steps: 1. Initialize Ranges: Define initial visible ranges for the volume. 2. Define Envelopes: Users adjust the min/max values for specific regions using visible range sliders or painting tools. 3. Carving/Peeling: To hide data or expose internal features, specify an empty range where min = max. 4. Render: For each voxel, check if its density value v falls within any defined interval [mini, maxi]. 5. Interact: Users can rotate, move, and adjust parameters within the context of the selected envelope. Formulas: A voxel with density v is visible if: \exists i: mini \le v \le maxi Parameters: Visible Range Sliders: Controls the min/max visualized values for specific regions. Empty Range: A special case where min = max effectively carves away the selected region. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fuzzy Data: In data with low intensity variability (e.g., MRI soft tissues), partial volume effects make it difficult to isolate features. Ambiguity: Semi-translucent representations can lead to ambiguities in spatial relationships, especially when closer features clash with further ones. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isvisible(density, envelopes): """ Check if a voxel density is within any of the defined visible envelopes. Args: density (float): The density value of the voxel. envelopes (list of tuples): List of (min, max) tuples defining visible ranges. Returns: bool: True if the density is within any envelope, False otherwise. """ for minval, maxval in envelopes: if minval <= density <= maxval: return True return False def rendervoxel(density, envelopes, opacityfunction): """ Render a single voxel based on its density and the current envelopes. Args: density (float): The density value of the voxel. envelopes (list of tuples): List of (min, max) tuples defining visible ranges. opacityfunction (function): A function that maps density to opacity. Returns: float: The opacity of the voxel (0 if invisible). """ if isvisible(density, envelopes): return opacityfunction(density) else: return 0.0 A technique for visualizing fuzzy data with low intensity variability (e.g., MRI scans of soft tissues) by painting an arbitrarily shaped 2D window on the screen to provide semi-translucent spatial representations and aid in understanding spatial relationships. It is chosen when 3D isolation is difficult due to partial volume effects and ambiguous depth cues. Steps include painting a 2D envelope on the screen and adjusting visualization parameters within that context. Pitfalls include difficulty in isolating features due to lack of clearly defined surfaces. Usage is common for MRI scans of soft tissues like brain matter or fruit pulp. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Flexibility in exploring internal features through carving and peeling; intuitive interaction via painting metaphors. Limitations: Ambiguities in spatial interpretation for fuzzy data; difficulty in isolating features in 3D space. When to Use: For volumes where users need to selectively visualize specific density ranges or carve away occluding parts. MIDA Visualization was introduced in the context of context-preserving volume image exploration using a 3D painting metaphor. It builds on the concept of density range windowing to allow more complex interactions such as carving and peeling. The method was evaluated through user studies, showing positive results in terms of ease of learning and control. name: Glyph Lines
head: Active Vector Field Arrow Rendering, ActiveVectorValuesOp, Vector Glyphs as Lines, Vector rendering
body: Glyph Lines visualizes a 3D vector field by sampling it on a 2D grid at a fixed coordinate and rendering each vector as a line segment centered at the sample point, scaled by magnitude and colored by magnitude. It builds on Grid Visualization with Thresholding by replacing the 3D scatter plot of grid cells with directed line glyphs that explicitly encode vector direction and magnitude, rather than just scalar presence. Unlike Density Range Windowing which focuses on scalar opacity, this method is specialized for vector field topology and flow visualization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D vector field grid (e.g., OpenVDB or texture), a fixed scalar coordinate x defining the 2D slice plane, and rendering parameters (glyphLength, magnitudeCtfNormalizeMult). Output: A set of line primitives (start and end vertices with associated colors) representing the vector field on the slice. Data Structures: Mask Tree: A boolean topology tree derived from the grid to identify active voxels. Vertex Buffer: Stores pairs of 3D coordinates (start and end points) for each glyph. Size: 2 \times \text{voxelCount} vertices. Color Buffer: Stores RGB colors for each vertex. Size: 2 \times \text{voxelCount} colors. Index Buffer: Indices for GLLINES primitive type. Size: 2 \times \text{voxelCount} indices. Parameters: x: The fixed x-coordinate for the 2D grid of glyphs. glyphLength: Scaling factor for the length of the glyph line. magnitudeCtfNormalizeMult: Normalization factor calculated as \text{vectorMagnitudeCtfLength} / \text{maxMagnitude}. worldSize: The physical dimensions of the volume. glyphsCount: The number of samples in the x and y dimensions of the 2D grid. Steps: 1. Topology Preparation: Create a boolean mask tree from the grid's topology using mask->topologyUnion(tree) and voxelize active tiles using mask->voxelizeActiveTiles(). 2. Global Maximum Calculation: Calculate the maximum vector length in the tree using openvdb::tools::minMax(tree).max().length() and store it in length. 3. Thread Execution (GPU Kernel): Calculate global thread ID id. Calculate total count totalCount = glyphsCount.x glyphsCount.y. If id >= totalCount, return. Calculate grid coordinates: col = id % glyphsCount.x, row = id / glyphsCount.x. Calculate position: position = makefloat3(x, col (worldSize.x / glyphsCount.x), row (worldSize.y / glyphsCount.y)). Sample vector field: vector = tex3D(vectorFieldTex, position.x volumeCoordSpaceMult.x, position.y volumeCoordSpaceMult.y, position.z volumeCoordSpaceMult.z). Set start vertex: outputPts[id] = position. Set end vertex: outputPts[id + 1] = position + normalize(makefloat3(vector.x, vector.y, vector.z)) glyphLength vector.w magnitudeCtfNormalizeMult 0.5. Sample color: color = tex1D(vectorMagnitudeCtfTex, vector.w magnitudeCtfNormalizeMult). Set colors: outVertexColors[id] and outVertexColors[id + 1] to makefloat3(color.x, color.y, color.z). 4. CPU/Alternative Iteration (OpenVDB specific): Allocate buffers for pointCount 2 points (start and end of each arrow), colors, and indices. pointCount is voxelCount 2. Iterate over all active voxels in the mask's leaf nodes. For each voxel at coordinate ijk: 1. Get the world position pos via grid->indexToWorld(ijk). 2. Store pos as the start point. 3. Get the vector value vec from the grid. 4. Calculate weight w = \text{vec.length()} / \text{length}. 5. Normalize vec. 6. Calculate end position pos += grid->voxelSize()[0] 0.9 vec. 7. Store end position. 8. Calculate color using interpolation: color = w \times (0.9, 0.3, 0.3) + (1.0 - w) \times (0.3, 0.3, 0.9). 9. Multiply final RGB values by 0.3 for the start point and 1.0 for the end point. 5. Buffer Generation: Generate GPU buffers for vertices, colors, and indices using mVectorBuffer->genVertexBuffer, genColorBuffer, and genIndexBuffer(indices, GLLINES). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderglyphlines(vectorfieldtex, worldsize, glyphscount, glyphlength, magnitudectfnormalizemult): """ Renders vector field glyphs on a 2D slice at a fixed x-coordinate. """ # Total number of glyphs to render totalcount = glyphscount.x glyphscount.y # Output buffers outputpts = [None] (totalcount 2) outvertexcolors = [None] (totalcount 2) for id in range(totalcount): # Calculate grid coordinates col = id % glyphscount.x row = id // glyphscount.x # Calculate position on the 2D slice # Note: x is fixed, y and z are derived from grid indices # Assuming worldSize.x/y correspond to the dimensions of the slice plane # and glyphscount.x/y define the resolution of that slice. posx = 0.0 # Fixed x-coordinate, typically passed as parameter or assumed 0.5 if normalized posy = col (worldsize.x / glyphscount.x) posz = row (worldsize.y / glyphscount.y) position = (posx, posy, posz) # Sample vector field # volumeCoordSpaceMult scales world coordinates to texture coordinates [0,1] # This is a placeholder for the actual texture sampling logic vector = samplevectorfield(vectorfieldtex, position) # Set start vertex outputpts[id] = position # Set end vertex # Normalize the vector direction vecnorm = normalize(vector) # Calculate end position # vector.w is used as magnitude in this specific implementation endpos = ( position[0] + vecnorm[0] glyphlength vector.w magnitudectfnormalizemult 0.5, position[1] + vecnorm[1] glyphlength vector.w magnitudectfnormalizemult 0.5, position[2] + vecnorm[2] glyphlength vector.w magnitudectfnormalizemult 0.5) outputpts[id + 1] = endpos # Sample color based on magnitude # vectorMangitudeCtfTex is a 1D texture mapping magnitude to color colorsample = samplecolortexture(vector.w magnitudectfnormalizemult) # Set colors for both start and end vertices outvertexcolors[id] = (colorsample.x, colorsample.y, colorsample.z) outvertexcolors[id + 1] = (colorsample.x, colorsample.y, colorsample.z) return outputpts, outvertexcolors def normalize(v): length = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 if length == 0: return (0, 0, 0) return (v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length) def samplevectorfield(tex, pos): # Placeholder for actual texture sampling # Returns a float4 (x, y, z, magnitude) return (0, 0, 0, 0) def samplecolortexture(t): # Placeholder for 1D texture sampling return (0, 0, 0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Magnitude: If the vector magnitude is zero, the direction is undefined. The implementation normalizes the vector, which may result in NaN or arbitrary direction if not handled. The sources do not explicitly define a guard for zero vectors, but normalization of a zero vector is a standard pitfall. Precision: The use of float3 and texture sampling may introduce precision errors in position calculation, especially for large volumes. Boundary Conditions: The fixed x-coordinate must be within the volume bounds. If it is outside, the texture sampling may return zero or undefined values. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of active voxels or grid samples. The GPU kernel runs in parallel for each glyph. Memory Complexity: O(N) for vertex, color, and index buffers. Performance: Performance depends on the number of active voxels and the efficiency of the texture sampling and GPU kernel execution. Strengths: Simple and efficient for visualizing vector fields on 2D slices. Provides clear direction and magnitude information. Limitations: Limited to 2D slices. Does not show 3D flow structures directly. Performance may degrade with very high resolution grids. When to use: When visualizing vector fields on specific planes or slices is required. When not to use: When 3D flow visualization or particle tracing is needed. Glyph Lines is a technique for visualizing vector fields, often implemented using GPU shaders and texture sampling. It is commonly used in scientific visualization to analyze fluid dynamics, electromagnetic fields, and other vector data. The implementation described here is based on CUDA and OpenVDB. name: 3D Table Computation on GPU
head: 3D Texture Lookup Volume Rendering, GPU-based 3D Texture Volume Rendering
body: This method computes a 3D pre-integration table for volume rendering by rasterizing 2D slices on the GPU, where each pixel represents a specific triplet of scalar values (sf, sm, sb) along a ray. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating the volume rendering integral for transfer functions defined on 8-bit scalar domains by pre-computing the integration results into a texture. It is distinguished from its parent method, 2D Visualization from 3D Grid (Slow), by utilizing GPU rasterization and pre-integration to accelerate the evaluation of the volume rendering equation, rather than performing per-ray sampling in software or on the CPU. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity, defined on an 8-bit domain. Output: A 3D texture (pre-integration table) of size 256 \times 256 \times 256, where each voxel (i, j, k) stores the accumulated color and opacity for a ray segment traversing scalar values i, j, k. Data Structures: Pre-integration Table: A 3D texture with dimensions 256 \times 256 \times 256. Each texel stores a 4-component floating-point vector (R, G, B, \alpha) representing the accumulated color and opacity. Viewport: 256 \times 256 pixels. Projection: Orthogonal projection matrix. Algorithm Steps: 1. Setup: Configure an orthogonal projection matrix and a viewport of size 256 \times 256. Initialize the 3D texture for the pre-integration table. 2. Slice Rendering Loop: For each depth index k from 0 to 255 (representing the back sample sb): a. Set a uniform variable in the fragment shader to the current back sample value sb = k. b. Render a quadrilateral parallel to the projection plane, filling the viewport. c. Fragment Shader Execution: For each pixel (x, y) in the viewport: i. Map screen coordinates to scalar values: sf = x (front sample), sm = y (middle sample). ii. Determine the coefficients A, B, C for the second-order polynomial approximation according to equation (2) in the source. iii. Initialize accumulated color C{acc} = (0, 0, 0) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0. iv. Iterate a fixed number of steps N over the interval [0, 1]. For each step t: 1. Compute the scalar value s at the current step using Horner's rule for numerical accuracy and performance: s = (A \cdot t + B) \cdot t + C. 2. Fetch the color c(s) and opacity \alpha(s) from the transfer function for scalar s. 3. Composite the result using a back-to-front algorithm with the previous accumulated color and opacity. v. Write the final (C{acc}, \alpha{acc}) to the frame buffer at pixel (x, y). d. Perform a copy-to-texture operation to store the rendered 2D slice into the k-th slice of the 3D pre-integration table. Parameters: Number of Iterations (N): User-defined. Determines the quality of the pre-integration. Scalar Domain: 8-bit (0-255). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Accumulation is performed in floating-point registers to avoid precision loss during compositing. Polynomial Approximation: The method uses a second-order polynomial approximation for the transfer function integration. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes scalar values map directly to integer indices 0-255. 3D Table Animation is a method for controlling the movement and shape of volumetric gases by storing control values in a 3D table surrounding the gas volume in world space. It solves the problem of directing gas flow by interpolating values from lattice points to determine sample-specific control parameters. It is distinguished from its parent method, 3D Table Computation on GPU, by its specific application to gas animation via functional flow fields and vector fields, rather than general volume shadowing or density computation. Time Complexity: O(256^3 \cdot N), where N is the number of integration steps per ray segment. The method requires rendering 256 slices, each with 256x256 pixels, and performing N iterations per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(256^3) for the pre-integration table, storing 4 floats per voxel. Performance: The method leverages GPU parallelism for the rasterization and compositing steps. The fixed number of iterations and polynomial evaluation allow for efficient shader execution. Strengths: Pre-computation allows for fast rendering during the final volume rendering pass, as the integration results are looked up from the texture. Limitations: The method is specific to 8-bit scalar domains and second-order polynomial approximations. It requires significant GPU memory for the 3D texture. The quality depends on the number of integration steps N. This method is described in the paper "Second Order Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering". It builds on the concept of pre-integrated volume rendering, adapting it for GPU implementation using rasterization techniques. The approach was presented at PacificVis 2008. Second Order Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering, https://people.freedesktop.org/~marcheu/pacificvis08.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: 3D Table Animation
head: Three-dimensional Table Animation, solid space animation, volume control tables
body: 3D Table Animation is a method for controlling the movement and shape of volumetric gases by storing control values in a 3D table surrounding the gas volume in world space. It solves the problem of directing gas flow by interpolating values from lattice points to determine sample-specific control parameters. It is distinguished from its parent method, 3D Table Computation on GPU, by its specific application to gas animation via functional flow fields and vector fields, rather than general volume shadowing or density computation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D table of control values stored at lattice points in world space; a sample point in screen space. Output: Interpolated control values (e.g., direction vector, density scaling, velocity) for the sample point. Data Structures: 3D Table: A 3D grid where each entry stores control data. Lattice Points: The vertices of the table grid. Parallelepiped: The volume defined by the eight lattice points surrounding a given sample point in table space. Indices: Entries are defined by integer indices (i, j, k). Steps: 1. Map Screen to World: Convert the 3D screen space coordinate of the ray sample point into world space coordinates (xw, yw, zw). 2. Map World to Table Space: Calculate the location of the point within the 3D table (xt, yt, zt) using the world space position and the table's spatial parameters. 3. Identify Surrounding Entries: Determine the eight table entries forming the parallelepiped surrounding the calculated table coordinate. 4. Interpolate: Perform tri-linear interpolation on the values from the eight surrounding entries to determine the final control value. Formulas: The location within the table (xt, yt, zt) is determined by the point in world space (xw, yw, zw): xt = (xw - x{start}) \cdot sx yt = (yw - y{start}) \cdot sy zt = (zw - z{start}) \cdot sz Where: (x{start}, y{start}, z{start}) is the location in world space of the starting table entry (origin of the table grid). sx, sy, sz is the inverse of the step size between table elements in each dimension (i.e., 1/\Delta x, 1/\Delta y, 1/\Delta z). Parameters: Table Bounds: Defined by the starting table entry location and the step size (resolution) in each dimension. Interpolation Method: Tri-linear interpolation is normally sufficient. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Sampling: The formula for table location involves mapping world space to table space. Incorrect mapping leads to sampling outside the table bounds. Implementers must clamp or handle out-of-bounds coordinates. Precision: Floating-point precision in the mapping step can affect which lattice points are selected for interpolation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gettablevalue(samplescreenpos, camera, tableorigin, tableinvstep, tabledata, tabledims): """ samplescreenpos: (x, y, z) in screen space camera: object with method to convert screen to world tableorigin: (xstart, ystart, zstart) in world space tableinvstep: (sx, sy, sz) inverse step sizes tabledata: 3D array of control values tabledims: (N, M, P) dimensions of the table """ # 1. Map screen to world worldpos = camera.screentoworld(samplescreenpos) xw, yw, zw = worldpos # 2. Map world to table space xt = (xw - tableorigin[0]) tableinvstep[0] yt = (yw - tableorigin[1]) tableinvstep[1] zt = (zw - tableorigin[2]) tableinvstep[2] # 3. Identify surrounding entries and clamp to valid range i = int(math.floor(xt)) j = int(math.floor(yt)) k = int(math.floor(zt)) i = max(0, min(i, tabledims[0] - 2)) j = max(0, min(j, tabledims[1] - 2)) k = max(0, min(k, tabledims[2] - 2)) # 4. Interpolate (Tri-linear) fx = xt - i fy = yt - j fz = zt - k v000 = tabledata[i, j, k] v100 = tabledata[i+1, j, k] v010 = tabledata[i, j+1, k] v110 = tabledata[i+1, j+1, k] v001 = tabledata[i, j, k+1] v101 = tabledata[i+1, j, k+1] v011 = tabledata[i, j+1, k+1] v111 = tabledata[i+1, j+1, k+1] v00 = lerp(v000, v100, fx) v01 = lerp(v010, v110, fx) v10 = lerp(v001, v101, fx) v11 = lerp(v011, v111, fx) v0 = lerp(v00, v01, fy) v1 = lerp(v10, v11, fy) finalvalue = lerp(v0, v1, fz) return finalvalue def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) A type of 3D table where each entry contains a reference to a function (or list of functions) that calculates direction, density scaling, velocity, and usage percentage for gas movement. It is chosen when choreographed animation of gases is required, offering infinite detail in motion compared to fixed-resolution vector field tables, at the cost of higher evaluation expense. Steps: 1. Calculate the default path and velocity for the gas movement. 2. Evaluate the vector field tables (if used) and the functional flow field functions at the current point. 3. Combine the default path vector, the vector from the vector field table, and the vector from the flow field function to produce the new path. Parameters: percentofvectortouse: A value used to smoothly transition between control sources (flow field, vector field, default path) and between different flow field functions. Pitfalls: The percenttouse value decreases as the sample point moves away from the center of control for a given flow field function. A type of 3D table that stores direction vectors, density scaling factors, and other information at each lattice point, suited for visualizing CFD simulations. Vector field tables are cheaper to evaluate than functional flow field tables but provide fixed resolution detail, whereas functional tables provide infinite detail. Evaluation Cost: Functional flow field functions are much more expensive to evaluate than simply interpolating values from a vector field table. Strengths: Allows for complex, choreographed gas animation with infinite detail via functional flow fields. Limitations: Functional flow field functions are computationally expensive to evaluate compared to vector field tables. When to use: When precise, artistic control over gas movement is needed, and computational budget allows for function evaluation per sample. When not to use: When performance is critical and simple, fixed-resolution control (vector field tables) is sufficient. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. 3D Table Animation was introduced by David Ebert in the context of procedural modeling, animation, and rendering of gases, fluids, and textures. It is an extension of previous work using three-dimensional tables for volume shadowing effects. The method is described in detail in Ebert's work on procedural gas rendering. Procedural Modeling, Animation, and Rendering of Gases, Fluids, and Textures, https://www.researchgate.net/profile/David-Ebert-4/publication/2786953ProceduralModelingAnimationandRenderingofGasesFluidsandTextures/links/00b7d51a73e42a3c4e000000/Procedural-Modeling-Animation-and-Rendering-of-Gases-Fluids-and-Textures.pdf, fetched 2026-10-31 (unofficial)

name: Rubbersheet Visualization
head: Height Map, Rubbersheet Projection
body: Rubbersheet Visualization is a technique for visualizing data collected on a 2-dimensional grid by elevating the grid into the third dimension (Z), where the height or Z-value given to each vertex is proportional to the specified scalar data value at that vertex. It leverages human familiarity with physical height to show "ups and downs" in data values, resulting in a relief map-like appearance. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on thresholding or complex 3D table computations, this method provides a direct geometric deformation of the input grid [S1, 1515-grid-visualization-with-thresholding.md, 2083-3d-table-computation-on-gpu.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2-dimensional Field (grid) with scalar data values associated with vertices. Optionally, a "normals" component may be present. Output: A 3-dimensional Field (height field) where vertices are displaced along the Z-axis. Data Structures: The input is a 2D grid lying in the X-Y plane. Each vertex v has coordinates (x, y, 0) and an associated scalar value s. The output grid retains the (x, y) coordinates but updates the Z coordinate to z'. Steps: 1. Check for Normals: Determine if the input Field contains a "normals" component. If no normals component exists, the method assumes the input grid is flat and projects values in a perpendicular direction (along the Z-axis). If a normals component exists, it is used to control the direction of projection. 2. Calculate Displacement: For each vertex, calculate the new Z-coordinate based on the scalar data value and a scale parameter. 3. Apply Projection: Displace the vertex from its original position (x, y, 0) to (x, y, z'). 4. Post-Processing (Optional): To improve rendering quality, generate real surface normals for the projected surface using a Normals module, as the original normals (if any) may not accurately reflect the deformed geometry. Formulas: Let si be the scalar data value at vertex i, and k be the scale parameter. If no custom normals are provided, the new Z-coordinate z'i is: z'i = k \cdot si The vertex moves from (xi, yi, 0) to (xi, yi, z'i). If custom normals \mathbf{n}i are provided, the displacement direction is determined by \mathbf{n}i. The exact formula for non-perpendicular projection is not specified in the sources, but the direction is controlled by the modified normals component. Parameters: Scale (k): Determines the proportionality between data values and Z-deflection. Example: if scale is 1.0 and minimum count is 0, a count of 2 results in a point at z=2. Minimum Count: Implicitly referenced as a baseline for displacement (e.g., if minimum count is 0, displacement is directly proportional to value). Not given in the sources if this is a configurable parameter or a fixed assumption. Pitfalls: Misinterpretation of Data: The 3-D representation is not a "realistic" image of the original 2-D sampling space. Data was collected at z=0, but is displayed at z=z'. It is the user's responsibility to make this clear to viewers. Flat Grid Assumption: Rubbersheet assumes the input grid is flat if no "normals" component is present. If the input grid is not flat in the X-Y plane (e.g., already has Z variation), the behavior may be undefined or incorrect. Vector Data: For vector data, the grid is elevated by the magnitude of the vector, as magnitude is a scalar value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rubbersheetprojection(field, scale=1.0): """ Projects a 2D field into 3D by elevating vertices based on scalar values. Args: field: A 2D grid with vertices having (x, y, 0) coordinates and scalar values. scale: Proportionality factor for Z-deflection. Returns: A 3D field with vertices displaced along Z. """ outputfield = copy(field) # Check for normals component hasnormals = "normals" in field.components for vertex in outputfield.vertices: scalarvalue = vertex.scalardata if hasnormals: # Use custom normals for projection direction # Note: Exact formula for non-perpendicular projection not specified in sources # Assuming displacement is along the normal direction scaled by scalar value normal = vertex.normals # Displacement vector = scalarvalue scale normal # New position = old position + displacement # However, sources imply Z-deflection is the primary mechanism for 2D grids # If normals are provided, they control the direction. # For simplicity, if normals are Z-aligned (0,0,1), it reduces to Z-deflection. # If not, the implementation must project along the normal. # Since exact formula is missing, we assume standard Z-elevation if normals are not explicitly handled for direction. # Guard: If normals are not Z-aligned, the displacement direction must be calculated. # For this implementation, we assume the common case of Z-elevation unless normals are explicitly used for direction. # If normals are present and not Z-aligned, the source does not specify the exact vector math. # We will assume the displacement is along the normal direction. displacement = scalarvalue scale normal vertex.position = vertex.position + displacement else: # Assume flat grid, project in perpendicular direction (Z-axis) znew = scale scalarvalue vertex.position.z = znew return outputfield A synonym for Rubbersheet Visualization, emphasizing the visual output resembling a topographic map. Emphasizes the geometric transformation process. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of vertices in the grid, as each vertex is processed independently. Memory Complexity: Linear, as the output field requires storing the same number of vertices with an additional Z-coordinate. Strengths: Leverages human familiarity with physical height; provides a powerful visualization technique for showing data variations. Combining color and elevation can be more instructive than either alone. Limitations: Can be misleading if viewers interpret the 3-D height as actual physical elevation in the sampling space. Assumes input grid is flat if no normals are provided. When to Use: When visualizing 2D grid data with scalar values and wanting to emphasize magnitude through height. When Not to Use: When the data is not on a 2D grid, or when the Z-dimension has a different physical meaning than the scalar value. Rubbersheet Visualization originated in the IBM Visualization Data Explorer (DX) as a module for generating height maps. It is part of the broader family of direct volume ray casting and proxy geometry rendering techniques, specifically under slice-based and proxy geometry rendering [S1, 1507-2d-visualization-from-3d-grid-slow.md]. The technique is used to visualize data collected on a 2-dimensional grid, such as ecological data (e.g., grass species count). User's Guide - Visualization Techniques, https://theochem.mercer.edu/dxdocs/pages/usrgu063.htm, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Anti-Aliasing and Filtering
head: Box filter, Gaussian filter, Volume Filter
body: Anti-Aliasing and Filtering addresses visual artifacts caused by undersampling, such as jagged edges, flickering, and high-frequency noise, by smoothing the transition between discrete samples and continuous geometry. This family encompasses methods that operate at different stages of the rendering pipeline: pre-filtering data to prevent discretization errors, spatial filtering during rasterization, and post-processing screen-space blurs. It is distinct from sibling methods like Interpolation and Sampling Techniques because it focuses on the suppression of high-frequency components in the final image or intermediate buffers rather than the accuracy of individual sample retrieval. The children share no single mathematical mechanism beyond operating on discrete signals. Methods are selected based on their pipeline stage: pre-filtering for participating media [2928-prefiltering.md], rasterization coverage for line primitives [3607-line-coverage-anti-aliasing.md], or screen-space post-processing for ambient occlusion and color buffers [8374-pseudoseparable-cross-bilateral-filter.md][8804-separable-ping-pong-blur-post-processing.md][9037-screen-space-image-filtering.md]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelinecoverageaa(fragmentworldpos, linestart, lineend, viewportheight, fovy): v = lineend - linestart w = fragmentworldpos - linestart c1 = dot(v, w) c2 = dot(v, v) if c2 == 0: distance = length(fragmentworldpos - linestart) else: b = c1 / c2 b = max(0.0, min(1.0, b)) closestpoint = linestart + b v distance = length(fragmentworldpos - closestpoint) alpha = distance / (viewportheight fovy) return alpha def blendlinecolor(alpha, linecolor, backgroundcolor): finalcolor = alpha linecolor + (1.0 - alpha) backgroundcolor return finalcolor class BilateralData: def init(self, ao, normal, tracedistance): self.Ao = ao self.Normal = normal self.TraceDistance = tracedistance def applypseudoseparablebilateralfilter(uv, direction, filtersize=14, epsilon=0.001, discreteweights=None): # Load texture values at uv centerao = LoadAmbientOcclusionAsFloat4(uv) centernormal = LoadNormal(uv) centerdepth = LoadTraceDistance(uv) centerdata = BilateralData(centerao, centernormal, centerdepth) gtid = GetGlobalThreadID() padoffset = CastDir(gtid.xy) + filtersize gsBilateralData = [None] ((2 filtersize) + 100) gsBilateralData[padoffset + gtid.xy] = centerdata uvstep = GetUVStep(direction) for i in range(1, filtersize + 1): uvlower = uv - (i uvstep) lowerao = LoadAmbientOcclusionAsFloat4(uvlower, sampler="pointclamp") lowernormal = LoadNormal(uvlower, sampler="pointclamp") lowerdepth = LoadTraceDistance(uvlower, sampler="pointclamp") gsBilateralData[padoffset + gtid.xy - i] = BilateralData(lowerao, lowernormal, lowerdepth) uvupper = uv + (i uvstep) upperao = LoadAmbientOcclusionAsFloat4(uvupper, sampler="pointclamp") uppernormal = LoadNormal(uvupper, sampler="pointclamp") upperdepth = LoadTraceDistance(uvupper, sampler="pointclamp") gsBilateralData[padoffset + gtid.xy + i] = BilateralData(upperao, uppernormal, upperdepth) SyncThreads() filteredao = centerdata.Ao discreteweights[0] totalweight = discreteweights[0] for i in range(1, filtersize + 1): for sign in [-1, 1]: neighboridx = padoffset + gtid.xy + (sign i) bdata = gsBilateralData[neighboridx] depthdiff = abs(centerdata.TraceDistance - bdata.TraceDistance) depthweight = 1.0 / (epsilon + centerdata.TraceDistance 0.01 + depthdiff) normaldot = dot(centerdata.Normal, bdata.Normal) normalweight = pow(abs(normaldot), 32) combinedweight = discreteweights[i] depthweight normalweight filteredao += bdata.Ao combinedweight totalweight += combinedweight finalao = filteredao / totalweight if totalweight > 0 else centerdata.Ao WriteToAmbientOcclusionTarget(uv, finalao) def initializepingpongblur(width=512, height=512): fbtexture0 = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] fbtexture1 = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] fb0 = {"texture": fbtexture0, "depth": True} fb1 = {"texture": fbtexture1} return fb0, fb1, fbtexture0, fbtexture1 def applyseparableblur(fb0, fb1, fbtexture0, fbtexture1, shader, fulltexturesize=512): w1 = 0.0555555 w2 = 0.2777777 baseoffset = 1.0 / fulltexturesize intraoffset = (w2 / (w1 + w2)) baseoffset finaloffset = baseoffset + intraoffset bindframebuffer(fb1) clearcolorbuffer() bindshader(shader) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsetx", finaloffset) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsety", 0.0) bindtexture(shader, "inputtexture", fbtexture0) drawfullscreenquad() bindframebuffer(fb0) clearcolorbuffer() bindshader(shader) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsetx", 0.0) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsety", finaloffset) bindtexture(shader, "inputtexture", fbtexture1) drawfullscreenquad() Prefiltering initializes radiance or scattering coefficients for discrete ordinates to remove singularity-like artifacts and avoid discretization errors in participating media with insufficient optical thickness. It differs from naive source illumination prefiltering by being adaptive, preserving background illumination features while smoothing the initial scattering distribution. Choose this method when rendering thin, strongly-scattering media where natural blurring is absent. Line Coverage Anti-Aliasing reduces jagged edges in rasterized lines by calculating the ratio of a line's occupancy within a pixel and blending the pixel's original color with the line's color based on that ratio. It differs from the all-or-nothing strategy by producing smoother edges, especially for wireframe models. Choose this method when rendering line-based or wireframe geometry. The PseudoSeparable Cross Bilateral Filter is a screen-space post-processing technique used to smooth Ambient Occlusion data in direct volume ray casting. It reduces computational cost by decomposing a 2D bilateral filter into two sequential 1D passes, leveraging precomputed depth and normal information to preserve edges and prevent bleeding across object boundaries. It sets itself apart from standard Gaussian blurs by weighting neighbors based on geometric consistency rather than spatial proximity. Choose this method when preserving sharp silhouettes in volumetric scenes is required. Separable Ping-Pong Blur Post-Processing applies a smoothing filter to a rendered image to reduce high-frequency noise and aliasing artifacts. It solves the problem of jagged edges and visual noise by treating the rendered image as a discrete function requiring spatial smoothing. It differs from sibling methods by operating exclusively on the final color buffer using a two-pass separable convolution with a ping-pong framebuffer switching technique. Choose this method when efficient constant-memory per-pass smoothing of the final color buffer is needed. Screen-Space Image Filtering refers to a family of techniques that modify a base image rendered in a vacuum by adding effects caused by participating media, using only information currently visible on the screen. It sets itself apart from its siblings by its exclusive reliance on the 2D image buffer, which cannot access data for objects behind the camera or occluded geometry. Choose this method when high parallelism on GPUs is prioritized over physical accuracy. Affine Arithmetic Filtering obtains an average value of a procedural shader with an error bound over a finite area using affine arithmetic. It differs from standard sampling by providing rigorous error bounds for procedural volume shading. Choose this method when deterministic error bounds for procedural volume evaluation are required. Calculates the Screen Space Ratio (SSR) for a texture coordinate to determine sampling density or filtering strength, optionally applying a perspective filter to soften the result. It calculates the SSR based on projection matrix, position, object scale, and screen dimensions, used for font scaling. If Filter is true: compute derivatives a = \text{float2}(\text{ddx}(UV.x), \text{ddy}(UV.x)) and b = \text{float2}(\text{ddx}(UV.y), \text{ddy}(UV.y)); compute s = \text{lerp}(\text{dot}(a,a), \text{dot}(b,b), 0.5); set \text{SSR} = \text{rsqrt}(s) / \text{TextureSize}. If Filter is false: compute s = \text{rsqrt}(|\text{ddx}(UV.x) \cdot \text{ddy}(UV.y) - \text{ddy}(UV.x) \cdot \text{ddx}(UV.y)|); set \text{SSR} = s / \text{TextureSize}. Set \text{pixelSize} = \text{position}.w; divide \text{pixelSize} by (\text{objectScale} \cdot \text{mul}((\text{float2x2})\text{projection}, \text{float2}(\text{screenWidth}, \text{screenHeight}))); compute \text{SSR} = \text{rsqrt}(\text{dot}(\text{pixelSize}, \text{pixelSize}) \cdot 2) \cdot \text{fontScale}. An anti-aliasing technique that precomputes MIP-filtered parameters at the surfel center during preprocessing to reduce per-pixel rasterization cost while eliminating aliasing artifacts. Stores the resulting MIP-filtered inverse covariance \Sigma^{-1}{\text{mip}} and normalization factor \alpha{\text{norm}} once per primitive. During rasterization, loads these four parameters from shared memory. Applies the parameters directly to the intersection coordinates via the quadratic form of equation 6. Rendering time is 50 ms per frame for the center-precomputed MIP filter, an overhead of only 8 ms (<20%) over the unfiltered baseline of 42 ms. Compared to per-pixel Jacobian evaluation (AA-2DGS), this method is visually indistinguishable but faster (50 ms vs 65 ms per frame) because it avoids computing the full 2x2 Jacobian, its outer product, and matrix inverse at every covered pixel. An invisible object that makes overlapping volume parts invisible. In PovRay rendering, it interacts with other objects. In preview, it interacts only with volume. Rendering quality must be set quite high because the volume shape becomes complicated rather than a simple box. An antialiasing method that operates on the final color buffer. It performs edge detection and applies perceptually correct edge filtering. It provides antialiasing for both geometry and volume in the composited image. FXAA is applied to the final composited image, whereas multisampled G-buffer antialiasing is applied during geometry rendering. They can be combined for improved quality. Applies inverse diffusion with a negative diffusion coefficient to correct z-direction blur in confocal microscopy data. Works only in preview. Filtered data must be exported to new.df3 files for PovRay rendering. Early methods relied on simple box filters for crisp edges in high-resolution volumes, while Gaussian filters were introduced to prevent banding artifacts. name: Prefiltering
head: Adaptive Prefiltering, Anisotropy Prefiltering
body: Prefiltering is a technique used in discrete ordinates rendering to remove singularity-like artifacts and avoid discretization errors, particularly in participating media with insufficient optical thickness to naturally blur sampled illumination. Unlike naive prefiltering of source illumination which blurs background features, this method is adaptive, allowing the perception of background illumination features while smoothing the initial scattering distribution. It operates on discrete signals prior to ray marching, distinguishing it from screen-space post-processing methods like Screen-Space Image Filtering or PseudoSeparable Cross Bilateral Filter, and from primitive-level coverage methods like Line Coverage Anti-Aliasing or Affine Arithmetic Filtering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An environment map or local light source distribution (e.g., VPLs) and a set of discrete ordinates (directions) for the radiative transfer equation. Output: A prefiltered initialization of the radiance or scattering coefficients for each ordinate, ready for ray marching. Data Structures: Ordinates: A set of N directions. For environment maps, these are arranged in radial grids or spherical grids. For local lights, spherical grids use angular and radial coordinates aligned with the point source. Importance Weights (wn): A scalar value for each ordinate n representing its contribution to the image, proportional to the solid angle \Omegan of the direction. Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Importance: Determine the importance wn for each ordinate n, which is proportional to the solid angle \Omegan subtended by the direction. 2. Map Importance to Anisotropy: Compute the initial anisotropy a{n,i} for each ordinate i using the heuristic formula: a{n,i} = \left(1 - \frac{wn}{N}\right)^\beta Where: N is the total number of ordinates. wn is the importance of ordinate n mapped from the solid angle proportion. \beta > 0 is a scalar factor defining proportionality. Important ordinates (high wn) are denser in the directional domain, have smaller solid angles, and result in higher initial anisotropy. 3. Clamp Singularities: Apply clamping to the resulting values to reduce any remaining singularities. 4. Propagation (Optional/Contextual): In Principal-Ordinates Propagation (POP), this prefiltered initialization is applied before sampling the medium. For local lights, VPLs with large importance receive high initial anisotropy. Parameters: \beta: Scalar factor defining the proportionality in the anisotropy mapping heuristic. Value: Tuned empirically once for each environment map. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Insufficient Optical Thickness: Without prefiltering, singularity-like artifacts appear in thin, strongly-scattering media. Grid Merging: When combining grids from different light sources, geometric misalignments may occur, requiring careful merging strategies. A prefilter applied to reduce aliasing artifacts, specifically preventing 'valleys' of rims from becoming shallower due to oversmoothing. It addresses reconstruction quality issues in isosurface raycasting. Performance: The prefiltering step is described as a simple and quick task. In the POP pipeline, prefiltering initialization is part of a sequence that includes propagation (e.g., 2 ms for residuum propagation) and ray marching (e.g., 5 ms). Strengths: Removes singularity artifacts in thin media; preserves background illumination features due to adaptivity; handles high anisotropy (e.g., g=0.98) effectively. Limitations: Requires empirical tuning of \beta for each environment map. Prefiltering originated in real-time rendering of participating media with high scattering anisotropy. The method was proposed to handle the shortcomings of current methods in handling highly anisotropic scattering, which is common in natural and artificial media. name: Line Coverage Anti-Aliasing
head: Anti-Aliasing Factor for Line Coverage, Coverage approach, Coverage-based Anti-Aliasing (Line), Sub-pixel averaging for lines
body: Line Coverage Anti-Aliasing reduces jagged edges (aliasing) in rasterized lines by calculating the ratio of a line's occupancy within a pixel and mixing the pixel's original color with the line's color based on that ratio. It differs from the "all or nothing" (winner-take-all) strategy where a pixel is set to the line's color if the line passes through it, and unchanged otherwise. This approach produces smoother edges, especially for wireframe models. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Fragment position in world space (\mathbf{p}), line segment endpoints in world space (\mathbf{l}0, \mathbf{l}1), viewport height in pixels (u{\text{ViewportSize}.y}), and vertical field of view (u{\text{FovY}}). Output: An anti-aliasing factor \alpha \in [0, 1] used to blend the line color with the background. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required; the method operates on standard vertex/fragment shader uniforms and temporary scalar/vector variables. Steps: 1. Compute the Euclidean distance d from the fragment's world position to the line segment defined by endpoints \mathbf{l}0 and \mathbf{l}1. 2. Calculate the anti-aliasing factor \alpha using the formula: \alpha = \frac{d}{u{\text{ViewportSize}.y} \cdot u{\text{FovY}}} 3. The factor \alpha represents the pixel size relative to the distance; smaller projected distance results in smaller anti-aliasing influence. 4. Blend the final pixel color C{\text{final}} with the line color C{\text{line}} and the original background color C{\text{bg}} using \alpha as the background weight: C{\text{final}} = (1 - \alpha) \cdot C{\text{line}} + \alpha \cdot C{\text{bg}} Parameters: u{\text{FovY}}: Vertical field of view. u{\text{ViewportSize}.y}: Viewport height in pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If \mathbf{l}0 = \mathbf{l}1, the line segment has zero length. The distance calculation c2 = \text{dot}(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v}) becomes 0, causing division by zero in b = c1 / c2. The implementation must check if the segment length is near zero before division. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelinecoverageaa(fragmentworldpos, linestart, lineend, viewportheight, fovy): v = lineend - linestart w = fragmentworldpos - linestart c1 = dot(v, w) c2 = dot(v, v) if c2 == 0: distance = length(fragmentworldpos - linestart) else: b = c1 / c2 b = max(0.0, min(1.0, b)) closestpoint = linestart + b v distance = length(fragmentworldpos - closestpoint) alpha = distance / (viewportheight fovy) return alpha def blendlinecolor(alpha, linecolor, backgroundcolor): return (1.0 - alpha) linecolor + alpha backgroundcolor Breaks each pixel into smaller sub-pixels (e.g., 10×10), renders with an all-or-nothing strategy, and averages the results. It differs from direct coverage by using discrete sub-pixel sampling rather than continuous distance projection. Choose it when hardware supports sub-pixel rendering and maximum edge smoothness is required. Link: Not given in the sources. Renders a large image (e.g., 6000×6000) and scales it down using bilinear interpolation to approximate sub-pixel coverage. It differs from direct coverage by avoiding per-fragment distance calculations in favor of post-rendering downsampling. Choose it when hardware sub-pixel rendering is unavailable but high-quality results are needed. Link: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The sub-pixel averaging variant requires approximately 10 times the memory and rendering time for a 10×10 sub-pixel grid. Strengths: Produces smoother edges for wireframe models compared to all-or-nothing rasterization. Limitations: The sub-pixel variant is computationally expensive. The direct coverage method relies on accurate distance calculations and proper scaling factors. When to Use: Rendering wireframe models or lines where jagged edges are prominent and hardware sub-pixel rendering is unavailable or costly. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and the visual improvement of anti-aliasing is not worth the cost. The technique is described in the context of advanced computer graphics, specifically addressing aliasing problems in rasterization. It is presented as an alternative to the "all or nothing" rasterization strategy. The implementation details are found in an unofficial GitHub repository simulating graphics primitives.
