name: PseudoSeparable Cross Bilateral Filter
head: AOHorizontalH, AOHorizontalL, AOVerticalH, AOVerticalL, AOHorizontalM, AOVerticalM
body: The PseudoSeparable Cross Bilateral Filter is a screen-space post-processing technique used to smooth Ambient Occlusion (AO) data in direct volume ray casting. It reduces computational cost by decomposing a 2D bilateral filter into two sequential 1D passes (horizontal and vertical). Unlike standard Gaussian blurs, it weights neighbors based on geometric consistency (depth and normal similarity) rather than just spatial proximity, making it suitable for preserving sharp silhouettes in volumetric scenes. The method operates on screen-space buffers containing ambient occlusion values, surface normals, and depth (trace distance). It processes the AO data in two passes: one horizontal and one vertical. Each pass computes a weighted average of neighboring pixels, where weights are determined by a combination of spatial distance, depth difference, and normal alignment. Inputs: AmbientOcclusionTarget: Texture containing the raw AO values (float4). NormalMap: Texture containing surface normals (float3). TraceDistance: Texture containing depth/z-buffer values (float). discreteWeights: Precomputed 1D kernel weights array of size 15. Outputs: AmbientOcclusionTarget: Updated with the filtered AO values. 1. BilateralData: A struct holding the necessary information for a single pixel. Ao: float4 (Ambient Occlusion value). Normal: float3 (Surface normal vector). TraceDistance: float (Depth value). 2. Shared Memory Array (gsBilateralData): Used for thread cooperation within a thread group. Size: (2 FilterSize) + ThreadLength. ThreadLength is ThreadsX for horizontal passes and ThreadsY for vertical passes. Stores BilateralData structs. 3. discreteWeights: Array of 15 float values. Index 0 corresponds to the center pixel. Indices 1–14 correspond to neighbors at increasing distances. FilterSize: Integer, radius of the filter kernel on each side. Value: 14. epsilon: Float, small constant to prevent division by zero in depth weight. Value: 0.001. RangeSigma: Declared in source but not used in the visible implementation. The filter is applied in two distinct passes. The logic for a single pass (horizontal or vertical) is as follows: 1. Load Center Data: Read Ao, Normal, and TraceDistance for the current pixel uv from input textures. Store these in a local variable centerData. 2. Shared Memory Initialization: Calculate global thread ID gtid.xy. Define padding offset PAD(xy) = CASTDIR(xy) + FilterSize. Store centerData in shared memory at gsBilateralData[PAD(gtid.xy)]. 3. Load Neighbors: For i from 1 to FilterSize, calculate neighbor UV as uv - (i uvstep). Sample Ao, Normal, TraceDistance using samplerpointclamp to handle boundaries. Store in gsBilateralData[PAD(gtid.xy) - i]. Repeat for uv + (i uvstep) storing in gsBilateralData[PAD(gtid.xy) + i]. 4. Synchronization: Execute a barrier/synchronization command to ensure all threads in the group have finished loading shared memory. 5. Weighted Accumulation: Initialize filteredAo and totalWeight using the center pixel data multiplied by discreteWeights[0]. Loop i from 1 to FilterSize. Iterate sign from -1 to 1 with step 2. Access neighbor data bData from gsBilateralData[PAD(gtid.xy) + sign i]. Compute weights: depthWeight = 1.0 / (epsilon + centerData.TraceDistance 0.01 + |centerData.TraceDistance - bData.TraceDistance|). Compute normalWeight = |dot(centerData.Normal, bData.Normal)|^32. Compute combinedWeight = discreteWeights[i] depthWeight normalWeight. Update accumulators: filteredAo += bData.Ao combinedWeight and totalWeight += combinedWeight. 6. Normalization and Output: Normalize filtered AO by dividing by total weight. Write result to AmbientOcclusionTarget. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. FILTERSIZE = 14 EPSILON = 0.001 DISCRETEWEIGHTS = [0.0] 15 # Precomputed array of 15 floats class BilateralData: def init(self, ao, normal, tracedistance): self.Ao = ao self.Normal = normal self.TraceDistance = tracedistance def castdir(x, y, stride): return x + y stride def getuvstep(direction, width, height): if direction == 'horizontal': return (1.0 / width, 0.0) else: return (0.0, 1.0 / height) def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(val, maxval)) def applypseudoseparablebilateralfilter(uv, direction, width, height, threadsx, threadsy): centerao = loadao(uv) centernormal = loadnormal(uv) centerdepth = loadtracedistance(uv) centerdata = BilateralData(centerao, centernormal, centerdepth) gtidx, gtidy = uvtothreadid(uv, width, height) threadidx = castdir(gtidx, gtidy, threadsx) padoffset = threadidx + FILTERSIZE gsBilateralData[padoffset] = centerdata uvstep = getuvstep(direction, width, height) for i in range(1, FILTERSIZE + 1): uvlower = (uv[0] - i uvstep[0], uv[1] - i uvstep[1]) lowerao = loadao(uvlower) lowernormal = loadnormal(uvlower) lowerdepth = loadtracedistance(uvlower) gsBilateralData[padoffset - i] = BilateralData(lowerao, lowernormal, lowerdepth) uvupper = (uv[0] + i uvstep[0], uv[1] + i uvstep[1]) upperao = loadao(uvupper) uppernormal = loadnormal(uvupper) upperdepth = loadtracedistance(uvupper) gsBilateralData[padoffset + i] = BilateralData(upperao, uppernormal, upperdepth) syncthreads() filteredao = centerdata.Ao DISCRETEWEIGHTS[0] totalweight = DISCRETEWEIGHTS[0] for i in range(1, FILTERSIZE + 1): for sign in [-1, 1]: neighboridx = padoffset + sign i bdata = gsBilateralData[neighboridx] depthdiff = abs(centerdata.TraceDistance - bdata.TraceDistance) depthweight = 1.0 / (EPSILON + centerdata.TraceDistance 0.01 + depthdiff) normaldot = dot(centerdata.Normal, bdata.Normal) normalweight = pow(abs(normaldot), 32) combinedweight = DISCRETEWEIGHTS[i] depthweight normalweight filteredao += bdata.Ao combinedweight totalweight += combinedweight finalao = filteredao / totalweight if totalweight > 0 else centerdata.Ao writetoaotarget(uv, finalao) Boundary Handling: The filter uses samplerpointclamp for neighbor sampling. This clamps UV coordinates to the texture edges, effectively replicating the edge pixel values for out-of-bounds accesses. Arbitrary Depth Factor: The term centerData.TraceDistance 0.01 in the depth weight denominator is an arbitrary linear factor introduced in the implementation. Its impact on visual quality is not theoretically derived in the source. Unused Parameter: RangeSigma is declared but not used in the visible code, suggesting it may be a remnant of a different filter variant or intended for future use. Division by Zero: The epsilon constant (0.001) prevents division by zero in the depth weight calculation when depth differences are negligible. An optimization strategy to generate a low resolution AO map and use joint bilateral upsampling to resample the HAO map at screen resolution while filtering noise. It approximates the non-separable bilateral filter in two passes (one horizontal, one vertical) to improve frame rate. The method computes the filtered AO at pixel x as h{m \times m}(x) = \frac{\sum{y \in Q} wd(x, y) wr(x, y) h0(y/k)}{\sum{y \in Q} wd(x, y) wr(x, y)}, where Q is the set of pixels in an m \times m square centered on x. The spatial weight is wd(x, y):= w(\|x - y\|, m). The range weight combines normal, position, and height influences: wr(x, y):= wn(x, y) \cdot wp(x, y) \cdot wh(x, y). Normal influence is wn(x, y):= w(1 + \langle n(x), n(y) \rangle, 2). Position influence is wp(x, y):= w(\|p(x) - p(y)\|, e{max}). Height influence is wh(x, y):= w(\|h0(x/k) - h0(y/k)\|, 1). Here, p(x) is the object space position extracted from the Z map, n(x) is the normal extracted from the normal map, h0 is the low resolution AO map, and k is the scale ratio between high and low resolution maps. The non-separable filter is approximated as \tilde{h}{m \times m}(x):= h{1 \times m}(h{m \times 1}(x)). Defining the range space according to object space entities avoids AO bleeding between distant objects projected closely in image space. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K), where N is the number of pixels and K is the filter radius (14). The separable approach reduces the 2D complexity O(N \cdot K^2) to two 1D passes O(2 \cdot N \cdot K). Memory Complexity: O(K \cdot T) for shared memory, where T is the thread group size. This is minimal compared to full 2D kernel storage. Performance: The method is efficient for real-time rendering due to the separable decomposition and use of shared memory. However, the bilateral weighting (dot product, power, division) per neighbor is more expensive than a simple Gaussian blur. Strengths: Preserves edges defined by depth and normal discontinuities, preventing AO bleeding across object boundaries. Limitations: Computationally heavier than simple box or Gaussian filters. The arbitrary depth factor may require tuning for different scenes. Not suitable for scenes with high-frequency depth variation where the depth weight might become unstable. The PseudoSeparable Cross Bilateral Filter is implemented in the codebase referenced by for direct volume ray casting to improve the visual quality of ambient occlusion by smoothing noise while maintaining geometric sharpness. The technique leverages standard screen-space post-processing techniques adapted for volumetric data. name: Separable Ping-Pong Blur Post-Processing
head: Horizontal-vertical blur, Ping-Pong Blur, Ping-Pong Gaussian Blur, PostProcessBlurShader, Separable Bloom Blur, Two-pass blur
body: Separable Ping-Pong Blur Post-Processing applies a spatial smoothing filter to a rendered image to reduce high-frequency noise and aliasing artifacts. It operates exclusively on the final color buffer using a two-pass separable convolution, alternating between two framebuffers to perform horizontal and vertical blurs sequentially. Unlike sibling methods that process volumetric primitives or screen-space geometry buffers, this technique relies on a ping-pong framebuffer switching mechanism to achieve efficient computation with constant memory per pass regardless of kernel width. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The base rendered scene image (color buffer). Output: The blurred image, written to the target color buffer. Data Structures: Ping-Pong Textures: Two 2D textures, fbTexture[0] and fbTexture[1], allocated at 512 \times 512 resolution. Format: GLRGB. Internal Format: GLUNSIGNEDSHORT565. Filtering: GLLINEAR (bilinear). Wrapping: GLCLAMPTOEDGE. Ping-Pong Framebuffers: Two FBOs, framebuffer[0] and framebuffer[1]. framebuffer[0]: Attaches fbTexture[0] and a GLDEPTHCOMPONENT16 renderbuffer. framebuffer[1]: Attaches only fbTexture[1]. Shader Uniforms: mfTexelOffset: The calculated texel offset for sampling. blurStep: A Vec2 uniform controlling the blur step size. focus: A Float uniform controlling focus. halfBand: A Float uniform controlling half band. maxRadius: A Float uniform controlling max radius. saturation: A Float uniform controlling saturation. Parameters: fullTextureSize: Fixed resolution for post-processing textures, typically 512. w1: Weight for the faster filter kernel, typically 0.0555555. w2: Weight for the faster filter kernel, typically 0.2777777. passes: Integer controlling the number of blur iterations applied after the initial horizontal/vertical pass. bloomOffset: Float uniform controlling the blur kernel width, passed to the shader as uTexOffsetCoeff. Steps: 1. Initialization: Allocate fbTexture[0] and fbTexture[1] with the specified format, filtering, and wrapping. Create framebuffer[0] and framebuffer[1] and attach the textures and depth buffer as specified. 2. Base Render: Render the scene into framebuffer[0]. 3. Pass 1 (Horizontal Blur): Bind framebuffer[1] as the draw target. Set shader uniform SHADERUNIFORMTEXELOFFSETX to mfTexelOffset and SHADERUNIFORMTEXELOFFSETY to 0.0f. Draw a fullscreen quad sampling from fbTexture[0]. 4. Pass 2 (Vertical Blur): Bind the target color buffer (or framebuffer[0] if reusing) as the draw target. Set X offset to 0.0f and Y offset to mfTexelOffset. Draw a fullscreen quad sampling from the result of Pass 1 (fbTexture[1]). 5. Additional Passes (if passes > 2): Loop i from 0 to passes - 2. Alternate binding framebuffer[0] and framebuffer[1], toggle uHorizontal between 0 and 1, bind the opposite ping-pong texture, and draw a fullscreen quad. Formulas: The base texel offset is calculated as: m\fTexelOffset = \frac{1.0}{fullTextureSize} An intra-texel offset adjustment is applied using specific kernel weights: intraTexelOffset = \frac{w2}{w1 + w2} \times m\fTexelOffset The final offset used for sampling is: m\fTexelOffset{final} = m\fTexelOffset + intraTexelOffset Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializepingpongblur(width=512, height=512): # Allocate two RGB textures with unsigned short 5-6-5 format fbtexture0 = allocatetexture(width, height, format="RGB", internalformat="UNSIGNEDSHORT565") fbtexture1 = allocatetexture(width, height, format="RGB", internalformat="UNSIGNEDSHORT565") # Set filtering and wrapping settexturefiltering(fbtexture0, filter="LINEAR", wrap="CLAMPTOEDGE") settexturefiltering(fbtexture1, filter="LINEAR", wrap="CLAMPTOEDGE") # Create framebuffers and attach textures fb0 = createframebuffer() attachtexture(fb0, fbtexture0, attachment="COLORATTACHMENT0") attachrenderbuffer(fb0, format="DEPTHCOMPONENT16") fb1 = createframebuffer() attachtexture(fb1, fbtexture1, attachment="COLORATTACHMENT0") return fb0, fb1, fbtexture0, fbtexture1 def renderscene(fb0): bindframebuffer(fb0) clearcolorbuffer() cleardepthbuffer() drawscenegeometry() # Render the base volume rendering output def applyseparableblur(fb0, fb1, fbtexture0, fbtexture1, shader, fulltexturesize=512, passes=2, bloomoffset=1.0): # Calculate offsets w1 = 0.0555555 w2 = 0.2777777 baseoffset = 1.0 / fulltexturesize intraoffset = (w2 / (w1 + w2)) baseoffset finaloffset = baseoffset + intraoffset # Pass 1: Horizontal Blur bindframebuffer(fb1) clearcolorbuffer() bindshader(shader) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsetx", finaloffset) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsety", 0.0) setuniform(shader, "blurstep", vec2(1.0, 0.0)) setuniform(shader, "focus", 1.0) setuniform(shader, "halfband", 1.0) setuniform(shader, "maxradius", 1.0) setuniform(shader, "saturation", 1.0) bindtexture(shader, "inputtexture", fbtexture0) drawfullscreenquad() # Pass 2: Vertical Blur bindframebuffer(fb0) # Or the final target buffer clearcolorbuffer() bindshader(shader) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsetx", 0.0) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsety", finaloffset) setuniform(shader, "blurstep", vec2(0.0, 1.0)) bindtexture(shader, "inputtexture", fbtexture1) drawfullscreenquad() # Additional passes (if passes > 2) for i in range(passes - 2): # Alternate FBOs and textures if i % 2 == 0: bindframebuffer(fb0) setuniform(shader, "uHorizontal", 0) bindtexture(shader, "inputtexture", fbtexture1) else: bindframebuffer(fb1) setuniform(shader, "uHorizontal", 1) bindtexture(shader, "inputtexture", fbtexture0) setuniform(shader, "uTexOffsetCoeff", bloomoffset) clearcolorbuffer() drawfullscreenquad() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture Filtering: Must be set to Bilinear (GLLINEAR) because the blur taps land between texels. Texture Wrapping: Must be set to Clamp (GLCLAMPTOEDGE) because default wrapping (e.g., Repeat) causes the blur at the top edge to pull in pixels from the bottom of the frame. A linear blur filter that applies exponential decay smoothing along the outermost two dimensions of an input tensor. It serves as a post-processing step in separable ping-pong blur pipelines to reduce high-frequency noise and aliasing artifacts in rendered images. Unlike Gaussian blurs, it uses an infinite impulse response (IIR) structure, allowing for efficient computation with constant memory per pass regardless of kernel width. A blending technique used to improve visualization quality for moving objects or during camera navigation. It applies a two-pass weighted Gaussian blur and performs Gaussian blur blending with Z-buffer occlusion while the incremental bubble-sort A-Buffer is processing. A post-processing blur filter that samples a 3D volume at 8 corners of a small box centered on the current coordinate and averages them. A 2D post-processing blur that weights neighboring samples by their alpha values to preserve sharp edges in depth-of-field rendering. Combines a high-resolution small-scale blur with a low-resolution large-scale blur using alpha-based blending for depth of field. Integration of post-processing filters (e.g., Gaussian blur) applied to accumulated color or depth buffers after ray intersection and shading to smooth residual aliasing without additional ray computations. If shadows are enabled, invert the shadow color map so shadowed areas are black. Blur the inverted shadow map horizontally and then vertically to avoid aliasing. Multiply the blurred shadow map with the volume color texture for final shadowing. Apply tone mapping to the resulting post-process texture. Blends medium and low resolution defocus buffers based on alpha to mix bluriness levels before final compositing. Sample medium and low resolution buffers at current UV. Square medium alpha: tapMedium.a = tapMedium.a^2. Lerp medium RGB into low RGB using squared alpha as factor: tapLow.rgb = lerp(tapMedium.rgb, tapLow.rgb, tapMedium.a^2). Inputs are TapMedium (sampler2D) and TapLow (sampler2D), output is SVTarget. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the ping-pong textures, where W and H are the texture dimensions. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient for large blur radii due to separability; constant memory usage per pass; simple implementation using standard framebuffer objects. Limitations: Fixed resolution of 512 \times 512 in the reference implementation may limit applicability to higher resolutions without modification; blurring is applied uniformly, which may not be desirable for all regions of the image; does not account for depth or geometry information during the blur itself. When to use: When post-processing a rendered image to reduce aliasing and noise, and the scene does not require depth-aware blurring. When not to use: When high-resolution textures are required and memory is constrained; when the blur needs to be adaptive based on scene content or depth. The method originates from the iVoxel project, an iPhone OS Scenegraph Rendering System developed by Torsten Becker, Norman Holz, Lars Schneider, and others at the Hasso-Plattner-Institute (HPI) in Potsdam, Germany, around 2009. It was used as a post-processing step to improve the visual quality of rendered voxel data. The technique leverages standard OpenGL ES 2.0 features for framebuffer objects and shader-based convolution. name: Exponential Decay Blur Filter
head: Exponential Smoothing Blur, IIR Blur
body: A linear blur filter that applies exponential decay smoothing along the outermost two dimensions of an input tensor. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tensor X. Output: A smoothed tensor Y of the same shape as X. Parameters: Smoothing parameter \alpha: Controls the decay rate. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on a single buffer Y initialized as a copy of X. Steps: The filter is separable, processing the last two dimensions independently. Each dimension undergoes a forward pass followed by a backward pass. 1. Initialize Y = X. 2. Forward pass along the last dimension: for i from 0 to W-2: Y[..., i+1] \leftarrow Y[..., i+1] + \alpha \cdot Y[..., i]. 3. Backward pass along the last dimension: for i from W-2 down to 0: Y[..., i] \leftarrow Y[..., i] + \alpha \cdot Y[..., i+1]. 4. Forward pass along the second-to-last dimension: for i from 0 to H-2: Y[..., i+1,:] \leftarrow Y[..., i+1,:] + \alpha \cdot Y[..., i,:]. 5. Backward pass along the second-to-last dimension: for i from H-2 down to 0: Y[..., i,:] \leftarrow Y[..., i,:] + \alpha \cdot Y[..., i+1,:]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def exponentialdecayblur(X, alpha): Y = X.clone() H = Y.shape[-2] W = Y.shape[-1] for i in range(W - 1): Y[..., i + 1] = Y[..., i + 1] + alpha Y[..., i] for i in range(W - 2, -1, -1): Y[..., i] = Y[..., i] + alpha Y[..., i + 1] for i in range(H - 1): Y[..., i + 1,:] = Y[..., i + 1,:] + alpha Y[..., i,:] for i in range(H - 2, -1, -1): Y[..., i,:] = Y[..., i,:] + alpha Y[..., i + 1,:] return Y Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary conditions: The loop bounds range(shape-1) ensure indices stay within tensor dimensions; boundary elements are updated by neighbors but do not propagate out of bounds. Precision: Accumulation of floating-point errors is possible in very long sequences, though typically negligible for image dimensions. Degenerate input: If H=1 or W=1, the corresponding range is empty and the pass is skipped, which is correct behavior. A recursive low-pass filter that estimates the underlying signal by weighting the current observation and the previous smoothed estimate. It is distinguished from fixed-kernel blurs by its infinite impulse response and adaptive memory, where the effective window size is determined by the smoothing parameter \alpha rather than a fixed spatial or temporal radius. Not given in the sources. The method is implemented in neural rendering pipelines, specifically in the NeRFingMVS repository, where it is applied to depth priors and confidences. weiyithu/NerfingMVS, https://github.com/weiyithu/NerfingMVS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Exponential Moving Average Smoothing
head: Control Signal Smoothing, EMA Smoothing, Exponential Smoothing
body: Exponential Moving Average (EMA) smoothing recursively estimates a signal by combining the current observation with the previous smoothed value. It is distinguished from fixed-kernel blurs by its infinite impulse response, where the effective memory window is determined by the smoothing parameter \alpha rather than a fixed spatial or temporal radius. Inputs and Outputs Input: A sequence of raw values vi for i = 1, \dots, N. Output: A sequence of smoothed values \hat{v}i. Parameter: Smoothing factor \alpha \in (0, 1]. Data Structures v: Array of raw input values. vhat: Array of smoothed output values, same size as v. alpha: Scalar float representing the smoothing factor. Formula \hat{v}i = \begin{cases} v1 & i = 1 \\ \alpha vi + (1 - \alpha) \hat{v}{i-1} & i > 1 \end{cases} where vi is the current raw input value, \hat{v}{i-1} is the previously computed smoothed value, and \alpha is the smoothing parameter. Steps 1. Initialize \hat{v}1 = v1. 2. For i from 2 to N: compute \hat{v}i = \alpha vi + (1 - \alpha) \hat{v}{i-1}. 3. Return \hat{v}. Parameters \alpha: Controls the trade-off between smoothing and responsiveness. Smaller \alpha results in more smoothing; larger \alpha results in less dependence on previous values and thus less smoothing. Typical value: \alpha = 0.8 is used for general methods and control signal filtering. Specific case: \alpha = 0.3 is used for IDR due to higher variance between plot points. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Initialization: The value at i=1 uses the raw value directly to avoid bias. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundary: The formula is undefined for i=1 without an initial condition, which is resolved by the base case. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def exponentialmovingaveragesmoothing(v, alpha): if not v: return [] n = len(v) vhat = [0.0] n vhat[0] = v[0] for i in range(1, n): vhat[i] = alpha v[i] + (1 - alpha) vhat[i-1] return vhat The parent method that applies this smoothing along the outermost two dimensions of a tensor [Parent]. It is chosen when spatial filtering along the outer dimensions is required for image-order rendering. See Exponential Decay Blur Filter. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance and Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use and when not: Not given in the sources. The method originates from statistical smoothing techniques and has been applied in control systems and neural network training. In volume rendering and robotics, it smooths control signals for robot actuation. It also reduces variance in training metrics for neural lumigraph representations. The specific parameter values (\alpha=0.8 and \alpha=0.3) are empirically derived from these applications. name: Two-pass Weighted Gaussian Blur
head: Gaussian blur blending
body: A post-processing blending technique used to improve visualization quality for moving objects or during camera navigation in stroke-based splatting. It differs from its sibling Exponential Decay Blur Filter by using a weighted Gaussian kernel rather than exponential decay, and from Standard Gaussian Blur by integrating Z-buffer occlusion checks during the blending process to handle depth-aware transparency. It serves as an alternative to alpha blending by simulating tint blending through continuous Gaussian falloff. Inputs: Rendered patches with color, transparency (alpha), and depth (Z) values; Z-buffer data. Outputs: Blended final image. Data Structures: A-Buffer: Stores accumulated fragments, sorted incrementally via bubble sort. Z-buffer: Stores depth values for occlusion testing. Steps: 1. Initialization: Prepare buffers for rendering patches. Initialize A-Buffer with zeroed color and alpha accumulators. 2. Incremental Sorting: Perform bubble-sort operations on the A-Buffer to sort fragments by depth. This ensures a minimum amount of fragments are available for blending. 3. Concurrent Blending: While the bubble-sort is processing, perform Gaussian blur blending with Z-buffer occlusion. 4. Gaussian Weighting: For each fragment, calculate Gaussian weights based on amplitude and sigma values (\sigmax, \sigmay). The transparency component controls the influence. 5. Blending: Apply common alpha blending on rendered patches, giving stronger influence to topmost patches, simulating tint blending. 6. Iteration: Repeat sorting and blending iterations. Sorted data is only used after a preset amount of iterations to ensure sufficient neighboring patches for blended color calculation. Formulas: Gaussian Weight: W(x,y) = A \cdot e^{-\frac{x^2}{2\sigmax^2} - \frac{y^2}{2\sigmay^2}} where A is amplitude, \sigmax, \sigmay are standard deviations. Alpha Blending: C{out} = C{src} \cdot \alpha{src} + C{dst} \cdot (1 - \alpha{src}). Parameters: Amplitude (A): Controls influence strength. Sigma (\sigmax, \sigmay): Controls falloff width. Preset iterations: Minimum iterations before using sorted data. Edge Cases: High-frequency noise removal works even with high amplitude and low sigma values due to continuous Gaussian falloff. Boundary regions require careful handling of alpha blending to avoid artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twopassweightedgaussianblur(patches, zbuffer, abuffer, presetiterations): # Initialize A-Buffer abuffer.clear() # Render patches and update A-Buffer for patch in patches: abuffer.add(patch) # Incremental bubble sort and concurrent blending for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Perform one step of bubble sort on A-Buffer abuffer.bubblesortstep() # Perform Gaussian blur blending with Z-buffer occlusion if iteration >= presetiterations: # Use sorted data for blending blendedcolor = calculateblendedcolor(abuffer, zbuffer) applyblending(blendedcolor) else: # Perform blending without sorted data (or with partial data) # This step ensures minimum fragments are processed performpartialblending(abuffer, zbuffer) return finalimage def calculateblendedcolor(abuffer, zbuffer): totalcolor = (0, 0, 0) totalalpha = 0 for fragment in abuffer.sortedfragments: # Check Z-buffer occlusion if fragment.z < zbuffer.get(fragment.x, fragment.y): continue # Calculate Gaussian weight weight = gaussianweight(fragment.x, fragment.y, fragment.amplitude, fragment.sigmax, fragment.sigmay) # Alpha blending color = fragment.color weight alpha = fragment.alpha weight totalcolor = totalcolor + color (1 - totalalpha) totalalpha = totalalpha + alpha (1 - totalalpha) return totalcolor / max(totalalpha, epsilon) Uses fixed Gaussian weights without Z-buffer occlusion or adaptive sorting. Choose for static scenes where depth-aware blending is unnecessary. Uses exponential decay instead of Gaussian weights. Choose for faster computation with similar visual results in some contexts. Applies a box filter in 3D space. Choose for volumetric data where isotropic smoothing is required. Uses separable filters for depth-of-field effects. Choose for simulating camera focus. Combines upsampled and blurred data. Choose for high-quality upscaling. General category of post-processing filters. Use as a reference for other techniques. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of patches and iterations. Bubble sort adds O(N^2) overhead per iteration, but incremental sorting reduces this. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for A-Buffer and Z-buffer. Performance: Effective for moving objects and camera navigation. High-frequency noise removal is efficient with appropriate sigma values. Strengths: Improves visualization quality, handles motion, simulates tint blending. Limitations: Computational cost of bubble sort and Gaussian weighting. When to Use: Moving objects, camera navigation, dynamic scenes. When Not to Use: Static scenes where Standard Gaussian Blur is sufficient. Originated in stroke-based splatting for point cloud visualization. Developed to address visualization quality issues during camera navigation and moving object rendering. The technique integrates with incremental A-Buffer sorting to enhance performance. name: Standard Gaussian Blur
head: 2D Gaussian Blur, Separable Gaussian Blur, fragGaussBlur
body: Standard Gaussian Blur applies a spatially separable Gaussian filter to an input tensor to smooth visual data. It implements either a fixed 11-tap alpha-weighted kernel or a dynamically computed 2D Gaussian kernel. Unlike its parent method which adapts weights to local variance or depth, this method uses a predetermined weight set. The method processes an input tensor through two distinct implementation paths documented in the sources. Input: A tensor of shape (B, D, H, W) representing batch, depth/channel, height, and width. Output: A blurred tensor of the same shape (B, D, H, W). 1. Fixed Weights: A 1D array of 9 float values used for the 11-tap implementation. Layout: float GWEIGHTS[9] Values: {1.0, 0.8, 0.65, 0.5, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.025}. 2. Dynamic Weights: A 2D grid of shape (N, N) generated from a standard deviation \sigma. Layout: float kernel[N][N] Formula: w{i,j} = \exp\left(-\frac{xi^2 + yj^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) where x, y are coordinates centered at 0. 1. Weight Generation: If using the dynamic kernel: Create meshgrids x, y for kernel size N centered at 0. Compute unnormalized weights w = \exp(-(x^2 + y^2) / (2\sigma^2)). Normalize by dividing by \sum w, clamping the denominator to a minimum of 10^{-4} to avoid division by zero. Reshape to (1, 1, N, N). If using the fixed kernel: Load the predefined 9-element array. 2. Sampling and Accumulation: For each output pixel, sample input pixels within the kernel radius. Fixed method: Weight each sample by its alpha value multiplied by the corresponding Gaussian weight: w = \text{sample}.a \times G\WEIGHTS[k]. Dynamic method: Weight by the precomputed kernel value. Accumulate weighted color and alpha values. 3. Normalization: Divide the accumulated sums by the total weight plus 10^{-4} to prevent division by zero. 4. Output: Write the normalized color and alpha values to the output buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def standardgaussianblur(inputtensor, kernelsize, sigma, usefixedweights): """ Applies Standard Gaussian Blur to inputtensor of shape (B, D, H, W). """ B, D, H, W = len(inputtensor), len(inputtensor[0]), len(inputtensor[0][0]), len(inputtensor[0][0][0]) outputtensor = [[[[0.0] W for in range(H)] for in range(D)] for in range(B)] halfk = kernelsize // 2 if usefixedweights: # Fixed 11-tap weights from (source provides 9 values for a 3x3 neighborhood) fixedweights = [1.0, 0.8, 0.65, 0.5, 0.4, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.025] for b in range(B): for d in range(D): for h in range(H): for w in range(W): sumcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] sumalpha = 0.0 sumweight = 0.0 for kh in range(-halfk, halfk + 1): for kw in range(-halfk, halfk + 1): nh, nw = h + kh, w + kw if nh < 0 or nh >= H or nw < 0 or nw >= W: continue sample = inputtensor[b][d][nh][nw] color, alpha = sample[:3], sample[3] # Map 3x3 offset to 1D index [0, 8] idx = (kh + halfk) 3 + (kw + halfk) weight = alpha fixedweights[idx] sumcolor = [sumcolor[i] + color[i] weight for i in range(3)] sumalpha += weight sumweight += weight norm = sumweight + 1e-4 outputtensor[b][d][h][w] = [c / norm for c in sumcolor] + [sumalpha / norm] else: # Dynamic 2D Gaussian weights from x = list(range(-halfk, halfk + 1)) y = list(range(-halfk, halfk + 1)) # Compute unnormalized weights w = exp(-(x^2 + y^2) / (2sigma^2)) weights = [[math.exp(-(xi2 + yi2) / (2 sigma2)) for xi in x] for yi in y] total = sum(sum(row) for row in weights) # Normalize weights by dividing by sum, clamped to min 1e-4 weights = [[w / max(total, 1e-4) for w in row] for row in weights] # Reshape input to (BD, 1, H, W) inputreshaped = [] for b in range(B): for d in range(D): inputreshaped.append(inputtensor[b][d]) blurred = [] for img in inputreshaped: blurredimg = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] # Apply 2D convolution with padding=N//2 for h in range(H): for w in range(W): acc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for kh in range(kernelsize): for kw in range(kernelsize): nh, nw = h - halfk + kh, w - halfk + kw # Zero-padding for boundary conditions if 0 <= nh < H and 0 <= nw < W: for c in range(4): acc[c] += img[nh][nw][c] weights[kh][kw] # else: add 0.0 (implicit) blurredimg[h][w] = acc blurred.append(blurredimg) # Reshape output back to (B, D, H, W) for b in range(B): for d in range(D): outputtensor[b][d] = blurred[b D + d] return outputtensor Kernel Size: N (typically odd). Sigma (\sigma): Standard deviation for the Gaussian distribution. Normalization Epsilon: 10^{-4}. Boundary Conditions: The fixed method implies sampling neighbors; boundary pixels require clamping or replication. The dynamic method uses zero-padding via padding=N//2. Alpha Handling: The fixed method explicitly weights by alpha before accumulation. The dynamic method treats the input as a tensor without explicit alpha weighting in the convolution step, potentially requiring alpha to be a separate channel or handled in post-processing. Precision: Division by zero is prevented by the epsilon clamp. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. The fixed-weight variant originates from the metaballs project. The tensor-based variant originates from the GPSplus framework for 3D reconstruction. dario-zubovic/metaballs, https://github.com/dario-zubovic/metaballs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) YaourtB/GPSplus, https://github.com/YaourtB/GPSplus, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: 3D Box Blur
head: blurFragShader
body: A post-processing blur filter that samples a 3D volume at the 8 corners of a small box centered on the current coordinate and averages them. It serves as a lightweight anti-aliasing and smoothing step in direct volume ray casting pipelines, distinct from its siblings by using a uniform 8-tap kernel rather than weighted or exponential decay functions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D texture (intensityVol) containing volume data, and uniform parameters defining the sampling geometry. Output: A blurred color value (FragColor) for the current fragment. Data Structures and Uniforms: The method relies on the following GLSL uniforms: highp sampler3D intensityVol: The 3D volume texture to sample. float coordZ: The Z-coordinate of the current sample point in volume space. float dX: The half-width of the box in the X dimension. float dY: The half-width of the box in the Y dimension. float dZ: The half-width of the box in the Z dimension. Algorithm Steps: 1. Construct Coordinate: Form the 3D sampling coordinate vx using the fragment's texture coordinates (TexCoord.xy) and the provided Z-coordinate. vx = (TexCoord.x, TexCoord.y, coordZ) 2. Define Offsets: The box corners are defined by the combinations of offsets \pm dX, \pm dY, \pm dZ. There are 8 corners. 3. Sample Corners: Sample the intensityVol at each of the 8 corners: (vx.x \pm dX, vx.y \pm dY, vx.z \pm dZ) 4. Average: Sum the 8 sampled values and divide by 8 (multiply by 0.125) to produce the final color. FragColor = \left( \sum{i=1}^{8} samplei \right) \times 0.125 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sample3dboxblur(TexCoord, coordZ, dX, dY, dZ, intensityVol): # 1. Construct 3D coordinate vx = vec3(TexCoord.x, TexCoord.y, coordZ) # 2. Define the 8 corner offsets offsets = [ vec3(-dX, -dY, -dZ), vec3(-dX, -dY, dZ), vec3(-dX, dY, -dZ), vec3(-dX, dY, dZ), vec3( dX, -dY, -dZ), vec3( dX, -dY, dZ), vec3( dX, dY, -dZ), vec3( dX, dY, dZ) ] # 3. Sample and sum total = vec4(0.0) for offset in offsets: samplepos = vx + offset # Assuming standard 3D texture sampling with wrapping/clamping handled by sampler total += texture(intensityVol, samplepos) # 4. Average FragColor = total 0.125 return FragColor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: If the box extends outside the volume bounds, texture sampling behavior (clamp, repeat, or border color) affects the result. Standard sampler3D behavior applies. Precision: Use highp for the sampler and coordinates to prevent precision artifacts in the volume lookup. Degenerate Input: If dX, dY, or dZ are zero, the box collapses to a line or point, effectively becoming a lower-dimensional blur or a single sample. A 12-tap variant that samples along a line with varying weights based on alpha and distance. It differs from the standard 8-tap box blur by using a weighted accumulation rather than a simple average, and by operating along a 1D line segment rather than a 3D cube. Choose this when alpha-based weighting is required for metaball rendering or specific visual effects. Definition: A 12-tap box blur that samples along a line with varying weights based on alpha and distance. Steps: 1. Initialize: Start with the center tap. Set sampleCount to the alpha of the center tap, and sum to the center tap multiplied by its alpha. sampleCount = centerTap.a sum = centerTap \times sampleCount 2. Calculate Step: Determine the step size for the 12 taps based on the center tap's alpha and the number of taps (TAPS). lenStep = centerTap.aa \times \left( \frac{1.0}{TAPS - 1.0} \right) (Note: centerTap.aa likely refers to a specific component or property of the center tap, possibly alpha or a derived value, as per source) 3. Loop and Sample: Iterate TAPS - 1 times. In each iteration, sample two points along the step vector. sampleUV = i.uv1.xyxy + steps \times l where l is the loop index. 4. Calculate Weights: Use smoothstep to determine weights based on the difference between the alpha and the step distance r. weight01 = smoothstep(vec2(-0.4, -0.4), vec2(0.0, 0.0), maxLen01 - r) 5. Accumulate: Add the weighted samples to the sum and the weights to the sample count. sum += sample0 \times weight01.x + sample1 \times weight01.y sampleCount += dot(weight01, vec2(1.0)) 6. Normalize: Divide the sum by the total weight (sample count) plus a small epsilon to avoid division by zero. returnValue = \frac{sum}{1e-5f + sampleCount} Parameters: TAPS: Number of taps (implied 12 from the name, but the loop runs TAPS-1 times sampling two points, suggesting 1 + 2(TAPS-1) samples? The source says "12-tap" and "loop TAPS-1 times... sampling two points". If TAPS=12, loop runs 11 times, sampling 22 points? This contradicts "12-tap". The source is ambiguous. We report the steps as given.) Edge Cases: Division by Zero: The epsilon 1e-5f prevents NaN results if sampleCount is zero. Alpha Dependency: The weights depend heavily on the alpha value of the center tap, making this method sensitive to the input volume's alpha channel. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment, as it performs a fixed number of texture lookups (8 for the standard method, 12+ for the variant). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, only requiring uniforms and local variables. Performance: Extremely fast due to the fixed, small kernel size and lack of complex weighting calculations in the standard version. The weighted variant is slightly more expensive due to the loop and smoothstep calculations. Strengths: Simple implementation, low computational cost, effective for mild smoothing and anti-aliasing. body: A 2D post-processing blur that weights neighboring samples by their alpha values to preserve sharp edges in depth-of-field rendering. It differs from its parent, Separable Ping-Pong Blur Post-Processing, by using a predefined non-separable kernel (typically 11-tap) where weights are dynamically modulated by pixel alpha, rather than applying independent 1D horizontal and vertical passes. This approach prevents alpha bleeding across object boundaries, a common artifact in standard Gaussian blurs. Inputs: A source texture containing RGBA color data, UV offset coordinates precomputed for the kernel taps, and Gaussian weight constants. Outputs: A blurred RGBA texture. Data Structures: The vertex shader or compute kernel populates a v2fBlur struct with UV coordinates for the kernel taps. The layout is: uv: Center pixel UV. uv01: UVs for taps B and C. uv23: UVs for taps D and E. uv45: UVs for taps F and G. uv67: UVs for taps H and I. uv89: UVs for taps J and K. Parameters: GWEIGHTS: Array of 6 floats defining the spatial decay: {1.0, 0.8, 0.675, 0.5, 0.2, 0.075}. ALPHAWEIGHT: Multiplier for alpha modulation, typically 2.0. EPSILON: Small constant for numerical stability, typically 1e-4f. Steps: 1. Sample the center pixel A at uv. 2. Sample the 10 neighbor pixels (B through K) using the corresponding uv fields in v2fBlur. 3. Initialize sumColor (RGB) to zero and sumWeight to zero. 4. For each neighbor pixel P \in \{B, \dots, K\} with index i (where B is index 1, C is index 2, etc.): a. Retrieve the spatial weight w{spatial} = G\WEIGHTS[i]. b. Calculate the alpha-modulated weight: w{alpha} = \text{saturate}(ALPHA\WEIGHT \cdot P.a). c. Calculate total weight: w = w{alpha} \cdot w{spatial}. d. Accumulate color: sumColor += P.rgb \cdot w. e. Accumulate weight: sumWeight += w. 5. Normalize the accumulated color: result.rgb = sumColor / (sumWeight + EPSILON). 6. Set the output alpha to the center pixel's alpha: result.a = A.a. 7. Edge Case: If the center pixel alpha is negligible (A.a < 1e-2f), restore the original RGB color from A to prevent darkening transparent areas. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The notes imply mapping neighbors to these weights. # Assuming a specific mapping where neighbors B-K use weights 1.0, 0.8, 0.675, 0.5, 0.2, 0.075 # and potentially repeating or clamping. The notes list 6 weights for 10 taps. # We assume the weights are applied cyclically or the first 6 are used for the first 6 taps, # and the remaining 4 taps use the last weight or zero. # However, standard implementation usually maps specific taps to specific weights. # Given "11-tap blur (center + 10 neighbors)" and "GWEIGHTS[6]", # we assume the weights are distributed. Let's assume a direct mapping for the first 6, # and the rest might be zero or reuse. # To be safe and implementable: we iterate 10 neighbors. for i in range(10): neighboruv = neighboruvs[i] samplep = texturesample(neighboruv) # Map index i to weight. # If i < len(GWEIGHTS), use GWEIGHTS[i]. # If i >= len(GWEIGHTS), use GWEIGHTS[-1] (0.075) or 0? # The notes don't specify the mapping for taps 7-10. # We will assume the weights are applied to the first 6 taps, # and taps 7-10 have zero weight or are not present in a 6-weight array context. # However, a 11-tap blur usually implies a cross or diamond shape. # Let's assume the weights array is indexed by tap distance/order. if i < len(gweights): wspatial = gweights[i] else: wspatial = 0.0 # Or reuse last weight? Notes are ambiguous. # "predefined Gaussian-like weight array" of size 6. # We assume taps beyond index 5 have 0 weight or are not sampled. # But it says 11-tap. # Let's assume the weights are: [1.0, 0.8, 0.675, 0.5, 0.2, 0.075] # and applied to taps B, C, D, E, F, G. # Taps H, I, J, K might have 0 weight or use the last weight. # Given "11-tap", we sample 10. # We will assume the weights are applied to the first 6 neighbors, # and the remaining 4 have 0 weight (effectively 7-tap). # Or, more likely, the weights are reused. # Without explicit mapping, we assume the first 6 neighbors get the 6 weights. # The remaining 4 neighbors get 0 weight. walpha = clamp(alphaweight samplep.a, 0.0, 1.0) w = walpha wspatial sumcolor += samplep.rgb w sumweight += w # Normalize resultrgb = sumcolor / (sumweight + epsilon) resulta = samplea.a # Edge case for transparent center if samplea.a < 0.01: resultrgb = samplea.rgb return vec4(resultrgb, resulta) A 4-tap blur used for spawning low-resolution effects, weighting neighbors by their alpha. It distinguishes itself from standard alpha-weighted blurs by using the smoothstep difference between neighbor and center alpha values as weights, effectively isolating foreground blur contributions. body: Insane HQ Bokeh Blur is a screen-space post-processing technique that simulates depth-of-field (DoF) or tilt-shift effects using Poisson-disk sampling with a disc kernel. It differs from its parent, Separable Weighted Blur (DoF), by employing a spatially varying kernel weight to control blur radius based on screen position and using a fixed set of Poisson-disk samples for uniform coverage, rather than a separable 1D convolution. It handles stereo rendering and alpha-weighted accumulation to preserve sharp edges in the final image. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A source texture MainTex containing the scene color and alpha. UV coordinates uv (normalized 0-1). Parameters: BlurSize: Maximum blur radius multiplier (scalar). BlurArea: Controls the falloff/gradient strength of the blur weight (scalar). Offsets: A vector where.w is a scale factor for Poisson disk size,.z is a minimum sample count floor. DiscKernel: An array of 28 float3 vectors. Layout: [x, y, weight]. Only x and y are used for offset calculation; z is ignored in the standard implementation. Output: A blurred color texture with the computed blur weight w stored in the alpha channel. Data Structures: DiscKernel: Array of size 28. Each element is a float3. DiscKernel[l].xy: Normalized offset coordinates for the l-th sample. DiscKernel[l].z: Precomputed weight (unused in the core sampling loop described in sources). Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Spatial Weight (w): Calculate the blur weight based on the normalized UV coordinates and the selected mode (Field or Iris). The weight determines the local blur radius. w = \text{clamp}(\text{WeightMode}(uv), 0, \BlurSize) Where WeightMode is either: Field Mode (Tilt-Shift): \text{WeightFieldMode}(uv) = |uvy \cdot 2 - 1| \cdot \BlurArea Iris Mode (DoF): \text{WeightIrisMode}(uv) = \text{dot}(uv \cdot 2 - 1, uv \cdot 2 - 1) \cdot \BlurArea 2. Early Exit Optimization: If w < 10^{-2} and the shader API is not DirectX 9, skip sampling and return the center tap immediately. This prevents compilation/runtime crashes on older D3D9 hardware which may fail on early returns or conditional compilation blocks. 3. Initialize Accumulators: Sample the center pixel: \text{centerTap} = \text{tex2D}(\MainTex, uv) Initialize the sum with the center tap: \text{sum} = \text{centerTap} Calculate the Poisson scale factor based on the center alpha and offsets: \text{poissonScale} = \MainTex\TexelSize.xy \cdot w (Note: Sources indicate poissonScale is multiplied by centerTap.a Offsets.w in some variants, but the core formula uses w derived from the weight function. The scale defines the radius of the disc kernel in texel space). 4. Calculate Sample Count: Determine the normalization divisor. A factor of 0.25 is used to handle high-frequency specular highlights: \text{sampleCount} = \max(\text{centerTap}.a \cdot 0.25, \Offsets.z) (Note: In the final normalization step, the denominator is 1.0 + N or 1.0 + 2N depending on the pass. The sampleCount variable here acts as a dynamic floor or accumulator base). 5. Poisson-Disk Sampling Loop: Loop l from 0 to 27 (28 iterations): a. Compute Sample UV: \text{sampleUV} = uv + \text{DiscKernel}[l].xy \cdot \text{poissonScale} For stereo rendering, this UV is adjusted for left and right eyes using UnityStereoScreenSpaceUVAdjust. b. Sample Texture: \text{sample0} = \text{tex2D}(\MainTex, \text{sampleUV}{\text{left}}) \text{sample1} = \text{tex2D}(\MainTex, \text{sampleUV}{\text{right}}) c. Accumulate: If either sample has non-zero alpha, compute Bokeh weights and accumulate: \text{weights} = \text{BokehWeightDisc2}(\text{sample0}, \text{sample1}, \dots, \text{centerTap}) \text{sum} += \text{sample0} \cdot \text{weights}.x + \text{sample1} \cdot \text{weights}.y \text{sampleCount} += \text{dot}(\text{weights}, 1) (Note: The exact implementation of BokehWeightDisc2 is not detailed in the provided notes, but it likely weights samples based on their depth/alpha relative to the center to simulate bokeh shape). 6. Normalize and Output: Divide the accumulated RGB sum by the sample count. For HQ passes, the divisor is 1.0 + 2.0 \cdot N (where N=28); for standard passes, it is 1.0 + N. \text{returnValue}.rgb = \frac{\text{sum}.rgb}{\text{sampleCount}} Preserve the center alpha: \text{returnValue}.a = \text{centerTap}.a Store the computed blur weight w in the output alpha channel for subsequent passes if needed. \text{output} = \text{float4}(\text{returnValue}.rgb, w) Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: uv: float2, normalized UV coordinates [0, 1]. maintex: Texture2D, input scene color/alpha. maintextexelsize: float2, (1/width, 1/height). blursize: float, max blur radius multiplier. blurarea: float, controls falloff strength. offsets: float4,.w is Poisson scale factor,.z is min sample count. disckernel: list of 28 float3, [x, y, weight]. Only xy used. Returns: float4, blurred color with blur weight in alpha. """ # 1. Compute Spatial Weight # Determine mode. Assuming Iris Mode (DoF) as default for "Bokeh". # Field Mode uses abs(uv.y 2 - 1). Iris Mode uses dot product. uvadjusted = uv 2.0 - 1.0 weightfield = abs(uv.y 2.0 - 1.0) blurarea weightiris = dot(uvadjusted, uvadjusted) blurarea # Select mode. The code snippet implies a switch or uniform selection. # We'll assume Iris Mode for "Bokeh" unless specified otherwise. wraw = weightiris # Clamp to max blur size w = clamp(wraw, 0.0, blursize) # 2. Early Exit Optimization # Guard against D3D9 compiler issues with early returns if w < 0.01: # 1e-2f # In a real shader, this would be #ifndef SHADERAPID3D9 # For this generic implementation, we proceed but note the optimization pass # 3. Sample Center centertap = maintex.sample(uv) # 4. Initialize Accumulators # Poisson scale: texel size blur weight poissonscale = maintextexelsize w # Sample count initialization # Factor 0.25 for high-frequency specular highlights samplecount = max(centertap.a 0.25, offsets.z) # Sum initialized with center tap sumrgb = centertap.rgb # 5. Poisson-Disk Sampling Loop numsamples = len(disckernel) # 28 for l in range(numsamples): # Compute sample UV # DiscKernel[l].xy poissonscale offset = disckernel[l].xy poissonscale sampleuv = uv + offset # Sample texture # Note: Stereo support requires adjusting UVs for left/right eye. # Assuming single-pass for this generic implementation. sample = maintex.sample(sampleuv) # Accumulate # If sample has alpha, add to sum. # The source mentions BokehWeightDisc2, which is not fully defined. # We assume a simple alpha-weighted accumulation for the generic case. if sample.a > 0.0: sumrgb += sample.rgb samplecount += 1.0 # Simplified accumulation logic based on source notes # 6. Normalize and Output # HQ pass divisor: 1.0 + 2.0 N # Standard pass divisor: 1.0 + N # We use HQ divisor as per the method name divisor = 1.0 + 2.0 numsamples blurredrgb = sumrgb / divisor # Preserve center alpha outputalpha = centertap.a # Store blur weight in alpha for potential downstream use outputalpha = w return float4(blurredrgb, outputalpha) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: D3D9 Compatibility: The early exit optimization (if w < 1e-2f) must be guarded with #ifndef SHADERAPID3D9 to prevent compilation or runtime crashes on older DirectX 9 hardware. Stereo Rendering: The method supports stereo rendering by sampling both left and right eye textures. UVs must be adjusted using UnityStereoScreenSpaceUVAdjust. Specular Highlights: The use of 0.25 factor in sampleCount calculation helps mitigate artifacts from high-frequency specular highlights. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of disc samples (28). The complexity is constant per pixel but depends on the resolution via texel size scaling. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel. The kernel is stored in constant memory. Performance: The early exit optimization significantly improves performance in regions with low blur weight (sharp focus areas). Stereo rendering doubles the texture fetches. body: Foreground CoC Blur is a post-processing blur that calculates the Circle of Confusion (CoC) for foreground elements in depth-of-field rendering. It distinguishes itself from standard alpha-weighted blurs by using the smoothstep difference between neighbor and center alpha values as weights. It builds on Separable Weighted Blur (DoF) to isolate foreground blur contributions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Alpha values of a center pixel and 11 neighboring pixels. Output: A normalized, weighted alpha sum representing the foreground CoC. Data Structures: GWEIGHTS: An array of floating-point weights; the exact size and values are not given, but GWEIGHTS[1] is used as a multiplier. Sample pattern: 11 pixels (labeled A–K) sampled similarly to Alpha-Weighted Blur. The exact spatial offsets are not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Sample the center pixel alpha (\alphac) and 11 neighbor alphas (\alphai). 2. Calculate the weight for each neighbor: wi = \text{smoothstep}(-0.5, 0.0, \alphai - \alphac) \times \text{G\WEIGHTS}[1]. 3. Accumulate the weighted alphas (S = \sum \alphai wi) and the weights (W = \sum wi). 4. Normalize the result: \text{result} = S / (W + 1\text{e-}4). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def foregroundcocblur(centeralpha, neighboralphas, gweights): """ centeralpha: float, alpha of the center pixel neighboralphas: list of floats, alpha values of 11 neighbors gweights: list of floats, GWEIGHTS array """ sumalpha = 0.0 sumweights = 0.0 weightscale = gweights[1] for neighboralpha in neighboralphas: diff = neighboralpha - centeralpha w = smoothstep(-0.5, 0.0, diff) weightscale sumalpha += neighboralpha w sumweights += w epsilon = 1e-4 result = sumalpha / (sumweights + epsilon) return result Parameters: GWEIGHTS[1]: A constant weight multiplier. Value not given in the sources. smoothstep bounds: Fixed at [-0.5, 0.0]. Epsilon: 1e-4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero is prevented by adding 1e-4 to the denominator. Boundary checks for sample indices are not specified in the sources. This variant integrates foreground CoC calculation with background CoC masking. It samples MainTex for background CoC and FgOverlap for foreground CoC. If the background CoC is negligible (< 0.01), it returns the saturated difference between foreground and background CoC: Result = (bgAndFgCoc < 0.01) \times \text{saturate}(fgOverlapCoc - bgAndFgCoc). body: Capture CoC calculates the unsigned magnitude of the Circle of Confusion (CoC) for a given pixel depth. It serves as the foundational step in depth-of-field post-processing by determining how much a pixel should blur based on its distance from the focal plane. It differs from Foreground CoC Blur by providing the raw magnitude value (stored in alpha) rather than performing the weighted blur specific to foreground elements. Inputs: Camera depth texture (CameraDepthTexture). Shader parameters packed in CurveParams: CurveParams.x: Maximum CoC value. CurveParams.y: Minimum CoC threshold (values below this become 0). CurveParams.z: Scale factor. CurveParams.w: Focal depth plane (linear depth). Current UV coordinates. Outputs: A color value where the alpha channel contains the clamped, unsigned CoC magnitude. Data Structures: The CoC is stored as a single floating-point value in the alpha channel of the output color. Steps: 1. Sample the camera depth texture at the current UV coordinates to obtain the raw depth value. 2. Convert the raw depth to linear 0-1 depth space. 3. Calculate the raw CoC magnitude using the scale factor, focal depth, and linear depth. 4. Subtract the minimum threshold. If the result is negative, clamp to 0. 5. Clamp the final result to the maximum CoC value. Formula: The raw CoC magnitude C{raw} is calculated as: C{raw} = \frac{\text{CurveParams.z} \times (\text{CurveParams.w} - d)}{d + 10^{-5}} Where: d is the linear depth in 0-1 range. CurveParams.z is the scale factor. CurveParams.w is the focal depth. The final alpha value \alpha is: \alpha = \text{clamp}(\max(0.0, C{raw} - \text{CurveParams.y}), 0.0, \text{CurveParams.x}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatecapturecoc(uv, cameradepthtexture, curveparams): # 1. Sample depth rawdepth = sampledepthtexture(cameradepthtexture, uv) # 2. Convert to linear 0-1 depth # Implementation detail: Linear01Depth converts non-linear depth to linear 0-1 range. # This depends on the specific graphics API and depth buffer format. d = linear01depth(rawdepth) # 3. Calculate raw CoC magnitude # Note: The source formula uses (focaldepth - d). # This implies positive CoC for objects closer than focal plane if scale is positive, # or it represents a specific directional convention. scalefactor = curveparams.z focaldepth = curveparams.w minthreshold = curveparams.y maxcoc = curveparams.x epsilon = 1e-5 numerator = scalefactor (focaldepth - d) denominator = d + epsilon rawcoc = numerator / denominator # 4. Clamp to unsigned magnitude # Subtract min threshold adjustedcoc = rawcoc - minthreshold # Clamp to max(0,...) to remove negative values (unsigned) clampedcoc = max(0.0, adjustedcoc) # Clamp to max CoC finalcoc = min(clampedcoc, maxcoc) return finalcoc Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: An epsilon (10^{-5}) is added to the denominator to prevent division by zero when depth d is 0. Negative Depth Differences: The formula (\text{CurveParams.w} - d) can yield negative values if the object is behind the focal plane (assuming standard depth conventions). The max(0.0,...) step ensures the output is unsigned, discarding the sign information. Precision: Linear depth conversion precision varies by platform and depth buffer format (e.g., 16-bit vs 24-bit/32-bit). Low precision can cause banding in the CoC gradient. It emphasizes that the raw CoC is derived from the difference between the focal depth and the linear depth, scaled by a factor. It is chosen when the implementation requires explicit control over the depth texture sampling and linearization process. It is the core calculation logic for Capture CoC. This variant calculates a signed CoC instead of an unsigned magnitude. It stores the sign based on whether the depth d is greater than or less than the focal depth CurveParams.w. body: This method calculates the magnitude of the Circle of Confusion (CoC) for a given pixel based on its linear depth relative to a focal plane, producing an unsigned blur radius used in depth-of-field post-processing. It differs from parent methods by converting scene depth into a specific blur metric using a parametric formula, rather than storing raw depth or performing the blur itself. It serves as the input generator for Foreground CoC Blur. Inputs: depthTexture: A texture containing non-linear depth values (e.g., OpenGL or DirectX clip-space depth) sampled at current UV coordinates. CurveParams: A vector of four floats: CurveParams.x: Maximum CoC value (clamping upper bound). CurveParams.y: Minimum CoC threshold (values below this become 0). CurveParams.z: Scale factor for the CoC calculation. CurveParams.w: Focal depth plane (linear depth value where CoC is 0). Outputs: coc: A single float representing the unsigned blur radius for the pixel. Data Structures: The implementation typically resides in a fragment shader. No persistent data structures are required; the calculation is per-pixel. Steps: 1. Sample Depth: Read the depth value from the depth texture at the current UV coordinates. 2. Linearize Depth: Convert the sampled depth d{sample} to linear 0-1 depth d. The source code uses a helper function Linear01Depth: d = \text{Linear01Depth}(d{sample}) In standard OpenGL, this typically involves d = \frac{2 \cdot near}{far + near - d{sample} \cdot (far - near)}. In DirectX, it involves d = d{sample} \cdot far. The exact conversion depends on the graphics API and depth buffer configuration, but the source assumes a Linear01Depth function exists that returns a value in [0, 1]. 3. Calculate Raw CoC: Compute the raw CoC value using the parametric formula: C{raw} = \frac{\text{CurveParams.z} \times (\text{CurveParams.w} - d)}{d + 10^{-5}} Here, 10^{-5} is a small epsilon added to the denominator to prevent division by zero when d \approx 0. 4. Apply Minimum Threshold: Subtract the minimum CoC threshold CurveParams.y from C{raw}. If the result is negative, clamp it to 0. C{thresh} = \max(0, C{raw} - \text{CurveParams.y}) 5. Apply Maximum Clamping: Clamp the result to the maximum CoC value CurveParams.x. \text{coc} = \min(C{thresh}, \text{CurveParams.x}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: depthsample: The non-linear depth value sampled from the depth texture. curveparams: A tuple or list [maxcoc, mincocthreshold, scalefactor, focaldepth]. curveparams[0]: CurveParams.x (Max CoC) curveparams[1]: CurveParams.y (Min CoC Threshold) curveparams[2]: CurveParams.z (Scale Factor) curveparams[3]: CurveParams.w (Focal Depth) Returns: float: The calculated unsigned CoC value. """ # 1. Sample and Linearize Depth # Note: Linear01Depth is API-specific. # OpenGL: d = 2.0 near / (far + near - depthsample (far - near)) # DirectX: d = depthsample far # The source assumes a function Linear01Depth(depthsample) exists. d = linear01depth(depthsample) # Extract parameters for clarity maxcoc = curveparams[0] mincocthreshold = curveparams[1] scalefactor = curveparams[2] focaldepth = curveparams[3] # 2. Calculate Raw CoC # Formula: Craw = (scalefactor (focaldepth - d)) / (d + epsilon) epsilon = 1e-5 craw = (scalefactor (focaldepth - d)) / (d + epsilon) # 3. Apply Minimum Threshold # Subtract min threshold and clamp to 0 cthresh = max(0.0, craw - mincocthreshold) # 4. Apply Maximum Clamping # Clamp to max CoC coc = min(cthresh, maxcoc) return coc Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: The denominator d + 10^{-5} prevents division by zero if d=0. Negative CoC: The formula can produce negative values if d > \text{CurveParams.w} (pixel is behind focal plane). The subtraction of CurveParams.y and subsequent clamping to \max(0, \dots) handles this, effectively treating out-of-focus regions symmetrically in magnitude but potentially requiring the blur kernel to handle directionality if signed CoC were needed (though this method outputs unsigned). Depth Precision: The accuracy of d depends on the depth buffer precision and the linearization function. Incorrect linearization leads to incorrect CoC values. This variant is not a calculation method but a calibration procedure to map a software focus parameter to physical focal distance. It is used to determine the CurveParams.w (focal depth) or to validate the scale factor CurveParams.z in real-world scenarios. Definition: Establishes a one-to-one correspondence between a software focus parameter (FParam) and physical focal distance for a fixed focal length. Steps: 1. Manually set the zoom (focal length). 2. Turn the focus ring to the far end until the camera is focused on the nearest objects, setting FParam = 0. 3. Launch DigicamControl software, vary FParam, and measure the focal distance for each value by recording the distance interval within which a printed grid is seen without blur. 4. Fit a curve between the mean values of the focused intervals and FParam to generate the final calibration mapping. Parameters: FParam: A focus parameter controlled via DigicamControl software, associated with focal distance. Initialized to 0 when the focus ring is turned to the far end. Calibration Data (Table I): | FParam | Focused Interval (meters) | |:--- |:--- | | 0 | 0.24-0.25 | | -500 | 0.27-0.28 | | -1000 | 0.30-0.32 | | -1500 | 0.35-0.37 | | -2000 | 0.41-0.43 | | -2500 | 0.49-0.51 | | -3000 | 0.60-0.63 | | -3500 | 0.79-0.82 | | -4000 | 1.20-1.27 | | -4500 | 2.0-2.7 | | -5000 | 15-25 | Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel. The calculation involves a few arithmetic operations and texture sampling. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Requires only the depth texture and the curve parameters. Strengths: Simple to implement; computationally inexpensive; provides a smooth transition of blur based on depth. Limitations: Assumes a thin-lens model; does not account for lens aberrations or complex bokeh shapes; relies on accurate depth information. When to Use: When a simple depth-of-field effect is needed in post-processing and the scene depth is available. When Not to Use: When physically accurate lens simulation is required, or when depth information is unavailable or unreliable. This method is derived from shader implementations found in the metaballs repository, specifically in the fragment shaders fragCaptureForegroundCoc and fragMergeCoc. The calibration procedure is described in the context of partial light field tomographic reconstruction, where accurate focus parameter mapping is essential for refocusing algorithms. dario-zubovic/metaballs, https://github.com/dario-zubovic/metaballs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Partial light field tomographic reconstruction from a fixed-camera focal stack, https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.01903v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: HQ Upsample Combine Blur
head: MQ Upsample Combine Blur, fragBlurUpsampleCombineHQ, fragBlurUpsampleCombineMQ
body: HQ Upsample Combine Blur combines a high-resolution small-scale blur with a low-resolution large-scale blur using alpha-based blending to achieve depth of field effects. It distinguishes itself from its siblings by using a larger disc kernel and specific blending thresholds compared to the Medium Quality (MQ) variant, while providing higher fidelity than the Cheap variant. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: MainTex: High-resolution source texture (float4). LowRez: Low-resolution pre-blurred texture (float4). Offsets.w: A scalar parameter controlling the blur scale. centerTap: The sample from MainTex at the current pixel. bigBlur: The sample from LowRez at the corresponding pixel. Outputs: float4: The final blended color and alpha. Data Structures: DiscKernel: An array of structures containing xy (float2 offset) and z (float radius/weight factor). The size is NumDiscSamples. PoissonScale: A float4 used to scale the kernel offsets. Steps: 1. Sample Base Textures: Retrieve bigBlur from LowRez. Retrieve centerTap from MainTex. 2. Calculate Scale and Initial Count: Compute poissonScale: \text{poissonScale} = \text{MainTex\TexelSize}.xyxy \times \text{centerTap}.a \times \text{Offsets}.w Where MainTexTexelSize.xy is the inverse of the texture dimensions (pixel width/height). Compute initial sampleCount: \text{sampleCount} = \max(\text{centerTap}.a \times 0.25, 0.1) 3. Accumulate Small Blur: Initialize smallBlur to zero. Loop i from 0 to NumDiscSamples - 1: Calculate sample UV: \text{sampleUV} = \text{centerTap}.uv + \text{DiscKernel}[i].xy \times \text{poissonScale}.xy Sample high-res texture: \text{sample0} = \text{tex2D}(\text{MainTex}, \text{sampleUV}) Calculate weight: \text{weight0} = \text{BokehWeightDisc}(\text{sample0}, \text{DiscKernel}[i].z, \text{centerTap}) Accumulate: \text{smallBlur} += \text{sample0} \times \text{weight0} \text{sampleCount} += \text{weight0} 4. Normalize Small Blur: \text{smallBlur} = \frac{\text{smallBlur}}{\text{sampleCount} + 10^{-5}} 5. Blend Low and High Resolution: Apply BlendLowWithHighHQ using centerTap.a, smallBlur, and bigBlur. Note: The exact implementation of BlendLowWithHighHQ is not provided in the sources, but it is distinct from BlendLowWithHighMQ used in the MQ variant. 6. Final Output: If centerTap.a < 10^{-2}: \text{return centerTap} Else: \text{return float4}(\text{smallBlur}.rgb, \text{centerTap}.a) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def HQUpsampleCombineBlur(centeruv, centertap, bigblur, offsetsw, maintex, lowrez, disckernel, numdiscsamples): # 1. Calculate Poisson Scale # Assuming maintextexelsize is (1/width, 1/height) texelsize = maintex.texelsize poissonscale = float4(texelsize.x, texelsize.y, texelsize.x, texelsize.y) centertap.a offsetsw # 2. Initial Sample Count samplecount = max(centertap.a 0.25, 0.1) # 3. Accumulate Small Blur smallblur = float4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for i in range(numdiscsamples): # Calculate sample UV sampleuv = centeruv + disckernel[i].xy poissonscale.xy # Sample Main Texture sample0 = maintex.sample(sampleuv) # Calculate Weight # BokehWeightDisc is a helper function defined elsewhere in the source context weight0 = BokehWeightDisc(sample0, disckernel[i].z, centertap) # Accumulate smallblur += sample0 weight0 samplecount += weight0 # 4. Normalize smallblur = smallblur / (samplecount + 1e-5) # 5. Blend # BlendLowWithHighHQ is a helper function defined elsewhere blended = BlendLowWithHighHQ(centertap.a, smallblur, bigblur) # 6. Return if centertap.a < 1e-2: return centertap else: return float4(blended.rgb, centertap.a) Parameters: NumDiscSamples: Number of samples in the disc kernel. Not given in the sources. Offsets.w: Scalar multiplier for blur radius. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Alpha: If centerTap.a is negligible (< 1e-2), the function returns the original centerTap to avoid unnecessary blending artifacts. Division by Zero: A small epsilon (1e-5) is added to the denominator during normalization to prevent division by zero. A low-cost blur variant that linearly interpolates between the center tap and the big blur based on alpha and foreground overlap. It differs from HQ by using a simple lerp instead of a disc kernel accumulation and blending function. Steps: 1. Sample Textures: centerTap: From MainTex. bigBlur: From LowRez. fgCoc: Foreground overlap alpha from FgOverlap texture. 2. Interpolate: Calculate blend factor: \text{factor} = \text{saturate}(\max(\text{centerTap}.a, \text{fgCoc}) \times 8.0) Compute result: \text{smallBlur} = \text{lerp}(\text{centerTap}, \text{bigBlur}, \text{factor}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def CheapUpsampleCombineBlur(centertap, bigblur, fgcoc): # Calculate blend factor maxalpha = max(centertap.a, fgcoc) factor = saturate(maxalpha 8.0) # Linear interpolation smallblur = lerp(centertap, bigblur, factor) return smallblur Time Complexity: Proportional to NumDiscSamples for HQ, constant for Cheap. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for MainTex, LowRez, and optionally FgOverlap. Performance: HQ is more expensive due to multiple texture samples and kernel accumulation. Cheap is significantly faster but lower quality. Strengths: HQ provides high-quality depth of field with proper bokeh shape. Cheap is suitable for performance-constrained scenarios. Limitations: HQ requires careful tuning of NumDiscSamples and kernel data. Cheap may exhibit visible artifacts in complex scenes due to linear interpolation. This method is part of a post-processing pipeline for depth of field, specifically within the context of Unity's built-in post-processing stack or similar implementations. The HQ variant is designed to balance quality and performance for high-end rendering, while the Cheap variant serves as a fallback for lower-end hardware. dario-zubovic/metaballs, https://github.com/dario-zubovic/metaballs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Post-Processing Filtering
head: Accumulation Buffer Filtering, Noise Removal in Region Growing, Post-Processing Blur, Region Growing Postprocessing
body: Post-processing filtering applies spatial filters to accumulated buffers to smooth residual aliasing after ray intersection and shading. It also refers to a cleanup step after region growing to remove noise-induced erroneous connections between features or fill gaps in segmented data. It is distinguished from pre-filtering or supersampling by operating on the final rendered image or extracted feature set rather than modifying the ray casting process itself. This method encompasses two primary workflows depending on the context: image-order smoothing and region-growing cleanup. Inputs: Accumulated color buffer C, depth buffer D, or both. Outputs: Filtered image C'. Data Structures: 2D arrays for color and depth values per pixel. 1. Ray Casting: Perform standard ray casting to generate the initial accumulated color and depth buffers. 2. Filter Application: Apply a spatial filter (e.g., Gaussian blur) directly to the accumulated buffers. This step smooths residual aliasing without additional ray computations. This is necessary because single-ray-per-pixel generation exacerbates aliasing. Inputs: Segmented volume data, feature map. Outputs: Cleaned feature map with erroneous connections removed. Data Structures: Voxel grid with feature labels. 1. Identify Thin Connections: Scan the segmented volume to identify connections between distinct features that are one- or two-voxels wide, caused by noise. 2. Filtering: Remove these thin connections to prevent features from growing into each other erroneously. 3. Gap Filling (Optional): Fill gaps introduced by noisy data if the filtering criteria allow. When defining the region growing criteria that necessitate post-processing, the cost function C{cc}(p) for a voxel p is defined as: C{cc}(p) = f{ca} p + f{cb} (1-p) Where: f{ca} and f{cb} are feature values. p is a weight specified by the user or system. Default weight: p = \frac{\sigmav}{\sigmav + \sigmag}, where \sigmav is the volume data standard deviation and \sigmag is the gradient magnitude standard deviation. Performance: Not given in the sources. Quality: Smooths residual aliasing in single-sample renders. Removes topological errors in segmented data. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Image-order post-processing filters are integrated with ray casting to handle aliasing in direct volume rendering. Region-growing post-processing techniques were developed to improve the robustness of feature extraction in noisy volumetric data, specifically for medical visualization tasks such as lung structure analysis. ray casting, https://grokipedia.com/page/Raycasting, fetched 2026-10-26 RGVis: Region Growing Based Visualization Techniques for Volume Visualization, https://escholarship.org/uc/item/3td71868, fetched 2026-11-03 (unofficial)

name: Screen-Space Image Filtering
head: Screen-space approaches
body: Screen-Space Image Filtering modifies a base image rendered in a vacuum by adding effects caused by participating media, using only information currently visible on the screen. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its exclusive reliance on the 2D image buffer; it cannot access data for objects behind the camera or occluded geometry that was not rendered in the base pass. The family shares no single mathematical mechanism beyond operating on discrete signals, with techniques selected based on their pipeline stage: pre-filtering for participating media, rasterization coverage for line primitives, or screen-space post-processing for ambient occlusion and color buffers. 1. Image Representation: The input is an image L, defined as a discrete two-dimensional function L: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Color Space and Range: The color channels (red, green, blue) are assumed to be non-negative real numbers, with HDR values ranging from 0 to +\infty. 3. Screen-Space Constraint: Techniques operate exclusively on information currently visible on the screen, limiting access to occluded geometry or data behind the camera. 4. Convolution Basis: Many techniques apply a filter to the original image, typically using neighborhood-based convolution. Uses screen-space splatting to handle small cells. Incorporates motion blur into the screen-space splatting process. Applies thresholding to slice data before screen-space filtering. Pre-computes filters to accelerate screen-space operations. Uses a pseudo-separable bilateral filter for edge-preserving smoothing. Implements blur via separable ping-pong passes. Uses affine arithmetic to track uncertainty during filtering. The term "screen-space" was introduced to describe methods that modify an image rendered in a vacuum by adding effects caused by participating media, relying solely on information "on the screen". These approaches became popular in real-time rendering on GPUs because they can often be executed for each output pixel individually in parallel. The limitation of not working with information not currently on the screen (e.g., objects behind the camera) is noted, though often considered not critical in certain conditions. The mathematical foundation treats the image as a discrete 2D function L: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3 with HDR values in [0, +\infty).
