name: Affine Arithmetic Filtering
head: Affine Arithmetic for Shader Averaging, Heidrich et al. filtering
body: Affine Arithmetic Filtering is a method to obtain an average value of a procedural shader with an error bound over a finite area using affine arithmetic. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Prefiltering by providing a rigorous mathematical error bound derived from the propagation of uncertainty, rather than relying on statistical variance estimates or sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A procedural shader function f(\mathbf{x}) where \mathbf{x} is the spatial coordinate; the finite area (e.g., pixel footprint) over which to average. Output: The average value of the shader over the area, along with an error bound \delta representing the loss in noise variance due to filtering. Data Structures: Affine arithmetic represents a value x as a linear form: x = x0 + \sum{i=1}^{n} xi \epsiloni where x0 is the central value, xi are coefficients, and \epsiloni are independent noise symbols taking values in [-1, 1]. Steps: 1. Represent the input coordinates of the shader as affine forms, capturing the uncertainty of the position within the pixel area. 2. Evaluate the procedural shader using affine arithmetic operations. This propagates the uncertainty through the shader's mathematical operations. 3. Extract the central value of the resulting affine form as the average shader value. 4. Compute the error bound \delta from the sum of the absolute values of the non-central coefficients of the resulting affine form. This bound quantifies the loss in noise variance due to filtering. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Provides a rigorous error bound for procedural shader averaging. When to use: When filtering procedural textures and an analytical expression of the noise variance is available. When not: Not given in the sources. Affine Arithmetic Filtering was presented by Heidrich et al. in [HSS98]. It is part of the broader investigation into general methods for filtering procedural textures. name: Neural volume rendering
head: SRN Rendering
body: Neural volume rendering is a family of differentiable rendering methods that synthesize novel views of 3D scenes by querying a neural network or neural representation along camera rays and integrating the outputs using classical volume rendering techniques. It solves the problem of representing complex, high-dimensional volumetric data or implicit scenes without explicit geometric meshes or large voxel grids, enabling view-dependent appearance and high-fidelity reconstruction from 2D images. This family sets itself apart from traditional direct volume ray casting by replacing the lookup of scalar voxel values with a neural function that predicts density and color, and from sibling methods by relying on specific architectural choices such as hierarchical sampling, direct voxel grids, or in-shader evaluation. All neural volume rendering methods share the following core mechanism: 1. Neural Representation: The 3D scene is represented by a neural network (typically a Multi-Layer Perceptron, MLP) or a neural data structure (e.g., hash grids, feature grids) parameterized by weights \theta. This network maps spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} (and optionally viewing directions \mathbf{d}) to raw density \tilde{\sigma} and color \tilde{\mathbf{c}}. 2. Differentiable Rendering: The rendering process is fully differentiable with respect to the network parameters \theta. This allows the method to be trained using gradient descent on the difference between rendered images and ground truth images. 3. Volume Rendering Equation: The final pixel color is computed by integrating the neural network's outputs along the ray using the front-to-back volume rendering equation, identical to the parent method Direct volume ray casting: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \mathbf{c}i and \alphai are derived from the neural network's output \tilde{\mathbf{c}}i and \tilde{\sigma}i via activation functions (e.g., sigmoid for color, softplus for density) and the Beer-Lambert law. 4. Positional Encoding: To enable the MLP to capture high-frequency details, input coordinates \mathbf{x} and viewing directions \mathbf{d} are typically mapped to higher-dimensional spaces using sinusoidal positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) before being fed into the network. A differentiable rendering method that synthesizes novel views by querying a neural radiance field along camera rays and integrating outputs using classical volume rendering. It sets itself apart from siblings like Iterative Ray Marching with Neural Volume Inference and DVGO Volume Rendering Forward Pass by relying on a simple, differentiable hierarchical sampling of coarse alpha weights without auxiliary acceleration structures. Choose it for high-fidelity novel view synthesis where view-dependent appearance is critical. A GPU-accelerated technique that splits neural volume evaluation along a ray into multiple kernel launches to handle rays that do not fully converge in a single pass. It distinguishes itself from single-pass methods by using a counter-based compaction mechanism to track active rays between launches, allowing dynamic handling of varying ray depths and complex occlusion without fixed iteration limits. Choose it when rendering complex scenes with deep occlusion or varying density. A direct volume rendering technique where the neural network (MLP) is evaluated directly inside the CUDA kernel for each sample point during ray marching, rather than pre-decoding the volume into a 3D texture or using sample-streaming. It supports multiple shading modes, including gradient shading and single-shade heuristics, allowing for real-time interactive visualization of neural radiance fields. Choose it for interactive applications requiring on-the-fly neural inference. Renders a 3D scene represented by a direct voxel grid of density and color features into a 2D image by querying the grid along camera rays and compositing the results. It differs from standard NeRF by replacing the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with a direct lookup in a 3D texture (voxel grid), enabling significantly faster training and inference while maintaining view-dependent color through auxiliary feature vectors. Choose it for fast training and inference of large-scale scenes. A path-tracing method for rendering scattering and emissive media represented by mixtures of kernel-based volumetric primitives (e.g., Gaussians, Epanechnikov) rather than voxel grids or point clouds. It modifies standard volumetric path tracing by replacing medium interaction routines with primitive-specific transmittance evaluation, free-flight distance sampling, and albedo evaluation. It distinguishes itself from its sibling, the Volumetric Primitive Tomography Integrator, by supporting scattering and emissive media via multiple importance sampling with PDF balancing, whereas the tomography integrator integrates density with no scattering. Choose it for physically-based rendering of participating media. Provides a diagnostic visualization pipeline for neural volume models by rendering individual sample points as instanced spheres, colored by the network's predicted radiance and filtered by an opacity threshold. It differs from standard rendering methods by bypassing front-to-back compositing to inspect the raw distribution and magnitude of neural network outputs in 3D space, serving as a tool to verify that the implicit representation is capturing scene geometry and appearance correctly. Choose it for debugging and analyzing neural volume training. Renders volumetric data by mapping a 3D texture to a stack of view-aligned polygons and executing a neural network classifier directly within the fragment shader for each pixel. It solves the problem of interactive, high-dimensional classification of volume data by offloading the inference logic to the GPU, allowing users to evaluate training results in real-time. Unlike standard volume rendering which uses fixed transfer functions, this approach uses a learned neural network to determine opacity and color, and it differs from In-Shader Neural Volume Ray Marching by relying on rasterization of textured polygons rather than explicit ray marching through the volume. Choose it for interactive classification and visualization of scalar fields. Learns to reconstruct high-quality images from noisy, low-sample path-traced volume renderings by exploiting spatial and volumetric correlations, trading unbiased Monte Carlo convergence for biased neural reconstruction. It is distinguished from surface-only denoisers by its requirement for specialized volumetric auxiliary features (such as optical thickness and scattering normals) because standard features like depth and albedo are ill-defined or unavailable throughout participating media. Choose it for accelerating Monte Carlo path tracing in volumetric scenes. Definition: A framework for high-fidelity 3D surface reconstruction from RGB images using neural volume rendering, combining multi-resolution 3D hash grids with neural surface rendering without auxiliary data. It uses numerical gradients to compute higher-order derivatives (e.g., surface normals) as a smoothing operation to stabilize optimization. It uses coarse-to-fine optimization on hash grids controlling different levels of details. Steps: Samples 3D locations along camera view directions. Encodes the sampled positions using a multi-resolution hash encoding. Feeds encoded features into an SDF MLP and a color MLP. Composites images using SDF-based volume rendering. Comparison: Unlike concurrent work which uses a displacement network to correct shape, Neuralangelo uses hierarchical hash grids and controls detail levels based on analysis of higher-order derivatives. Definition: An approach that uses cost volumes estimated from input views via multi-view stereo algorithms, processed by a CNN to create feature maps, from which visibility and local features are extracted during volume rendering. Steps: A CNN is used to create feature maps G from the estimated cost volumes. During volume rendering, visibility and local features are extracted from these features and processed using MLPs to extract color and alpha. Formula: Visibility is computed as a cumulative density function written as a weighted sum of sigmoid functions. Definition: A rendering acceleration technique that replaces slow neural volume rendering with a mesh-based approach by pre-computing appearance features and using a compact shape model for real-time frame generation. Steps: Use the marching cubes algorithm to extract a mesh as an iso-surface of the SDF. Store the features computed from the set of input images by the encoder as well as their associated depth maps. At render time, aggregate these features based on the target viewing direction. Evaluate the decoder on the aggregated features for each frame. Parameter: Decoder evaluation time: 8.7ms for DTU images and network architecture. Feature aggregation time: 22.3ms for DTU images and network architecture. Number: Total rendering time per frame is approximately 31ms (8.7ms + 22.3ms), enabling real-time rates. Comparison: Unlike neural volume rendering methods which cannot generate frames at nearly a real-time rate, this surface-based method renders in real time. Deep Volumetric Ambient Occlusion (DVAO) is a deep learning-based technique that predicts per-voxel ambient occlusion (AO) volumes for direct volume rendering (DVR). It solves the problem of computing realistic volumetric illumination efficiently by training a 3D convolutional neural network to map input scalar field data and transfer functions to an AO volume. Unlike traditional numerical integration methods, DVAO predicts the AO field once, which is then sampled via texture lookup during rendering, supporting real-time interaction when the transfer function changes. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its use of a global encoder-decoder architecture that incorporates transfer function information implicitly or explicitly, rather than computing occlusion locally per ray. Neural volume rendering builds on the principles of differentiable rendering and neural implicit representations. The core mechanism involves querying a neural network along camera rays and integrating the outputs using classical volume rendering techniques. The field has expanded to include various representations such as Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO) and hash-grid-based methods. It is applied in computer vision for 3D reconstruction and novel view synthesis. name: NeRF Volumetric Rendering (Coarse/Fine Sampling)
head: NeRF Coarse-to-Fine Rendering, NeRF Rendering Equation, NeRF Two-Stage Sampling, Standard NeRF, Vanilla NeRF, Volume Rendering (NeRF), Volumetric Rendering (NeRF)
body: NeRF Volumetric Rendering (Coarse/Fine Sampling) is a differentiable volume rendering technique that synthesizes novel views of 3D scenes by querying a neural radiance field along camera rays and accumulating outputs using classical volume rendering. It solves the problem of insufficient sampling in high-frequency regions by employing a two-stage sampling strategy: a coarse network estimates the density distribution to guide a fine network that concentrates samples in high-opacity regions. This method sets itself apart from its siblings, such as Iterative Ray Marching with Neural Volume Inference which uses learned acceleration structures, and DVGO Volume Rendering Forward Pass which uses hybrid voxel-MLP representations, by relying on a simple, differentiable stratified resampling of coarse alpha weights without auxiliary acceleration structures or complex data structures. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A batch of rays \mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}) where \mathbf{o} is the origin and \mathbf{d} is the direction; near and far plane bounds tn, tf; number of coarse samples Nc and fine samples Nf; boolean flags for lindisp (inverse depth sampling) and perturb (stratified jittering); and two neural networks: coarsemodel and finemodel. Outputs: Rendered RGB color \mathbf{C}{out}, accumulated opacity \alpha{out}, depth \mathbf{D}{out}, and optionally disparity maps. Data Structures: Ray Batch: Tensor of shape [R, 8] or [R, 9] containing ray origins (3), directions (3), near/far bounds (2), and optionally viewing directions (3) if view-dependent color is used. Sample Positions: Tensor of shape [R, N] containing depth values ti along the ray. 3D Points: Tensor of shape [R, N, 3] containing world coordinates \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d}. Network Output: Tensor of shape [R, N, 4] containing raw density \tilde{\sigma} (1 channel) and raw color \tilde{\mathbf{c}} (3 channels). Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Construction: For each pixel, construct the ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} using the camera pose and intrinsic parameters. Extract ray origins \mathbf{o}, directions \mathbf{d}, and near/far bounds tn, tf from the ray batch. 2. Coarse Sampling: Generate Nc linearly spaced values t{vals} \in [0, 1]. Map to depth bounds: If lindisp is False: z{vals} = tn (1 - t{vals}) + tf t{vals}. If lindisp is True: z{vals} = \left( \frac{1}{tn} (1 - t{vals}) + \frac{1}{tf} t{vals} \right)^{-1}. If perturb is True, apply stratified sampling: compute midpoints mids = 0.5 (z{vals}[:, 1:] + z{vals}[:,:-1]), define lower bounds [z{vals}[:,:1], mids] and upper bounds [mids, z{vals}[:, -1]], and jitter: z{vals} = lower + (upper - lower) \cdot \text{rand}(). Compute 3D points: \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + z{vals, i} \mathbf{d}. 3. Coarse Network Query: Apply positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to spatial coordinates \mathbf{x} and viewing directions \mathbf{d}. Query coarsemodel to obtain raw density \tilde{\sigma}c and raw color \tilde{\mathbf{c}}c. Apply activation functions: Density: \sigmac = \text{softplus}(\tilde{\sigma}c) or \text{relu}(\tilde{\sigma}c). Note: uses softplus with a bias, while uses ReLU. Standard NeRF typically uses softplus for density to ensure positivity. Color: \mathbf{c}c = \text{sigmoid}(\tilde{\mathbf{c}}c). 4. Coarse Rendering: Compute segment distances: \deltai = z{vals, i+1} - z{vals, i} for i < Nc-1, and \delta{Nc-1} = \infty (or a large value like 10^{10}) to handle the last interval. Compute alpha (opacity): \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigma{c,i} \deltai). Compute transmittance: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma{c,j} \deltaj\right). Compute weights: wi = Ti \alphai. Compute coarse color: \mathbf{C}{coarse} = \sum{i=1}^{Nc} wi \mathbf{c}{c,i}. Compute coarse depth: \mathbf{D}{coarse} = \sum{i=1}^{Nc} wi z{vals, i}. 5. Fine Sampling (Importance Resampling): Use the coarse weights wi (excluding the first sample i=0 to avoid bias) as a probability distribution. Draw Nf samples from this distribution using stratified sampling to generate finer depth values z{vals}^{fine}. Crucial Implementation Detail: Detach z{vals}^{fine} from the computation graph to prevent gradients from flowing back to the coarse network during the fine stage. 6. Fine Network Query: Compute 3D points for fine samples: \mathbf{x}i^{fine} = \mathbf{o} + z{vals, i}^{fine} \mathbf{d}. Apply positional encoding to \mathbf{x}^{fine} and \mathbf{d}. Query finemodel to obtain raw density \tilde{\sigma}f and raw color \tilde{\mathbf{c}}f. Apply activations: \sigmaf = \text{softplus}(\tilde{\sigma}f), \mathbf{c}f = \text{sigmoid}(\tilde{\mathbf{c}}f). 7. Fine Rendering: Compute distances \deltai^{fine} between fine samples. Compute alpha: \alphai^{fine} = 1 - \exp(-\sigma{f,i} \deltai^{fine}). Compute transmittance: Ti^{fine} = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma{f,j} \deltaj^{fine}\right). Compute weights: wi^{fine} = Ti^{fine} \alphai^{fine}. Compute final color: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{i=1}^{Nf} wi^{fine} \mathbf{c}{f,i}. Compute final depth: \mathbf{D}{out} = \sum{i=1}^{Nf} wi^{fine} z{vals, i}^{fine}. 8. Loss Computation: Compute photometric loss (MSE) between \mathbf{C}{coarse} and ground truth \mathbf{C}{gt}, and between \mathbf{C}{out} and \mathbf{C}{gt}. Backpropagate through both stages to update coarsemodel and finemodel parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The cumulative product for transmittance can underflow to zero, causing all subsequent weights to be zero. Add a small epsilon (\epsilon = 10^{-10}) to (1-\alpha). Boundaries: The last interval \delta{N-1} must be handled carefully. Setting it to \infty ensures the last sample contributes if it has non-zero density, effectively treating the ray as extending to infinity. Gradient Flow: Gradients must not flow from the fine stage back to the coarse model. Detach the fine sample positions z{vals}^{fine} from the computation graph before querying the fine model. Degenerate Input: If near and far bounds are equal or invalid, the sampling range collapses. Ensure tn < tf. NeRF Importance Sampling is a two-stage volume rendering strategy that refines the discrete sampling distribution along a ray by drawing additional points from a probability density function (PDF) derived from the coarse stage's opacity weights. It solves the problem of insufficient sampling in high-opacity regions, which leads to aliasing and noise, by concentrating fine samples where the volume contributes most to the final color. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as NerfAcc Rendering Pipeline which uses learned acceleration structures, and VF-NeRF which uses view-dependent feature grids, by relying on a simple, differentiable stratified resampling of the coarse alpha weights without auxiliary networks or complex data structures. NerfAcc is a standalone PyTorch library providing efficient sampling for volumetric rendering, decoupled from the radiance field representation. It accelerates Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by supporting Occupancy Grids and Proposal Networks to skip empty space and concentrate samples on surfaces. It builds on NeRF Volumetric Rendering (Coarse/Fine Sampling) by replacing fixed uniform sampling with a transmittance estimator that dynamically updates during training. VF-NeRF is a method for rigid registration between two Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) when the original camera positions are unknown. It introduces Viewshed Fields (VF), an implicit function that maps an oriented point (3D location and viewing direction) to a scalar indicating how well that point was covered by the original camera set. By using Normalizing Flows to generate high-scoring oriented points, VF-NeRF creates informative virtual camera viewpoints for photometric alignment, avoiding the noise and poor coverage associated with random sampling. It differs from NeRF Importance Sampling by focusing on registration via novel view generation rather than training efficiency, and from NerfAcc Rendering Pipeline by its specific application to inter-NeRF alignment. Voxel-based Volume Rendering is a technique that trains a dense or semi-dense voxel representation of a radiance field, where multiple voxels contribute to a single sample during rendering. It solves the problem of efficiently estimating scene opacity and color by using a structured 3D grid as a coarse model, often serving as the initial stage in two-tier sampling architectures to determine opaque regions in space. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as NeRF Importance Sampling which relies on learned probability distributions, and NerfAcc Rendering Pipeline which uses acceleration structures like hash grids, is its reliance on a fixed, dense (or semi-dense) volumetric grid where the volume integral is approximated by summing contributions from intersected voxels. Unlike VF-NeRF which may use sparse or hybrid representations, this method explicitly contrasts with sparse voxelization (octrees) by ensuring multiple voxels contribute to a single ray sample, providing structural consistency through opacity prediction independent of view direction. Deformable Volume Rendering extends the standard NeRF rendering equation to handle dynamic scenes by incorporating a time parameter t into the ray and density functions. The rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}(z), t) is computed as a weighted sum of color samples \mathbf{c}j along the ray \mathbf{r}(z) = \mathbf{o} + z\mathbf{d} at time t, where the weights wj are determined by the accumulated transmittance and local density \sigmaj. This allows the neural field to represent geometry and appearance that change over time, enabling novel view synthesis of non-rigidly deforming objects. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Training can take over 10 hours on a single GPU. Scaling: Performance degrades with increasing scene complexity and resolution due to the need for more samples Nc, Nf to capture high-frequency details. Strengths: High-quality novel view synthesis with view-dependent effects; simple implementation; differentiable end-to-end training. Limitations: Slow training. When to Use: High-quality offline rendering of static scenes with known camera poses. When Not to Use: Real-time applications, dynamic scenes (without extensions), or scenes with unknown camera poses. NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It represents a scene as a continuous volumetric radiance field parameterized by a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). The method was developed to address the limitations of previous neural rendering approaches, which often struggled with high-frequency details and view-dependent appearance. The coarse-to-fine sampling strategy was introduced to improve rendering quality by adaptively sampling points in high-density regions. NeRF has become a foundational technique in neural rendering, inspiring numerous variants and acceleration methods. head: Importance Sampling for NeRF, NeRF Integration, NeRF Sampling, Neural Radiance Field Rendering, Neural Volume Rendering Integration, Stratified Sampling with PDF Resampling
body: NeRF Importance Sampling is a two-stage volume rendering strategy that refines the distribution of sample points along a ray by drawing additional samples from a probability distribution defined by the opacity weights of a coarse neural network pass. It solves the inefficiency of uniform sampling by concentrating computational effort on regions with high expected density or opacity, thereby improving rendering quality with minimal overhead. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Near and far clipping bounds, z{near} and z{far}. Coarse neural network model f{coarse}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{v}) returning raw density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Number of coarse samples N{samples} (default 64). Number of importance samples N{importance} (default 0, disabling the fine stage). Perturbation flag perturb (boolean, typically True during training, False during inference). Noise standard deviation noisestd for regularization. Epsilon value eps for numerical stability (default 10^{-5}). Outputs: Final depth values z{final} sorted along the ray. 3D positions \mathbf{x}{final} corresponding to z{final}. Rendered color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}), opacity \alpha(\mathbf{r}), and depth D(\mathbf{r}) via volumetric integration [Parent]. Data Structures: zvals: Tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples}) storing depth values along rays. weights: Tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples}) storing alpha compositing weights. pdf: Probability density function tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples}). cdf: Cumulative distribution function tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples} + 1). Steps: 1. Coarse Uniform Sampling: Generate N{samples} depth values linearly spaced between z{near} and z{far}. z{steps} = \text{linspace}(0, 1, N{samples}) z{vals} = z{near} \cdot (1 - z{steps}) + z{far} \cdot z{steps} 2. Perturbation (Optional): If perturb is True, add random noise to break symmetry and aid gradient flow. Calculate midpoints: z{vals\mid} = 0.5 \cdot (z{vals}[:,:-1] + z{vals}[:, 1:]) Define interval bounds: lower = z{vals\mid} upper = z{vals\mid} Add noise: z{vals} = z{vals} + \text{perturb} \cdot \text{random\uniform}(z{vals}.shape) \cdot (upper - lower) 3. Coarse Network Query: Query f{coarse} at positions \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{o} + z{vals} \cdot \mathbf{d} to obtain raw densities \sigma. 4. Alpha and Weight Calculation: Compute deltas between samples: \Delta zi = z{vals{i+1}} - z{valsi} Add Gaussian noise to density: \sigma' = \text{relu}(\sigma + \mathcal{N}(0, \text{noise\std})) Compute alpha values: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\Delta zi \cdot \sigma'i) Compute transmittance and weights: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) wi = \alphai \cdot Ti (Implemented as weights = alphas torch.cumprod(alphasshifted, -1)[:,:-1] where alphasshifted is 1 - alphas padded with 1 at the start). 5. Importance Sampling (Fine Stage): If N{importance} > 0: a. Extract weights for sampling, excluding the first and last samples to avoid boundary issues: w{sample} = weights[:, 1:-1] b. Compute PDF: pi = \frac{w{sample, i} + \text{eps}}{\sumj (w{sample, j} + \text{eps})} c. Compute CDF: ci = \sum{k=1}^{i} pk Pad CDF with 0 at the start and 1 at the end (implicitly handled by concatenating zeros and using searchsorted). d. Generate uniform samples u in [0, 1]. If deterministic (det=True): u = \text{linspace}(0, 1, N{importance}) Else: u = \text{random\uniform}(N{importance}) e. Perform inverse transform sampling using searchsorted to find indices in the CDF. f. Linearly interpolate within the bin to get new depth values z{samples}. g. Stop gradient on z{samples} to prevent backpropagation through the sampling process. 6. Combine and Sort: Concatenate coarse and fine depth values: z{combined} = \text{concat}(z{vals}, z{samples}) Sort z{combined} in ascending order to form final z{final}. 7. Fine Network Query: Query the fine neural network f{fine} at positions \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{o} + z{final} \cdot \mathbf{d}. 8. Final Rendering: Compute final alphas and weights using the fine network's output. Perform volumetric integration: \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sumi wi \mathbf{c}i [Parent] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def samplepdf(bins, weights, Nimportance, det=False, eps=1e-5): """ Stratified sampling of bins based on weights. bins: (Nrays, Nsamples) depth values (midpoints or edges) weights: (Nrays, Nsamples) importance weights Nimportance: int, number of samples to draw det: bool, if True use linspace, else random eps: float, numerical stability constant """ Nrays, Nsamples = weights.shape # Add epsilon to prevent division by zero weights = weights + eps # Compute PDF pdf = weights / torch.sum(weights, -1, keepdim=True) # Compute CDF cdf = torch.cumsum(pdf, -1) # Pad CDF with 0 at the start and 1 at the end cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[:,:1]), cdf], -1) # Generate uniform samples if det: u = torch.linspace(0, 1, Nimportance, device=bins.device) u = u.expand(Nrays, Nimportance) else: u = torch.rand(Nrays, Nimportance, device=bins.device) # Find indices in CDF inds = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, side='right') # Clamp indices to valid range below = torch.clampmin(inds - 1, 0) above = torch.clampmax(inds, Nsamples) # Stack indices for interpolation indssampled = torch.stack([below, above], -1).view(Nrays, 2 Nimportance) # Gather CDF and bin values for the sampled indices cdfg = torch.gather(cdf, 1, indssampled).view(Nrays, Nimportance, 2) binsg = torch.gather(bins, 1, indssampled).view(Nrays, Nimportance, 2) # Linear interpolation denom = cdfg[..., 1] - cdfg[..., 0] denom[denom < eps] = 1.0 samples = binsg[..., 0] + (u - cdfg[..., 0]) / denom (binsg[..., 1] - binsg[..., 0]) return samples def rendernerfimportancesampling(rayo, rayd, znear, zfar, coarsenet, finenet, Nsamples=64, Nimportance=64, perturb=True, noisestd=1e-4, eps=1e-5): """ Render a ray using NeRF Importance Sampling. """ # 1. Coarse Uniform Sampling zsteps = torch.linspace(0, 1, Nsamples) zvals = znear (1 - zsteps) + zfar zsteps # 2. Perturbation if perturb: zvalsmid = 0.5 (zvals[:,:-1] + zvals[:, 1:]) lower = zvalsmid upper = zvalsmid noise = torch.randlike(zvals) zvals = zvals + noise (upper - lower) # 3. Coarse Network Query xyzcoarse = rayo.unsqueeze(1) + zvals.unsqueeze(2) rayd.unsqueeze(1) sigmaraw = coarsenet(xyzcoarse) # 4. Alpha and Weight Calculation # Align deltas and sigmas to Nsamples-1 intervals deltas = zvals[:, 1:] - zvals[:,:-1] sigmaintervals = sigmaraw[:,:-1] # Add noise to density sigmanoisy = torch.relu(sigmaintervals + torch.randnlike(sigmaintervals) noisestd) # Compute alphas alphas = 1 - torch.exp(-deltas sigmanoisy) # Compute weights: weights = alphas cumprod([1, 1-alpha1, 1-alpha2,...])[:-1] alphashifted = 1 - alphas alphashiftedpadded = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alphashifted[:,:1]), alphashifted], dim=-1) T = torch.cumprod(alphashiftedpadded, -1)[:,:-1] weights = alphas T # 5. Importance Sampling if Nimportance > 0: # Extract weights for sampling (exclude first and last) weightssample = weights[:, 1:-1] # Get midpoints for bins zvalsmid = 0.5 (zvals[:,:-1] + zvals[:, 1:]) # Sample zsamples = samplepdf(zvalsmid, weightssample, Nimportance, det=not perturb, eps=eps) # Concatenate and sort zvalscombined = torch.cat([zvals, zsamples], dim=-1) zvalssorted, = torch.sort(zvalscombined, dim=-1) else: zvalssorted = zvals # 6. Fine Network Query xyzfine = rayo.unsqueeze(1) + zvalssorted.unsqueeze(2) rayd.unsqueeze(1) xyzfine = xyzfine.detach() # Query fine net sigmafine = finenet(xyzfine) # 7. Final Rendering deltasfine = zvalssorted[:, 1:] - zvalssorted[:,:-1] sigmafinenoisy = torch.relu(sigmafine + torch.randnlike(sigmafine) noisestd) alphasfine = 1 - torch.exp(-deltasfine sigmafinenoisy) alphashiftedfine = 1 - alphasfine alphashiftedfinepadded = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alphashiftedfine[:,:1]), alphashiftedfine], dim=-1) Tfine = torch.cumprod(alphashiftedfinepadded, -1)[:,:-1] weightsfine = alphasfine Tfine # Integrate color (assuming finenet also returns color) # colorfine = finenetcolor(xyzfine) # C = sum(weightsfine colorfine) return zvalssorted, weightsfine Parameters: N{samples}: Number of coarse samples per ray. Default: 64. N{importance}: Number of fine samples per ray. Default: 0 (disables fine stage). perturb: Boolean flag to add noise to coarse samples. Default: True during training. noisestd: Standard deviation of Gaussian noise added to density. Default: Not given in the sources. eps: Epsilon for numerical stability in PDF/CDF calculation. Default: 10^{-5}. chunk: Chunk size for batched inference to manage memory. Default: 1024 \times 32. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero in PDF: Weights can be zero. Add eps to weights before computing PDF. Zero Denominator in Inverse CDF: If cdfg[...,1] - cdfg[...,0] is less than eps, set it to 1 to avoid division by zero, as bins with zero weight are not sampled anyway. Boundary Handling: The first and last samples are often excluded from importance sampling to avoid boundary artifacts. Gradient Flow: Gradients should be stopped on the sampled positions z{samples} to prevent backpropagation through the sampling process. Refines the sampling distribution by applying a 2-tap max filter, a 2-tap blur filter (blurpool), and a bias term to coarse weights before inverse transform sampling, ensuring robust sampling in empty regions and a smoother weight envelope. Explicitly defines procedural steps for binning, smoothing, and stratified sampling within a discrete partition of the ray, building on NeRF Importance Sampling. Time Complexity: O(N{samples} + N{importance}) per ray for sampling and network queries. The sorting step adds O((N{samples} + N{importance}) \log (N{samples} + N{importance})). Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot (N{samples} + N{importance})) to store depth values, weights, and intermediate tensors. Measured Performance: In the unofficial implementation, training on 8 GPUs finishes within 1 hour for synthetic datasets. The speed is ~100x faster than the original NeRF repo on an RTX 2080 Ti, with reduced GPU memory usage (3.2 GB vs 8.5 GB) due to batched inference. Strengths: Improves rendering quality by focusing samples on opaque regions with minimal overhead compared to uniform sampling. Simple to implement and integrate into existing NeRF pipelines. Limitations: Requires two network passes (coarse and fine). Performance gain depends on the scene's density distribution; uniform sampling may be sufficient for simple scenes. When to Use: When rendering quality is critical and the scene has varying density (e.g., thin structures, transparent objects). When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited, or the scene is uniformly dense. NeRF Importance Sampling was introduced in the original NeRF paper (Mildenhall et al., 2020). It is a standard technique in neural volume rendering to address the inefficiency of uniform sampling. kwea123/nerfpl, https://github.com/kwea123/nerfpl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) dgsmith7/nerf-mlp, https://github.com/dgsmith7/nerf-mlp, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical Sampling with Weight Modification
head: Fine sampling with blurpool
body: Hierarchical Sampling with Weight Modification refines the sampling distribution along rays by using alpha compositing weights from a coarse model to generate additional fine sample points, improving rendering quality with minimal overhead. It differs from standard NeRF importance sampling by applying a 2-tap max filter followed by a 2-tap blur filter (blurpool) and a bias term \alpha to the coarse weights before inverse transform sampling, ensuring robust sampling in empty regions and a smoother weight envelope. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Coarse sample positions \mathbf{t}^c along a ray, and their corresponding alpha compositing weights w derived from the coarse neural volume rendering model. Output: Refined fine sample positions \mathbf{t}^f. Data Structures: w: A 1D array of size Nc (number of coarse samples), containing the normalized alpha compositing weights such that \sum wk = 1. w': A 1D array of size Nc, containing the modified weights used for probability density estimation. Parameters: Nc: Number of coarse samples. Default: 128. Nf: Number of fine samples. Default: 128. \alpha: Hyperparameter added to the envelope to ensure sampling in empty regions. Default: 0.01. Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling: Produce coarse sample positions \mathbf{t}^c using stratified sampling along the ray segment. 2. Weight Computation: Compute the alpha compositing weights wk for each coarse sample k based on the neural network's output at \mathbf{t}^c. 3. Weight Modification: Apply the blurpool filter and bias to w to produce w': Apply a 2-tap max filter followed by a 2-tap blur filter to w. Add the hyperparameter \alpha to each element. The combined formula for the modified weight w'k is: w'k = \frac{1}{2}(\max(w{k-1}, wk) + \max(wk, w{k+1})) + \alpha Re-normalize w' so that \sum w'k = 1. 4. Fine Sampling: Sample fine sample positions \mathbf{t}^f from the distribution defined by w' using inverse transform sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicalsamplingwithweightmodification(w, alpha=0.01): """ Modifies coarse weights w using blurpool and bias, then returns normalized weights. w: list of floats, size Nc alpha: float, bias term Returns: list of floats, size Nc, normalized to sum to 1 """ n = len(w) if n == 0: return [] # 2-tap max filter followed by 2-tap blur # Boundary handling: clamp to nearest endpoint modified = [] for k in range(n): wprev = w[k-1] if k > 0 else w[0] wnext = w[k+1] if k < n-1 else w[n-1] maxleft = max(wprev, w[k]) maxright = max(w[k], wnext) blurred = 0.5 (maxleft + maxright) modified.append(blurred) # Add alpha and re-normalize biased = [x + alpha for x in modified] total = sum(biased) if total == 0: return [1.0 / n] n return [x / total for x in biased] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary conditions for indices -1 and Nc are not specified in the source; implementers typically clamp to the nearest endpoint. The bias \alpha guarantees non-zero weights in empty regions to prevent sampling failure. An enhanced sampling strategy that shapes the weight function w(t) to approximate the L0 distance, replacing piecewise constant interpolation with piecewise exponential functions to create a quasi-L0 PDF. It concentrates fine-stage sampling near surfaces without altering the underlying density field, providing a more precise distribution than Hierarchical Volume Sampling. Choose when surface-concentrated sampling is preferred over uniform interval distribution. See L0-Sampler. Performance: Uses 128 coarse and 128 fine samples per ray, yielding the same total number of MLP evaluations as standard NeRF for fair comparison. Strengths: The blurpool filter produces a wide, smooth upper envelope on the weights, and \alpha ensures sampling in empty regions. Time Complexity: Not given in. Memory Complexity: Not given in. Limitations: Not given in. Originated in mip-NeRF by Barron et al. (2021). It builds on NeRF's hierarchical sampling but introduces the blurpool technique to improve the quality of fine-stage sampling. Mip-NeRF: A Multiscale Representation for Anti-Aliasing Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.00580, fetched 2026-10-26

name: L0-Sampler
head: L0 Model Guided Volume Sampling
body: L0-Sampler is an enhanced sampling strategy for neural volume rendering that concentrates sampling points near surfaces by shaping the weight function w(t) to approximate the L0 distance form. It replaces the piecewise constant interpolation of Hierarchical Volume Sampling (HVS) with piecewise exponential functions, creating a quasi-L0 probability density function (PDF) that focuses fine-stage sampling near surfaces without altering the underlying density field. Unlike HVS, which results in a uniform distribution within intervals, L0-Sampler provides a more concentrated and precise sampling distribution. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Coarse-stage sampling positions \{ti\} along a ray, coarse-stage density outputs \{\sigmai\}, and the interval lengths \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. Outputs: A set of fine-stage sampling positions \{x\} derived from the normalized quasi-L0 weight PDF. Data Structures: Coarse Weights: A list of scalar weights wi corresponding to each coarse sample ti. Interpolated Function: A piecewise exponential function defined over intervals [ti, t{i+1}]. Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling and Weight Prediction: Uniformly sample points \{ti\} along the ray in the coarse stage. Predict weights \{wi\} using the coarse network outputs: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) wi = \alphai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where \sigmai is the density at ti and \deltai = t{i+1} - ti. 2. Maxblur Smoothing: Apply maxblur smoothing to coarse weights to broaden peak areas and generate a smoother weight distribution. For each weight wi, compute the smoothed weight w'i: w'i = \frac{1}{2 \cdot (\max(w{i-1}, wi) + \max(wi, w{i+1}) + 0.01)} where 0.01 is a small constant added to the denominator in the maxblur smoothing step to prevent division by zero. Use w'i for subsequent interpolation steps. 3. Interval Mapping: For each interval [ti, t{i+1}], map to a normalized interval s \in [0, 1] using the transformation: \hat{w}(s):= w((t{i+1} - ti)s + ti) where \hat{w}(0) = a = wi and \hat{w}(1) = b = w{i+1}. 4. Piecewise Exponential Interpolation: Interpolate \hat{w}(s) using the exponential function to create a quasi-L0 weight distribution: \hat{w}(s) = a \cdot \left(\frac{b}{a}\right)^s Concatenate these interpolated functions to form the global weight function w(t). 5. Normalization: Normalize the interpolated weight function w(t) into a probability density function (PDF) and use it for inverse transform sampling to guide the fine sampling process. 6. Inverse Transform Sampling: Use inverse transform sampling to find sampling positions x for residual probability r. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def l0sampler(tcoarse, sigmacoarse, epsilon=0.01, numfinesamples=128): """ Implements L0-Sampler for a single ray. Args: tcoarse: Array of coarse sampling positions [t0,..., tN]. sigmacoarse: Array of coarse density outputs [sigma0,..., sigmaN]. epsilon: Small constant for maxblur smoothing. numfinesamples: Number of fine samples to generate per ray. Returns: tfine: Array of fine sampling positions. """ N = len(tcoarse) delta = np.diff(tcoarse) # deltai = t{i+1} - ti, length N-1 # Step 1: Coarse Sampling and Weight Prediction # alphai = 1 - exp(-sigmai deltai) for i in 0..N-2 alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigmacoarse[:-1] delta) # Transmittance Ti = product{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) # T has length N. T[0] = 1.0 T = np.ones(N) if N > 1: T[1:] = np.cumprod(1.0 - alpha) # wi = alphai Ti for i in 0..N-2, w{N-1} = T{N-1} w = np.zeros(N) w[:-1] = alpha T[:-1] w[-1] = T[-1] # Step 2: Maxblur Smoothing # w'i = 1 / (2 (max(w{i-1}, wi) + max(wi, w{i+1}) + epsilon)) # Pad boundaries with edge values to handle i=0 and i=N-1 wpad = np.pad(w, (1, 1), mode='edge') maxprev = np.maximum(wpad[:-2], wpad[1:-1]) maxnext = np.maximum(wpad[1:-1], wpad[2:]) wsmoothed = 1.0 / (2.0 (maxprev + maxnext + epsilon)) # Step 3 & 4: Interval Mapping and Piecewise Exponential Interpolation # Compute integral of w(t) over each interval [ti, t{i+1}] intervalintegrals = np.zeros(N - 1) for i in range(N - 1): a = wsmoothed[i] b = wsmoothed[i+1] d = delta[i] if np.isclose(a, b): intervalintegrals[i] = d a else: ratio = b / a intervalintegrals[i] = d a (ratio - 1.0) / np.log(ratio) # Step 5: Normalization totalintegral = np.sum(intervalintegrals) if totalintegral == 0: return np.linspace(tcoarse[0], tcoarse[-1], numfinesamples) pdfweights = intervalintegrals / totalintegral cdf = np.cumsum(pdfweights) # Step 6: Inverse Transform Sampling r = np.random.uniform(0.0, 1.0, numfinesamples) tfine = np.zeros(numfinesamples) for k in range(numfinesamples): val = r[k] idx = np.searchsorted(cdf, val, side='right') if idx >= len(cdf): idx = len(cdf) - 1 cdfstart = cdf[idx-1] if idx > 0 else 0.0 cdfend = cdf[idx] localprob = (val - cdfstart) / (cdfend - cdfstart) a = wsmoothed[idx] b = wsmoothed[idx+1] d = delta[idx] if np.isclose(a, b): s = localprob else: ratio = b / a numerator = localprob (ratio - 1.0) + 1.0 numerator = np.clip(numerator, 1e-10, None) s = np.log(numerator) / np.log(ratio) tfine[k] = tcoarse[idx] + s d return tfine Parameters: epsilon: A small constant added to the denominator in the maxblur smoothing step to prevent division by zero. Value: 0.01. The method is parameter-free otherwise. Pitfalls: If a and b are very close, the exponential function behaves like a linear one, promoting uniform sampling. If the difference between a and b is too large, the integral approximates \min(a, b), reducing sampling concentration. Performance gains are not universal; some scenes or views may not show improvement. The method is currently optimized primarily for the fine sampling stage. Time Complexity: Adds less than 1% to training time due to closed-form solutions at each sampling step. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Achieves stable performance improvements on rendering and reconstruction tasks across NeRF, NeRF++, Instant NGP, mip-NeRF, and NeuS. Improves PSNR and LPIPS on Blender and LLFF datasets, and refines geometry extraction in DTU scans. Strengths: Parameter-free, easy to implement (around ten lines of code), no additional loss evaluation overhead, captures challenging details and thin structures. Limitations: Not all results are improved; primarily effective for fine-stage sampling. L0-Sampler was proposed in the paper "L0-Sampler: An L0 Model Guided Volume Sampling for NeRF". It builds on the observation that a well-trained weight function w(t) and the L0 distance between points and the surface have high similarity. The L0 distance is defined as d(p, S) = 1 if p \notin S, and 0 if p \in S. The method was applied to various NeRF frameworks to improve sampling efficiency and geometric detail capture. L0-Sampler: An L0Model Guided Volume Sampling for NeRF, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.02021, fetched 2026-11-04

name: Importance Ray Sampling
head: Importance Sampling for NeRF
body: Importance Ray Sampling is a technique used in neural volume rendering to refine the distribution of sample points along a ray. It uses initial density estimates (weights) to sample more densely from regions expected to have objects. The method partitions the ray into coarse bins, computes a probability mass function from the weights, samples bin indices, and interpolates within those bins. Inputs: volumerange: The spatial extent of the volume along the ray, partitioned into coarse bins. ts: Coarse timestamps defining the bin boundaries. weights: Raw density or opacity estimates for each coarse bin, derived from a coarse model. alpha: A small scalar added to weights to prevent zero-probability bins. blurpool: A boolean flag indicating whether to apply smoothing filters. nsamples: The number of fine sample points to generate. Outputs: ts: A sorted array of normalized parameter values t \in [0, 1] representing the positions of the fine sample points along the ray. Data Structures: weights: A tensor of shape (B, Nc), where B is batch size and Nc is the number of coarse bins. pmf: Probability Mass Function tensor of shape (B, Nc), normalized such that \sum{i} \text{pmf}i = 1. lower, upper: Tensors of shape (B, Nc) representing the start and end normalized parameters of each coarse bin. Steps: 1. Partition Volume: Divide the volume range into coarse bins using timestamps ts. Let lower and upper be the lower and upper bounds of these bins. 2. Retrieve Weights: Obtain the raw weights wi for each bin i from the coarse model's output. 3. Smooth Weights (Optional): If blurpool is true, apply a smoothing filter to w to reduce noise and prevent aliasing artifacts: Pad w with its first and last elements: w{padded} = \text{concat}(w[:,:1], w, w[:, -1:]). Compute adjacent maximums: mi = \max(w{padded, i}, w{padded, i+1}). Average adjacent maximums: w'i = 0.5 \times (mi + m{i+1}). Update weights: w \leftarrow w'. 4. Regularize Weights: Add \alpha to all weights to ensure non-zero probability: wi \leftarrow wi + \alpha. The default value for \alpha is 10^{-5}. 5. Compute PMF: Normalize the weights along the bin dimension to form a probability mass function: \text{pmf}i = \frac{wi}{\sum{j=1}^{Nc} wj}. 6. Sample Indices: Draw n{samples} indices k from the PMF using categorical sampling: k \sim \text{Categorical}(\text{pmf}). 7. Generate Noise: Generate random noise t{rand} with the same shape as the sampled indices k, uniformly distributed in [0, 1]. 8. Gather Bounds: Retrieve the lower and upper bounds for the sampled bins: lk = \text{gather}(lower, k), \quad uk = \text{gather}(upper, k). 9. Interpolate: Compute the final sample positions by linearly interpolating within the sampled bins: t = lk + (uk - lk) \times t{rand}. 10. Sort: Sort the resulting t values along the sample dimension to maintain monotonicity along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def importanceraysampling(volumerange, ts, weights, alpha=1e-5, blurpool=False, nsamples=64): # 1. Partition volume range into coarse bins lower, upper, = volumerange.partition(ts) # 2. Retrieve weights from coarse model w = weights.clone() # 3. Optional smoothing (mip-NeRF style 2-tap max + 2-tap blur) if blurpool: padded = concatenate([w[...,:1,:], w, w[..., -1:,:]], axis=-2) maxes = maximum(padded[...,:-1,:], padded[..., 1:,:]) w = 0.5 (maxes[...,:-1,:] + maxes[..., 1:,:]) # 4. Add alpha to prevent zero probabilities w = w + alpha # 5. Compute PMF pmf = w / sum(w, axis=-2, keepdims=True) # 6. Sample indices from PMF using inverse transform sampling cdf = cumsum(pmf, axis=-2) u = rand(shape=w.shape[:-1] + (nsamples,)) inds = argmax(cast(cdf >= u[..., None], dtype=bool), axis=-2) # 7. Generate random noise trand = rand(shape=inds.shape) # 8. Gather bounds for sampled indices lower = indexselect(lower, axis=-2, indices=inds) upper = indexselect(upper, axis=-2, indices=inds) # 9. Interpolate within bins ts = lower + (upper - lower) trand # 10. Sort along sample dimension ts = sort(ts, axis=-2) return ts Parameters: alpha: Default 10^{-5}. blurpool: Boolean, default False. Edge Cases: If all weights are zero, the addition of \alpha ensures valid probabilities. If volumerange has only one bin, sampling degenerates to uniform distribution within that bin. Time Complexity: Dominated by the categorical sampling and sorting steps, O(Nc + Nr \cdot Ns \log Ns), where Nc is coarse bins, Nr is rays, and Ns is samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(Nc) for storing weights and PMF per ray. Strengths: Reduces variance in regions of high density; computationally cheap compared to learning a separate importance network. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the coarse model's weights; may undersample if coarse weights are inaccurate. It adapts techniques from mip-NeRF's smoothing strategy for NeRF importance sampling. gsgen3d/gsgen, https://github.com/gsgen3d/gsgen, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: NerfAcc Rendering Pipeline
head: Efficient Sampling for Volumetric Rendering, NeRF Volume Rendering (CPU/PyTorch), NerfAcc, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with Coarse/Fine Sampling and NDC, Neural Volume Rendering (Coarse/Fine Sampling), Volume Rendering with Neural Fields[S3, unofficial]
body: NerfAcc is a standalone PyTorch library providing efficient sampling for volumetric rendering, decoupled from the radiance field representation. It accelerates Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by supporting Occupancy Grids and Proposal Networks to skip empty space and concentrate samples on surfaces. It builds on NeRF Volumetric Rendering (Coarse/Fine Sampling) by replacing fixed uniform sampling with a transmittance estimator that dynamically updates during training. Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{r}o (shape N{rays}, 3), normalized ray directions \mathbf{r}d (shape N{rays}, 3), near/far bounds, and a neural radiance field model providing density \sigma and RGB color. Outputs: Rendered color, opacity, depth, and auxiliary data for estimator updates. Data Structures: Packed Samples: Represented as intervals (t0, t1, r), where t0, t1 are start/end points along the r-th ray. This interval representation supports cone-based rays for anti-aliasing. Ray Array: Shape (N{rays}, 8). Columns 0-2: origin; 3-5: direction; 6: near depth; 7: far depth. Steps: 1. Initialize Estimator: Create a transmittance estimator (e.g., Proposal Network or Occupancy Grid). 2. Define Query Functions: Density function queries the radiance field for \sigma given intervals. RGB/Density function queries the radiance field for \sigma and RGB. 3. Efficient Sampling: Sample intervals along rays using the estimator and density function. 4. Differentiable Rendering: Integrate RGB and density over the sampled intervals. 5. Update Estimator: Update the transmittance estimator with the sampled intervals and auxiliary data every n steps. 6. Loss and Backprop: Compute loss (e.g., MSE) and backpropagate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. estimator = nerfacc.TransmittanceEstimator() def densityfn(t0, t1, rid): return nerf.density(ro[rid], rd[rid], t0, t1) def rgbdensityfn(t0, t1, rid): return nerf.forward(ro[rid], rd[rid], t0, t1) t0, t1, rid = nerfacc.sampling(ro, rd, estimator, densityfn=densityfn) color, opacity, depth, aux = nerfacc.rendering(t0, t1, rid, rgbdensityfn=rgbdensityfn) estimator.updateeverynsteps(t0, t1, rid, aux) loss = F.mseloss(color, colorgt) loss.backward() Formulas: Opacity: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\delta \sigma). Weight: wi = \alphai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Color: C = \sum wi ci. Depth: z = \sum wi \frac{z{i+1} + zi}{2}. Parameters: near: Near plane depth. Typical: 0.5. far: Far plane depth. Typical: 3.0. Nsamples: Number of coarse samples per ray. Default: 64. Nimportance: Number of fine samples per ray. Default: 0. usedisp: Boolean for linear sampling in depth (False) or disparity (True). perturb: Float factor for random jitter on coarse samples. Default: 0. noisestd: Float factor for Gaussian noise on \sigma. Default: 1. chunk: Integer chunk size for batched inference. Default: 102432. whiteback: Boolean. If True, adds unrendered background weight to RGB. Edge Cases: Division by Zero: In ray-box intersection, add epsilon (10^{-7}) to direction components. NaN in Hash Grid: Clamp points to [-bound, bound]. Gradient Leakage: Detach fine samples from coarse weights to prevent backpropagation. Zero Weight in PDF: Add epsilon (10^{-5}) to weights before computing PDF in samplepdf. Zero Denominator in Interpolation: Set denominator to 1 if it falls below epsilon during samplepdf linear interpolation. NeuSample replaces the coarse-to-fine stage with a neural sample field mapping rays directly to sample distributions, enabling single-shot inference and reducing inference time by ~25%. Uses a hash-based occupancy grid to skip empty space during ray marching, restricting samples to non-empty voxels within a bounding sphere. Unlike NeuSample, it relies on static spatial hashing. Computes deltas and alphas from coarse samples, derives weights for PDF sampling, and samples new zvals using samplepdf on midpoints and weights. A PyTorch renderer using NerfAcc for CUDA-accelerated marching, supporting progressive checkerboard rendering for 30-400 fps interactivity. Speedup: 1.5× to 20× faster training compared to standard NeRF. Memory: Minimizes GPU memory via chunked inference and progressive rendering. Interactivity: Achieves 30-400 fps with progressive rendering. Strengths: Decoupled from radiance field, supports multiple acceleration structures (Occupancy Grid, Proposal Network). Limitations: Not given in the sources. NerfAcc was introduced in 2023 to accelerate NeRF training by decoupling sampling from the radiance field. It builds on Instant-NGP and Mip-NeRF 360 concepts. name: NeuSample
head: Neural Sample Field, Sample Field Extraction
body: NeuSample is a neural volume rendering method that replaces the coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling stage of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) with a lightweight neural sample field. It maps a camera ray directly into a distribution of sample points, enabling single-shot inference without the intermediate coarse pass. This approach reduces inference time by approximately 25% compared to standard NeRF while maintaining or improving rendering quality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray defined by origin o = (xo, yo, zo) and normalized direction d, near bound tn, far bound tf, and number of samples N. Output: N 3D sample coordinates \{x1,..., xN\} along the ray, which are fed into a radiance field R\Theta to produce density \sigma and color c, resulting in a final pixel color via volume rendering. Data Structures: Neural Sample Field (S\Theta): A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). Input dimension: 6 (3 for origin, 3 for direction) before encoding. Hidden layers: 8 Fully Connected (FC) layers with ReLU activation. Hidden dimension: 256. Skip connection: Input concatenated with output of the 4th layer. Output layer: 1 FC layer mapping 256 dimensions to N dimensions, followed by Sigmoid activation. Radiance Field (R\Theta): Standard NeRF MLP (assumed standard NeRF architecture). Parameters: N: Number of samples. The source uses N=192 for the main experiments. This replaces the sum of coarse (Nc) and fine (Nf) samples in NeRF. Position Encoding: 10-frequency positional encoding applied to both origin and direction. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Compute ray origin o and direction d for the target pixel from the camera pose. 2. Position Encoding: Apply 10-frequency positional encoding \tilde{\tau} to o and d. Concatenate the encoded origin and direction to form the input vector v. 3. Sample Field Inference: Pass v through S\Theta. Pass through 8 FC layers with ReLU. Concatenate original input v with the output of the 4th layer (skip connection). Pass through final FC layer to get N-dimensional vector. Apply Sigmoid activation to obtain relative positions \hat{t}1,..., \hat{t}N \in [0, 1]. 4. Coordinate Transformation: Map relative positions to absolute distances ti using near/far bounds: ti = (1 - \hat{t}i)tn + \hat{t}i tf Compute 3D sample coordinates: xi = o + ti d 5. Radiance Field Query: For each xi, query R\Theta(xi, d) to obtain density \sigmai and color ci. 6. Volume Rendering: Accumulate color using standard volume rendering equation: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where \deltai = t{i+1} - ti (with t{N+1} = tf), and Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the accumulated transmittance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies=10): """ Standard NeRF positional encoding. x: tensor of shape (..., 3) Returns: tensor of shape (..., 3 + 32numfrequencies) """ scales = torch.tensor([2i for i in range(numfrequencies)], dtype=x.dtype, device=x.device) scaledx = torch.flatten(x[..., None,:] scales[None, None,:, None], -2) return torch.cat([x, torch.sin(scaledx), torch.cos(scaledx)], dim=-1) class NeuralSampleField(nn.Module): def init(self, N=192): super().init() self.N = N self.inputdim = 6 + 6 2 10 # 6 raw dims + 120 encoded dims self.hiddendim = 256 # 8 FC layers with ReLU self.fc1 = nn.Linear(self.inputdim, self.hiddendim) self.fc2 = nn.Linear(self.hiddendim, self.hiddendim) self.fc3 = nn.Linear(self.hiddendim, self.hiddendim) self.fc4 = nn.Linear(self.hiddendim, self.hiddendim) self.fc5 = nn.Linear(self.hiddendim, self.hiddendim) self.fc6 = nn.Linear(self.hiddendim, self.hiddendim) self.fc7 = nn.Linear(self.hiddendim, self.hiddendim) self.fc8 = nn.Linear(self.hiddendim, self.hiddendim) # Skip connection: concat input with h4 self.fc9 = nn.Linear(self.hiddendim + self.inputdim, self.hiddendim) # Output layer: 256 -> N, followed by Sigmoid self.fcout = nn.Linear(self.hiddendim, self.N) def forward(self, origin, direction): x = torch.cat([origin, direction], dim=-1) xenc = positionalencoding(x, numfrequencies=10) h1 = torch.relu(self.fc1(xenc)) h2 = torch.relu(self.fc2(h1)) h3 = torch.relu(self.fc3(h2)) h4 = torch.relu(self.fc4(h3)) hskip = torch.cat([xenc, h4], dim=-1) h5 = torch.relu(self.fc5(hskip)) h6 = torch.relu(self.fc6(h5)) h7 = torch.relu(self.fc7(h6)) h8 = torch.relu(self.fc8(h7)) logits = self.fcout(h8) return torch.sigmoid(logits) def renderneusample(rayorigins, raydirections, nearbound, farbound, N=192, radiancefield=None): """ rayorigins: (B, 3) raydirections: (B, 3) nearbound: float farbound: float radiancefield: callable Rtheta(x, d) -> (sigma, color) """ samplefield = NeuralSampleField(N=N) # 1. Get relative positions relativet = samplefield(rayorigins, raydirections) # (B, N) # 2. Map to absolute distances absolutet = (1 - relativet) nearbound + relativet farbound # (B, N) # 3. Compute 3D coordinates samples = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + absolutet.unsqueeze(2) raydirections.unsqueeze(1) # (B, N, 3) # 4. Query Radiance Field B, N, = samples.shape samplesflat = samples.view(-1, 3) dirsflat = raydirections.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, N, -1).view(-1, 3) sigma, color = radiancefield(samplesflat, dirsflat) sigma = sigma.view(B, N, 1) color = color.view(B, N, 3) # 5. Volume Rendering tpadded = torch.cat([absolutet, torch.full((B, 1), farbound, device=absolutet.device)], dim=1) delta = tpadded[:, 1:] - tpadded[:,:-1] # (B, N) alpha = 1 - torch.exp(-sigma delta) # (B, N, 1) sigmadelta = sigma delta # (B, N, 1) cumsigmadelta = torch.cumsum(sigmadelta, dim=1) # (B, N, 1) # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) T = torch.exp(-torch.cat([torch.zeros((B, 1, 1), device=sigmadelta.device), cumsigmadelta[:,:-1]], dim=1)) # (B, N, 1) weights = T alpha # (B, N, 1) coloracc = torch.sum(weights color, dim=1) # (B, 3) return coloracc Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The sigmoid activation ensures outputs are in [0, 1], preventing out-of-bounds sampling. Training: The sample field and radiance field are trained end-to-end by minimizing the MSE between rendered and ground truth colors. Initialization: The neural sample field requires pre-trained weights; untrained networks produce arbitrary distributions. Subtopics: Sample Field Extraction: A compression technique that reduces the number of samples (e.g., to 64) while maintaining competitive quality, achieving 25% of the inference time of the original NeuSample. It uses depth boost initialization to fit the mean value of the extracted field to depth predicted by a learned regular field. Comparison with NeRF: NeuSample discards the costly coarse stage of NeRF's hierarchical sampling, using single-shot inference instead. Time Complexity: Single-shot inference. Saves approximately 25% of inference time compared to NeRF. Sample Field Extraction reduces this further to 25% of the original NeuSample's time. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the parameters for the Neural Sample Field (MLP with ~8 layers, hidden dim 256) in addition to the Radiance Field. The source does not specify exact memory footprint in MB/GB. Performance: On Realistic Synthetic 360° and Real ForwardFacing benchmarks, NeuSample achieves better or similar PSNR to NeRF while being faster. Strengths: Faster inference than NeRF; simpler pipeline (no hierarchical sampling logic); end-to-end trainable. Limitations: Requires training a separate network for sampling; quality depends on the learned sampling distribution; may struggle with complex geometry if not properly initialized (addressed by Sample Field Extraction). When to use: When inference speed is critical and the scene geometry can be effectively modeled by a learned sampling distribution. When not to use: When hierarchical sampling is required for high-frequency details that a single MLP cannot capture efficiently, or when memory is extremely constrained (due to additional network parameters). NeuSample was proposed in the paper "NeuSample: Neural Sample Field for Efficient View Synthesis". It addresses the computational overhead of NeRF's inference stage, specifically the coarse-to-fine hierarchical sampling procedure. The method was developed to alleviate the burden of the coarse stage by replacing it with a lightweight neural sample field. name: Occupancy Grid Sampling
head: Grid-based Neural Radiance Field rendering, INGP-NeRF Volume Rendering, Sphere Sampling
body: Occupancy Grid Sampling is a spatial acceleration strategy for neural volume rendering that utilizes a hash-based occupancy grid to skip empty space during ray marching. It solves the inefficiency of uniform sampling in sparse scenes by restricting sample point selection to non-empty voxels within a predefined bounding sphere. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, scene bounding sphere radius r, occupancy grid data structure. Output: A set of sample distances \{ti\} along the ray that lie within non-empty voxels. Data Structures: The method uses a multiscale occupancy grid stored in a hash table. Grid Structure: Space is divided into grids of different resolutions. Voxel Storage: Feature vectors \Phi\theta are assigned to the corners of each voxel. Hash Table: Indices \mathbf{x} and feature vectors are stored in a hash table to allow O(1) lookup. Occupancy State: Each grid cell is dynamically labeled as empty or non-empty during training. Steps: 1. Define Sampling Bounds: Restrict candidate sample distances to a sphere of radius r. 2. Generate Candidates: Produce a set of candidate distances t along the ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. 3. Check Sphere Bounds: For each candidate point \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, compute its distance from the origin; if |\mathbf{p}| > r, discard it. 4. Query Occupancy Grid: Map \mathbf{p} to a voxel index and query the hash table for the cell's occupancy value. 5. Check Threshold: If the occupancy value is \le the threshold, discard the point. 6. Sample Non-Empty Cells: Retain only points passing the occupancy check. 7. Interpolate Features: Retrieve feature vectors from the 8 neighboring voxel corners and interpolate to obtain feature \mathbf{f}. 8. Predict Density and Color: Pass \mathbf{f} through an MLP to predict density \sigma and hidden state h, then predict color \mathbf{c}. 9. Volume Rendering: Compute opacity \alphai and transmittance Ti for the retained points. Formulas: The opacity \alphai for sample i is calculated as: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) where \sigmai is the predicted density and \deltai = t{i+1} - ti is the distance between adjacent sampled points. Parameters: Sphere Radius (r): Defines the bounding sphere for sampling. For the nerf-synthetic dataset, r = 1.5. Occupancy Threshold: Used to determine if a cell is non-empty. The value is 0.005. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision near boundaries: Floating-point rounding can cause points exactly on the sphere boundary or voxel edges to be misclassified; a small epsilon guard is recommended when comparing distances or indices. Degenerate rays: Rays with zero direction components require careful voxel index computation to avoid division-by-zero or infinite loops; clamping or using integer floor division avoids this. Hash collisions: Multiscale hash tables may collide; standard collision resolution (e.g., chaining or probing) must be implemented to maintain correctness. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def occupancygridsampling(rayo, rayd, radius, gridres, occupancygrid, threshold): """ rayo: (3,) array, ray origin rayd: (3,) array, ray direction radius: float, bounding sphere radius gridres: int, resolution of the occupancy grid occupancygrid: dict/HashTable, maps voxel indices to occupancy values threshold: float, occupancy threshold """ # Generate uniform candidate distances along the ray within [0, 2radius] numcandidates = 128 ts = [i 2.0 radius / numcandidates for i in range(numcandidates)] validts = [] for t in ts: p = rayo + t rayd # Check bounding sphere: discard points outside radius if dot(p, p) > radius radius: continue # Compute voxel index from point coordinates voxelidx = computevoxelindex(p, gridres, radius) # Check occupancy threshold if occupancygrid.get(voxelidx, 0.0) <= threshold: continue validts.append(t) return validts def computevoxelindex(point, gridres, radius): """Map a 3D point to a voxel index in a grid covering [-radius, radius]^3.""" # Normalize to [0, 1] nx = (point[0] + radius) / (2.0 radius) ny = (point[1] + radius) / (2.0 radius) nz = (point[2] + radius) / (2.0 radius) # Clamp to avoid out-of-bounds due to floating-point error nx = max(0.0, min(1.0, nx)) ny = max(0.0, min(1.0, ny)) nz = max(0.0, min(1.0, nz)) # Convert to integer indices ix = int(nx gridres) % gridres iy = int(ny gridres) % gridres iz = int(nz gridres) % gridres return (ix, iy, iz) A sampling strategy that reduces the number of sample points during rendering by modeling occupancy information explicitly. The method achieves a rendering speed that is 10 times faster than NGP. Time Complexity: Sampling is accelerated by skipping empty voxels, reducing the number of neural network queries. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the hash table for voxel features and occupancy states. Strengths: Markedly enhances sampling efficiency in sparse scenes by avoiding empty space. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the occupancy grid; if the grid is not properly trained, empty regions may be incorrectly sampled or vice versa. When to use: When rendering scenes with significant empty space and using a hash-based neural radiance field backbone like INGP-NeRF. The method is based on the INGP-NeRF model, which employs multiscale occupancy grids to expedite the sampling process. It was adopted in later works such as Rip-NeRF, which uses the OccupancyGrid from nerfacc. The approach is part of the broader family of grid-based neural radiance fields. name: VF-NeRF
head: Vector Field NeRF, Viewshed Fields for Rigid NeRF Registration
body: VF-NeRF is a method for rigid registration between two Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) when the original camera positions are unknown. It introduces Viewshed Fields (VF), an implicit function that maps an oriented point (3D location and viewing direction) to a scalar indicating how well that point was covered by the original camera set. By using Normalizing Flows to generate high-scoring oriented points, VF-NeRF creates informative virtual camera viewpoints for photometric alignment, avoiding the noise and poor coverage associated with random sampling. It differs from NeRF Importance Sampling by focusing on registration via novel view generation rather than training efficiency, and from NerfAcc Rendering Pipeline by its specific application to inter-NeRF alignment. VF-NeRF operates in two distinct modes: Registration (using Viewshed Fields to align two NeRFs) and Scene Representation (using Vector Fields to render scenes from posed images). The registration algorithm is detailed in, while the vector field rendering implementation is provided in. Registration Mode Inputs: Two pre-trained NeRFs (Source and Target), without camera poses. Registration Mode Outputs: A 6-DoF rigid transformation matrix aligning the Source NeRF to the Target NeRF. Rendering Mode Inputs: Multi-view posed images and monocular depth maps. Rendering Mode Outputs: Rendered RGB images and depth maps of the indoor scene. The model consists of the following components: 1. vectorfieldnetwork: A VectorFieldNetwork instance. 2. renderingnetwork: A RenderingNetwork instance. 3. density: A LaplaceDensity function initialized with parameters from config.densityconfig.todict(). 4. finevectorfieldnetwork: Optional VectorFieldNetwork instance, used if fine sampling is enabled. Defaults to sharing the vectorfieldnetwork instance if not explicitly configured. 5. raysampler: A UniformSampler with parameters nsamples, near, far, and perturb (inverted boolean). 6. finesampler: Optional RangeFineSampler with parameters nimportance, near, far, perturb (inverted), range (config.raysamplerconfig.finerange), and maxsamples (config.raysamplerconfig.maxsamples). This method aligns two NeRFs by generating virtual views from the source NeRF using VF and optimizing a rigid transform. 1. VF Network Initialization: Initialize a Normalizing Flows model using Real-NVP [13] with L=4 layers and H=128 hidden dimensions. The model maps 6D oriented points (x, d) to a 6-dimensional diagonal Gaussian in latent space z. 2. VF Training: During NeRF training, sample oriented points (x, d) around surfaces. The viewing direction d is constant along a ray, while the location x varies. Map sampled points to latent space z. Optimize the VF network by minimizing the unsupervised negative log-likelihood of the data distribution pX(x) through the change of variables formula: \log(px(x)) = \log(pz(f(x))) + \sum{i=1}^{K} \log \left| \det \left( \frac{dfi}{df{i-1}} \right) \right| Use the RAdam optimizer with a constant learning rate of 5 \times 10^{-5}. Real Scenes: Train the NeRF for 60,000 iterations total, and enable VF training on the last 10,000 iterations. Synthetic Scenes: Train the NeRF for 20,000 iterations total, enable VF training on the last 5,000 iterations, and ignore samples where the image alpha is less than 128. 3. Point Cloud Generation (PC Initialization): Sample 100,000 points from the learned VF distribution. Select points with density higher than 10. Use these points as input for a classic global registration method, specifically using FPFH for feature extraction. 4. Virtual Camera Generation: Sample from the 6D Gaussian in the latent space to generate high-visibility oriented points (\tilde{x}, \tilde{d}). Use the invertible Normalizing Flows model to recover the oriented point. Determine the position and orientation of a novel virtual camera using the recovered point and direction. 5. Photometric Optimization: Render images from the Source NeRF using the generated virtual cameras. Optimize the 6-DoF rigid transformation parameters to minimize photometric loss between the rendered Source images and the Target NeRF. Real Scenes: Optimize for 15,000 iterations with 32,000 samples per iteration using an SGD optimizer with an initial learning rate of 5 \times 10^{-3} and exponential decay. Synthetic Scenes: Optimize for 2,500 iterations with 8,128 samples per iteration using an SGD optimizer with an initial learning rate of 1 \times 10^{-3} and exponential decay. Photometric Initialization: Perform optimization over 25 random transformations to find a good starting point. During optimization, use VF to select high-quality rays to improve convergence. This method renders indoor scenes using vector fields learned from posed images and depth maps. 1. Configuration: Parse configuration for vfnetconfig, renderingnetconfig, raysamplerconfig, densityconfig, and schedulerconfig. 2. Network Initialization: Initialize vectorfieldnetwork and renderingnetwork. If config.raysamplerconfig.finesampling() is true, initialize finevectorfieldnetwork (defaulting to self.vectorfieldnetwork). Initialize density as LaplaceDensity. If config.cossimweightsanneal is not 'none', initialize LinearAnnealing with shape self.config.cossimweights.shape[0], duration self.config.annealend - self.config.annealstart, and soft mode based on self.config.cossimweightsanneal == 'soft'. 3. Parallelism: If config.cudaconfig.numgpus > 1, wrap networks in nn.DataParallel and move all networks to config.cudaconfig.device. 4. Ray Sampling: Create raysampler (UniformSampler) with nsamples, near, far, and perturb (inverted). If fine sampling is enabled, create finesampler (RangeFineSampler) with nimportance, near, far, perturb (inverted), range, and maxsamples. 5. Optimization: Initialize optimizer as torch.optim.Adam with learning rate config.schedulerconfig.lr and weight decay config.schedulerconfig.weightdecay. Initialize scheduler as torch.optim.lrscheduler.ExponentialLR with decay factor self.config.schedulerconfig.lrdecayfactor (1. / self.config.schedulerconfig.lrdecaysteps). Train the network to minimize reconstruction loss against posed images and depth maps. VF Network: Real-NVP, L=4 layers, H=128 hidden dims. VF Optimizer: RAdam, constant learning rate 5 \times 10^{-5}. NeRF Representation: Nerfacto. NeRF Training: 1,024 rays per iteration, Adam optimizer, initial learning rate 10^{-2}, exponential decay. Density: LaplaceDensity. Annealing: LinearAnnealing for cosine similarity weights if configured. Transparent Regions: In synthetic scenes, samples where the image alpha is less than 128 are ignored during VF training. Random Sampling Failure: Random sampling on a unit sphere often produces non-informative images with noise; VF-NeRF avoids this by generating informative views. Initialization: Photometric optimization requires a good initial guess; VF-NeRF provides this via PC initialization (FPFH+RANSAC) or photometric initialization over 25 random transformations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Training requires 60,000 or 20,000 NeRF iterations plus 10,000 or 5,000 VF iterations, followed by 15,000 or 2,500 registration optimization iterations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing NeRF weights, VF network weights, and latent space samples. Performance: Evaluated on LLFF and Objaverse datasets. LLFF Full Overlap on Trex yields \Delta t = 0.0205, \Delta R = 0.0122. LLFF No Overlap on Trex yields \Delta t = 0.0102, \Delta R = 0.0105. Objaverse results vary by object; e.g., Chair 4b05 yields \Delta R = 0.03, \Delta t = 2.43, while Piano 0e0d yields \Delta R = 6.89, \Delta t = 13.84. Strengths: Does not require user input at initialization unlike NeRF2NeRF, generates informative views better than random sampling, and is robust to noise. Limitations: Requires pre-trained NeRFs and is computationally intensive due to Normalizing Flows and iterative optimization. VF-NeRF was introduced to solve the problem of rigid registration between two NeRFs without original camera positions. It builds on NeRF Volumetric Rendering (Coarse/Fine Sampling) by using NeRF as the scene representation. The method was evaluated on LLFF and Objaverse datasets. The code implementation is available on GitHub.
