name: Neural Volume Scattering Prediction
head: Backbone Neural Network for Volume Rendering, Deep scattering for volumes, Radiance-predicting neural network for volumes
body: Neural Volume Scattering Prediction is a method for rendering participating media that uses a neural network to predict the scattering distribution at the centers of sampling templates, which is then used to solve the radiative transfer equation. It sets itself apart from its sibling Neural Radiative Transfer Equation Solver and the earlier Radiance-Predicting Neural Networks (RPNN) by decomposing input features into density, transmission, and phase, and by using specific sampling templates (diffuse and highlight) to simplify the network structure and input parameters. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Sampling features: Pre-calculated density, transmission, and phase features derived from particle position coordinates and template points. Configuration parameters: Asymmetry parameters of the Henyey-Greenstein (HG) phase function (g): 1, 2, or 3 parameters depending on material type. Albedo (\etac): A 3D vector for RGB channels, range 0–1, assumed homogeneous within the same material. Gaseous materials: 0 to 0.5. Solid, liquid, and skin materials: 0.5 to 1. Angle (\alpha): Between viewing direction (\omega) and light direction (l), calculated as \alpha = \cos^{-1}(\omega, l). Dataset: Annotated data Z = \{(F1, F(u1, l1)),..., (FN, F(uN, lN))\}, where N is the dataset size, Fi(p, l) is the annotation value, and T^c(F) is the estimated value. Outputs: Scattering distribution F(p, l) for the center point of each sampling template. These values are brought into the radiative transfer equation to render the volume medium. Data Structures Sampling Templates: Total of 4129 templates. Diffuse reflection sampling template: 8 layers. Specular (highlight) reflection sampling template: 4 layers. Feature Vectors: For the i-th layer input feature Hi^\tau, where \tau \in \{\rho, f, T\} represents density, phase function, and transmission field respectively: Average pooling: Bi^\tau = \frac{1}{ni} \sum{j=1}^{ni} H{i,j}^\tau. Maximum pooling: fi^\tau = \max H{i,j}^\tau. ni: Total number of points in the i-th layer template. Attention vector vi: 8-dimensional vector constructed from layer inputs: vi = \{Bi^\rho, Bi^f, Bi^T, fi^\rho, fi^f, fi^T, g, \alpha\}. Algorithm Steps The method uses a backbone neural network divided into two separate networks with identical structures: one for diffuse reflection and one for specular reflection. If density, transmittance, and phase are included, there are 6 identical network modules (2 per feature type: diffuse/specular). 1. Input Layer: Input sampling features (density, transmission, phase) from the pre-calculation table based on particle position and template points. Features are input in batches. There are 4129 sampling templates, so the network processes them 4129 times (or in parallel using multiple models). 2. Hidden Layer Processing (Layer-by-Layer): For each feature type (density, transmission, phase), process features layer-by-layer through identical network structures. Diffuse Reflection: Process 8 layers. Specular Reflection: Process 4 layers. Per Layer Operation: 1. Fuse current layer sampling features (e.g., density) with configuration parameters (g, \etac, \alpha). 2. Input the fused vector into an Attention Module (implemented as SENet) to determine channel importance. Construct vi from the current layer's pooled features and configuration parameters. Calculate weight coefficient wi^\tau = S(R(vi)), where R(vi) = \max(vi, 0) (ReLU) and S(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} (Sigmoid). Apply weights to features: Hi^\tau = wi^\tau \cdot \sum Hi^\tau. 3. Fuse the attention module output with the next layer's sampling features using Fully Connected layer FC-1 to match dimensions. 4. Pass the fused vector through Fully Connected layer FC-2. 5. Fuse the result with the current layer's sampling feature and output. 3. Merge Diffuse and Specular: Merge the diffuse reflection sampling density features (after 8 iterations) and specular reflection sampling density features (after 4 iterations) via a full connection. 4. Final Prediction: Input sampling transmission features and sampling phase features layer-by-layer (12 times each total across diffuse/specular paths). Fuse transmission and phase features together. Input the fused features into a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). Output the scattering distribution of the center point of the sampling template. 5. Rendering: Sample all 4129 volume medium particle points with the template. Predict output in parallel to obtain scattering distributions for all 4129 centers. Bring predicted scattering distribution values into the radiative transfer equation to render the volume medium. Loss Function The network is trained using a mean square error loss with logarithmic transformation to compress the radiation range and speed up training. LS = \frac{1}{B} \sum{i \in B} \left( \log \frac{T^c(F)}{\etac \gamma} + 1 - \log \frac{Fi(p, l)}{\etac \gamma} + 1 \right)^2 B: Batch size. T^c(F): Estimated value of the neural network. Fi(p, l): Annotation value of the scattering distribution. \etac: Albedo for RGB channel c. \gamma: Hyperparameter, typically \gamma = 4. c: RGB color channel. The total loss is minimized over the annotated dataset Z: L{total} = \argmin \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} LS. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def relu(x): return [max(0.0, v) for v in x] def sigmoid(x): return [1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-v)) for v in x] def averagepooling(features, npoints): dim = len(features[0]) avg = [0.0] dim for feat in features: for k in range(dim): avg[k] += feat[k] return [v / npoints for v in avg] def maxpooling(features): dim = len(features[0]) maxval = [float('-inf')] dim for feat in features: for k in range(dim): if feat[k] > maxval[k]: maxval[k] = feat[k] return maxval def attentionmodule(vi): rvi = relu(vi) return sigmoid(rvi) def fclayer(vecin, targetdim): # Standard linear projection with learned weights and bias # Returns a vector of length targetdim return [0.0] targetdim def processlayer(features, config, isdiffuse): # 1. Fuse current layer features with configuration parameters # Exact fusion operation not specified; assumed concatenation or addition fusedconfig = features[0] + config # 2. Attention Module (SENet) # Construct 8-dimensional vector vi npoints = len(features) # Assuming features contain density, phase, and transmission components Brho = averagepooling(features, npoints) frho = maxpooling(features) # Bf, BT, ff, fT would be computed similarly from respective feature streams Bf = [0.0] len(Brho) BT = [0.0] len(Brho) ff = [0.0] len(frho) fT = [0.0] len(frho) g = config[0] alpha = config[1] vi = Brho + Bf + BT + frho + ff + fT + [g, alpha] wi = attentionmodule(vi) # 3. FC-1: Fuse attention output with next layer features to match dimensions # Next layer features are not available in this single-layer function; # in practice, FC-1 projects the attention output to the dimension of the next layer nextlayerdim = len(features[0]) fc1out = fclayer(wi, nextlayerdim) # 4. FC-2 fc2out = fclayer(fc1out, nextlayerdim) # 5. Fuse with current layer feature and output output = [fc2out[k] + features[0][k] for k in range(nextlayerdim)] return output def neuralvolumescatteringprediction(densityfeats, transfeats, phasefeats, config): # config = [g, alpha, albedor, albedog, albedob] nlayersdiffuse = 8 nlayersspecular = 4 # Diffuse reflection path (8 layers) diffusefeats = densityfeats for in range(nlayersdiffuse): diffusefeats = processlayer(diffusefeats, config, isdiffuse=True) # Specular reflection path (4 layers) specularfeats = densityfeats for in range(nlayersspecular): specularfeats = processlayer(specularfeats, config, isdiffuse=False) # Merge diffuse and specular density features via FC mergeddensity = fclayer(diffusefeats, len(specularfeats)) # Transmission and phase features layer-by-layer (12 times each) transfeats12 = transfeats for in range(12): transfeats12 = processlayer(transfeats12, config, isdiffuse=True) phasefeats12 = phasefeats for in range(12): phasefeats12 = processlayer(phasefeats12, config, isdiffuse=True) # Fuse transmission and phase features fusedtransphase = [transfeats12[k] + phasefeats12[k] for k in range(len(transfeats12))] # Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) # Standard MLP with learned weights and ReLU activations mlpout = fclayer(fusedtransphase, 3) # Output 3 channels for RGB scattering scatteringdistribution = [max(0.0, v) for v in mlpout] return scatteringdistribution def computeloss(estimated, annotation, albedo, gamma=4): # LS = 1/B sum( (log(T^c(F)/(etacgamma)) + 1 - log(Fi(p,l)/(etacgamma)) + 1)^2) loss = 0.0 for c in range(3): # RGB channels term1 = math.log(estimated[c] / (albedo[c] gamma)) + 1.0 term2 = math.log(annotation[c] / (albedo[c] gamma)) + 1.0 loss += (term1 - term2) 2 return loss / 3.0 A real-time volume rendering method that uses a neural network to simulate the iterative integration process of solving the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE), replacing traditional path tracing to achieve real-time performance for high albedo anisotropic materials with multiple scattering. It sets itself apart from its sibling Neural Volume Scattering Prediction and the earlier Radiance-Predicting Neural Networks (RPNN) by decomposing input features into density, transmission, and phase, and by using specific sampling templates (diffuse and highlight) to simplify the network structure and input parameters, thereby addressing RPNN's inability to handle shadows and its requirement for large sampling. Time Complexity: The method processes 4129 sampling templates. To improve real-time rendering performance, multiple neural network models can be generated and calculated in parallel. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the pre-calculation table of sampling features and the neural network weights. The network structure includes 6 identical modules (2 per feature type: diffuse/specular) with 8 layers for diffuse and 4 for specular. Measured Performance: Designed for real-time rendering of high albedo anisotropic materials with multiple scattering. Strengths: Logarithmic transformation compresses radiation range, speeding up training and reducing bright mutations from high-frequency phase functions. Limitations: Requires pre-calculation of sampling features based on particle positions and template points. Assumes the 3D volume medium is homogeneous (albedo is equal everywhere within the same material). When to use: Suitable for real-time rendering of participating media with high albedo and anisotropic scattering properties. When not to use: Not suitable for heterogeneous media where albedo varies significantly within a single material type, or for real-time applications where parallel model generation is not feasible. Origin: The method is described in "A real-time rendering method for high albedo anisotropic materials with multiple scattering". History: Not given in the sources. Usage: Used for rendering participating media, specifically high albedo anisotropic materials with multiple scattering. A real-time rendering method for high albedo anisotropic materials with multiple scattering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2401.14051, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Neural Radiative Transfer Equation Solver
head: Neural network-based real-time volume rendering method, RPNN variant with hierarchical transmittance and sampling templates
body: A real-time volume rendering method that uses a neural network to simulate the iterative integration process of solving the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE), replacing traditional path tracing to achieve real-time performance for high albedo anisotropic materials with multiple scattering. It sets itself apart from its sibling Neural Volume Scattering Prediction and the earlier Radiance-Predicting Neural Networks (RPNN) by decomposing input features into density, transmission, and phase, and by using specific sampling templates (diffuse and highlight) to simplify the network structure and input parameters, thereby addressing RPNN's inability to handle shadows and its requirement for large sampling. Inputs: 1. Original 3D volumetric media density field, represented as a point cloud or voxel grid with resolution 1024 \times 1024 \times 1024. 2. Incident light direction (implied by the highlight template geometry). Outputs: 1. Scattering distribution for the center points of all sampling templates, which contributes to the final radiance calculation. Data Structures: 1. Hierarchical Density Fields: A set of 11 density fields \rhoi at resolutions Ri. i=0: 1024^3 i=1: 512^3 i=2: 256^3 i=3: 128^3 i=4: 64^3 (Note: Source text contains typo '624 64 64', corrected to 64^3 based on sequence). i=5: 32^3 i=6: 16^3 i=7: 8^3 i=8: 4^3 (Note: Source text contains typo '4 4 4 4', corrected to 4^3 based on sequence). i=9: 2^3 i=10: 1^3 2. Hierarchical Transmission Fields: A set of 11 transmission fields Ti(p, y), one for each density level. 3. Transmission Feature: A single feature map resulting from the 3D-CNN processing of the 11 transmission fields. 4. Diffuse Reflection Sampling Template (S{diff}): A set of 182 points distributed in a sphere around a center point, divided into 8 layers. Layer 0: 6 points (1 center, 5 inside). Layer 1: 8 points. Layer 2: 12 points. Layer 3: 16 points. Layer 4: 24 points. Layer 5: 32 points. Layer 6: 48 points. Layer 7: 48 points. Points in layers 1-7 are evenly distributed in the spherical shell between the current layer's surface and the previous layer's surface. 5. Highlight Sampling Template (S{high}): A set of 72 points distributed along the direction of incident light, divided into 4 layers. Layer 0: 32 points. Layer 1: 16 points. Layer 2: 16 points. Layer 3: 8 points. Points are evenly distributed by distance from the center. Parameters: \lambda{i+1}: Coefficient for transmittance calculation, range [0, 1], specific value 0.6. Steps: 1. Data Processing (Hierarchical Transmittance): For each density level i from 0 to 10: a. Obtain the density field \rhoi(x) at resolution Ri. b. Calculate the transmission field Ti(p, y) using the formula: Ti(p, y) = e^{-\int{p}^{y} \lambda{i+1} \rhoi(x) dx} where p is the starting point, y is the ending point along the path, and \lambda{i+1} = 0.6. c. Store the 11 transmission fields T0, \dots, T{10}. 2. Transmission Feature Extraction: a. Input the 11 hierarchical transmission fields into a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D-CNN). b. The 3D-CNN assigns a weight to each level of transmission field and superimposes them to produce a single combined transmission feature. 3. Sampling Template Generation: a. Create the diffuse reflection sampling template S{diff} using a sphere divided into 8 layers. b. Create the highlight sampling template S{high} divided into 4 layers along the incident light direction. 4. Feature Sampling: For a given center point in the volume: a. Sample the density features using both S{diff} and S{high} templates. b. Sample the transmission features (from the combined feature map generated in Step 2) using both S{diff} and S{high} templates. c. Sample the phase features (scattering phase function values) using both S{diff} and S{high} templates. d. This results in sampled phase features, sampled density features, and sampled transmission features for each template layer. 5. Network Input Preparation: a. Layer the three types of sampled features (density, transmission, phase) according to the layers of the diffuse reflection sampling template and the highlight sampling template. b. The sampled features of each layer are sent into the network for internal scattering estimation. 6. Attention Mechanism: a. Pass the layered features through an attention module. b. The module selects important channel features to pay more attention to light scattering, highlights, and shadows. 7. Scattering Prediction: a. name: Neural Cloud Shading with Triplane Encoding
head: Environmental Volumetric Neural Shading, Mesh-based Neural Volumetric Rendering, Neural Shading of Clouds, Neural Volumetric Shading for Clouds
body: Neural Cloud Shading with Triplane Encoding is a real-time rendering method that replaces explicit volumetric ray marching with a neural shading model applied to mesh geometry. It solves the problem of high-fidelity cloud relighting by approximating complex light scattering and atmospheric illumination using a multilayer perceptron (MLP) evaluated per pixel on a rasterized cloud mesh. Unlike density-field approaches such as Radiance-Predicting Neural Networks (RPNN) or traditional ray marching, this method eliminates volume integration entirely, relying instead on a rasterization-based pipeline with triplane feature encoding to capture view-dependent opacity and parallax. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a mesh representation of a volumetric cloud, a sky illumination model (Nishita sky model), and a sun direction defined by spherical coordinates (\theta, \phi). The output is a final color c{tilde} and transparency \alpha for each pixel, composited over the background. Data Structures: 1. Triplane Feature Maps: Six 32-bit floating-point RGBA textures at 512 \times 512 resolution. Three planes (XY, XZ, YZ) are used, with 8 features per plane (4 channels per texture). These are stored as learnable Parameter tensors in PyTorch during training and as textures during inference. 2. MLP Weights: Stored in 16-bit floating-point precision to support tensor core operations. 3. Depth/Position Attachments: Back-face position: 16-bit RGB color attachment storing normalized positions of the furthest visible surface. Front-face depth: Standard depth buffer storing the closest visible surface. Shadow map: Generated from the sun's perspective. Numbered Steps: 1. Mesh Conversion: Convert the volumetric cloud asset into a mesh representation. 2. Training Data Generation: Render the mesh in Blender under diverse viewing and lighting conditions using path tracing to generate ground-truth RGBA values. 3. Thickness Estimation (Training): Render the mesh back faces (front-face culling, greater-than depth test) and front faces (back-face culling, less-or-equal depth test) to compute per-pixel thickness \delta as the difference between front and back positions. 4. Visibility Computation (Training): Compute a diffuse direct light pass and apply a smoothstep function with lower bound 0.0 and upper bound 0.1 to produce soft visibility values. 5. Model Training: Train an MLP (4 hidden layers, 64 neurons, ReLU activations) using Adam optimizer (initial LR 10^{-3}, halved every 50 epochs, batch size 1024^2, 250 epochs). The input is the concatenation of triplane features, sun direction (\theta, \phi), and thickness \delta. The output is two RGB colors (cD, cI) and \alpha. The loss is the L2 distance between \log(\tilde{c} + 1) and \log(c{GT} + 1). 6. Back-Face Position Pre-Pass (Runtime): Render back faces with front-face culling and a greater-than depth test. Store normalized positions in a 16-bit RGB color attachment. 7. Front-Face Depth Pre-Pass (Runtime): Render front faces with back-face culling and a less-or-equal depth test to a depth map (Scene Depth). 8. Shadow Pre-Pass (Runtime): Generate a shadow map from the light source's point of view (sun direction) using back-face culling and disabled depth test. 9. Final Cloud Color Pass (Runtime): Use a depth test set to 'equal' against the front-face depth map to identify the visible surface. Reconstruct front-face position in the vertex shader and normalize it to the bounding box. Compute thickness \delta as the difference between the front-face position and the back-face position (from Step 6). Apply a smoothstep function to \delta with bounds 0.0 and 0.4 to prevent contouring artifacts. Project the normalized position onto XY, XZ, and YZ planes to obtain texture coordinates. Sample the 6 triplane textures using bilinear interpolation and sum the features. Concatenate summed triplane features, sun direction (\theta, \phi), and smoothed thickness \delta. Evaluate the MLP to output cD, cI, and \alpha. Interpolate between cD and cI based on precomputed visibility values (from shadow map using PCF) to obtain final color \tilde{c}. Blend \tilde{c} and \alpha with the background. Formulas: Triplane Encoding: For a point p, features F{XY}, F{YZ}, F{XZ} are sampled via bilinear interpolation and summed: F{total} = F{XY} + F{YZ} + F{XZ}. Output Activation: g(x) = e^{x-3} applied to the output layer. Loss Function: L = || \log(\tilde{c} + 1) - \log(c{GT} + 1) ||2^2. Visibility Interpolation: \tilde{c} = V \cdot cD + (1 - V) \cdot cI, where V is the smoothstep visibility value. Thickness Smoothing: \delta{smooth} = \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 0.4, \delta). Parameters: MLP Architecture: 4 hidden layers, 64 neurons per layer (4 \times 64). Triplane Resolution: 512 \times 512. Features per Plane: 8 (stored in 2 RGBA textures per plane). Sun Direction: 2D vector (\theta, \phi). Thickness Bounds: 0.0 to 0.4. Visibility Thresholds: 0.0 to 0.1. Mipmapping: Mipmap level 4 applied to triplane features for final rendering to reduce noise. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Thickness: Without the thickness parameter, the model fails to account for accumulated density, leading to inconsistent transparency and erroneous semi-transparent regions. Opacity Saturation: Opacity does not saturate sufficiently toward the cloud interior without smoothing, causing contouring artifacts. High-Frequency Noise: High-frequency components in triplane features introduce noise; mitigated by mipmapping at the cost of PSNR. View Direction: View direction is excluded from inputs as it was found less critical than thickness for view dependency. The foundational method for neural shading of assets using MLPs. Neural Cloud Shading adapts RNA by adding thickness and sky illumination. RNA The parent method where the MLP is evaluated during ray marching. Neural Cloud Shading differs by using rasterization and mesh geometry instead of ray marching. In-Shader Neural Volume Ray Marching Time Complexity: Real-time performance achieved. Frame times are 3.7 ms for high-poly meshes and 0.41 ms for low-poly meshes on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for 6 triplane textures (512 \times 512 \times 4 \times 32-bit) and MLP weights. Performance: Training takes ~20 minutes on NVIDIA A100 GPU. Quality: 22.315 dB PSNR and 0.059 FLIP error for the 4 \times 64 architecture with thickness. Strengths: Eliminates ray marching, enabling real-time performance; preserves volumetric appearance with full parallax; supports real-time relighting via sky model inputs. Limitations: Requires mesh conversion of volumetric assets; relies on rasterization shadows which may not capture complex volumetric self-shadowing as accurately as ray tracing; quality depends on training data diversity. When to Use: Real-time applications requiring high-fidelity, relightable clouds where ray marching is too expensive. When Not to Use: When exact volumetric integration is required or when assets cannot be converted to meshes. Neural Cloud Shading with Triplane Encoding was introduced by Rikard Olajos, Michael Doggett, and Prashant Goswami in 2026 in the paper "Environmental Volumetric Neural Shading of Clouds for Real-Time Rendering". It builds upon the Relightable Neural Assets (RNA) framework, adapting it for volumetric clouds by incorporating per-pixel thickness and sky illumination models. The method addresses the computational cost of traditional density-field ray marching approaches like those by Hillaire (2016) and Schneider (2023). name: DVGO Volume Rendering Forward Pass
head: DVGO forward, Direct Voxel Grid Optimization rendering
body: The DVGO forward pass renders a 3D scene represented by a direct voxel grid of density and color features into a 2D image by querying the grid along camera rays and compositing the results. It differs from standard NeRF by replacing the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with a direct lookup in a 3D texture (voxel grid), enabling significantly faster training and inference while maintaining view-dependent color through auxiliary feature vectors. Inputs: rayso: Origin of each ray, shape (N, 3), where N is the number of pixels (rays). raysd: Direction of each ray, shape (N, 3). near, far: Near and far clipping planes for ray marching. stepsize: Distance between sample points along the ray. renderkwargs: Dictionary containing optional flags (renderfeatures, renderdiffuse, renderdepth) and background color bg. Outputs: rgbmarched: Final rendered RGB image, shape (N, 3). alphainvlast: Accumulated transmittance at the end of the ray, shape (N). weights: Per-sample weights used for compositing, shape (M), where M is the number of valid samples. rawalpha: Raw alpha values before weighting, shape (M). rawrgb: Raw RGB values before weighting, shape (M, 3). rayid: Mapping from sample index to ray index, shape (M). depth (optional): Weighted average depth, shape (N). diffusemarched (optional): Rendered diffuse color, shape (N, 3). Density Grid (V\sigma): A 3D tensor of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz) storing raw density values. Color Feature Grid (Vc): A 3D tensor of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz, k0) storing feature vectors. k0 is the feature dimension. RGB Network (\text{rgbnet}): A small MLP (optional) that maps color features and view direction to final RGB. Diffuse Color Grid (Vd): A 3D tensor of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz, 3) storing diffuse color components (if usediffusecolor is enabled). Mask Cache: A boolean grid or hash map indicating free space, used to skip empty regions. interval: Sampling interval for density-to-alpha conversion. Calculated as stepsize voxelsizeratio. actshift: Shift parameter for the density activation function (e.g., sigmoid shift). fastcolorthres: Threshold for early ray termination. If alpha or weight exceeds this, subsequent samples are skipped. usediffusecolor: Boolean flag to enable diffuse color rendering. rgbnetfullimplicit: Boolean flag determining if view direction is concatenated with features before the RGB network. rgbnetdirect: Boolean flag determining if diffuse color is added directly to the network output. 1. Ray Sampling: Generate sample points along each ray. For each ray i \in [0, N-1], compute sample positions \mathbf{x}j = \mathbf{o}i + tj \mathbf{d}i, where tj are evenly spaced between near and far with spacing stepsize. Collect all points into raypts of shape (M, 3), along with corresponding rayid and stepid (index along the ray). 2. Free Space Culling: If maskcache is present, filter raypts, rayid, and stepid to keep only points where maskcache(raypts) is true. 3. Density Query: Query the density grid V\sigma at raypts using trilinear interpolation. Let \sigmaj be the raw density value for sample j. 4. Density to Alpha Conversion: Convert raw density \sigmaj to alpha \alphaj using the Raw2Alpha function: \alphaj = 1 - \exp(-(\sigmaj + \text{act\shift}) \cdot \text{interval}). 5. Early Termination (Alpha): If fastcolorthres > 0, filter samples where \alphaj > \text{fast\color\thres}. Remove these samples from raypts, rayid, stepid, density, and alpha. 6. Weight Computation: Compute accumulated transmittance Tj and weights wj for each sample. T1 = 1, T{j} = T{j-1} \cdot (1 - \alpha{j-1}) for j > 1 (assuming sorted by depth). wj = Tj \cdot \alphaj. Compute alphainvlast (total transmittance at the end of the ray): T{M+1} = TM \cdot (1 - \alphaM). 7. Early Termination (Weight): If fastcolorthres > 0, filter samples where wj > \text{fast\color\thres}. Remove these samples. 8. Color Query: Query the color feature grid Vc at raypts to get features \mathbf{k}j \in \mathbb{R}^{k0}. If usediffusecolor is true, query the diffuse color grid Vd to get \mathbf{d}j \in \mathbb{R}^3. 9. RGB Computation: If rgbnet is None, set \mathbf{c}j = \text{sigmoid}(\mathbf{d}j) (if diffuse is used) or use features directly. If rgbnet is not None, compute positional encoding of view direction \mathbf{d}i for the ray containing sample j, concatenate with \mathbf{k}j, pass through rgbnet, and apply sigmoid. If rgbnetdirect is true, add diffuse color: \mathbf{c}j = \mathbf{c}j + \mathbf{d}j. 10. Compositing: Compute final RGB for each ray i: \text{rgb}i = \sum{j \in \text{ray } i} wj \cdot \mathbf{c}j + T{M+1} \cdot \mathbf{bg}, where \mathbf{bg} is the background color. 11. Optional Outputs: If renderfeatures: Sum weights kj grouped by rayid. If renderdiffuse: Sum weights sigmoid(dj) grouped by rayid. If renderdepth: Sum weights stepid grouped by rayid. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def dvgoforwardpass(rayso, raysd, near, far, stepsize, model, renderkwargs): N = rayso.shape[0] numsamples = int((far - near) / stepsize) tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., numsamples, device=rayso.device) tvals = near + tvals (far - near) raypts = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(2) M = N numsamples rayptsflat = raypts.reshape(-1, 3) rayid = torch.arange(N, device=rayso.device).unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, numsamples).reshape(-1) stepid = torch.arange(numsamples, device=rayso.device).unsqueeze(0).expand(N, -1).reshape(-1) # 2. Free Space Culling if model.maskcache is not None: validmask = model.maskcache(rayptsflat) rayptsflat = rayptsflat[validmask] rayid = rayid[validmask] stepid = stepid[validmask] M = rayptsflat.shape[0] if M == 0: return { 'rgbmarched': torch.zeros(N, 3, device=rayso.device) + renderkwargs['bg'], 'alphainvlast': torch.ones(N, device=rayso.device), 'weights': torch.zeros(0, device=rayso.device), 'rawalpha': torch.zeros(0, device=rayso.device), 'rawrgb': torch.zeros(0, 3, device=rayso.device), 'rayid': torch.zeros(0, dtype=torch.long, device=rayso.device) } # 3. Density Query normpts = (rayptsflat - model.xyzmin) / (model.xyzmax - model.xyzmin) normpts = torch.clamp(normpts, 0.0, 1.0) density = trilinearinterpolate(model.densitygrid, normpts) # 4. Density to Alpha interval = stepsize model.voxelsizeratio alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-(density + model.actshift) interval) # 5. Early Termination (Alpha) if model.fastcolorthres > 0: keepmask = alpha > model.fastcolorthres rayptsflat = rayptsflat[keepmask] rayid = rayid[keepmask] stepid = stepid[keepmask] density = density[keepmask] alpha = alpha[keepmask] M = rayptsflat.shape[0] # 6. Weight Computation # Sort by rayid and stepid sortidx = torch.argsort(rayid 100000 + stepid) rayid = rayid[sortidx] stepid = stepid[sortidx] alpha = alpha[sortidx] oneminusalpha = 1.0 - alpha T = torch.ones(M, device=rayso.device) # Compute transmittance T per ray for j in range(1, M): if rayid[j] != rayid[j-1]: T[j] = 1.0 else: T[j] = T[j-1] oneminusalpha[j-1] weights = T alpha # Compute alphainvlast per ray counts = torch.bincount(rayid, minlength=N) raystarts = torch.cat([torch.tensor([0], device=rayid.device), torch.cumsum(counts[:-1], dim=0)]) lastindices = raystarts + counts - 1 alphainvlastperray = T[lastindices] (1 - alpha[lastindices]) # 7. Early Termination (Weight) if model.fastcolorthres > 0: weightmask = weights > model.fastcolorthres rayptsflat = rayptsflat[weightmask] rayid = rayid[weightmask] stepid = stepid[weightmask] alpha = alpha[weightmask] weights = weights[weightmask] T = T[weightmask] M = rayptsflat.shape[0] counts = torch.bincount(rayid, minlength=N) raystarts = torch.cat([torch.tensor([0], device=rayid.device), torch.cumsum(counts[:-1], dim=0)]) lastindices = raystarts + counts - 1 alphainvlastperray = T[lastindices] (1 - alpha[lastindices]) # 8. Color Query normptsfiltered = (rayptsflat - model.xyzmin) / (model.xyzmax - model.xyzmin) normptsfiltered = torch.clamp(normptsfiltered, 0.0, 1.0) colorfeatures = trilinearinterpolate(model.colorgrid, normptsfiltered) rgb = torch.zeros(M, 3, device=rayso.device) diffuse = torch.zeros(M, 3, device=rayso.device) if model.usediffusecolor: diffuse = trilinearinterpolate(model.diffusegrid, normptsfiltered) if model.rgbnet is None: if model.usediffusecolor: rgb = torch.sigmoid(diffuse) else: if colorfeatures.shape[1] == 3: rgb = colorfeatures else: rgb = torch.zeros(M, 3, device=rayso.device) else: viewdirs = raysd[rayid] viewdirspe = positionalencoding(viewdirs) inputcolor = torch.cat([colorfeatures, viewdirspe], dim=-1) rawrgb = model.rgbnet(inputcolor) rgb = torch.sigmoid(rawrgb) if model.rgbnetdirect and model.usediffusecolor: rgb = rgb + torch.sigmoid(diffuse) # 9. Compositing rgbmarched = segmentcoo( src=weights.unsqueeze(-1) rgb, index=rayid, out=torch.zeros(N, 3, device=rayso.device), reduce='sum') bg = renderkwargs['bg'].to(rayso.device) rgbmarched = rgbmarched + alphainvlastperray.unsqueeze(-1) bg # 10. Optional Outputs extras = {} if renderkwargs.get('renderfeatures', False): extras['featuresmarched'] = segmentcoo( src=weights.unsqueeze(-1) colorfeatures, index=rayid, out=torch.zeros(N, colorfeatures.shape[1], device=rayso.device), reduce='sum') if model.usediffusecolor and renderkwargs.get('renderdiffuse', False): extras['diffusemarched'] = segmentcoo( src=weights.unsqueeze(-1) torch.sigmoid(diffuse), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros(N, 3, device=rayso.device), reduce='sum') if renderkwargs.get('renderdepth', False): extras['depth'] = segmentcoo( src=weights.unsqueeze(-1) stepid.unsqueeze(-1).float(), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros(N, 1, device=rayso.device), reduce='sum').squeeze(-1) return { 'rgbmarched': rgbmarched, 'alphainvlast': alphainvlastperray, 'weights': weights, 'rawalpha': alpha, 'rawrgb': rgb, 'rayid': rayid, extras } def trilinearinterpolate(grid, points): """Standard trilinear interpolation.""" gridshape = torch.tensor(grid.shape, device=points.device, dtype=torch.float32) coords = points (gridshape - dx) + v100 dx v01 = v001 (1 - dx) + v101 dx v10 = v010 (1 - dx) + v110 dx v11 = v011 (1 - dx) + v111 dx v0 = v00 (1 - dy) + v10 dy v1 = v01 (1 - dy) + v11 dy return v0 (1 - dz) + v1 dz def positionalencoding(x, mindeg=0, maxdeg=10, scale=1, basefreq=2.0): """Standard sinusoidal positional encoding.""" numbands = maxdeg - This prevents guiding the agent to choose the next-best view with highest information gain in active vision tasks. Boundaries: Ray points outside the voxel grid bounds must be clamped or filtered to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. An additional entropy volume V(E,c) introduced to overcome the zero-entropy initialization issue of DVGO's density volume, allowing information gain calculation at the start. It stores \alpha(E,c), initialized with 0.5 to represent highest entropy. For voxels of V(\sigma,c) that have been updated in the reconstruction stage, \alpha(E,c) is synchronized with \alpha(\sigma,c). Not given in the sources. DVGO (Direct Voxel Grid Optimization) was introduced as a method to accelerate NeRF training by replacing the MLP with a direct voxel grid. It builds on the principles of neural volume rendering. The method was developed to address the computational bottleneck of MLP queries in NeRF, enabling real-time or near-real-time training and rendering. gkouros/ref-dvgo, https://github.com/gkouros/ref-dvgo, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) ActiveRMAP: Radiance Field for Active Mapping And Planning, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2211.12656, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Primitive Radiance Field Integrator
body: The Volumetric Primitive Radiance Field Integrator is a path-tracing method for rendering scattering and emissive media represented by mixtures of kernel-based volumetric primitives (e.g., Gaussians, Epanechnikov) rather than voxel grids or point clouds. It modifies standard volumetric path tracing by replacing medium interaction routines with primitive-specific transmittance evaluation, free-flight distance sampling, and albedo evaluation. It distinguishes itself from its sibling, the Volumetric Primitive Tomography Integrator, by supporting scattering and emissive media via multiple importance sampling with PDF balancing, whereas the tomography integrator integrates density with no scattering. The integrator inherits from RBIntegrator and operates on a scene containing EllipsoidMesh primitives. Each primitive is defined by a center, rotation, scale, and opacity, optionally accompanied by spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for emission. The method supports both primal (forward) and adjoint (backward) modes for differentiable rendering. Input: A scene graph containing EllipsoidMesh primitives. Each primitive stores geometric parameters (center \mathbf{c}, rotation matrix \mathbf{R}, scale vector \mathbf{s}), opacity \alpha, and optionally SH coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH} for emission. Output: Radiance L (primal) or differential radiance \delta L (adjoint). Primitive Attributes: center: 3D vector \mathbf{c}. rotation: 3 \times 3 rotation matrix \mathbf{R}. scale: 3D vector \mathbf{s}. opacity: Scalar \alpha \in [0, 1]. shcoeffs: Array of spherical harmonic coefficients. State Variables (per ray): L: Radiance accumulator. \delta L: Differential radiance accumulator (adjoint). \beta: Path throughput. depth: Current path depth. active: Boolean mask for active rays. maxdepth (int): Maximum path depth. -1 indicates no limit, mapped to 0xFFFFFFFF internally. rrdepth (int): Minimum path depth before enabling Russian roulette. -1 indicates no limit, mapped to 0xFFFFFFFF. kerneltype (str): Name of the kernel to use for rendering the volumetric primitives, one of ['gaussian', 'epanechnikov']. srgbprimitives (bool): If true, converts sRGB light transport to linear color space at the end. userr (bool): Whether to use Russian Roulette. Determined by rrdepth >= 0 and (rrdepth < maxdepth or maxdepth == -1). 1. Initialization: Set maxdepth to 0xFFFFFFFF if input is -1. Set rrdepth to 0xFFFFFFFF if input is -1. Determine userr based on rrdepth and maxdepth. Initialize kernel with kernelfullrange=True and kernelnormalized=True. For each pixel/ray: Initialize L = 0 (or state input), \delta L = 0 (or state input), \beta = 1.0, depth = 0. Generate ray \mathbf{r}. Set active mask to true for all rays. 2. Ray Intersection Loop: While active is not empty: Perform ray intersection with scene using scene.rayintersect with flags All | BackfaceCulling and coherent intersection for depth == 0. Filter active rays to only those intersecting ellipsoids: \text{active} \leftarrow \text{active} \ \& \ (\text{si.is\valid}() \ \& \ (\text{si.shape.shape\type}() == \text{ShapeType.Ellipsoids})) If no active rays remain, break loop. 3. Primitive Evaluation: For active rays intersecting ellipsoids: Evaluate Transmission: Gather ellipsoid parameters: center \mathbf{c}, rotation \mathbf{R}, scale \mathbf{s}, opacity \alpha. Transform ray origin and direction to local space: \mathbf{o}' = \mathbf{R}^T (\mathbf{r}.o - \mathbf{c}) / \mathbf{s} \mathbf{d}' = \mathbf{R}^T \mathbf{r}.d / \mathbf{s} Compute peak location along ray: t{peak} = -\frac{\mathbf{o}' \cdot \mathbf{d}'}{\mathbf{d}' \cdot \mathbf{d}'} Evaluate density at peak: \rho = \text{density}(t{peak}) based on kerneltype (Gaussian or Epanechnikov). Compute transmission: \text{transmission} = 1.0 - \min(\alpha \cdot \rho, 0.9999) Note: Clamping to 0.9999 avoids numerical issues with 1.0 - 1.0. Evaluate Emission: Gather SH coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH}. Compute SH degree: n = \sqrt{\text{sh\coeffs.shape}[0] / 3 - 1}. Evaluate SH basis for viewing direction \mathbf{d}: \mathbf{sh\dir\coef} = \text{sh\eval}(\mathbf{d}, n). Compute emission: \text{emission} = \max(\sum (\mathbf{c}{SH} \odot \mathbf{sh\dir\coef}) + 0.5, 0.0) Note: Adding 0.5 before clamping handles potential negative values from SH evaluation. Clamp Infinite Values: Le[\sim \text{dr.is\finite}(Le)] = 0.0 4. Accumulation and Throughput Update: Compute local emission contribution: Le = \beta \cdot (1.0 - \text{transmission}) \cdot \text{emission} Update radiance accumulator: L[\text{active}] = L[\text{active}] + Le \quad (\text{if primal}) L[\text{active}] = L[\text{active}] - Le \quad (\text{if adjoint}) Update path throughput: \beta[\text{active}] = \text{transmission} 5. Adjoint Indirect Radiance (Adjoint Mode Only): Compute differentiable reflected indirect radiance: L{r\ind} = L \cdot \text{transmission} / \text{dr.detach}(\text{transmission}) Compute total local contribution: Lo = Le + L{r\ind} Select finite values: Lo = \text{dr.select}(\text{active} \ \& \ \text{dr.is\finite}(Lo), Lo, 0.0) Propagate gradients: If Backward: dr.backwardfrom(δL Lo) If Forward: δL += dr.forwardto(Lo) 6. Ray Propagation and Termination: Spawn new ray origin to avoid self-intersection: \mathbf{r}.o[\text{active}] = \text{si.p} + \mathbf{r}.d \cdot 10^{-4} Update active mask and depth: \text{active} \leftarrow \text{active} \ \& \ \text{si.is\valid}() \text{depth}[\text{active}] += 1 Kill paths with insignificant contribution: \beta{max} = \text{dr.max}(\beta) \text{active} \leftarrow \text{active} \ \& \ (\beta{max} > 0.01) Russian Roulette (if primal and userr): Calculate probability: p{rr} = \max(\beta{max}, 0.1) Identify candidates: \text{rr\active} = (\text{depth} \ge \text{rr\depth}) \ \& \ (\beta{max} < 0.1) Scale throughput: \beta[\text{rr\active}] = 1.0 / p{rr} Determine continuation: \text{rr\continue} = \text{sample\rr} < p{rr} Update active: \text{active} \leftarrow \text{active} \ \& \ \text{rr\continue} Limit recursion depth: \text{active} \leftarrow \text{active} \ \& \ (\text{depth} < \text{max\depth}) 7. Final Output: If srgbprimitives is true, convert L to linear space: L = \text{mi.math.srgb\to\linear}(L). Return L if primal, else \delta L. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolprimprb(scene, rayso, raysd, mode='primal', maxdepth=-1, rrdepth=-1, kerneltype='gaussian', srgbprimitives=True): # Initialize parameters if maxdepth == -1: maxdepth = 0xFFFFFFFF if rrdepth == -1: rrdepth = 0xFFFFFFFF userr = (rrdepth >= 0) and ((rrdepth < maxdepth) or (maxdepth == 0xFFFFFFFF)) N = len(rayso) L = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(N)] deltaL = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(N)] beta = [1.0] N depth = [0] N active = [True] N kernel = Kernel(kerneltype, fullrange=True, normalized=True) while any(active): # Ray intersection si = scene.rayintersect(rayso, raysd, flags=ALL | BACKFACECULLING, coherent=(depth[0] == 0)) # Filter for ellipsoids isvalid = [si.isvalid(i) for i in range(N)] isellipsoid = [si.shape.shapetype(i) == SHAPEELLIPSOID for i in range(N)] active = [a & v & e for a, v, e in zip(active, isvalid, isellipsoid)] if not any(active): break idxs = [i for i in range(N) if active[i]] centers = [si.shape.centers[si.primitiveindex(i)] for i in idxs] rotations = [si.shape.rotations[si.primitiveindex(i)] for i in idxs] scales = [si.shape.scales[si.primitiveindex(i)] for i in idxs] opacities = [si.shape.opacities[si.primitiveindex(i)] for i in idxs] shcoeffs = [si.shape.shcoeffs[si.primitiveindex(i)] for i in idxs] # Transform to local space localo = [scalevector(dotproduct(transpose(rot), subtract(o, c)), 1.0/s) for rot, o, c, s in zip(rotations, [rayso[i] for i in idxs], centers, scales)] locald = [scalevector(dotproduct(transpose(rot), d), 1.0/s) for rot, d, s in zip(rotations, [raysd[i] for i in idxs], scales)] # Compute peak location tpeak = [-dotproduct(lo, ld) / dotproduct(ld, ld) for lo, ld in zip(localo, locald)] # Evaluate density at peak density = [kernel.evaluatedensity(lo, ld, tp) for lo, ld, tp in zip(localo, locald, tpeak)] # Compute transmission transmittance = [1.0 - min(op den, 0.9999) for op, den in zip(opacities, density)] # Evaluate emission emission = [] for i in range(len(idxs)): shdeg = sqrt(len(shcoeffs[i]) / 3.0 - 1.0) shbasis = sheval(raysd[idxs[i]], shdeg) val = sum(c b for c, b in zip(shcoeffs[i], shbasis)) + 0.5 emission.append(max(val, 0.0)) emission = [0.0 if not isfinite(e) else e for e in emission] # Compute local contribution Le = [beta[idxs[i]] (1.0 - transmittance[i]) emission[i] for i in range(len(idxs))] # Update radiance accumulator if mode == 'primal': for i, idx in enumerate(idxs): L[idx] = addvectors(L[idx], Le[i]) else: for i, idx in enumerate(idxs): L[idx] = subtractvectors(L[idx], Le[i]) # Update throughput for i, idx in enumerate(idxs): beta[idx] = transmittance[i] # Adjoint indirect radiance if mode == 'adjoint': Lrind = [] for i, idx in enumerate(idxs): Lrind.append(scalevector(addvectors(L[idx], Le[i]), transmittance[i] / transmittance[i])) Lo = [addvectors(Le[i], Lrind[i]) for i in range(len(idxs))] Lo = [0.0 if not isfinite(v) else v for v in Lo] for i, idx in enumerate(idxs): deltaL[idx] = addvectors(deltaL[idx], Lo[i]) # Spawn new ray origin for idx in idxs: rayso[idx] = addvectors(si.p[idx], scalevector(raysd[idx], 1e-4)) active[idx] = active[idx] & si.isvalid(idx) depth[idx] += 1 # Kill insignificant paths betamax = max(beta) for idx in range(N): active[idx] = active[idx] & (betamax > 0.01) # Russian Roulette if userr and any(active): rrprob = max(betamax, 0.1) rractive = [(depth[idx] >= rrdepth) and (beta[idx] < 0.1) for idx in range(N)] rrcandidates = [idx for idx in range(N) if active[idx] and rractive[idx]] for idx in rrcandidates: beta[idx] /= rrprob rrcontinue = [random() < rrprob for in rrcandidates] for i, idx in enumerate(rrcandidates): active[idx] = active[idx] & rrcontinue[i] # Limit depth for idx in range(N): active[idx] = active[idx] & (depth[idx] < maxdepth) # Convert to linear space if needed if srgbprimitives: L = [srgbtolinear(c) for c in L] return L if mode == 'primal' else deltaL def Kernel(kerneltype, fullrange, normalized): class K: def evaluatedensity(self, o, d, t): # Placeholder for kernel-specific density evaluation return 1.0 return K() def sheval(d, degree): # Standard spherical harmonic basis evaluation return [1.0] (degree + 1)2 def srgbtolinear(c): return [max(0, (x/12.92) if x <= 0.04045 else ((x+0.055)/1.055)2.4) for x in c] def scene.rayintersect(o, d, flags, coherent): class SI: def isvalid(self, i): return True def shape(self): class S: def shapetype(self, i): return SHAPEELLIPSOID def centers(self, i): return [0,0,0] def rotations(self, i): return [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]] def scales(self, i): return [1,1,1] def opacities(self, i): return 1.0 def shcoeffs(self, i): return [1.0] return S() def p(self, i): return [0,0,0] return SI() ALL, BACKFACECULLING, SHAPEELLIPSOID = 1, 2, 10 def transpose(m): return [list(row) for row in zip(m)] def subtract(a, b): return [a[i]-b[i] for i in range(3)] def scalevector(v, s): return [xs for x in v] def dotproduct(a, b): return sum(xy for x, y in zip(a, b)) def addvectors(a, b): return [a[i]+b[i] for i in range(3)] def subtractvectors(a, b): return [a[i]-b[i] for i in range(3)] def isfinite(x): return x == x def random(): return 0.5 Numerical Stability: Transmission calculation clips opacity density to 0.9999 to avoid 1.0 - 1.0 numerical issues. SH Emission: Emission calculation adds 0.5 before clamping to 0.0 to handle potential negative values from SH evaluation. Self-Intersection: Ray origin is offset by 10^{-4} along the ray direction to prevent self-intersection after scattering. The Volumetric Primitive Tomography Integrator is a simplified rendering method for volumetric primitives that accounts exclusively for absorption, ignoring scattering and emission. It is designed for tomography applications where the goal is to visualize density or attenuation rather than photometric appearance. Unlike its sibling Volumetric Primitive PRB Integrator, which handles scattering media, this integrator treats the volume as a purely absorbing medium. The Volumetric Primitive PRB Integrator is a path tracing method for rendering scattering and emissive media represented by mixtures of kernel-based volumetric primitives (e.g., Gaussians, Epanechnikov) rather than voxel grids or point clouds. It modifies standard volumetric path tracing by replacing medium interaction routines with primitive-specific transmittance evaluation, free-flight distance sampling, and albedo evaluation. It distinguishes itself from its sibling, the Volumetric Primitive Tomography Integrator, by supporting scattering and emissive media via multiple importance sampling with PDF balancing, whereas the tomography integrator integrates density with no scattering. The Epanechnikov kernel variant uses a closed-form solution for transmittance calculation. Free-flight distance sampling requires numerical root-finding methods (e.g., Newton-Raphson) due to the complexity of the analytical solution for multiple primitives. The 3D Epanechnikov kernel is defined as: Ei(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \frac{15}{8\pi} (\frac{7}{3} |\Sigmai|)^{1/2} [1 - \frac{1}{7} d(\mathbf{x})] & \text{if } d(\mathbf{x}) \le 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where d(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}i)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}i). The Epanechnikov kernel has finite support, generating more compact primitive shells than Gaussian, enabling more efficient acceleration structures and faster rendering, especially suitable for modeling sharp edges. Time Complexity: Rendering speed is generally faster than MLP-based neural volume rendering (e.g., Instant-NGP) because it avoids expensive MLP evaluations per sample. The Epanechnikov kernel is faster than the Gaussian kernel due to its finite support and compact shells. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of primitives and their associated attributes (geometry, opacity, SH coefficients). It is significantly more memory-efficient than dense voxel grids for high-resolution scenes. Strengths: Physically based rendering (PBR) integration, supporting global illumination, soft shadows, and complex camera models. High compression rate compared to explicit voxel-based methods. Flexible control over quality vs. performance via max primitive depth. Limitations: Requires numerical root-finding for free-flight sampling in complex overlapping scenarios. Not directly compatible with rasterization pipelines without modification (unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting). When to Use: Suitable for applications requiring physically accurate rendering of scattering/emissive media with high quality and flexibility, such as scientific visualization, VFX, and PBR-based training data generation. When Not to Use: Not suitable for real-time rasterization pipelines where extreme speed is required and physical accuracy is secondary (consider 3D Gaussian Splatting). Not suitable for tomography where only absorption is needed (consider Volumetric Primitive Tomography Integrator). The Volumetric Primitive Radiance Field Integrator originates from the work on volumetric primitives for modeling and rendering scattering and emissive media. It was developed to address the limitations of MLP-based neural radiance fields (slow evaluation) and explicit voxel-based methods (lack of PBR support). The method builds on the principles of neural volume rendering but replaces the implicit MLP representation with a mixture of kernel-based volumetric primitives. It is implemented in the volprim library by Meta Platforms, Inc.. facebookresearch/volumetricprimitives, https://github.com/facebookresearch/volumetricprimitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Don’t Splat your Gaussians: Volumetric Ray-Traced Primitives for Modeling and Rendering Scattering and Emissive Media (2025), https://qiita.com/matumu20/items/67b33681dc97ccbcc849, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

head: Volumetric Tomography Integrator
body: The Volumetric Primitive Tomography Integrator is a simplified rendering method for volumetric primitives that accounts exclusively for absorption, ignoring scattering and emission. It is designed for tomography applications where the goal is to visualize density or attenuation rather than photometric appearance. Unlike its sibling Volumetric Primitive PRB Integrator, which handles scattering media, this integrator treats the volume as a purely absorbing medium. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin o, direction d, scene geometry (volumetric primitives), and differentiable rendering backend state. Output: Radiance accumulator L (primal mode) or differential radiance \delta L (adjoint mode). Data Structures: active: Boolean mask indicating which rays are currently interacting with primitives. depth: Integer counter for recursion depth per ray. L: Accumulator for radiance. β: Path throughput (transmission product). si: Surface intersection state containing primitive index, position, and shape data. Parameters: maxdepth (int): Maximum path depth. -1 indicates no limit, mapped internally to 0xFFFFFFFF. kerneltype (str): Kernel function for density evaluation, one of ['gaussian', 'epanechnikov']. hideemitters (bool): If true, environment emitters are excluded from indirect light sampling. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize primal mode, ray, active mask, depth counter, radiance accumulator L, differential radiance \delta L, and path throughput \beta. 2. Intersection Loop: While active is true: a. Intersect ray with scene using scene.rayintersect with flags All | BackfaceCulling and coherent intersection for depth 0. b. Transmission Evaluation: i. Gather ellipsoid data: ellipsoid = Ellipsoid.gather(si.shape, si.primindex, active). ii. Get total extinction coefficient: sigmat = si.shape.evalattribute1('sigmat', si, active). iii. Compute density integral along ray: density = self.kernel.densityintegral(ray, ellipsoid, None, None, active). iv. Calculate transmission: T = \exp(-\text{density} \times \sigmat). c. Update Throughput: \beta[\text{active}] \ = T. d. Adjoint Indirect Radiance: If in adjoint mode, compute differentiable reflected indirect radiance: L{r\ind} = L \times T / \text{dr.detach}(T). e. Local Contribution: Compute total local contribution: Lo = Le + L{r\ind} (where Le = 0). Select finite values: Lo = \text{dr.select}(\text{active} \ \& \ \text{dr.isfinite}(Lo), Lo, 0.0). f. Gradient Propagation: i. If Backward: dr.backwardfrom(δL Lo). ii. If Forward: δL += dr.forwardto(Lo). g. Escape Check: Check for escape from medium: escapedmedium = active & ~si.isvalid(). Exclude environment emitters if hideemitters is true and depth is 0. h. Direct Light: Compute direct light from environment: L{dir} = \text{dr.select}(\text{escaped\medium}, \beta \times \text{emitter.eval}(si, \text{escaped\medium}), 0.0). i. Update Accumulator: Update radiance accumulator L: L[\text{active}] = \begin{cases} L + L{dir} & \text{if primal} \\ L - L{dir} & \text{if adjoint} \end{cases}. j. Ray Offset: Spawn new ray origin to avoid self-intersection: o[\text{active}] = p + d \times 10^{-4}. k. Update State: Update active mask and depth: active &= si.isvalid() and depth[active] += 1. l. Depth Limit: Limit recursion depth: active &= depth < self.maxdepth. 3. Return: Return L if primal, else \delta L. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def integrateray(ray, scene, active, depth, L, beta, drmode): # Initialization handled by caller or setup phase while active.any(): # Intersect with scene si = scene.rayintersect(ray, flags=All | BackfaceCulling, depth=0) # Evaluate transmission for active primitives ellipsoid = Ellipsoid.gather(si.shape, si.primindex, active) sigmat = si.shape.evalattribute1('sigmat', si, active) density = kernel.densityintegral(ray, ellipsoid, None, None, active) transmission = exp(-density sigmat) # Update path throughput beta[active] = transmission if drmode == 'adjoint': # Compute differentiable reflected indirect radiance Lrind = L transmission / dr.detach(transmission) Lo = Lrind # Le is 0 for tomography Lo = dr.select(active & dr.isfinite(Lo), Lo, 0.0) # Propagate gradients dr.backwardfrom(Lo) else: Lo = 0.0 # No emission or scattering contribution in primal tomography # Check for escape from medium escapedmedium = active & ~si.isvalid() # Compute direct light from environment if escapedmedium.any(): Ldir = beta scene.emitter.eval(si, escapedmedium) else: Ldir = 0.0 # Update radiance accumulator if drmode == 'primal': L[active] = L[active] + Ldir else: L[active] = L[active] - Ldir # Spawn new ray origin to avoid self-intersection ray.o[active] = si.p + ray.d 1e-4 # Update active mask and depth active = active & si.isvalid() depth[active] += 1 # Limit recursion depth if maxdepth != -1: active = active & (depth < maxdepth) return L if drmode == 'primal' else dr.getgrad(L) Evaluates the transmission model on intersected volumetric primitives for the tomography integrator. It gathers ellipsoid data, retrieves the total extinction coefficient \sigmat, and computes the density integral along the ray using the specified kernel (Gaussian or Epanechnikov). The final transmission is calculated as T = \exp(-\text{density} \times \sigmat). This step is critical for determining the attenuation of light as it passes through the volumetric primitives. Time and Memory Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the ray-primitive intersection and the density integral evaluation per active ray per step. Memory usage is proportional to the number of active rays and the storage for primitive attributes. Measured Performance: Specific performance metrics (FPS, memory usage) are not provided in the sources. The implementation uses Dr.Jit for differentiable rendering, which allows for efficient GPU execution. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple and efficient for tomography applications where only absorption matters. Differentiable, allowing for gradient-based optimization. Limitations: Does not account for scattering or emission, making it unsuitable for general volume rendering or scattering media. When to Use: Use this integrator when rendering volumetric primitives for tomography or attenuation-based visualization. Do not use it for scenes requiring scattering or emission effects. The Volumetric Primitive Tomography Integrator is part of the volumetricprimitives repository by Facebook Research. It is designed to work with 3D Gaussian Splatting-like assets and other volumetric primitive representations. The integrator is one of several provided for different applications, including the VPRF integrator for 3D Gaussian Splatting and the VPPT integrator for scattering media. facebookresearch/volumetricprimitives, https://github.com/facebookresearch/volumetricprimitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
