name: Field Output Prediction
head: Model Output Unpacking
body:
Field Output Prediction transforms raw neural network outputs into semantically meaningful values for a specific reconstruction target. It handles direct semantic unpacking of the MLP's final layer, differing from Sigma Network Layer which focuses specifically on density/opacity, and CNN Post-Processing Network which applies spatial filters. The method takes raw predictions from the preceding network layer and converts them based on the configured reconstructiontarget. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Raw tensor from the neural network model, shape (N, C) or (N,), where N is the number of samples and C is the channel dimension. Output: Unpacked tensor of semantically meaningful values (e.g., density, temperature, RGB). Data Structures: reconstructiontarget: A string or enum specifying the output type (e.g., "plasma", "rgb"). boundsdict: Optional dictionary containing lower and upper bounds for physical quantities, used in clamping variants. Steps: 1. Model Forward Pass: Compute raw outputs by passing input positions x{AABB} through the neural network model M. raw = M(x{AABB}) 2. Dimension Handling: If the output dimensionality of raw is one less than the input dimensionality of x{AABB}, append a singleton dimension to preserve spatial structure. 	ext{if } raw.ndim == x{AABB}.ndim - 1: \quad raw = raw[..., 	ext{None}] 3. Flattening: Reshape raw to a 2D tensor for batch processing. raw{flat} = raw.reshape(-1, raw.shape[-1]) 4. Unpacking: Apply the unpacking function specific to the reconstruction target. outs, log
e, log	emp = 	ext{unpack\plasma\outputs}(raw{flat}, 	ext{reconstruction	arget}) 5. Clamping: If enabled, clamp log
e to [log
e{min}, log
e{max}] and log	emp to [log	emp{min}, log	emp{max}]. log
e = 	ext{clamp}(log
e, log
e{min}, log
e{max}) log	emp = 	ext{clamp}(log	emp, log	emp{min}, log	emp{max}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fieldoutputprediction(model, xAABB, reconstructiontarget, clamp=False, lognemin=None, lognemax=None, logtempmin=None, logtempmax=None): raw = model(xAABB) if raw.ndim == xAABB.ndim - 1: raw = raw[..., None] rawflat = raw.reshape(-1, raw.shape[-1]) outs, logne, logtemp = unpackplasmaoutputs(rawflat, reconstructiontarget) if clamp: if logne is not None: logne = torch.clamp(logne, lognemin, lognemax) if logtemp is not None: logtemp = torch.clamp(logtemp, logtempmin, logtempmax) return outs, logne, logtemp def unpackplasmaoutputs(rawflat, reconstructiontarget): if reconstructiontarget == "plasma": logne = rawflat[:, 0] logtemp = rawflat[:, 1] outs = torch.stack([logne, logtemp], dim=-1) elif reconstructiontarget == "rgb": rgb = rawflat[:,:3] sigma = rawflat[:, 3] alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma) weights = alpha torch.cumprod(torch.oneslike(alpha) - alpha + 1e-10, dim=0) rgbmap = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) rgb, dim=0) return rgbmap, None, None else: raise ValueError(f"Target {reconstructiontarget} not implemented") Parameters and Edge Cases: reconstructiontarget: Determines the unpacking logic. Precision: Raw outputs can be numerically unstable. Boundaries: Unconstrained outputs may lead to physically impossible values (e.g., negative density). Clamping Bounds: Bounds are derived by combining PSI and atomic constraints, raising an error if the lower bound exceeds the upper bound. A baseline neural volume representation that maps 3D Cartesian positions to density using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with explicit positional encoding. It serves as a reference for density reconstruction capabilities in neural tomography, distinct from hash-grid or latent-feature approaches. This variant transforms raw network predictions into semantically meaningful values like RGB, depth, and weights for volume rendering. It extracts RGB values from the first three channels, converts raw sigma to alpha and weights using a raw2alpha function, and computes RGB, depth, disparity, and accumulated alpha maps by summing weighted contributions. If a white background is requested, it adds the difference between 1 and accumulated alpha to the RGB map. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples N, as it involves a single forward pass and element-wise operations. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to N, storing the raw and unpacked tensors. Strengths: Provides a flexible interface for different reconstruction targets; ensures physical validity in specialized domains like plasma simulation. Limitations: Performance depends on the underlying model's output dimension; clamping may introduce bias if bounds are too tight. When to use: When the application requires specific physical parameters (e.g., density, temperature) or standard rendering attributes (RGB, depth) from a neural field. The method originates from implementations in neural volume rendering repositories, specifically those dealing with plasma reconstruction and point-based NeRF variants. It addresses the need to map latent space representations to observable quantities. name: MLP Model (Density Baseline)
head: positional encoder + MLP
body: A baseline neural volume representation that maps 3D Cartesian positions to density using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with explicit positional encoding. It serves as a reference for density reconstruction capabilities in neural tomography, distinct from hash-grid or latent-feature approaches. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D Cartesian position vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, mapped to an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). Output: A single scalar representing the base-10 logarithm of the number density, \log{10} ne. Data Structures and Layout: The input to the MLP is a concatenated vector of dimension 48, formed by: 1. Raw Position: 3 dimensions. 2. Fourier Positional Encoding: Axis-wise Fourier features with L=6 bands, frequencies 2^0, \dots, 2^5. For each axis, this generates \sin(2^k \pi x) and \cos(2^k \pi x) for k \in \{0, \dots, 5\}, totaling 2 \times 3 \times 6 = 36 dimensions. 3. Spherical Harmonic Encoding: Degree 2 real spherical harmonics of the unit direction \hat{\mathbf{x}}, totaling (2+1)^2 = 9 dimensions. MLP Architecture: Hidden Layers: 4 layers, each with width 256. Activation: SiLU (Sigmoid Linear Unit) for hidden layers. Output Layer: Linear layer producing a single scalar. Initialization: The final layer bias is initialized to the midpoint of the configured \log{10} ne clamp range. Total Parameters: 210,177. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Map the input 3D position \mathbf{x} to the AABB. 2. Compute the Fourier positional encoding \mathbf{f}{\text{fourier}}(\mathbf{x}) using the specified frequencies and axes. 3. Compute the spherical harmonic encoding \mathbf{f}{\text{sh}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) where \hat{\mathbf{x}} is the normalized direction of \mathbf{x}. 4. Concatenate the raw position, Fourier encoding, and SH encoding: \mathbf{v} = [\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{f}{\text{fourier}}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{f}{\text{sh}}(\hat{\mathbf{x}})]. 5. Pass \mathbf{v} through the MLP to produce the output scalar: \mathbf{h}1 = \text{SiLU}(\mathbf{W}1 \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{b}1) \mathbf{h}2 = \text{SiLU}(\mathbf{W}2 \mathbf{h}1 + \mathbf{b}2) \mathbf{h}3 = \text{SiLU}(\mathbf{W}3 \mathbf{h}2 + \mathbf{b}3) \mathbf{h}4 = \text{SiLU}(\mathbf{W}4 \mathbf{h}3 + \mathbf{b}4) \log{10} ne = \mathbf{w}5 \cdot \mathbf{h}4 + b5 Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def fourierencoding(x, numbands=6): """ Computes axis-wise Fourier positional encoding. x: (3,) array Returns: (36,) array """ freqs = np.array([2k for k in range(numbands)]) args = 2.0 math.pi np.outer(freqs, x) sinvals = np.sin(args).flatten() cosvals = np.cos(args).flatten() return np.concatenate([sinvals, cosvals]) def sphericalharmonicdegree2(x): """ Computes degree 2 real spherical harmonics for the direction of x. x: (3,) array Returns: (9,) array """ norm = np.linalg.norm(x) if norm == 0: return np.zeros(9) d = x / norm x, y, z = d[0], d[1], d[2] y00 = 0.5 math.sqrt(1.0 / math.pi) y1m1 = math.sqrt(3.0 / (4.0 math.pi)) y y10 = math.sqrt(3.0 / (4.0 math.pi)) z y11 = math.sqrt(3.0 / (4.0 math.pi)) x y2m2 = math.sqrt(15.0 / math.pi) x y y2m1 = math.sqrt(15.0 / math.pi) y z y20 = math.sqrt(5.0 / (16.0 math.pi)) (3 z2 - 1) y21 = math.sqrt(15.0 / math.pi) z x y22 = math.sqrt(15.0 / math.pi) (x2 - y2) return np.array([y00, y1m1, y10, y11, y2m2, y2m1, y20, y21, y22]) def mlpmodelforward(x, weights, biases): """ Forward pass of the MLP baseline. x: (3,) raw position weights: list of 5 weight matrices [W1, W2, W3, W4, W5] biases: list of 5 bias vectors [b1, b2, b3, b4, b5] Returns: scalar log10ne """ rawpos = x fourierfeat = fourierencoding(x) shfeat = sphericalharmonicdegree2(x) inputvec = np.concatenate([rawpos, fourierfeat, shfeat]) h = inputvec for i in range(4): h = np.dot(h, weights[i]) + biases[i] h = h np.exp(h) / (1.0 + np.exp(h)) # SiLU activation log10ne = np.dot(h, weights[4]) + biases[4] return log10ne Parameters: Fourier bands L=6. MLP hidden width: 256. MLP hidden layers: 4. Final layer bias initialization: Midpoint of \log{10} ne clamp range. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero in spherical harmonic calculation if \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}. A variant where the expression vector ei and encoded position \boldsymbol{\mu} are fed directly into an MLP \boldsymbol{\rho}(\boldsymbol{\mu}) to predict color and opacity, without a basis of latent features. It uses 5 linear layers with leaky ReLU activations. On the INSTA dataset with 295k Gaussians, it achieves 32.08 PSNR with 0.010s rendering time. It is slower than the proposed HeadGaS method despite lacking MLP computation during rendering, due to the significantly larger number of Gaussians (295k vs 28k). Complexity: The model contains 210,177 trainable parameters. Evaluation time scales linearly with query frequency and is independent of scene complexity. Performance: On the INSTA dataset, the HeadGaS Baseline (295k Gaussians) renders in 0.010s, compared to 0.004s for the proposed HeadGaS method (28k Gaussians). Strengths: Simple architecture with explicit frequency control via positional encoding. Limitations: High parameter count relative to simple density functions; requires careful bias initialization. Originated as a baseline in neural tomography research to evaluate density reconstruction capabilities using positional encoders and MLPs. It contrasts with more complex representations like multiresolution hash grids. name: Sigma Network Layer
body: The Sigma Network Layer computes the volume density \sigma along a ray in neural volume rendering. It builds on the RGB Network Layer by applying the same multi-layer perceptron forward pass to predict density instead of color, enabling alpha compositing during ray marching. The layer executes a two-hidden-layer perceptron forward pass on coordinate embeddings to produce density values, using shared memory for thread-block parallelism. Inputs: xyzsembedding: Input coordinate embeddings of shape [N, d{in}], where N is the number of subnetworks/rays and d{in} is the input dimension. sigmaweights: Flattened weight tensor containing all parameters for the two hidden layers. blockdim: Thread block dimension. sigmaninput: Number of input neurons (d{in}). netwidth: Hidden layer width. sigmasmpreload: Number of weight elements preloaded to shared memory. sigmanoutput: Number of output neurons (typically 1 for density). sigmalayer1base: Base index in sigmaweights for the second hidden layer. didlaunchnum: Threshold indicating active subnetworks in the current launch. Outputs: out1: Density array indexed by temphit, storing \sigma values. finalembedding: Array storing hidden layer outputs hid2 for all subnetworks. weight: Shared memory array of size sigmasmpreload holding preloaded network weights. inputval: Shared memory array of shape [d{in}, \text{block\dim}] holding coordinate embeddings for the current block. hid1: Shared memory array of shape [\text{net\width}, \text{block\dim}] storing first hidden layer activations. hid2: Shared memory array of shape [\text{sigma\n\output}, \text{block\dim}] storing second hidden layer activations. blockdim, sigmaninput, sigmamodelsize, netwidth, sigmasmpreload, sigmanoutput, sigmalayer1base. 1. Iterate over each subnetwork index sn in self.paddblocknetwork[None]. 2. Calculate thread ID: tid = sn % blockdim. 3. Preload network weights into shared memory: weight[k] = self.sigmaweights[k] for k in range(self.sigmasmpreload). 4. Load input embeddings into shared memory: inputval[i, tid] = self.xyzsembedding[sn, i] for i in range(self.sigmaninput). 5. Synchronize threads within the block: ti.simt.block.sync(). 6. If sn < didlaunchnum, compute the first hidden layer: for each neuron i in range(self.netwidth), compute \text{temp} = \sum{j=0}^{d{in}-1} \text{input\val}[j, \text{tid}] \times \text{weight}[i \times d{in} + j], and store in hid1[i, tid]. 7. Compute the second hidden layer (density output): for each output i in range(self.sigmanoutput), compute \text{temp} = \sum{j=0}^{\text{net\width}-1} \text{ReLU}(\text{hid1}[j, \text{tid}]) \times \text{weight}[\text{sigma\layer1\base} + i \times \text{net\width} + j], and store in hid2[i, tid]. 8. Compute final density: self.out1[self.temphit[sn]] = \exp(\text{hid2}[0, \text{tid}]). 9. Store all hidden layer outputs: self.finalembedding[sn, i] = hid2[i, tid]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesigmadensity(sn, tid, xyzsembedding, sigmaweights, blockdim, sigmaninput, netwidth, sigmasmpreload, sigmanoutput, sigmalayer1base, didlaunchnum, hid1, hid2, out1, temphit, finalembedding): # Load input embeddings into shared memory for i in range(sigmaninput): inputval[i, tid] = xyzsembedding[sn, i] # Synchronize threads within the block syncblock() # First hidden layer computation if sn < didlaunchnum: for i in range(netwidth): temp = 0.0 for j in range(sigmaninput): temp += inputval[j, tid] sigmaweights[i sigmaninput + j] hid1[i, tid] = temp # Second hidden layer (output layer for sigma) for i in range(sigmanoutput): temp = 0.0 for j in range(netwidth): # ReLU activation: max(0.0, x) activated = max(0.0, hid1[j, tid]) temp += activated sigmaweights[sigmalayer1base + i netwidth + j] hid2[i, tid] = temp # Final density computation density = math.exp(hid2[0, tid]) out1[temphit[sn]] = density # Store hidden layer outputs for i in range(sigmanoutput): finalembedding[sn, i] = hid2[i, tid] Precision Casting: The source uses datatype wrappers around exp and max operations, indicating explicit type casting is required to match the target hardware's floating-point format. Boundary Conditions: The guard sn < didlaunchnum means inactive subnetworks skip the first hidden layer computation; hid1 and hid2 must be zero-initialized or properly scoped to avoid garbage values. Shared Memory Synchronization: The block synchronization step is mandatory before reading inputval and weight; omitting it causes race conditions across threads. A reparameterization technique that increases the number of depth samples during training by duplicating and rearranging weight and bias tensors in the last layer, preserving the network's output for existing rays. Choose this when training requires finer depth sampling without altering the radiance field representation. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot d{in} \cdot dh) per ray sample for the forward pass, where d{in} is input dimension and dh is hidden width. Memory Complexity: Shared memory usage is O(d{in} + dh + d{out}) per thread block, plus global storage for embeddings and outputs. Strengths: High parallelism via shared memory preloading; explicit control over thread-block execution; compatible with GPU compute shaders. Limitations: Requires careful shared memory management and explicit synchronization; precision casting adds minor overhead; inactive thread guards must be handled correctly. The Sigma Network Layer is used in neural volume rendering pipelines to predict volumetric density along rays, complementing color prediction networks. Its implementation details originate from a Taichi-based neural graphics pipeline renderer. Linyou/taichi-ngp-renderer, https://github.com/Linyou/taichi-ngp-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Subdivision of Output Layers
head: Subdiv output layers
body: Subdivision of Output Layers is a reparameterization technique in neural volume rendering that increases the number of depth samples during training without altering the final rendered color of existing rays. It modifies the last layer of each subnetwork by duplicating and rearranging weight and bias tensors, ensuring the network's output remains consistent with the previous resolution. This method is distinct from Subdivision of Input Layers, which preserves input ray colors by modifying the first and last layers to handle increased input dimensionality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Original weight tensor W{org} of shape [n{subnetworks}, d{out}, d{in}] and bias tensor B{org} of shape [n{subnetworks}, d{out}]. Output: Modified weight tensor W{new} and bias tensor B{new} with shapes [n{subnetworks}, 2d{out}, d{in}] and [n{subnetworks}, 2d{out}] respectively, containing reparameterized values. Data Structures: The method operates on tensor layouts where dimensions are explicitly split and concatenated. n{subnetworks}: Number of subnetworks. d{out}: Original output dimension (number of depth samples/channels). d{in}: Input dimension. Steps: 1. Bias Rearrangement: Split the output dimension d{out} of the bias tensor into c=4 channels. The shape [n{subnetworks}, d{out}] becomes [n{subnetworks}, d{out}/4, 4]. 2. Bias Duplication: Concatenate the rearranged bias with itself along the channel dimension (dim=2). The shape becomes [n{subnetworks}, d{out}/4, 8]. 3. Bias Reshape: Rearrange the concatenated bias back to a contiguous tensor structure. The shape becomes [n{subnetworks}, 2d{out}]. 4. Weight Rearrangement: Split the output dimension d{out} of the weight tensor into c=2 channels. The shape [n{subnetworks}, d{out}, d{in}] becomes [n{subnetworks}, d{out}/2, 2, d{in}]. 5. Weight Duplication: Concatenate the rearranged weight with itself along the channel dimension (dim=2). The shape becomes [n{subnetworks}, d{out}/2, 4, d{in}]. 6. Weight Reshape: Rearrange the concatenated weight back to a contiguous tensor structure. The shape becomes [n{subnetworks}, 2d{out}, d{in}]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rearrange(tensor, pattern, c=None): if pattern == 'n (d c) -> n d c': n, dout = tensor.shape d = dout // c return tensor.reshape(n, d, c) elif pattern == 'n d c -> n (d c)': n, d, c = tensor.shape return tensor.reshape(n, d c) elif pattern == 'n (d c) i -> n d c i': n, dout, din = tensor.shape d = dout // c return tensor.reshape(n, d, c, din) elif pattern == 'n d c i -> n (d c) i': n, d, c, din = tensor.shape return tensor.reshape(n, d c, din) raise ValueError("Unsupported pattern") def concatenate(tensors, dim): return np.concatenate(tensors, axis=dim) def subdivoutputlayers(orgweight, orgbias): bias = rearrange(orgbias, 'n (d c) -> n d c', c=4) bias = concatenate([bias, bias], dim=2) bias = rearrange(bias, 'n d c -> n (d c)') weight = rearrange(orgweight, 'n (d c) i -> n d c i', c=2) weight = concatenate([weight, weight], dim=2) weight = rearrange(weight, 'n d c i -> n (d c) i') return weight, bias Parameters: c=4 for bias splitting and c=2 for weight splitting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Divisibility: The original output dimension d{out} must be divisible by 4 for the bias operation and by 2 for the weight operation. Precision: The method relies on exact tensor reshaping and concatenation without scaling factors, unlike input subdivision which applies a 0.5 multiplier. A reparameterization technique to maintain unchanged input ray colors after depth subdivision by modifying the weight matrices and bias vectors of the first and last layer functions of the networks. It splits the input dimension d{in} into c=2 channels, duplicates the weights along the input dimension, and averages them by multiplying by 0.5 to ensure hidden features remain unaffected. The bias remains unchanged. This construction validates that the color of each input ray is kept unchanged. Time and Memory Complexity: The operation is O(n{subnetworks} \cdot d{out} \cdot d{in}) for weights and O(n{subnetworks} \cdot d{out}) for biases, as it involves tensor rearrangement and concatenation. Memory usage remains constant as the output tensor shapes are identical to the input shapes before subdivision. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method allows for progressive refinement of depth samples (Dk = D \times 2^k) during training stages. It scales with the number of subnetworks and the depth resolution. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Ensures consistency of rendered colors when increasing depth resolution, preventing artifacts from sudden changes in sampling density. Limitations: Requires d{out} to be divisible by 4 for bias operations. Only applies to the last layer of the subnetworks. When to use it and when not: Use when progressively increasing the number of depth samples in a neural volume rendering pipeline to improve rendering quality without disrupting the learned representation. Do not use if the output dimension is not divisible by 4 or if the goal is to modify input ray properties rather than output depth samples. Originated in the "Progressively-connected Light Field Network for Efficient View Synthesis" paper (2022). The technique is part of a broader strategy involving progressive connection and depth subdivision to enhance rendering quality in neural view synthesis. It is used in conjunction with consistency losses for regularization. name: CNN Post-Processing Network
head: Lightweight CNN
body: A post-processing convolutional neural network applied to MLP-decoded results to reduce boundary artifacts. It uses neighboring regions to improve texture detail without causing multiview inconsistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The rendered image or feature map produced by the preceding MLP-based volume rendering step. Output: The refined image with reduced boundary artifacts and enhanced texture detail. Data Structures: The network is shallow; one implementation uses five convolution layers, while another uses three. Each convolution layer uses 32 channels. No skip connections are added. Steps: 1. Input Padding: Apply "reflectance" padding to the input features to handle boundary conditions for convolution. 2. Convolutional Processing: Pass the padded input through the convolutional layers. Each layer uses 3×3 kernels and ReLU activations. 3. Output Trimming: Remove the padding values from the outputs of the convolutional layers to prevent checkerboard artifacts. 4. Feature-to-RGB Conversion: Apply a feed-forward perceptron layer to convert the representation from feature space to RGB space. Formulas: Loss Function (for training): Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the MLP-decoded results and the ground-truth (GT) volume. L = \text{MSE}(I{\text{MLP}}, I{\text{GT}}) Where I{\text{MLP}} is the image decoded by the MLP and I{\text{GT}} is the ground truth. Parameters: CNN Architecture: 5 convolution layers, 32 channels each. Kernel Size: 3×3. Activation: ReLU. Quantization: 9 bits applied at the end of CNN training without subsequent fine-tuning. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Checkerboard Artifacts: Prevented by removing padding values in the outputs. Multiview Inconsistency: Avoided because the CNN is very shallow and performs no upsampling. Artifact Removal Limit: Limited capacity does not guarantee removal of boundary artifacts when distortion is significant; remaining artifacts may still negatively impact rendering quality. Training Overhead: Adds approximately 5 minutes to encoding time and 100 KB to model size. Decoding Overhead: Adds approximately 50 seconds to decoding time due to sequential inference. A specific application of the CNN to mitigate rendering artifacts caused by inconsistent outputs between adjacent disjoint volumetric blocks along their boundaries. It sets itself apart by targeting the multiscale spatiotemporal representation's block-boundary issues. Choose this when using ECNR or similar block-based neural representations. It applies a lightweight CNN module to the output of the finest scale MLPs. The CNN consists of five convolution layers, each with 32 channels, with no skip connections. It is trained using an MSE loss between MLP-decoded results and ground-truth volume. After training, quantization with 9 bits is applied without fine-tuning. A technique where the super-resolution network accepts multiple feature maps alongside the low-resolution color image to improve reconstruction quality, specifically adapted for volumetric rendering. It sets itself apart from standard image super-resolution by incorporating volumetric-specific auxiliary data (depth, color-opacity vectors) to resolve ambiguities inherent in volume rendering, such as undefined depth in transparent regions. Supplementary Feature Input for Super-Resolution 2D Refinement Layers is an optional post-processing module applied to rendered images to enhance texture detail and prevent "texture sticking" artifacts under viewpoint changes. It builds on CNN Post-Processing Network by specifically employing alias-free convolutional layers to ensure temporal and spatial consistency when the camera moves. It addresses the limitation of standard CNNs where high-frequency details may appear to stick to the image plane rather than the 3D geometry. 2D Refinement Layers Time Complexity: Decoding adds approximately 50 seconds due to sequential inference. Despite this, it remains significantly faster than neurcomp. Memory Complexity: Adds approximately 100 KB to model size. Strengths: Reduces boundary artifacts; improves texture detail; avoids multiview inconsistency; prevents checkerboard artifacts. Limitations: Limited capacity may not remove significant distortion artifacts; adds sequential inference time; does not process each timestep independently in multiscale representations. When to Use: When using block-based neural representations (like ECNR) where boundary artifacts are prominent, and multiview consistency is critical. When Not to Use: When extreme distortion exists that exceeds the CNN's capacity to correct, or when minimal decoding overhead is required. Originated in the context of Efficient Compressive Neural Representation (ECNR) for time-varying volumetric datasets. It was introduced to address the issue of inconsistent outputs between adjacent blocks in multiscale spatiotemporal representations. The method was also explored in AligNeRF for high-fidelity neural radiance fields. name: Supplementary Feature Input for Super-Resolution
head: Multi-Channel Input for SR Network
body: A technique where the super-resolution network accepts multiple feature maps alongside the low-resolution color image to improve reconstruction quality, specifically adapted for volumetric rendering. It sets itself apart from standard image super-resolution by incorporating volumetric-specific auxiliary data (depth, color-opacity vectors) to resolve ambiguities inherent in volume rendering, such as undefined depth in transparent regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of feature maps concatenated along the channel dimension. Output: A single high-resolution RGB image. Data Structures: The input tensor has shape (H, W, C{total}), where H and W are the spatial dimensions and C{total} is the sum of channels from all supplementary features. The specific layout of the input channels is: 1. Final Rendered Color: 3 channels (RGB). 2. Depth Map: 1 channel. 3. Color-Opacity Vector: 4 channels (RGBA) at the position of maximum alpha along the ray, though the opacity channel is not shown in the source figures. 4. Motion Vector Image: 2 channels (typically u, v displacement components). Numbered Steps: 1. Render the standard RGB volume image. 2. Compute the depth value at the position of maximum alpha along each ray, as standard depth is not well-defined for volumetric data and this point contributes most to the final rendering. 3. Save the color and opacity values at this same maximum-alpha position. 4. Compute motion vectors between consecutive frames. 5. Concatenate the RGB image, depth map, color-opacity vector, and motion vectors into a single multi-channel tensor. 6. Pass the concatenated tensor through the CNN Post-Processing Network [7179-cnn-post-processing-network.md] to convert the feature space to RGB space. 7. Output the reconstructed high-resolution RGB image. Formulas: Let I{LR} be the low-resolution RGB image (3 channels). Let D be the depth map (1 channel). Let C{op} be the color-opacity vector at max alpha (4 channels). Let M be the motion vector field (2 channels). The input to the SR network is F{in} = \text{Concat}(I{LR}, D, C{op}, M). The output is I{HR} = \text{SR\Network}(F{in}). Parameters: Neighborhood Clamping: A 3 \times 3 neighborhood clamping is applied, which produced reasonably effective results for the volume rendering case. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Ambiguity: Standard depth is not well-defined for volumetric data, so using depth at maximum alpha mitigates ambiguity by selecting the most visually significant surface. Opacity Visibility: The opacity channel in the color-opacity vector is included in the input structure but is not visually distinct or explicitly shown in the source figures. This method is a deep learning pipeline for super-resolving volume-rendered images by supplementing the network with auxiliary volumetric features (depth, color, opacity at max alpha) and using temporal warping with a reweighting network to handle motion and lighting changes. It sets itself apart from standard image super-resolution by generating low-resolution inputs directly from the volume renderer without anti-aliasing and by incorporating volumetric-specific auxiliary features to resolve depth ambiguity inherent in volume rendering. It builds on Supplementary Feature Input for Super-Resolution by adding temporal consistency mechanisms. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves reconstruction quality by providing geometric and volumetric context that RGB alone lacks. Limitations: Requires rendering additional auxiliary buffers, increasing rendering time and memory bandwidth. Depth is still an approximation for complex volumetric structures. Developed for medical volume visualization using direct volume rendering. It builds on previous works showing that reconstruction networks for surface data benefit from depth inputs. It adapts these surface-based insights to volumetric data by using max-alpha depth as a proxy for surface depth. name: Volumetric Super-Resolution with Auxiliary Features and Temporal Warping
head: Deep Learning Based Super-Resolution for Medical Volume Visualization, SR-Volume
body: This method is a deep learning pipeline for super-resolving volume-rendered images by supplementing the network with auxiliary volumetric features (depth, color, opacity at max alpha) and using temporal warping with a reweighting network to handle motion and lighting changes. It sets itself apart from standard image super-resolution by generating low-resolution inputs directly from the volume renderer without anti-aliasing and by incorporating volumetric-specific auxiliary features to resolve depth ambiguity inherent in volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current low-resolution rendered frame, N previous low-resolution rendered frames, and auxiliary feature maps for all frames. Outputs: One high-resolution frame. Data Structures and Layouts: 1. Input Feature Images: For each frame, the following are provided: Final rendered color image: 3 channels (RGB). Depth: 1 channel. Defined as the depth at the point of maximum alpha value along the ray. Color-opacity vector: 4 channels (RGBA). Color and opacity values at the point of maximum alpha along the ray. Motion vector image: 2 channels (horizontal and vertical displacement) between the current frame and the previous frame. 2. Residual Block: Consists of two 3x3 convolutional layers, each followed by a ReLU activation. A 1x1 convolutional layer in the skip connection transforms the input shape for addition. The output of the second convolution is added to the input before the final ReLU. 3. Reweighting Network: A 3-layer convolutional network that generates a pixel-wise reweighting channel for each previous frame. 4. Autoencoder: A fully convolutional encoder-decoder hierarchy with skip connections, adopted from Hofmann et al.. Numbered Steps: 1. Generate Input Features: Render the volume to get a final color image (RGB). Calculate depth at the point of maximum alpha along the ray. Save color and opacity values at this same point. Generate a screen-space 2D motion vector image (2 channels) between current and previous frames. 2. Feature Extraction: Pass all input frames (current and previous, excluding motion vector) through a Residual Block to extract features. 3. Zero Upsampling: Upsample low-resolution input frames and extracted feature maps to the target high-resolution resolution using zero upsampling, where every low-res pixel is surrounded by zero values in high-res space. 4. Warping: Backward warp the upsampled previous frames and their feature maps to align with the current frame using the motion vectors. 5. Concatenation: Concatenate all warped previous frames/features with the current frame's features. 6. Reweighting: Pass concatenated data through a 3-layer Convolutional Reweighting Network to generate a pixel-wise reweighting channel for each previous frame. 7. Elementwise Product: Multiply each previous frame's feature maps (after zero upsampling and warping) by its corresponding reweighting channel. 8. Autoencoder Reconstruction: Concatenate the reweighted previous frames with the current frame's feature map and feed into an Autoencoder (fully convolutional encoder-decoder with skip connections) to produce the final high-resolution output. Formulas: The loss function used for training is the Charbonnier loss: L = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \rho(yi - zi) where: N is the number of pixels. yi is the output pixel value. zi is the ground truth high-resolution pixel value. \rho(x) = \sqrt{x^2 + \epsilon^2}. \epsilon = 1 \times 10^{-8} is the Charbonnier epsilon for numerical stability. Parameters: Charbonnier epsilon (\epsilon): 1 \times 10^{-8}. Input Resolution: Low-resolution inputs are rendered at 480x480, 240x240, or 120x120 without temporal anti-aliasing. Target Resolution: High-resolution ground truth and output resolution is 1920x1920. Upsampling Ratios: The network supports 4x4, 8x8, and 16x16 super-resolution. Temporal History: The network accepts N previous frames, with experiments using N=1, 2, \text{and } 3. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Depth Ambiguity: Depth is not well-defined for volumetric data. The method resolves this by using the depth at the point of maximum alpha value along the ray, as this point contributes most to the final rendering. Motion Vector Limitations: Motion vectors do not reflect shading and lighting changes between frames, nor do they handle disocclusion and ghosting directly. The reweighting network is used to weed out inconsistent samples caused by these factors. Low-Level Feature Loss: As the upsampling ratio increases (e.g., 16x16), the quality of reconstructed images deteriorates, and the network struggles to reconstruct low-level features. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class ResidualBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, inchannels, outchannels): super(ResidualBlock, self).init() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, outchannels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu1 = nn.ReLU() self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(outchannels, outchannels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu2 = nn.ReLU() self.skipconv = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, outchannels, kernelsize=1) def forward(self, x): identity = self.skipconv(x) out = self.relu1(self.conv1(x)) out = self.conv2(out) out = out + identity out = self.relu2(out) return out class ReweightingNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, inchannels): super(ReweightingNetwork, self).init() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, 32, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu1 = nn.ReLU() self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(32, 16, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu2 = nn.ReLU() self.conv3 = nn.Conv2d(16, 1, kernelsize=3, padding=1) def forward(self, x): out = self.relu1(self.conv1(x)) out = self.relu2(self.conv2(out)) out = self.conv3(out) return torch.sigmoid(out) class Autoencoder(nn.Module): def init(self, inchannels, outchannels): super(Autoencoder, self).init() self.enc1 = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.enc2 = nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.dec1 = nn.Conv2d(128, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.dec2 = nn.Conv2d(64, outchannels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu = nn.ReLU() self.skipconv1 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=1) self.skipconv2 = nn.Conv2d(128, 128, kernelsize=1) def forward(self, x): e1 = self.relu(self.enc1(x)) e2 = self.relu(self.enc2(e1)) d1 = self.relu(self.dec1(e2) + self.skipconv1(e1)) out = self.dec2(d1) return out def zeroupsample(x, scalefactor): h, w = x.shape[2], x.shape[3] newh, neww = h scalefactor, w scalefactor upscaled = torch.zeros((x.shape[0], x.shape[1], newh, neww), device=x.device) upscaled[:,:,::scalefactor,::scalefactor] = x return upscaled def backwardwarp(features, motionvectors): B, C, H, W = features.shape gridy, gridx = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(H), torch.arange(W), indexing='ij') gridy = gridy.float().unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).expand(B, 1, H, W).to(features.device) gridx = gridx.float().unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).expand(B, 1, H, W).to(features.device) flow = motionvectors.permute(0, 2, 3, 1) grid = torch.stack((gridx, gridy), dim=-1) grid = grid / torch.tensor([W - 1, H - 1], device=features.device) 2 - 1 grid = grid + flow / torch.tensor([W - 1, H - 1], device=features.device) 2 warped = F.gridsample(features, grid, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros') return warped def trainstep(currentlrfeatures, previouslrfeatures, motionvectors, groundtruthhr, scalefactor): N = len(previouslrfeatures) currentfeatures = ResidualBlock(8, 64)(currentlrfeatures) previousfeatures = [ResidualBlock(8, 64)(prev) for prev in previouslrfeatures] currentfeaturesup = zeroupsample(currentfeatures, scalefactor) previousfeaturesup = [zeroupsample(prev, scalefactor) for prev in previousfeatures] warpedpreviousfeaturesup = [backwardwarp(prev, motionvectors) for prev in previousfeaturesup] concatfeatures = torch.cat([currentfeaturesup] + warpedpreviousfeaturesup, dim=1) reweightingnet = ReweightingNetwork(concatfeatures.shape[1]) reweightingchannels = [] for i in range(N): startch = 64 + i 64 endch = startch + 64 reweightingchannels.append(reweightingnet(concatfeatures[:, startch:endch,:,:])) reweightedpreviousfeatures = [prev rew for prev, rew in zip(warpedpreviousfeaturesup, reweightingchannels)] finalinput = torch.cat([currentfeaturesup] + reweightedpreviousfeatures, dim=1) autoencoder = Autoencoder(finalinput.shape[1], 3) outputhr = autoencoder(finalinput) epsilon = 1e-8 loss = torch.mean(torch.sqrt((outputhr - groundtruthhr)2 + epsilon2)) return loss, outputhr Time and Memory Complexity: The method involves multiple convolutional operations (Residual Blocks, Reweighting Network, Autoencoder) and warping operations. The complexity is dominated by the convolutional layers and the number of previous frames N. Memory usage increases with N due to storing and processing previous frames. Measured Performance: CTA-Cardio (8x8): With additional RGBA features, PSNR 38.09 dB, SSIM 0.9705. Without, PSNR 37.07 dB, SSIM 0.9683. Manix (16x16): PSNR 33.65 dB, SSIM 0.9471. Runtime: 10 fps (0.1018 seconds per frame) on the current implementation. Scaling: Performance gains are observed with additional previous frames (N=1, 2, 3). However, as the upsampling ratio increases (e.g., 16x16), the quality of reconstructed images steadily deteriorates. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Incorporates volumetric-specific auxiliary features to handle depth ambiguity. Uses temporal warping and reweighting to handle motion and lighting changes. Generates low-res inputs directly from the volume renderer, avoiding artifacts from blurring/downscaling. Limitations: Designed for offline application; runtime performance is not optimized (10 fps). Quality deteriorates at high upsampling ratios (16x16). When to use it: Medical volume visualization where high-quality super-resolution is needed and offline processing is acceptable. When not to use it: Real-time applications requiring higher frame rates without hardware acceleration (e.g., TensorRT). Origin: The method was introduced by S. Devkota et al. in the paper "Deep Learning Based Super-Resolution for Medical Volume Visualization with Direct Volume Rendering". History and Development: The reconstruction network architecture was inspired by Xiao et al. [21], and the autoencoder architecture was adopted from Hofmann et al. [8]. The method was developed to address the specific challenges of super-resolving volume-rendered images, such as depth ambiguity and the lack of standard anti-aliasing in volume rendering. Usage: Used for medical volume visualization on datasets such as CTA-Cardio, Manix, and CTA Abdomen Panoramix. name: 2D Refinement Layers
head: Alias-free 2D CNN Refinement
body: 2D Refinement Layers is an optional post-processing module applied to rendered images to enhance texture detail and prevent texture sticking artifacts under viewpoint changes. It builds on CNN Post-Processing Network by employing alias-free convolutional layers to maintain spatial consistency during camera movement. Inputs and Outputs Input: The rendered RGB image I{rendered} of resolution H \times W. Output: The refined RGB image I{refined} of resolution H \times W. Data Structures The refinement network is a shallow 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). Architecture: 2 hidden layers. Layer Dimension: 16 channels per layer. Kernel Size: 3 \times 3. Activation: ReLU. Sampling: Critical sampling is used to maintain alias-free properties. Steps 1. Input Preparation: Take the rendered image I{rendered}. 2. First Convolutional Layer: Apply a 3 \times 3 convolution with 16 output channels to the input. The convolution uses alias-free layers with critical sampling. 3. Non-linearity: Apply a ReLU activation function to the output of the first layer. 4. Second Convolutional Layer: Apply a 3 \times 3 convolution with 16 output channels to the result of step 3. This layer also uses alias-free layers with critical sampling. 5. Final Convolution: Apply a 3 \times 3 convolution with 3 output channels (RGB) to produce the final refined image. 6. Output: Return I{refined}. Formulas Not given in the sources. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def conv2d(x, outchannels, kernelsize, padding): # Applies 2D convolution with zero-padding # Alias-free critical sampling is applied per H, W, C = x.shape out = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] for i in range(H): for j in range(W): for c in range(C): for ki in range(kernelsize): for kj in range(kernelsize): pi, pj = i + ki - padding, j + kj - padding if 0 <= pi < H and 0 <= pj < W: out[i][j] += x[pi][pj][c] return out def relu(x): return [[max(0, val) for val in row] for row in x] def refineimage(renderedimage): x = renderedimage x = conv2d(x, outchannels=16, kernelsize=3, padding=1) x = relu(x) x = conv2d(x, outchannels=16, kernelsize=3, padding=1) refinedimage = conv2d(x, outchannels=3, kernelsize=3, padding=1) return refinedimage Parameters Hidden Layers: 2. Hidden Layer Dimension: 16. Kernel Size: 3. Sampling: Critical sampling (alias-free). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Texture Sticking: Standard CNNs may cause textures to stick to the 2D image plane during viewpoint changes. Using alias-free layers with critical sampling mitigates this. Optional Application: The refinement is optional and depends on the dataset. It may not be necessary for all scenes or datasets. Renders a geometric mesh approximation and refines the image with a neural network to recover missing details and correct shading errors. It differs from voxel-based methods by using projective texturing for UV maps, though it shares limitations regarding GAN artifacts and shadow estimation. Choose it when mesh-based rendering is preferred over voxel grids. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. As a shallow CNN with small kernel sizes and low channel dimensions, it is computationally lightweight compared to the volume rendering process itself. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The network has a small number of parameters, fitting easily in memory. Measured Performance, Resolution, Scene, and Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Prevents texture sticking artifacts under viewpoint changes; improves texture detail. Limitations: Optional; may not be needed for all datasets; adds a post-processing step. When to use: When rendering images that exhibit texture sticking artifacts or when higher texture fidelity is required. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the visual improvement is negligible, or for datasets where the base rendering is already sufficient. The 2D Refinement Layers method was introduced in the context of VoxGRAF: Fast 3D-Aware Image Synthesis with Sparse Voxel Grids. It leverages alias-free layers to ensure that the refinement does not introduce artifacts that are inconsistent with 3D geometry. The approach is part of a broader effort to improve the visual quality of neural volume rendering methods. name: Textured Mesh Refinement
head: Deep Shading, Mesh Rendering Refinement
body: Textured Mesh Refinement is a neural rendering baseline that renders a geometric mesh approximation of a scene and refines the resulting image using a neural network to recover missing details and correct shading errors. It differs from voxel-based rerendering methods by using a mesh representation to estimate UV maps via projective texturing, though it faces similar limitations regarding GAN artifacts and shadow estimation. Inputs: 1. A textured mesh of the scene (vertices, faces, and texture coordinates). 2. Target camera viewpoint parameters. 3. Light position. 4. Target image T for optimization. Outputs: Refined image that roughly completes missing regions in the re-projected textured mesh. Data Structures: Mesh: Defined by vertex positions, face connectivity, and UV coordinates. Buffers: Diffuse color buffer and depth buffer rendered from the mesh. Network: A Pix2Pix network takes the rendered buffers and light position as input channels. Exact layouts, sizes, and bit packing are Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Estimate UV Map: Use projective texturing to estimate the UV map of the mesh relative to the target camera viewpoint. 2. Position Mesh: Place the mesh in the desired position corresponding to the target camera view. 3. Render Buffers: Render the scene to generate the diffuse color buffer and depth buffer. 4. Prepare Input Tensor: Concatenate the diffuse color buffer, depth buffer, and light position to form the input tensor. 5. Neural Refinement: Pass the input tensor through a neural network (e.g., Pix2Pix) to predict the refined image. 6. Optimization: Optimize the network parameters to minimize the difference between the network output and the target image T. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Regions: The re-projected textured mesh may have missing regions which the network must complete, though results are only roughly completed. Artifacts: The method may produce typical GAN artifacts and fail to estimate shadows properly, similar to Image Translation models. Detail Loss: While it completes missing regions, the refined result may have less detail compared to more advanced methods like Neural Point Cloud Rendering. Performance: On 'scene0010 00', the PSNR and SSIM of the refined images (re-projected textured mesh) are 22.208 and 0.86, respectively. This is lower than the authors' proposed method (PSNR 24.421, SSIM 0.901). Strengths: Can complete missing regions in the re-projected textured mesh. Limitations: Faces similar limitations to Image Translation, including GAN artifacts and poor shadow estimation, despite using a mesh representation instead of voxels. The results may lack fine details compared to other neural rendering approaches. Textured Mesh Refinement is used as a comparison method in neural rendering research to evaluate the effectiveness of mesh-based representations versus point cloud or voxel-based representations. It is also referred to as "Deep Shading" in some contexts, where it is compared against voxel-based rerendering methods. What it is: A specific implementation of Textured Mesh Refinement that uses projective texturing to estimate UV maps and a Pix2Pix network for refinement. Differentiation: Uses a mesh representation instead of voxels. When to choose: When a mesh representation is preferred over voxels, but similar limitations to image translation apply. name: MLP with Positional Encoding and IOR Activation
head: MLP with Skip Connections and Refractive Index Activation
body: A multi-layer perceptron that maps 3D coordinates to a scalar field (e.g., refractive index) using positional encoding, residual skip connections, and a domain-specific activation function to constrain output ranges. It is distinguished by a post-processing activation function that maps the MLP's raw output to a positive range [1, \infty), ensuring physical validity for light propagation. Inputs: x: Input feature vector, typically the positional encoding of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). degpoint: Integer degree for positional encoding. netdepth: Integer depth of the hidden layers. netwidth: Integer width of the hidden layers. doskip: Boolean flag for skip connections. activation: Choice of activation function (ReLU or ELU). iorden: Denominator for the IOR scaling factor. Outputs: eta: Scalar field representing the refractive index at the input position. Data Structures: The MLP consists of a sequence of dense (fully connected) layers. Weights are initialized using He uniform initialization. The final layer outputs a single scalar value (outchannel = 1). Parameters: netdepth: Default 4. netwidth: Default 128 (for dark matter simulations) or 256 (for gas/neural field simulations). degpoint: Default 4 or 6. iorden: Default 400. doskip: Default True for dark matter, False for gas/neural fields. activation: nn.relu for dark matter, nn.elu for gas/neural fields. Algorithm: 1. Positional Encoding: Apply positional encoding to the input coordinates x. Let x{enc} = \text{posenc}(x, \text{deg\point}). 2. Skip Connection Storage: Store the encoded input for potential skip connections: inputs = x{enc}. 3. Hidden Layers: Iterate i from 0 to \text{net\depth} - 1: a. Apply a dense layer with width \text{net\width}: x = \text{Dense}{\text{net\width}}(x). b. Apply the chosen activation function: x = \text{Activation}(x). c. Skip Connection Logic: If doskip is true, and i > 0, and i is a multiple of \lfloor \text{net\depth} / 2 \rfloor: i. Concatenate the current representation x with the original encoded input inputs along the feature axis: x = \text{concat}(x, inputs). 4. Output Layer: Apply a final dense layer with 1 output channel: y = \text{Dense}1(x). 5. IOR Activation: Apply the refractive index activation function to constrain the output: \eta = \frac{\text{softplus}(y - 2)}{\text{ior\den}} + 1 Where \text{softplus}(z) = \ln(1 + e^z). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp from jax import nn def posenc(x, degpoint): """Standard positional encoding.""" scales = jnp.array([2.0 (2 i / degpoint) for i in range(degpoint // 2)]) x = jnp.expanddims(x scales, axis=-1) return jnp.concatenate([jnp.sin(x), jnp.cos(x)], axis=-1) def denselayer(x, weight, bias): """Standard fully connected layer.""" return x @ weight + bias def mlpwithioractivation(x, params, degpoint, netdepth, netwidth, doskip, activationfn, iorden): """ x: Input coordinates, shape (..., 3) params: Dictionary containing weights and biases for the MLP degpoint: Degree of positional encoding netdepth: Number of hidden layers netwidth: Width of hidden layers doskip: Boolean, use skip connections activationfn: JAX activation function (e.g., nn.relu or nn.elu) iorden: Denominator for IOR scaling """ # 1. Positional Encoding xenc = posenc(x, degpoint) # 2. Store inputs for skip connections inputs = xenc # 3. Hidden Layers currentx = xenc skipinterval = netdepth // 2 for i in range(netdepth): # Apply dense layer with He uniform initialization (handled by params) currentx = denselayer(currentx, params[f'layer{i}weight'], params[f'layer{i}bias']) # Apply activation currentx = activationfn(currentx) # Skip connection logic if doskip and i > 0 and i % skipinterval == 0: # Concatenate with original encoded input currentx = jnp.concatenate([currentx, inputs], axis=-1) # 4. Final Dense Layer y = denselayer(currentx, params['outputweight'], params['outputbias']) # 5. IOR Activation eta = nn.softplus(jnp.squeeze(y) - 2) / iorden + 1.0 return eta Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The softplus function is numerically stable, but subtracting 2 before applying it is critical for the specific scaling used in the source implementation. Boundaries: The output \eta is strictly greater than 1.0 because \text{softplus}(z) > 0 for all real z, and \text{ior\den} > 0. This ensures the refractive index is physically valid (greater than vacuum). Degenerate Input: If netdepth is 0 or 1, the skip connection logic may not trigger or may behave unexpectedly depending on the modulo arithmetic. The default depth is 4. A dark matter variant of the MLP that uses netwidth=128, doskip=True, and activation=relu. It is distinguished from the gas variant by its shallower width and enabled skip connections, which optimize it for capturing the diffuse scattering properties of dark matter fields. Choose this variant when simulating dark matter distributions. See MLPactdm. A gas/neural field variant of the MLP that uses netwidth=256, doskip=False, and activation=elu. It is distinguished from the dark matter variant by its increased width, disabled skip connections, and ELU activation, which better model the continuous density gradients of gas. Choose this variant when simulating gas or neural field volumes. See MLPactgas. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. It adapts the standard MLP architecture used in NeRF-like models to predict refractive index fields instead of color or density. name: Neural Radiance Caching
head: NRC, Neural Surface Cache
body: Neural Radiance Caching (NRC) is a neural rendering technique that uses a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to predict photorealistic pixel colors from per-pixel feature buffers containing world-space positions and auxiliary features. It solves the problem of real-time indirect illumination by deferring shading computations to a trained neural model, allowing for online adaptation to dynamic scenes. Unlike sibling methods that may require scene-specific retraining or lack dynamic support, NRC continuously overfits to the current lighting and geometry using sparse light paths spawned from the camera view, enabling real-time performance with a strict training budget. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Per-pixel feature buffers containing the world-space position \mathbf{x} and additional auxiliary encoded dimensions (e.g., view direction, surface normals). Output: Predicted photorealistic pixel color (RGB). Data Structures: Feature Buffer: A per-pixel array storing the concatenated encoded position and auxiliary features. Multi-resolution Hash Encoding: A data structure mapping input coordinates to feature vectors across multiple grid resolutions. The encoding uses the same representational capacity as Neural Irradiance Volume (NIV). MLP: A non-convolutional network processing each pixel independently. Parameters: MLP Architecture: 2 hidden layers with 64 neurons each. Training Budget: 1 millisecond per frame to support animated content. Encoding: Multi-resolution hash encoding [MESK22]. Steps: 1. Feature Buffer Construction: For each pixel, retrieve the world-space position \mathbf{x} and any additional auxiliary features (e.g., view direction). 2. Position Encoding: Encode the world-space position \mathbf{x} using multi-resolution hash encoding. 3. Feature Concatenation: Concatenate the encoded position with the encoded auxiliary dimensions using the same encoding scheme as Müller et al. [2021]. 4. MLP Inference: Feed the concatenated vector into the MLP to predict the pixel color. 5. Online Training: Continuously update the MLP using sparse light paths spawned from the camera view, adhering to a 1 ms per frame training budget. 6. Dynamic Object Handling (Deferred Shading): If a ray hits a dynamic object not part of the static training domain, defer the cache query by one or more bounces until it hits a static surface where the neural cache is valid. 7. Denoising: Apply a denoiser to remove variance resulting from the deferred path depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neuralradiancecachingpixel(xworld, auxfeatures, mlp, hashencoder): """ Predicts color for a single pixel using Neural Radiance Caching. Args: xworld: World-space 3D position vector. auxfeatures: List of auxiliary feature vectors (e.g., view direction). mlp: The trained MLP model. hashencoder: Multi-resolution hash encoder instance. Returns: Predicted RGB color. """ # Step 2: Encode position encodedpos = hashencoder.encode(xworld) # Step 3: Encode auxiliary features and concatenate # Note: Auxiliary features are encoded using the same scheme as position encodedaux = [] for feat in auxfeatures: encodedaux.append(hashencoder.encode(feat)) # Concatenate encoded position and encoded auxiliary features inputvector = concatenate(encodedpos, encodedaux) # Step 4: MLP Inference color = mlp.forward(inputvector) return color def handledynamicobjectray(ray, cache, denoiser): """ Handles rays hitting dynamic objects by deferring shading. Args: ray: The current ray segment. cache: The neural radiance cache (MLP + Hash Encoder). denoiser: The denoising filter. Returns: Shaded color. """ # Check if ray hits a dynamic object not in training domain if isdynamicobject(ray.hit): # Step 6: Defer cache query # Trace ray further until it hits a static surface deferredray = tracerayuntilstatic(ray, cache.staticmeshes) if deferredray.hit: # Query cache for the deferred hit point color = neuralradiancecachingpixel( deferredray.hitpoint, deferredray.auxfeatures, cache.mlp, cache.hashencoder) # Step 7: Denoise to remove variance from deferral color = denoiser.filter(color) return color else: # Fallback if no static surface hit return backgroundcolor else: # Direct cache query for static objects return neuralradiancecachingpixel( ray.hitpoint, ray.auxfeatures, cache.mlp, cache.hashencoder) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hash Collisions: Hash collisions cause microstructure artifacts at the finest grid resolution. These artifacts do not disappear with longer training times. Dynamic Object Shading: Objects not part of the training domain (dynamic objects) cannot be directly shaded. Ray tracing is required to defer shading, which increases variance proportional to the deferred path depth. Variance: Increasing model capacity reduces bias but does not significantly improve quality because variance from deferring is the major source of error. Time Complexity: Runtime overhead is approximately 0.7 ms at 1920x1080 resolution, including training and runtime costs. However, when handling dynamic objects, ray tracing and denoising add 5-10 ms per frame overhead. Memory Complexity: Uses 2 or 4 grid levels, consuming 0.16 to 1.20 MB of memory. Performance: Achieves 133 FPS with multi-resolution hash encoding vs. 147 FPS with triangle wave encoding at 1920x1080 resolution. Strengths: Real-time performance, online adaptability to dynamic scenes, high quality for static scenes. Limitations: Requires ray tracing and denoising for dynamic objects, leading to higher variance and runtime overhead compared to methods like NIV. Hash collisions cause persistent artifacts. When to Use: Suitable for real-time rendering of scenes with static geometry and dynamic objects where online adaptation is needed. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes with many dynamic objects where low variance is critical, or when hardware ray tracing is unavailable. Neural Radiance Caching was introduced by Müller et al. in 2021. It builds on the concept of neural surface caches [RWG∗ 13, HCZ21, CDD∗ 24] but adapts it for real-time rendering with online learning. The method was later augmented with multi-resolution hash encoding [MESK22] to improve quality and performance. It is used in real-time rendering applications, particularly in the context of instant neural graphics primitives. Real-time Rendering with a Neural Irradiance Volume, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2602.12949, fetched 2026-10-26 Nvidia – learning representations of positions in a 3D scene [pdf], https://nvlabs.github.io/instant-ngp/assets/mueller2022instant.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
