name: Temporal Accumulation (Closest Hit)
body: Temporal Accumulation (Closest Hit) stabilizes stochastic or noisy direct volume ray casting results by blending the current frame with a history buffer of previous frames. Unlike simple frame averaging, this method specifically selects the "closest hit" (the sample with the smallest depth/opacity weight) between the current frame and the accumulated history to maintain geometric stability and reduce ghosting artifacts during camera movement. The method executes as a multi-pass rendering pipeline or fragment shader logic block that manages a history buffer. It requires the current frame's color/depth and the previous frame's reprojection data. Inputs: currentframe: Current render pass output (color and depth/opacity). currentdepth: Depth value for the current pixel. historybuffer: Accumulated data from previous frames. cameramatrices: Current and previous View-Projection matrices (V{curr}, P{curr}, V{prev}, P{prev}). cameraposition: World-space camera origin. Outputs: accumulatedframe: The final stabilized color buffer. The history is typically stored in a texture array or a circular buffer to save memory. 1. History Texture Array (historyframes): Dimensions: \{width, height, N\HISTORY\ACC\}. Format: RGBA32Float or equivalent surface format. Usage: RENDERATTACHMENT | TEXTUREBINDING. Indexing: Layer index is framecount % NHISTORYACC. 2. Normal/Depth Texture (normaldepthtexture): Dimensions: \{width, height, 1\}. Format: RGBA32Float. Stores depth and potentially normal/opacity info for reprojection. 3. Uniforms (for shader passes): uCurrent: Sampler for current frame. uCurrentDepth: Sampler for current depth. uHistory: Sampler for history buffer. uInvViewProj: Inverse of current View-Projection matrix. uPrevViewProj: Inverse of previous View-Projection matrix. uCamPos: Camera world position. uBlend: Blending weight (0.0 to 1.0). uHistoryValid: Boolean flag (0 or 1) indicating if history is valid. uInvFrameNumber: Inverse of current frame count (for running average). uMix: Mixing factor for accumulator/frame blend. 1. Initialization (Closest Hit Texture Initialization): Reset the accumulation buffer to a value indicating "no hit" (e.g., vec4(-1)) when the scene changes or at startup. Clear uHistoryValid to 0. 2. Ray Pass (Current Frame Generation): Render the volume using standard ray casting. Output the result to historyframes at layer framecount % NHISTORYACC and to normaldepthtexture. Store the current frame's depth/opacity in the w component of the color vector for closest-hit comparison. 3. Reprojection and Blending (Temporal Pass): Check Validity: If uHistoryValid == 0, output currentframe directly and set uHistoryValid = 1. World Position Reconstruction: Compute ray direction in world space from NDC coordinates (u, v): \mathbf{ndc} = (2u - 1, 2v - 1) \mathbf{p}{near} = V{curr}^{-1} P{curr}^{-1} (\mathbf{ndc}x, \mathbf{ndc}y, -1, 1) \mathbf{p}{far} = V{curr}^{-1} P{curr}^{-1} (\mathbf{ndc}x, \mathbf{ndc}y, 1, 1) \mathbf{rd} = \text{normalize}\left(\frac{\mathbf{p}{far}.xyz}{\mathbf{p}{far}.w} - \frac{\mathbf{p}{near}.xyz}{\mathbf{p}{near}.w}\right) Fetch depth d from uCurrentDepth. Compute world position \mathbf{worldPos}: \mathbf{worldPos} = \mathbf{uCamPos} + \mathbf{rd} \cdot (d > 0 ? d: 200000.0) Pitfall: Pixels with no cloud (d \le 0) cause large parallax errors during reprojection; substituting a far distance (200000.0) handles this. Project to Previous Frame: Transform \mathbf{worldPos} to previous clip space: \mathbf{prevClip} = V{prev} P{prev} (\mathbf{worldPos}, 1) Compute previous UV: \mathbf{prevUv} = \left(\frac{\mathbf{prevClip}.xy}{\mathbf{prevClip}.w}\right) \cdot 0.5 + 0.5 Boundary Check: Evaluate screen validity: onScreen = prevClip.w > 0.0 && all(greaterThanEqual(prevUv, vec2(0.0))) && all(lessThanEqual(prevUv, vec2(1.0))). If !onScreen (i.e., prevClip.w <= 0.0 or prevUv outside [0, 1]), output currentframe. Closest Hit Selection: Sample current frame: \mathbf{frame} = \text{texture}(\mathbf{uCurrent}, \mathbf{vUv}). Sample history: \mathbf{acc} = \text{texture}(\mathbf{uHistory}, \mathbf{prevUv}). Let w{frame} and w{acc} be the opacity/depth weights (typically the w component). If w{frame} > 0 and w{acc} > 0: \mathbf{oClosest} = (w{frame} < w{acc}) ? \mathbf{frame}: \mathbf{acc} If only w{frame} > 0: \mathbf{oClosest} = \mathbf{frame}. If only w{acc} > 0: \mathbf{oClosest} = \mathbf{acc}. If neither: \mathbf{oClosest} = \mathbf{acc}. Noise Clamping and Blending: Compute 3x3 neighborhood min/max of current sample to bound noise: \mathbf{lo} = \min{x,y \in \{-1,0,1\}} \text{texture}(\mathbf{uCurrent}, \mathbf{vUv} + (x,y)\Delta\mathbf{uv}) \mathbf{hi} = \max{x,y \in \{-1,0,1\}} \text{texture}(\mathbf{uCurrent}, \mathbf{vUv} + (x,y)\Delta\mathbf{uv}) Pad bounds: \mathbf{lo}' = \mathbf{lo} - (\mathbf{hi} - \mathbf{lo}) \cdot 0.25 - 0.002 \mathbf{hi}' = \mathbf{hi} + (\mathbf{hi} - \mathbf{lo}) \cdot 0.25 + 0.002 Clamp history sample: \mathbf{hist} = \text{clamp}(\mathbf{acc}, \mathbf{lo}', \mathbf{hi}') Blend: \mathbf{oColor} = \text{mix}(\mathbf{hist}, \mathbf{oClosest}, \mathbf{uBlend}) Alternative: Use running average: \mathbf{oColor} = \mathbf{acc} + (\mathbf{frame} - \mathbf{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{uInvFrameNumber}. Alternative: Use mixing factor: \mathbf{oColor} = \text{mix}(\mathbf{acc}, \mathbf{frame}, \mathbf{uMix}). 4. Final Output: Present the accumulated frame to the screen. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def temporalaccumulationclosesthit(currentframetex, currentframeuv, currentdepth, historybuffer, uinvviewproj, prevviewproj, campos, ublend, uhistoryvalid, framecount, nhistoryacc): # 1. Handle invalid history or first frame if framecount == 0 or uhistoryvalid == 0: return currentframetex[currentframeuv] # 2. Reconstruct world position from current depth ndc = vec2(currentframeuv.x 2.0 - 1.0, currentframeuv.y 2.0 - 1.0) pnear = uinvviewproj vec4(ndc.x, ndc.y, -1.0, 1.0) pfar = uinvviewproj vec4(ndc.x, ndc.y, 1.0, 1.0) raydir = normalize(pfar.xyz / pfar.w - pnear.xyz / pnear.w) depth = currentdepth if depth <= 0.0: depth = 200000.0 worldpos = campos + raydir depth # 3. Project to previous frame UV prevclip = prevviewproj vec4(worldpos, 1.0) prevuv = (prevclip.xy / prevclip.w) 0.5 + 0.5 # 4. Check bounds onscreen = prevclip.w > 0.0 and 0.0 <= prevuv.x <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= prevuv.y <= 1.0 if not onscreen: return currentframetex[currentframeuv] # 5. Sample history historysample = texture(historybuffer, prevuv) # 6. Closest Hit Selection wframe = currentframetex[currentframeuv].w whist = historysample.w if wframe > 0.0 and whist > 0.0: closest = currentframetex[currentframeuv] if wframe < whist else historysample elif wframe > 0.0: closest = currentframetex[currentframeuv] elif whist > 0.0: closest = historysample else: closest = historysample # 7. Noise Clamping texelsize = vec2(1.0 / currentframetex.width, 1.0 / currentframetex.height) lo = currentframetex[currentframeuv] hi = currentframetex[currentframeuv] for y in [-1, 0, 1]: for x in [-1, 0, 1]: neighbor = texture(currentframetex, currentframeuv + vec2(x, y) texelsize) lo = min(lo, neighbor) hi = max(hi, neighbor) pad = (hi - lo) 0.25 + 0.002 loclamped = lo - pad hiclamped = hi + pad histclamped = max(loclamped, min(hiclamped, historysample)) # 8. Blend result = mix(histclamped, closest, ublend) return result NHISTORYACC: Number of history frames stored. Must be >0. uBlend: Interpolation factor between clamped history and current closest hit. uMix: Blending factor between accumulator and frame. uInvFrameNumber: Inverse of current frame number for running average. uHistoryValid: Flag to skip reprojection on first frame or scene change. Disocclusion/Ghosting: Caused by camera movement or object animation. Handled by clamping history samples to the padded min/max neighborhood of the current frame. Empty Pixels: Depth \le 0 causes large parallax errors. Substitute a far distance (e.g., 200000.0). Buffer Overflow: If framecount overflows or NHISTORYACC is 0, layer indexing fails. Use modulo arithmetic framecount % NHISTORYACC. Scene Changes: Camera/object transformations invalidate history. Clear the buffer and reset uHistoryValid. Memory Limits: Multi-frame buffers require dynamic memory modification, which is limited. Single-buffer overwrite (circular buffer) is preferred. A fragment shader pass that initializes the closest hit texture to a value indicating no hit (e.g., vec4(-1)). This resets the accumulation buffer when scene conditions change or at startup. A rendering pass that blends an accumulated buffer with a new frame using a mixing factor. It samples the accumulator and current frame, selects the closest depth/position (smaller w value) if both are valid, and blends them using uMix. A technique to combine frames over time to reduce noise, using an exponential moving average or simple frame blending based on frame count. It updates the accumulator as acc + (frame - acc) uInvFrameNumber. A fragment shader pass that averages color values across multiple layers of a 2D texture array. It loops through all layers, sums the values, and divides by the number of layers. Used for temporal accumulation or history blending. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel per frame, assuming constant number of history layers and fixed neighborhood size for clamping. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H \times N\HISTORY\ACC) for the history buffer. Single-buffer overwrite reduces this to O(W \times H) if only the immediate previous frame is stored. Performance: Significantly reduces noise in stochastic ray casting, allowing for fewer samples per frame. Strengths: Stabilizes flickering, reduces noise, maintains sharp edges via closest-hit selection. Limitations: Ghosting artifacts during rapid motion or disocclusion if clamping is insufficient. Requires reprojection matrices and depth buffers. Temporal accumulation has been used in volume rendering to stabilize stochastic results, such as those from sparse voxel octrees or cloud rendering. The "Closest Hit" variant specifically addresses the issue of selecting the most relevant historical data to prevent ghosting of occluded geometry. Implementations vary from simple frame blending to complex reprojection with noise clamping. newDINO/voxelraydemo, https://github.com/newDINO/voxelraydemo, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) Estudio de la compresión y la eficiencia del Sparse Voxel Octree en el cálculo de la Iluminación Global, https://hdl.handle.net/2117/445971, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) rokcej/volumetric-ray-casting, https://github.com/rokcej/volumetric-ray-casting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) harkawataryan/Volumetric-Cloud-Renderer, https://github.com/harkawataryan/Volumetric-Cloud-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) terier/vpt, https://github.com/terier/vpt, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: DeepBrick
head: Deep Volume Raytracing
body: DeepBrick is a ray-marching kernel for deep volume raytracing that combines empty space skipping with front-to-back alpha blending to accumulate color and transmittance. It is distinguished from standard sparse voxel traversal by its explicit support for deep rendering outputs (depth, flow) and its specific handling of hierarchical brick data loading and evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin, ray direction, world position increment (wpt), voxel delta (gvdb->vdel[0]), and a pointer to the VDB leaf node. Output: A buffer (outBuf) containing 10 floats per pixel: indices 0-2 for color, 3 for mask, 4-6 for normal, 7 for depth, 8-9 for flow. Data Structures: VDB Leaf Node: Accessed via getNode and contains the voxel data. Sample Point (p): Index coordinates derived from the world position. Accumulators: val: Vector holding voxel properties (density, color components). clr: Accumulated color and transmittance. hit: Structure storing front hit point (hit.x) and weighted mean depth (hit.y). Parameters: SCNMINVAL: Threshold for skipping empty voxels during initial traversal. SCNALPHACUT: Threshold for stopping color accumulation based on current transmittance. MAXITER: Maximum iterations per ray. SCNEXTINCT: Extinction coefficient. SCNALBEDO: Albedo multiplier. SCNPSTEP: Step size. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Get the VDB leaf node using getNode. Compute the sample point in index coordinates p from the world position wp and voxel delta gvdb->vdel[0]. Compute the world position increment wpt. Initialize val and hclr (hit color) to zero. Initialize clr (accumulated color/transmittance) to zero. Record the front hit point hit.x if it is zero. 2. Empty Space Skipping: Loop while val.w < SCNMINVAL, iter < MAXITER, and p is within bounds. Fetch the voxel value and update val.w (density). If val.w < SCNMINVAL, advance p, wp, and t.x (ray parameter). Increment iter. This loop skips voxels with negligible density. 3. Color Accumulation (Ray Marching): Loop while clr.w > SCNALPHACUT, iter < MAXITER, and p is within bounds. Perform an optional depth buffer test to cull rays that have already been occluded. Transfer the current voxel's properties into val. Compute the transmittance through the current voxel step. Update hit.y using the transmittance and step size. Fetch the voxel color into hclr. Accumulate the color clr. Update clr.w by multiplying with the new voxel transmittance. Advance p, wp, and t.x. Increment iter. 4. Finalization: Clamp the final color and alpha values. Write results to outBuf. Formulas: Transmittance is computed as \tau = \exp(SCN\EXTINCT \cdot val.w \cdot SCN\PSTEP), where val.w is the voxel density, SCN\EXTINCT is the extinction coefficient, and SCN\PSTEP is the step size. (Note: The source reuses val.w for transmittance; this implementation renames it to \tau to prevent variable reuse bugs.) Color accumulation follows clr.x += val.x \cdot clr.w \cdot (1 - \tau) \cdot SCN\ALBEDO \cdot hclr.x, where val.x is the voxel color component, clr.w is current transmittance, and SCN\ALBEDO is the albedo multiplier. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def deepbrickraycast(rayorigin, raydirection, vdbleaf, outbuf, pixelidx): # Constants SCNMINVAL = 1e-6 SCNALPHACUT = 0.01 MAXITER = 1000 SCNEXTINCT = 1.0 SCNALBEDO = 1.0 SCNPSTEP = 1.0 # Step size parameter # Initialization voxeldelta = vdbleaf.vdel[0] wp = [rayorigin[i] for i in range(3)] wpt = [raydirection[i] voxeldelta for i in range(3)] p = [(wp[i] - vdbleaf.origin[i]) / voxeldelta for i in range(3)] val = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # x,y,z,w clr = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # clr[3] is transmittance hclr = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] hit = [0.0, 0.0] # hit[0] = front hit, hit[1] = weighted mean depth itercount = 0 # Fetch initial voxel val = getvoxel(vdbleaf, p) # Step 1: Empty Space Skipping while val[3] < SCNMINVAL and itercount < MAXITER and isinbounds(p, vdbleaf): p = [p[i] + 1.0 for i in range(3)] wp = [wp[i] + wpt[i] for i in range(3)] itercount += 1 val = getvoxel(vdbleaf, p) # Step 2: Color Accumulation while clr[3] > SCNALPHACUT and itercount < MAXITER and isinbounds(p, vdbleaf): if depthbuffertest(hit[1]): break val = getvoxel(vdbleaf, p) # Compute transmittance (renamed from val.w to tau to fix variable reuse) tau = math.exp(SCNEXTINCT val[3] SCNPSTEP) # Update weighted mean depth hit[1] = hit[1] clr[3] + (1.0 - tau) wp[2] hclr = getcolor(vdbleaf, p) # Accumulate color (applied to x, y, z channels) for c in range(3): clr[c] += val[c] clr[3] (1.0 - tau) SCNALBEDO hclr[c] clr[3] = tau p = [p[i] + 1.0 for i in range(3)] wp = [wp[i] + wpt[i] for i in range(3)] itercount += 1 # Finalization clr[0] = max(0.0, min(1.0, clr[0])) clr[1] = max(0.0, min(1.0, clr[1])) clr[2] = max(0.0, min(1.0, clr[2])) # Write to output buffer outbuf[pixelidx 10 + 0] = clr[0] outbuf[pixelidx 10 + 1] = clr[1] outbuf[pixelidx 10 + 2] = clr[2] outbuf[pixelidx 10 + 3] = 1.0 - clr[3] outbuf[pixelidx 10 + 7] = hit[1] def getvoxel(leaf, p): # Standard voxel fetch operation return leaf.getsample(p) def isinbounds(p, leaf): # Standard bounds check return all(0 <= p[i] < leaf.dimensions[i] for i in range(3)) def depthbuffertest(depth): # Standard depth test operation return depth < currentdepthbuffer def getcolor(leaf, p): # Standard color fetch operation return leaf.getcolor(p) A ray-marching kernel that samples a volumetric brick texture, adjusts alpha and RGB values for variable step sizes, and composites the result into a destination color using front-to-back alpha blending. It accounts for a "sample ratio" (r) between the ray step and the brick's internal resolution to adjust sampling density across hierarchical levels. Defines behavior based on node type: Loaded Brick: If the node is a brick with available data, perform regular ray-marching inside its data. Unloaded Brick: If the brick is not loaded (e.g., dynamic loading failure), use the average color stored in the node and accumulate it based on the distance the ray travels through the brick (using pre-integration). Empty Node: If the node is empty, ignore it (skip processing). A GPU-based process for constructing distance fields within bricks: Process: Each brick is processed by one thread group (size 8^3 = 512 threads). Each thread evaluates the edit list once to obtain a single sample. Evaluation: Iterates through the index buffer of the brick, evaluating each edit at the thread's corresponding location in space. Results are combined according to the CSG operation of each edit. Memory Optimization: Edits are loaded into group-shared memory in chunks of 256 to speed up evaluation, as 1024 edits do not fit in shared memory. Larger chunks limit occupancy; smaller chunks limit parallelism. Precision: Brick pool format is 8-bit signed normalized values (256 possible values per voxel). Distance range is [-4, 4] voxels, where magnitude 1 corresponds to 4 voxels. Surface representation precision is 1/32 of the brick size. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels traversed along the ray, optimized by empty space skipping and hierarchical brick structures. Memory Complexity: Depends on the brick pool size and shared memory usage. Shared memory usage is constrained to chunks of 256 edits to maintain occupancy. Strengths: Efficient handling of sparse data via empty space skipping; support for deep rendering (depth/flow output); flexible handling of unloaded bricks via pre-integration. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of thresholds (SCNMINVAL, SCNALPHACUT); brick evaluation stalls if hierarchical construction is not complete; shared memory constraints in brick evaluation limit parallelism. When to Use: Suitable for real-time volume rendering of sparse, hierarchical voxel data where depth information is required. DeepBrick is associated with deep volume raytracing techniques, often implemented in conjunction with VDB (Volume Database) structures. The concept of "brick" traversal and hierarchical processing is detailed in research on interactive exploration of procedural volumes. The specific brick evaluation method for signed distance fields (SDFs) was developed for real-time rendering applications, as described in dissertation work on modifiable SDFs. name: Brick Traversal
head: Ray Marching with Alpha Compositing & Sample Ratio Adjustment, TraverseBrick
body: Brick Traversal is a ray-marching kernel that samples a volumetric brick texture, adjusts alpha and RGB values for variable step sizes, and composites the result into a destination color using front-to-back alpha blending. It accounts for a "sample ratio" (r) between the ray step and the brick's internal resolution to adjust sampling density across hierarchical levels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin (\mathbf{O}), ray direction (\mathbf{D}), brick bounds, brick texture data, accumulated destination color/alpha (c{dst}, a{dst}), global ray step size (RayStepSize), current brick depth (curDepth), octree depth minus one (OctTreeDepthMinusOne), and brick step size scalar (k{BrickStepSizeScalar}). Output: Composite color (c{dst}) and accumulated alpha (a{dst}). Data Structures: The method operates on the following variables: dst: Accumulated destination color and alpha. src: Fetched texel color and alpha. rayWorldPosition: Current world-space ray position. curBrickRayPos: Current brick-local ray position. Parameters: r (sampleRatio): The ratio of the ray step size to the brick's effective voxel size. It is computed as r = k{BrickStepSizeScalar}^{OctTreeDepthMinusOne - curDepth} for constant nodes, or derived from curBrickDepth for textured bricks. Steps: 1. Compute Intersection: Calculate the time to exit the brick bounds (t{exit}) using a ray-box intersection routine. 2. Calculate Steps: Determine the ray step size in world space: rayStepSize = RayStepSize \times r. Calculate the number of steps: numSteps = \lfloor t{exit} / rayStepSize \rfloor + 1. 3. Initialize: Set rayWorldPosition and curBrickRayPos to the brick entry point. Initialize c{dst} = (0,0,0,0) and a{dst} = 0. 4. Loop: For i from 0 to numSteps - 1: a. Advance World Ray: Update the world position: rayWorldPosition += worldRayStep where worldRayStep = \mathbf{D} \times RayStepSize. b. Early Exit Check: If a{dst} > 0.995, subtract (i+1) from numSteps, advance rayWorldPosition by the remaining steps to the exit point, and return. c. Fetch Texel: Sample the brick texture at curBrickRayPos to get source color c{src} and alpha a{src}. d. Adjust Values: Compute adjusted alpha and color: a{adj} = 1 - (1 - a{src})^r and c{adj} = c{src} \times r. e. Composite: Update the destination using front-to-back blending: c{dst} = (1 - a{dst}) \times c{adj} + c{dst}. The accumulated alpha updates as a{dst} = a{dst} + a{adj} \times (1 - a{dst}). f. Advance Brick Ray: Update the brick-space ray position: curBrickRayPos += brickRayStep where brickRayStep = \mathbf{D} \times rayStepSize. Pseudocode: Unverified code. It is critical to advance rayWorldPosition to the exact exit point of the brick to prevent visual artifacts in subsequent rays or passes. Not given in the sources. name: Interpolation and Sampling Techniques
head: Trilinear Interpolation (DRR), Trilinear rendering
body: Interpolation and Sampling Techniques approximate continuous scalar fields from discrete voxel data during ray casting, determining the trade-off between computational cost and visual smoothness. This family is distinguished from Anti-Aliasing and Filtering by focusing on spatial reconstruction of the volume function rather than post-processing, and from Neural volume rendering by typically relying on explicit geometric kernels or lookup tables. A prominent example is trilinear interpolation, which offers significant speed advantages over exact intersection methods like Siddon's method for low sample counts. All methods in this family approximate a continuous scalar field V(\mathbf{p}) from discrete samples Vi at grid positions \mathbf{p}i. The core mechanism involves: 1. Query Positioning: Determining the 3D coordinate \mathbf{p} along the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} where a value is needed. 2. Kernel/Weight Application: Computing weights wi(\mathbf{p}) based on the distance between \mathbf{p} and sample centers \mathbf{p}i to calculate V(\mathbf{p}) = \sumi wi(\mathbf{p}) Vi. 3. Coordinate Transformation: Mapping world-space or camera-space coordinates to the volume's local coordinate system before interpolation. Transforms sampled depth values (z\vals) along a camera ray into physical segment lengths (dists) between consecutive samples. This conversion is necessary because uniform sampling in depth space does not correspond to uniform physical spacing in 3D space, particularly under perspective projection. It accounts for the geometric relationship between the ray direction and the viewing angle, ensuring that volume rendering integration weights samples correctly by their true spatial extent. Unlike NDC Points to Distance, which operates in Normalized Device Coordinates, this method operates directly on camera-space depth values. Samples voxel data with jittered step offsets to reduce banding, and composites the result using front-to-back alpha blending. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by perturbing sample locations with random offsets, transforming structured aliasing into less visually noticeable noise. It is particularly effective when using low sample counts or nearest-neighbor interpolation, where regular grid patterns are most visible. Warps 3D space towards the view cell center using radial distortion to bring the background closer for positional encoding, dampening high frequencies in the background while preserving foreground detail. It sets itself apart from its parent Interpolation and Sampling Techniques by explicitly warping the 3D coordinate space before encoding, and from its sibling NDC Warping by using a radial distortion function rather than a linear NDC squash. Approximates a continuous scalar field and its gradients from discrete samples (regular or irregular) using Moving Least Squares (MLS) approximation. It solves the problem of high-quality visualization of arbitrary volumetric datasets by providing a unified framework for function reconstruction that supports adaptive preintegration. Unlike Radial Basis Functions (RBFs), MLS does not require solving a global system of equations, making it more efficient for large datasets. It sets itself apart from standard interpolation methods by allowing tunable smoothing and interpolation control through basis and weighting functions, and from standard ray casting by integrating adaptive subdivision based on preintegration tables to handle the computational cost of the scalar field evaluation. Approximates a continuous volumetric field V(\mathbf{p}) from discrete samples Vi located at grid positions \mathbf{p}i to determine values along viewing rays. This family is distinguished from sibling methods like Depth to Distance Conversion and Sampling and Jittering by its exclusive focus on the spatial weighting and blending of data values, rather than coordinate mapping or noise reduction. It sets itself apart from Kernel-based Resampling by encompassing a broader range of techniques including non-kernel approaches (e.g., nearest neighbor, gradient-based splatting) and specialized hardware-accelerated primitives. A high-quality sampling technique for direct volume ray casting that improves reconstruction accuracy by compensating for the low-pass filtering effect of the cubic B-spline kernel. Unlike standard cubic B-spline interpolation, which can cause excessive blurring, this method pre-processes the voxel data to invert the kernel's frequency response, allowing for sharper results without increasing memory footprint. It is chosen when visual fidelity is prioritized over the raw performance of hardware-accelerated tri-linear interpolation. A direct volume ray casting technique that improves visual accuracy by interpolating the product of opacity and material color, rather than interpolating color and opacity separately. This method calculates the material color at a resampling point using opacity weighting before interpolation and computes lighting directly on the resampled points using interpolated normals, thereby avoiding color distortion and Mach band artifacts common in methods that interpolate shaded voxel colors. It sets itself apart from standard trilinear interpolation by preventing "intermediate colors" at material interfaces where transparent media would otherwise inappropriately influence the final color. A visibility optimization technique for Monte Carlo volume rendering that maps volume data to a discrete set of importance values after interpolation, rather than before. It solves the problem of accurately visualizing small, thin structures (e.g., bone periosteum) which are often lost or blurred by pre-interpolative importance functions due to smoothing artifacts. Unlike pre-interpolative methods that apply importance to continuous scalar values, this method creates a step function along the ray, preserving fine details and eliminating the need for smoothing discontinuities. Defines the computational framework for evaluating the volume rendering equation along a viewing ray, converting discrete volumetric data into a final pixel color. This family encompasses methods that determine where to sample the volume (stochastic vs. deterministic spacing) and how to aggregate those samples (compositing, projection, or approximation). It is distinguished from Interpolation and Sampling Techniques by focusing on the integration logic and sampling distribution rather than the spatial interpolation kernel, and from Ray Marching and Discretization by encompassing both the sampling strategy and the reduction phase. A technique to extend pre-integrated volume rendering to multidimensional transfer functions. A grid of irradiance samples is taken throughout the scene; at render time, the volume is queried and near-by irradiance samples are interpolated to estimate the global illumination at a point. The use of trilinear interpolation for volume rendering, particularly in the context of Digital Radiographic Reconstructions (DRR), has been highlighted for its significant speed advantage over exact intersection methods like Siddon's method. For instance, with 25 sample points, trilinear rendering takes approximately 737 μs, whereas Siddon's method takes ~25 ms; the costs match only when the sample count reaches ~2,000 points. name: Depth to Distance Conversion
head: Depth to Distance, depth2dist, z_vals to dists
body: Depth to Distance Conversion transforms sampled depth values (z\vals) along a camera ray into the physical segment lengths (dists) between consecutive samples. This conversion is necessary because uniform sampling in depth space does not correspond to uniform physical spacing in 3D space under perspective projection. It accounts for the geometric relationship between the ray direction and the viewing angle. Unlike NDC Points to Distance, which operates in Normalized Device Coordinates, this method operates directly on camera-space depth values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: zvals, a tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples}) containing the depth values for each sample point along each ray. Output: dists, a tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples}) containing the physical distance between consecutive samples. Data Structures: The input zvals is a contiguous tensor where zvals[i, j] represents the depth of the j-th sample along the i-th ray. The values are assumed to be sorted in increasing order of depth (near to far). Steps: 1. Compute Raw Differences: Calculate the difference between consecutive depth values to get the raw segment lengths. For a ray with samples z0, z1, \dots, z{N-1}, the raw distance between sample j and j+1 is z{j+1} - zj. 2. Handle Boundary: Append a large constant value (10^{10}) to the end of the distance array to represent the segment after the last sample. This ensures the output tensor has the same shape as the input zvals. 3. Cosine Scaling: Scale the raw distances by the cosine of the angle between the ray direction and the viewing direction. This step corrects for the perspective projection effect where depth intervals do not linearly map to Euclidean distances along the ray. Formulas: Let z{i,j} be the depth of the j-th sample on the i-th ray. The raw distance d'{i,j} between sample j and j+1 is: d'{i,j} = z{i,j+1} - z{i,j} For the last sample j = N{samples}-1, the distance is set to a large constant C = 10^{10}. The final distance d{i,j} is scaled by \cos \thetai, where \thetai is the angle between the ray direction \mathbf{d}i and the viewing direction (or the axis along which depth is measured): d{i,j} = d'{i,j} \cdot \cos \thetai If the rays are parallel to the viewing axis (orthographic), \cos \theta = 1. For perspective rays, this factor varies. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def depthtodistance(zvals, cosangle): """ Convert depth values (zvals) to distances between samples. Args: zvals: Tensor of shape (Nrays, Nsamples) containing depth values. cosangle: Tensor of shape (Nrays,) or (Nrays, 1) containing the cosine of the angle between the ray and the viewing direction. Returns: dists: Tensor of shape (Nrays, Nsamples) containing segment distances. """ # Step 1: Compute raw differences between consecutive samples distsraw = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] # Step 2: Append a large constant to the last segment to match input shape largeconstant = torch.tensor(1e10, device=zvals.device, dtype=zvals.dtype) lastsegment = largeconstant torch.oneslike(distsraw[...,:1]) dists = torch.cat([distsraw, lastsegment], dim=-1) # Step 3: Scale by cosine of the angle if cosangle.dim() == 1: cosangle = cosangle.unsqueeze(-1) dists = dists cosangle return dists Parameters: largeconstant: 10^{10}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shape Mismatch: Ensure cosangle is broadcastable to the last dimension of dists. If cosangle is per-ray, it must be unsqueezed to shape (N{rays}, 1). Last Segment: The last segment's distance is arbitrary since there is no next sample. The large constant is a convention to maintain tensor shape. Cosine Angle Definition: The exact definition of \cos \theta depends on the coordinate system. In many implementations, if the ray direction is normalized and the depth is measured along the camera's z-axis, this factor accounts for the projection geometry. Converts sampled Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) points to segment distances between consecutive samples along a ray, accounting for the cosine of the viewing angle. It operates directly in NDC space, where uniform sampling steps do not correspond to uniform physical distances, unlike linear depth-to-distance methods. Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{samples}). The operation involves simple subtraction and multiplication, which are linear in the number of samples. Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{samples}) for the output tensor dists. Strengths: Simple, efficient, and numerically stable. It correctly accounts for perspective projection effects when combined with the cosine scaling. Limitations: Assumes that the depth values are sorted and correspond to samples along a single ray. It does not handle non-linear depth mappings or complex coordinate transformations beyond the cosine scaling. When to Use: When using depth-based sampling in volume rendering or neural radiance fields where samples are generated in camera space. Not given in the sources. name: NDC Points to Distance
head: NDC to Distance, NDC to Distance Conversion, ndc2dist, ndc_pts to dists
body: Converts sampled Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) points to segment distances between consecutive samples along a ray, accounting for the cosine of the viewing angle. It operates directly in NDC space, where uniform sampling steps do not correspond to uniform physical distances, unlike linear depth-to-distance methods. Inputs and Outputs: Input: ndcpts, a tensor of shape [Nray, Nsample, 3] containing 3D points in NDC space, ordered along the ray. Input: cosangle, a tensor of shape [Nray] representing the cosine of the angle between the ray direction and the view direction. Output: dists, a tensor of shape [Nrays, Nsamples] containing the segment distances. Data Structures: ndcpts: Float tensor. Coordinates are in NDC space. dists: Float tensor. Steps: 1. Compute the Euclidean distance between consecutive NDC points along the ray: dists = torch.norm(ndcpts[:, 1:] - ndcpts[:,:-1], dim=-1). 2. Append a large value scaled by cosangle to the end of the distance array: dists = torch.cat([dists, 1e10 cosangle.unsqueeze(-1)], -1). Formulas: Let \mathbf{p}i be the i-th point in ndcpts for a given ray. The segment distance for i = 0, \dots, N-2 is: di = \|\mathbf{p}{i+1} - \mathbf{p}i\|2 The final distance is: d{N-1} = 10^{10} \cdot \cos(\theta) where \theta is the angle between the ray and the view direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def ndcptstodists(ndcpts, cosangle): # ndcpts: [Nray, Nsample, 3] # cosangle: [Nray] # Step 1: Compute Euclidean distances between consecutive points diffs = ndcpts[:, 1:] - ndcpts[:,:-1] dists = torch.norm(diffs, dim=-1) # Shape: [Nray, Nsample - 1] # Step 2: Append large value scaled by cosangle # cosangle.unsqueeze(-1) makes it [Nray, 1] for broadcasting sentinel = 1e10 cosangle.unsqueeze(-1) dists = torch.cat([dists, sentinel], dim=-1) # Shape: [Nray, Nsample] return dists Parameters: 1e10: A large constant appended to the distance array. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cosine Angle: If cosangle is zero, the sentinel becomes zero, which may affect integration logic. Standard forward-facing camera setups typically yield cosangle > 0. Batch Dimensions: The pseudocode assumes batched inputs [Nray,...]. For a single ray, unsqueeze dimensions appropriately before calling, or adjust slicing. Time and Memory Complexity: O(N) time and memory per ray, where N is the number of samples, dominated by vectorized tensor operations. Strengths and Limitations: Accurately computes physical distances from NDC samples for forward-facing scenes. Requires points to be in NDC space and does not apply to linear depth or world-space sampling without prior conversion. Originated in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and tensor-based variants for forward-facing scene reconstruction, where NDC space compresses the infinite depth range into a unit cube. The conversion is a standard step in the volume rendering pipeline to compute correct weights for alpha compositing. name: Sampling and Jittering
head: Jittered Ray Casting, Jittered Sampling Volume Rendering, Volume Ray Casting with Jittered Sampling and Front-to-Back Blending
body: Sampling and Jittering is a direct volume ray casting technique that casts rays from the camera through the volume, samples voxel data with jittered step offsets to reduce banding, and composites the result using front-to-back alpha blending. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by perturbing sample locations with random offsets, transforming structured aliasing into less visually noticeable noise. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position (\mathbf{o}), ray direction (\mathbf{d}), volume texture (V), jitter texture (J), volume bounding box ([\mathbf{VolExtentMin}, \mathbf{VolExtentMax}]), lighting parameters (\mathbf{k}{Ambient}, \mathbf{k}{Diffuse}, \mathbf{k}{Specular}, k{Shininess}), and control flags (ComputeLighting). Outputs: Final fragment color (\mathbf{dst}). Data Structures: Voxel Sampler: A 3D texture storing scalar or RGBA volume data. Jitter Texture: A 2D texture storing pre-computed random offsets. The width and height are defined by JitterTexSize. The red channel is used for the jitter value. Ray State: Current position \mathbf{p}, direction \mathbf{d}, step size s. Parameters: NumSamples: Maximum iterations per ray. RayStepSize: Distance between consecutive samples (s). JitterTexSize: Dimension of the jitter texture. ComputeLighting: Boolean flag for shading. \mathbf{k}{Ambient} = (0.05, 0.05, 0.05). \mathbf{k}{Diffuse} = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0). \mathbf{k}{Specular} = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0). k{Shininess} = 100.0. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set destination color \mathbf{dst} = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0). Calculate ray direction \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}{frag} - \mathbf{o}). Calculate step vector \mathbf{s} = \mathbf{d} \times RayStepSize. 2. Jitter Application: Determine texture coordinate from fragment coordinates modulo JitterTexSize. Fetch jitter value j from the red channel of J. Update ray position: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{s} \times j. 3. Boundary Check: Check if \mathbf{p} is inside the volume bounds. Using the bounding box defined by \mathbf{VolExtentMin} and \mathbf{VolExtentMax}, compute test vectors. If \text{dot}(\mathbf{test1}, \mathbf{test2}) \ge 3.0, the point is inside. 4. Sampling: Sample the volume at \mathbf{p} to get source color/alpha \mathbf{src}. 5. Lighting (Optional): If ComputeLighting is true: Estimate gradient normal using central differences on the alpha channel (a) of \mathbf{src}. Use offsets ivec4(1, 0, 0, -1) and permutations (yxz, yzx, wyz, ywz, yzw) to sample neighbors. Calculate \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{sample2} - \mathbf{sample1}). If \mathbf{n} is NaN, skip shading. Apply Phong shading to \mathbf{src}.rgb using ambient, diffuse, and specular components. 6. Compositing: Update destination using front-to-back blending: \mathbf{dst} = (1.0 - \mathbf{dst}.a) \times \mathbf{src} + \mathbf{dst} 7. Termination: If \mathbf{dst}.a > 0.95, break the loop (early ray termination). 8. Advance: Update \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{s}. Re-evaluate boundary check. Repeat until NumSamples is reached or ray exits. 9. Output: Return \mathbf{dst}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderjitteredvolume(rayposition, cameraposition, raystepsize, numsamples, jittertex, jittertexsize, voxeltex, volextentmin, volextentmax, computelighting, lightposition, fragcoord): # 1. Initialize dst = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) raydir = normalize(rayposition - cameraposition) raystep = raydir raystepsize # 2. Jitter offset application jitteruv = vec2(fragcoord.x % jittertexsize, fragcoord.y % jittertexsize) / jittertexsize jittervalue = texture(jittertex, jitteruv).r currentpos = rayposition + raystep jittervalue for i in range(numsamples): # 3. Boundary Check test1 = vec3(sign(currentpos - volextentmin)) test2 = vec3(sign(volextentmax - currentpos)) if dot(test1, test2) < 3.0: currentpos += raystep continue # 4. Sample Voxel Data src = texture(voxeltex, currentpos) # 5. Lighting (Optional) if computelighting: # Estimate gradient normal using central differences on the alpha channel # Source specifies using offset ivec4(1, 0, 0, -1) and permutations alphacenter = texture(voxeltex, currentpos).a alphaxp = texture(voxeltex, currentpos + vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)).a alphaxm = texture(voxeltex, currentpos + vec3(-1.0, 0.0, 0.0)).a alphayp = texture(voxeltex, currentpos + vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)).a alphaym = texture(voxeltex, currentpos + vec3(0.0, -1.0, 0.0)).a alphazp = texture(voxeltex, currentpos + vec3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0)).a alphazm = texture(voxeltex, currentpos + vec3(0.0, 0.0, -1.0)).a normal = normalize(vec3(alphaxp - alphaxm, alphayp - alphaym, alphazp - alphazm)) if not isnan(normal): tocamera = normalize(cameraposition - currentpos) tolight = normalize(lightposition - currentpos) src.rgb = shading(src.rgb, normal, tocamera, tolight) # 6. Front-to-Back Blending dst = (1.0 - dst.a) src + dst # 7. Early Ray Termination if dst.a > 0.95: break # 8. Advance Ray currentpos += raystep return dst def shading(rgb, normal, tocamera, tolight): halfway = normalize(tolight + tocamera) diffuselight = max(dot(tolight, normal), 0.0) diffuse = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) specular = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) if diffuselight > 0.0: diffuse = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) rgb diffuselight specularlight = pow(max(dot(halfway, normal), 0.0), 100.0) specular = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) rgb specularlight ambient = vec3(0.05, 0.05, 0.05) rgb return ambient + diffuse + specular Edge Cases and Pitfalls: NaN Normals: Gradient calculation may result in NaN if sample1 equals sample2 or if values are identical. This is handled by checking isnan(normal) and skipping shading. Early Termination: Early ray termination occurs when accumulated alpha exceeds 0.95, potentially missing faint structures behind dense ones. Stochastic jittering is a sampling technique used in direct volume ray casting to mitigate banding and quantization artifacts caused by regular, uniformly spaced sample positions. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by perturbing sample locations with random offsets, transforming structured aliasing into less visually noticeable noise. It is particularly effective when using low sample counts or nearest-neighbor interpolation, where regular grid patterns are most visible. Hierarchical sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling) is a method for generating importance samples along a ray in volume rendering by inverting the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the rendering contribution. It solves the problem of efficiently placing sample points in regions of high density without redundant radiance queries. Unlike standard hierarchical sampling which samples from a piecewise constant probability density defined by coarse weights, this method uses inverse transform sampling on a piecewise approximated density field (constant or linear), allowing gradients to back-propagate through the sampling process to the density parameters. It builds on Sampling and Jittering by providing a deterministic or stratified mechanism to concentrate fine samples where the coarse pass indicated high opacity. Uniform Ray Sampling is a ray traversal approach where samples are taken at equal distances along the ray as it passes through volume data stored on a regular grid. It serves as the baseline sampling method in NeRF, assuming every point along the ray contributes equally to the final rendering when no transmittance estimator is available. It sets itself apart from Stochastic Jittering by using fixed intervals rather than random offsets, and from Slab-based Ray Sampling by ignoring voxel boundaries and maintaining a constant step size regardless of scene geometry. Slab-based ray sampling is an image-order caching mechanism for direct volume ray casting that groups rays into rectangular screen regions to form stacked slabs, storing voxel samples in shared memory to optimize neighborhood access for lighting and compositing. Unlike object-order bricking, which struggles with GPU hardware mapping due to per-brick lists, this method leverages the regular structure of rays within a slab to reduce memory bandwidth and latency when calculating gradients or performing ambient occlusion. It is distinct from sibling methods like Uniform Ray Sampling by explicitly managing spatial locality in shared memory across multiple rays, and from Stochastic Jittering by prioritizing deterministic cache coherence over variance reduction. Supersampling is a technique to minimize aliasing artifacts by casting multiple rays per pixel and averaging the results. It handles high-frequency components in transfer functions by performing dense quadrature of the volume render integral, assuming linearity of the scalar field between sample points but not linearity of the integral itself. Unlike pre-integration, which requires equidistant sample points and fails for nonlinear integrals, supersampling accounts for the nonlinearity of the volume render integral while avoiding oversampling of the scalar field. It differs from Stochastic Jittering by using deterministic, fixed offsets for low sample counts (1x–4x) rather than random or stratified patterns, and from Monte Carlo Volume Rendering by relying on simple arithmetic averaging rather than importance-weighted integration. Importance Sampling for SPH Rendering is a technique to increase rendering performance by reducing the number of particles used during rendering, using a non-uniform sampling strategy based on data importance and view-dependent criteria. It solves the problem of high computational cost when rendering large, unstructured Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) datasets by ensuring that particles in complex regions (e.g., phase interfaces, vortices) are sampled more densely than those in homogeneous areas. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by avoiding equal-time high-error trade-offs. Epipolar sampling is a technique that places sample points along epipolar lines (rays emanating radially from a light source's projection on the screen or feature correspondences between views) to exploit the smooth variation of inscattered light or cross-view features along these lines. This reduces the number of expensive ray-marching or feature-interpolation steps required compared to uniform sampling. In volume rendering, it optimizes light shaft computation by leveraging the observation that light intensity varies smoothly orthogonally to epipolar rays. In multi-view reconstruction, it enables cross-view feature aggregation without full 3D volume rendering by correlating features along epipolar lines. Warp-based Sampling is a GPU optimization strategy for direct volume ray casting that improves texture cache performance by reorganizing thread warps to align sampling directions with the volume's memory strides. Unlike standard sampling where a warp processes a block of pixels, Warp Marching assigns a single warp to a single ray, marching through the volume in chunks equal to the warp size. This approach minimizes memory stride within the atomic scheduling unit (the warp), making it particularly effective for rendering large dynamic volumes at low resolutions where view-independent performance is critical. Hierarchical sampling is a two-stage strategy for volume rendering that improves image quality by concentrating samples in regions of high geometric or color complexity, addressing the bottleneck of point sampling in neural radiance fields. It sets itself apart from uniform sampling by using a coarse network to estimate density and guide importance sampling for a fine network. Resampling techniques align geometry and color between scenes along corresponding rays. Uniform sampling points evenly along the ray but can lead to misalignment. A strategy exists where points are valid only if density exceeds a threshold in both scenes, without resampling. Density-based resampling identifies density peaks along each ray and adjusts sampling to align key points in both scenes, ensuring improved color-geometry consistency. Consistent Ray Sampling ensures that ray sample intervals are consistent across all subvolumes to allow correct reconstruction of the original volume and prevent feature loss or enhancement. The starting sample location for each subvolume is calculated such that the distance between the first sample of the new subvolume and the last sample of the previous subvolume equals the predetermined interval. Incorrect calculation of sample locations causes small features in the data to be lost or enhanced erroneously. Ray Direction Jitter improves the generalizability of learned rendering models by applying sub-pixel noise to ray directions. It prevents the color network from overfitting to specific training viewing directions, which otherwise leads to artifacts in novel view synthesis and texture reproduction. Unlike Uniform Ray Sampling which distributes samples across a pixel area, this method perturbs the ray vector itself while ensuring the ray remains confined within the pixel's geometric boundaries. name: Stochastic Jittering
head: Jittered Ray Sampling, Ray Jittering, Stochastic Sample Jittering
body: Stochastic jittering is a sampling technique used in direct volume ray casting to mitigate banding and quantization artifacts caused by regular, uniformly spaced sample positions. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by perturbing sample locations with random offsets, transforming structured aliasing into less visually noticeable noise. It is particularly effective when using low sample counts or nearest-neighbor interpolation, where regular grid patterns are most visible. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Base step size \Delta t. A pre-computed jitter texture (2D noise texture). Pixel coordinates (u, v) or screen-space position. Maximum noise factor \alpha (optional, controls jitter magnitude). Outputs: Perturbed sample positions along the ray. Data Structures: Jitter Texture: A 2D texture storing noise values. Dimensions: Typically N \times N (e.g., 64 \times 64). Format: Single channel or RGB, sampled with nearest-neighbor filtering. Filtering: GLNEAREST (or equivalent) to preserve sharp noise patterns without interpolation. Wrapping: GLREPEAT to allow seamless tiling. Source: Often blue noise for better perceptual quality. Steps: 1. Initialize Ray: Compute the entry (t{near}) and exit (t{far}) parameters along the ray where it intersects the volume bounding box. 2. Loop for Samples: For each sample index n = 0, 1, 2, \dots: a. Fetch Jitter Value: Sample the jitter texture at coordinates derived from the pixel's screen position to obtain a value j \in [0, 1]. b. Compute Sample Position: Calculate the perturbed parameter along the ray: t{sample} = t{near} + \Delta t \cdot (n + j \cdot \alpha) \mathbf{p}{sample} = \mathbf{o} + t{sample} \cdot \mathbf{d} This places the sample at a random position within the segment [t{near} + n\Delta t, t{near} + (n+1)\Delta t]. c. Sample Volume: Evaluate the volume data at \mathbf{p}{sample} to retrieve color and opacity. d. Composite: Accumulate color and opacity using front-to-back compositing: C{out} = C{in} + c \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - T), T{out} = T{in} + \alpha \cdot (1 - T{in}), where c and \alpha are the sample's color and opacity, and T is the accumulated transmission. e. Advance: If the ray exits the volume (t{sample} \ge t{far}) or accumulated transmission drops below a threshold (e.g., 0.01), break. Otherwise, continue to the next n. Parameters: Jitter Texture Size (N): Typical value: 64. Max Noise Factor (\alpha): Typical value: 0.75. Controls the maximum displacement relative to step size. Noise Type: Blue noise is preferred over white noise because it is intrinsically tileable and easier to blur out, reducing visible dither patterns. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetnearfar(rayorigin, raydir, volmin, volmax): """Standard slab method for AABB intersection.""" tnear = -float('inf') tfar = float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] == 0: if rayorigin[i] < volmin[i] or rayorigin[i] > volmax[i]: return None, None else: t1 = (volmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] t2 = (volmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 if t1 > tnear: tnear = t1 if t2 < tfar: tfar = t2 if tnear > tfar: return None, None return tnear, tfar def stochasticjitteredraycast(rayorigin, raydir, volumedata, stepsize, jittertexture, pixeluv, maxnoisefactor=1.0, volmin=None, volmax=None, threshold=0.01): """ Casts a ray through a volume using stochastic jittering to reduce banding. Args: rayorigin: vec3, origin of the ray. raydir: vec3, normalized direction of the ray. volumedata: function, samples volume at (x,y,z) returning (color, opacity). stepsize: float, base distance between samples. jittertexture: function, samples 2D noise texture at (u,v) returning float in [0,1]. pixeluv: vec2, screen-space coordinates of the pixel. maxnoisefactor: float, multiplier for jitter magnitude (default 1.0). volmin, volmax: vec3, volume bounding box corners. threshold: float, transmission cutoff to break early. Returns: vec4, final accumulated color with alpha. """ if volmin is None or volmax is None: raise ValueError("Volume bounding box must be provided.") tnear, tfar = computetnearfar(rayorigin, raydir, volmin, volmax) if tnear is None: return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedcolor = vec4(0.0) transmission = 1.0 sampleindex = 0 # Fetch jitter value once per pixel/ray jitterval = jittertexture.sample(pixeluv.x, pixeluv.y) while tnear + stepsize (sampleindex + jitterval maxnoisefactor) < tfar and transmission > threshold: tsample = tnear + stepsize (sampleindex + jitterval maxnoisefactor) samplepos = rayorigin + tsample raydir color, opacity = volumedata(samplepos) alpha = opacity transmission accumulatedcolor += color alpha transmission -= alpha sampleindex += 1 return vec4(accumulatedcolor, 1.0 - transmission) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Banding vs. Noise: Jittering replaces visible banding artifacts with noise. While visually more pleasing, it introduces noise that may require further reduction techniques (e.g., temporal filtering). Sampling Rate Dependence: Ray jittering provides a slight improvement at low sampling rates (0.25, 0.5) but the benefit vanishes with higher sampling rates. Isosurface Errors: Without refinement, isosurface rendering errors are inevitable if sample distance is not reduced; jittering makes these artifacts less visible but does not eliminate them. Precision: At high sampling rates, the benefit of jittering vanishes as the regular sampling is sufficient to capture volume details. Slice Artifact Reduction is a stochastic sampling technique used in direct volume ray casting to mitigate "wood grain" artifacts—visible slice boundaries caused by regular ray start positions and discrete voxel grids. It differs from standard ray casting by randomizing the initial ray origin along the viewing direction and performing a localized "solidity check" to verify that a sampled voxel is truly part of the volume rather than an edge artifact. This method effectively breaks the regularity of sampling patterns that cause visible artifacts, regardless of the ray step size relative to voxel dimensions. Temporal Filtering and Jittering is a technique that smooths out noise and improves perceived volume resolution without extra raymarching steps. It addresses spatial banding artifacts caused by coarse slice resolution by combining sub-voxel depth jittering with temporal reprojection. It distinguishes itself from static spatial filters by leveraging camera motion vectors to blend frames, and from pure spatial sampling methods by accumulating jittered samples over time to improve perceived resolution without additional raymarching steps. Random Jitter with Reprojection is a technique to reduce banding artifacts caused by low sample counts in volume rendering by introducing stochastic jitter during ray marching and subsequently reducing the resulting noise via temporal accumulation. It distinguishes itself from pure spatial jittering methods by leveraging temporal coherence, projecting a pseudo-hit position from the current frame into the previous frame's screen space to blend the current result with a history buffer, thereby allowing for lower per-frame sample counts while maintaining visual stability. Ray Casting with Jittered Sampling is a direct volume rendering technique that casts rays through a 3D voxel grid to accumulate color and opacity along the ray path. It distinguishes itself from uniform ray sampling by perturbing sample positions with a pre-computed jitter texture to break up regular grid patterns and reduce aliasing artifacts. Unlike stochastic methods, it uses deterministic offsets stored in a 2D texture rather than runtime random number generation. An extension where sampling occurs at a lower resolution to reduce texture bandwidth requirements, combined with varying the sample pattern with stochastic sampling to reduce regular pattern artifacts where sampling density is reduced. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. Jittering adds negligible overhead (texture fetch and addition) compared to the volume sampling itself. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) for the jitter texture, where N is the texture dimension (e.g., 64 \times 64 floats = 16 KB). Measured Performance: On typical hardware, jittering has minimal impact on frame rate. The benefit is visual quality rather than speed. Scaling: The benefit of ray jittering vanishes with higher sampling rates (e.g., s \ge 2.0). It provides a slight improvement at low sampling rates (e.g., s = 0.25, 0.5). Strengths: Effectively reduces banding and wood-grain artifacts; simple to implement; works well with nearest-neighbor interpolation. Limitations: Introduces noise; does not improve accuracy, only visual quality; ineffective at high sample counts. When to Use: When using low sample counts, nearest-neighbor interpolation, or when banding artifacts are prominent. When Not to Use: When high sample counts are available, or when noise is unacceptable without temporal filtering. Stochastic jittering originated as a technique to address quantization errors in volume rendering. It is implemented in libraries such as VTK (Visualization Toolkit) under the name "Noise". The technique is widely used in real-time volume rendering to improve visual quality without significant performance cost. Blue noise textures for jittering are commonly sourced from libraries like 'free-blue-noise-textures'. name: Slice Artifact Reduction
head: Initial rays’ start positions randomization, Ray Start Position Randomization, Ray start jittering, Ray start jittering with solidity check, Wood grain artifact reduction
body: Slice Artifact Reduction is a stochastic sampling technique used in direct volume ray casting to mitigate "wood grain" artifacts—visible slice boundaries caused by regular ray start positions and discrete voxel grids. It differs from standard ray casting by randomizing the initial ray origin along the viewing direction and performing a localized "solidity check" to verify that a sampled voxel is truly part of the volume rather than an edge artifact. This method effectively breaks the regularity of sampling patterns that cause visible artifacts, regardless of the ray step size relative to voxel dimensions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset, transfer function parameters (Threshold), ray start position P{start}, ray direction vector \vec{d}, step length L, noise texture N, fragment coordinates (x, y), and far plane distance. Output: Final accumulated color dst for the pixel. Data Structures: Noise Texture: A 2D texture N of size 256 \times 256 containing random values in [0, 1]. Volume Data: Accessible via a sampling function returning scalar density V at a given position. Parameters: Threshold: Density threshold for voxel solidity. Typical value: Not given in the sources. StepLength (L): Distance between sampling points. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Noise Scale: Division factor for fragment coordinates to sample the noise texture. Typical value: 256. Algorithm Steps: 1. Jitter Ray Start: Calculate a random offset using the noise texture sampled at a scaled fragment coordinate. Add this offset to the ray start position along the view direction. P{start}' = P{start} + \vec{s} \cdot N(x/256, y/256) where \vec{s} is the step vector and N is the noise value. 2. Initialize Ray: Set current position P = P{start}', remaining ray length R = R{total}, and accumulated color dst = (0, 0, 0, 0). 3. Ray Casting Loop: While dst.a < 1 and R > 0: a. Sample density V = \text{lookup}(P). b. If V > \text{Threshold}: i. Solidity Check: Perform a localized check to ensure the voxel is solid. Move back by half-step: P \leftarrow P - \vec{s} \cdot 0.5, V \leftarrow \text{lookup}(P). If V > \text{Threshold}, scale offset forward by quarter-step: \vec{s}{offset} \leftarrow \vec{s}{offset} \cdot 0.5. Else, scale offset backward by quarter-step: \vec{s}{offset} \leftarrow \vec{s}{offset} \cdot (-0.5). Update position and sample: P \leftarrow P + \vec{s}{offset}, V \leftarrow \text{lookup}(P). ii. If V > \text{Threshold}, proceed with lighting calculations and accumulate color. Break loop if opaque. c. Advance ray: P \leftarrow P + \vec{s}, R \leftarrow R - L. 4. Temporal Accumulation (Optional): If the viewpoint is static, accumulate multiple frames over time to average out the stochastic noise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sliceartifactreduction(rayorigin, raydirection, steplength, threshold, noisetexture, fragcoord, farplanedist): # Compute step vector from direction and length stepvector = raydirection steplength # Jitter ray start position along view direction noiseval = noisetexture.sample(fragcoord / 256.0) rayorigin += stepvector noiseval pos = rayorigin raylength = farplanedist dst = vec4(0.0) # Standard volume sampling: returns density at pos def lookup(p): return volumedata.sample(p) while dst.a < 1.0 and raylength > 0: V = lookup(pos) if V > threshold: # Solidity check s = -stepvector 0.5 pos += s V = lookup(pos) if V > threshold: s = 0.5 else: s = -0.5 pos += s V = lookup(pos) if V > threshold: # Lighting calculations (gradient estimation, diffuse lighting) # src = vec4(color, 1.0) # dst = (1.0 - dst.a) src + dst break pos += stepvector raylength -= steplength return dst Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors may cause the solidity check to fail incorrectly if the step size is very small relative to the voxel size. Boundaries: Ensure the ray start jitter does not push the ray outside the volume bounding box. A specific variant focusing solely on randomizing the initial ray origin to break regularity, effective for low step counts or nearest-neighbor interpolation. Uses temporal accumulation to average out the noise introduced by stochastic jittering, requiring a static viewpoint. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of sampling steps per ray. The solidity check adds a constant overhead (2-3 extra samples) per voxel hit. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray, plus the noise texture storage. Measured Performance: Reduces visible artifacts significantly without requiring a reduction in step size, thus maintaining performance compared to high-resolution sampling. Strengths: Effective against "wood grain" artifacts; simple to implement; works well with low step counts. Limitations: Introduces stochastic noise, requiring temporal accumulation for a clean image if the viewpoint is static. When to Use: When regular sampling patterns cause visible artifacts, such as with nearest-neighbor interpolation or limited step counts. When Not to Use: When high performance is critical and artifacts are acceptable, or when using high-resolution sampling with trilinear/tricubic interpolation. The technique was popularized in the context of GPU-based volume rendering, specifically in tutorials and implementations such as "Volumetric Splatting at The Little Grasshopper". It addresses a common issue in early volume renderers where regular sampling patterns led to visible slice boundaries. The concept of randomizing ray start positions to break regularity was also discussed in academic literature on GPU volume rendering. name: Temporal Filtering and Jittering
head: Temporal Filtering, Temporal Supersampling
body: Temporal Filtering and Jittering is a technique that smooths out noise and improves perceived volume resolution without extra raymarching steps. It addresses spatial banding artifacts caused by coarse slice resolution by combining sub-voxel depth jittering with temporal reprojection. It distinguishes itself from static spatial filters by leveraging camera motion vectors to blend frames, and from pure spatial sampling methods by accumulating jittered samples over time to improve perceived resolution without additional raymarching steps. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current frame’s 3D texture (or accumulated volume data), previous frame’s 3D texture, camera motion vectors, and a pseudo-random sequence (e.g., blue noise or Halton sequence). Outputs: A final filtered 3D texture. Data Structures: 3D Texture: Stores volumetric data (e.g., transmittance, in-scattered light). Layout is not explicitly defined in sources, but standard hardware trilinear interpolation (GLLINEAR) is used for sampling. Motion Vectors: 2D vectors per pixel representing the displacement of scene points between frames, used for reprojection. Jitter Offset: A sub-voxel offset derived from the pseudo-random sequence. Steps: 1. Depth Jittering: Each frame, apply a sub-voxel offset to ray positions. The offset is derived from a pseudo-random sequence such as blue noise or a Halton sequence. This offsets the sampling positions to break up spatial aliasing patterns. 2. Raymarching/Accumulation: Execute the volume rendering pass (raymarching) using the jittered ray positions to generate the current frame’s 3D texture data. 3. Temporal Reprojection Compute Pass: Blend the current frame’s 3D texture with the previous frame's 3D texture using camera motion vectors. This step effectively smooths out noise by accumulating information over time. 4. Final Composition (Post-processing): The accumulated volumetric data is applied to the scene during post-processing or forward-lighting: Retrieve the linear depth of the opaque scene fragment from the scene's depth buffer. Convert the fragment's screen coordinates and linear depth into 3D texture coordinates (u, v, w) using the exponential depth equation. Sample the integrated 3D texture using hardware trilinear interpolation. Add the sampled in-scattered light to the scene color and attenuate the scene color by the sampled transmittance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def temporalfilteringandjittering(currentframetexture, previousframetexture, motionvectors, frameindex): """ Implements Temporal Filtering and Jittering for volume rendering. Args: currentframetexture (ndarray): Raw accumulated volume data for the current frame. previousframetexture (ndarray): The filtered 3D texture from the previous frame. motionvectors (ndarray): 2D motion vectors for the current frame. frameindex (int): Index of the current frame for jitter sequence lookup. Returns: ndarray: The final filtered 3D texture for the current frame. """ height, width = currentframetexture.shape[:2] filteredtexture = np.zeroslike(currentframetexture) # Step 1: Generate jitter offset for the current frame # Standard pseudo-random sequence lookup (e.g., blue noise or Halton sequence) jitteroffset = np.array([0.0, 0.0]) # Step 2 & 3: Temporal Reprojection and Blending for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Reproject previous frame's pixel to current screen space mv = motionvectors[y, x] prevx = int(x + mv[0]) prevy = int(y + mv[1]) # Clamp to bounds prevx = max(0, min(width - 1, prevx)) prevy = max(0, min(height - 1, prevy)) prevvalue = previousframetexture[prevy, prevx] currvalue = currentframetexture[y, x] # Blend current and previous data # Simple temporal accumulation blend; exact weights depend on implementation filteredvalue = 0.5 currvalue + 0.5 prevvalue filteredtexture[y, x] = filteredvalue return filteredtexture def finalcomposition(filteredtexture, scenedepthbuffer, screencoordinates, scenecolor): """ Applies the filtered volumetric data to the final scene. Args: filteredtexture (ndarray): The output from temporalfilteringandjittering. scenedepthbuffer (ndarray): Linear depth of the opaque scene. screencoordinates (tuple): Fragment's screen coordinates (u, v). scenecolor (tuple): Opaque scene color. Returns: tuple: The final scene color with volumetric effects. """ # Retrieve linear depth of the opaque scene fragment lineardepth = scenedepthbuffer[screencoordinates] # Convert screen coordinates and linear depth to 3D texture coordinates (u, v, w) # using the exponential depth equation # Standard exponential depth mapping: w = exp(-depth scale) normalized to [0,1] u, v = screencoordinates w = np.exp(-lineardepth 0.1) # Placeholder scale factor # Sample the integrated 3D texture using hardware trilinear interpolation # Standard trilinear interpolation over the 3D texture sampledlight = np.zeros(3) # Placeholder for trilinear sample # Sample transmittance (assumed to be stored in the same 3D texture or a companion texture) # Assuming transmittance is stored in the same 3D texture or a companion texture transmittance = 1.0 # Placeholder for trilinear transmittance sample # Add in-scattered light to scene color and attenuate by transmittance finalcolor = tuple(c transmittance + s for c, s in zip(scenecolor, sampledlight)) return finalcolor Parameters: Jitter Sequence: Blue noise or Halton sequence. Interpolation: Hardware trilinear interpolation (GLLINEAR). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Motion Vectors: Incorrect or missing motion vectors will cause ghosting or blurring in the temporal reprojection step. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Edge-Preserving Kawase Blur is a post-processing technique designed to remove dither patterns introduced by blue noise jittering in volume rendering while preserving cloud edge details. It distinguishes itself from standard box blurs by using edge-aware weighting to prevent the smoothing of sharp volumetric boundaries, and from temporal accumulation methods by operating on a single frame without requiring reprojection of previous frames. A post-processing technique that smooths noise artifacts from blue noise dithering by calculating a new pixel value using a cubic polynomial over 16 neighboring pixels. It is applied as a separate post-processing pass using Frame Buffer Objects (FBOs) to render the main scene into a texture, which is then sampled by a bicubic filtering material on a fullscreen triangle. A technique to replace weighted volume lookups (trilinear interpolation) with a single stochastically jittered sample to speed up rendering while maintaining unbiased results. It provides a roughly 3.5x speedup compared to trilinear filtering. At 32 samples per pixel, the PSNR difference between stochastic and trilinear filtering is less than 0.1 dB compared to a converged reference. It is virtually indistinguishable from trilinear filtering in converged images (PSNR 56.23 dB) but is significantly faster. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Stochastic filtering (a variant) provides a roughly 3.5x speedup compared to trilinear filtering. Timings were measured on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU at 1920 × 1080 resolution with three bounces of multiple (isotropic) scattering, using a Moana cloud at 1000 × 680 × 1224 voxel resolution. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Smooths out noise and improves perceived volume resolution without extra raymarching steps. Stochastic filtering variant is significantly faster. Limitations: Requires motion vectors for temporal reprojection. Stochastic filtering may introduce noise at low sample counts, though the difference is negligible at 32 samples per pixel. When to use: When spatial banding artifacts are visible due to coarse slice resolution and extra raymarching steps are undesirable. When not to use: When motion vectors are unavailable or unreliable. Origin: The technique is described in the context of volumetric fog using 3D textures in OpenGL and efficient unbiased volume path tracing on the GPU. History and Development: The use of depth jittering with blue noise or Halton sequences to hide spatial banding artifacts is a known technique in volume rendering. The integration of temporal reprojection for noise smoothing is an extension of this approach. Stochastic filtering as a replacement for trilinear interpolation was introduced to improve performance in volume path tracing. Where it is used: Real-time volumetric rendering, particularly for clouds and fog.
