name: Edge-Preserving Kawase Blur
head: Edge-Aware Kawase Blur, Kawase Blur with Blue Noise Jittering
body: Edge-Preserving Kawase Blur is a post-processing technique used to remove dither patterns introduced by blue noise jittering while preserving cloud edge details. It applies a weighted box-blur variant where samples are jittered with blue noise to prevent new dither patterns, and weighted by luminosity or depth differences to preserve edges. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A rendered frame buffer containing jittered volume samples. Input: A depth buffer (or luminance buffer) for edge detection. Input: Blue noise texture for jittering sample positions. Output: A smoothed frame buffer with preserved edges. Data Structures: FrameBuffer: 2D array of pixel colors (RGB or RGBA). DepthBuffer: 2D array of depth values corresponding to the FrameBuffer. BlueNoiseTexture: 2D texture containing precomputed blue noise values. Parameters: blurRadius: The radius of the blur kernel (e.g., 1, 2, 3). edgeThreshold: The luminance/depth difference threshold for edge preservation. extraBlurFactor: A multiplier for blurring distant surfaces. Steps: 1. Initialize Output: Create an output frame buffer of the same dimensions as the input. 2. Iterate Pixels: For each pixel (x, y) in the input frame: a. Get the center color Cc and depth Dc at (x, y). b. Initialize a weighted sum W{sum} = 0 and a weighted color sum C{sum} = (0, 0, 0). c. Kawase Passes: For each pass p from 1 to blurRadius: i. Define the 4 diagonal offsets for the current pass: (\pm p, \pm p). ii. For each offset (dx, dy): 1. Calculate the sample position (xs, ys) = (x + dx, y + dy). 2. Sample the blue noise value B at (xs, ys). 3. Jitter the sample position: (xj, yj) = (xs + B \cdot \epsilon, ys + B \cdot \epsilon), where \epsilon is a small jitter magnitude. 4. Clamp (xj, yj) to the image boundaries. 5. Get the sample color Cs and depth Ds at (xj, yj). 6. Calculate the edge weight w: w = \max\left(0, 1 - \frac{|Cs - Cc| + |Ds - Dc|}{\text{edgeThreshold}}\right) 7. Apply extra blur for distant surfaces: w{final} = w \cdot (1 + \text{extraBlurFactor} \cdot Dc) 8. Update sums: W{sum} += w{final} C{sum} += w{final} \cdot Cs d. Normalize: If W{sum} > 0, set the output color at (x, y) to C{sum} / W{sum}, otherwise keep Cc. 3. Output: Return the output frame buffer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: Clamp sample positions to image boundaries to avoid out-of-bounds access. Precision: Use floating-point arithmetic for color and depth calculations to avoid precision errors. Degenerate Input: If the depth buffer is unavailable, use luminance only for edge detection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def edgepreservingkawaseblur(inputframe, depthbuffer, bluenoisetexture, blurradius, edgethreshold, extrablurfactor): height, width = len(inputframe), len(inputframe[0]) outputframe = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): centercolor = inputframe[y][x] centerdepth = depthbuffer[y][x] weightedsumcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] weightedsum = 0.0 for p in range(1, blurradius + 1): offsets = [(p, p), (p, -p), (-p, p), (-p, -p)] for dx, dy in offsets: samplex = x + dx sampley = y + dy noiseval = bluenoisetexture[sampley % height][samplex % width] jitteredx = samplex + noiseval 0.5 jitteredy = sampley + noiseval 0.5 jitteredx = max(0, min(width - 1, jitteredx)) jitteredy = max(0, min(height - 1, jitteredy)) samplecolor = inputframe[int(jitteredy)][int(jitteredx)] sampledepth = depthbuffer[int(jitteredy)][int(jitteredx)] colordiff = sum(abs(samplecolor[c] - centercolor[c]) for c in range(3)) depthdiff = abs(sampledepth - centerdepth) weight = max(0.0, 1.0 - (colordiff + depthdiff) / edgethreshold) finalweight = weight (1.0 + extrablurfactor centerdepth) weightedsumcolor[0] += finalweight samplecolor[0] weightedsumcolor[1] += finalweight samplecolor[1] weightedsumcolor[2] += finalweight samplecolor[2] weightedsum += finalweight if weightedsum > 0: outputframe[y][x] = (weightedsumcolor[0] / weightedsum, weightedsumcolor[1] / weightedsum, weightedsumcolor[2] / weightedsum) else: outputframe[y][x] = centercolor return outputframe A post-processing technique used to reduce 'Salt and Pepper' noise caused by unpredictable precision errors in raycasting that result in wrong or missing pixel colors. It sets itself apart from its sibling Edge-Preserving Kawase Blur by operating on a fixed 3x3 neighborhood to remove isolated outliers (single-pixel errors) rather than blurring dither patterns, making it suitable for correcting discrete precision failures rather than high-frequency jitter. Time and Memory Complexity: Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R), where N is the number of pixels and R is the blur radius, since each pixel processes 4 \cdot R samples. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the input and output frame buffers, plus O(N) for the depth buffer and blue noise texture. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of pixels and the blur radius. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Cheap and effective blur; preserves cloud edge details; removes dither patterns introduced by blue noise jittering. Limitations: Can introduce banding patterns if not jittered; may not be suitable for hard surfaces where temporal accumulation is preferred. When to Use: Use when rendering volumetric clouds with blue noise jittering and edge preservation is desired. When Not to Use: Do not use when rendering hard surfaces where temporal accumulation (TAA) is more effective. Origin: The technique is described in a forum post by SimonDev on the three.js forum. History and Development: The technique builds on the Kawase blur method, which is a type of box-blur known for its efficiency but prone to banding patterns, mitigated here by blue noise jittering. Where it is Used: Used in efficient volumetric cloud rendering to smooth out noise and improve perceived resolution without extra raymarching steps. name: Median Filter Denoising
head: Postprocessing Shader Median Filter
body: A post-processing technique used to reduce 'Salt and Pepper' noise caused by unpredictable precision errors in raycasting that result in wrong or missing pixel colors. It operates on a fixed 3x3 neighborhood to remove extreme single-pixel outliers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The rendered image buffer (texture) from the raycasting step. Output: A denoised image buffer. Data Structures: colorStack: An array of 9 float4 color values. lookups: An array of 9 float2 offset vectors representing the relative coordinates of the 3x3 neighborhood. GRAYSCALEFACTORS: A constant vector used in a dot product to convert float4 colors to a scalar grayscale value for comparison. Steps: 1. Calculate the texture coordinate step sizes: dx = 1.0 / \text{width} and dy = 1.0 / \text{height}. 2. Define the 3x3 neighborhood offsets relative to the current pixel (0,0): \begin{aligned} &(-dx, -dy), (0, -dy), (dx, -dy), \\ &(-dx, 0), (0, 0), (dx, 0), \\ &(-dx, dy), (0, dy), (dx, dy) \end{aligned}. 3. For each pixel p{i,j}: a. Retrieve the 8 surrounding pixels and the center pixel using the offsets defined in step 2. b. Store these 9 colors in colorStack. c. Sort colorStack based on the grayscale luminance of the colors using the comparison function C(a, b) = \text{dot}(\text{GRAY\SCALE\FACTORS}, a) > \text{dot}(\text{GRAY\SCALE\FACTORS}, b). d. The median of 9 elements (n=9, m=4) is the element at index 4 (the 5th element) because arrays are zero-based. e. Set the output pixel color to colorStack[4]. Formula: For an odd number of elements n = 2m + 1, the median is the element at index m. For even n = 2m, it is the average of elements at m and m+1. In this 3x3 case (n=9, m=4), the median is x5 (stored at index 4). Parameters: GRAYSCALEFACTORS: Luminance weights for color comparison. Not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Indexing Error: Arrays are zero-based, so the 5th element (median of 9) is at index 4, not index 5. Boundary Conditions: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. GRAYSCALEFACTORS = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Not given in the sources width = 1920 # Image width in pixels height = 1080 # Image height in pixels def luminance(color: vec4) -> float: return dot(color, GRAYSCALEFACTORS) def comparecolors(a: vec4, b: vec4) -> bool: return luminance(a) > luminance(b) def texturefetch(uv: vec2) -> vec4: return vec4(0.0) # [G: Standard texture lookup operation] def medianfilterpixel(centeruv: vec2, dx: float, dy: float) -> vec4: offsets = [ vec2(-dx, -dy), vec2(0, -dy), vec2(dx, -dy), vec2(-dx, 0), vec2(0, 0), vec2(dx, 0), vec2(-dx, dy), vec2(0, dy), vec2(dx, dy) ] colorstack = [vec4(0.0) for in range(9)] currentcount = 0 for k in range(9): currentcolor = texturefetch(centeruv + offsets[k]) idx = currentcount while idx > 0 and comparecolors(colorstack[idx - 1], currentcolor): colorstack[idx] = colorstack[idx - 1] idx -= 1 colorstack[idx] = currentcolor currentcount += 1 return colorstack[4] def postprocessingshader(inputuv: vec2) -> vec4: dx = 1.0 / width dy = 1.0 / height return medianfilterpixel(inputuv, dx, dy) The Forgetful Selection Median Filter is a GPU-optimized algorithm for computing the median of a data set, specifically designed to overcome register pressure limitations on CUDA hardware. It solves the problem of high memory usage in classic histogram-based median filters, which require excessive registers per thread, thereby limiting parallelism on GPUs with limited low-latency memory (up to compute capability 3.5). It sets itself apart from histogram-based siblings by maintaining a small, fixed-size subset of values in registers rather than a full frequency distribution, allowing sorting operations to occur entirely within registers. Time and Memory Complexity: Time Complexity: O(1) because the loop always iterates through a fixed array of length 9, regardless of image size. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, requiring storage for 9 colors and a few scalar variables. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Effective at removing "Salt and Pepper" noise caused by precision errors in raycasting. Simple to implement as a post-processing shader. Limitations: Only considers a 3x3 neighborhood, which may not be sufficient for larger noise patterns. When to use it: Use when the primary noise source is single-pixel outliers (salt and pepper noise) resulting from raycasting precision issues. When not to use it: Not given in the sources. Origin: Developed as part of a raycasting-based voxel rendering system to handle noise from precision errors. The technique is described in a thesis/report by Enes Hergül (2022). name: Forgetful Selection Median Filter
head: Forgetful selection, Median filter via forgetful selection
body: The Forgetful Selection Median Filter is a GPU-optimized algorithm for computing the median of a data set, specifically designed to overcome register pressure limitations on CUDA hardware. It solves the problem of high memory usage in classic histogram-based median filters, which require excessive registers per thread, thereby limiting parallelism on GPUs with limited low-latency memory (up to compute capability 3.5). It sets itself apart from histogram-based siblings by maintaining a small, fixed-size subset of values in registers rather than a full frequency distribution, allowing sorting operations to occur entirely within registers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n numbers (typically voxel values in a local neighborhood). Output: The median value of the set. Data Layout: Values are stored as 8-bit unsigned integers. Data Structures: A register-based subset of size k = n/2 + 1. The subset holds the current candidate values for the median. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the subset with the first n/2 + 1 numbers from the input set. 2. Identify the minimum and maximum values (extrema) within the current subset. 3. Remove both the minimum and maximum values from the subset. 4. Add one additional value from the remaining input set to the subset. 5. Repeat steps 2–4 until the subset contains only one element. 6. The remaining element is the median. Implementation Details: The algorithm is applied iteratively in the slow scan direction. Each CUDA thread is assigned to a single pixel in a B-scan of the output volume. Shared memory blocking is used to hide memory access latencies, acting as explicit caching. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forgetfulselectionmedian(values): """ Computes the median of a list of values using the forgetful selection algorithm. values: list of numbers (e.g., 8-bit unsigned integers) returns: the median value """ n = len(values) # Step 1: Start with a subset of n/2 + 1 numbers subsetsize = n // 2 + 1 subset = values[:subsetsize] # Remaining values to process remaining = values[subsetsize:] # Step 5: Iterate until only the median remains while len(subset) > 1: # Step 2: Identify extrema minval = min(subset) maxval = max(subset) # Step 3: Remove extrema from the subset # Note: If minval == maxval, remove one instance of each # To ensure correctness, we remove one occurrence of min and one of max subset.remove(minval) subset.remove(maxval) # Step 4: Add an additional value from the original set if remaining: subset.append(remaining.pop(0)) return subset[0] Parameters: n: The number of input values (e.g., 27 for a 3x3x3 filter). Typical Value: For a 3x3x3 median filter, n=27, requiring 14 registers for the subset. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Register Limit: Classic histogram-based approaches fail on older CUDA hardware because they require more than 256 registers per thread, preventing sufficient parallel thread count. Precision: Data is saved as 8-bit unsigned integers, which may limit dynamic range compared to floating-point representations. Boundary Conditions: The algorithm assumes a valid input set of size n \ge 1. For even n, the standard median definition (average of two middle values) is not explicitly described; the algorithm returns one of the two middle values depending on removal order. A 5x5 2D Gaussian filter used for de-noising, implemented using the same blocking approach and thread structure as the median filter. Convolution is used instead of the 2D Fourier transform because the Gaussian kernel is small, making convolution faster. Both filters operate on data saved as 8-bit unsigned integers. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The algorithm requires only n/2 + 1 registers, allowing sorting operations to take place entirely within registers. This is significantly less than histogram-based methods which require a full frequency array. Time: The algorithm is iterative, requiring O(n \log n) or similar complexity depending on the sorting implementation within the subset, but the constant factor is low due to register locality. Measured Performance: The method enables sufficient parallel thread counts on CUDA hardware up to compute capability 3.5, leveraging the computational power of the GPU which was previously bottlenecked by register limits. Shared memory blocking effectively hides memory access latencies. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Low register footprint, high parallelism on older GPUs, efficient use of shared memory for caching. Limitations: Algorithmically more complicated than histogram-based approaches. Limited to 8-bit unsigned integer data in the cited implementation. When to Use: Use when implementing median filtering on CUDA GPUs with limited register space (compute capability \le 3.5) and when histogram-based methods cause register spilling or insufficient thread occupancy. When Not to Use: Avoid on modern GPUs with abundant registers where histogram-based methods might be simpler to implement and potentially faster due to parallel reduction techniques. Avoid if floating-point precision is required for the median calculation. The Forgetful Selection Median Filter was employed in the context of enhanced volumetric visualization for real-time 4D intraoperative ophthalmic swept-source OCT. It was chosen over classic histogram-based approaches due to the inadequate low-latency memory (registers) on CUDA cores at the time (up to compute capability 3.5). The method relies on the mathematical property that the median of a set of n numbers cannot be the extrema of an n/2 + 1 subset of those numbers. name: Random Jitter with Reprojection
head: Frame Accumulation, Temporal Reprojection
body: Random Jitter with Reprojection is a technique to reduce banding artifacts caused by low sample counts in volume rendering by introducing stochastic jitter during ray marching and subsequently reducing the resulting noise via temporal accumulation. It distinguishes itself from pure spatial jittering methods by leveraging temporal coherence, projecting a pseudo-hit position from the current frame into the previous frame's screen space to blend the current result with a history buffer, thereby allowing for lower per-frame sample counts while maintaining visual stability. The method modifies the standard marching loop to introduce jittered sampling positions and maintains a specific data structure for reprojection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current view matrix, previous view matrix, current frame's accumulated color, history buffer (previous frame's color), step size, density threshold. Output: Final accumulated color for the current pixel. Data Structures: reprojectionHitPosition: A float3 variable storing the 3D world position, updated during the march loop when the accumulated density falls below a threshold, serving as a proxy for the hit position in scenes without explicit geometry. Parameters: TRESHOLD: A density threshold used to determine if the ray is still within the volume (e.g., cloud) for reprojection purposes. weight: A blending factor between the history buffer and the current result, kept relatively high because volumetric elements like clouds do not reproject accurately due to their non-rigid nature. Steps: 1. Initialize reprojectionHitPosition to a default value (e.g., origin or previous frame's hit). 2. Iterate through the ray march loop: a. Calculate a jittered position by adding a random float multiplied by the step size to the current sample position. b. Update the base samplePosition by adding the step size (without jitter) to maintain a non-jittered progression track. c. Sample the density at the jittered position. d. Accumulate the density. e. If the accumulated density is below TRESHOLD, update reprojectionHitPosition to the current non-jittered samplePosition. 3. After the march loop completes, project reprojectionHitPosition to the previous screen space using the previous view matrix. 4. Sample the history buffer at the projected screen position to retrieve the previous frame's result. 5. Blend the history result and the current frame's result using the weight factor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpixel(rayorigin, prevview, historybuffer, stepsize, threshold, maxsteps): reprojectionhitposition = float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) sampleposition = rayorigin accumulateddensity = 0.0 currentresult = float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) weight = 0.8 # High weight for volumetrics for step in range(maxsteps): jitterposition = sampleposition + randomfloat() stepsize sampleposition += stepsize sampledensity = sampledensityfunction(jitterposition) # Renderer-specific density lookup accumulateddensity += sampledensity currentresult += computecolor(sampledensity) # Renderer-specific color accumulation if accumulateddensity < threshold: reprojectionhitposition = sampleposition prevscreenpos = worldtoscreen(reprojectionhitposition, prevview) history = historybuffer.sample(prevscreenpos) result = lerp(history, currentresult, weight) return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Clouds and Volumetrics: Since clouds lack a sharp geometric boundary, the hit position is an approximation. Inaccurate reprojection leads to ghosting or blurring. The blending weight must be tuned to balance noise reduction against motion artifacts. Threshold Selection: If TRESHOLD is too high, the reprojection position may be set too early (shallow in the cloud), leading to misalignment. Precision: Floating-point precision in world-to-screen projection can cause jitter in the history buffer sampling if the camera moves significantly between frames. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of march steps. The reprojection step adds a constant overhead for matrix multiplication and buffer sampling. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the history buffer, where W and H are the screen dimensions. Performance: Allows for a significant reduction in per-frame sample counts compared to non-jittered methods, reducing computational cost while maintaining visual quality through temporal accumulation. Strengths: Effective at reducing banding artifacts from low sample counts; leverages temporal coherence to smooth noise. Limitations: Introduces temporal latency and potential ghosting artifacts, especially with fast camera motion or dynamic volumetric changes. Requires a history buffer and reprojection logic. When to use: When rendering static or slowly moving volumetric scenes (e.g., clouds) where temporal coherence is high and banding from low sample counts is a concern. When not to use: In scenes with rapid camera motion or highly dynamic volumetric changes where ghosting artifacts would be distracting. This technique is described in the context of volumetric cloud rendering, specifically as an adaptive sampling technique to reduce the cost of high-quality cloud rendering by lowering sample counts and using temporal accumulation to mitigate noise. name: Ray Casting with Jittered Sampling
head: Jittered Sampling Volume Rendering
body: Ray Casting with Jittered Sampling is a direct volume rendering technique that casts rays through a 3D voxel grid to accumulate color and opacity along the ray path. It distinguishes itself from uniform ray sampling by perturbing sample positions with a pre-computed jitter texture to break up regular grid patterns and reduce aliasing artifacts. Unlike stochastic methods, it uses deterministic offsets stored in a 2D texture rather than runtime random number generation. Inputs: 3D Voxel Data Texture: Stores voxel colors and opacities. Camera parameters: Projection matrix, ModelView matrix, and camera position. Volume parameters: Bounding box extents, translation, and scale. Rendering parameters: Number of samples per ray, ray step size, and a lighting computation flag. Jitter Texture: A 2D texture storing pre-computed jitter offsets. Outputs: Color buffer: Accumulated RGBA color per pixel. Voxel Data Texture (textureIDs[0]) Target: GLTEXTURE3D. Format: GLRGBA32F for floating-point data, GLRGBA8 for unsigned byte data, or GLCOMPRESSEDRGBAS3TCDXT5EXT if the uncompressed size exceeds 1GB. Content: Voxel colors and opacities. Jitter Texture (textureIDs[1]) Target: GLTEXTURE2D. Size: 32x32 pixels. Content: 2D jitter offset vectors for sampling. Geometry Structure: Bounding box composed of 6 faces (front, back, left, right, top, bottom). Primitive: GLQUADS. Vertices: 4 vertices per face, defined by bounding box corners (x{min/max}, y{min/max}, z{min/max}). N{samples} (mnumSamples): Number of samples per ray. If voxel count is 0: N{samples} = \sqrt{dimX^2 + dimY^2 + dimZ^2} + 2. Clamped to a minimum of 32. JitterTexSize: Resolution of the jitter texture. Fixed at 32x32. RayStepSize: Distance between samples along the ray. Formula: RayStepSize = \frac{\sqrt{3.0}}{N{samples}}. Normalizes the step size relative to the diagonal of the unit cube. VolTranslation: Bounding box center. VolScale: Bounding box dimensions. VolExtentMin/Max: Bounding box minimum and maximum coordinates. 1. Coordinate Transformation Setup: Normalize the volume bounding box to a unit cube for shader calculations. Transform VolExtentMin, VolExtentMax, CameraPosition, and LightPosition into this local space using: coord{local} = \frac{coord{world} - VolTranslation}{VolScale} + 0.5 2. Near Plane Pass: Draw a near plane quad using a separate shader program (spCameraNearPlaneProg). Pass the same transformation matrices and parameters as the main ray caster. 3. Stencil Test Setup: Enable the stencil test. Set the function to GLEQUAL with a reference value of 0. Set the operation on pass to GLINCR. This ensures only one pixel modifies the color buffer per fragment. 4. Blending Setup: Enable alpha blending. Set blend factors to GLONE and GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA. 5. Ray Casting Shader Execution: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. Sample the 3D voxel texture along the ray path. Apply jitter offsets from the 2D jitter texture to sample positions to reduce aliasing. Accumulate color and opacity along the ray using front-to-back compositing. Optionally compute lighting if the ComputeLighting flag is set. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def transformtolocal(coord, voltranslation, volscale): """Transforms world coordinates to local unit cube space.""" return [(c - t) / s + 0.5 for c, t, s in zip(coord, voltranslation, volscale)] def samplejitter(jittertexture, u, v, jittertexsize): """Samples a 2D jitter offset from the pre-computed texture.""" # Normalize UV coordinates to [0, 1) range unorm = (u % jittertexsize) / jittertexsize vnorm = (v % jittertexsize) / jittertexsize # Return a 2D offset vector (dx, dy) return jittertexture[unorm, vnorm] def jitteredvolumeraycasting(camerapos, projmatrix, modelviewmatrix, voxeltexture, jittertexture, jittertexsize, voltranslation, volscale, volextentmin, volextentmax, lightpos, computelighting, numsamples): """Main ray casting loop for jittered volume rendering.""" # 1. Coordinate Transformation localextentmin = transformtolocal(volextentmin, voltranslation, volscale) localextentmax = transformtolocal(volextentmax, voltranslation, volscale) localcamerapos = transformtolocal(camerapos, voltranslation, volscale) locallightpos = transformtolocal(lightpos, voltranslation, volscale) # 2. Setup Rendering State enablestenciltest() setstencilfunction(GLEQUAL, ref=0) setstencilop(GLINCR, GLKEEP, GLKEEP) enablealphablending() setblendfactors(GLONE, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA) # 3. Near Plane Pass drawnearplanequad(projmatrix, modelviewmatrix, localcamerapos, locallightpos) # 4. Ray Casting Loop raystepsize = math.sqrt(3.0) / numsamples for v in range(height): for u in range(width): # Generate ray direction from camera to pixel raydir = generateraydirection(u, v, projmatrix, modelviewmatrix, localcamerapos) raydir = normalize(raydir) # Initialize accumulation (RGBA color, scalar opacity) acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accopacity = 0.0 # Determine ray start and end points in local space raystart = localcamerapos rayend = [raystart[i] + raydir[i] distancetofarplane for i in range(3)] # Get jitter offset for this pixel jitteroffset = samplejitter(jittertexture, u, v, jittertexsize) # Calculate number of steps raylength = math.sqrt(sum((rayend[i] - raystart[i])2 for i in range(3))) numsteps = int(raylength / raystepsize) # Sample along ray for i in range(numsteps): # Apply jitter as an offset to the step index t = (i + jitteroffset[0]) raystepsize samplepos = [raystart[i] + raydir[i] t for i in range(3)] # Check if sample is within volume bounds if all(localextentmin[i] <= samplepos[i] <= localextentmax[i] for i in range(3)): # Sample voxel texture voxelcolor = sample3dtexture(voxeltexture, samplepos) voxelopacity = voxelcolor[3] # Front-to-back compositing weight = voxelopacity (1.0 - accopacity) acccolor[0] += voxelcolor[0] weight acccolor[1] += voxelcolor[1] weight acccolor[2] += voxelcolor[2] weight acccolor[3] += voxelcolor[3] weight accopacity += weight # Early termination if fully opaque if accopacity >= 1.0: break # Write to color buffer writecolorbuffer(u, v, acccolor) Memory Limit: If the uncompressed voxel texture size exceeds 1GB, the format is automatically switched to GLCOMPRESSEDRGBAS3TCDXT5EXT to fit within GPU memory limits. Empty Volume: If the voxel data pointer is NULL and no subvolumes exist, a default color LUT is generated with 4 entries (transparent black, red, green, blue) and applied to the volume. Precision: The coordinate transformation formula (coord - translation) / scale + 0.5 assumes consistent units between world coordinates and volume dimensions. Uses runtime random number generation for jitter offsets instead of a pre-computed texture. Uses hierarchical data structures to sample based on probability distributions, useful for importance sampling. Samples at fixed intervals without jitter, leading to aliasing artifacts. Uses stochastic sampling with many samples to reduce noise, often for complex lighting. Uses jittered sampling with reprojection techniques for temporal stability in animations. Tailored for Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics data, sampling based on particle density. Uses warping techniques to adjust sampling patterns, possibly for adaptive resolution. Time Complexity: O(N{pixels} \times N{samples}) per frame. Memory Complexity: O(VoxelVolume + JitterTextureSize). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with resolution and number of samples. Strengths: Reduces aliasing artifacts compared to uniform sampling; deterministic jitter pattern ensures reproducibility. Limitations: Requires a pre-computed 32x32 jitter texture. When to use: When aliasing is a concern and deterministic results are preferred. When not to use: When memory is extremely constrained or when stochastic methods are preferred for other reasons. Origin: The specific implementation details are documented in a thesis by Apecoraro. History: The technique is part of the GigaVoxels framework for large-scale volume rendering. Usage: Used in the VoxViz visualization tool. apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, https://github.com/apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Direction Jitter
head: Direction Jitter, Ray Direction Noise
body: Ray Direction Jitter is a technique that improves the generalizability of learned rendering models by applying sub-pixel noise to ray directions. It prevents the color network from overfitting to specific training viewing directions, which otherwise leads to artifacts in novel view synthesis and texture reproduction. Unlike Uniform Ray Sampling which distributes samples across a pixel area, this method perturbs the ray vector itself while ensuring the ray remains confined within the pixel's geometric boundaries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, nominal ray direction \mathbf{d}, and pixel boundary constraints. Output: Jittered ray direction \mathbf{d}' = \mathbf{d} + \psi and the resulting ray equation. Data Structures: \mathbf{o}: 3D vector (ox, oy, oz) representing the camera origin. \mathbf{d}: 3D vector (dx, dy, dz) representing the nominal ray direction pointing through the pixel center. \psi: 3D vector representing the sub-pixel jitter noise. Steps: 1. Sample a jitter vector \psi uniformly. 2. The sampling distribution must ensure that the perturbed ray \mathbf{o} + t(\mathbf{d} + \psi) remains within the pixel boundaries for all t > 0. 3. Compute the jittered direction: \mathbf{d}' = \mathbf{d} + \psi. 4. Construct the ray equation: \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti (\mathbf{d} + \psi). Formula: \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti (\mathbf{d} + \psi) Where: \mathbf{x}i is the point on the ray at distance ti. \mathbf{o} is the camera origin. \mathbf{d} is the nominal ray direction (pointing through the pixel center). \psi is the sub-pixel jitter noise. ti is the distance along the ray. Parameters: The magnitude of \psi is determined by the pixel size and camera intrinsics to ensure boundary confinement. Specific numerical bounds for \psi are not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Without jitter, the color network tends to overfit training viewing directions, leading to visible artifacts in rendering and textures. The jitter must be sampled such that the ray does not exit the pixel boundaries; otherwise, the sample no longer corresponds to the intended pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def jitterraydirection(origin, nominaldirection, pixelsize, focallength): """ Generates a jittered ray direction confined to pixel boundaries. name: Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling)
head: Inverse CDF, Inverse CDF Sampling, PDF Sampling, PDF Sampling via Inverse CDF, PDF sampling from weights, Sorted Piecewise Constant PDF Sampling
body: Hierarchical sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling) is a method for generating importance samples along a ray in volume rendering by inverting the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the rendering contribution. It solves the problem of efficiently placing sample points in regions of high density without redundant radiance queries. It builds on Sampling and Jittering by providing a deterministic or stratified mechanism to concentrate fine samples where the coarse pass indicated high opacity. Inputs: bins: Tensor of shape (B, T) containing the depth boundaries (bin edges) of the coarse samples, where B is the batch size and T is the number of bin edges (N{coarse} + 1). weights: Tensor of shape (B, T-1) containing the unnormalized importance weights (typically density or opacity contribution) for each bin. Nsamples: Integer specifying the number of fine samples to generate per ray (N{importance}). det: Boolean flag. If True, uses deterministic stratified sampling (uniform u); if False, uses random uniform sampling. Outputs: samples: Tensor of shape [batchsize, numsamples] containing the new depth values sampled from the fine distribution. Data Structures: The method operates on batched tensors where the last dimension corresponds to the ray depth axis. pdf: Probability Density Function, shape (B, T-1). cdf: Cumulative Distribution Function, shape (B, T), padded with a leading zero. Parameters: eps: Small constant for numerical stability, added to weights to prevent division by zero during normalization. perturb: Controls jittering. 0 disables jittering (deterministic midpoints), 1 enables full stratified jittering. Note: In the inverse CDF context, det usually handles the stratification logic directly via linspace vs rand. Steps: 1. Stabilize Weights: Add a small epsilon to weights to prevent division by zero during normalization. weights = weights + \epsilon Typical value: \epsilon = 10^{-5}. 2. Compute PDF: Normalize the weights along the last dimension to form a Probability Density Function (PDF). pdf = \frac{weights}{\sum{j} weightsj} Where the sum is over the bin index (last dimension), keeping dimensions for batch and ray. 3. Compute CDF: Compute the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) by taking the cumulative sum of the PDF along the last dimension. Prepend a tensor of zeros to align the CDF indices with the bin edges (since CDF values correspond to bin boundaries, not centers). cdf = \text{cumsum}(pdf, \text{dim}=-1) cdf = \text{concat}([zeros\like(cdf[...,:1]), cdf], \text{dim}=-1) The resulting CDF has shape (B, T) and ranges from 0 to 1. 4. Generate Uniform Samples (u): Generate N{samples} uniform random numbers in [0, 1] for each ray. If det is True: Use deterministic stratified sampling. u = \text{linspace}(0, 1, N{samples}) Expand u to match the batch shape: (B, Nsamples). If det is False: Use random uniform sampling. u \sim U[0, 1] Shape: (B, Nsamples). 5. Find Bin Indices: Determine which bin each sample u falls into by searching the sorted CDF. inds = \text{searchsorted}(cdf, u, \text{side}=\text{'right'}) This returns indices in the range [0, T-1] indicating the position in the CDF array. 6. Determine Bin Boundaries: For each sample, identify the lower and upper CDF values and bin boundaries for interpolation. below = \max(0, inds - 1) above = \min(T - 1, inds) Stack these to form indices for gathering: inds\g = \text{stack}([below, above], \text{dim}=-1) Shape of indsg: (B, Nsamples, 2). 7. Gather CDF and Bin Values: Retrieve the CDF values and bin depth boundaries corresponding to the lower and upper indices. cdf\g = \text{gather}(cdf, inds\g) bins\g = \text{gather}(bins, inds\g) cdfg has shape (B, Nsamples, 2) containing [cdf{lower}, cdf{upper}]. binsg has shape (B, Nsamples, 2) containing [z{lower}, z{upper}]. 8. Interpolate (Inverse CDF): Calculate the relative position t within the bin and map it to the depth space. denom = cdf\g[..., 1] - cdf\g[..., 0] Handle zero-width bins (division by zero) by clamping the denominator: denom = \text{where}(denom < 10^{-5}, \text{ones\like}(denom), denom) t = \frac{u - cdf\g[..., 0]}{denom} samples = bins\g[..., 0] + t \times (bins\g[..., 1] - bins\g[..., 0]) The result samples has shape (B, Nsamples). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def hierarchicalsamplinginversecdf(bins, weights, Nsamples, det=False, eps=1e-5): """ Samples depth values from a probability distribution defined by weights using inverse transform sampling on the cumulative distribution function (CDF). Args: bins: Tensor of shape (B, T) containing bin edges (depth boundaries). weights: Tensor of shape (B, T-1) containing unnormalized weights for each bin. Nsamples: Integer, number of fine samples to generate per ray. det: Boolean, if True uses deterministic linspace, else random uniform. eps: Float, numerical stability constant. Returns: samples: Tensor of shape (B, Nsamples) containing sampled depths. """ # 1. Stabilize weights weights = weights + eps # 2. Compute PDF # Sum over the last dimension (bins), keep dimensions for broadcasting pdf = weights / torch.sum(weights, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # 3. Compute CDF and prepend zeros cdf = torch.cumsum(pdf, dim=-1) # Prepend a zero tensor to align CDF indices with bin edges cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[...,:1]), cdf], dim=-1) # 4. Generate uniform samples u # cdf shape: (B, T) # We want u shape: (B, Nsamples) batchshape = cdf.shape[:-1] if det: # Deterministic stratified sampling u = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, steps=Nsamples, device=bins.device) u = u.expand(batchshape + (Nsamples,)) else: # Random uniform sampling u = torch.rand(batchshape + (Nsamples,), device=bins.device) # 5. Find bin indices # searchsorted finds the index where u would be inserted to maintain order # side='right' means if u == cdf[i], it returns i+1 (or similar logic consistent with bin indexing) inds = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, side='right') # 6. Determine bin boundaries for interpolation # below is the index of the lower bin edge, above is the index of the upper bin edge # Clamp to valid range [0, T-1] below = torch.clamp(inds - 1, min=0) above = torch.clamp(inds, max=cdf.shape[-1] - 1) # Stack to create indices for gathering pairs indsg = torch.stack([below, above], dim=-1) # Shape: (B, Nsamples, 2) # 7. Gather CDF and Bin values # Expand indsg to match dimensions for gather if necessary, # but gather works on the last dim if dim=2 is specified for 3D tensor # cdf shape: (B, T), we want to gather from dim=1 (the T dim) # indsg shape: (B, Nsamples, 2) # To use torch.gather, we need to expand indsg to match the number of dims # cdf is (B, T). We gather from dim 1. # indsg needs to be (B, Nsamples, 2) and we gather 2 values. # Note: torch.gather(input, dim, index) # input: (B, T) # index: (B, Nsamples, 2) # output: (B, Nsamples, 2) cdfg = torch.gather(cdf.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, Nsamples, -1), 2, indsg) binsg = torch.gather(bins.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, Nsamples, -1), 2, indsg) # 8. Interpolate denom = cdfg[..., 1] - cdfg[..., 0] # Handle division by zero for zero-width bins denom = torch.where(denom < 1e-5, torch.oneslike(denom), denom) t = (u - cdfg[..., 0]) / denom samples = binsg[..., 0] + t (binsg[..., 1] - binsg[..., 0]) return samples Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Weights: If all weights in a ray are zero, normalization results in NaN. Adding \epsilon prevents this. Zero-Width Bins: If cdfg[..., 1] == cdfg[..., 0], the interpolation denominator is zero. Clamping the denominator to 10^{-5} or 1 prevents NaNs and returns the lower bound or a safe default. Index Out of Bounds: searchsorted can return out-of-bounds indices, which are clamped to valid ranges. Uses inverse transform sampling on a piecewise approximated density field (constant or linear) to allow gradients to back-propagate through the sampling process to the density parameters. Chosen when differentiable sampling is required for end-to-end optimization. Uses a coarse MLP to directly estimate the PDF, providing more accurate transmittance estimation at the cost of higher sample counts in empty regions. Chosen when a learned prior is available and computational budget allows for network inference per ray. Refines coarse samples by generating a dense uniform grid around the coarse sample with the highest weight, supplemented by random samples. Chosen when high-frequency details are missing between coarse samples and a deterministic geometric expansion is preferred over probabilistic CDF inversion. Explicitly constructs a discrete PDF from coarse weights using deterministic inverse CDF lookup. Chosen when a strict deterministic mapping from coarse weights to fine samples is needed without neural network overhead. The core primitive selecting indices from a finite set based on weights via CDF traversal. Chosen as the foundational building block for hierarchical sampling, supporting both stochastic and deterministic top-k selection. Generates deterministic, hierarchical point sets within a unit cube maintaining uniform density and minimum inter-point distance. Chosen for density control and LOD management in 3D space rather than 1D ray sampling. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: The piecewise constant assumption of the PDF may not perfectly match the true underlying density, leading to aliasing if the coarse grid is too sparse. When to use: When refining coarse samples in a hierarchical rendering pipeline, especially in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) where differentiability is crucial for training. When not to use: When the scene is extremely sparse and empty space skipping is more important than density estimation accuracy, or when the coarse grid is too fine to justify the overhead of CDF construction. Hierarchical sampling via inverse CDF was introduced in the seminal paper "NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis" by Mildenhall et al. (2020). It was designed to improve the quality of volume rendering by adding fine samples in regions of high opacity identified by a coarse pass. The method leverages the fact that the probability of a ray interacting with a volume element is proportional to its density, allowing the CDF of the coarse weights to guide the placement of fine samples. name: Inverse Opacity Calculation
head: inverse opacity sampling
body: Inverse Opacity Calculation is a method for generating importance samples along a ray in volume rendering by inverting the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the rendering contribution, which is mathematically equivalent to the transmittance function. It solves the problem of efficiently placing sample points in regions of high density without redundant radiance queries, enabling differentiable end-to-end optimization of neural radiance fields. Unlike standard hierarchical sampling which samples from a piecewise constant probability density defined by coarse weights, this method uses inverse transform sampling on a piecewise approximated density field (constant or linear), allowing gradients to back-propagate through the sampling process to the density parameters. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Near and far clipping planes tn, tf. A set of coarse sample positions t1, \dots, tm (where t1=tn, tm=tf). A neural network or function evaluating density \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(t) at any point along the ray. A target cumulative density value y \in [0, yf], where yf = 1 - \exp(-\int{tn}^{tf} \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(s) ds) is the total ray opacity. Outputs: A sample position t along the ray such that the cumulative opacity up to t equals y. Data Structures: Grid Points: Array t of size m+1, sorted t1 < t2 < \dots < t{m+1}. Density Values: Array \sigma of size m+1, where \sigmai = \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(ti). For piecewise constant approximation, an additional sample point \hat{t}i per bin [ti, t{i+1}] is used to evaluate density \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}i). Steps: 1. Compute Total Opacity (yf): Calculate the integral of density along the entire ray to determine the total opacity. yf = 1 - \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{tf} \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(s) ds\right) In practice, this integral is approximated using piecewise constant or linear approximations of \sigma{\mathbf{r}} over the grid intervals. 2. Generate Target Cumulative Values (y): Generate k independent uniform random samples ui \sim \mathcal{U}[0, 1]. Compute the target cumulative density for each sample: y{target, i} = yf \cdot ui For stratified sampling, use ui \sim \mathcal{U}[\frac{i-1}{k+1}, \frac{i}{k+1}]. 3. Numerical Stability for y (Optional but Recommended): To avoid numerical instability when computing y = -\log(1 - yf u) for opaque rays, use the logsumexp formulation: y = -\log \left( \exp(\log(1-u)) + \exp(\log u - \int{tn}^{tf} \sigmar(s) ds) \right) If the ray is opaque (\int{tn}^{tf} \sigmar(s) ds \approx 0), replace y with u. 4. Identify the Bin: Find the index i such that the cumulative integral up to ti is less than or equal to y, and the cumulative integral up to t{i+1} is greater than y. Let I(t) be the approximate integral of density from tn to t. Find i where I(ti) \le y < I(t{i+1}). 5. Solve for t within the Bin: Depending on the approximation used for density within the bin [ti, t{i+1}], solve for t. Case A: Piecewise Constant Approximation Assume \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(t) = \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}i) is constant within the bin. The integral approximation is: I0(t) = \sum{j=1}^i \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}j)(tj - t{j-1}) + \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}i)(t - ti) Set I0(t) = y and solve for t: t = ti + \frac{y - \sum{j=1}^i \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}j)(tj - t{j-1})}{\sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}i)} Add a small epsilon \epsilon to the denominator if \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(\hat{t}i) \approx 0 to prevent division by zero. Case B: Piecewise Linear Approximation Assume \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(t) varies linearly between ti and t{i+1}. The integral approximation I1(t) is piecewise quadratic. Let \Delta t = t - ti. Solve the quadratic equation 0 = a\Delta t^2 + b\Delta t + c for \Delta t: a = \frac{\sigma{\mathbf{r}}(t{i+1}) - \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(ti)}{2} b = \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(ti) \times (t{i+1} - ti) c = \left( \sum{j=1}^i \frac{\sigma{\mathbf{r}}(tj) + \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(t{j-1})}{2} (tj - t{j-1}) - y \right) \times (t{i+1} - ti) The valid root is: \Delta t = \frac{-b + \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} Handle edge cases where a \approx 0 or b \approx 0 by using appropriate limits (e.g., \Delta t = \sqrt{-c/a} if b \approx 0). Then t = ti + \Delta t. 6. Evaluate Radiance: Evaluate the color/radiance c{\mathbf{r}}(t) at the computed sample position t. 7. Compute Final Estimate: The expected radiance is estimated as: \hat{C}{MC}^R(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{yf}{k} \sum{i=1}^k c{\mathbf{r}}(ti) This estimate is unbiased and differentiable with respect to the density field parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def inverseopacitycalculation(tgrid, sigmagrid, ytarget, approxtype='piecewiseconstant'): """ Computes the ray parameter t for a given target cumulative density ytarget. Args: tgrid: Tensor of shape (m+1,), sorted grid points t1... t{m+1}. sigmagrid: Tensor of shape (m+1,), density values at grid points. ytarget: Scalar or Tensor, target cumulative density value. approxtype: 'piecewiseconstant' or 'piecewiselinear'. Returns: t: Tensor of same shape as ytarget, the computed ray parameter. """ # Step 1: Identify the bin i such that cumulativeintegral[i] <= ytarget < cumulativeintegral[i+1] # Compute cumulative integrals up to each grid point dt = tgrid[1:] - tgrid[:-1] if approxtype == 'piecewiseconstant': # For piecewise constant, density is constant per bin. # Assume sigmagrid has shape (m,) representing density in each bin, or (m+1) where we use left endpoints. # Following source, we use sigmagrid[:-1] for bin densities. binsigma = sigmagrid[:-1] # Cumulative integral at each grid point cumintegral = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(tgrid[:1]), torch.cumsum(binsigma dt, dim=0)]) else: # Piecewise linear: trapezoidal rule binsigmaavg = (sigmagrid[:-1] + sigmagrid[1:]) / 2.0 cumintegral = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(tgrid[:1]), torch.cumsum(binsigmaavg dt, dim=0)]) # Find bin index i where cumintegral[i] <= ytarget < cumintegral[i+1] # Use searchsorted to find the right bin i = torch.searchsorted(cumintegral, ytarget, side='right') - 1 i = torch.clamp(i, 0, len(tgrid) - 2) # Get values for the identified bin ti = tgrid[i] tip1 = tgrid[i+1] yprev = cumintegral[i] if approxtype == 'piecewiseconstant': sigmai = sigmagrid[i] # Solve linear equation: y = yprev + sigmai (t - ti) # t = ti + (y - yprev) / sigmai denom = sigmai + 1e-6 # Add epsilon for stability t = ti + (ytarget - yprev) / denom else: # Piecewise linear: solve quadratic 0 = adeltat^2 + bdeltat + c sigmai = sigmagrid[i] sigmaip1 = sigmagrid[i+1] a = (sigmaip1 - sigmai) / 2.0 b = sigmai (tip1 - ti) c = (yprev - ytarget) (tip1 - ti) # Handle degenerate cases if torch.abs(a) < 1e-6: # Linear case: bdeltat + c = 0 deltat = -c / (b + 1e-6) else: # Quadratic formula: deltat = (-b + sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) / 2a # We take the positive root since integral is monotonic increasing deltat = (-b + torch.sqrt(torch.clamp(b2 - 4ac, min=0.0))) / (2a) t = ti + deltat return t Inverse Transform Sampling with Piecewise Linear Density is a differentiable method for generating samples along a ray according to a distribution induced by linearly interpolating the volume density \sigma{\mathbf{r}}. It solves the problem of finding the ray parameter t corresponding to a target cumulative density value y, ensuring that samples strictly follow the Beer-Lambert law within each bin. Unlike NeRF's hierarchical sampling, which interpolates exponentiated densities (probabilities), this method interpolates the density field directly, offering better numerical stability for end-to-end optimization. Piecewise Linear Approximation Inverse is a technique for solving the inverse opacity integral to determine the ray parameter t for a given cumulative density value y during hierarchical volume sampling. It assumes that the density \sigmar(t) varies linearly within each sampling interval, resulting in a piecewise quadratic cumulative density function. This approach is a specific interpolation strategy within the L0-Sampler framework, designed to approximate the L0 property for more precise geometric detail capture compared to standard hierarchical volume sampling. It is simpler than piecewise exponential or inverse variants but focuses sampling less intensely at interval endpoints. Piecewise Constant Approximation Inverse is a method for computing the inverse of the density integral along a ray, used to determine sample positions in inverse opacity sampling. It assumes that the density \sigma{\mathbf{r}} is constant within each discrete sample interval [t{j-1}, tj]. This approach differs from its sibling, Piecewise Linear Approximation Inverse, by treating density as a step function rather than a linearly varying one, resulting in a linear equation for the ray parameter t instead of a quadratic one. It builds on Inverse Opacity Calculation by providing an explicit closed-form solution for the ray parameter given a target cumulative density value. Time complexity is O(m) for computing cumulative integrals and O(\log m) or O(1) for bin search depending on implementation, with O(1) for the final quadratic/linear solve. Memory complexity is O(m) to store grid points and densities. Measured performance on the Lego scene (Blender dataset) with (Np=16, Nf=32) achieves PSNR 29.18 vs NeRF 27.09, SSIM 0.928 vs 0.913, and LPIPS 0.112 vs 0.121, with relative training time 0.37 vs 0.39. On the Lego scene with (Np=64, Nf=192), it achieves PSNR 33.03 vs NeRF 32.69, SSIM 0.964 vs 0.962, and LPIPS 0.047 vs 0.048, with relative training time 0.98 vs 1.0. On the Blender dataset average with (Np=32, Nf=64), it achieves PSNR 30.26 vs NeRF 29.49, SSIM 0.939 vs 0.934, and LPIPS 0.082 vs 0.085. On the LLFF dataset average with (Np=32, Nf=64), it achieves PSNR 26.01 vs NeRF 26.01 (tie), SSIM 0.796 vs 0.796 (tie), and LPIPS 0.273 vs 0.273 (tie). Strengths include end-to-end differentiability without auxiliary losses and reduced redundant radiance queries. Limitations include numerical instability for near-zero densities or opaque rays, requiring epsilon additions or logsumexp reparameterization. It is best used when training neural radiance fields end-to-end and when avoiding auxiliary proposal networks is desired. Originated in the "Differentiable Rendering with Reparameterized Volume Sampling" paper (2023) by authors from AIRI. It was developed to improve upon the hierarchical sampling scheme in the original NeRF work by replacing sampling from piecewise constant PDF with inverse CDF sampling using piecewise linear density approximation, and by removing the auxiliary reconstruction loss on the coarse network. The method allows training NeRF end-to-end without auxiliary tasks by back-propagating gradients through the sampler. It is used in modern neural rendering pipelines for novel view synthesis. body: Inverse Transform Sampling with Piecewise Linear Density is a differentiable method for generating samples along a ray according to a distribution induced by linearly interpolating the volume density \sigma{\mathbf{r}}. It solves the problem of finding the ray parameter t corresponding to a target cumulative density value y, ensuring that samples strictly follow the Beer-Lambert law within each bin. Unlike NeRF's hierarchical sampling, which interpolates exponentiated densities (probabilities), this method interpolates the density field directly, offering better numerical stability for end-to-end optimization. Inputs: u: Uniform random variable, u \in [0, 1). \sigma{\mathbf{r}}: Array of density values at grid knots, size N. ts, te: Start and end parameters of the ray segment. t: Array of grid knots, size N, where t0 = ts and t{N-1} = te. Outputs: t{\text{sample}}: The sampled ray parameter. Data Structures: prefixintegrals: Array of size N, storing the cumulative integral of density from t0 to ti. binintegrals: Array of size N-1, storing the integral of density within each interval [ti, t{i+1}]. Steps: 1. Compute Bin Integrals and Prefix Sums: Calculate the integral of density over each interval using linear interpolation. \text{bin\integrals}i = \frac{\sigma{\mathbf{r}}(ti) + \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(t{i+1})}{2} (t{i+1} - ti) \text{prefix\integrals}0 = 0 \text{prefix\integrals}{i+1} = \text{prefix\integrals}i + \text{bin\integrals}i 2. Compute Inverse Opacity Input y: Calculate the target cumulative density value y from the uniform sample u and the total ray optical depth \tau = \int{tn}^{tf} \sigmar(s) ds using the numerically stable logsumexp operator. y = -\log \left( \exp(\log(1-u)) + \exp(\log u - \tau) \right) Edge Case: When the integral is approximately zero, the logsumexp implementation becomes computationally unstable, and y is replaced with a first-order approximation u \cdot \tau. 3. Find the Interval: Find the index i such that \text{prefix\integrals}i \le y < \text{prefix\integrals}{i+1}. If y \ge \text{prefix\integrals}{N-1}, set t{\text{sample}} = te. 4. Solve for \Delta t: Within the interval [ti, t{i+1}], assume linear density interpolation. We solve for \Delta t = t - ti in the quadratic equation: 0 = a \Delta t^2 + b \Delta t + c Where: a = \frac{\sigma{\mathbf{r}}(t{i+1}) - \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(ti)}{2} b = \sigma{\mathbf{r}}(ti) \times (t{i+1} - ti) c = \left( \text{prefix\integrals}i - y \right) \times (t{i+1} - ti) Compute the root using the stable formula to avoid cancellation when a \approx 0: \Delta t = \frac{2c}{b + \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}} Pitfall: If b^2 - 4ac < 0, clamp the discriminant to 0. If the denominator is 0, set \Delta t = 0. 5. Return Result: t{\text{sample}} = ti + \Delta t Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: u: Uniform random sample [0, 1). sigmas: Density values at knots, shape (N,). ts: Knot positions, shape (N,). Returns: tsample: Sampled position along the ray. """ N = len(ts) if N < 2: return ts[0] # 1. Compute Prefix Integrals (linear interpolation per source derivation) binintegrals = (sigmas[:-1] + sigmas[1:]) / 2.0 np.diff(ts) prefixintegrals = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(binintegrals)]) totaltau = prefixintegrals[-1] # 2. Compute y (Inverse Opacity Input) # Handle numerical stability for small optical depth (transparent rays) if totaltau < 1e-5: y = u totaltau else: term1 = np.log(1.0 - u) term2 = np.log(u) - totaltau maxval = np.maximum(term1, term2) y = - (maxval + np.log(np.exp(term1 - maxval) + np.exp(term2 - maxval))) # 3. Find interval i = np.searchsorted(prefixintegrals, y, side='right') - 1 i = np.clip(i, 0, N - 2) ti = ts[i] tip1 = ts[i+1] sigmai = sigmas[i] sigmaip1 = sigmas[i+1] dtinterval = tip1 - ti # 4. Solve Quadratic a = (sigmaip1 - sigmai) / 2.0 b = sigmai dtinterval c = (prefixintegrals[i] - y) dtinterval discriminant = bb - 4ac if discriminant < 0: discriminant = 0.0 denom = b + np.sqrt(discriminant) if denom == 0: deltat = 0.0 else: # Stable formula per source: Delta t = 2c / (b + sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)) deltat = (2.0 c) / denom # Clamp deltat to interval bounds deltat = np.clip(deltat, 0.0, dtinterval) return ti + deltat Time Complexity: O(N) to compute prefix integrals; O(\log N) to find the interval and O(1) to solve the quadratic. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store prefix integrals. Strengths: Differentiable; samples follow the Beer-Lambert law within bins; numerically stable for end-to-end optimization compared to exponentiated density interpolation. Limitations: Requires computing prefix integrals; quadratic solution has edge cases for a \approx 0 handled by the stable formula. When to use: When differentiable sampling from a linearly interpolated density field is required, particularly in neural volume rendering contexts like RVS. This method was introduced in "Differentiable Rendering with Reparameterized Volume Sampling" (2023). It contrasts with the original NeRF hierarchical sampling, which uses piecewise constant density interpolation and exponentiates densities. The RVS method interpolates the density field directly, leading to samples that adhere to the Beer-Lambert law within each bin, which is argued to be more suitable for end-to-end optimization due to better numerical stability. name: Precision Importance Sampling
head: Exact Inverse Transform Sampling under Piecewise Linear Opacity
body: Precision Importance Sampling is a method for generating samples from a continuous ray distribution in volume rendering by deriving an exact closed-form inverse for the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) under a piecewise linear opacity assumption. It solves the problem that piecewise constant opacity models produce a non-invertible and discontinuous CDF, which forces conversion to a discrete random variable and prevents exact continuous sampling. Unlike its sibling Inverse Transform Sampling with Piecewise Linear Density, which focuses on density interpolation, this method explicitly leverages the continuity of the CDF induced by linear opacity to allow direct inversion x = F^{-1}(u). Inputs: Uniform random variable u \sim U(0, 1). Pre-computed interval probabilities P1, \dots, PN derived from the ray distribution. Sample positions s1, \dots, sN defining the bins. Opacity values \tauk, \tau{k+1} at the boundaries of the identified bin. Transmittance T(sk) at the start of the identified bin. Outputs: Exact sample position x along the ray. Data Structures: The method relies on the cumulative probabilities Ck = \sum{j < k} Pj to identify the correct bin. Pj represents the probability mass of the j-th interval, summing to 1 assuming an opaque far plane (s{N+1}). Steps: 1. Identify the bin index k such that the uniform sample u falls within the cumulative probability range [Ck, C{k+1}], where Ck = \sum{j < k} Pj. This corresponds to finding the spatial interval [sk, s{k+1}]. 2. Reparameterize the position within the bin as x = sk + t, where t \in [0, s{k+1} - sk]. 3. Calculate the offset t using the closed-form solution derived from inverting the CDF under piecewise linear opacity: t = \frac{s{k+1} - sk}{\tau{k+1} - \tauk} \left[ -\tauk + \sqrt{\tauk^2 + \frac{2(\tau{k+1} - \tauk) \left( -\ln \frac{1-u}{T(sk)} \right)}{(s{k+1} - sk)}} \right] 4. Compute the final sample position x = sk + t. Formulas: The CDF F(t) for a continuous random variable t is defined as: F(t) = \int0^t p(s) \, ds = \sum{sj < t} Pj + \int{sj}^t \tau(s) T(s) \, ds where p(s) is the ray distribution, Pj are the interval probabilities, \tau(s) is the opacity, and T(s) is the transmittance. The assumption that opacity \tau \ge 0 everywhere ensures that F is strictly increasing and continuous, making it invertible. Parameters: Interval probabilities P1, \dots, PN. Opacities \tauk, \tau{k+1} at sample boundaries. Transmittance T(sk). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The derivation assumes \tau \ge 0 everywhere. The method requires the far plane to be opaque for the probabilities to sum to 1. Precision issues may arise if \tau{k+1} \approx \tauk, potentially causing division by zero in the coefficient \frac{s{k+1} - sk}{\tau{k+1} - \tauk}. The sources do not specify a guard for this case. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def precisionimportancesampling(u, s, P, tau, T): """ Generate an exact sample x using Precision Importance Sampling. Args: u: Uniform random variable in [0, 1]. s: List of sample positions [s1,..., sN]. P: List of interval probabilities [P1,..., PN]. tau: List of opacities at sample positions [tau1,..., tauN]. T: List of transmittances at sample positions [T(s1),..., T(sN)]. Returns: x: The exact sample position. """ # Step 1: Identify the bin k such that u is in [Ck, C{k+1}] # Ck = sum(Pj for j < k) cumulativeprob = 0.0 k = 0 for i in range(len(P)): if u < cumulativeprob + P[i]: k = i break cumulativeprob += P[i] # s[k] corresponds to sk, s[k+1] to s{k+1} # Note: The source uses 1-based indexing for s1...sN. # Assuming s is 0-indexed list of length N, s[k] is sk. # We need s{k+1}. If k is the last index, we assume s{N+1} is the far plane. # The source notes s{N+1} corresponds to the far plane. sk = s[k] if k + 1 < len(s): sk1 = s[k + 1] else: # Far plane position. Not given in sources. # Assuming s is extended or far plane is known. # For implementation, this value must be provided. raise ValueError("Far plane position not provided.") tauk = tau[k] tauk1 = tau[k + 1] if k + 1 < len(tau) else 0.0 # Opacity at far plane is 1 (opaque), so tau might be handled differently. # Source says "opaque far plane". Tau is opacity. T(s) is transmittance. # If far plane is opaque, T(s{N+1}) = 0. # The formula uses tauk and tau{k+1}. Tsk = T[k] # Step 2 & 3: Calculate t # t = (s{k+1} - sk) / (tau{k+1} - tauk) [ -tauk + sqrt( tauk^2 + 2(tau{k+1} - tauk)(-ln((1-u)/T(sk))) / (s{k+1} - sk)) ] deltas = sk1 - sk deltatau = tauk1 - tauk # Guard against division by zero if deltatau is 0 if abs(deltatau) < 1e-9: # If opacity is constant in the interval, linear interpolation of CDF might be needed. # Source does not specify this edge case. # Fallback to linear interpolation in probability space? # u is in [Ck, C{k+1}]. Linear interpolation: # t = deltas (u - Ck) / P[k] # But we need Ck. pass terminsidesqrt = tauk2 + (2 deltatau (-math.log((1 - u) / Tsk))) / deltas # Guard against negative sqrt argument due to precision if terminsidesqrt < 0: terminsidesqrt = 0 sqrtval = math.sqrt(terminsidesqrt) t = (deltas / deltatau) (-tauk + sqrtval) # Step 4: Final sample x = sk + t return x Time Complexity: O(N) to find the bin k if cumulative probabilities are not pre-indexed, or O(\log N) with binary search on the cumulative distribution. The calculation of t is O(1). Memory Complexity: Requires storing Pj, sj, \tauj, and T(sj) for all N samples. Performance: Enables better importance sampling and stronger depth supervision, allowing the use of fewer samples (128 coarse, 64 fine) while maintaining total sample count in PL-NeRF. Strengths: Provides an exact closed-form solution for inverse transform sampling, avoiding the discretization errors of piecewise constant opacity. Limitations: Requires piecewise linear opacity assumption and pre-computed interval probabilities. Origin: Introduced in "NeRF Revisited: Fixing Quadrature Instability in Volume Rendering". History: The method addresses the drawback of the CDF being non-invertible and discontinuous under piecewise constant opacity assumptions, which was previously noted in the same work. It builds on the piecewise linear opacity assumption to derive an exact inverse. Usage: Used in PL-NeRF for better importance sampling and depth supervision. name: Piecewise Linear Approximation Inverse
head: Interpolation Functions for L0-Sampler, Inverse Opacity Calculation with Piecewise Linear Density, Quadratic Inverse Sampling, Weight function interpolation, w(t) approximation
body: Piecewise Linear Approximation Inverse is a technique for solving the inverse opacity integral to determine the ray parameter t for a given cumulative density value y during hierarchical volume sampling. It assumes that the density \sigmar(t) varies linearly within each sampling interval, resulting in a piecewise quadratic cumulative density function. This approach is a specific interpolation strategy within the L0-Sampler framework, designed to approximate the L0 property for more precise geometric detail capture compared to standard hierarchical volume sampling. It is simpler than piecewise exponential or inverse variants but focuses sampling less intensely at interval endpoints. Inputs: Ray segment endpoints tn, tf. Pre-computed sample positions t0, t1, \dots, tk where tn = t0 < t1 < \dots < tk = tf. Density values at these positions \sigmar(t0), \sigmar(t1), \dots, \sigmar(tk). Target cumulative density value y (derived from uniform random number u and previous ray opacity). Outputs: Ray parameter t such that the integral of density from tn to t equals y. Data Structures: Arrays for t and \sigmar of size k+1. Scalar y. Steps: 1. Compute the cumulative density up to the start of the current interval i. Let i be the index such that Ci \le y < C{i+1}, where Ci = \sum{j=1}^{i} \frac{\sigmar(tj) + \sigmar(t{j-1})}{2} (tj - t{j-1}). 2. Define the remaining target density \Delta y = y - Ci. The goal is to find \Delta t = t - ti within the interval [ti, t{i+1}] such that the integral from ti to ti + \Delta t equals \Delta y. 3. Under the piecewise linear density assumption, the density at any point ti + \tau (where \tau \in [0, t{i+1}-ti]) is interpolated linearly between \sigmar(ti) and \sigmar(t{i+1}). The integral over this sub-interval results in a quadratic equation in \Delta t: 0 = a\Delta t^2 + b\Delta t + c. 4. Calculate the coefficients: a = \frac{\sigmar(t{i+1}) - \sigmar(ti)}{2}. b = \sigmar(ti) \times (t{i+1} - ti). c = \left( Ci - y \right) \times (t{i+1} - ti). 5. Solve for \Delta t. The standard quadratic formula is: \Delta t = \frac{-b + \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}. 6. Numerical Stability: The standard formula is computationally unstable when a \approx 0. Use the following stable variants: If a \approx 0: \Delta t = -c/b. If b \approx 0: \Delta t = \sqrt{c/a}. Add a small epsilon \epsilon to the square root and denominators for stability. 7. Compute t = ti + \Delta t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def piecewiselinearinverse(t, sigma, y): """ Solve for t given target cumulative density y, assuming piecewise linear density. t: array of sample positions [t0,..., tk] sigma: array of density values [sigma0,..., sigmak] y: target cumulative density value """ k = len(t) - 1 epsilon = 1e-6 # 1. Compute cumulative density up to each sample point C = [0.0] (k + 1) for j in range(1, k + 1): C[j] = C[j-1] + 0.5 (sigma[j] + sigma[j-1]) (t[j] - t[j-1]) # 2. Find the interval i such that C[i] <= y < C[i+1] i = 0 for idx in range(k): if y < C[idx+1]: i = idx break else: return t[k] # 3. Calculate coefficients for the quadratic equation in the current interval dtinterval = t[i+1] - t[i] a = 0.5 (sigma[i+1] - sigma[i]) b = sigma[i] dtinterval c = (C[i] - y) dtinterval # 4. Solve for deltat = t - t[i] with numerical stability if abs(a) < epsilon: deltat = -c / (b + epsilon) elif abs(b) < epsilon: deltat = math.sqrt(c / (a + epsilon)) else: discriminant = b2 - 4ac if discriminant < 0: discriminant = 0 deltat = 2 c / (b + epsilon + math.sqrt(discriminant + epsilon)) # 5. Return t return t[i] + deltat Uses the same density assumption but solves the forward sampling problem (finding y for a given t) or uses a different inversion strategy. Choose when forward mapping is preferred or when the specific L0 property fitting is not required. Assumes density is constant within intervals, leading to a linear cumulative density function. Simpler but less accurate than linear density approximation. Choose for very coarse sampling or when computational cost must be minimized. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Piecewise linear functions are simpler than exponential or inverse variants but focus sampling less intensely at interval endpoints. They provide steady improvements over standard hierarchical volume sampling but are generally outperformed by piecewise exponential functions in terms of consistency and stability across datasets. Strengths: Simple implementation, computationally efficient, better geometric detail capture than constant approximation. Limitations: Less effective at focusing samples at interval endpoints compared to exponential/inverse methods. Numerical stability requires careful handling of the quadratic root, especially when a \approx 0. When to use: When a balance between simplicity and accuracy is needed, or when implementing the L0-Sampler with a linear density assumption. When not to use: When maximum geometric detail capture or endpoint focusing is required, piecewise exponential or inverse variants are preferred. The method is part of the L0-Sampler framework, proposed to improve hierarchical volume sampling in NeRF-based methods. It was introduced in the paper "L0-Sampler: An L0Model Guided Volume Sampling for NeRF". The specific piecewise linear approximation is detailed in the supplementary material of "Differentiable Rendering With Reparameterized Volume Sampling". It is used in NeRF, mip-NeRF, Instant NGP, and NeuS to replace or augment standard sampling strategies. name: Piecewise Constant Approximation Inverse
head: Inverse CDF with Piecewise Constant Density, Piecewise Constant Inverse Sampling
body: Piecewise Constant Approximation Inverse computes the inverse of the density integral along a ray to determine sample positions in inverse opacity sampling. It assumes the density \sigma{\mathbf{r}} is constant within each discrete sample interval [t{j-1}, tj]. This approach differs from its sibling, Piecewise Linear Approximation Inverse, by treating density as a step function rather than a linearly varying one, resulting in a linear equation for the ray parameter t instead of a quadratic one. It builds on Inverse Opacity Calculation by providing an explicit closed-form solution for the ray parameter given a target cumulative density value. Inputs: y: The target cumulative density value (integral of density) to solve for. \{tj\}{j=0}^{N}: The sorted array of sample positions along the ray, where t0 is the entry point and tN is the exit point. \{\hat{\sigma}j\}{j=1}^{N}: The density values sampled at each interval, where \hat{\sigma}j represents the constant density in the interval [t{j-1}, tj]. Outputs: t: The ray parameter such that the integral of density from t0 to t equals y. Data Structures: Arrays t and sigma of size N+1 and N respectively. Precomputed prefix sums of the product \sigma \cdot \Delta t can be used to accelerate the summation, though the direct summation is O(N) per query. Steps: 1. Iterate through the sample intervals j=1, \dots, N to find the index i such that the cumulative integral up to ti is less than or equal to y, and the cumulative integral up to t{i+1} is greater than y. Specifically, find i where: \sum{j=1}^{i} \hat{\sigma}j (tj - t{j-1}) \le y < \sum{j=1}^{i+1} \hat{\sigma}j (tj - t{j-1}) If y exceeds the total integral, clamp t to tN. If y \le 0, return t0. 2. Calculate the cumulative integral up to the start of the identified interval ti: Ci = \sum{j=1}^{i} \hat{\sigma}j (tj - t{j-1}) 3. Solve for t using the linear relationship within the interval [ti, t{i+1}]. The density is assumed constant at \hat{\sigma}i. The formula is derived from: y = Ci + \hat{\sigma}i (t - ti) Rearranging for t: t = ti + \frac{y - Ci}{\hat{\sigma}i} Formula: The explicit solution for t is: t = ti + \frac{y - \sum{j=1}^{i} \hat{\sigma}j (tj - t{j-1})}{\hat{\sigma}i} where \hat{\sigma}i is the density in the interval containing t. (Note: The source text contains a typographical error in the denominator, listing \sigmar(\hat{t}j); the correct term is \sigmar(\hat{t}i) to match the linear derivation.) Parameters: Epsilon (\epsilon): A small positive constant added to the denominator \hat{\sigma}i to prevent division by zero or instability when density is near zero. Typical value: 10^{-6} or machine epsilon scaled by density range. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Density: If \hat{\sigma}i \approx 0, the denominator becomes unstable. The implementation must add a small epsilon value to the denominator to improve stability. Boundary Conditions: If y is outside the range [0, I{total}], the result should be clamped to [t0, tN]. Precision: Floating-point errors in the summation Ci can accumulate. Using Kahan summation or precomputed prefix sums can mitigate this. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def piecewiseconstantinverse(t, sigma, y, epsilon=1e-6): """ Compute the ray parameter t for a given cumulative density y using piecewise constant density approximation. Args: t: Array of sample positions [t0, t1,..., tN] sigma: Array of densities [sigma1,..., sigmaN] for intervals [t0, t1],..., [t{N-1}, tN] y: Target cumulative density value epsilon: Small value to add to denominator for stability Returns: tout: The computed ray parameter """ n = len(sigma) if n == 0: return t[0] # Compute cumulative integrals C[i] = integral from t0 to ti C = [0.0] (n + 1) for j in range(1, n + 1): deltat = t[j] - t[j-1] C[j] = C[j-1] + sigma[j-1] deltat totalintegral = C[n] # Clamp y to valid range if y <= 0.0: return t[0] if y >= totalintegral: return t[n] # Find interval index i such that C[i] <= y < C[i+1] i = 0 for j in range(1, n + 1): if C[j] > y: i = j - 1 break # Solve for t in interval [ti, t{i+1}] using the linear relationship # y = C[i] + sigma[i] (t - t[i]) # Add epsilon to denominator for stability when density is near zero tout = t[i] + (y - C[i]) / (sigma[i] + epsilon) return tout Uses linear interpolation between cumulative weight boundaries rather than assuming constant density within bins, providing smoother sampling distributions. Choose this when higher accuracy in sample placement is needed and the cost of solving a linear interpolation is acceptable. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Linear scan is O(N), binary search O(\log N). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. O(N) for cumulative array, O(1) if computed on the fly. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive per sample, explicit closed-form solution. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Assumes constant density within intervals, which can lead to sampling artifacts if the density varies significantly within an interval. When to use: Not given in the sources. When performance is critical and the density field is relatively smooth or the sampling rate is high enough that the piecewise constant assumption is reasonable. When not to use: Not given in the sources. When high accuracy in sample placement is required for highly varying density fields, or when the density is known to vary linearly within intervals. The method is described in "Differentiable Rendering With Reparameterized Volume Sampling", which derives explicit formulae for the density integral inverse used in inverse opacity sampling.
