name: Inverse CDF Interpolation
head: Inverse CDF Sampling
body: Inverse CDF Interpolation inverts a cumulative distribution function defined by bin endpoints t and weights w at query points u in 0, 1). It maps uniform samples u to the time domain t by [linear interpolation between cumulative weight boundaries. Inputs: wlogits: Raw density scores (logits) for each sample interval along the ray. Shape: (N,) or (B, N) where N is the number of intervals. t: Array of bin endpoints (time/depth values) corresponding to the intervals. Shape: (N+1,). u: Uniform random numbers in 0, 1). Shape: (M,) or (B, M). Outputs: tnew: Sampled time/depth values corresponding to the random inputs u. Data Structures: w: Normalized weights, shape (N,). cw: Cumulative weights ([CDF), shape (N+1,). Steps: 1. Normalize weights: Convert logits to weights using the Softmax function along the last axis. w = torch.softmax(wlogits, dim=-1). 2. Compute CDF: Integrate the weights to form the cumulative distribution function. cw = integrateweights(w). 3. Interpolate: Map the uniform random values u to the time domain t using the inverse CDF. tnew = math.sortedinterp(u, cw, t). Formulas: wi = \frac{\exp(w\logitsi)}{\sum{j} \exp(w\logitsj)} cw0 = 0, \quad cwi = cw{i-1} + w{i-1} \quad \text{for } i = 1 \dots N t\new = ti + (t{i+1} - ti) \frac{u - cwi}{cw{i+1} - cwi} \quad \text{where } cwi \le u < cw{i+1} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def inversecdfinterpolation(wlogits, t, u): # Step 1: Normalize weights using Softmax along the last axis # Source: w = torch.softmax(wlogits, dim=-1) w = torch.softmax(wlogits, dim=-1) # Step 2: Compute cumulative weights (CDF) # Source: cw = integrateweights(w) # cw has shape matching w with an extra element at the start: [0, w0, w0+w1,..., 1] cw = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(w[...,:1]), torch.cumsum(w, dim=-1)], dim=-1) # Step 3: Interpolate u into the inverse CDF using t and cw # Source: tnew = math.sortedinterp(u, cw, t) # Find interval index i such that cw[..., i] <= u < cw[..., i+1] # searchsorted with side='right' returns insertion point i where cw[..., i-1] <= u < cw[..., i] indices = torch.searchsorted(cw, u, side='right') - 1 indices = torch.clamp(indices, min=0, max=w.shape[-1] - 1) # Gather bounds cwlower = cw.gather(-1, indices.unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) cwupper = cw.gather(-1, (indices + 1).unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1) tlower = t[indices] tupper = t[indices + 1] # Linear interpolation denom = cwupper - cwlower denom = torch.where(denom == 0, 1.0, denom) fraction = (u - cwlower) / denom tnew = tlower + fraction (tupper - tlower) return tnew Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Weights: If a bin has zero weight, cwlower equals cwupper. The interpolation fraction becomes undefined. The code handles this by clamping the denominator to 1.0, effectively returning the lower bound tlower. Boundary Conditions: Uniform samples u must be strictly less than 1.0 to avoid index out-of-bounds when searching in cw which ends at 1.0. Clamping u to 1 - epsilon is recommended. Precision: Floating-point errors in cumulative sum may cause cw[-1] to deviate slightly from 1.0. Normalizing cw by cw[-1] can improve robustness. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. name: Proposal Network Sampling
head: Proposal Network, Proposal Network Sampler, PDF Approaches
body: Proposal Network Sampling is a method that uses a coarse Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to directly estimate the Probability Density Function (PDF) along a ray, enabling importance sampling that concentrates samples on high-contribution areas (surfaces) while spreading them in empty or occluded regions. Unlike spatial skipping methods (e.g., RangeFineSampler) which skip empty space entirely, proposal networks always spread samples throughout the space but with varying density, providing more accurate transmittance estimation at the cost of higher sample counts in empty regions. It builds on Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling) by providing the discrete probability distribution via a learned neural estimator rather than a static grid or uniform distribution. Inputs: Ray parameters (origin, direction, near/far planes), coarse MLP weights (trained parameters). Outputs: Sample locations ti along the ray, sampled according to the estimated PDF p(ti). Data Structures: Coarse MLP (Proposal Network): A standard MLP taking ray parameters (e.g., position, direction) as input and outputting density \sigma(t) at queried locations. The size is typically comparable to the shading network. Transmittance Estimator: Implicitly maintained via the density outputs and the exponential transmittance formula. Steps: 1. Training Phase: Train the coarse MLP using volumetric rendering loss to output densities \sigma(ti). 2. PDF Construction: Construct a piece-wise constant PDF from the discrete density outputs: p(ti) = \sigma(ti) \exp(-\sigma(ti) dt) where dt is the distance between samples. 3. Transmittance Estimation: Compute the piece-wise linear transmittance estimator T(ti) for importance sampling: T(ti) = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma(tj) dt\right). 4. Optimization: Update the transmittance estimator (and thus the MLP weights) through gradient descent using the rendering loss. 5. Inference/Sampling: Use the trained PDF p(ti) to sample new locations ti along the ray using inverse CDF sampling (as described in Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling)). Parameters: Network Size: The oracle/proposal network often uses an MLP of the same size as the shading network to generate consistent depth estimates. Update Schedule: In some implementations (e.g., GANeRF), proposal network updates are interpolated based on training steps to balance quality and speed. proposalwarmup: Number of steps for interpolation. proposalupdateevery: Maximum frequency (in steps) for updates. Sharing: A single proposal network can be shared across all proposal iterations via usesameproposalnetwork. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Discontinuities: Accurate estimates around depth discontinuities are difficult, leading to visual artifacts if the oracle predicts exact geometric structures. Mitigation: Allow the oracle to return the same result for all rays around discontinuities (sampling both foreground and background) to make the task easier to learn. Aliasing: Introduces aliasing effects due to the piece-wise linearity assumption for estimating transmittance along the ray. No Skipping: Samples are always spread out throughout the entire space without any skipping, which can be less efficient than spatial skipping in highly empty scenes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class ProposalNetwork(nn.Module): """Coarse MLP estimating density sigma(t) along a ray.""" def init(self, inputdim=6, hiddendim=256, numlayers=4): super().init() layers = [] for i in range(numlayers): layers.append(nn.Linear(inputdim if i == 0 else hiddendim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1)) self.network = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, rayorigins, raydirections, tvals): """Query density at sample points along rays. Args: rayorigins: (N, 3) raydirections: (N, 3) tvals: (N, K) distances along ray Returns: sigmas: (N, K) estimated density """ pts = rayorigins[:, None,:] + tvals[:,:, None] raydirections[:, None,:] ptsflat = pts.reshape(-1, 3) raydirsflat = raydirections[:, None,:].expand(-1, tvals.shape[1], -1).reshape(-1, 3) inputvec = torch.cat([ptsflat, raydirsflat], dim=-1) sigma = self.network(inputvec).squeeze(-1) return sigma.reshape(rayorigins.shape[0], tvals.shape[1]) def samplefromproposalnetwork(proposalnet, rayorigins, raydirections, numsamples, nearplane, farplane): """Sample locations along the ray using the proposal network's estimated PDF.""" # 1. Initialize initial samples (e.g., uniform) tvals = torch.linspace(nearplane, farplane, numsamples + 1).to(rayorigins.device) tmids = 0.5 (tvals[:-1] + tvals[1:]) # 2. Query proposal network for densities sigmas = proposalnet(rayorigins, raydirections, tmids) # 3. Compute dt and PDF dt = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] # PDF: p(ti) = sigma(ti) exp(-sigma(ti) dt) pdf = sigmas torch.exp(-sigmas dt) # Normalize PDF to sum to 1 over the ray pdfsum = pdf.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) pdfnormalized = pdf / (pdfsum + 1e-10) # 4. Inverse CDF sampling cdf = torch.cumsum(pdfnormalized, dim=-1) cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[:,:1]), cdf], dim=-1) # Generate uniform random numbers u = torch.randlike(cdf[:,:-1]) # Find bin indices indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf[:,:-1], u, right=True) # Interpolate t within the bin tlow = tmids[torch.arange(u.shape[0]), indices] thigh = tmids[torch.arange(u.shape[0]), indices + 1] cdflow = cdf[torch.arange(u.shape[0]), indices] cdfhigh = cdf[torch.arange(u.shape[0]), indices + 1] tsample = tlow + (u - cdflow) / (cdfhigh - cdflow + 1e-10) (thigh - tlow) return tsample A technique to dilate proposal histograms to reduce aliasing artifacts caused by the proposal MLP being supervised only on rays corresponding to input pixels. It widens the intervals of the proposal MLP to counteract rotational aliasing. Method: Compute probability density \hat{p}i = \hat{w}i / (\hat{s}{i+1} - \hat{s}i) from histogram (\hat{s}, \hat{w}). Dilate by computing \max{s-\epsilon \leq s' < s+\epsilon} \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}{\hat{\boldsymbol{s}}}(s'). Construct new intervals with endpoints \text{sort}(\hat{s} \cup \hat{s} - \epsilon \cup \hat{s} + \epsilon). Compute max of all intervals in expanded set. Convert dilated \hat{p} back to histogram by multiplying by interval size. Normalize histogram to sum to 1. Parameters: Dilation factor \epsilonk = \frac{a}{\prod{k'=1}^{k-1} n{k'}} + b where n{k'} is the sample count at level k'. Hyperparameters a = 0.5 and b = 0.0025. A chunked rendering pipeline that uses a PropNetEstimator to sample from a sequence of proposal networks, then composites results using the main radiance field. Method: Define propsigmafn to query proposal networks at midpoints. Define rgbsigmafn to query the radiance field for RGB and sigma at midpoints. Loop over rays in chunks. Call estimator.sampling with a list of proposal sigma functions, propsamples per network, total numsamples, and samplingtype. Call rendering with tstarts, tends, rayindices=None, nrays=None, and rgbsigmafn to composite. Collate chunk results using torch.cat for tensors and reshape to image dimensions. A mechanism to predict the importance of each proposal sample to reduce computational burden by querying the fine network only on important samples. Method: The proposer predicts importance scores by regressing another set of Nc + Nf scalars using the same mechanism as proposal generation (e.g., a fully connected head on the 'ray representation' vector). Training uses the weight wi that each fine sample contributes to the final rendering as the target signal. Threshold these weights at 0.03 to define positive (important) and negative (unimportant) samples. Train the predictor using balanced logistic regression loss. Parameters: Importance threshold: 0.03. A method where a deep neural network models the probability density function of samples to guide the ray's outgoing direction. It is independent from scenes and local point parameters (e.g., including the textured BRDF). However, the method is biased and sampling is very expensive. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples and the cost of querying the proposal MLP. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the proposal MLP weights. Performance: Provides more accurate transmittance estimation, concentrating samples on surfaces and spreading them in empty/occluded regions. However, it introduces aliasing effects due to piece-wise linearity assumptions. Strengths: Adaptive sampling based on learned scene structure; effective for complex scenes with varying density. Limitations: Samples are always spread out without skipping, which can be inefficient in highly empty scenes compared to spatial skipping methods. Difficult to learn accurate estimates around depth discontinuities. When to use: When accurate transmittance estimation is critical and the scene has complex density variations that uniform or grid-based sampling cannot efficiently capture. When not to use: When memory or compute is severely constrained and the scene is mostly empty (spatial skipping may be better). Proposal Network Sampling originated from the need to improve importance sampling in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). It was introduced in Mip-NeRF 360, which proposed using a smaller "Proposal Network" MLP to speed up PDF construction while maintaining accuracy. The method is part of a broader class of "PDF Approaches" that directly estimate the PDF along the ray, as opposed to "Spatial Skipping" approaches like Occupancy Grids. It builds on the concept of transmittance-based importance sampling, where the transmittance estimator is updated through gradient descent during optimization. Variants include using depth oracle networks for compact representations and learning sample importance to reduce fine network queries. name: Occupancy Proposal Sampling
head: Occupancy Proposal Network Sampling, Proposal Network Sampler
body: Occupancy Proposal Sampling is a ray sampling strategy that queries a lightweight occupancy proposal network at uniform intervals along each camera ray, then selects additional samples based on the initial samples to accelerate rendering. It differs from its parent, Proposal Network Sampling, by specifically utilizing an occupancy-based signal and employing separate hash table-backed static and dynamic branches for temporal scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray r, current time t (for dynamic scenes), and the lightweight proposal network parameters. Output: A set of sample positions \{ti\} and associated weights \{wi\} along the ray r for volume rendering integration. Data Structures: The proposal network is modeled with separate hash table-backed static and dynamic branches. Static Branch: Stores geometry that does not change over time. Dynamic Branch: Stores geometry that changes over time. Hash Table: Used for efficient spatial hashing of features in both branches. Steps: 1. Uniform Query: Query the lightweight occupancy proposal network at uniform intervals along the camera ray r within the viewing range (typically t0 \in [-1, 1]). 2. Sample Selection: Pick additional samples based on the initial samples, guided by occupancy values to concentrate samples in the area where the first surface intersects. 3. Branch Separation: Maintain separate static and dynamic branches, each backed by a hash table. 4. Histogram Loss Training: Train each branch using histogram loss with the weights of the respective branch of the main model as the target distribution. The loss is computed as Lf(r) = \sum{t0 \in [-1,1]} |F(r) - \hat{F}{t0}(r)|, where F(r) is the cumulative opacity from the main model and \hat{F}{t0}(r) is the cumulative opacity from the proposal network. 5. Distortion Loss Regularization: Regularize the resulting sample distances and weights using distortion loss. Parameters: Speedup Factor: 2-4x compared to uniform sampling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Hash table collisions may affect accuracy in high-density regions. Boundaries: The uniform query range must cover the entire visible scene; clipping errors can occur if the frustum is not correctly defined. Degenerate Input: If the scene is empty or fully transparent, the proposal network may return uniform occupancy, degrading to uniform sampling. A generalizable learned sampler conditioned on cheap low-resolution information to enable full-resolution rendering during training, replacing dense uniform sampling. The sampler is a scene-conditional proposal network that generalizes across scenes, inspired by density estimators, instead of being category-specific or optimized per-scene. It operates on a per-ray basis to adaptively accelerate rendering. The sampler allows the method to operate with just 20 samples per ray, compared to existing 3D GANs which must use at least 96 samples per ray. The approach uses up to 5 times fewer depth samples than dense sampling methods. Unlike acceleration structures like octrees which are limited to coarse or category-specific acceleration, this sampling-based method generalizes to every new scene. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of uniform query points plus the number of additional samples. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the hash tables for the static and dynamic branches. Measured Performance: Provides a 2-4x speedup compared to uniform sampling. Scaling: Scales well with dynamic scenes due to the separation of static and dynamic branches. Strengths: Significant speedup; handles dynamic scenes effectively via branch separation. Limitations: Requires training the proposal network; may introduce artifacts if the proposal network is poorly trained. When to Use: When rendering speed is critical and the scene has significant empty space or occluders. When Not to Use: When the scene is uniformly dense, as the overhead of the proposal network may not be justified. Originated in the context of scalable urban dynamic scenes, specifically in the SUDS method. It builds on the idea of using lightweight networks to guide sampling, extending it to dynamic scenes with separate static and dynamic branches. name: Ray-Conditioned Sample Prediction with Geometric Primitives
head: E_phi network, HyperReel sampling
body: This method predicts sample locations for volume rendering by intersecting input rays with predicted geometric primitives, ensuring multi-view consistency and efficient sampling. It differs from sibling methods like Occupancy Proposal Sampling by explicitly modeling sample positions as intersections with world-space primitives (planes or spheres) rather than discrete probability distributions or occupancy grids. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \vec{\omega}. Output: A set of n sample points \{\mathbf{x}k\}{k=1}^n and associated scalar values \{\deltak\}{k=1}^n used to compute weights. Data Structures: Ray Representation: Plücker coordinates \mathbf{r} = (\vec{\omega}, \vec{\omega} \times \mathbf{o}). Network E\phi: A 6-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with 256 hidden units and Leaky ReLU activations. Geometric Primitives Gk: Defined in the world coordinate frame. The network outputs parameters defining these primitives based on the input ray. For forward-facing scenes: n=32 axis-aligned z-planes. For other scenes: n=32 concentric spherical shells centered at the origin. Offsets: Per-sample displacement vectors \mathbf{e}k. Scalars: Per-sample scalar values \deltak. Steps: 1. Reparameterize Ray: Convert ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \vec{\omega} into Plücker coordinates: \mathbf{r} = \text{Plucker}(\mathbf{o}, \vec{\omega}) = (\vec{\omega}, \vec{\omega} \times \mathbf{o}) 2. Predict Primitives: Pass \mathbf{r} through network E\phi to predict parameters for n geometric primitives \{G1, \dots, Gn\}. 3. Intersect Ray: Compute initial sample points \mathbf{x}k by intersecting the ray with each primitive Gk: \mathbf{x}k = \text{inter}(Gk; \mathbf{o}, \vec{\omega}) Note: \text{inter} is a differentiable operation. 4. Predict Offsets and Scalars: The network also outputs per-sample displacement vectors \mathbf{e}k and scalar values \deltak. 5. Compute Displacement: Calculate the final displacement \mathbf{d}k by scaling the offset \mathbf{e}k with the sigmoid of \deltak: \mathbf{d}k = \gamma(\deltak) \mathbf{e}k where \gamma is the sigmoid operator. 6. Update Samples: Add the displacement to the initial intersection points: \mathbf{x}k^{\text{new}} = \mathbf{x}k + \mathbf{d}k Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class RayConditionedSampler(nn.Module): def init(self, numprimitives=32, scenetype='forward'): super().init() self.numprimitives = numprimitives self.scenetype = scenetype # 6-layer MLP, 256 hidden units, Leaky ReLU # Outputs: primitive params (varies by type), offsets (3 numprimitives), scalars (numprimitives) self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(6, 256), nn.LeakyReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.LeakyReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.LeakyReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.LeakyReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.LeakyReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 3 numprimitives + numprimitives + self.getprimitivedim())) def getprimitivedim(self): if self.scenetype == 'forward': return 1 # z-plane position else: return 1 # sphere radius def forward(self, rayorigins, raydirections): # 1. Reparameterize to Plucker coordinates # r = (omega, omega x o) cross = torch.cross(raydirections, rayorigins, dim=-1) plucker = torch.cat([raydirections, cross], dim=-1) # Shape: (..., 6) # 2. Predict network outputs # Note: In practice, primitive params might be shared or ray-dependent. # Based on, Ephi takes ray as input. # We assume the network outputs primitive parameters, offsets, and scalars. # For simplicity, assuming primitive params are also ray-dependent or fixed per scene type. # The source implies Ephi(o, w) -> (G1...Gn, e1...en, delta1...deltan). # Let's assume the last layer outputs primitive params + offsets + scalars. # Adjust input dim if primitive params are ray-dependent. # If primitives are fixed per scene (e.g. just z-planes at fixed z), # the network might only predict offsets/scalars. # However, says "predict a set of geometric primitives... defined in world coordinate frame". # And "primitive parameters themselves are a function of the input ray". # So we predict primitive params too. out = self.net(plucker) # Split outputs primdim = self.getprimitivedim() primparams = out[...,:self.numprimitives primdim] offsets = out[..., self.numprimitives primdim: self.numprimitives primdim + self.numprimitives 3] scalars = out[..., self.numprimitives primdim + self.numprimitives 3:] # Reshape primparams = primparams.view(-1, self.numprimitives, primdim) offsets = offsets.view(-1, self.numprimitives, 3) scalars = scalars.view(-1, self.numprimitives) # 3. Intersect ray with primitives to get initial points # This depends on primitive type. if self.scenetype == 'forward': # Axis-aligned z-planes. Plane equation: z = zk # Ray: o + t w. Intersection: t = (zk - oz) / wz zplanes = primparams[..., 0] # Shape: (..., numprimitives) # Avoid division by zero wz = raydirections[..., 2:3] t = (zplanes - rayorigins[..., 2:3]) / wz initialpoints = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + t.unsqueeze(-1) raydirections.unsqueeze(1) else: # Concentric spherical shells. Sphere: |x|^2 = rk^2 # Ray: o + t w. Intersection: |o + tw|^2 = r^2 => t^2 + 2(o.w)t + |o|^2 - r^2 = 0 radii = primparams[..., 0] # Shape: (..., numprimitives) radiisq = radii 2 odotw = torch.sum(rayorigins raydirections, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # (..., 1) osq = torch.sum(rayorigins 2, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # (..., 1) # Quadratic formula: t = (-B - sqrt(B^2 - 4AC)) / 2A, where A=1, B=2(o.w), C=|o|^2 - r^2 # We want the closest intersection in front of the camera (t > 0) # Discriminant disc = 4 odotw 2 - 4 (osq - radiisq) # Clamp disc to avoid NaNs disc = torch.clamp(disc, min=0.0) sqrtdisc = torch.sqrt(disc) # Two solutions t1 = (-2 odotw - sqrtdisc) / 2.0 t2 = (-2 odotw + sqrtdisc) / 2.0 # Choose the smallest positive t # If both negative, pick the least negative (closest to origin)? Or ignore? # Standard ray marching usually picks the first hit. # Let's pick the smallest t that is > 0. If none, pick smallest t. t = torch.where(t1 > 0, t1, t2) t = torch.where(t2 > 0, t2, t) # This logic is flawed if both > 0. # Correct logic: tcandidates = torch.stack([t1, t2], dim=-1) # (..., numprimitives, 2) # Filter for t > 0 valid = tcandidates > 0 # If no valid, use min(t1, t2) tmin = torch.min(t1, t2) t = torch.where(valid.any(dim=-1), tcandidates[valid].view(tcandidates.shape[0], -1).min(dim=-1)[0], tmin) initialpoints = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + t.unsqueeze(-1) raydirections.unsqueeze(1) # 4. Compute displacement # dk = sigmoid(deltak) ek weights = torch.sigmoid(scalars) # (..., numprimitives) weights = weights.unsqueeze(-1) # (..., numprimitives, 1) displacements = weights offsets # (..., numprimitives, 3) # 5. Update samples finalpoints = initialpoints + displacements return finalpoints, scalars Parameters: Network Architecture: 6-layer MLP, 256 hidden units, Leaky ReLU. Number of Primitives: 32. Initialization: Scalar values \deltak should be initialized to negative values to keep the sigmoid output close to 0 and gradients small, preventing premature unmasking of point offsets. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization: Failing to initialize \deltak to negative values may cause the network to unmask point offsets prematurely during training, leading to instability. Ray-Primitive Intersection: The intersection operation must be differentiable. Degenerate rays (e.g., wz=0 for z-planes) require handling to avoid division by zero. Time Complexity: The method requires a single forward pass through the network E\phi per ray, followed by n intersection calculations. This is significantly faster than importance sampling methods that require hundreds or thousands of queries. Memory Complexity: Depends on the network size (6-layer MLP) and the storage of primitive parameters and offsets. Performance: Enables real-time rendering with low sample counts. Strengths: Multi-view consistency is inherent because primitives are defined in world space; if two rays observe the same point, the network predicts the same primitive. Flexible modeling of complex view-dependent appearance, such as distorted refractions. Limitations: The initial sample points lie along the ray, which may be less flexible than other methods. Origin: Introduced in "HyperReel: High-Fidelity 6-DoF Video with Ray-Conditioned Sampling". History: Developed to address the high sample counts required by traditional importance sampling in volume rendering. Usage: Used for high-fidelity 6-DoF video synthesis, including static and dynamic scenes. name: RangeFineSampler
body: RangeFineSampler is a hierarchical sampling technique for direct volume ray casting that refines coarse samples by generating a dense uniform grid around the coarse sample with the highest weight, supplemented by random samples across the full ray extent. It addresses missing high-frequency details between coarse samples by concentrating computational effort near the most significant signal while maintaining global coverage through random jittering. Unlike Inverse Opacity Calculation which derives samples from opacity gradients, or Proposal Network Sampling which uses learned neural networks to predict sample locations, RangeFineSampler relies on a deterministic geometric expansion around the peak weight index combined with stochastic uniform sampling. The method takes coarse sample positions and weights as input and outputs a refined set of sample positions along the ray. It operates on batches of rays, where each ray has a set of coarse z-values (depths) and corresponding weights. Inputs: coarsezvals: Tensor of shape (numrays, numcoarsesamples) containing the depth positions of coarse samples. coarseweights: Tensor of shape (numrays, numcoarsesamples) containing the importance weights for each coarse sample. near: Float, the near plane distance of the ray. far: Float, the far plane distance of the ray. maxsamples: Integer, the maximum total number of samples allowed per ray. Nsamples: Integer, the number of fine samples to generate around the peak. range: Float, the total width of the interval around the max weight z-value where uniform samples are placed. Default is 0.5. deterministic: Boolean, whether to use stratified sampling or pure random jittering. Outputs: zvalsret: Tensor of shape (numrays, numtotalsamples) containing the sorted, refined sample positions. Data Structures: The implementation uses batched tensor indexing and sorting operations. Steps: 1. Determine Effective Sample Count: Calculate the number of fine samples to generate around the peak. This is bounded by maxsamples and Nsamples. N{fine} = \min(\text{max\samples}, N{samples}) 2. Find Peak Weight Index: Identify the index of the coarse sample with the maximum weight for each ray. \text{max\indices} = \text{argmax}{dim=-1}(\text{coarse\weights}) 3. Retrieve Peak Z-Value: Get the depth value corresponding to the peak weight for each ray. \text{max\z\vals} = \text{coarse\z\vals}[\text{arange}(\text{num\rays}), \text{max\indices}] 4. Generate Uniform Samples Around Peak: Create a uniform grid of N{fine} samples centered around maxzvals. The source defines range as the total width, but the code formula uses 2 range, effectively making range a half-width in implementation. The formula distributes points evenly across this interval. z{fine} = \text{max\z\vals}[:, \text{None}] - \text{range} + \frac{2 \cdot \text{range}}{N{fine} - 1} \cdot \text{arange}(N{fine}) 5. Apply Stratified Sampling (Optional): If deterministic is False, apply stratified jittering to the uniform samples to reduce aliasing. Compute midpoints between adjacent uniform samples: \text{mids} = 0.5 \cdot (z{fine}[:, 1:] + z{fine}[:,:-1]) Define intervals: \text{lower} = \text{concat}([z{fine}[:,:1], \text{mids}], \text{dim}=-1) \text{upper} = \text{concat}([\text{mids}, z{fine}[:, -1:]], \text{dim}=-1) Generate random jitter: t{rand} = \text{rand}(z{fine}.shape) Jitter the samples: z{fine} = \text{lower} + (\text{upper} - \text{lower}) \cdot t{rand} If deterministic is True, z{fine} remains the uniform grid from Step 4. 6. Generate Random Samples Across Full Range: Generate N{fine} random samples uniformly distributed between near and far for each ray. z{add} = \text{rand}((\text{num\rays}, N{fine})) \cdot (\text{far} - \text{near}) + \text{near} 7. Combine and Sort (Global): Concatenate the original coarse samples with the random samples z{add} and sort them. z{base} = \text{sort}(\text{concat}([\text{coarse\z\vals}, z{add}], \text{dim}=-1), \text{dim}=-1) 8. Inject Fine Samples for Non-Edge Rays: For rays where the peak index is not at the very beginning (index > 0), concatenate the structured fine samples z{fine} with the coarse samples and sort. \text{mask} = \text{max\indices} > 0 z{ret}[\text{mask}] = \text{sort}(\text{concat}([\text{coarse\z\vals}[\text{mask}], z{fine}[\text{mask}]], \text{dim}=-1), \text{dim}=-1) For rays where maxindices == 0, the sorted combination of coarse and random samples (z{base}) is used. 9. Return Result: The final tensor z{ret} contains the sorted sample positions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def rangefinesampler(coarsezvals, coarseweights, near, far, maxsamples, Nsamples, rangeval, deterministic=True): """ RangeFineSampler implementation. Args: coarsezvals: (numrays, numcoarse) Tensor of coarse sample depths. coarseweights: (numrays, numcoarse) Tensor of coarse sample weights. near: Float, near plane. far: Float, far plane. maxsamples: Int, max total samples. Nsamples: Int, number of fine samples to generate around peak. rangeval: Float, width of interval around peak. deterministic: Bool, use stratified sampling. Returns: zvalsret: (numrays, numtotal) Tensor of sorted sample depths. """ numrays, numcoarse = coarsezvals.shape # Step 1: Determine effective sample count Nfine = min(maxsamples, Nsamples) # Step 2: Find peak weight index maxindices = torch.argmax(coarseweights, dim=-1) # Step 3: Retrieve peak z-values arangerays = torch.arange(numrays).to(coarsezvals.device) maxzvals = coarsezvals[arangerays, maxindices] # Step 4: Generate uniform samples around peak # Handle Nfine = 1 case to avoid division by zero if Nfine == 1: zfine = maxzvals.unsqueeze(1) else: arangefine = torch.arange(Nfine).to(coarsezvals.device) zfine = maxzvals.unsqueeze(1) - rangeval + (2 rangeval / (Nfine - 1)) arangefine.unsqueeze(0) # Step 5: Stratified sampling if not deterministic: mids = 0.5 (zfine[:, 1:] + zfine[:,:-1]) lower = torch.cat([zfine[:,:1], mids], dim=-1) upper = torch.cat([mids, zfine[:, -1:]], dim=-1) trand = torch.rand(zfine.shape, device=coarsezvals.device) zfine = lower + (upper - lower) trand # Step 6: Generate random samples across full range zadd = torch.rand((numrays, Nfine), device=coarsezvals.device) (far - near) + near # Step 7: Combine coarse and random, sort zvalsret = torch.sort(torch.cat([coarsezvals, zadd], dim=-1), dim=-1)[0] # Step 8: Inject fine samples for rays where maxindices > 0 mask = maxindices > 0 if mask.any(): zcombined = torch.cat([coarsezvals[mask], zfine[mask]], dim=-1) zvalsret[mask] = torch.sort(zcombined, dim=-1)[0] return zvalsret Parameters: range: Float, default 0.5. body: Inverse Sampling for Fine Rays is a hierarchical sampling technique in volume rendering that generates fine-grained sample positions along a ray by leveraging the probability distribution derived from a prior coarse rendering pass. It concentrates samples in regions of high importance rather than using uniform spacing. It differs from its parent, Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling), by explicitly mapping discrete coarse weights to continuous fine depths via inverse CDF interpolation. It differs from Inverse Opacity Calculation by operating on pre-computed coarse weights rather than deriving probabilities from opacity accumulation during the fine pass. Inputs and Outputs: Input: zvals (coarse sample depths, shape [batch, numcoarsesamples]), weights (coarse sample importance weights, shape [batch, numcoarsesamples]), numfinesamples (integer, number of fine samples to generate per ray). Output: zvalsfine (fine sample depths, shape [batch, numfinesamples]). Data Structures: zvals: 1D array of depths along the ray. weights: 1D array of non-negative importance weights corresponding to zvals. Steps: 1. Normalize Weights: Compute the probability mass function (PMF) by normalizing the coarse weights. pi = \frac{wi}{\sum{j} wj} where wi is the weight at index i. If \sum wj = 0, use uniform distribution pi = 1/N. 2. Compute CDF: Compute the cumulative distribution function (CDF) from the PMF. ci = \sum{k=0}^{i} pk Ensure c{N-1} = 1.0 to handle floating-point errors. 3. Generate Uniform Random Numbers: Generate M uniform random numbers u \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1) for each ray in the batch. 4. Inverse CDF Sampling: For each random number u, find the index i such that c{i-1} < u \le ci. Interpolate between z{i-1} and zi to find the continuous depth. z{fine} = z{i-1} + \frac{u - c{i-1}}{ci - c{i-1}} (zi - z{i-1}) If u > c{N-1}, clamp to z{N-1}. 5. Sort and Concatenate: The parent class RaySampler concatenates additionaldepths to zvals if provided, sorts them, and computes points via points = (camloc.unsqueeze(1) + zvals.unsqueeze(2) raydirs.unsqueeze(1)). Flat CDF: Interpolation denominator becomes zero; handled by clamping or fallback. Boundary conditions: Clamping indices to valid range. body: Piecewise-Constant PDF Sampling generates sample coordinates from a discrete probability distribution defined by bin endpoints and logits by inverting the cumulative distribution function (CDF). It differs from sibling methods by explicitly constructing a step-wise CDF from softmax-normalized weights and using inverse interpolation to map uniform random variables to bin centers or intervals, ensuring samples respect the learned probability mass of each bin. Inputs: t: Tensor of shape [..., numbins + 1] containing sorted bin endpoint coordinates. wlogits: Tensor of shape [..., numbins] containing raw logits for bin weights. numsamples: Integer specifying the number of samples to draw. rng: Optional random number generator. If None, deterministic sampling is used. deterministiccenter: Boolean. If True, deterministic samples are centered within bins; otherwise, they span the full range. singlejitter: Boolean. If True, all samples along a ray share the same jitter offset; if False, each sample gets independent jitter. eps: Machine epsilon for the dtype of t, used to prevent boundary issues (e.g., torch.finfo(t.dtype).eps). Outputs: tsamples: Tensor of shape [..., numsamples] containing the sampled coordinates. Data Structures: CDF (cw): Cumulative sum of softmax weights, excluding the last bin, clamped to a maximum of 1. Shape [..., numbins]. Full CDF (cw0): Concatenation of 0, cw, and 1 along the last axis. Shape [..., numbins + 2]. Steps: 1. Compute Probabilities: Calculate the probability density function (PDF) weights w by applying softmax to wlogits along the last axis: w = \text{softmax}(w{\text{logits}}, \text{dim}=-1) 2. Construct CDF: Compute the cumulative distribution function cw by taking the cumulative sum of the weights excluding the last bin, and clamp the maximum value to 1: cw = \text{clamp}{\max}(1, \text{cumsum}(w[...,:-1], \text{dim}=-1)) 3. Generate Uniform Samples (u): Deterministic (rng is None): If deterministiccenter is True: Generate u using linspace over [pad, 1 - pad - eps], where pad = 1 / (2 numsamples). This centers samples within the PDF intervals. Else: Generate u using linspace over [0, 1 - eps]. Stochastic (rng is not None): Calculate umax = eps + (1 - eps) / numsamples. Calculate maxjitter = (1 - umax) / (numsamples - 1) - eps. Determine jitter dimension d: 1 if singlejitter is True, else numsamples. Generate base linspace ubase = \text{linspace}(0, 1 - u{\text{max}}, \text{num\samples}). Generate random jitter j = \text{rand}(t.\text{shape}[:-1] + (d,)). Compute final u: u = u{\text{base}} + j \times \text{max\jitter} Note: If rng is provided but singlejitter is False, the jitter shape must broadcast correctly with t's batch dimensions. 4. Interpolate Samples: Map the uniform samples u to the coordinate space t using the inverse CDF. This is implemented via sorted interpolation between the full CDF cw0 and the bin endpoints t: t{\text{samples}} = \text{sorted\interp}(u, cw0, t) The full CDF cw0 is constructed as: cw0 = \text{concat}([0, cw, 1], \text{dim}=-1) sortedinterp performs linear interpolation based on the sorted values of cw0. Args: t: [..., numbins + 1], sorted bin endpoint coordinates. wlogits: [..., numbins], logits for bin weights. numsamples: int, number of samples to draw. rng: Optional random number generator. If None, uses deterministic linspace. deterministiccenter: bool, if True, centers samples in bins for deterministic case. singlejitter: bool, if True, uses same jitter for all samples along a ray. eps: float, machine epsilon. cwleft # denom = torch.where(denom == 0, 1.0, denom) # Avoid division by zero # tsamples = tleft + (u - cwleft) / denom (tright - tleft) # Note: The source uses math.sortedinterp which likely handles this efficiently. # For pure Python/PyTorch implementation: # Expand u for searchsorted uexpanded = u.unsqueeze(-1) # [..., numsamples, 1] cw0expanded = cw0.unsqueeze(-2) # [..., 1, numbins+2] # Find indices indices = torch.searchsorted(cw0expanded, uexpanded, side='right') - The method operates on a set of weights associated with discrete elements, selecting a specified number of unique indices. It validates inputs, normalizes weights, and delegates the sampling operation to either PyTorch or NumPy based on the size of the input data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: weights (1D tensor of non-negative weights), n (integer, number of samples to draw), replacement (boolean, default True in general definition, but False in specific implementation context for unique selection). Output: A tensor of selected indices. Data Structures: weights: A 1D PyTorch tensor. If using the NumPy fallback, it is converted to a NumPy array. indices: The list or tensor of indices from which weights are drawn. In the specific implementation, weights are extracted corresponding to provided indices. Steps: 1. Validate n: Check if n is a non-negative integer. If n is 0, set n to the length of the weights. 2. Extract Weights: If indices are provided, extract the corresponding weights and convert them to a PyTorch tensor of type double (float64). 3. Check Size Threshold: Determine the number of elements (numelements) in the weight distribution. 4. Branch Execution: If numelements > 2^{24}: Normalize the weights so they sum to 1. Convert the weights to a NumPy array. Sample indices using np.random.choice with the normalized weights and replace=False (for unique sampling). Convert the resulting indices back to a PyTorch tensor. Move the tensor to the original device. Else: Use torch.multinomial with the weights, n, and replacement=False. Yield the corresponding indices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def multinomialsamplingfallback(weights, n, replacement=False): """ Selects n indices from weights using multinomial sampling. Falls back to NumPy for large tensors to avoid PyTorch limitations. Args: weights: 1D Tensor of weights. n: Integer, number of samples to draw. replacement: Boolean, whether to sample with replacement. Returns: Tensor of selected indices. """ # Validate n if not isinstance(n, int) or n < 0: raise ValueError("n must be a non-negative integer") # If n is 0, sample all elements if n == 0: n = len(weights) # Ensure weights are double precision for numerical stability weights = weights.double() # Threshold for fallback THRESHOLD = 224 if len(weights) > THRESHOLD: # Fallback to NumPy # Normalize weights sumweights = torch.sum(weights) if sumweights == 0: # Handle degenerate case: uniform distribution if all weights are zero probs = torch.oneslike(weights) / len(weights) else: probs = weights / sumweights # Convert to NumPy probsnp = probs.cpu().numpy() # Sample using NumPy # Note: np.random.choice does not support direct probability array in older versions, # but modern versions do. We assume standard behavior. indicesnp = np.random.choice(len(probsnp), size=n, replace=replacement, p=probsnp) # Convert back to Tensor and move to original device indices = torch.fromnumpy(indicesnp).to(weights.device) return indices else: # Native PyTorch sampling indices = torch.multinomial(weights, numsamples=n, replacement=replacement) return indices Parameters: weights: 1D Tensor of weights for each element. n: Integer, number of samples to draw. replacement: Boolean, whether to sample with replacement. Default True in general definition, but False in the specific implementation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Weights: If all weights are zero, normalization fails. The implementation should handle this by defaulting to a uniform distribution. Device Mismatch: The NumPy fallback requires moving data to CPU, which can be slow. Ensure the final tensor is moved back to the original device. Precision: Weights are converted to double to maintain precision during normalization and sampling. Time Complexity: O(N) for normalization and conversion, where N is the number of elements. Sampling is O(n) for n samples. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing weights and intermediate arrays. Performance: The fallback is triggered for N > 2^{24}, avoiding potential memory or performance issues in PyTorch's multinomial for very large tensors. Strengths: Robustness for large-scale data, compatibility with both PyTorch and NumPy ecosystems. Limitations: Device transfer overhead when using NumPy fallback. Not differentiable w.r.t. camera intrinsics in some contexts. The method is used in 3D Gaussian Splatting implementations, such as splatad and guassian-diffusion, to handle aliasing and efficient sampling of Gaussian primitives. It is part of a broader effort to optimize rendering pipelines for large-scale 3D scenes. carlinds/splatad, https://github.com/carlinds/splatad, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) pbonazzi/guassian-diffusion, https://github.com/pbonazzi/guassian-diffusion, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: PMF Sampling
head: Discrete Distribution Sampler with Replacement, Inverse CDF Sampling for Discrete PMF, Weighted Subset Random Sampler
body: PMF Sampling draws indices from a discrete probability mass function (PMF) with replacement, using inverse transform sampling via the cumulative distribution function (CDF). It differs from its sibling Multinomial Sampling Fallback by explicitly constructing the CDF and using search operations to map uniform random variables to indices, rather than relying on library-specific multinomial primitives or fallback logic. It is chosen when deterministic CDF-based mapping is required for gradient flow or reproducibility in stochastic sampling pipelines. Inputs: pmf: A tensor of shape [batchsize, shape, nsamples, 1] representing the probability mass function. The sum along dimension -2 (the nsamples dimension) must equal 1.0. nsamples: An integer specifying the number of samples to draw. If 0, the number of samples defaults to the length of the support dimension (nsamples in the input tensor). Outputs: indices: A tensor of sampled indices, reshaped to match the original batch and shape dimensions, with the last dimension being the number of drawn samples. Data Structures: cdf: A tensor of the same shape as pmf, where each element is the cumulative sum of pmf along the support dimension. Steps: 1. Filter Weights: If the sampler is initialized with a subset of indices, filter the pmf weights to match these indices. 2. Normalize: Ensure the pmf sums to 1 along the support dimension. 3. Compute CDF: Calculate the cumulative distribution function along the support dimension (dim=-2). \text{CDF}i = \sum{j=0}^{i} \text{PMF}j 4. Determine Sample Count: If nsamples is 0, set it to the size of the support dimension. Otherwise, use the provided nsamples. 5. Generate Randoms: Generate nsamples uniform random numbers u \in [0, 1) for each sample. 6. Search Sorted: Use searchsorted to find the index k in the CDF such that \text{CDF}{k-1} < u \leq \text{CDF}k. This maps the uniform random value to the corresponding index in the support. 7. Clamp and Reshape: Clamp the resulting indices to the valid range [0, \text{support\size} - 1] to handle edge cases (e.g., u=1.0 due to floating point precision). Reshape the indices to the original batch and shape dimensions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def pmfsampling(pmf: torch.Tensor, nsamples: int) -> torch.Tensor: """ Samples indices from a discrete PMF with replacement using inverse CDF. Args: pmf: Tensor of shape [batchsize, shape, nsupport, 1]. Sum along dim=-2 must be 1. nsamples: Number of samples to draw. If 0, defaults to nsupport. Returns: indices: Tensor of sampled indices. """ # 1. Ensure pmf sums to 1 along the support dimension (dim=-2) # Add small epsilon for numerical stability if needed, though source assumes valid input pmfsum = pmf.sum(dim=-2, keepdim=True) pmf = pmf / pmfsum # 2. Compute CDF along the support dimension cdf = torch.cumsum(pmf, dim=-2) # 3. Determine number of samples supportsize = pmf.shape[-2] if nsamples == 0: nsamples = supportsize # 4. Generate uniform random numbers # Shape: [batchsize, shape, nsamples, 1] # Assuming batch and shape dimensions are preserved for random generation batchshape = pmf.shape[:-2] u = torch.rand((batchshape, nsamples, 1), device=pmf.device) # 5. Searchsorted to find indices in CDF # searchsorted returns the index where u would be inserted to maintain order # This effectively finds the smallest k such that CDF[k] >= u indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf.squeeze(-1), u.squeeze(-1), side='right') # 6. Clamp indices to valid range [0, supportsize - 1] indices = torch.clamp(indices, 0, supportsize - 1) # 7. Reshape to original batch/shape dimensions with nsamples # The output shape should be [batchsize, shape, nsamples] return indices Parameters: pmf: Input probability mass tensor. Shape [batchsize, shape, nsamples, 1]. Sum along dim=-2 must be 1. nsamples: Number of samples to draw. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Summation Error: If the PMF does not sum to 1, the CDF will not reach 1.0, leading to incorrect sampling. Normalization is required. Boundary Conditions: Uniform random numbers can be exactly 1.0 due to floating-point representation. Clamping indices to supportsize - 1 prevents out-of-bounds access. Zero Weights: If some weights are zero, the CDF will have flat regions. searchsorted will return the first index in the flat region, which is a valid deterministic choice. Time Complexity: O(N \log M) where N is the number of samples and M is the support size, due to searchsorted. CDF computation is O(M). Memory Complexity: O(M) for storing the CDF. Strengths: Deterministic mapping from random seed to index (given fixed randoms), compatible with gradient-based optimization if using differentiable search approximations (though standard searchsorted is not differentiable). Limitations: Not differentiable through the sampling step. Slower than library-specific multinomial samplers for large M if N is small. When to use: When inverse transform sampling is explicitly required, or when integrating with systems that expect CDF-based sampling. When not to use: When performance is critical and M is very large, or when differentiability through the sampling step is required (consider Gumbel-Softmax or straight-through estimators). PMF Sampling is a standard technique in stochastic simulation and computer graphics for sampling from discrete distributions. It is implemented in various 3D generation frameworks, such as gsgen3d and guassian-diffusion, often as part of a larger Discrete Distribution Sampler class. gsgen3d/gsgen, https://github.com/gsgen3d/gsgen, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) pbonazzi/guassian-diffusion, https://github.com/pbonazzi/guassian-diffusion, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical 3D Sampling
head: Hierarchical Poisson-disk Sampling, Ordered 3D Dithering
body: Hierarchical 3D Sampling generates a sequence of points within a unit cube such that any prefix \{P0, \dots, P{n-1}\} maintains uniform density and a minimum inter-point distance. This property enables density control for volume rendering, serving as an alternative to opacity control or managing the level of detail (LOD) by selecting a subset of pre-computed points. The method provides hierarchical point sets where the priority of a point is defined by its serial number (index) in the generation sequence. Ordered dithering produces regular patterns, while Poisson-disk variants produce irregular patterns to mitigate aliasing. Inputs: Target number of points n. Sampling domain: A unit cube [0,1]^3 with periodic boundary conditions (each face treated identically to its opposite). Source data: Voxel grid for scalar value retrieval. Outputs: A sequence of 3D coordinates \{P0, P1, \dots, P{n-1}\} representing the hierarchical point set. Pre-computed histogram h(s): The count of sampled points falling into each scalar value bin s, used for estimating the total number of rendered primitives. 1. Point List: An array of 3D vectors storing coordinates (x, y, z). The index k corresponds to the priority number; smaller k implies higher priority. 2. Histogram: An array indexed by scalar value s, storing the integer count h(s) of points whose interpolated scalar value equals s. 1. Generate Point Set: Create the sequence of points using either Ordered 3D Dithering or Hierarchical Poisson-disk Sampling. 2. Interpolate Scalar Values: For each point Pk, calculate the scalar value sk by linear interpolation from the original voxel data. 3. Update Histogram: Increment the count h(sk) in the histogram for the calculated scalar value. 4. Estimate Total Points: Use the histogram to estimate the total number of candidates N for density control. This is the simplest implementation, extending 2D ordered dithering (digital halftoning) directly to 3D. Method: Divide the unit cube into a grid. Assign points to grid centers. Sort the grid cells based on a 3D dithering matrix value. The first n points in this sorted order form the subset \{P0, \dots, P{n-1}\}. Properties: Points are evenly distributed. The serial number k determines priority. Proposed by McCool and Fiume, this method creates irregular patterns to avoid aliasing. Parameters: Failure threshold T{\text{fail}} = 1000. Radius reduction factor \alpha = 0.99. Initial minimum distance limit L{\text{init}}: Not given in the sources. Procedure: 1. Initialize an empty list of placed points. 2. Set current limit length L = L{\text{init}}. 3. Repeat until n points are placed: a. Attempt to place a new point P{\text{new}} randomly in the unit cube. b. Check distance to all previously placed points. c. If distance to any existing point is less than L, discard P{\text{new}} and increment failure counter C. d. If C < T{\text{fail}}, repeat step 3a. e. If C \ge T{\text{fail}}, reduce L \leftarrow L \times \alpha and reset C = 0. f. If L becomes too small to place any point, terminate or adjust L{\text{init}}. Scalar Interpolation: The scalar value s at point P is calculated by linear interpolation from the original voxel data. s = \text{LinearInterpolate}(VoxelData, P) Note: Higher degree interpolation or interpolation from irregular meshed data is also possible. Total Candidate Estimation: For a density function dm(s), the estimated total number of points N is: N = \sum{s=s{\min}}^{s{\max}} dm(s) h(s) where s{\min} and s{\max} are the minimum and maximum scalar values, and h(s) is the histogram count. For other density functions requiring gradient magnitude, an approximation is used: N = \sum{s=s{\min}}^{s{\max}} \bar{g}(s) h(s) where \bar{g}(s) is the average gradient magnitude at scalar value s. Density Adjustment: If the number of candidates N is too large for interactivity, the actual point density d(x) is reduced: d(x) = dm(x) \min(1, S/N) where S represents a target scaling factor. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def calculateinitiallimit(n): """ Standard approximation for uniform spacing in a unit cube.""" return (1.0 / n) (1.0 / 3.0) def randompointinunitcube(): """ Standard uniform random generation in [0, 1)^3.""" return (random.random(), random.random(), random.random()) def distanceperiodic(p1, p2): """Euclidean distance on a 3D torus.""" diff = [min(abs(p1[i] - p2[i]), 1.0 - abs(p1[i] - p2[i])) for i in range(3)] return math.sqrt(diff[0]2 + diff[1]2 + diff[2]2) def generatehierarchicalpoissondisk(n): """ Generates n points using Hierarchical Poisson-disk sampling. Matches the dart-throwing algorithm with radius reduction from. """ points = [] L = calculateinitiallimit(n) failurecount = 0 Tfail = 1000 alpha = 0.99 while len(points) < n: candidate = randompointinunitcube() isvalid = True for existingpoint in points: if distanceperiodic(candidate, existingpoint) < L: isvalid = False break if isvalid: points.append(candidate) failurecount = 0 else: failurecount += 1 if failurecount >= Tfail: L = L alpha failurecount = 0 if L < 1e-6: break return points def estimatetotalpoints(histogram, densityfunction): """ Estimates total number of rendered primitives N. histogram: dict mapping scalar value s to count h(s) densityfunction: function dm(s) """ N = 0.0 for s, hs in histogram.items(): N += densityfunction(s) hs return N Regularity Artifact: If the total number of points n is too small, the regularity of the pattern becomes obvious, causing aliasing artifacts when correlated with object surfaces or screen coordinates. Aliasing: Ordered dithering creates severe aliasing artifacts due to its regularity. Irregular patterns (like Poisson-disk) are necessary for many applications to mitigate this. Performance: Hierarchical Poisson-disk sampling requires expensive computation during generation. However, points can be pre-computed and reused for any object. Time Complexity: Ordered Dithering generation involves simple grid assignment and sorting. Poisson-disk generation has high computational cost due to distance checks against all existing points. Exact asymptotic complexity is Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store the point list and O(S) for the histogram, where S is the number of scalar bins. Strengths: Provides hierarchical LOD control; subsets of points maintain uniform density. Irregular variants (Poisson-disk) reduce aliasing artifacts. Pre-computable; reusable across different objects. Limitations: Regular patterns (Dithering) suffer from aliasing. Poisson-disk generation is computationally expensive. Requires careful tuning of failure thresholds and radius reduction factors. When to Use: When density control is needed for opacity adaptation or LOD management, and pre-computation is feasible. Hierarchical 3D Sampling is used for density control and level-of-detail management in volume rendering. The method builds on 2D ordered dithering techniques used in digital halftoning. The irregular variant, Hierarchical Poisson-disk sampling, was proposed by McCool and Fiume. The technique is applied in real-time previewing for volume visualization. name: Uniform Ray Sampling
head: Fixed-step Ray Sampling, Regular Sampling, Uniform Distance Sampling, Uniform Point Sampling, Uniform Point Sampling along Rays, Uniform Sampling
body: Uniform Ray Sampling is a ray traversal approach where samples are taken at equal distances along the ray as it passes through volume data stored on a regular grid. It serves as the baseline sampling method in NeRF, assuming every point along the ray contributes equally to the final rendering when no transmittance estimator is available. It sets itself apart from Stochastic Jittering by using fixed intervals rather than random offsets, and from Slab-based Ray Sampling by ignoring voxel boundaries and maintaining a constant step size regardless of scene geometry. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} (3D vector). Ray direction \mathbf{d} (unit-norm 3D vector). Near clipping plane distance t{near} (scalar). Far clipping plane distance t{far} (scalar). Number of samples N (integer). Outputs: Sample positions \mathbf{x}i for i \in [0, N-1] (3D vectors). Sample depths ti (scalars). Segment lengths \Delta ti (scalars). Data Structures: tvals: 1D tensor/array of size N containing linearly spaced depth values. samplepoints: 3D tensor/array of shape (N, N, 3) containing the 3D coordinates of the samples. samplelengths: 1D tensor/array of size N (or (N, 1)) containing the distance between consecutive samples. Steps: 1. Generate N linearly spaced depth values ti between t{near} and t{far}: ti = t{near} + i \cdot \frac{t{far} - t{near}}{N - 1}, \quad i = 0, 1, \dots, N-1 Note: Some implementations use N+1 points or exclude endpoints depending on the integration rule, but the core spacing remains uniform. 2. Compute the 3D sample positions by scaling the ray direction by the depth values and adding the ray origin: \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \cdot \mathbf{d} 3. Calculate the segment lengths (deltas) for integration. For i < N-1: \Delta ti = t{i+1} - ti = \frac{t{far} - t{near}}{N - 1} For the last sample, \Delta t{N-1} is set to a large value (e.g., 10^{10}) to ensure transmittance reaches zero during compositing. 4. Evaluate the volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}i) and color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}i) at each sample position. 5. Compute opacity \alphai using the segment length and density: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{x}i) \cdot \Delta ti) 6. Render using front-to-back compositing: C = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}i), \quad Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def uniformraysampling(rayorigins, raydirections, near, far, numsamples): """ Generate uniform samples along rays. Args: rayorigins: Tensor of shape (N, 3) raydirections: Tensor of shape (N, 3), unit-norm near: Scalar or Tensor of shape (N,) far: Scalar or Tensor of shape (N,) numsamples: Integer Returns: samplepoints: Tensor of shape (N, numsamples, 3) samplelengths: Tensor of shape (N, numsamples, 1) """ # Step 1: Generate linearly spaced depth values # tvals shape: (numsamples,) tvals = torch.linspace(near, far, numsamples) # Broadcast tvals to match ray batch dimension # tvals shape: (1, numsamples, 1) tvals = tvals.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(-1) # Step 2: Compute 3D sample positions # rayorigins shape: (N, 1, 3) # raydirections shape: (N, 1, 3) # samplepoints shape: (N, numsamples, 3) samplepoints = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + tvals raydirections.unsqueeze(1) # Step 3: Compute segment lengths # deltas shape: (numsamples - 1,) deltas = tvals[0, 1:, 0] - tvals[0,:-1, 0] # Append a large value for the last segment to handle transmittance correctly lastdelta = torch.full((1,), 1e10, device=deltas.device) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, lastdelta], dim=0) # Reshape deltas to (N, numsamples, 1) samplelengths = deltas.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(-1) return samplepoints, samplelengths Parameters: numsamples (N): Number of points to sample along each ray. Typical value: 64. near (t{near}): Near clipping plane distance. Defined in config. far (t{far}): Far clipping plane distance. Defined in config. stepsize (\Delta t): Fixed distance between samples, calculated as (t{far} - t{near}) / (N - 1). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: If the step size is too large, features are missed and a banding effect appears. Mitigation: Add small random noise to sample positions (stratified sampling). Computational Cost: High computational cost due to the maximum number of interpolations required per sample point, especially in 3D where 7 interpolations are needed per sample for trilinear interpolation. Empty Space: Uniform sampling evaluates empty space equally to occupied space, leading to low efficiency compared to spatial skipping or PDF-based methods. This method ensures even spacing along rays within a voxel cell by using preprocessed ray data and a 4-bit depth-sampling indicator stored in the pixel opacity. It solves the problem of efficiently computing sampling coordinates for trilinear interpolation and evaluating the Riemann sum in front-to-back order. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by relying on a shared set of preprocessed rays and a stateful depth indicator to maintain sampling continuity across cells. Uniform NDC Point Sampling generates a fixed number of points uniformly distributed along each ray in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) space, mapping the ray parameter t from 0 to 1. Unlike standard uniform sampling which depends on scene bounding boxes or depth ranges, this method assumes a canonical camera frame, making it suitable for neural rendering pipelines that require consistent positional encoding inputs regardless of scene scale. It sets itself apart from Uniform Ray Sampling by decoupling sample density from physical depth, and from Non-linear (Logarithmic) Sampling by providing a linear sampling curve in NDC space that corresponds to a 1/x disparity distribution in original space. Local Sampling is a ray sampling strategy that concentrates evaluation points around a known surface representation (e.g., a depth texture) to minimize empty-space evaluations in volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Uniform Ray Sampling by leveraging geometric priors to achieve high quality with significantly fewer samples, though it relies on the availability of ground truth depth during training. Non-linear (Logarithmic) Sampling is a sample placement strategy that distributes points along a view ray using a logarithmic function to concentrate density near the camera while maintaining coverage over large depth ranges. It addresses the limitation of uniform sampling in large scenes, where linear spacing causes excessive evaluations in the distance or insufficient resolution near the viewer. Pixel-guided ray sampling is a non-uniform sampling strategy that calculates a prior probability distribution based on the color variation (standard deviation) within pixel neighborhoods to identify high-information regions. It solves the problem of inefficient ray casting in uniform sampling by concentrating computational resources on pixels with sharp color differences, which typically correspond to rich texture details or sharp density variations in the scene. Context-based Probability Ray Sampling is a non-uniform ray sampling strategy that allocates more rays to image regions with high visual complexity (edges, texture) and fewer rays to trivial regions (uniform backgrounds). It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by sampling more rays in areas with large probability (complex shapes/colors) and fewer rays in trivial areas (white background, walls, floors) rather than uniformly. Stratified Sampling partitions the ray depth interval [tn, tf] into k equal-sized bins and generates one sample per bin, avoiding the clustering and gaps inherent in pure uniform random sampling. It sets itself apart from its parent Uniform Ray Sampling by guaranteeing coverage of the entire depth range, and from its siblings by providing a structured variance reduction technique for the volume rendering integral. Samples points forward along the ray from the surface to get SDF values inside the object, used when latent space is not pretrained. It asserts numforwardsampling > 0, extracts valid camera rays and z-depths, and computes grid values to generate point samples at validzdepth + grid. When the camera ray reaches the translucent material after diffuse interactions, sample the ray randomly with a small number of samples, as low as one sample per camera ray. It computes k{max} sample points Pk using the formula: dk = -\frac{1}{\sigmat} \log \left( 1 - \frac{|k(1 - e^{-\sigmat d{\max}})|}{k{\max}} \right) where \sigmat is the extinction coefficient, k is the sample index, and k{max} is the total number of samples. This ensures exactly k{max} samples are placed, preventing undersampling for small object widths. Selects N\theta azimuthal directions and N\phi elevational directions to uniformly cover the sphere, then evenly places Nr points between near and far bounds for each direction, querying the network at N\theta \times N\phi \times Nr points. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. The cost scales linearly with the number of samples. Memory Complexity: O(N) per ray to store sample positions and densities. Performance: On RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, 1M rays, dragon dataset, fp32, cone=0: Speedup 1.06x (2.953ms -> 2.790ms) with optimizations. For a dataset with 1-unit grid spacing, a 0.1 step size took nearly 10 times as long as a 1.0 step size, which took twice as long as a 2.0 step size. Strengths: Simple to implement, accurate for regular grids, guaranteed even spacing. Limitations: Low efficiency in empty space, high computational cost due to interpolations, prone to aliasing if step size is large. When to use: Baseline for neural rendering (NeRF), small scenes, or when no transmittance estimator is available. When not to use: Large scenes with significant empty space, where spatial skipping or importance sampling is preferred. Uniform Ray Sampling originated as the default sampling strategy in NeRF. It is based on the assumption that every point along the ray contributes equally to the final rendering, leading to a constant PDF and linearly decaying transmittance. It is widely used in neural radiance field rendering and direct volume rendering on regular grids. name: Evenly Spaced Sampling with Preprocessed Rays and Depth Indicators
head: Depth Indicator Sampling, Preprocessed Ray Structure Sampling
body: This method ensures even spacing along rays within a voxel cell by using preprocessed ray data and a 4-bit depth-sampling indicator stored in the pixel opacity. It solves the problem of efficiently computing sampling coordinates for trilinear interpolation and evaluating the Riemann sum in front-to-back order. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by relying on a shared set of preprocessed rays and a stateful depth indicator to maintain sampling continuity across cells. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A RAY structure containing entry coordinates (xyz) and a precomputed Length parameter representing the maximum number of Unit Translation Vectors (UTVs) that fit within the cell. A PIXEL structure containing a density field. An integer samplingrate in the range [1, 16]. Output: Updated PIXEL.density with accumulated luminance/density and the updated depth indicator. Data Structures: 1. Preprocessed Ray Structure: Stores 3 entry coordinates (x, y, z) as 16-bit unsigned integers representing values in the range [0, 1], plus an additional ray.Length parameter representing the maximum number of UTVs that can be added to the entry point before going out of the cell. 2. Pixel Structure: Contains a density field. The lower 4 bits (mask 0xF) store the depth-sampling indicator (next sampling offset). The upper bits (mask 0xFFF0) store accumulated density/luminance values as 16-bit unsigned integers. Unit Translation Vector (UTV): The UTV is parallel to the viewing direction. It is defined as 1/16 of the longest vector crossing the cell. Consequently, its coordinate on the major projection axis is also equal to 1/16. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Extract the lower 4 bits of pixel.density to get nextsampling, a depth-sampling indicator representing the offset in UTVs. 2. Loop: While nextsampling is less than ray.Length: a. Calculate the sampling position: \text{xyz} = \text{ray.xyz} + \text{next\sampling} \times \text{UTV.xyz}. b. Interpolate the volume data at xyz and accumulate the result into the pixel. c. Increment nextsampling by samplingrate. 3. Finalize: Subtract ray.Length from nextsampling to wrap the indicator for the next traversal or frame. 4. Update: Clear the lower 4 bits of pixel.density and add the new nextsampling value to it. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def accumulate(ray, pixel, samplingrate, utv): # Extract lower 4 bits for depth-sampling indicator (offset in UTVs) nextsampling = pixel.density & 0xF # Normalize to [0, ray.Length) to handle out-of-bounds initialization if ray.Length > 0: nextsampling = nextsampling % ray.Length # Iterate while within the cell's precomputed length while nextsampling < ray.Length: # Calculate sampling position using preprocessed ray entry and UTV xyz = ray.xyz + nextsampling utv # Interpolate volume data at xyz and accumulate into pixel # (Standard trilinear interpolation and front-to-back compositing) # Implementation depends on volume data structure # Advance to next sampling point nextsampling += samplingrate # Wrap the indicator for the next cell traversal or frame nextsampling -= ray.Length # Update pixel density: keep upper bits (accumulated data), set lower bits (new indicator) pixel.density = (pixel.density & 0xFFF0) + nextsampling Parameters: samplingrate: An arbitrary integer value within the range [1, 16]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Approximation: Sampling positions and trilinear weights are approximated due to the limited set of preprocessed rays, limited projection lists, and the 4-bit depth indicator. Accuracy vs. Performance: Accuracy can be improved by increasing table sizes and depth bits, but this increases cache misses and reduces randomizing, trading noise for aliasing. A technique to reduce aliasing by using incoherent sampling depths between neighboring pixels. Half of the depth indicators are initialized to zero, and the others to half the sampling rate, ensuring every pixel differs from its four nearest neighbors. Unlike usual rectilinear sampling which causes staircase effects even at high rates, interleaving depth indicators clearly reduces aliasing. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sampling points per ray within the cell, as each step performs a constant-time lookup and accumulation. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the preprocessed ray table and the projection lists. The pixel structure is compact, storing 16-bit density with an embedded 4-bit state. Strengths: Efficient computation of sampling coordinates avoids complex ray-cell intersection calculations per sample. Reduces aliasing through interleaving. Limitations: Approximation errors due to limited preprocessed rays and 4-bit depth indicator. Increasing table sizes and depth bits increases cache misses and reduces randomizing, trading noise for aliasing. When to use: When rendering volumes with regular grid structures where even spacing is desired and computational efficiency is prioritized over perfect geometric accuracy. This method originates from a new object-order ray-casting algorithm. It addresses the difficulties of computing sampling coordinates quickly and ensuring even spacing for Riemann sum evaluation in front-to-back ray casting. The technique leverages the incoherency between rays to improve rendering accuracy, building on earlier work by Theufll et al..
