name: Uniform NDC Point Sampling
head: NDC Ray Sampling, NDC Sampling
body: Uniform NDC Point Sampling generates a fixed number of points uniformly distributed along each ray in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) space, mapping the ray parameter t from 0 to 1. Unlike standard uniform sampling which depends on scene bounding boxes or depth ranges, this method assumes a canonical camera frame, making it suitable for neural rendering pipelines that require consistent positional encoding inputs regardless of scene scale. It sets itself apart from Uniform Ray Sampling by decoupling sample density from physical depth, and from Non-linear (Logarithmic) Sampling by providing a linear sampling curve in NDC space that corresponds to a 1/x disparity distribution in original space. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: rayso: Tensor of shape (N, 3), ray origins in the average camera frame. raysd: Tensor of shape (N, 3), ray directions in the average camera frame. Nsamples: Integer, the fixed number of samples per ray. xyzmin, xyzmax: Tensors of shape (3), defining the bounding box for validity checks (optional but common in implementations like DirectVoxGO). ndcnearplane: Float, default 1.0, defining the near clipping plane in NDC space. Outputs: rayspts: Tensor of shape (N, N\samples, 3), the 3D coordinates of the sampled points. maskoutbbox: Tensor of shape (N, N\samples), boolean mask indicating points outside the bounding box. Data Structures: The method operates on standard floating-point tensors. The ray parameter t (or dist) is a scalar value in [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Transform to Average Camera Frame: Before sampling, rays must be transformed into an "average" camera frame. This involves rotating and translating the ray origins and directions such that the camera poses are centered and aligned. This step is critical; if the original rays are not in this frame, the NDC assumption fails. 2. Compute Normalized Distance: For each ray i and sample index j (where j \in \{0, \dots, N\samples-1\}), compute the normalized distance dist: dist = \frac{j}{N\samples - 1} This maps the samples linearly from t=0 to t=1. 3. Compute 3D Coordinates: Calculate the 3D point p for each sample using linear interpolation along the ray: px = ox + dx \times dist py = oy + dy \times dist pz = oz + dz \times dist where (ox, oy, oz) and (dx, dy, dz) are the components of the ray origin and direction in the average camera frame. 4. Bounding Box Check (Optional): If xyzmin and xyzmax are provided, check if any coordinate of p is less than the corresponding min or greater than the corresponding max. Set the corresponding bit in maskoutbbox to true if the point is outside. 5. Distance Scaling (Variant): In implementations like TensoRF, if NDC sampling is enabled, inter-sample distances are computed and scaled by the ray direction norm to approximate Euclidean distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def uniformndcpointsampling(rayso, raysd, Nsamples, xyzmin=None, xyzmax=None): """ Samples Nsamples uniformly spaced points along each ray in NDC space. Args: rayso: Tensor of shape (N, 3), ray origins in average camera frame. raysd: Tensor of shape (N, 3), ray directions in average camera frame. Nsamples: Integer, number of samples per ray. xyzmin: Tensor of shape (3), minimum bounding box coordinates. xyzmax: Tensor of shape (3), maximum bounding box coordinates. Returns: rayspts: Tensor of shape (N, Nsamples, 3), sampled points. maskoutbbox: Tensor of shape (N, Nsamples), True if point is outside bbox. """ N = rayso.shape[0] # Step 2: Compute normalized distance # dist ranges from 0.0 to 1.0, matching j / (Nsamples - 1) dists = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, Nsamples, device=rayso.device) # Expand dimensions for broadcasting # rayso: (N, 3) -> (N, 1, 3) # raysd: (N, 3) -> (N, 1, 3) # dists: (Nsamples,) -> (1, Nsamples, 1) raysoexp = rayso.unsqueeze(1) raysdexp = raysd.unsqueeze(1) distsexp = dists.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(2) # Step 3: Compute 3D coordinates # p = o + d dist rayspts = raysoexp + raysdexp distsexp maskoutbbox = torch.zeros((N, Nsamples), dtype=torch.bool, device=rayso.device) # Step 4: Bounding box check if xyzmin is not None and xyzmax is not None: # Check if any coordinate is less than min or greater than max # xyzmin: (3,) -> (1, 1, 3) # xyzmax: (3,) -> (1, 1, 3) xyzminexp = xyzmin.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) xyzmaxexp = xyzmax.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) outmin = rayspts < xyzminexp outmax = rayspts > xyzmaxexp # Any dimension out of bounds outbbox = outmin | outmax # Reduce over the last dimension (x, y, z) maskoutbbox = outbbox.any(dim=-1) return rayspts, maskoutbbox Parameters: Nsamples: The fixed number of samples per ray. ndcnearplane: Default 1.0. Defines the near clipping plane in NDC space. Used in distance scaling variants. dmin: 1. Lower bound for NDC depth. dmax: \infty. Upper bound for NDC depth. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Average Camera Frame: The method is only applicable if all samples lie strictly in the front hemisphere of the average camera frame. Large deviations from this frame lead to high non-linear perspective distortions, which can negatively impact the learning process. Ray Direction Norm: In NDC space, the ray direction norm may vary. If Euclidean distance accuracy is required, distances must be scaled by the ray direction norm. Bounding Box: If the bounding box is not provided, the method does not filter out-of-bounds points, which may lead to sampling empty space or invalid regions. A variant that computes inter-sample distances and scales them by the ray direction norm to approximate Euclidean distance in NDC space. It uses parameters ndcnearplane (default 1.0), simulateeuclidsample (bool), and simulateeucliddepth (float) to control depth simulation. This variant is chosen when accurate depth-based weighting is needed despite using NDC sampling. Time Complexity: O(N \times N\samples), where N is the number of rays and N\samples is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N \times N\samples \times 3) for storing the sampled points. Performance: NDC sampling only surpasses uniform sampling in quality at 128 samples in ablation studies. Strengths: Consistent sample distribution regardless of scene scale; simple linear interpolation; compatible with positional encoding that expects NDC inputs. Limitations: Requires transformation to an average camera frame; sensitive to large deviations from the average frame; less effective than logarithmic or local sampling for foreground-focused scenes with low sample counts. When to Use: When using positional encodings designed for NDC space; when a fixed number of samples is required regardless of depth. When Not to Use: When the scene cannot be easily transformed to an average camera frame; when samples must remain strictly in the front hemisphere of the average camera frame; when depth-aware sampling (e.g., logarithmic) is preferred. Uniform NDC Point Sampling was introduced in the context of NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) to address positional encoding applied equally to foreground and background frequencies. The method transforms rays into an average camera frame and samples uniformly in NDC space, allowing the network to learn consistent features regardless of the original camera configuration. It was proposed as an alternative to logarithmic sampling, offering a linear sampling curve in NDC space that corresponds to a 1/x disparity distribution in original space. The approach is detailed in the original NeRF paper and subsequent works like DONeRF. name: Local Sampling
head: Surface-aware Sampling
body: Local Sampling is a ray sampling strategy that concentrates evaluation points around a known surface representation (e.g., a depth texture) to minimize empty-space evaluations in volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Uniform Ray Sampling by leveraging geometric priors to achieve high quality with significantly fewer samples, though it relies on the availability of ground truth depth during training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray parameters, a trained neural radiance field (NeRF) or similar implicit representation, and a ground truth depth texture (or depth oracle network output) representing the scene surface. Output: A set of sample positions along the ray and the corresponding volume rendering result (color and alpha). Data Structures: Depth Texture: A 2D array storing the distance from the camera origin to the nearest surface intersection for each pixel. Ray: Defined by origin o and direction d. Steps: 1. Depth Retrieval: For a given pixel, retrieve the ground truth depth z{gt} from the depth texture. 2. Sample Placement: Place a fraction of the total samples N locally around z{gt}. The remaining samples are distributed uniformly or according to another strategy in the empty space before and after the surface. 3. Volume Rendering: Evaluate the neural network at the sample positions to obtain density \sigma and color c, then perform standard volume integration. Formulas: The depth z{gt} is used to define the local region. If N is the total number of samples, and N{local} is the number of samples placed locally, the positions are clustered around z{gt}. The exact distribution within the local cluster is not specified beyond "around the surface". Parameters: N: Total samples per ray. Tested values: [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128]. N{local}: Number of samples placed locally. Can be as low as 2 with nearly no decrease in quality. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Discontinuities: A depth oracle network with a single depth output may smooth depth around discontinuities, causing local sampling to mix foreground and background features and distort the result. Inference Availability: Ground truth depth is often unavailable during inference due to memory/computational constraints and the need for reprojection for novel views. NDC Sampling: Sampling in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) reaches competitive results only at high sample counts (>64) and falls behind uniform sampling at lower counts because the network must reconstruct the nonlinear transformation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def localsampling(rayorigin, raydirection, depthtexture, nerfmodel, totalsamples=64): # Get ground truth depth for the current pixel # Note: In practice, this requires a depth oracle or pre-computed depth map depthz = depthtexture[rayorigin.x, rayorigin.y] # Determine local sample range around depthz # The exact width of the local region is not specified in the source # Assuming a small epsilon range around depthz for demonstration epsilon = 0.1 localstart = max(0, depthz - epsilon) localend = depthz + epsilon # Place Nlocal samples locally nlocal = 2 localsamples = linspace(localstart, localend, nlocal) # Place remaining samples uniformly in the rest of the ray nuniform = totalsamples - nlocal # Assuming mindepth and maxdepth are defined for the scene uniformsamples = linspace(0, maxdepth, nuniform) # Combine samples allsamples = concatenate([uniformsamples, localsamples]) # Evaluate NeRF and render colors, alphas = volumerender(rayorigin, raydirection, allsamples, nerfmodel) return colors, alphas Uses mesh boundaries to localize surface evaluation, requiring only two samples per ray. It is efficient and applicable as a post-processing step to existing NeRF models. Time Complexity: Reduced compared to uniform sampling due to fewer total samples needed for equivalent quality. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the depth texture or depth oracle network. Performance: With local sampling, the number of samples can be reduced to two with nearly no decrease in quality. Log+warp adds about 1.3 dB in quality over uniform for local sampling. Strengths: Significant gains in quality-speed tradeoff given an ideal sampling oracle. Limitations: Ground truth depth is often not available during inference, making it a niche scenario without an oracle network. Originated in the context of NeRF optimization, specifically in the DONeRF paper, which explores using depth oracle networks to enable local sampling for real-time rendering of compact neural radiance fields. DONeRF: Towards Real‐Time Rendering of Compact Neural Radiance Fields using Depth Oracle Networks, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14340, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mesh-based Sampling
head: Wan et al. Mesh-based Sampling
body: Mesh-based Sampling localizes surface evaluation by estimating the volume density or Signed Distance Field (SDF) to define an inner and outer mesh boundary, using learned features attached to mesh vertices to estimate radiance. It builds on Local Sampling by placing samples around a known ground truth surface representation to reduce empty space evaluations. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by requiring only two samples per ray, significantly improving runtime efficiency while remaining applicable as a post-processing step to any existing NeRF models. Inputs: An implicit representation (volume density or SDF) defining the object geometry. Two meshes (inner and outer) derived from the implicit representation. Learned features attached to the vertices of these meshes. A viewing direction vector \mathbf{d} for the ray. Outputs: Estimated radiance for the ray. Data Structures: Inner Mesh: A triangular mesh representing the inner boundary of the surface region, with vertices storing learned feature vectors. Outer Mesh: A triangular mesh representing the outer boundary of the surface region, with vertices storing learned feature vectors. Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Steps: 1. Ray-Mesh Intersection: Compute the intersection points of the viewing ray with both the inner mesh and the outer mesh. Let these intersection points be \mathbf{p}{\text{in}} and \mathbf{p}{\text{out}} respectively. 2. Feature Interpolation: At each intersection point (\mathbf{p}{\text{in}} and \mathbf{p}{\text{out}}), interpolate the learned features from the surrounding mesh vertices. This yields feature vectors \mathbf{f}{\text{in}} and \mathbf{f}{\text{out}}. 3. Radiance Estimation: Feed the interpolated features (\mathbf{f}{\text{in}}, \mathbf{f}{\text{out}}) and the viewing direction \mathbf{d} into a shallow convolutional network. 4. Output: The network outputs the estimated radiance. Formulas: Feature interpolation: \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p}) = \text{Interpolate}(\mathcal{M}, \mathbf{p}), where \mathcal{M} is the mesh and \mathbf{p} is the intersection point. Radiance estimation: L = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p}{\text{in}}), \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p}{\text{out}}), \mathbf{d}), where \mathcal{N} is the shallow convolutional network. Parameters: Number of samples per ray: 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray-mesh intersection precision must be handled carefully to avoid missing thin surface regions or producing incorrect \mathbf{p}{\text{in}}/\mathbf{p}{\text{out}} ordering. The shallow convolutional network architecture must be explicitly designed to accept two spatial feature vectors and a direction vector as joint inputs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def meshbasedsampling(rayorigin, raydirection, innermesh, outermesh, network): # 1. Ray-mesh intersection pin = intersectraymesh(rayorigin, raydirection, innermesh) pout = intersectraymesh(rayorigin, raydirection, outermesh) # 2. Feature interpolation fin = interpolatefeatures(innermesh, pin) fout = interpolatefeatures(outermesh, pout) # 3. Radiance estimation radiance = network(fin, fout, raydirection) return radiance A query point sampling strategy where points are distributed along a displacement trajectory from a voxel grid to the surface closest point, designed to be more efficient than uniform or Gaussian sampling for mesh deformation tasks. It maintains performance with fewer query points (75k vs 200k) and is more efficient for mesh deformation. In unconstrained chair point cloud generation, Trajectory 75k achieved CD=56.12 and EMD=53.30, outperforming Uniform 75k (CD=56.88, EMD=54.93) and Gaussian 75k (CD=56.46, EMD=53.97). Compared to uniform sampling (query points uniformly from voxel shape space) and Gaussian sampling (points sampled with Gaussian distribution, mean=ground truth surface, variance=0.1 and 0.01), trajectory sampling maintains performance with fewer query points (75k vs 200k) and is more efficient for mesh deformation. Efficiency: Requires only two samples per ray, significantly improving runtime efficiency compared to methods that require dense sampling or multiple evaluations. Generality: Can be applied as a post-processing step to any existing NeRF models, making it a versatile addition to existing pipelines. Performance: Specific quantitative performance metrics (e.g., FPS, memory usage) for the Wan et al. method are not given in the sources. The method was proposed by Wan et al. [WRB 23] as a way to localize the surface between an inner and outer mesh using volume density or SDF estimates from an implicit representation. It is cited in recent surveys on learning-based 3D representations as a technique that improves runtime efficiency by minimizing the number of samples per ray. name: Non-linear (Logarithmic) Sampling
head: Logarithmic Sampling, Logarithmic Sampling for Volumetric Clouds, Logarithmic depth sampling
body: Non-linear (Logarithmic) Sampling is a sample placement strategy that distributes points along a view ray using a logarithmic function to concentrate density near the camera while maintaining coverage over large depth ranges. It addresses the limitation of uniform sampling in large scenes, where linear spacing causes excessive evaluations in the distance or insufficient resolution near the viewer. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Minimum depth d{min}, maximum depth d{max}, and the number of samples N. Outputs: A sequence of N depth values \tilde{d}i for i \in [0, N-1]. Data Structures: A contiguous array of floating-point numbers storing the computed depth values. Parameters: d{min}: The start of the ray segment (typically camera near plane). d{max}: The end of the ray segment (typically camera far plane). N: The total number of samples per ray. Formulas: The method first generates uniform depth indices di and then warps them logarithmically. 1. Uniform Depth Generation: di = d{min} + \frac{i}{N-1} (d{max} - d{min}) where i is the sample index from 0 to N-1. 2. Logarithmic Warping: \tilde{d}i = d{min} + \frac{\log(di - d{min} + 1)}{\log(d{max} - d{min} + 1)} \cdot (d{max} - d{min}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generatelogarithmicsamples(dmin, dmax, nsamples): """ Generates nsamples depth values along a ray from dmin to dmax using logarithmic non-linearity. Args: dmin (float): Minimum depth (near plane). dmax (float): Maximum depth (far plane). nsamples (int): Number of samples to generate. Returns: list[float]: List of warped depth values. """ if nsamples <= 0: return [] if dmax <= dmin: return [dmin] nsamples if nsamples == 1: return [dmin] samples = [] depthrange = dmax - dmin # Logarithmic base is arbitrary as long as numerator and denominator match logdenom = math.log(depthrange + 1) for i in range(nsamples): # Step 1: Calculate uniform depth di di = dmin + (i / (nsamples - 1)) depthrange # Step 2: Apply logarithmic warping numerator = math.log(di - dmin + 1) warpeddepth = dmin + (numerator / logdenom) depthrange samples.append(warpeddepth) return samples Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The addition of 1 inside the logarithm ensures the argument remains positive when di = d{min}. Balance: If the sampling density along the z-axis is not balanced with the x-y plane coverage, lighting will appear incorrect when the camera rotates, even if the static render looks acceptable. The goal is to keep the frustum covered by a single sample roughly cubic. Under-sampling: To maintain performance, the number of samples along the z-axis is typically set to approximately 10 times fewer than the number of samples covering the x-y plane area. Uses stratified sampling to reduce variance in radiance estimation. [1373-stratified-monte-carlo-radiance-estimate.md] Precomputes ray depths to ensure even spacing. [2335-evenly-spaced-sampling-with-preprocessed-rays-and-depth-indi.md] Samples in Normalized Device Coordinates. [2395-uniform-ndc-point-sampling.md] Applies stratification across batches of rays. [2730-batch-stratified-sampling.md] Stratifies the ray space directly. [3014-stratified-ray-sampling.md] Samples around a specific depth (e.g., ground truth or previous estimate). [5532-local-sampling.md] Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: In ablation studies, logarithmic sampling increases PSNR by 1.3 dB per doubling of N, compared to 1.8 dB for uniform sampling. Strengths: Reduces network evaluations in large depth ranges without losing quality near the camera. Limitations: Lower PSNR efficiency per sample compared to uniform sampling; requires careful balancing with x-y sampling density to avoid lighting artifacts. When to use: Large scenes with significant depth ranges; volumetric clouds; neural radiance fields where near-field detail is critical. When not to use: Small scenes with limited depth range; scenarios where uniform distribution is strictly required for theoretical guarantees. Non-linear logarithmic sampling was introduced in the context of compact neural radiance fields, specifically in the DONeRF paper. It was proposed as an intuitive first step to reduce network evaluations by focusing samples on objects closer to the camera. The technique was further popularized and adapted for real-time volumetric cloud rendering in game engines, where it is described as the "most important optimization for large scenes" to balance sample frustums. name: Pixel-guided ray sampling
head: Color-guided sampling, Pc sampling
body: Pixel-guided ray sampling is a non-uniform sampling strategy that calculates a prior probability distribution based on the color variation (standard deviation) within pixel neighborhoods to identify high-information regions. It solves the problem of inefficient ray casting in uniform sampling by concentrating computational resources on pixels with sharp color differences, which typically correspond to rich texture details or sharp density variations in the scene. Inputs: Source view image Ii with dimensions Hi \times Wi. Pixel coordinates (u, v) where u \in [0, Hi] and v \in [0, Wi]. Neighborhood size parameter n (default 3). Threshold scaling factor 0.01. Outputs: A set of sampled rays ri(u, v) for the image, where the probability of selecting a ray at (u, v) is proportional to the computed probability density P'c(u, v). Data Structures: The probability map Pc is a 2D array of size Hi \times Wi storing the raw standard deviation values. The normalized probability map P'c is a 2D array of size Hi \times Wi storing the final sampling weights. Steps: 1. For each pixel (u, v) in image Ii, compute the mean color \bar{c} of the n \times n neighborhood centered at (u, v). 2. Compute Pc(u, v) as the standard deviation of colors in that neighborhood. 3. Find the maximum value \max(Pc(u, v)) across the image. 4. Calculate threshold s = 0.01 \times \text{mean}(Pc), where \text{mean}(Pc) is the average of all Pc values across the image. 5. Apply normalization: P'c(u, v) = \text{clamp}(Pc(u, v), s, \max(Pc(u, v))) / \max(Pc(u, v)). 6. Sample rays ri(u, v) from pixel coordinates (u, v) according to the probability distribution P'c(u, v). Formulas: Raw probability calculation: Pc(u, v) = \text{std}(c(u, v)) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n^2} \sum{x', y'} [c(x', y') - \bar{c}]^2}, where c(u,v) is the pixel color, n is the neighborhood size (default 3), x' \in [u - \frac{n-1}{2}, u + \frac{n-1}{2}], y' \in [v - \frac{n-1}{2}, v + \frac{n-1}{2}], and \bar{c} is the mean color of the n \times n neighborhood. Computational implementation using variance identity: \text{std}(c(u, v)) = \sqrt{E(c(x', y')^2) - E(c(x', y'))^2}. Note: The source text contains a typo repeating E(c(x', y')^2), but the standard identity implies subtracting the square of the mean. Normalization to prevent underfitting: P'c(u, v) = \frac{\text{clamp}(Pc(u, v), s, \max(Pc(u, v)))}{\max(Pc(u, v))}, where s = 0.01 \times \text{mean}(Pc). Values below s are clamped to s. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pixelguidedraysampling(image: list, n: int = 3) -> list: """ Computes the normalized probability distribution for pixel-guided ray sampling. Args: image: 2D list of scalar color values (H, W). n: Neighborhood size (default 3). Returns: Pprimec: Normalized probability distribution (H, W). """ H = len(image) W = len(image[0]) halfn = (n - 1) // 2 meancolor = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] meansqcolor = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] for u in range(H): for v in range(W): ustart = max(0, u - halfn) uend = min(H, u + halfn + 1) vstart = max(0, v - halfn) vend = min(W, v + halfn + 1) count = (uend - ustart) (vend - vstart) sumc = 0.0 sumsq = 0.0 for i in range(ustart, uend): for j in range(vstart, vend): val = image[i][j] sumc += val sumsq += val val meancolor[u][v] = sumc / count meansqcolor[u][v] = sumsq / count Pc = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] for u in range(H): for v in range(W): var = meansqcolor[u][v] - meancolor[u][v] 2 Pc[u][v] = max(var, 0.0) 0.5 maxPc = max(max(row) for row in Pc) meanPc = sum(sum(row) for row in Pc) / (H W) s = 0.01 meanPc Pprimec = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] for u in range(H): for v in range(W): val = Pc[u][v] if val < s: val = s if val > maxPc: val = maxPc Pprimec[u][v] = val / maxPc return Pprimec Parameters: n: The size of the pixel neighborhood for computing standard deviation. Default value: 3. Threshold scaling factor: The multiplier for the lower bound threshold s. Default value: 0.01. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Handling: Not given in the sources. Implementers typically clamp indices to image bounds. Zero Variance: If a pixel and its neighborhood have identical colors, Pc(u, v) = 0. The clamping step ensures this value is raised to s, preventing zero probability. Precision: The variance identity E(c^2) - E(c)^2 can suffer from catastrophic cancellation if the color values are large and the variance is small. Using float64 for intermediate calculations is recommended. A ray sampling strategy that uses the standard deviation of depth values in pixel neighborhoods to guide ray sampling, targeting areas with abrupt depth changes. It obtains the depth probability volume Pi(u, v) from an ENeRF coarse-to-fine approach, computes the expected depth D(u, v) = \sum{i=1}^{Nd} Pi(u, v) \cdot Li(u, v) where Li are depth planes sampled from [L{min}, L{max}] and Nd is the number of sampled depth planes. It then computes Pd(u, v) = \text{std}(D(u, v)) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n^2} \sum{x', y'} [D(x', y') - \bar{D}]^2} over an n \times n neighborhood, applies the same normalization as pixel-guided sampling to get P'd(u, v), and fuses it with the color-guided distribution via P{samp}(u, v) = \beta P'c(u, v) + (1 - \beta)P'd(u, v) during training. Time Complexity: O(H \cdot W \cdot n^2) for computing the probability map, where H and W are image dimensions and n is the neighborhood size. Sampling rays is O(H \cdot W) assuming efficient sampling from the distribution. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) to store the probability maps Pc and P'c. Strengths: Focuses computational resources on pixels with sharp color differences, which correspond to rich texture details or sharp density variations in the scene. Limitations: Requires an initial pass to compute statistics. When to use: When training radiance fields or volume renderers where computational efficiency is critical and the scene has significant texture variation. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Pixel-guided ray sampling was introduced in the context of efficient ray sampling for radiance fields reconstruction. It is based on the intuition that pixels with identical colors to their neighborhood contain less information, while those with substantial color differences encompass more scene details. The method replaces the uniform distribution of sampled rays during training with a probability density function derived from color variation. name: Depth-guided ray sampling
head: Confidence and Depth-Guided Sampling, Depth Prior Sampling, Pd sampling
body: Depth-guided ray sampling is a ray sampling strategy that uses depth information to concentrate sample points near geometric boundaries and object surfaces. It complements pixel-guided sampling by targeting areas with abrupt depth changes rather than color variation. The method addresses the inefficiency of uniform sampling, which often misses object surfaces and degrades rendering quality. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Depth probability volume Pi(u, v) or per-view depth estimates Dj(p); ray origin o and direction g; near plane en and far plane ef; total sample count M; neighborhood size n; fusion weight \beta. Outputs: A set of M sample distances em along the ray. Data Structures: Depth Probability Volume: A 3D array Pi(u, v) storing the probability of depth at pixel (u, v) for each discrete depth plane Li. Expected Depth Map: A 2D array D(u, v) storing the expected depth value per pixel. Sampling Probability Map: A 2D array P'd(u, v) storing the normalized standard deviation of depth values in local neighborhoods. Confidence Range: A 1D interval \hat{U}(p) = [\hat{D}(p) - \hat{S}(p), \hat{D}(p) + \hat{S}(p)] defining the high-probability depth region for pixel p. Steps: 1. Compute Expected Depth: Calculate the expected depth D(u, v) by summing the products of depth probabilities and their corresponding plane distances: D(u, v) = \sum{i=1}^{Nd} Pi(u, v) \cdot Li where Nd is the number of depth planes and Li \in [L{\min}, L{\max}]. 2. Compute Depth Standard Deviation: Calculate the standard deviation of depth values within an n \times n neighborhood centered at (u, v) to form the sampling probability map: Pd(u, v) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{K} \sum{x', y'} [D(x', y') - \bar{D}]^2} where \bar{D} is the mean depth in the neighborhood, (x', y') iterates over valid neighborhood pixels, and K is the actual number of pixels in the patch (accounting for image boundaries). 3. Normalize Probability: Apply min-max normalization to Pd(u, v) to produce P'd(u, v), preventing underfitting for rays in low-variance regions. 4. Calculate Confidence Interval (Alternative Formulation): In multi-view stereo contexts, compute the standard deviation \hat{S}(p) directly from depth estimates and their confidence weights Pj(p): \hat{S}(p) = \sqrt{\sum{j=1}^{J} Pj(p) (Dj(p) - \hat{D}(p))^2} where J is the number of views/planes, Pj(p) are confidence weights, and Dj(p) are depth estimates from those views. The confidence range is \hat{U}(p) = [\hat{D}(p) - \hat{S}(p), \hat{D}(p) + \hat{S}(p)]. 5. Fuse Probabilities (Optional): Combine the depth-guided probability P'd(u, v) with pixel-guided probability P'c(u, v) using weight \beta: P{\text{samp}}(u, v) = \beta P'c(u, v) + (1 - \beta) P'd(u, v). 6. Sample Points: Distribute the M sample distances along the ray rp = o + e g: Place half of the M points uniformly between en and ef. Place the second half of the points uniformly within the clamped confidence range [\max(en, \hat{D}(p) - \hat{S}(p)), \min(ef, \hat{D}(p) + \hat{S}(p))]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def depthguidedsampling(D, n, M, en, ef, o, g, beta=None, Pc=None): """ D: 2D list of floats, expected depth map [H, W] n: int, neighborhood size for standard deviation M: int, total number of samples per ray en: float, near plane distance ef: float, far plane distance o: list of 3 floats, ray origin g: list of 3 floats, ray direction beta: float, fusion weight (optional) Pc: 2D list of floats, normalized pixel-guided probability (optional) Returns: list of 3D points along the ray """ H = len(D) W = len(D[0]) # Step 2: Compute depth standard deviation Pd(u, v) Pd = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] for u in range(H): for v in range(W): ystart = max(0, u - n // 2) yend = min(H, u + n // 2 + 1) xstart = max(0, v - n // 2) xend = min(W, v + n // 2 + 1) patch = [D[r][c] for r in range(ystart, yend) for c in range(xstart, xend)] K = len(patch) meanval = sum(patch) / K varval = sum((x - meanval) 2 for x in patch) / K Pd[u][v] = math.sqrt(varval) # Step 3: Normalize Pd to Pprimed minval = min(min(row) for row in Pd) maxval = max(max(row) for row in Pd) rangeval = maxval - minval Pprimed = [[(Pd[u][v] - minval) / rangeval if rangeval > 1e-8 else 0.0 for v in range(W)] for u in range(H)] # Step 5: Fuse probabilities if beta is provided if beta is not None and Pc is not None: Psamp = [[beta Pc[u][v] + (1 - beta) Pprimed[u][v] for v in range(W)] for u in range(H)] else: Psamp = Pprimed # Step 6: Sample points for a single ray (using center pixel as example) ucenter, vcenter = H // 2, W // 2 Dhat = D[ucenter][vcenter] Shat = Pd[ucenter][vcenter] halfM = M // 2 euniform = [en + (ef - en) (m / (halfM - 1)) for m in range(halfM)] enear = max(en, Dhat - Shat) efar = min(ef, Dhat + Shat) if enear >= efar: eguided = [en + (ef - en) (m / (M - halfM - 1)) for m in range(M - halfM)] else: eguided = [enear + (efar - enear) (m / (M - halfM - 1)) for m in range(M - halfM)] esamples = euniform + eguided points = [[o[0] + e g[0], o[1] + e g[1], o[2] + e g[2]] for e in esamples] return points Parameters: n: Neighborhood size for standard deviation calculation. Typical value not given in the sources. M: Number of sample points per ray. Typical value not given in the sources. \beta: Fusion weight for pixel-guided sampling. Typical value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: At image borders, the n \times n neighborhood is truncated, so the variance divisor must be the actual patch area K rather than n^2. Invalid Confidence Range: If \hat{U}(p) falls outside [en, ef] or becomes empty due to precision limits, the range must be clamped or fallback to uniform sampling. Precision: Small Nd or quantized depth probabilities can introduce discretization errors in D(u, v) and \hat{S}(p). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Concentrates samples near geometric boundaries and object surfaces, improving reconstruction quality in depth-ambiguous regions. Limitations: Performance degrades if the underlying depth estimation network produces inaccurate probabilities or confidence weights. When to Use: When reliable depth priors are available and geometric accuracy is prioritized over color variation. When Not to Use: When depth estimation is unreliable or when color/texture variation better indicates sampling importance. Depth-guided ray sampling was introduced to improve neural volume rendering and multi-view stereo reconstruction. It builds on the ENeRF coarse-to-fine depth prediction pipeline to generate depth probability volumes. The method was proposed to solve the inefficiency of uniform NeRF sampling, which fails to concentrate points on object surfaces and reduces rendering quality. It is frequently combined with pixel-guided sampling via weighted fusion during training. name: Context-based Probability Ray Sampling
head: Context-based probability distribution sampling, Probability-based sampling function, context-based ray allocation, probability sampling
body: Context-based Probability Ray Sampling is a non-uniform ray sampling strategy that allocates more rays to image regions with high visual complexity (edges, texture) and fewer rays to trivial regions (uniform backgrounds). It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by sampling more rays in areas with large probability (complex shapes/colors) and fewer rays in trivial areas (white background, walls, floors) rather than uniformly. Inputs: Input image Ii with height Hi and width Wi. Color channel data c(x, y) for each pixel. Threshold parameter s. Outputs: A set of rays ri(u, v) sampled from pixel coordinates (u, v) according to a probability distribution. Data Structures: A 2D probability map g'(u, v) of size Hi \times Wi, normalized to [0, 1]. A cumulative distribution function (CDF) derived from g'(u, v) for sampling. Steps: 1. Compute Local Mean Color: For each pixel (u, v), calculate the mean color \bar{c} of the 3 \times 3 patch centered at (u, v). The patch includes pixels (x, y) where x \in \{u-1, u, u+1\} and y \in \{v-1, v, v+1\}. 2. Compute Standard Deviation (Context Metric): Calculate the standard deviation g(u, v) of the color values within the same 3 \times 3 patch. This metric represents the local color variance, where high values indicate edges or texture and low values indicate uniform areas. 3. Normalize and Clamp: Normalize g(u, v) to the interval [0, 1] and apply a lower-bound clamp to prevent trivial areas from receiving zero rays. 4. Sample Rays: Generate rays ri(u, v) for pixel (u, v) by sampling from the distribution g'(u, v). In practice, this involves constructing a CDF from g' and using inverse transform sampling or stratified sampling to select ray origins or densities. Formulas: Mean color: \bar{c} = \frac{1}{9} \sum{x,y} c(x, y), where x \in \{u-1, u, u+1\} and y \in \{v-1, v, v+1\}. Context probability: g(u, v) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{9} \sum{x,y} [c(x, y) - \bar{c}]^2}. Normalized probability: g'(u, v) = \frac{\text{clamp}(s, g(u, v))}{\max(g)}, where \text{clamp}(s, g(u, v)) replaces any value in g(u, v) less than s with s. The result is distributed in [0, 1]. Ray sampling: ri(u, v) \sim g'(u, v) for u \in [0, Hi] and v \in [0, Wi]. Parameters: Threshold s: Ensures minimum ray allocation to avoid sampling too few rays in trivial areas. Typically s = 0.01 \times \text{mean}(g(u, v)). Patch Size: The spatial neighborhood scale used to calculate context information. The source primarily uses 3 \times 3 but tests 5 \times 5, 7 \times 7, 9 \times 9, 11 \times 11. Context Metric: The method uses Standard Deviation as the context metric. Alternatives tested include Entropy and Variance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Pixels: The formula requires neighbors outside the image for edge pixels. The source does not specify padding; implementers must choose a strategy (e.g., zero, replicate, or ignore). Uniform Regions: Without clamping s, uniform regions (e.g., white walls) would have g(u, v) \approx 0, leading to no rays being sampled and potential training instability. Metric Choice: Standard Deviation was selected over tested alternatives (Entropy, Variance). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeprobabilitymap(image, patchsize=3, thresholdfactor=0.01): H, W, C = image.shape probmap = np.zeros((H, W)) half = patchsize // 2 padded = np.pad(image, half, mode='reflect') # for u in range(H): for v in range(W): patch = padded[u:u+patchsize, v:v+patchsize,:] meanc = np.mean(patch) stdc = np.std(patch) # Matches sqrt(1/9 sum((c-mean)^2)) probmap[u, v] = stdc maxg = np.max(probmap) meang = np.mean(probmap) s = thresholdfactor meang probmap = np.clip(probmap, s, maxg) / maxg # return probmap def samplerays(probmap, numrays): flatprobs = probmap.flatten() flatprobs /= flatprobs.sum() # pixelindices = np.random.choice(flatprobs.size, size=numrays, p=flatprobs) # rays = np.unravelindex(pixelindices, probmap.shape) # return rays Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on Plenoxels, it significantly improves performance over methods without probability sampling. Reduces training time by sampling fewer rays in trivial areas while maintaining accuracy in complex regions. Hardware, resolution, and scene specifics are not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement; leverages existing image data; reduces computational load in low-information areas. Limitations: Requires access to the input image context; may not adapt to 3D geometry changes that do not affect 2D image variance; boundary handling is ambiguous. Originated in the paper "Fast Learning Radiance Fields by Shooting Much Fewer Rays" (2023). The method was evaluated as an ablation study on the Plenoxels radiance field method to demonstrate the benefit of context-aware ray allocation. It addresses the inefficiency of uniform sampling in neural radiance fields by recognizing that not all pixels contribute equally to the reconstruction of complex 3D structures. name: Stratified Sampling
head: Discrete Volume Rendering, Fragmental Approximate Volume Rendering Method, Stratified Sampling for Volume Rendering
body: Stratified Sampling partitions the ray depth interval [tn, tf] into N equal-sized bins and generates one sample per bin to approximate the continuous volume rendering integral. It sets itself apart from its parent Uniform Ray Sampling by guaranteeing coverage of the entire depth range without clustering or gaps, and from its siblings by providing a structured variance reduction technique for the volume rendering integral. Inputs: ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, near depth tn, far depth tf, number of samples N. Outputs: sampled 3D positions \mathbf{p}i, densities \sigmai, colors ci, transmittance Ti, opacity \alphai, accumulated color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}). Data structures: Arrays of size N+1 for bin boundaries, size N for samples, transmittance, and opacity. All values are stored as floating-point scalars or vectors depending on batch dimension. Numbered steps: 1. Compute N+1 uniform parameter values t{\text{vals}} \in [0, 1]. 2. Map parameters to physical distances z{\text{vals}} via linear interpolation between tn and tf. 3. Compute midpoints of adjacent intervals. 4. Define lower and upper boundaries for each of the N bins. 5. Generate N independent uniform random numbers ui \sim U[0, 1]. 6. Perturb sample positions within each bin: zi = \text{lower}i + ui (\text{upper}i - \text{lower}i). 7. Compute 3D positions: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + zi \mathbf{d}. 8. Query neural field or volume for density \sigmai and color ci at \mathbf{p}i. 9. Compute step sizes \deltai = z{i+1} - zi. 10. Compute opacity \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) and transmittance Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right). 11. Accumulate color: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci. Formulas: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) \deltai = t{i+1} - ti where \sigmai is the density at sample i, ci is the color contribution, and \deltai is the distance between neighboring sampling points. Parameters: N: Number of sampling points. Typical values range from 32 to 128 depending on scene complexity and hardware constraints. \deltai: Distance between neighboring sampling points along the ray. Edge cases and pitfalls: When N=1, stratification degenerates to uniform sampling. If \sigmai \deltai exceeds \approx 700, \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) underflows to zero, causing \alphai to saturate at 1 and Ti to drop to 0 prematurely. Boundary precision errors can cause gaps or overlaps if z{\text{vals}} are not computed with consistent interpolation. Degenerate rays (zero direction magnitude) must be normalized before sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def stratifiedsample(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, N): # 1. Compute uniform parameter values tvals = [i / N for i in range(N + 1)] # 2. Map to physical distances zvals = [tmin (1.0 - t) + tmax t for t in tvals] # 3. Compute midpoints mids = [0.5 (zvals[i] + zvals[i + 1]) for i in range(N)] # 4. Define interval boundaries lower = [zvals[0]] + mids[:-1] upper = mids[1:] + [zvals[-1]] # 5. Generate random noise u = [random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) for in range(N)] # 6. Sample within intervals zsamples = [lower[i] + u[i] (upper[i] - lower[i]) for i in range(N)] # 7. Compute 3D positions pts = [(rayorigin[0] + z raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + z raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + z raydirection[2]) for z in zsamples] # 8. Query densities and colors # Sources do not specify the neural field query; implement standard volume query here. sigma = [0.0] N color = [(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)] N # 9. Compute step sizes delta = [zvals[i + 1] - zvals[i] for i in range(N)] # 10. Compute opacity and transmittance alpha = [1.0 - math.exp(-sigma[i] delta[i]) for i in range(N)] T = [math.exp(-sum(sigma[j] delta[j] for j in range(i))) for i in range(N)] # 11. Accumulate color C = sum(T[i] alpha[i] color[i][0] for i in range(N)) return pts, sigma, color, T, alpha, C An unbiased radiance estimation technique that reduces variance compared to uniform sampling, particularly effective for degenerate distributions. It sets itself apart from its sibling Batch Stratified Sampling by focusing on the specific integration of radiance along a single ray's path segment using stratified bins, and from Stratified Ray Sampling by operating on the distance parameter t along the ray rather than stratifying the ray origins or directions themselves. Choose this variant when precise per-ray radiance integration is required for physically accurate synthesis. Partitions the ray depth interval [tn, tf] into Nc evenly-spaced bins and perturbs sample positions within each bin to reduce aliasing artifacts during volume rendering. It builds on Stratified Sampling by vectorizing the bin boundary and sampling operations to process multiple rays simultaneously. Unlike pure uniform sampling, it ensures one sample per stratum, avoiding clustering and gaps. Choose this variant for GPU-accelerated neural rendering pipelines where batch processing throughput is critical. Discretizes the integration interval along a camera ray by dividing it into equal-sized bins and drawing one sample uniformly at random from each bin. It is used to approximate acoustic integrals and to capture scene structure during the coarse training stage of neural radiance fields. Choose this variant when coarse scene structure capture or acoustic simulation is the primary objective. Compares surface rendering (PSNR 28.5), uniform sampling with 64 samples (PSNR 29.6), and proposed stratified sampling with 33 samples (PSNR 31.6) on novel view synthesis. Surface rendering produces severe geometric artifacts, while uniform sampling produces stratified artifacts due to discretized sampling. The proposed stratified approach avoids both artifacts and achieves better results with fewer samples. Choose this configuration when balancing reconstruction quality and sample efficiency is required. Computes weights for PDF estimation, normalizes them to form a PDF, computes the cumulative distribution function (CDF), pads the CDF with a zero, generates uniform samples u, finds corresponding indices via searchsorted, clamps denominators to prevent division by zero, and interpolates sample positions within selected bins. Choose this variant when scene density is highly non-uniform and adaptive sample placement is needed to concentrate queries in high-density regions. Time and memory complexity: O(N) time per ray and O(N) memory for storing samples, transmittance, and opacity arrays. The algorithm is highly parallelizable, scaling linearly with the number of rays R to O(N \cdot R) time and memory when vectorized. Measured performance: On novel view synthesis benchmarks, stratified sampling with 33 samples achieves a PSNR of 31.6, outperforming uniform sampling with 64 samples (PSNR 29.6) and surface rendering (PSNR 28.5). Scaling: Performance scales linearly with N; increasing N reduces variance and aliasing at the cost of higher compute and memory bandwidth. Strengths: Guarantees coverage of the integration interval, reduces variance and aliasing compared to pure uniform random sampling, and is computationally lightweight. Limitations: Can still exhibit stratified artifacts if N is too low or bins are too coarse for high-frequency scene details; does not adapt sample density to local scene complexity without PDF inversion. When to use: Standard direct volume ray casting, neural radiance field training, and acoustic integration where uniform coverage and low variance are prioritized. When not: Highly anisotropic or sparse scenes requiring adaptive importance sampling, or when strict unbiased Monte Carlo convergence over many passes is required. Originating from the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) framework, this method was proposed to approximate the continuous volume rendering integral by dividing the ray segment into parts and uniformly randomly sampling within each part. It addresses the limitation of fixed offline sampling locations by ensuring better coverage of the ray space. The technique has since been adopted in neural rendering pipelines, acoustic simulation, and batch-optimized GPU implementations. name: Stratified Monte Carlo Radiance Estimate
head: RVS Stratified Estimate
body: The Stratified Monte Carlo Radiance Estimate is an unbiased radiance estimation technique that reduces variance compared to uniform sampling, particularly effective for degenerate distributions. It operates by stratifying the distance parameter t along a single ray's path segment between near and far clipping planes, distinguishing it from Batch Stratified Sampling and Stratified Ray Sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, near clipping plane tn, far clipping plane tf, and number of samples k. Outputs: Estimated radiance \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for the ray \mathbf{r}. Data Structures: The method requires storing bin boundaries and sampled distances. Implementations typically store these in RayBundle.samplepoints (3D positions) and RayBundle.samplelengths (distances ti). Steps: 1. Define Bin Boundaries: Divide the integration interval [tn, tf] into k equal-sized bins. The boundaries ti for i=0, \dots, k are ti = tn + i \cdot \frac{tf - tn}{k}, where t0 = tn and tk = tf. 2. Generate Samples: For each bin i (i=1, \dots, k), generate a sample \taui within [t{i-1}, ti]. Randomized (Unbiased): Draw ui \sim U[0, 1] and compute \taui = t{i-1} + ui \cdot (ti - t{i-1}). Deterministic (Midpoint): Use \taui = 0.5 \cdot (t{i-1} + ti). 3. Compute 3D Positions: Calculate the 3D position \mathbf{p}i for each sample distance \taui as \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + \taui \mathbf{d}. 4. Evaluate Color: Evaluate the color contribution c{\mathbf{r}}(\taui) at each position \mathbf{p}i. 5. Accumulate Radiance: Compute the final radiance estimate by summing the contributions: \hat{C}{\text{IW}}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^k (ti - t{i-1}) c{\mathbf{r}}(\taui) \frac{dF{\mathbf{r}}}{dt} \bigg|{t=\taui} where \frac{dF{\mathbf{r}}}{dt} is the derivative of the cumulative distribution function for the ray's distance sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def stratifiedmontecarloradianceestimate(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, numsamples, pdffunc, colorfunc): """ Computes the stratified Monte Carlo radiance estimate for a single ray. name: Antithetic Sampling
head: Antithetic BSDF Sampling
body: Antithetic sampling is a variance reduction technique for estimating the derivative of a BSDF with respect to scene parameters when the integrand approximates an odd function. It exploits the symmetry of Normal Distribution Functions (NDFs) to make the derivative term an odd function, allowing paired samples to cancel out noise. It sets itself apart from general stratified sampling by targeting the specific symmetry of microfacet derivatives, whereas its sibling Decomposed sampling addresses cases where derivatives are even functions. Inputs: Outgoing direction \boldsymbol{\omega}o. Scene parameter \pi (e.g., roughness, position). NDF model D (assumed symmetric, e.g., Beckmann, GGX). Outputs: Two antithetic samples for the derivative estimate. Data Structures: Local coordinate system defined by the surface normal \mathbf{n} and tangent \mathbf{t}. Half-way vectors \boldsymbol{\omega}{h,1}, \boldsymbol{\omega}{h,2}. Steps: 1. Draw first half-way vector: Sample a half-way vector \boldsymbol{\omega}{h,1} based on the NDF D. 2. Generate antithetic half-way vector: Set \boldsymbol{\omega}{h,2} to be symmetric to \boldsymbol{\omega}{h,1} with respect to the z-axis in the local coordinate system. 3. Compute incident directions: Calculate the corresponding incident directions \boldsymbol{\omega}{i,1} and \boldsymbol{\omega}{i,2} using the reflection relation \boldsymbol{\omega}{h} = (\boldsymbol{\omega}i + \boldsymbol{\omega}o) / \|\boldsymbol{\omega}i + \boldsymbol{\omega}o\|. 4. Evaluate derivative: Compute the BSDF derivative \frac{\partial fs^{(0)}}{\partial \pi} for both samples. Formulas: The microfacet BSDF decomposes into: fs^{(0)}(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = D(\boldsymbol{\omega}h) fs^{(0)}(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) where fs^{(0)} represents other terms (e.g., Fresnel) and \boldsymbol{\omega}h:= (\boldsymbol{\omega}i + \boldsymbol{\omega}o) / \|\boldsymbol{\omega}i + \boldsymbol{\omega}o\|. The derivative with respect to parameter \pi follows the chain rule: \frac{\partial fs^{(0)}}{\partial \pi} = \frac{\partial D}{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}h} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}h}{\partial \pi} fs^{(0)} + D \frac{\partial fs^{(0)}}{\partial \pi} The first term dominates for glossy BSDFs. If D is symmetric, \frac{\partial D}{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}h} is an odd function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def antitheticbsdfsample(outgoingdirection, parameter, ndfmodel, localbasis): """Generates two antithetic samples for BSDF derivative estimation.""" normal, tangent, bitangent = localbasis # Step 1: Draw first half-way vector based on NDF omegah1 = ndfmodel.importancesample(outgoingdirection, localbasis) # Step 2: Generate antithetic half-way vector symmetric w.r.t. z-axis (normal) z1 = dot(omegah1, normal) x1 = dot(omegah1, tangent) y1 = dot(omegah1, bitangent) omegah2 = normal z1 - tangent x1 - bitangent y1 # Step 3: Compute incident directions omegai1 = reflectacrosshalfway(omegah1, outgoingdirection) omegai2 = reflectacrosshalfway(omegah2, outgoingdirection) # Step 4: Evaluate derivative deriv1 = computebsdfderivative(omegai1, outgoingdirection, parameter, ndfmodel, localbasis) deriv2 = computebsdfderivative(omegai2, outgoingdirection, parameter, ndfmodel, localbasis) return [(omegai1, deriv1), (omegai2, deriv2)] def reflectacrosshalfway(halfway, outgoing): """Computes incident direction from half-way and outgoing vectors.""" return 2.0 dot(halfway, outgoing) halfway - outgoing def computebsdfderivative(incident, outgoing, parameter, ndfmodel, localbasis): """Evaluates the derivative using the chain rule formula.""" wh = normalize(incident + outgoing) Dval = ndfmodel.value(wh) dDdwh = ndfmodel.gradient(wh) dwhdpi = computehalfwayjacobian(incident, outgoing, parameter) Fother = ndfmodel.otherterms(incident, outgoing) dFotherdpi = ndfmodel.othertermsgradient(incident, outgoing, parameter) return dot(dDdwh, dwhdpi) Fother + Dval dFotherdpi def computehalfwayjacobian(incident, outgoing, parameter): """Standard Jacobian for half-way vector w.r.t. parameter.""" return normalize(outgoing - incident) (1.0 / norm(incident + outgoing)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Exponential Path Growth: Applying antithetic sampling to every light bounce on glossy surfaces in scenes with multiple glossy surfaces causes exponential growth in the number of light paths. Even Functions: Antithetic sampling is not effective if the BSDF derivative is an even function (e.g., derivative w.r.t. roughness of GGX), as it produces high variance in such cases. A technique for cases where BSDF derivatives are even functions, where antithetic sampling fails. The parent method that provides the stratified framework within which antithetic sampling is applied to reduce variance. Variance Reduction: Significantly lowers variance when estimating the interior integral for glossy BSDFs where the NDF is symmetric. Complexity: Doubles the number of samples per bounce if applied naively, leading to exponential path counts in complex scenes with multiple glossy surfaces. Limitations: Ineffective for even-function derivatives (e.g., GGX roughness derivative). Usage Strategy: For complex scenes, apply antithetic sampling only once per light path, merge branched paths after a few bounces (when the surface is no longer glossy), and repeat the path k times to sample k different glossy surfaces. Antithetic sampling for BSDF derivatives was formally discussed by Zhang et al. [ZDDZ21], building on earlier mentions in [LHJ19] and [ZSGJ21]. It is a key technique in differentiable rendering to stabilize gradients for glossy materials. name: Batch Stratified Sampling
head: StratifiedSampler, Uniform Stratified Sampling
body: Batch Stratified Sampling partitions the ray depth interval [tn, tf] into Nc evenly-spaced bins and perturbs sample positions within each bin to reduce aliasing artifacts during volume rendering. It builds on Stratified Sampling by vectorizing the bin boundary and sampling operations to process multiple rays simultaneously. Unlike pure uniform sampling, it ensures one sample per stratum, avoiding clustering and gaps. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o} (shape [R, 3]), ray directions \mathbf{d} (shape [R, 3]), near plane tn (scalar or [R]), far plane tf (scalar or [R]), number of bins Nc (integer), and a boolean flag perturb (default True). Outputs: Sample depths \tau (shape (, Nc)) and 3D positions \mathbf{p} (shape (, Nc, 3)). Data Structures: Tensors store all values; depths are stored as floating-point values. Steps: 1. Normalize and Expand Bounds: If tn and tf are scalars or 1D arrays, they are broadcast or reshaped to match the batch dimension R with shape [R, 1]. 2. Compute Normalized Boundaries: Generate Nc + 1 evenly spaced values ui in the interval [0, 1] using linear spacing. 3. Interpolate to World Space: Map the normalized boundaries to the ray-specific near and far planes. For each ray r, the boundaries t^{(r)}i are computed as t^{(r)}i = tn^{(r)} \cdot (1 - ui) + tf^{(r)} \cdot ui, yielding a tensor of shape (, Nc + 1). 4. Define Interval Bounds: Construct lower bounds L^{(r)}i = t^{(r)}{i-1} and upper bounds U^{(r)}i = t^{(r)}i for i=1, \dots, Nc, yielding a tensor of shape (, Nc). 5. Sample Within Bins: Generate random uniform numbers v^{(r)}i \sim U[0, 1] for each ray and bin. If perturb is True, compute the sample depth \tau^{(r)}i = L^{(r)}i + v^{(r)}i \cdot (U^{(r)}i - L^{(r)}i). If perturb is False, use the midpoint \tau^{(r)}i = 0.5 \cdot (L^{(r)}i + U^{(r)}i). 6. Compute 3D Positions: For each sample, compute the 3D position \mathbf{p}^{(r)}i = \mathbf{o}^{(r)} + \tau^{(r)}i \cdot \mathbf{d}^{(r)}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def batchstratifiedsampling(rayso, raysd, near, far, numsamples, perturb=True): """ rayso: [R, 3] raysd: [R, 3] near: scalar or [R] far: scalar or [R] numsamples: int (Nc) perturb: bool """ # 1. Normalize and Expand Bounds if near.ndim == 0: near = near.expand(rayso.shape[0], 1) else: near = near.unsqueeze(-1) if far.ndim == 0: far = far.expand(rayso.shape[0], 1) else: far = far.unsqueeze(-1) # 2. Compute Normalized Boundaries in [0, 1] u = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples + 1, device=rayso.device) # 3. Interpolate to World Space tvals = near (1.0 - u) + far u # Shape: [R, Nc + 1] # 4. Define Interval Bounds lower = tvals[:,:-1] # Shape: [R, Nc] upper = tvals[:, 1:] # Shape: [R, Nc] # 5. Sample Within Bins if perturb: randvals = torch.randlike(lower) zvals = lower + (upper - lower) randvals else: zvals = 0.5 (lower + upper) # 6. Compute 3D Positions raysoexp = rayso.unsqueeze(1) # [R, 1, 3] raysdexp = raysd.unsqueeze(1) # [R, 1, 3] zvalsexp = zvals.unsqueeze(2) # [R, Nc, 1] pts = raysoexp + zvalsexp raysdexp # [R, Nc, 3] return zvals, pts Parameters: numsamples (Nc): The number of stratified bins. Typical values range from 32 to 128 in neural rendering pipelines. perturb: Boolean flag. True for unbiased randomized sampling, False for deterministic midpoint sampling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When tn \approx tf, the bin width becomes very small, potentially leading to numerical instability or duplicate samples. A small epsilon check or clamping of the bin width may be required. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes tn < tf. If tn \ge tf, the interval is invalid and the implementation should validate this input. Batch Dimensions: The method requires consistent batch dimensions for rayso, raysd, near, and far. Mismatched shapes will cause broadcasting errors. Generates a regular grid of samples per pixel with independent uniform random offsets within each grid cell to reduce aliasing while maintaining stratification. It enhances supersampling by introducing random offsets to ray origins within the pixel grid, distributing samples more evenly and reducing patterned artifacts compared to uniform grids. Unlike standard uniform ray sampling, it breaks the rigid alignment of sample positions, which prevents coherent aliasing patterns in volume rendering. A stratified sampling method where the unit interval is partitioned into c strata based on non-zero bins of a predicted distribution, and samples are allocated unevenly to strata based on the predicted probability mass to handle multimodal distributions. It allocates \lfloor s/c \rfloor samples to each stratum and distributes the remainder to bins with maximal predicted probability. It clips the distance between adjacent intra-stratum samples to the bin width to prevent outsized contributions from endpoints. It is biased if the sample budget s < c, but implementations ensure s \ge c via regularization. Typical sample budget s is 17.6 samples per ray at high resolutions. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: In neural rendering benchmarks, hierarchical sampling with Nc=64 coarse and Nf=128 fine samples per ray is commonly used, achieving high PSNR with mixed precision on CUDA. Strengths: Reduces aliasing artifacts compared to uniform sampling; supports efficient batch processing. Limitations: Does not adapt to scene complexity; may waste samples in empty space if not combined with hierarchical or adaptive strategies. When to Use: Standard direct volume rendering or neural rendering where uniform coverage is desired and computational efficiency is key. When Not to Use: Scenes with high variance or complex geometry where adaptive sampling is needed. name: Jittered Sampling
head: Grid-based Jittered Sampling
body: Jittered Sampling generates a regular grid of samples per pixel with independent uniform random offsets within each grid cell to reduce aliasing while maintaining stratification. It enhances supersampling by introducing random offsets to ray origins within the pixel grid, distributing samples more evenly and reducing patterned artifacts compared to uniform grids. Inputs: Adepth: The number of samples along each axis per pixel (integer, typically \ge 1). sample->getX(), sample->getY(): The base coordinates of the pixel or voxel center in the image or texture space. randf(): A function returning a uniform random float in [0, 1). Outputs: A set of 2D sample coordinates for the pixel. Data Structures: No complex structures required; the method operates on scalar coordinates. Steps: 1. Iterate ax from 0 to Adepth-1 and ay from 0 to Adepth-1. 2. Compute the normalized grid offsets: xOffset = \frac{ax}{Adepth} yOffset = \frac{ay}{Adepth}. 3. Generate independent random offsets: xOffsetRandom = randf() \times xOffset yOffsetRandom = randf() \times yOffset. 4. Compute the final sample position: x{final} = sample \rightarrow getX() + xOffset + xOffsetRandom y{final} = sample \rightarrow getY() + yOffset + yOffsetRandom. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def jitteredsample(Adepth, basex, basey, randf): samples = [] for ax in range(Adepth): for ay in range(Adepth): xoffset = ax / Adepth yoffset = ay / Adepth xjitter = randf() xoffset yjitter = randf() yoffset finalx = basex + xoffset + xjitter finaly = basey + yoffset + yjitter samples.append((finalx, finaly)) return samples Parameters: Adepth: Controls the density of samples. Typical values are Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: randf() must return uniform and independent values to maintain statistical benefits. Boundary Conditions: The source formula adds the jitter to the base offset. If Adepth is 1, xOffset is 0, resulting in no jitter. Time Complexity: O(N^2) per pixel, where N = Adepth. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per sample. Strengths: Reduces aliasing artifacts compared to uniform sampling by breaking up coherent patterns. Limitations: Performance scales quadratically with Adepth. When to use: When supersampling is needed to reduce aliasing in volume rendering. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Jittered sampling is an enhancement to supersampling introduced to reduce patterned artifacts in ray casting. It is used in volume rendering to improve the visual quality of ray-cast images by distributing samples more evenly within pixels. The method is part of the family of sampling and jittering techniques in direct volume ray casting. wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, https://github.com/wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ray casting, https://grokipedia.com/page/Raycasting, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Stratified Ray Sampling
head: Jittered Uniform Sampling, Ray Sampling for Acoustic Volume Rendering, Stratified Sample
body: Stratified Ray Sampling discretizes the integration interval along a camera ray by dividing it into equal-sized bins and drawing one sample uniformly at random from each bin. It is used to approximate acoustic integrals and to capture scene structure during the coarse training stage of neural radiance fields. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} (3D vector). Ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized 3D vector). Near plane distance tn (scalar). Far plane distance tf (scalar). Number of samples per ray k (integer). Optional: lindisp (boolean, whether to sample in disparity space). Optional: perturb (boolean, whether to add random jitter). Outputs: Array of sample depths \taui for i=1, \dots, k. Array of 3D sample positions \mathbf{p}i for i=1, \dots, k. Data Structures: zvals: A 1D array of size k storing the depth values along the ray. samplepoints: A 2D array of shape (k, 3) storing the Cartesian coordinates of the samples. Steps: 1. Define Interval and Bins: Determine the total length of the integration interval: L = tf - tn The boundaries of the k equal-sized bins are defined as: ti = tn + i \cdot \frac{L}{k}, \quad \text{for } i = 0, \dots, k. 2. Compute Base Depths (Linear or Disparity): If lindisp is False (standard depth sampling), compute the midpoints or boundaries linearly. If lindisp is True, compute in disparity space (1/t). Linear Depth: Generate k evenly spaced values between tn and tf. Let t{vals} be the boundaries: t{vals}[i] = tn + i \cdot \frac{tf - tn}{k}, \quad i=0,\dots,k. Disparity Depth: Compute boundaries in disparity space d = 1/t: d{vals}[i] = \frac{1}{tn} + i \cdot \frac{\frac{1}{tf} - \frac{1}{tn}}{k}, \quad i=0,\dots,k Convert back to depth: t{vals}[i] = \frac{1}{d{vals}[i]}. 3. Generate Stratified Samples: For each bin i from 1 to k: Identify the bin boundaries: [t{i-1}, ti]. Draw a uniform random number ui \sim U[0, 1]. Compute the sample depth \taui: \taui = t{i-1} + ui \cdot (ti - t{i-1}) Note on Perturbation: In some implementations (e.g., NeRF), jitter is applied to the midpoints of the bins rather than the boundaries to avoid sampling exactly at the edges, which can cause artifacts if the density function is discontinuous. If perturb is True: 1. Compute midpoints mi = 0.5 \cdot (t{i-1} + ti) for i=1, \dots, k-1. 2. Define upper and lower bounds for jitter: \text{lower} = [t0, m1, \dots, m{k-1}] \text{upper} = [m1, \dots, m{k-1}, tk] 3. Draw random t{rand} \sim U[0, 1] of size k. 4. Compute \taui = \text{lower}[i] + t{rand}[i] \cdot (\text{upper}[i] - \text{lower}[i]). 4. Compute 3D Positions: For each sample depth \taui, compute the 3D position \mathbf{p}i: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + \taui \mathbf{d}. 5. Render (Integration): The color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for the ray is approximated by volume rendering integration using the samples: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{k} Ti \alphai ci where: ci is the color contribution at \mathbf{p}i. \sigmai is the density at \mathbf{p}i. \deltai = ti - t{i-1} is the distance between bin boundaries. Note: In standard NeRF implementations, \deltai is often approximated as the distance between consecutive samples \taui - \tau{i-1}, but the theoretical definition relies on the bin width L/k for unbiased estimation of the integral over the bin. Opacity: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). Transmittance: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def stratifiedraysampling(origin, direction, near, far, numsamples, lindisp=False, perturb=True): """ Generates stratified samples along a single ray. Args: origin: Tuple (x, y, z) direction: Tuple (dx, dy, dz) near: Float, near plane distance far: Float, far plane distance numsamples: Int, number of samples per ray (k) lindisp: Bool, if True sample in disparity space perturb: Bool, if True add uniform jitter within bins Returns: depths: List of floats points: List of tuples (x, y, z) """ # Step 1 & 2: Compute bin boundaries boundaries = [] for i in range(numsamples + 1): t = i / numsamples if lindisp: dnear = 1.0 / near dfar = 1.0 / far dval = dnear (1.0 - t) + dfar t boundaries.append(1.0 / dval) else: boundaries.append(near (1.0 - t) + far t) # Step 3: Generate stratified samples depths = [] if perturb: # NeRF-style perturbation using midpoints mids = [0.5 (boundaries[i] + boundaries[i+1]) for i in range(numsamples)] lower = [boundaries[0]] + mids[:-1] upper = mids[1:] + [boundaries[-1]] for i in range(numsamples): u = random.random() depths.append(lower[i] + u (upper[i] - lower[i])) else: # Standard stratified sampling without perturbation for i in range(numsamples): u = random.random() depths.append(boundaries[i] + u (boundaries[i+1] - boundaries[i])) # Step 4: Compute 3D positions points = [] for t in depths: points.append((origin[0] + t direction[0], origin[1] + t direction[1], origin[2] + t direction[2])) return depths, points Parameters: numsamples (k): Typically 64 for coarse networks and 128 for fine networks in hierarchical schemes. near (tn): Minimum depth. Defined in cfg.mindepth. far (tf): Maximum depth. Defined in cfg.maxdepth. lindisp: Boolean. False by default. perturb: Boolean. True by default in many implementations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Near Zero Depth: If tn = 0, disparity sampling (1/t) results in division by zero. Ensure tn > 0 for disparity sampling. Bin Width vs Sample Distance: The opacity calculation \alphai uses \deltai. If using stratified sampling, \deltai should ideally be the bin width L/k to maintain the unbiased nature of the integral over the bin, rather than the distance between random samples \taui - \tau{i-1}, which varies. However, many implementations use sample-to-sample distances for simplicity. Boundary Sampling: Without perturbation, samples might fall exactly on bin boundaries, which can cause artifacts if the density function is discontinuous at those points. Hierarchical Stratified Sampling divides a camera ray into equally spaced bins, draws uniform samples from each, and adaptively refines regions that contributed to the final color using a probabilistic function. It builds on Stratified Ray Sampling by adding an importance-driven refinement layer to improve reconstruction quality and prevent overfitting. Time Complexity: O(k) per ray, where k is the number of samples. Generating random numbers and computing positions is linear in the number of samples. Memory Complexity: O(k) per ray to store sample depths and positions. Strengths: Simple to implement, unbiased (if random), ensures full coverage of the ray interval. Limitations: Does not adapt to scene content; may waste samples in empty space or under-sample in high-frequency regions. When to Use: As a baseline sampling strategy, particularly in the coarse stage of hierarchical rendering. In the context of volume rendering and Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), it was popularized by the original NeRF paper and subsequent implementations. It is used in various domains including acoustic volume rendering and neural surface reconstruction. The method is often employed in the coarse training stage to capture general scene structure before refining with importance sampling. name: Hierarchical Stratified Sampling
head: Importance Stratified Sampling
body: Hierarchical Stratified Sampling divides a camera ray into equally spaced bins, draws uniform samples from each, and adaptively refines regions that contributed to the final color using a probabilistic function. It builds on Stratified Ray Sampling by adding an importance-driven refinement layer to improve reconstruction quality and prevent overfitting. Inputs: Camera ray geometry (origin, direction, t{min}, t{max}), a volume representation, and a target number of initial strata N. Outputs: A sorted list of sample positions t along the ray used to predict the pixel color. Data Structures: 1. Ray Data Structure: One instance per camera ray tracking segment locations where the importance value changes. 2. Sample List: A sorted list of sample positions t and their corresponding contributions. Steps: 1. Initial Stratified Sampling: Divide the camera ray into N equally spaced bins. Draw one sample uniformly at random from each bin. 2. Contribution Analysis: Render the scene using the initial samples to identify which samples contributed to the final color. 3. Adaptive Refinement: Sample more points around the high-contribution regions using a probabilistic function to determine the expected color value along the ray. Maintain one data structure per ray and alternate between uniform strata sampling and adaptive sampling in subsequent progressive rendering passes. Adaptive sampling targets non-sampled regions between segments, within segments to detect splits, and non-sampled regions close to the begin and end of the ray. 4. Aggregation: Combine the initial stratified samples and the refined adaptive samples to predict the pixel color. Parameters: N: Number of initial strata. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Number of adaptive passes: In experiments, one uniform sampling pass followed by three adaptive sampling steps yielded extremely fast accuracy increases. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Using stratified samples generally improves reconstructions by helping to prevent overfitting. View Dependency: NeRFs may produce incorrect depth maps if they rely on all spatial points behind a reflecting surface rather than explaining view-dependent appearance directly. Precision: The accuracy of the estimated integral \tilde{k}(t) depends on the number of adaptive steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def hierarchicalstratifiedsampling(raymint, raymaxt, numinitialstrata=64, numadaptivepasses=3): # Step 1: Divide the camera ray into equally spaced bins and draw a uniform sample from each bin binsize = (raymaxt - raymint) / numinitialstrata samples = [] for i in range(numinitialstrata): t = raymint + i binsize + random.uniform(0, binsize) samples.append(t) # Step 2-3: Maintain one data structure per camera ray # Alternate between uniform strata sampling and adaptive sampling in progressive passes for in range(numadaptivepasses): # Identify which samples contributed to the final color # Sample more points around those regions using a probabilistic function to determine the expected color value along the ray # Adaptive sampling targets: non-sampled regions between segments, within segments to detect splits, and non-sampled regions close to the begin and end of the ray newsamples = [] # The sources do not specify the exact probabilistic function or segment tracking algorithm for t in samples: # Placeholder for probabilistic refinement step pass samples.extend(newsamples) samples.sort() # Step 4: Aggregate samples to predict the pixel color # The exact aggregation weights are not specified in the sources return samples This variant maintains one data structure per camera ray and uses stratified sampling by dividing the ray into N equally-sized regions to obtain a sorted list of new samples. It alternates between uniform strata sampling and adaptive sampling in subsequent progressive rendering passes. Adaptive sampling targets non-sampled regions between segments, within segments to detect splits, and non-sampled regions close to the begin and end of the ray. In experiments, accuracy of \tilde{k}(t) increased extremely fast when performing one uniform sampling, followed by three adaptive sampling steps in subsequent progressive rendering passes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method requires multiple progressive rendering passes, with experimental results showing fast convergence after one uniform pass and three adaptive passes. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing one data structure per camera ray and a sorted list of samples. Strengths: Reduces overfitting and improves reconstruction quality. Allows for progressive refinement and fast accuracy increases in adaptive passes. Limitations: More complex to implement than uniform or simple stratified sampling. Requires multiple passes for optimal results. When to Use: When high-quality reconstruction is needed and computational resources allow for multiple sampling passes. Hierarchical Stratified Sampling was introduced in the context of 3D geometric reconstruction and evaluation of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). It addresses the limitations of NeRFs in handling view-dependent appearance and incorrect depth maps by leveraging hierarchical sampling strategies. The method has been further developed in the context of view-dependent visibility optimization for Monte Carlo volume visualization.
