name: Slab-based Ray Sampling
head: Image-order caching, Slab Definition and Sampling, Slab Sampling, Slab-based approach
body: Slab-based ray sampling is an image-order caching mechanism for direct volume ray casting that groups rays into rectangular screen regions to form stacked slabs, storing voxel samples in shared memory to optimize neighborhood access for lighting and compositing. Unlike object-order bricking, which struggles with GPU hardware mapping due to per-brick lists, this method leverages the regular structure of rays within a slab to reduce memory bandwidth and latency when calculating gradients or performing ambient occlusion. It is distinct from sibling methods like Uniform Ray Sampling by explicitly managing spatial locality in shared memory across multiple rays, and from Stochastic Jittering by prioritizing deterministic cache coherence over variance reduction. Inputs: 3D volume texture (scalar field). Camera parameters (view matrix, projection type: orthogonal or perspective). Screen resolution and subdivision grid (rectangular regions). Slab depth parameter sd (number of samples written to cache per ray at once). Step length d (distance between samples). Outputs: Final pixel color and opacity via front-to-back compositing. Slab Cache: A three-dimensional array stored in GPU shared memory. Dimensions: [N{rays}, N{slices}, N{samples\per\slice}]. N{rays}: Number of rays in the slab (threads in the block). N{slices}: Determined by slab depth sd. N{samples\per\slice}: Determined by ray length and step size. Layout: Rays with the same distance to the camera lie on the same slice. Slab Definition: A slab of thickness 2d is defined by three successive samples (sf, sm, sb). The next slab is indexed by (sf, sm, sb) with the correlation sf = sb (front sample of the next slab equals the back sample of the current slab). d: Step length between samples. sd: Slab depth, controlling the number of samples written into the cache per ray simultaneously. Typical values: Not given in the sources. 1. Screen Subdivision and Slab Creation: The screen is subdivided into rectangular regions. For each region, a slab is created. For orthogonal projection, the slab is a cuboid; for perspective projection, it is a frustum. 2. Start Point Preprocessing: To ensure voxels adjacent in texture space lie close together in the cache, all ray start points in a slab are modified to have the same distance to the camera as the closest ray. Use shared memory and thread synchronization to find the minimum camera distance among all rays in the block. Move each ray's start point to this minimum distance. Pitfall: If the view plane is not parallel to one side of the proxy geometry cube, ray start positions have different distances, causing adjacent voxels to lie on different slices in the cache, resulting in incorrect gradients. Modifying start points resolves this. Texture coordinates will lie outside [0,1]^3; checks must be performed before each 3D texture fetch. 3. Main Loop Part 1 (Cache Filling): Traverse the ray from the modified start point. Retrieve scalar values for the current sample position from the 3D volume texture. Write the sample result into the shared memory slab cache. The slab depth sd controls how many samples are written per ray at a time. Border Handling: For rays adjacent to the slab boundary, execute only Part 1 to write samples into the cache. This ensures inner rays have access to neighbor voxels for gradient calculation, avoiding discontinuities (grid patterns). 4. Thread Synchronization: Perform a barrier synchronization after Part 1 to ensure all samples are written to shared memory before reading. 5. Main Loop Part 2 (Lighting and Compositing): Restart ray traversal from the beginning of the slab. Read samples directly from the shared memory cache instead of the texture. Gradient Calculation: Calculate gradients in eye space using adjacent samples on the same slice from top, left, bottom, and right rays (as seen from the viewpoint), and the next/previous samples on the current ray. Transform gradients to object space for lighting. Compositing: Apply lighting and front-to-back compositing. For pre-integration methods, fetch color/opacity from a 3D pre-integration table using the retrieved scalar values. 6. Early Ray Termination (ERT): ERT cannot stop a single ray independently because data sampled by one ray is used for gradient calculation in adjacent rays. Determine if all rays in the slab have reached the required alpha threshold. Use a flag in shared memory for synchronization to terminate further traversal for the entire slab if the condition is met. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def slabbasedraycasting(blockrays): # 1. Start Point Preprocessing mindist = infinity for i in range(blockrays): dist = length(raystartpositions[i]) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist # Synchronize to find global min in block syncthreads() # Move start points to mindist for i in range(blockrays): currentdist = length(raystartpositions[i]) if currentdist > mindist: # Adjust start point to be at mindist along the ray direction raystartpositions[i] = raystartpositions[i] + (mindist - currentdist) normalize(raydirections[i]) syncthreads() # 2. Main Loop Part 1: Fill Cache for slabindex in range(numslabs): # Define slab bounds based on thickness 2d # Next slab starts where previous ended (sf = sb) for i in range(blockrays): # Check if this is a border ray isborder = isadjacenttoslabboundary(i) # Traverse ray for slab depth sd for sampleidx in range(slabdepth): pos = raystartpositions[i] + sampleidx stepvector # Fetch from volume if isborder or isinnerray(i): val = texturefetch(volumetexture, pos) # Write to shared memory # Layout: rays with same camera distance on same slice sliceidx = getsliceindex(pos) slabcache[i][sliceidx][sampleidx] = val # Synchronize after filling cache syncthreads() # 3. Main Loop Part 2: Lighting and Compositing for i in range(blockrays): # Skip border rays for compositing if they only filled cache if isborder and not isinnerray(i): continue # Read from cache # Calculate Gradient grad = calculategradientfromcache(slabcache, i, sliceidx) # Transform gradient to object space gradobj = transformtoobjectspace(grad) # Lighting and Compositing color = applylightingandcompositing(slabcache, i, gradobj) # Early Ray Termination Check if allraysterminated(): break return finalpixelcolor def calculategradientfromcache(cache, rayidx, sliceidx): # Get adjacent samples on same slice from top, left, bottom, right rays # and next/previous on current ray # Note: Exact indexing depends on ray ordering in block pass def allraysterminated(): # Check shared memory flag set by threads pass Incorrect Gradients: If the view plane is not parallel to one side of the proxy geometry cube, ray start positions have different distances to the camera. This causes voxels adjacent in the volume to lie on different slices in the slab cache, leading to incorrect gradients. Solution: Modify all ray start points in a slab to have the same distance to the camera as the closest one. Discontinuities (Grid Pattern): Ignoring voxels not accessible through the cache for gradient calculation leads to discontinuities, visible as a grid pattern. Solution: Include surrounding voxels by adding all rays adjacent to the slab to the cache. For these border rays, only Part 1 of the main loop is executed. Texture Coordinates: Moving start points may result in texture coordinates outside [0,1]^3. Checks must be performed before each 3D texture fetch. Perspective Projection: Rays are not parallel, so the distance between sample points differs, making the relation between adjacent samples in the cache irregular. An approximation of the neighborhood is often sufficient. Memory: Uses shared memory for the slab cache. The size depends on the number of rays in a block, slab depth sd, and samples per slice. It avoids large global memory allocations for bricking lists. Time: Two passes per slab (fill cache, then read/composite). This doubles the traversal cost for the cached portion but saves memory bandwidth for gradient calculations. Implemented in the Voreen volume rendering framework (Meyer-Spradow et al., 2009) for CUDA version 2.1. Specific performance numbers are not provided in the sources, but it is noted to be better adapted to CUDA architecture features than bricking. Performance advantage is realized when lighting techniques (ambient occlusion, gradient calculation) access the same sample position multiple times. Caching provides no advantage if samples are accessed only once. Strengths: Efficient use of shared memory for image-order processing; reduces memory bandwidth for neighborhood-dependent lighting; avoids object-order bricking inefficiencies on GPUs. Limitations: Requires synchronization; ERT is slab-wide, not per-ray; irregular cache layout in perspective projection; increased complexity in border handling. Use when gradient-based lighting or ambient occlusion is required and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. Use when targeting GPU architectures with efficient shared memory access. Do not use if samples are accessed only once (no caching benefit) or if per-ray early termination is critical without slab-wide synchronization overhead. Introduced as an alternative to bricking (object-order) for CUDA implementation. Implemented in the Voreen volume rendering framework (Meyer-Spradow et al., 2009). Described in "An Advanced Volume Raycasting Technique Using GPU Stream Processing". Used in the Voreen volume rendering framework. Applicable to both orthogonal and perspective projections. name: Supersampling
head: Dense Quadrature Supersampling, Hardware Supersampling, Multi-sampling, NeRF-SR Supersampling, Oversampling, Sub-pixel Supersampling
body: Supersampling is a technique to minimize aliasing artifacts by casting multiple rays per pixel and averaging the results. It handles high-frequency components in transfer functions by performing dense quadrature of the volume render integral, assuming linearity of the scalar field between sample points but not linearity of the integral itself. Unlike pre-integration, which requires equidistant sample points and fails for nonlinear integrals, supersampling accounts for the nonlinearity of the volume render integral while avoiding oversampling of the scalar field. It differs from Stochastic Jittering by using deterministic, fixed offsets for low sample counts (1x–4x) rather than random or stratified patterns, and from Monte Carlo Volume Rendering by relying on simple arithmetic averaging rather than importance-weighted integration. Inputs: Volume data set V with voxel spacing \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z. Camera parameters defining the view ray \gamma(s) for each pixel. Supersampling factor k (number of samples per pixel or per slice). Outputs: Final pixel color C{\text{pixel}}. Data Structures: Sample positions: A set of offsets \{oi\}{i=1}^{k} within the pixel area or along the ray depth. Accumulator: Sum of ray contributions S = \sum{i=1}^{k} Ci. Steps: 1. Define Sample Pattern: Determine the spatial distribution of k sample points within the pixel footprint (x-y plane) or along the ray depth (z-direction). 2. Cast Rays: For each sample point i, cast a ray \gammai(s) through the volume. 3. Sample & Composite: Evaluate radiance along the ray and perform front-to-back or back-to-front compositing to obtain the color Ci for that specific sample ray. 4. Average: Compute the final pixel color by averaging the contributions: C{\text{pixel}} = \frac{1}{k} \sum{i=1}^{k} Ci Parameters: Sampling Rate: Typically 5 samples per pixel in software implementations. Max Supersampling Factor: In hardware (VolumePro), the maximum supersampling factor in the z-direction is eight. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Nonlinearity: Pre-integration fails if sample points are not equidistant because the volume render integral is nonlinear. Regular Spacing: Regular spacing where the distance between sample points in the x- and y-directions can result in aliasing; uniform distribution is desired. Hardware Limitations: Hardware supersampling is supported only in the z-direction in some architectures (e.g., VolumePro). Performance: Supersampling increases computational load. In VolumePro, supersampling by a factor of k reduces the rendering rate of a 256^3 data set to 30 frames per second. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesampleoffsets(k): """Generate k deterministic sample offsets within a unit square pixel.""" if k == 5: # Divide pixel into 4 parts, cast from centers and pixel center return [(-0.25, -0.25), (0.25, -0.25), (-0.25, 0.25), (0.25, 0.25), (0.0, 0.0)] # Standard stratified grid for arbitrary k n = int(k0.5) if n n < k: n += 1 offsets = [] for i in range(n): for j in range(n): if len(offsets) >= k: break offsets.append(((2 i + 1) / (2 n) - 0.5, (2 j + 1) / (2 n) - 0.5)) return offsets[:k] def castrayandcomposite(volume, origin, direction, tmax): """Standard front-to-back volume compositing.""" color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) alpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 step = 1.0 / volume.resolution # Simplified step size while t < tmax and alpha < 1.0: sample = volume.sample(origin + direction t) c, a = sample.color, sample.opacity transmittance = 1.0 - alpha color = tuple(c1 + c2 a transmittance for c1, c2 in zip(color, c)) alpha += a transmittance t += step return color def supersamplevolumeraycasting(volume, camera, pixel, k=5): """Renders a single pixel using supersampling.""" offsets = computesampleoffsets(k) totalcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for dx, dy in offsets: rayorigin, raydirection = camera.getray(pixel.x + dx, pixel.y + dy) color = castrayandcomposite(volume, rayorigin, raydirection, camera.farplane) totalcolor = tuple(c1 + c2 for c1, c2 in zip(totalcolor, color)) return tuple(c / k for c in totalcolor) Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing (MSAA) via Ray Distribution is an image-order rendering technique that reduces aliasing artifacts by casting multiple rays per pixel, distributed within the pixel area, and averaging the resulting color values. It solves the problem of jagged edges caused by abrupt intensity changes along object silhouettes, which occur when a single ray per pixel fails to capture the scene's high-frequency details. Unlike post-processing convolution filters, this method performs supersampling directly during ray traversal, offering higher quality at the cost of increased computational load. It differs from Stochastic Jittering by using deterministic, fixed offsets for low sample counts (1x–4x) rather than random or stratified patterns, and from Monte Carlo Volume Rendering by relying on simple arithmetic averaging rather than importance-weighted integration. Z-direction supersampling is a hardware-accelerated technique that reduces aliasing artifacts by increasing the number of sample slices per volume in the z-direction, interpolating additional sample slices between existing voxel slices. It is distinct from its sibling Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution because it operates by spatial interpolation of volume data along the view ray's depth axis rather than distributing multiple rays per pixel in the image plane. A technique to mitigate interpolation artifacts in sliced-based volume rendering by adjusting the super-sampling level per slab based on its distance to the viewpoint. It assigns a higher super-sampling level to slabs located closer to the viewpoint and a lower level to slabs farther away. VolumePro uses uniform super-sampling across all slabs, causing performance degradation; SWF VRS uses differential levels to balance image quality and rendering speed. A software-based technique to achieve supersampling in x and y directions by rendering the volume multiple times with sub-pixel offsets and blending the results. It renders the volume several times with slightly different sub-pixel accurate initial offsets of the base plane in the x and y dimensions, then blends the resulting images in software to create a smoother final supersampled image. The initial offsets of the base plane must be sub-pixel accurate. A technique to improve image quality by supersampling a 3D data set using a high-quality reconstruction filter in a pre-processing step, then rendering the higher-resolution data set using trilinear interpolation. This approach yields noticeable quality improvements without necessarily increasing rendering time, addressing the low quality of standard trilinear interpolation. A small Gaussian prefilter applied along each ray, sized to the sample step, to remove moiré artifacts and improve biological detail rendering. It applies a Gaussian prefilter along each ray, sized to the sample step, and pairs with hardware-filtered data textures to eliminate the kernel's cost: using R8 for uint8, and R16 via EXTtexturenorm16 for uint16, falling back to the integer path when the extension is missing. Each lookup performs one filtered fetch instead of eight, making the kernel's cost mostly disappear. It extends to float32 next; 32- and 64-bit integers stay on the exact integer path. On integer textures with manual trilinear filtering, the kernel is expensive (about 3–4× the GPU time per frame). Images produced by the filtered path match the integer path to within one 8-bit step. An antialiasing technique that renders geometry into a multisampled G-buffer where attributes like normals and view positions are evaluated at each subsample of a fragment. This allows specular lighting to be computed at a higher effective resolution, reducing specular aliasing that standard MSAA cannot fix. Unlike standard graphics hardware multisampling which only reduces aliasing at polygon edges, this method specifically targets aliased specular highlights introduced by the fragment shader by evaluating normals per subsample. Time Complexity: Increases linearly with the number of samples k per pixel. In hardware (VolumePro), supersampling by a factor of k reduces the rendering rate of a 256^3 data set to 30 frames per second. Memory Complexity: No additional memory required for the sampling pattern itself, but hardware implementations may require additional slice buffers for interpolation. Measured Performance: CUDA implementation capable of rendering 60 frames per second with high-end hardware. Strengths: Reduces wood-grain artifacts and increases image quality by capturing high frequencies of the transfer function. Minimizes aliasing effects significantly. Limitations: Increased computational load. Regular spacing can result in aliasing if not uniform. When to Use: When high image quality is required and computational resources allow. Particularly useful for reducing artifacts along silhouette edges. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and aliasing artifacts are acceptable. Supersampling originated as a general computer graphics technique to combat aliasing caused by coarse granularity of per-pixel sampling. In volume rendering, it was adopted to handle high-frequency components in transfer functions and reduce wood-grain artifacts. The VolumePro system implemented hardware-supported supersampling in the z-direction. CUDA implementations have demonstrated its effectiveness in real-time volume rendering. name: Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution
head: MSAA via Ray Distribution, Multi-ray AA, Multi-sample AA, Multi-sampling for rendering, Ray Distribution AA
body: Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution is an image-order rendering technique that reduces aliasing artifacts by casting multiple rays per pixel, distributed within the pixel area, and averaging the resulting color values. It solves the problem of jagged edges caused by abrupt intensity changes along object silhouettes, which occur when a single ray per pixel fails to capture high-frequency scene details. Unlike post-processing convolution filters, this method performs supersampling directly during ray traversal, offering higher quality at the cost of increased computational load. It differs from Stochastic Jittering by using deterministic, fixed offsets for low sample counts (1x–4x) rather than random patterns, and from Monte Carlo Volume Rendering by relying on simple arithmetic averaging rather than importance-weighted integration. Inputs: Pixel coordinates (x, y) from the rasterizer (e.g., glFragCoord). A uniform integer parameter AA selecting the sampling mode (1, 2, 3, or 4). A rendering function render(uv) that traces a single ray for a given normalized UV offset within the pixel and returns a vec3 color. Outputs: A single vec3 color value representing the averaged result of all distributed rays for the pixel. No complex data structures are required. The method uses scalar arithmetic for offset calculation and accumulation, and stores the AA mode selector as an integer uniform. 1. Select Mode: Determine the number of samples N based on the AA uniform. If AA is not 1, 2, or 3, default to 4. 2. Generate Offsets: Calculate 2D UV offsets (\delta u, \delta v) for each of the N rays. The offsets depend on the mode and, for 2x and 3x, the parity of the pixel coordinates. 3. Trace Rays: For each offset i \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}, pass the offset to getUV and call render to obtain color Ci. 4. Average: Sum all color values Ci and divide by N to produce the final pixel color. AAx1 (N=1): Offset: (0, 0). AAx2 (N=2): Let b{xy} = (x + y) \pmod 2. Let n{bxy} = 1 - b{xy}. Offsets: (0.33 \cdot n{bxy}, 0) and (0.33 \cdot b{xy}, 0.66). AAx3 (N=3): Let b{xy} = (x + y) \pmod 2. Let n{bxy} = 1 - b{xy}. Offsets: (0.66 \cdot n{bxy}, 0), (0.66 \cdot b{xy}, 0.66), and (0.33, 0.33). AAx4 (N=4): Define vector e = (0.125, -0.125, 0.375, -0.375). Offsets: (e.x, e.z), (e.y, e.w), (e.w, e.x), and (e.z, e.y). Averaging: C{final} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} Ci where Ci is the color returned by render(getUV(offseti)). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderaa(x: int, y: int, aamode: int, renderfunc) -> tuple: if aamode not in (1, 2, 3): aamode = 4 if aamode == 1: return renderfunc((0.0, 0.0)) elif aamode == 2: bxy = (x + y) & 1 nbxy = 1 - bxy c1 = renderfunc((0.33 nbxy, 0.0)) c2 = renderfunc((0.33 bxy, 0.66)) return ((c1[0] + c2[0]) / 2.0, (c1[1] + c2[1]) / 2.0, (c1[2] + c2[2]) / 2.0) elif aamode == 3: bxy = (x + y) & 1 nbxy = 1 - bxy c1 = renderfunc((0.66 nbxy, 0.0)) c2 = renderfunc((0.66 bxy, 0.66)) c3 = renderfunc((0.33, 0.33)) return ((c1[0] + c2[0] + c3[0]) / 3.0, (c1[1] + c2[1] + c3[1]) / 3.0, (c1[2] + c2[2] + c3[2]) / 3.0) elif aamode == 4: ex, ey, ez, ew = 0.125, -0.125, 0.375, -0.375 c1 = renderfunc((ex, ez)) c2 = renderfunc((ey, ew)) c3 = renderfunc((ew, ex)) c4 = renderfunc((ez, ey)) return ((c1[0] + c2[0] + c3[0] + c4[0]) / 4.0, (c1[1] + c2[1] + c3[1] + c4[1]) / 4.0, (c1[2] + c2[2] + c3[2] + c4[2]) / 4.0) Performance: This technique significantly reduces framerate due to the increased ray count, as rendering time increases linearly with the number of samples. Optimization: To mitigate performance loss, an optimization is to only perform AA if the iteration count (e.g., ray marching steps) is above average, as this likely indicates the ray is near an object edge. Precision: The source code uses floating-point literals 0.33 and 0.66 rather than exact fractions like 1/3 or 2/3. Boundary Conditions: The offsets are passed directly to getUV for coordinate transformation. Uses random offsets to break up regular aliasing patterns. Sets it apart by avoiding the fixed pattern bias of MSAA. Choose when you need to avoid structured artifacts. Link Uses cumulative distribution functions for importance sampling. Sets it apart by adapting to scene density and lighting. Choose when the scene has varying density or lighting that benefits from non-uniform sampling. Link Samples at regular grid points. Sets it apart by offering simplicity and predictability at the cost of potential moiré patterns. Choose for simplicity and predictability. Link Uses random sampling with statistical integration. Sets it apart by handling complex media and global illumination with higher variance. Choose for high-quality global illumination or complex media, accepting higher variance. Link Combines jittering with temporal reprojection for temporal anti-aliasing. Sets it apart by reducing flickering over time in dynamic scenes. Choose for dynamic scenes to reduce flickering over time. Link General term for sampling at higher resolution. Sets it apart as the parent category, with MSAA via Ray Distribution implementing it using fixed offsets. Choose when high-quality anti-aliasing is required and performance is not the primary constraint. Link Specialized sampling for Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics. Sets it apart by targeting particle-based fluid rendering. Choose for particle-based fluid rendering. Link Uses jittered offsets to reduce aliasing. Sets it apart by balancing regularity and randomness. Choose when you want a balance between regularity and randomness. Link Uses warp-level parallelism for sampling. Sets it apart by optimizing for GPU massive parallel contexts. Choose for GPU optimization in massive parallel contexts. Link Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of samples per pixel. Rendering time increases linearly proportional to the number of samples because the same number of interpolations are required for each sample. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as only the accumulated color sum is stored before averaging. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. However, it is noted that the technique "wrecks your framerate" if not optimized. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with N. AAx4 is 4x slower than AAx1. Strengths: Effective at removing jagged edges and aliasing artifacts, particularly along silhouette edges where intensity changes abruptly. Simple to implement. Limitations: High computational cost. Fixed offsets may not adapt to scene complexity, potentially wasting samples in uniform regions. When to Use: When high-quality anti-aliasing is required and performance is not the primary constraint, or when combined with edge-detection optimizations. When Not to Use: In real-time applications with strict performance budgets, or when the scene is largely uniform and aliasing is minimal. The technique is described in the context of raymarching distance fields and volume rendering. It is a form of supersampling, which is defined as sampling the scene at a higher resolution than displayed to combat aliasing. The specific offset patterns for 2x, 3x, and 4x sampling are derived from implementations in GLSL shaders, as seen in the kushchevd/RayMarching repository. The theoretical basis for supersampling as a method to reduce undersampling artifacts is discussed in literature on volume visualization. name: Z-direction Supersampling
head: Supersampling in z, VolumePro Supersampling
body: Z-direction supersampling is a hardware-accelerated technique that reduces aliasing artifacts by increasing the number of sample slices per volume in the z-direction, interpolating additional sample slices between existing voxel slices. It is distinct from its sibling Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution because it operates by interpolating additional sample slices between existing voxel slices along the volume's z-axis, rather than distributing multiple rays per pixel in the image plane. Inputs: Volume dataset stored in voxel memory; viewing parameters (viewing angle, sample spacing). Outputs: Rendered image with reduced aliasing artifacts. Data Structures: The volume data is stored in voxel memory. The hardware pipeline includes an Interpolation unit that processes slices in order. Steps: 1. Interpolation: The hardware interpolates additional sample slices between existing voxel slices in the z-direction. This is done by performing several interpolations from the same pair of adjacent voxel slices before moving to the next slice pair. Samples pass from the Interpolation unit in slice-by-slice order. 2. Opacity Correction: The software automatically corrects opacity according to the viewing angle and the new sample spacing by reloading the opacity table. 3. Rendering: The interpolated slices are composited along the ray. If the supersampling factor is k, the total number of sample slices exceeds the number of voxel slices by a factor of k. Parameters: Supersampling Factor (k): The maximum supersampling factor in z is eight. Typical values include 2x and 3x. Pitfalls: Pipeline Stall: The voxel memory stages of the pipeline must stall and wait for the additional, supersampled slices to clear, which reduces the rendering rate. Performance: For a 256^3 data set, supersampling reduces the rendering rate to 30 frames per second. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zdirectionsupersampling(volume, rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, supersamplingfactor): """ volume: 3D list [X][Y][Z] of (R, G, B, alpha) tuples. rayorigin: (ox, oy, oz) raydirection: (dx, dy, dz) stepsize: float supersamplingfactor: int k (max 8) Returns: (R, G, B, alpha) """ # Opacity correction factor for supersampling # Software reloads opacity table based on viewing angle and sample spacing def reloadopacitytable(viewingangle, samplespacing, k): return 1.0 / k # Interpolate between two adjacent voxel slices def interpolateslices(slicea, sliceb, fraction): return ( slicea[0] (1 - fraction) + sliceb[0] fraction, slicea[1] (1 - fraction) + sliceb[1] fraction, slicea[2] (1 - fraction) + sliceb[2] fraction, slicea[3] (1 - fraction) + sliceb[3] fraction) # Initialize compositing state alphaout = 0.0 colorout = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] opacityfactor = reloadopacitytable(0.0, stepsize, supersamplingfactor) # Volume dimensions volx = len(volume[0][0]) voly = len(volume[0]) volz = len(volume) # Ray parameters ox, oy, oz = rayorigin dx, dy, dz = raydirection t = 0.0 while True: x = ox + dx t y = oy + dy t z = oz + dz t # Check bounds if not (0 <= x < volx and 0 <= y < voly and 0 <= z < volz): break # Get voxel indices ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) # Clamp indices to valid range for interpolation if ix < 0: ix = 0 if iy < 0: iy = 0 if iz < 0: iz = 0 if ix >= volx - 1: ix = volx - 2 if iy >= voly - 1: iy = voly - 2 if iz >= volz - 1: iz = volz - 2 # Z-supersampling interpolation between adjacent slices fz = z - iz c1 = volume[ix][iy][iz] c2 = volume[ix][iy][iz + 1] sample = interpolateslices(c1, c2, fz) # Apply opacity correction for supersampling a = sample[3] opacityfactor # Front-to-back compositing alphaout += a (1 - alphaout) colorout[0] += sample[0] a (1 - alphaout) colorout[1] += sample[1] a (1 - alphaout) colorout[2] += sample[2] a (1 - alphaout) if alphaout >= 1.0: break t += stepsize return colorout[0], colorout[1], colorout[2], alphaout Time Complexity: Rendering time increases linearly with the supersampling factor k due to the increased number of slices to process and the pipeline stall. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional interpolated slices in the pipeline buffer, causing stalls. Performance: For a 256^3 dataset, rendering rate drops to 30 fps with supersampling. For a 152 \times 261 \times 200 CT scan, 3x supersampling reduces artifacts caused by insufficient sampling rate of high frequencies on the foot surface. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated, effective at reducing aliasing artifacts caused by insufficient sampling rate of high frequencies. Limitations: Limited to z-direction in hardware. Supersampling in x and y requires software-based multi-pass rendering and blending. Pipeline stalls reduce throughput. When to use: When aliasing artifacts are visible due to coarse z-sampling, especially for high-frequency surfaces. When not to use: When performance is critical and artifacts are acceptable, or when supersampling in x/y is required (requires software workaround). Z-direction supersampling was introduced in the VolumePro real-time ray-casting system. VolumePro is a hardware-accelerated volume rendering system. The technique was designed to address aliasing artifacts in real-time volume rendering by increasing the sampling density along the volume's z-axis. It is part of the VolumePro hardware's support for high-quality volume visualization. name: Adaptive Supersampling
head: Adaptive Ray Supersampling
body: Adaptive supersampling is a technique for direct volume ray casting that maintains a user-specified 3D sampling rate by recursively splitting rays when the projected pixel area exceeds the square of the linear sampling rate, thereby avoiding the wasted computation of uniform oversampling near the eye. Unlike uniform supersampling, which wastes computation on near-eye voxels by applying a constant high sampling rate regardless of distance, adaptive supersampling ensures no computation is wasted by oversampling regions close to the eyepoint while increasing density only where necessary. Inputs and Outputs Input: A volume dataset, camera parameters (eye position, view direction, field of view), a user-specified minimum linear sampling rate s, and a screen resolution. Output: A final pixel value for each screen pixel, computed by compositing ray fragments. Data Structures Ray Structure: Each ray object contains: Origin point \mathbf{o} and direction vector \mathbf{d}. Current position along the ray t. Accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} (initialized to 0). A child pointer to manage split rays. A queue or list of active rays (slab queue) for processing. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Compute the solid angle subtended by each screen pixel during initialization. Queue all rays for processing. 2. Ray Casting Loop: For each active ray, determine its current position along the ray axis. 3. Projected Area Calculation: Calculate the projected area A{proj} of the screen pixel at the current position along the ray. This area grows with distance from the eyepoint. 4. Split Condition Check: Compare A{proj} to the square of the linear sampling rate s^2. If A{proj} > s^2, the ray is split. If A{proj} \le s^2, the ray continues without splitting. 5. Ray Splitting: If the condition is met, split the current ray into four divergent child rays at the current split point. The specific geometric arrangement of the four divergent rays is not detailed in the sources, but they are generated to cover the pixel area more finely. 6. Recursion: Recursively apply the split condition to the child rays. This process continues until the ray exits the volume boundary. 7. Sampling: Maintain the sampling rate along the ray axis by taking samples at regular intervals along the ray direction. The sampling rate in the remaining two dimensions (transverse to the ray) is maintained by the adaptive splitting based on projected area. 8. Opacity Check: If the accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} of a ray approaches unity, halt the processing of its child rays by removing them from the slab queue to save computation. 9. Compositing: Composite the resulting ray fragments to yield the final pixel value. In the described implementation, all ray fragments are averaged uniformly during composition. Any filter function could be used in its place. Formulas Split Condition: A{proj}(t) > s^2 Where: A{proj}(t) is the projected area of the screen pixel at distance t along the ray from the eye. s is the user-specified linear sampling rate (samples per unit length in the transverse plane). s^2 is the square of the linear sampling rate, representing the maximum allowed projected pixel area before splitting is required. Parameters Linear Sampling Rate (s): User-specified threshold. The minimum volumetric sampling rate required before triggering a ray split. Uniform Averaging Weight: In the current implementation, fragments are averaged uniformly. The weight for each fragment is 1/N where N is the number of fragments contributing to the pixel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Opacity Cutoff: If accumulated opacity approaches unity, child rays may be halted. Implementers must define a threshold for "approaches unity" (e.g., \alpha{acc} > 0.99) to prevent unnecessary computation. Filter Function: While uniform averaging is used in the source implementation, other filter functions can be used. The choice of filter affects the final image quality and must be consistent with the sampling strategy. Depth of Field: If depth of field is simulated by jittering ray origins over a finite aperture, the slice processing order must be modified to account for the shifting ray origins, necessitating two passes through the slabs within the minimum and maximum z extents of the lens. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivesupersampling(volume, camera, s): """ volume: 3D array of density/opacity values camera: object with eyepos, viewdir, fov, screenwidth, screenheight s: linear sampling rate threshold """ # Initialize rays for each screen pixel rays = [] for y in range(camera.screenheight): for x in range(camera.screenwidth): ray = createrayfrompixel(camera, x, y) ray.accumulatedopacity = 0.0 ray.children = [] rays.append(ray) # Process rays through volume slabs # Note: The source mentions a slab processing order optimized to load each slice once. # We assume a simplified loop over slabs for clarity. for slab in volume.getslabsinorder(): activerays = [] for ray in rays: if ray.isinsidevolume(slab): # Calculate projected area at current ray position projectedarea = calculateprojectedarea(ray, camera) # Check split condition if projectedarea > s2: # Split ray into four divergent children children = splitray(ray) ray.children = children # Add children to active list for next slab activerays.extend(children) # Mark original ray as split, no longer process directly ray.processed = True else: # Continue with current ray activerays.append(ray) # Sample along ray axis at regular intervals samplevalue = samplevolume(ray, slab) ray.accumulatedopacity = compositeopacity(ray.accumulatedopacity, samplevalue) # Check opacity cutoff if ray.accumulatedopacity >= 0.99: # Halt processing of child rays ray.children = [] ray.processed = True rays = activerays # Composite final pixel values pixels = {} for ray in rays: pixelvalue = averagerayfragments(ray) pixels[ray.pixelcoords] = pixelvalue return pixels def calculateprojectedarea(ray, camera): """ Calculate the projected area of the screen pixel at the ray's current position. This area grows with distance from the eyepoint. """ # Distance from eye to current ray position dist = ray.distancefromeye() # Projected area is proportional to dist^2 # Assuming a pinhole camera model pixelsize = camera.screenwidth / camera.fov area = (pixelsize dist)2 return area def splitray(ray): """ Split a ray into four divergent child rays at the current position. The exact geometric distribution is not specified in the source. """ children = [] # Placeholder for specific divergence strategy # Typically, this might involve jittering or grid-based subdivision for i in range(4): child = Ray( origin=ray.currentposition, direction=ray.direction + getdivergencevector(i), accumulatedopacity=0.0, children=[]) children.append(child) return children def averagerayfragments(ray): """ Average the contributions of all ray fragments (children) uniformly. """ if not ray.children: return ray.samplevalue # Or final accumulated color total = 0 count = len(ray.children) for child in ray.children: total += averagerayfragments(child) return total / count Time Complexity: The number of samples is adaptive. In a test case on a 256x256 rendering of a 119x112x73 CT study, adaptive supersampling took about 6 million samples, compared to 12 million samples for uniform supersampling ensuring at least two samples per voxel. This represents a 50% reduction in sample count for the same minimum sampling rate guarantee. Memory Complexity: Requires storing ray structures with child pointers and a slab queue. The source notes that rays are queued during initialization and the slice processing order is optimized so that each slice of memory is loaded only once. Strengths: Automatically computes the number of child rays necessary to maintain a given sampling rate independent of screen resolution. No computation effort is wasted by oversampling the region close to the eyepoint. Limitations: Adds complexity to the ray tracer, which must pass through several sets of slabs and vary the sampling rate along the ray direction. The recursive splitting and management of child rays can increase implementation complexity compared to uniform supersampling. When to Use: When a guaranteed minimum sampling rate is necessary for precision, but uniform supersampling would result in excessive computation due to near-eye oversampling. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and a lower, non-adaptive sampling rate is acceptable, or when the volume data does not require high-frequency detail that would benefit from adaptive refinement. Adaptive supersampling was introduced in the paper "An efficient method for volume rendering using perspective projection". The method builds on the concept of supersampling to combat aliasing but adapts the sampling density based on the geometric projection of the pixel onto the volume. It is used in direct volume ray casting to ensure that voxels are taken into account when precision is absolutely necessary, providing a guarantee that all voxels are sampled adequately without the waste of uniform oversampling. The technique is implemented as an option to any ray tracer, allowing for easy integration. An efficient method for volume rendering using perspective projection, https://doi.org/10.1145/99308.99329, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Importance Sampling for SPH Rendering
head: Non-uniform particle sampling, Stochastic Sampling for SPH Rendering, Stochastic sampling
body: Importance Sampling for SPH Rendering is a technique to increase rendering performance by reducing the number of particles used during rendering, using a non-uniform sampling strategy based on data importance and view-dependent criteria. It solves the problem of high computational cost when rendering large, unstructured Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) datasets by ensuring that particles in complex regions (e.g., phase interfaces, vortices) are sampled more densely than those in homogeneous areas. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by avoiding equal-time high-error trade-offs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: SPH particle dataset (positions, attributes, phases), camera parameters, transfer functions, and sampling parameters p{min} and p{max}. Output: Rendered image with reduced noise and artifacts in critical regions, achieved by selectively accessing a subset of particles per ray. Data Structures: Particle Data: Standard SPH structure containing position \mathbf{x}i, attributes (e.g., density, temperature), and phase identifier. Data Importance Grid/Array: A precomputed value pi for each particle i, representing the static importance of that particle based on local attribute complexity and phase interface presence. View-Dependent Criterion: A dynamic value pt calculated per pixel or ray segment based on view-dependent factors (e.g., opacity, occlusion). Parameters: p{min}: Minimal sampling probability. Controls render time significantly. Recommended value is 0.01 to avoid high sampling error at phase interfaces. p{max}: Maximal sampling probability. Controls rendering error with least effect on render times. Should be assigned to high values to increase the range of sampling probabilities. Steps: 1. Precompute Data Importance (pi): Calculate a static importance value for each particle. This value is low for homogeneous areas and high for complex regions like phase interfaces and vortices. This step is fast (<30ms) compared to volume resampling preprocessing. 2. Determine Sampling Probability (p): For each ray marching step, combine the precomputed data importance pi with the view-dependent criterion pt to determine the per-pixel particle access probability p. The specific combination formula is not provided, but it results in varying probabilities. 3. Stochastic Particle Selection: Based on the calculated probability p, randomly decide whether to access and render the current particle. If accessed, use the particle's attributes for shading. 4. Handle Phase Interfaces and Shading: If a phase transition leading to surface shading is detected during ray marching, use a constant sampling probability of one (p=1) for the iterative search for the surface position xs and the resampling of SPH attributes at xs for shading. For single scattering occlusion rays cast from a sampling point in a volumetric area, reduce the particle sampling probability by a factor of 10% (i.e., p{new} = 0.9 \times p{old}). Do not reduce the probability if an occlusion ray stems from a ray segment containing surface shading, because surfaces have higher opacity and use irradiance influenced by occlusion for shading. 5. Render: Accumulate the contributions of sampled particles to form the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def rendersphimportancesampling(particles, camera, pmin, pmax): # Precompute static data importance pi for each particle # Not given in the sources. Typically involves analyzing local attribute variance and phase interfaces. pi = [0.0] len(particles) image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(camera.height)] for u in range(camera.width): for v in range(camera.height): ray = camera.generateray(u, v) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 while transmittance > 0.001 and ray.t < camera.maxdistance: # Find relevant particles near the current ray position # Not given in the sources. Typically uses spatial hashing or kd-tree. relevantparticles = findparticlesnearray(ray, particles) if not relevantparticles: ray.t += ray.stepsize continue selectedparticle = None for particle in relevantparticles: # Calculate view-dependent criterion pt # Not given in the sources. Typically relates to accumulated opacity or depth. pt = 1.0 - transmittance # Combine pi and pt to get sampling probability p # Formula not provided in the sources p = pi[particle.id] pt p = max(pmin, min(pmax, p)) # Stochastic selection if random.random() < p: selectedparticle = particle break if selectedparticle is None: ray.t += ray.stepsize continue # Check for phase transition if isphasetransition(selectedparticle, ray): # Use constant probability 1 for surface shading search surfacepos = findsurfaceposition(selectedparticle, ray) attributes = resamplesphattributes(surfacepos, particles) color = shadesurface(attributes, ray) transmittance = 0.0 break else: attributes = getparticleattributes(selectedparticle) # Reduce probability for secondary occlusion rays from volumetric areas if issecondaryocclusionray(ray): # Probability reduction factor of 10% applied to subsequent steps pass volumecolor = shadevolume(attributes, ray) color = [c + v transmittance for c, v in zip(color, volumecolor)] transmittance = (1.0 - selectedparticle.opacity) ray.t += ray.stepsize image[v][u] = color return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If p{min} approaches p{max}, the method collapses to uniform sampling, omitting performance advantages. Setting p{min} = 0 can lead to high sampling error at phase interfaces that were not correctly identified in the data importance pi. Therefore, p{min} should be set to at least 0.01 for high-quality renders. Temporal noise: Particle sampling and preprocessing do not currently consider temporal properties, so sampling noise may change between frames in time-dependent data. SPH Attribute Entropy for Importance Sampling is a precomputation technique that assigns sampling probabilities to SPH particles based on the local information complexity of their attributes and the presence of phase interfaces. It solves the problem of high-frequency shading errors and subsampling artifacts at phase boundaries by ensuring that regions with high attribute variation or discontinuous phase transitions are sampled more densely. It differs from naive random discarding by using a structured, data-driven importance grid that accounts for the spatial support of the SPH kernel, and it differs from its sibling Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data by explicitly computing entropy to quantify attribute variation rather than relying solely on stochastic selection heuristics. A direct volume rendering technique for large, unstructured smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) data that avoids intermediate grid representations by stochastically sampling a subset of particles during ray marching. It differs from standard DVR by using view-dependent and spatial-complexity-based probabilities to select particles, enabling continuous scaling from interactive previews to high-quality renders. It specifically addresses multi-phase flows by reconstructing interfaces between different fluid types using a combined volumetric and surface shading model. This method approximates Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) scalar fields along viewing rays using piecewise polynomial functions of higher order, addressing the challenge of rendering SPH data which has highly varying spatial resolution. It sets itself apart from linear or constant approximations by minimizing the L^2 distance between the approximation and the exact particle kernel contribution for each particle individually, allowing the representation resolution to adapt to the data resolution. Unlike sibling methods that focus on sampling strategies or entropy-based selection, this technique focuses on the mathematical fidelity of the field representation along the ray. This variant adapts sampling probabilities based on the type of shading being performed. If a phase transition leading to surface shading is detected during ray marching, it uses a constant sampling probability of one for the iterative search for the surface position xs and the resampling of SPH attributes at xs for shading. For single scattering occlusion, it reduces particle sampling probability by a factor of 10% if an occlusion ray is cast from a sampling point in a volumetric area. However, it does not reduce the probability if an occlusion ray stems from a ray segment containing surface shading, because surfaces have higher opacity and use irradiance influenced by occlusion for shading. Single scattering occlusion is low frequency and impervious to subsampling compared to surface shading, allowing reduced sampling probability for secondary rays which perform the majority of SPH approximations. Time Complexity: Rendering time is linearly dependent on the number of particle accesses. By reducing particle accesses through non-uniform sampling, performance is significantly improved. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for particle data and precomputed importance values pi. No intermediate grid representation is needed, unlike volume resampling. Measured Performance: Spray Nozzle (43.2M particles): Fast rendering <1s, High-quality 8s, No sampling 45s. Bubble (4.3M particles): Aggressive subsampling <1s, Reference >10s. Turbine: Equal-time rendering (5.3s) with uniform sampling had significantly higher error than the non-uniform sampling method. Preprocessing: Negligible preprocessing time (<30ms) compared to volume resampling which can take several minutes. Strengths: Handles dense multi-phase data with accurate phase interface reconstruction; avoids discretization errors associated with grid-based resampling; allows interactive exploration due to low preprocessing time. Limitations: Temporal noise may be visible in time-dependent data; requires careful tuning of p{min} and p{max} to balance error and performance. When to Use: When rendering large, unstructured SPH datasets with complex phase interfaces where uniform sampling is too slow or produces high error. When Not to Use: When temporal consistency is critical and preprocessing for temporal coherence is not implemented; when the dataset is very small and preprocessing overhead dominates. Originating from the paper "Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data", this method was developed to address the challenges of rendering large, unstructured SPH data without the need for expensive intermediate grid representations. It builds on the principles of direct volume ray casting and importance sampling, adapting them to the specific characteristics of SPH data, such as varying particle densities and multi-phase interfaces. The method has been applied to various SPH datasets, including spray nozzles, bubble flows, and turbine simulations, demonstrating significant performance improvements over uniform sampling and volume resampling. name: SPH Attribute Entropy for Importance Sampling
head: Data importance precomputation, Entropy-based importance
body: SPH Attribute Entropy for Importance Sampling is a precomputation technique that assigns sampling probabilities to SPH particles based on the local information complexity of their attributes and the presence of phase interfaces. It solves the problem of high-frequency shading errors and subsampling artifacts at phase boundaries by ensuring that regions with high attribute variation or discontinuous phase transitions are sampled more densely. It differs from naive random discarding by using a structured, data-driven importance grid that accounts for the spatial support of the SPH kernel, and it differs from its sibling Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data by explicitly computing entropy to quantify attribute variation rather than relying solely on stochastic selection heuristics. The method operates in two phases: a precomputation phase that builds an importance grid from the particle data, and a runtime phase that queries this grid during ray marching to determine particle sampling probabilities. Inputs: A particle set \mathcal{P} where each particle i has position \mathbf{x}i, phase \pii, and attribute values for the visualized SPH attribute A. The rendering SPH kernel function with finite support radius h. The importance grid resolution and bounds covering the spatial extent of the SPH data. The number of histogram bins N{\text{bins}} for entropy calculation. The dilation kernel width (in grid cells) and number of dilation iterations. Outputs: An importance grid storing scalar importance values pi(\mathbf{x}) for each cell. The runtime sampling probability p(\mathbf{x}) for any position \mathbf{x} during rendering. 1. Importance Grid: A 3D regular grid where each cell stores a single floating-point value representing the data importance pi(\mathbf{x}c) at the cell center \mathbf{x}c. The grid resolution is chosen to cover the bounding box of the particle set. 2. Histogram: A temporary array of size N{\text{bins}} used to compute the entropy of attribute values for particles within a local neighborhood. The precomputation determines the initial importance for each grid cell and then filters these values to account for the SPH kernel's spatial support and interface detection. 1. Initialize Grid: Create an importance grid of sufficient resolution to cover the particle domain. Initialize all cells to 0. 2. Compute Initial Importance: For each grid cell c with center \mathbf{x}c: a. Identify the set of particles \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) lying within this cell. b. If \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) is empty, set pi(\mathbf{x}c) = 0. c. If \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) contains particles with different phases (i.e., \exists i, j \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) such that \pii \neq \pij), set pi(\mathbf{x}c) = 1. d. Otherwise, if all particles in \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) have the same phase, compute the entropy of attribute A for these particles: i. Bin the attribute values of particles in \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) into a normalized histogram h(b) with N{\text{bins}} bins. ii. Compute the entropy: \mathbb{H}{\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)}(A) = - \sum{b=0}^{N{\text{bins}}-1} h(b) \log2 h(b) iii. Normalize the entropy to be independent of histogram size: \overline{\mathbb{H}}{\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)}(A) = \frac{2^{\mathbb{H}{\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)}(A)}}{N{\text{bins}}} iv. Set pi(\mathbf{x}c) = \mathbb{H}{\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)}(A). 3. Filter with Maximum Dilation: Apply a 3D maximum dilation filter to the importance grid to propagate importance values to neighboring cells, compensating for the fact that SPH approximation at a sampling point depends on particles in neighboring cells. a. Define a dilation kernel with width equal to the number of grid cells covered by the finite support of the SPH kernel function used in rendering. b. For each cell in the grid, update its importance value to the maximum importance value found in any cell within the dilation kernel. c. Interface Detection: During dilation, if more than half of the cells in the dilation kernel do not contain any particles, the cell is expected to contain a free-surface interface. In this case, set the cell's importance pi(\mathbf{x}c) to 1. 4. Iterate Dilation: Repeat the dilation step for a user-specified number of iterations. In practice, 1 or 2 iterations are sufficient. During ray marching, for a sampling position \mathbf{x}: 1. Query the precomputed importance value pi(\mathbf{x}) from the importance grid cell containing \mathbf{x}. 2. Combine pi(\mathbf{x}) with the view-dependent transmittance factor pt(\mathbf{x}) to determine the particle sampling probability p(\mathbf{x}) according to Equation 9 of the parent article. The exact combination formula depends on the parent article's definition of pt(\mathbf{x}). 3. Use p(\mathbf{x}) to stochastically select particles for the SPH approximation at \mathbf{x}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from collections import defaultdict class Particle: def init(self, x, y, z, phase, attr): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z self.phase = phase self.attr = attr def computeentropy(attributevalues, nbins): """Computes entropy for a set of attribute values per Eq. 11.""" if not attributevalues: return 0.0 minval = min(attributevalues) maxval = max(attributevalues) if minval == maxval: return 0.0 binwidth = (maxval - minval) / nbins hist = [0.0] nbins for v in attributevalues: b = int((v - minval) / binwidth) if b >= nbins: b = nbins - 1 hist[b] += 1.0 total = sum(hist) entropy = 0.0 for count in hist: if count > 0: p = count / total entropy -= p math.log2(p) return entropy def precomputeimportancegrid(particles, gridbounds, gridresolution, nbins, dilationradius): """Precomputes the importance grid for SPH attribute entropy sampling.""" nx, ny, nz = gridresolution (minx, maxx), (miny, maxy), (minz, maxz) = gridbounds dx = (maxx - minx) / nx dy = (maxy - miny) / ny dz = (maxz - minz) / nz importancegrid = [[[0.0] nz for in range(ny)] for in range(nx)] hasparticles = [[[False] nz for in range(ny)] for in range(nx)] cellparticles = defaultdict(list) for p in particles: i = int((p.x - minx) / dx) j = int((p.y - miny) / dy) k = int((p.z - minz) / dz) i = max(0, min(nx - 1, i)) j = max(0, min(ny - 1, j)) k = max(0, min(nz - 1, k)) cellparticles[(i, j, k)].append(p) hasparticles[i][j][k] = True for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): if (i, j, k) in cellparticles: plist = cellparticles[(i, j, k)] phases = set(p.phase for p in plist) if len(phases) > 1: importancegrid[i][j][k] = 1.0 else: attrs = [p.attr for p in plist] importancegrid[i][j][k] = computeentropy(attrs, nbins) for in range(dilationradius): newgrid = [[[0.0] nz for in range(ny)] for in range(nx)] for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): imin = max(0, i - dilationradius) imax = min(nx - 1, i + dilationradius) jmin = max(0, j - dilationradius) jmax = min(ny - 1, j + dilationradius) kmin = max(0, k - dilationradius) kmax = min(nz - 1, k + dilationradius) emptycount = 0 maximp = 0.0 totalcells = (imax - imin + 1) (jmax - jmin + 1) (kmax - kmin + 1) for ii in range(imin, imax + 1): for jj in range(jmin, jmax + 1): for kk in range(kmin, kmax + 1): if not hasparticles[ii][jj][kk]: emptycount += 1 else: if importancegrid[ii][jj][kk] > maximp: maximp = importancegrid[ii][jj][kk] if emptycount > totalcells / 2: newgrid[i][j][k] = 1.0 else: newgrid[i][j][k] = maximp importancegrid = newgrid return importancegrid N{\text{bins}}: Number of histogram bins for entropy calculation. Not given in the sources. Dilation kernel width: Equal to the number of grid cells covered by the finite support of the SPH kernel function used in rendering. Dilation iterations: User-specified number of iterations for the filtering process; 1 or 2 iterations are sufficient in practice. Phase Interface Discontinuity: The approximation of phases is discontinuous, leading to edge cases where false distinct phases may be assigned to a sampling point, causing poor surface shading due to high-frequency specular highlights and high opacities. Subsampling Errors at Interfaces: Regions with different phases contain phase interfaces provoking surface shading; small SPH subsampling errors lead to poor surface shading due to dependency on normals and high opacities. Empty Cells: Cells with no particles are assigned importance 0, which is handled correctly by the interface detection logic during dilation. Stratified Stochastic Particle Sampling reduces overall sampling error in SPH rendering by selecting well-distributed particle subsets within an acceleration structure's cells. It differs from naive random discarding by enforcing a structured selection process based on cell and position importance, ensuring that the statistical properties of the particle neighborhood are preserved more accurately during ray marching. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the paper "Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data". It addresses the challenges of rendering SPH data with multiple phases, where traditional uniform sampling can lead to artifacts at phase boundaries. The use of entropy to measure attribute variation is based on information theory [Sha48], and the normalization of entropy follows Wei et al. [WDS18]. name: Stratified Stochastic Particle Sampling
head: Stratification of particle samples
body: Stratified Stochastic Particle Sampling reduces overall sampling error in SPH rendering by selecting well-distributed particle subsets within an acceleration structure's cells. It differs from naive random discarding by enforcing a structured selection process based on cell and position importance, ensuring that the statistical properties of the particle neighborhood are preserved more accurately during ray marching. Inputs: Particle set \mathcal{P} organized in a uniform grid acceleration structure. Data importance grid pi(\mathbf{x}c), precomputed for each cell center \mathbf{x}c. Sampling position \mathbf{x} within the volume. Probability bounds p{\min} and p{\max}. Outputs: A subset of particles chosen from the relevant acceleration structure cells to evaluate the SPH approximation at \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: The acceleration structure is a uniform grid storing particles, aligned with the data importance grid. Both grids share equal cell sizes and perfect overlap, ensuring overlapping cells share the same center point \mathbf{x}c. Parameters: p{\min} and p{\max} define the sampling probability bounds. Grid resolution determines cell size; optimal cell width equals the kernel function support for efficient particle access. Finer grids increase the stratification factor but may decrease performance. Algorithm: 1. Identify all cells in the acceleration structure that contribute to the SPH approximation at \mathbf{x}. Let \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}) be this set. 2. For each cell center \mathbf{x}c \in \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}): a. Retrieve the particle count |\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)| in the cell. b. Retrieve the cell importance pi(\mathbf{x}c). c. Compute the position importance pi(\mathbf{x}) for the sampling location. d. Calculate the target number of particles n using n = p{\min} + (p{\max} - p{\min}) pi(\mathbf{x}c) pi(\mathbf{x}) |\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)|. e. Select \lfloor n \rfloor particles from \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c). f. Select one additional particle with probability n - \lfloor n \rfloor. (The source's "(n - n)" is a typographical error for the fractional part.) 3. Aggregate the selected particles from all cells in \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}) to perform the SPH approximation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def stratifiedstochasticsampling(particlesgrid, importancegrid, x, pmin, pmax, kernelradius): """ Selects particles for SPH approximation at position x using stratification. """ selectedparticles = [] cellsize = particlesgrid.cellsize # 1. Identify contributing cells for SPH approximation at x # Standard SPH kernel support determines which grid cells overlap the kernel sphere. startidx = (math.floor((x[0] - kernelradius) / cellsize), math.floor((x[1] - kernelradius) / cellsize), math.floor((x[2] - kernelradius) / cellsize)) endidx = (math.floor((x[0] + kernelradius) / cellsize), math.floor((x[1] + kernelradius) / cellsize), math.floor((x[2] + kernelradius) / cellsize)) # Precompute position importance pi(x) # Exact formula for position importance is not provided in the sources. positionimportance = 1.0 for i in range(startidx[0], endidx[0] + 1): for j in range(startidx[1], endidx[1] + 1): for k in range(startidx[2], endidx[2] + 1): xc = (i + 0.5) cellsize cellparticles = particlesgrid.getparticlesatcenter(xc) Nc = len(cellparticles) if Nc == 0: continue cellimportance = importancegrid.getvalueatcenter(xc) # 2d. Calculate target number n n = pmin + (pmax - pmin) cellimportance positionimportance Nc # 2e & 2f. Select integer part nint = math.floor(n) if nint > 0: indices = random.sample(range(Nc), min(nint, Nc)) selectedparticles.extend([cellparticles[idx] for idx in indices]) # 2g. Probabilistic additional particle remainder = n - nint if remainder > 0 and nint < Nc: if random.random() < remainder: remainingindices = [idx for idx in range(Nc) if idx not in indices] if remainingindices: selectedparticles.append(cellparticles[random.choice(remainingindices)]) return selectedparticles Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Cell Access: At each sampling position, multiple cells are accessed. The position importance pi(\mathbf{x}) remains constant across all accessed cells, but the cell importance pi(\mathbf{x}c) can differ between these cells during a single SPH approximation. Grid Alignment: The method assumes the acceleration structure and the data importance grid have equal cell sizes and perfect overlap, sharing the same center point \mathbf{x}c. Performance vs. Stratification: Using a finer grid resolution increases the stratification factor but can decrease performance. The optimal cell width is equal to the kernel function support. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of contributing cells and particles per cell. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the uniform grid acceleration structure and the data importance grid. Strengths: Reduces overall sampling error by ensuring well-distributed samples in the neighborhood. It avoids the variance associated with purely random discarding of particles. Limitations: Performance can degrade if the grid resolution is too fine. It requires precomputation of importance values. When to use: Used in SPH rendering to reduce sampling error in neighborhoods. The method is described in the context of stochastic volume rendering of multi-phase SPH data. It builds upon the concept of importance sampling using SPH attribute entropy [3626-sph-attribute-entropy-for-importance-sampling.md]. The technique was introduced to handle the high-frequency nature of surface shading and phase interfaces in SPH rendering. Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi‐Phase SPH Data, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14121, fetched 2026-10-27
