name: Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data
head: Coalesced Memory Access Sampling, GPU Ray Marching Implementation, OpenCL SPH Renderer
body: A direct volume rendering technique for large, unstructured smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) data that avoids intermediate grid representations by stochastically sampling a subset of particles during ray marching. It differs from standard DVR by using view-dependent and spatial-complexity-based probabilities to select particles, enabling continuous scaling from interactive previews to high-quality renders. It specifically addresses multi-phase flows by reconstructing interfaces between different fluid types using a combined volumetric and surface shading model. Inputs: SPH particle dataset containing positions, masses, densities, phase IDs, and attributes. Camera parameters: eye position, view direction, and projection matrix. Rendering parameters: number of ray march steps, kernel type (cubic spline or Epanechnikov), maximum number of particles to sample per cell, and a precomputed random value table. Transfer functions for volumetric opacity and color. Light sources for shading calculations. Outputs: Rendered image with color and opacity per pixel. 1. Particle Storage Flat array of particles grouped by the grid cell they reside in. Each particle i stores: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. mi: Mass. \rhoi: Density. \phii: Phase ID (integer). Other attributes (e.g., temperature Ti). 2. Acceleration Structure (3D Uniform Grid) A 3D uniform grid covering the simulation domain. Each cell stores a reference (pointer/index) to a contiguous block of memory in the Particle Storage array containing all particles within that cell. This structure allows O(1) access to the list of particles in a specific spatial region. The grid is used only for querying particles, not as a discrete signal for traversal. 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, generate a primary ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate along the ray for a fixed number of steps or until the ray exits the domain. a. Determine Sampling Position: Calculate the current sampling point \mathbf{x} on the ray. b. Identify Relevant Grid Cell: Find the grid cell containing \mathbf{x}. c. Stochastic Particle Sampling: i. Retrieve the list of particles in the current cell from the acceleration structure. ii. Select a subset of these particles using stochastic sampling. The probability of selecting a particle is determined by an importance measure based on view-dependent factors and spatial complexity. iii. To ensure coalesced memory access on GPUs, all threads in a work group share the same random offset, but their local work group index is added as an offset to the selection. The selected subset is always a contiguous block of particles in memory. d. SPH Evaluation: i. For each selected particle j, compute the kernel weight W(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}j) using the chosen kernel function (cubic spline or Epanechnikov). ii. Estimate the field value (e.g., density, phase indicator) at \mathbf{x} by summing contributions from selected particles. iii. Determine the dominant phase at \mathbf{x} based on the phase IDs of the contributing particles. iv. Compute gradients if needed for surface reconstruction. e. Shading: i. Volumetric Shading: If the ray segment is within a homogeneous phase, use pre-integrated transfer functions [EKE01] for opacity and color accumulation. Pre-integration assumes fixed segment length and cannot handle phase transitions. ii. Surface Shading: If the ray segment crosses a phase interface, use a multi-material model. Apply Blinn-Phong BRDF for surface shading. iii. Single Scattering: Optionally perform stochastic single scattering to improve spatial perception of phase interfaces. f. Accumulation: Accumulate color and opacity along the ray using standard volume rendering integral equations. 3. Final Color: Output the accumulated color for the pixel. SPH Kernel Functions: The exact mathematical expressions for the kernel functions are Not given in the sources. The cubic spline kernel is smoother but has twice the support width of the Epanechnikov kernel, requiring more particle accesses. Importance Sampling Probability: The probability Pi of selecting particle i is proportional to an importance measure Ii. The exact formula for Ii is Not given in the sources, but it is derived from view-dependent factors and spatial complexity. Pre-integrated Transfer Function: For homogeneous segments, the transmittance T and color C are pre-computed in a 2D texture based on segment length L and optical depth \tau = \int \sigmat ds [EKE01]. This is not applicable to segments with phase transitions. Kernel Function: User-specified. Options: Cubic spline (smoother, wider support, more accesses) or Epanechnikov. Shading Model: Blinn-Phong BRDF for surface, Henyey-Greenstein phase function for volume. Number of Particles to Sample: Controls quality vs. performance. Higher values yield more accurate results. Random Values: Precomputed pseudo-random values are used instead of generating them on the GPU. Random Number Generation: Generating pseudo-random numbers on GPUs is difficult and slow. The method uses precomputed random values to avoid this. Phase Transitions: Pre-integrated transfer functions cannot be used for ray segments that cross phase boundaries because they assume fixed segment length and homogeneous material. Grid Usage: The uniform grid is only for particle querying. Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) or higher-order traversal methods are not applicable because the grid does not represent a discrete signal. Memory Coalescing: To ensure efficient GPU memory access, the selected subset of particles must be contiguous in memory. This is achieved by sharing a random offset across a work group and adding the local work group index. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersphvolume(rayorigin, raydir, grid, particles, randomtable, numsteps, kerneltype, maxsamplespercell, workgroupid, localid, transferfunc): # Initialize accumulation variables color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 # Ray marching loop for step in range(numsteps): # 1. Determine sampling position x = rayorigin + t raydir # 2. Identify relevant grid cell cellidx = grid.querycell(x) cellparticles = grid.cells[cellidx].particleblock # 3. Stochastic particle sampling if len(cellparticles) == 0: continue # Use precomputed random table with work-group offset for coalesced access baseoffset = randomtable[workgroupid] offset = baseoffset + localid sampleidx = offset % len(cellparticles) # Select contiguous block of particles k = min(maxsamplespercell, len(cellparticles)) subset = cellparticles[sampleidx: sampleidx + k] # 4. SPH evaluation density = 0.0 phaseid = -1 gradient = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for p in subset: r = distance(x, p.position) w = evaluatekernel(r, p.h, kerneltype) density += p.mass w / p.density if phaseid == -1 or p.phaseid == phaseid: phaseid = p.phaseid gradient += p.mass w (x - p.position) / p.density # 5. Shading # Check for phase transition or homogeneous segment if isphasetransition(phaseid, previousphase): # Surface shading with Blinn-Phong BRDF shading = computesurfaceshading(x, gradient, lightsources) else: # Volumetric shading with pre-integrated transfer functions opticaldepth = computeopticaldepth(density, steplength) shading = lookuppreintegratedtransfer(opticaldepth, transferfunc) # Optional stochastic single scattering if enablesinglescattering: shading += computesinglescattering(x, raydir, subset) # 6. Accumulation color += shading alpha (1.0 - alpha) alpha += (1.0 - alpha) shading.alpha t += steplength if alpha >= 1.0: break return color Time Complexity: Depends on the number of particles sampled per step. By sampling a subset, it reduces the complexity from O(N) per step to O(k) where k \ll N. The overall complexity is O(R \cdot S \cdot k) where R is the number of rays, S is the number of steps per ray, and k is the number of sampled particles per step. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing particles and the grid. The grid adds minimal overhead as it only stores references. Performance: Scales continuously from fast, interactive previews to high-quality rendering by adjusting the number of sampled particles. Strengths: Minimal preprocessing, no intermediate grid representation, handles large datasets, supports multi-phase flows, efficient GPU implementation with coalesced memory access. Limitations: Stochastic sampling introduces noise; requires careful tuning of the importance measure and number of samples for quality. Pre-integration is limited to homogeneous segments. When to Use: Large SPH datasets where preprocessing time and memory are constraints, and interactive or semi-interactive visualization is desired. Particularly suitable for multi-phase flows. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data". History: It builds on previous work in SPH visualization and stochastic rendering. It addresses the computational complexity of rendering large, unstructured particle data by avoiding intermediate representations and using importance sampling. Usage: Used in scientific visualization for fluid dynamics, particularly for multi-phase flows like gas-liquid interactions. Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi‐Phase SPH Data, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14121, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Particle-Wise Higher-Order SPH Field Approximation for DVR
head: Higher-order SPH field approximation, Particle-Wise Higher-Order SPH Field Approximation, Piecewise polynomial SPH approximation
body: This method approximates Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) scalar fields along viewing rays using piecewise polynomial functions of higher order, addressing the challenge of rendering SPH data which has highly varying spatial resolution. It sets itself apart from linear or constant approximations by minimizing the L^2 distance between the approximation and the exact particle kernel contribution for each particle individually, allowing the representation resolution to adapt to the data resolution. Unlike sibling methods that focus on sampling strategies or entropy-based selection, this technique focuses on the mathematical fidelity of the field representation along the ray [S1, 3626-importance-sampling-for-sph-rendering.md, 3638-stochastic-volume-rendering-of-multi-phase-sph-data.md]. Inputs: SPH particle dataset: positions \chi, mass \mu, target field value \alpha, density \rho, smoothing radius \zeta. Viewing rays defined by base point b and unit direction vector v. Approximation parameters: maximum polynomial degree D and number of non-trivial pieces K. SPH kernel function w(r) (typically cubic B-spline). Outputs: Rendered image with scalar field values. 1. Look-up Table (LUT) for Optimal Approximations: Precomputed for equidistant values of \Lambda (normalized distance from particle to ray). Stores localized difference coefficients \hat{a}{kd} for the optimal approximation of the unit particle contribution B\Lambda. Structure: Array indexed by \Lambda, containing sequences of knots (tk, \hat{a}{k0}, \dots, \hat{a}{kD}). 2. Ray Contribution List: For each ray, a list of contributions from particles. Each contribution is encoded as a sequence of knots: (tk, \hat{a}{k0}, \dots, \hat{a}{kD}). tk: Ray parameter (knot position). \hat{a}{kd}: Localized difference coefficients representing the change in polynomial behavior at tk. 1. Precomputation: For the chosen kernel, generate closed-form symbolic formulas for inner products \langle A, B\Lambda \rangle for variable knot positions \thetak and distance \Lambda. For a range of equidistant \Lambda values, perform non-linear optimization to find optimal knot positions \thetak that minimize E\Lambda. For each \Lambda and its optimal knots, compute the orthogonal basis \mathcal{A} and the optimal approximation S\Lambda. Encode S\Lambda as a sequence of knots (tk, \hat{a}{k0}, \dots, \hat{a}{kD}) and store in LUT. 2. Pass 1: Particle Approximation: For each particle i with parameters \mui, \alphai, \rhoi, \zetai, \chii: For each viewing ray j: Compute t{\chi, ij} (closest point parameter) and \Lambda{ij} = \frac{1}{\zetai} \|\chii - xj(t{\chi, ij})\|. If \Lambda{ij} is within kernel support: Retrieve precomputed localized difference coefficients \hat{a}{kd} from LUT for \Lambda{ij}. Scale and translate coefficients to match particle parameters and ray position. The contribution is \frac{\mui\alphai}{\rhoi\zetai^3} B{\Lambda{ij}}\left(\frac{t - t{\chi, ij}}{\zetai}\right). The encoding in terms of knots (tk, \hat{a}{kd}) must be adjusted for scaling by \zetai and translation by t{\chi, ij}, and amplitude scaling by \frac{\mui\alphai}{\rhoi\zetai^3}. Add the encoded contribution (knots and coefficients) to the ray's contribution list. 3. Pass 2: Sorting: For each ray, sort all contributions in its list by knot position tk in increasing order. 4. Pass 3: Accumulation and Compositing: For each ray: Initialize current polynomial coefficients a{kd} = 0 for all d. Iterate through sorted knots (tk, \hat{a}{k0}, \dots, \hat{a}{kD}): Update coefficients for the current piece k using the update rule: a{kd} = \hat{a}{kd} + \sum{j=d}^D \binom{j}{d} a{(k-1)j} (tk - t{k-1})^{j-d} for d = 0, \dots, D, where t{-1} is the ray start or previous knot, and a{(k-1)j} are coefficients from the previous piece. Evaluate the polynomial Ak(t) = \sum{d=0}^D a{kd} (t - tk)^d at sample points within [tk, t{k+1}] (or integrate if using quadrature) to get the field value. Accumulate the field value along the ray for compositing (e.g., using standard DVR compositing equations with the computed field value as the density/opacity source). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def particlewisesphdvr(particles, rays, lut, D, K, raystart, rayend): # Data structures rayknots = {ray.id: [] for ray in rays} # Pass 1: Particle Approximation for p in particles: for ray in rays: tchi = closestpointparam(ray, p.pos) Lambda = norm(p.pos - ray.pointat(tchi)) / p.zeta if Lambda < lut.maxlambda: # Retrieve precomputed knots and localized difference coefficients knots, hata = lut.query(Lambda) # Scale and translate knots and coefficients for tk, coeffs in zip(knots, hata): scaledt = p.zeta tk + tchi scaledcoeffs = [p.amplitude c for c in coeffs] rayknots[ray.id].append((scaledt, scaledcoeffs)) # Pass 2: Sorting for rayid in rayknots: rayknots[rayid].sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Pass 3: Accumulation and Compositing for ray in rays: a = [0.0] (D + 1) prevt = raystart fieldvalue = 0.0 for tk, hata in rayknots[ray.id]: # Update coefficients using the constant-complexity rule for d in range(D + 1): sumval = 0.0 for j in range(d, D + 1): sumval += comb(j, d) a[j] (tk - prevt)(j - d) a[d] = hata[d] + sumval # Evaluate polynomial at sample points within [tk, t{k+1}] # (Standard DVR sampling step) fieldvalue = sum(a[d] (tsample - tk)d for d in range(D + 1)) # Accumulate field value for compositing # (Standard DVR compositing step) prevt = tk SPH Kernel: The cubic B-spline kernel is used: w(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi} \begin{cases} (2-r)^3 - 4(1-r)^3, & 0 \leq r < 1 \\ (2-r)^3, & 1 \leq r < 2 \\ 0, & 2 \leq r \end{cases} where r is the normalized distance. Particle Contribution: A particle's contribution to a scalar field at position x is: \frac{\mu\alpha}{\rho\zeta^3} w\left(\frac{\|x - \chi\|}{\zeta}\right) Normalized Particle Contribution on a Ray: For a ray x(t) = b + tv, let t\chi be the parameter of the point on the ray closest to particle position \chi. Let \Lambda = \frac{1}{\zeta} \|\chi - x(t\chi)\|. The normalized contribution (unit mass, density, field attribute, smoothing radius) is: B\Lambda(t) = w\left(\sqrt{\Lambda^2 + t^2}\right) The actual contribution of a data particle is: \frac{\mu\alpha}{\rho\zeta^3} B\Lambda\left(\frac{t - t\chi}{\zeta}\right) Polynomial Representation: A polynomial A(t) of order D is represented by coefficients ad: A(t) = \sum{d=0}^D ad t^d Localized coefficients ad at t are computed from standard coefficients aj as: a{d} = \sum{j=d}^D \binom{j}{d} aj t^{j-d} Such that A(t) = \sum{d=0}^D a{d} (t - t)^d. Piecewise Polynomial Encoding: A continuous piecewise polynomial function is defined by knots tk and localized difference coefficients \hat{a}{kd} such that the difference between polynomials Ak (right of tk) and A{k-1} (left of tk) is: Ak(t) - A{k-1}(t) = \sum{d=0}^D \hat{a}{kd} (t - tk)^d Summing piecewise polynomials reduces to sorting their joint knots. The localized coefficients a{kd} for piece k are updated from piece k-1 using: a{kd} = \hat{a}{kd} + \sum{j=d}^D \binom{j}{d} a{(k-1)j} (tk - t{k-1})^{j-d} \quad \text{for } d = 0, \dots, D Optimal Approximation: The goal is to minimize the L^2 distance error: E\Lambda(S) = \|S - B\Lambda\|2 = \left( \int{\mathbb{R}} [S(t) - B\Lambda(t)]^2 dt \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} The space \mathcal{S} consists of even, continuous, piecewise polynomial functions with compact support, maximal degree D, and K non-trivial pieces. The dimension of \mathcal{S} is \lfloor \frac{KD}{2} \rfloor. Basis Construction: 1. Define non-orthogonal basis \tilde{\mathcal{A}} = \{\tilde{A}{kd}\} where \mathcal{J} is the set of pairs (k, d) with k \leq \lceil K/2 \rceil and d \leq D, excluding (1, d) for uneven d if K is uneven. 2. Basis functions are: \tilde{A}{kd}(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } |t| \leq \theta{k-1} \\ 1 - \left( \frac{|t| - \theta{k-1}}{\thetak - \theta{k-1}} \right)^d & \text{if } \theta{k-1} \leq |t| \leq \thetak \\ 0 & \text{if } |t| \geq \thetak \end{cases} where \theta0 = 0 and \thetak are positive knot positions. 3. Convert to orthogonal basis \mathcal{A} using Gram-Schmidt in lexicographical order: A{k^d^} = \tilde{A}{d^k^} - \sum{\substack{(k,d) \in \mathcal{J} \\ k < k^ \vee (k = k \wedge d < d^)}} \text{proj}{A{kd}}(\tilde{A}{d^k^}) where \text{proj}B(A) = \frac{\langle A, B \rangle}{\langle B, B \rangle} B and \langle A, B \rangle = \int{\mathbb{R}} A(t) B(t) dt. Optimal Knot Positions: Find \theta1, \dots, \theta{\lceil K/2 \rceil} by minimizing E\Lambda via non-linear optimization over 0 < \theta1 < \dots < \theta{\lceil K/2 \rceil}. The objective function E\Lambda is computed using closed-form symbolic formulas for inner products \langle A, B\Lambda \rangle, generated once per kernel type using computer algebra systems. For \Lambda close to the upper bound, multiple precision arithmetic (e.g., GNU MPFR) is required for stability. The optimal approximation S\Lambda for fixed knots is the orthogonal projection of B\Lambda onto \mathcal{S}: S\Lambda = \sum{A \in \mathcal{A}} \text{proj}A(B\Lambda) D: Maximum polynomial degree (order of approximation). K: Number of non-trivial polynomial pieces per particle. Continuity and Symmetry: Approximation candidates must be continuous, even functions with compact support to match the target B\Lambda. Numerical Stability: For \Lambda close to the upper bound of the kernel support, evaluation of symbolic formulae becomes unstable. Use multiple precision arithmetic (e.g., GNU MPFR) for precomputation. Degenerate Input: If \zeta = 0, the particle contribution is undefined. Guard against zero smoothing radius. Time Complexity: The summation of piecewise polynomials reduces to a sorting task. The update rule for coefficients has constant complexity per piece, irrespective of the number of particles contributing. Precomputation is done offline. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the LUT (size depends on \Lambda resolution, D, K) and per-ray contribution lists. Strengths: Higher-order approximation provides better accuracy than linear/constant methods, adapting to data resolution. Efficient summation via sorting. Limitations: Precomputation is complex and requires computer algebra systems. Numerical instability for large \Lambda. When to use: When high-fidelity rendering of SPH data is required, and precomputation time is acceptable. When not to use: For real-time rendering with strict latency constraints where precomputation is not feasible, or for very low-resolution approximations where linear methods suffice. The method is based on the paper "Particle-Wise Higher-Order SPH Field Approximation for DVR". SPH was introduced by Gingold and Monaghan (1977) and Lucy (1977). Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) has a long-standing tradition (Drebin et al., 1988). The cubic B-spline kernel is referenced from Rosswog (2009). name: Epipolar Sampling
body: Epipolar sampling is a class of techniques that place sample points along epipolar lines to exploit geometric smoothness and reduce computation. In participating media rendering, it places samples along rays emanating radially from a light source's projection on the screen to exploit the smooth variation of inscattered light along these lines. In multi-view neural rendering, it samples features from other views along epipolar lines corresponding to a given ray, enabling cross-view feature aggregation without full 3D volume rendering. Both variants reduce the number of expensive ray-marching or feature-interpolation steps compared to uniform sampling. The method varies significantly depending on the application domain. The following describes the two primary implementations found in the sources. This variant optimizes the computation of inscattered light (light shafts) in participating media. Inputs: Screen resolution. Projected position of the light source on the screen (Lx, Ly). Depth buffer (z-buffer) of the scene. Number of initial ray-marching samples (N{init}) and interpolation samples (N{interp}) per line. Outputs: Ins scattered light intensity for each screen pixel. Auxiliary textures storing sample indices and coordinates. Data Structures: 1. Epipolar Texture: A 2D texture where each row corresponds to one epipolar line and each column to a sample location on that line. 2. Auxiliary Integer Texture: A two-channel texture storing the indices of the two closest ray-marching samples from the same slice for each interpolation sample. Steps: 1. Epipolar Line Generation: Determine the entry point E as the projected light position on the screen. If the light is behind the camera, E is the point at infinity where rays converge. If the light is on the screen, equidistantly place a user-defined number of exit points along the screen border and connect E to each exit point to form epipolar lines. If the light is outside the screen, cull lines completely outside the visible area and truncate remaining lines against screen borders. 2. Sample Placement: Place N{init} initial ray-marching samples equidistantly along each epipolar line to capture low-frequency variations. Detect depth breaks (discontinuities) in the depth buffer along each epipolar line and place additional ray-marching samples directly before and after each break to capture high-frequency details. Fill the remaining positions with interpolation samples. 3. Ray Marching: Perform expensive ray marching only at the initial and depth-break samples to compute inscattered light intensity. 4. Interpolation: For interpolation samples, compute intensity by linearly interpolating between the intensities of the two closest ray-marching samples. Use the auxiliary integer texture to retrieve the indices of the bounding ray-marching samples for efficient lookup. 5. Pixel Computation: For each screen pixel, cast an epipolar line through the pixel and compute its location in the epipolar texture. Perform bilateral filtering on the gathered inscattered light values. If no appropriate samples exist for filtering, mark the sample in a stencil and perform an additional ray-marching pass with fewer steps. Parameters: Number of initial ray-marching samples (N{init}) and interpolation samples (N{interp}) per line. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the light source is close to the screen boundary, epipolar line lengths vary significantly, causing dense sampling on short lines and redundant computations. Solution: Rescale epipolar lines by advancing the exit point to strive for a 1:1 correspondence between samples and screen pixels, which reduces computations and yields a more natural circular-shaped distribution of samples. This variant samples features from other views along epipolar lines for a given ray, enabling cross-view feature aggregation. Inputs: Image rays (origins, directions) for each pixel in the source view. Camera extrinsics and intrinsics for all views, used to project rays onto target views. Number of samples per epipolar line segment (s), typically 64. Outputs: Aggregated features from other views. Data Structures: EpipolarSampling dataclass containing: features: Float Tensor of shape (batch, view, otherview, ray, sample, channel). valid: Bool Tensor of shape (batch, view, otherview, ray). xyray: Float Tensor of shape (batch, view, ray, 2). xysample: Float Tensor of shape (batch, view, otherview, ray, sample, 2). xysamplenear: Float Tensor of shape (batch, view, otherview, ray, sample, 2). xysamplefar: Float Tensor of shape (batch, view, otherview, ray, sample, 2). origins: Float Tensor of shape (batch, view, ray, 3). directions: Float Tensor of shape (batch, view, ray, 3). Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Generate image rays for each pixel in the source view using sampleimagegrid and getworldrays. 2. Projection: Project rays onto all other views using projectrays with extrinsics, intrinsics, and near/far planes to obtain xymin, xymax, and overlapsimage masks. Clamp xymin and xymax to zero for infinite values and mask with overlapsimage. 3. Sample Depth Generation: Compute sample depths linearly spaced between 0 and 1: \text{sample\depth} = \frac{\text{torch.arange}(s) + 0.5}{s} 4. Coordinate Interpolation: Interpolate sample coordinates in the target view: \text{xy\sample} = \text{xy\min} + \text{sample\depth} \times (\text{xy\max} - \text{xy\min}) 5. Feature Sampling: Transpose sample coordinates so the 'view' dimension refers to the target view. Exclude the diagonal (self-view) using precomputed indices. Sample image features at xysample coordinates using bilinear gridsample with zero padding. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def epipolarsamplefeatures(origins, directions, extrinsics, intrinsics, near, far, s): # origins: (batch, view, ray, 3) # directions: (batch, view, ray, 3) # extrinsics: (batch, view, otherview, 4, 4) # intrinsics: (batch, view, otherview, 3, 3) # near, far: (batch, view, otherview, ray) # 1. Project rays to other views # Compute ray endpoints at near and far planes in world space nearpts = origins + directions near.unsqueeze(-1) farpts = origins + directions far.unsqueeze(-1) # Transform to target view space neartgt = torch.matmul(extrinsics, torch.cat([nearpts, torch.oneslike(nearpts[...,:1])], dim=-1).unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1)[...,:3] fartgt = torch.matmul(extrinsics, torch.cat([farpts, torch.oneslike(farpts[...,:1])], dim=-1).unsqueeze(-1)).squeeze(-1)[...,:3] # Project to screen coordinates nearproj = torch.matmul(intrinsics, neartgt.transpose(-2, -1)).transpose(-2, -1) farproj = torch.matmul(intrinsics, fartgt.transpose(-2, -1)).transpose(-2, -1) xymin = nearproj[...,:2] / nearproj[..., 2:3] xymax = farproj[...,:2] / farproj[..., 2:3] overlapsimage = (nearproj[..., 2] > 0) & (farproj[..., 2] > 0) # 2. Clamp and mask xymin = torch.where(torch.isinf(xymin), torch.zeroslike(xymin), xymin) xymax = torch.where(torch.isinf(xymax), torch.zeroslike(xymax), xymax) xymin = xymin overlapsimage.float() xymax = xymax overlapsimage.float() # 3. Generate sample depths sampledepth = (torch.arange(s) + 0.5) / s # shape: (s,) # 4. Interpolate coordinates # Broadcast sampledepth to (1, 1, 1, 1, s) xysample = xymin + sampledepth.view(1, 1, 1, 1, s) (xymax - xymin) # 5. Transpose and mask self-view xysample = xysample.transpose(1, 2) # (batch, otherview, view, ray, sample, 2) # Exclude diagonal via precomputed mask (implementation omitted as per source comment) # 6. Sample features using bilinear interpolation features = bilinearsample(xysample) return features def bilinearsample(coords): # coords: (batch, otherview, view, ray, sample, 2) in normalized grid coordinates # Standard bilinear texture sampling: sample nearest 2x2 grid points, # compute interpolation weights based on fractional coordinates, and return weighted sum. pass Parameters: Number of samples per epipolar line segment (s), typically 64. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. The Epipolar Encoder is a two-view (or multi-view) neural module that resolves scale ambiguity in 3D reconstruction by aggregating cross-view features along epipolar lines. It solves the problem where camera poses are scaled by an arbitrary factor si, preventing the inference of metric depth from a single view. Unlike standard volume rendering which samples along a ray, this method samples features from a reference pixel and correlates them with features sampled along the corresponding epipolar line in a second view, augmented with positionally encoded depths. This allows the encoder to memorize the correct depth consistent with the scene's arbitrary scale, which is then used for subsequent Gaussian parameter prediction. An extension of the rectification mapping for perspective cameras and local spot lights. The \gamma coordinate is set to the angle the light ray makes with the direction from the light to the camera. This results in nonuniform sampling density along the camera ray, causing the ds/d\gamma term in the integral I(\gamma, \beta) to vary with both \gamma and \beta, unlike directional lights where it varies only with \beta. An algorithm that exploits the geometric structure of epipolar plane images (EPIs) to render scenes from several views simultaneously. Its complexity is an order of magnitude lower than brute-force multiview rendering, but it cannot be applied with existing applications in a non-immersive way. Introduced by M. Halle in Computer Graphics, SIGGRAPH 98 Proceedings, ACM Press. Light Scattering: Dramatically reduces computation time by minimizing expensive ray-marching steps. Rescaling epipolar lines reduces redundant computations on short lines and results in a more natural circular-shaped distribution of samples. Multi-View Aggregation: Enables cross-view feature aggregation without full 3D volume rendering during the encoding phase. Limitations: If the light source is close to the screen boundary, epipolar line lengths vary significantly, causing dense sampling on short lines and redundant computations if not rescaled. Epipolar sampling for light scattering was proposed by Engelhardt and Dachsbacher to optimize the rendering of light shafts by exploiting the smooth variation of inscattered light along epipolar lines. The application of epipolar sampling to multi-view feature aggregation was introduced in pixelSplat to resolve scale ambiguity in 3D Gaussian Splatting from sparse views. dcharatan/pixelsplat, https://github.com/dcharatan/pixelsplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) High-Performance Light Scattering Rendering, https://www.scribd.com/document/748135031/822368Yusov-Egor-Practical-Implementation-of-Light, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) A hierarchical volumetric shadow algorithm for single scattering, https://doi.org/10.1145/1866158.1866200, fetched 2026-11-03 Distributed rendering for multiview parallax displays, https://doi.org/10.1117/12.650171, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Epipolar Encoder
body: The Epipolar Encoder is a two-view (or multi-view) neural module that resolves scale ambiguity in 3D reconstruction by aggregating cross-view features along epipolar lines. It solves the problem where camera poses are scaled by an arbitrary factor si, preventing the inference of metric depth from a single view. Unlike standard volume rendering which samples along a ray, this method samples features from a reference pixel and correlates them with features sampled along the corresponding epipolar line in a second view, augmented with positionally encoded depths. This allows the encoder to memorize the correct depth consistent with the scene's arbitrary scale, which is then used for subsequent Gaussian parameter prediction. The method operates on a pair of reference views, denoted as I (reference) and \tilde{I} (secondary), though it extends to N views. The core mechanism is epipolar cross-attention, which aligns features from I with potential correspondences in \tilde{I} using geometric depth constraints. Inputs: Reference image I and secondary image \tilde{I}. Camera poses for I and \tilde{I} (extrinsics E, \tilde{E} and intrinsics K, \tilde{K}). Feature volumes \mathbf{F} and \tilde{\mathbf{F}} of shape (H, W, C), where H, W are image dimensions and C is the feature dimension. These are produced by a per-image feature encoder applied to I and \tilde{I} separately. Outputs: Updated feature volume \mathbf{F}' of shape (H, W, C), where each pixel \mathbf{F}'[\mathbf{u}] contains aggregated cross-view information and encoded depth consistent with the scene scale. Feature Volumes: \mathbf{F}, \tilde{\mathbf{F}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}. Embedding Matrices: \mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C{head}}. These are learnable linear projection matrices. Positional Encoding: \gamma: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^{C{enc}}. A standard positional encoding function (e.g., sine/cosine or learned) mapping a scalar depth to a vector. Per-Image Embeddings: \mathbf{e}i \in \mathbb{R}^{C{emb}} for each view i (used in multi-view variant). 1. Per-Image Encoding: Encode each input view into a feature volume. \mathbf{F} = \text{Encoder}(I), \quad \tilde{\mathbf{F}} = \text{Encoder}(\tilde{I}) 2. Epipolar Line Computation: For each pixel \mathbf{u} = (ux, uy) in I, compute the epipolar line \ell in \tilde{I} induced by \mathbf{u}'s camera ray. 3. Epipolar Sampling: Sample pixel coordinates \{\tilde{\mathbf{u}}l\} along the epipolar line \ell in \tilde{I}. 4. Depth Triangulation: For each sample \tilde{\mathbf{u}}l, compute the distance \tilde{d}{\tilde{\mathbf{u}}l} from the sample to I's camera origin by triangulating \mathbf{u} and \tilde{\mathbf{u}}l. 5. Feature Augmentation: For each sample \tilde{\mathbf{u}}l, create an augmented feature vector \mathbf{s}: \mathbf{s} = \tilde{\mathbf{F}}[\tilde{\mathbf{u}}l] \oplus \gamma(\tilde{d}{\tilde{\mathbf{u}}l}) where \oplus denotes concatenation. 6. Attention Projection: Compute query, key, and value vectors for the epipolar attention: \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{Q} \cdot \mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}], \quad \mathbf{k}l = \mathbf{K} \cdot \mathbf{s}, \quad \mathbf{v}l = \mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{s} 7. Epipolar Cross-Attention: Update the feature \mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}] using softmax attention over the epipolar samples: \mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}] \leftarrow \mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}] + \text{Att}(\mathbf{q}, \{\mathbf{k}l\}, \{\mathbf{v}l\}) where \text{Att} denotes softmax attention and + denotes a skip connection. 8. Per-Image Self-Attention: Apply a self-attention layer to the entire feature volume \mathbf{F}: \mathbf{F} \leftarrow \mathbf{F} + \text{SelfAttention}(\mathbf{F}) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F import math class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module): def init(self, dim): super().init() self.dim = dim def forward(self, d): # d: (B, N, L) scalar depths divterm = torch.exp(torch.arange(0, self.dim, 2, dtype=torch.float).log() -(math.log(10000.0) / self.dim)) pe = torch.zeroslike(d).unsqueeze(-1) pe[..., 0::2] = torch.sin(d.unsqueeze(-1) divterm) pe[..., 1::2] = torch.cos(d.unsqueeze(-1) divterm) return pe def getpixelcoordinates(H, W, device): y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(H, device=device), torch.arange(W, device=device), indexing='ij') return torch.stack([x.float(), y.float()], dim=-1) def computeepipolarlines(ucoords, poseI, posetilde, K, Ktilde): # ucoords: (B, N, 2) uhom = torch.cat([ucoords, torch.oneslike(ucoords[...,:1])], dim=-1) # (B, N, 3) RI, tI = poseI[:,:,:3,:3], poseI[:,:,:3, 3] Rt, tt = posetilde[:,:,:3,:3], posetilde[:,:,:3, 3] # Essential matrix E = [tt]x Rt RI^T def skew(v): x, y, z = v.unbind(dim=-1) return torch.stack([torch.zeroslike(x), -z, y, z, torch.zeroslike(x), -x, -y, x, torch.zeroslike(x)], dim=-1).view(v.shape[0], 3, 3) E = torch.bmm(skew(tt), torch.bmm(Rt, RI.transpose(1, 2))) # Fundamental matrix F = Ktilde^-T E K^-1 Fmat = torch.bmm(torch.inverse(Ktilde).transpose(1, 2), torch.bmm(E, torch.inverse(K))) # Epipolar lines ltilde = F uhom ltilde = torch.bmm(Fmat, uhom.transpose(1, 2)).transpose(1, 2) # (B, N, 3) return ltilde def samplelinepoints(l, H, W, L): # l: (B, N, 3) line coefficients (a, b, c) ys = torch.linspace(0, H, L, device=l.device).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).expand(l.shape[0], l.shape[1], -1) xs = (-l[:,:, 1:2] ys - l[:,:, 2:3]) / (l[:,:, 0:1] + 1e-8) xs = torch.clamp(xs, 0, W - 1) ys = torch.clamp(ys, 0, H - 1) return torch.stack([xs, ys], dim=-1) # (B, N, L, 2) def triangulatedepths(ucoords, utildesamples, poseI, posetilde, K, Ktilde): # ucoords: (B, N, 2), utildesamples: (B, N, L, 2) # Unproject to rays in camera frames def unproject(u, K): uhom = torch.cat([u, torch.oneslike(u[...,:1])], dim=-1) rays = torch.bmm(uhom.unsqueeze(1), torch.inverse(K).unsqueeze(0)).squeeze(1) return F.normalize(rays, dim=-1) rI = unproject(ucoords, K) # (B, N, 3) rt = unproject(utildesamples, Ktilde) # (B, N, L, 3) # Transform to world frame RI, tI = poseI[:,:,:3,:3], poseI[:,:,:3, 3] Rt, tt = posetilde[:,:,:3,:3], posetilde[:,:,:3, 3] OI = -torch.bmm(RI.transpose(1, 2), tI.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2).unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, rI.shape[1], -1) DI = torch.bmm(RI.transpose(1, 2), rI.transpose(1, 2)).transpose(1, 2) Ot = -torch.bmm(Rt.transpose(1, 2), tt.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(2).expand(-1, rt.shape[1], rt.shape[2], -1) Dt = torch.bmm(Rt.transpose(1, 2), rt.transpose(2, 3)).transpose(2, 3) # Triangulation: solve for depth dI along DI diff = Ot - OI.unsqueeze(2) # (B, N, L, 3) crossprod = torch.cross(DI.unsqueeze(2), Dt, dim=3) # (B, N, L, 3) crossprodsq = torch.sum(crossprod 2, dim=3, keepdim=True) + 1e-8 numerator = torch.sum(diff crossprod, dim=3, keepdim=True) depths = numerator.squeeze(3) / crossprodsq.squeeze(3) # (B, N, L) return depths def samplefeaturesatcoords(F, coords, H, W): # F: (B, H, W, C), coords: (B, N, L, 2) in [0, W]x[0, H] Fperm = F.permute(0, 3, 1, 2) # (B, C, H, W) x = coords[..., 0] / (W - 1) 2 - 1 y = coords[..., 1] / (H - 1) 2 - 1 grid = torch.stack([x, y], dim=-1) # (B, N, L, 2) B, N, L, = coords.shape sampled = F.gridsample(Fperm.view(BN, Fperm.shape[1], H, W), grid.view(BN, L, 1, 2), aligncorners=True) # (BN, C, L, 1) return sampled.view(B, N, L, F.shape[-1]) class EpipolarEncoder(nn.Module): def init(self, featuredim, headdim=64, numheads=8, numsamples=64): super().init() self.numsamples = numsamples self.numheads = numheads self.headdim = headdim self.qproj = nn.Linear(featuredim, numheads headdim) self.kproj = nn.Linear(featuredim + 64, numheads headdim) self.vproj = nn.Linear(featuredim + 64, numheads headdim) self.selfattn = nn.MultiheadAttention(featuredim, numheads, batchfirst=True) self.posenc = PositionalEncoding(64) def forward(self, F, Ftilde, poseI, posetilde, K, Ktilde, H, W): B, H, W, C = F.shape ucoords = getpixelcoordinates(H, W, F.device) ucoordsflat = ucoords.view(1, 1, HW, 2).expand(B, -1, -1, -1) ltilde = computeepipolarlines(ucoordsflat, poseI, posetilde, K, Ktilde) utildesamples = samplelinepoints(ltilde, H, W, self.numsamples) depths = triangulatedepths(ucoordsflat, utildesamples, poseI, posetilde, K, Ktilde) Ftildesamples = samplefeaturesatcoords(Ftilde, utildesamples, H, W) depthenc = self.posenc(depths) s = torch.cat([Ftildesamples, depthenc], dim=-1) q = self.qproj(F.view(B, -1, C)) k = self.kproj(s) v = self.vproj(s) q = q.view(B, HW, self.numheads, self.headdim).transpose(1, 2) k = k.view(B, HW, self.numsamples, self.numheads, self.headdim).transpose(1, 3).transpose(2, 3) v = v.view(B, HW, self.numsamples, self.numheads, self.headdim).transpose(1, 3).transpose(2, 3) attnweights = F.softmax(torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.headdim), dim=-1) attnoutput = torch.matmul(attnweights, v) attnoutput = attnoutput.transpose(1, 2).view(B, HW, self.numheads self.headdim) Fflat = F.view(B, -1, C) Fupdatedflat = Fflat + attnoutput Fupdated = Fupdatedflat.view(B, H, W, C) Fselfinput = Fupdated.view(B, HW, C) Fselfout, = self.selfattn(Fselfinput, Fselfinput, Fselfinput) Ffinal = Fupdated + Fselfout Ffinal = Ffinal.view(B, H, W, C) return Ffinal Number of samples (L): Typically 64. Feature dimension (C): Depends on the backbone (e.g., 256, 512). Head dimension (C{head}): Typically 64. Positional Encoding: Standard sine/cosine or learned. Missing Correspondences: Pixels in I that have no match in \tilde{I} (occlusions, boundaries) will have no valid epipolar samples. The per-image self-attention layer propagates depth estimates from neighboring pixels to these regions. Triangulation Instability: If the rays from I and \tilde{I} are nearly parallel, the triangulation depth \tilde{d}{\tilde{\mathbf{u}}l} becomes noisy. This is mitigated by the attention mechanism, which learns to down-weight unreliable samples. Scale Ambiguity: Without the positional encoding of depth, the encoder cannot resolve the arbitrary scale factor si. The depth augmentation is critical. A multi-view encoder component that resolves scale ambiguity by finding cross-view pixel correspondences and associating them with positionally encoded depth values, allowing the inference of the per-scene scale factor si. It compares features belonging to a ray's corresponding pixel on one view with features sampled along the epipolar line on the other view. Epipolar samples are augmented with their positionally-encoded depths along the ray. Recorded depths are later used for depth prediction. Extends the epipolar encoder from pairs to an arbitrary number of reference views by taking epipolar samples from any number of images and using their union. For a given pixel coordinate, epipolar samples are taken from any number of images. The union of these samples is used in place of a single epipolar line's samples. A learnable per-image embedding is added to each sampled feature to allow the epipolar transformer to distinguish between samples taken from different views. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot L \cdot C^2) per pixel for the cross-attention, where N is the number of pixels, L is the number of epipolar samples, and C is the feature dimension. The self-attention layer adds O(N^2 \cdot C) if applied globally, but is typically applied per-image with linear complexity or reduced heads. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot L \cdot C) to store the epipolar samples and intermediate features. Performance: In 3-view settings, PSNR improves from 26.09 to 28.31 on the Real Estate 10k dataset, with SSIM improving from 0.863 to 0.908. Strengths: Resolves scale ambiguity without explicit depth supervision; leverages geometric constraints for robust feature aggregation. Limitations: Requires accurate camera poses; performance degrades if epipolar geometry is incorrect; self-attention may blur details in textureless regions. The Epipolar Encoder was introduced in "PixelSplat: 3D Gaussian Splats from Image Pairs for Scalable Generalizable 3D Reconstruction" (CVPR 2024). It addresses the limitation of diffusion models that rescale 3D scenes according to heuristics on depth statistics. By using an epipolar transformer, the method infers the scene scale directly from cross-view correspondences. It builds on the concept of epipolar attention [16] and is used in conjunction with 3D Gaussian Splatting [19] for novel view synthesis. PixelSplat: 3D Gaussian Splats from Image Pairs for Scalable Generalizable 3D Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.01840, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Multi-View Epipolar Encoder
head: Multi-View Epipolar Extension
body: The Multi-View Epipolar Encoder extends the standard epipolar encoder from pairs of images to an arbitrary number of reference views. It solves the problem of limited geometric context in two-view reconstruction by aggregating epipolar samples from multiple input images. It differs from its parent, the Epipolar Encoder, by replacing the single epipolar line's samples with the union of samples from N views and introducing view-specific embeddings to disambiguate the source of each sample. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A target pixel coordinate (u, v), N reference images with known camera poses, and the corresponding epipolar geometry. Output: A feature tensor representing the aggregated epipolar context for the target pixel, ready for the epipolar transformer. Data Structures: Learnable Per-Image Embedding: A vector ei \in \mathbb{R}^d for each reference image i \in \{1, \dots, N\}. These are trainable parameters shared across all pixels. Sampled Features: For each reference image i, a set of features Fi sampled along the epipolar line corresponding to (u, v). Bit packing and exact memory layout: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Epipolar Sampling: For each reference image i \in \{1, \dots, N\}, compute the epipolar line in image i corresponding to the target pixel (u, v) in the reference view. Sample features Fi along this line using the same sampling strategy as the base Epipolar Encoder. 2. View Embedding Addition: For each sampled feature f \in Fi, add the learnable per-image embedding ei to f. This allows the subsequent transformer to distinguish which reference image a sample originated from. f'i = fi + ei 3. Union Aggregation: Collect all modified features from all N images into a single set. \mathcal{F}{union} = \bigcup{i=1}^{N} F'i 4. Transformer Input: Pass \mathcal{F}{union} as the input sequence to the epipolar transformer. The transformer processes these samples to produce the final encoded representation. Parameters: N: Number of reference views. The method supports arbitrary N, though the source demonstrates N=3. Learning Rate: The source notes a reduction to 1 \times 10^{-4} from the default 3 \times 10^{-4} to prevent training collapse, but this is a training hyperparameter, not a method parameter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: The number of samples grows linearly with N. If the sampling density is high, memory and compute requirements increase significantly. Ambiguity: Without the learnable embeddings, the transformer cannot distinguish between samples from different views, leading to potential confusion in feature aggregation. The Plane Sweep Volume (PSV) is a 5D tensor representation that encodes the epipolar geometry between a set of input views and a target view by projecting input images onto a series of depth planes. It differs from standard volume representations by structuring data such that adjacent camera rays have adjacent encodings, allowing local operators to process epipolar lines efficiently. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of reference views N and the number of samples per view. Memory Complexity: Linear in N and the number of samples. Performance: The 3-view variant achieves higher PSNR (28.31 vs 26.09) and SSIM (0.908 vs 0.863) on the Real Estate 10k dataset compared to the 2-view baseline. Strengths: Improved reconstruction quality with additional views; scalable to arbitrary numbers of views. Limitations: Increased computational cost with more views; potential for training instability if learning rate is not adjusted. The Multi-View Epipolar Encoder was introduced in the PixelSplat paper (2024) as an extension to the original two-view epipolar encoder. It was developed to leverage more reference views for scalable generalizable 3D reconstruction from images. name: Plane Sweep Volume (PSV)
head: Plane Sweep Volume (PSV) Averaging
body: The Plane Sweep Volume (PSV) is a 5D tensor representation that encodes the epipolar geometry between a set of input views and a target view by projecting input images onto a series of depth planes. It differs from standard volume representations by structuring data such that adjacent camera rays have adjacent encodings, allowing local operators to process epipolar lines efficiently. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of V input images Iv with known camera intrinsics Kv and extrinsics (Rv, tv) relative to a target view. The target view has intrinsics K and normal n. A set of D depth planes is defined parallel to the target image plane, specified by distances \{ad\}{d=1}^D from the target camera center. Output: A 5D tensor X \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times V \times 3 \times H \times W}, where dimensions correspond to depth, view, color channels, height, and width. Data Structures The PSV tensor X is indexed as X{d,v,c,h,w}. d \in \{1, \dots, D\}: Depth plane index. v \in \{1, \dots, V\}: Input view index. c \in \{1, 2, 3\}: Color channel. h, w: Pixel coordinates in the target image plane. Numbered Steps 1. Define Depth Planes: Establish D planes parallel to the target image plane with normal n. The distance ad of each plane from the target camera center is chosen to cover the scene's depth range. 2. Compute Homographies: For each input view v and depth plane d, compute the homography matrix H{dv} that maps points from the target image plane to the input view plane at depth ad. Assuming the world origin is at the target camera center (R = I, t = 0), the homography is: H{dv} = Kv (Rv - tv n^T) K^{-1} where Kv, K are intrinsic matrices, and Rv, tv are the rotation and translation of view v relative to the target. 3. Project Images: Apply the homography H{dv} to each input image Iv to generate a projected image X{dv} for each depth plane. 4. Construct Tensor: Assemble the projected images into the 5D tensor X. The slice r{hw} for a target pixel (h,w) contains pixels sampled along the epipolar lines in all input views at all depths. Specifically: r{hw} = \left\{ \left\{ X{dv,c,h,w} \right\}{c=1}^3 \right\}{d=1}^D \right\}{v=1}^V This structure ensures that operations along the depth dimension correspond to operations along individual epipolar lines, and operations along the view dimension correspond to operations between corresponding epipolar lines. Parameters Typical values for D, V, H, and W are Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Depth Coverage: The distances \{ad\} must be chosen such that the scene of interest is adequately covered. Memory: The 5D structure requires significant memory, scaling as O(D \cdot V \cdot H \cdot W). Averaging Variants Mean PSV: Average the tensor X over the view dimension V to obtain a tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{D \times 3 \times H \times W}. This highlights epipolar geometry: parts of objects lying on a specific depth plane appear in focus, while others appear blurry. Blurry Estimate: Average X over both view and depth dimensions to produce a blurry estimate of the target view. Memory Complexity: O(D \cdot V \cdot H \cdot W). The tensor size grows linearly with the number of depth planes, views, and image resolution. Strengths: Encodes epipolar geometry explicitly, allowing efficient local processing via convolutions. Adjacent rays have adjacent encodings, facilitating the use of simple local operators. Limitations: High memory consumption for large D and V. Requires known camera intrinsics/extrinsics and depth bounds covering the scene. When to Use: Novel view synthesis where generalizable models are needed, and epipolar consistency is important. The Plane Sweep Volume was introduced in the context of generalizable novel view synthesis, specifically in the Global Latent Neural Rendering framework. The concept of averaging the PSV to highlight depth planes is closely related to the original plane sweep algorithm by Collins for depth estimation. The PSV generalizes the 4D tensor (single view) to a 5D tensor (multiple views) to leverage multi-view epipolar geometry. name: Halle’s Multiple Viewpoint Rendering
head: Epipolar Plane Image (EPI) based Multi-View Rendering, Perspective Shift Rendering
body: Halle’s Multiple Viewpoint Rendering is a technique for generating images from arbitrary viewing angles by exploiting the geometric structure of Epipolar Plane Images (EPIs). It solves the problem of efficient multi-view synthesis by treating the light field as a collection of 2D epipolar slices, allowing perspective shifts to be rendered by extracting and reassembling horizontal lines from these slices. Unlike brute-force ray casting, it achieves an order of magnitude lower complexity by avoiding full 3D volume traversal during the encoding phase, though it is restricted to specific epipolar geometries. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of reconstructed (x, u)-epipolar images, one for each vertical coordinate y. These are typically derived from a focal stack or a light field capture. Output: A series of novel perspective-shifted images, each corresponding to a specific viewing angle. Data Structures The core data structure is the Epipolar Plane Image (EPI) for a fixed y. Layout: A 2D image where the horizontal axis represents the spatial coordinate x and the vertical axis represents the view coordinate u (or camera position along the baseline). Size: Width W (spatial resolution), Height Hu (number of views or baseline samples). Content: Pixel value I(x, u, y) represents the intensity at spatial position x, view u, and vertical slice y. Steps 1. Construct EPIs: For every vertical scanline y in the scene, construct the corresponding (x, u)-epipolar image. This aggregates pixel values from multiple input views into a single 2D plane for that y. 2. Select Reference Line: Choose a fixed view coordinate u0 that defines the desired perspective shift. This u0 corresponds to a specific virtual camera position. 3. Extract Horizontal Lines: For each y, extract the horizontal line from the (x, u)-epipolar image at the fixed coordinate u0. The extracted line is Ly(x) = I(x, u0, y). 4. Pile Up Lines: Stack the extracted horizontal lines Ly(x) for all y to form the final rendered image. The resulting image has spatial coordinates (x, y) and represents the scene as seen from the perspective defined by u0. 5. Vary Perspective: To render a series of images from different perspectives, repeat steps 2–4 with different values of u0. Formulas The intensity of the rendered pixel at spatial location (x, y) for a given perspective u0 is: I{rendered}(x, y; u0) = I{EPI}(x, u0, y) Where: I{rendered} is the output image intensity. I{EPI} is the intensity in the epipolar plane image. u0 is the fixed view coordinate (perspective parameter). Parameters u0: The view coordinate index. Varying u0 changes the viewing angle. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Depth Range Violation: If the depth range of the object exceeds the depth range covered by the input focal stack or EPI construction, artifacts such as blurring and transparency may occur. Boundary Artifacts: Regions near object boundaries may become transparent or exhibit artifacts if the underlying assumptions about in-focus depth ranges are violated. Geometric Constraint: The method relies on the epipolar constraint; it cannot be directly applied to general multi-view setups without proper epipolar rectification. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hallemultipleviewpointrendering(epipolarimages, u0): """ Render a single perspective-shifted image from a set of EPIs. Args: epipolarimages: A list or 3D array of shape (Y, X, U) representing the (x, u)-epipolar images for each y. epipolarimages[y, x, u] is the intensity at x, u, y. u0: The fixed view coordinate (integer) defining the perspective. Returns: renderedimage: A 2D array of shape (Y, X) representing the novel view. """ Y, X, U = epipolarimages.shape # Validate u0 is within bounds if u0 < 0 or u0 >= U: raise ValueError("u0 is out of bounds for the epipolar images.") renderedimage = np.empty((Y, X), dtype=epipolarimages.dtype) # Step 3 & 4: Extract horizontal lines at u0 and pile them up # The line at y is epipolarimages[y,:, u0] # Stacking these lines vertically forms the image for y in range(Y): renderedimage[y,:] = epipolarimages[y,:, u0] return renderedimage def renderperspectiveseries(epipolarimages, uvalues): """ Render a series of images for different perspectives. Args: epipolarimages: 3D array (Y, X, U). uvalues: List of view coordinates to render. Returns: series: List of rendered images. """ series = [] for u0 in uvalues: img = hallemultipleviewpointrendering(epipolarimages, u0) series.append(img) return series Time Complexity: The complexity is an order of magnitude lower than brute-force multiview rendering. The extraction and stacking operation is linear with respect to the number of pixels in the output image. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the EPIs. The size depends on the number of views and spatial resolution. Strengths: Efficient for generating multiple perspectives from a single light field representation; avoids full 3D volume rendering during the encoding phase. Limitations: Cannot be applied to existing applications in a non-immersive way without specific support; limited to epipolar geometries. Sensitive to depth range mismatches between the input data and the scene. When to use: When efficient multi-view synthesis is required from a pre-constructed light field or focal stack, and the viewing angles are constrained to the epipolar plane. When not to use: For general 3D volume rendering with arbitrary camera paths; when the depth range of the scene is unknown or exceeds the capture range. Halle’s Multiple Viewpoint Rendering was introduced by M. Halle in the SIGGRAPH 98 Proceedings. It is based on the geometric properties of Epipolar Plane Images (EPIs). The method is often cited in the context of light field processing and multi-view display systems.
