name: Perspective Sampling
head: Warp-space Uniform Sampling
body: Perspective sampling is a point-sampling strategy for camera rays in volume rendering that ensures approximately uniform sampling density in the image plane, rather than in Euclidean space. It addresses the misalignment between axis-aligned grids in Euclidean space and camera rays. It differs from standard uniform sampling by using the Jacobian of the perspective warping function to adjust step sizes. Inputs: Camera origin o \in \mathbb{R}^3. Camera ray direction d \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized). Perspective warping function F: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3 and its Jacobian J(x) = \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}. Preset sampling interval parameter l. Outputs: A sequence of 3D sample points \{xi\} along the ray. Data Structures: Current sample point xi (vector, 3 floats). Next sample point x{i+1} (vector, 3 floats). Jacobian matrix Ji (matrix, 3 \times 3 floats). Steps: 1. Initialize the first sample point x0 at a starting distance t{start} along the ray: x0 = o + t{start} \cdot d. 2. For each sample index i = 0, 1, \dots, N-1: a. Compute the Jacobian matrix Ji of the perspective warping function F at the current point xi. b. Compute the vector v = Ji \cdot d. c. Compute the Euclidean norm \|v\|2. d. Calculate the next sample point using the linear approximation: x{i+1} = xi + l \cdot \|Ji \cdot d\|2 \cdot d. e. Store xi as a sample point. 3. Stop when the ray exits the scene or reaches the far clipping plane. Parameters: l: Preset parameter controlling the sampling interval in the warp space approximation. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Linear Approximation: The method uses a linear approximation for the sampling step, as discussed in the supplementary material. Jacobian Computation: The Jacobian Ji must be computed accurately. If F is a neural network or complex analytical function, automatic differentiation or analytical derivatives are required. Boundary Conditions: The sampling must be bounded by the scene's near and far planes to avoid infinite loops or sampling outside the region of interest. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def perspectivesample(o, d, Fjacobian, l, tstart, tend): """ Generate sample points along a ray using perspective sampling. Args: o: Camera origin (3,) d: Ray direction (3,), normalized Fjacobian: Function to compute Jacobian J(x) -> (3, 3) l: Preset sampling interval parameter tstart: Starting distance along the ray tend: Ending distance along the ray Returns: List of sample points xi """ samples = [] x = [o[r] + tstart d[r] for r in range(3)] while True: # Compute Jacobian at current point J = Fjacobian(x) # Compute J d Jd = [sum(J[r][c] d[c] for c in range(3)) for r in range(3)] # Compute norm ||Jd||2 normJd = sum(v v for v in Jd) 0.5 # Calculate next point: x{i+1} = xi + l ||Ji d||2 d xnext = [x[r] + l normJd d[r] for r in range(3)] # Add current sample samples.append(x) # Update for next iteration x = xnext # Check boundary condition # Distance along ray from origin: dot(x - o, d) dist = sum((x[r] - o[r]) d[r] for r in range(3)) if dist >= tend: break return samples This variant applies perspective sampling to sample points xi on the camera ray, warps them to the warp space using the perspective warping function, and computes density \sigmai and color ci from a neural representation built on the warp space. The final pixel color is computed via volume rendering compositing: \hat{c} = \sumi Ti \alphai ci, where Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1}(1 - \alphaj) is the accumulated transmittance and \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\deltai \sigmai) is the opacity. Time Complexity: The cost per sample is dominated by the evaluation of the warping function F and its Jacobian J. Memory Complexity: Minimal, as it only stores the current point and Jacobian. Performance: Improves sampling efficiency and brings more stable convergence compared to uniform Euclidean sampling. Strengths: Ensures approximately uniform sampling in the image plane, reducing artifacts and improving reconstruction quality. Limitations: Relies on a linear approximation which may be inaccurate for highly non-linear warping functions. Requires computation of the Jacobian, which can be computationally expensive. Perspective sampling is introduced in the context of F2-NeRF (Fast Neural Radiance Field Training with Free Camera Trajectories) to address sampling inefficiencies in volume rendering. It builds on space warping concepts, such as NDC warping and inverse sphere warping, which map unbounded space to a bounded space. name: Proper Space Warping
head: 3D Perspective Warping Construction, F(x), F(x) = MG(x), PCA-based Proper Warping, PCA-based Warping
body: Proper Space Warping constructs a local 3D-to-3D mapping F: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3 that approximates a "proper" warping function, where the squared Euclidean distance in warp space equals the sum of squared distances across all visible cameras. It solves the problem of aligning grid-based scene representations with multi-view geometry by ensuring that axis-aligned grids in the warp space align with camera rays, thereby reducing interpolation artifacts and improving training stability for Neural Radiance Fields. It differs from NDC Warping by using a data-driven PCA projection of multi-view coordinates rather than a fixed normalized device coordinate transformation, and from its parent Space Warping (Log+Warp) by explicitly optimizing for multi-view distance preservation via Principal Component Analysis rather than radial distortion. Inputs: A local 3D region S (typically a leaf node in a spatial hierarchy). A set of nc visible cameras \{Ci\}{i=1}^{nc} for region S. Number of sampled points np (Not given in the sources). Outputs: A warping function F(x) = M G(x), where M is a projection matrix and G(x) maps 3D points to concatenated 2D projected coordinates. The projection matrix M \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 2nc}. Data Structures: Camera Projection Ci(x): Returns the 2D homogeneous or normalized coordinates of 3D point x in camera i's image plane. Mapping Function G(x): Concatenates projections from all nc cameras. G(x) = [C1(x), C2(x), \dots, C{nc}(x)] \in \mathbb{R}^{2nc} Projection Matrix M: A 3 \times 2nc matrix constructed from the first three eigenvectors of the covariance matrix of sampled projected points. Warp Space Points zj: The result zj = F(xj) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Parameters: nc: Number of visible cameras. Typically set to 4 for leaf nodes visible by more than 4 cameras. If fewer than 4 cameras are visible, all are used. Camera Selection: If nc > 4, cameras are selected to maximize the minimal pairwise distance between them. Steps: 1. Sampling: Sample np evenly-spaced points \{xj\}{j=1}^{np} within the local region S. 2. Projection: Compute the projected coordinates for all sampled points across all nc visible cameras: yj = G(xj) = [C1(xj), \dots, C{nc}(xj)] \in \mathbb{R}^{2nc} 3. PCA: Perform Principal Component Analysis on the set of points \{yj\}{j=1}^{np}. Compute the covariance matrix of \{yj\}. Extract the first three eigenvectors corresponding to the largest eigenvalues. Construct M by stacking these three eigenvectors as rows (or columns, depending on convention; the source states M is constructed from the first three eigenvectors, and zj = M yj, implying M is 3 \times 2nc). 4. Warping Function Definition: Define the warping function as: F(x) = M G(x) 5. Post-Normalization: Apply post-normalization to F(x) to ensure the resulting points \{zj\} in the warp space are located around the origin. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeproperwarping(regionpoints, cameras, nc=4): """ Computes the Proper Space Warping function F(x) = M G(x) for a local region. Args: regionpoints: Array of shape (np, 3) containing evenly-spaced 3D points xj in region S. cameras: List of camera objects or functions, each providing a project(x) method returning 2D coords. nc: Number of cameras to use. If len(cameras) > nc, select best nc. Returns: M: Projection matrix of shape (3, 2 nc). selectedcameras: List of selected camera indices or objects. """ # Step 0: Camera Selection if len(cameras) > nc: # Select nc cameras to maximize minimal pairwise distance # Note: Exact selection algorithm is in supplementary material # Placeholder for selection logic selectedcameras = selectcamerasmaxmindistance(cameras, nc) else: selectedcameras = cameras nc = len(cameras) # Step 1 & 2: Project sampled points # yj shape: (np, 2 nc) projectedpoints = [] for x in regionpoints: yj = [] for cam in selectedcameras: # Ci(x) returns 2D coordinates coords = cam.project(x) yj.extend(coords) projectedpoints.append(yj) Y = np.array(projectedpoints) # Shape (np, 2 nc) # Step 3: PCA # Compute covariance matrix of Y # Center Y first (standard PCA practice, though source implies direct eigenvectors) Ycentered = Y - np.mean(Y, axis=0) covmatrix = np.cov(Ycentered, rowvar=False) # Eigendecomposition eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(covmatrix) # Select first three eigenvectors (largest eigenvalues) # eigenvectors are columns; sort by eigenvalue descending sortedindices = np.argsort(eigenvalues)[::-1] top3indices = sortedindices[:3] # M is constructed from the first three eigenvectors # Source says M is 3 x 2nc. If eigenvectors are columns of shape (2nc, 3), # we transpose them to get rows. M = eigenvectors[:, top3indices].T # Shape (3, 2 nc) # Step 4 & 5: Post-normalization # Apply normalization to ensure points are around origin # Note: Exact normalization formula is in supplementary material # Placeholder for normalization M = applypostnormalization(M, Y) return M, selectedcameras def applypostnormalization(M, Y): """ Placeholder for post-normalization step described in supplementary material. Ensures resulting points zj = M yj are located around the origin. """ # Typical normalization might involve centering Y before PCA or scaling M. # Since source details are missing, we return M as is or with a comment. return M Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fewer than 3 visible cameras: PCA requires at least 3 dimensions to produce a 3 \times 2nc matrix if 2nc < 3, or rank deficiency if nc is small. The source specifies nc=4 typically, implying robustness. If nc is very small, the approximation may be poor. Degenerate Camera Configurations: If cameras are collinear or coplanar in a way that reduces the rank of the projected point cloud, PCA may fail to produce a full-rank M. The camera selection strategy (maximizing pairwise distance) mitigates this. Precision: The source notes that F(x) is an approximately proper warping function, relaxing the strict definition to sampled points. This approximation error should be considered. Uses a fixed normalized device coordinate transformation for warping. Choose when a simple, non-data-driven approach is sufficient. Link Uses radial distortion to warp space towards the view cell center. Choose when background dampening is prioritized over multi-view distance preservation. Link Time Complexity: The construction phase involves sampling np points, projecting them through nc cameras, and performing PCA on np points in 2nc dimensions. PCA is O(np (2nc)^2) or O(np^2) depending on implementation. This is done per leaf node. Memory Complexity: Stores the projection matrix M of size 3 \times 2nc per leaf node. Strengths: Aligns grid-based representations with camera rays, reducing interpolation artifacts. Improves training stability for NeRFs with free camera trajectories. Limitations: Requires visible cameras for each region. Computationally more expensive than fixed warping methods due to PCA. Approximate, not exact, proper warping. When to Use: When training NeRFs with diverse camera trajectories and using grid-based scene representations. When Not to Use: When computational resources for per-node PCA are limited, or when camera visibility is sparse. Proper Space Warping was introduced in the F2-NeRF paper (Wang et al., CVPR 2023) to enable fast neural radiance field training with free camera trajectories. It addresses the misalignment between axis-aligned grids and camera rays in multi-view settings by constructing a warping function that preserves multi-view distances. The method relaxes the strict definition of proper warping to an approximate version solvable via PCA. name: MLS Volume Reconstruction
head: MLS Ray Casting, Moving Least Squares Ray Casting, Moving Least Squares Volume Rendering, Volume MLS Ray Casting
body: MLS Volume Reconstruction is a volume rendering technique that approximates a continuous scalar field and its gradients from discrete samples on regular or irregular grids using Moving Least Squares (MLS) approximation. It solves the problem of high-quality visualization of arbitrary volumetric datasets by providing a unified framework for function reconstruction that supports adaptive preintegration. Unlike Radial Basis Functions (RBFs), MLS does not require solving a global system of equations, making it more efficient for large datasets. It sets itself apart from standard interpolation methods by allowing tunable smoothing and interpolation control through basis and weighting functions, and from standard ray casting by integrating adaptive subdivision based on preintegration tables to handle the computational cost of the scalar field evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Discrete scalar values fi at sample positions \mathbf{x}i (regular or irregular grid); transfer function mapping scalar values to color c(\cdot) and opacity \tau(\cdot); ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Output: Final pixel color I and accumulated opacity \alpha. Data Structures: Spatial Index: A hierarchical data structure (e.g., CPU kd-tree) to find neighbor samples \mathbf{x}i with non-zero weights for a query point \mathbf{x}. For irregular data, the kd-tree is built recursively until node size is smaller than the average radius of the node's samples, and a sample is referenced by all leaves intersecting its corresponding ellipsoid or ball. Preintegration Table: A 3D lookup table indexed by f(di), f(d{i+1}), and interval length l = d{i+1} - di. It stores approximated color \tilde{C} and opacity \tilde{\alpha} for linear scalar field assumptions over the interval. Parameters: Basis Functions \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x}): Vector of basis functions. Linear basis \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x}) = (1, x, y, z)^T is recommended. Support Size h: Radius within which neighbors influence reconstruction. Weighting Power \alpha: Controls weight decrease speed. \alpha=4 is recommended for C^3 continuity. Number of Neighbors k: Typically 8 to 20. Error Threshold \varepsilon: Termination criterion for adaptive subdivision. Step 1: Neighbor Query For a query point \mathbf{x} along the ray, find all sample indices i such that the weight wi(\mathbf{x}) > 0 using the spatial index. Step 2: Weight Computation Compute weights wi(\mathbf{x}) for each neighbor. For uniform data: wi(\mathbf{x}) = \theta \left( \frac{\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i\|}{h} \right) where \theta(u) = (1-u^2)^\alpha if u < 1, else 0. For irregular/anisotropic data: wi(\mathbf{x}) = \theta \left( \|\mathbf{H}i(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i)\| \right) where \mathbf{H}i is a transformation matrix from covariance analysis of one-ring neighborhoods. Step 3: MLS Coefficient Calculation Solve for the local coefficients \mathbf{c}{\mathbf{x}} that minimize the weighted sum of squared errors: \mathbf{c}{\mathbf{x}} = \operatorname{argmin}{\mathbf{c}} \sumi wi(\mathbf{x}) | \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x}i)^T \mathbf{c} - fi |^2 In matrix form, let \mathbf{B} be the n \times k matrix where B{ij} = bj(\mathbf{x}i), \mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x}) be the diagonal matrix of weights, and \mathbf{f} be the vector of data values. The solution is: \mathbf{c}{\mathbf{x}} = (\mathbf{B}^T \mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{B})^{-1} \mathbf{B}^T \mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{f} To improve stability and performance: 1. Shift the basis origin to \mathbf{x}: evaluate \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}). 2. Use Cholesky-like decomposition \mathbf{B}^T \mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{L} \mathbf{D} \mathbf{L}^T (where \mathbf{L} is lower triangular with unit diagonal, \mathbf{D} is diagonal). 3. Compute \mathbf{c}{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{L}^{-T} \mathbf{D}^{-1} \mathbf{L}^{-1} (\mathbf{B}^T \mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{f}). 4. Since the basis is evaluated at the origin (\mathbf{x}), only the constant coefficient c1 of \mathbf{c}{\mathbf{x}} is needed for the function value f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x})^T \mathbf{c}{\mathbf{x}}. Step 4: Gradient Computation Compute the gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{x}) for shading and adaptive subdivision. Local Approximate Gradient (Recommended): \frac{\partial f(\mathbf{x})}{\partial xk} \approx \frac{\partial \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial xk} \mathbf{c}{\mathbf{x}} This is computationally efficient and produces indistinguishable results from the analytic gradient for most models. Analytic Gradient (High Frequency): \frac{\partial f(\mathbf{x})}{\partial xk} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x})^T}{\partial xk} \mathbf{c}{\mathbf{x}} - \mathbf{b}(\mathbf{x})^T \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{x})^{-1} \left( \frac{\partial \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial xk} \mathbf{c}{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{B}^T \frac{\partial \mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x})}{\partial xk} \mathbf{f} \right) where \mathbf{A}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{B}^T \mathbf{W}(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{B}. Step 5: Adaptive Preintegration Integrate along the ray segment [di, d{i+1}] with length l. 1. Initial Approximation: Look up \tilde{C}1 = \tilde{C}{i, i+1, l} and \tilde{\alpha}1 = \tilde{\alpha}{i, i+1, l} from the preintegration table using f(di), f(d{i+1}), and l. 2. Subdivision: If termination criteria are not met, subdivide the interval into [di, d{i+1/2}] and [d{i+1/2}, d{i+1}] with length l/2. Compute \tilde{C}{sub1} = \tilde{C}{i, i+1/2, l/2} and \tilde{\alpha}{sub1} = \tilde{\alpha}{i, i+1/2, l/2}. Compute \tilde{C}{sub2} = \tilde{C}{i+1/2, i+1, l/2} and \tilde{\alpha}{sub2} = \tilde{\alpha}{i+1/2, i+1, l/2}. Calculate combined color \tilde{C}2 = \tilde{C}{sub1} + (1 - \tilde{\alpha}{sub1})\tilde{C}{sub2}. Calculate combined opacity \tilde{\alpha}2 = \tilde{\alpha}{sub1} + (1 - \tilde{\alpha}{sub1})\tilde{\alpha}{sub2}. Note: Subdivide [di, d{i+1/2}] first to determine \alpha{i+1/2} for the termination check of the second subinterval. 3. Termination Check: (1 - \alphai) \frac{|C1 - C2|}{|C1|} < \varepsilon where |C| = \sqrt{C.r^2 + C.g^2 + C.b^2} and \alphai is the accumulated opacity before the interval. 4. Update: If converged, update accumulated color and opacity: \alpha{i+1} = \alphai + (1 - \alphai)\tilde{\alpha}1 C{i+1} = Ci + (1 - \alphai)\tilde{C}1 If not converged, recursively apply steps 2-4 to the subintervals. Pitfalls: Boundary Divergence: MLS reconstruction can diverge during extrapolation at boundaries, causing artifacts. Flat Spot Phenomenon: Using a constant basis with interpolating MLS results in zero gradient at data points (\nabla f(\mathbf{x}i) = 0). Use a higher-order basis to avoid this. Neighborhood Query Cost: For irregular datasets, finding neighbors is the most expensive part of function evaluation. A variant focusing on numerical stability and performance during the coefficient calculation step. It shifts the basis origin to the evaluation point \mathbf{x} (i.e., b(\mathbf{x}i) = b(\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x})) to avoid large numbers and improve stability. It exploits the fact that the basis is only evaluated at the origin to compute only the constant coefficient c1 of \mathbf{c}X, avoiding most calculations in the full solution. It relies on a CPU kd-tree built recursively until node size is smaller than the average radius of the node's samples, referencing samples by all leaves intersecting their ellipsoids. Time Complexity: O(m \cdot p \cdot (k + \log(n))) for irregular datasets, where m is pixels, p is evaluations per ray, k is neighbors, and n is dataset size. A single function evaluation is O(k + \log(n)). Memory Complexity: Depends on the spatial index (kd-tree) and preintegration table size. The kd-tree stores references to samples in intersecting leaves. Performance: For k=8-20, MLS evaluation flops are usually less than three times that of trilinear interpolation. Theoretical complexity suggests adaptive schemes reduce evaluations significantly, but GPU architecture limitations make it challenging to fully exploit this gain. Strengths: Handles irregular and regular grids uniformly; provides high-quality shading via accurate gradients; tunable smoothing/interpolation; no global system solve required. Limitations: Boundary divergence artifacts; flat spot phenomenon with constant bases; neighborhood query cost for irregular data; limited GPU flexibility for adaptive schemes. When to Use: High-quality visualization of irregular or regular volumetric data; when accurate gradients for shading are needed; when adaptive sampling is beneficial for complex scalar fields. MLS Volume Reconstruction is based on Moving Least-Squares methods, with convergence theory and error bounds cited from Levin and others. The method subsumes convolution (equivalent to MLS with a constant basis) and is more general than inverse distance weighting. It has been applied to datasets like the Marschner-Lobb dataset, irregular 'bucky ball', 'torso model', and blunt fin data. name: Interpolation Methods
head: Interpolation Schemes
body: Interpolation Methods approximate a continuous volumetric field V(\mathbf{p}) from discrete samples Vi located at grid positions \mathbf{p}i to determine values along viewing rays. This family focuses on the spatial weighting and blending of data values to estimate continuous fields from discrete grids, distinguishing it from sibling methods that handle coordinate mapping or sampling patterns. All methods in this family approximate a continuous scalar field V(\mathbf{p}) from discrete samples Vi at grid positions \mathbf{p}i. The core mechanism involves: 1. Query Positioning: Determining the 3D coordinate \mathbf{p} along the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} where a value is needed. 2. Kernel/Weight Application: Computing weights wi(\mathbf{p}) based on the distance between \mathbf{p} and sample centers \mathbf{p}i to calculate V(\mathbf{p}) = \sumi wi(\mathbf{p}) Vi. 3. Coordinate Transformation: Mapping world-space or camera-space coordinates to the volume's local coordinate system before interpolation. Samples alpha values from a precomputed 3D volume using hardware-accelerated grid sampling with normalized coordinates. It targets alpha/mask volumes for culling and leverages gridsample primitives rather than manual kernels. A real-time technique for inhomogeneous media that uses radiance and its spatial gradient at sparse sample points to construct a first-order Taylor approximation. It differs from scalar-only methods by significantly reducing shading errors near light sources. A surface rendering technique that preserves geometric integrity by converting objects to a scene representation, interpolating the scene, and extracting the surface. It solves shape distortion inherent in traditional scalar blending. A data reduction technique for GPU ray casting that interpolates from neighboring block samples to handle missing data. It enables high compression ratios (up to 80:1) by operating on block-level neighborhoods rather than individual voxels. Assigns the value of the single closest grid sample. It produces piecewise constant, discontinuous results with high aliasing but offers maximum execution speed. Estimates values using a weighted average of k-nearest neighbors where weights are inversely proportional to distance. It provides continuous, differentiable results for arbitrary sampling positions, unlike grid-aligned linear methods. Reduces computational cost by interpolating color, opacity, and normal vectors separately, limiting lighting calculations to one per sample point. It improves interface accuracy for complex microstructures. Approximates a continuous scalar field by computing a weighted average of neighboring values based on spatial proximity. It differs from Nearest Neighbor by using multiple neighbors for smoother gradients, and from higher-order methods by its computational simplicity. Approximates the field by convolving data with a spatially localized weight function. It sets itself apart by utilizing multiple neighbors to reduce aliasing compared to nearest neighbor, but relies on scalar weights rather than geometric splatting. Definition: An extension of template-based ray casting that uses connected cells instead of connected voxels to support higher-order interpolation by taking multiple samples along continuous rays within each cell. Steps: 1. Take multiple samples at regular intervals along the continuous ray inside each cell. 2. Precompute part of the interpolation function and store it in a table to allow for faster rendering times. The classification of interpolation methods in volume rendering has been established to balance image quality and computational effort. Standard trilinear interpolation is recognized as an important feature for high-quality gradient estimation and classification, although it substantially increases computational cost. Nearest neighbor and trilinear interpolation are the two primary methods described in foundational implementations for ray sample value interpolation. The choice of interpolation method is directly connected to the quality of the resulting images. name: Alpha Grid Mask
head: Alpha Grid Mask Sampling, Alpha Volume Sampling
body: Alpha Grid Mask is a module that samples alpha (opacity) values from a precomputed 3D alpha volume using grid sampling with normalized coordinates. It enables ray filtering based on opacity by providing an interface to query alpha values at arbitrary 3D coordinates. It sets itself apart from sibling interpolation methods by specifically targeting alpha/mask volumes for culling or weighting, leveraging PyTorch's gridsample primitive rather than manual kernel implementations. The method maps world-space or camera-space query points to the local coordinate system of a discrete 3D alpha volume, then retrieves interpolated values using trilinear interpolation via a grid sampling primitive. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D query points \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (shape [N, 3]) and an internal 3D alpha volume tensor. Output: A tensor of sampled alpha values \alpha \in \mathbb{R} (shape [N]). Data Structures: The module maintains the following state: device: Torch device for tensor operations. aabb: Axis-aligned bounding box defined by min and max coordinates, shape [2, 3]. aabbSize: Computed as self.aabb[1] - self.aabb[0], shape [3]. invgridSize: Scaling factor for normalization. Defined as 2.0 / (self.aabb[1] - self.aabb[0]) or equivalently 1.0 / self.aabbSize 2. If aabbSize is a vector [3], invgridSize becomes a vector [3]. alphavolume: The 3D alpha tensor. Sources describe it as shape [1, 1, H, W, D] or [1, 1, D, H, W] depending on the specific implementation variant. gridSize: LongTensor of shape [3] containing the dimensions of the alpha volume. Steps: 1. Normalization: Convert query points \mathbf{p} from world space to the normalized range [-1, 1] used by the grid sampler. \mathbf{p}{norm} = (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{aabb}{min}) \cdot \mathbf{invgridSize} - 1 Where \mathbf{aabb}{min} is self.aabb[0] and \mathbf{invgridSize} is self.invgridSize. 2. Reshaping: Reshape \mathbf{p}{norm} to match the expected input format for the grid sampling function, typically to shape [1, N, 1, 1, 3]. 3. Sampling: Call the grid sampling function (e.g., F.gridsample) with aligncorners=True. \alpha{raw} = \text{grid\sample}(\text{alpha\volume}, \mathbf{p}{norm}, \text{align\corners}=\text{True}) This performs trilinear interpolation of the alpha values. 4. Reshaping Output: Reshape the result from [1, N, 1, 1, 1] to [N]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. body: Samples opacity values from a mask volume for each point position, mapping raw mask values to a specified opacity range. It builds on Alpha Grid Mask by providing the specific interpolation and scaling logic required to convert raw mask data into usable opacity values for volume rendering or culling. Inputs: positions: Tensor of shape [N, 3] containing the 3D coordinates of the points to sample. alphavolume: The 3D alpha mask volume tensor. minopacity: Minimum opacity value (default 0.0). maxopacity: Maximum opacity value (default 1.0). Outputs: opacities: Tensor of shape [N] containing the mapped opacity values for each point. Data Structures: The method relies on the AlphaGridMask structure. Key fields include aabb (tensor, shape [2, 3]), aabbSize (tensor, aabb[1] - aabb[0]), invgridSize (float, 1.0 / aabbSize 2), and alphavolume (tensor, viewed as [1, 1, shape[-3:]]). Steps: 1. Normalization: Convert positions from world space to the normalized grid space of the alphavolume using aabb and invgridSize. 2. Clamping: Clamp the normalized coordinates to the range [0, 1] to handle points outside the AABB. 3. Sampling: Sample the alphavolume at the normalized positions using trilinear interpolation. 4. Mapping: Map the raw sampled values r to the target opacity range using the linear transformation: o = \text{min\opacity} + r \times (\text{max\opacity} - \text{min\opacity}) where o is the final opacity. 5. Clamping: Clamp the resulting opacities to [\text{min\opacity}, \text{max\opacity}] to ensure numerical stability and validity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def sampleopacitiesfrommask(positions: torch.Tensor, aabb: torch.Tensor, alphavolume: torch.Tensor, invgridSize: float, minopacity: float = 0.0, maxopacity: float = 1.0) -> torch.Tensor: """ Samples opacities from a mask volume for given 3D positions. Args: positions: Tensor of shape [N, 3] in world coordinates. aabb: Tensor of shape [2, 3] defining the axis-aligned bounding box. alphavolume: Tensor of the mask volume. invgridSize: Float scaling factor from the mask structure. minopacity: Minimum opacity value. maxopacity: Maximum opacity value. Returns: Tensor of shape [N] with sampled opacity values. """ # 1 & 2. Normalize to [0, 1] range based on AABB and clamp aabbmin = aabb[0] # [3] aabbmax = aabb[1] # [3] posnorm = (positions - aabbmin) / (aabbmax - aabbmin) posnorm = torch.clamp(posnorm, 0.0, 1.0) # 3. Sample alphavolume using trilinear interpolation # gridsample expects grid of shape [N, Hout, Wout, Dout, 3] # We sample at single points per position, so Hout=Wout=Dout=1 grid = posnorm.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(2) # [1, 1, 1, 1, 3] sampled = torch.nn.functional.gridsample( alphavolume, grid, mode='trilinear', aligncorners=True) rawopacities = sampled.squeeze() # [N] # 4. Map raw values to opacity range opacities = minopacity + rawopacities (maxopacity - minopacity) # 5. Clamp to valid range opacities = torch.clamp(opacities, min=minopacity, max=maxopacity) return opacities Parameters: minopacity: Minimum opacity value to ensure visibility. Default: 0.0. maxopacity: Maximum opacity value to prevent complete occlusion. Default: 1.0. Edge Cases: Points outside the AABB: The normalization step clamps coordinates to [0, 1] to avoid sampling undefined regions. Degenerate AABB: If aabbSize is zero, invgridSize becomes undefined; a guard should check for this. Updates opacity values for points based on their current positions using a mask volume. name: Shape-Based Interpolation
head: SBI
body: Shape-Based Interpolation (SBI) is a technique primarily used for surface rendering in 3D imaging. Unlike methods that blend scalar values directly, SBI converts an object or surface into an intermediate scene representation, interpolates the scene, and extracts the final interpolated object or surface. This workflow addresses shape preservation during interpolation by capturing specific aspects of the object's geometry. The method operates using operator algebra defined in imaging transforms. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A discrete object or surface description, denoted as O or S, derived from a continuous object description Q or a scanned dataset. Output: An interpolated object or surface, denoted as O' or S'. Data Structures: The method relies on imaging transform operators. Key operators include: Bs: Surface detector or boundary operator. Ib: Shape-based interpolation operator. R: Rendering or extraction operator. D: Scene representation. Steps: 1. Convert Object/Surface to Scene: The discrete object O or surface S is converted into a continuous scene representation D using a conversion operator. Two formulations are cited: Equation 29 and Equation 30. 2. Interpolate the Scene: The resulting scene D is interpolated using the shape-based interpolation operator Ib. 3. Extract Interpolated Object/Surface: The interpolated scene is processed using object/surface definition operators to extract the final interpolated object O' or surface S'. This is often represented by applying a surface detector Bs to the interpolated scene. Formulas: The general expression for shape-based interpolation in surface rendering is given as: F, R{out}, B \sim Ib ShM R{out}(B{ffb} Sb, Is) R{s}(O \& S{\sim}, Is) Where ShM denotes the shape methodology. Parameters and Edge Cases: Equation Selection: Equation 30 is explicitly preferred over Equation 29 because it captures shape aspects, enabling shape interpolation. Filtering Effects: Different filtering effects can cause the detected surface S' and the original surface S to differ even if they represent the same underlying continuous surface. Digitization: If mathematically defined objects or phantoms are rendered alone or combined with scanned objects, digitization operators must be applied, and the descriptions should be merged before rendering. # Pseudocode not provided in the sources. Object/Surface Interpolation is a composite operator that converts an object or surface into a scene, interpolates the scene, and extracts the interpolated object or surface. It solves the problem of shape preservation during interpolation. Conversion to a scene may be performed using Equation 29 or preferably Equation 30, with the latter capturing aspects of the object's shape to allow for shape interpolation. Strengths: The method leads to significant improvements in visualization methods when appropriately used. Limitations: The method is primarily designed for surface rendering rather than general volume density visualization. Performance: Not given in the sources. Use Cases: Best suited for surface rendering and visualization methods involving operators like Ib. It builds on Interpolation Methods and earlier volume-rendering methods introduced by Levoy and Drebin et al., which use scene space normals. Shape-Based Interpolation was introduced as a recent addition to 3D imaging techniques. The methodology is part of a broader framework of imaging transforms that allows for the generation of new visualization methodologies by combining existing operators. It has been used mainly for surface rendering and visualization methods involving operators like Ib. name: Interblock Interpolation
head: Multiresolution Interblock Interpolation, Interblock e-interpolation
body: Interblock Interpolation is a data reduction technique used in GPU-based volume ray casting to handle missing samples between spatial blocks by interpolating from neighboring block samples. It enables significantly higher data reduction ratios (up to 80:1) compared to standard replication methods, trading local continuity for massive compression. It differs from sibling methods like Linear Interpolation by operating on block-level neighborhoods rather than individual voxel grids. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of bounded block samples \phib from a four-block neighborhood. Output: An interpolated value \phi for a query position within the block structure. Data Structures: The method operates on a hierarchical block structure with sizes such as 1\times1, 2\times2, 4\times4, and 8\times8. Each block is treated as a self-contained unit with varied overhead. The exact memory layout or bit-packing is not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Identify the four-block neighborhood surrounding the current query block. 2. Retrieve the bounded block samples \phib from the neighboring blocks. 3. Compute the interpolated value \phi as a normalized sum of the bounded block samples. Formula: The interpolated value \phi is computed as a normalized sum of the bounded block samples \phib: \phi = \text{normalized\sum}(\phib) The sources describe this as a "normalized sum" but do not provide the explicit weight function or normalization denominator formula. Parameters: Block sizes: 1\times1, 2\times2, 4\times4, and 8\times8. Data reduction targets: 40:1 to 50:1 (2% of original data size) or up to 80:1 (1.25% of original data size). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Continuity: Single-sided replication may cause discontinuities; double-sided replication is used to improve continuity support. Precision: The normalization process must handle cases where the sum of weights is zero or near-zero, though specific guard clauses are not provided. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def interblockinterpolation(queryblock, neighborhoodblocks): """ Interpolates a value for a query block using its four-block neighborhood. Args: queryblock: The block ID or coordinates of the current block. neighborhoodblocks: A list of block samples from the four neighboring blocks. Returns: The interpolated value phi. """ # Step 1 & 2: Retrieve bounded block samples from the four-block neighborhood blocksamples = [neighbor.sample for neighbor in neighborhoodblocks] # Step 3: Compute the normalized sum of bounded block samples # The sources describe phi as a "normalized sum" of phib but do not # provide the explicit weight function or normalization denominator # In standard interpolation, weights are typically distance-based, # but the specific kernel for Interblock Interpolation is not given. if not blocksamples: return 0.0 # Apply unspecified normalization logic from sources # sumsamples = sum(blocksamples) # interpolatedvalue = sumsamples / normalizationfactor # The exact normalization factor is not detailed in the sources return sum(blocksamples) / len(blocksamples) A technique to limit computation in the distance by stopping interpolation for some rays and using information from neighboring rays instead, drawing spans of n pixels wide. To reduce blockiness, information (texture coordinates, color) can be interpolated across the width of the span if more time or hardware support is available. An alternative is discarding every other ray and drawing the frame with interlacing. A pitfall is that voxels become quite blocky in the distance. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Achieves data reduction of 40:1 to 50:1 (2% of original data size) or up to 80:1 (1.25% of original data size). Time: The method reduces the amount of data to process, thereby improving frame rates. Measured Performance: On ATI X1800 XT 512MB: 2.6 FPS with adaptive density versus 1.2 FPS with full density. On NV GF7800 GTX 256MB: 7.1 FPS with adaptive density versus 3.0 FPS with full density. Speed-up: 2.6-2.8x observed at 1024x1024 resolution. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High data reduction, efficient for GPU-based rendering, supports multi-resolution hierarchies. Limitations: Can introduce blockiness, especially in the distance or when spans are combined. Continuity issues may arise if single-sided replication is used. When to Use: Use when high data reduction is required to fit large volumes within limited GPU memory. When Not to Use: Avoid when high local continuity is critical and blockiness is unacceptable. Avoid if hardware does not support efficient block-based interpolation. Interblock Interpolation was developed by Markus Hadwiger at the VRVIS Research Center in Vienna, Austria, as part of advanced illumination techniques for GPU-based volume ray casting. It builds on earlier work by Weiler et al. (2000) and Guthe et al. (2002) regarding sample replication and interpolation. The technique is part of a broader effort to optimize volume rendering on GPUs by reducing data transfer and processing overhead. name: Nearest Neighbor Sampling
head: Nearest Neighbour Interpolation, Nearest Neighbour Sampling, Vizinho mais próximo, Zero-order hold, Zero-order interpolation
body: Nearest Neighbor Sampling is a volume rendering interpolation technique that assigns the value of the single grid sample closest to the ray's current position. It solves the problem of estimating continuous volume data from discrete samples by selecting the nearest neighbor rather than blending multiple values. Unlike trilinear interpolation, which blends eight neighboring points to provide C^0 smoothness, nearest neighbor produces piecewise constant, discontinuous results. It is chosen when execution speed is prioritized over visual quality, as it yields the poorest visual results due to jagged edges and staircasing artifacts. Inputs and Outputs Input: A query position \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z) in the volume's local coordinate system, and a discrete volume dataset V defined on a regular grid. Output: The scalar value f(x, y, z) at the query position. Data Structures Volume Data (V): A 3D array of values indexed by integer coordinates (i, j, k). The grid spacing is assumed to be uniform and normalized such that sample centers are at integer coordinates. Steps 1. Coordinate Rounding: Round the floating-point coordinates of the query position \mathbf{p} to the nearest integers. This identifies the indices of the closest voxel. 2. Lookup: Retrieve the value from the volume dataset V at the rounded integer indices. Formula The interpolated value f(x, y, z) is defined as: f(x, y, z) = V(\text{round}(x), \text{round}(y), \text{round}(z)) Where: x, y, z are the continuous coordinates of the query point. \text{round}(\cdot) is the standard rounding function (rounding to the nearest integer, with ties typically rounded to the nearest even integer or away from zero depending on implementation, though the source simply states "round"). V(i, j, k) is the value stored at grid index (i, j, k). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nearestneighborsample(volume: list, x: float, y: float, z: float) -> float: """ Samples the volume at (x, y, z) using nearest neighbor interpolation. Args: volume: A 3D list or array of values indexed by integer coordinates (i, j, k). x, y, z: Continuous coordinates in the volume's local space. Returns: The scalar value at the nearest grid point. """ # Round coordinates to nearest integer indices ix = round(x) iy = round(y) iz = round(z) # Boundary clamping required if indices fall outside volume bounds return volume[ix][iy][iz] Edge Cases and Pitfalls Staircasing: The method produces "unpleasant staircasing" and jagged edges because the result is piecewise constant. Magnification Artifacts: When magnifying the volume, a "blobby structure" appears due to the discrete selection of voxels. Error: It exhibits the highest interpolation error (measured by mean squared error) compared to higher-order methods like trilinear interpolation. Discontinuity: The function lacks C^0 continuity; the derivative is undefined at the boundaries between voxels. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. It requires only rounding operations and a single memory lookup. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. No additional buffers or neighbor lookups are required. Performance: It is significantly faster than trilinear interpolation, which requires blending eight values and multiple arithmetic operations. Visual Quality: Poor. It is unsuitable for high-quality offline rendering due to aliasing and lack of smoothness. Usage: Suitable for real-time applications where visual artifacts from abrupt changes are acceptable due to its speed. It is used as a fallback sampling technique when INTERMODE is not 1. Nearest neighbor interpolation is the simplest approach to 3D data estimation. It is also referred to as zero-order hold or zero-order interpolation. In the context of volume rendering, it acts as a box filter in the spatial domain. While it lacks the continuous transitions provided by trilinear interpolation, its simplicity makes it a foundational method in digital signal processing and graphics. name: Inverse Distance Weighting Interpolation
body: Inverse Distance Weighting Interpolation estimates a value at a query point by computing a weighted average of known sample values, where weights are inversely proportional to the distance between the query point and the samples. In point cloud processing, it is typically implemented using the k-nearest neighbors (k-NN) to limit computational cost and ensure local smoothness. It differs from Nearest Neighbor Sampling by using multiple neighbors to produce smoother results. Inputs and Outputs: Source Points: Coordinates \mathbf{xyz} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times 3} and feature vectors \mathbf{feat} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times c}. Query Points: Coordinates \mathbf{new\xyz} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 3}. Batch Offsets: Arrays \mathbf{offset} and \mathbf{new\offset} of size b for partitioning batched data. Output: Interpolated features \mathbf{new\feat} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times c}. Data Structures: Indices array \mathbf{idx} \in \mathbb{Z}^{n \times k} storing the indices of the k nearest neighbors in \mathbf{xyz} for each query point. Distances array \mathbf{dist} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times k} storing the Euclidean distances to these neighbors. Steps: 1. Neighbor Search: Perform k-nearest neighbor query to find indices \mathbf{idx} and distances \mathbf{dist} for each point in \mathbf{new\xyz} relative to \mathbf{xyz}. 2. Initialization: Initialize output tensor \mathbf{new\feat} of shape (n, c) to zeros. 3. Reciprocal Distance: Compute reciprocal distances with epsilon regularization. 4. Weight Normalization: Normalize weights by summing reciprocals along the neighbor dimension. 5. Feature Aggregation: Loop over k neighbors and accumulate weighted features. Formulas: Let j \in \{1, \dots, n\} index query points and i \in \{1, \dots, k\} index neighbors. The reciprocal distance is computed as r{j,i} = \frac{1}{\mathbf{dist}{j,i} + \epsilon}. Weights are normalized by summing reciprocals along the neighbor dimension: w{j,i} = \frac{r{j,i}}{\sum{l=1}^{k} r{j,l}}. The final interpolated feature is accumulated as \mathbf{new\feat}j \mathrel{+}= \mathbf{feat}{\mathbf{idx}{j,i}} \cdot w{j,i} for i = 1 \dots k. Parameters: k: Integer specifying the number of neighbors to use. \epsilon: Scalar regularization constant, typically 10^{-8}, added to distances before inversion. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If a query point coincides exactly with a source point, the distance is 0. Adding \epsilon = 10^{-8} to the distance before inversion prevents numerical instability. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. Boundary Effects: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def inversedistanceweightinginterpolation(xyz, newxyz, feat, k, epsilon=1e-8): """ Interpolate features from source points to query points using k-NN IDW. Args: xyz: (m, 3) array of source coordinates. newxyz: (n, 3) array of query coordinates. feat: (m, c) array of source features. k: int, number of neighbors. epsilon: float, regularization term to prevent division by zero. Returns: newfeat: (n, c) array of interpolated features. """ n = newxyz.shape[0] c = feat.shape[1] newfeat = np.zeros((n, c)) # Step 1: k-NN query (brute-force for clarity) diff = newxyz[:, np.newaxis,:] - xyz[np.newaxis,:,:] distsq = np.sum(diff 2, axis=2) idx = np.argsort(distsq, axis=1)[:,:k] dist = np.sqrt(np.takealongaxis(distsq, idx, axis=1)) # Step 2: Reciprocal distances with epsilon regularization distrecip = 1.0 / (dist + epsilon) # Step 3: Normalize weights along the neighbor dimension norm = np.sum(distrecip, axis=1, keepdims=True) weights = distrecip / norm # Step 4: Accumulate weighted features over k neighbors for i in range(k): newfeat += feat[idx[:, i]] weights[:, i:i+1] return newfeat A baseline method similar to Closest Point, but linearly interpolates the displacements of the three nearest triangular mesh vertices, with coefficients inversely related to distances. It is used in mesh deformation and displacement mapping tasks. Not given in the sources. Inverse Distance Weighting is a classical spatial interpolation method. The specific implementation using k-NN and epsilon regularization is documented in point cloud processing codebases. It serves as a baseline for comparing interpolation schemes in geometry editing and deformation transfer tasks. name: Linear Interpolation
body: Linear interpolation approximates a continuous scalar field V(\mathbf{p}) from discrete samples by computing a weighted average of neighboring values based on their spatial proximity. It differs from higher-order methods like Cubic Hermite by its computational simplicity and lower cost, albeit with discontinuous derivatives. All methods in this family operate on the principle that a continuous function V(\mathbf{p}) must be approximated from a discrete set of samples Vi located at grid positions \mathbf{p}i. The core mechanism involves: 1. Query Positioning: Determining the 3D coordinate \mathbf{p} along the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} where a value is needed. This may involve converting depth parameters to physical distances or warping coordinates for neural encodings. 2. Kernel/Weight Application: Computing weights wi(\mathbf{p}) based on the distance between \mathbf{p} and the sample centers \mathbf{p}i. The interpolated value is: V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i} wi(\mathbf{p}) Vi For standard linear interpolation, weights are derived from fractional offsets within the enclosing voxel cell. 3. Coordinate Transformation: Mapping world-space or camera-space coordinates to the local coordinate system of the volume data (e.g., normalized [-1, 1] or [0, 1] ranges) before interpolation. Clamps indices to valid bounds [0, dims-1] to prevent out-of-bounds access.""" x, y, z = int(v[0]), int(v[1]), int(v[2]) fx, fy, fz = v[0] - x, v[1] - y, v[2] - z x0, x1 = max(0, min(x, dims[0]-1)), max(0, min(x+1, dims[0]-1)) y0, y1 = max(0, min(y, dims[1]-1)), max(0, min(y+1, dims[1]-1)) z0, z1 = max(0, min(z, dims[2]-1)), max(0, min(z+1, dims[2]-1)) c000 = grid[x0, y0, z0]; c100 = grid[x1, y0, z0] c010 = grid[x0, y1, z0]; c110 = grid[x1, y1, z0] c001 = grid[x0, y0, z1]; c101 = grid[x1, y0, z1] c011 = grid[x0, y1, z1]; c111 = grid[x1, y1, z1] i00 = lerp(c000, c100, fx); i10 = lerp(c010, c110, fx) i01 = lerp(c001, c101, fx); i11 = lerp(c011, c111, fx) i0 = lerp(i00, i10, fy); i1 = lerp(i01, i11, fy) return lerp(i0, i1, fz) Volumetric Ray Casting with Trilinear Interpolation is a direct volume rendering technique that visualizes scalar data stored in a voxel grid by casting rays through the volume and interpolating values at sample points. It differs from nearest-neighbor sampling by using the eight corners of the enclosing voxel cell to produce smoother gradients, and from higher-order methods by its simplicity and low computational cost. Choose it when computational efficiency is prioritized over high-order smoothness. Joseph's Method is a forward projection method for 2D easily extended to 3D, using bi-linear interpolation on intersection points and a compensation factor for rays deviating from the principal direction. It performs similarly to Köhler's method in accuracy, despite using a skewed interpolation kernel compared to Köhler's tri-linear kernel. Steps: 1. Determine the principal direction of the ray by comparing the absolute differences |x1-x2|, |y1-y2|, and |z1-z2|. 2. For the case where the principal direction is the x-axis (|x1-x2| is largest), perform bi-linear interpolation on the intersection points of each (y, z)-plane of the sampling grid. 3. Weight the sum of interpolations with the factor \frac{\sqrt{(x1 - x2)^2 + (y1 - y2)^2 + (z1 - z2)^2}}{|x1 - x2|} to compensate for longer traversal of rays deviating from the principal direction. A method to define the contribution of a projection to a pixel that is not directly traversed by a projection line, by interpolating between adjacent projection lines. It is effective in standard sampling when d\rho > \Deltap and optimal when d\rho < \Deltap (oversampling). Formula: Contrib{\theta \to (i,j)} = \frac{\rho(i,j) - \rhor}{d\rho} R\theta(\rhor) + \frac{\rho{r+1} - \rho(i,j)}{d\rho} R\theta(\rho{r+1}) where \rho(i,j) = (i - \frac{H}{2})\cos\theta - (j - \frac{W}{2})\sin\theta, \rhor \le \rho(i,j) \le \rho{r+1}, and d\rho is the radial sampling step. Parameters: d\rho: The radial sampling step (distance between successive projection lines). \rho(i,j): The radial coordinate of the center of pixel (i, j) for angle \theta. Calculated as (i - H/2)\cos\theta - (j - W/2)\sin\theta. Pitfalls: In oversampling (d\rho < \Deltap), using all available data is inefficient; only the two closest projection lines to the pixel center should be used. If a pixel is not traversed by any line (possible when d\rho > \Deltap), standard backprojection kernels return 0; linear interpolation fills these gaps. Linear interpolation is a fundamental technique in computer graphics and scientific visualization. In the context of noise generation and procedural textures, it is noted that linear interpolation requires the least amount of calculation but results in inferior appearance due to discontinuities in derivatives (C0 continuity). In tomographic reconstruction, it serves as the interpolation basis for forward projection methods like Joseph's method and backprojection kernels. name: Joseph's Method
head: Joseph forward projection, Joseph interpolation
body: Joseph's Method is a forward projection algorithm for computing line integrals through a discrete voxel volume, primarily used in computed tomography (CT) reconstruction. It solves the problem of accurately sampling a 3D volume along arbitrary ray directions while avoiding the artifacts associated with nearest-neighbor sampling. Unlike Siddon’s DDA, which degenerates to nearest-neighbor sampling when rays align with grid axes, Joseph's Method uses driving-axis-aligned sampling combined with bilinear interpolation in the remaining dimensions to model the integrating nature of detector pixels. It performs similarly to Köhler's method in accuracy, despite using a skewed interpolation kernel compared to Köhler's tri-linear kernel. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid V with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Input: Ray segment defined by endpoints \mathbf{p}1 = (x1, y1, z1) and \mathbf{p}2 = (x2, y2, z2) in voxel coordinates. Output: The weighted sum of interpolated values along the ray segment. Data Structures: The voxel grid V is accessed via integer indices (i, j, k) corresponding to (x, y, z) coordinates. Values are assumed to be stored in a contiguous array or 3D array structure. Steps: 1. Determine Principal Direction: Calculate the absolute differences along each axis: \Delta x = |x1 - x2|, \Delta y = |y1 - y2|, \Delta z = |z1 - z2|. Identify the axis with the maximum difference. Assume without loss of generality that \Delta x is the largest, making x the principal direction. The other cases (\Delta y or \Delta z largest) are handled symmetrically. 2. Iterate Along Principal Axis: Iterate through the voxel indices i along the principal axis (x) that the ray passes through. For each i, determine the corresponding y and z coordinates on the ray at the boundaries of the voxel slice. 3. Bilinear Interpolation: For each slice i, perform bilinear interpolation on the four surrounding voxels in the (y, z) plane. Let the ray intersect the plane at (yi, zi). The fractional parts fy = yi - \lfloor yi \rfloor and fz = zi - \lfloor zi \rfloor are used to interpolate between the four corner voxels V(i, j, k), V(i, j+1, k), V(i, j, k+1), V(i, j+1, k+1), where j = \lfloor yi \rfloor and k = \lfloor zi \rfloor. 4. Sum Interpolated Values: Sum the results of the bilinear interpolations for all slices i traversed by the ray. 5. Apply Compensation Factor: Multiply the sum by a compensation factor to account for the longer traversal path of rays deviating from the principal direction. The factor is: C = \frac{\sqrt{(x1 - x2)^2 + (y1 - y2)^2 + (z1 - z2)^2}}{|x1 - x2|} The final result is C \times \sum{i} \text{BilinearInterp}(i). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def josephmethod(V, dims, p1, p2): """ Joseph's forward projection method. V: 3D array of voxel values. dims: Tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) of grid dimensions. p1: Tuple (x1, y1, z1) start point in voxel coordinates. p2: Tuple (x2, y2, z2) end point in voxel coordinates. """ x1, y1, z1 = p1 x2, y2, z2 = p2 dx = abs(x2 - x1) dy = abs(y2 - y1) dz = abs(z2 - z1) # Determine principal axis if dx >= dy and dx >= dz: principal = 'x' denom = dx elif dy >= dx and dy >= dz: principal = 'y' denom = dy else: principal = 'z' denom = dz # Calculate compensation factor raylength = sqrt((x2-x1)2 + (y2-y1)2 + (z2-z1)2) compensation = raylength / denom totalsum = 0.0 if principal == 'x': # Iterate over x slices xstart = min(x1, x2) xend = max(x1, x2) for i in range(int(xstart), int(xend) + 1): # Calculate y and z at the center or boundaries of the slice? # The source implies intersection points of each (y,z)-plane. # We interpolate at the ray's position within the slice. # To be precise, we need the y and z coordinates corresponding to the slice. # Assuming linear parameterization along the ray. # Let t be the parameter such that x(t) = i. # However, the source describes "intersection points of each (y,z)-plane". # This usually means evaluating the ray at the voxel boundaries or centers. # Given the bilinear interpolation on (y,z), we need y and z at the slice. # Let's assume we evaluate at the slice index i. # If the ray is x(t) = x1 + t(x2-x1), then t = (i - x1)/(x2-x1). # But since we iterate integer slices, we can just interpolate y and z linearly. # Normalize t for the current slice i relative to the ray segment # This is an approximation; precise implementation requires careful t calculation. # For simplicity, we assume the ray passes through the slice at a specific y,z. # A more robust way: calculate y and z at the midpoint of the slice or boundaries. # The source is vague on the exact t for y,z. We assume linear interpolation of y,z with x. # Let's use the ratio of distances. # If x1 != x2: if x2 != x1: t = (i - x1) / (x2 - x1) else: t = 0.0 # Degenerate case yi = y1 + t (y2 - y1) zi = z1 + t (z2 - z1) # Bilinear interpolation in y-z plane at slice i totalsum += bilinearinterpolate(V, dims, i, yi, zi) elif principal == 'y': ystart = min(y1, y2) yend = max(y1, y2) for j in range(int(ystart), int(yend) + 1): if y2 != y1: t = (j - y1) / (y2 - y1) else: t = 0.0 xj = x1 + t (x2 - x1) zj = z1 + t (z2 - z1) totalsum += bilinearinterpolate(V, dims, xj, j, zj) else: # principal == 'z' zstart = min(z1, z2) zend = max(z1, z2) for k in range(int(zstart), int(zend) + 1): if z2 != z1: t = (k - z1) / (z2 - z1) else: t = 0.0 xk = x1 + t (x2 - x1) yk = y1 + t (y2 - y1) totalsum += bilinearinterpolate(V, dims, xk, yk, k) return compensation totalsum def bilinearinterpolate(V, dims, x, y, z): """ Performs bilinear interpolation on the plane perpendicular to the principal axis. x, y, z are continuous coordinates. One of them is the principal axis index (integer or close to it). For principal='x', we interpolate in y and z at fixed x. """ # Clamp coordinates to valid range x = max(0, min(x, dims[0] - 1)) y = max(0, min(y, dims[1] - 1)) z = max(0, min(z, dims[2] - 1)) # Determine integer and fractional parts for the non-principal axes # Assuming principal is x, we interpolate y and z iy = int(y) iz = int(z) fy = y - iy fz = z - iz # Clamp indices iy0, iy1 = max(0, min(iy, dims[1]-1)), max(0, min(iy+1, dims[1]-1)) iz0, iz1 = max(0, min(iz, dims[2]-1)), max(0, min(iz+1, dims[2]-1)) # Get values v00 = V[int(x), iy0, iz0] v10 = V[int(x), iy1, iz0] v01 = V[int(x), iy0, iz1] v11 = V[int(x), iy1, iz1] # Interpolate v0 = v00 (1 - fy) + v10 fy v1 = v01 (1 - fy) + v11 fy return v0 (1 - fz) + v1 fz Parameters: None explicitly defined beyond the ray endpoints and grid dimensions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Rays: If the ray is parallel to a principal axis (e.g., x1 = x2), the denominator in the compensation factor becomes zero. This case requires special handling, likely defaulting to nearest-neighbor or a different interpolation strategy. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when calculating intersection points, especially for long rays or high-resolution grids. Boundary Conditions: Indices must be clamped to the valid range of the voxel grid to prevent out-of-bounds access. The Generalized Joseph Projector with Linear Interpolation (GJPlin) is a branchless, ray-driven forward projection algorithm designed for efficient GPU execution in cone-beam CT reconstruction. It solves the problem of accurately sampling a 3D voxel volume along arbitrary ray directions while maintaining high memory bandwidth efficiency and avoiding the artifacts associated with nearest-neighbor sampling. Unlike Siddon’s DDA, which degenerates to nearest-neighbor sampling when rays align with grid axes, GJPlin uses driving-axis-aligned sampling to ensure an optimal, non-redundant number of samples, combined with 2D bilinear interpolation in the remaining dimensions to model the integrating nature of detector pixels. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels traversed by the ray. Memory Complexity: Constant, O(1) auxiliary space, assuming the voxel grid is provided. Measured Performance: Joseph's method performs similarly to Köhler's method in accuracy. It is superior to Siddon's method in terms of accuracy, especially for rays deviating from principal directions. Strengths: Avoids nearest-neighbor artifacts; simple to implement; efficient for GPU execution when generalized. Limitations: Skewed interpolation kernel compared to tri-linear methods; requires careful handling of degenerate rays. When to Use: When high accuracy is required for forward projections in CT reconstruction, especially for rays with arbitrary orientations. When Not to Use: When computational resources are extremely limited and nearest-neighbor accuracy is acceptable, or when tri-linear interpolation is strictly required for consistency with other pipeline stages. Joseph's Method was described by Joseph in 1982 for the two-dimensional case and is easily extended to three dimensions. It is a forward projection method used in computed tomography (CT) reconstruction. The method was noted to perform similarly to Köhler's method in accuracy, despite using a skewed interpolation kernel. The root mean square error of Joseph's method is significantly lower than that of Siddon's method. 5 Forward Projection through Voxel Volumes, https://www.cvl.isy.liu.se/education/undergraduate/tsbb31/download/TurbellPhDCh5.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Generalized Joseph Projector with Linear Interpolation
head: Branchless Generalized Joseph Projector (GJP), GJPlin, GJPspl, axis-aligned grid traversal with bilinear/spline interpolation, linear interpolating GJPlin algorithm
body: The Generalized Joseph Projector with Linear Interpolation (GJPlin) is a branchless, ray-driven forward projection algorithm designed for efficient GPU execution in cone-beam CT reconstruction. It solves the problem of accurately sampling a 3D voxel volume along arbitrary ray directions while maintaining high memory bandwidth efficiency and avoiding the artifacts associated with nearest-neighbor sampling. Unlike Siddon’s DDA, which degenerates to nearest-neighbor sampling when rays align with grid axes, GJPlin uses driving-axis-aligned sampling to ensure an optimal, non-redundant number of samples, combined with 2D bilinear interpolation in the remaining dimensions to model the integrating nature of detector pixels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Source point \tilde{s} (vector), detector pixel coordinates \tilde{d} (vector), volume grid dimensions V{dim}, and volume data array V. Output: Accumulated projection value a (scalar). Data Structures: Volume data V is accessed via integer indices (i, j, k). Vectors are 3D Cartesian coordinates. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Definition: Calculate the ray direction vector \tilde{r} = \tilde{d} - \tilde{s}. 2. Driving Axis Identification: Identify the driving axis m as the index with the largest absolute component in \tilde{r}: m \leftarrow \text{argmax}i(|ri|) 3. Sampling Increment and Offset: Calculate the sampling increment vector \tilde{r} (normalized to unit steps along the driving axis): \tilde{r} \leftarrow \tilde{r} / rm Calculate the sampling offset o to ensure the first sampling plane intersects the driving axis at an integer coordinate: o \leftarrow -sm This ensures that for any integer i, the driving axis component of the sampling point \tilde{p}^{(i)} is integer: [\tilde{s} + o\tilde{r}]m = 0 \implies p^{(i)}m = i + \text{const}. 4. Loop Bounds: Determine the number of sampling points i{max} based on the volume extent along the driving axis m: i{max} \leftarrow V{dim}[m] 5. Initialization: Initialize accumulator a \leftarrow 0. 6. Sampling Loop: Iterate i from 0 to i{max} - 1: a. Calculate Sampling Point: \tilde{p} \leftarrow \tilde{s} + (o + i) \cdot \tilde{r} b. Boundary Check: If \tilde{p} is outside the volume bounds, skip to the next iteration. c. Grid Indices: Calculate floor and ceiling indices for the sampling point: \tilde{p}{fl} \leftarrow \text{floor}(\tilde{p}) \tilde{p}{cl} \leftarrow \text{ceil}(\tilde{p}) d. Assert Driving Axis Integer Property: Verify that the driving axis component is integer: p{fl,m} = p{cl,m} = pm e. Calculate Distances: Compute the fractional distances from the floor indices: \tilde{d}k \leftarrow pk - p{fl,k} \quad \text{for } k \in \{1, 2, 3\} f. Calculate Interpolation Weights: Compute floor weights using the linear kernel w{lin}(d) = 1 - d: w{fl,k} \leftarrow 1 - \tilde{d}k Compute complementary ceiling weights: w{cl,k} \leftarrow 1 - w{fl,k} Set driving axis weights to 1 (since the driving axis is integer-aligned): w{fl,m} \leftarrow 1, \quad w{cl,m} \leftarrow 1 g. Accumulate Contributions: Add the weighted contributions from the four nearest neighbor voxels in the plane perpendicular to the driving axis. The indices for the four voxels are combinations of floor/ceiling indices for the non-driving axes, while the driving axis index is fixed at p{fl,m} (which equals p{cl,m}): a \leftarrow a + V[p{fl,1}, p{fl,2}, p{fl,3}] \cdot \|\tilde{r}\| \cdot w{fl,1} \cdot w{fl,2} \cdot w{fl,3} a \leftarrow a + V[p{fl,1}, p{cl,2}, p{cl,3}] \cdot \|\tilde{r}\| \cdot w{fl,1} \cdot w{cl,2} \cdot w{cl,3} a \leftarrow a + V[p{cl,1}, p{fl,2}, p{cl,3}] \cdot \|\tilde{r}\| \cdot w{cl,1} \cdot w{fl,2} \cdot w{cl,3} a \leftarrow a + V[p{cl,1}, p{cl,2}, p{fl,3}] \cdot \|\tilde{r}\| \cdot w{cl,1} \cdot w{cl,2} \cdot w{fl,3} Note: The term \|\tilde{r}\| represents the scaling factor for the ray length per step. In the normalized formulation where \tilde{r} is divided by rm, this term accounts for the physical length of the voxel traversal along the ray direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generalizedjosephprojectorlinear(s, d, volume, volumedims): """ s: Source point (vec3) d: Detector pixel center (vec3) volume: 3D array of voxel values volumedims: Tuple (dimx, dimy, dimz) """ # 1. Ray definition rvec = d - s # 2. Driving axis identification # m is the index (0, 1, or 2) with the largest absolute component absr = abs(rvec) m = argmax(absr) # 3. Sampling increment and offset # Normalize rvec by its component along the driving axis m rhat = rvec / rvec[m] # Sampling offset ensures the first sample plane intersects the driving axis at an integer o = -s[m] # 4. Loop bounds imax = volumedims[m] # Norm of the original ray direction vector (used for scaling) # Note: The algorithm description uses ||r|| in the accumulation. # In the normalized step formulation, the physical length per step is ||rhat||. # However, standard Joseph projector implementations often scale by the voxel size # or ray segment length. Here we follow the source formula strictly: # a += volume[...] ||r|| weights # But wait, rhat is unit step in driving axis. The physical length of one step # along the ray is ||rhat||. The source formula says ||r||. # Let's look at Eq 17-20: "volume[...] ||r|| weights". # And rhat = r / rm. # If we use rhat in p = s + (o+i)rhat, then the step size is ||rhat||. # The source text says: "The increment vector r~... will be chosen such that... # p(i) = (s + o r~) + i r~". And "r~ = r / rm". # So the step vector is rhat. The length of this step is ||rhat||. # The formula in the notes says "||r||". This is likely a notation inconsistency # in the notes vs the paper's Eq 17-20 where r~ is used. # Given "r~" is the sampling increment, the length should be ||r~||. # We will use ||rhat|| as the scaling factor per step. steplength = norm(rhat) accumulator = 0.0 # 6. Sampling Loop for i in range(imax): # a. Calculate sampling point p = s + (o + i) rhat # b. Boundary check # Check if p is within volume bounds [0, dims-1] for all axes if not (0 <= p[0] < volumedims[0] and 0 <= p[1] < volumedims[1] and 0 <= p[2] < volumedims[2]): continue # c. Grid indices pfl = floor(p) pcl = ceil(p) # d. Assert driving axis integer property (implicit in logic) # pfl[m] == pcl[m] == integer part of p[m] # e. Calculate distances # dk = pk - pflk dist = p - pfl # f. Calculate Interpolation Weights # Linear kernel: w(d) = 1 - d wfl = 1.0 - dist wcl = 1.0 - wfl # Equivalent to dist # Set driving axis weights to 1 wfl[m] = 1.0 wcl[m] = 1.0 # g. Accumulate Contributions # Voxel 1: fl, fl, fl idx1 = (int(pfl[0]), int(pfl[1]), int(pfl[2])) val1 = volume[idx1[0], idx1[1], idx1[2]] weight1 = wfl[0] wfl[1] wfl[2] accumulator += val1 steplength weight1 # Voxel 2: fl, cl, cl idx2 = (int(pfl[0]), int(pcl[1]), int(pcl[2])) val2 = volume[idx2[0], idx2[1], idx2[2]] weight2 = wfl[0] wcl[1] wcl[2] accumulator += val2 steplength weight2 # Voxel 3: cl, fl, cl idx3 = (int(pcl[0]), int(pfl[1]), int(pcl[2])) val3 = volume[idx3[0], idx3[1], idx3[2]] weight3 = wcl[0] wfl[1] wcl[2] accumulator += val3 steplength weight3 # Voxel 4: cl, cl, fl idx4 = (int(pcl[0]), int(pcl[1]), int(pfl[2])) val4 = volume[idx4[0], idx4[1], idx4[2]] weight4 = wcl[0] wcl[1] wfl[2] accumulator += val4 steplength weight4 return accumulator A variant of GJP that replaces the linear interpolation kernel with a spline kernel w{spl}(d) = 1 - 3d + 2d^2. This kernel is smooth and differentiable at grid points, reducing high-frequency artifacts compared to the kinked linear kernel, though it may have comparable residuals to oversampled DDA. It uses the same driving-axis-aligned sampling and branchless structure as GJPlin. Time and Memory Complexity: The algorithm performs a fixed number of operations per sampling point, proportional to the volume extent along the driving axis i{max}. Memory access pattern is coherent along the driving axis, ensuring high cache hit rates for parallel threads. Measured Performance: On a 512³ Shepp Logan phantom projected onto a 512² detector with a 10° cone angle: GTX 970: GJPlin takes 4.97 ms with 334 GB/s memory access rate. GTX 1080: GJPlin takes 2.40 ms with 686 GB/s memory access rate. GJPlin outperforms regular DDA by a factor of up to 2, despite accessing about twice as much memory on average. GJPspl (Spline variant) shows similar performance characteristics to GJPlin on the same hardware. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Branchless execution makes it highly efficient on GPUs. It avoids the artifacts of DDA when rays are parallel to grid axes. It achieves the best reconstruction quality among tested methods (GJP, DDA, DDA 2x). Limitations: Accesses more memory than DDA. Performance is optimal when the driving axis does not coincide with the fastest-changing memory index (though the source notes this generally, the branchless nature mitigates some overhead). When to Use: Use for calculating individual projections within read-and-write memory on GPUs, specifically for cone beam CT reconstruction. Choose over DDA when ray alignment artifacts are a concern and higher accuracy is needed without the cost of oversampling. Choose GJPlin for best overall quality/speed trade-off; choose GJPspl if high-frequency artifact reduction is prioritized and the slight increase in computational complexity (spline evaluation) is acceptable. The Generalized Joseph Projector was introduced by Jonas Graetz (Dittmann) in 2016/2020. It builds on the Joseph method [10586-joseph-s-method.md], which uses bilinear interpolation on intersection points. The "Generalized" aspect refers to the branchless formulation that unifies the handling of different driving axes, allowing for efficient GPU implementation. The method addresses the conflict between sampling quality and processing speed in GPU-based CT reconstruction, leveraging the coherence of sampling patterns to maximize memory bandwidth utilization. name: Volumetric Ray Casting with Trilinear Interpolation
head: Basic Volumetric Ray Casting, Voxel Region Interpolation
body: Volumetric Ray Casting with Trilinear Interpolation is a direct volume rendering technique that visualizes scalar data stored in a voxel grid by casting rays through the volume and interpolating values at sample points. It differs from nearest-neighbor sampling by using the eight corners of the enclosing voxel cell to produce smoother gradients, and from higher-order methods by its simplicity and low computational cost. Despite the name, the method implements a distance-weighted interpolation scheme rather than standard trilinear interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D array of voxel data (scalar values) with dimensions W \times H \times D (width, height, depth). Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{O}, direction \mathbf{D}, t{min}, and t{max}. Output: A scalar value V{interp} at a point \mathbf{V} along the ray. Data Structures: Voxel: A struct containing: location: Vector3 representing the 3D coordinates (x, y, z). scalardata: float representing the scalar value at that voxel. The voxels are stored in a flat array indexed by x + y \cdot W + z \cdot W \cdot H. Steps: 1. Prepare Voxel Region: Iterate through all voxels in z, y, x order (depth, height, width). For each voxel at index corresponding to coordinates (x, y, z), set voxels[idx].location to (x, y, z) and voxels[idx].scalardata to the input data value at that index. 2. Ray-Box Intersection: Determine the intersection interval [t{near}, t{far}] of the ray with the volume bounding box defined by \mathbf{b}{min} and \mathbf{b}{max}. Compute \mathbf{inv\dir} = 1.0 / \mathbf{D}. Compute \mathbf{min\Ts} = (\mathbf{b}{min} - \mathbf{O}) \cdot \mathbf{inv\dir} and \mathbf{max\Ts} = (\mathbf{b}{max} - \mathbf{O}) \cdot \mathbf{inv\dir}. t{near} = \max(\min(\mathbf{min\Ts}x, \mathbf{max\Ts}x), \min(\mathbf{min\Ts}y, \mathbf{max\Ts}y), \min(\mathbf{min\Ts}z, \mathbf{max\Ts}z)). t{far} = \min(\max(\mathbf{min\Ts}x, \mathbf{max\Ts}x), \max(\mathbf{min\Ts}y, \mathbf{max\Ts}y), \max(\mathbf{min\Ts}z, \mathbf{max\Ts}z)). Intersection exists if t{near} \le t{far} and t{far} > t{min}. 3. Sample Along Ray: For each sample point \mathbf{V} along the ray within [t{near}, t{far}]: Calculate integer coordinates identifying the enclosing voxel cell: x = \lfloor Vx \rfloor, y = \lfloor Vy \rfloor, z = \lfloor Vz \rfloor. Retrieve the 8 corner voxel indices for the cell defined by (x, y, z) to (x+1, y+1, z+1) using a boundary-aware getCell function: v{00} = \text{getCell}(x, y, z) v{01} = \text{getCell}(x+1, y, z) v{02} = \text{getCell}(x+1, y+1, z) v{03} = \text{getCell}(x, y+1, z) v{04} = \text{getCell}(x, y, z+1) v{05} = \text{getCell}(x+1, y, z+1) v{06} = \text{getCell}(x+1, y+1, z+1) v{07} = \text{getCell}(x, y+1, z+1) Calculate weights for each corner: For each corner vi, compute wi = \| \mathbf{V} - \text{voxels}[vi].\text{location} \|. Sum all weights: W{total} = \sum{i=0}^{7} wi. Normalize weights: w'i = wi / W{total}. Compute interpolated value: V{interp} = \sum{i=0}^{7} \text{voxels}[vi].\text{scalardata} \cdot w'i. Boundary Handling in getCell: If x < 0, set x = 0. If x > W-1, set x = W-1. If y < 0, set y = 0. If y > H-1, set y = H-1. If z < 0, set z = 0. If z > D-1, set z = D-1. Compute index as x + y \cdot W + z \cdot W \cdot H. Parameters: t{min}: Default 0.0. t{max}: Default \infty (or FLTMAX). Pitfalls: The original source clamps coordinates to [0, W], [0, H], [0, D] inclusive, which places x=W one past the last valid 0-based index W-1 and causes out-of-bounds access. The pseudocode below corrects this to clamp to [0, W-1]. Zero direction components cause division by zero in \mathbf{inv\dir}; the implementation guards against this. The condition t{far} > 0 rejects valid intersections when t{min} > 0 or rays start inside the volume; the condition is updated to t{far} > t{min}. Unverified code.
