name: Multi-Dimensional Interpolation Extension
head: 3D Kernel Extension Methods, Separable and Radial Kernel Extension
body: This method extends one-dimensional reconstruction kernels to higher dimensions for volume rendering. It constructs a three-dimensional filter from a one-dimensional base kernel to correctly reconstruct signals on a regular mesh, distinguishing itself from radial extension methods by avoiding sample frequency ripple artifacts on structured grids. Input: A one-dimensional reconstruction kernel function h'(u), where u represents the distance from the kernel center. Output: A three-dimensional kernel function h(x, y, z) evaluated at offset coordinates (x, y, z) relative to the sample center. Not given in the sources. Method 1: Separable Extension (Recommended) This method treats each coordinate as an independent variable. It is the correct way to extend filters to higher dimensions for regular meshes. 1. Evaluate the one-dimensional kernel for each coordinate offset: h'(x), h'(y), and h'(z). 2. Multiply the results to form the three-dimensional kernel: h(x, y, z) = h'(x) \times h'(y) \times h'(z). Method 2: Radial Extension This method uses the Euclidean radius from the kernel center as the free variable. This produces rotationally-symmetric kernels. 1. Calculate the radius r from the kernel center: r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}. 2. Evaluate the one-dimensional kernel at the radius: h(x, y, z) = h'(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}). Not given in the sources. Sample Frequency Ripple: Method 2 suffers from sample frequency ripple on regular meshes. Even when input samples have equal amplitude, the output field will not be flat; it will differ from the constant amplitude at points between the equal-valued input samples. Reconstruction Accuracy: Rotationally-symmetric kernels (except for the Gaussian, which is also separable) do not correctly reconstruct a regular mesh. Therefore, Method 2 should generally not be used for standard volume rendering on structured grids. Definition: This variant applies separable kernels to enable two-pass and three-pass image warping. It is much less sensitive to kernel extent sizes because the computational amount is O(n) for a kernel extent of n, compared to O(n^3) for ray-casting methods. Procedure: When using three-pass approaches, the order of passes is critical. All magnification steps must be performed before any minification steps. If minification precedes magnification, multiple samples are collapsed into a single sample during minification and cannot be separated during subsequent passes, leading to signal loss. Usage: Typically employs high-quality reconstruction kernels for all image generation to retain maximum signal information. Complexity: Ray-casting methods require O(n^3) computation for a kernel extent of n, whereas affine transformation methods using separable kernels reduce this to O(n). Strengths: Method 1 correctly reconstructs regular meshes and avoids the ripple artifacts inherent in Method 2. Limitations: Affine transformation methods are much less sensitive to kernel extent sizes than ray-casting methods. However, affine methods require careful pass ordering to avoid information loss. When to use: Use Method 1 for all regular mesh reconstructions. Use Affine Transformation Interpolation when performing image warping or non-axis-aligned rendering where computational efficiency is prioritized and high-quality kernels are required. The extension of one-dimensional kernels to higher dimensions is described as having two primary methods. Volume renderers seldom generate images that are axis-aligned with identical sampling rates for input data and the image, so resampling and careful filter design are required. Hanrahan [Hanrahan 90] is cited as a key contributor who considered these signal processing concerns, specifically regarding the ordering of magnification and minification in affine transformations. A Parallel, Feed-Forward Volume Rendering Algorithm, https://www.cs.unc.edu/techreports/91-029.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: POCS Interpolation Hardware Implementation
head: POCS Filter Hardware Implementation
body: A hardware architecture for implementing POCS interpolation filters in volume rendering, designed to overcome the quality limitations of standard tri-linear interpolation while remaining feasible within VLSI constraints. It distinguishes itself from Bilinear Interpolation by supporting larger kernel sizes (3 \times 3 \times 3 and 5 \times 5 \times 5) using lookup tables and specialized memory banking to handle the high data throughput required for multi-voxel sampling. Input: Volume dataset (voxel grid), ray sampling positions (fractional coordinates). Output: Interpolated scalar value for the sampling position. Parameters: Filter size (3 \times 3 \times 3 or 5 \times 5 \times 5), RAM access time (assumed 100 ns in source), clock speed. 1. RAM Banks: Parallel memory modules storing voxel data. Layout: Voxel addresses are mapped to banks based on the parity (odd/even) of their row, column, and depth indices. Bank Count: 8 banks for the 3 \times 3 \times 3 filter, and 16 banks for the 5 \times 5 \times 5 filter (derived from 64 voxels divided by a 4x time multiplexing factor). 2. Lookup Table (LUT): Precomputed POCS function values stored in EPROM or similar static memory. Content: Interpolation weights or filter coefficients for specific fractional offsets. Precision: Determined by design requirements; values are precomputed to avoid runtime calculation overhead. 3. Interpolation Chip: Contains the LUT, addressing logic, and caching registers. 1. Address Parity Analysis: For a given sampling point with fractional address (x, y, z), determine the integer base address (xb, yb, zb) by truncation. 2. Bank Mapping: Calculate the target RAM bank for each of the N surrounding voxels required by the filter kernel. For each dimension d \in \{x, y, z\}, determine if the offset from the base address is odd or even. Map the combination of parities to a specific bank index B \in \{0, \dots, 7\} for the 8-voxel case. 3. Parallel Fetch (8-voxel case): Issue simultaneous read commands to the 8 RAM banks. Ensure all 8 required voxels reside in distinct banks to avoid bank conflicts. Wait for data return (approx. 100 ns access time). 4. Time Multiplexing (64-voxel case): If using a 5 \times 5 \times 5 filter (64 voxels), clock the RAM banks at 4x the system speed. Fetch voxels in groups of 4 over 4 clock cycles. This reduces the physical RAM bank count from 64 to 16, resulting in a 256-bit data path width. 5. Caching: Store the fetched 64 voxels in the interpolation chip's internal cache. Exploit the fact that 4 resampling points typically fall within the spatial extent of a voxel sub-cube defined by the 64 surrounding voxels. Reuse the cached 64 voxels for all 4 resampling points to minimize memory bandwidth. 6. Lookup and Interpolation: Use the fractional parts of the sampling coordinates as indices into the Lookup Table. Retrieve precomputed POCS weights. Multiply fetched voxel values by weights and sum to produce the output. Bank Assignment: For a voxel at integer coordinates (i, j, k), the bank index B is determined by the parity bits: B = 4 \cdot (i \bmod 2) + 2 \cdot (j \bmod 2) + 1 \cdot (k \bmod 2) (Note: This mapping ensures that the 8 neighbors of any grid point map to unique banks 0-7). Data Path Width: W{64} = \frac{64 \cdot w}{4} = 16 \cdot w Where w is the voxel bit-width. For 16-bit voxels, W{64} = 256 bits. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fetchvoxels8banks(basex, basey, basez, rambanks): """Fetches 8 surrounding voxels for a 3x3x3 filter using 8 parallel RAM banks.""" voxels = [] for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: ax, ay, az = basex + dx, basey + dy, basez + dz bankidx = ((ax % 2) << 2) | ((ay % 2) << 1) | (az % 2) voxels.append(rambanks[bankidx][ax, ay, az]) return voxels def fetchvoxels16bankstimemux(basex, basey, basez, rambanks): """Fetches 64 surrounding voxels for a 5x5x5 filter using 16 RAM banks clocked 4x faster.""" allvoxels = [] # 64 voxels total, 16 banks, 4 voxels per bank fetched over 4 cycles for cycle in range(4): for bankidx in range(16): # The exact cycle-to-voxel mapping logic is not specified in the sources. # In practice, extra addressing logic distinguishes cases based on # whether the truncated address is odd or even in any direction. voxel = rambanks[bankidx].readfast(cycle) allvoxels.append(voxel) return allvoxels def interpolatepocs(voxels, fractionalcoords, lut): """Perform POCS interpolation using precomputed LUT.""" weight = lut.get(fractionalcoords) result = 0.0 for i, v in enumerate(voxels): result += v weight[i] return result Address Truncation Mismatch: When sampling two points P1 and P2 with fractional addresses, the truncated address of P2 may not map to the same 8 RAM banks as P1 (e.g., banks B, D, F, H might differ). Extra addressing logic is needed to distinguish cases based on whether the truncated address is odd or even in any direction. VLSI Pin Count: A naive implementation of a 5 \times 5 \times 5 filter would require 64 RAM banks and a 1024-bit data path, which is infeasible with current VLSI technology. Time multiplexing is used to reduce the RAM bank count by a factor of 4, resulting in a 256-bit data path. Memory Bandwidth: Caching voxels in the interpolation chip exploits that 4 resampling points exist within one voxel sub-cube of 8 voxels, allowing reuse of the same 64 voxels. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point, dominated by memory access latency and LUT lookup. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the interpolation chip (LUT + cache). The RAM bank count scales with filter size and multiplexing factor. Performance: The 8-voxel parallel fetch achieves throughput limited by RAM access time (100 ns). The 64-voxel implementation reduces hardware complexity (pins/banks) by 4x at the cost of requiring 4x RAM clock speed. Strengths: Higher quality than tri-linear interpolation; feasible hardware implementation for large kernels. Limitations: Requires significant extra addressing logic to handle bank conflicts when sampling points are close; high RAM clock speed requirements for large filters. The method originates from research on hardware implementations of POCS filters for volume rendering, specifically addressing the inadequacy of tri-linear interpolation for high-quality visualization. It was proposed as a hardware-optimized alternative to software-based POCS filtering, leveraging lookup tables and memory banking to achieve real-time performance on VLSI hardware. Fourier volume rendering, https://shiftleft.com/mirrors/www.hpl.hp.com/techreports/95/HPL-95-73.pdf, fetched 2026-10-31 (unofficial)

name: Seamless Interpolation
head: TileTree seamless interpolation, n-leaf interpolation
body: Seamless Interpolation is a method for rendering smooth surfaces stored in hierarchical tile-based structures (TileTrees) that eliminates pixelated appearance and interpolation seams at tile boundaries. It solves the problem of discontinuous color transitions when sampling from partially covered faces or n-leaves by computing a weighted sum of contributions from up to three adjacent face tiles (Tx, Ty, Tz) based on the surface normal. It differs from standard bilinear interpolation by explicitly handling multi-face visibility via binary alpha flags and normal-based dampening to ensure continuity across adaptive resolution boundaries and partial coverage areas. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point P in 3D space, the surface normal \mathbf{n} at P, and the TileTree data structure containing tiles Tx, Ty, Tz. Output: A final color c at P. Data Structures: Tile: A block of texture data. Each sample within a tile stores: Color C (RGB). Alpha flag \alpha (binary or interpolated float): Indicates if the sample corresponds to the enclosed surface. Stored in the alpha channel. TileTree: Hierarchical structure of tiles. Tiles may have different resolutions (adaptive resolution). Neighboring tiles share a one-pixel border replication. Steps: 1. Identify Contributing Tiles: Determine the three tiles Tx, Ty, Tz corresponding to the faces aligned with the surface normal \mathbf{n}. At most three faces contribute, selected by the dominant components of \mathbf{n}. 2. Fetch Samples and Flags: For each contributing tile Ti (where i \in \{x, y, z\}), fetch the color ci and the interpolated alpha flag \alphai at the projection of P onto the tile face. If a sample is undefined (e.g., in boundary-leaves or n-leaves interior where the surface does not cover the entire tile), fill the undefined color by reading from the neighboring leaf tile. The flag \alphai is interpolated using hardware bilinear filtering. It equals 1 if the tile contains proper samples for the surface and drops to 0 when irrelevant. 3. Compute Dampening Factors: To ensure robustness and prevent multiple flags from being 1 simultaneously, dampen the flags using the surface normal \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz): di = \frac{|ni|}{\max(|nx|, |ny|, |nz|)} where i \in \{x, y, z\}. 4. Compute Weights: Calculate the weights wx, wy, wz using the dampened flags. Add a small epsilon \epsilon to \alphai to avoid division by zero: wx = \frac{\alphax dx (1 - \alphay dy) (1 - \alphaz dz)}{\alphax dx (1 - \alphay dy) (1 - \alphaz dz) + \alphay dy (1 - \alphaz dz) (1 - \alphax dx) + \alphaz dz (1 - \alphax dx) (1 - \alphay dy)} wy = \frac{\alphay dy (1 - \alphaz dz) (1 - \alphax dx)}{\text{denominator}} wz = \frac{\alphaz dz (1 - \alphax dx) (1 - \alphay dy)}{\text{denominator}} The denominator is the sum of the numerators. 5. Compute Final Color: c = \frac{cx wx + cy wy + cz wz}{wx + wy + wz} 6. Adaptive Resolution Handling: If tiles have different resolutions, force the color of higher-resolution border samples to match the bilinear interpolation of the lower-resolution samples to prevent high-frequency discontinuities. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def seamlessinterpolation(pointp, surfacenormaln, tiletree): nx, ny, nz = surfacenormaln maxabsn = max(abs(nx), abs(ny), abs(nz)) if maxabsn == 0: maxabsn = 1e-6 # Guard against zero-length normal # 1. Identify contributing tiles based on normal axes tilex = tiletree.gettilex(pointp) tiley = tiletree.gettiley(pointp) tilez = tiletree.gettilez(pointp) # 2. Fetch samples and flags cx, alphax = tilex.bilinearinterpolate(pointp) cy, alphay = tiley.bilinearinterpolate(pointp) cz, alphaz = tilez.bilinearinterpolate(pointp) # Fill undefined colors from neighbors if necessary if cx is None: cx = tilex.neighborsample(pointp) if cy is None: cy = tiley.neighborsample(pointp) if cz is None: cz = tilez.neighborsample(pointp) # 3. Compute dampening factors dx = abs(nx) / maxabsn dy = abs(ny) / maxabsn dz = abs(nz) / maxabsn # 4. Compute weights epsilon = 1e-6 # Small constant to prevent division by zero adx = (alphax + epsilon) dx ady = (alphay + epsilon) dy adz = (alphaz + epsilon) dz numx = adx (1 - ady) (1 - adz) numy = ady (1 - adz) (1 - adx) numz = adz (1 - adx) (1 - ady) denom = numx + numy + numz if denom == 0: return cx # Fallback if all dampened flags are zero wx = numx / denom wy = numy / denom wz = numz / denom # 5. Compute final color finalcolor = (cx wx + cy wy + cz wz) / (wx + wy + wz) return finalcolor Parameters: \epsilon: Small constant to prevent division by zero. Value not given in sources. Typical value: 10^{-6}. Tile resolution: 2k+1 pixels per side. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Flags = 1: If multiple flags equal 1, weights become null/undefined. Solved by dampening with surface normal. All Flags = 0: If all flags equal 0, weights are undefined. Solved by adding epsilon to flags. Discontinuous Normals: The method assumes a smooth surface normal field. Discontinuities in the normal field will cause discontinuities in the result. Adaptive Resolution Boundaries: Without specific treatment, boundaries between different resolution tiles produce high-frequency discontinuities. Solved by forcing higher-resolution border samples to match bilinear interpolation of lower-resolution samples. Time Complexity: Per-sample computation requires only a few multiplications and additions, relying on hardware bilinear filtering for flag interpolation. Memory Complexity: Increases space overhead due to one-pixel border replication between neighboring tiles, especially for thick layers. Strengths: Seamless interpolation over smooth surfaces; handles partial coverage and adaptive resolution; robust against geometric features between tile samples. Limitations: Limited to smooth surfaces with continuous normal fields; increased memory usage for border replication; requires storing binary flags in alpha channel. Seamless Interpolation was introduced in the context of TileTrees, a hierarchical data structure for volume rendering. It was proposed to address the limitations of standard hardware interpolation when dealing with partially covered faces and n-leaves in tile-based volume rendering. The method relies on the graphics hardware interpolation capabilities and extends them with specific handling for tile boundaries and surface normals. TileTrees, https://doi.org/10.1145/1230100.1230104, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Distance-driven Interpolation
head: DD model
body: Distance-driven (DD) interpolation is a geometrical discretization model for volume rendering that computes interpolation weights based on the overlap length between voxel and detector bin footprints, rather than relying on projection matrices or homographies. Unlike destination-driven models that use \beta^1 for both projection and backprojection, DD is neither source nor destination driven, resulting in a matched pair (up to normalization) for projection and backprojection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Voxel centers xj, voxel width (implicitly 1 unit in the normalized domain), detector bin centers ui, detector bin width \Deltai, and the geometric mapping function h^{-1} that maps detector coordinates to the common axis. Output: Interpolation weights \xi{\Deltai}^{0,0}(h^{-1}(ui) - xj) representing the contribution of voxel j to detector bin i. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: Defined by centers xj. In the 1D separable case, voxels are located by their edges. A voxel j spans the interval [xj - 0.5, xj + 0.5] assuming unit width. Detector Bins: Defined by centers ui and widths \Deltai. A bin i spans the interval [h^{-1}(ui) - \Deltai/2, h^{-1}(ui) + \Deltai/2] on the common axis. Numbered Steps: 1. Locate Edges: For planar parallel or fan-beam geometry (or when separability holds), identify the edges of each voxel and each detector bin on their respective axes. 2. Map to Common Axis: Map the detector bin locations onto the same axis as the voxels using the inverse geometric mapping h^{-1}. 3. Compute Overlap: For each pair of voxel j and detector bin i, compute the interpolation weight as the length of the overlapping segment between the voxel footprint and the mapped bin footprint. Formula: The interpolation weight is given by the convolution of two order-0 B-splines (box functions): \xi{\Deltai}^{0,0}(h^{-1}(ui) - xj) = \int{-\infty}^{+\infty} \beta1^0(\tau) \beta{\Deltai}^0(h^{-1}(ui) - xj - \tau) d\tau = \int{xj - \frac{1}{2}}^{xj + \frac{1}{2}} \beta{\Deltai}^0(h^{-1}(ui) - \tau) d\tau Where: \xi{\Deltai}^{0,0} is the DD kernel. h^{-1}(ui) is the mapped detector bin center on the common axis. xj is the voxel center. \beta1^0 is the order-0 B-spline (box function) of width 1, centered at xj, defined as 1 on [xj - 0.5, xj + 0.5] and 0 otherwise. \beta{\Deltai}^0 is the order-0 B-spline of width \Deltai, centered at h^{-1}(ui), defined as 1 on [h^{-1}(ui) - \Deltai/2, h^{-1}(ui) + \Deltai/2] and 0 otherwise. The integral \int{xj - \frac{1}{2}}^{xj + \frac{1}{2}} \beta{\Deltai}^0(h^{-1}(ui) - \tau) d\tau represents the intersection of the support of \beta1^0 centered at xj and the support of \beta{\Deltai}^0 centered at h^{-1}(ui). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distancedrivenweight(xj, hinvui, deltai): """ Computes the DD interpolation weight for a single voxel and detector bin pair. Args: xj (float): Center of the voxel. hinvui (float): Mapped center of the detector bin on the common axis. deltai (float): Width of the detector bin. Returns: float: The length of the overlapping segment between the voxel and the bin. """ # Voxel footprint: [xj - 0.5, xj + 0.5] voxelleft = xj - 0.5 voxelright = xj + 0.5 # Detector bin footprint on common axis: [hinvui - deltai/2, hinvui + deltai/2] binleft = hinvui - deltai / 2.0 binright = hinvui + deltai / 2.0 # Calculate intersection interval overlapleft = max(voxelleft, binleft) overlapright = min(voxelright, binright) # Calculate length of intersection overlaplength = overlapright - overlapleft # If no overlap, weight is 0 if overlaplength < 0: return 0.0 return overlaplength Parameters: \Deltai: Detector bin width. Not given in the sources. h^{-1}: Geometric mapping function. Specific implementation depends on the system geometry (e.g., flat panel, cone beam). Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Overlap: If the voxel and bin footprints do not intersect, the weight is 0. The pseudocode handles this by returning 0.0 if overlaplength < 0. Precision: Floating-point precision may affect the calculation of overlap boundaries, especially for very small overlaps. Degenerate Input: If \Deltai = 0, the bin has no width, and the overlap length is 0 unless the bin center exactly coincides with the voxel center, in which case the overlap is a point (measure 0). Optimizes trilinear interpolation for hardware efficiency. Choose when hardware constraints limit computational resources. Extends interpolation to higher dimensions. Choose when working with 3D or higher-dimensional data. Implements interpolation using Projection Onto Convex Sets (POCS) on hardware. Choose for hardware-accelerated iterative reconstruction. Ensures seamless transitions between interpolated regions. Choose when visual continuity is critical. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Geometrical discretization model that captures both voxel and detector bin sampling levels. Neither source nor destination driven, resulting in a matched pair for projection and backprojection. Not specific to flat panel detector and does not rely on projection matrices and homographies. Limitations: Requires geometric mapping h^{-1} which may be complex for non-standard geometries. Computationally intensive if many voxel-bin pairs need to be evaluated. When to Use: When a geometrical discretization model is preferred over matrix-based approaches. When a matched pair for projection and backprojection is required. When Not to Use: When projection matrices and homographies are already available and preferred. When computational efficiency is paramount and simpler interpolation methods suffice. Distance-driven interpolation was proposed as an alternative to bilinear interpolation. It was introduced in the context of cone beam projection and backprojection, specifically for magnification-driven B-spline interpolation. The method is particularly relevant for flat panel cone beam geometry. Magnification-driven B-spline Interpolation for Cone Beam Projection and Backprojection, https://doi.org/10.1002/mp.15179, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Hardware Interpolation Approximation
head: Piecewise Bilinear/Trilinear Interpolation via Polygon Subdivision
body: Hardware Interpolation Approximation approximates the volume rendering integral by leveraging graphics hardware rasterization to perform linear interpolation along ray segments. It sets itself apart from Trilinear Interpolation and Bilinear Interpolation by deriving its interpolation kernel from the geometric subdivision of view-plane polygons by the graphics pipeline rather than a fixed volume grid. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset, a camera model, and a polygon mesh representing volume cells projected onto the view plane. Output: A 2D image rendered via hardware rasterization. Data Structures: Polygon Mesh: Defined by vertices in screen or world space, relying on standard graphics API primitive definitions (quadrilaterals or triangles). Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Polygon Subdivision: The graphics hardware receives polygon primitives representing volume cells projected onto the view plane. 2. Rasterization Subdivision: The hardware subdivides these polygons according to two possibilities suggested in the OpenGL specifications: Case 1 (Triangles): The polygon is divided into triangles, and linear interpolation is performed across them. Case 2 (Trapezoids): The polygon is divided into trapezoids by horizontal lines through the vertices, with bilinear interpolation performed inside the trapezoids (or linear interpolation if a trapezoid degenerates into a triangle). 3. Ray Segment Interpolation: Along each ray segment corresponding to a polygon edge or face, the method assumes a further linear interpolation of the scalar field values. 4. Integration Approximation: The combination of polygon subdivision and linear ray-segment interpolation yields piecewise bilinear interpolation for Case 1, and piecewise trilinear interpolation for Case 2. Formulas: The interpolated value V(\mathbf{p}) at a point \mathbf{p} is computed by the hardware's interpolation function I{\text{hw}} applied to the vertex attributes of the subdivided primitive. For linear interpolation across a primitive, V(\mathbf{p}) = \sumi wi V{vi}, where wi are the hardware-generated interpolation weights and V{vi} are the scalar values at the primitive's vertices. Parameters: Subdivision Strategy: Determined by the graphics driver/hardware implementation. Polygon Type: Quadrilaterals are the standard input for this approximation. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View Dependence: The interpolation is view-dependent because the subdivision into pieces depends on the subdivision of the view plane into polygons. Non-planar Faces: The behavior with non-planar faces is complex; subdividing a non-planar quadrilateral by a diagonal affects the interpolation result and may introduce artifacts. Specification Ambiguity: The exact interpolation produced is hard to determine because interpolation across polygons is not completely determined in the OpenGL specifications. First Order Integration approximates the volume rendering integral along a ray segment by assuming linear scalar field variation between two discrete samples, corresponding to the trapezoid rule. It sets itself apart from its parent Hardware Interpolation Approximation by explicitly modeling linear variation to enable pre-computation of the integral into a lookup table, and from Second Order Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering by using a linear rather than quadratic polynomial, which yields higher approximation error for high-frequency fields but lower computational complexity. Choose this method when pre-integration is required and linear variation assumptions are sufficient for the transfer function frequencies. Time Complexity: Dependent on rasterization speed; generally fast as it leverages dedicated GPU pipelines. Memory Complexity: Low, requiring only the polygon mesh and vertex attributes. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient hardware rasterization; simple implementation via standard graphics APIs. Limitations: View-dependent interpolation quality; ambiguity with non-planar faces; lack of precise kernel control compared to software methods. When to use: When hardware acceleration is prioritized and approximate linear interpolation is sufficient. When not to use: When precise interpolation control is required or when non-planar geometry artifacts are unacceptable. The method originates from the observation that graphics hardware can approximate integration by assuming linear interpolation along ray segments. It was discussed in the context of cell projection of meshes with nonplanar faces. The approach highlights the gap between theoretical finite element interpolation functions and the practical, view-dependent interpolation provided by standard graphics hardware. Cell projection of meshes with nonplanar faces, https://www.sciweavers.org/publications/cell-projection-meshes-non-planar-faces, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: First Order Integration (Trapezoid Rule)
head: Linear Interpolation Approximation, Linear approximation, Linear interpolation integration, Standard pre-integrated volume rendering
body: First Order Integration approximates the volume rendering integral along a ray segment by assuming the scalar field varies linearly between two discrete samples, corresponding to the trapezoid rule. It solves the visual artifacts caused by piecewise-constant (zero-order) approximations by capturing higher frequencies of the transfer function, enabling the pre-computation of the integral into a lookup table. It sets itself apart from its parent, Hardware Interpolation Approximation, by explicitly modeling the linear variation of the scalar field to allow for pre-integration, and from Second Order Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering by using a linear rather than quadratic polynomial, resulting in higher approximation error for high-frequency fields but lower computational complexity. Inputs: Scalar field samples at the front (sf) and back (sb) endpoints of a ray segment. Sampling distance l = x{i+1} - xi. If the sampling distance is constant, l can be fixed. Transfer functions for opacity \kappa(s) and color/emission q(s). Outputs: Pre-integrated opacity Ti and color contribution Ci for the segment. Data Structures: A 3D lookup table (LUT) indexed by (sf, sb, l) storing the precomputed integrals. If l is constant, this reduces to a 2D table indexed by (sf, sb). Steps: 1. Linear Interpolation Assumption: Assume the scalar field s(x) varies linearly between the front sample sf and back sample sb over the interval [xi, x{i+1}]. 2. Composition: Compose the linearly interpolated scalar field with the transfer functions to obtain the extinction coefficient \kappa(s(x)) and chromaticity q(s(x)). 3. Integration: Compute the integrals for opacity and color over the segment length l. Opacity: Ti = \exp\left(-\int{xi}^{x{i+1}} \kappa(s(x)) dx\right). Color: Ci = \int{xi}^{x{i+1}} q(s(x)) \exp\left(-\int{xi}^{x} \kappa(s(x')) dx'\right) dx. 4. Tabulation: Pre-compute these integrals for all relevant combinations of (sf, sb, l) and store them in the LUT. 5. Rendering: During ray casting, look up the pre-integrated values using the sampled sf and sb (and l if variable) to composite the segment. Formulas: The continuous version for a sample interval [xi, x{i+1}] with linear s(x) simplifies the integrals by changing the integration variable from x to s: Ti = \exp\left(-\int{si}^{s{i+1}} \kappa(s) \frac{l}{s{i+1}-si} ds \right) Ci = \int{si}^{s{i+1}} q(s) \exp\left(-\int{si}^{s} \kappa(s') \frac{l}{s{i+1}-si} ds' \right) \frac{l}{s{i+1}-si} ds Parameters: sf, sb: Scalar values at front and back endpoints. l: Length of the ray segment. d: Sampling distance x{i+1} - xi. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The approximation error is significant if the scalar field has high curvature, as the linear assumption fails to capture C^1 continuity within a dual voxel. Boundaries: The method assumes the transfer functions do not depend on derivatives. Degenerate Input: If sf = sb, the linear interpolation is constant, reducing to zero-order integration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def precomputelut(smin, smax, numlevels, lengths, kappafunc, qfunc, numsteps=100): """ Precompute the lookup table for first order integration. smin, smax: Range of scalar values. numlevels: Number of discrete levels for sf and sb. lengths: List of possible segment lengths. kappafunc, qfunc: User-defined transfer functions for extinction and color. numsteps: Number of quadrature steps for numerical integration. name: Second Order Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering

body: Second Order Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering is a direct volume rendering technique that approximates the scalar field along a ray segment using a second-order Lagrange polynomial (quadratic) defined by three equispaced samples, allowing the volume rendering integral to be pre-computed into a lookup table. This method captures high-frequency transfer function details more accurately than linear approaches by reducing the discrepancy between the trilinearly interpolated volume and its piecewise polynomial approximation. It sets itself apart from its parent, First Order Integration (Trapezoid Rule), by using quadratic polynomials to model the non-zero curvature inherent in trilinear interpolation, thereby providing significantly reduced approximation error and faster convergence for scalar fields with high frequencies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset, a transfer function mapping scalar values to color \mathbf{c}(s) and opacity \tau(s), and a set of rays cast through the volume. Output: A 2D image where each pixel color is computed via front-to-back compositing of pre-integrated segment contributions. Data Structures: Pre-integration Table: A 3D texture storing pre-computed color and opacity values. Dimensions: 256 \times 256 \times 256 for an 8-bit scalar domain. Indices: (sf, sm, sb), representing the front, middle, and back sample values of a ray segment. Stored Values: A pair (\mathbf{c}2, \tau2) for each index combination. Note: While theoretically a 4D table indexed by (sf, sm, sb, l) is required for variable segment lengths, constant length sampling reduces this to a 3D table as l becomes constant. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-computation (Table Generation): 1. Iterate through all possible combinations of 8-bit scalar values for sf, sm, sb \in [0, 255]. 2. For each triplet, calculate the coefficients A, B, C of the quadratic polynomial P(t) that interpolates the samples at t=0, 0.5, 1. 3. Compute the pre-integrated color \mathbf{c}2 and opacity \tau2 for a segment of constant length l by numerically integrating the transfer function composed with P(t). 2. Ray Sampling: 1. Cast rays through the volume. 2. Sample the scalar field \mathcal{F} at three equispaced points along each ray segment to obtain sf, sm, sb. 3. Determine the segment length l = t{back} - t{front}. For constant length sampling, l is fixed. 3. Rendering (Compositing): 1. Initialize accumulated color C = 0 and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0. 2. Iterate through the ray samples in steps of 2 (forming triads i = 0, 2, \dots, n-3): 1. Quantize the floating-point samples to integers in [0, 255] for table lookup. 2. Retrieve the pre-integrated color \mathbf{c}2 and opacity \tau2 from the 3D table using indices (sf(i), sm(i), sb(i)). 3. Compute the contribution of the current segment: \text{contribution} = \mathbf{c}2 \times (1 - \alpha{acc}). 4. Update accumulated color: C \leftarrow C + \text{contribution}. 5. Update accumulated opacity using the product form from Eq. 3: \alpha{acc} \leftarrow 1 - (1 - \alpha{acc})(1 - \tau2). 3. The final pixel color is C. Formulas: Quadratic Interpolation: The scalar field P(t) along the segment (t \in [0,1]) is defined as P(t) = At^2 + Bt + C, where: \begin{cases} A = 2sf - 4sm + 2sb \\ B = -3sf + 4sm - sb \\ C = sf \end{cases} Pre-integrated Color and Opacity: For a segment of length l: \mathbf{c}2(sf, sm, sb, l) = \int0^1 \mathbf{c}(P(t)) \tau(P(t)) l \exp \left( \int0^t \tau(P(t')) l dt' \right) dt \tau2(sf, sm, sb, l) = 1 - \exp \left( \int0^1 \tau(P(t)) l dt \right) Front-to-Back Compositing: C \approx \sum{i=0}^{n-3} \mathbf{c}2(sf(i), sm(i), sb(i), l(i)) \times \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \tau2(sf(j), sm(j), sb(j), l(j))) Parameters: Scalar Domain: 8-bit (0-255). Table Size: 256^3 (3D texture). Sampling: Equispaced samples along the ray. Constant length sampling is preferred for performance and simplicity, despite theoretical imperfections at voxel boundaries. Integration Steps: A fixed number of iterations over the polynomial interval [0,1] during table generation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Voxel Boundary Artifacts: When using constant length sampling, ray segments may cross dual voxel boundaries, causing abrupt changes in the first derivative of the underlying trilinear interpolation. This can theoretically deteriorate the 2nd order approximation quality, although empirical tests show it still outperforms 1st order methods. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ if len(samples) < 3: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # Iterate in steps of 2 to form triads for i in range(0, len(samples) - 2, 2): # Quantize samples to 8-bit integer indices for table lookup sf = int(round(max(0, min(255, samples[i])))) sm = int(round(max(0, min(255, samples[i+1])))) sb = int(round(max(0, min(255, samples[i+2])))) # Lookup pre-integrated values c2, tau2 = table[(sf, sm, sb)] # Front-to-back compositing (equivalent to product form in Eq. 3) weight = 1.0 - accumulatedopacity accumulatedcolor[0] += c2[0] weight accumulatedcolor[1] += c2[1] weight accumulatedcolor[2] += c2[2] weight accumulatedopacity += tau2 weight return accumulatedcolor + [accumulatedopacity] A variant that replaces the piecewise linear segment with a second-order function to improve the accuracy of approximating the pre-integrated transfer function integral. Time Complexity: Pre-computation scales with the cube of the scalar domain size and the number of integration steps. Rendering requires N texture accesses per ray, with the back sample cached for the next segment to lower computational cost. Memory Complexity: O(S^3) for the pre-integration table, where S=256 for an 8-bit domain, specifically under constant length ray sampling. Measured Performance: Constant length sampling is more efficient with respect to performance than adaptive sampling. Strengths: Significantly reduced approximation error compared to 1st order pre-integration. Better convergence to the true trilinear signal, especially for scalar fields with high frequencies. Captures high-frequency transfer function details more accurately. Limitations: Higher memory consumption than 1st order (3D vs 2D table). Potential quality degradation at voxel boundaries with constant length sampling. When to Use: When high-frequency details in the transfer function or scalar field are critical, and sufficient GPU memory is available. Second Order Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering was introduced in the paper "Second Order Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering" (2008) by Marchesin et al.. It extends the concept of pre-integrated volume rendering, which was originally based on 1st order (linear) integration, to 2nd order (quadratic) integration. The method addresses the limitations of linear interpolation in capturing the curvature of trilinearly interpolated volumes, which can lead to significant errors in the presence of high-frequency scalar fields or transfer functions. The technique leverages GPU programmability for both table generation and rendering, utilizing 3D textures for efficient lookup. name: Analytic Integration for Linear Variation
head: Williams and Max method
body: Analytic Integration for Linear Variation computes the exact volume rendering integral for optical properties that vary linearly along a ray segment. It solves the approximation errors of numerical quadrature when the scalar field is interpolated linearly and transfer functions are linear. Unlike First Order Integration (Trapezoid Rule), which assumes constant or linearly averaged values, this method derives a closed-form solution for the exponential integral of a linear function, providing higher accuracy for linearly interpolated data. Inputs: Ray segment defined by start point \mathbf{r}0, direction \mathbf{d}, and length L. Scalar field values si at the vertices of the primitive (e.g., tetrahedron) intersected by the ray. Linear transfer functions mapping scalar s to extinction coefficient \tau(s) = a\tau s + b\tau and color c(s) = ac s + bc. Outputs: Accumulated color C and opacity \alpha for the segment. Data Structures: No complex data structures required beyond standard scalar values and ray parameters. The method relies on direct evaluation of the analytic formula. Steps: 1. Parameterize the Ray: Define the position along the ray as \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{r}0 + t\mathbf{d} for t \in [0, L]. 2. Evaluate Scalar Field: Determine the scalar value s(t) at any point t. If the scalar field is linearly interpolated from tetrahedron vertices, s(t) is a linear function of t: s(t) = s0 + t \cdot \Delta s, where s0 is the scalar at \mathbf{r}0 and \Delta s is the rate of change along the ray. 3. Define Optical Properties: Substitute s(t) into the linear transfer functions to get extinction \tau(t) and color c(t) as linear functions of t: \tau(t) = \tau0 + t \cdot \Delta \tau c(t) = c0 + t \cdot \Delta c where \tau0 = \tau(s0), \Delta \tau = \Delta s \cdot a\tau, etc.. 4. Compute Analytic Integral: Evaluate the volume rendering integral for the segment. The transmittance T(L) and accumulated color C(L) are given by closed-form expressions involving exponentials of \tau(t). For a linear extinction \tau(t) = \tau0 + t \Delta \tau, the transmittance is: T(L) = \exp\left(-\int0^L \tau(t) dt\right) = \exp\left(-\tau0 L - \frac{1}{2}\Delta \tau L^2\right) The accumulated color requires integrating c(t) T(t). This integral yields a rather complicated analytic expression that must be evaluated using symbolic integration techniques. 5. Handle Piecewise Linear Transfer Functions: If the transfer function is piecewise linear, divide the tetrahedron into sub-polyhedra where the transfer function is linear, and sum the contributions. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Zero Extinction Change: If \Delta \tau = 0, the formula simplifies to the constant extinction case. Numerical Stability: The original formulation by Williams and Max was complex and prone to numerical instability. Improved formulations [59] improve the numerical stability of the software evaluation. Visibility Sorting: When applied to tetrahedral meshes, a visibility sort is required to process primitives back-to-front. Cycles in tetrahedron overlap can make sorting impossible. Computes the exact integral for trilinearly varying scalar fields, accounting for cubic polynomial structures. Choose this when using trilinear interpolation on voxel grids instead of tetrahedral linear interpolation. Time Complexity: O(1) per segment, but involves expensive exponential and potentially error function evaluations. More complex than the Trapezoid Rule. Memory Complexity: O(1) if evaluated directly. Moreland and Angel [43] used GPU precomputed texture tables to accelerate evaluation, trading memory for speed. Strengths: Exact integration for linearly varying optical properties; reduces aliasing and approximation errors compared to numerical quadrature. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to transcendental functions; visibility sorting for tetrahedral meshes can be a bottleneck or impossible due to cycles. When to Use: High-quality rendering with tetrahedral data and linear transfer functions where accuracy is critical. When Not to Use: Real-time applications with limited GPU power, or when data is not linearly interpolated (e.g., trilinear voxel data). First presented by Williams and Max [58], this method was improved for numerical stability in [59]. Moreland and Angel [43] implemented it on the GPU using precomputed texture tables. It is a foundational technique for volume rendering with tetrahedral meshes and linear transfer functions. name: Analytic Integration for Trilinear Variation
head: Polynomial integration for trilinear basis, Trilinear Basis Function Integration
body: Analytic Integration for Trilinear Variation computes the exact integral of a scalar field varying according to a trilinear basis function along a ray segment within a voxel. It solves the problem of accurately evaluating volume rendering integrals when the underlying data is interpolated using trilinear filtering, avoiding approximation errors inherent in numerical quadrature. Unlike Analytic Integration for Linear Variation, which assumes linear variation along the ray, this method accounts for the full cubic polynomial structure introduced by the interaction of the ray's direction with the three-dimensional trilinear interpolation weights. Inputs: Ray segment defined by origin \mathbf{p} = (px, py, pz) and normalized direction vector \mathbf{r} = (rx, ry, rz) in voxel space. Intersection parameters s1 and s2 representing the entry and exit points of the ray with the current voxel, expressed in unit coordinates relative to the voxel's local space. Scalar values at the 8 corners of the voxel: p{000}, p{001}, p{010}, p{011}, p{100}, p{101}, p{110}, p{111}. These correspond to the unit cube corners in the order of p{zyx} (i.e., the least significant bit corresponds to the x-axis, middle to y, most significant to z). Outputs: The definite integral of the trilinearly interpolated function f(s) along the ray segment from s1 to s2. Data Structures: The method relies on precomputed coefficients a1 through a8 derived from the corner values. Steps: 1. Compute the constants a1 through a8 using the corner values p{ijk}: \begin{aligned} a1 &= -p{000} - p{001} + p{010} + p{011} - p{100} - p{101} + p{110} + p{111} \\ a2 &= -p{000} + p{001} + p{010} - p{011} \\ a3 &= -p{000} + p{001} - p{100} + p{101} \\ a4 &= -p{000} + p{010} - p{100} + p{110} \\ a5 &= -p{000} - p{001} \\ a6 &= p{000} - p{010} \\ a7 &= p{000} + p{100} \\ a8 &= -p{000} \end{aligned} 2. Construct the cubic polynomial P(s) = C3 s^3 + C2 s^2 + C1 s + C0 representing the integrand. The coefficients are defined as follows: Coefficient for s^3 (C3): C3 = a1 rx ry rz Coefficient for s^2 (C2): C2 = a1 (rx ry pz + px ry rz + py rx rz) + a2 rx ry + a3 rx rz + a4 ry rz Coefficient for s^1 (C1): C1 = a1 (pz px ry + pz py rx + px py rz) + a2 (px rz + py rx) + a3 (px rz + pz rx) + a4 (py rz + pz ry) + a5 rx + a6 ry + a7 rz Constant term (C0): C0 = a1 px py pz + a2 px py + a3 px py + a4 py pz + a5 px + a6 py + a7 pz + a8 3. Integrate the polynomial P(s) from s1 to s2: \text{Integral} = \left[ \frac{C3}{4}s^4 + \frac{C2}{3}s^3 + \frac{C1}{2}s^2 + C0 s \right]{s1}^{s2} Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: porigin: Tuple (px, py, pz) representing the ray origin in voxel space. rdirection: Tuple (rx, ry, rz) representing the ray direction. Source assumes this is normalized. s1: Float, entry parameter of the ray into the voxel. s2: Float, exit parameter of the ray into the voxel. pcorners: List of 8 floats [p000, p001, p010, p011, p100, p101, p110, p111]. Order is pzyx (index = z4 + y2 + x). Returns: Float, the value of the integral from s1 to s2. """ px, py, pz = porigin rx, ry, rz = rdirection p000, p001, p010, p011, p100, p101, p110, p111 = pcorners # Step 1: Compute constants a1...a8 a1 = -p000 - p001 + p010 + p011 - p100 - p101 + p110 + p111 a2 = -p000 + p001 + p010 - p011 a3 = -p000 + p001 - p100 + p101 a4 = -p000 + p010 - p100 + p110 a5 = -p000 - p001 a6 = p000 - p010 a7 = p000 + p100 a8 = -p000 # Step 2: Compute polynomial coefficients C3, C2, C1, C0 C3 = a1 rx ry rz C2 = a1 (rx ry pz + px ry rz + py rx rz) + a2 rx ry + a3 rx rz + a4 ry rz C1 = (a1 (pz px ry + pz py rx + px py rz) + a2 (px rz + py rx) + a3 (px rz + pz rx) + a4 (py rz + pz ry) + a5 rx + a6 ry + a7 rz) C0 = (a1 px py pz + a2 px py + a3 px py + a4 py pz + a5 px + a6 py + a7 pz + a8) # Step 3: Integrate from s1 to s2 # Antiderivative F(s) = (C3/4)s^4 + (C2/3)s^3 + (C1/2)s^2 + C0s def antiderivative(s): return (C3 / 4.0) (s 4) + \ (C2 / 3.0) (s 3) + \ (C1 / 2.0) (s 2) + \ C0 s return antiderivative(s2) - antiderivative(s1) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The proof for the transformation of curve integrals used to derive these coefficients is only valid for a linear curve cn and linear transformation T. If the ray is not linear or the transformation is non-linear, this method is invalid. The order of corner values p{000} \dots p{111} must strictly follow the p{zyx} indexing convention specified in the source. The ray direction vector must be normalized before computing coefficients, as the derivation assumes a unit direction vector. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. head: Interval Integration, Trilinear Integration
body: Deterministic Volume Integration is a ray-marching technique that improves upon standard point-sampling by integrating the trilinearly interpolated feature fields over the entire length of a ray segment within a voxel, rather than evaluating them at a single point. This method addresses the error introduced by assuming density and color fields are constant between samples, providing a more accurate estimation of the volume integral compared to Monte Carlo approaches. It is distinct from Second Order Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering which handles quadratic variations, and Analytic Integration for Linear Variation which may use different basis functions or constraints. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a voxel grid containing learned feature fields (density \sigma and intermediate features \mathbf{h}); a color decoder function \theta{color}; and a positional encoding function \gamma for the viewing direction. Output: The accumulated color \mathbf{C} and opacity \alpha for the pixel, derived from the integrated density and features. Data Structures: The method operates on a voxel grid where each voxel stores feature vectors. In the specific implementation described in the sources, the scene is divided into N=8 symmetric regions (cubes) sharing a single feature grid to reduce memory usage by a factor of N. Each voxel's features are accessed via trilinear interpolation. A data layout strategy places features symmetrically to the scene center to favor continuity between density fields and reduce the number of unique features needed. Steps: 1. Ray-Voxel Intersection: Determine the entry point tj^{in} and exit point tj^{out} for each voxel j intersected by the ray. 2. Feature Integration: For each interval [tj^{in}, tj^{out}], compute the integrated density \sigmaj and integrated intermediate features \mathbf{h}j by integrating the trilinearly interpolated fields over the interval. The integration is defined as: (\sigmaj, \mathbf{h}j) = \int{tj^{in}}^{tj^{out}} \hat{f}i(\mathbf{x}(t), \mathbf{d}) \, dt, \quad i \in [1, 8] where \hat{f}i represents the trilinearly interpolated feature field for region i, and \mathbf{x}(t) is the position on the ray at distance t. 3. Color Decoding: Decode the color \mathbf{c}j for the voxel interval using the integrated intermediate features \mathbf{h}j, the viewing direction \mathbf{d}j, and the color decoder \theta{color}: \mathbf{c}j = \theta{color}(\mathbf{h}j, \gamma(\mathbf{d}j)) where \gamma(\mathbf{d}j) is the positional encoding of the viewing direction. 4. Compositing: Composite the results (\sigmaj, \mathbf{h}j, \mathbf{c}j) along the ray using standard volume rendering accumulation equations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Compute ray-voxel intervals (standard slab traversal) intervals = computerayvoxelintervals(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid.bounds) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 for tin, tout in intervals: # 2. Integrate features over the interval sigmaj, hj = integratetrilinearfield(voxelgrid, rayorigin, raydirection, tin, tout) # 3. Decode color directionenc = positionalencoding(raydirection) cj = colordecoder(hj, directionenc) # 4. Accumulate # sigmaj is already the integrated density over [tin, tout] alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmaj) accumulatedcolor += alpha transmittance cj transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Early ray termination if transmittance < 1e-4: break return accumulatedcolor def computerayvoxelintervals(origin, direction, bounds): """Standard slab traversal to find tmin and tmax for each intersected voxel.""" # Standard implementation computes tmax on each axis, takes min/max, # and steps through voxels until exiting bounds. Returns list of (tin, tout). pass Parameters: N=8: Number of symmetric regions in the voxel grid configuration. Region size: Cube with side length equal to half the bounding box side. Decoder layers: Density decoders have an input layer, a hidden layer of 32 neurons, and an output layer of 33 neurons; the color decoder has an input layer of 32 neurons and an output layer of 3 neurons. All layers use ReLU activation except output layers, which have no activation for density. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The integration of trilinear fields is more computationally expensive than point sampling. Numerical integration errors may occur if the interval is large relative to the voxel size and low-order quadrature is used. Boundaries: The symmetric configuration is designed to ensure continuity between regions at boundaries, reducing artifacts. Transmittance Culling: Early ray termination should use a small epsilon threshold to avoid division by zero or infinite loops. A data layout strategy where features are placed symmetrically to the scene center. This favors continuity between density fields and feature pruning, reducing the number of unique features needed by a factor of N. Choose this when memory efficiency and inter-region continuity are priorities. Link: NeRFLight. Time Complexity: Higher than standard point-sampling trilinear interpolation because it requires integrating the feature field over the voxel interval rather than evaluating it at a single point. The cost depends on the integration method (analytic vs. numerical quadrature). Memory Complexity: Reduced by a factor of N (where N=8 in the cited implementation) due to the shared feature grid across symmetric regions. Performance: Produces better estimation than Monte Carlo sampling because it accounts for the variation of density and color fields within the voxel interval. Strengths: Improved visual quality over point-sampling; memory efficient via shared grids. Limitations: Increased computational cost per voxel compared to point sampling. When to use: When high-quality volume rendering is required and memory is constrained, particularly in neural radiance field contexts like NeRFLight. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and point-sampling quality is sufficient. The method was introduced in the context of NeRFLight, a fast and light Neural Radiance Fields approach using a shared feature grid. The technique was developed to improve the quality of the model by replacing random sampling with deterministic integration of trilinearly interpolated features. name: Trilinear Interpolation
head: 3D Linear Interpolation, Interpolação trilinear, Linear Interpolation (Trilinear), Trilinear Interpolant, Trilinear Sampling, Voxel Trilinear Interpolation
body: Trilinear interpolation estimates the scalar value at an arbitrary point within a voxel grid by computing a weighted average of the values of the 8 surrounding voxels, based on their distances to the sample point. It solves the problem of discretization artifacts (blockiness) inherent in nearest-neighbor sampling by providing a continuous, first-order approximation of the underlying scalar field. It produces softer, higher-quality images than nearest-neighbor interpolation but requires approximately 5 times more computation time. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field defined on a regular grid with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz, and a query position \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z) in voxel space. Output: A single scalar value V(\mathbf{p}). Data Structures: The volume data is stored in a 3D array (or flattened 1D array with row-major indexing). For a query point, the algorithm accesses the 8 corner values of the containing voxel: \begin{aligned} v{000} &= \text{Grid}(i0, j0, k0) \\ v{100} &= \text{Grid}(i1, j0, k0) \\ v{010} &= \text{Grid}(i0, j1, k0) \\ v{110} &= \text{Grid}(i1, j1, k0) \\ v{001} &= \text{Grid}(i0, j0, k1) \\ v{101} &= \text{Grid}(i1, j0, k1) \\ v{011} &= \text{Grid}(i0, j1, k1) \\ v{111} &= \text{Grid}(i1, j1, k1) \end{aligned} where i1 = i0 + 1, j1 = j0 + 1, k1 = k0 + 1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate System Alignment: Depending on the grid's coordinate convention, an offset (e.g., -0.5) may be applied to align voxel centers with integer coordinates. Standard implementations assume voxel corners at integer indices and skip this step. \mathbf{p}{\text{aligned}} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c} \quad (\text{where } \mathbf{c} \text{ is typically } (0,0,0) \text{ or } (0.5,0.5,0.5)) 2. Index Calculation: Compute the integer indices of the lower-left corner of the containing voxel using the floor function. i0 = \lfloor p{\text{aligned}, x} \rfloor, \quad j0 = \lfloor p{\text{aligned}, y} \rfloor, \quad k0 = \lfloor p{\text{aligned}, z} \rfloor 3. Boundary Clamping: Clamp the lower indices to prevent out-of-bounds access if the query point lies on the grid boundary. If i0 = Dx - 1, set i0 = Dx - 2 (and similarly for y, z). 4. Fractional Weights: Calculate the fractional offset (weights) within the voxel. wx = p{\text{aligned}, x} - i0, \quad wy = p{\text{aligned}, y} - j0, \quad wz = p{\text{aligned}, z} - k0 These weights lie in the range [0, 1]. 5. Interpolation: Perform linear interpolation sequentially along the x, y, and z axes. X-axis: Interpolate pairs along the x-dimension for the bottom (k0) and top (k1) faces. \begin{aligned} c{00} &= v{000}(1 - wx) + v{100}wx \\ c{10} &= v{010}(1 - wx) + v{110}wx \\ c{01} &= v{001}(1 - wx) + v{101}wx \\ c{11} &= v{011}(1 - wx) + v{111}wx \end{aligned} Y-axis: Interpolate the results from the X-step along the y-dimension. \begin{aligned} c0 &= c{00}(1 - wy) + c{10}wy \\ c1 &= c{01}(1 - wy) + c{11}wy \end{aligned} Z-axis: Interpolate the results from the Y-step along the z-dimension to get the final value. V(\mathbf{p}) = c0(1 - wz) + c1 wz Expanded Formula: The result can also be expressed as a weighted sum of the 8 corners: \begin{aligned} V(\mathbf{p}) = & \ v{000}(1-wx)(1-wy)(1-wz) + v{100}wx(1-wy)(1-wz) + \\ & \ v{010}(1-wx)wy(1-wz) + v{110}wx wy (1-wz) + \\ & \ v{001}(1-wx)(1-wy)wz + v{101}wx(1-wy)wz + \\ & \ v{011}(1-wx)wy wz + v{111}wx wy wz \end{aligned} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearinterpolation(grid, p, dims): """ grid: 3D array of shape (Dz, Dy, Dx) p: tuple (x, y, z) in voxel space dims: tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) """ x, y, z = p # 1. Compute lower indices i0 = int(x // 1) if x >= 0 else int(x // 1) - (1 if x != int(x) else 0) j0 = int(y // 1) if y >= 0 else int(y // 1) - (1 if y != int(y) else 0) k0 = int(z // 1) if z >= 0 else int(z // 1) - (1 if z != int(z) else 0) # 2. Handle boundaries: clamp lower index to valid range [0, dim-2] i0 = max(0, min(i0, dims[0] - 2)) j0 = max(0, min(j0, dims[1] - 2)) k0 = max(0, min(k0, dims[2] - 2)) i1 = i0 + 1 j1 = j0 + 1 k1 = k0 + 1 # 3. Compute fractional weights wx = x - i0 wy = y - j0 wz = z - k0 # 4. Fetch 8 corner values (assuming grid is indexed as [z, y, x]) v000 = grid[k0, j0, i0] v100 = grid[k0, j0, i1] v010 = grid[k0, j1, i0] v110 = grid[k0, j1, i1] v001 = grid[k1, j0, i0] v101 = grid[k1, j0, i1] v011 = grid[k1, j1, i0] v111 = grid[k1, j1, i1] # 5. Interpolate along X c00 = v000 (1 - wx) + v100 wx c10 = v010 (1 - wx) + v110 wx c01 = v001 (1 - wx) + v101 wx c11 = v011 (1 - wx) + v111 wx # 6. Interpolate along Y c0 = c00 (1 - wy) + c10 wy c1 = c01 (1 - wy) + c11 wy # 7. Interpolate along Z result = c0 (1 - wz) + c1 wz return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: If the query point lies exactly on the upper boundary of the grid, the upper neighbor index would exceed the array bounds. Clamping the lower index to dim - 2 ensures valid access. Zero-Width Voxels: If the grid has degenerate voxels (width 0), division by zero may occur if using explicit division for weights. The fractional weight calculation w = p - i0 avoids this, but boundary clamping is still necessary. Coordinate System Mismatch: Applying a -0.5 offset when the grid uses corner-aligned coordinates (or vice versa) shifts the sampling grid, causing incorrect interpolation weights and visual artifacts. Uses trilinear interpolation on a sparse grid of spherical harmonic coefficients to enable gradient-based optimization, differing from standard scalar trilinear interpolation by storing directional radiance data. Implements trilinear interpolation via a stack of 2D textures and dependent texturing to approximate 3D sampling on hardware that lacks native 3D texture support, relying on the Piecewise Regular Interval (PRI) data structure. Uses trilinear interpolation to define the scalar field within hexahedral cells but replaces uniform ray marching with analytical integration of the piecewise-linear function to avoid isosurface artifacts. Uses trilinear interpolation to approximate the line integral of the Linear Attenuation Coefficient for differentiable X-ray rendering, trading geometric precision for speed and regularization. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, requiring exactly 8 memory fetches and 7 linear interpolations (14 multiplications, 7 additions). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: Produces significantly higher quality images than nearest-neighbor interpolation but takes approximately 5 times longer to compute. It is faster than higher-order methods like tri-cubic interpolation. Strengths: Simple to implement, hardware-supported (via 3D texture sampling units in GPUs), and provides smoother results than nearest-neighbor. Limitations: Introduces blurring and high-frequency artifacts (false edges or "star patterns") due to the infinite extent of the triangular pulse kernel's Fourier transform. It is not suitable for applications requiring sharp feature preservation or exact geometric reconstruction. When to use: General-purpose volume rendering where visual smoothness is prioritized over sharpness, and computational resources are limited compared to higher-order methods. When not to use: When exact geometric intersection is required, as it approximates values rather than computing precise voxel boundaries. Trilinear interpolation is the direct 3D extension of bilinear interpolation, defined as the linear interpolation of two bilinear interpolations. It was widely adopted in early volume rendering techniques to improve upon the blocky artifacts of nearest-neighbor sampling. The method is fundamental to many volume rendering pipelines, including those implemented in OpenVDB and standard GPU texture sampling hardware. It is also used in related fields such as fluid simulation. name: Plenoxels Interpolation Methods
head: Plenoxel Grid with Trilinear Interpolation, Plenoxel Trilinear Interpolation, Trilinear Plenoxel, Trilinear Plenoxel Interpolation
body: Plenoxels Interpolation Methods define a continuous plenoptic function throughout a sparse 3D voxel grid by trilinearly interpolating density and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients stored at voxel centers. Unlike its sibling Trilinear Interpolation which handles general rectilinear grids, this method specifically targets the optimization stability and effective resolution of radiance field representations. It distinguishes itself from Multi-Texture Trilinear Estimation and Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering with Trilinear Interpolation by integrating SH-based view-dependent color directly into the interpolation weights, and from Radial Basis Function Interpolation by using a structured grid rather than scattered points. The primary advantage is that trilinear interpolation produces a continuous function approximation critical for stable gradient-based optimization, outperforming nearest-neighbor approaches even at lower resolutions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse 3D voxel grid containing optimized parameters; a ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; the viewing direction \mathbf{d} for SH evaluation. Output: Transmittance T, density \sigma, and color \mathbf{c} at sample points along the ray. Data Structures: The grid stores values at voxel centers. For each active voxel, the following data is stored: 1. Density (\sigma): A single scalar value. 2. Spherical Harmonic Coefficients: For each of the 3 color channels (RGB), 9 coefficients are stored (Degree 2 SH). Total: 27 coefficients per voxel. Layout: A flat array of 28 floats per voxel (1 density + 27 SH coefficients). Bit packing: Not specified in sources; typically stored as standard 32-bit floats. Parameters: Spherical Harmonics Degree: 2. This requires 9 coefficients per color channel, totaling 27 harmonic coefficients per voxel. Higher orders confer minimal benefit. Grid Resolution: Variable (e.g., 128^3, 256^3). Coarse-to-fine strategies may start at lower resolutions and upsample. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Marching Setup: Define sample points along the ray. 2. Voxel Lookup: For a sample point \mathbf{p}, identify the 8 nearest voxel centers surrounding \mathbf{p} in the 3D grid. 3. Barycentric Weights: Compute the trilinear interpolation weights based on the relative position of \mathbf{p} within the unit cube defined by the 8 voxels. Let \mathbf{w} = (wx, wy, wz) be the fractional coordinates of \mathbf{p} within the voxel cell, where 0 \le wi < 1. The weight for a corner voxel at offset (i, j, k) where i,j,k \in \{0,1\} is: W{ijk} = \begin{cases} (1-wx)(1-wy)(1-wz) & \text{if } i=0, j=0, k=0 \\ wx(1-wy)(1-wz) & \text{if } i=1, j=0, k=0 \\ (1-wx)wy(1-wz) & \text{if } i=0, j=1, k=0 \\ wx wy (1-wz) & \text{if } i=1, j=1, k=0 \\ (1-wx)(1-wy)wz & \text{if } i=0, j=0, k=1 \\ wx(1-wy)wz & \text{if } i=1, j=0, k=1 \\ (1-wx)wy wz & \text{if } i=0, j=1, k=1 \\ wx wy wz & \text{if } i=1, j=1, k=1 \end{cases} 4. Interpolate Density: Compute the density \sigma(\mathbf{p}) by summing the weighted density values \sigmav of the 8 neighbors: \sigma(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{v \in \text{neighbors}} Wv \cdot \sigmav 5. Interpolate SH Coefficients: For each color channel c \in \{R, G, B\}, compute the interpolated SH coefficients \mathbf{a}{c} by summing the weighted SH coefficient vectors \mathbf{a}{c,v} of the 8 neighbors: \mathbf{a}{c}(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{v \in \text{neighbors}} Wv \cdot \mathbf{a}{c,v} where \mathbf{a}{c,v} is the vector of 9 SH coefficients for channel c at voxel v. 6. Evaluate Color: Compute the color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}) by evaluating the spherical harmonic basis functions \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{d}) for the viewing direction \mathbf{d} and dotting with the interpolated coefficients: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{c \in \{R,G,B\}} \left( \mathbf{a}{c}(\mathbf{p}) \cdot \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{d}) \right) \hat{e}c where \hat{e}c is the basis vector for the color channel. 7. Volume Rendering: Use \sigma(\mathbf{p}) and \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}) in the standard volume rendering integral (e.g., front-to-back compositing) to compute the final pixel color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def evaluateplenoxeltrilinear(voxelgrid, rayorigin, raydirection, samplepoints): """ Evaluates the plenoptic function at sample points along a ray using trilinear interpolation. Args: voxelgrid: Sparse grid structure. grid.values: array of shape (N, 28), where N is number of active voxels. grid.coords: array of shape (N, 3), voxel center coordinates. grid.active: boolean mask or list of active indices. rayorigin: (3,) array, ray origin. raydirection: (3,) array, ray direction. samplepoints: (M, 3) array, M sample points along the ray. Returns: densities: (M,) array of interpolated densities. colors: (M, 3) array of interpolated colors. """ # Precompute SH basis functions for the viewing direction # Degree 2 SH has 9 basis functions. # Y(d) is a vector of shape (9,) Yd = computeshbasisdegree2(raydirection) densities = np.zeros(len(samplepoints)) colors = np.zeros((len(samplepoints), 3)) for i, p in enumerate(samplepoints): # 1. Find the 8 nearest voxel centers surrounding point p # In a dense grid, this is O(1) via integer division. # In a sparse grid, a spatial hash or k-d tree is needed. # Assuming we have a function to get the 8 neighbors and their weights: neighbors, weights = gettrilinearneighbors(p, voxelgrid) if not neighbors: densities[i] = 0.0 colors[i] = 0.0 continue # 2. Extract data from neighbors # Each neighbor has 28 values: 1 density + 27 SH coeffs (9 per channel) neighbordata = np.array([voxelgrid.values[v] for v in neighbors]) # 3. Interpolate Density # neighbordata[:, 0] is the density column densities[i] = np.dot(weights, neighbordata[:, 0]) # 4. Interpolate SH Coefficients # neighbordata[:, 1:28] contains the 27 SH coefficients # Reshape to (8 neighbors, 3 channels, 9 coeffs) shcoeffs = neighbordata[:, 1:].reshape(-1, 3, 9) # Interpolate weights for each channel # weights is shape (8,) # interpolatedsh is shape (3, 9) interpolatedsh = np.einsum('n,ncm->cm', weights, shcoeffs) # 5. Evaluate Color # Dot product of interpolated SH coeffs with SH basis Yd # Yd is shape (9,) # colorchannel = sum(interpolatedsh[c,:] Yd) colors[i, 0] = np.dot(interpolatedsh[0,:], Yd) colors[i, 1] = np.dot(interpolatedsh[1,:], Yd) colors[i, 2] = np.dot(interpolatedsh[2,:], Yd) return densities, colors def computeshbasisdegree2(direction): """ Computes the 9 spherical harmonic basis functions for degree 2 given a normalized direction vector. """ x, y, z = direction # Standard SH basis functions for l=0,1,2 # Y00 = 1/sqrt(4pi) # Y1-1, Y10, Y11 # Y2-2, Y2-1, Y20, Y21, Y22 # Note: Exact normalization constants depend on the convention used. # The sources do not specify the exact SH normalization, but standard # orthonormal SH is assumed. sqrt4pi = np.sqrt(4 np.pi) sqrt3pi = np.sqrt(3 np.pi) sqrt12pi = np.sqrt(12 np.pi) sqrt5pi = np.sqrt(5 np.pi) sqrt15pi = np.sqrt(15 np.pi) # Basis functions (unnormalized for brevity, assuming optimization handles scaling) # Or using standard orthonormal basis: # Y0 = 1 / sqrt(4pi) # Y1 = sqrt(3/4pi) z # Y2 = sqrt(3/4pi) x # Y3 = sqrt(3/4pi) y # Y4 = sqrt(15/4pi) x z # Y5 = sqrt(15/4pi) y z # Y6 = sqrt(5/16pi) (3z^2 - 1) # Y7 = sqrt(15/4pi) (x^2 - y^2) # Y8 = sqrt(15/4pi) 2xy # Using standard real SH basis for l=0,1,2 y0 = 1.0 / np.sqrt(4 np.pi) y1 = np.sqrt(3.0 / (4 np.pi)) z y2 = np.sqrt(3.0 / (4 np.pi)) x y3 = np.sqrt(3.0 / (4 np.pi)) y y4 = np.sqrt(15.0 / (4 np.pi)) x z y5 = np.sqrt(15.0 / (4 np.pi)) y z y6 = np.sqrt(5.0 / (16 np.pi)) (3 z2 - 1) y7 = np.sqrt(15.0 / (4 np.pi)) (x2 - y2) y8 = np.sqrt(15.0 / (4 np.pi)) 2 x y return np.array([y0, y1, y2, y3, y4, y5, y6, y7, y8]) def gettrilinearneighbors(point, voxelgrid): """ Finds the 8 nearest voxel centers and trilinear weights. This is a placeholder for the specific spatial indexing implementation. In a dense grid, this involves integer division of the point coordinate by the voxel size to find the grid cell, then accessing the 8 corners. """ # Implementation detail: # 1. Determine voxel size from grid bounds and resolution. # 2. Compute grid coordinates: idx = floor((point - origin) / voxelsize) # 3. Compute fractional part: frac = (point - origin) / voxelsize - idx # 4. Identify the 8 corner indices: (idxx, idxy, idxz) + (0/1, 0/1, 0/1) # 5. Retrieve voxel data for these indices. # 6. Compute weights based on frac. # If a voxel is inactive/empty, its contribution is 0. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Nearest Neighbor Instability: Using nearest neighbor interpolation creates a discontinuous model that is difficult to optimize and less stable with respect to learning rate variations. Tricubic Cost: Tricubic interpolation offers continuous and smooth approximation but incurs substantial computation with negligible quality gain compared to trilinear. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes a bounded grid. Handling unbounded scenes requires extensions like NDC or Multisphere Images (see Subtopics). Extends Plenoxels to unbounded scenes using NDC for forward-facing views or Multisphere Images for 360° scenes. Choose this when rendering outside the bounded voxel grid. (No other children listed in sources) Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Scales linearly with the number of active voxels. Each voxel stores 28 floats (1 density + 27 SH coefficients). Time: Per sample point, the cost is dominated by the lookup of 8 neighbors and the dot product of 9-element vectors. It is O(1) per sample point given efficient spatial indexing. Measured Performance: On 8 NeRF synthetic scenes, Trilinear Plenoxels at 128^3 resolution achieves PSNR 28.46, SSIM 0.926, LPIPS 0.100. Trilinear at 256^3 achieves PSNR 30.57, SSIM 0.950, LPIPS 0.065. Nearest Neighbor at 256^3 achieves PSNR 27.17, SSIM 0.914, LPIPS 0.119. Nearest Neighbor at 128^3 achieves PSNR 23.73, SSIM 0.866, LPIPS 0.176. Trilinear interpolation at 128^3 outperforms Nearest Neighbor at 256^3. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Increases effective resolution by representing sub-voxel variations; produces a continuous function approximation critical for successful optimization; more stable with respect to learning rate variations than nearest neighbor. Limitations: Tricubic interpolation, while smoother, is computationally expensive with negligible quality gain. Requires careful handling of unbounded scenes. When to Use: Use when optimizing a radiance field representation and stability/convergence is a concern. Use when higher effective resolution is needed without increasing the grid size significantly. Do not use if computational resources are extremely limited and nearest neighbor is acceptable (though quality will suffer). Plenoxels were introduced by Fridovich-Keil et al. in 2022. The method was developed as a sparse voxel-based alternative to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), aiming to eliminate the need for neural networks in radiance field representation. It builds on the concept of PlenOctrees but uses a regular grid with trilinear interpolation to define a continuous plenoptic function, contrasting with PlenOctrees which assumes constant values inside each voxel. The use of Spherical Harmonics (SH) for view-dependent color was inspired by PlenOctrees, but the trilinear interpolation of SH coefficients is a key innovation of Plenoxels. name: Unbounded Scene Handling (NDC and Background Model)
head: Background Spheres, NDC and Background Model
body: This method extends Plenoxels to real, unbounded scenes, both forward-facing and 360°. For forward-facing scenes, it uses normalized device coordinates (NDC) for the sparse voxel grid structure. For 360° scenes, it augments the sparse voxel grid foreground with a multisphere image (MSI) background model to represent distant geometry. The method adapts the discrete voxel representation based on the scene type. Inputs: Camera poses, image observations, and scene classification (forward-facing or 360°). Outputs: Radiance and density fields represented by a sparse voxel grid (foreground) and, for 360° scenes, multisphere layers (background). 1. Foreground Voxel Grid: A sparse 3D grid storing learned voxel colors and opacities or densities. Forward-facing: Coordinates are mapped to NDC space. 360°: Coordinates remain in standard Euclidean space, with the background handled separately. 2. Multisphere Image (MSI) Layers (360° only): Consists of 64 concentric spheres. Each sphere stores a 2D voxel grid indexed by spherical angles \theta and \phi via equirectangular projection. Storage: Only RGB channels (zero-order SH) are stored to conserve memory. Sparsity: Layers are stored sparsely using opacity thresholding or density thresholding. 1. Scene Classification: Determine if the scene is forward-facing or 360°. 2. Coordinate Transformation: If Forward-Facing: Use normalized device coordinates (NDC) for the sparse voxel grid structure, as defined in the original NeRF paper. If 360°: Keep coordinates in standard Euclidean space for the foreground. 3. Background Model Construction (360° only): Pre-scale the inner scene so it is approximately contained within the unit sphere. Place 64 spheres linearly in inverse radius from r=1 to r=\infty. For each sphere, voxels are indexed by spherical angles \theta and \phi using an equirectangular projection. Learn voxel colors (RGB) and opacities for each sphere layer using trilinear interpolation within and between spheres. 4. Rendering: For each pixel, cast a ray. If the ray intersects the foreground voxel grid, sample radiance and density using trilinear interpolation. If the ray extends beyond the foreground (or for 360° scenes), intersect the MSI layers. Sample the appropriate sphere based on distance, using equirectangular coordinates to index the 2D voxel grid. Number of Background Spheres: 64. Radius Distribution: Linear in inverse radius from 1 to \infty. Color Representation: RGB only (zero-order SH). Sparsity Threshold: Opacity thresholding or density thresholding is used to prune empty background layers. Precision: The pre-scaling of the inner scene to the unit sphere is critical for correct sphere placement and smooth foreground-background transitions. Memory: Storing 64 full-resolution spheres is memory-intensive, requiring sparsity pruning and zero-order SH storage to remain feasible. Forward-Facing Assumption: NDC is only valid for forward-facing scenes where the camera does not orbit 360° around the center. This variant refers to the implementation details in the Plenoxels paper for handling unbounded scenes. It distinguishes two modes: forward-facing scenes using NDC coordinates, and 360° scenes using a Multisphere Image (MSI) background model. The MSI model uses 64 spheres linearly spaced in inverse radius from 1 to \infty, with voxels warped into spheres via equirectangular projection. Colors are stored as RGB (zero-order SH) and layers are stored sparsely using opacity thresholding or density thresholding. Memory: Memory consumption is mitigated by storing only RGB channels (zero-order SH) and pruning layers via opacity thresholding or density thresholding. Strengths: Enables training on real, unbounded scenes, both forward-facing and 360°, without requiring manual bounding box estimation. Limitations: The NDC approach is restricted to forward-facing camera trajectories. This method was introduced in the Plenoxels paper (Fridovich-Keil et al., 2022) to extend radiance field representation without neural networks to real, unbounded scenes. It builds on the NDC coordinate system from the original NeRF paper and the multisphere background model from NeRF++.
