name: Intensity Interpolation
head: Anisotropic Volume Rendering Using Intensity Interpolation
body: Intensity Interpolation is an anisotropic volume rendering technique that computes the lighting intensity at a sample position between two consecutive slices by linearly interpolating the pre-computed intensity values of the voxels in those slices, rather than interpolating density values and recalculating normals for every sample. It is designed specifically for medical datasets where axial resolution is significantly higher than the resolution in the perpendicular (slice) direction, offering a speedup over density-interpolation methods without the storage overhead of pre-interpolated slices. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset with anisotropic resolution (high in X,Y, low in Z); a lighting model (ambient and diffuse); light vector L. Output: Rendered image with intensity values for samples located between original voxel slices. Data Structures: Original Voxels: Stored in a 3D grid. Each voxel v has a density value d(v) and a pre-computed normal vector N(v). Normals: Normal vectors are computed only for the original voxels in the dataset. No normals are stored for interpolated positions. Storage: The method requires no extra memory for interpolated slices, maintaining the same storage size as the original anisotropic data. Parameters: m: Interpolation weight (0 \le m \le 1) representing the position of the sample vi between voxel vk (slice k) and v{k+1} (slice k+1). The distance is divided as m: (1-m). Ka: Ambient reflection coefficient. Ia: Ambient-light intensity. Kd: Diffuse-reflection coefficient. L: Light vector. \lambda: Wavelength or scaling factor used in conventional normal calculation (contextual constant). Method Steps: 1. Pre-computation: For every original voxel v in the anisotropic volume, compute the normal vector N(v) based on its density neighbors. Compute the intensity I(v) using the lighting equation: I(v) = Ka Ia + Kd (L \cdot N(v)) Store I(v) for each original voxel. 2. Ray Casting: Cast rays through the volume. When a sample point vi falls between two adjacent slices k and k+1 (specifically between voxel vk in slice k and v{k+1} in slice k+1), determine the interpolation weight m based on the sample's position relative to the slices. 3. Intensity Interpolation: Calculate the intensity I(vi) at the sample position vi by linearly interpolating the pre-computed intensities of the two voxels: I(vi) = I(vk)(1 - m) + I(v{k+1})m Mathematical Equivalence: The method relies on the linearity of the diffuse lighting equation. Substituting the lighting equation into the interpolation formula proves that the interpolated intensity is equivalent to calculating intensity from an interpolated normal \tilde{N}(vi): \begin{aligned} I(vi) &= (Ka Ia + Kd (L \cdot N(vk)))(1 - m) + (Ka Ia + Kd (L \cdot N(v{k+1})))m \\ &= Ka Ia (1 - m + m) + Kd L \cdot (N(vk)(1 - m) + N(v{k+1})m) \\ &= Ka Ia + Kd (L \cdot \tilde{N}(vi)) \end{aligned} where the interpolated normal is: \tilde{N}(vi) = N(vk)(1 - m) + N(v{k+1})m [ S1 ] Normal Vector Comparison: The normal vector along the Z-axis for the interpolated sample using this method is: \tilde{N}Z(vi) = NZ(vk)(1 - m) + NZ(v{k+1})m In contrast, the conventional method references more samples (e.g., v{k-1}, vk, v{k+1}, v{k+2}) to calculate the normal, often using a formula such as: NZ(vi) = \frac{(d(v{k+1}) - d(v{k-1}))(1 - m) + (d(v{k+2}) - d(vk))m}{2\lambda} The intensity interpolation method uses fewer samples for normal estimation, resulting in smoother images but potentially different high-frequency behavior. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeintensityinterpolation(vk, vkplus1, m, Ka, Ia, Kd, L): """ Computes the intensity at an interpolated sample position between two voxels. Args: vk: Voxel object from slice k. Must have pre-computed intensity I(vk) and normal N(vk). vkplus1: Voxel object from slice k+1. Must have pre-computed intensity I(vkplus1) and normal N(vkplus1). m: Interpolation weight (0 to 1). Ka: Ambient reflection coefficient. Ia: Ambient light intensity. Kd: Diffuse reflection coefficient. L: Light vector. Returns: float: The interpolated intensity value I(vi). """ # Step 1: Linearly interpolate the pre-computed intensities # I(vi) = I(vk)(1 - m) + I(vk+1)m intensityinterpolated = vk.intensity (1 - m) + vkplus1.intensity m return intensityinterpolated def precomputevoxeldata(voxel): """ Pre-computes intensity and normal for an original voxel. This step is performed once per original voxel in the anisotropic volume. """ # Compute normal N(v) from density neighbors # Note: Specific density-based normal calculation is not detailed in the source # for the general case, but the source implies N(v) is computed for original voxels. # Assuming a standard gradient-based normal calculation from density d(v) # is performed here to get N(v). normal = computenormalfromdensity(voxel.density, voxel.neighbors) # Compute intensity using the lighting model # I(v) = Ka Ia + Kd (L. N(v)) dotproduct = dot(L, normal) intensity = Ka Ia + Kd dotproduct voxel.normal = normal voxel.intensity = intensity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overblurring: The method may cause overblurring in high-frequency areas. This is noted as a limitation, with the authors stating they are extending the approach to avoid it. Anisotropy Assumption: The method assumes the anisotropy is primarily along the Z-axis (slice direction). It is not designed for isotropic data or anisotropy in other directions without modification. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: The method requires no extra storage for interpolated slices, maintaining the same storage size as the original anisotropic data (e.g., 71.8 MB for airway data). This is significantly less than pre-interpolation methods (P-Interp), which require 240.8 MB for the same data. Preprocessing: No preprocessing time is required for interpolation, unlike P-Interp which took 12,684 ms for airway data. Rendering Speed: The method is faster than real-time density interpolation (R-Interp). On an 800 MHz Pentium III PC with 512 MB RAM: Colon data (512x512x141): 1.46x speedup with 0.6M samples, 1.68x with 8.1M samples, and 1.83x with 13.3M samples compared to R-Interp. Airway data: Average rendering time of 1108 ms, compared to 1486 ms for P-Interp and 1513 ms for R-Interp. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Fast rendering speed; no extra memory for interpolated slices; no preprocessing time; simpler normal calculation for interpolated samples (only uses two adjacent slices). Limitations: Potential overblurring in high-frequency areas; limited to anisotropic data with high axial resolution. When to Use: Use for medical applications with anisotropic volume datasets where the resolution in the axial plane is higher than in the perpendicular direction. Use when memory and preprocessing time are constraints, and real-time or near-real-time rendering is needed. When Not to Use: Do not use for isotropic data where the method's assumptions about anisotropy do not hold. Avoid if high-frequency detail preservation is critical and the overblurring limitation is unacceptable. Origin: The method was proposed by T. Kim, Y. Shin, and B. Shin from Seoul National University and Inha University, Korea. It was published in the paper "Anisotropic Volume Rendering Using Intensity Interpolation" in 2003. History and Development: The method was developed to address the inefficiency of conventional density interpolation methods for anisotropic medical data. Conventional methods require computing density values and normal vectors for every interpolated sample, which is computationally expensive. The intensity interpolation method simplifies this by pre-computing intensities for original voxels and interpolating those values directly. Usage: The method is primarily used in medical imaging applications for visualizing anisotropic volume data sets, such as CT scans where slice thickness is greater than in-plane resolution. Anisotropic Volume Rendering Using Intensity Interpolation, https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-45468-3163, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Plane-Based Sampling
head: Plan-Based Sampling Method, Plane-Based Sampling for Ray Casting
body: Plane-Based Sampling is a ray casting optimization technique that replaces per-voxel trilinear interpolation with a two-stage process: calculating ray-plane intersections and then interpolating between those intersection points using definite proportions. It solves the high computational cost of traditional Ray Casting Algorithms (RCA) by reducing the number of arithmetic operations required to determine optical properties at sampling points. Unlike standard methods that sample within every voxel individually, this method leverages the geometry of equidistant parallel planes to guarantee image density while significantly accelerating rendering speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset (discrete samples), a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and a sampling interval \Delta s. Output: The accumulated color and opacity for each pixel along the ray. Data Structures: The method relies on the geometric structure of the volume data, specifically treating it as a cluster of equidistant parallel planes. No additional complex data structures beyond the standard volume array are required. Steps: 1. Ray Casting: Cast a ray through the volume from back to front for each output image pixel. 2. Plane Identification: Identify the group of equidistant parallel planes in the volume data field that the ray travels through. 3. Intersection Calculation: Calculate the intersection points where the ray transacts with these parallel planes. 4. Proportional Interpolation: For sampling points located between adjacent intersection points, calculate their optical properties (color and opacity) using the formula of definite proportion and separated points, based on the properties of the intersection points. Formulas: The traditional RCA requires 17 additions and 16 multiplications per sampling point to locate the voxel and perform trilinear interpolation. The Plane-Based Sampling method replaces this with proportional interpolation between intersection points. If a sampling point S lies between two adjacent intersection points Ia and Ib with optical properties (\mathbf{c}a, \alphaa) and (\mathbf{c}b, \alphab), its properties are calculated as: \mathbf{c}S = \mathbf{c}a + \frac{d(S, Ia)}{d(Ia, Ib)} (\mathbf{c}b - \mathbf{c}a) \alphaS = \alphaa + \frac{d(S, Ia)}{d(Ia, Ib)} (\alphab - \alphaa) where d(\cdot, \cdot) denotes the Euclidean distance along the ray. Parameters: Sampling Interval (\Delta s): The distance between adjacent parallel planes. The method requires this distance to not far surpass the desired sampling interval to guarantee image density. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Plane Spacing: If the distance between adjacent parallel planes is significantly larger than the desired sampling interval, the method fails to guarantee image density, potentially leading to aliasing or loss of detail. Precision: The method relies on accurate intersection calculations, and standard floating-point precision issues in ray-plane intersection may apply. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def planebasedsampling(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, planespacing, numplanes): """ rayorigin: 3D vector (x, y, z) raydirection: 3D vector (x, y, z), normalized volumedata: 3D array with bounds.min/max and interpolate(point) method planespacing: float, distance between adjacent parallel planes numplanes: int, number of parallel planes in the cluster Returns: accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity """ # Step 1: Cast ray from back to front tmin, tmax = computerayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata) if tmin > tmax: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 frontopacity = 1.0 # Step 2 & 3: Identify parallel planes and calculate intersections # Assuming planes are aligned with the Z-axis planenormal = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) intersectionpoints = [] for i in range(numplanes): planeoriginz = i planespacing planeorigin = (0.0, 0.0, planeoriginz) denom = dot(planenormal, raydirection) if abs(denom) > 1e-8: tintersect = dot(planenormal, (planeorigin - rayorigin)) / denom if tmin <= tintersect <= tmax: point = rayorigin + tintersect raydirection color, opacity = volumedata.interpolate(point) intersectionpoints.append({'t': tintersect, 'color': color, 'opacity': opacity}) # Sort intersection points from back to front (decreasing t) intersectionpoints.sort(key=lambda k: k['t'], reverse=True) # Step 4: Interpolate between intersection points for i in range(len(intersectionpoints) - 1): p1 = intersectionpoints[i] p2 = intersectionpoints[i+1] distsegment = p2['t'] - p1['t'] if distsegment <= 0: continue # Determine sampling points within this segment based on planespacing numsamples = max(1, int(distsegment / planespacing)) for j in range(numsamples): ratio = j / numsamples # Definite proportion interpolation colorsample = lerpvec3(p1['color'], p2['color'], ratio) opacitysample = lerpscalar(p1['opacity'], p2['opacity'], ratio) # Front-to-back compositing alpha = opacitysample color = colorsample accumulatedcolor = ( accumulatedcolor[0] + frontopacity color[0] alpha, accumulatedcolor[1] + frontopacity color[1] alpha, accumulatedcolor[2] + frontopacity color[2] alpha) accumulatedopacity = accumulatedopacity + frontopacity alpha frontopacity = frontopacity (1.0 - alpha) if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def lerpvec3(a, b, t): return (a[0] + t(b[0]-a[0]), a[1] + t(b[1]-a[1]), a[2] + t(b[2]-a[2])) def lerpscalar(a, b, t): return a + t(b-a) def computerayboxintersection(origin, direction, volumedata): tmin, tmax = 0.0, float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < volumedata.bounds.min[i] or origin[i] > volumedata.bounds.max[i]: return float('inf'), 0.0 else: t1 = (volumedata.bounds.min[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (volumedata.bounds.max[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return tmin, tmax The baseline method that Plane-Based Sampling improves upon. It performs trilinear interpolation for every sampling point, requiring 17 additions and 16 multiplications per point. A related approach that replaces sampling points with intersection points along three groups of parallel planes along orthometric axes. However, it cannot guarantee image density when the distance between adjacent parallel planes far surpasses the sampling interval. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of arithmetic operations per sampling point compared to traditional trilinear interpolation. The traditional RCA takes 17 additions and 16 multiplications per point. The Plane-Based Sampling method is described as "faster" and improves rendering speed by over three times. The exact operation count is not given. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method does not appear to require additional large data structures beyond the volume data itself. Measured Performance: In the context of fast reconstruction of 3D biomedical models from sequential images, the method improves rendering speed by over three times compared with the conventional algorithm while maintaining image quality. Strengths: Significantly faster rendering speed; reduces computational load by using fewer intersection points and proportional division; maintains image quality. Limitations: If the distance between adjacent parallel planes is significantly larger than the desired sampling interval, the method fails to guarantee image density, potentially leading to aliasing or loss of detail. When to use: When fast reconstruction of 3D biomedical models from sequential images is required and the volume data can be effectively represented by equidistant parallel planes. When not to use: When high image density is critical and the plane spacing cannot be kept close to the sampling interval, as this leads to aliasing. The method was proposed to improve the traditional Ray Casting Algorithm (RCA) for the fast reconstruction of three-dimensional biomedical models from sequential images. It addresses the high proportion of time spent on sampling optical properties (about 39% of rendering time) in traditional RCA. The work cites Qian et al. [11] as prior art that used intersection points along three groups of parallel planes but failed to guarantee image density under certain conditions. Plane-Based Sampling for Ray Casting Algorithm in Sequential Medical Images, https://doi.org/10.1155/2013/874517, fetched 2026-10-25

name: Post-Interpolative Importance Function
body: The Post-Interpolative Importance Function is a visibility optimization technique for Monte Carlo volume rendering that maps volume data to a discrete set of importance values after interpolation, rather than before. It solves the problem of accurately visualizing small, thin structures (e.g., bone periosteum and endosteum) which are often lost or blurred by pre-interpolative importance functions due to smoothing artifacts. Unlike pre-interpolative methods that apply importance to continuous scalar values, this method creates a step function along the ray, preserving fine details and eliminating the need for smoothing discontinuities. The method defines the importance k(t) along a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} as a piecewise constant step function. This allows the renderer to identify segments of the ray with uniform importance, enabling efficient unbiased estimation for visibility optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray parameter t, volume data (scalar or segmentation), optional spatial attributes. Output: Importance value k(t) \in [0, 1]. Data Structures: The importance function is represented by a set of n mutually exclusive segments Ai along the ray, each associated with a distinct importance value \alphai. n: Number of segments (typically n=1 for binary optimization, or small for multi-class). \alphai: Importance value for segment i, where \alphai \in [0, 1]. Ai: Interval of t values defining the spatial extent of segment i. Formula: The importance function k(t) is defined as: k(t) = \sum{i=0}^n \alphai \chi{Ai}(t) where \chi{Ai}(t) is the indicator function for segment Ai: \chiA(t) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } t \in A \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Here, n is the number of segments, \alphai are the distinct importance values, and Ai are the mutually exclusive segments along the ray. Steps: 1. Interpolate Volume Data: Sample the volume data V(\mathbf{p}) at the query position \mathbf{p} = r(t) using trilinear interpolation and a box filter. This yields a continuous scalar value used for importance evaluation. 2. Determine Segment Boundaries: Identify the intervals Ai along the ray where the importance criteria are met. This can be done by: Attribute-based: Mapping the interpolated volume data (e.g., extinction) to importance values. Spatial/Segmentation-based: Using a pre-computed signed distance field (SDF) from segmentation data. Evaluate the SDF at \mathbf{p} and compare against a threshold (e.g., 0.5) to determine if the point belongs to an important region. 3. Assign Importance Values: Assign the discrete importance value \alphai to each segment Ai. Commonly, n=1 is sufficient, resulting in a binary importance map where \alphai \in \{0, 1\}. Values less than 1 (e.g., 0.75) can be used but may lead to inferior visibility compared to binary 0/1 assignments. 4. Evaluate k(t): For a given t, return the \alphai corresponding to the segment Ai that contains t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def postinterpolativeimportance(t, rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, sdfgrid, threshold=0.5): # 1. Query position along ray p = rayorigin + t raydirection # 2. Interpolate volume data at p using trilinear interpolation and box filter volumevalue = trilinearsample(volumedata, p) # 3. Evaluate importance criteria # Source specifies SDF thresholding as the primary example sdfvalue = trilinearsample(sdfgrid, p) if sdfvalue < threshold: alpha = 1.0 else: alpha = 0.0 # Attribute-based mapping (e.g., extinction) is mentioned but not detailed in sources # alpha = mapextinctiontoimportance(volumevalue) # 4. Return k(t) = alpha for the current segment return alpha Parameters: n: Number of distinct importance segments. Typically n=1 (binary) is sufficient for visibility optimization. \alphai: Importance values. Typically \{0, 1\}. Threshold: For SDF-based importance, a threshold (e.g., 0.5) is used to define boundaries. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Importance < 1: Using importance values strictly between 0 and 1 (e.g., 0.75) can lead to inferior visibility in the final visualization. It is recommended to use binary values (0 and 1) for most cases. Smooth Approximation: The step-function nature means smooth importance functions (e.g., Gaussian regions of interest) can only be approximated, not exactly represented. Discretization Artifacts: While it preserves details better than pre-interpolative methods, the step function may introduce hard edges in importance if the underlying data or segmentation is noisy. Applies importance to the continuous scalar value before interpolation, which fails to accurately discern small regions due to smoothing. It is chosen when smooth importance gradients are acceptable, but is not recommended for thin structures. See Interpolation Methods. Generates spatial attributes for importance determination via boundary criteria. It is chosen when segmentation-based spatial attributes are required. See Space Warping (Log+Warp) for related spatial transformations. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, assuming constant-time evaluation of the importance map (e.g., SDF lookup or scalar thresholding). Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the importance map (e.g., SDF grid or scalar volume). Performance: In the cited evaluation, rendering with 2000 samples per pixel and post-interpolative importance took 47.5 seconds for a complex scene (human pelvis). Strengths: Preserves fine details of small structures (e.g., bone layers) that pre-interpolative methods miss. Eliminates the need for smoothing discontinuities. Limitations: Cannot represent smooth importance gradients exactly. Importance values < 1 may reduce visibility quality. When to Use: When visualizing thin, high-contrast structures (e.g., periosteum, endosteum) where pre-interpolative smoothing causes loss of detail. When binary visibility optimization is sufficient. When Not to Use: When smooth, gradual importance transitions are required (e.g., soft region-of-interest highlighting). The Post-Interpolative Importance Function was introduced in the context of view-dependent visibility optimization for Monte Carlo volume visualization. It addresses limitations of previous importance sampling techniques that applied importance before interpolation, leading to inaccuracies in small regions. The method builds on the concept of using signed distance fields for boundary detection, similar to Green [Gre07], but applies the importance decision after the interpolation step. View‐Dependent Visibility Optimization for Monte Carlo Volume Visualization, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70064, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Sampling and Integration Schemes
body: Sampling and Integration Schemes define the computational framework for sampling volumetric data along camera rays and aggregating those samples into final pixel colors. This family encompasses methods that determine where to sample the volume (stochastic vs. deterministic spacing) and how to aggregate those samples (compositing, projection, or approximation). It is distinguished from Interpolation and Sampling Techniques by focusing on the integration logic and sampling distribution rather than the spatial interpolation kernel. Builds on Interpolation and Sampling Techniques, which covers the query positioning, kernel/weight application, and coordinate transformation common to all children. A stochastic approach that replaces uniform spatial sampling with probabilistic distance sampling and null-collision scattering events. It is chosen when simulating complex light transport phenomena like multiple scattering in heterogeneous media, where deterministic methods are computationally prohibitive. Defines the reduction logic that maps a sequence of discretized ray samples to a final pixel output via deterministic, grid-aligned traversal. It is chosen for standard direct volume ray casting where order-dependent integration (e.g., front-to-back compositing) is required. Accelerates rendering by replacing on-the-fly evaluation of non-linear transfer functions with pre-computed lookup tables. It is chosen to eliminate aliasing artifacts caused by low sampling frequencies and to decouple transfer function frequency from sampling rate. Resolves the order-dependence of sampling operations required for numerical solutions of integrals in volumetric lighting. It is chosen when illumination calculations depend on the specific sequence of samples relative to light sources, using iterative processing or precomputation. The family originates from the fundamental volume rendering equation formulated by Williams et al.. Early implementations relied on uniform sampling and front-to-back compositing. Monte Carlo methods were adapted from photon mapping techniques to handle participating media. Pre-integration was introduced to address the "missing peak" problem in transfer functions. Levoy, M., & Williams, J. (1973). Linear methods for volume rendering. Krivine, J. (2012). GPU-based Monte Carlo Volume Rendering. Krivine, J. (2012). Photon Tracing for Volume Rendering.

name: Monte Carlo Volume Rendering
head: Monte Carlo Scattering (MCS), Stochastic Volume Rendering
body: Monte Carlo Volume Rendering is a stochastic approach to volumetric visualization that avoids uniform sampling grids, instead using random number generation to determine scattering events and integration steps. It solves the problem of artifacts in homogeneous materials and the computational cost of dense uniform sampling by adaptively concentrating samples in non-homogeneous regions or along light paths. Unlike deterministic ray casting which samples fixed intervals, this method traces photon paths through participating media, accumulating radiance and transmittance estimates via multiple bounces and null-collision absorption/scattering events. The method implements two primary variants: a direct ray-casting approach using exponential distance sampling and a photon-marching approach using null-collision Monte Carlo. Both require unprojecting screen coordinates to world-space rays and intersecting them with the volume bounding box. Inputs: Volume data: 3D texture V containing density/opacity (alpha) and color (RGB). Environment map: 2D texture for background/lighting. Camera parameters: Inverse Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix for ray unprojection. Volume parameters: Extinction coefficient (\sigmat), albedo (\omega), scattering bias (g), majorant ratio. Rendering parameters: Maximum bounces (Nb), steps per ray (Ns), random seed offset. Outputs: Accumulated color buffer (RGBA). (Photon variant) Photon state buffers: position, direction, transmittance, radiance, bounce count, sample count. Photon State (Photon Variant): position: vec3 (world space). direction: vec3 (normalized). transmittance: vec3 (accumulated transmission). radiance: vec3 (accumulated emitted/scattered light). bounces: uint (scattering events). samples: uint (integration steps). Random Number Generator (RNG): A hash-based RNG is used to generate deterministic pseudo-random numbers from pixel coordinates and frame offsets. rand(p) = fract( (cos(M \times p)x, sin(M \times p)y) \times D) Where M is a 2 \times 2 constant matrix, D is a constant vec2, and p is the input coordinate (e.g., fragment position + offset). uSigmaMax: Maximum extinction coefficient (majorant). Typical: positive float representing max volume density. uExtinction: Total extinction coefficient \sigmat. uAbsorptionCoefficient: Base absorption multiplier. uScatteringCoefficient: Base scattering multiplier. uScatteringBias: Anisotropy parameter g for Henyey-Greenstein phase function. Default: 0. uMajorant: Majorant density \sigma{maj}. Typically \sigma{maj} \ge \sigmat. Default: 2. uMaxBounces: Maximum scattering bounces. Default: 8. uSteps: Integration steps per photon trace. Default: varies. uAlphaCorrection: Scaling factor for sampled alpha values. uOffset: Random offset uniform for temporal anti-aliasing. This variant traces a single ray per pixel, stochastically determining scattering points. 1. Ray Initialization: Unproject screen coordinates to get ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction endpoint \mathbf{d}{end}. Compute ray direction \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{d}{end} - \mathbf{o}. Intersect ray with volume bounding box to get entry t{min} and exit t{max}. If no intersection, sample environment map and return. Set ray segment start \mathbf{p}{start} = \mathbf{o} + t{min}\mathbf{d} and max distance L = t{max} - t{min}. 2. Stochastic Distance Sampling: Initialize distance dist = 0. Compute inverse majorant invSigmaMax = 1.0 / \sigma{maj}. Loop: Generate random number r1 \in 0, 1). Update distance: dist \leftarrow dist - \ln(1 - r1) \times invSigmaMax. If dist > L, break loop (ray exits volume). Sample volume color \mathbf{C}{vol} and alpha \alpha at position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}{start} + dist \cdot \mathbf{d}. Check scattering condition: If r2 < \alpha \times uAlphaCorrection \times invSigmaMax, break loop (scattering event occurred). 3. [Scattering and Integration: If dist > L, sample environment map in direction \mathbf{d} and return color. Sample diffuse color \mathbf{C}{diffuse} = \mathbf{C}{vol} at \mathbf{p}. Sample environment map \mathbf{C}{light} in direction \mathbf{d} (or use light sources). Compute transmittance T from \mathbf{p} to volume exit in direction \mathbf{d} using sampleTransmittance (see below). Final color: \mathbf{C}{out} = \mathbf{C}{diffuse} \times \mathbf{C}{light} \times T. 4. Transmittance Sampling (sampleTransmittance): Initialize T = 1.0. Loop: Generate random r1. Update dist \leftarrow dist - \ln(1 - r1) \times invSigmaMax. If dist > L{segment}, break. Sample volume alpha \alpha at current position. Update transmittance: T \leftarrow T \times (1 - \alpha \times uAlphaCorrection \times invSigmaMax). Return T. 5. Render Accumulation: To converge, accumulate frames over time: C{avg} = C{avg} + \frac{C{new} - C{avg}}{N{frame}} Where N{frame} is the current frame number. This variant traces photons through the volume, handling absorption and scattering via null-collision Monte Carlo. 1. Photon Initialization: Unproject screen position to ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Intersect with volume cube to get entry t{min}. Set photon position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t{min}\mathbf{d}. Initialize transmittance \mathbf{T} = (1, 1, 1), radiance \mathbf{L} = (0, 0, 0), bounces = 0, samples = 0. 2. Photon Loop (for i = 0 to uSteps): Generate random number r1. Compute step size t = -\ln(r1) / \sigma{maj}. Update position: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. Sample volume at \mathbf{p} to get color \mathbf{C}{vol} and alpha \alpha. Compute local coefficients: \mu{abs} = \alpha \times uAbsorptionCoefficient \mu{sca} = \alpha \times uScatteringCoefficient \mu{null} = \sigma{maj} - \mu{abs} - \mu{sca} \sigma{maj} = \mu{abs} + \mu{sca} + |\mu{null}|. Compute probabilities: P{null} = |\mu{null}| / \sigma{maj} P{abs} = \mu{abs} / \sigma{maj} P{sca} = \mu{sca} / \sigma{maj}. Check bounds: If \mathbf{p} is outside [0,1]^3, sample environment map in direction \mathbf{d}, add to radiance estimate \mathbf{L}, increment samples, reset photon, and continue to next step. Check collision type using random r2: If r2 < P{abs} + P{sca}: Update transmittance \mathbf{T} \leftarrow \mathbf{T} \times \mathbf{C}{vol} \times (\mu{sca} / (\sigma{maj} P{sca})). Sample new direction using Henyey-Greenstein with bias g. Increment bounces. If bounces > uMaxBounces, terminate. Else (Null Collision): Update transmittance \mathbf{T} \leftarrow \mathbf{T} \times (\mu{null} / (\sigma{maj} P{null})). Store photon state in output buffers. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def montecarlovolumerender(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, envmap, sigmamax, alphacorrection, seedoffset): # 1. Intersect with volume (standard slab method) tmin, tmax = rayboxintersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if tmin >= tmax: return sampleenvironmentmap(raydirection, envmap) raylength = tmax - tmin pstart = rayorigin + tmin raydirection invsigmamax = 1.0 / sigmamax # 2. Stochastic Sampling dist = 0.0 rngstate = hashseed(rayorigin, seedoffset) while dist < raylength: r1 = nextrandom(rngstate) # Exponential distance sampling dist -= log(1.0 - r1) invsigmamax if dist >= raylength: break # Sample volume at current position p = pstart + dist raydirection volsample = samplevolume(volumetexture, p) alpha = volsample.a alphacorrection # Check for scattering event r2 = nextrandom(rngstate) if r2 < alpha invsigmamax: break # 3. If no scattering within volume, return background if dist >= raylength: return sampleenvironmentmap(raydirection, envmap) # 4. Compute scattered radiance pscatter = pstart + dist raydirection diffusecolor = volsample.rgb # Sample light/environment lightcolor = sampleenvironmentmap(raydirection, envmap) # Compute transmittance to exit transmittance = sampletransmittance(pscatter, raydirection, tmax, volumetexture, sigmamax, alphacorrection, rngstate) return diffusecolor lightcolor transmittance def sampletransmittance(pstart, direction, tmax, volumetexture, sigmamax, alphacorrection, rngstate): # Calculate remaining distance to exit texitlocal = intersectboxlocal(pstart, direction, tmax) if texitlocal <= 0: return 1.0 invsigmamax = 1.0 / sigmamax transmittance = 1.0 dist = 0.0 while dist < texitlocal: r1 = nextrandom(rngstate) dist -= log(1.0 - r1) invsigmamax if dist >= texitlocal: break p = pstart + dist direction volsample = samplevolume(volumetexture, p) alpha = volsample.a alphacorrection transmittance = (1.0 - alpha invsigmamax) return transmittance def rayboxintersect(origin, direction): tmin = -1e9 tmax = 1e9 for i in range(3): if abs(direction[i]) > 1e-8: t1 = (0.0 - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (1.0 - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) else: if origin[i] < 0.0 or origin[i] > 1.0: return (1e9, -1e9) return (tmin, tmax) def hashseed(p, offset): M = [[2.3, 1.7], [1.1, 3.3]] D = [0.5, 0.7] x = cos(M[0][0]p.x + M[0][1]p.y) y = sin(M[1][0]p.x + M[1][1]p.y) return (x D[0] + offset, y D[1] + offset) def nextrandom(state): return fract(state[0] + state[1]) Not given in the sources. name: Ray Traversal and Integration Schemes
body: Ray Traversal and Integration Schemes define the aggregation logic applied to voxel samples collected along a ray to produce a final pixel value. While Ray Marching and Discretization determines where to sample, these schemes determine how to combine those samples. They are distinguished from standard front-to-back alpha compositing by their ability to perform non-compositional aggregations (such as Maximum or Average) or to simplify the compositing process for specific visualization goals like X-ray simulation. Builds on Interpolation and Sampling Techniques, which covers the query positioning, kernel/weight application, and coordinate transformation common to all children. Iterative numerical algorithm approximating the volume integral via discrete steps and alpha compositing. Chosen for real-time performance on GPUs. Fundamental control structure iterating over pixels to generate rays. Chosen for correct perspective projection and single-pass execution. Direct volume rendering with strict filtering on SOS, Attenuation, and Reflection values, and HSV color mapping. Chosen for specific scientific visualization pipelines requiring component-based filtering. Computes scalar physical quantities (e.g., column density) via direct line-of-sight integration. Chosen for solar physics to avoid chromospheric artifacts. Stochastic framework using Woodcock tracking for light attenuation and shadows. Chosen for photo-realistic rendering with complex lighting and depth-of-field. Defines aggregation logic (e.g., Maximum, Average) for voxel samples. Chosen for non-compositional visualizations or X-ray simulation. Single-pass GPU method managing traversal and compositing state explicitly. Chosen for deterministic, uniform step-size rendering without surface extraction. Dynamically splits rays to maintain sampling density under perspective divergence. Chosen to prevent aliasing in distant volume slices. Emits cones from the camera to sample isotropic spheres, avoiding distance-agnostic aliasing. Chosen for neural field rendering with pre-filtered encodings. Two-pass geometry-based traversal using back-face depth buffering. Chosen for parallel implementations where entry/exit points are determined via geometry. A strategy to optimize speed while reducing artifacts by varying segment length based on contribution to ray color. Uses smaller segments when the contribution to the ray color is large, and longer segments when the contribution is low. Originating from the foundational work on direct volume rendering in the late 1980s and early 1990s, ray traversal methods evolved from simple fixed-step marching to adaptive and stochastic techniques. The introduction of GPU fragment shaders enabled real-time image-order rendering loops. name: Ray Marching and Discretization
head: Front-to-Back Accumulation, Ray Marching (Core Algorithm), Ray Marching for Volume Rendering, Volume Ray Marching (Basic)
body: Ray marching is an iterative numerical algorithm used to approximate the volume rendering equation by casting rays from the camera, taking discrete steps along the ray, querying volumetric properties (density, color), and accumulating these samples via alpha compositing. It solves the problem of rendering 3D scalar fields or implicit surfaces by discretizing the continuous integral into a sequence of sample points. Unlike fixed-step traversal which samples uniformly, advanced variants adapt step sizes based on distance estimators to handle sparse or implicit data efficiently. It is distinguished from Discrete Ray Tracing by its ability to use variable step sizes and from Fixed Step Ray Marching by its general iterative framework that supports both uniform and adaptive stepping. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), volume data (3D texture or procedural function), transfer function (color/opacity mapping), and parameters (step size, max samples, bounds). Outputs: Final pixel color C{out} and accumulated alpha A{out}. Data Structures: Volume Texture: 3D texture storing scalar values (density/extinction). Layout is typically [0, 1]^3 normalized coordinates. Colormap/Transfer Function: 1D or 2D texture mapping scalar values to RGBA. Accumulators: fragColor (vec3, RGB), fragAlpha (float, A). Initialized to 0. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Calculate the ray origin and direction in the volume's local coordinate system. If using a fullscreen quad, compute the world position of the far plane using the inverse projection-view matrix: \mathbf{p}{far} = \text{inv}(P \cdot V) \cdot [2u-1, 2v-1, 1, 1]^T. Ray direction: \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}{far} - \mathbf{o}). Transform \mathbf{o} and \mathbf{d} into model space if the volume is not at the world origin: \mathbf{o}{model} = M^{-1}\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}{model} = \text{normalize}(M^{-1}\mathbf{d}). 2. Bounding Box Intersection: Determine the entry (t{near}) and exit (t{far}) points of the ray with the volume's bounding box. Compute t{min} = (\mathbf{boxMin} - \mathbf{o}) / \mathbf{d} and t{max} = (\mathbf{boxMax} - \mathbf{o}) / \mathbf{d}. t{near} = \max(\max(t{min}.x, t{min}.y), t{min}.z). t{far} = \min(\min(t{max}.x, t{max}.y), t{max}.z). If t{near} > t{far} or t{far} < 0, the ray misses the volume; return background color. 3. Step Calculation: Determine the step size \Delta s. Fixed Step: \Delta s = \frac{\text{length}(\mathbf{exit} - \mathbf{entry})}{N{steps}}, where N{steps} is a constant (e.g., 64 or 300). Adaptive Step: \Delta s = \max(\Delta s{min}, f(\mathbf{p})), where f(\mathbf{p}) is a distance estimator (e.g., SDF value). 4. Marching Loop: Iterate from t = t{near} to t = t{far} (or until early termination). Position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. Sampling: Query the volume at \mathbf{p} to get scalar value v. If procedural: v = \text{sampleFunction}(\mathbf{p}). If texture: v = \text{textureLod}(volume, \mathbf{p}{norm}, 0).r. Transfer Function: Map v to color c and opacity \alpha. \alpha = 1 - e^{-\sigmae \Delta s} (Beer-Lambert), where \sigmae is the extinction coefficient or scaled sampled value. c = \text{textureLod}(colormap, v, 0).rgb. Compositing (Front-to-Back): C{out} = C{in} + c \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - A{in}). A{out} = A{in} + \alpha \cdot (1 - A{in}). Where C{in}, A{in} are the accumulated color and alpha from previous steps. Early Termination: If A{out} > \tau{term} (e.g., 0.95 or 0.99), break loop. 5. Output: Write C{out} and A{out} to the framebuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, colormap, steplength, maxalpha=0.99, maxsteps=300): """ rayorigin: vec3, camera position in model space raydirection: vec3, normalized direction in model space volumetexture: 3D texture object colormap: 1D/2D texture object steplength: float, distance between samples maxalpha: float, threshold for early termination maxsteps: int, hard limit for loop iterations """ def isinsidevolume(pos): return 0.0 <= pos.x <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= pos.y <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= pos.z <= 1.0 def normalizetotexturecoords(pos): return pos # Assumes input is already in [0,1]^3 acccolor = vec3(0.0) accalpha = 0.0 position = rayorigin for i in range(maxsteps): if not isinsidevolume(position): break normpos = normalizetotexturecoords(position) density = texture(volumetexture, normpos).r sigmae = density alpha = 1.0 - exp(-sigmae steplength) color = texture(colormap, vec2(density, 0.5)).rgb contribution = color alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor += contribution accalpha += alpha (1.0 - accalpha) if accalpha >= maxalpha: break position += raydirection steplength return acccolor, accalpha Parameters: steplength: Controls resolution. Smaller values increase quality but reduce performance. Typical value: 1/256 or derived from volume diagonal. maxalpha: Early termination threshold. Default 0.95–0.99. MAXSTEPS: Hard limit to prevent infinite loops. Default 64–300. Edge Cases: Ray Miss: If the ray does not intersect the bounding box, return background immediately. Empty Space: If density is 0, alpha is 0, and compositing has no effect. Early termination helps skip large empty regions. Precision: Floating point errors in position accumulation can cause artifacts. Using relative step sizes or re-normalizing position periodically is recommended. The Discrete Volume Rendering Integral (VRI) is the fundamental numerical approximation used in direct volume ray casting to compute the color and opacity of a pixel by integrating the continuous Volume Rendering Equation (VRE) along a camera ray. It solves the problem of rendering 3D scalar or vector fields by discretizing the ray into fixed or variable segments, sampling the volume data at each step, and compositing the results front-to-back. It sets itself apart from analytical methods like Self-Attenuation Integral Evaluation by relying on Riemann sums rather than closed-form solutions, and from higher-order integration schemes like Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) Integration by assuming constant density and color within each segment (Zero Order Integration). The Exponential Approximation Method (EAM) is a direct volume ray casting technique that approximates the continuous light attenuation integral using discrete steps and an exponential transmittance model. It differs from standard linear alpha compositing by scaling sampled alpha values by a step-size-dependent correction factor, allowing larger steps while approximating exponential decay. It is typically chosen when performance is prioritized over exact physical accuracy, or when the volume data is sparse enough that early ray termination provides significant speedup. This method renders a 3D volume defined by a density texture by accumulating scattered light along a ray, utilizing the Henyey-Greenstein phase function to model anisotropic scattering and shadow rays for self-shadowing. It distinguishes itself from standard front-to-back volume rendering by explicitly incorporating directional light transport through the Henyey-Greenstein phase function, allowing for the visualization of forward or backward scattering effects in participating media. Ray Tracing (Binary Objects) is an image-order rendering technique for visualizing surfaces contained within binary volumetric data by determining only the first intersection points with a surface. It solves the problem of displaying opaque surfaces in binary volumes without requiring explicit boundary detection or hidden-surface removal algorithms. Unlike methods that composite translucent data or require gradient estimation from multi-valued volumes, this method treats the volume as a set of opaque objects where light stops at the first surface hit. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as Discrete Ray Tracing which uses voxel connectivity, and Fixed Step Ray Marching which integrates density, by its exclusive focus on the binary "first-hit" condition using zero-order interpolation. Discrete Ray Tracing (DRT) is a volume rendering technique that approximates continuous viewing rays with discrete, voxel-connected paths (voxelization) to traverse a 3D scalar field. Unlike methods that rely on geometric primitives or acceleration structures, DRT directly samples the voxel grid using a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) or Bresenham-like algorithm, guaranteeing that voxels are visited in the exact order of intersection. This approach limits intersection tests to Pythagorean complexity rather than cubic, ensuring the first opaque voxel found is the closest. It is distinguished from Fixed Step Ray Marching by its adaptive step size (always moving to the next voxel boundary) and from Exponential Approximation Method by its explicit traversal of every voxel along the ray path without skipping. Fixed Step Ray Marching is a direct volume rendering technique that integrates the volume rendering equation along camera rays using a constant step size, applying exponential absorption and gradient-based shading to fog-like participating media. It uniformly samples the ray, which simplifies implementation but requires tuning of stepsize to balance visual quality and performance. Unlike Exponential Approximation Method, which may use analytical approximations for transmittance, this method explicitly computes transmittance per step using the Beer-Lambert law. Per-primitive ray sampling is a rendering strategy where each geometric primitive (specifically ellipsoids) independently updates only the ray segments it intersects, avoiding redundant parameter loads and enabling accurate Transfer Function (TF) mapping by accumulating contributions in 3D space. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Fixed Step Ray Marching and Volume Ray Casting by organizing computation around primitives rather than rays, which eliminates the need for explicit per-tile sorting required in 2D rasterization because contributions accumulate in depth order as each ray segment corresponds to a discrete depth interval. Directional Derivative Diffuse Lighting is an approximation for diffuse lighting in volumetric raymarching that estimates light scattering by comparing density at the current point and an offset point in the light direction, avoiding the need for normal calculation. It sets itself apart from standard surface raymarching normals by requiring only two density samples instead of multiple gradient estimates, making it significantly cheaper for the resource-intensive volumetric loop. Specific Material and Geometry Rendering is a family of techniques that define how volumetric data is mapped to optical properties (density, color, emission) and how specific geometric constraints or material compositions are handled during ray traversal. It solves the problem of translating abstract simulation data or procedural definitions into physically plausible or artistically controlled radiance contributions within the volume rendering integral. It sets itself apart from general sampling schemes by focusing on the definition of material properties [5335-material-parameter-setting.md], the handling of complex global geometries like planetary cloud shells [3480-procedural-volumetric-cloud-rendering.md], or the specific compositing of multi-material scalar fields. DOSRender is a depth-ordered, slice-based volume rendering technique that accumulates color and occlusion along a ray while simultaneously tracking semantic instance and group IDs for segmentation. It distinguishes itself from standard front-to-back ray casting by integrating precomputed occlusion samples and hierarchical group membership buffers directly into the accumulation pass, allowing for efficient occlusion-aware rendering and semantic data extraction in a single pass. Light Transmittance Marching is a technique to compute physically accurate lighting in a volume by casting a secondary raymarch from each sample point on the primary view ray towards the light source to calculate absorbed light (transmittance). It solves the problem of volumetric occlusion, where light passing through the volume before reaching a sample point is attenuated by the medium itself. Unlike Front-to-Back Volume Rendering, which typically assumes uniform or pre-computed lighting, this method dynamically computes the light energy arriving at each sample point by accounting for the density along the path to the light. This method performs direct volume ray casting by sampling a 3D volume stored in a 2D texture atlas, computing surface normals via finite differences of sampled densities, and applying diffuse shading. It stops sampling when a high-density threshold is reached or the ray exits the bounding box. It is distinguished from standard ray marching by its specific use of a 2D texture atlas for 3D data storage and the explicit calculation of gradients for lighting, rather than relying solely on transmittance accumulation or pre-computed normals. Sphere-Guided Volume Rendering is a sampling strategy for neural implicit surface reconstruction that uses a trainable cloud of spheres to filter ray-marching samples. It solves the problem of inefficient sample distribution in standard volume rendering, where samples are often wasted in empty space or fail to capture thin geometry. Unlike fixed-step ray marching or methods relying on greedy optimization, this approach guides sampling by intersecting rays with a coarse surface approximation, ensuring samples are concentrated near the estimated surface. This improves sample efficiency and helps the implicit function converge to a better optimum. Ray marching with depth testing visualizes volumes by casting rays from the camera and sampling at discrete steps along each ray's path, traversing a voxel grid and applying transfer functions to map raw values to color and opacity. It solves the problem of correct occlusion between volumetric effects and solid geometry by integrating manual depth buffer comparisons into the ray marching loop. This method sets itself apart from sibling techniques like Fixed Step Ray Marching by explicitly discarding samples that lie behind opaque objects, thereby preventing visual artifacts where volume appears in front of or behind solid geometry incorrectly. Plane-Based Layered Volume Rendering is a direct volume ray casting technique that approximates continuous volume integration by sampling a discrete set of parallel planes aligned with the camera view direction. It differs from standard fixed-step ray marching by restricting samples to specific geometric planes, which allows for optional exclusion plane testing to skip empty or occluded regions, thereby reducing unnecessary texture lookups and shading computations. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is the number of pixels and P is the number of steps per ray. Performance scales linearly with the number of steps. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Fixed-step ray marching is predictable and GPU-friendly due to uniform loop lengths. Adaptive ray marching (e.g., sphere tracing) can be significantly faster in sparse volumes by skipping empty space. Strengths: Simple to implement, supports real-time performance on GPUs, handles implicit and procedural volumes naturally. Limitations: Fixed-step methods can be aliasing-prone or inefficient in sparse volumes. Early termination can miss subtle transparent details. Low simulation resolution causes blocky artifacts. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering, neural graphics (NeRF), SDF rendering. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Ray marching was introduced as an efficient method for volume rendering, extending the concept of ray casting to iterative sampling. It is widely used in modern differentiable rendering libraries like Jrender and GPU-based implementations. The technique is fundamental to rendering Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). Variants like sphere tracing were introduced for antialiased rendering of height fields and extended to general implicit volumes. name: Discrete Volume Rendering Integral
head: Discrete Volume Rendering Equation, Discretized Volume Rendering Integral, Levoy's Volume Rendering Integral, VRI
body: The Discrete Volume Rendering Integral (VRI) is the fundamental numerical approximation used in direct volume ray casting to compute the color and opacity of a pixel by integrating the continuous Volume Rendering Equation (VRE) along a camera ray. It solves the problem of rendering 3D scalar or vector fields by discretizing the ray into fixed or variable segments, sampling the volume data at each step, and compositing the results front-to-back. It sets itself apart from analytical methods like Self-Attenuation Integral Evaluation by relying on Riemann sums rather than closed-form solutions, and from higher-order integration schemes like Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) Integration by assuming constant density and color within each segment (Zero Order Integration). Inputs: Volume Data: A 3D grid of scalar or vector values (e.g., density \sigma, color c). Camera Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, intersecting the volume at entry parameter t{in} and exit parameter t{out}. Step Size (\Delta s): The distance between consecutive sample points along the ray. Transfer Function: Maps sampled scalar values to color ci and opacity \alphai. Outputs: Pixel Color (C): The accumulated radiance for the pixel. Pixel Opacity (\alpha): The accumulated transparency/opacity for the pixel. Volume Grid: Typically stored as a 3D array or texture. For CPU implementations, data is often stored in a linear array with indexing based on dimensions. For GPU implementations, this is often a 3D texture allowing hardware trilinear interpolation. Accumulators: Two variables per ray, accumulatedcolor (RGB) and accumulatedalpha (float), initialized to 0 and 0 respectively. Transmittance: A scalar variable T (or derived from accumulatedalpha) representing the light reaching the current sample, initialized to 1.0. 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, compute the camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Determine the intersection interval [t{in}, t{out}] with the volume bounding box or implicit surface. 2. Discretization: Divide the interval [t{in}, t{out}] into N segments of length \Delta s = (t{out} - t{in}) / N. 3. Loop Over Samples: Iterate i from 0 to N-1 (front-to-back): a. Sample Position: Calculate the position \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + (t{in} + i \cdot \Delta s) \mathbf{d}. b. Interpolation: Sample the volume data at \mathbf{p}i using trilinear interpolation to get the scalar value vi. c. Transfer Function: Map vi to color ci and opacity \alphai. d. Compute Weight: Calculate the contribution weight wi for the current segment. Using the exponential attenuation model: wi = Ti \cdot (1 - e^{-\sigmai \Delta s}) where \sigmai is the density (often equivalent to opacity per unit length or derived from \alphai) and Ti is the transmittance entering the segment. Note: In simpler implementations where \alphai is the opacity of the segment itself, the weight is often computed as: wi = Ti \cdot \alphai where Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). e. Accumulate: Update the accumulated color and opacity: C{new} = C{old} + wi \cdot ci \alpha{new} = \alpha{old} + wi Alternatively, using the standard front-to-back compositing equations: \hat{C}{out} = \hat{C}{in} + \hat{C}i (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + \alphai (1 - \alpha{in}) where \hat{C} denotes pre-multiplied color (C \cdot \alpha). f. Update Transmittance: Update T{i+1} = Ti \cdot (1 - \alphai) or T{i+1} = Ti \cdot e^{-\sigmai \Delta s}. g. Early Termination: If \alpha{out} \geq 1.0 (or a threshold like 0.95), break the loop. 4. Final Color: If the final accumulated opacity \alpha{out} < 1.0, blend with the background color C{bg}: C{final} = C{out} + C{bg} (1 - \alpha{out}) If a fully opaque background was composited, normalization is omitted. The discrete volume rendering integral for a ray \mathbf{r} is approximated as a Riemann sum: L{out} = \sum{i=0}^{n-1} ci \alphai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Where: L{out} is the final pixel color (radiance). ci is the color contribution of the i-th sample. \alphai is the opacity of the i-th sample/segment. \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the transmittance Ti from the camera to the start of the i-th segment, representing the fraction of light not absorbed by previous samples. For density-based rendering (e.g., NeRFs or physical media), the opacity \alphai is derived from density \sigmai and step size \Delta s: \alphai = 1 - e^{-\sigmai \Delta s} Ti = e^{-\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \sigmaj \Delta s} L{out} = \sum{i=0}^{n-1} ci (1 - e^{-\sigmai \Delta s}) e^{-\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \sigmaj \Delta s}. \Delta s (Step Size): Controls sampling density. Smaller \Delta s reduces aliasing and integration error but increases computation time. Typical values depend on volume resolution; e.g., 0.001 in normalized coordinates or fixed voxel steps. N (Number of Samples): N = (t{out} - t{in}) / \Delta s. Opacity Threshold: Early termination threshold, typically 0.95 or 1.0. Aliasing: If \Delta s is too large relative to the frequency of the volume data, visible artifacts (stair-stepping, moiré) occur. Precision: Accumulating many small opacity values can lead to floating-point precision errors. Using full precision for intermediate transmittance calculations is recommended. Boundary Conditions: Incorrectly calculating t{in} and t{out} leads to missing data or sampling outside the volume bounds. Degenerate Rays: Rays that do not intersect the volume should return the background color immediately. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def discretevolumerenderingintegral(volume, rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, stepsize, transferfunction): """ Computes the pixel color and opacity using the Discrete Volume Rendering Integral. Args: volume: 3D array or texture object with method sample(x, y, z) returning scalar value. rayorigin: vec3, camera position. raydirection: vec3, normalized ray direction. tmin: float, entry parameter of the ray into the volume. tmax: float, exit parameter of the ray from the volume. stepsize: float, distance between samples. transferfunction: function(scalar) -> (color, opacity). Returns: (color, opacity): vec3 and float representing the final pixel color and opacity. """ # Initialize accumulators accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 # Calculate number of steps # Note: Use a small epsilon to avoid floating point issues at tmax numsteps = int((tmax - tmin) / stepsize) for i in range(numsteps): # 1. Sample Position t = tmin + i stepsize pos = rayorigin + raydirection t # 2. Interpolation (Trilinear) # Assuming volume.sample returns a scalar density/value scalarvalue = volume.sample(pos.x, pos.y, pos.z) # 3. Transfer Function # Maps scalar value to color (RGB) and opacity (alpha) colorsample, alphasample = transferfunction(scalarvalue) # 4. Early Termination Check if accumulatedalpha >= 0.99: break # 5. Accumulate Color and Opacity (Front-to-Back) # Contribution of current sample: transmittance alphasample colorsample contribution = transmittance alphasample colorsample accumulatedcolor += contribution # Update accumulated alpha and transmittance accumulatedalpha += transmittance alphasample transmittance = (1.0 - alphasample) # 6. Final Color (Blend with background if necessary) # Assuming black background (0,0,0) finalcolor = accumulatedcolor return finalcolor, accumulatedalpha A sample placement strategy where the first sample point is calculated relative to the eye position, creating concentric sampling lines across pixels. It differs from Entry Align by aligning to the viewer, potentially introducing endpoint aliasing. Computes the self-attenuation integral using a normalized 3D Gaussian density and exponential attenuation, providing an exact closed-form solution that avoids discretization errors. Improves integration approximation by using a 2D lookup table (\psi table) independent of the transfer function, allowing interactive updates with minimal overhead. A direct volume rendering technique using explicit multithreaded pixel processing on the CPU with trilinear interpolation and early ray termination. A simplified technique averaging scalar intensities along rays, treating the volume as transparent and ignoring opacity/absorption, resulting in low contrast. Adapts sampling density along the ray based on view-dependent frequency to respect the Nyquist limit, using variable step sizes. Explicitly approximates the in-scattering term Li(x, \omega) using auxiliary light rays and Beer's law for non-homogeneous volumes. Assumes constant density and color within each segment, evaluating a Riemann sum with one sample per segment. Simple but prone to discontinuities. Extends ray tracing to handle geometric intersections and recursive paths for global illumination effects in volumetric scenes, introducing aliasing at grid locations. A forward projection algorithm that separates line-integral calculation into continuous volume construction via tri-linear interpolation and approximation by summing values at equidistant points along the ray. It constructs a continuous volume by tri-linear interpolation from the discrete voxel data, then approximates the line-integration by summing values at equidistant points along the ray. The oversampling factor is defined as N = \frac{\Delta x}{h}, where \Delta x is the voxel sampling distance and N=1 corresponds to a sampling distance equal to the voxel sampling distance. The step width h is a free parameter trading off between image quality and computation time. This method requires a high oversampling factor to match the accuracy of Köhler's method, resulting in substantially more computation time. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot N), where P is the number of pixels and N is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for storing the volume data, where V is the number of voxels. Performance: Highly dependent on \Delta s and early termination. Fast for sparse volumes or those with high opacity (early termination triggers quickly). Slow for dense, transparent volumes requiring full ray traversal. Strengths: Simple to implement, physically plausible (with proper transfer functions), supports arbitrary lighting and shading models per sample. Limitations: Prone to aliasing if \Delta s is not small enough; computationally expensive for high-resolution volumes or transparent media; requires careful handling of interpolation and boundary conditions. When to Use: Direct volume rendering of scalar fields where transparency and color mapping are key; suitable for GPU implementation via fragment shaders. When Not to Use: When analytical solutions are available and sufficient (e.g., Self-Attenuation Integral Evaluation); when high performance is critical and the volume is very sparse (consider Average Intensity Projection or CPU Volume Raycasting with optimizations). The Discrete Volume Rendering Integral is rooted in the foundational work of volume rendering in the late 1980s and early 1990s. The front-to-back compositing algorithm, which discretizes the volume rendering integral, was popularized by Levoy and others. The term "Volume Rendering Integral" (VRI) refers to the continuous integral, and its discretization into a Riemann sum is the standard approach for direct volume ray casting. It is widely used in medical imaging, scientific visualization, and computer graphics for rendering 3D scalar fields. name: Eye Align
body: Eye Align is a sample placement strategy for volume raycasting where the first sample point inside the volume is calculated relative to the eye position, creating a sampling pattern across pixels that forms concentric lines. It sets itself apart from siblings like Entry Align by aligning samples to the viewer's perspective rather than the volume entry boundary, which can introduce specific aliasing artifacts at the ray endpoints. Inputs: entryPoint: 3D vector, entry point of the ray into the volume (in texture coordinates). exitPoint: 3D vector, exit point of the ray from the volume (in texture coordinates). eyePos: 3D vector, position of the camera/eye (in texture coordinates). dim: 3D vector, dimensions of the volume grid. samplingRate: float, number of samples per unit length in texture space. Outputs: tStart: float, the parameter value for the first sample point inside the volume. tIncr: float, the step increment between consecutive samples. tEnd: float, the total length of the ray within the volume. Data Structures: Standard floating-point vectors and scalars. Steps: 1. Calculate the ray vector in texture coordinates: \vec{ray} = \text{exitPoint} - \text{entryPoint} 2. Calculate the total number of samples based on ray length, volume dimensions, and sampling rate: \text{samples} = \|\vec{ray} \odot \text{dim}\| \times \text{samplingRate} where \odot denotes element-wise multiplication, and \|\cdot\| is the Euclidean norm. 3. Calculate the total ray length: t{\text{End}} = \|\vec{ray}\| 4. Calculate the step increment: t{\text{Incr}} = \frac{t{\text{End}}}{\text{samples}} 5. Calculate the distance from the eye to the entry point to determine the offset for the first sample: \text{numSteps} = \frac{\|\text{entryPoint} - \text{eyePos}\|}{t{\text{Incr}}} 6. Calculate the start parameter for the first sample inside the volume by removing the fractional part of the steps from the eye: t{\text{Start}} = (1 - \text{fract}(\text{numSteps})) \times t{\text{Incr}} where \text{fract}(x) = x - \lfloor x \rfloor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def eyealign(entryPoint, exitPoint, eyePos, dim, samplingRate): # 1. Ray vector in texture coordinates ray = (exitPoint[0] - entryPoint[0], exitPoint[1] - entryPoint[1], exitPoint[2] - entryPoint[2]) # 2. Total number of samples (element-wise multiply then Euclidean norm) rayscaled = (ray[0] dim[0], ray[1] dim[1], ray[2] dim[2]) samples = (rayscaled[0]2 + rayscaled[1]2 + rayscaled[2]2)0.5 samplingRate # 3. Total ray length tEnd = (ray[0]2 + ray[1]2 + ray[2]2)0.5 # 4. Step increment if samples == 0: return 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # Guard against division by zero tIncr = tEnd / samples # 5. Distance from eye to entry in terms of steps disteyeentry = ((entryPoint[0] - eyePos[0])2 + (entryPoint[1] - eyePos[1])2 + (entryPoint[2] - eyePos[2])2)0.5 numSteps = disteyeentry / tIncr # 6. Start parameter frac = numSteps - math.floor(numSteps) # fract(x) = x - floor(x) tStart = (1.0 - frac) tIncr return tStart, tIncr, tEnd Parameters: samplingRate: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Endpoint Estimation Error: The Riemann sum mid-point estimate used in conjunction with this sampling strategy tends to over- or underestimate contributions at both the first and last sample points, visually indicated by overshooting artifacts. Zero Ray Length: If entryPoint equals exitPoint, tEnd and tIncr become zero, leading to division by zero in steps 4 and 5. This should be handled by skipping rendering or returning default values. A sample placement strategy for fixed-step volume raycasting that shifts the first sample point half a step away from the volume entry boundary to align with the Riemann sum midpoint estimate. Unlike Eye Align, which aligns samples relative to the eye position, Entry Align aligns the sampling grid relative to the volume geometry, eliminating the boundary estimation error at the entry point. Choose it when minimizing endpoint artifacts is prioritized over viewer-aligned sampling patterns. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Aligns sampling to the viewer's perspective, creating a concentric line pattern across pixels. Limitations: Prone to endpoint estimation errors (over/underestimation) due to the mid-point rule interaction. The concentric line pattern may be visually noticeable or undesirable in some contexts. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was described in the context of volume raycasting sampling strategies, specifically as a "first attempt" following work by Kruger et al. [6] (cited in). It is presented as an alternative to aligning samples with the volume entry point (Entry Align). Volume Raycasting Sampling Revisited, https://osf.io/download/u9qnz/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Entry Align
body: Entry Align is a sample placement strategy for fixed-step volume raycasting that shifts the first sample point half a step away from the volume entry boundary to align with the Riemann sum midpoint estimate. Unlike its sibling Eye Align, which aligns samples relative to the eye position, Entry Align aligns the sampling grid relative to the volume geometry, eliminating the boundary estimation error at the entry point. Inputs: entryPoint: The 3D position where the ray enters the volume, in texture coordinates. exitPoint: The 3D position where the ray exits the volume, in texture coordinates. dim: The dimensions of the volume texture (width, height, depth). samplingRate: The number of samples per unit length in texture space. Outputs: tStart: The starting parameter for the first sample along the ray. tIncr: The step increment between consecutive samples. tEnd: The total length of the ray in texture coordinates. Data Structures: ray: A 3D vector representing the direction and length of the ray in texture space. samples: A scalar representing the total number of samples to be taken. Steps: 1. Calculate the ray vector in texture coordinates: \text{ray} = \text{exitPoint} - \text{entryPoint} 2. Calculate the total number of samples required based on the ray length and sampling rate: \text{samples} = \|\text{ray} \times \text{dim}\| \times \text{samplingRate} The multiplication ray dim scales the texture coordinate ray to voxel indices. The function length() computes the Euclidean norm of the scaled vector. 3. Calculate the total length of the ray in texture coordinates: t{\text{End}} = \|\text{ray}\| 4. Calculate the step increment (distance between samples in parameter space): t{\text{Incr}} = \frac{t{\text{End}}}{\text{samples}} 5. Set the start parameter to half a step from the entry point: t{\text{Start}} = 0.5 \times t{\text{Incr}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def entryalign(entrypoint, exitpoint, dim, samplingrate): # 1. Calculate ray vector in texture coordinates ray = exitpoint - entrypoint # 2. Calculate total number of samples # ray dim scales texture coordinates to voxel indices # length() computes the Euclidean norm samples = length(ray dim) samplingrate # 3. Calculate total ray length in texture coordinates tend = length(ray) # 4. Calculate step increment tincr = tend / samples # 5. Set start parameter to half a step from entry tstart = 0.5 tincr return tstart, tincr, tend Parameters: samplingRate: Determines the density of samples. Typical values depend on the desired visual quality and performance constraints. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Back Boundary Error: While Entry Align corrects the estimation error at the entry point, the last sample may still under- or overestimate the contribution at the exit boundary, depending on how close the final sample is to the back side of the volume. This occurs because the step size is fixed based on the entry alignment, and the exit point is not necessarily aligned with a sample midpoint. A variant that aligns both the first and last samples to minimize boundary artifacts at entry and exit by adjusting the step size per ray. Recommended as best practice for zero performance impact and minimal errors. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates the boundary estimation error at the entry point, which is a common artifact in naive fixed-step raycasting. Limitations: Does not correct the boundary error at the exit point. The fixed step size may lead to suboptimal sampling density if the ray length varies significantly across pixels, though the step size is calculated per ray. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Entry Align was introduced to address Riemann sum midpoint estimation errors where samples over- or underestimate contributions at boundaries. It shifts samples half a step to align with the entry point, similar to techniques described in "Real-Time Volume Graphics" by Engel et al..
