name: Entry Exit Align
head: Entry Exit Align Corner, Entry Exit Align Corner Sampling, Recommended Sampling Strategy
body: Entry Exit Align is a sample placement strategy for fixed-length volume raycasting that aligns sample points with both the ray entry and exit points to minimize boundary artifacts. Unlike its sibling Entry Align, which only aligns the first sample, Entry Exit Align ensures that neither the first nor the last sample under- or overestimates the integral by adjusting the step size per ray. It is recommended as the best practice for volume raycasting due to zero performance impact and minimal errors. Inputs: entryPoint: The 3D coordinate where the ray enters the volume, given in texture coordinates. exitPoint: The 3D coordinate where the ray exits the volume, given in texture coordinates. samplingRate: The desired number of samples per unit volume dimension. dim: The dimensions of the volume texture (width, height, depth). Outputs: tStart: The starting parameter along the ray for the first sample. tIncr: The step increment (distance between samples) along the ray. tEnd: The total length of the ray vector. Data Structures: vec3: A 3D vector type holding x, y, z components. float: Standard floating-point number. Algorithm: The method calculates the number of samples required to cover the ray length while ensuring the first sample is half a step inside the entry and the last sample is half a step inside the exit. To handle corner rays where the length is smaller than the standard step size, it uses a ceiling function applied to the scaled length of the ray against the volume dimensions minus one, ensuring at least one sample is placed at the midpoint of such short rays. 1. Calculate the ray vector in texture coordinates: \text{ray} = \text{exitPoint} - \text{entryPoint} 2. Calculate the number of samples using the ceiling function applied to the scaled length of the ray against the volume dimensions minus one: \text{samples} = \lceil \text{samplingRate} \times \|\text{ray} \times (\text{dim} - \vec{1})\| \rceil Where \vec{1} is a vector (1, 1, 1) and \times denotes component-wise multiplication. 3. Calculate the total ray length: t{\text{End}} = \|\text{ray}\| 4. Calculate the step increment by dividing the total length by the number of samples: t{\text{Incr}} = \frac{t{\text{End}}}{\text{samples}} 5. Set the start parameter to half a step from the entry point: t{\text{Start}} = 0.5 \times t{\text{Incr}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def entryexitalign(entryPoint, exitPoint, samplingRate, dim): """ Calculates sampling parameters for Entry Exit Align Corner strategy. Args: entryPoint (tuple): Entry point in texture coordinates (x, y, z). exitPoint (tuple): Exit point in texture coordinates (x, y, z). samplingRate (float): Samples per unit dimension. dim (tuple): Volume dimensions (width, height, depth). Returns: tStart (float): Start parameter for first sample. tIncr (float): Step increment. tEnd (float): Total ray length. """ # 1. Ray vector in texture coordinates ray = (exitPoint[0] - entryPoint[0], exitPoint[1] - entryPoint[1], exitPoint[2] - entryPoint[2]) # 2. Number of samples adjusteddim = (dim[0] - 1.0, dim[1] - 1.0, dim[2] - 1.0) scaledray = (ray[0] adjusteddim[0], ray[1] adjusteddim[1], ray[2] adjusteddim[2]) scaledlength = math.sqrt(scaledray[0]2 + scaledray[1]2 + scaledray[2]2) samples = math.ceil(samplingRate scaledlength) # Ensure at least one sample is taken for degenerate rays if samples < 1: samples = 1 # 3. Total ray length raylength = math.sqrt(ray[0]2 + ray[1]2 + ray[2]2) tEnd = raylength # 4. Step increment tIncr = tEnd / samples # 5. Start parameter (half a step from entry) tStart = 0.5 tIncr return tStart, tIncr, tEnd Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Corner Rays: Standard strategies may exclude contributions at corners where the ray length is smaller than the step size. This method explicitly includes these by adjusting the step size to the ray length and placing a sample at the midpoint. Pre-integrated Rendering: Implementations using pre-integrated volume rendering reduced to two dimensions require all rays to use the same step length. Consequently, they cannot use this per-ray adaptive step size and must choose a strategy that under- or overestimates the integral. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Zero performance impact compared to simpler strategies. Strengths: Eliminates stepping artifacts and gaps at the bounding box. It does not suffer from over- or underestimation of first/last samples. Limitations: Requires per-ray calculation of step size, which may be incompatible with fixed-step pre-integrated rendering techniques. When to use: Recommended as the best practice for general volume raycasting. When not to use: When using pre-integrated volume rendering in 2D where a uniform step size across all rays is mandatory. The method was developed and evaluated in the Inviwo framework. It builds upon the "Eye Align" and "Entry Align" strategies, addressing their respective deficiencies regarding boundary estimation. The authors note that while errors due to sample placement can be significant for data at the borders, they are often marginal in real-world use cases with higher resolution volumes. However, artifacts can appear when zooming in on borders, justifying the recommendation of this method. name: Self-Attenuation Integral Evaluation
head: Proof for Equation used for Self-Attenuation
body: Self-Attenuation Integral Evaluation computes the self-attenuation integral for a ray passing through a pixel, where the integrand involves a normalized 3D Gaussian and an exponential attenuation term based on the cumulative integral of that Gaussian. It solves the problem of analytically evaluating the volume rendering integral for 3D Gaussian primitives, ensuring physical correctness in density estimation by explicitly modeling self-attenuation. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Eye Align and Partial Pre-Integration by its reliance on a closed-form substitution of the cumulative distribution function rather than numerical discretization or hardware-accelerated lookup tables. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray \mathcal{R} parameterized by t, where \mathcal{R}(t) maps to 3D space. A normalized 3D Gaussian density function \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{0}) centered at the origin (or transformed to the ray space). The ray enters the volume at t = -\infty and exits at t = \infty (conceptually, covering the support of the Gaussian). Output: The scalar value 1 - e^{-f0(\mathbf{p})}, where f0(\mathbf{p}) is the 2D extinction function (the integrated 2D Gaussian density) at pixel \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: No explicit data structures are required for the evaluation itself, as it is a mathematical derivation. The implementation requires access to the cumulative distribution function (CDF) or the ability to compute the definite integral of the Gaussian along the ray. Steps: 1. Define the Integrand: The volume rendering integral for a single Gaussian primitive with color c0(\mathcal{R}) and density \mathcal{G}3^n is given by: I(\mathbf{p}) = c0(\mathcal{R}) \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(t), 0) e^{-\int{-\infty}^t \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(\tau), 0) d\tau} dt 2. Define the Cumulative Integral: Let H(t) be the inner cumulative integral of the Gaussian density along the ray: H(t) = \int{-\infty}^t \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(\tau), 0) d\tau The derivative of H(t) with respect to t is the integrand of the inner integral: \frac{dH(t)}{dt} = \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(t), 0) 3. Substitution: Rewrite the outer integral using the substitution dH(t) = \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(t), 0) dt. The integral becomes: \int{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-H(t)} dH(t) 4. Change of Bounds: Determine the bounds for the new variable u = H(t). Since \mathcal{G}3^n is a normalized Gaussian, H(t) converges from 0 as t \to -\infty to f0(\mathbf{p}) as t \to \infty, where f0(\mathbf{p}) is the total integrated 2D Gaussian density (the 2D extinction function). The integral bounds change to [0, f0(\mathbf{p})]: \int0^{f0(\mathbf{p})} e^{-u} du 5. Evaluate: Compute the definite integral: \int0^{f0(\mathbf{p})} e^{-u} du = \left[ -e^{-u} \right]0^{f0(\mathbf{p})} = -e^{-f0(\mathbf{p})} - (-e^0) = 1 - e^{-f0(\mathbf{p})} Formulas: I(\mathbf{p}) = c0(\mathcal{R}) (1 - e^{-f0(\mathbf{p})}) f0(\mathbf{p}) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \mathcal{G}3^n(\mathcal{R}(t), 0) dt Parameters: c0(\mathcal{R}): The color of the Gaussian primitive at the ray intersection. Not given in the sources. \mathcal{G}3^n: The normalized 3D Gaussian density. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The derivation assumes the Gaussian is normalized and the integration bounds are effectively -\infty to \infty. In practice, the Gaussian support is truncated, but the error is negligible if the truncation is sufficiently large. Precision issues may arise if f0(\mathbf{p}) is very large, causing e^{-f0(\mathbf{p})} to underflow to 0, resulting in an opacity of 1. This is physically correct for high-density regions. Exponential Attenuation Computation calculates the final color of a sample point along a ray by applying colors and densities obtained from a query (such as an MLP network) via the discrete volume rendering formula. It solves the problem of accurately integrating light absorption and emission through a participating medium in a single pass. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its explicit use of the exponential attenuation term Tk to model self-attenuation, ensuring physical correctness in density estimation. Post color-attenuated classification is an algorithm that rapidly evaluates the optical properties of each segment by eliminating the extinction coefficient from the opacity-associated color integral and computing color attenuation segment by segment instead of point by point. It is distinguished from point-wise integration methods by its segment-based approach, which improves lookup table generation speed and accuracy. Time and Memory Complexity: The evaluation is O(1) with respect to the number of samples, as it uses a closed-form solution. Memory complexity is minimal, requiring only the storage of the 2D extinction function f0(\mathbf{p}) and the color c0. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales linearly with the number of primitives if evaluated per primitive, but the closed-form nature avoids the O(N) sampling cost of numerical integration. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Physically correct self-attenuation; computationally efficient due to closed-form solution; no need for numerical integration or lookup tables. Limitations: Specific to Gaussian primitives; requires the ability to compute the integrated 2D Gaussian density f0(\mathbf{p}). When to use it and when not: Use when rendering 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes where accurate volumetric rendering is required. Do not use for non-Gaussian primitives or when approximate rendering is acceptable and hardware acceleration (like Partial Pre-Integration) is preferred. The method originates from the analysis of 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering, specifically in the context of determining whether accurate volumetric rendering is necessary. The proof demonstrates that the self-attenuation integral for a 3D Gaussian can be solved analytically, leading to the term 1 - e^{-f0(\mathbf{p})}. It is used in modern neural graphics primitives and Gaussian splatting implementations to ensure physically plausible opacity accumulation. name: Exponential Attenuation Computation
head: Discrete Volume Rendering, Exponential Attenuation Evaluation, Radiance Absorption-Ray Stepping
body: Exponential Attenuation Computation calculates the final color of a sample point along a ray by applying colors and densities obtained from a query (such as an MLP network) via the discrete volume rendering formula. It solves the problem of accurately integrating light absorption and emission through a participating medium in a single pass. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its explicit use of the exponential attenuation term Tk to model self-attenuation, ensuring physical correctness in density estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of N sample points along a ray. For each sample k \in \{1, \dots, N\}, the inputs are the density \sigmak, the color ck, and the depth coordinates tk and t{k+1} defining the step interval. Outputs: The accumulated color C^(r) for the ray r. Data Structures: Arrays for \sigma, c, and t of size N+1 (for depths) or N (for densities/colors). Accumulators for transmittance T and color C. Formulas: The final color C^(r) is computed as: C^(r) = \sum{k=1}^{N} Tk (1 - \exp(-\sigmak (t{k+1} - tk))) ck where the transmittance Tk at sample k is: Tk = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigmaj (t{j+1} - tj)\right) Here, \sigma is density, c is color, t is depth, and T is transmittance. Parameters: N: Number of samples per ray. Typical values range from 10 to 100,000 depending on resolution and march step count. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeexponentialattenuation(densities, colors, depths): """ Computes the final color using exponential attenuation. Args: densities: List of N floats (sigmak). colors: List of N 3D vectors (ck). depths: List of N+1 floats (tk to t{N+1}). Returns: Final color vector. """ N = len(densities) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 for k in range(N): # Calculate step length steplength = depths[k+1] - depths[k] # Calculate opacity for this segment: 1 - exp(-sigma deltat) # Note: exp(-sigma deltat) is the transmittance through this segment segmenttransmittance = math.exp(-densities[k] steplength) segmentopacity = 1.0 - segmenttransmittance # Add contribution: Tk opacityk ck # Tk is the transmittance arriving at the start of segment k contribution = [accumulatedtransmittance segmentopacity colors[k][i] for i in range(3)] accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[i] + contribution[i] for i in range(3)] # Update transmittance for the next segment # T{k+1} = Tk exp(-sigmak deltat) accumulatedtransmittance = segmenttransmittance return accumulatedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: For large numbers of march steps (1000-100,000), repeated multiplication for transmittance can become expensive or suffer from underflow if not handled carefully. Performance: The choice of exponential function implementation matters. powf (fast single-precision) is generally fastest, followed by incremental multiplication, with pow (standard double-precision) being slowest. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples. The cost depends on the implementation of the exponential function. For small step counts (10-100), powf is fastest, followed by incremental multiplication. For large step counts (1000-100,000), powf remains fastest, while pow overtakes incremental multiplication because repeated multiplication becomes increasingly expensive as steps grow, whereas power functions maintain constant-time complexity. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store sample attributes, or O(1) if computed on-the-fly during ray marching. Strengths: Physically accurate modeling of light absorption; computationally efficient on general-purpose hardware (CPU/GPU) without specialized acceleration units. Limitations: Performance degrades with very high sample counts if incremental multiplication is used; precision issues may arise with extreme density/depth values. When to use: Standard direct volume rendering, neural rendering (NeRF-like tasks) requiring traditional volume rendering calculations. When not to use: When approximate rendering is sufficient and speed is critical over physical accuracy; when hardware-specific optimizations (like specialized ray tracing cores) are available and preferred. The method originates from the foundational principles of volume rendering, specifically the discrete approximation of the volume rendering integral. It is widely used in neural rendering tasks, particularly NeRF-like tasks, where it is applied to colors and densities obtained from querying MLP networks. The computational requirements align with general computational units and lookup table units, making it suitable for hardware acceleration in neural network computations. name: Partial Pre-Integration
body: Partial Pre-Integration is a volume ray integration technique that improves ray integration approximation by pre-integrating part of the volume rendering integral into a 2D lookup table (\Psi table) that is independent of the transfer function. Unlike previous pre-integration approaches that rely on specific transfer function attributes (requiring table recomputation upon changes), this method allows interactive transfer function updates without recomputing the table, while avoiding the heavy computational overhead of direct integral calculation. It provides superior accuracy compared to Average Color/Luminance approximations (eliminating artifacts like blue bleeding through yellow) and is visually indistinguishable from Linear Color/Luminance methods but an order of magnitude faster. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar field samples s(\bar{\rho}) along a ray segment, transfer function g(s) (color c) and \tau(s) (extinction coefficient), ray segment thickness l (or optical thickness parameters). Output: Final fragment color C{frag}. Data Structures: 2D \Psi Table: A pre-computed 2D texture or array indexed by \gammab and \gammaf. Indices: \gammab, \gammaf \in 0, 1). Values: \Psi{\gammab, \gammaf}, representing the pre-integrated transmittance contribution. Size: Not given in the sources. Parameters: \gamma (Gamma): A normalized optical thickness parameter defined as \gamma \equiv \frac{\tau D}{\tau D + 1}, where \tau D is the optical thickness. The valid range is [0, 1). Optical Thickness (\tau D): Recovered from \gamma via \tau D = \gamma / (1 - \gamma). Steps: 1. Retrieve Colors: For the current ray segment endpoints (or scalar values sf, sb), retrieve the [RGBA colors cf, cb and extinction coefficients \tauf, \taub from the transfer function. 2. Compute \gamma Indices: Calculate the \gamma values for the front and back of the segment: \gammaf = \frac{\tauf l}{\tauf l + 1} \gammab = \frac{\taub l}{\taub l + 1} (Note: The sources define \gamma generally for optical thickness \tau D. In the context of a segment of length l, \tau D becomes \tau l.). 3. Lookup \Psi: Use \gammab and \gammaf as indices to retrieve the value \Psi{\gammab, \gammaf} from the pre-compiled 2D \Psi table. 4. Compute Final Color: Use the retrieved \Psi value, along with the colors cf, cb and potentially other shading attributes, to compute the final fragment color. The exact combination formula is not explicitly detailed in the provided text, but it replaces the direct integration step. Formula: The core function \Psi{\gammab, \gammaf} is computed by integrating the transmittance over the interval [0, 1], where the extinction coefficient varies linearly between boundary values \gammab and \gammaf: \Psi{\gammab, \gammaf} = \int0^1 e^{-\ints^1 \left( \frac{\gammab}{1-\gammab}(1-t) + \frac{\gammaf}{1-\gammaf}t \right) dt} ds This integral represents the pre-integration of the transmittance term, assuming a linear variation of the optical thickness parameter \gamma across the segment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def partialpreintegration(raysegment, transferfunction, psitable): """ Computes the fragment color for a ray segment using Partial Pre-Integration. Args: raysegment: Object containing scalar values at endpoints sf, sb and length l. transferfunction: Function mapping scalar s to (color, extinction). psitable: 2D lookup table indexed by (gammab, gammaf). Returns: Final fragment color. """ # 1. Retrieve colors and extinction coefficients from transfer function cf, tauf = transferfunction(raysegment.sf) cb, taub = transferfunction(raysegment.sb) # 2. Compute gamma indices # gamma = (tau l) / (tau l + 1) gammaf = (tauf raysegment.l) / (tauf raysegment.l + 1) gammab = (taub raysegment.l) / (taub raysegment.l + 1) # 3. Lookup Psi value # Note: In implementation, gamma indices must be scaled to table resolution psival = psitable.lookup(gammaf, gammab) # 4. Compute final color # The exact combination of cf, cb, and psival is not specified in the sources. # Typically, this involves blending the colors weighted by the pre-integrated transmittance. # Placeholder for the specific color blending formula derived from the volume rendering equation. finalcolor = computecolorfrompsi(cf, cb, psival) return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Table Construction: The construction of the \Psi table is very compute intensive and can take hours to perform. However, it is computed once and reused. Precision: The sources do not specify precision issues, but the mapping from \tau D to \gamma handles the infinite domain of optical thickness by mapping it to 0, 1). Boundary Conditions: The range of \gamma is [0, 1). If \tau D \to \infty, \gamma \to 1. The table must handle the limit as \gamma \to 1 appropriately. A GPU-accelerated [cell projection method that combines direct volume rendering with multiple isosurfaces. It uses tetrahedral discretization and eliminates bus transfer overhead. Improves accuracy by adaptively subdividing the ray integration interval based on local extrema of scalar and shading polynomials, using front- and back-weighted tables. Time Complexity: The table construction is O(N^2) where N is the table resolution, but this is a one-time cost. Per-fragment cost involves two transfer function lookups, two gamma calculations, one 2D table lookup, and a color blend. It is slower than the simple average scalar method but faster than direct integration. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 2D \Psi table. Size depends on resolution, not given in sources. Performance: Rendering speeds vary with volume, classification, projection, and image size. It is an order of magnitude faster than Linear Color/Luminance methods. Strengths: Interactive transfer function changes without table recomputation; superior accuracy to Average Color/Luminance; applicable to any classification system (gradient shading, opacity, etc.). Limitations: Slower than simple average scalar methods; table construction is computationally expensive (though one-time). Partial Pre-Integration was introduced by Kenneth Moreland in 2004. It builds upon the original Pre-Integration (PT) method by Shirley and Tuchman, which required the pre-integration table to be computed based on the transfer function. Moreland's method decouples the table from the transfer function by using the \gamma parameterization, allowing a single universal table to be used for any classification algorithm. The method is used in fragment processors for volume ray integration and supports various shading techniques including gradient shading, gradient opacity, boundary highlights, silhouettes, and multidimensional transfer functions. name: Hybrid Volume and Isosurface Rendering with Partial Pre-Integration
head: PT with partial preintegration, PTINT
body: Hybrid Volume and Isosurface Rendering with Partial Pre-Integration (PTINT) is a GPU-accelerated cell projection method that combines direct volume rendering with multiple isosurfaces to achieve interactive frame rates. It builds on Partial Pre-Integration by eliminating bus transfer overhead and allowing the simultaneous rendering of opaque or semi-transparent isosurfaces within the same fragment shader passes. Unlike pure ray casting, PTINT uses a tetrahedral discretization that requires no cell connectivity, offering significantly lower memory usage than hardware-accelerated ray casting (HARC) variants. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar field defined on a set of n vertices and m tetrahedra. Output: A 2D image with combined volume shading and isosurface geometry. Data Structures and Memory Layout: The method requires no explicit cell connectivity, storing data in textures to optimize GPU access. Texture Element Size: 16 bytes per element. Total Storage: 16(2n + m) bytes for n vertices and m tetrahedra. Storage per Tetrahedron: Assuming an average of 4 tetrahedra per vertex, the storage is 24 bytes per tetrahedron. Memory Usage: Approximately 24 MB for one million cells (20 MB without illumination data). Operational Variants: The algorithm supports three operational variants: 1. Basic Average Scalar Method: Standard volume rendering without pre-integration. 2. Partial Pre-Integration Technique: Uses partial pre-integration for improved integration accuracy. 3. Partial Pre-Integration with Isosurface Rendering: A hybrid mode combining direct volume rendering with multiple isosurfaces to achieve interactive frame rates by eliminating bus transfer overhead. Algorithm Steps: The rendering is performed in two main passes, with all isosurface computation handled in the second fragment shader to avoid additional rendering passes. 1. First Pass (Volume/Pre-integration): Render the tetrahedra to intermediate framebuffers 2 and 3. Compute gradient vectors gf and gb if lighting or isosurfaces are enabled. If isosurfaces/lighting are not desired, skip gradient computations and skip rendering to framebuffers 2 and 3. 2. Intermediate CPU Pass: Update gradient arrays if they were computed in the first pass. If gradients were skipped, this step is omitted. 3. Second Pass (Hybrid Rendering): Interpolate gradients and compute normals. If gradients were skipped, skip interpolation and normal computation. Perform isosurface detection and shading in the second fragment shader. Apply Phong shading model with controllable diffuse, specular, and ambient coefficients for isosurfaces. Render isosurfaces as fully opaque or semi-transparent fragments. Optimizations and Pitfalls: Early Tetrahedral Discard: An early discard test is applied to improve performance by skipping tetrahedra that do not contribute to the final image. Small Pixel Area Degradation: On datasets like "Liquid Oxygen Post," PTINT may lose performance compared to ray casting at viewpoints where the model occupies a small pixel area, as cell projection approaches are unaffected by pixel area size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetetgradients(vertices): # Standard gradient estimation from vertex scalar values return gradientforward, gradientbackward def rasterizetoframebuffers(tetrahedra, gradients, fbids): # Project tetrahedra to screen and render to specified framebuffers pass def copytocpu(data): # Synchronize data from GPU to CPU memory return data def computenormalsfromgradients(tet, gradients): # Barycentric interpolation of gradients to fragment positions return normalvector def cullvisibletetrahedra(tetrahedra): # Cull tetrahedra outside view frustum or with zero screen projection return [t for t in tetrahedra if t.inviewfrustum] def checkisosurfaceintersection(tet, threshold): # Find intersection of scalar field with threshold inside tetrahedron return True def applyphongmodel(tet, normals, diffuse, specular, ambient): # Standard Phong model: ambient + diffuse + specular return color def accumulatevolumeshading(tet, normals): # Accumulate color and opacity using partial pre-integration return volumecolor def writefragment(color, opaque=False, alpha=1.0): # Output fragment to framebuffer pass def renderptint(vertices, tetrahedra, isosurfacethresholds, enablelighting, enableisosurfaces): # 1. First Pass: Volume/Pre-integration and Gradient Computation if enablelighting or enableisosurfaces: gradients = [] for tet in tetrahedra: gf, gb = computetetgradients(tet.vertices) gradients.append((gf, gb)) rasterizetoframebuffers(tetrahedra, gradients, fbids=[2, 3]) else: gradients = None rasterizetoframebuffers(tetrahedra, None, fbids=[]) # 2. Intermediate CPU Pass if enablelighting or enableisosurfaces: cpugradients = copytocpu(gradients) else: cpugradients = None # 3. Second Pass: Hybrid Isosurface and Volume Shading if enablelighting or enableisosurfaces: normals = [] for tet in tetrahedra: n = computenormalsfromgradients(tet, cpugradients) normals.append(n) else: normals = None # Apply early tetrahedral discard test visibletets = cullvisibletetrahedra(tetrahedra) # Render final image for tet in visibletets: if enableisosurfaces: for threshold in isosurfacethresholds: if checkisosurfaceintersection(tet, threshold): color = applyphongmodel(tet, normals, diffuse=0.8, specular=0.5, ambient=0.2) writefragment(color, opaque=True) volumecolor = accumulatevolumeshading(tet, normals) writefragment(volumecolor, alpha=0.5) Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined in sources, but achieves interactive frame rates on tested hardware. Memory Complexity: O(n + m) with a constant factor of 16 bytes per vertex/tet element. Total memory is 16(2n + m) bytes. Measured Performance: Hardware: Intel Pentium IV 3.6 GHz, 2 GB RAM, nVidia GeForce 6800 256 MB, PCI Express 16x. Viewport: 512 \times 512 pixels, constantly rotating model. Blunt Fin Dataset: PTINT outperforms all compared algorithms (GATOR, VICP, VICP Balanced, HARC, HARC INT, HAVIS, HAVS). Oxygen Post Dataset: PTINT loses to ray casting algorithms at certain viewpoints where the model has a small pixel area. Strengths: Low memory footprint (24 bytes/tet vs. 96-144 bytes/tet for HARC variants). No cell connectivity required, freeing GPU memory. Interactive frame rates via elimination of bus transfer overhead. Hybrid visualization allows underlying volumes to be hidden by opaque isosurfaces or enhanced by semi-transparent layers. Limitations: Performance degradation on small pixel area views compared to ray casting. Considerable performance loss if Phong shading is used for isosurfaces due to gradient computation overhead. When to Use: When interactive frame rates are required for large tetrahedral datasets and hybrid volume/isosurface visualization is desired, particularly on hardware with limited GPU memory. When Not to Use: When rendering datasets with small pixel area coverage where ray casting might be more efficient. Origin: Proposed by R. Marroquim et al. in the paper "Volume and Isosurface Rendering with GPU-Accelerated Cell Projection" (CGF 2008). Development: The method extends previous cell projection techniques (GATOR, VICP) and hardware-accelerated ray casting (HARC) by integrating partial pre-integration and isosurface rendering into a unified GPU pipeline. Usage: Tested on datasets including Blunt Fin, Combustion Chamber, Liquid Oxygen Post, Super Phoenix, Fuel Injection, and Electron Distribution Probability. Implemented in C++ with OpenGL 2.0 and GLSL under Linux. name: Semi-Analytical Fragment Shader Preintegration
body:
Semi-Analytical Fragment Shader Preintegration is a GPU-based rendering technique that improves the accuracy of discrete volume rendering integrals by adaptively subdividing the ray integration interval based on the local extrema of the underlying scalar and shading polynomials. The method computes the roots of the derivatives of the signal and shading functions within the fragment's bounding box to define integration sub-intervals, over which preintegration and shading interpolation are applied using front- and back-weighted tables. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray exit point, scalar field coefficients (cubic polynomial a,b,c,d), shading coefficients (quadratic polynomial e,f,g), and preintegration lookup tables. Output: Accumulated color and opacity for the fragment. Data Structures: Preintegration Table: A 256 × 256 × 32 RGBA texture where each component is 16-bit floating point. The dimensions correspond to the scalar values at the start and end of the interval (s1, s2) and the interval length (l). Logarithmic table access is used for the length dimension to provide greater precision at small lengths. Offscreen Buffer: A 16-bit floating point buffer used for intermediate blending to improve accuracy before copying to the front buffer. Polynomial Representation: The scalar signal s(t) and shading factor l(t) along the ray parameter t \in [0, 1] are approximated by polynomials: s(t) = at^3 + bt^2 + ct + d l(t) = et^2 + ft + g where a,b,c,d are cubic coefficients and e,f,g are quadratic coefficients derived from the cell data. Algorithm Steps: 1. Find Exit Point: Compute the ray exit point of the current cell or patch. 2. Compute Coefficients: Calculate a,b,c,d for the scalar signal and e,f,g for the shading factor. 3. Initialize Extrema List: Set T = \emptyset. 4. Find Scalar Extrema: If a 
eq 0 and b 
eq 0: Compute discriminant \Delta = 4b^2 - 12ac. Add roots of s'(t)=0 to T: t =  rac{-2b \pm \sqrt{\Delta}}{6a} Else if a = 0 and b 
eq 0: Add root of s'(t)=0 to T: t =  rac{-c}{2b} 5. Find Shading Extrema: If e 
eq 0: Add root of l'(t)=0 to T: t =  rac{-f}{2e} 6. Prune and Sort: Remove any t \in T such that t \le 0 or t \ge 1. Add boundary points 0 and 1 to T. Sort T in ascending order. 7. Adaptive Preintegration: For each consecutive pair (t1, t2) in T: Reconstruct scalar values s1 = s(t1) and s2 = s(t2). Reconstruct shading values l1 = l(t1) and l2 = l(t2). Compute interval length l = t2 - t1. Fetch preintegration values from the front and back weighted tables using (s1, s2, l). Combine the fetched values and accumulate color and opacity using standard overcompositing. The final fragment color and opacity are the result of this accumulation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def semianalyticalpreintegration(a, b, c, d, e, f, g): # T stores the sorted integration boundaries T = [] # Find extrema of scalar polynomial s(t) = at^3 + bt^2 + ct + d # s'(t) = 3at^2 + 2bt + c = 0 if a != 0 and b != 0: delta = 4 b2 - 12 a c if delta >= 0: sqrtdelta = math.sqrt(delta) t1 = (-2 b + sqrtdelta) / (6 a) t2 = (-2 b - sqrtdelta) / (6 a) T.append(t1) T.append(t2) elif a == 0 and b != 0: # s'(t) = 2bt + c = 0 t = -c / (2 b) T.append(t) # Find extrema of shading polynomial l(t) = et^2 + ft + g # l'(t) = 2et + f = 0 if e != 0: t = -f / (2 e) T.append(t) # Prune points outside (0, 1) T = [t for t in T if 0 < t < 1] # Add boundaries and sort T.append(0.0) T.append(1.0) T.sort() # Initialize accumulation variables accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # Iterate over intervals for i in range(len(T) - 1): t1 = T[i] t2 = T[i+1] # Reconstruct scalar values using Horner's method s1 = d + t1 (c + t1 (b + t1 a)) s2 = d + t2 (c + t2 (b + t2 a)) # Reconstruct shading values l1 = g + t1 (f + t1 e) l2 = g + t2 (f + t2 e) # Compute interval length length = t2 - t1 # Fetch preintegration tables (logarithmic indexing for length handled internally) frontval = fetchpreintegrationtable(s1, s2, length, type='front') backval = fetchpreintegrationtable(s1, s2, length, type='back') # Standard overcompositing accumulation # frontval and backval are assumed to be (colorrgb, opacity) tuples colorseg = frontval[0] alphaseg = frontval[1] accumulatedcolor[0] = accumulatedcolor[0] + (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) colorseg[0] accumulatedcolor[1] = accumulatedcolor[1] + (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) colorseg[1] accumulatedcolor[2] = accumulatedcolor[2] + (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) colorseg[2] accumulatedopacity = accumulatedopacity + (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) alphaseg return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity def fetchpreintegrationtable(s1, s2, l, type): # Standard 3D texture lookup with logarithmic length indexing # Maps linear length l to a logarithmic index for the 32-entry dimension idxl = max(0, min(31, int(math.log2(max(l, 1e-6)) scalefactor))) idxs1 = int(s1 255) idxs2 = int(s2 255) # Returns RGBA value from the 256x256x32 texture return texturelookup(idxs1, idxs2, idxl, type) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Small interval lengths require high precision. The use of 16-bit floating point textures and logarithmic indexing for the length dimension mitigates precision loss at small l. Degenerate Polynomials: If a=0 and b=0, the scalar function is linear, and no extrema exist within the interval (other than boundaries). Complex Roots: If the discriminant \Delta < 0, there are no real extrema, and no points are added to T from that polynomial. Interval Integration computes in-scattered radiance by decomposing the ray path into intervals defined by the front and back faces of a light volume, allowing analytical evaluation of the scattering integral for directional lights and numerical or lookup-based evaluation for point and spot lights. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly treating light volume boundaries as integration limits, enabling a "sum and difference" approach where contributions are added for front-face intersections and subtracted for back-face intersections. Time Complexity: The fragment shader performs a constant number of arithmetic operations to find roots and a number of texture fetches proportional to the number of extrema found. Memory Complexity: Requires a 256 × 256 × 32 16-bit RGBA texture for the preintegration table. Performance: The method is implemented on the GPU using OpenGL. It uses a 16-bit floating point offscreen buffer for blending accuracy. Performance measurements are presented in the source but specific frame rates are not detailed in the provided notes. Strengths: Perspective-correct sorting of cells is ensured. Limitations: Requires computing polynomial coefficients and roots in the fragment shader, which can be computationally intensive if many extrema are present. The method was implemented as part of a hybrid CPU-GPU Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) volume rendering system. The CPU traverses a KD-tree of AMR patches back-to-front, sending indices to the GPU. The geometry shader instantiates faces, and the fragment shader performs the semi-analytical preintegration. The approach builds on the concept of Partial Pre-Integration but adapts it for AMR data structures and fragment-shader execution. name: Interval Integration for Volumetric Light Scattering
head: Analytic Interval Integration, Sum & Difference of Intervals
body: Interval Integration computes in-scattered radiance by decomposing the integration path into intervals defined by the front and back faces of a light volume, allowing analytical evaluation for directional lights and numerical or lookup-based evaluation for point and spot lights. It sets itself apart from its parent Semi-Analytical Fragment Shader Preintegration by explicitly using the geometric boundaries of the light volume (front/back faces) to define integration limits, rather than relying solely on local extrema of scalar polynomials. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, light volume geometry (front and back faces), light type (directional, omnidirectional, spot), shadow map, and medium properties (density, phase function). Outputs: In-scattered radiance LS for the pixel. Data Structures: Light Volume Mesh: Defined by front faces (Gf) and back faces (Gb). Lookup Texture: For omnidirectional lights, a 2D texture mapping \cos^{-1}(v \cdot l) to precomputed differential values. Steps: 1. Decompose Ray into Intervals: Identify the intersection points of the view ray with the light volume. The ray is divided into segments based on entering (n \in Gf) and exiting (m \in Gb) the volume. 2. Evaluate In-Scattered Radiance per Light Type: The total in-scattered radiance LS is computed as the sum of contributions from lit intervals: LS = \sum{n \in Gf} L'S(tn) - \sum{m \in Gb} L'S(tm) where L'S(t) is the indefinite integral of the scattering term evaluated at distance t. Directional Lights: Assume constant direction and constant power (light distance >> medium depth). The integral simplifies to an analytic function evaluated in the pixel shader: L'S(d) = L(d, l) \rhom(xl, \omegax) \frac{1 - e^{-\tau{ex} d}}{\tau{ex}} where d is the distance along the ray, L is light intensity, \rhom is medium reflectance, and \tau{ex} is extinction coefficient. Omnidirectional Lights: Analytical solutions are too complex. Create a lookup texture mapping \cos^{-1}(v \cdot l) to 2D space. Evaluate the differential and numerically integrate using a Compute Shader. Spot Lights: Perform cone intersection to clamp the interval. For variable falloff, perform numerical integration using Newton-Cotes methods in the pixel shader. For fixed or no falloff, use modified point light lookups or treat as point lights. 3. Apply Attenuation: Ensure that the light reaching the camera is attenuated by the media. 4. Composite Results: Additively blend the resolved/filtered output with the scene. Use dual-source blending to attenuate based on medium and depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeintervalintegration(rayorigin, raydirection, lightvolumefaces, lighttype, shadowmapdata): # 1. Find intersections with light volume faces (front Gf and back Gb) # Standard ray-mesh intersection routine intersections = [] for face in lightvolumefaces: t = rayplaneintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, face) if t > 1e-6: intersections.append(t) intersections.sort() # 2. Decompose into intervals and sum contributions totalradiance = 0.0 for i in range(0, len(intersections) - 1, 2): tstart = intersections[i] tend = intersections[i + 1] # Check visibility using shadow map if isoccluded(rayorigin, raydirection, tstart, tend, shadowmapdata): continue if lighttype == "directional": termstart = analyticdirectionalintegral(tstart) termend = analyticdirectionalintegral(tend) contribution = termend - termstart elif lighttype == "omnidirectional": # Map cos^-1(v. l) to 2D space, evaluate differential, numerically integrate cosangle = math.acos(dotproduct(raydirection, normalize(lightdirection))) lookupval = samplelookuptexture(cosangle) contribution = numericalintegralomni(tstart, tend, lookupval) elif lighttype == "spot": # Cone intersection to clamp interval if checkconeintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, tstart, tend, lightdirection, spotangle): # Newton-Cotes integration for variable falloff contribution = newtoncotesintegration(tstart, tend, lightfalloff) else: contribution = 0.0 else: contribution = 0.0 # Apply attenuation to light reaching the camera in the media totalradiance += contribution math.exp(-extinctioncoefficient (tend - tstart)) return totalradiance def analyticdirectionalintegral(d): # L'S(d) = L(d, l) rhom (1 - exp(-tauex d)) / tauex return lightintensity mediumreflectance (1.0 - math.exp(-extinctioncoefficient d)) / extinctioncoefficient def rayplaneintersect(origin, direction, face): # Standard ray-plane intersection returning distance t return 0.0 def isoccluded(origin, direction, tstart, tend, shadowmapdata): # Sample shadow map at entry and exit points return False def normalize(v): return [x / math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in v)) for x in v] def dotproduct(v1, v2): return sum(ab for a,b in zip(v1, v2)) def samplelookuptexture(cosangle): # Lookup precomputed differential values return 0.0 def numericalintegralomni(tstart, tend, lookupval): # Numerical integration using Compute Shader results or precomputed table return 0.0 def checkconeintersection(origin, direction, tstart, tend, lightdir, angle): # Check if ray segment intersects light cone return True def newtoncotesintegration(tstart, tend, falloff): # Newton-Cotes numerical integration return 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shadow Map Inconsistencies: If only front faces are rendered to the shadow map, or if distant occluders are excluded, artifacts appear. Ensure shadow map contents are consistent with scene geometry (e.g., render both front and back faces if needed). Temporal AA Jitter: Temporal AA jitter causes flickering in down-sampled buffers. Add a separate TAA resolve to down-sampled buffers before compositing. High-Frequency Occluders: Performance drops at low angles due to dense occluders. Adjust tessellation factor based on view angle and pre-filter shadow maps. A method to compute the inscattering integral for a point light source by reducing the integral to a function of three variables (h, Sc, So) and using a 2D precomputed lookup table, avoiding the lack of a closed-form solution. It precomputes the inscattering integral for different values of h (distance from light to ray) and start distance Sc (signed distance from light projected position to camera) to infinity, storing results in a two-dimensional lookup table. The inscattering integral for a specific ray segment is computed as the integral from the camera towards infinity minus the integral from the object towards infinity, with attenuation applied to the light reaching the camera in the media. The phase function p(\theta) is assumed to be normalized to unity such that \frac{1}{4\pi} \frac{dp(\theta)}{dw} = 1 where integration is performed over the whole set of directions w. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of intervals (intersections with light volume) and the complexity of the light type. Directional lights are O(1) per interval (analytic). Omnidirectional and spot lights require lookup or numerical integration, which is more expensive. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the light volume mesh, shadow maps, and lookup textures for omnidirectional/spot lights. Performance: Fast enough for entire spec range and flexible enough for almost any engine. Compatible with physically-based engines and available in DirectX 11. Strengths: Analytic solution for directional lights is efficient. Handles complex light types via lookups and numerical integration. Limitations: Shadow map inconsistencies can cause artifacts. Temporal jitter requires additional resolve steps. High-frequency occluders can cause performance drops. When to Use: Real-time volumetric light scattering in games and interactive applications, particularly when directional lighting is dominant. Originated from work on volumetric light scattering in real-time rendering, specifically integrated into the game Fallout 4. The method builds on earlier analytic single scattering models. It was developed to provide a fast, flexible, and physically-based solution for volumetric lighting in modern game engines. Volumetric Light Scattering in Fallout 4, https://www.scribd.com/document/748135006/Fast-Flexible-Physically-Based-Volumetric-Light-Scattering, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) High-Performance Light Scattering Rendering, https://www.scribd.com/document/748135031/822368Yusov-Egor-Practical-Implementation-of-Light, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: CPU Volume Raycasting
head: CPU Ray Casting
body: CPU Volume Raycasting is a direct volume rendering technique that computes the volume rendering integral by casting rays from the camera through each pixel into a voxel grid, accumulating color and opacity using front-to-back compositing. It is distinguished from GPU-based raycasting by its explicit multithreaded pixel processing on the CPU and from sibling discretization methods by its specific implementation of trilinear interpolation and early ray termination. Unlike Eye Align which optimizes sampling positions, or Partial Pre-Integration which approximates integration over steps, this method performs per-sample evaluation with standard compositing. Inputs: Volume Data: A 3D grid of scalar values (density/intensity). Transfer Functions: Two 1D lookup tables mapping scalar values to RGBA color and opacity. Camera Parameters: Position, orientation (Euler angles or quaternion), and field of view. Lighting: Light direction and Phong lighting coefficients (ambient + diffuse). Rendering Settings: Step size, opacity multiplier, and alpha threshold for early termination. Outputs: Image Buffer: A 2D array of RGB pixels (8-bit per channel). Volume Data Layout: The volume is stored as a 3D array. Two distinct layouts are observed in source implementations: 1. Slice-based (S1): int[zSize][] where volumes[z] is a 1D array of size width width. Values are extracted from a 2D source image by masking the alpha channel: 0x00ffffff & imageInPixels[i + idi]. 2. Flat Row-Major (G): A std::vector<uint8t> within a Volume struct containing width, height, and depth. Data is stored in row-major order: data[x + y width + z width height]. Transfer Function Layout: Stored as two 1D integer arrays: int[] transferrgb and int[] transfera, typically loaded from 2D PNG images. In standard implementations, a lookup function transferFunction->lookup(val) returns a struct with.rgb and.a fields. Ray Structure: A Ray struct contains origin (Vector3) and direction (Vector3), where Vector3 has fields x, y, z (float). Pixel Buffer: A std::vector<uint8t> with 3 components per pixel (RGB). The index for pixel (i, j) in an image of width is (j width + i) 3. Rotation Matrix: Camera orientation is defined by Euler angles (roll, pitch, yaw). These are converted to a quaternion q[4]: \begin{aligned} c1 &= \cos(\text{yaw}/2), & s1 &= \sin(\text{yaw}/2) \\ c2 &= \cos(\text{pitch}/2), & s2 &= \sin(\text{pitch}/2) \\ c3 &= \cos(\text{roll}/2), & s3 &= \sin(\text{roll}/2) \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} q[0] &= c1 c2 c3 - s1 s2 s3 \\ q[1] &= c1 c2 s3 + s1 s2 c3 \\ q[2] &= s1 c2 c3 + c1 s2 s3 \\ q[3] &= c1 s2 c3 - s1 c2 s3 \end{aligned} The quaternion is then converted to a 3x3 rotation matrix M flattened to 9 numbers: \begin{aligned} M[0] &= 2(q0^2 + q1^2) - 1, & M[1] &= 2(q1 q2 - q0 q3), & M[2] &= 2(q1 q3 + q0 q2) \\ M[3] &= 2(q1 q2 + q0 q3), & M[4] &= 2(q0^2 + q2^2) - 1, & M[5] &= 2(q2 q3 - q0 q1) \\ M[6] &= 2(q1 q3 - q0 q2), & M[7] &= 2(q2 q3 + q0 q1), & M[8] &= 2(q0^2 + q3^2) - 1 \end{aligned} Intensity Mapping (S1 Specific): Precomputed squared and cubed values for intensity mapping are stored in arrays squared[256] and cubed[256]: \text{squared}[i] = \frac{(i/256.0)^2}{3.0}, \quad \text{cubed}[i] = (i/256.0)^3 \quad \text{for } i \in [0, 255] 1. Initialization: Split the image into tiles for multithreading. A common configuration is a 4x4 grid of tiles. For each tile (a, b), define bounds: startA = a width / 4, endA = startA + width / 4, startB = b height / 4, endB = startB + height / 4. Initialize ray origin and direction for each pixel (i, j) within the tile. Check intersection with the volume's bounding sphere. If no intersection, skip the pixel. Set ray parameter t to the entry point t0. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate while t < t1 (exit point) and accumulatedalpha < 0.99f (early termination threshold). Calculate sample point p = ray.origin + ray.direction t. Sampling: Map p to voxel coordinates, apply rotation matrix, and clamp to bounds. Retrieve value v from volumes[z][x + y width]. Handle out-of-bounds coordinates by clamping indices or returning 0. Transfer Function Lookup: Map val to color c and opacity a{sample} using the transfer function. Apply global opacity multiplier: asample = asample settings.opacity. Lighting: Compute gradient using central differences of neighboring voxels. Normalize gradient. Compute diffuse lighting: diffuse = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0). Combine ambient and diffuse to modulate color. Compositing (Front-to-Back): Update accumulated color Cout and alpha alphaout: \begin{aligned} C{out} &= C{in} + (1 - \alpha{in}) \cdot a{sample} \cdot c \\ \alpha{out} &= \alpha{in} + (1 - \alpha{in}) \cdot a{sample} \end{aligned} where C{in} and \alpha{in} are the accumulated values before this step. Step Advance: Increment t by settings.stepSize. Note: S1 uses a fixed step of 0.75 in its loop c += 0.75. S2 uses settings.stepSize, typically derived from rayLength / (samplingRate rayLength). 3. Finalization: Clamp final color components to [0, 1]. Convert to 8-bit integers: pixel[idx + k] = (uint8t)(min(color[k], 1.0f) 255) for k \in \{0, 1, 2\}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Vector3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Vector3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def mul(self, scalar): return Vector3(self.x scalar, self.y scalar, self.z scalar) def rmul(self, scalar): return self.mul(scalar) def cpuvolumeraycasting(volume, transferfunc, camera, light, settings, width, height, uselighting): pixels = [0] (width height 3) rotmatrix = eulertorotationmatrix(camera.roll, camera.pitch, camera.yaw) tilesizex = width // 4 tilesizey = height // 4 threads = [] for a in range(4): for b in range(4): startx = a tilesizex endx = startx + tilesizex starty = b tilesizey endy = starty + tilesizey threads.append(lambda sx=startx, ex=endx, sy=starty, ey=endy: rendertile( volume, transferfunc, camera, light, settings, sx, ex, sy, ey, width, height, pixels, rotmatrix, uselighting)) for t in threads: t() return pixels def rendertile(volume, transferfunc, camera, light, settings, startx, endx, starty, endy, width, height, pixels, rotmatrix, uselighting): for j in range(starty, endy): for i in range(startx, endx): rayorigin, raydirection = getrayforpixel(i, j, camera, width, height) t0, t1 = intersectsphere(rayorigin, raydirection, volume.boundingsphere) if t0 is None: continue t = t0 acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 while t < t1 and accalpha < 0.99: p = rayorigin + raydirection t val = volumesample(volume, p, rotmatrix) sample = transferfunc.lookup(val) samplecolor = sample.rgb samplealpha = sample.a settings.opacity if uselighting: normal = volumecomputegradient(volume, p) normal = normalize(normal) diffuse = max(dot(normal, light.direction), 0.0) samplecolor = samplecolor (light.ambient + light.diffuse diffuse) weight = (1.0 - accalpha) samplealpha acccolor[0] += weight samplecolor[0] acccolor[1] += weight samplecolor[1] acccolor[2] += weight samplecolor[2] accalpha += weight t += settings.stepsize idx = (j width + i) 3 pixels[idx] = int(min(acccolor[0], 1.0) 255) pixels[idx+1] = int(min(acccolor[1], 1.0) 255) pixels[idx+2] = int(min(acccolor[2], 1.0) 255) def volumesample(volume, p, rotmatrix): # Apply rotation matrix (flattened 9 floats) to point p rx = rotmatrix[0]p.x + rotmatrix[1]p.y + rotmatrix[2]p.z ry = rotmatrix[3]p.x + rotmatrix[4]p.y + rotmatrix[5]p.z rz = rotmatrix[6]p.x + rotmatrix[7]p.y + rotmatrix[8]p.z ix, iy, iz = int(rx), int(ry), int(rz) if not volume.isinside(ix, iy, iz): return 0.0 # Nearest-neighbor sampling as per S1 return volume.data[ix + iy volume.width + iz volume.width volume.height] def volumecomputegradient(volume, p): # Central differences as per S1 ix, iy, iz = int(p.x), int(p.y), int(p.z) def getval(x, y, z): if not volume.isinside(x, y, z): return 0.0 return volume.data[x + y volume.width + z volume.width volume.height] / 255.0 gradx = getval(ix+1, iy, iz) - getval(ix-1, iy, iz) grady = getval(ix, iy+1, iz) - getval(ix, iy-1, iz) gradz = getval(ix, iy, iz+1) - getval(ix, iy, iz-1) return Vector3(gradx, grady, gradz) def eulertorotationmatrix(roll, pitch, yaw): c1, s1 = math.cos(yaw/2), math.sin(yaw/2) c2, s2 = math.cos(pitch/2), math.sin(pitch/2) c3, s3 = math.cos(roll/2), math.sin(roll/2) q0 = c1c2c3 - s1s2s3 q1 = c1c2s3 + s1s2c3 q2 = s1c2c3 + c1s2s3 q3 = c1s2c3 - s1c2s3 return [ 2(q0q0 + q1q1) - 1, 2(q1q2 - q0q3), 2(q1q3 + q0q2), 2(q1q2 + q0q3), 2(q0q0 + q2q2) - 1, 2(q2q3 - q0q1), 2(q1q3 - q0q2), 2(q2q3 + q0q1), 2(q0q0 + q3q3) - 1 ] def getrayforpixel(i, j, camera, width, height): aspect = width / height fov = camera.fov ndcx = (2.0 (i + 0.5) / width) - 1.0 ndcy = 1.0 - (2.0 (j + 0.5) / height) raydir = Vector3(ndcx aspect math.tan(fov/2), ndcy math.tan(fov/2), -1.0) raydir = normalize(raydir) return camera.position, raydir def intersectsphere(origin, direction, sphere): oc = origin - sphere.center a = dot(direction, direction) b = 2.0 dot(oc, direction) c = dot(oc, oc) - sphere.radius sphere.radius disc = bb - 4ac if disc < 0: return None, None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t0 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a) t1 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a) if t0 < 0: t0 = max(t0, 0.0) return t0, t1 def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(v.xv.x + v.yv.y + v.zv.z) if l == 0: return Vector3(0,0,0) return Vector3(v.x/l, v.y/l, v.z/l) def dot(v1, v2): return v1.xv2.x + v1.yv2.y + v1.zv2.z Step Size (settings.stepSize): Distance between samples. In S1, calculated as 1.0 when samplingRate=1. In standard implementations, a configurable setting. Opacity Multiplier (settings.opacity): Global scalar applied to sample opacity from the transfer function. Alpha Threshold: Termination condition for early ray casting. Typically 0.99f. Ray Length: Diagonal length of the volume bounding box. In S1, approximated as width sqrt(2). Volume Distortion: If the source image is not square or height is not a multiple of width, the derived volume shape (zSize = height / width) may be distorted or truncated. Out-of-Bounds Sampling: If coordinates fall outside the volume bounds, implementations clamp indices or return 0. This affects interpolation weights at edges. Aliasing: S1 explicitly states "no pixel interpolation," relying on nearest-neighbor access which causes aliasing/blocky artifacts at oblique angles. Standard implementations use trilinear interpolation to mitigate this. Color Overflow: Final color values must be clamped to [0, 1] before 8-bit conversion to prevent overflow. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels, M is the number of samples per ray (determined by volume depth and step size), and S is the cost of sampling/compositing per sample. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, where V is the number of voxels. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Full control over rendering pipeline on CPU; supports complex transfer functions and Phong lighting without GPU shader constraints; suitable for interactive systems where GPU resources are unavailable or insufficient. Limitations: Prone to aliasing if step size is large or interpolation is poor; no built-in acceleration structures (like BVH) in the basic implementations described, leading to uniform sampling. When to Use: Interactive direct volume rendering on CPU-only systems; educational implementations; scenarios requiring custom lighting or transfer function logic not easily expressible in shaders. When Not to Use: High-performance real-time rendering of large volumes; scenes requiring complex light transport (e.g., full in-scattering) without approximation. CPU Volume Raycasting originated as a foundational technique in Direct Volume Rendering (DVR), allowing visualization of 3D scalar fields on standard hardware before GPU compute shaders became prevalent. The specific implementations cited here represent independent open-source projects: Pure CPU Direct Volume Rendering: Developed by Tomasz Hachaj, this implementation emphasizes a pure CPU approach with quaternion-based rotation and Phong lighting, explicitly avoiding 3rd party libraries and GPU acceleration. VTK CPU Mapper: The vtkVolumeRayCastMapper and vtkVolumeRayCastCompositeFunction provide a standardized CPU-based ray casting pipeline with configurable composite functions, shading coefficients (ambient=0.5, diffuse=1.0, specular=0.5, specularPower=25), and linear interpolation. These methods build upon the theoretical framework of the Volume Rendering Integral discretization [831-volume-raycasting-discretization.md], applying it via explicit ray marching loops on the CPU. browarsoftware/directvolumerenderingcpu, https://github.com/browarsoftware/directvolumerenderingcpu, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) manishaa1704/Interactive-DVR-System, https://github.com/manishaa1704/Interactive-DVR-System, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) chapering/PyVolRender, https://github.com/chapering/PyVolRender, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) superfan666/vtk-based-volume-rendering, https://github.com/superfan666/vtk-based-volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Average Intensity Projection
head: AIP, Average Depth, Average Intensity, Average Intensity Ray Traversal, Average Projection, Mean Density Projection, Ray Traversal -Average
body: Average Intensity Projection (AIP) is a ray traversal scheme that computes the image by averaging the scalar intensities of voxels along rays through the volume onto the image plane. It produces an X-ray-like picture equivalent to an additive reprojection. Unlike front-to-back compositing, AIP treats the volume as a transparent medium where every sample contributes equally to the final pixel value, making it computationally inexpensive but prone to low contrast and obscured structural details. Inputs: Volume Data: A 3D grid of scalar values. Sources describe two common layouts: 1. 3D Texture: Dimensions X \times Y \times Z (e.g., 256 \times 256 \times 109), stored in a GLTEXTURE3D with GLRGBA internal format but GLRED base format, using GLUNSIGNEDBYTE type. 2. Raw Array: 1D array of unsigned char values with dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz, stored in row-major order. Camera/View: Defined by a view position (viewPos) and a bounding box for the volume (e.g., min vec3(-1.0), max vec3(1.0) or centered at volume origin). Parameters: numsteps: Fixed number of sampling steps along the ray (e.g., 256). scale: Scaling factor for output image dimensions (ImageWidth = VolumeWidth \times scale). isoSurf: Optional uniform float for isosurface extraction mode, processed as iso = isoSurf - floor(isoSurf). Outputs: Image: A 2D grid of pixel values. Format: unsigned char (0-255 range). Dimensions: Scaled width and height. Value: The arithmetic mean of the sampled voxel intensities along the ray. Ray: Defined by origin or and direction dir. Transfer Function (Optional): A 1D texture (GLTEXTURE1D) mapping scalar values to color/opacity. In some implementations, color is accumulated per sample; in others, the mean scalar is mapped to color at the end. Accumulators: totalVoxelValue or meanSum: Accumulates the sum of sampled intensities. cnt or validSamples: Counts the number of valid samples taken. 1. Initialize: For each pixel, initialize totalVoxelValue = 0.0 and cnt = 1 (to avoid division by zero). 2. Ray Setup: Compute ray origin fpos (fragment position) and direction direction = normalize(fpos - viewPos). Alternatively, for orthographic projections, map pixel coordinates to volume space: originalX = pixelX / scale, originalY = pixelY / scale, with ray origin at (originalX, originalY, 0) and direction (0, 0, 1). 3. Intersection (Perspective): Intersect the ray with the volume bounding box to find entry (tenter) and exit (texit) distances using the slab method. 4. Step Calculation: Calculate ray length dist = distance(entry, exit) and step size stepsize = dist / numsteps. 5. Sampling Loop: Iterate i from 0 to numsteps - 1: Increment counter cnt++. Determine sample position curPos along the ray. Coordinate Transformation: Scale Z-coordinate if necessary: tmp.z = curPos.z 2.3486238532110093 (to handle non-isotropic data or texture normalization). Map to texture coordinates: texPos = (1 + tmp) / 2. Invert Y-axis: texPos.y = 1 - texPos.y (due to image data inversion). Sampling: Fetch value val = texture(texVol, texPos).x. Accumulation: If using raw array indexing (orthographic case): Translate sample to volume center, apply rotation matrix, translate back, check bounds, compute linear index, and fetch voxelIntensity = vol.data[index] / 255.0f. Add to sum: totalVoxelValue += val (or voxelIntensity). Advance: curPos = curPos + direction stepsize. 6. Finalize: Compute the average: meanValue = totalVoxelValue / cnt. 7. Color Mapping: Map meanValue to a final color using a transfer function or color map. If lighting is enabled, calculate normals from the mean position and apply lighting. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def averageintensityprojection(volumedata, viewpos, imagewidth, imageheight, numsteps=256, scale=1.0, fovdeg=60.0): """ Renders an Average Intensity Projection of a 3D volume. Args: volumedata: 3D array of shape (Z, Y, X) with values in [0, 1] viewpos: Camera position (list/tuple of 3 floats) imagewidth: Output image width imageheight: Output image height numsteps: Number of samples per ray scale: Scaling factor for image dimensions relative to volume fovdeg: Field of view in degrees for perspective projection Returns: imagedata: 2D array of floats (0.0 to 1.0) representing average intensity """ imagedata = [[0.0 for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] # Define bounding box for intersection (example: unit cube centered at origin) bboxmin = [-1.0, -1.0, -1.0] bboxmax = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): direction = computeraydirection(x, y, imagewidth, imageheight, fovdeg) result = intersectbox(viewpos, direction, bboxmin, bboxmax) if result is None: continue tenter, texit = result dist = texit - tenter stepsize = dist / numsteps totalvalue = 0.0 count = 1 # Avoid division by zero currentpos = [ viewpos[0] + direction[0] tenter, viewpos[1] + direction[1] tenter, viewpos[2] + direction[2] tenter ] for in range(numsteps): count += 1 # Coordinate transformation tmp = [currentpos[0], currentpos[1], currentpos[2] 2.3486238532110093] texpos = [(1.0 + tmp[0]) / 2.0, (1.0 + tmp[1]) / 2.0, (1.0 + tmp[2]) / 2.0] texpos[1] = 1.0 - texpos[1] # Invert Y-axis val = samplevolume(volumedata, texpos) totalvalue += val currentpos = [ currentpos[0] + direction[0] stepsize, currentpos[1] + direction[1] stepsize, currentpos[2] + direction[2] stepsize ] meanvalue = totalvalue / count # Compute average imagedata[y][x] = meanvalue return imagedata def computeraydirection(pixelx, pixely, imgw, imgh, fovdeg=60.0): aspect = imgw / imgh fovrad = math.radians(fovdeg) halfh = math.tan(fovrad / 2.0) halfw = halfh aspect dx = (pixelx / imgw - 0.5) 2.0 halfw dy = (0.5 - pixely / imgh) 2.0 halfh dirvec = [dx, dy, -1.0] length = math.sqrt(dirvec[0]2 + dirvec[1]2 + dirvec[2]2) return [dirvec[0]/length, dirvec[1]/length, dirvec[2]/length] def intersectbox(origin, direction, minb, maxb): tmin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0.0: if origin[i] < minb[i] or origin[i] > maxb[i]: return None tmin[i] = -float('inf') tmax[i] = float('inf') else: tmin[i] = (minb[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmax[i] = (maxb[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tenter = max(tmin[0], tmin[1], tmin[2]) texit = min(tmax[0], tmax[1], tmax[2]) if tenter > texit: return None if texit < 0: return None if tenter < 0: tenter = 0 return tenter, texit def samplevolume(volumedata, texcoords): c = [max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) for v in texcoords] zidx = int(c[2] (len(volumedata) - 1)) yidx = int(c[1] (len(volumedata[0]) - 1)) xidx = int(c[0] (len(volumedata[0][0]) - 1)) return volumedata[zidx][yidx][xidx] Division by Zero: The sample counter cnt is initialized to 1 and incremented before sampling to ensure color /= cnt never divides by zero. Coordinate Inversion: The texture Y-coordinate must be inverted (1 - texPos.y) because image data is often inverted on the Y-axis. Non-Isotropic Data: The Z-coordinate may require scaling by a specific constant (e.g., 2.3486238532110093) before mapping to texture space to handle non-isotropic voxels or specific normalization requirements. Low Contrast: Additive projection techniques suffer from a confused or unclear appearance because all information is projected, resulting in very little contrast to distinguish gradual variations or small abrupt changes. Occlusion: Unlike front-to-back compositing, AIP does not handle obscuration, which can hide structural details. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, where V is the number of voxels. Performance: Very fast due to the lack of complex compositing (opacity/alpha blending) and lighting calculations. Strengths: Simple implementation, fast rendering, useful for quick overviews or X-ray-like visualizations. Limitations: Low contrast, no depth cues from occlusion, sensitive to noise and background clutter. When to Use: When speed is critical and depth perception is not required, or for initial data exploration. When Not to Use: When detailed structural visualization, depth cues, or high contrast is needed. Average Intensity Projection, also known as additive reprojection, was developed by Hohne et al. for medical imaging applications, specifically stereotactic neurosurgery planning. It is one of their generalized projection images, designed to directly image the volume of data without surface shading. The technique is equivalent to an X-ray projection through the volume. It is often contrasted with techniques that use partial volume effects for surface shading or segmentation. Volume Rendering Volume Rendering. Lecture 21. Acknowledgements.
