name: Differential Sampling
head: Differential construction of T
body: Differential sampling is a ray discretization strategy for volume raycasting that adapts the sampling density along a ray based on the view-dependent frequency of the image plane, ensuring the sampling rate respects the Nyquist limit. Unlike uniform sampling methods, it uses a quadratic sampling function T(x) derived from ray differentials, allowing variable step sizes that are finer near the viewpoint and coarser further away, which prevents aliasing for features close to the camera. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera origin \vec{o}, central view direction \vec{w}, right vector \vec{u}, up vector \vec{v}, image plane resolution (\Delta x, \Delta y), scaling factor sk, volume data structure, and exit distance D{\text{exit}}. Outputs: A sequence of sample positions \vec{P}i along the ray and their corresponding transfer function evaluations. Data Structures: The method maintains the following state variables per ray during iteration: \vec{P}: Current 3D sample position. \vec{D}: Unitized ray direction vector. x: Current image-space coordinate index (integer). \Delta t: Current step size (derivative of T with respect to x). T: Cumulative distance along the ray corresponding to image coordinate x. maxtsampled: Greatest t value already sampled. Exact memory layouts and bit packing are not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Generate the ray direction vector \vec{d} for pixel coordinates (x, y) using the pinhole camera model. 2. Unitize the ray direction to obtain \vec{D}. 3. Compute the partial derivative of \vec{D} with respect to the image-space coordinate x. 4. Calculate the scalar coefficients k, a, and b based on the pixel footprint and differential magnitude. 5. Initialize the sampling state at x=0. 6. Iterate along the ray: sample the volume, handle macrocell entry boundaries, and increment the position and step size. Formulas: Ray generation: \vec{d}(x, y) = \vec{w} + x\vec{u} + y\vec{v}. Ray unitization: \vec{D}(x, y) = \vec{d} / \sqrt{\vec{d} \cdot \vec{d}}. Ray differential vector: \frac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial x} = \frac{(\vec{d} \cdot \vec{d})\vec{u} - (\vec{d} \cdot \vec{u})\vec{d}}{(\vec{d} \cdot \vec{d})^{3/2}}. Step size multiplier: k = sk |\vec{u}\Delta x + \vec{v}\Delta y|. Quadratic coefficients: a = k \left| \frac{\partial \vec{D}}{\partial x} \right|, b = k. Sampling function: T(x) = \frac{a}{2}x^2 + bx. Step size derivative: \frac{\partial T}{\partial x} = ax + b. Position update: \vec{P}{n+1} = \vec{P}n + \Delta tn \vec{D}. Step size update: \Delta t{n+1} = \Delta tn + a. Macrocell entry coordinate: x{\text{enter}} = \frac{-b + \sqrt{b^2 + 2aT{\text{enter}}}}{a}. Parameters: sk: Scaling factor for k. Typical value: 4. Theoretical Nyquist limit requires sk < 0.5, but this is excessive in practice. k0: Constant combining k and geometric factors. If k is arbitrarily chosen, k0 = k. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. d = w + xu + yv D = d / sqrt(dot(d, d)) Ddx = ((dot(d, d) u) - (dot(d, u) d)) / (dot(d, d) 1.5) magDdx = sqrt(dot(Ddx, Ddx)) k = sk sqrt(dot(udx + vdy, udx + vdy)) a = k magDdx b = k x = 0 dt = b P = o T = 0.0 maxtsampled = -inf # Guard for macrocell entry duplicates while P is inside volume and T < Dexit: # Sample volume at current position samplevolume(P) # Handle macrocell entry if crossing boundary if enteringnewmacrocell(Tenter): xenter = (-b + sqrt(b2 + 2aTenter)) / a x = floor(xenter) dt = b + a x T = 0.5 a x2 + b x P = o + T D maxtsampled = max(maxtsampled, T) # Increment per source equations P = P + dt D dt = dt + a x = x + 1 T = 0.5 a x2 + b x Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Duplicate Samples at Macrocell Boundaries: When entering a new macrocell, the sampling sequence might overlap with previously visited space. To avoid duplicate samples, store the greatest t already sampled and use the maximum of that value and T{\text{enter}}. Nyquist Limit: Using sk < 0.5 satisfies the Nyquist limit theoretically but is computationally expensive. sk=4 is a practical default. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples per ray. The number of samples adapts to view-dependent frequency, generally higher near the viewpoint and lower further away. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray for state variables. Strengths: Respects the Nyquist frequency of the image plane, reducing aliasing artifacts for structures close to the viewpoint. Avoids adaptive branching, maintaining thread coherence on GPUs. Limitations: Requires computation of ray differentials (\partial \vec{D} / \partial x) per pixel. Purely adaptive methods based on local gradients perform poorly on GPUs due to poor thread coherence, though per-macrocell adaptation is supported. When to Use: High-quality volume rendering where aliasing is a concern, particularly for large volumes viewed from varying distances. When Not to Use: Real-time applications with strict performance constraints where uniform sampling is sufficient, or when the volume lacks high-frequency features near the camera. Differential sampling was introduced in the context of volume ray casting with peak finding, building on the concept of ray differentials originally formulated by Igehy. The method addresses the issue that regular sampling in world-space undersamples features close to the viewpoint relative to those further away, due to the convolution of the volume rendering integral during the transformation from world-space to image-space. It was implemented in a GLSL fragment shader framework for OpenGL. Volume Ray Casting with Peak Finding and Differential..., https://www.sci.utah.edu/~knolla/avrc.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: In-Scattering Integral Approximation via Riemann Sum
head: Discrete In-Scattering Integral, Riemann Sum In-Scattering
body: This method approximates the continuous influx of light energy scattered toward the eye (in-scattering) along a camera ray segment by discretizing the integral into a sum of small rectangular areas. It solves the problem that the in-scattering integral has no analytical solution for general volume shapes and lighting scenarios, necessitating numerical approximation. Inputs: Camera ray segment defined by parametric distances t0 (entry) and t1 (exit). Step size dx. Volume density field to determine light travel distance. Light source direction. Outputs: Approximated in-scattered radiance accumulated over the segment. Data Structures: Accumulator variable for total in-scattered light (scalar). Current position x along the ray (scalar). Light travel distance (scalar). Steps: 1. Initialize the total in-scattered light accumulator to zero. 2. Divide the camera ray segment contained within the volume boundaries (from t0 to t1) into smaller sub-segments of length dx. 3. For each sub-segment, identify the sample point x at the middle of the interval. 4. Evaluate the incident light radiance Li(x, \omega) at point x: shoot a ray from x in the direction of the light source to determine the distance light traveled through the volume. Apply Beer's law to the light travel distance to determine the remaining light energy at point x. Note that the basic Riemann sum description does not account for the scattering phase function, which is required for the full calculation of Li(x, \omega). 5. Compute the area of the rectangle for the current sub-segment as Li(x, \omega) \times dx. 6. Accumulate the contribution of each small segment to the total in-scattered light. 7. Return the accumulated sum as the approximation of the integral. Formula: The integral to approximate is: \int{x=t0}^{t1} Li(x, \omega) dx where Li(x, \omega) is the radiance scattered towards the eye direction \omega at point x on the segment between parametric distances t0 and t1. The Riemann sum approximation is: \sum{i} Li(xi, \omega) \cdot dx Parameters: dx: The width of the rectangles in the Riemann sum approximation. Smaller dx yields higher accuracy but increases processing time. Pitfalls: The integral has no analytical solution for general volume shapes and lighting scenarios. The basic Riemann sum description provided does not yet account for the scattering phase function, which is required for the full calculation of Li(x, \omega). Precision issues may arise if dx is too large, leading to significant deviation from the true area under the curve. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def approximateinscattering(t0, t1, dx, densityfunc, lightdirection, lightradiance): """ Approximates the in-scattering integral using a Riemann sum. Args: t0: Parametric distance where ray enters volume. t1: Parametric distance where ray exits volume. dx: Step size (width of rectangles). densityfunc: Function returning volume density at a point. lightdirection: Direction vector to the light source. lightradiance: Intensity of the light source. Returns: Approximated in-scattered radiance. """ totalinscattered = 0.0 numsteps = int((t1 - t0) / dx) for i in range(numsteps): x = t0 + (i + 0.5) dx # Shoot ray from x in light direction to find distance through volume # Integrate density along path to compute optical depth lighttraveldistance = 0.0 t = 0.0 step = 0.01 while t < 100.0: lighttraveldistance += densityfunc(x + lightdirection t) step t += step # Apply Beer's law to determine remaining light energy lix = lightradiance exp(-lighttraveldistance) totalinscattered += lix dx return totalinscattered This method approximates the in-scattering integral for volumetric clouds by discretizing the continuous light propagation equation into a Riemann sum using fixed-step ray marching. It distinguishes itself from general in-scattering approximations by explicitly assuming that 50% of scattered light propagates in the forward direction within a small solid angle (~0.0001 steradians), ignoring the remaining 50% to reduce computational cost. It builds on In-Scattering Integral Approximation via Riemann Sum by providing the specific physical assumptions and numerical simplifications (Maclaurin expansion) required for real-time GPU implementation. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sub-segments (N = (t1 - t0) / dx). Each sub-segment requires a light ray traversal, making the complexity O(N \cdot M) where M is the number of steps for the light ray traversal. Memory Complexity: Constant, O(1), as it only requires storing the accumulator and current position. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Accuracy scales inversely with dx; smaller dx yields higher accuracy but increases processing time linearly. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides a foundational approximation for in-scattering. Limitations: Does not account for the scattering phase function in its basic form; computationally expensive due to the nested ray traversal for light. When to use: When a basic approximation of in-scattering is sufficient. When not to use: When the scattering phase function is negligible or can be approximated differently (e.g., using Discrete Ray-Marching with Forward Scattering Approximation). The concept of using a Riemann sum to approximate the in-scattering integral is discussed in "An Introduction to Volume Rendering". The method is presented as a practical solution to the problem that the in-scattering integral has no analytical solution for general volume shapes and lighting scenarios. The source emphasizes that while the result is an approximation, it becomes closer to the true area under the curve as the width of the rectangles (dx) decreases. An Introduction to Volume Rendering, https://scratchapixel.com/lessons/3d-basic-rendering/volume-rendering-for-developers/intro-volume-rendering.html, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Discrete Ray-Marching with Forward Scattering Approximation
head: Ray-marching with light propagation approximation
body: This method approximates the in-scattering integral for volumetric clouds by discretizing the continuous light propagation equation into a Riemann sum using fixed-step ray marching. It distinguishes itself from general in-scattering approximations by explicitly assuming that 50% of scattered light propagates in the forward direction within a small solid angle (~0.0001 steradians), ignoring the remaining 50% to reduce computational cost. It builds on In-Scattering Integral Approximation via Riemann Sum by applying the forward scattering assumption and Maclaurin expansion for transmittance. Inputs: Voxel grid lighting data, passed to the GPU as a 3D texture. Ray marching step size \Delta s. Asymmetry factor g for the phase function. Surface transmittance parameters. Outputs: Final pixel color I{total} for each frame buffer point, comprising reflected and scattered light components. 3D Texture: Stores voxel grid lighting values. This structure enables hardware-accelerated trilinear interpolation to sample lighting values along the marching ray. Ray State: Contains current position s, accumulated transmittance, and accumulated incident light. Let s be the position along the ray, starting from the cloud surface. Let L(si) be the illumination at intermediate point i. Let Ti be the transmittance from the surface to point i. 1. Forward Scattering Assumption: 50% of light scatters in the forward direction within a small solid angle of approximately 0.0001 steradians. The remaining 50% is ignored. 2. Incident Light (I{inc}): Calculated as the summation of light emitted by scattering from each intermediate point i, attenuated by transmittance: I{inc} = \sumi L(si) \cdot Ti \cdot \Delta si 3. Total Light (I{total}): The sum of reflected and scattered light, both affected by transmittance from the surface to point s: I{total} = I{reflected} + I{scattered} Where I{reflected} depends on illumination L(s) and occluded area, and I{scattered} includes a phase function p(\theta). 4. Segment Integral Approximation: The continuous integral is converted to a summation of segment integrals. The phase term is considered constant along the segment and factored out. 5. Differential Transmittance (dT): Denoted as the differential transmittance along the segment. 6. Transmittance Approximation: The exponential function e^{-\tau} is approximated using the first two terms of its Maclaurin series expansion: e^{-\tau} \approx 1 - \tau This simplifies the segment integral calculation. 7. Phase Function: The Henyey–Greenstein function is used to approximate refraction of light in water droplets: p(\theta) = \frac{1-g^2}{(1+g^2-2g\cos\theta)^{3/2}} Where \theta is the scattering angle and g is the asymmetry factor. Step Size (\Delta s): The fixed distance between ray march steps. Asymmetry Factor (g): Parameter for the Henyey–Greenstein phase function. Solid Angle: Assumed to be ~0.0001 steradians for the forward scattering component. The following pseudocode implements the ray-marching pass described in. It defines all required helpers inline and uses standard vector operations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intersectaabb(origin, direction, boundsmin, boundsmax): """Standard ray-AABB intersection returning tmin and tmax.""" tmin = max((boundsmin[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] for i in range(3)) tmax = min((boundsmax[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] for i in range(3)) return tmin, tmax def raymarchcloud(rayorigin, raydirection, boundsmin, boundsmax, stepsize, g, lightingtex, lightsourcepos): """ Renders a cloud volume using discrete ray-marching with forward scattering approximation. """ tmin, tmax = intersectaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, boundsmin, boundsmax) if tmax < 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) sstart = rayorigin + raydirection tmin send = rayorigin + raydirection tmax totalreflected = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) totalscattered = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) currenttransmittance = 1.0 currentpos = sstart while currentpos < send: # Sample lighting using hardware-accelerated trilinear interpolation illumination = lightingtex.sample(currentpos) lightdir = normalize(lightsourcepos - currentpos) viewdir = -raydirection costheta = dot(lightdir, viewdir) numerator = 1.0 - g g denominator = 1.0 + g g - 2.0 g costheta phase = numerator / (denominator 1.5) forwardscatteringfactor = 0.5 scatteredcontribution = illumination phase forwardscatteringfactor currenttransmittance stepsize totalscattered += scatteredcontribution # Reflected light depends on illumination and occluded area, affected by transmittance occludedareafactor = 1.0 # Not given in sources reflectedcontribution = illumination occludedareafactor currenttransmittance stepsize totalreflected += reflectedcontribution # Update transmittance: e^(-tau) approx 1 - tau sigmat = 1.0 # Extinction coefficient not given in sources tau = sigmat stepsize currenttransmittance = (1.0 - tau) currentpos += raydirection stepsize return totalreflected + totalscattered Transmittance Approximation: The method uses the linear Maclaurin approximation e^{-\tau} \approx 1 - \tau for transmittance. Scattering Loss: The method ignores 50% of scattered light to save computation. Missing Details: Specific numerical stability constraints, extinction coefficient values, and occluded area calculations are not given in the sources. Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. Measured performance metrics are not given in the sources. Strengths: Computationally efficient due to the forward scattering approximation (ignoring 50% of scattering) and the Maclaurin series approximation for transmittance. Limitations: Less physically accurate due to the 50% scattering loss and the linear transmittance approximation. When to use is not given in the sources. When not to use is not given in the sources. The method is described in the paper "Efficient Algorithms for Real-Time GPU Volumetric Cloud Rendering with Enhanced Geometry". The approach builds upon previous work on light propagation and scattering approximations, specifically referencing [13] for the forward scattering assumption and [33] for the segment integral conversion. It is used for GPU volumetric cloud rendering. Efficient Algorithms for Real-Time GPU Volumetric Cloud Rendering with Enhanced Geometry, https://doi.org/10.3390/sym10040125, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Zero Order Integration (Rectangle Rule)
head: Riemann sum with rectangle rule, Standard Numerical Quadrature (Rectangle Rule)
body: Zero Order Integration approximates the continuous volume rendering integral by discretizing the ray into n segments and assuming the extinction coefficient and emission are constant within each segment, effectively evaluating a Riemann sum using the rectangle rule. It sets itself apart from higher-order methods like Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) Integration by ignoring field variation within the step, and from Partial Pre-Integration by not requiring pre-computed lookup tables for transfer functions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, near/far bounds t{near}, t{far} (or total length D), number of samples n, volume data function s(\mathbf{x}), transfer function g(s) (emission), and opacity/extinction function \tau(s). Output: Composite color C and accumulated opacity A (or transmittance T) for the pixel. Data Structures: Samples: An array of n positions along the ray. For uniform sampling, position i is ti = t{near} + i \cdot \Delta t, where \Delta t = (t{far} - t{near}) / n. Attributes: For each sample i, store density \sigmai (or extinction \taui) and color ci (or emission Ci). Steps: 1. Discretize the Ray: Divide the ray interval [0, D] into n equal segments of length \Delta x = D/n. Sample points are chosen as xi = i \Delta x for i=1 \dots n (or 0 \dots n-1 depending on indexing). 2. Evaluate Volume Properties: At each sample point xi, evaluate the volume density \sigmai = \sigma(\mathbf{x}(xi)) and color/emission ci (or pre-multiplied color). 3. Compute Segment Opacity: Calculate the opacity \alphai for the i-th segment. The exact form uses the exponential attenuation: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \Delta x). A common approximation for efficiency, valid when \sigmai \Delta x \ll 1, is: \alphai \approx \sigmai \Delta x. 4. Compute Transmittance: Calculate the accumulated transmittance Ti up to sample i. This represents the probability that light passes through all previous segments: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj). Note: T1 = 1. 5. Composite Color: Combine the contributions. The standard front-to-back compositing equation is: C{out} = \sum{i=1}^{n} Ti \alphai ci. Alternatively, back-to-front compositing can be used: C'i = \alphai ci + (1 - \alphai) C'{i+1} with C'{n+1} = 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zeroorderintegration(rayorigin, raydirection, volumesampler, nsamples, near, far): """ Approximates the volume rendering integral using the rectangle rule (zero-order hold). Args: rayorigin: (3,) array, ray origin. raydirection: (3,) array, normalized ray direction. volumesampler: callable, returns (density, color) at a 3D point. nsamples: int, number of segments. near: float, near plane distance. far: float, far plane distance. Returns: color: (3,) array, composite color. opacity: float, accumulated opacity. """ totaldist = far - near deltat = totaldist / nsamples # Pre-compute sample positions # Positions: near + deltat, near + 2deltat,..., far # Note: Some implementations use left endpoints (near + ideltat for i=0..n-1) # We use right endpoints or centers depending on convention; # Standard Riemann sum often uses sample point within segment. # Here we use the sample point at the start of the segment (left Riemann sum) # or end. S7 uses left endpoint for T(si) calculation in Iteration A. # S8 uses xi = idx. accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # Front-to-back iteration for i in range(nsamples): # Sample position t = near + (i + 0.5) deltat # Midpoint is often better, but S7/S8 imply left/right endpoints. # S7: si = iDeltaS (left endpoint). # Let's stick to left endpoint as per S7/S8 for consistency with "rectangle rule" definition. t = near + i deltat # Evaluate volume properties pos = rayorigin + raydirection t density, color = volumesampler(pos) # Compute opacity for this segment # Exact: alpha = 1 - exp(-density deltat) # Approx: alpha = density deltat (if small) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-density deltat) # Accumulate color # Contribution = Transmittance Alpha Color weight = accumulatedtransmittance alpha accumulatedcolor[0] += weight color[0] accumulatedcolor[1] += weight color[1] accumulatedcolor[2] += weight color[2] # Update transmittance for next segment accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Optional: Early ray termination if transmittance is negligible if accumulatedtransmittance < 1e-5: break accumulatedopacity = 1.0 - accumulatedtransmittance return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuities: The reconstructed signal is not C^0 continuous, leading to visible artifacts (staircasing) where density changes abruptly between samples. Approximation Error: The assumption of constant density/color within a segment causes significant error if the transfer function or density varies rapidly. Numerical Stability: When computing transmittance, adding a small epsilon (e.g., 10^{-10}) to (1 - \alpha) prevents numerical instability if \alpha is exactly 1.0. Early Termination: Front-to-back iteration supports early ray termination when transmittance becomes negligible, improving performance. Back-to-front does not. Uses four slope estimates to account for field variation within the step, providing higher accuracy than the constant assumption of the rectangle rule. Choose when density/refractive index varies significantly within a segment. Uses unequally weighted sums at unequally spaced points to achieve greater accuracy for smooth functions with the same number of samples. Choose when the transfer function and density vary smoothly. Time Complexity: O(n) per ray, where n is the number of samples. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray (excluding storage for the volume data). Performance: Fastest integration method due to simplicity and lack of pre-computation requirements. Accuracy: Low. It is a first-order approximation (piecewise constant). Accuracy improves linearly with n but suffers from aliasing and blockiness artifacts. Strengths: Simple to implement, no pre-computation needed, supports early ray termination. Limitations: Visible artifacts in high-frequency regions, inaccurate for non-linear transfer functions. When to use: Real-time rendering with limited sampling budget, or as a baseline method. When not to use: High-quality offline rendering, or when density/transfer functions vary rapidly within a single sample step. The method originates from standard numerical quadrature, specifically the Riemann sum using the rectangle rule. It is one of the simplest numerical integration techniques, historically used in early volume ray casting implementations due to its computational efficiency. It is widely cited in foundational volume rendering literature as the baseline for comparison against more advanced techniques like pre-integration. name: Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) Integration
head: Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4), RK4 method, RK4 integration, RK4 Integrator, Runge-Kutta 4 Integrator, 4th order Runge-Kutta, Runge-Kutta 4th order, Fourth Order Runge-Kutta, Order Four Runge-Kutta
body: Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) is a fourth-order explicit numerical integration method used to compute curved photon and ray trajectories in media with continuously varying properties, such as refractive index or flow velocity. It solves the initial value problem by taking four slope estimates within a single time step to reduce integration error over time, providing significantly higher accuracy than the first-order Euler method. It sets itself apart from its parent Zero Order Integration (Rectangle Rule) by accounting for the variation of the field within the step rather than assuming constancy, and from its sibling Gaussian Integration for Volume Rendering by using a deterministic weighted average of field samples rather than probabilistic sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current position p(t) (or xi), time step \Delta t (or \delta), and a vector field function f(p, t) (or \nu(x, t)) representing the derivative (e.g., velocity, gradient of refractive index). Output: New position p(t + \Delta t) (or x{i+1}). Data Structures: Position: A 3D vector (x, y, z). Slopes (k1, k2, k3, k4 or x1, x2, x3, x4): 3D vectors representing the field values at specific points. Time Step: A scalar value \Delta t. Formulas: The update rule for the position is: p(t + \Delta t) = p(t) + \frac{\Delta t}{6} (k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4) where the intermediate slopes are calculated as follows: For a steady flow field f(p): k1 = f(p(t)) k2 = f\left(p(t) + \frac{\Delta t}{2} k1\right) k3 = f\left(p(t) + \frac{\Delta t}{2} k2\right) k4 = f(p(t) + \Delta t \cdot k3) For an unsteady flow field f(p, t): k1 = f(p(t), t) k2 = f\left(p(t) + \frac{\Delta t}{2} k1, t + \frac{\Delta t}{2}\right) k3 = f\left(p(t) + \frac{\Delta t}{2} k2, t + \frac{\Delta t}{2}\right) k4 = f(p(t) + \Delta t \cdot k3, t + \Delta t) Note: In some formulations, the slopes ki include the multiplication by \Delta t (i.e., k1 = \Delta t \cdot f(p)), in which case the final update is p(t+\Delta t) = p(t) + \frac{1}{6}(k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4). The implementation below uses the form where ki are pure field derivatives, consistent with. Parameters: \Delta t: The time step size. Described as "small". In real-time applications, it is dynamic to maintain performance. t: Current time. For steady fields, this is ignored or fixed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rk4integrate(pos, dt, vectorfieldfunc, isunsteady=False, currenttime=0.0): """ Performs one step of Runge-Kutta 4 integration. Args: pos: Current position (vec3). dt: Time step size (float). vectorfieldfunc: Function f(p, t) returning vec3. isunsteady: Boolean flag for time-dependent fields. currenttime: Current time t (float). Returns: New position (vec3). """ # Step 1: Sample at current position k1 = vectorfieldfunc(pos, currenttime if isunsteady else 0.0) # Step 2: Sample at midpoint using k1 # Position: pos + (dt/2) k1 midpos1 = pos + (dt 0.5) k1 time1 = currenttime + (dt 0.5) if isunsteady else currenttime k2 = vectorfieldfunc(midpos1, time1) # Step 3: Sample at midpoint using k2 # Position: pos + (dt/2) k2 midpos2 = pos + (dt 0.5) k2 time2 = currenttime + (dt 0.5) if isunsteady else currenttime k3 = vectorfieldfunc(midpos2, time2) # Step 4: Sample at end using k3 # Position: pos + dt k3 endpos = pos + dt k3 time3 = currenttime + dt if isunsteady else currenttime k4 = vectorfieldfunc(endpos, time3) # Step 5: Weighted average # p(t + dt) = p(t) + (dt / 6) (k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4) weightedsum = k1 + (2.0 k2) + (2.0 k3) + k4 newpos = pos + (dt / 6.0) weightedsum return newpos Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unsteady Flow: Requires six texture reads (or function evaluations) instead of four because the flow field changes over time, requiring samples at intermediate time steps t + \Delta t/2 and t + \Delta t. Steady Flow: The time argument must be ignored or set to a fixed value. Precision: RK4 has an error of O(dt^5) per step, compared to O(dt^2) for Euler. However, it is approximately 4x slower than Euler. Vortices: RK4 stays within vortices better than Euler, but may sometimes converge to the center of vortices instead of escaping them. A numerical integration method used for volume deformation processes, specifically within tensor field visualization. name: Euler Integration
head: Euler Method, Forward Euler, Euler's Method, Explicit Euler, Euler Integrator, Order 1 Runge-Kutta, First-order Euler Integrator
body: Euler Integration is the most basic numerical method for solving initial value problems (IVPs) in vector fields, estimating the next state based on the derivative at the current single point. In volume rendering, it is numerically equivalent to traditional ray marching, where the radiance variation is evaluated using a single sample per segment. It serves as the baseline explicit integrator for streamline visualization and differential ray marching, distinguished from higher-order siblings like Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) Integration by its first-order accuracy and single-sample-per-step efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current position xn (or yi), vector field function v(x) (or derivative function f(y,t)), step size dt (or s). Output: Next position x{n+1} (or y{i+1}). Data Structures: Position: A 3D vector (e.g., double3 or float3) representing the current location in the volume. Vector Field: A 3D texture or grid storing the vector value at each voxel. Step Size: A scalar float representing the distance to march. Explicit Euler (Standard Ray Marching): The explicit method linearizes the Taylor series expansion, approximating the next position by moving along the vector field direction at the current position. 1. Sample the vector field at the current position xn. 2. Compute the displacement by multiplying the vector field value by the step size dt. 3. Add the displacement to the current position to get x{n+1}. Formula: x{n+1} = xn + dt \cdot v(xn) + O(dt^2) Where: xn is the current position. x{n+1} is the next position. dt is the time/step size. v(xn) is the vector field value at xn. O(dt^2) is the local truncation error per step. Implicit Euler (Backwards Euler): The implicit method replaces the explicit derivative evaluation with an implicit one at the next step to stabilize calculations in stiff regions. It solves a per-step system of equations. Formula: y{i+1} = yi + s \cdot f(y{i+1}, ti) Where: y{i+1} is the unknown value at the next step. yi is the current value. s is the step size. f is the derivative function evaluated at the next step's state y{i+1}. Algorithm (Explicit): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def eulerexplicit(pos, dt, vectorfieldsampler): """ Performs one step of explicit Euler integration. Args: pos: Current position (Vec3). dt: Step size (float). vectorfieldsampler: Function that returns vector (Vec3) at a given position. Returns: Next position (Vec3). """ # 1. Sample vector field at current position v = vectorfieldsampler(pos) # 2. Compute displacement: dt v displacement = v dt # 3. Return new position return pos + displacement Algorithm (Implicit): The implicit equation requires solving for y{i+1} using fixed-point iteration until the error is below a tolerance threshold. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def eulerimplicit(pos, dt, vectorfieldsampler, tolerance=1e-6, maxiterations=10): """ Performs one step of implicit Euler integration using fixed-point iteration. Args: pos: Current position (Vec3). dt: Step size (float). vectorfieldsampler: Function that returns vector (Vec3) at a given position. tolerance: Error threshold for convergence (float). maxiterations: Maximum number of fixed-point iterations (int). Returns: Next position (Vec3). """ # Initial guess: use explicit Euler result vcurrent = vectorfieldsampler(pos) nextpos = pos + vcurrent dt for i in range(maxiterations): # Evaluate derivative at the current estimate of the next position vnext = vectorfieldsampler(nextpos) # Calculate the new estimate based on the implicit formula: # y{i+1} = yi + s f(y{i+1}, ti) newnextpos = pos + vnext dt # Check for convergence error = (newnextpos - nextpos).length() if error < tolerance: return newnextpos nextpos = newnextpos # Return the last estimate if tolerance not reached return nextpos Parameters: Step size (s or dt): The distance between samples. Larger s results in faster calculation but lower accuracy. Fixed-point tolerance: The threshold for error in the fixed-point iteration for the implicit method. Configures the precision of the implicit solve. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: For inappropriately large step sizes, the error remains undesirably large even for higher-order schemes. Vortices: The Euler integrator tends to escape vortices even for very low time step values, whereas higher-order methods may converge to the center. Convergence: The implicit method may fail to converge to an adequate solution for bigger step sizes if the per-step error is too high. Stiffness: Explicit Euler is prone to instabilities in stiff regions; implicit Euler is used to overcome mathematical singularities (e.g., point lights) with little performance hit. A variant used for tracking white matter tracts in diffusion tensor imaging. It modifies the tracking process by taking both forward and backward steps from the seed point (reversing the time step sign \Delta t \to -\Delta t) to overcome the arbitrary choice between eigenvectors and their negatives when decomposing the tensor field. A numerical integration method for particle dynamics that is time-reversible and unconditionally stable, distinguishing it from Euler Integration by implicitly handling velocity through position differences. It updates particle positions based on current and previous positions without explicitly storing velocity. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per step. It requires only one vector field evaluation per step, making it the most efficient method for low accuracy requirements. Memory: O(1) auxiliary memory (storing current position and vector). Measured Performance: Euler is the most efficient method for low accuracies. Global error is proportional to the step size O(h), while local error is proportional to the square of the step size O(h^2). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simplest implementation (literally two lines of code), fastest execution per step, and numerically equivalent to traditional ray marching. Limitations: First-order accuracy leads to significant error accumulation over long paths; escapes vortices; unstable in stiff regions without implicit formulation. When to use/not use: Use as a baseline for comparison or when performance is critical and high accuracy is not required. Do not use when tracking complex flow features like vortices, as the Euler integrator tends to escape them even for very low time step values. Euler's method is the most basic numerical method for initial value problems, widely documented in existing literature. It was introduced as a standard technique for solving ordinary differential equations and has been applied in volume rendering as "traditional ray marching". It is used in streamline visualization and as a comparative baseline for more advanced integrators like Runge-Kutta methods. name: Verlet Integration
head: Position-Based Dynamics Integration, Störmer-Verlet, Velocity Verlet
body: Verlet Integration is a numerical integration method for particle dynamics that updates positions based on current and previous positions without explicitly storing velocity. It is time-reversible and unconditionally stable, distinguishing it from Euler Integration by implicitly handling velocity through position differences. Inputs: Current position pos Previous position oldPos Acceleration acc (accumulated from forces) Mass mass Damping factor damping (scalar, default 0.99) Pinned status pinned (boolean) Time step dt (squared as dt^2) Outputs: New position newPos Updated oldPos Reset acc to zero Data Structures: Each particle stores: pos: Vec3 (current position) oldPos: Vec3 (previous position) acc: Vec3 (accumulated acceleration) mass: float pinned: bool Steps: 1. If pinned is true, return immediately without updating. 2. Apply forces to calculate acceleration: acc = acc + force / mass. 3. Store current position in temporary variable: tempPos = pos. 4. Update position using the Verlet scheme: newPos = pos + (pos - oldPos) \times damping + acc \times dt^2 Note: The velocity term (pos - oldPos) is scaled by damping to simulate energy loss. 5. Update previous position: oldPos = tempPos. 6. Reset acceleration: acc = 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def verletstep(particle, force, damping, dtsq): if particle.pinned: return # Apply forces to acceleration particle.acc = particle.acc.addScaled(force, 1.0 / particle.mass) # Store current position tempPos = particle.pos.clone() # Calculate velocity term (pos - oldPos) velocity = particle.pos.sub(particle.oldPos) # Scale velocity by damping dampedVelocity = velocity.scale(damping) # Scale acceleration by squared timestep accelTerm = particle.acc.scale(dtsq) # Update position particle.pos = particle.pos.add(dampedVelocity).add(accelTerm) # Update old position particle.oldPos = tempPos # Reset acceleration particle.acc.set(0, 0, 0) Parameters: damping: Scalar multiplier for velocity term, default 0.99. dtsq: Squared time step value (dt^2). Edge Cases: Pinned particles do not update position or apply forces. Not given in the sources. Verlet Integration originates from particle dynamics simulations. name: Runge-Kutta 2/3 ODE Solver
head: Midpoint Method, Order 2 Runge-Kutta, Order Two Runge-Kutta, RK23, Runge-Kutta 2, Runge-Kutta 23
body: A 2nd/3rd order Runge-Kutta method for solving ODEs with adaptive step size control. It sets itself apart from its parent Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) Integration by using a lower-order formulation that requires fewer function evaluations per step, and from its sibling Dormand-Prince 5(4) Step by offering a balance of accuracy and performance with a minimum of four evaluations per step. Inputs: y: Current state vector (position/field value). w: Additional parameters (e.g., time, grid metadata). force: Function evaluating the derivative \frac{dy}{dt}. t: Current time/parameter. t{span}: End time/parameter. rtol: Relative tolerance (default 10^{-2}). atol: Absolute tolerance (default 10^{-4}). h{max}: Maximum step size (default 0.1 \times t{span}). Outputs: y{final}: State at t{span}. t{final}: Final time reached. Data Structures: Vectors k1, k2, k3, k4 of same dimension as y. Scalar h: Step size. Scalar e: Error estimate. Scalar er: Relative error. Steps: 1. Compute k1 = force(y, w). 2. Estimate initial error r using k1 and a threshold. 3. Initialize step size h = 0.8 \times rtol^{1/3} / r. 4. While t < t{span}: a. Clamp h to [h{min}, h{max}], where h{min} = 16 \times \text{FLOAT\MIN} \times |t|. b. If 1.1 \times h \ge t{span} - t, set h = t{span} - t. c. Compute k2 = force(y + (h/2)k1, w). d. Compute k3 = force(y + (3h/4)k2, w). e. Compute y{next} = y + (2h/9)k1 + (h/3)k2 + (4h/9)k3. f. Compute k4 = force(y{next}, w). g. Compute error estimate e = (-5k1 + 6k2 + 8k3 - 9k4) \times h / 72.0. h. Compute relative error er using e, \max(|y|, |y{next}|), and threshold. i. If er \le rtol: Accept step: t = t + h, y = y{next}, k1 = k4. Update h = h \times \min(5.0, 0.8 \times (rtol/er)^{1/3}). j. If h \le h{min}, break loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import sys def rk23solve(y, w, force, t, tspan, rtol=1e-2, atol=1e-4, hmax=None): if hmax is None: hmax = 0.1 tspan # Initial step setup k1 = force(y, w) # Estimate initial error r based on k1 and threshold r = max(abs(k1) / max(abs(y), atol, 1e-12)) h = 0.8 (rtol (1/3)) / r while t < tspan: # Clamp step size hmin = 16 sys.floatinfo.min abs(t) h = max(hmin, min(h, hmax)) # Adjust for end of span if 1.1 h >= tspan - t: h = tspan - t # Stage evaluations k2 = force(y + (h / 2) k1, w) k3 = force(y + (3 h / 4) k2, w) # 3rd order solution ynext = y + (2 h / 9) k1 + (h / 3) k2 + (4 h / 9) k3 # 2nd order error estimate stage k4 = force(ynext, w) # Error calculation e = (-5 k1 + 6 k2 + 8 k3 - 9 k4) h / 72.0 # Relative error maxval = max(abs(y), abs(ynext), atol) er = max(abs(e) / maxval) if er <= rtol: # Accept step t = t + h y = ynext k1 = k4 # Update step size h = h min(5.0, 0.8 (rtol / er) (1/3)) else: # Reject step, reduce h h = h 0.5 if h <= hmin: break return y, t A hybrid integration strategy that uses an adaptive Runge-Kutta integrator when the sphere radius S(\hat{x}) is large compared to the error threshold \hat{\epsilon}, and falls back to simple Euler integration when S(\hat{x}) is small to reduce overhead. It evaluates RKF45, DP54, and BS23, selecting BS23 for its balance of accuracy (minimum four evaluations per step) and performance. If S(\hat{x}) < a \cdot \hat{\epsilon} (where a=3), it falls back to forward Euler. Implicit solvers are avoided because the equations are not stiff, constant speed prevents runaway error, and implicit solvers incur difficult-to-control performance overhead compared to BS23's small minimum overhead. Automatically selects appropriate step sizes h during integration by comparing results from different h or approximation orders to estimate accuracy. It computes x(t+h) for different h or orders; if the error (e.g., angular deviation) exceeds a threshold, it repeats with decreased h. The error is measured as E(t; h0, h1) = 1 - (x(t + h0) - x(t)) \cdot (x(t + h1) - x(t)). This leads to an increased number of field evaluations but yields higher accuracy in turbulent regions. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of adaptive steps. Each accepted step requires a minimum of four function evaluations. Memory Complexity: O(d) where d is the dimension of the state vector, storing k1, k2, k3, k4 and intermediate states. Performance: BS23 requires a minimum of four evaluations per step, which is lower than RKF45 and DP54. Strengths: Balance of accuracy and performance; adaptive step size handles varying field complexity. Limitations: Increased field evaluations in turbulent regions compared to fixed-step methods. The method is based on the Bogacki-Shampine (BS23) scheme. It is used in volume rendering for ray trajectory integration, particularly in non-linear sphere tracing for rendering deformed signed distance fields. tink-expo/ntsl-graphics, https://github.com/tink-expo/ntsl-graphics, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Differential Ray Marching, https://doi.org/10.2312/localchapterevents/ceig/ceig12/091-098, fetched 2026-10-26 Non-linear sphere tracing for rendering deformed signed distance fields, https://doi.org/10.1145/3355089.3356502, fetched 2026-10-29 Multi-Field Visualization, https://kluedo.ub.rptu.de/files/2291/diss.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Trapezoidal Method
head: Euler-Trapezoidal, Predictor-corrector Trapezoidal, Quadrature Warp, V^q
body: The Trapezoidal Method is a second-order implicit predictor-corrector technique used for ray marching and integration in volume rendering. It solves the ordinary differential equation (ODE) governing light transport by combining the speed of an explicit Euler predictor with the accuracy of an implicit trapezoidal corrector. Unlike explicit methods, it can overcome black hole singularities caused by point lights, though it may fail to converge on non-stiff equations with large step sizes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current state yi (accumulated color/transmittance), current position ti, step size s, and derivative function f(y, t) (typically density or absorption coefficient). Output: Next state y{i+1}. Data Structures: Scalar values for yi, y{i+1}, ti, t{i+1}, s. Function f evaluating the integrand at a given position and state. Steps: 1. Predictor Step: Estimate y{i+1} using Euler's method to provide a fast initial guess. y{i+1}^{(0)} = yi + s \cdot f(yi, ti) 2. Corrector Step (Fixed-Point Iteration): Solve the implicit trapezoidal equation using the predictor as the initial value for iteration. y{i+1}^{(k+1)} = yi + \frac{s}{2} \left( f(yi, ti) + f(y{i+1}^{(k)}, ti + s) \right) Iterate until convergence or a maximum number of iterations is reached. Formula: The core implicit equation is: y{i+1} = yi + \frac{s}{2} (f(yi, ti) + f(y{i+1}, ti + s)) Where: y{i+1} is the unknown next state. yi is the current state. s is the step size. f is the derivative function (e.g., density). ti is the current position along the ray. Parameters: Step size s: Determined by adaptive step control or fixed marching. Convergence tolerance: Not specified in sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Convergence Failure: The method may not converge, particularly when the equation is not stiff or when step sizes are too large relative to the tolerance. Singularities: Implicit nature allows it to handle singularities (e.g., point lights) that break explicit methods. Bias: In the context of differentiable rendering, trapezoidal quadrature is a biased estimator of the integral, though it becomes consistent at silhouettes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trapezoidalmethod(yi, ti, s, f, maxiter=10, tol=1e-6): """ Perform one step of the Euler-Trapezoidal method. Args: yi: Current accumulated value (scalar or vector). ti: Current position along the ray. s: Step size. f: Function returning the derivative (e.g., density) at (y, t). maxiter: Maximum fixed-point iterations. tol: Convergence tolerance. Returns: yi+1: The updated accumulated value. """ # Predictor: Euler's method ypred = yi + s f(yi, ti) # Corrector: Fixed-point iteration ynext = ypred for k in range(maxiter): # Evaluate derivative at current estimate fnext = f(ynext, ti + s) fcurrent = f(yi, ti) # Update estimate using trapezoidal rule ynew = yi + (s / 2.0) (fcurrent + fnext) # Check convergence if abs(ynew - ynext) < tol: return ynew ynext = ynew # Return last estimate if not converged return ynext Estimates error by comparing solutions of different orders to adjust step size. A specific application in differentiable rendering where trapezoidal quadrature is used to define a continuous warp function that satisfies boundary consistency at silhouettes. Time Complexity: Slower than explicit methods due to fixed-point iteration, but faster than pure implicit methods because the Euler predictor provides a good initial guess. Memory Complexity: Low, requiring storage for current and next state values. Performance: Similar to Order Two Runge-Kutta (RK2). Strengths: Handles black hole singularities from point lights better than explicit methods. Limitations: May fail to converge on non-stiff equations or with large step sizes. Biased estimator in general cases, though consistent at boundaries. When to Use: When handling singularities is critical and step sizes are controlled. When Not to Use: For non-stiff problems where explicit methods are sufficient and faster. The method was tested in the context of differential ray marching, specifically the "Euler-Trapezoidal" variant, which uses an explicit Euler step as a predictor for the implicit trapezoidal corrector. It is also referenced in differentiable rendering of neural SDFs as a quadrature rule for warp estimation. name: Tensorline Integration
head: Discrete Volume Rendering (Compositing), Riemann Sum Approximation
body: Tensorline Integration visualizes directional information in volumetric tensor fields by integrating streamlines through masked focus regions. It combines fourth-order Runge-Kutta geometric integration with a discrete Riemann sum approximation of the volume rendering integral to composite color and opacity along the ray. It differs from sibling methods like Euler Integration by using RK4 for higher accuracy in complex flow structures, while relying on discrete compositing for image synthesis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset storing a color vector (RGB triple) and an alpha value at each grid point. A binary mask defining focus regions. Seed points randomly placed inside the masked volume. Output: A 2D image containing composited tensorlines with color and opacity. Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D grid where each voxel stores a color vector and an alpha value. Seed Points: A list of 3D coordinates randomly distributed within the masked volume. Parameters: Step Size: The ray interpolation distance \Delta s. Transfer Functions: Mapping functions R(d), G(d), B(d), A(d) that map scalar densities to color and opacity values. Steps: 1. Randomly place seed points inside the masked volume (focus region). 2. For each seed, initialize the current position x0 to the seed coordinate. 3. Check if the current position lies in an isotropic region; if so, terminate integration for this line. 4. Compute the next position x{i+1} using a fourth-order Runge-Kutta scheme based on the local tensor field. 5. Sample the precomputed color C(i\Delta s) and opacity \alpha(i\Delta s) at the new position. 6. Update accumulated color c and opacity \alpha using the front-to-back compositing equation. 7. Update xi = x{i+1} and repeat from step 3 until a boundary, isotropic region, or maximum step count is reached. Formulas: The rendering uses a discrete Riemann sum approximation of the analytic volume rendering integral. For each sample point i spaced by \Delta s: 1. Transparency: t(i\Delta s) = \exp(-\mu(i\Delta s)\Delta s) where \mu is the mass density or light extinction coefficient of the volume particles. 2. Opacity: \alpha(i\Delta s) = 1 - t(i\Delta s). 3. Compositing (Front-to-Back): The color c and accumulated opacity \alpha are updated as follows: c = C(i\Delta s)\alpha(i\Delta s)(1-\alpha) + c \alpha = \alpha(i\Delta s)(1-\alpha) + \alpha(i\Delta s) Alternatively, using the equivalent standard form: c = c(1-\alpha(i\Delta s)) + C(i\Delta s) \alpha = \alpha(1-\alpha(i\Delta s)) + \alpha(i\Delta s) Here, C(i\Delta s) is the color of the sample, obtained by shading the grid point using transfer functions. Pitfalls: Isotropic Regions: If the tensor is isotropic, the integration terminates immediately because it does not provide directional information. Precision: The source notes a Taylor series approximation t(i\Delta s) \approx 1 - \mu(i\Delta s)\Delta s, but the exact exponential form is standard for compositing. Back-to-Front Compositing: This is a generalization of the Painter's algorithm but lacks early ray termination speed-ups, making it less frequently used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tensorlineintegration(volumergbalpha, mask, seedpoints, maxsteps=1000): """ Renders tensorlines by integrating from seed points in focus regions. Args: volumergbalpha: 3D array of (R, G, B, A) tuples per voxel. mask: 3D boolean array indicating focus regions. seedpoints: List of (x, y, z) coordinates. maxsteps: Maximum integration steps per ray. Returns: List of (color, alpha) tuples for each seed. """ results = [] for seed in seedpoints: if not mask[seed]: results.append(([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0)) continue pos = seed acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): if isisotropic(volumergbalpha[pos]): break nextpos = rk4step(volumergbalpha, pos) if not inbounds(nextpos, volumergbalpha.shape): break csample, asample = samplevolume(volumergbalpha, nextpos) acccolor = [csample[k] asample (1.0 - accalpha) + acccolor[k] for k in range(3)] accalpha = asample (1.0 - accalpha) + asample pos = nextpos results.append((acccolor, accalpha)) return results def isisotropic(tensor): # Checks if tensor is proportional to identity matrix return numpy.allclose(tensor, numpy.eye(3) numpy.trace(tensor)/3) def rk4step(tensorfield, pos): # Standard RK4 integration using dominant eigenvector direction # Computes k1, k2, k3, k4 and returns weighted average position k1 = getdirection(tensorfield, pos) k2 = getdirection(tensorfield, pos + 0.5 k1) k3 = getdirection(tensorfield, pos + 0.5 k2) k4 = getdirection(tensorfield, pos + k3) return pos + (k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4) / 6.0 def getdirection(tensorfield, pos): # Extracts dominant eigenvector from tensor at pos return numpy.linalg.eig(tensorfield[pos])[1][:, 0] def inbounds(pos, shape): return all(0 <= p < s for p, s in zip(pos, shape)) def samplevolume(volumergbalpha, pos): # Bilinear interpolation of voxel data return volumergbalpha[pos] Time Complexity: Depends on the number of seed points and the length of integration paths. Integration uses RK4, requiring multiple tensor evaluations per step. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the tensor field, mask, and image buffer. Strengths: Provides high-quality visualization of directional structures in stress tensor fields. Limitations: Computationally expensive for long paths; terminates immediately in isotropic regions. When to use: Visualizing directional information in stress tensor fields or datasets where flow-like structures are important. When not to use: When isotropic regions dominate or real-time performance is critical. name: Dormand-Prince 5(4) Step
head: DP5(4), DP5(4) ODE Step, Dormand-Prince 5(4) method, Runge-Kutta-Fehlberg 7(8) Variant, dormandPrinceStep
body: The Dormand-Prince 5(4) step is an explicit Runge-Kutta method providing 5th-order accuracy with embedded 4th-order error estimation, used for integrating ordinary differential equations (ODEs) in volume rendering. It sets itself apart from its sibling Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) Integration by computing an embedded error estimate to control step acceptance, whereas RK4 uses a fixed step size. Inputs and Outputs: rhs: A function representing the right-hand side of the ODE y' = f(t, y), returning the derivative vector. y: The current state vector (position in the volume field). h: The step size (can be negative for backward integration). Output: A DPStepResult object containing: ok: Boolean flag indicating success or failure. ynew: The updated state vector (if ok is true). failedStage: The index of the stage that failed (if ok is false). Data Structures: The method uses the FSAL (First Same As Last) property: the first stage derivative k0 is carried over from the previous step's final derivative k{\text{last}}, which equals f(y{\text{new}}), avoiding a redundant function evaluation. No additional complex data structures are required beyond standard vectors for the state and stage derivatives. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Stage 0: If this is the first step, compute k0 = \text{rhs}(y). Otherwise, set k0 to the final derivative from the previous step. 2. Evaluate Stages 1–5: Compute the remaining five stage derivatives using the standard Dormand-Prince coefficients and the previously computed k values. 3. Check RHS Validity: If the RHS function returns null or an invalid value during any stage evaluation, the step fails immediately at that stage. 4. Compute Solution: Calculate the new state y{\text{new}} using the weighted sum of the stage derivatives and the step size h. 5. Error Estimation: Compute the local truncation error estimate using the difference between the 5th-order and 4th-order solutions. 6. Check Acceptance: Compare the error estimate against the ONESTEPTRUNCATION threshold (default 10^{-9}). 7. Return Result: If the error is within bounds, return DPStepResult(ok=true, ynew=y{\text{new}}). Otherwise, return DPStepResult(ok=false, failedStage=stageindex). Formulas: Local truncation error is O(h^6). Global error converges at 5th order (\propto h^5). Halving step size h reduces global error by \ge 24\times (theoretical 2^5 = 32\times). Parameters: ONESTEPTRUNCATION: Expected truncation error bound for one step. Value: 10^{-9}. ENERGYDRIFT1000STEPS: Expected energy drift bound for 1000 steps. Value: 10^{-6}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stage Failures: If the RHS function returns null or invalid data during any stage evaluation, the step fails. The method reports the failing stage index in failedStage. Precision: One step of y' = -y over h=0.1 lands \sim 10^{-10} from the analytic e^{-h}. Drift: 1000 steps of a harmonic oscillator (x'=v, v'=-x) with h=0.05 drift \sim 10^{-7} in energy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class DPStepResult: def init(self, ok, ynew=None, failedstage=None): self.ok = ok self.ynew = ynew self.failedstage = failedstage def dormandPrinceStep(rhs, y, h, k0=None): # FSAL: k0 is carried over from the previous step's final derivative if k0 is None: k0 = rhs(y) if k0 is None: return DPStepResult(ok=False, failedstage=0) # Standard Dormand-Prince 5(4) Butcher tableau coefficients # Stage 2 k1 = rhs(y + h (1/5 k0)) if k1 is None: return DPStepResult(ok=False, failedstage=1) # Stage 3 k2 = rhs(y + h (3/40 k0 + 9/40 k1)) if k2 is None: return DPStepResult(ok=False, failedstage=2) # Stage 4 k3 = rhs(y + h (44/45 k0 - 56/15 k1 + 32/9 k2)) if k3 is None: return DPStepResult(ok=False, failedstage=3) # Stage 5 k4 = rhs(y + h (19372/6561 k0 - 25360/2187 k1 + 64443/6561 k2 - 212/729 k3)) if k4 is None: return DPStepResult(ok=False, failedstage=4) # Stage 6 k5 = rhs(y + h (9017/3168 k0 - 355/33 k1 + 46732/5247 k2 + 49/176 k3 - 5103/18656 k4)) if k5 is None: return DPStepResult(ok=False, failedstage=5) # 5th-order solution # Weights: [25/216, 0, 1408/2565, 2197/4104, 1/5, 0] ynew = y + h (25/216 k0 + 1408/2565 k2 + 2197/4104 k3 + 1/5 k4) # Error estimation uses the embedded 4th-order pair # 4th-order weights: [5179/57600, 0, 1525/16587, 3759/4104, 125/1152, -1/4] ynew4th = y + h (5179/57600 k0 + 1525/16587 k2 + 3759/4104 k3 + 125/1152 k4 - 1/4 k5) error = abs(ynew - ynew4th) # Check Acceptance if error > 1e-9: # ONESTEPTRUNCATION return DPStepResult(ok=False, failedstage=5) # Step rejected # Store k5 for FSAL in the next step # In practice, the caller stores k5 and passes it as k0 in the next call return DPStepResult(ok=True, ynew=ynew) A first-order explicit method that computes the next state using a single derivative evaluation. Choose it when computational resources are extremely limited and low accuracy is acceptable. A third-order method with embedded second-order error estimation requiring fewer RHS evaluations than DP5(4). Choose it when a balance between accuracy and computational cost is needed. Integrates along higher-order tensor fields rather than vector fields. Choose it when dealing with tensor data, as it employs integration methods like Euler's method with adaptive stepsize control, second order Runge-Kutta, and dopri5/RK45 to prevent flipping of eigenvector directions in regions of high isotropy. Integration methods used to get correct interpolation of eigenvectors and prevent flipping of eigenvector directions in regions of high isotropy. Implemented methods include Euler’s method with adaptive stepsize control, second order Runge-Kutta, and dopri5/RK45. Time Complexity: Each step requires 6 evaluations of the RHS function. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the state vector and stage derivatives. Measured Performance: One step of y' = -y over h=0.1 lands \sim 10^{-10} from the analytic e^{-h}. 1000 steps of a harmonic oscillator (x'=v, v'=-x) with h=0.05 drift \sim 10^{-7} in energy. Scaling: Halving step size h reduces global error by \ge 24\times (theoretical 2^5 = 32\times). Strengths: High accuracy (5th-order) with adaptive step control via embedded error estimation. Limitations: Higher computational cost per step compared to lower-order methods due to 6 RHS evaluations. name: Modified 4th Order Runge-Kutta Integration
head: Modified RK4 for Spring Models, RK4 with Force-Position Equivalence
body: A numerical integration method used in volume deformation for tensor visualization, based on the 4th order Runge-Kutta (RK4) method. It solves the initial value problem for point positions by treating position adjustment as equal to the force field at the same time step. Unlike standard RK4 which integrates a vector field over time, this variant modifies the definition of the force function F to accelerate processing while preserving the correct resting states (equilibrium) of the spring models. It is distinct from standard RK4 Runge-Kutta 4 (RK4) Integration by relaxing the requirement for accurate intermediate stages, focusing solely on the final equilibrium configuration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Initial position P(x, t0) of a point x at time t0, force function F(x, P), time step h. Output: Updated position P(x, t0 + h). Data Structures: Point position P: 3D vector (x, y, z). Force function F: Returns a 3D vector based on current position and spatial coordinates x. Formulas: The core differential equation is defined as: \frac{\partial P(x, t)}{\partial t} = F(x, P(t)) \quad (16) This implies that the rate of change of position is equal to the force field evaluated at the current position. Steps: 1. Evaluate the force at the current position: k1 = F(x, P). 2. Evaluate the force at the midpoint using half the step of k1: k2 = F(x, P + \frac{h}{2}k1). 3. Evaluate the force at the midpoint using half the step of k2: k3 = F(x, P + \frac{h}{2}k2). 4. Evaluate the force at the end point using the full step of k3: k4 = F(x, P + h k3). 5. Update the position using the weighted average: P{new} = P + \frac{h}{6}(k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4) Modifications: The standard RK4 algorithm is modified by redefining F to speed up processing. The modification is valid as long as F retains the same resting states (where F=0) as the original physical spring model. This allows for simplified force calculations that do not accurately represent intermediate dynamic stages but converge to the correct static equilibrium. Parameters: Time step h: Must be chosen wisely to ensure stability and prevent destruction of the connection structure. Adaptive time stepping is recommended. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If h is too small, processing time increases unnecessarily. If h is too large, the integration may become unstable or destroy the structural integrity of the spring model. The method does not guarantee accurate intermediate stages; it is only valid for finding the resting state. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def modifiedrk4step(P, x, F, h): """ Perform one step of Modified RK4 integration for volume deformation. Args: P: Current position vector (3D) x: Spatial coordinate parameter (3D) F: Force function F(x, P) returning a 3D vector h: Time step size Returns: New position vector """ # k1 = F(x, P) k1 = F(x, P) # k2 = F(x, P + h/2 k1) k2 = F(x, P + (h / 2.0) k1) # k3 = F(x, P + h/2 k2) k3 = F(x, P + (h / 2.0) k2) # k4 = F(x, P + h k3) k4 = F(x, P + h k3) # Pnew = P + h/6 (k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4) Pnew = P + (h / 6.0) (k1 + 2.0 k2 + 2.0 k3 + k4) return Pnew An algorithm to determine the time step T for integrating the position adjustment of points in a spring model, ensuring stability and preventing destruction of the connection structure during deformation. It sets the step size based on the ratio of displacement to force magnitude, scaled by a user parameter, to balance convergence speed against structural integrity. Time Complexity: O(1) per step, requiring four evaluations of the force function F. Memory Complexity: O(1), storing only current position and four force vectors. Performance: Faster than standard RK4 if F is simplified, as intermediate accuracy is not required. Strengths: Efficient for finding equilibrium states in spring models; stable with appropriate time stepping. Limitations: Not suitable for scenarios requiring accurate dynamic trajectories; sensitive to time step size. When to use: When visualizing tensor fields via volume deformation and only the final resting state of spring models is needed. When not to use: When accurate intermediate stages of the deformation process are required. Originated in the context of tensor field visualization, specifically for volume deformation techniques. The method was proposed to address implementation issues in visualizing tensor fields, where numerical stability and processing speed are critical. It adapts the standard 4th order Runge-Kutta method, which is commonly used for numerical integration, to the specific constraints of spring model deformation in tensor visualization. name: Adaptive Time Step for Spring Model Integration
head: Adaptive Time Step for Spring Model, Spring Model Adaptive Step
body: An algorithm to determine the time step T for integrating the position adjustment of points in a spring model, ensuring stability and preventing destruction of the connection structure during deformation. It sets the step size based on the ratio of displacement to force magnitude, scaled by a user parameter, to balance convergence speed against structural integrity. Inputs: Force field F(x) for each point x in the mesh. Original position x0 for each point. Current position x for each point. User parameter \gamma (gamma). Outputs: Time step T. Data Structures: Points are indexed by x. Positions x and x0 are vectors in \mathbb{R}^3. Forces F(x) are vectors in \mathbb{R}^3. Steps: 1. For each point x, calculate the displacement vector d = x - x0. 2. Calculate the magnitude of the displacement \|d\| = \|x - x0\|. 3. For each point x, calculate the magnitude of the force \|F(x)\|. 4. Compute the ratio rx = \frac{\|x - x0\|}{\|F(x)\|} for each point x. 5. Find the minimum ratio across all points: r{min} = \minx (rx). 6. Calculate the time step T = \gamma \cdot r{min}. Formula: T = \gamma \cdot \minx \left( \frac{\max{x0} \|x - x0\|}{\|F(x)\|} \right) Where: \gamma is the user-specified parameter. \minx is the minimum over all points x. \|x - x0\| is the Euclidean distance from the original position x0 to the current position x. \|F(x)\| is the magnitude of the force at x. Parameters: \gamma: A user-specified parameter controlling the time step magnitude. Typical value: 0.1. Pitfalls: If T is too small, integration takes too many iterations (slow). If T is too big, the solution may never stabilize. The adaptive step prevents destroying the connection structure by constraining maximum deformation per iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateadaptivetimestep(points, forces, gamma=0.1): """ Calculate the adaptive time step for spring model integration. Args: points: List of current positions x. forces: List of force vectors F(x) corresponding to each point. gamma: User-specified parameter (default 0.1). Returns: T: The calculated time step. """ minratio = float('inf') for x, F in zip(points, forces): # Calculate displacement magnitude dx = [x[i] - pointsoriginal[i] for i in range(3)] # Note: pointsoriginal must be available displacementmag = math.sqrt(sum(d2 for d in dx)) # Calculate force magnitude forcemag = math.sqrt(sum(f2 for f in F)) # Avoid division by zero if forcemag == 0: continue ratio = displacementmag / forcemag if ratio < minratio: minratio = ratio T = gamma minratio return T Note: The pseudocode assumes pointsoriginal is accessible. The source formula uses \max{x0} \|x - x0\|, which implies the maximum distance from the original position. In the context of the algorithm described, this is interpreted as the displacement magnitude for each point. The "max" notation in the source formula might refer to the maximum over all points in the minimization step, or it might be a typo for just \|x - x0\|. Given the step description "maximum distance from its original position x0 to its current position x", it likely means the displacement magnitude. The minimization is over all points. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of points, as it requires a single pass to compute ratios and find the minimum. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory beyond storing the points and forces. Strengths: Prevents structural destruction during deformation by constraining maximum deformation per iteration. Balances convergence speed and stability. Limitations: Requires calculation of force magnitudes and displacements for all points. Performance depends on the choice of \gamma. When to use: When integrating spring models for volume deformation, especially where stability is critical. When not to use: When computational cost of calculating forces for all points is prohibitive, or when a fixed time step is sufficient and known to be stable. Originated in the context of volume deformation for tensor visualization. The method was employed to ensure a reasonable time step for each round of integration in spring models, addressing the trade-off between integration speed and solution stability. Tested on data sets including single point load, delta wing, and cylinder with hemispherical cap. name: Gaussian Integration for Volume Rendering
head: Gaussian Quadrature Integration, Gaussian Quadrature for Volume Rendering
body: Gaussian integration approximates the volume rendering integral as an unequally weighted sum of the integrand evaluated at n unequally spaced sample points. It is chosen over equally spaced sampling when the transfer function and density vary smoothly, as it achieves greater accuracy for the same number of sample points by exploiting the degrees of freedom in sample positions and weights. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{x} and direction \boldsymbol{\omega}0. Near and far bounds tn, tf defining the integration interval. Number of quadrature points N. Precomputed quadrature nodes \xik \in [-1, 1] and weights wk for the chosen order N. Outputs: Estimated radiance L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0). Data Structures: Quadrature nodes: Array of size N, values in [-1, 1]. Quadrature weights: Array of size N, summing to 2 for standard Legendre-Gauss quadrature. Sample positions: Array of size N, computed in world space. Steps: 1. Map nodes to ray interval: Transform the standard quadrature nodes \xik \in [-1, 1] to the ray parameter interval [tn, tf]. The sample position \mathbf{x}k along the ray is computed as \mathbf{x}k = \mathbf{x} + \frac{tf - tn}{2} (\xik + 1) \boldsymbol{\omega}0. 2. Compute segment distances: Calculate the distance between adjacent quadrature points as \Delta \mathbf{x}j = \|\mathbf{x}{j+1} - \mathbf{x}j\|. 3. Evaluate integrand: For each sample point k=1 \dots N, sample the volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}k) and source radiance Ls(\mathbf{x}k, \boldsymbol{\omega}0). 4. Compute transmittance: Calculate the accumulated transmittance \hat{T}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}k) from the ray origin to sample k as the product of extinction factors for all preceding segments: \hat{T}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}k) = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} e^{-\sigma(\mathbf{x}j) \Delta \mathbf{x}j}. For k=1, \hat{T}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}1) = 1. 5. Compute contribution: Calculate the radiance contribution for each sample using the term (1 - e^{-\sigma(\mathbf{x}k) \Delta \mathbf{x}k}), which represents the probability of scattering within the segment associated with sample k. 6. Sum: Accumulate the final radiance as the sum of all sample contributions. Formulas: The core approximation is: L(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}0) \approx \sum{k=1}^N \hat{T}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}k) (1 - e^{-\sigma(\mathbf{x}k) \Delta \mathbf{x}k}) Ls(\mathbf{x}k, \boldsymbol{\omega}0) where \hat{T}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}k) = \prod{j=1}^{k-1} e^{-\sigma(\mathbf{x}j) \Delta \mathbf{x}j} and \Delta \mathbf{x}j = \|\mathbf{x}{j+1} - \mathbf{x}j\|. The sample locations and weights are chosen such that the integral is exact for polynomials of maximum degree 2N-1, utilizing the 2N degrees of freedom in the positions and weights. Parameters: N: Number of quadrature points. Typical values depend on the smoothness of the transfer function; higher N yields higher accuracy for smooth functions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-smooth Transfer Functions: Gaussian integration performs poorly for non-smooth transfer functions selected to emphasize specific contour surfaces. In these cases, the integrand is not well-approximated by high-degree polynomials, and the method fails to capture sharp features accurately. Precision: The exponential terms in transmittance can suffer from underflow or overflow if density is very high or low; standard double-precision arithmetic is recommended. Boundary Segments: The formula defines \Delta \mathbf{x}j strictly as the distance between adjacent quadrature points, leaving the segment length for the final sample k=N undefined in the source notation. Implementations typically reuse the distance to the previous point or adjust weights to account for the interval boundary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def gaussianvolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, densityfield, emissionfield, N): # Source does not provide node/weight generation algorithm; standard Legendre-Gauss routine nodes, weights = getlegendregaussquadrature(N) # Map nodes from [-1, 1] to ray interval [tnear, tfar] samplepositions = [] for xi in nodes: t = 0.5 (tfar - tnear) (xi + 1) + tnear samplepositions.append(rayorigin + t raydirection) # Compute distances between adjacent quadrature points: deltax[j] = ||x{j+1} - xj|| deltax = [] for j in range(N - 1): deltax.append(math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(samplepositions[j + 1], samplepositions[j])))) radiance = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 for k in range(N): xk = samplepositions[k] sigma = densityfield.sample(xk) Ls = emissionfield.sample(xk, raydirection) # Determine segment length for sample k # Formula defines deltaxj for j < N; reuse previous distance for last point if k < N - 1: dxk = deltax[k] else: dxk = deltax[N - 2] if N > 1 else 0.0 # Contribution: That (1 - exp(-sigma dx)) Ls scatteringprob = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma dxk) radiance += transmittance scatteringprob Ls # Update transmittance for next sample: That{k+1} = Thatk exp(-sigmak dxk) transmittance = math.exp(-sigma dxk) return radiance Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of quadrature points, as evaluating density and emission at N points dominates the computation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, excluding the volume data structure. Performance: Provides higher accuracy than equally spaced sampling for the same N when the transfer function and density are smooth. Strengths: High accuracy for smooth integrands; fewer samples are needed compared to uniform sampling for the same error tolerance in smooth regions. Limitations: Poor performance for non-smooth transfer functions or sharp contours. Requires precomputed quadrature nodes and weights. When to use: Smooth density and transfer functions. When not to use: Sharp edges, discontinuities, or contour-based visualization where exact intersection is preferred. Gaussian integration is a classical numerical analysis technique applied to volume rendering to improve the accuracy of the discrete ray marching integral. It was discussed in the context of volume rendering by Williams et al., who noted its superiority over equally spaced sampling for smoothly varying transfer functions. The method leverages the properties of Legendre polynomials to place sample points optimally for polynomial approximation.
