name: Volumetric Ray Tracing with Global Illumination
body: A rendering method for scenes containing both volumetric and geometric data that extends the standard ray tracing illumination equation to capture global illumination effects (shadows, reflections) and volume rendering effects (compositing, maximum-value projections) in a single image. It differs from pure volume rendering methods by explicitly handling geometric intersections and recursive ray paths, and from pure geometric ray tracing by forcing volumetric intersections to occur at grid locations, which introduces aliasing artifacts that increase with recursion depth. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene containing both geometric primitives and volumetric data (grids); a global illumination equation defining the light transport model. Output: A final pixel intensity value. Data Structures: Intersection Results: Standard intersection points (for geometry) and intersection segments (for volumes). Ray Tree: A recursive structure of rays, where the "level" of a ray corresponds to its depth in the recursion. Steps: 1. Sort Objects: Sort all objects along the current ray according to distance and intersection classification (point vs. segment) before performing any intersection calculations. 2. Calculate Intersections: Perform intersection calculations. For volumetric data, the intersection is forced to occur at grid locations in the data. 3. Evaluate Shader: Pass the intersection results (points or segments) to a shader. The shader evaluates the intensity equation defined by the illumination model to determine the final pixel value. Formulas: The method extends the standard ray tracing illumination equation. The specific mathematical formulation of the extended equation is not provided in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Forcing volumetric intersections to occur at grid locations produces aliasing effects. These effects increase in severity as the level of the ray in the recursive ray tracing tree increases. An approach using gradients to realize a volumetric ray-tracer supporting physically correct illumination, considering only first-order rays. It simulates mirror-like reflections by casting a ray and computing its deflection, performing an environment texture lookup. It simulates refraction by computing ray deflection. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Captures realistic global effects (e.g., mirrors) and practical volume rendering effects (compositing, maximum-value projections) in a single image. Limitations: Aliasing effects increase with ray recursion depth due to grid-locked volumetric intersections. The method was developed to create a useful global illumination model and efficient rendering technique for scenes containing both volumetric and geometric data. It was motivated by the desire to include global effects in scientific applications, such as placing mirrors in the scene. name: Exponential Approximation Method
head: EAMGenerate, EAMRender, EAMRenderer, Exponential Attenuation Model
body: The Exponential Approximation Method (EAM) is a direct volume ray casting technique that approximates the continuous light attenuation integral using discrete steps and an exponential transmittance model. It differs from standard linear alpha compositing by scaling sampled alpha values by a step-size-dependent correction factor, allowing larger steps while approximating exponential decay. It is typically chosen when performance is prioritized over exact physical accuracy, or when the volume data is sparse enough that early ray termination provides significant speedup. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume texture (scalar density field), a transfer function (mapping density to color and opacity), camera parameters (unprojected ray endpoints vRayFrom and vRayTo), and rendering parameters (uStepSize, uAlphaCorrection or uExtinction, uOffset). Output: A 2D image pixel (RGBA color). Data Structures Volume Texture: A 3D texture object storing scalar density values, sampled at the red channel (.r). Transfer Function: A 1D or 2D texture mapping density values to RGBA color, sampled at vec2(val, 0.5). Ray Parameters: vRayFrom, vRayTo: Unprojected ray endpoints in volume space. tbounds: Intersection interval [t{min}, t{max}] of the ray with the unit cube, normalized to [0, 1]. uStepSize: Normalized step size in the range [0, 1] representing the fraction of the total ray length per step. uAlphaCorrection / uExtinction: Correction factor applied to alpha. In it is uAlphaCorrection. In it is uExtinction. uOffset: Initial offset parameter used in. Numbered Steps 1. Unproject and Intersect: Unproject the screen coordinate to obtain the ray endpoints vRayFrom and vRayTo. Intersect the ray with the unit cube. If no intersection is found (t{min} \ge t{max}), output black. 2. Initialize Ray Segment: Compute the start and end points of the ray segment within the volume: \text{from} = \text{mix}(vRayFrom, vRayTo, t{min}) and \text{to} = \text{mix}(vRayFrom, vRayTo, t{max}). Compute the physical length of the ray segment: L = \text{distance}(\text{from}, \text{to}). Compute the step length in world units: \text{rayStepLength} = L \times uStepSize. 3. Initialize Accumulator and Progress: Initialize the accumulator acc to (0, 0, 0, 0). Initialize the normalized progress parameter t. In, t starts at 0.0. In, t starts at uStepSize \times uOffset. 4. Ray Marching Loop: While t < 1.0 and acc.a < 0.99: 1. Compute position: \text{pos} = \text{mix}(\text{from}, \text{to}, t). 2. Sample volume: \text{val} = \text{texture}(uVolume, \text{pos}).r. 3. Sample transfer function: \text{colorSample} = \text{texture}(uTransferFunction, \text{vec2}(\text{val}, 0.5)). 4. Compute effective alpha: \alpha = \text{colorSample}.a \times \text{rayStepLength} \times uAlphaCorrection (or uExtinction in). 5. Scale color and alpha: \text{colorSample}.rgb \times= \alpha and \text{colorSample}.a \times= \alpha. 6. Composite using front-to-back: \text{acc}.rgb += (1.0 - \text{acc}.a) \times \text{colorSample}.rgb and \text{acc}.a += (1.0 - \text{acc}.a) \times \text{colorSample}.a. 7. Increment progress: t += uStepSize. 5. Post-Processing: If acc.a > 1.0, divide acc.rgb by acc.a to correct over-saturation. Set acc.a to 1.0. Output acc.rgb. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderexponentialapproximation(screenuv, invprojview, vrayfrom, vrayto, tbounds, ustepsize, ualphacorrection, uoffset): # 1. Unproject screen UV to ray endpoints in volume space rayorigin = invprojview @ vec4(screenuv.x, screenuv.y, 0.0, 1.0) rayorigin /= rayorigin.w raydir = invprojview @ vec4(screenuv.x, screenuv.y, 1.0, 1.0) raydir /= raydir.w raydir = normalize(raydir - rayorigin) # 2. Intersect ray with unit cube [0,1]^3, returning normalized bounds [0,1] tmin, tmax = intersectraycubenormalized(rayorigin, raydir) if tmin >= tmax: return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 3. Initialize ray segment frompoint = mix(vrayfrom, vrayto, tmin) topoint = mix(vrayfrom, vrayto, tmax) raylength = distance(frompoint, topoint) raysteplength = raylength ustepsize accumulator = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Sources disagree on initial t: S1 uses 0.0, S2 uses ustepsize uoffset t = 0.0 # 4. Ray marching loop while t < 1.0 and accumulator.a < 0.99: pos = mix(frompoint, topoint, t) val = texture(uvolume, pos).r colorsample = texture(utransferfunction, vec2(val, 0.5)) # Scale alpha and RGB by step length and correction factor alpha = colorsample.a raysteplength ualphacorrection colorsample.rgb = alpha colorsample.a = alpha # Front-to-back compositing accumulator.rgb += (1.0 - accumulator.a) colorsample.rgb accumulator.a += (1.0 - accumulator.a) colorsample.a t += ustepsize # 5. Post-processing if accumulator.a > 1.0: accumulator.rgb /= accumulator.a accumulator.a = 1.0 return accumulator.rgb def intersectraycubenormalized(origin, direction): tmin = 0.0 tmax = 1.0 for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0.0: if origin[i] < 0.0 or origin[i] > 1.0: return 1.0, 0.0 else: t1 = (0.0 - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (1.0 - origin[i]) / direction[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) return tmin, tmax Parameters uStepSize: Normalized step size in the range [0, 1]. uAlphaCorrection / uExtinction: Correction factor applied to alpha. In it is uAlphaCorrection. In it is uExtinction. uOffset: Initial offset parameter used in. Edge Cases and Pitfalls No Intersection: If the ray does not intersect the volume cube, the method outputs black. Over-saturation: If the step size or correction factor is too high, accumulator.a can exceed 1.0, requiring RGB normalization. Early Termination: The loop stops when accumulator.a exceeds 0.99. Precision: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Exponential Approximation Method is a practical approach to direct volume rendering based on the principle of alpha compositing with an approximation of the transmittance integral. It is implemented in open-source projects such as rokcej/volumetric-ray-casting and terier/vpt. The specific implementation details (e.g., uAlphaCorrection vs uExtinction and initial t offset) vary between projects, but the core algorithm remains consistent. rokcej/volumetric-ray-casting, https://github.com/rokcej/volumetric-ray-casting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) terier/vpt, https://github.com/terier/vpt, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray Tracing (Binary Objects)
head: Binary Object Ray Tracing, Binary Ray Casting, First-hit Ray Casting for Binary Volumes, Tuy's binary ray casting
body: Ray Tracing (Binary Objects) is an image-order rendering technique for visualizing surfaces contained within binary volumetric data by determining only the first intersection points with a surface. It solves the problem of displaying opaque surfaces in binary volumes without requiring explicit boundary detection or hidden-surface removal algorithms. Unlike methods that composite translucent data or require gradient estimation from multi-valued volumes, this method treats the volume as a set of opaque objects where light stops at the first surface hit. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as Discrete Ray Tracing which uses voxel connectivity, and Fixed Step Ray Marching which integrates density, by its exclusive focus on the binary "first-hit" condition using zero-order interpolation. Inputs: Binary volumetric data V, where V(x,y,z) \in \{0, 1\}. Value 1 indicates object interior, 0 indicates background. Camera parameters: projection type (parallel or perspective), view direction, field of view (for perspective), and image plane resolution. Step size d for sampling along the ray. Lighting model parameters (light direction, view direction) for shading. Outputs: Image pixels with color values determined by shading the first intersection point. Data Structures: Binary Volume: Can be stored as a binary array of 0s and 1s, or optimized as a scan-line representation where each scan-line stores a list of end points representing segments belonging to the object. The scan-line representation is compact and reduces memory usage, critical for early implementations with limited RAM. Bounding Box: The axis-aligned bounding box of the data volume is used to limit ray traversal. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel on the image plane, cast a ray. For parallel projection, all rays are parallel to the view direction. For perspective projection, rays originate from the eye point and pass through the pixel, defined by the view direction and field of view. 2. Ray Clipping: Traverse only the segment of the ray contained within the bounding box of the data to reduce the number of steps. 3. Sampling: Traverse the clipped ray segment using a fixed step size d. The i-th sample point pi is located at a distance i \cdot d along the ray from the start of the traversal. 4. Interpolation: Determine the value of the volume at each sample point pi using zero-order interpolation. The value is 0 if the location is not in any voxel, otherwise it is the value of the closest data sample (nearest voxel). 5. Intersection Test: Check the sampled values sequentially. If all samples along the ray have a value of 0, the ray missed the object. If there exists a sample pi such that all previous samples pj (where j < i) have a value of 0, and pi has a value of 1, then pi is the first intersection point. Work progresses from the screen toward the object (from the near plane of the bounding box) to find the first hit. 6. Shading: If an intersection is found at pi, calculate the surface normal at pi and apply a shading model (e.g., depth shading, light direction, gradient estimate) to determine the pixel color. Place the resulting color in the pixel. Formulas: Sample position: pi = \text{ray\origin} + i \cdot d \cdot \text{ray\direction}, where pi is the i-th sample point, d is the step size, and i is the sample index. First intersection condition: \exists i such that V(pi) = 1 and \forall j < i, V(pj) = 0. Parameters: Step size d: Must be chosen carefully. If d is too large, small features may not be detected. If d is small, computation time increases. Typical values depend on the voxel size and desired accuracy, but no specific numerical value is given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing/Feature Loss: If the step size d is too large relative to the voxel size or feature size, small objects or thin structures may be missed entirely. Precision: The method relies on exact binary values. Floating-point errors in ray position calculation could theoretically lead to incorrect voxel lookups if not handled with robust integer arithmetic or careful rounding. Bounding Box: Rays must be correctly clipped to the data bounding box to avoid unnecessary computation and out-of-bounds memory access. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytracebinaryvolume(volume, volumeorigin, volumespacing, volumedims, camera, stepsize, lightdir): width, height = camera.resolution image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height)] bbox = camera.getboundingbox() for y in range(height): for x in range(width): ray = camera.getray(x, y) tnear, tfar = intersectaabb(ray, bbox) if tnear > tfar: image[y][x] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] continue t = tnear hit = False while t <= tfar: point = ray.origin + ray.direction t voxelcoords = [ int(round((point[0] - volumeorigin[0]) / volumespacing[0])), int(round((point[1] - volumeorigin[1]) / volumespacing[1])), int(round((point[2] - volumeorigin[2]) / volumespacing[2])) ] if 0 <= voxelcoords[0] < volumedims[0] and \ 0 <= voxelcoords[1] < volumedims[1] and \ 0 <= voxelcoords[2] < volumedims[2]: value = volume[voxelcoords[0]][voxelcoords[1]][voxelcoords[2]] else: value = 0 if value == 1: normal = estimatenormal(volume, voxelcoords, volumespacing, volumedims) color = shade(point, normal, lightdir) image[y][x] = color hit = True break t += stepsize if not hit: image[y][x] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return image def intersectaabb(ray, bbox): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if ray.direction[i] == 0: if ray.origin[i] < bbox.min[i] or ray.origin[i] > bbox.max[i]: return (float('inf'), -float('inf')) else: t1 = (bbox.min[i] - ray.origin[i]) / ray.direction[i] t2 = (bbox.max[i] - ray.origin[i]) / ray.direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return (tmin, tmax) def estimatenormal(volume, voxelcoords, volumespacing, volumedims): # Central difference gradient estimation for binary volume with boundary clamping def clamp(v, minv, maxv): return max(minv, min(v, maxv)) x, y, z = voxelcoords nx = volume[clamp(x+1, 0, volumedims[0]-1)][y][z] - volume[clamp(x-1, 0, volumedims[0]-1)][y][z] ny = volume[x][clamp(y+1, 0, volumedims[1]-1)][z] - volume[x][clamp(y-1, 0, volumedims[1]-1)][z] nz = volume[x][y][clamp(z+1, 0, volumedims[2]-1)] - volume[x][y][clamp(z-1, 0, volumedims[2]-1)] return normalize([nx volumespacing[0], ny volumespacing[1], nz volumespacing[2]]) def normalize(v): length = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 if length == 0: return [0, 0, 0] return [v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length] def shade(point, normal, lightdir): # Simple diffuse shading diff = max(0, dot(normal, lightdir)) return [diff, diff, diff] def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of steps per ray. M is determined by the depth of the volume along the ray divided by the step size d. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, where V is the number of voxels. Using scan-line representation can reduce memory footprint for sparse data. Performance: The method is computationally intensive due to the large number of steps required to achieve accurate intersection points, especially if a small step size is used. Optimizations like bounding box clipping and scan-line representation help reduce computation time and memory usage. Strengths: Simple to implement; does not require explicit surface extraction or boundary detection; handles opaque surfaces directly. Limitations: Cannot render translucent volumes; sensitive to step size choice; may miss small features if step size is too large; shading is limited to depth and gradient estimates. When to use: When visualizing opaque surfaces in binary volumetric data is required, and computational resources are limited or explicit surface extraction is undesirable. The method was developed in 1984 by Tuy et al. as "binary ray casting" to visualize surfaces in binary volumetric data. It was one of the first image-order volume rendering techniques, designed to generate images without explicit boundary detection or hidden-surface removal. The algorithm was originally developed on a machine with only 32K of RAM, leading to the use of data compression techniques like scan-line representation. It is a direct method for identifying visible points by simulating light rays, where light stops at the surface of opaque objects. name: Discrete Ray Tracing
head: 3D DDA Voxel Traversal, Naive Voxel-Raycasting
body: Discrete Ray Tracing (DRT) approximates continuous viewing rays with discrete, voxel-connected paths (voxelization) to traverse a 3D scalar field. Unlike methods that rely on geometric primitives or acceleration structures, DRT directly samples the voxel grid using a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) or Bresenham-like algorithm, guaranteeing that voxels are visited in the exact order of intersection. This approach limits intersection tests to Pythagorean complexity rather than cubic, ensuring the first opaque voxel found is the closest. It is distinguished from Fixed Step Ray Marching by its adaptive step size (always moving to the next voxel boundary) and from Exponential Approximation Method by its explicit traversal of every voxel along the ray path without skipping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid (scalar field) V of dimensions W \times H \times D; camera parameters (position, view vectors, near/far planes); transfer function T(v) \rightarrow (r, g, b, \alpha); projection type (surface, maximum, sum, or composite). Output: A 2D image where each pixel (x, y) holds the accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D array V[i, j, k] where indices are integers. A voxel is defined as an index in an axis-aligned grid, not a geometric cube with independent position. Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. In DRT, the ray is represented as a sequence of integer voxel coordinates (i, j, k). Pixel Accumulator: A 4-tuple (R, G, B, A) initialized to (0, 0, 0, 0). Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Setup: For each pixel (x, y) in the image plane: Calculate the ray direction \mathbf{d} using bilinear interpolation of the four viewport corner normals. Set ray origin \mathbf{o} to the camera position (for perspective) or a point on the near plane (for orthographic). Note: For orthographic projection along the Z-axis, \mathbf{d} = (0, 0, 1) and \mathbf{o} = (x/W, y/H, \text{near\plane}). 2. Voxelization (Ray Traversal): Generate a discrete path of voxels intersected by the ray using a 3D DDA algorithm. Initialize current voxel coordinates (i, j, k) to the voxel containing \mathbf{o}: i = \lfloor \mathbf{o}x \cdot W - 0.5 \rfloor, \quad j = \lfloor \mathbf{o}y \cdot H - 0.5 \rfloor, \quad k = \lfloor \mathbf{o}z \cdot D - 0.5 \rfloor The -0.5 offset centers the sampling within the voxel. Determine the step direction (\Delta i, \Delta j, \Delta k) \in \{-1, 0, 1\} based on the sign of \mathbf{d}. Calculate the distance to the next voxel boundary in each axis: t{i} = \frac{\text{boundary}i - \mathbf{o}x}{\mathbf{d}x} \quad \text{(if } \mathbf{d}x \neq 0 \text{)} (Similar formulas for tj, tk). While the ray is within the volume bounds: 1. Sample the scalar value v = V[i, j, k]. 2. Apply the transfer function to get color \mathbf{c} = (r, g, b) and opacity \alpha. 3. Composite the sample into the pixel accumulator using the front-to-back over operator: \mathbf{C}{out} = \mathbf{C}{in} + (1 - A{in}) \cdot \mathbf{c} \cdot \alpha A{out} = A{in} + (1 - A{in}) \cdot \alpha 4. If using surface projection, stop at the first non-transparent voxel. 5. Advance to the next voxel: Find the axis with the smallest positive t (distance to next boundary). Increment/decrement the coordinate on that axis by 1. Update the boundary distance for that axis. 3. Projection Variants: Composite: Accumulate all samples along the ray using the over operator. Maximum: Store the maximum scalar value encountered. Sum/Average: Accumulate scalar values (X-ray simulation). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def discreteraytracing(volume, width, height, depth, camerapos, viewvectors): """ volume: 3D list of lists of lists (W, H, D) camerapos: (ox, oy, oz) viewvectors: dict with 'upperLeft', 'upperRight', 'lowerLeft', 'lowerRight' (tuples) """ image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height width)] invh = 1.0 / height invw = 1.0 / width uln = normalize(viewvectors['upperLeft']) urn = normalize(viewvectors['upperRight']) lln = normalize(viewvectors['lowerLeft']) lrn = normalize(viewvectors['lowerRight']) leftydelta = tuple(lln[i] - uln[i] for i in range(3)) invh rightydelta = tuple(lrn[i] - urn[i] for i in range(3)) invh leftnormal = uln rightnormal = urn for y in range(height): xdelta = tuple(rightnormal[i] - leftnormal[i] for i in range(3)) invw raydir = leftnormal for x in range(width): accr, accg, accb, acca = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # Map ray to voxel space for traversal # In practice, origin is mapped from world to voxel coordinates. rayorigin = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for i, j, k in getvoxelpath(rayorigin, raydir, width, height, depth): val = volume[i][j][k] # Transfer function (Gaussian Mixtures from S4) r = math.exp(-((val - 9.0)2) / 1.0) + 0.1 math.exp(-((val - 3.0)2) / 0.1) + 0.1 math.exp(-((val + 3.0)2) / 0.5) g = math.exp(-((val - 9.0)2) / 1.0) + math.exp(-((val - 3.0)2) / 0.1) + 0.1 math.exp(-((val + 3.0)2) / 0.5) b = 0.1 math.exp(-((val - 9.0)2) / 1.0) + 0.1 math.exp(-((val - 3.0)2) / 0.1) + math.exp(-((val + 3.0)2) / 0.5) a = 0.6 math.exp(-((val - 9.0)2) / 1.0) + 0.1 math.exp(-((val - 3.0)2) / 0.1) + 0.01 math.exp(-((val + 3.0)2) / 0.5) accr += (1.0 - acca) r a accg += (1.0 - acca) g a accb += (1.0 - acca) b a acca += (1.0 - acca) a if acca >= 1.0: break image[y width + x] = [accr, accg, accb, acca] raydir = tuple(raydir[i] + xdelta[i] for i in range(3)) leftnormal = tuple(leftnormal[i] + leftydelta[i] for i in range(3)) rightnormal = tuple(rightnormal[i] + rightydelta[i] for i in range(3)) return image def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in v)) return tuple(c/mag for c in v) def getvoxelpath(origin, direction, w, h, d): """ Yields voxel indices (i, j, k) along the ray defined by direction. Uses 3D DDA. """ ix = math.floor(origin[0]) iy = math.floor(origin[1]) iz = math.floor(origin[2]) stepx = 1 if direction[0] > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if direction[1] > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if direction[2] > 0 else -1 tmaxx = ( (ix + (1 if stepx > 0 else 0)) - origin[0]) / direction[0] if direction[0] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = ( (iy + (1 if stepy > 0 else 0)) - origin[1]) / direction[1] if direction[1] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxz = ( (iz + (1 if stepz > 0 else 0)) - origin[2]) / direction[2] if direction[2] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltax = abs(1.0 / direction[0]) if direction[0] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltay = abs(1.0 / direction[1]) if direction[1] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltaz = abs(1.0 / direction[2]) if direction[2] != 0 else float('inf') while 0 <= ix < w and 0 <= iy < h and 0 <= iz < d: yield ix, iy, iz if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: ix += stepx tmaxx += tdeltax else: iz += stepz tmaxz += tdeltaz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: iy += stepy tmaxy += tdeltay else: iz += stepz tmaxz += tdeltaz Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Using nearest-neighbor sampling (flooring coordinates) can result in blocky artifacts at low resolutions. Connectivity: The choice of 6-, 18-, or 26-connected paths affects accuracy and performance. 6-connected paths contain almost twice as many voxels as 26-connected paths. 26-connected paths are faster but may miss intersections detected by 6-connected paths. Performance: High number of texture accesses and multiplications per ray leads to low frame rates for large or sparse volumes. Voxel Definition: Voxels are indices, not geometric cubes. They do not move. A hardware-oriented hybrid algorithm for real-time visualization of high-resolution volumes (512^3). It ensures each voxel is read at most once per projection using a Cubic Frame Buffer and global communication network, exploiting spatial coherency. Choose when memory bandwidth is the bottleneck and hardware support for skewed memory organization exists. Time Complexity: O(n), where n is the number of voxels traversed along the ray. In the worst case, n is proportional to the volume dimension in the view direction. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per ray (excluding the volume storage). Performance: Suitable for small, dense voxel entities (e.g., 50^3 or 100^3) where modifications are frequent and acceleration structures cannot be updated efficiently. Performance degrades significantly for large, sparse volumes due to the lack of acceleration structures. Strengths: Simple implementation; no need for acceleration structures; guarantees closest intersection; insensitive to scene complexity (only one primitive type: voxel). Limitations: Low frame rates for large or sparse volumes due to high texture accesses and multiplications. Discrete Ray Tracing was proposed by Yagel, Cohen, and Kaufman as a method for fast parallel implementation of volume rendering. It allows rendering 3D sampled datasets like MRI or fluid dynamics simulations directly, avoiding the approximation of sampled data with geometric primitives. The method leverages the 3D DDA algorithm, originally used in computer graphics for line rasterization, to traverse voxel grids efficiently. name: Cube-3 Hybrid Ray-Casting
head: Cube-1, Cube-3
body: Cube-3 is a hardware-oriented hybrid ray-casting algorithm designed for the real-time visualization of high-resolution volumetric datasets (e.g., 512^3 voxels). It solves the traditional memory access bottleneck in volume rendering by ensuring that each voxel is read from memory at most once per projection, without pre-processing or data-dependent optimizations. Unlike object-order methods like VIRIM or image-order methods like VOGUE, Cube-3 exploits spatial coherency by processing all sample values of a ray simultaneously in a fully pipelined architecture. It is distinguished by its use of a Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB) with skewed memory organization and a global communication network (Fast Bus) to align discrete rays for parallel processing. The algorithm combines object-order data access with image-order projection. It generates discrete voxel-rays from continuous viewing rays, fetches them as beams from a skewed memory structure, and composites them into a base-plane image, which is subsequently warped to the final view plane. Input: A volumetric dataset of size n \times n \times n voxels (typically 16 bits per voxel). Viewing direction (parallel or perspective). Output: A 2D base-plane image, which is transformed and warped by the host CPU/GPU into the final view plane image. 1. Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB): The volume memory is organized into n dual-access memory modules, each storing n^2 voxels. Memory Mapping: A voxel at coordinates (x, y, z) is mapped to memory module k using: k = (x + y + z) \bmod n where 0 \leq k, x, y, z \leq n-1. Internal Mapping: Within module k, the voxel is stored at internal coordinates (i, j) where i=x and j=y. Skewing: This skewed organization ensures conflict-free access to any beam of n voxels parallel to a primary axis. 2. Discrete Ray Templates: Lookup tables storing the steps in non-major directions (e.g., X and Y) for Bresenham's line drawing algorithm, ensuring constant stepping along the major axis (e.g., Z) and avoiding voxel overlap between neighboring rays. 3. 2D Buffers: Memory structures with 2D skewing (similar to CFB) used to store beams fetched from the CFB and retrieve axis-aligned discrete rays conflict-free. 4. ABC Sample Buffers: Stores three continuous planes of ray samples: Above, Below, and Current. 5. Ray Projection Cone (RPC): A circular cross-linked binary tree of n-1 Voxel Combination Units (VCUs) that composites samples into final pixel values. 1. Discrete Ray Generation: Generate discrete voxel-rays from continuous viewing rays using a 3D variation of Bresenham's line drawing algorithm. This guarantees a constant step of distance 1 along the major axis of the viewing direction. Steps in non-major directions are retrieved from lookup tables (templates). 2. Base-Plane Projection: Cast discrete rays from each pixel on the base-plane, defined as the volume face most perpendicular to the viewing direction. A set of discrete rays belonging to a scanline forms a Projection Ray Plane (PRP). 3. Beam Fetching: Fetch PRPs as a sequence of voxel beams from the CFB. The beams are stored in discrete ray buffers within the TRILIN units. 4. Ray Alignment: Use a high-bandwidth global bus (Fast Bus) to align all discrete rays in each PRP parallel to a main axis of the 2D buffers. 5. Interpolation (Sheared Trilinear): Consecutive discrete rays are fetched each clock cycle and placed into n Tri-linear Interpolation units (TRI-LINs). Two discrete PRPs (top and bottom) are used to generate sample values for the original continuous rays. Perform sheared trilinear interpolation using voxels from neighboring discrete rays of the top and bottom PRPs. Overlapping voxels of neighboring discrete rays are shared between neighboring TRI-LIN units. 6. Sample Storage and Gradient Estimation: Store the resulting continuous planes of ray samples in the Above, Below, and Current (ABC) sample buffers. Estimate the gradient at each sample location using central differences between samples of rays on the immediate left, right, above, below, and along the current ray. This allows sharing of already computed ray samples and avoids additional voxel accesses. 7. Shading and Classification: Forward interpolated sample and gradient values to shading units (Shaders). Assign opacity values using a user-controlled look-up table (transfer function). Calculate color values at each sample location according to a local illumination model (e.g., Phong lighting). 8. Compositing (RPC): Connect the n shading units as leaves of a folded and circular binary tree containing n-1 Voxel Combination Units (VCUs). The RPC takes one ray of opacity and color samples and generates one projected pixel value per clock cycle. Implement projection schemes such as first/last opaque projection, maximum voxel value, weighted summation, or front-to-back compositing within the RPC. 9. Warping: Transmit the resulting pixel of the base-plane to the host. The host transforms and interpolates it into the final view plane image. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cube3render(volume, origin, direction, stepsize): # 1. Determine major axis for discrete stepping absd = [abs(direction[0]), abs(direction[1]), abs(direction[2])] majoraxis = 0 if absd[0] >= absd[1] and absd[0] >= absd[2] else (1 if absd[1] >= absd[2] else 2) # 2. Generate discrete voxel-rays using 3D Bresenham's algorithm # Guarantees constant stepping of 1 along the major axis discreteray = bresenham3d(origin, direction, majoraxis) # 3. Fetch beams from CFB (simulated direct access for software reference) # Hardware uses skewed memory mapping: k = (x+y+z) mod n beam = [] for voxel in discreteray: if isinsidevolume(voxel, volume.shape): beam.append(volume[voxel[0]][voxel[1]][voxel[2]]) else: beam.append(0.0) # 4. Sheared trilinear interpolation to generate continuous samples # Uses top and bottom PRPs (simulated by offsetting the beam) samples = [] for i in range(len(beam)): sample = shearedtrilinearinterpolate(beam, i) samples.append(sample) # 5. Gradient estimation using central differences gradients = [] for i in range(len(samples)): grad = centraldifference(samples, i) gradients.append(grad) # 6. Shading and classification opacities = [] colors = [] for i in range(len(samples)): opacity = applytransferfunction(samples[i]) color = calculateillumination(samples[i], gradients[i]) opacities.append(opacity) colors.append(color) # 7. Compositing via RPC (Ray Projection Cone) # Front-to-back compositing implemented in a circular binary tree finalcolor = 0.0 alpha = 0.0 for i in range(len(opacities)): alpha += (1.0 - alpha) opacities[i] finalcolor += colors[i] opacities[i] (1.0 - alpha) if alpha >= 1.0: break return samples # Hardware returns finalcolor after RPC compositing def bresenham3d(origin, direction, majoraxis): # Standard 3D Bresenham line drawing algorithm # Returns list of voxel coordinates along the ray voxels = [] x, y, z = float(origin[0]), float(origin[1]), float(origin[2]) dx, dy, dz = direction steps = int(max(abs(x), abs(y), abs(z)) 2) + 1 for in range(steps): voxels.append((int(x), int(y), int(z))) x += dx y += dy z += dz return voxels def isinsidevolume(voxel, shape): return 0 <= voxel[0] < shape[0] and 0 <= voxel[1] < shape[1] and 0 <= voxel[2] < shape[2] def shearedtrilinearinterpolate(beam, index): # Simulates sheared trilinear interpolation using neighboring PRPs # Returns a continuous sample value current = beam[index] prev = beam[index-1] if index > 0 else 0.0 nextval = beam[index+1] if index < len(beam)-1 else 0.0 return current 0.5 + prev 0.25 + nextval 0.25 def centraldifference(samples, index): # Central difference gradient estimation left = samples[index-1] if index > 0 else samples[index] right = samples[index+1] if index < len(samples)-1 else samples[index] return (right - left) / 2.0 def applytransferfunction(sample): # User-controlled transfer function return min(1.0, sample 0.1) def calculateillumination(sample, gradient): # Local illumination model (e.g., Phong) return sample 0.8 + abs(gradient) 0.2 def warptoviewplane(baseplanepixels, viewdirection): # Host-side transformation and interpolation return baseplanepixels Dataset Size: 512^3 voxels, 16 bits per voxel. Memory Modules: n modules for an n^3 dataset. Pipelines: 8 identical rendering pipelines in EM-Cube (commercial variant). Cube-3 uses a fully distributed memory system. Bus Frequency: Performance scales with bus frequency. 125 MHz yields 30 Hz for 512^3. Frame Rate: Target 30 frames per second for 512^3 datasets. Perspective Projections: While Cube-3 supports arbitrary parallel and perspective projections, certain viewpoints under perspective projections may adversely affect performance for hybrid order algorithms. The commercial EM-Cube variant does not support perspective projections. Memory Conflicts: Avoided by the skewed organization of the CFB and 2D skewing of the 2D buffers. Voxel Re-fetch: In section-based processing (used to reduce on-chip storage), boundary voxels of a section must be re-fetched, increasing average voxel re-fetch. Extends the original Cube architecture to support arbitrary viewing directions by shearing data into a 2D memory structure, overcoming the distortion limitations of rotating the Cubic Frame Buffer for non-orthographic views. Time Complexity: The algorithm is limited only by the data-transfer rate on the Fast Bus due to its fully pipelined implementation. Memory Complexity: Requires n memory modules for an n^3 dataset. Memory utilization is 100% when synchronous memory accesses are sustained for each voxel. Performance: Cube-3 implementation for 512^3 16-bit dataset requires 8 custom boards and a specially fabricated bus backplane. Performance estimates: 128^3 at 8 MHz bus yields 30 Hz; 256^3 at 33 MHz yields 30 Hz; 512^3 at 66 MHz yields 15 Hz; 512^3 at 125 MHz yields 30 Hz. EM-Cube (Cube-4 variant) processes ~533 million samples per second, sufficient for 256^3 at 30 fps. Strengths: Solves the memory access bottleneck by reading each voxel at most once per projection. High degree of parallelism; processes all sample values of a ray simultaneously. Supports arbitrary parallel and perspective projections (theoretically). Limitations: Requires specialized hardware (Fast Bus, skewed memory). Perspective projections can cause performance issues. EM-Cube does not support perspective projections. The Cube project, pioneered at the State University of New York at Stony Brook, aims to realize high-performance volume rendering systems for large datasets. Cube-1 was the first generation hardware prototype based on specially interleaved memory organization. Cube-2 was a single-chip VLSI implementation of Cube-1. Cube-3 introduced a high-speed global communication network (Fast Bus) and a circular cross-linked binary tree for compositing to reduce the memory access bottleneck further. EM-Cube is a commercial version of the Cube-4 architecture, which uses local interconnections for scalability. name: Extended Cube Architecture for Arbitrary Parallel Projection
head: Arbitrary Parallel Viewing Architecture
body: The Extended Cube Architecture is a special-purpose computer architecture designed to enable real-time arbitrary parallel projection of volumetric data, overcoming the distortion limitations of rotating the Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB) for non-orthographic views. It extends the original Cube architecture, which only supported orthographic projection, by introducing a 2D Skewed Buffer (2DSB) and a Ray Projection Tree (RPT) to fetch and process slanted planes of projection rays without pre-processing. Unlike the original Cube, which accesses axial beams directly, this method handles arbitrary viewing directions by shearing the data into a 2D memory structure, aligning rays, and projecting them in parallel. The method transforms arbitrary parallel projection rays into a format suitable for parallel hardware processing. It operates on a dataset stored in a Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB) and produces a 2D projected image. Input: A volumetric dataset of size n \times n \times n voxels stored in the CFB. The viewing direction is arbitrary (parallel projection). Output: A 2D image where each pixel corresponds to a projection ray passing through the volume. 1. Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB) Layout: A 3D modular memory organization. Size: For a 512^3 dataset, the CFB holds 128M voxels. Access: Supports conflict-free access to full beams of n voxels in any orthographic direction. 2. 2D Skewed Buffer (2DSB) Purpose: Stores the slanted Projection Ray Plane (PRP) and performs de-skewing. Layout: Physically divided into n modules, diagonally skewed to allow conflict-free writing of horizontal beams and reading of vertical rays. Dimensions: Width is at least 2n-1 columns to accommodate parallel rays entering the slanted PRP. Modules: Contains n modules. Each module connects to neighbors via conveyors (barrel shifters) with 256 lines (16 bits \times 16 shift places). Pipelining: Uses multiple planes (e.g., 4 planes) to allow concurrent loading of the next PRP while processing the current one. 3. Ray Projection Tree (RPT) Purpose: Parallel processing of viewing rays to compute pixel values. Layout: A hierarchical binary tree of n-1 Voxel Combination Units (VCUs). Leaves: Accept n voxels along a viewing ray. Root: Produces the final color for the corresponding pixel. 4. Voxel Combination Unit (VCU) Input: Two voxel values. Operation: Combines inputs into an output voxel value. Latency: 7 time units per combination. 1. Retrieve Projection Ray Plane (PRP): Identify the set of projection rays belonging to the same scan line of the projected 2D frame buffer. These rays form a slanted plane (PRP) within the CFB. 2. Fetch Beams: Retrieve the PRP from the CFB as n beams parallel to a primary axis. 3. Store in 2DSB: Store the slanted PRP into the 2DSB one beam at a time, from closest to furthest. 4. De-skew (Shear): Shift each beam left or right within the 2DSB to align all viewing rays vertically (parallel to a 2D axis) using a barrel shifter (Conveyor). 5. Retrieve Rays: Retrieve vertical viewing rays from the 2DSB in parallel. 6. Transfer to RPT: Transfer rays to the RPT, shifting them during transfer to ensure the closest voxel appears at the desired position. 7. Process Rays: Process rays in parallel through the RPT. Each VCU combines two voxels in 7 time units. For algorithms requiring a 27-voxel neighborhood (central voxel + 26 neighbors), use multiple parallel 2DSBs to extract and transfer the cube in parallel. 8. Pipeline: Use a fourth plane in the 2DSB to load the next slanted PRP while three planes are used for extracting the 27-voxel cube for concurrent projection. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extendedcubepipeline(volume, viewdir, n): dsbwidth = 2 n - 1 dsb = [[[None] dsbwidth for in range(n)] for in range(4)] for scany in range(n): plane = scany % 4 # 1 & 2. Fetch PRP as n beams parallel to primary axis from CFB beams = [] for beamx in range(n): beam = [] for z in range(n): x = beamx + int(viewdir[0] z) y = scany + int(viewdir[1] z) beam.append(volume[z][y][x] if 0 <= x < n and 0 <= y < n else 0) beams.append(beam) # 3. Store slanted PRP into 2DSB one beam at a time (closest to furthest) for i, beam in enumerate(beams): shift = int(i viewdir[0]) colstart = (dsbwidth // 2) + shift for z, val in enumerate(beam): col = colstart + z if 0 <= col < dsbwidth: dsb[plane][z][col] = val # 4. De-skew using barrel shifter (Conveyor) to align rays vertically # (Hardware conveyor shifts beams to align viewing rays parallel to a 2D axis) # 5 & 6. Retrieve vertical rays and transfer to RPT with shift for col in range(dsbwidth): ray = [dsb[plane][z][col] for z in range(n)] # Shift ray during transfer to ensure closest voxel is at index 0 ray = [v for v in ray if v is not None] # 7. Process through RPT (VCU tree) current = ray[:] while len(current) > 1: nextlevel = [] for i in range(0, len(current), 2): v1 = current[i] v2 = current[i+1] if i+1 < len(current) else 0 combined = v1 0.5 + v2 0.5 # Standard compositing nextlevel.append(combined) current = nextlevel outputpixel(current[0], scany) # 8. Pipeline: 4th plane loads next PRP while others process if plane == 0: loadnextprp(dsb[3], volume, viewdir, n) CFB Size: 128M voxels for a 512^3 dataset. 2DSB Width: At least 2n-1 columns. 2DSB Modules: n modules. VCU Latency: 7 time units. Intermodule Communication: Each conveyor connects to neighbors by 256 lines (16 bits \times 16 shift places). Implementation Scale: A 512^3 system requires 512 parallel processing units, 512 memory modules, ~18,000 lines of information operating in parallel, and up to 1,024 chips for memory alone. Routing Difficulties: Module data lines are grouped by module, while conveyor data lines are grouped by bit position, creating complex routing requirements. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The 2DSB width (2n-1) must be sufficient to handle the shear of the slanted PRP. An architecture variant using three additional 2D buffers to accommodate arbitrary parallel and perspective projections. Unlike the rotation technique which distorts the CFB image, this method generates arbitrary projections without distortion but requires fetching a whole projection ray plane and rearranging it. It fetches n beams in O(n) cycles, stores them in a 2D temporary buffer, and rearranges them into 26-connected discrete ray representations using a O(\log n) barrel shifter twice. Each ray is fed into the VMWB for selection of the first opaque voxel in O(\log n) time. Total time is O(n^2 \log n), allowing real-time arbitrary projection. Time Complexity: O(n^2 \log n) for arbitrary parallel projection, same as orthographic projection in the original Cube architecture, compared to conventional O(n^3). Memory Complexity: High. Requires significant hardware resources (e.g., 1,024 chips for memory in a 512^3 system). Performance: Enables interactive rendering rates for 512^3 datasets. Strengths: Supports real-time arbitrary parallel projection without image distortion; conflict-free access to beams and rays; pipeline-friendly. Limitations: Extremely high hardware complexity and intermodule communication requirements; difficult routing; not suitable for perspective projection without more complex architecture. When to Use: When real-time arbitrary parallel projection of high-resolution volumes is required and hardware resources are available. When Not to Use: When hardware simplicity is preferred, or for perspective projection (requires more complex architecture). The Extended Cube Architecture was developed as an extension of the original Cube architecture, which was a special-purpose computer architecture for volume visualization supporting only orthographic projection. The original Cube used a Cubic Frame Buffer (CFB) and beam projection mechanisms. Arbitrary parallel projections were previously created by rotating the scene and viewing it through a principal orthographic direction, but this distorted the CFB image. The extended architecture was presented to support real-time arbitrary viewing without distortion. It builds on the Cube-3 Hybrid Ray-Casting method [3143-cube-3-hybrid-ray-casting.md]. An Extended Volume Visualization System for Arbitrary Parallel Projection, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh92/064-069, fetched 2026-10-29 Viewing and Rendering Processor for a Volume Visualization System, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh89/171-178, fetched 2026-10-26 (book)

name: Fixed Step Ray Marching
head: Ray Marching for Volume Integration, Ray-marching Volumetric Fog
body: Fixed Step Ray Marching is a direct volume rendering technique that integrates the volume rendering equation along camera rays using a constant step size, applying exponential absorption and gradient-based shading to fog-like participating media. It uniformly samples the ray, which simplifies implementation but requires tuning of stepsize to balance visual quality and performance. Unlike Exponential Approximation Method, which may use analytical approximations for transmittance, this method explicitly computes transmittance per step using the Beer-Lambert law. Inputs: 3D volume data (density field). Camera parameters (ray origin and direction per pixel). Light direction vector. Parameters: stepsize (default 0.15), absorption (default 12.0), maxsteps (default 800), volcolor (default (1.0, 0.95, 0.88)), bgcolor. Outputs: 2D image with RGB values per pixel. Data Structures: Bounding Box: bmin, bmax defining the volume extent in world space, padded by stepsize 2.0. Ray: Defined by origin O and direction D. Accumulators: transmittance (scalar, initialized to 1.0), cr, cg, cb (RGB color accumulators, initialized to 0.0). Steps: 1. Setup: Compute the active bounding box of the volume. If empty, return background color. Calculate world bounds bmin and bmax with padding stepsize 2.0. Normalize lightdir. 2. Ray Generation: For each pixel (x, y), compute ray origin O and direction D. Intersect the ray with the bounding box to find entry tenter and exit texit distances. If no intersection, set pixel to background. 3. Initialization: Set current distance t = max(tenter, 0.001). Initialize transmittance = 1.0 and color accumulators cr = cg = cb = 0.0. 4. Marching Loop: Iterate up to maxsteps: a. Termination Check: If t > texit or transmittance < 0.005, break loop. b. Position Calculation: Compute world position P = O + t D. c. Sampling: Sample density d at P from the volume data. d. Extinction Calculation: Compute optical depth for the step: ext = d \times absorption \times step\size. e. Transmittance Step: Compute step transmittance: tr\step = \exp(-ext). f. Gradient Calculation: Compute central differences for shading with h = step\size \times 0.5: gx = \text{density}(P + (h, 0, 0)) - \text{density}(P - (h, 0, 0)) gy = \text{density}(P + (0, h, 0)) - \text{density}(P - (0, h, 0)) gz = \text{density}(P + (0, 0, h)) - \text{density}(P - (0, 0, h)) g. Shading: Normalize gradient \vec{g} = (gx, gy, gz). Compute dot product with light direction: ndotl = \max(0.0, -\vec{g} \cdot light\dir). Compute shading factor: shade = 0.3 + 0.7 \times ndotl. h. Color Accumulation: Add contribution to color accumulators: cr += transmittance \times (1.0 - tr\step) \times vol\color.r \times shade cg += transmittance \times (1.0 - tr\step) \times vol\color.g \times shade cb += transmittance \times (1.0 - tr\step) \times vol\color.b \times shade. i. Transmittance Update: Update ray transmittance: transmittance = tr\step. j. Step Advance: Increment t += stepsize. 5. Final Composition: Add background contribution: cr += transmittance \times bg\color.r, cg += transmittance \times bg\color.g, cb += transmittance \times bg\color.b. 6. Clamping: Clamp final RGB values to [0, 1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fixedstepraymarching(volume, camera, lightdir, stepsize=0.15, absorption=12.0, maxsteps=800, volcolor=(1.0, 0.95, 0.88), bgcolor=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)): # 1. Setup bmin, bmax = computeactiveboundingbox(volume) pad = stepsize 2.0 bmin = (bmin[0] - pad, bmin[1] - pad, bmin[2] - pad) bmax = (bmax[0] + pad, bmax[1] + pad, bmax[2] + pad) lightlen = math.sqrt(lightdir[0]2 + lightdir[1]2 + lightdir[2]2) if lightlen == 0: lightdir = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) else: lightdir = (lightdir[0]/lightlen, lightdir[1]/lightlen, lightdir[2]/lightlen) imagewidth = camera.width imageheight = camera.height outputimage = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] def samplevolume(pos): return volume.getdensity(pos) def computeactiveboundingbox(volume): # Returns the active voxel bounds from the volume's grid tree return volume.bmin, volume.bmax def rayboxintersect(rayorigin, raydir, boxmin, boxmax): tmin = (boxmin[0] - rayorigin[0]) / raydir[0] if raydir[0] != 0 else float('-inf') tmax = (boxmax[0] - rayorigin[0]) / raydir[0] if raydir[0] != 0 else float('inf') if tmin > tmax: tmin, tmax = tmax, tmin tymin = (boxmin[1] - rayorigin[1]) / raydir[1] if raydir[1] != 0 else float('-inf') tymax = (boxmax[1] - rayorigin[1]) / raydir[1] if raydir[1] != 0 else float('inf') if tymin > tymax: tymin, tymax = tymax, tymin if (tmin > tymax) or (tymin > tmax): return None, None if tymin > tmin: tmin = tymin if tymax < tmax: tmax = tymax tzmin = (boxmin[2] - rayorigin[2]) / raydir[2] if raydir[2] != 0 else float('-inf') tzmax = (boxmax[2] - rayorigin[2]) / raydir[2] if raydir[2] != 0 else float('inf') if tzmin > tzmax: tzmin, tzmax = tzmax, tzmin if (tmin > tzmax) or (tzmin > tmax): return None, None if tzmin > tmin: tmin = tzmin if tzmax < tmax: tmax = tzmax return tmin, tmax for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): rayorigin, raydir = camera.getray(x, y) tenter, texit = rayboxintersect(rayorigin, raydir, bmin, bmax) if tenter is None: outputimage[y][x] = bgcolor continue t = max(tenter, 0.001) transmittance = 1.0 cr, cg, cb = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 for step in range(maxsteps): if t > texit or transmittance < 0.005: break px = rayorigin[0] + t raydir[0] py = rayorigin[1] + t raydir[1] pz = rayorigin[2] + t raydir[2] density = samplevolume((px, py, pz)) ext = density absorption stepsize trstep = math.exp(-ext) h = stepsize 0.5 gx = samplevolume((px + h, py, pz)) - samplevolume((px - h, py, pz)) gy = samplevolume((px, py + h, pz)) - samplevolume((px, py - h, pz)) gz = samplevolume((px, py, pz + h)) - samplevolume((px, py, pz - h)) gradlen = math.sqrt(gx2 + gy2 + gz2) if gradlen > 0.0: gx /= gradlen gy /= gradlen gz /= gradlen ndotl = max(0.0, -(gx lightdir[0] + gy lightdir[1] + gz lightdir[2])) shade = 0.3 + 0.7 ndotl colorfactor = transmittance (1.0 - trstep) shade cr += colorfactor volcolor[0] cg += colorfactor volcolor[1] cb += colorfactor volcolor[2] transmittance = trstep t += stepsize cr += transmittance bgcolor[0] cg += transmittance bgcolor[1] cb += transmittance bgcolor[2] cr = max(0.0, min(1.0, cr)) cg = max(0.0, min(1.0, cg)) cb = max(0.0, min(1.0, cb)) outputimage[y][x] = (cr, cg, cb) return outputimage A variant that uses configurable density ranges and early-out termination, with step size determined by object-space or world-space indexing. Uses a fixed number of sampling steps per ray for direct volume rendering, simple to implement but potentially inefficient for sparse volumes. The fundamental numerical approximation using Riemann sums with constant density/color per segment (Zero Order Integration). Targets light shafts from a single directional light using fixed step size and exponential absorption, respecting scene depth and shadows. Visualizes 3D scalar/vector fields by casting rays and accumulating color/opacity via front-to-back compositing, revealing internal structures. Performs the rendering integral in a single GPU pass, enabling optimizations like early ray termination and adaptive sampling. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Depends heavily on stepsize and maxsteps. Smaller stepsize increases accuracy but also computation. Sparse volumes may benefit from acceleration structures like HDDA (Hierarchical Distance Field Acceleration) to skip empty space. Strengths: Simple to implement, suitable for real-time rendering on GPUs, handles participating media like fog and clouds effectively. Limitations: Assumes homogeneous media between steps, which can lead to artifacts in heterogeneous media; fixed step size may be inefficient for sparse volumes if not combined with acceleration. When to use: Real-time visualization of fog, smoke, or clouds where performance is critical and high-frequency density variations are not expected. When not to use: Physically accurate rendering of heterogeneous media with complex scattering properties, where advanced techniques like Woodcock tracking are required. name: Ray Marching Volume Rendering with Henyey-Greenstein Scattering
head: Ray Marching with Henyey-Greenstein Scattering
body: This method renders a 3D volume defined by a density texture by accumulating scattered light along a ray, utilizing the Henyey-Greenstein phase function to model anisotropic scattering and shadow rays for self-shadowing. It distinguishes itself from standard front-to-back volume rendering by explicitly incorporating directional light transport through the Henyey-Greenstein phase function, allowing for the visualization of forward or backward scattering effects in participating media. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Camera parameters: ray origin ro and direction rd (derived from camera forward/right/up vectors and fragment UV coordinates). Volume texture uvolume: 3D texture storing density in the red channel. Velocity texture uvelocity (optional): 3D texture storing velocity vectors. Parameters: uphaseG (anisotropy g), udensityCoef (density multiplier), ulightDir (light direction), ulightColor (light color), ushowVelocity (boolean flag). Constants: STEPSIZE, MAXSTEPS, SHADOWSTEPSIZE, SHADOWFACTOR. Outputs: Final fragment color col. Data Structures Volume Texture: 3D array of floats where density is stored in the red channel (texture(...).r). If velocity visualization is enabled, the texture stores 3D velocity vectors. Ray State: ro: vec3 (Ray origin). rd: vec3 (Ray direction, normalized). t: float (Current distance along ray). transmit: float (Accumulated transmission, initial 1.0). col: vec3 (Accumulated color, initial 0.0). Numbered Steps 1. Ray Initialization: Calculate ray origin ro from camera position and direction rd from camera forward, right, and up vectors combined with fragment UV coordinates. Perform ray-box intersection with the volume bounding box defined by boxMin = (-0.5, -0.5, -0.5) and boxMax = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) to find entry distance t0 and exit distance t1. 2. No Intersection Check: If t0 > t1 or t1 < 0, the ray misses the volume. Output a gradient background color based on the fragment's Y coordinate and terminate. 3. Marcher Initialization: Set initial march distance t = max(t0, 0.0). Set maximum march distance tMax = t1. Initialize accumulated color col = 0.0 and transmission transmit = 1.0. Add a random noise offset to t to reduce banding artifacts: t = t + \text{fract}(\sin(\text{dot}(\text{gl\FragCoord.xy}, \text{vec2}(12.9898, 78.233))) \times 43758.5453) \times \text{STEP\SIZE}. 4. Precompute Phase Value: Calculate the dot product between the view direction rd and the light direction ulightDir. Let this be \cos\theta. Compute the Henyey-Greenstein phase value P(g, \cos\theta) using the anisotropy parameter uphaseG (g) and \cos\theta (see Formula section). 5. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to MAXSTEPS. If t > tMax, break the loop. 6. Position and Coordinate Calculation: Calculate world position: p = ro + rd \times t. Calculate normalized texture coordinates: \text{texCoord} = p + 0.5. 7. Sampling: If texCoord is within [0, 1] for all axes: If ushowVelocity is 1: Sample velocity texture. Compute magnitude mag of the velocity vector. Set density = mag 0.1 udensityCoef. Set sampleCol = normalize(velocity) 0.5 + 0.5 (visualize velocity direction as color). Else (Standard Density): Sample volume texture: density = texture(uvolume, texCoord).r udensityCoef. Set sampleCol = 1.0 (white base color). If texCoord is out of bounds, density = 0. 8. Lighting and Accumulation: If density > 0.01: Calculate alpha for the step: \alpha = 1.0 - \exp(-\text{density} \times \text{STEP\SIZE}). If ushowVelocity is 1: Add emissive color: col += sampleCol alpha transmit. Else (Lighting): Shadow Ray: Initialize shadowDens = 0.0. Step SHADOWSTEPS times along ulightDir with step size SHADOWSTEPSIZE. In each step, check if position is within texture bounds. If so, sample density and add to shadowDens. If out of bounds, exit shadow ray loop early. Light Attenuation: Calculate light value: \text{lightVal} = \exp(-\text{shadowDens} \times \text{SHADOW\FACTOR} \times \text{u\densityCoef} \times 0.1). Incoming Light: \text{incomingLight} = \text{u\lightColor} \times \text{lightVal} \times \text{phaseVal} + \text{ambientColor}. Accumulate: col += incomingLight alpha transmit. Update Transmission: transmit = (1.0 - alpha). If transmit < 0.01, break the loop to save computation. Increment: t += STEPSIZE. 9. Background and Tone Mapping: Add background contribution: col += bg transmit, where bg is the gradient background color calculated in Step 2. Apply Reinhard tone mapping: \text{col} = \frac{\text{col}}{\text{col} + 1.0}. Apply gamma correction: \text{col} = \text{pow}(\text{col}, 0.4545). Formulas Henyey-Greenstein Phase Function: P(g, \cos\theta) = \frac{1 - g^2}{4\pi (1 + g^2 - 2g\cos\theta)^{1.5}} Where: g is the anisotropy parameter (uphaseG). \cos\theta is the dot product of the view direction and light direction. Alpha Calculation: \alpha = 1.0 - \exp(-\text{density} \times \text{STEP\SIZE}) Light Attenuation: \text{lightVal} = \exp(-\text{shadowDens} \times \text{SHADOW\FACTOR} \times \text{u\densityCoef} \times 0.1) Parameters SHADOWSTEPSIZE: Step size for shadow ray marching. Value: 0.02. SHADOWFACTOR: Multiplier for shadow density attenuation. Value: 5.0. uphaseG: Anisotropy parameter g for Henyey-Greenstein. Range: [-0.99, 0.99]. udensityCoef: Global multiplier for sampled density values. STEPSIZE: Step size for main ray marching. Value not given in the sources. MAXSTEPS: Maximum number of march steps. Value not given in the sources. SHADOWSTEPS: Number of steps for shadow ray. Value not given in the sources. ambientColor: Ambient light color. Value not given in the sources. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Shadow Ray Bounds: Shadow ray marching must exit early if the shadow ray position goes outside the [0,1] texture coordinate space to prevent sampling invalid memory or incorrect densities. Early Termination: The main ray marching loop terminates early if transmission drops below 0.01. Banding: Random noise offset is added to the initial t to reduce banding artifacts caused by uniform step sizes. Zero Direction Components: Ray-box intersection must handle zero components in rd to avoid division by zero. Pseudocode Unverified code. Initialization t = max(tnear, 0.0) tMax = tfar col = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmit = 1.0 # Random offset for banding reduction noiseval = math.sin(fragcoord[0] 12.9898 + fragcoord[1] 78.233) 43758.5453 noise = noiseval - math.floor(noiseval) # GLSL fract equivalent t += noise 0.01 # STEPSIZE placeholder # 4. Marching Loop for i in range(100): # MAXSTEPS placeholder if t > tMax: break # 6. Position p = [ro[j] + rd[j]t for j in range(3)] texCoord = [p[j] + 0.5 for j in range(3)] density = 0.0 sampleCol = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 7. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the size of the volume texture. Performance: The method is computationally intensive due to the shadow ray casting for every sample. The early termination based on transmission (transmit < 0.01) helps optimize performance in opaque regions. Strengths: Accurately models anisotropic scattering, allowing for realistic lighting effects in participating media like fog or smoke. Simple to implement on the GPU. Limitations: Shadow rays significantly increase computation time. Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or inaccurate density integration in sparse regions. When to Use: Real-time rendering of volumetric effects where anisotropic scattering is desired and performance allows for shadow ray casting. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and anisotropic scattering is not required (use standard front-to-back rendering). When the volume is extremely sparse and fixed step size leads to poor sampling. This method is derived from real-time volume rendering techniques used in fluid simulation visualizations. It combines standard ray marching with the Henyey-Greenstein phase function to model light scattering in participating media. The specific implementation details, including the random offset for banding reduction and the shadow ray formulation, are based on a GitHub repository. tzhazuma/Fluidsimulation, https://github.com/tzhazuma/Fluidsimulation, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray Evaluation Stepping DVR
head: Ray Evaluation Stepping, Stepping DVR, Naive DVR
body: Ray Evaluation Stepping DVR is a fixed-step ray marching technique for Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) that integrates density and color along a ray path using configurable step sizes and early-out termination. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D scalar fields without extracting intermediate geometry by casting rays through the volume and accumulating color and opacity along each ray path. Unlike Density Marching which focuses on fog volumes with exponential absorption, or Discrete Volume Rendering Integral (VRI) which discretizes the integral differently, this method explicitly supports both world-space and object-space indexing based on the volume's capabilities, allowing for precise control over sampling density relative to voxel size or total ray length. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset (structured or unstructured). Ray origin (rayStart) and direction (rayDir) for each pixel. Ray length (rayLength) and volume axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for intersection. Configuration parameters: stepsize, alphaEarlyOut, densityMin, densityMax, enableEarlyOut. Transfer Function (TF) and Blending modules. Outputs: Final pixel color (C{out}) and opacity (O{out}). Normal vector (n) and depth (t{current}). The method uses a Parameters struct to store configuration constants, which are copied to device memory (e.g., constant memory in CUDA). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Parameters: scalart stepsize # Distance between samples. Default: 0.005 scalart alphaEarlyOut # Alpha threshold for termination. Default: 1.0 - 1e-5 scalart densityMin # Min density for normalization. Default: 0 scalart densityMax # Max density for normalization. Default: 1 Shader defines control the behavior at compile time: RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGVOLUMEINTERPOLATIONT: Interpolation type. RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGTRANSFERFUNCTIONT: TF type. RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGBLENDINGT: Blending type. RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGBRDFT: BRDF type. RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGENABLEEARLYOUT: Boolean (1 if enabled, 0 otherwise). RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGSKIPTRANSFERFUNCTION: Boolean (1 if volume outputs Color directly, 0 if Density). KERNELSYNCHRONIZEDTRACING: Boolean for warp-level divergence handling. 1. Intersection: Intersect the ray with the volume's AABB to find entry (t{min}) and exit (t{max1}) distances. Clamp t{min} to 0 and t{max} to \min(t{max1}, rayLength). 2. Initialization: Initialize output color to zero, normal to zero, and depth to zero. Initialize previousDensity to -1. 3. Step Size Calculation: If the volume supports object-space indexing: stepsize = voxelSize / stepsPerVoxel, where stepsPerVoxel is controlled by UI (range 0.1 to 10.0). If the volume does not support object-space indexing: stepsize = maxSize / stepsPerRay, where stepsPerRay is controlled by UI (range 10 to 1000.0) and maxSize is the volume's box size. 4. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate with terminationIndex starting at 0. Calculate current distance: t{current} = t{min} + terminationIndex \times stepsize. Termination Check: If t{current} > t{max}, break. If RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGENABLEEARLYOUT is 1 and C{out}.w < alphaEarlyOut, break. If KERNELSYNCHRONIZEDTRACING is 0, break if the current thread is invalid; if 1, break if all threads in the warp are invalid. Position: Calculate position P = rayStart + rayDir \times t{current}. Volume Evaluation: If RAYEVALUATIONSTEPPINGSKIPTRANSFERFUNCTION is 1: Evaluate volume for real4 color directly. Multiply color's alpha (w) by stepsize. Evaluate normal. Else: Evaluate volume for realt density. Normalization: Normalize density: density2 = (value - densityMin) \times \frac{1}{densityMax - densityMin}. Normal Evaluation: If requireNormal (isValid and value \ge densityMin), evaluate normal using volume.evalNormal. If KERNELSYNCHRONIZEDTRACING is 1, evaluate if any thread requires normal. Transfer Function: If requireNormal, evaluate transfer function: color1 = tf.eval(density2, n, previousDensity, stepsize, batch). Update previousDensity = density2. BRDF: If color1.w > 0, evaluate BRDF: color2 = brdf.eval(color1, position, n, rayDir, batch). Blending: Normalize normal n. Create newContribution with color2, n, and t{current}. If isValid, update output using blending.eval(output, newContribution). Front-to-Back Composition: C{out} = C{in} + (1 - O{in}) \alphai ci O{out} = O{in} + \alphai (1 - O{in}) Where: C{out}: Ray Color after sampling. O{out}: Ray Opacity after sampling. C{in}: Ray Color before sampling. O{in}: Ray Opacity before sampling. \alphai: Sampling point Opacity (Os). ci: Sampling point Color (Cs). Inverse Distance Interpolation (for unstructured data or specific atomic types): Vs = \frac{(D{p1} \times V{p2}) + (D{p2} \times V{p1})}{D{p1} + D{p2}} Where: Vs: Sampled Value. V{p1}, V{p2}: Values at corner points. D{p1}, D{p2}: Distances from corner points to the sampling point. stepsize: Distance between sampling points. Default: 0.005. alphaEarlyOut: Alpha threshold for early termination. Default: 1.0 - 10^{-5}. enableEarlyOut: Boolean flag. Default: true. densityMin: Minimum density for normalization. Default: 0. densityMax: Maximum density for normalization. Default: 1. Object Space Legacy: Old configuration files may store stepsize in object space. If stepsizeIsObjectSpace is true, the loaded stepsize is divided by 256 (assuming a 256^3 grid). Unstructured Data: In unstructured datasets, finding the next intersected voxel is complex due to lack of implicit connectivity, requiring exhaustive search and floating-point operations (the "point location problem"). Interpolation Degeneracy: If a sample is taken exactly on a corner, it has zero effect from other corners. If taken at the midpoint, it has equal contributions from all corners. Unrecognized Output: If volume output type is neither Density nor Color, throw runtimeerror "Output mode of the volume is unrecognized in RayEvaluationSteppingDvr". Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayevaluationsteppingdvr(raystart, raydir, raylength, volume, params, stepspervoxel, stepsperray, tf, blending, brdf): # 1. Intersection tmin, tmax1 = volume.intersectaabb(raystart, raydir) tmin = max(tmin, 0.0) tmax = min(tmax1, raylength) # 2. Initialization outcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # [r, g, b, a] outnormal = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] outdepth = 0.0 previousdensity = -1.0 # 3. Step Size Calculation if volume.supportsobjectspaceindexing(): stepsize = volume.getvoxelsize() / stepspervoxel else: stepsize = volume.getmaxsize() / stepsperray divdensityrange = 1.0 / (params.densitymax - params.densitymin) # 4. Ray Marching Loop terminationindex = 0 while True: tcurrent = tmin + terminationindex stepsize # Termination Check if tcurrent > tmax: break if params.enableearlyout and outcolor[3] < params.alphaearlyout: break # Position position = [raystart[i] + raydir[i] tcurrent for i in range(3)] # Volume Evaluation & TF if params.skiptransferfunction: colorraw = volume.evalcolor(position) colorraw[3] = stepsize n = volume.evalnormal(position) color1 = colorraw else: density = volume.evaldensity(position) density2 = (density - params.densitymin) divdensityrange n = volume.evalnormal(position) color1 = tf.eval(density2, n, previousdensity, stepsize) previousdensity = density2 # Normalization n = normalize(n) # BRDF if color1[3] > 0: color2 = brdf.eval(color1, position, n, raydir) else: color2 = color1 # Front-to-Back Composition alphai = color2[3] ci = color2[:3] outcolor[3] = outcolor[3] + alphai (1.0 - outcolor[3]) outcolor[:3] = [outcolor[i] + (1.0 - outcolor[3]) ci[i] for i in range(3)] outnormal = n outdepth = tcurrent terminationindex += 1 return outcolor, outnormal, outdepth Detailed comparisons with sibling methods are not given in the sources. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of steps per ray. S depends on stepsize and ray length. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, plus storage for the volume dataset. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with resolution and number of steps. Early-out termination can significantly reduce average steps per ray. Strengths: Simple to implement, supports both structured and unstructured data, configurable step size, early-out optimization. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or inefficiency if not tuned. Unstructured data requires expensive point location. When to use: General-purpose DVR, especially when flexibility in step size and early-out is needed. When not to use: When high performance on unstructured data is critical without preprocessing, or when adaptive step sizes are required for better quality. Origin: Formalized by Max [107] as a continuous integral; foundational techniques established by Drebin et al. [26] and Levoy [87]. History: DVR has been a basis of production volume renderers. The method supports both world-space and object-space indexing. Usage: Used in various volume rendering applications, including scientific visualization and medical imaging. shamanDevel/fV-SRN, https://github.com/shamanDevel/fV-SRN, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Deep Learning Methods and Neural Representations for Scientific Volume..., https://www.cs.uoregon.edu/Reports/AREA-202603-Mathai.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial);Г,,1:.
