name: Front-to-Back Ray Casting
head: RayCastSimple
body: Front-to-Back Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that accumulates color and opacity along a ray traversing a 3D texture space, starting from the viewer and moving toward the back of the volume. It solves the problem of compositing semi-transparent volumetric data into a 2D image by applying the standard front-to-back alpha blending equation at each sample step. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit use of a fixed iteration count combined with boundary checks, and its specific normalization of raw volume values to a fixed [0, 1] range before blending, rather than relying solely on the transfer function's alpha channel for opacity weighting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume texture (Volume), a front-face position texture (Front), a back-face position texture (Back), and a fragment shader input containing projective texture coordinates. Output: A float4 color value representing the accumulated ray color and opacity. Data Structures: Front / Back: 2D textures storing the 3D world coordinates of the entry and exit points of the ray through the volume bounding box. Volume: 3D texture storing scalar density values. dst: Accumulator buffer, initialized to (0, 0, 0, 0). src: Temporary sample buffer, initialized to (0, 0, 0, 0). pos: Current ray position, initialized to float4(front, 0). dir: Ray direction vector. Step: Step vector calculated as dir StepSize. Parameters: Iterations: Fixed number of steps (e.g., 1500). StepSize: Distance between samples. ThresholdMin: Lower bound for value clamping (40). ThresholdMax: Upper bound for value clamping (60). AlphaScale: Divisor for alpha normalization (Iterations / 50.0). EarlyTerminationThreshold: Alpha threshold to stop rendering (0.95). Steps: 1. Compute Ray Geometry: Calculate projective texture coordinates from the vertex shader output: texC.x = 0.5 \times \left(\frac{input.pos.xy.x}{input.pos.w}\right) + 0.5 texC.y = -0.5 \times \left(\frac{input.pos.xy.y}{input.pos.w}\right) + 0.5 Sample the front and back positions: front = Front.Sample(texC).rgb back = Back.Sample(texC).rgb Compute direction and initialize position: dir = normalize(back - front) pos = float4(front, 0) Compute step vector: Step = dir \times StepSize 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to Iterations - 1: Sample Volume: value = TrilinearSample(pos.xyz) TrilinearSample performs standard trilinear interpolation on the 3D volume texture at pos.xyz. Clamp and Normalize: Clamp value to [40, 60]: value = \max(40, \min(60, value)) Normalize to [0, 1]: value = \frac{value - 40.0}{20.0} Prepare Source Color/Alpha: Set source components to the normalized value: src = (value, value, value, value) Calculate source alpha: src.a = \frac{src.a}{Iterations / 50.0} Front-to-Back Blending: Modulate color by alpha: src.rgb = src.rgb \times src.a Update destination: dst = (1.0 - dst.a) \times src + dst Early Termination: If dst.a \ge 0.95, break loop. Advance Ray: pos.xyz = pos.xyz + Step Boundary Check: If any component of pos.xyz is outside [0.0, 1.0], break loop. 3. Return Result: Return dst. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def RayCastSimple(inputpos, fronttex, backtex, volumetex, iterations=1500, stepsize=0.01): # 1. Compute Ray Geometry texcx = 0.5 (inputpos.xy.x / inputpos.w) + 0.5 texcy = -0.5 (inputpos.xy.y / inputpos.w) + 0.5 front = fronttex.sample(texcx, texcy) back = backtex.sample(texcx, texcy) dir = normalize(back - front) pos = vec4(front, 0.0) dst = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) src = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) step = dir stepsize # 2. Ray Marching Loop for i in range(iterations): value = volumetex.trilinearsample(pos.xyz) value = max(40.0, min(60.0, value)) value = (value - 40.0) / 20.0 src = vec4(value, value, value, value) src.a /= (iterations / 50.0) src.rgb = src.a dst = (1.0 - dst.a) src + dst if dst.a >= 0.95: break pos.xyz += step if pos.x < 0.0 or pos.x > 1.0 or pos.y < 0.0 or pos.y > 1.0 or pos.z < 0.0 or pos.z > 1.0: break return dst Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The normalization relies on fixed thresholds (40, 60). If the volume data does not contain values in this range, the output will be uniformly black or white. Boundary Exit: The boundary check pos.x > 1.0f ||... assumes the volume texture coordinates are normalized to [0, 1]. If the volume is larger or smaller, this check may terminate rays prematurely or allow them to sample outside the texture bounds. Alpha Saturation: The early termination threshold of 0.95 may cause visible artifacts (banding) in transparent regions if the step size is too large, as the ray stops before fully integrating the back of the volume. Uses gradient information to determine isovalue boundaries for rendering, offering sharper edges than simple density-based raycasting. Combines gradient magnitude and density for transfer function evaluation, providing better material differentiation than density-only methods. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of iterations (steps) per pixel. The complexity is linear with respect to the number of samples taken along the ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as only the current position, direction, and accumulation buffers are stored. The volume texture is accessed via streaming. Measured Performance: Performance depends heavily on the Iterations parameter and early termination. With Iterations = 1500 and early termination at dst.a >= 0.95, average steps per pixel may be significantly lower than 1500 in opaque regions, but full 1500 steps in transparent regions. Strengths: Simple to implement; efficient early termination; fixed iteration count ensures consistent performance across frames. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or missing thin structures; normalization thresholds are hardcoded and not adaptive; boundary checks are simplistic. When to Use: Real-time rendering of volumetric data with known density ranges; when computational resources are limited and a simple, fast approximation is acceptable. When Not to Use: High-fidelity scientific visualization requiring adaptive step sizes; volumes with density ranges outside the hardcoded [40, 60] range; scenes requiring accurate transparency blending across large distances. The method originates from a specific implementation discussed in a GameDev Stack Exchange post titled "3D Texture Only interpolates on Y-Axis". The code snippet provided in the source demonstrates a fragment shader (RayCastSimplePS) that performs front-to-back raycasting using a fixed number of iterations and specific normalization thresholds. It is part of a broader family of direct volume rendering techniques that map 3D texture coordinates to screen space and accumulate color along rays. The technique is often used in real-time applications where performance is critical, and the volume data has a known, limited range of values. 3D Texture Only interpolates on Y-Axis, https://gamedev.stackexchange.com/questions/166205, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Light Shafts (URP Raymarching)
head: God Rays, Light Shafts, VolumetricLightURP
body: Volumetric Light Shafts (URP Raymarching) is a real-time post-processing technique for rendering volumetric light scattering (fog beams, atmospheric lighting) in the Unity Universal Render Pipeline (URP) by performing per-pixel raymarching through a main light's shadow map. It approximates single in-scattering from a single directional light source, modulated by a Henyey-Greenstein phase function and estimated occlusion derived from realtime shadow sampling. Unlike slice-based volume rendering or complex shadow-map methods, it requires no preprocessing, extra scene geometry, or high fill rate, making it significantly cheaper than full volumetric ray marching. However, it is limited to a single light source and lacks full volumetric depth information, leading to artifacts when foreground objects obscure background light shafts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Screen-space position (fragment world position), camera world position, main light realtime shadow map, light position, light color/intensity, and material parameters (density, step count, max distance, scattering multiplier). Output: Accumulated volumetric light color and alpha, added additively to the screen buffer. Data Structures: Shader Constants: BaseColor (float4): Base color of the volumetric effect. Default: (1, 1, 1, 1). Density (float): Density of the volume. Default: 0.5. Range: 0 to 1. StepCount (int): Number of raymarching steps. Default: 64. Range: 16 to 128. MaxDistance (float): Maximum distance for raymarching. Default: 20. Scattering (float): Scattering multiplier for the final color. Default: 1.2. LightPos (float4): Position of the light source in world space (xyz position, w=1). Updated dynamically by a C# controller. LightColor (float4): Color of the light source multiplied by intensity. Updated dynamically by a C# controller. Vertex Shader Output: positionHCS (float4): Clip space position. positionWS (float3): World space position of the fragment, passed to the fragment shader via TEXCOORD0. Numbered Steps: 1. Vertex Transformation: Input vertex position in object space (positionOS). Transform to clip space (positionCS) and world space (positionWS) using standard vertex utilities. Pass positionWS to the fragment shader via TEXCOORD0. 2. Ray Direction Calculation: In the fragment shader, retrieve the camera world position (camPos). Calculate the ray direction by normalizing the vector from the camera to the fragment's world position: \text{rayDir} = \text{normalize}(\text{positionWS} - \text{camPos}). 3. Initialization: Initialize accumulation variable accum = 0.0. Determine the number of steps: steps = max(StepCount, 1). This prevents division by zero or invalid loop behavior if StepCount is less than 1. Calculate step size: stepSize = MaxDistance / steps. 4. Raymarching Loop: Loop i from 0 to steps - 1. Calculate distance along the ray: dist = i stepSize. Calculate sample position in world space: \text{samplePos} = \text{camPos} + \text{rayDir} \times \text{dist}. 5. Shadow Sampling: Transform samplePos to shadow coordinates: shadowCoord = TransformWorldToShadowCoord(samplePos). Sample the main light realtime shadow: shadow = MainLightRealtimeShadow(shadowCoord). This value represents the occlusion factor (1.0 if lit, 0.0 if shadowed, or intermediate values for soft shadows). 6. Phase Function Calculation: Calculate the light direction from the sample position to the light position: \text{lightDir} = \text{normalize}(\LightPos.xyz - \text{samplePos}). Calculate the cosine of the angle between the ray direction and the light direction: \cos\theta = \text{dot}(\text{rayDir}, \text{lightDir}). Compute the Henyey-Greenstein phase function with hardcoded asymmetry parameter g = 0.35: P(\theta) = \frac{1 - g^2}{(1 + g^2 - 2g \cos\theta)^{1.5}}. 7. Accumulation: Add to accum: \text{accum} += \text{shadow} \times P(\theta) \times \Density \times \text{stepSize}. 8. Final Color Computation: Compute the final light amount: lightAmount = accum. Multiply LightColor.rgb by lightAmount and Scattering. Compute alpha: alpha = saturate(lightAmount). Output the result as an additive blend to the screen buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def heneygreenstein(costheta: float, g: float) -> float: g2 = g g return (1.0 - g2) / math.pow(1.0 + g2 - 2.0 g costheta, 1.5) def normalize(x, y, z): length = math.sqrt(xx + yy + zz) return (x/length, y/length, z/length) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def raymarchfragments(positionsws, campos, lightpos, lightcolor, density, stepcount, maxdistance, scattering): steps = max(stepcount, 1) stepsize = maxdistance / steps results = [] for fragws in positionsws: raydir = normalize(fragws[0] - campos[0], fragws[1] - campos[1], fragws[2] - campos[2]) accum = 0.0 for i in range(steps): dist = i stepsize samplepos = (campos[0] + raydir[0] dist, campos[1] + raydir[1] dist, campos[2] + raydir[2] dist) # Unity's TransformWorldToShadowCoord and MainLightRealtimeShadow are built-in; not given in sources. shadow = 1.0 lightdir = normalize(lightpos[0] - samplepos[0], lightpos[1] - samplepos[1], lightpos[2] - samplepos[2]) costheta = dot(raydir, lightdir) phase = heneygreenstein(costheta, 0.35) accum += shadow phase density stepsize lightamount = accum finalcolor = (lightcolor[0] lightamount scattering, lightcolor[1] lightamount scattering, lightcolor[2] lightamount scattering) alpha = min(1.0, max(0.0, lightamount)) results.append((finalcolor, alpha)) return results Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If StepCount is less than 1, it is clamped to 1 to prevent division by zero or invalid loop behavior. The method uses a single directional light with shadow sampling and does not support multiple lights or complex volume textures. Performance cost is significant; enabling god rays adds 2.30 ms to a 5.0 ms frame in benchmarked scenes. Screen-Space God Rays is a real-time post-processing technique that approximates volumetric light scattering (crepuscular rays) by performing per-pixel additive sampling of an image light source in screen space. name: Screen-Space God Rays
head: Screen-Space Radial Blur, Screen-Space Light Shafts, Radial Blur God Rays
body: Screen-Space God Rays is a real-time post-processing technique that approximates volumetric light scattering (crepuscular rays) by performing per-pixel additive sampling of an image light source in screen space. It builds on Volumetric Light Shafts (URP Raymarching) by simplifying the volume rendering equation to estimate single in-scattering from a single light source, modulated by an estimated occlusion factor derived from radial sampling. Unlike slice-based volume rendering or shadow-map methods, it requires no preprocessing, extra scene geometry, or high fill rate, making it significantly cheaper than volumetric ray marching. However, it is limited to single light sources and lacks full volumetric depth information, leading to artifacts when foreground objects obscure background light shafts. The method operates in three passes: an occlusion pre-pass, a radial blur accumulation pass, and a compositing pass. Inputs: scenetexture: The rendered scene color buffer or occlusion map. lightposscreen: The 2D screen-space coordinates of the light source (UV space [0,1] or NDC [-1,1]). density: Controls sample separation and ray spread. decay: Exponential falloff factor per sample. weight: Per-sample intensity multiplier. exposure: Final output brightness multiplier. numsamples: Number of iterations for the radial accumulation loop. Outputs: finalcolor: The final composited color with god rays added. The technique uses standard 2D textures (sampler2D) for the scene buffer and occlusion map. Uniforms are passed to the fragment shader. No complex volumetric grids or sparse structures are used. 1. Light Position Projection: Project the 3D world position of the light source into screen space. Transform the light's world position by the View-Projection matrix. Perform perspective division by w to obtain NDC coordinates. Scale and bias to the texture coordinate range [0, 1] (or [-1, 1] depending on implementation). Edge Case: If the light is behind the camera (clip w \le 0 or very small), clamp the screen position to the center of the screen (0.5, 0.5) and mark the light as not in front. 2. Occlusion Pre-Pass (Optional but Recommended): To improve occlusion accuracy, render the scene geometry as solid black and the light source as a bright shape (circle/sphere) into a separate render target. This creates a binary-like occlusion map where bright pixels indicate direct visibility of the light and black pixels indicate occlusion by geometry. This pass reduces streaking artifacts caused by surface texture variations in the main scene buffer. 3. Radial Accumulation (Fragment Shader): For each pixel in the output texture: Calculate the direction vector from the current pixel's texture coordinate (uv) to the light's screen position (light\pos). Compute the step size (delta\uv) by scaling the direction vector by the density and dividing by the number of samples. Initialize the accumulated color to zero (if using occlusion map) or the base scene color (if using direct scene buffer). Initialize the illumination decay factor to 1.0. Iterate num\samples times: Step the texture coordinate backwards along the direction vector: uv \leftarrow uv - delta\uv. Sample the texture at the new coordinate. Clamp coordinates to [0, 1] to handle boundary conditions. Multiply the sample color by the current illumination decay and the weight constant. Add the result to the accumulated color. Update the illumination decay: illumination \leftarrow illumination \times decay. The accumulation approximates the integral of in-scattered light, where the decay simulates absorption/scattering over distance. 4. Compositing: If an occlusion map was used in Step 2, add the accumulated god ray color to the original scene color using additive blending. Multiply the final color by the exposure constant. Output the result with alpha 1.0. The following is a self-contained Python-like implementation for the radial accumulation pass, assuming an occlusion map input. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegodrays(uv, lightpos, density, decay, weight, exposure, numsamples, texturesampler): # Calculate step vector from current pixel to light source deltauv = (uv - lightpos) density / numsamples currentuv = uv illumination = 1.0 color = vec3(0.0) # Initialize to zero for occlusion map; use texturesampler(uv) for direct scene buffer for i in range(numsamples): currentuv = currentuv - deltauv # Clamp to [0, 1] to handle screen boundaries samp = texturesampler(clamp(currentuv, 0.0, 1.0)) samp = samp illumination weight color = color + samp illumination = illumination decay return color exposure If using the direct scene buffer without an occlusion pre-pass, the initialization changes to color = texturesampler(uv) and the accumulation adds to this base color. NUMSAMPLES: Controls sampling density and smoothness. Typical value: 64 or 100. Higher values increase cost. density: Controls the separation between samples. Higher values decrease separation, resulting in brighter rays covering a shorter range. Typical value: 0.92. decay: Exponential falloff factor per sample. Range [0, 1]. Values close to 1.0 (e.g., 0.97) produce long, gradual rays; lower values produce short, punchy rays. Typical value: 0.96815. weight: Per-sample contribution factor. Typical value: 0.1 or 0.58. exposure: Final color multiplier. Typical value: 0.3. Light Behind Camera: If the light is behind the camera, the screen position projection may be invalid. Handle by clamping to screen center and disabling the effect or returning a default value. Off-Screen Lights: The technique only works for visible light sources. If the light moves off-screen, the rays disappear or become distorted. Depth Artifacts: Since the method lacks full volumetric depth, light shafts from background objects may appear in front of foreground objects when the light source is relatively near. This is often perceived as a lens flare effect but can break immersion. Streaking: Sampling the main scene buffer directly can cause streaks due to high-frequency surface textures. Using an occlusion pre-pass (black geometry, bright light) mitigates this. Single Light Source: The method assumes single scattering from a single light source. It does not handle multiple light sources or complex multiple scattering effects. A post-processing technique that draws light sources to a separate render target, then processes this target using a post-processing shader to create light scattering, merging it with the back buffer. Designed originally for one very strong light. Main loop: For each pixel, get texCoord. For each light, if Type == SPOTLIGHT: Calculate deltaTexCoord = (texCoord - projectedLightPos.xy) / (NUMSAMPLES Density). Initialize illuminationDecay = 1.0. Loop j from 0 to NUMSAMPLES-1: Decrease texCoord by deltaTexCoord. Sample inputTexture at modifiedPixel. Add to color: color += sample illuminationDecay Weight. Update decay: illuminationDecay = Decay. Add result to output: result += color Exposure. Pitfall: Applying this method to multiple lights resulted in a simple 'Blur' of the light source map rather than correct volumetric scattering. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the image resolution (pixels) and M is the number of samples (NUM\SAMPLES). Memory Complexity: O(N) for the temporary render targets (occlusion map, god ray buffer). Performance: Very fast. Requires only two extra render passes (occlusion pre-pass and radial blur) and a handful of texture samples per pixel. It is significantly cheaper than volumetric ray marching. Strengths: Simple to implement, low hardware requirements, no preprocessing, works with arbitrary scene complexity. Limitations: Limited to single light sources, inaccurate occlusion estimation (screen-space only), depth artifacts (background rays in front of foreground objects), fails if light is off-screen. When to Use: Real-time rendering on mobile or lower-end hardware, scenes with a dominant single light source (e.g., sun), where performance is critical and perfect physical accuracy is not required. When Not to Use: Scenes with multiple light sources, scenes requiring accurate volumetric depth interaction, or when the light source is frequently off-screen. The technique was published by Kenny Mitchell in 2007 in GPU Gems 3 as "Volumetric Light Scattering as a Post-Process". It gained widespread adoption in the gaming industry, notably in Crysis (2007), setting a standard for high-end PC games. It dominated god ray implementations for over a decade due to its speed and simplicity. The method approximates the volume rendering equation by simplifying the in-scattering term and estimating occlusion through radial sampling in screen space. name: Volumetric Sun Shafts (God Rays)
head: Haze volumetrics, In-scattered light shafts
body: A post-processing technique that renders volumetric light shafts (sun shafts) by marching a view ray through a sun shadow map, accumulating in-scattered light where the ray is lit and no light where it is shadowed, modulated by ground-hugging haze density. It differs from screen-space alternatives like Screen-Space God Rays by relying on a dedicated shadow map for occlusion rather than screen-space depth, allowing accurate volumetric occlusion from geometry outside the current view frustum, while trading off higher memory bandwidth for the shadow map. It builds on Volumetric Light Shafts (URP Raymarching) and contrasts with Image-Based Light Shaft (Dobashi) by using explicit ray marching instead of screen-space blurring. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Depth buffer, inverse projection matrix, inverse view matrix, sun shadow map, sun color, sun direction, ground plane height, global intensity multiplier, and camera position. Outputs: A post-processing texture containing the accumulated sun shafts, composited over the scene. Data Structures: VolumetricPass Target: A render target with HalfFloatType precision, no depth buffer, sized at half the screen resolution. Shadow Map: A texture storing depth or binary lit/shadowed status for the sun light source. Parameters: STEPS: Number of march steps, set to 16. uIntensity: Global intensity multiplier, calculated as 0.07 \times \text{strength}. uGround: Height of the ground plane for density calculation. MARCHLENGTH: The last 32 units of the ray are used for marching, or 0 if the ray is shorter than 32 units. Algorithm Steps: 1. Resolution Reduction: Render the effect at half resolution to quarter the per-pixel shadow-map sampling cost, relying on the soft nature of the haze effect to hide aliasing. 2. Jittering: To hide banding artifacts in the volumetric march, jitter the start position of the ray march using interleaved gradient noise. 3. Ray Reconstruction: For each pixel, reconstruct the world position from the depth buffer using the inverse projection and view matrices. 4. Ray Definition: Compute the view ray direction \mathbf{rd} from the camera position to the reconstructed world position and its length L. 5. March Setup: Determine the march start distance as the last 32 units of the ray (or 0 if L < 32). Calculate the step length \Delta s based on 16 steps over the march length: \Delta s = \frac{\text{MARCH\LENGTH}}{\text{STEPS}} 6. Integration Loop: Loop STEPS (16) times: a. Compute sample position \mathbf{p} along the ray. b. Transform \mathbf{p} to shadow map space. c. Determine if the sample is lit by checking shadow map bounds and depth. Let S \in \{0, 1\} be the shadow factor (1 if lit, 0 if shadowed). d. Calculate ground-hugging density \rho using exponential falloff based on sample height y relative to ground level uGround: \rho = e^{-k(y - uGround)} (Note: The exact decay constant k is not specified in the sources.) e. Apply forward scattering phase function P(\theta), which is brighter when looking toward the sun. f. Scale the contribution by distance attenuation and density. g. Accumulate the result: Accum += S \cdot \rho \cdot P(\theta) \cdot \text{attenuation}. 7. Output: Output final color as sun color multiplied by the accumulated amount, phase, and intensity uIntensity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendervolumetricsunshafts(depthbuffer, invproj, invview, shadowmap, shadowmatrix, suncolor, sundir, uground, strength, camerapos): STEPS = 16 MARCHLENGTH = 32.0 uintensity = 0.07 strength outw = depthbuffer.width // 2 outh = depthbuffer.height // 2 output = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(outw)] for in range(outh)] for y in range(outh): for x in range(outw): depthval = depthbuffer.get(x, y) # Reconstruct world position from depth buffer using inverse projection and view matrices clipx = 2.0 (x + 0.5) / outw - 1.0 clipy = 2.0 (y + 0.5) / outh - 1.0 clipz = depthval 2.0 - 1.0 clippos = (clipx, clipy, clipz, 1.0) viewpos = invproj @ clippos viewpos = (viewpos[0]/viewpos[3], viewpos[1]/viewpos[3], viewpos[2]/viewpos[3]) worldpos = invview @ (viewpos[0], viewpos[1], viewpos[2], 1.0) raydir = normalize(worldpos[:3] - camerapos) raylen = length(worldpos[:3] - camerapos) # March start distance as the last 32 units of the ray (or 0 if L < 32) startdist = max(0.0, raylen - MARCHLENGTH) steplen = MARCHLENGTH / STEPS if steplen <= 0.0: continue # Jitter start position using interleaved gradient noise to hide banding artifacts jitter = ((x 12.9898 + y 78.233) % 1.0) 2.0 - 1.0 t = startdist + jitter steplen 0.5 accumulated = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(STEPS): samplepos = camerapos + raydir t # Transform to shadow map space shadowclip = shadowmatrix @ (samplepos[0], samplepos[1], samplepos[2], 1.0) shadowuv = (shadowclip[0] / shadowclip[3], shadowclip[1] / shadowclip[3]) # Determine if the sample is lit by checking shadow map bounds and depth if 0.0 <= shadowuv[0] <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= shadowuv[1] <= 1.0: storeddepth = shadowmap.get(shadowuv) S = 1.0 if samplepos[2] < storeddepth else 0.0 else: S = 0.0 # Calculate ground-hugging density using exponential falloff based on sample height relative to ground level heightdiff = samplepos[1] - uground density = math.exp(-max(0.0, heightdiff)) # Decay constant not given # Apply forward scattering phase function (brighter when looking toward sun) phase = max(0.0, dot(raydir, sundir)) # Scale by distance attenuation attenuation = 1.0 / (t + 1.0) # contrib = S density phase attenuation steplen accumulated[0] += contrib suncolor[0] accumulated[1] += contrib suncolor[1] accumulated[2] += contrib suncolor[2] output[y][x] = (accumulated[0] uintensity, accumulated[1] uintensity, accumulated[2] uintensity) return output def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) if l > 0 else (0,0,0) def length(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Banding: Banding artifacts in the volumetric march are hidden by jittering the start position using interleaved gradient noise. Short Rays: If the ray length is less than 32 units, the march length is 0, and no light is accumulated. Resolution: Running at half resolution is critical for performance; running at full resolution would significantly increase cost without proportional visual benefit due to the soft nature of the effect. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot \text{STEPS}), where W and H are the output resolution (half screen) and STEPS is 16. The cost is dominated by shadow map lookups. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the output texture (half float, 3 channels) plus the shadow map size. Performance: Runs at half resolution to reduce cost, relying on the soft nature of the haze effect. Strengths: Accurate volumetric occlusion from shadow maps, allowing shafts to be cast by geometry outside the view frustum. Limitations: Requires a dedicated shadow map and post-processing pass. Performance scales with resolution and step count. This technique is part of the volumetric rendering pipeline in a custom WebAssembly-based voxel engine, specifically implemented in src/volumetric.ts. It is designed to render atmospheric lighting effects in a browser environment. 12.8B destructible voxels rendered in the browser with Rust WASM custom engine, https://github.com/cktang88/2.5d-experiment, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Image-Based Light Shaft (Dobashi)
head: Dobashi Light Shafts, Parallel Slice Light Shafts
body: A method that displays light shafts with a shadow map using texture-mapping hardware by placing parallel slices in front of the screen to compute light scattering induced by atmospheric particles. It uses the color buffer of light received by visible objects to calculate the light frustum from a shadow map and the average extinction of participating media. It sets itself apart from siblings like Screen-Space God Rays by explicitly modeling the volumetric light transport equation via parallel slices rather than post-processing screen-space artifacts, and from Volumetric Sun Shafts (God Rays) by relying on hardware-accelerated shadow mapping for occlusion rather than simple radial blurring. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: View ray, light source position, shadow map, color buffer of visible objects, particle density distribution, light frustum parameters. Outputs: Final image with light shafts. Data Structures: Parallel Slices: A series of planes positioned in front of the screen. The number of slices is proportional to the desired quality and inversely proportional to the sampling error. Shadow Map: Standard depth buffer storing depth of opaque objects from the light's perspective. Color Buffer: Stores the color of light received by visible objects. Steps: 1. Render Shadow Map: Generate a shadow map from the light source's perspective, storing depths of opaque objects. 2. Calculate Light Frustum: Determine the light frustum using the shadow map and the average extinction of participating media. 3. Intersect Eye Ray: Calculate the intersection of the eye ray with the light frustum to determine the length of the light path through the frustum. 4. Render Parallel Slices: Place parallel slices in front of the screen. For each slice: a. Sample the shadow map to determine if the slice is in shadow. b. Compute light scattering induced by atmospheric particles using the rendering light transport equation. c. Integrate in-scattering along the view ray. d. Compute light attenuation reaching the viewpoint based on particle density. 5. Composite: Combine the results from all slices to form the final image. Formulas: Light Transport Equation: The method integrates the in-scattering along the view ray and light attenuation reaching the viewpoint. The extra intensity is computed from information that represents light scattering, where leads to appear columns of scattered radiance visible with space is partly in shadow. Light Path Length: L = \text{Intersection}(EyeRay, LightFrustum). Parameters: Number of Virtual Planes: Proportional to the number of passes required. Particle Density: Determines the density of particles in the atmosphere. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sampling Error: Requires multiple passes proportional to the number of virtual planes, which leads to error sampling. Aliasing: The method tries to avoid aliasing problems, but the multiple passes can introduce sampling artifacts. Performance: Adding sub-planes to overcome sampling error requires more computation, making it time-consuming. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderlightshaftsdobashi(viewray, lightsource, shadowmap, colorbuffer, particledensity, numslices): # Step 1: Render Shadow Map (Assumed pre-computed) shadowmap = rendershadowmap(lightsource) # Step 2: Calculate Light Frustum lightfrustum = calculatelightfrustum(shadowmap, particledensity) # Step 3 & 4: Render Parallel Slices finalimage = zeroslike(colorbuffer) for i in range(numslices): # Place slice in front of screen sliceplane = getsliceplane(i, numslices) # Intersect eye ray with light frustum lightpathlength = intersecteyeraywithfrustum(viewray, lightfrustum) # Sample shadow map for this slice isinshadow = sampleshadowmap(shadowmap, sliceplane.position) # Compute light scattering if not isinshadow: scattering = computescattering(sliceplane, particledensity, lightsource) attenuation = computeattenuation(particledensity, lightpathlength) finalimage += scattering attenuation else: # Slice is in shadow, no scattering pass # Step 5: Composite return finalimage A method based on stochastic transparency that casts shadows between any aggregation of colored transmissive, opaque, and partial coverage surfaces, consistent with hardware shadow mapping. It applies an infinite number of surfaces on GPUs and consoles, using the depth buffer to store the depth of opaque surfaces and blending RGB channels to emulate a depth test for translucent surfaces. It extends Dobashi's method by allowing translucent objects to cast shadows, which Dobashi's original method could not do. A method to render sunlight and illumination effects induced by attenuated light reaching the viewpoint at different altitudes. It computes lit segments from the view ray and ignores dark parts through a shadow test to reduce the cost of the integral equation of light. It differs from Dobashi by focusing on altitude-based attenuation and optimizing the integral calculation by skipping dark segments. A method that restores intensity points in space as a texture put in an array, using shadow sampling to calculate intensity for interactive rate images. It lacks calculation of multiple scattering. It differs from Dobashi by using a geometric approach with intensity points in an array rather than parallel slices, and is optimized for interactive rates but sacrifices physical accuracy in multiple scattering. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of virtual planes (slices). Adding sub-planes increases computation time, making it time-consuming. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of slices and the resolution of the shadow map and color buffer. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance degrades linearly with the number of slices. Strengths: Uses hardware-accelerated shadow mapping; physically based on light transport equation. Limitations: Multiple passes lead to sampling errors and aliasing; time-consuming if sub-planes are added. When to use: When physically accurate light shafts are needed and hardware shadow mapping is available. When not to use: When performance is critical and sampling errors can be tolerated or mitigated by other means. Dobashi proposed the method to display light shafts with a shadow map using texture-mapping hardware. The method includes rendering light shafts by placing parallel slices in front of the screen to compute light scattering induced by atmospheric particles. The principle fundamental of participating media to interact with light is based on rendering the light transport equation for generating effects of atmospheric phenomena such as light shaft. Therefore, when light travels from the light source through space in variety directions hits particles of atmosphere, based on physical properties of particles yield effects such as scattering and absorption of light. The integration of the in-scattering along the view ray and light attenuation that reaches to viewpoint will appear light volume according to the density of particles in atmosphere. Moreover, the presence of objects inside the light volume leads to generate shadow with light shaft. This method has been exploited graphics hardware rendering light shaft and shadow map. However, this method tried avoiding aliasing problem, but it needs multiple passes for number virtual planes that must proportional to the number of passes which lead to error sampling. Dobashi later modified the method by adding sub-planes to overcome the sampling error, but this method requires more computation which time-consuming. Mitchell presented a method which based on work by Dobashi for simulating light shafts. This method renders a traditional shadow map from opaque objects merely and then fills the scene with hundreds of translucent fog planes that receive the shadowing. This provides convincing light shafts, which can have color if the light has a projective texture or fog planes have colored texture. But this method, translucent objects cannot cast shadows. Then Morgan proposed a method based on develop technique presented by stochastic transparency, for shadow cast between any aggregation of colored transmissive, opaque, and partial coverage surfaces which it consistent with hardware shadow mapping techniques. This method used number infinity of surfaces that apply on GPUs and consoles. However it use depth buffer to store a depth of opaque surfaces and use to blending RGB channels to emulate a depth test for translucent surfaces. Gautron presented technique to use color buffer to light received by visible objects to calculate light frustum form shadow map and average extinction of participating media. The intersection of an eye ray is calculated in order to determine length of the light path through frustum. Bruneton proposed method to render sunlight and illumination effects induced of attenuated light until reach to viewpoint and at different altitude from level ground for atmosphere. However, it based on compute the lit segments from view ray and ignore the dark parts through shadow test that reduce cost of integral equation of light. name: Ray Marching Volume Rendering (GLSL)
head: Fragment Shader Ray Marching, GLSL Ray Marching Volume Rendering, GPU Ray Marching, GPU-Based Ray Marching, Ray Marching on the GPU, Ray Marching with Trilinear Interpolation, vol-fs.glsl raymarch, vol-fs2.glsl raymarch
body: Ray Marching Volume Rendering is a direct volume rendering technique that discretizes viewing rays into fixed steps to sample a 3D texture, accumulating color and opacity via front-to-back compositing within a fragment shader. It solves the problem of real-time volumetric visualization by performing the entire rendering integral in a single pass on the GPU, avoiding the memory bandwidth bottlenecks of slice-based methods like Shear-Warp. Unlike its siblings, it processes rays independently, enabling optimizations such as early ray termination, and is generally faster than Shear-Warp for equivalent visual quality. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D volume texture (density/scalar field), a transfer function (optional, for color mapping), camera position and orientation matrices, and a bounding box defining the volume extent (typically a unit cube centered at origin or [0,1]^3). Outputs: A final pixel color (vec4) with accumulated alpha. Data Structures: Volume Texture: Stored as a 3D texture (sampler3D) or a 2D texture atlas where slices are packed. If using a 2D atlas, the z-coordinate is mapped to slice index. Uniforms: uvolumesize (ivec3): Dimensions of the volume. umatrixtranslation (mat4): World-to-local transform. umatrixcameratranslation (mat4): Camera-to-world transform. uTexDim (vec3): Texture dimensions (width, height, depth). uTMK / uTMK2 (float): Transmittance multiplier constant for exponential absorption. uenablemaxvaluesampling (int): 1 for max-value sampling, 0 for standard compositing. MAXSTEPS (int): Maximum iteration count (e.g., 128, 200, 256). STEPSIZE (float): Fixed step distance (e.g., 0.01). TMMIN (float): Minimum transmittance threshold for early termination (e.g., 0.25 or 0.0). Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Read volume data from disk and estimate normals if required for shading. 2. Ray Setup: Compute ray origin in local volume space: rayOrigin = (invModel vec4(cameraPos, 1.0)).xyz. Compute ray direction in camera space: rayDircam = normalize(camrelpos.xyz). Transform ray direction to local volume space: rayDirlocal = normalize((camToLocal vec4(rayDircam, 0.0)).xyz). Alternatively, compute direction as normalize(rayOrigin - cameraPos). 3. Ray-Box Intersection: Define bounding box: boxMin = vec3(-0.5), boxMax = vec3(0.5) (or [0,1]). Compute intersection interval [tMin, tMax] using the slab method: invDir = 1.0 / (rayDir + \epsilon) t0s = (boxMin - rayOrigin) invDir t1s = (boxMax - rayOrigin) invDir tSmaller = min(t0s, t1s) tLarger = max(t0s, t1s) tMin = max(max(tSmaller.x, tSmaller.y), max(tSmaller.z, 0.0)) tMax = min(min(tLarger.x, tLarger.y), tLarger.z) If tMin >= tMax, discard the fragment (ray misses volume). Clamp tMin to 0.0. 4. Step Size Calculation: Fixed Step: Use a constant STEPSIZE (e.g., 0.01) or derive from MAXSTEPS and diagonal length: gStepSize = sqrt(3.0) / float(MAXSTEPS). Voxel-Aligned Step: Calculate dt to ensure at least one sample per voxel dimension: size = u\volume\size abs(rayDir\local) dt\vec = 1.0 / size dt = min(dt\vec.x, min(dt\vec.y, dt\vec.z)). 5. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize t = tMin, accumulatedColor = vec4(0.0), tm = 1.0 (transmittance). Loop for i from 0 to MAXSTEPS while t < tMax: a. Sample Position: pos = rayOrigin + t rayDirlocal. b. Texture Sampling: Map pos to texture coordinates (0.0 to 1.0): samplePos = pos + vec3(0.5). If using 2D atlas: Calculate zSlice = (1.0 - pos.y) (uTexDim.z - 1.0), sample two slices with texture2D, and lerp using fract(zSlice). Read density: density = texture(volumeTexture, samplePos).r. c. Color/Alpha Mapping: Map density to color: voxelcolor = texture(transferfn, vec2(density, 0.5)). Calculate alpha contribution: a = density voxelcolor.a. (Note: applies an opacity correction a{corrected} = 1.0 - (1.0 - a{val})^{dt\scale}.) d. Compositing: Standard Front-to-Back: accumulatedColor.rgb += (1.0 - accumulatedColor.a) a voxel\color.rgb accumulatedColor.a += (1.0 - accumulatedColor.a) a. Max-Value Sampling: If a > accumulatedColor.a, update accumulatedColor.rgb = voxelcolor.rgb a and accumulatedColor.a = max(a, accumulatedColor.a). Lighting (Optional): Compute light direction ld, light transmittance ltm, and add: col += (1.0 - dtm) uColor2 uLightC[k] tm ltm. e. Update Transmittance: tm = exp(-uTMK density step). f. Advance Ray: t += step. g. Early Termination: If accumulatedColor.a >= 0.95, break loop. If tm < TMMIN, break loop. If pos is outside bounds, break loop. 6. Final Output: Compute final alpha: alpha = 1.0 - tm. Return vec4(accumulatedColor.rgb / alpha, alpha). Discard if FragColor.a <= 0.001. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarch(volumetexture, transferfn, camerapos, invmodel, camtolocal, boxmin, boxmax, maxsteps, stepsize, tmmin, utmk, uenablemaxvaluesampling): # 1. Ray Setup rayorigin = (invmodel @ vec4(camerapos, 1.0)).xyz raydircam = normalize(vec3(0, 0, -1)) # Assuming camera looks down -Z, or use camrelpos raydirlocal = normalize((camtolocal @ vec4(raydircam, 0.0)).xyz) # 2. Ray-Box Intersection invdir = 1.0 / (raydirlocal + 0.0000001) # Epsilon for division by zero t0s = (boxmin - rayorigin) invdir t1s = (boxmax - rayorigin) invdir tsmaller = min(t0s, t1s) tlarger = max(t0s, t1s) tmin = max(max(tsmaller.x, tsmaller.y), max(tsmaller.z, 0.0)) tmax = min(min(tlarger.x, tlarger.y), tlarger.z) if tmin >= tmax: return None # Discard fragment tmin = max(tmin, 0.0) traveldistance = tmax - tmin step = stepsize # Or traveldistance / maxsteps # 3. Initialization accumulatedcolor = vec4(0.0) tm = 1.0 t = tmin # 4. Ray Marching Loop for i in range(maxsteps): if t >= tmax: break pos = rayorigin + t raydirlocal samplepos = pos + vec3(0.5) # Offset for texture coords # Sample volume density = volumetexture.sample(samplepos).r # Map to color voxelcolor = transferfn.sample(vec2(density, 0.5)) a = density voxelcolor.a # Compositing if uenablemaxvaluesampling == 1: if a > accumulatedcolor.a: accumulatedcolor.rgb = voxelcolor.rgb a accumulatedcolor.a = max(a, accumulatedcolor.a) else: accumulatedcolor.rgb += (1.0 - accumulatedcolor.a) a voxelcolor.rgb accumulatedcolor.a += (1.0 - accumulatedcolor.a) a # Update transmittance tm = exp(-utmk density step) # Advance t += step # Early Termination if accumulatedcolor.a >= 0.95: break if tm < tmmin: break # 5. Final Output alpha = 1.0 - tm if alpha <= 0.001: return None # Discard return vec4(accumulatedcolor.rgb / alpha, alpha) Parameters: MAXSTEPS: 128 (vol-fs.glsl), 200 (vol-fs2.glsl), 256. STEPSIZE: 0.01. TMMIN: 0.25 (vol-fs.glsl), 0.0 (vol-fs2.glsl). Early Ray Termination Threshold: 0.95. Sampling Rate (s): In Shear-Warp context, equivalent to virtual slices; for Ray Marching, this corresponds to MAXSTEPS or inverse step size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: Ray direction components can be zero; handle with epsilon in invDir. Aliasing: Uniform fixed-step sampling causes aliasing artifacts if the sampling rate is too low. Visible Slices: Low sampling rates make individual slices visible; solved by increasing steps or using interpolation. Texture Coordinate Layout: Non-standard layouts (e.g., z-up in tex coords) require specific handling in sampleVolTex. Adaptive stepping based on density gradients rather than fixed intervals. Choose when volume density varies significantly and uniform sampling wastes compute. Link Marching based on density thresholds rather than fixed steps. Choose when sparse volumes benefit from skipping empty regions. Link Analytical integration over steps. Choose when exact integration over fixed intervals is required for high accuracy. Link Ray marching for light scattering in URP. Choose when rendering volumetric light effects in Unity's Universal Render Pipeline. Link Specific optimizations for cloud volumes. Choose when rendering large-scale atmospheric phenomena. Link Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of steps per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the 3D volume texture, where V is the number of voxels. Measured Performance: On a 3.8GHz Pentium 4 with GeForce FX7950 GX2, GPU Ray Marching achieved 44 fps for a 512x512x73 Knee model at 500 steps, compared to 134 fps for Shear-Warp at sampling rate 1, but Ray Marching at 400 steps (48 fps) was faster than Shear-Warp at sampling rate 10 (10 fps). Scaling: Frame rate drops linearly with increased steps or sampling rate. Strengths: Single-pass rendering, independent ray processing allows early termination and empty space skipping, higher quality than low-rate Shear-Warp. Limitations: Aliasing artifacts at low sampling rates, performance degrades with high step counts, fixed step size may oversample empty space or undersample dense regions. When to Use: Real-time visualization on standard PC hardware where simplicity and single-pass efficiency are prioritized over adaptive sampling. When Not to Use: When adaptive sampling or empty space skipping is strictly required for performance, as fixed-step marching samples uniformly along the ray. Originated in the context of GPU-based volume rendering for medical imagery, specifically as a comparison to the Shear-Warp algorithm. The method leverages the fragment shader's ability to perform parallel ray traversal, moving computational load from CPU to GPU. It was implemented to address the limitations of slice-based methods, such as visible artifacts at low sampling rates and lower frame rates for high-quality rendering. jaanonim/volume-rendering, https://github.com/jaanonim/volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) rbaravalle/webgl-volumetric, https://github.com/rbaravalle/webgl-volumetric, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) sunjianxin/rendnerwebgl, https://github.com/sunjianxin/rendnerwebgl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GPU-Based Volume Rendering for Medical Imagery, https://scholarly.org/pdf/display/gpu-based-volume-rendering-for-medical-imagery, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching with Depth Testing
head: GPU Ray Marching, Manual Depth Testing, Ray Marching for Volume Rendering, Sequential Ray Marching
body: Ray marching with depth testing visualizes volumes by casting rays from the camera and sampling at discrete steps along each ray's path, traversing a voxel grid and applying transfer functions to map raw values to color and opacity. It solves the problem of correct occlusion between volumetric effects and solid geometry by integrating manual depth buffer comparisons into the ray marching loop. This method sets itself apart from sibling techniques like Fixed Step Ray Marching by explicitly discarding samples that lie behind opaque objects, thereby preventing visual artifacts where volume appears in front of or behind solid geometry incorrectly. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera matrices (view and projection), ray origin o, normalized ray direction d, volume textures (density and temperature), depth buffer from the geometry pass, step count N, and a user-adjustable opacity scale factor \alpha{scale}. Outputs: Final accumulated color C{acc} and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} for the pixel. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin o and direction d. Volume Texture: 3D texture storing density and temperature values. Depth Buffer: Stores depth values zb for each pixel from the preceding geometry pass. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Derive the ray origin o and direction d from camera matrices. Calculate the intersection of the ray with the volume's bounding box to determine the entry point t{min} and exit point t{max}. 2. Step Size Calculation: Compute the step size \Delta t using the formula: \Delta t = \frac{t{max} - t{min}}{N} where N is the configurable step count. 3. Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to N-1. For each step: a. Position Update: Calculate the current world position p(t): p(t) = o + t d where p(t) is the current position, o is the ray origin, and d is the normalized direction. b. Depth Testing: Transform the sample's world position p(t) to clip space to obtain screen depth z. Compare z against the stored depth buffer value zb with a small bias \epsilon to determine the depth weight dw: dw:= \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } z < f(zb + \epsilon) \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where f is the depth mapping function, z is the screen depth, zb is the stored depth buffer value, and \epsilon is a small bias (e.g., 0.004) to handle precision issues. c. Sample and Weight: If dw = 0, discard the sample. If dw = 1, sample the density texture \tilde{d} and temperature at p(t). Apply the depth weight to the density: w:= \tilde{d} \cdot dw where w is the weighted density and \tilde{d} is the density value of the volume sample. d. Interpolation: Use quasi-cubic sampling to enhance interpolation quality. e. Accumulation: Update the accumulated color and opacity using alpha blending adapted from Max [13]: \alpha{acc}:= 1 - (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot (1 - \alpha{current}) C{acc}:= C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot C{current} \cdot \alpha{current} where \alpha{current} and C{current} are the opacity and color of the current voxel, derived from the weighted density w and temperature via transfer functions. f. Termination: Continue marching until the ray exits the volume (t > t{max}) or the accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} reaches a threshold (e.g., 1.0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def mul(self, s): return Vec3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def getitem(self, i): return (self.x, self.y, self.z)[i] class Vec4: def init(self, x, y, z, w): self.x, self.y, self.z, self.w = x, y, z, w def getitem(self, i): return (self.x, self.y, self.z, self.w)[i] def raymarchwithdepthtesting(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, depthbuffer, stepcount, alphascale): # 1. Calculate bounding box intersections (standard slab method) tmin, tmax = 0.0, 1.0 for axis in range(3): if abs(raydirection[axis]) > 1e-6: t1 = (0.0 - rayorigin[axis]) / raydirection[axis] t2 = (1.0 - rayorigin[axis]) / raydirection[axis] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) else: if rayorigin[axis] < 0.0 or rayorigin[axis] > 1.0: return Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 if tmin > tmax: return Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 # 2. Calculate step size stepsize = (tmax - tmin) / stepcount # Initialize accumulation acccolor = Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # 3. Marching loop for i in range(stepcount): t = tmin + i stepsize position = rayorigin + t raydirection # Transform to clip space to get screen depth clippos = applyviewprojection(position) z = clippos.z / clippos.w # Get stored depth buffer value for this pixel pixeluv = clippos.xy / clippos.w zb = depthbuffer[pixeluv] # Bias to avoid precision issues epsilon = 0.004 depthweight = 1.0 if z < zb + epsilon else 0.0 # Discard if behind opaque geometry if depthweight == 0.0: continue # Sample volume using quasi-cubic sampling density = quasicubicsample(volumetexture, position) temperature = quasicubicsample(volumetexture, position, channel='temperature') # Apply depth weight to density weighteddensity = density depthweight # Map to color and opacity via transfer functions currentalpha = weighteddensity alphascale currentcolor = lookuptemperaturepalette(temperature) # Alpha blending (Max's formula) accalpha = 1.0 - (1.0 - accalpha) (1.0 - currentalpha) acccolor = acccolor + (1.0 - accalpha) currentcolor currentalpha # Early exit if fully opaque if accalpha >= 1.0: break return acccolor, accalpha def quasicubicsample(texture, uv, channel='density'): # Implementation from Listing 1 in R = texture.dimensions() U = uv R + Vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) F = Vec3(U.x % 1.0, U.y % 1.0, U.z % 1.0) U = Vec3( (U.x - F.x) + F.x F.x (3.0 - 2.0 F.x), (U.y - F.y) + F.y F.y (3.0 - 2.0 F.y), (U.z - F.z) + F.z F.z (3.0 - 2.0 F.z)) C = Vec3((U.x - 0.5) / R, (U.y - 0.5) / R, (U.z - 0.5) / R) return texture.lookup(C, channel) def applyviewprojection(position): # Standard view-projection matrix multiplication viewpos = applyviewmatrix(position) clippos = applyprojectionmatrix(viewpos) return clippos def lookuptemperaturepalette(temperature): # 1D texture lookup mapping temperature to explosion colors return Vec3(temperature, temperature, temperature) Parameters: Step Count (N): Configurable value with options 16, 32, 64, 128, or 256. 128-256 steps provide a balance between performance and visual quality. Bias (\epsilon): A small value (e.g., 0.004) added to the depth buffer value to prevent precision issues in depth comparison. Opacity Scale (\alpha{scale}): User-adjustable factor controlling the contribution of each sample to the accumulated opacity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Issues: Without a bias \epsilon, depth comparison can fail due to floating-point precision errors, causing the volume to appear incorrectly behind or in front of opaque objects. Occlusion: If depth testing is omitted, volumetric effects may render incorrectly relative to solid geometry. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps N and the number of pixels. Each pixel requires N samples in the worst case. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the volume texture and the depth buffer. The depth buffer is required from the previous pass. Performance: 128-256 steps are recommended for a balance between performance and visual quality. Strengths: Correctly handles occlusion between volumes and solid geometry, reducing artifacts. Quasi-cubic sampling improves interpolation quality over linear sampling. Limitations: Requires a pre-pass to generate the depth buffer. Precision issues can occur without proper biasing. This method is described in the context of real-time volumetric explosion special effects for games, implemented using WebGPU and WGSL shaders. The accumulation formula adapts classical alpha blending principles described by Max [13]. The specific implementation details, including manual depth testing and quasi-cubic sampling, are presented in the WSCG 2025 Proceedings. Real-time volumetric explosion special effects for games, https://doi.org/10.24132/csrn.2025-34, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Per-primitive Ray Sampling
head: Primitive-centric ray marching
body: Per-primitive ray sampling is a rendering strategy where each geometric primitive (specifically ellipsoids) independently updates only the ray segments it intersects, avoiding redundant parameter loads and enabling accurate Transfer Function (TF) mapping by accumulating contributions in 3D space. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Fixed Step Ray Marching and Volume Ray Casting by organizing computation around primitives rather than rays, which eliminates the need for explicit per-tile sorting required in 2D rasterization because contributions accumulate in depth order as each ray segment corresponds to a discrete depth interval. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a set of primitives, each defined by center \mu, covariance \Sigma, support radius factor r{supp}, intensity I, and scaling factor k; a sampling step size \Delta t; a projection matrix; and a pixel grid. The output is a set of accumulated ray segments rayi for each pixel, which are subsequently traversed front-to-back for alpha blending to produce the final pixel color. Data Structures: Each primitive is defined by \mu = (\mux, \muy, \muz), covariance matrix \Sigma, support radius factor r{supp}, and intensity I. Each ray segment is a 1D array rayi for pixel i, discretized with step size \Delta t, where the j-th entry stores the accumulated intensity at depth t = j\Delta t. Steps: 1. Transform and Cull: Transform primitives by the projection matrix and process only those visible in screen space. 2. Cache Parameters: Cache ellipsoid parameters in tile-level shared memory to minimize redundant global memory accesses across pixels. 3. Determine Depth Range: For a primitive with center \mu and covariance \Sigma, determine the valid depth range. Segments within |t - \muz| \le r{supp} \cdot \sqrt{\Sigma'{zz}} are considered, where \sqrt{\Sigma'{zz}} is the standard deviation along the z-axis after projection. 4. Update Ray Segments: For each primitive, calculate the start and end indices of the affected ray segments and update them with the primitive's contribution. Formulas: Ray Parameterization: In ray space, the ray for pixel (xi, yi) is ri(t) = (xi, yi, 0) + t \cdot (0, 0, 1), where t varies along the z-axis. Sample Position: The sample position for index j is rayi[j] = \hat{V}(ri(j\Delta t)) = \hat{V}(xi, yi, j\Delta t). Primitive Contribution: The contribution of a primitive to ray segment j is: \tilde{P}(xi, yi, j \cdot \Delta t) = I \cdot \frac{\sigma(k \cdot (1 - \mathbf{d}^\top \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{d}))}{\sigma(k)} where \mathbf{d} = [xi, yi, j\Delta t] - [\mux, \muy, \muz] is the displacement from the primitive center, k is a scaling factor, and \sigma is the sigmoid function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def perprimitiveraysampling(primitives, deltat, raysegments, pixelcoords): """ primitives: List of primitives with attributes mu, Sigma, rsupp, I, k, screenxmin, screenxmax, screenymin, screenymax deltat: float, sampling step size raysegments: 2D list [H][W] of lists of floats, initialized to 0.0 pixelcoords: list of (xi, yi) tuples for each pixel """ for prim in primitives: muz = prim.mu[2] sigmazz = prim.Sigma[2, 2] rsupp = prim.rsupp I = prim.I k = prim.k Sigmainv = inverse(prim.Sigma) # Calculate depth range indices zmin = muz - rsupp sqrt(sigmazz) zmax = muz + rsupp sqrt(sigmazz) indexstart = floor(zmin / deltat) indexend = floor(zmax / deltat) # Sources do not specify the exact pixel culling loop; standard screen-space bounding box iteration is used. for y in range(prim.screenymin, prim.screenymax + 1): for x in range(prim.screenxmin, prim.screenxmax + 1): pixelid = y W + x xi, yi = pixelcoords[pixelid] for j in range(indexstart, indexend + 1): dx = xi - prim.mu[0] dy = yi - prim.mu[1] dz = (j deltat) - prim.mu[2] d = [dx, dy, dz] quadratic = dot(d, dot(Sigmainv, d)) numerator = 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-k (1.0 - quadratic))) denominator = 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-k)) contribution = I (numerator / denominator) raysegments[pixelid][j] += contribution Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision in calculating d^T \Sigma^{-1} d can affect the sigmoid evaluation, especially for large displacements. Boundaries: The support radius factor r{supp} determines the cutoff; if too small, contributions are truncated, and if too large, unnecessary computations occur. Degenerate Input: If \Sigma is singular, \Sigma^{-1} is undefined, requiring a small regularization term. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of primitives and the average number of ray segments they intersect, avoiding the O(N{rays} \cdot N{steps}) complexity of naive ray marching by only processing relevant primitives for each segment. Memory Complexity: Requires storing ray segments for all pixels and caching primitive parameters in shared memory. Performance: Eliminates redundant global memory traffic by processing each primitive once and caching parameters in tile-level shared memory. Strengths: Accurate TF evaluation in 3D space, no explicit sorting required, and reduced memory traffic. Limitations: Requires efficient culling and bounding box calculation to avoid processing non-intersecting primitives, and performance may degrade with high primitive density and overlap. Per-primitive ray sampling was introduced in the context of 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering (ESVR). It addresses the overhead of naively adopting ray marching for learned primitives, where each ray step requires checking intersections and repeatedly fetching ellipsoid parameters from memory. By organizing computation around primitives, it enables real-time rendering with accurate TF mapping. ESVR: 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering via Structure-aware Primitive Learning and Per-primitive Ray Sampling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05564v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Directional Derivative Diffuse Lighting
head: Density Gradient Diffuse Approximation, Inigo Quilez's directional derivatives
body: Directional Derivative Diffuse Lighting is an approximation for diffuse lighting in volumetric raymarching that estimates light scattering by comparing density at the current point and an offset point in the light direction, avoiding the need for normal calculation. It sets itself apart from standard surface raymarching normals by requiring only two density samples instead of multiple gradient estimates, making it significantly cheaper for the resource-intensive volumetric loop. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes the current 3D position p, a normalized light direction sunDirection, and a density function scene(p) that returns the scalar density at position p as inputs. It outputs a diffuse lighting factor and a linear lighting color vector to modulate the accumulated volume color. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required beyond the density function and standard vector types. The method relies on scalar arithmetic and vector addition. Parameters: Offset Scale: 0.3 (distance along the light direction for the second sample). Ambient Color: vec3(0.60, 0.60, 0.75). Ambient Multiplier: 1.1. Diffuse Color: vec3(1.0, 0.6, 0.3). Diffuse Multiplier: 0.8. Clamp Range: [0.0, 1.0]. Steps: 1. Sample the density at the current point p. 2. Sample the density at an offset point p' located further along the light direction. 3. Calculate the diffuse factor by taking the difference between the two density samples, dividing by the offset scale, and clamping the result to [0.0, 1.0]. Formula: diffuse = clamp((scene(p) - scene(p + 0.3 sunDirection)) / 0.3, 0.0, 1.0) Interpretation: If density increases along the light path (dcurrent > doffset), the result is positive, indicating more scattering. If density decreases, the result is lower or zero, indicating less scattering. 4. Compute the linear lighting color by mixing ambient light and the calculated diffuse light. Formula: lin = vec3(0.60, 0.60, 0.75) 1.1 + vec3(1.0, 0.6, 0.3) diffuse 0.8 5. Determine the base color of the volume slice by mixing white and black based on the current density dcurrent. Formula: basecolor = mix(vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0), vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), dcurrent) 6. Combine the base color with the linear lighting and the density alpha, then accumulate into the final result using the over operator. Formula: color = vec4(basecolor lin, dcurrent) Accumulation: color.rgb = color.a; res += color (1.0 - res.a);. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def directionalderivativediffuselightingraymarch(origin, direction, stepsize, maxsteps, sundirection, scenefunc): """ Marches a ray through a volume applying directional derivative diffuse lighting. Args: origin (vec3): Ray origin. direction (vec3): Ray direction (normalized). stepsize (float): Constant step size for marching. maxsteps (int): Maximum number of steps to prevent infinite loops. sundirection (vec3): Normalized light direction vector. scenefunc (callable): Returns scalar density at a 3D position. Returns: vec4: Accumulated result (rgb, a). """ # Initialize accumulated result to zero (fixes bug where res was undefined/zeroed incorrectly) res = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # March along the ray for i in range(maxsteps): p = origin + direction (i stepsize) dcurrent = scenefunc(p) # Only process if density is present if dcurrent > 0.0: # Directional derivative approximation offsetscale = 0.3 poffset = p + offsetscale sundirection doffset = scenefunc(poffset) # Calculate diffuse factor diffuse = (dcurrent - doffset) / offsetscale if diffuse < 0.0: diffuse = 0.0 elif diffuse > 1.0: diffuse = 1.0 # Compute linear lighting color ambient = vec3(0.60, 0.60, 0.75) 1.1 diffuselight = vec3(1.0, 0.6, 0.3) diffuse 0.8 lin = ambient + diffuselight # Determine base color basecolor = mix(vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0), vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), dcurrent) # Form slice color and apply lighting color = vec4(basecolor lin, dcurrent) color.rgb = color.a # Accumulate using over operator res.rgb += color.rgb (1.0 - res.a) res.a += color.a (1.0 - res.a) # Exit early if fully opaque if res.a >= 1.0: break return res Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Calculation Suboptimality: Standard normal calculation using getNormal requires 4-6 sample points to estimate the gradient, which is resource-intensive given the heavy volumetric loop. This method avoids that by using only 2 samples. Loop Inclusion: Unlike surface raymarching where diffuse is computed once at the surface, this calculation must be included inside the volumetric raymarching loop because density varies throughout the volume. Precision: The division by 0.3 can amplify noise if the density function is noisy. Clamping to [0.0, 1.0] prevents negative lighting contributions but may clip valid gradients if the density change is very steep. Initialization and Loop Bounds: The accumulation variable res must be explicitly initialized to vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) before the marching loop, and the loop must iterate over the ray path using the specified step size; failure to do so results in a zero output for all rays. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point, requiring exactly 2 density function evaluations per lighting calculation. This is significantly faster than gradient-based normal estimation which requires 4-6 evaluations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory, as it only stores a few scalar and vector variables. Strengths: Low computational cost, easy to implement, provides a visually plausible approximation of diffuse lighting in volumes without explicit normals. Limitations: Approximation may not capture complex scattering effects accurately. When to use: Real-time volumetric rendering where performance is critical and approximate diffuse lighting is sufficient. When not to use: Offline rendering requiring high physical accuracy, or volumes with very fine details where the fixed offset might miss significant density changes. The method is attributed to Inigo Quilez and presented in his article on directional derivatives. It was developed as an alternative to standard normal calculation in volumetric raymarching to reduce the computational cost associated with gradient estimation. Real-time dreamy Cloudscapes with Volumetric Raymarching, https://blog.maximeheckel.com/posts/real-time-cloudscapes-with-volumetric-raymarching/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Specific Material and Geometry Rendering
body: Specific Material and Geometry Rendering is a family of techniques that define how volumetric data is mapped to optical properties and how specific geometric constraints or material compositions are handled during ray traversal. It solves the problem of translating abstract simulation data into physically plausible radiance contributions within the volume rendering integral, setting itself apart from general sampling schemes by focusing on material definitions Material Parameter Setting, global geometric constraints Procedural Volumetric Cloud Rendering, or multi-material compositing. The family shares the fundamental volume rendering equation, where the final color C(r) along a ray r is the integral of emitted and in-scattered light attenuated by transmittance: C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigmat(t) c(t) dt where T(t) = \exp(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigmat(\tau) d\tau) is the transmittance, \sigmat is the extinction coefficient (density), and c(t) is the color/emission term Material Parameter Setting. Key shared mechanisms include: 1. Material Definition: Mapping raw data (scalar grids, noise fields) to \sigmat and c(t) via transfer functions, procedural noise, or neural networks Material Parameter SettingDVGO Density and Color Rendering. 2. Geometric Constraints: Defining the spatial bounds of the volume, whether as a local box, a spherical shell, or a procedural mask Procedural Volumetric Cloud RenderingRay-marched Volumetric Fog. 3. Integration: Discretizing the integral via ray marching, accumulating radiance and transmittance step-by-step Mr-Voxel Volume RenderingRay-marched Volumetric Fog. Procedural Volumetric Cloud Rendering is a real-time technique that renders planetary-scale cloud layers using ray marching through 3D noise fields, combining atmospheric lighting models with adaptive density shaping. It solves the problem of rendering large, physically plausible cloudscapes that conform to a planet's curvature, supporting cameras inside, outside, or between cloud shells. It sets itself apart from local volumetrics (like Ray-marched Volumetric Fog) by treating clouds as a global spherical shell rather than a local box, and from grid-based methods (like Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering) by using procedural noise for density rather than sampled voxel data. Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering is a direct volume ray casting method implemented in the VolumeIntegrator::Li function that performs ray marching through a single volume region, accumulating emitted light and computing transmittance and scattering contributions from a single light source. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific implementation of Russian Roulette for early termination and its assumption of a single-volume, single-light scene structure, serving as the core integration logic within the Mr-Voxel accelerated voxel data structure. Ray-marched volumetric fog simulates aerial perspective and light shafts by treating fog as a 3D volume of participating media traced via forward ray-marching from the camera to the scene. It solves the problem of rendering dynamic, light-interacting fog that absorbs and scatters light, distinguishing itself from backward ray-marching by allowing early-out optimizations when transmittance becomes negligible. Material Parameter Setting defines the optical and geometric properties of volumetric media by mapping raw data grids to physical attributes such as density, color, and emission. It solves the problem of converting abstract simulation data (e.g., density, temperature) into renderable radiance contributions within the volume rendering integral. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the definition of these properties via explicit channel bindings and parameter sliders (Standard Volume Material) or low-level API calls (VolPack), rather than the traversal or shading algorithms themselves. DVGO (Direct Volume Gaussian Optimization) is a method for rendering 3D scenes from images by combining a sparse voxel grid with neural networks to represent density and view-dependent color. It solves the problem of efficiently synthesizing novel views of complex scenes by decoupling the representation of geometry (density) from appearance (color). Unlike standard NeRF which uses a single MLP for both, DVGO uses a voxel grid for density and a shallow MLP for color, allowing for faster training and inference while maintaining high fidelity. It is distinct from Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering by its specific use of shifted softplus activation for density and post-activation interpolation to achieve sharp surfaces with fewer cells. Definition: Surface rendering mode computes color C(s) according to the Phong equation using the volume gradient. Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs (DRRs) mode sets C(s) = (0,0,0), attenuating only the backlight by accumulated transmittance t. Maximum Intensity Projections (MIPs) output the opacity \alpha of the maximum-opacity interval along the ray. Parameter: A uniform variable tells the fragment shader which rendering mode to use. Definition: A technique for rendering volumes with mixtures of materials (e.g., bone, muscle) by creating material percentage volumes and compositing them. Steps: Assume the scalar field was sampled above Nyquist frequency or low-pass filtered. Differentiate materials by scalar value or additional composition info. Create material percentage volumes, where each is a scalar field representing one material. Associate color and opacity with each material. Obtain composite color and opacity by linearly combining the color and opacity for each material percentage volume. Use a matte volume (scalar field 0-1) to slice the volume or perform spatial set operations. Transform the volume so one axis is perpendicular to the image plane. Project plane by plane in a back-to-front manner and composite to form the final image. Definition: Produces the same result as Volumetric Geometry but adds a heat haze refraction effect. Requires V-Ray. Uses Surface channel gradient to change ray direction. Parameter: Heat Haze (hhfactor): Multiplier for refraction based on Surface channel gradient. 1 approximates normal air heat haze from temperature. 0 produces no effect. Larger values needed if using smoke/other channels as source. Only available in Volumetric Heat Haze mode. Pitfall: Heat Haze only affects camera view, not shadows cast through volume. If Heat Haze shader intersects with VRayMtl refraction, Max depth of VRayMtl may need increase. Definition: Produces the same visual result as Volumetric mode but uses procedural geometry made of multiple transparent layers. Requires V-Ray. Used for exporting deep images and render elements (normals, velocity, multi matte) not available in standard Volumetric mode. Pitfall: Approximate and Approximate+Shadows options for Scattering in Smoke color window are not supported in this mode. Cutter Geom does not work when Mode is set to Volumetric Geometry. The concept of rendering specific materials within volumes dates back to early volume visualization work. Drebin, Carpenter, and Hanrahan developed techniques for rendering volumes containing mixtures of materials, such as CT data containing bone, muscle, and flesh, by creating material percentage volumes. Modern implementations extend this to procedural generation for clouds Procedural Volumetric Cloud Rendering and neural representations like DVGO DVGO Density and Color Rendering. Specific rendering modes like DRRs and MIPs are implemented in GPU volume renderers, while heat haze and volumetric geometry modes are specialized features in production renderers like V-Ray for 3ds Max.
