name: Procedural Volumetric Cloud Rendering
head: Nubis³, Nubis Cubed, Nubis Evolved
body: Procedural Volumetric Cloud Rendering is a real-time technique that renders planetary-scale cloud layers using ray marching through 3D noise fields, combining atmospheric lighting models with adaptive density shaping. It solves the problem of rendering large, physically plausible cloudscapes that conform to a planet's curvature, supporting cameras inside, outside, or between cloud shells. It sets itself apart from local volumetrics (like Ray-marched Volumetric Fog) by treating clouds as a global spherical shell rather than a local box, and from grid-based methods (like Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering) by using procedural noise for density rather than sampled voxel data. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position, view-projection matrix, sun direction, sun color, cloud layer parameters (base height, thickness, coverage, wind speed/direction), and noise textures (shape, detail, weather map). Outputs: In-scattered radiance, transmittance, and transmittance-weighted mean depth. Data Structures: Shape Texture: 3D texture (e.g., 128^3) containing Perlin fBm dilated by Worley noise plus three Worley octaves. Detail Texture: 3D texture (e.g., 32^3) containing Worley noise. Weather Map: 2D texture (e.g., 512^2) storing coverage and cloud type (stratus, cumulus, cumulonimbus) per region. Cloud FBO: Two color attachments: GLCOLORATTACHMENT0 bound to cloudColor (GLRGBA16F) and GLCOLORATTACHMENT1 bound to cloudDepth (GLR32F). Resolve FBO: Array of two framebuffers, each with one color attachment resolveColor[i] (GLRGBA16F) for temporal history ping-ponging. Output FBO: Single color attachment outputTex (GLRGBA8) used when rendering offscreen. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Setup: Convert vertex UV to ray direction based on frustum corners. Normalize ray direction in world space. Intersect ray with the spherical cloud shell defined by inner radius R{inner} and outer radius R{outer}. Let O be camera position, C be planet center (e.g., (0, -R{Earth}, 0)). oc = O - C. b = dot(oc, rd). c = dot(oc, oc). h{outer} = b^2 - (c - R{outer}^2). If h{outer} < 0, no intersection. s{outer} = \sqrt{h{outer}}. t{outer\near} = -b - s{outer}. t{outer\far} = -b + s{outer}. h{inner} = b^2 - (c - R{inner}^2). If h{inner} > 0, s{inner} = \sqrt{h{inner}}, else s{inner} = 0. Determine entry tn and exit tf within the shell. 2. Density Sampling: Calculate world position P at current step. Transform P for high-res noise sampling: hiResPosition = P \times hiResS + hiResT, where hiResT = 0.1f \times hiResNoiseTranslate and hiResS = 0.1f \times hiResNoiseScaling. Sample 4 textures from volumeHighRes at hiResPosition[0..3]. Compute hiResDensity = dot(hiResNoise, normalizeL1(hiResChannelWeights)). Apply falloff: falloff = yFalloff(P) \times xzFalloff(P). hiResDensity = falloff. Add offset: hiResDensityWithOffset = hiResDensity + hiResDensityOffset. If hiResDensityWithOffset \le 0, return 0. Sample low-res noise: loResPosition = P \times loResNoiseScaling \times 0.1f + loResNoiseTranslate. loResDensity = dot(texture(volumeLowRes, loResPosition), normalizeL1(loResChannelWeights)). Compute erosion weight: erosionWeight = pow(1.f - hiResDensity, 6) (quintic). Final density: density = hiResDensityWithOffset - erosionWeight \times loResDensityWeight \times loResDensity. Return \max(density \times densityMult \times 5.f, 0.f). 3. Lighting and Integration: For each step, calculate optical depth to the sun by taking 6 samples toward the sun direction. Compute light transmittance: lightTransmittance = \exp(\tau), where \tau is accumulated optical depth scaled by absorption. Evaluate multiple-scattering approximation (4 octaves) using attenuated extinction, contribution, and phase eccentricity. Apply phase function (e.g., two-lobe Henyey-Greenstein or Mie). Calculate in-scattered radiance analytically over the step size so the result does not depend on step size. Apply powder term (darkens back-lit edges) and ambient term (fades from blue at top to grey at bottom). Update transmittance: T{new} = T{old} \times \exp(-density \times stepSize). 4. Termination: Stop marching if transmittance drops below 0.5% (or log threshold -4.6). Accumulate radiance and transmittance. 5. Temporal Reprojection: Render cloud pass at reduced resolution (e.g., 0.5x) with sub-pixel jitter (Halton sequence). Reconstruct world position from depth. Project previous frame's position using previous view-projection matrix. Blend history sample (e.g., 92% current, 8% history). Clamp history to 3x3 neighborhood to prevent ghosting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchclouds(camerapos, cameradir, sundir, suncolor, cloudparams, shapetex, detailtex, weathertex): # 1. Ray-Sphere Intersection (per) oc = camerapos - cloudparams.planetcenter b = dot(oc, cameradir) c = dot(oc, oc) houter = b b - (c - cloudparams.router 2) if houter < 0.0: return vec3(0.0), 1.0, 0.0 souter = sqrt(houter) touternear = -b - souter touterfar = -b + souter hinner = b b - (c - cloudparams.rinner 2) if hinner > 0.0: sinner = sqrt(hinner) tinnernear = -b - sinner tinnerfar = -b + sinner tstart = max(touternear, tinnernear) tend = min(touterfar, tinnerfar) else: tstart = touternear tend = touterfar if tstart > tend or tend < 0.0: return vec3(0.0), 1.0, 0.0 # 2. Setup stepsize = (tend - tstart) / cloudparams.maxsteps # Jitter per pixel/frame (per) jitter = (hash32(camerapos.x 12.9898 + camerapos.y 78.233) % 1000) / 1000.0 - 0.5 pos = camerapos + (tstart + jitter stepsize) cameradir radiance = vec3(0.0) transmittance = 1.0 depthaccum = 0.0 transmittanceweighteddepth = 0.0 for i in range(cloudparams.maxsteps): if transmittance < cloudparams.earlystopthreshold: break # 3. Density Sampling (per) density = sampledensity(pos, shapetex, detailtex, weathertex, cloudparams) if density > 0.0: # 4. Lighting & Integration (per) # Optical depth to sun (6 samples) tau = 0.0 sunpos = pos for j in range(6): sunpos += sundir stepsize tau += sampledensity(sunpos, shapetex, detailtex, weathertex, cloudparams) stepsize lighttrans = exp(-tau cloudparams.absorptioncoeff) # Phase function (per) cosangle = dot(normalize(cameradir), normalize(sundir)) g = cloudparams.anisotropy g2 = g g phase = (1.0 - g2) / (4.0 3.14159 pow(1.0 + g2 - 2.0 g cosangle, 1.5)) # Multiple scattering approximation (per) ms = 1.0 # Simplified 4-octave approximation per evidence # In-scattering integrated analytically per step (per) inscatter = suncolor lighttrans phase ms cloudparams.sunintensity # Ambient term (per) heightratio = (length(pos - cloudparams.planetcenter) - cloudparams.rinner) / (cloudparams.router - cloudparams.rinner) ambient = mix(cloudparams.ambienttop, cloudparams.ambientbottom, clamp(heightratio, 0.0, 1.0)) # Powder term (per) powder = 1.0 - exp(-cloudparams.powderstrength (1.0 - cosangle)) totallight = inscatter powder + ambient cloudparams.ambientintensity # Discrete integration (Beer-Lambert) sigmat = density dt = stepsize Tstep = exp(-sigmat dt) radiance += totallight transmittance (1.0 - Tstep) transmittance = Tstep depthaccum += dt transmittanceweighteddepth += dt transmittance pos += cameradir stepsize meandepth = transmittanceweighteddepth / (1.0 - transmittance) if transmittance < 0.995 else 0.0 return radiance, transmittance, meandepth def sampledensity(pos, shapetex, detailtex, weathertex, cloudparams): # High-res transform (per) hiResS = vec4(0.1 cloudparams.hiResNoiseScaling.x, 0.1 cloudparams.hiResNoiseScaling.y, 0.1 cloudparams.hiResNoiseScaling.z, 0.0) hiResT = vec4(0.1 cloudparams.hiResNoiseTranslate.x, 0.1 cloudparams.hiResNoiseTranslate.y, 0.1 cloudparams.hiResNoiseTranslate.z, 1.0) hiResPosition = pos hiResS + hiResT hiResNoise = vec4(texture(shapetex, hiResPosition[0]), texture(shapetex, hiResPosition[1]), texture(shapetex, hiResPosition[2]), texture(shapetex, hiResPosition[3])) hiResDensity = dot(hiResNoise, normalizeL1(cloudparams.hiResChannelWeights)) if cloudparams.invertdensity: hiResDensity = 1.0 - hiResDensity # Falloff (per) ymin = -0.5 cloudparams.volumeScaling.y + cloudparams.volumeTranslate.y ymax = ymin + cloudparams.volumeScaling.y distY = min(cloudparams.yfalloffdist, min(pos.y - ymin, ymax - pos.y)) yfalloff = distY / cloudparams.yfalloffdist xmin = -0.5 cloudparams.volumeScaling.x + cloudparams.volumeTranslate.x xmax = xmin + cloudparams.volumeScaling.x zmin = -0.5 cloudparams.volumeScaling.z + cloudparams.volumeTranslate.z zmax = zmin + cloudparams.volumeScaling.z distX = min(cloudparams.xzfalloffdist, min(pos.x - xmin, xmax - pos.x)) distZ = min(cloudparams.xzfalloffdist, min(pos.z - zmin, zmax - pos.z)) xzfalloff = min(distX, distZ) / cloudparams.xzfalloffdist falloff = yfalloff xzfalloff hiResDensity = falloff hiResDensityWithOffset = hiResDensity + cloudparams.hiResDensityOffset if hiResDensityWithOffset <= 0.0: return 0.0 # Low-res (per) loResPosition = pos cloudparams.loResNoiseScaling 0.1 + cloudparams.loResNoiseTranslate loResNoise = texture(detailtex, loResPosition) loResDensity = dot(loResNoise, normalizeL1(cloudparams.loResChannelWeights)) loResDensity = 1.0 - loResDensity # Erosion (per) erosionWeight = pow(1.0 - hiResDensity, 6.0) density = hiResDensityWithOffset - erosionWeight cloudparams.loResDensityWeight loResDensity return max(density cloudparams.densityMult 5.0, 0.0) def normalizeL1(v): return v / dot(v, vec4(1.0)) def hash32(x): seed = int(x) seed = (seed ^ 61) ^ (seed >> 16) seed = 9 seed = seed ^ (seed >> 4) seed = 0x27d4eb2d seed = seed ^ (seed >> 15) return seed % 2147483647 Parameters: shapenoisescale: Default 6.4 km. Controls cloud size. coverage: Scales weather coverage. densityThreshold: Minimum noise value for density. absorptionCoefficient: Default 1.0. scatterFactor: Forward scattering strength [0.0, 1.0]. windSpeed: Controls noise scroll speed. maxSteps: Default 128. EARLYSTOPTHRESHOLD: 1e-2f. EARLYSTOPLOGTHRESHOLD: -4.6f. MINNUMFINESTEPS: 16. COARSESTEPSIZEMULTIPLIER: 4.f. MAXNUMMISSEDSTEPS: 5. STEPSIZEFINE: 0.02f. SMALLDENSITY: 0.005f. MAXSUNINTENSITY: 4.f. SUNRADIUS: 100.f. XZFALLOFFDIST: 1.f. YFALLOFFDIST: 1.f. EARTHRADIUS: 6371000.0 metres. SHAPESCALE: 1.0 / 9000.0 metres per noise tile. DETAILSCALE: 1.0 / 900.0. WEATHERSCALE: 1.0 / 48000.0. AMBIENTTOP: vec3(0.62, 0.74, 0.95). AMBIENTBOTTOM: vec3(0.36, 0.42, 0.52). uBlend: 0.08f. s.scale: Resolution scale factor, default 0.5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture History Validity: History textures must be checked for identity; reallocation or resize invalidates history. Shadow Map Basis Error: Cloud shadow maps are traced along the first directional light. Using them for non-parallel lights causes displaced shadows. Viewport Depth Mismatch: Depth reads must be offset by viewport origin to avoid tracing wrong parts of the view. Reprojection Depth Compromise: Mean cloud depth is used for reprojection; overlapping thin/far clouds cause depth ambiguity, mitigated by history clamping. HLSL Compilation: point is a reserved keyword; rename to cellPoint. Preprocessor Float Comparison: #if does not support floating point comparisons; remove preprocessor float comparison for CLOUDJITTERSTRENGTH. Visible Seams: Caused by sin()-based hash functions with precision issues at large values and improper negative coordinate handling in tiling; fixed by replacing with pure arithmetic hashes and proper wrapCoords() using floor division. Time Scaling: Clouds not visibly moving due to lack of time scaling in wind offset calculation; add time scaling factor 0.05 to convert game time to visible motion. Floating Point Precision: Use fmod to prevent precision issues with large time values. Renders clouds as a spherical shell using 3D noise, combining Nubis density with Frostbite light transport. Choose for planetary-scale clouds. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) where N is number of steps and M is samples per step for lighting. Memory Complexity: O(T{shape} + T{detail} + T{weather}) for noise textures. Performance: On Mesa llvmpipe at 640×360, full-res 128 steps takes 927 ms. Half-res with temporal reprojection takes 266 ms (29% of full-res). Strengths: Physically plausible, supports arbitrary camera positions, efficient with temporal reprojection. Limitations: Approximate multiple scattering, hand-tuned sun color at low elevation, single cloud layer limit in some implementations. Originated from techniques described in "The Real-time Volumetric Cloudscapes of Horizon: Zero Dawn" (Schneider, 2015) and "Physically Based Sky, Atmosphere and Cloud Rendering in Frostbite" (Hillaire, 2016). Implemented in various open-source projects like Bevy atmosphere plugin, Depersonalizc/volumetric-clouds, and harkawataryan/Volumetric-Cloud-Renderer. feat: Implement physically-inspired volumetric clouds with raymarching, https://github.com/jasonjgardner/open-rtx/pull/5, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) WIP: Nubis-based volumetric clouds, https://github.com/mate-h/bevy/pull/26, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Depersonalizc/volumetric-clouds, https://github.com/Depersonalizc/volumetric-clouds, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) harkawataryan/Volumetric-Cloud-Renderer, https://github.com/harkawataryan/Volumetric-Cloud-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ldarnbr/volumetric-cloud-renderer, https://github.com/ldarnbr/volumetric-cloud-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Clouds from Base Shape (Nubis/Frostbite Hybrid)
head: Hillaire 2016 light, Nubis density, Planetary Cloud Layer, Spherical Shell Clouds, Volumetric Clouds as a Spherical Shell, Wrenninge multiple scattering
body: This technique renders volumetric clouds as a spherical shell surrounding a planet, using raymarching between defined inner and outer radii with density derived from 3D noise fields rather than finite 2D textures. It combines Schneider’s density model from Horizon Zero Dawn’s Nubis system with Hillaire 2016 light transport from Frostbite, allowing the cloud layer to conform to any base shape by sampling noise at 3D points in the shading frame. Unlike local volumetrics or ground fog, this method treats clouds as a planetary-scale feature, supporting multiple planets and camera positions inside, outside, or between shells. Inputs: Planet center and radius. Cloud layer inner and outer altitudes relative to planet radius. Noise textures: 128³ Perlin-Worley shape noise and 32³ Worley detail noise. Camera position and view direction. Sun direction and intensity. Atmosphere transmittance data required for correct lighting. Outputs: Cloud color and opacity per pixel. Transmittance and distance buffers for the camera-centered direction grid. CloudLayer Component Parameters: innerradius: Float. The inner boundary of the cloud shell. outerradius: Float. The outer boundary of the cloud shell. coverage: Float. Authored parameter controlling cloud density. density: Float. Global density multiplier. wind: Vector3. Render-space wind direction vector. noisematerial: Asset reference. Contains noise parameters. Camera-Centred Direction Grid: Dimensions: 1536 × 768 texels, centered around the base's up vector. Resolution: ~0.23° per texel. Texel Layout: cloudlight: Vector3. Cloud light contribution including air in front. transmittance: Float. Light transmittance through the cloud. frontdistance: Float. Distance to the front of the cloud shell. meandistance: Float. Mean distance of scattering events. opacity: Float. Accumulated opacity. Shadow Map: Dimensions: 512². Alignment: Aligned along the sun vector around the camera. Reach: Shadows do not extend past the map boundary (e.g., 64 km on Earth, or 4 camera altitudes). 1. Ray-Sphere Intersection: Calculate the entry and exit points of the view ray relative to the cloud shell's inner and outer radii using the shared AtmosphereVolume intersection logic. If the ray misses the shell, the shader early-outs. 2. Layer Scaling and Lifting: Scale the cloud layer height relative to the planet's radius. Lift the layer so its bottom is at least 1.25 times the ground's maximum relief to ensure the marcher is unaware of terrain features. For Earth (3.3 km relief), the layer is lifted to 4.1–6.6 km. For a 2 km planet, it is 78–208 m. 3. Density Calculation (Schneider/Nubis): Sample the 128³ Perlin-Worley shape noise at the current 3D ray position. Determine cloud cover and type based on thresholds measured directly on the noise values at a "weather scale". Apply erosion from separate noise fields if available. 4. Ray Marching: March the ray through the shell volume using a fixed step size and empty-space skipping inherited from the parent sampling scheme. The marcher does not account for terrain occlusion; a depth-aware march is required to fix clouds wrapping peaks. 5. Light Transport (Hillaire 2016): Calculate sun transmittance through the atmosphere using the atmosphere's transmittance march, then through the cloud using progressive shadow samples from the 512² shadow map. Use a dual-lobe Henyey-Greenstein phase function for scattering. Implement Wrenninge's multiple-scattering octaves for the cloud interior. Compute lighting using a few in-scattering samples rather than a second full march. Sample the sky's light contribution from the atmosphere's multiple-scattering table. 6. Integration: Integrate scattering such that light scattering applies to the light reaching the clouds and the light they send on. Clouds are marched in the same pass as the atmosphere or ordered against it, as clouds sit inside the atmosphere. 7. Compositing: The sky shader places clouds over the atmosphere's sky. The page shader adds clouds in front of a fragment to its FOG buffer. The light() function reads the shadow map (one fetch) to determine cloud shadows. 8. Distance Policy: From orbit, render the cloud layer as a texture on a sphere. From the ground, render as a fly-through volume. The transition must be continuous and measured, not guessed. Ray-Sphere Intersection: Given ray origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, sphere center \mathbf{c}, and radius r: \mathbf{m} = \mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c} b = \mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{d} c = \mathbf{m} \cdot \mathbf{m} - r^2 \Delta = b^2 - c If \Delta < 0, the ray misses. Otherwise, t{entry} = -b - \sqrt{\Delta} and t{exit} = -b + \sqrt{\Delta}. Beer-Lambert Integration: T(t) = \exp\left(-\int0^t \sigmat(s) \, ds\right) L = \int0^t \sigmas(s) \, T(s) \, ds where \sigmat is the extinction coefficient, \sigmas is the scattering coefficient, T(t) is transmittance, and L is accumulated radiance. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolumetricclouds(camerapos, planetcenter, planetradius, inneraltitude, outeraltitude, shapenoisetex, detailnoisetex, sundirection, atmospheredata, shadowmaptex): # 1. Allocate camera-centred direction grid (1536x768) grid = allocate2darray(1536, 768) # 2. Compute layer bounds maxterrainrelief = computemaxterrainheight(planetcenter) layerthickness = 3000.0 # Typical Earth value innerradius = planetradius + maxterrainrelief 1.25 outerradius = innerradius + layerthickness # 3. March grid texels (one invocation per 2x2 block) for block in grid.blocks2x2: for texel in block: rayorigin = camerapos raydirection = computeraydirection(texel.uv, camerapos) # Ray-sphere intersection entry, exit = intersectsphereshell(rayorigin, raydirection, planetcenter, innerradius, outerradius) if entry is None: continue # Early-out if ray misses shell transmittance = 1.0 cloudlight = vec3(0.0) frontdistance = 0.0 meandistance = 0.0 opacity = 0.0 stepsize = computefixedstepsize(entry, exit) pos = entry while pos < exit and transmittance > 0.01: # Density calculation (Schneider/Nubis) noiseval = sample3dnoise(shapenoisetex, pos) density = computedensityfromnoise(noiseval) if density > 0.0: # Light transport (Hillaire 2016) atmtransmittance = atmospheredata.gettransmittance(pos, sundirection) cloudshadow = sampleshadowmap(shadowmaptex, pos, sundirection) phase = duallobehenyeygreensteinphase(sundirection, raydirection) multiscatter = getmultiplescatteringoctaves(pos) skylight = atmospheredata.getmultiplescatteringtable(pos) scattering = density (atmtransmittance cloudshadow phase + skylight multiscatter) cloudlight += scattering stepsize transmittance transmittance = exp(-density stepsize) frontdistance = length(pos - rayorigin) meandistance = (meandistance opacity + frontdistance density stepsize) / (opacity + density stepsize) opacity += density stepsize pos += raydirection stepsize texel.cloudlight = cloudlight texel.transmittance = transmittance texel.frontdistance = frontdistance texel.meandistance = meandistance texel.opacity = opacity # 4. Compositing for pixeluv in screenuv: texel = grid.sample2d(pixeluv) finalcolor = atmospheredata.skycolor texel.transmittance + texel.cloudlight fogbuffer.add(finalcolor, texel.opacity) Noise Resolution: Shape noise 128³, Detail noise 32³. Layer Height (Earth): 1.5 to 4 km. Grid Resolution: 1536 × 768. Shadow Map: 512². Wind: Render-space vector. Terrain Occlusion: The layer is lifted, not composited. The march knows nothing of the terrain, so clouds do not wrap peaks. A depth-aware march is required to fix this. Jagged Edges: The grid's resolution (0.23° per texel) shows as jagged edges on a small planet seen whole. Shadow Reach: Shadows do not extend past the shadow map boundary (64 km on Earth, or 4 camera altitudes). Color Accuracy: Clouds take the scene's warm sun color, reddened again by the air, resulting in a pinkish-tan appearance. There is no white balance. Fixing this requires setting the scene's light to white, which is a scene change. Wind Direction: The wind is a render-space vector. On a planet, the noise drifts through the shell away from the pole. It is now aligned with the wind; the old cloud layer drifted against it. Grid Limits: The froxel grid ends at ClusterSettings::far (200 m default). Planetary clouds are kilometres out, outside the grid by two orders of magnitude. Assuming the grid covers the clouds is a mistake. Atmosphere Dependency: Clouds lit by a sun that ignores the atmosphere look wrong. The atmosphere component must be implemented first. Time and Memory Complexity: The technique inherits sampling techniques from the parent scheme: 3D noise textures, empty-space skipping, and fixed step size. The camera-centered direction grid requires 1536 × 768 texels, with one invocation per 2×2 block. Shadow map updates are per-frame. Measured Performance: OneXFly (10 W): Current implementation cost is 39 ms when switched off, which is the only reason the frame meets the 13.9 ms budget. Direct lighting alone is at twice budget. RTX 3070 Laptop (Power-Saver): Forest5cm, steady, 300 frames: Clouds off 19.05 ms, Clouds on 21.21 ms (+2.2 ms). Earth's pole: 4.8 → 8.1 ms (sky full of clouds). Earth from 100 km: 5.2 → 11 ms. The first version read cloud shadow per fragment, costing +33 ms in the forest. The shadow map optimization removed this cost. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Conforms to any base shape; supports multiple planets; efficient lighting via few in-scattering samples and shadow maps; continuous transition between orbit and ground views. Limitations: No terrain occlusion (clouds float above peaks); jagged edges on small planets; limited shadow reach; color accuracy issues due to lack of white balance; high cost on low-power hardware. When to Use: Planetary-scale cloud rendering where clouds must follow the curvature of the planet. Real-time engines requiring efficient volumetric lighting with shadow maps. When Not to Use: Local volumetrics or ground fog (use froxel buffer instead). Scenes requiring precise terrain interaction with clouds (requires depth-aware march). Low-power hardware where the 39 ms overhead is prohibitive. Origin: The technique is based on Guerrilla's Nubis work for Horizon Zero Dawn (Schneider, SIGGRAPH 2015), which models clouds as a spherical shell over the planet. The lighting model is derived from Hillaire 2016 (Frostbite). History and Development: SIGGRAPH 2015: Schneider published "The Real-Time Volumetric Cloudscapes of Horizon Zero Dawn," establishing the spherical shell model and Nubis density. Frostbite: Hillaire 2016 introduced the energy-conserving light transport and dual-lobe Henyey-Greenstein phase function. Wrenninge: Multiple-scattering octaves were adapted for cloud interior lighting. Implementation: The technique was implemented in the opti-voxel engine (ov::Clouds component), integrated with Godot sky and page shaders, and owned by World with the atmosphere. Usage: Used in the opti-voxel engine, integrated with Godot sky and page shaders. Owned by World with the atmosphere. feat(render): volumetric clouds as a spherical shell, per planet, https://github.com/lobinuxsoft/kooch/issues/731, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volumetric clouds from the base's shape, https://github.com/aobayama-gaming/opti-voxel/pull/145, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering
head: VolumeIntegrator::Li
body: Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering is a direct volume ray casting method implemented in the VolumeIntegrator::Li function that performs ray marching through a single volume region, accumulating emitted light and computing transmittance and scattering contributions from a single light source. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific implementation of Russian Roulette for early termination and its assumption of a single-volume, single-light scene structure, serving as the core integration logic within the Mr-Voxel accelerated voxel data structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A camera ray r defined by origin and direction, and a pointer to a transmittance variable T to be updated. Output: A Spectrum representing the accumulated radiance Lv along the ray. Scene Data: Access to a single volume object (volumes[0]) and a single light source (lights[0]) via the scene graph. Data Structures: The method operates within the VolumeIntegrator class. It relies on scene queries: mScene->getVolumeCount(): Returns the number of volumes (assumed to be 1). mScene->getVolumes(): Returns the array of volume objects. mScene->getLightSources(): Returns the array of light sources. volumes[0]->tau(ray, length,...): Computes optical depth (tau) for a given ray segment. volumes[0]->Lve(p): Returns emitted light at position p. volumes[0]->sigmas(p): Returns the scattering coefficient at position p. mScene->intersect(ray, &surface): Checks for surface intersections for shadow rays. Parameters: mStepSize: The nominal step size for ray marching. Russian Roulette Threshold: Transmittance value below which termination occurs (10^{-3}). Russian Roulette Probability: Probability of continuing if threshold is met (0.5). Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Sample Count: Determine the number of steps based on the ray segment length inside the volume (t1 - t0) and mStepSize. If the calculated count is 0, set it to 1. N = \max\left(1, \left\lfloor \frac{t1 - t0}{\text{mStepSize}} \right\rfloor \right) 2. Calculate Actual Step Length: Compute the precise step size \Delta t to ensure the ray exits exactly at t1. \Delta t = \frac{t1 - t0}{N} 3. Random Offset: Apply a random offset to the starting position t0 to reduce banding artifacts. The offset is uniformly distributed between 0 and \Delta t. t0' = t0 + U[0, 1) \cdot \Delta t 4. Initialize Accumulators: Set accumulated radiance Lv = 0 and transmittance Tr = 1. 5. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to N-1: a. Position Update: Let p{prev} be the position at the start of the step. Calculate the new position p = r(t0' + i \cdot \Delta t). b. Step Ray: Define a short ray segment from p{prev} to p with length \Delta t. c. Optical Depth: Compute the optical depth \tau{step} for this segment. The source code passes 0.5 step as the length argument to tau, implying the function might expect a radius or half-length, or it is a specific implementation detail of volumes[0]->tau. We assume standard optical depth calculation: \tau{step} = \text{volumes}[0].\text{tau}(p{prev} \to p, \Delta t, 0) d. Update Transmittance: Update the ray transmittance. Tr = Tr \cdot e^{-\tau{step}} e. Accumulate Emission: Add emitted light from the current position. Lv = Lv + \text{volumes}[0].Le(p) f. Scattering Check: Retrieve the scattering coefficient \sigmas(p) = \text{volumes}[0].\sigmas(p). If \sigmas(p) is non-zero (not black): i. Light Direction: Compute the normalized direction vector \omegaL from p to the light source position. ii. Shadow Ray: Cast a shadow ray from p in direction \omegaL. Check if it intersects a surface closer than the distance to the light. Let dL be the distance to the light. If no intersection occurs or the intersection distance t{surf} > dL, the point is unshadowed. iii. Light Transmittance: If unshadowed, compute the transmittance of light through the volume from p to the light. The source code uses mStepSize 2 as the length argument. T{light} = e^{-\text{volumes}[0].\text{tau}(\text{shadowRay}, 2 \cdot \text{mStepSize}, 0)} iv. Direct Lighting: Compute the direct lighting contribution Ld using the light's color CL and the light transmittance. Ld = T{light} \cdot CL v. Accumulate Scattering: Add the scattered light to Lv. Lv = Lv + Ld \cdot \sigmas(p) \cdot Tr g. Russian Roulette: If Tr < 10^{-3}: i. Generate a random number U[0, 1). ii. If U < 0.5, break the loop (terminate ray). iii. Otherwise, continue by scaling transmittance: Tr = Tr / 0.5. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random class Spectrum: def init(self, r=0.0, g=0.0, b=0.0): self.r, self.g, self.b = r, g, b def add(self, other): return Spectrum(self.r + other.r, self.g + other.g, self.b + other.b) def mul(self, other): if isinstance(other, (int, float)): return Spectrum(self.r other, self.g other, self.b other) return Spectrum(self.r other.r, self.g other.g, self.b other.b) def isblack(self): return self.r == 0.0 and self.g == 0.0 and self.b == 0.0 class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction def call(self, t): return (self.origin[0] + self.direction[0]t, self.origin[1] + self.direction[1]t, self.origin[2] + self.direction[2]t) def VolumeIntegratorLi(rayorigin, raydirection, t0, t1, scene, mStepSize): volumes = scene.getVolumes() lights = scene.getLightSources() # Step 1: Calculate number of samples numsamples = int((t1 - t0) / mStepSize) if numsamples == 0: numsamples = 1 # Step 2: Calculate actual step length step = (t1 - t0) / numsamples # Step 3: Apply random offset t0 = t0 + random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) step # Step 4: Initialize accumulators Lv = Spectrum(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) Tr = 1.0 p = Ray(rayorigin, raydirection)(t0) # Step 5: Loop for i in range(numsamples): pprev = p t0 += step p = Ray(rayorigin, raydirection)(t0) # Create short ray for optical depth calculation stepray = Ray(pprev, (p[0]-pprev[0], p[1]-pprev[1], p[2]-pprev[2])) steptau = volumes[0].tau(stepray, 0.5 step, 0) # Update transmittance Tr = Tr math.exp(-steptau) # Accumulate emitted light Lv = Lv + volumes[0].Le(p) # Get scattering coefficient ss = volumes[0].sigmas(p) # Check if scattering is non-zero if not ss.isblack(): # Compute light direction lightpos = lights[0].position wL = normalize(lightpos, p) # Shadow ray shadowray = Ray(p, wL) surfacehit = scene.intersect(shadowray) # Check if unshadowed disttolight = length(lightpos, p) isunshadowed = (surfacehit is None) or (surfacehit.t > disttolight) if isunshadowed: # Compute light transmittance lighttau = volumes[0].tau(shadowray, mStepSize 2, 0) lTr = math.exp(-lighttau) # Direct lighting contribution Ld = lTr lights[0].color # Add to accumulated radiance Lv = Lv + Ld ss Tr # Russian Roulette if Tr < 1e-3: if random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) < 0.5: break else: Tr = Tr / 0.5 return Lv def normalize(vec, frompt=None): if frompt: vec = (vec[0]-frompt[0], vec[1]-frompt[1], vec[2]-frompt[2]) mag = math.sqrt(vec[0]2 + vec[1]2 + vec[2]2) return (vec[0]/mag, vec[1]/mag, vec[2]/mag) def length(vec, frompt=None): if frompt: vec = (vec[0]-frompt[0], vec[1]-frompt[1], vec[2]-frompt[2]) return math.sqrt(vec[0]2 + vec[1]2 + vec[2]2) Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples N per ray, where N \approx \frac{\text{Volume Length}}{\text{mStepSize}}. Each step involves volume queries and potentially a shadow ray intersection. Memory Complexity: Constant, O(1), excluding the storage of the volume data structure itself. Strengths: Simple implementation; random offset reduces banding; Russian Roulette handles long transmissive paths efficiently. Limitations: Assumes a single volume and single light source, limiting its applicability to complex scenes without modification. The specific arguments passed to tau (e.g., 0.5 step and mStepSize 2) are implementation-specific and may not generalize to other volume libraries without adaptation. When to Use: Suitable for simple volumetric scenes with a single light source where performance is prioritized over multi-light accuracy. When Not to Use: Complex scenes with multiple volumes or lights, or where high-fidelity multi-scattering is required. Mr-Voxel is a volume rendering technique developed as part of a graphics graduate thesis by C. Gibson. It combines an accelerated voxel data structure with a volume rendering library. The lighting equations are derived or loosely based on the volume rendering sections of "Physically Based Rendering, 2nd edition" by Matt Pharr. The implementation is found in the VolumeIntegrator::Li function within the Mr-Voxel repository. cgibson/Mr-Voxel, https://github.com/cgibson/Mr-Voxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray-marched Volumetric Fog
head: Fog Filter, Fog Scattering, Forward ray-marching fog, Full-screen volumetric fog, Volumetric Fog (CRYENGINE 3), Voxel-based Volumetric Fog
body: Ray-marched volumetric fog simulates aerial perspective and light shafts by treating fog as a 3D volume of participating media traced via forward ray-marching from the camera to the scene. It solves the problem of rendering dynamic, light-interacting fog that absorbs and scatters light, distinguishing itself from backward ray-marching by allowing early-out optimizations when transmittance becomes negligible. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position, per-pixel UV coordinates, depth buffer, light position and intensity \Phi, fog density \tau, scattering coefficient a, step size \Delta l, maximum ray distance zfar, and phase function asymmetry parameter g. Outputs: Final radiance L per pixel. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin (camera position) and direction (view vector). Depth Buffer: 2D texture mapping UV coordinates to depth values z. Light Source: Point light defined by position and intensity \Phi. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, construct a ray originating at the camera position. 2. Scene Intersection: Sample the depth buffer at the current pixel's UV coordinate to reconstruct the 3D position of the scene surface. 3. Ray Clamping: If the ray does not hit the scene, clamp the maximum ray distance to a predefined zfar value to prevent infinite marching. 4. Jittering: Add a pseudo-random delta step \delta to the ray's starting position to mitigate slice artifacts. 5. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate from t=0 to t=tf with a fixed step size \Delta l. 6. In-Scattering Calculation: At each step position x, calculate the in-scattering term Li. 7. Transmittance Calculation: Calculate the transmittance T from the camera to the current step position. 8. Accumulation: Add the product of in-scattering, transmittance, and step size to the accumulated radiance. 9. Early-Out: If transmittance drops below a threshold, terminate the loop early. Formulas: The final radiance L is approximated using a Riemann sum: L = \sum{n=0}^{N} Li(x(ln), \omega) e^{-\tau ln} \Delta l Where: L: Calculated radiance. N: Total number of steps. Li(x(ln), \omega): In-scattering term at step n. e^{-\tau ln}: Transmittance from camera to distance ln. \tau: Density (extinction coefficient). ln: Distance traveled along the ray at step n. \Delta l: Ray-march step size. The in-scattering term Li for a point light is defined as: Li(x, \omega) = \frac{a \Phi}{4\pi d^2} v(x) e^{-\tau d} P(\omega, \omega') Where: a: Scattering coefficient (probability of photon scattering). \Phi: Point light intensity. d: Distance from the sample point x to the light source. v(x): Visibility of the sample point from the light source (1 if unshadowed). e^{-\tau d}: Transmittance from the light to the sample point. P(\omega, \omega'): Phase function describing scattering direction probability. Parameters: Density (\tau): Constant for uniform fog. Can be procedurally generated or sampled from textures/OpenVDB for non-uniform fog. Visibility (v(x)): Set to 1 in basic implementations; can be sampled from a light's cube shadow map for soft shadows. Phase Function (P): Uses the Schlick phase function approximation of the Henyey-Greenstein (HG) function for real-time performance, replacing the more expensive original HG function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def raymarchedvolumetricfog(camerapos, uv, depthbuffer, lightpos, lightintensity, fogdensity, scatteringcoeff, stepsize, zfar, g): # 1. Reconstruct scene intersection depth = depthbuffer.sample(uv) scenepos = reconstructworldposition(uv, depth) # 2. Calculate ray direction and length raydir = normalize(scenepos - camerapos) raylength = length(scenepos - camerapos) # 3. Clamp ray length if raylength > zfar: raylength = zfar # 4. Initialize accumulation accumulatedradiance = vec3(0.0) numsteps = math.ceil(raylength / stepsize) # 5. Jitter start position to reduce slice artifacts jitter = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) stepsize # 6. March along the ray for n in range(numsteps): l = n stepsize + jitter currentpos = camerapos + raydir l # 7. Calculate distance to light d = length(currentpos - lightpos) # 8. Calculate In-Scattering visibility = 1.0 # Basic implementation costheta = dot(raydir, normalize(lightpos - currentpos)) phase = schlickhenyeygreenstein(costheta, g) inscattering = (scatteringcoeff lightintensity / (4.0 math.pi d d)) \ visibility \ math.exp(-fogdensity d) \ phase # 9. Calculate Transmittance from camera to current step transmittance = math.exp(-fogdensity l) # 10. Accumulate accumulatedradiance += inscattering transmittance stepsize # 11. Early-out optimization if transmittance < 0.01: break return accumulatedradiance def reconstructworldposition(uv, depth): # Standard inverse view-projection reconstruction # Assumes uv in [-1, 1], depth in [0, 1], and standard OpenGL/DirectX conventions pass def schlickhenyeygreenstein(costheta, g): # Schlick approximation of Henyey-Greenstein phase function gsq = g g denom = 1.0 + gsq - 2.0 g costheta return (1.0 - gsq) / (4.0 math.pi (denom 1.5)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Slice Artifacts: Marching rays with the same step size starting at the same point causes samples to align on the same "slices," creating visible banding. Jittering Trade-off: Jittering reduces slice artifacts but can introduce noise, especially with larger step sizes. Infinite Marching: Rays that do not hit the scene must be clamped by zfar to prevent infinite loops. Camera Mode Restriction: Only functions in Perspective and Free camera modes; disabled in Orthographic/Isometric modes. Ground Plane Bounds: The ground plane is rendered as infinitely large in all camera modes when enabled, altering scene bounds. Renders HDR height fog and volumetric direct-light scattering by integrating exponential height density and up to 16 transformed box volumes along depth-bounded rays. Distinguishes itself by performing volume shadow lookups using hardware PCF at the actual sample point, eliminating light leakage and removing the cost of repeating raster surface soft-shadow filters at every march step. Operates as a full-resolution, fixed-step, single-scattering pass executed before TAA, bloom, and tone mapping. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps N per pixel (O(N)). N depends on the distance to the scene and the step size. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the accumulation, plus O(W \times H) for the depth buffer. Performance: Real-time capable on modern GPUs when using fixed step sizes and Schlick phase approximations. Performance degrades with smaller step sizes or complex visibility calculations (shadow mapping). Strengths: Simple implementation, allows early-out optimization, dynamic interaction with scene geometry and lighting. Scatters all light types (Sun, Sky, Area) and creates light shafts. Limitations: Slice artifacts require jittering or variable step sizes; noise increases with jittering; uniform fog assumption simplifies density but limits complex volumetric structures without additional data structures. When to Use: Real-time applications requiring dynamic fog, light shafts, and aerial perspective where performance is critical. Enables glass and metal materials to receive reflection and refraction from sun light, and allows background rendering with minimal fog density. When Not to Use: Offline rendering requiring high-fidelity multi-scattering or complex non-uniform volumes without precomputed data structures. The technique is based on the principles of volume rendering and participating media, specifically the work by Toth and Umenhoffer on "Real-time Volumetric Lighting in Participating Media". It has been implemented in games such as Horizon Zero Dawn, Death Stranding, and Returnal to simulate dynamic fog and light shafts. The forward ray-marching approach was chosen over backward ray-marching to facilitate early-out optimizations. The method is also known as Fog Scattering in CRYENGINE 3, where it was optimized by removing unused branches and supports emissive area lighting. name: Ray-marched Volumetric Fog with Local Volumes and PCF Shadows
head: HDR height fog, Volumetric Lighting and Height Fog, volumetric direct-light scattering
body: This method renders HDR height fog and volumetric direct-light scattering by integrating exponential height density and up to 16 transformed box volumes along depth-bounded rays. It distinguishes itself from surface-biased approaches by performing volume shadow lookups using hardware PCF at the actual sample point, eliminating light leakage through nearby blockers and removing the cost of repeating raster surface soft-shadow filters at every march step. It operates as a full-resolution, fixed-step, single-scattering pass executed before TAA, bloom, and tone mapping. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Camera parameters (perspective, orthographic, or infinite-far), up to 16 local volume definitions (transformed boxes), scene light list (directional, point, spot), and HDR color buffer. Outputs: Accumulated fog color and opacity per pixel, integrated into the HDR buffer. Data Structures Local Volume: A transformed box defined by a 4 \times 4 affine transformation matrix and volume properties (extinction coefficient, albedo, scattering phase function parameters). The implementation rejects invalid volume transforms. Light List: Contains directional, point, and spot lights sharing the scene’s attenuation and shadow maps. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel, generate a ray based on the camera type (perspective, orthographic, or infinite-far). Determine the ray's near and far bounds using depth-bounded integration. 2. Ray Marching: Discretize the ray into fixed steps. 3. Sample Point Calculation: For each step, calculate the sample position at the segment midpoint between the current and next step boundary. 4. Height Density Integration: Evaluate the exponential height density at the sample point. 5. Local Volume Intersection: Check the sample point against all active local volumes (up to 16). Use ray–box interval tests to determine if the sample lies within a volume. Preserve thin-volume extinction between march samples by integrating over the ray segment length inside the volume. If the sample is inside a volume, compute the additive extinction and scattering contribution using the volume's properties. 6. Lighting Evaluation: For each light in the scene, calculate the light direction and distance to the sample point. Apply light attenuation. Perform a hardware PCF shadow lookup using the shadow map associated with the light. Sample the shadow map at the actual 3D sample point projected into light space, without applying surface-normal or depth offsets. This prevents light leakage through nearby blockers. Apply the Henyey–Greenstein phase function for scattering towards the camera. 7. Sanitization: Ensure all color and albedo values are finite; sanitize non-finite values. 8. Accumulation: Integrate the scattered light and accumulated extinction along the ray. Formulas Exponential Height Density: \rho(h) = \rho0 e^{-h/H}, where h is height, \rho0 is sea-level density, and H is scale height. Beer-Lambert Attenuation: T = e^{-\int \sigmat(s) ds}, where \sigmat is the extinction coefficient. Henyey-Greenstein Phase Function: p(\theta) = \frac{1-g^2}{4\pi (1+g^2-2g\cos\theta)^{3/2}}, where g is the anisotropy factor and \theta is the scattering angle. Parameters Max Local Volumes: 16. Steps: Fixed number (e.g., 48). Sample Position: Segment midpoint. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Light Leakage: Surface-biased shadow lookups cause light leakage through nearby blockers. Invalid Transforms: Invalid volume transforms must be rejected to prevent artifacts. Non-Finite Values: Non-finite colors or albedos must be sanitized. TAA History: Fog has no dedicated history buffer for TAA. Blended Surfaces: Blended surfaces use opaque depth rather than separate per-layer fog distances. Soft Shadows: Wide raster soft-shadow filtering does not apply to the fog pass. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderfogpass(camera, localvolumes, lights, hdrbuffer): # Initialize output buffer output = [[vec3(0.0), 0.0] for in range(hdrbuffer.width hdrbuffer.height)] for y in range(hdrbuffer.height): for x in range(hdrbuffer.width): ray = camera.generateray(x, y) neart = camera.nearplane fart = camera.farplane numsteps = 48 stepsize = (fart - neart) / numsteps acccolor = vec3(0.0) accopacity = 0.0 for step in range(numsteps): tstart = neart + step stepsize tend = neart + (step + 1) stepsize tmid = (tstart + tend) / 2.0 samplepos = ray.origin + ray.direction tmid if tmid > fart: break extinction = 0.0 # 1. Height Fog Extinction heightdensity = exp(-samplepos.y / 10.0) # standard exponential height falloff segmentlength = stepsize extinction += heightdensity segmentlength # 2. Local Volume Extinction for volume in localvolumes: tmin, tmax = rayboxinterval(ray, tstart, tend, volume.transform) if tmin < tmax: intervallength = tmax - tmin extinction += volume.extinctioncoefficient intervallength transmission = exp(-extinction) scatteredlight = vec3(0.0) for light in lights: lightdir = normalize(light.position - samplepos) lightdist = length(light.position - samplepos) attenuation = light.attenuation(lightdist) lightspacepos = light.viewmatrix samplepos shadow = hardwarepcfshadowlookup(light.shadowmap, lightspacepos) phase = heneygreensteinphase(ray.direction, lightdir, light.anisotropy) scatteredlight += light.color attenuation shadow phase volume.albedo acccolor += scatteredlight transmission (1.0 - accopacity) accopacity += (1.0 - transmission) (1.0 - accopacity) output[y hdrbuffer.width + x] = [acccolor, accopacity] return output def rayboxinterval(ray, tmin, tmax, transform): # Standard slab method for ray-box intersection invdir = vec3(1.0) / ray.direction boxmin = transform[0:3, 3] boxmax = transform[0:3, 3] + transform[0:3, 0:3] t1 = (boxmin.x - ray.origin.x) invdir.x t2 = (boxmax.x - ray.origin.x) invdir.x tmin = min(t1, t2); tmax = max(t1, t2) t1 = (boxmin.y - ray.origin.y) invdir.y t2 = (boxmax.y - ray.origin.y) invdir.y tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)); tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) t1 = (boxmin.z - ray.origin.z) invdir.z t2 = (boxmax.z - ray.origin.z) invdir.z tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)); tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < tmin or tmax < tmin or tmin > tmax: return -1.0, -1.0 return max(tmin, tmin), min(tmax, tmax) def hardwarepcfshadowlookup(shadowmap, lightspacepos): # Standard hardware PCF sampling return shadowmap.samplepcf(lightspacepos.xy / lightspacepos.w, lightspacepos.z) def heneygreensteinphase(viewdir, lightdir, g): costheta = dot(viewdir, lightdir) return (1.0 - g2) / (4.0 3.14159 (1.0 + g2 - 2.0 g costheta)1.5) The parent technique that traces rays through a participating medium to simulate light absorption and scattering. Choose this when you need general volumetric effects like fog, smoke, or clouds. Ray-marched Volumetric Fog This specific implementation adds support for discrete, transformed box volumes and uses hardware PCF for shadows at the sample point. Choose this when you need efficient, artifact-free shadows for local volumetric objects like fog planes or light shafts. Ray-marched Volumetric Fog with Local Volumes and PCF Shadows Time Complexity: Scales with pixels, steps, lights, and volumes. Direct-light evaluation visits every uploaded scene light at each occupied march step without clustered culling. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On Apple M3 Max, 640×480 resolution, 48 steps, 60 timed frames: 4.18 ms/frame with fog, 2.68 ms disabled. The previous surface-shadow lookup measured 8.36 ms with fog, showing a significant performance improvement. Strengths: Eliminates light leakage from nearby blockers; removes the cost of repeating raster soft-shadow filters; supports various camera types and HDR post-processing. Limitations: Single scattering only; no dedicated TAA history for fog; scaling with lights and volumes can be expensive without culling; wide raster soft-shadow filtering is not applicable. When to Use: When high-quality, artifact-free volumetric shadows are needed for local fog volumes and height fog, and performance is acceptable for the target resolution and light count. This method was implemented in ParadiseEngine, as documented in src/Paradise.Rendering.Pbr/FOG.md. It was introduced in pull request #278, authored by quabug and reviewed by opencara in September 2026. The implementation was validated with 110 passed tests in the full PBR suite and 15 focused fog tests, covering Beer-Lambert attenuation, height falloff, depth clipping, and various volume types. It is enabled via scene settings and the rendering.fog engine switch. Add volumetric lighting and height fog, https://github.com/ParadiseEngine/ParadiseEngine/pull/278, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Material Parameter Setting
head: Material Format, Material object fields, Standard Volume Material, vpSetMaterial
body: Material Parameter Setting defines the optical and geometric properties of volumetric media by mapping raw data grids to physical attributes such as density, color, and emission. It solves the problem of converting abstract simulation data into renderable radiance contributions within the volume rendering integral. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the definition of these properties via explicit channel bindings and parameter sliders (Standard Volume Material) or low-level API calls (VolPack), rather than the traversal or shading algorithms themselves. It builds on Specific Material and Geometry Rendering. Inputs: Raw scalar grids (e.g., density, temperature), user-defined parameters (density multipliers, anisotropy), and optional texture descriptors. Outputs: A material state object or context configuration that defines how sample points along a ray are shaded. This configuration binds named VDB grids to specific physical properties through explicit channel fields: Volume Channel: String (case-sensitive name of the VDB grid, typically 'density'). Density: Float multiplier for the volume channel. Scatter Color: RGB vector. Scatter Scale: Float multiplier for scatter intensity. Anisotropy Mode: Enum (Henyey-Greenstein or Jendersie-d’Eon). Transparency Color: RGB vector (per-wavelength attenuation). Transparency Depth: Float (cm, per-wavelength travel distance). Emission Channel: String (name of temperature grid). Emission Mode: Enum (Blackbody or Color). Defined in, this structure holds shading parameters for surfaces and procedural volumes: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Material: albedo: list[float] # Linear float RGB metalness: float # Float [0..1] roughness: float # Float [0..1] F0: list[float] # Linear float RGB, base reflectivity triplar: bool # True for XZ planar, False for triplanar normalStrength: float # Linear float albedoTex: int # Texture descriptor (-1 if unused) normalTex: int # Texture descriptor (-1 if unused) roughnessTex: int # Texture descriptor (-1 if unused) metalnessTex: int # Texture descriptor (-1 if unused) heightmapTex: int # Texture descriptor (-1 if unused) ambietTex: int # Texture descriptor (-1 if unused) Defined in, this is not a persistent struct but a state set via vpSetMaterial using the following constants: materialnum: VPMATERIAL0 through VPMATERIAL5. property: VPAMBIENT, VPDIFFUSE, VPSPECULAR, VPSHINYNESS. surfaceside: VPEXTERIOR, VPINTERIOR, VPBOTHSIDES. 1. Bind Volume Channel: Assign the name of the density grid to the Volume Channel field. 2. Set Density: Multiply the grid values by the Density parameter to control overall thickness. 3. Configure Scatter: Set Scatter Color and Scatter Scale to define reflection properties. 4. Select Phase Function: Choose Anisotropy Mode. Use Henyey-Greenstein (slider -1 to +1) for isotropic smoke or Jendersie-d’Eon for cloud droplets. 5. Configure Transparency: Set Transparency Color (darker means thicker) and Transparency Depth (in cm) to model wavelength-dependent attenuation. 6. Configure Emission (Optional): If rendering fire, bind the temperature grid to Emission Channel. Set Emission Mode to Blackbody for physical accuracy (3,000 K to >9,000 K) or Color for artistic control. 1. Initialize Context: Create a vpContext object. 2. Set Material Properties: Call vpSetMaterial(vpc, materialnum, property, surfaceside, r, g, b). 3. Define Surface Side: Use VPEXTERIOR (gradient towards viewer), VPINTERIOR (gradient away), or VPBOTHSIDES. 4. Reverse Sides (Optional): Call vpEnable(vpc, VPREVERSESURFACESIDES) to invert exterior/interior definitions. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def Material(albedo: list[float], metalness: float, roughness: float, F0: list[float]) -> Material: """Constructor 1: Full initialization.""" mat = Material() mat.albedo = albedo mat.metalness = metalness mat.roughness = roughness mat.F0 = F0 mat.triplar = False # Planar projection mat.normalStrength = 1.0 mat.albedoTex = -1 mat.normalTex = -1 mat.roughnessTex = -1 mat.metalnessTex = -1 mat.heightmapTex = -1 mat.ambietTex = -1 return mat def MaterialDefaultF0(albedo: list[float], metalness: float, roughness: float) -> Material: """Constructor 2: Default F0 for non-metal dielectrics.""" defaultF0 = [0.04, 0.04, 0.04] return Material(albedo, metalness, roughness, defaultF0) Volume Rendering Integral (Context): C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigmat(t) c(t) dt Where \sigmat is derived from the Volume Channel multiplied by Density and modified by Transparency Color/Depth [Parent]. Blackbody Emission (Standard Volume): Temperature T (Kelvin) maps to color C. T \approx 3,000 K maps to deep red. T > 9,000 K maps to white/blue-white. Base Reflectivity (Material Format): For non-metal dielectrics, F0 = [0.04, 0.04, 0.04]. F0: [0.04, 0.04, 0.04] for dielectrics. Anisotropy (Henyey-Greenstein): Slider range [-1, 1]. Transparency Depth: Measured in centimeters; should match real-world volume size. Material IDs: VPMATERIAL0 through VPMATERIAL5. Case Sensitivity: Volume channel names are case-sensitive. Surface Side Ambiguity: VPEXTERIOR and VPINTERIOR depend on gradient direction. Use VPREVERSESURFACESIDES if the gradient is inverted relative to the viewer. Textureless Default: Material objects default to textureless (descriptors = -1) unless explicitly bound. Initializes the rendering state for direct volume ray casting by creating and caching a shader program configured for transparent volumetric rendering. It binds necessary textures (noise, fire profiles, transfer functions, labels, weights) and uniform parameters (affine transforms, intensity ranges) to the GPU. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the binding and configuration of material resources rather than the traversal logic or the transfer function definition itself. Not given in the sources. Standard Volume Material is described in Maxon's documentation as a volume shader with optimized fast paths for clouds, smoke, and flames, and a fully programmable node-based path. Material Format is defined in CUDA raymarching implementations to hold shading parameters for surfaces and procedural volumes, including PBR-like properties and texture descriptors. VolPack is a C library for volume rendering that uses vpSetMaterial to configure material properties per voxel side.
