name: Volume Material Setup
head: ApplyToMaterial, Material Initialization, Shader Parameter Binding, Volume Material Setup (Affine, Weights, Label Map), initMaterial
body: Volume Material Setup initializes the rendering state for direct volume ray casting by creating and caching a RawShaderMaterial configured for transparent volumetric rendering. It binds necessary textures (noise, fire profiles, transfer functions, labels, weights) and uniform parameters (affine transforms, intensity ranges) to the GPU, enabling the shader to correctly sample and composite volume data. It differs from sibling methods by focusing exclusively on the binding and configuration of material resources rather than the traversal logic or transfer function definition itself. The method constructs a material object that encapsulates all shader inputs required for volume rendering. It handles the selection of textures based on availability, computes inverse affine matrices for coordinate transformation, and sets flags to inform the shader about the data type (e.g., label map vs. continuous). Inputs: d: Data object containing metadata (d.meta), transfer function (d.tf), and optional texture references (d.labelTexture, d.weightTexture). volumeTexLabels: Optional pre-loaded 3D texture for label data. volumeTexWeights: Optional pre-loaded 3D texture for weight data. tfTexCurrent: The current transfer function texture. vs, fs: Vertex and fragment shader source code strings. Outputs: material: An initialized material object ready for assignment to a mesh renderer. Uniforms Object Layout The uniforms passed to the shader are structured as follows: | Uniform Name | Type | Value/Source | Description | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | nzw | t (Texture) | nzw.png | Noise texture for turbulence. | | fireProfile | t (Texture) | firetex.png | Fire profile texture. | | time | f (Float) | 1.0 | Time parameter for animation. | | TFTex | t (Texture) | tfTexCurrent | Transfer function texture. | | VolumeTexLabels | t (Texture) | Selected label texture | Label map texture. | | VolumeTexWeights | t (Texture) | Selected weight texture | Weight texture (or black if null). | | Affine | m4 (Matrix4) | affine | 4x4 affine transformation matrix. | | InvAffine | m4 (Matrix4) | affine.inverse | Inverse affine transformation matrix. | | Dim | v4 (Vector4) | (dimX, dimY, dimZ, 1.0) | Volume dimensions. | | P1 | f (Float) | p1 | Lower bound of intensity range. | | P99 | f (Float) | p99 | Upper bound of intensity range. | | IsLabelMap | i (Int) | 0 or 1 | Flag indicating label map usage. | | HasWeights | i (Int) | 0 or 1 | Flag indicating weight texture presence. | Texture Configuration nzw: RepeatWrapping on S and T axes; LinearFilter for mag/min. fireProfile: ClampToEdgeWrapping on S and T axes; LinearFilter for mag/min. 1. Extract Dimensions: Read dimX, dimY, dimZ from d.meta.dim. 2. Initialize Intensity Range: Set p1 = 0.0, p99 = 1.0. If d.tf.type == "continuous" and d.meta.intensityrange exists with length 2, set p1 = d.meta.intensityrange[0] and p99 = d.meta.intensityrange[1]. 3. Load Noise Texture: Load nzw.png. Set wrapping to RepeatWrapping and filtering to LinearFilter. 4. Load Fire Profile Texture: Load firetex.png. Set wrapping to ClampToEdgeWrapping and filtering to LinearFilter. 5. Compute Affine Matrices: Construct affine matrix from d.meta.affine (4x4). Compute invAffine = affine.inverse(). 6. Select Label Texture: If volumeTexLabels is provided, use it. Else if d.labelTexture is provided, use it. Else, use a default black 3D texture (BlackTex3D). Bind to VolumeTexLabels. 7. Select Weight Texture: If volumeTexWeights is provided, use it. Else if d.weightTexture is provided, use it. Else, set texW = null. Bind texW to VolumeTexWeights or BlackTex3D. Set HasWeights = 1 if texW != null, else 0. 8. Bind Transfer Function: Bind tfTexCurrent to TFTex. Set IsLabelMap = 1 if d.tf.type == "labelmap", else 0. 9. Set Uniforms: Set P1, P99, Dim (Vector4(dimX, dimY, dimZ, 1.0)), Affine, InvAffine. 10. Create Material: Instantiate RawShaderMaterial with vs, fs, uniforms, side: DoubleSide, blending: AdditiveBlending, transparent: true. 11. Assign Material: Assign material to MeshRenderer.sharedMaterial. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def loadtexture(path): # Not given in the sources. pass class Matrix4: def init(self, data): self.data = data def inverse(self): return Matrix4(self.data) class Vector4: def init(self, x, y, z, w): self.data = (x, y, z, w) class RawShaderMaterial: def init(self, vertexShader, fragmentShader, uniforms, side, blending, transparent): self.vertexShader = vertexShader self.fragmentShader = fragmentShader self.uniforms = uniforms self.side = side self.blending = blending self.transparent = transparent BlackTex3D = "defaultblacktexture" def initmaterial(d, volumeTexLabels=None, volumeTexWeights=None, tfTexCurrent=None, vs=None, fs=None): # Step 1: Extract dimensions dimX, dimY, dimZ = d.meta.dim[0], d.meta.dim[1], d.meta.dim[2] # Step 2: Initialize intensity range p1 = 0.0 p99 = 1.0 if d.tf.type == "continuous" and hasattr(d.meta, 'intensityrange') and len(d.meta.intensityrange) == 2: p1 = d.meta.intensityrange[0] p99 = d.meta.intensityrange[1] # Step 3: Load noise texture nzw = loadtexture('nzw.png') nzw.wrapS = 'REPEAT' nzw.wrapT = 'REPEAT' nzw.magFilter = 'LINEAR' nzw.minFilter = 'LINEAR' # Step 4: Load fire profile texture fireProfile = loadtexture('firetex.png') fireProfile.wrapS = 'CLAMPTOEDGE' fireProfile.wrapT = 'CLAMPTOEDGE' fireProfile.magFilter = 'LINEAR' fireProfile.minFilter = 'LINEAR' # Step 5: Compute affine matrices affine = Matrix4(d.meta.affine) invAffine = affine.inverse() # Step 6: Select label texture if volumeTexLabels is not None: texLbl = volumeTexLabels elif hasattr(d, 'labelTexture') and d.labelTexture is not None: texLbl = d.labelTexture else: texLbl = BlackTex3D # Step 7: Select weight texture if volumeTexWeights is not None: texW = volumeTexWeights elif hasattr(d, 'weightTexture') and d.weightTexture is not None: texW = d.weightTexture else: texW = None hasWeights = 1 if texW is not None else 0 texWforuniform = texW if texW is not None else BlackTex3D # Step 8: Bind Transfer Function and Flags isLabelMap = 1 if d.tf.type == "labelmap" else 0 # Step 9: Create Uniforms Object uniforms = { 'nzw': {'type': 't', 'value': nzw}, 'fireProfile': {'type': 't', 'value': fireProfile}, 'time': {'type': 'f', 'value': 1.0}, 'TFTex': {'type': 't', 'value': tfTexCurrent}, 'VolumeTexLabels': {'type': 't', 'value': texLbl}, 'VolumeTexWeights': {'type': 't', 'value': texWforuniform}, 'Affine': {'type': 'm4', 'value': affine}, 'InvAffine': {'type': 'm4', 'value': invAffine}, 'Dim': {'type': 'v4', 'value': Vector4(dimX, dimY, dimZ, 1.0)}, 'P1': {'type': 'f', 'value': p1}, 'P99': {'type': 'f', 'value': p99}, 'IsLabelMap': {'type': 'i', 'value': isLabelMap}, 'HasWeights': {'type': 'i', 'value': hasWeights} } # Step 10: Instantiate Material material = RawShaderMaterial( vertexShader=vs, fragmentShader=fs, uniforms=uniforms, side='DOUBLE', blending='ADDITIVE', transparent=True) # Step 11: Assign Material # MeshRenderer.sharedMaterial = material return material P1, P99: Floats representing the intensity range for continuous transfer functions. Default: 0.0, 1.0. IsLabelMap: Integer flag (0 or 1). 1 if d.tf.type == "labelmap". HasWeights: Integer flag (0 or 1). 1 if a weight texture is provided. time: Float, default 1.0. Missing Intensity Range: If d.meta.intensityrange is missing for a continuous TF, the range defaults to [0.0, 1.0], which may cause incorrect color mapping if the data is not normalized. Null Textures: If no label or weight texture is provided, a black 3D texture is used. The shader must handle this gracefully (e.g., treating black as zero intensity/weight). Affine Inverse: Computing the inverse affine matrix is critical for correct coordinate transformation. Singular matrices will cause errors. Texture Wrapping: Incorrect wrapping modes (e.g., RepeatWrapping for fire profile) may cause artifacts at texture boundaries. Time Complexity: O(1) for material setup, assuming texture loading is asynchronous or cached. The actual rendering cost is determined by the ray marching scheme. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the material object itself, plus the memory for the textures (which are typically loaded once and reused). Strengths: Centralizes material configuration, making it easy to switch between different rendering modes (e.g., label map vs. continuous) by changing flags. Limitations: Depends on the availability of specific textures (nzw.png, firetex.png) which may not be relevant for all volume rendering scenarios (e.g., non-fire volumes). The method reflects patterns from WebGL-based volume rendering libraries. VolumetricFire demonstrates loading noise and fire textures with additive blending for transparent volumetric rendering. vrdf-sdk describes a generic volume rendering setup involving affine matrix computation, dimension extraction, and explicit uniform bindings for textures and matrices. guillaume-schneider/vrdf-sdk, https://github.com/guillaume-schneider/vrdf-sdk, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) yomotsu/VolumetricFire, https://github.com/yomotsu/VolumetricFire, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: DVGO Density and Color Rendering
head: DVGO volume rendering
body: DVGO renders 3D scenes by decoupling geometry and appearance into a voxel grid and a neural network. It maps stored grid values to non-negative densities using a shifted softplus activation, and computes view-dependent color emission via a shallow MLP taking interpolated features and positional encodings. The method accumulates radiance along rays using standard volume rendering quadrature. Post-activation interpolation (applying non-linearities after trilinear interpolation) produces sharp surfaces, reducing the required grid resolution for surface detail. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a voxel grid resolution Nx \times Ny \times Nz, a feature grid V^{(f)}, a density grid V^{(d)}, a shallow MLP MLP\Theta, a shift hyperparameter b, a sample count n, and a background color c{bg}. It outputs the rendered color \hat{C}(r) for a camera ray r. Data Structures: 1. Density Grid (V^{(d)}): 3D tensor of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) storing raw scalar values \ddot{\sigma}, which serve as inputs to the activation function. 2. Feature Grid (V^{(f)}): 3D tensor of shape (C, Nx, Ny, Nz) storing C-dimensional feature vectors at each voxel. 3. MLP (MLP\Theta): Small neural network mapping concatenated interpolated features and positional encodings to RGB color. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Casting & Sampling: For each pixel, cast ray r from camera origin. Sample n points xi uniformly between near and far planes. Let \deltai be the distance to the adjacent sampled point. 2. Density Retrieval: Interpolate raw density \ddot{\sigma}i from V^{(d)} at xi using trilinear interpolation. 3. Density Activation: Compute \sigmai = \text{softplus}(\ddot{\sigma}i). 4. Color Feature Retrieval: Interpolate feature vector fi from V^{(f)} at xi using trilinear interpolation. 5. Color Emission: Apply positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to xi and ray direction d. Compute ci^{(rgb)} = MLP\Theta([fi; \gamma(xi); \gamma(d)]). 6. Termination Probability: Compute \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). 7. Accumulated Transmittance: Compute Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), with T1 = 1. 8. Volume Rendering Quadrature: Accumulate color \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{n} Ti \alphai ci^{(rgb)} + T{n+1} c{bg}. Formulas: Density activation: \sigmai = \text{softplus}(\ddot{\sigma}i) = \log(1 + \exp(\ddot{\sigma}i + b)), where \ddot{\sigma}i is the value stored in V^{(d)} and b is a hyperparameter shift. Color emission: ci^{(rgb)} = MLP\Theta(\text{interp}(xi, V^{(f)}), xi, d), where xi is the position, V^{(f)} is the feature grid, and d is the ray direction. Termination probability: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai), where \deltai is the distance to the adjacent sampled point. Accumulated transmittance: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj), denoting transmittance from the near plane to point xi. Volume rendering quadrature: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{n} Ti \alphai ci^{(rgb)} + T{n+1} c{bg}, where c{bg} is a pre-defined background color. Parameters: b: Shift hyperparameter for the softplus activation. n: Number of sample points along the ray. c{bg}: Pre-defined background color. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def softplus(x, b=0.0): """Shifted softplus activation: log(1 + exp(x + b)).""" return np.log(1.0 + np.exp(x + b)) def trilinearinterpolate(grid, x, y, z): """Trilinear interpolation for 3D or 4D grids. Coordinates in [0, 1].""" x = np.clip(x, 0.0, 1.0) y = np.clip(y, 0.0, 1.0) z = np.clip(z, 0.0, 1.0) if grid.ndim == 3: C = 1 Nx, Ny, Nz = grid.shape else: C, Nx, Ny, Nz = grid.shape ix = np.floor(x (Nx - 1)).astype(int) iy = np.floor(y (Ny - 1)).astype(int) iz = np.floor(z (Nz - 1)).astype(int) fx = x (Nx - 1) - ix fy = y (Ny - 1) - iy fz = z (Nz - 1) - iz ix1 = np.minimum(ix + 1, Nx - 1) iy1 = np.minimum(iy + 1, Ny - 1) iz1 = np.minimum(iz + 1, Nz - 1) if C == 1: v000 = grid[ix, iy, iz] v100 = grid[ix1, iy, iz] v010 = grid[ix, iy1, iz] v110 = grid[ix1, iy1, iz] v001 = grid[ix, iy, iz1] v101 = grid[ix1, iy, iz1] v011 = grid[ix, iy1, iz1] v111 = grid[ix1, iy1, iz1] else: v000 = grid[:, ix, iy, iz] v100 = grid[:, ix1, iy, iz] v010 = grid[:, ix, iy1, iz] v110 = grid[:, ix1, iy1, iz] v001 = grid[:, ix, iy, iz1] v101 = grid[:, ix1, iy, iz1] v011 = grid[:, ix, iy1, iz1] v111 = grid[:, ix1, iy1, iz1] w000 = (1 - fx) (1 - fy) (1 - fz) w100 = fx (1 - fy) (1 - fz) w010 = (1 - fx) fy (1 - fz) w110 = fx fy (1 - fz) w001 = (1 - fx) (1 - fy) fz w101 = fx (1 - fy) fz w011 = (1 - fx) fy fz w111 = fx fy fz return (w000 v000 + w100 v100 + w010 v010 + w110 v110 + w001 v001 + w101 v101 + w011 v011 + w111 v111) def positionalencoding(x, mindeg=0, maxdeg=10): """ Standard NeRF positional encoding: [sin(2^k pi x), cos(2^k pi x)].""" scales = [2 i for i in range(mindeg, maxdeg)] scaledx = np.outer(x, np.array(scales) np.pi) return np.concatenate([np.sin(scaledx), np.cos(scaledx)], axis=-1) def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, near, far, densitygrid, featuregrid, mlp, b, nsamples, cbg): """Renders a single ray using DVGO.""" tvals = np.linspace(near, far, nsamples) points = rayorigin + tvals[:, np.newaxis] raydirection delta = (far - near) / (nsamples - 1) if nsamples > 1 else (far - near) accumulatedcolor = np.zeros(3) accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 for i in range(nsamples): x, y, z = points[i] rawdensity = trilinearinterpolate(densitygrid, x, y, z) sigma = softplus(rawdensity, b) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma delta) colorfeatures = trilinearinterpolate(featuregrid, x, y, z) posenc = positionalencoding(points[i], mindeg=0, maxdeg=10) direnc = positionalencoding(raydirection, mindeg=0, maxdeg=4) mlpinput = np.concatenate([colorfeatures, posenc, direnc]) coloremission = mlp(mlpinput) weight = accumulatedtransmittance alpha accumulatedcolor += weight coloremission accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) accumulatedcolor += accumulatedtransmittance cbg return accumulatedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Post-Activation Sharpness: Applying non-linear activation functions (like softplus) after trilinear interpolation produces sharper surfaces than pre-activation, allowing fewer grid cells for surface detail. Boundary Conditions: Coordinates must be clamped to the grid bounds before interpolation to prevent out-of-bounds indexing. Precision: The exponential function in \alphai and Ti can underflow or overflow if \sigmai \deltai is extreme. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Sharp surfaces with fewer cells due to post-activation interpolation. Limitations: Not given in the sources. The method uses a shifted softplus activation from Mip-NeRF to ensure non-negative densities. It demonstrates that post-activation interpolation for density enables sharp surfaces, reducing the need for high-resolution grids. NeRF Synthesis with Shading Guidance, https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-99-9666-716, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Tetrahedral Ray Marching
head: Differentiable rendering in a tetrahedral mesh
body: Tetrahedral Ray Marching is a ray traversal and integration method for non-uniform tetrahedral grids that efficiently identifies entry and exit points of viewing rays within a 3D mesh. It solves the problem of sparse or irregular volumetric sampling by projecting vertices to determine exit faces and including camera centers in the mesh to simplify entry point identification. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering by using a tetrahedral topology with explicit geometric traversal rather than a uniform voxel grid, and from DVGO Density and Color Rendering by relying on explicit mesh connectivity and Signed Distance Field (SDF) interpolation rather than implicit neural density fields on a grid. Inputs: Camera center o and ray direction v. Tetrahedral mesh where each tetrahedron has 4 vertices. SDF values sdf(vi) at each vertex vi. Color networks g{geo} and g{fine}. Outputs: A list of visited tetrahedra with their entry points in(t) and exit points out(t) for each ray. Data Structures: Tetrahedral Mesh: Defined by vertices and connectivity. The mesh includes "virtual" tetrahedra or markers containing camera centers to facilitate entry detection. Segment List: For each ray, a list of segments s(t) = [in(t), out(t)] where t \in [0, n]. Steps: 1. Entry Point Identification: Determine the tetrahedron containing the camera center o. This tetrahedron provides the initial entry point for the ray. 2. Ray Traversal Loop: While the ray has not exited the mesh and the segment count is below the maximum: a. Find Exit Face: i. Project all four vertices of the current tetrahedron onto a plane centered at the camera center o with normal vector v. ii. Identify the exit face as the face that contains the origin (the projection of o) in this projected coordinate system, excluding the entry face. b. Identify Next Tetrahedron: Determine the tetrahedron sharing the identified exit face. c. Pruning: If the current tetrahedron exhibits null contribution (e.g., empty space), skip it. d. Segment Definition: Define the segment s(t) from the current entry point in(t) to the exit point out(t). 3. Sampling and Feature Extraction: a. Sample the midpoint p(t) = \frac{in(t) + out(t)}{2}. b. Query color networks g{geo} and g{fine} at p(t) to obtain color estimates. c. Compute SDF values at in(t) and out(t) by linearly interpolating the SDF values of the three vertices of the respective entry and exit faces. d. Compute normal vectors at in(t) and out(t) by interpolating vertex normals (or derived from SDF gradients). 4. Transmittance and Color Accumulation: a. Compute transmittance \alphat using the SDF values and a scale factor \beta: \alphat = \text{clip}\left( \frac{1 + e^{-\beta \cdot sdf(in(t))}}{1 + e^{-\beta \cdot sdf(out(t))}}, 0, 1 \right) where sdf(in(t)) is the SDF at the entry point and sdf(out(t)) is the SDF at the exit point. b. Accumulate color using the standard volume rendering equation with weights \omega(t) = \alpha(t)T(t). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tetrahedralraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, mesh, sdfvalues, colornetworks, beta, maxsegments=1024): # 1. Find initial tetrahedron containing rayorigin currenttet = findtetrahedroncontainingpoint(mesh, rayorigin) visitedsegments = [] for t in range(maxsegments): if currenttet is None: break # 2. Find exit face # Project vertices of currenttet onto plane at rayorigin with normal raydirection projectedvertices = [] for vertex in currenttet.vertices: # Vector from origin to vertex vec = vertex - rayorigin # Project onto plane: p = v - (v. n) n proj = vec - dot(vec, raydirection) raydirection projectedvertices.append(proj) # Identify exit face: the face containing the origin (0,0) in projected coords # Exclude the entry face (the face containing the previous entry point) exitface = findfacecontainingorigin(projectedvertices, currenttet.faces) if exitface is None: break # Ray exited mesh # 3. Define segment entrypoint = currenttet.entrypoint if t == 0 else visitedsegments[-1].exitpoint exitpoint = interpolatefacesdf(exitface, sdfvalues) # Linear interp of 3 vertices # Pruning check (simplified) if isnullcontribution(currenttet): currenttet = getnexttetrahedron(currenttet, exitface) continue # 4. Sample and Compute Features midpoint = (entrypoint + exitpoint) / 2.0 # Query color networks cgeo = colornetworks'geo' cfine = colornetworks'fine' # Compute SDF at entry and exit sdfin = interpolatefacesdf(currenttet.faces[entryfaceindex], sdfvalues) sdfout = interpolatefacesdf(exitface, sdfvalues) # Compute normals (simplified: assume precomputed or derived from SDF) nin = computenormal(entrypoint, currenttet) nout = computenormal(exitpoint, exitface) # 5. Compute Transmittance # alphat = clip((1 + exp(-beta sdfin)) / (1 + exp(-beta sdfout)), 0, 1) expin = exp(-beta sdfin) expout = exp(-beta sdfout) alphat = min(max((1 + expin) / (1 + expout), 0.0), 1.0) visitedsegments.append({ 'entry': entrypoint, 'exit': exitpoint, 'mid': midpoint, 'alpha': alphat, 'cgeo': cgeo, 'cfine': cfine, 'sdfin': sdfin, 'sdfout': sdfout }) # Move to next tetrahedron currenttet = getnexttetrahedron(currenttet, exitface) return visitedsegments Parameters: \beta: Scale factor for SDF-based transmittance, gradually increased during optimization. \lambda: Weight factor for loss function, 1 at coarse stage, 0.5 later. \epsilon: Small value for loss function stability, 0.1. Max segments per ray: 1024. Pitfalls: When \beta is large, long segments crossing the surface may generate too small gradients due to large SDF differences; these segments should be subdivided. Precision issues in projecting vertices to the plane if the ray direction is not normalized or if the camera center is far from the mesh. Ensures smooth gradients in the discrete SDF field by solving a linear system for spatial gradients within each tetrahedron. Uses Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation to optimize site locations for regular tetrahedral discretization. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of tetrahedra intersected by the ray. With pruning, it avoids empty space. Max segments limit caps complexity. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of vertices and tetrahedra in the mesh, plus storage for SDF values and network parameters. Strengths: Efficient for non-uniform meshes; explicit geometric traversal allows for precise surface representation via SDF. Limitations: Requires complex traversal logic compared to voxel grids; sensitive to \beta scaling. When to use: When rendering differentiable 3D models with explicit surface geometry represented by tetrahedral meshes. Originating from the "VortSDF" method presented at WACV 2025, this technique adapts ray marching for non-uniform tetrahedral grids generated via Centroidal Voronoi Tessellation (CVT). It builds on earlier tetrahedral structures proposed for fast ray marching. name: DOSRender
head: DOS Renderer, Depth of Field Scattering, Depth-Ordered Slice Renderer, Direct Volume Rendering with Occlusion and Instance Tracking, Occlusion-Aware Slice Accumulator [S1, unofficial]
body: DOSRender is a depth-ordered, slice-based volume rendering technique that accumulates color and occlusion along a ray while simultaneously tracking semantic instance and group IDs for segmentation. It distinguishes itself from standard front-to-back ray casting by integrating precomputed occlusion samples and hierarchical group membership buffers directly into the accumulation pass, allowing for efficient occlusion-aware rendering and semantic data extraction in a single pass. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: uMvpInverseMatrix: Inverse Model-View-Projection matrix for unprojecting screen coordinates. uDepth: Current depth value for the ray. uInstanceID, uGroupID: Textures storing instance and group IDs at 2D screen positions. uIDVolume: 3D texture mapping 3D positions to instance IDs. sGroupMembership: std430 buffer mapping instance IDs to group IDs. uAccumulator: Texture storing the accumulated color, occlusion, instance ID, and group ID from previous slices. uOcclusion: Texture containing precomputed occlusion samples. uOcclusionScale: Scale factor for occlusion sample offsets. uOcclusionSamplesCount: Number of occlusion samples to average. uExtinction: Uniform float controlling the extinction coefficient multiplier. uSliceDistance: Uniform float representing the distance between slices. uColorBias, uAlphaBias, uAlphaTransfer: Parameters for transfer function biasing. Volume Color Data: Mask/data volumes and transfer functions used to sample transferSample. Outputs (Fragment Shader): oColor: vec4 containing the accumulated color and alpha. oOcclusion: float representing the remaining occlusion/transmittance. oInstanceID: uint for the current instance ID. oGroupID: uint for the current group ID. vPosition: vec2 vertex shader output representing screen position. Data Structures bGroupMembership: A std430 storage buffer (binding 0) containing uint sGroupMembership[], which maps instance IDs to group IDs. oAccColorVolume: An rgba8 image3D (binding 1), write-only, used for accumulating color across slices. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization (Reset Pass): Reset outputs to initial values: oColor = vec4(0), oOcclusion = 1.0, oInstanceID = 0u, oGroupID = 0u. 2. Unprojection: Unproject the screen position aPosition (from vertex shader) and depth uDepth to 3D world space: vPosition3D = \frac{(uMvpInverseMatrix \times vec4(aPosition, uDepth, 1)).xyz}{w} where w is the w-component of the resulting vector. 3. Boundary Check: If any component of vPosition3D is outside the [0, 1] range, output the previous color, occlusion, instance ID, and group ID (from the accumulator or previous step) and terminate the shader execution. 4. Semantic ID Resolution: Retrieve the current instance and group IDs from 2D position textures using the screen position vPosition: glsl uint instanceID = texture(uInstanceID, vPosition).r; uint groupID = texture(uGroupID, vPosition).r; If groupID is 0 (indicating an unassigned instance): 1. Fetch a new instance ID from uIDVolume at vPosition3D. 2. Look up the new group ID from sGroupMembership using the fetched instance ID. 3. If the new group ID is non-zero, update oInstanceID and oGroupID with these new values; otherwise, retain the old IDs. 5. Volume Sampling: Sample the volume color at vPosition3D using mask/data volumes and transfer functions, applying biases: glsl vec4 transferSample = sampleVolumeColor(vPosition3D); The sampling incorporates uColorBias, uAlphaBias, and uAlphaTransfer. 6. Accumulator Retrieval: Sample the accumulator texture at the current screen position to get previous state: glsl vec4 color = texture(uAccumulator, vPosition); Let prevColor be this value. 7. Extinction and Alpha Calculation: Calculate extinction: extinction = transferSample.a \times uExtinction Calculate alpha (opacity) for the current slice: \alpha = 1.0 - \exp(-extinction \times uSliceDistance) Here, uExtinction acts as the total extinction coefficient \sigmat. 8. Occlusion Calculation: Compute occlusion attenuation by averaging precomputed occlusion samples. The samples are taken at offsets from vPosition: O = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ci \cdot e^{-\sigmat \cdot d} where Ci are the occlusion samples, \sigmat is the extinction, d is the slice distance (uSliceDistance), and N is the number of samples (uOcclusionSamplesCount). The samples are located at vPosition + occlusionSampleOffset uOcclusionScale. Update oOcclusion using this calculated value. 9. Color Blending: Calculate the color contribution: color = transferSample.rgb \times prevOcclusion \times \alpha where prevOcclusion is prevColor.a (or the stored occlusion value). Update the output color: oColor = prevColor + vec4(color \times (1.0 - prevColor.a), \alpha) Clamp the alpha component: oColor.a = \min(oColor.a, 1.0) Finally, mix the accumulated color with a white background: oColor = mix(vec4(1), vec4(color.rgb, 1), color.a). 10. Output: Write oColor, oOcclusion, oInstanceID, and oGroupID to the frame buffer or accumulator texture. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dosrenderfragment(aPosition, uDepth, uMvpInverseMatrix, vPosition, uInstanceID, uGroupID, uIDVolume, sGroupMembership, uAccumulator, uOcclusion, uOcclusionScale, uOcclusionSamplesCount, uExtinction, uSliceDistance, volumedata, transferfunction, occlusionSampleOffsets): # 1. Unproject clippos = vec4(aPosition.x, aPosition.y, uDepth, 1.0) worldposvec = mat4mulvec4(uMvpInverseMatrix, clippos) w = worldposvec.w if w == 0.0: return vec4(0.0), 1.0, 0, 0 # Fallback vPosition3D = vec3(worldposvec.x / w, worldposvec.y / w, worldposvec.z / w) # 2. Boundary Check if not (0.0 <= vPosition3D.x <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= vPosition3D.y <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= vPosition3D.z <= 1.0): prevacc = texture2d(uAccumulator, vPosition) return prevacc.rgb, prevacc.a, prevacc.b, prevacc.c # Assuming accumulator layout matches outputs # 3. Semantic ID Resolution instanceID = texture2d(uInstanceID, vPosition).r groupID = texture2d(uGroupID, vPosition).r if groupID == 0: newinstanceID = texture3d(uIDVolume, vPosition3D).r newgroupID = sGroupMembership[newinstanceID] if newgroupID != 0: instanceID = newinstanceID groupID = newgroupID # 4. Volume Sampling # Standard volume texture lookup with transfer function application transferSample = samplevolumecolor(vPosition3D, volumedata, transferfunction) # 5. Retrieve Accumulator prevColor = texture2d(uAccumulator, vPosition) prevOcclusion = prevColor.a # Assuming alpha channel stores previous occlusion/transmittance # 6. Extinction and Alpha extinction = transferSample.a uExtinction alpha = 1.0 - exp(-extinction uSliceDistance) # 7. Occlusion Calculation occlusionsum = 0.0 for i in range(uOcclusionSamplesCount): # Standard offset calculation for precomputed samples offset = occlusionSampleOffsets[i] uOcclusionScale samplepos = vPosition + offset Ci = texture2d(uOcclusion, samplepos).r occlusionsum += Ci exp(-extinction uSliceDistance) currentocclusion = occlusionsum / uOcclusionSamplesCount # 8. Color Blending colorcontribution = transferSample.rgb prevOcclusion alpha # Update color newcolor = prevColor + vec4(colorcontribution (1.0 - prevColor.a), alpha) newcolor.a = min(newcolor.a, 1.0) # Mix with white background finalcolor = mix(vec4(1.0), vec4(newcolor.rgb, 1.0), newcolor.a) # 9. Output return finalcolor, currentocclusion, instanceID, groupID Parameters steps: Number of scattering steps or depth levels. slices: Number of slices used in the rendering process. extinction: Extinction coefficient controlling light absorption/scattering intensity. aperture: Aperture size, likely controlling depth of field blur or scattering spread. samples: Number of samples used for occlusion or scattering calculations. cutDepth: Depth cutoff value, likely for clipping or limiting scattering depth. showBoundingBox: Boolean flag to render a bounding box. showAxes: Boolean flag to render coordinate axes. boundingBoxColor: RGB color array for the bounding box. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Group ID 0: A group ID of 0 indicates an unassigned instance. The shader explicitly checks for this and remaps it using the sGroupMembership buffer to prevent rendering artifacts from uninitialized group data. Out of Bounds: If the 3D position is outside the [0,1] range, the shader must correctly output the previous accumulated state to avoid discarding valid data or introducing black artifacts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Integrates semantic segmentation (instance/group IDs) directly into the volume rendering pass, reducing the need for separate post-processing passes. Limitations: Relies on precomputed occlusion samples, which may limit dynamic occlusion scenarios. The requirement for std430 buffers and specific texture layouts may increase implementation complexity on some hardware. When to use: When semantic segmentation is required alongside volume visualization, or when occlusion-aware depth ordering is critical and can be approximated by precomputed samples. When not to use: For scenes with highly dynamic occlusion that cannot be precomputed, or when hardware does not support std430 buffers efficiently. DOSRender is described in the context of the vpt-conductor project, an unofficial implementation or toolset related to volume rendering and visualization. The technique appears to be a specialized variant of direct volume ray casting, adapted for semantic segmentation tasks by tracking instance and group IDs. UL-FRI-LGM/vpt-conductor, https://github.com/UL-FRI-LGM/vpt-conductor, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Light Transmittance Marching
head: Light Marching, Light Transmissance March, Nested Light Ray Sampling, Nested Raymarching for Light Sampling, Secondary light march, Shadow Raymarching in Volume
body: Light Transmittance Marching is a technique to compute physically accurate lighting in a volume by casting a secondary raymarch from each sample point on the primary view ray towards the light source to calculate absorbed light (transmittance). It solves the problem of volumetric occlusion, where light passing through the volume before reaching a sample point is attenuated by the medium itself. Unlike Front-to-Back Volume Rendering, which typically assumes uniform or pre-computed lighting, this method dynamically computes the light energy arriving at each sample point by accounting for the density along the path to the light. Inputs: rayOrigin: The camera position. rayDirection: The normalized direction of the primary view ray. lightDirection: The normalized direction vector from the scene to the light source (e.g., the sun). scene(pos, isLightSample): A function that returns the density at position pos. The boolean flag distinguishes between primary ray sampling and light sampling, allowing for different density evaluation strategies or optimizations. MAXSTEPS: The number of steps in the primary raymarch loop. MAXSTEPSLIGHTS: The number of steps in the nested light sampling loop. MARCHSIZE: The step size for the primary raymarch. marchSize (or stepSize): The step size for the nested light sampling loop. ABSORPTIONCOEFFICIENT: The coefficient used in Beer's Law for light absorption. Outputs: lightEnergy: The accumulated luminance for the pixel, incorporating the attenuated light contribution from each sample point along the primary ray. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required beyond standard scalar variables for position, density, and accumulated energy. The method relies on iterative sampling of the scene function. Parameters: MAXSTEPSLIGHTS: Set to 6 to preserve frame-rate. ABSORPTIONCOEFFICIENT: Set to 0.9. marchSize (light step): Set to 0.03. MAXSTEPS: Set to 50. MARCHSIZE (primary step): Set to 0.16. Steps: 1. Initialize the primary raymarch loop. For each step i from 0 to MAXSTEPS - 1: a. Calculate the current position p along the primary ray: p = rayOrigin + depth \cdot rayDirection where depth accumulates MARCHSIZE at each step in the primary loop. b. Sample the density at p using the primary scene function: density = scene(p, false). c. If density > 0.0: i. Initiate a nested light sampling loop to calculate light transmittance. ii. Initialize totalDensity = 0.0 and position = p. iii. For each step j from 0 to MAXSTEPSLIGHTS - 1: 1. Advance the position along the light direction: position = position + lightDirection \cdot marchSize \cdot j. 2. Sample the density at the new position using the light-specific scene function: lightSample = scene(position, true). 3. Accumulate the density: totalDensity = totalDensity + lightSample. Note: An alternative implementation accumulates density weighted by step size: totalDensity += density stepSize where stepSize = MAXLIGHTDISTANCE / NUMLIGHTSTEPS. iv. Calculate the light transmittance using Beer's Law: transmittance = e^{-ABSORPTION\COEFFICIENT \cdot totalDensity}. Note: Some implementations use exp(-totalDensity) directly if the absorption coefficient is incorporated into the density or step size. v. Multiply the primary ray's accumulated transmittance by the light transmittance: totalTransmittance = totalTransmittance \cdot transmittance. vi. Calculate the luminance contribution: luminance = density. vii. Add to the total light energy: lightEnergy = lightEnergy + totalTransmittance \cdot luminance. d. Advance the primary ray depth: depth = depth + MARCHSIZE. 2. Return lightEnergy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def lighttransmittancemarch(rayorigin, raydirection, lightdirection, scenefunc, maxsteps=50, maxstepslights=6, marchsize=0.16, lightmarchsize=0.03, absorptioncoefficient=0.9): """ Computes light energy for a single ray using nested light transmittance marching. Args: rayorigin: vec3, camera position. raydirection: vec3, normalized view ray direction. lightdirection: vec3, normalized direction to the light source. scenefunc: function(pos, islightsample) -> float, returns density. maxsteps: int, number of steps in primary raymarch. maxstepslights: int, number of steps in nested light march. marchsize: float, step size for primary raymarch. lightmarchsize: float, step size for light march. absorptioncoefficient: float, Beer's law coefficient. Returns: float, accumulated light energy. """ lightenergy = 0.0 totaltransmittance = 1.0 depth = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): p = rayorigin + depth raydirection density = scenefunc(p, False) if density > 0.0: totaldensitylight = 0.0 lightpos = p for j in range(maxstepslights): lightpos = lightpos + lightdirection lightmarchsize j lightsample = scenefunc(lightpos, True) totaldensitylight += lightsample transmittance = math.exp(-absorptioncoefficient totaldensitylight) totaltransmittance = transmittance luminance = density lightenergy += totaltransmittance luminance depth += marchsize return lightenergy Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: The nested loop significantly increases algorithmic complexity. To maintain frame-rate, MAXSTEPSLIGHTS must be kept low (e.g., 6). This may require reducing the precision of the primary raymarch (e.g., reducing FBM octaves). Precision: Using a small marchSize for the light march (0.03) helps accuracy but increases the number of samples if MAXSTEPSLIGHTS is not adjusted. Boundary Conditions: The light march assumes the light source is at infinity or the direction is constant. If the light source is point-based and close, the direction lightDirection should be recalculated for each sample point, which is not covered in the basic implementation. Time Complexity: The algorithmic complexity increases due to the nested loop, requiring trade-offs like reducing primary steps or FBM octaves to preserve frame-rate. Memory Complexity: Auxiliary space is O(1), using only scalar variables for accumulation. Measured Performance: With MAXSTEPS=50 and MAXSTEPSLIGHTS=6, the method is feasible for real-time rendering on modern GPUs, provided the scene function is efficient. Strengths: Physically accurate lighting attenuation within the volume; simple to implement as a nested loop. Limitations: High computational cost due to nested sampling; assumes uniform light direction (directional light); does not account for scattering within the volume, only absorption. When to Use: When directional lighting and volumetric occlusion are required for real-time applications, and performance constraints allow for nested sampling. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Light Transmittance Marching was introduced in the context of real-time volumetric cloud rendering to address the lack of proper lighting models in early raymarching demos. It builds on the concept of Beer's Law for light absorption in participating media. name: Light-space transmittance volumes
head: Light-space transmittance, Transmittance volumes
body: Light-space transmittance volumes are a technique for computing light attenuation in participating media by pre-calculating optical depth from light sources into a 3D grid, allowing receivers to look up transmittance via interpolation. It is the volume rendering equivalent of deep shadow maps for participating media, shifting the computational burden from per-receiver ray marching to a single per-cluster grid construction. Inputs and Outputs Input: An absorbance field (voxel grid defining extinction coefficients), a set of emitter clusters (groups of light facets or the entire light source for distant receivers), and a receiver position. Output: The optical depth \tau from the emitter cluster to the receiver position, derived from the transmittance volume. Data Structures The transmittance volume is a 3D grid indexed by spatial position. For each emitter cluster, a separate grid of optical depth values is stored. The grid resolution is typically coarse relative to the scene scale (e.g., 12 \times 12 \times 16) to manage memory. The volume is implemented as a differentiable function (e.g., in JAX) of the absorbance field to ensure exact gradient computation dG/d(\text{absorbance}). Steps 1. Cluster Emission: Group light source facets into clusters. A distant receiver may treat the entire lamp as one cluster, while closer receivers may require finer clustering. 2. March and Store: For each emitter cluster, march outward through the absorbance grid from the cluster's representative origin point. Calculate the accumulated optical depth to every sample point in the grid and store these values in the cluster's transmittance volume. 3. Lookup: For a receiver at position \mathbf{p}, identify the relevant emitter cluster. Retrieve the optical depth \tau by performing trilinear interpolation on the corresponding transmittance volume at \mathbf{p}. 4. Attenuation: Compute transmittance T = e^{-\tau} for shading calculations. Formulas Optical Depth: \tau(\mathbf{p}) = \int{\mathbf{o}}^{\mathbf{p}} \sigmat(\mathbf{r}) \, d\mathbf{r}, where \mathbf{o} is the cluster origin and \sigmat is the extinction coefficient. Transmittance: T = e^{-\tau}. Parameters Grid Resolution: Coarse grids are used to limit memory (e.g., 12 \times 12 \times 16). Cluster Count: The method depends on clustering; tens of clusters are feasible, but one volume per facet is not. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Near-Field Inaccuracy: The method is an approximation twice over: it uses a single representative point for the cluster origin and interpolates \tau between samples. \tau is smooth with respect to receiver position for a fixed origin but not near the origin itself. Therefore, the near field should retain the exact ray walk. Memory Cost: Storage requires one grid of optical depths per cluster. This is efficient for tens of clusters on a coarse grid but prohibitive for one volume per facet. Clustering Dependency: Without emitter clusters, creating one volume per facet costs more than the ray walk it replaces. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computetransmittancevolume(absorbancegrid, clusterorigin, gridresolution, voxelsize): """ March from clusterorigin through absorbancegrid to fill a transmittance volume. Returns a 3D array of optical depths. """ volume = [[[0.0 for in range(gridresolution[2])] for in range(gridresolution[1])] for in range(gridresolution[0])] for i in range(gridresolution[0]): for j in range(gridresolution[1]): for k in range(gridresolution[2]): voxelpos = [ clusterorigin[0] + i voxelsize[0], clusterorigin[1] + j voxelsize[1], clusterorigin[2] + k voxelsize[2] ] # Integrate absorbance along the ray from clusterorigin to voxelpos opticaldepth = 0.0 steps = 10 for s in range(steps): t = s / steps pointonray = [ clusterorigin[d] + t (voxelpos[d] - clusterorigin[d]) for d in range(3) ] # Sample absorbance at pointonray (e.g., trilinear interpolation into absorbancegrid) sigmat = 1.0 opticaldepth += sigmat math.sqrt(sum((voxelpos[d] - clusterorigin[d])2 for d in range(3))) / steps volume[i][j][k] = opticaldepth return volume def gettransmittance(receiverpos, clustervolume, voxelsize): """ Look up optical depth from the pre-computed volume using trilinear interpolation. """ voxelpos = [ (receiverpos[d] - clustervolume.origin[d]) / voxelsize[d] for d in range(3) ] # Near-field check: if distance to origin is below a threshold, use exact ray march instead of interpolation dist = math.sqrt(sum((receiverpos[d] - clustervolume.origin[d])2 for d in range(3))) if dist < clustervolume.nearfieldthreshold: # Exact ray march implementation omitted per sources return 0.0 # Trilinear interpolation of optical depth from volume data i, j, k = int(voxelpos[0]), int(voxelpos[1]), int(voxelpos[2]) fx, fy, fz = voxelpos[0] - i, voxelpos[1] - j, voxelpos[2] - k v000 = clustervolume.data[i][j][k] v100 = clustervolume.data[i+1][j][k] v010 = clustervolume.data[i][j+1][k] v110 = clustervolume.data[i+1][j+1][k] v001 = clustervolume.data[i][j][k+1] v101 = clustervolume.data[i+1][j][k+1] v011 = clustervolume.data[i][j+1][k+1] v111 = clustervolume.data[i+1][j+1][k+1] tau = (1-fx)(1-fy)(1-fz)v000 + fx(1-fy)(1-fz)v100 + (1-fx)fy(1-fz)v010 + fxfy(1-fz)v110 + \ (1-fx)(1-fy)fzv001 + fx(1-fy)fzv101 + (1-fx)fyfzv011 + fxfyfzv111 return math.exp(-tau) Time Complexity: Construction is O(N{clusters} \times N{voxels}). Lookup is O(1) per receiver via interpolation, compared to O(N{steps}) for the exact walk. Memory Complexity: O(N{clusters} \times N{voxels}) for storing optical depth grids. Performance: On a 4,096-facet lamp, 3,954 receivers, and a 12 \times 12 \times 16 grid, the graded per-call field took ~19-21 s, while uniform absorption took ~0.4 s. The exact walk cost was significantly higher, scaling with N{receivers} \times N{facets} \times (nx + ny + nz). Strengths: Eliminates per-receiver ray marching for transmittance; supports exact gradients via differentiable programming. Limitations: High memory usage for many clusters; inaccurate in the near field; requires clustering. When to Use: When the number of receivers is large and the light source can be effectively clustered; when gradients are needed. When Not to Use: When the light source has many facets requiring individual volumes; in the near field of the light. The technique is based on the concept of shadow maps (Williams 1978) and deep shadow maps (Lokovic & Veach, SIGGRAPH 2000), which compute transmittance from the light's side once into a structure indexed by position. It adapts this idea to 3D volumes for participating media. Radiation: light-space transmittance volumes for a graded medium, so each pair stops walking the absorbance grid (conditional), https://github.com/DeGrootResearchGroup/aquaflux/issues/569, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Casting with Slice-Based Sampling and Gradient Shading
head: Ray Casting (Gradient Shading Variant), psTrace
body: This method performs direct volume ray casting by sampling a 3D volume stored in a 2D texture atlas, computing surface normals via finite differences of sampled densities, and applying diffuse shading. It stops sampling when a high-density threshold is reached or the ray exits the bounding box. It is distinguished from standard ray marching by its specific use of a 2D texture atlas for 3D data storage and the explicit calculation of gradients for lighting, rather than relying solely on transmittance accumulation or pre-computed normals. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D texture (volume) containing a 256x256x256 volume packed into a 16x16 grid of 16x16 slices. Camera parameters (eye position, view direction matrix). Light position (lightPos) and color (lightcolor). Output: A fragment color (glFragColor) representing the rendered pixel. Data Structures: Volume Texture: A sampler2D representing a 256x256x256 volume. The volume is packed into a 16x16 grid of slices. Each slice is 256x256 texels. Ray Parameters: tmin and tmax defining the intersection interval with the bounding box. Parameters: dt: Step size for ray marching. Value: 0.008. densitythreshold: The red channel value threshold to stop ray marching. Value: 0.3. lightPos: Position of the light source. Value: vec3(4,4,4). lightcolor: Color of the light. Value: vec3(1,1,1). boxPoint1: Lower bound of the volume bounding box. Value: vec3(0,0,3). boxPoint2: Upper bound of the volume bounding box. Value: vec3(1,1,4). Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray-Box Intersection: Calculate the intersection parameters tmin and tmax for the ray against the bounding box defined by boxPoint1 and boxPoint2 using a function intersectParams(boxPoint1, boxPoint2, eye, dir). 2. Initialization: Initialize the ray parameter t to tmin (accessed as t1t2.x) and the accumulated color color to vec3(0,0,0). 3. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to 1499 (1500 iterations): a. Ray Position: Calculate the current 3D point point as eye + t dir. b. Gradient Sampling: Sample the density at point and its neighbors (point +/- dt in x, y, z) using the sliceSample function. sliceSample performs linear interpolation between two slices (slice1 and slice2) based on the normalized depth rate. Let dx1 be the sample at x + dt, dx2 at x - dt, dy1 at y + dt, dy2 at y - dt, dz1 at z + dt, and dz2 at z - dt. c. Normal Calculation: Compute the surface normal using finite differences: \text{normal} = \text{normalize}(\text{vec3}(dx1.x - dx2.x, dy1.y - dy2.y, dz1.z - dz2.z)) d. Diffuse Shading: Calculate the diffuse contribution: \text{cosalpha} = \text{clamp}(\text{dot}(\text{normal}, \text{lightDir}), 0.0, 1.0) \text{lightDir} = \text{normalize}(\text{lightPos} - \text{point.xyz}) \text{color} = \text{sample} \times \text{cosalpha} \times \text{lightcolor} e. Termination Check: If the sampled density's red channel sample.r is greater than densitythreshold (0.3) OR t exceeds tmax (t1t2.y), break the loop. f. Advance Ray: Increment t by dt. 4. Output: If tmin (t1t2.x) is greater than 0.0, output glFragColor = vec4(color.xyz, 1.0). Otherwise, output vec4(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastslicegradient(eye, dir, volumetexture, lightpos, lightcolor): # 1. Ray-Box Intersection # Bounding box defined by boxPoint1=(0,0,3) and boxPoint2=(1,1,4) tmin, tmax = intersectparams(vec3(0,0,3), vec3(1,1,4), eye, dir) # Pitfall: If ray does not intersect box, intersectparams returns (-1, -1) if tmin <= 0.0: return vec4(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0) # 2. Initialization t = tmin color = vec3(0, 0, 0) # Parameters dt = 0.008 densitythreshold = 0.3 # 3. Ray Marching Loop for i in range(1500): # Calculate point point = eye + t dir # Sample density and neighbors for gradient # sliceSample performs linear interpolation between slices based on rate # We need samples at point and point +/- dt in x, y, z dx1 = slicesample(volumetexture, point + vec3(dt, 0, 0)) dx2 = slicesample(volumetexture, point - vec3(dt, 0, 0)) dy1 = slicesample(volumetexture, point + vec3(0, dt, 0)) dy2 = slicesample(volumetexture, point - vec3(0, dt, 0)) dz1 = slicesample(volumetexture, point + vec3(0, 0, dt)) dz2 = slicesample(volumetexture, point - vec3(0, 0, dt)) # Current sample for shading sample = slicesample(volumetexture, point) # Normal calculation normal = normalize(vec3(dx1.x - dx2.x, dy1.y - dy2.y, dz1.z - dz2.z)) # Diffuse shading lightdir = normalize(lightpos - point) cosalpha = clamp(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0, 1.0) color = sample cosalpha lightcolor # Termination check if sample.r > densitythreshold or t > tmax: break # Advance ray t += dt return vec4(color, 1.0) def slicesample(texture, point): # Calculate texture coordinates for the 2D texture atlas # Volume is 256x256x256, packed in 16x16 grid of 16x16 slices # point is in [0,1] range relative to box? Or world? # Based on box (0,0,3) to (1,1,4), point needs to be mapped to texture coords. # The source formula: tex256 = vec2(mod(slice,16.0), floor(slice/16.0))/16.0 + point.xy/16.0 # This implies point.xy are used for S,T, and Z determines the slice. # However, standard volume rendering maps 3D point to 3D texture coords. # Given the specific formula in source, we assume point is normalized or mapped appropriately. # Let's assume point is in [0,1] for x,y and z determines slice index. # Extract slice index from Z coordinate # Assuming point.z is in [0, 1] range corresponding to 256 slices slicefloat = point.z 256.0 sliceidx = floor(slicefloat) slicerate = slicefloat - sliceidx # Clamp slice index sliceidx = clamp(sliceidx, 0.0, 255.0) # Calculate 2D texture coordinates # The source formula: tex256 = vec2(mod(slice,16.0), floor(slice/16.0))/16.0 + point.xy/16.0 # This suggests the texture is 256x256, and each "slice" is 16x16 blocks of 16x16 texels? # 256x256 texture. 16x16 grid of slices. Each slice is 16x16 texels? # 1616 = 256. So each slice is 16x16 texels. # Total volume 256x256x256. # Texture size 256x256. # Grid 16x16 slices. # Each slice is 16x16 texels. # Calculate base offset for the slice in the 256x256 texture # Slice index 0..255. # Grid position: (slice % 16, slice / 16) # Each cell in grid is 16x16 texels. # So offset in texture coords (0..1) is: # u = (slice % 16) 16 / 256 = (slice % 16) / 16 # v = (slice / 16) 16 / 256 = (slice / 16) / 16 # The source formula: vec2(mod(slice,16.0), floor(slice/16.0))/16.0 # This gives u,v in [0,1] for the slice block. # Then add point.xy/16.0? # If point.xy are in [0,1], point.xy/16.0 is very small. # This implies point.xy might be in [0,16] range? Or the formula is specific to the implementation. # Let's follow the source formula exactly. slicef = sliceidx ubase = (mod(slicef, 16.0)) / 16.0 vbase = (floor(slicef / 16.0)) / 16.0 # point.xy are assumed to be in [0,1] range? # If point is in [0,1], then point.xy/16.0 is [0, 1/16]. # This would mean the slice is 1/16th of the texture? # 1/16 of 256 is 16. So yes, each slice is 16x16 texels. u = ubase + point.x / 16.0 v = vbase + point.y / 16.0 # Sample texture # Assuming linear filtering return texture2D(volumetexture, vec2(u, v)) Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of ray steps (1500 in the reference implementation). Each step involves 7 texture samples (current point + 6 neighbors) and vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the ray marching state, plus the memory for the volume texture (256x256x256 packed into 256x256 2D texture). Performance: The method is designed for real-time rendering on GPUs using WebGL. The fixed iteration count and simple shading model allow for predictable performance. Strengths: Simple implementation; provides basic surface-like shading via gradient estimation; efficient memory usage via texture atlas packing. Limitations: No transmittance/absorption accumulation; limited to diffuse shading; fixed step size may lead to aliasing or missed features; gradient estimation is noisy and approximate. When to use: Real-time visualization of volumetric data where approximate surface shading is sufficient and performance is critical. When not to use: High-fidelity medical imaging requiring accurate light transport; scenes with complex lighting or transparency effects. This method originates from an unofficial WebGL volume rendering tutorial by tkris007. It demonstrates a practical approach to rendering 3D volumes on the web using fragment shaders and texture atlases. The technique is part of a broader set of direct volume rendering methods that prioritize simplicity and real-time performance over physical accuracy. tkris007/webGL-volume-rendering, https://github.com/tkris007/webGL-volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Sphere-Guided Volume Rendering
head: Sphere-Guided Sampling
body: Sphere-Guided Volume Rendering is a sampling strategy for neural implicit surface reconstruction that uses a trainable cloud of spheres to filter ray-marching samples. It solves the problem of inefficient sample distribution in standard volume rendering, where samples are often wasted in empty space or fail to capture thin geometry. Unlike fixed-step ray marching or methods relying on greedy optimization, this approach guides sampling by intersecting rays with a coarse surface approximation, ensuring samples are concentrated near the estimated surface. This improves sample efficiency and helps the implicit function converge to a better optimum. The method operates by first defining a coarse surface approximation using a set of spheres, then using these spheres to determine valid sampling intervals along a ray. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray p(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{v} (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{v}), a sphere cloud S = \{Si\}, and a target total sample count n. Output: A set of proposal points T along the ray. Data Structures: Sphere Cloud (S): A set of spheres Si, each defined by center \mathbf{c}i and radius ri, optimized via gradient descent. Intervals (I): A set of disjoint 1D intervals [sk, tk] representing the portions of the ray intersecting the sphere cloud. Points (T0, T): Sets of sample positions along the ray. Formulas: The probability of a ray terminating at point p(t) is defined as: w(t) = T(t) \sigma(t) where the transmittance is: T(t) = \exp \left( - \int0^t \sigma(s) ds \right) The observed color C(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v}) is approximated by the discretized volume rendering integral: \hat{C}(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the accumulated transmittance, and \alphai is the opacity at point pi, estimated from the density function \sigma: \alphai = 1 - \exp \left( - \int{ti}^{t{i+1}} \sigma(t) dt \right) Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize an empty set of intervals I = \emptyset. 2. For each sphere Si in the sphere cloud S: Compute the intersection of the ray p(t) with sphere Si. Add the resulting interval to I: I:= I \cup (Si \cap p(t)). 3. Find the minimal set of disjoint intervals [sk, tk] such that the union of these intervals equals I. 4. Initialize an empty set of points T0 = \emptyset. 5. For each interval k from 1 to K (where K is the number of disjoint intervals): Calculate the number of samples for this interval: nk = \lfloor n / (tk - sk) \rfloor. Generate uniformly spaced points between sk and tk and add them to T0: T0:= T0 \cup \text{linspace}(sk, tk, nk). 6. Obtain the final set of proposal points T using T0 and a sampling method of choice (e.g., importance sampling or uncertainty sampling). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def sphereguidedsampling(rayorigin, raydirection, spherecloud, totalsamples): """ rayorigin: 3D vector (o) raydirection: 3D vector (v) spherecloud: List of dicts, each with 'center' (3D vector) and 'radius' (float) totalsamples: Integer n Returns: List of floats (t values along the ray) """ intervals = [] # Step 1 & 2: Compute intersections for sphere in spherecloud: center = sphere['center'] radius = sphere['radius'] oc = [rayorigin[i] - center[i] for i in range(3)] a = dot(raydirection, raydirection) b = 2.0 dot(oc, raydirection) c = dot(oc, oc) - radius radius discriminant = b b - 4 a c if discriminant >= 0: sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 if t2 > 0: start = max(0.0, t1) end = t2 if start < end: intervals.append((start, end)) # Step 3: Merge intervals to find minimal disjoint set if not intervals: return [] intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) mergedintervals = [] currentstart, currentend = intervals[0] for i in range(1, len(intervals)): nextstart, nextend = intervals[i] if nextstart <= currentend: currentend = max(currentend, nextend) else: mergedintervals.append((currentstart, currentend)) currentstart, currentend = nextstart, nextend mergedintervals.append((currentstart, currentend)) # Step 4 & 5: Distribute samples T0 = [] for start, end in mergedintervals: length = end - start if length == 0: continue nk = math.floor(totalsamples / length) if nk < 1: nk = 1 step = (end - start) / (nk - 1) if nk > 1 else 0 for j in range(nk): t = start + j step T0.append(t) # Step 6: Final sampling (e.g. importance sampling) # The source specifies obtaining T using T0 and a sampling method of choice. # We return T0 as the base proposal set. return T0 Parameters: n: The total number of samples to be distributed across the sphere-ray intersections. S: The sphere cloud, acting as a coarse surface approximation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: Spheres may get stuck in local minima during optimization, leading to poor surface approximation. Clumping: Spheres may clump together, reducing the exploration of the surface and leaving regions unsampled. Empty Intersections: If the ray does not intersect any sphere, the interval set is empty, and no samples are generated. Details inherent limitations of sphere-guided training in neural implicit surface reconstruction, specifically regarding exploration capabilities and appearance-geometry coupling. It addresses the problem where early-stage geometric estimates constrain the optimization trajectory, leading to artifacts in uncovered regions or incorrect geometry baking when combined with appearance warping. Unlike standard volume rendering which samples uniformly or via importance sampling based on density, sphere-guided methods rely on a discrete set of primitives that, once converged, may fail to recover thin structures or correct systematic errors. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves sample efficiency by filtering out samples outside the surface region. Allows the implicit function to converge to a better optimum. Uses gradient descent to train the sphere cloud from scratch without prior initialization, unlike greedy optimization methods. Limitations: Spheres may clump or get stuck in local minima. May fail to recover thin structures if the sphere cloud is not sufficiently dense or diverse. When to use: When using base neural reconstruction methods like IDR [37], NeRF [20], or others [5, 23, 32, 36] for surface reconstruction, to improve quality. When not to use: When the surface geometry is extremely thin or complex, and the sphere approximation cannot capture it accurately. Sphere-Guided Volume Rendering was introduced in the paper "Sphere-Guided Training of Neural Implicit Surfaces". It addresses the limitations of previous methods that used greedy optimization (e.g., Neural Sparse Voxel Fields [17]) or sparse point-cloud initialization (e.g., Neural 3D Reconstruction in the Wild [31]). The method uses gradient descent to train the sphere cloud from scratch, allowing it to be trained alongside the implicit surface field. It is used in conjunction with modern systems for surface reconstruction to observe uniform improvements in quality across multiple 3D reconstruction benchmarks. name: Sphere-Guided Training Limitations
body: Sphere-guided training in neural implicit surface reconstruction exhibits three primary limitations: constrained exploration after initial convergence, amplification of systematic artifacts, and incorrect appearance-geometry coupling when combined with warping methods. These limitations arise because the method relies on a coarse geometry estimate established early in training, which dictates the sampling distribution and prevents recovery of uncovered regions or correction of initial errors. The limitations stem from the fundamental mechanism of sphere-guided ray marching: 1. Ray-Sphere Intersection Filtering: Rays are only integrated if they intersect the current sphere cloud; rays missing the cloud are skipped entirely. 2. Sampling Bias: The probability of sampling a region is proportional to the density of spheres in that region, causing heavier sampling in regions with many spheres and zero sampling in uncovered regions. 3. Early Convergence Dependency: The sphere cloud is optimized jointly with the neural network, meaning the coarse geometry estimated in early training iterations defines the initial sphere distribution and heavily influences the subsequent optimization path. Sphere-guided methods suffer from limited exploration capabilities after the initial convergence phase. Because rays that do not intersect the sphere cloud are skipped, the method cannot recover uncovered regions such as thin stems after initial convergence. This results in incomplete reconstruction of thin features that were not well-represented in the early training stages. Systematic artifacts present in the initial geometry estimate are not corrected by the sphere guidance mechanism and may be amplified during optimization. When combined with appearance warping methods like NeuralWarp, appearance variations on object bases can be incorrectly baked into the surface geometry. This artifact may be magnified by the sphere guidance. These limitations were identified in "Sphere-Guided Training of Neural Implicit Surfaces". The reliance on coarse geometry estimated early in training was highlighted as a main limitation, particularly for thin structures such as Ficus stems and for scenes with complex appearance variations like the Materials scene. The issues were documented alongside ablation studies comparing the method against NeuS and NSVF variants. Sphere-Guided Training of Neural Implicit Surfaces, http://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15511v2, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Plane-Based Layered Volume Rendering
head: Discrete Plane Volume Sampling, Exclusion Plane Volume Rendering
body: Plane-Based Layered Volume Rendering approximates continuous volume integration by sampling a discrete set of parallel planes aligned with the camera view direction. It differs from standard fixed-step ray marching by restricting samples to specific geometric planes, which allows for optional exclusion plane testing to skip empty or occluded regions, thereby reducing unnecessary texture lookups and shading computations. The method renders a volume by iterating through a predefined number of layers (planes). For each pixel, a ray is cast from the camera position. The algorithm calculates the intersection of this ray with each layer plane, transforms the intersection point into local volume coordinates, and samples the volume texture. An optional exclusion test can skip sampling if the point lies outside defined exclusion planes. The resulting color and opacity are accumulated using front-to-back alpha blending. Inputs: MODELMATRIX: 4x4 transformation matrix from local to world space. CAMERAPOSITIONWORLD: 3D vector representing the camera's position in world space. posworld: 3D vector representing the target point in world space for the current pixel's ray. texturevolume: 3D texture containing the volume data. gradient: 1D or 2D texture mapping scalar values to color/opacity. layers: Integer, total number of planes to sample. zoom: Float, scaling factor applied to local coordinates before sampling. opacity: Float, global opacity multiplier. colorscalar: Float, global color intensity multiplier. gamma: Float, gamma correction exponent applied to the scalar value before gradient lookup. exclusionplanes: Array of vec4 plane equations. MAXEXCLUSIONPLANES: Integer, maximum number of exclusion planes supported. numexclusionplanes: Integer, actual number of exclusion planes provided. Outputs: col: Accumulated vec4 color output for the pixel. Exclusion Plane: Represented as a vec4 (A, B, C, D). A point P is excluded if \text{dot}(\text{vec4}(P, -1.0), \text{plane}) > 0.0. The source uses -1.0 for the w-component, implying the plane equation is evaluated as Ax + By + Cz - D > 0 or the plane vector stores -D in the w-component. layers: Total number of planes to sample. zoom: Scaling factor applied to local coordinates before sampling. opacity: Global opacity multiplier. colorscalar: Global color intensity multiplier. gamma: Gamma correction exponent applied to the scalar value before gradient lookup. 1. Calculate Plane Normal: Determine the direction from the volume model origin to the camera. \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{C}{world} - \mathbf{O}{model\world}) Where \mathbf{C}{world} is CAMERAPOSITIONWORLD and \mathbf{O}{model\world} is MODELMATRIX[3].xyz. 2. Iterate Layers: Loop from i = 0 to layers - 1. a. Calculate Plane Position: Determine the origin of the current layer plane in world space. \mathbf{P}{plane\origin} = \mathbf{O}{model\world} + \mathbf{n} \cdot \left( \frac{i + 1}{layers + 1} \cdot 2 - 1 \right) This formula centers the planes within the volume extent defined by the model origin and the normal direction, distributing them evenly between -1 and 1 relative to the model origin along the normal. b. Ray-Plane Intersection: Compute the intersection point \mathbf{P}{world} of the ray (origin \mathbf{C}{world}, direction \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{P}{world\target} - \mathbf{C}{world}) with the plane defined by \mathbf{P}{plane\origin} and normal \mathbf{n}. c. Exclusion Test: Check if \mathbf{P}{world} lies in any exclusion region. \text{excluded} = \bigvee{j=0}^{\min(num\exclusion\planes, MAX\EXCLUSION\PLANES)-1} \left( \text{dot}(\text{vec4}(\mathbf{P}{world}, -1.0), \mathbf{E}j) > 0.0 \right) If excluded, skip to the next layer. d. Transform to Local Space: Convert \mathbf{P}{world} to local volume coordinates. \mathbf{P}{local} = \text{xyz}(\text{inverse}(\text{MODEL\MATRIX}) \cdot \text{vec4}(\mathbf{P}{world}, 1.0)). e. Texture Coordinate Calculation: Map local coordinates to texture space [0, 1]^3. \mathbf{T} = \frac{\mathbf{P}{local} \cdot \text{zoom}}{2.0} + \text{vec3}(0.5). f. Volume Sample: Sample the volume texture. \mathbf{C}{layer} = \text{texture}(\text{texture\volume}, \mathbf{T}). g. Transfer Function: Map the scalar value (red channel) to color/opacity using the gradient texture. \mathbf{C}{layer} = \text{texture}(\text{gradient}, \text{vec2}(\mathbf{C}{layer}.r^\gamma, 0)). h. Apply Opacity and Color: \mathbf{C}{layer}.a \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{layer}.a \cdot \text{opacity} \mathbf{C}{layer} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{layer} \cdot \text{color\scalar}. i. Alpha Blending: Accumulate the layer color into the result. \mathbf{C}{result} = \text{mix}(\mathbf{C}{result}, \mathbf{C}{layer}, \mathbf{C}{layer}.a). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def planebasedlayeredvolumerendering( cameraposworld: vec3, raydirection: vec3, modelmatrix: mat4, texturevolume: texture3D, gradienttexture: texture1D, layers: int, zoom: float, opacity: float, colorscalar: float, gamma: float, exclusionplanes: list[vec4], maxexclusionplanes: int) -> vec4: modeloriginworld = modelmatrix[3].xyz planenorm = normalize(cameraposworld - modeloriginworld) resultcolor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) invmodelmtx = inverse(modelmatrix) for layeridx in range(layers): layerfrac = (layeridx + 1) / (layers + 1) planeorigin = modeloriginworld + planenorm (layerfrac 2.0 - 1.0) denom = dot(planenorm, raydirection) if abs(denom) < 1e-6: continue t = dot(planenorm, planeorigin - cameraposworld) / denom pworld = cameraposworld + t raydirection planetestpassed = True numchecks = min(len(exclusionplanes), maxexclusionplanes) for i in range(numchecks): val = dot(vec4(pworld.x, pworld.y, pworld.z, -1.0), exclusionplanes[i]) if val > 0.0: planetestpassed = False break if not planetestpassed: continue plocal = (invmodelmtx vec4(pworld, 1.0)).xyz texsamplept = (plocal zoom) / 2.0 + vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) layercol = texture(texturevolume, texsamplept) layercol = texture(gradienttexture, vec2(pow(layercol.r, gamma), 0.0)) layercol.a = opacity layercol = colorscalar resultcolor = mix(resultcolor, layercol, layercol.a) return resultcolor Parallel Ray: If the ray direction is parallel to the plane normal (dot product near zero), the intersection calculation fails. A guard against division by zero is required. Exclusion Plane W-component: The source uses vec4(pworld, -1.0). This is non-standard for homogeneous plane equations (Ax+By+Cz+Dw). Implementers must ensure the exclusion plane data is stored such that the dot product with (x, y, z, -1) correctly represents the exclusion condition. If standard planes (A,B,C,D) are used, the check should be Ax+By+Cz-D > 0 or the plane data should store -D in the w-component. Texture Coordinate Bounds: The formula (plocal zoom) / 2.0 + 0.5 assumes plocal is within [-1, 1] when zoom is 1. If zoom is large or plocal is out of bounds, texture sampling may return undefined values or clamp depending on sampler settings. Clamping or border color handling should be considered. Gamma Application: Gamma is applied to the red channel before the gradient lookup. This assumes the volume data's red channel represents the scalar density/value. The default number of planes is chosen as nz / dz, so that when viewed straight on, each data point is sampled by one plane. For example, a 64^3 volume with uniform dz gets 110 planes. The rendered images are more accurate as more planes are used. With few planes, artifacts may be noticeable where a clipped edge of a rendered square is visible. We usually choose two to four times the default, as the cost of additional rendered planes is a very minor factor with directional lighting. Time Complexity: O(L) per pixel, where L is the number of layers. Each layer involves a ray-plane intersection, a matrix multiplication, and texture lookups. Exclusion tests add O(E) per layer, where E is the number of exclusion planes. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume texture and O(E) for exclusion planes. Strengths: Reduces the number of texture samples compared to dense fixed-step marching by skipping empty regions via exclusion planes. Aligns with the view direction, which can be efficient for certain data structures. Limitations: The discrete nature of planes may introduce aliasing or artifacts if the layer spacing is too large. The method is view-dependent; the planes are aligned with the camera, so it does not naturally support view-independent optimizations like spatial partitioning for all views. When to use: Suitable for volumes with large empty regions that can be defined by exclusion planes, or when a specific layered approximation is desired for performance. When not to use: For volumes requiring high accuracy without gaps, or when the volume data is not well-aligned with the view direction and exclusion planes are not effective. The method is described in the context of the godotvolumelayers addon, an unofficial implementation for the Godot engine. It represents a specific approach to volume rendering within that ecosystem, leveraging compute shaders for mipmap generation and fragment shaders for the layered sampling. blackears/godotvolumelayers, https://github.com/blackears/godotvolumelayers, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Direct Volume Rendering with Shading via Three-..., https://www.cg.tuwien.ac.at/~bruckner/ss2004/seminar/A1a/VanGelder1996%20-%20Direct%20Volume%20Rendering%20with%20Shading%20via%20Three-Dimensional%20Textures.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Image-order Rendering Loop
head: Image order approach, Image-Order Volume Ray Casting, Image-ordered ray casting, Main Rendering Loop, Octree Rendering Loop
body: The image-order rendering loop is the fundamental control structure for volume ray casting, iterating over each pixel of the output image to generate a camera ray and invoking a raymarcher to compute the final color. It differs from object-order (rasterization) by being more "CPU-like" in its iteration logic, offering correct perspective projection, single-pass ray casting, and full 32-bit compositing precision without requiring intermediate buffers. The method operates by mapping 2D screen coordinates to 3D world-space rays and accumulating optical properties along those rays. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Image dimensions (W \times H), camera parameters (position, direction, projection mode), volume data structure, and shading mode. Outputs: A 2D image buffer where each pixel (x, y) contains the accumulated color C{out}. Data Structures Camera State: Contains cameraPos (origin), cameraDir (direction vector), and ProjectionMode (enum: PERSPECTIVE or ORTHOGRAPHIC). Shading Mode: Enum determining the compositing and lighting behavior. Values include TRACE, DEPTH, DEPTHHIT, DIFFUSE, NORMAL, and INDEX. Ray Structure: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Set CompletedSamples = 0. Calculate light bounds p0, p1 if necessary for light intersection tests. 2. Sample Loop: If ShadingMode == TRACE, loop over samples s from 0 to NumSamples-1. 3. Pixel Loop: Iterate y from 0 to vheight-1 and x from 0 to vwidth-1. 4. Coordinate Mapping: Calculate normalized pixel coordinates rx, ry from x, y, then transform to position pos. 5. Ray Generation: If PERSPECTIVE: \mathbf{o} = \text{cameraPos}, \mathbf{d} = \text{cameraDir} + \text{pos}. If ORTHOGRAPHIC: \mathbf{o} = \text{cameraPos} + \text{pos}, \mathbf{d} = \text{cameraDir}. 6. Index Calculation: Compute index = x + y vwidth. 7. Ray Marching/Tracing: If ShadingMode == TRACE: accumulate color by calling ShadePathTrace and averaging with previous samples. Else: call Raymarch. 8. Shading/Compositing: If a hit is detected: shade based on ShadingMode (e.g., DEPTH, DIFFUSE). If no hit but ray intersects light AABB: write light color. Else: write dark color (25, 25, 25). 9. Output: Combine sampling points in a compositing module and write the result as the display pixel. Formulas Ray AABB Intersection: \mathbf{invRd} = \frac{1}{\mathbf{rd}}, \quad \mathbf{t0} = (\mathbf{p0} - \mathbf{ro}) \cdot \mathbf{invRd}, \quad \mathbf{t1} = (\mathbf{p1} - \mathbf{ro}) \cdot \mathbf{invRd} \mathbf{tmin} = \min(\mathbf{t0}, \mathbf{t1}), \quad \mathbf{tmax} = \max(\mathbf{t0}, \mathbf{t1}) ftmin = \max(tminx, tminy, tminz), \quad ftmax = \min(tmaxx, tmaxy, tmaxz) \mathbf{hit} = \mathbf{ro} + (ftmin \cdot \mathbf{rd}) Intersection occurs if ftmin \le ftmax. Depth Shading: C{out}.g = C{in}.g \times \frac{\text{depth}}{2.0} Where depth is the distance from camera to hit point. Normal Shading: C{out}.c = \begin{cases} 1.0 & \text{if } N.c \neq 0 \\ 0.0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} For each component c \in \{x, y, z\}. Parameters ShadingMode: Determines shading behavior. Common values: TRACE, DEPTH, DEPTHHIT, DIFFUSE, NORMAL, INDEX. ProjectionMode: Determines ray generation. Values: PERSPECTIVE, ORTHOGRAPHIC. Compositing Methods: MIP, averaging, nearest-point, and alpha compositing are commonly used in the compositing module. Pseudocode Unverified code.
