Precision: Image-order allows for 32-bit compositing precision, avoiding the need for a compositing buffer. Empty Space: In sparse volumes (e.g., octrees), empty space must be skipped efficiently to avoid performance degradation. The Terminal Rendering Pipeline renders a 3D scene to a text-based terminal buffer by iterating over pixels, mapping them to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC), casting rays via a raymarcher, and applying ASCII/ANSI styling based on depth and lighting. It differs from standard terminal rendering by explicitly accounting for character aspect ratio when converting pixel indices to NDC and using ANSI escape codes to modulate brightness based on depth percentage, effectively acting as a low-resolution, text-based raymarcher. Diffuse Octree Rendering is an image-order raycasting technique that traverses an octree to locate the first leaf node containing data for each pixel, then computes surface lighting using a diffuse and Phong specular model with distance attenuation. It differs from sibling methods by relying on a coarse-to-fine octree traversal to skip empty space entirely, rather than marching through a dense voxel grid. Renders an image by casting rays per pixel through a scene, with optional multi-sample anti-aliasing using uniform sub-pixel jittering. It extends the basic Image-order Rendering Loop by introducing a sampling loop that averages multiple jittered ray samples per pixel to reduce aliasing artifacts. The Renderer configuration is a top-level controller that manages global rendering parameters such as ray depth, sampling rates, and background color. It serves as the static interface for adjusting image-order rendering behavior, including exposure, gamma correction, and post-processing flags like FXAA, diffuse shading, shadows, and Screen Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO). It differs from sibling methods by centralizing these global state variables rather than implementing the ray traversal or shading logic itself. Time Complexity: O(W \times H \times S), where W and H are image dimensions and S is the number of samples per pixel (or steps in ray marching). Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the output image buffer, plus the memory required for the volume data structure. Performance: Image-order is described as more "CPU-like" but offers correct perspective and single-pass ray casting with 32-bit compositing. It is flexible, supporting adaptive sampling. Strengths: Correct perspective, single-pass, 32-bit compositing precision, flexibility (adaptive sampling). When to Use: When correct perspective and high-quality compositing are required, and when the hardware supports conditional loops in shaders (Shader Model 3.0+). The image-order approach is a fundamental technique in volume rendering, often contrasted with object-order (rasterization) methods. It has been widely used in GPU-based volume ray casting, with notable implementations in the NVIDIA SDK and various research papers. The use of image-order rendering on FPGAs has been explored for its flexibility and cost-effectiveness in prototype development, specifically for systems capturing endomicroscopic images from biological tissue. name: Terminal Rendering Pipeline
head: ASCII Raymarcher Display, ASCII/ANSI Volume Rendering, Character-based Screen Buffer, Terminal ASCII Rendering Pipeline
body: The Terminal Rendering Pipeline renders a 3D scene to a text-based terminal buffer by iterating over pixels, mapping them to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC), casting rays via a raymarcher, and applying ASCII/ANSI styling based on depth and lighting. It differs from standard terminal rendering by explicitly accounting for character aspect ratio when converting pixel indices to NDC and using ANSI escape codes to modulate brightness based on depth percentage, effectively acting as a low-resolution, text-based raymarcher. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position and orientation, raymarcher instance (step count, max distance, epsilon), list of lights, screen height, aspect ratio, and ASCII gradient string. Outputs: Terminal screen buffer containing ASCII characters and ANSI escape codes. Data Structures: Screen Buffer: Two vectors of size width height. pixelsvector: std::vector<char>, stores the ASCII character for each pixel. modifiersvector: std::vector<std::string>, stores per-pixel ANSI escape codes. Dimensions: height: Number of rows. width: Number of columns, calculated as height aspect CHARASPECT. CHARASPECT: Constant value 2.0 to account for character aspect ratio. pixels: Total pixel count width height. NDC Constants: halfpixelwidth: 1.0 / (2.0 width). halfpixelheight: 1.0 / (2.0 height). Gradient: gradient: String of ASCII characters representing brightness levels. gradientsize: Length of the gradient string. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Screen: Determine screen height, calculate width using width = height aspect CHARASPECT, initialize pixelsvector with EMPTYCHAR and modifiersvector with empty strings, calculate halfpixelwidth and halfpixelheight, and set gradientsize to the length of the gradient string. 2. Render Loop (per frame): Clear the terminal screen and hide cursor using static methods, clear the screen buffer, and iterate over all pixel indices i from 0 to screen.getpixelcount() - 1. For each pixel: a. Convert Pixel Index to NDC: Calculate column and row from index i: col = i \pmod{width}, row = \lfloor i / width \rfloor. Calculate NDC coordinates: ndcx = \frac{col}{width} + \frac{1}{2 \cdot width}, ndcy = \frac{row}{height} - \frac{1}{2 \cdot height}. b. Map NDC to World Position: Use camera projection to map (ndcx, ndcy) to world position pixelwpos. c. Raymarch: Cast ray from cam.pos to pixelwpos. If hit: compute normalized light intensity light based on surface normal and lights, compute depth percentage D{perc} = \frac{hit\distance}{MAX\DIST}, and set pixel color based on brightness and depth. If D{perc} > 0.666, apply dim modifier \u001b[2m; if D{perc} > 0.333, apply no modifier; else apply bright modifier \u001b[1m. Map brightness to gradient character index: idx = \lfloor \max(brightness - 0.0001, 0.0) \times gradient\size \rfloor, clamp idx to [0, gradient\size - 1], set pixelsvector[i] to gradient[idx], and set modifiersvector[i] to the selected ANSI modifier. If no hit: set pixelsvector[i] to EMPTYCHAR and modifiersvector[i] to empty string. 3. Output: Print the buffer to the terminal using printbuffer(), which outputs each character with its corresponding ANSI modifier. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderframe(height, aspect, raymarcher, lights, gradient): CHARASPECT = 2.0 width = height aspect CHARASPECT numpixels = width height gradientsize = len(gradient) EMPTYCHAR = ' ' pixelsvector = [EMPTYCHAR] numpixels modifiersvector = [''] numpixels # Clear terminal and hide cursor using ANSI escape codes. print('\033[2J\033[H', end='') print('\033[?25l', end='') for i in range(numpixels): col = i % width row = i // width ndcx = (col / width) + (1.0 / (2.0 width)) ndcy = (row / height) - (1.0 / (2.0 height)) # Standard camera projection maps NDC to world coordinates. pixelwpos = camera.ndctoworldpos(ndcx, ndcy) # Raymarch from camera position to pixelwpos. # Raymarching step loop and hit detection not detailed in sources. hit, normal, hitdistance = raymarcher.raymarch(camera.pos, pixelwpos) if hit: # Diffuse lighting calculation from scene lights. light = sum(l.calculatediffuse(normal) for l in lights) maxdist = raymarcher.getmaxdist() depthpercentage = hitdistance / maxdist if depthpercentage > 0.666: modifier = "\u001b[2m" elif depthpercentage > 0.333: modifier = "" else: modifier = "\u001b[1m" brightness = light idx = int(max(brightness - 0.0001, 0.0) gradientsize) idx = max(0, min(idx, gradientsize - 1)) pixelsvector[i] = gradient[idx] modifiersvector[i] = modifier else: pixelsvector[i] = EMPTYCHAR modifiersvector[i] = "" # Output buffer to terminal for i in range(numpixels): print(f"{modifiersvector[i]}{pixelsvector[i]}", end='') if (i + 1) % width == 0: print() print('\033?25h', end='') Parameters: [FPS: Target frame rate is 30. FRAMETIME = 1.0 / FPS. CHARASPECT: 2.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aspect Ratio: Failure to account for character aspect ratio (CHARASPECT) results in distorted scenes. The width is scaled by CHARASPECT to compensate for the taller-than-wide nature of terminal characters. Precision: The brightness mapping uses a small epsilon (0.0001) to avoid index out-of-bounds errors due to floating-point inaccuracies. It differs from standard terminal rendering by employing ordered dithering via a Bayer matrix to simulate grayscale intensity and color depth within the constraints of a fixed 80x24 character grid, effectively acting as a low-resolution, text-based raymarcher. name: ASCII Rendering with Dithering
head: ASCII Ray Tracing, ASCII Tracing with Ordered Dithering, Terminal Ray Tracing, Terminal Raymarching, VT100 Rendering
body: ASCII Rendering with Dithering renders 3D scenes to a text-based terminal buffer by casting rays, computing lighting, and mapping the resulting continuous-tone color to a limited set of ASCII characters (typically # and space) using ANSI escape codes. It differs from standard terminal rendering by employing ordered dithering via a Bayer matrix to simulate grayscale intensity and color depth within the constraints of a fixed 80x24 character grid, effectively acting as a low-resolution, text-based raymarcher. Inputs: Scene defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for primitives (e.g., planes, tori, spheres). Camera position (campos) and orientation. Light position (lightpos) and color (lcol). Material properties: diffuse color (mcol) and shininess (mshiny) for each material index. Resolution: Fixed at 80 columns (x) and 24 rows (y). Outputs: A terminal buffer containing ANSI escape sequences for foreground/background colors and ASCII characters (# or space). Bayer Matrix: A 4x4 integer array used for ordered dithering offsets, stored in row-major order: {1, 9, 3, 11, 13, 5, 15, 7, 4, 12, 2, 10, 16, 8, 14, 6} Color Lookup Table (LUT): A precomputed table colorLUT[161616] mapping quantized RGB indices (0-15 per channel) to a packed integer representing foreground and background ANSI color indices. Material Arrays: mcol (diffuse colors) and mshiny (shininess exponents). Light Color: lcol = {0.7, 0.5, 0.5}. 1. Initialization: Call renderinit() to populate the colorLUT. This iterates over all 16^3 possible quantized RGB combinations, finds the nearest ANSI foreground/background pair using a brute-force search over 17 palette entries (indices 0-16) with an error metric based on squared Euclidean distance in RGB space, and stores the result. 2. Loop: Iterate through each frame. 3. Camera Setup: Define camera position campos and view direction camz = normalize(campos -1). Compute camera basis vectors: camx = normalize(cross(camz, vec3(0, 1, 0))) and camy = normalize(cross(camx, camz)). 4. Pixel Loop: For each pixel (x, y) where x ∈ [0, 79] and y ∈ [0, 23]: 5. Accumulate Color: Initialize color = vec3(0, 0, 0). 6. Multi-sampling (AA): Perform 8 samples per pixel to reduce aliasing. Iterate xx in {-0.25, 0.25} (2 samples). Iterate yy in {-0.75, -0.25, 0.25, 0.75} (4 samples). Construct ray direction dir in screen space: dir{screen} = \text{normalize}(v3(x - 40.0 + xx, 25.0 - 2.0 \cdot y + yy, 40.0)). Transform dir to camera space: dir = camx \cdot dir.x + camy \cdot dir.y + camz \cdot dir.z. Ray Marching: Initialize t = 0, m = -1 (no material). Loop up to 64 iterations or until t > 1e6: Compute point p = dir t + campos. Compute distance d = dist(p, &m) using SDFs. If d < 0.001, a hit occurred. Compute lighting L = lighting(p, m, lightpos) and add to accumulator: color = color + L. Break loop. Else, t += d. 7. Scale: Multiply accumulated color by 0.125 (divide by 8) to average the 8 samples. 8. Dithering and Color Mapping: Compute dithering offset o using the Bayer matrix B. The source code uses o = B[(x \bmod 4) + (y \bmod 4) \cdot 4] \cdot \frac{1}{8}. (The notes mention an alternative formula o = -48 + 4 \cdot B[(x \bmod 4) + (y \bmod 4) \cdot 4], but the code implementation is as stated). Quantize RGB channels to 0-15 range with offset: r = \text{clamp}(\lfloor c.x \cdot 15.0 - o \rfloor, 0, 15), g = \text{clamp}(\lfloor c.y \cdot 15.0 - o \rfloor, 0, 15), b = \text{clamp}(\lfloor c.z \cdot 15.0 - o \rfloor, 0, 15). Lookup ANSI codes in colorLUT[r + g16 + b256] to get fg and bg. 9. Render Character: If fg is valid (>=0), print # with ANSI foreground color 30 + (fg & 7) and bold flag !!(fg & 8). If fg is invalid (-1), print space. The rendercolor function tracks previous curfg and curbg to avoid printing escape sequences when attributes are identical to the previous pixel. 10. End of Row: After x loop, print newline \n and reset attributes \x1b[0m. 11. Frame Update: Flush stdout, sleep 20ms, increment frame counter, and move cursor up 24 lines (\x1b[24A) to redraw. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderinit(): colorLUT = [0] (16 16 16) for r in range(16): for g in range(16): for b in range(16): color = vec3(r / 15.0, g / 15.0, b / 15.0) fg, bg = nearestcolor(color) colorLUT[r + g 16 + b 256] = (bg << 5) | fg return colorLUT def dist(p, mout): dplane = p.y + 50.0 mout[0] = ((int(p.x 0.01) & 1) ^ (int(p.z 0.01) & 1)) d = dplane # Add other SDFs (torus, etc.) and update d, mout if closer return d def lighting(p, m, lightpos): lightdir = normalize(lightpos - p) eps = 0.1 mtemp = [-1] diffuse = max(0.0, 10.0 dist(p + lightdir eps, mtemp)) s = shadow(p, lightdir, 0.01, length(lightpos - p)) l = max(0.1, diffuse s) return MCOL[m] l + LCOL pow(l, MSHINY[m]) def shadow(ro, rd, mint, maxt): res = 1.0 t = mint while t < maxt: mtemp = [-1] h = dist(ro + rd t, mtemp) if h < 0.001: return 0.0 res = min(res, 10.0 h / t) t += h return res def renderframe(frame): campos = vec3(120 sin(frame 0.01), 40 + 30 sin(frame 0.03), -120 cos(frame 0.01)) camz = normalize(campos -1) camx = normalize(cross(camz, vec3(0, 1, 0))) camy = normalize(cross(camx, camz)) curfg = 7 curbg = 0 colorLUT = renderinit() for y in range(24): for x in range(80): color = vec3(0, 0, 0) for xx in [-0.25, 0.25]: for yy in [-0.75, -0.25, 0.25, 0.75]: dirscreen = normalize(vec3(x - 40.0 + xx, 25.0 - 2.0 y + yy, 40.0)) dir = camx dirscreen.x + camy dirscreen.y + camz dirscreen.z t = 0.0 m = [-1] for in range(64): if t > 1e6: break p = dir t + campos d = dist(p, m) if d < 0.001: color = color + lighting(p, m[0], vec3(0, 40, 0)) break t += d color = color 0.125 bayerval = BAYERMATRIX[(x & 3) + ((y & 3) 4)] o = bayerval (1.0 / 8.0) r = clamp(int(color.x 15.0 - o), 0, 15) g = clamp(int(color.y 15.0 - o), 0, 15) b = clamp(int(color.z 15.0 - o), 0, 15) entry = colorLUT[r + g 16 + b 256] fg = entry & 31 bg = entry >> 5 if fg >= 0: # Print '#' with ANSI codes pass else: # Print space pass print("\n") print("\x1b0m") print("\x1b[24A") flush() sleep(0.02) Resolution: 80x24 characters. Samples per Pixel: 8 (2 in x, 4 in y). [Gamma Correction: Not explicitly applied in the provided code, but standard gamma is 2.2. Color Scaling: 0.125 for AA averaging. Light Color: {0.7, 0.5, 0.5}. Shininess: The notes specify {10, 10, 10} for materials 0, 1, 2, but the source code uses {100, 10, 10}. Material Colors: The notes specify mcol[0]={0.0,1.6,0.0}, mcol[1]={0.0,0.0,0.0}, mcol[2]={1.0,0.0,0.0}, but the source code uses mcol[0]={1.5, 1.5, 1.5}, mcol[1]={0.6, 0.6, 0.6}, mcol[2]={0.0, 0.4, 1.0}. Precision: The distance field check uses a threshold of 0.001. If the ray step t accumulates floating-point errors, the ray might miss the surface or jitter. The source uses a fixed iteration limit (64) and a max distance (1e6 or 6000) to prevent infinite loops. Color Mapping: The nearest color function uses a brute-force search over 17 palette entries. If no close match is found, it returns -1, resulting in a space character (background). ANSI State: Failing to track curfg and curbg correctly will result in excessive escape sequence emission, slowing down rendering. Camera Basis: The camera basis calculation camx = normalize(cross(camz, vec3(0,1,0))) assumes the camera is not looking exactly up or down (parallel to the Y-axis). If camz is parallel to (0,1,0), the cross product is zero, causing a division by zero in normalization. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot S \cdot I), where W=80, H=24, S=8 (samples), and I=64 (max ray march iterations). The complexity is dominated by the ray marching loop. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the scene (SDFs are procedural), plus O(1) for the LUT (16^3 entries). Performance: Described as "pretty slow and unoptimized". The use of Python-like pseudocode suggests it is intended for clarity rather than speed, but the original C implementation runs in real-time on modern CPUs for simple scenes. Strengths: Simple implementation, no external assets, portable to any terminal. Limitations: Low resolution (80x24), limited color palette, no transparency/reflections (only diffuse/specular), fixed camera movement. ASCII Rendering with Dithering is a technique popularized by obfuscated C programming contests and terminal art enthusiasts. The specific implementation described here is from the a1k0n/asciitracing repository, which demonstrates raymarching in a terminal using ANSI escape codes. It builds on the principles of raymarching (as seen in Shadertoy) but adapts the output to a text-based medium using ordered dithering to simulate grayscale. a1k0n/asciitracing, https://github.com/a1k0n/asciitracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Diffuse Octree Rendering
body: Diffuse Octree Rendering is an image-order raycasting technique that traverses an octree to locate the first leaf node containing data for each pixel, then computes surface lighting using a diffuse and Phong specular model with distance attenuation. It differs from sibling methods by relying on a coarse-to-fine octree traversal to skip empty space entirely, rather than marching through a dense voxel grid. Inputs and Outputs Input: An octree where leaf nodes contain VoxelData; a camera configuration providing eye position and a ray generation function; a list of lights with attenuation constants and shininess; image dimensions (rc.n\x, rc.n\y). Output: A texture array (RGBA) where each pixel stores the final color and an alpha value of 1. Data Structures The core data structure is VoxelData, stored in leaf nodes. Its layout contains a morton code (uint64t), a color vector (vec3), and a normal vector (vec3). The total size is sizeof(uint64t) + 2 (3 sizeof(float)) bytes. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize OpenMP threads using the number of available processors. 2. Pixel Loop: Parallelize the loop over pixel coordinates (x, y). 3. Ray Generation: For each pixel (x, y), generate a ray using the camera's ray generation function. 4. Traversal: Initialize a ray traverser with the octree and the generated ray. 5. Search: Iterate while the traverser is not terminated: if the current node is a leaf and has data, break; otherwise step to the next node. 6. Lighting Calculation: For each active light i: Compute light vector: \vec{to\light} = \text{light}[i].\text{position} - \text{current\position}. Compute half vector: \vec{s} = \vec{to\light} + (\text{camera\eye} - \text{current\position}), then normalize \vec{s}. Compute distance attenuation: \text{distancecut} = \frac{1.0}{\text{CONSTANT\ATTENUATION} + \text{LINEAR\ATTENUATION} \cdot \|\vec{to\light}\| + \text{QUADRATIC\ATTENUATION} \cdot \|\vec{to\light}\|^2}. Normalize \vec{to\light}. Compute diffuse factor: f{diff} = \text{leaf\normal} \cdot \vec{to\light}. Accumulate diffuse color: C{diff} += \max(0.0, f{diff}) \cdot \text{distancecut} \cdot \text{light}[i].\text{diffuse}. Compute Phong specular factor: f{spec} = (\vec{to\light} \cdot \text{leaf\normal})^{\text{SHININESS}}. Accumulate specular color: C{spec} += \max(0.0, f{spec}) \cdot \text{distancecut} \cdot \text{light}[i].\text{specular}. 7. Final Color: Combine contributions: \text{FinalColor} = \text{leaf\color} \cdot (C{diff} + C{spec} + 0.25), clamp to [0, 255], and store in the texture array. 8. Alpha: Set alpha to 1. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def clamp(value, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(value, maxval)) class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def dot(self, other): return self.x other.x + self.y other.y + self.z other.z def len(self): return math.sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2) def normalized(self): l = self.len() return Vec3(self.x / l, self.y / l, self.z / l) if l > 0 else Vec3(0, 0, 0) def diffuseoctreerender(tree, rc): # Initialize OpenMP threads: numprocs = ompgetnumprocs(); ompsetnumthreads(numprocs) texturearray = [0] (rc.nx rc.ny 4) # Parallel pixel loop for y in range(rc.ny): for x in range(rc.nx): ray = rc.getRayForPixel(x, y) t = TreeTraverser(tree, ray) # The sources do not provide the internal octree traversal logic while not t.isTerminated(): node = t.getCurrentNode() if node.isLeaf() and node.hasData(): break t.step() if t.isTerminated(): continue currentpos = t.getCurrentPosition() leafdata = tree.data[node.data] normal = leafdata.normal color = leafdata.color r, g, b = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 for light in rc.lights: tolight = light.position - currentpos dist = tolight.len() # Compute half vector (computed in source but unused in final accumulation) s = tolight + (rc.camera.e - currentpos) s = s.normalized() denom = light.CONSTANTATTENUATION + light.LINEARATTENUATION dist + light.QUADRATICATTENUATION (dist 2) distancecut = 1.0 / denom if denom != 0 else 0.0 tolight = tolight.normalized() diffusefactor = normal.dot(tolight) r += max(0.0, diffusefactor) distancecut light.diffuse[0] g += max(0.0, diffusefactor) distancecut light.diffuse[1] b += max(0.0, diffusefactor) distancecut light.diffuse[2] phongfactor = max(0.0, normal.dot(tolight)) light.SHININESS r += max(0.0, phongfactor) distancecut light.specular[0] g += max(0.0, phongfactor) distancecut light.specular[1] b += max(0.0, phongfactor) distancecut light.specular[2] index = (y rc.nx + x) 4 texturearray[index] = clamp(255 (color[0] (r + 0.25)), 0, 255) texturearray[index + 1] = clamp(255 (color[1] (g + 0.25)), 0, 255) texturearray[index + 2] = clamp(255 (color[2] (b + 0.25)), 0, 255) texturearray[index + 3] = 1 return texturearray Parameters CONSTANTATTENUATION, LINEARATTENUATION, QUADRATICATTENUATION: Light attenuation constants. SHININESS: Exponent for the specular term. Ambient factor: Fixed at 0.25. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Termination: If the ray traverses the entire octree without finding a leaf with data, the loop terminates without shading. Division by Zero: The distance attenuation denominator must be checked for zero to avoid division by zero errors. Precision: The source uses float for color and vector calculations throughout. name: Ray Casting Loop with Supersampling
head: Image-order Rendering Loop with Supersampling
body: Renders an image by casting rays per pixel through a scene, with optional multi-sample anti-aliasing using uniform sub-pixel jittering. It extends the basic Image-order Rendering Loop by introducing a sampling loop that averages multiple jittered ray samples per pixel to reduce aliasing artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera object (providing getWidth(), getHeight(), drawPixel()), boolean flag SAMPLING, integer SN, and a trace(x, y) function returning a Color. Output: Image drawn via camera->drawPixel(). Data Structures: Color: A vector-like structure supporting initialization to zero, addition, scalar division, and clamping. Vector3D: A 3D vector structure supporting arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division). Ray: Contains origin, direction, and hit information, handled internally by trace. Parameters: SN: Number of samples per axis for supersampling. Typical value: 5. SAMPLING: Boolean flag enabling/disabling supersampling. Typical value: false. Steps: 1. Initialize pixel index i = 0. 2. Loop while renderLoop() returns false. 3. Inside renderLoop(), parallelize over the vertical pixel coordinate j from 0 to camera->getHeight() - 1. 4. If SAMPLING is false: call trace(i, j), clamp the color, and draw the pixel at (i, j). 5. If SAMPLING is true: initialize color to zero, loop p from 0 to SN - 1, loop q from 0 to SN - 1, generate random e via randGen(1), compute sub-pixel coordinates x = i + (p + e) / SN and y = j + (q + e) / SN, call trace(x, y), clamp the sample color, and accumulate it into color. After the inner loops, draw the pixel at (i, j) with color / (SN SN). 6. Increment i. If i == camera->getWidth(), reset i = 0 and return true to terminate the loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random class Color: def init(self, r=0.0, g=0.0, b=0.0): self.r, self.g, self.b = r, g, b def iadd(self, other): self.r += other.r; self.g += other.g; self.b += other.b return self def truediv(self, scalar): return Color(self.r/scalar, self.g/scalar, self.b/scalar) def clamp(self): self.r = max(0.0, min(1.0, self.r)) self.g = max(0.0, min(1.0, self.g)) self.b = max(0.0, min(1.0, self.b)) return self def renderloop(camera, trace, sampling=False, sn=5): width = camera.getWidth() height = camera.getHeight() i = 0 while True: # Parallelized over j per for j in range(height): if not sampling: color = trace(i, j) color.clamp() camera.drawPixel(i, j, color) else: color = Color(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for p in range(sn): for q in range(sn): e = random.random() # Maps to randGen(1) x = i + (p + e) / sn y = j + (q + e) / sn c = trace(x, y) c.clamp() color += c camera.drawPixel(i, j, color / (sn sn)) i += 1 if i == width: i = 0 return True # renderLoop() returns true to terminate Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The sub-pixel coordinates x and y are floating-point values; trace must handle sub-pixel sampling correctly. Boundaries: The loop assumes i and j remain within valid camera dimensions; the reset logic if i == width ensures i wraps around. Randomness: randGen(1) is assumed to return a value in [0, 1). name: MPIRE Raycasting on Tera MTA
head: MPIRE, Tera MTA Raycasting
body: MPIRE is a massively parallel direct volume raycasting implementation designed for the Tera MTA architecture, leveraging a flat global memory model and hardware multithreading to hide memory latency. It distinguishes itself from distributed-memory alternatives like the Cray T3E by eliminating the need for a pixel composition step and avoiding the overhead of message passing and local memory partitioning. Inputs and Outputs Input: Image raster dimensions (xsize, ysize), a shaded volume data structure (v), and a ray structure (R) containing camera parameters. Output: An image buffer (image) containing the final color and opacity for each pixel. Data Structures image: A linear array indexed by index. The size is xsize ysize. R: A structure of type ray passed to the sampling function. v: The volume data structure containing the scalar field and transfer functions. Numbered Steps 1. Initialize a double loop iterating over the image raster dimensions. 2. Calculate the linear index for the current pixel in the image buffer using the formula: index = i + j \times xsize 3. Invoke the SampleRay function with the ray R and volume v to compute the final color and opacity. 4. Store the result in the image buffer at the calculated index: image[index] = SampleRay(R, v) 5. Attach the pragma #pragma tera assert parallel to both the outer and inner loops to explicitly instruct the Tera compiler to multithread the execution. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. image = [0.0] (xsize ysize) #pragma tera assert parallel for i in range(xsize): # Inner loop over y-dimension # Note: The source code places the pragma on the inner loop as well. # In a standard Python context, this pragma is ignored, but it represents # the instruction for the Tera compiler. # #pragma tera assert parallel for j in range(ysize): # Calculate linear index index = i + j xsize # Create ray R based on camera parameters and pixel coordinates (i, j) # This step is implicit in the source's abstraction of SampleRay R = createray(i, j, cameraparams) # Sample the volume and composite color/opacity # SampleRay steps through the volume v compositing color and opacity color, opacity = SampleRay(R, v) # Store result image[index] = color Parameters Image Resolution: Typically 400 x 400 pixels, resulting in 160,000 rays (threads). Hardware Thread Capacity: 128 threads per processor. Memory Size: 4 gigabytes of globally addressable, physically distributed memory with no local memory. Processor-Memory Bandwidth: 8 bytes per cycle. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Compiler Parallelization Uncertainty: The Tera compiler may refuse to automatically parallelize the loop if it cannot verify the absence of side effects in called functions like SampleRay. Explicit pragmas are required to force multithreading. Thread Granularity: Since there are 128 threads per processor, it is only efficient to use more than one processor if there are more than 128 calls to SampleRay (i.e., more than 128 pixels). Time and Memory Complexity Time Complexity: The algorithm scales linearly with the number of pixels (N = xsize \times ysize) and the number of processors (P), assuming sufficient parallelism. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the image buffer and O(V) for the volume data, where V is the volume size. The flat memory model requires all data to be globally addressable. Measured Performance MTA Performance: On a 256^3 sample data volume and 400x400 pixel image: 1 processor: 3.67s 2 processors: 1.89s (97% efficiency) 3 processors: 1.32s (93% efficiency) 4 processors: 0.97s (95% efficiency) T3E Performance (Comparison): On the same problem: 1 processor: 16.31s 2 processors: 8.56s (95% efficiency) 3 processors: 6.82s (80% efficiency) 4 processors: 5.45s (75% efficiency) 8 processors: 3.19s (64% efficiency) 16 processors: 2.08s (49% efficiency) Scaling and Trade-offs Scalability: The MTA scales well with problem size due to fine-grained parallelism (one thread per ray). Strengths: The MTA outperforms the T3E by more than 4:1 on single processors due to higher memory bandwidth (8 bytes/cycle vs. 2 bytes/cycle on cache miss) and hardware multithreading that hides latency. It avoids the pixel composition step required by distributed-memory machines. Limitations: The MTA configuration described has only 4 gigabytes of main memory, compared to the T3E's aggregate total of more than 36 gigabytes. This makes the T3E the machine of choice for truly large renders that exceed the MTA's memory capacity. When to use: Small to medium-sized problems where memory bandwidth and low-latency parallelism are critical, and the volume fits within 4GB. When not to use: Very large renders that exceed the MTA's 4GB memory limit, or problems where the overhead of message passing on the T3E is amortized by a sufficiently large problem size. MPIRE was developed for the Tera MTA architecture, a massively parallel machine designed to handle memory-intensive problems like raycasting. The implementation highlights the advantages of a flat global memory model over distributed-memory architectures like the Cray T3E, which require complex decomposition and message passing. The work was presented in the context of comparing data-intensive volume visualization on the Tera MTA and Cray T3E. name: Front-to-Back Volume Ray Casting with HSV Shading and SOS/Attenuation/Reflection Filtering
head: Front-to-Back Volume Ray Casting
body: This method performs direct volume rendering by casting rays from the camera through each pixel into a 3D volume, sampling voxel values along the ray, and compositing them using a front-to-back alpha blending algorithm. It distinguishes itself from standard ray casting by applying strict filtering based on Scalar Output Scalar (SOS), Attenuation, and Reflection values to discard irrelevant samples, and by converting the resulting scalar data into RGB color via an HSV color space mapping. Unlike adaptive step methods, this implementation uses a fixed number of steps with early termination upon opacity saturation or boundary exit. Inputs: Geometry: A screen-aligned quad representing the viewport. Entry/Exit Points: For each pixel, the 3D coordinates where the ray enters and exits the volume bounding box, passed as varying attributes (frontColor, pos) from a vertex shader. Volume Data: Stored as a series of 2D texture slices (uSliceMaps) arranged in a sprite sheet format, indexed by Z-coordinate. Back Coordination Texture: A 2D texture (uBackCoord) storing the exit point coordinates for each pixel, sampled using normalized fragment coordinates. Parameters: uStepsI: Integer constant for the number of steps per ray (default: 144). uOpacityVal: Uniform float controlling opacity scaling (default: 40). uSlicesOverX, uSlicesOverY: Dimensions of the texture sprite sheet (e.g., 16x16). uNumberOfSlices: Total number of volume slices. minSos, maxSos: Thresholds for the SOS component. minAtten, maxAtten: Thresholds for the Attenuation component. minRefl, maxRefl: Thresholds for the Reflection component. bgColor: Background color (default: vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0)). Outputs: Final Color: The composited RGB color and alpha for each pixel (glFragColor). Volume Texture: A set of 2D textures (uSliceMaps). Each texture contains a grid of slices. The Z-coordinate of the volume is mapped to an index within this sprite sheet. slicesPerSprite = uSlicesOverX uSlicesOverY. Texture coordinate calculation for a volume position volpos: s1Original = floor(volpos.z uNumberOfSlices). tex1Index = int(floor(s1Original / slicesPerSprite)). s1 = mod(s1Original, slicesPerSprite). dx1 = fract(s1 / uSlicesOverX). dy1 = floor(s1 / uSlicesOverY) / uSlicesOverY. texpos1.x = dx1 + (volpos.x / uSlicesOverX). texpos1.y = dy1 + (volpos.y / uSlicesOverY). Sample Value: A 3-component vector grayval returned by getVolumeValue, representing [SOS, Attenuation, Reflection]. 1. Ray Initialization: Calculate normalized texture coordinates texC from the fragment position pos: \text{texC} = \frac{(\text{pos}.xy / \text{pos}.w) + 1.0}{2.0} Sample the exit point from the back coordination texture: \text{backColor} = \text{texture2D}(uBackCoord, \text{texC}) Compute the ray direction vector: \mathbf{dir} = \text{backColor}.rgb - \text{frontColor}.rgb Initialize the current position: \mathbf{vpos} = \text{frontColor} Compute the step size vector: \mathbf{Step} = \frac{\mathbf{dir}}{uStepsF} \quad \text{where } uStepsF = \text{float}(uStepsI) Initialize accumulation buffers: \text{accum} = \text{vec4}(0, 0, 0, 0) \text{sample} = \text{vec4}(0, 0, 0, 0) 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to uStepsI - 1: Sample Volume: Retrieve the volume value at the current position: \text{gray\val} = \text{getVolumeValue}(\mathbf{vpos}.xyz) Filtering: If any component of grayval is outside its defined thresholds, skip shading for this step: \text{if } (\text{gray\val}.z < 0.05 \lor \text{gray\val}.x < \text{minSos} \lor \text{gray\val}.x > \text{maxSos} \lor \text{gray\val}.y < \text{minAtten} \lor \text{gray\val}.y > \text{maxAtten} \lor \text{gray\val}.z < \text{minRefl} \lor \text{gray\val}.z > \text{maxRefl}) Set \text{colorValue} = \text{vec4}(0.0) and continue to the next iteration. Shading (HSV Conversion): Compute the intermediate color value vector: \text{colorValue}.x = \text{gray\val}.x \text{colorValue}.y = 1.0 - \frac{\text{gray\val}.y}{0.6} \text{colorValue}.z = \text{gray\val}.z \text{colorValue}.w = 0.1 Convert HSV to RGB: \text{rgb\color} = \text{hsv2rgb}(\text{colorValue}.rgb) Alpha Calculation: Compute the sample alpha: \text{sample}.a = \text{colorValue}.w \times \text{uOpacityVal} \times \left(\frac{1.0}{uStepsF}\right) Compositing: Compute the sample RGB contribution: \text{sample}.rgb = (1.0 - \text{accum}.a) \times \text{rgb\color} \times \text{sample}.a Update the accumulation buffer: \text{accum}.rgb += \text{sample}.rgb \text{accum}.a += (1.0 - \text{accum}.a) \times \text{sample}.a Termination Checks: If \text{accum}.a \ge 1.0, break the loop. Advance position: \mathbf{vpos}.xyz += \mathbf{Step}. If \mathbf{vpos}.x, \mathbf{vpos}.y, or \mathbf{vpos}.z is outside [0.0, 1.0], break the loop. 3. Output: Set glFragColor to accum. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackhsvraycasting(frontcolor, pos, backcoordtexture, volumeslices, params): """ frontcolor: list of 4 floats [r, g, b, a] representing entry point pos: list of 4 floats [x, y, z, w] clip-space position backcoordtexture: list of lists of lists (texture array) volumeslices: list of texture arrays params: dict containing uStepsI, uOpacityVal, uSlicesOverX, uSlicesOverY, uNumberOfSlices, minSos, maxSos, minAtten, maxAtten, minRefl, maxRefl """ # 1. Ray Initialization texc = ((pos[0] / pos[3]) + 1.0) / 2.0 backcolor = texture2D(backcoordtexture, [texc, texc]) dirvec = [backcolor[0] - frontcolor[0], backcolor[1] - frontcolor[1], backcolor[2] - frontcolor[2]] vpos = [frontcolor[0], frontcolor[1], frontcolor[2]] step = [dirvec[0] / params['uStepsI'], dirvec[1] / params['uStepsI'], dirvec[2] / params['uStepsI']] accum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 2. Ray Marching for i in range(params['uStepsI']): grayval = getvolumevalue(vpos, volumeslices, params) # Filtering if (grayval[2] < 0.05 or grayval[0] < params['minSos'] or grayval[0] > params['maxSos'] or grayval[1] < params['minAtten'] or grayval[1] > params['maxAtten'] or grayval[2] < params['minRefl'] or grayval[2] > params['maxRefl']): colorvalue = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: # Shading colorvalue = [ grayval[0], 1.0 - grayval[1] / 0.6, grayval[2], 0.1 ] # Alpha Calculation samplealpha = colorvalue[3] params['uOpacityVal'] (1.0 / params['uStepsI']) # Compositing rgbcolor = hsvtorgb(colorvalue[:3]) samplergb = [(1.0 - accum[3]) rgbcolor[0] samplealpha, (1.0 - accum[3]) rgbcolor[1] samplealpha, (1.0 - accum[3]) rgbcolor[2] samplealpha] accum[0] += samplergb[0] accum[1] += samplergb[1] accum[2] += samplergb[2] accum[3] += (1.0 - accum[3]) samplealpha # Termination if accum[3] >= 1.0: break vpos[0] += step[0] vpos[1] += step[1] vpos[2] += step[2] # Boundary Check if not (0.0 <= vpos[0] <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= vpos[1] <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= vpos[2] <= 1.0): break return accum def getvolumevalue(volpos, volumeslices, params): """ Simulates 3D texture lookup using 2D slice textures. Returns vec3 (SOS, Attenuation, Reflection) """ slicespersprite = params['uSlicesOverX'] params['uSlicesOverY'] s1original = int(volpos[2] params['uNumberOfSlices']) tex1index = int(s1original // slicespersprite) s1 = s1original % slicespersprite dx1 = (s1 / params['uSlicesOverX']) % 1.0 dy1 = (s1 // params['uSlicesOverY']) / params['uSlicesOverY'] texpos1 = [ dx1 + (volpos[0] / params['uSlicesOverX']), dy1 + (volpos[1] / params['uSlicesOverY']) ] # Clamp index to avoid out-of-bounds access tex1index = max(0, min(tex1index, len(volumeslices) - 1)) value = texture2D(volumeslices[tex1index], texpos1) return value[:3] def hsvtorgb(hsv): """ Standard HSV to RGB conversion. H in [0,1], S in [0,1], V in [0,1] """ h, s, v = hsv if s == 0.0: return [v, v, v] i = int(h 6.0) % 6 f = h 6.0 - int(h 6.0) p = v (1.0 - s) q = v (1.0 - f s) t = v (1.0 - (1.0 - f) s) if i == 0: return [v, t, p] elif i == 1: return [q, v, p] elif i == 2: return [p, v, t] elif i == 3: return [p, q, v] elif i == 4: return [t, p, v] else: return [v, p, q] def texture2D(tex, uv): # Standard 2D texture lookup returning vec4 # Returns a list of 4 floats [r, g, b, a] return [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0] Out-of-Bounds Access: The loop must check if vpos coordinates exceed [0.0, 1.0] to prevent memory access errors. Alpha Clamping: Accumulated alpha can exceed 1.0 due to floating-point precision or high opacity. It should be clamped to 1.0, and the loop should break. Ray Length: Termination must account for the exact ray length to avoid sampling outside the volume. Filtering Thresholds: Incorrectly set thresholds for SOS, Attenuation, or Reflection can result in empty renders or visual artifacts. The source uses a hardcoded check for grayval.z < 0.05 in addition to the configurable thresholds. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of steps per ray (fixed at 144 in the reference implementation). Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the size of the volume data stored in 2D texture slices. Performance: The fixed step count (144) provides predictable performance but lacks the efficiency of adaptive stepping. Early termination on opacity saturation (\alpha \ge 1.0) reduces average computation time for opaque regions. Strengths: Simple implementation, efficient early termination, flexible color mapping via HSV. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or slow convergence in sparse regions; reliance on 2D texture slices for 3D lookup can be complex to manage. This method is derived from direct volume rendering techniques that use front-to-back compositing. It builds on the principles of ray casting and compositing, adapting them for specific data types where scalar values need to be mapped to color via HSV space. levl-dev/VolumeRayCasting0, https://github.com/levl-dev/VolumeRayCasting0, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: LOS-integration for visualization
head: LUT-based Line-of-Sight Integration, column_ne integration, emission integration, ewt_temp integration
body: LOS-integration for visualization computes scalar physical quantities (electron column density, integrated emissivity, or emission-weighted temperature) along camera rays by integrating sampled neural field outputs or ground truth data. It differs from standard volume rendering compositing by performing a direct line-of-sight integral of the physical quantity itself, rather than compositing color and opacity to produce an image. This method is specifically designed for solar physics visualization to avoid artifacts from the saturated chromospheric base by restricting integration to the corona shell. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape (N, 3). raysd: Ray directions, shape (N, 3). ts: Start times/parameters for segments, shape (M,). te: End times/parameters for segments, shape (M,). rayidx: Indices mapping segment samples to rays, shape (M,). valid: Boolean mask for valid rays, shape (N,). quantity: String specifying the integrand: 'columnne', 'emission', or 'ewttemp'. uniformsamples: Integer; if >0, uniform sampling is used; otherwise point sampling is used. rminrsun, rmaxrsun: Floats or None; radial bounds in solar radii to restrict integration. channels: List, tuple, int, or None; spectral line indices to select for emission quantities. aabbscale: Scaling factor to convert AABB coordinates to physical units. rsuntocm: Conversion constant, default 6.957 \times 10^{10} cm/R{\odot}. wavelengths: List of wavelengths in Angstroms for photon-to-erg conversion. nefield, tempfield: Optional ground truth field query functions. ccoeffield: Neural network or field mapping (\log ne, \log T, \log r) to emissivity coefficients. Outputs: full: Tensor of shape (N, C), where C is the number of intensity channels (or 1 for column density). Contains NaN for invalid rays. The method operates on PyTorch tensors. The core data structure for integration is the output accumulator, initialized to zeros for valid rays. The intermediate values are computed per sample point. 1. Ray Initialization: Convert rayso and raysd to the renderer's dtype and device. 2. Sampling: If uniformsamples > 0, call sampleuniformshell to obtain ts, te, rayidx, and valid. Otherwise, call samplepointsalongrays to obtain these values. 3. Coordinate Computation: Compute segment midpoints: t{mid} = 0.5 \times (ts + te). Compute Cartesian coordinates in AABB space: \mathbf{x}{AABB} = \text{rays\o}[\text{valid}][\text{ray\idx}] + t{mid} \times \text{rays\d}[\text{valid}][\text{ray\idx}]. Convert to physical units: \mathbf{x}{xyz} = \mathbf{x}{AABB} \times \text{aabb\scale}. 4. Radial Masking: Compute sample radius: r{samp} = \|\mathbf{x}{xyz}\|. Initialize mask keepw to ones. If rminrsun is not None, multiply keepw by (r{samp} \ge r{min\rsun}). If rmaxrsun is not None, multiply keepw by (r{samp} \le r{max\rsun}). This prevents artifacts from the saturated chromospheric base. 5. Integration Helper: Define integ(vals) which initializes an output tensor of size N{valid} and accumulates values using out.indexadd(0, rayidx, vals seglen keepw). 8. Quantity Calculation: If quantity == 'columnne': Compute per-ray column density: P{ray} = \text{integ}(10^{\log ne}). P{ray} = N / \max(D, 10^{-30}). 9. Finalization: Initialize full tensor of shape (N, C) with NaN. Set full[valid] = P{ray}. Return full. Unverified code. name: Monte Carlo Path Tracing for Volume Rendering
head: MC VPT, Monte Carlo Path Tracing, Monte Carlo Volumetric Path Tracing, P=KU Implementation, Path Tracing Volume Rendering, VPT
body: Monte Carlo Path Tracing for Volume Rendering is a unified, brute-force, progressive stochastic rendering framework that produces photo-realistic images of volumetric data without relying on pre-computed quantities or auxiliary volumes. It distinguishes itself from traditional ray marching by using Woodcock tracking to efficiently handle light attenuation and shadows, and by integrating depth-of-field and hybrid surface/volumetric scattering through stochastic sampling rather than slice-based approximations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data (typically 16-bit unsigned short), camera parameters (MVP matrix, lens aperture), lighting configuration (environment, point, area lights), transfer function (opacity \alpha, color), and maximum extinction coefficient \sigma{max}. Output: A Low Dynamic Range (LDR) image, accumulated progressively over frames. Data Structures: Accumulator Buffer: Stores the running Monte Carlo estimate of the High Dynamic Range (HDR) color. Frame Buffer: Stores the current frame's HDR estimate. Camera Parameters: Stored in constant memory for fast access. Lights: Stored in constant memory. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Unproject screen position to get ray origin vRayFrom and ray end vRayTo using the inverse MVP matrix. Construct a camera ray using a thin lens model: sample a point on the lens and a perturbed point within the pixel area on the film plane using stratified sampling. Intersect the ray with the volume’s bounding box to obtain parametric range [t{bounds}.x, t{bounds}.y]. If t{bounds}.x \ge t{bounds}.y, the ray misses the volume; sample the environment map and output as color. 2. Initialization: Calculate ray segment from and to within the cube and maxDistance. Initialize seed: seed = vPosition + rand(vec2(uOffset, uOffset)). Initialize from to the ray origin at the bounding box entry point. 3. Scattering Point Selection (Woodcock Tracking): To find the first scattering point, use Woodcock tracking: 1. Generate a path length s using the maximum extinction coefficient \sigma{max}. 2. Accept the tentative collision point with probability \sigmat(p(s)) / \sigma{max}, where \sigmat is the extinction coefficient at point p(s). 3. Repeat until a collision is accepted. Alternatively, implemented via sampleDistance(from, to, seed): 1. Initialize dist = 0.0, invSigmaMax = 1.0 / uSigmaMax, invMaxDistance = 1.0 / maxDistance. 2. Loop: generate random seed, update dist -= log(1.0 - seed.x) invSigmaMax. 3. If dist > maxDistance, break loop. 4. Calculate samplingPosition = mix(from, to, dist invMaxDistance). 5. Get alphaSample = transferSample.a uAlphaCorrection. 6. If seed.y < alphaSample invSigmaMax, break loop. If the loop breaks due to dist > maxDistance, sample the environment map and output. 4. Lighting and Transmittance Calculation: Update from to the scattering point: from = mix(from, to, dist / maxDistance). Calculate transmittance from from to to using sampleTransmittance(from, to, seed): 1. Initialize transmittance = 1.0. 2. Loop similarly to sampleDistance, updating transmittance = 1.0 - alphaSample invSigmaMax. Compute direct lighting contribution: 1. Form light ray R{light} connecting scattering point ps to a stochastically sampled point on a stochastically chosen light source. 2. Apply Woodcock tracking to R{light} to determine if blocked. If the resulting scattering point p's is beyond ps, the ray is unblocked; add light's exitant radiance Le. 3. Sample scattering function yielding scattering ray R{scattering}; intersect with light to compute contribution. 4. Combine contributions using Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) with the power heuristic. Hybrid Scattering Decision: 1. Draw random number j from uniform distribution. 2. Compare j to P{brdf}. If j < P{brdf}, treat as surface scattering (BRDF); otherwise, treat as volumetric scattering (Phase function). 3. P{brdf} = \alphax \cdot (1 - \exp(-25 \cdot g \cdot \|\nabla{tn}(x)\|)), where \alphax is opacity, \|\nabla{tn}(x)\| is normalized gradient magnitude, and g \in [0,1] is gradient factor. 4. For surface scattering, use Fresnel blend shading model. For volumetric, use isotropic phase function (or Schlick's). 5. Color Accumulation: Sample diffuse color at from: diffuseColor = sampleVolumeColor(from). Sample light color: lightColor = sampleEnvironmentMap(uScatteringDirection). Calculate final color: oColor = diffuseColor \times lightColor \times transmittance. Accumulate frame: acc = texture(uAccumulator, vPosition), frame = texture(uFrame, vPosition). Update accumulator: oColor = acc + (frame - acc) uInvFrameNumber. 6. Post-Processing: Filter HDR MC estimate with separable Gaussian kernel (standard deviation 1.5, window 5x5 pixels) to reduce anti-aliasing. Compute cumulative moving average for Monte Carlo integration. Tone map HDR estimate to compress dynamic range. Gamma correct. An-isotropically filter LDR image to reduce noise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def mix(a, b, t): return a + (b - a) t def samplephasefunction(direction): phi = random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) costheta = random.uniform(-1, 1) sintheta = math.sqrt(1 - costheta2) return (sintheta math.cos(phi), sintheta math.sin(phi), costheta) def woodcocktrackingray(origin, direction, maxdist, sigmamax, volumesampler): dist = 0.0 invsigmamax = 1.0 / sigmamax while dist < maxdist: r = random.uniform(0, 1) dist -= math.log(1.0 - r) invsigmamax if dist >= maxdist: return False, None pos = mix(origin, origin + direction maxdist, dist / maxdist) sigmat = volumesampler.getextinction(pos) raccept = random.uniform(0, 1) if raccept < sigmat / sigmamax: return True, pos return False, None def montecarlovolumerendering(pixelpos, cameraparams, volumedata, transferfunc, lights, sigmamax, alphacorrection, gradientfactor, framenumber): # 1. Ray Generation rayorigin = cameraparams.unproject(pixelpos) raydirection = cameraparams.samplelensandpixel(pixelpos) tmin, tmax = intersectboundingbox(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata.bbox) if tmin >= tmax: return sampleenvironmentmap(raydirection) maxdistance = tmax - tmin frompoint = rayorigin + tmin raydirection topoint = rayorigin + tmax raydirection seed = pixelpos + random.uniform(0, 1) cameraparams.uOffset # 2. Scattering Point Selection (Woodcock Tracking / sampleDistance) dist = 0.0 invsigmamax = 1.0 / sigmamax invmaxdistance = 1.0 / maxdistance while dist < maxdistance: r1 = random.uniform(0, 1) dist -= math.log(1.0 - r1) invsigmamax if dist >= maxdistance: break samplingpos = mix(frompoint, topoint, dist invmaxdistance) alphasample = transferfunc.samplealpha(samplingpos) alphacorrection r2 = random.uniform(0, 1) if r2 < alphasample invsigmamax: break if dist >= maxdistance: return sampleenvironmentmap(raydirection) scatteringpoint = mix(frompoint, topoint, dist invmaxdistance) # 3. Transmittance Calculation transmittance = 1.0 distt = 0.0 while distt < maxdistance: r1 = random.uniform(0, 1) distt -= math.log(1.0 - r1) invsigmamax if distt >= maxdistance: break samplingpost = mix(frompoint, topoint, distt invmaxdistance) alphasamplet = transferfunc.samplealpha(samplingpost) alphacorrection transmittance = 1.0 - alphasamplet invsigmamax # 4. Lighting and Hybrid Scattering gradmag = computenormalizedgradient(scatteringpoint, volumedata) pbrdf = transferfunc.samplealpha(scatteringpoint) (1.0 - math.exp(-25.0 gradientfactor gradmag)) rhybrid = random.uniform(0, 1) if rhybrid < pbrdf: color = samplefresnelblendbrdf(scatteringpoint, raydirection, lights) else: scatteringdir = samplephasefunction(raydirection) lightcolor = sampleenvironmentmap(scatteringdir) diffusecolor = samplevolumecolor(scatteringpoint, transferfunc) # Light attenuation via Woodcock tracking on light ray isunblocked, = woodcocktrackingray(scatteringpoint, scatteringdir, maxdistance, sigmamax, volumedata) if isunblocked: color = diffusecolor lightcolor transmittance else: color = vec4(0.0) # 5. Accumulation currentacc = getaccumulatorbuffer(pixelpos) currentframe = color invframenumber = 1.0 / framenumber newacc = currentacc + (currentframe - currentacc) invframenumber setaccumulatorbuffer(pixelpos, newacc) # 6. Post-Processing filteredacc = gaussianfilter(newacc, std=1.5, window=5) tonemapped = tonemap(filteredacc) gammacorrected = tonemapped (1.0 / 2.2) finalcolor = anisotropicfilter(gammacorrected) return finalcolor Parameters: sigmamax (uSigmaMax): Maximum scattering coefficient used for distance sampling. alphacorrection (uAlphaCorrection): Correction factor for alpha values from transfer function. gradientfactor (g): Controls surface/volumetric scattering amount, range [0-1]. uOffset: Offset for random seed generation. uInvFrameNumber: Inverse of current frame number for exponential moving average accumulation. Gaussian kernel: Standard deviation 1.5, window 5x5 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise at Startup: Objectionable noise occurs at the start of the MC algorithm. A noise reduction filter is applied during initial iterations, increasing blurring initially, with influence reducing based on the error in the running estimate. Ray Marching Performance: Standard Ray Marching becomes prohibitively slow for shadow calculations at every sample. Woodcock tracking is used to yield far fewer shadow computations and remains unbiased. Reset Condition: If transfer function, lighting, or camera position changes, the Monte Carlo integrated estimate buffer must be cleared and the algorithm restarted. A real-time denoising algorithm for DVR in MR systems that exploits temporal coherence between adjacent frames and spatial coherence between HMD screens to reduce noise from MC estimation. It identifies three corresponding reprojected pixels for a target pixel: one on the other HMD screen in the current frame, and two on the left and right HMD screens in the previous frame. It calculates their contribution using a weight function and performs spatio-temporal denoising to reduce visual discomfort caused by MC estimation noise. Time Complexity: Progressive convergence. Performance is measured in frame estimates per second. Memory Complexity: Insensitive to lighting, material, camera, and transfer function configurations. Does not require pre-computed quantities or additional volumes. Measured Performance (800x600 resolution, 16-bit unsigned short data): Mecanix (512x743x512): 35.2 (Front), 34.1 (Left), 36.3 (Top) fps. Manix (512x460x512): 32.7 (Front), 39.7 (Left), 42.4 (Top) fps. Engine (256x256x128): 65.5 (Front), 53.7 (Left), 65.7 (Top) fps. Bonsai (256x256x257): 57.7 (Front), 66.6 (Left), 68.1 (Top) fps. Artifix (512x347x512): 47.3 (Front), 40.3 (Left), 50.8 (Top) fps. Strengths: Photo-realism, unified handling of isosurfaces and volumes, support for complex lighting (directional, point, environment), depth-of-field via stochastic sampling, unbiased. Limitations: Noise at low frame counts requires filtering; progressive nature means no single-frame instant result without accumulation. Origin: Developed by Csébfalvi et al. as part of the Exposure Render framework. History: Csébfalvi et al. were the first to apply Monte Carlo integration to volume rendering to solve depth-of-field effects and achieve photo-realism. The method was demonstrated on datasets including Mecanix, Manix, Engine, Bonsai, Artifix, and a bat CT scan. Usage: Implemented in the Exposure Render framework. name: Ray Traversal Schemes
head: Accumulate Projection, Depth Projection, Max Intensity Projection, Projection Methods, Ray Traversal -Accumulate
body: Ray Traversal Schemes define the aggregation logic applied to voxel samples collected along a ray to produce a final pixel value. While Ray Marching and Discretization determines where to sample, these schemes determine how to combine those samples. They are distinguished from standard front-to-back alpha compositing by their ability to perform non-compositional aggregations (such as Maximum or Average) or to simplify the compositing process for specific visualization goals like X-ray simulation. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, step size \Delta t, volume data grid with voxel colors Ci and opacities \alphai (or scalar intensities), and transfer functions mapping scalar values to Ci, \alphai. Outputs: Final pixel color C and accumulated opacity \alpha. Data structures: A 3D texture or grid storing voxel attributes; per-ray accumulators for color C and opacity \alpha. Steps: 1. Initialize accumulators: C \leftarrow (0, 0, 0), \alpha \leftarrow 0. 2. Iterate along the ray from the near clipping plane to the far clipping plane with step \Delta t. 3. At each step, query the volume at position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to obtain sample color Cs and opacity \alphas using interpolation (e.g., trilinear). 4. Apply the selected aggregation scheme to update C and \alpha. 5. Terminate early if \alpha \geq 1.0 (for Accumulate) or after traversing the full volume extent. Formulas (Accumulate/Front-to-Back): C \leftarrow Cs \alphas (1 - \alpha) + C \alpha \leftarrow \alphas (1 - \alpha) + \alpha where C is the accumulated color, \alpha is the accumulated opacity, Cs is the sample color, \alphas is the sample opacity, and t is the current ray parameter. Other schemes modify step 4: First: Stop at the first voxel where \alphas > \tau (threshold). Max: C \leftarrow \max(C, Cs), \alpha \leftarrow 1.0. Average: Sum Cs and count steps, return \frac{1}{N}\sum Cs. Depth: Accumulate t values weighted by \alphas. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytraversal(rayorigin, raydir, farplane, stepsize, scheme, threshold=0.5): C = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 intensitysum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] stepcount = 0 depthaccum = 0.0 while t <= farplane: p = rayorigin + raydir t # Interpolate Cs, alphas at p from volume grid Cs, alphas = samplevolume(p) if scheme == "accumulate": C = [Cs[i] alphas (1.0 - alpha) + C[i] for i in range(3)] alpha = alphas (1.0 - alpha) + alpha if alpha >= 1.0: break elif scheme == "first": if alphas > threshold: return Cs elif scheme == "max": C = [max(C[i], Cs[i]) for i in range(3)] alpha = 1.0 elif scheme == "average": intensitysum = [intensitysum[i] + Cs[i] for i in range(3)] stepcount += 1 elif scheme == "depth": depthaccum += t alphas alpha += alphas t += stepsize if scheme == "average": return [intensitysum[i] / stepcount for i in range(3)] if stepcount > 0 else C elif scheme == "depth": return [depthaccum / alpha] if alpha > 0 else [0.0] return C Edge cases and pitfalls: Zero direction components require axis-aligned traversal logic to avoid division by zero; precision loss in deep volumes requires normalized depth or early termination; degenerate rays (origin inside volume) need near-plane clamping. Integrates radiance over a pixel footprint using aggregated visibility functions to handle inter-voxel correlation and background blending without order-dependent ray marching. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by precomputing visibility terms to approximate complex integration, allowing efficient level-of-detail rendering. Choose it when rendering scenes with complex background interactions or when inter-voxel correlation matters. Simulates a transmission view (such as a CT scan) by linearly accumulating or averaging voxel intensity values along a ray, ignoring alpha compositing for the final accumulation logic. It differs from its sibling Pixel Intensity Evaluation with Scene Aggregates by operating directly on volumetric data via ray traversal rather than scene aggregates. Choose it when a transparent/transmissive appearance representing mean or sum of densities is required. Casts a ray from the pixel, samples all associated voxels, and chooses the one with the highest occupancy probability. Choose it for binary occupancy visualization. Computes the probability that a ray stops at a certain distance, allowing rendering of depth maps, color images, and foreground masks. Choose it when differentiable depth/color outputs are needed. Introduces a bidirectional emission-absorption (EA) light radiation model for emitting materials, in addition to visual hull (VH) and absorption-only (AO) models. Choose it for scenes with self-illuminating volumetric materials. Casts a ray from each pixel and iteratively accumulates color and opacity probabilities. Remaining voxels are discarded when cumulative opacity reaches a maximum value. Choose it for differentiable rendering with early termination. Casts a ray from the pixel and locates the surface voxel closest to the camera. The final pixel color is computed as a weighted sum of the surface voxel and its neighboring voxels, with shading based on normals computed from voxel values. Choose it for differentiable surface rendering from signed distance fields. Time and memory complexity per ray are not given in the sources. Measured performance on specific hardware and resolution scaling are not given in the sources. Strengths include hardware-friendly early termination for the Accumulate scheme, specialized visualization modes for MIP in angiography, and X-ray simulation for Average. Limitations include order-dependence in standard accumulation and potential aliasing without proper sampling rates. The classification of ray traversal schemes into Intensity, Max, Average, Accumulate, First, and Depth was established in early direct volume rendering literature. The "Accumulate" scheme, which performs front-to-back compositing, is attributed to Levoy (1988) and is designed to make transparent layers visible. The "Max" scheme, or Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP), is widely used in Magnetic Resonance Angiography. The "Average" scheme produces an X-ray-like picture by averaging values along the ray. The "First" scheme extracts iso-surfaces. These schemes form the basis of the compositing stage in the volume rendering pipeline, following ray-tracing/resampling and preceding image pixel output. name: Voxel Aggregation Methods
body: Voxel aggregation methods determine the final pixel color and properties by combining voxel values along a ray cast from the camera. They solve the problem of mapping 3D volumetric data to a 2D image while maintaining differentiability with respect to the voxel inputs, enabling gradient-based optimization in differentiable rendering pipelines. Unlike sibling methods such as Pixel Intensity Evaluation with Scene Aggregates or X-Ray Volume Rendering, these methods explicitly traverse the voxel grid along viewing rays to accumulate or select values. Inputs: Voxel grid storing per-voxel attributes (occupancy probability, SDF, color, opacity) and camera parameters (origin, direction). Outputs: Pixel color, opacity, depth, and optionally normals. Data structures: 3D array for voxel grid; ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. The general process involves casting a ray from each pixel through the voxel grid and applying a specific aggregation function to the sampled voxels. Yan et al. [7] associate an occupancy probability with each pixel. 1. Cast a ray from the pixel. 2. Sample all voxels intersected by the ray. 3. Compute the pixel value as the maximum occupancy probability among the sampled voxels. C{\text{pixel}} = \max{v \in \text{ray}} P{\text{occ}}(v) Where P{\text{occ}}(v) is the occupancy probability of voxel v. Tulsiani et al. [29] compute the probability that a ray stops at a certain distance, allowing rendering of depth maps, color images, and foreground masks. 1. Cast a ray. 2. For each voxel v at distance dv with opacity \alphav, compute the probability that the ray terminates at v. 3. Aggregate color and depth weighted by these termination probabilities. This method extends simple max-aggregation by modeling the ray as a probabilistic event stopping at a specific depth. Henzler et al. [30] introduce bidirectional emission-absorption (EA) light radiation models, in addition to visual hull (VH) and absorption-only (AO) models similar to Tulsiani et al.. AO: Standard volume rendering where light is absorbed. EA: Voxels can emit light, requiring integration of emission and absorption along the ray. C{\text{out}} = \int{tn}^{tf} \sigma(t) c(t) e^{-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(s) \, ds} \, dt + C{\text{bg}} e^{-\int{tn}^{tf} \sigma(s) \, ds} Where \sigma is density, c is color/emission, and C{\text{bg}} is background color. Lombardi et al. [31] iteratively accumulate color and opacity probabilities. 1. Cast a ray. 2. Iterate through voxels vi along the ray. 3. Accumulate color C and opacity \alpha: C{\text{accum}} = \sum{i} ci \alphai \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) \alpha{\text{accum}} = \sum{i} \alphai \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) 4. Pitfall/Guard: Discard remaining voxels when cumulative opacity \alpha{\text{accum}} reaches a maximum threshold (e.g., 1.0) to prevent further impact on color and save computation. Jiang et al. [32] handle voxels representing Signed Distance Functions (SDF). 1. Cast a ray. 2. Locate the surface voxel vs closest to the camera (where SDF value is near zero). Note: Locating the surface point is not a differentiable operation. 3. Compute final pixel color as a weighted sum of the surface voxel and its neighboring voxels. 4. Compute normal vector \mathbf{n} at the surface point based on voxel values around the surface point for shading. Note: Although surface location is non-differentiable, the pixel color is differentiable with respect to the voxels around the surface point. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def aggregateraymarch(voxelgrid, rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, maxsteps=100, alphathreshold=0.99): """ Aggregates voxel values along a ray using iterative accumulation. voxelgrid: 3D array of (color, opacity) tuples. rayorigin: (x, y, z) raydirection: (dx, dy, dz) normalized. stepsize: float, distance between consecutive samples. """ currentpos = list(rayorigin) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 for in range(maxsteps): # Sample voxel at currentpos, return (0,0) if out of bounds color, opacity = samplevoxel(voxelgrid, currentpos) # Contribution of this voxel contribution = [c opacity transmittance for c in color] accumulatedcolor = [a + c for a, c in zip(accumulatedcolor, contribution)] accumulatedopacity += opacity transmittance # Update transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - opacity) # Early termination if cumulative opacity reaches threshold if accumulatedopacity >= alphathreshold: break # Move along ray currentpos = [p + d stepsize for p, d in zip(currentpos, raydirection)] return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity def samplevoxel(grid, pos): # Bounds check and nearest-neighbor lookup if not (0 <= pos[0] < grid.shape[0] and 0 <= pos[1] < grid.shape[1] and 0 <= pos[2] < grid.shape[2]): return (0.0, 0.0) ix, iy, iz = int(pos[0]), int(pos[1]), int(pos[2]) return grid[ix][iy][iz] A streaming dense voxel aggregation module that performs temporal warping of cached voxel features and aggregates them with current frame features to predict 3D occupancy. It aligns past voxel features to the current ego frame using motion-aware warping and rectifies interpolation artifacts introduced during warping or aggregation using adaptive residual refinement. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by propagating dense voxel features through a recurrent streaming buffer rather than relying solely on static spatial aggregation or query-based instance propagation. A rendering integration technique using a K-D tree structure to aggregate point features, normals, and IST (Intensity/Signal Transmission) along ray segments for color modeling. For rendering integration, uniformly select s points on the ray intersect interval (including endpoints). Apply spline integration using the features of the selected points. For each selected point, use its K nearest neighbors (KNN) to interpolate features, normals, and IST. Calculate average point feature, average normal vector, and average IST for each segment. Use the average point feature, average normal vector, and average IST in the color modeling of the representative point. Parameters: K-D tree depth is 21 layers, containing up to 2^{21} (~2 million) points. Voxel layers for rendering use the bottom 4 non-leaf layers, and the 5th layer from the bottom is used only for point cloud growing. Integration sample counts s are 8, 11, 16, 22, 22 for the 5 used layers from the bottom. KNN size for interpolation is K=32. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Differentiable with respect to voxel inputs, enabling gradient-based optimization. Flexible support for various output types (depth, color, masks). Limitations: Locating surface points (SDF methods) is non-differentiable, though gradients can be approximated via neighboring voxels. When to use: Differentiable rendering pipelines, neural rendering, and optimization tasks where gradients through the volume are required. Originating from differentiable rendering research, these methods were developed to enable gradient-based optimization of 3D representations. Key contributions include Yan et al. [7] for occupancy probability, Tulsiani et al. [29] for depth/color probability, Henzler et al. [30] for emission-absorption models, Lombardi et al. [31] for differentiable ray marching, and Jiang et al. [32] for SDF-based surface extraction.
