name: Depth Compositing Speculated Intersections
head: Closest Hit Selection, Speculation Depth Compositing
body: This method performs depth compositing on a set of potential intersections found for each ray during speculative ray traversal. It iterates through N{Spec} candidates to select the closest valid hit and writes the result to the framebuffer, marking rays that exit the volume without a hit as terminated. It differs from non-speculative compositing by handling multiple block IDs per ray ID, requiring an offset buffer to resolve unique ray-block pairs. Inputs: N{Spec}: Speculation count per ray. RID: Buffer of ray IDs, where each active ray ID appears N{Spec} times. O{Spec}: Offset buffer providing the index into the intersection data for each ray-block pair. Intersection data: Depth values and other attributes for the N{Spec} blocks traversed by each ray. w, h: Image width and height. N{Act}: Number of currently active rays. Outputs: Framebuffer: Final color/depth for each pixel. Termination status: Marks rays that did not hit a surface. Data Structures: RID: Array of size N{Act} \times N{Spec}. Contains ray identifiers. Not unique per entry; duplicates indicate multiple speculation slots for the same ray. O{Spec}: Array of size N{Act} \times N{Spec}. Stores offsets into the intersection results buffer, allowing the kernel to access the correct depth/value for each specific ray-block intersection. Parameters: N{Spec} = \lfloor \frac{w \times h}{N{Act}} \rfloor. Maximum N{Spec} = 64. Steps: 1. For each active ray r in the active set: 2. Initialize closest\hit = \infty and hit\found = false. 3. For i from 0 to N{Spec} - 1: 4. Retrieve the ray ID rid = RID[r \times N{Spec} + i]. 5. Retrieve the offset offset = O{Spec}[r \times N{Spec} + i]. 6. Retrieve the depth d and attributes from the intersection data at offset. 7. If d < closest\hit: 8. closest\hit = d 9. best\result = attributes 10. hit\found = true 11. If hit\found: 12. Write the attributes from best\result to the framebuffer at the pixel corresponding to ray r. 13. Else: 14. Mark ray r as terminated. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthcompositingspeculatedintersections(RID, OSpec, intersectiondata, NSpec, NAct): """ Selects the closest intersection for each active ray from NSpec candidates. """ framebuffer = [None] NAct terminated = [False] NAct for r in range(NAct): closestdepth = float('inf') bestresult = None hitfound = False for i in range(NSpec): offset = OSpec[r NSpec + i] depth, attributes = intersectiondata[offset] if depth < closestdepth: closestdepth = depth bestresult = attributes hitfound = True if hitfound: framebuffer[r] = bestresult else: terminated[r] = True return framebuffer, terminated Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Without 64-bit atomics, depth sorting must be performed in this compositing step rather than during traversal. The speculation count is capped at 64 to balance between terminating rays in fewer passes and performing unnecessary computation. This method constructs the input buffers required for a raytracing kernel when speculative intersection detection is enabled. Time Complexity: O(N{Act} \times N{Spec}) per pass. Since N{Spec} \approx \frac{w \times h}{N{Act}}, total work is O(w \times h) per pass, independent of N{Act}. Memory Complexity: Requires buffers for RID and O{Spec} of size N{Act} \times N{Spec} \approx w \times h. Performance: Evaluated on datasets from 256^3 to 2048 \times 2048 \times 1920 voxels. Strengths: Allows efficient use of GPU resources by reusing terminated ray slots for speculation. Limitations: Requires multiple passes if N{Spec} is small; limited to 64 speculation slots. Described as the final compositing step in speculative progressive raycasting for memory-constrained isosurface visualization of massive volumes. The method addresses the non-uniqueness of ray IDs in speculative traversal by introducing offset buffers. name: Speculated Raytracing Kernel Inputs Construction
head: Build Speculated Raytracing Kernel Inputs
body: This method constructs the input buffers required for a raytracing kernel when speculative intersection detection is enabled. It solves the problem of non-unique ray identifiers in the active ray ID buffer, where a single ray ID may appear multiple times corresponding to potential intersections in different blocks. It differs from the non-speculative input construction by introducing an offset buffer to uniquely index each ray-block intersection pair, enabling the kernel to output multiple results per ray for later compositing. Inputs: M{RAct}: Buffer marking active ray-block intersections, produced during the compaction of active ray IDs. I{RAct}: Active ray ID buffer, containing ray IDs repeated N{Spec} times. Outputs: O{Spec}: Offset buffer assigning a unique index to each ray-block intersection. I{BVis}: List of visible block IDs. N{BRays}: Number of rays to process for each visible block. O{BRays}: Offsets into the ray ID buffer for each visible block. Data Structures: O{Spec}: An integer buffer with the same layout as I{RAct}, storing unique indices for each entry in I{RAct}. I{RAct}: Array of ray IDs, compacted to active entries and sorted by block ID. Steps: 1. Scan M{RAct} to produce O{Spec}: Iterate through the buffer M{RAct} which marks active ray-block intersections. Assign a unique sequential index to each active intersection. This index serves as the unique identifier for that specific ray-block pair, resolving the ambiguity caused by repeated ray IDs in I{RAct}. 2. Compact and Sort O{Spec}: Compact O{Spec} to retain only entries corresponding to active ray-block intersections. Sort these entries by block ID to ensure alignment with the sorted order of I{RAct}. 3. Produce Block Metadata: Generate the list of visible block IDs (I{BVis}), the count of rays per block (N{BRays}), and the starting offsets for each block's rays (O{BRays}) using the same logic as the non-speculative case, but operating on the now-aligned and unique data structures. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildspeculatedkernelinputs(MRAct, IRAct): # Step 1: Scan MRAct to produce unique indices # MRAct marks which entries in IRAct are active intersections OSpec = [] uniqueindex = 0 for i in range(len(MRAct)): if MRAct[i] is active: OSpec.append(uniqueindex) uniqueindex += 1 else: # Placeholder for inactive entries, to be removed in compaction OSpec.append(None) # Step 2: Compact OSpec to active entries only OSpeccompact = [idx for idx in OSpec if idx is not None] # Step 3: Sort OSpeccompact by block ID # This requires pairing OSpeccompact with the corresponding block IDs from IRAct # Assuming IRAct is already sorted by block ID or we have a parallel block ID array # For clarity, we assume IRAct and OSpeccompact are aligned by index # We need to sort them together based on block ID # Extract block IDs corresponding to active rays # This step assumes access to block ID mapping for each ray in IRAct # Let's assume we have a function getblockid(rayid) or a parallel array # Since the source says "sorted by block ID to match the order of IRAct", # we perform a stable sort or re-indexing. # Simplified representation of sorting: # Create pairs of (blockid, uniqueindex) pairs = [] for i, idx in enumerate(OSpeccompact): # Placeholder: In practice, block ID is derived from the ray or block context # The source implies IRAct is sorted by block ID, so we sort OSpec accordingly blockid = getblockidforactiveentry(i) # Helper to retrieve block ID pairs.append((blockid, idx)) # Sort by block ID pairs.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Extract sorted unique indices OSpecsorted = [idx for, idx in pairs] # Step 3: Produce block metadata (IBVis, NBRays, OBRays) # This is done "as before" using the sorted IRAct and OSpecsorted IBVis, NBRays, OBRays = produceblockmetadata(IRAct, OSpecsorted) return OSpecsorted, IBVis, NBRays, OBRays Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The number of speculated intersections N{Spec} must be consistent across all rays to ensure buffer sizes are predictable. Degenerate Input: If M{RAct} is empty, the output buffers will be empty, and no raytracing kernel launch is required. This variant modifies the raytracing kernel to output intersection results to a new RGBZ buffer instead of directly to the framebuffer. This allows multiple intersections per ray to be stored for later depth compositing. The kernel writes color and depth values for intersections at offsets given in O{Spec} for the ray-block intersection. Time and Memory Complexity: The construction involves a scan and a sort, which are linear and O(N \log N) respectively with respect to the number of active ray-block intersections. Memory overhead includes the additional O{Spec} buffer, which has the same size as the active portion of I{RAct}. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enables handling of multiple intersections per ray, which is necessary for accurate isosurface visualization in massive volumes where a ray may intersect the same isosurface in multiple blocks. Limitations: Requires additional memory for O{Spec} and a subsequent depth compositing step to resolve the multiple intersections. When to Use: Use when visualizing isosurfaces in massive volumes where rays may intersect the same surface in multiple blocks, and memory constraints prevent storing all intersections in the framebuffer directly. This method is part of a speculative progressive raycasting pipeline for memory-constrained isosurface visualization of massive volumes. It was introduced in the context of browser-based visualization of 1TB volumes. The approach allows for efficient handling of large datasets by deferring the final pixel color determination to a compositing step, thereby reducing memory bandwidth pressure during the raytracing phase. name: Ray Casting with Ray Subdividing
head: Adaptive Ray Subdivision, Ray Splitting for Perspective Rendering, Ray Subdividing
body: Ray Casting with Ray Subdividing maintains adequate spatial sampling rates in volume rendering under perspective projection, where rays diverge as they travel deeper into the scene. It addresses undersampling in distant volume slices by dynamically splitting rays when local ray density falls below a threshold, ensuring sample footprints remain consistent with the target resolution. Unlike fixed-step ray marching, this method adapts integration granularity based on geometric divergence rather than local data features. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Perspective camera rays r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, a volume dataset V, and a target maximum screen-space footprint size \delta{max}. Output: Color and opacity values for each pixel, computed via front-to-back compositing. Data Structures: Active Ray List: A queue of ray segments, each storing origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, current depth t, original screen-space position, accumulated color C, accumulated opacity \alpha, and pixel identifier. Steps: 1. Initialization: Generate one ray per pixel from the camera center through the pixel center. 2. Divergence Check: For each ray, compute the screen-space distance to its original pixel center or nearest sibling at the current depth t. 3. Splitting: If the distance exceeds \delta{max}, split the ray into two or more sub-rays. The new origins are offset in screen space, and directions are adjusted to maintain perspective consistency. The original ray is removed and replaced by the sub-rays in the list. 4. Integration: For each ray segment, sample the volume, interpolate values, and composite along the segment until the next split point or volume exit. 5. Merging: When rays converge or density exceeds requirements, adjacent segments can be merged to reduce computation, tracking ancestry for correct compositing. 6. Final Compositing: Combine results from all leaf rays contributing to each pixel. Formulas: Ray Divergence Metric: Let d{screen}(ri, rj) be the Euclidean distance between the screen-space projections of rays ri and rj at depth t. Split if: d{screen}(ri, rj) > \delta{max} where \delta{max} is the maximum allowed screen-space footprint size. Parameters: \delta{max}: Typically set to the pixel pitch or a fraction thereof, depending on desired anti-aliasing quality. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite Splitting: If \delta{max} is too small, rays may split indefinitely. Enforce a maximum recursion depth or minimum ray segment length. Merging Complexity: Merging requires careful handling of compositing order to avoid artifacts. Efficient spatial partitioning may be needed to find nearest neighbors quickly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raycastingwithsubdivision(camerarays, volume, deltamax, maxdepth): # Active ray queue: (origin, direction, depth, pixelid, origscreenpos, accc, acca) activerays = [] for r in camerarays: activerays.append((r.origin, r.direction, 0.0, r.pixelid, [r.origin[0], r.origin[1]], [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0)) pixelresults = {} while activerays: nextrays = [] for origin, direction, depth, pixelid, origscreen, accc, acca in activerays: # 1. Compute screen-space position at current depth pos = [origin[i] + direction[i] depth for i in range(3)] screenpos = [pos[0], pos[1]] # 2. Check divergence against original pixel center dist = math.sqrt((screenpos[0] - origscreen[0])2 + (screenpos[1] - origscreen[1])2) if dist > deltamax and depth < maxdepth: # 3. Split ray into two sub-rays with offset origins offset = deltamax 0.5 r1origin = [origin[0] + offset, origin[1] + offset, origin[2]] r2origin = [origin[0] - offset, origin[1] - offset, origin[2]] nextrays.append((r1origin, direction, depth, pixelid, origscreen, accc, acca)) nextrays.append((r2origin, direction, depth, pixelid, origscreen, accc, acca)) else: # 4. Integrate ray segment through volume stepsize = 0.1 t = depth segc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] sega = 0.0 while t < depth + 1.0: samplept = [origin[i] + direction[i] t for i in range(3)] val = volume.query(samplept) # Standard volume query c, a = val.color, val.opacity segc = [segc[i] + c[i] a (1.0 - sega) for i in range(3)] sega = sega + a (1.0 - sega) t += stepsize # 5. Composite segment result into pixel accumulator nc = [accc[i] + segc[i] sega (1.0 - acca) for i in range(3)] na = acca + sega (1.0 - acca) pixelresults[pixelid] = (nc, na) activerays = nextrays return pixelresults Focuses on the dynamic adjustment of ray density based on screen-space metrics. Choose when perspective distortion causes significant sampling variation. Link Emphasizes the geometric necessity of splitting in perspective views. Choose when fixed-step methods fail to capture distant details. Link Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the average number of splits per ray. Splits increase S in distant regions. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where D is the maximum depth of ray splitting. The ray queue grows with the number of active sub-rays. Performance: Improves image quality in distant regions compared to fixed-step ray marching. However, it is more complex to implement and may have higher overhead due to queue management. Strengths: Maintains consistent sampling density across the entire volume, reducing aliasing in perspective views. Limitations: Complex implementation; potential for high memory usage if many rays split; merging is non-trivial. When to Use: Perspective volume rendering where distant details are important and fixed-step sampling leads to aliasing. When Not to Use: Parallel projection (where rays do not diverge) or when performance is critical and some aliasing is acceptable. The concept of ray subdividing was introduced as a solution to the undersampling problem in perspective volume rendering. It is considered an equivalent approach to Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) splatting for raycasting, which handles screen-space footprint mapping. Kreeger et al. proposed improvements involving optimal splitting and merging of rays. The method operates on the principle that continuous volume functions must be approximated from discrete samples, adapting the sampling grid to camera geometry rather than data density. name: Cone Casting with Inscribed Sphere Sampling
head: Cone casting, MipNeRF Cone Sampling, Tri-MipRF Cone Casting
body: Cone casting with inscribed sphere sampling is a rendering technique that formulates a pixel as a disc on the image plane and emits a cone from the camera's projection center to sample the volume, avoiding the aliasing artifacts of distance-agnostic ray casting. Unlike sibling methods that treat pixels as points or use anisotropic Gaussian distributions for area sampling, this method uses isotropic spheres inscribed within the cone to match pre-filtered feature encodings. Inputs: Camera parameters: optical center \mathbf{o}, focal length f, pixel dimensions in world coordinates \Delta x, \Delta y. Ray direction \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{p}o - \mathbf{o}, where \mathbf{p}o is the pixel center. Sampling distances ti along the ray. Model parameters: Tri-Mip encoding maps \mathcal{M}, tiny MLP weights \Theta. Scene bounds: near plane tn, far plane tf (or AABB intersections). Outputs: Final pixel color C. Data Structures: Sphere Si: Defined by center \mathbf{x}i and radius ri. Tri-Mip Encoding: Three 2D mipmap arrays representing orthogonal planes (XY, YZ, XZ). Tiny MLP: A shallow neural network mapping feature vectors to density and color. Steps: 1. Pixel Disc and Cone Definition: Calculate the pixel disc radius \tilde{r} in world coordinates: \tilde{r} = \frac{\Delta x \cdot \Delta y}{\pi} Emit a cone C from the camera projection center \mathbf{o} along the direction \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{p}o - \mathbf{o}. The apex is at \mathbf{o} and the intersection with the image plane is the disc. The central axis of the cone is defined as: \mathbf{a}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. 2. Sampling Distance Selection: Determine a set of sampling distances ti by uniformly sampling between the camera's near tn and far tf planes, or the intersections of the cone's central axis with the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the 3D space. A binary occupancy grid may be used to skip samples in empty areas and concentrate samples near surfaces. 3. Sphere Parameterization: For each distance ti, calculate the sphere center \mathbf{x}i and inscribed radius ri. The center lies on the central axis: \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d}. The radius ri is calculated to ensure the sphere is inscribed within the cone: ri = \frac{\|\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{o}\|2 \cdot f \cdot \beta}{\|\mathbf{d}\|2 \cdot \sqrt{\left(\sqrt{\|\mathbf{d}\|2^2 - f^2} - \beta\right)^2 + f^2}} where f is the focal length and \beta is a base radius parameter. 4. Featurization (Tri-Mip Encoding): Orthogonally project each sphere Si(\mathbf{x}i, ri) onto the three Tri-Mip planes (XY, YZ, XZ). Sample the corresponding mipmaps based on the sphere's occupied area to generate a feature vector \mathbf{f}i. This step leverages the isotropic pre-filtering of the Tri-Mip encoding. 5. Density and Color Prediction: Feed the feature vector \mathbf{f}i and the view direction \mathbf{d} into a tiny MLP to predict density \taui and color \mathbf{c}i: [\taui, \mathbf{c}i] = \text{MLP}(\mathbf{f}i, \mathbf{d}; \Theta) where \Theta are the MLP weights. 6. Volume Rendering Integration: Integrate the density and color of the sampled spheres using standard front-to-back volume rendering to produce the final pixel color: C = \sum{i} Ti \left(1 - \exp(-\taui (t{i+1} - ti))\right) \mathbf{c}i with Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{k < i} \tauk (t{k+1} - tk)\right) where t represents the distance between sampled spheres. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def conecastingwithinscribedspheres(o, d, pixelwidthworld, pixelheightworld, focallength, baseradius, tnear, tfar, numsamples, trimipmaps, mlpmodel): """ Renders a single pixel using cone casting with inscribed sphere sampling. Args: o: Camera optical center (list/tuple of 3 floats). d: Ray direction vector (list/tuple of 3 floats). pixelwidthworld: Width of pixel in world units. pixelheightworld: Height of pixel in world units. focallength: Camera focal length f. baseradius: Base radius parameter beta. tnear: Near plane distance. tfar: Far plane distance. numsamples: Number of spheres to sample along the cone. trimipmaps: Dictionary of 2D mipmap arrays for XY, YZ, XZ planes. mlpmodel: Function implementing the tiny MLP. Returns: finalcolor: Rendered color of the pixel. """ # 1. Calculate pixel disc radius rtilde = (pixelwidthworld pixelheightworld) / math.pi # 2. Define sampling distances tvalues = [tnear + i (tfar - tnear) / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 for i in range(numsamples): ti = tvalues[i] tnext = tvalues[i+1] if i < numsamples - 1 else tfar # 3. Sphere Center and Radius xi = [o[j] + ti d[j] for j in range(3)] distfromorigin = math.sqrt(sum((xi[j] - o[j])2 for j in range(3))) normd = math.sqrt(sum(d[j]2 for j in range(3))) # Guard against negative value inside sqrt if ||d|| < f innersqrtarg = normd2 - focallength2 if innersqrtarg < 0: innersqrtarg = 0 term = math.sqrt(innersqrtarg) - baseradius denominator = normd math.sqrt(term2 + focallength2) if denominator == 0: ri = 0.0 else: ri = (distfromorigin focallength baseradius) / denominator # 4. Featurization via Tri-Mip fxy = samplemipmap(trimipmaps['XY'], xi[0], xi[1], ri) fyz = samplemipmap(trimipmaps['YZ'], xi[1], xi[2], ri) fxz = samplemipmap(trimipmaps['XZ'], xi[0], xi[2], ri) fi = fxy + fyz + fxz # 5. Predict Density and Color taui, ci = mlpmodel(fi, d) # 6. Volume Rendering Step deltat = tnext - ti alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-taui deltat) contribution = [transmittance alpha ci[j] for j in range(3)] finalcolor = [finalcolor[j] + contribution[j] for j in range(3)] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Early termination if transmittance is negligible if transmittance < 1e-4: break return finalcolor def samplemipmap(mipmaparray, u, v, radius): """ Samples a 2D mipmap array at (u, v) with radius r. Selects mipmap level based on projected radius and performs bilinear interpolation. """ # Map world coordinates to normalized texture coordinates # Select appropriate mipmap level based on radius # Perform bilinear interpolation at the selected level # Return feature vector return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for specific Tri-Mip sampling logic Parameters: baseradius (\beta): A base radius parameter controlling the scale of inscribed spheres. numsamples: Number of spheres along the cone. Not given in the sources. tiny MLP: A shallow neural network. Specific architecture (layers, activation functions) is not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Focal Length vs Ray Direction Norm: The formula for ri involves \sqrt{\|\mathbf{d}\|2^2 - f^2}. The source defines \mathbf{d} as the unnormalized vector \mathbf{p}o - \mathbf{o}, so \|\mathbf{d}\| scales with pixel size and camera intrinsics. Isotropy: The method relies on isotropic pre-filtering, which is why inscribed spheres are used instead of anisotropic multivariate Gaussians. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sampled spheres per pixel. The use of a binary occupancy grid allows skipping empty space, reducing effective complexity in sparse scenes. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the Tri-Mip maps (three 2D mipmap arrays) and the tiny MLP. The Tri-Mip encoding is described as compact, requiring only three 2D maps for base levels. Strengths: Produces anti-aliased high-fidelity renderings in both close-up and distant views. Avoids the high cost of super-sampling techniques which require casting multiple rays per pixel. Limitations: Requires the specific Tri-Mip encoding structure. Incorporating pre-filtering with hash encoding is non-trivial due to hash collisions, and multivariate Gaussians are anisotropic while Tri-Mip pre-filtering is isotropic. Cone casting with inscribed sphere sampling was introduced in the Tri-MipRF paper (2023) as a rendering strategy for efficient anti-aliased neural radiance fields. It addresses the flaw in previous methods (like NeRF) that formulate pixels as single points, causing blurring in close-up views and aliasing in distant views. It differs from MipNeRF, which uses multivariate Gaussians, by using inscribed spheres to match the isotropic pre-filtering of the Tri-Mip encoding. name: Local Implicit Ray Function (LIRF) Rendering
head: cone-based ray sampling
body: Local Implicit Ray Function (LIRF) is a rendering technique that represents the feature aggregation of samples within a ray conical frustum in a continuous manner, enabling arbitrary supersampling of rays for novel view synthesis at multiple scales. Unlike standard ray casting which treats a pixel as an infinitesimal line, LIRF constructs each target ray by aggregating information from a cone (represented by vertices), allowing for better handling of thin structures and multi-scale synthesis. It sets itself apart from its sibling Cone Casting with Inscribed Sphere Sampling by explicitly defining a continuous implicit function over the frustum's volume to interpolate features, rather than relying solely on geometric sampling strategies. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D coordinate \mathbf{p} of a sampled position within a conical frustum. Features of the M vertices defining the conical frustum. Image feature maps extracted from V nearby source views. Outputs: Aggregated feature for the sample at \mathbf{p} in a continuous manner. Predicted density and color for the sample. Final rendered color via volume rendering. Data Structures: Conical Frustum: Represented by M=8 vertices. The vertices are defined based on neighbor rays through neighbor pixels. Feature Maps: Extracted image feature maps with C=32 channels, sized same as the original image. Visibility Patches: Feature patches of size 7 \times 7 used to predict visibility weights. Parameters: V = 8: Number of nearby source views selected for training and testing. M = 8: Number of vertices used to represent a conical frustum. rm: Cone radius, set to the pixel width of the target image with the minimum resolution. N = 128: Number of points directly sampled on a ray. Patch size: 7 \times 7. Algorithm Steps: 1. Select Source Views: For a target view, select V=8 nearby source views. 2. Extract Features: Extract image feature maps with 32 channels from the source views, maintaining the original image dimensions. 3. Define Conical Frustum: Construct a conical frustum for the target pixel. The frustum is defined by M=8 vertices. The radius rm is determined by the pixel width of the target image at minimum resolution. 4. Sample Points: Directly sample N=128 points along the target ray. 5. Compute Visibility Weights: For each sample, match local multi-view feature patches of size 7 \times 7 from the source views to estimate visibility weights, mitigating occlusion artifacts. 6. Evaluate LIRF: For each sampled 3D position \mathbf{p} within the frustum: Input \mathbf{p} and the features of the M=8 frustum vertices into the Local Implicit Ray Function. The function outputs the aggregated feature continuously. Note: The specific mathematical formulation of the LIRF function (e.g., Eq. 5 and 6 in the source) involves scale s and relative position \Delta x. 7. Predict Radiance: Use the aggregated features to predict the density and color of the sample. 8. Volume Rendering: Render the final color of the target ray using the predicted densities and colors via standard volume rendering integration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def LIRFRendering(targetview, sourceviews): # 1. Select V=8 nearby source views selectedviews = SelectNearbyViews(targetview, sourceviews, V=8) # 2. Extract 32-channel feature maps from selected views featuremaps = ExtractFeatures(selectedviews, channels=32) # 3. Define conical frustum vertices (M=8) # Radius rm is pixel width of target image at min resolution frustumvertices = DefineFrustumVertices(targetview, rm=pixelwidthminres) # 4. Sample N=128 points on the ray points = SamplePointsOnRay(targetview, N=128) renderedcolor = 0.0 accumulatedweight = 0.0 for point in points: # 5. Estimate visibility weights using 7x7 patches visibility = EstimateVisibility(point, featuremaps, patchsize=7) # 6. Get aggregated feature via LIRF # Input: 3D coordinate 'point' and features of 'frustumvertices' aggregatedfeature = LIRFEvaluate(point, frustumvertices, featuremaps) # 7. Predict density and color density, color = PredictRadiance(aggregatedfeature) # 8. Volume rendering step (simplified alpha compositing) # Note: Standard volume rendering equation (Eq. 1 in source) is used alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density stepsize) weight = alpha exp(-sum(densitiessofar)) renderedcolor += weight color visibility accumulatedweight += weight return renderedcolor def LIRFEvaluate(point, vertices, featuremaps): """ Computes the aggregated feature for a point within the conical frustum. Uses the continuous nature of LIRF to interpolate based on relative position and scale. """ # The source mentions Eq. 5 and 6 involving scale s and relative position dx. # Specific implementation details of the MLP or interpolation function # are not fully detailed in the provided text beyond the inputs. # Assuming a standard MLP or interpolation layer takes the point # coordinates and vertex features as input to produce the aggregated feature. return InterpolateFeatures(point, vertices, featuremaps) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Rendering regions occluded in all input views is impossible. View Consistency: View consistency is weaker than NeRF because selected input views vary with the novel view position. Computational Cost: Rendering a pixel requires casting four rays to approximate a cone, increasing computational cost. Scale Sensitivity: Performance degrades significantly if the scale parameter or relative position components of the LIRF are removed, especially at extreme scales (\times 0.5 and \times 4). Time Complexity: Increases due to the requirement of casting four rays to approximate a cone for each pixel. Training takes approximately two days on eight V100 GPUs for 250k iterations with a batch size of 512 rays. Memory Complexity: Requires storing feature maps for V=8 source views and processing N=128 samples per ray. Performance: The full LIRF model performs better than the "single ray" variant on all scales, especially at \times 0.5 and \times 4. It outperforms IBRNet, NeuRay, and GeoNeRF in quantitative metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) on real forward-facing scenes. Using the method's own feature extraction yields significantly better performance than using U-Net features from IBRNet. Strengths: Enables arbitrary supersampling for novel view synthesis at multiple levels of detail (anti-blurring and anti-aliasing). Better handling of thin structures compared to single-ray methods. Limitations: Cannot render fully occluded regions; weaker view consistency compared to NeRF; higher computational cost due to cone approximation. Local Implicit Ray Function (LIRF) was proposed as a novel method for generalizable radiance field representation and novel view synthesis of unseen scenes. It addresses the limitations of single-ray representations by introducing a continuous aggregation of features within a conical frustum. The method was supported by NSFC under Grant 62031023. Local Implicit Ray Function for Generalizable Radiance Field Representation, http://arxiv.org/abs/2304.12746v1, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Cone Discrete Sampling
head: IES Cone Sampling
body: Cone Discrete Sampling is a volume rendering technique that alleviates aliasing by treating a camera pixel as a disc and casting a cone from the projection center, rather than a single ray. It integrates features within a series of conical frustums by blending data from the frustum's vertices using distance-dependent weights. It differs from its parent, Cone Casting with Inscribed Sphere Sampling, by explicitly discretizing the cone into frustums and using vertex-based blending with learnable decay, and from Local Implicit Ray Function (LIRF) Rendering by relying on explicit tri-plane featurization and discrete vertex aggregation rather than continuous ray function approximation. Inputs: Camera parameters (projection center, pixel corners). A tri-plane based scene representation with L levels of detail. A set of sample points \mathbf{x} along a ray within a conical frustum. Outputs: A Level-of-Detail (LoD) feature vector \mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{x}) for each sample point, which is subsequently passed to an MLP to predict color and signed distance. Data Structures: Conical Frustum: Defined by 8 vertices \{\mathbf{x}v\}{v=1}^8. These are obtained by casting rays through the pixel center and its four corners, intersected with the near and far planes of the frustum segment. Tri-plane Features: For each vertex \mathbf{x}v, features are projected onto three 2D planes (XY, YZ, XZ) to query base feature vectors \mathbf{F}l. Parameters: k: Learnable weight decay parameter. Initial value is 80. \{\taul\}{l=1}^L: Kernel sizes for Gaussian convolution at each tri-plane level l. V: Number of vertices in a conical frustum, fixed at 8. Steps: 1. Frustum Construction: Divide the ray through the pixel into a series of conical frustums. For each frustum, determine the 8 vertices \mathbf{x}v by intersecting rays from the camera center through the pixel corners and center with the frustum's near and far boundaries. 2. Multi-Convolved Featurization: For each vertex \mathbf{x}v, compute the multi-scale multi-convolved feature \mathbf{G}v(\mathbf{x}v). Project \mathbf{x}v onto the tri-planes to query base feature vectors \mathbf{F}l for each level l \in \{1, \dots, L\}. Apply 2D Gaussian convolution \mathcal{G}(\cdot, \taul) to each \mathbf{F}l using kernel size \taul. This aggregates features within a 3D sphere centered at \mathbf{x}v by leveraging the compressed 2D planes. Concatenate the convolved features from all levels: \mathbf{G}v(\mathbf{x}v) = \bigcup{l=1}^L \mathcal{G}(\mathbf{F}l, \taul) \quad (5) where \bigcup denotes concatenation. 3. Weight Calculation: For a sample point \mathbf{x} within the frustum, calculate the blending weight W(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}v) for each vertex \mathbf{x}v based on the Euclidean distance: W(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}v) = \exp(-k \|\mathbf{x}v - \mathbf{x}\|) \quad (4) The parameter k controls the decay rate. It must be aware of the frustum size; smaller frustums require a more rapid decrease (larger k) to maintain accuracy. 4. LoD Feature Aggregation: Compute the final LoD feature \mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{x}) by summing the weighted vertex features: \mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{v=1}^V W(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{x}v) \mathbf{G}v(\mathbf{x}v) \quad (6) where V=8. 5. Prediction: Pass \mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{x}) through a shallow 8-layer MLP to predict the signed distance f and feature vector \Theta, from which color is derived. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def conediscretesampling(samplex, frustumvertices, triplanes, k, kernelsizes): """ Computes the LoD feature for a sample point within a conical frustum. Args: samplex: 3D point (x, y, z) within the frustum. frustumvertices: List of 8 vertices (xv) defining the conical frustum. triplanes: Dictionary or array containing the 2D feature planes for each level l. k: Learnable weight decay parameter (initially 80). kernelsizes: List of L kernel sizes {taul} for Gaussian convolution. Returns: Z: Aggregated LoD feature vector. """ V = 8 L = len(kernelsizes) Z = np.zeroslike(samplex) # Placeholder for feature dimension; actual dim depends on tri-plane output # Step 2: Multi-Convolved Featurization for each vertex Gvlist = [] for v in range(V): xv = frustumvertices[v] # Query base features from tri-planes for this vertex # Note: Implementation of tri-plane projection and querying is assumed to be handled by the # underlying tri-plane representation structure. Fllist = [] for l in range(L): # Project xv onto the 3 planes (XY, YZ, XZ) and query features # This returns a feature vector Fl for level l Fl = querytriplane(xv, triplanes[l]) Fllist.append(Fl) # Apply Gaussian convolution with different kernel sizes Gv = None for l in range(L): taul = kernelsizes[l] # Apply 2D Gaussian convolution to Fl # The convolution aggregates features in the 2D plane, approximating 3D spherical aggregation Gl = gaussianconvolve2d(Fllist[l], taul) # Concatenate features from all levels if Gv is None: Gv = Gl else: Gv = np.concatenate([Gv, Gl], axis=-1) Gvlist.append(Gv) # Step 3 & 4: Weight Calculation and Aggregation Z = np.zeroslike(Gvlist[0]) for v in range(V): xv = frustumvertices[v] Gv = Gvlist[v] # Calculate weight based on distance dist = np.linalg.norm(xv - samplex) W = np.exp(-k dist) # Add weighted feature to sum Z += W Gv return Z def querytriplane(point, planefeatures): """ Helper to simulate querying a tri-plane. Projects a 3D point onto 2D planes and interpolates features. Returns a feature vector. """ # Project point (x,y,z) to XY, YZ, XZ xycoords = (point[0], point[1]) yzcoords = (point[1], point[2]) xzcoords = (point[0], point[2]) # Bilinear interpolation on each plane fxy = interpolate2d(planefeatures['xy'], xycoords) fyz = interpolate2d(planefeatures['yz'], yzcoords) fxz = interpolate2d(planefeatures['xz'], xzcoords) # Concatenate plane features return np.concatenate([fxy, fyz, fxz], axis=-1) def gaussianconvolve2d(featuremap, kernelsize): """ Applies a 2D Gaussian convolution to a feature map. """ # Create Gaussian kernel sigma = kernelsize / 2.0 # Standard implementation of Gaussian kernel generation and convolution #... return featuremap # Placeholder for actual convolution result Uses 2D Gaussian convolution on each tri-plane to represent the region of integration for a conical frustum. For a vertex \mathbf{x}v, the multi-scale multi-convolved feature \mathbf{G}v is defined by applying Gaussian convolutions with different kernel sizes \{\taul\} for each level l. Features are combined using concatenation. Different kernel sizes cover various frequency details, allowing the representation to handle sparse samples within the frustum efficiently without increasing discretization density. The final step where the Level-of-Detail feature \mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{x}) is computed for a sample \mathbf{x} by summing the weighted multi-convolved features of the frustum's vertices. This aggregates the continuous features from the vertices into a single representation for the sample point, enabling the subsequent MLP to predict color and geometry. Complexity: Reduces computational cost compared to increasing the number of sampled rays and points, as it integrates features within conical frustums using a fixed number of vertices (8) and levels. Performance: Offers faster inference time than methods that increase ray counts to mitigate aliasing. Strengths: Efficiently represents ray sampling within a cone using explicit tri-plane featurization. Avoids the complexity of shape-adaptive 3D Gaussian kernels by using a single learnable parameter k. Limitations: The accuracy of the weight decay function k is sensitive to the size of the conical frustum; improper tuning can lead to artifacts. When to use: When rendering with tri-plane representations and needing to balance aliasing reduction with computational efficiency. Cone Discrete Sampling was introduced in "Anti-Aliased Neural Implicit Surfaces with Encoding Level of Detail" (2024) by the authors of. It draws inspiration from Mip-NeRF but adapts the concept for tri-plane-based representations and explicit level-of-detail encoding rather than multi-resolution rendering. The method addresses the high computational costs associated with increasing sampled rays and points in volume rendering. name: Raycasting Phase
head: Data sampling, Two-Pass Raycasting with Back-Face Depth Buffering
body: The Raycasting Phase samples volumetric data along camera rays and applies shading to compute optical properties. It is implemented using a two-pass rasterization strategy to determine ray entry and exit points via back-face depth buffering. In parallel implementations, its performance is highly sensitive to the interaction between decomposition geometry and camera direction. Inputs: Volumetric data grid V. Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, field of view). Decomposition geometry (block structure for parallel processing). Predefined step length parameter d. Outputs: Final pixel color C{\text{pixel}}. Intermediate fragment buffers (back-face and front-face coordinates). Data Structures: 1. Auxiliary Buffers: Two texture buffers bound to distinct texture units; one stores back-face depth/coordinates, the other stores front-face coordinates. 2. Fragment Buffer: Temporary storage for image fragments; size constraints may require scaling down data volume if the buffer overflows (e.g., at image size 23040^3). Algorithm Steps: 1. Pass 1: Back-Face Depth Buffering Render the volume bounding box or decomposition blocks. Bind auxiliary buffers for multiple render targets using GLARBdrawbuffers. For each fragment generated by a back-facing polygon, store its texture coordinates in the back-face buffer. 2. Pass 2: Ray Initialization and Integration Setup Bind the two auxiliary buffers to distinct texture units. Project a viewport-filling quadrilateral. For each pixel: Fetch back-face texture coordinates from the first buffer. If invalid (no back-face hit), discard the fragment. Otherwise, retrieve the corresponding front-face texture coordinates from the second buffer. Compute the step vector \Delta \mathbf{p} along the ray based on the predefined step length d and the distance between front and back faces. Calculate the total number of iterations N required to traverse the ray segment. 3. Integration Loop Initialize ray position \mathbf{p} at the front-face entry point. For i = 0 to N-1: Sample the volume data V(\mathbf{p}) using trilinear interpolation. Apply a Phong-style shader to compute optical properties (color, opacity). Integrate the contribution into the accumulated color and opacity. Advance \mathbf{p} by the step vector \Delta \mathbf{p}. The integration is structured in slabs: each slab of thickness 2d is defined by three successive samples (sf, sm, sb), with the next slab indexed by shifting these samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastingphase(volumedata, camera, steplengthd, decomposition): # Pass 1: Determine entry and exit points via back-face buffering backfacecoords = renderbackfaces(volumedata, camera, decomposition) # Pass 2: Initialize rays and integrate finalcolors = [None] camera.resolution for pixel in camera.viewport: bfcoord = backfacecoords[pixel] if bfcoord is None: continue # Discard fragment if no back-face hit ffcoord = getfrontfacecoord(pixel) rayorigin = ffcoord raydirection = normalize(camera.direction) stepvector = computestepvector(raydirection, steplengthd, ffcoord, bfcoord) numsteps = computenumsteps(rayorigin, bfcoord, stepvector) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 currentpos = rayorigin for i in range(numsteps): # Sample volume data using trilinear interpolation samplevalue = trilinearinterpolate(volumedata, currentpos) # Apply Phong-style shading color, opacity = applyphongshading(samplevalue, currentpos, camera) # Integrate contribution into accumulated color and opacity weight = (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[j] + weight color[j] for j in range(3)] accumulatedopacity += weight # Advance position by step vector currentpos = [currentpos[j] + stepvector[j] for j in range(3)] finalcolors[pixel] = accumulatedcolor return finalcolors def renderbackfaces(volumedata, camera, decomposition): # Rasterize decomposition blocks; store back-face texture coordinates in auxiliary buffer return [[None for in range(camera.resolution[1])] for in range(camera.resolution[0])] def getfrontfacecoord(pixel): # Retrieve front-face coordinates from second auxiliary buffer return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def computestepvector(raydirection, steplengthd, ffcoord, bfcoord): # Compute step vector along the ray based on predefined step length d and geometry return [steplengthd raydirection[j] for j in range(3)] def computenumsteps(rayorigin, bfcoord, stepvector): # Calculate total iterations to traverse the ray segment dist = ((bfcoord[0]-rayorigin[0])2 + (bfcoord[1]-rayorigin[1])2 + (bfcoord[2]-rayorigin[2])2)0.5 stepmag = ((stepvector[0]2 + stepvector[1]2 + stepvector[2]2)0.5) return int(dist / stepmag) if stepmag > 0 else 0 def trilinearinterpolate(volumedata, pos): # Standard trilinear interpolation from discrete grid samples return 0.0 # Not given in the sources. def applyphongshading(samplevalue, pos, camera): # Apply Phong-style shading to compute optical properties return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0 # Not given in the sources. def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return [v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag] Parameters: d: Predefined step length; slabs are defined with thickness 2d. Interpolation: Trilinear interpolation is used for data sampling along the ray. Shading: Phong-style shading is applied during the integration process. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Thread Divergence: The final raycasting time is determined by the runtime of the thread that takes the most integration steps, which depends on the view and decomposition geometry interaction. Weak Scaling Degradation: Perspective projection causes variation in the number of samples each thread must calculate; this variation increases at scale as each core operates on a smaller portion of the view frustum, accounting for a 20% performance degradation. Memory Overflow: Increasing image size to 23040^3 causes temporary buffers for image fragments to overflow; to accommodate the fragment buffer, data size had to be scaled down to 19200^3 (7.1 trillion cells) instead of 23040^3 (12.2 trillion cells). Hybrid Memory Performance: At higher concurrencies, the interaction between decomposition geometry and camera direction causes the hybrid-memory implementation to underperform distributed memory by 10% due to irregular block sizes in GPU clusters. Time Complexity: Performance is bounded by the maximum integration steps among all threads. Memory Complexity: Fragment buffer size constraints force data downsampling to avoid overflow. Scalability: Distributed memory achieves linear scaling up to 216,000-way concurrency for the raycasting phase. Hybrid-memory implementations maintain ~80% scalability in weak scaling up to 216,000 cores but exhibit sublinear scaling in strong scaling due to irregular decomposition geometry. Performance: At 448-way concurrency with a 4608^3 dataset, the hybrid/CUDA implementation averaged 1.18s for raycasting. Strengths: No message passing is involved in the raycasting phase itself, allowing for efficient scaling in distributed memory systems. Limitations: Performance is highly sensitive to view direction relative to decomposition geometry, and perspective projection exacerbates load imbalance in weak scaling. The method originated in the context of large-scale parallel volume rendering on multi- and many-core systems. It was developed to address the challenges of scaling raycasting across distributed and hybrid memory architectures. The two-pass approach with back-face depth buffering was introduced to efficiently determine ray entry and exit points without complex ray-volume intersection algorithms, leveraging GPU rasterization capabilities. name: Pre-integration and Approximation Methods
body: Pre-integration and Approximation Methods accelerate direct volume ray casting by replacing on-the-fly integration of non-linear transfer functions with pre-computed lookup tables or efficient mathematical approximations. This family addresses aliasing artifacts and performance bottlenecks caused by low sampling frequencies and high-frequency transfer functions. It sets itself apart from siblings like Monte Carlo Volume Rendering and Ray Traversal and Integration Schemes by explicitly pre-computing segment contributions or approximating blending functions, rather than evaluating transfer functions at discrete sample points or using stochastic sampling. Pre-integrated Volume Rendering (PIVR) accelerates direct volume rendering by pre-computing the volume rendering integral for a ray segment and storing the results in a lookup table for fast retrieval. It solves the problem of aliasing artifacts caused by high-frequency, non-linear transfer functions when sampling sparse ray segments. Unlike standard classification which applies the transfer function to individual sample points, PIVR decouples the integration of the transfer function contribution from the sampling process, allowing the sampling to focus only on volume reconstruction while the pre-computed table handles the optical properties. It sets itself apart from Pre-integration of Transfer Function Contribution by specifically addressing the scalar field interpolation between segment endpoints to compute accurate color and opacity contributions. Pre-integration of transfer function contribution is a technique that replaces on-the-fly interpolation and integration with pre-computed lookup tables to perform fully-shaded semi-transparent and iso-surface volume rendering. It addresses the dichotomy between image quality and performance by pre-integrating the transfer function's contribution along ray segments, thereby smoothing image imperfections caused by low sampling frequencies. It sets itself apart from standard ray casting by mapping pairs of scalar density values directly to pre-integrated color and opacity, decoupling the integration of the transfer function from the sampling process. A technique to approximate the exponential light attenuation and blending function in volume rendering with a quadratic function to allow efficient hardware implementation using Gouraud shading, while maintaining accuracy for small cell depths. Set the first coefficient a0 = 0 to simplify the blend function structure. The target exponential function is f(z) = 1 - e^{-\tau z}, where \tau is the opacity-per-unit-distance and z is the depth. The approximation is g(z) = (c0 + c1 z)(a0 + a1 z). The quadratic approximation for exponential blending was proposed to facilitate hardware acceleration using Gouraud shading. It was tested on a Silicon Graphics uniprocessor VGX, with rendering times measured in CPU seconds for grid sizes up to 40,960 samples. The concept of pre-integrating transfer function contributions was developed to address the dichotomy between image quality and performance in volume rendering. name: Pre-integrated Volume Rendering
head: PIVR, Pre-integration, Precomputed volume rendering integral, Preintegration Volume Rendering, Pré-integração, Engel, Kraus & Ertl 2001, Pre-integrated transfer function
body: Pre-integrated Volume Rendering (PIVR) accelerates direct volume rendering by pre-computing the volume rendering integral for a ray segment and storing the results in a lookup table for fast retrieval. It solves the problem of aliasing artifacts caused by high-frequency, non-linear transfer functions when sampling sparse ray segments. Unlike standard classification which applies the transfer function to individual sample points, PIVR decouples the integration of the transfer function contribution from the sampling process, allowing the sampling to focus only on volume reconstruction while the pre-computed table handles the optical properties. It sets itself apart from Pre-integration of Transfer Function Contribution by specifically addressing the scalar field interpolation between segment endpoints to compute accurate color and opacity contributions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scalar volume data V, transfer functions for extinction density \tau(s) and color density \tilde{c}(s), ray segment length d (assumed constant per frame), and scalar values at segment endpoints sb (back) and sf (front). Outputs: Accumulated color \tilde{C} and opacity \alpha for the segment, which are composited into the final image. Data Structures: 1. Integral Table: A 1D lookup table of size 256 entries (for 8-bit scalar data). Each entry stores four 32-bit floating-point numbers: accumulated color components (\tilde{R}A, \tilde{G}A, \tilde{B}A) and accumulated opacity TA. Layout: Contiguous memory, [R, G, B, A] per entry. Values: T(s) = \int0^s \tau(s) ds and K(s) = \int0^s \tilde{c}(s) ds are pre-computed and stored. 2. Exponential Approximation Parameters: Four linear segments defined by slopes mi and intercepts bi (i=0..3) to approximate 1 - \exp(-x). Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-computation (Offline/Setup): Compute the integral functions T(s) and K(s) for all possible scalar values s \in [0, 255] using the user-supplied transfer functions \tau(s) and \tilde{c}(s). Store these values in the 256-entry 1D table. Compute the linear approximation parameters mi, bi for 1 - \exp(-x) using a brute-force minimization method for x \ge 0. 2. Ray Casting Loop (Per Ray): Iterate through the volume along the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. For each segment of length d, sample the scalar field at the start (s{prev}) and end (s{curr}) of the segment. Thresholding Check: If s{max} = \max(s{prev}, s{curr}) is below a user-supplied threshold (assuming clamped transfer functions), skip the segment. 3. Segment Evaluation: Determine s{max} = \max(s{prev}, s{curr}) and s{min} = \min(s{prev}, s{curr}). Compute the difference diff = s{max} - s{min}. Compute the reciprocal invDiff = 1.0 / diff. Table Lookup: Access the integral table at indices s{max} and s{min} to retrieve T(s{max}), K(s{max}) and T(s{min}), K(s{min}). Color Computation: \Delta K = K(s{max}) - K(s{min}) \tilde{C} = d \cdot invDiff \cdot \Delta K This yields the positive raypoint light emission. Opacity Computation: x = invDiff \cdot (T(s{max}) - T(s{min})) Note that x \ge 0. Approximate the opacity using the linear segments: yi = mi \cdot x + bi \quad \text{for } i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\} \alpha = \min(y0, y1, y2, y3) This approximates 1 - \exp(-x). 4. Compositing: Combine the computed \tilde{C} and \alpha with the accumulated color and opacity from previous segments using front-to-back compositing. Formulas: The approximate opacity \alpha and emitted light intensity \tilde{C} for an interval between two raypoints with distance d and scalar values sb and sf are given by: \alpha(sf, sb, d) \approx 1 - \exp\left(\frac{d}{sb - sf} \cdot (T(sf) - T(sb))\right) \tilde{C}(sf, sb, d) \approx \frac{d}{sb - sf} \cdot (K(sb) - K(sf)) where T(s) = \int0^s \tau(s) ds and K(s) = \int0^s \tilde{c}(s) ds. Here \tau(s) is the extinction density and \tilde{c}(s) is the color density. The general volume rendering integral for opacity is: \alpha = 1 - \exp \left( - \int{li}^{lo} \lambda(V(R(l))) \times dl \right) where \lambda is the extinction coefficient function, V is the volume field, R(l) is the ray position, and li, lo are the start and end points of the segment. Parameters: Raypoint distance d: Assumed constant for all rays during a frame. Typical values tested: 0.45 and 0.9 grid units. Linear Approximation Parameters (mi, bi): Computed once via brute-force method. Specific numerical values are not provided in the sources, only that they minimize error for x \ge 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Simplified Alpha Loss: Using a simplified linear approximation for opacity (e.g., \alpha \approx \frac{d}{sb - sf} (T(sb) - T(sf))) instead of the exponential approximation results in a visible loss in contrast. Thresholding: Raypoints below a threshold should not be simply discarded if the previous point was above the threshold, as linear interpolation might exceed the threshold within the interval. However, if s{max} is below the threshold, the entire interval can be safely skipped (assuming clamped transfer functions). Discretization Artifacts: The method assumes a linear progression of scalar values between samples, which can introduce artifacts if the scalar field varies non-linearly. High-Dimensional Transfer Functions: Pre-integration is not applicable without restrictions to transfer functions of dimension greater than one due to the large memory and processing time required to build tables with at least four dimensions (for 2D TFs). Adaptive Pre-integration is a technique applied to texture slicing that pre-computes optimal step sizes for each ray based on pre-integrated emission, opacity, and second-order gradients to guarantee error bounds on ray integration. It is an adaptive approach that overcomes pre-integration artifacts by using an adaptive sampling rate based on the actual information stored in the volume and the transfer function used. It builds on Pre-integrated Volume Rendering by dynamically adjusting the discretization of the pre-integration integral rather than using a fixed slab thickness. Choose it when scalar fields vary highly non-linearly and fixed-step pre-integration artifacts are unacceptable. Direct Volume Rendering with Pre-integration renders adapted tetrahedral meshes using direct volume ray casting, accelerated by pre-integration computed in shaders. It extends pre-integrated volume rendering, which allows for faster evaluation by pre-computing all possible results from the integral and storing them in a table for lookup [Parent], to unstructured volumetric data (tetrahedral meshes). Unlike methods limited to regular grids, this approach handles the geometric complexity of unstructured grids by storing the mesh data structure in textures and using barycentric interpolation for value estimation. Choose it when rendering unstructured tetrahedral meshes requires the speedup of pre-integration. Time Complexity: The per-raypoint computation is dominated by SIMD arithmetic operations (MULPS, ADDPS, SUBPS, MINPS, RCPPS) with latencies of 4-6 cycles. The pre-computation of the lookup table is time-consuming, especially for high-dimensional transfer functions. Memory Complexity: The 1D table implementation uses 4 Kbytes (256 entries \times 4 floats \times 4 bytes), which fits in the L1 cache, avoiding cache misses associated with larger 2D tables (e.g., 512 Kbytes). Measured Performance: On a Pentium-4 2GHz, pre-integrated rendering (d=0.45, simplified alpha) took 0.158s for a 256x256 viewport, compared to 0.295s for standard classification with empty-space skipping. Pre-integration increases speed by a factor of 10 for the linear model compared to baseline. Strengths: Reduces aliasing artifacts caused by high frequencies in non-linear transfer functions. Allows for larger ray step sizes (coarser sampling) while maintaining image quality. Decouples sampling from transfer function evaluation. Limitations: Assumes linear scalar progression between samples, which can cause artifacts. Not directly applicable to high-dimensional transfer functions without restrictions. The simplified alpha approximation may reduce contrast. When to use: Suitable for interactive volume rendering on CPUs or GPUs where transfer functions are non-linear and high-frequency, and where memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. When not to use: When the scalar field varies highly non-linearly within segments and adaptive sampling is not used. When rendering requires high-dimensional transfer functions without applying restrictions, as pre-integration is not applicable to TFs of dimension greater than one without significant memory and processing overhead. Pre-integrated volume rendering was introduced by Engel et al. in 2001. It was developed to overcome the problem of high Nyquist frequencies resulting from non-linear transfer functions in texture-based volume rendering. The method splits the numerical integration into two parts: one for the continuous scalar field and one for the transfer function. It was later combined with volumetric clipping and advanced lighting effects by Röttger et al.. The technique has been implemented in software systems like UltraVis and adapted for unstructured grids. name: Adaptive Pre-integration
body: Adaptive Pre-integration is a technique applied to texture slicing that pre-computes optimal step sizes for each ray based on pre-integrated emission, opacity, and second-order gradients to guarantee error bounds on ray integration. It is an adaptive approach that overcomes pre-integration artifacts by using an adaptive sampling rate based on the actual information stored in the volume and the transfer function used. It builds on Pre-integrated Volume Rendering by dynamically adjusting the discretization of the pre-integration integral rather than using a fixed slab thickness. Inputs: Volume dataset, transfer functions for opacity and color, and camera parameters. Outputs: Final color image. Data Structures: Importance volume, a floating-point texture storing the pre-computed optimal step size for each ray. Ray traversal parameters, floating-point textures storing current ray positions and accumulated opacity/color. Z-buffer, used to track ray termination. Steps: 1. Initialization: Render the bounding box of the volume in front-to-back order to provide starting locations for all rays. Initialize ray traversal parameters in floating-point textures. 2. Step Size Computation: For each ray, compute the optimal step size. This size depends on the pre-integrated emission and opacity value as well as second-order gradients. The step size is stored in the importance volume. 3. Ray Traversal: Update ray positions using the step sizes from the importance volume. 4. Pre-integration: Apply pre-integration of opacity and color transfer functions to the volume slabs defined by the entry and exit points and the distance between slices. 5. Blending (Multi-step Slicing): Internally blend the results of multiple pre-integrated slabs before writing to the framebuffer to improve image quality. 6. Termination: Rays are terminated early or when they leave the volume by setting the z-buffer for the corresponding pixels, avoiding further computation. 7. Accumulation: Resampled RGB\alpha textures are accumulated into the frame buffer using back-to-front compositing. If front-to-back compositing is used, accumulated opacities need to be stored for each pixel in the image. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Over-sampling factor: Two-times over-sampling has almost the same performance as no over-sampling due to increased cache coherency. Four-times over-sampling yields the best quality-performance tradeoff. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Artifacts: Standard pre-integration assumes a linear progression of scalar values between slices, which can introduce artifacts. Adaptive sampling mitigates this by adjusting to the actual information in the volume. Precision: Not given in the sources. Performance: Two-times over-sampling has almost the same performance as no over-sampling because of increased cache coherency. Quality: Four-times over-sampling yields the best quality-performance tradeoff using multi-step slicing. Accuracy: Guarantees error bounds on ray integration by adapting step sizes to local volume properties. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Adaptive sampling rate based on volume information and transfer function reduces artifacts from linear progression assumptions. Limitations: Requires additional rendering passes to determine if all rays have terminated. Adaptive Pre-integration was proposed by Roettger et al.. It extends the work of Engel et al. who applied pre-integration of opacity and color transfer functions to texture slicing. Roettger et al. improved image quality by internally blending results of multiple pre-integrated slabs. name: Direct Volume Rendering with Pre-integration
head: GPU-accelerated raycasting for tetrahedral meshes, PIVR, Pre-integrated Volume Rendering for Tetrahedral Meshes, Pre-integrated tetrahedral rendering
body: Direct Volume Rendering with Pre-integration renders adapted tetrahedral meshes using direct volume ray casting, accelerated by pre-integration computed in shaders. It extends pre-integrated volume rendering, which allows for faster evaluation by pre-computing all possible results from the integral and storing them in a table for lookup [Parent], to unstructured volumetric data (tetrahedral meshes). Unlike methods limited to regular grids, this approach handles the geometric complexity of unstructured grids by storing the mesh data structure in textures and using barycentric interpolation for value estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An adapted tetrahedral mesh defined by vertex positions, vertex scalar values, and connectivity. Camera parameters including the view vector. Transfer function parameters defining opacity \alpha and color \tilde{C}. Output: A 2D image with color and opacity per pixel. Data Structures: 1. Tetrahedral Mesh Textures: The tetrahedral mesh data structure is stored in a set of textures. These textures allow the shader to calculate the current tetrahedron and its entry/exit points for each ray integral iteration. 2. Pre-integration Table: A 3D texture storing pre-computed ray integral results. The standard table is indexed by (s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l), where s^{(f)} and s^{(b)} are the scalar values at the ray entry and exit points, and l is the thickness (distance between entry and exit). Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-computation (Table Generation): 1. Iterate over all possible combinations of entry scalar value s^{(f)}, exit scalar value s^{(b)}, and thickness l. 2. For each combination, compute the pre-integrated color \tilde{C}(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l) and opacity \alpha(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l) using the transfer function and the volume rendering integral. 3. Store these values in the pre-integration table texture. 4. Logarithmic sampling is implemented for the thickness dimension l to handle varying scales efficiently. 2. Rendering (Ray Casting): 1. For each pixel, cast a ray through the scene. 2. Intersect the ray with the tetrahedral mesh using the texture-based mesh representation. 3. For each tetrahedron intersected by the ray segment: a. Determine the entry point and exit point of the ray within the tetrahedron. b. Estimate the scalar values s^{(f)} (at entry) and s^{(b)} (at exit) using barycentric interpolation from the vertex values of the tetrahedron. This assumes datasets with good resolution where regions of interest are highly sampled. c. Calculate the thickness l as the distance between the entry and exit points. d. Use (s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l) as indices to fetch the pre-computed color \tilde{C} and opacity \alpha from the pre-integration table. e. Composite the fetched color and opacity into the ray accumulator using standard volume rendering blending equations. 4. Repeat for all intersected tetrahedra until the ray exits the volume or is fully opaque. Formulas: Barycentric Interpolation: Scalar value s at a point inside a tetrahedron is computed as s = \sum{i=1}^{4} wi si, where wi are barycentric coordinates and si are vertex scalar values. Thickness: l = \| \vec{p}{exit} - \vec{p}{entry} \|. Parameters: Logarithmic Sampling: Used for the thickness dimension l in the pre-integration table. Illustrative Effect Parameters: Various parameters (\omega, p, oo) control specific illustrative effects (see Subtopics). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Constant Gradient Artifacts: A constant gradient within each tetrahedron causes artifacts. This is noted as an issue to be solved in future work. Resolution Dependency: Barycentric interpolation for gradient estimation is sufficient only for datasets with good resolution. Occlusion: The system currently does not take occlusion by the segments into account when adapting the mesh, considering attribute errors only. An illustrative effect that highlights essential high-gradient dataset features by masking pre-integrated table entries using an approximated view-dependent gradient magnitude. It is chosen when one wants to emphasize regions of rapid scalar change without computing full gradients. It differs from full gradient enhancement by using the approximated gradient (s^{(b)} - s^{(f)})/l. Mask Calculation: m = \tilde{\omega} \cdot \left( \left| \frac{s(f) - s(b)}{l} \right| \right)^p, where \tilde{\omega} is an artificial user-defined opacity scaling factor and p is a scalar controlling gradient magnitude's effect on opacity. Masked Opacity: \alpha^{(m)}(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l) = 1 - e^{(m \log(1 - \alpha(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l)))}. Masked Color: \tilde{C}^{(m)}(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l) = \frac{\alpha^{(m)}(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l)}{\alpha(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l)} \tilde{C}(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l). Implementation: The mask is applied during pre-integrated table computation, requiring no modification to the raycaster. An effect that highlights areas where the view vector and gradient vector are near orthogonal, showing contour lines of a surface, by using a pre-integrated table indexed by phi values. It is chosen for silhouette extraction. It differs from other gradient effects by indexing the table by \phi instead of scalar values. Phi Calculation: \phi = \langle \vec{n}, \vec{v} \rangle, where \vec{n} is the normalized gradient vector and \vec{v} is the view vector. Implementation: The pre-integrated table is constructed indexed by (\phi(f), \phi(b), l) instead of (s(f), s(b), l). A one-dimensional opacity transfer function \alpha(\phi) is used to highlight areas where \phi is close to 0. An illustrative effect obtained by estimating the curvature for the segment between entry and exit points to generate contour effects. It is chosen to highlight regions of high curvature change. Mask Calculation: m = \omega \cdot \left( \frac{\|\vec{n}^{(f)} - \vec{n}^{(b)}\|}{l} \right)^p, where \vec{n}^{(f)} and \vec{n}^{(b)} are normal vectors at entry and exit, l is thickness, \omega is opacity scaling factor, and p is a scalar. Implementation: The mask is applied during rendering by modifying the shader. An effect that restricts contour detection to interfaces between different materials by masking pre-integrated table entries during rendering using a windowing function and phi value. It is chosen for masked silhouettes. Mask Calculation: m = g(\|\nabla f\|) \cdot (1 - |\phi|)^p, where \nabla f is the gradient, g(\cdot) is a windowing function (usually linear clamped to [0,1]), and \phi = \langle \vec{n}, \vec{v} \rangle. Implementation: \phi is calculated in the fragment shader, and masking is applied during rendering using Equations 1 and 2. A technique that scales the entries of the pre-integrated table using a mask based on a specific value (e.g., scalar value, gradient magnitude) to create effects like banding. It is chosen for banding effects. Mask Calculation: m = ((1 + \sin(oo \pi k)) \cdot 0.5)^p, where oo is the value to mask (e.g., scalar value, gradient magnitude) and p is a scalar. Implementation: The masking is done during table computation; no modification is introduced into the rendering process. Time Complexity: Performance is primarily limited by the volume rendering stage. The method processes the adapted mesh, with performance depending on the number of tetrahedra and the complexity of illustrative effects. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the tetrahedral mesh in textures and the pre-integration table. Measured Performance: On a standard PC with an NVidia GeForce 7800 GTX (512MB) at 640x480 resolution, the direct volume renderer has a peak performance of about 800,000 tetrahedra per second. The performance change due to illustration techniques is negligible even for datasets with millions of tetrahedra. Strengths: GPU-accelerated, handles unstructured grids (tetrahedral meshes), supports various illustrative effects, negligible performance overhead for effects. Limitations: Artifacts due to constant gradient within each tetrahedron. Does not account for occlusion during mesh adaptation. Requires good resolution for accurate gradient estimation via barycentric interpolation. When to Use: When rendering unstructured volumetric data (tetrahedral meshes) with a need for fast, GPU-accelerated volume rendering and illustrative effects. When Not to Use: When high accuracy in gradient estimation is critical for low-resolution data, or when occlusion-aware mesh adaptation is required. Originating from work on pre-integrated volume rendering for regular grids [Parent], this method extends the technique to unstructured volumetric data (tetrahedral meshes). It was presented in the context of flow visualization, aiming to apply illustrative techniques to unstructured grids which had previously been limited to uniform grids. The implementation modifies a single-pass raycaster for tetrahedral meshes.
