name: Interpolated Pre-Integrated Lighting
head: Lighting method for pre-integrated volume rendering
body: Interpolated Pre-Integrated Lighting is a technique for achieving high-quality, discontinuity-free lighting in pre-integrated volume rendering by approximating the lighting integral through linear interpolation between front and back sample planes. Unlike standard pre-integrated rendering which applies lighting to a single representative sample, this method eliminates lighting artifacts at transparent boundaries and allows an unlimited number of possibly transparent isosurfaces without ordering problems. It sets itself apart from Incremental Subrange Integration by focusing on the spatial interpolation of lighting contributions across a sampling slab rather than optimizing the accumulation of the volume rendering integral itself. Inputs: A volume dataset with a defined transfer function mapping scalar values to color (r, g, b) and opacity \alpha. A sampling scheme defining front sample index i and back sample index j for each ray segment (slab). Normals Ni and Nj at the front and back sampling points, either looked up from a gradient field or computed. Lighting parameters (light position, view direction, material properties). Outputs: Final pixel color C{output} and opacity \alpha{output}. The method relies on two 2D RGBA lookup tables indexed by the pair of sample indices (i, j), where i and j represent the scalar values or indices of the front and back samples of a slab. The tables pack five pieces of information into four components across two textures: 1. Front Lookup Table: (r, g, b): Diffusely-lit, front-weighted color integral. \alpha: Full pre-integrated opacity (unweighted). 2. Back Lookup Table: (r, g, b): Diffusely-lit, back-weighted color integral. \alpha: Specularly-lit, back-weighted color intensity. The front-weighted specular color is not stored directly but is derived during rendering by subtracting the back-weighted specular intensity (from the Back Table's \alpha) from the full pre-integrated opacity (from the Front Table's \alpha). This relies on the constraint that the sum of front-weighted and back-weighted integrals equals the unweighted integral. The tables are pre-computed with O(n^2) complexity, where n is the number of discrete sample values. 1. Unweighted Integrals: Compute the standard pre-integrated color and opacity for all pairs (i, j): C{i \rightarrow j}^1 = \sum{k=i}^{j} Ak Ck \alpha{i \rightarrow j} = \sum{k=i}^{j} Ak Where Ak is the opacity and Ck is the color at index k. 2. Globally Ramped Integrals: Compute the integral weighted by the index k: C{i \rightarrow j}^G = \sum{k=i}^{j} k Ak Ck 3. Weighted Color Calculation: Derive the front-weighted color C{i \rightarrow j}^W (which corresponds to the contribution weighted toward the front sample i) using the formula: C{i \rightarrow j}^W = \frac{C{i \rightarrow j}^G - i C{i \rightarrow j}^1}{j - i} This operation removes the dependence on i from each term and scales the result by the slab thickness (j-i). 4. Table Population: Diffuse Tables: Compute C{i \rightarrow j}^W using the transfer function's color Ck. Store front-weighted diffuse in Front Table RGB and back-weighted diffuse in Back Table RGB. Specular Tables: Compute C{i \rightarrow j}^W using white color (1, 1, 1) for Ck. Store back-weighted specular intensity in Back Table \alpha. Opacity: Store \alpha{i \rightarrow j} in Front Table \alpha. For each ray and sampling slab defined by front sample i and back sample j: 1. Retrieve Indices: Identify the scalar values or indices i and j at the front and back of the current slab. 2. Lookup Pre-integrated Data: Read Front Table at (i, j) to get C{diffuse, front}^{RGB} and \alpha{full}. Read Back Table at (i, j) to get C{diffuse, back}^{RGB} and I{specular, back}. 3. Compute Specular Components: Calculate front-weighted specular intensity: I{specular, front} = \alpha{full} - I{specular, back}. Note: The specular color is assumed to be white (1,1,1) in the integration, so the intensity values can be used directly as scalar multipliers for the specular lighting model. 4. Compute Lighting Contributions: Compute diffuse lighting contribution for front sample: L{diffuse, i} = \text{DiffuseLight}(Ni, \text{material}). Compute specular lighting contribution for front sample: L{specular, i} = \text{SpecularLight}(Ni, \text{material}). Compute diffuse lighting contribution for back sample: L{diffuse, j} = \text{DiffuseLight}(Nj, \text{material}). Compute specular lighting contribution for back sample: L{specular, j} = \text{SpecularLight}(Nj, \text{material}). 5. Apply Weights: Front-weighted lit color: Ci = C{diffuse, front}^{RGB} \cdot L{diffuse, i} + \mathbf{1} \cdot I{specular, front} \cdot L{specular, i}. Back-weighted lit color: Cj = C{diffuse, back}^{RGB} \cdot L{diffuse, j} + \mathbf{1} \cdot I{specular, back} \cdot L{specular, j}. Note: The source describes multiplying the table values by the lighting contribution. The table values represent the integrated color/opacity. The lighting model is applied to these integrated values. 6. Composite: C{output} = Ci + Cj. \alpha{output} = \alpha{full}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderslab(i, j, Ni, Nj, lightpos, viewdir, material): """ Renders a single slab between sample indices i and j. i, j: Scalar values or indices of front and back samples. Ni, Nj: Normals at front and back samples. """ # 1. Lookup pre-integrated data from 2D RGBA tables # Front Table: RGB = Front Diffuse Color, Alpha = Full Opacity frontdata = lookuptablefront[i, j] Cdifffront = frontdata.rgb alphafull = frontdata.a # Back Table: RGB = Back Diffuse Color, Alpha = Back Specular Intensity backdata = lookuptableback[i, j] Cdiffback = backdata.rgb Ispecback = backdata.a # 2. Derive Front Specular Intensity # Constraint: Front Specular + Back Specular = Full Opacity (assuming white specular integration) Ispecfront = alphafull - Ispecback # 3. Compute Lighting Models # Standard Blinn-Phong or similar Ldiffi = computediffuse(Ni, lightpos, material) Lspeci = computespecular(Ni, lightpos, viewdir, material) Ldiffj = computediffuse(Nj, lightpos, material) Lspecj = computespecular(Nj, lightpos, viewdir, material) # 4. Apply Lighting to Pre-integrated Colors # The table values are colors (RGB). Lighting is applied as a multiplier. # Specular is an intensity added to the color. # Front contribution: Diffuse color Diffuse light + Specular intensity Specular light Ci = Cdifffront Ldiffi + vec3(Ispecfront) Lspeci # Back contribution: Diffuse color Diffuse light + Specular intensity Specular light Cj = Cdiffback Ldiffj + vec3(Ispecback) Lspecj # 5. Output Coutput = Ci + Cj alphaoutput = alphafull return Coutput, alphaoutput Table Size: Larger tables reduce interpolation error when sample values fall between discrete entries. The source provides performance data for tables up to n=2048. Degenerate Input (i=j): If the front and back samples are identical, the denominator (j-i) in the weighted color formula becomes zero. This case represents a zero-thickness slab and should result in zero color contribution and zero opacity, or be handled as a single-sample case. The source notes that i > j cases exist but does not detail the handling, implying standard ray casting order (i < j) is maintained. Rapid Normal Changes: If normals change rapidly or are poorly defined (e.g., at sharp boundaries between homogeneous materials), the method may introduce minor lighting artifacts compared to special-case isosurface rendering. Complexity: The lookup table generation has O(n^2) complexity, a significant improvement over the O(n^3) brute-force method. Performance: The rendering algorithm is slower than traditional pre-integrated rendering because it requires computing two lighting values per slab and an extra texture read (fill-rate dependent). Vortex Dataset (128³, 512² window): 8.1 fps with masking, 5.4 fps without (vs 10.5/8.1 fps for single-sample). Limitations: Fill-rate dependent; slightly slower than standard pre-integration; potential artifacts at sharp material boundaries with rapidly changing normals. This method approximates the lighting integral by interpolating between front and back samples, analogous to Gouraud shading but applied to pre-integrated volumes. It builds on the concept of pre-integrated volume rendering [MHC90, EKE01] and complements techniques like Incremental Subrange Integration for efficient table generation. name: Incremental Subrange Integration
body: Incremental Subrange Integration is an algorithm for computing the exact n \times n pre-integration lookup table in O(n^2) time, avoiding the O(n^3) cost of brute-force integration. It solves the problem that standard incremental composition fails because the non-linear opacity correction depends on the number of composited intervals |j-i|, which varies across the lookup table. Unlike brute-force methods, it reuses previously computed subrange integrals by organizing them along diagonals where |j-i| is constant. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A transfer function with nt entries (sample values). Output: An n \times n pre-integration lookup table, where n is typically equal to or a small constant factor of nt. Data Structures: Lookup Table: An n \times n matrix storing pre-integrated color and opacity values for all pairs of transfer function endpoints (i, j). Subrange-Integral Table: For each diagonal of length nr (where nr = |j-i|), a table is constructed to store intermediate integration results. The transfer function (size nt) is separated into bins of length nr. Each bin stores 2nr integration values: computed incrementally from left-to-right and right-to-left. Total entries per sub-integral table: O(nt). Formulas: The core challenge is the non-linear opacity correction required when compositing intervals of different lengths. The opacity value from the transfer function (\alpha{\text{from xfer func}}) represents opacity per unit in world space. To composite it correctly over a range of |j-i| intervals with world-space sampling slab width \Delta, the opacity must be corrected before compositing: \alpha{\text{for compositing}} = 1 - (1 - \alpha{\text{from xfer func}})^{\frac{\Delta}{|j - i|}} This correction must be applied to the \alpha values before compositing; it cannot be applied to a composited sequence of color values. Steps: 1. Diagonal Processing: Iterate through all 2n diagonals of the n \times n lookup table. Each diagonal corresponds to a fixed difference nr = |j - i|. 2. Bin Construction: For a diagonal of length nr, divide the transfer function into bins of length nr. 3. Subrange Computation: For each bin, compute subrange integrals incrementally: Left-hand subrange: Start with a subrange i \rightarrow x. Expand it to i \rightarrow (x + 1) by compositing a new value behind it (using the corrected opacity). Right-hand subrange: Start with a subrange x \rightarrow j. Expand it to (x - 1) \rightarrow j by compositing one value in the front (using the corrected opacity). Store the 2nr intermediate results in the sub-integral table for this bin. 4. Bin Composition: Composite two subrange-integral pairs from adjacent bins to construct the final integral of length nr for the diagonal. 5. Reverse Direction: For entries where i > j (below the main diagonal), reverse the view direction. Compute integrals and composite operations in the opposite direction (back-to-front). Returns: lookuptable: n x n matrix of (color, opacity) tuples. Composite the relevant subranges. # This is more complex and may require multiple steps. # The source states "Two subrange-integral pairs from adjacent bins # can then be composited". This suggests the diagonal is built # by combining O(1) pre-computed values. lookuptable[i][j] = retrievesubrangeintegral(subrangetables, i, j, numintervals, delta) return lookuptable def retrievesubrangeintegral(subrangetables, i, j, numintervals, delta): """ Retrieves the pre-computed integral for range [i, j] from the subrange tables. Handles bin boundaries and direction. """ # Implementation detail: # This function would map i and j to the specific pre-computed values # in the left/right lists of the relevant bins and composite them if necessary. # Since the source does not provide the exact indexing formula, # we note that the complexity is O(1) per entry. pass Parameters: n: Number of sample values (transfer function entries). \Delta: World-space sampling slab width. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-linear Opacity Correction: Simple addition of new intervals to previously computed integrals is invalid because the opacity scaling depends on |j-i|. If the number of ranges changes, the scaling for previously computed color values becomes incorrect. Ordering Problems: Simplifying the integration to occur within a single sampling slab can cause ordering problems, especially with multiple spikes in the transfer function (e.g., thin "isoslabs"). Below Diagonal: For i > j, the view direction must be reversed, and compositing must be performed in the opposite direction. A method for generating pre-integrated lookup tables that incorporate lighting effects by applying spatially varying scaling functions to transfer function colors. It uses Incremental Subrange Integration as a first step to compute the base tables in O(n^2) time, then combines three intermediate tables to handle linearly varying lighting. Time Complexity: O(n^2) for an n \times n lookup table, where n is the number of sample values. This is a significant improvement over the O(n^3) brute-force method. Memory Complexity: O(nt) per diagonal's subrange-integral table, where nt is the number of transfer function entries. Total memory is proportional to the number of diagonals times nt, which is O(n^2) overall. Performance: Allows interactive generation of lookup tables in software for transfer functions with a large number of entries, without approximation or hardware assistance. Strengths: Exact computation, no approximation, software-only implementation, interactive speed for large transfer functions. Limitations: Requires O(n^2) memory for the lookup table and intermediate tables. The algorithm is more complex to implement than brute-force due to bin management and direction handling. When to Use: When high-quality pre-integration is required for large transfer functions and interactive table generation is needed, and hardware acceleration for table generation is not available or desired. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained, or when approximate methods are acceptable and simpler to implement. Incremental Subrange Integration was proposed by Roettger and Ertl in 2004 as part of their work on high-quality lighting and efficient pre-integration for volume rendering. It was introduced to address the computational bottleneck of generating pre-integration lookup tables for large transfer functions, which previously required O(n^3) time or hardware assistance. The method is applicable to any pre-integrated rendering method, including cell projection, ray casting, and hardware-accelerated algorithms. name: Weighted Lookup Table Computation
head: Back-weighted lookup tables, Front-weighted lookup tables
body: Weighted Lookup Table Computation is a method for generating pre-integrated lookup tables that incorporate lighting effects (diffuse and specular) by applying spatially varying scaling functions (ramps) to transfer function colors during integration. It solves the problem that standard pre-integration assumes uniform lighting across a voxel interval, whereas weighted tables allow the lighting contribution to vary linearly from the front to the back of the interval. Unlike standard pre-integration, where the lookup table entry depends only on the opacity values at the endpoints, weighted tables depend on the integration range (i, j). This dependency is resolved by computing three intermediate tables and combining them, allowing the method to run in O(n^2) time, matching the complexity of standard pre-integration. Inputs: Transfer function size nt (number of bins). Pre-integration table size n \times n, where n = nt / nr and nr is the number of samples per bin. Opacity values \alphak and color values Ck for each transfer function sample k \in [0, nt-1]. Outputs: Three intermediate lookup tables: 1. C^1: Standard pre-integrated lookup table (unweighted). 2. C^G{front}: Table computed with a global ramp weighting function increasing from front to back (index k). 3. C^G{back}: Table computed with a global ramp weighting function decreasing from front to back (index nt - 1 - k). Final weighted lookup tables C^W derived from the intermediates. Data Structures: The lookup tables are 2D arrays of size n \times n. Each entry (i, j) stores a 3D color vector (r, g, b). Intermediate tables store the same format but represent integrals with modified color weights. Steps: 1. Compute Standard Table (C^1): Run the standard incremental subrange integration algorithm [Parent] on the original transfer function colors Ck to populate C^1. This represents the unweighted pre-integrated color. 2. Compute Globally Ramped Tables (C^G): Create a modified transfer function where each color Ck is multiplied by its index k (for front-weighted) or nt - 1 - k (for back-weighted). Note that opacity \alphak remains unchanged. Run the standard incremental subrange integration algorithm on these modified colors to populate C^G{front} and C^G{back} respectively. 3. Compute Final Weighted Tables (C^W): For each entry (i, j) in the lookup table where i < j: Calculate the weighted color using the formula: C{i \rightarrow j}^W = \frac{C{i \rightarrow j}^G - i C{i \rightarrow j}^1}{j - i} where C{i \rightarrow j}^G is the value from the appropriate globally ramped table (C^G{front} or C^G{back} depending on the desired weighting direction), C{i \rightarrow j}^1 is the value from the standard table, i is the front sample index, and j is the back sample index. Formulas: The opacity factor Ax for term x in the integration sum is defined as: Ax = (1 - \alphai)(1 - \alpha{i+1})\dots(1 - \alpha{x-1}) \alphax The derivation relies on the fact that the desired weighted integral C{i \rightarrow j}^W with a local ramp W(x) = \frac{x-i}{j-i} can be expressed as: C{i \rightarrow j}^W = \frac{1}{j-i} \sum{x=i}^{j} (x-i) Ax Cx This is equivalent to: C{i \rightarrow j}^W = \frac{1}{j-i} \left( \sum{x=i}^{j} x Ax Cx - i \sum{x=i}^{j} Ax Cx \right) The first sum is C{i \rightarrow j}^G and the second is C{i \rightarrow j}^1. Parameters: nt: Number of transfer function bins. Typical values depend on the transfer function complexity. nr: Number of samples per bin. Determines the resolution of the lookup table n = nt / nr. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero: If i = j, the denominator j-i is zero. This case corresponds to a single-sample interval and should be handled separately or avoided by ensuring i < j for weighted entries. Precision: The subtraction C^G - i C^1 may suffer from catastrophic cancellation if i is large and C^G \approx i C^1. Use high-precision arithmetic if necessary. Lighting direction: Front-weighted tables are used when lighting varies from front to back; back-weighted when it varies from back to front. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeweightedlookuptables(transferfunction, nr): """ transferfunction: list of tuples (alpha, r, g, b) for each bin. nr: number of samples per bin. Returns: weightedlookuptable (n x n array of (r, g, b)) """ nt = len(transferfunction) n = nt // nr # Step 1: Compute standard pre-integrated table C^1 # This uses the standard incremental subrange integration algorithm [Parent] C1 = computestandardpreintegration(transferfunction, nr) # Step 2: Compute globally ramped tables C^Gfront and C^Gback # Create modified transfer functions tffront = [] tfback = [] for k, (alpha, r, g, b) in enumerate(transferfunction): # Multiply color by index k for front-weighted tffront.append((alpha, r k, g k, b k)) # Multiply color by (nt - 1 - k) for back-weighted tfback.append((alpha, r (nt - 1 - k), g (nt - 1 - k), b (nt - 1 - k))) CGfront = computestandardpreintegration(tffront, nr) CGback = computestandardpreintegration(tfback, nr) # Step 3: Compute final weighted tables weightedtable = [[(0, 0, 0) for in range(n)] for in range(n)] for i in range(n): for j in range(i + 1, n): # Get values from intermediate tables c1 = C1[i][j] cgf = CGfront[i][j] cgb = CGback[i][j] # Compute front-weighted entry # Formula: (C^G - i C^1) / (j - i) denom = j - i rf = (cgf[0] - i c1[0]) / denom gf = (cgf[1] - i c1[1]) / denom bf = (cgf[2] - i c1[2]) / denom weightedtable[i][j] = (rf, gf, bf) # Compute back-weighted entry rb = (cgb[0] - i c1[0]) / denom gb = (cgb[1] - i c1[1]) / denom bb = (cgb[2] - i c1[2]) / denom # Note: The back-weighted table might be stored separately or combined # depending on implementation. Here we assume a single table for front-weighted # as per the primary formula derivation. return weightedtable Time Complexity: O(n^2), where n is the number of bins in the lookup table. This is because there are 2n diagonals in the n \times n table, and each requires a single range-integral table computation of O(nt) operations, leading to O(n \cdot nt) = O(n^2) total time. Memory Complexity: O(n^2) to store the three intermediate tables and the final weighted table. Performance: The method allows interactive generation of lit pre-integration tables, similar to standard pre-integration. Strengths: Incorporates lighting effects (diffuse and specular) into pre-integration, providing higher visual quality than unweighted pre-integration. Efficient O(n^2) computation makes it feasible for real-time applications. Limitations: More complex to implement than standard pre-integration due to the need for three intermediate tables and the combination step. The weighting function depends on the integration range, requiring the specific derivation to avoid O(n^4) complexity. The method was introduced in the paper "High-Quality Lighting and Efficient Pre-Integration for Volume Rendering" by Ma et al. (2004). It extends the concept of pre-integration to include lighting by applying scaling functions to transfer function colors during integration. The key insight is that the dependency of the weighting function on the integration range can be resolved using globally ramped intermediate tables, allowing efficient computation. name: Pre-integration of Transfer Function Contribution
head: Pre-integrated Transfer Function Tables
body: Pre-integration of transfer function contribution is a technique that replaces on-the-fly interpolation and integration with pre-computed lookup tables to perform fully-shaded semi-transparent and iso-surface volume rendering. It addresses the dichotomy between image quality and performance by pre-integrating the transfer function's contribution along ray segments, thereby smoothing image imperfections caused by low sampling frequencies. It sets itself apart from Pre-integrated Volume Rendering by mapping pairs of scalar density values directly to pre-integrated color and opacity, decoupling the integration of the transfer function from the sampling process. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume dataset V, a color transfer function C(v), an extinction coefficient transfer function \lambda(v), and a gradient volume for shading. Output: A rendered image with reduced aliasing artifacts. Data Structures: Pre-integrated Transfer Function Table: A 2D lookup table indexed by two scalar density values (e.g., vi and v{i+1}). The stored values are the pre-integrated color and opacity contributions for the segment between these two densities. Gradient Volume: Loaded into texture memory to compute gradients for shading. Note that interpolating a gradient volume without subsequent normalization is generally incorrect, though artifacts may not always be visible. Method Steps: 1. Pre-computation: Compute the analytical integration of the transfer function over the segment between two adjacent sample values. For a segment from li to lo, the resulting color C{res} and opacity \alpha are derived from the integrals: C{res} = \int{li}^{lo} C(V(R(l))) \times \exp \left( - \int{li}^l \lambda(V(R(j))) \times dj \right) \times dl \alpha = 1 - \exp \left( - \int{li}^{lo} \lambda(V(R(l))) \times dl \right) The integrals are evaluated for relevant density pairs and stored in the table. 2. Ray Casting: Decompose view rays into segments of homogeneous or very similar length. 3. Lookup: For each segment, determine the scalar density values at the endpoints. Use these values to index into the pre-integrated transfer function table to retrieve the pre-computed color and opacity contribution for that segment. 4. Composition: Composite the retrieved color and opacity contributions along the ray using standard front-to-back alpha blending. Note that in these approximations, color and extinction coefficient values often become absolute values rather than ratios per unit length due to the decomposition of rays into segments. 5. Shading: Load the gradient volume and compute shading. To eliminate artifacts from incorrect gradient interpolation, use a shading cube texture instead of standard texture mapping. Parameters: Table Resolution: Determined by the number of discrete density values stored. Segment Length: Should be homogeneous or very similar to ensure the validity of the pre-integrated values. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Interpolation: Interpolating a gradient volume without normalization yields incorrect results. Value Interpretation: The pre-integrated values are absolute contributions for the segment, not per-unit-length ratios. Solves aliasing artifacts in direct volume ray casting caused by low sampling frequencies, where narrow peaks in a transfer function are missed by discrete ray samples. It sets itself apart from standard ray casting by pre-computing the analytical integration of the transfer function over the segment between two adjacent samples, mapping the pair of scalar density values directly to a pre-integrated color and opacity. Choose it when low sampling frequencies cause aliasing but hardware supports fast 2D texture lookups. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The implementation can perform fully-shaded semi-transparent and iso-surface volume rendering at 1-4 frames per second for 256^3 volumes, using an NVidia GeForce3. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Overcomes undersampling problems associated with large inter-slice distances at off-angles. Smooths image imperfections caused by low sampling frequencies. Performance is inversely dependent on sampling frequency, and the sampled field behavior, when modulated by the transfer function, cannot be satisfactorily reconstructed using too low sampling frequencies. When to Use: Use when image quality must be maintained at low sampling frequencies without increasing computational cost per frame. When not: Avoid when hardware lacks efficient 2D texture lookup or when exact per-unit-length ratios are required. The technique was proposed by Engel et al. to smooth image imperfections caused by low sampling frequencies. It replaced earlier techniques that overcame undersampling problems by interpolating intermediate slices on-the-fly using register combiners in the fragment shader compartment. name: Pre-integrated Transfer Functions
head: 2-D dependent texture classification, Pre-integrated transfer function tables
body: Pre-integrated transfer functions solve aliasing artifacts in direct volume ray casting caused by low sampling frequencies, where narrow peaks in a transfer function are missed by discrete ray samples. It sets itself apart from standard ray casting by pre-computing the analytical integration of the transfer function over the segment between two adjacent samples, mapping the pair of scalar density values directly to a pre-integrated color and opacity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume dataset, a 1-D transfer function T(d) = (c(d), \alpha(d)) mapping density d to color c and opacity \alpha, and the ray step size \Delta s. Output: A 2-D lookup table (LUT) storing pre-integrated color and opacity for every pair of adjacent density values. Data Structures: The core data structure is a 2-D texture or array PreIntTable with dimensions N \times N. Each entry PreIntTable[i][j] stores a tuple (C{int}, \alpha{int}). Indices i and j correspond to the quantized density values of the back and front samples, respectively. Formulas: The method assumes the transfer function is piecewise linear between density values. For a ray segment of length \Delta s connecting two sample points with densities db (back) and df (front), the analytical integration of the volume rendering equation is pre-computed. The standard volume rendering equation for a segment is: C = \int{0}^{\Delta s} c(s) \alpha(s) e^{-\int{0}^{s} \alpha(t) dt} ds \alpha{total} = 1 - e^{-\int{0}^{\Delta s} \alpha(s) ds} Under the piecewise linear assumption, \alpha(s) and c(s) vary linearly between the values at db and df. The pre-integration computes the exact solution to these integrals for the specific segment defined by (db, df) and \Delta s. Parameters: \Delta s: The distance between adjacent ray samples. N: The resolution of the density quantization. Steps: 1. Pre-computation: 1. Iterate over all possible pairs of density values (di, dj) from the volume's range. 2. For each pair, treat them as the boundary values of a segment of length \Delta s. 3. Assume linear interpolation of opacity \alpha(s) and color c(s) between T(di) and T(dj) over the segment. 4. Compute the analytical integral for color C{int} and opacity \alpha{int} using the volume rendering equation with these linear functions. 5. Store (C{int}, \alpha{int}) in PreIntTable at index (i, j). 2. Rendering: 1. For each ray, sample the volume at two adjacent positions separated by \Delta s. 2. Retrieve the scalar density values db and df from the neighboring slices or samples. 3. Quantize db and df to indices i and j. 4. Perform a 2-D texture lookup (or array access) into PreIntTable using (i, j) to retrieve (C{int}, \alpha{int}). 5. Use the retrieved (C{int}, \alpha{int}) as the contribution of that segment in the front-to-back compositing loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def precomputetable(volumemin, volumemax, numlevels, deltas, transferfunction): """ Pre-compute the 2D lookup table for pre-integrated transfer functions. Args: volumemin: Minimum density value in the volume. volumemax: Maximum density value in the volume. numlevels: Number of discrete density levels (N). deltas: Distance between adjacent ray samples. transferfunction: A function T(d) returning (color, opacity) for density d. Returns: A 2D array PreIntTable[numlevels][numlevels] storing (color, opacity). """ PreIntTable = [[None for in range(numlevels)] for in range(numlevels)] # Map density values to indices densitystep = (volumemax - volumemin) / (numlevels - 1) for i in range(numlevels): db = volumemin + i densitystep for j in range(numlevels): df = volumemin + j densitystep # Get transfer function values at boundaries cb, alphab = transferfunction(db) cf, alphaf = transferfunction(df) # Compute analytical integration for the segment # Assuming linear variation of alpha and c between (db, alphab, cb) and (df, alphaf, cf) # over distance deltas. # This requires solving the volume rendering integral analytically. # Let alpha(s) = alphab + (alphaf - alphab) (s / deltas) # Let c(s) = cb + (cf - cb) (s / deltas) # Analytical solution for opacity integral: # A = integral(alpha(s) ds) from 0 to deltas # A = alphab deltas + 0.5 (alphaf - alphab) deltas A = (alphab + alphaf) 0.5 deltas alphaint = 1.0 - math.exp(-A) # Analytical solution for color integral: # Cint = integral(c(s) alpha(s) exp(-integral0^s alpha(t) dt) ds) # This is more complex. For constant alpha, it simplifies. # For linear alpha, the integral of c(s)alpha(s)exp(-A(s)) must be computed. # Standard implementation uses a high-accuracy numerical quadrature # for the color integral when the closed form is unwieldy, or the exact # Engel et al. closed form. We implement a robust 100-step Simpson's rule here. Cint = computecolorintegral(cb, alphab, cf, alphaf, deltas) PreIntTable[i][j] = (Cint, alphaint) return PreIntTable def computecolorintegral(cb, alphab, cf, alphaf, deltas): """ Computes the pre-integrated color for a segment with linearly varying opacity and color. Implements a 100-step Simpson's rule for the volume rendering color integral. """ if abs(alphab - alphaf) < 1e-6 and abs(cb[0] - cf[0]) < 1e-6: # Constant opacity and color case alpha = alphab if alpha == 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) avgc = ((cb[0] + cf[0]) / 2.0, (cb[1] + cf[1]) / 2.0, (cb[2] + cf[2]) / 2.0) return tuple(ch (1.0 - math.exp(-alpha deltas)) for ch in avgc) # General case: linear opacity and color # alpha(s) = alphab + k s, k = (alphaf - alphab) / deltas # c(s) = cb + m s, m = (cf - cb) / deltas # T(s) = exp(-alphab s - 0.5 k s^2) # Integrand: c(s) alpha(s) T(s) k = (alphaf - alphab) / deltas m = [(cf[ch] - cb[ch]) / deltas for ch in range(3)] n = 100 h = deltas / n integral = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(n + 1): s = i h alphas = alphab + k s cs = [cb[ch] + m[ch] s for ch in range(3)] Ts = math.exp(-alphab s - 0.5 k s s) coeff = 4.0 if i % 2 == 1 else 2.0 if i > 0 and i < n else 1.0 for ch in range(3): integral[ch] += coeff cs[ch] alphas Ts return tuple(ch h / 3.0 for ch in integral) def renderray(samples, PreIntTable, numlevels, volumemin, volumemax): """ Render a single ray using pre-integrated transfer functions. Args: samples: List of density values along the ray. PreIntTable: The pre-computed 2D table. numlevels: Number of density levels (N). volumemin: Minimum density value in the volume. volumemax: Maximum density value in the volume. Returns: Final color and transmittance. """ color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 densitystep = (volumemax - volumemin) / (numlevels - 1) for k in range(len(samples) - 1): db = samples[k] df = samples[k+1] # Quantize densities to indices i = int((db - volumemin) / densitystep) j = int((df - volumemin) / densitystep) # Clamp indices to valid range i = max(0, min(numlevels - 1, i)) j = max(0, min(numlevels - 1, j)) # Lookup pre-integrated color and opacity Cint, alphaint = PreIntTable[i][j] # Front-to-back compositing for ch in range(3): color[ch] += transmittance Cint[ch] transmittance = (1.0 - alphaint) if transmittance < 1e-4: break return tuple(color), transmittance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Quantization of density values into the N \times N table introduces discretization error. Higher N reduces this but increases memory. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes the segment is bounded by the two samples. If the ray starts or ends within a voxel, special handling is needed (e.g., treating the boundary density as the sample density). Non-linear Transfer Functions: The analytical integration assumes piecewise linearity. If the transfer function is highly non-linear within the segment, the approximation error increases. Extends the concept to 3-D transfer functions by using 3-D dependent textures, allowing mapping from multiple scalar values (e.g., density, gradient magnitude) to color and opacity. It offers more control but requires larger textures and more complex hardware support. The underlying assumption of the pre-integration method. It guarantees that no transfer function detail falling between two interpolated density pairs fails to be considered in the discrete ray integration. Not given in the sources. Pre-integrated transfer functions were proposed by Engel et al. in 2003. The method was introduced to address the dichotomy between image quality and performance in volume rendering, specifically targeting the image imperfections caused by low sampling frequencies. It builds on the idea of using dependent textures for transfer function classification. name: Order-Dependent Sampling Strategies
head: Order-Dependent Sampling
body: Order-Dependent Sampling Strategies are a category of volume illumination approaches designed to resolve the order-dependence of sampling operations required for the numerical solutions of integrals in volumetric lighting. They differ from Monte Carlo Volume Rendering and Ray Traversal and Integration Schemes by explicitly addressing illumination order-dependence through deterministic iterative processing or precomputation rather than stochastic sampling or traversal optimization. All methods in this family operate on the principle that the illumination integral is order-dependent with respect to the sampling operation. The core mechanism involves resolving this dependency through one of two primary strategies: 1. Iterative Processing: Determining a common sampling front based on camera and light positions to process all samples in the correct order, ensuring each sample is processed only once. 2. Precomputation: Performing precomputation for a sufficient number of samples and storing results in data structures such as illumination volumes or spherical harmonic representations, making them available during rendering. Iterative processing determines a common sampling front based on camera and light positions to process all samples in the correct order, whereby each sample is only processed once. This approach is typically implemented in combination with slice-based volume rendering. However, it prevents the use of early ray termination and empty space skipping, which are mandatory techniques when dealing with costly sampling operations. Precomputation facilitates solving the order-dependent illumination integral by performing calculations for a sufficient number of samples in advance, storing results in data structures ranging from simple illumination volumes to spherical harmonic representations. This method is viable for single light source scenarios but becomes non-viable for multimodal data with multiple light sources. Storing illumination information for all light sources and wavelengths results in huge data structures, and unnecessary computations are performed for occluded parts of the volumes since the precomputation is performed independently of the view-dependent visibility. The concept of order-dependent sampling arises in the context of multimodal volume illumination, where standard volume rendering techniques fail to provide the desired interactive experience due to the complexity of illumination integrals. The specific strategies of iterative processing and precomputation were identified and analyzed in the context of resolving order-dependence for advanced volumetric illumination. The limitations of these approaches, particularly regarding memory usage for multiple light sources and the inability to use early ray termination, motivated the development of alternative approaches for multimodal volume illumination. name: Simpson's Rule Integration
head: Simpson's Rule Integration for Extinction Sampling, Simpson's Rule Integration of scattering, Simpson's Rule for Extinction Sampling
body: Simpson's Rule Integration is a numerical integration technique used to sample the extinction function \sigmat(x) along a ray in direct volume ray casting, specifically to reduce aliasing artifacts when particles are large and few in number. It computes the scattered radiance C{scat} by approximating the integral of the extinction coefficient, chosen for its superior accuracy over Taylor series integration methods. It sets itself apart from Monte Carlo methods by providing deterministic, low-variance results for participating media with sparse large particles, and from pre-integration methods by operating directly on the ray without requiring precomputed volumes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray interval [z{min}, z{max}]; number of integration steps n; shadow map for visibility sampling; particle data for extinction calculation. Output: Approximated integral value for C{scat} (scattered radiance contribution). Data Structures: The method does not define a specific complex data structure beyond standard ray parameters and shader inputs. It relies on the ability to sample a shadow map for visibility Vis(z) and compute extinction \sigmat(z) at arbitrary points along the ray. Parameters: n: Number of Simpson's rule steps. Configurable integer. Default: 1 (single step spanning [z{min}, z{max}]). Range: 1 to 10. Note: Increasing from 1 to 2 causes a dramatic visual difference; further increases offer marginal improvements, most visible in volumetric shadows. Formulas: The basic Simpson's rule approximation for an interval [a, b] is: \inta^b f(x) dx \approx \frac{b-a}{6} \left( f(a) + 4f\left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right) + f(b) \right) where f(x) represents the integrand, which involves terms like TL(z), TV(z{min}, z), Vis(z), and \sigmat(z). To apply this to the full interval [z{min}, z{max}], the interval is divided into n sub-intervals. Simpson's rule is applied to each sub-interval, and the results are summed. For each step, the following quantities are computed: 1. TL(z): Computed using Equation 8 from the source. 2. TV(z{min}, z): Computed using Equation 10 from the source. 3. Vis(z): Sampled from a shadow map. 4. \sigmat(z): Extinction coefficient computed using Equation 9 from the source. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def simpsonsruleintegration(zmin, zmax, n, shadowmapsampler, extinctioncalculator): """ Computes the integral for Cscat using Simpson's rule over n steps. Args: zmin: Start of ray interval. zmax: End of ray interval. n: Number of integration steps (default 1, range 1-10). shadowmapsampler: Function to sample Vis(z) from shadow map. extinctioncalculator: Function to compute sigmat(z) using Equation 9. Returns: Approximated integral value. """ totalintegral = 0.0 stepsize = (zmax - zmin) / n for i in range(n): # Define sub-interval [a, b] a = zmin + i stepsize b = zmin + (i + 1) stepsize mid = (a + b) / 2.0 # Evaluate integrand f(x) at a, mid, b # Note: The exact form of f(x) involves TL, TV, Vis, and sigmat # as per Equations 8, 9, 10 from the source. # We assume a helper function integrand(z) encapsulates these calculations. fa = integrand(a, shadowmapsampler, extinctioncalculator) fmid = integrand(mid, shadowmapsampler, extinctioncalculator) fb = integrand(b, shadowmapsampler, extinctioncalculator) # Apply Simpson's rule for this sub-interval subintervalintegral = (b - a) / 6.0 (fa + 4.0 fmid + fb) totalintegral += subintervalintegral return totalintegral def integrand(z, shadowmapsampler, extinctioncalculator): """ Computes the value of the integrand f(z) at point z. This involves computing TL(z), TV(zmin, z), sampling Vis(z), and computing sigmat(z). Args: z: Position along the ray. shadowmapsampler: Function to sample Vis(z). extinctioncalculator: Function to compute sigmat(z). Returns: The value of the integrand at z. """ # Compute TL(z) using Equation 8 TL = computeTL(z) # Compute TV(zmin, z) using Equation 10 TV = computeTV(zmin, z) # Sample Vis(z) from shadow map Vis = shadowmapsampler(z) # Compute sigmat(z) using Equation 9 sigmat = extinctioncalculator(z) # The exact combination of these terms to form f(z) is defined in the source's # Equation 7 and related equations. Since the exact algebraic combination # is not fully explicit in the provided notes, we return a placeholder # representing the complex integrand. In a real implementation, this # would be the specific formula from the paper. # Assuming the integrand is a product or sum involving these terms # as per standard volume rendering integrals. A precise implementation # requires the full context of Equations 7-10 from. return TL TV Vis sigmat # Placeholder for actual integrand formula def computeTL(z): # Implementation of Equation 8 from # Not given in the sources. pass def computeTV(zmin, z): # Implementation of Equation 10 from # Not given in the sources. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Under-sampling: Low step counts (e.g., n=1) result in under-sampling of the extinction function \sigmat(x), causing tetrahedron edges to be visible as artifacts. Firefly Artifacts: Taylor series integration methods produce firefly artifacts, which Simpson's rule avoids. Hole-like Shadows: When viewing volumetric shadows head-on, they may appear as holes through the medium, especially when cast onto low extinction media. Performance: Increasing n increases frame time linearly. The slope is steeper for larger particle counts. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of integration steps n and the number of particles. Frame time increases linearly with n. Memory Complexity: Low, as it operates per-pixel in the shader and does not require large precomputed volumes. Memory usage scales with screen resolution. Measured Performance: At 800x600 resolution: 1.60 ms/frame. At 1920x1080 resolution: 3.80 ms/frame. At 2560x1600 resolution: 7.87 ms/frame. Base time (without large kernel PCF) is 3.24 ms/frame, increasing to 7.63 ms/frame with large kernel PCF. However, large kernel PCF is not recommended as increasing step count provides better softening at lower cost. Strengths: Reduces aliasing artifacts for large, sparse particles. Avoids firefly artifacts associated with Taylor series integration. Provides better shadow softening at lower computational cost compared to large kernel PCF. Limitations: Under-sampling leads to visible geometric artifacts (tetrahedron edges). Performance scales with resolution and particle count. Marginal visual improvements beyond n=2 or n=3. When to use: When rendering participating media with large, sparse particles where aliasing artifacts are a concern, and deterministic results are preferred over Monte Carlo methods. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and low step counts cause unacceptable artifacts, or when very high particle counts make the linear scaling prohibitive. Simpson's Rule Integration was explored as an alternative to Taylor series integration for computing scattered radiance C{scat} in particle-based volumetric rendering. The Taylor series method was found to be inaccurate and produced objectionable firefly artifacts. Simpson's rule was chosen for its higher accuracy. The method was implemented in a research artifact, with the step count n made configurable to balance visual quality and performance. It is used in the context of direct volume ray casting for particle-based participating media. name: Layered Volume Rendering with Light Propagation
head: Layer-based volumetric ray marching, Plane-sweep volume rendering
body:
Layered Volume Rendering with Light Propagation is a compute-shader-based technique that renders volumetric data by processing a stack of parallel planes (layers) rather than individual pixels or rays. It propagates light and view rays across these layers, accumulating color, alpha, and material properties while applying refraction gradients and transfer functions. It sets itself apart from standard direct volume ray casting by decoupling the light transport calculation from the view ray accumulation into distinct propagation passes, allowing for efficient screen-space approximation of scattering and refraction effects across discrete depth slices. The method operates on a stack of P parallel planes spaced by a constant distance. It uses two main phases per layer: a Light Propagation pass to compute attenuated light intensity and direction, and a Ray Propagation pass to accumulate the final image color using the propagated light. Inputs: ubo: Uniform buffer object containing: planepixelsize: Pixel size of the rendering planes in world units. distancebetweenplanes: Constant Z-distance between consecutive layers. lightVSPos: View-space position of the light source. lightcolor: View-space color/intensity of the light source. planecount: Total number of layers P. middleoffrontplanevs.z: Z-coordinate of the front plane in view space. Textures: volumedensity: Scalar volume data. volumetransfer: Transfer function texture, sampled with vec2(volumedensity, volumedensityprev) to output alpha. mediumtransfer: Tint transfer function texture, sampled with vec2(volumedensity, volumedensityprev) to output tint color. Buffers (from previous layer or initialization): lbin: Light color buffer (input). ldbin: Light direction buffer (input). vpbin: View position buffer (input). vdbin: View direction buffer (input). cbin: Color buffer (input). mbin: Material buffer (input). Outputs: lbout: Light color buffer (output). ldbout: Light direction buffer (output). cbout: Final color/alpha buffer (output). mbout: Material buffer (output). vpbout: Next view position buffer (output). vdbout: Next view direction buffer (output). All buffers are accessed via imageLoad/imageStore using ivec2 pixel coordinates corresponding to the screen resolution. The buffers store vec4 values for color/alpha/material and vec3 for directions/positions. For each layer l from 0 to P-1: 1. Coordinate Calculation: Compute current layer Z position: z{current} = 	ext{ubo.middle\of ront\plane\vs.z} - l \cdot 	ext{ubo.distance etween\planes}. 2. Light Ray Intersection: For each pixel (u, v), define a light ray starting at (0.5, 0.5, z{current} + d{plane}) with direction -\mathbf{L}{current} (sampled from ldbin at (u,v)). Intersect this ray with the plane at z{current} to find the hit point \mathbf{p}{prev}. 3. Light Sampling & Averaging: Sample light color \mathbf{L}{prev} from lbin at \mathbf{p}{prev}.xy. Sample light direction \mathbf{L}{prev\dir} from ldbin at \mathbf{p}{prev}.xy. Apply 4-tap averaging to \mathbf{L}{prev\dir}: center weight 0.5, four neighbors weight 0.125 each. Normalize the result. If length < 10^{-6}, set to (0,0,1). 4. Irradiance Scaling: Compute screen-space area factors: S{current} = | rac{\partial u}{\partial x}| \cdot | rac{\partial u}{\partial y}| and S{prev} = | rac{\partial p{prev}.x}{\partial x}| \cdot | rac{\partial p{prev}.y}{\partial y}| using dFdx/dFdy. Compute irradiance factor I: I =  egin{cases} S{prev} / S{current} & 	ext{if } S{current} > 10^{-8} \ 1.0 & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases}. 5. Transfer Function & Attenuation: Convert UV and \mathbf{p}{prev}.xy to world positions at z{current} and z{current} + d{plane}. Sample volumedensity at both positions to get ho{current} and ho{prev}. Sample volumetransfer with vec2(ρcurrent, ρprev) to get opacity \alpha. Sample mediumtransfer with vec2(ρcurrent, ρprev) to get tint \mathbf{T} via mix(vec3(1.0), mdata.rgb, mdata.a). Compute output light color: \mathbf{L}{out} = \mathbf{L}{prev} \cdot I \cdot (1.0 - \alpha) \cdot \mathbf{T}. Clamp \mathbf{L}{out} to minimum value 20.0. 6. Light Refraction Update: Compute midpoint \mathbf{m}{ws\light} = (\mathbf{p}{ws} + \mathbf{p}{prev\ws}) \cdot 0.5. Get refraction gradient 
abla \mathbf{L}{grad} from volume density at \mathbf{m}{ws\light}. Update light direction: \mathbf{L}{next} = \mathbf{L}{prev\dir} + 
abla \mathbf{L}{grad} \cdot d{plane}. Normalize and store to ldbout. For each layer l from 0 to P-1: 1. View Ray Intersection: Sample view position \mathbf{V}{pos} from vpbin and direction \mathbf{V}{dir} from vdbin at (u,v). Convert \mathbf{V}{pos} to world space. Intersect ray from \mathbf{V}{pos} with direction -\mathbf{V}{dir} with plane at z{current} + d{plane} to get previous hit point \mathbf{V}{prev}. Convert to world space. 2. Shading: Compute volume gradient \mathbf{N} at \mathbf{V}{ws} + 0.5. View vector \mathbf{V} = 	ext{normalize}(-\mathbf{V}{dir}). Light direction \mathbf{L}{dir} = 	ext{normalize}(	ext{ubo.lightVSPos} - \mathbf{V}{pos}). Half vector \mathbf{H} = 	ext{normalize}(\mathbf{L}{dir} + \mathbf{V}). Specular: 	ext{spec} = \max(\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{H}, 0.0)^{128.0}. Specular intensity: \mathbf{I}s = 	ext{ubo.lightcolor} \cdot 	ext{spec} \cdot 0.05. Material mask: m{mask} = 	ext{smoothstep}(0.0, 0.05, ho{current}). 3. Accumulation: Sample previous color \mathbf{C}{prev} and alpha A{prev} from cbin. Sample previous material \mathbf{M}{prev} from mbin. Sample light intensity \mathbf{I}d from lbin at current UV. Compute current color: \mathbf{C}{current} = \mathbf{C}{prev} + (1.0 - A{prev}) \cdot \mathbf{M}{prev} \cdot (\alpha \cdot \mathbf{I}d + \mathbf{I}s \cdot m{mask}). Update alpha: A{current} = A{prev} + (1.0 - A{prev}) \cdot \alpha. Update material: \mathbf{M}{current} = \mathbf{M}{prev} \cdot (1.0 - \mathbf{M}{prev}.w) + \mathbf{M}{prev} \cdot \mathbf{M}{prev}.xyz \cdot \mathbf{M}{prev}.w. 4. Refraction & Next Step: Compute midpoint \mathbf{m}{ws\view} = (\mathbf{V}{ws} + \mathbf{V}{prev\ws}) \cdot 0.5 + 0.5. Get refraction gradient 
abla \mathbf{V}{grad}. Update view direction: \mathbf{V}{next} = \mathbf{V}{dir} + 
abla \mathbf{V}{grad} \cdot d{plane}. Normalize. Intersect ray from \mathbf{V}{pos} with \mathbf{V}{next} to plane at z{current} - d{plane} to get \mathbf{V}{next\pos}. 5. Background Replacement (Last Layer): If l == P-1: Generate checkerboard background: scale=16, checkuv = \mathbf{V}{next}.xy \cdot 16, f = \lfloor 	ext{check\uv}.x floor + \lfloor 	ext{check\uv}.y floor \pmod 2, \mathbf{B} = 	ext{mix}((0.2,0.2,0.2), (0.5,0.5,0.5), f). Blend background: \mathbf{C}{current} = \mathbf{B} \cdot (1.0 - A{current}) + \mathbf{C}{current} \cdot A{current}. Set A{current} = 1.0. 6. Output Storage: Store \mathbf{C}{current}, A{current} to cbout. Store \mathbf{M}{current} to mbout. Store \mathbf{V}{next\pos} to vpbout. Store \mathbf{V}{next} to vdbout. Unverified code. e0) / (e1 - e0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def floorvec(v): return (math.floor(v[0]), math.floor(v[1]), math.floor(v[2])) def modvec(v, m): return (v[0] % m, v[1] % m, v[2] % m) def powvec(v, p): return (v[0]p, v[1]p, v[2]p) def maxvec(a, b): return (max(a[0], b[0]), max(a[1], b[1]), max(a[2], b[2])) def samplebuffer(buf, uv): return buf[uv[1]][uv[0]] def storebuffer(buf, uv, value): buf[uv[1]][uv[0]] = value def sampletexture(tex, uv): return tex[uv[1]][uv[0]] def intersectrayplane(origin, direction, planez): t = (planez - origin[2]) / direction[2] return (origin[0] + t direction[0], origin[1] + t direction[1], planez) def uvtoworld(uv, z, pixelsize): return (uv[0] pixelsize, uv[1] pixelsize, z) def vsptoworld(vsp, pixelsize): return (vsp[0] pixelsize, vsp[1] pixelsize, vsp[2]) def computegradient(voldata, pos): dx = voldata[pos[0]+1][pos[1]][pos[2]] - Zero-length light direction: If the normalized light direction after averaging has length < 10^{-6}, it is replaced with (0,0,1) to prevent NaN propagation or division by zero. Division by zero in irradiance scaling: If S{current} < 10^{-8}, the irradiance factor I is clamped to 1.0 to avoid NaN or infinite values. Performance: The method is designed for GPU execution via compute shaders, leveraging parallel processing for each pixel and layer. Strengths: Efficient handling of large volumes by reducing the 3D integration to a series of 2D plane sweeps; supports screen-space refraction and approximate scattering. Limitations: Approximate light transport due to screen-space propagation; quality depends on the number of layers and plane spacing. This method is described in the context of a Vulkan-based volume rendering implementation, specifically associated with the vis-magnus-2018 project. It represents a modern, hardware-accelerated approach to layered volume rendering, integrating light propagation with view ray casting in a compute shader environment. name: Customization Volume Integration
head: Customization Volume Integration in Ray Casting, Position-dependent Parameter Modification
body: Customization Volume Integration is a method that integrates a pre-computed customization volume into the volume rendering pipeline to apply position-dependent modifications to visualization parameters, such as gamma correction of intensity values. It enables localized control over rendering appearance without altering the underlying scalar field. Unlike global transfer function adjustments, this approach decouples the modification logic from the core compositing loop, allowing spatially coherent parameter fields to drive the visualization. Inputs and Outputs: InputVolume: The primary scalar volume dataset to be visualized. CustomizationVolume: A pre-computed 3D grid containing position-dependent visualization parameters (e.g., gamma values). Output: The final composited image with position-dependent parameter modifications applied. Data Structures: InputVolume: A 3D grid of scalar values representing the target dataset. CustomizationVolume: A 3D grid of scalar values representing the parameter field, typically with a resolution between 32^3 and 128^3. Linear Filtering Helper: A function that retrieves a value from a volume at a continuous 3D position using linear interpolation. Numbered Steps: 1. Pass Volumes: The CustomizationVolume is passed to the rendering shader alongside the InputVolume. 2. Ray Sampling: For each sample position along the ray segment, fetch the intensity value from the InputVolume. 3. Parameter Fetch: Fetch the visualization parameter from the CustomizationVolume at the identical sampling position using linear filtering. 4. Apply Modification: Apply the fetched parameter to the intensity value. For gamma correction, compute intensity{modified} = \text{pow}(intensity, \gamma). The intensity values are assumed to be normalized to the range [0, 1] to justify this operation. 5. Classification: Apply the transfer function to the modified intensity to obtain the color vector and opacity scalar. 6. Compositing: Accumulate the color and opacity using the standard front-to-back volume rendering equation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastingwithcustomization(InputVolume, CustomizationVolume, rayorigin, raydirection, raybegin, rayend, numsamples, transferfunction): """ Performs volume rendering with position-dependent customization. Args: InputVolume: Primary scalar volume. CustomizationVolume: Pre-computed parameter volume. rayorigin: Camera origin point. raydirection: Normalized viewing direction vector. raybegin: Entry t parameter of the ray segment. rayend: Exit t parameter of the ray segment. numsamples: Discretization count for the ray segment. transferfunction: Maps intensity to (color, opacity). Returns: Final composited color and accumulated opacity. """ acccolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accopacity = 0.0 deltat = (rayend - raybegin) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): t = raybegin + i deltat position = rayorigin + t raydirection # 1. Fetch intensity from input volume intensity = linearfiltersample(InputVolume, position) # 2. Fetch customization parameter (e.g., gamma) from customization volume gamma = linearfiltersample(CustomizationVolume, position) # 3. Apply modification (e.g., gamma correction) # Note: intensity is assumed to be in [0, 1] intensity = pow(intensity, gamma) # 4. Apply transfer function color, opacity = transferfunction(intensity) # 5. Front-to-back compositing alphaterm = opacity (1.0 - accopacity) acccolor += alphaterm color accopacity += alphaterm # Early ray termination optimization if accopacity >= 1.0: break return acccolor, accopacity def linearfiltersample(volume, position): # Standard trilinear interpolation of volume texture at position. # Implementation involves coordinate scaling, voxel indexing, and 7 lerp operations. pass Parameters: CustomizationVolume Resolution: Typically ranges from 32^3 to 128^3. Intensity Range: Input intensity values must be normalized to [0, 1] for operations like gamma correction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance Impact: Additional lookups and computations (e.g., the power function) reduce overall rendering performance. The impact scales with the number of samples and the complexity of the customization computation. Resolution Trade-off: Changing the customization volume resolution between 32^3 and 128^3 has no significant impact on rendering performance, but higher resolution increases interpolation complexity, diminishing interactivity when adjusting seed points. Mitigation: Use lower resolution for interactive customization and higher resolution for final rendering. Memory Bottleneck: For large out-of-core volume datasets, memory transfer to the GPU is the primary bottleneck, making the performance impact of the customization step negligible. Time Complexity: Adds O(1) overhead per sample for the additional lookup and parameter application. The total rendering time increases proportionally to the number of samples and the computational cost of the customization function. Memory Complexity: Requires storing an additional volume of size R^3, where R is the resolution of the customization volume. Performance: The performance impact is generally small, especially for large datasets where memory bandwidth limits throughput. Complex customization functions or high-resolution parameter fields can degrade interactivity. Strengths: Enables spatially varying, position-dependent control over visualization parameters without significantly altering the core ray-casting algorithm. Integrates easily into existing rendering pipelines. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of the customization volume (e.g., via Voronoi tessellation). Performance degrades with high customization volume resolution or complex per-sample functions. When to Use: When spatially varying adjustments to visualization parameters (gamma, opacity scaling, color mapping) are required, and the parameter field can be pre-computed or interactively adjusted at lower resolution. When Not to Use: When real-time, per-sample dynamic parameter generation without pre-computation is required, or when the customization function is extremely complex and strict performance constraints exist. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Interactive Position-dependent Customization of Transfer Function Classification Parameters in Volume Rendering". History: The technique was developed to address the need for localized control over volume rendering parameters, allowing users to adjust visualization aspects in specific regions without affecting the entire dataset. Usage: It is employed in interactive volume rendering systems where users require fine-tuned control over the appearance of specific structures or regions within a volume dataset. name: Adaptive Undersampling
head: Adaptive undersampling with pre-computed interval integrals, Fast Adaptive Undersampling, Two-Pass Adaptive Undersampling with G-Buffer, Two-pass Adaptive Undersampling with Pre-computed Intervals, Two-pass adaptive screen sampling, Two-pass adaptive undersampling with interval G-buffer
body: Adaptive Undersampling is a two-pass rendering technique that accelerates direct volume ray casting by partitioning the integration domain into equal intervals and storing partial integrals in a G-buffer. Unlike standard adaptive undersampling which interpolates final pixel colors, this method interpolates pre-computed interval integrals, allowing the second pass to calculate integrals only over specific intervals where coherence fails, rather than integrating over the entire ray. This approach increases frames per second (FPS) by a factor of 1.5 on average compared to standard adaptive undersampling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D volume texture (unit cube, side length 1), transfer function f, ray origin s, ray end f, block size n, number of intervals M, color threshold \delta. Outputs: Final pixel color C and accumulated opacity A. Data Structures: G-Buffer: A set of M+1 parallel textures with resolution 1/n of the viewport along each side. Each entry is a 4-component vector (RGBA). Index 0: G[0].a stores the distance to the start of the non-zero transfer function domain; G[0].rgb stores the final composited color. Indices 1 \dots M: G[i].rgb stores the color contribution of the i-th interval; G[i].a stores the opacity contribution of the i-th interval. Parameters: M: Maximum number of intervals. Typical value: 8. n: Side length of square blocks for pixel partitioning. One pixel is processed per n \times n block in Pass 1. \delta: Threshold for color difference comparison. Typical value: 0.05. Algorithm Steps: Pass 1: Pre-computation 1. Partition pixels into n \times n blocks. Select one pixel per block. 2. For each selected pixel, calculate the distance a from ray start s to the first point v where the transfer function is non-zero using GetDistanceForStart(s, f). 3. If a \le 0 (no volume hit), set G[0].rgb = \text{BackgroundColor} and halt for this pixel. 4. Initialize G = 0, i = 0, C = 0, A = 0. 5. Calculate step size: \text{step} = \sqrt{3} / M. This assumes the volume is in a unit cube, so the maximum ray length is \sqrt{3}. 6. Calculate maximum iterations: \text{imax} = \lfloor \text{length}(f - s) / \text{step} \rfloor. 7. Calculate last step remainder: \text{lastStep} = \text{length}(f - s) - \text{step} \times \text{imax}. 8. Normalize ray direction: r = \text{normalize}(f - s). 9. Set start point: v = s + G[0].a \times r. 10. Loop while A < 1 and i < \text{imax}: a. Compute partial integral: G[i + 1] = \text{VolumeIntegral}(v, \text{step}). b. Update color: C = C + (1 - A) \times G[i + 1].\text{rgb} \times G[i + 1].a. c. Update opacity: A = A + (1 - A) \times G[i + 1].a. d. Advance ray: v = v + \text{step} \times r. e. Increment i. 11. If A < 1 after the loop, compute final partial integral with lastStep: a. G[\text{imax} + 1] = \text{VolumeIntegral}(v, \text{lastStep}). b. C = C + (1 - A) \times G[\text{imax} + 1].\text{rgb} \times G[\text{imax} + 1].a. 12. Store final color: G[0].\text{rgb} = C. Pass 2: Interpolation or Partial Integration 1. For each remaining pixel, check if adjacent pixels' colors are sufficiently close. Condition: \maxj \| Gj[0].\text{rgb} - Gi[0].\text{rgb} \| < \delta for all neighbors j. 2. If true, perform bilinear interpolation of neighbor colors: C = \text{BilinearInterpolation}(Gi.\text{rgb}). 3. If false, calculate C using recurrence relation: a. Initialize A = 0, C = 0. b. Accelerate start point search: t = r \times \min\{Gi[0].a\}. c. Calculate new start: v = s + r \times \text{GetDistanceForStart}(s + t, f). d. Loop k from 1 to M: i. Check if neighbors' interval k integrals are close: \maxj \| Gj[k].\text{rgb} - Gi[k].\text{rgb} \| < \delta / M. ii. If true, I = \text{BilinearInterpolation}(Gi[k]). iii. If false, determine length: if k = M, \text{Length} = \text{lastStep}, else \text{Length} = \text{step}. Calculate I = \text{VolumeIntegral}(v, \text{Length}). iv. Update color: C = C + (1 - A) \times I.\text{rgb} \times I.a. v. Update opacity: A = A + (1 - A) \times I.a. vi. Advance ray: v = v + \text{step} \times r. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pass1(s, f, M, volumeintegralfunc): # Find distance to first non-zero transfer function value a = getdistanceforstart(s, f) if a <= 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0 C = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] A = 0.0 i = 0 step = sqrt(3.0) / M raylength = length(f - s) imax = floor(raylength / step) laststep = raylength - step imax r = normalize(f - s) v = s + a r while A < 1.0 and i < imax: rgb, alpha = volumeintegralfunc(v, step) C = [C[k] + (1.0 - A) alpha rgb[k] for k in range(3)] A = A + (1.0 - A) alpha v = v + step r i += 1 if A < 1.0: rgb, alpha = volumeintegralfunc(v, laststep) C = [C[k] + (1.0 - A) alpha rgb[k] for k in range(3)] A = A + (1.0 - A) alpha return C, A def pass2(s, f, M, delta, neighborsgbuffer, volumeintegralfunc): # neighborsgbuffer is a list of 4 tuples: (rgb, a) for indices 0..M # Check color coherence maxdiff = max(length(n[0].rgb - neighborsgbuffer[j][0].rgb) for j in range(4)) if maxdiff < delta: # Bilinear interpolation of neighbor colors C = bilinearinterpolatecolors(neighborsgbuffer) return C, 0.0 # Incoherent: partial integration C = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] A = 0.0 step = sqrt(3.0) / M raylength = length(f - s) imax = floor(raylength / step) laststep = raylength - step imax r = normalize(f - s) # Accelerate start point search mina = min(n[0].a for n in neighborsgbuffer) t = r mina v = s + r getdistanceforstart(s + t, f) for k in range(1, M + 1): # Check interval coherence maxintervaldiff = max(length(n[k].rgb - neighborsgbuffer[j][k].rgb) for j in range(4)) if maxintervaldiff < delta / M: rgb, alpha = bilinearinterpolateinterval(neighborsgbuffer, k) else: lengthval = laststep if k == M else step rgb, alpha = volumeintegralfunc(v, lengthval) C = [C[j] + (1.0 - A) alpha rgb[j] for j in range(3)] A = A + (1.0 - A) alpha v = v + step r return C, A def getdistanceforstart(s, f): # Standard ray-marching or analytical step to find first non-zero transfer function value along ray [s, f] pass def bilinearinterpolatecolors(neighbors): # Standard bilinear interpolation of 4 corner colors pass def bilinearinterpolateinterval(neighbors, k): # Standard bilinear interpolation of interval k values from 4 neighbors pass This method accelerates volume integral calculation by partitioning the ray integration interval into M equal pieces and using a second pass to interpolate or recompute integrals for pixels based on neighborhood coherence. It builds on Adaptive Undersampling by increasing the adaptive undersampling factor, allowing fewer pixels to be processed in the first pass while maintaining image quality through spatial interpolation in the second pass. Compared to standard adaptive undersampling, it increases frames per second (FPS) by a factor of 1.5 on average, and provides further acceleration over two-pass adaptive screen sampling without interval partitioning. Time Complexity: Depends on data coherence. In the best case (high coherence), most pixels are interpolated in Pass 2. In the worst case, integrals are calculated for many intervals. Memory Complexity: Requires a G-buffer with M+1 textures of resolution 1/n of the viewport. Performance: On a 3.4GHz Intel Core i7 2600, GTX 780 Ti, 1200x900 viewport, with M=8 and \delta=0.05, the method accelerates standard adaptive undersampling by a factor of 1.5 to 3.7 depending on the dataset. In tested datasets, 91.7% of pixels were interpolated, 5.7% required 1 interval calculation, 2.1% required 2, 0.1% required 3, and 0.4% required >3 intervals. Strengths: Reduces redundant calculations by leveraging spatial coherence of interval integrals. Avoids recursive subdivision overhead on GPUs. Limitations: Efficiency decreases on low coherence datasets. Acceleration factor decreases if many rays end early (e.g., bones), as intervals become short and harder to partition. When to use: High-resolution volume rendering where coherence exists between adjacent rays. When not to use: Highly incoherent data or scenes with rapid geometry changes in screen space. The method was proposed by Smirnova and Shubnikov in 2019, published in the Journal of WSCG. It builds upon earlier adaptive undersampling techniques. The authors implemented it in Unity3D using OpenGL ES 3.1 and tested it on CT datasets (head, lungs, bones). The technique addresses the computational expense of direct volume rendering, which is proportional to the number of pixels. name: Two-pass Adaptive Screen Sampling with Interval Partitioning
head: Two-pass Adaptive Undersampling with Interval Partitioning, Two-pass adaptive screen sampling plus partitioning the interval of integration into M pieces
body: This method accelerates volume integral calculation by partitioning the ray integration interval into M equal pieces and using a second pass to interpolate or recompute integrals for pixels based on neighborhood coherence. It builds on Adaptive Undersampling by increasing the adaptive undersampling factor, allowing fewer pixels to be processed in the first pass while maintaining image quality through spatial interpolation in the second pass. Compared to standard adaptive undersampling, it increases frames per second (FPS) by a factor of 1.5 on average, and provides further acceleration over two-pass adaptive screen sampling without interval partitioning. The method consists of two passes. The first pass computes volume integrals over M equal-length intervals for a subset of pixels (typically one per n \times n block, as defined in the parent article). The second pass processes the remaining pixels, using data from the G-buffer of neighboring pixels to either interpolate colors or compute integrals for specific intervals. Inputs: 3D texture data (volume), transfer function, ray origin s, ray end f, maximum number of intervals M, color difference threshold \delta. Outputs: Final pixel color C{final} and alpha A{final} for each pixel. The G-buffer G stores integration results per pixel. The layout is defined as follows: G[0].rgb: Final pixel color. G[0].a: Distance to the start of the volume (transparency) or background distance. G[i] for i > 0: Intermediate integral results for the i-th interval. Each G[i] contains: G[i].rgb: Color contribution of the interval. G[i].a: Alpha (opacity) contribution of the interval. Note: On hardware with limited G-buffer size (e.g., GTX 780 Ti with 8 elements), multiple integrals can be stored in one element by using only one color component, effectively increasing M. M: User-selected maximum number of intervals for partitioning the ray. Typical value: 8. \delta: Threshold for color difference to determine if bilinear interpolation is sufficient. Typical value: 0.05. For selected pixels (e.g., one per n \times n block): 1. Calculate the distance to the start of the volume d{start} using GetDistanceForStart(s, f). 2. If d{start} \le 0, set G[0].rgb = BackgroundColor and terminate. 3. Initialize G = 0, i = 0, accumulated color C = 0, accumulated alpha A = 0. 4. Calculate step size: step = \sqrt{3} / M. (The longest ray in texture space is \sqrt{3}, the diagonal of the unit cube). 5. Calculate maximum number of full steps: imax = \lfloor length(f - s) / step \rfloor. 6. Calculate length of the last interval: lastStep = length(f - s) - step \times imax. 7. Normalize ray direction: r = normalize(f - s). 8. Set current position: v = s + d{start} \cdot r. 9. Loop while A < 1 and i \le imax: a. Determine current step length: curStep = step if i < imax else lastStep. b. Compute interval integral: G[i+1] = VolumeIntegral(v, curStep). c. Update accumulated color: C = C + (1 - A) \cdot G[i+1].rgb \times G[i+1].a. d. Update accumulated alpha: A = A + (1 - A) \cdot G[i+1].a. e. Advance position: v = v + curStep \cdot r. f. Increment i. 10. Store final color: G[0].rgb = C. For pixels not processed in Pass 1: 1. Get distance to start for current pixel: G[0].a = GetDistanceForStart(s, f). 2. If G[0].a \le 0, set G[0].rgb = BackgroundColor and terminate. 3. Initialize G = 0, i = 0, C = 0, A = 0. 4. Optimization: Determine accelerated start point by casting the ray from s + r \cdot \min\{G{neighbor}[0].a\} using the minimum start distance from the 4 neighboring pixels. 5. Calculate step size: step = \sqrt{3} / M. 6. Calculate imax = \lfloor length(f - s) / step \rfloor. 7. Calculate lastStep = length(f - s) - step \times imax. 8. Normalize ray direction: r = normalize(f - s). 9. Set current position: v = s + G[0].a \cdot r. 10. Loop for each interval k from 1 to imax: a. Check neighborhood coherence using the colors of the 4 neighboring pixels. b. If \max(|C{neighbor} - C{current}|) < \delta / M: i. Use bilinear interpolation of neighbor colors for this interval's contribution. ii. Update C and A using interpolated values. c. Else: i. Compute integral I = VolumeIntegral(v, curStep) where curStep = step if k < imax else lastStep. ii. Update C = C + (1 - A) \cdot I.rgb \times I.a. iii. Update A = A + (1 - A) \cdot I.a. d. Advance position: v = v + curStep \cdot r. 11. Store final color: G[0].rgb = C. Unverified code.
