A) integral["rgb"] integral["a"] A = A + (1.0 - A) integral["a"] G[i + 1] = integral v = v + curstep r i += 1 G[0]["rgb"] = C return G[0] def pass2interpolation(volumedata, transferfunc, rayorigin, rayend, M, delta, neighborcolors): dstart = getdistanceforstart(rayorigin, rayend, volumedata, transferfunc) if dstart <= 0: return {"rgb": Vec3(0, 0, 0), "a": 0} G = [{"rgb": Vec3(0, 0, 0), "a": 0.0} for in range(M + 1)] G[0]["a"] = dstart # Optimization: Accelerate start point calculation using neighbor start distances neighbordstarts = [n["a"] for n in neighborcolors] mindstart = min(neighbordstarts) C = Vec3(0, 0, 0) A = 0.0 step = math.sqrt(3) / M raylen = (rayend - rayorigin).norm() imax = math.floor(raylen / step) laststep = raylen - step imax r = (rayend - rayorigin) / raylen v = rayorigin + mindstart r i = 0 while A < 1.0 and i <= imax: curstep = step if i < imax else laststep # Check neighborhood coherence maxdiff = max((c["rgb"] - C).norm() for c in neighborcolors) if maxdiff < delta / M: # Standard bilinear interpolation of neighbor colors for this interval interprgb = bilinearinterpolate( neighborcolors[0]["rgb"], neighborcolors[1]["rgb"], neighborcolors[2]["rgb"], neighborcolors[3]["rgb"], 0.5, 0.5) integral = {"rgb": interprgb, "a": 0.0} else: integral = volumeintegral(v, curstep, volumedata, transferfunc) C = C + (1.0 - A) integral["rgb"] integral["a"] A = A + (1.0 - A) integral["a"] G[i + 1] = integral v = v + curstep r i += 1 G[0]["rgb"] = C return G[0] High Coherence: Performance decreases if data has high coherence because many pixels are interpolated, reducing the benefit of the second pass. Low Coherence: Performance decreases if data has low coherence because many pixels require full recomputation in the second pass. Optimal performance is at medium coherence. Early Ray Termination: If a significant number of rays end early (e.g., bones), acceleration factor decreases because intervals are short and harder to partition. Visibility Prefiltering is a technique used in hierarchical volumetric shadowing to reduce correlated artifacts inherent in Riemann sum integration by storing a distribution of blocker depths rather than a single depth value per integration sample. It approximates the percentage of visibility changes along the angular axis (\beta) for each sample, converting structured aliasing into less objectionable noise similar to Monte Carlo sampling while requiring significantly fewer light rays. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of pixels processed in the first pass, but adds a second pass. The complexity depends on the coherence of the data. For medium coherence, it provides significant speedup. Memory Complexity: Requires a G-buffer of size M+1 per pixel. On hardware with limited G-buffer size (e.g., 8 elements), multiple integrals can be stored in one element. Measured Performance: On a 3.4GHz Intel Core i7 2600, 4.0GB RAM, NVidia GForce GTX 780 Ti, at 1200x900 resolution, with dataset (a) 256x256x256: Standard adaptive undersampling (A): 32 FPS Two-pass adaptive screen sampling without interval partitioning (B): 72 FPS Proposed method (C): 118 FPS Acceleration C/A = 3.69, C/B = 1.64. Scaling: Increasing M from 8 to 16 increases performance by ~21% on average, but further increases are ineffective. Strengths: Increases FPS by a factor of 1.5 on average compared to standard adaptive undersampling. Most efficient when input data has medium coherence and the transfer function excludes early ray termination. Limitations: Inherits the limitation of adaptive undersampling: input data must be spatially coherent. Performance degrades with high or low coherence. The method was proposed in "Fast Adaptive Undersampling for Volume Rendering". It is implemented in Unity3D using OpenGL ES 3.1. The volume integrals were calculated using the standard method [KW03] with 1/4 of the voxel size as the step size. The bounding volume was chosen as a box. name: Visibility Prefiltering
head: Depth Distribution Prefiltering, Mode-based Depth Storage
body: Visibility Prefiltering is a technique used in hierarchical volumetric shadowing to reduce correlated artifacts inherent in Riemann sum integration by storing a distribution of blocker depths rather than a single depth value per integration sample. It approximates the percentage of visibility changes along the angular axis (\beta) for each sample, converting structured aliasing into less objectionable noise similar to Monte Carlo sampling while requiring significantly fewer light rays. Visibility Prefiltering modifies the standard Riemann sum integration by replacing the scalar blocker depth S[\gamma] with a weighted set of depth modes. This allows the integration step to account for partial visibility within a single integration interval \Delta \gamma, rather than assuming binary occlusion based on a single depth query. Input: The rectified coordinate \gamma for a light ray segment and the integration interval \Delta \gamma. Output: A set of depth modes \{(di, wi)\} inserted into the termination depths structure, where di is the depth and wi is the fractional weight of the mode. The method updates the termination depths structure. While the specific internal layout of this structure is defined in the parent article Two-pass Adaptive Screen Sampling with Interval Partitioning, Visibility Prefiltering interacts with it by performing fractional updates. If a segment yields k modes, the corresponding tree node is updated k times, each time with a fraction of the light intensity equal to the mode's weight wi. 1. Sample: For each integration interval \Delta \gamma in the rectification loop, sample the blocker depth four times along the interval. 2. Cluster: Group the four depth values into one or more modes by clustering values that differ by at most a small constant. For each cluster, calculate the mode depth (e.g., the mean of the cluster) and the weight wj equal to the fraction of samples comprising that mode. 3. Insert: For each mode (dj, wj), update the termination depths structure at the segment's location. When there is more than one mode, the tree node at the segment's location is updated once for every mode at different \beta coordinates, assigning a fraction of the light corresponding to the mode's weight. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def visibilityprefiltering(segmentgamma, deltagamma, sampleblockerdepth, epsilon): """ Prefilters visibility for a single integration interval. Args: segmentgamma: The base rectified gamma coordinate for the segment. deltagamma: The width of the integration interval. sampleblockerdepth: A function that returns the blocker depth at a given gamma. epsilon: A small constant for clustering depth values. Returns: A list of tuples (depth, weight) representing the depth distribution. """ # Step 1: Sample blocker depth four times along the interval # Exact sampling positions along Δγ are implementation-defined samples = [] for i in range(4): offset = (i + 0.5) deltagamma / 4.0 gammapos = segmentgamma + offset depth = sampleblockerdepth(gammapos) samples.append(depth) # Step 2: Cluster nearby depths into modes samples.sort() modes = [] if not samples: return modes currentcluster = [samples[0]] for i in range(1, len(samples)): if samples[i] - samples[i-1] <= epsilon: currentcluster.append(samples[i]) else: # Finalize previous cluster modedepth = sum(currentcluster) / len(currentcluster) modeweight = len(currentcluster) / 4.0 modes.append((modedepth, modeweight)) currentcluster = [samples[i]] # Finalize last cluster modedepth = sum(currentcluster) / len(currentcluster) modeweight = len(currentcluster) / 4.0 modes.append((modedepth, modeweight)) return modes Number of samples: 4. Clustering threshold (\epsilon): "A small constant". Not given in the sources. A value relative to the depth precision or scene scale is required. Single Mode: In the common case where a segment hits a single continuous surface, all four depth values are close to each other, resulting in a single mode with weight 1.0. Multiple Modes: Multiple modes only occur for light rays that terminate on depth discontinuities as seen from the light. Precision: The method relies on the ability to distinguish depth values. If the clustering threshold is too large, distinct occluders may be merged, causing overestimation of visibility. Complexity: The prefiltering step adds a constant overhead (4 samples and clustering) per integration interval. The insertion into the termination depths structure scales with the number of modes (typically 1, occasionally >1). Performance: Compared to basic Riemann sums, which require approximately 10x the number of samples for equal visual quality, Visibility Prefiltering reduces the required number of light rays significantly. It converts correlated artifacts to less objectionable noise, similar to Monte Carlo sampling, but with fewer rays. Visual Quality: The improvements are particularly noticeable in animated sequences, where correlated artifacts manifest as flickering, while differences are hard to spot in still images. Limitations: It does not eliminate aliasing entirely but mitigates its visual impact. It is specific to the hierarchical shadowing context and relies on the underlying termination depths structure. Visibility Prefiltering was introduced in the context of hierarchical volumetric shadow algorithms for single scattering. The general idea is similar to shadow mapping techniques that store depth distributions to enable linear filtering of shadow maps. It addresses the limitation of Riemann sums in volumetric integration, which produce correlated artifacts unless a very large number of samples is used. A hierarchical volumetric shadow algorithm for single scattering, https://doi.org/10.1145/1866158.1866200, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Slice-based and Proxy Geometry Rendering
body: Slice-based and Proxy Geometry Rendering is a direct volume ray casting technique that converts 3D volumetric data into a sequence of 2D polygonal slices (proxy geometry) which are rasterized and composited using standard graphics hardware. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large volumetric datasets by leveraging the fixed-function pipeline or fragment shaders for alpha blending, avoiding the computational cost of per-pixel ray marching loops. It sets itself apart from Texture-Based Volume Rendering by explicitly generating geometric primitives (polygons) for each slice rather than relying solely on texture coordinate generation within a single pass, and from Direct volume ray casting by replacing the continuous sampling integral with discrete, view-dependent or object-aligned polygon rasterization. The method relies on the decomposition of the 3D volume into a set of 2D planar slices. These slices are treated as geometric primitives (typically triangles or quads) that are rasterized by the GPU. The core mechanism involves: 1. Slice Generation: The volume is intersected by a series of parallel planes. The intersection of these planes with the volume bounding box defines the polygonal shape of each slice. 2. Texture Mapping: Each slice vertex is assigned 3D texture coordinates that map to the volumetric data. The volume data is stored as a 3D texture on the GPU. 3. Rasterization and Shading: The polygons are rasterized. In the fragment shader, the 3D texture is sampled at the interpolated texture coordinates to retrieve the scalar value. 4. Classification and Blending: The scalar value is mapped to color and opacity via a transfer function. The fragments are composited using alpha blending (typically GLSRCALPHA, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA). 5. Sorting: The slices must be rendered in the correct depth order relative to the camera (back-to-front for standard alpha blending) to ensure correct compositing. Hybrid Ray Tracing mixes geometric and volumetric data by casting rays through both, drawing samples of each, and compositing them in depth-sorted order. It solves the problem of rendering scenes containing both polygonal models and scalar fields without conversion. It sets itself apart from Texture-Based Volume Rendering by explicitly handling polygon intersections within the ray traversal loop, and from Mixed Geometry Rendering by using a unified ray-casting framework with adaptive supersampling for geometric events rather than separate rendering passes or fixed scan-conversion. Surface rendering is a volume rendering mode that stops at the first voxel inside a threshold and shades it with a normal taken from the value gradient. It generates no mesh or triangles, avoiding invented shapes between voxels. Unlike volume rendering which integrates over slice spacing, surface rendering exposes the slice spacing as terracing artifacts. Mixed geometry rendering integrates explicit geometric primitives (isosurfaces, bounding boxes, wireframes) with volumetric data in a single image to provide spatial context and structural clarity. It solves the problem of isolating volumetric features from their surrounding environment by allowing users to see both the internal scalar field distribution and the discrete boundaries or grid structures that define the data domain. Unlike pure volume rendering, which treats the dataset as a continuous medium, this method explicitly renders surface geometry, often using the hardware depth buffer to occlude volume data behind opaque surfaces. A two-pass algorithm that renders volumetric shadows on the GPU by modifying proxy geometry slicing to render from both the eye and the light's point of view. It improves depth perception and amplifies surface structure by simulating light attenuation without the cost of secondary raymarching. It sets apart from standard slice-based rendering by decoupling the lighting calculation into a separate pass that computes light transmissivity, allowing for interactive hard and translucent shadows. Steps: Set the slice axis half-way between the view direction and the light direction. First Pass: Render from the eye. In the fragment shader, look up light color from a light buffer bound as a texture and multiply material color by light color. Second Pass: Render from the light. In the fragment shader, only blend alpha values to compute light transmissivity. Parameters: Render order for light: front-to-back. Render order for eye: front-to-back or back-to-front. View-Aligned Slicing is a direct volume rendering technique that decomposes a 3D volume into a set of 2D triangular proxy geometry slices aligned with the view direction. It solves the problem of maintaining consistent sampling density and minimizing sampling artifacts inherent in standard ray casting by dynamically regenerating geometry per frame based on the camera transform. Unlike standard ray casting which samples the volume texture directly via shader loops, this method rasterizes explicit geometry, requiring regeneration of geometry when the view changes. This method integrates volume rendering into a polygonal virtual environment by treating rendered volume images as image-based primitives (impostors) within the scene. It decouples the computationally expensive volume rendering from the client-side polygonal rendering, distributing the workload to a separate server while maintaining interactive frame rates for the virtual environment. Unlike direct ray casting performed on the client, this approach renders the volume as 2D images (often stereoscopic pairs) and maps them onto quads that track the viewer's orientation, allowing seamless mixing of volume and polygonal geometry. Vector Icon Volume Rendering is a 3D raster resampling technique that integrates vector field visualization into scalar volume rendering by embedding small billboard images containing vector icons within splat footprints. It solves the problem of visualizing flow direction and magnitude within volumetric data by creating an illusion of coherent flow through stochastic placement and compositing of these icons. It differs from standard direct volume ray casting by replacing or augmenting the scalar sampling integral with discrete, oriented billboard primitives that indicate vector orientation, rather than relying solely on color or opacity transfer functions for directionality. Image-Based Volume Rendering (IBVR) is a technique that separates the computationally expensive volume rendering process from the interactive viewing stage, enabling the interactive exploration of arbitrarily large datasets on standard graphics hardware. It achieves this by precomputing "ray slices" from multiple viewpoints and combining them with a geometric proxy surface to form "opacity light fields," which allow users to clip into the volume and reveal internal structure without re-rendering the volumetric data. Unlike previous image-based methods that were restricted to external viewpoints or lacked opacity, IBVR supports unrestricted viewpoints and arbitrary clipping surfaces. Key View Generation is a preprocessing step in image-based volume rendering that synthesizes intermediate views from a sparse set of pre-rendered ray slices using a geometric proxy surface. It solves the problem of real-time interactive viewing by replacing expensive ray-casting with fast 2D interpolation of precomputed data. Unlike direct ray casting, it decouples the volume integration from the viewing angle, relying on the accuracy of the proxy surface to minimize interpolation artifacts. Rendering occurs only inside the selected geometric object's volume. If Fire Lights are enabled, only those inside the cutter are rendered. Parameters: usegizmo (enable), gizmo (object). Invert Cutter (invgizmo): When enabled, rendering occurs only outside the render cutter. Rays not intersecting the cutter are shaded as well. Distinct from cutter with inverted geometry. Cutter Geom does not work in Volumetric Geometry mode. A raster display technique that generates several 2D slices of 3D data and combines them to produce a 3D image. Leaves gaps between the slices, forcing the user to guess about flow field conditions in those gaps. The technique originated with the advent of 3D texture support in graphics hardware, allowing volumetric data to be stored directly in GPU memory. Early implementations used object-aligned slicing, where the volume was sliced along the principal axes (x, y, z). This approach was fast but suffered from memory overhead (requiring replication of data in three directions) and view-dependent artifacts such as intensity variations and image popping when switching between texture stacks. View-aligned slicing was introduced to address these issues by dynamically generating slice geometry aligned with the camera view, ensuring consistent sampling distance and reducing artifacts, albeit at the cost of increased CPU/GPU geometry generation overhead. name: Surface Rendering Pipeline
head: Surface Rendering (R_so, Surface Rendering from Volume
body: Surface rendering is a volume rendering mode that stops at the first voxel inside a threshold and shades it with a normal taken from the value gradient. It generates no mesh or triangles, avoiding invented shapes between voxels. Unlike volume rendering which integrates over slice spacing, surface rendering exposes the slice spacing as terracing artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field (volume data), a threshold value, a camera configuration (position, orientation, image size W \times H), and a light direction. Output: A 2D color image of size H \times W \times 3. Data Structures: RayBundle: Contains origins, directions, and sample points for each pixel. SurfaceModel: Contains implicitfn, sampler, and renderer modules initialized from configuration dictionaries. Volume Data: Stored as a scalar field accessible via the implicit function or sampler. Method Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the SurfaceModel with an implicit function, a sampler, and a renderer from configuration dictionaries. 2. Coordinate Generation: For each camera, generate normalized image plane coordinates xy\grid based on the image dimensions. x = \text{linspace}(-1, 1, W) y = \text{linspace}(-1, 1, H) xy\grid = \text{meshgrid}(y, x) 3. Ray Generation: Generate a ray bundle from the pixel coordinates using the camera's inverse projection matrix to obtain ray origins and directions. 4. Ray Marching: March each ray until the first voxel value exceeds the specified threshold. 5. Normal Estimation: Compute the surface normal at the hit point using the gradient of the scalar field. The method is classified as scene space, object space, or view space depending on the normal estimation technique. 6. Rendering: Pass the ray bundle and light direction through the model to compute the final color. Reshape the output tensor to H \times W \times 3 and convert to a standard image array. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def getnormalizedimageplanecoordinates(imagesize): W, H = imagesize x = torch.linspace(-1, 1, steps=W) y = torch.linspace(-1, 1, steps=H) gridy, gridx = torch.meshgrid(y, x) xygrid = torch.stack((gridx, gridy), dim=-1).view(W H, 2) return -xygrid def getraysfrompixels(xygrid, camera): N = xygrid.shape[0] xygridcopy = xygrid.clone().to(camera.device) ndcptsip = torch.cat([xygridcopy, torch.ones([N, 1], device=camera.device)], dim=-1) # Standard inverse projection: world = invproj @ ndc unprojected = camera.inverseprojection @ ndcptsip.T origins = unprojected[:3,:] directions = unprojected[3:,:] directions = directions / torch.norm(directions, dim=0, keepdim=True) return origins.T, directions.T def marchtosurface(origins, directions, implicitfn, threshold, maxsteps=1000, stepsize=0.01): # Advance along ray until implicitfn value > threshold t = torch.arange(maxsteps, device=origins.device).unsqueeze(1) stepsize samplepoints = origins.unsqueeze(1) + directions.unsqueeze(1) t.unsqueeze(2) values = implicitfn(samplepoints) hitmask = values > threshold hitindices = hitmask.argmax(dim=1) hitpoints = samplepoints[torch.arange(len(origins)), hitindices] return hitpoints def computegradientatpoint(point, implicitfn): # Central finite differences for normal estimation eps = 1e-4 dx = (implicitfn(point + torch.tensor([eps, 0, 0])) - implicitfn(point + torch.tensor([-eps, 0, 0]))) / (2 eps) dy = (implicitfn(point + torch.tensor([0, eps, 0])) - implicitfn(point + torch.tensor([0, -eps, 0]))) / (2 eps) dz = (implicitfn(point + torch.tensor([0, 0, eps])) - implicitfn(point + torch.tensor([0, 0, -eps]))) / (2 eps) return torch.stack([dx, dy, dz]) def surfacerenderpipeline(volumedata, threshold, camera, imagesize, lightdir): # 1. Generate rays xygrid = getnormalizedimageplanecoordinates(imagesize) origins, directions = getraysfrompixels(xygrid, camera) # 2. March to first surface hit hitpoints = marchtosurface(origins, directions, volumedata, threshold) # 3. Compute normals via gradient normals = computegradientatpoint(hitpoints, volumedata) normals = normals / torch.norm(normals, dim=1, keepdim=True) # 4. Shade and composite diffuse = torch.clamp(torch.sum(normals lightdir, dim=1), 0, 1) colors = volumedata(hitpoints) diffuse.unsqueeze(1) # 5. Reshape to image image = colors.view(imagesize[1], imagesize[0], 3) return image Parameters: Threshold: The scalar value separating background from surface voxels. Slice Spacing: The physical distance between voxels along the depth axis, which directly determines the magnitude of terracing artifacts. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Terracing: Discrete voxel sampling exposes slice spacing as visible stair-step artifacts, particularly when spacing is large (e.g., 3 mm). Gradient Noise: Computing normals via finite differences on unsmoothed scalar fields produces jagged normals and shading artifacts. Threshold Sensitivity: Incorrect threshold selection either fragments the surface or includes background noise. Real Time Cutting Operations clips volume surfaces using cutting planes by maintaining near and far depth buffers per pixel, avoiding full re-rendering when planes change. It differs from static cutting methods by dynamically filtering voxels per frame via halfspace checks, whereas static methods pre-filter and discard cut voxels. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Measured at 390×844 on a synthetic 700 HU sphere: surface rendering exposed 9.8% of the canvas at peak intensity 255, compared to volume rendering's 9.3% at 238. Strengths: No mesh generation overhead; avoids shape invention between voxels. Limitations: Terracing artifacts due to discrete sampling; sensitive to threshold selection; does not reveal internal structure. Surface rendering is classified as a scene space, object space, or view space operation depending on the normal estimation technique used. It is discussed within the framework of imaging transforms for visualizing surfaces and volumes, where it operates on explicit hard sets of volume or surface elements. feat(body-exposure): render a DICOM series in 3D, not a description of one, https://github.com/rizkyazhar486/Panacea/pull/1585, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, https://github.com/Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Imaging transforms for visualizing surfaces and volumes, https://doi.org/10.1007/bf03168529, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Real Time Cutting Operations
head: Cutting Planes via Depth Buffers
body: Real Time Cutting Operations is a technique for clipping volume surfaces using cutting planes by maintaining near and far depth buffers per pixel, avoiding full re-rendering when planes change. It differs from static cutting methods by avoiding full re-rendering through per-pixel depth buffer updates, whereas static methods typically pre-filter and discard cut voxels. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of cutting planes Ci defined by normal vectors Ni and implicit equations, a volume dataset, and an image plane with resolution W \times H. Outputs: A rendered image where surface points are displayed only if they lie within the valid depth range defined by the cutting planes. Data Structures: 1. Near Depth Buffer (D{near}): A 2D array of size W \times H, initialized to 0. 2. Far Depth Buffer (D{far}): A 2D array of size W \times H, initialized to \text{MAX\DEPTH}. 3. Intersection Buffer: Stores per-pixel data for all surface intersections along the ray, including depth D(i,j), intensity I(i,j), and intersection count k for pixel (i,j). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Buffers: Set all elements in D{near} to 0 and all elements in D{far} to \text{MAX\DEPTH}. 2. Classify Planes per Pixel: For each pixel p in the image plane, classify each cutting plane Ci relative to the ray R(p) as parallel (R(p)\cdot Ni=0), facing the same direction (R(p)\cdot Ni>0), or facing the opposite direction (R(p)\cdot Ni<0). 3. Update Depth Buffers: For each pixel p and each cutting plane Ci: If Ci is parallel to R(p) and pixel p is in the negative halfspace defined by the plane (Ci(p)<0), then: D{near}(p) \leftarrow \text{MAX\DEPTH} D{far}(p) \leftarrow 0 If Ci is facing the same direction as R(p): Compute the intersection depth d between ray R(p) and plane Ci. D{near}(p) \leftarrow \max(D{near}(p), d) If Ci is facing the opposite direction to R(p): Compute the intersection depth d between ray R(p) and plane Ci. D{far}(p) \leftarrow \min(D{far}(p), d) 4. Ray Casting and Clipping: Cast rays into the volume, storing all surface intersections in the Intersection Buffer. A surface point with depth d{surf} is displayed if and only if: D{near}(p) \le d{surf} \le D{far}(p) Points with depth in front of D{near}(p) or behind D{far}(p) are cut away. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def realtimecuttingoperations(volume, cuttingplanes, imagewidth, imageheight, maxdepth, rayoriginfunc, raydirectionfunc, stepsize, threshold): """ Renders volume with real-time cutting planes using depth buffers. Args: volume: Volume dataset object with method sample(point) cuttingplanes: List of plane objects, each having normal N, constant Dplane, and implicit(p) method imagewidth: int imageheight: int maxdepth: float, maximum possible depth in the scene rayoriginfunc: function(x, y) -> [x, y, z] raydirectionfunc: function(x, y) -> [dx, dy, dz] stepsize: float, marching step along ray threshold: float, volume value threshold for surface detection Returns: image: 2D array of rendered intensities """ # 1. Initialize Depth Buffers Dnear = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] Dfar = [[maxdepth] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] # 2. Update Depth Buffers based on Cutting Planes for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): rayo = rayoriginfunc(x, y) rayd = raydirectionfunc(x, y) for plane in cuttingplanes: # Dot product of ray direction and plane normal dotprod = rayd[0]plane.normal[0] + rayd[1]plane.normal[1] + rayd[2]plane.normal[2] if abs(dotprod) < 1e-9: # Parallel # Check if pixel ray origin is in negative halfspace if plane.implicit(rayo) < 0: Dnear[y][x] = maxdepth Dfar[y][x] = 0.0 elif dotprod > 0: # Facing same direction # Intersection t = (plane.Dplane - dot(plane.normal, rayo)) / dotprod t = (plane.Dplane - (plane.normal[0]rayo[0] + plane.normal[1]rayo[1] + plane.normal[2]rayo[2])) / dotprod if t > 0: Dnear[y][x] = max(Dnear[y][x], t) else: # Facing opposite direction t = (plane.Dplane - (plane.normal[0]rayo[0] + plane.normal[1]rayo[1] + plane.normal[2]rayo[2])) / dotprod if t > 0: Dfar[y][x] = min(Dfar[y][x], t) # 3. Ray Casting and Clipping image = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): rayo = rayoriginfunc(x, y) rayd = raydirectionfunc(x, y) # Collect intersections along the ray intersections = [] t = 0.0 while t < maxdepth: pos = [rayo[0] + trayd[0], rayo[1] + trayd[1], rayo[2] + trayd[2]] val = volume.sample(pos) if val > threshold: intersections.append((t, val)) t += stepsize # Display first valid intersection within depth range for depth, intensity in intersections: if Dnear[y][x] <= depth <= Dfar[y][x]: image[y][x] = intensity break return image Parameters: \text{MAX\DEPTH}: The maximum depth value in the scene or camera frustum. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Planes: If a plane is parallel to the ray and the pixel is in the negative halfspace, the valid depth range becomes empty (D{near} > D{far}), effectively hiding the pixel. Degenerate Input: If no cutting planes are provided, D{near} remains 0 and D{far} remains \text{MAX\DEPTH}, rendering the full volume. Time Complexity: The depth buffer update step is O(W \cdot H \cdot P), where W, H are image dimensions and P is the number of cutting planes. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the two depth buffers plus O(W \cdot H \cdot S{max}) for the intersection buffer, where S{max} is the maximum number of intersections per pixel. Performance: This method avoids re-preprocessing the volume data when cutting planes change, allowing for interactive modification of plane location and orientation. Strengths: Real-time performance for dynamic cutting without modifying the underlying volume data structure. Limitations: Requires storing all surface intersections for each ray, which can be memory-intensive for complex volumes with many intersections. This method was described in the paper "Fast Cutting Operations on Three Dimensional Volume Datasets". It is used in direct volume ray casting to enable interactive exploration of volume data by revealing internal structures through cutting planes. Fast Cutting Operations on Three Dimensional Volume Datasets, https://zenodo.org/records/14173364, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Interactive Cutting Operations
head: Cutting Planes via Halfspace Check, Interactive Cutting Plane
body: Interactive Cutting Operations is a method for real-time modification of cutting plane location and orientation in direct volume ray casting without re-preprocessing the volume data. It solves the performance bottleneck of static cutting by keeping the original volume in main memory and projecting surface points and internal voxels separately, allowing the cutting plane to be updated interactively. It differs from static cutting methods by maintaining the full volume dataset and using a halfspace check to dynamically filter voxels per frame, whereas static methods pre-filter and discard cut voxels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Original volume data V(x,y,z), cutting plane defined by normal \mathbf{n}=(a,b,c) and distance d (equation ax+by+cz+d=0), viewing direction, segmentation function for surface extraction b(i,j,k), and optional segmentation function for region of interest s(i,j,k). Output: Rendered image with interactive cutting plane. Data Structures: Volume V: 3D array of voxel values, indexed by (x,y,z). Surface Points: List of (x,y,z) coordinates extracted during preprocessing, potentially sorted by z then y. Cutting Plane: Parameters (a,b,c,d). Steps: 1. Halfspace Check for Internal Voxels: For each potentially visible voxel (x,y,z), determine if it lies in the visible halfspace. Substitute coordinates into the plane equation: r = a \cdot x + b \cdot y + c \cdot z + d The sign of the residual r indicates whether the voxel is rendered or ignored. Optimization: Since voxels are stored sorted by z, evaluate c \cdot z + d once per z-slice. Further Optimization: Sort surface points within a slice by y coordinates to optimize elimination. This sorting occurs automatically during row-continuous visibility calculation in preprocessing, adding negligible cost. 2. Projection of Intersected Voxels: Voxels intersected by the cutting plane must be rendered to show the cut surface. Assume the principal component of the plane normal is z (i.e., |c| is largest). Iterate over all discrete (x,y) pairs in the volume bounds (x \in \{0, \dots, X-1\}, y \in \{0, \dots, Y-1\}). Substitute (x,y) into the explicit plane equation to solve for z: z = \frac{-a \cdot x - b \cdot y - d}{c} Use the calculated z to address the original volume V(x,y,z). Render these voxels using gray-scaled data values. 3. Region of Interest Check: Before projecting intersected voxels, check if they belong to the region of interest using an additional segmentation function s(i,j,k). This function may differ from the surface extraction function b(i,j,k). Purpose: Prevent low-density voxels (e.g., surrounding air) from hiding surface points. For example, if rendering the skull surface, a bone threshold segmentation function is not suitable for the cut slice because it may contain low-density voxels below the bone threshold. 4. Rendering Order: If surface points are in the halfspace containing the viewpoint, render internal voxels intersected by the cutting plane first, then project surface points. Otherwise, reverse the order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderinteractivecutting(volume, surfacepoints, planenormal, planedist, camerapos, surfacesegfunc, roisegfunc): a, b, c = planenormal d = planedist # Determine which halfspace contains the camera rcam = a camerapos[0] + b camerapos[1] + c camerapos[2] + d positivehalfspace = rcam > 0 # 1. Halfspace check for internal voxels zsliceterms = [c z + d for z in range(volume.depth)] voxelstorender = [] for z in range(volume.depth): zterm = zsliceterms[z] for y in range(volume.height): for x in range(volume.width): r = a x + b y + zterm if (r > 0) == positivehalfspace: if surfacesegfunc(x, y, z): voxelstorender.append(('surface', x, y, z, volume[x, y, z])) else: voxelstorender.append(('internal', x, y, z, volume[x, y, z])) # 2. Projection of intersected voxels intersectedvoxels = [] for x in range(volume.width): for y in range(volume.height): if c != 0: zfloat = (-a x - b y - d) / c z = round(zfloat) if 0 <= z < volume.depth: if roisegfunc(x, y, z): intersectedvoxels.append((x, y, z, volume[x, y, z])) # 3. Determine rendering order based on viewpoint if positivehalfspace: renderlist = intersectedvoxels + voxelstorender else: renderlist = voxelstorender + intersectedvoxels return renderlist Time Complexity: The halfspace check is optimized to O(1) per voxel with precomputed z-slice terms, adding one multiplication and one conditional instruction per voxel. Sorting surface points by y adds no preprocessing time. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the original volume in main memory, unlike static cutting methods that discard cut voxels. Performance: The extension does not significantly affect performance due to the optimized halfspace check. Strengths: Allows interactive modification of cutting planes without re-preprocessing. Limitations: Requires keeping the full volume in memory. The method assumes the principal component of the plane normal is z for the intersected voxel projection, which may require coordinate transformation for other orientations. Interactive Cutting Operations was proposed to address the limitation of static cutting methods where cut voxels are discarded, preventing interactive modification of cutting planes. It is particularly important in medical imaging applications where interactive adjustment of cutting planes is crucial. The method was described in a dissertation on interactive volume-rendering techniques for medical data visualization. name: Two-Pass Volume Rendering with Shadows
head: GPU Volumetric Shadows
body: A two-pass algorithm that renders volumetric shadows on the GPU by modifying proxy geometry slicing to render from both the eye and the light's point of view. It improves depth perception and amplifies surface structure by simulating light attenuation without the cost of secondary raymarching. It differs from standard slice-based rendering by computing light transmissivity in a dedicated pass, enabling interactive hard and translucent shadows. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volume texture, slice geometry (proxy triangles/quads), view matrix, light position/direction. Output: Final color buffer with shadows. Data Structures: 3D Texture: Stores scalar volume data. Light Buffer: A texture (framebuffer object) storing light color/transmissivity values computed in the second pass. Slice Geometry: Planar polygons intersecting the volume bounding box, with 3D texture coordinates mapped to the volume. Steps: 1. Slice Axis Calculation: Set the slice axis half-way between the view direction and the light direction. This orientation allows each slice to be rendered effectively from both the eye and light points of view. 2. First Pass (Eye View): Render slices from the eye's point of view. Render order: Front-to-back or back-to-front. In the fragment shader: Sample the 3D texture to get material color/opacity. Look up the light color from the Light Buffer (bound as a texture). Multiply material color by light color: C{final} = C{material} \times C{light}. Composite using standard alpha blending. 3. Second Pass (Light View): Render slices from the light's point of view. Render order: Front-to-back. In the fragment shader: Sample the 3D texture to get opacity. Only blend alpha values to compute light transmissivity (shadowing). Store the result in the Light Buffer. This pass simulates light attenuation from the light's perspective. Parameters: Slice axis: Bisector of view and light directions. Light render order: Front-to-back. Eye render order: Front-to-back or back-to-front. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Large fragment/pixel operations and texture access can lead to precision issues in the light buffer if not handled with sufficient bit depth. Memory Usage: Requires additional framebuffer objects for the light buffer, increasing memory usage. Degenerate Input: If the view and light directions are parallel, the slice axis calculation may become ambiguous; however, the bisector remains well-defined unless vectors are identical or opposite. A technique for simulating shadows in texture-based volume rendering that avoids expensive lighting computations by computing shadow maps per volume slice and rendering them with a specific blending function. It computes a shadow map for each slice, renders these into the framebuffer, and applies a specific blending function to modulate shading based on the shadow maps. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of slices and S is the number of fragments per slice. Two passes double the rasterization cost compared to single-pass volume rendering. Memory: Requires storage for the 3D volume texture plus an additional framebuffer/texture for the light buffer. Measured Performance: Performance is limited by the huge amount of fragment/pixel operations, texture access, lighting calculation, and blending. It maintains interactivity compared to full raymarching. The second pass increases computational cost over standard slice-based rendering. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Interactive performance, improved depth perception, simulation of hard and translucent shadows. Limitations: High fragment/pixel operation count, large memory usage, potential for artifacts if light buffer precision is insufficient. When to Use: Use when interactive volumetric shadows are needed and full raymarching is too slow. Originating from research on GPU-based volume rendering, this method modifies proxy geometry slicing to handle illumination. It addresses the complexity of general scattering effects, which are too complex for interactive rendering, by focusing on incoming light from the direction of the light source. The approach is part of a broader effort to improve perception in volume visualization through illumination techniques. Related acceleration techniques for GPU-based volume rendering were discussed by Krüger and Westermann in 2003. name: Vector Icon Volume Rendering
head: Billboard vector icons, Vector Icon Splatting with Billboard Textures, Vector icons embedded in splat footprint, Volume Rendering with Embedded Vector Icons
body: Vector Icon Volume Rendering is a 3D raster resampling technique that integrates vector field visualization into scalar volume rendering by embedding small billboard images containing vector icons within the splat footprint of the volume rendering sheets. It solves the problem of visualizing flow direction and magnitude within a volumetric scalar field by creating an illusion of coherent flow through stochastic placement and orientation of these icons. It sets itself apart from continuous integration methods by modifying the volume integral to include rendering of tiny cylinders within a small neighborhood of each sampling point, and differs from pure vector field visualization by merging the rendering of a scalar field with that of a vector field in a single compositing pass. The method builds on the slice-based rendering principles defined in Slice-based and Proxy Geometry Rendering. It modifies the standard volume integral to include the rendering of tiny cylinders (vector icons) within a small neighborhood of each sampling point. Inputs: 3D scalar field data (e.g., density clouds). 3D vector field data (e.g., wind velocity). Grid spacing for sheet sampling. Stochastic threshold for icon placement. Icon size limits (maximum and minimum). Color mapping parameters (e.g., altitude to color). Time step for time-varying fields. Outputs: A 2D image where the scalar volume is rendered via alpha blending, and vector flow is indicated by colored, oriented billboard icons. Volume Texture: 3D texture storing scalar values. Icon Texture Set: A set of 2D textures containing pre-rendered vector icons that move across the texture and fade in/out to simulate motion. Billboard Geometry: Implicitly defined by the splat footprint; each billboard image is oriented perpendicular to the viewing ray and parallel to the projected vector direction at the splat's center. Grid Spacing: Regular grid sampling on the current sheet. Stochastic Threshold: Heuristic determining whether a splat includes a cylinder/icon. Icon Size Scaling: Maximum size when flow is parallel to the screen plane; minimum size (dot) when flow is parallel to the viewer’s line of sight. Color Mapping: Scalar value (e.g., altitude) mapped to icon color. 1. Decompose the volume into sheets oriented parallel to the image plane. 2. Sort the sheets in back-to-front order relative to the camera for correct alpha blending compositing. 3. For each sheet, take a regular grid sampling of the vector field data. 4. Place an image reconstruction operator (splat) over each grid point. 5. Use a stochastic heuristic to determine if the current splat should include a vector icon (cylinder). 6. If included, randomly offset the icon from the splat center. 7. Orient the billboard image such that it lies perpendicular to the viewing ray and parallel to the projected vector direction at the splat's center point. 8. Scale the icon size based on the angle between the flow vector and the view direction: largest when parallel to the screen, reduced to a dot when parallel to the line of sight. 9. Render the scalar volume for the sheet using standard volume rendering techniques (texture mapping, classification, blending). 10. Add the volume integral for each pixel under both the splat and the cylinder. 11. Composite the results back-to-front. 12. For time-varying fields, produce a new rendering for each time step and animate in a movie loop. 13. Cycle through the icon texture set at rendering time, where icons move across the texture and fade in/out, to achieve the illusion of motion. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def rendervectoriconvolume(scalarvolume, vectorfield, camera, timestep, gridspacing, stochasticthreshold, maxiconsize, miniconsize): # 1. Generate sheets parallel to image plane sheets = generatesheetsparalleltoimageplane(scalarvolume.boundingbox, camera.viewdirection) # 2. Sort sheets back-to-front sheets.sort(key=lambda s: math.dist(s.center, camera.position)) framebuffer = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for sheet in sheets: # 9. Render scalar volume for sheet sheetcolor = renderscalarsheetstandard(scalarvolume, sheet, camera) # 3. Regular grid sampling on the current sheet gridpoints = sampleregulargridonsheet(sheet, gridspacing) iconlayer = [] for point in gridpoints: # 5. Stochastic heuristic if random.random() < stochasticthreshold: # 6. Random offset from center offset = (random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5), random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5)) iconpos = (point.x + offset[0], point.y + offset[1]) # 7. Orientation: perpendicular to viewing ray, parallel to projected vector flowvec = vectorfield.sample(point) projecteddir = projectvectortoscreen(flowvec, camera) billboard = createbillboard(iconpos, projecteddir, camera.viewdirection) # 8. Icon size scaling viewdir = normalize(camera.viewdirection) flownorm = normalize(flowvec) angle = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, math.dot(flownorm, viewdir)))) if abs(angle - math.pi/2) < 0.1: size = maxiconsize elif abs(angle) < 0.1 or abs(angle - math.pi) < 0.1: size = miniconsize else: size = maxiconsize math.sin(angle) billboard.size = size # 13. Texture cycling for motion illusion textureframe = gettextureframe(timestep, point, iconlayer) billboard.texture = textureframe # Color by altitude altitude = scalarvolume.sample(point) billboard.color = mapaltitudetocolor(altitude) iconlayer.append(billboard) # 10 & 11. Add volume integral and composite back-to-front sheetcolor = alphablendsplats(sheetcolor, iconlayer) framebuffer = alphablend(framebuffer, sheetcolor) return framebuffer def generatesheetsparalleltoimageplane(boundingbox, viewdirection): # Standard slice generation from parent method return [Sheet(center=boundingbox.min + i step, normal=viewdirection) for i in range(numslices)] def sampleregulargridonsheet(sheet, spacing): return [Point(x, y, sheet.center) for x in range(sheet.minx, sheet.maxx, spacing) for y in range(sheet.miny, sheet.maxy, spacing)] def projectvectortoscreen(vec, camera): # Standard projection to screen space return vec - math.dot(vec, normalize(camera.viewdirection)) normalize(camera.viewdirection) def createbillboard(position, direction, viewdirection): return {"position": position, "direction": direction, "viewdirection": viewdirection, "size": 1.0, "texture": None, "color": (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0)} def gettextureframe(timestep, point, iconlayer): # Cycle through texture set based on time and point index return iconlayer.index(point) % len(textureset) def mapaltitudetocolor(altitude): # Standard transfer function mapping return (altitude, 1.0 - altitude, 0.0, 1.0) def alphablendsplats(basecolor, splats): # Standard alpha compositing color = list(basecolor) for s in splats: color = blendtwocolors(color, s.color) return color def alphablend(a, b): return blendtwocolors(a, b) def blendtwocolors(c1, c2): return (c1[0]c1[3] + c2[0]c2[3](1-c1[3]), c1[1]c1[3] + c2[1]c2[3](1-c1[3]), c1[2]c1[3] + c2[2]c2[3](1-c1[3]), c1[3] + c2[3](1-c1[3])) def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in v)) return [x/mag for x in v] if mag > 0 else v Sparse Representation: The discrete and sparse nature of the icons can make the flow difficult to understand. This is mitigated by the texture cycling technique to create an illusion of motion. View Alignment: Icon size must be carefully scaled to avoid occlusion or invisibility when the flow is parallel to the view direction. Uses discrete billboard images to represent flow. Sets itself apart by being purely discrete and stochastic, unlike continuous vector fields. Choose when visual clarity of individual flow elements is preferred over dense field representation. Link Enhances the basic billboard method by using animated textures to simulate motion. Choose when animation is required to convey flow direction in a sparse representation. Link Integrates icons directly into the volume rendering splat footprint. Sets itself apart by merging scalar and vector rendering in a single pass per splat. Choose for tight integration of scalar context and vector direction. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Efficient on GPU due to rasterization of billboards. Performance scales with the number of sheets and grid resolution. Strengths: Intuitive representation of flow direction; integrates well with scalar volume rendering; creates illusion of motion through animation. Limitations: Sparse representation can obscure flow; stochastic placement may lead to visual artifacts; difficult to understand flow in complex regions due to discrete nature. When to Use: Time-varying wind or fluid flow visualization where direction and magnitude are critical, and scalar context (e.g., clouds) is also needed. When Not to Use: When precise quantitative flow analysis is required, or when the flow is dense and continuous (use streamlines or pathlines instead). The technique was developed by R. Crawfis, H. Shen, and N. Max. It is described in the paper "Flow Visualization Techniques for CDF using Volume Rendering" presented at the 9th International Symposium on Flow Visualization, Heriot-Watt University, Edinburgh, 2000. The authors previously developed related techniques such as Line Bundles. The method was applied to global climate simulation data, merging white density clouds (cloudiness) with colored vector icons (wind velocity). name: Hybrid and Mixed Geometry
head: Hybrid ray-volume rendering
body: Hybrid and Mixed Geometry rendering intermixes explicit polygonal geometry with implicit volumetric data in a single image, ensuring correct visibility and attenuation. It is distinguished from pure slice-based rasterization by explicitly combining ray-casting or slab compositing with polygon rendering, and from pure ray tracing by leveraging GPU-accelerated volume sampling. This family builds on Slice-based and Proxy Geometry Rendering. All methods intermix polygonal geometry and volumetric data by compositing them in depth-sorted order, handling both opaque and translucent surfaces alongside volumetric samples. The core mechanism involves sampling the volume along viewing rays or through slabs, intersecting or rasterizing polygons, and blending contributions using front-to-back alpha compositing. Polygonal surfaces are shaded to yield color and opacity, while volumetric samples are classified via transfer functions to yield matching color and opacity values. The final image is assembled by iterating through depth-sorted events (volume slivers and polygons) and applying the over operator to accumulate color and opacity. Hybrid Volume Rendering mixes geometric and volumetric data by casting rays through both, drawing samples of each, and compositing them in depth-sorted order. It solves the problem of rendering scenes containing both polygonal models and volumetric data in a single pass with correct visibility and attenuation. Unlike pure volume rendering which rasterizes slices, or pure ray tracing which handles only geometry, this method simultaneously traces rays through volumetric sample arrays and polygonal databases, resampling both at equally spaced intervals to handle mixtures of geometric and volumetric data. It is distinguished from slice-based or proxy-geometry rasterization by its explicit ray-casting approach to mixing. The Hybrid Volume Rendering Scheme is a parallel volume rendering algorithm for unstructured grids that combines object-order and image-order techniques to handle complex block boundaries, dramatic cell size variations, and camera-induced load imbalances. Unlike pure image-order methods, which suffer from replicated cell loading and unequal cell distribution, or pure object-order methods, where image compositing becomes a bottleneck, this approach bounds the computation of each processing phase to adapt dynamically to the workload. Artifact-Based Rendering (ABR) is a hybrid visualization technique for Diffusion-Tensor MRI (DT-MRI) data that combines volume rendering for anatomical context with sparsely sampled, texture-encoded glyphs and oriented ellipsoids to represent crossing fibers and microstructural parameters. It solves the problem of occlusion in 3D representations of complex white matter by using a "magic lens" design: volume rendering and sparse glyphs provide global context, while high-resolution glyph data is presented in an interactively defined small volume. It differs from prior slice-based approaches by encoding fiber orientation via glyph texture variations instead of color, freeing the color channel to encode a derived variable (similarity between primary and secondary directions). Flow Volume Rendering visualizes steady 3D vector fields by rendering a "flow volume"—the space swept by a generating polygon P as it is advected by the flow velocity field. It solves the problem of efficiently visualizing phenomena like smoke or wind in steady flows without the computational cost of full-volume ray casting or the sorting overhead of standard polyhedron compositing. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific use of the Shirley and Tuchman tetrahedron projection method to enable order-independent hardware compositing for constant-color tracers, allowing interactive performance by rendering only the swept volume rather than the entire data set. Image-order parallel volume rendering is a distributed rendering technique that decomposes the final image into non-overlapping spatial regions, assigning each region to a separate processor. Unlike object-order methods that distribute the volume dataset, this approach assigns distinct regions of screen space to each processor, allowing the resulting partial images to be combined without an ordered composition step. It is distinguished from its siblings by its screen-space decomposition strategy, which eliminates the need for global depth sorting of fragments but introduces significant data duplication and view-dependent load imbalance. Rendering occurs only inside the selected geometric object's volume. If Fire Lights are enabled, only those inside the cutter are rendered. Parameters: usegizmo (enable), gizmo (object). Invert Cutter (invgizmo): When enabled, rendering occurs only outside the render cutter. Rays not intersecting the cutter are shaded. This is distinct from a cutter with inverted geometry. Pitfall: Cutter Geom does not work in Volumetric Geometry mode. A technique that achieves interactive rendering by avoiding full volume rerendering per frame, instead computing arbitrary views from nearby prerendered images. Steps: Partition the volume data using slab decomposition. Volume render each data slab to generate a set of prerendered source images. Warp and blend images from the known prerendered views to synthesize what would be seen from an arbitrary new view. Parameter: The total number of source images equals the number of data slabs created by the partitioning. Comparison: Trades off the cost of prerendering slabs for interactive frame rates, eliminating the need to completely rerender the volume for every frame. A method to intermix opaque and translucent geometry with volumetric data by interlacing slab images. This ensures all contributing objects are composited in the correct order. Steps: For opaque polygons: Render geometry into the framebuffer, then draw slab images with z-depth test to correctly occlude volume samples behind the geometry. For translucent polygons: Draw polygons between each slab image in between texture mapping the individual slab images. The concept of hybrid rendering, specifically blending OpenGL-rendered volumes with ray-traced non-volume objects, is implemented in software such as PyMOL via the rayvolume setting. Ray trace specific features like shadows or outlines (raytracemode) are not available with the base approach; the rayvolume setting activates the hybrid solution instead. Image sizes other than the current window size are not possible with the hybrid ray-volume solution, and neither solution works in headless (batch) mode. name: Hybrid Volume Rendering
head: Mixed Geometry Rendering, Hybrid Ray Tracing
body: Hybrid Volume Rendering is a method for mixing geometric and volumetric data by casting rays through the ensemble of both, drawing samples of each, and compositing them in depth-sorted order. It solves the problem of rendering scenes containing both polygonal models (e.g., surgical instruments, surface meshes) and volumetric data (e.g., CT/MR scans) in a single pass with correct visibility and attenuation. Unlike pure volume rendering which rasterizes slices, or pure ray tracing which handles only geometry, this method simultaneously traces rays through volumetric sample arrays and polygonal databases, resampling both at equally spaced intervals to handle mixtures of geometric and volumetric data. It is distinguished from slice-based or proxy-geometry rasterization by its explicit ray-casting approach to mixing. The method consists of two primary variants: the Hybrid Ray Tracer (direct ray casting through mixed data) and 3D Scan-Conversion (converting geometry to volume). The Hybrid Ray Tracer is the core method described below. Inputs: A 3D voxel array of scalar values (volume data). A set of embedded polygons (geometric data). Camera position and viewing direction. Transfer functions mapping scalar values to color cv and opacity ov for voxels. Shading parameters for polygons (color cp, opacity op). Supersampling threshold \theta. Outputs: A 2D image where each pixel contains the final composited color. Volumetric Data: Stored as a 3D array. Each voxel has an associated color and opacity derived from classification. Geometric Data: A list of polygons (triangles/quads) with surface normals for shading. Ray State: For each pixel, a viewing ray is defined by origin and direction. The Hybrid Ray Tracer casts rays through both data types and composites them. 1. Preprocessing: Shade and classify volumetric data to yield color cv and opacity ov for each voxel. Independently, shade polygons to yield color cp and opacity op. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel, trace a parallel viewing ray from the observer position into the data. 3. Volumetric Sampling: Compute a vector of colors cv and opacities ov by resampling the volumetric data at equally spaced positions along the ray. Use tri-linear interpolation from the colors and opacities in the eight voxels surrounding each sample location. The spacing between samples along the ray equals the slab thickness. The spacing between adjacent rays equals the slab width. 4. Geometric Intersection: Independently compute all intersections between the ray and polygons in the environment. 5. Slab Handling: The volume is conceptually divided into slabs of thickness equal to the sample spacing. When a ray intersects a polygon within a slab: Treat the polygon locally as a plane perpendicular to the ray at the intersection point. Calculate the opacity of the volumetric sliver immediately in front of the plane (of) and immediately behind the plane (ob) using exponential attenuation formulas. 6. Compositing: Composite the contributions in depth-sorted order (front-to-back). If a ray intersects more than one polygon within a slab, compute and composite the contribution of each polygon and each sliver of volumetric gel separately. Order: Composite front volumetric sliver (cv, of), then the polygon (cp, op), then the back volumetric sliver (cv, ob). 7. Adaptive Supersampling: To avoid aliasing at polygonal edges, intersections, and highlights, increase the number of rays per pixel in specific regions. Compute two auxiliary colors during ray tracing: Cx: Contributions only from polygons (set ov=0 for all volumetric samples). Cq: Contributions only from polygons, attenuated by passage through volumetric data (set ov=0 for all volumetric samples). Determine if supersampling is needed based on the range of these colors within a sample region: If range(Cx) > \theta and range(Cq) \le \theta: Color difference is due to volumetric data. Do not supersample. If range(Cq) > \theta and range(Cx) \le \theta: Geometric event is hidden by opaque volumetric data. Do not supersample. If range(Cx) > \theta and range(Cq) > \theta: Region contains a visible geometric event. Cast more rays (supersample). This variant converts geometry to volume to bypass explicit ray-polygon intersection tests during compositing. 1. Shading: Shade the polygons. 2. Bandlimiting: Bandlimit the object to the Nyquist frequency in all three dimensions to avoid aliasing artifacts. 3. Scan-Conversion: Use efficient 3D scan-conversion algorithms (e.g., Kaufman 1987b) to create a binary voxel representation of the geometry. 4. Sampling: Sample the object to limit quantization losses. 5. Filtering: Filter the sampled geometry. 6. Combining: Combine the filtered geometry with the volumetric data. 7. Rendering: Render the composite dataset using standard volume rendering techniques. Slab Opacity: The opacity ov of a slab is related to density dv and thickness tv by: ov = 1 - e^{-dv tv} where 0 < ov < 1 and ov = 1 signifies complete attenuation. Front Sliver Opacity: The opacity of of the portion of a slab lying immediately in front of an embedded plane perpendicular to the viewing ray is: of = 1 - (1 - ov)^{tf/tv} where tf is the thickness of the front portion and tv is the total slab thickness. Back Sliver Opacity: The opacity ob of the portion of a slab lying immediately behind an embedded plane perpendicular to the viewing ray is: ob = 1 - (1 - ov)^{tb/tv} where tb is the thickness of the back portion. Slab Thickness: Equal to the spacing between samples along a viewing ray. Slab Width: Equal to the spacing between adjacent rays. Threshold \theta: Used in adaptive supersampling to determine if geometric events are visible. Value not given in the sources. Visibility Errors: Volumetric samples lying immediately in front of and behind polygons require special treatment to avoid errors in visibility. The slab splitting method addresses this. Aliasing: Binary voxel representations in scan-conversion result in aliasing. This is handled by bandlimiting the object to the Nyquist frequency before sampling. Supersampling Ambiguity: Distinguishing whether color difference is due to volumetric data or geometric data is difficult. The use of Cx and Cq resolves this. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridvolumerendering(volumedata, polygons, rayorigin, raydirection, step, theta): """ Renders a mixture of volumetric and geometric data using hybrid ray tracing. volumedata: dict mapping (x,y,z) -> scalar polygons: list of dicts with 'verts' (3x3) and 'normal' (3) rayorigin, raydirection: 3D vectors step: slab thickness / sample spacing theta: supersampling threshold """ def trilinearsample(pos, voldata): # Standard tri-linear interpolation from 8 surrounding voxels # Returns (color, opacity) based on transfer functions pass # Implementation depends on transfer function; assumed available def rayintersect(origin, dir, poly): # Möller–Trumbore or similar triangle intersection # Returns {'t': float, 'u': float, 'v': float} or None pass # Standard geometric primitive intersection def shadepolygon(poly, origin, dir): # Compute color and opacity from surface shading model pass # Standard Phong/Blinn-Phong or similar def overoperator(c1, o1, c2, o2): # Front-to-back alpha compositing alpha = o2 (1.0 - auxxopacity) auxxcolor = [auxxcolor[i] + c[i] alphax for i in range(3)] auxxopacity += alphax # Cq: polygons only, attenuated by volume attenuation = 1.0 - accumopacity alphaq = o attenuation (1.0 - auxqopacity) auxqcolor = [auxqcolor[i] + c[i] alphaq for i in range(3)] auxqopacity += alphaq # Adaptive supersampling check would happen here per pixel neighborhood # If range(auxxcolor) > theta and range(auxqcolor) > theta: supersample return accumcolor A rendering method that combines shaded polygons with volumetric data by treating surfaces as infinitesimally thin solids, using a binary voxel representation for the geometry, and rendering the composite dataset using volume rendering techniques to avoid aliasing artifacts. Unlike the direct ray-tracing variant, this approach does not require supersampling if polygons are sufficiently bandlimited prior to sampling. It is chosen when hardware acceleration for volume rendering is available and polygonal aliasing can be mitigated by pre-filtering. Time Complexity: The hybrid ray tracer is computationally expensive due to ray-polygon intersection tests and adaptive supersampling. The 3D scan-conversion method requires 3D scan-conversion and filtering of polygons, which can be costly for complex meshes. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for both the volumetric data and the polygonal database. The scan-conversion method requires additional memory for the binary voxel representation of the geometry. Performance: The hybrid ray tracer provides high-quality images with correct visibility but is slow due to supersampling. The scan-conversion method is faster if efficient 3D scan-conversion algorithms are used, but may suffer from aliasing if bandlimiting is insufficient. Strengths: Handles mixtures of geometry and volume correctly; avoids errors in visibility with proper slab handling. Scan-conversion avoids ray-polygon intersection complexity by rasterizing geometry into a voxel grid. Limitations: Supersampling increases rendering time significantly. Scan-conversion may lose geometric detail if not bandlimited properly. When to use: Use when high-quality mixing of geometry and volume is required and performance is not the primary constraint. Use scan-conversion when hardware acceleration for volume rendering is available and geometry is simple enough to be bandlimited effectively. The concept of a hybrid ray tracer handling both scalar fields and polygons was proposed by multiple researchers including Kajiya (1984), Levoy (1988a), DeRose (1988), and Upson (1988). However, no implementation was reported until Kaufman et al. published their methods. The hybrid ray tracer was described in detail by Kaufman et al. in 1990. The 3D scan-conversion method was also developed by Kaufman et al. as an alternative to avoid aliasing and supersampling costs. These methods are foundational for applications such as virtual endoscopy, where synthetic objects (probes, catheters) must be mixed with anatomical volume data (CT/MR). name: Hybrid Scanline A-Buffer Volume Rendering
head: Scanline A-Buffer with Volume Fragments
body: Hybrid Scanline A-Buffer Volume Rendering integrates surface-defined geometry and procedural volume data (such as gases) into a single image by combining a fast scanline a-buffer algorithm for solids with volume rendering for translucent media. It distinguishes itself from pure ray casting by using an a-buffer to manage fragment overlap and from pure polygon rendering by explicitly handling volumetric opacity and attenuation through sorted volume fragments. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A scene containing surface-defined objects (polygons) and volume-defined objects (procedural gases or fluids), a camera view, and lighting parameters. Outputs: A final 2D image with correct blending of surfaces and volumes. Data Structures: A-Buffer: A data structure associated with a scanline that maintains a list for each pixel containing all fragments that partially or fully cover that pixel. Volume Fragments: Sub-sections of the volume data that cover the current scanline, treated as fragments with average Z-depth values. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize A-Buffer: Create an a-buffer for the current scanline containing a list for each pixel to hold fragments that partially or fully cover the pixel. 2. Process Surface Geometry: Render surface-defined objects into the a-buffer by storing their fragments in the pixel lists based on coverage and depth. 3. Process Volumes: For each volume object that intersects the current scanline, perform volume rendering calculations for the sections covering the scanline and generate a-buffer fragments for those sections. Cease volume rendering for a specific pixel once full coverage of that pixel is achieved by either volume or surface-defined elements. 4. Sort Fragments: Sort the volume a-buffer fragments into the a-buffer fragment list for each pixel based on their average Z-depth values. 5. Composite: Render the final a-buffer fragment list for each pixel to produce the final color by combining the contributions of all sorted fragments. Illumination and Shadows: The system uses a physically-based low-albedo illumination and atmospheric attenuation model for gases. Volumetric shadows are combined efficiently using three-dimensional shadow tables. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridscanlineabufferrendering(scene, scanliney): # 1. Initialize A-Buffer for the scanline abuffer = {pixelid: [] for pixelid in range(scene.width)} # 2. Render surface-defined objects for surface in scene.surfaces: if surface.intersectsscanline(scanliney): for frag in surface.getfragments(scanliney): abuffer[frag.pixelid].append(frag) # 3. Render volume-defined objects for volume in scene.volumes: if volume.intersectsscanline(scanliney): for section in volume.getsections(scanliney): for vfrag in volume.rendersection(section, scanliney): if not ispixelfullycovered(abuffer[vfrag.pixelid]): abuffer[vfrag.pixelid].append(vfrag) # 4. Sort fragments by average Z-depth for each pixel for pixelid, fragments in abuffer.items(): fragments.sort(key=lambda f: f.averagezdepth) # 5. Composite final image image = {} for pixelid, fragments in abuffer.items(): image[pixelid] = compositefragments(fragments) return image def ispixelfullycovered(fragments): # Check if accumulated coverage sum >= 1.0 or # if opaque surface fragments exist at front-most depth. coveragesum = sum(f.coverage for f in fragments) if coveragesum >= 1.0: return True for f in fragments: if f.isopaque and f.issurface: return True return False def compositefragments(fragments): # Standard front-to-back volume rendering composition # using sorted fragments by average Z-depth. # Illumination and shadow application details are not given in the sources. color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) alpha = 0.0 for frag in fragments: c = frag.color a = frag.opacity color = color + c a (1.0 - alpha) alpha = alpha + a (1.0 - alpha) if alpha >= 1.0: break return color A rendering algorithm for surface-defined objects in hybrid scenes that creates an a-buffer for a scanline containing a list for each pixel of all fragments that partially or fully cover the pixel. It sets itself apart by explicitly managing fragment lists per pixel to support hybrid volume rendering, unlike standard scanline renderers that discard depth information early. A hybrid volume rendering method that traverses the volume in object order and accumulates contributions in image order (object-then-image traversal) using a 2D scan-plane buffer to store information perpendicular to a scanline. It discretizes the z-dimension due to the scan-plane buffer. The algorithm processes scanlines from top to bottom and determines the intersections of the cells with the respective scan-plane in an incremental manner using a list of active cells whose y-extents cover the current scanline. The volume elements intersecting the current scan-plane are sliced by finding the edge intersections of faces of volume elements with the current scan-plane. Then, each slice is divided into triangles and each triangle is further decomposed into line segments in the z direction. The composition is carried out by processing the line segments in front-to-back order and linearly interpolating them along the ray. The quality of the images and the performance of the algorithm are heavily dependent on the discretization level of the scan-plane buffer. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Described as a "fast" algorithm for surface-defined objects. Strengths: Efficiently combines surface and volume rendering and uses 3D shadow tables for efficient volumetric shadowing. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When visualizing procedural gases or fluids alongside surface-defined objects in a hybrid scene. The method was developed by David Ebert as part of a system for procedural modeling, animation, and rendering of gases, fluids, and textures. It builds upon work in solid texturing and procedural noise functions (such as Perlin’s turbulence). The approach was presented in the context of visualizing computational fluid dynamics and hybrid scenes.
