name: Scanline A-buffer rendering
head: Ebert and Parent method, Scanline Rendering, スキャンラインレンダリング
body: A rendering algorithm for surface-defined objects in hybrid scenes, creating an A-buffer for a scanline containing a list of all fragments that partially or fully cover each pixel. It sets itself apart by explicitly managing per-pixel fragment lists to support hybrid volume rendering, combining scanline rasterization with volume rendering passes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scanline of pixels, geometry data for surface-defined objects in a hybrid scene. Output: An A-buffer data structure for the scanline, containing fragment lists for each pixel. Data Structures: A-buffer: An array indexed by pixel column for the current scanline. Each entry holds a linked list of fragments. Fragment: Represents a surface patch covering part of a pixel. Fields include: zmin, zmax: Depth range of the fragment. color, opacity: Surface appearance properties. coverage: Fraction of the pixel area covered by the fragment. next: Pointer to the next fragment in the list. Steps: 1. For each pixel in the scanline, initialize an empty fragment list in the A-buffer. 2. For each surface-defined object intersecting the scanline: a. Determine all fragments that partially or fully cover the pixel. b. For each fragment, compute its depth range and coverage. c. Insert the fragment into the pixel's list in the A-buffer, sorted by depth (back-to-front). 3. After processing all objects, the A-buffer contains all fragments for the scanline, ready for volume rendering compositing. Formulas: Fragment coverage: C = \frac{\text{Area of intersection}}{\text{Pixel Area}}. Depth sorting: Fragments are sorted such that z{i} \le z{i+1} for back-to-front rendering. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Precision: Depth values must be precise to avoid z-fighting in fragment sorting. Boundaries: Fragments covering partial pixels must be handled correctly to avoid artifacts. Degenerate input: Objects with no intersection with the scanline should be skipped. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def scanlineabufferrendering(scanlinepixels, geometryobjects): # Initialize A-buffer: array of linked lists for each pixel in the scanline abuffer = [None] len(scanlinepixels) for obj in geometryobjects: # Determine fragments covering the scanline # (Standard rasterization/intersection step) fragments = [] for pixel in scanlinepixels: if intersects(obj, pixel): fragments.append(createfragment(obj, pixel)) for frag in fragments: # Compute depth range and coverage zmin, zmax = computedepthrange(frag) coverage = computecoverage(frag) # Create fragment node node = {'zmin': zmin, 'zmax': zmax, 'coverage': coverage, 'next': None} # Insert into pixel's list sorted by depth (back-to-front) pixelidx = frag.pixelindex prev = None curr = abuffer[pixelidx] while curr and curr['zmin'] > zmin: prev = curr curr = curr['next'] if prev is None: node['next'] = curr abuffer[pixelidx] = node else: prev['next'] = node node['next'] = curr return abuffer A hybrid rendering system that uses a fast scanline a-buffer algorithm for surface-defined objects and volume rendering for procedural gases, combining them via Z-sorted a-buffer fragments [Parent]. It sets itself apart by explicitly managing per-pixel fragment lists to support hybrid volume rendering, unlike standard scanline renderers that discard depth information early. When to choose: Hybrid scenes with surface-defined objects and volumetric data. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance degrades with high fragment density per pixel. Strengths: Explicit management of fragments allows for hybrid rendering with volume data; offers higher quality than rasterization and faster performance than full ray tracing. Limitations: High memory usage for scenes with many overlapping surfaces; complex processing pipeline results in low affinity with modern GPUs. When to use: Hybrid scenes with surface-defined objects and volumetric data. When not to use: Scenes requiring strict optical consistency or physical-based rendering workflows. Originated by Ebert and Parent in the pre-shader era, combining scanline A-buffer rendering with volume rendering to handle hybrid scenes. It was used for visualizing surface-defined objects in conjunction with procedural gases like clouds. During the 1980s and 1990s, it became a mainstream technique in film and television CG, notably in Terminator 2 and early ILM productions, achieving film quality by combining raster processing with localized ray casting. It declined with the adoption of physical-based rendering due to optical consistency limitations and complex pipeline requirements. name: Hybrid Volume Rendering Scheme
head: Scalable Hybrid Scheme, Hybrid between classical object order and image order
body: The Hybrid Volume Rendering Scheme is a parallel volume rendering algorithm for unstructured grids that combines object-order and image-order techniques to handle complex block boundaries, dramatic cell size variations, and camera-induced load imbalances. Unlike pure image-order methods, which suffer from replicated cell loading and unequal cell distribution, or pure object-order methods, where image compositing becomes a bottleneck, this approach bounds the computation of each processing phase to adapt dynamically to the workload. The algorithm operates on unstructured grids (and structured ones) by dividing work over resources such that each phase of processing is bounded in the amount of computation it can perform. The method addresses the memory footprint issues of the original 2006 Childs et al. technique by introducing the concept of partial composites. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unstructured volume data (mesh), camera parameters, transfer function, and image resolution. Output: Final composited image. Data Structures: Unstructured Grid: Defined by cells and vertices, with sizes and shapes that may vary dramatically. Partial Composites: Intermediate image tiles stored to reduce memory footprint compared to storing full intermediate results. Processor Partitioning: Work is distributed across P processors. Steps: 1. Phase 1: Object-Order Ray Casting (Bounded): Processors perform ray casting on their local portion of the unstructured grid. To prevent load imbalance caused by large cells or camera focus, the processing of large cells is deferred. Each processor bounds the amount of computation it performs in this phase to ensure balanced workload distribution. Rays are cast through the cells owned by the processor. For each ray, the scalar values are sampled along the ray path within the cell. The sampled values are mapped to color and opacity using the transfer function. Instead of compositing into a single final image immediately, processors generate partial composites for their assigned tiles. 2. Phase 2: Image Compositing (Bounded): The partial composites from all processors are collected and composited to produce the final image. This phase handles the depth ordering and blending of the partial results. The amount of computation in this phase is also bounded to maintain balance. 3. Handling Load Imbalance: If a processor owns larger cells or the camera view focuses on a region owned by one processor, the workload would normally be unequal. The hybrid approach solves this by deferring the processing of large cells in Phase 1 and distributing the workload among processors in Phase 2. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Number of Processors (P): Scaled up to 8,192 processors. Data Size: Operated on data sets with more than one billion cells. Partial Composite Size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Footprint: The original 2006 technique required unnecessarily large amounts of memory to store intermediate results, affecting timing and causing crashes. The scalable hybrid scheme introduces partial composites to mitigate this. Load Imbalance: Caused by varying cell sizes or camera positions focusing on specific regions. The hybrid approach manages this by bounding computation per phase. Many-Core Architectures: The algorithm was adapted to support many-core architectures, accounting for the changed balance of computing and communication inherent in these environments. Time Complexity: The algorithm adapts its computation based on workload, performing well in all cases tested (varying camera position, data set size, transfer function, image size, and processor count). Memory Complexity: Reduced memory footprint compared to the original 2006 technique due to the use of partial composites. Scalability: Scaled up to 8,192 processors and operated on data sets with more than one billion cells. Strengths: Handles complex block boundaries, dramatic cell size variations, and camera-induced load imbalances effectively. It can operate like either an object-order or image-order technique depending on the scenario. Limitations: The original technique had high memory requirements (addressed in the scalable version). When to Use: When dealing with unstructured grids with varying cell sizes or when camera position causes load imbalance in traditional methods. When Not to Use: Not specified in the sources. The approach is based on a 2006 method by Childs et al., which was a hybrid between object-order and image-order techniques for unstructured meshes. The original work was lacking in three major respects: insufficient evaluation, high memory requirements for intermediate results, and no consideration for many-core architectures. The scalable hybrid scheme addresses these shortcomings by providing a comprehensive evaluation, introducing partial composites to reduce memory footprint, and adding support for many-core architectures. name: ABR Glyph-Volume Hybrid Visualization
head: Artifact-Based Rendering (ABR) for Brain Microstructure, Magic Lens Glyph-Volume Rendering
body: Artifact-Based Rendering (ABR) is a hybrid visualization technique for Diffusion-Tensor MRI (DT-MRI) data that combines volume rendering for anatomical context with sparsely sampled, texture-encoded glyphs and oriented ellipsoids to represent crossing fibers and microstructural parameters. It solves the problem of occlusion in 3D representations of complex white matter by using a "magic lens" design: volume rendering and sparse glyphs provide global context, while high-resolution glyph data is presented in an interactively defined small volume. It differs from prior slice-based approaches by encoding fiber orientation via glyph texture variations instead of color, freeing the color channel to encode a derived variable (similarity between primary and secondary directions). Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D Diffusion-Tensor MRI volume data; user-defined interaction region (magic lens); parameters for axonal density and axonal radius. Output: Composite image containing volume-rendered anatomical context, sparse oriented glyphs for crossing fibers, and oriented ellipsoids for leftover diffusion. Data Structures: Voxel Data: Each voxel contains diffusion tensor information, from which primary and secondary fiber orientations are derived. Glyph Profile: A 2D texture or geometry profile shared by all glyphs. The profile has a linear texture whose density varies along its length. Ellipsoid Geometry: An oriented ellipsoid geometry per voxel, scaled and rotated to depict leftover diffusion. Steps: 1. Filter Voxels: Identify voxels containing crossing fibers. Only these voxels are processed for glyph rendering. 2. Compute Orientations: For each selected voxel, compute the primary and secondary fiber orientations from the diffusion tensor data. 3. Compute Derived Variable: Calculate the similarity between the primary and secondary directions. 4. Configure Glyphs: Scale the glyph size based on the axonal radius parameter. Adjust the linear texture density along the glyph length based on the axonal density variable. Orient the glyph to align with the primary and secondary fiber orientations. Map the derived similarity variable to color, using a red color range to highlight nearly perpendicular crossings. 5. Configure Ellipsoids: For each selected voxel, generate an oriented ellipsoid that depicts the "leftover" diffusion after accounting for the two primary fiber orientations. 6. Render Context: Render the full volume using standard volume rendering techniques to provide anatomical context. 7. Render Magic Lens: Define an interactively specified small volume (the magic lens). Within this region, render the configured glyphs and ellipsoids at high resolution. Outside this region, render only the sparse glyphs for context. 8. Composite: Combine the volume-rendered context, the sparse context glyphs, and the high-resolution magic lens content into the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: volumedata: 3D array of diffusion tensors. camera: Camera position and orientation. magiclensregion: Bounding box or sphere defining the high-res interaction volume. axonaldensityvar: Scalar controlling glyph texture density. axonalradiusparam: Scalar controlling glyph size. """ # 1. Render Volume Context # Standard volume rendering for anatomical context contextimage = volumerender(volumedata, camera) # 2. Identify Crossing Fiber Voxels crossingvoxels = [] for voxel in volumedata: if hascrossingfibers(voxel): crossingvoxels.append(voxel) # 3. Prepare Glyphs and Ellipsoids glyphs = [] ellipsoids = [] for voxel in crossingvoxels: primarydir, secondarydir = computeprimarysecondaryorientations(voxel) similarity = computesimilarity(primarydir, secondarydir) # Configure Glyph glyph = createglyph( profile=getsharedglyphprofile(), size=axonalradiusparam, texturedensity=axonaldensityvar, orientation=primarydir, # Simplified; actual implementation may use both dirs color=mapsimilaritytocolor(similarity) # Red for perpendicular) # Configure Ellipsoid for leftover diffusion ellipsoid = createorientedellipsoid( voxel.tensor, primarydir, secondarydir) glyphs.append(glyph) ellipsoids.append(ellipsoid) # 4. Render Magic Lens (High-Res) # Render glyphs and ellipsoids inside the magic lens region lenscontent = renderemptyimage() for glyph in glyphs: if isinside(glyph.position, magiclensregion): renderglyph(lenscontent, glyph) for ellipsoid in ellipsoids: if isinside(ellipsoid.position, magiclensregion): renderellipsoid(lenscontent, ellipsoid) # 5. Render Sparse Context Glyphs (Outside Magic Lens) # Render only glyphs outside the magic lens to provide context contextglyphs = renderemptyimage() for glyph in glyphs: if not isinside(glyph.position, magiclensregion): renderglyph(contextglyphs, glyph) # 6. Composite # Combine volume context, sparse context glyphs, and high-res lens content finalimage = alphablend(contextimage, contextglyphs) finalimage = alphablend(finalimage, lenscontent) return finalimage def hascrossingfibers(voxel): # Implementation detail: Check eigenvalues or angular separation of eigenvectors # to determine if fibers cross. Not specified in sources. return True # Placeholder for actual DT-MRI crossing detection logic def computeprimarysecondaryorientations(voxel): # Extract dominant eigenvectors from the diffusion tensor # Not specified in sources. return (Vector(1,0,0), Vector(0,1,0)) # Placeholder def computesimilarity(dir1, dir2): # Compute angular similarity or dot product # Not specified in sources. return 0.5 # Placeholder def mapsimilaritytocolor(similarity): # Red color range for nearly perpendicular crossings # Specific color mapping function not detailed in sources return Color(1, 0, 0) # Placeholder for red def createglyph(profile, size, texturedensity, orientation, color): # Create geometry/texture for the glyph # Not specified in sources. return {"profile": profile, "size": size, "texturedensity": texturedensity, "orientation": orientation, "color": color} def createorientedellipsoid(tensor, primary, secondary): # Create ellipsoid geometry representing leftover diffusion # Not specified in sources. return {"position": Vector(0,0,0), "orientation": primary} # Placeholder def renderglyph(image, glyph): # Rasterize glyph onto image pass def renderellipsoid(image, ellipsoid): # Rasterize ellipsoid onto image pass def isinside(position, region): # Check if position is within magic lens region return True # Placeholder Parameters: axonal density variable: Controls the density of the linear texture along the length of each glyph. axonal radius parameter: Controls the size of each glyph. similarity between primary and secondary directions: Derived variable encoded via color mapping to highlight nearly perpendicular crossings (red color range). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Severe occlusion degrades 3D representations of complex white matter. Mitigated by using the magic lens design to isolate high-resolution data in an interactively defined small volume while glyphs provide surrounding context. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a natural, organic visual language. Allows visualization of structure not possible in 2D slice-based visualizations, particularly in VR. Frees the color channel by encoding fiber orientation in texture, allowing color to encode a new derived variable (direction similarity). Limitations: Occlusion is a major factor in 3D representation design. Relies on user interaction (magic lens) to manage complexity. When to use: Visualizing brain microstructure (Diffusion-Tensor MRI) in VR, specifically regions with high fiber crossings like the centrum semiovale. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Origin: Artifact-Based Rendering (ABR) was introduced in the paper "Artifact-Based Rendering: Harnessing Natural and Traditional Visual Media for More Expressive and Engaging 3D Visualizations". History and Development: Prior to ABR, DT-MRI data had only been visualized using slice-based approaches. A straightforward translation of slice-based visualizations to 3D failed due to occlusion. ABR was developed to address this by combining volume rendering with sparsely sampled glyphs and oriented ellipsoids. The technique was applied to the centrum semiovale region, a region with high fiber crossings. The collaborating domain scientist confirmed expected brain structure and noted that the 3D VR visualization revealed structure not visible in 2D slice-based visualizations. Usage: Applied to brain microstructure imaging (Diffusion-Tensor MRI) in VR. name: Flow Volume Rendering
head: Flow Volumes with Hardware Compositing, Shirley and Tuchman Method, Tetrahedron Projection Method
body: Flow Volume Rendering visualizes steady 3D vector fields by rendering a "flow volume"—the space swept by a generating polygon P as it is advected by the flow velocity field. It solves the problem of efficiently visualizing phenomena like smoke or wind in steady flows without the computational cost of full-volume ray casting or the sorting overhead of standard polyhedron compositing. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific use of the Shirley and Tuchman tetrahedron projection method to enable order-independent hardware compositing for constant-color tracers, allowing interactive performance by rendering only the swept volume rather than the entire data set. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A steady 3D vector field \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}); a user-defined generating polygon P (typically a small planar shape) positioned in the flow; a constant smoke color C; and an absorption coefficient a. Output: A 2D image of the flow volume with correct transparency and occlusion against opaque background geometry. Data Structures: 1. Flow Volume Representation: The volume is represented as a set of tetrahedra. The flow volume is bounded by the initial generating polygon P, the final polygon Pt (carried by the flow for time t), and the stream ribbons generated by the sides of P. 2. Tetrahedral Mesh: The flow volume is subdivided into tetrahedra using the adaptive 3D subdivision method of Max Becker and Crawfis. 3. Projection Data: For each tetrahedron, the projection into screen space is decomposed into triangles. Each triangle vertex stores screen coordinates (x, y, z) and the texture coordinate u = L \cdot a, where L is the path length integral factor along the flow direction. The value L is zero at the "profile" vertices (those on the boundary ribbons) and non-zero only at the "thick" interior vertex A. 4. 1-D Texture Table: A 1D texture map storing the function f(u) = 1 - \exp(-u). Numbered Steps: 1. Generate Flow Volume Geometry: Position the generating polygon P such that it orients itself normal to the local flow velocity \mathbf{v}. Advect the vertices of P through the vector field to generate the stream ribbons and the final polygon Pt. Subdivide the resulting polyhedron (bounded by P, Pt, and the ribbons) into tetrahedra using the Becker and Crawfis adaptive subdivision algorithm. 2. Project and Decompose Tetrahedra: For each tetrahedron, project its vertices into screen space. Apply the Shirley and Tuchman method to decompose the projected tetrahedron into triangles. Identify the "thick" interior vertex A in the projection. This is the vertex where the path length integral L is non-zero. At all other vertices (profile vertices), L=0. In non-degenerate cases, the projection is divided into three or four triangles. In degenerate cases, the thick vertex may lie on the profile. 3. Compute Vertex Attributes: For each vertex of the projected triangles, compute the texture coordinate u using u = L \cdot a, where L is the integrated path length along the flow direction for that vertex, and a is the constant absorption coefficient. For profile vertices, u = 0. For the thick vertex A, u = LA \cdot a. 4. Hardware Compositing Setup: Load the function 1 - \exp(-u) into a 1D texture table. Configure the graphics hardware to use this 1D texture. The hardware will linearly interpolate the texture coordinate u across each triangle and sample the texture to retrieve the alpha value \alpha = 1 - \exp(-u). This alpha value corresponds to 1 - T, where T is the transmittance. 5. Render Opaque Background: Render all opaque surface polygons of the scene first to populate the depth buffer (z-buffer). 6. Composite Flow Volume Triangles: Render the triangles generated from the flow volume tetrahedra. Use the hardware's alpha blending capabilities. The alpha value for each fragment is derived from the 1D texture lookup based on the interpolated u. Compare the fragment's z-value with the z-buffer to determine if the fragment is visible. If visible, composite it using the retrieved alpha. Do not update the z-buffer with the flow volume fragments. Because the smoke color C is constant, the resulting image is independent of the compositing order of the triangles. Therefore, no back-to-front sorting of the tetrahedra is required. Formulas: Transmittance at vertex A: T = \exp(-L \cdot a) where L is the path length integral and a is the absorption coefficient. Color at vertex A: I = C \cdot (1 - T) where C is the constant smoke color and I is the computed color. Alpha Value for Hardware: \alpha = 1 - \exp(-u) where u = L \cdot a. This value is stored in the 1D texture table and sampled by the hardware. Parameters: Smoke Color C: Must be constant for the order-independence proof to hold. Typically specified by the user via interface sliders. Absorption Coefficient a: A scalar value controlling opacity density. Generating Polygon P: User-positioned; orients normal to flow velocity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Linear Interpolation Artifacts: Linearly interpolating T and I directly across triangles produces artifacts because the exponential function is non-linear. This is avoided by using the 1D texture lookup for 1 - \exp(-u). Degenerate Projections: In degenerate cases, the thick vertex may lie on the profile. Unsteady Flows: The method assumes steady flows (velocity independent of time) to achieve near real-time interaction. Compressible Flow: To visualize compressible flow, opacity can be made to vary inversely with the volume of the tetrahedral cell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderflowvolume(vectorfield, generatingpolygonP, smokecolorC, absorptioncoefficienta, timestept, cameramatrix): # Step 1: Generate Flow Volume Geometry # Advect polygon vertices through the steady vector field Pt = [] dt = 0.1 steps = max(1, int(timestept / dt)) for vertex in generatingpolygonP: pos = list(vertex) for in range(steps): vel = vectorfield(pos) pos = [pos[i] + vel[i] dt for i in range(3)] Pt.append(pos) ribbons = list(zip(generatingpolygonP, Pt)) # Subdivide the flow volume into tetrahedra # The sources do not give the exact subdivision algorithm details tetrahedra = [] # Populated by Becker and Crawfis adaptive subdivision # Step 2 & 3: Project, Decompose, and Compute Attributes projectedtriangles = [] for tet in tetrahedra: # Project vertices to screen space using standard perspective projection screenverts = [] for v in tet.vertices: h = [cameramatrix[i][0]v[0] + cameramatrix[i][1]v[1] + cameramatrix[i][2]v[2] + cameramatrix[i][3] for i in range(4)] screenverts.append([h[0]/h[3], h[1]/h[3], h[2]/h[3]]) # Identify thick vertex (max depth) thickidx = max(range(4), key=lambda i: screenverts[i][2]) # Decompose into triangles (Shirley-Tuchman method) others = sorted([i for i in range(4) if i != thickidx], key=lambda i: screenverts[i][2]) triangles = [ [thickidx, others[0], others[1]], [thickidx, others[1], others[2]] ] if len(others) == 3: triangles.append([thickidx, others[2], others[0]]) for tri in triangles: tridata = [] for vidx in tri: # L is zero at profile vertices, non-zero only at thick vertex L = 0.0 if vidx != thickidx else tet.pathlengthat(thickidx) u = L absorptioncoefficienta tridata.append({'screenpos': screenverts[vidx], 'u': u}) projectedtriangles.append(tridata) # Step 4: Hardware Compositing Setup def texturelookup(u): return 1.0 - math.exp(-u) # Step 5: Render Opaque Background renderopaquegeometry(cameramatrix) # Step 6: Composite Flow Volume Triangles zbuffer = {} zbufferwriteenabled = False for tridata in projectedtriangles: for frag in rasterizetriangle(tridata): alpha = texturelookup(frag['u']) if frag['z'] < zbuffer.get((frag['x'], frag['y']), float('inf')): # Composite fragment using alpha compositefragment(frag, alpha) # Do not update the z-buffer # zbuffer[(frag['x'], frag['y'])] = frag['z'] # Skipped per source def rasterizetriangle(tridata): # Standard triangle rasterization producing fragments with interpolated u and z pass def compositefragment(frag, alpha): # Standard front-to-back alpha compositing using retrieved alpha pass def renderopaquegeometry(cameramatrix): # Renders opaque surfaces, populating z-buffer pass The method of Max Becker and Crawfis used to subdivide the flow volume into tetrahedra. It ensures efficient representation of the flow volume geometry by adapting to flow complexity. The specific algorithm for decomposing a projected tetrahedron into triangles, identifying the "thick" vertex, and enabling the hardware compositing trick. Time Complexity: Near real-time interaction is achieved because only the small cells inside the flow volume are rendered, rather than the whole data volume. The hardware pipeline handles shading and compositing efficiently. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of tetrahedra in the flow volume. The technique avoids accessing or storing the whole data volume. Measured Performance: The source notes "near real time interaction" for steady flows. Specific frame rates are not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales with the number of tetrahedra in the flow volume and the resolution of the screen, avoiding access to the whole data volume. Strengths: Order-independent compositing for constant-color tracers eliminates the need for expensive back-to-front sorting. Efficient hardware compositing using 1D texture lookups avoids per-pixel exponential calculations. Interactive visualization of steady flows. Limitations: Assumes steady flows. Unsteady flows require more complex handling. Artifacts can occur if linear interpolation of transmittance is used directly instead of the texture lookup method. Requires constant smoke color for order-independence proof. When to Use: Visualizing steady 3D vector fields (e.g., wind, ocean currents) where the user wants to see the path of tracers (smoke/dye) in real-time. When Not to Use: Unsteady flows, non-constant color tracers (without sorting), or when full-volume rendering is required for other data attributes. Origin: Developed by researchers at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, specifically mentioned in the context of visualizing climate data (typhoons). Key Paper: "New techniques in 3D scalar and vector field visualization" by Shirley and Tuchman (and others), published in 1994 (based on the source date and context). History: The method builds on earlier work by Max Becker and Crawfis on adaptive 3D subdivision into tetrahedra. It also references the polyhedron compositing algorithms that previously required software scan conversion. Usage: Used for visualizing climate data, specifically showing the effect of a typhoon over the Pacific/Indian Ocean. name: Image-order parallel volume rendering
head: Parallel image-order rendering, Screen-space decomposition volume rendering
body: Image-order parallel volume rendering is a distributed rendering technique that decomposes the final image into non-overlapping spatial regions, assigning each region to a separate processor. Unlike object-order methods that distribute the volume dataset, this approach assigns distinct regions of screen space to each processor, allowing the resulting partial images to be combined without an ordered composition step. It is distinguished from its siblings by its screen-space decomposition strategy, which eliminates the need for global depth sorting of fragments but introduces significant data duplication and view-dependent load imbalance. The method relies on the shared principles of the parent family Hybrid and Mixed Geometry, specifically the use of planar slice proxies rasterized on the GPU. The parallelization occurs at the image level. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric dataset V, a camera view matrix M, and a set of P processors. Output: A single composite image I. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored as a 3D texture on each processor's local memory. Screen Partition: The image plane is divided into P non-overlapping rectangular regions R1, R2, \dots, RP. Steps: 1. Partition Assignment: The screen space is divided into P non-overlapping regions. Each processor p is assigned a unique region Rp. 2. Data Distribution: The entire volume dataset (or the necessary subset for the current view) is duplicated and stored on every processor. This is required because the set of volume slices intersecting the viewing frustum for a specific screen region changes dynamically with view orientation. 3. Local Rendering: Each processor p renders the volume slices using the shared proxy geometry technique. It rasterizes the slices and performs classification and blending, but restricts its output to the pixels within its assigned region Rp. The result is a partial image Ip. 4. Image Combination: The partial images I1, I2, \dots, IP are combined. Since the regions Rp are non-overlapping and cover the entire screen, the final image I is formed by placing each Ip into its corresponding spatial location in the output buffer. No ordered alpha blending or depth sorting is required between the processors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Data Redistribution: As the model or view orientation changes, the volume data required by a specific processor to render its screen region may change. This necessitates dynamic data redistribution across the network, which can become a bottleneck. Idle Processors: In certain view orientations, some processors may have little or no work if their assigned screen regions do not intersect the volume's projection. Scalability: Due to the requirement of duplicating the volume dataset on all processors, scalability is limited by the available memory and bandwidth, especially for large datasets. Decomposes the task by distributing the volume dataset across processors rather than screen space. It avoids data duplication and scales better with data size, but requires ordered image composition. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of pixels in the assigned region and the number of samples per ray. However, communication overhead for data redistribution can dominate as the number of processors increases. Memory Complexity: Each processor must store a copy of the volume dataset. Total memory usage is P \times |V|, where |V| is the size of the volume. Performance: Performance is highly sensitive to view orientation. Views that result in uneven distribution of volume pixels across screen regions cause load imbalance, leaving some processors idle while others are overloaded. Strengths: Eliminates the need for complex ordered image composition or global depth sorting between processors. Limitations: Poor scalability with data size due to data duplication; high communication overhead for dynamic data redistribution; sensitivity to view orientation. When to use: Suitable for small to medium datasets where view changes are infrequent or predictable, and where the overhead of data redistribution is acceptable. When not to use: Unsuitable for very large datasets due to memory constraints, or for interactive applications with frequent, arbitrary view changes that cause frequent data redistribution and load imbalance. The concept of image-order parallel volume rendering was described in the context of enabling remote and distributed visualization over high-speed WANs. It is presented as an alternative to object-order methods, highlighting the trade-offs between communication overhead (data duplication) and synchronization complexity (ordered composition). Using High-Speed WANs and Network Data Caches to Enable Remote and Distributed Visualization, https://doi.org/10.5555/370049.370397, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Object-order parallel volume rendering
head: Data-parallel volume rendering, Domain decomposition volume rendering
body: Object-order parallel volume rendering is a distributed rendering approach that decomposes the computational task by distributing the volume dataset itself across multiple processors, rather than partitioning the screen space. Unlike Image-order parallel volume rendering, which assigns distinct regions of screen space to each processor, this method avoids data duplication across processors, scales better with increasing data size, and is less sensitive to view orientation. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset V and a set of P processors. Outputs: A single composite 2D image. Data Structures: The volume data is partitioned using a domain decomposition strategy. Common strategies include: Slab decomposition: The volume is split into planar slabs along one axis. Shaft decomposition: The volume is split into vertical shafts (columns). Block decomposition: The volume is split into 3D blocks. Each processor p holds a subset Vp \subset V. Algorithm Steps: 1. Decomposition: Distribute the volume data V across the P processors using a chosen domain decomposition strategy. 2. Local Rendering: Each processor p renders its assigned subset Vp independently. This produces an intermediate image Ip for that processor. The rendering process typically involves ray casting or projection through the local data subset. 3. Gathering: Collect all intermediate images \{I0, I1,..., I{P-1}\} from the processors. This may involve network communication depending on the architecture. 4. Recombination: Recombine the gathered intermediate images into a final image I{final} using alpha blending. This step must occur in a prescribed order (either back-to-front or front-to-back) to ensure correct transparency handling. Pitfalls: Screen Space Overlap: Intermediate images from different processors may overlap in screen space. This necessitates the ordered composition step in the recombination phase, unlike image-order methods where processor images do not overlap. Communication Overhead: Gathering and recombining images requires synchronization and data transfer, which can become a bottleneck if not managed efficiently. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def objectorderparallelrendering(volumedata, processors, decompositionstrategy): # Step 1: Decompose volume data # Each processor gets a subset of the volume based on the strategy (Slab, Shaft, Block) localvolumes = decompose(volumedata, processors, decompositionstrategy) # Step 2: Each processor renders its local volume # This produces an intermediate image for each processor intermediateimages = [] for p in processors: # Render the local subset to an image # The specific ray-casting or projection method is implementation-dependent img = rendervolume(localvolumes[p]) intermediateimages.append((p, img)) # Step 3: Gather all intermediate images # In a distributed system, this involves collecting images from all nodes gatheredimages = collectall(intermediateimages) # Step 4: Recombine images using alpha blending in prescribed order # Order must be back-to-front or front-to-front relative to the view finalimage = recombinealphablend(gatheredimages, order="back-to-front") return finalimage Scaling: Scales better with data size than image-order methods because it avoids data duplication across processors. View Sensitivity: Less sensitive to view orientation than image-order methods. In image-order methods, certain views may leave some processors with little or no work, and data redistribution may be required as the model moves. Complexity: The recombination step adds complexity due to the need for ordered composition of overlapping intermediate images. Strengths: Efficient for large datasets where data duplication is prohibitive; robust to view changes. Limitations: Requires careful management of overlapping intermediate images during recombination; potential communication overhead in gathering images. The classification of parallel volume rendering algorithms into image-order and object-order categories was established to address the challenges of rendering large datasets. Object-order methods were developed as a solution to the data duplication and view-sensitivity issues inherent in image-order approaches. The term "scene graph" is sometimes associated with the management of displayable data and rendering services in such distributed visualization systems. name: Proxy Geometry and Slicing
body: Proxy Geometry and Slicing renders volumetric data by decomposing the 3D volume into a set of 2D planar slices, which are treated as explicit geometric primitives (typically triangles or quads) and rasterized by the GPU. This method solves the problem of interactive volume visualization by leveraging fixed-function rasterization and hardware alpha blending, avoiding the per-pixel ray-marching overhead of direct volume ray casting. It sets itself apart from Direct Volume Ray Casting by using explicit geometry and fixed-function blending, and from Surface Rendering Pipeline by rendering the entire volume interior rather than just isosurfaces. See Slice-based and Proxy Geometry Rendering for shared principles. Inputs: 3D volume data (stored as a 3D texture on the GPU), camera view direction, volume bounding box, slice spacing/distance. Outputs: Rasterized 2D slices composited into a 2D image. Data structures: An array of BufferGeometry objects pre-allocated to MAXSLICESCOUNT. Each geometry holds a position attribute array of 21 floats (7 vertices × 3 components) and an index array of 18 integers (6 triangles × 3 indices). Steps: 1. Bounding Box Setup: Calculate the minimum and maximum coordinates of the volume bounding box. Store the 8 corners in a corners array and create 12 Line3 edge objects connecting them. 2. Plane Generation: Create a clipping plane aligned with the camera view direction. Initialize a plane.constant value based on the camera position and view distance. 3. Slice Intersection Loop: While sliceIndex < MAXSLICESCOUNT, decrement plane.constant by window.sliceDistance. For each of the 12 edges, compute the intersection of the plane with the edge line segment. Collect valid intersection points into intersectionVertices. 4. Polygon Sorting & Triangulation: If intersectionVertices contains points, compute the centroid by summing the vertices and dividing by the count. Calculate the 2D angle of each vertex relative to the centroid using atan2(y - centroid.y, x - centroid.x). Sort the vertices by this angle. Push the centroid to the end of the sorted array to form a fan. 5. Geometry Update: Update the geometry's position attribute with the sorted vertices and centroid. Build the index array for fan triangulation. Set the draw range to the number of vertices. Mark attributes for update and compute the bounding sphere. Increment sliceIndex. 6. Texture Mapping: Each slice vertex is assigned 3D texture coordinates that map to the volumetric data. 7. Rasterization and Shading: The polygons are rasterized. In the fragment shader, the 3D texture is sampled at the interpolated texture coordinates to retrieve the scalar value. 8. Classification and Blending: The scalar value is mapped to color and opacity via a transfer function. The fragments are composited using alpha blending (typically GLSRCALPHA, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA). 9. Sorting: The slices must be rendered in the correct depth order relative to the camera (back-to-front for standard alpha blending) to ensure correct compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class BufferGeometry: def init(self): self.position = [0.0] 21 self.index = [0] 18 self.drawrange = (0, 0) def markattributesforupdate(self): pass def computeboundingsphere(self): pass class Line3: def init(self, start, end): self.start = start self.end = end class Plane: def init(self, normal, constant): self.normal = normal self.constant = constant def intersectline(self, line): # Returns intersection point or None return None class ProxyGeometrySlicer: def init(self, maxslicescount): self.maxslicescount = maxslicescount self.geometries = [BufferGeometry() for in range(maxslicescount)] self.corners = [] self.edges = [] self.sliceindex = 0 self.intersectionvertices = [] def setboundingbox(self, boxmin, boxmax): self.corners = [ boxmin, [boxmin[0], boxmin[1], boxmax[2]], [boxmin[0], boxmax[1], boxmin[2]], [boxmin[0], boxmax[1], boxmax[2]], [boxmax[0], boxmin[1], boxmin[2]], [boxmax[0], boxmin[1], boxmax[2]], [boxmax[0], boxmax[1], boxmin[2]], boxmax ] cornerpairs = [(0,1), (0,2), (0,4), (1,3), (1,5), (2,3), (2,6), (3,7), (4,5), (4,6), (5,7), (6,7)] self.edges = [Line3(self.corners[i], self.corners[j]) for i, j in cornerpairs] def updateproxygeometries(self, cameradir, viewplaneconstant, slicedistance): self.sliceindex = 0 plane = Plane(normal=cameradir, constant=viewplaneconstant) while (len(self.intersectionvertices) > 0 or self.sliceindex == 0) and self.sliceindex < self.maxslicescount: plane.constant -= slicedistance self.intersectionvertices = [] for edge in self.edges: pt = plane.intersectline(edge) if pt is not None: self.intersectionvertices.append(pt) if len(self.intersectionvertices) > 0: self.sortpolygonedges(self.intersectionvertices) self.updategeometry(self.sliceindex, self.intersectionvertices) self.sliceindex += 1 def sortpolygonedges(self, vertices): centroid = [sum(v[i] for v in vertices) / len(vertices) for i in range(3)] angles = [math.atan2(v[1] - centroid[1], v[0] - centroid[0]) for v in vertices] sortedvertices = [v for, v in sorted(zip(angles, vertices))] sortedvertices.append(centroid) vertices[:] = sortedvertices def updategeometry(self, index, vertices): self.geometries[index].position = [coord for v in vertices for coord in v] # Fan triangulation indices: (0,1,2), (0,2,3),... n = len(vertices) indices = [] for i in range(1, n - 1): indices.extend([0, i, i + 1]) self.geometries[index].index = indices + [0] (18 - len(indices)) self.geometries[index].drawrange = (0, len(vertices)) self.geometries[index].markattributesforupdate() self.geometries[index].computeboundingsphere() Parameters: MAXSLICESCOUNT (maximum number of slices supported, used to pre-allocate the geometries array). window.sliceDistance (spacing between consecutive planes). Edge cases and pitfalls: If plane.intersectLine returns undefined (degenerate intersection), the intersection is skipped. The geometries are pre-allocated with fixed sizes (7 vertices, 18 indices), so intersectionVertices.length must not exceed 7; otherwise, index bounds errors occur. Texture-Based Volume Rendering (TBVR) is a direct volume rendering technique that accelerates image-order ray casting by decomposing the 3D volume into a set of 2D planar slices. These slices are treated as geometric primitives (proxy geometry) that are rasterized by the GPU, with the volumetric data stored in 3D or 2D texture memory. Unlike View-Aligned Slicing, which dynamically computes slice geometry to maintain constant sampling distance, TBVR typically relies on fixed object-aligned slices or view-aligned slices that may vary in sampling density, trading memory efficiency and artifact susceptibility for rendering speed. Choose TBVR when maximum rendering throughput on standard graphics hardware is required and slight sampling artifacts are acceptable. View-aligned slicing is a direct volume rendering technique that decomposes a 3D volume into a series of 2D planar slices (proxy geometry) aligned with the camera's view direction. Unlike standard ray casting which samples the volume texture directly per pixel, this method generates explicit geometric primitives (triangles or quads) that are rasterized by the GPU. The primary advantage is consistent sampling distance relative to the camera, which minimizes sampling artifacts and maintains uniform slice thickness regardless of viewing angle. Choose this variant when visual fidelity and uniform sampling are prioritized over the performance cost of per-frame geometry regeneration. A raster display technique that generates several 2D slices of 3D data and combines them to produce a 3D image. It leaves gaps between the slices, forcing the user to guess about flow field conditions in those gaps. A volume rendering technique using the Volumizer library to polygonize volume data and render it in layers from back to front. The volume data is stored in a 3D texture map, and the subregion corresponding to the newly acquired slice is loaded with the new image data immediately after reconstruction. The volume data is polygonized using trilinear interpolation, then rendered in layers from back to front. A predefined blend function combines the new layer with the existing display buffer: alpha blending weights each new layer by scalar alpha and the existing buffer by 1-alpha, imparting translucency, while MIP selects the maximum of the new layer and display buffer contents regardless of alpha, used for contrast agent visualization. Not given in the sources. The technique originated from early efforts to visualize 3D data on raster display systems. Smith, Sperry, and Everton extended two-dimensional techniques by generating several two-dimensional slices and combining them to produce a three-dimensional image, marking an early application of this family. This approach leveraged the advancement of raster display systems and computer graphics techniques like ray tracing to create images that exploited higher resolution systems. Later implementations integrated real-time MRI imaging guidance, utilizing the Volumizer library and OpenGL to polygonize and render volume data in layers with alpha blending or MIP for contrast agent visualization. name: Texture-Based Volume Rendering
head: Geometry-based volume visualization, Proxy Geometry Rendering, Slice-based rendering, TBVR, Texture Based Ray Casting, Texture-based visualization
body: Texture-Based Volume Rendering (TBVR) is a direct volume rendering technique that accelerates image-order ray casting by decomposing the 3D volume into a set of 2D planar slices. These slices are treated as geometric primitives (proxy geometry) that are rasterized by the GPU, with the volumetric data stored in 3D or 2D texture memory. Unlike View-Aligned Slicing, which dynamically computes slice geometry to maintain constant sampling distance, TBVR typically relies on fixed object-aligned slices or view-aligned slices that may vary in sampling density, trading memory efficiency and artifact susceptibility for rendering speed. The method operates in three stages: Initialize, Update, and Draw. Input: Volumetric scalar field data (regular grid), transfer function (TF), camera parameters (view/projection matrices), and rendering mode (transparent/solid). Output: 2D color buffer with composited volume image. 1. Volume Texture: 3D Texture: Stores the entire volume in GPU memory. Format: GLRGBA or GLRED (for scalar data). Type: GLUNSIGNEDBYTE or GLFLOAT. Filters: GLLINEAR (trilinear interpolation). 2D Texture Stack: Stores slices as a stack of 2D textures. Requires replication along X, Y, and Z axes for object-aligned rendering, consuming 3x memory. 2. Transfer Function Texture: 1D texture mapping scalar values to RGBA color/opacity. 3. Proxy Geometry: Array of vertices defining planar polygons (quads or triangle fans) intersecting the volume bounding box. Object-Aligned: Rectangles aligned with principal axes (X, Y, Z). View-Aligned: Polygons orthogonal to the viewing direction, constructed by intersecting slicing planes with the volume bounding box. 4. Uniforms/Constants: uslices: vec3 containing texture dimensions (Dx, Dy, Dz) for coordinate normalization. uthresh: float threshold for fragment discard. ualphaScale: float multiplier for opacity. uclipPlaneX/Y/Z, uclipCubeMax/Min: Clipping parameters. 1. Initialize: Load volume data into CPU memory. Process data (e.g., compute gradients, downsample) if required. Create transfer function lookup tables (1D textures). Download volume data to GPU as 3D texture or 2D texture stack. Compile fragment shaders. 2. Update (Per Frame): Compute proxy geometry: For View-Aligned: Intersect slicing planes with the volume bounding box. Sort resulting vertices in counter-clockwise order. Construct polygon primitives (e.g., triangle fan from centroid). For Object-Aligned: Select the texture stack (X, Y, or Z) closest to the camera viewpoint. Update vertex arrays with proxy geometry vertices and their corresponding 3D texture coordinates. Texture coordinates are assigned to vertices, either on CPU or via vertex shader. Refresh textures if rendering mode or transfer function parameters change. 3. Draw: Set up rendering state: Disable lighting and culling. Enable alpha blending. For Over operator (back-to-front): Source = 1, Destination = 1 - Source Alpha. For Under operator (front-to-back): Source = 1 - Destination Alpha, Destination = 1. Disable depth testing or disable depth buffer writing if blending with opaque geometry. Bind volume texture and transfer function texture. Specify shader input parameters (matrices, uniforms). Draw slice polygons in sorted order (back-to-front for Over operator). Restore rendering state. For each fragment of a proxy polygon: 1. Interpolate Texture Coordinates: Receive interpolated 3D texture coordinates from vertex attributes. 2. Data Lookup: Sample the volume texture at the interpolated coordinates to retrieve the scalar value v. Note: If using 2D textures, bilinear interpolation is used within slices, causing artifacts at slice boundaries. 3D textures use trilinear interpolation. 3. Transfer Function Lookup: Use the scalar value v as a texture coordinate for a dependent lookup into the 1D transfer function texture to retrieve color C and opacity \alpha. 4. Illumination (Optional): Compute surface normal using central differences (finite differences) between neighboring voxels. Apply lighting model (e.g., Blinn-Phong) to modify color. 5. Compositing: The resulting color and alpha are sent to the hardware compositing stage (alpha blending). Unverified code. Precision: Trilinear interpolation in 3D textures is slightly slower than bilinear in 2D but provides better quality. Boundaries: Object-aligned slices suffer from "pop-up" artifacts when switching between texture stacks (X, Y, Z) due to changes in sampling points. Intensity Variations: As the camera moves, the sampling distance changes in object-aligned rendering, causing intensity variations. Viewing Angle: 2D texture stacks suffer from sampling artifacts when the viewing angle approaches 45 degrees relative to the slices, as the viewer sees between slice gaps. Memory: Object-aligned slices require 3x memory consumption due to data replication along principal directions. Uses fixed proxy geometry aligned with the principal axes (X, Y, Z) of the volume. Requires storing the volume as three stacks of 2D textures (replicated data), consuming 3x memory. Fast and simple to implement but suffers from memory overhead, image popping artifacts during stack swaps, and intensity variations as the camera moves. Uses proxy geometry that is orthogonal to the viewing direction. Requires 3D textures (or on-the-fly reconstruction from 2D stacks). Slower to compute geometry but more memory efficient (no replication) and provides consistent sampling distance, eliminating 45-degree viewing artifacts. A variant of object-aligned rendering where data is stored as a set of 2D texture slices. Proxy polygons are simple rectangles aligned with slices. To avoid data replication, slices can be reconstructed on the fly, incurring performance overhead. Sampling rate depends on volume resolution, which can be mitigated by adding intermediate slices and using trilinear interpolation. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of slices and the resolution of the image. Fragment shader execution is parallelized on the GPU. Memory Complexity: 3D Textures: O(N) where N is the number of voxels. 2D Textures (Object-Aligned): O(3N) due to replication along X, Y, Z axes. Measured Performance: Achieves interactive frame rates on modern GPUs by leveraging hardware texture sampling and alpha blending. 2D textures are faster than 3D textures due to simpler bilinear interpolation, but 3D textures provide better image quality. Strengths: High performance on GPUs; simple implementation; leverages standard graphics pipeline. Limitations: Artifacts at slice boundaries (2D); memory usage (2D replication); sampling artifacts at oblique angles (2D); dependency on sampling rate. When to Use: Interactive visualization where performance is critical and artifacts are acceptable or mitigated (e.g., view-aligned slices). When Not to Use: High-quality offline rendering requiring precise sampling (use ray casting); memory-constrained environments with large volumes using 2D textures. Texture-Based Volume Rendering was developed to accelerate volume rendering on graphics hardware. Early implementations used 2D textures due to hardware limitations, leading to object-aligned slicing techniques. The advent of 3D texture support in GPUs allowed for view-aligned slicing and trilinear interpolation, significantly improving image quality and eliminating viewing angle artifacts. The technique is widely used in medical imaging and scientific visualization for interactive exploration of volumetric data. name: View-Aligned Slicing
head: 3D-Texture Based Slicing, View-Aligned 3D Texture Slicing, View-Aligned Proxy Geometry Sampling, View-Aligned Slice Rendering
body: View-aligned slicing is a direct volume rendering technique that decomposes a 3D volume into a series of 2D planar slices (proxy geometry) aligned with the camera's view direction. Unlike standard ray casting which samples the volume texture directly per pixel, this method generates explicit geometric primitives (triangles or quads) that are rasterized by the GPU. The primary advantage is consistent sampling distance relative to the camera, which minimizes sampling artifacts and maintains uniform slice thickness regardless of viewing angle. It builds on Proxy Geometry and Slicing by dynamically regenerating geometry every frame to maintain view alignment. The method renders the volume by intersecting parallel slicing planes with the volume bounding box, generating billboards that face the camera. These billboards are rasterized, and fragment shaders sample the 3D volume texture at interpolated 3D texture coordinates. Inputs: 3D volume data (scalar field), camera position (eyePos), view matrix (mtx), volume dimensions (res), and sampling rate (sampleRate or numberOfSlices). Outputs: 2D image with color and opacity composited via alpha blending. 1. Volume Texture (tex3D): Format: GLRGBA32F (or 8-bit precision in some implementations). Dimensions: rawinf->res.x, rawinf->res.y, rawinf->res.z. Wrap Mode: GLCLAMPTOBORDER to avoid artifacts from texture coordinate transformation. Filter: GLNEAREST. Binding: GLTEXTURE0. 2. Transfer Function (tex1D): Format: GLRGBA32F. Size: 256 entries. Wrap Mode: GLCLAMP. Filter: GLLINEAR. Binding: GLTEXTURE1. 3. Vertex Buffer (aposition): Type: Float32Array (flat array of [x, y, z] coordinates). Layout: Concatenated vertices for all slices. 4. Offset Array (offsetslength): Type: Array of tuples [offset, length]. offset: Byte offset in the vertex buffer (multiplied by 4 for Float32 alignment). length: Number of vertices for that specific slice. 1. Initialization: Load 3D volume data into tex3D. Load transfer function into tex1D. Define volume bounds: x{bound} = res.x, y{bound} = res.y, z{bound} = res.z. Define the 8 corners of the volume bounding box in local coordinates: corner[8][3] = \left\{ \pm \frac{x{bound}}{2}, \pm \frac{y{bound}}{2}, \pm \frac{z{bound}}{2} \right\}. 2. Geometry Generation (Per Frame): Calculate the distance d from the eye to the origin along the view normal (z-axis of the view matrix mtx): d = mtx[2] \cdot eyePos[0] + mtx[6] \cdot eyePos[1] + mtx[10] \cdot eyePos[2]. Find the furthest and nearest intersection distances by iterating over the 8 corners: distancei = \left| -mtx[2] \cdot corner[i][0] - mtx[6] \cdot corner[i][1] - mtx[10] \cdot corner[i][2] + d \right|. nearest = \min(distancei) furthest = \max(distancei) Calculate the step size (slice thickness): \delta D = \frac{furthest - nearest}{sampleRate}. Calculate the billboard size (diagonal of the bounding box): size = 2 \cdot \sqrt{x{bound}^2 + y{bound}^2 + z{bound}^2}. Generate slice geometry: Loop from i = furthest down to nearest with step \delta D (back-to-front order). Calculate billboard center: billboardCenter[0] = eyePos[0] - i \cdot mtx[2] billboardCenter[1] = eyePos[1] - i \cdot mtx[6] billboardCenter[2] = eyePos[2] - i \cdot mtx[10]. Construct a polygon primitive (triangle fan or quad) centered at billboardCenter with size. Assign 3D texture coordinates to vertices. The coordinates map the unit quad to the volume bounds. In some implementations, a rotation matrix transforms texture coordinates in the vertex shader to align with the view, keeping the slice geometry stationary while changing the texture content. Store vertices in aposition and record [offset, length] in offsetslength. 3. Rendering: Enable blending and set blend function to standard alpha compositing. Bind vertex buffer and enable vertex attribute array for aposition. Iterate through offsetslength: Set vertex pointer with size 3, type FLOAT, normalized false, stride 0, and offset calculated as offset 4 (for Float32 byte alignment). Draw slice using triangle primitives with the recorded vertex count. Fragment Shader: Sample tex3D at interpolated 3D texture coordinates to get scalar value. Map scalar value to color and opacity using a 1D transfer function texture. Composite using alpha blending. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateviewalignedslices(numberofslices, eyepos, mtx, res): # 1. Define volume bounds and 8 corners xbound, ybound, zbound = res.x, res.y, res.z corners = [] for dx in [-1, 1]: for dy in [-1, 1]: for dz in [-1, 1]: corners.append([dx xbound / 2, dy ybound / 2, dz zbound / 2]) # 2. Calculate distance from eye to origin along view normal d = mtx[2] eyepos[0] + mtx[6] eyepos[1] + mtx[10] eyepos[2] # 3. Find nearest and furthest intersection distances distances = [] for corner in corners: dist = abs(-mtx[2] corner[0] - mtx[6] corner[1] - mtx[10] corner[2] + d) distances.append(dist) nearest = min(distances) furthest = max(distances) # 4. Calculate step size and billboard size deltad = (furthest - nearest) / numberofslices size = 2.0 sqrt(xbound2 + ybound2 + zbound2) # 5. Generate slice geometry vertices = [] offsets = [] for i in range(furthest, nearest - deltad, -deltad): # Billboard center calculation using view direction components center = [ eyepos[0] - i mtx[2], eyepos[1] - i mtx[6], eyepos[2] - i mtx[10] ] # Construct polygon primitive (triangle fan or quad) centered at billboardCenter with size # Assign 3D texture coordinates mapping unit quad to volume bounds # Transform texture coordinates in vertex shader to align with view slicevertices = constructbillboard(center, size) vertices.extend(slicevertices) offsets.append([len(vertices) 4, len(slicevertices)]) # offset in bytes for Float32 return vertices, offsets def renderslices(vertices, offsets, tex3d, tex1d): # Enable blending and set blend function to standard alpha compositing enableblending() setblendfunc(SRCALPHA, ONEMINUSSRCALPHA) # Bind vertex buffer and enable vertex attribute array for aposition bindbuffer(vertices) enablevertexattribute("aposition") # Iterate through offsetslength to draw each slice individually for offset, length in offsets: # Set vertex pointer: size=3, type=FLOAT, normalize=False, stride=0, offset=offset4 setvertexpointer(location=0, size=3, type=FLOAT, normalize=False, stride=0, offset=offset 4) # Draw slice using triangle primitives drawarrays(TRIANGLES, start=0, count=length) numberOfSlices / sampleRate: Determines the number of slices. nearClip: Near plane of the orthographic projection, default 200.0. farClip: Far plane of the orthographic projection, default 600.0. viewBound: Half-width of the orthographic projection box, default 50, adjustable by keys 'z' (multiply by 0.9) and 'x' (multiply by 10/9). boundary: Integer flag passed to shader, default 0, toggled by keys '1' (0) and '2' (1). Texture Artifacts: Using GLCLAMPTOBORDER is critical when transforming texture coordinates to avoid sampling artifacts at slice edges. Index Wrapping: When constructing triangles from slice vertices, ensure the index for the third vertex wraps correctly (e.g., to index 1) if k + 1 exceeds the array length to form closed polygons. View Alignment: The proxy geometry must be strictly view-aligned to ensure samples can be correctly read from the frame buffer if post-processing or compositing relies on buffer reads. Performance Management: The number of slices is automatically reduced during rotation to guarantee interactive rates. Object-aligned slicing divides the volume into slices along the principal axes (x, y, z) rather than the view direction. It uses fixed texture coordinates assigned to slice vertices and avoids per-ray intersection calculations. It is distinguished from its parent View-Aligned Slicing by its simplicity and speed, but suffers from higher memory consumption and visual artifacts due to inconsistent sampling distances and stack swapping. Arbitrary slicing uses a plane as proxy geometry to sample arbitrary planes for removing depth complexity and exploring volumes. The plane is view-aligned (rotated to be parallel to the image plane) and rendered to the back buffer. Results can be displayed in a separate viewport or as a textured polygon in object space. This allows for interactive probing and slicing without regenerating the full volume geometry. R-GC is a volume slicing strategy where parallel cutting planes are oriented perpendicular to the straight line connecting the point of reflection to the gravity center of the volume domain. It is used to generate Layered Polygonal Area Lights (LPALs) for indirect illumination. Compared to Ray-of-Regular-Reflection (R-RR) slicing, R-GC ensures LPALs face properly to the point of reflection regardless of the regular reflection direction, correctly rendering the upper part of the reflected appearance when the reflection point is apart from the volume. This variant implements view-aligned slicing on the GPU with pre-integration. It uses two levels of pre-integration: simplified (neglecting color attenuation, faster) for interactive transfer function editing, and full pre-integration for final rendering. Volume shading can be enabled using a per-fragment Phong lighting model based on the gradient of the scalar field. The number of slices is automatically reduced during rotation to guarantee interactive rates. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Interactive rates are achievable; the number of slices is automatically reduced during rotation to guarantee interactive rates. Strengths: Consistent sampling distance, minimal aliasing artifacts compared to object-aligned methods, efficient use of GPU rasterization. Limitations: Requires geometry regeneration every frame. When to use: Interactive volume visualization where view alignment is critical for quality and performance is acceptable. When not to use: When extreme lighting complexity (e.g., accurate indirect illumination) is required without additional techniques, or when memory bandwidth is severely constrained. name: Object-Aligned Slicing
head: Object-Aligned Slices, Three-Stack Slicing
body: Object-Aligned Slicing is a proxy geometry method for direct volume rendering that renders 3D voxel data by projecting pre-defined planar slices aligned with the world axes. It solves the problem of efficient GPU-based volume rendering by avoiding per-ray intersection calculations, instead relying on fixed texture coordinates assigned to slice vertices. It is distinguished from its parent View-Aligned Slicing by its simplicity and speed, but suffers from higher memory consumption and visual artifacts due to inconsistent sampling distances and stack swapping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D voxel data. Output: 2D rendered image. Data Structures: Three stacks of 2D textures, corresponding to the X, Y, and Z principal directions of the volume. Each stack contains slices perpendicular to the respective axis. The 3D voxel data is replicated into these three sets of 2D textures. Steps: 1. Texture Preparation: Create three stacks of 2D textures from the 3D voxel data, one for each principal axis. 2. Viewpoint Analysis: Determine the viewpoint's closest principal direction (the axis with the smallest angle to the view vector). 3. Stack Selection: Swap the active texture stack to the one corresponding to the closest principal direction. 4. Rendering: For each slice in the selected stack: intersect the slice plane with the view frustum or bounding box, assign texture coordinates to the slice vertices, render the slice as a textured quad (or triangle fan) using the GPU, and accumulate color and opacity using alpha blending, sorting slices by distance from the camera to handle transparency correctly. Formulas: Texture coordinate assignment: For a slice at position p along the normal axis, the texture coordinates (u, v) for a vertex at position \mathbf{x} are calculated based on the projection of \mathbf{x} onto the slice plane, normalized to the texture dimensions. Sorting: Slices are sorted by their distance from the camera: di = \mathbf{v}i \cdot \mathbf{c}, where \mathbf{v}i is the slice center and \mathbf{c} is the camera position. Parameters: Number of slices per stack: Determined by the volume resolution along each axis. Sampling distance: Fixed per stack, but varies between stacks. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Image Popping: Swapping texture stacks can cause visible artifacts if not handled smoothly. Lag: Downloading new textures during stack swaps can cause performance lag. Intensity Variations: Sampling distance changes with viewpoint, leading to intensity variations as the camera moves. Memory Consumption: Requires 3x memory for storing the volume data in three orientations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderobjectaligned(volumedata, camera): # Create three stacks of 2D textures stackx = [create2dtexture(volumedata, axis='x', idx=i) for i in range(volumedata.dimx)] stacky = [create2dtexture(volumedata, axis='y', idx=i) for i in range(volumedata.dimy)] stackz = [create2dtexture(volumedata, axis='z', idx=i) for i in range(volumedata.dimz)] # Determine closest principal direction viewvector = normalize(camera.direction) anglex = abs(dot(viewvector, [1, 0, 0])) angley = abs(dot(viewvector, [0, 1, 0])) anglez = abs(dot(viewvector, [0, 0, 1])) # Select stack based on closest direction (smallest angle) if anglex >= angley and anglex >= anglez: activestack = stackx elif angley >= anglex and angley >= anglez: activestack = stacky else: activestack = stackz # Sort slices by distance from camera sortedslices = sorted(activestack, key=lambda s: dot(s.center, camera.position)) # Render slices for slice in sortedslices: # Assign texture coordinates u, v = assigntexturecoordinates(slice, volumedata.dimensions) # Render slice as textured quad renderquad(slice.vertices, u, v, slice.texture) def create2dtexture(volumedata, axis, idx): # Extract 2D slice perpendicular to axis at index idx if axis == 'x': return volumedata[idx,:,:] elif axis == 'y': return volumedata[:, idx,:] else: return volumedata[:,:, idx] def assigntexturecoordinates(slice, dimensions): # Map slice vertex positions to [0,1] texture space u = slice.vertexx / dimensions.x v = slice.vertexy / dimensions.y return u, v def renderquad(vertices, u, v, texture): # Draw textured quad using GPU rasterizer gpudraw(vertices, u, v, texture) SlicingBlockRenderer is a slice-based direct volume rendering method that organizes volume data into subvolumes (blocks) and renders them as textured quads (slices) sorted by distance from the camera to handle transparency correctly. It builds on Object-Aligned Slicing by introducing explicit blocking to improve memory locality and culling efficiency, distinguishing itself from non-blocking slice renderers by managing discrete GPU resources per block. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of slices and the cost of texture sampling. Stack swapping adds overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires 3x the memory of the original volume data due to replication along three axes. Performance: Fast and simple to implement. However, performance can degrade due to texture swapping and memory bandwidth limitations. Strengths: Simple implementation, fast rendering speed for static views. Limitations: High memory usage, visual artifacts during stack swaps, inconsistent sampling distances leading to intensity variations. When to Use: Suitable for applications where memory is not a constraint and view changes are infrequent or can be smoothed. When Not to Use: Not suitable for interactive applications with frequent view changes or memory-constrained environments. Object-Aligned Slicing is a technique used in GPU-based volume rendering, particularly in early implementations using OpenGL. It is discussed in the context of proxy geometry methods for volume rendering. name: SlicingBlockRenderer
head: Slice-based direct volume renderer with subvolume blocking
body: SlicingBlockRenderer is a slice-based direct volume rendering method that organizes volume data into subvolumes (blocks) and renders them as textured quads (slices) sorted by distance from the camera to handle transparency correctly. It builds on Object-Aligned Slicing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data partitioned into blocks, camera position and view direction, transfer function parameters. Output: Rendered image with correct alpha blending. Data Structures: Block: Represents a subvolume. Contains a status flag GPURES indicating if texture data is uploaded to the GPU. Vertex Buffer: A single buffer containing geometry for all possible slice orientations. Layout: 6 sets of quads corresponding to 3 axes (YZ, XZ, XY) and 2 viewing directions (positive/negative) per axis. Each set contains numSlices slices. Each slice is a quad (4 vertices). Total vertices = 6 \times \text{numSlices} \times 4. Indices are structured to draw these quads sequentially. Sampler: Configured with linear min/mag filtering and clamp-to-border wrapping for S, T, and R axes. Bound to BLOCKTEXTUREUNIT. Parameters: mtfuncScaleValue: Scale factor for the transfer function. Default: 1.0. Passed to shader uniform VOLUMETRANSFSCALERUNIFORMSTR. mshouldUseLighting: Boolean flag to toggle lighting. Default: false. mdrawNonEmptySlices: Boolean flag to toggle slice rendering. Default: true. mdrawNonEmptyBoundingBoxes: Boolean flag to toggle bounding box rendering. Default: false. Numbered Steps: 1. Sampler Setup: Create a sampler object with linear min/mag filtering and clamp-to-border wrapping for S, T, and R axes. Bind it to BLOCKTEXTUREUNIT. 2. Block Sorting: In the draw loop, identify non-empty blocks. Sort these blocks by distance from the camera eye using the block's origin in descending order (furthest first) to satisfy the painters algorithm for transparency. 3. View Axis Determination: Compute the base vertex and element offset for the vertex buffer based on the view direction. Determine the axis with the largest absolute component in the view vector to select the slice set (YZ, XZ, or XY). Determine if viewing in the positive or negative direction to select the correct vertex range within that set. 4. Rendering Loop: For each non-empty block in the sorted list: Check if the block's status includes GPURES. If not, skip the block. Set the world matrix for the block. Bind the block's texture to BLOCKTEXTUREUNIT. Set the MVP matrix uniform. Draw the slices using glDrawElementsBaseVertex with the computed base vertex and element offset. Formulas: Let N be the number of slices along the viewing axis (numSlicesPerBlock). Let V{quad} = 4 be the vertices per quad. The base vertex index for the vertex buffer is calculated as follows: View along X (YZ slices): Positive X: BaseVertex = 0 Negative X: BaseVertex = 1 \times V{quad} \times N View along Y (XZ slices): Positive Y: BaseVertex = 2 \times V{quad} \times N Negative Y: BaseVertex = 3 \times V{quad} \times N View along Z (XY slices): Positive Z: BaseVertex = 4 \times V{quad} \times N Negative Z: BaseVertex = 5 \times V{quad} \times N Where N is numSlicesPerBlock.x for X-view,.y for Y-view, and.z for Z-view. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Sort blocks by distance from camera eye, descending (furthest first) sortedblocks = sorted(blocks, key=lambda b: ((b.origin.x - cameraeye.x)2 + (b.origin.y - cameraeye.y)2 + (b.origin.z - cameraeye.z)2)0.5, reverse=True) # 2. name: VoxelBlur Depth-of-Field Volume Rendering
head: Depth of Field Effects for Interactive Direct Volume Rendering implementation
body: VoxelBlur is an interactive direct volume rendering method that provides a depth-of-field effect by selectively blurring voxels based on their distance from a predefined focus plane, simulating real-world camera lens systems. It extends the view-aligned slicing technique by splitting the rendering pipeline into front-to-back and back-to-front passes, each maintaining an intermediate buffer where blur is applied during compositing. Unlike standard back-to-front blending which relies on native GPU blending, VoxelBlur uses custom shader-based blending to enable the blur effect, allowing users to enhance depth perception and separate focus from context. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volume data (8 or 16-bit integers), camera parameters (position, orientation, focal plane, strength), and a focus plane definition. Output: A 2D image with depth-of-field blur effects. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored in 3D textures. Supports arbitrary dimensions, byte skipping, and gzip-compressed raw data via a custom metadata format. Intermediate Buffers: Two framebuffer objects (FBOs) are used: one for the front slices (front-to-back) and one for the back slices (back-to-front). Circle of Confusion (CoC): A radius value derived from camera parameters and distance to the focal plane, transformed into clip-space for sampling. Preprocessing: 1. Load volume data into a 3D texture. 2. Apply 3D Gaussian convolution using a compute shader to reduce noise and smooth surfaces. 3. Calculate gradients using another compute shader and optionally rescale data to [0, 1] range. Rendering Steps: 1. Slice Generation: Intersect several view-aligned planes with the volume's bounding box to create polygons. 2. Tessellation: Tessellate polygons into triangles. 3. Splitting: Divide slices into two sets: those in front of the focal plane and those behind it. 4. Front Pass: Process front slices in front-to-back order. For each slice, render the slice to the front intermediate buffer. Sample the previous content of the front intermediate buffer with blur (using 4 samples on the CoC radius) and combine with the current slice using custom blending. 5. Back Pass: Process back slices in back-to-front order. For each slice, render the slice to the back intermediate buffer. Sample the previous content of the back intermediate buffer with blur (using 4 samples on the CoC radius) and combine with the current slice using custom blending. 6. Final Compositing: Combine the two intermediate buffers to produce the final output image. Pseudocode: Unverified code.
