Setup intermediate buffers frontbuffer = createfbo() backbuffer = createfbo() # Generate slices slices = generateviewalignedslices(rescaledvolume, cameraparams) # Split slices frontslices = [s for s in slices if s.distancetofocusplane < 0] backslices = [s for s in slices if s.distancetofocusplane >= 0] # Sort front slices front-to-back frontslices.sort(key=lambda s: s.distancetocamera) # Sort back slices back-to-front backslices.sort(key=lambda s: -s.distancetocamera) # Front pass for slice in frontslices: renderslicetofbo(slice, frontbuffer, rescaledvolume, gradients) cocradius = calculatecocradius(slice, focusplane, cameraparams, strength) clipspacecoc = transformtoclipspace(cocradius, cameraparams) blurredprev = samplewithblur(frontbuffer, clipspacecoc, numsamples=4) compositewithblur(frontbuffer, blurredprev) # Back pass for slice in backslices: renderslicetofbo(slice, backbuffer, rescaledvolume, gradients) cocradius = calculatecocradius(slice, focusplane, cameraparams, strength) clipspacecoc = transformtoclipspace(cocradius, cameraparams) blurredprev = samplewithblur(backbuffer, clipspacecoc, numsamples=4) compositewithblur(backbuffer, blurredprev) # Final compositing finalimage = combinebuffers(frontbuffer, backbuffer) return finalimage def gaussianconvolution3d(volume): # Apply standard 3D Gaussian blur kernel to volume return volume # Kernel convolution omitted def calculategradients(volume): # Compute volume gradients using central finite differences return volume # Gradient computation omitted def rescaleto01(volume, gradients): # Normalize volume data to [0, 1] range return volume # Min-max normalization omitted def createfbo(): # Allocate 2D framebuffer object buffer return [] def generateviewalignedslices(volume, camera): # Intersect view-aligned planes with volume bounding box to form polygons return [] def renderslicetofbo(slice, buffer, volume, gradients): # Evaluate volume along slice, apply Blinn-Phong shading using gradient normals pass def calculatecocradius(slice, focusplane, camera, strength): # Compute blur radius proportional to distance from focus plane scaled by strength return abs(slice.distancetofocusplane) strength def transformtoclipspace(radius, camera): # Scale radius to clip-space coordinates return radius camera.aspectratio def getsampleoffset(index, clipspacecoc): # Generate 4 sample points on the circle of confusion import math angle = index math.pi / 2 return (clipspacecoc math.cos(angle), clipspacecoc math.sin(angle)) def samplewithblur(buffer, clipspacecoc, numsamples=4): # Sample previous buffer at multiple points around original point samples = [] for i in range(numsamples): offset = getsampleoffset(i, clipspacecoc) samples.append(buffer.sample(offset)) return average(samples) def average(samples): return sum(samples) / len(samples) def compositewithblur(buffer, blurredprev): # Apply custom blending shader to combine current slice with blurred previous buffer buffer.blend(blurredprev) def combinebuffers(front, back): # Merge front and back intermediate buffers into final output return front.merge(back) Parameters: Strength: User-defined parameter governing the increase of blurring with distance. Focus Plane: Predefined plane in the scene, adjustable via UI. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: FTB Compositing: Requires custom blending method and shader support, unlike native GPU blending for back-to-front compositing. Manual Sync: Manual synchronization for data upload of each slice is used to increase GPU asynchronous performance. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: WebGL Volume Ray Casting (Slice Tiling)
head: 2D slice tiling volume rendering, Mosaic Volume Rendering, Volume Ray Casting in WebGL, Volume Ray Casting with Mosaic Texture and Post-Classification
body: WebGL Volume Ray Casting (Slice Tiling) is a direct volume rendering method adapted for web browsers that replaces native 3D volume textures with a 2D tiling map of volume slices to simulate 3D data while preserving tri-linear interpolation. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric data in environments lacking hardware support for 3D textures by running entirely on the client side, leveraging the GPU's accelerated graphics pipeline while avoiding server-side rendering overhead. The method builds on Direct volume ray casting but modifies the data structure and sampling mechanism to accommodate WebGL's texture limitations. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset V of dimensions W \times H \times D, a 2D tiling map texture T{tile} constructed from the slices of V, camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), transfer function T(V) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha), mosaic dimensions (total slices S, images per row Mx, rows My), and step count S. Output: A 2D image buffer containing the composited color \mathbf{C}{out} and opacity \alpha{out} for each pixel. Data Structures 1. 2D Tiling Map (T{tile}): A 2D texture where the volume slices are arranged in a matrix configuration. Not given in the sources. Typical sizes are 4096 \times 4096 for PC and 1024 \times 1024 for handheld devices. 2. Ray Parameters: For each pixel, the entry t{near} and exit t{far} parameters of the ray intersecting the volume bounding box, extracted from a two-pass color cube render. Numbered Steps 1. Data Preprocessing: Tile all slices of the 3D volume dataset beside each other in a matrix configuration to form a single 2D texture object. Medical datasets are typically reduced to 8 bits per pixel to match WebGL format limitations. 2. Ray Coordinate Identification (Geometry Pass): Render a unit cube with coordinates (0,0,0) to (1,1,1) representing the volume boundary in two passes with modified depth functions. The first pass captures the closest region to the camera (ray start), and the second captures the far region (ray end). Coordinates are stored in the r, g, b color components of each pixel as 24-bit RGB values. 3. Ray Generation: Extract the start and end positions of the ray for each pixel from the previous render passes. Divide the ray interval into S equi-parametric steps. 4. Volume Value Interpolation: For each sample point, calculate the slice indices and fractional parts to map the 3D coordinate to the 2D tiling map texture coordinates. Sample the two adjacent slices and perform linear interpolation between them. 5. Transfer Function Application (Post-Classification): Apply the transfer function to the interpolated raw scalar value to obtain color \mathbf{V}{rgb} and opacity Sa. Post-classification interpolates raw data first, then applies the transfer function, which is considered correct for continuous scalar fields despite higher computational cost. 6. Compositing and Early Termination: Accumulate the color and opacity using the front-to-back composition function. The ray is interrupted when the composition reaches the end of the cube or the accumulated alpha Aa reaches its maximum value of 1. Formulas The algorithm complexity is: O(M \times S) where M is the number of pixels to be drawn (resolution width \times height) and S is the number of steps of the ray that traverses the volume. Slice index and coordinate mapping: s1 = \lfloor z \cdot S \rfloor, \quad s2 = s1 + 1 dx1 = \text{fract}(s1/Mx), \quad dy1 = \text{fract}(s1/My) dx2 = \text{fract}(s2/Mx), \quad dy2 = \text{fract}(s2/My) tx1 = dx1 + x/Mx, \quad ty1 = dy1 + y/My tx2 = dx2 + x/Mx, \quad ty2 = dy2 + y/My where x, y are the normalized coordinates within the slice (0 \le x, y \le 1), and \text{fract}(\cdot) returns the fractional part. Texture sampling and scalar interpolation: v1 = \text{tex2D}(tx1, ty1), \quad v2 = \text{tex2D}(tx2, ty2) Va(x,y,z) = \text{mix}(v1, v2, (z \cdot S) - s1) where the source uses (x \cdot S) - s1 but x is a typo for the slice coordinate z. Accumulation and transfer function: Sa = Va \cdot Of, \quad S{rgb} = V{rgb} \cdot Sa \cdot Lf A{rgb}^k = A{rgb}^{k-1} + (1 - Aa^{k-1}) \cdot S{rgb} Aa^k = Aa^{k-1} + Sa where Of and Lf are general opacity and light factors, and the final pixel alpha Aa is set to 1 at the end of the render process. (Note: The source includes a factor (1/s) in Sa, which is treated as a typo for 1 or omitted for standard compositing.) Parameters M: Number of pixels to be drawn. Typical resolutions tested: 512px, 1024px, 2048px, 4096px. S: Number of ray steps. Typical values tested: 30, 80, 140, 200. Texture Size: 4096 \times 4096 for PC, 1024 \times 1024 for handheld devices. Bit Depth: 8 bits per pixel. Mosaic Dimensions: Total slices S, images per row Mx, rows My. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Precision: Storing ray coordinates in 24-bit RGB color components provides sufficient precision for ray coordinates despite the seemingly small range, due to color interpolation. Shader Compilation Limits: Browser shader compilers may fail to compile larger shader programs due to inadequate or restricted shader language implementations. Interpolation Overhead: The use of 2D slice tiling introduces a slight interpolation overhead compared to native 3D textures, though it is minimal and imperceptible in browser environments. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intersectraybox(o, d, boxmin, boxmax): # Standard slab method; handles grazing cases and zero direction components correctly tmin = (boxmin - o) / d tmax = (boxmax - o) / d t1 = min(tmin, tmax) t2 = max(tmin, tmax) tnear = max(t1) tfar = min(t2) if tnear > tfar: return None return tnear, tfar def getslicecoords(xnorm, ynorm, z, S, Mx, My): s1 = int(z S) s2 = s1 + 1 dx1 = (s1 / Mx) % 1.0 dy1 = (s1 / My) % 1.0 dx2 = (s2 / Mx) % 1.0 dy2 = (s2 / My) % 1.0 tx1 = dx1 + xnorm / Mx ty1 = dy1 + ynorm / My tx2 = dx2 + xnorm / Mx ty2 = dy2 + ynorm / My return (tx1, ty1), (tx2, ty2) def sample2D(texture, u, v): # Standard 2D texture lookup with tri-linear interpolation return texture.lookup(u, v) def renderwebglvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds, ttile, transferfunction, numsteps, S, Mx, My): tnear, tfar = intersectraybox(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds.min, volumebounds.max) if tnear is None: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 stepsize = (tfar - tnear) / numsteps acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 for i in range(numsteps): t = tnear + i stepsize p = rayorigin + raydirection t xnorm, ynorm, z = p coords1, coords2 = getslicecoords(xnorm, ynorm, z, S, Mx, My) u1, v1 = coords1 u2, v2 = coords2 v1val = sample2D(ttile, u1, v1) v2val = sample2D(ttile, u2, v2) fracz = (z S) - int(z S) Va = mix(v1val, v2val, fracz) color, alpha = transferfunction(Va) weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = tuple(acccolor[k] + weight color[k] for k in range(3)) accalpha = accalpha + alpha if accalpha >= 1.0: break return acccolor, 1.0 A software-based approach that iterates through slices in CPU memory. It was implemented in a web-based volume rendering system for medical (Aorta) and radar datasets, tested on the Mozilla Firefox/Fennec mobile browser. name: Slicing Plane Volume Rendering
head: slicing plane framework, three-pass volume rendering
body: Slicing Plane Volume Rendering is an image-order direct volume ray casting method that decomposes a 3D density volume into a series of view-aligned 2D planes. It solves the problem of efficient hardware-accelerated volume visualization by rasterizing these planes front-to-back and blending the results, allowing complex lighting models (such as single and multiple scattering) to be applied per fragment. It differs from standard texture-based volume rendering by explicitly generating geometric slice primitives rather than relying solely on ray-marching through a 3D texture, and it differs from proxy geometry methods by using planes that are strictly aligned to the camera view direction for every frame. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D density volume (stored as a 3D texture map). Output: A 2D image with accumulated lighting contributions. Data Structures: 3D Texture: Stores the scalar density values of the volume. Slice Geometry: A series of planar polygons (quads or triangles) intersecting the volume bounding box. Precomputed Data: The distance from each sample point to the light source (llight) is precomputed and stored for all sample points in the volume. Parameters: Slice Spacing: Planes are equally spaced along the view direction. Scattering Phase Function: The Henyey-Greenstein phase function is used, defined by the mean cosine of the scattering angle g. Blending: Front-to-back alpha blending is used to accumulate results. Steps: 1. View-Aligned Slice Generation: For each frame, generate a series of planes equally spaced along the view direction that intersect the volume. 2. Texture Coordinate Assignment: Assign 3D texture coordinates to the vertices of each plane corresponding to the density volume. 3. Front-to-Back Rendering: Render the planes in front-to-back order relative to the camera. 4. Fragment Processing (Per Slice): For each fragment inside the medium volume on a slice, execute the following lighting passes: Pass 1 (Preliminary): Compute leye (distance from fragment to eye) and seye (distance from light to eye path). Determine the blur width w based on leye and seye. Pass 2 (Single Scattering): Compute the direct lighting contribution L{direct}. Pass 3 (Multiple Scattering): Compute the indirect lighting contribution L{indirect}. 5. Accumulation: Add the contributions to the total accumulated lighting L{total}: L{total} = L{total} + L{direct} + L{indirect} Formulas: Henyey-Greenstein Phase Function: P(\theta) = \frac{1 - g^2}{4\pi(1 + g^2 - 2g \cos \theta)^{3/2}} where g is the mean cosine of the scattering angle. Direct Lighting (L{direct}): L{direct} = L \cdot sm \cdot P \cdot atten \cdot \Delta l where L is light intensity, sm is material scattering coefficient, P is the phase function, atten is attenuation, and \Delta l is the slice thickness. Attenuation: atten = \exp(-(c/b) \cdot l) where l is the path length. Multiple Scattering (L{indirect}): L{indirect} = L{blurred} \cdot 2\langle hb \theta \ranglew \cdot P{MS} \cdot atten \cdot \Delta l where L{blurred} is the blurred light image, P{MS} is the multiple scattering phase function, and atten = \exp(-\gamma (c/b) \cdot l)^2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderslices(volume3dtexture, lightsource, camera): # 1. Generate view-aligned planes slices = generateviewalignedplanes(volume3dtexture.bounds, camera.viewdirection, spacing) # 2. Sort slices front-to-back relative to camera slices.sortbydepth(camera.position) # Initialize total accumulated lighting Ltotal = 0 for slice in slices: # 3. Assign texture coordinates to slice vertices assigntexturecoordinates(slice, volume3dtexture) # 4. Rasterize slice and execute fragment program for each fragment for fragment in slice.fragments: # Get 3D position from texture coordinates pos = fragment.worldposition # Pass 1: Preliminary computation leye = distance(fragment.position, camera.position) seye = distance(lightsource.position, fragment.position) # Simplified; actual seye depends on light path geometry # Compute blur width w based on leye and seye w = computeblurwidth(leye, seye) # Sample blurred light image Lblurred = samplelightimage(fragment.uv, w) # Pass 2: Single Scattering # Compute angle theta between view direction and light direction viewdir = normalize(camera.position - fragment.position) lightdir = normalize(lightsource.position - fragment.position) costheta = dot(viewdir, lightdir) # Henyey-Greenstein phase function P = heneygreensteinphase(costheta, g) # Attenuation along eye path # Note: llight is precomputed, but attenuation formula uses l (path length) # In the context of the slice, l is approximated by leye or slice thickness atten = exp(-(c/b) leye) Ldirect = computedirectlighting(L, sm, P, atten, slicethickness) # Pass 3: Multiple Scattering # Compute multiple scattering phase function PMS PMS = multiplescatteringphase(costheta, g) # Attenuation for multiple scattering (squared term in source) attenms = exp(-gamma (c/b) leye) 2 # Compute indirect contribution # 2<hb theta>w is a precomputed or sampled factor related to blur width factor = 2 sampleblurfactor(w) Lindirect = Lblurred factor PMS attenms slicethickness # Composite Ltotal = Ltotal + Ldirect + Lindirect return Ltotal Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Orthogonal View: When the viewing direction becomes orthogonal to the slice planes, the slices may disappear due to back-face culling. This requires enabling double-sided rendering. Performance: Implementing single and multiple scattering in separate passes is less efficient. Combining Passes 2 and 3 into a single rendering pass provides a 40% performance increase. Precision: The attenuation formula involves exponential decay; precision issues may arise for large path lengths or high density values. A technique to prevent volume rendering slices from disappearing when they become orthogonal to the viewing direction by enabling rendering of both front and back faces of the plane geometry. It is chosen when the camera view angle causes standard back-face culling to hide the slice planes. Implementation involves setting the material side property to DoubleSide (e.g., THREE.DoubleSide in Three.js). Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of slices and the number of fragments per slice. The complexity of the fragment shader depends on the number of passes (1-3) and the cost of sampling the blurred light image. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D volume texture and precomputed llight data for all sample points. Measured Performance: Combining single and multiple scattering passes yields a 40% performance increase over the three-pass method. Strengths: Leverages standard GPU rasterization hardware; allows for complex lighting models (scattering) to be applied efficiently per fragment. Limitations: Requires regeneration of slice geometry every frame to maintain view-alignment; performance degrades if the number of slices is very high or if the fragment shader is complex. When to Use: Suitable for real-time visualization of participating media where lighting effects are important and hardware rasterization is preferred over ray marching. When Not to Use: When the view direction changes frequently and geometry generation overhead is prohibitive, or when the volume is extremely large and memory bandwidth for 3D texture sampling is a bottleneck. The method was introduced by Cabral et al. in 1994 as a texture-based volume rendering approach using graphics hardware. It was later extended by to include a lighting model for general participating media, incorporating single and multiple scattering effects. The method is widely used in scientific visualization and medical imaging for real-time volume rendering with lighting effects. name: Slice Plane Rendering via Shader Interception
body: Slice Plane Rendering via Shader Interception is a technique to render orthogonal slice planes inside a 3D volume by intercepting the volume rendering draw call, swapping the shader to a dedicated slice shader, and disabling depth testing to ensure visibility. It builds on Slicing Plane Volume Rendering by modifying the rendering pipeline state rather than changing the geometry generation logic, allowing slice planes to be composited over the volume without depth conflicts. The method operates by overriding a specific volume rendering function (nv.drawImage3D) to inject a secondary rendering pass for slice planes. It saves the current OpenGL state, configures a dedicated slice shader with specific uniforms, disables depth testing to allow the slices to be seen through the volume, renders the slices, and then restores the original state. Inputs: The current volume rendering context (nv), the voxel data, the volume scale, and the slice configuration. Outputs: A rendered frame where orthogonal slice planes are visible over the volume rendering. The implementation relies on the nv object, which contains: nv.gl: The WebGL 2 context. nv.drawImage3D: The original volume rendering function. nv.renderSliceShader: The shader program dedicated to rendering slice planes. nv.renderShader: The current volume rendering shader. nv.gradientTextureAmount: The current gradient texture amount uniform. nv.sliceScale(enabled: boolean): A function that returns the voxel scale and volume scale. Opacity: The opacity of the slice planes is set to 0.65. Overlays: The overlays uniform is set to 0 to prevent the native shader from drawing difference overlays, as those are handled by the preceding volume pass. Clip Plane Color: Set to [0, 0, 0, 0]. Render Overlay Blend: Set to 0. 1. Store the original drawImage3D method. 2. Override nv.drawImage3D to call the original method first. 3. name: Image-based rendering integration
head: Image-Based Rendering with Impostors, Impostor rendering
body: This method integrates volume rendering into a polygonal virtual environment by treating rendered volume images as image-based primitives (impostors) within the scene. It solves the problem of combining high-fidelity volume visualization with interactive polygonal environments by offloading the computationally expensive volume rendering to a separate server, while the client handles the polygonal scene and impostor management. It sets itself apart from direct ray casting or slice-based rendering by decoupling the volume rendering computation from the display geometry, using 2D quads textured with pre-rendered volume images as the visual representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volumetric data set, camera positions for left and right eyes (stereoscopic), head-tracker updates. Output: Stereo pair of images rendered on impostor quads within the polygonal virtual environment. Data Structures: Impostor: A geometric primitive (quad) used to represent the volume object. Texture: The rendered volume image mapped onto the impostor quad. Server State: Holds the volume data and rendering logic. Client State: Holds the polygonal environment, impostor geometry, and network communication logic. Steps: 1. Distribution: The volume rendering process is distributed to a separate server (a fast PC with sufficient memory for the volume data sets). 2. Communication: The client (implemented as a Studierstube application) communicates with the server via a Local Area Network (LAN). 3. View Request: When the user moves or the view changes, the head-tracker reports the change to the impostors on the client. The impostors update their orientation so their surface normal faces the respective eye and send a request for new volume renderings to the server for the two viewing directions (one for each eye). 4. Volume Rendering: The server receives the two viewing directions and renders the volume data for those directions. 5. Image Transmission: The server sends the rendered images back to the client. 6. Impostor Integration: The client integrates these images into the polygonal renderings of the virtual environment by mapping them as textures onto quads that act as impostors for the volume object. 7. Stereoscopic Display: Two quads act as impostors, one for each stereoscopic view. The quads are rotated around their center so their surface normal always faces the respective eye of the user. The size of the impostors does not need to be varied, as normal perspective rendering of the quads takes place afterwards. 8. Asynchronous Update: The update process happens asynchronously in a background thread to prevent the virtual environment from freezing during the rendering time (20ms to 500ms). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import threading import time from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Tuple, List @dataclass class Pose: position: Tuple[float, float, float] orientation: Tuple[float, float, float] @dataclass class Image: pixels: List[List[int]] width: int height: int @dataclass class RenderRequest: volumeid: str eyeleftpose: Pose eyerightpose: Pose @dataclass class RenderResponse: imageleft: Image imageright: Image def drawquad(normal: Tuple[float, float, float], texture: Image) -> None: """Renders a quad with the given surface normal and texture mapping.""" pass def bindtexture(image: Image) -> None: """Uploads image data to GPU texture memory.""" pass class ImpostorManager: def init(self, volumeid: str, serveraddress: str): self.volumeid = volumeid self.serveraddress = serveraddress self.leftquadnormal = Pose((0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1)) self.rightquadnormal = Pose((0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1)) self.lefttexture = None self.righttexture = None self.lock = threading.Lock() self.updatethread = threading.Thread(target=self.updateloop, daemon=True) self.updatethread.start() def updateloop(self): while True: # Read head-tracker for 6DoF pose lefteye, righteye = self.readheadtracker() # Update impostor orientation to face respective eyes self.leftquadnormal.orientation = self.computenormal(lefteye.position) self.rightquadnormal.orientation = self.computenormal(righteye.position) # Send request to server request = RenderRequest(self.volumeid, lefteye, righteye) response = self.sendnetworkrequest(self.serveraddress, request) # Apply textures asynchronously with self.lock: self.lefttexture = response.imageleft self.righttexture = response.imageright def readheadtracker(self) -> Tuple[Pose, Pose]: # Standard 6DoF head-tracker polling (step not detailed in sources) return Pose((0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 0)), Pose((0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 0)) def computenormal(self, eyepos: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: # Returns normalized vector from quad center to eye return eyepos def sendnetworkrequest(self, address: str, req: RenderRequest) -> RenderResponse: # Standard TCP/UDP LAN socket request (step not detailed in sources) return RenderResponse(Image([], 0, 0), Image([], 0, 0)) def render(self): # Render polygonal environment pass with self.lock: if self.lefttexture: bindtexture(self.lefttexture) drawquad(self.leftquadnormal.orientation, self.lefttexture) if self.righttexture: bindtexture(self.righttexture) drawquad(self.rightquadnormal.orientation, self.righttexture) class VolumeServer: def init(self, volumedata): self.volumedata = volumedata def rendervolume(self, viewdirection: Pose) -> Image: # Software-based volume rendering (RTVR) return Image([], 0, 0) def handlerequest(self, request: RenderRequest) -> RenderResponse: imgleft = self.rendervolume(request.eyeleftpose) imgright = self.rendervolume(request.eyerightpose) return RenderResponse(imgleft, imgright) Parameters: Rendering Time: 20ms to 500ms, depending on the complexity of the volume data set and the rendering mode. Frame Rate: Up to 25fps for a resolution of 128^3 or approximately 11fps for 256^3, depending on complexity and rendering modes (e.g., surface shaded, maximum intensity projection, or non-photorealistic). Polygonal Environment Frame Rate: 60fps, independent of the volume rendering rate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Network Delay: The main problem besides the rendering rate is the network delay (lag), which results in a delayed response when manipulating the volume data. Quick Turning: The decoupling between image update and impostor display becomes visible when turning the volume object quickly, as the textures may not update fast enough to match the rapid change in viewpoint. Freezing: Without asynchronous updates, the virtual environment would freeze during the rendering time. Time Complexity: The volume rendering time varies from 20ms to 500ms per stereo pair, depending on data complexity and rendering mode. The polygonal environment continues to update at 60fps independently. Memory Complexity: The server requires enough memory to hold the volume data sets. Performance: Interactive frame (stereo pair) rates of up to 25fps for a resolution of 128^3 or approximately 11fps for 256^3. Strengths: Adds flexibility and scalability to the system by distributing volume rendering to a separate server. Allows seamless integration of volume visualization and polygonal rendering. Prevents the virtual environment from freezing during volume rendering updates. Limitations: Network delay (lag) causes delayed response when manipulating volume data. Visual artifacts may occur when turning the volume object quickly due to the asynchronous update process. When to Use: When integrating volume rendering into a polygonal virtual environment with limited client-side rendering power for volume data, and when stereoscopic visualization is required. When Not to Use: When low latency is critical and network delay is unacceptable, or when the volume data is too large for the server to handle efficiently. This method was developed by A.L. Fuhrmann et al. and presented in the paper "Distributed Software-Based Volume Visualization in a Virtual Environment" at Eurographics 2005. It builds on previous VR techniques employed in visualization settings. The system uses the Real Time Volume Rendering Library (RTVR) and the Studierstube virtual environment. It was applied to heterogeneous display settings, mixing volume rendering and polygonal rendering. Distributed Software-Based Volume Visualization in a Virtual Environment, https://doi.org/10.2312/egve/iptegve2005/129-140, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Image-Based Volume Rendering
head: Image-Based Volume Rendering (IBVR) with Opacity Light Fields, Opacity Light Field Rendering
body: Image-Based Volume Rendering (IBVR) is a technique for interactively exploring arbitrarily large volumetric datasets on standard graphics hardware by decoupling the expensive volume integration from the interactive viewing phase. It solves the performance bottleneck of direct ray casting on large datasets by precomputing "ray slices" from multiple viewpoints and compositing them as opacity light fields during interaction. Unlike previous image-based methods that restricted viewpoints to a limited cone or lacked opacity for internal structure, IBVR allows unrestricted external viewpoints and arbitrary clipping surfaces to reveal interior details without re-rendering the volume. The method operates in three distinct phases: Volume Rendering (preprocessing), Key View Generation, and Interactive Viewing. It is independent of the underlying volume rendering system and dataset representation (e.g., rectilinear or irregular grids). Inputs: Volumetric dataset (scalar field). Geometric proxy surface bounding the volume (initially a bounding sphere or isosurface). Set of original viewpoints for preprocessing. User-defined parameters: number of ray slices per viewpoint, slice spacing. Outputs: Interactive 3D visualization allowing camera movement and dynamic clipping surface modification. 1. Ray Slice A Ray Slice is a 2D image where each pixel represents a partial ray projected from a specific slice location through the volume. Layout: A 2D array of RGBA values. Content: The color and opacity at each pixel correspond to the accumulated values generated by the volume integral along a viewing ray starting at the slice plane and extending through the remainder of the volumetric data towards the original viewpoint. Storage: Stored as compressed images (e.g., PNG for lossless, JPEG 2000 for lossy). 2. Geometric Proxy Surface A surface bounding the volume used to define clipping planes during interactive viewing. Layout: Standard triangle mesh or implicit surface representation. Function: Defines the boundary between the pre-rendered interior (behind the proxy relative to the camera) and the interactive exterior. The user can modify this surface (e.g., add clipping planes) to reveal internal structure. 3. Key View A composite image generated from a set of ray slices and the proxy surface for a specific viewing location. Step 1: Volume Rendering (Preprocessing) 1. Select a set of original viewpoints from which to pre-render the volume. 2. For each viewpoint, define a series of image-aligned clipping planes moving back-to-front through the volume. 3. For each clipping plane position (slice): a. Clip the volume between the clipping plane and the viewpoint. b. Render the remaining volume (from the clipping plane to the far end of the data) using a standard volume rendering algorithm with back-to-front compositing. c. Store the resulting RGBA image as a Ray Slice. Note: The number of slices per viewpoint is adjustable and dataset-dependent. Anisotropic data may require more slices along one axis. Spacing can be adapted to skip empty space or capture detail. 4. Define a Geometric Proxy Surface bounding the volume. Step 2: Key View Generation 1. Input: The set of Ray Slices, their associated viewpoint parameters, and the Geometric Proxy Surface. 2. For each desired interactive viewing location (Key View): a. Determine the intersection of the viewing rays with the Geometric Proxy Surface. b. Identify which Ray Slices are "behind" the proxy surface relative to the new viewpoint. c. Composite the relevant Ray Slices and the proxy surface to generate a Key View image. This image represents the volume intersected by the proxy surface from that specific location. Step 3: Interactive Viewing 1. Load the Key Views and the Geometric Proxy Surface into the graphics hardware. 2. Render the scene interactively: a. Render the Geometric Proxy Surface. b. Render the Key Views as Opacity Light Fields behind the proxy surface. c. Allow the user to modify the Geometric Proxy Surface (e.g., via clipping planes) to reveal interior structure. d. Because the interior structure is pre-computed in the Ray Slices/Key Views, changes to the proxy do not require volumetric re-rendering. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ibvrpipeline(volumedata, transferfunction, proxysurface, viewpoints, sliceparams): rayslices = {} for viewpoint in viewpoints: rayslices[viewpoint] = [] # Determine slice positions along the view direction viewdir = normalize(viewpoint.position - volumedata.center) numslices = sliceparams.get('numslices', 10) spacing = sliceparams.get('spacing', 1.0) slicepositions = [viewpoint.position + viewdir (i spacing) for i in range(numslices)] for pos in slicepositions: # Delegate to any arbitrary volume rendering system that computes RGBA images with back-to-front compositing for arbitrary image-aligned clipping planes. rgbaimage = rendervolumebacktofront(volumedata, transferfunction, pos, viewpoint) # Standard lossless image compression (e.g., PNG). compressedslice = compresstopng(rgbaimage) rayslices[viewpoint].append({'position': pos, 'image': compressedslice}) return rayslices def generatekeyviews(rayslices, proxysurface, keyviewpoints): keyviews = {} for kv in keyviewpoints: relevantslices = [] for vp, slices in rayslices.items(): for s in slices: # Determine if slice position is occluded by proxy surface from key viewpoint. if isbehindproxy(s['position'], kv.position, proxysurface): relevantslices.append(s) # Back-to-front alpha compositing of selected ray slices. keyviews[kv] = compositeslices(relevantslices, kv) return keyviews def renderinteractive(keyviews, proxysurface, currentcamera): # Rasterize proxy surface geometry. rasterize(proxysurface, currentcamera) # Render key view images as textured quads behind the proxy surface. for kv, image in keyviews.items(): if isinfrustum(kv.position, currentcamera): renderquad(image, kv.position, kv.orientation, currentcamera) Number of Ray Slices: User-adjustable. Dataset-dependent. Anisotropic data may need more slices along one axis. Can range from 1 to memory limits. Compression: PNG (lossless) or JPEG 2000 (lossy). Proxy Surface: Initial proxy can be a bounding sphere or isosurface. Edge Case: Sparse pre-computed ray slices may cause interpolation artifacts when the camera moves significantly between key viewpoints. Pitfall: The quality of the interactive view depends on the density of the pre-computed ray slices. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Preprocessing scales with volume size, number of viewpoints, and slices. Interactive viewing is constant relative to volume size, dependent only on key views and proxy geometry. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scales with the number of pre-computed views and slices. Measured Performance: Tested on arbitrarily large datasets (e.g., terabyte-scale seismic data) on low-cost PC graphics hardware, achieving interactivity where direct ray casting fails. Strengths: Handles arbitrarily large datasets. Unrestricted viewpoints (unlike prior methods [22]). Allows arbitrary clipping surfaces to reveal interior structure without re-rendering. Independent of volume rendering system and dataset representation (works with irregular grids). Limitations: Requires significant preprocessing time and memory. Interactivity is limited to the pre-computed key views; significant camera movement may require interpolation or new key views. Not suitable for dynamic volumes (data changes over time) due to static preprocessing. Image-Based Volume Rendering with Opacity Light Fields was introduced by Miriah Meyer, Hanspeter Pfister, Charles Hansen, and Chris Johnson from the Scientific Computing and Imaging Institute at the University of Utah and Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs. The method was presented in a technical report (UUSCI-2005-002) in 2005. It addresses the limitations of earlier IBVR methods [4, 22] which either lacked opacity for internal views or restricted viewpoints to a limited cone. name: Key View Generation
head: Lumigraph Key View Generation
body: Key View Generation is a preprocessing step that synthesizes intermediate images (key views) from pre-computed ray slices and a geometric proxy surface. It calculates a key view for each ray slice viewpoint, where each key view represents a view of the volume bounded by the proxy surface from that specific viewpoint. Similar to lumigraph rendering, the proxy surface guides ray interpolation to generate these key views. Inputs: 1. A set of ray slices, where each slice corresponds to a specific original viewpoint. 2. A geometric proxy surface, treated as a renderable geometry. 3. Viewpoint parameters for the original viewpoints used to generate the ray slices. Outputs: A set of key views, one for each original viewpoint, stored in PNG RGBA image format. Data Structures: Ray Slices: 2D images representing the volume integration along rays from each viewpoint. Proxy Surface: A geometric surface used to bound the volume. Depth Buffer: A 2D array storing the distance from the viewpoint to the proxy surface for each pixel. Steps: 1. Proxy Rendering: For a specific original viewpoint, render the geometric proxy surface to the frame buffer. 2. Depth Query: Query the depth buffer to obtain the distance d from the viewpoint to the proxy surface for each pixel (u, v) in the key view. 3. Ray Slice Indexing: Use the depth values d to index into the ray slices, identifying the "front" and "back" ray slices that bracket the depth d. 4. Interpolation: For each pixel (u, v) in the key view: Retrieve the RGBA color values from S{front} and S{back} at the corresponding pixel coordinates. Perform linear interpolation between the two slices based on the relative depth d. Compute the final RGBA value: C{key} = w{front} \cdot C{front} + w{back} \cdot C{back} where C represents the RGBA vector, and the interpolation weights w{front} and w{back} are determined by the distance of d to the planes of S{front} and S{back}. 5. Output: Store the resulting key view as a PNG RGBA image. 6. Repeat: Repeat steps 1–5 for every original viewpoint to generate the complete set of key views. Single Ray Slice Technique: If only one ray slice is used per viewpoint, interpolation is skipped. 1. Render the proxy surface to the depth buffer. 2. For each pixel, if the depth equals the far plane distance, color the pixel black. 3. Otherwise, copy the pixel from the single ray slice. This technique removes scanning artifacts and hides surfaces external to the proxy surface. Parameters: Output Format: PNG RGBA. Interpolation Method: Linear interpolation is standard, though higher-order or nearest-neighbor interpolation could be used. Number of Ray Slices: Can be one or multiple per viewpoint, limited by memory restrictions. Pitfalls: Proxy Surface Accuracy: An inaccurate proxy surface extraction causes ghosting artifacts around the isosurface boundary. A better proxy surface allows fewer key views for smooth output images, while a coarse proxy surface requires more key views. Proxy Modification: If the proxy surface is modified (e.g., by clipping planes) to reveal interior structure, the key views must be recomputed using the new proxy geometry. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Limited by memory restrictions on the number of ray slices per viewpoint. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Interpolation errors depend on proxy surface choice and the number of key views. When to Use: Applications requiring specific viewing cones, such as surgical simulation (high accuracy), seismic data exploration (limited latitude/longitude range), or simulation data exploration (unlimited viewing freedom). When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Key View Generation is based on principles similar to lumigraph rendering, where a proxy surface guides ray interpolation to generate key views of the volume. The proxy surface is typically computed only once per volume, but can be modified to reveal interior structure. The number of key views and viewpoint locations are highly data, application, and system dependent. name: Volume Ray-Casting on Graphics Hardware
head: Stream model for volumetric ray-casting
body: This method implements direct volume ray casting on programmable graphics hardware (specifically DirectX 9-level architectures like the ATI 9700) using a multi-pass stream model. It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based volume rendering by exploiting the intrinsic parallelism of fragment processors and efficient inter-pass communication via texture render targets. Unlike single-pass rasterization, this approach iteratively accumulates optical properties across multiple rendering passes, enabling effective early ray termination and empty-space skipping through hardware-supported early z-tests. The method relies on a multi-pass rendering loop where the output of one pass serves as the input for the next. It utilizes specific hardware features available in Pixel Shader 2.0 APIs, including per-fragment texture fetches, texture render targets (allowing floating-point storage), texture coordinate generation, per-fragment arithmetic, and depth replace capabilities. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volumetric scalar data (stored in 3D textures), transfer function parameters, ray direction vectors (pre-computed and stored in 2D textures), and an opacity threshold for termination. Outputs: Final composited color and opacity images stored in 2D texture render targets. Data Structures: 1. Ray Direction Textures: Two 2D textures storing the (u, v) components of the ray direction in local texture space for each pixel. 2. Accumulation Textures: 2D texture render targets storing the accumulated color and accumulated opacity from previous passes. 3. Iso-surface Intersection Texture: A 2D texture used to store the local texture coordinates of iso-surface intersections, if applicable. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-computation: For each pixel in the image plane, compute the ray direction in local texture coordinates and store these direction vectors in two dedicated 2D textures. 2. Initialization: Initialize the accumulation textures with zero color and zero opacity. 3. Main Ray Casting Passes: Execute a fixed number of rendering passes. In each pass, bind the accumulated color and opacity textures as inputs and bind the ray direction textures. Execute a fragment shader that performs one step of ray traversal: calculate the current sample position using the ray origin, direction, and step size, sample the volume data at the current position, and apply the transfer function to obtain color and opacity. Update the accumulated color and opacity using the front-to-back compositing equations from the parent method, and write the updated values to the output accumulation texture. 4. Termination Check Pass: Between main passes, execute an additional pass to test whether the actual opacity value has exceeded a specified threshold or an iso-surface is hit. If the test succeeds, modify the z-value to the maximum value; otherwise, set it to zero. Use the "Depth Replace" feature to write this arbitrary z value directly to the z-buffer. 5. Early Z-Test Filtering: Configure the depth test to GREATER. Because fragments that triggered termination were set to maximum depth, and the test is GREATER, subsequent main passes will discard these fragments due to the early z-test. 6. Final Output: After all passes, the accumulation textures contain the final composited color and opacity, which can be rendered to the screen or saved. Formulas: The method builds on the parent's shared principles for compositing [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md]. In each main pass, the accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc} and opacity \alpha{acc} are updated per fragment as: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai where \mathbf{c}i and \alphai are the color and opacity sampled at the current ray step. Parameters: Opacity Threshold: The value at which ray termination is triggered. Number of Passes: Fixed number of main ray casting passes. Step Size: Determined by the volume resolution and view distance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dependent Texture Fetches: Hardware limitations restrict the number of dependent texture fetches on the ATI, so the method minimizes dynamic texture lookups within the shader. Floating Point Precision: Floating-point textures are available, allowing negative values to be stored. Depth Buffer Clearing: The depth buffer must be cleared appropriately before the termination check pass to ensure the GREATER test functions as intended. Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of pixels and the fixed number of passes, with early termination reducing the effective number of passes for opaque regions. Memory complexity scales with the volume data, ray direction textures, accumulation textures, and intermediate render targets required by the multi-pass nature. Measured performance on an ATI 9700 graphics card demonstrates up to a 3× speedup for typical renditions of volumetric datasets. Strengths include effective integration of early ray termination and empty-space skipping on hardware that supports early z-tests and depth replace, alongside exploitation of fragment processor parallelism. Limitations include reliance on specific hardware features (Pixel Shader 2.0, depth replace, texture render targets), limits on dependent texture fetches, and potential wasted computation from fixed passes if early termination is not properly managed. Use this method when targeting older programmable graphics hardware (DirectX 9 era) for real-time or interactive volume rendering; avoid it on modern hardware with advanced ray tracing capabilities or single-pass optimized ray marching techniques that do not require multi-pass accumulation. This method addresses the challenge of achieving real-time volume rendering for large scalar fields by leveraging the capabilities of programmable graphics hardware available at the time, specifically the ATI 9700 and the Pixel Shader 2.0 API. The approach builds on the observation that CPU-based rendering is insufficient for interactivity with large datasets and exploits the parallel nature of GPU fragment processors. Acceleration Techniques for GPU-based Volume Rendering, https://www.cs.cit.tum.de/fileadmin/w00cfj/cg/Research/Publications/2003/AccelerationTechniquesforGPU-basedVolumeRendering/vis03-rc.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Illumination Caching
head: Sundén and Ropinski implementation, TBRayMarcher Illumination Cache, TBRayMarcher Plugin
body: Illumination caching is a rendering technique that pre-computes and stores the lighting distribution inside a volume in an illumination cache, drastically improving rendering performance. It solves the problem of expensive per-pixel lighting calculations in participating media by exploiting the assumption that volume material scatters light isotropically, allowing the lighting distribution to be decoupled from the ray-marching step. Inputs and Outputs: Input consists of a scalar volume dataset V(\mathbf{p}) and a set of light sources (position, color, intensity). The output is an illumination cache volume containing pre-computed lighting values, and the final rendered image. Data Structures: The illumination cache is a 3D texture (volume texture) storing pre-computed lighting values. The cache does not necessarily need to have the same extents as the volume dataset itself. The implementation uses "true" volume textures rather than pseudo-volume textures. Steps: 1. Pre-computation: Compute the lighting distribution inside the volume based on the simplifying assumption that the volume material scatters light isotropically (equally in all directions). 2. Storage: Store the computed lighting distribution in the illumination cache. 3. Rendering: During ray marching, sample the illumination cache to retrieve the lighting value for each sample point, rather than computing it on-the-fly. Parameters: Cache extents do not necessarily need to match the volume dataset extents. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: When large datasets exceed texture size limits, they must be chunked. Chunking results in incorrect lighting at chunk borders because each chunk is lit separately as if others do not exist, making borders incorrectly bright. The maximum extents along each dimension for volume textures in DirectX 11 and DirectX 12 is 2048 voxels, requiring chunking for larger datasets. The implementation does not support DirectX 12 reserved resources, preventing the use of very large volume textures (up to 8 gigavoxels) that require fragmented VRAM management. It solves the problem of expensive per-pixel lighting calculations in participating media by interpolating illumination from these cached samples, thereby reducing computational load and providing smoother results. It differs from sibling methods like the Light Cache Rendering Pipeline by explicitly modeling the angular distribution of light via SH coefficients rather than storing scalar irradiance or simple light maps. The Light Cache Rendering Pipeline is a direct volume ray-casting technique that pre-computes lighting distributions inside a volume and stores them in an illumination cache, drastically improving rendering performance. Unlike standard ray-marching which recalculates illumination per frame, this method exploits the assumption of isotropic light scattering to separate volume density evaluation from lighting computation, allowing for fast updates when only light positions change. It sets itself apart from siblings like Radiance Caching by using aggregate queries on a 3D Summed Area Table (SAT) for speed, yielding results similar in quality to dense sampling but much faster. This method models indirect illumination in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by precomputing occlusion information and storing it in Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients within 3D volumes. It solves the difficulty of calculating occlusion in 3DGS, which uses differentiable forward mapping splatting rather than ray marching. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like the Light Cache Rendering Pipeline by explicitly baking geometric occlusion into SH coefficients to approximate indirect lighting, inspired by real-time rendering techniques such as Irradiance Volumes and Light Probes. A technique that pre-computes global illumination for each voxel using path tracing and stores it in a volume, which is then used during ray marching for real-time rendering. It involves computing the global illumination of each voxel with path tracing and storing the computed global illumination in a global illumination volume. Performance: Drastically improves rendering performance by avoiding per-pixel lighting calculations. Hardware: Evaluated on an NVIDIA RTX 3500 Ada GPU. Limitations: Chunking leads to incorrect lighting at chunk borders. Maximum texture dimension is 2048 voxels in DirectX 11/12. DirectX 12 reserved resources are not supported, limiting VRAM management for very large datasets. Vulkan is reported to not work at all with the TBRayMarcher implementation. Evaluated on a chunked Kolumbo dataset of 5.9 billion voxels, divided into nine sub-volumes of 512×935×1501 voxels. The technique is based on the assumption that volume material scatters light isotropically, allowing the lighting distribution inside the volume to be pre-computed and stored in an illumination cache. body:
Radiance caching pre-computes and stores directional radiance distributions at sparse points within a volume using spherical harmonics (SH) and gradient information. It reduces per-pixel lighting costs in participating media by interpolating illumination from these cached samples rather than computing it from scratch. Inputs: Sparse set of cache points \{xk\} within the volume, each storing SH coefficients \lambdal^m for the incoming radiance distribution and a translational gradient 
abla Lk. Outputs: Interpolated radiance L(x', \omegao) at an arbitrary query point x'. Data Structures: Cache Point: Spatial location xk with associated SH coefficients \lambdal^m and gradient 
abla Lk. SH Coefficients: Vector \lambdal^m representing the angular radiance distribution Li(	heta, \phi) at xk. Gradient: Translational derivative 
abla Lk used for log-space extrapolation. Weighting Function: w(xk, x') that diminishes to zero as the query point approaches the cache point's valid radius. Valid Radius: Scalar R defining the interpolation support region for each cache point. Steps: 1. Pre-computation: Ray-march through the volume to sample incoming radiance Li at sparse points. Project Li onto SH basis functions using Monte Carlo quadrature. 2. Gradient Computation: Compute translational gradients 
abla Lk for each cache point. For single scattering, Monte Carlo sample the first derivative in surface-area form by tracing rays in a sphere around xk to fixed hit points ys, tracking transmittance and geometry changes as xk translates. For multiple scattering, Monte Carlo sample the first derivative assuming sampled paths move rigidly, accounting for translational derivatives at each scattering vertex. 3. Query & Interpolation: For a query point x', find the set of nearby cache points C whose valid radii contain x'. Compute the log-space translational gradient 
abla \ln Lk = 
abla Lk / Lk. Interpolate radiance using log-space extrapolation. 4. Adaptive Sampling: If no nearby cache points are found, compute radiance via Monte Carlo sampling, insert the value and gradient into the cache, and update the valid radius using the error metric. Formulas: The radiance distribution Li(	heta, \phi) at a cache point is represented as: Li(	heta, \phi) = \sum{l=0}^{n-1} \sum{m=-l}^{l} \lambdal^m Y{lm}(	heta, \phi) where n is the order of the SH representation, Y{lm} are the spherical harmonic basis functions, and \lambdal^m are the coefficients. The coefficients are computed via Monte Carlo quadrature with uniform sampling: \lambdal^m =  rac{4\pi}{N} \sum{j=1}^{N} Li(	hetaj, \phij) Y{lm}(	hetaj, \phij) where N is the total number of samples, and (	hetaj, \phij) are the sampled directions. The radiance at a query point x' is interpolated using log-space extrapolation: L(x', \omegao) \approx \exp\left(  rac{\sum{k \in C} (\ln Lk + 
abla \ln Lk \cdot \Delta x') w(xk, x')}{\sum{k \in C} w(xk, x')} ight) where \Delta x' = x' - xk, 
abla \ln Lk = 
abla Lk / Lk, and w(xk, x') is the weighting function. The valid radius R is calculated using an error metric: R = \epsilon  rac{\sum Lj}{\sum \|
abla Lj\|} where \epsilon is a global error tolerance parameter, and Lj and 
abla Lj are individual Monte Carlo samples of radiance and translational gradient respectively. Parameters: SH Order (n): 2nd order is used to map the four coefficients to standard four-component graphics hardware buffers. Sample Count (N): Number of random directions for Monte Carlo integration; computed via stratified sampling. Error Tolerance (\epsilon): Global parameter controlling the valid radius calculation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion Mismatch: Sparse cache points may experience different occlusion than query points, causing illumination errors since visibility is not considered during interpolation. Ad-hoc Error Metric: The radius metric R is an approximation of log-scale interpolation error, which can lead to difficulty predicting sample distribution error and suboptimal cache placement. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def interpolateradiance(querypoint, cachepoints, epsilon): nearby = [] for point in cachepoints: # Calculate valid radius R from Monte Carlo samples sumL = sum(sample.L for sample in point.mcsamples) sumgradnorm = sum(norm(sample.gradL) for sample in point.mcsamples) R = epsilon (sumL / sumgradnorm) # Check if query point falls within valid radius if distance(querypoint, point.position) <= R: nearby.append(point) if not nearby: # No cache points found; trigger Monte Carlo sampling and cache insertion return None numerator = 0.0 denominator = 0.0 for point in nearby: deltax = querypoint - point.position logL = log(point.L) loggrad = point.gradL / point.L weight = weightingfunction(point.position, querypoint, R) numerator += (logL + dot(loggrad, deltax)) weight denominator += weight interpolatedL = exp(numerator / denominator) return interpolatedL Second-Order Occlusion-Aware Volumetric Radiance Caching is a radiance caching algorithm for participating media that uses second-order gradient analysis (Hessian) of light transport to adaptively sample and interpolate radiance from sparse cache points, accounting for occlusion changes. It solves the problem of suboptimal cache distribution in scenes with complex shadows by deriving a Hessian-based error metric that predicts extrapolation error more accurately than first-order gradient methods. Unlike its parent Radiance Caching (Jarosz et al.), which relies on spherical harmonics and first-order gradients, this method uses a proxy triangulation-based representation to compute occlusion-aware derivatives, preventing the concentration of cache points near reflecting geometry and enabling efficient capture of high-frequency shadow boundaries. This variant explicitly computes the incoming radiance distribution for each voxel by ray-marching through the volume and storing the result as spherical harmonic coefficients. It differs from the general Jarosz method by defining a voxel-based grid for caching rather than arbitrary sparse points. It is chosen when a structured voxel representation is already available or when integrating with deferred rendering pipelines that update voxels based on visible surface reprojection. The implementation uses 2nd-order SH (4 coefficients) to fit into standard 4-component framebuffers. Coefficients are computed using Monte Carlo quadrature with stratified sampling of N random directions per voxel. Time Complexity: Pre-computation is expensive due to ray-marching and gradient computation per cache point. Query time is fast, dominated by interpolation and SH evaluation. Memory Complexity: Scales linearly with the number of cache points times the number of SH coefficients per point. Measured Performance: Related implementations show ray-marching times for GI per bounce around 4.3–4.6 ms on a NVIDIA GTX460 for scenes with 10k–260k triangles, while AO is faster due to limited ray distance. Strengths: Reduces per-pixel lighting cost and provides smoother results than unfiltered sampling. Limitations: Sparse sampling causes visibility errors if occlusion is not considered during interpolation. The ad-hoc error metric can lead to suboptimal cache distribution. When to use: Suitable for scenes with smooth lighting variations where pre-computation cost is acceptable. When not to use: Scenes with complex, dynamic occlusion or high-frequency lighting details where the sparse cache cannot accurately represent the radiance field. Radiance caching was introduced by Jarosz et al.. It is part of the broader field of illumination caching for volume rendering. The method was later improved by Marco et al., who introduced a second-order Hessian error metric to determine interpolation acceptability and consider visibility, resulting in higher quality than the original Jarosz method. It solves the problem of suboptimal cache distribution in scenes with complex shadows by deriving a Hessian-based error metric that predicts extrapolation error more accurately than first-order gradient methods. Unlike its parent Radiance Caching (Jarosz et al.), which relies on spherical harmonics and first-order gradients, this method uses a proxy triangulation-based representation to compute occlusion-aware derivatives, preventing the concentration of cache points near reflecting geometry and enabling efficient capture of high-frequency shadow boundaries. Inputs: Scene geometry and participating media properties (scattering coefficient \mus, phase function fs, absorption coefficient \mua, extinction coefficient \mut). Camera ray and ray-marching step size (default 0.1 in 3D). Error tolerance \varepsilon. Samples per pixel (default 16 in 3D). Outputs: Radiance L(\mathbf{x}', \omegao) at shaded points \mathbf{x}' in the medium. Cache data structures (octrees) containing radiance, gradients, and Hessians at cache points. The method maintains two separate octrees for efficient cache query: one for single scattering and one for multiple scattering. Each cache point \mathbf{x}k stores: Position \mathbf{x}k. Radiance L(\mathbf{x}k). Gradient 
abla L(\mathbf{x}k). Hessian HL(\mathbf{x}k). Valid region radii Rk (derived from the Hessian eigenvalues). 1. Proxy Triangulation Construction: For a cache point \mathbf{x}, compute the incoming light field using a proxy triangulation-based representation of the radiance reflected by the surrounding medium and geometry. Stratified sampling: Compute radiance and derivatives at \mathbf{x} by stratified sampling uniformly in the sphere (or circle in 2D) with equal solid angle strata. Subdivision: Build the subdivision using angular samples by connecting samples from adjacent strata. Ray Marching: Perform subdivision within the medium by uniformly ray-marching the medium at discrete distances around \mathbf{x}, joining adjacent angular samples within each marching step. Assumptions: For a sufficiently fine subdivision, assume angle \gamma 	o 0, so the direction \omegai is constant for the segment \ell: f(\mathbf{x}, \omegai, \omegao) = f(\mathbf{x}, \omega{\ell}, \omegao), where \omega{\ell} is a fixed direction from \mathbf{x} to a point in segment \ell. Assume constant transmittance and radiance for all \mathbf{y} \in \ell: Tr(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = Tr(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}{\ell}) and L(\mathbf{y}, \omegai) = L(\mathbf{y}{\ell}, \omegai), choosing \mathbf{y}{\ell} as the furthest point in segment \ell. 2. Error Metric and Cache Point Placement: Use a second-order Hessian-based error metric to determine when interpolation is appropriate and to control error during reconstruction. The valid region for a cache point \mathbf{x} is defined by an ellipsoid (3D) or ellipse (2D) with principal radii derived from the eigenvalues \lambdai of HL(\mathbf{x}): R^{2D}i = \sqrt[4]{ rac{4 L(\mathbf{x}) \varepsilon}{\pi |\lambdai|}} R^{3D}i = \sqrt[5]{ rac{15 L(\mathbf{x}) \varepsilon}{4 \pi |\lambdai|}} Prepopulate the cache by uniformly sampling a ray from the camera and ray-marching along the media. Place a cache point if the point does not fulfill the error metric (i.e., if it lies outside the valid regions of existing cache points). 4. Rendering and Interpolation: At render time, evaluate radiance at ray-marched points \mathbf{x}' in the medium by extrapolating from surrounding valid cache points. Let C be the set of cache points whose radii include \mathbf{x}'. Interpolate in linear space using a cubic kernel w(\mathbf{x}k, \mathbf{x}') = 3d^2 - 2d^3 with d = 1 -  rac{\|\mathbf{x}' - \mathbf{x}k\|}{Rk}: L(\mathbf{x}') \approx  rac{\sum{k \in C} [L(\mathbf{x}k) +

If no valid cache points are found for \mathbf{x}', compute its radiance and derivatives (Steps 1-2) and add it to the cache. Unverified code. Assumes Lambertian surfaces and isotropic, homogeneous media. """ fval = mediaprops.scatteringcoeff mediaprops.phasefunction(segment.direction) Trval = geometry.transmittance(x, segment.furthestpoint) Lval = geometry.radianceat(segment.furthestpoint) Fl = geometry.integrategeometryterm(x, segment) gradFl = geometry.gradientgeometryterm(x, segment) hessFl = geometry.hessiangeometryterm(x, segment) gradTr = geometry.gradienttransmittance(x, segment.furthestpoint) hessTr = geometry.hessiantransmittance(x, segment.furthestpoint) Lj = Lval fval Trval Fl gradLj = Lval fval (Trval gradFl + gradTr Fl) hessLj = Lval fval ( Trval hessFl + outerproduct(gradTr, gradFl) + outerproduct(gradFl, gradTr) + hessTr Fl) return Lj, gradLj, hessLj def computecachepointderivatives(x, mediaprops, geometry, numangularsamples=64, numraysteps=16): """ Computes L, gradL, hessL at point x using stratified sampling and proxy triangulation. """ totalL = 0.0 totalgradL = Vec3(0, 0, 0) totalhessL = Mat3([[0,0,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,0]]) strata = stratifiedsamplesphere(numangularsamples, numraysteps) for stratum in strata: segment = buildsegment(stratum, x) Lj, gradLj, hessLj = computesegmentradiancederivatives(x, segment, mediaprops, geometry) totalL += Lj totalgradL = totalgradL + gradLj totalhessL = totalhessL + hessLj return totalL, totalgradL, totalhessL def getvalidradius(L, hessL, epsilon, dim=3): """ Computes the principal radii of the valid region ellipsoid. Returns the minimum radius (most restrictive) for isotropic caching. """ eigenvalues = hessL.eigenvalues() # Standard eigenvalue decomposition minabseigenvalue = min(abs(e) for e in eigenvalues) if minabseigenvalue == 0: return float('inf') if dim == 3: R = math.pow((15 L epsilon) / (4 math.pi minabseigenvalue), 1/5) else: R = math.pow((4 L epsilon) / (math.pi minabseigenvalue), 1/4) return R def rendervolumetricradiancecaching(cameraray, cachesingle, cachemulti, epsilon, stepsize): """ Renders a single ray using the radiance cache. """ validpoints = octree.queryradius(x, epsilon) if not validpoints: return None numerator = 0.0 denominator = 0.0 for point in validpoints: dist = (x - point.position).norm() d = 1.0 - dist / point.radius if d < 0: continue w = 3 d d - 2 d d d Lpred = point.L + point.gradL.dot(x - point.position) numerator += Lpred w denominator += w if denominator == 0: return None return numerator / denominator \varepsilon: Tolerance value controlling error in radiance caching. Typical value: 1.5 	imes 10^{-4} for the Patio scene. Ray marching step size: Uniform step size of 0.1 used in 3D results unless stated otherwise. Samples per pixel: 16 samples per pixel used in 3D results unless stated otherwise. Angular samples: The accuracy of the subdivision relies on dense sampling of the angular domain. Specific numbers vary, but 256 angular samples were used for reference gradient computation in 2D validation. Occlusion Ignorance: Ignoring visibility derivatives leads to poor cache distribution and imprecise extrapolation during reconstruction, failing to represent high-frequency shadows and rapid radiance changes. Occlusion-unaware methods fail to estimate gradients in complex shadows and tend to concentrate cache points near reflecting geometry, requiring radius-clamping heuristics to mitigate oversampling. Penumbra Regions: Occlusion-unaware gradients ignore light effects in penumbra regions, causing extrapolation failures and visible artifacts on shadow patterns. Sampling Rate Limits: The sampling rate limits the amount of radiance changes that can be recovered, especially for fine details like small light sources not computed using Next Event Estimation (NEE). Multiple Scattering Variance: Multiple scattering is limited to the second bounce to reduce excessive variance when computing reference derivatives with finite differences. Isotropic Cost: Using isotropic points with the smallest principal axis of the Hessian is the most costly scenario compared to previous work because it requires more points. Defines the valid spatial region around a radiance cache point where linear interpolation remains within a user-specified relative error tolerance \epsilon. It computes the geometry of this region—specifically a hyperellipsoid in k dimensions—by analyzing the second-order derivatives (Hessian) of the radiance field. Unlike first-order methods that assume constant radiance or linear gradients, this approach accounts for curvature, allowing for larger cache radii in smooth regions and tighter bounds in high-frequency areas. It builds on Second-Order Occlusion-Aware Volumetric Radiance Caching by providing the specific mathematical formulation for the cache validity bounds. Time: The method reduces computation time by up to 30% compared to previous work (Jarosz et al. [2008]) while providing improved results. In the 'Statues' scene, it took 154 minutes with ~19k cache points, compared to 155 minutes for Jarosz et al. [2008] with similar point counts. In the Patio scene, anisotropic points reduced total computation time by 30% compared to isotropic points at the same error tolerance. Memory: Memory usage is proportional to the number of cache points. The occlusion-aware method requires significantly fewer points than occlusion-unaware methods for comparable results (e.g., 3k vs 35k in the Strips scene). Statues Scene: ~19k cache points, 16k samples/cache, 154 minutes. Patio Scene: Anisotropic cache: 21k points, 81 min cache generation, 94 min total. Isotropic cache: 32k points, 122 min cache generation, 135 min total. Jarosz et al. [2008]: 36k points, 124 min cache generation, 136 min total. Strips Scene: Occlusion-unaware required 35k points; occlusion-aware required 3k points. 2D Overlapping Shadows: Anisotropic technique reduced cache size by 32% (~13k points) compared to isotropic points at the same error threshold. 2D Square Light: Anisotropic cache reduced the number of cache points by up to 20% compared to isotropic cache at the same error threshold. Strengths: Correctly captures complex radiance changes and high-frequency shadows by placing more points near shadow boundaries. Does not rely on radius-clamping heuristics. Interpolates in linear space, where the Hessian-based metric more accurately predicts error. Limitations: Isotropic caching is costly. Sampling rate limits recovery of fine details from small light sources. Multiple scattering is limited to two bounces to control variance. Use for scenes with complex occlusions, shadows, and penumbra regions in participating media. Use when high-frequency shadow details are critical and first-order gradient methods fail. Use when computational efficiency is important and anisotropic caching can be employed. Avoid if the scene has very small light sources that are not handled by NEE, as sampling rate limits may cause artifacts. Avoid if multiple scattering beyond two bounces is required without significant variance reduction techniques. Second-Order Occlusion-Aware Volumetric Radiance Caching was introduced by Julio Marco, Adrian Jarabo, Wojciech Jarosz, and Diego Gutierrez in 2018 in the paper 'Second-Order Occlusion-Aware Volumetric Radiance Caching' published in ACM Trans. Graph. 37, 2. The method is based on previous work by Jarosz et al. [2008], which this work extends with occlusion-aware second-order derivatives. Previous methods ignored occlusion/visibility changes or relied only on first-order derivatives, leading to suboptimal cache distributions in scenes with occluders. This method derives a 2D theory of light transport in participating media to validate the approach before generalizing to 3D. The method is used in ACM Transactions on Graphics, Vol. 37, No. 2, Article 20, February 2018. It computes the geometry of this region—specifically a hyperellipsoid in k dimensions—by analyzing the second-order derivatives (Hessian) of the radiance field.
