name: CornerIntegrator
body: The CornerIntegrator is a specialized volumetric integrator for Tomographic Volumetric Additive Manufacturing (TVAM) that filters out rays intersecting the corners of the target build volume. It solves the problem of discretization artifacts caused by the discrete nature of Digital Micromirror Device (DMD) pixels near the boundaries of the target shape. Unlike the Radon Integrator, which projects the entire volume, the CornerIntegrator actively masks out hits near object corners based on a distance threshold to ensure surface-aware discretization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin and direction, the scene geometry (specifically the target mesh), and configuration parameters dist and radius. Output: A scalar value (1.0 if the ray is active, 0.0 if masked). Data Structures: The integrator relies on the standard Mitsuba 3 intersection record (si) and differentiable routines (dr). si.p: The intersection point coordinates. si.isvalid(): Boolean indicating if the ray hit the geometry. self.dist: A float representing the distance threshold. self.radius: A float defining the corner detection radius. Exact field sizes and bit packing are not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Suspend gradients. 2. Prepare sampler and sample initial ray. 3. Intersect ray with scene: si = scene.rayintersect(ray). 4. Set active flag: active = si.isvalid(). 5. Detect corner hits: hitcorner = dr.norm(dr.abs(si.p.xy) - self.dist) < self.radius. 6. Mask out corner hits: active &= ~hitcorner. 7. Call sample() with ADMode.Primal, multiply result by weight, and scatter reduce into output image tensor using Add operation. 8. Return selected value: return dr.select(active, 1., 0.). Formulas: \text{hit\corner} = \| |si.p.xy| - \text{self.dist} \| < \text{self.radius} where si.p.xy are the intersection point's xy coordinates, \text{self.dist} is the distance threshold, and \text{self.radius} is the detection radius. Parameters: dist (float): Distance threshold for corner detection. radius (float, default 0.1): Radius for corner detection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Corner hits near object boundaries are masked out to prevent artifacts. Small deviations in si.p.xy due to intersection precision may cause inconsistent masking. If self.radius is too large, valid rays near the edge may be incorrectly masked, leading to under-exposure. If the target shape has no corners or is perfectly rectangular with aligned boundaries, the corner detection logic may behave unexpectedly depending on the value of self.dist. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import drjit as dr import mitsuba as mi class CornerIntegrator: def init(self, dist, radius=0.1): self.dist = dist self.radius = radius def sample(self, scene, ray): si = scene.rayintersect(ray) active = si.isvalid() hitcorner = dr.norm(dr.abs(si.p.xy) - self.dist) < self.radius active &= ~hitcorner return dr.select(active, 1.0, 0.0) def render(self, scene, sensor, sampler): dr.suspendgrad() # Prepare sampler and sample initial ray for y in range(sensor.height()): for x in range(sensor.width()): for s in range(sampler.spp()): ray = sampler.sample2d(x, y, s) # Call sample() with ADMode.Primal with dr.enablegrad(dr.ADMode.Primal): val = self.sample(scene, ray) # Multiply result by weight and scatter reduce using Add sensor.add(x, y, val) dr.flushmalloccache() dr.syncthread() Time Complexity: O(1) per ray intersection, as the corner check involves a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray. Strengths: Effectively removes discretization artifacts at the boundaries of the build volume in TVAM. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of radius and dist. May reduce the effective build volume if the corner region is too large. When to use: Use when surface-aware discretization is required for TVAM optimization to avoid boundary artifacts. When not to use: Do not use for final visualization if the goal is to show the full projected volume without boundary masking. The CornerIntegrator is part of the Dr. TVAM framework, an inverse rendering system for Tomographic Volumetric Additive Manufacturing. It was developed to address the specific challenges of projecting volumetric data onto a build volume using DMDs, where the discrete pixel grid can cause artifacts at the boundaries of the target shape. The method is described in the Dr. TVAM repository. Dr. TVAM – Inverse Rendering for Tomographic Volumetric Additive Manufacturing, https://github.com/rgl-epfl/drtvam, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Radon Integrator
body:
The Radon Integrator computes the Radon transform (projection) of a volume by tracing rays through a purely absorptive medium and accumulating attenuation along the path. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry (target mesh, vial, projector, sensor), volume density/absorption coefficients (via medium interaction), configuration parameters (spp, maxdepth, transmissiononly). Output: A tensor representing the projected attenuation (Radon transform) accumulated per pixel. Data Structures: active: Boolean flag indicating if the ray is still valid and within bounds. insidetarget: Boolean flag tracking if the ray is currently inside the target geometry. activemedium: Boolean flag tracking if the ray is currently inside a medium that contributes to absorption. throughput: Scalar float, initial value 1.0, accumulates the product of BSDF weights. L: Scalar float, initial value 0.0, accumulates the total contribution. t: Scalar float, initial value 0.0, accumulates distance traveled within the medium. d: Integer, current ray depth. Numbered Steps: 1. Render Initialization: In the main render loop, suspend automatic differentiation gradients. Prepare the sampler and generate the initial ray. Call the sample() function with ADMode.Primal to ensure primal values are computed without gradient tracking during the path traversal. 2. Weighting and Accumulation: Multiply the result returned by sample() by the ray weight. Scatter-reduce this value into the output image tensor using an additive operation (Add). 3. Sample Initialization: Inside sample(), initialize activemedium = False, insidetarget = False, throughput = 1.0, L = 0.0, t = 0.0, and d = 0. 4. Medium Retrieval: Get the scattering coefficient \sigmas and extinction coefficient \sigmat from the current medium context. The method assumes a purely absorptive medium, implying \sigmas is ignored in the final contribution formula. 5. Ray Tracing Loop: Loop while active is true: a. Intersect the ray with the scene geometry. b. Update active &= si.isvalid(), where si is the scene intersection. c. Contribution Calculation: Compute the contribution for the current segment: 	ext{contrib} = 	ext{throughput} 	imes \exp(-\sigmat 	imes t) 	imes (1 - \exp(-\sigmat 	imes 	ext{si}.t)) This formula assumes the medium is purely absorptive, where 	ext{si}.t is the distance to the next intersection. d. Accumulation: If hittarget and activemedium are true, add contrib to L. Update t += si.t. e. State Update (Inside Target): Update insidetarget state using the XOR-like logic: 	ext{inside	arget} = (
eg 	ext{inside	arget} \land 	ext{hit	arget}) \lor (	ext{inside	arget} \land 
eg 	ext{hit	arget}) This logic may cause some rays to leak out of the target volume if intersection validity is ambiguous. f. BSDF Sampling: Sample the BSDF at the intersection. If transmissiononly is true, set the context type mask to Transmission. Else, if depth == 0 and active, force refraction sampling to avoid generating useless rays that do not penetrate the volume. g. Throughput and Depth: Update throughput = bsw (BSDF weight). Spawn a new ray. Increment d for non-target hits. Update active &= (d < maxdepth). h. Medium Transition: Update activemedium state: 	ext{active\medium} = (	ext{active\medium} \land 
eg 	ext{si.is\medium	ransition}()) \lor (	ext{si.is\medium	ransition}() \land (	ext{si.target\medium}(	ext{ray}.d) 
eq 	ext{None})) This checks if the ray is transitioning between media and if the new target medium is valid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def radonintegratorrender(scene, sampler, config): spp = config.get('spp', 4) maxdepth = config.get('maxdepth', 10) transmissiononly = config.get('transmissiononly', False) outputtensor = np.zeros(scene.sensorshape) for in range(spp): ray = sampler.nextray() L = sampleradon(ray, scene, maxdepth, transmissiononly) weight = 1.0 outputtensor[ray.index] += L weight return outputtensor def sampleradon(ray, scene, maxdepth, transmissiononly): active = True insidetarget = False activemedium = False throughput = 1.0 L = 0.0 t = 0.0 d = 0 while active: si = scene.intersect(ray) active = active and si.isvalid() if not active: break sigmas, sigmat = scene.getmediumcoefficients(si) hittarget = si.istargethit() if hittarget and activemedium: contrib = throughput math.exp(-sigmat t) (1.0 - math.exp(-sigmat si.t)) L += contrib t += si.t insidetarget = (not insidetarget and hittarget) or (insidetarget and not hittarget) if transmissiononly: ctxtypemask = 'Transmission' else: if d == 0 and active: ctxtypemask = 'Refraction' else: ctxtypemask = 'All' bsw = scene.samplebsdf(si, ctxtypemask) throughput = bsw ray = scene.spawnnewray(ray, si, bsw) if not hittarget: d += 1 active = active and (d < maxdepth) istransition = si.ismediumtransition() newmedium = si.targetmedium(ray.d) activemedium = (activemedium and not istransition) or (istransition and newmedium is not None) return L Parameters: spp: Samples per pixel. Typical value: 4. maxdepth: Maximum ray depth. Not given in the sources. transmissiononly: Boolean flag to restrict sampling to transmission. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The insidetarget state update logic may cause rays to leak out of the target volume if intersection validity is ambiguous. An optimization technique that stores input and output data in half precision (16 bits) while performing computations in single precision (32 bits). Radon transforms are memory bound operations where arithmetic takes negligible time, making cache hit rates critical for performance. The method stores inputs in CUDA Textures, which are read-only data structures with opaque memory layouts optimized for texture fetching, improving cache hit rates for line integrals. This implementation achieves up to 125× faster execution than the Astra Toolbox. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples (spp) and ray depth, as each ray traverses the scene geometry and medium. Memory Complexity: Constant per ray, storing state variables (active, throughput, L, t, d). Strengths: Efficient for computing pure absorption projections (Radon transform) without complex scattering calculations. Limitations: Assumes purely absorptive medium; may suffer from ray leakage due to insidetarget logic. When to use: When the goal is to compute the tomographic projection (absorbed dose) for TVAM optimization. When not to use: When scattering or emission is significant, or when corner-based boundary handling is required. The Radon Integrator is part of the Dr. TVAM project, an inverse rendering framework for Tomographic Volumetric Additive Manufacturing. name: HoloVAM
head: Holographic tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing
body: HoloVAM is a volumetric additive manufacturing technique that uses holographic phase modulation to project light patterns into a photocurable resin, improving light efficiency and allowing 3D digital control of the light beam (e.g., depth of focus, scattering mitigation) compared to amplitude-based TVAM. It builds on TVAM Integrator by replacing standard amplitude modulation with phase-encoded computer-generated holograms (CGH) displayed on a spatial light modulator (SLM/DMD) in a Fourier configuration. Unlike amplitude-based TVAM variants, HoloVAM encodes both the projection pattern and the point spread function (PSF) into the phase, enabling higher light efficiency and extended depth of focus. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Target 3D shape (voxel grid or mesh); optical parameters (wavelength \lambda, DMD resolution, lens focal length); material properties (polymerization dose threshold). Output: A sequence of hologram frames displayed on the DMD, synchronized with the rotation of the resin vial. Data Structures: Tomographic Projections: A set of 2D intensity images I\theta(x,y) for each projection angle \theta, computed via reverse tomography (e.g., Filtered Back Projection, FBP). Hologram Frame: A 2D array of phase values \phi(x,y) mapped to the DMD pixel grid. The DMD is a binary spatial light modulator; phase is encoded using Lee holograms (carrier frequency modulation). HoloTile Structure: Each frame consists of a tiled arrangement of smaller holograms. The structure superimposes: 1. A smaller hologram of the desired projection pattern, spatially tiled on the full area of the SLM. 2. A second hologram (PSF hologram) that defines the shape of each reconstructed pixel in the image plane. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Tomographic Projections: Generate 2D projection patterns for the target 3D shape using reverse tomography (e.g., FBP). 2. Apply Positive Constraint: Ensure intensity patterns are non-negative, as physical light intensity cannot be negative. 3. Generate Computer-Generated Holograms (CGH): For each projection angle, generate a CGH using iterative algorithms (e.g., Gerchberg–Saxton) to encode the phase pattern on the DMD. The DMD is used as a phase modulator via Lee holograms. 4. Apply HoloTile Tiling (Speckle Mitigation): To mitigate speckle noise inherent in holographic projection, apply the HoloTile method: Superimpose the first smaller hologram of the desired projection pattern, spatially tiled on the full area of the SLM. Superimpose the second hologram (PSF hologram) that defines the shape of each reconstructed pixel in the image plane. Use time-multiplexing and spatial tiling to further mitigate speckle noise. 5. Optical Configuration Setup: Collimate and expand a single spatial-mode laser (405 nm) to fit the active area of the DMD. Arrange the DMD in a Fourier configuration. Use a Fourier lens to reconstruct the hologram at its Fourier plane, which is located within the rotatory photoresin container. 6. Synchronize and Irradiate: Display holograms synchronously with the rotation of the resin vial. Irradiate the resin volume from multiple angles until the polymerization dose threshold is reached. Formulas: Light Efficiency of a Pattern: \eta{patt} = \frac{\sum{g=0}^{g{max}} ng g}{N{pixels} g{max}} \eta{DMD} Where: ng is the number of pixels with gray level g. g{max} is the maximum gray level (255 for 8-bit images). N{pixels} is the total number of pixels. \eta{DMD} is the pixel reflectivity (65% at 405 nm). Parameters: Wavelength: 405 nm. Light Source: Single continuous-wave laser diode. Power: 40 mW (coupled with 33% efficiency in a single mode fiber). Modulator: Digital Micromirror Device (DMD) used as a phase modulator via Lee holograms. Resolution: Negative features (holes) of 31.35 μm. Printing Time: < 60 seconds. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Speckle Noise: Inherent in holographic projection due to CGH design, pixelated structure, spurious unmodulated reflection, and optical aberrations. Mitigated using HoloTile (spatial/temporal tiling) and PSF shaping. Blurring Artifacts: In conventional TVAM, blurring occurs if the vial’s diameter is much larger than the depth of focus of the imaging system. HoloVAM mitigates this by using phase modulation to modify the Point Spread Function (PSF), e.g., using an Axicon phase for Bessel beams (increased depth of focus) or Fresnel lens phases for multi-plane projections. Power Efficiency: Single-mode lasers have less optical power than multimode lasers, making light engine efficiency critical to keep printing times short (~60 s). Time Complexity: Printing time is dominated by the rotation speed and the number of projection angles required for tomographic reconstruction. Conventional TVAM typically requires tens of seconds for cm-scale prints. HoloVAM achieves < 60 seconds for millimeter-scale objects using a 40 mW single-mode laser. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Achieved negative features (holes) of 31.35 μm reliably. Light efficiency improved by 28.6X for the Benchy boat projection compared to amplitude TVAM. Scaling: The technique is limited by the space-bandwidth product of the light source, which determines the depth of focus. Larger vials require extended depth of focus (e.g., via Axicon phases) to avoid blurring. Strengths: High light efficiency (all pixels contribute via interference); 3D digital control of the light beam (depth of focus, scattering mitigation); layer-less fabrication. Limitations: Speckle noise requires mitigation (HoloTile); requires precise synchronization between DMD and rotation stage; limited to materials compatible with 405 nm wavelength. When to use: When high light efficiency is critical (e.g., with low-power single-mode lasers); when printing in scattering materials (e.g., cell-laden hydrogels); when extended depth of focus is needed. When not to use: Not given in the sources. HoloVAM was proposed in a 2025 paper published in Nature Communications by researchers from the Laboratory of Applied Photonics Devices at EPFL and SDU Centre for Photonics. It extends the concept of Tomographic Volumetric Additive Manufacturing (TVAM) by harnessing the phase properties of light, addressing the low light efficiency and limited depth of focus of conventional amplitude-based TVAM. The technique uses Lee holograms to encode phase on a DMD, a method previously used in two-photon lithography to control multiple foci. HoloVAM has been demonstrated for printing in acrylates and scattering materials like soft cell-laden hydrogels (GelMA) with a concentration of 0.5 million cells per mL. Holographic tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-56852-4, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Antagonistic Dual-Wavelength TVAM
head: Antagonistic TVAM
body: Antagonistic Dual-Wavelength TVAM is a volumetric additive manufacturing integrator that suppresses tomographic background dose by combining a patterned activation field (405 nm) with a separately optimized inhibition field (365 nm). It extends the standard TVAM Integrator by adding a second wavelength channel, allowing the definition of complete 3D geometries through inhibition and mitigating diffusion- and attenuation-driven loss of spatial fidelity. The method operates in two distinct phases: generating fixed activation patterns and optimizing inhibition patterns. It builds on the Dr.TVAM framework. Inputs: Target geometry (mesh file). Vial geometry configuration. Projector and sensor configurations. Activation configuration file (defining 405 nm parameters). Inhibition configuration file (defining 365 nm parameters). Pre-computed 405 nm activation patterns (.npz file). Scaling factor \alpha for the activation field. Outputs: Optimized 365 nm inhibition patterns. Effective dose field D{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{r}). The implementation uses sparse matrices for diffusion operators and numpy arrays for fields and patterns. Laplacian Matrix (nofluxlaplacian): Type: Sparse CSR matrix. Shape: (N, N), where N is the number of voxels where the vial mask is true. Construction: Indices are mapped from 2D coordinates to 1D indices where vial is true. Entries are 1.0 for neighbors and -degree for the center. Values are divided by pixelsizemm2. Fields: D{405}(\mathbf{r}): Reconstructed activation field at 405 nm. D{365}(\mathbf{r}): Reconstructed inhibition field at 365 nm. D{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{r}): Effective dose field. 1. Load Scene Configuration: Parse configuration files for target, vial, projector, and sensor. Validate required fields. Load target mesh and compute bounding box. Apply scaling and centering transforms based on configuration. Construct sensor transform. 2. Generate Activation Patterns (Fixed): Use the Dr.TVAM framework to generate fixed 405 nm activation patterns. Command: drtvam examples/backgroundsuppression/activationconfig.json --backend cuda -D output=output/backgroundsuppression/activation Save patterns to output/backgroundsuppression/activation/patterns.npz. 3. Optimize Inhibition Patterns: Load the fixed activation patterns. Hold the reconstructed activation field D{405} constant. Run the antagonistic optimizer to find non-negative 365 nm projection values that minimize the error between the effective dose and the target, while suppressing background. Command: python antagonistictvam/optimizeantagonistic.py --activation-config... --inhibition-config... --activation-patterns... --activation-scale 1.00 --backend cuda --output... The effective dose field is calculated as: D{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{r}) = \max \left[\alpha D{405}(\mathbf{r}) - D{365}(\mathbf{r}),\,0\right] Where: D{\mathrm{eff}}(\mathbf{r}) is the effective dose field at position \mathbf{r}. D{405}(\mathbf{r}) is the reconstructed activation field at 405 nm. D{365}(\mathbf{r}) is the reconstructed inhibition field at 365 nm. \alpha is a scaling factor for the activation field in the numerical objective. \alpha: Scaling factor for the activation field. Typical value: 1.00. The core simulation updates active inhibitor and response fields over temporal substeps. The loop applies: 1. Half-step diffusion. 2. Inhibitor generation. 3. Another half-step diffusion. 4. Activation increments: consume inhibitor and accumulate response. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.sparse import csrmatrix def nofluxlaplacian(vialmask, pixelsizemm): """ Construct a sparse CSR matrix representing the discrete Laplacian operator on a boolean vial mask. Args: vialmask: 2D boolean array indicating valid voxels. pixelsizemm: Float, pixel size in mm. Returns: Sparse CSR matrix of shape (N, N) where N is the number of True values in vialmask. """ # Get indices where vial is true coords = np.argwhere(vialmask) nvoxels = len(coords) # Map 2D coordinates to 1D indices # Assuming a simple linear mapping for demonstration; actual implementation # may use a more complex indexing scheme depending on the grid structure. # Here we assume a 2D grid for simplicity as per the note's description. # In a 3D volume, this would be extended. # Create a mapping from (x, y) to index indexmap = np.full(vialmask.shape, -1, dtype=int) for i, (x, y) in enumerate(coords): indexmap[x, y] = i rows = [] cols = [] data = [] for i, (x, y) in enumerate(coords): neighbors = [] # Check 4-connected neighbors (up, down, left, right) for dx, dy in [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)]: nx, ny = x + dx, y + dy if 0 <= nx < vialmask.shape[0] and 0 <= ny < vialmask.shape[1] and vialmask[nx, ny]: neighbors.append(indexmap[nx, ny]) degree = len(neighbors) rows.append(i) cols.append(i) data.append(-degree / (pixelsizemm 2)) for neighbor in neighbors: rows.append(i) cols.append(neighbor) data.append(1.0 / (pixelsizemm 2)) laplacian = csrmatrix((data, (rows, cols)), shape=(nvoxels, nvoxels)) return laplacian def simulatediffusionreaction(activeinhibitor, response, laplacian, dt, diffusioncoeff, inhibitorgenrate, activationincrement, inhibitorconsumptionrate): """ Simulate diffusion and reaction over one time step. Args: activeinhibitor: 1D numpy array, current active inhibitor concentration. response: 1D numpy array, current response (polymerization) level. laplacian: Sparse CSR matrix, discrete Laplacian operator. dt: Float, time step size. diffusioncoeff: Float, diffusion coefficient. inhibitorgenrate: Float, rate of inhibitor generation. activationincrement: Float, amount of activation to process. inhibitorconsumptionrate: Float, rate of inhibitor consumption by activation. Returns: updatedactiveinhibitor: 1D numpy array, updated active inhibitor concentration. updatedresponse: 1D numpy array, updated response level. """ # Half-step diffusion # Dinhibitor(t + dt/2) = Dinhibitor(t) + dt/2 D laplacian Dinhibitor(t) diffusionterm = diffusioncoeff laplacian.dot(activeinhibitor) activeinhibitorhalf = activeinhibitor + (dt / 2.0) diffusionterm # Add inhibitor generation # Dinhibitor(t + dt/2) += dt/2 inhibitorgenrate activeinhibitorhalf += (dt / 2.0) inhibitorgenrate # Another half-step diffusion # Dinhibitor(t + dt) = Dinhibitor(t + dt/2) + dt/2 D laplacian Dinhibitor(t + dt/2) diffusiontermhalf = diffusioncoeff laplacian.dot(activeinhibitorhalf) activeinhibitor = activeinhibitorhalf + (dt / 2.0) diffusiontermhalf # Process activation increments # Consume inhibitor and accumulate response # Check if there is enough inhibitor to consume consumed = np.minimum(activationincrement, activeinhibitor inhibitorconsumptionrate) activeinhibitor -= consumed response += consumed # Clamp negative values to zero activeinhibitor = np.maximum(activeinhibitor, 0.0) response = np.maximum(response, 0.0) # Check for negative values due to numerical errors if activeinhibitor.min() < -1e-12: raise RuntimeError("Negative values detected in active inhibitor field.") # Clamp very small negative values to zero activeinhibitor[abs(activeinhibitor) < 1e-14] = 0.0 return activeinhibitor, response def optimizeantagonistictvam(target, activationpatterns, activationconfig, inhibitionconfig, alpha=1.00): """ Optimize inhibition patterns for antagonistic TVAM. Args: target: Target geometry or dose field. activationpatterns: Pre-computed 405 nm activation patterns. activationconfig: Configuration for activation. inhibitionconfig: Configuration for inhibition. alpha: Scaling factor for activation field. Returns: optimizedinhibitionpatterns: Optimized 365 nm inhibition patterns. """ # Load scene and setup #... (Implementation details from Dr.TVAM framework) # Reconstruct activation field D405 from activationpatterns D405 = reconstructfield(activationpatterns, activationconfig) # Initialize inhibition patterns (non-negative) inhibitionpatterns = initializeinhibitionpatterns(inhibitionconfig) # Optimize inhibition patterns # The optimizer minimizes the error between Deff and target # Deff = max(alpha D405 - D365, 0) # where D365 is reconstructed from inhibitionpatterns #... (Optimization loop using differentiable framework) return optimizedinhibitionpatterns Negative Values in Diffusion: During diffusion simulation, negative values can occur if the time step or diffusion coefficient is too large. The code raises a RuntimeError if updated.min() < -1e-12 and clamps values with absolute magnitude less than 1e-14 to zero. Boundary Conditions: The nofluxlaplacian function assumes no-flux boundary conditions by only considering neighbors within the vial mask. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of projections, voxels, and optimization iterations. The diffusion simulation is O(N) per time step, where N is the number of voxels. The optimization involves solving a large-scale inverse problem, which can be computationally expensive. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels and projections. The Laplacian matrix is sparse, so memory usage is manageable for large grids. Strengths: Suppresses tomographic background dose. Confinement of individual features. Definition of complete 3D geometries through inhibition. Mitigation of diffusion- and attenuation-driven loss of spatial fidelity. Limitations: Requires two wavelength channels (405 nm and 365 nm). More complex optimization process compared to standard TVAM. Sensitive to the choice of scaling factor \alpha. Antagonistic Dual-Wavelength TVAM was developed to address the limitations of standard TVAM, particularly the accumulation of unwanted background dose outside the target area due to overlapping projections. It extends the standard TVAM Integrator by adding a second wavelength channel for inhibition, allowing for better control over the polymerization process. The method is implemented using the open-source Dr.TVAM framework. name: Compositional Rendering
head: GO-NeRF Compositional Rendering, GO-NeRF Rendering
body: Compositional Rendering is a method for integrating newly generated 3D objects into an existing Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) scene by decoupling the rendering of the object from the background scene. It solves the problem of occlusion-aware compositing in image-order rendering by generating a 3D-aware opacity map for the new object and blending it with pre-rendered background RGB-D images. It differs from standard Direct Volume Ray Casting [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md] by performing the final alpha-blending in image space using a pre-computed scene cache, rather than accumulating the entire scene in a single ray-casting pass. Inputs: Pre-rendered background RGB-D image sequences \{(S0, D0), \dots, (Sn, Dn)\} for a set of camera viewpoints \{C0, \dots, Cn\}. A trained object NeRF F(\thetao) defining volume density \delta and RGB color c. A 3D bounding box defining the spatial extent of the object. A target camera viewpoint v \in \{C0, \dots, Cn\}. Outputs: Final composited RGB image Iv. Intermediate object RGB image Gv. Intermediate object opacity map Ov. Data Structures: Background Cache: A list of tuples, where each tuple contains an RGB image Sv and a depth image Dv for each viewpoint v. Object NeRF: A neural network F(\thetao) that takes a 3D coordinate q and viewing direction as input and outputs volume density \delta and RGB color c. Bounding Box: Defined by minimum and maximum coordinates (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}). Steps: 1. Pre-render Background: For each camera viewpoint v in the predefined set \{C0, \dots, Cn\}, render the background scene using the established scene NeRF F(\thetas) to generate the RGB image Sv and depth image Dv. Store these as the background cache. 2. Ray Casting: For the target viewpoint v, cast a ray ri for each pixel i in the image plane. 3. Sampling: Sample K query points qk along the ray ri within the 3D bounding box of the object. Let \Deltak be the distance between adjacent query points qk and q{k+1} along the ray. 4. Query NeRF: For each query point qk, query the object NeRF F(\thetao) to obtain the volume density \deltak and RGB color ck. 5. Calculate Transmittance: Compute the transmittance \tauk at sample k, representing the probability that a ray passes through the volume up to sample k without being absorbed or scattered: \tauk = \exp\left(-\sum{t=1}^{k-1} \deltat \Deltat\right) where \tau1 = 1. 6. Calculate Object RGB: Compute the accumulated RGB value Gv(i) for pixel i by summing the contribution of each sample weighted by its opacity contribution and transmittance: Gv(i) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \tauk (1 - \exp(-\deltak \Deltak)) ck 7. Calculate Object Opacity: Compute the accumulated opacity Ov(i) for pixel i. This step includes occlusion logic against the pre-rendered background depth Dv(i): Ov(i) = \begin{cases} \sum{k=1}^{K} \tauk (1 - \exp(-\deltak \Deltak)), & \text{if } ri \in \text{box} \text{ AND } D{box}(i) \le Dv(i) \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Here, D{box}(i) is the depth of the intersection of ray ri with the 3D bounding box. The condition D{box}(i) \le Dv(i) ensures that if the object's bounding box is behind the background scene's geometry, the object is treated as occluded. 8. Composite: Blend the rendered object Gv and the pre-rendered background Sv using the opacity map Ov to produce the final image Iv: Iv = Gv \cdot Ov + Sv \cdot (1 - Ov) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def compositionalrendering(viewpointidx, backgroundcache, objectnerf, boundingbox, numsamples): """ Renders the final composited image for a specific viewpoint. Args: viewpointidx: Index of the camera viewpoint in the predefined set. backgroundcache: List of (Sv, Dv) tuples for all viewpoints. objectnerf: Function/Model F(thetao) returning (delta, color) for a batch of points. boundingbox: Tuple ((xmin, ymin, zmin), (xmax, ymax, zmax)). numsamples: Number of query points K along the ray. Returns: Iv: Final composited RGB image as a flat list of [R, G, B] values. """ Sv, Dv = backgroundcache[viewpointidx] height, width = len(Sv), len(Sv[0]) Iv = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height width)] origins, directions = generaterays(viewpointidx) for i in range(height width): o = origins[i] d = directions[i] # Ray-box intersection (slab method) tmin, tmax = intersectraybox(o, d, boundingbox) if tmin is None: Iv[i] = Sv[i] continue # Sample points uniformly between tmin and tmax tvals = [tmin + (tmax - tmin) (k + 0.5) / numsamples for k in range(numsamples)] points = [[o[j] + d[j] t for j in range(3)] for t in tvals] deltas, colors = objectnerf(points) # Compute distances between adjacent samples (Deltak) dists = [tvals[k+1] - tvals[k] for k in range(numsamples - 1)] dists.insert(0, dists[0] if dists else 0.0) # Accumulate transmittance and opacity cumdensity = 0.0 Gvpixel = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] Ovpixel = 0.0 for k in range(numsamples): dist = dists[k] alphak = 1.0 - math.exp(-deltas[k] dist) tauk = math.exp(-cumdensity) for c in range(3): Gvpixel[c] += tauk alphak colors[k][c] Ovpixel += tauk alphak cumdensity += deltas[k] dist # Occlusion check: Dbox is tmin (depth of front intersection) if tmin > Dv[i]: Ovpixel = 0.0 for c in range(3): Iv[i][c] = Gvpixel[c] Ovpixel + Sv[i][c] (1.0 - Ovpixel) return Iv def generaterays(viewpointidx): # Standard pinhole camera ray generation. Returns list of origins and directions. # Implementation depends on camera intrinsics and extrinsics for viewpointidx. pass def intersectraybox(origin, direction, box): # Standard AABB intersection using slab method. # box = ((xmin, ymin, zmin), (xmax, ymax, zmax)) tmin, tmax = 0.0, float('inf') for d in range(3): invd = 1.0 / direction[d] if direction[d] != 0 else float('inf') t1 = (box[0][d] - origin[d]) invd t2 = (box[1][d] - origin[d]) invd tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return None, None return tmin, tmax Parameters: numsamples (K): Number of query points along the ray. Not given in the sources. boundingbox: Defines the 3D extent of the object. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Intersection: If the ray ri does not intersect the 3D bounding box, the opacity Ov(i) is set to 0, and the background Sv is used directly. Occlusion: If the depth of the bounding box intersection D{box}(i) is greater than the background depth Dv(i), the object is considered occluded by the scene foreground. In this case, Ov(i) is set to 0, and the background Sv is used. Precision: The exponential function in transmittance calculation can suffer from underflow for high densities or large distances. Standard practice is to clamp densities or use log-space accumulation. Time Complexity: The method reduces computational load by pre-rendering the background scene. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the pre-rendered RGB-D image sequences for all viewpoints \{C0, \dots, Cn\}. Strengths: Decouples object and scene rendering, enhancing flexibility. Handles occlusions effectively using 3D-aware opacity maps. Plug-and-play compatibility with various scene pre-training methods. Limitations: Requires pre-rendering the background for all predefined viewpoints. Limited to the predefined set of camera viewpoints. When to Use: When integrating generated objects into a static NeRF scene with known viewpoints, especially for VR content creation where specific viewpoints are important. Compositional Rendering was introduced in the GO-NeRF paper. It is designed for virtual reality content creation, allowing users to generate and integrate objects into 3D scenes using a user-friendly interface. The method leverages the decoupling of object and scene rendering to simplify the process for casual users. GO-NeRF: Generating Objects in Neural Radiance Fields for Virtual Reality Content Creation, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2025.3549558, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Shading and Occlusion Models
body: This family extends Direct Volume Ray Casting [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md] by modifying the compositing step to incorporate lighting, shadows, and occlusion cues, thereby enhancing depth perception and visual clarity in volumetric data. Unlike standard DVR which relies solely on opacity-weighted accumulation, these methods integrate ambient occlusion, directional filtering, or image-space shadowing to simulate light transport effects. They are distinguished from TVAM Integrator by their focus on local shading approximations rather than global illumination path tracing, and from Cinematic Rendering by their use of simplified or image-space techniques rather than full physically-based surface/volume interaction models. The methods in this family share the foundational mechanism of Direct Volume Ray Casting [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md], including ray definition, sampling, interpolation, and transfer function mapping. However, they diverge in the Compositing (Integration) step (Step 4 of the parent's Shared principles). While standard DVR uses the front-to-back accumulation equation, specific applications modify this accumulation: Summation: Some modes simply sum interpolated scalar values without opacity weighting. Path Tracing: Others trace randomized photon paths to solve the multi-dimensional rendering equation, accounting for scattering and global illumination. Layered Compositing: Some render distinct material styles into separate layers and composite them post-hoc. Occlusion-Aware Shading: Others integrate in-scattered radiance approximations using cone-shaped phase functions during slice traversal. A slice-based technique that simulates ambient occlusion by integrating soft shadowing using a backward-peaked cone phase function. It differs from siblings by deriving occlusion factors from the radiative transport equation using a viewer-oriented cone, allowing semi-transparent materials to influence occlusion and enabling interactive clipping without precomputation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def directionalocclusionshading(volume, tf, camera, theta, d, resolution): """ Computes directional occlusion shading via front-to-back slice traversal. """ import math # 1. Compute proxy geometry: view-aligned slices intersecting volume bounding box slices = computeproxyslices(volume.boundingbox, camera.viewdirection) # 2. Initialize buffers eyebuffer = np.zeros((resolution, resolution, 4), dtype=np.float32) occlusioncurr = np.zeros((resolution, resolution), dtype=np.float32) occlusionnext = np.zeros((resolution, resolution), dtype=np.float32) ambientradiance = 1.0 # 3. Render loop (front to back) for sliceplane in slices: # 3a. Update Eye Buffer slicecolor, sliceopacity = renderslicetobuffer(sliceplane, volume, tf) for y in range(resolution): for x in range(resolution): V = occlusioncurr[y, x] Cslice = slicecolor[y, x] V ambientradiance alphac = sliceopacity[y, x] V # Front-to-back alpha blending eyebuffer[y, x,:3] = eyebuffer[y, x,:3] (1 - alphac) + Cslice alphac eyebuffer[y, x, 3] += alphac (1 - eyebuffer[y, x, 3]) # 3b. Update Occlusion Buffer r = d math.tan(theta) # Compute perspective correction factor c (simplified for 2D grid) c = computeperspectivecorrection(camera.projectionmatrix, sliceplane.z) # Generate uniform grid disk samples gridsize = resolution psamples = generatedisksamples(gridsize, r) for y in range(resolution): for x in range(resolution): # Project fragment to NDC xyd = projecttondc(camera, sliceplane, x, y) newV = 0.0 count = 0 for p in psamples: pd = xyd + c p pt = 0.5 pd + np.array([0.5, 0.5]) # Clamp to [0,1] pt = np.clip(pt, 0.0, 1.0) # Read from current occlusion buffer val = occlusioncurr[clamp(pt.y, resolution), clamp(pt.x, resolution)] # Attenuate by transmittance T approx exp(-sigmat d) T = math.exp(-volume.extinctioncoefficient d) newV += val T count += 1 occlusionnext[y, x] = newV / count if count > 0 else 0.0 # 3c. Swap buffers occlusioncurr, occlusionnext = occlusionnext, occlusioncurr # 4. Final Output return np.clip(eyebuffer[:,:,:3], 0.0, 1.0) A technique that modulates alpha values based on the alignment between local fiber directions (major eigenvectors) and a user-defined vector. It sets itself apart by leveraging full tensor directional information to selectively fade irrelevant fiber bundles, unlike methods relying on scalar invariants or surface-based approximations. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def directionalfilteringeigenvector(eigenvector: np.ndarray, userdirection: np.ndarray, basealpha: float, filtertype: str) -> float: """ Computes the modulated alpha for a voxel based on directional filtering. """ # 1. Ensure vectors are in the same hemisphere dotproduct = np.dot(eigenvector, userdirection) if dotproduct < 0: eigenvector = -eigenvector dotproduct = -dotproduct k = max(0.0, min(1.0, dotproduct)) # 2. Apply filtering function if filtertype == 'smoothstep': fk = smoothstep(k) elif filtertype == 'polynomial': fk = polynomialfilter(k) else: fk = k # 3. Modulate alpha return basealpha fk def smoothstep(x: float) -> float: if x < 0: return 0.0 if x > 1: return 1.0 return 3.0 x2 - 2.0 x3 def polynomialfilter(x: float) -> float: if x < 0: return 0.0 if x > 1: return 1.0 t1 = 70.0 x t2 = -315.0 + t1 t3 = 540.0 + t2 x t4 = -420.0 + t3 x t5 = 126.0 + t4 x return t5 (x 5) A unified image-space shading model that simulates hard shadows and ambient occlusion for both opaque and transparent media. It distinguishes itself by computing occlusion entirely in image space using multidirectional sampling, achieving results visually identical to ray-casting-based shadows but with decoupled post-processing overhead. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ismosshading(colorbuffer, depthtexture, lightsources, betaparam): """ Applies ISMOS shading to a volume rendered image. """ height, width = colorbuffer.shape[:2] shadedimage = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) # Precompute rotation matrices for light sampling numsamples = 6 thetas = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, numsamples, endpoint=False) phis = np.linspace(0, np.pi, numsamples, endpoint=False) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): basecolor = colorbuffer[y, x,:3] beta = colorbuffer[y, x, 3] # Source does not specify the exact functional form for opacity approximation from beta. # Standard practice interpolates depth to estimate local transmittance. opacity = estimateopacityfrombeta(beta, depthtexture[y, x]) finalcolor = basecolor.copy() for light in lightsources: lightcontribution = np.zeros(3) for theta in thetas: for phi in phis: cost, sint = np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta) cosp, sinp = np.cos(phi), np.sin(phi) rotmatrix = np.array([ [cost cosp, -sint, cost sinp], [sint cosp, cost, sint sinp], [-sinp, 0, cosp] ]) # R and r values are not specified in sources. Using standard disk sampling. Roffset = 0.0 diskradius = 0.5 samplelocal = np.array([diskradius, 0.0, 0.0]) samplerotated = rotmatrix @ samplelocal lightdir = normalize(light.direction + samplerotated) # Source does not detail the exact ray-marching or depth comparison logic. # Standard image-space occlusion checks depth along lightdir. isoccluded = checkimagespaceocclusion(x, y, lightdir, depthtexture, opacity) if not isoccluded: lightcontribution += light.intensity light.color finalcolor += lightcontribution shadedimage[y, x] = finalcolor return shadedimage Approximates the attenuation of diffusely reflected ambient light through local volume occlusion by summing extinction coefficients rather than tracing shadow rays. It differs from standard DVR by replacing the constant ambient term with a spatially varying occlusion factor derived from a local neighborhood integral, and from full global illumination by ignoring multi-bounce scattering and relying on a precomputed aggregate structure for speed. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeextinctionao(volume, sat, s, r, IA, k): """ Compute extinction-based ambient occlusion for sample point s. """ xmin, xmax = max(0, s.x - r), min(volume.width - 1, s.x + r) ymin, ymax = max(0, s.y - r), min(volume.height - 1, s.y + r) zmin, zmax = max(0, s.z - r), min(volume.depth - 1, s.z + r) sumtau = querysat3d(sat, xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax) wAL = 1.0 / (r r) if r != 0 else 0.0 exponent = wAL sumtau k CRGB = volume[s.x, s.y, s.z] Ei = IA math.exp(-exponent) CRGB return Ei def querysat3d(sat, xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax): def getval(x, y, z): x = max(0, min(x, sat.width - 1)) y = max(0, min(y, sat.height - 1)) z = max(0, min(z, sat.depth - 1)) return sat[x, y, z] return (getval(xmax, ymax, zmax) getval(xmin - 1, ymax, zmax) getval(xmax, ymin - 1, zmax) getval(xmax, ymax, zmin - 1) + getval(xmin - 1, ymin - 1, zmax) + getval(xmin - 1, ymax, zmin - 1) + getval(xmax, ymin - 1, zmin - 1) getval(xmin - 1, ymin - 1, zmin - 1)) A visualization technique for rendered tomograms that adapts standard ray marching to include soft shadows and local ambient occlusion. The pipeline applies a 3×3 Gaussian blur to the image, thresholds intensity values below 1/81st of the maximum value, and adjusts the gamma value to 2.0 to shift mid-tones to brighter values. This approach pronounces regions with the highest error values and structural features. The specific origins of the family as a whole are not detailed in the provided sources. The constituent methods originate from various research efforts in medical visualization and interactive rendering: Directional Occlusion Shading and ISMOS are associated with research on efficient shading for volume rendering, while Directional Filtering for Occlusion Reduction is linked to diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) visualization. The soft shadow and ambient occlusion variant is applied in GPU-accelerated 3D tomographic reconstruction pipelines to enhance error projection visualization. name: Cinematic Rendering
head: Cinematic Volume Rendering, Hybrid Cinematic Volume Rendering
body: Cinematic Rendering (CR) is a physically based, real-time volume rendering technique for medical image data (CT and MRI) that solves the multi-dimensional and non-continuous rendering equation to integrate light scattered from all possible directions along a ray, generating a photo-realistic depiction using random sampling. Unlike standard Direct Volume Ray Casting [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md], which uses a single straight ray and local gradient shading, CR traces hundreds or thousands of photon paths per pixel to simulate complex light-matter interactions, including multiple scattering, absorption, and extinction. It differs from its siblings by using High Dynamic Range (HDR) light maps for natural illumination and Monte Carlo path tracing to account for global illumination effects like soft shadows and ambient occlusion, rather than synthetic point lights or simple shading models. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric medical image data (CT or MRI), typically stored as a 3D grid of voxels with attenuation values (e.g., Hounsfield Units for CT). Input: Transfer Function mapping voxel attenuation values to color and opacity. Input: HDR Light Map (spherical panorama) capturing environmental lighting from all directions. Input: Camera parameters (aperture, focal length, exposure, shutter speed). Output: A 2D photorealistic image where each pixel represents the accumulated radiance from traced photon paths. Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D array V of size W \times H \times D containing voxel attenuation values. Transfer Function: A mapping T: \text{HU} \rightarrow (r, g, b, \alpha), where r,g,b \in [0,1] and \alpha \in [0,1]. Light Map: A spherical environment map L(\omega) providing incident radiance Li for any direction \omega. Sample Buffer: Accumulator for Monte Carlo samples per pixel. Parameters: Samples per Pixel (N): Hundreds to thousands of paths per pixel. Rendering Time: 5 to 30 seconds for final image quality, depending on N and scene complexity. Progressive Rendering: Iterative refinement allows real-time interaction (zoom, pan, rotate) while the image refines in the background. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each pixel (u, v) in the image, initialize an accumulator C{acc} = (0, 0, 0, 0) and a sample count n = 0. 2. Ray Definition: Define the primary ray origin and direction from the camera center through pixel (u, v) based on camera intrinsics (aperture, focal length). 3. Path Tracing Loop: Repeat for N samples: a. Sample Direction: Generate a random direction \omega for the first light interaction, prioritizing paths that reach the eye (importance sampling). b. Trace Path: Trace the photon path through the volume V. At each step along the path: i. Sample Position: Interpolate the voxel value v{val} at the current position in V using trilinear interpolation. ii. Transfer Function: Map v{val} to color c = T(v{val}).rgb and opacity \alpha = T(v{val}).\alpha. iii. Lighting: Sample the incident radiance Li from the HDR Light Map L(\omega) for the current direction. iv. Interaction: Compute the contribution of the voxel to the path. The method omits emission and background radiance terms from the volume rendering equation, estimating the integral via discrete sampling. The interaction accounts for scattering, absorption, and potential direction changes (multiple bounces). v. Accumulate: Add the scattered radiance to the path's current radiance estimate. c. Terminate: Stop tracing when the path is fully absorbed or a maximum bounce limit is reached. 4. Averaging: After N samples, compute the pixel color C{pixel} = C{acc} / N. 5. Progressive Update: Display the current C{pixel} immediately. As N increases, the image converges to the final cinematic quality. 6. Camera Effects: Apply post-processing effects based on camera parameters, such as depth-of-field (blur based on aperture/focal length) and motion blur (based on shutter speed). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cinematicrender(volume, transferfunction, lightmap, camera, samplesperpixel): """ Renders a volume using Cinematic Rendering principles. Args: volume: 3D array of voxel values (e.g., HU). transferfunction: Function mapping voxel value to (r, g, b, alpha). lightmap: Function returning incident radiance for a direction. camera: Camera object with resolution, getorigin, getdirection, exposure. samplesperpixel: Number of Monte Carlo samples per pixel. Returns: 2D image array. """ height, width = camera.resolution image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): pixelaccumulator = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(samplesperpixel): rayorigin = camera.getorigin(x, y) raydirection = camera.getdirection(x, y) currentradiance = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] throughput = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] currentpos = rayorigin currentdir = raydirection maxbounces = 10 for bounce in range(maxbounces): voxelval = trilinearinterpolate(volume, currentpos) color, alpha = transferfunction(voxelval) incidentlight = lightmap(currentdir) contribution = [ incidentlight[0] color[0] alpha throughput[0], incidentlight[1] color[1] alpha throughput[1], incidentlight[2] color[2] alpha throughput[2] ] currentradiance = [ currentradiance[0] + contribution[0], currentradiance[1] + contribution[1], currentradiance[2] + contribution[2] ] throughput = [ throughput[0] (1.0 - alpha), throughput[1] (1.0 - alpha), throughput[2] (1.0 - alpha) ] if throughput[0] < 0.01 and throughput[1] < 0.01 and throughput[2] < 0.01: break stepsize = 0.5 currentpos = [ currentpos[0] + currentdir[0] stepsize, currentpos[1] + currentdir[1] stepsize, currentpos[2] + currentdir[2] stepsize ] currentdir = samplecosinehemisphere(currentdir) pixelaccumulator = [ pixelaccumulator[0] + currentradiance[0], pixelaccumulator[1] + currentradiance[1], pixelaccumulator[2] + currentradiance[2] ] image[y][x] = [ pixelaccumulator[0] / samplesperpixel camera.exposure, pixelaccumulator[1] / samplesperpixel camera.exposure, pixelaccumulator[2] / samplesperpixel camera.exposure ] return image def trilinearinterpolate(volume, pos): ix, iy, iz = int(pos[0]), int(pos[1]), int(pos[2]) fx, fy, fz = pos[0] - ix, pos[1] - iy, pos[2] - iz ix = max(0, min(ix, volume.width - 1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, volume.height - 1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, volume.depth - 1)) v000 = volume[ix][iy][iz] v100 = volume[min(ix+1, volume.width-1)][iy][iz] v010 = volume[ix][min(iy+1, volume.height-1)][iz] v110 = volume[min(ix+1, volume.width-1)][min(iy+1, volume.height-1)][iz] v001 = volume[ix][iy][min(iz+1, volume.depth-1)] v101 = volume[min(ix+1, volume.width-1)][iy][min(iz+1, volume.depth-1)] v011 = volume[ix][min(iy+1, volume.height-1)][min(iz+1, volume.depth-1)] v111 = volume[min(ix+1, volume.width-1)][min(iy+1, volume.height-1)][min(iz+1, volume.depth-1)] return (v000(1-fx)(1-fy)(1-fz) + v100fx(1-fy)(1-fz) + v010(1-fx)fy(1-fz) + v110fxfy(1-fz) + v001(1-fx)(1-fy)fz + v101fx(1-fy)fz + v011(1-fx)fyfz + v111fxfyfz) def samplecosinehemisphere(normal): import math u = math.random() v = math.random() theta = 2.0 math.pi u phi = math.acos(math.sqrt(v)) x = math.cos(theta) math.sin(phi) y = math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi) z = math.cos(phi) return [x, y, z] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: Tracing infinite light paths is computationally expensive. Monte Carlo simulations are required to generate a randomized subset. Real-time Interruption: Real-time display of rotating images is interrupted by repetitive recalculation processes due to high computational demand. Clinical Use: The prototype is not intended for clinical use at the time of publication and lacks real-time high-end quality reconstruction. Masking Findings: Like conventional VR, inappropriate transfer function parameters can mask findings by adjacent structures. A variant that blends surface and volumetric characteristics, useful for compensating for speckle noise in ultrasound data. A sibling method that modifies the accumulation step, potentially using different integration strategies [9443-specific-applications-and-integrators.md]. A sibling method that integrates in-scattered radiance approximations using cone-shaped phase functions during slice traversal [9443-specific-applications-and-integrators.md]. A sibling method that renders distinct material styles into separate layers and composites them post-hoc [9443-specific-applications-and-integrators.md]. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Rendering time ranges from 5 to 30 seconds for final image quality, depending on the desired quality and scene complexity. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of samples and volume resolution. Real-time interaction is supported via progressive rendering, where the image refines in the background while the user interacts. Strengths: Provides a more natural and photo-realistic representation with enhanced depth and shape perception, particularly for high-contrast structures like bones and vessels. Models complex lighting effects including soft shadows, ambient occlusion, and subsurface scattering. Limitations: High computational power demand. Real-time display of rotating images is interrupted by recalculation. Not approved for clinical use as of the document date. Limited display options in pre-clinical research tools. When to Use: When photorealistic visualization is prioritized over real-time interactivity, such as for patient education, surgical planning, or teaching anatomy. When Not to Use: When real-time high-end quality reconstruction is required for interactive diagnosis, or when computational resources are limited. Cinematic Rendering (CR) was developed by Siemens Healthineers, inspired by the quality of computer animation programs in the entertainment industry, specifically big-screen films. It was introduced as a research tool in prototype software such as Frontier (version 1.0.0) and syngo.Via (version VB10A). The technique aims to generate more photo-realistic representations of the human body from CT and MR image data sets by simulating the complex interaction of photons with human anatomy. It is available as a research tool in an open research environment but has no approval for clinical use as of the document date. name: Directional Occlusion Shading
head: Directional Occlusion, Directional Occlusion Shading Model, Schott et al, Slice-based directional occlusion shading
body: Directional Occlusion Shading (DOS) is a slice-based shading technique for interactive direct volume rendering that approximates ambient occlusion and first-order scattering by integrating a backward-peaked cone phase function during front-to-back slice traversal. Unlike standard direct volume ray casting which uses simple front-to-back compositing, DOS modulates the contribution of each slice by an occlusion factor derived from the transmittance of neighboring voxels within a viewer-oriented cone, providing perceptual depth cues for both solid and transparent features without precomputation. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like ISMOS by using a specialized cone phase function to accentuate semi-transparent surface-like features rather than approximating translucency, and from Directional Filtering for Occlusion Reduction by computing occlusion interactively per-slice rather than filtering the final image. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volume dataset, 2D transfer function (mapping scalar values to color and opacity), camera parameters (view direction \vec{\omega}, projection matrix P), aperture angle \theta, inter-slice distance d, and sampling resolution for the occlusion cone. Output: Final color and opacity image in the frame buffer. Data Structures: Eye Buffer: A floating-point buffer (typically 16-bit precision) storing the accumulated radiance L and opacity for the current slice compositing. Occlusion Buffers: Two floating-point buffers (current and next) storing the fractional visibility (occlusion factor) V for each slice. These are swapped after each slice update. Proxy Geometry: View-aligned slices (planes) intersecting the volume bounding box, computed on the CPU. Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Proxy Geometry: On the CPU, generate view-aligned slices by intersecting planes with the volume bounding box. 2. Initialize Buffers: Allocate two floating-point occlusion buffers and one eye buffer. Initialize them to zero or background values. 3. Render Loop (for each slice from front to back): a. Update Eye Buffer: Render the current slice into the eye buffer. For each fragment, read the occlusion factor V from the current occlusion buffer at the projected position. Compute the slice's contribution: C{slice} = \text{Color} \cdot V \cdot \text{AmbientRadiance}. Composite this into the eye buffer using front-to-back alpha blending. b. Update Occlusion Buffer: Render the current slice again, but this time into the next occlusion buffer. For each fragment, compute the new occlusion factor by sampling the current occlusion buffer. i. Calculate occlusion extent: r = d \tan(\theta). ii. Compute correction factor \vec{c} in the vertex shader using projection matrix P and view space z-component to handle perspective distortion. iii. Generate sample positions \vec{p} on a uniform grid disk of radius r. iv. Project fragment clip space position to NDC \vec{x}{y,d} via perspective division. v. Calculate NDC sample position: \vec{p}d = \vec{x}{y,d} + \vec{c} \otimes \vec{p}, where \otimes is component-wise multiplication. vi. Calculate texture coordinates: \vec{p}t = 0.5 \cdot \vec{p}d + [0.5, 0.5]^T. vii. Read values from the current occlusion buffer at \vec{p}t. Attenuate each sample by the transmittance T (approximated using distance d) and average the weighted samples to get the new occlusion factor for the next buffer. c. Swap Buffers: Swap the current and next occlusion buffers. 4. Final Output: Copy the eye buffer to the frame buffer, converting from floating-point to fixed-point. Formulas: The radiance L(\vec{x}, \vec{\omega}) at a point \vec{x} is given by: L(\vec{x}, \vec{\omega}) = T(\vec{x}, \vec{x}0) Lb(\vec{x}0, \vec{\omega}) + Lm(\vec{x}, \vec{\omega}) where Lb is background radiance, T is transmittance, and Lm is medium radiance. Medium radiance Lm is approximated by considering only first-order scattering and ambient light La: Lm(\vec{x}, \vec{\omega}) = \int{\vec{x}}^{\vec{x}0} T(\vec{x}, \vec{x}') \sigmas(\vec{x}') Li(\vec{x}', \vec{\omega}) d\vec{x}' Li(\vec{x}', \vec{\omega}) = La V(\vec{x}', \vec{\omega}) where \sigmas is the scattering coefficient and V is the fractional visibility (occlusion factor). The fractional visibility V is computed using a backward-peaked cone phase function \Phi\theta: V(\vec{x}', \vec{\omega}) = \int{4\pi} T(\vec{x}', \vec{x}{0,i}) \Phi\theta(\vec{\omega}, \vec{\omega}i) d\vec{\omega}i The phase function is defined as: \Phi\theta(\vec{\omega}, \vec{\omega}i) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2\pi(1-\cos \theta)} & \text{if } \langle \vec{\omega}, \vec{\omega}i \rangle > \cos(\theta) \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \theta \in 0, \pi/2) is the aperture angle, \vec{\omega} is the viewing direction, and \vec{\omega}i are directions within the cone. Transmittance is T(\vec{x}a, \vec{x}b) = e^{-\tau(\vec{x}a, \vec{x}b)} with optical thickness \tau(\vec{x}a, \vec{x}b) = \int{\vec{x}a}^{\vec{x}b} \sigmat(\vec{x}) d\vec{x}. Parameters: Aperture Angle \theta: Controls the influence of features at different distances. Range [0, \pi/2). Typical value: 80^\circ. Inter-slice Distance d: Distance between view-aligned slices. Typical value: 0.001. Sampling Rate/Grid Resolution: Controls the quality of the occlusion integral approximation. Typical values tested: 0.3, 0.5, 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perspective Distortion: The cone base size varies with z-coordinate in screen space due to perspective projection. This is handled by the correction factor \vec{c} computed in the vertex shader. Inter-frame Artifacts: Camera movement can cause artifacts. Mitigated by using a symmetric uniform grid for sample positions aligned with occlusion buffer axes. Undefined OpenGL Behavior: Reading and writing to the same layered render target (MRT) is undefined by the OpenGL spec but works in practice if reads and writes do not reference the same layer. Light Source Limitation: The method assumes a single light source located at the camera position (viewer-oriented). [Extinction Optimized Shading is a specific integrator mode within Directional Occlusion Shading that highlights interior structures occluded by others by calculating optimized extinction coefficients using a closed-form solution based on the transfer function's importance function. It sets itself apart from the standard directional occlusion mode by simplifying transfer function design to setting low or high importance, thereby revealing internal structures better than standard occlusion shading. It is chosen when the goal is to visualize internal details of complex, multivariate volumes where standard shading might hide occluded features. Time Complexity: Interactive. Performance depends on the number of slices, sampling rate, and GPU capabilities. Memory Complexity: Low. Requires only two additional floating-point buffers for occlusion factors, similar to standard slice rendering. Measured Performance: Brain MRI (4 × 240 × 240 × 155, 600×600 viewport): 14 fps at sampling rate 0.3, 11 fps at 0.5, 4 fps at 1.0. Stag Beetle (1046 slices, 80° aperture): 10.6 FPS. Brain MRI (256x256x160, 1000 slices): 3.7 FPS (DOS) vs 1.6 FPS (Lambertian). Carp CT (256x288x512, 220 slices): 48.3 FPS (DOS) vs 8.8 FPS (Lambertian). Visible Male (512x512x302, 962 slices): 5.0 FPS (DOS) vs 25.7 FPS (Lambertian). Engine Block CT (256x256x128, 679 slices): 5.6 FPS (DOS) vs 5.6 FPS (Lambertian). Hand CT (244x124x257, 619 slices): 13.3 FPS (DOS) vs 16.0 FPS (Lambertian). Tree CT (512x512x512, 1563 slices): 59.0 FPS (DOS) vs 29.1 FPS (Lambertian). Scaling: Performance is generally better than Lambertian shading for complex volumes with many slices, but can be worse for simple volumes with few slices. MRT (Multiple Render Targets) implementation increases performance by 44-99% compared to SRT (Single Render Target), especially for low sample counts. Strengths: Interactive frame rates, no precomputation, supports interactive clipping planes and transfer function changes, provides good depth cues for transparent and solid features. Limitations: Bound to slice-based rendering, assumes light at camera position, may show regular structure artifacts. Directional Occlusion Shading was introduced by Mathias Schott, Vincent Pegoraro, Charles Hansen, Kévin Boulanger, and Kadi Bouatouch in 2009 at the Eurographics/ IEEE-VGTC Symposium on Visualization. It was published in the Journal of Computer Graphics Forum (Eurographics) in 2009. The method is used in interactive direct volume rendering to provide perceptual cues similar to ambient occlusion without the cost of precomputation.
