name: Volume Rendering in 3D Slicer
head: VTK CPU Ray Casting, VTK GPU Ray Casting, VTK Multi-Volume
body: Volume rendering in 3D Slicer is a visualization technique for displaying image volumes as 3D objects directly without requiring segmentation, accomplished by specifying color and opacity for each voxel based on its image intensity. It builds on Direct volume ray casting by providing a user interface for transfer function tuning and multiple rendering backends (CPU, GPU, Multi-Volume). It distinguishes itself from general implementations by its integration with the Slicer data model, allowing for synchronized color mapping with slice views, interactive segmentation-based masking, and specific handling of medical imaging modalities (CT/MR) via presets. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A vtkMRMLVolumeNode containing scalar, RGB, or RGBA data. The volume may be associated with a segmentation mask (via the Segment Editor) to blank out regions. Output: A rendered 3D view displaying the volume with applied transfer functions, shading, and compositing. Data Structures: Transfer Functions: Defined by control points (X, O, M, S) where X is the scalar value, O is opacity, M is the mid-point, and S is sharpness. Cropping Box (ROI): A bounding box defining the region of interest. Partitions: A tuple (px, py, pz) used to split the volume into smaller chunks for GPU rendering stability. Numbered Steps: 1. Volume Preparation: If the volume is warped (affine or non-linear), the transform must be hardened on the volume data before rendering. If regions need to be hidden, a segmentation is created using Paint/Scissors effects, and the Mask volume effect fills the region with "empty" values (e.g., -1000 HU for CT air). The original volume rendering is hidden, and rendering is applied to the masked volume. 2. Backend Selection: The user selects one of three techniques in the "Rendering" section: VTK CPU Ray Casting, VTK GPU Ray Casting (default), or VTK Multi-Volume. 3. Transfer Function Application: Scalar Opacity Mapping maps scalar values to opacity and supports threshold mode with range sliders. Scalar Color Mapping maps scalar values to color but is hidden for RGB/RGBA volumes, where voxel colors are used directly. Gradient Opacity controls opacity based on the magnitude of the density gradient next to the voxel. The Shift parameter moves inner control points left/right to adjust the intensity range (e.g., shifting a 0–200 ramp to 1000–1200). 4. Sampling and Interpolation: Linear interpolation is used (default for scalar volumes) or nearest neighbor (default for labelmaps). Shading is enabled/disabled; when disabled, the output resembles an X-ray-like projection. 5. Compositing and Technique: The renderer applies one of three techniques: Composite with shading (default, standard front-to-back accumulation), Maximum Intensity Projection (brightest voxel per line), or Minimum Intensity Projection (darkest voxel per line). 6. Quality and Performance Tuning: Quality is set to Adaptive (reduces quality during interaction to maintain frame rate, optimized for CPU), Interactive speed (enforces target FPS by lowering resolution), Normal (fixed quality, default), or Maximum (oversamples for higher quality). Surface smoothing adds random noise (jitter) to raycasting lines to reduce staircase artifacts. Auto-release resources controls whether GPU memory and precomputed gradients are freed when the volume is hidden. Formulas: Compositing follows the standard front-to-back emission-absorption model defined in the parent article Direct volume ray casting. Control point interpolation uses mid-point M and sharpness S parameters to shape the transfer function ramps. Parameters: Preset: Pre-defined sets of opacity, color, and gradient transfer functions tuned for specific modalities and organs. Shift: Horizontal offset for inner transfer function control points. Quality: Adaptive, Interactive speed, Normal, Maximum. Interpolation: Linear, Nearest neighbor. Shade: Boolean (enabled/disabled). Auto-release resources: Boolean (enabled/disabled). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: TDR Error: The application crashes when rotating/zooming if the OS shuts down the app for keeping the GPU busy too long due to large volume size. Workarounds include splitting the volume into partitions, cropping/downsampling, increasing the TDR registry delay, switching to CPU rendering, or upgrading the GPU. Warped Volumes: Volumes under affine or non-linear transformations must have the transform hardened before rendering. Multi-Volume Limitations: Cropping is ignored, RGB volume rendering is unsupported, and only "Composite with shading" is allowed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getnodebyname(name):... def getactivethreedview():... volumenode = getnodebyname('skull') threedview = getactivethreedview() displaymanager = threedview.getdisplaymanagerbyclass('vtkMRMLVolumeRenderingDisplayableManager') volumemapper = displaymanager.getvolumemapper(volumenode) volumemapper.setpartitions(1, 1, 2) A rendering technique entirely realized on the CPU. It is slower than GPU options but available on all computers regardless of graphics hardware capabilities. Choose this when GPU resources are unavailable or when debugging rendering logic on hardware with limited GPU support. The default rendering technique using graphics hardware. It is typically much faster than CPU rendering and supports surface smoothing to remove staircase artifacts. Choose this for standard interactive visualization of medical volumes. A GPU-based technique that can render multiple overlapping volumes. It has significant limitations: cropping (ROI) is not supported (ignored), RGB volume rendering is not supported, and only the "Composite with shading" technique is supported. Choose this only when visualizing multiple scalar volumes simultaneously and cropping is not required. A variant where volume visualization is performed using GPU-based ray-casting on colored medical images, replacing manual transfer function tuning. The pipeline involves obtaining colored versions of monochromatic images via a color transfer pipeline and then rendering the stack. A pitfall is the appearance of unwanted dark patches in the colored volume if the reference image contains unwanted structures, which are transferred to the target. Time Complexity: Dependent on the backend. CPU rendering is predictable but slow. GPU rendering is faster but subject to TDR (Timeout Detection and Recovery) errors if the volume is too large for the GPU, causing the OS to shut down the application. Memory Complexity: GPU rendering allocates GPU memory, precomputed gradients, and space-leaping volumes. The "Auto-release resources" flag controls whether these are freed when hidden, trading memory usage for reload time. Performance: VTK GPU Ray Casting is typically much faster than CPU rendering. Quality settings like "Adaptive" or "Interactive speed" can dynamically adjust sampling to maintain frame rates. Strengths: Direct visualization without segmentation; support for multiple modalities via presets; interactive transfer function editing; synchronization with slice view color maps. Limitations: Warped volumes must be hardened before rendering; Multi-Volume backend lacks cropping and RGB support; Large volumes may cause TDR crashes on GPU. When to use: Interactive visualization of CT/MR data; when segmentation is not desired or available; when multiple overlapping volumes need to be shown (Multi-Volume). When not to use: When cropping is required with multiple volumes (Multi-Volume limitation); when RGB volume rendering is required with multiple volumes (Multi-Volume limitation); when the volume is too large for the GPU and TDR cannot be adjusted (use CPU or split partitions). Volume rendering in 3D Slicer is a visualization technique for displaying image volumes as 3D objects directly, a technique originally described as volume ray casting. The module integrates with the Slicer data model to provide presets tuned for CT and MR modalities, and synchronization with the Volumes module for consistent color mapping. The colored medical images variant extends this pipeline to include automatic colorization via deep image analogy or guided filtering, as explored in recent research. What Is Volumetric Rendering? name: GPU Based Single-Pass Raycasting
head: Single-pass raycaster, Volume Rendering Component
body: GPU Based Single-Pass Raycasting is a volume rendering technique where the volume is traversed along a single ray per pixel, implemented within the Volume Rendering Component framework. It solves the limitations of polygonal-based methods (which are limited in expressive power) and slicing techniques (which can lead to artifacts) by providing high-quality visual results. It is distinguished from its siblings by its implementation as a single-pass fragment shader execution on modern graphics hardware. It builds on Hardware-Accelerated and GPU Implementations and implements the emission-absorption optical model defined in Direct volume ray casting. The method operates within the Volume Rendering Component, separating scene graph responsibilities into data representation (VolumeData) and rendering styles (VolumeRenderStyle). The core algorithm executes a ray marching loop in the fragment shader for each pixel. Input: A 3D texture volume (voxels), camera parameters, ray generation settings (stepSize, type), acceleration settings (boundingVolumeType, traversalFunction), normal calculation settings (algorithm), and transfer functions (OpacityMap). Output: A 2D image with accumulated color and opacity per pixel. The primary data structure is the VolumeData node, which holds the volume data in its voxels field (an MFNode holding a 3D texture). Additional fields include: sliceThickness (SFVec3f): Default (1,1,1). Used to handle non-equidistant grids. dimensions (SFVec3f): Currently unused. swapped (SFBool): Helper for 16-bit volume byte swapping. Rendering settings are encapsulated in: AccelerationVolumeSettings: Contains boundingVolumeType ("boxGeometry" or "boundaryGeometry") for outer space skipping and traversalFunction ("simple" or "blockSkipping") for inner space skipping. NormalVolumeSettings: Contains algorithm ("precomputedCentralDifferences", "onlineCentralDifferences", or "onlineSobel"). RayGenerationVolumeSettings: Contains type ("simple" or "interleaved") and stepSize (e.g., 0.0039). OpacityMapVolumeStyle: Contains transferFunction (an ImageTexture) and type ("simple" or "preintegrated"). 1. Volume Loading: Load the volume data into a 3D texture. Handle byte swapping if necessary using the swapped field. Adjust sampling coordinates based on sliceThickness if the grid is non-equidistant. 2. Ray Generation: For each pixel, generate a ray. The type parameter determines the generation strategy: "simple": Standard per-pixel ray generation. "interleaved": Interleaved ray generation to mitigate wood artifacts. 3. Acceleration (Outer Space Skipping): Determine the entry and exit points of the ray through the volume bounding box. The boundingVolumeType in AccelerationVolumeSettings selects between "boxGeometry" or "boundaryGeometry". 4. Acceleration (Inner Space Skipping): Traverse the volume from entry to exit. The traversalFunction in AccelerationVolumeSettings selects between "simple" or "blockSkipping". 5. Sampling and Classification: At each step along the ray, sample the 3D texture using hardware-accelerated trilinear interpolation. Apply the transfer function (defined in OpacityMapVolumeStyle) to determine color Ci and opacity \alphai. The type in OpacityMapVolumeStyle selects between "simple" or "preintegrated". 6. Normal Calculation: If lighting is enabled (ShadedVolumeStyle.lighting = TRUE), calculate surface normals. The algorithm in NormalVolumeSettings determines the method: "precomputedCentralDifferences": Fastest. "onlineCentralDifferences": Usually most appropriate. "onlineSobel": Nicest. 7. Compositing: Perform front-to-back compositing using the standard emission-absorption model: C'{i} = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Ci \alpha'{i} = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycast(volume, origin, direction, stepsize, boundsmin, boundsmax, transferfunction, lightingenabled=False): # Normalize direction dirlen = (direction[0]2 + direction[1]2 + direction[2]2)0.5 if dirlen == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] d = [direction[i] / dirlen for i in range(3)] # Compute entry and exit t values for AABB tmin = 0.0 tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if d[i] == 0: if origin[i] < boundsmin[i] or origin[i] > boundsmax[i]: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: t1 = (boundsmin[i] - origin[i]) / d[i] t2 = (boundsmax[i] - origin[i]) / d[i] tenter = min(t1, t2) texit = max(t1, t2) tmin = max(tmin, tenter) tmax = min(tmax, texit) if tmin >= tmax: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 t = tmin while t < tmax and accumulatedopacity < 0.95: # Sample position pos = [origin[i] + t d[i] for i in range(3)] # Sample volume (assume trilinear interpolation handled by volume access) value = volume.sample(pos) # Apply transfer function alpha, color = transferfunction(value, stepsize) # Lighting (if enabled) if lightingenabled: normal = volume.computenormal(pos) # Lighting model applied here # Compositing if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break accumulatedcolor[0] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) alpha color[0] accumulatedcolor[1] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) alpha color[1] accumulatedcolor[2] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) alpha color[2] accumulatedopacity += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) alpha t += stepsize return accumulatedcolor + [accumulatedopacity] stepSize: Controls the distance between samples. Example value: 0.0039. A smaller value increases quality but reduces performance. type (RayGeneration): "simple" or "interleaved". "interleaved" reduces wood artifacts. boundingVolumeType: "boxGeometry" or "boundaryGeometry". Used for outer space skipping. traversalFunction: "simple" or "blockSkipping". Used for inner space skipping to improve performance. type (OpacityMap): "simple" or "preintegrated". "preintegrated" often leads to a much better look. algorithm (NormalVolumeSettings): "precomputedCentralDifferences" (fastest), "onlineCentralDifferences" (usually most appropriate), "onlineSobel" (nicest). lighting: Boolean. If TRUE, lighting effects are calculated. Wood Artifacts: Can occur in raycasting. Mitigated by using the "interleaved" ray generation type. Non-equidistant Grids: Handled by the sliceThickness field in VolumeData, defaulting to (1,1,1). 16-bit Volume Byte Swapping: Handled by the swapped field in VolumeData. Hardware Requirements: Requires modern graphics hardware. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: High visual quality compared to polygonal methods and slicing, which can be limited or artifact-prone. Limitations: Requires modern graphics hardware; current implementation is limited to one volume per scene. When to Use: When high-quality volume visualization is required and modern graphics hardware is available. When Not to Use: When hardware does not support 3D textures or fragment shaders, or when real-time performance on low-end hardware is critical. The GPU Based Single-Pass Raycasting method is implemented within the Volume Rendering Component, an X3D extension proposal. It was developed to alleviate the drawbacks of polygonal-based methods and slicing techniques. The component separates scene graph responsibilities into data representation and rendering styles, allowing for flexible configuration of rendering parameters. The implementation relies on GPU-based single-pass raycasting, traversing the volume along a single ray per pixel. instantreality 1.0 - tutorial - Volume Rendering, https://doc.instantreality.org/tutorial/volume-rendering/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: GPU Implementation Architecture
head: OpenGL/GLSL Volume Rendering Implementation
body: This article describes the standard software architecture for implementing direct volume ray casting on modern GPUs using OpenGL and GLSL. It details the pipeline for generating spherical harmonic (SH) coefficient volumes and performing ray marching via fragment shaders. It distinguishes itself from generic hardware-accelerated approaches by focusing on the specific data structures (3D coefficient volumes) and rendering techniques (slice-by-slice ray marching with Monte Carlo sampling) required for advanced light-material interaction. The implementation uses C++ with OpenGL and GLSL. The core challenge addressed is the integration of three functions (material function M, incoming light L{mi}, and outgoing light L{mi}^0) which is complex for direct SH integration. The solution approximates this integration to achieve convincing visual results. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data, material properties, lighting conditions (represented as SH coefficients), and pre-generated random sample directions. Output: Rendered image with advanced lighting interactions, specifically SH coefficient volumes for L{mi} and L{mi}^0. Data Structures: 1. 3D Coefficient Volumes: SH coefficients for L{mi} and L{mi}^0 are stored in 3D texture volumes. 2. 2D Textures: Used for uploading pre-computed data from the CPU, including normalized Cartesian vectors for Monte Carlo sampling and spherical harmonic basis functions Y{lm}(\vartheta, \phi) for each sample direction. Algorithm Steps: 1. Generate SH Coefficient Volumes: Use Framebuffer Objects (FBOs) in conjunction with Multiple Render Targets (MRT) to generate the 3D coefficient volumes. 2. Discard Unused Coefficients: Coefficients for L{mi} can be discarded after L{mi}^0 has been computed, as they are not accessed during rendering. 3. Prepare Sampling Data (CPU Side): Generate random samples for Monte Carlo sampling on the CPU as normalized Cartesian vectors. 4. Compute Basis Functions: Compute Y{lm}(\vartheta, \phi) for each sample direction. 5. Upload to GPU: Upload the normalized Cartesian vectors and basis functions to the GPU as 2D textures. 6. Ray Marching (Fragment Shader): Render the volume slice by slice. 7. Cast Rays: In the fragment shader, use the uploaded random samples to cast rays. 8. Perform Integration: Execute the approximate integration of light-material interaction. 9. Finalize Contribution: After a ray terminates, multiply its contribution with the values Y{lm}(\varthetas, \phis) obtained from the second 2D texture. Formulas and Symbols: M: Material function. L{mi}: Incoming light. L{mi}^0: Outgoing light. Y{lm}(\vartheta, \phi): Spherical harmonic basis functions evaluated at sample directions. The integration of M, L{mi}, and L{mi}^0 is approximated rather than computed directly due to complexity. Parameters: Samples: The number of samples affects quality. Example: 1250 samples distributed over the hemisphere. Implementation Language: C++ with OpenGL and GLSL. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Random Number Generation: The GLSL specification describes functionality for generating random numbers, but this feature was not implemented in the referenced environment. Therefore, random samples must be generated on the CPU and uploaded. Approximation: The integration technique used is not physically correct but provides convincing visual results. Direct volume rendering on GPUs that integrates rays by accumulating gradients across sequential cutting planes of the volume stored as 2D textures, bypassing GPU memory limits by paging data from CPU main memory. Definition: Stores the volume out-of-core in CPU main memory and pages it into GPU memory. Performance: Medium-sized volumes up to 512^3 can be viewed at interactive rates. Context: This approach addresses the limitation that larger volumes are restricted by GPU memory, unlike standard in-core rendering. Memory: Standard implementations are limited by GPU memory capacity. Out-of-core variants mitigate this by paging data. Performance: GPU volume rendering is fast, permitting interactive rates for medium-sized volumes (512^3). Complexity: Handling three-function SH integration is complex; the described architecture uses an approximation to maintain performance. The concepts described in this paper have been integrated into a GPU-based volume ray-caster implemented in C++ using OpenGL and GLSL. The approach builds on the effectiveness of direct volume rendering on GPUs, which is faster than ray tracing for this purpose. name: In-shader neural network inference
head: Tiny-CUDA-NN in-shader routine, fully fused MLP inference
body: This method performs neural network inference directly within a GPU shader program to eliminate global memory access overhead, specifically by fusing the hash grid encoding layer into the Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) calculation. It differs from standard approaches by managing data locally within threadblocks via shared memory and utilizing GPU tensor cores for acceleration, setting it apart from CPU-based or standard GPU inference pipelines that rely on global memory transfers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray-generation kernel (callback) and network parameters (weights, biases, grid dimensions). Output: Rendered image pixels with neural network evaluations integrated into the ray-casting loop. Data Structures: Shared Memory: Used to store inputs and outputs locally within each threadblock to avoid global memory latency. Threadblock Configuration: Configured to process exactly 16 inputs (feature vectors) per block. Warp Configuration: Each warp consists of 32 threads. Parameters: Group Size: MLP layers are broken into groups of 16 neurons. Matrix Dimensions: Tensor cores accelerate multiplications between two 16 \times 16 matrices. Warp Iterations: In a standard ray tracer where one thread handles one ray, each warp iterates W/8 times to compensate for producing only one input coordinate per thread, where W is the total number of 16-neuron groups in the layer. Algorithm Steps: 1. Eliminate Global Memory Access: Remove all global GPU memory reads/writes for network weights and activations. Fuse the hash grid encoding layer fully into the MLP calculation logic. 2. Local Management: Manage inputs and outputs locally within each threadblock. Pass data to the network via shared memory. 3. Layer Decomposition: Break an MLP layer into W groups of 16 neurons each. 4. Warp Execution: Assign each 32-thread warp to compute the operations for one 16-neuron group. The warp processes 16 consecutive feature vectors. This results in the warp handling multiplications between two 16 \times 16 matrices, leveraging GPU tensor cores. 5. Threadblock Aggregation: Combine all W groups to form a single GPU threadblock. Execute these groups in parallel within the block. Each threadblock processes exactly 16 inputs at a time. 6. Iteration Compensation: If the rendering kernel assigns one ray to one thread (producing one input coordinate), configure each warp to iterate W/8 times to cover all W groups. 7. Control Flow Management: GPU tensor cores require all threads in a calling warp to be active. Manage control flow carefully to ensure warp divergence does not stall execution. Use a blockany helper function: this function evaluates to true for all threads in a threadblock if any of the thread-local predicates v evaluates to true. 8. Kernel Launch: Use a templated CUDA wrapper function that accepts the ray-generation kernel as a callback. This wrapper initializes the correct threadblock configurations and shared memory sizes, allowing integration into standard GPU volume ray tracing algorithms. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def launchinferencekernel(raygenkernel, networkparams): """ Templated wrapper to launch the rendering kernel with in-shader inference. """ # Determine W: number of 16-neuron groups in the MLP layer W = networkparams.numneurons // 16 # Configure threadblock to handle 16 inputs # Each warp (32 threads) handles one 16x16 matrix multiplication # Total warps per block = W threadsperblock = 32 W # Shared memory allocation for inputs/outputs sharedmemsize = calculatesharedmemorysize(16, networkparams) # Launch kernel with callback raygenkernelthreadsperblock, 1 def raygenkernel(networkparams, sharedmemsize): """ Main rendering kernel with fused inference. """ # 1. Manage inputs/outputs in shared memory sharedinputs = getsharedmemoryblock(0, 16) sharedoutputs = getsharedmemoryblock(16, 16) # 2. Load input coordinate (one per thread) # In standard ray tracing, threadid maps to one ray coord = getraycoordinate(threadid()) # 3. Encode and prepare for MLP # Hash grid encoding is fused here encodedfeatures = fusehashencoding(coord, networkparams.grid) # 4. Warp-level iteration # Each warp handles one 16-neuron group # Warp needs to iterate W/8 times if 1 thread = 1 ray # Note: 32 threads / 16 features = 2 threads per feature # But the text says "warp handles multiplications between two 16x16 matrices" # and "iterate for W/8 times". warpid = threadid() // 32 laneid = threadid() % 32 # Determine if this thread is active for the current iteration # Using blockany for control flow management active = True # Iterate through all W groups for groupidx in range(W): # Check if we need to iterate again (compensation for 1 ray/thread) # The text implies the warp itself iterates W/8 times. # This suggests a loop structure within the warp or block logic. # Load 16 features into shared memory for the warp to process # Assuming 16 features are loaded per iteration loadfeaturesintoshared(sharedinputs, encodedfeatures, groupidx) # Tensor Core Operation: 16x16 matrix multiplication # Input: 16x16 matrix from shared memory # Weight: 16x16 matrix from fused parameters (no global memory) output = tensorcorematmul(sharedinputs, networkparams.weights[groupidx]) # Store result sharedoutputs[groupidx] = output # Control flow check # blockany evaluates true if any thread-local predicate is true # This ensures warp synchronization if branching occurs if not blockany(active): break # 5. Finalize and write output writepixel(sharedoutputs, threadid()) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Warp Divergence: GPU tensor cores require all threads in the calling warp to be active. Divergent control flow can stall execution. Use blockany to manage predicates. Memory Limits: Shared memory usage must be calculated precisely to fit within the hardware limits of the GPU. Input Mismatch: If the number of neurons is not divisible by 16, padding or handling of the remainder is required (Not given in the sources). What it is: The integration of the hash grid encoding step directly into the MLP shader code, removing separate memory lookups. Differentiation: Eliminates the overhead of fetching encoded features from global memory before MLP computation. When to choose: When memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and the encoding scheme is static or can be computed on-the-fly efficiently. Link: Fully Fused Hash Encoding What it is: Utilizing specialized GPU hardware (tensor cores) for matrix multiplications of specific dimensions (16 \times 16). Differentiation: Provides significant speedup over standard CUDA cores for dense linear algebra operations. When to choose: When running on NVIDIA GPUs with Volta architecture or newer that support tensor cores. Link: Tensor Core Acceleration Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of neurons and layers, but with a significantly reduced constant factor due to tensor core acceleration and eliminated memory latency. Memory Complexity: O(1) per threadblock for shared memory (fixed size for 16 inputs), plus the size of the network weights which are embedded in the shader code. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of threadblocks. Each block processes 16 inputs independently. Strengths: Eliminates global memory access overhead; leverages hardware tensor cores; integrates seamlessly into existing ray tracing pipelines via the wrapper function. Limitations: Requires careful control flow management to avoid warp divergence; limited to NVIDIA GPUs with tensor cores; rigid structure (16-neuron groups). When to use: High-performance real-time volume rendering where neural networks are used for density/opacity prediction and memory bandwidth is a constraint. When not: When using non-NVIDIA hardware; when the network architecture does not fit the 16-neuron group structure easily; when dynamic control flow is prevalent and cannot be masked by blockany. This method was developed as part of the Tiny-CUDA-NN framework to enable efficient neural network inference in GPU shaders. It was concurrently and independently developed by Lovegrove et al. (Deepsdf) and Weiss et al., though based on different network architectures. The technique addresses the bottleneck of global memory access in neural rendering pipelines. Interactive Volume Visualization via Multi-Resolution Hash Encoding, https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.11620, fetched 2026-10-26

name: CUDA GPU Implementation
head: CUDA Raycast Backend, cvc::volren CUDA backend
body: The CUDA GPU Implementation is a direct volume ray casting method that offloads the per-ray sampling, classification, and compositing loop to the NVIDIA CUDA architecture, mirroring the semantic behavior of a reference CPU marcher while leveraging hardware acceleration for real-time performance. It sets itself apart from CPU-based ray casting by utilizing the GPU's parallel thread architecture to significantly reduce computational complexity for intersection calculation, resampling, and compositing, and differs from generic hardware-accelerated approaches by explicitly decoupling ray traversal logic from the volume data structure to allow for adaptive algorithms and custom spatial indices. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data (scalar field or SDF), transfer function (LUT), camera parameters, and rendering options (isosurface threshold, lighting model, cut planes). Output: Final 2D image (color and depth) and optional accumulated opacity. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored in device memory (texture or linear buffer). For SDF volumes, gradient computation uses de Boor splines. Transfer Function: Baked Lookup Table (LUT) stored in device memory. Spatial Index: A dynamic redundant octree (Guennebaud et al.) used for efficient neighbor sampling and adaptive traversal. Marching Cubes Tables: constant memory storage for isosurface geometry, tracked per-device to avoid cross-GPU aliasing issues. Ray Stack: A small stack stored in local memory to manage recursion for adaptive ray traversal. Parameters: Block Size: 16x16 threads per block. Ray Cap: 32 hits per ray (historically documented as unreachable due to opacity cutoff, but implemented as a hard limit for DDA collection). Isosurface Limit: Up to 8 isosurfaces/lights/cut planes per scene. Volume Limit: Exactly one volume per render in version 1. Backend Selection: backend::cpu (default), backend::cuda (demands GPU), backend::automatic (uses GPU if available, falls back silently). Math Precision: Compiled with --usefastmath. Steps: 1. Initialization: Upload volume data and LUT from host to device (H2D) for each render pass. Ensure CUDA error state is cleared before launch to prevent spurious fallbacks from previous unrelated errors. 2. Kernel Launch: Launch one CUDA thread per pixel in 16x16 blocks. 3. Ray Generation: Each thread computes ray parameters from camera matrices and determines entry/exit points via slab intersection. 4. Ray Traversal: Isosurface Path: Use Amanatides-Woo DDA to traverse cells, enumerating every crossed cell to avoid silhouette holes. General Path: Implement either constant step size or adaptive algorithm. Adaptive recursion is managed via a local memory stack. Neighbor Access: Use the dynamic redundant octree to find neighbor samples efficiently. 5. Sampling: Sample volume data using trilinear interpolation. Compute gradients using de Boor splines for SDF volumes. 6. Classification: Apply transfer functions using the baked LUT. Apply gradient ramp, density window, and cut planes. Handle NaN corners correctly by using std::min/std::max semantics (keeping NaN accumulator) rather than fminf/fmaxf (which discard NaN) for corner min/max folds. 7. Compositing: Perform front-to-back compositing on a per-cell basis. Update accumulated color C' and opacity \alpha': C'{i} = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Ci \alpha'{i} = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Apply Blinn-Phong lighting model if enabled. 8. Depth Latch: Store depth information for the final pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intersectslab(rayorigin, raydirection, boundsmin, boundsmax): """Returns (hit, tentry, texit) for ray vs axis-aligned slab.""" tentry = -float('inf') texit = float('inf') for i in range(3): invd = 1.0 / raydirection[i] if raydirection[i] != 0.0 else float('inf') t1 = (boundsmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) invd t2 = (boundsmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) invd if invd >= 0: tentry = max(tentry, t1) texit = min(texit, t2) else: tentry = max(tentry, t2) texit = min(texit, t1) if tentry > texit or texit < 0: return False, 0.0, 0.0 return True, tentry, texit def raycastkernel(volumedata, lut, cam, isovalue, cutplanes, width, height): # Simulates execution of a single CUDA thread x, y = getthreadindex() if x >= width or y >= height: return ray = generateray(cam, x, y) hit, tentry, texit = intersectslab(ray.origin, ray.direction, volumeboundsmin, volumeboundsmax) if not hit: outcolor[y width + x] = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 t = tentry stepsize = computestepsize(ray, tentry, texit) while t < texit: pos = [ray.origin[i] + t ray.direction[i] for i in range(3)] density = samplevolumetrilinear(volumedata, pos) if issdfmode: grad = computegradientdeboor(volumedata, pos) else: grad = computegradienttrilinear(volumedata, pos) alpha, color = lookuplut(lut, density) if isisosurfacemode: if containsisosurface(pos, isovalue): lightdir = normalize(lightpos - pos) viewdir = normalize([-d for d in ray.direction]) halfdir = normalize([lightdir[i] + viewdir[i] for i in range(3)]) NdotH = max(0.0, dot(grad, halfdir)) specular = NdotH shininess color = [c diffuse + specular specfactor for c in color] else: t += stepsize continue else: if applycutplanes(pos, cutplanes): t += stepsize continue weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = [acccolor[i] + weight color[i] for i in range(3)] accalpha += weight if accalpha > 0.95: break t += stepsize outcolor[y width + x] = (acccolor[0], acccolor[1], acccolor[2], accalpha) outdepth[y width + x] = texit Slab-based raycasting is a CUDA GPU optimization for direct volume rendering that caches sampled voxels in shared memory as "slabs" to improve performance when volume data is accessed multiple times, such as for gradient calculation in Phong lighting. It sets itself apart from basic raycasting by trading increased shared memory overhead and reduced early ray termination granularity for cache hits on repeated voxel access. Unlike hardware texture caches, which benefit from large viewports where adjacent rays hit the same voxels, the slab cache is most efficient when the data set resolution is high compared to the viewport size. GPU-accelerated ray casting is a direct volume rendering method that offloads the per-ray sampling and integration loop to the graphics processor, enabling real-time interaction with volumetric datasets. It differs from CPU-based ray casting by leveraging the GPU's parallel architecture to significantly reduce computational complexity for intersection calculation, resampling, and compositing. As a standard image-order approach, it is embarrassingly parallel and supports numerous performance and quality enhancements. The Jittor Volume Render Cuvol Wrapper is a custom Jittor function that fuses the forward and backward passes of volume rendering into a single CUDA kernel launch sequence, managing memory aliases and gradient propagation for a sparse grid representation. It differs from standard CPU-based ray marchers by executing the core ray casting logic on the GPU via CUDA, while maintaining compatibility with Jittor's automatic differentiation engine. It builds on the CUDA GPU Implementation by providing a high-level API that handles the integration of sparse grid data structures (offsets, scaling, links) into the CUDA kernels. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Linear with respect to the number of rays (pixels) and the number of samples per ray. The GPU implementation provides significant speedups over CPU counterparts due to massive parallelism. Memory: Requires storage for the volume data, LUT, and spatial index (octree) in device memory. The octree allows for dynamic updates and control of memory footprint versus performance. Measured Performance: Hardware: NVIDIA GTX 1650. Resolution: 512x512. Results: Isosurface rendering: 160 ms (CPU) vs 65 ms (CUDA). Shaded Transfer Function + Gradient Ramp + Cut Plane: 270 ms (CPU) vs 113 ms (CUDA). Image Parity: 100% of pixels within 1 LSB with identical depth compared to CPU reference. Throughput: 16.5 Mray/s at 640x360 resolution for a single bunny model. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High performance for single-volume scenes; image-level parity with CPU reference; flexible traversal strategies (constant/adaptive); efficient neighbor access via octree. Limitations: Version 1 is limited to a single volume; limited to 8 isosurfaces/lights/cut planes; requires GPU memory for H2D uploads per render; constant memory management requires per-device tracking. When to Use: Real-time interactive volume rendering on NVIDIA hardware. Single-volume scenes with complex lighting or isosurface extraction. When image-level parity with a CPU reference is required. When Not to Use: Multi-volume scenes (v1 limitation). Non-NVIDIA hardware. Scenes requiring more than 8 isosurfaces/lights/cut planes. The CUDA GPU Implementation was developed as part of the libcvc library, specifically within the cvc::volren module, to provide a high-performance alternative to CPU-based volume rendering. It was introduced in pull request #323, which added the cvcGL VolRenNode and the volrenbunny demo. The implementation mirrors the semantic behavior of the existing CPU marcher, ensuring visual consistency while leveraging CUDA for speed. It builds on the principles of hardware-accelerated volume rendering, specifically utilizing the fragment shader-like parallelism of CUDA threads. cvcGL VolRenNode, CUDA raycast backend, and the volrenbunny demo, https://github.com/transfix/libcvc/pull/323, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Volume MLS Ray Casting, https://miriah.github.io/publications/volumemls.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Slab-based Raycasting
head: Slab-based Raycaster
body: Slab-based raycasting is a CUDA GPU optimization for direct volume rendering that caches sampled voxels in shared memory as "slabs" to improve performance when volume data is accessed multiple times, such as for gradient calculation in Phong lighting. It sets itself apart from basic raycasting by trading increased shared memory overhead and reduced early ray termination granularity for cache hits on repeated voxel access. Unlike hardware texture caches, which benefit from large viewports where adjacent rays hit the same voxels, the slab cache is most efficient when the data set resolution is high compared to the viewport size. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset (e.g., 16-bit or 8-bit), ray origin and direction per pixel, thread block configuration (bsx, bsy), slab depth (sd). Output: Rendered image with lighting (e.g., Phong) applied. Data Structures: Shared Memory Cache: A contiguous block of shared memory storing bsx \times bsy \times sd sampled voxels. Voxel Layout: The cache stores the voxel values (and potentially gradients) for the slab. The exact bit-packing depends on the data type (e.g., 16-bit integers for vmhead, 8-bit for engine). Parameters: bsx, bsy: Thread block dimensions. sd: Slab depth (number of voxels along the ray stored in the cache). sd{opt}: Optimal slab depth, which depends on the specific dataset. Algorithm Steps: 1. Block Initialization: Each thread in the block determines its ray parameters. The block calculates the spatial extent of the slab it needs to fetch. 2. Slab Fetch: The threads cooperatively fetch the volume data corresponding to the slab depth sd along their rays into the shared memory cache. This involves calculating global memory addresses for the start of the slab and fetching bsx \times bsy \times sd voxels. 3. Border Handling: Additional border voxels may be fetched to handle gradient calculations at the edges of the slab, introducing overhead. 4. Synchronization: All threads in the block synchronize (syncthreads()) to ensure the slab is fully loaded into shared memory before any thread begins processing. 5. Ray Casting Loop: Threads iterate through the slab depth sd. For each step: Read voxel value and gradient from shared memory. Compute lighting (e.g., Phong) using the gradient. Perform volume integration (compositing). Check for early ray termination. Note: Termination can only occur at the end of a complete slab, not after individual rays within the slab, reducing efficiency for solid data. 6. Next Slab: If the ray has not terminated and more volume remains, the block fetches the next slab into shared memory and repeats Step 3-5. 7. Write Output: Write the final accumulated color and opacity to global memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Calculate slab bounds # Determine the range of t values for the current slab slabstartt = currentslabindex sd raystepsize slabendt = (currentslabindex + 1) sd raystepsize # 2. Fetch slab into shared memory # Each thread fetches its portion of the slab tid = threadIdx.x + threadIdx.y bsx numthreads = bsx bsy # Cooperative fetch logic # Threads iterate to fill sharedvoxels and sharedgradients for i in range(0, sd): # Calculate global memory index for the voxel at current step globalidx = getvolumeindex(rayorigin + raydirection (slabstartt + i raystepsize)) # Fetch voxel value sharedvoxels[tid sd + i] = volumedata[globalidx] # Fetch gradient for lighting (if using Phong) # Note: Gradient calculation may require neighbor fetches, handled via border logic sharedgradients[(tid sd + i) 3: (tid sd + i) 3 + 3] = computegradient(volumedata, globalidx) syncthreads() # Ensure all threads have fetched their part before next step? # Actually, usually fetch is done in parallel, then sync. # Simplified: Fetch all, then sync. syncthreads() # Ensure entire slab is in shared memory # 3. Increment slab index and repeat if needed currentslabindex += 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overhead: For basic raycasting (no lighting/gradient), caching adds 23-67% overhead because each voxel is accessed only once. Early Termination: Early ray termination is less efficient because only complete slabs can be terminated, not individual rays. This leads to performance decreases with solid/non-transparent data. Shared Memory Limits: The cache size is bsx \times bsy \times sd. For optimal configurations, this can reach 15,360 bytes, close to the 16 kB maximum on older GPUs (e.g., GTX 280), limiting occupancy to one thread block per multiprocessor. Gradient Accuracy: Gradients computed from slab data may be less exact than those from direct global memory access. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of slabs traversed. Each slab fetch is O(bsx \times bsy \times sd), and processing is O(sd). Overhead is significant for basic raycasting (23-67% slower) but beneficial for Phong lighting (12-78% faster). Memory Complexity: Shared memory usage is bsx \times bsy \times sd voxels. For vmhead, this is 15,360 bytes; for engine, up to 7,936 bytes. Larger viewports increase hardware texture cache hit rates due to spatial locality, reducing the relative benefit of the slab cache. Strengths: Significant speedup for large, semi-transparent datasets with high resolution relative to viewport size, especially when lighting calculations require multiple voxel accesses. Limitations: Poor performance for small, solid datasets or basic raycasting due to overhead and inefficient early termination. Limited by shared memory size, potentially reducing occupancy. When to Use: Direct volume rendering of semi-transparent, high-resolution data with Phong lighting on GPUs with sufficient shared memory. When Not to Use: Basic raycasting, small solid datasets, or when early ray termination is critical for performance. It was designed to address the inefficiency of repeated volume data access for lighting calculations (e.g., gradients for Phong shading) by leveraging shared memory. The method is particularly relevant for medical imaging applications, where data sets typically have high resolution and are semi-transparent. body: GPU-accelerated ray casting is a direct volume rendering method that offloads ray traversal and compositing to a graphics processing unit (GPU) to achieve real-time frame rates. It differs from CPU-based approaches by leveraging massive parallelism, where each thread handles a single pixel, making it an embarrassingly parallel standard image-order approach. It builds on CUDA GPU Implementation by explicitly mapping the image grid to CUDA thread blocks and utilizing hardware features like context switching to hide memory latency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric data set V, a camera view (eye point, direction), and a transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Output: A 2D image of resolution W \times H. Data Structures: Thread Block Layout: The image is treated as a 2D CUDA grid divided into thread blocks. An M \times N thread block corresponds to an M \times N pixel image tile. Memory Layout: The source volume S can be stored in array-order or Z-order. Array-order: S[i, j, k] is at memory location i + j \cdot xsize + k \cdot xsize \cdot ysize. Z-order: A 1D layout of a 2^n tree where nearby index space points are nearby in physical memory, computed via the formulation by Pascucci and Frank. Steps: 1. Ray-Bounding Box Intersection: Calculate the entry (p{in}) and exit (p{out}) points of the ray intersecting the volume bounding box by rendering the bounding box twice: once culling front faces and once culling back faces. 2. Thread Assignment: The CUDA runtime dynamically schedules thread blocks, assigning up to eight blocks at a time to each of the GPU’s multiprocessors. 3. Ray Marching and Compositing: Each individual CUDA thread performs raycasting for a single pixel. 4. Resampling and Shading: Perform resampling and compositing on the shader to reduce running time. 5. Optimizations: The method uses parallelization, empty space skipping, early ray termination, and pre-integration for quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpuraycastkernel(threadid, blockid, blockdims, imagedims, volumetexture, transferfunction, cameramatrix, boundingbox, resolution, framebuffer): blockwidth, blockheight = blockdims imagewidth, imageheight = imagedims pixelx = blockid.x blockwidth + threadid.x pixely = blockid.y blockheight + threadid.y if pixelx >= imagewidth or pixely >= imageheight: return # Standard camera setup rayorigin = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) raydirection = normalize(cameramatrix (pixelx, pixely, 0.0)) # Calculate ray-bounding box intersections pin, pout = calculateraybboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, boundingbox) # Initialize compositing accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) t = 0.0 stepsize = distance(pin, pout) / resolution # Ray march and compositing while t < distance(pin, pout): currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t scalarvalue = samplevolume(volumetexture, currentpos) color, opacity = applytransferfunction(scalarvalue, transferfunction) accumulatedcolor = composite(accumulatedcolor, color, opacity) t += stepsize # Write result framebuffer[pixely imagewidth + pixelx] = accumulatedcolor def calculateraybboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, boundingbox): # Render bounding box twice: front culling for pin, back culling for pout pin = renderbboxfrontculled(rayorigin, raydirection, boundingbox) pout = renderbboxbackculled(rayorigin, raydirection, boundingbox) return pin, pout def normalize(v): length = sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length) def distance(a, b): return sqrt((a[0]-b[0])2 + (a[1]-b[1])2 + (a[2]-b[2])2) def samplevolume(texture, pos): # Tri-linear interpolation return texture.trilinearsample(pos) def applytransferfunction(scalar, tf): # Transfer function lookup return tf.lookup(scalar) def composite(acc, color, opacity): # Front-to-back compositing alphaout = acc[3] + (1.0 - acc[3]) opacity colorout = acc[:3] + (1.0 - acc[3]) opacity color return colorout + (0.0,) + (alphaout,) Parameters: CUDA Version: 3.2 compiler and runtime. NVIDIA Driver: Version 270.41.19. Compute Capability: Targeted at 2.0 (Fermi-series) for additional optimizations. Shared Memory: Configured to be used as L1 cache for global memory requests. ECC Support: Enabled. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Latency: The GPU uses hardware context switches between blocks within a multiprocessor to hide memory latency. Data Size Scaling: While computational complexity for interpolation and compositing is approximately constant for the same viewpoint, processing time shows a slowly wavelike rising trend as data set size increases due to increased RAM/graphics card memory addressing time and varying computing resources. Performance Variance: Final speed is dependent on the nature of volumetric data and classification settings. The foundational hardware-accelerated method defining the data flow between CPU-side texture preparation and GPU-side ray execution. Chosen when explicit pipeline control is needed for real-time displays like HTC Vive. Enhances visual quality by applying anisotropic shading models (Ward or Lafortune BRDFs) using precomputed covariance matrices. Chosen when surface orientation and anisotropy are critical. Supports Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data with wavelength-dependent absorption. Chosen for complex light models and higher quality compared to slicing-based approaches. Time Complexity: The computational complexity for tri-linear interpolation and compositing is approximately constant regardless of data set size increase, as the number of resampling points does not grow with data set size for the same viewpoint. Performance: In experiments with a 101 \times 101 \times 250 seismic data volume at 10 viewpoints (50 trials each, removing max/min), the GPU average time was 14.9947 ms (range [14.1886, 15.7046]), compared to a CPU average of 9486.24 ms (range [9250.04, 9737.42]). Scaling: When the data set size increased ten times (increment 10 \times 28 \times 25) at the same viewpoint, both GPU and CPU processing times showed a slowly wavelike rising trend due to increased memory addressing time and varying computing resources, despite constant computational complexity for interpolation and compositing. Strengths: Significantly faster than CPU algorithms due to lower computational complexity for intersection calculation, resampling, and compositing. It is an embarrassingly parallel standard image-order approach that supports many performance and quality enhancements. Limitations: Processing time can fluctuate based on the number of resampling points required for different viewpoints and intersections. GPU-accelerated ray casting was introduced by Röttger et al. in 2003 and Krüger and Westermann in 2003. It emerged as a standard image-order approach to overcome the limitations of earlier texture slicing methods, which suffered from visual artifacts and less flexibility. It is widely used in interactive visualization and real-time applications requiring high frame rates. body: The GPU Ray Casting Pipeline is a hardware-accelerated direct volume rendering method that offloads ray traversal and front-to-back compositing to the graphics processing unit to generate a 2D image from volumetric data. It differs from CPU-based implementations by leveraging massive parallelism to achieve real-time frame rates. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data sets (typically from CT and MRI images). Output: A final 2D image generated by the GPU. Data Structures: 1. Volume Model: The volumetric data is stored in a 3D texture on the GPU. The CPU reads the original data set and builds a volume model stored in a 3D texture. 2. Ray Definition: Implicitly defined by the camera position and viewport geometry for each pixel. Optical and Illumination Models: Optical Model: The emission-absorption model is used to estimate the volume-rendering integral. Illumination Model: The Blinn-Phong illumination model is used to approximate the scattering of light. Algorithm Steps: 1. Data Preparation (CPU): Read the original volumetric data set. 2. Texture Upload (CPU): Build a volume model from the data and store it in a 3D texture. 3. Transfer: Pass the 3D texture to the GPU. 4. Ray Casting (GPU): Perform ray casting on the 3D texture to generate the final image. This involves casting rays from the camera through the volume and accumulating color and opacity along each ray path using front-to-back compositing. Formulas: The rendering integral is estimated using the emission-absorption model: C = \int{t0}^{t1} c(t) e^{-\int{t0}^t \alpha(\tau) d\tau} dt where c(t) is the emitted color and \alpha(t) is the absorption coefficient at position t. Discretized with step size \Delta t, the front-to-back compositing updates are: C{out} = C{in} + ci (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + \alphai (1 - \alpha{in}) where \alphai = 1 - e^{-\alpha(ti) \Delta t} is the segment opacity. The illumination L at a sample point is calculated using the Blinn-Phong model: L = ka Ia + \sum kd Id \max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) + ks Is (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v})^p where \mathbf{n} is the surface normal, \mathbf{l} is the light direction, \mathbf{v} is the view direction, and \mathbf{r} is the reflection vector. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpuraycastingpipeline(volumedata, cameraorigin, raydirections, resx, resy, stepsize): # volumedata: 3D array of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz) with values in [0, 1] # cameraorigin: (ox, oy, oz) # raydirections: 2D list of (dx, dy, dz) for each pixel # resx, resy: integer dimensions # stepsize: float distance between samples outputcolor = [[vec3(0.0) for in range(resx)] for in range(resy)] outputalpha = [[0.0 for in range(resx)] for in range(resy)] for y in range(resy): for x in range(resx): rayo = cameraorigin rayd = normalize(raydirections[y][x]) color = vec3(0.0) alpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < 1000.0: # Ray position in world space pos = (rayo[0] + t rayd[0], rayo[1] + t rayd[1], rayo[2] + t rayd[2]) # Boundary check (assuming volume occupies [0, 1]^3) if not (0.0 <= pos[0] < 1.0 and 0.0 <= pos[1] < 1.0 and 0.0 <= pos[2] < 1.0): break # Tri-linear interpolation to get density density = trilinearsample(volumedata, pos) # Segment opacity via Beer-Lambert law alphaseg = 1.0 - exp(-density stepsize) # Gradient for normal estimation grad = computegradient(volumedata, pos) normal = normalize(grad) viewdir = normalize((-rayd[0], -rayd[1], -rayd[2])) lightdir = normalize((0.5, 1.0, 0.3)) halfvec = normalize((lightdir[0] + viewdir[0], lightdir[1] + viewdir[1], lightdir[2] + viewdir[2])) diff = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) spec = pow(max(dot(normal, halfvec), 0.0), 32.0) colorseg = vec3(0.8, 0.8, 0.8) (0.2 + 0.6 diff + 0.2 spec) # Front-to-back compositing weight = alphaseg (1.0 - alpha) color = color + colorseg weight alpha = alpha + weight if alpha >= 0.99: break t += stepsize outputcolor[y][x] = color outputalpha[y][x] = alpha return outputcolor, outputalpha def trilinearsample(data, p): ix, iy, iz = p[0] (data.shape[0]-1), p[1] (data.shape[1]-1), p[2] (data.shape[2]-1) x0, y0, z0 = floor(ix), floor(iy), floor(iz) x1, y1, z1 = x0+1, y0+1, z0+1 dx, dy, dz = ix-x0, iy-y0, iz-z0 def v(x, y, z): return data[min(x, data.shape[0]-1)][min(y, data.shape[1]-1)][min(z, data.shape[2]-1)] c00 = v(x0, y0, z0) (1-dx) + v(x1, y0, z0) dx c10 = v(x0, y1, z0) (1-dx) + v(x1, y1, z0) dx c01 = v(x0, y0, z1) (1-dx) + v(x1, y0, z1) dx c11 = v(x0, y1, z1) (1-dx) + v(x1, y1, z1) dx return c00 (1-dy) (1-dz) + c10 dx (1-dy) (1-dz) + c01 (1-dy) dz + c11 dx (1-dy) dz def computegradient(data, p): eps = 0.001 def v(x, y, z): return data[min(max(floor(x(data.shape[0]-1)),0), data.shape[0]-1)][min(max(floor(y(data.shape[1]-1)),0), data.shape[1]-1)][min(max(floor(z(data.shape[2]-1)),0), data.shape[2]-1)] gx = v(p[0]+eps, p[1], p[2]) - v(p[0]-eps, p[1], p[2]) gy = v(p[0], p[1]+eps, p[2]) - v(p[0], p[1]-eps, p[2]) gz = v(p[0], p[1], p[2]+eps) - v(p[0], p[1], p[2]-eps) return (gx, gy, gz) def normalize(v): l = sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) if l > 0 else (0,0,0) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def vec3(r, g, b): return (r, g, b) def floor(x): return int(x) if x >= 0 else int(x) - name: GPU-based Raycasting Rendering
head: GPU-accelerated volume ray casting, Hardware-accelerated direct volume rendering
body: GPU-based raycasting renders volumetric datasets by casting rays from the camera through the volume on the GPU, accumulating color and opacity along each ray path. It differs from CPU-based raycasting by leveraging massive parallelism to achieve real-time frame rates, which is mandatory for high-refresh-rate displays like the HTC Vive (90 Hz). It builds on the GPU Ray Casting Pipeline. Inputs: Volumetric dataset (scalar field). Camera parameters (position, orientation, projection). Transfer function (mapping scalar values to color and opacity). Optional pre-computed gradient data. Outputs: Final image (color and alpha per pixel). Data Structures: Volume Texture: 3D texture storing scalar values. Gradient Texture: 3D RGBA texture storing pre-computed gradients, where each voxel stores gradient direction and magnitude. Transfer Function Texture: 1D or 2D texture mapping scalar values to RGBA. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel in the viewport, generate a ray originating from the camera position and passing through the pixel center in world space. 2. Ray-Volume Intersection: Determine the entry (t{min}) and exit (t{max}) distances of the ray with the volume bounding box. If t{max} < 0 or t{min} > t{max}, the ray misses the volume or points away from it. 3. Step Size Calculation: Determine the step size along the ray. This may be fixed or adaptive based on resolution and desired accuracy. 4. Sampling Loop: a. Sample the volume texture at the current ray position to get the scalar value v. b. Sample the transfer function using v to get color c and opacity \alpha. c. If pre-computed gradients are used, sample the gradient texture at the current position to get \nabla v. Otherwise, compute gradients on-the-fly using finite differences, which requires 6 extra texture fetches. d. Compositing: Update the accumulated color C{acc} and opacity A{acc} using front-to-back compositing: C{acc} = C{acc} + c \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - A{acc}) A{acc} = A{acc} + \alpha \cdot (1 - A{acc}) e. Advance the ray position by the step size. f. If A{acc} \geq 1 or the ray has exited the volume, terminate the loop. 5. Post-Processing: Apply any final image processing (e.g., tone mapping, anti-aliasing). Parameters: Step Size: Determines sampling density. Smaller steps increase accuracy but reduce performance. Gradient Pre-computation: Trade-off between memory usage and computational cost. Pre-computing gradients saves texture fetches but increases memory bandwidth requirements. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overlapping Material Ranges: When transfer functions for different materials have overlapping scalar ranges, the color contribution should be set as the average of the non-transparent materials for the sample, rather than a sum. Empty-Space Skipping: Rays traversing transparent regions can be skipped to avoid unnecessary sampling. Boundary Conditions: Ensure correct handling of rays that do not intersect the volume or intersect only at the boundary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpuraycasting(volumetex, gradienttex, tftex, camera, viewport, volumebbox, stepsize, backgroundcolor, useprecomputedgradients): image = [[backgroundcolor] viewport.width for in range(viewport.height)] for y in range(viewport.height): for x in range(viewport.width): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.generateray(x, y, viewport) tmin, tmax = rayboxintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebbox) if tmax < 0 or tmin > tmax: continue acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 t = tmin while t < tmax and accalpha < 1.0: pos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] v = volumetex.sample(pos) c, alpha = tftex.sample(v) if useprecomputedgradients: grad = gradienttex.sample(pos) else: grad = computegradientonfly(volumetex, pos) weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor[0] += c[0] weight acccolor[1] += c[1] weight acccolor[2] += c[2] weight accalpha += weight t += stepsize image[y][x] = acccolor + [accalpha] return image def rayboxintersect(origin, direction, bbox): tmin, tmax = -float('inf'), float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bbox.min[i] or origin[i] > bbox.max[i]: return -float('inf'), -float('inf') else: t1 = (bbox.min[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bbox.max[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return tmin, tmax def computegradientonfly(tex, pos): # Standard central differences requiring 6 texture fetches dx = tex.sample([pos[0]+0.5, pos[1], pos[2]]) - tex.sample([pos[0]-0.5, pos[1], pos[2]]) dy = tex.sample([pos[0], pos[1]+0.5, pos[2]]) - tex.sample([pos[0], pos[1]-0.5, pos[2]]) dz = tex.sample([pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]+0.5]) - tex.sample([pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]-0.5]) return [dx, dy, dz] Renders the volume at a lower resolution viewport and scales the result up to the target display resolution using interpolation to reduce computational cost. It differs from full-resolution raycasting by trading spatial resolution for performance; effective because raycasting is a screen-space algorithm. Used in Unity 3D VR systems for HTC Vive to achieve real-time rendering at 90 fps, allowing comfortable movement without motion sickness. Renders function-based microstructure models directly using accelerated ray-tracing/ray-casting on the GPU, avoiding intermediate representations like BRep or voxels. Performance reaches approximately 20 frames per second on an NVidia 9600 graphics card for a 512x512 image size, independent of microstructure complexity. Rendering time remains almost identical for lattices with different densities because the complexity of the underlying mathematical function does not depend on the density of the microstructures. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the average number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: Scales with the volume dataset size, plus additional memory for pre-computed gradient textures if used. Performance: Achieves real-time frame rates (e.g., 90 fps) on modern GPUs, essential for VR applications. Function-based models achieve ~20 fps on an NVidia 9600 for 512x512 resolution. Strengths: High parallelism, real-time capability, flexible transfer functions, and effective optimization via reduced viewports or pre-computed gradients. Limitations: Pre-computed gradients increase memory usage, while reduced viewports trade spatial resolution for performance. Performance depends on step size and transfer function complexity. When to Use: Real-time visualization of volumetric data, especially in VR/AR environments or for interactive inspection. When Not to Use: When high spatial resolution is critical and performance is not a constraint, or when memory bandwidth is severely limited. GPU-based raycasting was developed to overcome the performance limitations of CPU-based raycasting for volume visualization. It is used in medical imaging for tasks such as MR bile duct examination and in VR/AR applications with head-mounted displays like the HTC Vive. The technique has also been applied to the direct rendering of function-based microstructure models for digital fabrication workflows. name: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains
head: Direct Volume Rendering of Stack-Based Terrains, GPU Raycasting for SBRT, SBRT Raycasting
body: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains (SBRT) is a direct volume rendering technique adapted for geoscientific terrain data, implemented on the GPU to enable real-time visualization. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering complex, layered subsurface structures by casting rays from a virtual camera through each output buffer pixel and composing sampled colors along the ray path. What sets it apart from standard raycasting is its specific adaptation to the SBRT data structure, which uses a stack-based representation of geological intervals, and its hybrid deferred strategy for normal calculation to avoid the performance bottlenecks associated with 3D convolution on sparse stack data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: SBRT dataset (grid dimensions grid{ancho} \times grid{alto}, maximum intervals m), camera parameters, light source position, Transfer Function (discrete lookup table), and rendering resolution. Output: Final color image buffer. Data Structures: The volumetric data is encoded into one or two GPU structures (textures or buffers). The specific layout depends on the chosen memory approach (see Subtopics). Common components include: Index Structure: Maps 2D grid coordinates to stack start positions and sizes. Interval Structure: Stores material attributes and accumulated heights for each interval. Transfer Function: Discrete lookup table mapping material values to colors. Numbered Steps: 1. Proxy Geometry Setup: Use the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the terrain dataset as the proxy geometry for ray intersection. This maintains simplicity and fits the terrain shape. 2. Data Encoding: Encode the SBRT data into the chosen GPU structure(s) (e.g., 2D textures, 3D texture, or SSBOs). The data is organized such that the stack is extracted first, then iterated over its intervals. 3. Ray Casting Loop: For each pixel in the output buffer, cast a ray from the virtual camera. 4. Ray-Box Intersection: Intersect the ray with the bounding box to determine the entry and exit points of the ray within the terrain volume. 5. Adaptive Ray Marching: Traverse the SBRT stack along the ray to sample attributes and compose color: Empty Space: When the ray is in empty space, the step length equals the terrain cell resolution. Non-Empty Material: Once the ray collides with non-empty material, increase the sampling frequency to avoid artifacts. Stack Traversal: For each step, identify the current stack using the index structure, then iterate through its intervals to find the active material. 6. Color Composition: Map the sampled material values to colors using the discrete Transfer Function. Use front-to-back alpha blending for composition. 7. Termination: Stop the ray algorithm when the accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold of 1 - \epsilon, assuming new contributions are irrelevant. 8. Deferred Normal Calculation (Hybrid Strategy): Pass 1: Render the color from the Transfer Function and store the ray-collision distance (depth) in a depth map. Pass 2: Calculate surface normals and compose the final pixel color. Obtain the 3D position of the convolution mask center by performing inverse projection from the depth map. Determine if a voxel is occupied: project the inverse projection value again; if the resulting depth is less than the camera-to-inverse-projection distance, the voxel is part of the surface. Calculate normals based on occupied neighbors in the mask. 9. Lighting: Apply the Lambertian diffuse BRDF lighting model to the final color. Formulas: Lambertian Diffuse BRDF: Ip = ia + kd (\vec{L} \cdot \vec{N}) id Where: Ip: Final intensity at point p. ia: Ambient light intensity. id: Diffuse light intensity. kd: Lambertian reflectance. \vec{L}: Vector from the object to the light source. \vec{N}: Surface normal vector at point p. Super-texels Dimensions (Approach 2): texture{ancho} = grid{ancho} \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil texture{alto} = grid{alto} \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil Where \lceil \cdot \rceil is the ceiling operator and m is the maximum number of intervals among all stacks. Rectangular Optimization (Approach 2 Variant): Minimize rec{ancho} rec{alto} subject to: rec{ancho} + rec{alto} \text{ is minimized (implied by context of minimizing area/overhead)} rec{ancho} rec{alto} \ge m rec{ancho} > 0, rec{alto} > 0 Where rec{ancho} and rec{alto} are the dimensions of the rectangular super-texel region. Parameters: \epsilon: Threshold for opacity termination. Not given in the sources. m: Maximum number of intervals among all stacks in the SBRT. SSBO Minimum Size: OpenGL implementations must support SSBOs of at least 128 MB (read/write). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Calculation Bottleneck: Using 3D convolution for normal calculation in SBRT causes a performance bottleneck because each voxel access may require locating a new stack and iterating it sequentially. The hybrid deferred strategy avoids this. Memory Waste: Approach 1 (Two 2D Textures) wastes memory because the last cells of the last row usually remain unoccupied. Precision/Boundaries: The ray intersection with the bounding box must be handled correctly to avoid sampling outside the valid data range. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersbrt(camera, lightposition, gridancho, gridalto, m, epsilon): # Pass 1: Color and Depth for y in range(gridalto): for x in range(gridancho): rayorigin = camera.getorigin() raydirection = camera.getraydirection(x, y) # Intersect with bounding box tmin, tmax = intersectaabb(rayorigin, raydirection) if tmin > tmax: continue # Ray misses terrain # Adaptive ray marching t = tmin accumulatedopacity = 0.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) while t < tmax and accumulatedopacity < 1.0 - epsilon: # Determine step size if isemptyspace(rayorigin + raydirection t): step = terraincellresolution else: step = smallstepsize # Increased frequency for non-empty # Sample SBRT at current position material, height = samplesbrt(rayorigin + raydirection t, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m) # Map to color samplecolor = transferfunction[material] # Front-to-back alpha blending alpha = samplecolor[3] # Assuming RGBA color = color + samplecolor (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedopacity += alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) t += step # Store depth for normal calculation depthmap[x, y] = t # Ray-collision distance # Store intermediate color (or final if no normals needed, but here we do deferred) # Note: The source says "obtenemos el color devuelto por la FT" in pass 1 # and "componemos el color final" in pass 2. # We store the unlit color for pass 2. finalcolorbuffer[x, y] = color # Pass 2: Normal Calculation and Final Lighting for y in range(gridalto): for x in range(gridancho): # Get depth from pass 1 depth = depthmap[x, y] # Inverse projection to get 3D position pos3d = inverseproject(camera, x, y, depth) # Calculate normal using hybrid deferred strategy # Check neighbors in a mask around pos3d normal = calculatenormalhybrid(pos3d, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m) # Get unlit color from pass 1 unlitcolor = finalcolorbuffer[x, y] # Apply Lambertian lighting L = normalize(lightposition - pos3d) N = normalize(normal) kd = 1.0 # Example reflectance ia = 0.2 # Ambient intensity id = 0.8 # Diffuse intensity diffuse = kd dot(L, N) id finalintensity = ia + diffuse # Apply lighting to color finalcolor = unlitcolor finalintensity # Write to final buffer writetooutputbuffer(x, y, finalcolor) def samplesbrt(position, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m): # Project position to grid coordinates gx, gz = projecttogrid(position) # Get stack index and size from index buffer stackstart = indexbuffer[gx, gz].R stacksize = indexbuffer[gx, gz].G # Iterate through intervals in interval buffer # Interval buffer stores [material (R), accumulatedheight (G)] currentheight = 0.0 for i in range(stacksize): intervalidx = stackstart + i material = intervalbuffer[intervalidx].R intervalheight = intervalbuffer[intervalidx].G # Check if position is within this interval # Note: The source says "comparar esta altura con G2" # Assuming G2 is the accumulated height of the current interval # and we need to check if the ray's height relative to the stack start is within this interval # This is a simplified interpretation; exact logic depends on SBRT height encoding if currentheight <= position.y < currentheight + intervalheight: return material, intervalheight currentheight += intervalheight return EMPTYMATERIAL, 0.0 def calculatenormalhybrid(pos3d, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m): # Define mask size (e.g., 3x3x3) masksize = 1 normal = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Check neighbors in the mask for dx in range(-masksize, masksize + 1): for dy in range(-masksize, masksize + 1): for dz in range(-masksize, masksize + 1): neighborpos = pos3d + (dx, dy, dz) # Check if neighbor is occupied # "Un vóxel se considera ocupado si no está ocluido por el modelo real" # "si al proyectar de nuevo el valor obtenido por la proyección inversa, # se obtiene un valor de profundidad menor que la distancia de la cámara # a la posición de la proyección inversa" # This implies checking if the neighbor's depth in the depth map is valid # and corresponds to a surface voxel # Simplified: Check if the neighbor is part of the surface if issurfacevoxel(neighborpos, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m): # Add vector to normal normal += normalize(neighborpos - pos3d) return normalize(normal) def issurfacevoxel(pos, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m): # Check if voxel is occupied and not occluded # This requires checking the SBRT data at pos material, = samplesbrt(pos, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m) if material == EMPTYMATERIAL: return False # Check occlusion: project pos again and compare depths # This is a simplified check; actual implementation requires access to depth map # and camera parameters return True # Placeholder for complex occlusion check Uses an Index Texture (grid{ancho} \times grid{alto}) storing stack start (R) and size (G), and an Interval Texture storing material (R) and accumulated height (G). Stacks are stored row-order in the Interval Texture. Sets apart: Simple indexing but wastes memory in the last row. Choose when: Memory is not a critical constraint and simplicity is preferred. Link: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains Uses a single 2D Texture with dimensions grid{ancho} \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil \times grid{alto} \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil. Regions of size \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil \times \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil act as super-texels. Sets apart: Pseudo-indexing via regions. Choose when: m is small and square regions are efficient. Link: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains Uses a 2D Texture of dimensions (grid{ancho} m) \times grid{alto}. Intervals stored along x-axis. Sets apart: Checks spatial coherence against 3D textures. Choose when: Spatial coherence is a priority. Link: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains Uses a 3D Texture of dimensions grid{ancho} \times grid{alto} \times m. Intervals stored along z-axis. Sets apart: Standard 3D texture access. Choose when: 3D texture hardware is efficient. Link: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains Uses two Shader Storage Buffer Objects (SSBOs) for indices and intervals, using OpenGL std430 layout. Sets apart: Flexible array sizes, large memory support (128 MB min). Choose when: Large datasets or dynamic stack sizes. Link: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays (pixels) and the average stack depth. Adaptive marching reduces steps in empty space. Normal calculation is deferred and depends on output buffer size, not data size. Memory Complexity: Depends on the chosen approach. Approach 1 wastes memory in the last row. Approach 5 requires SSBOs of at least 128 MB. Measured Performance: Enables real-time rendering and visual operations such as cross-sections, material layer attenuation, and borehole visualization. Scaling: Scales with GPU hardware capabilities. Avoids CPU-GPU data transfer bottleneck. Strengths: Real-time performance, efficient memory usage with SSBOs, avoids 3D convolution bottleneck for normals. Limitations: Normal calculation is limited in number compared to gradient-based methods, though sufficient for scientific applications. Approach 1 wastes memory. When to use: Geoscientific visualization requiring real-time interaction with layered terrain data. When not: When high-fidelity, gradient-based normals are critical and performance is not a constraint. Origin: Proposed by A. Graciano, A.J. Rueda & F.R. Feito in 2017. History: Developed to address the bottleneck of data transfer between CPU and GPU in visualization systems and to enable real-time operations on SBRT data. Usage: Geoscientific applications, terrain visualization, subsurface structure visualization.
