name: GPU Direct Volume Rendering with Anisotropic Shading
head: CUDA DVR
body: A GPU-based direct volume ray casting algorithm that enhances visual quality by applying anisotropic shading models (Ward or Lafortune BRDFs) to volumetric data. It distinguishes itself from standard isotropic shading by precomputing and storing covariance matrices alongside gradients, allowing the reconstruction of local surface orientation and anisotropy axes on-the-fly during ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D scalar field data, precomputed 3D textures for normals and covariance matrices, transfer function TF, list of light sources LS, Henyey-Greenstein phase function f{d,hg}, Ward BRDF function f{s,w}, background radiance Lb, glossiness parameter \kappaw, scaling factor \gammaw, and diffuse coefficient kd. Outputs: Final color image with accumulated radiance and opacity. Data Structures: Scalar Field: Stored in a 3D texture. Prefiltered Normals: Stored in a 3D texture, quantized to 8 bits per channel. Covariance Matrices: Stored in a 3D texture as symmetric 2x2 matrices, quantized to 8 bits per channel. Eigenvectors are not stored; they are computed during rendering to avoid interpolation inconsistencies. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Optional): If prefiltering is enabled, iterate over all voxels x, read the symmetric 2x2 matrix C, apply Gaussian filtering, and store the result back. 2. Ray Casting Loop: For each pixel P: a. Initialize accumulated radiance L = 0 and transmittance T = 0. b. Compute the eye ray and set view direction \omega = -\text{ray.direction}. c. While the ray has not finished traversing the volume: i. Get the current ray position x. ii. Sample the symmetric 2x2 covariance matrix C and the gradient G{\sigma t} from their respective 3D textures at x. iii. Compute the surface normal N{\sigma t} = G{\sigma t} / \text{length}(G{\sigma t}). iv. Perform eigenanalysis on C to obtain eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and eigenvectors \Lambda1, \Lambda2. v. Transform eigenvectors \Lambda1, \Lambda2 to world space and normalize them using N{\sigma t} to obtain tangent vectors U and V. vi. Compute Ward anisotropy parameters uw, vw from \lambda1, \lambda2, \kappaw, \gammaw. (For Lafortune BRDF, compute corresponding parameters analogously). vii. Compute the specular coefficient ks = \text{length}(G{\sigma t}). viii. Initialize light contribution Li = 0. ix. For each light source ls \in LS: 1. Compute light direction \omega0 = \text{lightDirection}(x, ls). 2. Compute the BRDF value: f = kd f{d,hg}(\omega0, \omega) + ks f{s,w}(U, V, N{\sigma t}, uw, vw, \omega0, \omega) (\omega0 \cdot N{\sigma t}) 3. Add to light contribution: Li = Li + f \cdot \text{incomingRadianceFromLightSource}(x, ls) x. Composite the light contribution into the accumulator using the transfer function: (L, T) = \text{composite}(x, TF, L, T, Li) d. Return the final color: T \cdot Lb + L. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpuanisotropicvolumerendering( scalarfieldtexture, normaltexture, covariancetexture, transferfunction, lightsources, kappaw, gammaw, kd, backgroundradiance, lightdirectionfunc, incomingradiancefunc, compositefunc): # Preprocessing step (optional, done once) # for x in allvoxels: # C = readsymmetric2x2matrix(covariancetexture, x) # C = filtergaussian(C) # writesymmetric2x2matrix(covariancetexture, C, x) for pixel in screen: L = 0.0 T = 0.0 ray = computeeyeray(pixel) omega = -ray.direction # View direction while raycastingnotfinished(ray): x = getrayposition(ray) # Sample precomputed data C = samplesymmetric2x2matrix(covariancetexture, x) Gsigmat = samplegradient(normaltexture, x) # Compute normal Nsigmat = normalize(Gsigmat) # Eigenanalysis of covariance matrix # Sources do not provide explicit eigenanalysis formulas lambda1, lambda2, Lambda1, Lambda2 = computeeigenanalysis(C) # Transform eigenvectors to world space and normalize # Sources do not provide explicit transformation formulas U, V = transformtoworldspaceandnormalize(Lambda1, Lambda2, Nsigmat) # Compute Ward parameters # Sources do not provide explicit Ward parameter formulas uw, vw = computewardparameters(lambda1, lambda2, kappaw, gammaw) # Specular coefficient from gradient magnitude ks = length(Gsigmat) Li = 0.0 for ls in lightsources: omega0 = lightdirectionfunc(x, ls) # Diffuse term using Henyey-Greenstein phase function # Sources do not provide explicit phase function formula fdiffuse = kd henyeygreensteinphase(omega0, omega) # Specular term using Ward BRDF # Sources do not provide explicit BRDF formula fspecular = ks wardbrdf(U, V, Nsigmat, uw, vw, omega0, omega) dot(omega0, Nsigmat) f = fdiffuse + fspecular Li += f incomingradiancefunc(x, ls) # Composite step L, T = compositefunc(x, transferfunction, L, T, Li) return T backgroundradiance + L Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Eigenvector Interpolation: Eigenvectors must not be stored or interpolated directly. Interpolating eigenvectors leads to inconsistent results due to sign ambiguity and discontinuities. Instead, the covariance matrix components are interpolated, and eigenanalysis is performed on-the-fly. Gradient Normalization: The normal N{\sigma t} is derived from the gradient G{\sigma t}. If the gradient magnitude is zero, normalization fails. Quantization: Values are quantized to 8 bits per channel. This may introduce artifacts in high-precision requirements, though it is generally sufficient for gradient-based shading. Performance: Interactive visualization is achievable on GPU hardware. On-the-fly eigenanalysis is preferred over precomputing eigenvectors to balance memory usage and computational cost. Strengths: Provides realistic anisotropic shading effects for volumetric data, enhancing the perception of structure and orientation. Limitations: Prefiltering increases the memory footprint, which can become problematic for medium-sized data sets. On-the-fly curvature estimation is too expensive for interactive visualization. The method is described in "Anisotropic Ambient Volume Shading". It builds on the concept of using geometry tensors (covariance matrices) to estimate local surface orientation and anisotropy in volumetric data. The approach avoids the high cost of on-the-fly curvature estimation by prefiltering and storing the necessary tensor data. name: GPU-based Parallel Ray Casting
head: Volume Ray Casting using Different GPU based Parallel APIs
body: GPU-based parallel ray casting implements volume rendering algorithms by leveraging various GPU parallel Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) to optimize performance. It differs from CPU-based approaches by exploiting the highly parallel nature of the GPU to accelerate ray traversal and shading. Unlike hardware-accelerated APIs such as OptiX or DirectX Raytracing, standard CUDA implementations require the programmer to manually write all code for acceleration structure construction, ray traversal, and intersection logic. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset (scalar field), camera parameters (origin, direction), and rendering resolution. Output: Final framebuffer image. Data Structures: Acceleration Structure: Typically a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) or similar spatial partitioning structure, built manually by the programmer. Ray Data: Origin and direction vectors for each pixel or thread. Volume Data: 3D texture or linear array representing the scalar field. Intersection Approaches: The intersection of the ray with the volume object is calculated using one of two primary approaches: 1. Rasterization: Uses back-face culling to find the entry point (first hit) and front-face culling to find the exit point (last hit). 2. Ray/Box Intersection Test: Uses a divide-and-conquer approach to determine intersections with volume elements. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Launch parallel threads (one per pixel or ray) on the GPU. 2. Acceleration Structure Build: Construct the BVH or similar structure on the GPU memory. 3. Ray Traversal: Traverse the acceleration structure to find the entry and exit points of the ray within the volume. If using rasterization, calculate entry/exit via culling. If using ray/box intersection, perform the divide-and-conquer test. 4. Sampling and Shading: For each step along the ray between entry and exit, sample the volume data and apply transfer functions. 5. Compositing: Accumulate color and opacity along the ray to produce the final pixel value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastkernel(volumedata, accelerationstructure, camera, width, height, x, y): # 1. Calculate ray origin and direction for this pixel rayorigin = camera.getorigin(x, y) raydirection = camera.getdirection(x, y) # 2. Find entry and exit points # Approach A: Rasterization (if applicable) # entrypoint = findfirsthitbackfaceculled(volume, rayorigin, raydirection) # exitpoint = findlasthitfrontfaceculled(volume, rayorigin, raydirection) # Approach B: Ray/Box Intersection with BVH (Manual Implementation) # Programmer must implement BVH traversal and ray-box intersection entrypoint, exitpoint = traversebvhandintersect(accelerationstructure, rayorigin, raydirection) # 3. Sample and Composite color = vec3(0.0) alpha = 0.0 t = entrypoint stepsize = (exitpoint - entrypoint) / numsamples while t < exitpoint: # Sample volume at current ray position density = samplevolume(volumedata, rayorigin + t raydirection) # Apply transfer function and shading samplecolor, samplealpha = applytransferfunction(density) # Front-to-back compositing color = color + samplecolor samplealpha (1.0 - alpha) alpha = alpha + samplealpha (1.0 - alpha) t += stepsize return color Parameters: Num Samples: Number of steps between entry and exit points. Not given in the sources. Transfer Function: Maps density to color and opacity. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors in ray-box intersection tests may cause gaps or artifacts. Empty Space: Rays passing through empty space should be skipped efficiently using the acceleration structure. Memory Coalescing: Ensure volume data access patterns are coalesced for optimal memory bandwidth. Describes the general pipeline stages for GPU ray casting. Link Focuses on anisotropic shading techniques within GPU ray casting. Link Adapts GPU ray casting for Adaptive Mesh Refinement data. Link Time Complexity: Theoretical complexity is reduced to O(\log n / \log 2) compared to conventional ray casting due to the binary tree-like structure of the acceleration structure. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the volume data and the acceleration structure. Not given in the sources. Performance: Performance varies across APIs. Comparisons are made among OpenCL, OpenGL with fragment shader, CUDA, and OpenGL with compute shader. Strengths: High parallelism allows for significant speedup over CPU implementations. Limitations: Requires manual implementation of traversal and intersection logic in CUDA, increasing development effort. Does not utilize specialized RTX hardware accelerators unless using APIs like OptiX. When to Use: When hardware-accelerated APIs (OptiX, DXR) are not available or when custom traversal logic is required. When Not to Use: When maximum performance is needed and RTX hardware is available; consider OptiX instead. GPU-based parallel ray casting has been implemented using various APIs including OpenCL, OpenGL (fragment and compute shaders), and CUDA. CUDA, as a general-purpose compute API, does not have built-in raycasting facilities or access to RTX hardware accelerators, requiring programmers to write all code for acceleration structure building, traversal, and intersection. This contrasts with APIs like OptiX, which provide built-in acceleration for ray traversal and intersection using specialized hardware. name: Jittor Volume Render Cuvol Wrapper
body: The Jittor Volume Render Cuvol Wrapper is a custom Jittor function that fuses the forward and backward passes of volume rendering into a single CUDA kernel launch sequence, managing memory aliases and gradient propagation for a sparse grid representation. It differs from standard CPU-based ray marchers by executing the core ray casting logic on the GPU via CUDA while maintaining compatibility with Jittor's automatic differentiation engine. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse grid object (containing density, SH coefficients, basis data, links, offsets, scaling), ray origins and directions (tensors), and a RenderOptions struct. Outputs: Rendered color buffer, confidence/confidence map, and optionally a log-transparency buffer if background rendering is enabled. Data Structures: RenderOptions: A struct passed to CUDA kernels containing: backgroundbrightness (float), stepsize (float), sigmathresh (float), stopthresh (float), nearclip (float), usesphericclip (bool), lastsampleopaque (bool). Sparse Grid: Contains links (connectivity), offset, scaling, basisdim, basistype, basisdata, densitydata, shdata, backgroundlinks, backgrounddata. Steps: 1. Prepare Grid Offsets and Scaling: If gridcoords is true, use identity scaling. Otherwise, scale grid offsets and scaling by the number of links: gsz = jt.array(np.array(grid.links.shape[0])); self.gridoffset = grid.offsetgsz-0.5; self.gridscaling = grid.scalinggsz;. 2. Initialize Log Transmit Buffer: If background rendering is enabled, create an empty buffer logtransmit with shape [rays.origins.shape[0]] and dtype matching rays.origins, then call.stopgrad() to prevent gradient flow through this buffer during backpropagation. 3. Launch Forward CUDA Kernel: Pass grid data (density, SH, links, offset, scaling, background links/data, basis info), ray origins/directions, RenderOptions, output buffer, and logtransmit pointer (or nullptr if no background) to renderraykernel. 4. Launch Background Kernel: If background is used, launch renderbackgroundkernel subsequently to handle background color integration using the logtransmit buffer. 5. Gradient Computation: Initialize gradient buffers for density, SH, basis, and background data. Determine if gradients are needed for basis and background data based on requiresgrad flags. 6. Launch Backward CUDA Kernel: Pass gradients, color cache, rays, RenderOptions, and output gradient structure to renderraybackwardkernel. 7. Launch Background Backward Kernel: If background is used, launch renderbackgroundbackwardkernel to compute gradients related to background parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jittor as jt import numpy as np class VolumeRenderCuvol(jt.Function): def execute(self, grid, rays, opt, usebackground=False): # 1. Prepare grid offsets and scaling if grid.gridcoords: self.gridoffset = 0.0 self.gridscaling = 1.0 else: gsz = jt.array(np.array(grid.links.shape[0])) self.gridoffset = grid.offset gsz - 0.5 self.gridscaling = grid.scaling gsz # 2. Initialize logtransmit buffer if background is used if usebackground: self.logtransmit = jt.empty([rays.origins.shape[0]], dtype=rays.origins.dtype).stopgrad() else: self.logtransmit = None # 3. Initialize output and cache buffers N = rays.origins.shape[0] output = jt.zeros([N, 4], dtype=rays.origins.dtype) colorcache = jt.zeros([N, 4], dtype=rays.origins.dtype) # 4. Ray marching loop (orchestrated by CUDA kernel, shown here for correctness) # The actual traversal and sampling are fused into a single CUDA kernel launch. for i in range(N): o = rays.origins[i] d = rays.dirs[i] # Compute ray-box intersection with the scaled grid bounds tmin, tmax = computerayboxintersection(o, d, self.gridoffset, self.gridscaling) tstart = max(opt.nearclip, tmin) if tstart > tmax: output[i] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] continue t = tstart transmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = jt.zeros(3, dtype=rays.origins.dtype) maxalpha = 0.0 while t < tmax and transmittance > opt.stopthresh: pos = o + d t # Sparse grid traversal and trilinear interpolation density = samplesparsegrid(grid, pos, self.gridoffset, self.gridscaling) if density < opt.sigmathresh: t += opt.stepsize continue alpha = 1.0 - jt.exp(-density opt.stepsize) color = computecolor(grid, pos) accumulatedcolor += transmittance alpha color transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) maxalpha = max(maxalpha, alpha) t += opt.stepsize output[i,:3] = accumulatedcolor output[i, 3] = 1.0 - transmittance colorcache[i] = [accumulatedcolor[0], accumulatedcolor[1], accumulatedcolor[2], maxalpha] # 5. Launch background kernel if needed if usebackground: # renderbackgroundkernel uses logtransmit to integrate background color pass return output, colorcache def grad(self, gradoutput): # 6. Initialize gradient buffers graddensity = jt.zeroslike(self.grid.densitydata) gradsh = jt.zeroslike(self.grid.shdata) gradbasis = jt.zeroslike(self.grid.basisdata) gradbackground = jt.zeroslike(self.grid.backgrounddata) if self.grid.requiresgradbackground else None # 7. Launch backward CUDA kernel # renderraybackwardkernel computes gradients for density, SH, and basis data pass # 8. Launch background backward kernel if needed if self.usebackground: # renderbackgroundbackwardkernel computes gradients for background parameters pass return graddensity, gradsh, gradbasis, gradbackground def computerayboxintersection(o, d, offset, scaling): # Standard axis-aligned bounding box intersection invd = 1.0 / d t1 = (offset - o) invd t2 = (offset + scaling - o) invd tmin = max(min(t1), min(t2)) tmax = min(max(t1), max(t2)) return tmin, tmax def samplesparsegrid(grid, pos, offset, scaling): # Sparse grid traversal and trilinear interpolation is handled by the CUDA kernel return 0.0 # Placeholder for grid lookup logic def computecolor(grid, pos): # SH/basis evaluation is handled by the CUDA kernel return jt.zeros(3, dtype=pos.dtype) Parameters: opt: RenderOptions struct passed to CUDA kernels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision depends on the underlying CUDA compilation flags and hardware. Memory Aliases: The wrapper manages memory aliases for sparse grid data; incorrect handling of links and offset can lead to out-of-bounds access. Background Rendering: If usebackground is true, the logtransmit buffer must be correctly initialized and passed to both forward and backward kernels. Uses slab-based traversal for efficient ray-grid intersection. Choose when the grid is dense and regular. [11383-slab-based-raycasting.md] General GPU acceleration techniques. Choose when hardware acceleration is needed but specific sparse grid optimizations are not required. [12256-gpu-accelerated-ray-casting.md] Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and samples per ray. Early ray termination (controlled by sigmathresh and stopthresh) reduces the average number of samples. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of non-zero grid cells and rays. The sparse grid representation reduces memory usage compared to dense volumes. Performance: High performance on NVIDIA GPUs due to CUDA optimization. Performance scales with the number of CUDA cores and memory bandwidth. Strengths: Efficient handling of sparse data, integration with Jittor's autograd, support for background rendering. Limitations: Requires NVIDIA GPU, dependent on Jittor framework. When to use: When using Jittor for differentiable volume rendering with sparse data and needing GPU acceleration. When not to use: When using other frameworks or when CPU-only execution is required. The Jittor Volume Render Cuvol Wrapper is a custom function developed to leverage Jittor's custom function capabilities for efficient GPU-accelerated volume rendering with automatic differentiation. It builds on the CUDA GPU Implementation to provide seamless integration with Jittor's computational graph. Jittor/JNeRF, https://github.com/Jittor/JNeRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Bricked Single-Pass Ray-Casting
head: 3D Brick Cache Ray Casting, Brick cache raycasting, Brick-based Ray Casting, Bricked Ray-casting, Single-pass raycasting for bricked volumes
body: Bricked single-pass ray-casting is a hardware-accelerated technique for rendering volumetric datasets that exceed the capacity of GPU video memory. It solves the out-of-core rendering problem by storing a dynamic working set of volume bricks in a large "brick cache" texture and performing ray-marching in a single fragment shader pass. Unlike multi-pass approaches that render each brick separately, this method translates virtual volume coordinates to physical cache coordinates on-the-fly, enabling efficient rendering of large datasets while maintaining the visual quality of direct ray-casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A large 3D volume dataset partitioned into fixed-size bricks (sub-volumes). Input: A camera view (position, orientation, field of view). Input: A transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Input: A brick cache texture (3D texture) containing the currently loaded bricks. Output: A 2D image (color and opacity per pixel). Data Structures: 1. Volume Grid: The logical volume is divided into a regular grid of bricks. Each brick has a fixed resolution (e.g., N \times N \times N voxels). The total volume dimensions are Vx \times Vy \times Vz. 2. Brick Cache Texture: A large 3D texture object in GPU memory. Its dimensions are determined by the maximum number of bricks that can fit in available VRAM, not the total volume size. The texture stores the voxel data of the active bricks. 3. Virtual-to-Physical Mapping: A mechanism to map a voxel coordinate (x, y, z) in the logical volume to a coordinate (u, v, w) in the brick cache texture. This involves: Calculating the brick ID: bx = \lfloor x / N \rfloor, by = \lfloor y / N \rfloor, bz = \lfloor z / N \rfloor. Calculating the local offset within the brick: lx = x \mod N, ly = y \mod N, lz = z \mod N. Mapping the brick ID to a position in the cache texture. The cache layout must be consistent (e.g., row-major or column-major) and known to the shader. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Setup: For each pixel, compute the ray origin and direction in object space. Perform object-space culling to determine the entry and exit points of the ray into the volume bounding box. Perform empty space skipping if the volume has an associated empty-space indicator (e.g., a sparse structure or a separate empty-space texture) to skip non-voxel regions. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate along the ray from the entry point to the exit point. The step size is typically determined by the voxel size or a multiple thereof to ensure proper sampling. 3. Coordinate Translation: For each sample point P along the ray: Convert P to integer brick coordinates (bx, by, bz) and local fractional coordinates (lx, ly, lz). Determine the physical location of the brick (bx, by, bz) in the brick cache texture. This requires a dynamic lookup or a precomputed mapping table if the cache layout is complex. Compute the texture coordinates (u, v, w) in the brick cache texture corresponding to the sample point. This includes the base offset of the brick in the cache plus the local offset. 4. Sampling: Sample the scalar value S at (u, v, w) from the brick cache texture using trilinear interpolation. The hardware texture unit handles the interpolation across the brick boundaries, ensuring correct tri-linear interpolation between adjacent bricks. 5. Classification: Map the scalar value S to color C and opacity \alpha using the transfer function. 6. Compositing: Update the accumulated color C' and opacity \alpha' using the front-to-back compositing equation: C'{i} = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Ci \alpha'{i} = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai 7. Early Ray Termination (ERT): If \alpha' exceeds a threshold (e.g., 0.95 or 1.0), terminate the ray marching loop early. 8. Output: Write the final C' and \alpha' to the framebuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fragmentshader(rayorigin, raydirection): # 1. Ray Setup entryt, exitt = computeentryexit(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds) if entryt > exitt: return backgroundcolor, 0.0 # 2. Initialize compositing acccolor = vec3(0.0) accopacity = 0.0 t = entryt # 3. Ray Marching Loop while t < exitt and accopacity < 0.95: # ERT threshold # Sample point in world/object space samplepoint = rayorigin + raydirection t # 4. Coordinate Translation # Convert to brick coordinates brickcoords = floor(samplepoint / bricksize) localcoords = fract(samplepoint / bricksize) # Map brick coordinates to cache texture coordinates # cachelayoutmap is a function or texture that maps (bx, by, bz) to (u, v, w) in cache cachecoords = cachelayoutmap(brickcoords) # Add local offset to cache coordinates # Note: localcoords are in 0,1), need to scale by bricksize if cache texture is not normalized # Assuming cache texture uses normalized coordinates for the brick finalcachecoords = cachecoords + localcoords # 5. Sampling scalarvalue = texture(brickcachetexture, finalcachecoords).r # 6. Classification color, opacity = transferfunction(scalarvalue) # 7. Compositing acccolor = acccolor + (1.0 - accopacity) opacity color accopacity = accopacity + (1.0 - accopacity) opacity # 8. Advance ray t += stepsize # stepsize is typically voxelsize or a multiple return acccolor, accopacity Parameters: Brick Size: The resolution of each brick (e.g., 32^3, 64^3). Larger bricks reduce the number of cache misses but increase memory usage per brick. Not given in the sources. Cache Size: The maximum number of bricks that can fit in GPU memory. Determined by available VRAM and brick size. Not given in the sources. Step Size: The distance between samples along the ray. Typically equal to the voxel size or a fraction thereof. Not given in the sources. ERT Threshold: The opacity threshold for early ray termination. Typically 0.95 or 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cache Management: The brick cache must be managed fully dynamically to accommodate changes in the current view and the current transfer function. If the view changes, the set of visible bricks changes, requiring cache updates. If the transfer function changes, the classification step changes, but the cache data itself may not need to change, though the rendering pipeline must handle this. Interpolation at Brick Boundaries: Correct tri-linear interpolation between bricks is essential to avoid visual artifacts. The hardware texture unit handles this if the brick cache texture is constructed such that adjacent bricks are adjacent in texture memory, or if the shader correctly handles the wrapping/offsetting. [Address Translation Overhead: The on-the-fly address translation from virtual to physical coordinates can be computationally expensive. Efficient mapping strategies are required to minimize this overhead. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of samples along the ray. The address translation adds a constant overhead per sample. Memory Complexity: O(B), where B is the number of bricks in the cache. This is much smaller than the total volume size, allowing rendering of volumes larger than GPU memory. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with volume size, limited by GPU memory and cache management efficiency. Performance is sensitive to cache hit rates. Strengths: Supports volumes larger than GPU memory; single-pass rendering is efficient; correct interpolation between bricks. Limitations: Requires dynamic cache management; address translation overhead; complex implementation. When to Use: When rendering large volumetric datasets that do not fit in GPU memory. When Not to Use: When the volume fits in GPU memory, simpler 3D texture ray-casting may be more efficient. Bricked single-pass ray-casting was introduced by Hadwiger et al. in 2005 and Beyer et al. in 2007. It was developed to address the limitations of earlier out-of-core rendering techniques, such as texture slicing, which suffered from visual artifacts and limited flexibility. The method builds on the principles of hardware-accelerated ray-casting and extends them to handle large-scale data by leveraging a brick cache architecture. It is widely used in scientific visualization for large datasets, such as medical imaging and climate data. name: Volume Fragment Shader (Direct Ray Marching)
head: Fragment Shader Implementation, Ray-box volume rendering, Volume Rendering Shader
body: This method implements direct volume ray casting entirely within a GPU fragment shader, computing per-pixel ray parameters from camera matrices and executing the emission-absorption compositing loop directly in the fragment shader. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on hardware-accelerated texture sampling for trilinear interpolation and its specific handling of mask-based context visualization (ghosting) and intensity normalization within the shader logic itself. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D volume texture (volumeTex), 3D mask texture (maskTex), 1D lookup table (lut), 1D color transfer function (CTF), 1D gradient magnitude transfer function (GMTF), camera matrices (implicit via NDC), and UI parameters (beta, surfaceVoxelsOnly, colorGhosting, roiMin, roiMax, isoValue, quality, dithering, rangeMin, rangeMax, gamma). Outputs: Final fragment color (glFragColor). Data Structures: volumeTex: sampler3D, stores scalar volume values normalized to [0, 1]. maskTex: sampler3D, stores classification/mask data. lut: sampler1D, maps volume intensity to color/opacity. CTF: sampler1D, maps mask data to color. GMTF: sampler1D, maps gradient magnitude to shading weight. transferTex: sampler2D, used in some implementations to store 1-D LUTs as a single-row 2-D texture. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate Generation: Compute Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) from fragment coordinates to ensure robustness across platforms (e.g., macOS). 2. Ray-AABB Intersection: Define the bounding box (AABB) centered at the origin with half-extents boxHalf. Compute ray direction rayDir and origin rayOrigin from camera parameters. Calculate inverse direction: invDir = 1.0 / rayDir, handling zero components to avoid division-by-zero. Compute intersection intervals for each slab: t0 = (-\text{boxHalf} - \text{rayOrigin}) \times \text{invDir} t1 = (\text{boxHalf} - \text{rayOrigin}) \times \text{invDir} Determine t{\text{min}} and t{\text{max}}: t{\text{min}} = \max(\min(t0.x, t1.x), \min(t0.y, t1.y), \min(t0.z, t1.z)) t{\text{max}} = \min(\max(t0.x, t1.x), \max(t0.y, t1.y), \max(t0.z, t1.z)) The ray intersects the box if t{\text{max}} > \max(t{\text{min}}, 0.0). 3. Volume & Mask Sampling: Sample the volume texture at the fragment's position (glTexCoord[0].stp) to get p. Extract gradient vector grad from p.rgb. Sample the Lookup Table (LUT) using p.a to get volume color colvol. Sample the mask texture at the current fragment's texture coordinates (glTexCoord[1].stp) to get value r. Sample the Color Transfer Function (CTF) using the alpha channel of r (r.a) to obtain the mask color colmask. Sample the Gradient Magnitude Transfer Function (GMTF) using r.a to get gradweight. 4. Intensity Normalization: Before sampling, raw volume values are normalized: v{\text{norm}} = \frac{v{\text{raw}} - \text{rangeMin}}{\text{rangeMax} - \text{rangeMin}} Clamped to [0, 1]. If \text{rangeMax} - \text{rangeMin} < 10^{-6}, return 0.0 to avoid division by zero. Gamma correction is applied: v{\text{final}} = v{\text{norm}}^{\text{gamma}}. 5. Ray Marching & Compositing: Initialize the output color and opacity accumulator dest to vec4(0). Initialize the ray position at the far plane: position = eye + raydir tfar. Execute the volume rendering loop, advancing the position along the ray direction: position = position - raydir stepsize. Implement opacity correction within the rendering loop. Update accumulated color C' and opacity \alpha' using front-to-back compositing: C'{i} = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Ci \alpha'{i} = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Implement Early Ray Termination to stop sampling when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold (typically 0.95 or 1.0) [Parent notes, G]. 6. Mask/Context Blending Logic: If colmask.a is 0.0, discard the fragment. If colmask.a is 1.0: \text{color} = \text{col\vol} \times \beta + (1 - \beta) \times \text{col\mask}. Else (partial mask): If surfaceVoxelsOnly is true AND the gradient magnitude is small (checked via LargeGradient(grad, gradweight)): \text{color}.a = 0.0. Else if colorGhosting is true: \text{color} = \text{col\mask}. Else: \text{color} = \text{col\vol} \times \beta + (1 - \beta) \times \text{col\mask}. 7. Final Shading: Calculate normals using central differences to enable shading. Call the shade function with color, grad, and gradweight to produce glFragColor. Dithering: To prevent banding artifacts, a pseudo-random hash using noiseSeed adds a random offset to the ray start position. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderfragment(fragcoord, eye, raydir, volumetex, masktex, lut, ctf, gmtf, beta, surfacevoxelsonly, colorghosting, quality, dithering, rangemin, rangemax, gamma): # 1. Ray-AABB Intersection (Slab Method) boxmin = vec3(-1.0) boxmax = vec3(1.0) # Handle zero direction components to prevent inf/-inf propagation invdir = vec3(1.0 / raydir.x if raydir.x != 0.0 else 1e30, 1.0 / raydir.y if raydir.y != 0.0 else 1e30, 1.0 / raydir.z if raydir.z != 0.0 else 1e30) t0 = (boxmin - eye) invdir t1 = (boxmax - eye) invdir tnear = max(min(t0.x, t1.x), min(t0.y, t1.y), min(t0.z, t1.z)) tfar = min(max(t0.x, t1.x), max(t0.y, t1.y), max(t0.z, t1.z)) if tfar < tnear or tfar < 0.0: return vec4(0.0) tnear = max(tnear, 0.0) tnear = max(tnear, -1.0) # Clamp entry distance # 2. Dithering & Step Size ditheroffset = dithering pseudorandomhash(fragcoord.xy) stepsize = (tfar - tnear) quality # Controls step count # 3. Initialization dest = vec4(0.0) # Accumulated color and opacity position = eye + raydir tfar # Start at far plane # 4. Ray Marching Loop while tnear < tfar: # World-to-texture mapping texcoord = (position / (2.0 boxmax)) + vec3(0.5) # Sample textures p = texturelookup(volumetex, texcoord) r = texturelookup(masktex, texcoord) colmask = texturelookup(ctf, r.a) if colmask.a == 0.0: return vec4(0.0) # Discard fragment # Intensity normalization rawval = p.a denom = rangemax - rangemin val = 0.0 if denom < 1e-6 else clamp((rawval - rangemin) / denom, 0.0, 1.0) val = pow(val, gamma) # Sample transfer functions colvol = texturelookup(lut, val) grad = p.rgb gradweight = texturelookup(gmtf, r.a) # Opacity correction and compositing [Parent notes, S3, unofficial] alpha = colvol.a correctedalpha = alpha (1.0 / (1.0 - alpha stepsize)) # Standard opacity correction correctedalpha = min(correctedalpha, 1.0) dest.rgb += (1.0 - dest.a) correctedalpha colvol.rgb dest.a += (1.0 - dest.a) correctedalpha # Early Ray Termination [Parent notes, G] if dest.a > 0.95: break # Advance position position = position - raydir stepsize tnear += stepsize # 5. Mask/Context Blending Logic finalcolor = dest if colmask.a == 1.0: finalcolor = colvol beta + (1.0 - beta) colmask else: if surfacevoxelsonly and not largegradient(grad, gradweight): finalcolor.a = 0.0 elif colorghosting: finalcolor = colmask else: finalcolor = colvol beta + (1.0 - beta) colmask # 6. Shading finalcolor = shade(finalcolor, grad, gradweight) return finalcolor def largegradient(grad, gradweight): return gradweight > 0.5 # Threshold check inferred from context def shade(color, grad, gradweight): return color gradweight # Simplified shading model based on gradient weight Parameters: beta: Float, modulates the blend between volume color and mask color. Default 1.0. surfaceVoxelsOnly: Boolean, hides interior voxels if gradient is small. colorGhosting: Boolean, displays mask color for context nodes. roiMin, roiMax: vec3, texture coordinate bounds for Region of Interest clipping, default (0,0,0) to (1,1,1). isoValue: Float, threshold for isosurface mode. quality: Float, controls step count (0.1 coarse, 1.0 fine). dithering: Float, controls random ray-start offset strength. A variant that handles colormap and inversion logic differently, specifically separating inversion application for colormap vs scalar modes. It uses integer-based fragment coordinates to determine inversion state. Definition: Uses highp usampler3D for volume and highp sampler2D for colormap. Inversion is determined by comparing comp uniform with glFragCoord. Logic: 1. Initialize invert = false. If comp.x == int(glFragCoord.x) or comp.y == int(glFragCoord.y), set invert = true. 2. Sample volume at samp. Convert red channel to float and divide by 65536.0. If samp is outside [0.0, 1.0], set value to 0.0. 3. Default color is white RGB with alpha val. 4. If usecolormap is true: Sample colormap at vec2(val, 0.5). Set color to RGB from colormap and alpha from val. 5. If invert is true AND usecolormap is false: Set color to white RGB and alpha 1.0 - val. 6. If invert is true AND usecolormap is true: Set color to white RGB and alpha 1.0. When to choose: When integer-based coordinate inversion is required for specific visualization modes or when using 16-bit integer volume data mapped to colormap. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray, which is controlled by the quality parameter. Memory Complexity: Low, as it operates per-fragment without storing large intermediate buffers, relying on GPU texture memory. Performance: Fast for small volumes or low quality settings; performance degrades with high quality (fine step count) and large volumes. Strengths: Simple implementation, leverages hardware texture sampling, supports real-time interaction via UI parameters. Limitations: Limited to direct ray casting; does not support advanced lighting or global illumination without additional shader complexity. Banding artifacts may occur without dithering. When to use: Real-time visualization of scalar volumes with simple transfer functions. When not to use: Complex lighting requirements or very large volumes requiring hierarchical traversal. This method originates from implementations in open-source visualization tools and educational assignments, adapting direct volume ray casting to fragment shaders. It builds on the principles of hardware-accelerated volume rendering Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering. name: Multithreaded Volume Rendering Pipeline
head: Context Switching for Data Hazards, Ray Multithreading
body: The Multithreaded Volume Rendering Pipeline is a hardware optimization technique designed to overcome data hazards in pipelined volume rendering architectures. It solves the problem where subsequent sample point addresses depend on the distance value of the current sample point, which causes pipeline stalls due to memory read delays. By processing multiple rays (threads) in a round-robin order, it maintains high pipeline utilization where sequential processing would drop below 10%. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume dataset, camera parameters, and a ray queue structure. Output: A 2D image where each pixel's brightness is the accumulated contribution of all rays passing through it. Data Structures Ray Queue: Implemented as a shift register. Each slot in the register stores the parameters of a single ray. Slot Layout: Not given in the sources. Capacity: Up to 64 rays are processed simultaneously. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel of the final image, a ray is cast into the volume. 2. Sample Point Generation: Sample points are generated at regular intervals starting from the viewing plane (nearest to the viewer). 3. Position Calculation: The position of the sample point in the data volume is calculated. 4. Voxel Sampling: The 8 neighboring voxels are read out from volume memory. 5. Interpolation: Trilinear interpolation is performed on the 8 voxels to obtain the gray value (interpreted as opacity) of the sample point. 6. Gradient Calculation: A gradient is calculated by determining the gray value change between neighboring sample points. This gradient serves as the normal of a possible plane in the volume. 7. Shading: Using the plane normal, shading is performed to calculate how much light is reflected toward the viewer direction by diffuse and specular reflection. 8. Absorption Calculation: It is calculated how much of the reflected light intensity reaches the viewing plane due to absorption. 9. Compositing: Each contribution of a ray is accumulated to represent the brightness of the considered pixel. The standard compositing equation updates accumulated color C' and opacity \alpha': C'{i} = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Ci \alpha'{i} = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai where Ci and \alphai are the color and opacity of the current sample point. 10. Data Hazard Detection: The system detects that the next sample point address depends on the distance value of the current sample point, which requires reading from volume memory with a delay of 3 clock cycles plus calculation delay. 11. Context Switching: Instead of inserting no-operations (stalls), the hardware switches context to the next ray in the queue to hide the memory latency. 12. Queue Management: When a new sample point is calculated for a ray, the ray is added to the end of the ray queue (shift register). 13. Early Ray Termination (ERT): If the intensity of a ray falls below a user-defined threshold, the ray is deleted from the queue. Pseudocode The following pseudocode implements the round-robin processing logic within the hardware pipeline, focusing on the queue management, context switching, and pipeline stages required to hide latency. It uses standard front-to-back compositing from the parent method. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trilinearinterpolate(grid, x, y, z): """Standard trilinear interpolation of 8 neighboring voxels.""" # Clamp coordinates to grid bounds x, y, z = max(0, min(x, grid.width-1)), max(0, min(y, grid.height-1)), max(0, min(z, grid.depth-1)) # Extract 8 voxels and interpolate (standard implementation omitted for brevity) return grid.sample(x, y, z) def calculategradientalongray(grid, pos, direction, step): """Gradient calculated by determining gray value change between neighboring sample points along the ray.""" posnext = (pos[0] + direction[0] step, pos[1] + direction[1] step, pos[2] + direction[2] step) posprev = (pos[0] - direction[0] step, pos[1] - direction[1] step, pos[2] - direction[2] step) valcurr = grid.sample(pos) valnext = grid.sample(posnext) valprev = grid.sample(posprev) return (valnext - valprev) / (2.0 step) def calculateshading(gradientmagnitude, viewdir, lightdir): """Phong shading model for diffuse and specular reflection.""" # Simplified to return light intensity factor return 0.5 + 0.5 max(0.0, viewdir.dot(lightdir)) def calculateabsorption(lightintensity, opacity): """Beer-Lambert absorption model.""" return lightintensity (1.0 - math.exp(-opacity)) def accumulatepixel(pixelcolor, pixelalpha, color, alpha): """Front-to-back compositing equation.""" newalpha = pixelalpha + (1.0 - pixelalpha) alpha newcolor = pixelcolor + (1.0 - pixelalpha) alpha color return newcolor, newalpha class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction, stepsize): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction self.stepsize = stepsize self.position = origin self.color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) self.alpha = 0.0 self.intensity = 0.0 def advance(self): self.position = (self.position[0] + self.direction[0] self.stepsize, self.position[1] + self.direction[1] self.stepsize, self.position[2] + self.direction[2] self.stepsize) def insidevolume(self, bounds): return bounds[0] <= self.position[0] <= bounds[3] and \ bounds[1] <= self.position[1] <= bounds[4] and \ bounds[2] <= self.position[2] <= bounds[5] class RayQueue: """Shift register implementation for round-robin ray processing.""" def init(self, capacity): self.capacity = capacity self.rays = [None] capacity self.head = 0 self.tail = 0 self.count = 0 def isempty(self): return self.count == 0 def isfull(self): return self.count == self.capacity def enqueue(self, ray): if self.isfull(): # Shift register drops oldest entry when full self.head = (self.head + 1) % self.capacity self.count -= 1 self.rays[self.tail] = ray self.tail = (self.tail + 1) % self.capacity self.count += 1 def dequeue(self): if self.isempty(): return None ray = self.rays[self.head] self.head = (self.head + 1) % self.capacity self.count -= 1 return ray def peek(self): if self.isempty(): return None return self.rays[self.head] def processpipeline(volume, rays, bounds, maxrays=64, threshold=0.95): """Multithreaded pipeline processing with round-robin context switching.""" queue = RayQueue(maxrays) # Initialize rays for ray in rays: queue.enqueue(ray) if queue.isfull(): break # Round-robin processing loop while not queue.isempty(): ray = queue.peek() # Skip rays that have exited the volume if not ray.insidevolume(bounds): queue.dequeue() continue # Hardware pipeline stages executed per sample point pos = ray.position opacity = trilinearinterpolate(volume, pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]) gradientval = calculategradientalongray(volume, pos, ray.direction, ray.stepsize) light = calculateshading(gradientval, ray.direction, (0.0, 0.0, 1.0)) absorbed = calculateabsorption(light, opacity) ray.color, ray.alpha = accumulatepixel(ray.color, ray.alpha, absorbed, opacity) ray.intensity = ray.alpha # Simplified intensity metric for ERT ray.advance() # Early Ray Termination if ray.alpha >= threshold: queue.dequeue() continue # Context switch: re-add to end of shift register queue for next cycle queue.enqueue(ray) return rays Parameters Max Concurrent Rays: 64 rays are processed simultaneously in the round-robin queue. Memory Delay: 3 clock cycles from addressing to data out. ERT Threshold: User-defined threshold for ray intensity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Data Hazard: Sequential processing of sample points causes pipeline stalls because the next address depends on the current distance value. Without multithreading, pipeline utilization drops to less than 10% due to the 3-cycle memory delay and address calculation delay. Queue Overflow: The source describes the queue as a shift register with a fixed capacity (64 rays). If more rays are generated than the queue can hold, older rays may be displaced or processing may stall if the queue management logic is not explicitly defined for overflow. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The ray queue requires storage for up to 64 rays. Measured Performance: Without multithreading, pipeline utilization drops to less than 10% due to 3-cycle memory delay and address calculation delay. With multithreading, pipeline utilization is maintained at a high level by calculating sample points for other rays instead of inserting no-operations. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Overcomes data hazards in pipelined volume rendering; maintains high pipeline utilization; hides memory latency. Limitations: Requires hardware support for context switching and a ray queue (shift register); limited to 64 concurrent rays in the described implementation. When to use: Use in hardware-accelerated volume rendering pipelines where data hazards cause significant stalls. When not: Use when the hardware does not support multithreading or when the volume data access pattern does not exhibit the described data hazard. What it is: A method that divides the volume data into spatial domains, assigning each domain to a different processor or thread group. Difference: Unlike the multithreaded pipeline which focuses on hiding latency within a single pipeline by switching rays, domain decomposition focuses on parallelizing the workload across multiple processing units by splitting the data space. When to choose: Use when the volume is large and can be effectively partitioned, and when hardware supports distributed memory or multi-core parallelism. Link: Parallel Domain-Decomposed Ray Casting What it is: The general architectural design for implementing volume rendering on GPUs, including memory hierarchies and shader models. Difference: The multithreaded pipeline is a specific optimization technique for pipelined hardware (often FPGA or custom ASIC), whereas GPU architecture is a broader framework that may use different parallelism models (SIMT). When to choose: Use when designing the overall system for a GPU, rather than optimizing a specific pipelined hardware unit. Link: GPU Implementation Architecture What it is: A specific implementation of volume rendering using NVIDIA's CUDA programming model. Difference: CUDA uses a SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Thread) model with warp scheduling, which is conceptually similar to multithreading but managed by the GPU driver and hardware differently than the explicit round-robin shift register described in the multithreaded pipeline. When to choose: Use when targeting NVIDIA GPUs and leveraging CUDA's high-level parallelism. Link: CUDA GPU Implementation The Multithreaded Volume Rendering Pipeline was introduced in the paper "Volume Rendering FPGA Hardware" by Lacroute et al. (1999). It was developed to address the performance bottlenecks in pipelined volume rendering hardware, specifically the data hazards caused by the dependency of sample point addresses on previous distance values. The technique is particularly relevant for FPGA-based volume rendering implementations where pipeline efficiency is critical.
