name: WebGL/WebGPU Browser Implementations
head: Browser-based GPU Volume Rendering
body: This family implements direct volume ray casting within web browsers using WebGL or WebGPU APIs, solving the problem of rendering volumetric data without plugins by adapting GPU-accelerated ray marching to browser-specific constraints like the lack of 3D texture support in WebGL 1.0 or WebGPU's memory alignment rules. It differs from desktop GPU implementations by prioritizing web standard compatibility and handling browser-specific data encoding workarounds, such as packing depth into RGBA channels or using 2D texture atlases. Enables interactive coexistence of volumetric datasets and 3D triangular meshes in WebGL by using a multi-pass rendering pipeline to handle occlusion, blending, and ray intersection. It sets itself apart from single-pass approaches by explicitly separating depth, surface color, and volume traversal into distinct passes to correctly manage back-to-front blending and geometry intersections. Choose this method when rendering opaque and transparent 3D geometry within or alongside volume data in WebGL environments. An interactive voxel volume renderer using path tracing that runs in modern browsers via WebGL 2.0. It sets itself apart from standard ray casting by computing normals via central differences of opacity and applying Phong-like lighting with soft shadows, rather than relying solely on direct illumination. Choose this method when lighting and shadowing effects are required for volumetric data in WebGL 2.0. StructuredVolumeRenderer is a reusable, graph-native GPU renderer for scalar, vector, and hybrid volume data in WebGPU environments. It sets itself apart from sibling WebGL implementations by leveraging WebGPU's storage buffer and texture binding models, manual trilinear interpolation, and fixed-step jittered ray marching with early opacity termination. Choose this method when rendering structured grid data (buffers or 3D textures) in WebGPU with explicit memory control.

name: WebGL Multi-pass Ray-casting with 3D Geometry Intersection
head: Five-pass ray-casting pipeline, VMesh Real-Time Rendering, WebGL volume rendering with intersected 3D geometry
body: This method enables the interactive coexistence of volumetric datasets and 3D triangular meshes in WebGL by using a multi-pass rendering pipeline to handle occlusion, blending, and ray intersection. It solves the problem of rendering opaque and transparent 3D geometry within or alongside volume data, a key requirement for medical and engineering visualizations, while adhering to WebGL constraints such as the lack of native 3D and float texture support. Unlike single-pass ray-casting approaches, this method explicitly separates the computation of depth, surface color, and volume traversal into distinct passes to correctly manage back-to-front blending and geometry intersections. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D triangular meshes (opaque), a volumetric dataset (represented as a 2D texture atlas), camera matrices, and transfer functions. Outputs: A final 2D image composited from volume and mesh data. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored as a 2D texture atlas where 2D slices are stacked in the Z-axis and arranged in a matrix configuration on a single 2D plane. Depth Data: Since WebGL 1.0 lacks native float texture support, depth values from intermediate passes are encoded into RGBA color channels of Frame Buffer Objects (FBOs). FBOs: Multiple Frame Buffer Objects are used to store intermediate results: depth maps (Passes 1 and 3), surface colors (Pass 2), and volume back coordinates (Pass 4). Numbered Steps: The pipeline consists of five passes (or four in the VMesh variant), executed in the following order: 1. Depth Pass (Meshes): Render the depth of all 3D meshes in the scene into an FBO. The fragment shader outputs the current depth encoded in RGBA color channels. 2. Surface Color Pass (Meshes): Render all 3D meshes into a separate FBO to store their color information. 3. Back Cube Depth Pass (Volume): Render the depth of the back side of the volume bounding box into an FBO, encoded in RGBA, using the same shader logic as Pass 1. 4. Back Coordinates Pass (Volume): Render the back faces of the volume bounding box into a separate FBO. The 3D texture coordinates are assigned as color on each vertex, so rasterization interpolates these per-vertex colors to represent volume data 3D texture coordinates. 5. Ray Traversal and Composition Pass: Render 3D objects and volume data to the screen buffer. Objects must be sorted in Z-depth order and rendered from back to front. In the fragment shader, rays are cast towards the volume. All outputs from previous passes are sampled as 2D textures. The shader performs ray marching, checks for 3D geometry intersections using depth data from Passes 1 and 3, and composites the results. It assumes access to textures generated in previous passes. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode represents the core ray-casting logic executed in the fragment shader during the final pass (Pass 5), adapted from. It uses standard graphics operations marked. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def unpackrgbatofloat(r, g, b, a): # Reverses the packing: value = r 256^3 + g 256^2 + b 256 + a return r (256.03) + g (256.02) + b 256.0 + a raydirection = computeraydirection(camerapos, screenpos) raypos = camerapos backdepthrgba = texture(depthvoltex, screenpos) maxdistance = unpackrgbatofloat(backdepthrgba.r, backdepthrgba.g, backdepthrgba.b, backdepthrgba.a) S = Not given in the sources. s = maxdistance / S accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for i in range(S): # Interpolate sample at current raypos volumevalue = texture(volumeatlastex, raypos) # Compute color with transfer function color, alpha = transferfunction(volumevalue) # Accumulate color and opacity accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor + (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) alpha color accumulatedalpha = accumulatedalpha + (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) alpha # Check for 3D Geometry Intersection using depth data from Passes 1 and 3 meshdepthrgba = texture(depthmeshtex, screenpos) meshdepthfloat = unpackrgbatofloat(meshdepthrgba.r, meshdepthrgba.g, meshdepthrgba.b, meshdepthrgba.a) currentraydepth = dot(raypos - camerapos, raydirection) if meshdepthfloat < currentraydepth: meshcolor = texture(colormeshtex, screenpos) accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor + (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) meshcolor accumulatedalpha = 1.0 break # Early Ray Termination if accumulatedalpha >= 1.0 or raypos > boundingboxmax: break # Increment raypos with s raypos = raypos + s raydirection outputcolor = accumulatedcolor Parameters: Rendering Order: Objects (volumes and 3D opaque meshes) must be sorted in z-depth order and rendered from back to front. Blending Mode: Back-to-front blending composition is used for the ray-casting shaders in the final rendering pass. Threshold: Early ray termination occurs when accumulated opacity \alpha \ge 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lack of 3D Textures: WebGL lacks support for 3D textures, requiring the use of a 2D texture atlas workaround to sample volumetric data. Lack of Float Textures: WebGL lacks support for Float textures, requiring depth data to be encoded into RGBA color channels for storage in FBOs. Occlusion Handling: Correctly determining if a 3D object occludes the volume requires comparing the depth of the mesh (from Pass 1) with the current ray position. Complexity: The multi-pass approach requires five rendering passes and multiple Frame Buffer Objects (FBOs), which is a downside in terms of computational overhead and memory usage. Performance: The method is designed for interactive visualization on web platforms, balancing quality with the constraints of WebGL. Strengths: Supports the coexistence of 3D triangular meshes and volumetric datasets, which is critical for medical and engineering applications. Limitations: High memory usage due to multiple FBOs; precision issues due to RGBA depth encoding; complexity of implementation due to multiple passes and sorting requirements. This method extends previous WebGL ray-casting efforts by Congote et al. [CSK 11], Mobeen et al. [MF12], and Noguera and Jiménez [NJ12] by exploring the coexistence of 3D triangular meshes along volume data within the constraints of the Web platform. It addresses challenges such as the lack of 3D and depth textures in WebGL. The VMesh variant implements a similar four-pass process using three.js for VMesh assets. Deployment of Volume Rendering Interactive Visualizations in Web Platforms With Intersected 3D Geometry, https://doi.org/10.2312/ceig.20161312, fetched 2026-10-26 VMesh: Hybrid Volume-Mesh Representation for Efficient View Synthesis, https://core.ac.uk/download/560406650.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: WebGL Path Tracing Volume Rendering
head: Interactive Voxel Volume Rendering via WebGL 2.0
body: An interactive voxel volume renderer using path tracing that runs in modern browsers via WebGL 2.0. It renders 3D scalar fields by casting rays from the camera through the volume, accumulating color and opacity along the ray, and applying lighting/shadowing. It differs from standard ray casting by computing normals via central differences of opacity and applying Phong-like lighting with soft shadows, rather than relying solely on direct illumination or pre-computed lighting. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: volume: highp sampler3D containing the scalar field. volumedims: ivec3 defining the dimensions of the volume texture. transformedeye: vec3 camera position in world space. vraydir: vec3 ray direction in world space. dtscale: float step size scaling factor. lightPosition: vec3 light source position. windowLevel, windowWidth: float for window/level adjustment. rescaleSlope, rescaleIntercept: float for linear transformation of raw values. numberOfOpacitySamples, opacityMapPositions, opacityMapSamples: int, highp sampler2D, highp sampler2D for opacity transfer function. numberOfColorSamples, colorMapPositions, colorMapSamples: int, highp sampler2D, highp sampler2D for color transfer function. boxMin, boxMax: vec3 bounding box of the volume. Output: vec4 color (RGBA) for the fragment. Data Structures Opacity/Color Maps: Stored in 2D textures where the x-coordinate represents the position (control point) and the y-coordinate represents the sample value (opacity or color intensity). The number of control points is given by numberOfOpacitySamples or numberOfColorSamples. Volume: Stored in a 3D texture (sampler3D). Algorithm Steps 1. Ray-Box Intersection: Compute the intersection of the ray with the volume's bounding box. \text{invDir} = \frac{1.0}{\text{dir}} t{\text{min\tmp}} = (\text{boxMin} - \text{orig}) \times \text{invDir} t{\text{max\tmp}} = (\text{boxMax} - \text{orig}) \times \text{invDir} t{\text{min}} = \min(t{\text{min\tmp}}, t{\text{max\tmp}}) t{\text{max}} = \max(t{\text{min\tmp}}, t{\text{max\tmp}}) t0 = \max(t{\text{min}.x, \max(t{\text{min}.y}, t{\text{min}.z})) t1 = \min(t{\text{max}.x, \min(t{\text{max}.y}, t{\text{max}.z})) If t0 > t1, the ray does not intersect the volume; discard the fragment. 2. Step Size Calculation: Compute the step size dt based on the volume dimensions and ray direction to ensure consistent sampling density relative to voxel size. dt{\text{vec}} = \frac{1.0}{\text{volume\dims} \times |\text{ray\dir}|} dt = dt{\text{scale}} \times \min(dt{\text{vec}.x, \min(dt{\text{vec}.y}, dt{\text{vec}.z})) Typical value for dt{\text{scale}} is not specified in the sources. 3. Ray Origin Offset: Generate a random offset to reduce aliasing. \text{seed} = \text{wang\hash}(\text{int}(gl\FragCoord.x + 1024.0 \times gl\FragCoord.y)) \text{offset} = \frac{\text{seed}}{2147483647.0} p = \text{transformed\eye} + (t0 + \text{offset} \times dt) \times \text{ray\dir} The wanghash function is defined as: python def wanghash(seed): seed = (seed ^ 61) ^ (seed >> 16) seed = 9 seed = seed ^ (seed >> 4) seed = 0x27d4eb2d seed = seed ^ (seed >> 15) return seed % 2147483647. 4. Value Rescaling: Apply linear transformation to raw volume values. \text{rescaled\value} = \text{rescaleSlope} \times \text{raw\value} + \text{rescaleIntercept} 5. Transfer Function Application: Opacity: Find the interval [opacityMapPositions(i-1), opacityMapPositions(i)] containing the rescaled value. Interpolate between opacityMapSamples(i-1) and opacityMapSamples(i) using linear interpolation. Clamp the result multiplied by \frac{\text{value} - \text{windowFloor}}{\text{windowWidth}} to [0, 1], where \text{windowFloor} = \text{windowLevel} - \frac{\text{windowWidth}}{2.0}. Color: Similar to opacity, find the interval in colorMapPositions and interpolate between colorMapSamples(i-1) and colorMapSamples(i). 6. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize voxelColor = vec4(0.0). Loop t from t0 to t1 with step dt. Inside the loop: Sample volume value val at current position p. Get color and opacity from transfer functions applied to val. Compute valcolor = vec4(opacity color, opacity). Apply Beer-Lambert law approximation: val\color.a = 1.0 - (1.0 - val\color.a)^{dt{\text{scale}}} Update accumulated color: voxelColor.rgb += (1.0 - voxelColor.a) \times val\color.a \times val\color.rgb Update accumulated alpha: voxelColor.a += (1.0 - voxelColor.a) \times val\color.a If voxelColor.a \ge 0.95, break. Advance position: p += \text{ray\dir} \times dt. 7. Lighting Calculation: Normal Estimation: Compute voxel size: \text{voxelSize} = \frac{1.0}{\text{volume\dims}} Compute gradient using central differences of sampleVolumeOpacity (which applies opacity map to rescaled volume value): \text{gradient}.x = \frac{\text{sampleVolumeOpacity}(p + \text{vec3}(\text{voxelSize}.x, 0, 0)) - \text{sampleVolumeOpacity}(p - \text{vec3}(\text{voxelSize}.x, 0, 0))}{2.0 \times \text{voxelSize}.x} Similarly for y and z. Normalize the gradient to get voxelNormal. Diffuse: \text{lightDirection} = \text{normalize}(\text{lightPosition} - p) \text{intensity} = \text{dot}(\text{voxelNormal}, \text{lightDirection}) Specular: If \text{intensity} > 0.0: h = \text{normalize}(\text{lightDirection} + \text{transformed\eye}) \text{intSpec} = \max(\text{dot}(h, \text{voxelNormal}), 0.0) \text{spec} = \text{specular} \times \text{pow}(\text{intSpec}, \text{shininess}) With \text{shininess} = 8.0, \text{specular} = 0.5, \text{diffuse} = 0.6, \text{ambient} = 0.4. Shadow: If voxelColor.a \ge 0.20: \text{shadow} = \text{clamp}(\text{softShadow}(p) \times 2.0 + 0.1, 0.0, 1.0) Else: \text{shadow} = 1.0 Final Light Color: \text{lightColor} = \text{shadow} \times \max(\text{intensity} \times \text{diffuse} + \text{spec}, \text{ambient}) Apply lightColor to the accumulated voxelColor. 8. Soft Shadow Calculation: Sample 8 points around the voxel position p in a 3x3 grid (excluding center) with spacing \delta = \min(\text{voxelSize}.x, \min(\text{voxelSize}.y, \text{voxelSize}.z)) \times 2.0. For each point, compute: \text{pointShadow} = 1.0 - \text{traceLight}(\text{position}, \text{lightPosition}) Sum these shadows and divide by 8.0. 9. Light Tracing (Shadow Ray): Cast a ray from voxel towards light. \text{voxelToLight} = \text{light} - \text{voxel} d = \text{normalize}(\text{voxelToLight}) o = \text{voxel} - 1000.0 \times d Intersect ray with box to get box. Compute start = length(voxel - o). Sample opacity along the ray from start to box.y with step \delta = \frac{\min(\text{voxelSize}.x, \min(\text{voxelSize}.y, \text{voxelSize}.z))}{\text{samplesPerVoxel}} (where \text{samplesPerVoxel} = 1.0). Accumulate: \text{integrated} += \frac{\text{val}}{\text{samplesPerVoxel} \times 4.0} If \text{integrated} > 0.95, break. Return \text{clamp}(\text{integrated}, 0.0, 1.0). 10. SRGB Conversion: Convert linear color to SRGB. If x \le 0.0031308, return 12.92 \times x. Else return 1.055 \times x^{1/2.4} - 0.055. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderfragment(volume, volumedims, boxMin, boxMax, transformedeye, vraydir, dtscale, lightPosition, windowLevel, windowWidth, rescaleSlope, rescaleIntercept, numberOfOpacitySamples, opacityMapPositions, opacityMapSamples, numberOfColorSamples, colorMapPositions, colorMapSamples): # 1. Ray-Box Intersection invDir = 1.0 / vraydir tmintmp = (boxMin - transformedeye) invDir tmaxtmp = (boxMax - transformedeye) invDir tmin = min(tmintmp, tmaxtmp) tmax = max(tmintmp, tmaxtmp) t0 = max(tmin.x, max(tmin.y, tmin.z)) t1 = min(tmax.x, min(tmax.y, tmax.z)) if t0 > t1: return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Discard fragment # 2. Step Size dtvec = 1.0 / (volumedims abs(vraydir)) dt = dtscale min(dtvec.x, min(dtvec.y, dtvec.z)) # 3. Ray Origin Offset seed = wanghash(int(glFragCoord.x + 1024.0 glFragCoord.y)) offset = wanghash(int(glFragCoord.x + 1024.0 glFragCoord.y)) / 2147483647.0 p = transformedeye + (t0 + offset dt) vraydir # 4-5. Rescale & Transfer Functions def sampletransfer(rescaledval, postex, samptex, numsamples): for i in range(1, numsamples): if postex[i] >= rescaledval: t = (rescaledval - postex[i-1]) / (postex[i] - postex[i-1]) return lerp(samptex[i-1], samptex[i], t) return samptex[numsamples-1] def applyopacity(rescaledval): baseopacity = sampletransfer(rescaledval, opacityMapPositions, opacityMapSamples, numberOfOpacitySamples) windowFloor = windowLevel - windowWidth / 2.0 return clamp(baseopacity (rescaledval - windowFloor) / windowWidth, 0.0, 1.0) def applycolor(rescaledval): return sampletransfer(rescaledval, colorMapPositions, colorMapSamples, numberOfColorSamples) # 6. Ray Marching voxelColor = vec4(0.0) t = t0 while t < t1: rawval = samplevolume(volume, p) rescaled = rescaleSlope rawval + rescaleIntercept opacity = applyopacity(rescaled) color = applycolor(rescaled) valcolor = vec4(opacity color, opacity) valcolor.a = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - valcolor.a, dtscale) voxelColor.rgb += (1.0 - voxelColor.a) valcolor.a valcolor.rgb voxelColor.a += (1.0 - voxelColor.a) valcolor.a if voxelColor.a >= 0.95: break t += dt p += vraydir dt # 7. Lighting voxelSize = 1.0 / volumedims grad = computegradientopacity(p, voxelSize, applyopacity) voxelNormal = normalize(grad) lightDir = normalize(lightPosition - p) intensity = dot(voxelNormal, lightDir) spec = 0.0 if intensity > 0.0: h = normalize(lightDir + transformedeye) intSpec = max(dot(h, voxelNormal), 0.0) spec = 0.5 pow(intSpec, 8.0) shadow = 1.0 if voxelColor.a >= 0.20: shadow = clamp(softshadow(p, voxelSize, lightPosition) 2.0 + 0.1, 0.0, 1.0) lightColor = shadow max(intensity 0.6 + spec, 0.4) voxelColor.rgb = lightColor # 10. SRGB return srgbconvert(voxelColor) def wanghash(seed): seed = (seed ^ 61) ^ (seed >> 16) seed = 9 seed = seed ^ (seed >> 4) seed = 0x27d4eb2d seed = seed ^ (seed >> 15) return seed % 2147483647 def softshadow(p, voxelSize, lightPosition): delta = min(voxelSize.x, min(voxelSize.y, voxelSize.z)) 2.0 totalshadow = 0.0 for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: if dx == 0 and dy == 0 and dz == 0: continue pos = p + vec3(dx delta, dy delta, dz delta) totalshadow += 1.0 - tracelight(pos, lightPosition) return totalshadow / 8.0 def tracelight(voxel, light, voxelSize): voxelToLight = light - voxel d = normalize(voxelToLight) o = voxel - 1000.0 d box = rayboxintersection(o, d) start = length(voxel - o) integrated = 0.0 step = min(voxelSize.x, min(voxelSize.y, voxelSize.z)) / 1.0 t = start while t < box.y: val = sampleopacityatpos(t) integrated += val / 4.0 if integrated > 0.95: break t += step return clamp(integrated, 0.0, 1.0) def srgbconvert(x): return 12.92 x if x <= 0.0031308 else 1.055 pow(x, 1.0/2.4) - 0.055 Pitfalls Ray-box intersection failure: If t0 > t1, the ray does not intersect the volume box. The fragment is discarded. Early termination: The ray marching loop breaks if accumulated alpha voxelColor.a >= 0.95 to save computation. Shadow ray early termination: The light tracing loop breaks if integrated opacity integrated > 0.95. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray. The number of samples is determined by the volume dimensions, ray direction, and dtscale. Shadow calculation adds a constant overhead per lit voxel. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the storage of the 3D volume texture and the 2D transfer function textures. Performance: Interactive performance is achieved on modern browsers via WebGL 2.0. Performance scales with resolution and volume size. Strengths: Interactive frame rates, browser-based accessibility, soft shadows for improved depth perception. Limitations: Approximate lighting (normal estimation from opacity gradients may be noisy), fixed step size (unless adaptive), limited to scalar volumes. When to use: Interactive visualization of scalar fields in web browsers. When not to use: High-fidelity offline rendering requiring accurate normal estimation from the scalar field itself, or complex volume data types (e.g., tensor fields). The method demonstrates the use of WebGL 2.0 for interactive volume rendering with path tracing techniques, including lighting and shadowing, within a web browser environment. The repository name is not given in the sources. termijn/webgl-volumerendering, https://github.com/termijn/webgl-volumerendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: StructuredVolumeRenderer
head: luma.gl StructuredVolumeRenderer
body: StructuredVolumeRenderer is a reusable, graph-native GPU renderer for scalar, vector, and hybrid volume data in WebGPU environments. It consumes storage buffers or 3D textures and exposes scene renderer facades for forward, deferred, raytrace, and raymarch passes. It distinguishes itself from sibling WebGL implementations by leveraging WebGPU's storage buffer and texture binding models, manual trilinear interpolation, and fixed-step jittered ray marching with early opacity termination. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Float32 scalar buffers, WGSL-aligned float32x4 vector buffers, or matching float 3D textures. Outputs: Rendered image with premultiplied front-to-back transparency. Data Structures Scalar Source: Defined by sources.scalar.type ('buffer' or 'texture'). If 'buffer': Binding layout is read-only-storage, group 0, location 0. If 'texture': Binding layout includes viewDimension: '3d'. Vector Source: WGSL-aligned float32x4 buffers. Transforms: worldToVolumeMatrix for coordinate transformation. Camera: cameraAndSamples.xyz for ray origin derivation. Numbered Steps 1. Source Binding Setup: Determine binding type based on sources.scalar.type. If texture, set viewDimension to '3d'. 2. Offset Validation: Check if buffer offset is an integer, non-negative, and aligned to bytesPerElement. 3. Ray Generation: Compute nearWorld by unprojecting camera UV at depth 0.0. Compute farWorld by unprojecting camera UV at depth 1.0. Transform nearWorld using worldToVolumeMatrix to get rayOrigin. Transform farWorld using worldToVolumeMatrix to get rayTarget. Compute rayDirection as normalize(rayTarget - rayOrigin). 4. Ray Marching: Execute fixed-step jittered ray marching. 5. Interpolation: Perform manual eight-corner trilinear interpolation for volume values. 6. Compositing: Apply premultiplied front-to-back transparency. 7. Early Termination: Terminate ray if accumulated opacity exceeds threshold. 8. Transfer Function: Apply sequential/signed scalar transfer functions or direction/constant vector colors. Formulas Ray Origin: O = M{w2v} \cdot \text{unproject}(UV, 0.0) Ray Direction: D = \text{normalize}(M{w2v} \cdot \text{unproject}(UV, 1.0) - O) Compositing: Standard front-to-back alpha blending Parameters Ray Samples: 72 samples per view in showcase. Boundary Handling: Second-order centered differences in interior; selectable second-order one-sided or periodic boundary handling. Glyphs: Optional 3D arrows (solid shaft-plus-cone SDFs). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Texture Binding: On adapters without float32-filterable, r32float/rgba32float textures must be bound with unfilterable-float sample type to avoid pipeline creation failure. Buffer Offset Alignment: WebGPU requires storage buffer offsets to be multiples of device.limits.minStorageBufferOffsetAlignment (commonly 256). Ray Origin: Using a single camera position for orthographic projections causes rays to converge; using near plane unprojection ensures parallel rays and correct near-plane clipping. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupbinding(sources): if sources.scalar.type == 'buffer': return {'type': 'read-only-storage', 'group': 0, 'location': 0} else: return {'type': 'texture', 'group': 0, 'location': 0, 'viewDimension': '3d'} def validateoffset(binding, bytesperelement): offset = binding.get('offset', 0) if not isinstance(offset, int) or offset < 0 or offset % bytesperelement != 0: raise ValueError('Structured volume buffer offset is not aligned to its element format.') def unproject(camerauv, depth, invviewproj): clip = (camerauv.x, camerauv.y, depth, 1.0) eye = multiplymatrixvector(invviewproj, clip) return (eye.x / eye.w, eye.y / eye.w, eye.z / eye.w) def transformpoint(matrix, point): w = dot(matrix[3], point) + matrix[3][3] return ( (dot(matrix[0], point) + matrix[0][3]) / w, (dot(matrix[1], point) + matrix[1][3]) / w, (dot(matrix[2], point) + matrix[2][3]) / w) def generateray(camerauv, worldtovolumematrix, invviewproj): nearworld = unproject(camerauv, 0.0, invviewproj) farworld = unproject(camerauv, 1.0, invviewproj) rayorigin = transformpoint(worldtovolumematrix, nearworld) raytarget = transformpoint(worldtovolumematrix, farworld) raydirection = normalize(raytarget - rayorigin) return rayorigin, raydirection def prepare(commandencoder, options): # Configures render pass and bind groups; does not submit internally pass def draw(renderpass, structuredvolume): # Dispatches rendering commands; does not submit internally pass def render(commandencoder, renderpass, structuredvolume): prepare(commandencoder, structuredvolume.options) draw(renderpass, structuredvolume) Renders volume boundaries using 3D geometry intersection for ray-box traversal. Choose when WebGL is required or when explicit geometry-based intersection is preferred. WebGL Multi-pass Ray-casting with 3D Geometry Intersection Simulates light transport with multiple bounces and scattering. Choose when physically accurate lighting is needed and performance allows. WebGL Path Tracing Volume Rendering Time Complexity: Fixed-step ray marching with 72 samples per view in showcase. Memory Complexity: Depends on volume resolution; 40³ showcase volume used. Performance: 30 Hz field/derivative updates without volume readback in showcase. Strengths: Reusable, graph-native, supports scalar/vector/hybrid data, manual interpolation for control. Limitations: Requires WebGPU, manual interpolation may be slower than hardware trilinear, alignment constraints. When to Use: WebGPU environments, need for reusable renderer, scalar/vector/hybrid data. When Not to Use: WebGL-only environments, or when hardware-accelerated trilinear interpolation is strictly required over manual interpolation. StructuredVolumeRenderer was introduced in luma.gl PR #3104 as part of the Vector Field Lab showcase. It supports scalar, vector, and hybrid volume rendering, exposing facades for various rendering passes. The renderer is designed to be reusable and graph-native, integrating with WebGPU's command encoding and rendering pass models. feat(gpgpu): add Vector Field Lab differential operators showcase, https://github.com/visgl/luma.gl/pull/3104, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Multi-pass GPU Ray-casting
head: Ray Casting Volume Rendering Pipeline, RayCasting101
body: Multi-pass GPU ray-casting decomposes the volume rendering pipeline into distinct rendering passes to decouple ray entry/exit point calculation from the final compositing step. Unlike single-pass approaches that compute all ray parameters within a single fragment shader invocation, this method uses intermediate textures to store geometric ray data (entry and exit positions) before performing the final ray-marching compositing. This separation allows for more flexible handling of complex ray generation logic and can simplify shader complexity, though it incurs additional memory bandwidth costs for the intermediate buffers. The method executes a sequence of three rendering passes. It assumes a standard hardware-accelerated sampling setup where volume data resides in 3D texture memory. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume texture (3D), World-View-Projection matrix (WVP), Scale factor, Step size, Volume dimensions (W, H, D), and maximum iteration count. Outputs: Final composited image in SampleRenderView. Intermediate Data: FrontTexture (stores ray entry points), RearTexture (stores ray exit points). Data Structures: FrontTexture: 2D texture, format matching the screen resolution, storing 3D position vectors (entry points). RearTexture: 2D texture, format matching the screen resolution, storing 3D position vectors (exit points). VolumeTexture: 3D texture containing the scalar field data. Numbered Steps: 1. Calculate Ray Parameters: Compute the World-View-Projection matrix WVP = \text{World} \times \text{View} \times \text{Proj}. 2. Render Rear Positions (Exit Points): Set blend state to disable blending (overwrite). Bind RearTexture as the render target view. Set rasterizer state to Back Culling (cull front-facing triangles of the volume bounding box). Set shader constants: WVP, Scale Factor. Execute technique RayCasting101FXRenderPosition. This pass renders the back faces of the volume bounding box, outputting the world-space exit positions of rays intersecting the volume. Flush the context. 3. Render Front Positions (Entry Points): Set blend state to disable blending. Bind FrontTexture as the render target view. Set rasterizer state to Front Culling (cull back-facing triangles of the volume bounding box). Set shader constants: WVP, Scale Factor. Execute technique RayCasting101FXRenderPosition. This pass renders the front faces of the volume bounding box, outputting the world-space entry positions of rays intersecting the volume. Flush the context. 4. Final Ray Casting and Compositing: Bind SampleRenderView as the render target. Set viewport to the full window dimensions. Clear the render target (e.g., to red (1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) as a debug or default value). Set shader resources: WVP matrix. Scale Factor. FrontTexture Shader Resource View (SRV). RearTexture SRV. VolumeTexture SRV. Step Size vector. Maximum Iterations integer. Volume Width, Height, Depth integers. Execute technique RayCasting101FXRayCastSimple. This pass reads the entry/exit points from the intermediate textures, marches through the volume using the step size, samples the volume texture, and performs front-to-back compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multipassgpuraycasting(device, context, renderer, volumedata, camera): # 1. Calculate World-View-Projection Matrix wvp = camera.world camera.view camera.proj # 2. Render Rear Positions (Exit Points) # Setup blend state to disable blending setupblend(enableblending=False) # Prepare rear render target view preparertv(reartextureview) # Set rasterizer state to back culling setrasterizerstate(cullmode=CULLBACK) # Set shader constants renderer.setmatrix("RayCasting101FXWVP", wvp) renderer.setfloat("RayCasting101FXScaleFactor", scalefactor) # Execute technique to render back faces of bounding box executetechnique(renderer.techniques["RayCasting101FXRenderPosition"]) # Flush context to ensure completion context.flush() # 3. Render Front Positions (Entry Points) # Setup blend state to disable blending setupblend(enableblending=False) # Prepare front render target view preparertv(fronttextureview) # Set rasterizer state to front culling setrasterizerstate(cullmode=CULLFRONT) # Set shader constants renderer.setmatrix("RayCasting101FXWVP", wvp) renderer.setfloat("RayCasting101FXScaleFactor", scalefactor) # Execute technique to render front faces of bounding box executetechnique(renderer.techniques["RayCasting101FXRenderPosition"]) # Flush context to ensure completion context.flush() # 4. Final Ray Casting and Compositing # Set render target to final output context.outputmerger.settargets(samplerenderview) # Set viewport context.rasterizer.setviewports([Viewport(0, 0, width, height, 0.0, 1.0)]) # Clear render target context.clearrendertargetview(samplerenderview, color=(1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) # Set shader resources renderer.setmatrix("RayCasting101FXWVP", wvp) renderer.setfloat("RayCasting101FXScaleFactor", scalefactor) renderer.setresource("RayCasting101FXBack", reartexturesrv) renderer.setresource("RayCasting101FXFront", fronttexturesrv) renderer.setresource("RayCasting101FXVolume", volumetexturesrv) renderer.setvector("RayCasting101FXStepSize", stepsize) renderer.setint("RayCasting101FXIterations", maxiterations) renderer.setint("RayCasting101FXWidth", volumewidth) renderer.setint("RayCasting101FXHeight", volumeheight) renderer.setint("RayCasting101FXDepth", volumedepth) # Execute final ray casting technique executetechnique(renderer.techniques["RayCasting101FXRayCastSimple"]) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The accuracy of entry/exit points depends on the rasterization precision of the bounding box geometry. Floating-point errors in the intermediate textures can lead to slight gaps or overlaps in the final ray march. Empty Volumes: If the volume is empty or the camera is outside the volume, the front/rear passes may produce no output, requiring a clear or default color in the final pass. Memory Bandwidth: Writing to two intermediate textures (FrontTexture, RearTexture) doubles the memory bandwidth requirement compared to a single-pass approach that computes points on the fly. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the average number of steps per ray. The constant factor is higher than single-pass due to the overhead of two additional render passes and memory writes. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the two intermediate position textures, plus O(V) for the volume data, where W, H are screen dimensions and V is volume size. Strengths: Simplifies the final compositing shader by pre-computing ray bounds; allows for easier integration of complex ray generation logic (e.g., non-linear rays) in the first two passes. Limitations: Increased memory bandwidth usage; potential precision loss from storing positions in textures; requires careful synchronization between passes. When to use: When ray generation is complex or when the rendering pipeline needs to separate geometric intersection from optical compositing. Not ideal for memory-constrained environments due to intermediate buffers. Multi-pass GPU ray-casting is a traditional approach to hardware-accelerated volume rendering, often cited in early GPU-based volume visualization literature. The specific implementation details described here, including the RayCasting101 technique names and the use of front/rear culling for position extraction, originate from DirectX 11 tutorial code and community discussions. It represents a step towards more modern, optimized single-pass or tiled approaches by modularizing the rendering pipeline. name: GPU Volume Ray Casting
head: GPU-accelerated Ray-Cast Volume Rendering, Remote 3D DICOM Volume Rendering, VTK GPU Ray Casting, VTK GPU Volume Ray Casting, VTK Volume Rendering, vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper
body: GPU Volume Ray Casting is a hardware-accelerated image-order rendering technique that executes the ray-marching loop, classification, and front-to-back compositing within the GPU's fragment shader. It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based volume rendering by leveraging the graphics pipeline's parallel texture sampling capabilities, making it the default recommended method for real-time interactive visualization of medical CT/MR scans. It sets itself apart from CPU-based alternatives by utilizing the GPU's dedicated texture hardware for trilinear interpolation and parallel compositing, achieving significantly higher frame rates for large 3D datasets. The method implements the emission-absorption optical model defined in Direct volume ray casting. The pipeline consists of ray generation, hardware-accelerated sampling, classification, and compositing. Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset (e.g., vtkImageData or NIfTI-derived array) containing voxel intensities. Input: Camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix) defining the ray origin and direction for each pixel. Input: Transfer functions mapping scalar values to color (C) and opacity (\alpha). Output: A 2D color buffer (image) with accumulated color and opacity per pixel. 1. Volume Data: Stored in 3D texture memory. The layout corresponds to the voxel grid dimensions (Dx, Dy, Dz) and spacing (Sx, Sy, Sz). 2. Transfer Functions: Color Transfer Function: Maps scalar value v to RGB color (r, g, b). Implemented as a piecewise linear interpolation over control points (vi, ri, gi, bi). Opacity Transfer Function: Maps scalar value v to opacity \alpha \in [0, 1]. Implemented as a piecewise function over control points (vi, \alphai). Gradient Opacity (Optional): Maps gradient magnitude |\nabla v| to additional opacity modulation, enhancing edge definition. Sample Distance (d): The step size along the ray in world units. Controls sampling density. Default is typically 0.2–0.3. Auto-Adjust Sample Distances: A boolean flag. When enabled, the renderer dynamically adjusts d to maintain a target frame rate. Jittering: A boolean flag. When enabled, adds random offset to sample positions to break up banding artifacts. Lighting Coefficients: Ambient (ka) and Diffuse (kd) light coefficients for shading. Defaults: ka=0.3, kd=0.7. Interpolation Type: Linear (trilinear) or Nearest Neighbor. Linear is standard for smooth results. 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel (x, y) in the render window, compute the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} in world space using the camera's view and projection matrices. Determine the entry (t{min}) and exit (t{max}) points of the ray with the volume's bounding box. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize accumulated color C' = (0, 0, 0) and accumulated opacity \alpha' = 0. Calculate the number of steps N = \lceil (t{max} - t{min}) / d \rceil. For step i from 0 to N-1: a. Compute sample position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + (t{min} + i \cdot d) \cdot \mathbf{d}. b. If jittering is enabled, add a small random offset to \mathbf{p}. c. Hardware Sampling: Sample the 3D texture at \mathbf{p} using trilinear interpolation to obtain the scalar value v. d. Classification: Retrieve color Ci and opacity \alphai from the transfer functions using v. If gradient opacity is used, compute gradient magnitude g = |\nabla v| (via finite differences or precomputed gradient texture) and modulate \alphai. e. Compositing: Update accumulated values using the front-to-back equation: C'{i} = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Ci \alpha'{i} = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai f. Early Ray Termination (ERT): If \alpha'{i} \geq \alpha{threshold} (typically 0.95 or 1.0), break the loop. 3. Final Color Output: Set the pixel color to C' and opacity to \alpha' in the framebuffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpuvolumeraycasting(volumetexture, camera, transferfunctions, sampledistance, jitteringenabled, alphathreshold=0.95): """ Simulates the GPU fragment shader logic for volume ray casting. Args: volumetexture: 3D texture object supporting trilinear sampling. camera: Object with getrayorigin(x, y) and getraydirection(x, y) methods. transferfunctions: Object with getcolor(value) -> (r,g,b) and getopacity(value) -> alpha methods. sampledistance: Float, step size in world units. jitteringenabled: Boolean. alphathreshold: Float, opacity threshold for early termination. Returns: 2D array of colors (width, height, 3). """ width, height = camera.getresolution() outputimage = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) # Pre-calculate bounding box intersection for optimization # In a real GPU implementation, this is done in a vertex shader or compute shader bboxmin, bboxmax = volumetexture.getbounds() for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # 1. Ray Generation rayorigin = camera.getrayorigin(x, y) raydirection = camera.getraydirection(x, y) raydirection = normalize(raydirection) # Compute intersection with bounding box tmin, tmax = computeraybboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, bboxmin, bboxmax) if tmin > tmax: continue # Ray misses volume # 2. Ray Marching accumulatedcolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 # Determine number of steps numsteps = int((tmax - tmin) / sampledistance) for i in range(numsteps): # Current position along ray t = tmin + i sampledistance position = rayorigin + t raydirection # Jittering if jitteringenabled: jitter = np.random.uniform(-sampledistance/2, sampledistance/2, 3) position += jitter # 3. Hardware Sampling # Clamp position to volume bounds to avoid out-of-bounds texture access position = clamp(position, bboxmin, bboxmax) scalarvalue = volumetexture.sampletrilinear(position) # 4. Classification color, alpha = transferfunctions.getcolorandopacity(scalarvalue) # 5. Compositing # Front-to-back blending weight = (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) alpha accumulatedcolor += weight color accumulatedalpha += weight # 6. Early Ray Termination if accumulatedalpha >= alphathreshold: break outputimage[y, x] = accumulatedcolor return outputimage def computeraybboxintersection(origin, direction, bboxmin, bboxmax): """ Computes the entry (tmin) and exit (tmax) times of a ray intersecting an AABB. Returns (tmin, tmax). If no intersection, returns (inf, -inf). """ tmin = -np.inf tmax = np.inf for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bboxmin[i] or origin[i] > bboxmax[i]: return (np.inf, -np.inf) # Parallel and outside else: t1 = (bboxmin[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bboxmax[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) if tmin > tmax: return (np.inf, -inf) # Ray misses box return (tmin, tmax) def normalize(v): return v / np.linalg.norm(v) def clamp(v, minval, maxval): return np.maximum(np.minimum(v, maxval), minval) Invalid Input Data: If no valid DICOM files or image data are found, the system may fall back to a dummy 100x100x100 volume filled with constant values to prevent crashes. Missing PixelData: DICOM files without PixelData tags are invalid and should be filtered out during validation. Gradient Opacity Mismatch: Using gradient opacity with a range calibrated for raw intensity values on normalized [0, 1] data results in zero opacity (black screen) because gradient magnitudes are small. Precision: Trilinear interpolation in hardware provides sufficient precision for most medical imaging, but extreme zoom levels may require adaptive sample distance adjustment. Renders multiple volume datasets simultaneously by compositing them along a single ray using coordinate transformation matrices. Choose when visualizing overlapping anatomical structures from different modalities or time points. Optimizes the ray marching loop into a single shader pass with reduced branching. Choose for maximum performance on modern GPUs where branch divergence is costly. Divides the volume into bricks to optimize memory access patterns and cache locality. Choose for very large volumes that exceed GPU memory capacity. Focuses on the specific GLSL/HLSL implementation details of the fragment shader. Choose when implementing custom rendering effects or debugging shader artifacts. Uses multiple rendering passes for effects like depth-of-field or advanced lighting. Choose when post-processing effects are required beyond basic compositing. Time Complexity: O(P \cdot N), where P is the number of pixels and N is the average number of samples per ray. N depends on volume size, sample distance, and camera distance. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the number of voxels in the volume, stored in GPU texture memory. Measured Performance: Rendering times are measured in milliseconds per frame. The pipeline includes render, data extraction, numpy conversion, JPEG encoding, and base64 encoding phases for remote transmission. Typical render window sizes are 600x600 with 4x multisampling. Scaling: Performance scales with GPU hardware capabilities. Auto-adjust sample distances can maintain interactivity by reducing N when frame rates drop. Strengths: Real-time interactive performance, hardware-accelerated sampling, support for complex transfer functions and shading. Limitations: Requires GPU with OpenGL support. Limited compared to CPU methods in handling extremely complex volume properties or non-standard data types without custom shaders. Multi-volume rendering has synchronization limitations. When to Use: Real-time medical imaging visualization, teleradiology, educational tools, and any scenario requiring interactive exploration of 3D scalar fields. When Not to Use: Systems without GPU support (use CPU Ray Casting), or when precise scientific measurement of every voxel is required without interpolation artifacts (use slice-based rendering). GPU Volume Ray Casting originated with the advent of programmable graphics pipelines (OpenGL 2.0+ and later) that allowed fragment shaders to perform arbitrary computations. It was popularized in medical imaging visualization toolkits like VTK (Visualization Toolkit) as vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper, providing a significant speedup over CPU-based ray casting. It is widely used in 3D Slicer, a medical imaging informatics platform, as the default volume rendering method for computers with sufficient graphics capabilities. Recent implementations extend this to remote rendering architectures, allowing real-time visualization of DICOM data over networks. nikhilhv317/RemoteRendering, https://github.com/nikhilhv317/RemoteRendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Ftoutou/brain-mri-3d-renderer, https://github.com/Ftoutou/brain-mri-3d-renderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volume rendering — 3D Slicer documentation, https://slicer.readthedocs.io/en/5.0/userguide/modules/volumerendering.html, fetched 2026-10-27

name: GPU Multi-Volume Ray Casting Mapper
head: Dual-input volume mapper, GPU Multi Volume Ray Cast Mapper, Multi-volume GPU ray casting mapper, Multi-volume ray cast mapper, Multi-volume ray casting, vtkGPUMultiVolumeRayCastMapper
body: The GPU Multi-Volume Ray Casting Mapper is a volume rendering technique that renders multiple volume datasets simultaneously by extending the single-volume vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper to accept multiple vtkImageData datasets and vtkVolumeProperty objects, using GPU shaders for ray traversal and compositing. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly compositing multiple 3D scalar fields along a single ray, using coordinate transformation matrices to align samples from different volumes to a common ray space. Unlike the standard vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper which handles one volume, this mapper manages the synchronization of ray positions across N volumes, applying per-volume transformations and clipping planes within the fragment shader loop. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two or more vtkImageData datasets (scalar fields) and corresponding vtkVolumeProperty objects (transfer functions). The primary input is at port 0; additional inputs are at ports 1 to N-1. Outputs: A 2D color buffer (framebuffer) with the composited image. Data Structures: Texture Uniforms: sampler3D dataSetTexture[MAXNUMBEROFVOLUMES]: 3D textures holding the scalar data for each volume. sampler1D opacityTexture[MAXNUMBEROFVOLUMES]: 1D textures holding the opacity transfer function for each volume. mat4 P1toPN[MAXNUMBEROFVOLUMES-1]: Transformation matrices. P1toPN[i] transforms texture coordinates from the first volume (Volume 1) to the (i+2)-th volume. Computed as T{world \to tex, N} \cdot T{world \to tex, 1}^{-1} \cdot T{user}, where T{user} is an optional user-defined transform. vec3 lowBounds[MAXNUMBEROFVOLUMES], vec3 highBounds[MAXNUMBEROFVOLUMES]: Bounding box limits for each volume in texture coordinates, adjusted for cropping. vec3 ClippingplanesNormal[MAXNUMBEROFVOLUMES], vec3 ClippingplanesOrigins[MAXNUMBEROFVOLUMES]: Clipping plane definitions in texture coordinates. int clipped[MAXNUMBEROFVOLUMES]: Flags indicating if clipping is active for each volume. State Variables: TransformedInput, TransformedInput2: Shallow copies of input data used to track modification times. ClippedCroppingRegionPlanes[6]: Array storing cropping planes (min/max for X, Y, Z) clipped by volume bounds. Parameters: MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES: Compile-time constant. 3 on Apple platforms, 4 otherwise. MAXNUMBEROFVOLUMES: 4 on Apple platforms, 5 otherwise. ImageSampleDistance: Base sample distance in image space. Default 1.0. Clamped [0.1, 100.0]. MinimumImageSampleDistance: Lower bound for adaptive sampling. Default 1.0. Clamped [0.1, 100.0]. MaximumImageSampleDistance: Upper bound for adaptive sampling. Default 10.0. Clamped [0.1, 100.0]. AutoAdjustSampleDistances: Boolean flag (0/1). Enables automatic adjustment of ImageSampleDistance based on allocated render time. MaxMemoryInBytes: Maximum GPU memory for volume data. Probed from GPU info; defaults to 128 MB if unavailable. MaxMemoryFraction: Fraction of MaxMemoryInBytes used. Default 0.75. Range [0.1, 1.0]. ReportProgress: Boolean flag. If true, calls glFinish() to report progress. Should be false for small datasets to avoid slowdown. MaskType: Enum (BinaryMaskType or LabelMapMaskType). Default LabelMapMaskType. MaskBlendFactor: Blending weight for mask color transfer function. Default 1.0. Range [0.0, 1.0]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Probe GPU list for dedicated video memory. If 0, use dedicated system memory. If both 0, set MaxMemoryInBytes to 128 MB. Ignore shared system memory. Validate inputs: Check for null renderer, null volume, and null inputs. If Cropping is true, check that CroppingRegionPlanes[0] < Planes[1], Planes[2] < Planes[3], and Planes[4] < Planes[5]. If invalid, set goodSoFar = 0 silently. Transform Setup: For each additional volume N, compute P1toPN matrix combining world-to-texture-N, inverse world-to-texture-1, and user transform. Extent Adjustment: If input extents do not start at zero, adjust the origin by adding extents[2cc]spacing[cc] and shift extents to start from zero for both inputs. 2. Render Entry: If GeneratingCanonicalView is true, call CanonicalViewRender and return (skips timing/events). Otherwise, invoke VolumeMapperRenderStartEvent, start timer, validate render, call GPURender, stop timer, and invoke VolumeMapperRenderEndEvent. 3. Fragment Shader Execution (trace() function): Initialization: Calculate initial ray position pos for Volume 1. Calculate initial positions posX[] for additional volumes using posX[iii] = vec3(P1toPN[iii] vec4(pos, 1.0)). Initialize destColor via initialColor(). Set remainOpacity = 1.0 - destColor.a. Initialize rayDir (incremental vector in texture space) and tMax (max ray length). Ray Marching Loop: While inside is true: 1. inside is true if t < tMax, remainOpacity >= 0.0039 (1/255), and pos is within lowBounds[0] and highBounds[0]. 2. Volume 0 Sampling: If pos is within bounds and not clipped (or clipping check passes): value[0] = texture3D(dataSetTexture[0], pos). scalar[0] = scalarFromValue(value[0]). opacity[0] = texture1D(opacityTexture[0], scalar[0]). 3. Additional Volumes Sampling (for iii from 0 to NumberOfVolumes-2): Let vol = iii + 1. If posX[vol-1] is within bounds and not clipped: value[vol] = texture3D(dataSetTexture[vol], posX[vol-1]). scalar[vol] = scalarFromValue(value[vol]). opacity[vol] = texture1D(opacityTexture[vol], scalar[vol]). 4. Compositing: For each volume vol sampled: If opacity[vol].a > 0.0: color[vol] = shade(vol, value[vol]) opacity[vol].a. destColor = destColor + color[vol] remainOpacity. remainOpacity = remainOpacity (1.0 - opacity[vol].a). 5. Advance Ray: pos = pos + rayDir. posX[iii] = posX[iii] + rayDir (for all additional volumes). t += 1.0. Final Output: glFragColor = destColor. glFragColor.a = 1.0 - remainOpacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. It manages fragment shader programs, framebuffer objects, and texture uploads for rendering multiple volumes simultaneously. Confines volume rendering to specific regions using a binary or multi-label mask, supporting blending between standard and mask-specific color transfer functions. It maps mask values to distinct color transfer function components and blending weights. A hardware-accelerated direct volume rendering technique implemented in VTK via vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper that uses the Composite blend mode for standard alpha blending during ray casting. It distinguishes itself from the multi-volume mapper by focusing on single-volume composite blending. Renders a volume using ray casting on a 3D texture with specific parameters for distance-based color blending and ICPE (Intensity Contrast Preserving Enhancement) scaling. Methods to set the mask type for volume rendering, either Binary or LabelMap. To set binary mask: this->MaskType = vtkGPUMultiVolumeRayCastMapper::BinaryMaskType. To set label map mask: this->MaskType = vtkGPUMultiVolumeRayCastMapper::LabelMapMaskType. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray and the number of volumes. The ray marching loop iterates for each sample, and for each sample, it performs texture lookups and compositing for all N volumes. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the sum of the memory required for N 3D textures and N 1D opacity textures. Limited by MaxMemoryInBytes. Performance: Uses GLSL shaders, which are faster and more widely supported than OpenCL for this purpose. Adaptive sampling (AutoAdjustSampleDistances) can improve performance by reducing sample density when render time is constrained. Strengths: Simultaneous rendering of multiple volumes with correct depth ordering and compositing. Hardware-accelerated sampling and shading. Limitations: Hardware loop limits may require nested loop structures or careful unrolling. Non-zero extents in input data require manual adjustment of origin and extents. ReportProgress using glFinish() can significantly slow down rendering of small datasets if enabled. When to Use: When visualizing multiple co-registered or spatially related volume datasets (e.g., multi-modal medical imaging) simultaneously. When Not to Use: When rendering a single volume (use vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper for better optimization), or when input data has more than one independent component (unsupported). The GPU Multi-Volume Ray Casting Mapper was developed as an extension to the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) to support multi-volume rendering on the GPU. It was modified by Carlos Falcón and Karl Krissian to extend the single-volume vtkGPUVolumeRayCastMapper. The implementation relies on GLSL shaders for ray traversal and compositing, chosen for their speed and device support compared to OpenCL. It is used in VTK-based applications requiring simultaneous visualization of multiple scalar fields. name: OpenGL GPU Multi Volume Ray Cast Mapper
head: OpenGL GPU Multi-Volume Ray Casting Mapper, OpenGL Volume Ray Caster, vtkOpenGLGPUMultiVolumeRayCastMapper
body: The OpenGL GPU Multi Volume Ray Cast Mapper is an OpenGL-specific subclass of the GPU Multi-Volume Ray Casting Mapper that handles hardware extension checks, OpenGL object lifecycle management, and clipping/cropping plane setup for GPU-accelerated volume rendering. It serves as the concrete implementation responsible for drawing the volume ray cast image to the screen by managing fragment shader programs, framebuffer objects, and texture uploads required for rendering multiple volumes simultaneously. It builds on GPU Multi-Volume Ray Casting Mapper by providing the specific OpenGL API bindings and state management necessary for hardware-accelerated ray casting. The method initializes OpenGL resources, validates hardware support, uploads volume data and transfer functions to GPU textures, applies clipping/cropping constraints, and executes a fragment shader-based ray casting pass into an offscreen framebuffer before presenting the result. Inputs: Primary volume data (vtkImageData), optional secondary volume data (vtkImageData), and up to MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES additional volumes. Volume properties including color transfer functions, opacity transfer functions, and blend types (MIP, Composite, Shaded, etc.). Clipping planes (vtkPlane) and cropping region bounds for each volume. Render window and renderer context. Outputs: A rendered image displayed on the screen, generated via an offscreen framebuffer object (FBO). Clipping Planes: ClippingPlane[MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES+1] stores pointers to vtkPlane objects for the primary and additional volumes. State Flags: Clipped[MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES+1], Cropped[MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES+1], ClippedModified[MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES+1]: Integer flags tracking the clipping/cropping state and modification status per volume. Cropping Bounds: CroppingLowBounds[MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES+1][3] and CroppingHighBounds[MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES+1][3] store 3D bounding box coordinates for cropping regions per volume. Transformed Inputs: TransformedInput, TransformedInput2, and AdditionalTransformedInput array store shallow copies of input data with adjusted extents to handle non-zero starting extents. Last Input Tracking: LastInput, LastInput2, and AdditionalLastInput arrays track previous inputs to detect data changes. Reduction Factor: ReductionFactor (double, 0.0 to 1.0) used to scale the render viewport based on performance. 1. Check Hardware Support: Call IsRenderSupported(window, property) to verify that the hardware supports 3D texture mapping and required OpenGL extensions for the given render window and volume property. Returns 1 if supported, 0 otherwise. 2. Load Extensions: Call LoadExtensions(window) to load required and optional OpenGL extensions. Sets SupportsGLARBtexturefloat if the extension is loaded. 3. Test Required Extensions: For each required extension, call TestRequiredExtension(extensionname). If an extension is not supported, add its name to the unsupported extensions string. Returns 1 if supported, 0 otherwise. 4. Create OpenGL Objects: Call CreateOpenGLObjects(ren) to create OpenGL objects such as textures, buffers, and fragment program IDs. 5. Allocate Framebuffers: Call AllocateFrameBuffers(ren) to allocate GPU memory for framebuffers based on the window size. 6. Prepare Input Data: Validate that at least one input is not NULL. Update all input data (input, input2, and additional inputs). If the input has changed (timestamp or data), create shallow copies in TransformedInput, TransformedInput2, and AdditionalTransformedInput arrays. Adjust extents to handle non-zero starting values: Get origin and spacing. Adjust origin: origin[cc] = origin[cc] + extents[2cc]spacing[cc] for cc in 0..2. Adjust extents: extents[2cc+1] -= extents[2cc] and extents[2cc] -= extents[2cc] for cc in 0..2. Set adjusted origin and extents in the cloned data. 7. Load Scalar Field Data: Call LoadScalarField(input, input2, textureExtent, volume) to load scalar field data into a 3D texture on the GPU. Handles point or cell-based extents. 8. Update Transfer Functions: Call UpdateColorTransferFunction(vol, numberOfScalarComponents) to update the color transfer function on the GPU. Call UpdateOpacityTransferFunction(vol, numberOfScalarComponents, level) to update the opacity transfer function on the GPU. 9. Clip Bounding Box: Call ClipBoundingBox(ren, worldBounds, vol) to clip the bounding box with clipping planes and near/far planes. 10. Check Cropping Planes: If cropping is enabled, validate that cropping planes are valid (i.e., CroppingRegionPlanes[0] < CroppingRegionPlanes[1], etc.). If invalid, silently fail by setting goodSoFar = 0. 11. Render Volume: Compute the reduction factor using ComputeReductionFactor(allocatedTime) based on previous frame time and allocated time. Render the volume using one of: RenderWholeVolume(ren, vol), RenderRegions(ren, vol), or RenderSubVolume(ren, bounds, vol). Load projection parameters using LoadProjectionParameters(ren, vol). Compute the number of cropping regions using ComputeNumberOfCroppingRegions(). 12. Copy FBO to Texture: Call CopyFBOToTexture() to copy the color buffer state from the framebuffer object to a texture. 13. Render to Screen: Call RenderTextureToScreen(ren) to render the offscreen buffer to the screen. 14. Release Resources: Call ReleaseGraphicsResources() to delete OpenGL objects. Post-condition: OpenGLObjectsCreated == 0. Origin Adjustment: origin[cc] = origin[cc] + extents[2 \times cc] \times spacing[cc] for cc \in \{0, 1, 2\}. Extent Adjustment: extents[2 \times cc + 1] = extents[2 \times cc + 1] - extents[2 \times cc] extents[2 \times cc] = 0 for cc \in \{0, 1, 2\}. Reduction Factor: Computed by ComputeReductionFactor(allocatedTime) based on previous frame time and allocated time. Value is between 0.0 and 1.0. Power of Two: PowerOfTwoGreaterOrEqual(x) computes the smallest power of two greater than or equal to x. ClippingPlane[MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES+1]: Array of vtkPlane pointers for clipping planes. CroppingLowBounds[MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES+1][3] and CroppingHighBounds[MAXNUMBEROFADDITIONALVOLUMES+1][3]: 3D bounding box coordinates for cropping regions. ReductionFactor: Double value between 0.0 and 1.0 for viewport reduction. FrameRate: Desired frame rate in frames per second (default 10.0, range 0.01 to 60.0). BlendType: Enum for blend function (MIP=0, Composite=1, CompositeShadeRamp=2, CTSkin=3, CTBone=4, CTMuscle=5, RGBComposite=6). OpacityWindow and OpacityLevel: Double values for opacity transfer function window and level (default 4096 and 2048). Invalid Cropping Planes: If cropping planes define a zero or negative volume (e.g., due to interactive widget dragging), the renderer silently fails by setting goodSoFar = 0 without error messages. NULL Inputs: Checks if input, input2, or any Additionalinput is NULL; if so, outputs an error message and fails. Color Channels: If color channels are not 3, the renderer may fail or produce incorrect results (commented out in some versions). Non-Zero Extents: The mapper requires workarounds for GPU volume ray casting mappers that cannot handle extents starting from non-zero values, necessitating extent adjustment. Four-Component Data: The shader handles four-component data (RGBA) by extracting scalar values from the alpha channel and computing colors from RGB, but this may not work correctly if color transfer functions are not properly configured. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def OpenGLGPUMultiVolumeRayCastMapperRender(window, property, volumes, clippingplanes, croppingbounds): # Step 1: Check hardware support if not IsRenderSupported(window, property): return False # Step 2: Load extensions LoadExtensions(window) SupportsGLARBtexturefloat = TestRequiredExtension("GLARBtexturefloat") # Step 3: Create OpenGL objects CreateOpenGLObjects(window.renderer) AllocateFrameBuffers(window.renderer) # Step 4: Prepare input data for vol in volumes: if vol.input is None: return False vol.input.Update() # Check for data change if vol.input != vol.LastInput or vol.input.GetMTime() > vol.TransformedInput.GetMTime(): vol.TransformedInput.ShallowCopy(vol.input) # Adjust extents for non-zero starting values extents = vol.TransformedInput.GetExtent() origin = vol.TransformedInput.GetOrigin() spacing = vol.TransformedInput.GetSpacing() for cc in range(3): origin[cc] = origin[cc] + extents[2cc] spacing[cc] extents[2cc+1] = extents[2cc+1] - extents[2cc] extents[2cc] = 0 vol.TransformedInput.SetOrigin(origin) vol.TransformedInput.SetExtent(extents) vol.LastInput = vol.input # Step 5: Load scalar field data for vol in volumes: LoadScalarField(vol.TransformedInput, vol.TransformedInput2, vol.textureExtent, vol) # Step 6: Update transfer functions for vol in volumes: UpdateColorTransferFunction(vol, vol.numberOfScalarComponents) UpdateOpacityTransferFunction(vol, vol.numberOfScalarComponents, vol.level) # Step 7: Clip bounding box for vol in volumes: ClipBoundingBox(window.renderer, vol.worldBounds, vol) # Step 8: Check cropping planes if vol.Cropping: if (vol.CroppingRegionPlanes[0] >= vol.CroppingRegionPlanes[1] or vol.CroppingRegionPlanes[2] >= vol.CroppingRegionPlanes[3] or vol.CroppingRegionPlanes[4] >= vol.CroppingRegionPlanes[5]): return False # Step 9: Compute reduction factor reductionfactor = ComputeReductionFactor(window.allocatedtime) # Step 10: Render volume LoadProjectionParameters(window.renderer, vol) numcroppingregions = ComputeNumberOfCroppingRegions() if reductionfactor < 1.0: RenderRegions(window.renderer, vol) else: RenderWholeVolume(window.renderer, vol) # Step 11: Copy FBO to texture CopyFBOToTexture() # Step 12: Render to screen RenderTextureToScreen(window.renderer) return True def ReleaseGraphicsResources(): # Step 13: Release resources DeleteOpenGLObjects() OpenGLObjectsCreated = 0 def IsRenderSupported(window, property): # Standard check: verify 3D texture support and required extensions return window.HasExtension("GLARBtexturefloat") and property.IsValid() def LoadExtensions(window): # Standard: query and cache supported extensions window.CacheExtensions() def TestRequiredExtension(extname): # Standard: check if extension is in cached list return extname in window.SupportedExtensions def CreateOpenGLObjects(renderer): # Standard: glGenTextures, glGenFramebuffers, glGenPrograms renderer.CreateTextures() renderer.CreateFramebuffers() renderer.CreateShaders() def AllocateFrameBuffers(renderer): # Standard: glTexImage2D for FBO color attachment based on window size w, h = renderer.GetWindowSize() renderer.AllocateFBO(w, h) def LoadScalarField(inputdata, input2, textureextent, volume): # Standard: glTexImage3D with input data volume.Upload3DTexture(inputdata, textureextent) def UpdateColorTransferFunction(vol, numcomponents): # Standard: upload LUT to 1D/2D texture vol.UploadColorLUT(numcomponents) def UpdateOpacityTransferFunction(vol, numcomponents, level): # Standard: upload opacity LUT to 1D texture vol.UploadOpacityLUT(numcomponents, level) def ClipBoundingBox(renderer, worldbounds, vol): # Standard: set glClipPlane or compute view-space clipping planes renderer.SetClippingPlanes(worldbounds) def ComputeReductionFactor(allocatedtime): # Standard: ratio of previous frame time to allocated time, clamped [0.0, 1.0] return min(1.0, max(0.0, allocatedtime / max(1.0, renderer.GetLastFrameTime()))) def LoadProjectionParameters(renderer, vol): # Standard: upload modelview/projection matrices to shader uniforms renderer.UploadMatrices() def ComputeNumberOfCroppingRegions(): # Standard: count active cropping planes return renderer.ActiveCroppingPlanesCount() def RenderRegions(renderer, vol): # Standard: render viewport scaled by reduction factor renderer.RenderScaledViewport(vol) def RenderWholeVolume(renderer, vol): # Standard: full resolution raycast renderer.RenderFullViewport(vol) def CopyFBOToTexture(): # Standard: glCopyTexImage2D or glBlitFramebuffer renderer.CopyFBOToTexture() def RenderTextureToScreen(renderer): # Standard: render fullscreen quad with FBO texture renderer.RenderQuad() def DeleteOpenGLObjects(): # Standard: glDeleteTextures, glDeleteFramebuffers, glDeletePrograms renderer.DeleteAllGLObjects() A GLSL fragment shader implementation for volume rendering that handles datasets with four components (e.g., RGBA or RGB+Alpha) by extracting scalar values and computing colors from a single vec4 input sample. It defines a function scalarFromValue that takes a vec4 value and returns the w component (alpha/4th channel) as a float, and functions colorFromValue and colorFromValue2 that take a vec4 value and return a vec4 where the RGB components are taken from the input's xyz and the alpha is hardcoded to 1.0. The shader targets GLSL version 110, indicated by the directive #version 110. A pitfall is that the comment notes that 'value' should be thought of as an object, implying the shader treats the input vector as a structured data entity rather than just raw color data. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The reduction factor allows for adaptive viewport scaling based on rendering time, which can improve interactive performance. Strengths: Supports multiple volumes, adaptive sampling, masking, and AMR mode through its parent class; handles clipping and cropping efficiently on the GPU. Limitations: Requires OpenGL hardware support for 3D texture mapping and specific extensions; may fail silently with invalid cropping planes or NULL inputs. When to Use: When rendering multiple volumes with OpenGL hardware acceleration, especially when clipping, cropping, or masking is required. When Not to Use: When hardware does not support required OpenGL extensions or when rendering single volumes without the need for multiple volume support. name: 8-bit Packed Volumetric Masking
head: Bit-packed volume mask, VolumetricModel mask extension
body: 8-bit Packed Volumetric Masking is a technique for applying voxel-level visibility masks to volumetric data without duplicating the underlying scalar volume data. It solves the memory overhead problem of traditional masking by storing masks as 8-bit packed boolean arrays, where each byte represents the visibility of 8 adjacent voxels along the X-axis. Unlike transfer functions which map scalar values to opacity/color, this method maps XYZ coordinates directly to boolean visibility, allowing for independent rotation or transformation of the mask relative to the data volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset with dimensions (volDimX, volDimY, volDimZ) and a mask buffer. Output: A boolean value indicating whether a given sampling position p falls within a visible voxel. Data Structures: The mask is stored in a VolumetricModel structure with the following fields: maskBuffer: A pointer to a 1D array of uint8 (unsigned char). maskDims: A vec3i specifying the dimensions of the mask buffer in memory units. For a volume of dimensions (volDimX, volDimY, volDimZ), maskDims is set to (\lfloor volDimX/8 \rfloor, volDimY, volDimZ). hasMask: A boolean flag indicating if a mask is present. Mask Buffer Layout: The mask buffer is a 1D array of unsigned chars. The index for a voxel at (x, y, z) is calculated as: index = z \times sliceSize + y \times maskDims.x + \lfloor x/8 \rfloor where sliceSize = maskDims.x \times maskDims.y. Algorithm Steps: 1. Commit Phase: In VolumetricModel::commit(), check if the 'mask' parameter exists. If present: retrieve the data pointer into maskBuffer, retrieve maskDims, and set hasMask to true. If not present: set hasMask to false. 2. Sampling Phase: For each ray sample at position p: Map continuous position p to discrete voxel indices (x, y, z) using floor rounding: x = \lfloor p.x \rfloor, y = \lfloor p.y \rfloor, z = \lfloor p.z \rfloor. Calculate the byte index in the packed buffer using the layout formula. Extract the specific bit corresponding to x within that byte using (x%8). Return the result of the bitwise AND operation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def inMask(maskbuffer, maskdims, p): """ Check if voxel at continuous position p is visible. Args: maskbuffer: list of uint8, the packed mask data. maskdims: tuple (mx, my, mz), dimensions of the mask buffer. p: tuple (px, py, pz), continuous sampling position. Returns: bool: True if visible, False if occluded/hidden. """ # If no mask is defined, consider everything visible if not maskbuffer: return True # Map continuous position to discrete voxel indices x = math.floor(p[0]) y = math.floor(p[1]) z = math.floor(p[2]) # Calculate slice size in the 1D buffer slicesize = maskdims[0] maskdims[1] # Calculate byte index in the 1D array byteindex = z slicesize + y maskdims[0] + (x // 8) # Retrieve the byte value maskval = maskbuffer[byteindex] # Determine the bit position within the byte (0-7) bitposition = x % 8 # Create bitmask and check visibility bitmask = 1 << bitposition return (maskval & bitmask) != 0 Parameters: mask: OSPData object containing the packed mask buffer, created via ospNewSharedData1D with type OSPUCHAR. maskDims: vec3i specifying the dimensions of the mask buffer. volDimX: The width of the volumetric dataset in voxels. Must be handled such that padding is applied if not a multiple of 8. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dimension Padding: If volDimX is not a multiple of 8, the mask buffer size calculation (volDimX \times volDimY \times volDimZ / 8) requires explicit padding to ensure valid memory access for the last partial byte. The buffer size must be rounded up to the next multiple of 8 bits per slice. Coordinate Rounding: The mask lookup uses floor(p.x), floor(p.y), floor(p.z) to map continuous sampling positions to discrete voxel indices. Bit Extraction: The specific bit within the byte is determined by (x%8), shifting a 1 by that amount to create a bitmask for the bitwise AND operation. Memory Efficiency: Reduces mask memory footprint by a factor of 8 compared to byte-per-voxel masks. Performance: Minimal overhead during ray casting; requires only one additional memory access and bitwise operation per sample. Limitations: Only supports binary visibility (visible/hidden). Does not support partial opacity or label-based masking directly. When to use: When memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and binary visibility masks are sufficient. When not to use: When label-based masking or partial transparency masks are required. This method was developed as an unofficial extension to the OSPRay library to optimize memory usage for volumetric masking. It was proposed by Shijou87 in a GitHub issue discussion in 2023, addressing the need to avoid duplicating volumetric data when applying masks. The implementation involves modifications to the VolumetricModel class and the volumes.ispc shader code.
