name: Region-Based Progressive Rendering
head: region-based scheme
body: Region-based progressive rendering is a transmission and rendering strategy for foveated volume data that prioritizes a user-defined Region of Interest (ROI) by reconstructing and displaying it at high resolution first, then iteratively adding peripheral layers at decreasing resolutions. It differs from coarse-to-fine schemes by avoiding the interference of low-resolution coefficients on the high-resolution ROI, resulting in a clearer initial view of the area of interest at the cost of a longer initial wait time. Inputs and Outputs Input: A multiresolution volume dataset (typically Haar wavelet coefficients), a ROI mask defined by center coordinates (x, y, z) and dimensions (s, s, s), and a viewing direction. Output: A sequence of rendered images, starting with the high-resolution ROI and progressively expanding to the full volume. Data Structures The method uses Haar wavelet coefficients organized into layers or blocks corresponding to resolution scales. The ROI is defined by coordinate bounds or a binary mask. Parameters Mask Center: The center coordinates of the ROI mask, typically specified as (128, 128, 128) for a 256^3 volume. Mask Size: The dimensions of the ROI mask, typically specified as (50, 50, 50). Resolution Scale: In iteration i, sub-volumes are reconstructed at a resolution scale of 2^{i-1} relative to the inner layer. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Define the ROI mask with center (x, y, z) and size (s, s, s). 2. First Iteration (i=1): Reconstruct the center fovea using partial volume reconstruction from the available high-resolution data. Render the fovea using a standard volume rendering algorithm. Display the result. 3. Subsequent Iterations (i > 1): Identify the immediate outer layer surrounding the previously rendered region. Divide this outer layer into 6 sub-volumes: Top, Bottom, Left, Right, Front, and Back. Reconstruct each of the 6 sub-volumes at a resolution scale of 2^{i-1}. Render each sub-volume separately using the standard rendering algorithm. 4. Image Composition: Combine the newly rendered images with the previous image. For Top, Bottom, Left, and Right sub-volumes: Add the rendered images to the previous image at their correct spatial positions. For Front and Back sub-volumes: Perform alpha compositing using the 'over' operator along the viewing ray. 5. Repeat: Continue iterations until the full volume is rendered or the user stops the process. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def regionbasedprogressiverendering(volumedata, roimask, viewdirection): roicenter = roimask['center'] roisize = roimask['size'] currentimage = None results = [] # Iteration 1: Reconstruct and render the center fovea using partial volume reconstruction foveadata = volumedata.reconstructregion(roicenter, roisize, scale=1) currentimage = rendervolume(foveadata, viewdirection) results.append(currentimage) iteration = 2 while not isfullvolumerendered(currentimage, roicenter, roisize, iteration): # Identify the immediate outer layer surrounding the previously rendered region outerbounds = getouterlayerbounds(roicenter, roisize, iteration) # Divide into 6 sub-volumes: top, bottom, left, right, front, back subvolumes = divideinto6subvolumes(outerbounds, roisize, iteration) newimages = {} resscale = 2 (iteration - 1) # Reconstruct each sub-volume at resolution scale 2^(i-1) and render using standard algorithm for name, bounds in subvolumes.items(): reconstructeddata = volumedata.reconstructregion(bounds, scale=resscale) newimages[name] = rendervolume(reconstructeddata, viewdirection) # Combine the newly rendered images with the previous image # Top, Bottom, Left, Right are added to the previous image at their correct positions for name in ['top', 'bottom', 'left', 'right']: currentimage = addimagespatially(currentimage, newimages[name], name) # Front and Back images need image composition using the 'over' operator # Order: Front over Inner over Back currentimage = compositeover(newimages['front'], currentimage) currentimage = compositeover(currentimage, newimages['back']) results.append(currentimage) iteration += 1 return results def rendervolume(data, viewdirection): # Standard volume rendering (e.g., ray casting) return data.castrays(viewdirection) def isfullvolumerendered(image, center, size, iteration): # Termination condition based on volume dimensions return False def getouterlayerbounds(center, prevsize, iteration): # Outer layer expands by factor of 2 in resolution scale each iteration outersize = prevsize (2 (iteration - 1)) return (center[0] - outersize/2, center[1] - outersize/2, center[2] - outersize/2, center[0] + outersize/2, center[1] + outersize/2, center[2] + outersize/2) def divideinto6subvolumes(outerbounds, prevsize, iteration): # Source does not specify exact subdivision logic; typically splits the bounding box into 6 face-aligned sub-volumes return {} def addimagespatially(base, overlay, position): # Standard image compositing/pasting operation return base.paste(overlay, position) def compositeover(pixela, pixelb): """ Performs the 'over' compositing operation on two pixels. Given pixel A(da, alphaa) and B(db, alphab). Result C(dc, alphac) where dc = da + (1 - alphaa) db. """ da, alphaa = pixela db, alphab = pixelb dc = da + (1 - alphaa) db alphac = alphaa + (1 - alphaa) alphab return (dc, alphac) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Non-Orthogonal Viewing: When viewing from a non-orthogonal direction, slices must be transformed to a sheared object space to allow efficient projection, then warped to the image plane. Precision: The 'over' operator is performed pixel-by-pixel, and floating-point precision issues may accumulate during compositing across many layers. Boundary Conditions: The definition of the "outer layer" must be precise to avoid gaps or overlaps between iterations. A variant where rendering starts with a rough average image of the entire volume and iteratively refines the fovea area. It divides each layer (excluding the innermost) into 7 parts: Top, Bottom, Left, Right, Front, Back, and Center. The Center part is saved for the next iteration, and the Front/Back results are combined with the next iteration's result using the refinement equation R = (RFi + (1 - \alpha{RFi}) R{i+1}) + (1 - \alpha{RFi} \alpha{R{i+1}}) RBi. It is chosen when a very fast initial preview is prioritized over ROI clarity, as it has a shorter initial wait time (0.1468s vs 0.381s) but suffers from low-resolution interference in the ROI. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but involves iterative reconstruction and rendering of expanding layers. Memory Complexity: Depends on the multiresolution data structure (e.g., octree/wavelet) and the current rendered image buffer. Measured Performance: The initial wait time is 0.381 seconds for the innermost ROI to arrive and be displayed. Coarse-to-fine has a shorter initial wait time of 0.1468 seconds. Strengths: Provides a clearer result for the ROI because it avoids interference from low-resolution coefficients that arrive early in coarse-to-fine schemes. Limitations: Longer initial wait time compared to coarse-to-fine schemes. When to Use: When the user's primary interest is the clarity of a specific region of interest and they are willing to wait longer for the initial high-quality view. Originated in the context of progressive transmission and rendering of foveated volume data, based on wavelet foveation and Haar wavelet transforms for data compression and multiresolution searching. The method is part of a broader effort to handle large-scale volume data stored on server repositories and progressively rendered on client sites., https://www.scitepress.org/PublishedPapers/2006/13574/pdf/index.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Reduced Volume Texture with Box Average
head: Box average reduction, Coarse grid representation, Multi-resolution volume textures, Reduced slice store
body: Reduced Volume Texture with Box Average is a technique for handling volumetric datasets that exceed the maximum texture dimensions supported by the GPU (e.g., 2048 voxels per axis). It solves the problem of rendering failure and main-thread stalling by maintaining multiple representations of the data: a full-resolution grid for high-quality rendering and a coarser grid created by box averaging for preview or low-resolution display. This approach allows the viewport to select the representation that fits the device's texture limits, ensuring continuous rendering even when the full volume cannot be loaded into GPU memory. It builds on Multiresolution Rendering with Data Reduction and complements ROI-based High-Resolution Rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of source frames (slices) delivered by a loader, potentially arriving asynchronously. Output: A reduced volume texture (coarse grid) stored in CPU memory, which is uploaded to the GPU as needed. The size of this reduced copy is bounded by the maximum texture size supported by the hardware (e.g., 256 \times 256 \times 256 int16, which is 32 MB). Data Structures: VoxelGrid: A type representing the grid descriptor and the box average arithmetic. CompositeVoxelManager: An object that holds the different representations (full and reduced) and reads the best one for the current viewport. Quality Record: Tracks what the loader has delivered and at which quality level. Reduced Texture: A 3D texture array or volume texture where each slice corresponds to a reduced representation of the source data. Algorithm Steps: 1. Box Averaging Reduction: Reduce a grid by a box on each axis to compute the coarser representation. For a target voxel at (i, j, k) in the reduced grid, the value is the average of the source voxels within the corresponding box. 2. Batch Derivation: The volume reduces each delivered frame into a reduced representation in CPU memory in batches, outside the render loop. This is managed by CompositeVoxelManager.createVoxelRepresentation, refreshDerivedFrames, and deriveInBatches with scheduleIdle. 3. Handling Missing Frames: If a frame has not arrived, it must not be treated as zero, which would incorrectly lower the average. A reduced slice reads only the frames that have arrived. A replicate (previous value) counts only when no frame of the box arrived. 4. Rounding and Storage: To prevent integer truncation, the reduction uses fillPlaneByAverage, which reads the target column from a table, keeps one row of sums, and applies rounding before storing in an integer texture. 5. Incremental Fill: A render fills at most 16 reduced slices that hold data. The render stops after 8 ms, but only after filling one slice. The texture requests another render, and the next fill starts where the last fill stopped. This is controlled by the rendering.reducedTextureFill configuration object. 6. Fast Path Optimization: The derived path uses the fillPlane fast path of the statistic. The getAtIJK reducer is identified as slow for i or j factors and should be avoided in the derived path. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def boxaveragereduce(sourcegrid, reductionfactor): """ Reduces a source grid by averaging blocks of voxels. sourcegrid: 3D list of shape (D, H, W) containing numeric values for arrived frames and None for missing frames. reductionfactor: integer, the factor by which to reduce each axis. """ srcd = len(sourcegrid) srch = len(sourcegrid[0]) srcw = len(sourcegrid[0][0]) dstd = srcd // reductionfactor dsth = srch // reductionfactor dstw = srcw // reductionfactor sums = [[[0.0 for in range(dstw)] for in range(dsth)] for in range(dstd)] counts = [[[0 for in range(dstw)] for in range(dsth)] for in range(dstd)] for d in range(dstd): for h in range(dsth): for w in range(dstw): dstart = d reductionfactor hstart = h reductionfactor wstart = w reductionfactor blocksum = 0.0 blockcount = 0 for sd in range(dstart, dstart + reductionfactor): for sh in range(hstart, hstart + reductionfactor): for sw in range(wstart, wstart + reductionfactor): val = sourcegrid[sd][sh][sw] if val is not None: blocksum += val blockcount += 1 sums[d][h][w] = blocksum counts[d][h][w] = blockcount reducedgrid = [[[0 for in range(dstw)] for in range(dsth)] for in range(dstd)] for d in range(dstd): for h in range(dsth): for w in range(dstw): if counts[d][h][w] > 0: avg = sums[d][h][w] / counts[d][h][w] reducedgrid[d][h][w] = int(avg + 0.5) else: reducedgrid[d][h][w] = 0 return reducedgrid def fillreducedsliceincrementally(reducedtexture, startslice, maxslices=16, maxtimems=8): """ Fills reduced slices incrementally to avoid stalling the main thread. reducedtexture: 3D list to fill. startslice: index of the first slice to fill. maxslices: maximum number of slices to fill per call. maxtimems: maximum time in milliseconds per call. """ filledcount = 0 currentslice = startslice elapsedms = 0 while currentslice < len(reducedtexture) and filledcount < maxslices: # Standard pacing logic checks wall-clock time; here simulated by elapsedms if elapsedms >= maxtimems: break fillplane(reducedtexture, currentslice) currentslice += 1 filledcount += 1 elapsedms += 1 return currentslice def fillplane(texture, sliceindex): """Fills a single slice plane in the reduced texture.""" # Standard plane upload logic; implementation depends on GPU API pass Parameters: rendering.reducedTextureFill: Configuration object that sets the limits for reduced texture fill work per render. Specifically, it limits the number of slices filled per render (e.g., 16) and the time spent (e.g., 8 ms). Maximum Texture Size: The size of the reduced copy is at most the size of the texture supported by the device (e.g., 2048 voxels/axis limit, or a reduced size like 256 \times 256 \times 256). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Frames: If a frame has not arrived, treating it as zero causes the average to be too low. The fix is to read only the frames that arrived and count replicates only when no frame of the box arrived. Integer Truncation: Integer textures previously truncated the average value. The fix is to use fillPlaneByAverage which applies rounding. Main Thread Stall: Deriving the full volume previously stalled the main thread for seconds. This is avoided by deriving for each delivery in batches. Slow Reducer: The getAtIJK reducer is slow for i or j factors. The fillPlane fast path should be used instead. Time Complexity: The reduction is performed in batches on the CPU, outside the render loop, to avoid stalling the main thread. The fill of the reduced texture is incremental, limited to 16 slices or 8 ms per render. Memory Complexity: The reduced texture size is bounded by the maximum texture size supported by the GPU (e.g., 32 MB for a 256 \times 256 \times 256 int16 texture). Performance: This method allows rendering of volumes that exceed GPU texture limits by providing a lower-quality preview. It prevents rendering stalls and failures. Strengths: Enables rendering of large volumes on devices with limited texture memory. Prevents main-thread blocking during derivation. Limitations: The reduced texture is a lower-quality approximation. Requires CPU-based reduction. Incremental filling may result in partial updates if the render is interrupted. When to Use: When the volume size exceeds the GPU's maximum texture dimensions or when a quick preview is needed before full loading. When Not to Use: When high-fidelity rendering of the full resolution is required and the device supports it. This technique was developed as part of the cornerstone3D project, specifically in PR #2931 and Issue #2966. It addresses the limitation of 2048 voxels per axis on known devices, which previously caused texture allocation failures and empty viewers. The work is based on task T2 of PR #2931 and includes refactoring of the IVoxelManager interface, addition of VoxelGrid and box average arithmetic, and the creation of CompositeVoxelManager. The approach was refined to avoid main-thread stalls by moving reduction to CPU batches and implementing incremental texture filling. feat(core): multi-resolution volume textures, the base for task T2, https://github.com/cornerstonejs/cornerstone3D/pull/2931, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volume textures: brick copies in the render, a recorded update copy, paced renders, and a preload that states its loader, https://github.com/cornerstonejs/cornerstone3D/issues/2966, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Distributed AMR Volume Rendering with Cost-Range Decomposition
head: Cost-range Decomposition, Distributed Texture-Based Slicing, Kreylos et al. (2002) method, Remote Interactive AMR Rendering Framework, Remote Interactive Rendering Framework, Slicing-Based AMR Rendering, Texture-Based AMR Volume Rendering
body: Distributed AMR Volume Rendering with Cost-Range Decomposition is a framework for remote, interactive volume rendering of Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data. It solves the problem of efficiently distributing heterogeneous, view-dependent AMR hierarchies across multiple processing nodes to achieve perfect load balancing. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Domain Block Decomposition by prioritizing computational load balance over memory efficiency, using a view-dependent cost interval splitting strategy rather than static spatial partitioning. The framework operates in three phases: data homogenization, cost-range decomposition, and distributed rendering with compositing. Input: An AMR dataset (typically Berger-Colella format) and a current camera viewpoint. Output: A composite image rendered across n distributed nodes. 1. Homogenized k-d Tree: The AMR hierarchy is partitioned into blocks of constant resolution. Each node in the k-d tree stores a cost field. Leaf Node: Represents a grid patch of constant resolution. cost is the estimated rendering cost of that patch. Interior Node: cost is the sum of the cost fields of its two children. Leaves are represented as intervals with width equal to their cost. These intervals are stacked in back-to-front rendering order. 1. Resample Data: Resample the AMR data to a node-centered format. 2. Homogenize Hierarchy: Partition the AMR hierarchy into blocks of constant resolution using a k-d tree. 3. Estimate Cost: Calculate the estimated rendering cost for each leaf. The cost of rendering a grid patch is roughly proportional to the number of cells it contains and to the projected size of each cell. Formula: Cost \propto N{cells} \times S{projected}, where N{cells} is the number of cells and S{projected} is the projected size. 4. Decompose Cost Range: Determine the back-to-front rendering order of the k-d tree leaves based on the current viewpoint. Split the total cost interval into n equal-sized sub-intervals, where n is the number of rendering nodes. Assign a leaf to node i if at least half of its cost interval lies within sub-interval i. 5. Distribute Data: Distribute the resulting blocks of constant resolution among the processors according to the assignment. This may result in data duplication if grid patches from the same original grid are assigned to multiple nodes. 6. Render: Each node renders its assigned blocks using either texture-based hardware-accelerated slicing or software-based cell-projection rendering. If using texture-based rendering, adapt slice spacing and correct opacity to handle varying resolution levels. During rendering, all decisions about traversing or skipping parts of the k-d tree are made during back-to-front traversal without requiring additional communication between nodes. 7. Composite: Composite partial images in order of increasing node index. Because of the cost-range assignment, no grid patch rendered by node i can be occluded by any grid patch rendered by node i-1, and no grid patch rendered by node i can occlude any grid patch rendered by node i+1. Use a binary tree compositing algorithm requiring \lceil \log2 n \rceil compositing rounds for n nodes. In each round, a node either sends its image to another node, receives an image and composites it into its own image, or is idle. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distributedamrrendering(AMRdata, viewpoint, numnodes): # Step 1: Resample to node-centered format nodecentereddata = resampletonodecentered(AMRdata) # Step 2: Homogenize hierarchy into constant-resolution blocks using a k-d tree kdtree = buildhomogenizationkdtree(nodecentereddata) # Step 3: Calculate costs # Cost is proportional to number of cells and projected size, ignoring perspective foreshortening for leaf in kdtree.leaves: leaf.cost = leaf.numcells calculateprojectedsize(leaf.boundingbox, viewpoint) for node in kdtree.interiornodes: node.cost = node.leftchild.cost + node.rightchild.cost totalcost = kdtree.root.cost intervalsize = totalcost / numnodes # Step 4 & 5: Distributed traversal and assignment # Each node traverses the tree back-to-front, deciding on the fly without communication partialimages = {} for nodeid in range(numnodes): nodestart = nodeid intervalsize nodeend = (nodeid + 1) intervalsize nodemid = (nodestart + nodeend) / 2.0 currentcost = 0.0 leavestorender = [] def traversebacktofront(kdnode): nonlocal currentcost if kdnode.isleaf(): leafstart = currentcost leafend = currentcost + kdnode.cost leafmid = (leafstart + leafend) / 2.0 # Assign if at least half inside node's interval if nodestart <= leafmid < nodeend: leavestorender.append(kdnode) currentcost = leafend else: # Standard back-to-front traversal logic if isfurther(kdnode.rightchild, viewpoint): traversebacktofront(kdnode.rightchild) traversebacktofront(kdnode.leftchild) else: traversebacktofront(kdnode.leftchild) traversebacktofront(kdnode.rightchild) traversebacktofront(kdtree.root) # Step 6: Render assigned leaves partialimages[nodeid] = renderleaves(leavestorender, viewpoint) # Step 7: Composite return binarytreecomposite(partialimages, numnodes) def resampletonodecentered(AMRdata): # Resample AMR data to node-centered format return AMRdata.tonodecentered() def buildhomogenizationkdtree(nodecentereddata): # Partition AMR hierarchy into blocks of constant resolution using a k-d tree return kdtreefromamr(nodecentereddata) def calculateprojectedsize(boundingbox, viewpoint): # Project bounding box to screen space to estimate pixel coverage return boundingbox.projectarea(viewpoint) def isfurther(node, viewpoint): # Compare distance of node's center to viewpoint return node.center.distanceto(viewpoint) > 0.0 def renderleaves(leaves, viewpoint): # Render leaves using texture-based slicing or cell-projection # Adapt slice spacing and correct opacity for varying resolutions image = emptyimage() for leaf in leaves: slice = leaf.generateslice(viewpoint) image = alphablend(image, slice) return image def binarytreecomposite(images, numnodes): # Composite partial images in order of increasing node index # Requires ceil(log2(numnodes)) rounds currentimages = list(images.values()) while len(currentimages) > 1: nextround = [] for i in range(0, len(currentimages), 2): if i + 1 < len(currentimages): # Composite in order: earlier node (further back) is destination, later node (closer) is source combined = alphablend(currentimages[i+1], currentimages[i]) nextround.append(combined) else: nextround.append(currentimages[i]) currentimages = nextround return currentimages[0] def alphablend(src, dst): # Standard over compositing: dst = src alpha + dst (1 - alpha) return src src.alpha + dst (1.0 - src.alpha) Number of Nodes (n): Determines the granularity of cost intervals. Cost Estimation Accuracy: Perfect load balancing depends on accurate cost estimates. Viewpoint Changes: Changing viewpoints alters the back-to-front order, causing grid patches to change assignment. Memory Efficiency: Poor memory efficiency is a known pitfall. Grid patches from the same grid may be assigned to multiple nodes, forcing each to load all associated data. After several viewpoint changes, the entire dataset might be replicated at every node. This method partitions Berger-Colella AMR data into homogeneous resolution regions to enable texture-based, hardware-accelerated volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from k-d tree-based or cost-range decomposition approaches by using a heuristic based on refining grid placement assumptions to minimize the total number of constant-resolution blocks. This reduction in block count is specifically beneficial for single-machine rendering scenarios where overhead from managing numerous small textures is detrimental. Load Balancing: Achieves perfect load balancing during rendering if cost estimates are accurate. Memory Efficiency: Poor. Data duplication is common, especially with viewpoint changes. Compositing Time: Comparable to Domain Block Decomposition. Communication: Minimal during rendering (decisions made locally during traversal). Compositing requires \lceil \log2 n \rceil rounds of communication. Strengths: Excellent load balancing, simple compositing logic due to ordered assignment. Limitations: High memory usage due to data replication, sensitive to viewpoint changes. When to Use: When load balancing is critical and memory bandwidth/storage is not a bottleneck. When Not to Use: When memory efficiency is paramount or when viewpoint changes are frequent and data replication is costly. The method was introduced by Kreylos et al. in 2002 as part of a framework for remote, interactive rendering of AMR data. It builds on earlier work by Weber et al. (2003a, 2003b) who compared various AMR partitioning strategies. The framework consists of a lightweight viewer and a renderer running on remote machines. It has been used in applications such as Virtual Director and CAVE for rendering astrophysical data sets like 'The First Star of the Universe'. name: Heuristic Partitioning for Texture-Based Volume Rendering
head: Berger-Colella AMR Partitioning, Kähler & Hege (2002) method
body: This method partitions Berger-Colella Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data into homogeneous resolution regions to enable texture-based, hardware-accelerated volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from k-d tree-based or cost-range decomposition approaches by using a heuristic based on refining grid placement assumptions to minimize the total number of constant-resolution blocks. This reduction in block count is specifically beneficial for single-machine rendering scenarios. The approach builds on the broader distributed AMR volume rendering framework [10508-distributed-amr-volume-rendering-with-cost-range-decompositi.md]. Inputs and Outputs Input: A Berger-Colella AMR dataset consisting of nested grids with uniform resolution per grid and associated refinement levels. Output: A list of homogeneous resolution blocks, each representing a sub-volume with constant refinement level, ready for texture mapping. Data Structures The method operates on the standard Berger-Colella AMR hierarchy where each grid stores its spatial bounds, cell resolution, and refinement level. Algorithm Steps 1. Traverse the AMR hierarchy to collect all grids sorted by refinement level. 2. Apply a heuristic based on assumptions about refining grid placement to identify regions that can be merged into constant-resolution blocks. 3. Partition the dataset into homogeneous resolution regions, minimizing the total block count by merging adjacent cells of identical resolution. 4. Generate 3D textures for each resulting homogeneous block for hardware-accelerated volume rendering. Pseudocode The sources do not provide the exact algorithmic steps or pseudocode for the heuristic partitioning scheme. Parameters and Edge Cases Heuristic Assumptions: The method's effectiveness depends on assumptions concerning the placement of refining grids to minimize constant-resolution blocks. Single-Machine Optimization: The approach generates fewer blocks than k-d tree, Weber et al. (2001a), and Kreylos et al. (2002) approaches, which is beneficial for single-machine rendering. Precision: Not given in the sources. Distributed Rendering: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of homogeneous blocks generated. Performance: Generates fewer blocks than k-d tree approaches, Weber et al. (2001a), and Kreylos et al. (2002). This reduction is beneficial for single-machine rendering. Strengths: Minimizes block count for single-machine rendering; enables hardware-accelerated texture-based volume rendering. Limitations: Effectiveness depends on the validity of heuristic assumptions regarding refining grid placement. Origin: Introduced by Kähler & Hege in 2002. Development: Later work by Kähler et al. (2002) applied the method to render simulations of forming stars in a CAVE environment using the Virtual Director interface. Usage: Used for texture-based volume rendering of AMR data, particularly optimized for single-machine contexts. name: Cluster Hierarchy-based Volume Rendering
head: Cluster Tree Widget Rendering, Interactive Visual Exploration of Multi-variate Volume Data
body: This method renders multi-variate volume data by mapping hierarchical clusters of feature vectors to transfer function parameters (color, opacity, size) for direct volume rendering, enabling interactive exploration via cluster tree and parallel coordinates widgets. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by decoupling the classification/clustering logic (CPU) from the rendering loop (GPU), using a mask-based post-classification approach to maintain interactive frame rates, whereas Multiresolution Volume Rendering focuses on spatial LOD and In-Core Volume Rendering focuses on memory management for large datasets. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A multi-variate volume dataset (scalar fields or derived properties) and a hierarchical clustering of the data's feature space. Output: A rendered image with clusters visualized according to user-defined transfer functions. Data Structures: 1. Cluster Hierarchy: A tree structure where nodes represent clusters. Each node contains: A set of data points (voxels) belonging to the cluster. Default color and opacity assigned by the automatic clustering algorithm. A density slider value used to filter voxels within the cluster based on density thresholds. 2. Mask Volume: A volume data structure with the same spatial dimensions as the input data. Value 1: The voxel belongs to a selected cluster and meets the density criteria. Value 0: The voxel is hidden (fully transparent). Steps: 1. Clustering Initialization: If pre-clustering exists, use the automatic clustering algorithm's output to assign default color and opacity to each cluster. If no pre-clustering exists, place all data points into a single root cluster. 2. User Interaction (CPU): Cluster Tree Widget: Users adjust density sliders for specific clusters. This modifies the effective size of the cluster by defining density thresholds. Parallel Coordinates Widget: Users brush intervals in the multi-variate feature space. Data points falling within selected intervals are marked; others are marked with zero. Reclustering: Users can split or merge nodes in the cluster hierarchy. This operation is performed on the CPU. 3. Mask Generation (CPU): For each voxel, determine if it belongs to a selected cluster and satisfies the current density/brushing criteria. Set the corresponding value in the Mask Volume to 1 if true, 0 if false. 4. Rendering (GPU): Perform direct volume ray casting using a 3D texture-based renderer. Masking: Voxels with a mask value of 0 are rendered fully transparent (hidden). Compositing: Combine the mask with the transfer function. The transfer function maps the cluster's properties (e.g., physical properties like ionization state) to color and opacity. Illumination: Use precomputed surface normals for lighting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. clustertree = buildclustertree(multivariatedata) maskvolume = createzerovolume(spatialdimensions) while userinteracting: # 1. Update cluster properties based on UI for node in clustertree.nodes: node.densitythreshold = getslidervalue(node.id) node.color = getcolormapping(node.physicalproperties) node.opacity = getopacitymapping(node.physicalproperties) # 2. Generate Mask (CPU) # Note: In practice, this might be optimized, but the source implies CPU-side classification/masking for voxel in spatialvoxels: featurevector = getmultivariatefeatures(voxel) cluster = findclusterforfeature(featurevector, clustertree) # Check if voxel is in a selected cluster and meets density criteria isselected = cluster.isselectedintreewidget meetsdensity = featurevector.density >= cluster.densitythreshold meetsbrushing = isinparallelcoordinatesbrush(featurevector) if isselected and meetsdensity and meetsbrushing: maskvolume[voxel] = 1 else: maskvolume[voxel] = 0 # 3. Render (GPU) # Direct volume ray casting with post-classification for ray in screenrays: accumulatedcolor = 0 accumulatedopacity = 0 for samplepoint along ray: if maskvolume[samplepoint] == 0: continue # Fully transparent # Get transfer function parameters for the cluster this point belongs to cluster = findclusterforfeature(getmultivariatefeatures(samplepoint), clustertree) color = cluster.color opacity = cluster.opacity # Standard volume compositing # Note: Source mentions post-classification with nearest-neighbor interpolation # This implies the transfer function is applied per-voxel based on its cluster alpha = opacity accumulatedcolor += color alpha (1 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedopacity += alpha (1 - accumulatedopacity) setpixelcolor(ray.screenpos, accumulatedcolor) def splitmergenodes(clustertree, operation): # Perform split or merge on the cluster hierarchy # Takes < 0.5 seconds on modern hardware pass Parameters: Rendering Hardware: nVIDIA GTX260. Screen Resolution: 1680x1050 pixels. Performance Target: 20-30 frames per second. Reclustering Time: < 0.5 seconds on modern hardware. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Post-classification with nearest-neighbor interpolation causes aliasing artifacts at cluster boundaries. Performance: Pre-classification (computing colors/opacities for all voxels on CPU and transmitting to GPU) inhibits interactive frame rates with marginal quality gain. Normals: On-the-fly surface normal computation significantly slows down rendering; normals must be precomputed. Illumination: If no density values are available, illumination cannot be applied. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on dataset resolution, zoom level, and sampling rate. Reclustering operations (splitting/merging) take < 0.5 seconds on modern hardware. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the multi-variate data, the cluster hierarchy, and the mask volume. Measured Performance: Achieved 20-30 fps at 1680x1050 resolution on an nVIDIA GTX260. Strengths: Interactive exploration of multi-variate data; intuitive UI with cluster tree and parallel coordinates; fast reclustering. Limitations: Aliasing artifacts at cluster boundaries; requires precomputed normals; no illumination if density is unavailable. When to Use: Interactive exploration of multi-variate volume data where user-driven clustering and filtering are needed. When Not to Use: When pre-computed classification is required for maximum quality (due to performance costs) or when density-based illumination is critical but density data is absent. Origin: Presented by Dobrev et al. in 2011. History: Applied to various datasets including Bonsai tree, ionization front instability, medical MRI, tornado flow field, and white dwarf/black hole simulations. Usage: Implemented in C++ using QT, OpenGL, and GLSL. A Cluster Hierarchy-based Volume Rendering Approach for Interactive Visual Exploration of Multi-variate Volume Data, https://doi.org/10.2312/pe/vmv/vmv11/137-144, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: In-Core Volume Rendering
head: In-core volume rendering for Cartesian grid fluid dynamics simulations, Srend, Srend In-Core Volume Rendering
body: In-core volume rendering, specifically implemented as Srend, is a method for visualizing computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations using Cartesian grids by compiling the rendering code directly into the simulation application. It solves the problem of high data I/O overhead and latency in post-processing by generating images in real-time during the simulation. Unlike general-purpose in-situ visualization frameworks that often employ load balancing or supervisory mechanisms, Srend relies on a user-defined "rendering tree" and time-partitioned rendering where every simulation process renders its own data brick, followed by space-partitioned compositing by dedicated processes. Inputs: Simulation Data: 3D arrays of variable values representing rectangular "bricks" of the volume. Data Format: The source data must be scaled to arrays of bytes (Fortran character1) and mapped to a user-defined color table. Rendering Parameters: View index, number of sources, MPI target rank, and image finishing parameters (e.g., output file name). Geometry: Spatial coordinates for interpolation if the simulation uses stretched grids or terrain-following coordinates. Outputs: Final Image: A 2D rendered image written to disk by the finisher at the root of the rendering tree. Brick: A rectangular sub-volume represented by a 3D array of byte values. Rendering Tree: A user-defined hierarchy of MPI ranks where leaves are simulation worker ranks, internal nodes are "composers", and the root is the "finisher". Message Payload: Contains the 2D rendered pre-multiplied alpha plane, view index, number of sources, and redundant image finishing parameters (file name). 1. Data Partitioning: The simulation domain is partitioned into rectangular bricks, and each simulation worker rank holds one or more bricks. 2. Local Rendering (Time Partitioning): Each worker rank renders its assigned brick using all available threads as if the brick were the entire volume. The rendering uses ray casting, collecting emissions along rays from the eye through the volume. The result is a 2D pre-multiplied alpha plane. 3. Compositing (Space Partitioning): Composers receive 2D renderings from their child ranks. Composers exploit the associativity of compositing pre-multiplied alpha planes to merge the incoming planes with their own local render (if they are also workers) or with previously composited results. The composited result is sent to the parent rank in the rendering tree. 4. Finalization: The finisher at the root of the rendering tree receives the final composited image and writes it to disk. The rendering process uses standard ray casting for volume rendering. The compositing of pre-multiplied alpha planes relies on the associativity of the compositing operator. For two adjacent alpha planes A and B (where A is closer to the eye), the composite C is calculated as: C = A + (1 - \alphaA) B where \alphaA is the alpha channel of A, and B is the pre-multiplied color/alpha of the further plane. Data Scaling: Users must manually scale real-valued simulation data to bytes and define a color table. View Index: Identifies the camera perspective. Number of Sources: Used by composers to track how many children have sent data. MPI Target Rank: The destination rank for sending composited results. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vec4(r, g, b, a): return (r, g, b, a) def zeros(shape): # Returns a 2D list of vec4 initialized to (0,0,0,0) return [[vec4(0, 0, 0, 0) for in range(shape[1])] for in range(shape[0])] def computeray(pixelx, pixely, viewparams): # Returns (origin: vec3, direction: vec3) based on camera parameters return viewparams['origin'], viewparams['directions'][pixely][pixelx] def raybrickintersection(rayorigin, raydir, brickbounds): # Returns (tmin, tmax) for ray intersecting brick axis-aligned bounds tmin, tmax = 0.0, float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] == 0: if rayorigin[i] < brickbounds[i2] or rayorigin[i] > brickbounds[i2+1]: return None, None else: t1 = (brickbounds[i2] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] t2 = (brickbounds[i2+1] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return tmin, tmax def interpolatescalar(rayorigin, raydir, t, brickdata, gridgeometry): # Interpolates byte value from 3D brick at ray position # Assumes gridgeometry maps brick indices to world coordinates # Returns a byte value (0-255) return 128 # Placeholder for interpolation logic def compositealpha(base, source): # Composites source onto base using pre-multiplied alpha # base is closer to the eye. Both are 2D lists of vec4. result = zeros((len(base), len(base[0]))) for y in range(len(base)): for x in range(len(base[y])): abase = base[y][x][3] / 255.0 rbase, gbase, bbase, abase = base[y][x] rsrc, gsrc, bsrc, asrc = source[y][x] asrcnorm = asrc / 255.0 # C = A + (1 - alphaA) B rnew = rbase + (1.0 - abase) rsrc gnew = gbase + (1.0 - abase) gsrc bnew = bbase + (1.0 - abase) bsrc anew = abase + (1.0 - abase) asrcnorm result[y][x] = vec4(rnew, gnew, bnew, anew 255.0) return result def renderbrick(brickdata3d, viewparams, colortable, brickbounds, gridgeometry): # Renders a single brick using ray casting imageheight = viewparams['height'] imagewidth = viewparams['width'] image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) raystepsize = viewparams['stepsize'] # for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): origin, direction = computeray(x, y, viewparams) tstart, tend = raybrickintersection(origin, direction, brickbounds) if tstart is None: continue coloraccum = vec4(0, 0, 0, 0) t = tstart while t < tend: val = interpolatescalar(origin, direction, t, brickdata3d, gridgeometry) rgba = colortable[val] # Returns vec4 # Front-to-back compositing for pre-multiplied alpha aaccum = coloraccum[3] / 255.0 rnew = coloraccum[0] + (1.0 - aaccum) rgba[0] gnew = coloraccum[1] + (1.0 - aaccum) rgba[1] bnew = coloraccum[2] + (1.0 - aaccum) rgba[2] anew = aaccum + (1.0 - aaccum) (rgba[3] / 255.0) coloraccum = vec4(rnew, gnew, bnew, anew 255.0) t += raystepsize image[y][x] = coloraccum return image def srendworker(brickdata, viewindex, numsources, targetrank, colortable, viewparams, brickbounds, gridgeometry): # Executed by simulation worker ranks localimage = renderbrick(brickdata, viewparams, colortable, brickbounds, gridgeometry) payload = { 'image': localimage, 'viewindex': viewindex, 'numsources': numsources, 'filename': 'output.png' # Redundant but simplifies usage } # MPI non-blocking send mpisend(targetrank, payload) def srendcomposer(childranks, viewindex, numsources, parentrank, colortable, viewparams, brickbounds, gridgeometry): # Executed by intermediate ranks in the rendering tree compositeimage = zeros((viewparams['height'], viewparams['width'])) for childrank in childranks: msg = mpirecv(childrank) compositeimage = compositealpha(compositeimage, msg['image']) # If this rank also holds data (hybrid worker/composer), render and composite if haslocalbrick(): localimage = renderbrick(getlocalbrick(), viewparams, colortable, brickbounds, gridgeometry) compositeimage = compositealpha(compositeimage, localimage) if parentrank is not None: payload = { 'image': compositeimage, 'viewindex': viewindex, 'numsources': numsources, 'filename': 'output.png' } mpisend(parentrank, payload) def srendfinisher(childranks, viewindex, numsources, outputfilename, viewparams): # Executed by the root rank compositeimage = zeros((viewparams['height'], viewparams['width'])) for childrank in childranks: msg = mpirecv(childrank) compositeimage = compositealpha(compositeimage, msg['image']) # Write final image to disk saveimage(outputfilename, compositeimage) def mpisend(rank, data): pass def mpirecv(rank): return {'image': zeros((1,1)), 'viewindex': 0, 'numsources': 0, 'filename': ''} def haslocalbrick(): return False def getlocalbrick(): return [] def saveimage(filename, data): pass Grid Interpolation: If the simulation uses stretched grids or terrain-following vertical coordinates, data arrays must be interpolated to spatial arrays for Srend to maintain spatial accuracy. Redundant Information: The output file name and other image finishing parameters are sent by every renderer, even though only the finisher uses them. This is a design choice to simplify usage, accepting a light data payload overhead. Data Scaling: Users must manually scale real data to bytes and define a color table. This requires knowledge of the data distribution and appearance requirements. Time Complexity: Rendering completion time (simulation halt time) depends primarily on the rendering work itself. There is no synchronization or management overhead beyond that imposed by MPI messaging. Memory Complexity: Data is kept in-core. The memory footprint includes the simulation data and the intermediate 2D rendered planes. Performance: Results show modest rendering overhead and high potential for scaling. The 3D data is already in CPU memory, requiring only movement to registers, making it efficient on CPUs compared to GPUs for this specific workflow where cluster communications are well-established for the lighter 2D results. Strengths: Immediate, quality imagery; reduces data output and storage requirements; no reliance on special visualization hardware or external programs; convenient integration into Fortran simulation codes. Limitations: No load balancing or supervisory mechanism; rendering and compositing are defined by the user's incorporation of Srend calls; requires manual data scaling and color table definition. When to Use: When embedding visualization directly into Fortran-based CFD simulations (e.g., PPMstar, CM1, WRF) to reduce I/O overhead and enable real-time exploration. When Not to Use: When dynamic load balancing is required or when the simulation code is not in Fortran or cannot be easily modified to include Srend calls. Srend was developed at the University of Minnesota / LCSE. It was modified from its original form, which was used within a terrain flow code developed to study the advection of smoke and pollen in the St. Louis River region. The "S" in Srend originally stood for spherical data rendering, supporting longitude/latitude views for full spherical rendering of stellar data from the center, though perspective views and other features were retained for general use. It was embedded in three major codes: Piecewise Parabolic Method (PPMstar), Cloud Model 1 (CM1), and Weather Research Forecast model (WRF). The code was implemented in Fortran to allow convenient inclusion within Fortran simulation codes using ordinary subroutine calls and familiar Fortran arrays. name: Spherical Harmonic Volume Ray Casting
head: GPU-based volume ray-caster with SH coefficients, SH Volume Ray Casting with Hybrid CPU/GPU Projection, SH-based interactive volume rendering, Spherical Harmonic (SH) Volume Ray Casting with Hybrid CPU/GPU Projection
body: Spherical Harmonic Volume Ray Casting is a technique for interactive volume rendering that approximates complex light-material interactions (such as subsurface scattering and color bleeding) by pre-computing Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients for material and light functions on the CPU, storing them in 3D volumes, and evaluating the rendering integral via Monte-Carlo ray marching in a GPU fragment shader. It sets itself apart from standard direct volume ray casting by replacing expensive per-sample shading integrals with a pre-convolved SH representation, allowing for real-time performance at the cost of low-frequency approximation. The method operates in two distinct phases: an offline (or pre-computation) phase on the CPU to generate SH coefficient volumes, and an online rendering phase on the GPU using fragment shaders. Inputs: Scalar volume data V(\mathbf{x}). Transfer function T(V) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha) mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Material function M(\mathbf{x}, \omegai, \omegao) and incoming light Li(\mathbf{x}, \omegai). Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}). Outputs: Final image color \mathbf{C}{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out}. 3D coefficient volumes containing SH coefficients for the modulated material/light interactions. 1. BRDF Coefficient Texture (CPU-side) A partitioned 2D texture used to store SH coefficients for the material function M and incoming light Li. Dimensions: 3 columns, 4 quadrants per column. Each quadrant is N \times N texels, where N is the number of random samples. Coordinate System: X-axis of each quadrant: \vartheta of outgoing direction \omegao, ranging from 0 to \pi. Y-axis of each quadrant: \phi of outgoing direction \omegao, ranging from 0 to 2\pi. Content Layout (for Band Limit L=3, 16 coefficients): Lower-Left Quadrant: First 4 coefficients (Bands 0 and 1). Lower-Right Quadrant: Next 4 coefficients (First 4 of Band 2). Upper-Left Quadrant: Next 4 coefficients (One of Band 2, three of Band 3). Upper-Right Quadrant: Final 4 coefficients (Remaining 4 of Band 3). Purpose: Allows the GPU to look up the necessary SH coefficients for any outgoing direction \omegao. 2. SH Coefficient Volumes (GPU-side) 3D textures storing the pre-computed SH coefficients for the volume. Standard Layout: 16 coefficients per color channel (for L=3). Rendered into 4 slices with 4 channels simultaneously using Multiple Render Targets (MRTs). Optimized Chromaticity/Luminance Layout: To reduce memory and MRT usage, chromaticity uses a 2-band projection (4 coefficients) and luminance uses a 4-band projection. Total coefficients: 3 \times 4 = 12 (3 color channels \times 4 coefficients for chroma/luma split logic described as 3 sets of 4, totaling 12 coefficients handled by three FBO-attached textures). This fits within the 8 MRT limit (using 7 targets). 3. Random Sample Textures (GPU-side) Sample Directions: Normalized Cartesian vectors generated on the CPU, uploaded as a 2D texture. Basis Values: Values of spherical harmonic basis functions Y{lm}(\vartheta, \phi) for each sample direction, uploaded as a second 2D texture. 1. Generate Random Samples: Create N random normalized Cartesian vectors on the CPU for Monte-Carlo integration. 2. Compute Basis Values: Calculate Y{lm}(\vartheta, \phi) for each sample direction. 3. Compute SH Coefficients: Project the material function M and light Li onto the SH basis. The physical triple product integral is approximated by two successive double products to simplify computation: first integrating over Material M and Incoming Light Li to get local material effects, then modulating by Environmental Illumination L{mi}. Store the resulting coefficients in the partitioned 2D BRDF texture. 4. Generate Coefficient Volumes: Use GPU framebuffer objects (FBOs) and MRTs to ray march slice-by-slice into 3D coefficient textures, distributing the (L+1)^2 SH coefficients for each voxel to the attached render targets. For each pixel, cast a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} intersecting the volume bounding box [0,1]^3. 1. Initialization: Initialize accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc} = (0,0,0) and opacity \alpha{acc} = 0. 2. Ray Marching Loop: While t < t{far} and \alpha{acc} < 0.95 (early termination threshold): a. Sample Volume: Retrieve scalar value V(\mathbf{p}) at current ray position \mathbf{p} = r(t) using trilinear interpolation. b. Check Boundaries: If any coordinate of \mathbf{p} in volume space [0,1]^3 reaches 0 or 1, terminate ray. c. Classification: Map V(\mathbf{p}) to color \mathbf{c} and opacity \alpha using the transfer function. d. SH Evaluation: i. Retrieve the SH coefficients for the current voxel from the 3D coefficient volume. ii. Retrieve the pre-computed Y{lm} values for the current sample direction from the 2D texture. iii. Compute the contribution of the current sample by taking the dot product of the SH coefficients and Y{lm} values, then multiply by the ray's contribution and add to the total integration sum. e. Compositing: Update \mathbf{C}{acc} and \alpha{acc} using the front-to-back equation: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c} \cdot \alpha \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alpha f. Advance: Increase t by the ray step size \Delta t. 3. Output: Write \mathbf{C}{acc} and \alpha{acc} to the framebuffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastshvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, volumetexture, coefficientvolume, ylmtex, transferfunc, stepsize): cacc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] aacc = 0.0 t = tnear while t < tfar: pworld = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] pvol = transformtovolumespace(pworld) if pvol[0] < 0.0 or pvol[0] > 1.0 or pvol[1] < 0.0 or pvol[1] > 1.0 or pvol[2] < 0.0 or pvol[2] > 1.0: break vval = trilinearsample(volumetexture, pvol) csample, alpha = transferfunc(vval) shcoeffs = sample3dtexture(coefficientvolume, pvol) yvals = sample2dtexture(ylmtex, raydirection) colorcontrib = sum(shcoeffs[i] yvals[i] for i in range(len(shcoeffs))) cacc = [cacc[i] + (1.0 - aacc) colorcontrib[i] alpha for i in range(3)] aacc = aacc + (1.0 - aacc) alpha if aacc > 0.95: break t += stepsize return cacc, aacc Ray Opacity Threshold: 95% for early ray termination. Boundary Condition: Ray terminates if any position coordinate reaches 0 or 1 in volume space [0,1]^3. SH Band Limit (L): Typically 3, yielding 16 coefficients per color channel. Coefficient Downsampling: Coefficient volumes are downsampled to ~33% of the original size to optimize performance, assuming low-frequency radiance transfer. Ray Step Size: Can be increased to speed up computation. Pitfalls: GLSL Random Numbers: GLSL random number generation was not implemented in the target driver at the time of the source, necessitating CPU-side generation. MRT Limit: Limited to 8 simultaneous output targets, constraining the max coefficients written per fragment (hence the choice of L=3 or chromaticity/luminance split). Gibbs Ringing: SH approximation restricts representation to low-frequency functions. Materials with sharp specular highlights may cause Gibbs ringing artifacts. Time Complexity: The pre-computation phase is expensive, scaling with the number of voxels and the complexity of the material/light integration. Rendering is interactive for simple effects (shadows only) but degrades with scattering and color bleeding. Memory Complexity: Requires storing 3D coefficient volumes. Downsampling to 33% size mitigates this. Measured Performance: Hardware: Intel Core2 Quad Q9450 (2.66 GHz), 4GB RAM, nVidia GeForce 9800 GTX (512MB RAM). Resolution: 400x400 window. 128^3 voxels: Shadows only: 0.9s projection / 24 fps. +Scattering: 21.3s / 17 fps. +Bleeding: 58.9s / 13 fps. 256^2x128 voxels: Shadows only: 2.6s / 20 fps. +Scattering: 70.2s / 14 fps. +Bleeding: 180s / 5 fps. 256^3 voxels: Shadows only: 3.4s / 6 fps. +Scattering: 149s / 3 fps. +Bleeding: 388s / 1 fps. Strengths: Enables interactive frame rates for complex lighting effects (shadows, scattering, color bleeding) that would otherwise be too slow for real-time ray casting. Limitations: Restricted to low-frequency functions; unsuitable for materials with sharp specular highlights due to Gibbs ringing. Performance degrades significantly with color bleeding. Origin: The method was introduced by F. Lindemann and T. Ropinski in the paper "Advanced Light Material Interaction for Direct Volume Rendering" (2010). History: It was implemented in the Voreen volume rendering engine. Usage: Applied in medical imaging and computational fluid dynamics, where predefined transfer functions are common. name: Sliced Ray Casting with On-Demand Volume Reconstruction
head: On-Demand Density Sampling, Sliced Ray Casting
body: Sliced Ray Casting with On-Demand Volume Reconstruction is a direct volume rendering technique that reconstructs particle density on-demand in screen space at viewport resolution and sampling depths, combining splatting, texture slicing, and ray casting to avoid aliasing artifacts and large memory footprints without pre-computation. It sets itself apart from traditional object-space volume ray casting by performing density reconstruction in image space, thereby moving perspective correction from the rendering stage to the data reconstruction stage. The method executes an iterative loop for #s times containing three inner steps: sampling position update, density reconstruction through splatting, and volume ray-casting. Inputs: Particle positions \mathbf{p}j, particle masses mj, kernel support radius h, volume sampling distance \Delta \lambda, eye position \mathbf{e}, ray direction \mathbf{v}, maximum ray length \lambda{max}, and number of iterations \#s. Outputs: Final composited color and opacity for each pixel. Particle Data: List of particles with fields \mathbf{p}j (position) and mj (mass). Ray Parameters: \mathbf{e}: Eye position. \mathbf{v}: Ray direction. \lambda{min}: Minimal distance between \mathbf{e} and the particle bounding box. \lambda{max}: Maximum ray length, calculated based on the back-side of the particle bounding box. \Delta \lambda: Volume sampling distance. \#s: Number of iterations for the inner loop. 1. Ray Setup: Determine \lambda{min} as the minimal distance between the eye \mathbf{e} and the bounding box of the particles. Determine \lambda{max} based on the back-side of the particle bounding box. Store ray direction \mathbf{v} and start position at the front face of the bounding box. 2. Shell Subdivision: Subdivide the viewing volume in the viewing direction into concentric spherical shells centered at the eye \mathbf{e}. Place the shells equally separated by the volume sampling distance \Delta \lambda. Position the first slice at \lambda{min} to skip empty space in front of the camera. 3. Iterative Loop: Execute a loop for \#s times. Each iteration performs three inner steps: a. Sampling Position Update: Update the sampling position along the ray based on the current shell distance. b. Density Reconstruction: Reconstruct the density field from particles via perspectively correct splatting of particle density footprints at the sampling depths used by volume ray casting. This is performed in screen space at viewport resolution. c. Volume Ray-Casting: Perform the standard ray casting steps (sampling, classification, compositing) using the reconstructed density. The density \bar{\rho}(\mathbf{p}) at a point \mathbf{p} is reconstructed using a radial symmetric kernel function W \in C^2[0, h] with support radius h, particle positions \mathbf{p}j, and particle masses mj: \bar{\rho}(\mathbf{p}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{j} mj W(\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}j\|) The result is normalized so that the average density evaluates to 1 for easier iso-value evaluation, i.e., \bar{\rho}(\mathbf{p}) = 1. For each particle j, a symmetric polynomial density kernel function (the smooth step function) with finite support radius h is used, though any other function with finite support could be used. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def slicedraycasting(particles, eye, raydirection, lambdamin, lambdamax, deltalambda, numiterations, h): """ Performs sliced ray casting with on-demand volume reconstruction. Args: particles: List of dicts with 'pos' (vector) and 'mass' (float). eye: Vector, position of the camera eye. raydirection: Vector, direction of the ray. lambdamin: Float, minimal distance to particle bounding box. lambdamax: Float, maximum ray length. deltalambda: Float, volume sampling distance. numiterations: Int, number of inner loop iterations. h: Float, support radius of the kernel function. Returns: color: Vector, final composited color. opacity: Float, final opacity. """ # Initialize compositing variables accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 numparticles = len(particles) # Iterate through sampling depths (concentric shells) for i in range(numiterations): # 1. Sampling Position Update currentlambda = lambdamin + i deltalambda # Check if we have exceeded the maximum ray length if currentlambda > lambdamax: break # Sample point on the ray (shells centered at eye) samplepoint = [ eye[0] + raydirection[0] currentlambda, eye[1] + raydirection[1] currentlambda, eye[2] + raydirection[2] currentlambda ] # 2. Density Reconstruction (On-Demand Splatting) # Note: In practice, this is performed via perspectively correct # screen-space splatting at viewport resolution. density = 0.0 for particle in particles: dx = samplepoint[0] - particle['pos'][0] dy = samplepoint[1] - particle['pos'][1] dz = samplepoint[2] - particle['pos'][2] dist = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) # Check if particle is within support radius h if dist <= h: roverh = dist / h # Smooth step function kernel (symmetric polynomial) w = 1.0 - 3.0 roverh roverh + 2.0 roverh roverh roverh density += particle['mass'] w # Normalize density to average 1 as specified by the source density = density / numparticles # 3. Volume Ray-Casting # Classification: Map density to color and opacity via transfer function # transferfunction(density) -> (colorsample, alphasample) colorsample = [density, density, density] alphasample = 1.0 - math.exp(-density deltalambda) # Compositing (front-to-back iterative form) weight = (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) alphasample accumulatedcolor[0] += weight colorsample[0] accumulatedcolor[1] += weight colorsample[1] accumulatedcolor[2] += weight colorsample[2] accumulatedopacity += weight # Early-z-test culling / Termination based on inter-frame occlusion queries if accumulatedopacity > 0.99: break return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity \Delta \lambda: Volume sampling distance that equally separates the concentric spherical shells. \lambda{min}: Minimal distance between the eye \mathbf{e} and the bounding box of the particles; determines the first slice position. \lambda{max}: Maximum ray length, calculated based on the back-side of the particles bounding box. \#s: Number of iterations for the inner loop that performs sampling position update, density reconstruction, and volume ray-casting. h: Support radius of the kernel function. Perspective Correction: Perspective correction is handled by moving the correction step from volume rendering to data reconstruction, performing density reconstruction in screen space at viewport resolution. Empty Space: The first slice is placed at \lambda{min} to skip empty space in front of the camera. Memory Footprint: The method avoids large memory footprints because volume data is only partially created on-demand. Performance: The method maintains comparative rendering performance to traditional methods while reducing memory requirements. Quality: It yields superior image quality due to image-space evaluation, avoiding aliasing artifacts common in particle visualization and object-space volume ray casting. Memory: Memory requirements are reduced because the volume data is only partially created on-demand. Hardware: The process is controlled by the CPU but the inner steps are performed solely on the GPU. Optimization: A novel method for termination of the ray casting based on inter-frame occlusion queries is employed to optimize overall performance, exploiting frame-to-frame coherency to compensate for overhead and latencies. The method was proposed in the paper "Interactive Image-Space Volume Visualization for Dynamic Particle Simulations" by Falk, Grottel, and Ertl. It is applied to systems biology (cell signaling propagation), biochemistry (protein surface visualization), and molecular dynamics (laser ablation processes). The approach combines ideas from texture slicing, ray casting, and splatting. Early implementations blended object-space-aligned texture stacks, and view-aligned texture stacks were superseded by single-pass volume ray casting. name: Standard Ray Casting
head: Fixed-step ray casting, Direct volume ray casting (baseline), Image-order volume rendering
body: Standard Ray Casting is the foundational direct volume rendering technique that generates images by casting rays from the camera through each pixel, sampling a 3D scalar field at regular intervals, and accumulating color and opacity via front-to-back compositing. It solves the problem of visualizing internal structures in scalar fields (e.g., CT scans) without extracting explicit geometric surfaces, serving as the baseline for more complex traversal or scattering variants. It differs from Exponential Approximation Method by using discrete alpha compositing rather than exponential transmittance approximations, and from Ray Marching Volume Rendering with Henyey-Greenstein Scattering by typically neglecting scattering effects in its standard form. All children of Standard Ray Casting share the following mechanism, terms, and mathematical formulation. Ray Definition: For each pixel (x, y) in the image plane, a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is defined, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. The ray is intersected with the volume bounding box to determine the entry parameter t{near} and exit parameter t{far}. Sampling: The ray segment [t{near}, t{far}] is discretized into N samples at positions ti = t{near} + i \cdot \Delta t, where \Delta t = (t{far} - t{near}) / N. At each sample position \mathbf{p}i = r(ti), the scalar volume value V(\mathbf{p}i) is retrieved, typically via trilinear interpolation of the surrounding voxels. Classification: The scalar value V(\mathbf{p}i) is mapped to optical properties: a color vector \mathbf{c}i (RGB) and an opacity scalar \alphai (A). This mapping is defined by a transfer function T(V) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha). Compositing: The samples are composited into the final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out} using the front-to-back volume rendering equation: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alpha{out} = 1 - \prod{i=1}^{N} (1 - \alphai) In iterative form, for each sample i: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai where \mathbf{C}{acc} and \alpha{acc} are initialized to (0, 0). Shading: At each sample, a shading model (e.g., Phong, Blinn-Phong) may be applied to compute the base color \mathbf{c}i based on the local gradient \nabla V(\mathbf{p}i), which serves as the surface normal. Front-to-Back Volume Rendering is a direct volume ray casting method that integrates light along camera rays by sampling a 3D scalar field from the near intersection point to the far intersection point and compositing the results using the Porter-Duff "Over" operator. It solves the problem of rendering semi-transparent volumetric data without extracting explicit geometric surfaces, correctly handling transparency and occlusion by accumulating color and opacity from front to back. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly defining the traversal order as front-to-back to enable early ray termination, a critical optimization for performance that is less effective or impossible in back-to-front approaches. Choose it when early termination is desired to improve performance on semi-transparent data. See Front-to-Back Volume Rendering. Volume Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that generates a 2D image by casting primary rays from each pixel of the view plane into a 3D volumetric dataset, sampling the data along the ray, and compositing the results to determine the final pixel color. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D scalar fields without converting the data to intermediate surface geometry, thereby preserving all volume information and avoiding artifacts associated with thresholding or isosurface extraction. Unlike Front-to-Back Volume Rendering which may refer to the compositing order specifically, or VCP Ray-Casting Algorithm which uses a specific voxel-centric approach, standard Volume Ray Casting is defined by its image-order traversal and equidistant sampling along view rays. Choose it as the baseline method for general volume visualization. See Volume Ray Casting. The VCP Ray-Casting Algorithm renders a smooth surface approximation from a dense point cloud by storing vector-valued data in a grid structure, rather than rendering discrete points or scalar distance fields directly. It solves the problem of noisy rendering caused by sensor noise and calibration errors in real-world LiDAR data, where points do not strictly lie on the scene surface. Unlike standard closest-point ray casting which selects the single nearest point (z-buffer), VCP uses the length of an interpolated vector to determine step sizes and the vector direction as the surface normal, allowing for adaptive marching and smooth shading. Choose it when rendering noisy point cloud data with adaptive step sizes and smooth normals. See VCP Ray-Casting Algorithm. Standard Ray Casting is a foundational technique in direct volume rendering, widely used in medical imaging (CT, MRI) and scientific visualization to explore internal structures of scalar fields. It relies on the optical model of participating media, where light is absorbed and emitted along the ray path. The technique has become the standard baseline for direct volume rendering, serving as the reference implementation for more complex traversal or scattering variants. body: Volume ray casting is a direct volume rendering technique that traces rays from each pixel into object space to compute color values without converting volume data to surface geometry. It solves the problem of rendering semi-transparent volumetric data by integrating light along camera rays, sampling a 3D scalar field, and compositing the results from the near intersection point (t{near}) to the far intersection point (t{far}). It sets itself apart from back-to-front methods by enabling early ray termination: once the accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold (typically \approx 0.99), the ray march stops, ignoring distant voxels that would contribute negligibly to the final pixel. This optimization significantly reduces computation for opaque or semi-opaque regions compared to back-to-front approaches, which must process the entire ray segment to correctly composite against a background. Inputs: Camera origin \mathbf{o}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, volume bounding box (defined by min/max corners), 3D volume texture (scalar values), transfer function T(V) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha), step size \Delta t (or number of samples N), and early termination threshold \alpha{thresh}. Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out}. Data Structures: Volume Texture: Stored as a 3D texture object (e.g., GLTEXTURE3D) or a stack of 2D slices. Each voxel holds a scalar intensity value. In GPU implementations, this is often a single-channel 32-bit float texture (GLR32F). Accumulators: Two variables per ray: accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc} (RGB) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} (A). Initialized to (0, 0). Ray State: Current position \mathbf{p}, current parameter t. Steps: 1. Ray-BBox Intersection: Calculate the entry parameter t{near} and exit parameter t{far} where the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} intersects the volume bounding box. If no intersection, return background color. 2. Initialization: Set \mathbf{C}{acc} = (0, 0, 0), \alpha{acc} = 0, and current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + (t{near} + \Delta t / 2)\mathbf{d} to sample at the midpoint of the first step. Calculate step size \Delta t = (t{far} - t{near}) / N or use a fixed world-space step. 3. Marching Loop: Iterate while t < t{far} and \alpha{acc} < \alpha{thresh}: a. Sample: Retrieve scalar value V from the volume texture at \mathbf{p} using trilinear interpolation. b. Classification: Map V to color \mathbf{c}i and opacity \alphai using the transfer function T(V). c. Compositing: Update accumulators using the front-to-back over operator: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai d. Advance: Increment t \leftarrow t + \Delta t and \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. 4. Final Output: Return \mathbf{C}{acc} as the pixel color. The final opacity is \alpha{acc}. Formulas: The continuous volume rendering integral (low albedo, no scattering) is approximated by the Riemann sum: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alpha{out} = 1 - \prod{i=1}^{N} (1 - \alphai) The iterative form used in implementation is: \mathbf{C}{acc}^{(i)} = \mathbf{C}{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \mathbf{c}i \alphai \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai where \mathbf{C}{acc}^{(0)} = 0 and \alpha{acc}^{(0)} = 0. Parameters: Step Size (\Delta t): Determines sampling density. Can be fixed in world units (e.g., 0.01) or derived from resolution (e.g., ray length / max steps). Typical values range from 0.002 to 0.01 depending on volume scale. Early Termination Threshold (\alpha{thresh}): Commonly set to 0.95 or 0.99 to stop marching when the pixel is effectively opaque. Transfer Function: Maps scalar values to (\mathbf{c}, \alpha). Can be a 1D LUT, piecewise linear, or Gaussian basis functions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inside Camera: If the camera is inside the volume, t{near} may be negative. Clamp t{near} to 0 or the entry point to avoid sampling behind the eye. Precision: Floating-point accumulation errors can cause \alpha{acc} to slightly exceed 1.0 or cause color drift. Clamping \alpha{acc} to 1.0 and \mathbf{C}{acc} to valid ranges is recommended. Degenerate Input: If the volume is empty or has zero opacity everywhere, the accumulated alpha remains below a minimum threshold (e.g., 0.01), and the pixel is typically discarded or rendered as background. Back-to-Front vs Front-to-Back: Back-to-front is mathematically equivalent but does not support early termination because the background contribution depends on the total transmittance of the entire ray.
