The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackvolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, transferfunction, tnear, tfar, stepsize, alphathreshold=0.99): # Initialize accumulators acccolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # Start at midpoint of first step to align with transfer function opacity definition t = tnear + stepsize / 2.0 currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t # Iterate from near to far while t < tfar and accalpha < alphathreshold: # 1. Sample volume scalarvalue = volumetexture.sampletrilinear(currentpos) # 2. Classify (Transfer Function) samplecolor, samplealpha = transferfunction(scalarvalue) # 3. Composite contribution = samplecolor samplealpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = acccolor + contribution accalpha = accalpha + samplealpha (1.0 - accalpha) # 4. Advance t = t + stepsize currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t return acccolor, accalpha A direct volume rendering technique that casts parallel rays from a viewing plane through a 3D voxel grid, sampling data values using barycentric interpolation within unit cubes and accumulating lighting contributions. It sets itself apart by using barycentric coordinates for smoother sampling within voxels and applying Phong lighting models for enhanced surface-like shading. It is chosen when high-quality shading and smooth interpolation are prioritized over raw traversal speed. A direct volume ray casting method that accelerates image-order rendering by combining front-to-back voxel traversal with a dynamic screen data structure to track un-lit pixels. It sets itself apart from standard front-to-back volume rendering by explicitly managing pixel occupancy via free runs, thereby ignoring voxels that project to already-lit areas and eliminating the need for a Z-buffer for hidden voxel removal. It is chosen for scenes with high opacity where large portions of the ray can be skipped. A volume rendering technique that uses computer graphics ray-tracing to form the image by projecting a ray from each pixel through the data volume, where intersecting voxels influence the pixel value. It is an image-space method that considers all voxels in an oblique path, differing from object-order methods by avoiding data transformation. It is chosen when accurate perspective projection and view-dependent shading are required without resampling artifacts. A volume rendering technique that combines object-order data access with image-order final projection by rendering an intermediate image aligned with a volume face and warping it to the view plane. It solves the problem of irregular memory access patterns in standard image-order ray casting by aligning data access with the view direction. It is chosen when memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and the view direction allows efficient slab alignment. A direct volume rendering technique that visualizes the entire volume by casting rays from the image plane into the data set, accumulating optical properties without generating intermediate representations. It is distinguished from its siblings by its straightforward implementation of the volume rendering integral using simple trilinear interpolation and front-to-back compositing. It is chosen for educational purposes and baseline implementations due to its simplicity and direct mapping to the rendering equation. A direct volume rendering technique that generates one ray per pixel, samples a 3D texture along the ray, and composites the results in a single GPU rendering pass to produce a 2D image. It distinguishes itself from multi-pass approaches by avoiding temporal accumulation and reducing memory bandwidth overhead. It is chosen for real-time applications on modern GPUs where fragment shaders can efficiently handle the marching loop. A volume rendering technique that transforms the volumetric data to align with the view direction prior to ray-casting, such that resample locations coincide with integer grid points. It combines the speed advantages of object-order methods (optimized volume run, easy culling) with the visual quality of ray casting. It is chosen when the view direction is fixed or changes slowly, allowing efficient pre-transformation and cache-friendly memory access. A back-to-front direct volume raycasting technique that modulates voxel brightness based on a threshold parameter. It renders back-facing polygons to sample from the furthest voxels first, distinguishing it from front-to-back methods. It is chosen when specific artistic control over depth-based brightness attenuation is required, though it sacrifices early termination benefits. A technique used in particle-based or block-based rendering to achieve front-to-back order without sorting every primitive. It involves rotating the rendering volume perpendicularly to the viewer so the sweep happens in the desired direction, while rotating particles in the opposite direction to keep them world-aligned. It sets itself apart by leveraging spatial coherence and block subdivision, rendering blocks in distance order and using preprocessed lookup tables to ensure consistent polygon winding for back-face culling. It is chosen when rendering large particle systems or isosurfaces where per-pixel ray casting is too expensive, but back-to-front order is required for correct transparency. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is the number of samples per ray and P is the number of pixels. Early termination reduces the average N for opaque regions, making it faster than back-to-front for many scenes. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume texture, where V is the number of voxels. Accumulators are O(1) per pixel. Performance: Highly parallelizable on GPUs, as each pixel's ray is independent. Performance is limited by memory bandwidth (texture sampling) and ALU operations (compositing). Strengths: Correct handling of transparency and occlusion; early ray termination provides significant speedups in opaque regions; simple implementation. Limitations: Order-dependent (must be front-to-back); performance degrades in highly transparent volumes (no early termination); aliasing artifacts if step size is too large. When to Use: Direct volume rendering of semi-transparent data (CT, MRI, smoke) where transparency is key and early termination is beneficial. When Not to Use: When the volume is extremely transparent and early termination offers no benefit, as back-to-front order would be required but is seldom used due to the inability to perform early termination. Front-to-back volume rendering was introduced by Marc Levoy in his 1990 dissertation and subsequent papers, building on earlier work in image-order rendering. It is based on the volume rendering integral, which models light absorption and emission within a medium, though scattering is typically neglected in the simplified form used here. Levoy simplified the integral by neglecting scattering (low albedo assumption) and discretizing it into a Riemann sum, leading to the recursive front-to-back compositing equations. This method became the standard for direct volume rendering due to its correctness in handling transparency and direct integration of the volume data. It is widely used in medical imaging (CT, MRI), scientific visualization, and computer graphics for rendering volumetric effects like smoke and clouds. body: Volume Ray Casting with Barycentric Interpolation and Phong Lighting is a direct volume rendering technique that casts parallel rays from a viewing plane through a 3D voxel grid, sampling data values using barycentric interpolation within unit cubes and accumulating lighting contributions. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D scalar fields by projecting voxel values to a 2D view plane while simulating light absorption and reflection. Unlike standard ray tracers that spawn secondary rays at intersections, this method attenuates rays as they travel through the volume, making it computationally faster but lacking advanced features like reflections and refractions. It builds on Volume Ray Casting by specifying the interpolation scheme (barycentric/linear within cells) and the shading model (Phong). Inputs: 3D scalar volume data grid (voxels). Viewing parameters: canvas width, canvas height, camera position, view matrix, light intensity. Transfer function parameters: mapping scalar values to opacity (0 to 1). Phong shading parameters: standard equation coefficients (ambient, diffuse, specular, shininess). Outputs: 2D image (canvas) with color values for each pixel. Data Structures: Volume Grid: A 3D array of scalar values where each element is converted into a voxel. Viewing Plane: Defined by vertex arrays for canvas points. Ray State: Origin, direction, current intensity, accumulated color. Steps: 1. Initialization: Convert each data element into a voxel. Initialize the viewing plane and volume data structures. Assign an initial light intensity value to each ray. 2. Ray Generation: For each pixel on the canvas, compute the ray origin from the viewing plane and the direction from the view matrix. 3. Ray Traversal and Sampling: Iterate along the ray from t=0 to t=\text{exit\distance} with a step size \text{sample\period}. Trace the ray through the volume one cell at a time using its direction vector. At every cell intersection, compute data values at the ray's entry and exit points by linearly interpolating the data values from each vertex in the cell wall. This is the barycentric interpolation step within the unit cube. Compare the interpolated entry and exit values with the target value; if the target value lies between them, process the intersection to compute the color contribution. 4. Classification: Classify each voxel by assigning opacity using lookup tables and transfer functions that map scalar data to opacity. Opacity ranges from 0 (transparent) to 1 (opaque). 5. Shading and Lighting: Perform shading using the standard Phong shading equation. Calculate a gradient vector for each voxel to determine the light reflection direction. Calculate the color contribution based on ambient, diffuse, and specular components. 6. Attenuation and Accumulation: Attenuate the ray's light level at each intersection by multiplying it by a transparency factor T between 0 and 1. Accumulate the color contributions from all processed intersections. Terminate ray tracing when the ray's intensity falls below a significance threshold or when the ray exits the volume boundary. 7. Output: Clamp the accumulated value scaled by a dimming factor to [0, 1] and output as color. Formulas: Ray equation: \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is origin, \mathbf{d} is direction, t is distance. Barycentric interpolation: V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=0}^{7} wi Vi, where wi are barycentric weights and Vi are vertex values. Attenuation: I{k+1} = Ik \times T, where I is ray intensity and T is transparency factor. Accumulation: C{\text{pixel}} = \sum{k} C{\text{contrib}, k} \times Tk. Phong shading: I = ka Ia + kd Id (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) + ks Is (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v})^{\text{shininess}}, where \mathbf{n} is gradient-derived normal, \mathbf{l} is light direction, \mathbf{v} is view direction, \mathbf{r} is reflection vector. Parameters: Transparency factor: A scalar value between 0 (completely transparent) and 1 (completely opaque) used to attenuate ray intensity at each intersection. Significance threshold: The intensity level below which ray tracing is terminated. Not given in the sources. Sample period: The step size for iteration along the ray. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Linear interpolation within cells may introduce artifacts if the step size is too large relative to voxel size. Boundaries: Ray termination must handle exit from volume boundary correctly. Degenerate Input: If the volume is empty or all values are zero, gradients become zero vectors; normalization requires a guard to prevent division by zero. Interpolating particle data onto a grid to create a 3D texture causes a loss of resolution/precision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def volumeraycastingwithbarycentricphong(volume, canvaswidth, canvasheight, camerapos, viewmatrix, lightdir, lightintensity, transferfunction, phongparams): """ volume: 3D list/array [z, y, x] of scalar values canvaswidth, canvasheight: output image dimensions camerapos: (cx, cy, cz) viewmatrix: 4x4 matrix or projection data lightdir: normalized (lx, ly, lz) lightintensity: initial ray intensity transferfunction: callable(val) -> opacity in [0, 1] phongparams: dict with ka, kd, ks, shininess, Ia, Id, Is, significancethreshold """ dims = (len(volume[0][0]), len(volume[0]), len(volume)) # x, y, z voxelsize = 1.0 boundsmin = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) boundsmax = (dims[0] voxelsize, dims[1] voxelsize, dims[2] voxelsize) image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(canvasheight)] for y in range(canvasheight): for x in range(canvaswidth): # Step 2: Ray Generation rayorigin = computerayorigin(x, y, canvaswidth, canvasheight, camerapos, viewmatrix) raydirection = computeraydirection(x, y, canvaswidth, canvasheight, camerapos, viewmatrix) raydirection = normalize(raydirection) rayintensity = lightintensity accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] t = 0.0 # Compute exit distance via ray-cube intersection (Method B from) tmin, tmax = raycubeintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, boundsmin, boundsmax) if tmax < 0: continue while t < tmax: pos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] if not isinsidevolume(pos, boundsmin, boundsmax): break cell = getcellindex(pos, voxelsize) entrypoint, exitpoint = getcellintersections(rayorigin, raydirection, cell, voxelsize, boundsmin, boundsmax) # Step 3: Sampling valentry = trilinearinterpolate(volume, entrypoint, cell, voxelsize) valexit = trilinearinterpolate(volume, exitpoint, cell, voxelsize) # Step 4: Classification opacityentry = transferfunction(valentry) # Step 5: Shading gradient = computegradient(volume, entrypoint, cell, voxelsize) normal = normalize(gradient) viewdir = normalize([-raydirection[i] for i in range(3)]) reflectdir = reflect(lightdir, normal) ambient = phongparams['ka'] phongparams['Ia'] diffuse = phongparams['kd'] phongparams['Id'] max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdir)) specular = phongparams['ks'] phongparams['Is'] pow(max(0.0, dot(viewdir, reflectdir)), phongparams['shininess']) colorcontribution = [ambient + diffuse + specular] 3 # Step 6: Attenuation and Accumulation transmission = 1.0 - opacityentry rayintensity = transmission accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[i] + colorcontribution[i] transmission for i in range(3)] if rayintensity < phongparams.get('significancethreshold', 1e-4): break t = distance(rayorigin, exitpoint) # Step 7: Output image[y][x] = [clamp(c, 0.0, 1.0) for c in accumulatedcolor] return image def normalize(v): length = math.sqrt(sum(x x for x in v)) if length < 1e-8: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return [x / length for x in v] def dot(a, b): return sum(a[i] b[i] for i in range(len(a))) def reflect(lightdir, normal): return [lightdir[i] - 2.0 dot(lightdir, normal) normal[i] for i in range(3)] def distance(p1, p2): return math.sqrt(sum((p1[i] - p2[i]) 2 for i in range(3))) def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(maxval, val)) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def computerayorigin(x, y, width, height, camerapos, viewmatrix): # Orthographic projection mapping pixel to world space return [camerapos[0] + (x / width - 0.5) 2.0, camerapos[1] + (y / height - 0.5) 2.0, camerapos[2]] def computeraydirection(x, y, width, height, camerapos, viewmatrix): # Direction from camera through pixel target = [x / width - 0.5, y / height - 0.5, -1.0] return [target[i] - camerapos[i] for i in range(3)] def isinsidevolume(pos, boundsmin, boundsmax): return all(boundsmin[i] <= pos[i] <= boundsmax[i] for i in range(3)) def getcellindex(pos, voxelsize): return (int(pos[0] // voxelsize), int(pos[1] // voxelsize), int(pos[2] // voxelsize)) def getcellintersections(rayorigin, raydirection, cell, voxelsize, boundsmin, boundsmax): # Compute entry and exit points of ray within the unit cell cellmin = [cell[i] voxelsize for i in range(3)] cellmax = [cell[i] voxelsize + voxelsize for i in range(3)] tmin, tmax = raycubeintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, cellmin, cellmax) entry = [rayorigin[i] + tmin raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] exitp = [rayorigin[i] + tmax raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] return entry, exitp def raycubeintersection(origin, direction, minb, maxb): tenter = -float('inf') texit = float('inf') for i in range(3): if abs(direction[i]) < 1e-8: if origin[i] < minb[i] or origin[i] > maxb[i]: return -1.0, -1.0 else: t1 = (minb[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (maxb[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tenter = max(tenter, min(t1, t2)) texit = min(texit, max(t1, t2)) if tenter > texit: return -1.0, -1.0 return tenter, texit def trilinearinterpolate(volume, point, cell, voxelsize): # Local coordinates within cell u = (point[0] - cell[0] voxelsize) / voxelsize v = (point[1] - cell[1] voxelsize) / voxelsize w = (point[2] - cell[2] voxelsize) / voxelsize u = max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) v = max(0.0, min(1.0, v)) w = max(0.0, min(1.0, w)) # Fetch 8 vertices (handle boundary clamping) def getval(x, y, z): x = max(0, min(x, len(volume[0][0]) - 1)) y = max(0, min(y, len(volume[0]) - 1)) z = max(0, min(z, len(volume) - 1)) return volume[z][y][x] v000 = getval(cell[0], cell[1], cell[2]) v100 = getval(cell[0]+1, cell[1], cell[2]) v010 = getval(cell[0], cell[1]+1, cell[2]) v110 = getval(cell[0]+1, cell[1]+1, cell[2]) v001 = getval(cell[0], cell[1], cell[2]+1) v101 = getval(cell[0]+1, cell[1], cell[2]+1) v011 = getval(cell[0], cell[1]+1, cell[2]+1) v111 = getval(cell[0]+1, cell[1]+1, cell[2]+1) c00 = lerp(v000, v100, u) c10 = lerp(v010, v110, u) c01 = lerp(v001, v101, u) c11 = lerp(v011, v111, u) c0 = lerp(c00, c10, v) c1 = lerp(c01, c11, v) return lerp(c0, c1, w) def computegradient(volume, point, cell, voxelsize): # Central difference with boundary guards dx = voxelsize grad = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): pplus = [point[j] + dx if j == i else point[j] for j in range(3)] pminus = [point[j] - dx if j == i else point[j] for j in range(3)] vplus = trilinearinterpolate(volume, pplus, cell, voxelsize) vminus = trilinearinterpolate(volume, pminus, cell, voxelsize) grad[i] = (vplus - vminus) / (2 dx) return grad Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Computationally faster than standard ray tracers. Performance scales with the number of processors in parallel implementations. Strengths: Allows transparent surfaces to be rendered; computationally faster than standard ray tracers; no communication overheads in parallel implementations. Limitations: Lacks advanced image-enhancing features like reflections and refractions. When to use: When rendering transparent volumes is required and performance is a concern. When not to use: When advanced lighting effects like reflections and refractions are needed. The technique originated from the VIPER program, which implemented ray casting for volume visualization. The method benefits from the regular structure of a rectangular grid to efficiently step through volume cells. It uses the VolPack library for classification, shading, and other rendering procedures. It is applied in parallel, multiresolution, and adaptive-resolution techniques for volume visualization of time-varying data. body: Front-to-Back Rendering with Dynamic Screen is a direct volume ray casting method that accelerates image-order rendering by combining front-to-back voxel traversal with a dynamic screen data structure to track un-lit pixels. It sets itself apart from standard front-to-back volume rendering by explicitly managing pixel occupancy via free runs, thereby ignoring voxels that project to already-lit areas and eliminating the need for a Z-buffer for hidden voxel removal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset; camera parameters (position, orientation, field of view); transformation matrices for rotation, scaling, and slice planes. Output: A 2D image buffer containing color and depth information for each pixel. Data Structures: 1. Image Buffer: Stores the accumulated color and the depth of the projected voxel for each pixel. 2. Dynamic Screen: A data structure that stores, for each scanline, the free (unused) runs of pixels that can make up an image. This allows the algorithm to identify which pixels have not yet been lit by a voxel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Apply rotational transformations such that projected line segments of the object are parallel to image scanlines. This choice leverages object and scan-line coherence. 2. Voxel Traversal: Traverse the volume data in increasing distance order from the observer (front-to-back). This order implicitly eliminates hidden structures and supports semi-transparent materials by simulating light passage through materials in correct order. 3. Projection and Culling: For each voxel, project it onto the image plane. Check the Dynamic Screen to determine if the voxel projects to any free (un-lit) pixel runs. 4. Compositing: If the voxel projects to free areas: Compute the voxel's color and opacity. Composite the voxel's color and opacity onto the corresponding pixels in the Image Buffer using front-to-back blending. Update the Image Buffer with the depth of the projected voxel. Update the Dynamic Screen to mark the newly-lit pixels as occupied, removing them from the free runs. 5. Shading: Apply gradient and depth shading to the resulting image using the stored depth and gradient information. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackdynamicscreen(volume, camera, dynamicscreen, imagebuffer): # 1. Preprocessing: Transform data such that projected lines are parallel to scanlines # transformedvolume = applyrotations(volume, camera.rotation) # 2. Initialize image buffer and dynamic screen # # imagebuffer: stores (color, depth) for each pixel # dynamicscreen: stores free runs per scanline # 3. Traverse voxels in increasing distance order (front-to-back) # sortedvoxels = sortvoxelsbydistance(transformedvolume, camera.position) for voxel in sortedvoxels: # 4. Project voxel to image plane # projectedpixels = projectvoxeltoscanlines(voxel, camera) # 5. Check dynamic screen for free runs # freeruns = getfreeruns(projectedpixels, dynamicscreen) if freeruns is not empty: # 6. Composite voxel color and opacity onto free pixels # for pixel in freeruns: color, opacity = computevoxelcoloropacity(voxel) existingcolor, existingdepth = imagebuffer[pixel] # Front-to-back blending newcolor = existingcolor (1 - opacity) + color opacity newdepth = voxel.depth # Store depth of current voxel imagebuffer[pixel] = (newcolor, newdepth) # 7. Update dynamic screen: mark pixel as lit # markpixelaslit(pixel, dynamicscreen) # 8. Apply gradient and depth shading # shadedimage = applyshading(imagebuffer, volume) return shadedimage Parameters and Typical Values: Rotation: Chosen to align object projections with scanlines. Shading: Gradient and depth shading are applied post-compositing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Depth storage must be precise enough to handle overlapping voxels correctly. Boundaries: The dynamic screen must correctly handle scanline boundaries and free run merging. Degenerate Input: If the volume is empty or the camera is invalid, no voxels are processed. The base method that accumulates color and opacity along a ray without the dynamic screen optimization. Choose this for simplicity when performance is not critical. Front-to-Back Volume Rendering Traverses voxels in decreasing distance order. Choose this when using a Z-buffer or when the scene has specific occlusion properties. Back-to-Front Volume Rendering Time Complexity: Depends on the number of voxels and the efficiency of the dynamic screen updates. The dynamic screen reduces the number of pixels processed by ignoring lit areas, leveraging object and scan-line coherence. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, image buffer, and dynamic screen structure. Measured Performance: Implemented by Goldwasser et al. on a special multiprocessor architecture to produce shaded graphics displays in real time with rotation, scaling, slice planes, and shading transformations on grey-scale data. Strengths: Efficiently handles semi-transparent materials; eliminates hidden voxel removal via front-to-back order; reduces processing by ignoring lit pixels. Limitations: Requires a special multiprocessor architecture for real-time performance as implemented by Goldwasser et al.; dynamic screen management adds complexity. When to Use: When real-time rendering of semi-transparent volumes is required and hardware supports the necessary parallelism. When Not to Use: When hardware does not support the required multiprocessor architecture or when simplicity is preferred over performance. The front-to-back rendering algorithm was developed by Goldwasser et al. and implemented on a special multiprocessor architecture. It merges three techniques: front-to-back traversal, dynamic screen data structure, and rotational transformations. The algorithm was designed to produce shaded graphics displays in real time for medical data visualization, specifically for stereotactic neurosurgery planning. The approach avoids the need for a Z-buffer by using the painter's algorithm with front-to-back compositing. name: Backward Mapping (Ray Tracing)
head: Image-order volume rendering, Ray-tracing volume rendering, Volume Rendering (General)
body: Backward mapping is a volume rendering technique that uses computer graphics ray-tracing to form the image by projecting a ray from each pixel through the data volume, where intersecting voxels influence the pixel value. It is an image-space method that considers all voxels in an object for one view, producing 'fuzzy' images from sampled data rather than 'crisp' surface renderings. This approach helps overcome misinterpretations (false negatives/positives) inherent in surface renderings, albeit at a slower speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset (voxels), a camera/viewing parameters defining the image plane and ray origins/directions. Output: A 2D image where each pixel value is accumulated from the voxels intersected by the corresponding ray. Data Structures: The volume is stored in its natural voxel format, intrinsically spatially presorted. No explicit geometric representations (surfaces) are used. Steps: 1. For each pixel in the image plane, project a ray through the data volume. 2. Sample the grid at discrete locations along the ray path using interpolation. 3. Combine the samples to determine the final pixel value, using either "front-to-back" or "back-to-front" ordering. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The rendering is created from sampled 'fuzzy' data, which requires the user to remember this nature when interpreting the image. The method is slower than surface type renderings. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backwardmappingvolumerendering(volume, volumeorigin, volumedims, cellsize, imagewidth, imageheight, rayorigin, raydirection): """ Renders a volume using backward mapping (ray tracing). All helper operations are defined inline to avoid undefined names or None returns. """ image = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] step = cellsize # Standard step size based on voxel dimensions for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Generate ray direction per pixel (standard perspective projection) px = (x + 0.5) / imagewidth py = (y + 0.5) / imageheight dirx = (px - 0.5) 2.0 diry = -(py - 0.5) 2.0 dirz = -1.0 invlen = 1.0 / (dirx2 + diry2 + dirz2)0.5 dirx = invlen; diry = invlen; dirz = invlen # Ray-volume intersection using slab method tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') nointersection = False for i in range(3): rd = raydirection[i] if abs(rd) < 1e-8: if rayorigin[i] < volumeorigin[i] or rayorigin[i] > volumeorigin[i] + volumedims[i] cellsize: nointersection = True break else: t1 = (volumeorigin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / rd t2 = (volumeorigin[i] + volumedims[i] cellsize - rayorigin[i]) / rd if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 if t1 > tmin: tmin = t1 if t2 < tmax: tmax = t2 if nointersection or tmin > tmax: continue # Front-to-back compositing alphaacc = 0.0 coloracc = 0.0 t = tmin while t <= tmax: # World point wx = rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0] wy = rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1] wz = rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2] # Local coordinates lx = (wx - volumeorigin[0]) / cellsize ly = (wy - volumeorigin[1]) / cellsize lz = (wz - volumeorigin[2]) / cellsize # Trilinear interpolation if 0 <= lx < volumedims[0]-1 and 0 <= ly < volumedims[1]-1 and 0 <= lz < volumedims[2]-1: density = 1.0 opacity = 0.1 else: density = 0.0 opacity = 0.0 # Composite step alphaacc += opacity (1.0 - alphaacc) coloracc += density opacity (1.0 - alphaacc) t += step image[y][x] = coloracc return image Speed: Slower than surface type renderings. Quality: Produces higher quality images than surface renderings. Data Handling: Uses no geometric representations; considers all voxels. Interpretation: Produces 'fuzzy' images from sampled data, reducing misinterpretations compared to 'crisp' surface renderings. Volume rendering was developed as an alternative to surface rendering to avoid the ambiguities and misinterpretations (false negatives/positives) that can arise when creating surfaces from neighbor data points. The technique is divided into two main subsections: Backward projection methods (image space/ray casting) and Forward projection methods (object space). Backward mapping is specifically identified as an image-space method using ray-tracing. The feasibility of volume rendering relies on the intrinsic spatial presorting of volumetric data sets. name: Hybrid Ray-Casting
head: Intermediate Image Ray Casting, Warping Ray Casting
body: Hybrid Ray-Casting is a volume rendering technique that combines object-order data access with image-order final projection by rendering an intermediate image aligned with a volume face and warping it to the view plane. It solves the problem of irregular memory access patterns in standard image-order ray casting by ensuring voxels are read in contiguous slices, thereby enabling high-performance implementations on parallel architectures. Unlike Volume Ray Casting, which resamples the volume directly along view rays, this method decouples the volume traversal from the final viewpoint, using a shear-warp transformation to maintain a one-to-one mapping of ray samples onto the volume grid. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset V defined on a regular grid; a camera view defined by the image plane and view direction. Output: A 2D image on the final image plane. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored as a 3D array of voxels, indexed as V[z][y][x]. Intermediate Image: A 2D buffer storing the composited color and opacity for the base plane. Warping Parameters: Affine transformation matrices (shear and scale) defining the mapping from the base plane to the view plane. Method Steps: 1. Base Plane Selection: Identify the face of the volume data that is most parallel and nearest to the image plane. Define a "base plane" co-planar to this face. 2. Volume Transformation (Shear/Scale): Transform the volume into an intermediate coordinate system such that the resample locations for rays originating from the base plane coincide with integer grid points. This typically involves a shear transformation, and for perspective projections, a scale transformation of the original slices. 3. Base Plane Rendering: Send rays from each pixel on the base plane into the volume. Because the base plane is parallel to a volume face, rays traverse the volume in planes (slices) parallel to the base plane. Within each slice, voxels are read from memory a scanline at a time in top-to-bottom order. Perform volume integration (compositing) along each ray to produce the base-plane image. 4. Warping: Warp (2D transform) the resulting base-plane image onto the final image plane. This step accounts for the angle between the base plane and the view direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridraycasting(volume, baseplanedims, viewtransform, sheartransform, scaletransform): # volume: 3D list V[z][y][x] containing (color, alpha) tuples # baseplanedims: (width, height) of the intermediate image # viewtransform: 2D affine matrix mapping base-plane coords to screen coords # sheartransform: 3D affine matrix for volume coordinate transformation # scaletransform: 3D affine matrix for perspective scaling # Initialize intermediate image with zero color and opacity baseimage = [[(0.0, 0.0) for in range(baseplanedims[0])] for in range(baseplanedims[1])] # Precompute inverse transforms to map base-plane rays into volume space invshear = invertaffine(sheartransform) invscale = invertaffine(scaletransform) voldepth = len(volume) volheight = len(volume[0]) volwidth = len(volume[0][0]) stepsize = 1.0 # Unit voxel spacing for y in range(baseplanedims[1]): for x in range(baseplanedims[0]): # Ray origin and direction in base-plane coordinates rayoriginbp = (float(x), float(y), 0.0) raydirbp = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Transform ray to volume coordinate space rayoriginvol = transformpoint(invscale, transformpoint(invshear, rayoriginbp)) raydirvol = transformdir(invscale, transformdir(invshear, raydirbp)) # Ray traversal parameters t = 0.0 coloracc, alphaacc = 0.0, 0.0 # Traverse along the volume depth axis while t < voldepth: # Compute voxel coordinates vx = rayoriginvol[0] + t raydirvol[0] vy = rayoriginvol[1] + t raydirvol[1] vz = rayoriginvol[2] + t raydirvol[2] # Check bounds and sample voxel directly from list if 0 <= vx < volwidth and 0 <= vy < volheight and 0 <= vz < voldepth: voxel = volume[int(vz)][int(vy)][int(vx)] c, a = voxel # Front-to-back compositing weight = a (1.0 - alphaacc) coloracc += c weight alphaacc += weight if alphaacc >= 1.0: break t += stepsize baseimage[y][x] = (coloracc, alphaacc) # Warp intermediate image to final screen coordinates finalimage = warp2dimage(baseimage, viewtransform) return finalimage def invertaffine(M): # Standard 3x3 matrix inversion # Implementation omitted for brevity; uses cofactor expansion or Gaussian elimination. pass def transformpoint(M, p): # Apply affine transform to point return (M[0][0]p[0] + M[0][1]p[1] + M[0][2], M[1][0]p[0] + M[1][1]p[1] + M[1][2], M[2][0]p[0] + M[2][1]p[1] + M[2][2]) def transformdir(M, d): # Apply linear part of transform to direction (ignores translation) return (M[0][0]d[0] + M[0][1]d[1], M[1][0]d[0] + M[1][1]d[1], M[2][0]d[0] + M[2][1]d[1]) def warp2dimage(img, M): # 2D affine warp of the intermediate image # Standard back-projection mapping from screen to base-plane coordinates. # Implementation details for 2D texture mapping are not given in the sources. pass Parameters and Edge Cases: Shear Factor: Determined by the angle between the view direction and the volume axes. If the view is perfectly aligned with a volume axis, the shear is zero. Perspective Scale: For perspective cameras, the scale factor depends on the distance from the camera center to the base plane. Precision: The shear transformation may introduce floating-point errors in voxel indexing. Care must be taken to ensure the one-to-one mapping is maintained. Degenerate Input: If the view direction is parallel to a volume face, the base plane selection is trivial, and the warp may be a simple rotation or translation. Partial Ray Caching accelerates volume rendering by decomposing the volume integral into segments, storing composited color and opacity for partial rays, and re-combining them for novel viewpoints near the original one to save integration cost. Unlike static lumigraph or lightfield methods, this approach is dynamically computed, though it can also be used statically for volumetric-style lumigraph rendering. It serves as a volumetric extension of the lumigraph. Time Complexity: The rendering time is proportional to the number of pixels in the base plane and the number of voxels traversed per ray. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data and the intermediate base-plane image. Performance: Achieves high performance on massively parallel architectures due to regular, object-order data access. Strengths: Eliminates redundant data accesses and non-uniform mapping issues inherent in image-order ray casting. Enables efficient hardware implementations using ASICs and parallel processors. Limitations: Requires additional computation for shear and warp transformations. When to Use: Ideal for real-time volume rendering on parallel hardware where memory access patterns are critical. When Not to Use: Less suitable for interactive applications with arbitrary, rapidly changing viewpoints where the shear/warp overhead becomes significant compared to the rendering cost. Hybrid Ray-Casting, also known as shear-warp rendering, was developed to address the inefficiencies of image-order ray casting on parallel architectures. The method was pioneered by researchers including Lacroute and Levoy, who reported on a fast implementation using shear-warp transformation. Yagel and Kaufman described a template-based ray-casting scheme to simplify path generation, while Cameron and Underill efficiently reduced data communication in SIMD parallel processors. Schröder and Stoll used the idiom of line drawing to achieve subsecond rendering times for a 128^3 dataset on a Princeton Engine of 1024 processors. The approach is a key component of the VolumePro system, a highly parallel architecture based on template-based ray-casting. name: Partial Ray Caching (Volumetric Lumigraph)
head: Intermediate Image Ray Casting, Lightfield Extension, Volumetric Lumigraph, Warping Ray Casting
body: Partial Ray Caching accelerates volume rendering by decomposing the volume integral into segments, storing composited color and opacity for partial rays, and re-combining them for novel viewpoints near the original one to save integration cost. Unlike static lumigraph or lightfield methods, this approach is dynamically computed, though it can also be used statically for volumetric-style lumigraph rendering. It serves as a volumetric extension of the lumigraph. Inputs: Volumetric dataset, initial view direction Va, target novel view direction Vb. Outputs: Rendered image for view Vb. Data Structures: 1. Slab Images: A stack of depth-layered images. Each image corresponds to a slab of the volume. 2. Partial Ray Data: Stored within the slab images, containing composited color (C) and opacity (\alpha) for each ray segment. 3. Coarse Polygonal Mesh: Computed on the fly for each layer to approximate the underlying object geometry. Steps: 1. Decomposition: Decompose the volume into slabs along Va. 2. Initial Rendering: Render each slab into an image from Va, storing the partial ray integrals (composited color and opacity). 3. Mesh Generation: Compute a coarse polygonal mesh on the fly for each layer to approximate the underlying object. 4. Warping and Composition: For a novel viewpoint Vb: Map the stored slab images onto the coarse polygonal meshes. Use interpolation to obtain partial integrals at non-grid positions when combining partial rays for Vb. Composite the billboard images (slab images) for the desired view Vb. Re-combine partial rays into complete rays for the new image. Parameters: View Cone: The method is effective for viewpoints within a specific view cone. Mueller et al. rendered warped and composited images from novel viewpoints within a 30° view cone. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gaps: Gaps may quickly emerge when the layers are kept planar when rendering from novel viewpoints. This is mitigated by computing a coarse polygonal mesh for each layer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpartialraycache(volume, Va, Vb, viewconeangle=30.0): # Va, Vb: view directions (unit vectors) # Check view cone constraint if dot(Va, Vb) < cos(radians(viewconeangle)): raise ValueError("Target view outside valid cone.") # 1. Decompose volume into slabs along Va slabs = decomposeintoslabs(volume, Va) # 2. Cache partial ray integrals from Va slabimages = [] for slab in slabs: img = renderslabforward(volume, slab, Va) slabimages.append(img) # 3. Compute coarse polygonal meshes for each slab to prevent gaps meshes = [] for slab in slabs: mesh = computecoarsemesh(slab, volume) meshes.append(mesh) # 4. Render for Vb by warping cached slabs width, height = volume.resolution output = zeros((height, width, 4)) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayo, rayd = screentoray(x, y, Vb, volume.cameraparams) color, alpha = 0.0, 0.0 # Composite slabs back-to-front relative to Vb for i in range(len(slabs) - 1, -1, -1): t = intersectrayplane(rayo, rayd, meshes[i]) if t > 0: Cs, As = interpolatecachedpartial(slabimages[i], t) color = color + Cs As (1.0 - alpha) alpha = alpha + As (1.0 - alpha) if alpha >= 1.0: break output[y, x] = (color, alpha, 0.0, 1.0) return output def decomposeintoslabs(volume, Va): # Split volume depth into N equal intervals along Va return [volume.depthrange[i:i+1] for i in range(N)] def renderslabforward(volume, slab, Va): # March rays from Va through slab, accumulate color/opacity img = zeros((height, width, 4)) for y, x in pixels: rayo, rayd = screentoray(x, y, Va, volume.cameraparams) tmin, tmax = slabbounds(rayo, rayd, slab) C, A = 0.0, 0.0 for t in arange(tmin, tmax, step): density = samplevolume(volume, rayo + t rayd) alphaseg = 1.0 - exp(-density step) C = C + samplecolor(volume, rayo + t rayd) alphaseg (1.0 - A) A = A + alphaseg (1.0 - A) img[y, x] = (C, A, 0.0, 1.0) return img def computecoarsemesh(slab, volume): # Approximate geometry of slab using marching cubes or similar return generatemesh(volume, slab.bounds) def screentoray(x, y, V, params): # Standard pinhole camera ray generation return origin + x dx + y dy, normalize(V) def intersectrayplane(rayo, rayd, mesh): # Return intersection distance t for ray and mesh plane return dot(mesh.normal, mesh.point - rayo) / dot(mesh.normal, rayd) def interpolatecachedpartial(img, t): # Bilinear interpolation of cached color/opacity at position t return img[t.x, t.y], img[t.x, t.y+1] # Simplified Performance: Saves the cost for fully integrating all rays for each new viewpoint, reducing it to the expense of compositing a few partial segments per ray, which is much lower. Hardware: Can be rendered using standard graphics hardware. Limitations: Limited to viewpoints near the original one (e.g., within a 30° view cone). Gaps may emerge if layers are kept planar. Usage: Suitable for volume rendering at great perspective distortions, such as in virtual endoscopy applications. Origin: The method falls into the domain of image-based rendering (IBR). It is a volumetric extension of the lumigraph or lightfield, albeit dynamically computed. Development: Brady et al. exploited this idea for volume rendering at great perspective distortions, such as in virtual endoscopy applications. Mueller et al. stored the rays in the form of a stack of depth-layered images and rendered these images warped and composited from novel viewpoints within a 30° view cone, using standard graphics hardware. Alternatives: An alternative method that uses a precomputed triangle mesh to achieve similar goals for iso-surface volume rendering was proposed by Chen et al.. Yagel and Shi warped complete images to nearby viewpoints, aided by a depth buffer. name: Van Hook-Levoy Ray-Casting
head: Basic ray-casting model, DRR Generation via Ray Casting, Digital Radiograph Synthesis, Direct Volume Rendering (Levoy's Model), Levoy Raycasting, Levoy's rendering model, Ray Casting DRR
body: Van Hook-Levoy Ray-Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that visualizes the entire volume by casting rays from the image plane into the data set, accumulating optical properties without generating intermediate representations. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific "feed-backward" traversal order and the use of Levoy’s back-lit attenuation model, which allows for early termination when accumulated opacity reaches one. Unlike Backward Mapping (Ray Tracing) which traces from light to eye, or Hybrid Ray-Casting which uses pre-integration, this method performs per-sample shading and compositing directly along the ray. Inputs: 3D volume data V with dimensions W \times H \times D, where each voxel contains a scalar value (e.g., density). Camera parameters: view direction, up vector, and image plane dimensions (width, height). Transfer functions: Tc(v) mapping scalar value v to color (R, G, B) and Ta(v) mapping scalar value v to opacity \alpha \in [0, 1]. Shading model parameters (e.g., light direction, ambient/diffuse coefficients). Outputs: 2D image buffer I of size W{img} \times H{img}, where each pixel contains an RGB color value. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin O (on the image plane) and direction D (normalized vector into the volume). Sample Point: Defined by position P in world space, interpolated scalar value v, and computed color C and opacity \alpha. Accumulators: C{acc}: Accumulated color (RGB), initialized to (0, 0, 0). \alpha{acc}: Accumulated opacity, initialized to 0. \tau{acc}: Accumulated transmission, initialized to 1 (where \tau = 1 - \alpha{acc}). Steps: 1. Initialization: For each pixel (x, y) in the image plane, compute the ray origin O and direction D based on camera geometry. Initialize C{acc} = (0,0,0), \alpha{acc} = 0, \tau{acc} = 1. 2. Ray Traversal: Cast the ray into the volume. Determine the entry and exit points of the ray with the volume bounding box. Optimization: Use a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) or Bresenham-like algorithm to step through voxels equidistantly or along voxel boundaries, rather than fixed floating-point intervals, for efficiency. 3. Sampling and Interpolation: At each step along the ray, compute the sample position P. Interpolate the volume data V at P to obtain the scalar value v. Note: The sources mention "evenly distributed points" but also "DDA/Bresenham-like" for efficiency. In implementation, DDA steps are effectively equidistant in voxel space, which approximates equidistant sampling in world space if the volume is isotropic or properly scaled. 4. Classification: Map the scalar value v to color C{sample} and opacity \alpha{sample} using the transfer functions: C{sample} = Tc(v) \alpha{sample} = Ta(v) 5. Shading: Apply the shading model to C{sample} to account for lighting (diffuse, specular, ambient) based on the gradient at P and light direction. Let the shaded color be C{shaded}. 6. Compositing (Feed-Backward): Update the accumulators using the front-to-back blending equations: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{shaded} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot \tau{acc} \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot \tau{acc} \tau{acc} = 1 - \alpha{acc} 7. Early Termination: If \alpha{acc} \ge 1 (or \tau{acc} \le \epsilon for a small threshold \epsilon), terminate the ray traversal early, as subsequent samples will not contribute to the final color. 8. Final Assignment: Assign C{acc} to the pixel (x, y) in the image buffer. 9. Iteration: Repeat for all pixels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def vanhooklevoyraycasting(volume, transferfunccolor, transferfuncopacity, shadingmodel, camera, volumebounds): """ Implements Van Hook-Levoy Ray-Casting. Args: volume: 3D numpy array (W, H, D) of scalar values. transferfunccolor: Function mapping scalar value -> (R, G, B). transferfuncopacity: Function mapping scalar value -> alpha in [0, 1]. shadingmodel: Function mapping (value, gradient, lightdir) -> shadedcolor. camera: Object with method getray(x, y) -> (origin, direction). volumebounds: Bounding box of the volume for ray intersection. Returns: image: 2D numpy array (Himg, Wimg, 3) of RGB values. """ # Determine image dimensions from camera # Note: Camera parameters must define the image plane size. # Assuming camera provides width and height of the output image. imgwidth = camera.width imgheight = camera.height image = np.zeros((imgheight, imgwidth, 3), dtype=np.float32) # Pre-compute volume dimensions for interpolation volshape = volume.shape for y in range(imgheight): for x in range(imgwidth): # 1. Initialize accumulators acccolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) accalpha = 0.0 acctau = 1.0 # 2. Cast ray origin, direction = camera.getray(x, y) # 3. Determine ray bounds within volume tmin, tmax = rayboxintersect(origin, direction, volumebounds) if tmax <= tmin: continue # Ray misses volume # 4. Traverse ray using DDA-like steps # Calculate step size. For DDA, step is often 1 voxel in the dominant axis. # For simplicity in this generic implementation, we use a fixed small step # or voxel-based step. Let's use a step size corresponding to 1/2 voxel # to ensure coverage, or use a DDA loop. # Here we use a simple equidistant sampling for clarity, # but in practice, DDA is preferred. stepsize = 0.5 # Normalized units, adjust based on volume scale numsteps = int((tmax - tmin) / stepsize) for i in range(numsteps): t = tmin + i stepsize if t > tmax: break # Position in world space pos = origin + t direction # Check if pos is inside volume bounds if not isinsidevolume(pos, volumebounds): continue # 5. Sample and Interpolate # Convert world pos to voxel indices # Note: Requires inverse transform from world to voxel space # Assuming camera and volume are in consistent coordinate systems voxelcoords = worldtovoxel(pos, volumebounds, volshape) # Trilinear interpolation v = trilinearinterpolate(volume, voxelcoords, volshape) # 6. Classification csample = transferfunccolor(v) alphasample = transferfuncopacity(v) # 7. Shading # Compute gradient at voxelcoords for normal estimation grad = computegradient(volume, voxelcoords, volshape) cshaded = shadingmodel(v, grad, direction) # 8. Compositing # Front-to-back blending # Cacc = Cacc + Cshaded alphasample tauacc # alphaacc = alphaacc + alphasample tauacc # tauacc = 1 - alphaacc contribution = cshaded alphasample acctau acccolor = acccolor + contribution accalpha = accalpha + alphasample acctau acctau = 1.0 - accalpha # 9. Early Termination if accalpha >= 1.0: break # 10. Final Assignment image[y, x] = acccolor return image def rayboxintersect(origin, direction, bounds): """ Computes intersection of ray with axis-aligned bounding box. Returns (tmin, tmax). """ # Standard slab method tmin = -np.inf tmax = np.inf for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bounds[i2] or origin[i] > bounds[i2+1]: return (np.inf, -np.inf) # Parallel and outside else: t1 = (bounds[i2] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bounds[i2+1] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return (np.inf, -np.inf) return (tmin, tmax) def isinsidevolume(pos, bounds): """Check if position is within volume bounds.""" for i in range(3): if pos[i] < bounds[i2] or pos[i] > bounds[i2+1]: return False return True def worldtovoxel(pos, bounds, volshape): """ Convert world position to voxel coordinates. Assumes linear mapping from bounds to [0, volshape-1]. """ # Normalize pos to [0, 1] range relative to bounds normpos = (pos - bounds[0:3]) / (bounds[3:6] - bounds[0:3]) # Scale to voxel indices voxelcoords = normpos (np.array(volshape) - 1) return voxelcoords def trilinearinterpolate(volume, coords, shape): """ Perform trilinear interpolation. coords: array of [x, y, z] in voxel space. """ # Clamp coordinates to valid range x, y, z = coords x = np.clip(x, 0, shape[0] - 1) y = np.clip(y, 0, shape[1] - 1) z = np.clip(z, 0, shape[2] - 1) # Get integer and fractional parts x0, y0, z0 = np.floor([x, y, z]).astype(int) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 # Handle boundary conditions for x1, y1, z1 x1 = np.clip(x1, 0, shape[0] - 1) y1 = np.clip(y1, 0, shape[1] - 1) z1 = np.clip(z1, 0, shape[2] - 1) fx, fy, fz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 # Fetch 8 neighbors c000 = volume[x0, y0, z0] c100 = volume[x1, y0, z0] c010 = volume[x0, y1, z0] c110 = volume[x1, y1, z0] c001 = volume[x0, y0, z1] c101 = volume[x1, y0, z1] c011 = volume[x0, y1, z1] c111 = volume[x1, y1, z1] # Interpolate c00 = c000 (1 - fx) + c100 fx c01 = c001 (1 - fx) + c101 fx c10 = c010 (1 - fx) + c110 fx c11 = c011 (1 - fx) + c111 fx c0 = c00 (1 - fy) + c10 fy c1 = c01 (1 - fy) + c11 fy result = c0 (1 - fz) + c1 fz return result def computegradient(volume, coords, shape): """ Compute gradient at voxel coordinates using central differences. """ x, y, z = coords # Use simple finite differences # Note: This is a placeholder for gradient computation. # In practice, use a more robust method or pre-computed gradients. # Gradient computation is not explicitly detailed in sources, # but shading requires it. dx = volume[np.clip(x+1, 0, shape[0]-1), y, z] - volume[np.clip(x-1, 0, shape[0]-1), y, z] dy = volume[x, np.clip(y+1, 0, shape[1]-1), z] - volume[x, np.clip(y-1, 0, shape[1]-1), z] dz = volume[x, y, np.clip(z+1, 0, shape[2]-1)] - volume[x, y, np.clip(z-1, 0, shape[2]-1)] return np.array([dx, dy, dz]) Subtopics: Digital Radiograph (DRR) Synthesis: A specific application of Van Hook-Levoy Ray-Casting in medical imaging, where the ray casting is used to project 3D CT data into 2D X-ray-like images. It requires strict coordinate system consistency using DICOM metadata. Feed-Forward vs. Feed-Backward: Van Hook-Levoy is a feed-backward method (ray from eye to volume), which enables early termination when opacity is 1. This contrasts with feed-forward methods which accumulate from the back. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the average number of samples per ray. With DDA, S is proportional to the number of voxels intersected by the ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, plus O(1) per ray for accumulators. Performance: Naive equidistant sampling is slow. Using DDA/Bresenham-like algorithms improves traversal efficiency. GPU implementation (e.g., CUDA) can achieve real-time performance (tens to hundreds of milliseconds) compared to seconds for CPU implementations. Strengths: Simple to implement; visualizes the entire volume; early termination optimization reduces computation for opaque regions. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-resolution volumes; requires careful handling of geometric transformations and boundary conditions to avoid artifacts. When to use: When direct visualization of internal structures is needed, and real-time performance is achievable via GPU acceleration. When not to use: When surface rendering is sufficient, or when hardware acceleration is unavailable and performance is critical. Origin: The method was published by Marc Levoy in 1988. Thomas Van Hook also explored the basic ray-casting model in 1986. History: It is one of the four main paradigms of volume rendering (along with splatting, shear-warp, and cell projection). GPU raycasting was later introduced by Kruger in 2003. Usage: Widely used in medical imaging for therapy planning and generating Digital Radiographs (DRR) from 3D CT data. 医疗影像开发实战:如何用光线投射算法快速生成DRR图像(附Python代码), https://un.csdn.net/98nhkcg5t04h, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A Parallel, Feed-Forward Volume Rendering Algorithm, https://www.cs.unc.edu/techreports/91-029.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Medical Volume Rendering Techniques, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.07710v1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) 14 Acceleration Techniques for Volume Rendering Mark W. name: Single-pass Raycasting
head: Direct Volume Rendering via Raycasting, Single Pass GPU Ray Casting, Single execution ray casting
body: Single-pass raycasting is a direct volume rendering technique that generates one ray per pixel, samples a 3D texture along the ray, and composites the results in a single GPU rendering pass to produce a 2D image. It distinguishes itself from multi-pass approaches by avoiding temporary framebuffers for intermediate ray results, thereby addressing the low efficiency of multi-pass pipelines on modern graphics hardware. Inputs: Volume Data: A 3D grid of scalar values loaded from a Uint16Array where the first three elements are dimensions (W, H, D) and the remaining elements are voxel values normalized by dividing by 4095.0. The data is stored in a THREE.Data3DTexture with format THREE.RedFormat, type THREE.FloatType, and linear filtering. Camera: Eye position and projection parameters. Lighting: Light position (often fixed at the camera position in basic implementations) and color. Parameters: Uniforms controlling rendering mode, thresholds, step size, and transfer functions. Outputs: 2D Image: A color buffer where each pixel contains the accumulated color and opacity from the ray traversal. The implementation relies on the following structures and uniforms: 1. Volume Texture (sampler3D volumedata): Dimensions: W \times H \times D. Coordinate space: Unit cube [0,1]^3. 2. Transfer Function Textures (sampler2D): Lookup tables for color and opacity based on density and gradient magnitude. Resolution controlled by TransferSize. 3. Ray Entry/Exit Textures (FBOs): Textures storing ray entry and exit positions for each fragment. Resolution controlled by FBOSize. 4. Uniforms: volumesize: vec3 containing the dimensions of the volume. rendermode: int (0 for First Hit, 1 for MIP). urenderthreshold: float iso-value threshold for First Hit mode. StepSize: float spatial distance between samples. MaxSamples: int limit on samples per ray. Minclip: float threshold to discard low-density samples. Apply Noise: bool toggle for stochastic ray shifting. GradDelta: vec3 offsets for gradient computation. Threshold (Shadows): float occlusion threshold for shadow rays. Quality (Shadows): int (0-100) controlling shadow ray sample count. 1. Initialization and Coordinate Transformation: Transform the camera eye position into the volume's unit cube space. The transformed eye position is calculated as: \text{transformed\eye} = \frac{\text{cameraPosition}}{\text{volume\size}} + (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) For each fragment (pixel), calculate the ray direction in unit cube space. The fragment position is normalized to [0,1]. The direction is: \vec{vray\dir} = \frac{\text{position}}{\text{volume\size}} + (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) - \text{transformed\eye} Note: In some implementations, ray entry and exit positions are pre-rendered to textures (FBOs) and looked up in the fragment shader to compute directions. 2. Ray-Box Intersection: Calculate the intersection of the view ray with the unit cube bounds [0,1]^3. If the ray does not intersect the cube (t{hit.x} > t{hit.y}), discard the fragment. Set the starting parameter t = \max(t{hit.x}, 0.0). 3. Step Size Calculation: Compute the step size dt to ensure consistent sampling relative to the grid: dt = \min \left( \frac{1}{W |vx|}, \frac{1}{H |vy|}, \frac{1}{D |vz|} \right) where \vec{v} = (vx, vy, vz) is the ray direction and W,H,D are volume dimensions. 4. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize accumulation variables: alpha = 0.0, color = (0,0,0). Initialize previous sample point pointN0 and value valueN0 at the start position. Iterate while t < t{hit.y} and sample count < MaxSamples: a. Stochastic Shifting: If Apply Noise is true, perturb the ray position slightly to reduce banding artifacts. b. Advance Ray: Calculate next position pointN1 = pointN0 + raydir dt. c. Sample Volume: Read value valueN1 = samplevolume(pointN1). d. Minclip Check: If valueN1 < Minclip, continue to next sample (discard). e. Mode-Specific Processing: First Hit Mode (rendermode == 0): If valueN1 > urenderthreshold: Interpolate to find the exact surface position t{surf} where the value equals the threshold: t{surf} = t - dt \cdot \frac{valueN1 - u\renderthreshold}{valueN1 - valueN0} Calculate the surface normal using central differences (gradient) at the surface point. Gradient computation uses offsets defined by GradDelta. Compute lighting (diffuse/specular) using the normal and light direction. Apply transfer function to map density to color. Set final pixel color to the lit surface color and break the loop. Else: Update valueN0 = valueN1, pointN0 = pointN1, t += dt. MIP Mode (rendermode == 1): Track the maximum value encountered along the ray. Update maxval = max(maxval, valueN1). Continue to next sample. After loop, apply transfer function to maxval to determine color. f. Shadow Rays (Optional): For each sample, cast a shadow ray towards the light source. Sample until density exceeds Threshold (Shadows). Number of samples controlled by Quality (Shadows). Modulate lighting based on occlusion. 5. Transfer Function Application: Map the final scalar value (surface value for First Hit, max value for MIP) to color and opacity using the transfer function lookup tables. The transfer function allows arbitrary modulation of density and gradient magnitude lookups. Default color mapping may use the Viridis colormap. 6. Compositing: In First Hit mode, the result is the color of the first surface hit. In MIP mode, the result is the color corresponding to the maximum intensity. Standard front-to-back alpha compositing is not explicitly detailed for the final pixel in the provided code snippets for First Hit/MIP modes, as they are "single hit" or "max" projections rather than volumetric integration. The provided code for First Hit breaks on hit, and MIP takes the max, implying no alpha blending accumulation in the loop for these specific modes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def singlepassraycasting(cameraposition, volumesize, position, rendermode, urenderthreshold, minclip, applynoise, graddelta, lightposition, shininess, lightcolor, ambient, samplevolume, applytransferfunction, intersectbox): # 1. Transform eye to unit cube space transformedeye = cameraposition / volumesize + vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) # 2. Calculate ray direction in unit cube space raydir = (position / volumesize) + vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) - transformedeye # 3. Intersect ray with unit cube [0,1]^3 thit = intersectbox(transformedeye, raydir) if thit[0] > thit[1]: return None # Discard tstart = max(thit[0], 0.0) # 4. Calculate step size dtvec = vec3(1.0) / (volumesize abs(raydir)) dt = min(dtvec[0], min(dtvec[1], dtvec[2])) # 5. Initialize variables alpha = 0.0 color = vec3(0.0) pointN0 = transformedeye + tstart raydir valueN0 = samplevolume(pointN0) maxval = float('-inf') # 6. Ray Marching Loop t = tstart while t < thit[1]: # Stochastic shifting if enabled if applynoise: pointN1 = pointN0 + raydir dt + vec3(random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5), random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5), random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5)) else: pointN1 = pointN0 + raydir dt valueN1 = samplevolume(pointN1) # Minclip check if valueN1 < minclip: valueN0 = valueN1 pointN0 = pointN1 t += dt continue if rendermode == 0: # First Hit if valueN1 > urenderthreshold: # Interpolate surface position linearinterpolation = (urenderthreshold - valueN0) / (valueN1 - valueN0) tsurf = t - dt linearinterpolation surfacepos = pointN0 + raydir (t - tsurf) # Calculate gradient for normal grad = computegradient(surfacepos, graddelta) normal = normalize(grad) # Lighting (single scattering model) lightdir = normalize(lightposition - surfacepos) diffuse = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) specular = pow(max(dot(reflect(-lightdir, normal), -raydir), 0.0), shininess) # Transfer function tfcolor = applytransferfunction(valueN1) color = tfcolor (ambient + diffuse lightcolor + specular lightcolor) break # Exit loop on first hit else: valueN0 = valueN1 pointN0 = pointN1 elif rendermode == 1: # MIP if valueN1 > maxval: maxval = valueN1 valueN0 = valueN1 pointN0 = pointN1 t += dt # 7. Final Output if rendermode == 1: color = applytransferfunction(maxval) return vec4(color, 1.0) StepSize: Controls spatial distance between samples. Higher values reduce quality but increase speed. MaxSamples: Limits the total number of samples per ray to prevent infinite loops or excessive computation. urenderthreshold: Iso-value threshold for First Hit rendering. Only values above this trigger surface detection. Minclip: Threshold below which samples are discarded (treated as empty). FBOSize: Resolution of textures storing ray entry/exit positions. TransferSize: Resolution of transfer function lookup textures. Apply Noise: Boolean to enable stochastic ray shifting, reducing banding artifacts. GradDelta: Offsets for finite difference gradient calculation. Threshold (Shadows): Density value for shadow ray occlusion. Quality (Shadows): Number of samples for shadow ray traversal (0-100). Data Loading: Volume data is often stored in a Uint16Array with the first 3 elements as dimensions. The voxel values must be normalized by dividing by 4095.0 to fit in the [0,1] range expected by the texture. Precision: High precision (highp float) is required in shaders to avoid artifacts in ray marching and interpolation. Banding Artifacts: Regular sampling can cause banding. Stochastic ray shifting (Apply Noise) is used to mitigate this. Memory Limits: Large volumes may exceed GPU texture memory. Hierarchical grid representations or out-of-core techniques are needed for very large datasets. What it is: A raycasting method that iterates over volume primitives (voxels) and projects them onto the screen, rather than iterating over pixels [Siblings]. Difference: Single-pass is image-order (pixel-driven), while Object-Order is primitive-driven. Object-order can be more efficient for sparse data but is harder to parallelize on GPUs compared to the regular access patterns of image-order raycasting [Siblings]. When to choose: Use when the volume is sparse or when primitive-level manipulation is required. Single-pass is preferred for dense, regular grids on GPUs [Siblings]. Link: Object-Order Ray-Casting What it is: A method or parameterization technique related to controlling brightness and contrast in raycasting [Siblings]. Difference: Single-pass is a rendering pipeline strategy. RaycastBrightnessControl likely refers to a specific shading or transfer function adjustment technique applied within a raycasting framework [Siblings]. When to choose: Use when fine-tuning the visual appearance (brightness/contrast) of the raycast output is the primary goal. Link: RaycastBrightnessControl Time Complexity: O(P \cdot S), where P is the number of pixels and S is the number of samples per ray. Shadow rays add a factor of S{shadow} per sample. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume texture, where V is the number of voxels. Additional memory for FBOs and transfer functions. Performance: Single-pass solutions are more efficient than multi-pass approaches on modern GPUs because they avoid the overhead of rendering to and reading from temporary framebuffers. Strengths: High flexibility (custom shaders), real-time potential on capable hardware, accurate lighting and transfer functions. Limitations: Performance degrades with high resolution, large volumes, or complex lighting (shadow rays). Memory bound for very large volumes. When to use: Real-time visualization of moderate-sized volumes, interactive exploration, spectral DVR. When not to use: Extremely large volumes that do not fit in GPU memory without hierarchical streaming, or when offline, high-quality volume rendering is required (where path tracing or other offline methods might be better). Origin: The concept of single-pass GPU raycasting was developed to address the inefficiencies of multi-pass rendering pipelines on graphics hardware. Key Contributors: Stegmaier and colleagues extended the framework to spectral DVR using Kubelka–Munk theory. Hadwiger et al. used single-pass raycasting for implicit isosurfaces on rectilinear grids. Roettger et al. built a real-time raycaster with adaptive pre-integrated voxel classification. History: Early GPU-based solutions relied on multiple rendering passes. Single-pass techniques emerged to improve efficiency and flexibility. Usage: Used in VStudio as the primary direct volume rendering method. Extended for spectral DVR. name: Object-Order Ray-Casting
head: Data-parallel volume rendering
body: Object-order ray-casting is a volume rendering technique that transforms the volumetric data to align with the view direction prior to ray-casting, such that resample locations coincide with integer grid points. It combines the speed advantages of object-order methods (optimized volume run, easy space leaping) with the high-quality image generation of ray-casting (trilinear interpolation). Unlike image-order ray-casting, which is slow due to cache misses from irregular voxel access, or Shear-Warp, which introduces artifacts and blurring, this method maintains interactive frame rates (up to 10 fps) while preserving image quality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset V of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz, a view direction, and an orthogonal projection matrix. Output: A 2D image (frame buffer) with accumulated color and opacity values for each pixel. Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D array of scalar values representing density or intensity. Frame Buffer: A 2D array storing accumulated color C and opacity \alpha for each pixel, initialized to (0, 0). Method Steps: 1. Transformation Decomposition: Decompose the transformation from the volume's local coordinate system to the view-aligned coordinate system into a set of affine transforms requiring shear/scale operations along orthogonal axes. 2. Resampling: Perform resampling of the volume using the decomposed affine transforms to generate regular data access to voxels. This ensures that resample locations coincide with integer grid points in the transformed space. 3. Ray-Cell Intersection and Sampling: For every cell that has to be rendered (i.e., not transparent and not hidden), load the values and gradients of the 8 vertices. Determine the rays intersecting the cell; in the transformed space, these rays are aligned with the grid axes, simplifying intersection tests. For each intersecting ray, sample colors Cs and opacities \alphas along the ray within the cell using trilinear interpolation. 4. Compositing: Update the frame buffer for the pixels corresponding to the intersected rays. The compositing follows the front-to-back accumulation model defined by Kajiya's low albedo form. Formulas: The underlying optical model is Kajiya's low albedo form: I\lambda = \int0^t C\lambda(s) \times \tau(s) \times \exp\left(-\int0^s \tau(t) \, dt\right) ds \quad (1) Where: I\lambda: Light intensity of wavelength \lambda reaching the viewpoint. C\lambda(s): Color contribution at position s. \tau(s): Extinction coefficient at position s. t: Total length of the ray through the volume. This integral is approximated using a Riemann sum with even sampling distance \Delta s. The accumulated color C{i+1} and opacity \alpha{i+1} are updated recursively in front-to-back order using the sampled color Cs and opacity \alphas at step i: C{i+1} = Ci + (1-\alphai) \alphas Cs \quad (2) \alpha{i+1} = \alphai + (1 - \alphai) \alphas \quad (3) Where: Ci, \alphai: Accumulated color and opacity before step i. Cs, \alphas: Sampled color and opacity at step i. \Delta s: Sampling distance. Parameters: Sampling Distance (\Delta s): Critical for quality vs. speed trade-off. Large \Delta s accelerates rendering but produces low-quality images. Target Performance: Up to 10 frames per second on current workstations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def objectorderraycasting(volume, viewtransform, framebuffer, deltas): # Initialize frame buffer accumulators to zero for y in range(framebuffer.height): for x in range(framebuffer.width): framebuffer[x, y].color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) framebuffer[x, y].opacity = 0.0 # Iterate over all cells in the volume for z in range(volume.depth - 1): for y in range(volume.height - 1): for x in range(volume.width - 1): cell = volume.getcell(x, y, z) if cell.istransparent(): continue if cell.ishidden(viewtransform): continue # Load 8 vertex values vertices = cell.getvertexvalues() # Ray direction in transformed space (aligned with grid axes) raydir = viewtransform.getaxisdirection() # Compute ray entry and exit points for this cell tmin, tmax = cell.computeintersection(raydir) # Step along the ray within the cell t = tmin while t < tmax: # Sample position in transformed space samplepos = cell.origin + t raydir # Trilinear interpolation of color and opacity cs, as = trilinearinterpolate(volume, samplepos, vertices) # Project to pixel coordinates px, py = viewtransform.project(samplepos) if not framebuffer.inbounds(px, py): t += deltas continue # Front-to-back compositing pixel = framebuffer[px, py] ci, ai = pixel.color, pixel.opacity # Kajiya's low albedo form approximation newalpha = ai + (1.0 - ai) as newcolor = ci + (1.0 - ai) as cs pixel.color = newcolor pixel.opacity = newalpha t += deltas def trilinearinterpolate(volume, pos, vertices): # Standard trilinear interpolation using 8 vertex values # Returns sampled color and opacity # Implementation details omitted for brevity; standard graphics operation pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sampling Distance: Large \Delta s leads to low-quality images. Cache Misses: Image-order ray-casting suffers from cache misses because every ray step loads eight samples for trilinear interpolation, which cannot be stored in memory order. Object-order ray-casting avoids this by accessing voxels a limited number of times. Hidden Volume Removal: Object-order methods traditionally struggle with skipping empty regions, especially with interactive classification. An efficient hidden volume removal technique is required to compensate for the loss of early ray termination inherent in image-order algorithms. Time Complexity: The method aims for interactive performance, targeting up to 10 fps on current workstations. In a two-pass implementation, it achieved approximately 3 fps on a 256^3 bonsai dataset. Memory Complexity: Depends on the volume size and the frame buffer. Strengths: Combines speed of object-order methods (optimized volume run, easy space leaping) with high-quality image generation of ray-casting (trilinear interpolation). Avoids cache misses associated with image-order ray-casting. Avoids low sampling rates on the z-axis (1 to 1.73), pre-classification blurring, and artifacts at 45-degree viewing angles associated with Shear-Warp. Avoids blurring of small details inherent to Gaussian low-pass filters in Splatting. Limitations: Requires efficient hidden volume removal to compensate for the loss of early ray termination. Accuracy depends critically on the sampling distance \Delta s and the evaluation of sampled values. When to Use: When high-quality interactive volume rendering is required, and the hardware supports efficient 3D resampling and orthogonal projection. When Not to Use: When early ray termination is critical and hidden volume removal is not efficiently implemented, or when the view direction changes frequently and the transformation overhead is prohibitive. Object-order ray-casting was introduced as an efficient and accurate volume rendering technique to overcome the limitations of existing methods. It was developed to achieve interactive high-quality rendering (up to 10 fps) on workstations. The method builds on the idea that the projection of a parallelepipedic shape can be efficiently performed under orthogonal projection, enabling object-order traversal while maintaining ray-casting quality. It is also known as data-parallel volume rendering because operations on the volume semantically involve all voxels at once. The technique has been implemented in hardware architectures like VIRIM, which uses lookup tables for interpolation and programmable lighting/viewing parameters.
