name: RaycastBrightnessControl
head: RaycastColorControl
body: RaycastBrightnessControl is a back-to-front direct volume raycasting technique that modulates voxel brightness based on a threshold parameter. It renders back-facing polygons to sample from the furthest voxels first, distinguishing it from front-to-back methods. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume texture, camera position (eye.xyz), fragment position (fragment.xyz), scalar valthreshold, and step size SAMPLESTEP. Output: A 2D color buffer. Data Structures: The volume is stored in a 3D texture. The fragment shader receives interpolated screen coordinates and uniform camera data. Steps: 1. Render the volume bounding box using back-facing polygons only to ensure sampling starts at the furthest entry point relative to the camera. 2. Compute the ray direction vector \vec{d} in the fragment shader: \vec{d} = \text{eye.xyz} - \text{fragment.xyz}. 3. March along \vec{d} with a fixed step size SAMPLESTEP. 4. At each step, sample the scalar value v from the volume texture. 5. Apply valthreshold to modulate the voxel's brightness contribution. 6. Accumulate the result back-to-front and output the final color. Parameters: valthreshold: Controls the brightness of the voxels. SAMPLESTEP: Controls ray-advancement precision; smaller values improve quality but increase rendering time. Pitfalls: Requires back-facing polygon rendering; using front-facing polygons requires inverting the ray direction to fragment.xyz - eye.xyz and switching to front-to-back marching. The exact transfer function mapping v and valthreshold to brightness is not specified in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastbrightnesscontrol(eye, fragmentpos, volumetexture, valthreshold, samplestep, maxsteps): raydir = (eye[0] - fragmentpos[0], eye[1] - fragmentpos[1], eye[2] - fragmentpos[2]) length = (raydir[0]2 + raydir[1]2 + raydir[2]2)0.5 stepvec = (raydir[0]/length samplestep, raydir[1]/length samplestep, raydir[2]/length samplestep) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] currentpos = (fragmentpos[0] + stepvec[0], fragmentpos[1] + stepvec[1], fragmentpos[2] + stepvec[2]) for in range(maxsteps): if not (0.0 <= currentpos[0] <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= currentpos[1] <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= currentpos[2] <= 1.0): break v = volumetexture[currentpos] brightness = v if v > valthreshold else 0.0 accumulatedcolor[0] += brightness accumulatedcolor[1] += brightness accumulatedcolor[2] += brightness currentpos = (currentpos[0] + stepvec[0], currentpos[1] + stepvec[1], currentpos[2] + stepvec[2]) return accumulatedcolor A back-to-front raycasting technique using the fragment shader volumeraycast02.fs. It uses valthreshold to control the density of the voxels. It requires back-facing polygon rendering and computes the ray direction as eye.xyz - fragment.xyz. Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray, determined by volume depth and SAMPLESTEP. Memory complexity is dominated by 3D volume texture storage. Smaller SAMPLESTEP improves quality but increases rendering time. Strengths include simple implementation for visualizing brightness variations. Limitations include the requirement for back-facing polygon rendering and the unspecified exact transfer function. name: VCP Ray-Casting Algorithm
head: Vector-to-Closest-Point Ray Casting
body: The VCP Ray-Casting Algorithm renders a smooth surface approximation from a dense point cloud by storing vector-valued data in a grid structure, rather than rendering discrete points or scalar distance fields directly. It solves the problem of noisy rendering caused by sensor noise and calibration errors in real-world LiDAR data, where points do not strictly lie on the scene surface. Unlike standard closest-point ray casting which selects the single nearest point (z-buffer), VCP uses the length of an interpolated vector to determine step sizes and the vector direction as the surface normal, allowing for adaptive marching and smooth shading. Inputs and Outputs Input: A VCP grid where each block stores either a scalar distance d{empty} (empty block) or a 3D vector \vec{V} (non-empty block). Input: Camera ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and threshold \epsilon > 0. Output: Pixel color and surface normal at the intersection point. Data Structures The VCP grid stores per block: 1. Empty Block: Stores a scalar distance d{empty} representing the distance from the block center to the nearest surface point. 2. Non-Empty Block: Stores a 3D vector \vec{V} = (Vx, Vy, Vz) pointing from the block center to the closest surface point; its length |\vec{V}| is the distance to the surface. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray-AABB Intersection: Compute entry t{near} and exit t{far} where the ray intersects the volume bounding box. 2. Adaptive Marching: Initialize t = t{near}. At each sampling position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, query the grid. If the block is empty, read d = d{empty}. If non-empty, interpolate \vec{V} from neighboring blocks and compute d = |\vec{V}|. 3. Step & Termination: If d < \epsilon, assume a ray-surface intersection. Otherwise, use d as the step size \Delta t = d / |\mathbf{d}| (assuming unit direction, \Delta t = d) and advance t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. 4. Intersection Refinement: When d < \epsilon, interpolate linearly between the previous sampling position \mathbf{p}{prev} (where distance was d{prev} \ge \epsilon) and the current position \mathbf{p}{curr} to find \mathbf{p}{hit} where the distance equals exactly \epsilon. 5. Normal & Lighting: The surface normal \mathbf{n} at \mathbf{p}{hit} is the normalized interpolated VCP vector \vec{V} / |\vec{V}|. Evaluate a local lighting model using \mathbf{n} to compute the final pixel color. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vcpraycasting(rayorigin, raydir, vcpgrid, epsilon): # 1. Intersect ray with AABB tnear, tfar = intersectaabb(rayorigin, raydir, vcpgrid.bboxmin, vcpgrid.bboxmax) if tnear > tfar: return None t = tnear pprev = add(rayorigin, scale(raydir, t)) dprev, vprev = samplevcpgrid(pprev, vcpgrid) while t < tfar: pcurr = add(rayorigin, scale(raydir, t)) dcurr, vcurr = samplevcpgrid(pcurr, vcpgrid) if dcurr < epsilon: # 4. Refine intersection if dprev == dcurr: phit = pcurr else: lam = (dprev - epsilon) / (dprev - dcurr) phit = add(pprev, scale(sub(pcurr, pprev), lam)) # Normal is normalized VCP vector at hit point, vhit = samplevcpgrid(phit, vcpgrid) normal = normalize(vhit) # Lighting model lightdir = normalize(vec(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) color = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdir)) return color # 3. Advance using distance as step size step = dcurr pprev = pcurr dprev = dcurr t += step return None def intersectaabb(origin, direction, bboxmin, bboxmax): tmin = sub(bboxmin, origin) / direction tmax = sub(bboxmax, origin) / direction t1 = compmin(tmin, tmax) t2 = compmax(tmin, tmax) return max(t1), min(t2) def samplevcpgrid(p, grid): # Query block containing p. If empty, return scalar distance dempty. # If non-empty, return length |V| and vector V from trilinear interpolation. # Grid traversal details depend on sparse/uniform layout pass # The sources do not specify the exact block lookup or interpolation implementation. def vec(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def add(a, b): return (a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]) def sub(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) def scale(v, s): return (v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def norm(v): return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 def normalize(v): n = norm(v); return (v[0]/n, v[1]/n, v[2]/n) def compmin(a, b): return tuple(min(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b)) def compmax(a, b): return tuple(max(x, y) for x, y in zip(a, b)) def max(a, b): return a if a > b else b def min(a, b): return a if a < b else b Parameters \epsilon: Threshold for surface intersection. Decreasing \epsilon allows the rendered surface to come arbitrarily close to the exact surface. Typical value: Not given in the sources. FPA is a variant used in LiDAR rendering (e.g., PCGen) to handle noise where points do not strictly lie on the surface. Instead of selecting the single closest point (standard CP ray-casting), FPA averages multiple points within a certain distance threshold near the closest point, weighting them by their inverse distance. This reduces noise in the rendered range image. It is often combined with a Ray-drop MLP to model return probability p = MLP(\theta', d, i), where \theta' is the viewing direction, d is distance, and i is intensity. The MLP has 4 layers, width 128, trained with Adam (lr 5e-3) for 10k iterations. Time Complexity: Depends on the density of the point cloud and the step size; adaptive stepping can skip empty space, potentially speeding up rendering compared to fixed-step ray casting. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the VCP grid. Strengths: Produces smooth surfaces from noisy point clouds; provides explicit surface normals for lighting; adaptive stepping allows efficient traversal of empty space. Limitations: Accuracy depends on the choice of \epsilon. When to use: When rendering surfaces from dense, noisy LiDAR point clouds where smooth shading and normals are required. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The VCP (Vector-to-Closest-Point) method was introduced in the paper "Vector-to-Closest-Point Octree for Surface Ray-Casting". It addresses the limitations of standard closest-point ray casting, which is sensitive to noise and produces jagged surfaces. The method uses a grid structure to store vector data, allowing for efficient ray traversal and smooth surface reconstruction. It has been applied in computer graphics for surface rendering from point clouds. name: Hardware-Based Volume Ray Casting with Early Termination and Z-Updates
head: Cell-Projection based Ray Casting, Hardware-Based Ray Casting
body: This method is a hardware-accelerated technique for volume rendering that exploits programmable graphics features, specifically early z-tests and occlusion queries, to manage ray traversal and termination efficiently. It differs from software ray casting by leveraging rasterization hardware to reduce fragment operations, though it introduces more complex rasterization logic. The method uses a loop of traversal and z-update passes to advance rays through the volume data. It relies on a specific cell index value to manage state and termination. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data, ray traversal parameters, and current depth buffer state. Output: Final rendered image stored in texture set 0. Data Structures: Current Cell Index: An integer value associated with each ray or fragment. A value of -1 indicates an "imaginary cell," used to signal reentries or termination conditions. Depth Buffer: Stores depth values to facilitate early z-testing. Color Buffer: Stores the accumulated color for each ray. Parameters: Current Cell Index: -1 is the sentinel value for imaginary cells. Comparison Function: GLLESS (or equivalent) for early z-tests. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Set up the first traversal pass and ensure the final result is stored in texture set 0. 2. Traversal Pass: For each fragment, determine the current cell index. Use an early z-test (GLLESS) to stop fragment processing for rays that have already been terminated or occluded. If the current cell index equals -1, write znear to the depth buffer and copy the current accumulated color into the result buffer. Update the ray position and cell index based on neighbor cell data. 3. Z-Update Pass: Perform a z-update pass to update the depth buffer. Only perform z-update passes after even traversal passes (i.e., after 2, 4, 6... traversal passes) to ensure correct state synchronization. 4. Termination Check: Use DirectX 9 occlusion queries (or equivalent) to determine when rendering is complete. Check if any pixels are still set. Do not wait for the asynchronous delivery of occlusion query results to avoid pipeline stalls; proceed based on the assumption that rendering is complete when no pixels are set. 5. Repeat: Continue the loop of traversal and z-update passes until the termination condition is met. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolume(volumedata, rayparams, depthbuffer, colorbuffer): currentcellindex = [0] len(rayparams) iscomplete = False traversalcount = 0 while not iscomplete: # Traversal pass for i in range(len(rayparams)): # Early z-test (GLLESS) stops processing for occluded/terminated rays if depthbuffer[i] < rayparams.znear[i]: continue if currentcellindex[i] == -1: # Imaginary cell handling: reentry or termination depthbuffer[i] = rayparams.znear[i] colorbuffer[i] = colorbuffer[i] # Copy accumulated color to result buffer else: # Update ray position and cell index from neighbor cell data pass traversalcount += 1 # Z-update pass: only after even traversal passes if traversalcount % 2 == 0: # Synchronize depth buffer state pass # Termination check via occlusion query # Do not wait for asynchronous delivery; assume complete when no pixels set if not any(depthbuffer[i] != rayparams.znear[i] for i in range(len(rayparams))): iscomplete = True # Final result is always stored in texture set 0 return colorbuffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Imaginary Cells: The use of -1 for cell index requires careful handling to distinguish between reentry and termination. Synchronization: Z-updates must only occur after even traversal passes to maintain correct state. Asynchronous Stalls: Waiting for occlusion query results can cause pipeline stalls. The method avoids this by assuming completion when no pixels are set. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Benefits from a reduced number of fragment operations due to early ray termination, space leaping, and adaptive sampling. Strengths: Leverages hardware features for efficiency and reduces fragment processing overhead. Limitations: Rasterization logic is more complex than software ray casting. The overhead of additional rendering passes is considered negligible. This method was introduced by Manfred Weiler, M. Kraus, M. Merz, and T. Ertl in the paper "Hardware-Based Ray Casting for Tetrahedral Meshes" presented at IEEE Visualization 2003. It is part of the broader effort to accelerate volume rendering using programmable graphics hardware, building upon earlier work such as "Hardware-Accelerated Volume and Isosurface Rendering Based On Cell-Projection" by Röttger et al. (2000). Hardware-Based Volume Ray Casting, https://doi.org/10.2312/egt.20031107, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Volume Raycasting (Ray Driven)
head: Basic Ray Casting, Ray Driven Ray Casting
body: Volume Raycasting (Ray Driven) is a direct volume rendering method that samples along rays through the entire dataset to render three-dimensional scalar fields. It differs from splatting by accumulating samples interpolated between voxels surrounding the ray. While it builds on the standard front-to-back compositing of Standard Ray Casting, this specific implementation variant is characterized by its simplicity, sometimes omitting interpolation in favor of direct voxel access, and supporting specific modes like limited depth raycasting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume V, camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), and rendering mode (Basic or Limited Depth). Output: A 2D image with accumulated color and opacity per pixel. Data Structures: Volume: A 3D array of scalar values. The non-interpolated implementation accesses voxel values directly without interpolation. Ray: Defined by entry t{near} and exit t{far} bounds within the volume bounding box. Steps: 1. Prefiltering: Apply a threshold and cutoff limit to the volume data. Voxels with values exceeding the cutoff limit are replaced with zeros (black) to eliminate reconstruction noise. 2. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, define the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and compute intersection with the volume bounding box to find t{near} and t{far}. 3. Sampling and Compositing: Iterate along the ray from t{near} to t{far}. If Basic Mode is selected, cast all voxels along the ray trace. If Limited Depth Mode is selected, start raycasting with a voxel value threshold condition. The ray continues only up to the selected depth where the condition is met, resulting in a partially transparent model. Retrieve the scalar value V(\mathbf{p}i) at the current sample position. Map V(\mathbf{p}i) to color \mathbf{c}i and opacity \alphai using a transfer function. Composite using the front-to-back equation: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai 4. Post-filtering: Apply gamma correction and saturation level to the final image. Optionally disable automatic white level control for manual white level, or invert the image. Parameters: Cutoff limit: Threshold for prefiltering noise. Depth threshold: Condition for stopping ray in Limited Depth mode. Gamma: Post-processing gamma correction value. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Basic Mode Transparency: In Basic mode, casting all voxels along the ray trace results in a fully transparent model. Bounding Box: Reducing the bounding area may increase performance but risks clipping valid data if not aligned with the volume extent. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeraycasting(volume, cameraorigin, cameradirection, volumebounds, mode, cutoffthreshold, depththreshold, gamma): # Initialize output image with zeros image = zeroslike(cameraimageshape) # Pre-filter volume: replace values exceeding cutoff with zero volumefiltered = where(volume > cutoffthreshold, 0, volume) for each pixel (x, y): rayo = cameraorigin(x, y) rayd = cameradirection(x, y) tnear, tfar = intersectbox(rayo, rayd, volumebounds) Cacc = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) alphaacc = 0.0 t = tnear # Step size not given in sources; typically derived from ray length and sample count dt = (tfar - tnear) / samplecount while t < tfar: p = rayo + t rayd v = samplevolume(volumefiltered, p) if mode == "limiteddepth" and v < depththreshold: break c, alpha = transferfunction(v) Cacc = Cacc + (1.0 - alphaacc) c alpha alphaacc = alphaacc + (1.0 - alphaacc) alpha t += dt image[x, y] = applypostfilter(Cacc, gamma) return image Time Complexity: O(n^3) for an n \times n \times n volume, as it requires sampling along rays through the entire dataset. Memory: Large volumes demand substantial storage; a 512^3 dataset requires ~0.5 GB for 32-bit precision. Performance: Rendering a 256^3 volume at 1080p can achieve interactive frame rates (20–60 fps) on modern GPUs with optimized pipelines. Strengths: Simple implementation; effective for viewing 3D volumes without external tools. Limitations: High computational cost for large volumes; undersampling leads to aliasing and blur. Origin: The ray casting model was introduced by Levoy in 1988. Development: It is a fundamental technique in volume rendering, often contrasted with splatting [Westover89]. Usage: Used in various visualization tools, including custom implementations to avoid dependencies on external software like 3D Slicer. A broader category that may include optimizations and variations. A specific optimized ray-casting algorithm. name: Front-to-Back Ray Casting with Iso-value Thresholding
head: RayCastSimplePS, Simple Volume Ray Casting, Standard Ray Casting with Iso-value Thresholding
body: Front-to-Back Ray Casting with Iso-value Thresholding is a direct volume rendering technique that accumulates color and opacity along a ray, but restricts contribution to samples where the scalar density exceeds a specific iso-value threshold. Unlike standard ray casting which blends all samples, this method acts as a hard or soft filter, rendering only structures above the threshold. It differs from Volume Ray Casting by explicitly enforcing a density cutoff before compositing, and from VCP Ray-Casting Algorithm by using a simpler, fixed-step sampling loop rather than variable-step traversal. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scalar volume texture V, a 1D transfer function texture T, 2D precomputed front/back intersection textures F and B, camera parameters (pixel position, ray direction), and rendering parameters: IsoValue, SampleDist, Iterations. Output: Final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out}. Data Structures 1. Volume Texture (V): 3D texture. Linear filtering. Border address mode with border color (1, 0, 0, 1). 2. Transfer Function Texture (T): 1D texture. Linear filtering. Clamp address mode. Maps scalar density to (\mathbf{c}, \alpha). 3. Front/Back Textures (F, B): 2D textures. Linear filtering. Border address mode with border color (0, 0, 0, 0). Store the entry and exit points of the ray through the volume bounding box for each pixel. 4. Accumulators: \mathbf{C}{acc} (RGB) and \alpha{acc} (A), initialized to (0, 0). Parameters IsoValue: The threshold density value. Typical value: 0.0 (compared against value.a 255.0). SampleDist: Distance between samples along the ray. Typical value: 0.5. Iterations: Maximum number of samples per ray. BaseSampleDist: Reference sample distance used for opacity correction. Not given in the sources. ActualSampleDist: The actual physical distance between samples, derived from SampleDist and view geometry. Not given in the sources. Steps 1. Ray Setup: For each pixel, retrieve the front intersection point \mathbf{p}{front} from F and the back intersection point \mathbf{p}{back} from B using projective texture coordinates. 2. Direction Calculation: Compute the normalized ray direction \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}{back} - \mathbf{p}{front}). 3. Initialization: Set current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p}{front}, accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc} = (0, 0, 0), and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0. Compute step vector \mathbf{s} = \mathbf{d} \cdot \text{SampleDist}. 4. Sampling Loop: For i = 0 to \text{Iterations} - 1: a. Sample Volume: Retrieve the scalar value v from the volume texture at position \mathbf{p}: v = \text{tex3Dlod}(V, \mathbf{p}). b. Threshold Check: If v.a \cdot 255.0 < \text{IsoValue}, skip blending for this step and proceed to step 4d. c. Transfer Function: Sample the transfer function using the density value: \mathbf{src} = \text{tex1Dlod}(T, v.a). d. Opacity Correction: Adjust the sampled opacity \mathbf{src}.a to account for the sampling distance: \mathbf{src}.a = 1 - |1 - \mathbf{src}.a|^{\frac{\text{ActualSampleDist}}{\text{BaseSampleDist}}}. e. Front-to-Back Blending: Update accumulators: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{src}.rgb \cdot \mathbf{src}.a + \mathbf{C}{acc} \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{src}.a. f. Advance Position: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{s}. g. Termination: If \alpha{acc} \ge 0.95 or \mathbf{p} exceeds the unit cube bounds (\mathbf{p}.x > 1.0, \mathbf{p}.y > 1.0, \mathbf{p}.z > 1.0), break the loop. 5. Output: Return \mathbf{C}{acc} and \alpha{acc} as the final pixel color and opacity. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpixelfronttobackisothreshold(pixelpos, volumetex, transfertex, fronttex, backtex, isovalue, sampledist, iterations, basesampledist): # 1. Ray Setup # Calculate projective texture coordinates texc = pixelpos.xy / pixelpos.w texc.x = 0.5 texc.x + 0.5 texc.y = -0.5 texc.y + 0.5 # Retrieve front and back intersection points frontpoint = fronttex.samplelinear(texc).xyz backpoint = backtex.samplelinear(texc).xyz # 2. Direction Calculation raydir = normalize(backpoint - frontpoint) # 3. Initialization currentpos = frontpoint acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 stepvec = raydir sampledist # 4. Sampling Loop for i in range(iterations): # a. Sample Volume # Note: tex3Dlod expects normalized coordinates or specific format depending on implementation. # Assuming currentpos is already in the correct coordinate space for the texture. sampleval = volumetex.samplelevellinear(currentpos, 0) density = sampleval.a # b. Threshold Check if density 255.0 < isovalue: # Skip blending currentpos += stepvec continue # c. Transfer Function srcrgba = transfertex.samplelevellinear(density, 0) srccolor = srcrgba.rgb srcalpha = srcrgba.a # d. Opacity Correction # ActualSampleDist and BaseSampleDist are assumed to be available or derived # For simplicity, assuming ActualSampleDist == sampledist if not provided actualsampledist = sampledist correctionfactor = actualsampledist / basesampledist srcalpha = 1.0 - abs(1.0 - srcalpha) correctionfactor # e. Front-to-Back Blending # dst = (1.0 - dst.a) src + dst acccolor = (1.0 - accalpha) srccolor srcalpha + acccolor accalpha = accalpha + (1.0 - accalpha) srcalpha # f. Advance Position currentpos += stepvec # g. Termination if accalpha >= 0.95: break if currentpos.x > 1.0 or currentpos.y > 1.0 or currentpos.z > 1.0: break return acccolor, accalpha Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The opacity correction formula uses absolute values and powers, which can introduce numerical instability if \mathbf{src}.a is very close to 1 or 0. Boundaries: The termination condition checks against the unit cube bounds (1.0). If the volume bounding box is not normalized to [0,1]^3, this check will fail to terminate rays correctly. Thresholding: If the IsoValue is set too high, no samples may contribute, resulting in a black image. If set too low, the method degrades to standard ray casting. Sampling Distance: The opacity correction requires BaseSampleDist. If this parameter is not provided or mismatched with SampleDist, the resulting opacity will be incorrect, leading to over- or under-saturation. The general category of casting rays and accumulating color. This method is a specific implementation using iso-thresholding. Simple Volume Ray Casting Uses variable step sizes and more complex traversal. Choose this for higher performance on sparse volumes. VCP Ray-Casting Algorithm A broader term for ray-driven rendering. This method is a specific ray-driven approach with fixed steps. Volume Raycasting (Ray Driven) Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of iterations (samples) per ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for accumulators, plus storage for textures. Performance: The method is computationally intensive due to the fixed number of iterations and texture lookups per sample. The threshold check can skip blending, but sampling and transfer function lookup still occur. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective for isolating specific structures within a volume. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or missed features if not tuned; opacity correction requires careful parameter tuning. When to Use: When the goal is to visualize only high-density structures (e.g., bones in CT scans) and performance is not the primary constraint. When Not to Use: When the volume has low contrast or when smooth, semi-transparent visualization of all structures is required. The technique is described in early online resources as a "reasonable introduction to simple raycasting". It is implemented in the Digital Volume Library (DVL) by Mihai Popescu, which uses cubic splines for transfer functions and a fixed-step ray casting loop with iso-value thresholding. The method is often cited in the context of simple volume rendering tutorials. name: Block-based Volume Rendering
head: Independent block rendering, Resource-independent volume rendering
body: Block-based volume rendering divides a scene into independent blocks, renders each block separately, and blends the results. It solves the problem of resource isolation in distributed or web-based rendering environments where multiple shaders cannot communicate or share intermediate state. Unlike methods that integrate all samples globally before deferred processing (e.g., MERF), this method uses segmented integration followed by inter-block blending, ensuring seamless boundaries and correct occlusion without requiring global synchronization. The method decomposes a ray traversal into two phases: intra-block rendering and inter-block compositing. It assumes a hierarchical representation of the scene with L Levels of Detail (LODs), where 2\times2 blocks are merged into one block between consecutive LODs l \in \{1, \dots, L\}. Inputs: Ray r(t) defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Scene representation: A set of K blocks intersected by the ray. Each block k contains Nk sample points. Per-sample data for block k: diffuse color \boldsymbol{c}i^k, specular feature \boldsymbol{f}i^k, and opacity \alphai^k for i=1 \dots Nk. These are retrieved from baked sparse voxel or triplane textures via an attribute query function f^{k,l}. Optional: A tiny deferred MLP \Phi^{k,l} for view-dependent effects and a proposal MLP \psi^{k,l} for sampling. Outputs: Final ray color \boldsymbol{C}(r), composed of diffuse color \boldsymbol{C}d(r) and specular feature \boldsymbol{F}(r). Data Structures: Block: A spatial partition of the volume. In hierarchical LODs, block size increases with LOD level l. Sample Point: Contains scalar opacity \alpha and vector attributes (color/feature). Algorithm Steps: 1. Intra-block Rendering: For each block k intersected by the ray, perform standard front-to-back volume rendering over its Nk samples to compute the block's aggregate properties. Calculate block diffuse color \boldsymbol{C}d^k: \boldsymbol{C}d^k = \sum{i=1}^{Nk} \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj^k) \right) \alphai^k \boldsymbol{c}i^k Calculate block specular feature \boldsymbol{F}^k: \boldsymbol{F}^k = \sum{i=1}^{Nk} \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj^k) \right) \alphai^k \boldsymbol{f}i^k Calculate block opacity \alpha^k: \alpha^k = \sum{i=1}^{Nk} \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj^k) \right) \alphai^k Note: The block opacity is equivalent to the product of individual transmittances: 1 - \alpha^k = \prod{i=1}^{Nk} (1 - \alphai^k) 2. Inter-block Compositing: Depth-sort the K blocks along the ray from near to far. Blend the results of the blocks using the standard volume rendering equation, treating each block's aggregate opacity \alpha^k as a single "super-sample". Calculate final diffuse color: \boldsymbol{C}d(r) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \left( \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alpha^j) \right) \boldsymbol{C}d^k Calculate final specular feature: \boldsymbol{F}(r) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \left( \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alpha^j) \right) \boldsymbol{F}^k The final color \boldsymbol{C}(r) combines these components, potentially applying the deferred MLP \Phi if view-dependent effects are required. Pseudocode: def blockbasedvolumerendering(ray, blocks): """ ray: object with origin, direction, and intersection range [tnear, tfar] blocks: list of Block objects intersected by the ray, sorted by distance from camera """ # Initialize accumulators for the final ray accdiffuse = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accspecular = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accopacity = 0.0 # Transmittance from previous blocks (initially 1.0, meaning no occlusion yet) transmittance = 1.0 for block in blocks: # Step 1: Intra-block rendering blockdiffuse = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] blockspecular = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] blockopacity = 0.0 blocktransmittance = 1.0 # Iterate through samples within this block for sample in block.samples: alpha = sample.opacity cdiffuse = sample.diffusecolor fspecular = sample.specularfeature # Contribution of this sample to the block's aggregates contribution = blocktransmittance alpha blockdiffuse += contribution cdiffuse blockspecular += contribution fspecular blockopacity += contribution # Update block transmittance for next sample blocktransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Step 2: Inter-block blending # Blend the block's result into the ray using the ray's current transmittance accdiffuse += transmittance blockdiffuse accspecular += transmittance blockspecular accopacity += transmittance blockopacity # Update ray transmittance for next block transmittance = (1.0 - blockopacity) # Combine diffuse and specular components for final color finalcolor = accdiffuse + accspecular return finalcolor, accopacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ordering: Blocks must be strictly depth-sorted along the ray to ensure correct occlusion at inter-block edges. Lambertian Assumption: The equivalence to traditional volume rendering (where segmented integration equals global integration) holds strictly under Lambertian surface conditions where specular color is zero. Training/Rendering Consistency: To avoid discrepancies between training and inference, the same block-based pipeline must be used during training as during rendering. A specific implementation variant that emphasizes the blending mechanism across block boundaries. It ensures seamless boundaries and correct occlusion at inter-block edges, avoiding seams caused by simple averaging or incorrect depth sorting. It differs from MERF, which integrates all sample points together followed by deferred rendering, by using segmented integration (block-by-block) followed by inter-block blending. Without deferred rendering, this variant is entirely equivalent to traditional volume rendering. It supports hierarchical LODs where L is the total number of levels, and blocks are merged between consecutive LODs. Resource Independence: The primary advantage is that each block can be rendered independently by separate shaders or processes that cannot communicate, making it suitable for web-based or distributed rendering environments. Complexity: The computational complexity is linear with respect to the total number of samples N across all blocks, similar to standard volume rendering. Accuracy: Maintains 3D consistency and correct occlusion. Under Lambertian conditions, it is mathematically equivalent to global volume rendering. The method was introduced in the paper "City-on-Web: Real-Time Neural Rendering of Large-Scale Scenes on the Web". It addresses the limitations of previous neural rendering methods (like MERF) that required global integration and deferred rendering, which are difficult to implement in resource-constrained or isolated shader environments. The approach proves that segmented integration followed by alpha blending is equivalent to traditional volume rendering under Lambertian conditions, allowing for efficient, parallelizable rendering pipelines. name: Pre-filtered Cubic B-spline Interpolation
head: Pre-filtered B-spline Interpolation
body: Pre-filtered Cubic B-spline Interpolation is an on-the-fly interpolation approach combined with a pre-filtering step to perform more accurate interpolations without larger data storage. It is chosen when reconstruction accuracy is prioritized over the raw performance of hardware-accelerated tri-linear interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Discrete volume data V{raw} on a 3D grid. Output: Interpolated scalar value V(\mathbf{p}) at query position \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: Pre-filtered volume V{pf}: Same dimensions and layout as V{raw}, storing pre-processed voxel values. Steps: 1. Pre-filtering (Offline/Pre-processing): Pre-process all voxel values in V{raw} to produce V{pf}. The exact mathematical inversion or filter coefficients are not detailed in the sources [G: Typically involves separable deconvolution or inverse filtering in 1D applied across dimensions, but exact coefficients are Not given in the sources]. 2. Ray Casting and Sampling: For each ray sample position \mathbf{p}, perform local lookups in V{pf}. 3. Interpolation: Combine the surrounding voxel values using cubic B-spline basis functions to compute V(\mathbf{p}). Parameters: Kernel: Cubic B-spline. Pre-filtering: Applied once per volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: The method incurs a "performance penalty" compared to tri-linear interpolation. Implementation: Requires custom shader code for the B-spline weights and pre-filtered data access, bypassing standard hardware texture filtering which defaults to tri-linear. Precision: Standard floating-point precision is assumed; no specific bit-packing is mentioned. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cubicbsplinebasis(u): """Standard 1D cubic B-spline basis function for u in [0, 1].""" u2 = u u u3 = u2 u w0 = (1.0 - u)3 / 6.0 w1 = (3.0 u3 - 6.0 u2 + 4.0) / 6.0 w2 = (-3.0 u3 + 3.0 u2 + 3.0 u + 1.0) / 6.0 w3 = u3 / 6.0 return w0, w1, w2, w3 def worldtovolumegrid(p, origin, spacing): """Transform world coordinates to volume grid coordinates.""" return [(p[i] - origin[i]) / spacing[i] for i in range(3)] def applyinversebsplinefilter(Vraw): # Exact inverse filter coefficients for cubic B-spline are not given in sources # This function represents the pre-processing step described in return Vraw # Placeholder for deconvolution step def prefiltervolume(Vraw, origin, spacing): """Pre-process all voxel values to produce Vpf.""" Vpf = applyinversebsplinefilter(Vraw) return Vpf def sampleprefilteredbspline(Vpf, p, origin, spacing): """Interpolate value at query position p using pre-filtered volume.""" gridp = worldtovolumegrid(p, origin, spacing) x0, y0, z0 = math.floor(gridp[0]), math.floor(gridp[1]), math.floor(gridp[2]) fx, fy, fz = gridp[0] - x0, gridp[1] - y0, gridp[2] - z0 w0x, w1x, w2x, w3x = cubicbsplinebasis(fx) w0y, w1y, w2y, w3y = cubicbsplinebasis(fy) w0z, w1z, w2z, w3z = cubicbsplinebasis(fz) weightsx = [w0x, w1x, w2x, w3x] weightsy = [w0y, w1y, w2y, w3y] weightsz = [w0z, w1z, w2z, w3z] val = 0.0 for i in range(4): for j in range(4): for k in range(4): val += weightsx[i] weightsy[j] weightsz[k] Vpf[x0 + i, y0 + j, z0 + k] return val Extends spline-based representation to geometry and scalar fields for pixel-accurate surfaces. Chosen when geometric exactness is critical. Time Complexity: Higher than tri-linear interpolation due to a performance penalty. Memory Complexity: Same as raw volume data; no larger storage footprint is required. Strengths: Provides more accurate interpolations than tri-linear methods. Limitations: Performance penalty; requires pre-processing step; more complex implementation than standard texture sampling. When to use: High-quality rendering where reconstruction accuracy is prioritized over raw performance. When not to use: Real-time applications with strict performance constraints where tri-linear interpolation is acceptable. The method is cited as an example of advanced on-the-fly interpolation combined with pre-filtering to address artifacts in volume rendering. It is discussed in the context of common artifacts, specifically as an alternative to tri-linear interpolation which remains popular due to hardware support. name: Isogeometric Volume Rendering
head: Direct Isogeometric Volume Visualization, Pixel-Accurate Isogeometric Volume Rendering
body: Isogeometric Volume Rendering is a method for the interactive visualization of isogeometric analysis (IGA) results, ensuring correct, pixel-accurate geometry of the volume including its bounding surfaces. It extends classic volume rendering to isogeometric volumes where both geometry and scalar field are given in terms of splines (NURBS, B-splines). Unlike voxelized methods which suffer from block-like structures and high memory demands, this method provides pixel-accurate outer surfaces and avoids the loss of geometrically exact representation. It builds on Pre-filtered Cubic B-spline Interpolation. The algorithm uses the entire OpenGL pipeline in a multi-stage approach leveraging techniques from surface rendering, order-independent transparency, and ODE theory. Inputs: An isogeometric model defined by control points, knot vectors, and basis functions for both geometry and scalar field; camera parameters. Outputs: A rendered image with pixel-accurate boundaries. The scalar field f(x,y,z) is defined via the inverse parameterization of the geometry. If \phi is the geometry mapping and \rho is the scalar field in parameter space, the field in physical space is f(x,y,z) = \rho(\phi^{-1}(x,y,z)). A 3D B-spline of degree p is defined as: f(u,v,w) = \sum{k=1}^{n} \sum{j=1}^{m} \sum{i=1}^{l} Ki^p(u) Lj^p(v) Mk^p(w) C{i,j,k} where C{i,j,k} \in \mathbb{R}^d are control points, and Ki^p, Lj^p, Mk^p are recursively defined i-th B-splines of degree p in the corresponding directions defined by knot vectors U, V, W. 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. 2. Root Finding: To determine entry and exit points of the volume boundary accurately, solve for the roots of the implicit surface function defined by the isogeometric geometry. This involves solving nonlinear equations, potentially using ODE-based numerical methods. 3. Integration: Integrate the scalar field along the ray segment inside the volume. The scalar field is evaluated using the spline basis functions in parameter space, requiring the mapping of physical ray points back to parameter space via \phi^{-1}. 4. Compositing: Use order-independent transparency techniques to composite the accumulated color and opacity along the ray. Voxelization of isogeometric models leads to spurious block-like structures at outer surfaces because standard volume rendering (tri-linear interpolation) cannot represent the sharp transition of the smooth outer surface. The approximation error for linear interpolation p1(x) of a function f(x) between points a, b is bounded by: |f(x) - p1(x)| \le \frac{(b-a)^2}{8} \max{x \in [a,b]} \|f''(x)\| In IGA, f(x,y,z) = \rho(\phi^{-1}(x,y,z)), so linear interpolation can have arbitrarily large error depending on second-order derivatives. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method is designed for interactive visualization. Strengths: Pixel-accurate outer surfaces; geometrically exact representation. Limitations: Requires solving nonlinear equations for boundary intersection; complex implementation involving multiple OpenGL stages. Isogeometric analysis (IGA) provides a unified approach for design, analysis and optimization of functional products in industry. Traditional volume rendering methods for inspecting the results from the numerical simulations cannot be applied directly to isogeometric models. This method was presented to address this gap, ensuring that the advantage of geometrically exact representation is not lost in the visualization stage. name: Partial Segment Handling
head: Reduced Segment Length Opacity Adjustment, Segmental Replacement, Segmental Replacer Node
body: Partial Segment Handling addresses the "jerky edges" or stair-stepping artifacts that occur at volume boundaries or cutting surfaces when rays are sampled at fixed intervals, leaving an incomplete segment at the end of the ray march. It solves this by introducing a smaller final segment to fill the remaining distance to the boundary and adjusting its opacity to preserve the correct accumulated attenuation. A variant, Segmental Replacement, uses surface models to partially replace volume models to exhibit internal information while avoiding the rendering of the entire volume, facilitating real-time simulation. Inputs: Original segment length d1 (typically the fixed step size \Delta t used in the ray march). Original segment opacity \alpha1 (derived from the transfer function and extinction coefficient for length d1). Remaining distance to the volume boundary or cutting surface d2 (where 0 < d2 < d1). Optional surface model data for the replacement region. Outputs: Adjusted opacity \alpha2 for the partial segment. Rendered pixel color using either the adjusted volume segment or the surface counterpart. No specific complex data structures are required beyond the standard ray marching state. The method operates on scalar values associated with the current ray step. Segment State: Contains current position t, accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc}, and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}. Boundary Check: A boolean or distance value indicating if the next full step t + d1 exceeds the volume exit t{far} or a cutting plane. 1. Ray Marching: Perform standard front-to-back compositing for full segments of length d1 as defined in Direct volume ray casting. 2. Boundary Detection: At each step, check if the next sample position t{next} = t{current} + d1 exceeds the volume exit parameter t{far} or intersects a cutting plane. 3. Partial Segment Calculation: If a boundary is crossed: Calculate the remaining distance d2 = t{far} - t{current} (or distance to cutting plane). Sample the volume at the midpoint of the segment t{current} + d2/2. Determine the original opacity \alpha1 that would have been applied if the segment length were d1. Calculate the adjusted opacity \alpha2 for the shorter length d2 using the formula below. Composite the partial segment using \alpha2 and the color \mathbf{c} derived from the sampled data. Terminate the ray march. 4. Segmental Replacement (Variant): If using the Segmental Replacer Node strategy: Clip the volume model along vertical and horizontal planes to generate quadruple sub-parts of the original model. Identify regions where the volume model is replaced by a surface counterpart. Render the surface counterpart for the darker areas to exhibit internal information while avoiding the cost of rendering the entire volume model. The core adjustment for reduced segment length is: \alpha2 = 1 - (1 - \alpha1)^{\frac{d2}{d1}} Where: \alpha1 is the opacity of the original full segment of length d1. d1 is the original segment length (step size). d2 is the new, reduced segment length (remaining distance to boundary). \alpha2 is the adjusted opacity for the partial segment. This formula ensures that the transmission (1 - \alpha2) equals the transmission of the original segment raised to the power of the length ratio, preserving the Beer-Lambert law's exponential attenuation property for the partial distance. Segment Length (d1): Typically the fixed step size \Delta t used in the ray march. Adaptive strategies may vary d1 based on contribution. Transfer Function: Maps scalar values to extinction coefficient \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Zero Remaining Distance: If d2 \approx 0, \alpha2 should be 0 to avoid division by zero or numerical instability in the exponent. Precision: Ensure floating-point precision is sufficient for the exponentiation, especially when d2 \ll d1. Adaptive Segments: Smaller segments are used when the contribution to the ray color is large, and longer segments when the contribution is low, to optimize for speed while yielding few artifacts. def partialsegmenthandling(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, stepsize, transferfunction, volumegrid, gridspacing, gridorigin): """ Renders a ray with partial segment handling at boundaries. Implements standard front-to-back compositing with opacity adjustment. """ def trilinearinterpolate(pos): # Standard trilinear interpolation gx = (pos[0] - gridorigin[0]) / gridspacing[0] gy = (pos[1] - gridorigin[1]) / gridspacing[1] gz = (pos[2] - gridorigin[2]) / gridspacing[2] gx = max(0.0, min(gx, volumegrid.shape[0] - 1.0)) gy = max(0.0, min(gy, volumegrid.shape[1] - 1.0)) gz = max(0.0, min(gz, volumegrid.shape[2] - 1.0)) x0, y0, z0 = int(gx), int(gy), int(gz) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 dx, dy, dz = gx - x0, gy - y0, gz - z0 v000 = volumegrid[x0, y0, z0] v100 = volumegrid[x1, y0, z0] v010 = volumegrid[x0, y1, z0] v110 = volumegrid[x1, y1, z0] v001 = volumegrid[x0, y0, z1] v101 = volumegrid[x1, y0, z1] v011 = volumegrid[x0, y1, z1] v111 = volumegrid[x1, y1, z1] c00 = v000 + dx (v100 - v000) c10 = v010 + dx (v110 - v010) c01 = v001 + dx (v101 - v001) c11 = v011 + dx (v111 - v011) c0 = c00 + dy (c10 - c00) c1 = c01 + dy (c11 - c01) return c0 + dz (c1 - c0) t = tnear acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accopacity = 0.0 while t < tfar: tnext = t + stepsize ispartial = tnext > tfar d1 = stepsize d2 = tfar - t if ispartial else d1 tsample = t + d2 / 2.0 val = trilinearinterpolate(rayorigin + tsample raydirection) color, sigma = transferfunction(val) # Compute original opacity for full step alpha1 = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma d1) # Compute adjusted opacity for partial step using source formula alpha2 = 1.0 - math.pow((1.0 - alpha1), d2 / d1) alpha = alpha2 if ispartial else alpha1 # Front-to-back compositing weight = (1.0 - accopacity) alpha acccolor = ( acccolor[0] + weight color[0], acccolor[1] + weight color[1], acccolor[2] + weight color[2]) accopacity = accopacity + weight t = tnext if not ispartial else tfar return acccolor, accopacity A strategy where a surface model partially replaces a volume model to exhibit internal information while avoiding the rendering of the entire volume model. It is chosen when real-time simulation requires avoiding the cost of full volume rendering, and the trade-off is acceptable. An optimization where smaller segments are used when the contribution to the ray color is large, and longer segments when the contribution is low. This reduces artifacts while optimizing for speed. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples. The partial segment handling adds a constant-time check and calculation at the end of the ray march. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory. No new data structures are required. Performance: The method is computationally inexpensive, adding minimal overhead to the ray march. It is suitable for real-time applications. Strengths: Eliminates jerky edges at boundaries without requiring global resampling or increased sampling density. Limitations: Only addresses artifacts at the end of the ray march. Partial Segment Handling was identified as a solution to common artifacts in volume rendering, specifically jerky edges caused by incomplete segments at volume boundaries. The technique is based on the Beer-Lambert law's exponential attenuation properties. The concept of using surface models to partially replace volume models (Segmental Replacement) was explored in hybrid rendering frameworks for real-time manipulation of volume and surface models. name: Improved Ray Casting Volume Rendering
head: Improved light projected volume rendering, Light projected volume rendering method
body: Improved Ray Casting Volume Rendering is a direct volume rendering technique optimized for large-scale, regular 3D spatial data fields (specifically seismic data) by prioritizing rendering speed and high-frequency component preservation over physical lighting accuracy. It distinguishes itself from standard ray casting by reversing the classification and interpolation order (interpolating raw data before classification) and replacing floating-point arithmetic with fixed-point operations to accelerate trilinear interpolation. Unlike Standard Ray Casting, which classifies data first and risks filtering high-frequency color components, this method ensures the convolution operation acts on the original discrete data field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A regular 3D scalar data field V (e.g., seismic data in SEGY format), camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), a transfer function T mapping scalar values to color \mathbf{c} and opacity \alpha, and an empty voxel marker value. Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains a synthesized RGBA color value. Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D array of scalar values stored using fixed-point number representation for interpolation calculations to avoid time-consuming floating-point operations. Sampling Points: K equal-interval points along the ray. Parameters: K: The number of equal-interval sampling points selected along the ray for each pixel. Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Definition: For each pixel, define a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} intersecting the volume bounding box. 2. Sampling: Select K equal-interval sampling points along the ray segment within the volume. 3. Interpolation (First): For each sampling point \mathbf{p}i, perform trilinear interpolation on the original discrete 3D scalar data field V using the eight closest grid points. This yields an interpolated scalar value V{interp}. Note: This step avoids the high-frequency component loss associated with classifying discrete data before interpolation. Implementation Detail: Use fixed-point arithmetic for the interpolation weights and value accumulation to improve performance. 4. Classification (Second): Apply the transfer function T to the interpolated scalar value V{interp} to obtain the color \mathbf{c}i and opacity \alphai for the sample. \mathbf{c}i, \alphai = T(V{interp}). 5. Shading (Ignored): Explicitly ignore lighting effects and gradient calculations. The source states that for seismic data, gradient values change disorderly and lighting effects are weak, so this step is skipped to minimize computation. 6. Compositing: Synthesize the color and opacity values from front to rear using the front-to-back compositing equation. Initialize accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc} = (0,0,0) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0. For each sample i from front to back: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai 7. Early Termination: If \alpha{acc} approaches 1 (indicating the pixel is effectively opaque), skip the remaining voxels/samples for that ray to eliminate invalid computation. 8. Empty Voxel Skipping: Skip sampling points that fall within empty voxels (voxels with no data contribution) to accelerate rendering speed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def improvedraycasting(volumedata, volumebounds, camera, transferfunction, K, emptyvalue): """ volumedata: 3D list/array of scalar values (fixed-point representation preferred) volumebounds: tuple (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) camera: object with origin o, direction d, resolution, and getray(x, y) method transferfunction: callable scalar -> (colortuple, opacityfloat) K: int, number of sampling points per ray emptyvalue: scalar value representing empty space in volumedata """ height, width = camera.resolution # Initialize output image with RGBA tuples output = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] def intersectvolume(rayo, rayd, bounds): # Slab method to find entry (tnear) and exit (tfar) parameters tmin, tmax = 0.0, float('inf') for i in range(3): if rayd[i] == 0.0: if rayo[i] < bounds[2i] or rayo[i] > bounds[2i+1]: return None, None else: t1 = (bounds[2i] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] t2 = (bounds[2i+1] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return None, None return tmin, tmax def isemptyvoxel(p, bounds, data, emptyval): # Check if point is within volume bounds if not (bounds[0] <= p[0] <= bounds[1] and bounds[2] <= p[1] <= bounds[3] and bounds[4] <= p[2] <= bounds[5]): return False # Map continuous coordinate to integer grid indices ix, iy, iz = int(p[0]), int(p[1]), int(p[2]) # Clamp to valid array bounds ix = max(0, min(ix, len(data)-1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, len(data[0])-1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, len(data[0][0])-1)) return data[ix][iy][iz] == emptyval for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayo, rayd = camera.getray(x, y) tnear, tfar = intersectvolume(rayo, rayd, volumebounds) if tnear is None: continue dt = (tfar - tnear) / K acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accopacity = 0.0 for k in range(K): t = tnear + k dt p = (rayo[0] + t rayd[0], rayo[1] + t rayd[1], rayo[2] + t rayd[2]) # Safety bounds check if not (volumebounds[0] <= p[0] <= volumebounds[1] and volumebounds[2] <= p[1] <= volumebounds[3] and volumebounds[4] <= p[2] <= volumebounds[5]): continue # Skip empty voxels if isemptyvoxel(p, volumebounds, volumedata, emptyvalue): continue # Step 3: Interpolate original data first (fixed-point arithmetic) vinterp = trilinearinterpolatefixedpoint(p, volumedata) # Step 4: Classify after interpolation color, opacity = transferfunction(vinterp) # Step 7: Early termination check if accopacity >= 0.99: break # Step 6: Front-to-back compositing weight = (1.0 - accopacity) opacity acccolor = (acccolor[0] + weight color[0], acccolor[1] + weight color[1], acccolor[2] + weight color[2]) accopacity = accopacity + weight output[y][x] = (acccolor[0], acccolor[1], acccolor[2], accopacity) return output def trilinearinterpolatefixedpoint(p, volumedata): """ Performs trilinear interpolation using fixed-point arithmetic logic. p: 3D coordinate (x, y, z) volumedata: 3D array of scalars """ ix, iy, iz = int(p[0]), int(p[1]), int(p[2]) fx, fy, fz = p[0] - ix, p[1] - iy, p[2] - iz # Boundary clamping for indices ix = max(0, min(ix, len(volumedata)-1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, len(volumedata[0])-1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, len(volumedata[0][0])-1)) # Fetch 8 surrounding voxels v000 = volumedata[ix][iy][iz] v100 = volumedata[min(ix+1, len(volumedata)-1)][iy][iz] v010 = volumedata[ix][min(iy+1, len(volumedata[0])-1)][iz] v110 = volumedata[min(ix+1, len(volumedata)-1)][min(iy+1, len(volumedata[0])-1)][iz] v001 = volumedata[ix][iy][min(iz+1, len(volumedata[0][0])-1)] v101 = volumedata[min(ix+1, len(volumedata)-1)][iy][min(iz+1, len(volumedata[0][0])-1)] v011 = volumedata[ix][min(iy+1, len(volumedata[0])-1)][min(iz+1, len(volumedata[0][0])-1)] v111 = volumedata[min(ix+1, len(volumedata)-1)][min(iy+1, len(volumedata[0])-1)][min(iz+1, len(volumedata[0][0])-1)] # Interpolation using fixed-point math (logical structure) # In practice, weights and values are scaled integers to avoid floating-point arithmetic w000 = (1-fx)(1-fy)(1-fz) w100 = fx(1-fy)(1-fz) w010 = (1-fx)fy(1-fz) w110 = fxfy(1-fz) w001 = (1-fx)(1-fy)fz w101 = fx(1-fy)fz w011 = (1-fx)fyfz w111 = fxfyfz return (w000v000 + w100v100 + w010v010 + w110v110 + w001v001 + w101v101 + w011v011 + w111v111) Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K) per pixel, where N is the number of pixels and K is the number of samples. The use of fixed-point arithmetic reduces the constant factor for interpolation compared to floating-point. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, where V is the number of voxels. Strengths: Significantly faster rendering speed for large-scale seismic data due to skipped lighting calculations, fixed-point interpolation, and early termination. Preserves high-frequency color components better than standard ray casting by interpolating before classification. Limitations: Not physically accurate due to ignored lighting/shading. When to use: Ideal for real-time or near-real-time visualization of large-scale, regular 3D scalar fields (like seismic data) where interpretive clarity and speed are prioritized over photorealistic lighting. When not to use: Not suitable for scenes requiring accurate surface shading, specular highlights, or where gradient-based normal estimation is critical for visual understanding. The method was introduced in the context of 3D visualization for seismic data processing. It addresses the inherent defects of standard ray casting, specifically its heavy calculation overhead and time/space complexity which increases with data volume. Seismic data is characterized as large-scale, distributed, scattered material with different eigenvalues, no clear interfaces, and disorderly gradient directions, making traditional lighting models ineffective. The method was implemented using the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) and MFC under Microsoft Windows to display SEGY format data.
