name: Multi-pass multi-view PBR
head: 8 MV, Conventional Multi-View Rendering
body: Multi-pass multi-view PBR is a rendering approach that generates N distinct perspective views of a 3D dataset by executing N separate rendering passes, storing each view in a render target texture, and subsequently compositing them into a final spatial image. It is primarily used for auto-stereoscopic displays (e.g., lenticular sheets or wavelength-selective filters) requiring multiple viewpoints. It differs from single-pass multi-view techniques (such as Half-angle slicing or Two-pass volume rendering) by isolating each view into its own rasterization pass, which simplifies the shader logic but incurs a significant performance penalty proportional to N. Inputs: 3D volume dataset. Number of views N (commonly 8). Display type (lenticular sheet or wavelength-selective filter array). View frustum configurations for each of the N views. Outputs: Final spatial image I(x, y) conforming to the auto-stereoscopic display device. Data Structures: N target textures (render targets) Ii, where i \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}. Each texture holds the rendered image for one view. Mask function Mask(x, y), initialized once during setup based on the display type. Steps: 1. Setup: Initialize the mask function Mask(x, y) based on the target display hardware. For lenticular sheets, Mask(x, y) = x \mod N. For wavelength-selective filter arrays, the mask incorporates RGB component masking and diagonal shifts. 2. Render Views: For each view i from 0 to N-1: a. Set the view frustum to the configuration for view i. b. Render the 3D data into target texture Ii using standard rasterization or ray-splatting techniques. 3. Composite: Combine the N target images into the final spatial image I(x, y) using the mask: I(x, y) = I{Mask(x, y)}(x, y) where Ik(x, y) denotes the pixel at (x, y) in texture Ik. Pitfalls: Performance: The method requires N separate rendering passes, leading to an N-fold cost increase compared to single-view rendering. Memory Bandwidth: Compositing N high-resolution images (e.g., 8 views of 1900 \times 1600) requires transferring significant data (e.g., ~70MB/frame), which can bottleneck the pipeline. Blurring: If pixel-fill rate is limiting, intermediate images may be rendered at sub-resolution and up-sampled during compositing, causing blurring artifacts. Geometry Overhead: Geometry processing cost overhead remains at N-1 times the single-view cost, which is a major limiting factor for large datasets. A conventional approach that renders 3D data in N passes using N different perspective (off-axis asymmetric sheared) view frustum configurations, then combines the resulting N images into a spatial image via masking. It is chosen when shader complexity is high or when using hardware that does not support efficient single-pass multi-view rasterization. The masking function for lenticular sheets is Mask(x, y) = x \mod N. For wavelength-selective filter arrays, masking involves individual RGB component masking and diagonal shifts. It suffers from an N-times cost increase compared to single-view rendering. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot T{render}), where T{render} is the time to render one view. Performance decreases by a factor of approximately 8 compared to single-view rendering for N=8. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for N full-resolution target images. For N=8 and resolution 1900 \times 1600, this involves transferring ~70MB per frame. Strengths: Simple implementation; leverages standard render-to-texture pipelines; no complex single-pass multi-view shader logic required. Limitations: Immense performance penalty due to separate passes; geometry processing overhead scales with N; potential for blurring if sub-resolution rendering is used. When to use: When N is small, or when the rendering pipeline cannot support efficient single-pass multi-view techniques (e.g., Half-angle slicing). When not to use: When pixel-fill rate or memory bandwidth is a bottleneck, or when N is large, as the N-fold cost increase becomes prohibitive. The conventional multi-view rendering approach has been used in systems such as those by SGI, Portoni et al. (2000), Schmidt and Grasnick (2002), and Miniel et al. (2004). It was implemented and tested for 8-view auto-stereoscopic displays using wavelength-selective filter arrays with a resolution of 1900 \times 1200. The method was compared against single-pass vertex-based (GPU VS) and fragment-based (GPU FS) implementations, showing significant performance degradation relative to single-view rendering. Multi-view point splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/1174429.1174479, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Compositing and Output Generation
body: Compositing and Output Generation defines the final stage of direct volume ray casting, where discrete volumetric samples are aggregated into a 2D image pixel. It solves the problem of optical integration, determining how light emitted or scattered by volume elements is attenuated by absorption and combined with background light. This family builds on Multi-Pass and Compositing Techniques and is distinct from Projection and MIP Techniques because it explicitly tracks opacity and transmittance for alpha blending, preserving depth cues, whereas MIP methods discard opacity for order-independent extremum aggregation. It differs from Volume Raycasting Output Generation by focusing on the mathematical accumulation logic itself, while the sibling article covers the broader implementation pipeline including ray traversal and transfer function sampling. All methods in this family operate on a sequence of samples (ci, \alphai) encountered along a ray, where ci is the sample color (RGB) and \alphai is the sample opacity (A). The core mechanism involves an accumulator state (C{acc}, \alpha{acc}) initialized to (0, 0) (or background color/opacity) and updated iteratively for each sample. The standard optical model assumes that light is emitted or scattered by the volume and attenuated by absorption. The standard front-to-back compositing equation updates these accumulators for each sample i from front to back: C{acc}^{(i)} = C{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai Ci \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai where C{acc}^{(0)} = 0 and \alpha{acc}^{(0)} = 0. The term (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) represents the transmittance, i.e., the fraction of light reaching sample i from the camera side. In iterative form using transmittance T = 1 - \alpha{acc}: \begin{aligned} C{final} &\leftarrow C{final} + ci \cdot \alphai \cdot T \\ T &\leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai) \end{aligned} Where T is initialized to 1.0 and represents the accumulated transparency \prod (1-\alphaj). The final pixel color is often composited over a background color C{bg} using C{final} = C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{bg}. Early ray termination is a common optimization where the loop breaks if \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1.0), as further samples contribute negligibly to the color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositingloop(samples, backgroundcolor): """ Standard front-to-back compositing loop shared by the family. samples: list of (color: list[float], opacity: float) sorted front-to-back. backgroundcolor: list[float] for the scene background. """ Cacc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphaacc = 0.0 for ci, alphai in samples: transmittance = 1.0 - alphaacc Cacc = [Cacc[j] + transmittance alphai ci[j] for j in range(3)] alphaacc = alphaacc + transmittance alphai # Early ray termination if alphaacc >= 1.0: break # Composite over background return [Cacc[j] + (1.0 - alphaacc) backgroundcolor[j] for j in range(3)] Defines the mathematical rules for combining volumetric samples into a final pixel color and opacity. Sets itself apart by focusing on the accumulation logic and alpha blending, explicitly tracking transmittance, unlike Projection and MIP Techniques which discard opacity for extremum projection. Choose when depth-aware blending and accurate light attenuation modeling are required. The core image-order rendering technique that traverses a 3D volume along rays, accumulating color and opacity from front to back. Differs from Compositing and Blending by explicitly handling the ray traversal loop, boundary checks, and transfer function sampling within the output generation step. Choose for standard direct volume rendering pipelines requiring full ray marching. A family of methods that generate 2D images by aggregating scalar values using operators other than standard emission-absorption compositing (e.g., Maximum, Minimum, Sum). Solves the problem of visualizing specific features (like bones or vessels) by emphasizing extremal values while suppressing intermediate background data. Distinct because it discards opacity accumulation and depth cues in favor of order-independent aggregation. Choose when highlighting high-density or high-intensity structures is prioritized over depth cues. Modulates sample opacity based on the angle between the surface normal and the view vector, making regions orthogonal to the viewer more transparent and regions curving towards or away from the viewer more opaque. Differs from standard compositing by dynamically adjusting transparency per sample based on geometric orientation to improve readability of nested structures. Choose when visualizing complex nested geometries or surface details requires enhanced transparency control. Not given in the sources. The front-to-back compositing equation is a standard result in volume rendering, derived from the Beer-Lambert law for light attenuation. Early ray termination was introduced as an optimization to reduce computational cost by skipping samples behind opaque regions. MIP techniques originated in medical imaging to visualize high-density structures like bones without the occlusion caused by soft tissue.

name: Compositing and Blending
head: Accumulate, Alternative Compositing Schemes, Blending Modes, First Hit, Front-to-back blending, Maximum Intensity blending, Minimum Intensity blending
body: Compositing and Blending defines the final stage of direct volume ray casting where per-ray sample contributions (color and opacity) are integrated into a 2D pixel value. It solves the problem of correctly blending semi-transparent, overlapping density fields to produce visually accurate renderings. All methods in this family operate on a sequence of samples (ci, \alphai) encountered along a ray, where ci is the sample color (RGB) and \alphai is the sample opacity (A). The core mechanism involves an accumulator state (C{acc}, \alpha{acc}) initialized to (0, 0) (or background color/opacity) and updated iteratively for each sample. The standard optical model assumes that light is emitted or scattered by the volume and attenuated by absorption. The standard front-to-back compositing equation updates these accumulators for each sample i from front to back: C{acc}^{(i)} = C{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai Ci \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai where C{acc}^{(0)} = 0 and \alpha{acc}^{(0)} = 0. The term (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) represents the transmittance, i.e., the fraction of light reaching sample i from the camera side. In iterative form using transmittance T = 1 - \alpha{acc}: \begin{aligned} C{final} &\leftarrow C{final} + ci \cdot \alphai \cdot T \\ T &\leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai) \end{aligned} Where T is initialized to 1.0 and represents the accumulated transparency \prod (1-\alphaj). The final pixel color is often composited over a background color C{bg} using C{final} = C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{bg}. Early ray termination is a common optimization where the loop breaks if T falls below a small threshold (e.g., 10^{-6}), as further samples contribute negligibly to the color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositingloop(samples, backgroundcolor): """ Standard front-to-back compositing loop shared by the family. samples: list of (color: vec3, opacity: float) sorted front-to-back. backgroundcolor: vec3 for the scene background. """ Cacc = vec3(0.0) T = 1.0 for ci, alphai in samples: Cacc = Cacc + T alphai ci T = T (1.0 - alphai) # Early ray termination if T <= 1e-6: break # Composite over background return Cacc + T backgroundcolor Pre-integration lookup is a technique in direct volume ray casting that replaces the iterative accumulation of color and opacity within a volume slab with a single texture fetch from a pre-computed table. It solves the problem of shading and color inaccuracies caused by linear interpolation of scalar values across a slab, which violates the non-linear optical properties of light attenuation. It sets itself apart from standard ray casting by moving the integration step from the rendering loop to an offline or on-the-fly pre-computation phase, and from Simplified Pre-integration by accounting for color attenuation within the slab rather than neglecting it. See Pre-Integration Lookup. Binary Swap Compositing is a parallel image compositing scheme for distributed-memory volume rendering that reduces network congestion by dividing communication between processors over multiple rounds. Unlike naive binary compositing where many processors become idle at the top of the tree, Binary Swap ensures every processor participates in all stages of the compositing process by splitting the image plane into two pieces and having each processor take responsibility for one piece during exchange and compositing. It is particularly suitable for massively parallel processing because it keeps all processors busy and decreases the image size for sending/compositing at each stage. See Binary Swap Compositing. Screen-space post-processing is a full-screen rendering stage that applies aspect-ratio preserving UV covering, luminance-based bright passes, color grading, spatial blurring, and dithering to a scene texture to produce a display-ready image. It differs from direct volume compositing methods by operating entirely in screen space on the final display image rather than during ray traversal, allowing for complex aesthetic effects like bloom and vignette without modifying the volume rendering pipeline. See Screen-space Post-processing. Layered SDF Compositing is a technique for rendering Signed Distance Field (SDF) glyphs by compositing multiple pre-multiplied alpha layers (typically a face and one or more outline layers) into a final pixel color. It solves the problem of rendering crisp, scalable text or icons with anti-aliased edges and colored outlines by treating each visual component as a distinct alpha-blended layer. It differs from standard SDF rendering by explicitly managing a fixed number of discrete layers (1, 2, or 4) using specific linear interpolation logic on pre-multiplied colors, rather than a continuous ray-casting integration. See Layered SDF Compositing. Reconstruction and Compositing Techniques constitute the final stage of direct volume ray casting, where 3D volumetric data is projected into a 2D image by integrating sample contributions along viewing rays. This family solves the problem of correctly blending semi-transparent, overlapping density fields to produce visually accurate renderings. See Reconstruction and Compositing Techniques. Lighting-Specific Compositing is a family of volume rendering techniques that integrate illumination models (such as in-scattering, Phong shading, or boundary enhancement) directly into the compositing loop, rather than treating lighting as a post-processing step or a simple per-sample color multiplication. It solves the problem of physically inaccurate or visually flat rendering by allowing light transport effects to influence the accumulation of opacity and color at the sample level. It differs from standard direct volume ray casting by modifying the color and opacity terms (ci, \alphai) before they enter the front-to-back accumulator, and from image-level compositing by preserving depth coherence for complex lighting interactions like occlusion and shadowing. See Lighting-Specific Compositing. The Layer-Centric Volume Rendering Framework is a visualization architecture that constructs the final image by compositing multiple distinct renderings, each treated as an independent layer. It solves the rigidity of traditional single-pass volume rendering by segmenting the workflow into a rendering phase for small regions of interest and a subsequent compositing phase. This approach provides a rich set of 2D operators and interactions, allowing for greater freedom and more intuitive user interaction compared to standard volume rendering techniques. See Layer-Centric Volume Rendering Framework. MAB compositing is a gaze-contingent rendering technique that maps framebuffer fragments to a Multi-Anchor Buffer (MAB) to retrieve and blend color values from different resolution levels based on the distance to the center of gaze. It solves the performance bottleneck in immersive VR volume rendering by dynamically adjusting resolution distribution to maintain high frame rates, thereby preventing cybersickness caused by performance fluctuations. Unlike standard fixed-resolution ray casting, it blends multiple resolution levels simultaneously using a smooth-step function to ensure unnoticeable transitions between detail levels. See MAB Compositing with Gaze-Contingent Blending. Multi-view image blending reduces artifacts caused by single-view fading, such as ghosting and transparency variation, by combining a set of images taken from various view angles. It sets itself apart from single-texture approaches by requiring the selection and blending of at least three textures, trading increased rendering cost for improved visual fidelity across viewpoints. See Multi-view image blending. Dynamic Job-Scheduling for Grid Volume Rendering is a distributed rendering technique that determines the processing order of sub-volumes based on their real-time visibility rather than a static sequence. It solves the bottleneck caused by heterogeneous agent speeds in grid computing, where static sequential scheduling forces fast agents to wait for slow agents to complete prior steps. By using obstacle-flags to track obscuration, the method allows agents to immediately process newly visible sub-volumes, significantly improving efficiency over sequential approaches. See Dynamic Job-Scheduling for Grid Volume Rendering. HardSoftRas Blending is a pixel-wise compositing strategy for differentiable rendering that distinguishes between edge pixels (silhouettes and vertical surfaces) and non-edge pixels to balance anti-aliasing with texture sharpness. Unlike SoftRas, which blends all faces in non-edge regions, HardSoftRas retains the most frontal color for non-edges while applying weighted averaging for edges, thereby maintaining sharp textures inside silhouettes and generating far-range gradients around boundaries. See HardSoftRas Blending. A pass that simply copies the current frame to the output, acting as a simple integration or blit step for the LAO renderer. Step: Sample frame buffer: oColor = texture(uFrame, vPosition);. A post-processing step where partial images rendered from blocks of different resolutions are expanded to a common 'virtual dimension' (the highest resolution dimension of the block) before compositing. This allows standard compositing algorithms to work despite varying input resolutions. Step: Determine the virtual dimensions for each block. For a block with original high-res dimensions (Hx, Hy, Hz), the virtual dimensions are (Hx, Hy, Hz). Render the block at its assigned resolution (e.g., Medium: Hx/2, Hy/2, Hz/2). This produces a partial image with actual dimensions smaller than the virtual dimensions. Expand the partial image to the virtual dimensions. This typically involves interpolating or replicating pixels to fill the larger grid, or simply placing the smaller image into a larger buffer with appropriate scaling factors during compositing. Parameter: Virtual Dimension Selection: The virtual dimension can be set to the dimension of the largest subimage in the scene to minimize padding, or fixed to the global high-resolution block size. A rendering compositing strategy where the scene is rendered part-by-part (one Voronoi cell at a time) and the resulting cell images are composited back-to-front to generate the final image. It relies on the proof that Voronoi cells admit a partial ordering compatible with occlusion. Step: 1. Define partial ordering on Voronoi cells based on distance from camera Q to the Voronoi sites P: V{P'} <Q VP iff d(P', Q) < d(P, Q). 2. Render each Voronoi cell independently. 3. Composite the rendered cell images in the order defined by <Q (back-to-front) to ensure closer objects occlude further ones. Formula: V{P'} <Q VP if and only if d(P', Q) < d(P, Q). Comparison: Standard Painter's Algorithm fails on cyclic occlusion graphs. Voronoi Painter's is always compatible because the distance-to-camera ordering is a strict partial order. Squaring the denominator emphasizes differences. Parameter: Blend factor r: Scalar factor used to blend between the two chosen tensor directions. Lighting function: A separate lighting function light manipulates intensity without affecting the base color of the mesh structure. Blinn-Phong shading is mentioned as providing required depth cues. The standard front-to-back accumulation model treats volume rendering as an integration of light emission and absorption along rays. Early systems like VolumePro supported multiple blending modes including Front-to-back blending, Minimum Intensity, and Maximum Intensity blending. Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) became widely used for extracting vessel structures in magnetic resonance angiograms. The field has since expanded to include distributed compositing strategies like Binary Swap for scalability, gaze-contingent rendering for VR performance, and differentiable compositing for neural rendering. name: Pre-Integration Lookup
head: 2D Pre-Integration, 2D Pre-integration Lookup, 3D Pre-integration, 3D Pre-integration Table
body: Pre-integration lookup is a technique in direct volume ray casting that replaces iterative per-sample accumulation within a volume slab with a single texture fetch from a pre-computed table. It provides optical properties for volume slices assuming linear data evolution within the slab. It sets itself apart from standard ray casting by moving the integration step to a pre-computation phase, and from Simplified Pre-integration by accounting for color attenuation within the slab rather than neglecting it. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset, a transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity, and ray samples (sf, sm, sb) representing the scalar values at the front, middle, and back of a slab (or entry/exit densities and slab thickness). Output: The pre-integrated color C{slab} and opacity \alpha{slab} contribution of the slab, which is then composited with other slabs. Data Structures: Pre-integration Lookup Table: A texture (2D or 3D) storing pre-calculated optical properties. 3D Table Layout: Dimensions 256 \times 256 \times 256 for 8-bit scalar domains. The axes correspond to front sample value (sf), middle sample value (sm), and back sample value (sb). 2D Table Layout: Dimensions dependent on entry density, exit density, and slab thickness. The axes typically correspond to these three parameters. Stored Values: Color (C) and Opacity (\alpha) resulting from the pre-calculated optical properties for the slab. Steps: 1. Pre-computation (Offline or On-the-fly): For a 3D table, render a quadrilateral parallel to the projection plane 256 times, filling the viewport. In the fragment shader, map screen coordinates to front (sf) and middle (sm) sample values, while the back sample (sb) is provided as a uniform variable. Compute the optical properties for the slab defined by sf, sm, sb using the pre-calculated functions. Store the result in the 3D texture at coordinate (sf, sm, sb). Note: 2D tables are preferred on hardware with faster 2D texturing capabilities, as 3D texturing can be slower. 2. Rendering (Per Ray): For each ray, divide the volume into slabs of thickness 2d. For each slab, retrieve the three scalar samples (sf, sm, sb) from the volume. Perform a 3D (or 2D) texture lookup using these samples as coordinates to fetch the pre-integrated color C{slab} and opacity \alpha{slab}. Composite the fetched slab contribution using the standard front-to-back compositing equation: C{acc}^{(i)} = C{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alpha{slab} C{slab} \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alpha{slab} Repeat for all slabs along the ray. Parameters: Slab Thickness: Defined as 2d, where d is the distance between samples. Table Resolution: 256^3 for 8-bit data. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Performance: 3D texture lookups may be slower than 2D lookups on some GPUs, making 2D pre-integration a practical choice despite potential artifacts. Linear Assumption: The method assumes linear evolution of data within the slice, which may introduce errors if the data varies non-linearly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preintegrationlookup(raysamples, backgroundcolor, lookuptable): """ Renders a ray using pre-integration lookup tables. raysamples: list of (sf, sm, sb) tuples for each slab along the ray. backgroundcolor: vec3 for the scene background. lookuptable: 3D texture or array supporting coordinate-based fetch. """ Cacc = vec3(0.0) alphaacc = 0.0 for sf, sm, sb in raysamples: # Standard hardware texture fetch operation Cslab, alphaslab = texturefetch(lookuptable, (sf, sm, sb)) transmittance = 1.0 - alphaacc Cacc = Cacc + transmittance alphaslab Cslab alphaacc = alphaacc + transmittance alphaslab # Early ray termination if alphaacc >= 1.0: break # Composite over background as per standard optical model finalcolor = Cacc + (1.0 - alphaacc) backgroundcolor return finalcolor, alphaacc This method computes the diffuse component of Blinn-Phong shading in pre-integrated volume rendering by decomposing the integral into four 2D look-up tables weighted by coefficients dependent on light direction and gradient angles. It avoids the prohibitive memory cost of full 4D normal-based pre-integration while reducing shading errors caused by large angles between consecutive sample gradients compared to linear interpolation. Non-linear gradient interpolation is a technique for pre-integrated direct volume rendering that reduces shading errors by interpolating gradients between front and back samples along a quadratic curve instead of a linear segment, allowing accurate computation of 2D pre-integration look-up tables. It sets itself apart from linear gradient interpolation by approximating the non-linear path of a normalized gradient vector as a quadratic polynomial, thereby avoiding the energy loss and shading errors inherent in linear interpolation which assumes the normalization term \eta(t)=1. Simplified Pre-integration is a faster approximation of full pre-integration used in direct volume ray casting. It solves the performance bottleneck of computing pre-integrated transfer function (TF) lookups by neglecting color attenuation inside volume slabs. It sets itself apart from full pre-integration Pre-Integration Lookup by trading accuracy for speed, making it suitable for interactive interfaces where multiple TFs are modified simultaneously. This method corrects rendering artifacts that occur at clip boundaries when using pre-integrated volume rendering with low sampling rates. It computes the optical contribution of the ray segment between a clipping surface and the first volume slice behind it, avoiding the need for interleaved rendering or complex boundary layer models. It differs from sibling methods by specifically addressing the discontinuity in sampling distance at clip planes rather than general gradient interpolation errors. A method for efficiently reconstructing 3D medical images that combines pre-integrated volume rendering with the Shear-Warp algorithm to eliminate aliasing artifacts from under-sampling and improve reconstruction quality via Phong lighting shading. It implements classification coding for volume data by utilizing the correlation of the opacity transfer function (OTF) and a min-max Octree data structure, establishing a new run-length encoded (RLE) data structure for fast reconstruction when OTF and view angle change. Time Complexity: The per-slab cost is reduced to a single texture lookup and compositing step, significantly faster than iterative integration per sample. Memory Complexity: Requires storing a large lookup table. For 8-bit data, a 3D table of size 256^3 is needed. Measured Performance: On ATI 9700 Pro with 5x5 tiles: spx1 dataset: 609-750 ms (2D), 688-907 ms (3D). blunt dataset: 141-391 ms (2D), 344-500 ms (3D). f117 dataset: 359-640 ms (2D), 453-719 ms (3D). On GeForce 6800 GT with 5x5 tiles: spx1 dataset: 312-531 ms (2D), 313-547 ms (3D). blunt dataset: 109-1094 ms (2D), 109-1032 ms (3D). f117 dataset: 266-563 ms (2D), 172-438 ms (3D). Ray casting passes (2D pre-integration): spx1: Min 571, Max 601. blunt: Min 341, Max 439. f117: Min 571, Max 601. Strengths: Reduces aliasing artifacts from under-sampling; improves shading accuracy; suitable for interactive rendering when combined with tiling. Limitations: High memory usage for 3D tables; 2D tables may introduce artifacts if not carefully designed; assumes linear data evolution within slabs. When to Use: When fast texture lookups are available and interactive medical image reconstruction is required. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained and 3D tables are too large; when non-linear data variation within slabs is significant. Pre-integration lookup was introduced to address the inaccuracies of linear interpolation in volume rendering. It is based on the principle that optical properties can be pre-calculated for volume slices assuming linear data evolution. The method has been implemented on GPU hardware. Variants include 2D and 3D lookup tables, with 2D often preferred for performance on certain hardware. It has been applied to medical image reconstruction and implemented on GPU hardware. name: Pre-Integrated Diffuse Shading with Non-Linear Gradient Interpolation
head: Pre-Integrated Diffuse Shading
body: This method computes the diffuse component of Blinn-Phong shading in pre-integrated volume rendering by decomposing the integral into four 2D look-up tables weighted by coefficients dependent on light direction and gradient angles. It avoids the prohibitive memory cost of full 4D normal-based pre-integration while reducing shading errors caused by large angles between consecutive sample gradients compared to linear interpolation. Inputs: Front scalar value Sf and back scalar value Sb for the current sampling step of length D. Front normal \mathbf{N}f and back normal \mathbf{N}b (gradients of the scalar field). Light direction \mathbf{L}. Diffuse coefficient Kd. Pre-computed 2D LUTs for I0, I1, I2, I3. Outputs: Pre-integrated diffuse color \tilde{C}d. Lookup Tables: Four 2D arrays indexed by quantized front and back scalar values. The exact array dimensions and binning strategy are not given in the sources. The pre-integrated diffuse color is calculated as: \tilde{C}d = Kd \cdot (a0(\mathbf{L})I0 + a1(\mathbf{L})I1 + a2(\mathbf{L})I2 + a3(\mathbf{L})I3) where Kd is the diffuse coefficient. The integral terms Ik(Sf, Sb) are defined as: Ik(Sf, Sb) = d \int{Sf}^{Sb} c(s0) \cdot s^k \cdot \exp(-d \cdot \sigma(Sf, s0)) \, ds0 where: k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\} is the polynomial exponent. c(s0) is the classification color at scalar value s0. \sigma(Sf, s0) is the accumulated absorption from Sf to s0. d = \frac{D}{Sb - Sf} is the normalized step length. s = \frac{s0 - Sf}{Sb - Sf} is the normalized position within the step. The coefficients ak(\mathbf{L}) depend on the light direction and normals: \begin{aligned} a0(\mathbf{L}) &= \mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{L} \\ a1(\mathbf{L}) &= \mathbf{N}b \cdot \mathbf{L} - (1 + r)\mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{L} \\ a2(\mathbf{L}) &= r(2\mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{L} - \mathbf{N}b \cdot \mathbf{L}) \\ a3(\mathbf{L}) &= r(\mathbf{N}b \cdot \mathbf{L} - \mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{L}) \end{aligned} where r is a factor derived from the angle \alpha between the front and back normals: r = \frac{4(\cos(\alpha) - 1)}{\cos(\alpha)} \alpha = \frac{1}{2} \arccos(\mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{N}b) All coefficients and the factor r are computed per sampling step. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def precomputeluts(numbins, scalarmin, scalarmax, classificationfunc, absorptionfunc): """ Pre-compute the four 2D lookup tables I0, I1, I2, I3. classificationfunc(s) returns color c(s) as a list/tuple of 3 floats. absorptionfunc(sf, s) returns sigma(Sf, s) as a float. """ # Initialize 2D tables with zeros LUTI0 = [[None] numbins for in range(numbins)] LUTI1 = [[None] numbins for in range(numbins)] LUTI2 = [[None] numbins for in range(numbins)] LUTI3 = [[None] numbins for in range(numbins)] # Discretize scalar range scalars = [scalarmin + i (scalarmax - scalarmin) / (numbins - 1) for i in range(numbins)] for i, Sf in enumerate(scalars): for j, Sb in enumerate(scalars): if Sb <= Sf: continue # Degenerate case # Normalized step length for table indexing Dnorm = 1.0 d = Dnorm / (Sb - Sf) # Accumulators for RGB channels accI0 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accI1 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accI2 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accI3 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] numsteps = 100 # Resolution for pre-computation integration ds0 = (Sb - Sf) / numsteps for stepidx in range(numsteps): s0 = Sf + stepidx ds0 s = (s0 - Sf) / (Sb - Sf) cs0 = classificationfunc(s0) sigma = absorptionfunc(Sf, s0) weight = math.exp(-d sigma) # Ik = d integral(c(s0) s^k exp(-dsigma) ds0) for ch in range(3): term = cs0[ch] weight ds0 d accI0[ch] += term (s 0) accI1[ch] += term (s 1) accI2[ch] += term (s 2) accI3[ch] += term (s 3) LUTI0[i][j] = accI0 LUTI1[i][j] = accI1 LUTI2[i][j] = accI2 LUTI3[i][j] = accI3 return LUTI0, LUTI1, LUTI2, LUTI3 def computediffuseshading(LUTI0, LUTI1, LUTI2, LUTI3, Sf, Sb, Nf, Nb, L, Kd, numbins, scalarmin, scalarmax): """ Compute pre-integrated diffuse shading for a single step. """ if Sb <= Sf: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 1. Compute angle alpha and factor r cosalpharaw = Nf[0]Nb[0] + Nf[1]Nb[1] + Nf[2]Nb[2] cosalpharaw = max(-1.0, min(1.0, cosalpharaw)) # Clamp for numerical stability alpha = math.acos(cosalpharaw) / 2.0 cosalpha = math.cos(alpha) # Handle division by zero when alpha approaches 90 degrees if abs(cosalpha) < 1e-6: r = -4.0 # Limit approximation else: r = 4.0 (cosalpha - 1.0) / cosalpha # 2. Compute coefficients a0 to a3 NfdotL = Nf[0]L[0] + Nf[1]L[1] + Nf[2]L[2] NbdotL = Nb[0]L[0] + Nb[1]L[1] + Nb[2]L[2] a0 = NfdotL a1 = NbdotL - (1.0 + r) NfdotL a2 = r (2.0 NfdotL - NbdotL) a3 = r (NbdotL - NfdotL) # 3. Quantize indices idxSf = int((Sf - scalarmin) / (scalarmax - scalarmin) (numbins - 1)) idxSb = int((Sb - scalarmin) / (scalarmax - scalarmin) (numbins - 1)) idxSf = max(0, min(numbins - 1, idxSf)) idxSb = max(0, min(numbins - 1, idxSb)) I0 = LUTI0[idxSf][idxSb] I1 = LUTI1[idxSf][idxSb] I2 = LUTI2[idxSf][idxSb] I3 = LUTI3[idxSf][idxSb] # 4. Compute final color sumI = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for ch in range(3): sumI[ch] = a0 I0[ch] + a1 I1[ch] + a2 I2[ch] + a3 I3[ch] Cd = [Kd sumI[ch] for ch in range(3)] return Cd Negative Dot Products: The dot product between the light direction and the normalized gradient may become negative, which is physically invalid for diffuse shading. Two solutions are common: applying max(0, dot) to the dot products before computing coefficients, or mirroring the gradient if the dot product is negative. Applying max(0, dot) makes exact pre-integration difficult, so the source distinguishes three cases but does not detail them. Degenerate Normals: If \mathbf{N}f and \mathbf{N}b are identical, \alpha = 0, r = 0, and the method reduces to standard linear shading. If they are orthogonal, \alpha = \pi/4. Precision: The factor r can become large negative values for large angles, potentially amplifying numerical errors in the coefficient calculation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. This method was proposed by Lum et al. in 2010 as an improvement over linear gradient interpolation in pre-integrated volume rendering. It addresses visual discontinuities and errors that arise when gradients change significantly between sample points, which linear interpolation fails to capture accurately. The approach builds on the concept of pre-integration lookup tables introduced in earlier work, extending it to handle diffuse shading with a non-linear gradient model. name: Non-Linear Gradient Interpolation for Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering
head: Non-linear gradient interpolation, Non-linear polynomial interpolation, Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering with Non-Linear Gradient Interpolation, Pre-integration with quadratic gradient interpolation, Quadratic gradient interpolation
body:
Non-linear gradient interpolation is a technique for pre-integrated direct volume rendering that reduces shading errors by interpolating gradients between front and back samples along a quadratic curve instead of a linear segment, allowing accurate computation of 2D pre-integration look-up tables. It sets itself apart from linear gradient interpolation by approximating the non-linear path of a normalized gradient vector as a quadratic polynomial, thereby avoiding the energy loss and shading errors inherent in linear interpolation which assumes the normalization term \eta(t)=1. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Front sample properties Sf, Back sample properties Sb, Front normalized gradient Nf, Back normalized gradient Nb, Light direction L, Specular half-vector H, Shininess n\delta, Slab size D, normalization factor r, and pre-computed 2D lookup tables. Outputs: Diffuse shading coefficient 	ilde{C}d, Specular shading coefficient 	ilde{C}s. Data Structures: Lookup Tables: Four 2D tables for the diffuse term (I0, I1, I2, I3) and five 2D tables for the specular term (I{00}, I{10}, I{20}, I{30}). Representation: 16-bit unsigned short in GPU memory. Indexing: Tables are indexed by Sf and Sb. Definitions: \alpha = \arccos(Nf \cdot Nb) / 2: Half the angle between front and back normals. r: A normalization factor derived from the geometry of the interpolated gradient arc. s = t/D: Normalized distance along the slab, t \in [0, D]. s0 = Sf + s(Sb - Sf): Normalized scalar value at position s. d = D / (Sb - Sf): Scaling factor for the integral substitution. \eta(t) \approx  rac{\cos(\alpha) \cdot x^2}{x^2 (\cos(\alpha) - 1) + 1}: Quadratic approximation of the normalization term, where x =  rac{2t}{D} - 1 = 2s - 1.

Compute Diffuse Coefficients (ak): Calculate coefficients using Nf, Nb, L, \alpha, and r: a0 =  rac{4(\cos(\alpha) - 1)}{\cos(\alpha)} a1 = Nb \cdot L - Nf \cdot L a2 =  rac{Nb \cdot L - (1 + r)Nf \cdot L}{r(2Nf \cdot L - Nb \cdot L)} a3 =  rac{Nf \cdot L}{r} 3. Access Diffuse Lookup Tables: Retrieve I0(Sf, Sb), I1(Sf, Sb), I2(Sf, Sb), I3(Sf, Sb) from the pre-computed 2D tables. Ik(Sf, Sb) = d \int{Sf}^{Sb} c(s0) \cdot s^k \cdot \exp(-d \sigma(Sf, s0)) \, ds0 4. Compute Diffuse Shading: Calculate 	ilde{C}d = Kd (a0 I0 + a1 I1 + a2 I2 + a3 I3). 5. Handle Negative Dot Products (Diffuse): If Nf \cdot L < 0 or Nb \cdot L < 0, apply case-based handling: if both are positive, use the standard formulation; if either is negative, fade in/out the non-negative value; if both are negative, the result is 0. 6. Specular Term Approximation: Replace the Phong lobe \cos(	heta)^{n\delta} with a Phong cone approximation: \cos(	heta)^{n\delta} \approx 1 + n\delta (\cos(	heta) - 1), where \cos(	heta) = N \cdot H. 7. Compute Specular Coefficients: Calculate a0(H), a1(H), a2(H), a3(H) using H instead of L with the same formulas as step 2. 8. Access Specular Lookup Tables: Retrieve I{00}, I{10}, I{20}, I{30}. I{00}(Sf, Sb) = d \int{Sf}^{Sb} (s < 0.5 ? 2s: 2 - 2s) \cdot \exp(-d \sigma(Sf, s0)) \, ds0 9. Compute Specular Shading: Calculate 	ilde{C}s = Ks (I{00} + n\delta (a0(H)I{00} + a1(H)I{10} + a2(H)I{20} + a3(H)I{30}) - n\delta I{00}). 10. Handle Negative Dot Products (Specular): Specular values become negative if N(s0) \cdot H < 	ext{thresh} = (n\delta - 1)/n\delta. If both Nf \cdot H > 	ext{thresh} and Nb \cdot H > 	ext{thresh}, use the standard formulation. If either is below the threshold, use a fading approximation. If both Nf \cdot L < 0 and Nb \cdot L < 0, a highlight may exist between samples; use the I{00} approximation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sample2dtable(table, sf, sb): """Helper to access a pre-computed 2D lookup table indexed by sf and sb.""" return table[sf][sb] def computeshading(Nf, Nb, Sf, Sb, L, H, ndelta, Ka, Kd, Ks, D, r, TI0, TI1, TI2, TI3, TI00, TI10, TI20, TI30): # 1. Compute angle alpha cosalpha = dot(Nf, Nb) alpha = acos(cosalpha) / 2.0 # 2. Compute Diffuse Coefficients NfdotL = dot(Nf, L) NbdotL = dot(Nb, L) a0 = 4.0 (cos(alpha) - 1.0) / cosalpha a1 = NbdotL - NfdotL denoma2 = r (2.0 NfdotL - NbdotL) a2 = (NbdotL - (1.0 + r) NfdotL) / denoma2 if abs(denoma2) > 1e-9 else 0.0 a3 = NfdotL / r # 3. Handle Negative Dot Products (Diffuse) if NfdotL < 0 and NbdotL < 0: Cd = 0.0 elif NfdotL > 0 and NbdotL > 0: # 4. Access Diffuse Lookup Tables I0 = sample2dtable(TI0, Sf, Sb) I1 = sample2dtable(TI1, Sf, Sb) I2 = sample2dtable(TI2, Sf, Sb) I3 = sample2dtable(TI3, Sf, Sb) # 5. Compute Diffuse Shading Cd = Kd (a0 I0 + a1 I1 + a2 I2 + a3 I3) else: # Fading approximation for mixed signs I0 = sample2dtable(TI0, Sf, Sb) I1 = sample2dtable(TI1, Sf, Sb) Cd = Kd (a0 I0 + a1 I1) # Simplified fading per source guidelines # 6. Specular Coefficients (using H) NfdotH = dot(Nf, H) NbdotH = dot(Nb, H) thresh = (ndelta - 1.0) / ndelta a0s = 4.0 (cos(alpha) - 1.0) / cosalpha a1s = NbdotH - NfdotH denoma2s = r (2.0 NfdotH - NbdotH) a2s = (NbdotH - (1.0 + r) NfdotH) / denoma2s if abs(denoma2s) > 1e-9 else 0.0 a3s = NfdotH / r # 7. Access Specular Lookup Tables I00 = sample2dtable(TI00, Sf, Sb) I10 = sample2dtable(TI10, Sf, Sb) I20 = sample2dtable(TI20, Sf, Sb) I30 = sample2dtable(TI30, Sf, Sb) # 8. Handle Negative Dot Products (Specular) if NfdotH > thresh and NbdotH > thresh: # Standard formulation Cs = Ks (I00 + ndelta (a0s I00 + a1s I10 + a2s I20 + a3s I30) - ndelta I00) elif NfdotL < 0 and NbdotL < 0: # Highlight may exist between samples; use I00 approximation Cs = Ks (I00 + ndelta (a0s I00 + a1s I10 + a2s I20 + a3s I30) - ndelta I00) else: # Fading approximation for threshold crossing I0 = sample2dtable(TI0, Sf, Sb) I1 = sample2dtable(TI1, Sf, Sb) Cs = Ks (I0 (1.0 - ndelta) + ndelta NbdotL I1) return Cd, Cs Time Complexity: The method requires four texture accesses for the diffuse term and five for the specular term (including I{00}). It is 10% to 20% slower than linear gradient interpolation due to these additional texture accesses. Memory Complexity: Uses 2D lookup tables, keeping memory usage low compared to 3D tables (which would depend on \alpha) and allowing real-time updates during transfer function changes. Tables use 16-bit unsigned short representation. Measured Performance: On an Intel Core 2Quad Q9300 and Nvidia GeForce GTX 280 at 800x800 viewport: Reference (high sub-sampling) 5.1 fps; Constant gradient 56.3 fps; Linear gradient 51.2 fps; Non-linear gradient 47.19 fps. Strengths: Reduces maximal shading error to approximately 0.3% for a 90-degree angle between normals, compared to 41% error with linear interpolation (assuming \eta(t)=1). Accurately depicts contours of specular highlights. Limitations: The quadratic curve interpolation is not exactly an arc of a circle, causing the normalization term to be potentially too low, resulting in vectors with norm > 1 and added energy around specular highlights. Mirroring gradients for negative values introduces approximation errors for slabs where one gradient is correctly oriented and the other is inverted. Origin: Proposed by Amel Guetat, Alexandre Ancel, Stephane Marchesin, and Jean-Michel Dischler in 2010. History: Builds on pre-integrated volume rendering techniques (e.g., Lum et al.) which used linear gradient interpolation. This method addresses the luminous energy loss in high-frequency gradient variations and high-frequency shading functions (like specular highlights) inherent in linear interpolation. Usage: Used in direct volume rendering with Blinn-Phong illumination and non-photorealistic models like Gooch shading. Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering with Non-Linear..., https://dpt-info.u-strasbg.fr/~dischler/papers/Vis2010.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Simplified Pre-integration
head: Pré-integração Simplificada, Simplified Pre-integrated Volume Rendering
body: Simplified pre-integration is a faster approximation of full pre-integration used in direct volume ray casting to accelerate interactive transfer function (TF) editing. It solves the performance bottleneck of computing volume rendering integrals in real-time by neglecting color attenuation inside volume slabs, allowing for the pre-computation of color and opacity contributions based on scalar values and distance. It is distinguished from full pre-integration by its omission of the exponential attenuation term within the lookup table calculation, trading visual accuracy for significant performance gains. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume texture, a transfer function (TF) mapping scalar values to color and opacity, and the distance between sample points. Output: A pre-integration lookup table (LUT) containing pre-computed color and opacity values. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored in GPU memory as a 3D texture with 8-bit precision per component. Transfer Function: Represented as a lookup table with 256 entries. Pre-integration Table: Typically stored as a 3D texture accessed by scalar values (s1, s2) on the x/y-axes and distance d on the z-axis. In the cited implementation, simplified pre-integration results are stored as 2D RGBA textures. Method Steps: 1. Pre-computation: For each pair of scalar values (s1, s2) sampled at two different positions along a ray and the distance d between them, compute the color and opacity contributions using the transfer function. 2. Simplified Integral Calculation: Compute the integral approximation by neglecting the color attenuation term. In full pre-integration, the contribution of a segment is weighted by the accumulated opacity of previous segments. In simplified pre-integration, this attenuation is disregarded. The standard volume rendering integral C = \int c(s) \alpha(s) e^{-\int0^s \alpha(t) dt} ds is approximated by removing the exponential decay factor. 3. Storage: Store the resulting color and opacity values in the lookup table. 4. Rasterization: During rendering, access the pre-integration table using the scalar values sampled at the ray segment endpoints and the segment distance. 5. Compositing: Combine the retrieved pre-computed color and opacity values into the accumulated final color for the pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesimplifiedpreintegrationtable(smin, smax, dmax, nums, numd, transferfunction): """ Pre-computes the simplified pre-integration lookup table. Args: smin, smax: Scalar value range. dmax: Maximum segment distance. nums, numd: Discretization steps for scalars and distance. transferfunction: Callable mapping scalar -> (color, opacity). Returns: LUT: 3D list of (color, opacity) tuples. """ # Initialize 3D LUT: LUT[s1idx, didx, s2idx] LUT = [[[None for in range(numd)] for in range(nums)] for in range(nums)] svalues = [smin + i (smax - smin) / (nums - 1) for i in range(nums)] dvalues = [i dmax / (numd - 1) for i in range(numd)] for i, s1 in enumerate(svalues): c1, a1 = transferfunction(s1) for j, s2 in enumerate(svalues): c2, a2 = transferfunction(s2) for k, d in enumerate(dvalues): # Simplified calculation: linear interpolation of color and opacity # without the exponential attenuation term t = d / dmax if dmax > 0 else 0.0 avgcolor = (c1 (1 - t) + c2 t) avgopacity = a1 (1 - t) + a2 t # Accumulate linearly over distance without attenuation contributioncolor = avgcolor avgopacity d contributionopacity = avgopacity d LUT[i][k][j] = (contributioncolor, contributionopacity) return LUT Parameters: TF Entries: 256 entries are typical for the transfer function lookup tables. Volume Precision: 8-bit precision is used for the 3D texture storage. Interaction Level: Simplified pre-integration is applied when multiple TFs are modified simultaneously (e.g., 36 TFs) to maintain interactivity. Full pre-integration is used when a single TF is modified. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discretization Artifacts: The method assumes a linear progression of scalar values between slices, which can introduce discretization artifacts. An adaptive sampling approach can mitigate this by adjusting the sampling rate based on volume and TF information. Color Deviation: Neglecting attenuation results in a deviation in the calculation of the total color contribution at each pixel compared to the physically correct result. Performance vs. Quality: While it guarantees superior performance, the visual quality is lower than full pre-integration. Time Complexity: Faster than full pre-integration due to the omission of the attenuation term. Memory Complexity: Stores pre-computed values in textures. The cited implementation uses 2D RGBA textures for the simplified case, whereas full pre-integration typically uses 3D textures. Performance: Guarantees superior performance, although of the same order of magnitude as efficient full pre-integration algorithms like Lum et al.. Strengths: Enables real-time interaction when modifying multiple transfer functions simultaneously. Limitations: Introduces visual artifacts due to the neglect of color attenuation and linear scalar interpolation assumptions. When to Use: Interactive editing interfaces where multiple TFs are adjusted at once. When Not to Use: Single-TF editing or final rendering where higher visual fidelity is required, as full pre-integration is applied in those contexts. Origin: The concept is described in the context of volume visualization and exploration through flexible transfer function design. It is also discussed in surveys of GPU-based volume rendering and in the specification of 1D and multidimensional transfer functions. History: The technique is presented as an alternative to full pre-integration to handle the computational cost of per-fragment operations. It is used in dual-domain interaction interfaces for TF design. Usage: Used in volume visualization tools to allow interactive modification of multiple transfer functions.
