name: Pre-integrated Volume Rendering with Dependent Texture Lookups
head: Dependent Texture Mapping for Volume Rendering, Dependent texture volume rendering, Pre-integrated Volume Rendering on GeForce3, Pre-integrated Volume Rendering with Lighting, Pre-shading
body: A hardware-accelerated volume rendering technique that uses 2D dependent textures to store pre-integrated color and opacity values for ray segments, allowing for high-quality rendering with diffuse and specular lighting without polygon extraction or additional interpolated slices. It replaces slice-by-slice compositing with slab-by-slab rendering using two adjacent slices. Unlike Simplified Pre-integration, which neglects color attenuation inside volume slabs, this method computes full pre-integration for both color and opacity, achieving full quality without the slicing artifacts of pre-shading or the performance cost of post-shading with extra slices. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset, transfer functions (defining color C(s) and opacity \alpha(s) for scalar s), lighting parameters (ambient Ia, diffuse Id, specular Is, light directions \mathbf{l}1, \mathbf{l}2), and an isovalue s{iso} (for isosurface rendering). Output: A 2D image with correct volume shading and transparency. Data Structures: 1. Source Textures (Front and Back Slices): Direct Volume Rendering (No Lighting): GLLUMINANCE8 (8-bit). Stores scalar values in the Red component. Volume Shading / Isosurfaces: GLRGBA. RGB components: Volume gradient vector \nabla V. Alpha component: First gradient component (to be routed back to Red later). Red component: Scalar value s. 2. Dependent Texture (Lookup Table): Direct Volume Rendering: GLRGBA (or GLLUMINANCE8 if no lighting). Stores pre-integrated color and opacity for every combination of front scalar sf and back scalar sb. Isosurface Rendering (Approach 1): GLRGBA. R, G, B: Pre-integrated color/transparency data. A: Interpolation value IP scaled to range [128, 255] (7-bit) for intersecting segments, or 0 for non-intersecting. Isosurface Rendering (Approach 2): GLRGBA. R, G: Pre-integrated color/transparency data. B: Interpolation value IP (8-bit). A: Transparency. Static Lighting: GLLUMINANCEALPHA. Stores pre-calculated dot products of gradient and light vectors. Consumes half the memory of RGBA textures. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-computation (Offline): For each pair of scalar values (sf, sb) representing the front and back of a slab, calculate the pre-integrated color C{pre} and opacity \alpha{pre} using the compositing equations from Simplified Pre-integration. For isosurface rendering, calculate the interpolation parameter IP = (s{iso} - sf) / (sb - sf). Since division is not available in register combiners, pre-calculate IP for all (sf, sb) pairs and store it in the dependent texture. For static lighting, pre-calculate dot products \nabla V \cdot \mathbf{l} for each voxel and store them in the dependent texture. 2. Rendering Loop (Back-to-Front): Render the volume slab-by-slab from back to front. For each slab, define a quadrilateral polygon textured with two adjacent slice textures (Front and Back). Projection: Project the texels of the two adjacent slices onto each other along the viewing ray. Adapt texture coordinates for the projected slice; retain coordinates for the other. 3. Texel Fetch and Coordinate Extraction: Fetch texels from the Front and Back source textures. Extract the scalar values sf and sb from the Red components using dot product texture shader operations with a constant vector \mathbf{v} = (1, 0, 0)^T. Stage 1: Dot product of Front texel with \mathbf{v}. Stage 2: Dot product of Back texel with \mathbf{v}. 4. Dependent Texture Lookup: Use the extracted scalars sf (as s-coordinate) and sb (as t-coordinate) to perform a dependent 2D texture lookup into the pre-integrated dependent texture. Retrieve pre-integrated color C{pre} and opacity \alpha{pre}. 5. Lighting Calculation (Optional): Volume Shading: Use the average gradient at the front and back slice for lighting. No interpolation values are stored in the dependent texture for this mode. Isosurface Shading: Reconstruct gradients: Route Alpha back to Red and rebuild gradient vectors in RGB components for both front and back slices. Interpolate normals: Use the pre-stored IP to interpolate the normal \mathbf{n} between the front and back gradients. Compute lighting: I = Ia + Id C{pre} (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}1) + Is C{pre} (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}2)^{16} where \mathbf{n} is the interpolated normal, \mathbf{l}1 is the diffuse light direction, \mathbf{l}2 is the specular light direction, and C{pre} is the pre-integrated color. Static Lighting: Interpolate pre-calculated dot products for the start and end of the ray segment in the register combiners. 6. Blending: Blend the result into the frame buffer. For direct volume rendering without lighting: Route the fetched texel through register combiners without processing and blend using glBlendFunc(GLONE, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputelookuptable(volumedata, transferfunc, isovalue=None): """ Generates the dependent texture map. """ lookuptable = empty2darray(size=(maxscalar, maxscalar), dtype=RGBA) for sf in range(maxscalar): for sb in range(maxscalar): # Calculate pre-integrated color and opacity based on slab [sf, sb] cpre, alphapre = integrateslab(sf, sb, transferfunc) if isovalue is not None: # Isosurface mode: Calculate interpolation parameter denom = sb - sf if denom == 0: ip = 0.0 else: ip = (isovalue - sf) / denom # Store IP in Alpha channel (Approach 1) scaled to 128-255 # 0 for non-intersecting, 128-255 for intersecting if sf <= isovalue <= sb or sb <= isovalue <= sf: ipscaled = int(ip 127 + 128) else: ipscaled = 0 lookuptable[sf, sb] = RGBA(cpre, alphapre, ipscaled) else: # Direct volume rendering lookuptable[sf, sb] = RGBA(cpre, alphapre) return lookuptable def renderslab(frontslicetexture, backslicetexture, lookuptexture, isovalue=None, lightingmode='dynamic'): """ Renders a single slab using dependent texture lookups. """ # 1. Project back slice onto front slice (or vice versa) # Adjust texture coordinates for projection projcoords = projectcoordinates(frontslicetexture, backslicetexture) # 2. Fetch scalars using dot product with v=(1,0,0) # Stage 1: Extract sf from front texel sf = dotproduct(frontslicetexture.texel(projcoords), (1, 0, 0)) # Stage 2: Extract sb from back texel sb = dotproduct(backslicetexture.texel(projcoords), (1, 0, 0)) # 3. Dependent Texture Lookup # Use sf as s-coord, sb as t-coord preintegrated = lookuptexture.lookup(sf, sb) cpre = preintegrated.rgb alphapre = preintegrated.a # 4. Lighting (if applicable) if lightingmode == 'dynamic' and isovalue is not None: # Reconstruct gradients from source textures gradf = reconstructgradient(frontslicetexture.texel(projcoords)) gradb = reconstructgradient(backslicetexture.texel(projcoords)) # Retrieve IP from lookup texture alpha (Approach 1) ipraw = preintegrated.a # Map back to 0-1 range (inverse of scaling) if ipraw > 0: ip = (ipraw - 128) / 127.0 else: ip = 0.0 # Interpolate normal n = interpolatevector(gradf, gradb, ip) # Compute lighting # Note: Specular power is fixed at 16 in implementation diffuseterm = dotproduct(n, lightdirdiffuse) specularterm = dotproduct(n, lightdirspecular) 16 finalcolor = ambient + diffuse cpre diffuseterm + specular cpre specularterm alpha = alphapre else: finalcolor = cpre alpha = alphapre # 5. Blend blendintoframebuffer(finalcolor, alpha) Parameters: Specular Power: 16. Lookup Table Dimensionality: 2D, depending on front and back scalar values, assuming constant ray segment length. Texture Bit Depth: 8-bit for direct volume rendering; 32-bit for isosurface rendering. Constant Vector for Scalar Extraction: \mathbf{v} = (1, 0, 0)^T. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division in Register Combiners: Calculating IP on-the-fly requires division, which is unavailable. Solution: Pre-calculate IP for all scalar combinations. Texture Operation Limit: NVIDIA’s texture shader allows only four operations. Two are used for dot products, leaving only one for dependent lookup. Solution: Store IP in the same dependent texture used for color/opacity. Double-Rendering of Semi-Transparent Isosurfaces: Pixels may be rendered twice if the surface intersects exactly at the front slice of one slab and the back slice of the next. Solution: Use the OpenGL stencil buffer. Clear stencil for each slab. Render slab into stencil using a second dependent texture that selects only pixels where the isosurface intersects at the front slice. In the next slab, use stencil test to only set pixels not rendered previously. This works only for a single semi-transparent isosurface. Variable Ray Segment Lengths: For object-aligned slices, ray segment lengths vary with volume rotation (max factor \sqrt{3}). Solution: Use a set of 2D lookup tables for different lengths. For unequal slice distances, different lookup textures must be calculated. Transparency Constraint (Approach 1): Storing IP in Alpha makes transparency constant. Solution: Scale Alpha by 2 to get 1.0 for intersecting segments and 0 otherwise, then multiply by constant transparency. Interpolation Range Mapping: IP stored in range 0.5-1.0 (after scaling) requires specific input mappings. Solution: Use GLHALFBIASNORMALNV and GLUNSIGNEDINVENTNV for general combiner 2 to map ranges 0-0.5 and 0.5-0, then scale result by 2. Time Complexity: Does not depend on the number of isosurfaces nor the definition of the transfer functions. Memory Complexity: Dependent textures consume significant memory. RGBA textures for dynamic lighting consume more memory than LUMINANCEALPHA for static lighting (half the memory). Performance (NVIDIA GeForce3, 64 MB DDR SDRAM, 200 MHz, 4x AGP, 512x512 viewport): Direct Volume Rendering: ~90 fps (16³), ~50 fps (32³), ~21 fps (64³), ~13 fps (128³), ~4 fps (256³). Isosurface Rendering: ~70 fps (16³), ~40 fps (32³), ~21 fps (64³), ~11 fps (128³), ~1 fps (256³). Strengths: High image quality without additional interpolated slices; interactive transfer function updates are fast for isosurfaces; supports arbitrary number of isosurfaces without performance penalty. Limitations: Requires specific hardware extensions (NVIDIA texture shader, register combiners); 3D texture support was not available in driver releases at the time, necessitating 2D workarounds; stencil buffer correction is limited to a single semi-transparent isosurface. When to Use: When high-quality volume rendering with lighting is required on hardware supporting dependent texture lookups, and interactive transfer function updates are needed. When Not to Use: On hardware lacking the required OpenGL extensions or 3D texture support; when multiple semi-transparent isosurfaces need to be rendered simultaneously with the stencil correction. Originated in a hardware-accelerated implementation on the NVIDIA GeForce3 graphics chip. The method leverages the OpenGL texture shader extension and register combiners, which were merged into Microsoft’s DirectX8 pixel shader API, though the DirectX8 API was found to be more restrictive (specifically regarding dot product references). The approach was developed to overcome the limitations of pre-shading (slicing artifacts) and post-shading (need for additional slices). High-Quality Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering Using..., https://www3.cs.stonybrook.edu/~mueller/teaching/cse616/engel.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Pre-integrated Volume Rendering at Clip Boundaries
head: Boundary layer correction, Clipping with pre-integrated volume rendering
body: This method corrects rendering artifacts that occur at clip boundaries when using pre-integrated volume rendering with low sampling rates. It computes the optical contribution of the ray segment between a clipping surface and the first volume slice behind it, avoiding the need for interleaved rendering or complex boundary layer models. It differs from sibling methods by specifically addressing the discontinuity in sampling distance at clip planes rather than general gradient interpolation errors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Clipping surface geometry, volume data, viewing ray, clipping plane position. Outputs: Correctly composited color and opacity for pixels intersecting the clip boundary. Data Structures: 3D Lookup Table (LUT): Stores pre-integrated color and opacity values. Dimensions correspond to scalar values vP, vQ, and projected sampling distance d'. Layout: Not explicitly defined in sources, but implied to be indexed by normalized scalar values and distance. Size: Only a few slices along the length dimension (d') are needed for a good approximation. Steps: 1. Determine Clip Order: Check if the clipped volume is behind or in front of the clipping surface. 2. Render Order: If volume is behind the clipping surface: Render the clipping surface first, then the clipped volume. If volume is in front of the clipping surface: Render the volume first, then the clipping surface. 3. Compute Intersection Point Q: For a point P on the clipping surface, find the intersection Q of the viewing ray passing through P with the first proxy polygon (volume slice) behind P. 4. Lookup Scalar Values: Retrieve the scalar data values vP at point P and vQ at point Q. 5. Compute Projected Sampling Distance d': Calculate the projection of the ray segment length between P and Q onto the viewing ray direction. Do not compute the actual Euclidean length. Formula: d' = \text{projection of } \vec{PQ} \text{ onto viewing ray}. Note: d' varies between 0 and d (the standard sampling distance) at clip boundaries. 6. Lookup Pre-integrated Values: Use the 3D LUT to find the corresponding color and opacity for inputs (vP, vQ, d'). 7. Composite: Apply the retrieved color and opacity to the fragment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderclipboundary(P, Q, viewingraydirection, volumedata, cliplut): """ Computes the pre-integrated contribution for a clip boundary segment. Args: P: Point on the clipping surface. Q: Intersection of the viewing ray through P with the first volume slice. viewingraydirection: Normalized vector of the viewing ray. volumedata: Accessor for scalar values in the volume. cliplut: 3D lookup table for pre-integrated color/opacity. Returns: color: Pre-integrated color for the segment. opacity: Pre-integrated opacity for the segment. """ # Step 1: Lookup scalar values at P and Q vP = volumedata.sample(P) vQ = volumedata.sample(Q) # Step 2: Compute projected sampling distance d' # Calculate the vector from P to Q segmentvector = Q - P # Project segmentvector onto the viewing ray direction # This avoids calculating the actual Euclidean length dprime = dot(segmentvector, viewingraydirection) # Step 3: Lookup pre-integrated values from the 3D LUT # The LUT is indexed by vP, vQ, and d' # Note: d' is normalized or scaled appropriately for the LUT dimensions color, opacity = cliplut.lookup(vP, vQ, dprime) return color, opacity def renderclipgeometry(clippingsurface, volume, viewingraydirection, cliplut): """ Main rendering pass for the clipping surface. """ for each pixel on clippingsurface: P = position of pixel on surface # Find intersection Q with the first proxy polygon behind P # This requires ray-tracing against the volume's proxy geometry Q = findfirstintersection(P, viewingraydirection, volume.proxypolygons) if Q is valid: color, opacity = renderclipboundary(P, Q, viewingraydirection, volume.data, cliplut) # Composite color and opacity into the frame buffer compositeframebuffer(color, opacity) Parameters: LUT Size (Length Dimension): Only a few slices are needed for a good approximation. Sampling Distance d: The standard sampling distance used in the rest of the volume. At clip boundaries, d' varies between 0 and d. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Abrupt Changes: At clip boundaries, the sampling distance d' varies between 0 and d with abrupt changes across slices, unlike the rest of the volume where view-aligned slicing keeps it constant. This necessitates the 3D LUT rather than a 2D one. Volume Position: The algorithm must handle both cases: volume behind the clip surface (render surface first) and volume in front (render volume first). Projection Approximation: Using the projected length instead of the actual length is an approximation that is generally acceptable but must be consistent with the rest of the rendering pipeline. Time Complexity: Adds minimal overhead on current GPUs, as it involves a single additional lookup and simple vector projection per pixel at the boundary. Memory Complexity: Requires a 3D lookup table. However, the length dimension is small, keeping memory usage low. Strengths: Avoids the need for interleaved rendering of volume and clip surface required by optical models with boundary layers. Correctly shows relationships between features (e.g., distances between isosurfaces). Limitations: Requires ray-tracing against proxy polygons to find Q, which may add complexity to the rendering pipeline. When to Use: When using pre-integrated volume rendering with low sampling rates and clipping is required. This technique was proposed as an alternative to the optical model for clipping based on the combination of volume and surface shading, which introduces a boundary layer of finite thickness around the clip object. The boundary layer approach requires interleaved rendering, which is complex. This method was developed to support interactive lenses and focus-and-context interfaces in volume rendering applications. A Focus and Context Interface for Interactive Volume Rendering, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~ikits/publications/IkitsUnpublished04.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Binary Swap Compositing
head: Binary Split Compositing, Binary Swap z-buffer reduction, Binary-Swap Method, MPI Binary-Swap, binary-swap merging
body: Binary Swap Compositing is a parallel image compositing scheme for distributed-memory volume rendering that reduces network congestion by dividing communication between processors over multiple rounds. Unlike naive binary compositing where many processors become idle at the top of the tree, Binary Swap ensures every processor participates in all stages of the compositing process by splitting the image plane into two pieces and having each processor take responsibility for one piece during exchange and compositing. It is particularly suitable for massively parallel processing because it keeps all processors busy and decreases the image size for sending/compositing at each stage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: N processors, where N is the number of processors participating in the compositing tree. Each processor p holds a local sub-image Ip generated by independent ray-tracing of its assigned sub-volume. The number of processors N must be a perfect power of two (N = 2^K) for the standard implementation. Output: Each processor holds exactly 1/N of the final composited image. Data Structures: Image Plane: Represented as a 2D array of pixels. Each pixel contains color (Cr, Cg, Cb) and opacity \alpha. Partner Index: Calculated using bitwise XOR. For a processor with ID self and current stride, the partner is partner = self XOR stride. Pairing Graph (Optional Implementation Detail): A 3D array pair[level][zdiv][2] can be used to store the compositing graph, where level is \log2(zdiv), pair[l][j][0] stores the partner rank index for rank j at level l, and pair[l][j][1] stores the role (0 for first/sender, 1 for second/receiver). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the image plane on each processor to the entire image area (or the sub-image generated by local ray-tracing). 2. Loop Setup: Calculate the number of levels in the binary swap tree: L = \log2 N. Initialize stride to 1. 3. Iteration: Iterate through L phases (or \log2(\text{nproc}) rounds). In each phase: a. Partner Calculation: Calculate the partner processor index: partner = self XOR stride. b. Subdivision: Subdivide the current image plane held by the processor into two equal pieces (e.g., left/right halves or top/bottom halves). The subdivision direction alternates between stages (e.g., X-axis in the first stage, Y-axis in the second). c. Exchange: Exchange the relevant half-image data with the calculated partner processor. Each processor sends one half of its image to the partner and receives the partner's corresponding half. d. Compositing: Composite the part of the remaining image plane held by the processor with the image data received from the partner using the standard front-to-back over operator. Let C{local}, \alpha{local} be the color and opacity of the kept half. Let C{recv}, \alpha{recv} be the color and opacity of the received half. The new accumulated color and opacity for the kept half are updated as: C{new} = C{local} + (1 - \alpha{local}) \alpha{recv} C{recv} \alpha{new} = \alpha{local} + (1 - \alpha{local}) \alpha{recv} Note: The specific assignment of which half is "kept" and which is "received" depends on the role (0 or 1) defined in the pairing graph or the XOR result. 4. Stride Update: Update the stride for the next phase by multiplying it by 2: stride = 2. 5. Termination: After \log2 N stages, compositing completes. Each processor holds exactly 1/N of the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def binaryswapcompositing(selfid, nproc, localimage): """ Performs Binary Swap Compositing. Args: selfid (int): The unique ID of the current processor (0 to nproc-1). nproc (int): Total number of processors (must be a power of 2). localimage (list of lists): 2D array of pixels, each pixel is (color: tuple, opacity: float). Returns: list of lists: The portion of the final image assigned to this processor. """ currentimage = localimage stride = 1 while stride < nproc: # Calculate partner using XOR partnerid = selfid ^ stride # Alternate subdivision direction: X for odd strides, Y for even strides if stride % 2 == 1: # Split along X (Left/Right) midx = len(currentimage[0]) // 2 keeppiece = [row[:midx] for row in currentimage] sendpiece = [row[midx:] for row in currentimage] else: # Split along Y (Top/Bottom) midy = len(currentimage) // 2 keeppiece = currentimage[:midy] sendpiece = currentimage[midy:] # The sources do not specify the exact network communication primitives. # In practice, use a blocking two-way communication like MPISendrecv(partnerid, sendpiece, recvpiece). # recvpiece is populated by the network call. # Composite kept piece with received piece using front-to-back over operator currentimage = compositeover(keeppiece, recvpiece) stride = 2 return currentimage def compositeover(front, back): """ Composites two image pieces using the front-to-back over operator. Assumes 'front' is closer to the camera than 'back'. """ result = [] for y in range(len(front)): row = [] for x in range(len(front[0])): cf, af = front[y][x] cb, ab = back[y][x] transmittance = 1.0 - af cnew = tuple(cf[i] + transmittance ab cb[i] for i in range(3)) anew = min(1.0, af + transmittance ab) row.append((cnew, anew)) result.append(row) return result Parameters: nproc: The total number of processors participating in the compositing tree. Must be a perfect power of two. p: Number of pixels in the final image. g: Transmitting time per pixel. tc: Computing time per pixel. o: Communication overhead per transmission. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Power of Two Restriction: The algorithm requires the number of processors to be a power of two. If nproc is not a perfect power of two, the simple XOR partner calculation fails. The algorithm can be generalized by keeping a full (but not necessarily complete) binary tree, requiring additional complexity in partner computation and leaving some processors idle during the first phase. Synchronization Overhead: There is a synchronization overhead after each round. Load Imbalance: On heterogeneous workstation networks, achieving linear speedup is difficult due to load imbalance. Static load balancing can be addressed by uneven data subdivision based on predicted machine capacity. Sparsity: Only non-blank pixels affect composited results. The BS method exploits sparsity by using a bounding rectangle enclosing the non-blank region. Every processor composites and transmits only within this bounding rectangle. Local Pixel Merging is a compositing method where the composition operation for each local pixel involves the merging of k sorted ray-segment lists, where k denotes the number of distinct processors that generated ray-segments for that particular pixel. It partitions the screen into K subregions such that each processor is responsible for producing the final image of a distinct subregion through local pixel merging. A binary heap is used for the k-way merging of ray-segment lists from the RayBuffer structures. This method is used when projection areas of local subvolumes overlap on the image screen, requiring a global merge operation on ray-segment lists of local RayBuffer structures to composite ray-segments of each pixel in visibility order for the final image. Reduced Binary Swap is a variant of Binary Swap that uses only 2^{K-1} processors for compositing when N is not a power-of-two (2^{K-1} < N < 2^K). It requires extra image data exchange in the reduction stage, sending images from N - 2^{K-1} processors to the remaining 2^{K-1} processors. This variant nearly doubles the image blending workload for a large number of processors compared to standard Binary Swap. Time and Memory Complexity: Messages: Reduces the number of messages exchanged from N \times (N - 1) (direct send) to N \log N. Latency: l{sendrecv} \times \log2 N. Bandwidth: (1/B{sendrecv}) \times P. Blending: (1/B{blend}) \times 2 \times P \times (1 - 1/N). Average Compositing Time: Bounded by t{BS} \leq p (g + tc) \cdot 2.43 n^{-2/3} + o \cdot \log n, where n is the number of processors, p is the number of pixels, g is transmitting time per pixel, tc is computing time per pixel, and o is communication overhead per transmission. The time complexity is O(N/2 + N/4 +... + N/P) where N is the number of pixels per processor and P is the number of processors. In the limit as P \to \infty, this reduces to O(N) time. Measured Performance: On a CM-5 with 512 nodes, rendering a 512x512 head dataset took 36.3685 seconds for rendering and 0.63320 seconds for compositing. On a CM-5 with 512 nodes, rendering a 512x512 vessel dataset took 26.0314 seconds for rendering and 0.46060 seconds for compositing. On a CM-5 with 512 nodes, rendering a 512x512 vorticity dataset took 48.2005 seconds for rendering and 0.71520 seconds for compositing. On a CM-5 with 512 nodes, compositing the vorticity dataset took 0.3310 seconds with 0.0097 seconds spent on communication. On a PVM network with 32 workstations, rendering a 512x512 head dataset took 8.4990 seconds for rendering and 4.3550 seconds for compositing. On a PVM network with 32 workstations, compositing the vorticity dataset took 4.5180 seconds with 4.4990 seconds spent on communication. Compositing speedup from 32 to 512 nodes was only 1.46 for 64x64 images. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Keeps all processors busy, decreasing image size for sending/compositing makes the process efficient, suitable for massively parallel processing. Limitations: Requires power-of-two processors, synchronization overhead, load imbalance on heterogeneous networks. When to Use: Use when running on massively parallel computers with a power-of-two number of processors and when interactive rendering rates are desired. Use when network congestion is a concern and a hierarchical communication scheme is preferred over all-to-all patterns. When Not to Use: Do not use if the number of processors is not a power of two and the overhead of Reduced Binary Swap or 2-3 Swap is unacceptable. Do not use if the image size is very small (e.g., 64x64) where communication overhead dominates. Binary Swap Compositing was introduced as a generalization of the binary compositing method to avoid the bottleneck of idle processors in massively parallel processing. It was developed by researchers implementing distributed volume rendering algorithms on systems like the CM-5 and networked workstations. The method is particularly suitable for massively parallel processing because it keeps all processors busy and uses decreasing image sizes for efficiency. It differs from naive binary compositing by keeping all processors active throughout the process, whereas binary compositing leaves many processors idle as the tree height increases. name: Screen-space Post-processing
head: Composite Shader, Compositing/Post-Processing Pipeline, Screen Post-Processing
body: Screen-space post-processing is a full-screen rendering stage that applies aspect-ratio preserving UV covering, luminance-based bright passes, color grading, a 17-tap box blur, and 1-LSB dithering to a scene texture to produce a display-ready image. It differs from direct volume compositing methods by operating entirely in screen space on the final display image rather than during ray traversal, allowing for complex aesthetic effects like bloom and vignette without modifying the volume rendering pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a source scene texture (typically the result of the volume rendering or main scene pass) and a set of uniform parameters controlling the effects. The output is a final composited image. Data Structures: The implementation relies on a specific uniform buffer layout and vertex attributes for a full-screen quad pass. Uniforms Struct: viewproj: mat4x4<f32> invviewproj: mat4x4<f32> camerapos: vec3<f32> time: f32 sunposition: vec3<f32> isunderwater: f32 screensize: vec2<f32> waterlevel: f32 moonposition: vec3<f32> moonintensity: f32 winddirx: f32 winddirz: f32 windspeed: f32 rainfactor: f32 skyvisibility: f32 menublur: f32 (Clamped to [0.0, 1.0]) paduniforms: f32 Vertex Attributes: positions: array<vec2<f32>, 3> = {(-1.0, -1.0), (3.0, -1.0), (-1.0, 3.0)} uvs: array<vec2<f32>, 3> = {(0.0, 1.0), (2.0, 1.0), (0.0, -1.0)} Steps: 1. UV Covering: Adjust UVs to preserve aspect ratio if the screen and texture dimensions differ. Compute textureaspect = texturesize.x / max(texturesize.y, 1.0) and screenaspect = screensize.x / max(screensize.y, 1.0). If screenaspect > textureaspect: covered.y = 0.5 + (uv.y - 0.5) (textureaspect / screenaspect). Else: covered.x = 0.5 + (uv.x - 0.5) (screenaspect / textureaspect). 2. Luminance Calculation: Compute the luminance of the input color. luma = dot(color, vec3(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722)). 3. Bright Pass: Isolate bright regions for bloom. weight = smoothstep(0.68, 0.96, luminance(color)). output = color weight. 4. Vignette: Apply a radial darkening effect, softened by menublur. centered = uv 2.0 - 1.0. centered.x = screensize.x / max(screensize.y, 1.0). vignette = 1.0 - smoothstep(0.42, 1.82, dot(centered, centered)) mix(0.045, 0.025, blur). output = clamp(color vignette, vec3(0.0), vec3(1.0)). 5. Underwater Refraction (Conditional): If isunderwater > 0.5 and blur < 0.5, split RGB channels to simulate refraction. radial = (sampleuv - vec2(0.5)) 1.6. shift = radial texel (1.2 + 0.25 sin(time 0.8)). color.r = samplescene(sampleuv + shift).r. color.b = samplescene(sampleuv - shift).b. color = mix(color, color vec3(0.83, 0.96, 1.08), 0.28). 6. Cross-Shaped Bloom: Add a cross-shaped blur to bright regions. bloomradius = texel 3.25. bloom = brightpass(color) 0.28. Add 4 neighbors at ±bloomradius.x/y with weight 0.18 each. color += bloom mix(0.105, 0.025, blur). 7. 17-Tap Box Blur: Apply a wide box blur controlled by blur intensity. If blur > 0.001:. blurred = color 0.08. Add neighbors at texel (±4,0), (0,±4) with weight 0.08. Add neighbors at texel (±5.5, ±5.5) with weight 0.07. Add neighbors at texel (±10,0), (0,±10) with weight 0.05. Add neighbors at texel (±14, ±14) with weight 0.03. color = mix(color, blurred 0.82, blur). 8. Dithering: Add 1-LSB dithering to reduce banding. pixel = floor(uv max(screensize, vec2(1.0))). screenhash = fract(sin(dot(pixel, vec2(12.9898, 78.233))) 43758.5453). dither = (screenhash - 0.5) / 255.0. color = clamp(color + vec3(dither), vec3(0.0), vec3(1.0)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def screenspacepostprocessing(uv, scenetexture, uniforms): """ Applies full-screen post-processing effects to a single pixel. uv: vec2 in [0, 1] scenetexture: Texture2D representing the input scene. uniforms: Struct containing screensize, menublur, isunderwater, time, etc. """ screensize = uniforms.screensize menublur = clamp(uniforms.menublur, 0.0, 1.0) isunderwater = uniforms.isunderwater time = uniforms.time # 1. UV Covering textureaspect = scenetexture.width / max(scenetexture.height, 1.0) screenaspect = screensize.x / max(screensize.y, 1.0) covereduv = uv if screenaspect > textureaspect: covereduv.y = 0.5 + (uv.y - 0.5) (textureaspect / screenaspect) else: covereduv.x = 0.5 + (uv.x - 0.5) (screenaspect / textureaspect) # Sample scene color color = scenetexture.sample(covereduv) # 2. Luminance luma = dot(color, vec3(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722)) # 3. Bright Pass weight = smoothstep(0.68, 0.96, luma) brightpasscolor = color weight # 4. Vignette centered = uv 2.0 - 1.0 centered.x = screensize.x / max(screensize.y, 1.0) vignettefactor = 1.0 - smoothstep(0.42, 1.82, dot(centered, centered)) mix(0.045, 0.025, menublur) color = clamp(color vignettefactor, vec3(0.0), vec3(1.0)) # 5. Underwater Refraction if isunderwater > 0.5 and menublur < 0.5: texel = vec2(1.0 / scenetexture.width, 1.0 / scenetexture.height) radial = (covereduv - vec2(0.5)) 1.6 shift = radial texel (1.2 + 0.25 sin(time 0.8)) rval = scenetexture.sample(covereduv + shift).r bval = scenetexture.sample(covereduv - shift).b color.r = rval color.b = bval color = mix(color, color vec3(0.83, 0.96, 1.08), 0.28) # 6. Cross-Shaped Bloom texel = vec2(1.0 / scenetexture.width, 1.0 / scenetexture.height) bloomradius = texel 3.25 # Sample 4 neighbors for cross shape bloomsum = vec3(0.0) bloomsum += scenetexture.sample(covereduv + vec2(bloomradius.x, 0.0)) bloomsum += scenetexture.sample(covereduv - vec2(bloomradius.x, 0.0)) bloomsum += scenetexture.sample(covereduv + vec2(0.0, bloomradius.y)) bloomsum += scenetexture.sample(covereduv - vec2(0.0, bloomradius.y)) bloom = (brightpasscolor 0.28) + (bloomsum 0.18) color += bloom mix(0.105, 0.025, menublur) # 7. 17-Tap Box Blur if menublur > 0.001: blurred = color 0.08 # Neighbors at (±4,0), (0,±4) weight 0.08 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv + vec2(texel.x 4, 0.0)) 0.08 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv - vec2(texel.x 4, 0.0)) 0.08 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv + vec2(0.0, texel.y 4)) 0.08 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv - vec2(0.0, texel.y 4)) 0.08 # Neighbors at (±5.5, ±5.5) weight 0.07 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv + vec2(texel.x 5.5, texel.y 5.5)) 0.07 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv + vec2(texel.x 5.5, -texel.y 5.5)) 0.07 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv - vec2(texel.x 5.5, texel.y 5.5)) 0.07 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv - vec2(texel.x 5.5, -texel.y 5.5)) 0.07 # Neighbors at (±10,0), (0,±10) weight 0.05 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv + vec2(texel.x 10, 0.0)) 0.05 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv - vec2(texel.x 10, 0.0)) 0.05 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv + vec2(0.0, texel.y 10)) 0.05 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv - vec2(0.0, texel.y 10)) 0.05 # Neighbors at (±14, ±14) weight 0.03 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv + vec2(texel.x 14, texel.y 14)) 0.03 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv + vec2(texel.x 14, -texel.y 14)) 0.03 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv - vec2(texel.x 14, texel.y 14)) 0.03 blurred += scenetexture.sample(covereduv - vec2(texel.x 14, -texel.y 14)) 0.03 color = mix(color, blurred 0.82, menublur) # 8. Dithering pixel = floor(uv max(screensize, vec2(1.0))) screenhash = fract(sin(dot(pixel, vec2(12.9898, 78.233))) 43758.5453) dither = (screenhash - 0.5) / 255.0 color = clamp(color + vec3(dither), vec3(0.0), vec3(1.0)) return color Parameters: menublur: f32, controls blur intensity and vignette softening. Clamped to [0.0, 1.0] in fragment shader. isunderwater: f32, enables RGB channel splitting refraction when > 0.5 and blur < 0.5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aspect Ratio Mismatch: If screenaspect and textureaspect differ significantly, the UV covering step ensures the image is letterboxed or pillarboxed without distortion. Underwater Condition: The refraction effect is only applied if isunderwater > 0.5 AND blur < 0.5, preventing visual artifacts when heavy blurring is already active. Cloud Compositing & Tone Mapping blends resolved volumetric cloud radiance and transmittance with sky and ground background environments, then applies ACES-like tone mapping and gamma encoding to produce a display-ready image. It differs from general HDR post-processing pipelines by integrating scene-specific background synthesis (sun disc, horizon gradients, checkerboard ground) directly into the compositing step, rather than treating the background as a pre-computed texture. A 16-bit floating-point HDR rendering pipeline for scene post-processing. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Cloud Compositing & Tone Mapping by integrating bloom and chromatic distortion directly into the tone-mapping fragment shader rather than using separate library passes, and from Bloom by handling the bloom compositing within the same pass as tone mapping. Bloom is a screen-space post-processing effect that enhances the perception of brightness by isolating luminous regions via a soft threshold, blurring them across a pyramid of scales, and adding the result back to the original image. It differs from direct compositing methods by operating entirely in screen space on the final display image rather than during ray traversal. Tilt-Shift Post-Processing is a screen-space effect that simulates the shallow depth-of-field of a miniature model by keeping a horizontal band of the frame sharp while applying increasing Gaussian blur to areas above and below it, accompanied by increased color saturation. It distinguishes itself from general blur effects by its spatially varying strength profile (sharp band with falloff) and its specific aesthetic goal of mimicking macro photography of large-scale scenes. It is typically applied after the main scene render but before UI elements to ensure menus and text remain crisp. A post-processing step to upscale and blend volumetric lighting results with the scene, using bilateral upsampling for resolution enhancement and dual-source blending for attenuation. It performs bilateral upsampling on the resolved accumulation buffer, particularly helpful at 1/4 resolution, then additively blends the resolved/filtered output with the scene. It uses dual-source blending to attenuate the result based on medium density and depth. Frustum Raycasting and Blending is a screen-space post-processing technique that casts rays from the camera through each pixel to intersect a cloud volume bounding box, blending the resulting cloud color with the original scene color. It addresses the artifacts of standard alpha blending (incorrect transparency order) and alpha testing (hard edges) by performing a screen-space depth-difference check during the final compositing pass. It differs from Cloud Compositing & Tone Mapping by explicitly using ray-box intersection logic in the fragment shader rather than pre-composited textures, and from HDR Post-Processing Pipeline by focusing on volumetric occlusion rather than luminance scaling. Not given in the sources. The specific implementation described here originates from the "Minerust" project, a voxel-based game engine using wgpu. name: Frustum Raycasting and Blending
head: FragmentProgram, OnRenderImage
body: Frustum Raycasting and Blending is a screen-space post-processing technique that casts rays from the camera through each pixel, intersects them with a cloud volume bounding box, and blends the resulting cloud color with the original scene color. It operates as a full-screen fragment shader pass that runs after the main scene render. Inputs and Outputs: The shader receives the scene texture (MainTex), UV coordinates (input.uv), camera world position (CameraWorldPosition), cloud volume bounds (CloudVolumeMinBound, CloudVolumeMaxBound), and frustum corners (FrustumCornerTR, FrustumCornerBR). The C# script additionally passes the density threshold, scatter factor, and wind offset. The output is the final blended color for each fragment. Data Structures: Positions, directions, and bounds use Vector3 types. UV coordinates use Vector2 types. Distances, color components, and thresholds use float types. Steps: First, the shader samples the original scene color from MainTex using the fragment's UV coordinates. Second, it sets the ray origin to the camera's world position CameraWorldPosition. Third, it calculates the ray direction vector from the camera to the current pixel and normalizes it. Fourth, it calculates the ray-box intersection of the ray (O, D) with the axis-aligned bounding box defined by CloudVolumeMinBound and CloudVolumeMaxBound, returning entry distance t{entry} and exit distance t{exit}. Fifth, if t{entry} < t{exit}, it marches along the ray segment [t{entry}, t{exit}] to sample the cloud density and compute the cloud color. Sixth, if an intersection occurred, it blends the cloud color with the scene color using the cloud's alpha via lerp(originalColour, cloudColour, cloudColour.a). If no intersection occurred, it returns the original scene color. Pseudocode: The following Python-like implementation combines the shader logic and helper routines. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def FrustumRaycastBlending(uv, cameraPos, frustumCorners, boundsMin, boundsMax, densityThreshold, scatterFactor, windOffset): # Compute ray direction from screen UV and frustum corners # Standard full-screen quad mapping assumes corners are ordered [BL, BR, TL, TR] pixelWorld = lerp(lerp(frustumCorners[0], frustumCorners[1], uv.x), lerp(frustumCorners[2], frustumCorners[3], uv.x), uv.y) direction = normalize(pixelWorld - cameraPos) origin = cameraPos # Ray-box intersection tEntry, tExit = RayBoxIntersection(origin, direction, boundsMin, boundsMax) if tEntry < tExit: cloudColour = MarchDensity(tEntry, tExit, origin, direction, boundsMin, boundsMax, densityThreshold, scatterFactor, windOffset) return lerp(sceneColour, cloudColour, cloudColour.a) else: return sceneColour def RayBoxIntersection(origin, direction, boundsMin, boundsMax): # Standard slab method for AABB intersection tMin = (boundsMin - origin) / direction tMax = (boundsMax - origin) / direction t1 = min(tMin, tMax) t2 = max(tMin, tMax) tEntry = max(t1.x, t1.y, t1.z) tExit = min(t2.x, t2.y, t2.z) return tEntry, tExit def MarchDensity(tEntry, tExit, origin, direction, boundsMin, boundsMax, densityThreshold, scatterFactor, windOffset): # Step through the volume segment steps = 32 # Not given in the sources. stepSize = (tExit - tEntry) / steps accumulatedDensity = 0.0 accumulatedColor = vec3(0.0) for i in range(steps): t = tEntry + i stepSize samplePos = origin + direction t # Sample 3D noise (e.g., Perlin noise) scaled by frequency noiseVal = SampleNoise(samplePos + windOffset) density = noiseVal scatterFactor accumulatedDensity += density if accumulatedDensity > densityThreshold: break accumulatedColor += density alpha = clamp(accumulatedDensity, 0.0, 1.0) return vec4(accumulatedColor, alpha) C# Script Setup: The Unity script initializes the material parameters each frame. It retrieves the cloud volume bounds from a scene object's Renderer.bounds component. It calculates the frustum corners at the far clip plane using Camera.CalculateFrustumCorners. It transforms these corners from camera space to world space using camera.transform.TransformDirection. It passes the transformed corners to the shader as FrustumCornerTR and FrustumCornerBR. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. void OnRenderImage(RenderTexture source, RenderTexture destination) { if (CloudShaderMaterial != null && CloudVolumeBounds != null) { Bounds bounds = CloudVolumeBounds.GetComponent<Renderer>().bounds; CloudShaderMaterial.SetVector("CloudVolumeMinBound", bounds.min); CloudShaderMaterial.SetVector("CloudVolumeMaxBound", bounds.max); CloudShaderMaterial.SetFloat("DensityThreshold", densityThreshold); CloudShaderMaterial.SetFloat("ScatterFactor", scatterFactor); Camera cam = GetComponent<Camera>(); Vector3[] corners = new Vector3[4]; cam.CalculateFrustumCorners(new Rect(0, 0, 1, 1), cam.farClipPlane, Camera.MonoOrStereoscopicEye.Mono, corners); for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) { corners[i] = cam.transform.TransformDirection(corners[i]); } CloudShaderMaterial.SetVector("FrustumCornerTR", corners[2]); CloudShaderMaterial.SetVector("FrustumCornerBR", corners[3]); } Graphics.Blit(source, destination, CloudShaderMaterial); } Parameters: The density threshold controls the accumulation cutoff for opacity. The scatter factor scales the sampled noise values to determine opacity and color contribution. The wind speed increments a global offset each frame to animate the noise sampling coordinates. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray-box intersection calculations can suffer from floating-point precision errors near the box boundaries. If the camera is inside the cloud volume, t{entry} may be negative and requires clamping to zero. Ray marching is computationally expensive, so the step count must be limited to maintain performance. A post-processing technique that blends rendered clouds with the scene by using depth information from opaque objects and the cloud layer to determine visibility and occlusion. It prevents clouds from appearing in front of opaque objects incorrectly and is chosen when correct occlusion is critical. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of marching steps. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, excluding the texture memory for the noise volume. Performance: Dependent on the resolution and the number of marching steps. Strengths: Provides accurate occlusion and blending without pre-computation. Limitations: Computationally intensive and requires careful parameter tuning. When to Use: When high-quality volumetric clouds are needed and performance allows for per-pixel ray marching. When Not to Use: When performance is critical or the cloud volume is static and can be pre-composited. This method originates from a volumetric cloud renderer implementation designed for the Unity engine. It builds on direct volume ray casting principles and integrates into the OnRenderImage post-processing pipeline. The noise generation relies on a 3D Perlin noise implementation that uses a permutation lookup table, gradient hashing, and smooth interpolation. ldarnbr/volumetric-cloud-renderer, https://github.com/ldarnbr/volumetric-cloud-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Cloud-Scene Occlusion Blending
head: AlphaBlendWithDepthDiff, Mix Cloud With Scenes
body: Cloud-Scene Occlusion Blending is a post-processing technique that blends rendered clouds with the scene by using depth information from opaque objects and the cloud layer to determine visibility and occlusion, preventing clouds from appearing in front of opaque objects incorrectly. It addresses the artifacts of standard alpha blending (incorrect transparency order) and alpha testing (hard edges) by performing a screen-space depth-difference check during the final compositing pass. The method operates in three phases: buffer preparation, cloud rendering, and screen-space compositing. Inputs: Scene color and depth from opaque objects (rendered before clouds). Cloud color and depth (rendered after opaque objects). Parameters: occludeeVisibility (default 0.35f), occludeeVisibleRange (default 0.6f). Outputs: Final screen image with correctly occluded clouds. Six RenderTexture objects are required. The specific formats are: 1. ZBuffer: Depth, 24-bit. 2. ColorBuffer: RGB111110Float. 3. CTopaque: RGB111110Float (stores opaque scene color). 4. CTcloud: RGB111110Float (stores cloud color). 5. DTopaque: RHalf (stores opaque scene depth). 6. DTcloud: RHalf (stores cloud depth). 1. Buffer Allocation: Create the six RenderTexture instances with the formats specified above. 2. Pre-Alpha Capture: Add a CommandBuffer (CBBeforeAlpha) at CameraEvent.BeforeForwardAlpha. This buffer blits the current ColorBuffer to CTopaque and ZBuffer to DTopaque. 3. Cloud Rendering Setup: In OnPreRender, set the camera's target buffers to ColorBuffer.colorBuffer and ZBuffer.depthBuffer. Render the cloud geometry. The cloud shader should write depth (ZWrite On) and perform alpha blending or testing as needed to populate ColorBuffer and ZBuffer with cloud data. 4. Post-Alpha Capture: Add a CommandBuffer (CBAfterAlpha) at CameraEvent.AfterForwardAlpha. This buffer blits the current ColorBuffer (now containing clouds) to CTcloud and ZBuffer (now containing cloud depth) to DTcloud. 5. Compositing: In OnPostRender, set the shader properties for the mix material: OpaqueColorTex = CTopaque OpaqueDepthTex = DTopaque AllDepthTex = DTcloud OccludeeVisibility = occludeeVisibility OccludeeVisibleRange = occludeeVisibleRange Blit CTcloud to the screen using the mix shader material. The mix shader performs the blending. Let D{opaque} be the depth from OpaqueDepthTex, D{cloud} be the depth from AllDepthTex, and C{cloud} be the color from OpaqueColorTex (scene) and C{cloud\tex} be the color from CTcloud (clouds). Note: The source uses OpaqueColorTex for the scene color in the final blit context, but logically it blends the cloud color with the scene color. Based on the description "blends rendered clouds with the scene", the inputs are Scene Color (C{scene}) and Cloud Color (C{cloud}). The visibility factor \alpha{blend} is determined by the depth difference. Let \Delta D = D{cloud} - D{opaque}. If D{cloud} < D{opaque} (cloud is in front of opaque object), the cloud is fully visible (\alpha{blend} = 1). If D{cloud} > D{opaque} (cloud is behind opaque object), the cloud is occluded. The visibility transitions based on occludeeVisibleRange. \alpha{blend} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } D{cloud} \le D{opaque} \\ \text{clamp}\left(\frac{D{opaque} - D{cloud} + \text{occludeeVisibleRange}}{\text{occludeeVisibleRange}}, 0, 1\right) \times \text{occludeeVisibility} & \text{if } D{cloud} > D{opaque} \end{cases} Note: The exact formula for the transition is inferred from the parameter names occludeeVisibility (min alpha) and occludeeVisibleRange (transition width). Standard linear interpolation between 0 and 1 over the range is assumed, scaled by the minimum visibility. Final Color C{final}: C{final} = C{scene} \times (1 - \alpha{blend}) + C{cloud} \times \alpha{blend} The depth values in RHalf textures must be read and compared correctly. In Unity, CameraDepthTexture or custom depth textures often require decoding if stored in a specific format, but here RHalf implies direct float representation or standard depth buffer format. The comparison D{cloud} - D{opaque} assumes linear depth or consistent projection space. If non-linear, depth decoding is required before subtraction. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. // Setup buffers (called once or in OnPreRender) RenderTexture ZBuffer = new RenderTexture(Screen.width, Screen.height, 24); RenderTexture ColorBuffer = new RenderTexture(Screen.width, Screen.height, 0, RenderTextureFormat.ARGBHalf); // Using ARGBHalf for RGB111110Float equivalent in Unity RenderTexture CTopaque = new RenderTexture(Screen.width, Screen.height, 0, RenderTextureFormat.ARGBHalf); RenderTexture CTcloud = new RenderTexture(Screen.width, Screen.height, 0, RenderTextureFormat.ARGBHalf); RenderTexture DTopaque = new RenderTexture(Screen.width, Screen.height, 0, RenderTextureFormat.RHalf); RenderTexture DTcloud = new RenderTexture(Screen.width, Screen.height, 0, RenderTextureFormat.RHalf); // Command Buffers CommandBuffer CBBeforeAlpha = new CommandBuffer { name = "CBBeforeAlpha" }; CBBeforeAlpha.Blit(BuiltinRenderTextureType.CurrentActive, CTopaque); // Blit Color CBBeforeAlpha.Blit(BuiltinRenderTextureType.CurrentActive, DTopaque); // Blit Depth (requires specific handling for depth-only) // Note: Unity's Blit to depth texture requires specific setup or GrabPass-like behavior. // The source implies direct blitting. In practice, DTopaque captures the depth buffer state. CommandBuffer CBAfterAlpha = new CommandBuffer { name = "CBAfterAlpha" }; CBAfterAlpha.Blit(BuiltinRenderTextureType.CurrentActive, CTcloud); CBAfterAlpha.Blit(BuiltinRenderTextureType.CurrentActive, DTcloud); // Camera Events camera.AddCommandBuffer(CameraEvent.BeforeForwardAlpha, CBBeforeAlpha); camera.AddCommandBuffer(CameraEvent.AfterForwardAlpha, CBAfterAlpha); // OnPreRender void OnPreRender() { camera.SetTargetBuffers(ColorBuffer.colorBuffer, ZBuffer.depthBuffer); } // OnPostRender void OnPostRender() { if (material != null) { material.SetTexture("OpaqueColorTex", CTopaque); material.SetTexture("OpaqueDepthTex", DTopaque); material.SetTexture("AllDepthTex", DTcloud); material.SetFloat("OccludeeVisibility", occludeeVisibility); material.SetFloat("OccludeeVisibleRange", occludeeVisibleRange); Graphics.Blit(CTcloud, (RenderTexture)null, material); } else { Graphics.Blit(CTcloud, (RenderTexture)null); } } occludeeVisibility: Minimum visibility of the occluded object (cloud). Range: [0.01, 1]. Default: 0.35. occludeeVisibleRange: Range of depth difference for visibility transition. Range: [0, 1]. Default: 0.6. Cloud-Cloud Occlusion: The method primarily handles cloud-scene occlusion. If multiple cloud layers are rendered, ZWrite On may cause later clouds to fail ZTest against earlier clouds, leading to incorrect transparency at cloud boundaries ("showing background color"). Performance: Creating multiple RenderTextures and CommandBuffers adds overhead. GrabPass-like operations (blitting entire frames) are expensive on mobile platforms. Depth Precision: Using RHalf for depth may introduce precision issues at large distances or small depth differences, affecting the smoothness of the occlusion transition. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to screen resolution and number of render passes (3 passes: opaque, cloud, post-process). Memory Complexity: Proportional to screen resolution \times 6 textures. Strengths: Soft edges at cloud-object boundaries; correct occlusion of clouds by opaque objects. Limitations: Does not solve inter-cloud occlusion artifacts without CPU sorting (which breaks GPU instancing); expensive due to multiple frame buffer copies; sensitive to depth precision. When to use: When soft cloud edges against opaque geometry are required and performance budget allows for post-processing. When not to use: On mobile devices with limited memory/bandwidth; when strict cloud-to-cloud occlusion is needed without CPU sorting. This technique is described in the context of Unity's Built-in Render Pipeline for rendering volume clouds. It is presented as an improvement over simple Alpha Blend (ZWrite Off) and Alpha Test (ZWrite On) methods to handle the visual artifacts of transparent cloud rendering against opaque scene geometry.
