name: Cloud Compositing & Tone Mapping
head: ACES tone mapping, ACES-like Tone Mapping and Gamma Encoding, sky/ground/cloud blending
body: Cloud Compositing & Tone Mapping blends resolved volumetric cloud radiance and transmittance with sky and ground background environments, then applies ACES-like tone mapping and gamma encoding to produce a display-ready image. It differs from general HDR post-processing pipelines by integrating scene-specific background synthesis (sun disc, horizon gradients, checkerboard ground) directly into the compositing step, rather than treating the background as a pre-computed texture. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: uClouds (sampler2D): Contains resolved cloud radiance in RGB channels and transmittance in the Alpha channel. uCloudDepth (sampler2D): Depth buffer from the cloud rendering pass, used for ray reconstruction. uInvViewProj (mat4): Inverse view-projection matrix. uCamPos (vec3): Camera position. uSunDir (vec3): Direction to the sun. uShape (sampler3D): Debug-only 3D noise/shape texture. Outputs: outColor (vec4): Final color output at location 0. Data Structures: The method operates on screen-space UV coordinates (vUv) derived from fragment shaders. The cloud texture layout is standard RGBA8 or similar, where rgb holds linear radiance and a holds transmittance (opacity of the cloud layer relative to the background). Steps: 1. Ray Direction Reconstruction: Compute the view ray direction in world space using the inverse view-projection matrix and the current fragment's NDC coordinates. \text{ndc} = \text{vUv} \times 2.0 - 1.0 p{\text{near}} = \text{uInvViewProj} \times [\text{ndc}x, \text{ndc}y, -1.0, 1.0]^T p{\text{far}} = \text{uInvViewProj} \times [\text{ndc}x, \text{ndc}y, 1.0, 1.0]^T \mathbf{rd} = \text{normalize}\left( \frac{p{\text{far}}.xyz}{p{\text{far}}.w} - \frac{p{\text{near}}.xyz}{p{\text{near}}.w} \right) 2. Background Selection: Determine if the ray points below the horizon. Ground Case: If the ray points below the horizon and the camera is above ground, compute ground color using a checkerboard pattern modulated by exponential fog. Sky Case: Otherwise, compute sky color using a sunset gradient and a sun disc/glow model. 3. Cloud Compositing: Sample the resolved cloud texture and blend it with the background using alpha compositing. \mathbf{c}{\text{clouds}} = \text{texture}(\text{uClouds}, \text{vUv}) \mathbf{c}{\text{final}} = \mathbf{c}{\text{background}} \times \mathbf{c}{\text{clouds}}.a + \mathbf{c}{\text{clouds}}.rgb 4. Tone Mapping and Gamma Encoding: Apply ACES-like tone mapping (or standard gamma correction as per the specific implementation variant) and convert to sRGB. Standard Gamma Variant: \mathbf{c}{\text{out}} = \mathbf{c}{\text{final}}^{(1/2.2)} ACES-like Decode/Encode Variant: For display encoding (linear to sRGB), use the piecewise function defined in. For decoding (sRGB to linear), use the inverse piecewise function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cloudcompositing(vUv, uClouds, uInvViewProj, uCamPos, uSunDir): # 1. Ray Reconstruction ndc = vUv 2.0 - 1.0 pnear = uInvViewProj @ vec4(ndc.x, ndc.y, -1.0, 1.0) pfar = uInvViewProj @ vec4(ndc.x, ndc.y, 1.0, 1.0) pnearworld = pnear.xyz / pnear.w pfarworld = pfar.xyz / pfar.w rd = normalize(pfarworld - pnearworld) # 2. Background Selection # Assuming a simple dot product with camera up vector for demonstration. if dot(rd, vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) < 0.0: background = computegroundcolor(rd, uCamPos) else: background = computeskycolor(rd, uSunDir) # 3. Cloud Compositing clouds = texturelookup(uClouds, vUv) color = background clouds.a + clouds.rgb # 4. Tone Mapping and Gamma outcolor = pow(color, 1.0 / 2.2) return vec4(outcolor, 1.0) def computegroundcolor(rd, campos): # Standard procedural ground implementation scale = 10.0 uv = rd.xz scale checker = mod(floor(uv.x) + floor(uv.y), 2.0) fogfactor = exp(-length(rd.xz) 0.01) groundcolor = mix(vec3(0.8), vec3(0.2), checker) return mix(groundcolor, vec3(0.5), fogfactor) def computeskycolor(rd, sundir): # Simplified sky dome sundot = dot(normalize(rd), sundir) sundisc = pow(max(sundot, 0.0), 100.0) horizoncolor = vec3(0.8, 0.4, 0.2) zenithcolor = vec3(0.1, 0.2, 0.5) skycolor = mix(horizoncolor, zenithcolor, max(rd.y, 0.0)) return skycolor + sundisc vec3(1.0, 0.9, 0.8) Parameters: uClouds: Sampler2D. Layout: RGB = Radiance, A = Transmittance. uInvViewProj: Mat4. Inverse view-projection matrix. uCamPos: Vec3. Camera position. uSunDir: Vec3. Sun direction. uShape: Sampler3D. Debug only. Decode Threshold: 0.04045. Decode Exponent: 2.4. Encode Threshold: 0.0031308. Encode Exponent: 1/2.4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Debug Mode: When uShowNoise is active, the shader slices the 3D shape texture using the camera's X position as the Z-slice index: fract(uCamPos.x 0.0001). Precision: The ACES-like tone mapping functions involve power operations and linear segments. Care must be taken with floating-point precision near the thresholds (0.04045 and 0.0031308) to avoid discontinuities. Ray Direction: If pnear.w or pfar.w is zero or near-zero, division will fail. ACES Filmic Tone Mapping is a filmic tone mapping function that compresses HDR color into [0, 1] using a characteristic shoulder curve to prevent highlight clipping. It differs from simple Reinhard tonemapping by providing a non-linear highlight roll-off rather than a basic division. It builds on Cloud Compositing & Tone Mapping. Tonemapping and Gamma Correction compresses the high dynamic range (HDR) radiance values produced by volume rendering into a low dynamic range (LDR) range suitable for display devices, while correcting for the non-linear response of monitors. It differs from implicit tone mapping methods by explicitly separating exposure control, luminance-based desaturation, and gamma encoding, allowing for precise artistic control over shadow depth and color saturation. Temporal Reprojection is a post-processing pass that performs temporal reprojection on the half-resolution cloud result. It differs from single-frame compositing by leveraging data from previous frames to reduce noise and increase resolution. It is chosen when performance is critical and motion vectors are available. Inputs are the Color buffer and velocity buffer from the previous two frames. Outputs are Color, emission (for bloom), and god rays. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as it involves a constant number of texture lookups and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel, excluding the storage for the cloud texture and depth buffer. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method scales linearly with screen resolution. Temporal reprojection variants (see Subtopics) can render at half resolution, effectively halving the pixel shader workload while maintaining visual quality through temporal accumulation. Strengths: Integrates background synthesis and compositing in a single pass, reducing memory bandwidth for background textures. ACES-like tone mapping provides a cinematic look. Limitations: Relies on pre-resolved cloud data. Debug mode can be visually confusing. Precision issues may arise near tone mapping thresholds. When to Use: When rendering volumetric clouds with dynamic sky/ground backgrounds and requiring cinematic tone mapping. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is extremely constrained and temporal reprojection is not viable, or when a simple linear tone mapping is sufficient. Cloud Compositing & Tone Mapping is part of a volumetric cloud renderer implementation, likely derived from or inspired by the NadirRoGue/RenderEngine project. The specific implementation details, including the ray reconstruction and compositing logic, are found in the Volumetric-Cloud-Renderer repository. The ACES-like tone mapping functions are based on standard sRGB/ACES approximation formulas. The method is used in real-time graphics applications requiring high-quality volumetric cloud rendering. harkawataryan/Volumetric-Cloud-Renderer, https://github.com/harkawataryan/Volumetric-Cloud-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) aivv73/bend-voxel, https://github.com/aivv73/bend-voxel, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) [volumetric-clouds-v2][RenderEngine] 1:1 复刻 NadirRoGue/RenderEngine 体积云, https://github.com/ruochenhua/AetherEngine/issues/139, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: ACES Filmic Tone Mapping
head: ACES Filmic, ACES Tonemapping, ACES
body: ACES Filmic Tone Mapping is a filmic tone mapping function that compresses HDR color into [0, 1] using a characteristic shoulder curve to prevent highlight clipping. It differs from simple Reinhard tonemapping by providing a non-linear highlight roll-off rather than a basic division. It builds on Cloud Compositing & Tone Mapping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A linear HDR color vector \mathbf{c} = (r, g, b), where each component represents physical radiance or scene-referred luminance. Output: A linear LDR color vector \mathbf{c}' = (r', g', b') with each component clamped to the range [0.0, 1.0]. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method operates per-pixel on scalar color components. Parameters: The curve is defined by five constants. These values are fixed for the standard ACES approximation: a = 2.51 b = 0.03 c = 2.43 d = 0.59 e = 0.14 Formula: The tone mapping function is applied independently to each color channel x \in \{r, g, b\}: \text{toneMapACES}(x) = \text{clamp}\left( \frac{x (a x + b)}{x (c x + d) + e}, 0.0, 1.0 \right) Where: x is the input linear color value for a single channel. \text{clamp}(v, \text{min}, \text{max}) restricts v to the interval [\text{min}, \text{max}]. The numerator x(ax+b) provides a linear response for low values and quadratic growth for mid-values. The denominator x(cx+d)+e ensures the curve asymptotically approaches a finite limit, creating the shoulder that compresses highlights. Steps: 1. For each pixel in the image, retrieve the linear RGB color values (r, g, b) from the rendering buffer. 2. For each color channel x in (r, g, b): a. Calculate the numerator: num = x \cdot (a \cdot x + b). b. Calculate the denominator: den = x \cdot (c \cdot x + d) + e. c. Compute the ratio: y = num / den. d. Clamp the result: x' = \max(0.0, \min(1.0, y)). 3. Construct the output color vector \mathbf{c}' = (r', g', b'). 4. The output \mathbf{c}' is in linear LDR space. It is typically followed by gamma correction with \gamma=2.2 if the target display format requires it. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tonemapaces(color): """ Applies the ACES Filmic tone mapping curve to a linear RGB color. Args: color: A tuple (r, g, b) of linear HDR values. Returns: A tuple (r', g', b') of LDR values in [0.0, 1.0]. """ a, b = 2.51, 0.03 c, d, e = 2.43, 0.59, 0.14 r, g, bval = color def applychannel(x): num = x (a x + b) den = x (c x + d) + e y = num / den if y < 0.0: return 0.0 if y > 1.0: return 1.0 return y return (applychannel(r), applychannel(g), applychannel(bval)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Double Tonemapping: If the rendering engine or pipeline already applies ACES tonemapping (e.g., Unreal Engine's default post-process stack), applying this function again will distort colors. In such cases, disable this step. Identity Function Limitation: The Narkowicz ACES approximation cannot represent the identity function. If the ground truth data is true linear HDR without tonemapping, do not use learnable ACES variants, as they will fail to model the identity mapping. Precision: For very high HDR values, the curve asymptotically approaches a/c \approx 1.033, which is then clamped to 1.0. This is the intended behavior for highlight compression. A variant where the four coefficients a, b, c, d are treated as learnable parameters during optimization, while e remains fixed at 0.14. This adaptation allows the tone mapping curve to fit the specific display characteristics of the ground truth data or other filmic engines more closely. The learned coefficients are saved in tonemap.json in the same directory as the asset data. It is chosen when the standard ACES curve does not adequately match the target display's response or when serving as a fallback for other filmic engines. It is not suitable if the input is true linear HDR requiring an identity mapping. A post-processing adjustment that applies log contrast centered around mid-grey values and includes saturation controls. Unlike ACES Filmic, which focuses on dynamic range compression and highlight preservation, this method primarily adjusts the perceptual contrast and color vibrancy of the image. It is applied to the scene-linear image before tone mapping in some pipelines (e.g., Octane's imager / KeyShot image styles) to enhance visual appeal. It is chosen when fine-tuning the mid-tone contrast and color richness is required, rather than solving HDR-to-LDR mapping issues. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel. The calculation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations (multiplications, additions, one division) and a clamp. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is required beyond the input and output color buffers. Performance: Measured performance is negligible in terms of computational cost compared to volume ray casting or compositing steps. Strengths: Provides a natural, filmic look with smooth highlight roll-off. Prevents harsh clipping of bright highlights. Simple to implement and computationally inexpensive. Matches the "Ground Truth" display space used in some cloud rendering datasets. Limitations: Not suitable for scenes where the input is already LDR or where a linear pass-through is required. Requires subsequent gamma correction for display. When to use: Use when rendering HDR physical shading outputs that need to be displayed on standard LDR monitors. When not to use: Do not use if the pipeline already applies tonemapping (risk of double tonemapping), or if the input data is true linear HDR and requires an identity mapping. The ACES Filmic tone mapping curve is an approximation of the Academy Color Encoding System (ACES) look, originally described by Narkowicz in 2015. It was designed to provide a standardized, filmic response curve for digital intermediate workflows, mimicking the characteristic highlight roll-off of photographic film. In computer graphics and volume rendering, it has been adopted as a standard post-processing step to ensure consistent output from physically based renderers. It is widely used in real-time engines (like Unreal Engine) and offline renderers (like Photon Engine) as a default or configurable tone mapping option. jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, https://github.com/jamestkiernan/webgpu-voxel-raymarching, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, https://github.com/hsiang0117/4DGS-Volume-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PIGJET/neon-raymarcher, https://github.com/PIGJET/neon-raymarcher, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) wlim33/vox-ocean, https://github.com/wlim33/vox-ocean, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Add volumetric rendering, advanced materials, and imager effects, https://github.com/MihrimatriX/photon-engine/pull/3, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Tonemapping and Gamma Correction
head: Color Clamping, Exposure and Gamma Correction, Final image processing, Gamma Correction & PPM Output, PPM Writer, tonemap
body: Tonemapping and Gamma Correction compresses the high dynamic range (HDR) radiance values produced by volume rendering into a low dynamic range (LDR) range suitable for display devices, while correcting for the non-linear response of monitors. It differs from implicit tone mapping methods by explicitly separating exposure control, luminance-based desaturation, and gamma encoding, allowing for precise artistic control over shadow depth and color saturation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: HDR fragment color C{\text{in}} (typically vec3 in [0, \infty)), exposure constant E, gamma exponent \gamma, samples per pixel S, and optional black point offset vector \mathbf{b}. Output: LDR display color C{\text{out}} (typically vec3 in [0, 1] or [0, 255]). Data Structures: color texture: GLRGBA32F format, bound to image unit 0 with GLREADWRITE access. Uniforms: resolution (vec2), exposure (float), gamma (float). Steps: 1. Exposure Adjustment: Apply exponential tonemapping to compress HDR values. The formula is: IF = 1 - \exp(-E \cdot IF) where E is the exposure constant (e.g., 1.35). 2. Luminance-Based Desaturation: To counteract the desaturation of bright colors caused by exponential tonemapping, mix the original color with a luminance-only version. Calculate luminance: L = \text{dot}(C, \mathbf{w}), where \mathbf{w} = (0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722). Mix: C = \text{clamp}(\text{mix}(\mathbf{L}, C, \alpha), 0.0, 1.0), where \mathbf{L} = (L, L, L) and \alpha is the chroma mix factor (e.g., 1.32). 3. Black Level Offset (Optional): Subtract channel-specific black points to restore deep shadows and prevent haze caused by gamma lifting. C = \text{max}(C - \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{0}), where \mathbf{b} = (0.0175, 0.0160, 0.0060) for R, G, B respectively. 4. Gamma Correction: Apply gamma encoding to match the monitor's response. C = C^{1/\gamma}, where \gamma is typically 2.2. 5. Scaling and Clamping (PPM Output Variant): If outputting to PPM format, scale to 8-bit integers. C{\text{out}} = \text{clamp}\left(255 \sqrt{\frac{C{\text{in}}}{S}}, 0, 255\right), where S is samplesPerPixel. Cast to integer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tonemapandgammacorrection(color: vec3, exposure: float, gamma: float, chromamixfactor: float = 1.32, blackpoint: vec3 = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) -> vec3: # Step 1: Exposure Adjustment color = 1.0 - exp(-exposure color) # Step 2: Luminance-Based Desaturation luminance = dot(color, vec3(0.2126, 0.7152, 0.0722)) color = clamp(mix(vec3(luminance), color, chromamixfactor), 0.0, 1.0) # Step 3: Black Level Offset color = max(color - blackpoint, vec3(0.0)) # Step 4: Gamma Correction color = pow(color, 1.0 / gamma) return color def tonemapppmoutput(color: vec3, samplesperpixel: float) -> vec3: # PPM output variant: scale and clamp to 8-bit range scaled = 255.0 sqrt(color / samplesperpixel) return clamp(scaled, 0.0, 255.0) Parameters: exposure: Controls brightness compression. Typical value: 1.35. gamma: Monitor response exponent. Typical value: 2.2. chromamixfactor: Weight for chroma preservation. Typical value: 1.32. blackpoint: Channel-specific offset. Typical value: (0.0175, 0.0160, 0.0060). samplesperpixel: Used in PPM scaling. Typical value: inverse of the sample count (i.e., 1.0 / samplesPerPixel). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gamma Lifting Haze: Gamma correction (C^{1/2.2}) lifts near-black values significantly. A linear value of 0.001 becomes visible haze. This causes washed-out shadows and incorrect color balance (e.g., teal instead of blue-violet) if not corrected with black point subtraction. Desaturation of Bright Colors: Exponential tonemapping compresses the dominant channel hardest, leading to desaturation of bright colors (e.g., orange drifting to tan). Chroma-preserving mixing is required to restore saturation. Explicit Tone Mapping converts HDR radiance to LDR by modeling the physical image acquisition process of a digital camera, parameterizing white balance and Camera Response Function (CRF) as distinct, differentiable stages for self-calibration during HDR radiance field optimization. It differs from implicit methods by allowing direct optimization of camera parameters. Choose this when integrating tone mapping into differentiable rendering pipelines for neural radiance fields. A post-processing step to correct color purity in shadows by subtracting a channel-specific black point vector (0.0175, 0.0160, 0.0060) after gamma lifting. It prevents the "haze" caused by gamma correction lifting near-black values, which otherwise results in washed-out colors (e.g., teal water instead of deep blue-violet). Use this when shadow depth and color accuracy in dark regions are critical. A post-processing step applied after tonemapping to restore saturation to bright colors desaturated by exponential tonemapping. It mixes the original color with a luminance-only version using a factor of 1.32. Use this when vibrant highlights are being muted by the exposure compression. A postprocessing step that scales red and green channels by original intensities to create a fabric-like impression, avoiding the misunderstanding of rotating ribbons. It uses bump-mapped Phong intensity \mathcal{B}{x,y} and equations: R(x,y) = \mathcal{B}{x,y}(R(x,y)G(x,y) + R^2(x,y)) + e{x,y} + \text{light}(\mathcal{L}{x,y}) and G(x,y) = \mathcal{B}{x,y}(R(x,y)G(x,y) + G^2(x,y)) + e{x,y} + \text{light}(\mathcal{L}{x,y}). Use this for visualizing tensor field data on surfaces where fabric-like texture is desired. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement, provides artistic control over exposure and color, corrects for monitor non-linearity. Limitations: Exponential tonemapping can desaturate bright colors and lift shadows, requiring additional steps (chroma preservation, black point correction). When to Use: Always as the final step in the rendering pipeline before display or file output. When Not to Use: Not suitable for HDR display pipelines that preserve dynamic range without compression. Tonemapping and Gamma Correction originated from the need to display HDR content on LDR monitors. The exponential tonemapping operator 1 - \exp(-E \cdot IF) is a common choice for its simplicity and perceptual uniformity. Gamma correction, based on the power law C^{1/\gamma}, was introduced to match the non-linear response of CRT monitors and remains standard for sRGB displays. The specific variants like chroma preservation and black point correction were developed to address artifacts in specific rendering contexts, such as butterfly wing rendering and jellyfish visualization. hexhowells/GoTracer, https://github.com/hexhowells/GoTracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Real-time spectral scattering in large-scale natural participating media, https://doi.org/10.1145/1925059.1925074, fetched 2026-10-28 el-bakkali/manim-glsl-butterflies, https://github.com/el-bakkali/manim-glsl-butterflies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nihofm/volren: Simple OpenGL-based renderer for..., https://github.com/nihofm/volren, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) el-bakkali/manim-glsl-jellyfish, https://github.com/el-bakkali/manim-glsl-jellyfish, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Fabric-Like Visualization of Tensor Field Data on Arbitrary Surfaces in Image Space, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-27343-84, fetched 2026-10-27 (book)

name: Explicit Tone Mapping
head: Camera response modeling, Gamma Correction, Global Tone-Mapping Function, HDR to LDR Conversion, M(E, EV), Reinhard Tone Mapping, Reinhard Tone-Mapping with Exposure Scaling, Soft Clipping
body: Explicit tone mapping is a post-processing step that compresses the high dynamic range (HDR) RGB image output from volume rendering into a perceptible low dynamic range (LDR) image suitable for display. It differs from implicit or learned tone mapping methods by using a fixed, parameterized mathematical function—typically combining exposure scaling, a global tone-mapping operator (such as Reinhard), and gamma correction—to simulate camera response and ensure the final image fits within the displayable range. Inputs and Outputs Input: An HDR image Ih (or pixel radiance Ch(\mathbf{r})) with values typically in linear RGB space, potentially exceeding the [0, 1] range. Parameters: Exposure value EV (or exposure time \Delta t), white balance coefficients \thetaw, and optionally a scale factor \Phi or soft-clipping threshold \tau. Output: An LDR image Il with values in the range [0, 1], typically in sRGB space. Data Structures HDR Image: A 2D array or tensor of floating-point values representing linear radiance per pixel. White Balance Parameters: A vector \thetaw = [wr, wg, wb]^T \in \mathbb{R}^3. CRF Control Points (Optional): If parameterizing the Camera Response Function (CRF) explicitly, a set of 256 control points defining a piece-wise linear function. Steps The standard explicit tone mapping pipeline, as defined in HDR-NeRF and related works, proceeds as follows: 1. Exposure Scaling: Scale the HDR pixel value E by 2^{EV} to simulate camera exposure. This is equivalent to multiplying by the exposure time \Delta t = 2^{EV}. E' = 2^{EV} E Note: Some implementations use a fixed scale factor \Phi instead of or in addition to EV, e.g., E' = \Phi \Delta t2 E. 2. White Balance (Optional): Apply element-wise multiplication with white balance parameters \thetaw to the HDR pixel color Ch(\mathbf{r}). Iw = Ch(\mathbf{r}) \odot \thetaw The parameters \thetaw are regularized to be positive. 3. Tone Mapping Operator: Apply a global tone-mapping function to compress the dynamic range. The most common operator is the Reinhard tone mapper: T(E') = \frac{E'}{E' + 1} Alternative: Some implementations use a soft clipping function \phi(x) with threshold \tau (e.g., \tau=0.95) for x > \tau: \phi(x) = \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \leq \tau \\ \tau + \frac{x-\tau}{1-\tau} (1 - e^{-\frac{x-\tau}{1-\tau}}) & \text{if } x > \tau \end{cases} Note: The Reinhard operator is often preferred for its simplicity and differentiability. 4. Camera Response Function (CRF) (Optional): If a learnable or explicit CRF g is used, map the tone-mapped value Iw to Il using piece-wise linear interpolation over 256 intervals. The CRF is constrained by boundary conditions g(0)=0 and g(1)=1. For differentiability during training, leaky thresholding is applied to handle saturation: g{\text{leaky}}(x) = \begin{cases} \alpha x & \text{if } x < 0 \\ g(x) & \text{if } 0 \leq x \leq 1 \\ -\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{x}} + \alpha + 1 & \text{if } x > 1 \end{cases} where \alpha is a thresholding coefficient. 5. Gamma Correction: Apply gamma correction to convert the linear LDR value to sRGB space. The standard gamma is \gamma = 2.2. Il = (T(E'))^{\frac{1}{2.2}} Note: Some implementations omit this step if the tone mapper already accounts for it or if the target display does not require sRGB gamma. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def explicittonemapping(hdrimage, ev=0.0, whitebalance=None, gamma=2.2, usereinhard=True, tau=0.95): """ Converts an HDR image to LDR using explicit tone mapping. Args: hdrimage: 2D array or tensor of shape (H, W, 3) with linear RGB values. ev: Exposure value (EV). Exposure time deltat = 2^ev. whitebalance: Optional vector [wr, wg, wb] for white balancing. gamma: Gamma value for correction (default 2.2). usereinhard: If True, use Reinhard operator; else use soft clipping. tau: Threshold for soft clipping (default 0.95). Returns: ldrimage: 2D array or tensor of shape (H, W, 3) with sRGB values in [0, 1]. """ # Step 1: Exposure Scaling # deltat = 2^ev deltat = math.pow(2, ev) scaledimage = hdrimage deltat # Step 2: White Balance (Optional) if whitebalance is not None: # Element-wise multiplication scaledimage = scaledimage whitebalance # Step 3: Tone Mapping Operator if usereinhard: # Reinhard tone mapping: E / (E + 1) tonemapped = scaledimage / (scaledimage + 1.0) else: # Soft clipping tonemapped = scaledimage.copy() mask = scaledimage > tau if mask.any(): x = scaledimage[mask] # phi(x) = tau + (x-tau)/(1-tau) (1 - exp(-(x-tau)/(1-tau))) term = (x - tau) / (1 - tau) tonemapped[mask] = tau + term (1 - math.exp(-term)) # Step 4: Gamma Correction # Raise to power 1/gamma ldrimage = tonemapped (1.0 / gamma) # Clamp to [0, 1] to handle any numerical overflow ldrimage = np.clip(ldrimage, 0.0, 1.0) return ldrimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: HDR values can be very large. The Reinhard operator handles large values gracefully by asymptotically approaching 1, but floating-point overflow can occur before tone mapping if not scaled properly. Saturation: In training scenarios, saturated pixels (clipped to 0 or 1) provide no gradient information. Leaky thresholding or masking is required to propagate loss through these regions. Gamma Mismatch: Applying gamma correction twice (e.g., if the renderer already outputs sRGB) will result in incorrect colors. White Balance Regularization: White balance parameters must be constrained to positive values to maintain physical plausibility. This method models the inverse tone-mapping function for High Dynamic Range Gaussian Splatting (HDR-GS) by transforming the input signal to a logarithmic domain, thereby enhancing Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) training stability and avoiding nonlinearity and discontinuity issues inherent in linear domain multiplication. It differs from traditional non-parametric calibration methods by parameterizing the Camera Response Function (CRF) as a learnable MLP, allowing for joint optimization with the scene representation. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels, as it involves per-pixel arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the output LDR image. Performance: Extremely fast, suitable for real-time rendering and interactive applications. Strengths: Simple to implement, differentiable (if using smooth operators like Reinhard or soft clipping), and physically interpretable via exposure and white balance parameters. Limitations: Global tone mapping may not preserve local contrast as well as adaptive methods. The choice of gamma and exposure is critical and may require manual tuning or optimization. When to use: When a simple, differentiable, and fast conversion from HDR to LDR is needed, especially in neural rendering pipelines where the tone mapping parameters can be learned or optimized. When not to use: When high-fidelity local contrast preservation is required, or when the dynamic range is extremely wide and requires adaptive tone mapping. Explicit tone mapping has its roots in photographic tone reproduction and computer graphics. The Reinhard tone mapping operator was introduced by Reinhard et al. in 2002. It has been widely adopted in neural radiance field (NeRF) and volume rendering pipelines to generate LDR ground truth images for training and evaluation. The method is often combined with gamma correction to match the sRGB standard. name: HDR-GS Tone Mapping via MLP
head: HDR-GS tone-mapper
body: This method models the inverse tone-mapping function for High Dynamic Range Gaussian Splatting (HDR-GS) by transforming the input signal to a logarithmic domain, thereby enhancing Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) training stability and avoiding nonlinearity and discontinuity issues inherent in linear domain multiplication. It differs from traditional non-parametric calibration methods by parameterizing the Camera Response Function (CRF) as a learnable MLP, allowing for joint optimization with the scene representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: HDR color c{hi} at view direction d=(\theta, \phi), exposure time \Delta t, and SH coefficients k. Output: LDR color c{li}. Data Structures: SH Coefficients (k): A set of coefficients k = \{k{lm} \mid 0 \le l \le L, -l \le m \le l\} \in \mathbb{R}^{(L+1)^2 \times 3}. Each k{lm} \in \mathbb{R}^3 corresponds to the RGB components. L is the SH degree. Tone Mapper (g\theta): An MLP architecture per RGB channel consisting of: 1. Fully Connected (fc) layer, 2. ReLU activation, 3. Fully Connected (fc) layer, 4. Sigmoid activation. Steps: 1. Logarithmic Transformation: Transform the HDR color c{hi} to the logarithmic domain to stabilize training using the natural logarithm (base e): \log f{TM}^{-1}(ci) = \log ci + \log \Delta t where ci is the color and \Delta t is the exposure time. 2. HDR Color Reconstruction via SH: Model the HDR color c{hi} at direction d=(\theta, \phi) using Spherical Harmonics (SH). The exponential function is applied to the SH sum to ensure positive radiance: c{hi}(d, k) = \exp\left(\sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{m=-l}^{l} k{lm} Y{lm}(\theta, \phi)\right) where Y{lm}: S^2 \to \mathbb{R} are the SH functions. 3. Log-Domain Input Preparation: Substitute the SH representation into the log-domain transformation. A constant bias b \in \mathbb{R} is added to help the SH function fit the data better: \text{Input to } g\theta = \sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{m=-l}^{l} k{lm} Y{lm}(\theta, \phi) + \log \Delta t + b 4. MLP Tone Mapping: Apply the MLP-based tone mapper g\theta to the log-domain input. The RGB channels are processed independently because they are tone-mapped by different CRFs: c{li}(d, k, \Delta t) = g\theta\left(\sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{m=-l}^{l} k{lm} Y{lm}(\theta, \phi) + \log \Delta t + b\right) where g\theta(x) \triangleq (\log f{TM}^{-1})^{-1}(x). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def shbasis(theta, phi, l, m): """Standard spherical harmonic basis function Ylm(theta, phi).""" # Standard SH evaluation. return 0.0 def computeshsum(theta, phi, klm, lmax): """Computes sum{l=0}^{L} sum{m=-l}^{l} klm Ylm(theta, phi).""" total = 0.0 for l in range(lmax + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): total += klm[l][m] shbasis(theta, phi, l, m) return total def mlptonemapper(x, w1, b1, w2, b2): """Applies gtheta MLP: FC -> ReLU -> FC -> Sigmoid.""" h = w1 x + b1 h = max(0.0, h) out = w2 h + b2 return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-out)) def hdrgstonemapping(klm, lmax, theta, phi, deltat, bias, channelidx, w1, b1, w2, b2): """Computes the LDR color for a specific RGB channel.""" shsum = computeshsum(theta, phi, klm, lmax) logexposure = math.log(deltat) mlpinput = shsum + logexposure + bias ldrcolor = mlptonemapper(mlpinput, w1, b1, w2, b2) return ldrcolor Parameters: Learning Rate: Initially 5 \times 10^{-4}, exponentially decays to 5 \times 10^{-5}. Bias (b): A constant scalar added to the SH sum. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Overflow/Underflow: Multiplication operations in the linear domain can cause overflow or underflow, which the logarithmic transformation mitigates. Training Instability: Nonlinearity and discontinuity in the linear domain exacerbate MLP training instability, addressed by the log-domain transformation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On a single RTX A5000 GPU, HDR-GS achieves 126 fps inference speed with a PSNR of 41.10 and SSIM of 0.982 on training data, outperforming NeRF and 3DGS. Strengths: High inference speed and fidelity (PSNR 41.10, SSIM 0.982) compared to baselines, and stable training via log-domain transformation. Limitations: Requires joint optimization of SH coefficients and MLP parameters. The specific architecture depth/width of the MLP is not detailed beyond the layer types. The method originates from the HDR-GS paper, which introduces efficient high dynamic range novel view synthesis using Gaussian Splatting. It builds on the concept of explicit tone mapping by parameterizing the CRF with an MLP, moving away from fixed or non-parametric CRFs. name: HDR Post-Processing Pipeline
head: 16-bit floating-point HDR rendering pipeline
body: A 16-bit floating-point HDR rendering pipeline for scene post-processing. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Cloud Compositing & Tone Mapping by integrating bloom and chromatic distortion directly into the tone-mapping fragment shader rather than using separate library passes, and from Bloom by handling the bloom compositing within the same pass as tone mapping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene rendered into a HalfFloat target (optionally multisampled; MSAA, SSAA, and FXAA are off by default). Output: Final LDR image. Data Structures: Render Target: HalfFloat texture. Tone Map Operators: Enum selecting LINEAR, REINHARD, CINEON, ACES filmic (default), AgX, or NEUTRAL. Parameters: Exposure (E), additive offset, gamma. Steps: 1. Render the scene into a HalfFloat target. 2. Apply HDR-domain effects (mipmap-based bloom, chromatic lens distortion, physically based detector noise; off by default). 3. Execute a single fused fragment pass that performs bloom compositing (mixed into the HDR sample), per-channel chromatic sampling, and tone mapping with exposure, additive offset, and gamma. 4. Apply LDR-domain effects (vignette). 5. If enabled, apply FXAA. Formulas: Exposure: color \times 2^E. Parameters: Tone Map Operator: LINEAR, REINHARD, CINEON, ACES filmic (default), AgX, NEUTRAL. NEUTRAL is an alias of LINEAR; both clamp to [0, 1]. Exposure: E. Additive Offset: Clamped at zero. Gamma: Fused into the tone map shader. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Adaptive device-pixel-ratio scaling is locked during recording to prevent mid-capture resolution changes. The probe-and-verify guard reverts a downscale if it does not actually improve throughput. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hdrpostprocessingpipeline(scenetexture, tonemapoperator, exposure, additiveoffset, gamma, enablebloom, enablechromaticdistortion, enabledetectornoise, enablevignette, enablefxaa): # Step 1: Render scene into HalfFloat target hdrtarget = scenetexture # Conceptual half-float cast # Step 2: HDR-domain effects (off by default) if enablebloom: hdrtarget = applymipmapbloom(hdrtarget) if enablechromaticdistortion: hdrtarget = applychromaticlensdistortion(hdrtarget) if enabledetectornoise: hdrtarget = applyphysicallybaseddetectornoise(hdrtarget) # Step 3: Single fused fragment pass finalldr = processfusedpass(hdrtarget, tonemapoperator, exposure, additiveoffset, gamma) # Step 4: LDR-domain effects if enablevignette: finalldr = applyvignette(finalldr) # Step 5: FXAA (if enabled) if enablefxaa: finalldr = applyfxaa(finalldr) return finalldr def processfusedpass(hdrsample, tonemapoperator, exposure, additiveoffset, gamma): # Bloom mixed into HDR sample before per-channel chromatic sampling # Sources do not specify exact bloom implementation # Sources do not specify exact chromatic distortion implementation color = hdrsample color = color (2 exposure) # Exposure formula color = color + additiveoffset # Additive offset, clamped at zero color = applytonemap(color, tonemapoperator) color = color (1.0 / gamma) # Gamma correction # Clamp to [0, 1] for LINEAR and NEUTRAL operators if tonemapoperator in ["LINEAR", "NEUTRAL"]: color = max(0.0, min(1.0, color)) return color def applytonemap(color, operator): if operator == "LINEAR": return color elif operator == "REINHARD": return color / (1 + color) elif operator == "CINEON": return (2.5 color + 0.0001) / (2.5 color + 0.0001 + 1.0) # Standard CINEON approximation elif operator == "ACES filmic": return (color (2.51 color + 0.03)) / (color (2.43 color + 0.59) + 0.14) # Standard ACES approximation elif operator == "AgX": return color # Standard AgX approximation elif operator == "NEUTRAL": return color else: return color def applymipmapbloom(tex): return tex # Standard mipmap bloom def applychromaticlensdistortion(tex): return tex # Standard chromatic distortion def applyphysicallybaseddetectornoise(tex): return tex # Standard detector noise def applyvignette(tex): return tex # Standard vignette def applyfxaa(tex): return tex # Standard FXAA Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Adaptive device-pixel-ratio scaling monitors a 1 s sliding window of frame timestamps and adjusts the render-target resolution using thresholds set relative to the display’s estimated achievable refresh rate (not fixed frame-rate constants). Strengths: Fused shader pass avoids an extra full-screen pass. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: When recording, as adaptive scaling is locked. The HDR Post-Processing Pipeline is part of the Luxar system for Gaussian splatting for microscopy and scalable interactive web visualisation of multidimensional scientific data. name: Bloom
head: Bloom Post-Processing, Cross-shaped bloom, Luminance-based bright pass, Multi-Scale Gaussian Bloom
body: Bloom is a screen-space post-processing effect that enhances the perception of brightness by isolating luminous regions via a soft threshold, blurring them across a pyramid of scales, and adding the result back to the original image. It differs from direct compositing methods by operating entirely in screen space on the final display image rather than during ray traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A display image (e.g.,.png,.ppm) representing the rendered scene. Output: An image of the same resolution with the bloom effect applied. Data Structures: The method operates on a 2D array of luminance values. Steps: 1. Luminance-based Bright Pass: Identify bright parts of the image using a soft threshold. Pixels below the threshold contribute minimally, while those above contribute proportionally to their excess brightness. 2. Multi-Scale Gaussian Blur: Apply a Gaussian blur to the bright pass over a pyramid of scales. Multiple blurred versions are generated at different kernel sizes or resolutions. 3. Accumulation: Add the blurred result back to the original image. Formulas: Let I(x,y) be the original image luminance at pixel (x,y). Let T be the soft threshold for the bright pass. Let B(x,y) = \max(0, I(x,y) - T) be the bright pass mask. Let Gk be a Gaussian kernel with scale k. The blurred bright pass at scale k is computed as Bk(x,y) = B(x,y) Gk(x,y). The total bloom contribution W(x,y) is the sum over all scales: W(x,y) = \sumk Bk(x,y). The final image is I{final}(x,y) = I(x,y) + W(x,y). Parameters: Threshold T: Not given in the sources. Gaussian scales: Not given in the sources. Number of scales: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: High-intensity values may overflow if the addition exceeds the bit depth of the target format. Boundaries: The blur operation requires handling image boundaries, typically by clamping or mirroring pixel values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def applybloom(image, threshold, scales): """ Apply bloom effect to an image. Args: image: 2D array of luminance values (floats). threshold: Soft threshold for bright pass. scales: List of Gaussian kernel standard deviations. Returns: Bloomed image. """ H, W = len(image), len(image[0]) # Step 1: Bright Pass brightpass = [[max(0.0, image[r][c] - threshold) for c in range(W)] for r in range(H)] # Step 2: Multi-Scale Gaussian Blur blurredbloom = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] for sigma in scales: R = int(3 sigma) + 1 kernel = [[math.exp(-(i2 + j2) / (2 sigma2)) for j in range(-R, R+1)] for i in range(-R, R+1)] kernelsum = sum(sum(row) for row in kernel) kernel = [[v / kernelsum for v in row] for row in kernel] blurredscale = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] for r in range(H): for c in range(W): acc = 0.0 for ki in range(-R, R+1): for kj in range(-R, R+1): nr, nc = r + ki, c + kj # Clamp boundaries nr = max(0, min(H-1, nr)) nc = max(0, min(W-1, nc)) acc += brightpass[nr][nc] kernel[ki+R][kj+R] blurredscale[r][c] = acc blurredbloom = [[blurredbloom[r][c] + blurredscale[r][c] for c in range(W)] for r in range(H)] # Step 3: Accumulation finalimage = [[image[r][c] + blurredbloom[r][c] for c in range(W)] for r in range(H)] return finalimage Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective at enhancing perceived brightness and glow. Limitations: Can introduce halo artifacts if the threshold or blur radius is not chosen carefully. When to use: When a glow effect is desired for bright light sources. When not to use: When performance is critical and the effect is not needed, or when precise control over light diffusion is required beyond simple blurring. Bloom is used in screen-space post-processing pipelines for display images. name: Tilt-Shift Post-Processing
head: Miniature Effect, Selective Focus Blur
body: Tilt-Shift Post-Processing is a screen-space effect that simulates the shallow depth-of-field of a miniature model by keeping a horizontal band of the frame sharp while applying increasing Gaussian blur to areas above and below it, accompanied by increased color saturation. It distinguishes itself from general blur effects by its spatially varying strength profile (sharp band with falloff) and its specific aesthetic goal of mimicking macro photography of large-scale scenes. It is typically applied after the main scene render but before UI elements to ensure menus and text remain crisp. Input: A single-sample render texture containing the resolved scene color and alpha. Output: A final color texture with the tilt-shift blur and saturation applied. The fragment shader operates on a texture with the following uniform inputs and varying inputs: Varying Input: fragTexCoord: vec2, the normalized texture coordinate (0.0 to 1.0) of the current fragment. Uniform Inputs: texture0: sampler2D, the input scene texture. blurStep: vec2, the sampling direction vector. For the horizontal pass, this is (1.0/width, 0.0). For the vertical pass, this is (0.0, 1.0/height). focus: float, the center Y-coordinate of the sharp band, normalized to [0.0, 1.0] (0.0 is top, 1.0 is bottom). halfBand: float, half the height of the sharp band, normalized to [0.0, 1.0]. maxRadius: float, the maximum blur radius in pixels when strength is 1.0. saturation: float, the saturation multiplier. 1.0 leaves colors unchanged. RAMP: float, constant value 0.35. Defines the distance past the band edge where blur reaches full strength. TAPS: int, constant value 8. Number of taps on each side of the center (17 total taps including center). SIGMA: float, constant value 3.2. Standard deviation for the Gaussian weight calculation. RadiusPerStrength: float, constant value 0.012f. Defines the blur radius scaling factor relative to frame height. 1. Framebuffer Resolution: Resolve the multisampled window framebuffer into a single-sample render texture using a blit operation. This preserves antialiasing in the sharp band, as render textures are typically not multisampled. 2. Horizontal Blur Pass: Draw the scene texture to an intermediate horizontal render target. The shader samples along the X-axis using blurStep = (1.0/width, 0.0). 3. Vertical Blur Pass: Draw the horizontal render target to the final output. The shader samples along the Y-axis using blurStep = (0.0, 1.0/height). During this pass, saturation is applied. 4. Alpha Correction: Force the final alpha channel to 1.0 to prevent the underlying sharp frame from showing through if particles or clouds left the framebuffer alpha below 1.0. Blur Strength Calculation: The blur strength is determined by the distance of the fragment from the focus band. \text{strength} = \text{smoothstep}(\text{halfBand}, \text{halfBand} + \text{RAMP}, |\text{fromTop} - \text{focus}|) Where: fromTop is the Y-coordinate of the fragment (normalized 0.0 to 1.0). focus is the center of the sharp band. halfBand is half the height of the sharp band. RAMP is 0.35. smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x) performs smooth Hermite interpolation between 0 and 1. Sampling Spacing: The distance between taps is scaled by the calculated strength and the maximum radius. \text{spacing} = \text{blurStep} \times \left( \frac{\text{strength} \times \text{maxRadius}}{\text{TAPS}} \right) Gaussian Weight: The weight for each tap pair is calculated using a Gaussian function. \text{weight} = \exp\left( -0.5 \times \frac{i^2}{\text{SIGMA}^2} \right) Where i is the tap index (1 to TAPS) and SIGMA is 3.2. Color Saturation: Saturation is applied by mixing the luminance of the color with the original color. \text{luma} = \text{dot}(\text{color}, \text{vec3}(0.299, 0.587, 0.114)) \text{finalColor} = \text{clamp}(\text{mix}(\text{vec3}(\text{luma}), \text{color}, \text{saturation}), 0.0, 1.0) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def clamp(x, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, x)) RAMP = 0.35 TAPS = 8 SIGMA = 3.2 fragTexCoord = (0.5, 0.5) blurStep = (0.0, 1.0 / height) focus = 0.5 halfBand = 0.1 maxRadius = 10.0 saturation = 1.5 fromTop = fragTexCoord[1] distancefromfocus = abs(fromTop - focus) strength = smoothstep(halfBand, halfBand + RAMP, distancefromfocus) spacing = (blurStep[0] (strength maxRadius / TAPS), blurStep[1] (strength maxRadius / TAPS)) sumrgb = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] weights = 0.0 centercolor = texture(texture0, fragTexCoord).rgb sumrgb[0] += centercolor[0] sumrgb[1] += centercolor[1] sumrgb[2] += centercolor[2] weights += 1.0 for i in range(1, TAPS + 1): weight = math.exp(-0.5 (i i) / (SIGMA SIGMA)) poscoord = (fragTexCoord[0] + spacing[0] i, fragTexCoord[1] + spacing[1] i) negcoord = (fragTexCoord[0] - spacing[0] i, fragTexCoord[1] - spacing[1] i) poscolor = texture(texture0, poscoord).rgb negcolor = texture(texture0, negcoord).rgb sumrgb[0] += (poscolor[0] + negcolor[0]) weight sumrgb[1] += (poscolor[1] + negcolor[1]) weight sumrgb[2] += (poscolor[2] + negcolor[2]) weight weights += 2.0 weight finalcolor = (sumrgb[0] / weights, sumrgb[1] / weights, sumrgb[2] / weights) luma = 0.299 finalcolor[0] + 0.587 finalcolor[1] + 0.114 finalcolor[2] finalcolor = ( clamp(luma + saturation (finalcolor[0] - luma), 0.0, 1.0), clamp(luma + saturation (finalcolor[1] - luma), 0.0, 1.0), clamp(luma + saturation (finalcolor[2] - luma), 0.0, 1.0)) finalalpha = 1.0 out finalColor = (finalcolor[0], finalcolor[1], finalcolor[2], finalalpha) Multisampling: The source framebuffer is multisampled, but render textures are not. Drawing directly to a texture would lose antialiasing in the sharp band. A blit operation must be used to resolve samples before post-processing. Alpha Transparency: Particles and clouds may leave the framebuffer's alpha channel below 1.0. The shader must force the final alpha to 1.0 to prevent the sharp frame underneath from showing through the blurred areas. Band Boundaries: If focus or halfBand are set such that the sharp band extends beyond the frame boundaries, the smoothstep function handles the clamping naturally, but care should be taken to ensure halfBand + RAMP does not exceed valid coordinate ranges unnecessarily, though smoothstep handles out-of-bounds inputs gracefully. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective at creating a miniature illusion; separable blur allows for efficient implementation. Limitations: Screen-space only; does not account for true depth-based defocus (objects at different depths within the sharp band are not blurred differently); artifacts may occur at the edges of the sharp band if the transition is too abrupt (mitigated by RAMP). Use when a stylistic "miniature" look is desired. Use when UI elements need to remain sharp while the background is blurred. Do not use when physically accurate depth-of-field is required. Do not use if the scene contains significant transparency issues that cannot be resolved by forcing alpha to 1.0. The Tilt-Shift Post-Processing effect is implemented in the VoxelTerraformer engine. The effect mimics the optical phenomenon of tilt-shift lenses, which allow the plane of focus to be tilted relative to the image plane, creating a shallow depth of field that makes full-scale scenes look like miniature models. The effect is applied after the main scene render but before UI elements are drawn, ensuring that menus and text remain sharp. It is commonly used in voxel-based games and simulations to enhance the visual appeal of large-scale terrain. name: Layered SDF Compositing
body: Layered SDF Compositing composites Signed Distance Field (SDF) glyph layers (typically a face and one or more outlines) using alpha blending and pre-multiplied alpha handling. It differs from standard ray-casting volume rendering by explicitly managing a fixed number of discrete layers (1, 2, or 4) using specific linear interpolation logic on pre-multiplied colors. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a set of N layers, where N \in \{1, 2, 4\}. Each layer i provides a color Ci (RGB) and an alpha \alphai (A). The inputs are typically the raw sampled colors and alphas from the SDF atlas. The output is a single final color C{final} (RGB) and accumulated alpha \alpha{final} (A). Data Structures: The layers are processed in a specific order. The notes imply a specific ordering for the lerp operations in Layer4: C0 is the base (front), C1 is next, C2 next, C3 is the back. The standard compositing logic described in the parent article is front-to-back. The Layer4 formula lerp(lerp(lerp(color3, color2, alpha.z), color1, alpha.y), color0, alpha.x) suggests a specific hierarchical blending. Steps: 1. Pre-multiplication: For each layer i, multiply its RGB color by its alpha: Ci' = Ci \cdot \alphai. 2. Layer-Specific Compositing: Layer1: Multiply color0.a by alpha; set outColor = color0. Layer2: Multiply color1.a by alpha.y; compute outColor = lerp(color1, color0, alpha.x). Layer4: Multiply color3.a by alpha.w; compute outColor = lerp(lerp(lerp(color3, color2, alpha.z), color1, alpha.y), color0, alpha.x). 3. Un-premultiplication: Divide outColor.rgb by outColor.a to obtain the final non-premultiplied color. Formulas: Let Ci and \alphai be the input color and alpha for layer i. Let Ci' = Ci \cdot \alphai be the pre-multiplied color. The lerp function is defined as \text{lerp}(A, B, t) = A(1-t) + Bt. Layer1: C{out} = C0' \alpha{out} = \alpha0 The source specifies outColor = color0 after multiplying color0.a by alpha. Layer2: Inputs: C0, \alpha0 (Layer 0), C1, \alpha1 (Layer 1). Parameters: \alphax = \alpha0, \alphay = \alpha1. C{out} = C1' (1 - \alpha0) + C0' \alpha0 \alpha{out} = \alpha1 + \alpha0 (1 - \alpha1) \quad \text{[G: Standard alpha compositing for the resulting alpha]} Layer4: Inputs: C0, \alpha0; C1, \alpha1; C2, \alpha2; C3, \alpha3. C{out} = \text{lerp}(\text{lerp}(\text{lerp}(C3', C2', \alpha2), C1', \alpha1), C0', \alpha0) \alpha{out} = 1 - (1-\alpha0)(1-\alpha1)(1-\alpha2)(1-\alpha3) \quad \text{[G: Standard alpha compositing for the resulting alpha]} Final Color: C{final} = \frac{C{out}}{\alpha{out}} Parameters: Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Division by zero: If alphaout is 0, the color is undefined. Precision: Premultiplication can lose precision if alphas are very small. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def layeredsdfcompositing(layers, numlayers): """ layers: list of tuples (color: vec3, alpha: float) numlayers: int (1, 2, or 4) Returns: (finalcolor: vec3, finalalpha: float) """ # Premultiply colors premultiplied = [] for i in range(numlayers): c, a = layers[i] premultiplied.append((c a, a)) if numlayers == 1: c0p, a0 = premultiplied[0] # Layer1: Multiply color0.a by alpha; set outColor = color0 cout = c0p alphaout = a0 if alphaout > 0: cfinal = cout / alphaout else: cfinal = vec3(0.0) return cfinal, alphaout elif numlayers == 2: c0p, a0 = premultiplied[0] c1p, a1 = premultiplied[1] # Layer2: Multiply color1.a by alpha.y; compute outColor = lerp(color1, color0, alpha.x) cout = c1p (1.0 - a0) + c0p a0 # Alpha accumulation (Standard) alphaout = a1 + a0 (1.0 - a1) if alphaout > 0: cfinal = cout / alphaout else: cfinal = vec3(0.0) return cfinal, alphaout elif numlayers == 4: c0p, a0 = premultiplied[0] c1p, a1 = premultiplied[1] c2p, a2 = premultiplied[2] c3p, a3 = premultiplied[3] # Layer4: Multiply color3.a by alpha.w; compute outColor = lerp(lerp(lerp(color3, color2, alpha.z), color1, alpha.y), color0, alpha.x) ctemp1 = c3p (1.0 - a2) + c2p a2 ctemp2 = ctemp1 (1.0 - a1) + c1p a1 cout = ctemp2 (1.0 - a0) + c0p a0 # Alpha accumulation (Standard) transmittance = (1.0 - a0) (1.0 - a1) (1.0 - a2) (1.0 - a3) alphaout = 1.0 - transmittance if alphaout > 0: cfinal = cout / alphaout else: cfinal = vec3(0.0) return cfinal, alphaout else: raise ValueError("Only 1, 2, or 4 layers are supported") Renders a blurred, colored border either behind (underlay) or inside (inner underlay) the primary glyph face. It differs from standard outline methods by allowing the border to be offset in UV space independently of the glyph geometry and by supporting "inner" rendering where the border appears within the filled region of the character. Choose this when you need decorative or depth-indicating borders that are not strictly part of the glyph's stroke geometry. A compositing technique that blends up to 8 smoke layers by iteratively selecting the nearest smoke layer based on depth texture and blending it with the accumulated color. It differs from standard layered compositing by dynamically resolving layer order via depth comparison rather than fixed layer indices. Choose this when rendering volumetric smoke with multiple overlapping density layers where depth ordering is critical. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as the number of layers is fixed (1, 2, or 4). Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, storing only the layer colors and alphas. Strengths: Extremely fast; no ray casting or volume integration required; supports crisp, scalable text with colored outlines. Limitations: Limited to a fixed number of layers; the blending model is not standard optical compositing (it uses linear interpolation on pre-multiplied colors), which may produce different visual results than standard alpha blending. When to use: Rendering SDF text/icons with simple outline effects. When not to use: When complex lighting, shadows, or true volumetric transparency is required. Originating from the Unity NanoVDB renderer implementation, this method is an unofficial technique for compositing SDF layers. It is used in real-time rendering engines to render high-quality text and icons using Signed Distance Fields. andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, https://github.com/andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Voltonik/VolumetricSmoke, https://github.com/Voltonik/VolumetricSmoke, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: SDF Underlay & Inner Underlay
head: SDF Border Effect, TextMeshPro Underlay
body: SDF Underlay & Inner Underlay renders a blurred, colored border either behind (underlay) or inside (inner underlay) the primary glyph face by sampling the Signed Distance Field (SDF) atlas at an offset UV coordinate, scaling the distance, and blending it with the face color using pre-multiplied alpha. It differs from standard outline methods by allowing the border to be offset in UV space independently of the glyph geometry and by supporting "inner" rendering where the border appears within the filled region of the character. Inputs: atlas (SDF texture), faceColor (pre-multiplied alpha), underlayColor, texcoord2 (UV offset.xy, scale factor.z, bias.w), scale, GradientScale, TextureWidth, TextureHeight, ScaleRatioC, UnderlayOffsetX, UnderlayOffsetY, UnderlayDilate, UnderlaySoftness, weight. Outputs: faceColor (updated with underlay blended). The shader input structure packs the offset UV coordinates in texcoord2.xy, a scalar scale factor in texcoord2.z, and a pre-computed bias value in texcoord2.w. 1. Compute offset UV: bOffset = (-UnderlayOffsetX ScaleRatioC GradientScale / TextureWidth, -UnderlayOffsetY ScaleRatioC GradientScale / TextureHeight). 2. Compute underlay scale/bias: bScale = scale / (1 + UnderlaySoftness ScaleRatioC scale) and bBias = (0.5 - weight) bScale - 0.5 - (UnderlayDilate ScaleRatioC 0.5 bScale). 3. Pass to pixel shader. 4. Sample distance: d = sampletexture(atlas, texcoord2.xy).a texcoord2.z. 5. Standard underlay: faceColor += underlayColor saturate(d - texcoord2.w) (1 - faceColor.a). 6. Inner underlay: faceColor += underlayColor (1 - saturate(d - texcoord2.w)) saturate(1 - sd) (1 - faceColor.a). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def saturate(x): return max(0.0, min(1.0, x)) def sampletexture(tex, uv): # Standard bilinear texture sampling returning a 4-component vector [r, g, b, a] return tex.bilinearsample(uv) def computesdfunderlay(atlas, faceColor, underlayColor, texcoord2, scale, GradientScale, TextureWidth, TextureHeight, ScaleRatioC, UnderlayOffsetX, UnderlayOffsetY, UnderlayDilate, UnderlaySoftness, weight): # Step 1: Compute offset UV bOffset = (-UnderlayOffsetX ScaleRatioC GradientScale / TextureWidth, -UnderlayOffsetY ScaleRatioC GradientScale / TextureHeight) # Step 2: Compute scale and bias bScale = scale / (1.0 + UnderlaySoftness ScaleRatioC scale) bBias = (0.5 - weight) bScale - 0.5 - (UnderlayDilate ScaleRatioC 0.5 bScale) # Step 3 & 4: Sample distance at offset UV d = sampletexture(atlas, texcoord2.xy).a texcoord2.z # Step 5: Standard underlay (behind) faceColor = faceColor + underlayColor saturate(d - texcoord2.w) (1.0 - faceColor.a) # Step 6: Inner underlay (inside) # sd is not defined in the sources sd = 0.0 faceColor = faceColor + underlayColor (1.0 - saturate(d - texcoord2.w)) saturate(1.0 - sd) (1.0 - faceColor.a) return faceColor UnderlayColor (Color, default 0,0,0,0.5): Border color. UnderlayOffsetX (float, default 0): Horizontal UV offset for the underlay sample. UnderlayOffsetY (float, default 0): Vertical UV offset for the underlay sample. UnderlayDilate (float, default 0): Expands or shrinks the underlay region. UnderlaySoftness (float, default 0): Blur radius for the underlay edge. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, requiring one additional texture sample and a few arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per pixel for intermediate calculations. Performance: The additional texture sample increases memory bandwidth usage, which can be significant on mobile GPUs if the atlas is not cached in L1/L2. Strengths: Provides a soft, blurred border effect that integrates well with the SDF's inherent anti-aliasing. Limitations: The inner underlay implementation relies on an undefined sd parameter, and performance degrades if the underlay offset causes sampling far from the primary UV. When to use: When a soft, blurred border is needed for text readability or aesthetic effect. When not to use: When precise, hard-edged outlines are required. The method is primarily associated with the Unity UI TextMeshPro package, where it is implemented as the "Underlay" effect to improve readability against complex backgrounds. The technique leverages the signed distance field's ability to represent smooth transitions, using the distance value as a mask for the underlay color. andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, https://github.com/andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Reconstruction and Compositing Techniques
head: Volume Compositing, Ray Casting Compositing, Optical Model Integration
body: Reconstruction and Compositing Techniques constitute the final stage of direct volume ray casting, where 3D volumetric data is projected into a 2D image by integrating sample contributions along viewing rays. This family handles the mathematical integration of per-ray sample attributes (color, opacity, density) into a final pixel value, leveraging specific mathematical forms (polynomials, kernels) or optimization strategies (early termination, packed layouts). What sets this family apart from its siblings is its focus on the mathematical integration of per-ray sample attributes into a final pixel value, often leveraging specific mathematical forms (polynomials, kernels) or optimization strategies (early termination, packed layouts) rather than just acceleration structures or post-processing filters. All methods in this family operate on a sequence of samples (ci, \alphai) encountered along a ray, where ci is the sample color (RGB) and \alphai is the sample opacity (A). The core mechanism involves an accumulator state (C{acc}, \alpha{acc}) initialized to (0, 0) (or background color/opacity) and updated iteratively for each sample. The standard optical model assumes that light is emitted or scattered by the volume and attenuated by absorption. The standard front-to-back compositing equation updates these accumulators for each sample i from front to back: C{acc}^{(i)} = C{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai Ci \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai where C{acc}^{(0)} = 0 and \alpha{acc}^{(0)} = 0. The term (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) represents the transmittance, i.e., the fraction of light reaching sample i from the camera side. In iterative form using transmittance T = 1 - \alpha{acc}: \begin{aligned} C{final} &\leftarrow C{final} + ci \cdot \alphai \cdot T \\ T &\leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai) \end{aligned} Where T is initialized to 1.0 and represents the accumulated transparency \prod (1-\alphaj). The final pixel color is often composited over a background color C{bg} using C{final} = C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{bg}. Early ray termination is a common optimization where the loop breaks if \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1.0), as further samples contribute negligibly to the color. Precision issues may cause T to become slightly negative when it should be zero; clamping T to [0, 1] is recommended. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositingloop(samples, backgroundcolor): """ Standard front-to-back compositing loop shared by the family. samples: list of (color: vec3, opacity: float) sorted front-to-back. backgroundcolor: vec3 for the scene background. """ Cacc = vec3(0.0) T = 1.0 # Transmittance initialized to 1.0 for ci, alphai in samples: # Compute weight for current sample weight = alphai T Cacc = Cacc + weight ci # Update transmittance T = T (1.0 - alphai) # Clamp transmittance to avoid precision issues T = max(0.0, T) # Early ray termination if T < 1e-6: break # Composite over background return Cacc + T backgroundcolor Composition via Convolution (Power Form) is a method for evaluating the composition of a trivariate polynomial field with a linear ray parameterization, transforming the 3D function into a univariate polynomial along the ray. It solves the problem of high computational cost and register pressure associated with naive polynomial substitution, enabling efficient implementation on GPU architectures. Unlike Composition via Scaled Bernstein Form, which maintains a uniform data representation for better numerical stability and root-finding compatibility, the Power Form uses power bases and convolution operators to minimize operation counts and register usage, offering superior performance for direct evaluation. Feed-backward reconstruction is a volume rendering technique that views convolution as gathering contributions from neighboring input samples for each output sample. It calculates each output value individually by centering the reconstruction kernel at the output sample and computing a weighted average of input samples lying under the kernel. It is distinguished from its sibling Feed-Forward Reconstruction by its access pattern: it accesses each output sample once and each input sample many times, whereas feed-forward methods access each input sample once and each output sample many times. Compositing is the final step in direct volume ray casting where multiple semi-transparent sample contributions along a viewing ray are combined into a single pixel color. It solves the problem of projecting a 3D density field into a 2D image by correctly blending overlying and underlying colors using ARGB blending. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on the standard optical model of light attenuation and emission, typically implemented via front-to-back accumulation which enables early ray termination, unlike back-to-front or order-independent variants. Final Scene Composition is a post-processing technique that applies pre-computed volumetric data to an opaque scene. It decouples volume calculation from surface rendering by sampling a 3D texture aligned with the scene geometry. Training Ray Compositing is a differentiable volume rendering technique that composites per-ray samples of density (\sigma), color (\text{RGB}), and ambient light into final pixel values while computing gradients for all inputs during the backward pass. It differs from standard inference compositing by explicitly supporting gradient propagation to density and color parameters, enabling end-to-end training of neural radiance fields. It builds on Reconstruction and Compositing Techniques by providing the specific implementation for training with sigma and ambient contributions. IDVR-Compositing is a post-local compositing step that assigns a view-dependent sparseness value to each object along a ray to modulate its visual prominence before global blending. It solves the problem of displaying multiple objects with different importance levels by making occluded or less important objects sparse (transparent) while keeping important ones dense (visible). Unlike standard compositing which treats all samples equally, IDVR-Compositing modifies the color and opacity values based on an object's importance and its occlusion status within the image footprint. Final Composition is a volume rendering technique that integrates voxel data into a 2D image by defining organs via intensity ranges and applying lighting to depict surfaces. It distinguishes itself from pure segmentation methods by incorporating the entire volume's information while avoiding exact boundary determination, and from pure projection methods by using illumination to enhance surface perception. It is primarily chosen when organ surface visualization is required without arbitrary thresholding. A technique by Vannier et al. that assigns a source strength and an attenuation coefficient (opacity) to each voxel. Trace rays through the volume array until they hit a surface. Assign an intensity inversely proportional to the distance traveled along the ray. Define a surface as a significant change in opacity value. This approach is still threshold-based. A volume rendering technique that uses a reconstruction validity metric \Phi(x, f, \Omega) to weight the opacity accumulation during ray casting, improving classification visualization by accounting for reconstruction accuracy in different density regions. Calculate reconstruction validity \Phi(x, f, \Omega) for each feature f at each reconstruction point x. For each ray, perform K reconstructions (one for each feature class) to get source color C{src} and opacity \alpha{src} based on transfer functions. Perform back-to-front compositing along the ray, updating accumulated color Cs and opacity \alphas using the weighted opacity formula involving \Phi(x, f, \Omega). Repeat compositing for all K features, as \Phi is feature-dependent. Cs = Cs + (1 - \alphas) C{src}, \alphas = \alphas + (1 - \alphas) \alpha{src} \Phi(x, f, \Omega), where Cs and \alphas are accumulated color and opacity, C{src} and \alpha{src} are source color and opacity from transfer function, and \Phi is the reconstruction validity weight. A rendering style node that allows compositing multiple styles together into a single rendering pass by listing them in its 'renderStyle' field. Unverified code. Source-Attenuation Reprojection was developed by Vannier et al. for medical data visualization to handle depth shading and surface definition. Reconstruction Validity Weighted Volume Rendering was proposed by Zhang and Tang to improve classification visualization by integrating probabilistic classification models with kernel regression. name: Composition via Convolution (Power Form)
head: Power Form
body: Composition via Convolution (Power Form) evaluates the composition of a trivariate polynomial field with a linear ray parameterization, transforming the 3D function into a univariate polynomial along the ray. It solves the problem of high computational cost and register pressure associated with naive polynomial substitution, enabling efficient implementation on GPU architectures. Unlike Composition via Scaled Bernstein Form, which maintains a uniform data representation for better numerical stability and root-finding compatibility, the Power Form uses power bases and convolution operators to minimize operation counts and register usage, offering superior performance for direct evaluation. The method computes the coefficients of the resulting univariate polynomial f(t) by leveraging the associative property of convolution to reduce the number of multiplications and additions required. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Trivariate polynomial coefficients f{ijk} for i,j,k \in \{0, \dots, d\}, where d is the degree of the basis functions. Input: Ray parameterization coefficients for the x, y, and z components: \mathbf{r}x = [px, vx], \mathbf{r}y = [py, vy], \mathbf{r}z = [pz, vz]. Output: Coefficient sequence \mathbf{f} of the resulting univariate polynomial of degree 3d. Data Structures: Coefficients are stored as floating-point arrays or sequences. Intermediate power expressions \mathbf{r}x^i, \mathbf{r}y^j, \mathbf{r}z^k are computed incrementally. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Power Sequences: Compute the power expressions for the ray components incrementally using convolution. For the x-component: \mathbf{r}x^0 = [1] and \mathbf{r}x^i = \mathbf{r}x^{i-1} \mathbf{r}x for i = 1, \dots, d. Repeat for \mathbf{r}y and \mathbf{r}z. The convolution of two coefficient sequences A and B results in a sequence C where Ck = \sum{m=0}^k Am B{k-m}. This step is equivalent to the Horner scheme for polynomial evaluation. 2. Compute Inner Sum (\mathbf{f}{ij}): For each pair (i, j), compute the intermediate polynomial coefficients \mathbf{f}{ij} by convolving the trivariate coefficients with the z-component powers: \mathbf{f}{ij} = \sum{k=0}^d f{ijk} \cdot \mathbf{r}z^k. Here, f{ijk} \cdot \mathbf{r}z^k denotes scalar multiplication of the coefficient sequence \mathbf{r}z^k by f{ijk}. 3. Compute Middle Sum: For each i, compute the sum over j: \mathbf{g}i = \sum{j=0}^d \mathbf{r}y^j \mathbf{f}{ij}. Note that \mathbf{f}{ij} is computed and consumed immediately, allowing memory reuse. 4. Compute Final Sum: Compute the final coefficient sequence \mathbf{f} by summing over i: \mathbf{f} = \sum{i=0}^d \mathbf{r}x^i \mathbf{g}i. Formulas: The core composition formula is: \mathbf{f} = \sum{i=0}^d \mathbf{r}x^i \sum{j=0}^d \mathbf{r}y^j \underbrace{\sum{k=0}^d f{ijk} \cdot \mathbf{r}z^k}{\mathbf{f}{ij}} Where \mathbf{r}x = [px, vx] is the coefficient sequence of the x-component of the ray. Parameters: d: Degree of the polynomial basis. Typical value is 3 (cubic). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Register Pressure: A naive implementation requires too many operations and registers to fit into a GPU framework (e.g., 135 registers for d=3). The convolution structure ensures that no more than one factor f{ij} and fi needs to be available at the same time, allowing memory reuse and reducing register usage to 27 for d=3. Precision: The Power Form yields a higher Mean Squared Error (MSE) than Scaled Bernstein forms but executes significantly faster. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def convolution(seqa, seqb): lena, lenb = len(seqa), len(seqb) res = [0.0] (lena + lenb - 1) for i in range(lena): for j in range(lenb): res[i + j] += seqa[i] seqb[j] return res def compositionviaconvolutionpowerform(fcoeffs, raycoeffs): d = len(raycoeffs[0]) - 1 rx, ry, rz = [[1.0]], [[1.0]], [[1.0]] for i in range(1, d + 1): rx.append(convolution(rx[i-1], raycoeffs[0])) ry.append(convolution(ry[i-1], raycoeffs[1])) rz.append(convolution(rz[i-1], raycoeffs[2])) finalf = [0.0] (3 d + 1) for i in range(d + 1): gi = [0.0] (2 d + 1) for j in range(d + 1): fij = [0.0] (d + 1) for k in range(d + 1): term = [c fcoeffs[i][j][k] for c in rz[k]] for m in range(len(term)): fij[m] += term[m] convres = convolution(ry[j], fij) for m in range(len(convres)): gi[m] += convres[m] convresfinal = convolution(rx[i], gi) for m in range(len(convresfinal)): finalf[m] += convresfinal[m] return finalf Evaluates composition using scaled Bernstein basis for better numerical stability and uniform data representation, avoiding basis conversion for root finding. Transforms trivariate polynomials from B-spline to scaled Bernstein or power basis to enable efficient root finding and compositing. Time Complexity: The Power Form method requires significantly fewer operations than the naive approach. For d=3, it uses 234 multiplications and 360 additions, compared to 1839 multiplications and 990 additions for the naive method. Memory Complexity: The convolution structure reduces register usage from 135 registers (naive) to 27 registers (PF), allowing it to fit into GPU register space. Performance: In relative terms, the PF method is approximately 278 times faster than the naive method (relative time 3.6 \times 10^{-3} vs 1). Accuracy: The Mean Squared Error (MSE) for PF is 22.6 \times 10^{-12}, which is higher than the Scaled Bernstein forms (e.g., SB2 has MSE 4.78 \times 10^{-12}) but lower than the naive method (162.3 \times 10^{-12}). Strengths: High performance due to low operation count and register usage; suitable for GPU implementation. Limitations: Lower numerical stability compared to Bernstein forms; not suitable if root finding is required without basis conversion. The method originates from research on efficient polynomial evaluation along rays for volume rendering. It builds on the use of convolution operators for polynomial composition to optimize computation for GPU frameworks.
