name: Composition via Scaled Bernstein Form
body: Composition via Scaled Bernstein Form (SB) evaluates the composition of a trivariate polynomial field with a ray parameterization, transforming a 3D function into a univariate function along a ray. It solves the problem of efficient numerical evaluation in direct volume ray casting by leveraging the scaled Bernstein basis. Unlike Composition via Convolution (Power Form), which uses power bases and convolution operators, SB maintains a uniform data representation throughout the pipeline, offering better numerical stability and avoiding the need for basis conversion when root finding is required. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Trivariate polynomial coefficients \tilde{b}{ijk} for i,j,k \in [0, d]; ray direction components ux, uy, uz; ray origin components qx, qy, qz; polynomial degree d. Output: Univariate polynomial coefficients \tilde{\mathbf{f}} representing the field values along the ray. Data Structures: Coefficients \tilde{b}{ijk}: Stored as a 3D array of size (d+1) \times (d+1) \times (d+1). Ray components: Scalars ue, qe for e \in \{x, y, z\}, where qe = 1 - ue. Intermediate terms: Precomputed powers of ue and qe. Formulas: The scaled Bernstein form uses basis functions defined by ray components ue and qe = 1 - ue. The composed polynomial \tilde{\mathbf{f}} is given by: \tilde{\mathbf{f}} = \sum{i,j,k=0}^d \tilde{b}{ijk} \cdot \tilde{\mathbf{q}}x^{d-i} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}x^i \tilde{\mathbf{q}}y^{d-j} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}y^j \tilde{\mathbf{q}}z^{d-k} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}z^k This can be factored to reduce operations: \tilde{\mathbf{f}} = \sum{i=0}^d \tilde{\mathbf{q}}x^{d-i} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}x^i \sum{j=0}^d \tilde{\mathbf{q}}y^{d-j} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}y^j \sum{k=0}^d \tilde{b}{ijk} \tilde{\mathbf{q}}z^{d-k} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}z^k For a single dimension, the composed coefficient sequence \tilde{\mathbf{c}} is computed recursively (Horner-like): \tilde{\mathbf{c}} = \sum{i=0}^d \tilde{b}i \tilde{\mathbf{q}}^{d-i} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}^i = \tilde{b}d \tilde{\mathbf{u}}^d + \tilde{\mathbf{q}} (\tilde{b}{d-1} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}^{d-1} + \dots + \tilde{\mathbf{q}} (\tilde{b}1 \tilde{\mathbf{u}} + \tilde{b}0 \tilde{\mathbf{q}})) Steps: 1. Precompute powers of ue and qe for e \in \{x, y, z\} and exponents 0 \dots d. Specifically, compute \tilde{\mathbf{u}}e^k and \tilde{\mathbf{q}}e^{d-k} for all k. 2. For each i from 0 to d: a. For each j from 0 to d: i. Compute the inner sum over k: S{ij} = \sum{k=0}^d \tilde{b}{ijk} \tilde{\mathbf{q}}z^{d-k} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}z^k. This can be done using the Horner-like recursion. ii. Multiply S{ij} by \tilde{\mathbf{q}}y^{d-j} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}y^j. b. Sum the results from step 2.a.ii over j. c. Multiply by \tilde{\mathbf{q}}x^{d-i} \tilde{\mathbf{u}}x^i. 3. Sum the results from step 2.c over i to get \tilde{\mathbf{f}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Ray components: ue, qe derived from ray direction and origin. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical stability: The scaled Bernstein form offers better stability than power form, especially for high degrees. Register usage: Naive implementation requires many registers. Optimized versions (SB1, SB2) reduce register pressure by reusing memory for intermediate coefficients. Precision: The operator denotes multiplication of basis terms; ensure floating-point precision is maintained during nested multiplications to avoid accumulation errors. Time Complexity: Significantly lower than naive evaluation. Operation counts for d=3 (from): SB0 (no precomputation): 741 muls, 483 adds. SB1 (precomputed x innermost): 687 muls, 490 adds. SB2 (precomputed x innermost, variant): 720 muls, 558 adds. Memory Complexity: Register usage is reduced compared to naive approach. SB0 uses 72 regs, SB1 uses 60 regs, SB2 uses 66 regs. Performance: Relative execution times (normalized to slowest) for d=3: SB0: 26e-3, SB1: 23e-3, SB2: 22e-3. Accuracy: Mean Squared Error (MSE) scaled by 10^{-12}: SB0: 5.15, SB1: 4.78, SB2: 4.78. Strengths: Uniform data representation, better numerical stability, avoids basis changes for root finding, fits well in GPU register space. Limitations: More complex implementation than power form. Precomputation adds memory overhead. When to use: When numerical stability is critical, or when root finding is needed later in the pipeline. When GPU register pressure is a bottleneck. When not to use: If simplicity is preferred and stability is not a concern. If memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck and precomputation overhead is too high. The scaled Bernstein form was proposed in [SR03] (cited in) as an alternative to the power form for polynomial evaluation in rendering. It is particularly useful in volume rendering where trivariate polynomials are composed with ray parameterizations. The method was highlighted in for its ability to reduce register usage and improve parallelism on GPUs by fitting the computation into limited register space. name: Basis Transform for Trivariate Polynomials
head: B-spline to Bernstein/Power Basis Transform
body: This method transforms a trivariate polynomial representation from the B-spline basis (used in tri-linear or tri-cubic filtering) to either the scaled Bernstein basis or the power basis. This transformation enables efficient root finding and composition via a Horner scheme, avoiding the memory overhead of storing explicit polynomial descriptions for every voxel in large datasets. It sets itself apart from naive substitution by leveraging the tensor product structure of the basis to reduce computational complexity and register usage. The method converts local voxel data, initially defined by surrounding data values in a B-spline basis, into a form suitable for efficient evaluation. Inputs: Voxel data values (coefficients in B-spline basis). Polynomial degree d (supported values: 0, 1, 2). Evaluation point coordinates (x, y, z). Outputs: Transformed coefficients in the target basis (scaled Bernstein or power basis). Evaluated polynomial value (when integrated with Horner scheme). Data Structures: Basis Vector (b): A vector containing the monomial or Bernstein basis terms. For degree 0: b = [1]. For degree 1: b = [1, x, y, z]. For degree 2: b = [1, x, y, z, xy, xz, yz, x^2, y^2, z^2]. Basis Matrix (B): A matrix where each row corresponds to the basis vector of a specific point. Size is P.rows() \times b.size(). Steps: 1. One-Dimensional Basis Transform: The transformation from 1D B-spline basis to the target basis is a matrix multiplication of the basis vector with a (d+1) \times (d+1) matrix. To scaled Bernstein basis: Requires 6 multiplications. To power basis: Requires 8 multiplications. Matrices are constructed to contain zeros and ones, scaled by a constant factor to minimize operations. 2. N-Dimensional Basis Transform Construction: The N-dimensional basis is a tensor product of the 1D bases. The full transform is constructed from N \cdot (d+1)^{N-1} one-dimensional basis transforms. For trivariate polynomials (N=3), this involves combining the 1D transforms across dimensions. 3. Integration with Horner Scheme: The basis transform is integrated into a Horner scheme for composition. This separation of single dimensions allows for efficient on-the-fly transformation during rendering, avoiding the storage of explicit polynomial descriptions which would increase memory consumption by a factor of (d+1)^3. Returns: transformed coefficients. name: Feed-Backward Reconstruction
head: Gather-based reconstruction, Ray-casting approach
body: Feed-backward reconstruction is a volume rendering technique that views convolution as gathering contributions from neighboring input samples for each output sample. It calculates each output value individually by centering the reconstruction kernel at the output sample and computing a weighted average of input samples lying under the kernel. It is distinguished from its sibling Feed-Forward Reconstruction by its access pattern: it accesses each output sample once and each input sample many times, whereas feed-forward methods access each input sample once and each output sample many times. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of discrete input samples Xj with positions Pj and values Vj. Input: A reconstruction kernel K(u), defined by its shape and support width. Input: A set of output sample positions I. Output: A sequence of output values Ai corresponding to each position I. Data Structures: inputpositions: Array of coordinates Pj. inputvalues: Array of values Vj. kernelfunc: Function or lookup table defining K(u). outputpositions: Array of coordinates I. outputvalues: Array of values Ai. Steps: 1. For each output sample position I: a. Initialize accumulator Ai = 0. b. Identify all input samples Xj that lie within the support of the kernel centered at I. c. For each such input sample Xj: i. Calculate the relative distance u = I - Pj. ii. Evaluate the kernel weight w = K(u). iii. Update the output sample: Ai \leftarrow Ai + Vj \cdot w. 2. Return the array of output samples Ai. Formulas: The value of output sample i is given by: Ai = \sum{j \in \text{support}(I)} Vj \cdot K(I - Pj) Where: Ai is the value of the i-th output sample. Vj is the value of the j-th input sample. K(\cdot) is the reconstruction kernel function. \text{support}(I) is the set of input indices j such that K(I - Pj) \neq 0. Parameters: Kernel type: Commonly linear (triangular pulse) for simplicity, but can be higher-order B-splines. Kernel support: Determines the number of input samples accessed per output sample. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Kernel Support Boundaries: Ensure that the loop over input samples correctly handles cases where the kernel support extends beyond the input data boundaries. Samples outside the input range should be treated as zero or handled via boundary conditions. Precision: Accumulating many small weights can lead to floating-point precision issues. Use compensated summation if high precision is required and the number of contributing samples is large. Degenerate Input: If input samples are not uniformly spaced, the distance calculation I - Pj must account for the actual coordinate of Pj, not just the index. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def feedbackwardreconstruction(inputpositions, inputvalues, kernelfunc, outputpositions): """ Performs feed-backward reconstruction. Args: inputpositions: List of coordinates Pj. inputvalues: List of values Vj. kernelfunc: Function K(u) that returns the kernel weight for distance u. outputpositions: List of output positions I. Returns: List of output values Ai. """ numoutputs = len(outputpositions) outputvalues = [0.0] numoutputs for i, Ipos in enumerate(outputpositions): accumulator = 0.0 for j, Pj in enumerate(inputpositions): u = Ipos - Pj w = kernelfunc(u) if w != 0.0: accumulator += inputvalues[j] w outputvalues[i] = accumulator return outputvalues Spatial convolution is a neighborhood-based operation where output values are calculated as a weighted average of neighboring input samples using a filter kernel. In volume rendering, it is used to convolve discrete samples with a reconstruction kernel in the spatial domain. It is distinguished from frequency-domain methods (like FFT-based convolution) by operating directly on spatial data, which is preferred for discrete kernels of limited extent because transforming to and from the frequency domain is more compute-intensive than direct spatial convolution. The Area-based Pixel Kernel is a reconstruction kernel used in feed-backward reconstruction that assigns pixel contributions proportional to the geometric area of intersection between a pixel and a thick projection line. It solves the artifact issues inherent in Dirac and B-Spline kernels, which leave unreconstructed pixels during subsampling, and linear kernels, which fail to fully exploit available data during oversampling. It is distinguished from its sibling Spatial Convolution by its specific geometric interpretation of projection thickness and its optimization via rotation-based approximation. Feed-forward reconstruction is a reconstruction method that views convolution as distributing contributions from a given input sample to its neighboring output samples. It centers the reconstruction kernel at an input value and spreads the energy to each output lying under the kernel. It is distinguished from feed-backward reconstruction by its access pattern: it accesses each input sample once and each output sample many times. Time and Memory Complexity: Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In an example with 4 input samples, 13 output samples, and linear reconstruction, feed-backward reconstruction results in 39 sample accesses (2 input accesses per output 13 outputs + 13 output writes). Feed-forward reconstruction in the same scenario results in 24 sample accesses (5 output accesses per input 4 inputs + 4 input reads). Scaling: The total number of accesses depends on the kernel extent and the number of intermediate samples. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple implementation, direct spatial domain operation, suitable for non-uniform sampling if coordinates are tracked. Limitations: Can be less cache-friendly than feed-forward methods due to repeated access to input samples. When to Use: Use when the output resolution is significantly higher than the input resolution, or when the kernel support is small relative to the input size. When Not to Use: Avoid when the input size is very large and the kernel support is wide, as the repeated access to input samples can become a bottleneck. Feed-backward reconstruction was described by Feibush in 1980. A Parallel, Feed-Forward Volume Rendering Algorithm, https://www.cs.unc.edu/techreports/91-029.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Spatial Convolution
head: Continuous Signal Reconstruction by Convolution, Direct Spatial Convolution, Discrete Convolution, Kernel Convolution, Spatial Domain Convolution
body: Spatial convolution is a neighborhood-based reconstruction method that calculates each output sample by computing a weighted average of neighboring input samples using a filter kernel. It solves the problem of reconstructing a continuous signal from discrete samples in the spatial domain, serving as the primary compositing step in direct volume ray casting when small kernels are used. Unlike frequency-domain methods (FFT), it is preferred for discrete kernels of limited extent because direct spatial summation is less compute-intensive than transforming to and from the frequency domain. It differs from Area-based Pixel Kernel by centering the kernel at the output sample and summing contributions from input samples, rather than distributing contributions from input samples to output pixels. Inputs: Discrete input signal f (e.g., volume samples f(i,j,k) or image pixels \mathbf{L}(\mathbf{x})). Reconstruction kernel h (or \mathbf{K}), defined over a support region. Outputs: Reconstructed continuous or discrete signal g (or (\mathbf{L} \mathbf{K})). Data Structures: Input Signal: Array of values indexed by integer coordinates. In 3D volume rendering, typically stored as a 3D grid or texture. Kernel: Array of floating-point weights. For a kernel of support N, the array size is N \times N \times N (or N \times N for 2D). Output Signal: Array of values with the same dimensions as the input (for discrete output) or a continuous function representation. Steps: 1. Kernel Normalization: If the kernel is derived from a continuous function (e.g., Gaussian), sum all kernel values S = \sum{\mathbf{x}'} K(\mathbf{x}'). Multiply every element of the kernel by 1/S to ensure energy conservation (\sum K(\mathbf{x}) = 1). 2. Iterate Output Positions: For each output position \mathbf{x} (or (x,y,z)): 3. Initialize Sum: Set accumulator g(\mathbf{x}) = 0. 4. Iterate Kernel Support: For each offset \mathbf{x}' within the kernel's support: Calculate the corresponding input sample position \mathbf{x}{in} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}' (or \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{x}' depending on kernel definition convention; standard convolution uses h(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{x}')). Boundary Check: If \mathbf{x}{in} is outside the input domain, handle boundary conditions (e.g., clamp, wrap, or zero-pad). Sample Input: Retrieve input value f(\mathbf{x}{in}). If \mathbf{x}{in} is not an integer coordinate, apply an interpolation method (e.g., trilinear) or treat as zero if outside support. Weight and Accumulate: g(\mathbf{x}) \leftarrow g(\mathbf{x}) + f(\mathbf{x}{in}) \cdot K(\mathbf{x}'). 5. Store Output: Assign g(\mathbf{x}) to the output buffer. Formulas: The continuous convolution integral in 1D is: g(t) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} f(u)h(t-u) du In 2D: g(x, y) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} f(u, v) h(x - u, y - v) du dv In 3D: g(x, y, z) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \int{-\infty}^{\infty} f(u, v, w) h(x - u, y - v, z - w) du dv dw For discrete signals, represented as v(x) = \sumi v[i]\delta(x - i), the convolution sum is: g(x, y, z) = \sum{i=-\infty}^{\infty} \sum{j=-\infty}^{\infty} \sum{k=-\infty}^{\infty} f(i, j, k) h(x - i, y - j, z - k) In 2D discrete notation: (\mathbf{L} \mathbf{K})(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{\mathbf{x}'} \mathbf{L}(\mathbf{x}') \mathbf{K}(\mathbf{x}' - \mathbf{x}) Parameters: Kernel Support: The range of positions for which h(x) is nonzero. Typical small kernels are 3 \times 3 \times 3 or 5 \times 5 \times 5. Large supports (e.g., 10 \times 10 \times 10) incur performance penalties. Kernel Type: Trilinear: De facto norm, poor aliasing. BC Splines (Mitchell-Netravali): Two-parameter cubic family. Catmull-Rom at (B,C)=(0, 0.5); Uniform cubic B-spline at (B,C)=(1, 0). Windowed Sinc: Close to ideal frequency response but large support. Pitfalls: Normalization Error: Sampling a normalized continuous function (like Gaussian) at discrete points breaks normalization, violating energy conservation. Explicit normalization is required. Memory Latency: Large kernel supports cause non-local memory accesses, leading to cache misses and performance degradation. Aliasing: Simple linear interpolation suffers from poor aliasing characteristics. Spatially Varying Kernel Filtering is a technique where the reconstruction kernel or weighting function differs for each pixel, rather than being stationary as in standard convolution. It solves the problem of applying spatially dependent blurring or smoothing (e.g., varying Point Spread Functions) which cannot be solved using standard convolution algorithms or FFT. Unlike Separable Convolution, which optimizes a single stationary kernel, this method requires per-pixel kernel evaluation. Separable convolution is a method to accelerate hologram computation by exploiting the linear separability of the lens phase function fz into independent horizontal and vertical components. It solves the performance bottleneck of point-wise integration in direct volume ray casting for holographic displays by reducing the computational complexity of the spatial convolution operation. It is distinguished from FFT-based convolution by its reliance on spatial separability rather than frequency-domain transformation, making it faster for smaller sub-hologram sizes but inapplicable when the phase function is not separable. DDA Convolution is a specific application of spatial convolution used for Line Integral Convolution (LIC) of vector fields. For each output pixel position, a filter kernel is defined along the vector direction (tangential to the flow) for a fixed distance L in both positive and negative directions. Input texture pixels falling within this kernel are sampled, summed, and normalized by the kernel length 2L to produce the output pixel value. While often implemented as a box filter, arbitrary filter shapes can be used. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K^d), where N is the number of output samples, K is the kernel support size, and d is the dimensionality (2 or 3). Memory Complexity: O(N + K^d) for input/output buffers and kernel storage. Performance: Preferred over FFT for small kernels because the overhead of forward and inverse transforms exceeds the cost of direct spatial summation. Large kernels (10 \times 10 \times 10) suffer from memory access latency. Strengths: Simple implementation; intuitive spatial interpretation; efficient for small, localized kernels; supports non-stationary kernels (with variants). Limitations: Poor aliasing with simple kernels (e.g., trilinear); large kernels are slow; normalization must be handled manually for sampled continuous kernels. When to Use: Direct volume ray casting with small reconstruction kernels (e.g., B-splines, windowed sinc); real-time rendering where FFT overhead is prohibitive. When Not to Use: Large kernel sizes where FFT is faster; scenarios requiring exact frequency-domain multiplication. Originating from signal processing theory (Oppenheim 75), spatial convolution is applied in volume rendering to reconstruct continuous signals from discrete voxel samples. In computer graphics, it is used for image filtering and reconstruction, with B-splines and windowed sinc kernels being common choices to balance smoothing and aliasing. The method is central to feed-backward reconstruction techniques in volume rendering. DDA Convolution was introduced for visualizing vector fields via Line Integral Convolution. name: Spatially Varying Kernel Filtering
head: Non-Stationary Filtering, Spatially Varying Convolution
body: Spatially Varying Kernel Filtering is a technique where the reconstruction kernel or weighting function differs for each pixel, rather than being stationary as in standard convolution. It solves the problem of applying spatially dependent blurring or smoothing (e.g., varying Point Spread Functions) which cannot be solved using standard convolution algorithms or FFT. Unlike Separable Convolution, which optimizes a single stationary kernel, this method requires per-pixel kernel evaluation. Inputs: Input image \mathbf{L} of size n \times n. A set of weighting functions w{\mathbf{x}'}(\mathbf{x}' - \mathbf{x}) that define the contribution of neighbor \mathbf{x}' to the target pixel \mathbf{x}. Outputs: Filtered image \mathbf{L}'. Data Structures: Kernel size is typically small (e.g., m \times m) to manage computational cost. Storage for weighting functions is Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Iterate over each pixel \mathbf{x} in the output image. 2. For each pixel \mathbf{x}, identify the neighborhood of source pixels \mathbf{x}'. 3. Compute the weighted sum of the input image values using the specific weighting function for that location: \mathbf{L}'(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{\mathbf{x}'} w{\mathbf{x}'}(\mathbf{x}' - \mathbf{x})\mathbf{L}(\mathbf{x}') where w{\mathbf{x}'} is the weight assigned to neighbor \mathbf{x}' for target \mathbf{x}. 4. Normalize the result if the kernel is not pre-normalized by summing the kernel values and multiplying the kernel by the reciprocal value to conserve energy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spatiallyvaryingfilter(L, getweights): """ L: Input image (n x n) getweights: Function that returns a list of (dx, dy, weight) for a given center pixel """ n = len(L) Lprime = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] for x in range(n): for y in range(n): weights = getweights(x, y) sumval = 0.0 sumweights = 0.0 for dx, dy, w in weights: nx, ny = x + dx, y + dy if 0 <= nx < n and 0 <= ny < n: sumval += w L[nx][ny] sumweights += w if sumweights != 0: Lprime[x][y] = sumval / sumweights else: Lprime[x][y] = 0.0 return Lprime Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normalization: If the sum of weights is zero or near-zero, division by zero occurs; guard against this. Boundary Conditions: The neighborhood \mathbf{x}' may fall outside the image bounds; explicit handling (e.g., clamping, mirroring, or ignoring out-of-bounds contributions) is required. Complexity: The naive implementation is O(n^2 m^2), where m is the kernel radius; FFT cannot be used. A specific variant of spatially varying filtering that convolves in the neighborhood of the analyzed point (not just along a vector direction) to obtain a smooth result rich in local dynamic information. It uses a local filtering kernel pattern rotated to the direction assumed by the vector field at each point. Unlike Line Integral Convolution (LIC), which convolves along lines, FAD convolves spatially in the local environment. Iterating FAD independently does not produce changes/improvements. It can use reduced kernels (e.g., 3x3) for low computational cost. Example asymmetric filter: \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. Example symmetric filter: \begin{pmatrix} -1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 3 & 2 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}. Time Complexity: Generally O(n^2 m^2) for an image of size n \times n and kernel size m \times m. It cannot be accelerated by FFT or standard convolution optimizations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows for spatially dependent effects like varying blur or directional emphasis based on local features. Limitations: High computational cost compared to stationary convolution; requires careful normalization. Originated in the context of image processing and light transport simulation, specifically addressing the need to handle spatially varying Point Spread Functions (PSF). The term "Dynamic Adaptive Filtering" (FAD) was developed in the context of vector field visualization, combining texture convolution with local dynamic information. name: Separable Convolution
head: Linearly separable convolution, Two-pass convolution
body: Separable convolution is a method to accelerate hologram computation by exploiting the linear separability of the lens phase function fz into independent horizontal and vertical components. It solves the performance bottleneck of point-wise integration in direct volume ray casting for holographic displays by reducing the computational complexity of the spatial convolution operation. It is distinguished from FFT-based convolution by its reliance on spatial separability rather than frequency-domain transformation, making it faster for smaller sub-hologram sizes but inapplicable when the phase function is not separable. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Target image data A (containing the square root of image intensities) and the lens phase function fz. Output: Computed hologram H. Data Structures: A: A 2D array of complex or real values representing the source image intensities. f{zx}: A 1D vector representing the horizontal component of the lens phase function. f{zy}: A 1D vector representing the vertical component of the lens phase function. H: A 2D array of the same dimensions as A, storing the resulting hologram. Prerequisites: The lens phase function fz must be linearly separable into vectors f{zx} and f{zy}. This condition holds for lens phase functions of any focal power and certain aberrations, such as horizontal astigmatism or vertical astigmatism. If fz is not linearly separable, this method cannot be applied. Formulas: The hologram H is computed by convolving the image A with the separable components sequentially: H = (A f{zx}) f{zy} where denotes the convolution operation. Parameters: Sub-hologram width: The runtime scales linearly with the sub-hologram size. Typical Performance: Calculation of a hologram with 2 million object points takes just a few milliseconds on a GPU. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Non-separable Phase Functions: If the lens phase function contains aberrations or focal properties that cannot be decomposed into independent horizontal and vertical vectors, this method fails. Spatial Variance: This method assumes the lens phase function is spatially invariant (constant over the image) to allow standard convolution. It does not support per-pixel focal control or spatially variant aberration correction. Sub-hologram Size Scaling: Unlike FFT-based convolution, the runtime of separable convolution scales linearly with the sub-hologram width. It is faster than FFT-based convolution for smaller sub-hologram sizes, but the crossover point depends on the specific hardware and implementation. Pseudocode: The implementation operates in two passes, one for each linearly separable axis. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def separableconvolution(A, fzx, fzy): """ Computes hologram H using separable convolution. Args: A: 2D array of image intensities (square root). fzx: 1D vector for horizontal phase component. fzy: 1D vector for vertical phase component. Returns: H: 2D array representing the hologram. """ # Pass 1: Convolve image A with horizontal kernel fzx # Result is stored in intermediate buffer Temp Temp = convolve2dhorizontal(A, fzx) # Pass 2: Convolve intermediate result Temp with vertical kernel fzy # Result is stored in H H = convolve2dvertical(Temp, fzy) return H def convolve2dhorizontal(Image, Kernel): """ Convolves each row of the image with the 1D horizontal kernel. """ Height, Width = Image.shape KernelLength = len(Kernel) Output = zeroslike(Image) for y in range(Height): for x in range(Width): Sum = 0 for k in range(KernelLength): # Handle boundary conditions (e.g., zero-padding or replication) # Not specified in sources; assume standard convolution boundary handling xidx = x - k + (KernelLength - 1) // 2 if 0 <= xidx < Width: Sum += Image[y, xidx] Kernel[k] Output[y, x] = Sum return Output def convolve2dvertical(Image, Kernel): """ Convolves each column of the image with the 1D vertical kernel. """ Height, Width = Image.shape KernelLength = len(Kernel) Output = zeroslike(Image) for y in range(Height): for x in range(Width): Sum = 0 for k in range(KernelLength): # Handle boundary conditions yidx = y - k + (KernelLength - 1) // 2 if 0 <= yidx < Height: Sum += Image[yidx, x] Kernel[k] Output[y, x] = Sum return Output A method to speed up hologram calculation by removing spatial variance of the lens phase function fz so it is the same for all object points, allowing substitution of point-wise integration with standard spatially invariant convolution. It computes H = A fz using the Fast Fourier Transform: H = FFT^{-1}(FFT(A) \times FFT(fz)), where \times indicates point-wise multiplication. It requires a spatially invariant lens phase function, implying focus and aberration correction is constant over the image. A key pitfall is that it does not support per-pixel focal control because the lens phase function is not spatially variant. It runs in just a few milliseconds for 2 million object points on a GPU. Unlike separable convolution, FFT convolution does not depend on sub-hologram size, whereas separable convolution scales linearly with it. Time Complexity: Scales linearly with the sub-hologram size. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the image A, the hologram H, and intermediate buffers for the two-pass convolution. Measured Performance: For a 1920x1080 hologram with 2 million object points, computation takes just a few milliseconds on a GPU. Scaling: Runtime increases linearly with sub-hologram width. Strengths: Significantly faster than point-wise integration (orders of magnitude). Faster than FFT-based convolution for smaller sub-hologram sizes. Limitations: Only applicable when the lens phase function is linearly separable. Does not support per-pixel focal control or spatially variant aberration correction. When to use: When the lens phase function is linearly separable and sub-hologram sizes are small to moderate. When not to use: When the lens phase function is not linearly separable or when per-pixel focal control is required. Separable convolution was introduced in the context of holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality by Maimone et al. in 2017. The method leverages a common simplification in image processing, applying it to hologram computation for the first time in this context. It is used in real-time holographic displays to generate holograms directly from rendered polygonal models, enabling frame rates exceeding the display refresh rate. name: Area-based Pixel Kernel
head: Area kernel, Noyau de Pixel basé sur l’aire (Area-based Pixel Kernel), Noyau d’interpolation sur l’aire des pixels
body: The Area-based Pixel Kernel is a reconstruction kernel that assigns pixel contributions proportional to the geometric area of intersection between a pixel and a thick projection line. It solves the artifact issues inherent in Dirac and B-Spline kernels, which leave unreconstructed pixels during subsampling, and linear kernels, which fail to fully exploit available data during oversampling. It is distinguished from its sibling Spatial Convolution by its specific geometric interpretation of projection thickness and its optimization via a rotation-based approximation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Projection data p(\theta, \rho), where \theta is the angle and \rho is the radial coordinate; pixel grid coordinates (i, j); projection line thickness d\rho; pixel size \Delta p. Outputs: Reconstructed image intensity I(i, j). Data Structures: Projection Buffer: Array of values indexed by (\theta, \rho). Temporary Image I\theta: A 2D array used to store the backprojected contributions for a specific angle \theta before rotation. Result Image I: The final accumulated 2D array. Parameters: d\rho: Thickness of the projection line. \Delta p: Pixel width. \theta: Current projection angle. \rho: Radial position of the projection line. i, j: Integer pixel coordinates. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the result image I to zero. 2. For each projection angle \theta: a. Create a temporary image I\theta of the same dimensions as I, initialized to zero. b. For each radial sample \rho in the projection p(\theta, \cdot): i. Calculate the kernel weight \Lambda(\phi=0, \rho, i, j) for every pixel (i, j) in I\theta using the formula below. ii. Add the contribution p(\theta, \rho) \times \Lambda(\phi=0, \rho, i, j) to I\theta(i, j). c. Rotate the temporary image I\theta by the angle -\theta. d. Add the rotated I\theta to the result image I. Formula: The kernel \Lambda(\phi=0, \rho, i, j) for the approximation where the projection is aligned with the axes (\phi=0) is defined as: \Lambda(\phi=0, \rho, i, j) = \begin{cases} d\rho & \text{if } [\rho - d\rho/2] = [\rho + d\rho/2] = [\rho] = i \\ \frac{d\rho + \Delta p}{2} + |\rho - i| & \text{if } [\rho - d\rho/2] < i \land [\rho + d\rho/2] = i \\ 1 & \text{if } [\rho - d\rho/2] < i \land [\rho + d\rho/2] > i \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where [\cdot] is the round function returning the nearest integer to the real parameter. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def areakernelweight(rho, drho, deltap, pixeli): """Calculates the kernel weight for a single pixel i given rho, drho, and deltap.""" def roundtoint(x): return int(math.floor(x + 0.5)) rholow = rho - drho / 2.0 rhohigh = rho + drho / 2.0 ilow = roundtoint(rholow) ihigh = roundtoint(rhohigh) imid = roundtoint(rho) if ilow == ihigh == imid == pixeli: return drho if ilow < pixeli and ihigh == pixeli: return (drho + deltap) / 2.0 + abs(rho - pixeli) if ilow < pixeli and ihigh > pixeli: return 1.0 return 0.0 def backprojectareakernel(projections, imageshape, drho, deltap): """Reconstructs an image using the Area-based Pixel Kernel approximation.""" height, width = imageshape resultimage = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for theta, rhovalues in projections: tempimage = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for rho, value in rhovalues: rholow = rho - drho / 2.0 rhohigh = rho + drho / 2.0 starti = max(0, int(math.floor(min(rholow, rhohigh) - 1))) endi = min(width, int(math.ceil(max(rholow, rhohigh) + 1))) for i in range(starti, endi): weight = areakernelweight(rho, drho, deltap, i) if weight > 0: for j in range(height): tempimage[j][i] += value weight # Rotation by -theta and accumulation. # The source does not specify the interpolation method for rotation. # Using nearest-neighbor sampling as a standard fallback. cost = math.cos(-theta) sint = math.sin(-theta) cxcenter = width / 2.0 cycenter = height / 2.0 for r in range(height): for c in range(width): dx = c - cxcenter dy = r - cycenter srcc = dx cost - dy sint + cxcenter srcr = dx sint + dy cost + cycenter srccint = int(math.floor(srcc + 0.5)) srcrint = int(math.floor(srcr + 0.5)) if 0 <= srcrint < height and 0 <= srccint < width: resultimage[r][c] += tempimage[srcrint][srccint] return resultimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex Geometry: The exact calculation of the common area between a thick line and a pixel generates complex shapes requiring non-trivial decomposition into simple shapes, which is why the rotation approximation is used. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates unreconstructed pixels (holes) present in Dirac and B-Spline kernels during subsampling. Fully exploits data in oversampling scenarios, unlike linear kernels. Limitations: The rotation approximation avoids exact geometric integration, which may lead to slight inaccuracies compared to a true area calculation. The Area-based Pixel Kernel was introduced in the context of tomographic reconstruction to address the limitations of standard interpolators. It is described in the thesis "Précision et qualité en reconstruction tomographique: algorithmes et applications". name: Compositing
head: Composite ARGB
body: Compositing is the final step in direct volume ray casting where multiple semi-transparent sample contributions along a viewing ray are combined into a single pixel color. It solves the problem of projecting a 3D density field into a 2D image by correctly blending overlying and underlying colors using ARGB blending. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on the standard optical model of light attenuation and emission, typically implemented via front-to-back accumulation which enables early ray termination, unlike back-to-front or order-independent variants. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of samples (ci, \alphai) encountered along a ray, where ci is the sample color (RGB) and \alphai is the sample opacity (A). The samples are sorted front-to-back. Input: A background color C{bg} (default black). Output: The final pixel color C{final}. Data Structures: The method maintains an accumulator state (C{acc}, \alpha{acc}) initialized to (0, 0). C{acc}: Accumulated color, a 3-component vector (RGB). \alpha{acc}: Accumulated opacity, a scalar. Formulas: The standard front-to-back compositing equation updates the accumulators for each sample i: C{acc}^{(i)} = C{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai ci \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai where C{acc}^{(0)} = 0 and \alpha{acc}^{(0)} = 0. The term (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) represents the transmittance T, i.e., the fraction of light reaching sample i from the camera side. In iterative form using transmittance T = 1 - \alpha{acc}: \begin{aligned} C{final} &\leftarrow C{final} + ci \cdot \alphai \cdot T \\ T &\leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai) \end{aligned} Where T is initialized to 1.0 and represents the accumulated transparency \prod (1-\alphaj). The final pixel color is composited over the background color C{bg} using: C{final} = C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{bg}. Parameters: Early ray termination threshold: Typically 1.0 (or a value slightly less, e.g., 0.99, to avoid precision issues). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If \alpha{acc} approaches 1.0, the transmittance approaches 0. Floating-point precision errors may cause T to become slightly negative or non-zero when it should be zero, leading to minor artifacts. Clamping T to [0, 1] is recommended. Boundary: If the ray exits the volume before \alpha{acc} reaches 1.0, the remaining transmittance is applied to the background color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositingloop(samples, backgroundcolor): """ Standard front-to-back compositing loop. samples: list of (color: vec3, opacity: float) sorted front-to-back. backgroundcolor: vec3 for the scene background. """ Cacc = vec3(0.0) alphaacc = 0.0 for ci, alphai in samples: transmittance = max(0.0, 1.0 - alphaacc) Cacc = Cacc + transmittance alphai ci alphaacc = min(1.0, alphaacc + transmittance alphai) # Early ray termination if alphaacc >= 1.0: break # Composite over background return Cacc + (1.0 - alphaacc) backgroundcolor Alpha compositing ray casting evaluates the volume rendering integral by marching along viewing rays and iteratively blending semi-transparent samples from the front of the ray to the back. It solves the problem of projecting a 3D density field into a 2D image without requiring binary classification, thereby eliminating false positives and false negatives. It is distinguished from its siblings by its recursive accumulation of color and opacity using the OVER operator, which enables early ray termination when the accumulated opacity reaches unity, a feature not available in back-to-front compositing. Alpha Compositing Ray Casting Ray Compositing and Accumulation is a hardware-accelerated method for aggregating color and opacity contributions into final pixel values during direct volume ray casting, specifically designed to handle sample streams that are not presented in strict ray order. Unlike software-based approaches that require sorting or random access memory for per-ray buffers, this method uses dedicated hardware structures (FIFOs and shift registers) to buffer partially accumulated values and resolve predecessor dependencies based on view direction and spatial coordinates. It is distinguished from Alpha Compositing Ray Casting by its explicit hardware implementation for non-ordered data streams, and from Raymarch Blending by its focus on fixed-function accumulation logic within the VolumePro architecture. Ray Compositing and Accumulation Average Compositing is a volume rendering technique that produces an X-ray-like image by sending a ray through the volume and compositing all found values with the same weight, taking no opacity into account. It differs from Alpha Compositing and Accumulation methods by treating every sample equally regardless of depth or transparency. Average Compositing Raymarch Blending combines a ray-marched volumetric result with an existing background scene texture using standard alpha compositing. It solves the problem of integrating semi-transparent volumetric data into a pre-rendered scene containing opaque geometry, ensuring correct occlusion where the volume interacts with the solid meshes. Unlike Alpha Compositing Ray Casting which typically handles volume-to-volume or volume-to-black blending, this method explicitly blends against a pre-existing framebuffer color. Raymarch Blending Alpha blending is a compositing technique used in direct volume ray casting to combine multiple semi-transparent contributions along a viewing ray into a final pixel color. It solves the problem of rendering translucent volumes by discretizing the continuous light transport equation, allowing for physically plausible accumulation of emitted and attenuated light. It is distinguished from simple averaging or maximum intensity projection by its use of an associative, non-commutative operator that preserves depth ordering, enabling correct compositing of independent sub-volumes or distributed rendering nodes. Alpha Blending Front-to-Back Compositing is a direct volume rendering technique that projects semi-transparent volume data to the screen by traversing viewing rays from the camera viewpoint toward the far plane, accumulating color and opacity contributions. It is distinguished from its sibling Alpha Compositing Ray Casting and Back-to-Front Compositing by its ability to exploit early ray termination, allowing the renderer to stop processing a ray once the accumulated opacity approaches 1.0, thereby significantly reducing computational cost for opaque or dense regions. Front-to-Back Compositing This method composites semi-transparent volumetric samples in an order-independent manner by employing a visibility function that represents the total transmittance between a sample and the camera. It solves the order-dependent transparency problem in direct volume rendering, enabling correct visibility composition beyond simple Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) or X-ray representations. Unlike its siblings which often rely on sorting or front-to-back accumulation, this approach refactors the alpha-blending equation to avoid recursion and sorting, allowing light sources to be processed independently of the camera location. Order-Independent Volumetric Compositing via Visibility Function Definition: A projection technique that composites samples along the ray using alpha blending until the ray exits the volume or becomes fully opaque. Steps: 1. Initialize contribution = 1.0f. 2. Composite each sample: outputColor.rgb += contribution transfer.a transfer.rgb. contribution = (1 - transfer.a). Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. Early ray termination reduces the average N for opaque regions. Memory: O(1) per ray for the accumulator state. Measured Performance: Performance depends heavily on the density of the volume and the effectiveness of early ray termination. For sparse volumes, the cost is proportional to the number of occupied samples. For dense volumes, the loop may terminate early, reducing cost. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays (pixels). Parallelization is straightforward across pixels. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Physically plausible results for semi-transparent volumes; efficient early ray termination; simple implementation. Limitations: Order-dependent (requires front-to-back sorting or traversal); not suitable for order-independent transparency without modification; early ray termination can cause artifacts if not handled carefully (e.g., in distributed rendering). When to Use: Use for standard direct volume rendering where semi-transparency is required and early ray termination is beneficial. Do not use when order-independent transparency is required or when samples are not available in front-to-back order without additional buffering. Compositing in volume rendering originated from the need to combine multiple semi-transparent samples along a ray to produce a realistic 2D projection. The front-to-back approach is used in interactive volume ray tracing. The technique is fundamental to direct volume rendering and is implemented in various graphics pipelines and hardware accelerators. name: Alpha Compositing Ray Casting
head: Alpha Compositing A+(1-A)*B, Blend2 Compositing, OVER compositing, OVER operator, Porter-Duff over operator, Standard Over Blend
body: Alpha compositing ray casting evaluates the volume rendering integral by marching a ray through the volume and accumulating color contributions from front to back using the "Over" operator. It solves the problem of projecting semi-transparent volumetric data into a 2D image without requiring binary classification, thereby avoiding false positives/negatives associated with thresholding. Unlike Back-to-Front Compositing, which lacks early termination support, this method tracks accumulated opacity to enable early ray termination, significantly reducing computation for opaque regions. It differs from Ray Compositing and Accumulation primarily in its specific recursive application of the Porter-Duff Over equation to discrete samples. Inputs: 3D volume grid V with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Transfer function TF(v) \rightarrow (R, G, B, \alpha) mapping scalar voxel values to color and opacity. Camera parameters: eye position E, view direction r, and volume bounds (typically [0,1]^3). Background color C{bg} (default black [0,0,0] or white [1,1,1]). Outputs: Final pixel color C{final} and accumulated opacity \alpha{final} for each pixel. Data Structures: Accumulators: Two variables per pixel: accumulated color C{acc} (RGB) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} (scalar). Initialized to C{acc} = [0,0,0] and \alpha{acc} = 0.0. Ray State: Current position p, step size dt, entry distance t{near}, exit distance t{far}. Steps: 1. Ray Setup: For each pixel, construct the view ray. Normalize the direction vector: \vec{d} = \text{normalize}(\vec{v}{ray}). Intersect the ray with the volume bounding box to find entry t{near} and exit t{far}. If t{near} > t{far}, discard the pixel (no intersection). If the eye is inside the volume, clamp t{near} = 0.0. 2. Step Size Calculation: Compute the step size dt based on the volume dimensions and ray direction to ensure consistent sampling density: \vec{dt}{vec} = \frac{1.0}{\text{vec3}(Dx, Dy, Dz) \cdot |\vec{d}|} dt = \min(dt{vec.x}, dt{vec.y}, dt{vec.z}) Alternatively, dt may be derived from the physical spacing or a fixed number of samples. 3. Initialization: Set C{acc} = [0,0,0] and \alpha{acc} = 0.0. 4. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate from t = t{near} to t < t{far} with increment dt: a. Sample: Evaluate the volume at position p = E + t \cdot \vec{d}. Use trilinear interpolation if p is not on a grid vertex. b. Transfer Function: Map the sampled scalar value v to color C{src} and opacity \alpha{src} using the transfer function. Note: Some implementations use the scalar value directly as opacity, ignoring the TF's alpha channel. Other implementations apply lighting/shading to the base color before compositing. c. Compositing (Over Operator): Update accumulators using the front-to-back equations: C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{src} \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{src} If colors are not pre-multiplied, C{src} must be multiplied by \alpha{src} before addition, or the equation adjusted accordingly. The sources indicate C{src} is often treated as the color contribution, and the term (1-\alpha{acc}) acts as the transmittance weight. d. Early Termination: If \alpha{acc} \geq \alpha{thresh} (typically 0.95 to 0.99), break the loop. This optimization is valid because further samples contribute negligibly to the final color. 5. Background Blending: After the loop, blend the accumulated result with the background color C{bg}: C{final} = C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{bg} If a white background is assumed (C{bg} = [1,1,1]), this simplifies to adding (1-\alpha{acc}) to the RGB channels if the image is stored as RGB with implicit alpha. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def alphacompositingraycasting(volume, transferfunction, eye, raydir, volumedims, bgcolor=[0.0, 0.0, 0.0]): # 1. Normalize ray and intersect bounds d = normalize(raydir) tnear, tfar = intersectbox(eye, d, volumedims) # Discard if no intersection if tnear > tfar: return None, 0.0 # Clamp start if eye is inside tnear = max(tnear, 0.0) # 2. Compute step size # Ensure d components are not zero to avoid division by zero absd = abs(d) dtvec = 1.0 / (volumedims absd) dt = min(dtvec.x, min(dtvec.y, dtvec.z)) # 3. Initialize accumulators acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 # 4. March ray t = tnear while t < tfar: # Sample position p = eye + d t # Sample volume (trilinear interpolation assumed) val = samplevolume(volume, p) # Map to color and opacity # Note: Some TFs return pre-multiplied color, others do not. # Standard Over operator assumes Csrc is the color contribution. # If TF returns (R,G,B, alpha), we use it directly. srccolor, srcalpha = transferfunction(val) # 5. Composite # Cdst <- Cdst + (1 - alphadst) Csrc # alphadst <- alphadst + (1 - alphadst) alphasrc weight = 1.0 - accalpha acccolor[0] += weight srccolor[0] acccolor[1] += weight srccolor[1] acccolor[2] += weight srccolor[2] accalpha += weight srcalpha # 6. Early termination if accalpha >= 0.99: break t += dt # 7. Blend with background finalcolor = [ acccolor[0] + (1.0 - accalpha) bgcolor[0], acccolor[1] + (1.0 - accalpha) bgcolor[1], acccolor[2] + (1.0 - accalpha) bgcolor[2] ] return finalcolor, accalpha Parameters: Early Termination Threshold: 0.95 to 0.99. Lower values (e.g., 0.95) optimize performance but may slightly underestimate color in transparent regions. Step Size: Determined by volume resolution and ray angle. Adaptive step sizes or density-based sampling are also used. Opacity Scaling: In some implementations, base alpha is scaled by step size or sampling density to compensate for discrete integration. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: When computing transmittance via cumulative products (e.g., in differentiable rendering), add epsilon (10^{-10}) to (1-\alpha) to prevent NaNs in cumprod. Order Dependence: The compositing operation is not commutative; front-to-back order is strictly required for the Over operator. Eye Inside Volume: If the camera is inside the volume, starting sampling at t{near} (which may be negative) causes sampling behind the eye. Clamp t{near} to 0.0. Transfer Function Alpha: Some pipelines ignore the alpha channel of the transfer function and use the scalar density/value directly as opacity. Back-to-front compositing accumulates samples from the far boundary to the camera. It uses the equation C'i = Ci + (1 - Ai)C'{i+1}. It is simpler as it does not track accumulated opacity for the color calculation but lacks early ray termination support. Choose it when hardware supports back-to-front blending or when early termination is not needed. Back-to-Front Compositing. Renders a localized region by walking a fixed number of voxels deep along a ray and compositing back-to-front. Differs from full ray casting by limiting trace depth to maxDepth. Choose for interactive exploration of specific volume regions. Subvolume Tracing. Modifies standard DVR to prevent high-intensity structures from being occluded by foreground material. It modulates accumulated color/opacity based on intensity difference, combining DVR context with MIP visibility. Choose for medical imaging where bone/edge visibility is critical. Maximum Intensity Difference Accumulation. Converts RGBA rendering to RGB by blending over a fixed white background (1.0, 1.0, 1.0). Simplifies the equation to rgb = rgb alpha + (1 - alpha). Choose for medical/scientific visualization requiring high contrast on white. White Background Compositing. Leverages GPU fixed-function pipeline to perform Over/Under compositing during rasterization of proxy geometry (slices/splats). Offloads arithmetic to hardware blend unit. Differs from software accumulation by using depth buffer and blend state rather than shader loops. Choose for real-time performance on standard graphics hardware. Hardware Alpha Blending Compositing. A weight function F(l, A) = 1 - (1 - A)^l proves equivalence between recursive blending and conventional ray casting over l cells. The blending formula is Bi = F(l{i+1}, A{i+1})C{i+1} + (1 - F(l{i+1}, A{i+1}))B{i+1}. Used to justify compositing approximations in octree-based rendering. Time Complexity: O(L) per ray, where L is the number of steps along the ray. Early ray termination reduces the average number of steps, especially in opaque regions. Memory Complexity: O(X \cdot Y) for the output frame buffer (color and opacity per pixel). Volume data storage is external. Performance: Depends heavily on volume density and transfer function opacity. Highly transparent volumes require full ray traversal; opaque volumes terminate early. Strengths: Physically plausible (approximates volume rendering integral); supports early termination; no binary classification required. Limitations: Order-dependent (must be front-to-back); sensitive to sampling density (aliasing if steps are too large); early termination threshold may cause slight color inaccuracies in transparent regions. When to Use: Standard direct volume rendering for semi-transparent data where physical accuracy and early termination are desired. When Not to Use: When order-independent transparency is required (use Order-Independent Volumetric Compositing via Visibility Function) or when maximum intensity projection is preferred for high-contrast structures. Originated from the volume rendering integral in light transport theory. The "Over" operator is derived from the Porter-Duff compositing model. It was popularized in direct volume rendering by Drebin, Torrance, and Cull in 1988, who introduced pre-classification (volumetric compositing) to avoid binary classification artifacts. The method is implemented in fragment shaders for GPU acceleration and is foundational for modern neural radiance fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipelines. name: Back-to-Front Compositing
head: Back-to-Front Alpha Blending, Back-to-Front Blending Formula, BTF Compositing
body: Back-to-front compositing is a volume rendering technique that determines the final pixel color by accumulating samples along a viewing ray from the far boundary (back) to the camera (front). It solves the problem of blending semi-transparent layers to produce a coherent image while enabling hardware alpha blending implementation where objects approach the viewer. Unlike its sibling Front-to-Back Compositing (Over Operator), which tracks accumulated opacity to enable early ray termination, back-to-front compositing does not require tracking accumulated opacity for the color calculation but consequently lacks early termination support. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n samples along a ray, sorted in back-to-front order (from i=0 at the far boundary to i=n-1 at the near boundary). Each sample i provides a pre-multiplied color Ci and an opacity \alphai. An initial background color C{dst} (or I0) is required. Output: The final accumulated color C{dst}. Data Structures: Sample Array: An array of structures or parallel arrays storing color (C) and opacity (\alpha) for each segment i=0 \dots n-1. Accumulators: Scalar variables for the destination/background color C{dst} and, optionally, accumulated transparency \hat{t} (if compositing over a new background is required). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Set the accumulated destination color C{dst} to the background color C{bg} (or I0). If accumulated transparency is needed for subsequent compositing, initialize \hat{t} = 1.0. 2. Iteration: For each sample i from 0 to n-1 (back to front): a. Retrieve the sample color C{src} (or Ci) and opacity \alpha{src} (or \alphai). b. Update the accumulated color using the back-to-front compositing equation: C{dst} \leftarrow (1 - \alpha{src})C{dst} + C{src}. c. If accumulated transparency is being tracked, update it: \hat{t} \leftarrow \hat{t} (1 - \alpha{src}). 3. Finalization: The result is C{dst}. If accumulated transparency \hat{t} was tracked, the final opacity of the composite is 1 - \hat{t}. Formulas: The core iterative update rule for color is: C{dst} \leftarrow (1 - \alpha{src})C{dst} + C{src} Where: C{dst} is the accumulated color from samples behind the current one. \alpha{src} is the opacity of the current sample (segment i). C{src} is the pre-multiplied color of the current sample. In terms of accumulated transparency \hat{t} and accumulated color \hat{C}, the recursive formulation for n samples is: \hat{t}n = (1 - \alphan) \hat{C}n = \tilde{C}n \hat{C}i = \hat{C}{i-1}(1 - \alphai) + \tilde{C}i \hat{t}i = \hat{t}{i-1}(1 - \alphai) Where \tilde{C}i is the sample color and \alphai is the sample opacity at index i. Parameters: Alpha Scale: Opacity values \alpha are typically in the range [0, 1], where 0 is transparent and 1 is opaque. Opacity Correction: If sample spacing d{new} differs from the storage spacing d{old}, opacity must be corrected: \alpha{corrected} = 1 - (1 - \alpha{stored})^{d{new}/d{old}}. Associated colors must also be corrected: \tilde{C}{corrected} = \tilde{C}{stored} \frac{\alpha{corrected}}{\alpha{stored}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backtofrontcompositing(samples, backgroundcolor): """ samples: list of tuples (color, opacity) sorted from back (index 0) to front (index n-1). color is pre-multiplied by opacity. backgroundcolor: tuple (r, g, b) """ acccolor = list(backgroundcolor) # Iterate from back (index 0) to front (index n-1) for samplecolor, samplealpha in samples: acccolor[0] = (1.0 - samplealpha) acccolor[0] + samplecolor[0] acccolor[1] = (1.0 - samplealpha) acccolor[1] + samplecolor[1] acccolor[2] = (1.0 - samplealpha) acccolor[2] + samplecolor[2] return acccolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ordering: Polygons must be rendered in strict back-to-front order. If rendered front-to-back or out of order, the z-buffer comparison will incorrectly reject or blend polygons, resulting in incorrect final colors because the frame buffer cannot be updated to insert a polygon in the middle of the stack. Precision: When rendering thousands of polygons with small alpha values using 8-bit per component storage, round-off errors accumulate over many polygons, resulting in gross errors in the output image. Early Termination: Back-to-front rendering does not allow for early ray termination because the accumulated opacity is not tracked/updated in the same way as front-to-back, and the final color depends on all subsequent samples. Front-to-Back Compositing is a volume rendering technique that determines the final pixel color by accumulating samples along a viewing ray from the camera (front) to the far boundary (back) using the alpha compositing "over" operator. It solves the problem of blending semi-transparent layers to produce a coherent image while enabling early ray termination, a significant performance optimization where ray traversal stops once the accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold. Unlike its sibling Back-to-Front Compositing, which does not require tracking accumulated opacity for color calculation but lacks early termination, front-to-back compositing explicitly maintains accumulated opacity to drive the termination condition. Time Complexity: O(n) per ray, where n is the number of samples. All samples must be processed. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray (excluding sample storage). Performance: Back-to-front compositing is suitable for hardware implementation where objects approach the viewer. It maps directly to standard hardware alpha blending functions (e.g., GLSRCALPHA, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA). However, it is generally considered less efficient for interactive perspective ray casting compared to front-to-back because it cannot use early ray termination. Strengths: Simple hardware implementation; correct optical accumulation for semi-transparent surfaces when ordered correctly; useful if the final image needs to be composited over a new background (requires tracking accumulated transparency). Limitations: No early ray termination; sensitive to rendering order in object-order approaches; prone to precision errors with many low-opacity layers in low-bit-depth buffers. When to use: When hardware alpha blending is the primary rendering path and early termination is not critical; when compositing volumes with opaque geometry (geometry drawn before volume); when the final image must be composited over a different background. When not to use: For interactive perspective ray casting where performance is critical and early termination is desired; when sample order cannot be guaranteed. Back-to-front compositing originates from the fundamental alpha compositing equations used in computer graphics to blend semi-transparent layers. It is a numerical integration method for the absorption plus emission model using a Riemann sum approximation. The technique is widely used in volume rendering pipelines, particularly in hardware-accelerated implementations such as splatting and slice-based rendering. It is also known as "forward rendering" in the context of object-order approaches. name: Front-to-Back Compositing (Over Operator)
head: Front-to-Back Accumulation, Over Operator, Recursive Front-to-Back Compositing, Sorted Front-to-Back Compositing, Sorted compositing, over-operator compositing
body: Front-to-Back Compositing is a ray-casting accumulation technique that computes the final pixel color by iteratively blending semi-transparent samples along a viewing ray, starting from the camera and moving toward the background. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric data by approximating the volume rendering integral through discrete emission-absorption modeling. Unlike its sibling Back-to-Front Compositing, which requires storing only the accumulated color but prohibits early termination, this method maintains accumulated opacity to enable early ray termination. This allows the ray to stop processing once the accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold, significantly reducing computation for opaque regions. Input: A 3D volume dataset (scalar field), a transfer function mapping scalar values to color C and opacity \alpha, a viewing ray defined by origin, direction, and length, a background color C{bg} (typically fully opaque, \alpha=1), and a sampling step size \Delta s. Output: A final pixel color C{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out}. The method maintains two accumulators for each ray: 1. C{acc}: Accumulated color (RGB), initialized to \mathbf{0}. 2. \alpha{acc}: Accumulated opacity (scalar), initialized to 0. Some formulations track transmission T{acc} = 1 - \alpha{acc} instead, where T{acc} is initialized to 1. Source computes transmission per segment as T \leftarrow (1 - \alpha{src})^{\Delta si / \xi}, where \xi is a standard length parameter. 1. Initialization: Set C{acc} = \mathbf{0} and \alpha{acc} = 0 (or T{acc} = 1). 2. Ray Traversal: Iterate through sample points i = 1 \dots n along the ray from front to back. 3. Sampling: For each sample position, retrieve the scalar value from the volume and apply the transfer function to obtain the sample color Ci and sample opacity \alphai. Opacity Correction: If the sampling step size \Delta s differs from the transfer function's assumed resolution, correct the opacity to maintain physical consistency. The corrected opacity is \alpha{corrected} = 1 - (1 - \alpha{original})^{\Delta s}. Some implementations use a hardcoded exponent multiplier for the step size, e.g., 1.0 - pow(1.0 - ain, stepsize 200.0). 4. Compositing (The Over Operator): Update the accumulators using the current sample's contribution, weighted by the remaining transmission (1 - \alpha{acc}): \Delta \alphai = \alphai (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + \Delta \alphai Ci \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + \Delta \alphai Alternatively, using transmission T{acc}: C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + T{acc} \alphai Ci T{acc} \leftarrow T{acc} (1 - \alphai) 5. Early Ray Termination (Optional): If \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1 - \epsilon or 0.95), terminate the ray loop. 6. Background Blending: If the ray terminates early or completes, blend the accumulated result with the background color C{bg}: C{final} = C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{bg} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackcompositing(rayorigin, raydirection, raylength, volumemin, volumemax, transferfunction, backgroundcolor, stepsize=0.01, threshold=0.99): # Initialize accumulators acccolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # Precompute number of samples numsamples = int(ceil(raylength / stepsize)) for i in range(numsamples): t = i stepsize samplepos = rayorigin + raydirection t # Check if sample is within volume bounds if not (all(volumemin <= samplepos) and all(samplepos <= volumemax)): continue # Sample scalar value and apply transfer function scalarval = volume.sample(samplepos) # Standard trilinear/bilinear interpolation samplecolor, samplealpha = transferfunction(scalarval) # Opacity correction for step size if stepsize != 1.0: samplealpha = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - samplealpha, stepsize) # Compositing (Over Operator) weight = samplealpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor += weight samplecolor accalpha += weight # Early ray termination if accalpha >= threshold: break # Blend with background finalcolor = acccolor + (1.0 - accalpha) backgroundcolor return finalcolor, accalpha Threshold: The early termination threshold determines the trade-off between speed and accuracy. A value of 0.95–0.99 is common. Step Size: Fixed step sizes require opacity correction to prevent transparency artifacts when zooming or changing resolution. Non-Premultiplied Alpha: If using non-premultiplied color values, the formula must explicitly multiply color by alpha before accumulation to prevent overflow or incorrect blending. The pseudocode above assumes Ci is the emitted color, and the weight handles the alpha blending. Associativity: The over operator is associative, allowing chunks to be composited independently before final assembly, provided they are processed in front-to-back order. IBATM is a volume rendering compositing technique that highlights specific features by modulating accumulated transparency along a viewing ray based on the difference between an incoming sample's importance and the accumulated result's importance. It generalizes Maximum Intensity Difference Accumulation (MIDA) by decoupling transparency modulation from color accumulation, thereby avoiding the need for complex tone-mapping of color values while allowing the final image to exist in a high dynamic range. Unlike MIDA, which modulates both color and transparency, IBATM only modulates transparency, ensuring that opacity remains bounded by 1 while color accumulates naturally. Visibility Field Computation calculates the specific contribution of each voxel to the final 2D image, accounting for its own opacity and the occlusion caused by preceding voxels along the viewing ray. It builds on Front-to-Back Compositing (Over Operator) by explicitly storing these per-voxel visibility weights in a data structure, enabling analysis of which parts of the volume contribute most to the image and how tissues occlude one another. The Cube-4 COM unit composes shaded volumetric samples into final pixel values using a slice-by-slice front-to-back compositing order. It solves the accumulation of color and opacity for rays traversing a volume by storing intermediate results in a base-plane buffer, enabling parallel processing across multiple rendering pipelines. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its dedicated hardware implementation on the Teramac custom computing machine, which uses specific traversal and addressing units to manage skewing and partial-beam dependencies. Merging subimages using the over compositing operator in a front-to-back order determined hierarchically by a recursive traversal of a k-D tree structure. The algorithm stores both color and accumulated opacity at each pixel to enable the over compositing operator. It traverses the k-D tree recursively, visiting the 'front' child before the 'back' child to determine the compositing order. Sibling nodes can be processed concurrently to accomplish compositing in parallel. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. With early ray termination, the average case is significantly faster, especially for opaque volumes. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray for accumulators. Requires storage for composited color and composited opacity at each sampling location. Performance: Highly efficient on GPUs due to the iterative, branch-heavy nature of early termination, which can be managed via warp-level primitives. Strengths: Supports early ray termination, allowing for significant speedups in opaque regions. Physically plausible under the emission-absorption model. Limitations: Requires tracking accumulated opacity, increasing register pressure compared to back-to-front. Sensitive to sampling density; incorrect step sizes lead to transparency artifacts without correction. Requires sorted chunks or falls back to order-independent transparency (OIT) when preconditions fail. Front-to-back compositing is derived from the volume rendering integral, specifically the emission-absorption model described by Levoy. It is the standard compositing scheme for direct volume ray casting. The method was formalized in the context of image-order rendering to allow for efficient hardware implementation and early termination. It is distinct from back-to-front compositing, which is often preferred for texture-based rendering or hardware alpha blending without early termination.
