name: Scatter-Add Accumulation
head: Accumulation Renderer, Accumulation Rendering, Ray Accumulation
body: Scatter-Add Accumulation is a compositing technique used in direct volume ray casting and neural rendering to aggregate per-sample color and opacity values into final pixel colors when samples are not processed in strict ray order. It solves the problem of non-deterministic or parallelized sample generation by using atomic scatter-add operations to sum weighted contributions into a per-ray output buffer. Unlike standard front-to-back compositing which requires sorted samples, this method supports both packed (ray-indexed) and unpacked layouts, handling feature accumulation and weight-only accumulation. Inputs: weights: Tensor of shape [M, 1] or [M, C] containing per-sample weights (e.g., opacity or density). values: Optional Tensor of shape [M, C] containing per-sample features (e.g., color). rayindices: Tensor of shape [M] mapping each sample to a specific ray index. numrays: Integer, total number of rays. C: Number of feature channels (default 1 for weight-only). Outputs: accumulatedvalues: Tensor of shape [num\rays, C] containing the final accumulated result per ray. Data Structures: Output buffer initialized to zeros: O \in \mathbb{R}^{num\rays \times C}. Steps: 1. Check Layout: Determine if samples are packed (associated with rayindices) or unpacked (sequential per ray). 2. Packed Samples (Scatter-Add): If rayindices and numrays are provided: Initialize output buffer: O = \text{zeros}((num\rays, C), \text{dtype}=float32) If values is provided: Compute weighted features: W{val} = weights[:, \text{None}] \times values \quad \text{shape: } [M, C] Perform scatter-add: O = O.\text{at}[ray\indices].\text{add}(W{val}) If values is None (weight-only accumulation): Compute weight contribution: W{only} = weights[:, \text{None}] \quad \text{shape: } [M, 1] Perform scatter-add into buffer of shape [num\rays, 1]: O = O.\text{at}[ray\indices].\text{add}(W{only}) Alternatively, use optimized library routines such as nerfacc.accumulatealongrays(weights, rayindices, values, numrays). 3. Unpacked Samples (Sequential Sum): If samples are ordered by ray (no rayindices needed): Sum weights along the sample dimension (typically dim=-2): O = \text{sum}(weights, \text{dim}=-2) If values are present, sum weighted values similarly: O = \text{sum}(weights[:, \text{None}] \times values, \text{dim}=-2) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def scatteraddaccumulation(weights, values, rayindices, numrays, C=1): """ Accumulate weighted values along rays using scatter-add. Args: weights: Tensor [M, 1] or [M, C], sample weights. values: Tensor [M, C] or None, sample features. rayindices: Tensor [M], ray index for each sample. numrays: int, total number of rays. C: int, number of feature channels. Returns: Tensor [numrays, C], accumulated results. """ # Initialize output buffer with zeros output = torch.zeros((numrays, C), dtype=weights.dtype, device=weights.device) if values is not None: # Compute weighted features: weights[:, None] values # Ensure weights has shape [M, 1] for broadcasting if weights.dim() == 1: wexpanded = weights.unsqueeze(1) else: wexpanded = weights weightedfeatures = wexpanded values # Shape: [M, C] # Scatter-add operation # output[rayindices] += weightedfeatures # Using advanced indexing for scatter-add output.indexadd(0, rayindices, weightedfeatures) else: # Weight-only accumulation if weights.dim() == 1: wexpanded = weights.unsqueeze(1) else: wexpanded = weights # If C=1, ensure shape is [M, 1] if C == 1 and wexpanded.dim() == 2 and wexpanded.shape[1] != 1: wexpanded = wexpanded[:,:1] output.indexadd(0, rayindices, wexpanded) return output def sequentialaccumulation(weights, values): """ Accumulate weighted values along rays when samples are ordered. Args: weights: Tensor [numrays, numsamples] or [numrays, numsamples, C] values: Tensor [numrays, numsamples, C] or None Returns: Tensor [numrays, C] """ if values is not None: # Weighted sum along sample dimension (dim=1) # weights shape: [numrays, numsamples, 1] or [numrays, numsamples] # values shape: [numrays, numsamples, C] if weights.dim() == 2: wexpanded = weights.unsqueeze(2) else: wexpanded = weights weightedvalues = wexpanded values return torch.sum(weightedvalues, dim=1) else: # Sum weights along sample dimension if weights.dim() == 2: return torch.sum(weights, dim=1) else: return torch.sum(weights, dim=1) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Use float32 for accumulation to balance precision and performance. float16 may cause overflow or underflow in large accumulations. Boundary Conditions: Ensure rayindices are within [0, num\rays - 1]. Out-of-bounds indices cause undefined behavior or errors. Degenerate Input: If weights is empty, return zero-initialized output. Atomicity: In GPU implementations, scatter-add must be atomic to handle concurrent writes to the same ray index. A multipass approach where pixel shader summation is performed by accumulating results from concentric rectangular bands emanating from the light source into successive outer bands. The accumulation formula is L(s, \theta, \phi) = L{i-1}(s, \theta, \phi) + Li(s, \theta, \phi), where L represents accumulated light and i is the band index. This method is described as the minimal required sampling and computation limit but may not be optimal for current hardware design compared to single-pass execution. Time Complexity: O(M) for scatter-add, where M is the number of samples. Parallelizable on GPU via atomic operations. Memory Complexity: O(num\rays \times C) for the output buffer. Performance: Efficient for large-scale neural rendering where samples are generated in parallel batches. Strengths: Supports non-ray-order sample presentation; flexible for both packed and unpacked data. Limitations: Requires atomic operations which may cause contention on GPU; not suitable for front-to-back compositing where transparency blending is required. When to Use: When samples are generated out of order or in parallel batches; when only weight or feature accumulation is needed without transparency blending. When Not to Use: When front-to-back compositing with transparency is required; when samples are already sorted by ray. Scatter-Add Accumulation is widely used in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and related neural rendering techniques to handle parallel sample generation. It is implemented in libraries such as nerfacc and gsplat-mlx. The method is also referenced in volumetric light scattering post-processing as a multipass accumulation technique. nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) autonomousvision/sdfstudio, https://github.com/autonomousvision/sdfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) RobotFlow-Labs/gsplat-mlx, https://github.com/RobotFlow-Labs/gsplat-mlx, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) barbararoessle/ganerf, https://github.com/barbararoessle/ganerf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volumetric Light Scattering as a Post-Process, https://developer.nvidia.com/gpugems/gpugems3/part-ii-light-and-shadows/chapter-13-volumetric-light-scattering-post-process, fetched 2026-10-27 (book)

name: Average Compositing
head: Linear Compositing
body: Average Compositing is a volume rendering technique that produces an X-ray-like image by sending a ray through the volume and compositing all found values with the same weight, taking no opacity into account. It differs from Alpha Compositing and Accumulation methods by treating every sample equally regardless of depth or transparency. Inputs: Ray defined by origin and direction; scalar volume dataset. Outputs: Single scalar intensity value for the pixel. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Send a ray through the volume. 2. Composite all found values with the same weight. Formulas: The output intensity I is the arithmetic mean of N sampled values vi along the ray: I = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} vi. Parameters: Step size and sampling density are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the ray does not intersect the volume, the sample count is zero; a guard must return a background value to avoid division by zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def averagecompositing(rayorigin, raydirection, volumesamplefn, stepsize, volumemin, volumemax): sumvalues = 0.0 count = 0 t = 0.0 while True: x = rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0] t y = rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1] t z = rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2] t if not (volumemin[0] <= x <= volumemax[0] and volumemin[1] <= y <= volumemax[1] and volumemin[2] <= z <= volumemax[2]): break value = volumesamplefn(x, y, z) sumvalues += value count += 1 t += stepsize if count == 0: return 0.0 return sumvalues / count Uses the over operator with opacity; choose when transparency and depth cues are needed. Accumulates intensity until opacity threshold is met; choose for emission-absorption models. General blending of samples; choose for flexible compositing rules. Standard alpha blending; choose for 2D/3D overlay compositing. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of samples along the ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, requiring only a running sum and count. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement; produces an X-ray-like overview of the entire volume. Limitations: Ignores opacity and depth cues; does not highlight high-intensity structures. When to use: When an X-ray-like overview of the entire volume is desired, and opacity or depth cues are not critical. When not to use: When transparency, occlusion, or highlighting of specific high-intensity features is required. Average Compositing is a compositing scheme used in Direct Volume Rendering. It is described alongside Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) and Accumulation compositing in introductory literature. name: Raymarch Blending
head: Alpha Blending Raymarch
body: Raymarch Blending combines a ray-marched volumetric result with an existing background scene texture using standard alpha compositing. It solves the problem of integrating semi-transparent volumetric data into a pre-rendered scene containing opaque geometry, ensuring correct occlusion where the volume interacts with the solid meshes. Unlike Alpha Compositing Ray Casting which typically handles volume-to-volume or volume-to-black blending, this method explicitly blends against a pre-existing framebuffer color. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-rendered scene texture containing the background color and opaque geometry; ray origin (ro) and ray direction (rd) for the current fragment. Output: A final fragment color that blends the raymarched volume over the background. Data Structures: Scene texture: A 2D texture sampling the scene color prior to this shader pass. raymarch(ro, rd): A function returning a 4D vector where the first three components are the accumulated color and the fourth component is the accumulated opacity (alpha) of the volume along the ray. Steps: 1. Sample Background: Retrieve the existing scene color from the background texture at the current UV coordinates. C{bg} = \text{tex2D}(\text{scene\texture}, uv) 2. Raymarch Volume: Compute the volumetric contribution by marching along the ray. C{vol}, \alpha{vol} = \text{raymarch}(ro, rd) 3. Blend: Combine the background color and the volumetric result using the standard alpha blending equation. C{final} = C{bg} \cdot (1.0 - \alpha{vol}) + C{vol} \cdot \alpha{vol} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def normalize(v): length = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return [v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length] def sampletexture(tex, uv): # Returns a 3D list [r, g, b] return tex.sample(uv) def raymarch(ro, rd): # Returns a 4D list [r, g, b, a] # Implementation details are in the raymarching method return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def fragshader(i, cameraws, maintex): # 1. Calculate ray parameters rd = normalize(i.ray) ro = cameraws # 2. Sample the existing scene color from the background texture colbg = sampletexture(maintex, i.uv) # 3. Perform raymarching to get volumetric color and alpha add = raymarch(ro, rd) # 4. Blend the volumetric result with the background # Formula: Cbg (1 - a) + Cvol a finalrgb = [ colbg[0] (1.0 - add[3]) + add[0] add[3], colbg[1] (1.0 - add[3]) + add[1] add[3], colbg[2] (1.0 - add[3]) + add[2] add[3] ] # Return 4D color with alpha = 1.0 return finalrgb + [1.0] Parameters: maxstep: The maximum number of samples for the raymarch. The source notes that 64 samples were used for a simple torus example, but suggests tweaking this value based on performance and accuracy needs. raymarch parameters: Step size, density thresholds, and other marching logic are handled internally by the raymarch function and are not specified in the blending context. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: Increasing maxstep increases accuracy but incurs a proportional performance cost. Pipeline Dependency: This method assumes the background texture already contains the correct opaque geometry from previous rendering passes. Composites a ray-marched volume over pre-rendered opaque 3D polygonal geometry by leveraging standard graphics pipeline alpha blending. It solves the occlusion problem where volumetric data must correctly interact with solid meshes, ensuring that the volume is blended against the background color already present in the framebuffer from previous rendering passes. Unlike standard ray casting which only evaluates volume density, this approach ensures correct occlusion of the volume by solid geometry, solving the problem of rendering transparent volumes over opaque meshes in a single pass or specific pipeline configuration. Time Complexity: Dominated by the raymarch function, which is O(N) where N is the number of samples (maxstep). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per fragment for the blending calculation, assuming the background texture is already in memory. Strengths: Simple to implement; allows for easy integration of volumes into existing scenes with opaque geometry; leverages standard alpha blending hardware. Limitations: Performance depends heavily on the raymarch implementation. When to use: When rendering semi-transparent volumes over opaque 3D models in a deferred or multi-pass pipeline. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method is described in an unofficial tutorial on raymarching distance fields. It is presented as a practical technique for integrating raymarched volumes into a standard graphics pipeline, specifically addressing the common scenario of adding volumetric effects to scenes with pre-existing geometry. name: Back-to-Front Alpha Blending with 3D Geometry
head: WebGL blending for volume-geometry intersection
body: This method composites a ray-marched volume over pre-rendered opaque 3D polygonal geometry by leveraging standard graphics pipeline alpha blending. It solves the occlusion problem where volumetric data must correctly interact with solid meshes, ensuring that the volume is blended against the background color already present in the framebuffer from previous rendering passes. Unlike standard ray casting which only evaluates volume density, this approach ensures correct occlusion of the volume by solid geometry, solving the problem of rendering transparent volumes over opaque meshes in a specific pipeline configuration. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume texture (3D scalar field). Depth textures (RGBA packed) from previous passes rendering the 3D geometry. Color buffer containing the rendered 3D geometry from previous passes. Ray origin and direction (derived from camera and screen coordinates). Outputs: Final color and alpha for each pixel, composited into the screen buffer. Data Structures: Depth Texture: Since WebGL 1.0 lacks native float depth texture support on all devices, depth information from passes 1 and 3 is packed into RGBA textures. The fragment shader must unpack this depth value to determine if a ray intersects a 3D object at a specific step. Frame Buffer Objects (FBO): Used to store the intermediate depth and color data from the geometry passes. Parameters: Blend Function: gl.SRCALPHA for source and gl.ONEMINUSSRCALPHA for destination. Early Ray Termination Threshold: Accumulated alpha equal to 1.0 (opaque). Steps: 1. Geometry Passes (Passes 1 and 3): Render the opaque 3D polygonal objects and store the depth information in RGBA textures. 2. Volume Ray Casting (Pass 5): Execute the ray-casting fragment shader. 3. Depth Unpacking: In the ray-casting shader, unpack the depth value from the RGBA texture sampled at the current pixel coordinate. 4. Ray Traversal: Traverse the volume along the ray. 5. Accumulation: Accumulate volume color and alpha along the ray. 6. Early Ray Termination: If the accumulated alpha reaches 1.0, terminate the ray traversal early. 7. Blending: Output the accumulated volume color and alpha. The graphics pipeline applies the blend function to composite this result with the existing color in the framebuffer (which contains the 3D geometry color). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vec3(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def vec4(x, y, z, w): return (x, y, z, w) def unpackdepth(rgba): return rgba[0] + rgba[1] 256.0 + rgba[2] 65536.0 + rgba[3] 16777216.0 def samplevolume(tex, pos): return tex.trilinearsample(pos) def sampledepth(tex, uv): return tex.sample(uv) def raycastfragmentshader(depthtexture, volumetexture, rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, maxdistance, resolution): # 1. Unpack depth from previous geometry passes uv = (glFragCoord[0] / resolution[0], glFragCoord[1] / resolution[1]) depthrgba = sampledepth(depthtexture, uv) depthvalue = unpackdepth(depthrgba) # 2. Initialize accumulation acccolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # 3. Ray traversal t = 0.0 while t < maxdistance: samplepos = vec3(rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0] t, rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1] t, rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2] t) density = samplevolume(volumetexture, samplepos) # Convert density to step alpha stepalpha = density stepsize # 4. Early Ray Termination if accalpha >= 1.0: break # 5. Accumulate color and alpha (Front-to-Back) weight = stepalpha (1.0 - accalpha) samplecolor = vec3(density, density, density) # Simplified transfer function acccolor = vec3(acccolor[0] + weight samplecolor[0], acccolor[1] + weight samplecolor[1], acccolor[2] + weight samplecolor[2]) accalpha += weight t += stepsize # 6. Output for blending # The pipeline applies: gl.blendFunc(gl.SRCALPHA, gl.ONEMINUSSRCALPHA) return vec4(acccolor[0], acccolor[1], acccolor[2], accalpha) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transparent Geometry: The base implementation assumes opaque 3D objects. Transparent 3D polygonal objects are not supported. Depth Precision: Packing depth into RGBA may introduce precision loss compared to native float depth textures. WebGL Compatibility: Native depth texture support is not universal in WebGL 1.0, necessitating the RGBA packing fallback. This method extends standard direct volume ray casting by integrating pre-rendered 3D polygonal geometry depth data, allowing volumetric rays to detect intersections with opaque solid objects and terminate or blend correctly. Unlike standard ray casting which only evaluates volume density, this approach ensures correct occlusion of the volume by solid geometry, solving the problem of rendering transparent volumes over opaque meshes in a single pass or specific pipeline configuration. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume texture and the depth textures from previous passes. Strengths: Correctly handles occlusion of volume by opaque geometry; leverages standard hardware blending. Limitations: Does not support transparent 3D geometry in the base implementation; dependent on WebGL version and extensions for depth texture support. When to use: When rendering volumetric data over opaque 3D meshes in a WebGL environment where standard blending is desired. When not to use: When transparent 3D geometry is present in the scene. This method was described in the context of deploying volume rendering interactive visualizations in web platforms with intersected 3D geometry. It utilizes WebGL directives to enable blending and perform back-to-front composition. The approach was tested with opaque 3D objects. Deployment of Volume Rendering Interactive Visualizations in Web Platforms With Intersected 3D Geometry, https://doi.org/10.2312/ceig.20161312, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Ray-Casting with 3D Geometry Intersection
head: Volume-Geometry Ray Casting
body: This method extends direct volume ray casting by integrating pre-rendered 3D polygonal geometry depth data, allowing volumetric rays to detect intersections with opaque solid objects and terminate or blend correctly. Unlike standard ray casting which only evaluates volume density, this approach ensures correct occlusion of the volume by solid geometry, solving the problem of rendering transparent volumes over opaque meshes in a specific pipeline configuration. The algorithm modifies the ray-casting traversal loop to compare the ray's current depth against the depth of 3D surfaces fetched from previous rendering passes. It assumes the scene contains no transparent 3D polygonal objects, though minor adjustments could support them. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume texture, 3D surface depth texture (uDepthSurface), back surface depth texture (uBackDepth), current fragment coordinates (texD, glFragCoord), number of ray steps (nsteps), and object color (objectColor.rgb). Outputs: Accumulated color (accum.rgb), accumulated alpha (accum.a), and final depth (finaldepth). Data Structures and Layouts: uBackDepth: Texture storing the depth of the volume's back boundary. uDepthSurface: Texture storing the depth of the 3D mesh surface. glFragCoord: Built-in GLSL variable containing window-relative coordinates, where.z is depth and.w is used in the depth calculation. raydepth: The current depth of the ray along its path in scene space. Parameters: nsteps: The number of discrete steps the ray takes through the volume. objectColor: The RGB color of the opaque 3D object hit by the ray. Step-by-Step Procedure: 1. Initialization: For each pixel, initialize ray parameters (rayorigin, raydirection, raystep). Fetch depth data from previous passes to establish the depth range in scene space. 2. Depth Calculation: Calculate the specific depth values required for intersection testing using the following formulas: \text{backDepth} = 1.0 - \text{unpackFloat}(\text{texture2D}(uBackDepth, \text{texD})) \text{frontDepth} = 1.0 - \text{gl\FragCoord.z} \times \text{gl\FragCoord.w} \text{surfDepth} = 1.0 - \text{unpackFloat}(\text{texture2D}(uDepthSurface, \text{texD})) \text{depthStep} = \frac{\text{backDepth} - \text{frontDepth}}{n\steps} Note: unpackFloat converts the stored texture value to a linear depth value. The subtraction from 1.0 suggests the textures may store depth in a non-standard or inverted format, or this is a specific implementation detail of the source. 3. Ray Traversal Loop: Iterate through the volume from frontDepth to backDepth in increments of depthStep. At each step, update raydepth. 4. Intersection Test: Compare the current raydepth with surfDepth. If the ray has intersected the surface thickness, execute the blending and termination logic: \text{if } (\text{ray\depth} - \text{surfDepth} > -\text{depthStep}) Pitfall: The intersection check uses the specific inequality (raydepth - surfDepth) > -(depthStep) to determine if the ray has hit the surface thickness. 5. Blending and Termination: Upon intersection, update the accumulated color and alpha using front-to-back blending, update the final depth, and break the loop: \text{accum.rgb} = (\text{accum.a} \times \text{accum.rgb}) + ((1.0 - \text{accum.a}) \times \text{objectColor.rgb}) \text{accum.a} = (\text{accum.a} \times \text{accum.a}) + (1.0 - \text{accum.a}) \text{final\depth} = \text{surfDepth} \text{break} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastwithgeometry(backdepth, frontdepth, surfdepth, nsteps, objectcolor, volumesampler): # Depth calculations depthstep = (backdepth - frontdepth) / nsteps # Initialization raydepth = frontdepth accumrgb = vec3(0.0) accuma = 0.0 finaldepth = backdepth # Ray Traversal for in range(nsteps): raydepth += depthstep # Increment depth per step # Standard volume ray casting: sample volume at raydepth, update accumrgb and accuma based on density/color # Intersection Test if (raydepth - surfdepth) > -depthstep: # Blend volume color with object color accumrgb = (accuma accumrgb) + ((1.0 - accuma) objectcolor) # Update alpha accuma = (accuma accuma) + (1.0 - accuma) finaldepth = surfdepth break return accumrgb, accuma, finaldepth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intersection Precision: The check (raydepth - surfDepth) > -(depthStep) is critical. Opaque Assumption: The method assumes opaque 3D objects. Depth Space Consistency: All depth values (backDepth, frontDepth, surfDepth, raydepth) must be in the same coordinate space (scene space) for the comparison to be valid. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Correctly handles occlusion of volume by solid geometry, which is difficult to achieve with pure volume ray casting alone without complex depth peeling or multiple passes. Limitations: Assumes opaque geometry. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Front-to-Back Alpha Blending
head: Alpha Blending DVR, Blended Compositing, First-Hit Projection, Front-to-Back Volume Rendering
body: Front-to-Back Alpha Blending is a direct volume rendering technique that projects volumetric data by compositing samples or textured slices along a viewing ray using alpha blending. It solves the problem of synthesizing a final pixel color from semi-transparent data by accumulating color and opacity contributions from front to back until the ray exits the volume or becomes fully opaque. It is distinguished from back-to-front methods by its correct handling of occlusion and alpha accumulation, which produces accurate results when the rendering order is strictly maintained. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset, a viewing ray defined by origin and direction, and a transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Output: A final pixel color and accumulated opacity. Data Structures: Ray State: A floating-point accumulator for the current color (C{acc}) and the current contribution factor (\alpha{contrib}). Sample/Block: A structure containing the interpolated color (C{sample}) and opacity (\alpha{sample}) from the transfer function. Formulas: The continuous rendering equation for constant extinction \kappa and constant emissivity \varepsilon reduces to: I(s) = I(s0) \cdot \alpha + S \cdot (1 - \alpha), \quad \text{where } \alpha = e^{-\kappa(s-s0)} where I(s) is the intensity at position s, I(s0) is the initial intensity, S = \varepsilon/\kappa is the source function, and \alpha is the transmittance. The discrete compositing step updates the accumulated color C{acc} and contribution factor \alpha{contrib} as: C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + \alpha{contrib} \cdot Ci \cdot \alphai \alpha{contrib} \leftarrow \alpha{contrib} \cdot (1 - \alphai) where Ci and \alphai are the color and opacity of the current sample. Steps: 1. Initialize the contribution factor \alpha{contrib} = 1.0 and the accumulated color C{acc} = (0, 0, 0). 2. Iterate through the volume samples (or textured slices) along the ray in front-to-back order relative to the camera. 3. For each sample i: a. Evaluate the transfer function to get color Ci and opacity \alphai. b. Update the accumulated color: C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + \alpha{contrib} \cdot Ci \cdot \alphai. c. Update the contribution factor: \alpha{contrib} \leftarrow \alpha{contrib} \cdot (1 - \alphai). 4. If the ray exits the volume or \alpha{contrib} becomes negligible, terminate the loop. 5. Assign C{acc} to the pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackalphablending(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds, stepsize, transferfunction): # Initialize accumulators accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] contribution = 1.0 # Compute ray-box intersection to find entry and exit distances invdir = [1.0 / d if d != 0.0 else float('inf') for d in raydirection] tmin = max((volumebounds[0][i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)) tmax = min((volumebounds[1][i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)) # If ray misses volume or starts inside, adjust tmin if tmin > tmax: return accumulatedcolor if tmin < 0.0: tmin = 0.0 # March along the ray t = tmin while t <= tmax: # Compute current position pos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] # Sample volume at pos; returns scalar value scalar = 0.5 color, alpha = transferfunction(scalar) # Composite sample accumulatedcolor = [ accumulatedcolor[i] + contribution color[i] alpha for i in range(3) ] contribution = (1.0 - alpha) # Advance step t += stepsize # Early termination if fully opaque if contribution < 1e-6: break return accumulatedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ordering: Incorrect rendering order (e.g., back-to-front without proper depth sorting) produces inaccurate results due to incorrect alpha accumulation and occlusion handling. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise if \alpha{contrib} becomes extremely small but non-zero, potentially causing visual artifacts in deep volumes. Uses the same blending equation but often implies a specific ray-casting loop structure. General term for accumulating contributions; front-to-back is a specific order. A different blending strategy that averages contributions rather than weighting by opacity. Often refers to the integration step in ray marching; front-to-back is the standard compositing order used within. The fundamental graphical operation used by this method. Synonymous with this method, emphasizing the compositing order. An alternative approach that avoids strict front-to-back ordering requirements. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Physically plausible for participating media under constant extinction and emissivity assumptions. Limitations: Requires strict front-to-back ordering to correctly evaluate the rendering equation. When to use: Standard direct volume rendering for semi-transparent data. When not to use: When order-independent transparency is required. The method originates from standard alpha compositing theory applied to volume rendering. It is derived from the rendering equation by Kajiya (1986). It is used in medical imaging for CT visualization, where accurate representation of semi-transparent anatomical structures is critical. name: Alpha Blending
head: Alpha Blending Compositing, Over Operator, Porter-Duff, Porter-Duff compositing, Porter-Duff over operator, The Over Operator
body: Alpha blending is a compositing technique used in direct volume ray casting to combine multiple semi-transparent contributions along a viewing ray into a final pixel color. It solves the problem of rendering translucent volumes by discretizing the continuous light transport equation, allowing for physically plausible accumulation of emitted and attenuated light. It is distinguished from simple averaging or maximum intensity projection by its use of an associative, non-commutative operator that preserves depth ordering, enabling correct compositing of independent sub-volumes or distributed rendering nodes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of volume samples along a ray, ordered from back to front (farthest to nearest). Each sample i provides a color Ci (or I(i)) and an opacity \alphai. An initial background color C{in} (typically ambient light or black) is required. Outputs: The final composited color C{out}. For front-to-back compositing, the final accumulated opacity \alpha{out} is also maintained. Data Structures: Sample: A structure containing color (RGB vector) and opacity (scalar in [0, 1]). Accumulators: accumulatedcolor (RGB vector) and accumulatedopacity (scalar). Formulas: The method is based on the discrete approximation of the light transport equation: I = \sum{0 \leq i \leq n} \left( \prod{0 \leq j \leq i} e^{-\intj^{j+1} \sigma(t) dt} \right) I(i) where \sigma(t) is the differential attenuation coefficient. The opacity of a ray segment [j, j+1] is defined as: \alpha(j) = 1 - e^{-\intj^{j+1} \sigma(t) dt} There are two primary recursive strategies: 1. Back-to-Front (Porter-Duff Over Operator): This strategy is associative, allowing distributed rendering where independent image tiles can be composited without global synchronization. It requires maintaining only the color accumulator, with the background explicitly provided as the initial value. C{out} = \alphai Ci + (1 - \alphai) C{in} Where: C{out} is the output color after sample i. C{in} is the input color (accumulated from samples behind i). \alphai is the opacity of sample i. Ci is the color of sample i. Initial C{in} is the ambient/background color. 2. Front-to-Back: This strategy is often used in hardware-accelerated ray casting where early ray termination is desired. It requires maintaining both color and accumulated opacity. C{out} = C{in} + (1 - \alpha{in}) \alphai Ci^{pre} \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + (1 - \alpha{in}) \alphai Where: C{in} is the accumulated color from samples in front of i. \alpha{in} is the accumulated opacity from samples in front of i. Ci^{pre} is the pre-multiplied color of sample i (\alphai Ci). Initial C{in} = 0, \alpha{in} = 0. Parameters: Opacity (\alpha): Defined in the interval [0, 1], where 0 is completely transparent and 1 is completely opaque. Transparency (T): T = 1 - \alpha, range [0, 1]. Threshold: A small value for early ray termination in front-to-back blending when accumulated opacity approaches 1. Pseudocode (Back-to-Front): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def alphablendingbacktofront(samples, backgroundcolor): """ Composites volume samples in back-to-front order using the Porter-Duff over operator. samples: list of dicts {'color': [r,g,b], 'opacity': float}, ordered far to near. backgroundcolor: [r,g,b] initial color (e.g., black or ambient light). Returns: [r,g,b] final color. """ accumulatedcolor = list(backgroundcolor) # Iterate from back (index 0) to front (last index) for sample in samples: alpha = sample['opacity'] color = sample['color'] # Porter-Duff Over Operator: Cout = alpha Csample + (1 - alpha) Cin for channel in range(3): accumulatedcolor[channel] = alpha color[channel] + (1.0 - alpha) accumulatedcolor[channel] return accumulatedcolor Pseudocode (Front-to-Back with Early Termination): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def alphablendingfronttoback(samples, threshold=0.99): """ Composites volume samples in front-to-back order with early ray termination. samples: list of dicts {'color': [r,g,b], 'opacity': float}, ordered near to far. threshold: float, stop when accumulated opacity exceeds this value. Returns: [r,g,b] final color. """ accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # Iterate from front (index 0) to back (last index) for sample in samples: alpha = sample['opacity'] color = sample['color'] # Pre-multiply color premultipliedcolor = [alpha c for c in color] # Update color and opacity # Cout = Cin + (1 - alphain) Csamplepre # alphaout = alphain + (1 - alphain) alpha for channel in range(3): accumulatedcolor[channel] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) premultipliedcolor[channel] accumulatedopacity += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) alpha # Early termination if accumulatedopacity >= threshold: break return accumulatedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Associativity of Painter's Equation: The simple equation O = \alphaF F + (1 - \alphaF) B is not associative because it ignores the background opacity. Using this for distributed compositing yields incorrect results. The associative over operator must be used. Ordering: The operator is associative but not commutative. Samples must be processed in strict back-to-front or front-to-back order depending on the implementation. Precision: Floating-point precision errors can accumulate in long rays. Standard practice uses pre-multiplied arithmetic to maintain numerical stability. Multi-pass blending is a hardware-accelerated technique for direct volume ray casting that approximates the correct intensity and opacity of semi-transparent cells using standard polygon rasterization. It solves the problem where linear interpolation (Gouraud shading) produces incorrect estimates of intensity and opacity across projected polygons, even when vertex values are accurate. By decomposing the rendering of a single cell into three passes, it uses quadratic functions to approximate the exponential decay of background opacity and the nonlinear contribution of cell color, allowing for correct compositing without software-based ray casting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Distributed implementations reduce network bandwidth by compositing only neighboring nodes. Hardware acceleration is commonly used for shading computations. Strengths: Associative nature enables efficient distributed rendering and hierarchical compositing. Limitations: Requires strict depth ordering. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Alpha blending in volume rendering was developed by Levoy in 1988, building on the Porter-Duff compositing operators introduced in 1984. Levoy's work adapted the "over" operator from 2D image compositing to 3D volume rendering, providing a physically based method for accumulating light along rays. It has become the standard compositing technique in direct volume ray casting due to its simplicity and associativity. name: Multi-pass Blending
head: Hardware Polygon Blending with Quadratic Approximation, Multi-pass Quadratic Blending, Quadratic Alpha Blending, Quadratic Fit to Exponential
body: Multi-pass blending is a hardware-accelerated technique for direct volume ray casting that approximates the correct intensity and opacity of semi-transparent cells using standard polygon rasterization. It solves the problem where linear interpolation (Gouraud shading) produces incorrect estimates of intensity and opacity across projected polygons, even when vertex values are accurate. By decomposing the rendering of a single cell into three passes, it uses quadratic functions to approximate the exponential decay of background opacity and the nonlinear contribution of cell color, allowing for correct compositing without software-based ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A visibility-ordered cell (e.g., from a curvilinear or tetrahedral grid) with vertex attributes: color \mathbf{C} and opacity \alpha. Output: The composited color and alpha in the framebuffer, correctly accounting for the exponential transmission of light through the cell's depth. Data Structures: The method relies on standard hardware polygon attributes. For each vertex v of the projected cell, the following values are computed and passed to the rasterizer: Color Vector (\mathbf{c}): The interpolated color contribution. Alpha Scalar (\alpha): The interpolated opacity weight. Depth (z): The physical depth of the vertex within the cell, ranging from 0 (nearest) to A (thickest point of the cell projection). Formulas: The physical model assumes that for a semi-transparent light-emitting medium with planar faces, the depth z varies linearly along any line, but the effective transmission of color varies exponentially. The accumulated light contribution f(z) at depth z is: f(z) = 1 - e^{-a z} where a is the absorption coefficient and z is the depth. This exponential function is approximated by a quadratic function g(z) over the interval [0, A], where A is the depth of the thickest vertex: g(z) = (c0 + c1 z)(a0 + a1 z) The approximation is constrained such that g(0) = f(0) and g(A) = f(A). 1. f(0) = 0, so g(0) = c0 a0 = 0. The source sets a0 = 0. 2. To maintain generality and scale, a1 is set to 1/A. The alpha term is computed as (a0 + a1 z) = (0 + (1/A)z). 3. The quadratic function g(z) as a whole is chosen to minimize the squared error between g(z) and f(z) on [0, A], subject to the constraint g(A) = f(A). The exact closed-form solution for the color coefficients c0 and c1 is detailed in Appendix A of the source. The hardware blend function used is one minus source alpha for attenuation passes, and source color x source alpha (or equivalent additive blend with alpha weighting) for the final color addition. Numbered Steps: The rendering of a single cell requires three distinct passes over the same polygon geometry: 1. Pass 1 (First Opacity Attenuation): Vertex Attributes: Color: \mathbf{c}1 = \mathbf{C}{vertex} (arbitrary, as it will be multiplied by the blend factor). Alpha: \alpha1(z) = a0 + a1 z = (1/A)z (Linear interpolation of depth normalized by max depth). Blend Function: one minus source alpha. Effect: Multiplies the current framebuffer background by (1 - \frac{z}{A}). This is the first linear factor of the quadratic approximation. 2. Pass 2 (Second Opacity Attenuation): Vertex Attributes: Color: \mathbf{c}2 = \mathbf{C}{vertex} (arbitrary). Alpha: \alpha2(z) = (1/A)z (Same linear interpolation). Blend Function: one minus source alpha. Effect: Multiplies the result of Pass 1 by (1 - \frac{z}{A}) again. The combined attenuation is (1 - \frac{z}{A})^2, which serves as a quadratic approximation to the exponential decay of the background. The source states that using a linear function twice with this blend function yields a quadratic approximation to the desired exponential decay. 3. Pass 3 (Color Addition): Vertex Attributes: Color: \mathbf{c}3(z) = \mathbf{C}{vertex} \cdot (c0 + c1 z) (Color modulated by the linear color term of the quadratic approximation). Alpha: \alpha3(z) = (1/A)z (Used to weight the color addition). Blend Function: source color x source alpha (or equivalent additive blend with alpha weighting). Effect: Adds the cell's color contribution to the attenuated background. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def rendercellmultipass(vertexcolors, vertexdepths, A, absorptioncoeff, fb): """ Renders a single cell using multi-pass blending. vertexcolors: List of (R, G, B) tuples for each vertex. vertexdepths: List of z-depths for each vertex (0 to A). A: Max depth of the cell (thickest vertex). absorptioncoeff: The 'a' in the exponential model. fb: 2D array of shape (H, W, 3) representing the framebuffer. """ # Precompute quadratic coefficients c0, c1 for the color term. # g(z) = (c0 + c1z) (z/A) # Constraint g(A) = f(A) => c0 + c1A = 1 - exp(-aA) targetval = 1.0 - math.exp(-absorptioncoeff A) bestc1 = 0.0 minerror = float('inf') # Numerical minimization of squared error over [0, A] as described in the source for c1 in range(-1000, 1000): c1f = c1 / 100.0 c0f = targetval - c1f A error = 0.0 for z in [i A / 100.0 for i in range(101)]: fz = 1.0 - math.exp(-absorptioncoeff z) gz = (c0f + c1f z) (z / A) error += (fz - gz) 2 if error < minerror: minerror = error bestc1 = c1f bestc0 = targetval - bestc1 A # Pass 1: First opacity attenuation applypass(vertexcolors, [z / A for z in vertexdepths], 'ONEMINUSSRCALPHA', fb, A) # Pass 2: Second opacity attenuation applypass(vertexcolors, [z / A for z in vertexdepths], 'ONEMINUSSRCALPHA', fb, A) # Pass 3: Color addition modulatedcolors = [] for i, z in enumerate(vertexdepths): colorterm = bestc0 + bestc1 z modulatedcolors.append(tuple(c colorterm for c in vertexcolors[i])) applypass(modulatedcolors, [z / A for z in vertexdepths], 'SRCALPHA', fb, A) def applypass(colors, alphas, blendfunc, fb, A): """ Simulates a hardware rendering pass with explicit blend math. Assumes a global framebuffer fb of shape (H, W, 3) initialized to background. """ # Rasterization interpolates vertex attributes across the polygon. # We simulate this by iterating over sample points (z) within the cell's depth range. for z in [i A / 100.0 for i in range(101)]: srcalpha = z / A srccolor = interpolatecolor(z, colors, [0.0, A]) if blendfunc == 'ONEMINUSSRCALPHA': # Hardware blend: dst = dst (1 - srcalpha) fb[:] = fb[:] (1.0 - srcalpha) elif blendfunc == 'SRCALPHA': # Hardware blend: dst = dst + srccolor srcalpha fb[:] = fb[:] + srccolor srcalpha def interpolatecolor(z, colors, depths): """Linear interpolation of vertex colors based on depth z.""" # In practice, this is handled by the GPU rasterizer if depths[1] == depths[0]: return colors[0] t = (z - depths[0]) / (depths[1] - depths[0]) return tuple(c0 (1 - t) + c1 t for c0, c1 in zip(colors[0], colors[1])) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the hardware's ability to accurately interpolate linear attributes and perform the blend operations. Precision errors in the quadratic approximation can lead to visible artifacts, especially with high absorption coefficients where the exponential decay is steep. Visibility Ordering: Correctness depends on a valid visibility ordering where no earlier cell occludes a later cell in screen space. Thick Cells: The approximation is valid on the interval [0, A]. If the cell projection is not convex or the depth variation is complex, the linear interpolation of z may not accurately represent the path length, leading to errors. The prerequisite for correct compositing. Ensures that cells are processed in an order such that earlier cells do not occlude later ones in screen space. Link The underlying hardware rasterization technique used for linear interpolation of vertex attributes, which multi-pass blending extends via multiple passes. Link Time Complexity: Three passes per cell, making it significantly slower than single-pass linear blending. The source notes "The extra time in computation and rendering are substantial". Memory Complexity: Low, as it uses standard framebuffer operations and does not require storing intermediate volume data per pixel. Strengths: Allows the use of standard hardware polygon renderers for volume rendering, avoiding the need for software ray casting. Provides a much better approximation of opacity and intensity than linear interpolation. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to multiple passes. Approximation errors exist, particularly for cells with high absorption or complex geometry. Requires careful visibility ordering. When to Use: When hardware acceleration is required and the visual quality of linear blending is insufficient, and software ray casting is too slow. When Not to Use: For real-time applications with very high frame rate requirements, or when exact physical accuracy is required. Multi-pass blending was introduced in the context of rapid exploration of curvilinear grids using direct volume rendering. It addresses the limitations of earlier methods that used linear interpolation (Gouraud shading) for color and opacity, which produced incorrect intensity and opacity estimates. The method was developed to leverage existing hardware polygon renderers while achieving higher fidelity in volume visualization. name: Front-to-Back Compositing
head: FTB Compositing, Front-to-back algorithm, Front-to-Back Integration, Front-to-Back Accumulation, Levoy's front-to-back method, Levoy's Front-to-Back Ray Casting, Recursive front-to-back compositing, Front-to-back volume rendering integral, front-to-back image-order volume rendering, Ray Marching with Front-to-Back Alpha Compositing
body: Front-to-Back Compositing is a direct volume rendering technique that projects semi-transparent volume data to the screen by traversing viewing rays from the camera viewpoint toward the far plane, accumulating color and opacity contributions. It is distinguished from its sibling Alpha Compositing Ray Casting and back-to-front compositing by its ability to exploit early ray termination, allowing the renderer to stop processing a ray once the accumulated opacity approaches 1.0 or transparency drops below a threshold, thereby reducing computational cost for opaque regions. Input: A volume dataset V defined on a grid, a transfer function mapping data values to optical properties (color C and opacity \alpha), and a set of viewing rays defined by origin O and direction D. Output: A final pixel color C{final} for each pixel on the image plane. For each pixel, the compositing state consists of two accumulators: 1. C{dst}: Accumulated color (RGB vector). 2. \alpha{dst}: Accumulated opacity (scalar, range [0, 1]). The method approximates the volume rendering integral using a discrete Riemann sum. 1. Initialization: For each pixel, initialize the accumulated color C{dst} = (0, 0, 0) and the accumulated opacity \alpha{dst} = 0. Alternatively, initialize transparency T = 1.0. 2. Ray Marching: Cast a ray from the camera origin along the pixel direction, sampling the volume at discrete intervals \Delta s from the near plane to the far plane. 3. Classification: For each sample point i, determine the data value and map it to color Ci and opacity \alphai using the transfer function and a local illumination model. 4. Compositing Update: Update the accumulated color and opacity using the recursive front-to-back formulas: C{dst}^{(i)} = C{dst}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{dst}^{(i-1)}) \cdot \alphai \cdot Ci \alpha{dst}^{(i)} = \alpha{dst}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{dst}^{(i-1)}) \cdot \alphai where C{dst}^{(i-1)} and \alpha{dst}^{(i-1)} are the values from the previous sample step. 5. Early Termination Check: After each update, check if the accumulated opacity \alpha{dst} approaches 1.0 or if the remaining transparency 1 - \alpha{dst} drops below a threshold (e.g., 0.01). If the condition is met, terminate the ray processing for this pixel. 6. Termination Conditions: The ray also terminates if it exits the volume bounding box, or hits a specific surface (e.g., isosurface) in caching or hybrid rendering setups. 7. Final Output: The final pixel color is C{final} = C{dst}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackcompositing(rayorigin, raydirection, volumemin, volumemax, volumeinterpolator, transferfunction, stepsize=1.0, transparencythreshold=0.01): acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accopacity = 0.0 t = 0.0 while True: pos = (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) inside = (volumemin[0] <= pos[0] <= volumemax[0] and volumemin[1] <= pos[1] <= volumemax[1] and volumemin[2] <= pos[2] <= volumemax[2]) if not inside: break density = volumeinterpolator(pos) color, opacity = transferfunction(density) if 1.0 - accopacity < transparencythreshold: break weight = (1.0 - accopacity) opacity acccolor[0] += weight color[0] acccolor[1] += weight color[1] acccolor[2] += weight color[2] accopacity += weight t += stepsize return acccolor Opacity/Transparency Threshold: Early termination triggers when accumulated opacity approaches 1.0 or transparency drops below a threshold such as 0.01. Step Size (\Delta s): Determines sampling density along the ray. Not given in the sources as a fixed value, but depends on volume resolution and view distance. Precision: Accumulating opacity can suffer from floating-point precision issues if many samples have very low opacity, though standard single-precision is generally sufficient for typical volume rendering. Order Dependency: The method requires samples to be processed in strict front-to-back order; back-to-front compositing does not support early termination. Degenerate Input: If the volume has no opacity (all \alpha = 0), the ray traverses fully without contributing color, resulting in the background color (black or clear). A sibling method that traverses rays from back to front. It does not require tracking accumulated opacity for color calculation but cannot use early ray termination, making it slower for opaque volumes. A sibling method that projects the maximum density value along the ray. It is order-independent and does not accumulate color or opacity, making it faster but less realistic for semi-transparent data. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel in the worst case, where N is the number of samples along the ray, but early ray termination significantly reduces the average number of processed samples for opaque regions. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for accumulators, plus O(V) memory for the volume dataset. Performance: Early ray termination provides substantial speedups, especially in volumes with high opacity regions. Strengths: Real-time capable due to early termination; physically plausible for semi-transparent media; simple recursive implementation. Limitations: Order-dependent (cannot be easily parallelized across samples for a single pixel without atomic operations or reduction); less efficient for fully transparent volumes where all samples must be processed. When to Use: Ideal for direct volume rendering of semi-transparent data where early termination is beneficial (e.g., medical CT/MRI with high-density structures). When Not to Use: When the volume is fully transparent (no early termination benefit) or when order-independent transparency is required (use back-to-front or other techniques). Front-to-Back Compositing is derived from the volume rendering equation, which models the transport of light through participating media. It is a recursive implementation of the discrete Riemann sum approximation of the volume rendering integral. The method is a fundamental technique in image-order volume rendering (ray casting). name: Order-Independent Volumetric Compositing via Visibility Function
head: Adaptive Transparency for Volume Rendering, Order-independent sample composition, Visibility-based compositing
body: This method composites semi-transparent volumetric samples in an order-independent manner by employing a visibility function that represents the total transmittance between a sample and the camera. It solves the order-dependent transparency problem in direct volume rendering, enabling correct visibility composition beyond simple Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) or X-ray representations. Unlike its siblings which often rely on sorting or front-to-back accumulation, this approach refactors the alpha-blending equation to avoid recursion and sorting, allowing light sources to be processed independently of the camera location. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volumetric data (modalities), light source positions, camera position (xe), and the visibility function v(xe, x) for each sample x along a ray. Outputs: A final composited color value for each pixel, representing the direct volume rendering result. Data Structures: Visibility Function: A scalar value associated with each sample x in the volume, representing the transmittance from x to the camera xe. Not given in the sources how this is stored (e.g., texture, cache), but it is computed or accessed per sample. Sample List: A collection of samples projected into camera space. The method allows these to be processed in any order. Formulas: The core compositing term for a sample x illuminated by light source si and viewed from camera xe is defined as: \rho(x, xe - x) \cdot \tau(si(x)) \cdot v(xe, x) Where: \rho(x, xe - x) is the scattering/emission term of the sample x towards the camera. \tau(si(x)) is the illumination term from light source si at sample x. v(xe, x) is the visibility function for x as seen from the camera at xe, representing the total transmittance between the sample and the camera. Steps: 1. Compute Visibility: Determine the visibility function v(xe, x) for each sample x along the view ray. 2. Project Samples: Project samples towards the camera in an order-independent manner using the visibility function. 3. Render Modalities Unordered: Render individual modalities unordered as seen from the light view. 4. Composite: Composite all samples along a ray in an order-independent manner. 5. Handle Illumination: Use the visibility function to achieve correct compositing without storing light contribution in an illumination cache. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def orderindependentcompositing(samples, camerapos, visibilityfunction): """ Composite volumetric samples order-independently. Args: samples: List of sample objects, each having: x: 3D position rho: scattering/emission term towards camera tau: illumination term from light source camerapos: 3D position of the camera (xe) visibilityfunction: A function or lookup that returns v(xe, x) for a given sample x Returns: compositedcolor: The final color value for the pixel """ compositedcolor = 0.0 # Process samples in any order (order-independent) for sample in samples: x = sample.x rho = sample.rho tau = sample.tau # Get visibility (transmittance from sample to camera) v = visibilityfunction(camerapos, x) # Compute contribution using the visibility-based formula contribution = rho tau v # Accumulate contributions # The exact refactored alpha-blending equation to avoid recursion is not detailed in the sources. compositedcolor += contribution return compositedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility Computation: The method relies on knowing v(xe, x). The source mentions avoiding the storage of a shadow data structure, implying v(xe, x) might be computed on-the-fly or via a simplified model. Early Ray Termination: The method can incorporate early ray termination to ensure only visible samples receive illumination (Observation 1), reducing sampling overhead. Occluded Illumination: Without the visibility function, samples illuminated by light but occluded from the camera would still contribute. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. However, by avoiding sorting and recursion, it may reduce overhead compared to order-dependent methods. The complexity depends on the cost of computing the visibility function v(xe, x). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method avoids storing an illumination cache, potentially reducing memory usage compared to methods that cache light contributions. Strengths: Enables correct direct volume rendering visibility composition beyond MIP and X-ray representations. Supports multimodal volumetric illumination with multiple light sources and colored shadows without extensions. Allows processing light sources in an order independent of the camera location. Limitations: Requires the computation or availability of the visibility function v(xe, x) for each sample. The exact implementation details of computing this function efficiently are not provided in the source. When to use: When correct semi-transparent volumetric compositing is required, and order-independence is desired to simplify rendering pipelines or support dynamic light/camera changes. Particularly useful for multimodal volume illumination. When not to use: If the visibility function is expensive to compute and performance is critical, or if simple MIP/X-ray representations are sufficient. This method is based on the theory of adaptive transparency, first introduced by Sintorn and Assarson. They applied this to hair rendering and later to arbitrary transparent geometries. The approach was extended to direct volume rendering by Sundén et al. in their work on multimodal volume illumination. It exploits the dualism between semi-transparent shadow rendering and semi-transparent volumetric rendering, as pointed out by Enderton et al.. Unlike previous order-independent approaches for volume rendering, this method enables true, semi-transparent volumetric compositing. name: Final Scene Composition
body: Final Scene Composition is a post-processing technique that applies pre-computed volumetric data to an opaque scene. It decouples volume calculation from surface rendering by sampling a 3D texture aligned with the scene geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Opaque scene depth buffer, fragment screen coordinates, linear depth, pre-computed 3D texture containing transmittance T and in-scattered light L{in}, and opaque scene color C{scene}. Output: Final composited pixel color C{final}. Data Structures: 3D Texture: A volumetric texture storing at least two components per voxel: transmittance T and in-scattered light L{in}. Steps: 1. Retrieve Depth: For each fragment in the opaque scene pass, retrieve the linear depth z{linear} from the scene's depth buffer. 2. Convert Coordinates: Convert the fragment's screen coordinates and linear depth into 3D texture coordinates (u, v, w) using the exponential depth equation. 3. Sample Texture: Sample the 3D texture at (u, v, w) using hardware trilinear interpolation (GLLINEAR) to obtain the transmittance T and in-scattered light L{in} for that point in the volume. 4. Composite: Combine the sampled volumetric data with the opaque scene color using the following equation: C{final} = C{scene} \times T + L{in} Where: C{scene} is the color of the opaque geometry at the fragment. T is the transmittance sampled from the texture. L{in} is the in-scattered light sampled from the texture. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def finalscenecomposition(scenecolor, lineardepth, texture3d): # 1. Retrieve linear depth from depth buffer (passed as input) zlinear = lineardepth # 2. Convert screen coordinates and linear depth to 3D texture coordinates (u, v, w) # The exact exponential depth equation is not provided in the sources. u, v, w = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # Coordinate conversion step omitted per sources # 3. Sample the integrated 3D texture using hardware trilinear interpolation T, Lin = texture3d.sampletrilinear(u, v, w) # 4. Composite: Final Color = Scene Color Transmittance + InScattered Light finalcolor = scenecolor T + Lin return finalcolor Parameters: Texture Resolution: Not given in the sources. Interpolation: Trilinear (GLLINEAR) is specified. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Opaque Scene Requirement: This method requires a pre-existing opaque scene depth buffer for coordinate mapping. Coordinate Precision: The accuracy of the composition depends on the precision of the depth-to-texture coordinate conversion. A variant that composites direct illumination, volumetric shadows, and caustic buffers. It renders surface caustics to a separate render target to allow for low-pass filtering before composition. A variant used in editable Gaussian splatting models (iVR-GS). It allows real-time editing by replacing palette color cp with a new palette color c'p, adjusting opacity by directly scaling the opacity term, and scaling attributes ka, kd, ks, \beta to adjust shading magnitudes. It renders with a new light direction using the Blinn-Phong equation based on primitive normals n. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the composition step, as it involves a single texture lookup and arithmetic operation. The overall complexity is dominated by the pre-computation of the 3D texture. Memory Complexity: Depends on the resolution of the 3D texture, requiring storage for transmittance and in-scattered light volumes. Strengths: High performance due to hardware interpolation and decoupling of volume and surface rendering. Limitations: Limited to volumes that can be pre-computed into a 3D texture. This method is described in the context of implementing volumetric fog in OpenGL using 3D textures. It leverages hardware capabilities for 3D texture sampling to achieve real-time performance for participating media.
