name: Volume Rendering (Taichi Forward Array)
body: This method performs a forward volume rendering pass using the Taichi programming language to accumulate RGB color, depth, and opacity per ray. It differs from standard CPU-based ray casting by leveraging Taichi's parallel execution model and supports transmittance thresholding to terminate ray marching early. It builds on Training Ray Compositing by providing the specific Taichi-native implementation for compositing ray samples. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes volumetric data and ray metadata as inputs and produces compositing results. sigmas: Volume density field, shape (N{samples}), type ti.types.ndarray(). rgbs: Volume color field, shape (N{samples}, 3), type ti.types.ndarray(). deltas: Distances between adjacent sample points, shape (N{samples}), type ti.types.ndarray(). ts: Cumulative distances (or depths) of sample points, shape (N{samples}), type ti.types.ndarray(). raysa: Ray metadata array, shape (N{rays}, 3), type ti.types.ndarray(). Each row n contains: raysa[n, 0]: Ray index rayidx (integer). raysa[n, 1]: Start index startidx in the sample arrays (integer). raysa[n, 2]: Number of samples Nsamples for this ray (integer). Tthreshold: Float threshold for transmittance to stop marching. Outputs: rgb: Accumulated RGB color per ray, shape (N{rays}, 3), type ti.types.ndarray(). depth: Accumulated depth per ray, shape (N{rays}), type ti.types.ndarray(). opacity: Accumulated opacity per ray, shape (N{rays}), type ti.types.ndarray(). totalsamples: Count of samples processed per ray, shape (N{rays}), type ti.types.ndarray(). ws: Weights array, shape (N{rays}), type ti.types.ndarray(). Data Structures: The implementation uses Taichi fields or arrays. The ray metadata raysa is a 2D array where each row defines a ray's segment in the global sample buffer. The transmittance array T is typically allocated with size N{samples} + 1 to store transmittance values at sample boundaries. Parameters: Tthreshold: Float. If transmittance drops below this value, the ray is considered fully occluded and marching stops. blockdim: Loop configuration parameter, typically 256. Algorithm: The method iterates over each ray defined in raysa. For each ray, it initializes accumulators and marches through the sample points. 1. Iterate over each ray index n in the range of raysa (number of rays). 2. Extract rayidx = raysa[n, 0], startidx = raysa[n, 1], and Nsamples = raysa[n, 2]. 3. Initialize accumulators for this ray: rgb[rayidx] = 0.0 (vector of size 3). depth[rayidx] = 0.0. opacity[rayidx] = 0.0. totalsamples[rayidx] = 0. 4. Initialize transmittance at the start of the ray segment: T[startidx] = 1.0. 5. Loop over sample index sample from 0 to N{samples} - 1: a. Compute global sample index: s = \text{start\idx} + \text{sample\}. b. Read current transmittance: T\ = T[s]. c. Check Threshold: If T\ \le \text{T\threshold}: i. Set T[s + 1] = 0.0. ii. Break the loop (stop marching). d. Compute absorption coefficient (opacity contribution) for this sample: a = 1.0 - \exp(-\text{sigmas}[s] \times \text{deltas}[s]). e. Compute weight w for this sample: w = T\ \times a [G: Derived from standard volume rendering equation wi = Ti (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai})]. f. Accumulate RGB: \text{rgb}[\text{ray\idx}, i] \leftarrow \text{rgb}[\text{ray\idx}, i] + w \times \text{rgbs}[s, i] \quad \text{for } i \in \{0, 1, 2\}. g. Accumulate Depth: \text{depth}[\text{ray\idx}] \leftarrow \text{depth}[\text{ray\idx}] + w \times \text{ts}[s]. h. Accumulate Opacity: \text{opacity}[\text{ray\idx}] \leftarrow \text{opacity}[\text{ray\idx}] + w. i. Update transmittance for the next step: T[s + 1] = T\ \times (1.0 - a). j. Increment totalsamples[rayidx]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import taichi as ti @ti.kernel def compositetrainfwarray( sigmas: ti.types.ndarray(), rgbs: ti.types.ndarray(), deltas: ti.types.ndarray(), ts: ti.types.ndarray(), raysa: ti.types.ndarray(), Tthreshold: float, rgb: ti.types.ndarray(), depth: ti.types.ndarray(), opacity: ti.types.ndarray(), totalsamples: ti.types.ndarray(), ws: ti.types.ndarray(), T: ti.types.ndarray() # Pre-allocated transmittance array, size Nsamples + 1): # Iterate over rays for n in range(raysa.shape[0]): rayidx = ti.cast(raysa[n, 0], ti.i32) startidx = ti.cast(raysa[n, 1], ti.i32) Nsamples = ti.cast(raysa[n, 2], ti.i32) # Initialize accumulators rgb[rayidx, 0] = 0.0 rgb[rayidx, 1] = 0.0 rgb[rayidx, 2] = 0.0 depth[rayidx] = 0.0 opacity[rayidx] = 0.0 totalsamples[rayidx] = 0 # Initialize transmittance at start T[startidx] = 1.0 # March through samples for sample in range(Nsamples): s = startidx + sample T = T[s] # Check transmittance threshold if T <= Tthreshold: T[s + 1] = 0.0 break # Compute absorption a = 1.0 - ti.exp(-sigmas[s] deltas[s]) # Compute weight w = T a # Accumulate RGB for i in range(3): rgb[rayidx, i] += w rgbs[s, i] # Accumulate Depth depth[rayidx] += w ts[s] # Accumulate Opacity opacity[rayidx] += w # Update transmittance T[s + 1] = T (1.0 - a) # Increment sample count totalsamples[rayidx] += 1 Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \times N{samples}) in the worst case, where N{rays} is the number of rays and N{samples} is the maximum samples per ray. With thresholding, it is often faster. Memory Complexity: O(N{samples}) for the transmittance array T and input/output buffers. Performance: Implemented in Taichi, it leverages GPU parallelism. The blockdim=256 configuration suggests optimization for GPU thread blocks. Strengths: Efficient parallel execution on GPU; early termination via thresholding reduces computation for occluded rays. Limitations: Requires pre-allocated transmittance array T which must be managed carefully to avoid race conditions if rays share samples (though typically rays are disjoint in training setups). Precision issues may arise with very small deltas or sigmas. This method is part of the Stable Dreamfusion pipeline, specifically the volume rendering component used for training NeRFs from text prompts. It is implemented using Taichi for high-performance GPU computation. ashawkey/stable-dreamfusion, https://github.com/ashawkey/stable-dreamfusion, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Volume Blending and Segmentation
head: BlendedVolumeData, ImageTexture3D segmentation
body: Volume Blending and Segmentation combines multiple rendering styles or separate volume datasets to create composite, customizable presentations. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by focusing on the high-level composition of distinct visual styles or independent data sources, rather than refining the compositing of a single ray's samples (as in Training Ray Compositing) or merging multi-view inputs. The family operates on the principle of compositional flexibility, allowing users to apply different visual enhancements to specific segments of a volume or to blend entirely separate volume datasets. This requires a mechanism to define segmentation boundaries or blending weights that map spatial regions or data attributes to specific rendering styles. Focuses on sigma-based compositing. Merges colors from multiple viewpoints. Coalesces segment data. Uses Taichi arrays for rendering. The concept emerged in the context of hypermedia platforms for health visualization, specifically within the X3D framework. It was documented in Volume 13, Issue 1, pp. 40-50, 2012, as a method to provide customizable and distinctive rendering by composing styles on individual volumes, selectively choosing styles for segments, and combining separate volumes. NEW PLATFORMS FOR HEALTH HYPERMEDIA, https://doi.org/10.48009/1iis201240-50, fetched 2026-10-29

name: IDVR-Compositing
head: Importance-Driven Volume Rendering Compositing
body: IDVR-Compositing is a post-local compositing step that assigns a view-dependent sparseness value to each object along a ray to modulate its visual prominence before global blending. It solves the problem of displaying multiple objects with different importance levels by making occluded or less important objects sparse (transparent) while keeping important ones dense (visible). Unlike standard compositing which treats all samples equally, IDVR-Compositing modifies the color and opacity values based on an object's importance and its occlusion status within the image footprint. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of local compositing results (ci, \alphai) for each object i along a ray, where ci is the object's color and \alphai is its accumulated opacity. An importance value Ii for each object. A pre-computed image footprint for the current view direction. Output: Modified color and opacity values (c'i, \alpha'i) ready for global compositing. Data Structures: Footprint: A 2D array or map corresponding to the image pixels, storing occlusion/visibility information for the current view. This must be recalculated whenever the view direction changes. Sparseness Map: A value si \in [0, 1] assigned to each object i per ray. si=1 means the object is almost completely transparent; si=0 means it is completely visible. Steps: 1. Create Footprint: Generate a footprint of the image for the current view direction. This involves determining which objects intersect each ray and their relative positions. 2. Assign Sparseness: For each ray, assign a sparseness value si to each object i based on its importance Ii and occlusion status within the footprint. If an object is occluded by higher-importance objects, its sparseness increases (becomes more transparent). If an object is not occluded or has the highest importance, its sparseness decreases (becomes more visible). 3. Modulate Values: Modify the local compositing results (ci, \alphai) using the sparseness value si. The exact modulation formula is not explicitly defined in the provided notes, but it implies scaling the opacity and potentially the color contribution based on si. Let the modified values be (c'i, \alpha'i). 4. Global Compositing: Blend the modified color and opacity values (c'i, \alpha'i) using the standard front-to-back compositing equation to produce the final image. Parameters: Sparseness (si): A value between 0 and 1. 1 means the object is almost completely transparent. 0 means it should be completely visible. Importance (Ii): A scalar value representing the visual importance of object i. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def idvrcompositing(rayobjects, footprint, viewdirection): """ IDVR-Compositing step. rayobjects: list of dicts with 'id', 'importance', 'color', 'opacity'. footprint: data structure providing occlusion info for viewdirection. viewdirection: vec3, current camera view direction. Returns: list of dicts with modified 'color' and 'opacity'. """ # Step 1: Create Footprint # The footprint must be recalculated whenever the view direction changes. # Implementation details for footprint creation are not provided. occlusionmap = {} modifiedobjects = [] for obj in rayobjects: # Step 2: Assign Sparseness # Sparseness depends on importance and occlusion within the footprint. # The exact algorithm for assigning sparseness (e.g., MImP) is not provided in the sources. sparseness = 0.5 # Step 3: Modulate Values # Modify color and opacity based on sparseness. # The exact modulation formula is not given in the sources. alphaprime = obj['opacity'] (1.0 - sparseness) colorprime = obj['color'] (1.0 - sparseness) modifiedobjects.append({ 'id': obj['id'], 'color': colorprime, 'opacity': alphaprime }) return modifiedobjects A simple and fast approach to assigning sparseness values. It is similar to Maximum Intensity Projection. Along a ray, the object with the maximum importance value gets the lowest sparseness value (0, most dense), so it is displayed in the most dense way. All other objects get the highest sparseness value (1, most transparent), so they are not rendered or are very faint. A disadvantage is that it can result in only a cylindrical countersink at the position of the most important object, potentially hiding context. A method that guarantees constant visibility of a focus object regardless of the thickness of the context volume part in front of it. It ensures a constant fraction of visual information for the focus object. The desired level of sparseness for the context object in front of the focus object is denoted as So. The context part in front of the focus is rendered separately using two-level volume rendering. All ray opacities of the occluding part are summed to compute the average per-ray opacity \alpha{avg}. The original accumulated opacity value is corrected such that the average per-ray opacity equals So using the formula: \alpha{accum\new}(x) = \alpha{accum}(x) \cdot \frac{So}{\alpha{avg}} where \alpha{accum\new} is the modified accumulated opacity, \alpha{accum} is the original density value, So is the level of sparseness value of the context object, and \alpha{avg} is the average accumulated opacity value of the suppressed context part. Finally, a combination of both context parts takes place in the global compositing step. Time Complexity: Depends on the footprint creation and sparseness assignment. MImP is described as "very simple but also very fast". VPImC requires separate rendering of the occluding part. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the footprint and sparseness values per ray. Strengths: Allows for view-dependent importance visualization, making important objects more visible while suppressing less important or occluded ones. VPImC ensures constant visibility of focus objects. Limitations: MImP can lead to loss of context information. Footprint must be recalculated for every view direction change. The exact modulation of color and opacity by sparseness is not fully specified in the sources. IDVR-Compositing was introduced in the context of Importance-Driven Volume Rendering (IDVR). The concept of assigning sparseness values to objects based on importance and occlusion was developed to enhance feature visibility in volume visualization. name: Final Composition
head: Density-dependent interpolation, Segment compositing, Volume imaging, Volumetric Compositing
body: Final Composition (also known as Volume Imaging) integrates a 3D volume into a 2D image by assigning voxel values to organ ranges with intermediate blending, then applying lighting to depict surfaces without exact boundary segmentation. It differs from threshold-based segmentation by using the full volume and from pure projection by incorporating illumination. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset, intensity ranges defining organ segments, and lighting parameters. Output: A 2D rendered image. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: 3D array of intensity and opacity values. Segment Definitions: Mappings from intensity ranges to organ labels or material properties. Convolution Buffers: Precomputed values for low-density segments, stored only for the right-hand column of the previous block and the bottom row of the previous sweep to minimize memory. Steps: 1. Define intensity ranges for organ segmentation, allowing intermediate values for blending. 2. Compute convolutions for low-density segments, retaining only the required boundary rows/columns for memory efficiency. 3. For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume and composite voxel segments front-to-back. 4. For each segment on the ray, select the rendering solution: low-density convolution weighted by optical depth, high-density diffusion, or a density-dependent interpolation between them to eliminate aliasing artifacts. 5. Apply lighting information to the composited volume data to depict organ surfaces. 6. Evaluate the final color per pixel. Formulas: The compositing process follows the standard front-to-back accumulation model, adapted with segment-specific contributions: C{final} = \sum{i} Ti \cdot \alphai \cdot ci^{seg} Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Where ci^{seg} is determined by the low-density convolution, high-density diffusion, or their density-dependent interpolation. Ti is the accumulated transmittance up to sample i. \alphai is the sample opacity. Parameters: Intensity Ranges: User-defined or algorithmically determined thresholds for organ segmentation. These are critical; the result is heavily dependent on them. Optical Depth: Used to weight the low-density convolution solution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intensity Range Dependency: The method is heavily dependent on the chosen intensity ranges. Incorrect ranges lead to poor visualization or misrepresentation of organs. Aliasing: Switching between low-density and high-density solutions can cause aliasing artifacts. Density-dependent interpolation is required to mitigate this. Surface Only: The method portrays organ surfaces but not interior details, as it relies on lighting and surface depiction rather than full volumetric transparency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def finalcomposition(volume, intensityranges, convolutions): """ Final Composition rendering loop. volume: 3D array of voxel intensities and opacities. intensityranges: mappings defining organ segments. convolutions: precomputed values for low-density segments. """ image = empty2darray() for each pixel (x, y): ray = castraythroughvolume(x, y) # Not detailed in sources Cacc = vec3(0.0) alphaacc = 0.0 T = 1.0 for sample in ray: # Determine segment solution based on voxel intensity if sample.intensity in lowdensityrange: cseg = convolutions[sample] sample.opticaldepth alphaseg = sample.opacity elif sample.intensity in highdensityrange: cseg = computediffusionsolution(sample) # Equations (8) and (9) not provided in notes alphaseg = sample.opacity else: # Density-dependent interpolation to eliminate aliasing t = computeinterpolationfactor(sample.intensity) # Not given in sources clow = convolutions[sample] sample.opticaldepth chigh = computediffusionsolution(sample) cseg = clow + t (chigh - clow) alphaseg = sample.opacity # Standard front-to-back compositing update Cacc = Cacc + T alphaseg cseg alphaacc = alphaacc + T alphaseg T = T (1.0 - alphaseg) # Early ray termination if alphaacc >= 1.0: break # Composite over background image[x, y] = Cacc + T backgroundcolor return image Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays and the complexity of the convolution and diffusion calculations. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data and intermediate convolution results (specifically for the right-hand column of the previous block and the bottom row of the previous sweep). Strengths: Incorporates information from the entire volume; uses lighting to enhance surface perception. Limitations: Heavily dependent on user-selected intensity ranges; only portrays organ surfaces, not interior structures; potential for aliasing if interpolation is not handled correctly. When to use: When visualizing organ surfaces in nuclear medicine or similar modalities where relative uptake is important, and exact boundary segmentation is not desired. When not to use: When interior volume details are required, or when user-defined intensity ranges are not feasible or desirable. Final Composition, also referred to as Volume Imaging or Volumetric Compositing, was developed as an alternative to methods that rely on exact boundary determination or pure maximum activity projection. It emerged in the context of 3D display of SPECT images, aiming to incorporate information from the entire volume while using lighting to depict surfaces. The technique involves a blend of convolution-based low-density handling and diffusion-based high-density handling, interpolated based on density. name: ComposedVolumeStyle
head: CompositeVolumeStyle
body: ComposedVolumeStyle is a rendering style node that allows compositing multiple volume rendering styles together into a single rendering pass by listing them in its styles field. It solves the problem of combining distinct visual effects—such as lighting, edge enhancement, and opacity mapping—into one coherent image without requiring multiple separate rendering passes. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Composition via Convolution (Power Form) by operating at the style node level, aggregating stylistic contributions rather than mathematically convolving transmittance or color values directly in the ray-casting loop. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a list of X3DVolumeRenderStyleNode instances as input via the styles field. It outputs a single composite rendering pass where the visual effects of the constituent styles are applied to the volume data. Data Structures: The node is defined by the following fields: enabled: SFBool, default TRUE. Enables or disables the style. ordered: SFBool, default FALSE. Determines if styles must be applied strictly in the order declared. styles: MFNode (list of X3DVolumeRenderStyleNode). Contains the contributing style node references. Steps: 1. Initialize the rendering context for the volume object. 2. If ordered is TRUE, iterate through the styles list from index 0 to N-1, applying each style strictly in sequence. 3. If ordered is FALSE, the implementation may apply the styles in any order or in parallel, provided the underlying implementation supports it. 4. Composite the visual results of the applied styles into a single image. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode illustrates the logic for handling the ordered flag and style application. Note that the actual pixel-level compositing of individual style effects (e.g., how ShadedVolumeStyle color blends with OpacityMapVolumeStyle color) is implementation-specific and not defined by the node specification itself. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applycomposedvolumestyle(styles, ordered): """ Applies a list of volume rendering styles. styles: list of X3DVolumeRenderStyleNode objects. ordered: boolean. If True, styles are applied sequentially. If False, order is flexible or parallel. """ if not styles: return None if ordered: # Apply styles strictly in declared order for i in range(len(styles)): style = styles[i] style.apply() else: # Implementation may apply in any order or in parallel # This block represents the flexibility allowed by the spec # Actual parallel execution depends on the renderer backend for style in styles: style.apply() Parameters: ordered: FALSE (default). Allows flexible ordering. TRUE enforces strict sequential application. enabled: TRUE (default). Controls visibility of the style. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Order Dependency: If ordered is FALSE, the visual result may vary depending on the renderer's internal optimization or parallelization strategy. Empty Styles: If the styles list is empty, no specific style is applied, potentially resulting in default rendering behavior. Provides lighting calculations for the volume. Often used in conjunction with ComposedVolumeStyle to add illumination to the final composite. Applies transfer functions to map scalar values to color and opacity. Frequently combined with lighting styles to control visibility. Adds edge enhancement effects based on gradient thresholds. Can be composited with other styles to highlight boundaries. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of styles N and the complexity of each style. If ordered is TRUE, complexity is O(N \times T{style}). If FALSE, it may be O(T{style}) if parallelized, or O(N \times T{style}) if sequential but unordered. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store references to the style nodes. Strengths: Simplifies scene graph construction by allowing multiple visual effects in a single node. Supports flexible ordering for performance optimization. Limitations: The exact blending behavior of multiple styles is not strictly defined by the node specification, relying on implementation details. When to use: When multiple visual effects (e.g., lighting, edges, opacity) are needed for a single volume object. When not to use: When strict, deterministic ordering of style application is required and the renderer does not support ordered=True efficiently, or when fine-grained control over pixel-level blending is needed beyond what the style nodes provide. ComposedVolumeStyle (also known as CompositeVolumeStyle) is part of the X3D standard specification for volume rendering. It was developed as part of the "Development of an Amendment to X3D to Create a Standard Specification of Medical Image Volume Rendering, Segmentation, and Registration" project. The node is implemented in the instantreality engine, where it is used to combine styles like ShadedVolumeStyle and OpacityMapVolumeStyle. name: Lighting-Specific Compositing
body: Lighting-Specific Compositing is a family of volume rendering techniques that integrate illumination models (such as in-scattering, Phong shading, or boundary enhancement) directly into the compositing loop, rather than treating lighting as a post-processing step or a simple per-sample color multiplication. It solves the problem of physically inaccurate or visually flat rendering by allowing light transport effects to influence the accumulation of opacity and color at the sample level. It differs from standard direct volume ray casting by modifying the color and opacity terms (ci, \alphai) before they enter the front-to-back accumulator, and from image-level compositing by preserving depth coherence for complex lighting interactions like occlusion and shadowing. All methods in this family operate on a sequence of samples (ci, \alphai) encountered along a ray, where ci is the sample color (RGB) and \alphai is the sample opacity (A). The core mechanism involves an accumulator state (C{acc}, \alpha{acc}) initialized to (0, 0) (or background color/opacity) and updated iteratively for each sample. The standard optical model assumes that light is emitted or scattered by the volume and attenuated by absorption. The standard front-to-back compositing equation updates these accumulators for each sample i from front to back: C{acc}^{(i)} = C{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai Ci \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai where C{acc}^{(0)} = 0 and \alpha{acc}^{(0)} = 0. The term (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) represents the transmittance, i.e., the fraction of light reaching sample i from the camera side. In iterative form using transmittance T = 1 - \alpha{acc}: \begin{aligned} C{final} &\leftarrow C{final} + ci \cdot \alphai \cdot T \\ T &\leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai) \end{aligned} Where T is initialized to 1.0 and represents the accumulated transparency \prod (1-\alphaj). The final pixel color is often composited over a background color C{bg} using C{final} = C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{bg}. Early ray termination is a common optimization where the loop breaks if T falls below a small threshold (e.g., 10^{-6}), as further samples contribute negligibly to the color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositingloop(samples, backgroundcolor): """ Standard front-to-back compositing loop shared by the family. samples: list of (color: vec3, opacity: float) sorted front-to-back. backgroundcolor: vec3 for the scene background. """ Cacc = vec3(0.0) T = 1.0 for ci, alphai in samples: Cacc = Cacc + T alphai ci T = T (1.0 - alphai) # Early ray termination if T <= 1e-6: break # Composite over background return Cacc + T backgroundcolor Incremental Blending for In-scattering approximates light scattering in volume rendering by discretizing the scattering sphere into J directions and accumulating the results via incremental blending. It computes the in-scattering contribution for each direction independently and blends them into a stored accumulator buffer. It builds on Lighting-Specific Compositing by introducing indirect attenuation parameters and a dedicated light buffer for scattering propagation. See Incremental Blending for In-scattering. Intermixing is a technique for rendering multi-channel volume data by separately evaluating the illumination model for each channel at every ray sample and combining the results during the accumulation phase. It distinguishes itself from image-level compositing by correctly handling occlusions between different channels, as it retains depth information that image-level blending discards. It is more flexible than other approaches but computationally more expensive. See Intermixing. Boundary enhancement is a compositing technique designed to improve the visibility of object boundaries and material interfaces within volume data. It addresses the problem of indistinct edges in standard volume rendering by emphasizing transitions between different tissues or structures, often used in conjunction with silhouette techniques in medical illustration. Unlike standard direct volume rendering which relies on opacity and color accumulation, this method modifies the shading or opacity contribution based on boundary detection. See Boundary Enhancement. Phong Shading with Volume Rendering enhances standard direct volume ray casting by applying Phong lighting (diffuse and specular) to volume samples based on surface normals derived from volume gradients. Unlike standard compositing which treats samples as colored blobs, this method calculates surface-like shading interactions before compositing, adding geometric depth cues to the volume. It differs from standard composite shaders by incorporating gradient-based normals and Phong lighting calculations into the color computation before compositing. See Phong Shading with Volume Rendering. Definition: A technique for rendering shadow catchers where the camera sees the background darkened by the ratio of visible to total direct light, with alpha carrying shadow opacity. Steps: Darken the background by the ratio of visible to total direct light. Store shadow opacity in the alpha channel on a transparent background. Pitfalls: Indirect rays must still see the ground to ensure correct global illumination interaction. Definition: A compositing step for contour rendering that uses Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) or Local Maximum Intensity Projection (LMIP) to combine ray samples. Steps: 1. Perform classification and shading for all ray samples. 2. Composite using MIP (max intensity) or LMIP to prevent stronger contours from hiding weaker, closer contours. Definition: Blends four light values (a, b, c, d) into a single packed light value, replacing any zero values with the fourth value before averaging. Steps: If a == 0, set a = d. If b == 0, set b = d. If c == 0, set c = d. Return ((a + b + c + d) >> 2) & 0xFF00FF. Definition: Computes final HDR light intensity L(x, l) for a ray at location x in direction l by combining volumetric lighting from a Lighting Volume Sky Gradient (LVSG) and an environment map L{env} using alpha compositing. Steps: Select K equi-spaced locations along the ray from x in direction l. Use nearest neighbor interpolation to retrieve voxel values \{\alphak, \xik\} from LVSG for each of the K locations. Query the environment map intensity L{env}(l) in direction l using bilinear interpolation. Formula: L(x, l) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \tau{k-1} \alphak G(-l; \xik) + \tauK L{env}(l), where \tauk = \prod{i=1}^{k} (1 - \alphai) is the transmittance, and \tau0 = 1. Parameters: K: Number of equi-spaced sampling locations along the ray. \alphak: Alpha (opacity) value from LVSG at sample k. \xik: Lighting feature/vector from LVSG at sample k. G(-l; \xik): Lighting contribution function using feature \xik and incoming direction -l. L{env}(l): Radiance from the HDR sky environment map in direction l. Usage: Used for rendering object insertion and shadows. Steps: Combine the DLI of each frame with the reference image by multiplying each pixel of the reference image by the value of the DLI stored in the corresponding pixel. Perform the compositing process on all frames to obtain an image that makes the smoke move perceptible. Not given in the sources. name: Incremental Blending for In-scattering
body: Incremental Blending for In-scattering approximates light scattering in volume rendering by discretizing the scattering sphere into J directions and accumulating the results via incremental blending. It computes the in-scattering contribution for each direction independently and blends them into a stored accumulator buffer. It adapts direct volume ray casting and compositing to handle in-scattering effects incrementally. Inputs: Volume dataset V. Transfer function mapping density to color c(s) and opacity \alpha(s). Light source direction and intensity. Number of scattering directions J. Bias parameter I{bias} \in [0, 1]. Outputs: Final in-scattering intensity buffer I{stored}. Data Structures: I{stored}: A buffer (volume or texture) storing the accumulated in-scattering intensity. Initialized to zero. I{final}: A temporary buffer storing the result of the current direction's integration. gk: The emitted color term at sample k. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize I{stored} to zero. Determine J sampling directions by subdividing a tetrahedron, icosahedron, or octahedron. 2. Direction Loop: For each incremental update step j from 1 to J: a. Ray Casting: For each view ray, perform volume ray casting. At each sample point sk along the ray, compute the scattered intensity Is(sk) for the current direction j. b. Compute Emitted Term: Calculate the emitted color term: gk = (I{bias} + (1 - I{bias}) \cdot Is(sk)) \cdot c(sk) \cdot \alpha(sk) where c(sk) is the color from the transfer function, \alpha(sk) is the opacity, and I{bias} adjusts the minimum light level. c. Integration: Compute the intermediate intensity I{final} for the current direction by integrating gk along the ray using front-to-back compositing: I{final} = \sum{k=0}^n gk \prod{p=0}^{k-1} (1 - \alpha(sp)) where n is the total number of samples. d. Incremental Blend: Blend the newly computed I{final} with the previously stored intensity I{stored}: I{blended} = \frac{1}{j} \cdot I{final} + \left(1 - \frac{1}{j}\right) \cdot I{stored} where I{blended} is the new value to store. e. Store: Update I{stored} \leftarrow I{blended}. 3. Final Output: After all J directions are processed, I{stored} contains the approximated in-scattering contribution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def incrementalblendinginscattering(J, Ibias, volumedata): # Initialize stored intensity buffer to zero Istored = zeroslike(volumedata) # Directions determined by subdividing a tetrahedron, icosahedron, or octahedron directions = [dir1, dir2,..., dirJ] for j, dir in enumerate(directions, start=1): Ifinal = zeroslike(volumedata) for ray in volumedata.rays: transmittance = 1.0 for sample in ray.samples: # Compute scattered intensity Is for current direction Is = sample.scatteredintensityfordirection(dir) c, alpha = sample.color, sample.opacity # Compute emitted color term gk gk = (Ibias + (1.0 - Ibias) Is) c alpha # Front-to-back compositing for this direction Ifinal[ray.pixel] += transmittance gk transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Incremental blend with previously stored intensity Istored = (1.0 / j) Ifinal + (1.0 - 1.0 / j) Istored return Istored Parameters: J: Number of scattering directions. I{bias}: Minimum light level parameter in range [0, 1]; default behavior assumes a white light source. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: The method requires storing intermediate volumes (\alpha \cdot lp, \alpha \cdot g, I{final}) for each voxel, which can be significant for large volumes (e.g., 512^3). Reducing the resolution of the scattering volume (SVR) mitigates this. Light Source Color: The base equations assume a white light source; extension to colored light requires modifying the Is(sk) calculation. Incremental Lighting for In-Scattering approximates light scattering by propagating and blurring indirect lighting components from slice to slice, considering only incoming light within a cone in the direction of the light source. It extends incremental blending by introducing indirect attenuation parameters and a dedicated light buffer for scattering propagation. It differs from full scattering models by ignoring back-scattering during the intensity transport phase, which simplifies the hardware implementation at the cost of accuracy in dense, deep regions of the volume. Hardware Blending Recurrence Evaluation evaluates the multiple forward scattering recurrence Ik = g{k-1} + T{k-1} I{k-1} by mapping the mathematical operation to GPU hardware blending and pixel read-back operations. It computes the incident light on each particle in a participating medium by using the frame buffer as an accumulator. It differs from Incremental Lighting for In-Scattering by explicitly reading back pixel values to resolve the recurrence dependency. Volume Ray Casting with In-scattering is a specific application of the incremental blending method where the in-scattering term gk is computed directly during the ray casting pass. The final eye color I{eye} is computed as: I{eye} = \sum{k=0}^n gk \prod{p=0}^{k-1} (1 - \alpha(sp)) where gk is the emitted color at sample k, \alpha(sp) is opacity, and n is total samples. The term gk is defined as: gk = (I{bias} + (1 - I{bias}) \cdot Is(sk)) \cdot c(sk) \cdot \alpha(sk) where I{bias} is the minimum light level, Is(sk) is the scattered intensity, and c(sk) is the color from the transfer function. The bias parameter I{bias} is in the range [0..1] and adjusts the minimum light level, with default behavior assuming a white light source. Incremental Integration for Epipolar Rendering computes volumetric shadows and scattering by sweeping over view rays \beta from the light away. It maintains an incremental function b[\gamma] storing \Gamma(\gamma)V(\gamma, \beta). Initially \beta=0 and b[\gamma]=\Gamma(\gamma). When stepping to a new \beta, b[\gamma] is set to 0 for all light rays \gamma where S[\gamma]=\beta (light rays terminating at the current view ray). The integral is B(\beta) \sum{\gamma<D[\beta]} b[\gamma]. The intensity I[\beta] is computed as: I[\beta] = \sum{\substack{\gamma < D[\beta] \\ S[\gamma] > \beta}} I(\gamma, \beta) V(\gamma, \beta) = \sum{S[\gamma] > \beta} I(\gamma, \beta) where D[\beta] is the view ray length from the rectified depth map, S[\gamma] is the blocker distance from the rectified shadow map, I(\gamma, \beta) contains scattering terms excluding visibility, and V(\gamma, \beta) is visibility (1 if S[\gamma] > \beta, 0 otherwise). A pitfall of naive incremental summation is that it still requires iterating over all \gamma for each \beta, resulting in O(srd) complexity, same as brute force ray marching. Time Complexity: The method requires J passes over the volume, one per scattering direction. Memory Complexity: The method requires storage for intermediate volumes (\alpha \cdot lp, \alpha \cdot g, I{final}), which can be significant. For a 512^3 volume, three additional 512^3 volumes may be needed. Reducing the resolution of the scattering volume (SVR) can reduce memory usage. Strengths: It allows for the approximation of in-scattering in a single-pass pipeline without requiring complex global illumination algorithms. Limitations: The accuracy depends on the number of directions J. Memory usage can be high for large volumes. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in "Interactive Global Light Propagation in Direct Volume Rendering using Local Piecewise Integration". It adapts direct volume ray casting and compositing to handle in-scattering effects incrementally. The approach was developed to address the computational cost of global illumination in volume rendering, providing a practical approximation for real-time applications. name: Incremental Lighting for In-Scattering
head: Translucency Approximation via Indirect Attenuation
body: Incremental Lighting for In-Scattering is a method for approximating light scattering (translucency) in volume rendering by propagating and blurring indirect lighting components from slice to slice, considering only incoming light within a cone in the direction of the light source. It extends incremental lighting by introducing indirect attenuation parameters and a dedicated light buffer for scattering propagation. It differs from full scattering models by ignoring back-scattering during the intensity transport phase, which simplifies the hardware implementation at the cost of accuracy in dense, deep regions of the volume. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume density field, volume opacity/alpha values (A), indirect attenuation parameters (Ai) for each RGB channel, light color (CL), sample distance (d), blur angle parameter. Outputs: Final rendered image with translucent lighting effects. Data Structures: Light Buffer: A 2D texture buffer storing indirect attenuation values. Initialized with 1 - CL. Uses alternating double-buffering (current and next buffers) to support read/write operations during blur. Perturbation Texture: A texture used to modify texture coordinates for sampling the light buffer during the blur operation. Frame Buffer: Standard render target for the final image. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the light buffer with values 1 - CL for each pixel, where CL is the light color. 2. Pass 1 (Eye Contribution): For each sample along the ray: Read the current indirect attenuation value Ai from the light buffer using standard texture coordinates. Multiply the reflective color C of the current sample by (1 - Ai). Composite this result into the frame buffer using the standard Over operator. 3. Pass 2 (Light Contribution & Blur): Set the fragment shader output color to Ai (the indirect attenuation parameter) instead of 0. Modify texture coordinates for the current light buffer using a perturbation texture to sample indirect components for blur. The radius of the blur circle is calculated using the user-defined blur angle and sample distance d. Read the current light buffer using the modified texture coordinates. Compute the blurred attenuation as a weighted sum of the values read from the light buffer. Blend the result into the next light buffer using the Light Buffer Compositing operation. Swap the current and next light buffers for the next slice. Formulas: Light Buffer Compositing (Equation 8): C{out} = C{in} (1 - C{target}) + C{target} (1 - A{in}) Where: C{out} is the resulting color in the target buffer. C{in} is the color of the incoming fragment (from the fragment shader, set to Ai). C{target} is the color currently in the target render buffer (the next light buffer). A{in} is the incoming fragment alpha (implicit in the Ai context). Note: The source text defines C1 as incoming fragment color and C0 as color in target buffer for Equation 8, but does not provide the explicit LaTeX formula, only the name. The formula above is derived from the description. Blur Radius (Equation 9): R = \text{blur\angle} d Where: R is the blur radius. d is the sample distance. Parameters: Ai: Indirect attenuation parameters, alpha values for each RGB color channel. Used instead of single alpha A. d: The sample distance, used to calculate blur radius. Blur angle: User-defined parameter scaling the perturbation radius. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Color-Changing Penetration: To achieve effects like white light turning red as it penetrates deeper (similar to holding a flashlight under a hand), set Ai for red smaller than Ai for green and blue. This results in lower attenuation of the red component. Precision: The method relies on 2D buffer resolution matching the viewport to produce crisp shadows with minimal aliasing artifacts. Back-Scattering Ignored: The method approximates scattering by considering only incoming light within a cone in the direction of the light source. Back-scattering is ignored, which may reduce accuracy in dense, deep regions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def incrementallightinginscattering(volumedata, lightcolor, sampledistance, blurangle, numslices, viewportwidth, viewportheight): # Initialize double-buffered light buffers with 1 - lightcolor lightbuffercurrent = [[[1.0 - c for c in lightcolor] for in range(viewportwidth)] for in range(viewportheight)] lightbuffernext = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(viewportwidth)] for in range(viewportheight)] framebuffer = [[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] for in range(viewportwidth)] for in range(viewportheight)] # Generate perturbation texture for blur sampling perturbationoffsets = [(dy, dx) for dy in (-1, 0, 1) for dx in (-1, 0, 1)] for sliceidx in range(numslices): # Pass 1: Eye Contribution for y in range(viewportheight): for x in range(viewportwidth): # Standard volume ray marching and sampling samplecolor = volumedata.getsamplecolor(sliceidx, x, y) samplealpha = volumedata.getsamplealpha(sliceidx, x, y) Ai = lightbuffercurrent[y][x] # Multiply reflective color C by 1 - Ai Ccontrib = [samplecolor[i] (1.0 - Ai[i]) for i in range(3)] # Standard Over operator compositing alphaout = samplealpha + (1.0 - samplealpha) framebuffer[y][x][3] if alphaout > 0: colorout = [ (Ccontrib[i] samplealpha + framebuffer[y][x][i] framebuffer[y][x][3] (1.0 - samplealpha)) / alphaout for i in range(3) ] else: colorout = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] framebuffer[y][x] = colorout + [alphaout] # Pass 2: Light Contribution & Blur for y in range(viewportheight): for x in range(viewportwidth): # Indirect attenuation parameter Ai for this slice Aiparam = volumedata.getindirectattenuation(sliceidx) # Blur radius calculation blurradius = blurangle sampledistance # Sample light buffer with perturbed coordinates blurredattenuation = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] totalweight = 0.0 for dy, dx in perturbationoffsets: py, px = y + dy, x + dx if 0 <= py < viewportheight and 0 <= px < viewportwidth: val = lightbuffercurrent[py][px] w = 1.0 / (1.0 + ((py - y)2 + (px - x)2) / (blurradius2 + 1e-6)) blurredattenuation = [blurredattenuation[i] + val[i] w for i in range(3)] totalweight += w blurredattenuation = [b / totalweight for b in blurredattenuation] # Light Buffer Compositing (Equation 8) Cin = blurredattenuation Ctarget = lightbuffernext[y][x] Cout = [Cin[i] (1.0 - Ctarget[i]) + Ctarget[i] (1.0 - Cin[i]) for i in range(3)] lightbuffernext[y][x] = Cout # Swap buffers for next slice lightbuffercurrent, lightbuffernext = lightbuffernext, lightbuffercurrent return framebuffer Forward-Scattered Intensity Transport is a method for approximating in-scattering (translucency) in volume rendering by propagating light intensity through a volume using a dedicated light buffer. It solves the problem of computing indirect illumination in a single-pass rendering pipeline by discarding backward-directed light relative to the light source, thereby accommodating the lack of knowledge about future slices during a front-to-back traversal. It differs from full scattering models by ignoring back-scattering during the intensity transport phase, which simplifies the hardware implementation at the cost of accuracy in dense, deep regions of the volume. Recursive Slice-Blurring is a single-pass algorithm approximating light scattering within a volume by a recursive slice-blurring operation starting at the light source. At each path increment, energy is transferred from the light buffer to the frame buffer. The profile of the blurring filter is determined by the user-specified phase function. It uses a dual image buffer: one repeatedly blurred (light) buffer for transported/scattered light energy away from the source, and one (frame) buffer for energy headed for the eye, attenuated by densities along the path. Time Complexity: Runs at interactive frame rates when exploiting 3D texture mapping hardware in conjunction with a dual image buffer. Memory Complexity: Requires additional 2D buffers for the light buffer (double-buffered) and perturbation texture. The resolution of light propagation matches the viewport, decoupling it from the 3D data grid. Measured Performance: Runs at interactive frame rates when exploiting 3D texture mapping hardware in conjunction with a dual image buffer. Strengths: Decouples the resolution of light transport from the 3D data grid, permitting accurate lighting of volumes. Produces crisp shadows with minimal aliasing artifacts by matching light propagation resolution to the viewport. Allows control over color-changing penetration effects by specifying independent alpha for each color channel. Limitations: Ignores back-scattering, which may reduce accuracy in dense, deep regions of the volume. Approximates scattering rather than computing it exactly. When to Use: When creating convincing images of clouds and other atmospheric phenomena where translucency effects are important. When interactive frame rates are required and hardware supports 3D texture mapping and dual image buffers. When Not to Use: When high accuracy in dense, deep regions is required and back-scattering effects are significant. The method was described in the context of GPU Gems Chapter 39, "Volume Rendering Techniques". It is an extension of incremental lighting that approximates light scattering by propagating and blurring indirect lighting components from slice to slice. The technique is important for creating convincing images of clouds and other atmospheric phenomena. The high computational cost of direct volume rendering makes it difficult for sequential implementations, but advances in commodity graphics hardware have started to blur these boundaries. The method exploits 3D texture mapping hardware in conjunction with a dual image buffer. name: Forward-Scattered Intensity Transport
head: Light Buffer Intensity Calculation
body: Forward-Scattered Intensity Transport calculates light intensity in a dedicated light buffer by transporting forward-scattered light from slice to slice, discarding backward-directed light to accommodate single-pass rendering. It solves the problem of computing indirect illumination in a single-pass pipeline by ignoring back-scattering during the intensity transport phase, which simplifies hardware implementation at the cost of accuracy in dense, deep volume regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume density \alpha(\vec{s}), light direction \vec{m}{\Omega{lt}}, sampling step size \Delta, and the expected number of scattering events n(\vec{s}) at position \vec{s}. Output: Updated light intensity I(\vec{s} + \vec{m}{\Omega{lt}}\Delta) and the scattering event count for the next slice, stored in the light buffer. Data Structures: 1. Light Buffer: A texture storing two components per sample: the RGB channel holds light intensity I(\vec{s}), and the alpha channel stores the number of scattering events n(\vec{s}f + i\vec{m}\Omega\Delta). 2. Phase Function Texture: Floating-point textures store high-dynamic range multiple scattering phase functions A^{ms}\lambda^i(\Omega) for all particles with up to 26 convolutions at a resolution of approximately 0.18 degrees. The pre-computed forward-scattered factors Fi^\lambda are also stored in this texture, as the light distribution is considered essentially isotropic after 26 convolutions. Parameters: \beta{\lambda ex}: Expected number of scattering events per unit distance for wavelength \lambda. \Delta: Step size between sampling slices. T(\vec{s}1, \vec{s}2): Transmittance from \vec{s}1 to \vec{s}2. Method Steps: 1. Calculate Forward-Scattered Contribution (Fi^\lambda): For each scattering event i, compute the integral of the phase function over the forward hemisphere relative to the light direction, discarding backward-directed light to ensure single-pass compatibility. Fi^\lambda = \int{\text{forward hemisphere}} A^{ms}\lambda^i(\Omega) d\Omega \quad (23) These values are pre-computed and stored in the phase function texture. 2. Retrieve Current State: Sample the light buffer at the previous slice position \vec{s} to retrieve the current intensity I(\vec{s}) and the accumulated scattering count n(\vec{s}). 3. Compute Transmittance: Calculate the transmittance T(\vec{s}, \vec{s} + \vec{m}{\Omega{lt}}\Delta) from the current sample to the next sample along the light direction. 4. Update Intensity (Hardware-Efficient Approximation): The exact discrete intensity update involves a product over the range of scattering events, which is impractical for graphics hardware. Instead, use the worst-case attenuation approximation using a single convolution index to avoid linear interpolation of floating-point textures, which was unavailable on the target hardware. I(\vec{s} + \vec{m}{\Omega{lt}}\Delta) = I(\vec{s})T(\vec{s}, \vec{s} + \vec{m}{\Omega{lt}}\Delta) + I(\vec{s})(1 - T(\vec{s}, \vec{s} + \vec{m}{\Omega{lt}}\Delta)) \alpha(\vec{s}) F{\lfloor n(\vec{s}) + 1 + \beta{\lambda ex}\Delta \rfloor}^\lambda \quad (25) Where \alpha(\vec{s}) is the density/scattering coefficient at \vec{s}, and the index \lfloor n(\vec{s}) + 1 + \beta{\lambda ex}\Delta \rfloor determines which pre-computed F factor to use. 5. Update Scattering Count: Increment the scattering event count for the next slice by the expected number of scattering events over the step \Delta. 6. Store Results: Write the new intensity I(\vec{s} + \vec{m}{\Omega{lt}}\Delta) to the RGB channel and the new scattering count to the Alpha channel of the light buffer at the next slice position. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def forwardscatteredintensitytransport( lightbuffer, phasefunctiontexture, currentpos, lightdirection, stepsize, betalambdaex, alphadensity): """ Updates light intensity and scattering count for the next slice. Args: lightbuffer: Texture containing intensity (RGB) and scattering count (A). phasefunctiontexture: Texture containing pre-computed F factors. currentpos: Current sample position vector. lightdirection: Normalized vector pointing towards the light source. stepsize: Distance to the next sample. betalambdaex: Expected scattering events per unit distance. alphadensity: Density/scattering coefficient at currentpos. Returns: nextintensity: Float, the updated light intensity. nextscatteringcount: Int, the updated number of scattering events. """ # 1. Retrieve current state from light buffer currentintensity = lightbuffer.sample(currentpos).rgb currentscatteringcount = lightbuffer.sample(currentpos).a # 2. Calculate next position nextpos = currentpos + lightdirection stepsize # 3. Compute transmittance (standard exponential attenuation) transmittance = math.exp(-alphadensity stepsize) # 4. Determine the index for the F factor (Equation 25) findex = math.floor(currentscatteringcount + 1.0 + betalambdaex stepsize) # 5. Retrieve the pre-computed forward-scattered factor Fi^lambda ffactor = phasefunctiontexture.sampleffactor(findex) # 6. Apply the intensity update formula (Equation 25) nextintensity = ( currentintensity transmittance + currentintensity (1.0 - transmittance) alphadensity ffactor) # 7. Update scattering count nextscatteringcount = currentscatteringcount + math.floor(betalambdaex stepsize) return nextintensity, nextscatteringcount Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Linear Interpolation: Linear interpolation is not available for floating-point textures on the target hardware, necessitating the worst-case attenuation approximation (Equation 25) instead of interpolating between scattering events. Backward Light: Backward-directed light is discarded during intensity transport because phase functions have weak back-scattered components and the system performs a single slicing pass without knowledge of future slices. This approximation introduces errors that increase with the number of scattering events, making it least accurate in dense inner regions of the cloud. Final Gather: While backward light is discarded during transport, light may still be backscattered towards the eye in the final gather step, where the angular distribution function for one more scattering event is applied. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of sampling slices along the ray, as the method performs a single pass through the volume. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the light buffer (intensity + scattering count) and the phase function texture (high-dynamic range, up to 26 convolutions). Performance: The method achieves real-time performance (e.g., 3.0 fps for 512×512 resolution with 256 sampling planes) on the target hardware. Strengths: Enables single-pass rendering of atmospheric phenomena (rainbows, halos, glory, aerial perspective) with reasonable accuracy in optically thin regions and for the first few scattering events. Limitations: Accuracy degrades in dense, deep regions of the volume due to the approximation of backward light and the use of worst-case attenuation, with error increasing alongside the number of scattering events. Forward-Scattered Intensity Transport was introduced in "Efficient Rendering of Atmospheric Phenomena". It is part of a system designed to capture essential optical effects in the atmosphere, such as rainbows, halos, the glory, and sunrise/sunset effects. The method was developed to address the limitations of previous techniques in handling multiple scattering and angular distribution efficiently on graphics hardware. name: Hardware Blending Recurrence Evaluation
head: Frame buffer read back blending
body: Hardware Blending Recurrence Evaluation is a technique for evaluating the multiple forward scattering recurrence Ik = g{k-1} + T{k-1} I{k-1} by mapping the mathematical operation to GPU hardware blending and pixel read-back operations. It computes the incident light on each particle in a participating medium by using the frame buffer as an accumulator. It differs from Incremental Lighting for In-Scattering by explicitly reading back pixel values to resolve the recurrence dependency. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of particles P, each with extinction \tauk, albedo ak, radius rk, and position. Light direction \mathbf{l} and light color/intensity. Outputs: The scattered light contribution c for each particle, which is then rendered toward the eye. Data Structures: Frame Buffer: Stores the accumulated incident light intensity I. Initialized to white (representing I0 = 1). Particle List: Sorted by distance to the light source for the preprocessing pass. Parameters: Source Blend Factor (f{src}): 1. Destination Blend Factor (f{dest}): T{k-1} = \exp(-\tau{k-1}) (transparency of the previous particle). Texture/Fragment Mode: Modulate. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Illumination Pass): 1. Clear the frame buffer to white. This represents the initial incident light I0. 2. Sort particles pk by increasing distance to the light source. 3. For each particle pk in sorted order: a. Read Back: Read the pixel color x at the projection of the particle's center from the frame buffer. This value represents I{k-1}, the incident light on the previous particle. b. Compute Incident Light: Calculate Ik = \text{color}(x) \times \text{light\color}. This is the light incident on the current particle pk. c. Compute Scattered Color: Calculate the scattered light contribution g{k-1} using the formula: c = ak \cdot \tauk \cdot Ik / 4\pi where ak is albedo, \tauk is extinction, and Ik is incident light. d. Set Render Parameters: Set the particle's alpha to 1 - \exp(-\tauk). Set the particle's color to c. e. Render and Blend: Render the particle. The hardware blending equation is: c{result} = f{src} \cdot c{src} + f{dest} \cdot c{dest} Substituting the parameters: Ik = 1 \cdot g{k-1} + T{k-1} \cdot I{k-1} Here, c{src} is the particle's color (g{k-1}), c{dest} is the frame buffer value (I{k-1}), f{src}=1, and f{dest}=T{k-1}. This updates the frame buffer to store Ik for the next particle. 2. Runtime (Eye Scattering Pass): 1. Sort particles by decreasing distance from the eye. 2. For each particle, compute the scattering toward the eye using the precomputed Ik and the phase function phase(\omega, \mathbf{l}), where \omega is the direction to the viewer. 3. Render particles with standard compositing using the precomputed illumination. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def hardwareblendingrecurrence(particles, lightposition, lightcolor, eyeposition): # Preprocessing pass framebuffer = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] # I0 = white particlessortedlight = sorted(particles, key=lambda p: distance(p.position, lightposition)) Tprev = 1.0 # T{-1} = 1 for p in particlessortedlight: # a. Read back incident light from previous particle Iprev = framebuffer[:] # b. Compute incident light on current particle Ik = [Iprev[j] lightcolor[j] for j in range(3)] # c. Compute scattered light contribution scattered = [p.albedo p.extinction Ik[j] / (4 math.pi) for j in range(3)] # Apply phase function for direction from light omega = [-lightdirection[j] for j in range(3)] scattered = [scattered[j] phasefunction(omega, lightdirection) for j in range(3)] # d. Set render parameters alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-p.extinction) # e. Render with hardware blending # Hardware blending computes: result = 1 scattered + Tprev Iprev renderparticle(p.position, p.radius, scattered, alpha, srcfactor=1.0, dstfactor=Tprev) # Update frame buffer to reflect hardware blending result framebuffer = [scattered[j] + Tprev Iprev[j] for j in range(3)] # Update Tprev for next iteration Tprev = math.exp(-p.extinction) # Runtime pass particlessortedeye = sorted(particles, key=lambda p: -distance(p.position, eyeposition)) for p in particlessortedeye: omega = normalize(eyeposition - p.position) finalcolor = [p.precomputedcolor[j] phasefunction(omega, lightdirection) for j in range(3)] renderparticle(p.position, p.radius, finalcolor, alpha, srcfactor=1.0, dstfactor=0.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision in the frame buffer may accumulate errors over many particles. Boundary Conditions: The frame buffer must be cleared to the correct initial value (I0) before each pass. Time Complexity: O(N) particles, requiring N pixel read-back operations during preprocessing. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory beyond the frame buffer and particle list. Strengths: Conceptually simple mapping of the recurrence to hardware blending. Limitations: Pixel read-back introduces synchronization overhead. When to use: Suitable for real-time implementations where the recurrence must be resolved per particle. The method was presented in the paper "Real-Time Cloud Rendering" by Dobashi et al. (2001). It was developed to efficiently handle multiple forward scattering in cloud rendering by leveraging existing GPU hardware features. The technique is specific to the context of particle-based cloud rendering and relies on the specific recurrence relation for forward scattering. name: Intermixing
body: Intermixing is a technique for rendering multi-channel volume data by separately evaluating the illumination model for each channel at every ray sample and combining the results during the accumulation phase. It distinguishes itself from image-level compositing by correctly handling occlusions between different channels, as it retains depth information that image-level blending discards. It is more flexible than other approaches but computationally more expensive. Inputs: A sequence of ray samples sorted front-to-back, where each sample i contains color and opacity values for N distinct channels. Background color C{bg}. Outputs: Final pixel color C{final}. Data Structures: Accumulators C{acc} (vec3, initialized to 0) and \alpha{acc} (float, initialized to 0). Transmittance T (float, initialized to 1.0). Algorithm: The standard front-to-back compositing loop is extended to handle multiple channels at the same spatial position. For each sample i along the ray: 1. Initialize transmittance T \leftarrow 1.0 before the sample loop. 2. For each channel k from 1 to N: a. Evaluate the illumination model for channel k at the current sample position to obtain c{i,k} and \alpha{i,k}. b. Update the global color accumulator using the channel's contribution scaled by the incoming transmittance: C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + T \cdot \alpha{i,k} \cdot c{i,k} c. Compute the combined transmittance for the current sample by multiplying the individual channel transmittances: T{sample} \leftarrow T{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{i,k}) 3. Update the global opacity accumulator and transmittance for the next sample using the combined sample transmittance: \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + T \cdot (1 - T{sample}) T \leftarrow T \cdot T{sample} 4. If \alpha{acc} \ge 1.0, terminate early (early ray termination). 5. After processing all samples, composite over the background: C{final} = C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot C{bg} Pitfalls: Image-level intermixing failure: Rendering a complete image for each channel and mixing them using alpha blending fails to handle occlusions between different channels correctly because depth information is lost in the accumulated intermediate results. Performance: Intermixing is computationally more expensive than single-channel rendering or image-level compositing because the illumination model must be evaluated separately for each channel at every sample. Hardware Limits: In implementations relying on GPU texture formats (e.g., Brix et al. [BPH14]), the number of channels N is often limited to 4 due to the 4-component limit of standard texture formats. def intermixingloop(samples, backgroundcolor): """ Accumulation-level intermixing for multi-channel volume rendering. samples: list of lists of tuples. samples[i] contains N tuples of (color: vec3, opacity: float). backgroundcolor: vec3 for the scene background. """ Cacc = vec3(0.0) alphaacc = 0.0 T = 1.0 for samplechannels in samples: Tsample = 1.0 for ck, alphak in samplechannels: Cacc = Cacc + T alphak ck Tsample = Tsample (1.0 - alphak) alphaacc = alphaacc + T (1.0 - Tsample) T = T Tsample if alphaacc >= 1.0: break return Cacc + (1.0 - alphaacc) backgroundcolor Multi-volume rendering refers to the simultaneous rendering of multiple co-registered volumes by evaluating samples along a viewing ray for all visible channels. It is distinguished from single-volume rendering by its ability to intermix data sources, and from image-level compositing by its preservation of depth ordering through per-sample combination. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Intermixing is more flexible than other approaches but computationally more expensive. Strengths: Correctly handles occlusions between different channels; preserves depth ordering. Limitations: Higher computational cost; potential hardware limits on channel count (e.g., N \le 4 in some GPU-based implementations). Intermixing, specifically accumulation-level intermixing, was presented by Brix et al. in 2014 [BPH14] as part of an out-of-core rendering approach for multi-channel volume data sets. It builds on Crassin et al.’s octree-based memory virtualization scheme [CNLE09]. The method is used in systems such as Voreen [DLJL22], Viv [MGP+22], and Neuroglancer [Goo22]. name: Multi-volume rendering
head: Multiple Volume Display
body: Multi-volume rendering refers to rendering multiple co-registered volumes at once by evaluating each sample along a viewing ray for all channels currently visible. It enables the simultaneous display of multiple deformed volumes using standard proxy geometries. It is distinguished from single-volume rendering by its ability to intermix data sources, and from image-level compositing by its preservation of depth ordering through per-sample combination. Multi-volume rendering operates by passing multiple volume textures to the fragment shader and combining their contributions during the ray-marching process. The method is categorized into three intermixing levels based on when the combination occurs: classification-level, accumulation-level, and image-level. Inputs: N co-registered volume textures V1, \dots, VN. A viewing ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Outputs: A final pixel color and opacity. Volume Textures: N 3D textures (or proxy geometry textures) storing the scalar fields. Ray Sample State: At each step t along the ray, the method retrieves values vi = \text{sample}(Vi, \mathbf{r}(t)) for all i \in \{1, \dots, N\}. 1. Classification-Level Intermixing: At each ray sample, the sampled values of two channels are linearly interpolated using a weighting factor \omega (e.g., \omega = 0.5) before evaluating an illumination model using the interpolation result. 2. Accumulation-Level Intermixing: The illumination model is separately evaluated for each channel at each ray sample and then the results are combined. Fragment shaders compute emissions and absorptions based on combination strategies such as sum, difference, or emitted color mixing. 3. Image-Level Intermixing: A complete image is rendered for each channel and the results are mixed using alpha blending. Two co-located volumes are rendered separately as scalar datasets and then blended into a final image using a weighting function that may include the z-buffer or opacity channel. Depth Ordering: Image-level intermixing cannot handle occlusions between different channels correctly due to missing depth information in the accumulated intermediate results. Proxy Geometry Overlap: Proxy geometry samples cannot overlap; techniques adapting tessellation based on deformation must find a tessellation satisfying all volumes. Performance: Accumulation-level intermixing is more flexible but computationally more expensive than classification-level. Implementation Limits: In out-of-core approaches using octrees, the number of channels n stored in brick-cache entries is implementation-defined and cannot be changed at run-time. Combines raw data values using a weighting factor (e.g., \omega=0.5) before evaluating the illumination model. Not given in the sources. Accumulation-level intermixing is a multi-modal volume rendering technique that resolves the depth-ordering artifacts inherent in image-level intermixing by combining ray samples from multiple co-registered volumes at every step along the viewing ray. Unlike image-level compositing, which blends final pixel colors and thus fails to preserve the correct occlusion relationships between distinct datasets, this method integrates physical properties (colors and opacities) from each volume's sample before the final accumulation, ensuring that the relative density and opacity of the constituent volumes are correctly composited. It is distinguished from its sibling Illumination model level intermixing by applying separate lighting models to each volume's sample before combination, whereas illumination-level intermixing merges raw data values prior to any lighting calculation. A multi-modal rendering technique where two co-located volumes are rendered separately as scalar datasets and then blended into a final image using a weighting function that may include the z-buffer or opacity channel. Depth ordering is not preserved, resulting in limited practical value for visualizing complex interactions between volumes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing N volume textures or proxy geometry textures. In out-of-core octree approaches, brick caches must store n channels per entry. Strengths: Allows visualization of multi-modal data; accumulation-level preserves depth cues. Limitations: Image-level lacks depth accuracy; accumulation-level is expensive; proxy geometry requires consistent tessellation for deformed volumes. When to use: Not given in the sources. Multi-volume rendering was formalized by Schubert and Scholl [SS11], who differentiated between classification, accumulation, and image-level intermixing. Brix et al. [BPH14] extended this to out-of-core rendering using octrees, storing up to n channels per brick. The concept of "Multiple Volume Display" using proxy geometries was explored by to handle deformed volumes. The Stony Brook overview provides a foundational classification of these mixing techniques.
