name: Attenuated Maximum-Intensity Projection
body: Attenuated Maximum-Intensity Projection (AMIP) is a CPU-emulated volume rendering technique that enhances the visibility of high-intensity structures by suppressing background noise and weaker signals that typically obscure details in standard Maximum-Intensity Projection (MIP). Unlike standard MIP, which simply selects the highest intensity value along a ray regardless of depth, AMIP weights samples by an exponential falloff based on the accumulated intensity encountered so far, ensuring that only strong, isolated peaks survive while dimmer, deeper contributions are attenuated. This method prevents background haze from bleeding over everything by dimming deeper or weaker samples. Inputs: volume: A 3D array of shape (nx, ny, nz) containing float32 voxel values. The data must be display-scaled and free of NaN values. origin: A length-3 tuple (ox, oy, oz) representing the world-space coordinates of the voxel at index (0, 0, 0). spacing: A length-3 tuple (sx, sy, sz) representing the physical size of each voxel along each axis. If any component is < 10^{-12}, it is replaced with 1.0. nearpts, farpts: Arrays of shape (H, W, 3) containing the world-space entry and exit points of the ray for each pixel in the output image of height H and width W. valuerange: A tuple (lo, hi) defining the contrast window for normalization. attenuation: A float coefficient controlling the strength of the exponential falloff. Default is 0.05. nsamples: An integer specifying the number of samples taken along each ray. Default is 256. colormap: A string specifying the colormap name. If None, grayscale is used. Outputs: outrgb: An (H, W, 3) uint8 array representing the final rendered image. outval: An array of shape (H, W) initialized to -\infty, storing the running maximum attenuated intensity for each pixel. acc: An array of shape (H, W) initialized to 0.0, storing the sum of normalized intensities encountered along each ray. invspan: A scalar calculated as 1.0 / (hi - lo). If hi \le lo, hi is set to lo + 1.0 to prevent division by zero. 1. Initialization: Initialize outval with -\infty and acc with 0.0. 2. Ray Parameterization: For each sample index s from 0 to n{samples}-1: Calculate the normalized depth parameter t: t = \begin{cases} \frac{s}{n{samples} - 1} & \text{if } n{samples} > 1 \\ 0.0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Calculate the world-space point P along the ray: P = P{near} + (P{far} - P{near}) \cdot t where P{near} and P{far} are the near and far points for the current pixel. 3. Voxel Indexing: Convert world point P to continuous voxel coordinates (fx, fy, fz): fx = \frac{Px - ox}{sx}, \quad fy = \frac{Py - oy}{sy}, \quad fz = \frac{Pz - oz}{sz} Determine valid voxels where 0 \le fx \le nx-1, 0 \le fy \le ny-1, and 0 \le fz \le nz-1. 4. Trilinear Interpolation: For valid voxels, compute integer floor (x0, y0, z0) and ceiling (x1, y1, z1) coordinates, clamped to the volume dimensions. Compute fractional parts dx = fx - x0, dy = fy - y0, dz = fz - z0. Perform trilinear interpolation of the 8 surrounding voxels: \begin{aligned} c{00} &= V(x0, y0, z0)(1-dx) + V(x1, y0, z0)dx \\ c{10} &= V(x0, y1, z0)(1-dx) + V(x1, y1, z0)dx \\ c{01} &= V(x0, y0, z1)(1-dx) + V(x1, y0, z1)dx \\ c{11} &= V(x0, y1, z1)(1-dx) + V(x1, y1, z1)dx \\ c0 &= c{00}(1-dy) + c{10}dy \\ c1 &= c{01}(1-dy) + c{11}dy \\ V{interp} &= c0(1-dz) + c1dz \end{aligned} where V(x,y,z) is the voxel value at integer coordinates. 5. Normalization: Normalize the interpolated value to [0, 1]: nval = \text{clip}\left( (V{interp} - lo) \cdot inv\span, 0.0, 1.0 \right) For invalid voxels, the normalized value is set to 0.0 so it does not contribute to accumulation or candidate calculation. 6. Weighting and Accumulation: Calculate the attenuation weight: w = e^{-\text{attenuation} \cdot acc} Calculate the candidate value: cand = \begin{cases} nval \cdot w & \text{for valid voxels} \\ -\infty & \text{for invalid voxels} \end{cases} Update the running maximum for the pixel: out\val = \max(out\val, cand) Update the intensity accumulator: acc = acc + nval. 7. Post-processing: Normalize the output: norm = \text{clip}\left( \text{where}(\text{isfinite}(out\val), out\val, 0.0), 0.0, 1.0 \right) Map to 8-bit index: idx = \text{clip}\left( \text{int32}(norm \cdot 255.0), 0, 255 \right) Lookup colors from the colormap using idx. If no colormap is specified, use grayscale [norm, norm, norm]. Convert to uint8 RGB. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def attenuatedmip(volume, origin, spacing, nearpts, farpts, valuerange, attenuation=0.05, nsamples=256, colormap=None): """ Attenuated Maximum-Intensity Projection rendering. Args: volume: (nx, ny, nz) float32 array. origin: (ox, oy, oz) tuple. spacing: (sx, sy, sz) tuple. nearpts: (H, W, 3) float array. farpts: (H, W, 3) float array. valuerange: (lo, hi) tuple. attenuation: float. nsamples: int. colormap: str or None. Returns: outrgb: (H, W, 3) uint8 array. """ H, W = nearpts.shape[:2] nx, ny, nz = volume.shape # Initialize output arrays outval = np.full((H, W), -np.inf) acc = np.zeros((H, W)) # Per-pixel accumulator # Handle value range lo, hi = valuerange if hi <= lo: hi = lo + 1.0 invspan = 1.0 / (hi - lo) # Handle spacing sx, sy, sz = spacing if sx < 1e-12: sx = 1.0 if sy < 1e-12: sy = 1.0 if sz < 1e-12: sz = 1.0 ox, oy, oz = origin # Loop over samples for s in range(nsamples): # Calculate t if nsamples > 1: t = s / (nsamples - 1) else: t = 0.0 # Calculate world point P for all pixels P = nearpts + (farpts - nearpts) t # Convert to voxel coordinates fx = (P[:,:, 0] - ox) / sx fy = (P[:,:, 1] - oy) / sy fz = (P[:,:, 2] - oz) / sz # Determine valid voxels (0 <= coord <= maxindex) valid = (fx >= 0) & (fx <= nx - 1) & \ (fy >= 0) & (fy <= ny - 1) & \ (fz >= 0) & (fz <= nz - 1) if not np.any(valid): continue # Integer coordinates x0 = np.floor(fx).astype(np.int32) y0 = np.floor(fy).astype(np.int32) z0 = np.floor(fz).astype(np.int32) x1 = np.minimum(x0 + 1, nx - 1) y1 = np.minimum(y0 + 1, ny - 1) z1 = np.minimum(z0 + 1, nz - 1) # Fractional parts dx = fx - x0 dy = fy - y0 dz = fz - z0 # Trilinear interpolation v000 = volume[x0, y0, z0] v100 = volume[x1, y0, z0] v010 = volume[x0, y1, z0] v110 = volume[x1, y1, z0] v001 = volume[x0, y0, z1] v101 = volume[x1, y0, z1] v011 = volume[x0, y1, z1] v111 = volume[x1, y1, z1] c00 = v000 (1 - dx) + v100 dx c10 = v010 (1 - dx) + v110 dx c01 = v001 (1 - dx) + v101 dx c11 = v011 (1 - dx) + v111 dx c0 = c00 (1 - dy) + c10 dy c1 = c01 (1 - dy) + c11 dy interp = c0 (1 - dz) + c1 dz # Normalize nval = np.clip((interp - lo) invspan, 0.0, 1.0) # Invalidate contribution for out-of-bounds voxels nval[~valid] = 0.0 # Calculate weight based on per-pixel accumulator weight = np.exp(-attenuation acc) # Candidate value: valid voxels contribute, invalid get -inf cand = np.where(valid, nval weight, -np.inf) # Update running maximum outval = np.maximum(outval, cand) # Update accumulator acc += nval # Post-processing norm = np.clip(np.where(np.isfinite(outval), outval, 0.0), 0.0, 1.0) idx = np.clip((norm 255.0).astype(np.int32), 0, 255) # Colormap lookup if colormap is None: outrgb = np.stack([norm, norm, norm], axis=-1) else: cmaprgb = cmaprgb(colormap) # Standard colormap table resolution outrgb = cmaprgb[idx] return outrgb.astype(np.uint8) def cmaprgb(name): """Resolve colormap name to a (256, 3) uint8 array.""" # Standard implementation placeholder for colormap resolution return np.zeros((256, 3), dtype=np.uint8) attenuation: Default 0.05. nsamples: Default 256. Division by Zero: If hi \le lo in valuerange, hi is set to lo + 1.0. Zero Spacing: If any axis spacing is < 10^{-12}, it is replaced with 1.0. NaN Values: The input volume must be NaN-free. Accumulator Scope: The source describes acc as a single variable, but physically it must be per-pixel to correctly attenuate rays independently. Time Complexity: O(H \cdot W \cdot n{samples}), where H and W are image dimensions and n{samples} is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) for the output arrays outval and acc. Strengths: Effectively suppresses background noise and haze, highlighting strong intensity peaks. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than standard MIP due to the accumulation and weighting step. When to Use: When visualizing dense volumes where background haze would otherwise bleed over everything. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and background haze is not a significant issue. Attenuated Maximum-Intensity Projection is described as a CPU-emulated rendering technique in the context of the voxel library. It is designed to improve upon standard MIP by introducing an attenuation factor based on accumulated intensity. stacy-zhang/voxel, https://github.com/stacy-zhang/voxel, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Projected Slabs Approximation
head: Parallel projected slabs, Perspective Baseplane Blending, Projected Slabs Approximation for Perspective Volume Rendering, Slab approximation
body: Projected Slabs Approximation is a technique that approximates perspective volume rendering by rendering slabs using parallel volume rendering hardware and blending the slab images perspectively on the graphics card. It enables acceleration on hardware designed for parallel projection by introducing an analytical error bound. The method approximates the perspective viewing frustum as a sequence of parallel slabs. The core inputs are the volume dataset, the camera position, and the view direction. The output is a rendered image. 1. Slab Decomposition: The volume is divided into slabs perpendicular to the view direction. For perspective projection, these slabs are not equidistant in depth but are chosen to bound the approximation error. For best quality, all slabs must be parallel to the image plane. Slab thicknesses are selected to trade off between quality (with a large number of thin slabs) and speed (with a small number of thick slabs). 2. Parallel Projection Approximation: Each slab is rendered using parallel projection techniques. 3. Error Analysis: An analytical study of the maximum and average error is performed to determine the optimal slab thickness and distribution. 4. Compositing: The results from the parallel projected slabs are composited together. The standard front-to-back compositing equation from the parent Projection and MIP Techniques is applied to the samples derived from these slabs. The approximation error is bounded by adjusting the slab boundaries based on the analytical error model. The improvement increases frame rate while keeping the global maximum error bounded. Pseudocode for the error-bounded slab selection and rendering: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projectedslabsapproximation(volumedata, camerapos, viewdir, imageplane, maxerrorthreshold): # 1. Cut volume into slabs parallel to the image plane slabs = [] currentdepth = 0.0 slabthickness = 32.0 # Cube-4/VolumePro requires borders to be multiples of 32 voxels while currentdepth < volumedepth: # Analytical study of maximum and average error bounds global maximum error # The specific analytical formula is not given in the sources # error = estimateperspectiveapproximationerror(...) # Not given in the sources if error > maxerrorthreshold: slabthickness = 0.5 # Reduce thickness to bound error slabs.append({'depth': currentdepth, 'thickness': slabthickness}) currentdepth += slabthickness # 2. Render each slab using parallel projection techniques slabresults = [] for slab in slabs: # Standard front-to-back compositing for the slab subvolume # generateraysthroughslab is not given in the sources for ray in generateraysthroughslab(slab, imageplane): cacc = vec3(0.0) alphaacc = 0.0 for sample in volumedata.traceray(ray, slab): transmittance = 1.0 - alphaacc cacc = cacc + transmittance sample.alpha sample.color alphaacc = alphaacc + transmittance sample.alpha if alphaacc >= 1.0: break slabresults.append(cacc) # 3. Blend the slab images perspectively on the graphics card # perspectiveblendsamples is not given in the sources # 4. Interlace and blend the slab images together to form the final image # interlaceandblend is not given in the sources return finalimage A method for performing perspective volume rendering on hardware originally designed for parallel projection, such as the Cube-4/VolumePro architecture. It sets itself apart from Projected Slabs Approximation by relying on hardware texture mapping for perspective correction rather than analytical error bounds for parallel projection approximation. It is chosen when hardware supports efficient texture-based perspective scaling. Perspective Slab Rendering via Texture Mapping A tool for out-of-core data processing where a consecutive series of data is gathered into an orthographic projection. It is used in conjunction with a slab-projected kd-tree partitioning to find partitions using nonempty voxel information represented by a series of slab-projection slices. It is chosen when memory constraints require processing large volumes that exceed free memory on rendering hardware or CPU main memory. The method enables acceleration on hardware designed for parallel projection. It increases frame rate while keeping the global maximum error bounded. Slab thicknesses are selected to trade off between quality (with a large number of thin slabs) and speed (with a small number of thick slabs). The exact time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. The method was introduced in 2001 for virtual endoscopy, a medical application where perspective projection is mandatory. It was applied to the VolumePro 500 hardware. The work focused on investigating the introduced error and improving the basic algorithm based on error analysis. name: Perspective Slab Rendering via Texture Mapping
head: Cube-4/VolumePro Perspective Rendering via Slabbing
body: Perspective Slab Rendering via Texture Mapping is a method for performing perspective volume rendering on hardware originally designed for parallel projection, such as the Cube-4/VolumePro architecture. It solves the problem of perspective distortion in volume data by partitioning the volume into slabs and using graphics card texture mapping to handle the perspective scaling of each slab individually. It sets itself apart from its sibling, Projected Slabs Approximation, by relying on hardware texture mapping for perspective correction rather than analytical error bounds for parallel projection approximation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset, a perspective camera definition, and a partitioning strategy for slabs. Output: A final composited image in the framebuffer. Data Structures: Slab: A subset of volume slices aligned either along a major volume axis or parallel to the image plane. Slab Image: A 2D RGB image rendered from the slab data. Geometry Plane: A polygon used to map the slab image onto the screen. Steps: 1. Partition Volume: Divide the volume into slabs of slices. Alignment is chosen along a major volume axis or parallel to the image plane. 2. Render Slab Images: For each slab, compute the RGB slab image. This step typically involves volume rendering techniques suitable for the hardware. 3. Perspective Scaling via Texture Mapping: Map each computed slab image onto a geometry plane using the graphics card's texture mapping unit. The texture mapping handles the perspective scaling required for that specific slab. 4. Depth Positioning: Set the depth position of each slab's geometry plane to the center of the slab it represents. 5. Compositing: Draw the slab images from back to front. Blend them into the framebuffer using channel compositing. Parameters: Slab Thickness: Determines the number of slabs. Thinner slabs reduce perspective distortion but increase rendering cost. A large number of thin slabs are required when perspective distortion is great. Number of Planes (for artifact elimination): The number of geometric planes used to map a single slab image to reduce artifacts at oblique angles. Pitfalls: Perspective Distortion: If slabs are too thick, significant perspective distortion artifacts occur, especially at oblique viewing angles. Fill Rate: Using multiple planes for artifact elimination increases texture mapping fill rate on the geometry processing side. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def perspectiveslabrendering(volume, camera, slabthickness): # Partition volume into slabs slabs = partitionvolume(volume, slabthickness) # Sort slabs back-to-front relative to camera slabs = sortbacktofront(slabs, camera) # Initialize framebuffer framebuffer = initializeframebuffer() for slab in slabs: # Render slab image slabimage = renderslabimage(slab) # Determine geometry plane for texture mapping # Depth is set to the center of the slab plane = creategeometryplane(slab.center, slab.imageplane) # Apply perspective scaling via texture mapping # The hardware handles the perspective projection mappedimage = texturemap(slabimage, plane, camera) # Composite into framebuffer framebuffer = channelcomposite(framebuffer, mappedimage) return framebuffer A method to eliminate artifacts caused by viewing slabs at oblique angles (where adjacent slabs project more than one pixel apart) by texture mapping the slab image onto multiple geometric planes, without increasing the burden on the volume rendering hardware. It reduces the values of the computed RGB slab image and modifies the values of the slab polygon during texture mapping to compensate for the reduced image values. The tradeoffs are evaluated based on ultimate frame rate to determine both slab thickness and the number of planes for texture mapping. This technique increases texture mapping fill rate on the geometry processing side, but is only used when slabs are more oblique so that slab images project to smaller areas on the screen. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of slabs and pixels per slab. The number of slabs is inversely proportional to slab thickness. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the volume size and slab count. Performance: Achieves real-time performance on specialized hardware like Cube-4/VolumePro. Strengths: Enables perspective rendering on parallel projection hardware; leverages hardware texture mapping for efficiency. Limitations: Requires many thin slabs for high perspective accuracy, increasing fill rate; artifacts at oblique angles if not mitigated. When to Use: When perspective volume rendering is needed on hardware with strong texture mapping capabilities but limited perspective volume rendering support. When Not to Use: When high accuracy at extreme oblique angles is required without the overhead of multi-plane mapping; when hardware lacks efficient texture mapping. This method is associated with the Cube-4/VolumePro hardware and the CTK (CtK) software framework. It was developed to enable perspective volume rendering on hardware originally designed for parallel projection, addressing the limitations of parallel projection approximations in perspective scenarios. It is used in applications such as virtual colonoscopy, where real-time navigation and high-resolution volume rendering are critical. name: Minimum Intensity Projection
head: Intensity Projection (MinIP), min intensity projection
body: Minimum Intensity Projection (MinIP) is a volume rendering technique that projects the lowest intensity value encountered along each viewing ray to the two-dimensional image plane. Unlike standard front-to-back compositing which blends all samples based on opacity, MinIP discards all but the single minimum sample, effectively highlighting low-density or dark structures such as air-filled spaces, bronchi, or hypodense ducts against brighter surrounding tissue. It serves as the inverse counterpart to Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP). MinIP operates as a raycasting projection mode that searches for the global minimum scalar value along the ray path. It does not use the standard optical compositing model (transmittance/opacity accumulation) because it selects a single voxel rather than blending a volume. Inputs: volume: 3D scalar field (texture). startcoord: Ray origin in texture coordinates. stepcoord: Ray step vector in texture coordinates. nsteps: Number of discrete samples along the ray. sizef: Volume dimensions (width, height, depth) used for coordinate normalization. umaterial: Material properties including opacity multiplier and color space setting. Outputs: outcolor: Final pixel color (RGB) and opacity (A). out.coord: The 3D texture coordinate of the minimum voxel. out.depth: The normalized device coordinate (NDC) depth (z/w) for the minimum voxel. The algorithm maintains three state variables during the ray traversal: 1. theref: The minimum intensity value found so far (scalar). 2. thecoord: The 3D texture coordinate corresponding to theref (vec3). 3. thevalue: The full sample data (e.g., RGBA vec4) at thecoord. 1. Initialization: Set theref to positive infinity (or a sufficiently large value, e.g., 999999.0). Set thecoord to startcoord. Initialize thevalue to zero. 2. Primary Coarse Search: Iterate iter from 0 to nsteps - 1: Calculate sample coordinate: coord = start\coord + iter \cdot step\coord. Sample the volume: value = \text{sample\vol}(coord, sizef). Extract scalar reference: reff = value.r (assuming scalar is stored in the red channel). Update minimum: If reff < the\ref, update the\ref = reff, the\coord = coord, and the\value = value. 3. Refinement Loop: To improve positional accuracy of the minimum, perform a binary search-like refinement: Initialize substepcoord = stepcoord. Iterate iter2 from 0 to 3 (4 iterations): Halve the step: substep\coord = substep\coord \cdot 0.5. Define candidate coordinates: coord1 = the\coord - substep\coord and coord2 = the\coord + substep\coord. Sample candidates: value1 = \text{sample\vol}(coord1, sizef) and value2 = \text{sample\vol}(coord2, sizef). Extract references: ref1 = value1.r and ref2 = value2.r. Update minimum: If ref1 \le the\ref, update state with ref1, coord1, value1. Else if ref2 > the\ref, update state with ref2, coord2, value2. 4. Color Mapping: Map the scalar value to color: color = \text{sampled\value\to\color}(the\value). Convert to physical (linear) color space: If colorspace is 'srgb': physical\color = \text{srgb2physical}(color.rgb). Else: physical\color = color.rgb. Calculate final opacity: opacity = color.a \cdot u\material.opacity. Set output color: out\color = vec4(physical\color, opacity). 5. Depth and Coordinate Output: Convert texture coordinate to data position: data\pos = the\coord \cdot sizef - vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5). Transform to world space: world\pos = u\wobject.world\transform \cdot vec4(data\pos, 1.0). Transform to NDC: ndc\pos = u\stdinfo.projection\transform \cdot u\stdinfo.cam\transform \cdot world\pos. Set output depth: out.depth = ndc\pos.z / ndc\pos.w. Set output coordinate: out.coord = the\coord. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def minipraycast(startcoord, stepcoord, nsteps, volumesampler, sizef, material): """ Minimum Intensity Projection raycasting. volumesampler(coord, sizef) returns a vec4 (rgba) where r is the scalar intensity. """ # 1. Initialization theref = float('inf') thecoord = startcoord thevalue = vec4(0.0) # 2. Primary Coarse Search for iter in range(nsteps): coord = startcoord + iter stepcoord value = volumesampler(coord, sizef) reff = value.r if reff < theref: theref = reff thecoord = coord thevalue = value # 3. Refinement Loop (4 iterations) substepcoord = stepcoord for iter2 in range(4): substepcoord = substepcoord 0.5 coord1 = thecoord - substepcoord coord2 = thecoord + substepcoord value1 = volumesampler(coord1, sizef) value2 = volumesampler(coord2, sizef) ref1 = value1.r ref2 = value2.r # Source uses exact operators: <= for first candidate, > for second if ref1 <= theref: theref = ref1 thecoord = coord1 thevalue = value1 elif ref2 > theref: theref = ref2 thecoord = coord2 thevalue = value2 # 4. Color Mapping color = colormap(thevalue) if material.colorspace == 'srgb': physicalcolor = srgbtolinear(color.rgb) else: physicalcolor = color.rgb opacity = color.a material.opacity outcolor = vec4(physicalcolor, opacity) # 5. Depth and Coordinate Calculation datapos = thecoord sizef - vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) worldpos = material.worldtransform vec4(datapos, 1.0) ndcpos = material.projectiontransform material.camtransform worldpos outcoord = thecoord outdepth = ndcpos.z / ndcpos.w return outcolor, outcoord, outdepth def colormap(value): """Maps a scalar vec4 sample to an RGBA color using a standard lookup table.""" # Standard implementation: lookup intensity in transfer function return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Placeholder for actual LUT lookup def srgbtolinear(srgb): """Converts sRGB color components to linear physical color space.""" # Standard implementation: apply sRGB gamma expansion return vec3( 1.055 pow(max(srgb.x, 0.04045), 1.0/2.4) - 0.055 if srgb.x > 0.04045 else srgb.x / 12.92, 1.055 pow(max(srgb.y, 0.04045), 1.0/2.4) - 0.055 if srgb.y > 0.04045 else srgb.y / 12.92, 1.055 pow(max(srgb.z, 0.04045), 1.0/2.4) - 0.055 if srgb.z > 0.04045 else srgb.z / 12.92) nsteps: Determines the resolution of the initial search. Refinement Iterations: Fixed at 4 in the reference implementation, providing a 1/16th precision improvement over the initial step size. Scalar Channel: The implementation assumes the scalar intensity is stored in the red channel (value.r). Infinity Initialization: theref must be initialized to a value larger than any possible intensity in the volume. No Compositing: Since only one voxel is selected, standard opacity accumulation and early ray termination are not applicable. The opacity is derived from the colormap alpha and material settings. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of steps. The refinement loop adds a constant overhead (4 \times 2 samples). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray (storing only the current best reference, coordinate, and value). Strengths: Rapidly highlights low-intensity structures such as lungs, vessels in contrast-enhanced scans where background is bright, or hypodense ducts. Hardware acceleration is feasible due to simple comparison logic. Limitations: Loses all depth information for the selected voxel, making it difficult to perceive the 3D structure of the scene. Static images lack depth cues. Only a small fraction of the data is used, potentially discarding relevant contextual information. When to Use: Angiography, bone visualization (if inverted), or highlighting air-filled spaces and hypodense structures like the bile tree or pancreatic duct. When Not to Use: When depth perception is critical or when the volume contains mixed densities where the minimum is not the feature of interest. MinIP was developed alongside MIP for projective diagnostic imaging, particularly in 3D CT and MR angiography. It allows for the rapid generation of images that clearly display vessels, tumors, or bones by selecting the extremal intensity values along the ray. While static MinIPs suffer from a lack of depth information, they are useful in interactive exploration or animation sequences where the drawback is less obvious. The technique is particularly valuable for analyzing the bronchial tree before contrast administration, as air-filled bronchi are the least dense structures in the thorax. name: Perspective Approximation via Orthogonal Slices
head: Perspective Volume Rendering Approximation
body: This method approximates perspective volume rendering by using view-orthogonal slices instead of the concentric spherical shells required for exact ray casting. It enables interactive frame rates on standard graphics hardware by leveraging optimized texture mapping, trading the geometric precision of spherical sampling for significant performance gains. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data set and perspective camera parameters. Output: A 2D image where each pixel color is composited from the volume samples along the corresponding perspective ray. Data Structures: The volume is accessed via 3D texture mapping. Slices are generated as 2D textures (or rendered as quads) orthogonal to the view direction. Unlike exact perspective ray casting, where sample positions form concentric spherical shells, this method assumes sample positions lie on planes orthogonal to the view. Steps: 1. Camera Setup: Define the perspective projection matrix based on the eye position and view parameters. 2. Slice Generation: Generate a sequence of 2D slices orthogonal to the view direction. The spacing between slices is determined by the desired sampling density. 3. Ray Sampling Approximation: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. Instead of calculating the exact intersection with spherical shells, sample the volume at regular intervals along the view-orthogonal slices. The distances of sample positions along a ray depend on the ray's orientation relative to the view direction. 4. Compositing: Perform front-to-back compositing using the standard optical model. The transmittance T and accumulated color C{acc} are updated for each sample i: C{acc}^{(i)} = C{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai Ci \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai where Ci and \alphai are the color and opacity of the sample at the i-th slice intersection. 5. Rendering: Render the composited result to the screen. Pitfalls: The approximation introduces error because the distances of sample positions along a ray depend on the ray's orientation relative to the view direction. Generating exact concentric spherical shells is expensive; this method avoids that cost but sacrifices geometric accuracy. Precision issues may arise if the slice spacing is too coarse relative to the volume features, leading to aliasing or missing details. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def perspectiveapproximationslicerendering(volume, camera, slicespacing): """ Approximates perspective volume rendering using view-orthogonal slices. volume: 3D texture or array representing the volumetric data. camera: Object containing eyeposition, focalpoint, xaxis, yaxis, width, height, and backgroundcolor. slicespacing: Distance between consecutive view-orthogonal slices along the view direction. """ image = [[vec3(0.0) for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] n = normalize(camera.focalpoint - camera.eyeposition) o = camera.eyeposition # Determine slice range based on volume bounds projected onto n. # Not given in sources, standard bounding box projection. kmin = floor(dot(n, volume.minbound - o) / slicespacing) kmax = ceil(dot(n, volume.maxbound - o) / slicespacing) slicepositions = [o + (k slicespacing) n for k in range(kmin, kmax + 1)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): # Generate perspective ray from eye through pixel rayo = camera.eyeposition rayd = normalize(camera.focalpoint - camera.eyeposition + (x - camera.width 0.5) camera.xaxis + (y - camera.height 0.5) camera.yaxis) Cacc = vec3(0.0) alphaacc = 0.0 T = 1.0 # Handle degenerate case where ray is parallel to slice planes denom = dot(n, rayd) if abs(denom) < 1e-6: image[y][x] = camera.backgroundcolor continue # Sort slices by distance along the ray to ensure front-to-back order # Intersection parameter t for plane at pk: t = dot(n, pk - rayo) / dot(n, rayd) sortedslices = sorted(slicepositions, key=lambda p: dot(n, p - rayo) / denom) for pk in sortedslices: t = dot(n, pk - rayo) / denom if t < 0: continue samplepos = rayo + t rayd color, opacity = volume.sample(samplepos) transmittance = T Cacc = Cacc + transmittance opacity color T = T (1.0 - opacity) alphaacc = 1.0 - T if alphaacc >= 1.0: break image[y][x] = Cacc + T camera.backgroundcolor return image Multi-view Depth Perception via Slice Multiplexing is a technique for recovering depth perception in virtual microscopy by projecting different slices of a volume onto multiple views, effectively simulating off-centered parallel cameras. Unlike orbital camera approaches that allow different view angles, this method positions views on the same plane as the slices, using a depth step parameter to determine slice selection for each view. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the number of slices intersected by the rays. Significantly faster than exact perspective ray casting due to the avoidance of spherical shell generation and intersection calculations. Memory Complexity: Depends on the volume data size and the number of slices stored in texture memory. Performance: Allows interactive frame rates even on "cheap" graphics boards due to hardware optimization for texture mapping. Strengths: High speed, suitability for real-time applications like Virtual Reality. Limitations: Approximation error due to the assumption of planar slices instead of spherical shells; quality may degrade for large field-of-view perspectives or when high geometric accuracy is required. When to use: When interactive performance is critical and the volume is viewed with a perspective camera, especially in Virtual Reality applications. When not to use: When exact geometric accuracy of the ray casting is required, or when the volume features are very small relative to the slice spacing. This technique was discussed in the context of texture-based volume rendering for parallel projections and extended to perspective projections. It addresses the computational expense of generating concentric spherical shells for exact perspective ray casting. The method leverages the fact that using view-orthogonal slices is a "good-enough" approximation for many applications, particularly in Virtual Reality. name: Multi-view Depth Perception via Slice Multiplexing
head: Off-centered parallel camera simulation, Slice selection for depth perception
body: Multi-view Depth Perception via Slice Multiplexing recovers depth perception in virtual microscopy by projecting different volume slices onto multiple views, simulating off-centered parallel cameras. Unlike orbital camera approaches that allow different view angles, this method positions views on the same plane as the slices and uses a depth step parameter to determine slice selection for each view. It builds on Perspective Approximation via Orthogonal Slices. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset (potentially anisotropic), a point of interest, and a depth step parameter \Delta z. Output: A set of images (views), each corresponding to a specific slice of the volume. Data Structures: The method relies on an out-of-core data structure using GPU texture memory, which allows trilinear interpolation of volume data using normalized coordinates. Exact layouts, fields, sizes, and bit packing are Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Identify Central Slice: Determine the slice index Iz containing the point of interest. This slice is always projected onto the first view (view index i=0). 2. Calculate Slice Indices: For each subsequent view i, calculate the associated slice index s using the formula: s = Iz + i \times \Delta z. Here, s is the slice index for view i, Iz is the central slice index, i is the view index, and \Delta z is the depth step parameter. 3. Alpha Generation: Perform alpha generation using a two-step process. First, classify each pixel into categories such as background, interest tissues, non-interest tissues, and artifacts. Second, assign each pixel an alpha value corresponding to its closest predefined class alpha value. 4. Projection: Project the identified slice s onto view i. The choice of \Delta z is at the user's discretion but must be adapted to data characteristics. Parameters: \Delta z: The depth step parameter determining the separation between slices projected on adjacent views. Typical values depend on data characteristics. For example, \Delta z = 3 was used for dataset (b) where slice differences were small, while \Delta z < 1 was required for dataset (a) due to significant volume anisotropy. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Anisotropy: High anisotropy requires \Delta z < 1, which is possible because the data is addressed using normalized coordinates and trilinear interpolation. Slice Visibility: If \Delta z < 1 is used, the number of visible slices in a multi-view frame may be drastically reduced, though the final result is softened. Misuse of \Delta z: A non-optimal \Delta z may induce uncomfortable visualization, reduce the depth effect, and make the approach irrelevant. Grayscale Data: Visualizing grayscale data works better with high-contrast or color data, and an extra step may be required to colorize the data via LUTs if the data is grayscale. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateviews(volume, pointofinterest, deltaz, numviews, alphaclasses): # 1. Identify central slice containing point of interest Iz = getsliceindexcontaining(pointofinterest) # views = [] for i in range(numviews): # 2. Calculate slice index for view i s = Iz + i deltaz # 3. Alpha generation: two-step classification pixelclasses = classifypixels(volume, s, alphaclasses) # alphamap = assignclosestalpha(pixelclasses, alphaclasses) # # 4. Projection: combine color and alpha views.append(combinergba(volume, s, alphamap)) # return views Performance: Pixel assignment is performed faster on grayscale pixels compared to RGBA pixels. Hardware: Tested on an autostereoscopic display where the user moves in front of the display to move inside the multi-view frame, and suggested for tablet devices where moving the device left and right is more convenient. Strengths: Recovers depth perception in virtual microscopy and simulates off-centered parallel cameras. Limitations: Views are positioned on the same plane as the slices, limiting view angles compared to orbital cameras, and data anisotropy is a critical factor that complicates the choice of \Delta z. Complexity & Scaling: Time and memory complexity, measured performance with specific hardware/resolution/scene, and scaling behavior are Not given in the sources. Usage Guidelines: Use when recovering depth perception in virtual microscopy with anisotropic data on autostereoscopic or tablet displays, and avoid when orbital camera angles are required due to anisotropy concerns. The method was proposed in the context of virtual microscopy to simulate depth perception using an autostereoscopic display. It addresses the challenge of visualizing volumetric data with significant anisotropy by using a slice selection strategy based on a depth step parameter. name: Projection
head: Direct Volume Rendering via Projection, Orthographic Projection (Summation), Summation Projection, Summed Reprojection, Summed projection, Total Intensity Projection, Voxel Projection
body: Projection is a direct volume rendering technique that visualizes the total accumulated intensity of a 3D volume along a specific axis by summing voxel values. It compresses volumetric data into a 2D representation where pixel brightness corresponds to the line integral of the scalar field along the viewing ray. Unlike Maximum Intensity Projection, which highlights the highest density structures, projection sums all contributions along the ray, which decreases noise but significantly reduces image contrast due to cumulative background activity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume V represented as a discrete grid of voxels, typically stored as a 3D array where each element V(x, y, z) holds a scalar intensity value. Output: A 2D accumulator array initialized to zero, with dimensions matching the volume perpendicular to the projection axis. Data Structures: The input volume is stored as a 3D array. The output is a 2D array of shape (Dy, Dz) when projecting along the X-axis. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize a 2D output array vr with zeros, matching the dimensions of the volume perpendicular to the projection axis. 2. Iterate through each slice index i along the projection axis (X-axis). 3. Extract the 2D slice at index i. 4. Add the slice values to the corresponding positions in the output accumulator. Formula: The accumulated intensity for each output pixel (y, z) is computed as: I(y, z) = \sum{x=0}^{Dx-1} V(x, y, z) where Dx is the number of voxels along the projection axis, and V(x, y, z) is the scalar intensity at voxel coordinates (x, y, z). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projection(volume): """ Computes the orthographic projection (summation) of a 3D volume along the first axis. Args: volume: 3D list or array of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz). Returns: 2D list or array of shape (Dy, Dz) containing the summed intensities. """ dx, dy, dz = len(volume), len(volume[0]), len(volume[0][0]) # Initialize output array with zeros matching the Y and Z dimensions vr = [[0.0 for in range(dz)] for in range(dy)] # Iterate through each slice along the X-axis (first dimension) for i in range(dx): # Extract the 2D slice at index i imgslice = volume[i] # Add the slice to the accumulator for y in range(dy): for z in range(dz): vr[y][z] += imgslice[y][z] return vr Parameters and Edge Cases: Axis Selection: The projection direction is determined by which axis is iterated over. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The method assumes the volume is fully contained within the grid bounds; out-of-bounds access is not handled. Degenerate Input: If the volume contains only zero-valued voxels, the output will be uniformly zero. A viewpoint-independent technique for visualizing 3D vector fields on surfaces, specifically designed for generating film loops where the viewpoint rotates about the vertical z-axis. It projects the 3D vector onto the surface along a direction pointing radially away from the rotational axis. It is chosen when preserving the z-component of a vector field during rotational motion is required, yielding results similar to XY Normal Projection but with more intuitive visualization for this specific motion. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N), where N is the total number of voxels in the volume, since each voxel is visited exactly once. Memory: O(Dy \times Dz) for the output image, plus the input volume storage, with no additional per-ray buffers required. Performance and Scaling: The method is extremely fast and highly parallelizable, as each output pixel is independent of others. It scales linearly with volume size. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement and computationally inexpensive. Summed reprojection decreases noise, but at the expense of image contrast. Limitations: Produces images with inferior contrast compared to slice display and Maximum Intensity Projection. It suffers from cumulative background activity, where structures far from the viewing plane interfere with the assessment of closer structures. The projection method, specifically referred to as "summed reprojection" or "raw projection," has been evaluated in clinical studies comparing lesion contrast in SPECT images. It is often contrasted with Maximum Activity Projection, which provides superior lesion contrast and decreased image noise compared to summed reprojection. mneela/Volume-Rendering, https://github.com/mneela/Volume-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volume Rendering Volume Rendering, https://docslib.org/doc/1400821/volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) "Volume rendering in three-dimensional display of SPECT images", http://jnm.snmjournals.org/cgi/pmidlookup?view=long&pmid=2384811, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Cylinder Projection
head: Normal projection, Vieweye projection, XY Normal Projection
body: Cylinder projection is a viewpoint-independent technique for visualizing 3D vector fields on surfaces, specifically designed for generating film loops where the viewpoint rotates about the vertical z-axis. It projects the 3D vector onto the surface along a direction pointing radially away from the rotational axis. It yields results very similar to XY Normal Projection, though it preserves the z-component of the vector field, which gives a somewhat more intuitive visualization for this specific rotational motion. The uniformity of the vector field is still not readily apparent with this projection. Inputs: A 3D vector field \mathbf{V} defined on or near a surface S. Outputs: A 2D projection of the vector field on the screen for each frame of the film loop. Data Structures: Surface point \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z), surface normal \mathbf{N} = (Nx, Ny, Nz) at \mathbf{p}, and vector field value \mathbf{V} = (Vx, Vy, Vz) at \mathbf{p}. Steps: 1. Determine the rotational axis, which is fixed as the z-axis. 2. Calculate the vector pointing away from the rotational axis at the current surface point \mathbf{p}. This radial direction \mathbf{R} lies in the xy-plane and is defined by the x and y coordinates of the point: \mathbf{R} = (x, y, 0). 3. Project the 3D velocity vector \mathbf{V} onto the surface along the direction \mathbf{R}. The projection \mathbf{V}{proj} is computed by removing the component of \mathbf{V} parallel to \mathbf{R}: \mathbf{V}{proj} = \mathbf{V} - \frac{\mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{R}}{\|\mathbf{R}\|^2} \mathbf{R}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cylinderprojection(p, V): # p = (x, y, z), V = (Vx, Vy, Vz) R = (p[0], p[1], 0) # Radial direction in xy-plane RdotR = R[0]2 + R[1]2 if RdotR == 0: return V # Guard for points on the z-axis Vproj = ( V[0] - (V[0]R[0] + V[1]R[1]) / RdotR R[0], V[1] - (V[0]R[0] + V[1]R[1]) / RdotR R[1], V[2]) return Vproj Parameters: Rotational axis: Fixed as z-axis (0,0,1). Surface centering: The surface must be centered on the rotational axis. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Surface Geometry: The method is only suitable for simple surfaces which are centered on the rotational axis. Uniformity: The uniformity of the vector field is still not readily apparent with this projection. Z-Component: It preserves the z component of the vector field. Projects the 3D vector onto the surface in the direction of the x and y components of the surface normal. It is viewpoint-independent and designed for z-axis rotation. It preserves the z-component but is also limited to simple surfaces. Choose it when radial symmetry is not required and standard normal alignment is preferred. See Projection. Projects vectors parallel to the viewing direction. It provides the most intuitive representation for a single image but changes significantly with viewpoint rotation, making it less suitable for film loops without additional seed point management. Choose it for static views or when dynamic viewpoint alignment is acceptable. See Projection. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Viewpoint-independent; preserves the z-component of the vector field, providing a more intuitive visualization for z-axis rotation than standard normal projection. Limitations: Only suitable for simple surfaces centered on the rotational axis; uniformity of the vector field is not readily apparent. When to use: When generating film loops with rotation about the z-axis for simple, axis-centered surfaces. When not to use: For complex surfaces not centered on the axis, or when uniformity of the vector field is the primary visualization goal. Cylinder projection was introduced in the context of visualizing 3D velocity fields near contour surfaces. It is designed specifically for producing film loops where the viewpoint is rotated about the z (vertical) axis. The technique was developed to address the limitations of other projection methods (like Eye Projection) which change significantly with viewpoint, while offering a slight improvement in intuition over XY Normal Projection by preserving the z-component. name: MPI Defocus Rendering
head: Multiplane image defocus, Synthetic Defocus Rendering, Synthetic Defocus Rendering from MPI
body: MPI Defocus Rendering synthesizes images with depth-of-field blur and lateral camera translation by compositing a precomputed Multi-Plane Image (MPI) representation. It differs from standard ray casting by operating on discrete disparity planes rather than continuous volumetric samples, allowing for efficient simulation of defocus blur via 2D image-space convolutions. Inputs: N: Number of planes in the MPI. \mathbf{c}{mpi}^{(i)}: Color tensor for plane i (RGB, linear HDR space). \alpha{mpi}^{(i)}: Opacity tensor for plane i. i{focus}: Index of the focal plane. \Delta r: Scalar controlling the simulated aperture size (defocus strength). \Delta \mathbf{d}: 2D vector controlling lateral camera translation parallel to the image plane. Outputs: C: The final composited image. The MPI consists of N fronto-parallel RGBA planes. The planes are indexed from back to front (i = 0 to N-1). Colors are stored in linear HDR space. 1. Precompute MPI: Generate the MPI representation from the trained model. The MPI comprises a series of fronto-parallel RGBA planes sampled linearly in disparity within a camera frustum at a central camera pose. 2. Initialize Accumulator: Set the output color accumulator C \leftarrow 0. 3. Iterate Planes: For each plane i from 0 to N-1 (back to front): a. Calculate Blur Radius: Compute the blur radius r based on the distance of the current plane from the focal plane: r = \Delta r \cdot |i - i{focus}| b. Generate Kernel: Create a blur kernel k{blur} using a circular mask of radius r centered at the origin. This is implemented as a 2D Fourier space convolution. c. Blur Color: Premultiply the plane's color by its alpha (\mathbf{c}{mpi}^{(i)} \cdot \alpha{mpi}^{(i)}) and convolve with the kernel: \mathbf{c}{blur} = \text{convolve}(\mathbf{c}{mpi}^{(i)} \cdot \alpha{mpi}^{(i)}, k{blur}) d. Blur Alpha: Convolve the plane's alpha with the kernel: \alpha{blur} = \text{convolve}(\alpha{mpi}^{(i)}, k{blur}) e. Calculate Translation Offset: Compute the translation vector \mathbf{d} for the current plane: \mathbf{d} = \Delta \mathbf{d} \cdot i f. Translate Blurred Layers: Apply continuous 2D image translation using bilinear resampling to the blurred color and alpha: \mathbf{c}{trans} = \text{translate}(\mathbf{c}{blur}, \mathbf{d}) \alpha{trans} = \text{translate}(\alpha{blur}, \mathbf{d}) g. Composite: Add the translated color to the accumulator using the transmittance (1 - \alpha{trans}): C \leftarrow \mathbf{c}{trans} + (1 - \alpha{trans}) C The color \mathbf{c}{trans} is not multiplied by \alpha{trans} here because the color was already premultiplied by alpha in step 3c. 4. Return Result: Output C. i{focus}: Controls the focal plane depth. \Delta r: Controls the simulated aperture size, determining defocus strength. \Delta \mathbf{d}: A 2D vector controlling camera translation parallel to the image plane. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def mpidefocusrendering(cmpi, alphampi, ifocus, deltar, deltad): """ Synthetic defocus rendering from a Multi-Plane Image. cmpi: list of N arrays (H, W, 3), colors in linear HDR space. alphampi: list of N arrays (H, W), opacities. ifocus: int, focal plane index. deltar: float, simulated aperture size. deltad: tuple (dx, dy), 2D vector for lateral camera translation. """ N = len(cmpi) H, W, = cmpi[0].shape C = np.zeros((H, W, 3)) for i in range(N): # 1. Calculate blur radius based on distance from focal plane r = deltar abs(i - ifocus) # 2. Generate blur kernel (circular mask, radius r) kblur = makecircularkernel(r) # 3. Premultiply color by alpha before blurring cpremult = cmpi[i] alphampi[i][..., np.newaxis] # 4. Convolve color and alpha with kernel cblur = convolve2d(cpremult, kblur) alphablur = convolve2d(alphampi[i], kblur) # 5. Calculate translation offset for this plane d = (deltad[0] i, deltad[1] i) # 6. Translate blurred layers using bilinear resampling ctrans = bilineartranslate(cblur, d) alphatrans = bilineartranslate(alphablur, d) # 7. Composite: C = ctrans + (1 - alphatrans) C transmittance = 1.0 - alphatrans[..., np.newaxis] C = ctrans + transmittance C return C def makecircularkernel(r): """Returns a normalized circular mask of radius r.""" size = int(2 r) + 1 y, x = np.ogrid[:size,:size] center = size // 2 mask = (x - center)2 + (y - center)2 <= r2 return mask.astype(float) / mask.sum() def convolve2d(image, kernel): """2D convolution using FFT for efficiency.""" # Apply FFT convolution per channel out = np.zeroslike(image) for c in range(image.shape[2]): out[:,:, c] = np.fft.ifft2( np.fft.fft2(image[:,:, c]) np.fft.fft2(kernel, s=image.shape[:2])).real return out def bilineartranslate(image, offset): """Continuous 2D translation using bilinear resampling.""" H, W = image.shape[:2] dy, dx = offset # Create coordinate grids y, x = np.mgrid[0:H, 0:W] ynew = y - dy xnew = x - dx # Clip to valid range for bilinear interpolation y0 = np.clip(ynew.astype(int), 0, H - 2) x0 = np.clip(xnew.astype(int), 0, W - 2) y1 = y0 + 1 x1 = x0 + 1 # Interpolation weights sy = ynew - y0 sx = xnew - x0 # Bilinear interpolation val = (image[y0, x0] (1 - sy) (1 - sx) + image[y0, x1] (1 - sy) sx + image[y1, x0] sy (1 - sx) + image[y1, x1] sy sx) return val Premultiplication: The color must be premultiplied by alpha before blurring. The accumulation step does not apply alpha to \mathbf{c}{trans} because the premultiplication in the blur step already accounts for it. Indexing: MPI planes are indexed from back to front (i=0 is back). Color Space: Colors must be in linear HDR space during processing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient simulation of defocus blur and lateral translation without per-pixel ray marching. Suitable for high dynamic range (HDR) raw image synthesis. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the precomputed MPI. Defocus blur is approximated via 2D convolution, which assumes thin-lens optics. When to use: When synthetic defocus and camera translation are required for view synthesis from an MPI. When not to use: Not given in the sources. MPI Defocus Rendering was introduced in the context of "NeRF in the Dark," a method for high dynamic range view synthesis from noisy raw images. The approach leverages the efficiency of Multi-Plane Images (MPIs). It builds on prior work addressing synthetic defocus. The method was developed to handle the challenges of low-light photography, where Bayer masking and raw domain processing are necessary to mitigate noise artifacts. name: View-Dependent Transparency
head: Angle-Based Transparency, Image fading with incidence angle, Incidence angle fading
body: View-Dependent Transparency (VDT) is a compositing technique that modulates sample opacity based on the geometric relationship between the surface normal and the viewer's direction, rather than relying solely on intrinsic material properties. It solves the problem of visual clutter in integral surface rendering by making regions orthogonal to the viewer more transparent and regions curving towards or away from the viewer more opaque, thereby improving the readability of nested structures and silhouettes. It differs from standard Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) by introducing view-dependent opacity modulation to enhance shape perception, and from billboard-based fading which suffers from ghosting artifacts when moving around complex objects. The method operates on the output of the ray casting loop, specifically modifying the opacity \alphai of each sample before or during the compositing step. Two primary variants are defined: Angle-Based Transparency and Normal-Variation Transparency. Inputs: Surface normal vector \mathbf{n} at the sample point. Normalized view vector \mathbf{v} from the camera to the sample point. Pixel coordinates (i, j) for image-space derivatives. Parameter \gamma \in [0, 1] for Normal-Variation Transparency. User-adjustable transparency range [\alpha{min}, \alpha{max}]. Outputs: Modified view-dependent opacity \alpha{view} or final opacity \alpha. No specific complex data structures are required beyond the standard sample attributes (ci, \alphai, \mathbf{n}i, \mathbf{v}i). The normal \mathbf{n} must be available in the same coordinate space as \mathbf{v} (typically view space or world space, provided they are consistent). This method computes transparency based on the incidence angle between the surface normal and the view vector. 1. Compute the dot product of the surface normal \mathbf{n} and the normalized view vector \mathbf{v}: d = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} 2. Apply the arccosine function to the dot product result to obtain the angle \theta \in [0, \pi]: \theta = \arccos(d) 3. Scale the result by 2/\pi to normalize the transparency to the range [0, 1]: \alpha{view} = \frac{2}{\pi} \arccos(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}) Interpretation: The source refers to \alpha{view} as "transparency", but notes that transparency "decreases as the object silhouette is approached". At the silhouette, \mathbf{n} \perp \mathbf{v}, so \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0, \arccos(0) = \pi/2, and \alpha{view} = 1. In standard alpha blending, \alpha=1 is opaque. Therefore, \alpha{view} functions as the opacity contribution in the compositing equation, where regions orthogonal to the viewer (\alpha{view} \approx 1) are actually opaque, and front-facing regions (\alpha{view} \approx 0) are transparent, matching the source's description of decreasing transparency at the silhouette. This method approximates local surface curvature perpendicular to the viewer using image-space partial derivatives. 1. Retrieve the surface normal \mathbf{n}(i,j) at pixel (i,j) and extract its z-component nz (assuming view space where z is the view direction). 2. Compute the partial derivatives of nz with respect to pixel coordinates i and j: \frac{\partial nz}{\partial i}, \quad \frac{\partial nz}{\partial j} 3. Calculate the base view-dependent term \alpha{view}: \alpha{view} = \left( \left(\frac{\partial nz}{\partial i}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial nz}{\partial j}\right)^2 \right)^{\gamma/2} Note: The source states that \alpha{view} is not necessarily limited to the unit interval and must be clamped before \gamma is applied. In practice, the gradient magnitude B = \sqrt{(\partial nz/\partial i)^2 + (\partial nz/\partial j)^2} is clamped to [0, 1] before raising to the power of \gamma/2 to ensure valid opacity values. 4. Constrain the final opacity \alpha to the user-adjustable interval [\alpha{min}, \alpha{max}]: \alpha = (1 - \alpha{view}) \cdot \alpha{min} + \alpha{view} \cdot \alpha{max} This linear interpolation assumes \alpha{view} is normalized to [0,1] after clamping. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math PI = 3.141592653589793 def anglebasedvdt(n: list, v: list) -> float: """ Computes view-dependent opacity using the angle between normal and view vector. n: Surface normal [nx, ny, nz] (normalized). v: View vector [vx, vy, vz] (normalized). Returns: Opacity alphaview in [0, 1]. """ dotproduct = n[0]v[0] + n[1]v[1] + n[2]v[2] dotproduct = max(-1.0, min(1.0, dotproduct)) angle = math.acos(dotproduct) alphaview = (2.0 / PI) angle return max(0.0, min(1.0, alphaview)) def computenormalderivatives(nbuffer: list, i: int, j: int) -> tuple: """ Computes finite differences for the z-component of normals at pixel (i, j). nbuffer: 2D array of normals [nx, ny, nz] indexed by (row, col). """ # Assuming nbuffer is indexed as nbuffer[row][col] # For simplicity, assume row corresponds to j and col to i nzcurr = nbuffer[j][i][2] nzright = nbuffer[j][i+1][2] if i+1 < len(nbuffer[j]) else nzcurr nzdown = nbuffer[j+1][i][2] if j+1 < len(nbuffer) else nzcurr dnzdi = nzright - nzcurr dnzdj = nzdown - nzcurr return dnzdi, dnzdj def normalvariationvdt(dnzdi: float, dnzdj: float, gamma: float, alphamin: float, alphamax: float) -> float: """ Computes view-dependent opacity using pre-computed normal derivatives. """ gradmag = math.sqrt(dnzdi2 + dnzdj2) gradmag = max(0.0, min(1.0, gradmag)) alphaview = gradmag (gamma / 2.0) alpha = (1.0 - alphaview) alphamin + alphaview alphamax return alpha def compositingwithvdt(samples, backgroundcolor, vdtmethod, gamma=1.0, alphamin=0.1, alphamax=0.9): """ Standard front-to-back compositing with View-Dependent Transparency. samples: list of dicts with keys 'color', 'opacity', 'normal', 'viewvector', 'pixelcoords' """ Cacc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphaacc = 0.0 for sample in samples: ci = sample['color'] alpharaw = sample['opacity'] n = sample['normal'] v = sample['viewvector'] i, j = sample['pixelcoords'] if vdtmethod == "angle": alphavdt = anglebasedvdt(n, v) elif vdtmethod == "normalvariation": # In a real implementation, nbuffer would be populated from the ray-casting pass. # Here we assume a helper buffer is available. dnzdi, dnzdj = computenormalderivatives(nbuffer, i, j) alphavdt = normalvariationvdt(dnzdi, dnzdj, gamma, alphamin, alphamax) else: alphavdt = alpharaw alphai = alpharaw alphavdt transmittance = 1.0 - alphaacc Cacc[0] += transmittance alphai ci[0] Cacc[1] += transmittance alphai ci[1] Cacc[2] += transmittance alphai ci[2] alphaacc = alphaacc + transmittance alphai if alphaacc >= 1.0: break bg = backgroundcolor Cacc[0] += (1.0 - alphaacc) bg[0] Cacc[1] += (1.0 - alphaacc) bg[1] Cacc[2] += (1.0 - alphaacc) bg[2] return Cacc Ghosting and Transparency Variation Artifacts: When using billboard-based fading (a related technique), moving the camera causes ghosting (duplicated features) and transparency variation artifacts because blending two half-faded textures is not equivalent to a single opaque texture. Flat Surface Opacity: In Angle-Based Transparency, large, almost flat parts of the integral surface result in high opacity, which can obscure the layers below. Unbounded Values: In Normal-Variation Transparency, \alpha{view} is not necessarily limited to the unit interval and must be clamped before the exponent \gamma is applied. Derivative Calculation: Normal-Variation Transparency requires accurate image-space partial derivatives of the normal's z-component. A transparency variation technique that approximates local surface curvature perpendicular to the viewer using image-space partial derivatives of the normal's z-component, making the surface more opaque where it curves away and more transparent when oriented perpendicular to the viewer. It is chosen when the goal is to emphasize surface details like creases and small features, or when viewing nested structures (e.g., flow tubes) where curvature indicates depth. It differs from Angle-Based Transparency by providing stronger opacity gradients at silhouettes and being less dependent on the global view direction, allowing curved features to be identified even when viewed frontally. Time Complexity: Angle-Based Transparency is O(1) per sample, requiring only a dot product and arccosine. Normal-Variation Transparency requires computing image-space derivatives, which adds overhead for neighbor lookups and derivative calculations, potentially requiring a post-processing pass or specific buffer layouts. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory for Angle-Based. Normal-Variation requires storing normals and potentially neighbor normals or derivative buffers. Performance: Angle-Based is very cheap. Normal-Variation is also cheap but depends on derivative accuracy. Billboard fading is 2-3 times slower than single texture fetches and requires blending multiple textures. Strengths: Improves readability of complex shapes and nested structures; highlights silhouettes and curvature. Limitations: Can obscure layers below if surfaces are large and flat (Angle-Based); prone to ghosting artifacts if implemented via billboards; requires accurate normals. When to use: When visualizing integral surfaces or volumes where shape perception and layer separation are critical. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and derivative computation is too expensive, or when the geometry is highly fragmented (billboard artifacts). View-Dependent Transparency was introduced to improve the readability of volumetric and integral surface visualizations. Bruckner and Gröller (2007) cited it as a composition strategy for direct volume rendering to enhance shape perception. The specific Angle-Based and Normal-Variation formulas were proposed in the context of the IRIS (Illustrative Rendering for Integral Surfaces) system, which aimed to provide cheap, effective transparency variation for large surfaces. Earlier work by Jakobsen (2000) discussed fading billboards based on incidence angle, noting the associated artifacts. name: Energy Region Compositing
head: Energy Compositing
body: Energy Region Compositing is a volume rendering technique that composites multiple energy volumes within a specific region of interest defined by a magnitude volume. It renders a volume using multiple energy volumes, blending colors based on normalized intensities above a threshold. It differs from standard composite rendering by using a separate magnitude volume to define visibility and applying a threshold to energy intensity before compositing. Inputs and Outputs: viewmatrix: A 3x3 or 4x4 matrix containing view vectors. Indices 0:3 are the U vector, 4:7 are the V vector, and 8:11 are the View vector. volume: The main magnitude volume object with attributes dimx, dimy, dimz and a method getmaximum(). imagesize: Integer width and height of the output image (assumed square). image: Output array of size imagesize imagesize 4 (RGBA). energyvolumes: Dictionary mapping integer energy IDs to Volume objects. magnitudeVolume: A separate volume object used to define the region of interest. interactivemode: Boolean flag determining step size. Data Structures: colorDictionary: Maps energy IDs to RGB colors. Colors are generated from permutations of [1, 0, 0.5, 1] taken 3 at a time. voxelcords: 3D coordinates calculated per ray step. Parameters: step: Loop step size. Set to 20 if interactivemode is true, otherwise 1. Note: Source snippets show conflicting values (2 or 10), but the primary definition states 20. threshold: Energy intensity threshold. Set to 0.3 (30%). Formulas: Ray extent diagonal: \text{diagonal} = \lfloor \sqrt{3} \times \max(\text{dim}x, \text{dim}y, \text{dim}z) / 2 \rfloor + 1 Voxel coordinates: \text{voxel\cords} = \mathbf{u} \times (i - \text{image\center}) + \mathbf{v} \times (j - \text{image\center}) + \mathbf{view} \times k + \text{volume\center} Composite color update: \text{current\r} = \text{color\a} \times \text{color\voxel}[0] + (1 - \text{color\a}) \times \text{initial\r} (Same for g and b) Steps: 1. Initialize image to zeros. 2. Generate colorDictionary: Generate permutations of [1, 0, 0.5, 1] taken 3 at a time. Map each energy ID in energyvolumes to a unique permutation. Set ID 0 to [0, 0, 0]. 3. Extract vectors from viewmatrix: \mathbf{u} = \text{view\matrix}[0:3]. \mathbf{v} = \text{view\matrix}[4:7]. \mathbf{view} = \text{view\matrix}[8:11]. 4. Calculate centers: \text{image\center} = \text{image\size} / 2. \text{volume\center} = [\text{volume.dim\x}/2, \text{volume.dim\y}/2, \text{volume.dim\z}/2]. 5. Calculate diagonal using the formula above. 6. Set step: 20 if interactivemode else 1. 7. Loop over pixel coordinates (i, j) with step size. 8. Initialize initialr, initialg, initialb to 0. 9. Loop along ray depth k from diagonal down to -diagonal. 10. Compute voxelcords using the formula above. 11. Sample magnitudeVolume at voxelcords to get g. 12. If g \neq 0: Set colorvoxel to the output of a transfer function evaluated at g (e.g., tfunc.getcolor(g)); otherwise, set colorvoxel to [0, 0, 0]. 13. Sample the main volume at voxelcords. If value > 0: Iterate through all energyvolumes. For each energy, get intensitymax (from volume) and energyintensity (interpolated at voxelcords). If energyintensity / intensitymax > 0.3: Update colorvoxel: \text{color\voxel} = \text{color\voxel} \times (1 - \text{ratio}) + \text{colorDictionary}[key] \times \text{ratio} where \text{ratio} = \text{energy\intensity} / \text{intensity\max}. 14. Calculate colora as the maximum component of colorvoxel. 15. Update accumulated color: \text{current\r} = \text{color\a} \times \text{color\voxel}[0] + (1 - \text{color\a}) \times \text{initial\r} (Same for g and b) \text{initial\r}, \text{initial\g}, \text{initial\b} = \text{current\r}, \text{current\g}, \text{current\b} 16. After ray loop, clamp and convert final colors to 8-bit integers: \text{red} = \lfloor \text{current\r} \times 255 \rfloor \text{ if } < 255 \text{ else } 255 (Same for g, b) 17. Assign RGBA values to image at index (j \times \text{image\size} + i) \times 4. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np from itertools import permutations def getvoxelInterpolated(volume, x, y, z): # Standard trilinear interpolation or nearest neighbor lookup return 0.0 def renderenergyregioncompositing(viewmatrix, volume, imagesize, image, energyvolumes, magnitudeVolume, interactivemode): # Clear image image.fill(0) # Generate color dictionary perm = np.asarray(list(permutations([1, 0, 0.5, 1], 3))) ids = list(energyvolumes.keys()) colorDictionary = {0: [0, 0, 0]} for i in range(len(ids)): colorDictionary[ids[i]] = perm[i] # Extract vectors uvector = viewmatrix[0:3].reshape(-1, 1) vvector = viewmatrix[4:7].reshape(-1, 1) viewvector = viewmatrix[8:11].reshape(-1, 1) # Centers imagecenter = imagesize / 2 volumecenter = np.asarray([volume.dimx / 2, volume.dimy / 2, volume.dimz / 2]).reshape(-1, 1) # Diagonal diagonal = np.sqrt(3) np.max([volume.dimx, volume.dimy, volume.dimz]) / 2 diagonal = int(math.floor(diagonal)) + 1 # Step size (sources show conflicting values: 2, 10, or 20; using 20 per primary definition) step = 20 if interactivemode else 1 for i in range(0, imagesize, step): for j in range(0, imagesize, step): initialr, initialg, initialb = 0, 0, 0 for k in range(diagonal, -diagonal, -1): # Compute voxel coordinates voxelcords = (np.dot(uvector, i - imagecenter) + np.dot(vvector, j - imagecenter) + np.dot(viewvector, k) + volumecenter) # Sample magnitude volume g = getvoxelInterpolated(magnitudeVolume, voxelcords[0], voxelcords[1], voxelcords[2]) # Initialize colorvoxel per voxel colorvoxel = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) if g != 0: # Transfer function not defined in source; applies magnitude to color colorvoxel = transferfunction(g) # Sample main volume value = getvoxelInterpolated(volume, voxelcords[0], voxelcords[1], voxelcords[2]) if value > 0: for key, energyvol in energyvolumes.items(): intensitymax = energyvol.getmaximum() if intensitymax > 0: energyintensity = getvoxelInterpolated(energyvol, voxelcords[0], voxelcords[1], voxelcords[2]) ratio = energyintensity / intensitymax if ratio > 0.3: colorvoxel = np.add(np.multiply(colorvoxel, 1 - ratio), np.multiply(colorDictionary[key], ratio)) colora = np.max(colorvoxel) currentr = colora colorvoxel[0] + (1 - colora) initialr currentg = colora colorvoxel[1] + (1 - colora) initialg currentb = colora colorvoxel[2] + (1 - colora) initialb initialr, initialg, initialb = currentr, currentg, currentb # Clamp and convert red = math.floor(currentr 255) if currentr < 255 else 255 green = math.floor(currentg 255) if currentg < 255 else 255 blue = math.floor(currentb 255) if currentb < 255 else 255 alpha = math.floor(np.max(colorvoxel) 255) if np.max(colorvoxel) < 255 else 255 # Assign to image idx = (j imagesize + i) 4 image[idx] = red image[idx + 1] = green image[idx + 2] = blue image[idx + 3] = alpha Time Complexity: O(\text{image\size}^2 \times \text{diagonal} \times N), where N is the number of energy volumes. Memory Complexity: O(\text{image\size}^2) for the output image, plus storage for all volume data. Performance: Uses a large step size (20) in interactive mode to speed up rendering. Strengths: Allows visualization of specific energy types within a defined region of interest. Limitations: Relies on a separate magnitude volume for region definition; thresholding is fixed at 30%.
