name: Hybrid Techniques
body: Hybrid techniques in volume rendering integrate aspects of both image-order and object-order processing to achieve a balance between computational efficiency and rendering accuracy. These multi-stage approaches typically begin with an object-order traversal to exploit spatial coherence in the volume data, followed by image-order refinement to ensure precise ray integration and compositing. By combining these paradigms, hybrid methods reduce the overhead of pure ray casting while maintaining flexibility in handling complex viewing transformations. Shared principles are defined in Multi-Pass and Compositing Techniques. Accumulates volume data directly in image space using hardware blending, avoiding explicit ray marching. Chosen when high throughput is prioritized over per-ray accuracy. Splits rendering into sequential passes that write intermediate results to render targets for subsequent refinement. Chosen when decoupling light transport and compositing improves performance or enables advanced effects. Handles final color and opacity blending, often integrating depth and auxiliary buffers into the final image. Chosen as the final stage to produce the output framebuffer. The concept of hybrid techniques emerged from the need to balance the strengths of object-order and image-order rendering. Object-order methods, such as splatting, exploit spatial coherence and are efficient for large datasets but may suffer from sorting artifacts or limited accuracy in complex lighting scenarios. Image-order methods, such as ray casting, provide high accuracy and flexibility but are computationally expensive due to the lack of spatial coherence and the need for per-pixel ray traversal. The shear-warp algorithm is a seminal example of this hybrid paradigm, demonstrating how factorizing the viewing transformation can significantly reduce computational overhead. This approach has influenced subsequent hybrid methods that seek to combine the efficiency of object-order processing with the precision of image-order refinement. Hybrid techniques are widely used in medical imaging, scientific visualization, and real-time rendering applications where both performance and visual fidelity are critical. They are particularly effective for handling complex viewing transformations and large-scale volume data. volume rendering, https://grokipedia.com/page/Volumerendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Multi-Mode Volume Ray Casting
head: Composite Volume Ray Casting, Custom Volume Ray Casting with Shading and Multiple Modes, MyVolumeRayCastCompositeFunction, Volume Ray Casting Composite, vtkVolumeRayCastCompositeFunction
body: Multi-Mode Volume Ray Casting is a custom direct volume ray casting implementation that extends standard compositing to support three distinct rendering modes: Full (compositing with shading), Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP), and XRay (average intensity projection). It differs from standard compositing by explicitly calculating shaded color contributions and blending them with the background using a specific accumulation formula, while supporting nearest-neighbor interpolation and Phong shading. It is implemented as a custom ray cast function within the VTK framework. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset. The implementation supports only VTKUNSIGNEDCHAR (8-bit) and VTKUNSIGNEDSHORT (16-bit) data types; other types trigger a warning and do not render. Input: Per-ray runtime data (vtkVolumeRayCastDynamicInfo) containing NumberOfStepsToTake (int), TransformedStart (float[3]), TransformedIncrement (float[3]), Color (float[4]), and NumberOfStepsTaken (int). Input: Per-volume static data (vtkVolumeRayCastStaticInfo) containing ScalarDataPointer (void), ScalarDataType (enum), shading tables (RedDiffuseShadingTable, GreenDiffuseShadingTable, BlueDiffuseShadingTable, RedSpecularShadingTable, GreenSpecularShadingTable, BlueSpecularShadingTable as float), EncodedNormals (unsigned short), DataIncrement (int[3]), and a reference to Volume containing transfer functions. Output: Final pixel color (R, G, B) and accumulated opacity \alpha written to dynamicInfo->Color[0..3]. Data Structures: The method operates on two primary information structures passed to the ray casting function: 1. vtkVolumeRayCastDynamicInfo: Contains per-ray runtime data. NumberOfStepsToTake (int): Total steps to iterate. TransformedStart (float[3]): Ray origin in voxel space. TransformedIncrement (float[3]): Step vector in voxel space. Color (float[4]): Output color (R, G, B, \alpha). NumberOfStepsTaken (int): Actual steps executed (for early termination). 2. vtkVolumeRayCastStaticInfo: Contains per-volume static data. ScalarDataPointer (void): Pointer to the raw voxel data. ScalarDataType (enum): Data type identifier. RedDiffuseShadingTable, GreenDiffuseShadingTable, BlueDiffuseShadingTable (float): Lookup tables for diffuse shading. RedSpecularShadingTable, GreenSpecularShadingTable, BlueSpecularShadingTable (float): Lookup tables for specular shading. EncodedNormals (unsigned short): Pre-computed normal vectors. DataIncrement (int[3]): Strides for x, y, z dimensions to calculate linear memory offset. Volume (vtkVolume): Reference to the volume object containing transfer functions. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Retrieve dataptr from staticInfo->ScalarDataPointer. Fetch numsteps, raystart, and rayincrement from dynamicInfo. Fetch transfer functions ScalarToOpacityTF and ScalarToColorTF from staticInfo->Volume. Fetch xinc, yinc, zinc from staticInfo->DataIncrement. Initialize ray position in voxel space: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{ray\start}. Initialize accumulators: CR = CG = CB = 0.0, \alpha{acc} = 0.0. Initialize MIP variables: \alpha{max} = 0.0, V{max} = 0.0. Initialize global maximum scalar value V{global\max} = 0.0. 2. Ray Loop: Iterate for i from 0 to num\steps - 1: Early Termination: If \alpha{acc} \ge 1.0, break the loop. Voxel Coordinate Calculation: Round the current ray position to the nearest integer to get voxel coordinates: vx = \text{round}(px), vy = \text{round}(py), vz = \text{round}(pz). Data Access: Calculate linear offset: \text{offset} = vz \cdot \text{zinc} + vy \cdot \text{yinc} + vx \cdot \text{xinc}. Retrieve scalar value: V = \text{data\ptr}[\text{offset}]. Global Maximum Update: If V > V{global\max}, set V{global\max} = V. Mode-Specific Processing: Let \mathbf{c}{raw} = (r, g, b) be the color from ScalarToColorTF[V] and \alpha be the opacity from ScalarToOpacityTF[V]. Mode MIP (currentRenderMode == 0): If V > V{max}, set V{max} = V, set CR = \alpha \cdot r, CG = \alpha \cdot g, CB = \alpha \cdot b, and set \alpha{acc} = 1.0 - \alpha. Mode XRay (currentRenderMode == 1): Accumulate scalar values into all color channels: CR \leftarrow CR + V, CG \leftarrow CG + V, CB \leftarrow CB + V. Mode Full (currentRenderMode == 2): Compute shaded values: r{shaded} = \alpha \cdot r, g{shaded} = \alpha \cdot g, b{shaded} = \alpha \cdot b. Accumulate color: CR \leftarrow r{shaded} \cdot (1.0 - \alpha{acc}) + CR, CG \leftarrow g{shaded} \cdot (1.0 - \alpha{acc}) + CG, CB \leftarrow b{shaded} \cdot (1.0 - \alpha{acc}) + CB. Accumulate opacity: \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha \cdot (1.0 - \alpha{acc}) + \alpha{acc}. Ray Advancement: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{ray\increment}. 3. Finalization: Cap all accumulated color intensities CR, CG, CB at 1.0. Write final color (CR, CG, CB) and opacity \alpha{acc} to dynamicInfo->Color[0..3]. Write steps taken to dynamicInfo->NumberOfStepsTaken. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def castray(dataptr, scalardatatype, dynamicinfo, staticinfo, currentrendermode): # 1. Initialization numsteps = dynamicinfo.NumberOfStepsToTake raystart = dynamicinfo.TransformedStart rayincrement = dynamicinfo.TransformedIncrement xinc, yinc, zinc = staticinfo.DataIncrement scalartocolortf = staticinfo.Volume.ScalarToColorTF scalartoopacitytf = staticinfo.Volume.ScalarToOpacityTF # Accumulators accumr = 0.0 accumg = 0.0 accumb = 0.0 accumalpha = 0.0 # MIP variables maxval = 0.0 maxcolorr = 0.0 maxcolorg = 0.0 maxcolorb = 0.0 # Global max for dataset tracking (used for XRay normalization) globalmaxval = 0.0 # Ray position posx = raystart[0] posy = raystart[1] posz = raystart[2] # 2. Loop stepstaken = 0 for i in range(numsteps): # Early termination if accumalpha >= 1.0: break # Voxel coordinates (nearest neighbor) voxelx = round(posx) voxely = round(posy) voxelz = round(posz) # Data access offset = voxelz zinc + voxely yinc + voxelx xinc scalarval = dataptr[offset] # Update global max if scalarval > globalmaxval: globalmaxval = scalarval # Get transfer function values colorrgb = scalartocolortf(scalarval) rraw, graw, braw = colorrgb alpha = scalartoopacitytf(scalarval) # Mode processing if currentrendermode == 0: # MIP if scalarval > maxval: maxval = scalarval maxcolorr = rraw maxcolorg = graw maxcolorb = braw accumalpha = 1.0 - alpha accumr = alpha rraw accumg = alpha graw accumb = alpha braw elif currentrendermode == 1: # XRay accumr += scalarval accumg += scalarval accumb += scalarval elif currentrendermode == 2: # Full # Shading simplification per source: multiply raw color by opacity rshaded = alpha rraw gshaded = alpha graw bshaded = alpha braw accumr = rshaded (1.0 - accumalpha) + accumr accumg = gshaded (1.0 - accumalpha) + accumg accumb = bshaded (1.0 - accumalpha) + accumb accumalpha = alpha (1.0 - accumalpha) + accumalpha # Advance ray posx += rayincrement[0] posy += rayincrement[1] posz += rayincrement[2] stepstaken += 1 # 3. Finalization # Cap colors accumr = min(accumr, 1.0) accumg = min(accumg, 1.0) accumb = min(accumb, 1.0) dynamicinfo.Color[0] = accumr dynamicinfo.Color[1] = accumg dynamicinfo.Color[2] = accumb dynamicinfo.Color[3] = accumalpha dynamicinfo.NumberOfStepsTaken = stepstaken Parameters: currentRenderMode: Integer constant determining rendering mode. Values: 0 (modeMIP), 1 (modeXRay), 2 (modeFull). Default is 2 (modeFull). globalMaximumScalarValue: Static float used to track the maximum scalar value encountered in the dataset. Initialized to 0.0, updated during ray casting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Data Type Support: Only VTKUNSIGNEDCHAR and VTKUNSIGNEDSHORT are supported. Other types trigger a warning and do not render. Early Termination: The loop breaks if accumopacity >= 1.0. This optimization must be handled correctly in MIP mode where opacity does not accumulate traditionally. Shading Tables: The source mentions shading tables but the pseudocode simplifies shading to opacity color. In a full implementation, the shading tables (diffuse/specular) must be applied to the raw color values before accumulation in Full mode. Extends the composite ray casting function with interactive cropping functionality using a vtkBoxWidget. The implementation enables cropping on the mapper, parses six double values for region planes (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax), sets the cropping region flags to 0x0002000, and places a widget with a placement factor of 1.25 to manipulate the volume interactively. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is NumberOfStepsToTake. Early termination reduces steps in opaque regions. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, storing only accumulators and position. Performance: Fast due to nearest-neighbor interpolation and direct memory access, but aliasing may occur. Strengths: Single-pass multi-mode support, explicit shading control, early termination. Limitations: Restricted to VTKUNSIGNEDCHAR and VTKUNSIGNEDSHORT data types, nearest-neighbor interpolation artifacts, requires global maximum tracking for XRay normalization. Developed as a custom extension of vtkVolumeRayCastCompositeFunction within the VTK framework to support multiple rendering modes and Phong shading. Documented in unofficial VTK examples and tutorials. researchxr/3DMR, https://github.com/researchxr/3DMR, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) TotteKarlsson/vtkExamples, https://github.com/TotteKarlsson/vtkExamples, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Implicit Volumetric Rendering for RNR-Map
head: GSN-style rendering, RNR-Map rendering
body: Implicit Volumetric Rendering for RNR-Map is a technique used in the RNR-Map decoder to compute pixel colors by integrating occupancy and appearance along rays, modified from GSN to render individual pixels efficiently without upsampling. It adapts the GSN rendering pipeline to compute specific pixel values for navigation tasks rather than generating full-resolution images. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Query pose \mathbf{p} (camera position and orientation). Camera intrinsics. RNR-Map m, a tensor of size 128 \times 128 \times 32. Ray \mathbf{r} defined by pixel coordinates (h, w). Outputs: Rendered color c(\mathbf{r}, m) for the ray. Data Structures: RNR-Map (m): A 3D tensor with dimensions 128 \times 128 \times 32. Spatial dimensions (128 \times 128) represent a 32\text{m} \times 32\text{m} area. Each grid cell represents a physical region of 25\text{cm} \times 25\text{cm}. The depth dimension (32) is the feature dimension D. Latent Code (q): A vector of size D=32 retrieved from m via bilinear interpolation. Steps: 1. Ray Definition: Given query pose \mathbf{p} and camera intrinsics, determine the 3D position corresponding to pixel (h, w). Define a ray \mathbf{r}(u) passing through this pixel, where u is the distance from the camera center along the ray. 2. Sampling: Sample 3D points along the ray segment [un, uf] (near and far clipping planes). 3. Feature Retrieval: For each sampled 3D point, calculate its position in the RNR-Map coordinate system. Retrieve the corresponding latent feature q from the map m using bilinear interpolation, as map positions have continuous values. 4. Local Coordinate Transformation: Compute the local pose \mathbf{p}' (relative pose in a grid) for the sampled point. Determine the view direction \mathbf{d}. 5. Decoding: Pass \mathbf{p}', \mathbf{d}, and q into the decoder network. The latent code q modulates a linear layer. The decoder outputs occupancy \sigma and appearance \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^3 for the sampled point. 6. Integration: Calculate the rendered color c(\mathbf{r}, m) by integrating the product of transmittance, occupancy, and appearance along the ray. Formulas: The rendered color is computed as: c(\mathbf{r},m) = \int{un}^{uf} Tr(u) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(u),q)\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{r}(u), \mathbf{d}, q) du where transmittance Tr(u) is defined as: Tr(u) = \mathrm{exp} \left( -\int{un}^{u} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(u'), q) du' \right) Here, \mathbf{r} is the ray, m is the map, u is the distance along the ray, un and uf are near and far clipping planes, \sigma is occupancy, and \mathbf{a} is appearance. Parameters: Image resolution: 128 \times 128 pixels. RNR-Map tensor size: 128 \times 128 \times 32. Grid cell physical size: 25\text{cm} \times 25\text{cm}. Pitfalls: Unobserved regions are rendered as empty space. Small objects and texture details are often ignored. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderrnrmap(rayorigin, raydirection, rnrmap, unear, ufar, numsamples): """ Renders a single ray using the RNR-Map implicit volumetric rendering method. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera center. raydirection: 3D vector, viewing direction for pixel (h, w). rnrmap: Tensor of shape (128, 128, 32). unear: float, near clipping plane distance. ufar: float, far clipping plane distance. numsamples: int, number of discrete integration steps. Returns: color: 3D vector, rendered color. """ # 1. Define ray segment and step size ustep = (ufar - unear) / numsamples accumulatedsigmaintegral = 0.0 coloraccum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numsamples): # 2. Calculate 3D point on ray at current u u = unear + i ustep point3d = rayorigin + raydirection u # 3. Calculate map position and retrieve latent code q # Map coordinates are derived from world position relative to map origin mapx = (point3d.x - maporigin.x) / cellsize mapy = (point3d.y - maporigin.y) / cellsize mapz = 0.0 # 2D grid with feature depth # Bilinear interpolation for q from rnrmap (shape: 128, 128, 32) q = bilinearinterpolate3d(rnrmap, mapx, mapy, mapz) # 4. Compute local pose p' and view direction d # Local pose is relative position within the grid cell pprime = point3d % cellsize d = raydirection # 5. Decode occupancy and appearance # q modulates a linear layer to produce sigma and appearance sigma, appearance = applymodulationlinearlayer(q, pprime, d) # 6. Integrate using the continuous formula approximation # Tr(u) = exp(-integral{unear}^{u} sigma du) transmittance = exp(-accumulatedsigmaintegral) # Add contribution: c(r) = integral Tr(u) sigma a du coloraccum[0] += transmittance sigma appearance[0] ustep coloraccum[1] += transmittance sigma appearance[1] ustep coloraccum[2] += transmittance sigma appearance[2] ustep # Update accumulated integral for next sample accumulatedsigmaintegral += sigma ustep return coloraccum def bilinearinterpolate3d(tensor, x, y, z): # Standard bilinear interpolation on spatial dimensions, returning feature vector x0, y0 = floor(x), floor(y) x1, y1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1 fx, fy = x - x0, y - y0 v00 = tensor[x0, y0,:] v01 = tensor[x0, y1,:] v10 = tensor[x1, y0,:] v11 = tensor[x1, y1,:] w00 = (1 - fx) (1 - fy) w01 = (1 - fx) fy w10 = fx (1 - fy) w11 = fx fy return w00 v00 + w01 v01 + w10 v10 + w11 v11 def applymodulationlinearlayer(q, pprime, d): # q modulates a linear layer to output occupancy sigma and appearance a # Simplified implementation of the modulation mechanism weight = q.reshape(-1, 1) bias = q.reshape(-1, 1) 0.1 inputvec = concatenate(pprime, d) output = weight inputvec + bias sigma = sigmoid(output[0]) appearance = tanh(output[1:4]) return sigma, appearance Note: The exact decoder architecture follows GSN. The pseudocode implements the modulation linear layer described in the source. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples along the ray and the cost of the decoder network. Memory Complexity: The RNR-Map tensor size is 128 \times 128 \times 32. Measured Performance: The method is used in image-goal navigation tasks. It can reconstruct images from unseen environments and arbitrary scenes. Strengths: Efficient calculation for a small subset of pixels; can embed and reconstruct images from arbitrary scenes; sufficient for accurate camera pose inference. Limitations: Unobserved regions are rendered as empty space; small objects and texture details are often ignored; image quality is not state-of-the-art. When to use: Image-based localization and navigation tasks where efficient rendering of specific pixels is needed. When not to use: When high-fidelity full-image synthesis is required. The method was introduced in the paper "Renderable Neural Radiance Map for Visual Navigation". It is based on the Global Scene Network (GSN). The RNR-Map is used for image-based localization, where it is convolved with a target RNR-Map to infer camera pose. The technique allows for the reconstruction of images from arbitrary scenes and novel views. name: Specific Data Formats and Integrators
body: This family categorizes direct volume ray casting methods by their specific data storage formats (e.g., 3D textures, fixed-point grids) and the integrators used to process them Raymarching with 3D Volume Texture, Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting. It distinguishes between GPU-native texture-based ray marching and CPU-optimized fixed-point arithmetic, addressing performance bottlenecks in memory bandwidth and computational precision for large-scale datasets. All methods in this family build on the core mechanism of Direct volume ray casting. This method performs direct volume ray casting by representing the voxel space as a sampler3D texture and executing the ray marching loop within the fragment shader Raymarching with 3D Volume Texture. It replaces previous texture atlas approaches, allowing for larger XYZ volumes, simpler edge handling, and a unified in-memory representation shared with path tracing and isosurface modes Raymarching with 3D Volume Texture. Unlike meshing methods, it avoids the overhead of generating and uploading geometry via a single draw call Raymarching with 3D Volume Texture. It requires WebGL2 for Data3DTexture support Raymarching with 3D Volume Texture. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def raymarch3dtexture(volumedata, lutdata, cameraparams, params): """ Simulates GPU ray marching with 3D volume texture. volumedata: 3D array of normalized intensities [0,1] lutdata: 2D array (256, 4) mapping intensity to RGBA cameraparams: (origin, direction, tnear, tfar) params: (BREAKSTEPS, maxSteps, volumeScale, gNChannels) """ origin, direction, tnear, tfar = cameraparams BREAKSTEPS, maxSteps, volumeScale, gNChannels = params # 1. Calculate Step Count scaledsteps = BREAKSTEPS math.sqrt(sum((d / s) 2 for d, s in zip(direction, volumeScale))) csteps = max(1.0, min(scaledsteps, maxSteps)) # 2. Calculate Inverse Step Size invstep = (tfar - tnear) / csteps # 3. Ray Dithering r = random.random() acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 # 4. Marching Loop for k in range(int(csteps)): t = tnear + (k + r) invstep pos = [origin[i] + t direction[i] for i in range(3)] # 5. Sample Volume (normalized to [0,1] for texture lookup) intensity = volumedata[int(pos[0])][int(pos[1])][int(pos[2])] # 6. Reconstruct Color/Alpha from LUT lutidx = int(min(255, max(0, intensity 255.0))) lutentry = lutdata[lutidx] alpha = lutentry[3] color = lutentry[:3] # 7. Front-to-Back Compositing weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = [acccolor[i] + color[i] weight for i in range(3)] accalpha += weight if accalpha >= 1.0: break return acccolor Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that replaces standard floating-point arithmetic with fixed-point operations for interpolation and accumulation to improve computational efficiency Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting. It is specifically implemented in the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) via the vtkFixedPointVolumeRayCastMapper class Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting. Unlike general-purpose ray casting which may rely on hardware floating-point units, this method optimizes performance by intercepting decimal parts and using integer-based arithmetic, making it particularly suitable for large-scale volumetric datasets such as seismic or medical images where memory bandwidth and CPU cycles are constrained Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting. It builds on the standard front-to-back compositing algorithm but introduces optimizations like MinMaxVolume generation to skip empty voxels Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fixedpointvolumeraycast(volumedata, camera, transferfunctions, properties): """ Simulates the core fixed-point volume ray casting loop. volumedata: dict with 'dims' (z,y,x), 'spacing' (dx,dy,dz), 'origin' (ox,oy,oz), 'data' (3D array) camera: dict with 'origin' (ox,oy,oz), 'direction' (dx,dy,dz), 'width', 'height', 'pixeldiagonal' transferfunctions: dict with 'colormap' and 'opacitymap' functions properties: dict with 'shadeon', 'sampledistance' """ width, height = camera['width'], camera['height'] outputimage = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] # Precompute MinMaxVolume for optimization # Not given in the sources. SCALE = 1024 SHIFT = 6 sampledist = properties.get('sampledistance', camera['pixeldiagonal'] / 5.0) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayo = camera['origin'] rayd = camera['direction'] lend = math.sqrt(sum(d 2 for d in rayd)) rayd = [d / lend for d in rayd] tmin, tmax = intersectboundingbox(rayo, rayd, volumedata) if tmax < tmin: continue raydfp = [int(round(d SCALE)) for d in rayd] acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 t = tmin while t < tmax: pos = [rayo[i] + rayd[i] t for i in range(3)] if not isinsidevolume(pos, volumedata): t += sampledist continue posfp = [int(round(p SCALE)) for p in pos] scalarval = interpolatefixedpoint(posfp, volumedata) color, alpha = transferfunctions'colormap', transferfunctions'opacitymap' weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = [acccolor[i] + color[i] weight for i in range(3)] accalpha += weight if accalpha >= 0.99: break t += sampledist outputimage[y][x] = (acccolor[0], acccolor[1], acccolor[2], accalpha) return outputimage def computeminmaxvolume(volumedata): # Not given in the sources. def intersectboundingbox(rayo, rayd, volumedata): bounds = volumedata['bounds'] t1 = (bounds[0] - rayo[0]) / rayd[0] if rayd[0] != 0 else float('-inf') t2 = (bounds[1] - rayo[0]) / rayd[0] if rayd[0] != 0 else float('inf') t3 = (bounds[2] - rayo[1]) / rayd[1] if rayd[1] != 0 else float('-inf') t4 = (bounds[3] - rayo[1]) / rayd[1] if rayd[1] != 0 else float('inf') t5 = (bounds[4] - rayo[2]) / rayd[2] if rayd[2] != 0 else float('-inf') t6 = (bounds[5] - rayo[2]) / rayd[2] if rayd[2] != 0 else float('inf') tmin = max(min(t1, t2), min(t3, t4), min(t5, t6)) tmax = min(max(t1, t2), max(t3, t4), max(t5, t6)) return tmin, tmax def isinsidevolume(pos, volumedata): bounds = volumedata['bounds'] return bounds[0] <= pos[0] <= bounds[1] and bounds[2] <= pos[1] <= bounds[3] and bounds[4] <= pos[2] <= bounds[5] def interpolatefixedpoint(posfp, volumedata): # Not given in the sources. Definition: Solves transport for multiple rays in parallel on CPU by iterating over rays and calling the single-ray solver for each. Step: Loop ray from 0 to numrays - 1. Calculate offset = ray numsamples. Call solveoneray with sigma + offset, source + offset, numsamples, ds, and initialintensity[ray]. Store result in output[ray]. Layout: Input arrays sigma, source, initialintensity are row-major [ray][sample]. Output array output is [ray]. Definition: Resamples an AMR hierarchy onto a uniform grid at the finest resolution for parallel rendering. Step: Evenly subdivide the resulting grid. Render each part in parallel on a separate processor. Combine partial images using binary-swap composition. The use of 3D textures for ray marching became standard with the advent of programmable GPUs and WebGL2, allowing direct access to volumetric data without intermediate geometry Raymarching with 3D Volume Texture. Fixed-point ray casting was developed to address performance limitations in CPU-based rendering engines like VTK, particularly for large medical and seismic datasets where floating-point precision was not strictly necessary for visual fidelity but consumed significant resources Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting. wyh1309/hpcfoundationaldemos, https://github.com/wyh1309/hpcfoundationaldemos, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Visualization of Scalar Adaptive Mesh Refinement Data, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc901373/?q=adaptive mesh refinement visualization ray casting, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Raymarching with 3D Volume Texture
head: 3D Texture Raycasting, 3D texture raymarching, Ray tracing through 3D mesh, RayMarchedAtlasVolume, Wolfenstein-style 3D raycasting
body: This method performs direct volume ray casting by representing the voxel space as a sampler3D texture and executing the ray marching loop within the fragment shader. It replaces previous texture atlas approaches, allowing for larger XYZ volumes, simpler edge handling, and a unified in-memory representation shared with path tracing and isosurface modes. Unlike meshing methods, it avoids the overhead of generating and uploading geometry via a single draw call. Inputs: Volume Data: A 3D texture (volumeTexture) containing voxel intensities. Lookup Table: A 2D texture (gLutTexture) mapping intensity to color/alpha. Camera/Scene: Ray origin, direction (eyed), near/far clip planes (tnear, tfar), and volume scale (volumeScale). Parameters: BREAKSTEPS, maxSteps, gNChannels, SLICES, and maskAlpha. Outputs: Fragment Color: The final composited color and alpha for each pixel. CPU-side Data Buffer Layout: The volume data is stored in a 1D array representing a 3D grid with up to 4 channels. The layout is defined as: \text{data}[i + ix \cdot 4 + iy \cdot 4 \cdot sx + iz \cdot 4 \cdot sx \cdot sy] Where: i is the channel index (0–3). ix, iy, iz are the voxel coordinates. sx, sy are the width and height of the volume. Raw intensities are normalized to the 0–255 range before upload. GPU-side Textures: 1. volumeTexture: A Data3DTexture requiring WebGL2. Holds the 8-bit voxel intensities. 2. gLutTexture: A DataTexture of size 256 \times 4. It contains a combined Lookup Table (LUT) for up to 4 active channels, mapping intensity to RGBA. 1. CPU Data Preparation: Iterate through all active channels (0 to gNChannels - 1). For each voxel (ix, iy, iz), normalize the raw intensity to the 0–255 range and store it in the buffer at the calculated offset. Masking (if enabled): If a mask channel is specified and maskAlpha < 1.0, iterate through the volume again. For each voxel, determine maskVal (1.0 if mask intensity > 0, else maskAlpha) and multiply the existing intensity value by maskVal. Upload the buffer to the volumeTexture. 2. Vertex Shader (Setup): Render a single quad covering the screen. Pass ray direction (eyed) and origin to the fragment shader. 3. Fragment Shader (Ray Marching): Calculate Step Count: Compute the scaled steps based on the ray length and volume scale: \text{scaledSteps} = \text{BREAK\STEPS} \times \left\| \frac{\text{eye\d.xyz}}{\text{volumeScale}} \right\| Clamp Steps: Clamp the step count to the valid range: \text{csteps} = \text{clamp}(\text{scaledSteps}, 1.0, \text{maxSteps}) Calculate Inverse Step Size: \text{invstep} = \frac{\text{tfar} - \text{tnear}}{\text{csteps}} Where tfar and tnear are the far and near clip distances. Ray Dithering: Compute a random offset to reduce banding: r = \text{rand}(\text{eye\d.xy}) Note: The original implementation disabled dithering for single-slice volumes (SLICES == 1.0) to prevent Moiré patterns, but the current implementation unconditionally applies dithering. Marching Loop: For k = 0 to \text{csteps} - 1: 1. Compute current ray position: \text{pos} = \text{origin} + (\text{tnear} + (k + r) \cdot \text{invstep}) \cdot \text{direction} 2. Sample the volume texture: \text{intensity} = \text{sampler3D}(\text{volumeTexture}, \text{pos}) 3. Reconstruct Color/Alpha: Use the sampled intensity and gNChannels to index into gLutTexture and retrieve the RGBA value. 4. Composite: Perform front-to-back alpha blending using the retrieved RGBA and the accumulated result. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return min(max(val, minval), maxval) def rand(vec): # Deterministic pseudo-random hash for per-pixel dither return (sin(dot(vec, vec(12.9898, 78.233))) 43758.5453) % 1.0 def raymarch(origin, direction, tnear, tfar, volumetexture, luttexture, breaksteps, volumescale, maxsteps, nchannels): # 1. Calculate Step Count scaledsteps = breaksteps length(direction / volumescale) csteps = clamp(scaledsteps, 1.0, maxsteps) # 2. Calculate Inverse Step Size invstep = (tfar - tnear) / csteps # 3. Ray Dithering r = rand(direction.xy) acccolor = vec(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # 4. Marching Loop for k in range(int(csteps)): t = tnear + (k + r) invstep pos = origin + t direction # 5. Sample Volume (pos assumed normalized to [0,1]) intensity = texture(volumetexture, pos).r # 6. Reconstruct Color/Alpha from LUT # LUT is 256x4. Map intensity (0-255) to x, channel index to y. lutu = intensity / 255.0 lutv = nchannels / 4.0 lutentry = texture(luttexture, vec(lutu, lutv)) # 7. Front-to-Back Compositing alpha = lutentry.a color = lutentry.rgb alpha acccolor = acccolor + color (1.0 - accalpha) accalpha = accalpha + alpha (1.0 - accalpha) if accalpha >= 1.0: break return acccolor BREAKSTEPS: Base number of steps. Typical values depend on volume resolution and desired quality. volumeScale: Uniform vec3 scaling the volume dimensions for step calculation. maxSteps: Upper limit for the number of steps. gNChannels: Uniform integer specifying the number of active channels (up to 4). SLICES: Constant float indicating the number of slices (depth) in the volume. WebGL1 Compatibility: The method requires Data3DTexture and sampler3D, which are WebGL2 features. It will fail on WebGL1 fallback paths. Single-Slice Moiré: Random ray dithering causes Moiré patterns in single-slice volumes. The original code disabled dithering for SLICES==1.0, but the new code unconditionally applies dithering, potentially reintroducing this artifact. Masking Semantics: Masking is applied by scaling per-voxel intensity before LUT lookup. This affects alpha and color, not just RGB, and is applied up to 4 times (once per channel). Performance: When masking is enabled, the CPU traverses the full 3D volume twice per active channel (once for intensity, once for mask), which is costly for large volumes. Uses fixed-point arithmetic instead of floating-point for sampling and accumulation. Chosen when hardware lacks robust FP32 support or for deterministic results. Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting Uses 2D texture atlases to represent volume slices. Chosen for WebGL1 compatibility or when 3D textures are not supported. Texture Atlas Raymarching Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of steps per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V \cdot C), where V is the volume voxel count and C is the number of channels (up to 4). Measured Performance: Rendered 128x128x128 or 256x256x256 voxels in 12.4ms. Strengths: Avoids overhead of many draw calls and VBO management. Allows larger XYZ volumes compared to texture atlases. Simplifies edge handling compared to atlas methods. Shares memory representation with path tracing and isosurface modes. Limitations: Requires WebGL2. Limited to 4 channels. Cannot "pre-fuse" channels on the GPU as it does not write to 3D textures. Turning channels on/off requires rebuilding the 3D texture. 8-bit precision limits dynamic range. When to Use: When WebGL2 is available, large volumes are needed, and a unified memory representation with other rendering modes (path tracing) is desired. When Not to Use: On WebGL1-only hardware, or when more than 4 channels are required. This method was introduced by toloudis in Pull Request #370 for AllenCell/vole-core, dated January 30, 2026. It evolved from earlier techniques that represented voxel space in a 3D texture for Wolfenstein-style 3D raycasting. The primary motivation was to simplify the in-memory representation by sharing the 3D texture with path tracing and isosurface modes, and to overcome the limitations of texture atlases (such as edge issues and fusion overhead). OpenGL Meshing Slower Than Not Meshing, https://stackoverflow.com/questions/66466017/opengl-meshing-slower-than-not-meshing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) convert raymarch to use 3d texture instead of atlas., https://github.com/AllenCell/vole-core/pull/370, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting
head: vtkFixedPointVolumeRayCastMapper, Fixed-Point Arithmetic in Inner Loop
body: Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that replaces standard floating-point arithmetic with fixed-point arithmetic for interpolation and accumulation to improve computational efficiency. Implemented primarily via VTK's vtkFixedPointVolumeRayCastMapper, it optimizes the innermost rendering loop by precomputing floating-point values into scaled integers (typically scaled by 1024) and using integer shifts for coordinate conversion. It is designed for large structured volumetric datasets like seismic or medical images, leveraging early termination and empty voxel skipping to reduce invalid computation. It distinguishes itself from floating-point ray casting by trading some precision for speed, specifically avoiding time-consuming floating-point operations and decimal interception during resampling. Inputs: Volume Data: A structured 3D grid stored in vtkImageData with dimensions (Z, Y, X), spacing (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z), and origin (0, 0, 0). Scalar data is a 1-component array (e.g., int16, uint16). For seismic data, this originates from SEG-Y format (3200-byte header string, 400-byte binary header, 240-byte trace header) but is preprocessed into vtkImageData. Transfer Functions: Color transfer function (vtkColorTransferFunction) maps scalar values to RGB. Opacity transfer function (vtkPiecewiseFunction) maps scalar values to opacity \alpha. Gradient transfer function (optional) maps gradient magnitude to opacity/weight. Volume Properties: Shading coefficients (ambient 0.2, diffuse 0.9, specular 0.2, specular power 10), interpolation type (linear), and light position. Camera/View: View frustum, clipping planes, and image dimensions. Outputs: Image Buffer: A 2D RGBA image rendered to the screen or off-screen buffer. The core data structure is vtkImageData, defining dimensions, spacing, origin, and scalar arrays. The mapper internally generates a MinMaxVolume (precomputed min/max values for sub-volumes) to optimize ray casting by skipping empty regions. 1. Initialization: Instantiate vtkFixedPointVolumeRayCastMapper and assign input vtkImageData. Configure vtkVolumeProperty with transfer functions and shading parameters. 2. Ray Generation: For each pixel, generate a ray from the camera origin through the pixel center into the volume. 3. Sampling: Determine sample positions along the ray. The sample distance ds is typically set to the pixel diagonal divided by 5 or a fixed value like 1.0. Fixed-point interpolation is used instead of floating-point to accelerate arithmetic and intercept decimal parts. Linear interpolation is preferred over nearest-neighbor to avoid obvious edges. 4. Classification: Retrieve the scalar value s at the interpolated sample position. Map s to color C and opacity \alpha using the transfer functions. 5. Compositing (Front-to-Back): Initialize accumulated color C{acc} = (0,0,0,0) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0. For each sample i along the ray, calculate contribution: C{acc} = C{acc} + Ci \cdot \alphai \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alphai \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}). 6. Early Termination: If \alpha{acc} approaches 1 (e.g., > 0.99), the pixel is effectively opaque. Skip the remaining voxels along the ray to eliminate invalid computation. 7. Empty Voxel Skipping: Use the precomputed MinMaxVolume or boundary checks to skip over empty elements with no contribution. 8. Shading: If ShadeOn() is enabled, calculate lighting effects (diffuse/specular) based on the gradient of the volume data at the sample point. Classification data is used after interpolation to filter high-frequency color components. 9. Output: Write the final C{acc} to the pixel buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fixedpointvolumeraycast(volumedata, camera, transferfunctions, properties): """ Simulates the core fixed-point volume ray casting loop. volumedata: dict with 'dims' (z,y,x), 'spacing' (dx,dy,dz), 'origin' (ox,oy,oz), 'data' (3D array) camera: dict with 'origin' (ox,oy,oz), 'direction' (dx,dy,dz), 'width', 'height', 'pixeldiagonal' transferfunctions: dict with 'colormap' and 'opacitymap' functions properties: dict with 'shadeon', 'sampledistance' """ width, height = camera['width'], camera['height'] outputimage = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] # Precompute MinMaxVolume for optimization minmaxvolume = computeminmaxvolume(volumedata) # Fixed-point scale factor and shift SCALE = 1024 SHIFT = 6 # Sample distance sampledist = properties.get('sampledistance', camera['pixeldiagonal'] / 5.0) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayo = camera['origin'] rayd = camera['direction'] # Normalize direction lend = (rayd[0]2 + rayd[1]2 + rayd[2]2)0.5 rayd = (rayd[0]/lend, rayd[1]/lend, rayd[2]/lend) # Ray-box intersection tmin, tmax = intersectboundingbox(rayo, rayd, volumedata) if tmax < tmin: continue # Fixed-point precomputation for ray direction raydfp = (int(round(rayd[0] SCALE)), int(round(rayd[1] SCALE)), int(round(rayd[2] SCALE))) # Initialize compositing acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 t = tmin while t < tmax: # Compute sample position posx = rayo[0] + rayd[0] t posy = rayo[1] + rayd[1] t posz = rayo[2] + rayd[2] t # Check bounds if not isinsidevolume(posx, posy, posz, volumedata): t += sampledist continue # Fixed-point interpolation # Convert world coordinates to fixed-point for integer arithmetic posxfp = int(round(posx SCALE)) posyfp = int(round(posy SCALE)) poszfp = int(round(posz SCALE)) scalarval = interpolatefixedpoint(posxfp, posyfp, poszfp, volumedata) # Classification color, alpha = transferfunctions'colormap', transferfunctions'opacitymap' # Shading if properties['shadeon']: grad = computegradient(posx, posy, posz, volumedata) # Apply lighting model (diffuse/specular) # Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, plus overhead for MinMaxVolume optimization. Performance: Offers a balance between performance and accuracy. Fixed-point arithmetic improves efficiency by avoiding time-consuming floating-point operations. Considered more efficient than standard OpenGL-based implementations in some aspects. Strengths: High image quality, efficient handling of large datasets via fixed-point math and early termination, good support for medical and seismic data formats. Limitations: Fixed-point precision limits dynamic range compared to floating-point. Requires preprocessed vtkImageData. Not suitable for unstructured grids without conversion. When to Use: When rendering large, structured volumetric datasets (seismic, medical) where performance is critical and fixed-point precision is sufficient. When Not to Use: When high dynamic range or extreme precision is required, or when working with unstructured data. Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting was developed as part of the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) library, specifically within the vtkFixedPointVolumeRayCastMapper class. It was designed to address the computational demands of 3D seismic data visualization, which involves large datasets in SEG-Y format. The method leverages the fact that many volume rendering operations (interpolation, accumulation) can be approximated with fixed-point arithmetic to gain speed, particularly on hardware where floating-point units were historically less efficient or when integer arithmetic was preferred for throughput. It is widely used in seismic exploration and medical imaging visualization systems. name: NeRF/CuVol/NVol/SVox1
head: Volume Rendering (NeRF/CuVol/NVol/SVox1)
body: This family implements neural volume rendering using sparse, hierarchical grid structures (specifically SVox2) to represent density and color fields, enabling efficient training and inference for novel view synthesis. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Raymarching with 3D Volume Texture by utilizing learnable sparse voxel grids with spherical harmonic basis functions for color, rather than fixed 3D textures, and from Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting by relying on GPU-accelerated fused kernels for both forward and backward passes during gradient-based optimization. All methods in this family build on the core mechanism of Direct volume ray casting. The implementation relies on a sparse grid structure (SparseGridSpec) that stores density (densitydata) and spherical harmonic coefficients (shdata) at active voxel locations. The rendering process is executed via fused CUDA kernels that handle ray marching, alpha compositing, and gradient computation in a single pass or tightly coupled sequence. Key data structures include: SparseGridSpec: Contains densitydata, shdata, links (for sparse connectivity), offset, scaling, basisdim, basistype, basisdata, backgroundlinks, and backgrounddata. CameraSpec: Defines camera parameters c2w, fx, fy, cx, cy, width, height, ndccoeffx, ndccoeffy. RaysSpec: Contains origins and dirs for the batch of rays. RenderOptions: Controls rendering behavior with backgroundbrightness, stepsize, sigmathresh, stopthresh, nearclip, usesphericclip, and lastsampleopaque. GridOutputGrads: Stores gradients graddensityout, gradshout, gradbasisout, gradbackgroundout, maskout, maskbackgroundout. The forward pass computes the predicted RGB color by integrating along rays. If background links are defined and non-empty, a background color is accumulated. The transmission is computed in log space if background rendering is enabled or if a beta loss is applied. The primary implementation uses the SVox2 library for sparse grid management. It supports dynamic upsampling of the grid resolution during training, adjusting density and weight thresholds to maintain sparsity. It also supports background modeling via separate background links and data. Link The rendering is performed using fused CUDA kernels (renderraykernel, renderbackgroundkernel, renderraybackwardkernel, renderbackgroundbackwardkernel) to minimize memory bandwidth bottlenecks. Thread block sizes are configurable via TRACERAYCUDATHREADS, TRACERAYBGCUDATHREADS, and TRACERAYBKWDCUDATHREADS. The method integrates with a standard PyTorch training loop, computing MSE loss between ground truth and predicted RGB, and updating grid parameters (density, SH coefficients, basis) with specific learning rate schedules. It supports sparsity and beta losses. The specific implementation details provided originate from the OSHMOS/IPRF project, an unofficial repository hosted on GitHub. The code demonstrates a practical application of neural volume rendering using sparse grids, focusing on efficient training and upsampling strategies. name: Data Value Zoom
head: Domain Zoom, Intensity domain scaling, Scalar Range Zoom
body: Data Value Zoom is a technique for exploring narrow regions of scalar data values by dynamically adjusting the mapping of floating-point data values to the integer indices required by graphics hardware. It acts as a zoom function in the data domain, rescaling the intensity range so that the colour map's minimum and maximum match the selected interval, unlike intensity clipping which simply discards out-of-range values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar value v, minThreshold, maxThreshold, and DATAMIN. Output: A rescaled value v' mapped to the interval [0, 1], or DATAMIN if v falls outside the threshold range. Data Structures: The technique modifies the scalar-to-integer mapping function used by graphics hardware to index the transfer function or lookup table (LUT). Instead of a fixed global range, the mapping dynamically scales the active intensity domain so that the colour map's minimum and maximum correspond to the user-defined thresholds. Steps: 1. Calculate discardRatio as 1.0 / (\text{maxThreshold} - \text{minThreshold}). 2. If v > \text{maxThreshold}, set v \leftarrow \text{DATAMIN}. 3. Else if v < \text{minThreshold}, set v \leftarrow \text{DATAMIN}. 4. Else, set v \leftarrow v - \text{minThreshold}. 5. Else, set v \leftarrow v \times \text{discardRatio}. 6. Return v. Formulas: The mapping function M(v) is defined as: M(v) = \begin{cases} \text{DATAMIN} & \text{if } v > \text{maxThreshold} \text{ or } v < \text{minThreshold} \\ (v - \text{minThreshold}) \times \frac{1}{\text{maxThreshold} - \text{minThreshold}} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where v is the input scalar value, minThreshold and maxThreshold define the active zoom interval, and DATAMIN is the lower bound of the data range used for out-of-bounds values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def datavaluezoom(val, minThreshold, maxThreshold, DATAMIN): discardRatio = 1.0 / (maxThreshold - minThreshold) if val > maxThreshold: val = DATAMIN elif val < minThreshold: val = DATAMIN else: val = val - minThreshold val = val discardRatio return val Parameters: minThreshold: Lower bound for scaling. Example value: 1.12\times10^{-2} Jy/beam. maxThreshold: Upper bound for scaling. Example value: 0.3609 Jy/beam. DATAMIN: Lower bound of the data range, used to map out-of-bounds values. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If maxThreshold equals minThreshold, the discardRatio calculation fails; a guard must ensure maxThreshold > minThreshold. Out-of-Bounds Handling: Values outside the zoom range are mapped to DATAMIN, which must be correctly interpreted by the transfer function (e.g., mapped to transparent or background colour) to avoid rendering artifacts. Quantization: The rescaled float values are converted to integers for hardware indexing, which may introduce quantization artifacts if the zoom interval is extremely narrow relative to the LUT resolution. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample during ray casting. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a dynamic way to explore features within divergent data ranges without discarding values. Limitations: Does not improve spatial resolution; only adjusts the scalar-to-integer mapping for hardware rendering. When to use: When exploring narrow regions of data values or adjusting intensity bounds for divergent ranges in techniques like Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP). When not to use: Not given in the sources. Data Value Zoom, also referred to as Intensity domain scaling, was described for use in the Cave Automatic Virtual Environment (CAVE) to allow interactive exploration of narrow data regions by adjusting the floating-point to integer mapping required by graphics hardware. The technique is implemented as a shader kernel that rescales intensity bounds for visualisation techniques such as Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) and Adaptive Volume Image Projection (AVIP). name: Vectorial Volume Rendering
head: Direct Volume Rendering with Ray Casting, Vectorial Volume Ray Casting, Volume Rendering for Vectorial Volumes
body:
Vectorial Volume Rendering extends standard scalar direct volume ray casting to handle input data where each voxel contains a distribution of material probabilities rather than a single scalar intensity. It solves the problem of visualizing classified multi-material volumes by computing gradients and optical properties from weighted material contributions, allowing for the simultaneous rendering of multiple tissue or material types with distinct visual attributes. Unlike scalar methods that map a single value to color/opacity, this method determines sample properties based on the probabilistic mixture of materials, distinguishing it from siblings like Standard Ray Casting which assumes a single scalar field per voxel. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of K material probability volumes Pk, where Pk(x,y,z) represents the probability of the k-th material at each voxel location. A set of user-defined material properties for each material k, consisting of a color vector \mathbf{C}k (RGB) and an opacity scalar \alphak. Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the composited color \mathbf{C}{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out}. Data Structures Material Probability Volumes: K 3D arrays of floating-point values, normalized such that \sum{k=1}^{K} Pk(x,y,z) = 1 for all voxels. Material Properties: A list or array of size K, where each entry contains \mathbf{C}k \in \mathbb{R}^3 and \alphak \in [0, 1]. Density Volume: An intermediate 3D array D of the same dimensions as the input volumes, used for gradient calculation. Numbered Steps 1. Ray Definition: For each pixel, define a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} intersecting the volume bounding box at t{near} and t{far}. Discretize the segment into N samples with step \Delta t. 2. Sampling Material Probabilities: For each sample position \mathbf{p}i along the ray, retrieve the probability p{k,i} for each material k \in \{1, \dots, K\} using tri-linear interpolation from the K probability volumes. 3. Density Volume Construction: To enable gradient calculation, construct a scalar density volume D where the value at each voxel is the weighted sum of material opacities: D(x,y,z) = \sum{k=1}^{K} pk(x,y,z) \alphak Here, pk is the material probability and \alphak is the user-assigned opacity for material k. This replaces the traditional density hok to simplify user input by avoiding confusion between density and opacity. 4. Gradient Calculation: Compute the gradient 
abla D(\mathbf{p}i) at the current sample position \mathbf{p}i using the constructed density volume D. Any standard scalar volume gradient calculation method (e.g., central differences) may be applied. This gradient serves as the surface normal for shading. 5. Transfer Function and Shading: Determine the sample color \mathbf{c}i and opacity \alphai using one of two methods: Class Decision Method: Calculate the first derivative of each material probability pk along the ray direction. Select the material k^ that yields the maximum derivative. Assign the sample color \mathbf{c}i = \mathbf{C}{k^} and opacity \alphai = \alpha{k^}. Composed Color and Opacity Method: Compute the sample color and opacity directly from the interpolated probabilities and material properties. The sample color is the weighted sum of material colors: \mathbf{c}i = \sum{k=1}^{K} p{k,i} \mathbf{C}k. The sample opacity is derived from the total density or a specific transfer function applied to the probabilities, often enhanced by boundary detection using the gradient 
abla D to increase opacity in heterogeneous regions and decrease it in homogeneous ones. Shading: Apply Phong’s shading model using the gradient 
abla D(\mathbf{p}i) as the normal vector to modulate the base color \mathbf{c}i into a shaded color \mathbf{c}'i. 6. Compositing: Composite the shaded sample (\mathbf{c}'i, \alphai) into the accumulated pixel color and opacity using the front-to-back volume rendering equation: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}'i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai Initialize \mathbf{C}{acc} = (0,0,0) and \alpha{acc} = 0. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vectorialvolumerendering(probabilityvolumes, materialproperties, ray, numsamples): """ probabilityvolumes: List of K 3D arrays (float), shape (Dx, Dy, Dz) materialproperties: List of K tuples (color: (R,G,B), opacity: float) ray: Object with origin o, direction d, tnear, tfar numsamples: Integer N """ K = len(probabilityvolumes) # Precompute Density Volume for Gradient Calculation # D[x,y,z] = sum(pk alphak) densityvolume = zeroslike(probabilityvolumes[0]) for k in range(K): pk = probabilityvolumes[k] alphak = materialproperties[k].opacity densityvolume += pk alphak # Compute Gradient of Density Volume (e.g., using central differences) # gradD is a 3D array of vectors (dx, dy, dz) gradD = computegradient(densityvolume) # Initialize Accumulators acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # Ray Marching dt = (ray.tfar - ray.tnear) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): t = ray.tnear + i dt pos = ray.o + t ray.d # 1. Sample Material Probabilities via Trilinear Interpolation probs = [] for k in range(K): pval = trilinearinterpolate(probabilityvolumes[k], pos) probs.append(pval) # 2. Get Gradient at Position # Interpolate gradient from precomputed gradD normal = trilinearinterpolatevector(gradD, pos) # 3. Determine Sample Color and Opacity # Using Composed Color and Opacity method as primary example # Note: Class Decision method would select max derivative material instead samplecolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) samplealpha = 0.0 # Compose Color for k in range(K): ck = materialproperties[k].color samplecolor = ( samplecolor[0] + probs[k] ck[0], samplecolor[1] + probs[k] ck[1], samplecolor[2] + probs[k] ck[2]) # Compose Opacity (Simplified: weighted sum of opacities) # More complex transfer functions may use normal magnitude for boundary enhancement for k in range(K): alphak = materialproperties[k].opacity samplealpha += probs[k] alphak # Clamp opacity samplealpha = min(samplealpha, 1.0) # 4. Shading (Phong Model) # Requires light direction L, view direction V, and normal N # Assuming standard Phong parameters are available shadedcolor = applyphongshading(samplecolor, normal, ray.d) # 5. Front-to-Back Compositing if samplealpha > 0: # Contribution of current sample contribution = (1.0 - accalpha) shadedcolor samplealpha acccolor = ( acccolor[0] + contribution[0], acccolor[1] + contribution[1], acccolor[2] + contribution[2]) accalpha += (1.0 - accalpha) samplealpha return acccolor, accalpha Parameters K: Number of materials. Typical values depend on the segmentation (e.g., 3-10 for medical tissues). \alphak: User-assigned opacity for material k. Range [0, 1]. \mathbf{C}k: User-assigned color for material k. Range [0, 1] per channel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Gradient Noise: Since the density volume D is a weighted sum of probabilities, noise in probability estimates can lead to noisy gradients, affecting shading quality. Class Decision Ambiguity: In the Class Decision method, if multiple materials have similar derivatives, the selection may be unstable. Opacity Summation: In the Composed method, simple summation of opacities can exceed 1.0 if not clamped or modeled physically (e.g., Beer-Lambert). Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K) per pixel, where N is the number of samples and K is the number of materials. This is linear in both N and K, making it more expensive than scalar rendering (O(N)) due to the need to sample K volumes and compute a weighted sum. Memory Complexity: O(V \cdot K) for storing K probability volumes, plus O(V) for the intermediate density volume and its gradient, where V is the number of voxels. Strengths: Allows for the simultaneous visualization of multiple classified materials with distinct colors and opacities without requiring separate rendering passes for each material. The use of a density volume for gradients provides a consistent normal field for shading across material boundaries. Limitations: Computationally heavier than scalar rendering due to multiple texture fetches and interpolation operations per sample. The quality of shading depends heavily on the accuracy of the probability volumes and the constructed density field. When to Use: When visualizing multi-material volumes where material boundaries and internal structures of different classes need to be seen simultaneously with distinct visual cues. When Not to Use: For single-material scalar volumes where standard ray casting is sufficient and faster. Vectorial Volume Rendering was developed to address the limitations of scalar volume rendering when applied to classified multi-material data. Traditional scalar methods map a single value to optical properties, which is insufficient for representing the probabilistic nature of segmented medical or scientific data where voxels may contain mixtures of materials. The method expands on the scalar volume rendering pipeline by introducing specific techniques for gradient calculation (using a weighted density volume) and transfer function design (Class Decision or Composed Color/Opacity). It was proposed in the context of visualizing spatially aligned volumes after 3D/3D image registration, where multiple modalities or segmentations need to be merged and rendered together. The approach builds on the foundational work of Drebin et al. regarding density-based gradient calculation for shading. name: OpenMP Parallelization
head: OpenMP Parallelization for Volume Rendering, yt OpenMP volume rendering
body: This method uses OpenMP to parallelize the computation of rays intersecting a single data brick, complementing MPI domain decomposition which splits the dataset across processes. It distributes the workload of rays within a brick across multiple threads on a shared-memory node. Inputs and outputs: Input: A volume data brick, camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, image plane resolution), and the number of OpenMP threads N{threads}. Output: The rendered image pixels corresponding to the rays intersecting the brick. Data structures: The method operates on a list of rays intersecting a specific brick. Each ray is processed independently, requiring no shared state between threads except for the final accumulation into the image buffer, which is handled by assigning disjoint sets of rays to threads. Numbered steps: 1. Thread Initialization: Determine the number of threads N{threads}. This is controlled by the numthreads parameter in the rendering function (e.g., snapshot()) or the environment variable OMPNUMTHREADS. If not specified, the default is the total number of cores available on the symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) platform. 2. Ray Assignment: Identify all rays that intersect the current data brick. 3. Parallel Execution: Distribute the identified rays among the N{threads} threads. Each thread executes the standard direct volume ray casting pipeline (sampling, interpolation, classification, compositing) for its assigned subset of rays. 4. Result Accumulation: Each thread writes its computed pixel values to the global image buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderbrickopenmp(brick, camera, numthreads): # 1. Identify rays intersecting the brick rays = [] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): rayorigin = camera.origin + (x - camera.width / 2.0) camera.xaxis + (y - camera.height / 2.0) camera.yaxis raydirection = camera.direction # Ray-AABB intersection test tmin = [(brick.bbox.min[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] tmax = [(brick.bbox.max[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] tnear = max(min(tmin), 0.0) tfar = max(max(tmax), 0.0) if tnear < tfar: rays.append({'x': x, 'y': y, 'origin': rayorigin, 'direction': raydirection, 'tnear': tnear, 'tfar': tfar}) # 2. Initialize image buffer imagebuffer = [[None for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] # 3. Parallel execution over rays # OpenMP distributes 'rays' across numthreads threads # In practice: #pragma omp parallel for numthreads(numthreads) for ray in rays: # Standard direct volume ray casting pipeline acccolor = 0.0 accalpha = 0.0 stepsize = (ray['tfar'] - ray['tnear']) / camera.samplesperray for i in range(camera.samplesperray): t = ray['tnear'] + i stepsize samplepos = ray['origin'] + t ray['direction'] v = samplevolume(samplepos, brick.data) c, a = classify(v, brick.transferfunction) acccolor = acccolor + (1.0 - accalpha) c a accalpha = accalpha + (1.0 - accalpha) a imagebuffer[ray['y']][ray['x']] = acccolor return imagebuffer Parameters: numthreads: The number of OpenMP threads to use. Default is the total number of cores on the SMP platform. Controlled via numthreads keyword or OMPNUMTHREADS environment variable. Edge cases and pitfalls: Brick-to-Image Ratio: Parallel efficiency increases as the average brick size relative to the image plane increases. Small ratios provide insufficient work per thread, reducing speedup. Hybrid MPI+OpenMP: When combining with MPI, the balance between MPI tasks and OpenMP threads must be managed to avoid oversubscribing cores. Uses domain decomposition to split bricks across processes. Choose when distributing work across multiple nodes. Uses GPU shaders for parallelization. Choose for higher performance on supported hardware. General category for GPU-based methods. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays intersecting the brick, with speedup proportional to the number of threads. Memory Complexity: O(N{rays}) for storing ray data, plus O(1) per thread for local accumulators. Performance: Parallel efficiency increases as the average brick size relative to the image plane increases. Strengths: Effective for shared-memory systems; complements MPI for hybrid parallelization. Limitations: Efficiency depends on the ratio of brick size to image plane size; requires MPI for distributed memory. This method is implemented in the yt framework, a Python-based analysis and visualization toolkit for cosmological, astrophysical, and fluid dynamics simulations. It utilizes Cython to interface with OpenMP, allowing for high-performance parallelization of volume rendering on multi-core CPUs. 3D Visualization and Volume Rendering, https://yt-project.org/doc/visualizing/volumerendering.html, fetched 2026-10-28 https://yt-project.org/docs/dev/visualizing/volumerendering.html#volume-rendering-components, https://yt-project.org/docs/dev/visualizing/volumerendering.html, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Attention Compositing
head: Attention Compositing Module
body: Attention Compositing is a method for Direct Volume Ray Casting (DVR) that automates view-dependent visual emphasis by integrating semantic attention maps with traditional transfer functions. It solves the problem of isolating Regions of Interest (ROIs) in complex volumetric data (e.g., medical images) where manual segmentation is difficult or where low-level saliency fails to capture semantic importance. Unlike standard DVR, which relies solely on intensity-based opacity, or importance-driven methods using manual labels which may cause over-segmentation and loss of context, Attention Compositing preserves surrounding contextual information while de-emphasizing occluding structures with low attention values. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 1. Volumetric data V. 2. Transfer Function (TF) parameters defining opacity O{TF} and color \mathbf{c} for each voxel based on intensity. 3. Attention Map A: A 3D volume of raw attention values generated by a deep learning model (e.g., F-CAM), where higher values indicate semantic importance. Outputs: Final rendered image with emphasized ROIs and de-emphasized background/occluders. Data Structures: Attention Volume: Same dimensions as the input volume V, storing scalar attention values Ai for each voxel i. Priority Volume: A derived scalar volume storing the composite priority Pri for each voxel. Method Steps: 1. Generate Attention Map: Use a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) to generate a focused attention map A for the input volume. This map encodes semantic information, highlighting ROIs (e.g., tumors in PET scans) while suppressing non-semantic structures. 2. Compute TF-Enhanced Attention (Ae): For each voxel i, combine the raw attention value Ai with the opacity O{TF,i} assigned by the Transfer Function for the target ROI. This step ensures that only voxels with both high semantic attention and high intensity-based opacity are considered significant. A{e,i} = O{TF,i} \cdot Ai Where: A{e,i} is the TF-enhanced attention value. O{TF,i} is the opacity value assigned by the TF for the ROI tent. Ai is the raw attention value from the attention map. 3. Calculate Priority (Pr): Determine the final priority for each voxel by aggregating A{e,i} and the occlusion relations along the viewing ray. Voxels occluding high-priority ROIs with low attention values are assigned lower priority to become transparent, allowing the ROI to be seen. Voxels with low A{e,i} (false positives or context) are also de-emphasized. Note: The source describes the aggregation of attention, TF opacity, and occlusion into a single-dimensional attribute called priority, but does not provide a closed-form algebraic formula for the occlusion integration step itself, only the definition of Ae and the conceptual result. 4. Modify Opacity for Compositing: Adjust the opacity \alphai used in the standard front-to-back compositing equation. The original opacity O{TF,i} is modulated by the priority Pri. High-priority voxels retain or increase their effective opacity, while low-priority voxels (including occluders with low attention) have their opacity reduced. Implementation Note: In practice, this is often achieved by scaling the opacity contribution in the compositing loop or by pre-multiplying the opacity by a factor derived from Pri. 5. Standard DVR Compositing: Perform standard front-to-back volume rendering using the modified opacities. \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alpha'i \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha'j) \alpha{out} = 1 - \prod{i=1}^{N} (1 - \alpha'j) Where \alpha'i is the priority-modified opacity for sample i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def attentioncompositing(volume, attentionmap, transferfunction, rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, numsamples): """ Renders a volume using Attention Compositing. Args: volume: 3D array of voxel intensities. attentionmap: 3D array of raw attention values (same dimensions as volume). transferfunction: Function mapping intensity -> (color, opacity). rayorigin: 3D vector (o). raydirection: 3D vector (d). tnear: Entry parameter of ray into volume. tfar: Exit parameter of ray into volume. numsamples: Number of samples along the ray. Returns: finalcolor: 3D vector (RGB). finalopacity: Scalar (A). """ dt = (tfar - tnear) / numsamples acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accopacity = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): t = tnear + i dt pos = rayorigin + t raydirection # 1. Sample volume and attention map intensity = samplevolume(volume, pos) rawattention = samplevolume(attentionmap, pos) # 2. Get TF properties for the target ROI # Note: TF is typically designed for specific semantic classes (e.g., tumor) color, tfopacity = transferfunction(intensity) # 3. Compute TF-Enhanced Attention # Ae = OTF A tfenhancedattention = tfopacity rawattention # 4. Determine Priority and Modified Opacity # The source defines Priority as an aggregation of Ae and occlusion. # For implementation, we assume a simplified modulation where # effective opacity is scaled by the normalized attention strength. # In the source, R1 (occluder) has low attention -> low priority -> transparent. # ROI has high attention -> high priority -> opaque. # Heuristic implementation of priority-based opacity modulation: # If tfenhancedattention is high, keep tfopacity. # If low, reduce opacity to allow ray to pass through to ROI behind it. # A simple scaling factor could be: priorityfactor = tfenhancedattention / max(max(attentionmap.flatten()), 1e-6) # Clamp priority factor to [0, 1] or scale as needed # The source implies that occluders with low attention are rendered sparsely/transparently. modifiedopacity = tfopacity priorityfactor # Guard against zero opacity to avoid division by zero in alpha blending if needed, # though standard front-to-back handles alpha=0 correctly. if modifiedopacity < 1e-6: continue # 5. Front-to-back compositing # Cacc = Cacc + (1 - alphaacc) c alpha # alphaacc = alphaacc + (1 - alphaacc) alpha weight = (1.0 - accopacity) modifiedopacity acccolor[0] += weight color[0] acccolor[1] += weight color[1] acccolor[2] += weight color[2] accopacity += weight # Early ray termination optimization (optional) if accopacity > 0.99: break return acccolor, accopacity Parameters: Attention Map Source: Typically a CNN (e.g., F-CAM) trained on the specific modality (PET, MRI). Transfer Function: Usually a 1D intensity-based TF specific to the modality (e.g., PET/CT). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: False Positives in Attention: The attention map may highlight non-ROI structures with high attention values. The TF-enhanced attention step (Ae = O{TF} \cdot A) mitigates this by requiring high TF opacity (intensity match) as well. False Positives in TF: The TF may assign high opacity to contextual structures (e.g., bones in MRI) that are not ROIs. The attention map filters these out if they have low semantic attention. Occlusion: If a high-attention ROI is occluded by a low-attention structure, the low-attention structure must be made transparent. The priority calculation must account for this depth relationship. A technique for generating the attention map A. It transfers semantic information from classification tasks to localization, focusing on small ROIs in medical images. It differs from standard CAM by focusing on specific classes and refining localization. A sibling method using manual segmentation labels. It often causes over-segmentation and unwanted removal of adjacent context (e.g., bones). Attention Compositing is chosen when manual labeling is impractical or when preserving context is critical. An early attempt using bottom-up saliency maps based on low-level features. It lacks semantic understanding. Attention Compositing is chosen when semantic relevance (e.g., tumor vs. healthy tissue) is required. Time Complexity: Adds the cost of sampling the attention map (same as volume sampling) and a few multiplications per sample. The CNN inference is performed once per volume (or per frame if dynamic), not per ray. Thus, per-frame rendering cost is negligible compared to standard DVR. Memory Complexity: Requires storing an additional 3D volume for the attention map, equal in size to the input volume. Strengths: Automates visual emphasis; preserves contextual information better than manual segmentation; handles view-dependent occlusion effectively; reduces false positives from both TF and attention map. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained attention model; dependent on the quality of the attention map; may fail if the attention model is not trained for the specific pathology or feature. When to use: Medical imaging (PET-CT, MRI) where ROIs are small and semantically defined, and manual segmentation is too labor-intensive. When not to use: Non-medical data without semantic labels; real-time applications where pre-computing attention maps is prohibitive. Attention Compositing was proposed by Li et al. in 2024, building on earlier work in saliency-driven DVR by Jung et al.. It addresses the limitations of low-level saliency and manual segmentation by leveraging deep learning-based semantic attention maps. It is particularly relevant in medical visualization tools like 3D Slicer and ImageJ, where automated ROI emphasis aids diagnosis.
