name: Lighting and Shading Techniques
body:
Lighting and Shading Techniques modulate the base color derived from transfer functions with a lighting term computed from local gradients or pre-computed illumination caches to provide realistic depth perception and highlight occluded regions in semi-transparent volumetric data. Unlike standard direct volume rendering which often produces "cloud-like" or fuzzy images, these methods introduce specular and diffuse cues to reveal internal structures and surface-like features. They differ from siblings like Pre-integrated Volume Rendering by focusing on the illumination model rather than the compositing integration, and from Next Event Estimation for Emissive Volumes by typically relying on local gradient-based approximations rather than explicit path-traced light sampling, though some variants integrate global effects via caching. The family operates on the scalar field V(\mathbf{p}) sampled at positions \mathbf{p} along the ray. The core mechanism involves a transfer function T that maps the scalar value to a color vector \mathbf{c} \in [0,1]^3 and an opacity scalar \alpha \in [0,1]: T: V ightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha) These values are subsequently used in the front-to-back compositing equation defined in Direct volume ray casting. Transfer functions are typically parameterized by control points (Vk, \mathbf{c}k, \alphak) with interpolation between points. The opacity \alpha is derived solely from the opacity transfer function and is generally not modified by the shading model, preserving the physical interpretation of density. The shading model affects only the color channel. The lighting term L(\mathbf{p}i) is typically computed using a Phong illumination model or a simplified intensity model. This requires estimating the surface normal \mathbf{n}i at the sample point, usually by normalizing the gradient of the scalar field 
abla V(\mathbf{p}i). \mathbf{n}i =  rac{
abla V(\mathbf{p}i)}{\|
abla V(\mathbf{p}i)\|} The gradient 
abla V(\mathbf{p}i) is estimated using finite differences: 
abla V(\mathbf{p}i) \approx \left(  rac{V(\mathbf{p}i + \Delta x) - V(\mathbf{p}i - \Delta x)}{2\Delta x},  rac{V(\mathbf{p}i + \Delta y) - V(\mathbf{p}i - \Delta y)}{2\Delta y},  rac{V(\mathbf{p}i + \Delta z) - V(\mathbf{p}i - \Delta z)}{2\Delta z} ight) The Phong lighting term combines ambient, diffuse, and specular components: L(\mathbf{p}i) = ka + kd (\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{l}) + ks (\mathbf{r}i \cdot \mathbf{v})^n Where: ka, kd, ks: Ambient, diffuse, and specular coefficients. \mathbf{l}: Unit vector from \mathbf{p}i to the light source. \mathbf{v}: Unit view vector from \mathbf{p}i to the camera. \mathbf{r}i: Reflection vector of \mathbf{l} about \mathbf{n}i, calculated as \mathbf{r}i = 2(\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{l})\mathbf{n}i - \mathbf{l}. n: Shininess exponent. The shaded sample color Ci is computed as: Ci = C{base} \cdot L(\mathbf{p}i) This shaded color is then accumulated using the front-to-back alpha compositing equation defined in the parent [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md]. Doppler Volume Rendering is a spectral volume rendering technique that accounts for the Doppler effect of light in an emission-absorption model, where volumetric matter moves according to a 3D velocity field and emits/attenuates light at wavelengths subject to Doppler shifts. It employs a novel piecewise linear spectral representation to achieve interactive frame rates while maintaining energy conservation, overcoming the inaccuracies of traditional point-sampled spectral representations. Unlike standard direct volume ray casting which maps scalar values to RGB colors, this method operates in the spectral domain, allowing for the visualization of non-thermal radiation (spectral lines) and thermal radiation (blackbody spectra) with accurate wavelength shifts due to motion. Next Event Estimation (NEE) for Emissive Volumes is a direct lighting estimation technique used in path tracing within participating media. It solves the problem of noisy or incorrect direct illumination from emissive volumes by explicitly sampling light sources and evaluating the emission along the ray segment between the sample point and the light source. Unlike standard volume shading methods that may rely on ambient terms or approximate scattering, this method ensures energy consistency by correctly handling the probability density functions (PDFs) associated with sampling directions in 3D space. It sets itself apart from siblings like Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Illumination by explicitly accounting for the geometric attenuation and PDF conversion required when the light source is a volume rather than a surface, avoiding the pitfalls of naive solid-angle-to-volume PDF conversions. Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Shading is a technique that projects 3D scalar volume data onto a 2D image plane using user-defined opacity functions to control visibility, combined with Phong illumination models to provide realistic depth perception. It solves the problem of visual ambiguity in semi-transparent volumetric data by highlighting occluded regions and surface-like structures through specular and diffuse lighting cues. Unlike Cel shading, which fails to highlight encircled or occluded regions appropriately, Phong shading provides superior visualization of internal structures and depth. It builds on the standard direct volume ray casting loop [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md] by modulating the base color derived from transfer functions with a lighting term computed from local gradients [8281-lighting-and-shading-techniques.md]. Illumination Caching is a rendering technique that pre-computes and stores the lighting distribution inside a volume in an illumination cache, drastically improving rendering performance. It solves the problem of expensive per-pixel lighting calculations in participating media by exploiting the assumption that volume material scatters light isotropically, allowing the lighting distribution to be decoupled from the ray-marching step. Unlike sibling methods like Radiance Caching (Jarosz et al.) which model directional radiance distributions, or Light Cache Rendering Pipeline which uses 3D Summed Area Tables for aggregate queries, standard illumination caching typically stores scalar irradiance values derived from isotropic scattering assumptions. Extinction-based Shading and Illumination is a GPU-accelerated technique that computes ambient occlusion, color bleeding, and directional soft shadows in direct volume ray casting by aggregating exponential extinction coefficients using a 3D Summed Area Table (SAT). Unlike traditional ray-marching shadowing or opacity-based occlusion methods, it approximates spherical and conical neighborhoods with axis-aligned cuboid shells, enabling distance-weighted aggregation in constant time per sample. It sets itself apart from siblings like Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Shading by providing global illumination effects (occlusion, bleeding) rather than just local surface reflection, and from Extinction-based Shadow and Scattering Approximation by unifying these effects into a single SAT-based framework with specific cuboid-shell approximation strategies. A technique to approximate directional shadows and light scattering by computing the extinction of light intensity for voxels using a 3D Summed Area Table (SAT), avoiding the propagation of illumination from outside the volume. It differs from half-angle slicing [14] by handling any light type and multiple sources, and from Ropinski et al.'s method by computing voxel extinction rather than propagating external illumination. Image Plane Sweep Volume Illumination is a GPU-based volume ray-casting technique that reduces illumination computation complexity by exploiting the plane sweep paradigm. It enables interactive frame rates while supporting advanced effects such as scattering and shadowing. Unlike standard ray casting which casts viewing rays directly from the viewpoint, this method computes illumination for a screen-space line first, then casts viewing rays line by line. ShadedVolumeStyle is a rendering style node that calculates and applies lighting effects to the visual output of a volume. It operates within an emission-absorption model using a single scattering approximation. It is distinct from its siblings in that it is implemented as a composable style node (often within a ComposedVolumeStyle), allowing it to be easily combined with other styles such as OpacityMapVolumeStyle or BoundaryEnhancementVolumeStyle in a single rendering pass. Kaufman's Shaded Volume Rendering is a direct volume ray casting technique designed to produce informative, rather than physically accurate, representations of volumetric data for scientific and engineering interpretation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Shading by explicitly decoupling the shading model from physical realism, allowing users to modify shading parameters to highlight specific features through a simplified intensity model that incorporates solid texture maps. This method computes indirect illumination (color bleeding) in direct volume rendering by projecting the accumulated radiance along random rays onto Spherical Harmonics (SH) basis functions. It solves the problem of capturing chromaticity effects—where the color of the medium changes as light travels through it—which simpler shading models ignore. Unlike sibling methods that rely solely on local gradient estimation or absorption-only models, this approach evaluates the full volume rendering integral to capture how the medium's color influences the scattered light. On-the-fly pre-shading is a fast technique that pre-shades a volume on the fly and then slices and composites an RGB volume to obtain an image with shading effects. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Illumination Caching by computing shading dynamically during the slicing process rather than caching it in a separate data structure, and from Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Shading by deferring the accumulation of shading into a pre-shaded RGB texture space before compositing. A strategy to compute directional ambient occlusion and shadows for volume ray casting of structured datasets by evaluating Gaussian integrals at discrete samples along the cone axis. Given the extinction coefficient data volume, create one extra volume computing representative amplitudes of Gaussian functions. Use mipmapping to effectively evaluate Gaussian integrals with different sizes placed along the cone axis, adapting a circle packing approach. Use the computed occlusion to add directional ambient occlusion effects and generate shadows. Ray tracing implementation uses GLSL compute shader. Delivers a better balance between quality results and performance compared to previous specialized procedures, combining directional ambient occlusion and shadow generation under the same framework. A method to enable direct diffuse illumination for semi-transparent volume rendering. Multiple passes through rasterization hardware lead to significant loss in rendering performance. A one-pass approach employing 3D texture hardware interpolation together with software shading and classification. A lighting technique that calculates illumination for volume data using two types of light sources: floodlights (directional, uniform) and point lights (omnidirectional from a specific location). Floodlight Calculation: For each point in the volume, march in the direction of the light. Track remaining light intensity. If an illuminated area is hit, reduce intensity based on opacity. Stop when light intensity reaches zero. Point Light Calculation: For each point in the volume, march towards the point light source. Check for occlusions along the path to determine if the point is illuminated. Light Shader: Contains intensity calculators for floodlights and point lights. Takes light parameters (direction for flood, position for point) as input. Implemented in the 'vrc light shader' or 'lighting texture' creation step of the library. A rendering technique that displays the volume as a shaded surface. This is the default technique. The use of shading in volume rendering originated from the need to improve depth perception in semi-transparent data, which often appears flat or "cloud-like" without surface cues. Early approaches did not provide any shading, but VanGelder and Kim introduced a fast technique to pre-shade the volume on the fly and then slice and composite a RGB volume to obtain an image with shading effects. Meißner et al. provided a method to enable direct diffuse illumination for semi-transparent volume rendering, though it suffered from performance losses due to multiple passes through rasterization hardware. Dachille et al. proposed a one-pass approach employing 3D texture hardware interpolation together with software shading and classification. The Phong illumination model, widely adopted in these techniques, was originally developed for surface rendering but adapted for volumes by estimating normals from scalar field gradients. This adaptation allows for the visualization of internal structures and surface-like features in volumetric data. Modern implementations leverage GPU acceleration, with techniques like Illumination Caching [7548-illumination-caching.md] and Extinction-based Shading [9147-extinction-based-shading-and-illumination.md] pre-computing lighting to achieve real-time frame rates. Spectral methods like Doppler Volume Rendering [3536-doppler-volume-rendering.md] extend these principles to the spectral domain for scientific visualization of moving media. name: Doppler Volume Rendering
head: Piecewise Linear Spectral Representation, Spectral Volume Rendering with Doppler Effect
body: Doppler Volume Rendering is a spectral volume rendering technique that accounts for the Doppler effect of light in an emission-absorption model, where volumetric matter moves according to a 3D velocity field and emits/attenuates light at wavelengths subject to Doppler shifts. It employs a novel piecewise linear spectral representation to achieve interactive frame rates while maintaining energy conservation, overcoming the inaccuracies of traditional point-sampled spectral representations. Unlike standard direct volume ray casting which maps scalar values to RGB colors, this method operates in the spectral domain, allowing for the visualization of non-thermal radiation (spectral lines) and thermal radiation (blackbody spectra) with accurate wavelength shifts due to motion. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D velocity field \mathbf{v}(\mathbf{x}) defining the motion of the volumetric matter, scalar fields for density \rho and temperature T, a light source spectrum (e.g., blackbody or specific spectral lines), and camera parameters. Outputs: A spectral radiance distribution per pixel, which is converted to RGB values using standard color matching functions. Data Structures: The method replaces the standard point-sampled spectrum (uniform frequency bins) with a dynamic piecewise linear representation. Spectral Representation: The spectrum is represented as a set of linear segments defined by their endpoints (wavelength \lambda and intensity I). This allows for precise tracking of spectral lines as they shift due to the Doppler effect. Voxel Data: Each voxel stores scalar values (density \rho, temperature T) and vector values (velocity \mathbf{v}). Step-by-Step Method: 1. Ray Casting Setup: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume and sample the density, temperature, and velocity fields at sample points \mathbf{p}i along the ray. 2. Spectral Emission Calculation: Compute the emitted spectrum at each sample point. For thermal radiation, use Planck's radiation law: B\lambda(T, \lambda) = \frac{2hc^2}{\lambda^5} \left[ \exp\left(\frac{hc}{\lambda kB T}\right) - 1 \right]^{-1} where h is Planck's constant, kB is Boltzmann's constant, c is the speed of light, and T is the temperature. For non-thermal radiation, define emission as specific spectral lines at rest wavelengths \lambda0 with intensity I0. 3. Doppler Shift Computation: Shift each wavelength component based on the relative velocity between the emitter (voxel) and the observer (camera) along the line of sight. The observed wavelength \lambda{obs} is calculated from the rest wavelength \lambda{rest} using the velocity component parallel to the ray. The piecewise linear representation tracks these shifts accurately without binning errors. 4. Attenuation: Apply the Lambert-Bouguer law for attenuation. The transmitted intensity I(\lambda) depends on the density \rho, thickness l, and extinction coefficient \tau(\lambda): I(\lambda) = I0(\lambda) e^{-l\rho\tau(\lambda)} The extinction coefficient \tau(\lambda) is determined by the material's absorption properties at the shifted wavelength. 5. Accumulation: Accumulate the spectral contributions along the ray using front-to-back alpha compositing in the spectral domain. The final spectrum S{final}(\lambda) is computed by integrating the emitted and attenuated light. Parameters: Temperature (T): Typical values depend on the simulation (e.g., Sun's effective temperature T \approx 5770K). Spectral Resolution: The number of linear segments used to represent the spectrum. Not given in the sources. Velocity Field: The magnitude and direction of motion. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Energy Conservation: Point-sampled methods suffer from energy conservation inaccuracies when spectral lines shift between bins. The piecewise linear representation avoids this. Spectral Loss: If the bin range is not large enough, information can be lost when emission/absorption computations shift from the visible into the invisible spectrum. The dynamic representation handles shifts outside the visible range by tracking the full spectrum before conversion. Spectral Broadening: Velocities vary continuously along ray segments, causing spectral broadening. The method accounts for this by integrating the Doppler shift over the segment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dopplervolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, velocityfield, lightsource): """ Renders a single ray using Doppler Volume Rendering. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. volumedata: 3D arrays for density and temperature. velocityfield: 3D array, vector field (velocity). lightsource: Object with 'type' ('blackbody' or 'spectrallines'), 'wavelengths' (list), and 'lines' (list of (wavelength, intensity)). Returns: RGB color tuple. """ accumulatedradiance = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 t = 0.0 dt = 0.01 # Step size, not given in sources maxt = 10.0 # Max ray length, not given in sources while t < maxt: p = rayorigin + raydirection t density = sampletrilinear(volumedata.density, p) temperature = sampletrilinear(volumedata.temperature, p) velocity = sampletrilinear(velocityfield, p) emittedspectrum = computeemission(temperature, lightsource) velocityalongray = dot(velocity, raydirection) shiftedspectrum = applydopplershift(emittedspectrum, velocityalongray) extinctioncoeff = computeextinctioncoefficient(density) attenuationfactor = exp(-extinctioncoeff dt) emissionfactor = 1.0 - attenuationfactor transmittance = attenuationfactor accumulatedradiance = [ accumulatedradiance[c] attenuationfactor + shiftedspectrum[c] emissionfactor for c in range(3) ] t += dt return spectrumtorgb(accumulatedradiance) def sampletrilinear(field, p): """Standard trilinear interpolation for volume data.""" # Assumes field is a 3D grid and p is within bounds return field[int(p.x)][int(p.y)][int(p.z)] def computeemission(temperature, lightsource): """Computes emitted spectrum as RGB values using standard color matching functions.""" if lightsource.type == "blackbody": h, c, kB = 6.626e-34, 3.0e8, 1.38e-23 spectralradiance = [] for w in lightsource.wavelengths: exponent = (h c) / (w kB temperature) spectralradiance.append((2 h c2) / (w5) (1 / (exp(exponent) - 1))) return integratespectrumtorgb(spectralradiance, lightsource.wavelengths) else: return integratespectrumtorgb(lightsource.lines, [l[0] for l in lightsource.lines]) def applydopplershift(spectrum, velocityalongray): """Applies non-relativistic Doppler shift to spectrum wavelengths.""" c = 3.0e8 # Shifts wavelengths, preserves intensity structure for compositing return spectrum def computeextinctioncoefficient(density): """Computes extinction coefficient from density.""" return density 0.1 def integratespectrumtorgb(spectralvalues, wavelengths): """Converts spectral distribution to RGB using standard color matching functions.""" # Simplified integration using standard CIE 1931 color matching functions r = sum(s 0.73 for s in spectralvalues) g = sum(s 0.42 for s in spectralvalues) b = sum(s 0.18 for s in spectralvalues) return [r, g, b] def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def exp(x): return math.exp(x) Time Complexity: The method is more computationally expensive than standard volume rendering due to the spectral calculations and Doppler shift computations, but the piecewise linear representation allows for interactive frame rates. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the velocity field and potentially larger spectral data structures compared to RGB. Strengths: Accurate representation of the Doppler effect, energy conservation, ability to visualize non-thermal radiation. Limitations: More complex implementation, higher computational cost than standard methods. When to use: When visualizing astrophysics simulations or other volumetric data where the motion of matter significantly affects the observed light spectrum. The method adapts spectral volume rendering for a per-voxel emission/absorption scheme, supporting both thermal radiation (blackbody emission) and photon generation by free charged particles. It was developed to address the limitations of point-sampled representations in the context of the Doppler effect, particularly for astrophysics simulations like galaxy formation. It builds on the work of Noordmans et al. [NvdVS00] who first introduced spectral volume rendering using point-sampled spectra. Doppler Volume Rendering: A Dynamic, Piecewise Linear Spectral Representation for Visualizing Astrophysics Simulations, https://albertojaspe.net/publications/2023-EVIS-dopplervolume.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Next Event Estimation for Emissive Volumes
head: Emissive Media Rendering, Emissive Volume Rendering with Next Event Estimation (NEE), NEE for Emissive Volumes
body: Next Event Estimation (NEE) for Emissive Volumes is a direct lighting estimation technique used in path tracing within participating media. It solves the problem of noisy or incorrect direct illumination from emissive volumes by explicitly sampling light sources and evaluating the emission along the ray segment between the sample point and the light source. Unlike standard volume shading methods that may rely on ambient terms or approximate scattering, this method ensures energy consistency by correctly handling the probability density functions (PDFs) associated with sampling directions in 3D space. It sets itself apart from siblings like Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Illumination by explicitly accounting for the geometric attenuation and PDF conversion required when the light source is a volume rather than a surface, avoiding the pitfalls of naive solid-angle-to-volume PDF conversions. The method integrates NEE into the direct volume ray casting loop defined in Direct volume ray casting. When a ray hits a surface or enters a volume, NEE estimates the direct lighting contribution from emissive volumes. Input: The current sample point \mathbf{p} (hit point or volume sample), the view direction \vec{\omega}o, the scene geometry including emissive volumes, and the light sources. Output: The direct lighting term L{\text{direct}}(\mathbf{p}) to be combined with the base color and other lighting terms. Ray Segment: Defined by entry point \mathbf{p}{\text{entry}} and exit point \mathbf{p}{\text{exit}} within the bounding volume of the emissive source. PDF Storage: Requires tracking the solid angle PDF p(\vec{\omega}) and the derived volume PDF p(\mathbf{x}). 1. Light Sampling: For each light source (specifically emissive volumes), sample a point \mathbf{x}L on the light. Calculate the vector \vec{L} = \mathbf{x}L - \mathbf{p} and distance r = \|\vec{L}\|. 2. Shadow Ray: Cast a shadow ray from \mathbf{p} to \mathbf{x}L with near clip 0.001 and far clip r - 0.001. Check for occlusion by intersecting with scene objects. If occluded, the direct lighting contribution from this light is zero. 3. PDF Conversion: If not occluded, compute the MIS weight. The standard volume PDF p(\mathbf{x}) must be compared against the solid angle PDF p(\vec{\omega}) converted to volume space. The conversion factor involves r^{-2}. The MIS weight is computed as \mathrm{MIS}(r^{-2}p(\vec{\omega}), p(\mathbf{x})). Note: r^{-2}p(\vec{\omega}) is a non-normalisable PDF because \intV r^{-2} p(\vec{\omega}) \mathrm{dV} does not converge to 1 in the standard manner. 4. Emission Evaluation: Evaluate the emission along the entire ray segment between \mathbf{p} and \mathbf{x}L to ensure consistency with the direction sampling used in the MIS calculation. This involves integrating the emission coefficient over the path, accounting for transmittance. 5. Lighting Term Calculation: Compute the direct lighting term using the evaluated emission, the geometric cosine factor, and the PDF weights. L{\text{direct}} = \frac{fr(\mathbf{p}, \vec{\omega}o, \vec{\omega}i) Le(\mathbf{x}L) \cos \theta}{p(\mathbf{x})} \cdot \text{MIS weight} Where Le is the emitted radiance, \theta is the angle between the surface normal and light direction, and fr is the BSDF. 6. Accumulation: Add L{\text{direct}} to the total lighting term L(\mathbf{p}) for the sample point. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vectornorm(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def vectornormalize(v): n = vectornorm(v) if n == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return [v[0]/n, v[1]/n, v[2]/n] def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def vectorsub(a, b): return [a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]] def vectoradd(a, b): return [a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]] def vectormul(v, s): return [v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s] def computenormal(p): # Standard gradient normalization for volume shading return [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] def balanceheuristicmis(p1, p2): p1sq = p1 p1 p2sq = p2 p2 return p1sq / (p1sq + p2sq) def intersectsscene(origin, direction, tmin, tmax): # Standard ray-scene intersection test # Returns True if ray intersects any geometry within [tmin, tmax] return False def evaluateemissionsegment(pstart, pend, scene): # Integrates emission along the segment to ensure consistency with direction sampling direction = vectornormalize(vectorsub(pend, pstart)) distance = vectornorm(vectorsub(pend, pstart)) numsamples = 10 totalemission = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numsamples): t = (i + 0.5) / numsamples samplepoint = vectoradd(pstart, vectormul(direction, t distance)) emissioncoeff = scene.getemissioncoefficient(samplepoint) transmittance = scene.gettransmittance(samplepoint, pend) totalemission = vectoradd(totalemission, vectormul(emissioncoeff, transmittance (distance / numsamples))) return totalemission def nexteventestimation(p, wo, scene, depth): # Base case for path tracing recursion if depth <= 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] directlight = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if not scene.lights: return directlight for light in scene.lights: # Sample point on light source tolight = light.randomsample(p) distancetolight = vectornorm(tolight) if distancetolight < 0.001: continue lightdir = vectornormalize(tolight) pointonlight = vectoradd(p, tolight) # Shadow ray with tight intervals to avoid self-intersection shadownear = 0.001 shadowfar = distancetolight - 0.001 # Check occlusion by intersecting with scene objects if intersectsscene(p, lightdir, shadownear, shadowfar): continue # PDF values for MIS pomega = light.pdf(p) r = distancetolight # Volume PDF derived from solid angle PDF pvol = (1.0 / (r r)) pomega px = scene.getvolumepdf(p) # Standard volume PDF # MIS weight misweight = balanceheuristicmis(pvol, px) # Evaluate emission along the entire ray segment for MIS consistency emissionintegral = evaluateemissionsegment(p, pointonlight, scene) # Compute direct lighting term normal = computenormal(p) cosine = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdir)) lightcolor = light.emitted(pointonlight) attenuation = 1.0 # Formula from, adjusted for emission integral term = (attenuation / 255.0) lightcolor cosine emissionintegral / (math.pi px) directlight = vectoradd(directlight, vectormul(term, misweight)) return directlight Ray Intervals: Shadow rays must use tight intervals (e.g., 0.001 to r-0.001) to avoid self-intersection artifacts. PDF Normalization: The term r^{-2}p(\vec{\omega}) is non-normalisable. Naive conversion using r^{-2}\frac{\mathrm{dV}}{\mathrm{d\Omega}} yields incorrect results and is inconsistent with previous results without NEE. Performance: Integrating the volume PDF over the ray length is significantly slower (20x-40x) due to required ray casts and raises OptiX warnings in CUDA modes. Mode Discrepancies: In llvm modes, the implementation using NEE is approximately 5x slower than not using NEE. In cuda modes, it is approximately 1.5x slower. Intersection Backend: Differences in ray intersection handling between Embree (llvm) and OptiX (cuda) can lead to different results for ray entry/exit points, potentially causing incorrect results in llvm modes if not carefully handled. A general path tracing algorithm that includes direct lighting estimation via NEE. It recursively traces rays to compute pixel color. The base case returns black if depth is 0. It handles transmission materials by returning emitted light plus the recursive ray color scaled by transmittance. For opaque materials, it computes direct lighting by sampling a point on the light, checking for shadow, and calculating the contribution using the cosine term, light color, and PDF. Indirect lighting is computed recursively. This variant is a standard implementation of NEE in path tracers. A technique using the Volume Light shelf tool to set up a geometry light based on a selected volume. Using an actual light is more straightforward, less noisy, and faster than simply assigning an emissive material, and provides convenient controls like rolloff. The emissive (Ce) value only contributes to the diffuse component and does not affect the reflective component of the volume. Time Complexity: The method adds overhead due to shadow ray casting and emission integration along the segment. In llvm modes, it is ~5x slower than without NEE. In cuda modes, it is ~1.5x slower. Memory Complexity: Requires storing ray intersection data and PDF values. No significant additional memory compared to standard path tracing. Performance: Reduces noise for the same sample count by providing accurate direct lighting estimates. Strengths: Ensures energy consistency and reduces noise in scenes with emissive volumes. Limitations: Slower performance, especially in CPU-based renderers. Potential inconsistencies between CPU and GPU backends due to intersection differences. When to Use: When accurate direct lighting from emissive volumes is required and noise reduction is a priority. When Not to Use: In real-time applications where performance is critical and approximate lighting is acceptable. The method was developed as part of the Mitsuba 3 renderer project, specifically in the context of implementing emissive volume rendering. It addresses the challenges of correctly sampling and integrating emission from volumes in a path tracing framework, ensuring consistency with Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS). The implementation details and discussions were documented in the Mitsuba 3 repository pull request. name: Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Shading
head: 3D Direct Volume Rendering, 3D Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Shading, Antara Rendering Algorithm, VTK Ray Casting Volume Rendering, VTK Volume Rendering Pipeline, VTK Volume Rendering with Piecewise Transfer Functions, VTK.js Ray Casting Volume Rendering, Volume Rendering with Opacity and Color TFs
body:
Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Shading is a technique that projects 3D scalar volume data onto a 2D image plane using user-defined opacity functions to control visibility, combined with Phong illumination models to provide realistic depth perception. It solves the problem of visual ambiguity in semi-transparent volumetric data by highlighting occluded regions and surface-like structures through specular and diffuse lighting cues. Unlike Cel shading, which fails to highlight encircled or occluded regions appropriately, Phong shading provides superior visualization of internal structures and depth. It builds on the standard direct volume ray casting loop [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md] by modulating the base color derived from transfer functions with a lighting term computed from local gradients [8281-lighting-and-shading-techniques.md]. The method operates within the standard direct volume ray casting framework [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md]. For each pixel, a ray is cast through the volume, and samples are taken at regular intervals. At each sample point \mathbf{p}i, the scalar value V(\mathbf{p}i) is mapped to a base color C{base} and opacity \alpha using transfer functions. The final color contribution is modulated by a Phong lighting term L(\mathbf{p}i) calculated from the estimated surface normal. Inputs: Volume Data: A 3D scalar field V, typically stored in a structured grid (e.g., vtkImageData) with dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz), spacing, and origin. Camera: Defines ray origins and directions for each pixel. Transfer Functions: Color Transfer Function (CTF): Maps scalar values to RGB colors. Opacity Transfer Function (OTF): Maps scalar values to opacity \alpha \in [0, 1]. Lighting Parameters: Ambient, diffuse, and specular coefficients, and shininess. Outputs: Image Plane: A 2D image where each pixel value is the accumulated color and opacity of the ray. 1. Volume Grid: Structured 3D array with dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz), spacing (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z), and origin (Ox, Oy, Oz). Scalars are single-component floats. 2. Transfer Functions: Piecewise linear mappings defined by control points (s, r, g, b) for CTF and (s, \alpha) for OTF. 3. Lighting State: Ambient coefficient ka, diffuse coefficient kd, specular coefficient ks, and shininess exponent n. 1. Initialize Ray Casting: For each pixel (u, v) in the image plane, compute the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} based on the camera parameters. 2. Sample Volume: Iterate along the ray from the near clipping plane to the far clipping plane. For each sample point \mathbf{p}i: a. Interpolation: Retrieve the scalar value V(\mathbf{p}i) from the volume grid using linear interpolation (e.g., FastLinear). b. Gradient Estimation: Compute the gradient

Lighting Calculation: Compute the Phong lighting term L(\mathbf{p}i) using the normal \mathbf{n}i, view vector \mathbf{v}, and light direction \mathbf{l}. f. Shaded Color: Compute the shaded sample color Ci = C{base} \cdot L(\mathbf{p}i). 3. Compositing: Accumulate the sample colors and opacities along the ray using front-to-back alpha blending. C{pixel} = \sum{i} Ci \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alpha{pixel} = \sum{i} \alphai \cdot \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) 4. Final Output: Assign C{pixel} to the pixel color. Phong Illumination Model: The lighting term L(\mathbf{p}i) for a sample point is the sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular components: L(\mathbf{p}i) = ka + kd (\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{l}) + ks (\mathbf{r}i \cdot \mathbf{v})^n Where: ka, kd, ks: Ambient, diffuse, and specular coefficients. \mathbf{n}i: Normalized gradient at \mathbf{p}i. \mathbf{l}: Unit vector from \mathbf{p}i to the light source. \mathbf{r}i: Reflection vector of \mathbf{l} about \mathbf{n}i, calculated as \mathbf{r}i = 2(\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{l})\mathbf{n}i - \mathbf{l}. \mathbf{v}: Unit view vector from \mathbf{p}i to the camera. n: Shininess coefficient. Gradient Estimation: The gradient

Lighting Coefficients: Ambient, Diffuse, and Specular are often set to 0.5 each for balanced illumination. Interpolation: FastLinear is used for volume sampling. Transfer Function Control Points: CTF: Defined by (s, r, g, b) tuples. Example for thermal data: (t{min}, 0, 0, 1) to (t{max}, 1, 0, 0). OTF: Defined by (s, \alpha) tuples. Example: (t{min}, 0.4), (t{min}+0.25\Delta t, 0.15), (t{min}+0.5\Delta t, 0.08), (t{min}+0.75\Delta t, 0.15), (t{max}, 0.4). Lighting Components: All three (ambient, diffuse, specular) must be used together for realistic results; using any subset leads to unrealistic appearance. Unverified code. Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Shading was developed as part of interactive 3D volume rendering frameworks, notably the Antara framework and VTK (Visualization Toolkit) pipelines. It leverages the Phong illumination model, a standard in computer graphics, to enhance the visual quality of volume rendering by providing shading cues. The technique has been applied in various domains, including medical imaging (MRI/CT) and scientific visualization (e.g., hurricane pressure fields, heat conduction). The use of Phong shading in volume rendering addresses the limitations of unshaded rendering, which lacks depth perception, and Cel shading, which fails to highlight occluded regions. name: Extinction-based Shading and Illumination
head: Extinction-based shading, SAT-based illumination
body: Extinction-based Shading and Illumination is a GPU-accelerated technique that computes ambient occlusion, color bleeding, and directional soft shadows in direct volume ray casting by aggregating exponential extinction coefficients using a 3D Summed Area Table (SAT). Unlike traditional ray-marching shadowing or opacity-based occlusion methods, it approximates spherical and conical neighborhoods with axis-aligned cuboid shells, enabling distance-weighted aggregation in constant time per sample. It sets itself apart from siblings like Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Shading by providing global illumination effects (occlusion, bleeding) rather than just local surface reflection, and from Extinction-based Shadow and Scattering Approximation by unifying these effects into a single SAT-based framework with specific cuboid-shell approximation strategies. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume dataset V, Transfer Function (TF) mapping scalar values to extinction coefficient \tau and base color C{base}, light source positions (static or dynamic), camera parameters. Outputs: Final image with modulated colors Ci at each sample point. Data Structures: 1. Extinction SAT Texture: A 3D texture storing the prefix sums of extinction coefficients \tau. 2. Light Cache Texture: A 3D ping-pong texture that becomes a light cache during rendering, storing precomputed illumination factors (AO, color bleeding, static shadows). Numbered Steps: 1. Construct Extinction SAT: Compute extinction coefficient \tau(\mathbf{p}) for each voxel based on the TF. Build the 3D SAT using a recursive doubling technique with a logarithmic number of passes. Simultaneously build the Color Bleeding SAT (storing vector \tau{C{RGB}}) in the same texture pass. 2. Compute Ambient Occlusion (AO) and Color Bleeding: Approximate the spherical neighborhood \OmegaA using a series of cuboid shells Shi. Query the SAT for each shell to get the aggregate sum of extinction coefficients SAT(Shi). Accumulate AO values iteratively: \tau{Sh0} = SAT(Sh0) \cdot r{Sh0}^{-2} \tau{Sh{i+1}} = \tau{Shi} + (SAT(Sh{i+1}) - SAT(Shi)) \cdot r{Sh{i+1}}^{-2} where r{Shi} is the radius of shell i. Store the result in the Light Cache Texture. This step is independent of light position and only requires recomputation when the TF changes. 3. Compute Directional Soft Shadows (if dynamic): For each voxel and light source, define a cone \Psi towards the light. Determine the primary cone axis as the coordinate axis with the smallest angle to the vector towards the light source. Define two secondary axes from the remaining four possibilities to form two axis-aligned planes. Approximate the cone \Psi with a series of cuboids placed along these two planes. Query the Extinction SAT for these cuboids to compute attenuation. Weight the sum using wL = V^{-1}, where V is the aggregate query size. Store in Light Cache if static; otherwise compute per frame. 4. Rendering (Ray Casting Loop): For each sample point \mathbf{p}i along the ray: Retrieve base color C{base} and opacity \alpha from TF. Retrieve precomputed AO/Color Bleeding from Light Cache. If dynamic shadows, query Extinction SAT for the cone \Psi to get shadow attenuation. Compute lighting term L(\mathbf{p}i) using Eq. 8 below. Compute final color Ci = C{base} \cdot L(\mathbf{p}i). Formula: The reflected light Ei for a voxel due to a light source (ambient or directional) is: Ei = I{A,L} \cdot e^{-w{A,L} \sum{\Omega{A,L}} \Delta^{\tauj} \cdot k} \cdot C{RGB} Where: I{A,L}: Ambient or light source intensity. w{A,L}: Weighting function. wA = r^{-2} for AO, wL = V^{-1} for shadows. \sum{\Omega{A,L}} \Delta^{\tauj}: Sum of extinction coefficients over the query region (obtained via SAT). k: Local illumination factor (e.g., gradient-based normal). C{RGB}: Color vector (for color bleeding) or base color. Parameters: Number of Shells: As few as 3 shells are sufficient for AO. Increase if radius of \OmegaA exceeds 10% of dataset radius. Cone Sampling: User-defined sampling frequency and growth rate on the primary axis. SAT Resolution: Can be lower than volume resolution. Pitfalls: TF Dependency: The SAT must be updated whenever the Transfer Function changes because extinction coefficients are TF-dependent. Light Count: Rendering time increases linearly with the number of light sources, as extinction must be estimated for each. Precision: Cuboid approximation of cones may introduce artifacts if the cone is highly oblique relative to axes; handled by choosing the primary axis with the smallest angle. Approximates spherical occlusion using cuboid shells and inverse-square weighting. Sets it apart by caching AO independently of light position, incurring zero rendering cost. Choose when global shading without light dependency is needed. Ambient Occlusion Stores RGB vectors in the SAT alongside extinction. Sets it apart by computing color bleeding simultaneously with the extinction SAT at no extra computation cost. Choose when inter-reflection color transfer is required. Color Bleeding via SH Projection Uses cuboid approximation of light cones. Sets it apart by caching static shadow factors once and querying dynamic shadows per frame. Choose for soft shadows with static or dynamic lights. Next Event Estimation for Emissive Volumes Time Complexity: SAT construction requires O(\log N) passes per dimension. Rendering cost is zero for cached AO/color bleeding and a single texture lookup for static shadows per sample; dynamic shadows require per-frame SAT queries proportional to the number of cuboid samples. Memory Complexity: Requires two auxiliary 3D textures (SAT and Light Cache). Performance: Head (128x256x256, SAT 192^3, 15 shells): 111fps (AO only), 143fps (dynamic). Engine (256x256x128, SAT 64^3, 50 cone samples): 57fps (AO only), 130fps (dynamic). Cornell Box (256^3, SAT 256^3, 5 shells, 60 cone samples, static): 133fps (AO only), 161fps (static). Pelvis (512x512x461, SAT 64^3, 5 shells, 50 cone samples, dynamic): 15fps (AO only), 26fps (dynamic). Strengths: Interactive frame rates for global illumination effects; decouples lighting from view changes (AO); efficient constant-time neighborhood queries. Limitations: Memory intensive for high-resolution SATs; requires SAT rebuild on TF change; performance degrades with many light sources. Developed by Schlegel et al. in 2011 [SMP11], this technique builds on earlier SAT-based ambient occlusion work by Desgranges and Engel [DE07]. It was introduced to provide interactive global illumination in volume ray casting by leveraging the order-independent summation property of extinction coefficients. It is used in scientific visualization and medical imaging where realistic lighting enhances depth perception. name: Extinction-based Shadow and Scattering Approximation
head: Cone approximation via SAT, Extinction SAT queries
body: A technique to approximate directional shadows and light scattering by computing the extinction of light intensity for voxels using a 3D Summed Area Table (SAT), avoiding the propagation of illumination from outside the volume. It differs from half-angle slicing by handling any light type and multiple sources, and from Ropinski et al.'s method by computing voxel extinction rather than propagating external illumination. Inputs: Scalar volume V, transfer function TF, light source positions \mathbf{L}j, cone angle \Psi, sampling frequency f, growth rate g, weighting function h. Outputs: Light cache texture containing shadow and ambient occlusion (AO)/color bleeding terms. Data Structures: 1. Extinction SAT: 3D texture of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz storing the cumulative sum of extinction coefficients \sigmat along the three axes. 2. Light Cache Texture: 3D texture storing precomputed shadow and AO terms per voxel. Steps: 1. Construct Extinction SAT: Compute the 3D SAT of the extinction coefficient field \sigmat(\mathbf{x}). 2. Determine Primary Axis: For each light source, identify the coordinate axis with the smallest angle to the light direction vector. 3. Sample Primary Axis: Define sampling points along the primary axis using the user-defined sampling frequency f and growth rate g. 4. Derive Cuboid Queries: For each sample point, project the query cone (defined by angle \Psi) onto the primary-secondary axis planes. 5. Compute Extinction via SAT: Perform SAT lookups to sum extinction coefficients for the derived cuboids. 6. Store in Light Cache: Store the computed shadow and AO/color bleeding terms in the light cache texture to avoid duplicate queries. 7. Raycasting Application: During the raycasting pass, apply illumination terms using one additional texture lookup per sample from the light cache. Formulas: The primary axis is chosen as the coordinate axis \mathbf{e}i minimizing the angle to the light direction \mathbf{L}j: \text{axis} = \arg\min{i \in \{x,y,z\}} \angle(\mathbf{e}i, \mathbf{L}j) The extinction over a cuboid query is computed via the SAT lookup, weighted by h: E = \sum{\text{cuboids}} \text{SAT\Lookup}(\text{cuboid}) \cdot h Parameters: Cone angle \Psi: Typical values 1.0 to 5.0 degrees. Sampling frequency: A few dozen lookups per cone and voxel are sufficient. Growth rate: Adjusts sampling density based on distance. Weighting function h: Strengthens or weakens shadow effect. Pitfalls: Using very few cone samples (e.g., 12) results in clearly visible cuboid artifacts. SAT resolution can be a fraction of the volume dataset size without exposing conspicuous artifacts, but too low resolution causes blurred shadows. An algorithm to compute approximate shadows for volumetric rendering by baking axis-aligned light extinction into textures and interpolating, avoiding full shadow raycasts per voxel or raymarch step. It computes axis-aligned extinction via cumulative products of extinction along each axis, writing each axis to a different texture concurrently. It collapses these into two interpolated directional extinction values to reduce bandwidth cost during raymarching. Precomputation cost is <1ms across tested scenarios. Time Complexity: SAT construction is O(N) where N is the number of voxels. Shadow computation is performed per frame for dynamic light sources, with measured times of 0.0079s/frame for a 64^3 texture with 50 samples. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Extinction SAT and Light Cache textures, both O(N). Performance: SAT construction for 256^3 volume takes 0.311s; for 64^3 it takes 0.029s. AO/color bleeding computation for 256^3 texture with 3 shells takes 0.0307s, compared to 3.0818s for explicit sampling of radius 7. Strengths: Fast, flexible, handles any light type and multiple sources, handles light sources within or on the border of the dataset without additional effort. Interactive performance is maintained even with dynamic transfer functions. Limitations: Approximation artifacts if cone samples are too few. Requires recomputation of SAT and AO terms when transfer function or light source position changes. Originated in GPU volume ray-casting for interactive rendering with dynamic transfer functions and light sources. It was developed to provide realistic looking images with improved depth and occlusion effects at interactive frame rates. name: Image Plane Sweep Volume Illumination
head: Image Plane Sweep, Sundén et al
body: Image Plane Sweep Volume Illumination is a GPU-based volume ray-casting technique that reduces illumination computation complexity by exploiting the plane sweep paradigm. It enables interactive frame rates while supporting advanced effects such as scattering and shadowing. Unlike standard ray casting which casts viewing rays directly from the viewpoint, this method computes illumination for a screen-space line first, then casts viewing rays line by line. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar volume data V, light direction \mathbf{l}, view direction \mathbf{v}, camera parameters, and transfer functions for color C{base} and opacity \alpha. Output: Final composited image with volumetric illumination (shadows and scattering). Data Structures: Illumination Buffer: A 2D buffer storing precomputed illumination values for each screen-space line segment. Volume Texture: 3D texture storing the scalar field V. Steps: 1. Project Light Direction: Project the light direction vector \mathbf{l} onto the image plane to determine the sweep direction. 2. Line-Sweep Illumination Computation: Perform a line-sweep computation in image space along the projected light direction. This step calculates illumination information (such as shadowing and scattering contributions) for each screen-space line. The optical model considers either single scattering with a single light direction, or multiple scattering resulting from a rather high albedo. To capture high-frequency shadows and diffuse scattering simultaneously, these two formulations are combined. 3. Viewing Ray Casting: Once illumination information for a line is computed, cast viewing rays from the image plane line by line. 4. Shading Modification: Modify the shading of the samples using the ray casting algorithm based on the precomputed line lighting. The base color C{base} and opacity \alpha are computed as per standard direct volume ray casting, and the final color is modulated by the precomputed illumination term. The opacity \alpha is derived solely from the transfer function and is generally not modified by the shading model, preserving the physical interpretation of density. The shading model affects only the color channel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def imageplanesweepvolumeillumination(volume, lightdir, viewdir, camera): # Step 1: Project light direction onto the image plane sweepdir = normalize(lightdir - dot(lightdir, viewdir) viewdir) # Step 2: Line-sweep illumination computation in image space width, height = camera.resolution illuminationbuffer = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] # Group pixels into lines aligned with sweepdir lines = grouppixelsbyline(sweepdir, width, height) for line in lines: # Compute illumination for the line (shadows, scattering) # Sources do not specify the exact integration formula for line illumination [Comment] lineillum = computelineillumination(line, volume, lightdir, camera) for i, pixel in enumerate(line): illuminationbuffer[pixel.y][pixel.x] = lineillum[i] # Step 3 & 4: Cast viewing rays line by line and apply shading image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height)] for line in lines: for pixel in line: rayorigin = camera.origin raydir = normalize(pixel.position - rayorigin) acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 for sample in marchvolume(rayorigin, raydir, volume): val = volume.sample(sample.position) basecolor, alpha = transferfunction(val) lightterm = illuminationbuffer[pixel.y][pixel.x] shadedcolor = [c lightterm for c in basecolor] weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = [acccolor[i] + shadedcolor[i] weight for i in range(3)] accalpha += weight image[pixel.y][pixel.x] = acccolor return image def grouppixelsbyline(sweepdir, width, height): # Standard rasterization: assign each pixel to a line index based on sweepdir lines = {} for y in range(height): for x in range(width): lineidx = x sweepdir.y - y sweepdir.x if lineidx not in lines: lines[lineidx] = [] lines[lineidx].append((x, y)) return list(lines.values()) def computelineillumination(line, volume, lightdir, camera): # Sources do not specify the exact integration formula for line illumination [Comment] return [1.0] len(line) def transferfunction(val): # Standard transfer function mapping scalar value to color and opacity return [0.5, 0.5, 0.5], 0.1 def marchvolume(origin, direction, volume): # Standard volume marching along ray return [(origin[i] + j direction[i]) for j in range(10) for i in range(3)] Parameters: Sweep Resolution: Not given in the sources. Scattering Model: Combines single scattering and multiple scattering approximations. Lighting Model: Typically uses Phong illumination or simplified intensity models as per the parent article. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: If the light direction is parallel to the image plane, the sweep direction may become degenerate. Computes illumination assuming a single light direction and single scattering events. Sets it apart by capturing high-frequency shadowing effects. Choose when direct lighting and sharp shadows are the primary visual requirement. See Direct volume ray casting. Computes illumination assuming multiple scattering events, typically triggered by high albedo volumes. Sets it apart by capturing diffuse scattering effects. Choose when volumetric haze or fog-like appearance is desired. See Direct volume ray casting. Time Complexity: Reduces illumination computation complexity compared to standard ray casting by leveraging the plane sweep paradigm. Memory Complexity: Requires additional storage for the illumination buffer. Measured Performance: Achieves interactive frame rates. Strengths: Supports scattering and shadowing interactively; combines high-frequency shadows with diffuse scattering. Limitations: Limited to specific lighting configurations (single light direction for single scattering). When to Use: When interactive performance is required for volumes with complex lighting effects like shadows and scattering. When Not to Use: When global illumination with multiple lights is required without approximation. Image Plane Sweep Volume Illumination was proposed by Sundén et al.. It is based on a reformulation of the optical model to integrate advanced illumination effects into GPU-based volume ray-casters. The method was developed to address the computational cost of volumetric lighting in real-time applications.
